# Yevamot 3

## Intro: Nashim & Yibum

### Nashim Definition

We begin *Seder Nashim*. The word *nashim* is generally translated as "women," but a very reasonable suggestion has been made that the more proper translation is actually "wives." The word *isha* in the plural yields *nashim*, and when we say, for instance, that *Shlomo* had many *nashim*, it does not mean women in general — it means wives. Indeed, so much of the tractates in this *seder* concern issues relating to wives: *Yevamot*, *Gittin*, *Kiddushin*, and even *Nedarim*, where, though the *Torah* also addresses young daughters and the rights of fathers to annul vows, the primary subject is husbands and fathers exercising those powers. It is worth pausing to reflect on what it means that women are treated largely as subject matter rather than as subjects in their own right.

### Masechet Structure

*Yevamot* is a very challenging *masechta* with which to open the *seder*. For *Daf Yomi* purposes, the ordering — largest *masechtos* first, as judged by number of chapters — is not easy on the learner. One begins with *Shabbat* and *Eruvin*, enormous tractates, and now with *Yevamot*, which will occupy us for many months. It would have been more pedagogically gentle to build up gradually. Nevertheless, that is the order, and we proceed.

### Yevamot Scope

While a good part of this *masechta* deals with the actual *mitzvah* of *yibum*, an equally important section addresses general issues of personal status. Questions of *mamzer*, of who may marry whom, of *patzu daka* and *krus shepcha* (those with certain physical disqualifications from the congregation), questions about individuals of uncertain Jewish status or uncertain paternity — all of these appear here. So too do matters concerning the women whom *kohanim* are forbidden to marry, extensive discussion of conversion (*gerus*), and even questions of *agunah*, which one might expect to find in *Gittin*. The question of whether a husband has died and whether a single witness suffices to establish that fact is treated at length in *Yevamot*. It is therefore more accurate to approach this tractate as the comprehensive treatment of personal status law, with the *mitzvah* of *yibum* as its central organizing theme rather than its only concern.

### Yabam Terminology

The literal meaning of *yabam* and *yevama* deserves mention: these terms mean brother-in-law and sister-in-law respectively. The word *yibum* is rendered in English as "levirate marriage" — and it turns out that "levirate" derives from the Latin *levir*, meaning a husband's brother. The Hebrew terms, however, carry a broader meaning beyond the technical *mitzvah* context; *yevama* simply means sister-in-law and *yabam* simply means brother-in-law, though both obviously also carry their specific technical legal senses.

### Yibum History

The practice of *yibum* is attested before *matan Torah*: we find it in the story of *Yehuda* and *Tamar*, and there are echoes of something like it in the book of *Rut*, though that case does not involve brothers. The *Ramban* draws on the *Rut* story to argue that *yibum* existed as an ancient cultural practice predating *matan Torah*, and that it originally applied not only to brothers but to any male relative. The *Torah* then came and, because of the prohibitions of *arayot*, restricted this practice generally — but preserved it in the one specific case of brothers.

### Lehakim Shem

This raises a profound question: what does it truly mean *lehakim shem achiv hamet* — to establish the name of the dead brother? It certainly cannot mean merely giving the child the dead brother's literal name, since we find no such practice in the *Torah* and none in the story of *Yehuda* and *Tamar* — indeed, *Yehuda* himself named the children. So why does the act of *yibum* specifically accomplish this purpose?

The *Ramban* hints at the idea of *gilgul neshamot* — some form of reincarnation of the dead brother's soul. The suggestion is that when conception occurs through a family member, it may allow for some continuity of the dead brother's soul in the child born from that union, even if one does not adopt a full doctrine of *gilgul neshamot*. There clearly seems to be something deeper operating on a metaphysical level: when this happens through a family member, the child represents a more genuine continuity of the dead father than would otherwise be possible.

### Yibum Halakha

For *halacha* purposes, the implications of *yibum* touch heavily on questions of inheritance — who inherits the dead brother's property — though we will see that this is not a matter of complete consensus. The entire complex of laws surrounding *yibum* is animated by this underlying tension between perpetuating the dead brother's name and line, and the network of legal relationships the act creates.

### Asei/Lo Taase

The central legal challenge of *yibum* is striking: the *mitzvah* of *yibum* requires a man to marry his dead brother's wife — yet the prohibition of *eshet ach* (a brother's wife) is among the most serious *arayot*, carrying the penalty of *kares*. How is this resolved? The non-simple answer is that this may be one of those cases where the *Torah* states two things that are essentially contradictory *be-dibbur echad* — as a single unified declaration. We find a parallel in *shamor ve-zachor*, though those two are not contradictory, merely two dimensions of *Shabbat*. More pertinently, there are cases where the *Torah* states two things that genuinely contradict one another and yet both are true — and *yevama yavo aleha* alongside the prohibition of *eshet ach* is one of the most powerful examples of this. Whether *yibum* fits the standard pattern of *asei doche lo ta'asei* — a positive commandment overriding a prohibition — or represents a more radical *chiddush* where the *Torah* itself holds the contradiction in simultaneous validity, is one of the foundational conceptual questions this *masechta* will address.

### Karaite Views

Non-rabbinic groups found their own solutions to this apparent contradiction. The *Karaites* offered a fascinating approach: they argued that the *Torah* only permits *yibum* precisely in the case where the man is *not* the actual brother — that when the *Torah* uses the word *achim*, it uses it loosely, as in *Avraham*'s words to *Lot*, *halo anashim achim anachnu*, where it does not mean literal brothers. On their reading, the *mitzvah* of *yibum* would apply only in a case like *Rut* — where the parties are related but not in a relationship of *issur erva*. That is how they resolve the apparent collision with the prohibition of a brother's wife. The *Essenes* (or another such group) proposed yet another solution — that *yibum* applied only to *eirusin* (betrothal) rather than *nissu'in* (full marriage) — another way of defusing the conflict with the *issur erva* of *eshet ach*. For *Chazal*, of course, that collision is precisely the point and the *chiddush*.

---

## Mishna Order

### Opening Sugya

At the beginning of this *masechta* we encounter what we find at the opening of many *masechtot*: an initial *stam* passage that is technically oriented and hyper-attentive to questions of language and grammatical precision in the *mishna*, rather than engaging with conceptual substance. Just as *Kiddushin* opens by asking why the *mishna* uses the formulation *ha-isha nikneit* rather than *ha-ish koneh*, and why the language of *kinyan* is employed, so too here. This type of opening is generally understood to represent one of the latest layers of the *Gemara*, perhaps added even after the main *stam* editorial work. *Rav Sherira Gaon*, in his famous letter, notes that these opening passages frequently serve as an opportunity to quote material that will appear later or to introduce ideas relevant to future discussions — they do not develop new ideas themselves. That is precisely what we will find here, as this *sugya* opens a window onto some of the complex material we will encounter later in the tractate.

The question the *Gemara* takes up is: what is the organizing principle behind the *mishna*'s list of the fifteen women whose status as *arayot* exempts them — and their *tzarot* (co-wives) — from *yibum* and *chalitza*? The *mishna* begins with *bito* (his daughter) and proceeds through granddaughter, then to wife's daughter and her descendants, then mother-in-law and grandmother-in-law, then sisters, and finally the various categories of wives. What determines this sequence?

### Bito Priority

The *Gemara* at the bottom of 2b says: *ella bito, keivan de'ati midrasha chaviva lei* — the reason the *mishna* begins with a daughter is that this prohibition is learned from *derasha* rather than being explicit in the verse, and it is therefore dear to the *tanna*. Tannaim show greater interest in foregrounding material they have themselves uncovered or derived through interpretation, rather than what is explicit in the text.

### Bito vs Bat Ishto

What does this mean — that the prohibition of a man's daughter is not explicit? *Rashi* quotes the relevant *pasuk*: *ervat isha u'vitah lo tegaleh, et bat bnah v'et bat bitah lo tikach legalot ervatah* — you shall not uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter, nor take her son's daughter or her daughter's daughter. Every time the *Torah* addresses this category, it speaks about a man's wife and *her* daughter, or *her* descendants. The most natural reading of *isha u'vitah* — a woman and her daughter — is: your wife and her daughter. The *rabbis* interpret this as: you are forbidden from your wife's daughter.

But what about his biological daughter who is not his wife's daughter — born, for instance, from a non-marital union? That prohibition nowhere appears explicit in the *Torah*. The *Gemara* therefore designates it a *milta de'ita bidrasha* — something learned through Rabbinic interpretation — and that is why the *tanna* opens with it. The *Gemara* refers to this case specifically as *bito me'anusato* (his daughter from a woman he violated), a formulation that is, it must be said, disturbing. Why the *Gemara* chose this example rather than *bito mi'mefutato* (his daughter from a woman he seduced) — itself already a painful category, but at least one that implies some measure of consent — is not entirely clear.

### Gezeira Shava

The *Gemara* then asks: *kulu nami midrasha atu* — but isn't everything in the *mishna* learned from *derasha*? The entire principle that *arayot* are exempt from *yibum* is derived through Rabbinic interpretation, not stated explicitly. So why should *bito* be privileged for this reason?

The *Gemara* answers: *nehi de'inyan yibum atyan midrasha* — true, the *yibum* exemption of all these *arayot* is learned from *derasha*, but *ikkar issuraihu bahedaya ketiv v'hu* — the fundamental fact that they are *arayot* at all is explicit in the text. Except for *bito*: *ikkar issura midrasha* — the very foundation of the prohibition of his biological daughter is itself a *derasha*. *De'amar Rava*, as *Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi* taught him: *atya heina heina, atya zima zima* — we derive it through a *gezeira shava* from the words *heina-heina* and *zima-zima*.

How does this work? The *Torah* states concerning biological granddaughter: *ervat bat bincha o bat bitecha lo tegaleh ervatan ki ervat-cha heina* — the nakedness of your son's daughter or your daughter's daughter you shall not uncover, for their nakedness is your own. Notably, this verse addresses biological grandchildren — there is no mention of wife. The word *heina* appears here. Separately, in the passage about a wife's daughter and granddaughter, the *Torah* states: *isha u'vito lo tegaleh, sh'eira heina zima hi* — a woman and her daughter, their nakedness is *heina*, and it is *zima*. And in yet another verse: *zima hi, ba-esh yisrefu oto v'et-hen* — it is *zima*, they shall be burned in fire. And: *v'lo tihye zima betochechem* — there shall be no *zima* among you.

The *gezeira shava* operates as follows: the word *heina* in the verse about biological granddaughter links it to the verse about wife's daughter and granddaughter, where *heina* also appears. In the latter context, daughter is explicitly prohibited and the punishment of *sreifa* (burning) is stated. Through the *heina-heina* link, we establish that just as the wife's granddaughter is forbidden, so too is the biological granddaughter — and, by daisy-chaining, since the biological is linked via *heina* to a context where daughter is mentioned, daughter is also forbidden. Furthermore, since that context contains the word *zima*, and *zima* is linked to *sreifa*, the biological daughter is also subject to the same punishment. The prohibition of biological daughter is thus learned entirely from this *gezeira shava* — hence *ikkar issura midrasha*, and hence its pride of place at the opening of the *mishna*.

The *Gemara* then observes: *hashta de'amarta kol milta de'atya midrasha chaviva lei* — now that we have said the *tanna* favors things learned from *derasha*, *lisni la'achot ishto libasof* — the *mishna* should then have placed *achot ishto* (wife's sister) at the very end of the list. The reason is that *achot ishto* is the one *erva* in the list whose exemption from *yibum* is most explicit in the *pasuk* — as we will see when we turn the page. If the organizing principle is to lead with *derasha*-derived categories and defer what is explicit, wife's sister should come last.

The *Gemara* responds: *aidei de'ayei be'issur achvaso, tana achot ishto* — since we had already moved into discussing the category of siblings, the *mishna* included wife's sister there naturally. The organization shifted from being governed by *derasha* to being governed by logical grouping. Fine. But the *Gemara* pushes further: *lisni lehai bava libasof* — even if we accept that wife's sister belongs in the sibling section, why doesn't the entire sibling section come after the wife-category section, given that *drashot* should dominate?

### Korvei Ordering

At this point the *Gemara* abandons the *derasha* theory entirely and offers what is clearly the straightforward explanation: *tana korvei korvei nakat* — the *mishna* lists the categories in order of closeness of relationship.

*Tana bito u'bat bito u'bat bno de'korvei atzmo* — first come his own descendants: daughter, granddaughter. These are the people most closely related to him. *Ve'aidei de'tana shlosha dorot lemata didei, tana nami shlosha dorot lemata didah* — once having dealt with three generations downward on his own side, the *mishna* naturally turns to three generations downward on his wife's side — wife's daughter and granddaughter.

### Three Generations

*Ve'aidei de'tana shlosha dorot lemata didah, tana shlosha dorot lemala didah* — and having gone three generations downward on her side, the *mishna* goes three generations upward on her side: mother-in-law and grandmother-in-law. The vertical dimension is thus exhausted — down three generations on his side, down three on hers, and up three on hers.

### Sister Inclusion

Then: *ve'tana achota* — we move horizontally to siblings. *Ve'achot ima, shekrovei atzma* — mother's sister, who is a blood relative of his wife. *Ve'achot ishto, achot ishto* — and then wife's sister, who is not his blood relative but fits within the horizontal relational category. The ordering is thus: vertical (downward, his side), vertical (downward, her side), vertical (upward, her side), horizontal (blood relatives — sisters), horizontal (his wife's sister by association with the sibling category).

### Wives Ordering

Having exhausted the sibling category, the *mishna* turns to wives. Here a further wrinkle emerges: *badin hu dilekadmei lekallato mikamei eshet achiv shelo haya beolamo, delav mishum korva hu de-assira* — it would have been logical to list *kallato* (daughter-in-law, i.e., his son's wife) before *eshet achiv shelo haya beolamo* (the wife of a brother who was not yet born when the dead brother married her). The reason *kallato* should come first is that her prohibition is rooted in *korva* — closeness of relationship, the core organizing principle. *Eshet achiv shelo haya beolamo*, by contrast, is not primarily an *issur* of kinship; it arises from the absence of any *mitzat yibum* (obligation of *yibum*).

To clarify: if *Shimon* was married and died, *Reuven* performed *yibum*, and then *Levi* was subsequently born — when *Reuven* later dies, *Levi* has no obligation of *yibum* toward *Reuven*'s first wife (who was originally *Shimon*'s wife), because *Levi* was never in the world at the time of that original marriage. There was never a potential *mitzat yibum* between them. This is what *eshet achiv shelo haya beolamo* means: the wife of a brother toward whom he never had any obligation of *yibum*.

Logically, then, *kallato* should have preceded this case. But the *Gemara* explains: *ela aidei de'ayrei be'issur achva, tani eshet achiv shelo haya beolamo* — since we were already dealing with wives of siblings in the sibling section, the *mishna* listed the wives of siblings first: *eshet achiv me'imo* (wife of a maternal half-brother) and *eshet achiv shelo haya beolamo* both belong in the sibling-wives category. *Ve'hadar tani kallato* — only then does the *mishna* reach daughter-in-law. And this, the *Gemara* concludes, is entirely cogent: the organization proceeds by vertical relations, then horizontal relations, leading naturally into wives of those horizontal relatives, and finally arriving at *kallato*.

---

## Language: Potrot

### Potrot Mechanism

Having resolved the questions of ordering, the *Gemara* turns to a different linguistic issue: *u-mai irya detani potrot* — why does the *mishna* use the language "they exempt" (*potrot*) their *tzarot*, rather than "they forbid" (*osrot*) their *tzarot* from *yibum*?

### Assur vs Patur

*Ei tana osrot* — had the *mishna* said "they forbid," *hava amina assur leyabbem aval michlatz chaltza* — one might have thought it is forbidden to perform *yibum* but perhaps *chalitza* is still required. This is not an idle concern: there are indeed categories of women for whom, due to *safek* or rabbinic considerations, one does not perform *yibum* but does perform *chalitza*. If the *mishna* merely said "forbidden," a reader might conclude that a biblical obligation still lurks and requires *chalitza* to discharge it. The word "exempt" (*potrot*) forecloses that misunderstanding: these women are entirely exempt, from both *yibum* and *chalitza*.

The *Gemara* immediately challenges: *u-litni assura lachlotz* — be explicit then, say it is forbidden to perform *chalitza*, which conveys the same total exemption. The *Gemara* replies: *mai ka avid?* — but how could it be forbidden to perform *chalitza*? *Yibum* is forbidden because it is an act of sexual relations with *arayot*, carrying *kares* absent the *mitzvah*. But what *issur* attaches to removing a shoe and spitting in a court proceeding? *Alma lo? Im ata omer choletzes, misyabbemes* — because if we say she may perform *chalitza*, the next person will come along and perform *yibum*, reasoning that if there is a *chalitza* option there must be a *yibum* option. So while we cannot properly say it is *assur* to perform *chalitza* (since *chalitza* itself is a neutral act), we also cannot allow it, lest it signal that *yibum* is on the table.

### Tzara Mechanism

So why not simply say *assur lachlotz* to communicate this? The *Gemara* explains: *kevan debimakom mitzvah hu de-assira tzara, ve-shelo bimakom mitzvah sharya, mishum hachi tana potrot* — because the *tzara* becomes forbidden specifically in the context of *mitzva*, that is, in the context of a brother's wife. If there is no *mitzat yibum*, then the *tzara* of an *erva* is perfectly permitted to the man — as long as they were not married to his brother.

This distinction is crucial. The mechanism is not that an *erva* renders her co-wife forbidden to the man as such. Rather, the *erva* removes the *mitzat yibum* entirely. Once the *mitzvah* of *yibum* is removed, the other woman defaults back to being prohibited as a brother's wife — because there is no *mitzva* to override that prohibition. But in a case where the same woman is an *erva* to someone she is not related to through a brother — say, her father is married to two women and one of them is his daughter — the daughter does not make the other wife forbidden to the father, because there was never any *mitzat yibum* to remove in the first place.

This is why the *mishna* had to say *potrot* — "exempt" — rather than anything conveying a direct prohibition on the *tzara*. The mechanism is the removal of the *mitzva*, not the imposition of a new *issur*. *Mishum hachi tana potrot*: that is precisely the conceptual reality being described.

### Chalitza Priority

*U-mai arya detani min hachalitzah u-min hayibbum* — the *Gemara* next asks: why does the *mishna* list *chalitza* before *yibum*? Since *yibum* is the primary *mitzvah*, should it not have been mentioned first? *Ei tani min hayibbum, hava amina michlatz chaltza yibumi lo mivama* — if the *mishna* said only "exempt from *yibum*," one might have thought: do not perform *yibum* but do perform *chalitza*, since perhaps the *yibum* exemption is only rabbinic while a biblical *chalitza* obligation remains. *Ka mashma lan* that this is not so: *kol ha'oleh leyibum oleh lachalitza, ve-chol she'eino oleh leyibum eino oleh lachalitza* — whoever is subject to *yibum* is subject to *chalitza*, and whoever is not subject to *yibum* is not subject to *chalitza*. At the biblical level they are a package: one implies the other. Hence the *mishna* must mention both, to prevent any inference that exemption from one leaves the other in place.

But then the *Gemara* asks: *ve-litni min hayibum umin hachalitza* — fine, say both, but why list *chalitza* first? *Abba Shaul hi* — the *mishna* follows the position of *Abba Shaul*, *de'amar mitzvat chalitza kodemet lemitzvat yibum* — who held that *chalitza* is the preferred mode, taking precedence over *yibum*.

### Leshem Mitzvah

*Rashi* at this juncture quotes *Abba Shaul* from a later chapter: *Abba Shaul omer hachones yevamto leshum noy leshum ishut ke'ilu pogeah be'erva* — one who takes his *yevama* in marriage for reasons of attraction or desire for marriage is as one who transgresses the *issur erva*. The concern is that if a man actually wishes to marry this woman — because he finds her attractive or genuinely desires to wed her — the act of *yibum* is no longer *leshem mitzvah*, no longer performed as a religious obligation, but as an ordinary marital pursuit. *Ve-karov be'einai lihyot ha-vlad mamzer* — and it is close in his view to the child being a *mamzer*, because it approaches the quality of *issur eshet ach* when the act is not performed entirely for the sake of the *mitzvah*. This is a striking position: one might assume that genuine mutual interest between the parties would be a positive factor, yet *Abba Shaul* regards motivation by attraction as what transforms the act from *mitzvah* to something approaching transgression. Following *Abba Shaul*'s view, the *mishna* places *chalitza* first to underscore that it is the preferred approach.

---

## Fifteen Women

### Rav Disputes

The *Gemara* now turns to the number itself: *minyana derisha lema'utei mai, minyana deseifa lema'utei mai* — why does the *mishna* need to specify fifteen? And why does it reiterate at the end "these women are exempt"? These specifications serve to exclude certain positions: *lema'utei derav vederav Assi* — to exclude the views of *Rav* and *Rav Assi*, who wished to add additional categories of women exempt from *yibum* to the list.

### Suta/Aylonit

*Rav* proposed the case of *tzarat sotah* — the co-wife of a woman who has committed adultery (or is at minimum suspected of it). A *sotah* is forbidden to her husband; their relationship is, in terms of conjugal life and the possibility of conceiving a child together, broken. The principle of *yibum* exists because the surviving brother steps into the dead brother's place to continue the possibility of children and continuity. A dead brother who could not have had licit relations with his wife — because she was a *sotah* — never had that viable conjugal relationship. Therefore, *Rav* argued, the surviving brother has no *mitzat yibum* with her. Fine. But *Rav* went further: if there is no *yibum* obligation with respect to the *sotah* herself, her *tzara* (co-wife) should likewise be exempt. This is the case of *tzarat sotah*. Crucially, the *sotah* is not an *erva* — the *issur* does not arise from kinship but from the state of the marital relationship. *Rav* nonetheless maintained that the *tzara* principle applies.

*Rav Assi*'s case is *tzarat aylonit* — the co-wife of a woman who is incapable of bearing children. An *aylonit* presents a different kind of problem: not a marital breakdown through prohibited conduct, but a physical impossibility of conception. *Rav Assi* held that since there is no viable prospect of progeny from the union with the *aylonit*, there is no *mitzat yibum* to her, and therefore her *tzara* is also exempt. Again, the *aylonit* is not an *erva*; the exemption arises from the nature of the relationship's inability to fulfill the purpose of *yibum*.

Both *Rav* and *Rav Assi* thus held that the *tzara* principle — which the *mishna* applies only to cases of *arayot* — extends to cases where there is no *yibum* obligation for a different reason. The *mishna*'s specification of precisely fifteen women, the *Gemara* argues, rejects this expansion: the co-wife of a *sotah* and the co-wife of an *aylonit* are not exempt; *yibum* would still apply to them because the *tzara* principle operates only where the primary woman is an *erva*.

### Tzara Exclusions

The *Gemara* then poses the question from *Rav* and *Rav Assi*'s perspective: *u'l'Rav u'l'Rav Assi l'mautei mai?* If they believe their cases are correct and not excluded by the *mishna*, why does the *mishna* specify only fifteen? What do *they* say the number is excluding?

The *Gemara* answers: *ei sevira lehu d'hadadei* — if *Rav* holds of *Rav Assi*'s case and *Rav Assi* holds of *Rav*'s case, so that they agree with one another on both, then the two instances of numerical specification in the *mishna* — "fifteen" at the beginning and "these women" at the close — each exclude one of two other cases: *chada l'mautei tzarat m'ma'enet v'chada l'mautei tzarat machzir gerushato* — one excludes the *tzara* of a *mema'enet* and the other excludes the *tzara* of a *machzir gerushato*.

And if they do not hold of one another — if *Rav* does not accept *Rav Assi*'s case and vice versa — then *chada l'mautei d'chavreih* — one specification excludes the other's case, and *v'chada l'mautei idach m'ma'enet o tzarat machzir gerushato* — the other specification excludes one of the remaining two cases: either *mema'enet* or *machzir gerushato*.

### Mema'enes Case

What are these two cases? *Mema'enet* refers to an underage girl who was married off by her brothers or mother (rather than by her father) after her father's death. Such a marriage is only rabbinic in character, and the girl retains the right of *mi'un* — refusal — to dissolve the marriage. The connection between *Reuven* and this underage wife is, at every level, a creation of rabbinic law. When *Reuven* dies, a *zika* — a quasi-marital attachment — transfers in some sense to *Shimon*, the surviving brother. But just as the girl could have performed *mi'un* to dissolve her marriage to *Reuven*, she can perform *mi'un* against *Shimon* and walk away from the *zika*. Once she does *mi'un*, *Shimon* can no longer perform *yibum* with her. The case of *tzarat mema'enet* would be: *Reuven* had two wives, and one was this underage girl who did *mi'un* — can *Shimon* still perform *yibum* with the other wife? The answer is yes. The entire structure here is rabbinic: the girl's marriage was rabbinic, her *mi'un* is rabbinic, the effect on the *zika* is rabbinic. It is therefore not at all surprising that her *mi'un* does not exempt the *tzara*, and the *mishna*'s fifteen cases necessarily exclude this scenario.

### Machzir Grushaso

The case of *machzir gerushato* — remarrying one's divorced wife — is more straightforward. The *Torah* prohibits a man from remarrying a woman he divorced if in the interim she was married to another man. In this scenario, *Yaakov* was married to *Leah*, divorced her, and then remarried her after she had been with another man (he was not permitted to do so, but he did). He was also always married to *Rachel*, whom he never divorced. When *Yaakov* dies, *Leah* cannot be subject to *yibum* because of the prohibition of *machzir gerushato*. But would *Rachel*'s obligation of *yibum* be affected? No. The *tzara* principle does not apply here. The *issur* of *machzir gerushato* differs in quality from that of *sotah*: the *sotah* prohibition bears primarily on sexual relations, whereas *machzir gerushato* is more precisely an *issur* on the act of remarriage itself. For that reason — which the *Gemara* leaves for later elaboration — the *issur* does not create a *tzara* effect that would exempt *Rachel*.

### Tzarat Tzara

The *Gemara* concludes by asking why *Rav* and *Rav Assi* did not simply include their cases in the list in the *mishna* if they believed the *tzara* principle applies there. The answer is: *lefi she'eino betzaras tzara* — because even according to *Rav* and *Rav Assi*, the *tzara* in their cases (whether *sotah* or *aylonit*) would not go further. In the *mishna*'s fifteen cases, the *erva* exempts not only her direct *tzara* but also the *tzarat tzara* — the co-wife of the co-wife — and this extends indefinitely. In the cases of *sotah* and *aylonit*, even if one accepts that the immediate *tzara* is exempt, that exemption does not propagate to subsequent levels. Since the *mishna*'s principle encompasses *tzarat tzara* and theirs does not, their cases are categorically different and were therefore deliberately excluded from the list.

*Rashi*, in his comment on the *mishna*, notes on the phrase *tzarat tzarata ad sof ha'olam* — the co-wife of the co-wife to the end of the world — that this is explained *b'masnisin meforesh*: the *mishna* itself, further along, will spell out what this means. *Rashi* normally writes *b'gemara meforesh* — the *Gemara* will explain — but here he notes that it is the *mishna* itself that provides the explanation, in a remarkably self-referential way, with the *mishna* later formulating its own question and then answering it by spelling out the scenario in detail.

---

---

# Yevamot 4

## Arayot Exemption

### Mana Hani Milei

The *Gemara* on 3b opens with a foundational question: *Mana hani milei?* — where do all these laws come from? Specifically, the question targets two distinct principles established in the *mishna*: first, that there is no *mitzvah* of *yibbum* when one of the women is an *ervah* to the *yavam*; and second, that the *tzara* — the co-wife — of such a woman is equally exempt. The *Gemara* signals that it will now provide the scriptural and exegetical basis for everything discussed thus far.

### Isha El Achota

*Detanu rabanan* — the Rabbis taught in a *baraita*: *Isha el achota lo tikach* — do not take a woman and her sister, *litzror* — to create friction or agitation between them — *legalot ervata aleha bechayeha* — to uncover her nakedness upon her, in her lifetime. The qualification *bechayeha* — in her lifetime — is significant: the prohibition of a woman and her sister applies specifically while the original wife is still alive. The verse thus establishes the general prohibition. The *baraita* then asks: *Ma talmud lomar?* — what does the verse come to teach? *Lefi shene'emar* — because the verse says *yevama yavo aleha* — the brother-in-law shall come upon her — one might have thought even in the case of *yibbum*, the *mitzvah* could override the prohibition of *arayot*. That is the *hava amina*.

### Aleha Drasha

The *baraita* resolves this through a *gezeirah shavah*-like verbal link on the word *aleha*. *Ne'emar kan aleha* — it says here, in the case of the wife's sister: *legalot ervata aleha* — to uncover her nakedness *aleha*. *Vene'emar lehalan aleha* — and it says there, in the case of *yibbum*: *yevama yavo aleha*. The word *aleha* appears in both contexts.

The method of inference works as follows: since in the context of *yibbum* the word *aleha* refers to a case in which there is a *mitzvah* of *yibbum*, so too when the verse forbidding a woman and her sister uses the word *aleha*, it means: even in a case of *aleha* — even in a case of *yibbum*. *Ma lehalan bemakom mitzvah* — just as *aleha* there denotes the *mitzvah* of *yibbum*, *af kan bemakom mitzvah* — so too here it means even in a context of *yibbum*. The Torah then says *ve'amar rachmana lo tikach* — even in that case, you may not proceed. The verse thus teaches unambiguously that the prohibition of a wife's sister is not displaced by the *mitzvah* of *yibbum*.

### Wife's Sister

The *baraita* continues: *Ve'ein li ela hi* — I know only that there is no *mitzvah* of *yibbum* in the case of the wife's sister herself. *Tzaratah minayin?* — from where do I know that the *tzara* — the co-wife of the wife's sister — is also exempt from *yibbum*? *Talmud lomar litzror* — the verse teaches through the word *litzror*. The word *litzror*, meaning to create friction or agitation, is read as encoding the word *tzara* — co-wife — just as we find by Hannah and Penina: *ve'ki'asata tzaratah gam ka'as*. This is a *drasha* on the word, not a verse from the Torah itself. Thus *litzror* signals that the exemption extends to the co-wife as well.

The *baraita* then continues: *Ve'ein li ela tzaratah* — I know only the direct co-wife. *Tzarat tzaratah minayin?* — what about the co-wife's co-wife? If this *tzara* subsequently marries another brother who then dies, does her co-wife also become exempt? *Talmud lomar litzror velo litzor* — the verse says *litzror* with a doubled *resh* rather than *litzor* with a single one. The doubled form indicates: even the *tzara* of a *tzara*.

This generates an interesting conceptual question that the *Gemara* will return to: is the *tzarat tzarah* really a distinct category, or does the mechanism work differently? Once there is no *mitzvah* of *yibbum*, the woman becomes an *eshet ach* — a forbidden relation in her own right. So when the *tzara* subsequently enters a *yibbum* situation with another brother, perhaps her co-wife is exempt not because of the category of *tzarat tzarah* per se, but simply because the *tzara* has herself become an *ervah* through her status as *eshet ach*. Whether these are truly distinct conceptual categories or simply generate overlapping cases of *eshet ach* remains an open question, though the *Gemara*'s textual derivation from *litzror* stands.

### Mah Matzinu

*Ve'ein li ela achot ishah* — I know only that the exemption and the exemption of the *tzara* apply in the case of the wife's sister. *She'ar arayot minayin?* — from where do I know the same applies to all other *arayot*? The *baraita* employs a *mah matzinu* — a paradigm inference: *mah achot ishah miyuchedet shehi ervah vechayavin al zedonah kareit ve'al shigegatah chatat ve'asurah leyavam* — just as the wife's sister is an *ervah* for which intentional transgression carries *kareit* and unintentional transgression requires a *chatat* offering, and she is forbidden to the *yavam* — *af kol shehi ervah vechayavin al zedonah kareit ve'al shigegatah chatat ve'asurah leyavam* — so too any other woman who is an *ervah* of comparable severity is likewise forbidden to the *yavam*. There is nothing distinctive about the wife's sister that should make her unique. The relevant criterion is simply: *ervah* with a *kareit* penalty. Any such case falls under the same rule.

### Tzarot Exemption

Once the exemption is extended to all *arayot*, the *baraita* asks: *Tzaroteihen minayin?* — from where do I know that the co-wives of all such *arayot* are also exempt? The same paradigmatic reasoning applies: *mah achot ishah miyuchedet shehi ervah vechayavin al zedonah kareit ve'al shigegatah chatat ve'asurah leyavam vetzaratah asurah* — just as the wife's sister, being an *ervah* of that severity, is forbidden to the *yavam* and her *tzara* is also forbidden — *af kol* — so too any similarly situated *ervah* exempts her co-wife as well. This establishes the general principle: *ha'arayot pturot vepoterot tzaroteihen* — *arayot* are themselves exempt and they exempt their co-wives. The entire principle is derived from the wife's sister as paradigm, and then generalized to all fifteen *arayot* enumerated in the *mishna*.

### Chamesh Esrei

The *baraita* then articulates this conclusion formally: *Mikan amru chachamim* — from here the Sages said: *chamesh esrei nashim poterot tzaroteihen vetzarat tzaroteihen min hachalitzah umin hayibbum ad sof kol ha'olam* — fifteen women exempt their co-wives and co-co-wives from *chalitzah* and *yibbum* indefinitely. The *baraita* then raises a further question: *yachol she'ani marbeh af sheish arayot hachamurot me'elu sheyihiyu tzaroteihen asurot* — perhaps I should include even the six more weighty *arayot*, those more severe than the fifteen, and say that their co-wives are also forbidden.

### Sheish Chamurot

A brief look at *Daf* 13 clarifies what the "six more weighty" cases are. The *mishna* there states: *sheish arayot chamurot me'elu mipnei shenesuot l'acherim* — six *arayot* are more weighty than those fifteen because they are married to other people — specifically because they could never be married to one's brother. Examples include one's mother and one's sister. In these cases, since the brother could never have been married to such a woman, there is never a context of *yibbum* to begin with. Since there is no *yibbum* context, the co-wife does not become an *eshet ach*, and therefore she remains permitted.

### Tzara Context

The *baraita* now answers the question it raised: *amrat* — you respond. *Mah achot ishah miyuchedet shehi ervah vechayavin al zedonah kareit ve'al shigegatah chatat ve'efshar l'hinasay l'ach* — what is distinctive about the wife's sister is that she is an *ervah*, carries a *kareit* penalty, and — crucially — she *could* have been married to a brother. *Im ken asurah leyavam vetzaratah asurah* — in such a case she is forbidden to the *yavam* and her co-wife is forbidden. *Af kol shehi ervah vechayavin al zedonah kareit ve'al shigegatah chatat ve'efshar l'hinasay l'ach* — similarly, any *ervah* that could have been married to a brother: *asurah leyavam vetzaratah asurah* — she is forbidden and her *tzara* is forbidden. *Yatz'u sheish arayot hachamurot me'elu sheharei ee efshar l'hinasay l'ach* — this excludes the six more severe cases, since they cannot be married to a brother. *Tzaroteihen mutarot* — their co-wives are therefore permitted. *She'ein tzara ela mei'ach* — the entire concept of a *tzara* creating a *yibbum* exemption exists only in the context of a co-wife of one's brother.

---

## Onesh Punishment

### Onesh Minayin

The *baraita* now transitions from prohibition to punishment. *Azharah shamanu* — we have heard that there is a prohibition: from the verse *isha el achota lo tikach litzror* read in light of the word *aleha*, we learn that a wife's sister remains forbidden even in a *yibbum* context. But how do we know what punishment applies? *Onesh minayin?* — from where do we derive that if one nonetheless goes ahead and performs *yibbum* with an *ervah*, the full punishment is in force? One might have thought that since a *mitzvah* is involved, the punishment is somehow attenuated.

### Kareit Yibbum

The verse provides the answer: *amar kra ki kol asher ya'aseh mikol hato'evot ha'eleh venichretu* — the verse says, whoever does any of these abominations shall be cut off. This *kareit* passage comes at the conclusion of the entire enumeration of *arayot*, and that enumeration includes *isha el achota lo tikach litzror*. Since the prohibition of the wife's sister includes the *yibbum* context — as we established through the word *aleha* — and the punishment of *kareit* is attached to the entire list of *arayot*, the *kareit* applies equally in the *yibbum* context. The word *litzror* further teaches that the prohibition and its punishment extend to the *tzara* as well. And once we know that having relations with the *tzara* in a *yibbum* context is forbidden and carries *kareit*, it follows that the *tzara* herself acquires the status of *eshet ach* — a forbidden relation — once there is no *mitzvah* of *yibbum* attaching to her.

---

## Hava Amina

### Meichdi Reasoning

With the *baraita* concluded, the *Gemara* steps back to analyze the logical foundations of the entire exercise. *Meichdi* — let us think about this: *ta'ama dechtav rachmana aleha* — it is because the Torah wrote *aleha* that we know *yibbum* does not apply in the case of an *ervah*. *Halav hacha hava amina achot isha meyabemet* — were it not for that verse, I would have thought that you could indeed perform *yibbum* with a wife's sister. But why would I have thought such a thing?

### Asei Dochei

*Mai ta'ama?* — what was the reasoning behind that *hava amina*? *Amrinan ati asei vedachi lo ta'asei* — I might have said: a positive *mitzvah* comes and overrides a negative prohibition. The *mitzvah* of *yibbum* is a positive commandment; the prohibition of a wife's sister is a negative prohibition. Hence the *hava amina* that the *mitzvah* might override the prohibition.

### Kareit Exception

But the *Gemara* immediately pushes back on this *hava amina*: *eima de'amrinan asei vidachei lo ta'asei* — when do we say a positive *mitzvah* overrides a negative? *Lo ta'asei greida* — only when it is a straightforward negative prohibition, not a particularly weighty one. *Lo ta'asei she'yesh bo kareit* — a negative prohibition that carries *kareit* — *mi dachi?* — does a positive *mitzvah* ever override that? The principle of *asei dochei lo ta'asei* does not apply to prohibitions of such severity.

One might respond: but the *mitzvah* of *yibbum* already overrides one prohibition that carries *kareit* — namely *eshet ach*. If it overrides that, perhaps it could override other *arayot* as well? That is indeed the most natural formulation of the *hava amina*. However, the *Gemara* has not yet reached that point. First it wants to establish the more fundamental question: where do we know the principle of *asei dochei lo ta'asei* at all? Understanding that principle is essential to understanding why anyone might have thought *yibbum* could override *arayot* — and why ultimately it cannot when *kareit* is involved.

---

## Shatnez-Tzitzit

### Velo Litzor

The *Gemara* now opens a broader inquiry: *lo ta'asei greida minalan de'dachi?* — from where do we even know that a positive *mitzvah* overrides a straightforward negative prohibition? This takes the discussion temporarily away from *yibbum*, but the purpose is clear: to establish the principle of *asei dochei lo ta'asei* so that we can understand the *hava amina* that *yibbum* might have overridden the prohibition of *arayot*.

### Lo Tilbash

The *Gemara* answers: *de'ksiv lo tilbash shatnez, gedilim ta'aseh lach* — because the verse says do not wear *shatnez*, and the very next verse says make yourself fringes. *Shatnez* is the prohibition of mixing wool and linen; *tzitzit* may require a wool string on a linen garment, which would constitute *shatnez*. The juxtaposition teaches that the positive *mitzvah* of *tzitzit* overrides the negative prohibition of *shatnez*.

### Smuchim Drasha

But how do we know that juxtaposition in the Torah is a legitimate hermeneutic tool? *Ve'amar Rabbi Elazar: smuchin min hatorah minayin?* — from where is the principle of *smuchin* — learning from textual juxtapositions — itself derived? *Shene'emar smuchim la'ad le'olam asuyim be'emes veyashar* — as the verse in *Tehillim* says, they are joined forever, made in truth and uprightness — which the *Gemara* reads as endorsing the method of *smuchin*. Thus the juxtaposition of *shatnez* and *gedilim ta'aseh lach* is a valid source for the principle that *asei dochei lo ta'aseh*.

At this point the *Gemara* introduces a related teaching. *Ve'amar Rav Sheshes amar Rabbi Elazar mishum Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah: minayin leyevama she'nafla lifnei Mukeh Shechin she'ein chosmin oto* — from where do we know that if a *yevama* falls before a *yavam* who is a repugnant person, such as one afflicted with severe boils, you do not silence her? *Shene'emar lo tachsom shor be'disho* — do not muzzle an ox while it threshes — *vesamich lei ki yeshvu achim yachdav* — and immediately juxtaposed to it is the passage establishing the *mitzvah* of *yibbum*. This *smuchin* teaches that we attend to the woman's objections and ensure that *chalitzah* is performed rather than *yibbum*. This is a significant point: although so much of this entire *tractate* is framed from the man's perspective — who is permitted to whom, where a *mitzvah* applies — this *drasha* establishes at the very outset that the woman has a voice and that her protest is legally cognizable.

---

## Smuchim General

### Reb Yehuda Position

The *Gemara* then notes: *afilu lema'an delo darash smuchin be'alma, be'Mishneh Torah darash* — even one who does not generally make *drashot* from *smuchin* will do so in *Mishneh Torah* — that is, in *Devarim*, where *Moshe Rabbeinu* recaps the earlier laws. This is directly relevant because the juxtaposition of *shatnez* and *tzitzit* appears in *Devarim*, which means that even those who reject *smuchin* as a general hermeneutic accept this particular *drasha* and therefore accept the principle of *asei dochei lo ta'aseh*.

Who is it that generally rejects *smuchin*? *Detanya: Rabbi Yehuda be'alma lo darash* — we know from a *baraita* that *Rabbi Yehuda* in general does not derive *halacha* from juxtaposition.

### Ben Azzai vs Yehuda

The *baraita* spells this out: *Ben Azzai omer: ne'emar machasheifa lo techayeh* — it says, do not suffer a sorceress to live — *vene'emar kol shochev im behemah mot yumat* — and it is juxtaposed to: whoever lies with an animal shall be put to death. *Samchu inyan lo* — they juxtaposed the two. *Mah shochev im behemah be'skilah* — just as lying with an animal is punishable by stoning — *af machasheifa be'skilah* — so too a sorceress is executed by stoning. This *smuchin* derivation appears in *Shemot* in *Parshat Mishpatim*, not in *Devarim*.

*Amar lei Rabbi Yehuda: ve'chi mipnei she'samchu inyan lo notzi zeh le'skilah?* — *Rabbi Yehuda* objects: just because they are juxtaposed we are going to stone someone? Juxtaposition alone is not a sufficient basis for a ruling of such gravity. Many things are juxtaposed in the Torah — in *Parshat Kedoshim* alone, the most disparate subjects appear side by side — and that cannot automatically serve as the basis for a *drasha*.

*Ela* — rather, says *Rabbi Yehuda*, I agree the sorceress is stoned, but not because of *smuchin*. *Ov veyidoni be'chlal machasheifim hayu* — the *ov* and *yidoni*, two forms of necromancy, were in the general category of sorcery. *Velama yatz'u* — why were they singled out? *Ba'even yirgemu otam dmeihem bam* — because the Torah states explicitly that they are stoned. *Lehakish lahem* — they were extracted from the general category in order to serve as a comparison: *mah ov veyidoni be'skilah af machasheifa be'skilah* — just as *ov* and *yidoni* are stoned, so too the sorceress. This is not *smuchin* but rather the standard hermeneutic of a *davar shehaya be'chlal veyatza min hakhlal lelamed* — a matter included in a general rule that was singled out to teach about the whole category — which is one of the standard thirteen hermeneutic principles. *Smuchin*, by contrast, is not among those thirteen principles, which is why *Rabbi Yehuda* refuses to employ it.

### Mishneh Torah Rule

*U've'Mishneh Torah minalan de'darash?* — but how do we know that *Rabbi Yehuda* is willing to use *smuchin* in *Devarim*? *De'tanan* — because we learned in the *mishna* what follows.

---

## Anusas Aviw

### Mefutat Aviv

The *mishna* states: *noseh adam anusat aviv umefutat aviv, anusat beno umefutat beno* — a man may marry a woman his father raped or seduced, and a woman his son raped or seduced. The prohibition of *eshet av* — father's wife — and *eshet beno* — daughter-in-law — does not extend to women with whom the father or son had non-marital sexual relations. These are simply not included in those prohibitions.

### Reb Yehuda Assur

*Rabbi Yehuda oser be'anusat aviv umefutat aviv* — *Rabbi Yehuda* disagrees in the case of a woman the father had sexual relations with, whether by rape or seduction, and holds she is forbidden. He agrees, however, that a woman the son had relations with does not become forbidden to the father.

### Knaf Interpretation

*Ve'amar Rav Gidal amar Rav: mai ta'ama de'Rebbe Yehuda?* — what is the basis for *Rabbi Yehuda's* position? The verse says: *lo yikach ish et eshet aviv velo yigaleh knaf aviv* — a man shall not marry his father's wife and shall not uncover the hem of his father. The phrase *velo yigaleh knaf aviv* — shall not uncover his father's hem — is initially puzzling. On one reading, it describes the wrongness of the act: this is the woman under whose garment-hem the father was; she is, as it were, *knaf aviv* — the covering of his father. On *Rabbi Yehuda's* reading, the phrase *velo yigaleh knaf aviv* — he shall not uncover any nakedness that was his father's — extends the prohibition beyond the formal category of *eshet av* to any woman the father had sexual relations with. The logic follows from the very meaning of *knaf*: what matters is not the formal marital bond but the fact of the father's intimacy with this woman.

### Smuchim Anusa

Now the *smuchin* dimension enters. *U'mimai de'be'anusa ktiv?* — how do we know that the verse is referring specifically to a woman the father had relations with outside of marriage? *Me'iluya de'kraya* — because of what is written immediately before the verse in question. The *parasha* preceding *lo yikach ish et eshet aviv* is the passage about a man who rapes an unmarried woman: *venatan ha'ish hashochev imah la'avi hana'arah chamishim kasef* — and the man who lay with her shall pay fifty pieces of silver to the girl's father. It is the case of *anusa* — a raped woman — that is discussed just before *lo yikach ish et eshet aviv*. *Vesamich lei* — and then this prohibition is juxtaposed to it. Thus, *Rabbi Yehuda*, reading *velo yigaleh knaf aviv* in light of the immediately preceding context of *anusa*, understands the phrase as extending the prohibition to women the father had extra-marital relations with.

This is, in fact, a use of *smuchin*. But it is *smuchin* in *Devarim* — this passage appears in *Parshat Ki Tetzei* in *Devarim* — which is exactly the point the *Gemara* is making: *Rabbi Yehuda*, who rejects *smuchin* in general, accepts it in *Mishneh Torah*.

### Rabbis Counter

*Ve'rabbanan* — and what would the Rabbis respond? They would say: *ee hava samich lei ke'de'ka'amrat* — if it were truly juxtaposed immediately, as you say, you would be right. *Hashata de'lo samich lei* — but now that it is not directly juxtaposed, as the gloss makes clear — *de'chtiv lo yikach ish et eshet aviv beintayim* — since the verse *lo yikach ish et eshet aviv* intervenes between the *anusa* passage and *velo yigaleh knaf aviv* — it is not sufficiently proximate to derive the teaching through *smuchin*.

### Shomeret Yavam

If so, what does the Rabbis' reading of *velo yigaleh knaf aviv* refer to? *Beshomeret yavam hakatuv medaber* — the verse is speaking of a *shomeret yavam*, a woman who is quasi-married to the father by virtue of the bond of *zikah*. That is: if the father's brother died childless, the father now has a *mitzvah* of *yibbum* toward his brother's widow. That widow is in a quasi-marital relationship with the father, since *zikah* — the *yibbum* bond — is like a form of inchoate marriage. *Velo yigaleh knaf aviv* then teaches that the son may not have relations with that woman either — she is effectively in the domain of the father.

The *Gemara* then notes: but you do not really need a verse to prohibit this, because that woman is the son's aunt. The son is already forbidden to his aunt by a separate *issur*. The verse must therefore be coming to add a second prohibition — *lav aleiha bishnei lavin* — so that there are two distinct negative prohibitions applying to the act, not merely to spell out a novel *halacha*.

---

## Muchach Mufneh

### Muchach Argument

The *Gemara* now returns to the question of why *smuchin* is valid in *Mishneh Torah* in the first place. *U've'Mishneh Torah mai ta'ama de'darash?* — why does everybody agree to *smuchin* in *Devarim*? *Ee ba'it eima mishum de'muchach* — one answer: because it is evident from context. What does that mean?

*De'im ken lichtov rachmana gabei arayot* — if the Torah wished to introduce the prohibition of *velo yigaleh knaf aviv* as a free-standing *ervah*, it should have written it back where it lists the *arayot* in *Acharei Mot* and *Kedoshim*. Why is it appearing here for the first time, in a different context, in *Devarim*? The very fact that this prohibition is introduced here — and not in its more natural location among the *arayot* — signals that it is here to communicate something specific to this context. The juxtaposition itself is communicating. When *Moshe Rabbeinu* recaps the laws of the Torah in *Devarim*, he sometimes frames things differently, places them in new sequences, and introduces them in new contexts. The *Gemara* treats this as hermeneutically significant: if something appears in *Devarim* that was not present in its natural earlier context, it is appearing here because this context is intended to teach us something that the earlier context could not. The new placement is itself the message.

### Mufneh Argument

*Ve'ee ba'it eima mishum de'mufni* — alternatively, because it is superfluous. *De'im ken lichtov rachmana lo yikach ish et eshet aviv velo yigaleh knaf* — the Torah could have simply said do not uncover the hem, without the word *aviv* — of his father. That is already obvious from the surrounding context. So the word *aviv* is extra, and something extra invites *drasha*. By being extra, it licenses us to read it in light of the adjacent *parasha* about *anusa* and derive a law from the juxtaposition.

The *Gemara* acknowledges, however, that this second argument — *mufneh* — is less distinctive to *Mishneh Torah*. Extra words appear throughout the Torah, and learning from *smuchin* on the basis of a superfluous word is not something unique to *Devarim*. By contrast, the argument from *muchach* — the idea that something newly appearing in *Devarim* without having been in its original context must be communicating something specific to its new surroundings — is genuinely distinctive to *Mishneh Torah*. That is what makes *Devarim* a uniquely rich context for *smuchin*-based *drashot*.

### Tzemer Upishtim

The *Gemara* now applies the same two arguments — *muchach* and *mufneh* — to the case of *shatnez* and *tzitzit* in *Devarim*. *Ee ba'it eima mishum de'muchach: de'im ken lichtov rachmana gabei parashat tzitzit* — if there was nothing to derive from context, why is the prohibition of *shatnez* appearing here in *Devarim* alongside *tzitzit*? *Gedilim ta'aseh lach* was already written back in *Parshat Shelach* in *Bamidbar*. Why repeat it here? The new context itself communicates: the juxtaposition is intentional, and it teaches that the *mitzvah* of *tzitzit* overrides the prohibition of *shatnez*.

*Ve'ee ba'it eima mishum de'mufni* — or alternatively, something in the verse is superfluous. The Torah already wrote in *Vayikra: uveged kilayim shatnez lo ya'aleh alecha*. The prohibition of *shatnez* is already there. *Lo tilbash shatnez lama li?* — why does it need to repeat the prohibition here in *Devarim*? The repetition is superfluous, and that superfluity licenses the *drasha* from *smuchin*. *Shema mina le'afnuyei* — conclude from this that it was made extra for the purpose of enabling the *drasha*.

### Tilbash Elevation

The *Gemara* challenges this: *hani mitzterechei* — you actually need both verses, and neither is superfluous. Here is why. *Dichasav rachmana lo ya'aleh alecha* — the verse in *Vayikra* says do not put [*shatnez*] upon you. *Hava amina kol derech ha'ala'ah asrah rachmana* — I would have thought: any form of placing *shatnez* on oneself is forbidden, even if it is not in a mode of wearing. *Va'afilu mochrei chsut* — even the fabric merchants who carry many garments stacked on their bodies in order to transport them. *Kasav rachmana lo tilbash shatnez* — therefore the Torah says in *Devarim*: do not *wear* *shatnez*. The verb *tilbash* — to wear — tells me it must be something comparable to genuine wearing: *dumya de'levisha de'it bah hana'ah* — similar to wearing in that there is tangible benefit and pleasure, not merely the act of placing it on oneself for transport purposes.

### Hana'ah Levels

Conversely: *de'ai khasav rachmana lo tilbash* — had the Torah only said do not wear, *hava amina davka levisha de'nafish hana'ah* — I would have said only actual wearing, where the benefit is substantial, is forbidden. *Aval ha'ala'ah* — but a blanket placed over oneself, *de'lo nafish hana'ah* — where the benefit is lesser — *la* — perhaps that would not be forbidden under *shatnez*. So *kasav rachmana lo ya'aleh alecha* — the verse in *Vayikra* comes to extend the prohibition to cases of placing on oneself that are not technically *levisha* but still involve a recognizable benefit. Each verse therefore carries independent work: *lo ya'aleh alecha* extends the prohibition beyond wearing; *lo tilbash* restricts it to acts that involve genuine personal benefit, excluding mere transport.

### Gezeirah Shavah

But the *Gemara* then identifies what truly is superfluous. *Im kein lichtov rachmana lo tilbash shatnez — tzemer ufishtim lama li?* — if that is so, why does the verse in *Devarim* need to say *tzemer ufishtim yachdav* — wool and linen together? Why specify the composition of *shatnez*?

One would think this is the least superfluous element — after all, without *tzemer ufishtim yachdav* we would not know what *shatnez* is. But the *Gemara* argues otherwise: *michdi kasav uveged kilayim shatnez lo ya'aleh alecha* — since the verse in *Vayikra* already says *uveged kilayim shatnez*, and *de'tana de'vei Rabbi Yishmael* — the school of *Rabbi Yishmael* teaches — *kol bi nimru baTorah stam begadim uferat lecha hakatuv be'echad meihem tzemer ufishtim* — wherever the Torah speaks of garments without specification, it means wool or linen garments, as established by the one instance where the Torah explicitly mentions *veged tzemer o veged pishtim* in the context of *tzara'at*. Thus, when *Vayikra* says *uveged kilayim shatnez* — a mixed garment — by the rule of *Rabbi Yishmael*, that means a garment mixing wool and linen. I would already have known *shatnez* means wool and linen. *Af kol tzemer ufishtim* — every garment is either wool or linen, and the mixing can only be wool with linen.

Why then does *Devarim* repeat *tzemer ufishtim yachdav*? The *Gemara* says it is still needed: *salka da'atach amina ha'ala'ah hi de'lo nafish hana'ah* — I might have thought that the act of *ha'ala'ah* — placing on oneself — involves lesser benefit and pleasure, and in that context the derivation from *Rabbi Yishmael* about the composition of garments applies, so *shatnez* there means only wool and linen. *Aval levisha de'nafish hana'ah* — but wearing, where there is greater pleasure, *kol terei minei asar rachmana* — perhaps the Torah prohibited any two different types of fiber mixed together, not just wool and linen. The word *tzemer ufishtim yachdav* is therefore needed even in *Devarim*, to explicitly confirm that the definition of *shatnez* as wool-and-linen specifically applies to the more pleasurable act of *levisha* just as much as to *ha'ala'ah*.

So *tzemer ufishtim* is still not superfluous? The *Gemara* responds: *im kein lishtok kera minei veteisei shatnez shatnez mehala* — if so, let the verse in *Devarim* be silent about *tzemer ufishtim* and I would have derived it from a *gezeirah shavah*: the word *shatnez* appears in *Vayikra* and the word *shatnez* appears in *Devarim*; from the verbal analogy I would have learned that the definition of *shatnez* is the same in both verses — wool and linen — even for the act of *levisha*. Therefore, the explicit mention of *tzemer ufishtim yachdav* in the verse about *levisha* in *Devarim* is in fact superfluous. *Shema mina le'afnuyei* — it must be that it was made extra, in order to enable the *drasha* from the juxtaposition with *tzitzit*. And that *drasha* is what establishes the principle of *asei dochei lo ta'aseh*.

---

## Summary Asei

### Established Principle

We can now draw together the threads of this entire *sugya*. The *Gemara* set out to explain why a *pasuk* was needed to prohibit *yibbum* in the case of *arayot* — that is, why the *hava amina* existed at all that *yibbum* might override those prohibitions. The answer begins with the principle of *asei dochei lo ta'aseh*: a positive *mitzvah* overrides a negative prohibition. We derive this principle from the juxtaposition in *Devarim* of the prohibition of *shatnez* and the *mitzvah* of *tzitzit*, which teaches that one may attach a wool string to a linen garment even though that constitutes *shatnez*, because the positive *mitzvah* of *tzitzit* overrides the negative prohibition of *shatnez*.

This principle is accepted by everyone, including those who generally reject *smuchin* as a hermeneutic, because the juxtaposition appears in *Mishneh Torah* — in *Devarim* — where *smuchin* is universally valid. It is valid there either because something newly appearing in *Devarim* in a different context from its original setting is evidently communicating something by means of that new context (*muchach*), or because the repetition of material already stated elsewhere renders the repeated passage superfluous (*mufneh*), specifically the phrase *tzemer ufishtim yachdav*, which could have been derived from a *gezeirah shavah* of *shatnez*–*shatnez* and therefore need not have been written out explicitly here.

With the principle of *asei dochei lo ta'aseh* thus firmly established and universally accepted, we have the foundation for the *hava amina*: one could have thought that the positive *mitzvah* of *yibbum* would override the negative prohibition of *arayot* in the *yibbum* context. The reason that *hava amina* does not hold in practice — because the prohibition of *arayot* carries *kareit*, and *asei dochei lo ta'aseh* does not apply to prohibitions of such severity — is precisely the point the opening *baraita* of the *sugya* established through its derivation from the word *aleha*. The full picture is now in place, and the discussion will continue from here.

---

---

# Yevamot 8

## Yibum & Arayot

### Review: Yibum Override

The daf begins approximately fifteen lines down, at the words *amar lei Rav Acha mi-Difti*. To recall where we left off: after many dappin establishing why one might have thought that the *mitzvah* of *yibum* would apply even in a case of *arayot*, the Gemara worked through the entire framework of *asei docheh lo ta'asei*, ultimately concluding that this principle could not serve as a valid basis, since it does not apply where *karet* is at stake.

The Gemara then arrived at a different *hava amina* entirely. The very case of *yibum* is itself a case of *arayot* — namely, *eshet ach*, one's brother's wife — and this fact might have provided a basis for assuming that *yibum* could apply even in the presence of other *arayot*. The reasoning: either through the principle of *keivan de-ishtari ishtari* — once something is permitted to enable a particular outcome, other related obstacles should similarly be set aside — or through the logic that since a verse links all the *arayot* to one another, what is true of one may be true of the rest.

It is on this basis that we require the verse containing the word *aleha*. That verse is in the prohibition of the wife's sister: *ve-ishah el achotah lo tikach litzror legalot ervatah aleha be-chayeha* — do not take a woman alongside her sister as a rival wife, to uncover her nakedness upon her, during her lifetime. The word *aleha* links this verse to *yevamah yavo aleha*, the operative phrase of *yibum*, thereby establishing that the prohibition of *achos ishah* applies even in the context of *yibum*.

### Rav Acha's Question

Rav Acha mi-Difti raised a pointed question to Ravina: *mikdi kol arayot itka'u le-eshet ach ve-itka'u le-achos ishah* — the verse links all *arayot* to one another, and we now have two *arayot* in play: *eshet ach*, which tells us that *yibum* is operative, and *achos ishah*, which tells us, via *aleha*, that *yibum* does not apply. Given this equipoise, why do we assume that *achos ishah* sets the rule? Why not link all other *arayot* to *eshet ach* and conclude that *yibum* applies in all such cases, with *achos ishah* standing as the sole exception?

### Two-Prohibition Rule

The Gemara offers two responses. The first is simply a matter of interpretive default: *le-kula u-le-chumra, le-chumra makshinan* — when one has a choice between linking toward leniency or stringency, one defaults to stringency.

The second answer is conceptually richer: *hacha terei issurei ve-hacha chad issura, trei mi-trei yalfanan*. Any other *ervah* arising in a *yibum* context carries two distinct prohibitions — the standing prohibition of *eshet ach* that always applies to a brother's wife, plus the additional prohibition specific to that *ervah* — daughter-in-law, mother-in-law, or whichever it might be. *Achos ishah* in a *yibum* context is exactly analogous: it too carries the prohibition of *eshet ach* combined with the prohibition of *achos ishah*. The simple case of *yibum* — *eshet ach* alone — carries only one prohibition. It is therefore far more apt to derive the rule for other *arayot* in a *yibum* context from *achos ishah*, which like them carries two prohibitions, than from the isolated case of *eshet ach* with its single prohibition. One does not derive a two-prohibition case from a one-prohibition case: *terei mi-terei yalfanan, aval me-chad lo yalfanan*.

### Rava: No Verse Needed

Rava now stakes out a more radical position: *erva gufah lo tzericha kra de-ein asei docheh lo ta'asei she-yesh bo karet*. The prohibition of *ervah* requires no verse at all, because it would never have occurred to anyone that *yibum* — a positive commandment — could override a *lo ta'asei* that carries *karet*. The principle of *asei docheh lo ta'asei* simply does not operate in the presence of *karet*, and so no *hava amina* exists in the first place.

One might immediately object: but we just established a stronger *hava amina*, the argument of *keivan de-ishtari ishtari* — once one prohibition has been set aside to enable *yibum*, perhaps another should be as well. Tosafot addresses this directly. First, Rava may simply not hold of Ulla's principle of *keivan de-ishtari ishtari* at all. But Tosafot goes further and offers a more precise conceptual distinction: the case where *keivan de-ishtari ishtari* operates — the classic example involving a *ba'al keri* and a *metzora* — involves a single shared *issur*, namely a *tamei* person entering the *Beis HaMikdash*. Regardless of the source of one's *tumah*, the prohibition being waived is one and the same. By contrast, in our case, the Torah waives the prohibition of *eshet ach* to enable *yibum*, but the prohibition of *achos ishah* is an entirely separate *issur* with its own name and status. Allowing one *issur ervah* does not entail allowing a different *issur ervah*. The two prohibitions are not merely different degrees of intensity of one thing; they are categorically distinct. Even if one accepts *keivan de-ishtari ishtari* in principle, it would not apply across categorically distinct *issurim*.

Rava's conclusion, then, is that one never had a genuine *hava amina* that *yibum* could override *ervah*. What, then, does the verse accomplish? *Ki itztarich kra le-maseir tzarah* — the verse was needed not to exclude *ervah*, which we knew, but to establish the law of the *tzarah*, the co-wife. This is precisely the *chiddush* that our Mishnah opens with: *chamesh esrei nashim potrot tzaroteihen* — fifteen women exempt their co-wives. The Mishnah highlights the exemption of the *tzarah*, not the exemption of the *ervah* herself, because the latter is taken for granted.

The mechanism works as follows: the word *aleha* links the verse to *yibum*, placing the verse in the context of *yibum*. Once the verse is speaking about a *yibum* context, it is positioned to address the *litzror* clause — that not only does the *ervah* herself not undergo *yibum*, but her co-wife does not either.

---

## Rava: Tzarah is Key

### Gemara Objects

The Gemara raises an objection to Rava's reading. If *ervah* requires no verse, why does the *braisa* itself appear to be proving precisely that point? The *braisa* uses the *aleha* linkage to conclude that *yibum* does not apply in the case of *achos ishah*, and only then proceeds to ask: *ein li ela hi — tzarasa minayin?* The *braisa*'s very structure seems to treat the *ervah* exclusion as the primary *chiddush* requiring derivation, with the *tzarah* exclusion following as a secondary consequence.

### Rava Responds

Rava's answer is that the *braisa* is not trying to prove the *ervah* case on its merits. It establishes the *ervah* context only as a necessary step toward proving the case of *tzarah*. The *braisa* must first get the verse talking about *yibum* and *ervah* — not because we needed proof of the *ervah* rule, which we could have derived ourselves — but in order to introduce the *litzror* clause and derive from it the law of the *tzarah*.

The objection is then extended: the *braisa* does not stop with *achos ishah*. It then asks how we know the rule applies to all other *arayot*, and derives this through a *mah matzinu* — reasoning by analogy from *achos ishah* to other *arayot*. And similarly, it asks how we know that the *tzarot* of those other *arayot* are also excluded, and again uses analogy. The Gemara suggests that this expanded structure also seems to prove the *arayot* exclusion as a primary *chiddush*. Rava's response is the same: the entire progression through *achos ishah* and the other *arayot* serves only to set up the corresponding *tzarah* cases. At each stage, the *braisa* is moving toward the law of *tzarah*; the *ervah* cases are vehicles, not destinations.

### Original Braisa Cited

To ground this discussion, it is worth recalling the *braisa* as it appears on 3b. The text reads: *isha el achosah lo tikach litzror* — the verse against marrying a wife's sister. Then: *aleha* — *mah talmud lomar?* What does this teach? The verse is juxtaposed with *yevamah yavo aleha* — the operative language of *yibum* — through a *gezeirah shavah* on the shared word *aleha*. The *braisa* concludes that this prohibition applies *bimkom mitzvah*, in a context of *yibum*, and the Torah says: *lo sikach*. It then asks: *ein li ela hi, tzaratah minayin?* — I have derived only her; from where do I derive the co-wife? The answer: *talmud lomar litzror*. And then: *ein li ela tzaratah, tzaras tzaratah minayin?* — from where do I derive the co-wife of the co-wife? The answer: the doubled form *litzror* rather than the simple *latzor*.

The *braisa* then extends to all other *arayot* through a *mah matzinu*: just as *achos ishah* is a *ervah* for which one is liable, so too all other *arayot* are excluded from *yibum*, and so too their co-wives.

Rava reads the entire structure as oriented toward *tzarah*. The *braisa* needed to get *achos ishah* into a *yibum* context in order to generate the *litzror* derivation; it needed to extend the *arayot* framework in order to cover the *tzarot* of those other *arayot*. None of it was proving something we didn't already know about *ervah* itself.

### Rabbi's Drasha

The Gemara now introduces a competing tradition: *Rabbi omer* — Rabbi derives the same laws from different verses. The relevant verses in the *yibum* passage read: *velakachah lo leishah veyibmah* — and he shall take her to be his wife and perform *yibum* with her. Rabbi notes that the Torah could have written *velakach* and *veyibam* — and he shall take, and he shall perform *yibum* — without the pronominal suffix. Instead it writes *velakachah* and *veyibmah* — her specifically. The feminine suffix, Rabbi argues, is exclusionary: it is *her* he takes and performs *yibum* with, not others in certain related situations. Specifically: one *heh* excludes the *ervah* herself from *yibum*, and the other excludes the *tzaras ervah*.

The reading thus yields: *velakachah* — her but not an *ervah*; *veyibmah* — her but not the co-wife of an *ervah*. This is an entirely different *drasha* from the *achos ishah* — *aleha* derivation. The weakness of Rabbi's *drasha* is readily apparent: there is nothing in *velakachah* or *veyibmah* that hints specifically at *ervah* or *tzaras ervah*; one must import those concepts entirely from without.

### Two Drashas

Rava reads Rabbi's *drasha* through his own lens. Since Rava holds that *ervah* needs no verse, he reinterprets the two suffixed forms accordingly. *Velakachah* means: her, and not the *tzarah* — there is no *yibum* for the co-wife of an *ervah*. *Veyibmah* specifies that this exclusion operates *bimkom yibum*, in a *yibum* context. The practical upshot of this second specification is critical: it tells us that the concept of *tzarah* as a problem is limited to the *yibum* context. Outside of *yibum*, the co-wife of a woman forbidden to me as an *ervah* is not forbidden to me by virtue of being her *tzarah*.

Thus, according to Rava, Rabbi's two words together teach: no *yibum* for a *tzarah* in a *yibum* context — and the implication that outside a *yibum* context, the *tzarah* relationship creates no prohibition. The *ervah* herself, meanwhile, we already knew was excluded without any verse.

### Rav Ashi Observes

Rav Ashi adds that Rava's reading is implicit in the Mishnah itself. The Mishnah opens: *chamesh esrei nashim potrot tzaroteihen* — fifteen women exempt their *tzarot*. Crucially, the Mishnah does not say "fifteen women are themselves exempt *and* exempt their *tzarot*." It simply states that they exempt their *tzarot*, taking their own exemption entirely for granted. *Shema mina* — this confirms that the *chiddush* of the Mishnah is the law of *tzarah*, not the law of *ervah*.

---

## Tzarah Logic Problem

### Challenge to Rava

Having established that the verse is needed for *tzarah* rather than *ervah*, the Gemara poses a symmetrical challenge: *tzarah nami lo tiba'i kra* — perhaps *tzarah* likewise needs no verse. Just as *ervah* needs no verse because *asei* cannot override *lo ta'asei she-yesh bo karet*, perhaps the same is true of *tzarah*. If *tzarah* is itself an *issur* carrying *karet*, one should have been able to derive the same conclusion without a special derivation.

### Rashi Explains

Rashi clarifies the Gemara's reasoning. Without linking the verse to a *yibum* context, one would have read the verse straightforwardly: the prohibition of *achos ishah* and her *tzarah* apply as a general *issur ervah* in all cases. And since *karet* is stated at the end of the *arayot* section — *ve-nichresu* — one would have concluded that *tzaras ervah* is independently forbidden with *karet* in all circumstances, not only in a *yibum* context. Therefore, just as *ervah* itself needs no verse since *asei* cannot override a *karet*-bearing prohibition, so too *tzarah* should need no verse on the same grounds.

The Gemara's question, then, is: what work does the *drasha* actually do?

### Tzarah Contexts

To appreciate the answer, it is essential to distinguish two scenarios. In one scenario — *bimkom mitzvah* — the *tzarah* arises within a *yibum* context. For example: Reuven is married to Rachel and Dvorah, and Shimon is married to Leah. Reuven and Shimon are brothers, and Rachel and Leah are sisters. When Shimon dies childless, Reuven cannot perform *yibum* with Leah, his wife's sister. Since there is no *mitzvat yibum* with Leah, Dvorah — who is Reuven's co-wife to Leah, his brother's wife — also has no *mitzvat yibum*. Once the *mitzvah* falls away, Dvorah reverts to the default status of *eshet ach* with no operative *mitzvah*, and she becomes forbidden. This is the law of *tzaras ervah bimkom mitzvah*.

In the second scenario — *shelo bimkom mitzvah* — a different man, Gideon, is married to Rachel and Dvorah, with no brother-sister relationship to Reuven's wife. When Gideon dies, Reuven cannot marry Rachel because she is his wife's sister. But Dvorah? She is permitted. She was a co-wife to someone who was an *ervah* to Reuven, but the context of *yibum* is entirely absent. The concept of *tzaras ervah* as an exclusion from *yibum* simply does not apply here.

### Rami bar Chama Objects

Rami bar Chama now poses a sharp question to Rava: *eima ha-ervah gufah shelo bimkom mitzvah tishteri* — if *tzarah* is permitted outside the *yibum* context, why not say the same about *ervah* itself? If the verse's role is to limit the *tzarah* prohibition to a *yibum* context, perhaps all *arayot* prohibitions are similarly limited to *yibum* contexts. Outside of *yibum*, perhaps the wife's sister and all other *arayot* should be permitted.

### Rava's Answer

The Gemara immediately rejects the suggestion regarding *ervah* itself: *lav kal va-chomer hu?* — is this not a *kal va-chomer*? If *ervah* is forbidden even *bimkom mitzvah*, all the more so is she forbidden *shelo bimkom mitzvah*. Rava responds to the parallel question about *tzarah*: *tatim alecha kra* — the verse bears you down. The verse says *be-chayeha* — during her lifetime. This phrase establishes a sweeping, time-bound prohibition of *achos ishah* in all contexts: as long as one's wife is alive, the sister is categorically forbidden regardless of circumstance. The word *aleha* in the verse then specifically links this prohibition to *yibum*, limiting the *tzarah* exclusion to that context. *Bimkom aleha hu de-asira* — it is in the *yibum* context that the *tzarah* is also forbidden; *shelo bimkom aleha sharya* — outside that context, the *tzarah* is permitted.

---

## Verse Contradiction

### Rav Huna: Trei Krai

At this point the Gemara identifies a deeper textual problem. Rav Huna bar Tachlifa, citing Rava, observes: *trei krai ktivi* — the verse of *achos ishah* contains, in effect, two distinct textual sections that appear to contradict one another.

Before examining the contradiction, the Gemara notes that *be-chayeha* is needed for a more fundamental *halacha*: to tell us that the prohibition of *achos ishah* applies even after the first wife has been divorced, not only during marriage.
