This is a profoundly counterintuitive position. We are accustomed to saying that matrilineal descent settles the matter: if the mother is Jewish, the child is Jewish, full stop. Yet here is an opinion that this child is not merely Jewish, but Jewish and a *mamzer*.

It should be emphasized at the outset that we do not rule this way. But the opinion exists in the Gemara, and its implications are striking.

### Tosafot Analysis

Tosafot, in the *dibur hamatchil* *kasavar*, takes up the challenge of explaining this opinion and raises a pointed difficulty. The first possible explanation is that this position follows Rabbi Akiva's view that *mamzerut* results from any violation of a negative prohibition — *mamzer mechayavei lavin*. A union with a slave carries a biblical *lav*, and thus the child would be a *mamzer* according to Rabbi Akiva. But the case of a non-Jewish man is more complicated. On the one hand, such a union is treated with the utmost gravity — communities would sit *shiva* for a child who intermarried — yet the technical biblical prohibition of sexual relations with a non-Jew may in fact be only rabbinic, at least when the non-Jew is not from one of the *shiva amamim*, the seven Canaanite nations. Relations in public invoke *kana'im pog'in bo*, as in the story of Pinchas — but that applies specifically to the public act. In private, if there is no biblical *lav*, why would the child be a *mamzer*?

Tosafot offers one answer: perhaps the *mamzerut* is only *miderabbanan*. But he then develops a second, more penetrating answer, which reframes the entire question. Moving to the passage beginning *ve'im tomar*, Tosafot writes: granted that for the case of a slave there is a *lav*, making sense of *mamzerut* along Rabbi Akiva's lines; but for a non-Jew, where relations may be *bias heter* from a biblical standpoint in private — *mikol makom*, since *kiddushin* cannot take effect with a non-Jew (*keivan delo tafsi bah kiddushin havay mamzer, kemo be'eved*) — the child is a *mamzer* in a sense that has nothing to do with the weight of the transgression at all.

This is a fundamental reconceptualization of *mamzerut*. The standard understanding is that *mamzerut* results from a prohibited union — a *lav* or a *karet* relationship. But Tosafot here articulates an alternative framework: *mamzerut* may be a function not of the severity of the transgression but of the impossibility of *kiddushin* taking effect. In all cases of *issurei karet*, *kiddushin* does not take effect. Here too, with a non-Jew, *kiddushin* does not take effect — not because of a weighty transgression, but because the Torah does not recognize such a *kiddushin*. And in this sense, the union with a non-Jew resembles the *karet* category structurally, even if not in terms of the gravity of the sin.

This framework also resolves an apparent paradox: a union that is *issur karet*, namely *nidda*, does not produce a *mamzer* — because *kiddushin* could take effect in that relationship and indeed may even be present. Conversely, a union with no biblical prohibition whatsoever can, according to this view, produce a *mamzer* — because *kiddushin* is categorically impossible. The determining factor is not transgression but the impossibility of marital bond.

Again, we do not rule this way. The *halakhah* is that the child of a Jewish mother and a non-Jewish father is simply Jewish, without any taint of *mamzerut*. The practical stakes are significant: *mamzerut* cannot be solved, whereas questions of Jewish identity — say, where one parent was not Jewish — can be resolved through conversion. That said, it is worth noting that even according to our normative position, the question of *pagum le'kehunah* — whether such a child is *pasul* to marry a *kohen* — is not entirely without discussion.

### Patrilineal Descent

An even more shocking possibility now emerges. The Gemara shifts to discussing the case of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Assi: *oved kochavim shekidesh b'zman hazeh chosheshin l'kiddushin shema me'aseret shevatim hu* — a non-Jew who betroths a Jewish woman nowadays, we are concerned that the *kiddushin* may be binding, lest this person turns out to be a descendant of the ten tribes and is therefore Jewish. The Gemara asks: surely we follow the principle that anyone who separates from a group is assumed to have come from the majority — and the majority of non-Jews are genuinely non-Jews? The Gemara answers that the case is specifically in places where we know the ten tribes were exiled, citing Rabbi Abba bar Kahana's identification of the locations — *Chalach* is *Chalazon*, *Chavor* is *Chadyav*, *Nehar Gozan* is *Ginzak*, and *arei Madai* is *Chemdan*.

One might assume that the concern about these people being descendants of the ten tribes is a concern about matrilineal descent — perhaps a great-great-great-grandmother all the way back through the maternal line was Jewish, and therefore the concern is that there is an unbroken chain of Jewish mothers. That is indeed one way of reading the Gemara, and it is ultimately what Tosafot concludes.

But Rashi reads the Gemara differently, and his reading is genuinely startling. In the passage beginning *measeret shevatim hu* (toward the bottom of 17b), Rashi explains: *shenasu ovdot kochavim* — the Jewish men of the ten tribes married non-Jewish women, and Rashi then states: *dekasavar ovedet kochavim sheyalda mi'Yisrael havlad mamzer vechoshshin lekiddushei mamzer* — there is a view that the child born of a non-Jewish woman from a Jewish father is a *mamzer*, and we are concerned about the *kiddushin* of a *mamzer*. That is: Rashi understands the Gemara to be entertaining the possibility that patrilineal descent — Jewish father, non-Jewish mother — produces not a non-Jew, but a Jew who is a *mamzer*.

Tosafot is understandably troubled. Multiple *mishnayot* establish clearly that Jewishness follows the mother, not the father. How can Rashi be reading this Gemara as suggesting patrilineal descent with *mamzerut*? Tosafot offers two resolutions. The first is that if one accepts the earlier principle — that a Jewish mother and non-Jewish father produce a *mamzer* because *kiddushin* cannot take effect — then perhaps by the same logic the mirror image holds: a Jewish father and non-Jewish mother would also produce a *mamzer*, because that union too admits no possibility of *kiddushin*. In that case, Rashi's reading is coherent, but only within the framework of that radical earlier opinion. Since we do not rule that way in the first case — we say the child is simply Jewish — we certainly do not say so in this direction either; we say the child is simply not Jewish. Tosafot's second resolution, which he treats as more straightforward, is that the concern is simply about matrilineal descent: perhaps these people are descendants of Jewish women from the ten tribes, and therefore the concern is an unbroken maternal line.

The result of this discussion is that two radical positions have now been articulated, both rejected in normative *halakhah*: first, that any union between a Jew and a non-Jew — regardless of which parent is Jewish — produces a child who is both Jewish and a *mamzer*; and second, that there is something akin to patrilineal descent, at least in the sense that the child retains Jewish identity from the father. We do not rule either way. We rule that a Jewish mother produces a Jewish child without any *mamzerut* issue, and a Jewish father with a non-Jewish mother produces a non-Jewish child — also without any *mamzerut* issue.

### Benot Yerushalayim

The Gemara now turns to the second explanation for the concern about Tarmod — *benot Yerushalayim*. The Gemara asks: *mai hi*? What is this about? Rav Yosef and the Rabbis debate, both in the name of Rabbah bar bar Chana. One says 12,000 men and 6,000 archers; the other says 18,000. The substance: when the non-Jews entered the Beit HaMikdash to destroy it at the time of the *churban*, everyone else went for the gold and silver, but this group — whether 12,000 or 18,000 men — *nitnu al benot Yerushalayim*, they went to seize the young women of Jerusalem. As the verse in Eichah says: *nashim be-Tziyon inu, betulot be-arei Yehudah* — the women of Jerusalem were subjected to assault, which is understood as referring to rape.

The *halakhic* question is thus the same one we have already been examining: what is the status of children born from these unions of non-Jewish men and Jewish women? According to one view, entirely unproblematic — the children are Jewish. According to the radical opinion we have discussed, the children would be *mamzerim*. The concern about the descendants of these events thus explains why there was a question about accepting *geirim* from Tarmod, or indeed about the status of people from that region generally.

---

## Enemy Drasha

### Metatron Passage

The Gemara interpolates a *derasha* from Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: the verse *naar hayiti gam zakanti* — "I was a youth and now have grown old" — was said by the *sar ha'olam*, the steward or prince of the world. The strong inclination among commentators is to identify this figure with Metatron, understood as a supreme angelic being or perhaps something beyond that. The Gemara's reasoning is: if it were God who said *gam zakanti*, that is impossible — God would not say He has grown old. And if it were David who said it, David was not so old that the phrase *gam zakanti* would be appropriate. The conclusion is therefore *shema mina sar ha'olam amro*. The precise theological implications of this passage are a matter for deeper exploration; the Gemara itself moves quickly past it to the next and more legally significant *derasha*.

### Sefer Torah Burned

The Gemara then states, again from Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: what is meant by the verse *yado paras tzar al kol machmadeha* — the hand of the enemy stretched out over all its precious things? *Zeh Amon u'Moav* — this refers to Ammon and Moab. When the non-Jews entered the *heichal* to destroy it, everyone else went for the gold and silver, but *heim nitnu al sefer Torah* — they, Ammon and Moab, turned to the Sefer Torah, for the Sefer Torah is *machmadeha*, the most precious and desirous thing of all. Why did they attack the Sefer Torah specifically? *Amru*: because it is written there, *lo yavo Amoni u'Moavi b'kehal Hashem* — Ammon and Moab may not enter the congregation of God. So *Amon u'Moav yisrofu ba'eish* — they burned it. The Maharsha points out a play on words: the word *paras* read backwards spells *saraf* — burned. There is also a verse in Eichah that reads *asher tzivita lo yavo'u b'kahalecha* — those whom You commanded shall not enter Your congregation — which in its plain sense means that enemies came into the Temple, the very ones excluded from the community. The *drasha* sharpens this: the specific enemy who burned the Sefer Torah was Ammon and Moab, precisely those excluded by the text they destroyed.

### Ammon & Moab

The verse in Eichah, *tzivah Hashem l'Yaakov sevivav tzarav* — God commanded for Jacob that enemies would surround it — is connected by Rav to cities such as Humanya and Pum Nahara. Rashi notes that Humanya was populated by Greeks and Pum Nahara by Jews, and the Greeks of that city were oppressive toward the Jewish residents. The broader theme is the same: the enemies of Israel and the problem of mixed ancestry and the intertwining of peoples at the time of the *churban* — Ammon and Moab being paradigmatic cases of peoples whose lineage was itself the product of illicit unions, and who were therefore excluded from the *kahal*, and who then sought to destroy the very text that excluded them.

---

## Matrilineal Descent

### Ten Tribes Concern

The Gemara now returns explicitly to the issue of descendants of the ten tribes. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav Assi: *oved kochavim shekidesh b'zman hazeh chosheshin l'kiddushin shema me'aseret shevatim hu* — if a non-Jew betroths a Jewish woman in our time, we are concerned that his *kiddushin* might be binding, lest he is in fact a descendant of the ten tribes and therefore Jewish. The Gemara objects: do we not ordinarily say that anyone who separates from a group separates from the majority, and since most non-Jews are genuinely non-Jewish, there is no concern? The Gemara answers: *b'duchta d'kviei* — the concern applies specifically in places where the ten tribes are known to have been settled. The locations are identified by Rabbi Abba bar Kahana through a verse: *vayanaichem b'Chalach u'vChavor nehar Gozan v'arei Madai* — *Chalach* is *Chalazon*, *Chavor* is *Chadyav*, *Nehar Gozan* is *Ginzak*, and *arei Madai* is *Chemdan*. An alternative tradition identifies the area as Nehar and its surrounding cities, which Shmuel specifies as Moshchei, Chidkei, and Dumkaya.

At this point the question becomes more nuanced. If we are worried that a person might be a descendant of the ten tribes, what exactly are we picturing? Are we assuming that men and women of the ten tribes married only amongst themselves and descended in a pure line? Or are we allowing for intermarriage, in which case the concern would be about someone whose maternal great-great-great-grandmother was Jewish?

Tosafot ultimately explains that the concern tracks matrilineal descent: perhaps there is an unbroken chain of Jewish mothers, generation after generation, from the exiled Jewish women of the ten tribes through to the present day. That is the straightforward reading.

But as noted above, Rashi reads the Gemara differently — understanding the case as involving Jewish fathers with non-Jewish mothers, with the concern that such a child is Jewish and a *mamzer*. That reading is, as Tosafot observes, deeply difficult to reconcile with the standard *halakhah* established in numerous *mishnayot* that Jewish identity follows the mother. The resolution in Tosafot's first approach is that if one accepts the framework in which any Jew-plus-non-Jew union produces *mamzerut* (in either direction), then Rashi's reading is internally coherent — but since we reject that framework entirely, we are left with the simpler reading that the concern is about matrilineal descent.

### Shmuel's Response

The tradition continues: *ki amritah kamei d'Shmuel amar li* — when Rav Yehuda reported Rav Assi's ruling before Shmuel, Shmuel responded in the clearest possible terms. *Bincha haba min hayisraelit karuy bincha* — your son who comes from a Jewish woman is called your son. *Ve'ein bincha haba min ha'ovedet kochavim karuy bincha ella b'nah* — but your son who comes from a non-Jewish woman is not called your son; he is called her son. This is the definitive articulation of matrilineal descent. The child of a Jewish man and a non-Jewish woman is not Jewish — he is her son, not yours, in the sense that Jewish identity does not pass through you in that case.

This response also clarifies why the earlier Gemara was concerned about non-Jews in those places: if the concern had been about Jewish fathers (as Rashi read), Shmuel now rules that the children of those Jewish fathers are simply not Jewish, and there is therefore no concern at all. If the non-Jews there are descended from Jewish men who married non-Jewish women, their children are not Jewish, period.

### Scripture & Inheritance

The Gemara proceeds to identify the scriptural basis for this principle. The relevant verse is in Devarim 7: *lo titchaten bam, bitcha lo titen livno u'vito lo tikach livnecha* — do not intermarry with them; do not give your daughter to his son, and do not take his daughter for your son. The structure of the verse is telling: the daughter always follows the man she is with. The reason given is *ki yasir et bincha me'achai* — because he will turn your son away from Me.

The grammatical problem here is significant. *Ki yasir* is in the masculine — *he* will turn away. Who is the male who will turn your son away? If it were the non-Jewish daughter who leads your son astray, the verse should read *ki tasir et bincha*, using the feminine. If it were the non-Jewish man leading your daughter astray, it should read *ki yasir et bitcha*. But *ki yasir et bincha* — a male turning away your *son* — what does that mean?

The Rabbis read it as follows: *bincha* here does not mean your son but your grandson. When a non-Jewish man marries a Jewish woman, that non-Jew will lead your grandson — who will be Jewish through the Jewish mother — away from God. That grandson is called *bincha* because he is indeed Jewish through his mother. By contrast, when a Jewish man's daughter marries a non-Jewish man's son, there is no such concern — because the child of that union (Jewish father, non-Jewish mother) follows the mother and is not Jewish, so there is no Jewish grandson to be led astray. The Torah therefore does not say *ki yasir et bincha* in that direction, because there is no *bincha* — no Jewish grandson — at stake.

This *pasuk* is the textual peg upon which the principle of matrilineal descent is hung. As the Gemara notes, that is a great deal to derive from a single *yud* — the difference between the masculine *yasir* and the feminine *tasir* — but that is indeed what the *drashah* is built upon.

### Ravina's Inference

Ravina adds: *shema mina ben bitcha haba min oved kochavim karuy bincha* — we learn from this that the son of your daughter who was born from a non-Jewish man is still called your son. In other words, a Jewish daughter who has a child with a non-Jewish man produces a child who is Jewish — and that child is considered your descendant (*bincha*) through the maternal line. This is implicit in the Shmuel formula already stated, but Ravina makes it explicit: matrilineal descent means that your daughter's child is Jewish regardless of the father, and that child is in a real sense your son.

### Infertile Women

If the concern about the ten tribes could still be answered by saying: well, perhaps these people are descendants through an unbroken maternal line from Jewish women of the ten tribes — the Gemara closes that avenue with a tradition. *Gemiri* — we have received a tradition — *debanshei dehahu dara itztaruy itztaru* — the women of the generation exiled with the ten tribes became infertile; their wombs were somehow rendered incapable of bearing children. If that tradition is correct, then no descendants trace back to the Jewish women of the ten tribes. Any descendants of those exiled communities trace only through Jewish men, and since Jewish men with non-Jewish women produce non-Jewish children, all of those descendants are simply non-Jews. According to this Gemara, there are no remaining Jewish descendants of the ten tribes at all — a remarkable and sobering conclusion that stands in some tension with both popular imagination and certain *responsa* literature on communities like the Ethiopian Jews.

### Assimilation View

An alternative version of the tradition is also recorded. Some say that when Rav Yehuda reported Rav Assi's ruling before Shmuel, Shmuel responded differently: *lo zazu misham ad she-asa'um ovdei kochavim gemurim* — they did not leave those places until they had been made into complete non-Jews. The verse cited is from Hoshea: *ba-Hashem bagadu ki banim zarim yaldu* — they betrayed God, for they bore foreign, non-Jewish children. Whether this verse refers to deliberate assimilation that caused the ten tribes to lose their Jewish status as a matter of communal or rabbinic ruling, or whether it is simply another way of expressing that all children born of those communities were non-Jewish by matrilineal reckoning, is not entirely clear. The listener who noted that the verse in Hoshea is prophetic rather than descriptive — that it depicts intermarriage before the exile rather than after — raises an interesting point about the original context of the verse, though its application here in the Gemara is as described.

Either way, the upshot is the same: there is no viable concern that a non-Jew from those regions today is actually a Jewish descendant of the ten tribes. The door is closed.

---

## Yichus Cities

### Rav Hamnuna Story

The Gemara transitions to a series of vivid vignettes about cities of questionable lineage. Rav Hamnuna was sitting before Ulla, and Ulla was posing challenging questions in the course of their learning. Rav Hamnuna, impressed, exclaimed: *ma gavra* — what a man! And then, in what he presumably intended as a compliment with an unfortunate addendum: *u'ma gavra ilav deHarfanya ma'aseh* — and how much greater this man would be if he were not from Harfanya. Apparently, Harfanya was a city known for its questionable *yichus* — not necessarily outright *mamzerut*, but lineage that was questioned enough that others would not want to intermarry with its residents.

The remark caused Ulla to be *ichsif* — embarrassed. Ulla then asked, with a play on the words *ichsif* and *kesef*: *kesef gulgulta le'heika yahavas* — where do you pay your poll tax? Rav Hamnuna replied that he paid it to Pum Nahara. Ulla immediately said: *im ken mi-Pum Nahara at* — in that case, you're from Pum Nahara. Since Pum Nahara was a Jewish city of unquestioned lineage — indeed, we encountered it earlier as a Jewish city oppressed by the neighboring Greek city of Humanya — Rav Hamnuna's payment of taxes there indicated that he was affiliated with Pum Nahara, not truly of Harfanya. The embarrassment was thereby mitigated: Rav Hamnuna was not casting aspersions on a resident of Harfanya; he was speaking about a city without reference to his interlocutor's actual community.

### Harfanya City

The Gemara asks: *mai Harfanya?* What does this city's name mean? Rav Zeira offers a *drash*: *har she-kol ponim bo* — a mountain, or city, that everyone turns toward, in the sense that all *psulim*, all those with questionable parentage, migrate there. When no one else will marry you, when your lineage is in doubt, you gravitate toward a community of similarly situated people. A *Beraisa* reinforces this: *kol she-ein makir mishpachto ve-shivto nifneh le-sham* — anyone who does not know his family or his tribe ends up there.

This is a striking social portrait. Even outside the specific legal category of *mamzerut*, the intense focus on *yichus* and known ancestry meant that people with uncertain lineage were effectively shut out of normal communal life and marriage. They congregated in cities like Harfanya, creating communities defined by their exclusion from others.

### Hierarchy of Defect

Rava adds a grim metaphor: *ve-hi amuka mi-she'ol* — Harfanya is deeper than the netherworld. For, as the verse says, *mi-yad she'ol efdem mi-mavet eg'alem* — from the hand of *she'ol*, from death itself, God can redeem. But the invalidity of *Harfanya* — meaning the *mamzerut* that ultimately characterizes its residents — has no remedy. The Gemara then traces the genealogy of the problem. The *psulim* of Harfanya came from those of Meshang; the *psulim* of Meshang came from those of Tarmod; and the *psulim* of Tarmod came from the servants of Solomon who had intermarried with Jewish women. And as the folk saying goes: *kava raba vekava zuta, minda ve'azla lish'ol* — a large measure and a small measure, rolling and going down to *she'ol*. From *she'ol* to Tarmod, from Tarmod to Meshang, from Meshang to Harfanya — everything rolls downhill, and each stop is further from any possibility of redemption.

The image is deliberately bleak, and yet one should perhaps hear in it something more than mere legal taxonomy. These are communities of human beings whose condition the Gemara regards with the gravity it deserves — a gravity that comes precisely from the irreversibility of their situation.

### Mamzeirut Irredeemable

The Gemara makes this explicit: *leit lei takanta* — there is no remedy. Unlike someone who is merely from a city of unknown *yichus*, or even someone caught in *she'ol*, the *mamzer* has no path out. The law of *mamzerut* is absolute and hereditary — a *mamzer* cannot marry into the congregation, and the status passes to subsequent generations. The Gemara acknowledges what the earlier discussion made clear: the Rabbis were deeply aware of this irreversibility and worked to construct frameworks — such as the rule that *safek mamzerim mutar* (those of doubtful *mamzer* status are permitted) — that could offer some mitigation. But those efforts did not change the fundamental reality that genuine *mamzerut* carried with it a permanent exclusion that no remedy could undo.

This passage, taken together with everything that has preceded it on this *daf*, represents what the Gemara presents as a distillation of the major concerns of Masechet Yevamot beyond the specific laws of *yibum*: the definition of Jewish identity, the catastrophic consequences of *mamzerut*, the fierce communal concern with *yichus*, and the question of what happens to communities that have lived at the intersection of Jewish and non-Jewish worlds for generations.

---

## Eshet Achivu

### Scenario Setup

The Gemara now opens the next *perek* with the *mishna* that asks: *keitzad eshet achiv shelo haya be'olamo?* — what is the case of the wife of a brother who was not yet alive at the same time? The scenario requires careful tracking. Reuven and Shimon are brothers. Reuven marries Rachel. Reuven then dies. Subsequently, Levi is born. At this point, Shimon — who is still alive — performs *yibum* with Rachel: that is stage three. Then Shimon dies. Now Levi is the surviving brother. What is his relationship to Rachel?

Rachel is *erva* to Levi — specifically, *eshet ach shelo haya be'olamo*, the wife of a brother who was not in existence at the same time as that brother. Because Levi was born after Reuven died, Levi and Reuven were never alive simultaneously, which means Levi has no *mitzvah* of *yibum* with Rachel; she is simply a brother's wife, and therefore *erva*. Shimon was married to Sarah, making Sarah *tzarat erva* — the co-wife of a woman who is *erva* — and therefore Sarah is also exempt from *yibum* and forbidden to Levi.

### Rachel & Sarah Status

The *mishna* therefore rules that Rachel — the first wife in this scenario — is excluded from *yibum* on the grounds of *eshet achiv shelo haya be'olamo*, and Sarah is excluded as her *tzarat erva*. Rachel stands as *erva* and Sarah as *tzarat erva*. Both are forbidden to Levi: Rachel by direct prohibition, and Sarah derivatively by virtue of being the co-wife of a woman who is *erva*.

### Maamar Case

The *mishna* adds a further variation: what if Shimon performed *maamar* with Rachel — a quasi-betrothal, a rabbinic *kiddushin* intended as a precursor to full *yibum* — and then Shimon died before actually completing *yibum*? In this case, Rachel is not fully his wife even by rabbinic standard, and certainly not biblically. Biblically, Shimon was married only to Sarah, and the full obligation of *yibum* rests upon Sarah alone. Yet because Shimon performed *maamar* with Rachel, there is a quasi-marital bond to Rachel at a rabbinic level. Rachel therefore stands as something like a quasi-*erva* in the context of *yibum*, and Sarah becomes something like a quasi-*tzarat erva*. The practical consequence: Levi may not perform *yibum* with Sarah because of the quasi-*tzarat erva* concern, but he also cannot simply walk away, because his real biblical obligation is to Sarah. The resolution is *chalitza*: Sarah requires *chalitza* from Levi, but not *yibum*. Levi discharges his obligation through *chalitza* rather than marriage.

### Textual Variants

The Gemara notes a textual discrepancy. Some versions of the *mishna* refer to Rachel as *rishona* — the first — while others refer to her as *shniya* — the second. Rav Nachman rules that neither version is an error: *man de'tani rishona lo mishtabesh, man de'tani shniya lo mishtabesh*. What does *rishona* mean? *Rishona l'nefilah* — she was the first to fall to *yibum*, in the sense that from the very beginning of this chain of events, the first person involved in the *yibum* process was Rachel (when Reuven died). And what does *shniya* mean? *Shniya b'nisuim* — not "second" in the ordinal sense, but the one who has been married twice: Rachel was married first to Reuven and subsequently taken into the household of Shimon through *yibum*. Sarah, by contrast, was married only once. So while *shniya* seems counterintuitive as a label for Rachel — she was involved from the beginning — it refers to the fact that she is the doubly-married woman in this scenario.

---

## Ki Yeshvu Achim

### Simultaneous Living

The Gemara now asks: *heicha ketiva?* — where in the Torah is the principle of *eshet achiv shelo haya be'olamo* derived? Rav Yehuda answers: from the verse *ki yeshvu achim yachdav* — "if brothers dwell together." The phrase *yeshvu yachdav* — dwell together — requires *shehayta lahem yeshiva achat ba'olam*: they must have had a period of simultaneous coexistence in this world. *Prat le'eshet achiv shelo haya be'olamo* — this excludes the case where one brother was born only after the other had already died. The word *yachdav* is doing real halakhic work: it mandates contemporaneous existence as a precondition for the *mitzvah* of *yibum* to apply.

### Paternal Brothers

The same verse also teaches that only paternal brothers — not maternal brothers — are subject to *yibum*. The Gemara derives this from *yachdav* as well: *meyuchadim benachala* — they are unified by inheritance. Brothers who share a father inherit from one another; maternal half-brothers do not share inheritance. Therefore, *yachdav* excludes *achiv min ha'em* — a maternal half-brother — from the obligation of *yibum*.

Rabba adds a parallel derivation: we learn the meaning of *achim* — brothers — in the context of *yibum* from the sons of Jacob, not from the case of Lot. Joseph's brothers say *shneim asar achim anachnu* — we are twelve brothers — and those brothers are all paternal brothers. Therefore, *achim* in *ki yeshvu achim yachdav* means paternal brothers. This derivation tracks: *ma lehalan min ha'av velo min ha'em, af kan min ha'av velo min ha'em* — just as there (by Jacob's sons) it means paternal brothers only, so here too.

### Yachdav Meaning

The Gemara asks: why not learn *achim* from the case of *arayot*, where the Torah uses the word *achicha* — your brother — and where that term is understood to include even a maternal half-brother? If *achicha* in the context of *arayot* includes maternal brothers, perhaps *achim* in the context of *yibum* should also include them?

The Gemara responds: *danin achim me'achim ve'ein danin achim me'achicha* — we derive a rule using *achim* from another context that also uses *achim*, not from a context that uses *achicha*. The exact same word is a closer linguistic match.

The Gemara pushes back: what difference does it make whether the word is *achim* or *achicha*? They are close enough. The Gemara answers with the principle of Rabbi Yishmael regarding *tzara'at*: where one verse says *veshav hakohen* and another says *uva hakohen*, the Rabbis link them despite the different words — *zo hi shiva, zo hi via* — because essentially the same act is being described. So too here, *achim* and *achicha* might be close enough to learn from one another. The Gemara's reply is: that principle applies only where there is no equally close match available. Here, we have *achim* appearing both in the context of Jacob's sons and in the context of *yibum*, which is a closer and more direct match. *Midi dedami lei yalpinan* — we derive from the closer analogue.

### Both Words Needed

The Gemara then asks: given all this, why was it necessary for the verse to write both *achim* and *yachdav*? Could not one word have done the work of both? The Gemara responds that each is necessary to prevent a misreading. If the Torah had written only *achim*, we might have derived the meaning of *achim* from the case of Lot — where *ki anashim achim anachnu* refers not to brothers but to relatives or even a nephew-uncle relationship. Perhaps *yibum* therefore applies even to a nephew? In that case, the problem of *erva* could theoretically be "solved" by limiting *yibum* to cases where there is no *erva* prohibition — i.e., only to a nephew, not a brother. The Gemara notes that this was not merely a hypothetical concern; certain non-rabbinic sects of the Second Temple period actually interpreted the Torah's law of *yibum* this way, holding that *achim* means relatives-but-not-brothers, and that *yibum* applies specifically where there is no *issur erva*. The Gemara therefore requires *yachdav* — which indicates shared inheritance — to clarify that *achim* here means brothers in the strict paternal sense, not relatives more broadly.

And if the Torah had written only *yachdav*, we might have thought that the *mitzvah* requires brothers who share *both* a father and a mother — i.e., full brothers only. The word *achim* (interpreted in light of Jacob's sons, all of whom were paternal brothers but had different mothers) establishes that maternal relationship is irrelevant; paternal brothers suffice even without a shared mother.

### Yibum & Inheritance

The Gemara's explanation for why *yachdav* signals inheritance — *yibum banachala tala Rachmana* — is genuinely striking. The ordinarily cited rationale for *yibum* is *yakum al shem achiv hamet* — to establish the name of the deceased brother. Yet the Gemara here understands that part of the essential structure of *yibum* is tied to inheritance: the *yavam* takes over the brother's *nachala* and, by implication, is responsible for perpetuating the brother's line through inheritance. Since inheritance flows through the father, the relevant fraternal relationship for *yibum* is similarly paternal. Maternal brothers have no shared *nachala* and therefore fall outside the *yibum* framework. This is not a peripheral point; it reveals something about the Gemara's underlying understanding of what *yibum* is for.

### Closest Relationship

A final *hava amina* rounds out the discussion. One might have thought to limit the application of *yibum* — which does override the ordinary *erva* prohibition of a brother's wife — to only the very closest possible fraternal relationship: brothers who share both a father and a mother. The logic would be: *yibum* is a *chiddush*, an exceptional override of an *erva* prohibition. Since it is exceptional, perhaps we should require the absolute closest relationship — full brothers — before we invoke this exceptional permission. Therefore, we might have required *yachdav* to mean sharing both father and mother. The verse's use of *achim* (from Jacob's sons, who were paternal but not all maternal brothers) teaches us that this is not required — paternal alone is sufficient for *yibum*.

Ironically, the Gemara also notes that one sect resolved the tension between *yibum* and *erva* by going in the opposite direction — applying *yibum* only to a nephew rather than a brother, thereby eliminating the *erva* issue entirely. The Gemara rejects this reading entirely, but it is worth registering that the tension the Gemara is grappling with — the apparent collision between the obligation of *yibum* and the prohibition of *eshet ach* — was recognized as a genuine puzzle that attracted competing solutions in Jewish antiquity.

---

---

# Yevamot 16b

## Mixed Marriages & Mamzer

### Chaggai & Tarmod

The Gemara on 16b continues from where the previous daf left off. Two testimonies were attributed to *Chaggai HaNavi*: first, that *tzarat habat* is *muteret*, in accordance with the position of *Beit Hillel*; and second, that *geirim* may be accepted from the inhabitants of Tarmod and Karduyim. That second point implies that those inhabitants are presumed to be non-Jews — as distinct from a concern that they might be Jews afflicted with *mamzerus*. The significance of that distinction is considerable: *mamzerus* cannot be resolved, whereas non-Jewish identity can be addressed through conversion. The Gemara had already noted a contradiction in the statements of Rabbi Yochanan regarding whether *geirim* could be accepted from Tarmod, and it is precisely that tension the Gemara now moves to resolve.

The Gemara asks: *mai ta'ama* — what is the concern with Tarmod in the first place? *Pligi beih Rabbi Yochanan v'Savia* — Rabbi Yochanan and Savia, an exceedingly rare *Amora*, debate the matter. One holds the concern is *mishum avdei Shlomo* — because the non-Jewish servants of King Solomon had intermarried with Jewish women from that region. The other holds the concern is *mishum bnos Yerushalayim* — because of what was done to the young women of Jerusalem at the time of the *Churban Beit HaMikdash*. In both cases, the immediate question is: if there is a Jewish mother, what is the problem? If *yichus* follows the mother, these descendants should simply be Jewish. Why should *mamzerus* even enter the picture?

### Avdei Shlomo Debate

The Gemara itself acknowledges the tension: *bishlama l'man d'amar mishum avdei Shlomo* — the concern about the servants of Solomon is intelligible if one holds the view that *kasavar oveid kochavim v'eved haba al bat Yisrael havlad mamzer* — that a non-Jew or a slave who has relations with a Jewish woman produces a *mamzer*. This is, to put it plainly, a striking position. The conventional understanding, which is also the normative ruling, is that *matrilineal descent* governs: the child of a Jewish mother is Jewish, full stop. Yet here is a view that the child is not merely Jewish, but specifically a *mamzer*.

The logical mechanism driving this view requires explanation, and *Tosafot* provides it in a careful and layered analysis.

### Tosafot on Mamzer

*Tosafot* in the *dibur hamatchil* of *kasavar* first proposes that this position follows Rabbi Akiva's opinion that a child born from a union prohibited by a *lav* — a simple negative commandment — carries the status of *mamzer*. This is the principle of *mamzer m'chiyuvei lavin*. That reasoning works more naturally for the case of an *eved*, where at least some *pasuk* can be read to establish a biblical *lav* against relations with a slave. But the case of a non-Jew is more complicated. Counterintuitive as it may seem given the profound sociological weight attached to intermarriage — parents historically sitting *shiva*, communities ostracizing such unions — the technical prohibition of relations with a non-Jew may in fact be only *d'rabanan*, at least where the non-Jew is not from the seven Canaanite nations. The famous principle of *kana'im pog'im bo*, applied in the episode of Pinchas, operates only when the act is committed publicly; in private, the biblical prohibition may not exist. So *Tosafot* asks: if the act itself is not biblically forbidden, why would the child be a *mamzer*?

*Tosafot* offers one resolution: perhaps the *mamzer* status here is only *mid'rabanan*. But then *Tosafot* advances a second and more conceptually significant answer. The relevant passage begins approximately a third of the way into the line starting with *al bat Yisrael havlad mamzer v'al korchacha Rabbi Akiva hi*, at the words *v'im tomar*. There, *Tosafot* writes: *bishlema me-eved havai mamzer d'v'eved ika lav ela me-oved kochavim amai havai mamzer* — granted that a slave produces a *mamzer* because there is a *lav*, but a non-Jew, why should that produce a *mamzer*? One answer the Gemara suggests is a rabbinic enactment — *Beis Din shel Shem gazru*. And then: *u'me-d'oraisa bias heter hi* — biblically, the act may actually be entirely permitted in private. Yet despite that, *Tosafot* continues: *v'yesh lomar*, one can say, even though the act is technically permitted *me-d'oraisa* in private, *keivan de-lo tafsi bah kiddushin havai mamzer k'mo b'eved* — since *kiddushin* cannot take effect in such a union, the child is a *mamzer*, just as in the case of a slave.

This is the crucial insight. The standard framework for *mamzerus* links it to the weight of transgression — *issurei kares* or *issurei lavin* according to Rabbi Akiva. What *Tosafot* is pointing to here is an entirely different axis: not the weight of the prohibition, but the impossibility of *kiddushin*. In the case of *issurei kares*, *kiddushin ein tofsin* — the betrothal does not take effect. The same is true, *Tosafot* argues, with a non-Jew, even absent any biblical prohibition: there is simply no capacity for the *Torah* to recognize *kiddushin* in such a union. The *mamzer* status, on this reading, is not a consequence of having violated a prohibition; it is a consequence of having produced a child from a union in which the marital bond is structurally impossible.

This reframing has a striking implication: a child born from relations with a *niddah* — which is unquestionably an *issur kares* — is not a *mamzer*, precisely because *kiddushin* is possible with a *niddah* and may even be present simultaneously. Conversely, a child born from a union with a non-Jew — where there may be no biblical prohibition at all — is a *mamzer* on this view, because *kiddushin* cannot take effect. The defining characteristic of *mamzerus*, on this approach, may have less to do with the severity of transgression and more to do with the structural incapacity for a recognized marital bond.

It bears emphasis that we do not rule in accordance with this position. The normative *halakha* is that the child of a Jewish mother and a non-Jewish father is simply Jewish, without any taint of *mamzerus*. At most, there may be questions regarding *pagum l'kehuna* — the fitness of such a child to marry a *kohen* — and that is a genuinely contested issue that arises in contemporary cases involving children of Jewish mothers and non-Jewish fathers. But the underlying concern of *mamzerus* itself is not applied.

### Bnos Yerushalayim

The Gemara then turns to the second opinion — that the problem with Tarmod stems from *bnos Yerushalayim*. The *meimra* of Rav Yosef and the *rabbanan*, both in the name of Rabbah bar bar Channah, describes what occurred when the nations entered the *Heichal*. The debate between Rav Yosef and *rabbanan* is relatively minor — one says twelve thousand men and six thousand archers, the other says twelve thousand men among whom were six thousand archers, amounting to either twelve thousand or eighteen thousand total. What matters is the act they committed: *hakol nifnu al kesef vezahav* — everyone else rushed for the gold and the silver, *vehem nifnu al bnos Yerushalayim* — this group turned specifically to the young women of Jerusalem. The verse invoked is *nashim beTzion inu, betulot b'arei Yehuda* — the women of Zion were violated, the young women of Judah's cities. The plain meaning of *inu* here is rape.

The halachic consequence is structurally identical to the *avdei Shlomo* scenario: in both cases we are dealing with offspring of Jewish women and non-Jewish men. According to the view that such unions produce *mamzerim* — whether on the basis of Rabbi Akiva's principle regarding *chiyuvei lavin* or on the basis of *kiddushin ein tofsin* — the descendants in Tarmod would be *mamzerim* and could not simply convert. According to the normative view, which does not recognize *mamzerus* in such cases, the descendants would simply be Jewish and there would be no bar to their accepting *geirim* from there, since there would be no one who requires conversion at all.

### Sefer Torah Drasha

The Gemara proceeds to a related *drasha* on the verse *yado parash tzar al kol machmadeha* — the enemy stretched out his hand over all her precious things. Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan identifies *tzar* here as Amon and Moav. When the non-Jews entered the *Heichal*, everyone else went for the gold and silver; Amon and Moav turned to the *Sefer Torah*. They declared: this is what it is written in — *lo yavo Amoni Moavi bi-kehal Hashem*, that we may not enter the congregation of God — and so they burned it. The *Maharsha* notes that the word *paras* read backwards yields *saras*, which is part of the wordplay operative in this passage. Additionally, the verse in *Eicha* states *asher tzivita lo yavo'u bi-kehalekha* — the enemies entered the Temple, the very enemies whom You commanded shall not enter Your congregation — and the *drasha* picks up on that resonance: those excluded from the *kahal* attacked the *Sefer Torah* that excluded them. The *machmada*, the most precious thing, was the *Sefer Torah* itself, and that is what Amon and Moav destroyed.

---

## Matrilineal Descent

### Rashi's Patrilineal

The Gemara then introduces a statement that, if anything, is even more striking. Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Rav Assi: *oveid kochavim she-kideish bi-zman ha-zeh, chosheshin le-kiddushin* — a non-Jew who betroths a Jewish woman nowadays, we are concerned that the betrothal may be binding. Why? *Shema me-aseret ha-shevatim hu* — perhaps this non-Jew is actually a descendant of the ten tribes, and therefore may in fact be Jewish.

The Gemara immediately objects: *kol de-parish me-rubah parish* — the principle is that anyone who separates from a group is assumed to come from the majority. The majority of non-Jews are genuinely non-Jews. Why should we entertain this concern? The Gemara responds: *be-duchta de-kavia* — this applies specifically in a place where the ten tribes are known to have been settled. In such a location, one cannot rely on *rov*, because the very composition of the population is in question. The biblical source for the locations of the exile is cited: Rav Abba bar Kahana identifies the places of the Assyrian exile — *Chalach, Chavor, nehar Gozan, and arei Madai* — with the identifiable cities of *Chalazon, Chadyav, Ginzak, and Chemdan* respectively. A second tradition, cited as *ve-ika d'amri*, gives an alternative set of locations centered around *Nihar* and its surrounding cities, which Shmuel identifies as *Mushkhei, Chidki, and Dumkaya*.

Now one must pause and ask: in what way might the descendants of the ten tribes still be Jewish? The ten tribes were exiled centuries earlier, and obviously intermarriage with the surrounding non-Jewish populations would have occurred extensively. If we are concerned that some of these apparent non-Jews carry Jewish ancestry, we are implicitly concerned about a matrilineal chain — some great-great-grandmother, several generations back, who was Jewish. That is the straightforward reading, and it is the reading that *Tosafot* ultimately endorses.

But *Rashi* reads it differently, and his reading is remarkable. On the words *shema me-aseret ha-shevatim hu*, approximately six lines from the bottom of 16b, *Rashi* explains: *shenasu ovdot kochavim* — the Jewish men there married non-Jewish women. That is, the concern is not about a matrilineal Jewish grandmother but about a patrilineal Jewish grandfather. And *Rashi* continues: *ve-kasvar de-ovedet kochavim she-yaldah mi-Yisrael ha-velad mamzer ve-chosheshin le-kiddushei mamzer* — the opinion being operated with here is that a child born of a non-Jewish mother and a Jewish father is a *mamzer*, and therefore we are concerned that the *kiddushin* with this apparent non-Jewish man might be *kiddushei mamzer*.

This is an astonishing move. *Rashi* is reading the Gemara as operating with an assumption of patrilineal Jewish identity — the child of a Jewish father and a non-Jewish mother is, on this view, still Jewish, and indeed a *mamzer*. One might think this opens some door: there is a Talmudic opinion, apparently, that patrilineal descent confers Jewish identity. But as will become immediately clear, that is precisely the wrong conclusion to draw. If this view says the child is a *mamzer*, then patrilineal descent, on this reading, is worse than no descent at all — a *mamzer* cannot be remedied, whereas a non-Jew can convert.

### Tosafot Rejects Patrilin…

*Tosafot* reacts with considerable force. In the *dibur hamatchil* beginning *oved kochav she-kidesh be-zman ha-zeh*, *Tosafot* writes: *peirush be-kuntres de-kasvar ovedet kochavim she-yaldah mi-Yisrael ha-velad mamzer ve-chosheshin le-kidushei mamzer* — so *Rashi* has explained it. But *Tosafot* objects: *u-teimah de-ve-kama mishnayot muchach de-ein ha-yachas ela achareha* — it is demonstrated from numerous *Mishnayot* that lineage follows the mother, not the father. When the father is Jewish and the mother is not Jewish, the child is not Jewish. The evidence from across *Shas* is overwhelming, and *Tosafot* marshals it.

*Tosafot* then attempts to defuse the difficulty: *ve-nireh de-lo kashya kol kach de-ha nami mishnah hi savira lei de-oved kochav ve-eved ha-ba al bat Yisrael ha-velad kasher* — the same position that says a non-Jewish man with a Jewish woman produces a *kasher* Jew would also say, in the mirror image, that a Jewish man with a non-Jewish woman produces a *kasher* child — just not Jewish. That is, if you accept the normative view that the Jewish-mother case produces a straightforward Jew with no *mamzer* issue, then logically you accept that the Jewish-father case produces a straightforward non-Jew with no *mamzer* issue either. *Ve-hu ha-din ipcha* — the same logic applies in reverse.

But *Tosafot* also explains what *Rashi's* reading would entail if followed through: *de-Rav Assi savar ke-Rabbi Akiva de-amar ein kiddushin tofsim be-chayvei lavin ve-ha-velad mamzer* — Rav Assi operates with Rabbi Akiva's position that *kiddushin* does not take effect with *chiyuvei lavin* and the child is a *mamzer*. If that were true in the case of a Jewish mother, *ve-hu ha-din* it would be true in the mirror image — the child of a Jewish father and non-Jewish mother would also be a *mamzer*. The two cases rise and fall together. Since we do not rule like this in the Jewish-mother case — the child is simply Jewish — we correspondingly do not apply it in the Jewish-father case — the child is simply non-Jewish. There is no *mamzer* in either direction.

*Tosafot's* final word on the matter is contained in the passage beginning with the word *Yehuda*: *ve-nireh de-tameih de-Rabbi Yehuda amar Rav Assi mishum banot* — the real reason for Rav Assi's concern is *mishum banot*, because of the Jewish women, that is, the concern is about a matrilineal chain through the Jewish mothers of the ten tribes, not through the Jewish fathers. This is the reading *Tosafot* ultimately endorses, and it is the reading consistent with the universal *halakhic* principle of matrilineal descent.

To summarize the two radical possibilities that have now emerged: one is that a Jewish mother combined with a non-Jewish father produces a *mamzer* — not on account of a biblical transgression, but because *kiddushin ein tofsin*. The other, following *Rashi's* reading, is that a Jewish father combined with a non-Jewish mother also produces a *mamzer* rather than a non-Jew. *Tosafot* shows that these two positions are interdependent: they stand or fall together, since they rest on the same underlying logic about the impossibility of *kiddushin*. The normative ruling rejects both: Jewish mother means Jewish child, Jewish father and non-Jewish mother means non-Jewish child, and *mamzerus* is not in play in either scenario.

### Shmuel's Ruling

The resolution is delivered by Shmuel himself. Rav Yehuda reports: when I stated this ruling before Shmuel, he said to me — *bincha haba min ha-Yisraelis kari bincha, v'ein bincha haba min ha-ovedet kochavim kari bincha ela bino* — your son who comes from a Jewish woman is called your son; the child who comes from a non-Jewish woman is not called your son, but her son.

This is the classical formulation of matrilineal descent in its most direct and unambiguous form. The child of a Jewish woman, regardless of who the father is, follows the mother and is Jewish. The child of a non-Jewish woman, regardless of who the father is, follows the mother and is not Jewish. The asymmetry is total and admits no qualification. This statement also retroactively explains why *Rashi* read the earlier Gemara the way he did: the Gemara was operating with an assumption that would be flatly denied by Shmuel, and Shmuel's ruling is precisely the rejection of that assumption.

One observation raised in discussion is worth noting here. It was pointed out that Shmuel's own daughters were reportedly kidnapped and violated, with the question of the status of their children being one that Shmuel himself would have faced with personal acuity. That biographical context lends an additional layer of significance to Shmuel's authoritative ruling on precisely this issue.

### Ki Yasir Pasuk

Having established the ruling, the Gemara provides its biblical anchor. The relevant verse is in *Devarim* 7, in the passage beginning *v'lo titchaten bam* — do not intermarry with them. The *pasuk* reads: *bitcha lo titein livno u-vito lo tikach l'vanecha* — do not give your daughter to his son, and do not take his daughter for your son. Note the structure: the daughter always follows the man she goes to. Now the reason given is *ki yasir et bincha me'acharai* — for he will turn your son away from Me.

There is a grammatical puzzle here. *Ki yasir* is masculine — "he will turn." But who is the "he" who will turn "your son"? If the concern is about your daughter marrying a non-Jewish man, then *he* — the non-Jewish man — will take your daughter away. But it says *yasir et bincha*, "will turn your son." Why would the non-Jewish man turn your son away?

The Rabbinic reading resolves this by understanding *bincha* not as your immediate son but as your grandson. The structure is: do not give your daughter to his son — because the non-Jewish husband (*yasir*, masculine) will turn your grandson (*bincha*, meaning your daughter's child) away from God. And that child is *bincha*, is called *your* (grand)son — meaning he is Jewish — because the mother is Jewish. By contrast, the case of taking a non-Jewish woman for your son carries no such warning, because in that case your grandchild through your son is not Jewish to begin with. There is no grandson to lead astray.

This derivation hangs on the word *yasir* — masculine, referring to the non-Jewish man taking your daughter — and the object *bincha* — the product of that union who is nonetheless still your Jewish (grand)son. The child of a Jewish daughter and a non-Jewish man is Jewish; the child of a Jewish son and a non-Jewish woman is not Jewish. That is the halakha, and this is the verse from which it is derived. The whole edifice of matrilineal descent rests, as the Gemara understands it, on this single grammatical turn.

### Ravina's Question

After Shmuel's ruling has established that descent from a non-Jewish mother renders a child non-Jewish regardless of paternal Jewish lineage, *Ravina* raises the obvious follow-up question. The Gemara's argument for dismissing concern about the inhabitants of the exiled-tribes' cities was that if Jewish fathers intermarried with non-Jewish women, the children would simply be non-Jewish — no cause for concern. But what about the reverse? What about the Jewish women of the ten tribes? Surely some of them also remained and had children. Those children, born of Jewish mothers, would be Jewish by matrilineal descent. And their descendants, several generations later, might still carry a matrilineal Jewish identity even while appearing fully assimilated into the surrounding non-Jewish population. Should we not be concerned that the apparent non-Jew in one of those cities is actually the matrilineal descendant of a Jewish woman from the ten tribes?

*Ravina* makes this point explicit: *shma mina, ben bitcha haba min ha-oved kochavim kari bincha* — we derive from the previous ruling that the son of your daughter, who had relations with a non-Jewish man, is called your son. That child is Jewish. So the concern about matrilineal descent from the women of the ten tribes is real and pressing.

### Women's Infertility

The Gemara provides a definitive answer: *Gemiri, de-b'nesha de-hadora ishtaruei ishtaru* — we have a received tradition that the women of that generation — the women of the ten tribes who were exiled — experienced some form of rupture or infertility. *Rashi* understands this to mean that their wombs were somehow burst, rendering them unable to bear children. As a result, there are no matrilineal descendants of the ten tribes whatsoever. Any descendants that exist come only through the Jewish men, not the Jewish women — and since the Jewish men intermarried with non-Jewish women, those descendants are all non-Jewish. There is, therefore, no living person with a matrilineal claim to Jewish identity through the women of the ten tribes.

This is a striking and theologically loaded *gemara*. If taken at face value, it means that the ten tribes are genuinely and irrevocably lost — not merely assimilated, but without any surviving matrilineal line. Various eschatological traditions posit the return of the ten tribes at the end of days; this *gemara* would seem to complicate such a vision considerably. The identification of, for example, the Ethiopian Jewish community as descendants of *shevet Dan* by the *Radbaz* raises the question of how he navigated this tradition — whether he understood it narrowly, as applying only to those specific exiled populations, or in some other way.

An alternative version of Shmuel's response to the same question is also cited: *lo zazu misham ad she-asam ovdei kochavim gemurim* — they did not leave there until they had been rendered completely non-Jewish. Whether this means a *halakhic* ruling was issued declaring them non-Jews, or whether it reflects the factual claim that all remaining descendants were patrilineal only, is not entirely clear. The verse cited in support is from *Hoshea*: *ba-Hashem bagadu ki banim zarim yaldu* — they betrayed God, for they bore foreign children. This could be read as describing deep assimilation destroying Jewish identity in a more diffuse sense, or as a restatement of the factual claim that all children born were non-Jewish because all were born of non-Jewish mothers.

---

## Cities of Defect

### Tarmod Destruction

The Gemara now shifts to a vivid scene of *amora'ic* discourse. Rav Yosef sat behind Rav Kahana, who sat in front of Rav Yehuda in the *beis midrash*. Rav Yehuda was teaching: *asidin Yisrael de-avdi yoma tava ki charvi Tarmod* — the Jewish people will celebrate a holiday when Tarmod is destroyed. The basis for this sentiment is the very material we have been studying: there was a persistent concern about the population of Tarmod, whether they were *mamzerim* or non-Jews, and according to *Rashi* they were regarded as *mamzerim* who were seeping into the Jewish community through intermarriage. The prospect of that city's elimination would be cause for celebration — though one might charitably understand "destroyed" to mean dispersed rather than anything more severe.

### Tarmod Persistent

The Gemara responds with a practical challenge: *ha-charuv?* — but it has already been destroyed! Rav Yehuda distinguishes: the city that was destroyed was *Tamod*, not *Tarmod*; they are different cities. The Gemara, however, objects that we have said elsewhere these are in fact the same city. The answer is that the city was rebuilt: *ichpulei d'ichpal* — it redoubled. *Chariv m'hai gisa, yativ m'hai gisa* — if one side of the city is destroyed, the other side is built up, and vice versa. Tarmod is persistent in the way the *tzinim u-pachim* of the *Torah* are persistent — a recurring affliction that does not disappear. And so Rav Yehuda's hope for its eventual destruction remains very much aspirational.

### Harfanya Issue

Rav Hamnuna sat before Ulla, engaged in *halacha*. Ulla was posing difficult questions, and Rav Hamnuna was struggling with them. Rav Hamnuna then remarked admiringly — though the remark was actually made about him, by Ulla: *mah gavra* — what a great person this is! *Mah gavra ila d'maharfanya mah avvad* — imagine how great he would be if he were not from Harfanya, if his lineage were not pulled down by his connection to that problematic city. Harfanya, like Tarmod, was a city with questions of *yichus*, though the concern there appears to be not *mamzerus* specifically but rather genealogical uncertainty more broadly.

Upon hearing this, Rav Hamnuna was embarrassed. Ulla sought to reassure him. He asked: *kesaf gulgalta l'heicha yahavat* — where do you pay your poll tax? Rav Hamnuna replied: to *Pum Nahara*. Just as an American living abroad might still file taxes with the United States, Rav Hamnuna, though residing in Harfanya, was registered as a subject of *Pum Nahara* — and we noted earlier that *Pum Nahara* was identified as a Jewish city. Ulla therefore concluded: *im ken mi-Pum Nahara at* — if so, you are really from *Pum Nahara*, not from Harfanya. His lineage is intact.

### Harfanya Definition

The Gemara then explains the name *Harfanya* through a form of *drash*. Rav Zeira says: *har she-hakol ponim bo* — a mountain toward which everyone turns, meaning everyone who has been excluded elsewhere, anyone with questionable parentage, converges there. The *Beraita* reinforces this: *kol she-ein makir mishpachto v'shivto nifne l'sham* — whoever cannot identify his family and tribal lineage goes to that city, because no one else will have him. This is a striking sociological observation embedded in the Talmudic text. Even setting aside the formal legal category of *mamzerus*, the community's insistence on *yichus* — knowing with certainty one's genealogical origins — was so acute that those who lacked such clarity were socially marginalized and effectively driven to settle among others in the same situation. This heightened concern with *yichus* will prove to be one of the central recurring themes of *Masechet Yevamot*.

### Worse Than Sheol

Rava then delivers a sharp epigram: *v'hi amuka mi-she'ol* — Harfanya is deeper than *Sheol*, the netherworld. His source is the verse: *mi-yad she'ol efdem mi-mavet eg'alem* — from the hand of *Sheol* I will redeem them, from death I will ransom them. The logic is painful in its clarity: those in *Sheol* can be redeemed. Those afflicted with the *psulot* of Harfanya cannot be redeemed; their disqualification is more permanent than death itself.

### Defect Chain

The Gemara then traces a cascade of genealogical defect that flows from one city to the next. The *psulim* of Harfanya came from the *psulim* of Meshan. The *psulim* of Meshan came from the *psulim* of Tarmod. The *psulim* of Tarmod came from the servants of Solomon — *mishum avdei Shlomo* — the non-Jewish slaves who had intermarried with Jewish women at the beginning of this entire discussion. And the folk saying captures this cascading descent: *kava rabba v'kava zuta, minder ve-azil li-she'ol, u-mi-she'ol le-Tarmod, u-mi-Tarmod le-Meshan, u-mi-Meshan le-Harfanya* — a large measure and a small measure rolling downhill, from *Sheol* to Tarmod to Meshan to Harfanya — each stage more irredeemable than the last.

One cannot help but sense, beneath this imagery, the human reality it describes: communities of people, generation after generation, for whom there was no return, no remedy, no reintegration into the broader Jewish community. *Chazal* were deeply aware of this, and their efforts to introduce leniencies — the principle of *safek mamzer mutar*, and the many *halakhic* mechanisms for dissolving *mamzerus* concerns — reflect their discomfort with this severity. But those leniencies did not erase the underlying social reality in which *yichus* functioned as a form of communal gatekeeping, and those without it were effectively exiled to cities of the rejected.

---

## Brother Not Alive

### Four-Stage Scenario

With the words *hadran alach chamisha asar nashim*, the *perek* concludes and the next one begins. The opening Mishnah asks: *keitzad eshet achiv shelo haya b'olamo* — how does the case of a brother's wife who was not alive at the same time as the deceased brother work? The scenario is built in four stages.

Stage one: Reuven and Shimon are alive. Reuven marries Rachel. Reuven then dies. Stage two: Levi is born. Because Levi was not alive when Reuven was alive — they never shared existence in this world — Levi has no *mitzva* of *yibum* with Rachel. For him, Rachel is simply his brother's wife, which is an *erva*. Stage three: Shimon, who was alive at the same time as Reuven, does *yibum* with Rachel. He is already married to Sarah. So now Shimon is married to both Sarah and Rachel. Stage four: Shimon dies. Now the question of Levi's obligations comes into full focus.

### Ervah & Tzarat

The Mishnah's ruling is as follows. *Ha-rishona* — Rachel, the first woman — *yotzeis mishum eshet achiv shelo haya b'olamo* — is exempt from *yibum* with Levi because she is an *erva* to him, being the wife of a brother he never coexisted with. *Ve-ha-shniya mishum tzarasah* — Sarah, the second woman, is exempt because she is the *tzarat erva*: the co-wife of an *erva* is herself exempt from *yibum* just as the *erva* herself is.

### Maamar Case

The Mishnah continues with a further complication. Suppose Shimon did not actually perform *yibum* with Rachel but instead performed *maamar* — the rabbinic act of betrothal intended as a preliminary step toward *yibum*, which creates a quasi-*kiddushin* status for the *yevama* — and then he died. The halachic picture shifts. *De'oraita*, Shimon was fully and biblically married only to Sarah. Rachel was not biblically his wife; she was simply the *yevama* with whom he had performed a rabbinic betrothal. Biblically, the *yibum* obligation rests entirely with Sarah.

Yet because of the *maamar*, Rachel has a quasi-marital status vis-à-vis Shimon. That means that from Levi's perspective, Rachel is something of a quasi-*erva* — not a full biblical *erva*, since Shimon's marriage to her was only rabbinic, but sufficiently complicated to generate a concern resembling *tzarat erva*. Sarah, in turn, becomes a quasi-*tzarat erva*. The result: Levi cannot perform *yibum* with Sarah because it looks like a *tzarat erva* situation, but he also cannot simply walk away from his obligation to Sarah, because biblically Sarah is his true *yevama*. The resolution is *chalitza*: Levi must perform *chalitza* with Sarah, releasing her, without performing *yibum*. She is neither available for *yibum* nor free without *chalitza*.

A question was raised here: would not the *zika* — the quasi-betrothal bond that exists between a *yavam* and his *yevamot* even before any *maamar* is performed — create a similar concern even without the *maamar*? The answer is that in this case *zika* alone does not generate the same status as *maamar*, though the question of *zika* as quasi-*kiddushin* is a broader sugya that will be addressed as the *masechet* continues.

### Rishona/Shniya

Rav Nachman then addresses a textual question about the Mishnah's terminology. *Man d'sani rishona v'lo mishtabesh* — one who has the text reading *rishona* (the first one) to describe Rachel is not in error. *Man d'sani shniya v'lo mishtabesh* — one who has the text reading *shniya* (the second one) to describe Rachel is also not in error.

Why might Rachel be called *rishona*? *Rishona l'nefila* — she was the first one to enter the picture when Reuven died, and when describing the situation to Levi, she is the first woman discussed. Why might Rachel be called *shniya*? One might think this means she was Shimon's second wife, but the Gemara objects: who says Shimon married her after Sarah? Perhaps he performed *yibum* with Rachel first and then married Sarah. The Gemara therefore resolves that *shniya* here means *shniya b'nisuim* — not the second in sequence but the one who has been married twice: Rachel was first married to Reuven and then, through *yibum*, to Shimon. That double-married status is what *shniya* refers to.

---

## Paternal Brotherhood

### Yachdov Source

The Gemara now seeks the biblical source for the rule that a brother who was not alive at the same time as the deceased has no *mitzva* of *yibum* and his sister-in-law is an *erva* to him. Rav Yehuda identifies the verse: *ki yeshvu achim yachdov* — "when brothers dwell together." The word *yachdov* — "together" — teaches *she-hayta lahem yeshiva achat ba-olam* — that they must have shared simultaneous existence in the world. *Prat l'eshet achiv shelo haya b'olamo* — this excludes the case where a brother is born only after the other has already died. The word *yachdov* insists on contemporaneity.

### Paternal Inheritance

Having established what *yachdov* teaches about temporal coexistence, the Gemara derives a second principle from the same word: *meyuchadim b'nachala* — they must be united in inheritance. *Prat l'achiv min ha-em* — this excludes a maternal brother. A maternal brother does not inherit together with his half-siblings through the father; inheritance flows through the paternal line. *Yachdov*, the togetherness required, is specifically the togetherness of those who share an inheritance — and that is a paternal, not a maternal, connection. Therefore, *yibum* applies only to paternal brothers, not to maternal ones.

### Rejecting Lot

Rabbah offers an alternative derivation of paternal brotherhood: *achi min ha-av yalif achva achva mi-bnei Yaakov* — the principle that "brother" in this context means paternal brother is learned through a *gezerah shava* of *achva-achva* from the sons of Yaakov. When the sons of Yaakov say *shneim asar achim anachnu* — we are twelve brothers — they are referring exclusively to paternal brothers. From that usage, the meaning of *achim* in *ki yeshvu achim yachdov* is also restricted to paternal brothers.

The Gemara asks: why not derive the meaning of *achim* from *arayot*, where the verse says *eshet achicha* — your brother's wife — and where *achicha* refers even to a maternal brother? If we learn the scope of *yibum* from *arayot*, we might include maternal brothers as well. The Gemara responds: *danim achim me-achim v'ein danim achim me-achicha* — we prefer to derive *achim* from *achim*, the same word, rather than from the related but distinct *achicha*.

The Gemara then presses further: what is the difference? One might argue that these are close enough to be linked through the principle of *Rabbi Yishmael's school*, which in the context of *tzara'at* links *veshav ha-kohen* and *u-va ha-kohen* — "the kohen shall return" and "the kohen shall come" — as referring to the same act even though the words differ. The Gemara answers: *hani mili heicha de-laika de-dami lei* — that principle applies only when there is no closer match. *Aval heicha de-ika de-dami lei, mi-de-dami lei yalfinan* — when a closer verbal parallel is available, we learn from the closer match. Since *achim* is available in the context of Yaakov's sons, we derive from there rather than from *arayot*.

But why not derive from Lot, where the word *achim* appears to refer to relatives more broadly? When Lot says to Abraham *ki anashim achim anachnu*, the word *achim* there seems to mean simply kinsmen or relatives — not brothers in the strict sense, and certainly not paternal brothers.

### Jacob's Declaration

The answer is that the word *achim* in the declaration of Yaakov's sons is a demonstrably superfluous word, and therefore it must be there to teach something. *Michdi hava lei le-michtav shneim asar avdecha bnei avinu* — they could have said simply "we are twelve, servants, sons of our father." Why add *achim* — brothers — at all? *V'ichtiv achim, shma mina le-afnuyei* — the extra word *achim* is there to serve as the source-word for the *gezerah shava*, teaching that *achim* means specifically paternal brothers. The word by Lot, by contrast, may or may not be superfluous — the Gemara acknowledges it might be — and indeed *le-afnuyei mifnei*: even the word by Lot can be shown to be extra, since Lot could have said "we are friends" (*reim*) rather than brothers.

### Both Words Needed

The Gemara concludes that both *achim* and *yachdov* are necessary and neither could serve alone. Had the verse said only *achim*, we might have learned from Lot that *achim* means any relative, including a nephew. Had the verse said only *yachdov*, it might have implied that we require brothers who share both mother and father — an even stricter requirement than paternal brotherhood alone. *Tzaricha* — each word is required to do its own work. *Achim* confirms, through the *gezerah shava* from Yaakov's sons, that paternal brotherhood is sufficient and that *yachdov* does not demand a shared mother. And *yachdov* confirms that the brothers must share an inheritance — ruling out the derivation from Lot that *achim* might mean any relative.

But one might still ask: why would I have thought *yachdov* requires shared parentage on both sides? The Gemara's answer is fundamental:

### Yibum & Inheritance

*Yibum b'nachala talya rachamana* — the Torah has tied *yibum* to inheritance. This is a striking claim. The surface rationale for *yibum* given by the Torah is *yakum al shem achiv ha-met* — the child born of the *yibum* will perpetuate the name of the deceased brother. But the Gemara understands that embedded within this rationale is the idea of inheritance: the *yavam* takes the deceased brother's *nachala* and passes it on through the child. *Yibum* is therefore structurally connected to inheritance law, and since inheritance flows through the father — *nachala min ha-av v'lo min ha-em* — maternal brothers, who do not share in the paternal inheritance, fall outside the scope of *yibum* altogether.

One might have thought to push in the opposite direction: since *yibum* involves overriding what would otherwise be an *erva* — a normally forbidden relationship — perhaps we should limit its application to only the closest possible fraternal bond, which would be brothers who share both mother and father. *Yibum* is a *chiddush*, an exception to the ordinary rules of *ervah*; perhaps we should minimize the exception and apply it only in the most intimate brotherly relationship. The Gemara rejects this through the dual derivation: *achim* from Yaakov's sons establishes that paternal brotherhood alone suffices, and *yachdov* rules out the extension to mere relatives. The result is the ruling as we know it: *yibum* applies to paternal brothers, not maternal ones, and only when both brothers were alive simultaneously.

---

---

# Yevamot 18

## Zika & Mother

### Yibum & Inheritance

The previous discussion concluded with a remarkable line in the *gemara*: *yibum b'nachala tala rachmana* — the obligation of *yibum* is somehow directly connected to the concept of inheritance. That connection is worth keeping in mind as we proceed, because it will circle back in subsequent discussions. We now turn to a new topic — or rather, one that is not entirely new — which brings us back to the end of the *mishna* that dealt with the concepts of *zika* and *maamar*. Before that, however, we had revisited the case of *eshes achiv shelo haya b'olamo*, derived from the word *yachdav*, which teaches us that *yibum* applies only when both brothers were alive at the same time, and that the patrilineal relationship alone — even without shared maternity — suffices to create the *yibum* bond.

### Zika Concept

The *gemara* opens with the statement of Rav Huna in the name of Rav. The concept at the center of this discussion is *zika* — a quasi-marital connection that the surviving brother inherits from his deceased brother with respect to the *yevama*. This is not a concept that appears explicitly anywhere in the *psukim*; the *psukim* simply legislate the *mitzvah* of *yibum*. Yet *Chazal* understand *zika* to be the underlying biblical mechanism — the metaphysical or legal reality that makes *yibum* possible. It is what allows the *yibum* act to be a continuation of the previous relationship rather than a new *issur* of *eshes achiv*. Because of this *zika*, the *yevama*'s status is transferred in some quasi-marital sense to the surviving brother, and this transfer then requires actualization through either *yibum* or *chalitza*. Importantly, *zika* is understood as a *d'oraisa* concept, not *derabbanan* — though, as we shall see, the question of exactly which implications flow from it at the *d'oraisa* level is precisely what is being debated.

### Shomeres Yavam Dies

Against this backdrop, Rav Huna states in the name of Rav: *shomeres yavam shemeisa muteres b'ima* — if a *shomeres yavam* dies, the *yavam* is permitted to marry her mother. The case is straightforward: Reuven is married to Rachel, Reuven dies, and Shimon now stands obligated in *yibum* to Rachel. Rachel, in her waiting status, is called a *shomeres yavam*. She then dies. The question is whether Shimon may now marry Rachel's mother.

One might think this is prohibited, since if Shimon had actually been married to Rachel and she died, he could not marry her mother — the prohibition of *isha v'ima* applies even to a deceased wife's mother. The question, then, is whether Rachel's status as Shimon's *zekuka* — as the woman to whom he has a *zika*, a quasi-marital connection inherited from Reuven — is sufficient to render her mother forbidden as the mother of his *zekukaso*, presumably at the *d'oraisa* level.

Rav's ruling is that this is permitted. The ruling is interpreted as reflecting the position of *ein zika*: either the concept of *zika* is denied altogether, or — more precisely — whatever *zika* exists is not substantial enough to carry the implication of rendering the woman's relatives forbidden as *erva*. There is also a distinct possible reading: even if one accepts *yesh zika* while the *shomeres yavam* is alive, one might argue that once she dies, the *mitzvah* of *yibum* no longer exists and the *zika* dissolves with it. After all, *zika* was tied to an obligation that needed to be actualized; once she is dead, there is no longer anything to actualize. However, as we will see, the *gemara* here is not limiting its statement in that way. It understands Rav's ruling as reflecting *ein zika* categorically — or at least, *ein zika* in any sense meaningful enough to create prohibited relationships.

### Ein vs. Yesh Zika

The *gemara* then asks: given that this ruling reflects *ein zika*, why not simply state the general principle — *halacha k'divrei ha'omer ein zika* — and be done with it? Why construct a specific case about marrying the mother?

The *gemara* answers with a two-step narrowing argument. First, had we only ruled *ein zika* in the context of the case involving two brothers — a case where Levi is engaged to Leah (Rachel's sister) but has not yet consummated the marriage, while Shimon also stands obligated to Rachel — one might have said: *ein zika* applies there because with two brothers, the *zika* is indeterminate. It is not clear that Rachel is specifically bound to Levi, since Shimon might be the one to perform *yibum* or *chalitza*. Perhaps with only one surviving brother, the *zika* is fully concentrated in him, and we would say *yesh zika* in that case. Therefore, Rav had to state a case of a single surviving *yavam* to demonstrate *ein zika* even there.

Second, had Rav simply ruled *ein zika* even in the case of one brother — without limiting his ruling to the scenario after her death — one might conclude that Shimon may marry Rachel's mother even while Rachel is still alive.
