### Torah Two-Generation

The *gemara* now turns to the list of Rabbi Chiya's school, which had been invoked in the preceding discussion. To understand what Rabbi Chiya adds, one must first appreciate the baseline. The *Torah* itself already prohibits relationships spanning two generations: a man may not marry a woman and also her granddaughter, and he may not marry his own granddaughter. Similarly, a man may not marry his wife's grandmother. These two-generation prohibitions are *arayot de'oraita*.

### Great-Granddaughters Down

Rabbi Chiya's innovation begins with the ruling *shlishi she-bivno ve-she-bivito* — the third generation downward through one's son or through one's daughter. The key *chiddush* is this: when the *Torah* prohibits one's granddaughter, it forbids the second generation going straight down through daughters — *bat bito* and *bat beno* are both explicitly biblical. If one continued downward through daughters alone, that would simply be an application of *ein lahem hefsek*. But Rabbi Chiya addresses a different case: where the second generation is a son — a grandson — and then the third generation produces a granddaughter. At the second generation, there is no biblical prohibition, since a grandson's relationship to his grandfather does not generate a restriction. Yet Rabbi Chiya teaches that the great-granddaughter — the third generation, even where the intervening link is a grandson — is nevertheless forbidden as a *shnia*.

Rashi makes this precise: *shlishi she-bivno* refers to *bat ben beno* — one's son's son's daughter; and *shlishi she-bivito* refers to *bat ben bito* — one's daughter's son's daughter. In both cases, the second generation is a son (*ben*), breaking the direct daughter-to-daughter chain, yet the third generation great-granddaughter is still rabbinically prohibited. This accounts for two of Rabbi Chiya's six additions.

### Wife's Great-Granddaught…

The next two entries are parallel, but applied to one's wife. The *Torah* prohibits a man from marrying a woman along with her granddaughter — which means, structurally, one may not marry one's wife's granddaughter, whether through the wife's son or through the wife's daughter. Those are *de'oraita* prohibitions. But again, where the second generation is a grandson — the wife's grandson — the biblical prohibition does not attach at that level. Rabbi Chiya extends the prohibition to the wife's great-granddaughter in such a case: *she-be-ven ishto ve-she-be-bat ishto* — whether the great-granddaughter descends through the wife's son or through the wife's daughter, she is rabbinically forbidden. This yields two more entries, for a running total of four.

### Wife's Great-Grandmother

The final two entries of Rabbi Chiya's list extend the prohibitions upward rather than downward: *revi'i she-be-chamiv ve-she-be-chamoto* — the fourth generation ascending through one's father-in-law or through one's mother-in-law. Here too the *Torah* already forbids a man from marrying a woman's grandmother, meaning one's wife's grandmother is biblically forbidden. Going one generation further upward yields one's wife's great-grandmother. Rabbi Chiya teaches that this too is rabbinically prohibited, whether the great-grandmother descends through the wife's paternal line or her maternal line.

The *chiddush* is most significant when the great-grandmother is reached through a grandfather — that is, where the intervening generation is a grandfather rather than a grandmother, at which level there is no independent biblical prohibition — yet even then, the great-grandmother is a *shnia*. Rashi describes these cases specifically in terms of the mother of the mother of the father-in-law (*em em chamiv*) and the mother of the mother of the mother-in-law (*em em chamoto*), though one might equally apply the reasoning to the paternal grandfather's mother.

These final two entries complete Rabbi Chiya's list of six additions: two forms of one's own great-granddaughters, two forms of one's wife's great-granddaughters, and two forms of one's wife's great-grandmothers.

### Generation Counting

Ravina posed a question to Rav Ashi about the terminology: *mai shna lemala de-chashiv lei ishto, mai shna lemata de-lo kachashiv lei ishto* — why when counting upward is one's wife counted as generation one (making her great-grandmother "generation four"), while when counting downward one is not counted as generation zero (making one's great-granddaughter "generation three")?

Rav Ashi explains: *lemala, de-issura mikoch ishto ka'ati chashiv lah* — going upward, the prohibition derives entirely from one's relationship to one's wife; she is the anchor of the relationship, and so she is counted as generation one, her mother as two, her grandmother as three, her great-grandmother as four. *Lemata, de-issura lav mikoch ishto ka'ati, lo kachashiv lah* — going downward, one's own great-granddaughter, the prohibition does not stem from the wife; one counts beginning with the first generation after oneself, so son or daughter is generation one, grandchild generation two, great-grandchild generation three.

The *gemara* then raises a difficulty: what of one's wife's great-granddaughters? That prohibition also derives from one's relationship to the wife — *de-issura mikoch ishto ka'ati* — so by the same logic, the wife should be counted as generation one, making the great-granddaughter generation four, not three. The *gemara* answers: *aidei de-tani tlat daragei lemata didei* — since when we counted generations below oneself we called it "three" and did not count ourselves, we likewise do not count the wife when going below her, and so her great-granddaughter is called "three" as well, for consistency of formulation.

### Hefsek Question

Rav Ashi poses the question to Avimi of Hagronya: *shniyot de-Rabbi Chiya yesh lahen hefsek o ein lahen hefsek* — do Rabbi Chiya's additional prohibitions have a cutoff, or do they continue indefinitely? The *gemara* considers a proof from Rav's statement that there are four women whose *shniyot* prohibitions stop — *arba nashim yesh lahen hefsek* — and since Rabbi Chiya's categories were not among those four, perhaps they continue without limit. The *gemara* deflects: perhaps Rav was only speaking about the original *baraita* of eight, and Rabbi Chiya's list may have its own cutoff.

An attempt is then made from Rabbi Chiya's own language: he specified *shlishi* — the third generation below — and *revi'i* — the fourth generation above. These are specific numbers, suggesting the prohibition stops there. The *gemara* again is unconvinced: *dilma mi-shlishi va-eilakh u-me-revi'i va-eilakh* — perhaps "third" means starting from the third generation onward, not limited to it. The question of *hefsek* for Rabbi Chiya's list is thus left without resolution.

---

## Converts & Shniyot

### Converts Status

A rabbi who came from the west — from *Eretz Yisrael* — reported to Rava, who conveyed the matter to Rav Nachman: *be'ei be-ma'arva* — they posed the following question in *Eretz Yisrael*: *gazru shniyot be-gerim* — did the Rabbis extend the secondary *arayot* prohibitions to converts? The question arises from the principle of *kegar she-nitgayer ke-katan she-nolad dami* — a convert is legally as a newborn child, severed from prior family relationships. But does this principle interact with the rabbinic secondary prohibitions, and if so, how?

### Eretz Yisrael Ruling

The ruling that emerges from *Eretz Yisrael* is that *shniyot* do not apply to converts. To explain why, the *gemara* first addresses the more basic question of biblical *arayot* for converts.

### Holiness Concern

Even at the level of biblical *arayot*, a convert is technically no longer related to his pre-conversion family members. A convert and his sister who converted together could, strictly speaking, marry one another. Yet the Rabbis prohibited this. The *gemara* explains: *ee lav d'lo yomru banu mi-kdusha chamura li-kdusha kala* — were it not for the concern that people would say "we moved from a stricter religion to a more lenient one," the Rabbis would not have enacted the prohibition at all. The prohibition of biblical-level *arayot* for converts was thus a targeted decree, motivated entirely by the concern that converts not perceive Judaism as less holy than their religion of origin, in which such unions were also forbidden.

### Shniyot Permitted

Given this reasoning, the *gemara* concludes that *shniyot* present no problem: *shniyot miba'ya* — is there even a question? A non-Jew is not bound by the rabbinic *shniyot*. If a convert's great-great-grandmother were to convert along with him, she was never forbidden to him even as a non-Jew. There is therefore no appearance of leniency — no one will say Judaism permits something that his prior religion forbade. Accordingly, *shniyot* are entirely permitted to converts. The concern of *kedusha kala mi-kedusha chamura* does not arise, and the technical principle of *ke-katan she-nolad dami* operates without restriction in this domain.

---

## Convert Testimony

### Maternal Brothers

Since the discussion has turned to converts, Rav Nachman adds a related ruling: *achi min ha'em lo ya'idu* — brothers on the maternal side who have both converted may not testify together *lechatchila*. However, *v'im he'idu, edutan edut* — if they did testify together *bedi'avad*, their testimony is valid, since *ke-katan she-nolad dami* renders them legally unrelated.

### Paternal Brothers

By contrast, *achi min ha'av me'idin lechatchila* — paternal brothers who have both converted may testify together from the outset, without any *lechatchila* restriction.

### Bio Relationship

This distinction is somewhat counterintuitive. Throughout the laws of *arayot*, paternal relationships carry greater legal weight than maternal ones. Why, then, is the maternal bond treated more stringently here for purposes of testimony? The answer lies not in legal weight but in biological visibility. When two people share the same mother, the biological relationship is plain and apparent to all — there is a clear, enduring physical bond. Even after conversion, it is obvious to observers that these two individuals are biological brothers. The concern is therefore that it will appear as though related parties are testifying together, even though *halakhically* they are not.

Paternal brotherhood, by contrast, rests not merely on biology but substantially on the social construct of family membership — being recognized as part of the same father's household. That social construct dissolves upon conversion in a more complete and perceptible way. The *halakhic* severance is therefore more evident to onlookers, and there is less concern that allowing paternal brothers to testify will create a false appearance of impropriety. Rashi notes in this context that among non-Jews, the maternal bond carried particular significance even prior to conversion, which further explains why the *lechatchila* restriction attaches specifically to maternal brothers.

### Court Control

The *gemara* pushes further: *afilu hachi min em nami me'idim lechatchila* — even maternal brothers who have converted may testify together from the outset. This is because testimony is a court-controlled matter, not a private one.

### Arayot Concerns

The *gemara* draws a formal distinction: *erva lechol mesura* — marital decisions are made by individuals and are not subject to court supervision. If a convert were permitted to marry his sister, other people might follow suit and believe they could do the same. The prohibition must therefore be maintained as an absolute rule, regardless of whether those particular individuals know they are permitted. Testimony, by contrast, is *edut levei dina mesura* — entirely under the jurisdiction of the *beit din*. The court knows that *kegar she-nitgayer ke-katan she-nolad dami* and that converts are not *halakhically* related. There is therefore no risk of error spreading, and even maternal brothers may testify together *lechatchila*.

This represents a shift from the earlier concern — where the issue was the convert's perception of relative religious stringency — to a new concern about the potential for the public to draw incorrect inferences. The two rationales operate in different domains, which is why the *gemara*'s application differs between *arayot* and testimony.

---

## Brother & Son

### Any Brother

The *mishnah* states: *mi she-yesh lo ach mikol makom, zokek et eshet achiv l'yibum* — whoever has any type of brother, that brother creates a *yibum* obligation upon the widow in the event of death. The *mishnah* adds that the brother is considered a full brother *l'chol davar* — for all purposes — with one exception: a half-brother born of a non-Jewish woman or a slave-woman is not considered a legal brother and does not create the *yibum* obligation.

### Mamzer Brother

The *gemara* asks: *mikol makom la'atuyei mai* — what does the phrase "any type" come to include? Rav Yehuda answers: *la'atuyei mamzer* — it includes even a brother who is a *mamzer*. That is, if one's father had a child through a forbidden union, producing a *mamzer*, that *mamzer* half-brother still creates a *yibum* obligation upon his brother's widow.

One might have thought to exclude the *mamzer* by applying a *gezeira shava* from the brothers of Yaakov — *shneim asar achim anachnu* — reasoning that just as those brothers were all legally fit (*kesharim*), the term "brother" in the context of *yibum* should likewise be restricted to fit (*kasher*) individuals, excluding a *mamzer*. The *gemara* rejects this: since a *mamzer* son exempts his father's wife from *yibum* — as we are about to see — it follows that *mamzer* status has full relevance within the laws of *yibum*, and therefore a *mamzer* brother likewise creates the *yibum* obligation.

### Mamzer Full Brother

The *mishnah* further states that the *mamzer* brother is considered a full brother *l'chol davar* — for all purposes. The *gemara* identifies two concrete applications: *l'yarsho* — a *mamzer* brother inherits from his brother just as any other brother would — and *l'tamei lo* — a *kohen* whose brother is a *mamzer* is still obligated to render himself *tamei* for the burial of that brother.

The second application requires elaboration. One might have thought to exclude it based on the verse *ki im l'she'ero ha-karov eilav* — a *kohen* renders himself *tamei* only for close flesh — and the teaching that *she'ero* refers to one's wife. Since a *kohen* does not render himself *tamei* for a wife who is a *grusha*, one might analogize: just as the *kohen* is not *metamei* for a wife of disqualified status, so too he should not be *metamei* for a brother of disqualified status such as a *mamzer*.

### Kashering Parallel

The *gemara* rejects this analogy: *hatam l'afukei kaima* — in the case of the *grusha*, the reason the *kohen* is not *metamei* for her is not that she is a person of diminished status, but that the relationship itself is one he should be dissolving. She should not be his wife at all; the marital bond is therefore weakened and does not support the obligation of *tumah*. The *mamzer* brother, however, is not a relationship that one should be ending or severing. He is simply always one's brother. The quality of the relationship — as distinct from the personal status of the relative — determines the *tumah* obligation. Since the fraternal relationship is intact and permanent, the *kohen* is fully obligated to render himself *tamei* for his *mamzer* brother.

---

## Son Exemption

### Any Son

The *mishnah* states: *mi she-yesh lo ben mikol makom poter eshet aviv min ha-yibum* — whoever has any type of son, even a *mamzer*, that son exempts his father's wife from *yibum*. The biblical law of *yibum* applies only when a man dies *without a son*; if any legally recognized son exists, the *yibum* obligation does not arise. The *mishnah* specifies that the exception is again a son born of a non-Jewish woman or slave-woman.

### Mamzer Son

Again the *gemara* asks what "any type" comes to include, and again Rav Yehuda answers: *la'atuyei mamzer*. The derivation comes from the phrase *u-ven ein lo* — "and he has no son" — which the *gemara* reads as *ayen alav*, inviting a broader investigation into what constitutes a son for this purpose. By this expansive reading, any person who falls within the category of son exempts the father's wife from *yibum*.

### Daughters & Grandchildren

The same *drashah* of *ayen alav* yields further expansions. Not only a son but even a daughter exempts the father's wife from *yibum*. Moreover, a grandson or granddaughter — indeed any descendant — also exempts. The *Torah*'s language of "son" is thus read broadly to encompass the full range of descendants, such that so long as any descendant of the deceased exists, the *yibum* obligation is displaced.

### Honor & Teshuva

The *mishnah* further states that if the *mamzer* son were to strike or curse his father, he would be liable (*chayav mita* for striking, and the equivalent prohibition for cursing). The *gemara* questions this. The verse *v'nasi be'amcha lo ta'or* is interpreted to mean that the prohibition against cursing — and by extension, striking — applies only to one who acts as part of the community: *be'oseh ma'aseh amcha*. A sinner who has placed himself outside the community would not be protected by this prohibition. Since the *mamzer*'s father committed a grave transgression to produce the *mamzer*, perhaps the father should not qualify as *oseh ma'aseh amcha* and should therefore not be protected.

The *gemara* cites Rav Pinchas in the name of Rav Pappa: *be'oseh teshuvah* — the *mishnah* speaks of a father who has done *teshuvah*. Once the father has repented, he is again within the community, and the son's obligation of honor is restored.

### Oseh Ma'aseh Amcha

The *gemara* then questions whether *teshuvah* is even possible in such a case. A *baraita* cited by Shimon ben Menasya identifies the verse *me'uvat lo yuchal litkon* — that which is crooked cannot be made straight — as referring specifically to one who had forbidden relations and produced a *mamzer*. The effects of the sin persist permanently in the world in the form of the *mamzer* child; full rectification seems impossible.

The *gemara* resolves this: *hashta miha oseh ma'aseh amcha hu* — the question of *oseh ma'aseh amcha* is not about whether the father has achieved complete metaphysical atonement or whether God has fully erased the sin from his account. The question is simply whether, at present, the father is living an observant life and conducting himself within the norms of the community. As long as he is presently acting within the framework of the Jewish people, the prohibition against striking and cursing him applies in full, regardless of whether complete atonement for the original transgression has been or can be achieved.

---

## Double Transgression

### Two Prohibitions

The *gemara* now introduces a *baraita*: *ha-ba al achoto ve-hi bat eshet aviv* — one who engages in relations with his sister who is also his father's wife's daughter transgresses a double prohibition, *chayav mishum achoto u-mishum bat eshet aviv* — liable for both "his sister" and "his father's wife's daughter."

### Tanna Kamma

The *tanna kamma* holds that in such a case, two distinct prohibitions are violated. Each prohibition — "sister" and "father's wife's daughter" — is an independent biblical *issur*, and when a single act violates both simultaneously, the transgressions are counted separately. This would mean, for instance, that if the act were done *be-shogeg*, two separate *korbanos* would be required, or if warnings were given, two sets of lashes would be administered.

The case requires clarification. A sister who is not the daughter of one's father's wife is possible: she could be the daughter of a woman one's father had a child with but never married. Conversely, a father's wife's daughter who is not one's sister would simply be a stepsister, and stepsister alone — that is, one's father's wife's daughter who is not also one's sister — is not biblically prohibited. The prohibition of "father's wife's daughter" only attaches when she is also one's sister. The question, then, is whether the fact that the father was married to the mother creates a new and additional prohibition on top of the existing prohibition of "sister."

### Rabbi Yose Opinion

Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda disagrees. He holds that there is only one prohibition: *mishum achoto ata mechayvo ve'ei ata mechayvo mishum bat eshet aviv* — the liability is only for "his sister," and the fact that the father was married to the mother does not create any additional *issur*. The father's marriage to the mother does not transform the sister into a more prohibited relative; she is prohibited only as a sister, full stop.

### Verse Redundancy

The *tanna kamma*'s reasoning proceeds as follows. The *Torah* writes in one verse: *ervat achotecha bat avicha o bat imecha* — the prohibition of one's sister, whether paternal or maternal. In a separate verse, the *Torah* writes: *bat eshet avicha moledes avicha, achotecha hi* — your father's wife's daughter, born of your father, she is your sister. If the sister prohibition already covers all sisters whether the father was married to the mother or not, why did the *Torah* need to write a separate verse about the father's wife's daughter? The redundancy teaches that in the case where the father *is* married to the mother, a second and distinct prohibition applies — the prohibition of "father's wife's daughter" — in addition to the prohibition of "sister." Thus: *shema mina, le-chayvo mishum achoto u-mishum bat eshet aviv*.

### Achosecha Hi

Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda reads the second verse differently. The verse states *achotecha hi* — she is your sister. He understands this phrase as restrictive: it tells you that in this case, the liability is as for *your sister*, and no more. The father's marriage to the mother adds nothing to the prohibition; it remains solely the prohibition of sister.

### Full Sister Derivation

The *tanna kamma* then accounts for the phrase *achotecha hi* differently: it is needed to teach that a full sister — one who shares both the same father and same mother — is also prohibited. One might have thought that since the *Torah* specifies the paternal sister in one verse and the maternal sister in another, a sister who is both — a full sister — might somehow fall between the categories and require separate derivation. The phrase *achotecha hi* serves to establish that a full sister is also prohibited, a fact one could not derive by *kal va-chomer* alone, and therefore requires explicit scriptural statement.

### Placement Question

Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda responds: if the purpose of *achotecha hi* were simply to establish the prohibition of a full sister, why would the *Torah* place it in the verse dealing specifically with one's father's wife's daughter? If the point were only about full sisters, the phrase should appear in the verse about sisters generally — the verse that begins *ervat achotecha bat avicha o bat imecha*. The fact that *achotecha hi* appears specifically in the verse about the father's wife's daughter indicates that its function is restrictive: it is telling you that even in that case — even where the father is married to the mother — the prohibition remains only that of "sister," and no new prohibition is generated by the marital relationship.

The *tanna kamma* responds in turn: *af al gav de-chtiv achotecha, itzterich le-michtav hi* — even granting that the word *achotecha* on its own could teach the prohibition of a full sister, the additional word *hi* was still necessary. *Shelo tomar be'alma mazhir min hadin* — one might have argued in principle that since the prohibition of full sister could have been derived by *kal va-chomer* from the partial-sister prohibitions, no explicit verse was needed, and that the verse could instead function restrictively. The *Torah* therefore writes *hi* to make clear that the verse does require an explicit statement — and is not merely restrictive — leaving it available to teach the double prohibition.

Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda closes: *im kein, lichtov Rachmana achotecha hi be'idach kra* — if all the *Torah* intended with *achotecha hi* was to establish the prohibition of a full sister, it should have written that phrase in the other verse, the general verse about sisters. The fact that it placed *achotecha hi* specifically in the verse about the father's wife's daughter signals that its message is directed at that very case — and the message is that in that case, the liability is *only* for sister, not for any additional prohibition. The debate is left standing, with both positions textually anchored, and the *gemara* will continue from this point in the following session.

---

---

# Yevamot 23

## Yossi: Marriageability

### Setup: Daughter Verse

The Gemara on 27b returns to the position of Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Yehuda, addressing a pointed question: given that Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Yehuda holds there is only a single prohibition of *achot* (sister) regardless of whether the father was married to the sister's mother, what does he do with the verse that specifically mentions *bat eshet avicha* — the daughter of your father's wife? If the prohibition of *achot* applies in all cases, the additional specification seems superfluous. What work, then, does that verse perform?

### Ishus Le'Avicha

The Gemara answers: *miba'ei lei mi sheyesh lo ishus le'avicha* — the verse is needed to establish that the only woman who qualifies as your sister in a halachic sense is one whose mother your father could have married. The operative concept is *ishus* — the theoretical availability of a marital bond between the woman's mother and the father.

### Exclude Shifcha, Akum

The practical consequence is stated explicitly: *perat l'achoiso mi'shifcha ve'akum she'ein ishus le'avicha bah* — this excludes a half-sibling whose mother is a *shifcha* (female slave) or a non-Jewish woman, since marriage with such a woman was not legally available to your father. Such a child is therefore not considered one's legal sibling — and, by extension, not one's legal child in the full halachic sense.

---

## Wedlock vs. Marriage

### Anusa Objection

The Gemara immediately presses: could one not have said that the verse excludes a child born from an *anusa* — a woman who was not the father's wife at all, without any formal prohibition, simply outside the context of marriage? In broader usage, of course, a child born outside of marriage is considered illegitimate. Perhaps halacha follows the same logic, treating the child of any non-wife as not the father's legal child?

### Arayos Proof

The Gemara rejects this: *hahi lo matzit amrit* — you cannot say this. The proof comes from Rava, who identifies an apparent contradiction between two verses. One verse states *ervat bat bincha o bat bitecha lo tegaleh* — do not uncover the nakedness of your son's daughter or your daughter's daughter — with an emphasis on *your* granddaughter. This might imply that only your own granddaughter is forbidden, not your wife's granddaughter from another man. Yet a second verse states *ervat isha u'vitah lo tegaleh*, including *bat b'nah ve'at bat bitah* — forbidding a woman and her daughter and her granddaughter. How are these reconciled? *Kan be'onsin, kan benissuin* — one verse refers to a context outside of marriage, the other to a marital context. The upshot is that in a non-marital union, the resulting grandchild is still *your* granddaughter for purposes of the *arayos* prohibition.

This is the essential point: it is not the *mamzer* question being addressed here, nor the question of a child's moral legitimacy in the colloquial sense. The question is whether the child is halachically reckoned as a legal child of the father. English intuition about "bastard" conflates the question of legal status with birth outside of wedlock, but halacha treats them entirely separately. As our *mishnah* makes clear, *kol makom* — every child, including a *mamzer*, is the father's legal child. The only exceptions are children born of a *shifcha* or a non-Jewish mother. The Gemara's concern here is thus: if even a child born out of wedlock in the *arayos* context remains a legal grandchild, one cannot simply say that birth outside of marriage strips a child of legal status. The non-marital origin does not change the child's legal standing.

---

## Lavin Don't Exclude

### Lavin Challenge

The Gemara advances to a second objection: perhaps the exclusion from legal sibling status applies not only to non-marital unions but to any union prohibited even by a simple negative prohibition — *chayvei lavin*. For example, a *kohen* who marries a *grusha*, or a case involving a *mamzer* or *mamzeres*. Should the child of such a prohibited union not be considered a legal child?

### Marriage Binding

Rav Pappa responds: *chayvei lavin tafsei behu kiddushin* — in cases where the union is prohibited only by a *lav*, marriage is nonetheless fully binding. Since marriage takes effect in such cases, the child's status as a legal child is not in question. The child is no different from any other — the prohibition affected the act of marriage, but the legal reality of marriage, and thus of parenthood, stands.

The proof text: *ki tiheina le'ish shtei nashim* — if a man has two wives, one beloved and one hated. The Gemara raises a curious question: is there really a beloved and a hated before God? What is the verse actually teaching? The answer is that *ahuvah b'nisueha, snuah b'nisueha* — one is beloved in her marriage, meaning the marriage was entirely legitimate; the other is hated in her marriage, meaning the marriage should not have taken place due to a *lav*. Nevertheless, the Torah uses the word *tiheina* — they *are* his wives — indicating through the language of *havayah* that even a marriage entered into in violation of a negative prohibition is a binding marriage. The verse thus teaches a *chiddush*: even in such a case, where there is an objective reason the marriage was problematic, the child retains full inheritance rights and legal status.

### Beloved/Hated Wives

The logic is now clarified. The progression of categories is as follows. First, a union that is simply extra-marital — birth outside of wedlock — clearly does not strip a child of legal status, as shown from the *arayos* granddaughter case. Second, a union that is prohibited by a *lav* — marriage was forbidden but would have been binding — likewise does not affect the child's legal standing, as shown from the beloved-and-hated verse. The next category to examine is therefore the one where not only is the union prohibited, but marriage would not even be binding — the *issurei karet*, the *arayos* prohibitions themselves, which produce *mamzerim*.

---

## Kares Unions

### Kares Challenge

The Gemara raises the third and most serious objection: *ve'eima perat l'chayvei kerisos* — perhaps the exclusion applies to children born from unions where the prohibition carries *karet*, where marriage is not merely forbidden but is entirely non-binding. In these cases, the man had relations with a woman he could never have legally married. Should such a child not be considered a legal child?

### Rava's Sister Verse

Rava responds with a verse: *ervat achotecha bat avicha o bat imecha moledes bayis o moledes chutz* — the nakedness of your sister, the daughter of your father or your mother, whether born in the house or born outside. The phrase *moledes bayis o moledes chutz* — born in the house or born outside — is interpreted as follows: *bein she'omrim lo le'avicha kayem, bein she'omrim lo le'avicha hotze* — whether they told your father to keep his wife, or whether they told him to send her away. Even in a case where the father was told to divorce the woman — because the marriage was forbidden — the child resulting from that union is still called *achosechi hi*, your sister. The Torah thus explicitly designates the offspring of even a prohibited union as one's legal sibling.

### Moledes Chutz

The phrase *moledes chutz* — born outside — refers to a child born from a union in which marriage was not binding at all, as in cases of *issur karet*. Even such a child is Torah-designated as one's sister. One might object that *omrim lo le'avicha hotze* could refer to a case of a *lav*, where the marriage is binding but should be dissolved — that might not be a case of *karet* at all. But since the previous objection regarding *lavin* was already addressed, the Gemara reads this verse as moving to the next level: even in *karet* cases, the child is a legal sibling.

This leads to an important observation. A *mamzer* — a child produced from an *issur karet* such as incest or adultery — is still the father's legal child in every halachic dimension other than the single restriction on whom the *mamzer* may marry. The *mamzer* inherits, fulfills *pru u'revu* for the father, and is counted as a sibling for purposes of *yibum* and *chalitzah*. If a man's only brother was a *mamzer* and that man died, his widow would be obligated in *yibum* with that *mamzer* brother, or *chalitzah* — though of course *yibum* in such a case would be prohibited, it would still be binding. The category of *mamzer* is thus, perhaps counterintuitively, not a category of "non-legal child" — it is a single halachic restriction on marriage. One helpful comparison is the category of *p'tzu'a daka*, which similarly carries a specific marital restriction without affecting the person's fundamental legal status. The only category of non-legal child, halachically, is the child of a *shifcha* or a non-Jewish mother.

---

## Final Distinctions

### Two Categories

Having established that the offspring of *karet* unions are still legal children and siblings, the Gemara now confronts the obvious question: both *arayos* unions and unions with a non-Jewish woman or a slave share the feature that marriage is not binding — indeed, not even possible. Why should the child of an *arayos* union be a legal sibling while the child of a non-Jewish mother is not? The Gemara formulates the question sharply: the verse *moledes chutz* seems to include the offspring of a woman who could not be in the house — but how do we know this refers to the *arayos* case rather than the *shifcha* or *akum* case?

### Arayos Marriageable

The Gemara's answer: *mistabra* — it stands to reason — that *chayvei kerisos* should be included as legal children. Why? *Sheken tofsin bah kiddushin l'achreini* — because such a woman is still marriageable within the Jewish world. Your sister, forbidden to you by *karet*, can nonetheless legally marry another Jewish man. She is not excluded from the category of those capable of *kiddushin*. She remains, in principle, a member of the marriageable world.

### Completely Excluded

The non-Jewish woman and the slave, by contrast, cannot marry any Jew at all. They are entirely outside the category of those with whom *kiddushin* can take effect. The Gemara anticipates the objection: could one not argue that a non-Jewish woman or slave is *more* theoretically marriageable to you personally, since conversion or manumission is at least conceivable — whereas your own sister you could never marry under any circumstances? The Gemara dismisses this: *lichi migayra gufa achrina hi* — when she converts, she becomes legally a different person. The principle of *kekatan shenolad* applies: a convert is as one newly born, legally a distinct individual. Therefore the theoretical possibility of conversion does not render the non-Jewish woman marriageable as *this* person. As this person, in her current state, she is entirely and irrevocably outside the category of those to whom any Jew could be married.

### Logic Summary

The organizing principle is thus: legal sibling status requires that the mother belong to the category of the potentially marriageable — not necessarily to *you*, but to some Jew. A woman forbidden to you by *karet*, such as your sister, remains marriageable to others and is therefore within the broader category. A non-Jewish woman or a slave is marriageable to no Jew in her current state, and her post-conversion identity would be legally a different person. She is therefore categorically excluded, and the child born of such a union is not your legal child.

---

## Rabbis' Sources

### Slave from Verse

The Gemara now asks: those who disagree with Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Yehuda — who use the verse *bat eshet avicha* for a different purpose entirely — where do *they* derive the principle that the child of a *shifcha* or non-Jewish woman is not a legal child?

The answer regarding the *shifcha* is straightforward: *nafka lehu me'ha'ishah ve'yeladeha tihyeh la'adoneha* — from the verse in the context of a slave woman who has borne children, the Torah states that the children belong to the master, not to the father. This establishes explicitly that the offspring of a slave woman are not legally reckoned as the father's children.

### Two Verses Needed

However, this verse covers only the *shifcha*. The non-Jewish woman requires a separate source, and one cannot simply learn the non-Jewish case from the slave case. The Gemara explains why both are needed: *de'ei ashmeinan shifcha, mishum de'leit lehu chayis* — had the Torah told us only about the slave, one might have said the reason is because slave families lack recognized familial relationships; slave society was characterized by broken families and the legal non-recognition of kinship. But a non-Jewish woman does have recognized familial relationships, and her children know their parents and siblings. One might therefore have thought the offspring with a non-Jewish woman is a legal child. Conversely, *de'ei ashmeinan avodat kochavim, mishum de'lo shaycha be'mitzvot* — had the Torah told us only about the non-Jewish woman, one might have attributed the exclusion to her being entirely outside the sphere of Jewish obligation. But a *shifcha*, an *eved kena'ani*, is obligated in negative commandments and positive non-time-bound commandments, placing her in a quasi-Jewish status. One might have thought her child with a Jewish man retains full legal child status. Therefore both verses are required.

### One Verse Covers Both

Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, derives both exclusions from the single verse of *bat eshet avicha* and the principle of *ishus le'avicha*. Since neither a *shifcha* nor a non-Jewish woman can enter into a marriage with a Jewish man that has any legal effect, both are excluded by the same principle, and no separate verse for each is required. This elegant economy is the hallmark of his reading: one verse, one principle, both cases covered.

---

## Matrilineal Descent

### Non-Intermarriage Verse

The Gemara now turns to the rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Yehuda: having established from the verse about the slave woman that *shifcha* offspring are not a man's legal children, where do they derive that the offspring of a non-Jewish mother likewise are not his legal children — and by extension, are not Jewish? This is the foundational question of matrilineal descent as treated in the Gemara.

Rabbi Yochanan, in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, cites the verse governing intermarriage with the seven Canaanite nations.

### Ki Yasir Derivation

The verse in question contains the prohibition *lo titchaten bam* — do not intermarry with them — including the directive *uvito lo tikach le'vincha*, do not take their daughter for your son. The reason given is *ki yasir et bincha me'acharai* — for he will turn your son away from Me. Here lies the crux of the *drasha*: the subject of *yasir* is masculine — *he* will lead astray — yet the subject of the clause is the non-Jewish daughter taken for your son. Grammatically, a non-Jewish daughter-in-law would be *she* who leads astray. The masculine *yasir* redirects the reading: it refers to the non-Jewish husband, pointing us back to the earlier clause about your daughter being given to their son. The non-Jewish son-in-law will lead your son — meaning your grandson — away from Me.

The conclusion: *bincha mi'Yisraelit itkarei bincha* — your grandson born of a Jewish daughter and a non-Jewish husband is still called your son. The fact that *yasir* refers to this man leading your grandson astray presupposes that the grandson is indeed yours. And therefore, by reversal: *ve'ein bincha haba min ha'ovedet kochavim itkarei bincha ela bna* — the child born of your son and a non-Jewish woman is not called your son but her son. Since she is not Jewish, the child follows the mother and is not your son, not Jewish.

### Matrilineal Rule

This is the Talmudic basis for matrilineal descent, derived from a single *yud* — the *yasir* versus the expected *tasir*. The principle establishes two things simultaneously: that the child of a Jewish mother and non-Jewish father remains legally your grandchild, and that the child of a Jewish father and non-Jewish mother is not legally your child — and is therefore not Jewish.

### Ravina's Psul

Ravina raises a sharp question: *shma mina ben bitcha haba min oved kochavim itkarei bincha* — we learn from this that your daughter's son from a non-Jewish father is still called your son. Does this mean Ravina holds that a child born of a non-Jewish father and Jewish mother is entirely *kasher*, with no halachic blemish whatsoever?

### Yisrael Pasul

The Gemara responds: the child is not a *mamzer* — that position was considered and rejected — but neither is the child entirely *kasher* in every sense. *Yisrael pasul mikrei* — the child is designated an invalid Israelite, carrying some form of *psul*. The Gemara does not elaborate here on the nature of that *psul*, but this becomes a substantial discussion elsewhere — in other *gemarot*, among the *rishonim*, and in practical *halacha*. The major issue that flows from this is whether a woman born of a Jewish mother and non-Jewish father is permitted to marry a *kohen*, given that some form of *psul* is hinted to here. This is a significant and debated question that is only alluded to in this *sugya*.

---

## Scope of Matrilineal

### Seven Nations Q

The Gemara raises an important objection: the verse *lo titchaten bam* is written in the context of the seven Canaanite nations. Perhaps the entire derivation — including the rule of matrilineal descent — applies only to intermarriage with the *sheva umot*, not with non-Jews generally. If so, a child born of a Jewish father and, say, a non-Canaanite non-Jewish mother might retain legal child status.

### Rabbi Shimon Method

The Gemara's resolution invokes the methodological principle of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: *darash ta'ama de'kra* — Rabbi Shimon derives halacha by identifying the reason embedded in the verse and applying the law wherever that reason applies. The classic illustration of this method is the prohibition against taking a widow's garment as collateral: Rabbi Shimon holds that if the widow is wealthy, the reason for the prohibition does not apply, and therefore the prohibition itself does not apply. The *rabbanan* disagree, holding that the verse's language defines its scope categorically, without reference to the underlying reason. Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, reads the reason as integral to the law's application.

### Ki Yasir Extension

Applied here: the verse states *ki yasir* — for he will lead astray. Rabbi Shimon identifies this as the reason for the prohibition on intermarriage. And the reason — the potential to lead your offspring away from God — applies to *kol hamessirim*, anyone capable of leading your son astray. This is not limited to the seven Canaanite nations; any non-Jewish spouse can lead your children from the path. Therefore, according to Rabbi Shimon, the verse and its derivation extend to all non-Jews, and matrilineal descent applies universally.

### Rabbis' Source

This leaves a significant question for those who do not share Rabbi Shimon's methodology: the *rabbanan* who do not *darash ta'ama de'kra* cannot extend the verse beyond the *sheva umot* on the basis of its rationale. Where, then, do they derive the universal rule of matrilineal descent?

The Gemara's answer: the opinion that argues with Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Yehuda is precisely Rabbi Shimon. Those who do not adopt Rabbi Shimon's methodology and do not agree with Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Yehuda's reading of *bat eshet avicha* will, in fact, use the verse of *bat eshet avicha* as Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Yehuda does — that is, they will hold like Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Yehuda for this derivation. The question of where *rabbanan* who reject both approaches find their source is thus resolved: the *tanna* who argues with Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Yehuda is Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Shimon has his own source — *ki yasir* extended via *ta'ama de'kra*. Those who do not hold like either will simply learn it from the verse of *ishus le'avicha* as Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Yehuda does.

---

## Two Sisters Case

### Setup: One Man

The *mishnah* on 23b opens a new section, returning to the practical territory of *yibum* and *chalitzah*. The foundational case: a man performed *kiddushin* with one of two sisters but does not know which one he married. He cannot continue to live with either woman, because whichever one he approaches might be his wife's sister — forbidden to him.

### Get to Both

To free the women to marry other men, the husband must give a *get* to each of them. Since either one might be his wife, each requires a *get* from him. He gives two *gittin* and releases them both.

### One Bro: Chalitza

If this man then dies and leaves only one brother, that brother must perform *chalitzah* with both sisters. He cannot perform *yibum* with either one, because whichever one he approaches might be *achot zekukato* — the sister of the woman to whom he stands in a *zika* relationship from *yibum*. *Achas zekukato* is forbidden to him like a married woman's sister; having sex with her would be a serious prohibition.

### Chalitza & Yibum

If, however, the man dies leaving two brothers, one performs *chalitzah* and the other performs *yibum*. The mechanism works as follows. Say the first brother performs *chalitzah* with one sister. This act either fulfilled his obligation — in which case she was the actual *yevamah* — or was performed with the wrong woman, in which case it was an inconsequential act. Either way, the second brother can now perform *yibum* with the other sister: if she was the real *yevamah*, he is fulfilling the *mitzvah* of *yibum*; if she was not the *yevamah*, the first *chalitzah* was real, and this is simply an ordinary marriage.

The critical point is that the second brother's *yibum* cannot precede the first brother's *chalitzah*. If the second brother performs *yibum* first, he risks having relations with *achot zekukato* — the sister of the woman who may actually be the real *yevamah* — which is forbidden. Only after the first brother has performed *chalitzah*, removing one woman from the state of *zika*, can the second brother safely perform *yibum* with the other.

---

## Two Men, Two Sisters

### Setup: Two Men

The *mishnah* now complicates the scenario: two men — say, two unrelated individuals — each performed *kiddushin* with one of the two sisters, and neither man knows which sister he married. Now each man faces the same dilemma as before: he cannot consummate the marriage. Each man must therefore give a *get* to both sisters — two *gittin* from each man, four *gittin* in total.

### Both Chalitza

If both men die, each man's surviving brother must perform *chalitzah* with both sisters. The presence of the second possible husband compounds the uncertainty: each surviving brother must address the possibility that his deceased brother was married to either of the sisters.

### One vs. Two Bros

If each deceased man left a single brother, each of those brothers performs *chalitzah* with both sisters. If one of the deceased men left a single brother and the other left two brothers, the single brother performs *chalitzah* with both sisters to neutralize his family's involvement — and once he has done so, we return in effect to the prior scenario. The two brothers of the other deceased man can then arrange one *chalitzah* and one *yibum* among themselves, as in the earlier case.

---

## Both Sides: Two Bros

### Dual-Family Setup

The *mishnah* adds yet another layer: each of the two deceased men left two brothers. On one side are two brothers — call them Shimon and Levi — and on the other side are two other brothers. Each pair of brothers represents the heirs of one of the deceased husbands, each of whom was married to one (unknown) sister.

### Cross-Chalitza

The solution is a cross-*chalitzah* strategy. One brother from the first family performs *chalitzah* with one sister, and one brother from the second family performs *chalitzah* with the other sister. Then the remaining brother from each family performs *yibum* with the respective sister freed by the other family's *chalitzah*.

### Why It Works

The logic: consider Shimon's performing *chalitzah* with one sister and Levi's subsequently performing *yibum* with the other. This is precisely the arrangement established in the earlier case — one *chalitzah*, one *yibum* — and it works for all the reasons already explained. The complication introduced by the second family is that the sister Levi wishes to perform *yibum* with may have been married to the second deceased man, in which case she stands in *zika* to his brothers and cannot simply marry Levi. But once one brother from the second family has performed *chalitzah* with her, that *zika* is dissolved, and Levi can perform *yibum* without any concern of *achot zekukato*. The same logic operates symmetrically for the other pair. Each side's *chalitzah* clears the path for the other side's *yibum*.

---

## Both Yibum

### Risk: Achat Zekuka

The *mishnah* addresses a final scenario: what if, rather than following the prescribed cross-*chalitzah* strategy, one brother went ahead and performed *yibum* directly — before any *chalitzah* had taken place? This is problematic because at the moment he performs *yibum*, the woman he approaches might be *achot zekukato* — the sister of the woman genuinely obligated to him through *yibum*. He has thus potentially transgressed a serious prohibition.

### Resolution

Nonetheless, once the second brother from the other family then goes ahead and performs *yibum* with the other sister, the situation is retroactively resolved. The first brother's woman is no longer his *achat zekukato* — she has no remaining relationship of *zika* to him — because the second *yibum* completed the discharge of the other obligation. Since the *zika* no longer exists, the first brother may remain married to the woman he took. The principle is the same one articulated earlier: *ein motzi'in miyadam* — once *yibum* has been performed by both, even if the order was wrong and the first act was technically problematic, the parties are not required to separate. The second *yibum* retroactively eliminates the basis of the prohibition that attached to the first.

---

---

# Yevamot 23b

## Unknown Marriage Cas (II)

### Opening & Context

The daf begins after the *mishnah* on 23b, with the *gemara* picking up approximately two lines before the text widens on the page. The *mishnah* addressed the case of a man who married two women without knowing which one he had married: before his death he must give a *get* to each, and after his death *chalitzah* is performed with each. The *mishnah* then extends the discussion to scenarios involving two brothers or two separate men in parallel situations. The *gemara* now proceeds to analyze the underlying halachic assumptions of this *mishnah*.

### Two Sisters Scenario

The opening scenario of the *mishnah* concerns a man who married one of two sisters without knowing which one he had married. The *gemara* initially infers from this case that *kiddushin she'einam re'uyim le'biah* — an act of betrothal that can never lead to marital relations — is nonetheless halachically binding. This inference follows because the scenario assumes that from the very moment of *kiddushin*, it was impossible to determine which woman was his wife, and therefore it was never possible to be intimate with either sister, since one might be one's wife's sister.

## Kiddushin Unsuitable (II)

### Binding Nature Question

The *gemara* draws the inference that *kiddushin she'einam re'uyim le'biah havei kiddushin* — betrothal that is inherently incapable of leading to intimacy is still a valid act of *kiddushin*. This question touches on the centrality of marital relations within the institution of marriage itself. One may recall that earlier in the tractate, the *gemara* discussed at length cases involving women for whom pregnancy posed a danger, or cases of underage girls and pregnant women, and the discussion there concerned the use of contraception — but never the option of complete abstention from relations. That itself reflects how fundamental intimacy is to the definition of marriage.

One might ask: if *kiddushin* that cannot lead to relations is still binding, why is *kiddushin* with an *ervah* not binding? After all, relations with an *ervah* are also forbidden. The answer — and this is indeed the question that Tosafot addresses — is that in the case of standard *issurei lavin*, the prohibition exists independently of the *kiddushin* itself. By contrast, in the two-sisters case, it is the very act of *kiddushin* that generates the impossibility: by creating an act of betrothal to one of the two sisters, one immediately renders the other a potential *achot ishto*, making relations with either woman impossible. As Tosafot states: *kiddushin she'einam re'uyim le'biah peirush she'al yedei kiddushin kamafsida biviah* — the *kiddushin* itself is what precludes the possibility of relations. By contrast, with *chayavei lavin* or *chayavei aseh*, the *kiddushin* does not generate the prohibition; the prohibition exists prior to and independent of the act of betrothal.

## Unknown Marriage Cas (II)

### Rashi's Explanation

Rashi's explanation of how the *kiddushin* could be indeterminate from the very outset is as follows. He writes: *she'ein sofam lavo lidei biah* — at the moment of *kiddushin* it was never possible for relations to follow. The scenario Rashi envisions is one in which the man declared *harei achas mikem mekudeshet li* — "one of you is betrothed to me" — without specifying which sister. Both sisters had appointed a single agent to receive the *kiddushin* on their behalf, and the man gave the money to that agent without designating which sister he intended. As a result, the betrothal was indeterminate from its very inception, and since neither woman could be identified as his wife, relations with either would always have been forbidden as potentially intimacy with one's wife's sister.

It should be noted that this scenario is somewhat distinct from a case where the identity was knowable in principle but happened to be unknown. One can imagine an alternative scenario — for example, where the parties agreed that the outcome would be determined by a coin flip, but the coin rolled away and its result was never observed. In that case, there was at least a definite intended recipient under each possible outcome, even if the result was unobserved. In Rashi's case, however, no specific woman was ever designated at all. Either way, the conceptual question of whether *kiddushin* that cannot lead to relations is binding remains significant.

## Kiddushin Unsuitable (II)

### Arayos vs. Lo Ta'aseh

One might press further: in the case of an *ervah* — a woman with whom relations are biblically forbidden as *arayot* — the *kiddushin* is likewise not binding. Why, then, should the two-sisters case, where relations are also forbidden, lead to a different conclusion? The distinction, as noted above and addressed explicitly by Tosafot, is that the *kiddushin* in the two-sisters case is itself the source of the problem. The act of betrothal is what creates the *issur*, not a pre-existing prohibition.

### Tosafot's Distinction

Tosafot formulates this clearly: *kiddushin she'einam re'uyim le'biah peirush she'al yedei kiddushin kamafsida biviah* — the category of *kiddushin* that cannot lead to relations refers specifically to a case where the *kiddushin* itself destroys the possibility of relations. By contrast, in cases of *chayavei lavin* or *chayavei aseh* — such as a *kohen* marrying a *gerushah*, or a *mamzer*, or a *petzu'a daka* — the prohibition on relations does not arise from the *kiddushin*. Indeed, in a somewhat ironic framing, those are considered *kiddushin ha-re'uyim le'biah* — betrothal that is in some sense oriented toward relations — because the *kiddushin* itself does not generate the impossibility.

### Gemara's Resolution

The *gemara* resolves its initial inference by reframing the *mishnah*'s case: *hacha bemai askinan keshe-hukru basof nit'arvu* — we are dealing here with a situation where the identities were originally known and then subsequently became confused. The man did intend a specific woman at the moment of betrothal, the *kiddushin* was therefore unambiguously valid, and only afterwards did confusion arise as to which sister he had married. Accordingly, no proof can be derived from this *mishnah* regarding *kiddushin she'einam re'uyim le'biah*, since the *mishnah* is not addressing that case at all.

## Mishnah Language & Seifa

### Language Analysis

The *gemara* notes that this reading is also supported by the precise language of the *mishnah* itself. The *mishnah* uses the formulation *ve'eino yodeia* — "and he does not know" — rather than *ve'eino yadu'a*, which would mean "and it is not known." The active construction indicates that *he* does not know, but the information exists and was once known. This linguistic precision confirms that the scenario is one of subsequent confusion, not original indeterminacy.

### Seifa's Role

Given that the *kiddushin* is clearly valid and this point requires no special derivation, the *gemara* asks: what is the *chiddush* of the *mishnah*? The answer is *seifa itztricha lei* — the *mishnah* is needed for the practical rulings found in its concluding portion, which spell out how *chalitzah* and *yibum* are to be conducted once the husband dies.

### One Brother Case

If the husband died and there is one surviving brother, he performs *chalitzah* with both women, since it is unknown which one creates the obligation.

### Two Brothers Case

If there were two brothers, one performs *chalitzah* and the other performs *yibum*. However, this must be done in a specific order: *davka mechaleitz ve'hadar yabumei* — the *chalitzah* must precede the *yibum*. The reason is that if the brother were to perform *yibum* first — say, with one of the sisters — and that sister turns out not to be the one to whom he is *zakuk*, then he would have engaged in relations with the sister of the woman to whom he is *zakuk*, violating the prohibition of *achot zikukato*.

To illustrate: suppose the deceased was married to either Rachel or Leah, and the surviving brothers are Shimon and Levi. If Shimon performs *chalitzah* with Rachel, and it turns out Rachel was indeed the obligated *yevamah*, Levi can then perform *yibum* with Leah without any concern. If, on the other hand, Leah was the obligated *yevamah*, then Shimon's *chalitzah* was technically superfluous but harmless, and Shimon himself has fulfilled the *mitzvah* of *yibum* with Leah. In either scenario, proceeding in the order of *chalitzah* first ensures that no violation occurs. But if Levi were to begin with *yibum* to Leah, and Rachel was in fact the obligated woman, then Levi would have had relations with *achot zikukato* — the sister of the woman to whom he bears a *zikah*.

## Two Men & Two Sisters

### Scenario Setup

The *mishnah* then presents a more complex scenario involving two unrelated men — each of whom married one of two sisters without knowing which — who both die. One man has a single surviving brother and the other has two surviving brothers.

### One Brother Dies

When one of the husbands dies leaving a single brother, that brother performs *chalitzah* with both women and thereby removes himself entirely from the picture, since he cannot perform *yibum* in any case: even if he were to perform *chalitzah* with one woman and then *yibum* with the other, the second would be *achot chalutzato* — the sister of the woman with whom he performed *chalitzah* — rendering the *yibum* forbidden.

### Both Men Die

When both husbands die — one leaving one brother and one leaving two brothers — the single brother performs *chalitzah* with both women and steps aside. This allows the two brothers of the other husband to proceed: one performs *chalitzah* and the other performs *yibum*, just as in the earlier case. The *gemara* then asks whether there is any novelty in stating this, given that the earlier portion of the *mishnah* already established the same principle. The answer is that without this ruling one might have feared a precedent — perhaps one of the parties would reason that since two brothers in the other family can do *chalitzah* and then *yibum*, perhaps the single brother could also do *chalitzah* with one woman and *yibum* with the other. The *mishnah* therefore states explicitly that this is not permitted.

### Why No Yibum First

Furthermore, the reason the single brother cannot perform *yibum* at all — even after *chalitzah* with one of the women — is that if he were to do so, it could constitute relations with *achot chalutzato*. And before he has performed *chalitzah* and exited the picture, if one of the two brothers of the other husband were to perform *yibum*, that brother might be performing *yibum* with a *yevamah lashuk* — a woman who is awaiting resolution with the single brother — since the *zikah* of the single brother has not yet been dissolved. Thus, the single brother must perform *chalitzah* with both women first, clearing the way for the remaining two brothers to proceed with one performing *chalitzah* and the other performing *yibum*.

## Two Brothers & Sisters

### Complex Setup

The final scenario of this section involves two unrelated men, each with two surviving brothers, both of whom had married two sisters without knowing which sister each had married.

### Solution Strategy

The *mishnah* prescribes a specific solution: each pair of brothers coordinates so that one member of each pair performs *chalitzah* with one woman while the other performs *yibum* with the other. Specifically, the first brother performs *chalitzah* with Leah and the second brother of the other pair performs *chalitzah* with Rachel; then the respective partners in each pair perform *yibum* with the other woman.

### Removing the Problem

This arrangement systematically removes the problem of *achot zikukato*. By performing *chalitzah* with Leah, the first brother dissolves whatever *zikah* he might have had to Leah from the first husband's marriage, so that Leah is no longer in a state of *zikukato* with respect to Levi. By performing *chalitzah* with Rachel, Shimon removes Rachel from the state of *zikukato* with respect to Levi, so that Levi may now perform *yibum* with Leah. The same logic operates symmetrically for the other pair and Rachel. The *gemara* asks why this ruling was necessary given that earlier rulings covered similar ground, and answers that one might otherwise have thought a concern exists that, since *chalitzah* and *yibum* are being performed in each pair, participants might bypass the *chalitzah* and rush directly to *yibum*. The *mishnah* therefore teaches explicitly that the ordered sequence is mandatory.

## Mishnah Language & Seifa

### Language Analysis

The *mishnah*'s language — *ve'eino yodeia* rather than *ve'eino yadu'a* — was already shown to confirm that the *mishnah* deals with a case of subsequent confusion, not original indeterminacy. This precision permeates the entire structure of the *mishnah*'s rulings.

## Certain Case Contrast

### Certain Marriage Case

The *gemara* now compares the foregoing uncertain scenarios to a distinct case taught elsewhere in the *mishnah*: four brothers, two of whom are married to two sisters. This is not a case of doubt — it is known that Reuven is married to Rachel and Shimon is married to Leah. Both Reuven and Shimon die. The *mishnah* rules: *harei elu choltzot velo mityabmot* — the surviving brothers Levi and Yehuda must perform *chalitzah* with both women; neither may perform *yibum*.

### Why Both Chalitzah

This ruling requires explanation. One might have supposed that the same solution applied in the uncertain case would apply here: Levi performs *chalitzah* with Rachel, thereby releasing Rachel from the state of *zikukato*, and then proceeds to perform *yibum* with Leah. Why is that not permitted here?

The *gemara* offers two distinct rationales, each tied to a different position in an underlying dispute.

### Rashi's Explanation

According to the position that *yesh zikah* — that the *zikah* creates a quasi-marital bond — Rashi explains the distinction as follows. At the very moment both Reuven and Shimon die, Rachel becomes forbidden to Levi as *achot zikukato*: she is the sister of Leah, to whom he is *zakuk* via the *zikah* from Shimon's marriage. Now, a woman who is *achot zikukato* is not merely a woman he may not currently have relations with — she is a *yevamah* to whom there is no *mitzvah* of *yibum*, and therefore she takes on the status of *eshet ach* without the redemptive possibility of *yibum*. That makes her an *ervah*.

When Levi then performs *chalitzah* with Rachel, the *zikah* to Rachel is dissolved, and she is no longer *zikukato*. But this dissolution does not undo the original *issur*: at the moment that Rachel became *achot zikukato* she simultaneously became *eshet ach* without *mitzvat yibum*, and that status of *ervah* does not disappear merely because the *zikah* has now been resolved. Rachel remains forbidden. By the same logic, Leah is also *achot zikukato* from the moment of Reuven's death — she is forbidden as the sister of the woman to whom Levi is *zakuk* via Reuven's *zikah*. Even after *chalitzah* is performed with Rachel, Leah retains her status as *ervah* because she too, at the moment of death, was a *yevamah* with no *mitzvah* of *yibum*, making her an *eshet ach* with *ervah* status. That status endures.

This is the critical difference from the uncertain case. In the uncertain case, only one of the two sisters was actually Reuven's wife. The other sister bore no marital connection to Reuven whatsoever. If the *zikah* ran to Rachel, then Leah was *achot zikukato* — but she was not an *eshet ach* of anyone. She had no marital tie to either Reuven or Shimon. Once the *zikah* to Rachel is dissolved, Leah has no residual forbidden status. In the certain case, by contrast, both sisters are simultaneously *yevamot* — both were wives of a deceased brother — and both became simultaneously *asurot* as *ervah* the moment the *zikah* created a conflict. That simultaneous *issur* remains even after *chalitzah*.

### Bitul Mitzvas Yevamim

The *gemara* also cites a second rationale, tied to the position of *ein zikah*. According to that position, there is no quasi-marital bond created by the *zikah*, and therefore there is no concept of *achot zikukato* as an *ervah*. Under that view, why couldn't Levi perform *yibum* with Rachel? If there is no *zikah*, there is no prohibition. Yet the *mishnah* still prohibits it.

The concern in this case is *bitul mitzvas yevamim* — the nullification of the *mitzvah* of *yibbum*. If Levi were to perform *yibum* with Rachel and then Yehuda were to die before performing *yibum* or *chalitzah* with Leah, Leah would be left as *eshet ach* of Levi — his wife's sister — and neither *yibum* nor *chalitzah* could be performed with her. The *mitzvah* of *yibbum* would be entirely nullified for her, which is prohibited. To prevent this outcome, the *mishnah* mandates that both surviving brothers perform *chalitzah*, ensuring that no one proceeds with *yibum* in a way that could lead to the complete frustration of the other woman's *mitzvah*.

### Uncertain Case Tolerated

One might then ask: why does the uncertain case tolerate both brothers proceeding with *chalitzah* and then *yibum*, given the same theoretical concern about *bitul mitzvas yevamim*? The answer is that in the uncertain case, only one of the two women was ever genuinely obligated in *yibum* or *chalitzah*. The other woman had no actual obligation at all. Since each brother can say *didi kamei ramyah* — "the obligated woman falls to me" — and since we do not know who the true *yevamah* is, there is no certainty that both women are genuinely owed *yibum* or *chalitzah*. The concern of *bitul mitzvas yevamim* therefore applies with far less force in a case built on *safek*, and accordingly the *mishnah* permits the more flexible approach in the uncertain case while forbidding it in the certain case.

## Both Yibum & Kohanim

### Yibum Allowed

The *mishnah* further states: *kidmu ve-khnasu ein motzi'in* — if both brothers went ahead and performed *yibum*, they are permitted to remain married. Although the proper procedure required one to perform *chalitzah* before the other performed *yibum*, once both have acted, the *yibum* takes effect. The reasoning is that while the first brother to act may have initially violated the prohibition of *achot zikukato*, once his brother performed *yibum* with the other sister, the *zikah* to that sister was dissolved, removing retroactively whatever problem had existed. The marriages may therefore stand.

### Kohanim Question

A *baraita* taught by Sheshila adds: *ve'afilu sheneihem kohanim* — this is true even if both brothers are *kohanim*. This requires explanation. In the scenario under discussion, both brothers have each received a *chalitzah* — since the resolution involved each pair performing a *chalitzah* with one woman and a *yibum* with the other. If both brothers are *kohanim*, the concern arises that one of the women they have now married may be a *chalutza*, and a *kohen* is forbidden to marry a *chalutza*.

### Chalutza Status

The *baraita* rules that they may remain married. The *gemara* asks: is the prohibition of *chalutza* to a *kohen* only rabbinic? The *gemara* affirms: *chalutza d'rabanan hi* — yes, the prohibition is rabbinic in nature, and the biblical verse that includes *chalutza* alongside *gerushah* in the prohibition for *kohanim* is treated as a mere *asmakhta*.

### Safek Chalutza Leniency

Since the prohibition is only rabbinic, a *safek chalutza* — a woman who may or may not be a *chalutza* — is treated leniently. In the present case, *chalitzah* was performed with both women, but only one of them actually required it. An act of *chalitzah* performed upon a woman who did not require it is halachically meaningless. Therefore, one of the two women is a genuine *chalutza* and the other is not; it is simply unknown which is which. Since each brother is married to only a *safek chalutza*, and *safek chalutza lo gazru bah rabanan* — the Rabbis did not extend their decree of *issur* to a *safek chalutza* — both brothers may remain married.

### Chalutza Source Debate

The *gemara* challenges whether *chalutza* is truly only rabbinic, citing a *baraita* that derives the prohibition from a biblical verse. The *gemara* resolves that the derivation is an *asmakhta* alone. It should be noted that a significant body of Tannaitic material appears to treat *chalutza* as *d'oraisa*, and indeed this may be the position of the Yerushalmi. Nevertheless, the Bavli consistently maintains that *chalutza* is *d'rabanan*, which allows for the leniency in the *safek* case.

The broader question of *chalutza*'s status is also illuminating conceptually. A *chalutza* occupies a status analogous to a *gerushah* — a divorcee — in that the *zikah* was a quasi-marriage and the *chalitzah* was its dissolution. Since widowhood is not forbidden to an ordinary *kohen* — only to a *kohen gadol* — it is the quasi-divorce aspect of *chalutza* that is halachically relevant for *kohanim*, and it is that dimension which the Rabbis addressed with their decree.

## Yibum Mitzvah Order

### Gadol Preference

The next *mishnah* states: *mitzvah be-gadol le-yabbem* — the *mitzvah* of *yibum* falls first upon the eldest surviving brother.

### Younger Brother Valid

Nevertheless, *ve'im kadam ha-katan zakha* — if the younger brother rushed ahead and performed *yibum*, his act is fully valid. The preference for the eldest brother does not render *yibum* by a younger brother ineffective; it establishes a proper order, but does not create an exclusive entitlement.

## Bechor Verse Drashah

### Verse Reading

The *tanna'im* teach: *ve-haya ha-bechor asher teleid yakum al shem achiv ha-met* — the plain reading of this verse would seem to say that the firstborn son born from the *yibum* union will be named after his dead father. The *gemara*, however, reads the verse entirely differently. *Ve-haya ha-bechor* is read not as a reference to the firstborn child who will be born, but as a directive that the *bechor* — the oldest brother — is the one who performs the *yibum*. The phrase *ve-yibma* — "and he shall perform *yibum*" — is followed by *ve-haya ha-bechor*, meaning: it is the *bechor* among the brothers who performs the *yibum*.

### Fertile Woman Requirement

*Asher teleid* — "who will bear" — is read as a qualification on the *yevamah*: the *bechor* performs *yibum* specifically with a woman who is capable of bearing children. This excludes an *ilonit* — a woman who is constitutionally infertile — from the *mitzvah* of *yibum*: *prat le'ilonit she'eina yoledet*.

### Inheritance Aspect

*Yakum al shem achiv* — the verse continues — is read as *lenachala*: inheritance. A *gezeirah shavah* connects this phrase to a parallel usage elsewhere — *al shem acheihem yikare'u be-nachalatam*, referring to Ephraim and Menashe and the inheritance of tribal portions — establishing that *al shem* in both contexts means assuming an inheritance. Thus *yakum al shem achiv* means that the brother who performs *yibum* assumes his dead brother's portion of the estate. None of this is about naming a child; it is all about the brother performing the act of *yibum*.

### Name Continuation

*Ve-lo yimache shemo mi-Yisrael* — "and his name shall not be blotted out from Israel" — is similarly read as a qualification on the brother, not as a reference to perpetuating the dead brother's name through a child. It is read as excluding a *saris* — a sterile man — from the *mitzvah* of *yibum*: *prat le-saris she-shemo machui*, for a *saris* cannot have children, his name is already as if blotted out, and the rationale underlying the *mitzvah* does not apply to him.

## Rava's Peshat Observation

### No Peshat Value

Rava makes a striking observation: *af al gav de-ve-chol ha-Torah kullah ein mikra yotze mi-yedey peshuto* — in the entire Torah, even when a *derashah* is made from a verse, the *peshat* of the verse retains some meaningful value. One may derive a halacha that overrides the plain reading, yet the plain reading continues to express something of the underlying values or spirit of the text. Rava's point is that this principle does not hold here.

### Gezeirah Shavah Effect

The *gezeirah shavah* connecting *yakum al shem achiv* to *lenachala* — inheritance — completely removes the verse from its apparent meaning. There is no residual *peshat* that remains operative.

### Peshat Eradication

As Rashi explains: *she-ein tzarich likro shemo be-shem achiv ha-met* — there is no requirement, nor even a meaningful expression of an idea, that the child born of the *yibum* be named after the deceased father. Under ordinary circumstances, even when a *derashah* re-reads a verse technically, one might still say: the spirit of the verse suggests naming the child after the dead father, and while this is not a halacha, it is a praiseworthy practice, analogous to the way some authorities treat *ve-re'item oto* by the *tzitzit* as suggesting they should be worn visibly, or the way some understand *ayin tachat ayin* as conveying a conceptual value even when the operative halacha is monetary compensation. Here, Rava teaches, no such residual spirit of the *peshat* applies. The *peshat* has been entirely eradicated.

## Verse Audience Question

### Direct Address Issue

The *gemara* probes the matter further. If the *peshat* of the verse were that the child should be named after the dead father, who exactly would the Torah be addressing? If it is speaking to the *yavam* — the brother-in-law — then the verse should have said *yakum al shem achicha*, "you shall name him after your brother," speaking in the second person.

### General Address

Alternatively, the verse may be addressing the *beit din* or *klal Yisrael* generally, prescribing what shall be done in this situation. Under that reading, the verse is not a directive to the *yavam* personally, but a general statement of how things are to be ordered.

### Brother vs. Father

But even under that reading, a difficulty remains: the verse says *al shem achiv* — after his brother — rather than *al shem aviv* — after his father. If the verse is about a child being named after the deceased, the deceased is the child's father, and the verse should have said *al shem aviv ha-met*, or alternatively, from the perspective of the *beit din* addressing the yavam's child, *al shem achi aviv* — "after his father's brother." The use of *achiv* — his brother — is inexplicable on the *peshat* reading, which further supports Rava's conclusion that the *peshat* has been entirely displaced.

## Brother Focus Resolution

### Beit Din Address

The *gemara* resolves the matter: the verse speaks to the *beit din*, directing them to ensure that the *yavam* — referred to as the *bechor* because he is the eldest — performs *yibum* and assumes his dead brother's portion of the inheritance. *Yakum al shem achiv* refers not to naming a child but to the *yavam* rising to take his brother's place with respect to *nachala*.

### All About Brother

Every element of the verse — *ve-haya ha-bechor*, *asher teleid*, *yakum al shem achiv*, *ve-lo yimache shemo* — refers to the brother performing *yibum*, not to any child who may be born. The verse is entirely about the *yavam* and his obligations and entitlements, with no residual reference to a child's name.

## Bechor Exclusivity T (II)

### Bechor Exclusivity T (II)heory

Now that the verse is established as speaking about the eldest brother, the *gemara* raises a series of further questions. Perhaps the verse intends that *only* a *bechor* — a halachic firstborn — may perform *yibum*, and non-firstborn brothers may not.

### Proof from Shelo Haya

This is disproved from the concept of *eshet achiv shelo haya be-olamo* — the wife of a brother who was born after the deceased brother had already died. The Torah established a special exclusion for this case, teaching that there is no *mitzvat yibum* in such a situation.
