The daf opens on 25a with a *mishna* that, at first glance, seems more at home in *Masechet Gittin* than in *Yevamos*. *Ha-mevi get mi-medinat ha-yam* — the one who brings a *get* from overseas. As is familiar from the opening *mishna* of *Gittin*, a messenger who delivers a *get* from *chutz la'aretz* must declare *bifnei nechtav bifnei nechtam* — that the document was written and signed in his presence, in order to validate its authenticity. The *mishna* here rules that such a messenger, *lo yisa ishto* — may not subsequently marry the newly divorced woman. The reason is evident: his interest in marrying her would cast retroactive suspicion on the validity of his testimony.

### Murder Confession

The *mishna* extends this principle in a striking direction. If the witness declares *haragti* — I killed the husband — or *haragnu* — we killed the husband — he likewise cannot marry the wife. What is remarkable is that the *mishna* makes no move to prosecute him for murder; the entire concern is the integrity of the testimony that permits the woman to remarry. *Rabbi Yehuda* draws a distinction: if he says *haragti*, I killed him, she may not remarry from his testimony; but if he says *haragnu*, we killed him, she may. The precise basis of this distinction will emerge in the *gemara*.

### Reason for Restriction

The *gemara* articulates the logic underlying the *mishna*'s ruling about the overseas *get*: *ta'ama de-medinat ha-yam* — the reason he cannot remarry applies specifically when he brings the *get* from overseas, *de-alei kasamchina*, because we are relying on his testimony. But *aval me-eretz yisrael*, if he delivers the *get* within *Eretz Yisrael*, where no such declaration is required, *de-lav alei kasamchina* — since we are not relying on his testimony — *yisa ishto*, he may marry the woman.

### Husband Death Testimony

The *gemara* then raises a challenge: in the case where the witness testifies that the husband has died, *de-lav alei kasamchina* — we do not ultimately rely on him in the same direct sense, because the principle established elsewhere is *isha dayka u-minsava* — the woman herself is trusted to investigate. The *gemara* elsewhere grapples with the conceptual difficulty of permitting remarriage on the basis of a single witness; the resolution it offers is that since the woman is fully aware of the severe consequences should the testimony prove false — should her husband turn out to be alive — we rely entirely on her own careful investigation following the testimony. On this reading, the operative reliability is hers, not the witness's.

If so, one might ask, why can he not marry her? If we are essentially relying on the woman rather than on him, why should his interest in the outcome disqualify him? The *gemara*'s answer brings us to the next distinction.

### Death vs Get

*Hatam leka ksava hacha ikka ksava* — there is still a critical difference between the case of testifying to the husband's death and the case of delivering a *get* within *Eretz Yisrael*. Even when the testimony about death is ultimately bolstered or even superseded by the woman's investigation, the witness is still testifying to facts; there is still some testimonial act that requires integrity. By contrast, when delivering a *get* within *Eretz Yisrael* — where no declaration is required — the document effectively validates itself. *Kidtnan, mah bein get l'misa — shehaksav mochiach* — what is the difference between divorce and death? The written document proves its own legitimacy.

The underlying principle is the well-known rule that *eidim shehachatumim al hashtar k'mi shenechkra edusan b'veis din* — witnesses whose signatures appear on a document are treated as if their testimony has already been examined before a court. Within *Eretz Yisrael*, the signatures are presumed reliable without external validation; the need for *bifnei nechtav uvifnei nechtam* arises only when the document originates from *chutz la'aretz*, where the reliability of signatures is less certain.

---

## Splitting Testimony

### Rape Witness Case

*Hu nihu d'lo yisav iteseih, ha l'acher tinasei* — he himself cannot marry her, but she may marry another man. With this the *gemara* transitions to a celebrated discussion, introduced by Rav Yosef. If a man testifies *ploni revani le'onsi* — a certain man had intercourse with me against my will — then *hu ve'acher mitztarfim le'hargo*: he may join with another witness to have that man executed by the court. Since he himself was a victim, he bears no culpability and retains his standing as a witness.

But if he says *birtzoni* — it was done willingly, I was a consenting participant — then *rasha hu*. He has admitted to a transgression. The Torah states *al tashet yadcha im rasha lihyot ed chamas* — do not place your hand with a wicked person to be a corrupt witness — which excludes a *rasha* from giving testimony. By his own admission he has rendered himself invalid, and his testimony implicating the other party cannot stand.

This introduces the concept of *palginan dibura* — the question of whether we may split a witness's statement, accepting the portion that relates to another person while discarding the self-incriminating portion. Here, Rav Yosef rules that we cannot: the moment he admits to willing participation, he has disqualified himself entirely, and we cannot bracket that admission and salvage the remainder of his testimony.

The parallel to the *mishna*'s case of murder is apparent. There, too, the witness is confessing to a serious crime. If we cannot split the testimony in the case of the rape witness, we might expect to be equally unable to split it in the murder case — and thus unable to use the testimony to permit the woman to remarry at all.

One might suggest a distinction: in the testimony about the murdered husband, we are operating in the domain of *edus isha*, about which the Rabbis were especially lenient. Perhaps in that domain, a more flexible standard applies, including the possibility of *palginan dibura*.

### Rav Yosef vs Menashe

The *gemara* now presents the positions of Rav Yosef and Rav Menashe in structured opposition, and this is a striking *gemara* to follow carefully.

Rav Menashe states: *gazlan de-divreihem kasher le-edus isha* — a person who is rabbinically invalid as a witness, such as a gambler, is nonetheless valid for testimony concerning a woman's ability to remarry. But *gazlan de-divrei Torah pasul le-edus isha* — one who is biblically invalid is excluded even in the more lenient domain of *edus isha*.

It is worth noting that *Tosafos* raises the question of whether the invalidity of a witness due to monetary corruption — where the logic is that such a person will shade testimony for financial gain — necessarily applies to one invalidated merely as a habitual sinner who poses no such temptation to lie about the death of a husband. The *gemara* does not distinguish along these lines.

The *gemara* then asks: should we say that Rav Menashe holds like *Rabbi Yehuda* in the *mishna* — who refuses to accept the testimony of one who says he is the murderer — while the *Tanna Kamma* permits it? The *gemara* rejects this forced identification. *Amar lach Rav Menashe* — Rav Menashe would say: *ve-ein adam mesim atzmo rasha*. A person cannot make himself into a *rasha* by his own testimony against himself. This is the principle of *palginan dibura* applied in the affirmative: because one cannot legally self-incriminate in matters of *misa* or *malkos* — confession of a criminal offense has no halachic standing — the self-incriminating portion of the statement is simply discarded. We retain only the relevant claim that the husband is dead.

But if Rav Menashe holds that we can do *palginan dibura* — split the testimony — why does he still rule that a biblically invalid witness is excluded from *edus isha*? And conversely, if Rav Yosef holds that *palginan dibura* is rejected, how can the *mishna's Tanna Kamma* accept the murderer's testimony at all?

The *gemara* resolves this by assigning each position a different hinge. Rav Menashe, who does *palginan dibura*, would therefore disagree with Rav Yosef in the rape case — he would split the testimony there as well and not disqualify the witness for the self-incriminating part. Conversely, Rav Yosef, who refuses *palginan dibura* in the rape case, can still accept the testimony in the *edus isha* context by holding that even a biblically invalid witness is acceptable there — and therefore the self-incriminating admission becomes irrelevant in any event.

The *gemara* also notes a possible synthesis: one might hold that neither *palginan dibura* alone nor the leniency of *edus isha* alone would suffice, but that the combination of both considerations together permits the testimony. Thus the *Tanna Kamma*, who accepts the murderer's testimony, could be understood as relying on the convergence of the two grounds — the unique latitude of *edus isha* and the doctrine of *palginan dibura* — each of which independently might not cross the threshold.

### Bandit Confession

A *baraisa* is then introduced in which the Rabbis challenge the position of *Rabbi Yehuda*. A bandit, *listis*, was being led out to execution in a place called Kaputkia. Before his death he instructed those present to go and tell the wife of Shimon ben Kohen: *ani haragti et ba'alah* — I murdered her husband. The story records that the woman's husband was subsequently declared dead and she was permitted to remarry. Here, then, is a clear case of accepting the testimony of someone who confesses to murder — precisely what *Rabbi Yehuda* would reject.

### Partial Responsibility

*Rabbi Yehuda* deflects the challenge: *be'omer ani hayiti im horgav* — I was with those who killed him. The statement attributed to the bandit, he maintains, did not mean that he personally committed the murder but rather that he was present, part of the group, a participant of some degree — but not the one who physically carried it out. Thus *Rabbi Yehuda* does not necessarily hold that one who directly admits to the killing can be used as a witness even for *edus isha*.

The *gemara* objects: but the *baraisa* explicitly identifies the man as a *listis*, a bandit, and says he was going out to execution — surely that implies he was convicted of murder? The *gemara* answers: *beit din shel ovdei kochavim delo dayki vekatli* — the non-Jewish courts would execute on the basis of suspicion without the rigorous evidentiary standards of a Jewish court. His being led to execution by a non-Jewish court does not halachically establish him as a murderer.

The upshot is that both the *Tanna Kamma* and *Rabbi Yehuda* agree that if a witness is clearly established as a murderer by proper *beit din* standards, the testimony cannot be relied upon — at least according to Rav Menashe's position. The disagreement between them is narrower: does the witness's own self-incriminating statement suffice to disqualify him? The *Tanna Kamma* says no, because we invoke *palginan dibura*, or because we are lenient in *edus isha*, or both. *Rabbi Yehuda* says yes — a self-incriminating admission of personal murder does disqualify, though not an admission of mere presence.

---

## Vow Annulment Case

### Vow Prohibition

The *mishna* turns to yet another scenario in the running theme of persons who are prohibited from marrying a woman they have in some way facilitated into being divorced. *He'chacham she'asar et ha'ishah b'neder al ba'alah* — a *chacham* who was asked to annul a vow and was unable to do so, with the result that the vow rendered the woman forbidden to her husband. This is actually a more extreme scenario than it might initially appear: it is not merely that the husband threatened divorce over the vow, but that the vow itself made cohabitation impossible. Such a *chacham* may not subsequently marry the woman.

### Beit Din Exception

However, the *mishna* adds important qualifications. If the *chacham* was involved in a *mi'un* proceeding — a minor girl who was married through the consent of her brothers or mother exercising her right of verbal refusal — or supervised a *chalitzah* ceremony, and he did so as part of a *beit din*, then *yisa'enah*, he may marry the woman afterward. The reason is *mipnei shehu beit din* — because he acted as part of a court. When he acts as one member of a three-person panel, the decision cannot be attributed to him personally, and there is far less reason to suspect that his judgment was distorted by personal interest.

### Expert Authority

The *gemara* now interrogates the precise configuration assumed by the *mishna*. If the *chacham* annulled the vow as a single authority, the *gemara* asks: *chad mi matzi matir* — can a single person annul a vow? After all, Rav, citing Rabbi Chiya or Rabbi Chiya bar Avin, taught: *tana hataras nedarim b'shlosha* — the release of vows requires three. Alternatively, if it was done by three, why is any one of them suspect at all?

The *gemara* resolves this by invoking a ruling of Rav Chisda in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *b'yachid mumcheh* — even where three laypeople are normally required, a single recognized expert, a *mumcheh*, may annul vows. The *mishna* is therefore discussing the case of such an individual expert. And the concluding clause — that if he acted as part of a *beit din*, he may marry the woman — is distinguished precisely because in the *beit din* context he was not acting unilaterally.

### Document Witnesses

The *gemara* extends the analysis. *Ta'ama d'beit din, ha bitrei lo* — if the exemption from suspicion applies specifically when there is a full *beit din*, then perhaps two witnesses acting jointly should still fall under suspicion? A *baraita* is cited: witnesses who signed a field-sale document or a woman's *get* — *lo chashu chachamim l'davar zeh* — the Sages were not concerned that a witness might have forged the document in order to profit from the transaction or marry the woman. Any time one is not acting entirely alone, the concern dissipates.

The *gemara* concludes that the *mishna*'s use of *beit din* language is incidentally conveying an additional ruling: do not think that *mi'un* may be performed before two — *mi'un b'gimmel*, it requires three. But for the purpose of permitting remarriage, even two witnesses acting together suffice.

---

## Marriage Occurred

### Divorce Required

*Ibaya lehu: knas mahu sheyotzi?* — the question is finally posed that has been lurking beneath all the preceding cases: if one of these men actually went ahead and married the woman despite the prohibition, must he now divorce her? This is the *knas* question — whether the Rabbis imposed a punitive requirement of divorce in cases where the initial marriage should not have taken place. Notably, *Rashi* understands this question as applying both to the case of the *chacham* and the *neder* and to the case of the one who brought the *get*. The *Rashba*, however, holds that the question applies only to the case of the *chacham* in the current *mishna*.

### Kahana vs Ashi

*Rav Kahana amar kanas motzi* — Rav Kahana rules that he must divorce. *Rav Ashi amar kanas eino motzi* — Rav Ashi rules that he need not. A tradition was taught in the school of Rav Papa supporting the position of Rav Ashi. When the Rabbis pressed Rav Ashi — is this a received tradition or a logical inference? — he replied: *matnitin hi* — I derive it from the *mishna* itself.

### Rumor Doctrine

The *mishna* cited as support is the ruling concerning one suspected of an affair who subsequently converted or whose circumstances changed: *harei zeh lo yichnos v'im kanas ein motzi* — he should not have married, but if he did, he need not divorce. From there the *gemara* draws the inference: *b'rinana lo mafkinan* — based on rumor and communal suspicion alone, we do not compel divorce.

*Hacha nami b'rinana lo mafkinan* — here too, the concern that the community might draw adverse conclusions does not rise to the level of requiring a divorce after the fact.

It is worth pausing on the disanalogy. In the case of the suspected affair, even if the rumor were true, the woman is still halachically permitted — the act was wrong but the marriage can stand. In the cases under discussion here, however, if the underlying concern is correct — if the *get* was forged or the husband is actually alive — the woman may be an *eishet ish*. The *Rashba*'s position that the question applies only to the *neder* case and not to the *get*-delivery case becomes understandable: in the *neder* case, even if the *chacham* manipulated matters, the husband still gave the woman a *get* of his own accord, and her divorce is fully valid. But in the *get*-delivery case, doubts about the legitimacy of the document or the testimony about death carry potentially severe consequences, making the *b'rinana* framework less clearly applicable.

---

## Remarriage Conditions

### Already Married

*V'kulam shehayu lahem nashim umetu mutarot l'hinasay lahem* — all these individuals, if they were already married at the time they delivered the *get* or testified to the husband's death, and their own wives subsequently died, the woman is permitted to marry them.

This is a remarkable *mishna*. Although *halacha* technically permits polygamy, the *mishna* operates on the sociological assumption that a man who already has a wife will not, as a practical matter, seek to take a second wife. This assumption is stated casually and taken for granted, which is itself striking — *halacha* permits something but the *mishna* treats it as effectively non-occurring for most men. Therefore, if a man was already married when he facilitated the divorce or testified about the husband's death, we do not suspect that he was manipulating events in order to free this woman for himself. He had a wife; he was not in the market for another.

One might counter: even if we assume he was not planning to take a second wife, he might have been planning to divorce his first wife unilaterally, which he is halachically entitled to do. This precise objection is taken up by the *gemara*.

### Divorce Distinction

*Metu in, nitgarshu lo* — the *gemara* infers from the *mishna* that if his wife died, the woman may marry him; but if he divorced his wife, she may not. A *baraita*, however, states *afilu nitgarshu* — even if they divorced their wives, the woman may marry them. The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya, ha d'havi ktata, ha d'la havi ktata* — there is no difficulty; the cases differ depending on whether there was preexisting marital strife.

### Pre-conflict Logic

*Rashi* explains the rule in a direction that may at first seem counterintuitive. Where there was preexisting strife — *d'havi ktata* — and he subsequently divorced his wife, the woman may marry him. Where there was no preexisting strife, she may not. The reasoning, as *Rashi* explains, is *d'achti lo natan da'ato*: if the couple was already in conflict before this woman came onto the scene, the decision to divorce was not generated by interest in the new woman. He would have divorced his wife regardless. The delivery of the *get* or the testimony about the husband's death was therefore not motivated by desire for this woman.

If there was no prior conflict, however, the divorce appears to have originated precisely when this woman became available — which creates the inference that the entire chain of events was engineered.

### Who Initiated

A second resolution is offered: *ha deargil hu, ha deargila hi* — in the case where he was the one pushing for divorce, she may not marry him; in the case where she was the one pushing for divorce, she may. If the wife initiated the desire to separate, then the husband was evidently committed to the marriage and his role in facilitating the other woman's divorce was not self-interested. If he was the one pressing for divorce, the suspicion is stronger.

The *gemara* elsewhere acknowledges that one can subtly maneuver a spouse into seeking divorce — but that level of psychological complexity is not developed further here.

### Intervening Marriage

*V'chulan shenisu l'acherim v'nitgarshu o shenit'almenu mutarot l'hinnase lahem* — if all these women went on to marry another man, and that second man then died or divorced them, the original messenger or witness may now marry the woman. Since she married an entirely different person in the interim, it is inconceivable that the witness's original act was designed to enable this eventual marriage to himself. No one fabricates an elaborate scheme to free a woman for another man's marriage, and then waits to see if that marriage will end, hoping eventually to marry her himself.

The *gemara* notes a further detail: the pairing of outcomes — husband testified dead, second husband divorces; or first husband gave *get*, second husband dies — should not necessarily be read as parallel. The *mishna* may intend a cross-matched reading, which also avoids any entanglement with the ruling of *Rabbi* that two deceased husbands may establish a *chazaka* of fatal ill fortune — a discussion reserved for later in *Yevamos*.

### Relatives Marriage

*V'chulan mutarot livneihem o l'acheihem* — all these women are permitted to marry the brother or the son of the person who brought the *get* or testified to the husband's death. The witness is not assumed to be lying and falsifying testimony so that a relative of his can benefit. The concern is confined to the witness's own potential interest; we do not project the suspicion outward to his family.

---

## Relative Analogy

### Affair Suspicion

The *gemara* challenges this ruling by comparing it to the law of one who is suspected of an illicit affair. The *gemara* cites: *ha'nitan min ha'isha asur be'ima uvevita* — one who is suspected of an affair with a woman is forbidden to marry her mother or her daughter — *uv'achotah* — and her sister. Once suspicion attaches, it is extended to close relatives. Why, then, are we not similarly concerned that the witness in our *mishna* might have delivered a false *get* or false testimony precisely in order that a brother or son could marry this woman, with the witness himself intending to continue an affair with her through access provided by the relative's household?

It is important to understand what the *issur* in the affair case actually is. *Rashi* clarifies: the Torah's prohibitions of a woman and her daughter, or of a wife's sister, are triggered only by marriage. One who had illicit relations with a woman before marrying her daughter has not technically violated *arayot* — that violation requires a marriage to be in place first. The concern in the affair case is therefore prospective: *shema le'achar sheyissa et imma o et bitta tizneh zo immo* — perhaps after marrying the mother or daughter, he will continue the affair with the original woman, and now it will constitute a full biblical violation of *issur arayot*. The family context creates opportunity and proximity.

So the question is: does the same logic apply here? If the witness's brother marries the woman, will the witness have opportunity — and motivation — to pursue an illicit relationship with her?

### Visit Frequency

The *gemara* offers a first answer: *nashi legabi nashi shechichan de'azlan, gavrei legabi gavrei lo shechichan* — women visit one another's homes frequently; mothers, sisters, and daughters spend time together and create natural opportunity for continued encounters. Men, however, do not visit their brothers' homes with comparable frequency. The access that the family-marriage dynamic creates is substantially less in the male-relative scenario.

### Wife Concern

*Ee nami* — alternatively, the *gemara* proposes: *nashi delo asran shechivotan ahadadei lo kapdi ahadadei; gavrei de'asran shechivotan ahadadei kapdi ahadadei* — women are not rendered halachically forbidden to one another by what one does with another woman's relative; therefore a wife is not especially vigilant about her husband's access to her own relatives. But a man whose brother's wife becomes sexually involved with his brother is in a serious situation: *she* becomes forbidden to *his brother*, potentially causing a forced divorce. Therefore brothers are acutely vigilant about one another's wives, which itself curtails opportunity.

This is a striking argument. The *gemara* is suggesting that the protective jealousy of the brother-in-law himself serves as a deterrent, in a way that does not operate in the case of a woman's female relatives.

### Father Exception

*Ee hachi, aviv nami* — if these are the operative distinctions, why does the *mishna* specify brothers and sons but not fathers? Should a father similarly be permitted to marry this woman? The *gemara* answers: *lo mibaya ka'amar, lo mibaya aviv* — of course the father may marry her, and the *mishna* need not even state it, because *de'bayit bereih mineih* — a son is embarrassed before his father and would not dare pursue an affair with his father's wife. *Aval beno delo bayit aviv mineih* — but a son's wife, regarding whom a father might feel he can take liberties with his own child — *eima lo*, one might have thought not to permit; *ka mashma lan* — the *mishna* teaches us that even so, the father is permitted to marry this woman.

The organizing concern throughout this entire section is thus not that someone would sin purely for the benefit of another person. We assume people sin for themselves. The question is whether marrying a relative would create opportunity and occasion for the witness to pursue an ongoing relationship with this woman. Given the distinctions in proximity, access, and marital stakes, the *gemara* finds sufficient grounds to confine the suspicion to the witness himself and not extend it to his male relatives.

---

## Achot Zekuka

### Setup Sisters

The daf concludes with a return to the *mishna* that has, in various forms, punctuated the entire discussion of *Yevamos*. *Arba'ah achim, shenayim mehem nesu'im shtei achayot* — four brothers, two of whom, Reuven and Shimon, are married to two sisters, Rachel and Leah. Reuven and Shimon both die.

### Yibum Restriction

Levi and Yehuda now face the *yibum* obligation. The *mishna* rules: *harei elu cholsot velo mityabmot* — these women must perform *chalitzah* and may not be taken in *yibum*. The reason is the configuration of *achot zekukato* — a *zika*, a quasi-marital bond, attaches each surviving brother to each of the widows. Levi cannot perform *yibum* with Rachel, because Rachel is connected through *zika* to Yehuda as well, making her *achot zekukato*. The same applies symmetrically to Yehuda with Leah. Even if Levi were to perform *chalitzah* with Rachel, he could not then proceed to *yibum* with Leah, because having performed *chalitzah* with Rachel, Leah would become *achot chalutzato* — the sister of his *chalutza* — which is itself rabbinically forbidden. The only resolution is *chalitzah* by both brothers with both women.

### Shammai Hillel

If one of them performed *yibum* in violation of this ruling, the question of whether the marriage stands becomes a matter of dispute between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel*. *Beit Shammai* permits the marriage to remain, holding that the prohibition may have been only rabbinic and therefore does not require dissolution *bedi'avad*. *Beit Hillel* rules *yotsiu* — they must divorce. And indeed, the severity of performing *yibum* improperly here may rise to the level of a *d'oraita* violation — the *zika* may constitute a quasi-marriage, making the completed *yibum* an act involving a woman who remains in some sense *eshet ach* to the other brother.

### One Ervah

*Hayeta achat mehen asura alav al ha'echad issur ervah* — if Rachel is actually Levi's daughter, Rachel is categorically an *ervah* to him, not merely a *zekukah*. In that case, the *ervah* removes the *zika*: Levi has no *yibum* bond to Rachel at all, and Rachel therefore does not function as *achot zekukato* in relation to Leah. Levi may perform *yibum* with Leah directly. Yehuda, however, still has *zika* to both and cannot do *yibum* with either.

### Both Eruvin

*Hayeta achat mehen asura al zeh issur ervah vehashniya asura al zeh issur ervah* — if Rachel is Levi's daughter and Leah is Yehuda's daughter, each woman is a full *ervah* to one brother, eliminating his *zika* to her. Rachel is out of the picture for Levi; he may do *yibum* with Leah. Leah is out of the picture for Yehuda; he may do *yibum* with Rachel. *Ha'asura lazeh muteret lazeh veha'asura lazeh muteret lazeh* — the one forbidden to this one is permitted to the other, and vice versa. This is the case the *mishna* describes with the phrase *achotah keshe'hi yevamtah* — her sister when she is also her sister-in-law: where one is an *ervah*, the other may do *chalitzah* or *yibum* freely.

### Zika Question

*Shma mina yesh zika* — the *gemara* infers from all of this that *zika* must be a real halachic bond, because the entire structure of the *mishna* depends upon it. If there were no *zika*, *hanei mitrei batei ka'atu* — these women come from two separate households, there is no *tzarah* relationship between them. *Hai liyabbem chad, vehai liyabbem chad* — Levi could simply take Rachel and Yehuda could simply take Leah, with no conflict at all. The fact that the *mishna* prohibits this entire arrangement must be because *zika* creates a cross-linkage that generates the problem of *achot zekukato*.

### Death Prevention

The *gemara* anticipates a counter-position: *le'olam eima lach ein zika* — perhaps there is in fact no *zika*, and yet *yibum* is still forbidden here. The reason would be *mishum dekasavar asur levatel mitzvat yevamin* — because performing *yibum* with one woman might lead to the *mitzva* of *yibum* for the other being lost entirely. *De'ad meyabbem chad meis idach* — while Levi is in the process of completing *yibum* with Rachel, Yehuda might die, and then Leah would have no one to perform either *yibum* or *chalitzah* for her.

By contrast, if both brothers perform *chalitzah* with both women, that possibility is foreclosed: once *chalitzah* has been performed with Rachel, even if Yehuda dies, *chalitzah* can still be completed with Leah. The prohibition on *yibum* is thus not rooted in *zika* per se, but in the protection of the *mitzva* from being rendered impossible through circumstance. The *gemara* notes that this is an exceedingly far-fetched explanation, and the discussion will continue on the following daf.

---

---

# Yevamot 25b

## Get from Overseas

### Get Overseas Intro

The *mishnah* at the bottom of 21a opens with a case that initially seems to belong in *Masechet Gittin*: *hamavee get mimedinat hayam* — someone who brings a *get* from overseas. As any student of *Gittin* knows, when delivering a *get* from overseas the messenger must declare *bifnay nechtav u'bifnay nechtam* — that the document was written and signed in his presence, thus validating its execution. The *mishnah* here establishes that this messenger, having delivered the testimony required to render the *get* valid, may not subsequently marry the newly divorced woman. Allowing him to do so would cast retrospective suspicion on the reliability and sincerity of his testimony.

### Death/Murder Cases

The *mishnah* continues with related cases. If the witness says *mes hu* — the husband died — or *haragtee* — I killed him — or *haragnu* — we killed him — he likewise may not marry the woman, because in each instance he has testified to the fact of the husband's death and thereby enabled the woman to remarry. Permitting him to marry her would undermine the credibility of his testimony.

What is striking, of course, is that the *mishnah* raises no concern about the confession of murder itself. The legal focus remains entirely on the question of whether his subsequent marriage to the woman would taint the testimony that allowed her to remarry. We will return to the confession below.

*Rabbi Yehuda* draws a distinction: if the witness says *haragtee* — I killed him — the woman may not remarry this particular man; but if he says *haragnu* — we killed him — she may. The precise meaning of this distinction is clarified by the *gemara*.

### Woman's Investigation

The *gemara* begins by probing the logic of the *mishnah*'s opening case. It observes: *ta'ama d'mimedinat hayam* — the reason the witness cannot marry the woman is that it is specifically because he comes from overseas, meaning we are relying on his testimony (*de-alav kasamchinan*). But if he delivers a *get* from within *Eretz Yisrael*, where no such declaration is required, and we are not formally relying on him (*d'lav alav kasamchinan*), then he may marry the woman.

The *gemara* then turns to the case of testifying to the husband's death, and here a sharp difficulty arises. When the *gemara* says *d'lav alav kasamchinan* — we are not relying on him — that seems plainly wrong. Of course we are relying on him; he is the one who said the husband is dead! The *gemara* resolves this by invoking a well-known principle: *isha dayka u'minsava* — the woman herself investigates before she remarries. Because the consequences of remarrying while a husband is still alive are so severe, we trust the woman to undertake her own thorough investigation following the witness's testimony. In this framing, it is ultimately her investigation, not his testimony alone, that bears the weight of the permission to remarry. This is quite a radical *gemara*: the entire operative mechanism is relocated to the woman's own diligence.

### Get vs. Death

If that is so, one might ask: if we are not really relying on the witness's testimony in the death case — since the woman's investigation is doing the real work — why can't he marry her? The *gemara* answers: *hatam leka ksava, hacha ika ksava* — there is still a meaningful difference between the two cases. When someone testifies to the husband's death, he is still presenting factual testimony, even if it is subsequently bolstered by the woman's investigation. Delivering a *get* within *Eretz Yisrael*, by contrast, requires no testimonial declaration whatsoever; the messenger is doing nothing more than physically transmitting a document.

As the *mishnah* itself puts it, *mah bein get lemita* — what is the difference between divorce and death? *She'haksav mochiach* — the written document proves itself. A signed document from *Eretz Yisrael* carries inherent presumptive validity.

### Document Validation

The basis for this presumption is the *gemara*'s principle that *edim she'bishtar kemi she'nechkerah edusam b'veis din* — witnesses whose signatures appear on a document are treated as though their testimony has already been fully examined in court. Even without what we might today call notarization, two signatures on a document establish its validity as a matter of law. It is only when a document arrives from outside *Eretz Yisrael* — from *chutz la'aretz* — that questions may arise about the reliability of the signatures, and external verification in the form of *bifnay nechtav u'bifnay nechtam* becomes necessary.

---

## Murder & Witness

### Murder Confession

The *gemara* now draws out a crucial implication from the *mishnah*. It states: *hu nihu d'lo yisa et ishto* — it is specifically he who may not marry the woman — *ha l'acher tinase* — but she may marry a different man. This makes clear that the testimony is in fact legally acceptable. The *mishnah* never says that because the man confessed to murder his testimony is disqualified. On the contrary, the testimony stands; the only concern is preventing *him* from marrying *her*, lest it appear that the testimony was self-serving.

This is consistent with the broader halachic principle — extensively developed throughout *Yevamot* — that for the purpose of *edut isha*, testimony enabling a woman to remarry, the usual standards of testimony are relaxed considerably. A single witness suffices, and the *gemara* elsewhere extends this to women, slaves, and even hearsay testimony.

### Rape Testimony

However, a difficulty arises from a ruling of *Rav Yosef*. *Rav Yosef* addresses a case where a man testifies that another man committed a sexual act with him *le'onsi* — against his will, meaning he was violated. In that case, he and a second witness may combine (*hu ve'acher mitztarfim lehargo*) to testify against the perpetrator and have him executed. Since the victim was not a willing participant, he bears no guilt and retains his status as a valid witness.

But if the man says the act was *birtzoni* — performed willingly — then he has admitted to being a willing participant in a grave transgression. The *Torah* declares *al tashet yadcha im rasha liheyot ed chamas* — do not join a wicked person to be a corrupt witness. He has effectively disqualified himself as a witness, and his testimony cannot be combined with that of another to prosecute anyone.

### Splitting Testimony

This raises the question at the heart of the *sugya*: the principle of *palginan dibura* — can we split his words? Can we take the portion of his testimony that concerns the other person and set aside the portion that incriminates himself? In *Rav Yosef*'s case, the answer is no. The man's declaration of willing participation renders him a *rasha* and invalidates him as a witness entirely; we cannot bracket his self-incrimination and retain the rest of his testimony. This would seem to apply equally to our case: if a man confesses to murder, he has declared himself a *rasha*, and should be disqualified for *edut isha* just as for any other testimony.

### Invalid Witnesses

*Rav Menashya* offers a position that adds a further layer. He holds that a *gazlan d'divreihem* — someone rabbinically disqualified as a witness, such as a gambler — is nonetheless valid for *edut isha*, because the rabbis were lenient in matters of testimony concerning a woman's ability to remarry. However, a *gazlan d'divrei Torah* — someone biblically disqualified as a witness — is invalid even for *edut isha*.

One might wonder, as *Tosafot* does, whether there is a distinction between different categories of biblical disqualification. One type of invalid witness is someone disqualified because he has sinned for financial gain — his testimony is suspect because it may be purchased. That concern is intelligible in the context of *edut isha*. But another type of disqualified witness is simply a habitual sinner (*neveila leteiavon*), someone who sins out of appetite rather than greed. Why should that person necessarily be invalid for *edut isha*? The *gemara* here does not draw that distinction, and the difficulty remains, at least implicitly.

In our case, if the witness confessed to murder, he would appear — by his own account — to be biblically disqualified, and according to *Rav Menashya* he should be invalid even for *edut isha*.

### Adam Karov

The *gemara* then raises the possibility that *Rav Menashya* must be following *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position in the *mishnah*, which disqualifies the witness who says *haragtee*. The *gemara* rejects this. *Rav Menashya* himself says: *ana de'amri afilu Rabbanon* — I can maintain my position even according to the Rabbis who accept the testimony. The reason the Rabbis accept it is based on *Rava*'s principle: *adam karov etzel atzmo, ve'ein adam mesim atzmo rasha* — a person is as close to himself as his nearest relative, and just as a relative's testimony about himself is inadmissible, a person cannot render himself a *rasha* through his own declaration. This is the mechanism of *palginan dibura*: we split his words, discard the self-incriminating portion as legally inert, and retain only the testimony concerning the other person — the fact that the husband is dead. Self-incrimination in matters of *mita* or *malkot* is halachically irrelevant; it requires external testimony to establish criminal status.

### Rav Yosef/Menashya

The *gemara* then considers whether *Rav Yosef* — who refuses to split the testimony in his case — must be following *Rabbi Yehuda* in the *mishnah*. Again the answer is no. *Rav Yosef* says *ana de'amri afilu Rabbanon*: I too can work with the position of the Rabbis. But my case is different: *shani edut isha de'akilu bah Rabbanon* — testimony concerning a woman's remarriage is a domain where the Rabbis were lenient, and it is specifically in that domain that we permit *palginan dibura*, splitting the testimony to retain only what is relevant. In the case of prosecuting someone for a capital offense, *Rav Yosef* holds, we do not split the words.

The *gemara* thus arrives at a nuanced picture. *Rav Menashya* holds that we do apply *palginan dibura* — he disagrees with *Rav Yosef* — and therefore even a witness who has testified against himself can have the relevant portion of his testimony accepted. But *Rav Menashya* also holds that a biblically disqualified witness cannot testify for *edut isha*; what saves the murderer-confessor is that his self-incrimination is discarded and he is therefore not treated as biblically disqualified. *Rav Yosef* holds that we do not apply *palginan dibura* — the testimony cannot be split — but is nonetheless lenient because even a biblically disqualified witness may testify for *edut isha*. The *gemara* suggests that one could in principle combine both leniencies, and in the *mishnah*'s case according to the *Tanna Kamma*, it is plausible that both factors work together: the *edut isha* context permits us to apply *palginan dibura*, thereby accepting the relevant portion of the testimony while discarding the self-incriminating portion.

---

## Tanna/R. Yehuda

### Haragi vs. Haragnu

Returning to *Rabbi Yehuda*'s distinction in the *mishnah*: why does it matter whether he says *haragtee* — I killed him — or *haragnu* — we killed him? Even in the latter case, he was part of a murder. The *gemara* answers: *amar Rav Yehuda be'omer ani hayisi im horgav* — it does not mean "I murdered him." It means "I was there, I was among those who killed him" — present, perhaps involved in the planning, but not the one who literally committed the act.

### Part of Group

On this reading, *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position is entirely coherent. When a man says "I was part of the group that killed him," he has not rendered himself a *rasha* in the biblical sense; he has not confessed to being the direct killer. His testimony about the husband's death therefore remains valid for *edut isha*, and the woman can remarry anyone except him.

### Bandit Case

The *gemara* then challenges *Rav Yehuda* — the *amora* who articulated this interpretation — with a *baraisa*. A certain bandit (*listis*) was being taken out for execution in *Kapotkia*, and he said to those present: go and tell the wife of *Shimon ben Kohen* that I killed her husband when I was entering *Lud*. They went and told her, and she was subsequently remarried on the basis of this testimony. Here, apparently, a man who was plainly being executed for murder — and who explicitly said *ani haragti*, I killed him — had his testimony accepted, and the woman remarried. This seems to contradict *Rav Yehuda*'s interpretation that *haragnu* is only acceptable because it means "I was part of the group, not the actual killer."

*Rav Yehuda* responds: *misham raya?* — do you bring a proof from that case? There too, the man was saying *ani hayisi im horgav* — I was among the killers — not that he personally committed the act.

### Non-Jewish Courts

But the *gemara* presses further: the text says he was being taken out to be executed (*hayotzei lehayeireig*). Does this not prove that he was a convicted murderer? The *gemara* answers: *bedina de'umot ha'olam dlo dayki vekatli* — non-Jewish courts do not apply the rigorous standards of evidence required by Jewish law; they may execute on the basis of suspicion or insufficient evidence. His execution by a non-Jewish court does not establish him as halachically defined as a *rasha*.

The *gemara* notes, however, that this caveat is instructive: according to *Rav Menashya*'s position that a biblically disqualified witness is invalid even for *edut isha*, everyone agrees that a witness definitively established as a murderer through proper *beit din* proceedings could not testify for *edut isha*. It is only because his status was established by a non-Jewish court — which is halachically insufficient — that his testimony remains acceptable. What divides the *Tanna Kamma* and *Rabbi Yehuda* is therefore the question of self-incriminating confession: the *Tanna Kamma* disregards it via *palginan dibura* and *adam karov etzel atzmo*, while *Rabbi Yehuda* treats the self-declaration of "I killed him" as effective self-disqualification, though he accepts "I was among the killers."

---

## Sage & Vow

### Vow Annulment

The next *mishnah* introduces another category of prohibited marriage. *Chacham she'asar et ha'ishah bineder al ba'alah* — a sage who, when asked to annul a woman's vow, ruled that the vow could not be annulled, with the consequence that the vow itself forbids her to her husband. The case is more extreme than simply a husband threatening divorce; the *neder* itself renders her halachically unavailable to her husband, making continued cohabitation impossible. Once the husband then divorces her, the sage who rendered that ruling may not marry her: *harei zeh lo yisaena*. His ruling directly brought about the divorce, and his subsequent marriage to the woman would cast retroactive doubt on the sincerity and integrity of his ruling.

### Beit Din Acts

The *mishnah* then carves out an exception. If the same sage was part of a *beit din* before which a minor performed *mi'un* — verbal refusal of a marriage contracted by her mother or brothers — or before which a *yevama* performed *chalitza*, in those cases he may subsequently marry the woman: *yisaena mipnei she'hu beis din*. The decisive factor is that he did not act alone; he was one member of a *beit din* and therefore cannot be said to have unilaterally engineered the woman's release. Whether the reasoning is that appearances are less problematic when a group acted together, or that collective deliberation is less susceptible to manipulation, the *mishnah* draws a clear line: independent action raises suspicion; action as part of a *beit din* does not.

### Mumcheh Expert

The *gemara* probes the *mishnah*'s case more carefully. If the *chacham* acted alone in ruling on the *neder*, how is that valid at all? Does not *hataras nedarim* require a *beit din* of three? The *gemara* cites the ruling: *tana hataras nedarim b'shlosha* — the annulment of vows requires three. And if we assume it was done by a *beit din* of three, why would any single member be suspect? The *gemara* answers: *le'olam b'chad* — the *mishnah* deals with a single individual. The basis for this is the ruling of *Rav Chisda* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: *b'yachid mumcheh* — a single recognized expert (*mumcheh*) can annul vows independently, just as three laypeople can. The *mishnah* is thus dealing with the case of a solitary *mumcheh* who ruled that the vow could not be annulled; since he acted alone, he is subject to suspicion and may not marry the woman.

### Witnesses Self-Interest

The *gemara* then raises a case to test how broadly we extend the concern for group composition. A *baraita* states: *ein hem me'idim* — when two witnesses have signed a sale document for a field, or signed a woman's *get*, the sages were not concerned (*lo chashu chachamim l'davar zeh*) that a witness might subsequently purchase the field or marry the woman. Even when only two are involved — which is less than a *beit din* of three — since the individual is not acting alone, there is no disqualifying suspicion.

The *gemara* resolves this by noting that the *mishnah*'s reference to *beit din* is not primarily about requiring three rather than two; rather, it is clarifying in passing that *mi'un* requires a *beit din* of three, against those who hold that two suffice. The underlying principle for permitting remarriage, however, is simply that the individual did not act independently — and two suffices for that purpose.

---

## Knas Yotzi Debate

### Kahana vs. Ashi

The *gemara* now turns to what appears to be the implicit question underlying all these *mishnayot*: *kanas mah she'yotsi* — if one of these men went ahead and married the woman despite the prohibition, must he divorce her? *Rashi* notes that the question applies to both the case of the *chacham* and the *neder*, and the case of the one who brought the *get* or testified to the husband's death, though the *Rashba* limits it to the final *mishnah* alone.

*Rav Kahana* says *kanas motzi* — he must divorce. *Rav Ashi* says *kanas eino motzi* — he need not divorce. A *baraisa* taught by *Rav Zuti* in the academy of *Rav Papa* supports *Rav Ashi*'s position. When the rabbis asked *Rav Ashi* whether his ruling was a received tradition (*gemara*) or a logical derivation (*sevara*), he replied that it can be inferred from the *mishnah* itself.

### Rumor Principle

The proof is from an earlier *mishnah* dealing with cases of suspected relationships — conversion, suspected adultery, and the like — where the *mishnah* rules: *im kanas eino motzi* — if he married her after the fact, he need not divorce. The principle derived is *birnana lo mafkinan* — we do not force divorce on the basis of rumor and communal suspicion alone. That same principle, the *gemara* concludes, applies here: *hacha nami birnana lo mafkinan*.

### Vow vs. Get

One might object, however, that the cases are not truly parallel. In the earlier cases of suspected adultery and conversion, even if the suspicion were true, the woman was still legally divorced or widowed; the only concern was reputational. Here, in the case of the *get* or the death testimony, if the underlying concern were true — if the *get* were invalid or the husband were still alive — the woman would be *eishes ish*, a married woman, which is a far more serious problem than mere appearances. This explains why the *Rashba* restricts the *gemara*'s ruling to the case of the *neder*: there, even if the *chacham* manipulated his ruling, the husband still gave a *get*, and the woman's divorce is halachically valid. The only issue is one of appearances and suspicion, to which *birnana lo mafkinan* properly applies. In the *get* and death-testimony cases, by contrast, there may be a genuine doubt about the woman's legal status — and that is a substantially weightier concern.

---

## Marriage Allowed

### Wife Dies

The following *mishnah* addresses when these same individuals — the *chacham* who could not annul the vow, the one who delivered the *get*, the one who testified to the husband's death — may in fact marry the woman. *Ve'kulam she'hoyu lahem nashim u'mesu mutarot le'hinasay lahem* — if all of these men were already married at the time they performed the relevant act, and their wives subsequently died, then the women they enabled to remarry are permitted to them. The logic is sociological: even in a society where polygamy was technically permitted, it was exceedingly rare in practice, and was essentially limited to men wealthy enough to support multiple households. The *mishnah* therefore takes it as a practical given that a married man would not seek to marry an additional woman. If he was already married when he delivered the *get* or testified to the husband's death, we do not suspect that he engineered the whole situation in order to marry her. One might ask: couldn't he simply have planned to divorce his own wife? The *mishnah* here says nothing about that scenario — and the *gemara* addresses it directly below.

### Marital Strife

The *gemara* draws a pointed inference: *mesu in, nisgarshu lo* — the *mishnah* permits marriage only when his wife died, not when he divorced her. If he divorced his wife, we can suspect that it was all part of a scheme: he manipulated the *get* or the death testimony, and then divorced his own wife so that he could marry this other woman, while the sequence created the appearance of propriety.

*Rav Hillel* then challenges this from a *baraisa* which states *afilu nisgarshu* — even if they divorced their wives, it is permitted. The *gemara* resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya, ha de-havei ketata, ha de-la havei ketata* — it depends on whether there was prior marital strife (*ketata*) or not.

*Rashi*'s reading here is counterintuitive and worth examining carefully. One might assume that if the couple was already fighting before the *get* was delivered, the suspicion would be heightened — the man was already contemplating divorce and could therefore have planned to marry this other woman all along. *Rashi* says the opposite: if they were already fighting beforehand, then his divorce of his wife was not precipitated by this woman. He would have divorced his wife regardless. The plan to leave his wife predated the woman's *get*, and therefore we do not say it was all engineered for her sake.

The *gemara* then offers a second answer: *iba'it eima, ha de'argil hu, ve'ha de'argilah hee* — even without any pre-existing fighting, it matters who was the one pressing for divorce. If he was the one pushing for the divorce of his own wife, he cannot then marry the woman, because it looks as though he engineered everything. If she — his own wife — was the one pushing for the divorce, we say he was not the architect of the situation, and he may marry the other woman. The *gemara* elsewhere acknowledges that interpersonal dynamics can be manipulated to induce one's spouse to seek a divorce, but the *mishnah* apparently does not press suspicion that far.

### Intervening Marriage

The *mishnah* further states: *ve'khulan she-nisu le'acherim ve'nisgarshu o she'nisalmenu mutarot le'hinase lahem* — if these women went ahead and married other men, and those second husbands then divorced them or died, the original witnesses may now marry them. Since the woman first married someone else, no one could reasonably conclude that the witness manipulated the original *get* or death testimony in order to marry her himself — for if he truly had wanted to marry her, he would not have wanted her to marry another man in the interim.

### Relatives Allow

Finally: *ve'khulan mutarot li'vneihem o le'acheihem* — all of these women may marry the sons or brothers of the witnesses who enabled their remarriage. We do not extend suspicion so far as to imagine that a man would falsify testimony or manipulate a vow ruling so that a *relative* of his could marry the woman. The concern we have is self-interested scheming; we do not carry it over to third parties.

### Women Visit; Men Don't

The *gemara* then raises a challenge from a *baraisa* that seems to go further in its prohibitions. Someone suspected of an affair with a woman is forbidden to marry her mother, daughter, or sister — *asur be'imah u've'vitah u've'achotah*. If we extend concern so broadly in that case, why do we not similarly prohibit the brother or son of the witness from marrying the woman?

The answer, as *Rashi* clarifies, is important. The prohibition against marrying the mother, daughter, or sister in the suspicion case is not because the man has already sinned by sleeping with the woman before marriage. Rather, the concern is prospective: once he is married to the mother or daughter, the woman herself will visit — *nashi l'gabei nashi shekichan de'azlan* — because women in a family regularly visit one another. He will then have opportunity to continue the affair, and at that point it will constitute the biblical prohibition of *eishes ish* or the forbidden union of a wife and her close female relative.

The same logic does not apply when it is a brother or son who marries the woman. *Gavri l'gabei gavri lo shekichan* — men do not visit each other's households with the same frequency and intimacy. The opportunity for an illicit encounter is therefore substantially less.

The *gemara* offers an additional distinction: *nashi d'lo asran shechivatan ahadadi lo kapdi ahadadi* — women are not halachically barred from their husbands simply because the husband slept with their relative, and therefore the wife is not vigilantly guarding against this. *Gavri d'asran shechivatan ahadadi kapdi ahadadi* — men, by contrast, are very much on guard, because if a brother-in-law were to sleep with his wife, she would become forbidden to her husband and the marriage would have to end. That vigilance itself diminishes the opportunity.

A further question: if so, why does the *mishnah* permit the *father* of the witness to marry the woman? Surely the father is also a male relative. The *gemara* answers: the *mishnah* uses the formulation *lo tzricha* — it need not even be stated. It is obvious that the father may marry the woman, because a son is embarrassed to initiate an affair with his own father's wife. The *mishnah* finds it necessary to state only the case of the son, where one might have thought that the father — feeling a parental sense of authority or access — might take advantage, and therefore comes to teach that even the son's case is permitted.

---

## Four Brothers

### Sisters & Death

The final *mishnah* of the *amud* returns to territory that has been covered multiple times in *Yevamot*, though it bears revisiting. *Arba'ah achim* — four brothers. Two of them, let us call them Reuven and Shimon, are married to two sisters, Rachel and Leah. Both Reuven and Shimon die. *Harei elu choltzot ve'lo mityabmot* — the surviving brothers, Levi and Yehuda, may not perform *yibum* with either sister; they may only perform *chalitza*.

### Achat Zekukato

The reason is the prohibition of *achot zekukato*. *Zika* — the quasi-marital bond that the *Torah* creates between a *yevama* and her *yavam* — connects Levi to both Rachel and Leah simultaneously. Rachel is the sister of the woman to whom Levi stands in a *zika* relationship, and *vice versa*. Therefore neither may be taken in *yibum*.

### One Ervah

The *mishnah* then refines the analysis. *Haysa achat me'hen asurah alav issur ervah* — if one of the women was an *ervah* to one of the brothers — his own daughter, for example — then that *yavam* is free to perform *yibum* with the other sister. An *issur ervah* removes the *zika* connection entirely, releasing him to marry the remaining *yevama*.

### Sister Options

In that case: *achota k'she'hi yevimtah, o choletzet o mityabmenet* — when the sister stands in the relationship of both sister and *yevama*, she has full options: either *chalitza* or *yibum*. With one woman an *ervah* and thus out of the picture, the other is a straightforward *yevama* with no competing *zika*.

### Zika Question

The *mishnah* also addresses the case where the prohibition is merely *issur mitzvah* or *issur kedusha* — a rabbinic prohibition or a lesser *lav* — rather than a full *issur ervah*. In that case, the weaker prohibition is insufficient to sever the *zika*, and the woman remains *zekukato*. Only a genuine *ervah* can remove the *zika* bond entirely.

One might naturally ask: even granting all of the above, why not simply have Levi perform *yibum* with Rachel and Yehuda perform *yibum* with Leah? They come from two separate marriages (*mi'trei batei ka'atu*), and there is no *tzara* issue. Let each *yavam* take one *yevama*.

### Rava Prevention

The *gemara* raises this question directly: *shma mina yesh zika* — the *mishnah*'s ruling implies that the concept of *zika* is operative, for otherwise, with no *zika*, there would be no obstacle to each *yavam* performing *yibum* with one of the sisters.

However, the *gemara* then considers the opposite position: *le'olam eima lach ein zika* — perhaps there is no *zika*. If so, what prevents each *yavam* from performing *yibum* with one woman? *Rava* offers an explanation: *mishum d'kasavar asur levatel mitzvas yavam* — it is prohibited to bring about a situation in which the *mitzvah* of *yibum* might be nullified. If, for example, Levi proceeds to perform *yibum* with Rachel, Leah now must wait for Yehuda. If Yehuda then dies in the interim, Leah is left without a *yavam* to perform either *yibum* or *chalitza*, and the *mitzvah* has been effectively nullified. If, on the other hand, Levi performs *chalitza* with Rachel, then even if Yehuda dies, Levi remains available and can perform *chalitza* with Leah as well, ensuring that neither woman is left in a state of unresolved *zika*. It is to prevent the potential nullification of the *mitzvah* that we require *chalitza* in this case — a far-reaching and admittedly somewhat attenuated rationale, but one that the *gemara* presents as Rava's resolution.

---

---

# Yevamot 26

## Four Brothers Case

### Intro: Four Brothers

The daf opens at the very bottom of 26a, where the Gemara is discussing the Mishnah concerning four brothers — two of whom die, leaving their widows to fall before the two surviving brothers — in a case where each surviving brother cannot perform *yibum* because each widow is *achot zekukato*, the sister of a woman to whom he stands in a *zikah* bond. The ruling of the Mishnah is that each surviving brother performs *chalitzah* with both women. We had already encountered an alternative explanation of this Mishnah: the real concern is *assur levatel mitzvat yabam* — it is forbidden to nullify the opportunity for *yibum*. According to this reading, if Levi were to perform *yibum* with Rachel, we fear that Yehuda might die, at which point Leah would become Levi's *achot ishto*, rendering her ineligible for either *yibum* or *chalitzah*. Therefore, Levi must perform *chalitzah* with Rachel, so that even if Yehuda dies, Levi retains the ability to perform *chalitzah* with Leah.

### Bittul Mitzvat Yabam

This alternative explanation — grounded in the concern of *assur levatel mitzvat yabam* rather than in the prohibition of *achot zekukato* — shifts the focus of the Mishnah's ruling from a structural *issur* to a prophylactic concern. The worry is not that the act of *yibum* is itself forbidden, but that performing it carelessly could eliminate the possibility of fulfilling the *mitzvah* for the other widow.

### Why Four Not Three?

The Gemara immediately challenges this reading: *i hachi, telata nami* — if the concern is *bittul mitzvat yabam*, why does the Mishnah require four brothers? Three would suffice to illustrate the point. If Levi alone survives and both women fall before him, he obviously cannot perform *yibum* with Rachel, since Leah would then be left with no recourse whatsoever. The problem is manifest even with three brothers.

### Zikah & Four Brothers

The Gemara responds that the Mishnah employs the principle of *lo miba'aya*: the case of three brothers is so obvious it goes without saying. The *chiddush* lies precisely in the case of four brothers. One might have thought that with two surviving brothers, the concern of *bittul mitzvat yabam* is attenuated — after all, even if Levi performs *yibum* with Rachel, Yehuda is still present and will likely be available to perform *yibum* or *chalitzah* with Leah. The Mishnah therefore teaches that even in this case, where there is a second brother standing by, we remain concerned that Yehuda might die before fulfilling his obligation.

Regarding the *achot zekukato* reading, the *chiddush* of four brothers is different: it is a more novel ruling that *achot zekukato* applies even when the *zikah* is distributed between two brothers, since one might have thought that a shared *zikah* is too weak to generate the prohibition.

### Fear of One Death

The Gemara then presses further: if we are worried that one brother might die, why not extend the case to five brothers — and fear that both Yehuda and a third brother might die, leaving Leah without *yibum* or *chalitzah*? The Gemara responds: *lemita de-trei lo chayshinan* — we do not entertain the fear that two people will die simultaneously before any act can be performed. The concern for one death is realistic enough to legislate around; the concern for two simultaneous deaths is too remote. With this, the Gemara closes the discussion of the four-brothers case.

---

## Three Sisters Case

### Setup: Three Sisters

The Gemara now introduces a new case, cited in the name of Rav: three sisters who are *yevamot* fall before two surviving brothers — Yissachar and Zebulun. Let us call the three sisters Rachel, Leah, and Sarah, all sisters of one another, each married to a different brother who has died, leaving the two survivors with a *zikah* obligation to all three women. Since all three women are sisters to one another, any act of *yibum* by either surviving brother would render the other two women *achot zekukato* — a rabbinic quasi-prohibition analogous to *achot ishto*.

The ruling of Rav is: *zeh choletz l'achas v'zeh choletz l'achas v'emtza'it tzericha chalitzah mishneihem* — one brother performs *chalitzah* with one sister, the other brother performs *chalitzah* with another, and the third woman — called *emtza'it*, "the middle one," though she is really the last to become available — requires *chalitzah* from both brothers. Tosafot notes that she is called "middle" because she stands, as it were, between Yissachar and Zebulun.

The case unfolds sequentially: the first husband dies, Yissachar performs *chalitzah* with Rachel; then the second husband dies, Zebulun performs *chalitzah* with Leah; then the third husband dies, and Sarah requires *chalitzah* from both of them. The question is why Sarah requires *chalitzah* from both brothers, and why there is a preference that Zebulun perform *chalitzah* with Leah rather than Yissachar.

### Chalitzah Psula Intro

Rava frames the logic as follows: *mideka'amret emtza'it tzericha chalitzah mishneihem, kasavar yesh zikah* — since Rav rules that the last sister requires *chalitzah* from both brothers, this ruling presupposes the position of *yesh zikah*, and moreover invokes a distinct principle: *chalitzah pesulah tzarich lachzor al kol ha'achim* — a defective, second-rate *chalitzah* must be obtained from all surviving brothers, not just one.

This is a governing principle that requires careful understanding. Ordinarily, when a man dies leaving multiple wives, *yibum* or *chalitzah* with one wife suffices to release all the others. But this rule applies only when the *zikah* is full and unimpaired. In cases where, for any reason, the *zikah* to a particular woman is weaker or altered in character, the resulting *chalitzah* is considered *pesulah* — not invalid in the sense of being null, but second-rate, a *chalitzah gru'ah*. Rashi explains it as a *chalitzah* performed in a situation where *yibum* is impossible. Tosafot refines this: the definition is not merely that *yibum* is impossible, but specifically that the reason *yibum* is impossible is because something has weakened or complicated the *zikah* itself. When the *zikah* is weakened, the *chalitzah* is correspondingly weakened, and a weakened *chalitzah* must be obtained from all brothers.

Tosafot enumerates the main categories that produce a *chalitzah pesulah*: (1) the woman is *achot zikukato* — for one who holds *yesh zikah*, this creates a quasi-*ervah* status that weakens the *zikah*; (2) the woman is *achot chalutzato* — her sister has already received *chalitzah* from this brother, making her a rabbinic quasi-*ervah*; (3) she is a *ba'alat haget* — the surviving brother gave her a *get*, which, though not halachically required and without full *d'oraita* effect in this context, nonetheless prevents *yibum* and shifts the character of the *zikah*; and (4) she is a *ba'alat ma'amar* — the surviving brother performed *maamar* with her, a rabbinic act of quasi-betrothal that strengthens the bond in one sense but simultaneously removes her from the simple center of the *zikah* relationship, making *chalitzah* less straightforwardly applicable.

In all these cases, the *zikah* has been displaced from its normal configuration — whether weakened by distance or complicated by prior action — and the *chalitzah* performed in such circumstances carries less force, requiring that it be obtained from each of the surviving brothers.

### Sequential Deaths

Returning to the three-sisters case, Rava asks: if every woman is *achot zekukato* and therefore in a weakened *zikah* relationship, why don't Rachel and Leah also require *chalitzah* from both brothers? The Gemara responds: *lo tzricha d'naphal zo achar zo* — the case is specifically one where the husbands died sequentially, not simultaneously.

When the first husband dies, only one woman — Rachel — falls before the two brothers. At that moment she is not *achot zekukato* to anyone, since no other woman has yet fallen. Her *zikah* is full and unimpaired. The *chalitzah* Yissachar performs with Rachel is therefore a complete, first-rate *chalitzah*. Then the second husband dies and Leah falls. What is Leah's status vis-à-vis Yissachar? She is *achot chalutzato* — her sister Rachel has just received *chalitzah* from Yissachar. But vis-à-vis Zebulun, she bears no such disability: the *zikah* was fully severed with respect to Yissachar by Rachel's *chalitzah*, and Leah is neither *achot chalutzato* nor *achot zekukato* relative to Zebulun. Therefore Zebulun performs a complete, first-rate *chalitzah* with Leah. By the time the third husband dies and Sarah becomes available, she is *achot chalutzato* of both Yissachar and Zebulun. Any *chalitzah* performed with her by either brother is therefore *pesulah*, and she requires the *chalitzah* to be performed by both.

If, however, all three men had died simultaneously, every woman would stand from the outset as *achot zekukato* to both brothers, and all three would require *chalitzah* from both — the Gemara concedes this point explicitly.

### Rachel & Sarah's Status

The Gemara then asks why Rachel is specifically called *achot zikukato* in Rav's formulation, since the application of that term is what sets the case in motion. The answer follows from the sequential structure of the case: before any death, Rachel stands in a full *zikah* with both brothers. Her status as *achot zikukato* exists only insofar as the *zikah* bond — which is a collective bond — implies that her sisters share in it. Once the deaths become sequential and *chalitzah* begins to be performed, Rachel's full *chalitzah* from Yissachar is the event that establishes Sarah as *achot chalutzato* of Yissachar, and Leah's *chalitzah* from Zebulun establishes Sarah as *achot chalutzato* of Zebulun as well. Sarah's need for *chalitzah* from both brothers thus flows from the sequential accumulation of *chalutzah* relationships as each act of *chalitzah* transforms the status of the remaining women.

---

## Rav vs. Shmuel

### Rav's Position

Having established the framework of *chalitzah pesulah* and its requirement of *chalitzah* from all brothers, the Gemara turns to the formal debate between Rav and Shmuel. The Gemara notes a potential tension: the ruling about the middle sister requiring *chalitzah* from both brothers was cited in Rav's name, yet we know from elsewhere that Rav holds *ein zikah* — he does not recognize the rabbinic category of *achot zekukato* as generating a true quasi-*ervah* relationship. The Gemara resolves this by clarifying that Rav articulated this ruling according to the position of *yesh zikah*, not necessarily as his own personal ruling.

### Shmuel's Position

Shmuel's position is stated simply: *echad choletz lekulan* — one brother performs *chalitzah* with all of the women. Shmuel apparently rejects both the requirement of first-rate *chalitzah* in every case and, more strikingly, the principle that *chalitzah pesulah* requires *chalitzah* from all brothers. According to Shmuel, if Reuven has already performed *chalitzah* with Rachel, making him unable to perform first-rate *chalitzah* with Leah — since she is now *achot chalutzato* — he may nonetheless go ahead and perform second-rate *chalitzah* with Leah, and then with Sarah as well. He need not defer to Shimon; one brother suffices throughout.

### Chalitzah Me'alya

The Gemara presses Shmuel: do we not know from elsewhere that Shmuel himself holds *chalitzah ma'alya beinun* — that a superior, first-rate *chalitzah* is required? The source for this is a ruling of Shmuel cited elsewhere (122a): *chalatz l'achayot lo nifteru tzarot* — if a man performs *chalitzah* with the sisters, the co-wives are not thereby released; but *chalatz litzarot nifteru achayot* — if he performs *chalitzah* with the co-wives, the sisters are released.

This ruling clearly presupposes that a first-rate *chalitzah* carries greater power than a second-rate one: a *chalitzah* performed with a woman whose status is *achot zekukato* (a second-rate *chalitzah*, grade B) does not release the co-wife, whereas a *chalitzah* performed with the co-wife — who, though herself subject to a one-degree-removed quasi-*ervah* status, stands in a fuller relationship with the *yavam* — does release the sister. If Shmuel values first-rate *chalitzah* to the point that only it can release a co-wife, why does he say that one brother may perform second-rate *chalitzah* with all the women when a first-rate option is available?

---

## Co-Wives & Chalitzah

### Weaker Chalitzah Insuffi…

To understand the stakes, the case that grounds Shmuel's ruling about co-wives must be spelled out carefully. Reuven dies leaving Rachel and her co-wife Devorah; Shimon dies leaving Leah and her co-wife Naomi. Yissachar alone survives. Of these four women, Rachel and Leah are sisters to one another, making each of them *achot zekukato* — a quasi-*ervah* — to the surviving brother. Devorah and Naomi are their respective co-wives.

Can Yissachar perform *yibum* with Rachel? No — she is *achot zekukato*. Can he perform *yibum* with Devorah? Devorah is a degree further removed: she is not *achot zekukato* herself, but *tzaras achot zekukato* — the co-wife of a quasi-*ervah*. This is a weaker prohibition, but it is still a prohibition. However, because Devorah's relationship to Yissachar is less attenuated by the quasi-*ervah* structure, his *chalitzah* with Devorah is of a higher grade than his *chalitzah* with Rachel. And it is this gradation that determines the outcome: a second-rate *chalitzah* with Rachel does not release Devorah, but a relatively better *chalitzah* with Devorah does release Rachel.

### Stronger Chalitzah Works

The question returns: if Shimon is available and could perform a full, first-rate *chalitzah* with Leah — since Leah is not *achot chalutzato* or *achot zekukato* relative to Shimon — why should we allow Reuven to perform a second-rate *chalitzah* with Leah? The *chalitzah* from Shimon would be *kesherah* in the fullest sense; *chalitzah* from Reuven would be *pesulah*. If Shmuel holds *chalitzah ma'alya beinun* — that a superior *chalitzah* is preferred — why does he permit the inferior option when the superior is available?

The Gemara offers a first reread of Shmuel: when Shmuel said *echad choletz lekulan*, perhaps he was not saying that one brother literally does *chalitzah* with all three women. Perhaps he meant only to dispute the requirement of obtaining *chalitzah* from all brothers in the case of the last woman, Sarah. He agrees that Reuven performs *chalitzah* with Rachel and Shimon performs *chalitzah* with Leah; his innovation is only that Sarah needs *chalitzah* from just one brother, not both. And since Shimon handled two of the three women, the Gemara permits calling him the one who did *chalitzah* "with all of them" — *keivan deruba gabeih, kari leh kulan*, since the majority was with him. This is acknowledged as a somewhat forced reading but at least allows Shmuel to maintain his preference for *chalitzah ma'alya* while disputing the *tzarich lachzor al kol ha'achim* principle.

### Achot Zikukato

The Gemara then attempts to defend the original, simpler reading of Shmuel, distinguishing when *chalitzah ma'alya* is required. The resolution offered is: *ki ka'amar Shmuel chalitzah ma'alya beinun, hanei mili limftar tzartah* — Shmuel's principle that a superior *chalitzah* is needed applies specifically when the goal is to release a co-wife. Only a first-rate *chalitzah* carries enough force to release another woman. But *aval limftar nafshah patrah* — to release the woman herself, a second-rate *chalitzah* is entirely sufficient. In the three-sisters case, Sarah has no co-wives. Therefore Shmuel sees no reason to insist on first-rate *chalitzah* for her; second-rate suffices, and the dispute with Rav reduces to whether *chalitzah pesulah* requires *chalitzah* from all brothers (Rav: yes; Shmuel: no) and whether a second-rate *chalitzah* is permissible when no co-wife is at stake (Shmuel: yes).

---

## Sequential Deaths Matter

### Simultaneous Deaths

The Gemara clarifies a fundamental structural point: the distinction between first-rate and second-rate *chalitzah*, and which woman receives *chalitzah* from which brother, depends entirely on whether the deaths occurred simultaneously or sequentially. If all three husbands had died at once, every woman would stand from the outset as *achot zekukato* to both surviving brothers. No one would have a privileged *chalitzah* relationship with either brother. All three women would occupy equal — and equally weakened — positions, and the question of ordering would carry no special significance.

### Status Changes Sequentia…

Once deaths are sequential, however, each act of *chalitzah* transforms the status of the remaining women for each of the surviving brothers. This is the key insight underlying Rav's ruling. When only Rachel has fallen — because only the first husband has died — she bears no *achot zekukato* disqualification, since no other sister has yet entered the *zikah*. Her *chalitzah* from Yissachar is complete. The moment that *chalitzah* is performed, however, the remaining sisters become *achot chalutzato* of Yissachar. They are not yet *achot chalutzato* of Zebulun — that status accrues only when he performs *chalitzah* with one of them. Thus the sequential nature of events generates a layered accumulation of statuses that varies between brothers.

### Rachel Becomes Achot Cha…

By the time Sarah requires *chalitzah*, she is *achot chalutzato* of Yissachar — because Yissachar performed *chalitzah* with Rachel — and simultaneously *achot chalutzato* of Zebulun — because Zebulun performed *chalitzah* with Leah. Any *chalitzah* performed with Sarah by either brother is therefore *pesulah*. Since both brothers generate only a *chalitzah pesulah* with her, the principle of *chalitzah pesulah tzarich lachzor al kol ha'achim* applies, and she must receive *chalitzah* from both. This is the complete logic underlying Rav's ruling: it is the sequential accumulation of *achot chalutzato* relationships across both brothers that locks Sarah into needing *chalitzah* from each of them.

---

## Beginning vs. Finishing

### Tzaras Krovat Chalitzato

At this point the Gemara introduces an entirely different reread of Shmuel's ruling — not based on the graduated strength of *chalitzah*, but on a distinct *issur*. The Mishnah elsewhere teaches: *assur adam bitzaras krovat chalitzato* — a man is forbidden to the co-wife of the relative of his *chalutza*.
