Rashi explains the case: if Reuven performed *chalitzah* with Leah and then a certain Barak — an entirely unrelated man — was married both to Leah's mother Rivkah and to Devorah, Reuven is forbidden to Devorah after Barak's death, because Devorah is the co-wife (*tzara*) of Rivkah, who is a relative of Reuven's *chalutza* Leah (*krovat chalitzato*). The reasoning, though complex, establishes that a *tzaras krovat chalitzato* is independently prohibited, not merely as a subset of the *chalitzah* relationship itself.

This prohibition has direct implications for the case at hand. After Yissachar performs *chalitzah* with Leah, Rachel becomes *achot chalutzato* of Yissachar — Yissachar's *krovat chalitzato*. Naomi, who was Reuven's co-wife alongside Rachel, now stands as *tzaras krovat chalitzato* of Yissachar. This is an independent *issur*, on equal footing with the *issur* of *achot chalutzato*, not a derivative one degree removed. Accordingly, both Rachel and Naomi are now problematic for Yissachar in their own independent ways, and performing *chalitzah* with one of them cannot release the other.

### Cannot Finish with Tzaros

Shmuel's ruling — on this reread — is not about the gradations of *chalitzah* quality at all. Rather, it is about the order in which one begins. *Hitchil ba'achayot, lo yigmor bitzarot* — if he began with the sisters (performing *chalitzah* with Leah first), he should not finish with the co-wives (attempting to use the *chalitzah* with Naomi to release Rachel). The reason is the *issur* of *tzaras krovat chalitzato*: once he has performed *chalitzah* with Leah, Naomi is forbidden to him as *tzaras krovat chalitzato*. A *chalitzah* with Naomi will not release Rachel, because both women are now independently prohibited. Rashi clarifies that *lo yigmor bitzarot* does not mean he cannot perform *chalitzah* with Naomi at all, but rather that doing so will not exempt Rachel; he must do both.

### Can Finish with Achayos

Conversely, *hitchil bitzarot, yigmor af ba'achayot* — if he is prudent and begins with Devorah (the co-wife), before any act of *chalitzah* with the sisters has been performed, then no *achot chalutzato* or *tzaras krovat chalitzato* relationship has yet been created. Both Rachel and Naomi remain fully available to him. In this case, a *chalitzah* with either woman will release the other, because *mutar adam bikrovas tzaras chalitzato* — a man is permitted to the relative of his *chalitzah*-co-wife. This is the mirror image of the earlier prohibition and explicitly not a concern. By beginning with the co-wives before any *achot chalutzato* relationship is established, he preserves the full effectiveness of each subsequent *chalitzah*. The lesson Shmuel is teaching, on this radical reread, is entirely about sequencing: the order in which one begins determines whether the remaining women can be released by a single subsequent *chalitzah*.

---

## Rav Ashi's Explanation

### Zikah Not Strong Enough

Having traversed Shmuel's radical reread, the Gemara finally offers what it presents as the straightforward explanation, attributed to Rav Ashi: *le'olam ked'kamris* — revert to the plain reading of Shmuel. Shmuel indeed holds that performing *chalitzah* with the co-wife (Devorah) is preferable to performing it with the sister (Leah), and that *chalitzah* with the co-wife releases the sister. The reason is not the elaborate sequencing analysis, but rather a principle about the strength of *zikah*: *umishum d'lo alima zika l'shavyei l'tzara k'erva* — the *zikah* is not strong enough to render the co-wife as significant an *ervah* as the sister herself.

Leah is *achot zekukato* — a quasi-*ervah* by rabbinic decree, one degree removed from *achot ishto*. Devorah is *tzaras achot zekukato* — the co-wife of a quasi-*ervah*. Ordinarily, the rule of *tzarat ervah* extends the *ervah* prohibition to co-wives, but that rule assumes a genuine, *d'oraita* *ervah*. Here, even the underlying *ervah* — *achot zekukato* — is only rabbinic. There is already a *chiddush* in declaring that *achot zekukato* generates any *ervah*-like status at all; extending that derivative status one further degree to the co-wife is too attenuated to carry full force. Devorah may therefore not be a *sug alef* (grade A) in the absolute sense, but she is a grade B relative to Leah's grade C. She stands in a fuller, less impaired relationship with the *yavam*, and *chalitzah* with her is therefore the stronger act — strong enough to release Leah.

### Chalitzah with Tzara

The practical application is thus: performing *chalitzah* with Devorah releases Leah, because the *zikah* between Devorah and the *yavam* is sufficiently unimpaired that the *chalitzah* carries full releasing force vis-à-vis a woman who, though *achot zekukato*, is not a true *ervah*. The graduated hierarchy — sisters (*achot zekukato*, grade B), co-wives of sisters (*tzaras achot zekukato*, grade B-plus relative to the sisters) — means that acting on the relatively stronger relationship releases the weaker one, but not vice versa.

---

## Beit Shammai View

### Beit Shammai Permits

Rabbi Abba bar Mammel proposes an entirely different approach to Shmuel's ruling. Rather than resolving the case through the logic of *zikah* strength and graduated *chalitzah* quality, he suggests: *ha mani Beis Shammai hi* — perhaps Shmuel is operating according to the position of Beit Shammai. The Mishnah records that Beit Shammai permits the co-wives (*tzaros*) to marry into the family of the surviving brothers — that is, Beit Shammai does not recognize the category of *tzarat ervah* at all in the context of *yibum*. On this view, Devorah is not subject to any prohibition whatsoever, and there is no tension between performing *chalitzah* with Devorah and subsequently releasing Leah. The preference for beginning with Devorah is simply that, according to Beit Shammai, there is a full *mitzvah* of *yibum* available with Devorah, making her the primary obligee.

### Covering All Views

The Gemara raises the obvious objection: if Shmuel follows Beit Shammai and Devorah is fully permitted, why not perform *yibum* with her rather than *chalitzah*? The Gemara responds by citing Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who ruled: *bo'u venisaken lahem l'tzaros sheyehu choltzot v'lo misyabmot* — let us enact a *takanah* that co-wives must receive *chalitzah* and may not undergo *yibum*. This ruling is designed to cover both positions: according to Beit Hillel, the co-wife is prohibited and can receive only *chalitzah*; according to Beit Shammai, she is permitted but we impose *chalitzah* rather than *yibum* as a compromise. By requiring *chalitzah*, we satisfy Beit Shammai's concern that the *mitzvah* be fulfilled in some form, without permitting the *yibum* that Beit Hillel would forbid.

### Final Stringency

The Gemara, however, notes a complication: the tradition records that the sages did not complete (*lo hispiku ligmor*) the enactment of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri before the moment passed. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak responds that a later session revisited the matter and the *takanah* was ultimately enacted — *achar kach chazru v'tiknu*. The force of stringency (*chumra*) ultimately prevailed.

The Gemara leaves this as a possible reading of Shmuel, but the explanation of Rav Ashi — that *zikah* is simply not strong enough to render the co-wife a full *ervah*, so *chalitzah* with the co-wife remains the superior act and releases the sister — is upheld by a *baraita* and stands as the primary resolution. The *baraita* confirms: *chalatz l'achayot lo nifteru tzarot, chalatz l'tzarot nifteru achayot*, and explains the reason as *d'kasavar yesh zikah v'lo almi zika l'shavyei l'tzara k'erva* — exactly as Rav Ashi formulated it. This closes the discussion on 26a.

---

---

# Yevamot 26b

## Four Brothers Case

### Mishnah Setup

The discussion opens at the very bottom of 26a, returning to a *mishnah* that has appeared several times: four brothers married to four women, two of whom are sisters. Because of the principle of *achos zekukaso* — the sister of one's *zekukah* — neither surviving brother may perform *yibum*, and both women require *chalitzah*. The *mishnah* thus far has been explained in two distinct ways. The first explanation focuses on *achos zekukaso* itself. The second explanation holds that the real concern is *assur levatel mitzvas yabmin*: if, for example, Levi performs *yibum* with Rachel, and Yehudah subsequently dies, Leah becomes *achos ishto* — forbidden to both Levi (as his wife's sister) and now unavailable for *chalitzah* or *yibum* from anyone. To prevent this, Levi is required to perform *chalitzah*, so that even in the event of Yehudah's death, Levi would still be able to perform *chalitzah* with Leah.

### Why Four Brothers?

The *Gemara* now presses a sharp question against the second explanation: *i hachi, tlosa nami* — if the concern is *assur levatel mitzvas yabmin*, why does the *mishnah* require four brothers? Three would suffice. With only three brothers and two sisters, if Levi performs *yibum* with Rachel, Leah is immediately left without any option — she becomes *achos ishto* to Levi and has no other brother to turn to. The prohibition is obvious even in the three-brother case.

### Zika Strength vs Mitzvah

The *Gemara* resolves this by invoking the principle of *lo mibaya ka'mar*: the three-brother case is the more obvious case and therefore need not be stated. The *chidush* of the four-brother case operates at a different level. When two brothers remain behind, there is reason to argue that the concern of *achos zekukaso* is attenuated — the *zika* is weaker when two brothers share it, since it is not exclusively Levi's *zika* nor exclusively Yehudah's. The *mishnah* therefore teaches that even with two remaining brothers, the *achos zekukaso* prohibition is operative. The alternative concern — *assur levatel mitzvas yabmin* — introduces a further *chidush* in the four-brother case: even though Yehudah is alive and presumably available, we nonetheless fear that he might die before performing *yibum* or *chalitzah*, leaving Leah stranded.

### One Death Fear

The *Gemara* then asks: if we fear Yehudah's death in the four-brother case, why not fear the deaths of both Yehudah and Yissachar in a five-brother case? The *Gemara* responds: *lemisa detrei lo chashinan* — we do not entertain the fear that two brothers will die simultaneously before any act of *yibum* or *chalitzah* can be performed. That possibility is too remote. We allow for the possibility of one death; two is beyond the scope of our concern. Thus in the four-brother scenario, where Leah depends on Yehudah alone, we do fear his death — but once two brothers stand between a woman and her potential *yibum*-less fate, we no longer worry.

---

## Three Sisters Case

### Three Sisters Setup

The *Gemara* now presents a new case: *shalosh achayos yevamos shenaplu lifnei shenei achim yevamim* — three sisters, all *yevamos*, who have fallen before two surviving brothers. To cast this concretely: three brothers — Reuven, Shimon, and Levi — each married one of three sisters, and all three have died. The two surviving brothers, Yissachar and Zevulun, now face three sisters — Rachel, Leah, and a third (call her Sarah) — all of whom stand in a relationship of *zika* to both of them. No woman is a genuine *ervah* to either brother, since each was married to a different man. But under the principle of *yesh zika*, any act of *yibum* would implicate *achos zekukaso*, since each woman is a sister of the others to whom the brother is also *zakuk*. The case is therefore a larger variant of *achos zekukaso*, and the question is how to distribute *chalitzah* between the two brothers and three women.

One might ask: why not simply allow Yissachar to perform *chalitzah* with all three women? As the *Gemara* will develop, the answer turns on a new principle — that not all *chalitzah* acts are of equal weight — and the distribution matters precisely because of differential strength in the *zika*.

### Distribution Pattern

The ruling, stated in the name of Rav via Rava bar Rav Huna, is as follows: one brother performs *chalitzah* with the first sister, the other brother performs *chalitzah* with the second sister, and the third sister — called the *emtza'it*, the "middle" one — requires *chalitzah* from both brothers. The term *emtza'it* is somewhat misleading: she is called "middle" not because she is the second to fall to *yibum*, but because she stands between both brothers in terms of their obligations. She has a claim on each of them and, as will be explained, requires *chalitzah* from each.

### Sequential Deaths

The *Gemara* refines the scenario. If all three brothers had died simultaneously, every sister would be *achos zekukaso* from the outset, and each woman would indeed require two *chalitzos*. But the case being discussed is one of sequential deaths — *denafelu zu achar zu*. When the first brother dies, one sister becomes subject to *yibum* with no complicating factor: there is no co-zekukah, the *zika* is complete, and the *chalitzah* performed by, say, Yissachar is fully valid. When the second brother dies, the next sister becomes available. At this point, from Yissachar's perspective, she is *achos chalutzaso* — the sister of the woman he just performed *chalitzah* with — making his *chalitzah* weaker. Zevulun, however, has no such problem: the first *chalitzah* was Yissachar's, not his. Zevulun's *chalitzah* with the second sister is therefore first-rate. By the time the third brother dies and Sarah becomes available, both brothers have each performed *chalitzah* with one of her sisters. She is *achos chalutzaso* to both Yissachar and to Zevulun. Any *chalitzah* she receives will be second-rate from either one of them. And this is precisely why she needs it from both.

### Chalitzah Pesulah

This brings us to a new and central principle that governs the remainder of the *daf*: the concept of *chalitzah pesulah*. The observation is this — when the *zika* between a brother and his *yevamah* is weakened, the *chalitzah* performed in that context is correspondingly weakened. A full, first-rate *chalitzah* by one brother frees a *yevamah* completely; all other brothers are discharged and she may go free. But a *chalitzah pesulah* — a second-rate *chalitzah* — does not accomplish this. It requires, instead, *chazor al kol ha'achim*: the woman must receive *chalitzah* from every surviving brother, each of whom must separately discharge his own *zika*.

---

## Chalitzah Pesulah

### Defining Pesulah

The principle of *chalitzah pesulah* thus emerges as the organizing concept for the cases that follow. When is a *chalitzah* considered *pesulah*? Rashi offers a general formulation: *chalitzah pesulah* is *chalitzah gerua*, a second-rate *chalitzah*, in any case where *yibum* was not possible — *she'im ratza leyabbem eino yachol*. If the brother could not have performed *yibum* with this woman, then the *chalitzah* he performs with her is by definition second-rate.

### Tosafos Refinement

Tosafos, however, sharpens this definition. Rashi's criterion is accurate as far as it goes, but it is somewhat overbroad. There are cases where *yibum* is impossible for reasons unrelated to any weakening of the *zika* — and Tosafos holds that such cases would not qualify as *chalitzah pesulah* in the operative sense. For *chalitzah pesulah* to apply, the specific reason *yibum* is impossible must be that the *zika* itself has been problematized or attenuated. It is not merely the impossibility of *yibum* that creates the category, but the particular mechanism: a *zika* that has been weakened, distorted, or displaced from its normative form.

### Examples of Weakening

Tosafos identifies three paradigmatic cases in which the *zika* is weakened in this operative sense, collected at the end of the relevant *dibur hamatchil*. The first is *achos zekukaso*: when among all the women to whom a brother is *zakuk*, one is the sister of another. She is not a genuine *ervah* — that would make her *achos ishto* and would generate full exemption — but she is a quasi-*ervah* through rabbinic extension. The *zika* to her is real, but it operates under a cloud, and any *chalitzah* performed with her is therefore *pesulah*. The second is *ba'alas haget*: if a brother gave the *yevamah* a *get* before performing *chalitzah*, the *get* has no Torah-level effect in this context — the woman is not his wife, and a *get* cannot dissolve the *zika* — but rabbinic law grants it enough weight to preclude *yibum*. Having now made *yibum* impossible, the subsequent *chalitzah* is second-rate. The third case is the inverse and is in some ways more striking: *ba'alas ma'amar*. Here the brother performed *ma'amar* — a rabbinic-level *kiddushin* with the *yevamah*, a formal act of partial acquisition that is the precursor to full *yibum* — thereby strengthening rather than weakening the apparent connection. Yet this too renders *chalitzah* second-rate. The dynamic is instructive: *chalitzah* is relevant to the middle zone of the *zika* relationship. Move the woman too far away — as with *achos zekukaso* or *ba'alas haget* — and *chalitzah* is less relevant because she is quasi-forbidden. Move her too close — as with *ma'amar* — and *chalitzah* is less relevant because she is quasi-his-wife. In either direction, the displacement from the normative *zika* weakens the *chalitzah*.

It should be noted that when *ma'amar* has been performed, the full procedure requires both a *get* (to undo the *ma'amar*) and *chalitzah* (to undo the underlying *zika*). But the *chalitzah* in that context is still regarded as second-rate because the woman's status has shifted from the classic *yevamah* who stands ready for *yibum* or *chalitzah* without prior complication.

### Multiple Chalitzos

The practical upshot of *chalitzah pesulah* is the rule of *chazor al kol ha'achim*: she must go around to all the brothers. Why? Because when a *chalitzah* is first-rate and complete, one brother's act fully extinguishes the entire nexus of *zika* — all brothers are discharged simultaneously, since the *zika* was a unified bond. But when the *chalitzah* is second-rate, it is only sufficient to remove the particular *zika* of the one brother who performed it. Each brother retains his own residual *zika*, and each must therefore act separately to discharge it. This explains the case of Sarah in the three-sisters scenario: since she is *achos chalutzaso* to both Yissachar and Zevulun, any *chalitzah* she receives is *pesulah*, and she must therefore obtain *chalitzah* from each of them individually.

---

## Rav vs Shmuel

### Rav Position

The *Gemara* raises an immediate difficulty: this entire analysis — *achos zekukaso*, *chalitzah pesulah*, *chazor al kol ha'achim* — is predicated on the position of *yesh zika*. But the ruling in question was stated by Rav, and Rav is on record elsewhere as holding *ein zika*. The *Gemara* resolves this: Rav was speaking *ledivrei ha'omer yesh zika* — he was articulating the *halacha* according to the position that holds *yesh zika*, not necessarily expressing his own view. Within that framework, the ruling stands: *chalitzah pesulah* requires *chalitzah* from all the brothers.

### Shmuel Position

Shmuel disagrees. His position is stated concisely: *echad choletz lekullan* — one brother may perform *chalitzah* for all of them. Shmuel apparently does not accept the *chazor al kol ha'achim* requirement. Even where a *chalitzah* would be second-rate — because the woman is *achos chalutzaso* — Shmuel maintains that one brother's *chalitzah* suffices, and the woman need not seek *chalitzah* from the remaining brothers.

---

## Rav vs Shmuel (II)

### Achos vs Tzaros

The *Gemara* now presses Shmuel's position from a different direction. We know from elsewhere on 26a that Shmuel himself holds *chalitzah ma'alya ba'inan* — that a first-rate *chalitzah* is required. Given this, there is a question about Shmuel's permitting one brother to perform *chalitzah* with all three sisters: even setting aside the question of *how many* brothers must participate, shouldn't we at least insist that the *better* *chalitzah* be used when available?

To see why this matters, consider the following case — stated by Shmuel on 26a — involving two sets of women. Yissachar is married to Rachel, and Rachel has a co-wife, Devorah. Zevulun is married to Leah, and Leah has a co-wife, Naomi. Both brothers die. Reuven is the sole surviving brother. All four women stand before him. He cannot perform *yibum* with Rachel, because Rachel is *achos zekukaso* — she is the sister of Leah, to whom he is also *zakuk*. He cannot perform *yibum* with Leah for the same reason. What about Devorah? Devorah is a co-wife of Rachel, who is herself a quasi-*ervah* by virtue of *achos zekukaso*. Devorah is therefore, in the language of the *Gemara*, *tzaras achos zekukaso* — a co-wife of a quasi-*ervah*. This is one degree removed from the problem, but Reuven still cannot perform *yibum* with her. Nevertheless, Reuven's relationship with Devorah is of a different character than his relationship with Rachel: his connection with Devorah is less problematized, and therefore a *chalitzah* with Devorah is stronger than a *chalitzah* with Rachel.

Shmuel's ruling: *chalatz l'achayos lo nifteru tzaros* — if Reuven performs *chalitzah* with the sisters (Rachel or Leah), the co-wives (Devorah, Naomi) are not freed. But *chalatz letzaros nipteru achayos* — if he performs *chalitzah* with the co-wives, the sisters are freed. This demonstrates that Shmuel does recognize a hierarchy of *chalitzah* quality, and that the stronger *chalitzah* — with the co-wife — is more powerful than the weaker one. The same principle applies to *ba'alas haget* and *ba'alas ma'amar*: in each case, *chalitz leba'alas haget* (or *ma'amar*) does not free her co-wife, but *chalatz letzarah* frees the *ba'alas haget* (or *ma'amar*).

### Shmuel's Logic

Given this, the *Gemara* objects: if Shmuel holds that a first-rate *chalitzah* is always preferable — indeed, necessary to free a co-wife — why does he permit one brother to perform all three *chalitzos* in the three-sisters case, including the weaker ones with the sisters who are *achos chalutzaso*? When Shimon's *chalitzah* with the second sister would be fully first-rate, why allow Reuven to do a second-rate *chalitzah* instead?

---

## Co-wives Case

### Co-wives Setup

To clarify the stakes of this debate, the *Gemara* works through the case involving co-wives directly. Here the scenario is as described above: two brothers married to two pairs of women (each wife having a co-wife), with only one brother surviving. All four women are now before Reuven.

### Pesulah Doesn't Free

Shmuel's ruling establishes a clear principle: a second-rate *chalitzah* — one performed in a context where the *zika* is weakened — lacks the force to free a co-wife. If Reuven performs *chalitzah* with Rachel, who is *achos zekukaso*, Devorah remains bound. The *chalitzah pesulah* is effective for Rachel herself — she is freed from the obligation — but it cannot discharge the obligation of a co-wife, because the co-wife's release depends on the *chalitzah* being fully valid.

### First-Rate Required

The inverse, however, holds: a first-rate *chalitzah* with Devorah — whose relationship to Reuven, while still not permitting *yibum*, is less burdened — does free Rachel. The logic is that Reuven's *zika* to Devorah, although precluded from *yibum* by virtue of her being *tzaras achos zekukaso*, is not as deeply problematized as his *zika* to Rachel. It is therefore a stronger act of *chalitzah*, and a stronger *chalitzah* has the power to discharge co-wives as well. This establishes that when co-wives are present, a first-rate *chalitzah* is not merely preferable but necessary to achieve their release.

---

## Chalitzah Pesulah (II)

### Strength Weakens

There is a striking irony embedded in the case of *ba'alas ma'amar* that is worth pausing on. When a brother performs *ma'amar* with his *yevamah*, he is strengthening the *zika* — he is moving closer to full *yibum*, not away from it. Yet this very strengthening renders the subsequent *chalitzah* weaker. The explanation, as noted above, is that *chalitzah* is calibrated to the specific relational zone of the *zika*: the woman stands in a liminal status, available for *yibum* but not yet his wife, available for *chalitzah* but not an *ervah*. Any movement from that liminal zone — whether toward greater distance (as in *achos zekukaso* or *ba'alas haget*) or toward greater closeness (as in *ma'amar*) — displaces the act of *chalitzah* from its normative context and weakens it. The *chalitzah* in a *ma'amar* case is therefore *pesulah*, even though the *zika* was, in one sense, intensified. The result is that both weakening and strengthening the *zika* produce the same outcome: a *chalitzah pesulah* that requires *chazor al kol ha'achim*.

---

## Shmuel Reread

### Challenge to Order

Returning now to the case of Reuven and the four women — Rachel, Leah, Devorah, and Naomi — the *Gemara* presses a deeper question. The *Gemara* had accepted that performing *chalitzah* with Devorah is preferable to doing so with Rachel, because Devorah is *tzaras achos zekukaso* (one degree removed) rather than *achos zekukaso* directly. But the *Gemara* now asks: if one holds *yesh zika*, doesn't this make Devorah *tzaras* a quasi-*ervah*? And if so, isn't she just as problematic in her own way as Rachel? Why is the *chalitzah* with Devorah considered stronger?

This challenge threatens the entire framework of Shmuel's ruling. If both Rachel and Devorah are problematic — one directly as *achos zekukaso* and the other as *tzaras achos zekukaso* — on what basis do we say that the *chalitzah* with Devorah is first-rate and gets Rachel off the hook, while the *chalitzah* with Rachel is second-rate and does not free Devorah?

The *Gemara* initially responds by suggesting that Shmuel holds *ein zika*. But this immediately generates a new difficulty: if there is no *zika*, then Rachel is not *achos zekukaso* at all, so why can't Reuven simply perform *yibum* with her? And if all four women stand on equal footing before him, what is the basis for distinguishing the *chalitzah* performed with Rachel from the *chalitzah* performed with Devorah?

### Beginning vs Ending

The *Gemara* therefore undertakes a radical re-reading of Shmuel's ruling. Rather than comparing Rachel and Devorah as two fixed alternatives and asking which is better, the *Gemara* proposes that Shmuel is addressing a sequential question: *hitchil velo hitchil* — the question of how one begins the process and how one ends it.

### Begin Sisters

If Reuven begins with the sisters — that is, he performs *chalitzah* first with Leah (one of the sisters) — then Leah becomes his *chalutzah*. Rachel is now *achos chalutzaso*. At this point, Naomi (Leah's co-wife) is *tzaras krovat chalutzaso* — the co-wife of a relative of his *chalutzah*. The *mishnah* teaches that a man is *assur* in *tzaras krovat chalutzaso*. Consequently, if Reuven started with Leah, he may not finish with Naomi, because doing so would implicate *tzaras krovat chalutzaso*. Doing *chalitzah* with Naomi would not free Rachel either, because she is independently problematic. He is therefore stuck and must still do *chalitzah* with Rachel — but that *chalitzah* will not get Naomi off the hook.

### Begin Co-wives

However, if Reuven begins with the co-wives — performing *chalitzah* first with Devorah — then the situation is entirely different. Devorah is now his *chalutzah*, and Rachel is not *achos chalutzaso* because no *chalitzah* has yet been performed with any sister. At this stage, the *mishnah* teaches *mutar adam bekrovat tzaras chalitzaso* — a man is permitted to the relative of his *chalutzah*'s co-wife. This is the mirror image of the previous case and is not considered problematic. With Devorah as his *chalutzah*, he may proceed with either Rachel or Naomi. If he does *chalitzah* with Rachel, it will free Naomi; if he does it with Naomi, it will free Rachel. By beginning with the co-wife, both options remain open, and first-rate *chalitzah* is available for each.

---

## Shmuel Reread (II)

### Rav Ashi

The *Gemara* ultimately abandons the radical re-reading and returns to the simpler original interpretation of Shmuel, through the intervention of Rav Ashi.

---

## Rav Ashi Resolution

### Zika Insufficient

Rav Ashi states: *leolam kidekamris* — Shmuel means exactly what we originally thought he meant. The *chalitzah* with Devorah is better than the *chalitzah* with Rachel, even within the framework of *yesh zika*. The key principle is: *umishum delo alima zika lishveiye litzarah ke'erva* — the *zika* is not strong enough to render the co-wife fully equivalent to an *ervah*. The reasoning proceeds as follows: Rachel, through *achos zekukaso*, is a quasi-*ervah* — a rabbinic extension of the prohibition of *achos isha*. She is not a genuine Torah-level *ervah*, but she is treated as one rabbinically. Normally, in a case of full *ervah*, the principle of *tzaras ervah* would apply — the co-wife of an *ervah* is also exempt from *yibum* and *chalitzah*. But in this case, since Rachel herself is only a quasi-*ervah* through rabbinic extension, the derivative principle — that her co-wife Devorah is *tzaras ervah* — does not carry the same weight. The *zika* generates the *achos zekukaso* prohibition, but it is not strong enough to then activate, in full, the *tzaras ervah* mechanism for Devorah.

### Co-wife Better

The practical consequence is that Devorah, although she cannot be taken in *yibum*, stands in a better position than Rachel for purposes of *chalitzah*. Rachel's *zika* is directly burdened by *achos zekukaso*, making her *chalitzah* second-rate. Devorah's *zika*, while indirectly affected, is not burdened to the same degree — because the chain of derivation (from *achos zekukaso* to *tzaras achos zekukaso*) attenuates the problem. She is, in the terms introduced earlier, perhaps a grade B rather than grade A, while Rachel is grade C. The *chalitzah* with Devorah is therefore relatively first-rate — stronger than the *chalitzah* with Rachel — and suffices to free Rachel.

### Mishna Alignment

The *Gemara* confirms that this understanding is in line with a *baraita*: *tanya kevasei deRav Ashi* — it was taught in accordance with Rav Ashi. The *baraita* states: *chalatz l'achayos lo nifteru tzaros, chalatz letzaros nifteru achayos* — performing *chalitzah* with the sisters does not free the co-wives, but performing *chalitzah* with the co-wives does free the sisters. And the reason given is precisely: *mishum dekasavar yesh zika velo alumi zika lishveiye litzara ke'erva* — because the *zika* exists but is insufficient to make the co-wife a full *ervah*. This is exactly what Rav Ashi said. The *baraita* resolves the debate in Rav Ashi's favor.

---

## Beis Shammai View

### Beis Shammai

Rabbi Abba bar Mamul offers an alternative account of why performing *chalitzah* with the co-wife is preferable. Rather than invoking the subtlety of *zika* strength, he proposes that Shmuel's ruling reflects the position of Beis Shammai. The *mishnah* elsewhere records: *Beis Shammai matirin hatzaros leachim* — Beis Shammai permit the co-wives to the brothers. According to Beis Shammai, the principle of *tzaras ervah* does not apply at all. Co-wives of an *ervah* are not exempt from *yibum*; they are fully obligated. On this view, Devorah is not problematic in any sense — she is simply another *yevamah* who may be taken in *yibum*. There is therefore no question of first-rate versus second-rate *chalitzah* with her; she stands in a fully normal *chalitzah* relationship with Reuven.

### Objection

The *Gemara* immediately objects: if Beis Shammai permits *yibum* with co-wives, and Shmuel is following Beis Shammai, then why is Shmuel requiring *chalitzah* with Devorah at all? Let Reuven perform *yibum* with her outright.

### Compromise

The *Gemara* responds by invoking the position of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who proposed: *bo'u unetaken lahem latzaros sheyihyu choltzos velo mityabmos* — let us enact for the co-wives that they perform *chalitzah* and not *yibum*. This ruling is a compromise designed to honor both Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel. Beis Hillel holds that co-wives of an *ervah* are exempt even from *chalitzah*; Beis Shammai holds that they are fully obligated and may even perform *yibum*. The enactment of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri requires *chalitzah* but forbids *yibum* — satisfying the concern of Beis Hillel (who would object to *yibum*) while acknowledging the Beis Shammai position that some obligation exists. The *Gemara* notes that the full ratification of this ruling was not completed in its time — *lo hispiku ligmor et hadavar* — but Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak replies that it was subsequently enacted. The position of Rabbi Abba bar Mamul is thus that Shmuel's ruling reflects this compromise: operating within a Beis Shammai framework modified by the later enactment requiring *chalitzah* rather than *yibum*.

---

---

# Yevamot 28

## Issur Mitzvah/Ervah

### Four Brothers Case

The daf begins at the very last line of 28a, with the conclusion of the *mishna* dealing with four brothers, two of whom died having been married to two sisters. The case under discussion is one in which the surviving brothers face the problem of *achos zekukaso* — the sister of a *zekuka*, a quasi-wife. Ordinarily, because each surviving brother has a *zika* (a quasi-marital bond) to each of the deceased brothers' widows, and those widows are sisters to one another, neither brother can perform *yibum* or *chalitza*, since each woman is the sister of the other's *zekuka*. The *mishna* teaches, however, that if one of the women is an *ervah* to one of the brothers — forbidden to him by a biblical incest prohibition — that *zika* is dissolved, and the other brother may then perform *yibum* with the remaining woman.

The canonical illustration: if Rachel is Levi's daughter, there is no *zika* between Levi and Rachel — she is an *ervah* to him outright — and therefore Leah is not Levi's *achos zekukaso*. He may perform *yibum* with Leah. One might wonder how Rachel and Leah can be sisters if one is Levi's daughter and the other is not. The answer, as the *gemara* will clarify, is that they share the same mother but have different fathers — Rachel's father being Levi himself, and Leah's father being another man.

### Issur Mitzvah vs. Ervah

The *gemara* on 28b opens by noting that we have already been taught the case of *issur mitzvah* and *issur kedushah* in a simpler context: *issur mitzvah choletzet v'lo misyabbemet* — a woman who is forbidden only by rabbinic prohibition, or by a *lav* such as the prohibition against a *kohen* marrying a *grushah*, does *chalitza* and does not do *yibum*. That earlier teaching addressed the straightforward scenario of a single deceased brother; the present teaching introduces the more complex hybrid case where two sisters are *zekukos* to two surviving brothers, and one of those sisters is an *issur mitzvah* — a rabbinic-level prohibition — to one of the brothers.

### Hava Amina

The *gemara* raises a compelling *hava amina*: since the entire problem of *achos zekukaso* is itself only a *derabbanan* prohibition — Rachel was never fully his wife, only a *zekuka*, a quasi-wife — perhaps if Rachel is an *issur derabbanan* to Levi, that should be sufficient to remove her from the picture. After all, we are operating entirely within the rabbinic domain: the *zika* is a rabbinic construct, and Rachel's forbidden status is also rabbinic. Let one *derabbanan* solve another *derabbanan* problem, and allow Levi to perform *yibum* with Leah.

### Rejection of Hava Amina

The *gemara* rejects this: *keivan demide'oraita ramya kamei* — since, on the biblical level, Levi still has a *zika* to Rachel, she remains his *zekuka de'oraita*, and Leah is therefore still the sister of his *zekuka* even if the *zika* is only actualized rabbinically. Rachel does not disappear from the scene merely because she is an *issur derabbanan* to him.

### Mishum Mitzvah

One might further suggest: since the entire problem is rabbinic, and the *rabbanan* instituted *achos zekukaso* in service of the *mitzva* of *yibum*, perhaps they would relax it in order to facilitate *yibum* in a case where the woman is already an *issur derabbanan*. The *gemara* dismisses this as well — *kamashma lan* — we are taught that the *rabbanan* would not override the *zika* problem in this fashion.

---

## Variations & Case Logic

### Pedagogical Logic

The *gemara* now asks why the *mishna* needed to state both the case where one of the two women is an *ervah* and the case where both women are each an *ervah* to the respective other brother. Is not the second case simply a doubled version of the first? *Hainu hach* — is it not the same point? The *gemara* answers that both cases are pedagogically necessary, and proceeds to explain the distinctive logical function each one serves.

### One Ervah Case

If the *mishna* had taught only the case where one woman is an *ervah* — say, Rachel is Levi's daughter, and Levi therefore performs *yibum* with Leah — one might fail to recognize that this is only permitted because of the special circumstance of *ervah*. Without the second case to illuminate the point, an observer might conclude that in any such configuration, the surviving brother is simply permitted to perform *yibum* with the other woman, regardless of whether an *ervah* relation is actually present. The singular case, standing alone, might be mistakenly read as establishing a general rule.

### Two Ervos Case

The case of two *ervos*, where each woman is an *ervah* to the respective other brother, allows each brother to perform *yibum* with the woman who is not his *ervah*. The presence of the second brother here is itself probative: because Yehuda performs *yibum* with Rachel and Levi performs *yibum* with Leah — each with a different woman — the mutual arrangement makes evident that something special is operative. This cross-pattern demonstrates that only because of the *ervah* relationship is each brother permitted to act.

### Sheni's Evidentiary Role

The *gemara* introduces the principle of *sheni demuchach* — the second one proves. In the case of two *ervos*, the second brother's restricted behavior demonstrates that a special circumstance accounts for why the first brother is permitted. Each brother's situation illuminates the other's. Conversely, if the *mishna* had taught only the two-*ervah* case, one might think the reason both brothers can perform *yibum* is self-evident from the symmetry alone, without realizing that each *yibum* is contingent on the *ervah* relation operating in that particular direction. The case of one *ervah* is then needed to establish that the permission is not structural but derives from the specific *ervah* status.

This analysis extends further: the *gemara* asks about the final line of the *mishna* — *zu hi she'amru*, "this is what they said" — and concludes that it comes to exclude the case where both women are an *issur mitzvah* to the respective brothers, rather than a true *ervah*. One might have thought that if each brother has a *derabbanan ervah* to one woman, and each can therefore perform *yibum* with the other, the symmetry of the situation should allow it — since neither brother is being disadvantaged and there is no concern about the *sheni*. The *mishna* teaches that even in this symmetric case, the *issur derabbanan* does not suffice to overcome the *zika*, and *yibum* remains forbidden.

---

## Fifteen Arayos Debate

### All Arayos Apply

The *gemara* now turns to a broader principle, one that may be recalled from early in the *masechet*. A *braita* teaches in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Rav, and likewise taught by Rabbi Hiyya: *v'chulan ani korei bahen ha'asurah lazeh muteret lazeh v'achosah k'shehi yevimtah o choletzes o misyabbemet* — in all of the fifteen forbidden relationships enumerated in the opening *mishna* of the *masechet*, one can construct the scenario in which the forbidden woman is forbidden to one brother but permitted to the other, and her sister who is simultaneously a sister-in-law may either do *chalitza* or *yibum*.

The puzzle being posed is essentially a combinatorial one: for each of the fifteen *arayos*, can one construct a configuration in which two sisters are each married to two brothers, such that one sister is an *ervah* to one brother but not the other, while the other sister is an *ervah* to the second brother but not the first? The claim is that this can be worked out for all fifteen cases. A simple illustration: if Leah is the mother-in-law of Yehuda (i.e., the mother of Yehuda's wife), she is an *ervah* to Yehuda but has no relationship to Levi. Similarly, Rachel is Levi's mother-in-law but not Yehuda's. Since Rachel and Leah are sisters through their father, the entire configuration is achieved.

### Rav Yehuda Excludes Six

However, Rav Yehuda himself restricts the application of this principle. He will only apply it beginning from the case of *chamot* — mother-in-law — and onward through the list. The first six cases of the *mishna* — which all derive from the category of *bat*, daughter — he excludes: *aval sheis bavi d'reisha lo*. He does not wish to teach that these six cases can be applied to the scenario of *achos zekukaso*.

### Daughter Cases Issue

The difficulty with the daughter cases is as follows. For Rachel to be Levi's daughter but not Yehuda's daughter, while Rachel and Leah are sisters, they must share the same mother. But if they share the same mother, and Levi fathered Rachel through that woman, then Leah — as the daughter of the same woman — would be Levi's wife's daughter, which is itself a forbidden relationship. The only way to avoid this is if Levi was never married to the mother. In other words, the case of daughter within this framework can only be constructed if the daughter was born out of wedlock. The *gemara* formulates this as: *keivan de'vita ba'onsin hu d'mishkachat lah, benisuin lo mishkachat lah* — the case of daughter is only workable when the child was born through an illicit union, not through marriage. Rav Yehuda, who prefers to speak only of cases that arise through legitimate marriage, excludes all six daughter-derived categories.

### Abayei Includes Daughter

Abaye disagrees and extends the principle to all fifteen cases, including the daughter categories. His reasoning is pragmatic: *keivan de'ashkachei mishkachat lah, ei ba'onsin teihavei ei benisuin teihavei* — since the scenario is achievable, whether through an out-of-wedlock birth or otherwise, it is legitimate to include it. Abaye is willing to speak even about cases that require positing an illicit origin for the daughter, provided the legal structure works.

### Eishet Achiv Exception

Abaye, however, carves out one exception of his own: the case of *eishet achiv shelo hayah be'olamo* — the wife of a brother who was not yet born when his brother was alive and married. Abaye says this case cannot be applied to the *achos zekukaso* scenario, because the only way to construct such a configuration is according to the position of Rabbi Shimon, and not according to the *rabbanan*. Since this is a matter of *machloket*, Abaye does not wish to build the scenario on a disputed foundation: *biflugeta lo ka'mira* — I do not speak of a case that is subject to dispute.

---

## Meis Nolad Yibem

### Initial Setup

The *gemara* then records that Rav Safra disagrees with Abaye on this last point, insisting that the case of *eishet achiv shelo hayah be'olamo* can indeed be applied to the *achos zekukaso* scenario — but only according to Rabbi Shimon, and it requires six brothers. The mnemonic given is *meis, nolad, v'yibem; meis, nolad, v'yibem* — died, born, did *yibum*; died, born, did *yibum*. The *gemara* then elaborates the case fully.

We begin with four brothers: Reuven and Shimon, who are married to two sisters — Rachel and Leah respectively. A second pair of brothers, Levi and Yehuda, are married to two unrelated women, Devorah and Channah.

### Stage 1: Reuven Dies

In the first stage, Reuven dies. In the second stage, a new brother, Yissachar, is born. Because Yissachar was born after Reuven had already died, Rachel — Reuven's widow — is an *ervah* to Yissachar as *eishet achiv shelo hayah be'olamo*: the wife of a brother who was never alive at the same time as him.

### Stage 2: Levi Yibums

In the third stage, Levi performs *yibum* with Rachel. He was already married to Devorah; now he takes Rachel as well through *yibum*. Rachel remains an *ervah* to Yissachar even after Levi's *yibum*, since the *eishet achiv shelo hayah be'olamo* prohibition is rooted in the relationship between Rachel and Reuven, not in Rachel's current marital status.

### Stages 3-4: Shimon Dies

In the fourth stage, Shimon dies. In the fifth stage, another new brother, Zevulun, is born. By the time Zevulun is born, Rachel is already married to Levi — she is not available as a *zekuka* to Zevulun, and therefore she is not an *ervah* to him. Leah, however, was Shimon's wife, and since Zevulun was born after Shimon died, Leah is *eishet achiv shelo hayah be'olamo* to Zevulun. Leah, by contrast, is not an *ervah* to Yissachar: Shimon and Yissachar were contemporaries, so there is a standard *zika* relationship — a *mitzva* obligation — not an *ervah*.

### Stage 5: Yehuda Yibums

In the sixth stage, Yehuda performs *yibum* with Leah. Now, when Levi and Yehuda die childless, their widows — Rachel and Leah — fall before Yissachar and Zevulun for *yibum*. The result is the desired cross-pattern: Rachel is an *ervah* to Yissachar (*eishet achiv shelo hayah be'olamo*) but permitted to Zevulun; Leah is an *ervah* to Zevulun (*eishet achiv shelo hayah be'olamo*) but permitted to Yissachar. Thus, *asurah lazeh muteret lazeh v'asurah lazeh muteret lazeh* — each woman is forbidden to one brother and permitted to the other. The full structure of the *achos zekukaso* ruling with *eishet achiv shelo hayah be'olamo* is thereby demonstrated.

### Rabbi Shimon Restriction

This construction, as was anticipated, works only according to Rabbi Shimon. The *rabbanan* would hold that even though Rachel was already married to Levi by the time Zevulun was born, Rachel's status as *eishet achiv shelo hayah be'olamo* vis-à-vis Reuven remains intact, and therefore she would be an *ervah* to Zevulun as well. Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, holds that once Rachel entered a fully consummated *yibum* with Levi — who was alive when Reuven was alive — her status with respect to Zevulun is redefined by her current marriage, not by her original connection to Reuven. Hence the scenario only functions according to Rabbi Shimon's position.

The *gemara* then asks why Yehuda's *yibum* with Leah was necessary to the construction, since it seems one could arrive at the same result without him. The answer is that Yehuda's presence is needed to generate the case of *tzarat ervah* — the co-wife of an *ervah* — as well. Without Yehuda in the picture, both women would be in an *ervah* relationship with the same brother, and there would be no way to introduce the co-wife scenario. The *gemara* further notes that with the addition of two more brothers, Gad and Asher, one can extend the case to include *tzarat tzarah* — the co-wife of a co-wife of an *ervah* — as well, though the details are left to the reader.

---

## Three Brothers Mishna

### Basic Setup

A new *mishna* opens: *sheloshah achim, shenayim meihem nesuim shtei achayos* — three brothers, two of them married to two sisters. The case is structurally similar to the four-brother case discussed previously, now simplified to three brothers. The third brother is *mufneh* — unattached, single.

### Types of Arayos

The *mishna* extends the ruling to apply not only to cases where the two women are sisters but also to any analogous *ervah* relationship between them: *o ishah u-vittah, o ishah u-vas bittah, o ishah u-vas binnah* — or a woman and her daughter, or a woman and her granddaughter (through the daughter or through the son). Any pair of women who could not both be married to the same man may stand in this configuration.

### Consensus Halacha

The baseline ruling of the *mishna* — consistent with what we have established — is that when such a configuration exists, *harei eilu choltzos v'lo misyabbemet*: these women do *chalitza* and do not do *yibum*. Since neither surviving brother can perform *yibum* with either woman without encountering the problem of *zika* to the other, they must each do *chalitza*. This is the standard position of the *rabbanan*, grounded in the rabbinic prohibition of *achos zekukaso*.

### Rabbi Shimon Position

Rabbi Shimon, however, takes a strikingly different position: *Rabbi Shimon poter* — Rabbi Shimon exempts entirely. In his view, both women are completely exempt from both *chalitza* and *yibum*. They simply walk away. This is a remarkable ruling, standing in sharp contrast to the majority position. Where the *rabbanan* treat *achos zekukaso* as a rabbinic prohibition requiring *chalitza* as a safeguard, Rabbi Shimon regards the entire configuration as generating a *de'oraita* exemption from the *yibum* obligation altogether. The *gemara* will proceed to examine his reasoning.

---

## Rabbi Shimon's Basis

### Prooftext Citation

The *gemara* cites the *braita*: Rabbi Shimon derives his position from the verse *v'ishah el achota lo tikach litzror* — "you shall not take a woman alongside her sister to create rivalry between them." This verse, which is the source of the prohibition against marrying two sisters simultaneously, is applied by Rabbi Shimon to the *yibum* context as well.

### Tzarot Principle

Rabbi Shimon reasons: *besha'ah shena'asu tzarot zu l'zu* — at the moment when these two women become *tzarot* to one another, co-sisters-in-law, each bound by the *mitzva* of *yibum* to different brothers who have now both died, they are as though they are co-wives competing for the same household. In such circumstances, *lo yihyeh lachem afilu b'achat meihen* — there is no *mitzva* relationship with even one of them. The prohibition of taking two sisters simultaneously extends, for Rabbi Shimon, to the *yibum* context, where the *zika* of each brother to each woman creates a functional co-wife relationship between the two sisters. Therefore, rather than a mere rabbinic enactment, Rabbi Shimon holds that there is a *de'oraita* exemption: the *mitzva* of *yibum* simply does not apply, and consequently neither does the obligation of *chalitza*.

### De'Oraita Status

This is a critical theological distinction. For the *rabbanan*, *achos zekukaso* is a *derabbanan* problem: biblically, one might argue that *yibum* should be performed with one of the women, and the rabbinic enactment merely prevents it for fear of complication. The *rabbanan* therefore require *chalitza* to discharge the residual *zika*. For Rabbi Shimon, the exemption is *de'oraita*: the *yibum* obligation does not arise at all in this configuration, and without a *mitzva* of *yibum*, there is no *yibum* obligation to discharge and therefore no need for *chalitza* either.

### Hava Amina Gezeirah

Given the severity of Rabbi Shimon's position — that this is a *de'oraita* exemption, and that performing *yibum* in such a case would constitute an actual *issur* of *eishet achiv* — one might have thought that even in the case where one of the women is a genuine *ervah* to one of the brothers, Rabbi Shimon would prohibit *yibum* with the other woman as well. The concern would be a *gezeirah*: if we allow *yibum* in this case, people might come to permit *yibum* in the ordinary case of *achos zekukaso*, which for Rabbi Shimon is a *de'oraita* prohibition.

### Rejection Gezeirah

The *gemara* rejects this *hava amina*: *kamashma lan* — we are taught that even Rabbi Shimon agrees that when one woman is a genuine *ervah* to one brother, the other brother may perform *yibum* with the remaining woman. There is no *gezeirah* in that case. When one woman is an *ervah* and is entirely removed from the picture, the remaining woman is simply a standard *yevama* to the other brother, and there is no circumstance that could generate a misunderstanding.

---

## Issur Mitzvah Gezeirah

### Public Perception Issue

The *mishna* continues: when one of the women is an *issur mitzvah* — a rabbinic-level prohibition, or a *lav* such as the prohibition against a *kohen* marrying a *grushah* — *choltzos v'lo misyabbemet* — both women do *chalitza* and neither does *yibum*. This ruling applies even according to Rabbi Shimon. The *gemara* notes that this seems surprising: in a plain case of two sisters with no other *issur* present, Rabbi Shimon says they walk away without *chalitza* at all. Why, when one of them is an *issur mitzvah*, should Rabbi Shimon require *chalitza*?

### Grusha/Kohen Example

The *gemara* answers: it is a *gezeirah* on account of *issur mitzvah d'alma* — a protective measure for the general category of *issur mitzvah* cases. Consider the following scenario: one of the women happens to be a *grushah* who was married to a *kohen*. Now, if both women are simply allowed to walk away without *chalitza* — as Rabbi Shimon would normally permit in a case of two sisters — observers will not focus on the sisters-and-brothers dimension of the case. They will focus on the specific fact that was salient to them: the woman was a *grushah* and the surviving brother was a *kohen*. They will conclude: "Apparently, when a woman is forbidden as an *issur mitzvah* to a *kohen*, no *chalitza* is required."

### Both Get Chalitza

This would be a catastrophically wrong inference, since the *halacha* requires *chalitza* whenever a woman is an *issur mitzvah* to the *yavam* in a standard *yibum* situation. To prevent this misunderstanding, the *rabbanan* require *chalitza* from both women even in the case of *achos zekukaso* where one is an *issur mitzvah* — specifically so that no one will infer that *issur mitzvah* cases are generally exempt from *chalitza*. The woman who is the *issur mitzvah* must do *chalitza* to remove the fear of a wrong public inference. And since we are requiring *chalitza* from her, the *gezeirah* extends to require *chalitza* from her sister as well.

### Ervah Clarity

The *gemara* then asks: in the case of a real *ervah* — say, the woman was Levi's daughter — Rabbi Shimon does not make a *gezeirah* and does not require *chalitza* from the sister. Why is a *gezeirah* not similarly needed there? The answer: *shani ervah d'mifarsma l'milsa* — the case of *ervah* is publicly known. When the woman is someone's daughter, or another clear *ervah* relationship, the nature of the prohibition is evident to all, and observers will correctly understand why the parties departed without *chalitza*. The confusion that would arise in the *issur mitzvah* case — where the reason is subtle and easily misattributed — does not arise when the *ervah* status is obvious. Therefore the *gezeirah* applies to *issur mitzvah* but not to genuine *ervah*.

---

## Ma'amar Before Death

### Setup Ma'amar

A new *mishna* introduces a fresh scenario. Three brothers again: two married to two sisters — call them Reuven married to Rachel, and Shimon married to Leah — and a third brother, Levi, who is *mufneh*, unattached. Reuven dies. Now Levi is the *yavam* for Rachel. At this point, before Shimon has died, there is no problem of *achos zekukaso*: Levi can straightforwardly perform *yibum* or *chalitza* with Rachel. Levi, instead of consummating *yibum*, performs *ma'amar* with Rachel — the rabbinic form of *kiddushin* that is a partial fulfillment of the *yibum* obligation. After this, Shimon dies.

### Ma'amar Strength

The question now before us is whether the *ma'amar* that Levi performed with Rachel is strong enough to alter the legal reality. Specifically: does the *ma'amar*, combined with the original *zika*, create a bond sufficiently robust to treat Rachel as Levi's wife for *de'oraita* purposes? If so, then once Shimon dies and Leah falls before Levi, Leah is the sister of Levi's wife — *achos isha* — and would simply depart without *chalitza*. If not, then Leah remains Levi's *zekuka* and there remains a *yibum* obligation to her, which cannot be discharged without *chalitza*.

There are really two separate questions embedded here. First, at the rabbinic level: does the *ma'amar* suffice to overcome the *derabbanan* problem of *achos zekukaso*, so that Levi may proceed to consummate *yibum* with Rachel? Second, at the *de'oraita* level: has the *ma'amar* transformed Rachel's status into that of a full wife, such that Leah — as the sister of Levi's wife — requires no *chalitza* at all?

### Beit Shammai View

Beit Shammai rules: *ishto imo v'halazu taitzei mishum achos isha* — Rachel is his wife, and Leah departs on account of being the sister of a wife. Beit Shammai grants the *ma'amar* full operative weight: it is sufficient to definitively establish Rachel as Levi's wife at the *de'oraita* level, such that Leah — now the sister of a married woman — is simply exempt from both *yibum* and *chalitza*. There is no *mitzva* and no need to discharge any bond.

### Beit Hillel View

Beit Hillel rules otherwise: *motzi et ishto be-get u-ve-chalitza, v'eshet achiv be-chalitza* — Levi must give Rachel a *get* on account of the *ma'amar*, and also *chalitza* on account of the residual *zika*; and he must give Leah *chalitza* as well. Beit Hillel refuses to grant the *ma'amar* the weight that Beit Shammai does. At the *de'oraita* level, Rachel is not yet Levi's wife in any full sense; the *zika* has not been converted into actual marriage. Therefore Leah still has a *zika* to Levi, which requires *chalitza*. And Rachel, whose relationship with Levi was deepened by the *ma'amar*, requires a *get* to dissolve the rabbinic *kiddushin*, plus *chalitza* to dissolve the *de'oraita* *zika*. Now, moreover, since Shimon has died and Leah is in the picture, the *achos zekukaso* problem is fully active: Levi cannot consummate with Rachel because Leah is her sister and Leah is his *zekuka*. Both women require *chalitza*; neither can be taken in *yibum*.

### Consequences Harm

This leads to the poignant statement of the *mishna*: *oy li al ishto v'oy li al eshet achiv* — woe to his wife and woe to his brother's wife. According to Beit Hillel, both Rachel and Leah are harmed. Rachel, who had the *ma'amar* and was on her way to being fully married, cannot be taken in *yibum* because of *achos zekukaso*; she must take a *get* and *chalitza* and goes away with nothing. Leah, who did nothing, is trapped and must also receive *chalitza* before she can remarry. According to Beit Shammai, by contrast, Levi consummates his marriage with Rachel and Leah departs freely.

One might ask — as indeed arises in the *gemara* — how, according to Beit Hillel, the *ma'amar* can be strong enough to require a *get* but not strong enough to solve the *achos zekukaso* problem. The answer, as the *gemara* makes clear, is that the *ma'amar* operates only at the rabbinic level, generating the rabbinic parallel to *kiddushin* that requires a *get* to dissolve — but the *de'oraita* *zika* to Leah persists and is not resolved by any amount of rabbinic *kiddushin* with Rachel. The *gemara* had already established this principle earlier: a *derabbanan ervah* does not resolve a *derabbanan* problem of *achos zekukaso* if the *de'oraita* *zika* remains intact.

---

## Ma'amar Analysis

### Partial Kinyan

Rabbi Elazar now clarifies the position of Beit Shammai more precisely. One should not say that *ma'amar*, according to Beit Shammai, creates a *kinyan gamur* — a complete, total acquisition — in the full sense of *yibum* consummation.

### Divorce Test

The test case is divorce. When a man consummated *yibum* with his *yevama* and subsequently wishes to divorce her, a *get* alone suffices — *chalitza* is not needed once the marriage has been consummated. If *ma'amar*, according to Beit Shammai, were a complete *kinyan gamur*, then dissolving it should similarly require only a *get*. But that is not the case.

### Partial Effect

Rather, the *ma'amar* according to Beit Shammai is sufficient to push Leah away and to permit consummation with Rachel — but it does not fully transform Rachel's legal status in every dimension. The relationship, while operative enough to displace the co-sister-in-law, has not fully converted from *yibum*-track to ordinary-marriage-track in every respect.

### Ma'amar Dachaya

Rabbi Elazar articulates the principle: *ma'amar le-Beit Shammai eino koneh ella lidchot be-tzarah bilvad* — the *ma'amar*, according to Beit Shammai, acquires only to the extent of pushing off the co-woman. This is *ma'amar dachaya*: the *ma'amar* operates by displacing Leah's claim rather than by fully constituting Rachel as Levi's wife in the ordinary sense. The relationship with Rachel has been meaningfully strengthened by the *ma'amar*, but it has not crossed the threshold of a *kinyan gamur* in the fullest sense.

---

## Ma'amar Solution Problem

### Why Not Ma'amar?

A sharp question now arises. If *ma'amar*, according to Beit Shammai, is strong enough to push Leah off the scene and allow Levi to consummate with Rachel — then why, in a standard case of *achos zekukaso* where no *ma'amar* has yet been done, should Levi not simply perform *ma'amar* with Rachel first, thereby displacing Leah, and then consummate *yibum* with Rachel? This would solve the entire *achos zekukaso* problem from the outset, without the need to suffer through the situation at all.

### Deheitera vs. Issura

The *gemara* answers by drawing a fundamental distinction: *ma'amar deheitera dachi* — only a *ma'amar* that was performed permissibly, without a competing *zika* problem at the time it was done, can have the effect of displacing the co-woman. In the case in our *mishna*, the *ma'amar* was performed with Rachel while Shimon was still alive. At that moment, there was no problem: Levi had a *zika* only to Rachel, Shimon was still married to Leah, and there was no *achos zekukaso* difficulty. The *ma'amar* was therefore a *ma'amar deheitera* — a permissible *ma'amar* done in legitimate circumstances. It is this *ma'amar* that, according to Beit Shammai, retains its effect even after Shimon dies and Leah enters the picture.

By contrast, if Levi were to perform *ma'amar* with Rachel after both brothers have already died — when there is already a *zika* to Leah and a *zika* to Rachel simultaneously, and *yibum* with Rachel is prohibited because of *achos zekukaso* — that *ma'amar* would be a *ma'amar de'issura*, performed in circumstances where the underlying *yibum* is forbidden. Such a *ma'amar* cannot have operative legal effect.

### Ma'amar Works Cleanly

The principle is that *ma'amar* is only meaningful when it is performed in a context where *yibum* itself would be permitted. The *ma'amar* is the rabbinic anticipation of *yibum* — a partial enactment of the relationship. If the relationship itself cannot be consummated because of a competing *zika* and the *achos zekukaso* prohibition, the *ma'amar* cannot bootstrap itself into creating legal reality.

### Zika Interference

Once Leah's *zika* is on the scene and *yibum* with Rachel is prohibited by reason of *achos zekukaso*, performing *ma'amar* with Rachel is itself problematic — it is a *ma'amar de'issura*. Such a *ma'amar* cannot create full marital status and cannot displace Leah's claim. The effect of *ma'amar* depends entirely on the legitimacy of the context in which it was done. This is why the *mishna*'s case is one where the *ma'amar* was done before the second brother died — that timing is not incidental but is the entire legal basis on which Beit Shammai's ruling operates.

---

## Ma'amar Status TBD

### Kinyan Degree

Having established that the *ma'amar* in the *mishna* was a *ma'amar deheitera* and that this is why it has operative effect according to Beit Shammai, the question remains: what precisely is the weight of that *ma'amar*? Does it create full marital status — a *kinyan gamur* — such that if Levi and Rachel subsequently wished to part ways, only a *get* would be needed? Or is it a partial status, sufficient to displace Leah, but insufficient to fully transform the relationship — so that *chalitza* would still be required in addition to a *get* if dissolution were sought?

### Divorce Implications

This question is not merely theoretical. It determines the practical consequences for the couple. If the *ma'amar deheitera* creates a *kinyan gamur*, then Levi and Rachel are fully married once he consummates, Leah walks away, and any future divorce would require only a *get*. If the *ma'amar deheitera* creates only a partial *kinyan* — enough to displace Leah but not enough to fully convert the relationship — then even after consummation, *chalitza* would remain a requirement should they ever divorce.

### Ongoing Debate

Rabbi Elazar's initial formulation — *ma'amar le-Beit Shammai eino koneh ella lidchot be-tzarah bilvad* — suggests it is not a full *kinyan*. However, the full weight of that ruling, and whether Beit Shammai could be read as granting a complete *kinyan gamur* under some interpretation, remains a point of ongoing discussion in the *gemara*. The daf concludes with Rav Ashi's version of Rabbi Elazar's statement beginning to be introduced, and the full analysis of the *ma'amar*'s degree of acquisition according to Beit Shammai will continue in the next shiur.

---

# Yevamot 28b

## Achot Zekukato

### Four Brothers Setup

The daf we take up begins at the very last line of 28a, with the word *issur mitzvah*. We are completing a *mishnah* that presented the case of four brothers, two of whom died having been married to two sisters. The question was whether the surviving brothers face the problem of *achot zekukato* — the sister of one's *zekukah*, a woman to whom one stands in a quasi-marital bond through the *mitzvah* of *yibbum*. The *mishnah* established that if one of the sisters is an *ervah* to one of the surviving brothers, that resolves the problem: since he has no *zikah* to her, she is entirely outside the picture, and his fellow brother may perform *yibbum* with the other sister without triggering the prohibition of *achot zekukato*.

### One Ervah Solution

To make the case concrete: suppose Reuven and Shimon died, having been married to Rachel and Leah, who are sisters. The surviving brothers are Levi and Yehudah. If Rachel is Levi's daughter — from a different mother than Leah — then Levi has no *zikah* to Rachel at all, since she is a forbidden relative. With no *zikah* connecting Levi to Rachel, Leah is not the sister of Levi's *zekukah*, and Yehudah may therefore perform *yibbum* with Rachel. This is the logic of the *ervah* solution.

### Issur Mitzvah Question

The question then arises: what if Rachel is not a biblical *ervah* to Levi, but is instead forbidden to him through a rabbinic prohibition — an *issur mitzvah*, such as being a *grushah* to a *kohen*, or some other *issur derabbanan*? The entire problem of *achot zekukato* is itself rabbinic in origin, since the *zikah* that creates the quasi-marital bond is a *derabbanan* construct. One might therefore reason that since we are operating in a *derabbanan* world — the *zikah* is *derabbanan*, the problem of *achot zekukato* is *derabbanan* — perhaps a *derabbanan ervah* should suffice to dissolve a *derabbanan* problem. Let the rabbinic prohibition against Rachel push her out of Levi's picture, thereby permitting Yehudah to perform *yibbum* with her.

### Issur Mitzvah Fails

This is the *hava amina* the *gemara* entertains at the top of 28b. The *gemara* cites the teaching: *issur mitzvah ve-issur kedushah — choletzet velo mityabemet* — a woman who is rabbinically forbidden performs *chalitzah* but not *yibbum*. The *gemara* distinguishes between that simpler case, where a single brother dies and the *yevamah* is forbidden to the surviving brother through a rabbinic prohibition alone, and the more complex case here, where we have both the *issur mitzvah* and the additional complication of *achot zekukato*.

The *gemara* responds: *kevan de-de'oraita ramya kammei* — since at the biblical level there still is a *zikah* connecting Levi to Rachel, the problem of *achot zekukato* persists. The reasoning that a *derabbanan ervah* might dissolve a *derabbanan* problem is rejected. Even though *achot zekukato* is rabbinic in character, the *zikah* that underlies it is a real *de'oraita* relationship, and no rabbinic-level prohibition on Rachel is sufficient to sever that connection. The *mishnah* thus teaches us — *kamashma lan* — that an *issur mitzvah* does not solve the *achot zekukato* problem, and *chalitzah* is still required.

This was a genuine and reasonable *hava amina*: if everything is *derabbanan*, let a *derabbanan ervah* resolve a *derabbanan* difficulty. The *gemara* rejects it cleanly, but it was not an unreasonable idea.

### One vs. Two Ervas

The *mishnah* then presents a further case: *haysah achas meihen zo ervah v'zu ervah* — if each sister is a forbidden relative to one of the surviving brothers. For instance, Rachel is Levi's daughter and Leah is Yehudah's daughter. In this scenario, each brother may perform *yibbum* with the sister who is not forbidden to him: Levi does *yibbum* with Leah, and Yehudah does *yibbum* with Rachel.

The *gemara* asks: *ha tu lama li? hainu hach* — why is this case necessary? It is essentially the same principle stated twice. What is added by doubling it? The *gemara* answers: *tzricha* — both cases are needed. If we only knew the case of one *ervah*, we might not appreciate that it is truly a case of *ervah* at work, because there is only one brother performing *yibbum* and the asymmetry is not fully evident. But because Yehudah is present in that scenario and *does not* perform *yibbum*, his restriction makes it clear that Levi's *yibbum* is a special case enabled by the *ervah* status. Conversely, if we only knew the case of two *ervas*, where both brothers each perform *yibbum* with the opposite sister, one might think this is simply the general rule and not a consequence of *ervah* status at all. Each case is therefore necessary to make the full picture clear to the reader.

### Final Mishnah Line

The final line of the *mishnah* reads: *zu hi she'amru* — "this is what the Sages meant when they said" that if a sister is also one's *yevamah*, and one of the sisters is an *ervah*, then the other may either perform *chalitzah* or *yibbum*. The *gemara* asks: *zu hi l'me'utei mai?* — what does this phrase come to exclude?

The answer: *l'me'utei issur mitzvah l'zeh v'issur mitzvah l'zeh* — to exclude the case where each sister is a *derabbanan ervah* to one of the brothers. The *gemara* already established that a single *derabbanan ervah* does not dissolve the *achot zekukato* problem. But might one think that if *both* sisters carry a *derabbanan* prohibition — each to one of the brothers — then perhaps together they are sufficient? Perhaps when each brother faces a *derabbanan* obstacle to one sister, we treat it as though both are effectively *ervas* to their respective brothers, and allow *yibbum* with the alternate sisters?

The *gemara* again asks: *mah li chad mah li l'trei* — what difference does doubling it make? And again the *gemara* provides a genuine *hava amina*: in the single case, a concern arises that we might confuse others if we allow *yibbum* based on a *derabbanan ervah*, since only one brother benefits and the second brother will not understand why. But in the symmetric case, where each brother does *yibbum* with one sister, there is no concern about the second brother — perhaps here we should allow the *derabbanan ervah* to function. The *mishnah* teaches us that even in this symmetric case we do not permit it. The *gezeirah* concern — that people will come to think a *derabbanan ervah* generally dissolves the *achot zekukato* problem — remains in force regardless.

---

## Fifteen Arayot

### Rav Yehuda Teaching

The *gemara* now turns to a famous teaching that readers may recall from much earlier in the *masechet*: applying all fifteen *arayot* of the opening *mishnah* to the scenario of sisters married to brothers. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav, and so too taught Rabbi Chiya: *v'chulan ani korei bahen* — in all fifteen cases of the *arayot* listed in the first *mishnah*, one can find a scenario where the rule applies: *asurah l'ze muteret l'ze v'achotah k'she-hi yevimtah o choletzet o mityabemet* — she is forbidden to this one and permitted to that one, and her sister, who is also her *yevamah*, either performs *chalitzah* or *yibbum*.

### Sisters Asymmetry

The puzzle embedded in this teaching is like a mind-bender: one needs to construct a case where two women are sisters, both share the same type of *ervah* relationship, yet each is forbidden only to one of the surviving brothers and permitted to the other. The women must be sisters, they must both carry the same category of *ervah*, and the *ervah* must fall asymmetrically — this one to that brother, that one to this brother. The claim is that for all fifteen categories listed in the opening *mishnah*, one can engineer such a scenario.

### Mother-in-Law Example

The easy case to begin with is *chamot* — mother-in-law. Leah is Yehudah's wife's mother, which obviously has no bearing on Levi. Rachel is Levi's wife's mother, equally irrelevant to Yehudah. Both women are sisters — through their father in such a scenario — and each carries the *ervah* of mother-in-law, but only to one brother. The *ervah* falls asymmetrically, and the sisters remain sisters. The teaching thus works straightforwardly for the mother-in-law case, and the claim is that one can similarly construct working cases for all fifteen categories.

### Rav Yehuda Excludes

However, Rav Yehuda restricts his own teaching: *metargem me-chamoso v'eilech* — he will only apply it starting from *chamot*, mother-in-law, the ninth entry in the list. *Aval shita bavei de-reisha* — the first six cases, which are all derived from the category of daughter, he does not wish to apply. The first six *arayot* of the opening *mishnah* are: one's daughter, one's granddaughter through one's daughter, one's granddaughter through one's son, one's wife's daughter, one's wife's granddaughter through her son, and one's wife's granddaughter through her daughter. All six are rooted in the daughter relationship.

### Daughter Problem

Why does Rav Yehuda exclude the first six? The difficulty becomes clear when one tries to construct the case of daughter. Suppose Rachel is Levi's daughter. For Rachel and Leah to be sisters, they must share the same mother — call her Chana. Since they have different fathers, Levi is Rachel's father and another man is Leah's father, while Chana is mother to both. So far so good: Leah is not Levi's daughter.

But here is the problem: if Chana was ever Levi's wife — even if he later divorced her — then Leah, as Chana's daughter, becomes Levi's wife's daughter, which is itself an *ervah*. Both sisters would then be *ervas* to Levi, not just one, and the asymmetry collapses. For the case to work — where Rachel is Levi's daughter but Leah is not any kind of *ervah* to him — Chana could never have been Levi's wife. Rachel must be a daughter born outside of marriage altogether.

The *gemara* states this explicitly: *kevan de-bita ba-onsin hu de-mishkachas lah* — the case of daughter only works when the daughter was born through an out-of-wedlock union. *Bi-nisuyin lo mishkachas lah* — through marriage one cannot find this case. And since Rav Yehuda says *bi-nisuyin kamairi, ba-onsin lo kamairi* — I want to speak of scenarios that arise through marriage, not through out-of-wedlock birth — he excludes the entire first six cases from his teaching.

### Abaye Includes All

Abaye disagrees: *metargem af bita be-anusato* — Abaye extends the teaching even to the case of daughter, even though it only arises through an out-of-wedlock scenario. *Kevan de-ashkochei mishkachas lah* — since one *can* find the case, it does not matter whether it arises through marriage or not: *ei ba-onsin tehvi, ei bi-nisuyin tehvi* — whether through an out-of-wedlock union or through marriage, either way the case is findable, and Abaye is willing to include it. Working out all fifteen cases is a genuine intellectual puzzle, and according to Abaye all fifteen yield valid scenarios.

### Brother's Wife Exception

However, Abaye himself draws a line at one case: *aval eishet achiv she-lo haya be-olamo* — the *ervah* of one's brother's wife in the case where the brother was not yet alive when she was married. This is the principle that a woman who was married to a brother who subsequently died, and then a new brother was born after the first brother's death — that new brother never coexisted with his deceased brother, and therefore the widow has a special *ervah* status toward him. Abaye says one cannot apply this category to the puzzle of the fifteen *arayot*, because *kevan de-aliba de-Rabbi Shimon hu de-mishkachas lah* — the case only works according to Rabbi Shimon. *Aliba de-rabbanan lo mishkachas lah* — according to the Rabbanan the case cannot be constructed. And since this is a matter of *machlokes*, *be-pilugta lo kamairi* — Abaye does not want to build his teaching on a position disputed among the authorities.

### Rav Safra Includes

Rav Safra goes further still: *metargem af eishet achiv she-lo haya be-olamo* — even this final case can be made to apply, and one can find it with six brothers according to Rabbi Shimon. The mnemonic for the construction is: *mes, nolad, ve-yibem, mes, nolad, ve-yibem* — died, was born, performed *yibbum*, died, was born, performed *yibbum*. The *gemara* will now spell out this elaborate scenario in full.

---

## Six-Brother Scenario

### Six Brother Setup

The *gemara* sets the stage: Reuven and Shimon are married to the two sisters, Rachel and Leah. Levi and Yehudah are also brothers, each married to unrelated women — Devorah and Chana respectively. These are four of the six brothers. Two more brothers, Yissachar and Zevulun, do not yet exist; they will be born in the course of the scenario.

### First Death-Birth

Step one: Reuven dies. Step two: Yissachar is born. Since Yissachar was born only after Reuven had already died, Reuven and Yissachar never coexisted. Rachel, who was Reuven's wife and is now his widow, was never married to a man who was alive at the same time as Yissachar. She is therefore *eishet achiv she-lo haya be-olamo* with respect to Yissachar — the wife of a brother who was not in the world when he was born — and she stands as an *ervah* to him.

### First Yibum

Step three: Levi performs *yibbum* with Rachel. Levi was already married to Devorah, and now he takes Rachel in *yibbum*. At this moment Rachel becomes Levi's wife. Crucially, Rachel had already become an *ervah* to Yissachar at step two — she was *eishet achiv she-lo haya be-olamo* to him — and this status remains even after Levi performs *yibbum* with her.
