An *ervah* relationship, once established, persists.

Now, looking ahead: when Zevulun will later be born, Levi will already be married to Rachel. Rachel will therefore not be *eishet achiv she-lo haya be-olamo* with respect to Zevulun, because by the time Zevulun enters the world she is already a married woman — Levi's wife — and not a free widow. Rachel is thus an *ervah* to Yissachar but not to Zevulun.

### Second Death-Birth

Step four: Shimon dies. Step five: Zevulun is born. Since Zevulun was born only after Shimon had already died, Leah — Shimon's widow — is *eishet achiv she-lo haya be-olamo* with respect to Zevulun. Leah is therefore an *ervah* to Zevulun.

### Crossed Ervah Status

Step six: Yehudah performs *yibbum* with Leah. Now consider the position of Yissachar and Zevulun. Rachel is an *ervah* to Yissachar but permitted to Zevulun; Leah is an *ervah* to Zevulun but permitted to Yissachar. The two sisters are crossed *ervas* — each forbidden to one of the brothers and permitted to the other.

When Levi and Yehudah subsequently die without children and their wives — Rachel and Leah — fall for *yibbum* before Yissachar and Zevulun, the situation is precisely: *asurah lazo muteret lazo va'asurah lazo muteret lazo achotah k'she-hi yevamtah* — each is forbidden to one and permitted to the other, and they are sisters who are each other's *yevamah*. The *gemara* concludes: *mes Levi vi-Yehudah belo banim venaflu lifnei Yissachar u-Zevulun*.

### Why Yehuda Needed

The *gemara* then asks: *lama li yibem Yehudah?* — why was it necessary to include Yehudah performing *yibbum* with Leah? Could one not achieve the same scenario with fewer brothers — simply having Shimon die, Zevulun be born, and let the two surviving original brothers both die, leaving Yissachar and Zevulun to face both widows? The *gemara* answers: *mishum tzarah* — because the purpose is also to generate a case of *tzarat ervah*, the co-wife of a forbidden relative. If Yehudah had not performed *yibbum* with Leah, and Shimon had had a co-wife, that co-wife too would have been *eishet achiv she-lo haya be-olamo* to Zevulun, making her also an *ervah* rather than merely a *tzarat ervah*. By including Yehudah's *yibbum*, Chana — Yehudah's original wife — becomes only a *tzarat ervah* rather than an *ervah* herself, and the scenario captures that additional case.

### Rabbi Shimon Only

This entire construction, the *gemara* notes, works only according to Rabbi Shimon. The dispute is this: once Rachel became Levi's wife, does Yissachar's *ervah* status toward her persist? According to Rabbi Shimon, it does: the *ervah* of *eishet achiv she-lo haya be-olamo* was established when Yissachar was born and Rachel was a free widow, and that status is not dissolved when Levi later takes her in *yibbum*. According to the Rabbanan, however, even they would say that once Rachel is Levi's wife when Zevulun is born, she stands as *eishet ach* — a brother's wife — to Zevulun through a current, ordinary marriage, and the *ervah* relationship of *eishet achiv she-lo haya be-olamo* that Yissachar has to her persists in their view as well. The precise contours of the dispute run through the whole elaborate scenario, and the conclusion is that this six-brother construction operates *aliba de-Rabbi Shimon* — according to Rabbi Shimon's position.

---

## Three Brothers Case

### Three Brother Setup

The *mishnah* now presents a new scenario: three brothers, two of whom are married to two sisters, and one who is unattached — *mufneh*, literally empty, unoccupied. This is the *mishnah* of *sheloshah achim, shenayim mehem nesuim shetei achayot, ve-echad mufneh*. The case builds on everything established before but introduces a new complication: *maamar*, the rabbinic form of *kiddushin* performed in the context of *yibbum*.

The broader point of this *mishnah* is largely to establish the ruling of Rabbi Shimon. The *mishnah* teaches that in all related cases — two sisters, or a woman and her daughter, or a woman and her granddaughter, or a woman and the daughter of her son — *harei elu choltzot velo mityabmot*, they all perform *chalitzah* and not *yibbum*. But Rabbi Shimon goes further: *aval Rabbi Shimon poter* — Rabbi Shimon exempts them even from *chalitzah*. Because when a *zikah* would, if consummated, create a forbidden union of two sisters or mother and daughter, Rabbi Shimon treats it as a complete *ervah* situation, deriving from the verse *ve-isha el achotah lo tikach litzror* — do not take a woman together with her sister to create friction — that when the sisters become co-*yevamot*, there is no bond of *yibbum* at all, not even one requiring *chalitzah*. This is a striking position: what the Rabbanan treat as a rabbinic prohibition, Rabbi Shimon regards as a complete biblical exemption from the *mitzvah* entirely.

### Death and Maamar

The *mishnah*'s specific case: Reuven and Shimon are married to Rachel and Leah; Levi is unattached. Reuven dies. At that point, with Shimon still alive, there is no problem of *achot zekukato* — Levi could perform *yibbum* with Rachel without difficulty. Instead, Levi performs *maamar* with Rachel — the rabbinic act of *kiddushin* that a *yavam* may perform with his *yevamah* in lieu of or as a prelude to *yibbum*. Then, after the *maamar*, Shimon dies.

### Maamar Marriage Status

Now the question crystallizes. If Levi had performed full *yibbum* — actual consummation — with Rachel, then when Shimon dies and Leah falls before him, Leah would simply go free as *achot ishto*, his wife's sister. There would be no issue. But Levi performed only *maamar*, not *yibbum*. Is *maamar* sufficient to transform Rachel into his wife at the biblical level, such that Leah is truly considered *achot ishto* and may leave without *chalitzah*? Or does the *maamar* leave his relationship with Rachel in a kind of intermediate state — enough to matter rabbinically, but insufficient to achieve the full biblical transformation that would fully exempt Leah?

Two questions arise: first, may Levi now consummate the relationship with Rachel despite the new *zikah* to Leah — that is, does the *maamar* dissolve the *achot zekukato* concern even at the rabbinic level? Second, and more strikingly, may Leah simply walk away without *chalitzah* at all — does the *maamar* transform Rachel into Levi's wife sufficiently at the biblical level to make Leah *achot ishto* in the full sense?

### Beit Shammai Allow

Beit Shammai rule: *ishto imo, ve-halazu teitzei mishum achot isha* — his wife is with him, meaning he may consummate the relationship with Rachel, and Leah goes free on account of being his wife's sister. Beit Shammai treats the combination of *zikah* plus *maamar* as sufficient to establish Rachel as his wife even at the biblical level. Leah does not require even *chalitzah*.

### Beit Hillel Stringent

Beit Hillel take the opposing stringent position: *motzi et ishto b'get u-v'chalitzah ve-et eshet achiv b'chalitzah*. Beit Hillel hold that *maamar* alone is not sufficient to dissolve the *achot zekukato* problem. Once Shimon dies, Leah falls into *zikah* with Levi, and since Levi has not fully consummated with Rachel through *yibbum*, his relationship with Rachel has not fully transformed. Leah is still enough of a *zekukah* to make Rachel *achot zekukato*, and therefore Levi may not consummate with Rachel either.

The result for Beit Hillel is that Levi must: first, give Rachel a *get* on account of the *maamar* — since *maamar* is a rabbinic *kiddushin* and the rabbinic dissolution of *maamar* requires a *get*; second, perform *chalitzah* with Rachel on account of the original *zikah* that was never resolved through *yibbum*; and third, perform *chalitzah* with Leah for her *zikah*. Everything requires formal dissolution.

### Consequences Stated

*Zu hi she'amru: oy li al ishto ve-oy li al eshet achiv* — this is what the Sages meant when they said, woe for my wife and woe for my brother's wife. According to Beit Shammai everyone benefits: Rachel and Levi consummate their relationship, and Leah goes free without *chalitzah*. According to Beit Hillel, both women — Rachel and Leah — lose out: neither gains a proper resolution, and both require formal proceedings to extricate themselves. Notably, even in this lament, Rachel is already called *ishto*, his wife — Beit Shammai calls her that, reflecting that *kiddushin* through *maamar* did take effect at the rabbinic level.

---

## Maamar Analysis

### Maamar Not Complete

Rabbi Elazar clarifies the precise position of Beit Shammai regarding *maamar*: *lo teima maamar l'Beit Shammai koneh kinyan gamur* — do not say that *maamar* for Beit Shammai is a complete *kinyan* that fully replaces *yibbum* in every respect.

### Divorce Requirements

The test case: if after performing *maamar* Levi wished to dissolve the relationship with Rachel, would a *get* alone suffice, or would he also need to perform *chalitzah*? If *maamar* were a complete *kinyan* equivalent to *yibbum*, then since consummated *yibbum* would require only a *get* upon divorce, *maamar* treated as complete *yibbum* should likewise require only a *get*. But Rabbi Elazar implies that even Beit Shammai would require *chalitzah* in addition to the *get* if the relationship were to be dissolved.

### Partial Transformation

The formulation is: *maamar l'Beit Shammai eino koneh ella lidchot b'tzarah bilvad* — *maamar* for Beit Shammai only achieves the effect of pushing away the co-wife. It is sufficient to treat Leah as *achot ishto* so that she need not perform *chalitzah*, and it is sufficient for Levi to consummate with Rachel without the obstacle of *achot zekukato*. But it does not fully transform the relationship with Rachel such that *chalitzah* is no longer relevant if they were to separate. The relationship stands in an intermediate state: enough to push Leah away, but not a complete *kinyan*.

### Rabbi Avin Support

Rabbi Avin adds: *af anan nami tanina* — we too have taught this from an earlier *mishnah*. In the previous case involving four brothers and two sisters, if the brothers went ahead and performed *yibbum* despite the *achot zekukah* situation — that is, in violation of the rabbinic prohibition — Beit Shammai says *yekayemu*, they may remain married. This is *be-di'avad* — after the fact, they did something impermissible but the marriage holds. The *achot zekukah* prohibition is rabbinic, and once *yibbum* was performed, the marriage stands.

### Why Not Maamar First

This raises an obvious question: given that Beit Shammai holds *maamar* pushes away the co-wife and lets the remaining *yibbum* proceed, why not do the following? In the original four-brother case where *achot zekukah* applies, have Levi perform *maamar* with Rachel first — not *yibbum*, just *maamar*, which nobody prohibited — and once *maamar* transforms Rachel into his wife (pushing Leah off the scene), then perform *yibbum* with Rachel legitimately. If *maamar* is enough to push Leah off entirely, why can one not do *maamar* first and then *yibbum*, thereby achieving a clean and fully permissible outcome?

The fact that the *mishnah* does not permit this, and instead says that doing *yibbum* in such a case is only permissible *be-di'avad*, must mean that this trick does not work.

### Maamar Timing

The answer: *maamar de-heiteira dachi; maamar de-issura lo dachi* — *maamar* that is performed permissibly works; *maamar* performed in the presence of a competing *zikah* does not work. In the case of the *mishnah* — the three-brother case — the *maamar* was done while Shimon was still alive and before any problem of *achot zekukato* arose. At the moment of the *maamar*, it was entirely permissible, and when Shimon subsequently dies, Leah falls before a man who already has a legitimate *maamar* with Rachel. The *maamar* was *de-heiteira* — done in a state of full permissibility.

But in the four-brother case, attempting to do *maamar* after both brothers have died and the *zikah* to both sisters already exists — that is a *maamar de-issura*. Since Levi is not permitted to perform *yibbum* with Rachel in the face of the *achot zekukato* problem, the *maamar* with Rachel cannot carry any legal weight. If *yibbum* itself is unavailable, *maamar* — which is a rabbinic shadow of *yibbum* — loses its significance. The trick is therefore unavailable.

### Timing Makes Difference

Having resolved that question, the analysis returns to whether *maamar* is a full *kinyan* or only a partial one. Whichever position one takes — whether *maamar* for Beit Shammai is a hundred percent or only ninety-five percent — the *maamar de-heiteira / maamar de-issura* distinction already disposes of the question of why the trick was not available. What remains is the separate, unresolved question: when *maamar* does work, how strong is it? Is it complete enough that if Levi and Rachel then separate, only a *get* is required — or does *chalitzah* remain necessary as well? That is the question Rabbi Elazar raised, and it continues to drive the analysis forward.

---

## Rav Ashi Analysis

### Rav Ashi Teaching

Rav Ashi presents a further version of this discussion, citing Rav Elazar's clarification directly: *lo teima maamar l'Beit Shammai dachi dechiyah gemurah ve-tzaratah chalitzah nami lo ba'aya* — do not say that *maamar* for Beit Shammai pushes the co-wife away completely such that she does not even require *chalitzah*. Rav Elazar's formulation in Rav Ashi's presentation refines the analysis of how much weight *maamar* carries for Beit Shammai, and the precise nature of its effect on both the woman herself and her co-wife. This discussion will be taken up and continued in the following session.

---

---

# Yevamot 29

## Maamar Status (Beit Sham…

### Maamar as Kinyan

The sugya opens by returning to the bottom of 29a in order to reframe the central question and correct a slightly imprecise reading from the previous session. The *mishna* had described a case involving three brothers — Reuven, Shimon, and Levi — where Reuven and Shimon are each married to one of two sisters, Rachel and Leah. Reuven dies, and before Shimon dies, Levi performs *maamar* with Rachel. Then Shimon dies. The dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel turns on the legal weight of that *maamar*.

Beit Shammai holds that Leah simply walks away — she is free without *yibum* or *chalitzah* — while Beit Hillel requires both a *get* and *chalitzah* with Leah (to counteract the *maamar*) and a *get* and *chalitzah* with Rachel. Beit Shammai's position implies that *maamar* carries a real *de-Oraita* status: it not only removes the problem of *achot zikukato*, which is itself only *derabbanan*, but it frees Leah to walk away entirely, as though she were an *erva* in the full sense. The *gemara* now wants to determine exactly how powerful that *maamar* is.

### Pushes Off Co-wife

The *gemara* introduces this question through Rabbi Elazar: *lo teima maamar l'Beit Shammai koneh kinyan gamur* — do not say that *maamar* according to Beit Shammai is a complete *kinyan*, equivalent in every respect to the consummation of *yibum* itself. The proof of a complete *kinyan gamur* would be that if Levi now wished to divorce Rachel, he would need only a *get*, just as in an ordinary marriage after *yibum*, where the *yibum* dimension is fully spent and no *chalitzah* is required for dissolution. Rabbi Elazar rejects this. Even if *maamar* frees Leah entirely, it does not complete the relationship with Rachel to that degree. Should Levi wish to divorce Rachel, he would require both a *get* and *chalitzah*, because there remains a residual dimension of the *yibum* bond.

The formulation is precise: *maamar l'Beit Shammai eino koneh ela lidechot bi-tzarah bilvad* — what the *maamar* accomplishes is to push off Leah, to give her a sufficiently strong *erva* status that she can walk away, while the relationship with Rachel remains not yet fully concluded. It is strong enough to free Leah but not strong enough to fully discharge the *yibum* obligation with Rachel.

### Maamar de-Heitera

Rav Avin then attempts to find support for Rabbi Elazar's position from the *mishna* itself. The earlier *mishna* had discussed a case where both brothers died more or less simultaneously, or where no *maamar* had been performed before either death, creating a situation in which Levi and Yehuda cannot perform *yibum* with Rachel and Leah because each is *achot zikukato* of the other. Beit Shammai says that if they went ahead and consummated the *yibum* anyway (*yekayemu*), they may remain married — *bidi'avad* yes, *l'chatchilah* no.

Rav Avin's argument is this: if *maamar* according to Beit Shammai were a *kinyan gamur*, there would be a ready solution in that lower case even *l'chatchilah*. Since nobody prohibits performing *maamar* — the prohibition is only on the act of intercourse with *achot zikukato* — one could simply do *maamar* with Rachel, thereby fully acquiring her and removing Leah from the *zika* picture entirely, and then consummate with Rachel. Then the other brother would do the same with Leah. If *maamar* were truly 100%, this should resolve the problem.

The *gemara* presses back: this objection applies equally whether you say *maamar* is *kinyan gamur* or whether you say it is merely *dechiya gemura* — that it fully pushes Leah off without constituting a complete acquisition of Rachel. Either way, the same question stands: why not use *maamar* to push the co-wife out of the picture and then consummate? The *gemara* therefore concludes that neither formulation can draw a proof from the structure of the case below, and offers a different resolution entirely.

The resolution is *maamar de-heteira dachi, de-issura lo dachi* — or in the parallel formulation, *maamar de-heteira kanei, de-issura lo kanei*. The *maamar* that Levi performed with Rachel in the *mishna* was done before Shimon died, at a point when *yibum* with Rachel was fully permissible. A *maamar* introduced into an uncomplicated, permitted situation carries legal force. In the case below, however, there is already a prohibition in place — the *achot zikukato* problem means *yibum* is already forbidden — and a *maamar* performed in that context of *issura* does not carry the same weight and cannot resolve the entanglement. This is what distinguishes the workable case from the unworkable one, regardless of whether *maamar* is *kinyan gamur* or merely *dechiya gemura*.

The upshot of the entire discussion to this point is that the core question remains open within Beit Shammai: is *maamar* a *kinyan gamur*, such that only a *get* would be needed from Rachel; or is it *dechiya gemura*, fully pushing Leah off but leaving the *yibum* dimension with Rachel incomplete, such that both a *get* and *chalitzah* would still be required?

### Meshayer Position

Rav Ashi now introduces a third, yet more restricted reading of Beit Shammai's position. Where the previous discussion debated whether *maamar* achieves *kinyan gamur* or merely *dechiya gemura* vis-à-vis Rachel, Rav Ashi teaches that the question is not about Rachel at all but rather about Leah. *Lo teimar maamar l'Beit Shammai dachi dechiya gemura* — do not say that *maamar* pushes Leah off completely, freeing her without any remaining need for *chalitzah*. Rather, *doche u-meshayyer hu* — the *maamar* pushes Leah off enough that Levi is not guilty of *achot zikukato* when he consummates with Rachel, but it leaves a residual connection to Leah such that she would still require *chalitzah* to be fully freed.

This reading is significantly more restrictive than what the *mishna* appears to say, and the *gemara* will challenge it on precisely those grounds.

### Meshayer Contradiction

Rav Avin responds by pointing directly to the *mishna*'s language. The *mishna* states explicitly: *ishto imo v'halazu teitzei mishum achot isha* — his wife Rachel remains with him, and Leah walks away as his wife's sister. The *mishna* says she walks away. There is no mention of any *chalitzah* required of Leah. The language of *teitzei* is unambiguous, and it undermines the *meshayer* position entirely. According to Beit Shammai as read in the *mishna*, Leah simply goes free; the *maamar* has effected a real *de-Oraita* change in her status.

### Yevama Distinction

The *gemara* does not abandon the *maamar de-heteira / maamar de-issura* framework but instead uses it to explain why the *meshayer* position fails in the lower case. The principle articulated is: *yevama de-chazya le-kulhu chazya le-miktzata* — a *yevama* who was eligible for *yibum* (from this *yavam*) can be affected by even a partial *maamar*. *Yevama de-lo chazya le-kulhu lo chazya le-miktzata* — a *yevama* who was ineligible for *yibum*, because the prohibition of *achot zikukato* was already in place, is not affected even by a partial *maamar*. This is simply another formulation of the *maamar de-heteira* principle.

The *gemara*'s final accounting on the *meshayer* question is that it clearly runs against the *mishna*. The *mishna* shows Leah walking away entirely. Of the remaining positions, the *gemara* has left open whether Beit Shammai holds *kinyan gamur* — in which case only a *get* is needed from Rachel — or *dechiya gemura* — in which case Leah is fully freed but a *get* and *chalitzah* are still needed from Rachel because the *yibum* dimension has not been fully discharged.

One might ask how a *maamar*, widely understood to be *derabbanan*, could produce the *de-Oraita* effect of freeing Leah without *chalitzah*. The *Yerushalmi* addresses this directly. It derives a biblical basis for Beit Shammai's position from the verse *yevamah yavo aleha ve-lakacha lo le-isha ve-yibbmah* — the *Yerushalmi* reads *ve-lakacha lo le-isha* as a reference to *maamar*-style acquisition, and *ve-yibbmah* as the act of *yibum* itself, identifying *lekicha l'ishah* as a *de-Oraita* component of the *yibum* process according to Beit Shammai.

---

## Maamar Completeness

### Nisuin Question

Rava now pushes the inquiry in an entirely different direction. Assuming Beit Shammai holds *maamar* to be a real *kinyan* — perhaps even *kinyan gamur* — the question becomes not merely whether it is stronger than standard *kiddushin* but whether it might accomplish something even beyond *kiddushin*: does *maamar* according to Beit Shammai achieve *nisuin* status, or only *eirusin*?

This is a striking question, given that *maamar* consists of a verbal declaration analogous to *kiddushin* and involves no act of consummation. But Rava is probing whether the unique *de-Oraita* framework of Beit Shammai might assign it a higher categorization.

### Abaye's Answer

Abaye asks: *le-mai hilchata* — what practical difference are you asking about? If the question is whether the rights associated with *nisuin* — inheritance, the husband's right to become *tamei* for her as a *kohen*, and annulment of vows without the father's participation — if that is what you mean, Abaye says those cannot apply to *maamar*.

### Eirusin Rights

The proof lies in the status of ordinary *eirusin*. A *baraita* taught in the school of Rabbi Chiyya specifies the rights that do *not* yet apply after *kiddushin* alone: the husband does not have *onen* status upon her death, does not become *tamei* for her even if he is a *kohen*, does not inherit her, and she does not inherit him (though she may collect her *ketuvah* if one was written). All of these belong to the *nisuin* stage.

Abaye's argument follows a *kal va-chomer*: if standard *eirusin*, which is *de-Oraita*, does not confer these rights, how could *maamar* — which is at most a *de-Oraita* institution of a different and arguably lesser character — do so? The *Ritva* presses on this, noting that within the *sugya* we are operating according to Beit Shammai who considers *maamar* to have biblical force, and therefore the question is not about its rabbinic versus biblical status but about its intrinsic weight. The *Ritva* points to another *gemara* indicating that a woman who has relations with another man after *maamar* but before the act of *yibum* does not incur the full penalty of *eishet ish*, even according to Beit Shammai — which shows that even where *maamar* may be *de-Oraita*, it does not carry the full gravity of an ordinary marital relationship.

### Chuppah Requirement

Rava refines the question. If *nisuin* rights are off the table regardless — since even *eirusin de-Oraita* does not produce them — then what is the actual question? The question, Rava clarifies, is about *mesirah la-chuppah*: does *maamar* itself constitute something equivalent to *chuppah*, so that no subsequent act of *nisuin* is required? Or does it function only as *eirusin*, meaning that after *maamar*, before proceeding to *yibum*, a formal act of *nisuin* — entrance under the *chuppah* — would also be required?

This question is not merely abstract. If, having performed *maamar*, the *yavam* is understood to have stepped onto the *kiddushin* track rather than the *yibum* track, then perhaps the rabbinic structure of *yibum* demands that *nisuin* follow *maamar* before consummation, just as *chuppah* follows *kiddushin* in ordinary marriage. Rava is asking: having done *maamar*, must one also perform an act of *nisuin* before proceeding?

### Bi'ah as Chuppah

The *gemara* responds by observing that in the ordinary case of *yibum* — where no *maamar* is performed — the *Torah* states *yevamah yavo aleha*, and this can take place *be'al korchah*, even against her will. The act of intercourse itself constitutes the completion of the *yibum* and brings with it whatever the equivalent of *nisuin* would be. This is because any consensual cohabitation naturally serves as *chuppah*, and even non-consensual *yibum* is halachically effective — a point the *gemara* acknowledges is deeply difficult but which it does not soften. The implication is that the act of intercourse itself, in any context of *yibum*, serves as *chuppah*.

Therefore, even if *maamar* places the parties on the *kiddushin* track, the subsequent act of *yibum* — the bi'ah — would itself constitute *chuppah*. The question of whether one would separately need an act of *mesirah la-chuppah* appears to dissolve, at least in the case without *maamar*, since bi'ah inherently is *chuppah*.

### Zikat Yevamim Removal

The deeper answer emerges from Rava's own statement, introduced with *sh'ani omer*: *kol ha-oseh maamar b'yevamto, parcha mimenu zikat yevamin* — whoever performs *maamar* with his *yevama*, the bond of *zikat yevamin* actually departs from him entirely, *v'chal alav zikat eirusin* — and is replaced entirely by the bond of *eirusin*. According to this view, once *maamar* is performed, the parties are no longer in the *yibum* track at all. The *zika* is gone and the relationship has been converted entirely into an *eirusin* relationship. This is a remarkable restructuring: the *maamar* does not supplement *yibum* but displaces it entirely and initiates a new marital trajectory.

If that is true, then the question of *chuppah* is genuine: they are now in an *eirusin* state, not a *yibum* state, and the subsequent act of consummation is no longer the act of *yibum be'al korchah* but must be framed as a *nisuin* within the ordinary marital model. This remains among the most fascinating theoretical positions within Beit Shammai's account of *maamar* — the idea that *maamar* does not merely strengthen or initiate the *yibum* process but fundamentally redirects it.

---

## Hafarat Nedarim

### Shomeret Yavam

The *gemara* now introduces a case involving *hafarat nedarim* — annulment of vows — as a means of probing the status of *maamar*. The case concerns a *shomeret yavam*, a woman waiting for her *yavam* to perform either *yibum* or *chalitzah*, who makes a vow. The question is whether the *yavam* (or *yevamin*, if there are more than one) can annul her vows.

### Rabbinic Dispute

Three *tanna'im* dispute this. Rabbi Eliezer says *yafer* — he can annul the vows. Rabbi Yehoshua says that only if there is a single *yavam* can he annul; if there are two *yevamin*, neither can annul. Rabbi Akiva says that not even a single *yavam* can annul — the *zika* alone is insufficient to confer the right of *hafarat nedarim*.

The *gemara* notes that Rabbi Akiva's position is internally coherent: he holds *ein zika* — the bond of *zika* is legally insufficient, even with a single *yavam*. Rabbi Yehoshua is also coherent: with one *yavam* there is *zika* directed clearly at him and he may annul; with two the *zika* is diffuse and neither has a strong enough individual relationship to annul alone. The difficulty is with Rabbi Eliezer, who evidently allows annulment even when there are two *yevamin*. One can understand why a single *yavam* could annul, but if there are two, neither has an exclusive claim — how can either one annul?

### Maamar Context

Rabbi Ami bar Abba resolves this by identifying the precise case under discussion: *kegon she-asah bah maamar* — it is a case where one of the two *yevamin* has already performed *maamar* with the woman, and the dispute reflects the position of Beit Shammai that *maamar koneh kinyan gamur*. The *maamar* singles out one of the *yevamin* as the one with the active relationship, which is why Rabbi Eliezer permits him to annul.

### Nisuin vs Eirusin

This identification has immediate implications. *Ei amart bishlama nisuin osah, mishum hachi mefer* — if *maamar* achieves *nisuin* status, one can readily explain why the *yavam* who performed *maamar* can annul her vows on his own, since a husband in the *nisuin* stage annuls alone. But if *maamar* only achieves *eirusin* status, there is a difficulty: the law (*mishna* in *Nedarim*) is that for a *na'arah me'orasah*, vows are annulled jointly by the *arus* and the father. If the *maamar* puts her in an *eirusin* state, the *yavam* should need the father's participation and could not annul alone.

This appears to be strong evidence that *maamar* achieves *nisuin*, not merely *eirusin*: the ability to annul alone is the hallmark of *nisuin* status.

### Partnership Annulment

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak challenges the inference. *Mai mefer? Mefer b'shutfut* — when the *tanna* says *yafer*, perhaps it means the *yavam* annuls in partnership with the father. The word *yafer* does not necessarily mean he annuls alone; it could be read as his participation in a joint annulment. On this reading, *maamar* achieves only *eirusin*, and the *yavam* annuls together with the father, which fully accords with the law of *na'arah me'orasah*.

### Meshayer & Hafara

The *gemara* then returns to Rabbi Elazar's position — the earlier view that *maamar* only pushes the co-wife off and does not even constitute *kinyan gamur* with Rachel. If that is the framework, how does *hafarat nedarim* work at all, even in partnership with the father? The *kinyan gamur* assumption was the prerequisite for any *eirusin*-level analysis; if we are below even that, neither alone nor with the father should suffice.

Rabbi Elazar responds: his statement — *eino koneh ela lidechot b'tzarah bilvad* — was only about the consequence of needing a *get* and *chalitzah* rather than just a *get* from Rachel. It does not mean the *kiddushin* itself is incomplete or lacking. The *kiddushin* component is fully present; what has not yet been discharged is the *yevama* dimension. On this reading, one can say she is simultaneously a full *arusah* — in which case he can annul with the father — while also retaining a residual status as *yevama* that requires *chalitzah* to discharge. These are two parallel statuses rather than a partially completed single status. This is a nuanced position: not partial acquisition, but dual status.

### Court Support Case

If this reading still seems strained — since Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's proposed answer requires him to annul in partnership, but the *baraita* uses the singular *yafer* — the *gemara* offers a different account of the entire case. *She'amda b'din u-fasku lah mezonot mishelo* — this is a case where the woman appeared before a court and the court ordered the *yavam* to support her financially until he performs either *yibum* or *chalitzah*. In that context, the *hafara* is not a formal act of *hafarat nedarim* at all but rather reflects the principle stated by Rav Pinchas in the name of Rava: *kol ha-noderet al da'at ba'alah hi noderet* — a woman who makes a vow does so implicitly with her husband's implicit consent in mind, and therefore vows made under conditions where she is financially dependent on him and seeking to preserve the relationship are understood as conditional on his agreement from the outset. This is not a technical *hafarat nedarim* within the *Torah*'s framework but an implicit stipulation, and the reason it is confined to this unusual case rather than applied universally is precisely that it depends on the particular type of relationship and financial dependency involved.

The broader takeaway from this entire section is a rich menu of possible standings for *maamar* according to Beit Shammai: full *kinyan gamur* requiring only a *get*; *kiddushin* with a residual *yevama* status requiring both *get* and *chalitzah*; and the radical option that *maamar* removes *zikat yevamin* entirely and places the couple on a pure *eirusin* track — potentially even requiring a formal *chuppah* before consummation.

---

## Complex Sibling Cases

### Case 1: Rachel Then Leah

The *mishna* now turns to a series of cases involving three brothers, two of whom are married to two sisters, and one of whom is married to an unrelated woman (*nochrit*). In the first case, Reuven is married to Rachel, Shimon is married to Leah, and Levi is married to Devorah.

In the sequence: Reuven dies; Levi performs *yibum* with Rachel (he is the only eligible *yavam*); then Levi dies. Now Shimon survives with two women before him: Rachel (Levi's now-wife, formerly Reuven's wife) and Devorah (Levi's original wife).

### Case 1 Result

*Ha-rishona yotzei'a mishum achot isha* — Rachel walks away because she is now Shimon's wife's sister (the sister of Leah, who is Shimon's wife). *Ve-ha-shniya mishum tzaratah* — Devorah requires *chalitzah* and may not have *yibum* because she is a co-wife of a woman who is forbidden to Shimon.

The *mishna* then addresses the scenario where Levi performed *maamar* rather than *yibum* with Rachel before dying. In that case, since we are now operating within the framework of Beit Hillel (not Beit Shammai), the *maamar* creates only a quasi-marital relationship. Rachel, being the quasi-wife of Levi, is effectively an *erva* in the *yibum* context for Shimon. Devorah therefore becomes a quasi-*tzarat erva*. The ruling is *nochrit choletzet ve-lo mityabemet* — Devorah must perform *chalitzah* and cannot have *yibum*, because the *maamar* has implicated her as a co-wife of a quasi-forbidden woman.

### No Zikat Proof

The *gemara* extracts a further inference. *Ta'ama de-avad bah maamar* — the reason Devorah is in a problematic status is specifically because Levi performed *maamar* with Rachel, creating that quasi-marital bond. *Ha lo avad bah maamar, nochrit yibumi nami mityabma* — had Levi not done *maamar*, the implication of the *mishna* is that Shimon could go ahead and perform full *yibum* with Devorah. But this requires attention: even without *maamar*, Levi had a *zika* with Rachel — a bond of the *yibum* relationship. After Levi dies with that *zika* intact, does that *zika* not create a quasi-marital connection to Rachel that would implicate Devorah as a quasi-*tzarat erva*?

The *mishna*'s implication that Shimon could do *yibum* with Devorah if no *maamar* was done answers this question. Rav Nachman draws the conclusion: *zot omeret ein zika va-afilu b'chad acha* — this demonstrates that there is no operative *zika*, even with a single *yavam*. The *zika* alone, without *maamar*, does not create a strong enough relationship to render Rachel a quasi-wife and Devorah a quasi-*tzarat erva*. This principle — *ein zika* — is one of the major *machlokot* in *masechet Yevamot*, and Rav Nachman here identifies this *mishna* as evidence for that position.

### Case 2: Devorah First

The second configuration: Levi (married to Devorah) dies first. Reuven, who is married to Rachel, performs *yibum* with Devorah. Then Reuven dies. Now Shimon has before him: Leah (his own wife, who is an *erva* to Reuven — his wife's sister — but is not a *yibum* candidate for Shimon since she is his own wife), Rachel (his wife's sister, an *erva* in the *yibum* context), and Devorah (Reuven's *yibum*-wife).

### Case 2 Result

The ruling: *ha-rishona yotzei'a mishum achot isha* — Rachel walks away as Shimon's wife's sister. *Ve-ha-shniya mishum tzaratah* — Devorah requires *chalitzah* as the co-wife of Rachel, who is an *erva*. As in case one, if Reuven had performed *maamar* with Devorah rather than *yibum* before dying, the result is that Devorah requires *chalitzah* and cannot have *yibum* — she is now the co-wife of a quasi-*erva*.

The structural difference from case one: in case one, the *maamar* was performed with Rachel (who is the *erva* — Shimon's wife's sister), and Devorah was implicated as *tzarat erva*. In case two, the real wife — Rachel, who is genuinely Shimon's wife's sister — is the *erva*, and Devorah is implicated through the *maamar* as a quasi-*tzarat erva*.

### Kal Va-Chomer

The *gemara* questions why the *mishna* needed to teach both cases. *Hainu hach* — are they not essentially the same ruling? The *gemara* responds with a *kal va-chomer*. In case one, the *erva* is the quasi-wife — brought in through *maamar* — and yet that was sufficient to render Devorah (who is the genuine *yibum* candidate, the real wife) forbidden to *yibum*. If even a quasi-*erva* suffices to block *yibum* with the real wife, then certainly in case two — where the *erva* is the full, genuine wife and Devorah is only quasi-implicated through *maamar* — one would expect the prohibition to apply. Case two, then, is the more obvious of the two, derivable by *kal va-chomer* from case one.

Why, then, were both cases taught? The *gemara* explains: *tana hacha tana bereisha* — the second case (case two, where the *erva* is the real wife) was actually taught first. And the reason is that the author initially entertained the possibility that in case one, where the basic *de-Oraita* obligation of *yibum* runs toward Devorah and the *erva* is only quasi-connected through *maamar*, perhaps the genuine *yibum* obligation should override the *maamar*-generated complication and *yibum* should be permitted. The *tanna* thought about it and then ruled no — even in that case, *chalitzah* is required. Because that was the more novel ruling — the greater *chiddush* — it was placed first. And once it was placed first, the subsequent *mishna* was retained even though it is technically superfluous, since once you prohibit the harder case, the easier case follows automatically. *Tosafot* notes that one might normally expect the formula *zu ve-ein tzarich lomar zu* to handle such redundancy, but that usage applies to a brief additional phrase, not an entire separately formulated *mishna* restating a full scenario.

---

## Status Lock at Death

### Sequence of Deaths

A third scenario unfolds. Once again: three brothers, two married to sisters, one to an unrelated woman. Reuven dies. Before Levi acts — before any *yibum* or *maamar* is performed — Leah dies. Then Levi dies. Now Rachel and Devorah stand before Shimon.

The question: Rachel was Shimon's wife's sister when Reuven died. But Leah has since died, and Leah's death dissolved the *achot isha* prohibition. By the time Levi dies and the *yibum* obligation crystallizes for Shimon, Rachel is no longer Shimon's wife's sister. May Shimon now perform *yibum* with Rachel?

### Olamit Forbidding

The *mishna* answers with striking finality: *harei zu asurah alav olamit ho'il ve-nesrah alav sha'ah achat* — she is permanently forbidden to him, because she was forbidden to him for even one moment. At the moment Reuven died — *sha'ah achat* — Rachel was Shimon's wife's sister and *yibum* was impossible. That original moment of prohibition is determinative. Even though the *achot isha* prohibition subsequently fell away with Leah's death, the status has been locked.

### Rav Yehuda's Rule

Rav Yehuda formulates a general principle in the name of Rav: *kol yevama she-eina nikraat bah bi-sha'at nefila yevama yavo aleha, harei hi ke-eshet ach she-yesh lah banim ve-asurah* — any *yevama* who cannot have the verse *yevama yavo aleha* applied to her at the moment she becomes a *yevama* (i.e., at the moment of the husband's death) is treated like a brother's wife who has children from her husband — an *eshet ach* for whom *yibum* is forbidden — and she remains permanently forbidden.

The logic is precise. The moment Reuven died, two things happened to Rachel simultaneously: she became a candidate for *yibum* with any eligible *yavam*, and she was prohibited as *achot isha* to Shimon. Since at that moment of *nefila* the verse *yevama yavo aleha* could not be applied to her in relation to Shimon, she acquired the status of an *eshet ach* forbidden as such — not merely the contingent status of *achot isha* — and that status does not dissolve when the *achot isha* prohibition later falls away.

### Attribution Question

The *gemara* asks: *mai kamashma lan?* What is Rav Yehuda adding beyond what the *mishna* itself already states? The *mishna* explicitly says *harei zu asurah lo olamit ho'il ve-nesrah alav sha'ah achat*. That is precisely what Rav Yehuda said.

### Status Finality

The *gemara* answers that Rav Yehuda's *chiddush* addresses a case not covered by the *mishna*. The *mishna* describes a situation where Rachel was continuously *asurah* to Shimon throughout the entire period that she was a *yevama* — from Reuven's death through Levi's *yibum* — and only after Levi married her did Leah die. Her *asur* status was unbroken. One might say this unbroken status is what makes the *issur* permanent.

But what if the status changed while she was still in the *yibum* process — before any *yavam* acted? For instance: Reuven dies, and then — before anyone performs *yibum* or *chalitzah* — Leah dies. Rachel's *achot isha* status dissolves. She is no longer *asurah* to Shimon. And she is still available for *yibum* from Levi. Perhaps now, since her status vis-à-vis Shimon has changed while she is still in the open *yibum* period, she should be permitted to Shimon if Levi later dies. This is the case Rav Yehuda rules on: even here, the status at the moment of death controls, and she remains forbidden.

### Death Status Lock

The *gemara* challenges this by citing yet another *mishna*: *shenei achim nesu'im shtei achayot* — two brothers married to two sisters. One dies; the other cannot perform *yibum* because his *yevama* is his wife's sister. Then his wife (the surviving sister) dies. Now the *yevama* is no longer his wife's sister. The *mishna* rules: *harei zu asurah lo olamit ho'il ve-nesrah alav sha'ah achat*. This is the same *halacha*, and it covers the very case Rav Yehuda is addressing — where the *achot isha* prohibition disappears before any *yibum* is done, and there is only one brother who could theoretically perform *yibum*.

The *gemara* distinguishes: in the case of only one surviving brother, when the first husband dies and the sole surviving brother cannot act because of *achot isha*, we might say the entire *yibum* process is finished for her vis-à-vis that household — she has been completely pushed away. The *mishna* tells us even then she remains forbidden. In Rav Yehuda's case, however — with multiple brothers — when Reuven dies, Rachel has not been completely rejected from the household. Levi remains and can perform *yibum*. She is still in process, still within the *yibum* framework. One might think that since she has not been closed off from the household entirely, a subsequent change in her *achot isha* status could permit her to Shimon. Rav Yehuda teaches that this reasoning fails: the status at the moment of *nefila* is final, and the process of being in flux does not reopen the question.

---

## Divorce Case

### Divorce Permits Yibum

The final *mishna* of this sequence introduces a variant: instead of death, *divorce*. The setup is the same — three brothers, Reuven married to Rachel, Shimon married to Leah, Levi married to Devorah. Now Shimon divorces Leah. Then Levi dies. Can Shimon perform *yibum* with Devorah?

Yes. Shimon divorced Leah; Devorah is not *achot ishto* in the relevant sense, and there is no obstacle to *yibum*. *Ve-chanas ha-migaresh* — Shimon performs *yibum* with Devorah. Then Shimon dies.

### Life vs Divorce

The prohibition of *achot isha* applies only *bechayeha* — while the sister-wife lives. Divorce has the same structural effect as death in removing the *achot isha* prohibition: once Leah has been divorced, Rachel ceases to be *achot ishto* in the operative sense (for purposes of the *yibum* framework), just as she would cease to be *achot ishto* if Leah had died. The *mishna* here demonstrates that it is the ongoing existence of the marital bond — not merely the woman's physical life — that generates the prohibition for the co-wife.

### All Permit Conclusion

The *mishna* concludes: *kulan she-metu o she-nitgareshu tzaroteihen mutarot* — in all the cases, if the sisters died or were divorced, their co-wives are permitted. This is the general principle: the *tzara* stands forbidden only as long as the *achot isha* prohibition is active — whether because the sister-wife is alive and still married. Once death or divorce removes that prohibition, the co-wife is freed, and there is no doctrine of *sha'ah achat* applying here to lock in a prior status. The *sha'ah achat* principle is operative only where a *yibum* status crystallized at a moment of death; divorce, operating prospectively, does not retroactively implicate the *tzara*.

---

---

# Yevamot 29b

## Ma'amar Status

### Opening & Reframing

We begin today with a brief return to the bottom of 29a, not because we have time to spare, but because yesterday's presentation of the *gemara* requires a small correction, and the core question needs to be reframed before we can proceed.

### Mishnah Setup

The *mishnah* before us presents the following scenario: Reuven and Shimon are brothers, married respectively to Rachel and Leah, who are sisters. Reuven dies. Before Shimon dies, Levi performs *ma'amar* with Rachel — a formal declaration of betrothal in the context of *yibum*, falling just short of the act of *yibum* itself. Then Shimon dies, leaving Leah as a second potential *yevamah*.

### Beit Shammai View

Beit Shammai holds that the *ma'amar* Levi performed with Rachel is sufficient to effectively complete the *yibum* relationship with her, so that when Leah subsequently becomes a widow, she walks away entirely. This is a striking position: it implies that *ma'amar* carries real *de'oraita* weight, powerful enough to free Leah not merely from a rabbinic restriction but from any *yibum* obligation whatsoever — she is released as an *ervah*, his wife's sister. Beit Hillel, by contrast, maintains that both Rachel and Leah now share the status of *achot zekukato*, and Levi must perform *chalitzah* with Leah and *chalitzah* with Rachel (along with a *get* to undo the *ma'amar*). The question the *gemara* now pursues is: precisely how powerful is this *ma'amar* according to Beit Shammai?

### Rabbi Elazar

Rabbi Elazar opens with a qualification. Do not say, he teaches — *lo teima ma'amar le-Veit Shammai koneh kinyan gamur* — that *ma'amar* for Beit Shammai constitutes a complete *kinyan*, the full equivalent of *yibum*. The evidence that it is not fully equivalent would be this: if it were a complete *kinyan*, then should Levi wish to separate from Rachel afterward, a *get* alone would suffice, just as in an ordinary marriage. But Rabbi Elazar holds that even after *ma'amar*, both a *get* and *chalitzah* would be required. What *ma'amar* accomplishes, he says, is *lidchot batzara bilvad* — it pushes off the *tzarah*, it frees Leah from any obligation — but the *yibum* component with Rachel has not been fully discharged. There remains some residue of the *yibum* relationship even as Leah walks free.

### Achot Zekukato Test

Rav Avin then brings a proof from the *mishnah* itself. In a different case — one where two brothers each face a sister-in-law who is the *achot zekukato* of the other's potential *yevamah* — Beit Shammai rules that if the brothers went ahead and performed *yibum* in that complicated scenario, the marriages stand *bedieved*, but *lechatchila* they may not. Now, if *ma'amar* were a complete *kinyan gamur*, there would be an obvious *lechatchila* solution available: let one brother perform *ma'amar* with his *yevamah*, thereby fully acquiring her and removing the other woman from the *zika* entirely, and then let the second brother proceed likewise. The fact that Beit Shammai offers no such solution suggests that *ma'amar* is not a complete *kinyan*.

But the *gemara* pushes back: this same question arises equally whether *ma'amar* is a *kinyan gamur* or merely a *dichiya gemura* — a complete pushing-off without full acquisition. Either way, if the *ma'amar* frees Leah, why can't the brothers use *ma'amar* to resolve the problem in the simultaneous case? The question applies symmetrically.

### Ma'amar DeHeteira

The resolution emerges from a crucial principle: *ma'amar de-heteira dachi, de-issura lo dachi*. A *ma'amar* performed in a legally uncomplicated situation — where *yibum* itself would have been permissible — carries weight and produces its legal effect. A *ma'amar* attempted to cut through an existing prohibition — *ma'amar de-issura* — accomplishes nothing. In the original *mishnah* case, Levi performed *ma'amar* with Rachel before Leah became a widow and before any problem of *achot zekukato* arose. That *ma'amar* came in at a moment of *heter* and therefore had the power to free Leah when she subsequently fell into the *yibum* pool. In the simultaneous case, the problem of *achot zekukato* already exists at the moment of the proposed *ma'amar*, and so the *ma'amar* cannot cut through it.

This principle applies identically whether *ma'amar* is framed as *kinyan gamur* or *dichiya gemura*: *ma'amar de-heteira kani, de-issura lo kani*. The distinction is not about the strength of *ma'amar* but about the circumstances into which it enters. So the unresolved question remains: does *ma'amar* constitute a complete *kinyan* requiring only a *get*, or is it *dichiya gemura* — Leah is fully out, but Rachel's relationship with Levi is incomplete, requiring both a *get* and *chalitzah*?

### Rav Ashi Reading

Rav Ashi now proposes a third reading, one that reduces the power of *ma'amar* even further. Do not say, teaches Rav Ashi in the name of Rabbi Elazar, that *ma'amar* for Beit Shammai is a *dichiya gemura* — a complete pushing-off of Leah. Rather, it is *docheh u-meshayer*: it pushes Leah off but leaves some remnant of connection even with respect to Leah herself. On this reading, the *ma'amar* is strong enough to weaken the *zika* to Leah so that the prohibition of *achot zekukato* no longer blocks consummation with Rachel — that rabbinic prohibition is sufficiently addressed. But the connection to Leah has not been entirely severed, and therefore Leah would still require *chalitzah*.

### Rejection of Rav Ashi

The *gemara* immediately rejects this reading from the *mishnah* itself. The *mishnah* states explicitly: *ishto imo, ve-halezu tetzei mi-shum achot isha* — his wife Rachel is his, and Leah walks away entirely because she is his wife's sister. There is no *chalitzah* required with Leah. The *mishnah* makes clear that Beit Shammai's *ma'amar* completely frees Leah, with no residual obligation. Rav Ashi's reading of *docheh u-meshayer* is simply incompatible with the *mishnah*'s language.

The *gemara* therefore restates the operative principle — *yevamah de-chazya le-kulhu chazya le-miktzatah, yevamah de-lo chazya le-kulhu lo chazya le-miktzatah* — a *yevamah* in respect of whom full *yibum* was possible, even a partial *ma'amar* is meaningful; a *yevamah* in respect of whom *yibum* was impossible at the time, not even a partial *ma'amar* has effect. This is another formulation of the same *ma'amar de-heteira* principle.

We are thus left with two live positions within Beit Shammai's view: either *ma'amar* is a *kinyan gamur* requiring only a *get* from Rachel, or it is a *dichiya gemura* — Leah is fully free but the relationship with Rachel is not complete, and therefore both a *get* and *chalitzah* are needed. The *gemara* will shortly revisit the first of these as a serious possibility.

### Yerushalmi Source

One might wonder how *ma'amar*, which has generally been treated as a rabbinic institution, could carry the *de'oraita* force that Beit Shammai's position seems to demand — freeing Leah without any *chalitzah*. The *Yerushalmi* supplies a biblical source for Beit Shammai's view, deriving it from the verse *ve-lakachah lo le-ishah ve-yivemah* (Deuteronomy 25:5). The *Yerushalmi* reads this as embedding two distinct acts within the *yibum* process: *ve-yivemah* refers to the act of *yibum* itself, and *ve-lakachah lo le-ishah* refers to *ma'amar* — a formal act of *kiddushin* — as a *de'oraita* component of the *yibum* process. On this reading, *ma'amar* is not purely rabbinic; it has a biblical grounding that explains why Beit Shammai grants it sufficient force to free Leah without *chalitzah*.

---

## Rava's Question

### Nisuin Question

With the *de'oraita* grounding of *ma'amar* established according to Beit Shammai, Rava now presses the question further. If *ma'amar* has real biblical standing, and if it may even be a *kinyan gamur*, perhaps it does not merely replicate the status of *kiddushin* — perhaps it goes all the way to *nissu'in*. The question Rava poses is: *ma'amar le-Veit Shammai — nissu'in oseh o erusin oseh?* Does *ma'amar* effect the status of full marriage (*nissu'in*), or does it produce only betrothal (*erusin*)?

### Abaye Response

Abaye responds by pressing for practical consequences: *le-mai hilcheta?* What difference would *nissu'in* make over *erusin*? He identifies three specific legal rights that *nissu'in* adds beyond *kiddushin*: the husband inherits his wife upon her death, a *kohen* husband may become *tamei* for her, and the husband may annul her vows unilaterally, without the participation of her father. These rights do not attach at the stage of *erusin* alone.

### Arusah vs Nesuah

Rav Chiyya teaches explicitly: if his wife is an *arusah* — betrothed but not yet fully married — the husband is not an *onen* upon her death, a *kohen* husband may not become *tamei* for her, and she similarly lacks the status of *onen* for him. Furthermore, if she predeceases him, he does not inherit her. If he predeceases her, she does collect her *ketubbah*, since that obligation arose at the time of *kiddushin*. These distinctions make clear how much *nissu'in* adds to *erusin* in terms of rights and statuses.

### Rava's Logic

This leads Rava to a *kal va-chomer*: if standard *kiddushin* — which is unambiguously *de'oraita* — does not confer these rights of inheritance, *tum'ah*, and unilateral vow annulment without *nissu'in*, then *ma'amar*, which (as Rashi notes) is fundamentally a rabbinic institution — even if Beit Shammai grants it *de'oraita* significance, it remains not as weighty as ordinary *kiddushin* in all its dimensions — why would *ma'amar* leap past *erusin* and confer the rights of *nissu'in*? The *gemara* cites Rashi's formulation: *ma'amar yavmi mi-derabanan hu, de-mi-de'oraita yevamah yavo alehah ketiv rachmana* — rabbinically the *ma'amar* is the prescribed mode, but the *Torah* itself speaks of *yibum* as the act of entering her. The *Ritva* notes a difficulty with Rashi here: according to Beit Shammai, we have just established that *ma'amar* has *de'oraita* grounding from *ve-lakachah lo le-ishah*. The *Ritva* therefore prefers a different formulation: even if *ma'amar* is *de'oraita* according to Beit Shammai, it does not carry the full weight of ordinary *kiddushin*. Evidence for this appears elsewhere in the *gemara*, where it is stated that if the *yevamah* were to sleep with another man after *ma'amar* but before the completion of *yibum*, she would not incur the capital penalty of *eshet ish* — the *ma'amar* does not impose the full weight of a married woman's status, even if it demands a *get*.

### Mesirah LeChuppah

At this point the *gemara* reframes Rava's question more precisely. The question is not about whether *ma'amar* confers the rights associated with *nissu'in* — those clearly do not apply. The real question is whether *ma'amar* itself constitutes an act of *nissu'in* such that no subsequent act of *mesirah le-chuppah* (formal conveyance to the *chuppah*) would be required before consummating the *yibum*. Or does *ma'amar* leave the couple at the level of *erusin*, such that the rabbinic framework would demand a formal act of *nissu'in* before they proceed? This is a subtle but important distinction: if one has put himself on the *ma'amar* track rather than going directly to *yibum*, has he accepted upon himself the full rabbinic structure of betrothal-followed-by-marriage, including the need for *chuppah*?

### Sex as Chuppah

The *gemara* then explores what the act of *yibum* itself accomplishes in the context of *nissu'in*. In a standard *yibum* case where no *ma'amar* was performed, the Torah says *yevamah yavo alehah* — the brother-in-law shall enter her. If the *yibum* is performed with the woman's consent and the couple proceed together willingly, that consensual act of intimacy itself constitutes *chuppah* and *nissu'in*. This is not unusual: in ordinary marriage as well, once a couple who have completed *kiddushin* begin living together as husband and wife, that shared act counts as *nissu'in*.

### Coercive Yibum

The *gemara* adds the difficult point that *yibum* works even *al korcha* — even without the woman's full consent. This is a deeply uncomfortable *halacha*, and one cannot minimize its difficulty. The *gemara* seems to be working with a distinction: an act of *yibum* that is not fully consensual would not itself carry the character of *chuppah*, but it would still be legally effective as *yibum*. *Kiddushin* cannot be performed *al korcha* — the woman's consent is required — but the act of *yibum* through intimacy retains its legal force even without it. The practical point being made is that any act of *yibum*, however it occurs, automatically produces the status of *nissu'in* for the woman, with no separate *chuppah* required.

### Rabba's Track Theory

Rabba now offers what emerges as the most compelling resolution. He proposes that once a man performs *ma'amar* with his *yevamah*, *parcha heimena zikas yivamin* — the entire *yibum* nexus flies away from her. She is no longer on the *yibum* track at all. According to Beit Shammai, the act of *ma'amar* does not merely supplement the *yibum* relationship — it displaces it entirely, *dechalah zikas erusin*, shifting the couple completely onto the *kiddushin* track. This is a remarkable structural point: the two possible paths — *yibum* via intimacy, or the *ve-lakachah* path via *ma'amar* — are genuinely alternative tracks. Once *ma'amar* is performed, the logic of *yibum* (including its special properties around *chuppah* and even *baal korcha*) no longer applies. The couple are now, in essence, in the position of a man and his betrothed, and if they are to proceed to full marriage, the regular apparatus of *nissu'in* through *mesirah le-chuppah* would apply. This model also reinforces the conclusion we reached earlier: since the *yibum* track has been abandoned in favor of the *kiddushin* track, presumably only a *get* would be needed for a separation — not a *get* plus *chalitzah*.

---

## Yibamah Nedarim

### Shomer Yavam

The *gemara* now introduces a *mishnah* to test the question of *ma'amar*'s legal strength. The *mishnah* discusses a woman who is a *shomeret yavam* — waiting for either *yibum* or *chalitzah* — and asks whether the *yavam* can annul her vows. The scenario specifies that the woman may be in a *zika* relationship with one *yavam* or with multiple brothers-in-law simultaneously.

### Vow Annulment Views

Three Tannaitic opinions are presented. Rabbi Eliezer says the *yavam* may annul her vows (*yafer*). Rabbi Yehoshua says he may annul if there is only one *yavam*, but not if there are two — in the case of two, neither individual has a sufficiently defined or exclusive relationship with her. Rabbi Akiva says neither one nor two can annul, because the *zika* itself is not strong enough to grant the *yavam* the legal standing to annul vows.

The positions of Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehoshua are each internally coherent. Rabbi Akiva holds there is no operative *zika* at all for purposes of vow annulment — *ein zika* even with one. Rabbi Yehoshua holds there is *zika* with one — *yesh zika le-echad* — but the *zika* becomes diluted when two brothers share it — *ein zika le-trei*. Both positions follow naturally from their respective understandings of *zika*.

### Annulment Problem

Rabbi Eliezer's position, however, is puzzling. Granting that he holds *yesh zika* even with two brothers, two difficulties arise. First, if the relationship is genuinely shared between two brothers, which of them has the standing to annul alone? Should both not be required? Second — and this is the deeper issue — even if one grants the *yavam* the standing of a *baal* for vow annulment purposes, the rule for a *na'arah me'orasah* is that her vows are annulled jointly by her father and her *arus*. If the *yevamah* stands at the level of an *arusah*, the *yavam* alone cannot annul — her father must participate. How then does Rabbi Eliezer permit the *yavam* to annul unilaterally?

### Rav Ami Solution

Rabbi Ami resolves the difficulty by reframing the *mishnah*'s case. The *mishnah* is not discussing a simple *shomeret yavam* waiting with only a *zika* in place. Rather, it is discussing a case *ke-gon de-avid bah ma'amar* — where *ma'amar* has already been performed, and moreover, the *mishnah* follows Beit Shammai's view that *ma'amar koneh kinyan gamur*. Once *ma'amar* has been performed and Beit Shammai treats it as a full *kinyan*, the *yevamah* is no longer merely betrothed — she has the status of a *nesu'ah*, a fully married woman. And a fully married woman's vows may be annulled by her husband alone, without the father's participation.

This resolves Rabbi Eliezer's position neatly: he permits vow annulment because one of the brothers performed *ma'amar*, giving her *nissu'in* status, and the other brother is no longer in the picture. The *gemara* adds that this reading feeds back into our earlier question: *i amarta bishlama nissu'in osah, mishum hachi meifer* — if *ma'amar* creates *nissu'in* status, that is precisely why the *yavam* can annul the vows. But *i amarta erusin osah — heichi mati meifer?* If *ma'amar* produces only *erusin*, vow annulment requires the father, and the *mishnah*'s ruling is unexplained.

### Rav Nachman Clarification

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak pushes back. Perhaps we need not concede that *ma'amar* creates *nissu'in*. One might re-read Rabbi Eliezer's *yafer* as referring not to solo annulment but to annulment performed together with the father — *meifer bi-reshus ha-av*. The *gemara* immediately challenges this reading on textual grounds: the *mishnah* says *yafer*, in the singular, not *yaferu* — "he annuls," not "they annul." Solo annulment is what is being described.

There is a further complication. Given that we have been working within Beit Shammai's framework and considering the view of Rabbi Eliezer (the earlier amora cited at the start) that *ma'amar* is not a *kinyan gamur* but only *lidchos batzara bilvad*, the question returns: even if we grant the *yevamah arusah* status, the *yavam* still cannot annul alone — and the *mishnah* attributes full annulment power to him. The *gemara* poses this difficulty directly: how does any of this work if we do not accept *kinyan gamur*? One response offered is that perhaps there is a dual status at play — she is both an *arusah* on the *kiddushin* track and still retains a *yevamah* dimension — and the *erusin* component, together with the father, would allow *hafarat nedarim*. This is a strained answer, and the *gemara* acknowledges it.

### Implicit Stipulation

The *gemara* therefore offers an alternative account of the *mishnah* that dispenses with *ma'amar* and *nissu'in* altogether. The case is one where the *yevamah* went to court (*amda be-din*), and the *beit din* ruled that since the *yavam* was refusing to perform either *yibum* or *chalitzah*, he must nonetheless support her financially — *pasku lah mezonot mi-shelo*. Once he is obligated to support her as a court-mandated dependent, we apply the principle stated by Rav Pinchas in the name of Rava: *kol ha-noderet al da'as ba'alah hi noderet* — any woman who makes a vow does so implicitly against the background of her husband's or quasi-husband's consent. Her vows are therefore understood as already implicitly conditional on his acceptance. This is not a technical *hafarat nedarim* in the formal sense — it is a presumption built into the structure of the relationship. The *gemara* recognizes the tension this creates: if such an implicit presumption always operates, why does the *Torah* need a formal mechanism for *hafarat nedarim* at all? The answer is that this implicit-stipulation framework applies specifically in the unusual relational context created by the court-ordered support arrangement — it is not a general rule displacing the *Torah*'s formal structure of vow annulment.

---

## Three Brothers

### Case 1: Reuven Dies

The *mishnah* now works through a series of cases involving three brothers — two married to two sisters, one married to an unrelated woman. Take the names: Reuven married to Rachel, Shimon married to Leah, Levi married to Dvorah. The cases will vary by who dies first, who performs *yibum*, and whether *ma'amar* is substituted for *yibum*.

**Case 1:** Reuven dies. Levi performs *yibum* with Rachel. Then Levi dies. Shimon now has before him both Rachel and Dvorah. Rachel is *achot ishto* — his wife's sister. Dvorah is *tzarat ervah*. The ruling: Rachel walks away as *achot isha*, and Dvorah is exempt because she is *tzaratah* — the co-wife of a forbidden relative.

### Case 1 Ma'amar

In the sub-case: instead of performing *yibum*, Levi performed *ma'amar* with Rachel and then died. Since this is now a case involving Beit Hillel's framework (not Beit Shammai's), Rachel is not actually fully married to Levi — the *ma'amar* creates a quasi-marital connection, not a complete *kinyan*. Rachel is thus a quasi-*ervah* in the *yibum* category. Dvorah, as the *tzarah* of a quasi-*ervah*, cannot be taken in *yibum* — but she does require *chalitzah*. Rachel walks away without obligation. The ruling: *nochrit choletzet ve-lo mityabemet* — Dvorah performs *chalitzah* but not *yibum*.

### No Zika Principle

The *gemara* draws a significant inference from this. The *mishnah* implies that if Levi had done neither *yibum* nor *ma'amar* — if he died without having acted at all — Dvorah would be entirely free for Shimon to perform *yibum* with her. The reason: Levi did have a *zika* to Rachel, but since he did nothing with it and Rachel is, in any case, *achot ishto* and off limits to Shimon, that *zika* carries no weight. Rav Nachman draws the explicit conclusion: *zot omeret ein zika, va-afilu be-chad acha* — this *mishnah* holds that there is no operative *zika*, even with a single brother-in-law. The *zika* alone — without any *ma'amar* and without *yibum* — does not bring Rachel into a problematic relationship with Shimon, and Dvorah is therefore free.

### Case 2: Levi Dies

**Case 2:** Now the order changes. Levi dies first. Reuven — married to Rachel — performs *yibum* with Dvorah and thus holds both Rachel (his wife) and Dvorah (his new *yevamah* via *yibum*). Then Reuven dies. Now Shimon faces Rachel and Dvorah. Rachel is *achot ishto*; Dvorah is *tzarat ervah*. The ruling is the same: Rachel walks away as *achot isha*, Dvorah is exempt as *tzaratah*.

### Case 2 Ma'amar

Sub-case: instead of *yibum*, Reuven performed *ma'amar* with Dvorah and then died. Shimon's situation mirrors Case 1: Rachel is the real *ervah* (his wife's sister and his own wife), Dvorah is the quasi *tzarat ervah* through the *ma'amar*. Dvorah requires *chalitzah* but cannot be taken in *yibum*.

### Redundancy Question

The *gemara* asks: why does the *mishnah* need to state this second case at all? Once we know the ruling in Case 1, Case 2 follows *a fortiori*. In Case 1, the *ervah* — Rachel — was only quasi-connected to Levi through *ma'amar*, and yet that was enough to make Dvorah a *tzarat ervah* requiring *chalitzah*. In Case 2, the *ervah* — Rachel — is Shimon's actual wife, and the quasi-connection runs only through Dvorah. If the weaker case (quasi-*ervah*) creates enough of a problem to block *yibum*, then the stronger case (real *ervah*) certainly does. The second *mishnah* appears to be a *kal va-chomer* from the first.

### Pedagogical Order

The *gemara* resolves this by explaining the actual compositional history. The second *mishnah* was in fact taught first — it is the case where the *ervah* is the real wife and Dvorah is brought in only quasi, through *ma'amar*. This case may have initially seemed permissible: after all, the core obligation was with Dvorah, and the *ervah* is only tangentially implicated through *ma'amar*. One might have thought to allow *yibum* with Dvorah in that scenario. The author therefore ruled that even this case is forbidden and requires only *chalitzah*. This was the *chiddush*. The first *mishnah* — where the quasi-wife is the *ervah* — followed later as an extension, and the ruling there is far more obvious. *Vahadur chazi le'issura* — the author came to see that even the easier-seeming case must be forbidden. Because that ruling was the dear *chiddush*, the author placed it first in the text. And *mishneh lo zaz mi-mekoma* — the second *mishnah* was not removed even after it became seemingly redundant, because it had an independent pedagogical history. *Tosafot* notes that this explanation is necessary: had the second case been just a brief addendum, one might have attributed it to an incidental *zu ve-ein tzarich lomar zu* formulation. But since it is a full, independently described *mishnah*, a fuller explanation of why both were retained is required.

---

## Death Moment Rule

### Case 3: Changed Status

**Case 3** introduces a critical new variable. Reuven dies. At this moment, Rachel — Shimon's wife — is still alive, so Rachel stands before Shimon as *achot ishto*. Levi is also present, and he could in principle perform *yibum* with Rachel. But rather than anyone acting, Leah then dies. And then Levi dies. Now, when Levi dies, Rachel falls before Shimon. At this point Leah is dead — Rachel is no longer *achot ishto*. Should Shimon now be permitted to perform *yibum* with Rachel?

The *mishnah* rules: *harei zu asurah alav olamit, ho'il ve-ne'esrah alav sha'at achat* — she remains forbidden to him permanently, because there was a moment at which she was forbidden. That moment was the instant Reuven died: at that point, Rachel became *achot ishto* — forbidden to Shimon. That initial prohibition fixes her status permanently.

### Rav's Rule

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav articulates the governing principle: *kol yevamah she-einah nikre'et bah be-sha'at nefilah yevamah yavo alehah, harei hi ke-eshet ach she-yesh lah banim ve-asurah* — any *yevamah* who could not be designated at the moment of her husband's death for the verse "the *yavam* shall enter her" — meaning *yibum* was impossible at that very moment — takes on the permanent status of a brother's wife for whom there is no *mitzvah* of *yibum*, and she remains forbidden indefinitely. The reason is not merely that she was *achot ishto* at that moment. When Reuven died, Rachel simultaneously became two things: *achot ishto* (forbidden for that reason) and *eshet achiv* (dead brother's wife, ordinarily calling for *yibum*). But since *yibum* was not possible — *lo chazya* — the *eshet achiv* status does not generate a *mitzvah* but rather an *issur*: she is a brother's wife for whom there is no *mitzvah* of *yibum*, which is the forbidden category of *eshet ach she-yesh lah banim*. That *issur* is permanent, surviving even the subsequent death of Leah.

### Why Different

One might ask why this case differs from the standard case of two brothers and two sisters, which was addressed in an earlier *mishnah*. There, when there was only one brother and one sister-in-law who was forbidden, the process ended entirely at the moment Reuven died — there was no one else to perform *yibum*, the *yibum* process was over, and the permanent *issur* of *eshet achiv* was unambiguously in place. Here, by contrast, when Reuven dies, Levi is still available — the *yibum* process with Rachel is not over. Rachel could still be taken by Levi. The process is ongoing. Perhaps, one might argue, the status that attaches to Shimon vis-à-vis Rachel should be reassessed once the *yibum* process plays out and Leah dies.

### Multiple Brothers

The *gemara* acknowledges this argument. When multiple brothers remain and the *yevamah* is still in process — *lo idchi lah me-hai beita le-gamrei* — one might have thought that a change in her status during the waiting period could open the door for another brother. Since she was not definitively excluded from the house — Levi could still act on her — perhaps Shimon's prohibition is not yet sealed. Rav's ruling establishes that this is not so.

### Dual Status

The reason lies in the dual status Rachel acquired at the moment of Reuven's death. She was *achot ishto* — that is why *yibum* was impossible for Shimon at that moment — and simultaneously she became *eshet achiv she-yesh lah banim*, a dead brother's wife for whom there is no *mitzvah of yibum*. The first status, *achot ishto*, can dissolve when Leah dies. The second status, *eshet achiv*, does not dissolve. It is fixed at the *sha'at nefilah*, the moment of death, and it persists. Even when Rachel stops being *achot ishto*, she remains permanently forbidden to Shimon as a brother's wife who was never amenable to *yibum*.

---

## Divorce Case

### Divorce Setup

The final *mishnah* introduces divorce in place of death. The same three brothers: Reuven married to Rachel, Shimon married to Leah, Levi married to Dvorah. Now: Shimon divorces Leah. Then Levi dies. Shimon performs *yibum* with Dvorah. Then Shimon dies.

### Leah Freed

The key move is Shimon's divorce of Leah. Once Leah is divorced, she is no longer Shimon's wife. The prohibition of *achot ishto* does not apply to a divorced woman when the original wife is no longer in the picture — or more precisely, the *issur* of *achot isha* applies only during the life of the wife (*bi-chayeha*), and a divorced woman's sister is technically not subject to that prohibition while the divorce stands. What matters for our purposes is that Leah is entirely outside the *yibum* equation: there is no *zika* to Leah because she was divorced, not widowed. She has no *yibum* obligation and brings no complications.

### Dvorah Permitted

When Levi dies, Dvorah falls into the *yibum* pool. Shimon — who has already divorced Leah — faces only Dvorah. There is no *ervah* in the picture. Dvorah is an unrelated woman whose husband (Levi) has died childless, and Shimon is the available *yavam*. There is nothing blocking *yibum* with Dvorah. The barrier of *achot ishto* that might have existed were Leah still his wife is absent. Shimon performs *yibum* with Dvorah. When Shimon subsequently dies, Reuven faces Dvorah. She is his brother Shimon's widow — an obligation of *yibum* — with no complicating *ervah* in the picture. *Yibum* with Dvorah is entirely permissible. As for Leah: she was divorced, not widowed, and so she never entered the *yibum* calculation at all. Reuven has no *yibum* obligation toward her, and the only prohibition that exists is the ordinary *ervah* of *achot isha* — he may not marry the sister of his wife Rachel, but that is an independent matter entirely unrelated to the *yibum* structure.

### Final Teaching

The *mishnah* closes with the general principle: *kulan she-meisu o nitgareshu, tzaroseihen mutarot* — in all cases where the forbidden wives have died or have been divorced, their *tzarot* — their co-wives who were blocked from *yibum* only because of their association with those forbidden women — become permitted. Once the *ervah* leaves the picture, whether through death or through divorce, the barrier that her presence created dissolves, and the remaining *yevamah* may be taken in *yibum* normally.

---

---

# Yevamot 30

## Mishnah Setup

### Three Brothers Setup

The Mishnah with which we begin deals with a scenario involving three brothers and two sisters. The Hebrew runs: *shlosha achim shnayim mehem nesuim shtei achayot ve-echad nasui achrit* — three brothers, two of whom are married to two sisters, and one who is married to an unrelated woman. For purposes of clarity, we will name the brothers Reuven, Shimon, and Levi. Reuven is married to Rachel, Shimon is married to Leah, and Levi is married to Devorah. Rachel and Leah are sisters, while Devorah is entirely unrelated.

### Three-Stage Sequence

The Mishnah then traces a three-stage sequence of events. Stage one: *gerash echad mibaalei ha-achayot et ishto* — one of the husbands of the sisters divorces his wife. Specifically, Shimon divorces Leah; a *get* is given and Leah exits the picture. Stage two: *u-met nasui achrit* — Levi, the brother who was married to Devorah, dies. At this point, Devorah falls before the surviving brothers for *yibbum*. Stage three: *u-kinesa ha-migaresh* — the one who had divorced, meaning Shimon, goes ahead and performs *yibbum* with Devorah, marrying her. Thereafter, *u-met* — Shimon himself dies.

### Devorah Permitted

The question now is what Reuven's status is with respect to Devorah. When Levi died, both Reuven and Shimon became potential *yevamim* for Devorah, and Shimon acted on that obligation and married her. Now that Shimon has died, Devorah once again falls before the remaining brother, Reuven. The Mishnah rules that Devorah is permitted to Reuven. The logic is straightforward: the potential complication would have been Leah, who is Rachel's sister and therefore an *ervah* to Reuven. Had Leah been present as Shimon's wife when Devorah entered the picture, Devorah could have become a *tzarat ervah*. But Leah was already gone — divorced by Shimon even before Levi died — so she was out of the picture from the very outset. With Leah removed, Devorah enters free of any taint, and when Shimon subsequently dies, Reuven may freely perform *yibbum* with Devorah.
