The Mishnah's closing formulation, *zu hi she-amru ve-khulan she-metu o nisgarshu tzaroteihen mutarot*, captures the principle: when the *ervot* have died or been divorced, their co-wives are permitted. This is presented as an extreme case — the easiest possible scenario — because Leah was removed from the picture entirely before any of the subsequent complications even arose.

---

## Zika Debate

### Extreme Case

The Gemara immediately focuses on the fact that the Mishnah chose to present this particular, most straightforward scenario. The Gemara says: *ta'ama de-geiraish ve-achar kakh met* — the reason this works is that Shimon first divorced Leah and only then did Levi die. Leah was out of the picture before Devorah even became relevant to the discussion. That is why everything proceeds smoothly. This is indeed an extreme case — Leah was removed at the first step before anything else had occurred.

### Middle Case

But the Gemara now asks about a more complicated middle case that the Mishnah did not address: *aval met ve-achar kakh geiraish* — what if Levi died first, and only afterward was Leah divorced? In that scenario, when Levi died, Devorah fell before the brothers for *yibbum*. At that moment, Leah had not yet been divorced. What is the legal status of that situation?

The issue is *zika*. Even before *yibbum* is performed, the death of Levi creates a bond — a *zika* — between Devorah and each of the surviving brothers. If *yesh zika*, if that bond has legal force, then at the moment Levi dies, Devorah becomes, in some sense, linked to both Reuven and Shimon. Since Leah is still present and is an *ervah* to Reuven, Devorah would immediately become a *tzarat ervah* by virtue of the *zika* alone. This would potentially problematize Devorah permanently for Reuven, even if Leah were subsequently divorced and Shimon later died.

The Gemara thus reads the Mishnah's choice to present the extreme case as implying that had the order been reversed — Levi dying before Leah's divorce — there would indeed have been a problem. This implication favors *yesh zika*.

### Rav Ashi vs Rav Nachman

From this reading of the Mishnah, Rav Ashi draws an explicit conclusion: *zot omeret, yesh zika afilu bitrei achai* — from here we infer that there is *zika* even in a case of two brothers. The significance of specifying "two brothers" is that the force of *zika* might be thought weaker when there are multiple potential *yevamim*, since no single brother is obviously designated to act. Yet Rav Ashi maintains that even so, the *zika* is operative the moment the *yavam* dies, and it is strong enough to render Devorah a *tzarat ervah* with respect to Reuven.

However, the Gemara immediately raises the difficulty from the contrary position: *u-le-Rav Ashi kashya de-Rav Nachman*. Rav Nachman had maintained *ein zika afilu be-chad* — that there is no operative *zika* even with a single brother. This was derived from a different Mishnah.

### Nachman's Source

To reconstruct Rav Nachman's source, the Gemara recalls an earlier Mishnah in which Reuven and Shimon are both married to sisters Rachel and Leah, while Levi is married to Devorah. Reuven dies, and Levi — now the relevant *yavam* for Rachel — does a *ma'amar* with Rachel. Levi then dies. The Mishnah states that Shimon cannot perform *yibbum* with Devorah, because Rachel has been drawn into the picture through the *ma'amar*.

Rav Nachman's question is sharp: why does it take a *ma'amar* to create the problem? If *zika* alone were operative, the moment Reuven died and Levi had a *zika* to Rachel, that *zika* would already have made Rachel a kind of *ervah* — and Devorah, as her co-wife, would already have been problematized for Shimon. The fact that the Mishnah required a *ma'amar* to bring Rachel into the equation implies that *zika* alone accomplishes nothing. Hence: *ein zika*.

### Ashi's Response

Rav Ashi responds: *amar lekha Rav Ashi, hu ha-din de-af al gav de-lo avid ma'amar* — you are correct that even without *ma'amar*, the *zika* alone would have created a problem. Even without the *ma'amar*, Rachel was already pulled into the equation by the *zika*, and Shimon would therefore have been unable to perform *yibbum* with Devorah. The *ma'amar* was not mentioned because it was necessary to create the prohibition; it was mentioned for a different reason entirely.

Why then did the Mishnah specify *ma'amar*? *Le-afukei mi-Beit Shammai de-amri ma'amar koneh kinyan gamur* — to exclude the view of Beit Shammai, who held that a *ma'amar* effects a complete acquisition of the woman, equivalent to full marriage. According to Beit Shammai, if Levi performed a *ma'amar* with Rachel, Rachel might be considered fully his wife. In that case, Leah's status as a *tzarat ervah* might be considered complete and unambiguous, and she might even be able to walk free without *chalitza*. The Mishnah therefore emphasizes *ma'amar* to tell us not that *ma'amar* is necessary to create a problem — the *zika* alone already did that — but that *ma'amar* does not function as a full *kinyan* in the manner Beit Shammai would suggest. Even with a *ma'amar*, Devorah still requires *chalitza* rather than being freed automatically.

This is, as one might note, a striking feature of this tractate: the opinions of Beit Shammai carry more weight in the context of *yibbum* than they tend to elsewhere, and the Mishnah explicitly legislates against their view in a way that presupposes their position as a real halakhic possibility.

---

## Mishnah Exclusions

### Nachman's Exclusion

Having established the two opposing positions — Rav Ashi maintaining *yesh zika* and Rav Nachman maintaining *ein zika* — the Gemara now asks how each position reads the Mishnah. Specifically, the Mishnah's formulation sounds as though it is permitting a specific case while implicitly excluding other cases. The Gemara asks: *zu le-ma'utei mai* — what is the Mishnah coming to exclude?

There are, upon analysis, three possible sequences of events to consider in this scenario. Case one is what the Mishnah actually presents: Leah is divorced first, then Levi dies, then Shimon performs *yibbum* with Devorah, then Shimon dies. Case two is: Levi dies first, creating a *zika*, and then Leah is divorced, and only after that Shimon performs *yibbum* with Devorah. Case three is: Levi dies, Shimon performs *yibbum* with Devorah so that he is now married simultaneously to both Leah and Devorah, and only then is Leah divorced — before Shimon himself dies.

According to Rav Nachman, who holds *ein zika*, the *zika* of case two is legally meaningless. Whether Levi died before or after Leah's divorce makes no difference, because the *zika* does not draw Devorah into any problematic status. Therefore, both case one and case two are equally permissible. What the Mishnah must be coming to exclude is case three — the scenario in which Shimon was simultaneously married to both Devorah and Leah, and only divorced Leah thereafter. That case remains problematic. But why?

### Nishuin/Mita Debate

This brings us to an important underlying debate: *nishuin rishonim mappilin* versus *mita mappelet*. The question is how we determine whether a *tzarat ervah* situation exists. Is it determined at the time of marriage — *nishuin rishonim mappilin* — meaning we look at who was married to whom simultaneously and that determines status? Or is it determined at the moment of death — *mita mappelet* — meaning we look at who is in the picture at the time the *yavam* dies, and that determines whether the co-wife is forbidden?

If we say *mita mappelet*, then what matters is only who is present at the moment Shimon dies. If Leah was divorced before Shimon died, she is out of the picture at the critical moment and Devorah is permitted. Under this view, case three would also be permissible, since Leah was gone before Shimon's death — and there would be nothing left for the Mishnah to exclude, since every scenario involving any divorce before death would be acceptable.

On the other hand, if we say *nishuin rishonim mappilin*, then the fact that Shimon was married to both Devorah and Leah simultaneously — even briefly — is what counts. In case three, they were co-wives under the same husband at the same time, and that status, once established at the time of marriage, cannot be undone by a subsequent divorce. Case three thus remains problematic, and that is precisely what the Mishnah is coming to exclude.

The Gemara therefore concludes that Rav Nachman, who holds *ein zika* and thus cannot distinguish between cases one and two, must hold *nishuin rishonim mappilin* in order to have something left to exclude — namely, case three. As the Gemara puts it: *al korchach ke-Rabbi Yirmiyah sevira leh* — he must hold like Rabbi Yirmiyah, who maintained that the two Mishnayot reflect different opinions, one holding *nishuin rishonim mappilin* and one holding *mita mappelet*.

### Rava's Exclusion

The Gemara then turns to Rava, who maintained that it is all one *tanna* and that we always go by *mita mappelet*. Under Rava's position, any divorce before death resolves the situation — and under *mita mappelet*, cases one, two, and three are all potentially permissible. So the Gemara asks: *zu le-ma'utei mai* — according to Rava, what does the Mishnah exclude?

The answer depends on whether Rava aligns with Rav Ashi (*yesh zika*) or Rav Nachman (*ein zika*). If Rava holds *yesh zika* like Rav Ashi, there is one scenario that remains problematic even under *mita mappelet*: the case in which Levi dies, creating a *zika* between Devorah and the surviving brothers, and Shimon then dies without ever divorcing Leah at all. In that case — *meis belo geiraish* — the *zika* alone was present, and since Leah was never divorced at any point before Shimon's death, the *zika* made Devorah a *tzarat ervah* and she is forbidden. This is the case the Mishnah excludes.

Paradoxically, this is the case where Shimon's connection to Devorah was at its weakest — a mere *zika*, not actual marriage — yet it is precisely this weak connection that creates the problem, because Leah was never removed from the picture at all.

### Rava's Position

The Gemara makes the conclusion explicit: *al korchach ke-Rav Ashi sevira lei* — Rava must hold like Rav Ashi, maintaining *yesh zika*. If Rava were to hold *ein zika* like Rav Nachman, there would be nothing left to exclude. Under *mita mappelet*, case three is permissible because the divorce occurred before death. Under *ein zika*, cases one and two are both permissible. There is literally no scenario involving a divorce at any point before death that would remain prohibited. The Mishnah would be excluding nothing, which is impossible.

Therefore, Rava must hold both *yesh zika* and *nishuin rishonim* — wait, not *nishuin rishonim*, but *mita mappelet* with *yesh zika*. It is the combination of *mita mappelet* and *yesh zika* that leaves exactly one case to be excluded: *meis belo geiraish*, dying without having divorced Leah, where the *zika* alone was operative and Leah was never removed from the picture.

---

## Safek Cases

### Safek Principle

The Mishnah now shifts to a different type of problem. Rather than cases where the *ervah* is definitively present or definitively absent, we encounter cases where her status is uncertain. The Mishnah introduces the category of *safek kiddushin* and *safek gerushin* — cases where we do not know whether the *ervah* was ever fully married or whether she was ever validly divorced. The Mishnah rules that in all such cases of uncertainty, the co-wife performs *chalitza* and does not do *yibbum*: *choltzot ve-lo misyabmot*. This is because perhaps the *ervah* is in the picture, in which case *yibbum* would involve an *issur ervah*, while if she is not in the picture, the co-wife still requires *chalitza* or *yibbum* to be released from the *zika*. Since we cannot know, we require *chalitza* without *yibbum*.

As for the *ervah* herself — Rachel in our scenario — she requires no action in any case. If she was never truly married, she has no obligation; if she is genuinely married and therefore an *ervah*, she is forbidden to the *yavam* entirely.

### Safek Kiddushin

The Mishnah illustrates *safek kiddushin* with the following case: *zaraka kiddushin, safek karov lo safek karov lah* — he threw the ring of *kiddushin*, and we do not know whether it landed closer to him or closer to her. The operative principle of acquisition here is the four-cubit radius of personal domain (*arba amot*). Rashi describes the scenario where the couple stands exactly eight *amot* apart, so the precise midpoint between them is where their respective four-cubit domains meet. The ring fell at or near that midpoint, and it is unknown whether it came to rest within her four *amot* — effecting a valid *kinyan* — or within his. This constitutes a genuine *safek kiddushin*.

### Safek Gerushin

For *safek gerushin*, the Mishnah takes a somewhat different approach. Rather than offering a parallel case of uncertainty about whether the *get* reached her — which would be the simple structural parallel to the *kiddushin* case — the Mishnah instead enumerates three types of *gittin* that are rabbinically invalid but Biblically valid. The Mishnah calls these *safek gerushin*, though in truth they represent a distinct category.

The three cases are: first, a *get* written in the husband's own handwriting but bearing no witnesses' signatures (*katav bi-khtav yado ve-ein alav eidim*); second, a *get* bearing witnesses but lacking a date (*yesh alav eidim ve-ein bo zman*); and third, a *get* bearing a date but signed by only one witness rather than two (*yesh bo zman ve-ein bo ella ed echad*). The Mishnah's formulation is notably crafted for mnemonic continuity: each clause picks up where the previous left off — "it has witnesses but no date," "it has a date but only one witness" — carrying the reader from one case to the next in a fluid chain.

Each of these *gittin* is Biblically valid as a *get* but rabbinically disqualified. The woman is therefore in a quasi-divorced state, treated as half-and-half, which is why the Mishnah classifies this as *safek gerushin* and requires *chalitza* rather than *yibbum* for the co-wife.

### Missing Parallel

The Gemara notes a conspicuous asymmetry: *ve-ilu be-gerushin safek karov lo safek karov lah lo katani* — the Mishnah did not include the parallel case for *gerushin* of a *get* thrown and of uncertain receipt, analogous to the thrown ring in *kiddushin*. The Gemara asks: *mai ta'ama* — what is the reason?

The answer, developed in detail in the next section, relates to the principle of *chazakah* — status quo. A *safek get* of the thrown variety would not alter the woman's existing status. Since she was definitely married before the uncertain act occurred, her status quo as a married woman remains intact. The uncertainty about whether the *get* reached her does not disturb that status quo. The Mishnah therefore had no reason to include this case, because Rava holds that we simply leave her with her prior status. The cases the Mishnah does bring — the three rabbinically defective *gittin* — are categorically different and warranted inclusion for their own reasons.

---

## Chazakah/Status Quo

### Rava's Logic

Rava now articulates the general principle underlying the Mishnah's selectivity. The principle is *chazakah*: a person's legal status before the uncertain event occurred remains her status after it, absent proof of change. One does not alter legal status on the basis of doubt.

### Get Status Quo

Applied to the case at hand: if Shimon was definitely married to Rachel and threw her a *get* that may or may not have reached her, Rachel's *chazakah* is that of a married woman — *bechezkat eshet ish*. We do not change that status based on doubt. Rachel remains presumed married. Correspondingly, Devorah's *chazakah* before the uncertain *get* was that she was a *tzarat ervah* — forbidden to the *yavam*. We do not change that status either. Rava formulates it as: *ishah zo bechezkat heter lashuk omedet u-misafek attah ba le-osrah al te'asrennah misafek* — this woman stands in a status of being permitted, and you are coming to forbid her on the basis of doubt; do not forbid her from doubt. Everyone retains their prior status.

### Challenge to Logic

The Gemara immediately presses this reasoning: *i hachi be-kiddushin nami neima* — if so, apply the same logic to *safek kiddushin*. Before the ring was thrown, Devorah's status was that she was permitted to the *yavam* for *yibbum*. The question of whether Rachel was married is now a *safek*. Why not say: Devorah stands in her prior status of being permitted to do *yibbum*, and we should not disturb that status based on doubt?

### Chalitza Required

The Gemara answers: *hatam le-chumra* — there it is a case of being stringent. The possibility that *yibbum* would be a violation of *issur ervah* — a prohibition carrying *karet* — is sufficiently serious that we do not allow *yibbum* to proceed even though in principle the status quo would permit it. We require *chalitza* instead. This is a *chumra de-rabbanan*: go ahead and do *chalitza* and forgo *yibbum* as a matter of caution.

---

## Chumra Costs

### No-Cost Chumra

The Gemara now engages in a sophisticated cost-benefit analysis of rabbinic stringencies, and the discussion is genuinely striking. The question is not only whether a *chumra* is warranted, but whether it comes at a cost — specifically, whether it sends a misleading message that will lead to real halakhic harm.

In the case of *safek kiddushin*, requiring *chalitza* rather than *yibbum* is a no-cost *chumra*. Here is why. The true status, based on *chazakah*, is that Rachel was not married to Shimon — the *safek kiddushin* did not alter her prior status as an unmarried woman. Devorah's true status is therefore that she is permitted to do *yibbum*. We are being stringent and not allowing *yibbum*, but we do require *chalitza*. What message does *chalitza* send? It sends the message that Rachel is out of the picture — not married to Shimon. That is precisely the true state of affairs according to *chazakah*. The act of *chalitza* is fully consistent with the correct legal reality. 

Moreover, if someone were to observe the *chalitza* and draw the conclusion that *yibbum* could have been performed — and were to go ahead and perform *yibbum* — even that mistake would not be a serious halakhic violation, because Rachel really was not married to Shimon in the first place. The *chumra* of requiring *chalitza* instead of permitting *yibbum* is thus entirely costless: it is consistent with the true status, it sends the right message, and even if the message is misread and leads to *yibbum*, the *yibbum* would in fact have been permissible. As the Gemara puts it: *v'keivan de-kamatzreikh chalitza, midei yada de-chumra be-alma hu* — since *chalitza* is demanded, it is understood to be a mere stringency, and the right message is communicated.

Furthermore, the concern about the absence of *yibbum* sending a wrong message is misplaced, because people do not observe the absence of *yibbum* — they observe the presence of *chalitza*. And *chalitza* here says exactly the right thing.

### Why Not Get Chumra

The Gemara then asks the natural question: why not apply the same reasoning to *safek get*? If a *get* of uncertain delivery was given, why not require *chalitza* as a *chumra* there as well? After all, perhaps Rachel was divorced and Devorah therefore needs to be freed from her obligation.

### Wrong Message

The answer is that in the case of *safek get*, *chalitza* sends exactly the wrong message. The true status based on *chazakah* is that Rachel remains married to Shimon. The *safek get* did not change that. Devorah's status as a *tzarat ervah* therefore remains. Now, if *chalitza* is performed, observers will reason: why is *chalitza* being done for Devorah? The only reason *chalitza* would be performed is that Rachel is out of the picture. But Rachel is not out of the picture — she is presumed married. *Chalitza* here therefore communicates that Rachel was successfully divorced, which is false. And that false message has serious consequences: people may conclude that Rachel is now free to remarry, when in fact she remains a married woman.

### Status Quo Solution

The solution, therefore, is to go by the status quo without requiring any *chalitza* at all. Devorah retains her status as a *tzarat ervah* — forbidden to the *yavam* — and no *chalitza* is performed. Not because we are being lenient about the *safek*, but because requiring *chalitza* here would actively mislead people into thinking Rachel was divorced when *chazakah* says otherwise. The cost of the *chumra* is too high: it would generate a false message that leads to precisely the wrong behavior. As Rava's logic is developed through the Gemara, the rule emerges: *chumrot* are appropriate only when they do not themselves produce a *kula* — a leniency in the wrong direction. A *chumra de-atya lidei kula* is not a genuine stringency; it is a counterproductive measure that halakha rejects.

---

## Building Collapse

### Setup

Abaye now challenges Rava's principle of *chazakah* with a case from a different Mishnah. The new case: *nafal ha-bayit alav ve-al bat achiv ve-ein yaduah eizeh meihem meis rishon* — a building fell on a man and on his niece, and we do not know which of them died first. Let us reconstruct the case. Shimon is married to Rachel, who is the daughter of Reuven — meaning Rachel is Reuven's daughter and therefore an *ervah* to Reuven. Shimon is also married to Devorah. The building then collapses on both Shimon and Rachel.

### Uncertainty

The uncertainty about the order of death creates a halakhic dilemma. If Rachel died first, then when Shimon subsequently died, Devorah was the only wife in the picture — no *ervah* was present — and Devorah is therefore permitted to Reuven for *yibbum*. But if Shimon died first, then at the moment of his death Rachel was still alive and present as his wife, making Devorah a *tzarat ervah*, forbidden to Reuven. We have a genuine *safek* about the order of death and therefore about Devorah's status.

### Mishnah Solution

The Mishnah rules: *tzarasah choletzet ve-lo misyabbemet* — in a case of *safek*, Devorah performs *chalitza* but does not do *yibbum*. This is the standard response to uncertainty about whether *tzarat ervah* applies.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye now applies Rava's own reasoning. Before the building collapsed, what was Devorah's status? She was *muteret la-shuk* — free of any *yibbum* obligation that would preclude her from the world. Her *chazakah* was that of a woman who had no issue of *tzarat ervah*. Why, asks Abaye, do we not apply Rava's principle? Let Devorah retain her prior status. The *safek* should not change it. She should be free to walk away without *chalitza*.

### No Wrong Message

One might try to answer Abaye's challenge the way the earlier cases were resolved: perhaps *chalitza* is required here because it is a no-cost *chumra*. After all, in the building-collapse case, Rachel is not visibly present in the way she would be in a divorce scenario. People are not walking around saying "but what about Rachel?" So *chalitza* does not send the same kind of wrong message here that it would in the *safek get* scenario. Performing *chalitza* in this case does not make people think Rachel was divorced; it merely suggests that the Rabbis took precautions about an uncertain situation.

### Frequency Principle

The Gemara's resolution, however, operates on a different principle altogether: *gerushin de-shkhikhei gazru bohu rabbanan; mapoles de-lo shkhikhei lo gazru bohu rabbanan* — cases of divorce are common, and the Rabbis therefore legislated concerning them; cases of a building collapse are rare, and the Rabbis did not legislate for them.

The import of this distinction is as follows. The reason the Rabbis were concerned about requiring *chalitza* in the *safek get* case was not merely the wrong message, but the cost that flows from that wrong message in a commonly recurring context. If the rule were that *chalitza* is required whenever a *get* might have been given, the message sent by *chalitza* — that Rachel is divorced and Devorah can potentially do *yibbum* — would propagate widely, generating real harm across many cases. The frequency of divorce as a social reality means that such a policy would lead to systematic violations: people would perform *yibbum* with genuine *ervot* based on the misleading implication of the *chalitza*.

In contrast, a building collapsing on a husband and his wife simultaneously is exceedingly rare. The scenario practically never arises. Therefore, even if requiring *chalitza* in this case sends a somewhat ambiguous message, the Rabbis did not need to create a general policy of leniency to address it. The risk of mass confusion and systematic violation simply does not exist. The Rabbis can afford to be stringent — requiring *chalitza* — in a case that is so unusual that it will generate no meaningful pattern of misleading behavior.

The Gemara adds a further nuance. In the *safek get* case, people seeing a *chalitza* being performed will ask: why is *chalitza* being done for Devorah? Rachel is still around. This actively prompts them to reason backward to the conclusion that Rachel must have been divorced — and that conclusion will then lead to harmful behavior. In the building-collapse case, by contrast, Rachel's absence from the scene (she is deceased, one way or another) means that no one is asking pointed questions that would lead them to draw dangerous conclusions. The Rabbis therefore determined that the calculus differs: *gerushin* is common and the wrong message spreads dangerously; *mapoles* is rare and the wrong message, to the extent it is even sent, causes no systemic harm.

---

---

# Yevamot 30b

## Three Brothers & Zika

### Mishna Setup

The *mishna* under discussion presents a case involving three brothers: two are married to two sisters, and one is married to a third, unrelated woman. Concretely, Reuven and Shimon are married to Rachel and Leah respectively, while Levi is married to Devorah.

### Sequence Analysis

The *mishna* then describes a sequence of events. First, Shimon divorces Leah — she is out of the picture from the very outset. Second, Levi dies, at which point either Reuven or Shimon could perform *yibum* with Devorah. Third, Shimon does in fact perform *yibum* with Devorah, bringing her into his household. Finally, Shimon dies.

The question is: what is Reuven's status vis-à-vis Devorah? Since Leah was already divorced before Levi died — before Devorah became relevant to the conversation at all — she was fully out of the picture by the time Shimon died. Devorah is therefore permitted to Reuven. This is the principle the *mishna* establishes: *zo hi she'amru, v'chulan shemetu o nisgareshu* — when the *ervah* has died or been divorced, her *tzarot* are permitted. In this case, since Leah was removed from the equation at the very first stage, Devorah is permitted to Reuven. The *mishna* deliberately chose an extreme case where Leah was out of the picture well before anything else occurred.

A more nuanced scenario — one the *mishna* does not directly address — would be if Shimon had first married Devorah and then divorced Leah afterward. The question in that scenario would be whether the period during which both women were simultaneously in Shimon's household created a permanent problem for Devorah vis-à-vis Reuven. But the *mishna*'s chosen case avoids that complication entirely.

### Yesh Zika Inference

The *gemara* now probes the *mishna*'s implicit logic. The *mishna* specifies that the reason the case works is *d'girash v'achar kach met* — Shimon first divorced Leah and only then did Levi die and *yibum* unfold. But what would have happened had Levi died first, creating a *zika* — a juridical connection — between Shimon and Devorah, before Leah was divorced? The *gemara* suggests that if Levi died first and Shimon thereby acquired a *zika* to Devorah, Devorah might immediately become a *tzarat ervah* relative to Reuven, even before any *yibum* had taken place. This would be problematic regardless of what followed.

Rav Ashi draws an explicit inference: *amar Rav Ashi, zos omeret, yesh zikah afilu b'trei achei* — from this *mishna* we can infer that *zika* applies even when there are two brothers. When Levi died, Reuven also had a claim on Devorah, not just Shimon. Even so, Shimon's *zika* is strong enough to render Devorah a quasi-*tzarat ervah*. This is a robust statement of *yesh zika*.

### Ein Zika Challenge

The *gemara* immediately raises a difficulty: Rav Nechman held *ein zika afilu b'chad* — that *zika* is not a legally operative connection, even when there is only a single surviving brother. He derived this from an earlier *mishna* in which Reuven and Shimon are married to Rachel and Leah, and Levi is married to Devorah. That *mishna* stated that if Reuven dies and Levi subsequently performs *ma'amar* with Rachel and then dies, Shimon cannot perform *yibum* with Devorah because she has become a *tzarat ervah*. Rav Nechman's reading is that Rachel only became problematic because of the *ma'amar* — the *zika* alone, without *ma'amar*, was insufficient to pull Rachel into the equation. Yet the *mishna* before us seems to imply that even *zika* alone — without *ma'amar* — creates a problem with Devorah. How are these two *mishnayot* to be reconciled?

---

## Zika & Tzarat Erva

### Rav Ashi's Response

Rav Ashi responds to Rav Nechman's challenge directly. He concedes the point: even without *ma'amar*, the *zika* itself would have made Rachel a problem. *Af al gav d'lo avad bah ma'amar, nachis michlal chalitzah, yibumi lo miyabma* — even without *ma'amar*, Devorah would have required *chalitza* and *yibum* would have been forbidden.

### Ma'amar's Role

If so, why did the *mishna* specifically mention that Levi performed *ma'amar* with Rachel? The *ma'amar* did not create the problem — *zika* alone was sufficient to pull Rachel in and render Devorah a *tzarat ervah*. The *ma'amar* is mentioned not to establish the prohibition but to address a different question entirely.

### Beit Shammai Debate

The *mishna*'s mention of *ma'amar* is *l'apuki mi'Beit Shammai d'amri ma'amar koneh kinyan gamur* — to exclude the position of Beit Shammai, who hold that *ma'amar* constitutes a full acquisition, equivalent to *nisuin*. According to Beit Shammai, one might have thought that if Levi performed *ma'amar* with Rachel, Rachel was now fully his wife. In that case, when Shimon subsequently became the surviving brother, Rachel would be a complete *tzarat ervah* — not merely a quasi-*tzarat ervah* on the strength of *zika* — and Devorah could theoretically walk free without *chalitza*, since she is the *tzarah* of a genuine *ervah*. The *mishna* teaches that we do not rule like Beit Shammai: even with *ma'amar*, Rachel is not fully acquired, *chalitza* remains necessary, and *yibum* with Devorah is forbidden.

So the *mishna*'s structure is this: *zika* itself pulls Rachel in and creates the problem; *ma'amar* does not solve it by making Rachel a complete *nisuin*-level wife. Doing *chalitza* with Devorah is required, and doing *yibum* with Devorah is forbidden.

### Rav Nechman's Logic

Having explained Rav Ashi's reading, the *gemara* now turns the tables. *U'l'Rav Nachman kashya d'Rav Ashi* — according to Rav Nechman, who holds *ein zika* and maintained that Rachel was only a problem because of *ma'amar*, how does our *mishna* work? If *zika* is legally inert, why does the *mishna* appear to exclude cases where Levi dies before Leah is divorced, implying that the *zika* at that moment creates a problem?

Rav Nechman's answer, as the *gemara* reconstructs it, is that the *mishna* does not necessarily exclude that scenario. One might say: *hu hadin d'afilu metat ach v'achar kach gerush, tzarata muteret* — even if Levi died first and only then Leah was divorced, the case would still be permissible, since *ein zika* and the *zika* creates no legal problem. If so, what is the *mishna* actually excluding?

---

## Three Scenarios

### Scenario A

The simplest scenario — Scenario A — is precisely the one the *mishna* describes: Leah is divorced before Levi dies, before anything else unfolds. Leah is out of the picture from the very beginning. This is the easiest case and clearly presents no problem.

### Scenario B

Scenario B is that Levi dies first and then Leah is divorced. According to those who hold *yesh zika*, this might immediately create a problem at the moment Levi dies, since Shimon acquires a *zika* to Devorah while Leah is still in the picture. According to those who hold *ein zika*, however, Scenario B is just as permissible as Scenario A — the *zika* is meaningless, and as long as Leah is out of the picture before Shimon dies, there is no issue.

### Scenario C

Scenario C is more complex: Levi dies, Shimon performs *yibum* with Devorah and thereby marries her, and then — while married to both Devorah and Leah — he divorces Leah before he himself dies. In this scenario, there was a period when Shimon was simultaneously married to both women. Even though Leah was out of the picture before Shimon died, the question is whether that matters. This scenario is what the *gemara* designates as *kanas v'achar kach geireish* — he married Devorah and only afterward divorced Leah.

### Nisuin vs. Mita

This brings the *gemara* to a fundamental dispute about when *tzarat ervah* is determined. One opinion holds *nisuin rishonim mappilin* — the relevant moment is the time of the original marriage; the question is whether the two women were ever simultaneously married to the same man. Another opinion holds *mita mapelet* — everything is determined at the moment of death; if the *ervah* is out of the picture when the husband dies, there is no problem regardless of the marital history. The *gemara* notes that this dispute was articulated by earlier *amoraim*: one position is associated with Rabbi Yirmiyah's reading (*mi sheshana zu lo shana zu*, that the different *mishnayot* reflect different *tannaim*), and the other with Rava's position that it is all one *tanna* and everything goes by the moment of death.

---

## Rabbi Yirmiyah & Rava

### Rabbi Yirmiyah View

If one follows Rabbi Yirmiyah's approach — that *tzarat ervah* is determined by the time of marriage, i.e., *nisuin rishonim mappilin* — then the criterion is whether the two women were ever simultaneously married to the same man. Under this view, Scenario A and Scenario B are both permitted: in neither case was Shimon simultaneously married to both Leah and Devorah. Scenario C, however, is problematic, because Shimon was indeed married to both women at the same time, even though Leah was eventually divorced before he died.

### What Mishna Excludes

This gives the *gemara* a clear answer to the question of what the *mishna* is excluding. Since, under *ein zika*, Scenario B is permissible — the *zika* creates no problem — what remains to be excluded is Scenario C, the case of *kanas v'achar kach geireish*: Shimon married Devorah and only later divorced Leah. That case is forbidden because they were simultaneously married at some point, and *nisuin rishonim* determines the status. The *mishna*'s emphasis that Leah was divorced first is not merely incidental — it is precisely excluding the scenario in which Shimon was ever married to both women at once.

The *gemara* makes this explicit: *al kurchak k'Rabbi Yirmiyah s'vira lei* — if one holds *ein zika* and reads the *mishna* consistently, one is compelled to follow Rabbi Yirmiyah's view that the critical moment is the time of marriage, not the time of death. Only then is there a meaningful case to exclude.

### Rava's View

Rava, however, holds that everything goes by the moment of death — *mita mapelet*. Under Rava's view, any divorce before the husband's death is sufficient, regardless of the marital history. If Leah was divorced at any point before Shimon died, Devorah is permitted. This means Scenario A, Scenario B, and even Scenario C are all permissible, because in all three cases Leah was out of the picture at the moment of Shimon's death.

### Rava's Conclusion

If Rava holds that all three scenarios of divorce work, the *gemara* asks: *zu hi l'me'utei mai?* — what does the *mishna*'s formulation actually exclude? There must be some case that does not work when *geirushin* is in play. The *gemara* answers: *meis b'lo geireish* — the case being excluded is one where Levi died and Shimon acquired a *zika* to Devorah, and then Shimon himself died without ever divorcing Leah. In that situation, if one holds *yesh zika* as Rav Ashi does, the *zika* alone was sufficient to render Devorah a *tzarat ervah* at the moment of Levi's death, and since Leah was never divorced, the problem was never resolved.

This is a striking conclusion. The one case excluded under Rava's view is precisely the case where Shimon's connection to Devorah was at its weakest — a mere *zika*, without *yibum*, without *ma'amar*. Yet that weak *zika*, on the view of *yesh zika*, is enough to create a lasting problem. All scenarios in which an actual divorce occurred at any point before Shimon's death are fine under Rava; the only failure case is the *zika* without any subsequent divorce whatsoever.

The *gemara* then asks: *ella i savra leh k'Rav Nachman* — but if one holds like Rav Nechman that *ein zika*, then under Rava's framework there is nothing left to exclude, because every scenario of divorce before death works and the *zika* is meaningless. *Al kurchak k'Rav Ashi s'vira lei* — therefore Rava must hold like Rav Ashi, that *yesh zika*. Only then can Rava's framework exclude anything at all, and the excluded case is the *zika* without any divorce.

---

## Safek & Status Quo

### Safek Introduction

The *mishna* now turns to a different category of cases. Up to this point, the discussion concerned *erva* who was definitively married or definitively divorced, and the question was about the sequence and timing of those events. The *mishna* now addresses situations where the *erva*'s status is itself uncertain — she may be married, or she may not be. The two categories of uncertainty are *safek kiddushin* (uncertain betrothal) and *safek gerushin* (uncertain divorce).

### Safek Solution

In all such cases, the *mishna* rules: *tzarotehen choltzot v'lo misyabmot* — the co-wife performs *chalitza* and does not do *yibum*. She cannot perform *yibum* because perhaps the *erva* is in the picture and that would create a forbidden situation. But she cannot simply walk away either, because perhaps the *erva* is not in the picture and some form of resolution is required. The solution is *chalitza* without *yibum*.

### Safek Kiddushin

The *mishna* defines *safek kiddushin* with the following scenario: a man declares betrothal to a woman and throws the ring between them, and it is unclear whether it fell closer to his domain or to hers — *safek karov lo safek karov lah*. As Rashi explains, the relevant *kinyan* here is that of *arba amos* — within a person's four cubits, objects can be acquired. If the couple were standing eight cubits apart, with their respective *arba amos* meeting at the midpoint, and the ring landed precisely at that midpoint, it is genuinely unclear whether the woman's *kinyan* of *arba amos* was effected. That is *safek kiddushin* — we do not know if she was ever betrothed to him.

### Safek Gerushin

*Safek gerushin* is defined differently. Rather than a parallel scenario of a *get* that fell ambiguously between the two parties, the *mishna* instead presents three cases of a *get* that is valid *d'oraisa* but invalidated *m'd'rabbanan*, and which is therefore treated as a quasi-*gerushin* of uncertain status. The three cases are: a *get* written in the husband's own handwriting but lacking witnesses (*kasav b'ksav yado v'ein alav edim*); a *get* bearing witnesses but lacking a date (*yesh alav edim v'ein bo zman*); and a *get* with a date but bearing only one witness rather than two (*yesh bo zman v'ein bo ela ed echad*). The *mishna*'s phrasing is worth noting: the language flows from one case into the next, with each statement introducing an element that the next case then takes as its starting point — a mnemonic elegance in the oral formulation.

---

## Gerushin vs. Kiddushin

### Missing Case

The *gemara* observes an asymmetry. By *kiddushin*, the *mishna* gave the parallel case of a ring thrown between them — a genuine *safek* about whether the *kinyan* was effected. By *gerushin*, however, the *mishna* did not give the parallel case of a *get* thrown toward the woman, where it is unclear whether it entered her domain or remained in his. Why not? *V'ilu b'gerushin safek karov lo safek karov lah lo katani* — this case is simply not mentioned.

### Rabba's Status Quo

Rava explains the omission on the basis of *chazakah* — the principle of status quo. In the case of a *get* thrown ambiguously between them, the woman was definitively married before the act. We do not know if that status changed. Since her status quo is that she remains married, we do not treat her as a *safek gerusha* — she retains the *chazakah* of a married woman, and there is no *safek* to speak of. The *get* that may or may not have reached her does not displace that presumption.

### Kiddushin Parallel

One might apply the same logic in reverse to *safek kiddushin*: before the ring was thrown, the woman was definitively unmarried. Her status quo is that she is single. If we keep everyone at their status quo, she should simply remain unmarried, and no *safek kiddushin* should be recognized at all. If that is so, her co-wife Devorah's status quo — that she was permitted to do *yibum* with the *yavam* — should equally be preserved, and there should be no reason to require *chalitza*.

### Gemara Challenge

The *gemara* presses this logic: *i hachi, b'kiddushin nami neima, isha zo b'chezkat heter l'yavam omedes* — apply the same status quo principle to Devorah in the *safek kiddushin* case. Before the questionable *kiddushin* took place, Devorah was permitted for *yibum*. *Umisafek ata ba u'osra* — why should a doubt change that? *Al tosrena misafek* — do not impose a prohibition on account of doubt. Let Devorah retain her status quo and allow *yibum* without restriction.

---

## Cost of Chumra

### Message Problem

The *gemara* responds: even though the status quo argument is valid in principle, in the case of *safek kiddushin* we are nonetheless stringent and require *chalitza* rather than permitting *yibum*. The concern is the message conveyed to the public. If Reuven declares his intent to perform *yibum* with Devorah and is told he may not, this prohibition sends a signal: people will infer that Rachel must in fact be married to Shimon, since that is the only reason *yibum* would be denied. If people conclude that Rachel is married to Shimon, they will draw consequences from that: any subsequent *kiddushin* that Rachel or someone close to her entered into will be viewed as having failed. *Ud'batar lav kiddushin* — those subsequent acts are actually valid, but the public message will lead people to treat them as void.

Specifically, the *gemara* identifies two problematic consequences: if Shimon subsequently performs a definite *kiddushin* to Leah (*kiddushei vadai l'achota*), people will assume it was ineffective because Rachel was already his wife; and if another man — let us say Barak — performs a definite *kiddushin* to Rachel herself after the ambiguous first *kiddushin*, people will assume that too was ineffective. Both of these real marriages will be undermined by the false inference that the first *safek kiddushin* was real.

### Chalitza Consistency

Here is the critical insight: the *gemara* notes that the relevant public signal is not the absence of *yibum* but the performance of *chalitza*. And *chalitza*, in the case of *safek kiddushin*, is entirely consistent with the true legal reality. What is the status quo? Rachel was not married to Shimon — that is the *chazakah*, since we go by the status quo of being unmarried. *Chalitza* with Devorah sends precisely that message: the reason *chalitza* was performed is that Rachel is not in the picture, that there was no operative *kiddushin*. People who see *chalitza* will understand that Rachel is out of the equation, and the subsequent *kiddushin* to Leah and to Rachel herself will be understood as valid.

This is what makes the *chumra* here cost-free. The *halacha* is that Rachel, by status quo, is not married to Shimon after a *safek kiddushin*. Demanding *chalitza* from Devorah conveys the accurate message. The only restriction is that Reuven is not permitted to do *yibum* — but the public does not see the absence of *yibum*; they see the performance of *chalitza*, which accurately reflects the underlying legal reality. *Meida yedaya d'chumra b'alma hu* — people will understand that this is simply a stringency. The *chumra* costs nothing because it sends no misleading signal. *V'kevan d'kamatba'ei chalitzah* — since *chalitza* is demanded, the right message is broadcast.

### Wrong Message

In the case of *safek gerushin*, however, the situation is reversed. Here Rachel was definitively married to Shimon, and the question is whether she was divorced. Her status quo is that she remains married. If Devorah were required to perform *chalitza*, people would ask: why is *chalitza* being done? Isn't Rachel still in the picture as a *tzarat ervah*? The answer they would draw is: the Rabbis must have investigated and determined that Rachel was in fact divorced — otherwise, why would *chalitza* be occurring at all? *Kamu bah rabbanan b'gita d'gita maalya hu* — they will assume that the Rabbis validated the *get* and established that Rachel is genuinely divorced.

### No Chalitza Demanded

That inference leads directly to harmful consequences. If people conclude that Rachel is divorced, they will then reason that *yibum* with Devorah is possible — since Rachel the *ervah* is out of the picture. Reuven or someone like him will come to perform *yibum* when Rachel is in fact not divorced and Devorah remains a genuine *tzarat ervah*. *V'asu l'yibumei l'tzarah* — this is a serious *issur*, potentially implicating *karet*. Performing *chalitza* in the case of *safek gerushin* is therefore not a no-cost *chumra* — it actively generates the most dangerous leniency imaginable.

Therefore, the *gemara* concludes, the Rabbis did not impose *chalitza* as a *chumra* in the case of *safek gerushin*. When the status quo says Rachel is married, Devorah retains her prior status of *tzarat ervah* and is simply permitted to go free — *muteret lashuk* — without any requirement of *chalitza*. The logic of status quo is preserved, and the dangerous message that *chalitza* would send is avoided entirely.

---

## Fallen House Case

### Setup

The *gemara* now introduces a challenge from Abaye based on the case of a fallen house. The scenario is this: Shimon is married to both Rachel and Devorah. Rachel is Reuven's daughter, making her an *ervah* to Reuven. Shimon and Rachel go together and a house falls upon them — *nafal habayit alav v'al bat achiv* — and it is unknown which of them died first. *V'ein yadua eizeh meihem meis rishon.* The *mishna* rules: *tzarata choletzet v'lo misyabemes* — Devorah performs *chalitza* and does not do *yibum* with Reuven.

The *safek* is this: if Rachel died first, then when Shimon subsequently died, only Devorah was his wife and Reuven could perform *yibum* normally. But if Shimon died first, then at the moment of his death both Rachel and Devorah were his wives, making Devorah a *tzarat ervah* to Reuven and forbidding *yibum* entirely. Since we do not know the order of death, the *mishna* requires *chalitza*.

### Devorah's Status

Abaye's challenge to Rava's status quo principle is immediate: before the house fell, what was Devorah's status quo? She was *muteret lashuk* — she was a *tzarat ervah* and therefore not subject to *yibum* at all, fully permitted to the outside world. That was her *chazakah*. *Umisafek ata ba l'osra* — why should the doubt created by the building collapse change that status? *Al tosrena misafek* — keep her at her status quo and let her go free without *chalitza*.

### Rare Event

The *gemara* acknowledges the force of this logic but answers on the basis of frequency. In this case, requiring *chalitza* is indeed a *chumra*, but it is a *chumra* whose cost is negligible because the underlying event is extraordinarily rare. How often does a house fall on a husband and his relative such that the order of death is unknown? Since the scenario almost never occurs, even if demanding *chalitza* sends a potentially misleading message, the real-world cost of that message is minimal. The Rabbis had no difficulty being stringent in a case that barely ever arises. *Mapoles d'lo shechiachi lo gazru behu rabbanan* — for a case of a building collapse, which is uncommon, the Rabbis did not issue the same decree as for a more common situation.

### Common vs. Rare

Divorce, by contrast, is unfortunately common. Cases of *safek gerushin* — where the validity of a *get* is uncertain — arise with sufficient regularity that the Rabbis had to think carefully about what message demanding *chalitza* would send to the public at large. The rarity of the *mapoles* case and the frequency of divorce cases thus lead to opposite outcomes.

### Rabbinic Verification Concern

The *gemara* makes this distinction explicit. In the case of *safek gerushin*, people understand that the Rabbis have the capacity and authority to investigate the validity of a *get*. If they see *chalitza* being performed in a case where Rachel is apparently still in the picture as a potential *ervah*, they will naturally assume that the Rabbis looked into it and determined that the *get* was in fact valid. *Kamu bah rabbanan b'gita* — they will conclude the Rabbis verified the divorce. And from that conclusion they will infer that *yibum* is permissible, when in truth Rachel remains married and Devorah is still a genuine *tzarat ervah*. The cost of demanding *chalitza* in the *safek gerushin* case is therefore real and substantial.

In the case of the fallen house, no such inference is available. Determining the order in which two people died when a building collapsed is not something people associate with Rabbinic investigation and verification. Nobody will assume the Rabbis conducted an inquiry into which death came first. *Mi kamu bei Rabbanan b'mapoles?* — the Rabbis are not understood as having the tools to determine that. Therefore, if *chalitza* is performed, people will accept that it is simply a precautionary measure under uncertainty, and no harmful inference will be drawn. The *chumra* of demanding *chalitza* in the *mapoles* case carries no risk of leading to the forbidden *yibum*.

---

---

# Yevamot 31

## Safek Gerushin intro

### Case overview

Today's daf is officially 34, but we continue from where we left off, picking up at the bottom of 31b. The *mishna* deals with a case of *safek kiddushin* and *safek gerushin* — doubtful betrothal and doubtful divorce — and addresses what is done with the *tzaras ervah*, the co-wife of a forbidden relative, in such circumstances: whether she requires *chalitza* or *yibum*.

### Safek vs. Psul

The *gemara* makes a pointed observation: the case of *safek gerushin* presented in the *mishna* is not, strictly speaking, a genuine *safek gerushin* at all. It is rather a case of a *gerushin* that is *pasul derabanan* — rabbinically invalid divorce. The *gemara* is therefore working from the assumption that a classic *safek gerushin* would carry different consequences entirely. In such a case, the woman would retain her *chazaka* — her presumed status — and remain *eshes ish*, a married woman, with the result that the *tzaras ervah* would retain her status as exempt from *yibum*.

### Chazaka principle

This is the tension the *gemara* is working through. Being *mechamir* — stringent — sometimes comes without cost, but in this case it would impose a serious burden: demanding *chalitza* where none is halachically required creates its own complications. Therefore the *gemara* leaves the matter on the *d'oraisa* level, holding that such a woman retains her status as *eshes ish*, her co-wife retains her status as *tzaras ervah*, and the co-wife walks away without *chalitza*.

---

## Gittin case

### Get thrown case

The *gemara* now challenges this framework by invoking a parallel case. It asks: is there not a case of genuine *safek gerushin* in the *mishna* in *Gittin*, which would produce the same consequence — namely, that the co-wife requires *chalitza*? The *mishna* there discusses the case of *ha-omedes bereshus harabim* — a woman standing in the public domain — where her husband throws a *get* toward her. If the *get* lands closer to her, she is divorced; if closer to him, she is not divorced; and if it lands exactly at the midpoint — *mechtza al mechtza* — she is in a state of doubt: *megureshes ve-eino megureshes*, divorced and not divorced.

The *gemara* in *Gittin* then asks: what is the practical significance of this doubtful status? Two implications are given. First, if the husband is a *kohen*, he cannot simply decide retrospectively that perhaps no divorce occurred and remain married — since she may in fact be divorced, she would be a *grusha*, whom a *kohen* cannot remarry. Second — and this is the *nafka mina* directly relevant here — if she is an *ervah*, her co-wife is a questionable *tzaras ervah* and therefore cannot simply walk away. She might be *megureshes*, in which case the co-wife is obligated in *yibum*, yet *yibum* cannot be performed because she might equally be *eina megureshes* and thus a true *tzaras ervah*. The ruling is therefore *ba'ei chalitza* — *chalitza* is required.

So the *gemara* asks: we see in *Gittin* that in a genuine case of *safek gerushin*, the *halacha* is *chalitza*, not that the woman simply retains her *chazaka* and walks away without anything. The *gemara* there does not say we fear that demanding *chalitza* will lead to *yibum* — it simply demands *chalitza*.

### Safeka D'Oraisa

To this the *gemara* responds: *haya itmara alah* — it was already said about that case. Both Rabba and Rav Yosef explain: *hacha bishtei kitei eidim askinan* — there we are actually dealing with two pairs of witnesses. One pair testifies that the *get* landed closer to her; another pair testifies that it landed closer to him. The reason the woman does not simply retain her *chazaka* of being married — and the co-wife her *chazaka* of being a *tzaras ervah* — is not because of an abstract doubt but because there is direct testimony opposing the *chazaka*. The testimony is contradicted, to be sure, but there is nevertheless direct testimony working against the presumed status.

This, the *gemara* says, creates a *sefika d'oraisa* — a genuine biblical-level doubt. The distinction is this: when there is merely an abstract doubt and nothing more, the principle is to rely on the *chazaka* and preserve the status quo. But when there is concrete testimony working against the *chazaka* — even if that testimony is itself contradicted — the *chazaka* is displaced, and one enters the domain of genuine *safek*. In such a case it is a real *d'oraisa* doubt, not a rabbinic stringency, and therefore *chalitza* is demanded. *Chalitza nibei bah*.

Our *mishna*, by contrast, is not talking about two pairs of witnesses. As the *gemara* explains: *u'masnisin d'hacha b'kas achas* — our *mishna* is dealing with a single pair of split witnesses, or with an abstract doubt, not with two opposing pairs of witnesses directly testifying against the *chazaka*. That would at most be a rabbinic *safek*, meaning that at the *d'oraisa* level one would still follow the status quo.

The *gemara* then anticipates the question: how do we know that the *mishna* in *Gittin* is discussing two pairs of witnesses, and how do we know that our *mishna*'s case of *kiddushin* is similarly a case of abstract doubt rather than contradictory testimony? The answer is that the cases are parallel: just as the *kiddushin* case involves a single pair whose members disagree — not two full pairs testifying in opposition — so too the *gerushin* case follows the same structure. *Mah kiddushin b'kas achas af geirushin b'kas achas.*

One might press further: how do we actually know the *kiddushin* case is one of abstract doubt? Perhaps it too involves contradictory pairs of witnesses. The *gemara* responds: if the *kiddushin* case involved two full pairs of contradictory witnesses, then how could it have been said earlier that we would not fear the *chalitza* leading to *yibum*? If there are witnesses testifying directly that the ring was clearly closer to her — that is, that she is genuinely married and the co-wife genuinely a *tzaras ervah* — then how could one be unconcerned about the possibility of *yibum* following? Rashi and Tosafot note the somewhat self-referential character of this argument, but the essential logic stands.

### Witnesses cancel

The *gemara* then makes a further and crucial point. Even granting the scenario of two contradictory pairs of witnesses, one might have thought that conflicting direct testimony displaces the *chazaka* and leaves a genuine blank-slate doubt. The *gemara* rejects this: *beshnei kitei eidim nami sefeika d'rabbanan* — even with two contradictory pairs of witnesses the result is only a rabbinic *safek*. The reason is that when witnesses contradict one another, one does not say "there is testimony against the *chazaka*, so the *chazaka* is undermined and we are left with a genuine doubt." Rather, one says: the testimonies contradict one another, so we reject all the testimony entirely, and we are restored to the *chazaka*. This is a fundamental principle: *okei terei bahadei terei* — put two against two — and return to the presumed status.

### Bar Shatya case

The *gemara* illustrates this principle with the case of the property of Bar Shatya. Bar Shatya was a person who experienced episodes of mental incapacity, and the question arose concerning transactions he conducted: was he of sound mind at the time? He sold some property. Two witnesses came and testified that he sold it while he was of clear mind — *keshu chalim zavin*. Another two witnesses came and said he sold it while he was of unsound mind — *keshu shoteh zavin*. What does one do? Rav Ashi ruled: *okei terei lahadei terei* — place two against two, cancel all the testimony, and restore the property to Bar Shatya's presumed ownership — *ve-ara okma be-chezkas Bar Shatya*. That was the default position. We wipe the testimony from the slate and return to the status quo.

This demonstrates that even in the face of contradictory witnesses, the *halacha* is to restore the *chazaka*, not to treat the situation as an open *safek*. This brings us back to the central difficulty: if the *halacha* in every case of *safek gerushin* — whether abstract doubt or contradictory witnesses — is to rely on the *chazaka*, then why does the *mishna* in *Gittin* rule that *chalitza* is required? And if the answer is that we are nevertheless *mechamir* and demand *chalitza* in such a case even though the *d'oraisa* principle would be to rely on the *chazaka*, why did our *mishna* not present a classic *safek get* to illustrate this rule?

---

## Safek resolution

### Abaye parallel

Abaye responds by invoking the principle *yagid alav rei'o* — let context and juxtaposition illuminate the matter. He argues: *tana be-kiddushin ve-hu hadin le-geirushin* — the *mishna* taught the rule by means of the *kiddushin* case, and the same applies equally to *geirushin*. The reason the *mishna* gave a different type of scenario by *get* was not to exclude the *kiddushin* example from applying to *gerushin*, but simply to add another scenario. Similarly, *tana be-geirushin ve-hu hadin le-kiddushin* — the *mishna* gave an example by *get* of a rabbinically invalid document, and the same would be true if one had a *kiddushin* that was rabbinically defective in a parallel way.

The essential point: do not read the scenarios in the *mishna* as mutually exclusive. The *mishna* gives one set of examples by *kiddushin* and another set by *geirushin*, but both sets of cases are halachically valid in both domains. And in terms of the underlying rule, even though the *d'oraisa* principle is to follow the *chazaka*, at the rabbinic level *chalitza* is demanded — and this is true for a classic *safek get* just as it is for a rabbinically defective one.

### Rava distinction

Rava, however, pushes back. If cases can simply be learned from one context to the other, what is the force of the word *zehu* — "this is the case" — which the *mishna* uses? That word implies precision: *these* are the cases, as though to exclude others. *Mai zehu d'katani?* — why does the *mishna* say "this is the case of *safek kiddushin*" and "this is the case of *safek geirushin*" if all cases apply in both directions?

Rava therefore offers a more nuanced formulation: *kol she'yesh be-kiddushin yesh be-geirushin* — every case of *safek* that applies to *kiddushin* applies equally to *geirushin*, but *yesh be-geirushin mah she-ein be-kiddushin* — there are cases in *geirushin* that do not apply to *kiddushin*. The *zehu* by *geirushin* is therefore *lav davka* — it is not exclusive; *geirushin* is a broader category and includes the classic *safek* as well. But the *zehu* by *kiddushin* is precise — it excludes the particular *psulim* of *get* that are not relevant to *kiddushin*.

### Zeman issue

What specifically is excluded? The *psul* of lacking a date — *ein bo zman* — which invalidates a *get* at a rabbinic level, does not apply to a *shtar kiddushin*. The other defects mentioned in the *mishna* — such as the document being written in the husband's handwriting without witnesses, or having only one witness — would equally apply to *kiddushei shtar*, betrothal effected by document. But the absence of a date: that *psul* is unique to *geirushin* and does not render a *shtar kiddushin* invalid. That is why the *mishna* uses *zehu* by *kiddushin* — not to exclude the classic *safek*, but to distinguish the cases that are genuinely unique to *get* from those that apply to both.

---

## Zeman reason

### Zeman reasons

Having established that the absence of a *zman* is a *psul* in *get* but not in *shtar kiddushin*, the *gemara* now asks directly: *u'mipnei mah lo tiknu zman be-kiddushin?* Why did the Rabbis not require a date in a *shtar kiddushin*, and correspondingly declare one invalid without it?

To answer this, the *gemara* first identifies the reasons for requiring a date in a *get*. Two reasons are given. The first is *mishum peirot*: from the moment a woman is divorced, the husband forfeits his right to benefit from the fruits of her *nichsei milug* — the property she brought into the marriage whose usufruct belonged to him during the marriage. Rashi cites the *gemara* in *Gittin*, in the chapter *Kol ha-Get*, which explains: the date is required so that it can be determined from when she may claim from her husband the fruits he consumed from her property. Since from the moment the husband wrote the *get* — the moment he set his mind to divorce her — he forfeits the right to the fruits, the woman needs to know precisely when that moment was. Without a date, the husband could always claim he had only just now given her the *get*, and dispute her claim to recover what he consumed over the years.

The second reason is *mishum bas achoso* — so that a husband cannot protect his wife from consequences. The scenario is this: a man divorces his wife, perhaps because she committed adultery and faces severe consequences, but he wishes to shield her. He might therefore give her an undated *get*, which she could then present and claim pre-dates the act. Once a date is required, this manipulation is impossible — the witnesses who signed the *get* ensure the date is accurate, and predating is prevented.

### Arusah no Peirot

Now the *gemara* asks: the first reason — *mishum peirot* — clearly does not apply to a *shtar kiddushin*, and this is straightforward. An *arusah* — a woman who is betrothed but not yet fully married — has no *peirot* rights. The husband's entitlement to the fruits of her property begins only from *nissu'in*, not from *kiddushin*. So there is no question of when to date the transition of those rights, and therefore no reason to require a date in the *shtar kiddushin* for this purpose.

### Kesef majority

But the second reason — *mishum bas achoso*, the concern about covering up adultery — would seem to apply equally to *kiddushin*. If a woman receives an undated *shtar kiddushin*, she could commit adultery and then claim she was only married afterward. Why then do the Rabbis not require a date in a *shtar kiddushin* to prevent this? The *gemara* answers: *mishum de-ika de-mikadesh be-chaspa ve-ika de-mikadesh be-shtara lo tiknu rabbanan zman* — because people perform *kiddushin* both with money and with a document, and since *kiddushei kesef* is far more common, in those cases there is no document and therefore no precise record of the date of *kiddushin* at all. Since we are already not worried about knowing the exact date when *kiddushin* is performed with money, it would be inconsistent to suddenly invalidate a *shtar kiddushin* for lacking a date. We are not going to impose a requirement of *zman* on the document simply because the parties chose to use a *shtar*.

### Slaves parallel

Rav Aha the son of Rav Yosef challenges this reasoning by pointing to the case of slaves: *ve-ha avadim* — slaves can also be acquired either with money or with a document, yet the Rabbis did require a date in a slave acquisition document. Why does the prevalence of non-document acquisition not similarly exempt the slave document from the *zman* requirement? The *gemara* responds: *hasam rova be-shtara* — there, the majority of slave acquisitions are in fact done with a document, since owners naturally want documented proof of property. Given that the majority use a *shtar*, the requirement of *zman* applies, and the minority who use *kesef* are simply not the reference point. *Hacha rova be-chesef* — here, by contrast, the vast majority of *kiddushin* are performed with money, and the document is the exception. The exception does not drive the requirement.

### Document loss

A second answer is offered: *ibayis eima mishum d'lo efshar* — or alternatively, it is simply not practically workable to require a date in a *shtar kiddushin*, because it would serve no purpose. *Heichi ne'avid?* — what would you do with such a document? If the *shtar kiddushin* is held by her — *nanchayei gabei didah* — she can simply erase it or claim to have lost it. She has every incentive to do so, since the whole purpose of the date would be to establish when she became married and thereby limit her ability to claim that a subsequent act of adultery predated the marriage. So she is not the right party to hold it. *Lihvei gabei didei* — perhaps the husband should hold it? But the same problem arises in reverse: *zimnin d'basar chosno mechapei lah* — perhaps he will want to protect her, and he too will lose or suppress the document. *Linhvei gabei eidim* — perhaps the witnesses should hold it?

### Witness testimony

This brings the *gemara* to a fundamental principle: if the witnesses remember the event, *leisavu v'lisahadu* — let them come and testify from memory. And if they do not remember, allowing them to look at the document creates a different problem: *zimnin d'chazu me'hai ksav* — they may see what is written and testify based on it, not on their actual recollection. And the *Torah* says *mipichem v'lo mipi ksavam* — testimony must come from your mouths, from your memory, not from what you read in a document. So having the witnesses hold the document does not help.

The *gemara* then challenges its own reasoning: *ei hachi be-geirushin nami* — if this is the problem, should the same not apply to a *get*? There too, people could lose or erase the document. The answer is obvious: *hasam le-hatzala didah ka'asi* — by a *get*, the document serves to protect her. She needs to produce the *get* to establish her status as a divorced woman eligible to remarry. She therefore has every incentive to preserve it. *Hacha le-chovsa didah ka'asi* — by *kiddushin*, the document is a liability for her, not a protection. So she will dispose of it.

Tosafot raise a pointed question about the *mipichem v'lo mipi ksavam* principle. They note: the entire purpose of a signed *shtar* is that it can be produced as evidence. Why would witnesses need to testify from memory at all? They could simply present the signed document to the court without saying anything, and the document itself would serve as the testimony. Tosafot answer: that would indeed work perfectly well, and if witnesses actually produced the document and refrained from testifying, the signed document would be accepted. The concern is rather that witnesses might not do this — they might read the document and then come to court and testify as though from memory when they do not in fact remember, essentially laundering their testimony through what they read. *Aval chaishinan shema lo ya'idu shekach ra'u bashtar ela shema ya'idu al hama'aseh atzmo k'ilu heim zochrim v'ein heim zochrim ela al pi haksav.*

Tosafot further clarify: if a witness wrote down notes and then re-reads them, such that reading them actually causes him genuinely to recall the event, and he testifies from that authentic recollection, that is permissible. The *gemara* in *Kesubos* (chapter 2) says a person may write down his testimony in a document and testify from it even many years later — *ve-hu shezochra me'atzmo* — provided that he genuinely remembers from himself. But *ein zochra me'atzmo lo* — if he does not actually remember and is merely relaying what he read, that testimony is invalid.

So the problematic case is narrow: testifying about an event one does not remember, not by producing the signed document, but by claiming to remember based on having read the document. Producing the document itself is fine. Testifying from genuine memory prompted by the document is also fine. Only the middle case — purporting to testify from memory when the "memory" is really just what one read — is invalid. Rabbeinu Tam adds that the contemporary practice of witnesses sending their written testimony to court by letter is similarly valid, since there they genuinely do remember — *keivan she-heim zochrim edusam* — and the written form is merely the medium of communication, not a substitute for memory.

---

## Maamar case

### Scenario setup

The *mishna* now presents a new scenario. Three brothers are married to three unrelated women — *gimmel achin nesuin gimmel nochriyos* — and one of them dies. The second brother then performs *maamar* with the first brother's widow, and then he too dies. To illustrate concretely: Reuven, Shimon, and Levi. Reuven is married to Rachel, Shimon to Devorah, Levi to another woman. Reuven dies. Shimon performs *maamar* — a quasi-betrothal in the context of *yibum*, effected like *kiddushin* with money, but not possessing full *d'oraisa* force — with Rachel. Then Shimon dies.

### Double connection

Levi now has a *mitzvah* of *yibum* to Devorah, coming from Shimon. He also has a *mitzvah* of *yibum* to Rachel, coming from Reuven. But since Shimon performed *maamar* with Rachel, Shimon has also created a quasi-connection to Rachel. Levi therefore has a dual connection to Rachel: one from Reuven and one from Shimon. He is connected to one woman through two separate deceased brothers.

### Chalitzah rule

The *mishna* rules: *harei elu choltzos v'lo mityabmos* — both women, Devorah and Rachel, do *chalitza* and not *yibum*. The *mishna* provides scriptural grounding: the verse states that when one brother dies, *yevamah yavo aleha* — the surviving brother comes upon his *yevama*. This is interpreted to mean *mi she'aleha zikas yavam echad* — only a woman connected to him through one brother, *v'lo she'aleha zikas shnei yevamin* — not a woman connected through two brothers-in-law. Rachel, with her dual connection, falls in the latter category and is therefore excluded from *yibum*.

It is worth noting that most authorities hold *maamar* to be entirely rabbinic in status, and accordingly this entire *derasha* is understood as a rabbinic enactment. But for those who hold, like Beis Shammai, that *maamar* carries some *d'oraisa* weight, Rachel's dual status might indeed have genuine biblical significance.

As for why Devorah cannot receive *yibum* — that will be addressed by the *gemara*.

### Rebbi Shimon

Rebbi Shimon takes a different position: *miyabem le-eizo she-yirtzeh v'choleitz la-shniya* — he may perform *yibum* with whichever one he wishes and *chalitza* with the other. Rebbi Shimon does not accept the intermediate position that *maamar* is "fifty percent." He holds that *maamar* is either fully valid — one hundred percent — or completely void. If *maamar* is fully valid, then Rachel was fully married to Shimon, Reuven is out of the picture, and Rachel's connection to Levi comes only from Shimon; Levi may then do *yibum* with either Rachel or Devorah. If *maamar* is void, then Rachel's only connection is to Reuven, she and Devorah come from different brothers, and Levi may do *yibum* with both. The problematic case only arises if *maamar* is exactly "fifty percent" — creating a dual status — which Rebbi Shimon rejects. Since it is either all or nothing, Levi can do *yibum* with one and must do *chalitza* with the other — because if *maamar* worked, both come from Shimon, and if it did not, only Rachel comes from Reuven. In either scenario one *yibum* and one *chalitza* suffices.

---

## Gezeira logic

### Doraita exclusion

The *gemara* now reframes the *mishna*'s reasoning. It observes: *ei zikas beit yevamin de'oraisa* — if the problem of Rachel having a dual connection were a genuine *d'oraisa* issue, then *chalitza nami lo tiba'ei* — not only would *yibum* be forbidden, but *chalitza* too would not be required. If the *Torah* is simply excluding a woman with this double status from the household of the surviving brother, she should simply be able to walk away without any ceremony. The very fact that *chalitza* is demanded indicates that the problem is not *d'oraisa*. *Ela miderabbanan* — the entire framework of the double *zikah* as a *psul* is rabbinic, which follows naturally from the fact that *maamar* itself is rabbinic.

### Gezeira Shema

Since the problem is rabbinic, why is *chalitza* demanded from Rachel? *Gezeira shema yomru shtei yevamos haba'os mibeit echad mityabmos* — it is a preventive rabbinic decree, lest people say that two *yevamos* from the same household may both be taken in *yibum*. The scenario is this: Reuven may have died years ago, and people have forgotten. Everyone sees Shimon as Rachel's husband — he performed *maamar* with her, a public act of quasi-betrothal. Now Shimon dies, and Levi performs *yibum* with both Devorah and Rachel. Observers will think that a surviving brother performed *yibum* with both of his deceased brother's wives — which is incorrect. The proper rule is that *yibum* is performed with one, and the others receive *chalitza*. To prevent this misunderstanding, the Rabbis enacted that Levi should not perform *yibum* with Rachel. She is the apparent source of the confusion, and so she is designated for *chalitza*. The *d'oraisa* level permits *yibum* with both; it is this *gezeira* that prevents it.

But if that is so, why not permit Levi to do *yibum* with Devorah and *chalitza* with Rachel? That would be accurate *halacha* with no false impression created.

### Wrong order fear

The *gemara* explains: *gezeira shema yomru beit echad miktzato banuy umiktzato chalutz* — there is a concern that people will observe Levi doing *yibum* with one woman and *chalitza* with the other, and will conclude that whenever a man dies leaving multiple wives, the surviving brother may perform *yibum* with one and *chalitza* with the others. This is a misunderstanding, but it is not without halachic cost.

The *gemara* probes this: why should we care if people draw that mistaken conclusion? The *gemara* responds: *ei de-miyabeim ve-hadar chalitz* — the problem is not the misunderstanding per se, but its practical consequence. If people believe that one performs *yibum* with one wife and *chalitza* with another, they may do them in the wrong order: *dilma chalitz bereisha ve-hadar miyabeim* — perhaps they will first perform *chalitza* with the woman they are less interested in, and only then perform *yibum* with the other. This sequence is halachically fatal. Once *chalitza* has been performed, the surviving brother enters the category of one who has *not* built up his brother's house — *ba'asher lo yivneh* — and *rachmana amar keivan shelo bana shuv lo yivneh*: once he has not built, he may no longer build. The *chalitza* disqualifies him from subsequently performing *yibum* with any of the remaining *yevamos*.

Therefore the Rabbis enacted the full stringency: both women must do *chalitza*, and neither may receive *yibum*. This comes at no halachic cost — an extra *chalitza* performed when not strictly required is far preferable to the risk that someone performs *chalitza* before *yibum* and thereby permanently forecloses the *yibum* option.

---

## Get negation

### Rava position

Rava now introduces a further question. Suppose that after performing *maamar* with Rachel, Shimon — before he died — decided he no longer wished to proceed, and gave Rachel a *get*. Does this *get*, which was intended to negate the *maamar*, free Levi to perform *yibum* with Devorah? And might Levi even be free to perform *yibum* with Rachel herself, who would revert to her status as a *yevama* awaiting *yibum* or *chalitza*?

Rava rules: *nosan get le-maamaro, hutra tzorasa, aval hi asurah* — if the second brother gave a *get* to negate his *maamar*, the co-wife Devorah is freed and becomes available for *yibum*, but Rachel herself remains forbidden to *yibum*. She requires *chalitza*, but not *yibum*.

### Confusion risk

Why? *Demichlifa be-baalas get* — because she is liable to be confused with a woman who received a *get* addressed to the *zika* itself. The relevant background: if no *maamar* was performed and the surviving brother wishes to decline *yibum*, he performs *chalitza*. But there also exists the option of giving the *yevama* a *get* addressed to the *zika* — a *get le-zika*. Such a *get* is a rabbinic mechanism: it does not dissolve the *zika* at the *d'oraisa* level (which only *chalitza* can do), but it rabbinically precludes the possibility of *yibum*, after which *chalitza* is still required. So there are two distinct uses of a *get* in this context: a *get le-maamar*, which only negates the quasi-betrothal, and a *get le-zika*, which precludes *yibum* for anyone. Since Rachel has now received a *get* from one of the brothers, observers cannot know which type of *get* it was.
