It looks like she received a *get* on the *zika* — and a woman who received such a *get* may not receive *yibum* from any of the surviving brothers. Therefore, even though Shimon's *get* was only intended to negate the *maamar*, Levi cannot perform *yibum* with Rachel, because she appears to be a woman for whom *yibum* has been foreclosed.

### Alternative view

*Ika d'amri* — some say Rava rules differently in this case: *nosan get le-maamaro, hutra, afilu hi* — even Rachel herself is permitted for *yibum*. Why? *Mah d'avad bah shaklei* — what he did to her, the *maamar*, he fully removed. The *get* is seen as precisely canceling the *maamar* and nothing more — it does not alter her status beyond that, and she is not treated as a *baalas ha-get* in any broader sense.

### Practical issue

The practical question underlying the dispute is: how does one distinguish between a *get le-maamar* and a *get le-zika*? Rashi explains that it depends on what is specified at the time the *get* is given. A *get* given without specification — *stama* — is presumed to apply to the *zika* as well and to prevent *yibum* by any of the brothers. Only a *get* explicitly given solely against the *maamar* is treated as limited in its effect.

This ambiguity, as the *gemara* itself makes evident, actually strengthens Rava's first position considerably. Given how unclear it typically is whether a *get* was given *le-maamar* or *le-zika*, it makes abundant sense to treat any *get* received by such a woman as potentially precluding *yibum* — and therefore to forbid Levi from performing *yibum* with Rachel even when the original intent was merely to cancel the *maamar*.

---

## Sisters case

### Scenario

The *mishna* moves to a further case: *shnei achim nesuim shtei achayos u-meis echad mehen* — two brothers married to two sisters, and one of them dies. *V'achar kach meitah ishto shel sheni* — and afterward, the wife of the second brother dies.

### Permanent status

The situation is this: Reuven married Rachel, Shimon married Leah. Reuven dies. Rachel's status relative to Shimon is immediately that of *achos isha* — the sister of his wife — which is an *ervah*, a forbidden relation. She walks away without any need for *yibum* or *chalitza*. Then Leah, Shimon's wife, dies. One might wonder: perhaps now that Leah is no longer alive, Rachel is no longer *achos isha* and Shimon could perform *yibum* with her. The *mishna* rules otherwise: *v'achar kach meitah ishto shel sheni harei zo asurah alav olamit* — Rachel remains eternally forbidden to Shimon. *Ho'il v'neasrah alav sha'ah achas* — because at that critical initial moment, when *yibum* first became relevant upon Reuven's death, she was forbidden to Shimon. That status does not dissolve when Leah subsequently dies.

### Obvious case

The *gemara* observes: *pshita* — this is obvious. If anything, the case just discussed in the previous *mishna* — where Rachel was not completely excluded from the household, because she was still relevant to Levi even if forbidden to Shimon — presents a harder question, and yet there too she remained forbidden to Shimon. Here, where Rachel is completely pushed away from the family — *d'ka midcheya mei-hai beisa l'gamrei* — there are only two brothers and she is forbidden to both, so she has no connection to the family whatsoever — *lo kol sheken* — is it not all the more obvious that she remains forbidden?

### Teaching order

The *gemara* explains why the *mishna* nevertheless teaches this case. *Tana hai tana b'reisha* — the *tana* taught this case first. And initially, when the *tana* was arranging the *mishna*, he considered the case of the more complex three-brother scenario and perhaps thought that after Levi married Rachel, her status relative to Shimon might have changed. *V'sharya* — he thought it might be permitted. *Ve-hadar chaza le-isura* — and then he concluded that no, even there, she was forbidden to Shimon from the moment of Reuven's death, and that initial forbidden status endures.

Once having resolved the complex case, the simpler two-brother case was clearly also forbidden. *V'aydi d'chaviva lei akdama* — but because this simpler case had seemed like a significant *chiddush* worth exploring, it had already been placed first in the arrangement of the *mishna*. *U-mishna lo zaza mimkomah* — and a *mishna* does not move from its place. Once it was included, it remained, even though by the time the full teaching was in its final form the case had become obvious given the other *mishna* that preceded it.

---

---

# Yevamot 31b

## Safek Gierushin Review

### Opening

Today's daf is officially 32, though we continue picking up from the bottom of 31b. The *mishnah* under discussion deals with cases of *safek kiddushin* and *safek gierushin*, examining what happens when there is a question about whether an *erva* is in the picture and what must be done with her *tzarat erva*. The *mishnah*'s ruling is *chalitza*, not *yibum*.

### Safek Gierushin Summary

The *gemara* pointedly observes that the case of *safek gierushin* discussed in the *mishnah* is not really a classic *safek gierushin* at all. Rather, it involves a *gierushin* that is *pasul d'rabbanan*. This distinction is consequential: the *gemara* operates on the assumption that a genuine *safek gierushin* would not be legally meaningful, because the woman would retain her *chazaka*—her status quo presumption—as an *eshet ish*. Correspondingly, the co-wife, the *tzarat erva*, would retain her status as exempt from *yibum*.

### Cost of Chalitza

The *gemara* works through the implications of being *machmir* in such a case. In some situations, one can demand *chalitza* without incurring any cost. Here, however, if we were to be *machmir* and demand *chalitza*, it would come with a serious cost. Therefore, we leave the matter on its *d'oraita* footing: such a woman is considered still an *eshet ish*, her co-wife is a *tzarat erva*, and the co-wife walks away without *chalitza*.

---

## Gittin Safek Cases

### Gittin Mishna

The *gemara* now raises an apparent challenge. When it comes to *get*, does the *gemara* not have a real case of *safek gierushin* with the same consequence—that the co-wife requires *chalitza*? The challenge is introduced with the formula *v'ha tnan*: we taught in the *mishnah* in Gittin the following classic case of *safek*.

A woman was standing in the public domain—*hayso omedet birshus harabbim*—and her husband threw a *get* toward her. If the *get* landed closer to her, *megureshet*; if closer to him, *eina megureshet*. And if it landed exactly at the midpoint—*mechtza al mechtza*—then she is in a state of doubt: *megureshet v'eina megureshet*.

### Nafka Minos

What are the practical consequences of this doubtful divorce? The *gemara* in Gittin identifies two *nafka minos*. First, if her husband is a *kohen*, he cannot simply decide that perhaps the divorce was invalid and remain married to her—she might be divorced, and remarrying a *gerusha* would be forbidden to him. Second, and directly relevant to our discussion, if she is an *erva*, her co-wife is a questionable *tzarat erva*. The co-wife cannot simply walk away, because the woman might indeed be divorced and the co-wife therefore obligated in *yibum*; yet *yibum* cannot be performed because the woman might not be divorced, making the co-wife a genuine *tzarat erva*. The resolution: *ba'ee chalitza*, she requires *chalitza*.

The *gemara* thus observes that in another tractate we rule that a genuine *safek gierushin* calls for *chalitza*, not that she simply retains her *chazaka* and walks off. The concern about being *machmir* leading to *yibum* does not deter us there—we demand *chalitza*.

### Two Pairs Witnesses

The *gemara* resolves this by invoking a teaching of Rabbah and Rav Yosef, who both said: *hacha b'shtei kitei edim askinan*—the case in Gittin is specifically one involving two pairs of witnesses. *Achas omeret karov la v'achas omeret karov lo*: one group of witnesses says definitively that it landed closer to her, and the other group says definitively it landed closer to him.

The reason the *chazaka* does not simply hold in that case—the woman's *chazaka* as an *eshet ish* and the co-wife's *chazaka* as a *tzarat erva*—is that there is something directly opposing the *chazaka*. It is not merely an abstract doubt: we don't know where the *get* fell, so we default to the status quo. Here there is direct testimony against the *chazaka*. The only complication is that the testimony is contradicted. Nevertheless, because *dahavei leh sefeika d'oraisa*—this creates a biblical-level doubt—it is sufficient to displace the *chazaka* and place us genuinely in the realm of uncertainty.

By contrast, our *mishnah* in Yevamot—*u'masnisin d'haka be'chas akhas*—is dealing with a single pair of witnesses, split between themselves. There is no two-against-two confrontation with the *chazaka*. At most this would generate *sefeika d'rabbanan*, a rabbinic-level doubt. At the *d'oraita* level, one simply follows the status quo, and in such a case *chalitza* would not even be required.

---

## Chazaka Principles

### D'Oraisa Doubt

This distinction—between an abstract doubt and direct contradictory testimony—raises a deeper question about how *chazaka* functions. If you have a *chazaka* and a *safek*, you follow the *chazaka*. If there are witnesses testifying against the *chazaka*, you follow the witnesses. But what if there is a *chazaka*, and witnesses against it, and those witnesses are themselves contradicted by other witnesses? Do you say: once there is direct testimony, even if ultimately contradicted, that is sufficient to undermine the *chazaka* and leave you with a blank slate—a genuine *safek*? Or do you say: throw out both pairs of witnesses, since they contradict one another, and return to the *chazaka*?

The *gemara* initially stated that contradictory witnesses displace the *chazaka* and create a real *d'oraita* doubt. It now revisits that claim and says: *v'su*—moreover, that is not actually correct. When two pairs of witnesses contradict each other—*okei trei l'bahadi trei*—we set them against one another, cancel them out, and restore the woman to her *chazaka*. This is the true *halacha*: contradictory witnesses are rejected entirely, and one returns to the status quo.

### Bar Shatya Case

The *gemara* supports this from a concrete legal story: *meidiy de-hava a-nichsei d'bar shatya*—like the case of the property of Bar Shatya. Bar Shatya was a person who apparently experienced intermittent episodes of mental incapacity—a *shoteh*—and the legal question concerned business transactions he had conducted: were they carried out during a period of lucidity or not?

Bar Shatya sold some property. Two witnesses came and testified: *k'she-hu chalim zavin*—he was of sound mind when he sold it. Then another two witnesses came and testified: *k'she-hu shoteh zavin*—he was not of sound mind when he sold it.

### Rav Ashi's Rule

Rav Ashi ruled: *okei trei l'bahadi trei v'ara okmah b'chazakas Bar Shatya*—set the two pairs against each other, cancel them out, and have the property remain under Bar Shatya's presumptive ownership. This is the default position: when testimony is irreconcilably contradicted, we reject all of it and revert to the *chazaka*.

One could observe that there is something to discuss about the difference between a *chazaka* rooted in property ownership and one rooted in a person's legal status, but the operative principle here is clear. If the doubt were genuine, one might expect a different outcome—perhaps dividing the property, as in the famous opening *mishnah* of Bava Metzia. Instead, we reject the witnesses and default to the status quo.

This brings the *gemara* back to the original difficulty. If even contradictory witnesses against a *chazaka* are thrown out and the *chazaka* is restored, how can the *mishnah* in Gittin say that in a case of *safek get* one requires *chalitza*? Whether the doubt arises from contradictory witnesses or from an abstract uncertainty, the *d'oraita* result should always be to follow the status quo and not require *chalitza*. If *chalitza* is nonetheless required, it must be a *chumra* even in the face of a *chazaka*. And if that is so, why does our *mishnah* in Yevamot not present a classic case of *safek get*?

---

## Mishnah Structure

### Abaye's Logic

Abaye responds with the principle of *yagid alav rei'o*—quoting the verse in Iyov, let his companion reveal it—meaning: learn one case from its context and juxtaposition with the other. His answer is: *tana b'kiddushin v'hu ha-din l'gerushin*. The *mishnah* taught a classic *safek* scenario in the context of *kiddushin*—a case where one did not know whether the object of *kiddushin* landed closer to the woman or closer to him—and the same *halacha* of *chalitza* without *yibum* applies to *gierushin* as well. Conversely, the *mishnah* taught certain cases in the context of *gierushin*—specifically, a *get* that was *pasul d'rabbanan*—and the same would be true if one had *kiddushin* that were *pasul d'rabbanan*.

The point is: do not read the two sets of scenarios as mutually exclusive. The *mishnah* gave one cluster of examples under *kiddushin* and another cluster under *gierushin*, but both sets of *halachot* apply in both directions. The different examples were given to add scenarios, not to exclude the applicability of the other category.

### Rava Objects

Rava pushes back. If one can simply learn one case from the other in both directions, why does the *mishnah* use the language *zehu*—"this is the case"—for both *safek kiddushin* and *safek gierushin*? That formulation sounds precise and exclusionary. When the *mishnah* says *zehu*, it implies: this and no more, not a broader category.

### Rava's Resolution

Rava therefore offers his own resolution: *kol she-yesh b'kiddushin yesh b'gerushin*. Whatever applies to *kiddushin* also applies to *gierushin*. Any classic *safek* scenario—one did not know whether the item landed closer or farther—would generate the same *halacha* in both cases. In that sense, the cases of *kiddushin* are not limited to the specific scenarios mentioned; a classic *safek* by *gierushin* would equally call for *chalitza*.

However, *v'yesh b'gerushin ma she-ein b'kiddushin*: there are defects specific to a *get*—the absence of a *zman*, the absence of two *eidim*, and so on—that do not apply to a *shtar kiddushin*. When the *mishnah* says *zehu safek gerushin*, the word *zehu* is *lav davka*—it is not meant to limit the category. Even a classic *safek* would apply. But when the *mishnah* says *zehu* regarding *kiddushin*, that *zehu* is *davka*, because the defects of a *get* that render it *pasul* do not carry over to *shtar kiddushin*.

Specifically, *le-ma'utei zman de-leita b'kiddushin*: to exclude the case of the missing *zman*, which invalidates a *get* but does not invalidate a *shtar kiddushin*. This explains why the *mishnah* uses exclusive language regarding *kiddushin*: it is not limiting *kiddushin* to only those scenarios, but rather signaling that the problems of *gierushin*—particularly the *zman* requirement—do not apply to *kiddushin*. That prompts the next question: why?

---

## Zman (Date) Requirement

### Two Reasons

Why did the Rabbis not require a *zman* in a *shtar kiddushin*? To answer this, the *gemara* first identifies why a *zman* is required in a *get* at all. Two reasons are offered. *Hani'cha l'man d'amar mishum peiri*: according to the view that the purpose of the date is to protect the woman's right to recover *peiros*—the usufruct—from her husband. And the second reason, which the *gemara* calls *mishum bas achoso*: to prevent a husband from backdating a *get* in order to protect his wife—perhaps his niece—from a charge of adultery.

Rashi explains the *peiros* reason as follows: from the moment a woman is divorced, her husband loses his entitlement to consume the fruit from her *nichsei melog*—her personal property. She is entitled to recover from him the fruit he consumed after the date of divorce. Since the husband may be tempted not to date the *get*, or to date it as late as possible, the Rabbis required a date to protect her. The question of why the husband would not be motivated to include an early date—since that would reduce his liability—is resolved by the observation that *mi-sha'ah she-nasan einav bah l'garshah shuv ein l'ba'al peiros*: from the moment he began writing the *get* with the intention of divorcing her, he forfeits his right to the fruit. So it is actually against his interest to have any date at all.

Similarly, once the Rabbis required a date, the concern about predating is neutralized, because witnesses who sign the *get* will not sign a false date. The date is therefore an effective protection: it establishes the precise moment from which the woman can recover her fruit, and it prevents false claims about timing in cases touching on adultery.

### Peiros Inapplicable

Given these two reasons, the *gemara* now asks why the *zman* was not required for a *shtar kiddushin* as well. Regarding the *peiros* reason, the answer is straightforward: *arusa leit lah peiros*. A husband's right to eat the fruit of his wife's property begins only at *nissu'in*, not at *kiddushin*. No transfer of property rights occurs at the moment of *kiddushin*, and therefore a date serves no function with respect to *peiros*.

### Adultery Challenge

But what of the second reason—*mishum bas achoso*, the concern about covering up adultery? If we require a date in a *get* so that one can know precisely when the divorce took place and prevent someone from claiming that a woman was already divorced before an act of adultery, the same logic would seem to apply to *kiddushin*. Without a date on the *shtar kiddushin*, a woman could claim she was only married after a particular event, thereby retroactively altering the legal picture. Should we not therefore require a date in a *shtar kiddushin* for the same reason?

### Money vs. Document

The *gemara*'s answer: *mishum d'ika d'mikadesh b'chaspa v'ika d'mikadesh b'shtara lo tiknu rabanan zeman*. Since people perform *kiddushin* with money far more often than with a document—and when *kiddushin* is performed with money there is no dated document at all—we would not have precise knowledge of the date of *kiddushin* in most cases anyway. It would therefore be inconsistent and practically ineffective to suddenly require a date when the minority of people who perform *kiddushin* with a *shtar* do so. The absence of a date would be the normal state of affairs, and the Rabbis did not impose a *zman* requirement for this reason.

As a practical observation, it is worth noting that among all the evidence recovered from the Cairo Geniza—the vast corpus of marriage documents and *ketubot* analyzed by scholars such as Mordechai Friedman—there appears to be not a single documented instance of *kiddushei shtara* in practice. The *gemara* acknowledges that some do *kiddushin* with money and some with a document, but the historical record suggests overwhelmingly that *kiddushei kesef* was the universal practice.

### Slave Analogy

Rav Acha the son of Rav Yosef raised a challenge to Rav Ashi: *v'ha avda*—what about a slave? A slave can be acquired either with money or with a document, just as *kiddushin* can be performed either way. Yet the Rabbis did require a *zman* in the document of slave acquisition. Why, then, does the same logic not apply to require a *zman* in a *shtar kiddushin*?

### Majority Principle

The *gemara* answers: *hatam ruba b'shtara*—there, the majority of slave acquisitions are done with a document, since owners naturally want documented proof of ownership of their property. Therefore, the Rabbis require a *zman* in that document, and we are not concerned about the minority cases done with money. *Hacha ruba b'chesef*—here, the majority of *kiddushin* are performed with money. We do not restructure the entire institution for the rare case of *kiddushei shtara*.

### Witness Testimony

The *gemara* offers an alternative reason why a *zman* in a *shtar kiddushin* would be impractical: *ibba'it eima mishum d'lo efshar*—because it would simply not be effective. The question is: who would hold onto the *shtar kiddushin*?

If she holds onto it—*lenacheihu gabi didah*—she could erase the date and deny when the *kiddushin* took place: *machkah lei*. If he holds onto it—the same problem arises in reverse: *zimnin de-bat achoto hee, mechaplei lah*, perhaps she is his niece and he will want to protect her by making the document disappear. And if the witnesses hold onto it as a neutral third party—*lincha gabei edim*—that also will not help. If they still remember the event, *leisu lisan*, they can testify from their own memory without needing the document. But if they do not remember, they might look at the document and testify based on what they read, not based on genuine recollection. And the Torah says *mi-pihem velo miksavam*: testimony must come from their mouths, from what they actually remember, and not from what they read in a document.

### Memory vs. Writing

This principle—*mi-pihem velo miksavam*—opens a genuinely striking discussion. Tosafot raises an obvious objection: the entire institution of a signed *shtar* is premised on the document serving as evidence. Why would witnesses need to testify at all? They should simply produce the signed document and let it speak for itself. Tosafot concedes the point entirely: if the witnesses actually produce the document and present it to the court without claiming independent memory, that is perfectly valid—*shapir havu avdi*. The signed witnesses on a *shtar* are treated as if their testimony has already been examined by a *beit din*—*de-edim ha-chasumim a-shetar na-asu ke-mi she-nechkerah edutan be-Veit Din*. The concern is specifically that they might not produce the document but instead claim to testify from memory when in fact they are relying on what they read—*ela shema ya-idu al ha-ma'aseh atzmo ke-ilu hem zochrim ve-einam zochrim, ela al pi ha-ksav*. That is the invalid case.

There is a further refinement: if reading a document actually prompts genuine recollection—not simply reading and asserting the event happened, but actually remembering it—then testifying based on that recalled memory is valid. The problematic case is the one in the middle: the witnesses do not genuinely remember, they are not producing the document, but they are testifying as if they remember because they read it. What is permitted, then, is either presenting the signed document directly, or using a written note to jog one's memory so that one genuinely recalls the event and testifies from actual recollection.

Tosafot also notes the practice cited by Rabbeinu Tam of witnesses writing out their testimony and sending it in writing to the *beit din*. This is different from the problematic case: since the witnesses do genuinely remember, *d'lo karinan bei mipihem velo mipi kesavam*, the mode of communication through writing does not render the testimony invalid—*keivan d'heim zochrim edusam*. The problem arises only when the written record is substituting for, rather than expressing, actual memory.

---

## Three Brothers Case

### Case Setup

The *mishnah* now presents: *gimel achin nesuin gimel nochriyos*—three brothers married to three unrelated women. One of them dies—*v'meis echad meihem*—and the second one performs *ma'amar* with the available *yevamah*—*v'asah bah hasheini ma'amar*—and then the second one dies as well.

To set out the case concretely: Reuven is married to Rochel, Shimon is married to Devorah, and Levi is married to Chuldah. Reuven dies. Shimon does *ma'amar* with Rochel. Shimon then dies. Levi now has an obligation of *yibum* toward Devorah, coming from Shimon, and an obligation of *yibum* toward Rochel, coming from Reuven—and additionally a quasi-obligation toward Rochel from Shimon, since *ma'amar* establishes a semi-marital bond. Rochel thus comes to him through two separate brothers.

### Zika Problem

The *mishnah* rules: *harei elu choltzos v'lo misyabmos*—both women, Devorah and Rochel, receive *chalitza* and may not undergo *yibum*. Why is Rochel problematic is clear from the *drashah* on the verse: *mi she'aleha zikas yavam echad*, the *yibum* obligation applies only to a woman connected through one deceased brother, *v'lo she'aleha zikas shnei yevamin*—not to a woman connected through two brothers. Since Shimon's *ma'amar* created a quasi-bond with Rochel while Reuven's original marriage also binds her to Levi, she arrives at Levi through two separate brothers, and that dual *zika* is excluded. If *ma'amar* carries some *d'oraita* weight—as the school of Beit Shammai maintains—then Rochel could genuinely stand in a quasi-status that creates a real double *zika*; even according to those who hold *ma'amar* is purely *d'rabbanan*, the *drashah* would be applied at the *d'rabbanan* level.

### Yibum Question

What is less obvious is why Devorah cannot undergo *yibum*. Devorah is connected to Levi through Shimon, straightforwardly, without any complication. Why does the *mishnah* require that she also receive only *chalitza*?

### Gezeira Decree

The *gemara* addresses this. If the prohibition on Rochel were a genuine *d'oraita* problem—a real biblical disqualification—then why does she require *chalitza* at all? If the Torah excludes a woman in such a double-*zika* situation, she should simply walk away without any *chalitza*. The *gemara* answers: *ela miderabbanan*—this entire prohibition is only rabbinic in origin, most likely because *ma'amar* itself is a *d'rabbanan* institution. Since it is a *d'rabbanan* matter, Rochel still requires *chalitza*.

The reason Devorah also requires only *chalitza*—and cannot undergo *yibum*—is a *gezeira*: *shema yomru shtei yevamot habaot mibayit echad mityabmot*. People will think that since Rochel was quasi-married to Shimon through *ma'amar*, and Devorah was actually married to Shimon, both are Shimon's wives. If Levi does *yibum* with one and *chalitza* with the other, observers will conclude that when a brother dies leaving two wives, the surviving brother may do *yibum* with both. That conclusion is of course wrong: one does *yibum* with one wife and *chalitza* with the others.

### Mixed Forbidden

The *gemara* then considers: why not simply allow *yibum* with Devorah and *chalitza* with Rochel? The *gemara* answers with a further *gezeira*: *shema yomru bayit echad miktzato banuy umiktzato chalutz*. People will see both women in the picture, and they will conclude that when a brother dies with multiple wives, one can do *yibum* with one and *chalitza* with another interchangeably.

One might respond: so what if people think that? What is the actual harm? The *gemara* answers: *ee d'miabem v'hadar chalitz*—if the normal practice were *yibum* first and then *chalitza* for the remaining wives, the error would carry no intrinsic cost. Perhaps people would perform unnecessary *chalitza*, and the women would be disqualified from *kehuna*, but the *beit din* would know better, and the act of *chalitza* itself would not be inherently harmful. But here the concern is different: *dilma chalitz be'reisha v'hadar miyabem*—perhaps, based on the mistaken understanding, someone will first perform *chalitza* with one and then attempt *yibum* with the other. That reversal is catastrophic. Once he has performed *chalitza* he enters the category of one who has not built up his brother's house—*v'kam lei b'asher lo yivneh*—and the Torah says *shuv lo yivneh*: once he has failed to build, he can no longer do so. The *chalitza* would render the subsequent *yibum* a violation.

It is therefore to prevent this catastrophic wrong-order scenario that the *gemara* requires both women to receive *chalitza* and permits neither to undergo *yibum*.

### Rava's Get Case

Rava now introduces a new variant: *nasan get l'maamaro*. What if, after performing *ma'amar* with Rochel, Shimon changed his mind and gave her a *get* to undo the *ma'amar*, and then died? Is Rochel now out of the picture, freeing Levi to perform *yibum* with Devorah? And might Levi even be free to perform *yibum* with Rochel herself, since she reverts to being a simple *yevamah* awaiting *yibum* or *chalitza*?

Rava rules: *nasan get l'maamaro, hutra tzarasah*—if he gave a *get* to counteract his *ma'amar*, the co-wife Devorah is released and may undergo *yibum*. *Aval hi asura*—but Rochel herself remains forbidden to *yibum*, and Levi can perform only *chalitza* with her. Why? *D'michalfa b'baalas get*—because people will confuse her situation with that of a woman who received a *get* on the *zika* itself, not on the *ma'amar*.

To clarify the relevant structure of *halacha*: if a man performed *ma'amar* and wishes to separate, he requires both a *get* for the *ma'amar* and *chalitza* for the *zika*. If he did no *ma'amar* and wishes to release the *yevamah*, only *chalitza* is required. There is also the concept of a *get l'zika*—a *get* addressed not to a *ma'amar* but to the *zika* itself—which is a rabbinic act that prevents *yibum* going forward, while still leaving the woman requiring *chalitza*. The critical distinction in Rava's ruling is that the *get* in this case was given *l'maamaro*—specifically to counteract the *ma'amar*—and not to the *zika*.

### Get Scope

A second opinion is cited: *icha d'amri*, some say Rava's ruling is that *nasan get l'maamaro, hutra afilu hi*—even Rochel herself is permitted, and Levi may perform *yibum* even with her. The reasoning: *ma d'avad bah shaklei*—what he did to her, the *ma'amar*, he completely removed. The *get* neutralizes the *ma'amar* entirely, and she is treated as if no *ma'amar* was ever performed. We do not view her as a *baalas get* who received a *get* on the *zika*; we see her simply as a *yevamah* who no longer has any *ma'amar* in the picture.

Rashi clarifies the distinction between the two opinions: the *get* must explicitly specify that it is directed at the *ma'amar* and not at the *zika*—*she-peresh l'maamaro v'lo l'zikato*. A *stam get*, one without explicit specification, is presumed to be directed at the *zika* as well, thereby preventing all the brothers from performing *yibum*: *aval stama kaima v'lo yivne kulu achim*.

This ambiguity actually lends force to Rava's first position. Since it is quite unclear in practice whether a given *get* is directed at the *ma'amar* or at the *zika*, the concern about confusion—about people thinking this is a case of receiving a *get* on the *zika*—is not at all far-fetched. The *gezeira* is well-grounded precisely because the distinction is subtle and practically difficult to maintain.

---

## Two Sisters Case

### First Status

The *mishnah* presents: *shnei achim nesuim shtei achayot*—two brothers married to two sisters—and one of them dies. Reuven is married to Rochel and Shimon is married to Leah. Reuven dies. What is Rochel's status with respect to Shimon? She is *achot isha*—his wife's sister—an *erva*, and she is forbidden. She walks away without *yibum* or *chalitza*.

### Permanent Prohibition

The *mishnah* then adds: *v'achar kach meta ishto shel sheni*—and afterwards the wife of the second brother, Leah, dies. Could it now be argued that Rochel is no longer *achot isha*, since the sister is no longer alive, and Shimon might now be permitted to perform *yibum* with Rochel? The *mishnah* rules emphatically: *harei zu asura alav l'olam*—Rochel remains forbidden to Shimon forever. *Ho'il v'nasra alav sha'a achas*—since she was forbidden to him at that critical moment when the *yibum* obligation first arose, that prohibition is permanent.

### Third Brother Case

The *gemara* asks: *p'shita*—this is obvious! The *gemara* supports this with a comparison to a case discussed just prior, involving three brothers. Reuven, Shimon, and Levi. Reuven dies. Levi then marries Rochel. Levi dies. Shimon is now confronted with the question: may he perform *yibum* with Rochel? Even though by the time of Levi's death Rochel is no longer Shimon's wife's sister in any direct sense—Leah may be dead, or Rochel is no longer in that relationship—Shimon remains forbidden. The reasoning: at the initial critical moment when Reuven died, Rochel was *achot isha* to Shimon. That status was fixed at that moment.

### Obviousness

If that case—where Rochel was not completely excluded from the family because Levi had married her and she was still *mutar* to Levi—already established that the initial forbidden status is permanent, how much more so in the case of our *mishnah*, where Rochel was completely pushed away from the family the moment Reuven died. *Hacha d'ka midchaya mehai beita legamrei*—here she was entirely excluded from the entire fraternal household at that moment. If even a partial connection was insufficient to undo the forbidden status, surely a complete exclusion from the household makes the permanence of the prohibition all the more obvious. *Lo kol sheken*—this is an *a fortiori* case that requires no independent teaching.

### Order of Teaching

The *gemara* explains why this *mishnah* was taught nonetheless: *tana hai tana be'reisha*—this case was actually taught first, before the more complex three-brother case. At the time it was initially taught, the *tana* thought the three-brother case might be *mutar*, because Rochel was not completely out of the family circle—Levi had married her and she remained relevant to that household. The *tana* therefore initially contemplated that her status might change once Levi married her. Only afterward did the *tana* reconsider and conclude that even in that case she remains forbidden to Shimon: once she was *asura* to him at that initial moment, she remains *asura*.

Once the three-brother case was decided, the present *mishnah* became superfluous—it is now an *a fortiori* case that teaches nothing new. But since the *mishnah* had already been taught and fixed in the tradition as an important ruling in its own right, it was not removed: *u-mishna lo zaza mi-mekoma*. The *mishnah* remains in place, even though its independent necessity has been superseded by the more complex case that was ultimately resolved.

---

---

# Yevamot 32

## Eshet Ach & Achot Isha

### Braita Setup

The Gemara on 32a, approximately six lines below where the daf begins, introduces a *braita* that shifts the discussion into entirely new terrain — away from the specific case of two brothers and two sisters, and into the broader question of *issur chal al issur*, whether one prohibition can take effect on top of another. The *braita* presents the following scenario: a man's brother married his wife's sister. The woman is thus, to this man, simultaneously *eshet ach* (his brother's wife) and *achot isha* (his wife's sister) — two independent prohibitions apply to the very same person. He then has relations with her. What is his liability?

### R. Yose vs. R. Shimon

The *braita* records a dispute between Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Yose takes the straightforward position: he has transgressed two prohibitions, *eshet ach* and *achot isha*, and is liable for both. Rabbi Shimon disagrees, holding that he is liable for only one. Before even analyzing the reasoning behind this dispute, however, the Gemara immediately confronts a contradiction: a second version of Rabbi Shimon's ruling states the exact opposite — that he is liable only for *achot isha*, not for *eshet ach*. So Rabbi Shimon consistently holds that only one prohibition applies, but the two versions disagree about which one.

### Order Matters

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya*. The two versions reflect two different factual sequences. In one case, the brother who ultimately dies married her first — making her *eshet ach* before she became *achot isha*. In the other case, the surviving brother married first, making her *achot isha* before she became *eshet ach*. Rabbi Shimon's position is that you follow whichever status was established first. This is the key principle: the first prohibition defines her status, and the second cannot displace it.

To make this concrete: Reuven married Rachel, and Shimon married Leah. Reuven then dies. From Shimon's perspective, Rachel is both *eshet ach* and *achot isha*. If Reuven married Rachel before Shimon married Leah, then Rachel's first status relative to Shimon was *eshet ach*; the subsequent marriage to Leah that created the *achot isha* status came later and, according to Rabbi Shimon, cannot take effect. Conversely, if Shimon married Leah first, Rachel was already *achot isha* before Reuven ever married her, and the subsequent *eshet ach* status cannot displace the earlier one.

### Ein Issur Chal

The operative principle behind Rabbi Shimon's position is *ein issur chal al issur*: one prohibition does not take effect on top of a prohibition that is already in force. The second status, whatever it may be, cannot replace or supplement the first. Rabbi Shimon applies this categorically — whichever status came first is the one that counts, and only its attendant consequences apply.

It is worth pausing to note what is practically at stake. Both prohibitions carry *karet*. The difference is not about going to hell once versus twice, as it were, but rather about whether one who acted *beshogeg* is obligated to bring one *korban* or two, and potentially about other related consequences. These are real *halakhic* distinctions that make the debate substantive.

### Two Scenarios

This also raises an important side point regarding *yibum*. According to Rabbi Shimon, if Reuven died without children, one might think Shimon could perform *yibum* with Rachel — after all, in the scenario where Rachel's first status was *eshet ach*, the *achot isha* prohibition never took effect. But Rav Ashi explains that the *issur* of *achot isha* is, as it were, hovering above, latent but present. Were the *issur eshet ach* to fall away — precisely what *yibum* would accomplish — the *issur achot isha* would immediately descend and take hold. Because performing *yibum* would only usher in the next prohibition, the first prohibition does not dissolve, and Rachel remains forbidden. This is a striking mechanism: the very act that would remove one prohibition would instantaneously activate another, so the system locks in place.

---

## R. Yose's Position

### Both Prohibitions

The Gemara now turns to Rabbi Yose, who says that both prohibitions apply simultaneously. Does Rabbi Yose truly hold that *issur chal al issur* — that one prohibition can take effect on top of another? This seems to be a striking claim, and the Gemara immediately raises a contradiction from Rabbi Yose's own rulings elsewhere.

### Two Deaths Braita

A *braita* teaches: if one commits a sin that carries two different death penalties, the court imposes only the more severe one — *nidon b'chamura*. Rabbi Yose disagrees: *nidon b'zika harishona haba'ah alav*, one is judged according to the first relationship that defined his liability. The term *zika* — connection or relationship — is significant here. Rabbi Yose says that the first relationship is what defines the punishment.

### Mother-in-Law Case

The *braita* then illustrates Rabbi Yose's view with a concrete case. A mother-in-law is subject to the penalty of *sreifa* (burning), while an *eshet ish* (married woman) is punishable by *chenek* (strangulation), the less severe death. Now consider a woman who is both a man's mother-in-law and a married woman — a natural scenario, since she is presumably married to his father-in-law.

### Zika Rishona

The *tanna kamma* would say he is punished by *sreifa*, the more severe penalty. Rabbi Yose says no — go by the first relationship. If she was his mother-in-law first and subsequently became a married woman (for instance, she was widowed or divorced and then remarried), then the first *zika* is mother-in-law, and he is punished by *sreifa*. But if she was a married woman first — that is, she was already married before he ever married her daughter — then the first *zika* is *eshet ish*, and he is punished only by *chenek*, not by *sreifa*.

This is the critical insight. The only way Rabbi Yose can arrive at the lighter penalty of *chenek* is if he genuinely holds that the mother-in-law status, though technically applicable, does not create a separate legal reality. He is not saying merely that we pick the lighter punishment while acknowledging both — he is saying the later status never took effect. This is structurally identical to *ein issur chal al issur*.

### R. Yose's Stance

But then we have the contradiction. The same Rabbi Yose who says in the mother-in-law case that you go by the first relationship — which implies *ein issur chal al issur* — says in the *eshet ach*/*achot isha* case that you are liable for both. Does Rabbi Yose hold *issur chal al issur* or not?

---

## Mosif vs. Kolel

### Issur Mosif Defined

The Gemara's answer, articulated by Rabbi Abahu, is: *modeh Rabbi Yosi be-issur mosif* — Rabbi Yose concedes that a second prohibition *can* take effect when it constitutes an *issur mosif*, a prohibition that broadens the scope of persons to whom the forbidden object or person is prohibited.

The concept requires careful exposition. The general rule is *ein issur chal al issur*: a second prohibition cannot descend onto an object already carrying a prohibition. But there is an exception: if the second prohibition extends the reach of that object's forbidden status to a wider class of people, it *can* take effect even on top of the existing one.

Consider the *eshet ach*/*achot isha* scenario. If Shimon married Leah first, Rachel became *achot isha* to Shimon. At that point, she was forbidden only to Shimon. Then Reuven married Rachel. By becoming *eshet ach*, Rachel's forbidden status now extends to all of Reuven's brothers — not just to Shimon, but to any other brothers as well. The scope of her prohibition has expanded: she was forbidden to one person, and now she is forbidden to a broader class of people. This is an *issur mosif*, and because it genuinely adds something — it reaches people who were not previously affected — it can take effect even on top of the existing *achot isha* prohibition. So in this sequence, Shimon is liable for both.

Why does it matter to Shimon that she is now forbidden to other brothers? The conceptual logic is that the new status has real operative content regarding other parties; since it takes effect vis-à-vis those others, it takes effect as a status altogether, including with respect to Shimon, even though she was already forbidden to him personally. The *issur mosif* creates an objectively new prohibition, not merely redundant with the one already in place.

If, on the other hand, Reuven married Rachel first, she was *eshet ach* from the outset, forbidden to all the brothers. Then Shimon married Leah. Now Rachel is *achot isha* — but the *achot isha* prohibition adds no new persons to whom Rachel is forbidden. She was already forbidden to all the brothers as *eshet ach*; the *achot isha* prohibition merely covers Shimon again, who was already covered. This is not an *issur mosif*, and thus the second prohibition cannot take effect.

The Gemara confirms: in the sequence where the surviving brother married first (wife's sister established first) and then the deceased brother married her (brother's wife established second), *migo de-itosif issur legabei achim* — since the new status broadens her prohibition to encompass the other brothers, *to-isif issur legabei dideih* — it also reinforces the prohibition with respect to Shimon himself. Both apply. In the reverse sequence, no such broadening occurs, and only the first prohibition counts.

### Issur Kolel Defined

Now the Gemara turns to a second category: *issur kolel*. This is a subtler and more contested concept. Whereas *issur mosif* means the forbidden object itself becomes prohibited to a wider class of people, *issur kolel* means the forbidden person finds themselves included within a larger population of people who are all now subject to the same prohibition — without the scope of the object's prohibition having changed at all.

The distinction can be illustrated as follows. With *issur mosif*: Rachel begins as *achot isha* — forbidden to Shimon. She then becomes *eshet ach* — now forbidden to all the brothers. Rachel herself has become prohibited to more people. Her own status has expanded outward. That is *issur mosif*.

With *issur kolel*: Rachel begins as *eshet ach* — forbidden to all the brothers. Shimon then marries Leah. Shimon is now forbidden not just to Rachel but to all of Leah's sisters. Rachel, as one of Leah's sisters, now finds herself among a larger class of women who are all forbidden to Shimon. But Rachel's own status has not changed — she was forbidden to all the brothers before, and she remains forbidden to all the brothers after. What changed is not Rachel's reach but Shimon's prohibitions: he is now subject to a broader class of women he cannot marry, and Rachel happens to be one of them. She becomes part of a *kolel*, a broader collective category, without her own status having expanded.

To crystallize the difference: *issur mosif* — the forbidden object is now prohibited to more people. *Issur kolel* — the person subject to the prohibition is now prohibited regarding a broader class of objects. The Gemara articulates this explicitly: *hai issur kolel hu* — this is an *issur kolel*, not an *issur mosif*. The object's scope has not changed; the subject's prohibited field has widened, sweeping the original object in.

### Why Mosif Works

Why does *issur mosif* allow a second prohibition to take effect but *issur kolel* does not? The Gemara's logic is that for the second prohibition to take effect on something already prohibited, it must bring something genuinely new that attaches to the object itself. With *issur mosif*, the object — Rachel — genuinely acquires a new dimension: she is now forbidden to people who were not previously forbidden from her. The new prohibition is a real, operative status change in the object. With *issur kolel*, the object itself has not changed; Rachel is still forbidden to exactly the same people as before. The change is in the subject's broader landscape of prohibitions, and that is not enough to generate a second, independent *issur* on the object.

The Gemara therefore concludes that Rabbi Yose holds of *issur mosif* but not *issur kolel*. This resolves the apparent contradiction: in the *eshet ach*/*achot isha* case, if the sequence creates an *issur mosif* — wife's sister first, then brother's wife — Rabbi Yose says both apply. In the mother-in-law and *eshet ish* case, when *eshet ish* comes first, mother-in-law is a narrower scope prohibition that cannot take effect on top of the broader one, so only the first applies.

The Gemara then raises a remaining difficulty: what does Rabbi Yose mean when he says both apply in the *eshet ach*/*achot isha* case in the opposite sequence, where no *issur mosif* exists? Rava answers: *ma'aleh ani alav ke'ilu asah shta'im bein chayav ela achas* — we consider it as if he committed two transgressions, even though he is formally liable for only one. This means that while the second prohibition does not create a second technical liability in terms of punishment, it still speaks to who this person is. The same formulation is confirmed by Rabbi Yochanan when Ravin transmitted his teaching: *ma'aleh ani alav ke'ilu asah shta'im ve'eino chayav ela achas*.

The Gemara asks: *mai nafka mina* — what is the practical consequence of this statement, which seems to say nothing more than "it's as if"? The answer is *likvoro bein resha'im gemurim* — it affects where he is buried. When the court executes a person, the severity of the sentence affects the section of the cemetery in which they are interred. The "as if" formulation means that in terms of his personal moral identity — what Briskers might call the *gavra* dimension — he is treated as one who committed two *aveiros*, even though the formal consequences of the act are determined by only one. This is how Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon are in fact arguing: Rabbi Shimon says it is purely one, even in this moral-identity sense; Rabbi Yose says it carries the character of two.

---

## R. Chiya vs. Bar Kappara

### Zar on Shabbos

The Gemara now connects the *issur chal al issur* discussion to a parallel series of debates between Rabbi Chiya and Bar Kappara. *Uviflukta* — this controversy, the Gemara says, is linked to another dispute. The first case: *zar she-shimesh be-Shabbos* — a non-*kohen* who performs the Temple service on *Shabbos*. The *halakha* is that a *zar* who performs the Temple service is liable with death *bidei shamayim*, and that performing *melacha* on *Shabbos* also incurs the death penalty, *bidei adam*. This person has done both: he has performed the Temple service as a non-*kohen*, and he has done so on *Shabbos*. Is he liable twice?

### Two vs. One

Rabbi Chiya says *chayav shta'im* — twice. Bar Kappara says *eino chayav ella achas* — only once. What follows is one of the more colorful passages in this section of the Gemara. Rabbi Chiya jumps up and takes an oath — *ha'avodah*, by the divine Temple service — that he heard from Rebbi (Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi) that the liability is twice. Bar Kappara immediately jumps up and takes his own oath — *ha'avodah* — that he heard from Rebbi exactly the opposite, that the liability is only once. Two Tannaim, two oaths, two contradictory reports. Rather than simply deferring to one or the other, both proceed to offer logical arguments in support of their positions.

### R. Chiya's Logic

Rabbi Chiya argues: *Shabbos* was forbidden to everyone. When it was permitted in the Temple — that is, when the Temple service overrides *Shabbos* — that dispensation was granted *etzel kohanim*, specifically to *kohanim*. For non-*kohanim*, no such dispensation was ever extended. Therefore, *yesh kan mishum zarus ve-yesh kan mishum Shabbos* — he has violated both the prohibition against a *zar* performing the Temple service and the prohibition of *Shabbos*.

### Bar Kappara Logic

Bar Kappara counters: *Shabbos* was forbidden to everyone; when it was permitted in the Temple, it was permitted *in the Temple* — that is, within the context of the Temple service, *melacha* on *Shabbos* does not apply at all. The premise of the *Shabbos* prohibition is simply set aside entirely in this context, not merely waived for *kohanim* specifically. Therefore, *ein kan ella zarus* — there is only the prohibition of *zar* performing the service; the *Shabbos* violation simply does not exist here.

This is a strange position on its face. One might ask: does this mean anyone can walk into the Temple and light a match on *Shabbos*? Bar Kappara's logic seems to push in that direction, and the Gemara is aware of the difficulty. The debate is ultimately about how to conceptualize the nature of the *heter*: is it a targeted dispensation for *kohanim* doing the *avodah*, leaving the *Shabbos* prohibition intact for everyone else? Or does the Temple context itself dissolve the *Shabbos* prohibition as an operative category, such that there is simply no *Shabbos* issue for any action performed there?

### Baal Mum & Tamei

The second parallel case: *baal mum she-shimesh be-tumah* — a *kohen* with a physical blemish who performs the Temple service in a state of *tumah* (ritual impurity), specifically in the context of a *korban tzibur* (communal offering). As background: a *baal mum* is normally forbidden from performing the *avodah*, and serving in a state of *tumah* is also normally forbidden. However, *tumah* is overridden for a *korban tzibur* — when the entire community is *tamei*, the communal sacrifice may still be brought. So were this *kohen* unblemished, the *tumah* would not be a problem. But he is a *baal mum*, so he cannot perform the *avodah* in any case. Has he violated only the prohibition of *baal mum*, or has he also violated the prohibition of *tumah*?

Rabbi Chiya says twice; Bar Kappara says once. They take the same oaths as before. Rabbi Chiya's argument: *tumah* was forbidden to all; when it was permitted in the Temple for a *korban tzibur*, that dispensation was granted *lekohanim tmimim* — to unblemished *kohanim* capable of performing the *avodah*, not to a *baal mum*. Since this *baal mum* was not the intended beneficiary of the dispensation, the *tumah* prohibition still applies to him in full. He therefore violates both. Bar Kappara's argument: when the Torah permits *tumah* in the Temple for a *korban tzibur*, it permits it for all Temple service in that context — the *tumah* prohibition is simply not operative in this situation, regardless of who is performing the *avodah*. Therefore only the *baal mum* prohibition applies.

It is worth noting that Bar Kappara's position here is somewhat more coherent than in the *Shabbos* case. The principle of *tumah hutra be-tzibur* — that *tumah* is broadly set aside when communal sacrifices are required — is a recognized *halakhic* category with genuine *sugyot* behind it, and one can plausibly argue that in such a context the prohibition of *tumah* is not merely waived for eligible *kohanim* but is categorically suspended.

### Melikah Case

The third case: *zeh she-achal melikah* — a non-*kohen* who ate from a bird *korban* that had been slaughtered by the *kohen* through *melikah* (the method of severing the bird's spine with the fingernail from behind the neck). *Melikah* is the valid method for bringing a bird sacrifice; when performed by a *kohen* on a qualifying *korban*, it renders the bird a legitimate offering, edible by *kohanim*. But this particular bird offering — a *chatas* — may only be eaten by *kohanim*. A non-*kohen* who eats it has certainly violated the prohibition against *zarim* eating from a *korban chatas*.

But has he also violated the prohibition of eating *neveilah*? Because *melikah*, unlike *shechita*, does not involve cutting the neck with a knife in a way that would render the bird a properly slaughtered animal for ordinary consumption. A bird slaughtered in this fashion outside the Temple context would indeed be a *neveilah*. Is this bird, then, simultaneously a kosher *korban* (permitted to *kohanim*) and a *neveilah* (with respect to *zarim*)? Rabbi Chiya says twice; Bar Kappara says once. The same oaths, the same structure.

Rabbi Chiya's argument: *neveilah* was forbidden to all; when it was permitted in the Temple through the vehicle of *melikah*, that permission was granted to *kohanim* specifically — *lekohanim hutra, velo le-zarim*. For this non-*kohen*, it remains a *neveilah*. He therefore violates both. Bar Kappara's argument: when the Torah established *melikah* as the mode of bringing a bird sacrifice, it was declaring that an animal prepared this way *is not a neveilah* — not that it is a *neveilah* for which there happens to be a special permit. The Torah redefined the category: done this way, in this context, it simply is not a *neveilah* at all. Therefore there is no *neveilah* issue, and only the *zarus* prohibition applies.

Bar Kappara's position in this third case is arguably the most compelling of the three. There is a coherent reading of *melikah* as a mode of preparation that is *sui generis* — the Torah, by prescribing it, defined the result as *not neveilah* rather than as *neveilah with a dispensation*. This is a meaningful conceptual distinction.

Despite the local coherence of each of Bar Kappara's arguments, the Gemara is going to reframe all three cases as expressing a single, unified *halakhic* debate rather than three separate local questions.

---

## Simultaneous Prohibi (II)

### All Three Are Kolel

The Gemara now asks: *be-mai kamiflagi* — what is the underlying dispute between Rabbi Chiya and Bar Kappara across all three cases? The answer proposed: *be-issur kolel ve-aliba de-Rabbi Yosi* — they are debating *issur kolel* according to Rabbi Yose. Recall that we established Rabbi Yose holds of *issur mosif* but the question remained whether he holds of *issur kolel*. All three cases, the Gemara now suggests, are structured as instances of *issur kolel*.

---

## Simultaneous Prohibi (II)

### R. Chiya on Kolel

Rabbi Chiya holds: *Rabbi Yosi be-issur kolel mechayev tartei* — Rabbi Yose says that even an *issur kolel* can take effect, generating liability for two prohibitions. This is why Rabbi Chiya rules twice across all three cases — he understands them as *issur kolel* scenarios in which Rabbi Yose would impose dual liability.

### Bar Kappara on Kolel

Bar Kappara holds: *lo mechayev ella chada* — even Rabbi Yose does not permit the second prohibition to take effect when it is only *issur kolel*. The second prohibition must genuinely expand the scope of the object itself (*issur mosif*); merely sweeping the object into a broader class of the subject's prohibitions (*issur kolel*) is insufficient. Hence only one.

The Gemara then demonstrates how each of the three cases can be understood as *issur kolel*. In the case of the *zar* on *Shabbos*: initially, the *zar* could perform *melacha* freely on weekdays — his only prohibition was the *avodah* in the Temple. When *Shabbos* arrives, he becomes forbidden in *melacha* generally; the class of things he cannot do expands, sweeping the Temple *avodah* into that broader class. His own forbidden status — the *avodah* prohibition — has not changed; he was forbidden from the *avodah* all along. But the range of activities he cannot engage in has broadened, and because the *avodah* falls within the same category of activity as *melacha*, it is now doubly prohibited, so to speak — once from *zarus* and once because it is a form of *melacha* that he cannot perform on *Shabbos*. This is *issur kolel*: the subject's prohibited activities have expanded, sweeping the already-forbidden act into a broader category.

In the case of the *baal mum* who became *tamei*: a *baal mum* cannot perform the *avodah* but may eat *korbanot*. Once he becomes *tamei*, he loses the ability to eat *korbanot* as well. Because he is now restricted in eating — and being restricted in eating *korbanot* is linked to being restricted in performing the *avodah* — the *tumah* status adds an additional dimension to his prohibition against performing the *avodah*. More of his activities are now forbidden; the *avodah* prohibition gets swept into this broader set of restrictions.

### Bat Achat Issue

But here a fundamental problem emerges with the *melikah* case. The Gemara states: *ella melikah be-vat achat hi de-mishkachat lah — be-issur kolel lo mishkachat lah*. In the *melikah* case, you cannot construct any sequence at all. The moment the *kohen* performs *melikah*, two things happen simultaneously: the bird becomes a *neveilah* (were it not a *korban*) and it becomes a *korban* prohibited to *zarim*. There is no prior moment when one prohibition existed without the other. You cannot say the *zarus* prohibition came first and the *neveilah* prohibition was added later, or vice versa — they arise in the same instant. The very act of *melikah* introduces both *issurin* in *bat achat*, at one and the same moment. *Issur kolel* requires at minimum a conceptual sequence; if both prohibitions arise simultaneously, *issur kolel* cannot be the operative framework.

### Real Debate

The Gemara therefore proposes a reframing: *kamiflagi be-issur bat achat* — the debate between Rabbi Chiya and Bar Kappara is actually about what happens when two prohibitions arise simultaneously. And the debate is *aliba de-Rabbi Yosi* — according to Rabbi Yose, who is already known to permit *issur chal al issur* in the case of *issur mosif*. Would Rabbi Yose also say that when two prohibitions arise at exactly the same moment — *bat achat* — both take effect? Rabbi Chiya says yes: *Rabbi Yosi be-issur bat achat mechayev tartei*. Bar Kappara says no: *lo mechayev ella chada* — even simultaneous prohibitions yield only one.

---

## Mosif vs. Kolel (II)

### Application to Yevamot

To close the loop back to our original case, we must now apply the framework of *issur mosif* and *issur kolel* to the question of *eshet ach* and *achot isha* that opened the discussion. We established that *issur mosif* works when the second prohibition broadens the scope of persons to whom the object is forbidden. In the sequence where *achot isha* comes first — she is forbidden to Shimon alone — and then she becomes *eshet ach* by marrying Reuven, she is now forbidden to all of the brothers. That expansion of scope constitutes *issur mosif*, and Rabbi Yose says both prohibitions apply. In the reverse sequence, where *eshet ach* comes first — she is already forbidden to all the brothers — the subsequent *achot isha* status, which merely sweeps her into the broader class of sisters forbidden to Shimon, constitutes *issur kolel*. Since Rabbi Yose does not hold of *issur kolel*, only the first prohibition applies, and the *ke'ilu asah shta'im* formulation of Rava addresses the residual moral dimension in that sequence.

---

## Reconciling Testimony

### The Contradiction

The Gemara returns to the most pressing structural puzzle: how can both Rabbi Chiya and Bar Kappara have taken oaths that they heard opposite rulings from the same teacher, Rebbi? They are not simply disagreeing about the law; each claims a direct personal tradition. Somebody heard incorrectly, but the Gemara resists attributing this to dishonesty — hence the need to reconstruct a scenario in which both could have genuinely misunderstood. And crucially, the Gemara is not satisfied with an explanation that works in only one direction; it needs an account that explains how each side could have innocently reached the wrong conclusion.

### Theory One

The first proposed resolution: *ki asnei l'dideih aliba de-Rabbi Yosi* — when Rebbi taught Rabbi Chiya, he was teaching according to Rabbi Yose, and said twice. *Ki asnei le-Bar Kappara aliba de-Rabbi Shimon* — when he taught Bar Kappara, he was presenting the view of Rabbi Shimon, and said once. Each student heard Rebbi's statement correctly but took it as Rebbi's definitive ruling rather than as a presentation of a particular Tanna's position. Rabbi Chiya heard twice and remembered twice; Bar Kappara heard once and remembered once. The mistake was one of attribution — each attached the ruling to Rebbi's own authority rather than to the Tanna whose position Rebbi was presenting.

### Theory Two

The Gemara is not fully satisfied with this explanation, however, and proposes a second framework. *Ela kamifligi be-issur bat achat aliba de-Rabbi Shimon* — perhaps the real debate is about *bat achat*, simultaneous prohibitions, according to Rabbi Shimon, not Rabbi Yose. The logic: Rabbi Yose is already known to permit *issur chal al issur* in certain cases. Rabbi Shimon categorically says *ein issur chal al issur*. Perhaps, however, even Rabbi Shimon would permit dual liability in the case of *bat achat* — when the prohibitions arise simultaneously, there is no moment where one preceded the other, and the logic of "one cannot take effect on top of the other" simply does not apply. They took hold together. Rabbi Chiya swears twice, maintaining that even Rabbi Shimon holds of liability in a *bat achat* scenario. Bar Kappara swears once, holding that Rabbi Shimon's position is consistent: even *bat achat* yields only one.

### Unresolved Problem

Yet the Gemara identifies a persistent difficulty with both frameworks. In either formulation — whether the debate is *bat achat aliba de-Rabbi Yosi* or *bat achat aliba de-Rabbi Shimon* — one can explain how one of the two scholars might have misunderstood. Under theory one, Rabbi Chiya could understand Bar Kappara's mistake: Rebbi said once according to Rabbi Shimon, and Bar Kappara mistakenly took it as Rebbi's general ruling; Rabbi Chiya knows the twice ruling was according to Rabbi Yose. But under the same theory, it is harder to explain from Bar Kappara's vantage point how Rabbi Chiya could have innocently arrived at twice if, according to Bar Kappara, even Rabbi Yose only yields once for *bat achat* — what would twice even be based on?

Under theory two, the problem is similarly asymmetric. If the debate is whether Rabbi Shimon allows *bat achat* to generate dual liability, then Rabbi Chiya is swearing that Rabbi Shimon permits twice in such a case, a position that contradicts the well-established understanding of Rabbi Shimon. One can understand why Bar Kappara would say once — that is simply Rabbi Shimon's known position. But *why* would Bar Kappara have needed to swear to that? It is the obvious, unremarkable reading of Rabbi Shimon. The oath adds nothing. And conversely, it becomes difficult to construct a plausible innocent mistake in the other direction. The Gemara leaves this *kashya* unresolved — *aliba de-Bar Kappara Rabbi Chiya shikurei ka-mishaker?* is asked but not answered to the Gemara's own satisfaction, and the discussion will continue.

---

---

# Yevamot 32b

## Achos Isha & Eshes Ach

### Two Prohibitions

The *gemara* on 32b picks up towards the bottom of the page, approximately six lines after the *gemara* begins, with *v'hashtah tanu rabbanan* — and now the Sages taught in a *baraita*. The case under discussion involves two brothers who have married two sisters, and the *gemara* has already established that even after one brother dies, his widow remains forbidden as *achos isha* — the surviving brother's wife's sister — to the surviving brother. Nothing here is dramatically new from what the *mishnah* has already introduced. But now the *gemara* presents a *baraita* that will open into a major conceptual discussion, taking us into very different territory.

The *baraita* describes a woman who is simultaneously forbidden in two distinct ways: she is both *eshes ach*, a brother's wife, and *achos isha*, a wife's sister. The scenario is not complicated to construct. One brother married a woman who happens to be the other brother's wife's sister. The brother dies — assume, for now, that there are children, so *yibbum* is not in play. This woman stands in two prohibited relationships to the surviving brother at once. If the surviving brother has relations with her, what is he liable for?

### Rabbi Yossi: Two

*Ba aleha chayav aleha mishum eshes ach umishum achos isha divrei Rabbi Yossi* — *Rabbi Yossi* says that he is liable under two headings: she is his brother's wife and she is his wife's sister. This seems entirely straightforward. She is in fact both, and the prohibition of each applies independently.

### Rabbi Shimon: One

*Rabbi Shimon omer eino chayav ela mishum eshes ach bilvad* — Rabbi Shimon says no: he is liable only for *eshes ach*, brother's wife, and not for *achos isha*, wife's sister. But this immediately generates a contradiction, because a second version of the *baraita* records Rabbi Shimon as saying precisely the reverse — *eino chayav ela mishum achos isha bilvad* — only wife's sister, not brother's wife. How can Rabbi Shimon say it is only one, and how can one version say it is *eshes ach* while the other says it is *achos isha*, if she is undeniably both?

### Lo Kashya Reconciliation

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction with *lo kashya*: there is no difficulty. The two versions of the *baraita* reflect two different factual sequences. *Kan shenasa chai v'achar kach nasa mes* — in one case, the surviving brother married first, and then the brother who would eventually die married her afterward. *Kan shenasa mes v'achar kach nasa chai* — in the other case, it was the reverse: the one who died married her first, and then the surviving brother married his own wife later.

The resolution flows from Rabbi Shimon's principle of *ein issur chal al issur* — one prohibited status does not take effect on top of a pre-existing one. The first prohibited relationship that was established is the operative one; the second cannot displace or supplement it.

### Marriage Sequence Example

To make this concrete: suppose Reuven is married to Rachel and Shimon is married to Leah, and Reuven and Shimon are brothers. Reuven dies. Rachel is now both *eshes ach* and *achos isha* to Shimon. Which status controls?

If Reuven married Rachel before Shimon married Leah — *nasa mes v'achar kach nasa chai* — then when Reuven married Rachel, she first became *eshes ach*, a brother's wife, to Shimon. Only later, when Shimon married Leah, did she become *achos isha*. Rabbi Shimon says the first status, *eshes ach*, is the operative one.

If the order was reversed — Shimon first married Leah, making Rachel his *achos isha*, and only afterward did Reuven marry Rachel — then when Reuven's marriage came about, she was already his *achos isha*, and the status of *eshes ach* was the second one to arrive. Rabbi Shimon again says go by the first status: she is *achos isha*. That explains why one version of the *baraita* records *eshes ach* as the operative prohibition and the other records *achos isha* — the difference is entirely a matter of which relationship was established first.

---

## Ein Issur Chal Issur

### Concept Introduction

This brings us to the central concept that will drive the *gemara* for the balance of today's material: *ein issur chal al issur*, one prohibited status does not take effect on top of another pre-existing one. It is the foundational principle behind Rabbi Shimon's ruling.

The obvious question is: what practical difference does it make? Both *eshes ach* and *achos isha* carry the penalty of *kares*. The person is going to the same fate regardless. But the difference is not trivial. If the act was performed *beshogeg* — without full awareness of the prohibition — the question of whether there is one prohibition or two determines whether one brings one *korban* or two. That is a concrete and significant *nafka minah*, as one of the students correctly observed, and it sets the table for why the disagreement matters at all.

The *gemara* also asks whether *ein issur chal al issur* operates in other familiar contexts — such as a person who eats *basar b'chalav* on Yom Kippur, stacking multiple prohibitions on a single act. The answer, as the *gemara* will clarify, depends on the precise nature of the second prohibition and its relationship to the first. But before reaching those distinctions, the *gemara* introduces another dimension to the problem.

### Rav Ashi: Hovering

*Amar Rav Ashi: issur achos isha miktala tali vekay.* Rav Ashi explains that the prohibition of *achos isha* does not simply disappear or become legally nonexistent merely because *eshes ach* was there first. Rather, it hovers. It is a real and applicable status — it simply cannot take effect because there is a pre-existing status occupying that space.

### Status Replacement Mechanism

The practical consequence of this hovering is striking. *Ee paka issur eshes ach* — if the prohibition of *eshes ach* were somehow removed, *asi issur achos isha vechayeil* — the hovering prohibition of *achos isha* would immediately descend and take effect. The moment the first status is vacated, the second rushes in.

### Yibbum Paradox

This creates a paradox for *yibbum*. Assume the order was: Reuven married Rachel first, making her *eshes ach* to Shimon; then Shimon married Leah, making Rachel *achos isha* as well, but that second status merely hovers. Now Reuven dies childless. Ordinarily, *eshes ach* would dissolve through the fulfillment of *yibbum*. But Rav Ashi explains: the very act of performing *yibbum* would vacate the *eshes ach* status, which would immediately invite the *achos isha* prohibition to land. Rachel would become Shimon's *achos isha* the moment *yibbum* is attempted.

*Vehilchach lo paka* — therefore the *eshes ach* status does not dissolve. Because *yibbum* would only trigger the hovering prohibition, it cannot be performed. Rachel remains forbidden under the operative prohibition of *eshes ach* even when Reuven dies childless, and the other wives in the *yibbum* structure are consequently treated as *tzaras erva* as well. The mechanism is self-sealing: *yibbum* is impossible precisely because it would activate the very *issur* it would otherwise seem to avoid.

---

## Rabbi Yossi Position

### Contradiction Question

The *gemara* now turns to a deep tension in Rabbi Yossi's position. Rabbi Yossi said in the *baraita* that the person who has relations with a woman who is both *eshes ach* and *achos isha* is liable for both. This implies that Rabbi Yossi holds *issur chal al issur* — that a second prohibition can indeed take effect on top of a first. But can that really be his view consistently?

### Mother-in-law Case

*Vehatanya* — and we have a *baraita* teaching that if someone committed a transgression that carries two different death penalties — *avar aveira sheyeish bah shtei misos* — the *halacha* is *nidon bachamura*, he is judged by the more severe punishment. A mother-in-law, *chamoso*, is punishable by *sreifa*, which is a weightier form of execution. A married woman, *eishet ish*, is punishable by *chenek*, which is considered the less severe form. Now consider a woman who is simultaneously a man's mother-in-law and a married woman — the most natural case being that his mother-in-law is married to his father-in-law.

The *tanna kamma* would say he is judged by *sreifa*, the heavier penalty, since that is the weightier of the two death sentences. But Rabbi Yossi says no: *nidon bezika harishona habaa alav* — he is judged according to the first relationship that defined their connection.

### First Relationship Rule

The *baraita* specifies how this plays out. If she was first his mother-in-law — she was widowed or divorced and then remarried — so that the *chamoso* status preceded the *eishet ish* status, then he is judged by *sreifa*. If, however, she was first a married woman to another man and then he married her daughter — so *eishet ish* came first and *chamoso* came later — then he is judged only by *chenek*, the penalty for *eishet ish*. The *chamoso* prohibition, though weightier, arrived second and does not displace the first.

The only coherent way to explain why Rabbi Yossi would ever impose the *lighter* penalty — *chenek* rather than *sreifa* — is to say that he holds the second prohibition simply does not attach when a first one is already in place. He is not punished by *sreifa* because, in his view, the *chamoso* status never legally took effect. That is precisely *ein issur chal al issur*.

### Sequence Determines Status

So we have a contradiction. In the case of *achos isha* and *eshes ach*, Rabbi Yossi seems to hold *issur chal al issur* — you can get both statuses. In the case of mother-in-law and married woman, he clearly holds *ein issur chal al issur* — the first status controls and the second does not take effect. Which is it?

### Rabbi Abbahu Resolution

*Amar Rabbi Abbahu: modeh Rabbi Yose be'issur mosif* — Rabbi Abbahu resolves the contradiction. Rabbi Yossi concedes, as a category, to *issur mosif*. This introduces the crucial distinction that will occupy the *gemara* from this point forward, and it opens the door to a broader taxonomy of how second prohibitions relate to first ones.

---

## Mosif vs. Kolel

### Issur Mosif Definition

There are, as the *gemara* now elaborates, multiple ways in which a second *issur* can relate to a first. The *gemara* identifies two principal categories: *issur mosif* and *issur kolel*. A third — *issur be'vas achas*, simultaneous prohibitions — will be addressed later.

*Issur mosif* means a prohibition that broadens the scope of *people* to whom the forbidden object or person is prohibited. The focus is on the *cheftza* — the object or person who is forbidden — and the question is whether that object or person has become forbidden to a wider circle of people under the second *issur* than it was under the first.

### Mosif Example

Return to the case of *achos isha* and *eshes ach*. Consider the sequence: Shimon first marries Leah, making Rachel forbidden to Shimon as *achos isha* — wife's sister. Subsequently, Reuven marries Rachel. At the moment Reuven marries Rachel, Rachel becomes *eshes ach* — brother's wife — not only to Shimon but to all of Reuven's brothers. Her status has expanded. Before Reuven's marriage, Rachel was forbidden to Shimon alone under the *achos isha* prohibition. After Reuven's marriage, she is forbidden to all of Reuven's brothers — a broader scope of people.

This is *issur mosif*: the second *issur*, *eshes ach*, is broader in scope than the first, *achos isha*, because it applies to a wider population. The logic is that since this new status, *eshes ach*, has genuine relevance to the other brothers — *migo d'itosaf issur legabei achim*, since an additional prohibition accrues with respect to the brothers — *itosaf issur legabei deidei* — it also takes effect with respect to Shimon, even though she was already forbidden to him under the first status. The new status has enough traction to be real because it matters to other people; and because it is real, it attaches even for Shimon.

This is why Rabbi Yossi can say, in one sequence, that the person is liable for both *eshes ach* and *achos isha*: when *achos isha* comes first and *eshes ach* comes second, the second *issur* is an *issur mosif* and can take effect despite the prior prohibition. Rabbi Yossi concedes to *issur mosif* — he agrees that a second *issur* of broader scope can impose itself on a first.

But a question immediately arises: what about the reverse sequence? If she first became *eshes ach* — Reuven married her first, making her the brother's wife, forbidden to all brothers — and then Shimon married Leah, now making Rachel his *achos isha* as well, why would Rabbi Yossi say both in that case? *Mai issur mosif ika?* — what broadening of scope is there here? She was already forbidden to all the brothers as *eshes ach*. *Achos isha* is actually a narrower *issur* — it applies only to Shimon, not to the other brothers. It adds no additional people. So there is no *issur mosif* in this sequence, and it seems Rabbi Yossi should agree that only the first status, *eshes ach*, applies.

Perhaps one might argue: *migu d'issar becholhu achvasa* — since when Shimon married Leah, all of her sisters became forbidden to Shimon, maybe Rachel now finds herself within a larger class of forbidden women, and that is a kind of broadening. But the *gemara* identifies this as something categorically different.

### Issur Kolel Definition

This brings us to *issur kolel*. While *issur mosif* focuses on the *cheftza* — the forbidden person's scope has broadened to include more people — *issur kolel* focuses on the *gavra*, the person who is prohibited. In *issur kolel*, the forbidden object has not become forbidden to more people. Rather, the person who is subject to the prohibition now finds himself prohibited in a broader range of activities or in a broader class of forbidden relationships.

The clearest way to distinguish them: in *issur mosif*, Rachel herself becomes forbidden to more people. In *issur kolel*, Shimon finds himself forbidden to more women — Rachel is now part of a larger category of women that Shimon cannot marry.
