She has not become prohibited to a wider circle; rather, she has been swept into a wider *klal* of things forbidden to him.

### Kolel Example

The example is exactly the scenario of the reverse sequence: Reuven married Rachel first, making her *eshes ach* to all the brothers. Then Shimon married Leah, making all of Leah's sisters — including Rachel — forbidden to Shimon as *achos isha*. Rachel's status vis-à-vis the brothers has not changed; she was forbidden to them all before and remains so. What has changed is that Shimon, by marrying Leah, now finds himself forbidden to a broader range of women: not only Rachel, but all of Leah's sisters. Rachel finds herself included in that broader class.

The question *issur kolel* asks is: since Rachel's sisters are now forbidden to Shimon, and Rachel is one of those sisters, does the fact that she has been drawn into this larger *klal* of forbidden women allow the *achos isha* prohibition to attach — even though she was already forbidden to Shimon under *eshes ach*? The argument would be: since the new *issur* covers a broader category of activities or relationships for the *gavra*, perhaps it can take hold even where a prior *issur* already exists, because it is operating at a different level.

The distinction between *mosif* and *kolel* can be summarized this way: *issur mosif* changes the status of the forbidden *cheftza* by expanding the scope of people to whom it is prohibited. *Issur kolel* changes the status of the *gavra* by expanding the range of things he is prohibited from. In the first case, the forbidden thing is now forbidden more broadly. In the second case, the forbidden person now has a broader set of prohibitions, of which this one is part.

### Kolel Application Question

The *gemara* then asks whether Rabbi Yossi, who concedes to *issur mosif*, would also hold of *issur kolel* — whether a second *issur* that broadens the *gavra*'s prohibited activities can also take effect on a pre-existing first *issur*. This question is what sets up Rava's intervention.

---

## Rava: As If Two

### Rava's Formulation

*Ella amar Rava* — Rava steps in with a formulation that is at once elegant and puzzling: *mah lani alav k'ilu asah shtayim v'eino chayav ela achas* — it is as if he transgressed two, but he is only liable for one.

Rava is acknowledging the force of the preceding analysis. Rabbi Yossi holds *issur mosif*, not *issur kolel*. In the sequence where *eshes ach* came first and *achos isha* came second, there is no *issur mosif* — the second *issur* does not broaden the scope of who is forbidden. And since Rabbi Yossi does not hold of *issur kolel* — that is clear from the mother-in-law case — technically, Rabbi Yossi in that reverse sequence ought to agree that only one prohibition applies. So why does he say you transgress both?

Rava's answer: in the reverse sequence, Rabbi Yossi does not mean that literally, technically, in terms of punishment and consequence, two prohibitions have taken effect. He means rather that *k'ilu* — it is *as if* — two prohibitions were transgressed. The same formulation is cited in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *ki ata Ravin amar Reb Yochanan mah lani leh k'ilu asah shtayim v'eino chayav ela achas*.

### Mah Nafka Mina

The *gemara* immediately presses the obvious question: *mah nafka mina?* If he is only liable for one, what difference does the *k'ilu* make? What is the practical meaning of saying it is *as if* he transgressed two, if in terms of punishment and legal consequence there is only one? If we strip away punishment entirely — imagine the *Torah* had imposed no penalty — would we say this person violated one prohibition or two? *Ein issur chal al issur*, as Rabbi Shimon frames it, might not mean the second prohibition literally does not exist; it might mean only that its consequences are subsumed by the first. The act may still be a genuine transgression of both, even if the practical consequences are assessed through the first status alone.

### Burial Application

*Likavro bein reshaim gemurim* — the *nafka minah* is where the person is buried after *beis din* executes him. The Sanhedrin would bury those it executed in designated sections of the cemetery, calibrated to the severity of their crime. This determination is not about punishment per se — it is about personal status and identity, about what this person's actions say about *who he is*. If he is treated *b'gavra*, in terms of personal standing, as someone who transgressed two prohibitions, he is buried among the fully wicked. This is the tangible consequence of the *k'ilu* — not an additional penalty imposed on the act, but a statement about the person.

This is a strikingly thin *nafka minah*, and the precise nature of the dispute with Rabbi Shimon remains somewhat elusive. But what the *gemara* has now established is a full conceptual map: Rabbi Shimon holds categorically *ein issur chal al issur*; Rabbi Yossi concedes to *issur mosif* — when the second *issur* broadens the scope of people who are forbidden — but does not hold of *issur kolel*; and in cases that fall into neither category, Rava explains Rabbi Yossi's position as a *k'ilu* — a matter of identity and status, not of additional punishment.

---

## Three Parallel Cases

### Zar BeShabbat

The *gemara* now connects the principle of *issur chal al issur* to a famous set of three parallel debates, each involving a situation where two prohibitions seem to converge on a single act. The first case: *zar sheshimmesh b'shabbos* — a non-*kohen* who performs the *avodah* in the *Beis Hamikdash* on *Shabbos*. A non-*kohen* who performs the Temple service is liable with the death penalty. Someone who performs *melacha* on *Shabbos* is also liable. Here both seem to apply simultaneously. Is he liable twice?

### Rabbi Chiyya vs. Bar Kappara

*Rabbi Chiyya omer chayav shtayim* — Rabbi Chiyya says he is liable for two. *Bar Kappara omer eino chayav ela achas* — Bar Kappara says only one. Both then take dramatic oaths. *Kafatz Rabbi Chiyya v'nishba: ha'avodah, kach shamati meRebbi shtayim* — Rabbi Chiyya jumped up and swore, by the Temple service itself: this is what I heard from Rebbe, that he is liable twice. *Kafatz Bar Kappara v'nishba: ha'avodah, kach shamati meRebbi achas* — Bar Kappara jumped up and swore the same oath in the opposite direction: this is what I heard from Rebbe, only once. The oaths make it impossible to dismiss either report as simple error of transmission — both are insisting with the utmost solemnity on having heard from the same source.

### Chiyya's Logic

Rabbi Chiyya then offers his reasoning. *Shabbos l'chol nitra* — *Shabbos* was forbidden to everyone. *K'shehutra b'Mikdash* — when it was permitted in the *Beis Hamikdash*, *etzel kohanim hutra* — it was permitted specifically for *kohanim*. *L'kohanim hutra v'lo l'zarim* — the dispensation applies to *kohanim*, not to non-*kohanim*. Therefore this person, as a *zar*, never received any dispensation from the *Shabbos* prohibition. *Yesh kan mishum zarus v'yesh kan mishum Shabbos* — there is a violation of performing unauthorized *avodah* as a non-*kohen*, and there is also a violation of *Shabbos*. Both apply.

### Bar Kappara Logic

Bar Kappara's counter-argument is structurally similar but arrives at an opposite conclusion. *Shabbos l'chola nasra* — *Shabbos* was forbidden to all. *K'shehutra, b'Mikdash hutra* — when a dispensation was given, it was given for the *Mikdash* as such, not specifically for *kohanim*. The *Mikdash* context itself waives the *Shabbos* concern. Therefore, anyone performing any activity in the *Mikdash* on *Shabbos* — even a *zar* performing unauthorized *avodah* — is operating in a context where *Shabbos* has been waived. *Ein kan ela zarus* — the only violation is the prohibition of a non-*kohen* performing the *avodah*.

This position is, as one might note, genuinely surprising. It seems to imply that anyone who walks into the *Beis Hamikdash* on *Shabbos* and strikes a match incurs no *Shabbos* violation — which is bizarre. But Bar Kappara is apparently conceptualizing the *Mikdash* as a space where the *Shabbos* prohibition does not apply, full stop, rather than as a space where *kohanim* receive a specific dispensation to perform the *avodah*.

### Ba'al Mum BeTemeiut

The second parallel case: *ba'al mum sheshimmesh b'tuma* — a *kohen* with a physical blemish who performs the *avodah* while *tamei*. A *ba'al mum* is ordinarily forbidden to perform the *avodah*, though he may eat from the *korbanot*. A *tamei* person is also forbidden to perform the *avodah*. Here the relevant background is that *tumah* can be overridden for a *korban tzibbur* — a communal sacrifice. Were this a normal *kohen*, he would have a dispensation to perform the *avodah* despite being *tamei* when there is a *korban tzibbur*. But this *kohen* has a blemish, which bars him from performing the *avodah* regardless. When he nonetheless performs the *avodah* while *tamei* in the context of a *korban tzibbur*, is he liable for both prohibitions — *ba'al mum* and *tumah* — or only for *ba'al mum*?

Again Rabbi Chiyya says twice and Bar Kappara says once, and both take the same solemn oath attributing their position to Rebbe.

Rabbi Chiyya's reasoning: *tumah l'chola nasra* — *tumah* was forbidden to all. *K'shehutra b'Mikdash l'kohanim temimim hutra* — when a dispensation was given, it was given to unblemished *kohanim* who are actually eligible to perform the *avodah*. A *ba'al mum* is not among those for whom the dispensation was granted. Therefore the *tumah* prohibition still applies to him. *Yesh kan mishum ba'al mum v'yesh kan mishum tumah* — both prohibitions are in force.

Bar Kappara counters: *k'shehutra b'Mikdash, b'Mikdash hutra* — when the dispensation was given, it was given for anything performed in the *Mikdash* in the context of *korban tzibbur*. The waiver is contextual, not person-specific. In this context, *tumah* as such is not a violation. *Ein kan ela mishum ba'al mum* — the only operative prohibition is that of the blemished *kohen* performing the *avodah*. This argument, notably, carries more intuitive weight than the *Shabbos* case. The principle of *tumah hutra b'tzibbur* is itself a known categorical rule; one can plausibly argue that in the context of communal sacrifice, *tumah* concerns are simply set aside.

### Zar Melikah

The third case: *zar she'achal melikah* — a non-*kohen* who ate from a bird offering that was slaughtered by *melikah*. The *kohen* pierces the back of the bird's neck with his fingernail. This is the prescribed method for a bird *chatas*. If this were done outside the context of a *korban*, the bird would be a *neveilah* — an animal that did not die through a valid *shechitah*. In the context of the *korban*, it is kosher and may be eaten by *kohanim*. A non-*kohen* ate this bird. He has certainly violated the prohibition against a *zar* eating a *korban chatas*. Has he also violated the prohibition against eating *neveilah*?

Again Rabbi Chiyya says twice and Bar Kappara says once; again both swear by *ha'avodah* that Rebbe said their version.

Rabbi Chiyya's reasoning: *neveilah lechol ne'esra* — *neveilah* was forbidden to all. *K'shehutra b'Mikdash, etzel kohanim hutra* — when it was permitted in the *Mikdash*, by virtue of *melikah* making it a valid *korban*, that permission was granted specifically to *kohanim*. For a *zar*, it remains *neveilah*. *Yesh kan mishum zarus v'yesh kan mishum melikah* — two violations.

Bar Kappara responds: *k'shehutra b'Mikdash hutrah* — the Torah itself, in prescribing *melikah* as the method for bird sacrifices, effectively declared that a bird killed this way is not a *neveilah*. It is simply not in the category of *neveilah*. *Ein kan ela mishum zarus* — there is only the violation of a non-*kohen* eating from a *korban*. This argument, as noted, carries real force: one can reasonably read the Torah's prescription of *melikah* as a wholesale redefinition of that act, such that the *neveilah* category simply does not apply.

---

## Issur Chal Analysis

### Reframing Question

Having presented all three parallel debates, the *gemara* steps back and asks: *bemai kamifligi?* — what is the underlying disagreement? On the surface, each case looks like a local question about how to conceptualize a specific halakhic dispensation. But the *gemara* suggests that these three parallel disputes reflect a unified deeper question, and it proposes that the real debate is: *be'issur kolel ve'aliba d'Rabbi Yosei* — it concerns the principle of *issur kolel*, and specifically whether Rabbi Yossi would apply it.

We have already established that Rabbi Yossi holds *issur mosif* — he allows a second *issur* to take effect when it broadens the scope of people to whom the *cheftza* is forbidden. The question now is whether Rabbi Yossi would also hold *issur kolel* — whether a second *issur* that broadens the class of *activities* forbidden to the person can take effect on a pre-existing prohibition.

### Chiyya: Kolel Applies

*Rabbi Chiyya savar Rabbi Yosei be'issur kolel mechayev* — Rabbi Chiyya holds that Rabbi Yossi would say *issur kolel* does allow a second prohibition to take effect, generating liability twice. All three of the parallel cases are instances of *issur kolel*, and Rabbi Chiyya is arguing that Rabbi Yossi's logic extends to them.

### Bar Kappara: Kolel Doesn't Apply

*Bar Kappara savar lo mechayev ela chada* — Bar Kappara holds that even Rabbi Yossi would not apply *issur kolel* to create double liability. Only one prohibition counts.

### Zar BeShabbat Analysis

The *gemara* works through each case to demonstrate where *issur kolel* appears. For the *zar* who performs *avodah* on *Shabbos*: *zar me'ikara shari bemelacha v'assur ba'avodah* — initially, on any weekday, the *zar* is permitted to perform *melacha* but is forbidden to perform the *avodah* in the *Mikdash*. That is his one prohibition. Then *Shabbos* arrives. *Asya leShabbos: migu d'kamitra bemelacha, itsar nami ba'avodah* — since he is now prohibited from *melacha* in general, and the *avodah* falls within the category of *melacha*, the broader prohibition of *Shabbos melacha* now encompasses the *avodah* as well.

This is *issur kolel*: the *zar*'s prohibited activities have broadened. Before *Shabbos*, he could do most things but not the *avodah*. On *Shabbos*, he cannot do a wide class of activities — *melacha* generally — and the *avodah* is included within that broader class. The *avodah* has not become forbidden to more people (*mosif*); rather, the *zar* now has a broader set of prohibited activities (*kolel*), into which the *avodah* is swept.

### Ba'al Mum Analysis

In the case of the *ba'al mum*: initially, he could eat from *korbanot* but could not perform the *avodah*. Then he became *tamei*. *Migu d'itassar ba'achila, itassar nami ba'avodah* — since he is now prohibited from eating *korbanot* due to *tumah*, and his relationship to *korbanot* has broadly changed, that broader prohibition also extends to performing the *avodah*. The class of activities related to *korbanot* that are now forbidden to him has widened, and the *avodah* is within that class. Again, *issur kolel*: his prohibited activities have broadened.

---

## Issur Chal Analysis (II)

### Melikah Problem

But when the *gemara* tries to apply the same *issur kolel* framework to the third case — the *zar* who ate *melikah* — it runs into a problem. *Ela: melikah be'vas achas hi* — the *melikah* case is one where everything happens at once. The moment the *kohen* performs *melikah* on the bird, two things occur simultaneously: the bird becomes a valid *korban*, triggering the prohibition of a *zar* eating it; and it also has the status of *neveilah* for those not eligible to eat it. There is no sequence — no prior state in which one prohibition existed before the other. *Be'issur kolel lo mishkachas lah* — you simply cannot construct an *issur kolel* scenario in this case, because *issur kolel* requires a first *issur* already in place before a second, broader one arrives. Here both arrive at the same instant. The *issur kolel* analysis, therefore, cannot be what is at stake in the *melikah* case.

---

## Bat Achat Debate

### Simultaneous Prohibition

This leads the *gemara* to a fresh formulation. *Kamipalgi be'issur be'vas achas* — the real debate underlying all three cases is not *issur kolel* but rather *issur be'vas achas*: what happens when two prohibitions arise simultaneously, at the exact same moment? According to Rabbi Yossi, who is prepared under some conditions to hold that a second *issur* takes effect despite a first, would he say the same when the two *issurim* arrive together, with no sequencing at all? *Rabbi Chiyya savar Rabbi Yosei be'issur be'vas achat mechayev tarti* — Rabbi Chiyya holds that Rabbi Yossi would impose double liability even when both prohibitions arise at once. *Bar Kappara savar lo mechayev ela chada* — Bar Kappara holds that even Rabbi Yossi would impose only one.

### Scenarios Constructed

The *gemara* then addresses an obvious challenge: if this is about simultaneous prohibitions, where does the simultaneity appear in the *Shabbos* and *ba'al mum* cases? Those seem to involve a prior condition (*zar*; *ba'al mum*) already in place before *Shabbos* arrives or before *tumah* supervenes. The *gemara* constructs specific scenarios to generate genuine *be'vas achas* situations.

### Zar Bar Mitzvah

*Kegon d'aysi shtei sa'aros b'Shabbos* — imagine a young man who reaches adulthood — acquiring his two pubic hairs, the halachic sign of majority — at the very moment *Shabbos* begins. Before that moment, he was a minor and was not subject to these prohibitions in the same way. At the instant he becomes an adult, it is simultaneously *Shabbos*, and simultaneously he is a *zar*. Both the prohibition of a non-*kohen* performing the *avodah* and the prohibition of *Shabbos* *melacha* descend upon him at the exact same moment. *D'havya leh zarus v'shabbos bahadi hadadi* — *zarus* and *Shabbos* come to him together.

### Kohein Bar Mitzvah

For the *ba'al mum* case: *kegon d'afik shtei sa'aros b'mum* — imagine a young man who had a blemish and who was also *tamei*, and who acquired his two pubic hairs — reached adulthood — at this moment. Before majority, neither prohibition was operative on him in the full sense. At the moment of majority, both the *ba'al mum* prohibition and the *tumah* prohibition descended simultaneously. *D'havya leh ba'al mum v'tumah bahadi hadadi* — both came at the same time.

### Knife Injury Alternative

Alternatively — and this is presented as a somewhat more interesting construction — *shechatach etzba'o b'sakin tme'iah* — he cut his finger with a *tamei* knife. At the very moment he was cut, he simultaneously acquired a *mum* — the blemish disqualifying him from the *avodah* — and became *tamei* through contact with the *tamei* knife. Both statuses arrived at the same instant, without any possibility of sequencing one before the other.

---

## Disagreement Reconstruct…

### Both Heard Rebbe

With the theoretical framework now constructed, the *gemara* returns to the immediate puzzle with which it began: how can Rabbi Chiyya and Bar Kappara take opposite oaths about what Rebbe said? Rebbe said one thing. The *gemara* is unwilling to say Rebbe changed his mind, and it is unwilling to say either rabbi is lying — particularly given the oaths. So it seeks to reconstruct how both could have heard accurately and still arrived at opposite conclusions.

### Different Tannaim

*Bishlama l'Rabbi Chiyya* — it works easily according to Rabbi Chiyya's perspective. *Ki asnei l'didei aliba d'Rabbi Yosei* — when Rebbe taught Rabbi Chiyya, saying you get double liability, he was presenting the position according to Rabbi Yossi, who is the one prepared to hold *issur chal al issur* and who, per Rabbi Chiyya, extends it even to *be'vas achas* cases. *Ki asnei l'Bar Kappara aliba d'Rabbi Shimon* — and when Rebbe taught Bar Kappara, saying only once, he was presenting the view of Rabbi Shimon, who categorically holds *ein issur chal al issur*. From Rabbi Chiyya's vantage point, Bar Kappara's mistake is entirely understandable: he heard the teaching according to Rabbi Shimon and mistook it for Rebbe's definitive ruling.

But the symmetrical problem arises immediately. According to Bar Kappara's understanding — that even Rabbi Yossi would hold only once in a *be'vas achas* case — how can he explain what Rabbi Chiyya heard? *Ela l'Bar Kappara Rabbi Chiyya shikurei kameshaker?* — is Rabbi Chiyya simply lying? He swore. The *gemara* cannot accept that either sworn testimony is fabricated.

### Mutual Truthfulness

The *gemara* grapples with the fact that both rabbis are insisting with equal conviction on having heard from the same master. Any reconstruction must be capable of accounting for both directions — explaining how each could have heard accurately, and how each could charitably understand where the other went wrong. Simply asserting one framework or the other always leaves one of the two swearing truthfully and the other irreconcilably mistaken in a way that is hard to explain.

### Rabbi Shimon Focus

The *gemara* therefore shifts the frame of the entire debate. *Ela k'mipalgi b'issur bas achas aliba d'Rabbi Shimon* — rather than asking whether Rabbi Yossi would extend *issur* to *be'vas achas* cases, the real dispute may concern Rabbi Shimon's position on simultaneous prohibitions. Rabbi Shimon ordinarily and categorically holds *ein issur chal al issur*. The question is whether *be'vas achas* might be an exception even for Rabbi Shimon — since when both prohibitions arrive at the exact same instant, neither can be said to pre-exist the other. There is no first *issur* for the second to overlay. Perhaps even Rabbi Shimon would concede that both take effect simultaneously.

On this reading: Rabbi Chiyya's oath that Rebbe said twice reflects Rebbe teaching that even Rabbi Shimon holds double liability in a *be'vas achas* case. Bar Kappara's oath that Rebbe said once reflects Rebbe teaching that Rabbi Shimon holds his usual position — *ein issur chal al issur* — even when they arrive together. Both could have heard Rebbe accurately, each in a different teaching session or context, each presenting Rabbi Shimon's position. Rabbi Chiyya is not saying Rabbi Yossi; both are debating what Rabbi Shimon holds about the *be'vas achas* scenario.

But the *gemara* then presses the same question in reverse: *bishlama l'Bar Kappara kamishhtava l'afuki l'Rabbi Shimon me'Chizkiya* — according to Bar Kappara, Rabbi Chiyya's oath makes sense as arguing that even Rabbi Shimon holds twice in a *be'vas achas* case, that being a non-trivial claim worth swearing about. *Ela l'Rabbi Chiyya lamma lei l'ishtabuei?* — but according to Rabbi Chiyya, why would Bar Kappara need to swear? Bar Kappara is simply saying Rabbi Shimon holds his normal position, one violation. That is not a controversial claim requiring an oath. *Kashya* — the *gemara* records this as a difficulty, unresolved at this point in the discussion. The full resolution of how both sworn testimonies can be vindicated simultaneously will be addressed as the *gemara* continues.

---

---

# Yevamot 33

## Chiya/Bar Kappara

### Three Scenarios

The Gemara on 33b picks up a dispute between Rabbi Chiya and Bar Kappara concerning three scenarios involving transgressions performed simultaneously or in sequence in the Temple context: a *zar* (non-kohen) who performs the *avodah* on *Shabbat*, a *baal mum* (physically blemished kohen) who performs the *avodah* in a state of *tumah* at a time when *tumah hutra betzibbur* (communal impurity is permitted), and a *zar* who eats from a bird upon which *melikah* (the nape-pinching slaughter unique to bird-offerings) was performed. The question was whether, in each scenario, the individual transgresses one prohibition or two. The Gemara sought to frame this disagreement as a debate about *issur chal al issur* — whether a second prohibition can take effect upon a preexisting one — and explored several explanatory models.

### Issur Kolel/Bevas Achas

The model of *issur kolel* — where a later prohibition encompasses a broader category and thus takes effect despite a prior prohibition already being in place — could account for the first two scenarios, which admit of a sequential reading: first one becomes a *zar*, and only thereafter does *Shabbat* arrive; first one is a *baal mum*, and only thereafter does *tumah* set in. The *melikah* case, however, cannot be sequential. The moment the bird's neck is pinched, it simultaneously becomes a *korban* forbidden to non-kohanim and becomes non-kosher for ordinary consumption. These two prohibitions arise at the exact same instant — *bevas achas* — making it impossible to say that one preceded the other. The Gemara therefore concluded that the underlying debate is whether *issur chal al issur* can operate *bevas achas*, and specifically whether Rabbi Shimon — who ordinarily rejects *issur chal al issur* — would concede that when two prohibitions arise simultaneously, both take effect.

### Bar Kappara's Error

This conclusion, however, creates a difficulty. Both Rabbi Chiya and Bar Kappara swore oaths that they had heard Rebbi's ruling directly: Rabbi Chiya maintained that Rebbi said two transgressions, Bar Kappara that Rebbi said one. If the *bevas achas* case genuinely yields two transgressions even according to the most lenient opinion — even according to Rabbi Shimon — then from Rabbi Chiya's perspective, how could Bar Kappara ever have heard from Rebbi that one only transgresses once? The Gemara poses this starkly: *ela l'Rabbi Chiya, Bar Kappara shikra ka meshaker?* — is Bar Kappara simply lying?

### Misremembering Theory

Rabbi Chiya's answer is that Bar Kappara is not lying — he genuinely misremembered. The Gemara explains: *ki asniyah Rebbi lidi-di tarti l'patur asniyah* — when Rebbi taught the ruling of "one transgression" to Bar Kappara, he was teaching only the first two cases, those of the *zar* on *Shabbat* and the *baal mum* in *tumah*. In those two cases, the sequence is that first one already has the status of *zar* or *baal mum*, and only afterward the additional prohibition of *Shabbat* or *tumah* arrives. This is a case of *issur kolel* — the later prohibition is broader in scope. According to Rabbi Shimon, who rejects *issur chal al issur*, if he even rejects *issur mosif* (a prohibition that extends the class of persons to whom the object is forbidden), he certainly rejects *issur kolel*. So Rebbi taught Bar Kappara that according to Rabbi Shimon, in these two sequential cases you transgress only once.

Then Bar Kappara encountered the third case — *vezar she'achal melicha*, the *zar* who ate from the *melikah* bird. Because it was structurally similar — again a non-kohen doing something ordinarily permitted when done correctly — he mixed it together with the first two in his mind: *ve'aydi d'damya lei arbav bahadeihu*. Now, treating all three as a single teaching, he noticed that the only common denominator across the newly combined set was *bevas achas*. He therefore concluded that the entire teaching was about *bevas achas*, and since Rebbi had exempted from a second transgression in those cases, he assumed Rebbi meant that *bevas achas* also yields only one transgression. In short, Bar Kappara misremembered — he inadvertently inserted the *melikah* case, which changed the character of the set, and drew a conclusion that Rebbi had never actually taught.

### Three Forms Summarized

This analysis occasions a useful summary of the three forms by which *issur chal al issur* can operate. *Issur mosif* is perhaps the most intuitively accessible: a second prohibition takes effect because it extends the forbidden status to a wider audience — more people, or more types of activity, are now prohibited with respect to this object. *Issur kolel* is harder: the object was already forbidden to everyone, but now more items within the same class are also forbidden, and by virtue of that expansion, the original prohibition is deemed to have been re-imposed in its fuller form. *Bevas achas* — when both prohibitions arise simultaneously — is in some respects the most conceptually straightforward, since there is no prior prohibition whose "territorial claim" would be challenged; both take effect together, and it is argued that even Rabbi Shimon would concede to this.

---

## Beraita Proof

### Zar/Baal Mum Beraita

Having established that the debate between Rabbi Chiya and Bar Kappara concerns whether *bevas achas* would cause even Rabbi Shimon to concede that two transgressions are incurred, the Gemara turns to a *beraita* that addresses almost precisely the same cases. The *beraita* states: *zar sheshimash b'Shabbat u'vaal mum sheshimash b'tumah* — a *zar* who performed the *avodah* on *Shabbat*, and a *baal mum* who performed the *avodah* in *tumah* even in a situation of *tumah hutra betzibbur*. In the first case, says the *beraita*, one transgresses both for being a *zar* and for *Shabbat*; in the second, for being a *baal mum* and for *tumah*. This is the position of Rabbi Yose. Rabbi Shimon disagrees: *ein kan ela mishum zar u'vaal mum bilvad* — there is only the first, original transgression of being a *zar* or *baal mum*; the subsequently arriving prohibition of *Shabbat* or *tumah* does not take further effect. This confirms that the debate is indeed between Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon, the very Tannaim known to disagree about *issur chal al issur*.

### Melikah Omitted

Crucially, the *beraita* discusses only two of the three scenarios — and conspicuously omits the *melikah* case. The Gemara asks: for whom was it omitted, and why? If the omission is from Rabbi Yose's perspective, that makes no sense. Rabbi Yose is prepared to say two transgressions even when the prohibitions arrive sequentially — how much more so would he say so when they arrive *bevas achas*, where there is no question of one preceding the other. *Hashta Rabbi Yose be'issur kolel mechayev shtayim, be'issur bevas achas mibaya?* — if Rabbi Yose obligates twice even in a sequential *kolel* case, would he ever hesitate regarding a *bevas achas* case? Clearly not. The *melikah* case must therefore have been omitted because it would yield a *different* ruling for the other disputant — Rabbi Shimon.

### Conclusion on Bevas Achas

The Gemara concludes: *ela lav Rabbi Shimon* — it is precisely because Rabbi Shimon would rule differently in the *melikah* case that it was left out. The *beraita* records Rabbi Shimon's leniency only for the sequential cases, where *issur kolel* is the operative mechanism. *Be'issur kolel hu d'patar* — it is specifically in the *kolel* scenario that Rabbi Shimon rules exempt. But *aval be'issur bevas achas mechayev* — in the *bevas achas* case, Rabbi Shimon would concede and hold the person liable for two transgressions. The Gemara therefore declares *tiyuvta d'Bar Kappara tiyuvta* — this is a refutation of Bar Kappara's position.

One might ask whether this proof is fully decisive. The *beraita* clearly treats three cases in the prior discussion, yet mentions only two. That something distinctive about the third case caused it to be omitted is a reasonable inference, and if one accepts *bevas achas* as the distinguishing feature, this constitutes a solid proof that Rabbi Shimon concedes in the *melikah* scenario. Whether the *beraita* also establishes precisely what the original dispute between Rabbi Chiya and Bar Kappara was about is a more open question — but the core ruling, that Rabbi Shimon holds *bevas achas chayav shtayim*, emerges clearly.

---

## Zar Shechita Analysis

### Shechita Permitted?

Before the Gemara moves to the next *Mishnah*, it pauses on a technical question that the *beraita*'s case raises: *bemai* — in what act exactly did the *zar* violate *Shabbat*? The problem is sharper than it first appears. If the *zar* performed *shechita* (slaughter of the *korban*), there is no *Shabbat* violation, because *shechita* of a *korban* by a non-kohen is actually *kasher*. This is a striking and perhaps unfamiliar *halacha*: even on *Shabbat*, when a communal *korban* overrides the day's restrictions, a non-kohen may perform the *shechita*, and that act is entirely valid. So there would be no secondary transgression there to speak of.

If instead the *zar* performed *kabbalah* (catching the blood) or *holachah* (carrying the blood to the *mizbeach*), this is essentially a matter of carrying within an enclosed area — a form of *tiltul b'alma*, simple moving of an object — and hardly the substantive *Shabbat* violation the *beraita* has in mind. If the act in question was *haktarah* — burning the limbs on the *mizbeach* — then, as Rav Yosef taught, *hav'ara l'lav yatza*: making a fire on *Shabbat* is, according to Rabbi Yose himself (one of the two disputants in the *beraita*), only a *lav* rather than a capital offense, because the Torah singled it out explicitly, and Rabbi Yose interprets that singling-out as a demotion in severity. This creates an inconsistency: are we seriously saying the two-transgression debate hinges on the lighter *lav* of *hav'ara*?

### Yom Kippur Exception

Rav Acha bar Yaakov resolves the difficulty by re-framing the scenario entirely: the case is not *Shabbat* in the ordinary sense but rather *Yom Kippur* — specifically the *shechita* of the High Priest's ox (*paro shel Kohen Gadol*). On *Yom Kippur*, the *avodah* is exclusive to the Kohen Gadol, and according to the opinion that the *shechita* of the Kohen Gadol's ox, when performed by a non-Kohen Gadol, is *pasul* — invalid — the act of *shechita* itself becomes a prohibited labor that the *zar* has no right to perform. Now we have a genuine *Shabbat*-category transgression through *shechita*, and it is a case where that *shechita* was specifically not *kasher b'zar*. The Gemara then pushes back: if that is the case, why specify a *zar* at all? Even a regular *kohen hedyot* would be disqualified from performing this particular *shechita* on *Yom Kippur* according to that opinion. The Gemara answers: *shezar etzlo ka'amar* — we mean someone who is like a *zar* with respect to this particular *korban*, i.e., anyone other than the Kohen Gadol. The Gemara itself acknowledges this is a stretch.

### Rav Ashi's Point

Rav Ashi cuts through the difficulty with a fundamentally clarifying observation. *Midi chatos katani? O lavin katani?* — did the *beraita* ever say anything about how many *chataot* one must bring, or how many sets of lashes? It did not. *Ela issurei be'alma ka chashiv* — the *beraita* was simply counting how many *issurim* (prohibitions) were violated, without specifying or implying anything about the legal consequences. The question of one or two is a question of how many wrong things the person did — *likro rabbeinu rasha gamur*, to assess how fully blameworthy a person is — not a question about capital liability or sin-offerings. Once that reframing is in place, there is no difficulty with *haktarah* and its *lav*-only status: we were never asked to equalize the penalties of the two transgressions, only to count them. This recalibration is not without irony: a sustained Tannaic dispute about *issur kolel*, *issur mosif*, and *bevas achas* ultimately resolves into a question about moral characterization rather than concrete legal obligation. But the Gemara had already flagged this dimension earlier, and Rav Ashi's point is that the earlier difficulty never should have arisen in the first place.

---

## Mixed-Up Wives

### Mishnah Setup

The Gemara now arrives at the *Mishnah* that actually motivates the entire preceding discussion of *issur chal al issur*. The *Mishnah* opens: *shnayim shekidshu shtei nashim* — two men betrothed two women. The men were unrelated to each other and the women were unrelated to each other. When the time came for the *chupah* — the consummation of the marriages — *hechlifu es shel zeh lazeh* — they mixed up the wives, each man going in to the other's wife. This is, in a sense, a worse situation than the *Rachel and Leah* episode, because there each man knows whose wife is whose — here, each man is unknowingly sleeping with the other man's wife.

### Multiple Transgressions

The *Mishnah* then systematically enumerates the potentially compounding transgressions. *Harei elu chayavim mishum eishet ish* — each man has transgressed the prohibition of adultery with a married woman. *Ve'im hayu achim, mishum eishet ach* — if the two men happened to be brothers, there is an additional transgression of *eishet ach*, the prohibition of a brother's wife. *Ve'im hayu achayot* — if the two women happened to be sisters, then each man is also in violation of *isha el achosah*, the prohibition of his wife's sister (*achat u'niddah* in the shorthand). *Ve'im hayu niddot, mishum niddah* — and if the women happen to be in a state of *niddah* at the time, that is yet a fourth transgression. In the worst configuration — brothers who have married sisters who are currently *niddot* — each man potentially incurs four separate prohibitions in a single act.

A natural question arises about the woman's role in this accounting. The answer is that the prohibitions of *arayot* are formulated from the man's perspective throughout the Torah, but the woman is a full participant in the act. She is therefore liable not as one who facilitates another's sin (*lifnei iver*) but as a direct party to the same transgression. Curiously, this is so even though the substantive definitions — married woman, brother's wife, wife's sister — are all defined from the male vantage point.

### Separation/Pregnancy

After the error is discovered, the *Mishnah* requires a period of enforced separation of three months — *shema me'ubarot hen* — lest the women be pregnant, which would create questions of *mamzerut*. There were no pregnancy tests; one waited three months to determine by external signs. If the women were minors (*ketanot*) who could not conceive, they are returned to their husbands immediately.

The Gemara establishes that the scenario described is one of inadvertent error, not deliberate wife-swapping. One proof: Rabbi Chiya teaches in a *beraita* that there would be sixteen *chataot* (sin-offerings) — four transgressions times four persons (each of the two men and each of the two women), all acting as *shogegin* (unwitting sinners). If the act had been intentional, there would be no *chata* obligation at all. Additionally, the *Mishnah*'s allowance for the women to return to their husbands after three months would be impossible if the act had been willful, since a woman who commits adultery voluntarily becomes forbidden to her husband. The Gemara therefore accepts the reading *huchlafu* — "they were exchanged" (passively, accidentally) — rather than *hechlifu*, "they exchanged."

One apparent exception: the Gemara notes that a minor's consent does not constitute legal consent — *pituy ketanah ones hu* — so even if a minor were to act willfully in such a scenario, she would be considered legally coerced and would not be forbidden to return to her husband. But that consideration does not apply here, where the entire case is one of unintentional error.

---

## Rabbi Meir Position

### Which Tanna?

With the *Mishnah*'s scenario established, the Gemara asks: *uman hai tanna d'is lei issur kolel ve'issur mosif ve'issur bas achas?* — which Tanna is it who accepts all three forms of *issur chal al issur*? The scenario involves *eishet ish* (married woman) and *eishet ach* (brother's wife) arising together — potentially *bevas achas* — and then *achos isha* (wife's sister) added through *issur kolel*, and *niddah* added through *issur mosif*. All three mechanisms must be operative for the *Mishnah* to yield four distinct transgressions. The Gemara, citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, identifies this as the position of Rabbi Meir.

### Rabbi Meir Example

The source is a *beraita*: *yesh ochel achilah achas ve'chayav aleha arba chataot ve'asham echad* — one can perform a single act of eating and thereby incur four *chataot* and one *asham*. The case: a person who is *tamei* eats the *cheilev* (forbidden fat) of a sanctified animal that has become *notar* (leftover sacrifice, which may no longer be consumed) on *Yom Kippur*. The four *chataot* correspond to: eating *cheilev* (forbidden fat in general), being *tamei* while eating consecrated food, eating *notar*, and eating on *Yom Kippur*. The *asham* corresponds to *me'ilah* — deriving benefit from consecrated property. Rabbi Meir adds: if it was *Shabbat* and the person carried this food in his mouth, he would be liable for that as well. The other Sages object — *eino min hashem* — carrying the food in one's mouth is not the same act as eating it; the additional *Shabbat* violation arises from a conceptually distinct action and should not be counted together. Tosafot, however, notes that Rabbi Meir may have held that the act of swallowing constitutes the *hanachah* (placement) required for the *melacha* of carrying, making it technically part of the same act.

### Three Forms Analysis

The *Rashi* on this passage assigns each of the three *issur chal al issur* mechanisms to a specific stage in this sequence. When the animal was plain *chullin* (unsanctified), its *cheilev* was forbidden to eat but permitted for other benefit. When it was sanctified — *hukdesha* — the *cheilev* acquired an additional dimension of prohibition: now benefit (*hana'ah*) from it is also forbidden. Rashi terms this *issur mosif*, since the sanctification extended the nature of the prohibition. It must be noted, however, that this is a somewhat unusual application of *issur mosif*: the standard understanding is that *issur mosif* means the forbidden object becomes forbidden to a wider circle of persons, whereas here it is the same persons who now face a stricter prohibition. Rashi's extension of the term to cover this case is worth flagging as genuinely questionable, even if it is the framework the Gemara works with.

When the animal became *notar*, the prohibition expanded to include the *mizbeach* itself — it can no longer be offered on the altar — and so the class of "entities" forbidden from it has grown. This is a more conventional *issur mosif*. When the person himself became *tamei*, he became forbidden from eating any consecrated food, not just this particular piece of *cheilev*; the expansion here is in the range of objects forbidden to him, not a change in the status of the object. This is *issur kolel* — the broader prohibition sweeps in this particular item along with everything else in its class. The *bevas achas* dimension, according to Tosafot, is illustrated by Rabbi Meir's addition of *Shabbat* to the case: when it is simultaneously *Yom Kippur* and *Shabbat*, both the *Yom Kippur* prohibition on eating and the *Shabbat* prohibition on carrying arise together, instantiating the *bevas achas* mechanism.

---

## Eliezer/Yehoshua

### Alignment Question

Having established that the *Mishnah* can be attributed to Rabbi Meir as the Tanna who accepts all three forms of *issur chal al issur*, the Gemara raises a further complication. There is a separate, well-known dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua about *to'eh bidvar mitzvah* — one who errs in the course of performing a *mitzvah*. The men in the *Mishnah* were attempting to sleep with their own wives — an act of marital relations, which is itself a *mitzvah*. If Rabbi Yehoshua holds that such a person is exempt from a *chata*, then the *Mishnah*'s assumption that *chataot* are owed becomes problematic. *Le-Rabbi Meir aliba de-man?* — according to which opinion of this second debate is Rabbi Meir's position in the *Mishnah* tenable?

The Gemara initially suggests it must align with Rabbi Eliezer, who does not grant an exemption for *mitzvah* errors. But the Gemara immediately offers an alternative: *ibba'it eima afilu aliba de-Rabbi Yehoshua* — one can maintain that even Rabbi Yehoshua would not exempt here.

### Bohul/Time Pressure

The key to reconciling Rabbi Meir with Rabbi Yehoshua lies in the precise conditions under which Rabbi Yehoshua grants the *mitzvah*-error exemption. The Gemara explains with a paradigmatic case: a *mohel* who has two children to circumcise on consecutive days — one whose eighth day falls on *Shabbat*, one whose eighth day falls on Sunday — accidentally performs the circumcision on *Shabbat* for the Sunday child. He has violated *Shabbat* through an act of *melacha*, yet he was attempting to perform a *mitzvah*. Rabbi Yehoshua exempts him from a *chata*.

The Gemara attributes this exemption to *bohul* — a sense of urgency or time pressure. The *mohel* operates under the pressure that today's circumcision must be done today; that ambient pressure, combined with the fact that he was acting in the service of a *mitzvah*, constitutes sufficient mitigation. The crucial point is that *bohul* and *mitzvah* together produce the exemption — neither alone is sufficient. In the case of the mixed-up wives, there is no *bohul*. A man does not face a deadline by which he must sleep with his wife on a particular night. Without time pressure, the combination that gives Rabbi Yehoshua's exemption its force is absent, and even Rabbi Yehoshua would say the man owes a *chata*.

The Gemara is careful here about what exactly is doing the exculpatory work. One reading is that *bohul* is a form of *ones* — unavoidable compulsion — and that the *mitzvah* context amplifies that *ones* to the point of exculpation. Another reading is that the *mitzvah* context is itself the primary exempting factor, but a high degree of negligence can override it; *bohul* functions to lower the threshold of apparent negligence. On either reading, the absence of *bohul* in the wife-mixing case is fatal to the exemption claim, and the *Mishnah*'s liability for a *chata* is consistent with Rabbi Yehoshua's view.

### Trumah Case

The Gemara challenges this framework by pointing to another case in which Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua debate, one that also lacks time pressure: a kohen eating *trumah* who is informed mid-meal that he is actually a *chalal* (a disqualified kohen, in this instance the son of a divorced woman or a *chalutzah*), and therefore unauthorized to eat *trumah* — he is, with respect to *trumah*, a *zar*. Rabbi Eliezer holds him liable for principal payment plus the additional *chomesh* penalty; Rabbi Yehoshua exempts him. Yet eating *trumah* is not a *mitzvah* under time pressure. Why then does Rabbi Yehoshua exempt him?

### Erev Pesach

The Gemara resolves this by the comment of Rabbi Abba bar Chiya: *hacha bitrumah be'erev pesach askinan* — the *trumah* case in question is specifically one that occurred on *erev Pesach*, when the kohen needed to eat his *trumah* (which was *chametz*) before the prohibition on *chametz* took effect. That creates a genuine *bohul* — a time-pressured context — and Rabbi Yehoshua's exemption fits the same framework as before. Alternatively, the Gemara suggests *ve'ibba'it eima* — even without that specific setting, one could resolve the *Mishnah* differently, by attributing it to Rabbi Shimon operating under a *bevas achas* framework, which would be a separate line of analysis altogether.

---

## Bevas Achas Reconcile

### Simultaneous Transgressi…

The final alternative the Gemara entertains is that the *Mishnah* need not be attributed to Rabbi Meir at all. Instead, one could read all four transgressions as arising literally simultaneously — *bevas achas* — in which case even Rabbi Shimon, who otherwise rejects *issur chal al issur*, would concede that all four apply. The challenge is constructing a scenario in which *eishet ish*, *eishet ach*, *achos isha*, and *niddah* can all genuinely take effect at the identical moment.

### Shlichim Synchronization

The synchronization of *eishet ish*, *eishet ach*, and *achos isha* is achievable through the mechanism of *shlichim* (agents). Suppose the two brothers — Reuven and Shimon — appoint a single agent, Michael, to perform two *kiddushin* simultaneously. Reuven's *kiddushin* is to Rachel, Shimon's is to Leah. Simultaneously, Rachel and Leah appoint their own agent, Devorah, to receive their *kiddushin*. Michael presents two *perutot* (coins) to Devorah in a single act — one for Rachel, one for Leah. In that exact instant, Rachel becomes Reuven's *eishet ish*, and since Shimon is Reuven's brother, she is also Shimon's *eishet ach*; Leah simultaneously becomes Shimon's wife and Rachel's sister, rendering her Reuven's *achos isha*. All three statuses crystallize in the same moment. This is the scenario the Gemara constructs: *d'shavyuhu shaliach ve'shavu inhu shaliach, u-faga shaliach b'shaliach* — the brothers made one agent, the women made another, and the two agents met.

### Niddah Age Three

The *niddah* prohibition, however, resists this synchronization. A woman is either already a *niddah* before the *kiddushin* moment — in which case the *niddah* prohibition predates *eishet ish* and is not simultaneous with it — or she becomes a *niddah* afterward, in which case it arrives later. Neither option gives us *bevas achas* for all four.

### Age Three Solution

The Gemara resolves this with a striking construction. *B'shofaat mitoch g' shanim* — we are dealing with women who began experiencing *niddah* bleeding before their third birthdays and who remained in *niddah* status continuously through their third birthday. The key is that halachic liability for acts of *biah* (intercourse) with a girl under three does not take effect — the act is not formally reckoned as *biah* under three years of age. So: the fathers of these girls (who are minors, and whose *kiddushin* may be effected by their fathers) arranged the *kiddushin* before the girls reached three. The girls were already in a state of *niddah* from before age three. For the brothers, all four prohibitions — *eishet ish*, *eishet ach*, *achos isha*, and *niddah* — crystallize at the single moment when the girls turn three, because only at that moment does the *biah* become formally actionable, and at that moment the *niddah* status is already present alongside the others. This is *bevas achas* for the brothers' liability.

For the women's own *chata* obligations, the relevant moment is when they themselves reach the age of *bat mitzvah* (twelve years). The Gemara's formulation — *v'chayiveinu mitoch shteim esrei l'achar shteim esrei l'chiyuvey inhei* — indicates that to create the women's liability, the *niddah* status established before age three (and never interrupted by *tevilah* in a *mikveh*) must persist continuously through their becoming *bat mitzvah*. At the moment they become obligated in *mitzvot*, the same set of simultaneous prohibitions is already in place, and the *niddah* component is the same continuous status that was operative from before age three. If they had immersed in the interim, the *niddah* status would have lapsed and the simultaneity would be broken. The scenario thus requires that neither woman immersed from before age three until after becoming *bat mitzvah* — a span of roughly nine years.

---

## Pregnancy/Tamar

### First Act Assumption

The *Mishnah* requires a three-month separation to ensure the women are not pregnant — *shema me'ubarot hen*. But a challenge arises: the Gemara operates on the assumption, widely held in the ancient world, that a woman cannot become pregnant from the first act of intercourse. If the men slept with the wrong wives only once, there is no risk of pregnancy. Rav Nachman, citing Rabba bar Avuha, resolves this: *shebau ve'shanu* — they had intercourse more than once. The second act is when pregnancy becomes possible.

A further objection presents itself: if we count each act separately, Rabbi Chiya's accounting of sixteen *chataot* would rapidly become incoherent, since Rabbi Eliezer holds that every distinct act of thrusting within a prolonged sexual encounter constitutes a separate act of *biah* — potentially multiplying the *chataot* enormously. The Gemara resolves this by explaining that the count of sixteen is based on the first act of *biah* alone — *b'via rishona kachashiv* — and that the three-month separation presupposes a second act having occurred. These are simply two separate framings of the scenario operating in parallel.

### Hymen Removal

The Gemara then raises the biblical case of Tamar, who became pregnant by Yehuda apparently from a single encounter — *d'b'via rishona iabra*. How does this square with the assumption that pregnancy cannot result from a first act? The answer offered is that Tamar had previously removed her hymen manually: *Tamar b'etzba miacha*. Rav Yitzchak adds that this practice was known from the household of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi — girls there would do so and were therefore given the name Tamar as a kind of epithet, reflecting what the original Tamar had done. The Gemara presupposes that the hymen, when intact, physically prevents conception on the first act; once it is removed, the obstacle is gone.

This connects to a broader halachic context: there is a rabbinic (post-Talmudic in its full development) treatment of *dam besulim* (hymenal blood) as resembling *niddah* blood, which historically gave rise to practices of pre-emptive hymen removal before the wedding night so as to avoid the resulting *niddah* status on the first night. The Gemara's assumptions about physiology reflect the medical understanding of the Talmudic period.

### Er/Onan Sin

But a new difficulty arises: Tamar had been married to Er and Onan before Yehuda. Was she not therefore no longer a virgin? The Gemara's answer is that *Er v'Onan shimshu shelo kedarkan* — Er and Onan had intercourse with her in a non-vaginal manner (*bi'ah shelo kedarkan*), which left her hymen intact. The Gemara then cites a *beraita*: *kol esrim ve'arba'ah chodesh dash mibifnim ve'zoreh mibachutz divrei Rabbi Eliezer* — for the twenty-four months of nursing, Rabbi Eliezer permits a form of early withdrawal (threshing on the inside, winnowing on the outside, to borrow the agricultural metaphor) to avoid impregnating the nursing mother. The Sages respond: *hallalu eino ela k'ma'aseh Er v'Onan* — this is nothing other than what Er and Onan did, and is forbidden.

The Gemara resolves the apparent tension between the *beraita* (which equates early withdrawal with the sin of Er and Onan) and its own characterization of Er and Onan's sin as *bi'ah shelo kedarkan* (non-vaginal sex, not early withdrawal): *k'ma'aseh Er v'Onan ve'lo k'ma'aseh Er v'Onan* — the nursing practice is *like* what they did in one respect (the semen is expelled outside the body, *ve'shichet artzah*) but *not* exactly what they did, because theirs was *bi'ah shelo kedarkan* while the nursing practice involves normal vaginal intercourse (*kedarkan*) with withdrawal at the end.

### Early Withdrawal Forbidd…

The Gemara then asks: we understand from the verse *ve'shichet artzah* that Onan practiced this form of emission, but what is the source that it was *bi'ah shelo kedarkan* rather than early withdrawal? And separately, the verse only explicitly describes Onan's act — what is the basis for assuming Er sinned in the same way? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers from the word *gam* in *vayamot gam oto* — "he too died." The word *gam* implies "also," meaning Er died by the same cause and in the same manner as Onan. The reason given for Onan's act is explicit: *lo lo yihyeh hazera* — he knew the child would be reckoned under his deceased brother's name, not his own, and he resisted that. Er's motive, by contrast, is inferred by the Gemara as having been aesthetic: *kedei shelo titaber ve'yachahish yofyah* — he did not want Tamar to become pregnant and lose her beauty. In both cases, the act was *bi'ah shelo kedarkan*.

---

## Zera Levatala Debate

### Tosafot First View

The discussion of *bi'ah shelo kedarkan* and the condemnation of Er and Onan's conduct opens onto a significant halakhic question that the Rishonim debate at length: in the context of marital relations, is a husband ever permitted to have a seminal emission outside of his wife? Two distinct *Gemara* passages appear to point in different directions. Here, early withdrawal is condemned as *k'ma'aseh Er v'Onan*; elsewhere (in tractate *Nedarim*), the Gemara appears to permit *bi'ah shelo kedarkan* in the marital setting without qualification. Tosafot addresses this tension directly. The first approach offered by Tosafot reconciles the sources by limiting the *Nedarim* permission to cases where *bi'ah shelo kedarkan* does not involve seminal emission: *mekivan d'leis hashchasas zera lo havei k'ma'aseh Er v'Onan* — only because there is no destruction of seed does it not constitute the sin of Er and Onan. On this reading, *bi'ah shelo kedarkan* is permissible in marriage only so long as it does not result in the semen being expelled outside the wife.

### Ri's View

The Ri (Rabbi Yitzchak, cited within the same Tosafot) offers a second, more permissive approach. *Velo chashiv k'ma'aseh Er v'Onan ela keshemitkavein lehashchis hazera ve'ragil la'asos kein tamid* — an act is only considered to be in the category of Er and Onan's sin when the person's *intention* is the destruction of seed as such, and when this is his habitual practice. If, on the other hand, the couple engages in *bi'ah shelo kedarkan* simply as part of their marital intimacy — *aval be'akrai be'alma umis'aveh lavo le'ishto* — without this being a calculated strategy to avoid procreation or destroy seed systematically, then *shelo kedarka shary*: it is permitted. The Ri grounds this in the *Nedarim* principle that *kol mah she'adam rotzeh la'asos be'ishto ya'aseh* — within the marital relationship a man may conduct himself with his wife as he wishes. On this view, the marital context transforms the character of the act: what would otherwise be *zera levatala* (wasted seed) is not so considered when it arises naturally from the couple's intimacy.

### Rema's Ruling

The practical *halakha* is shaped decisively by the *Rema* (Rabbi Moshe Isserles), who rules in accordance with the Ri's second approach. The implication is far-reaching: according to the *Rema*, the prohibition of *zera levatala* does not apply within the marital relationship regardless of whether seminal emission occurs during vaginal intercourse or otherwise, provided it is not a deliberate and habitual practice of seed destruction. This ruling has significant relevance for how marital relations are understood within *halakha*, and its basis in this passage of the Gemara — via the Ri in Tosafot — reflects the broader principle that contextual intention and relational setting are determinative in this domain.

---

---

# Yevamot 33b

## Rabbi Chiyya vs. Bar Kap…

### Three Prohibition Cases

The sugya on 33b picks up in the middle of a discussion concerning *issur chal al issur* — the question of whether a second prohibition can take effect upon an object or person already subject to a prior prohibition. Three specific cases had been presented: a *zar* (non-*kohen*) who performs the *avodah* in the *Beit HaMikdash* on *Shabbat*; a *kohen* who is a *ba'al mum* and performs the *avodah* in a state of *tumah* during a circumstance of *tumah hutrah b'tzibbur*; and a *zar* who eats a bird upon which *melikah* had been performed — an act of slaughter that is valid for *kohanim* but renders the bird forbidden to non-*kohanim* at the very same moment it takes effect. The question in each case was whether the individual transgresses two distinct prohibitions or only one.

### Misattribution Question

The debate was attributed to Rabbi Chiyya and Bar Kappara, both of whom swore that Rebbe had taught them his ruling — Rabbi Chiyya reporting that Rebbe said two transgressions, Bar Kappara reporting that Rebbe said one. The *Gemara* had concluded that their dispute was really about *issur b'vas achas* — prohibitions that take effect simultaneously — and whether Rabbi Shimon, who generally holds *ein issur chal al issur*, would concede that when two prohibitions arrive at exactly the same moment, both take effect. That explanation seems coherent. But it raises a sharp difficulty: if Rabbi Chiyya is correct that even Rabbi Shimon would agree to liability in a case of *b'vas achas*, from where did Bar Kappara ever hear that Rebbe taught only one transgression? The *Gemara* asks directly: *l'Rabbi Chiyya, Bar Kappara shikora kameshakeir* — is Bar Kappara simply lying?

### Kolel vs. Bas Achas

The *Gemara* resolves this by having Rabbi Chiyya explain that Bar Kappara did not misrepresent Rebbe deliberately — he misremembered. Specifically: *ki asnaya Rebbe l'didi, tarti l'ftor asnaya* — when Rebbe taught Bar Kappara, and said one is exempt (i.e., only one transgression), he was teaching only two of the three cases, not all three.

The first two cases — the *zar* performing *avodah* on *Shabbat*, and the *ba'al mum* performing *avodah* in a state of *tumah* — can each be understood as sequential. In the first, a person performs *avodah* and *Shabbat* then arrives; in the second, a person is a *ba'al mum* and then becomes *tamei*. In both cases, a first prohibition is already in place and a second prohibition descends upon it afterward. This is the domain of *issur kolel* — where the arriving prohibition does not render the object forbidden to a wider set of people, but rather expands the category of forbidden acts while something already forbidden to the whole world becomes forbidden in a broader sense. In cases of *issur kolel*, even opinions that are more permissive regarding *issur chal al issur* may not grant double liability. Rebbe taught Bar Kappara these two sequential cases according to the view of Rabbi Shimon, who says that even *issur mosif* does not take effect — and certainly *issur kolel*, which is a weaker category, would not — and therefore in these two cases one is liable only once.

The critical distinction is that *issur kolel* is a concept that applies only in sequential settings: first prohibition A, then prohibition B descends and encompasses a broader class of forbidden acts. It is incoherent to speak of *issur kolel* when both prohibitions arrive simultaneously — in a *b'vas achas* scenario, there is no "first" and "second," no earlier prohibition that could block a later one. Bar Kappara heard Rebbe's teaching about the two sequential cases, understood that in those cases (as *issur kolel*) one is liable only once according to Rabbi Shimon, and then — as the *Gemara* explains — inadvertently mixed in the third case of the *zar* who ate the bird on which *melikah* was performed.

### Third Case Confusion

That third case — *melikah* by a non-*kohen* — is categorically different. The moment *melikah* is performed, the bird simultaneously becomes a valid *korban* (and thus forbidden to non-*kohanim*) and becomes forbidden in the sense relevant to the act of *melikah* itself. This case cannot be sequential; it is inherently *b'vas achas*. When Bar Kappara added it to the set in his memory, the combined set of three cases could no longer be characterized as *issur kolel* operating sequentially. The only common denominator he could identify across all three was *b'vas achas*. He then reasoned: since Rebbe taught that in these cases one is liable only once, and these cases are all *b'vas achas*, Rebbe must have ruled that even *b'vas achas* yields only one transgression.

The *Gemara* states this explicitly: *v'aydi d'damya lei arvibihu* — because the third case was similar to the other two (all involving acts normally permitted when done correctly, all involving non-*kohanim* or disqualified *kohanim*), Bar Kappara mixed it in. *V'lo ashkach ela b'vas achas* — examining the merged set, the only explanatory framework he found was *b'vas achas*. *V'savar mid'ha b'vas achas, ha nami b'vas achas* — he concluded that since the *melikah* case is *b'vas achas*, the whole teaching must concern *b'vas achas*. *U'mid'ha l'pattur, ha nami l'pattur* — and since Rebbe had taught exemption, he concluded that *b'vas achas* generally yields only one transgression. He had honestly misremembered — not lied — and that misremembering is what the *Gemara* sets out to explain.

---

## Three Issur Types

### Mosif, Kolel, Achas

Having worked through the Bar Kappara episode, the *Gemara* pauses to present the systematic framework governing *issur chal al issur* in its three recognized forms. *Issur mosif* is when the newly arriving prohibition expands the range of persons to whom the object is forbidden — it "adds" to the audience of the prohibition. *Issur kolel* is when the new prohibition does not change who is forbidden the object, but broadens the category of acts forbidden in connection with it, encompassing it within a wider class. And *issur b'vas achas* refers to the case where two prohibitions descend simultaneously, with no temporal priority between them — the scenario where the very question of one prohibition "blocking" another loses its footing, because neither arrived first.

### Baraita Evidence

Having established that the debate of Rabbi Chiyya and Bar Kappara concerns whether Rabbi Shimon would concede double liability in a case of *b'vas achas*, the *Gemara* attempts to test this with a *baraita*. The *baraita* states: a *zar* who performs *avodah* on *Shabbat*, or a *ba'al mum* who performs *avodah* in a state of *tumah* even when there is a *korban tzibbur* — in each case there are two transgressions: transgressing as a *zar* and transgressing *Shabbat*, or transgressing as a *ba'al mum* and transgressing *tumah*. This is the position of Rabbi Yose. Rabbi Shimon, however, says one is liable only for the first prohibition — the *zar* status or the *ba'al mum* status — not for the prohibition that arrived afterward.

Crucially, the *baraita* discusses only two of the three cases. The *melikah* case — the *zar* who ate the bird — is absent. The *Gemara* asks: *l'man shiyarah* — for whom's sake was it left out? It cannot have been omitted on account of Rabbi Yose, since Rabbi Yose, who holds *issur chal al issur* even sequentially and even in *issur kolel*, would certainly hold it in a case of *b'vas achas* as well — *hashta Rabbi Yose b'issur kolel mechayev shtayim, b'vas achas mibaya*. If he permits double liability when prohibitions arrive sequentially, he would surely permit it when they arrive simultaneously. There is thus no reason the *baraita* would have omitted the *melikah* case on Rabbi Yose's account.

### Shimon Exemption

It must therefore be Rabbi Shimon for whose sake the case was left out — meaning that Rabbi Shimon would not have the same ruling in the *melikah* case as in the other two. Since Rabbi Shimon says only one transgression in the sequential cases, the *baraita*'s omission of the *melikah* case implies that Rabbi Shimon would say something different there — and the *Gemara* concludes that he would say *two* transgressions when prohibitions arrive simultaneously. *U'b'issur kolel hu d'pattar* — it is specifically in the *issur kolel* sequential scenario that Rabbi Shimon exempts from double liability. *Aval b'issur b'vas achas mechayev* — but in *b'vas achas*, he concedes double liability. This yields the conclusion: *tyufta d'Bar Kappara tyufta* — a refutation of Bar Kappara's position.

It is worth flagging that the force of this proof depends on accepting the *Gemara*'s prior conclusion that the distinction between the *melikah* case and the other two cases is precisely the *b'vas achas* character of the former. Given that, the omission of *melikah* from the *baraita* is indeed significant evidence that Rabbi Shimon treats *b'vas achas* differently — and would hold double liability there. Whether this cleanly refutes Bar Kappara's specific position (as opposed to simply proving that Rabbi Shimon agrees *b'vas achas* yields two transgressions) is a fair question, but the *Gemara* presents it as a refutation.

---

## Zar on Shabbat

### Which Act Violates

The *Gemara* now turns to a focused question that arises from one of the cases in the *baraita*: the *zar* who performs *avodah* on *Shabbat*. The ruling is that he transgresses twice — once for acting as a *zar* and once for *chillul Shabbat*. But this prompts a precise question: *b'mai* — in what act exactly did he violate *Shabbat*? Every prohibited *melachah* he might have performed in the context of *avodah* is subject to scrutiny.

If he performed *shechitah* — the answer is immediate: *shechitah b'zar kesherah* — a non-*kohen* may perform *shechitah* of a *korban*. This is actually a striking *halachah*: even in the *Beit HaMikdash*, even on *Shabbat* when the *avodah* is permitted, even a woman may perform *shechitah* of a *korban tzibbur*. So *shechitah* by a *zar* is not prohibited, and therefore cannot constitute a *Shabbat* violation in this context. If it was *kabalah* or *holachah* — catching the blood or carrying it to the *mizbeach* — that is merely *tiltul b'alma*, movement within an enclosed space, which does not rise to the level of a *Shabbat* violation in the usual sense. And if it was *haktarah* — burning the limbs on the *mizbeach* — one faces the position of Rabbi Yose himself, that *hava'arah l'lav nitna*: making a fire on *Shabbat*, according to Rabbi Yose, is only a *lav* and not a *chiyuv misah*, since the Torah singles it out explicitly — *lo tivaru eish b'chol moshvoseichem b'yom ha-Shabbat* — and Rabbi Yose derives from that singling-out that it was separated from the general category of *melachot* to teach that it is less severe. Since the discussion concerns equivalent-weight transgressions (carrying *chiyuv* for *korban* purposes), *haktarah* would not serve.

### Par on Yom Kippur

Rav Acha bar Yaakov resolves the difficulty: the case is not *Shabbat* in the ordinary sense but *Yom Kippur*, and the specific act is *shechitah* of the *par* — the ox of the *Kohen Gadol* on *Yom Kippur*. The *avodah* of *Yom Kippur* is performed exclusively by the *Kohen Gadol*, and according to the opinion that even *shechitah* of the *Kohen Gadol*'s *par* requires the *Kohen Gadol* himself, a *zar* performing that *shechitah* commits a prohibited act — and *shechitah* is universally agreed to constitute a *melachah* on *Shabbat* (or *Yom Kippur*). So the case involves a *zar* who performed the *shechitah* of the *par* on *Yom Kippur*: one transgression for acting as a *zar*, one for violating *Yom Kippur* through *shechitah*.

The *Gemara* then raises a further difficulty: *mai irya zar* — why is the case specifically a *zar*? If the ruling follows the opinion that any non-*Kohen Gadol* cannot perform this *shechitah*, then even an ordinary *kohen* (*kohen hedyot*) would be disqualified. The answer given is *she-zar etzlo ka'amar* — when the case says "*zar*," it means someone who is a *zar* relative to this particular *korban*, i.e., anyone who is not the *Kohen Gadol*. The *Gemara* itself notes that this is a significant stretch in the language.

### Rav Ashi Response

Rav Ashi cuts through the difficulty with a sharper observation. He asks: *midi chataos katani* — did the *baraita* say anything about how many *chataot* one must bring? *O lavei katani* — or about how many *lavin* were transgressed? *Ella issurei b'alma ka chashiv* — the *baraita* is simply counting how many prohibited acts were committed, not calibrating *chiyuvim* of lashes or *korbanos*. The *nafka mina*, Rav Ashi implies, is not the practical consequence of multiple sin-offerings or floggings — it is the more abstract question of how grievous a *rasha* one is for having committed one wrong or two. This observation, while somewhat reductionist in its immediate context, preserves the force of the debate: when the stakes are higher — multiple *chataot*, multiple sets of lashes — the same logic would apply with weightier consequences. Here, the practical implication is simply the moral accounting of the transgression.

---

## Wife Exchange Case

### Chuppah Exchange

The *Gemara* now turns to the *Mishnah*, whose subject matter is closely related to all that preceded it. The *Mishnah* states: *shenayim she-kiddeshu shtei nashim* — two men married two women; the men were unrelated to each other, the women were unrelated to each other. *Uvi-sh'at knisatan la-chuppah* — when the time came to enter the *chuppah* (a euphemism for the consummation of the marriage), *hechlifu et shel zeh la-zeh* — they accidentally exchanged wives. This is reminiscent of the exchange of Rachel and Leah, except that here it is more serious: each man has now had relations with the other man's wife. The critical point is that the *kiddushin* — the formal betrothal — had preceded the *chuppah*: each man was already fully married to his own wife when the exchange occurred. Whether the *chuppah* was a literal canopy under which faces were veiled or a euphemism for the bedroom, the legal reality is identical: each man had relations with another man's wife.

### Four Transgressions

The *Mishnah* then enumerates the transgressions. *Harei elu chayavim mishum eshet ish* — each man transgresses the prohibition of adultery with a married woman. *V'im hayu achim, mishum eshet ach* — if the two men happened to be brothers, there is an additional transgression of relations with a brother's wife. *V'im hayu achayot, mishum isha el achotah* — if the two women happened to be sisters, there is a further transgression, since each man's wife is the other woman's sister, making the illicit partner his wife's sister. *V'im hayu nidot, mishum niddah* — and if the women were *nidot* at the time, there is a fourth transgression. These four can combine in a single case: four transgressions arising from a single act.

### Minors Exception

The *Mishnah* adds: *ve-im hayu ketanot she-ein re-uyot le-yeled, machzirin otan mi-yad* — if the women were minors who were incapable of bearing children, they are returned immediately to their lawful husbands. This exception follows from the principle that *pituy ketanah ones ninhu* — the seduction of a minor is treated legally as coercion, regardless of any apparent consent. A minor's consent is legally meaningless; it constitutes statutory rape in *halachic* terms. Accordingly, even if the act were intentional on the man's part, the woman — being a minor — would not be rendered forbidden to her husband, since her status is that of one who was violated against her will.

### Accident Proof

The *Mishnah* also specifies: *u-mafrishin otan sheloshah chodashim, shema me-ubarot hen* — the women are kept separate from their husbands for three months lest they be pregnant, since a pregnancy by the wrong man would create serious questions of lineage. The *Gemara* engages with the word *hechlifu* — they exchanged — and asks whether this implies intentional wife-swapping, which would be incongruent with the rest of the *Mishnah*. Rav Yehudah rules that the correct reading is *huchlefu* — they were exchanged, passively, accidentally. This reading is confirmed by the *Gemara* from the clause requiring three months of separation: *ve-ei be-meizid, mi sharya* — if it were intentional, how could the women go back to their husbands at all? An intentional act of adultery renders a woman forbidden to her husband. The fact that the *Mishnah* contemplates their return — conditional only on confirming the absence of pregnancy — demonstrates conclusively that the act was unintentional, and the participants are liable to a *korban chatat* rather than subject to the severer consequences of deliberate transgression.

The *Gemara* also notes, from the *baraita* of Rabbi Chiyya, that if there are four prohibitions and four parties (two men, two women, each potentially liable), and each brings four *chataot*, the total is sixteen sin-offerings — *sheish esrei chataot*.

---

## Rabbi Meir Framework

### Four from One Act

With the *Mishnah* established as a case of *shogegin* (inadvertent transgressors), the *Gemara* raises a conceptual question. How can a single act give rise to four distinct transgressions? The case in the *Mishnah* involves prohibitions that did not all exist simultaneously at the moment of betrothal; they accrued at different times. The woman was first an *eshet ish* — a married woman — from the moment of *kiddushin*. She then became an *achot isha* — a sister to someone's wife — only when her sister was also married. She became a *niddah* at a different moment entirely. Each of these prohibitions arrived at a different time. This is precisely the domain of *issur chal al issur*: can a later prohibition take effect upon a person or object already subject to a prior prohibition?

*U-man hai tanna d'it leh issur kolel v'issur mosif v'issur bas achas* — which *tanna* holds that all three categories of *issur chal al issur* are operative? Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav: it is Rabbi Meir — *Rebbe Meir hi*.

### Chelev Example

The proof comes from a *baraita* in Rabbi Meir's name: *yesh ochel achilah achas v'chayav aleha arba chataot v'asham echad* — there is a case where one can eat a single item in a single act and incur four *chataot* and one *asham*. The scenario: one is *tamei* and eats *chelev* that comes from a *korban*, and this *chelev* is *notar* (left over beyond its permitted time), and it is from the sanctified *mukdashim*, and one does this on *Yom Kippur*. Each of these elements — eating *chelev*, eating as a *tamei* person from *kodshim*, eating *notar*, eating on *Yom Kippur* — independently carries *chiyuv karet* and obligates a *chatat*. The *asham* comes from *me'ilah*, the additional prohibition of deriving benefit from *hekdesh*. That is five in total — four *chataot* and one *asham*. Rabbi Meir adds: if it was *Shabbat* and the person was carrying the food in his mouth while walking through a public domain, there is a sixth. The Sages respond: *eino min ha-shem* — that is not of the same type, since the act of carrying is categorically distinct from the act of eating.

*Tosafot* engages seriously with the Sages' objection, suggesting that perhaps Rabbi Meir's point was that the act of swallowing constitutes a kind of *hanachah* — the placing-down that completes the *melachah* of carrying — making it more integrally connected to the act of eating than it might appear. This remains a somewhat difficult argument, and the *Gemara* does not fully resolve it.

### Chelev Analysis

The *baraita* involving Rabbi Meir's *chelev* case contains all three types of *issur chal al issur*. Rashi explains the structure as follows. The *chelev* begins as a non-sanctified animal (*chullin*), and at that stage the *chelev* is prohibited in eating but permitted in benefit. When the animal is sanctified (*hukdeshah*), an additional prohibition of *hana'ah* — benefit — takes effect on the *chelev*. Rashi identifies this as *issur mosif*, since the sanctification adds the prohibition of *issur hana'ah* on top of the existing *issur achilah*.
