It must be noted that this is a somewhat unusual application of *issur mosif*: the classic formulation of *issur mosif* involves the object becoming forbidden to a wider group of people, whereas here the object was already forbidden to everyone — the new prohibition simply adds a more stringent dimension (*issur hana'ah*) to the same object for the same people. Rashi's categorization should be noted as contested.

The *chelev* then becomes *notar*, left over past its permitted time. At that moment, as Rashi explains, the object becomes forbidden to the *mizbeach* as well — it can no longer be offered on the altar — *migo d'itosif issura la-mizbeach*. Since it is now forbidden to an additional party (the altar itself), this too constitutes *issur mosif* in the sense of expanding the domain of what is forbidden.

The *tamei* person then arrives and eats. Rashi identifies this as *issur kolel*: the *tamei* person was previously permitted to eat non-sanctified *chelev*, and now, having become *tamei*, he is forbidden from eating all *kodshim* — not just this piece of *chelev* but the entire category. The prohibition does not change the status of the *chelev* but expands the category of things forbidden to this person, which in turn includes this piece. That is the hallmark of *issur kolel*.

### Chelev Analysis

What, then, is the *issur bas achas* in the *chelev* case? Rashi's explanation is acknowledged to be complex. *Tosafot* proposes that Rabbi Meir's addition of *Shabbat* alongside *Yom Kippur* provides the *bas achas* element: on a day that is simultaneously *Shabbat* and *Yom Kippur*, the two prohibitions of *Yom Kippur* and *Shabbat* arrive at exactly the same moment and are not sequential. This is the case of *bas achas* — both *Shabbat* and *Yom Kippur* are in effect simultaneously, so there is no question of one blocking the other, and both are independently operative.

### Meir Following Whom

The *Gemara* then asks: *l'Rabbi Meir aliba d'man* — Rabbi Meir's ruling that all four transgressions in the *Mishnah* are operative: does it align with Rabbi Eliezer or with Rabbi Yehoshua on the separate question that must now be introduced?

---

## Mitzvah Attempt

### Yehoshua Exemption

There is an independent debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua: *to'eh bid'var mitzvah patur* — one who makes an error in the course of performing a *mitzvah* is exempt from bringing a *korban chatat*. Rabbi Yehoshua holds this exemption; Rabbi Eliezer does not. In the *Mishnah*'s case of the wife exchange, the man who inadvertently had relations with the wrong woman was attempting to fulfill the *mitzvah* of marital relations with his wife — *onah*, the conjugal obligation. If Rabbi Yehoshua exempts one who errs in the course of performing a *mitzvah*, why is the man in the *Mishnah* liable to a *chatat* at all?

The *Gemara* asks: if the *Mishnah* follows Rabbi Yehoshua, the four *chataot* should be inapplicable — since the man erred while attempting a *mitzvah*. It must therefore be that the *Mishnah* follows Rabbi Eliezer, who does not grant this exemption. Alternatively — *i ba'is eima* — even if it follows Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Yehoshua's exemption is not absolute.

### Brit Milah Case

Rabbi Yehoshua's exemption is illustrated by the case of a *mohel* who performs *brit milah* on *Shabbat* and accidentally circumcises the wrong infant — the baby born on Sunday rather than the one born on Saturday, whose *brit milah* is duly scheduled for that *Shabbat*. The *mohel* was attempting to perform a *mitzvah* and erred in its execution, and for this error he is exempt from a *chatat* according to Rabbi Yehoshua. Why? Because *d'zmano bahul* — there is a time pressure involved. The *Shabbat milah* must be performed on *Shabbat* specifically, and that urgency creates a mitigating context. Combined with the fact that the person was genuinely engaged in performing a *mitzvah*, the result is that the error falls into the category of an exempted inadvertence.

Two factors thus converge: the attempt to perform a *mitzvah*, and the urgency of a time-bound obligation. One may understand these as jointly producing a kind of *ones* — an externally imposed compulsion that reduces culpability — or alternatively as the *mitzvah*-attempt providing a moral dispensation that can only operate when the degree of negligence is sufficiently low. The time pressure reduces the fault level to the point where the *mitzvah* exemption can take hold.

### No Time Pressure

In the case of the wife exchange, neither mitigating factor is present in full. The man was indeed attempting to fulfill a *mitzvah* — marital relations — but there was no *zman u'vahul*, no time pressure compelling him to act at that moment. Marital relations are not a time-bound obligation in the same way as a *brit milah* scheduled for a specific *Shabbat*. Without the time pressure, the fault level is not mitigated enough for Rabbi Yehoshua's exemption to apply. Accordingly, even according to Rabbi Yehoshua, the man in the *Mishnah* would be liable to bring a *chatat*.

### Terumah Parallel

The *Gemara* raises what appears to be a challenge: the case of *terumah*. A *kohen* eating *terumah* — which is a *mitzvah* — subsequently discovers that he is actually a *chalal* (the son of a divorced woman or a *chalutzah*), and therefore disqualified from *kehunah* and prohibited from eating *terumah*. Rabbi Yehoshua exempts him from having to pay the principal plus the additional fifth (*keren v'chomesh*) that a *zar* who inadvertently eats *terumah* would normally owe. Yet there is no particular time pressure in eating *terumah* — one can eat it at any time. Does this not contradict the claim that Rabbi Yehoshua's exemption requires *zman u'vahul*?

Rav Bibi bar Abaye resolves this by positing that the *terumah* case in question was specifically on *Erev Pesach*: the *kohen* was eating *chametz terumah* before the deadline and was under time pressure to consume it before *Pesach* began, creating exactly the *zman u'vahul* needed. Alternatively — *v'ibayis eima* — the *Mishnah*'s case of the wife exchange may be read as *issur bas achas*, as will now be explored, and the entire preceding analysis may be reconfigured accordingly.

---

## Bas Achas Reading

### Simultaneous Kiddushin

The *Gemara* now offers an alternative reading of the entire *Mishnah*: perhaps all four prohibitions — *eshet ish*, *eshet ach*, *achot isha*, and *niddah* — applied simultaneously, making this a pure case of *issur bas achas*. If so, the *Mishnah* could hold even according to Rabbi Shimon, who normally denies *issur chal al issur* — since Rabbi Shimon concedes double liability in *bas achas* cases, as the *baraita* proved earlier.

The challenge is to construct a scenario in which all statuses applied at literally the same moment. *Eshet ish* and *eshet ach* are not difficult to synchronize in principle — if two brothers betroth two women simultaneously, both statuses (*married woman* and *brother's wife*) arise at the same instant. Simultaneity of *kiddushin* can be achieved through a *shaliach*: the two brothers appoint a single representative, and the two women appoint a single representative, and the two *shaliachs* execute the *kiddushin* in a single transaction — *paga shliach b'shliach*. In that moment, each woman becomes simultaneously an *eshet ish* and an *eshet ach*, and additionally an *achot isha* (the wife's sister to her brother-in-law).

### Niddah Simultaneity

The *niddah* status, however, is more difficult to synchronize. Either the woman was already a *niddah* before the *kiddushin* — in which case the *niddah* prohibition preceded the others and the question of *issur chal al issur* applies in reverse — or she became a *niddah* afterward, in which case it is again sequential. A stopwatch-precise coincidence of menstruation and *kiddushin* at the same moment seems impossible to engineer.

### Under Three Solution

The *Gemara* resolves this with a striking answer attributed to Rabram in the name of Rav: *b'shofet mitoch gimel l'achar gimel* — the girl was a *niddah* from before her third birthday, and that *niddah* status continued past her third birthday. In practical terms: the girl experienced her first menstrual flow before turning three, and it continued through that birthday. This means that at the moment she turned three years old, she was simultaneously a *niddah* and, for the first time, subject to the full legal consequences of the prohibitions that had already been formally created.

This solution exploits a fundamental *halachah*: sexual relations with a girl under the age of three are not considered *bi'ah* — a legally cognizable act of intercourse — from the Torah's perspective. Consequently, even though the brothers had formally married these girls (their father acting as *shaliach* to accept the *kiddushin* on their behalf), the prohibitions of *eshet ish*, *eshet ach*, and *achot isha* were technically in place but had no practical operative force — because any physical act with them would not constitute *bi'ah*. The *niddah* prohibition similarly was in place but not yet operative as a practical matter.

The moment the girls turned three, all of these prohibitions became simultaneously operative: the *bi'ah* prohibition of *eshet ish*, *eshet ach*, and *achot isha* took effect at that same instant, and the *niddah* prohibition — which had been in effect since before the third birthday and had never been removed by *tevilah* — was equally operative at that moment. Thus, from the standpoint of practical *chiyuv*, all four prohibitions descended simultaneously, constituting a genuine *issur bas achas*.

The *Gemara* further notes that this analysis applies to the men's liability — *l'chiyuvinuhu* — which takes effect when the girls turn three. For the women's own liability, the relevant moment is when they reach *bat mitzvah* (twelve years old). For the *bas achas* analysis to hold for the women as well, the *niddah* status must have been continuously in effect from before age three through age twelve without any intervening *tevilah* — an extended period of nine years. The *Gemara* accepts this as the structure of the case.

---

## Pregnancy Concern

### First Act

Returning to the three-month separation requirement, the *Gemara* confronts what might seem a logical difficulty. If the wife exchange was an isolated incident — a single mistaken act — why should there be a concern about pregnancy requiring three months of separation? The *Gemara* invokes a widespread belief of the ancient world: *ein ishah misaberet bi-vi'ah rishonah* — a woman does not conceive from the first act of intercourse. If this is so, the one-time error should not produce pregnancy, and no waiting period should be necessary.

The *Gemara* resolves this with the answer of Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha: *sheba'u v'shanu* — they did not err only once; they had relations a second time as well. That second act creates the possibility of pregnancy and justifies the three-month separation. The *Gemara* then notes that if they had relations twice, Rabbi Chiyya's count of sixteen *chataot* might seem too low — shouldn't there be thirty-two? The answer is that the count of sixteen is reckoned from the first act alone, and the question of how many subsequent acts there were (and indeed, according to Rabbi Eliezer, how many distinct *kochos* — thrusts — occurred within a single act) is left aside. The *baraita* counts from the initial *bi'ah*.

### Tamar Question

Rava raises a challenge to the principle that a woman cannot conceive from the first act of intercourse: *veha Tamar d'vi'ah rishonah i'abra* — Tamar became pregnant with Judah from what was apparently a single act, since the verse says *v'lo yasaf od lada'atah* — he did not know her again. If the first act cannot produce pregnancy, how did Tamar conceive?

This question presupposes that Tamar was a virgin when she had relations with Judah — otherwise she might have had prior acts of intercourse and this was not technically her "first." The *Gemara* will now address this presupposition.

### Hymen Removal

Rav answers: *Tamar b'etzba mi'acha* — Tamar had removed her own hymen with her finger before the encounter with Judah. The *Gemara* then cites Rav Yitzchak's tradition: *kol mu'achos shel beit Rebbi, Tamar sheman* — all the girls in the household of Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi who engaged in this practice were given the name Tamar, or were associated with this nickname, because this was understood to be what Tamar herself had done.

This *Gemara* is remarkable in its assumptions about ancient practice and touches on the *halachic* category of *dam besulim* — hymenal blood. The *halachah* (developed toward the end of the Talmudic period and formalized post-Talmudicaly) treats hymenal blood with *niddah*-like stringency rabbinically. The discussion here implicitly engages with the reality that hymenal blood would not be present if the hymen had been previously removed, which has *halachic* ramifications for the wedding night. The Gemara's concern is not the *halachah* of *dam besulim* per se but rather the question of whether Tamar could truly have been a virgin — and it answers that she was technically a virgin (in terms of never having had vaginal intercourse) while not having an intact hymen.

### Er Onan Sin

But if Tamar was a virgin in the relevant sense, what then were Er and Onan doing? The *Gemara* states: *Er v'Onan shimeshu shelo k'darkah* — they practiced non-vaginal intercourse (*bi'ah shelo k'darkah*, anal intercourse), which is why the hymen remained intact and why no conception occurred. This reading of the verse *va-yishchet artzah* — Onan "spoiled [his seed] to the ground" — differs from the *peshat*, which most naturally reads as a description of withdrawal and external ejaculation. The *Gemara* here reads the verse as describing the inherent nature of the act (non-vaginal intercourse necessarily results in the seed going to the ground), not as a separate act of withdrawal mid-intercourse.

---

## Zera Le-Vatalah

### Nursing Women

The *Gemara* now cites the teaching of Rabbi Eliezer regarding a nursing woman: *kol esrim v'arba chodesh dash m'bifnim v'zoreh m'bachutz* — for the full twenty-four months of nursing, a husband should thresh on the inside and winnow on the outside. The agricultural metaphor — *dash* refers to the threshing that loosens grain from chaff, *zoreh* to the winnowing that separates them through the wind — describes intercourse with external ejaculation (early withdrawal). Rabbi Eliezer's rationale is that pregnancy would endanger the nursing infant by potentially disrupting the milk supply, and he prescribes this method as a form of birth control for the nursing period.

### Withdrawal Critique

The Sages respond sharply: *halalu eino ela k'ma'aseh Er v'Onan* — this practice is like the sin of Er and Onan. The objection is categorical: early withdrawal, which results in seminal emission outside the wife, constitutes *zera l'vatalah* — the destruction of seed — and is prohibited.

### Tamar Proof

The *Gemara* then connects the Onan case to the earlier discussion of Tamar. Since Onan's sin is described as *va-yishchet artzah*, and we now know this meant *bi'ah shelo k'darkah* rather than simple withdrawal, the Sages' equation of Rabbi Eliezer's practice with *ma'aseh Er v'Onan* requires clarification: in what sense is early withdrawal "like" what Er and Onan did, if Er and Onan did something categorically different (non-vaginal intercourse)?

The *Gemara* resolves this with a careful formulation: *k'ma'aseh Er v'Onan v'lo k'ma'aseh Er v'Onan* — similar to but not identical with what Er and Onan did. The similarity is that in both cases the semen is emitted outside the body of the wife — *va-yishchet artzah*, the seed is destroyed. The difference is that Er and Onan engaged in *bi'ah shelo k'darkah* (non-vaginal intercourse), while Rabbi Eliezer's practice involves normal vaginal intercourse (*k'darkah*) with external ejaculation. The common thread is the destruction of seed; the manner differs.

As for Er's sin specifically — the *Gemara* asks: *Onan* we understand, since the verse says *va-yishchet artzah* of him explicitly. *Er minalan* — how do we know Er sinned in the same way? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives it from the word *gam* — *va-yamet gam oto*, "he also died": the *gam* indicates that Er died for the same sin as Onan. And why did Er do it? *K'dei shelo tisaber v'yachish yofyah* — so that Tamar would not become pregnant and her beauty would not be diminished by pregnancy.

### Tosafot Views

*Tosafot* engages directly with the apparent tension in this *Gemara*. On the one hand, the *Gemara* here condemns external ejaculation as akin to *ma'aseh Er v'Onan*. On the other hand, a *Gemara* in Nedarim appears to permit *bi'ah shelo k'darkah* as a legitimate mode of marital intercourse, which necessarily involves seminal emission outside the wife. *Tosafot* presents two answers in the name of the *Ri*. The first: the *Gemara* in Nedarim speaks only of *bi'ah shelo k'darkah* performed without seminal emission — *b'lo hotza'at zera d'shari* — and the prohibition of *ma'aseh Er v'Onan* applies only when there is actual destruction of seed. Without emission, the act is not *zera l'vatalah* regardless of the manner of intercourse. The second answer of the *Ri* is broader and more permissive: the prohibition of *zera l'vatalah* applies only when the husband specifically intends to destroy the seed — *k'she-mitkaven l'hashchit ha-zera* — and when this is a habitual practice — *v'ragil la'asot ken tamid*. But if the act arises spontaneously from desire for one's wife, and is not motivated by the purpose of avoiding procreation or destroying seed as such, then it is permitted — *d'amar b'Nedarim kol mah she-adam rotzeh la'asot b'ishto ya'aseh*.

### Rama's Ruling

This second position of the *Ri* is of considerable practical *halachic* significance. The *Rama* rules in accordance with this second interpretation of *Tosafot*: within the context of marital relations, the prohibition of *zera l'vatalah* is not triggered by the place or manner of seminal emission but only by the intent and habitual purpose of destroying seed to avoid procreation. Any form of sexual activity between husband and wife, without that specific intent, is not categorized as *zera l'vatalah*. This ruling is fundamental to understanding the *halachic* parameters of marital intimacy, and represents the authoritative *Ashkenazic* position on the question.

---

---

# Yevamot 36

## Pregnant Woman Debate

### Rabbi Yochanan's View

The daf opens on 35b, four lines before the wide lines begin, with a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish concerning the validity of *chalitzah* and *yibum* performed while the *yevama* is pregnant. The *mishnah* establishes that the outcome of such acts depends on whether the child born is viable (*ben kayama*) or not. The critical question, however, is whether Reish Lakish goes further than the *mishnah* and holds that even if the child turns out not to be viable — meaning, retroactively, that *chalitzah* was necessary — a *chalitzah* performed while the woman was pregnant is nonetheless not a valid *chalitzah* and must be repeated.

Rabbi Yochanan opens by challenging Reish Lakish from the *mishnah*: *ein ha-vlad shel kayama hu assur bi-krovoteha ve-hi assura bi-krovav u-psula min ha-kehuna* — if the child is not viable, the man who performed *chalitzah* is forbidden to her relatives, she is forbidden to his relatives, and she is disqualified from marrying a *kohen*. In other words, the *mishnah* treats the *chalitzah* as having rendered her a *chalutza*, with all its attendant consequences. Rabbi Yochanan presses: *bishlama ledidi* — this works out well according to me, who holds that *chalitzat me'uberet shema chalitzah*, that *chalitzah* performed on a pregnant woman is a valid *chalitzah* if the child subsequently proves non-viable. *Mishum hachi pasla* — that is why the *mishnah* disqualifies her to a *kohen*, because she has genuinely become a *chalutza*. *Ela ledidach* — but according to you, Reish Lakish, who holds that *chalitzat me'uberet lo shema chalitzah*, why does the *mishnah* impose the *chumra* of *psula min ha-kehunah*? By your account, the *chalitzah* was never meaningful to begin with.

### Reish Lakish Challenges

Reish Lakish responds: *miderabbanan u-lechumra*. The Rabbis can treat a *chalitzah* performed on a pregnant woman as a *chalitzah* for purposes of stringency — rendering her a *chalutza* with all the relevant prohibitions — without conceding that it is a valid *chalitzah* at the biblical level. Hence the *mishnah* imposes all the *chumrot* associated with *chalitzah* without affirming that the act actually freed her. She will still require a proper *chalitzah* from the brothers.

### Alt. Version of Dispute

The Gemara then presents the alternate version: *ika de-amri*, some say the exchange ran in the opposite direction, with Reish Lakish initiating the challenge to Rabbi Yochanan. Reish Lakish cites the same *mishnah* language and argues: *bishlama ledidi* — according to me, who holds that *chalitzat me'uberet lo shema chalitzah*, it makes sense that the *mishnah* teaches only the *chumrot*: she is forbidden to a *kohen*, she is forbidden to his relatives, and so on. *V'lo katni eina tzricha chalitzah min ha-achin* — but it does not tell you the major *chiddush* that she is now fully free and requires no further *chalitzah* from the brothers. That larger leniency is absent because it would be false according to my view. *Ela ledidach* — but according to you, Rabbi Yochanan, the *mishnah* should have led with the primary novelty: that *chalitzah* performed while she was pregnant, if the child proves non-viable, fully exempts her and she needs no further *chalitzah* from the brothers. Why did the *mishnah* omit that *kula*?

Rabbi Yochanan answers: *ein hachi nami*, you are correct that it could have said so. *Aidi detani reisha lo pasla* — but since the opening clause of the *mishnah* established that when the child turns out to be viable, the *chalitzah* carries no weight even *lechumra* — there are no *chumrot* at all, we treat the act as though it never occurred — the *mishnah* set up the parallel in the concluding clause by teaching the *chumra* of *psula min ha-kehunah* for the non-viable scenario. But you are correct, Rabbi Yochanan concedes: she would in fact need no further *chalitzah*, and that *kula* is implicit even if unstated.

### Yibum Case

Rabbi Yochanan now presses Reish Lakish from a different angle. If a man performed *yibum* with his *yevama* while she was pregnant, and she subsequently miscarried, the *mishnah* says he may remain married to her — *yikayem*. *Bishlama ledidi* — according to me, who holds that both *chalitzat me'uberet shema chalitzah* and *biat me'uberet shema biah*, the act of *yibum* is retrospectively valid if the child proves non-viable. Hence *mishum hachi tani yikayem* — that is why it says he may remain married. *Ela ledidach* — but according to you, Reish Lakish, who holds the act was not meaningful, the *mishnah* should not merely say *yikayem*; it should say *yachzor v'yibom* — let him go back and perform a proper act of *yibum*, and only then remain married. Why does it simply say *yikayem*?

### Reish Lakish's Response

Reish Lakish responds: *mai yikayem* — what do you think *yikayem* means? It means precisely *yachzor v'yibom v'yikayem* — let him perform another act of *bi'ah* to make the *yibum* binding, and then he may remain married. And there is no other option here: *d'lo sagi b'lav hachi* — there is no way forward without this step.

Rashi explains the reasoning: *d'lo mistra belo biah l'achar she'hipilah* — after she has miscarried, if he now wishes to either stay married or separate from her, he cannot simply give a *get*, because *biat me'uberet lav shema biah* — the earlier act did not constitute a valid act of *yibum*. Nor can a *chalitzah* follow, since he is in any case considered to have had relations with her and performing *chalitzah* after such contact would be entirely inappropriate at least at the rabbinic level. Therefore, his only available step is to have another act of *bi'ah*, which will then constitute binding *yibum*. After that, he may either remain married or give a *get*. Thus, *yikayem* is not merely permission to remain married — it is instruction that this is the only path forward regardless of what he ultimately chooses to do.

The Gemara then presents the alternative version of this exchange as well — *ika d'amri* — in which Reish Lakish uses the *yibum* case proactively to argue against Rabbi Yochanan, and Rabbi Yochanan responds *ein hachi nami*, that *ratza yotzi ratza yikayem* could have been stated, but the *mishnah* chose the parallel construction because the opening clause in the viable-child case required the language of *yotzi* — since there the man must divorce, as the woman is his brother's wife — and so the concluding clause correspondingly used *yikayem*, meaning he is permitted to remain married.

## Abaye Reframes

### Abaye's Solution

The Gemara then raises a *baraita*: *hakones et yevamto v'nimtzeit me'uberet harei zo lo tinasei tzaratah* — a man who performed *yibum* with his *yevama* and it turns out she was pregnant: her co-wife (*tzarah*) may not go ahead and remarry, lest the child be viable. This poses a question: if the child is viable, then *yibum* was unnecessary; if not viable, the *yibum* was valid. Either way, the *tzarah* seems to be released. Why then is she barred from remarrying?

The Gemara emends: the concern is *shema lo yehei havelad ben kayama* — perhaps the child will not be viable, meaning the *yibum* was necessary but invalid because performed during pregnancy. This seems to be strong support for Rabbi Yochanan's opponents. Abaye steps in with a reframing: *bebiat kulei alma lo pligi delo patra* — regarding *bi'ah* performed as *yibum* with a pregnant woman, everyone agrees it does not take effect. The logic is clear: since pregnancy creates a presumption that the child may be viable, the act of *bi'ah* would risk transgressing the prohibition of *eishet ach*, and therefore no retroactive validity can be granted. *Ki pligi bachalitzah* — the dispute is limited to *chalitzah*. Since *chalitzah* separates the man and woman rather than drawing them together, there is at least an argument that it could be valid even if performed during pregnancy. On this Rabbi Yochanan holds *chalitzat me'uberet shema chalitzah*, conceding that *biat me'uberet lo shema biah*; Reish Lakish holds both are invalid.

### Focus on Chalitzah

According to Abaye's reframing, the *tzarah* cannot remarry in the *yibum* case because everyone agrees the act of *bi'ah* did not work, and therefore if the child proves non-viable she remains bound and requires *chalitzah* or valid *yibum*. The dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish thus concerns only whether *chalitzah* performed during pregnancy is retrospectively valid.

## Rava's Objection

### Package Deal

Rava objects to Abaye's reframing: *mamma nafshach* — make up your mind. *I biah me'uberet shema biah, chalitzat me'uberet shema chalitzah* — if the *bi'ah* is valid, then the *chalitzah* is valid; *v'i biah me'uberet lo shema biah, chalitzat me'uberet nami lo shema chalitzah* — if the *bi'ah* is not valid, the *chalitzah* is not valid either. The principle is that *kol ha'oleh l'yibum oleh l'chalitzah, v'chol she'eino oleh l'yibum eino oleh l'chalitzah* — whatever is eligible for *yibum* is eligible for *chalitzah*, and whatever is ineligible for *yibum* is ineligible for *chalitzah*. They are a package deal. Abaye's bifurcation — that *yibum* fails but *chalitzah* succeeds — cannot be sustained.

### Child's Birth Factor

Having rejected Abaye's reframing, Rava now explains the *baraita* differently. *Hachi ka'amar* — here is what the *baraita* is actually saying: the *tzarah* cannot remarry *shema yihiyeh velad ben kayama* — lest the child be viable. Now, if the child is viable, why does it matter whether the *yibum* or *chalitzah* was valid? Because an entirely new principle now enters the discussion: *ha-velad eino poter ad sheyeitzei l'avir ha'olam* — the child does not release the wives from the *zikah* until he is actually born. Even if we know the child will be viable, the co-wives are not free until the moment of birth. Therefore, the *baraita*'s concern is precisely this: if the child turns out to be viable, neither *yibum* nor *chalitzah* was meaningful — everyone agrees on that — but furthermore, even knowing a viable child is coming, the co-wives remain bound until the birth actually occurs. Hence the *tzarah* cannot go ahead and remarry.

### Supporting Baraita

A *baraita* is then cited in direct support of Rava's framework: *tanya kevateih d'Rava* — we taught a *baraita* consistent with Rava. *Hakones yevamto v'nimtzeit me'uberet harei zo lo tinasei tzaratah shema yihiyeh velad ben kayama* — and now the *baraita* spells out why that is a problem: *v'ein biah v'chalitzah poteret* — neither *bi'ah* nor *chalitzah* exempts in the case of a viable child. *Ela velad poter* — it is the child that exempts. *She-ha-velad eino poter ad sheyeitzei l'avir ha'olam* — and the child does not exempt until he has actually entered the world.

## Co-Wife's Status

### Proof for Reish Lakish

The Gemara now draws an inference from the *baraita*: *taama d'shama yihiyeh velad ben kayama* — the reason the *tzarah* cannot remarry is specifically because the child might be viable and the birth has not yet occurred. *Ha lo havi velad ben kayama, miftar tzaratah* — but if the child were not viable, the *tzarah* would be permitted to remarry. This seems to be a proof in favor of Rabbi Yochanan: the *yibum* performed during pregnancy would be retroactively valid if the child proves non-viable, and the *tzarah* would then be released.

The Gemara therefore asks whether this constitutes a conclusive refutation of Reish Lakish. Reish Lakish responds: *hachi katani* — here is how the *baraita* is truly to be read. The *tzarah* cannot remarry for two independent reasons. First, *shema lo yehei havelad ben kayama* — maybe the child will not be viable, in which case *chalitzat me'uberet lo shema chalitzah u-viat me'uberet lo shema bi'ah* — neither the *chalitzah* nor the *yibum* was meaningful, and the *tzarah* remains bound. Second, even if you invoke *rov nashim velad malya yalden* — most pregnancies produce viable children, and one might assume the *tzarah* is effectively free — the answer is *velad eino poter ad sheyetzei l'avir ha'olam*: she is still not released until the child is born. Thus the *baraita* focused on the viable-child scenario because that is the one people might think resolves the problem, but in truth the *tzarah* is stuck either way — if non-viable, the *yibum* failed; if viable, she must wait for the birth. Nothing effective happens while the woman is pregnant.

### Husband Dies Away

Rabbi Elazar then remarks that Reish Lakish's position must have support in a *mishnah* somewhere, and upon investigation he finds it. The *mishnah* teaches: *ha-ishah she-halach ba'alah v'tzaratah limdinat ha-yam* — a woman whose husband went overseas together with her co-wife, and word came back that the husband died. *Harei zo lo tinasei v'lo tityabem* — she may neither remarry nor perform *yibum* with the brother, *ad shetedah shema me'uberet hi tzaratah* — until she knows whether the co-wife is pregnant.

The Gemara proceeds to analyze this. Why can she not perform *yibum* with the brother? *Shema yehei havelad ben kayama v'yifga b'issur eishet ach d'Oraita* — lest the co-wife carry a viable child, making the act of *yibum* a biblical transgression of *eishet ach*, since if a viable child exists there is no *mitzvah* of *yibum* at all. That is clear. But why can she not perform *chalitzah* and then remarry? That question requires careful examination.

### Nine-Month Question

The Gemara asks: *ela nechzei* — let us think about this. I understand that she cannot perform *chalitzah* and remarry *betoch tishah* — within nine months — since during that period we are uncertain whether the co-wife is pregnant with a viable child. *Ela tachlotz betoch tishah v'tinasei l'achar tishah* — but why not perform *chalitzah* right away and then remarry only after nine months have passed? At that point, either the *chalitzah* was valid because the co-wife was not pregnant, or if she was pregnant the child would by then have been born and the co-wife released in any event. This combined approach should satisfy all possibilities. Since the *mishnah* does not offer this option, it appears to prove like Reish Lakish — that *chalitzah* performed while the co-wife is pregnant is not valid, and therefore performing *chalitzah* now would be pointless if the co-wife turns out to be pregnant with a viable child.

The Gemara, however, questions whether this is a strong proof. Even if the *chalitzah* is valid, one might still object. The Gemara responds: *dilma ika inish d'havi b'chalitzah v'lo havi b'achraza* — the concern is that someone present at the *chalitzah* might later not hear the retraction. As stated by Abaye bar Avin and Rav Chanana bar Abaye: the reason we avoid performing *chalitzah* prematurely is *shema yehei velad ben kayama v'nimtza ata matricha kruz li-khehunah* — lest the child prove viable, in which case the *chalitzah* was meaningless, yet we would have to make a public announcement retracting it. The danger is that someone who was present at the *chalitzah* but missed the retraction might later see this woman marrying a *kohen* and conclude that a *chalutza* may marry a *kohen* — a grave error. To avoid this confusion, the Rabbis prefer not to perform *chalitzah* at all while there is uncertainty about the co-wife's pregnancy.

### Abaye's Reading

Abaye intervenes with a simpler resolution. He points out that the *mishnah* never in fact said she cannot perform *chalitzah*. *Lo tinasei v'lo tityabem tani* — the *mishnah* said only that she may not remarry and may not perform *yibum*, but it did not say she may not obtain *chalitzah*. Therefore the *mishnah* carries no implication about the validity of *chalitzah* during the co-wife's pregnancy, and thus provides no support for Reish Lakish. *Aval ee chalitz lah hachi nami desharya* — if she does obtain *chalitzah* and then waits nine months to remarry, that is perfectly permissible. The *mishnah* simply rules out *yibum* (due to the risk of *eishet ach*) and remarrying without any prior *chalitzah* — not *chalitzah* itself.

The result of Abaye's reading is that the *mishnah* offers no proof for Reish Lakish, and we are returned to the unresolved debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish.

## Rava's Ruling

### Baraita Proof

At last, a *baraita* is cited that supports Reish Lakish explicitly. *Ha-choletz l'me'uberet v'hipila* — one who performed *chalitzah* with a pregnant woman, and she subsequently miscarried: *tzricha chalitzah min ha-achim* — she still requires *chalitzah* from the brothers. The *chalitzah* performed during the pregnancy was not binding, even though it turned out retroactively that it would have been necessary.

### Rava Paskins

Rava rules: *hilchesa k'vasei d'Reish Lakish* — the *halacha* follows Reish Lakish. This is a striking ruling: the weight of the textual arguments throughout the *sugya* seemed to lean toward Rabbi Yochanan, yet in the end we have a *baraita* explicitly teaching Reish Lakish's position, and Rava rules accordingly. *Chalitzah* performed while the woman is pregnant is not binding.

### Parallel Cases

This ruling creates a clean and elegant symmetry. While the woman is pregnant, nothing binding or effective can occur — regardless of which way the pregnancy resolves. If the child will prove viable, then *chalitzah* and *yibum* are simply inapplicable, and moreover the co-wives are not released until the moment of birth. If the child will prove non-viable, then by Reish Lakish's ruling *chalitzah* or *yibum* during the pregnancy still do not take effect. In both scenarios, while she is pregnant, everything is in abeyance. Nothing binding happens until after the birth.

The Gemara then notes that this is one of three cases — *b'hani telat* — in which we rule like Reish Lakish against Rabbi Yochanan, notwithstanding the general principle that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yochanan in his disputes with Reish Lakish.

The second case involves a deathbed bequest. The *mishnah* rules that a dying man who distributes his property, enlarging one heir's share and diminishing another's, or equalizing the firstborn's portion with those of other sons, his words stand — provided the language of gift (*matana*) appears somewhere in the document, whether at the beginning, middle, or end. The dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish arises when a father uses the language of inheritance (*yerusha*) for one son and the language of gift (*matana*) for another. Rabbi Yochanan holds that the presence of gift language anywhere in the transaction validates the entire bequest, even the portion stated in the language of inheritance. Reish Lakish holds that it will not work unless the gift and inheritance language are bundled together — *ploni u-ploni yirshu sadeh ploni shenatatim lahem b'matana li-yerusha* — naming both heirs jointly. If he separated them, saying let Reuven inherit and let Shimon receive a gift, then Shimon's share is valid as a gift but Reuven's is not, since his portion was stated exclusively in the language of *yerusha*, which cannot override the Torah's inheritance law. We rule like Reish Lakish.

The third case is the major debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish that runs throughout *Shas*: *ha-kotev kol nechasav livno le-achar moto* — a father writes that he is giving his son a field "from now, effective after my death." The rabbis interpret this as: title (*kinyan ha-guf*) transfers to the son immediately, while the right to usufruct (*kinyan peirot*) — the ongoing benefit and produce of the field — remains with the father until death. If the son sells his interest in the field during the father's lifetime and the son subsequently predeceases the father, the question is whether the purchaser acquires anything.

Rabbi Yochanan holds *kinyan peirot ke-kinyan ha-guf dami* — the father's right to the produce is tantamount to full title, and therefore the son's sale of the bare legal title during the father's lifetime, when the father's *kinyan peirot* gave him effective ownership, was meaningless. Since the son is no longer alive when the father dies, the sale yields nothing to the purchaser. Reish Lakish holds *kinyan peirot lav ke-kinyan ha-guf dami* — the right to usufruct does not constitute title, the son was genuinely the title-holder and could validly sell his title even while the father retained *kinyan peirot*, and therefore the purchaser acquires the field upon the father's death. We rule like Reish Lakish.

## Pregnant/Nursing Wife

### Rabbi Eliezer Strict

The Gemara turns to the second section of the *mishnah*: *ein ha-vlad shelo kayama* — if the child proved non-viable and the *yibum* was therefore retrospectively valid, the man may remain married. A *baraita* then adds: *tana mishum Rabbi Eliezer amru, yotzi b'get* — they said in the name of Rabbi Eliezer that he must nonetheless divorce her with a *get*. Even though retroactively the *yibum* was entirely legitimate, the fact that he had relations with his *yevama* while she was pregnant — when in all likelihood it would have constituted a violation of *eishet ach*, a prohibition subject to *kares* — cannot be tolerated even *bedi'eved*. We demand a divorce regardless of how it resolved.

### Rava & R. Meir

Rava observes: *Rabbi Meir v'Rabbi Eliezer amru davar echad* — Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer share a common principle, namely that when someone enters a forbidden or problematic union, even if it resolves in a technically permissible direction, we demand that he divorce and separate, and we do not passively accept the fait accompli.

### Nursing Woman Case

The parallel from Rabbi Meir is sourced from a *baraita*: *lo yisa adam uberet chaveiro u-meineket chaveiro* — a man may not marry a woman who is pregnant or nursing from a previous marriage, whether the previous husband has died or divorced her. The concern — developed elsewhere in the Gemara — is that a new pregnancy while nursing poses a danger to the nursing infant. *V'im nasa yotzi v'lo yachazir olamit divrei Rabbi Meir* — if he went ahead and married her, he must divorce her and may never remarry her. Rabbi Meir is extraordinarily strict: even though the prohibition is violated, he will not permit the marriage to stand even after the problematic period has passed. The *Chachamim* are more lenient: *yotzi*, he must separate, but *u-che-sheyagia zmano lichnos, yichnos* — once the nursing period ends and the concern is resolved, he may remarry her.

### Abaye Distinguishes

Abaye challenges Rava's equation of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Meir: *dilma lo hi* — perhaps the cases are not parallel and the two *amora'im* do not in fact share the same principle.

One could argue in either direction. Perhaps Rabbi Eliezer is strict here specifically because the act in question — having relations with a pregnant *yevama* — risked a *d'Oraita* prohibition of *eishet ach* with its attendant *karet*. We will not tolerate even a retroactively valid *yibum* that was attended by such risk. But Rabbi Meir's case involves only a *d'rabbanan* prohibition — marrying a nursing woman — and perhaps Rabbi Eliezer would be lenient there and agree with the *Chachamim*.

Conversely, perhaps Rabbi Meir's stringency is confined to the *d'rabbanan* case, where the Rabbis applied *chizuk* — extra reinforcement of their own enactments — beyond even what would apply to a *d'Oraita* prohibition, since people tend to treat rabbinic rules lightly. But in the *d'Oraita* case of Rabbi Eliezer, where the prohibition is *eishet ach*, people naturally keep far away from it, and Rabbi Meir might well be lenient *bedi'eved* were it all resolved. The two cases thus cannot be assumed to express a single shared position.

## Divorce Requirement

### Get vs. Parshan

The Gemara addresses the precise meaning of *yotzi* in the *Chachamim*'s ruling regarding one who marries a pregnant or nursing woman. Rava clarifies: *ul'divrei Chachamim yotzi b'get* — the *Chachamim* require an actual *get*, a formal bill of divorce, not merely physical separation (*perisha*). This is not a trivial distinction: a *get* renders the woman a *gerusha*, with all consequent legal ramifications — most significantly, that if her husband is a *kohen*, he cannot divorce her with a *get* and subsequently remarry her.

### Mar Zutra's Analysis

Mar Zutra adds that this reading is supported by a close examination of the *mishnah*'s own language: *dika nami d'katani yotzi* — the *mishnah* uses the word *yotzi* (literally: he shall send her out / divorce her), *v'lo katani yafrish* — and not the word *yafrish* (he shall separate from her). *Yotzi* is the standard technical term for divorce, not mere separation. *Shema minah* — this close reading of the text confirms the ruling.

## Kohen Marriage Issue

### Kohen Problem

This raises an immediate difficulty. Rav Ashi poses the question to Rav Hoshaya son of Rav Idi: demanding a *get* is well and good when the husband is an ordinary *Yisrael*, who may always remarry the same woman. But would one actually demand a *get* when the husband is a *kohen*, thereby permanently severing the marriage? A *kohen* may not remarry a *gerusha*, and his wife — once divorced — acquires the disqualification of *gerusha* which follows her even with respect to other *kohanim*. The demand for a *get* thus carries far graver consequences for a *kohen* than for a *Yisrael*.

As a prelude to this question, the Gemara cites a *baraita* from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: *kol she-shaha b'adam shloshim yom, einu nefel* — if a newborn survives thirty days, he is no longer considered a *nefel* (non-viable infant). Rashi qualifies: this thirty-day rule applies specifically when it is uncertain whether the pregnancy was full-term. If it is known to be full-term, then *tinok ben yomo poter min ha-yibum* — a one-day-old infant, as soon as he is born, releases his mother from the obligation of *yibum*, as taught in Tractate Niddah.

### Safek Chalitza

The Gemara then develops the following scenario: a child was born, it was uncertain whether the pregnancy was full-term, and thus uncertain whether the child was viable. The child died within thirty days — without resolving the uncertainty — and the mother, assuming she was free because she had a child, went ahead and remarried. But in fact her status is uncertain: if the child was not viable, she was never released from *yibbum* and should have obtained *chalitzah* from the brothers-in-law first. She is thus a *safek* in need of *chalitzah*.

Ravina in the name of Rava rules: *im eshet Yisrael hi, choletzet* — if she is now married to a *Yisrael*, she must obtain *chalitzah* now to resolve the doubt. *V'im eshet kohen hi, eina choletzet* — but if she is married to a *kohen*, we do not demand that she obtain *chalitzah*, because doing so would make her a *chalutza* — or at least a *safek chalutza* — and render her permanently forbidden to her husband.

### Demand Chalitza?

Rav Mesharshiya, also in the name of Rava, disagrees: *achat zo v'achat zo choletzet* — in both cases she must obtain *chalitzah*, even if this means she must separate from her *kohen* husband.

Ravina then informs Rav Mesharshiya that he may have heard Rava say this at night, but *u-vetzafra hadar bei* — the next morning Rava reversed himself. Rav Mesharshiya responds with sharp skepticism — *sharyuta? yehei ra'ava d'tishrei afilu tarba* — you've found a leniency? Let it be God's will that you can permit even forbidden fat — expressing his refusal to credit the claimed retraction. He heard Rava's ruling from Rava himself, and will not accept a secondhand report of a reversal.

### Unresolved Kohen Q

This debate sets the stage for the governing question with which the daf concludes: *hacha gabi me'uberet chaveiro u-meineket chaveiro ha-nesu'ah l'kohen, mah — mi avadu rabbanan takanta l'kohen o lo?* In our case, where a man married a pregnant or nursing woman from a previous marriage and the Rabbis require him to issue a *get* — did the Rabbis create an exemption (*takana*) for a *kohen*, allowing him to remain married rather than be required to give a *get* that would forever prohibit remarriage? Or does the requirement of *get* apply equally to a *kohen*, at whatever cost? This question remains unresolved, and the Gemara will return to it.

---

---

# Yevamot 37

## Forced Divorce: Nursing

### Child Viability & 30 Days

The daf opens at 37a with a continuation of the discussion concerning forced divorce in cases where someone married against a rabbinic concern — specifically, the case of a woman who was pregnant or nursing a child from a previous relationship and subsequently remarried. The Gemara had established that such a woman must separate from her new husband, and if she was widowed or divorced she must wait until the child is no longer nursing before remarrying. The question now is what happens when the man who married her in violation of this concern is a *kohen*, for whom a divorce creates a permanent bar to remarriage.

This discussion overlaps with a parallel case involving a *yevamah* whose infant died within thirty days of birth, leaving uncertain whether the child was viable. The relevant background: if the child was born at full term, we assume viability without requiring the thirty-day period. If it was not a full-term pregnancy, we require thirty days to establish viability. Furthermore, the context assumes the child died from an external cause — some accident or tragedy — not a natural death, since a natural death within thirty days would itself be evidence of non-viability. According to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, in the non-full-term case, a death within thirty days leaves the child's status uncertain, and consequently, the mother's obligation of *chalitza* or *yibbum* remains unclear. If she then remarried, the question of whether to demand *chalitza* from her current situation is live — with the added complication that if she married a *kohen*, demanding *chalitza* at this point would permanently separate them.

### Kohen & Chalitza

The Gemara asks: *hacha gabei me'uberet chaveiro umineket chaveiro deniseit lekohen mai?* — what is the ruling when the woman who was pregnant or nursing has married a *kohen*? *Mi avdi Rabbanan takanta lekohen o lo?* — did the Rabbis make some accommodation to avoid forcing a divorce where remarriage would become permanently impossible?

The Gemara responds by sharply distinguishing the two cases: *amar lei hachi hashta?* — "How can you compare them?" In the *yevamah* case, where we refrain from demanding *chalitza*, there is a genuine halakhic position to rely upon. *Keivan de'ika Rabbanan dephaligi aleih deRabban Shimon ben Gamliel* — since there are Rabbis who disagree with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and hold that even a child who did not survive thirty days was a viable child (*velad malya hu*), we are not simply waiving the requirement because of the *kohen*'s predicament. Rather, we are relying on the existing rabbinic opinion — the principle that *kedai hu ploni lismokh alav bish'at hadechak*, a given opinion is worthy of reliance in a time of pressing need. Since demanding *chalitza* would force a permanent separation from her husband, we apply this minority — or in this case, majority — opinion when we need it.

### Why No Exception for Koh…

In the case of the nursing or pregnant woman, however, this logic does not apply. *Aval hacha, keman abdinnan?* — according to which opinion would we refrain from demanding a divorce? If we follow Rabbi Meir, he says *yotzi velo yachzir olamit* — he must divorce and may never remarry. If we follow the *Rabbanan*, they too require a *get*, even if remarriage is later permitted. There is simply no opinion in the debate over the nursing and pregnant case that permits the man to remain married without any divorce at all. We cannot invoke the "time of need" principle where no halakhic opinion actually supports the result we are trying to reach. Accordingly, even when the husband is a *kohen*, the divorce is required — and since the divorce creates a permanent bar to remarriage, the couple is permanently separated. This is a striking result: a *kohen* who technically entered a legitimate marriage, whose only violation was the timing with respect to the nursing period, loses his wife permanently.

---

## Kiddushin in 3 Months

### 3-Month Wait & Forced Get

The Gemara introduces a related case: *kiddesh b'toch shlosha u'varach* — a man performed *kiddushin* with a woman within the three-month waiting period required after the death or divorce of her prior husband, and then ran away. The rationale for the three-month waiting period is to establish clarity of paternity: if the woman remarries immediately, it will be unclear whose child she is carrying. The question is what happens when someone violated this by performing *kiddushin* within the three months, but did not yet proceed to *nisu'in*.

### Rafram's Running Away

*Pligi bah Rav Acha v'Rafram* — Rav Acha and Rafram disagree. One opinion holds that we place him in *cherem* until he gives a *get*. The assumption is that even *kiddushin* alone within the three-month period is serious enough to compel a forced divorce. The other opinion holds that *arukei mistayei* — his running away suffices. Since the fundamental concern is *nisu'in* — actual cohabitation which could result in a pregnancy and confusion about paternity — and since by running away he has made clear that *nisu'in* will not be taking place anytime soon, we need not pursue him and force a *get*.

The Gemara notes that a practical case came before Rafram, *havei uvda ramia l'Rafram*, and he ruled in accordance with his own position: *arukei mistayei*, the fact that he ran away is sufficient.

This raises the practical question — especially relevant for a *kohen* who performed *kiddushin* within the three-month period — of whether running away solves the problem. For a *kohen*, running away would be far preferable to being compelled to give a *get*, since a *get* would permanently bar him from remarrying this woman.

### Tosafot: Kiddushin Alone

The earlier discussion about the nursing mother gave no indication that *kiddushin* alone, without *nisu'in*, would be any different — the Gemara seemed to demand a *get* regardless, even when the husband was a *kohen*. Tosafot, however, on 36b, cite an interesting leniency. Rabbi Yosef of Orléans (*v'haRav Rabbi Yosef m'Orlinesh*) ruled that a man who performed *kiddushin* with a nursing woman (*b'echad shekiddesh meineket chaveiro*) need not be required to give a *get* — merely separation suffices (*ela hafrasha b'alma*). His reasoning: *keivan d'belav hachi assura lei* — since in any event they are prohibited from cohabiting, because *kallah belo bracha assura l'ba'alah k'niddah* — a bride without the recitation of *sheva brachot* and the consummation of *nisu'in* is forbidden to her husband like a *niddah* — there is no concern that they will live together as husband and wife during the nursing period. Without *nisu'in*, the fundamental problem does not arise, and therefore a formal *get* is not required. This constitutes a significant *kula*, though it does require reconciliation with the later Gemara that implies a *get* is necessary even in the *kohen* scenario.

---

## Unknown Paternity

### Case: 7 vs 9 Months

The Gemara now turns to a fascinating and detailed discussion about a woman who performed *yibbum* with her brother-in-law and subsequently gave birth at a time that left uncertain whether the child was fathered by the first husband or the *yavam*. The scenario: the first husband died, and the woman did *yibbum* before the three-month waiting period had elapsed. She then gave birth at a point in time that was consistent with either a seven-month pregnancy from the *yavam* or a nine-month pregnancy from the first husband. The child is not a *mamzer* in either case — if from the first husband, the child is legitimately the first husband's son; if from the *yavam*, then the *yibbum* was valid and the child is the *yavam*'s legitimate son. But the uncertainty of paternity has important practical consequences for inheritance and for determining whether the *yavam* is currently violating an *issur kares* by continuing to cohabit with his wife.

As Rashi notes, another implication concerns the *chatas* obligation. The Mishnah rules they bring an *asham talui* — the conditional guilt offering brought when one is unsure whether a sin was committed. But if we could establish that the child is indeed from the first husband, then the *yibbum* was clearly invalid, there is no *mitzvah* of *yibbum*, and the *yavam* is definitely cohabiting with an *arayos* — he would be required to bring a definite *chatas kavu'a* rather than a mere *asham talui*.

### Rava's Challenge

*Amar lei Rava l'Rav Nachman* — Rava challenged Rav Nachman: *leima halach achar rov nashim* — why not simply go by the majority? Most women give birth after nine months. If we apply the principle of *rov*, the majority, we should assume this child is a nine-month baby and therefore the son of the first husband. Why is there any doubt at all?

### Not Visibly Pregnant

Rav Nachman's initial response — *nashei didan beshiva yaldan*, our women give birth after seven months — provoked a sharp rejoinder from Rava: *nashei didichu havu ruba d'alma?* — are the women of your town the majority of the world? Even if a non-trivial minority of women give birth in the seventh month, the majority of women worldwide still give birth after nine months, so why not apply *rov*?

Rav Nachman then refined his answer. He said: *hachi ka'amina* — this is what I mean to say. *Rov nashim yaldan l'tisha* — yes, most women give birth after nine months, *u'miyuta l'shiva* — but a minority give birth in the seventh month. However, there is an additional critical factor: *v'chol hayoledes l'tisha ubra nikar l'shlish yameha* — any woman who will give birth after nine months will show visible signs of pregnancy by the end of the third month.

Now consider the case before us. If this woman had become visibly pregnant three months after the death of her first husband — that is, one month after the *yavam* married her — it would have been immediately apparent that she was pregnant from the first husband, and there would have been no uncertainty. The very existence of the doubt in this case means — implicitly — that she was *not* visibly pregnant three months after the first husband's death. And that fact undermines the *rov*. On the one hand, the majority suggests a nine-month pregnancy from the first husband; on the other hand, if it were a nine-month pregnancy, she would (in most cases) have been visibly pregnant by three months, which she was not. *V'zu ho'il v'lo hukeir ubra l'shlish yameha, itrei lah ruba* — since she was not visibly pregnant after three months, the majority is thrown into question.

### Visible Pregnancy

The Gemara presses the logic further. If every woman carrying a nine-month baby is visibly pregnant after three months (*kol hayoledes l'tisha ubra nikar l'shisha meha*), then the absence of visible pregnancy after three months would be conclusive proof in the *opposite* direction — we should know *for certain* that this is a seven-month baby from the *yavam*. *Ha me'delo u'kar l'shlisha meha, vadai bar sheva l'vastra hu* — if she was not visibly pregnant after three months, certainly the child is from the second husband.

The Gemara therefore amends the formulation: *ela eima rov* — say rather that *most* women carrying nine-month babies show visible pregnancy after three months, but not all. This yields the correct result: the absence of visible pregnancy at three months undermines but does not eliminate the *rov* that most babies are nine-month babies. We thus have two countervailing considerations — the *rov* pointing toward a nine-month pregnancy from the first husband, and the absence of visible pregnancy at three months creating serious doubt about that. The result is a genuine *safek*, and that is why the Mishnah treats the child's paternity as unknown.

---

## First & Second Child

### First: Kohen Gadol

The Gemara now turns to the legal consequences for the children born into this uncertain situation. The *Baraita* states: *rishon ra'uy lihyot kohen gadol* — the first child born in this ambiguous situation is fit to be a *kohen gadol*. Since both brothers are *kohanim* — if one is a *kohen* the other necessarily is as well — the child is certainly a *kohen* regardless of which man is his father. Moreover, the child was born within a legitimate marriage in any case: either he is the first husband's child, entirely legitimate; or he is the *yavam*'s child from a valid *yibbum*, equally legitimate. Tosafot raises the question of whether a *kohen* must be *miyuchas* — with fully known paternity — to serve as *kohen gadol*, but concludes that the requirement of *miyuchas* applies only where there is a question of illegitimate birth, not where the child was unquestionably born within marriage and the only uncertainty is which of two legitimate marriages he derives from.

### Second: Safek Mamzer

The *Baraita* continues: *v'sheni mamzer misafek* — but a second child, born after the first, is a doubtful *mamzer*. The reasoning: if the first child was indeed the first husband's son, then there was no obligation of *yibbum* and the *yavam* was living with a woman who is *arayos* to him. Any subsequent child born of that relationship would be a *mamzer*. If the first child was the *yavam*'s own child from a valid *yibbum*, then a subsequent child would also be legitimate. Since we do not know which is the case, the second child is a *safek mamzer*.

The striking contrast is thus established: the first child could be a *kohen gadol*, and yet his sibling is a *safek mamzer* — perhaps the most legally disadvantaged status in Jewish law.

---

## Safek Mamzer Debate

### Tanna Kamma Position

The *Tanna Kamma*'s position is that the second child is a *safek mamzer*, and as such is *asur b'mamzeret* — he cannot marry even a *mamzeret*. The logic of this is painful but straightforward: a *safek mamzer* cannot marry a regular *Yisrael* because he might be a *mamzer*; he cannot marry a *mamzeret* because he might not be a *mamzer*, and a *mamzeret* is forbidden to one who is not a *mamzer*. He is caught on both sides.

### R. Eliezer: Treat as Vad…

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov states: *ein mamzer misafek* — there is no such thing, halakhically, as a *mamzer from doubt*. This is not a factual dispute — he agrees the child's status is uncertain. It is a halakhic dispute about how to categorize and treat a person of doubtful *mamzer* status. His position, as elaborated by the Gemara, is *vadai mamzer u'mutar b'mamzeret* — we treat him as a definite *mamzer*, and therefore he is permitted to marry a *mamzeret*. The reasoning: the verse *lo yavo mamzer b'kehal Hashem* is understood to forbid entry into the "unblemished community." A person about whom there is a question mark — even if he may in truth be completely untainted — is by definition not part of the category of the "unblemished." The doubt itself removes him from the pristine category and places him in the category of the *mamzer*, so he may marry within that category. Thus, saying *vadai mamzer* is not a factual claim but a halakhic assignment: given the doubt, we treat him as a full *mamzer*, which is paradoxically a *leniency*.

### Abaye vs Rava Read

The question is then raised: who in this dispute is saying what? The Gemara notes that the debate between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the *Tanna Kamma* is parallel to a debate recorded in the name of Rabbi Elazar, who states: *vadan be'vadan muttar* — a definite *mamzer* may marry a definite *mamzer*; but *vadan bi'sfekan, sfekan be'vadan, sfekan be'sfekan asur* — a definite *mamzer* may not marry a *safek mamzer*, and two *safek mamzerim* may not marry each other. The categories of *safek* mentioned by Rabbi Elazar are *shtuki* (a child whose mother is known but whose father is not — she deflects the question), *asufi* (a foundling whose parents are unknown), and *kuti* (a Samaritan, since Samaritan practice regarding *kiddushin* differs from halakha and their children may unknowingly be *mamzerim*).

Rav Yehuda quoted Rav ruling *halacha ke'Rabbi Elazar* — that a *safek mamzer* is *asur*, cannot marry either a regular *Yisrael* or a definite *mamzer*. But when Rav Yehuda reported this ruling to Shmuel, Shmuel responded: *Hillel shana asara yuchasin* — Hillel taught that there are ten genealogical categories that came up from Babylonia, and all of them can intermarry in some combination (*v'chulan mutarin lavo zeh ba'zeh*). If a *safek mamzer* could marry no one at all, Hillel's teaching would be internally incoherent, for there would be no valid marriage partner for the *safek* categories.

This sets the stage for the central interpretive dispute. *Abaye savar lah k'Shmuel, d'amar halacha k'Hillel* — Abaye holds like Shmuel that we rule like Hillel, meaning a *safek mamzer* is *mutar* to marry another *mamzer*, and therefore he reads Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov as the one who is *lenient* — the one who says *vadai mamzer u'mutar b'mamzeret* — in order that the halakhic ruling in favor of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov not conflict with the ruling like Hillel. *Rava savar lah k'Rav, d'amar halacha ke'Rabbi Elazar* — Rava holds like Rav that the *safek mamzer* is *asur*, and he therefore reads Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov as the one who is *stringent* — the one who says *safek mamzer ve'asur b'mamzeret* — so that the ruling in favor of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov aligns with the ruling like Rabbi Elazar. Each Amora interprets the ambiguous dispute of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov so that it coincides with the halakhic ruling he holds, in order to avoid an internal contradiction between rulings.

---

## Ten Categories

### Halacha Ruling

Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, rules: *halacha ke'Rabbi Elazar* — the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar, meaning a *safek mamzer* is *asur* and cannot marry a definite *mamzer* or a *Yisrael*. This is the operative ruling.

### Hillel's Ten

Hillel's teaching lists ten genealogical categories that ascended from Babylonia: *kohanim, levi'im, yisraelim, chalalim* (a *kohen* who lost his priestly sanctity through prohibited union, such as the son of a *kohen* and a *grusha*), *geirim* (converts), *meshucharim* (freed slaves), *mamzerim, nesinim* (a group reduced to servitude in the time of Yehoshua or David, whose status as Jews is uncertain), *shtuki*, and *asufi*.

### Marriage Groups

Hillel's statement that all these groups can intermarry (*v'chulan mutarin lavo zeh ba'zeh*) does not mean that every group may marry every other group — it means that one can identify overlapping sub-groupings within which marriage is permitted. A male *kohen* cannot marry a convert; but *kohen*, *levi*, and *yisrael* may marry within their own group, and *chalal* may marry within that group as well. *Yisrael*, *chalal*, *ger*, and *meshuchrar* may marry one another. *Mamzer*, *ger*, and *meshuchrar* may marry one another. And the question is where the *safek* categories of *shtuki* and *asufi* fit.

If a *safek mamzer* is *mutar* to marry a definite *mamzer*, then the *shtuki* and *asufi* can marry *mamzer*, *ger*, and *meshuchrar* — an expansive sub-group. If, however, a *safek mamzer* is *asur* even to a definite *mamzer*, then the only option is *geirim*, but to reach *geirim* on the list, one would have to jump over *mamzer* and *ner*, which the Gemara does not contemplate. The *Rambam* (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 15:21) clarifies the underlying structure: *d'oraita*, a *safek mamzer* may actually marry into the general Jewish community, since the verse *lo yavo mamzer b'kehal Hashem* excludes only a *vadai mamzer* (*mamzer vaday assur lavo b'kahal v'lo safek*). Rabbinically, however, the sages enacted a higher standard for *yuchsin* and prohibited *safek mamzerim* from marrying *Yisrael* as well. A *vadai mamzer* may marry a *vadai mamzeret*. But a *safek mamzer, shtuki*, or *asufi* is forbidden to marry a *bas Yisrael* and, the *Rambam* rules, *v'assur lisa mamzeres, v'afilu mamzeres mi-safek assura lo* — even a *mamzeret misafek* is forbidden, lest one be a *mamzer vaday* and the other not. *V'ein li-sfekos elu takanah* — there is no remedy for such persons, except marriage to *geirim*. And even then, *vehavlad holech achar hapgam* — the child carries the same compromised status as the parent, so the problem is never fully resolved.

---

## R. Eliezer's Teachings

### World Filled Mamzerim

Abaye introduces a proof for his reading of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. He cites a *baraita*: *mina amina lei dechol safek le-Rebbi Elazar ben Yaakov kevadai mashvei lei* — from where do I derive that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov treats every *safek* as a *vadai*? From the following teaching: *harey sheba'al nashim harbeh, ve-eino yode'a eyzeh mehen ba'al* — a man had relations with many women and does not know which one he had relations with; and similarly, a woman had relations with many men and does not know from whom she conceived. *Nimtsa av nosei et bito ve-ach nosei et achoto* — the result is that a father might unknowingly marry his daughter, or a brother his sister. *Nimleh kol ha-olam kulo mamzerim* — the world would be filled with *mamzerim*. *Ve-al zeh ne'emar, umalah ha-arets zimah* — and concerning this the verse says, "the land will be filled with *zimah*."

This teaching is important on its own terms. It touches on the question of whether casual or promiscuous sexual relations outside marriage — even where neither party is formally married and thus no *mamzer* status would technically result from adultery — are nonetheless forbidden. The *Rambam* holds that any sexual union outside the context of marriage falls under the prohibition of *kedeshah*. Even for those who permit a *pilegesh* relationship in the context of commitment, it is clear from this passage that casual, indiscriminate sexual activity is the source of the prohibition *umalah ha-arets zimah* — the concern that the world will be filled with prohibited relationships, since no one knows who is related to whom.

But for our purposes, Abaye draws his proof from the phrasing: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov calls these children *mamzerim* even though technically they are *safek mamzerim*. This, says Abaye, demonstrates that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov treats *safek* status as *vadai* for halakhic purposes — which in context means a *leniency*, since a *vadai mamzer* may marry a *mamzeret*.

Rava disputes this reading. He says: *hachi ka'amar* — when Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says the world will be filled with *mamzerim*, he does not mean they will be halakhically categorized as *vadai mamzerim*. Rather, *zimah* in that verse is to be read as a *roshei teivos* (*ro'shei teivos*): *zo ma hi* — "who is this person?" — meaning the world will be filled with people of unknown parentage, genuine *safek mamzerim* whose identity is uncertain. There is no halakhic assignment of *vadai* status; there is only a description of a world in which doubt and uncertainty pervade.

The practical halakhic ruling is stringent: we rule that a *safek mamzer* is *assur bisafek, assur b'mamzeret, ve-assur b'Yisrael* — prohibited on all sides.

### Different Countries

The Gemara continues with additional teachings of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. *Lo yisa adam isha mi-medinah zu v'yelech v'yisa isha mi-medinah acheres* — a man should not marry a woman in one country and then go and marry a woman in another country. *Shema yizdavgu zeh l'zeh* — in an era without telecommunications or systematic record-keeping, the children of the two wives may one day meet and, with no awareness that they share a father, a brother may marry a sister. *Ve-nimtza ach nosei et achoto* — the result would be incest. The problem is not limited to illegitimate unions; it arises even from legitimate marriages when children are raised in ignorance of their full family structure.

### Rav's Temp Wives

One might object that the great Amoraim themselves seem to have practiced something like this. When Rav would travel to Darshier, he would announce: *man havya lei leyoma* — who wishes to be my wife for the day? Similarly, Rav Nachman, when he came to Shnichziv, would make the same announcement. These were not permanent unions but temporary marriages contracted for the duration of a visit. Did they not risk exactly the kind of confusion Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov warned against?

The Gemara answers: *shani rabbanan de-faki'a shemayhu* — great Torah scholars are so famous that their travels and temporary arrangements are publicly known. A child born of such a union would know: my mother was Rav's wife during his visit to this town. There would be no mystery about paternity.

A further question arises from Rava's ruling that *tevu'a linasei* — if a woman's *chatan* suddenly advanced the date of *nisu'in* without her prior expectation — *ve-nifaysa*, and she agreed — *tzrikha leishev shiva neki'im* — she must count seven clean days and go to the *mikvah*. The Gemara's assumption is that the sudden prospect of imminent intimacy may cause a woman to experience discharge sufficient to render her a *niddah*. If that is the halakha, how could Rav and Rav Nachman arrange same-day marriages?

The Gemara offers two answers. First, *rabbanan shluchei havu meshaderu u-modu lehu* — they would send advance notice, giving the woman adequate time to prepare and immerse, so that there would be a seven-day lead time. Second, *ve-iba'is eima, le-rabbanan yichuda be-alma hu de-meyachadi lehu* — alternatively, these arrangements involved *yichud* alone, not actual cohabitation. The Gemara then cites the principle *eino domeh mi she-yesh lo pas be-salo le-mi she-ein lo pas be-salo* — it is not the same to have bread in one's basket as to have none; the mere availability and closeness of a woman addresses the scholar's impulse even without consummation. The Rishonim offer various explanations for how *yichud* in this context could be permitted and how it might differ from the *tevu'a* scenario — some suggesting that a gradual, non-sudden transition to intimacy (as in *yichud* without an explicit announcement of imminent relations) would not cause the physiological response that triggers the concern.

### Don't Plan Divorce

A final teaching of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: *lo yisa adam et isha v'daato l'garsha* — a man should not marry a woman — or remain married to and cohabit with a woman — while planning to divorce her. *Mishum shene'emar: al tachrosh al re'acha ra'a v'hu yoshev lavetach itach* — as it is said, "Do not plot evil against your neighbor while he dwells in security with you." The treachery of a man who continues to enjoy the benefits of marriage — the companionship, the intimacy, the shared life — while privately planning to end it, without any transparency toward his wife, is a fundamental betrayal of trust. The verse addresses the corruption of such deceptive planning and demands that one not weaponize another person's confidence.

---

## Inheritance Dispute

### Safek vs Yavam

The Gemara now turns to the property implications of the uncertain paternity case. The child of unknown paternity — let us call him Gershon — and the *yavam* (let us call him Shimon) come to divide the estate of the deceased first husband (Reuven). Gershon claims: *ana bar mitna hu, v'nichsei didi hu* — I am Reuven's son, and the entire estate is mine. Shimon the *yavam* claims: *at beri didi at, v'leit lach v'lo midi b'nichsei* — you are my son, and you have no share in Reuven's estate. Both claims are entirely dependent on the unresolvable question of paternity; neither party has *chazakah* — prior possession — of the property, since Reuven held it and both Gershon and Shimon are claiming from Reuven's estate equally. This is *mamon hamutal b'safek* — money in doubtful ownership — and the rule is *cholkin*, they divide.

### Safek vs Sons

A second scenario: suppose Shimon himself has since died, leaving his own sons — Kehat and Merari. Now Gershon comes to divide Reuven's estate not with Shimon but with Shimon's sons. Gershon claims the entire estate as Reuven's son; Shimon's sons claim that Gershon is their brother, Shimon inherited Reuven's estate through valid *yibbum*, Shimon subsequently died, and therefore the three of them — Gershon, Kehat, and Merari — should divide it equally, with each getting a third.

### Mishnah Parallel

The Rabbis before Rav Mesharsheya thought to apply the principle of a different Mishnah: *hu eino yoresh otam v'hem yorshim oto* — he does not inherit them but they inherit him. That Mishnah involves a child of unknown paternity — say, the son of either Yehuda or Barak — who comes to claim a portion of Yehuda's estate. Yehuda's children say: you are Barak's son, go claim from him. He goes to Barak's children and they say: you are Yehuda's son, go claim from him. Each party deflects him to the other, *ayti ra'aya u'shkol* — bring proof and collect. Since he cannot prove his case, he collects nothing from either side. But when he dies, both families inherit from him, since each is a possible sibling. By analogy, the Rabbis suggested, Gershon should likewise get nothing — they will each tell him to prove his case, and he cannot.

### Both Parties Doubtful

Rav Mesharsheya rejects this comparison: *mi dami?* — the cases are not comparable. *Hatam inhu vaday v'ihu safek* — in the Mishnah case, each family he approaches has a definite, unquestionable claim as legitimate children of their father, and he alone has the uncertain claim. They are *vaday*; he is *safek*. They can therefore say: *ayti ra'aya* — you want from us, prove you belong. *Hacha idi v'idi safek* — here, however, all parties are in some sense doubtful. Gershon's claim is uncertain, but so is the claim of Shimon's sons, since they can only inherit Reuven's estate through Shimon's *yibbum*, and that *yibbum* is only valid if Gershon is not Reuven's son. Rav Mesharsheya adds — and Rashi amplifies this — that Gershon's claim, even if he is certain to have some stake in the property, rests on an uncertain basis: he cannot say whether he holds it as Reuven's son or as Shimon's son. The entirety of his claim is without a definite legal foundation, unlike the *vaday* claimants in the Mishnah case.

Rav Mesharsheya then notes what the present scenario actually does resemble: *l'safek u'vnei yavam sheba'u lachloke b'nichsei yavam gufei* — it resembles a case where Gershon and Shimon's sons come to divide *Shimon*'s estate, not Reuven's. There, Gershon claims to be their brother and demands a portion of their father Shimon's estate. They respond: *ayti ra'aya de'achuna at u'shkol* — prove you are our brother and collect. Since Gershon cannot prove paternity, he gets nothing from Shimon's estate, exactly parallel to the Mishnah.

### Rashi's Solution

For the original question — Gershon and Shimon's sons dividing Reuven's estate — Rashi proposes the following resolution. *Venireh be'einai, dehu mantsa dekamodu leh shakil* — the portion that all parties concede Gershon is entitled to, he takes outright. Since both Gershon and Shimon's sons would concede that Gershon holds at least a one-third share (Shimon's sons' own claim is that Gershon gets a third as a co-heir; Gershon claims the whole), that one-third is undisputed and goes directly to Gershon. *Ve'idach havei mamon hamutal besafek vecholkin* — the remaining two-thirds are in genuine dispute: Gershon claims all of it, Shimon's sons claim all of it as their father's inheritance. That disputed portion is divided equally, with Gershon receiving half and Shimon's sons receiving half between them. The practical result: Gershon receives the undisputed third plus half of the disputed two-thirds, giving him two-thirds of the total estate, while Shimon's sons together receive the remaining third.

---

---

# Yevamot 38

## Safek Veyavam

### Gershon vs. Shimon

The *gemara* opens at the top of 38a with the case of *safek veyavam* — a doubtful son and a *yavam* — who come to divide the inheritance of their grandfather Yaakov. The scenario is as follows. Yaakov owns a field. Gershon claims to be the son of Reuven, who has died, and on that basis demands half the field. Shimon, the *yavam*, is still alive, and his position is straightforward: Gershon is my son, not Reuven's, and therefore you have no claim to anything while I am living — the entire field is mine.

The *gemara* frames the competing claims in its own terms. Gershon declares, *hai gavra bar mitna hu u-palga didi hu* — I am the son of the deceased and half the field is mine. Shimon responds, *at bera didi at v-lo shayech lach v-lo midi* — you are my son and you have no portion in that field whatsoever.
