### Safek Motzi Rule

The *gemara* resolves this with a clean application of the principle *ein safek motzi mi-yedei vadai* — a doubtful claim cannot displace a certain one. Shimon has a definite claim: he is unquestionably an heir to this field, whether he takes half or the whole, his status as heir is certain. Gershon's claim, whatever he may assert with confidence, is in reality a *safek* — he is possibly an heir. Since one party has a definite standing and the other only a doubtful one, we apply *ha-motzi me-chaveiro alav ha-re'aya* and Shimon takes the entire field.

### Three-Way Division

The *gemara* then proceeds to *safek u-vnei yavam sheba'u lachlok bi-nichsei sabba* — the case where Shimon has died, and now Gershon is disputing with Shimon's sons Kehat and Merari over Yaakov's field. Gershon again claims to be Reuven's son and demands half. Kehat and Merari counter: you are our brother, *achuna*, and you take an equal share alongside us.

### Concessions Logic

Here the analysis turns on mutual concessions. Gershon concedes that the other half belongs to Kehat and Merari — his claim is only to his half. They in turn concede a third of the entire field to him — they acknowledge he is at least a brother entitled to a third. So each side has conceded something. Half and a third together account for five sixths of the field, leaving one sixth in dispute. About this remaining sixth, no one has a stronger claim than the other, and the rule is *havei mamon hamutal b'safek v-cholkin* — when money rests in genuine doubt, we divide it. So the contested sixth is split, giving Kehat and Merari together a half plus a twelfth — that is, seven twelfths — while Gershon receives a third plus a twelfth, which is five twelfths.

### Yaakov & Shimon

The *gemara* then considers the inverse scenario: *sabba v-yavam b-nichsei safek* — what happens when Gershon himself dies. Now Yaakov the grandfather and Shimon the *yavam* are both alive and both want to inherit Gershon's estate. Recall that Gershon had received half of Reuven's property. Shimon argues that Gershon was like his son and he therefore inherits from him. Yaakov argues that Gershon was Reuven's son, and since Reuven is gone, the inheritance flows back up to him. Neither claim is stronger than the other. And the parallel case — *sabba v-safek b-nichsei yavam* — arises when Shimon dies without Kehat and Merari yet in the picture: Gershon claims Shimon was his father, while Yaakov claims Reuven was Gershon's father and that Shimon's estate should come to him. In both configurations the *gemara* concludes: *havei mamon hamutal b'safek v-cholkin* — each side presents a claim without decisive advantage, and the property is divided.

---

## Shomeret Yavam

### Nafal Nechasim

The *gemara* turns to the *mishna* on *shomeret yavam* — a woman waiting for *yibbum* or *chalitzah* after her husband Reuven has died, while Shimon stands as the *yavam*. The question is: if she inherits property during this period of waiting — *naflo lah nechasim* — what is the *halacha* governing that property?

### Nechsei Milog

To understand the stakes, one must recall the framework of *nechsei milog*: property to which a wife holds title, while the husband enjoys the *peirot*, the usufruct. The principle of *kinyan peirot k'kinyan haguf* — that the right to the fruit is treated like ownership of the body of the asset itself — means that a husband's right to *peirot* is substantial. The question for the *shomeret yavam* is whether the *zika*, the bond tying her to Shimon, is strong enough to confer upon him the rights of a husband over her property. If the *zika* effectively makes her like his wife, he would be entitled to the *peirot*. If it does not, the property remains fully in her domain.

### Buying & Selling

The *mishna* opens with a ruling on which Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree: *modim Beit Shammai u-Veit Hillel she-mocheres u-nosenet v-kayam* — she may sell, give gifts, and transact with the property, and it all stands. This is itself a *chiddush*: not only does Shimon have no claim to the *peirot*, he lacks even the standing to block her sale of the principal. In this state, Shimon is entirely out of the picture — she holds the property freely, and the *zika* confers upon him no effective right.

### Upon Her Death

The *mishna* then asks: *meisa — ma ya'aseh bi-kesuvatah u-vi-nechasim ha-nichnasim v-yotzim imah* — if she dies, what becomes of her *kesubah* and the property she carried in and out? Two competing claimants emerge. Lavan, her father, argues that the property was hers, she died without heirs in the relevant sense, and it therefore reverts to him. Shimon argues that she was in some sense his wife, and though he may not have had rights to the property while she was alive, upon her death he ought to inherit.

The *kesubah* requires a word of clarification. When Reuven died, Rachel became entitled to collect her two hundred *zuz*. However, if Shimon performs *yibbum*, the marriage to Reuven is treated as continuing — it is not a new marriage — and she does not collect. The *kesubah* becomes collectable only if Shimon performs *chalitzah*, releasing her from the bond. So the question of who controls the uncollected *kesubah* is bound up with Shimon's ambiguous standing: if Shimon stands in Reuven's place, the *kesubah* has not yet been released and remains within Shimon's estate; if the *zika* relationship is not considered a genuine marriage, her claim against it is doubtful. One might also observe — and this point was raised in the course of study — that since this is a continuation of her *kesubah* against Reuven rather than a fresh obligation from Shimon, the amount remains two hundred *zuz* rather than one hundred, reflecting that this is not treated as the *kesubah* of a widow marrying anew, but as the original obligation carrying forward.

### Shammai Divide

Beit Shammai rules *yachloku yoresh ha-ba'al v-yoresh ha-av* — the husband's heirs and the father's heirs divide. Beit Hillel rules *nechasim b'chezkasan* — the property remains in its *chazakah*, its presumptive status. The underlying conceptual question is whether we apply *mamon hamutal b'safek cholkin* — disputed assets are split — or whether we follow *chazakah* and leave things where they stood.

Beit Hillel elaborates: the *kesubah* is *b'chezkat yorshei ha-ba'al* — it was never collected, it remained under Shimon's control, so it stays there. The *nechasim ha-nichnasim v-yotzim imah* — the property she carried — is *b'chezkat yorshei ha-av*, for it never entered Shimon's domain. She received it, held it, and controlled it throughout; it rightfully passes to her heirs. Beit Hillel's position is thus internally coherent: follow the *chazakah* in each case, and each category of property flows to the party who definitively held it. Beit Shammai, by contrast, holds that since Shimon's status is genuinely uncertain — he may or may not be treated as a husband — we treat this as a *safek* and divide.

### Arusa vs. Nesua

The *gemara* now asks: *mai shna reisha de-lo paligei u-mai shna seifa de-paligei* — why does Beit Shammai agree completely in the first case, where she is alive and in full control, yet contest the property in the second case after she dies? If Shimon has a doubtful claim as quasi-husband, why does that claim not surface while she is alive?

Ulla answers by introducing a distinction not stated explicitly in the *mishna*: *reisha d'nafla k'shehi arusa* — the first case is where she fell to *yibbum* having been an *arusa* to Reuven; *seifa d'nafla k'shehi nesua* — the second case is where she had been a *nesua*. Ulla holds *zikas arusa osa safek arusa* — the *zika* that derives from an *eirusin* relationship produces a doubtful *arusa* status for Shimon — and *zikas nesua osa safek nesua* — the *zika* that derives from a *nisuin* relationship produces a doubtful *nesua* status. Since a husband in an *eirusin* has no right to *peirot* in the first place, even a certain *eirusin* status would give Shimon no claim to the property. Hence in the *arusa* case, Beit Shammai fully concedes that she controls the property. But in the *nesua* case, the transferred *zika* creates at least a doubtful *nesua* bond, and upon her death Shimon can press a claim.

The *gemara* supplies the proofs. How do we know *zikas arusa osa safek arusa* and not *vadai arusa*? Because a *mishna* elsewhere teaches that if a woman received property *after* she became a regular (non-*yibbum*) *arusa*, Beit Hillel holds she may not sell it *l'chatchila*, even though *b'dieved* the sale stands. Yet here, the *shomeret yavam* may sell *l'chatchila*. This can only be because her *arusa* status through *zika* is merely a *safek*, and the weaker doubtful status does not even prohibit her from selling outright. Similarly, how do we know *zikas nesua osa safek nesua* and not *vadai nesua*? Because a *mishna* elsewhere teaches that if a woman received property after she became a *nesua*, both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that if she sold it the husband can reclaim it from the buyers — the husband is fully in control. Yet here, when she dies, Beit Shammai says only to split the property, not to award it entirely to Shimon. This confirms his status is only a *safek nesua*, not *vadai*: a *vadai* husband would take everything; since he takes only half, the *zika* must have produced only *safek nesua* standing.

### Rava Challenge

Rava challenges Ulla's construction directly: *atu mafalgi b'gufa v-le'achar mita* — is the *mishna* really discussing the body of the property and what happens after her death merely as a vehicle for distinguishing *arusa* from *nesua*? If that were the operative distinction, *liflug b'chayeha u-l'peirot* — the *mishna* should simply have discussed what happens to the *peirot* while she is alive, and distinguished between the two relationships there. Why does the *mishna* shift entirely to a case where she has died? Ulla's reading requires us to say that the difference between case one and case two has nothing to do with whether she is alive or dead — but the *mishna* plainly presents that as the pivotal distinction. Rava's objection is that you cannot explain away the *mishna*'s own structure.

### Title vs. Fruit

Rava therefore offers his own resolution: *eidi v'eidi d'nafla k'shehi nesua* — both cases of the *mishna* concern a woman who had been a *nesua* to Reuven. In both cases, *zikas nesua osa safek nesua*, and Shimon has a doubtful *nesua* claim throughout. So why does Beit Shammai concede that she controls the property while alive?

The answer is elegant and turns on a precise analysis of what is being claimed in each scenario. When she is alive: *reisha d'hee kayma, havya lah hee vadai v'ihu safek* — she is a *vadai* and he is a *safek*. She is the definite holder of *title* to the property — that is unquestioned even in *nechsei milog*. Shimon's claim is only to the *peirot*, the usufruct, and even that claim is doubtful because it depends on whether the *zika* is treated as a genuine *nisuin*. She says: I definitively own the land; you have a doubtful claim to the fruit. *V'ein safek motzi mi-yedei vadai* — a doubtful claim cannot displace a certain one. Therefore, Beit Shammai fully concedes while she is alive: her *vadai* title overrides his *safek* claim to *peirot*.

When she dies, the situation fundamentally changes. Now the debate is no longer about *peirot* but about the *title* itself — who inherits the principal. At that point, both Shimon and Lavan are coming to claim ownership. She is no longer present to assert her *vadai* title. Both claimants arrive with uncertain standing: Shimon may have been her husband, Lavan is her father. This is *mamon hamutal b'safek*, and Beit Shammai says *yachloku* — divide it.

### Abaye Question

Abaye presses a challenge: *u-l'Veit Shammai ein safek motzi mi-yedei vadai*? Does Beit Shammai truly hold that a *safek* cannot displace a *vadai*? The following *mishna* seems to present a counterexample.

### House Collapse

*Nafal ha-bayit alav v'al aviv* — a house collapsed on Reuven and his father Yaakov simultaneously, and it is unknown who died first. Reuven had creditors — a wife's *kesubah* or other debts. The *yorshim*, the heirs, argue that Reuven died first and then Yaakov, so the property never passed through Reuven and the creditors have no lien. The *ba'alei chov*, the creditors, argue that Yaakov died first, Reuven inherited from Yaakov, and the creditors acquired a lien on that inherited property before Reuven himself died. Beit Shammai rules *yachloku* — divide the contested property. Beit Hillel rules *nechasim b'chezkasam* — maintain the *chazakah*, which in this case favors the heirs, since the property was definitively under Yaakov's control and the creditors are outside claimants.

The *gemara* notes the apparent contradiction: *v'hacha yorshim vadai u-ba'alei chov safek* — the heirs have definite standing and the creditors have a doubtful claim. Yet Beit Shammai says divide! If Beit Shammai holds *ein safek motzi mi-yedei vadai*, why does a *safek* creditor get to press a claim against the *vadai* heirs?

### Shtar Rights

The *gemara* resolves this with an important principle: *kasvari Veit Shammai shtar ha'omed ligvos k'gavuy dami* — Beit Shammai holds that an outstanding *shtar*, a written debt instrument, is treated as though it has already been collected. This is what distinguishes the creditor case from the *shomeret yavam* case. Normally, one might conceptualize the creditor's situation as follows: the heirs inherit, and then the creditors come as outsiders attempting to take the property away — in which case the creditors would indeed be a *safek* pressing against the heirs' *vadai*, and *ein safek motzi mi-yedei vadai* would apply. But Beit Shammai does not conceptualize it that way. Because the creditors hold a *shtar*, their claim is treated as already realized — *k'gavuy dami*. When the heirs and the creditors present themselves before *beit din*, neither party is an outsider pressing against the other's established *chazakah*. Both stand at the same level, and since the facts are in doubt, you divide.

By contrast, in the *shomeret yavam* case while she is alive, Shimon holds no *shtar*. He has a doubtful claim to *peirot*, nothing more. She holds definite title. There is no instrument that elevates his standing to equal hers, and so *ein safek motzi mi-yedei vadai* applies in full force — he cannot press his doubtful claim against her certain ownership.

---

---

# Yevamot 39

## Shomeret Yavam Property

### Rachel's Property Status

Today's daf is 39, and we pick up in the middle of 38b. The *gemara* is engaged with the cases presented in the *mishnah*, where a woman — call her Rachel — is a *shomeret yavam*, waiting for her brother-in-law Shimon to either perform *yibum* or *chalitzah*. During this period, Rachel inherits property, which functions in the manner of *nichsei milug*: she holds title, and were she fully married, her husband would be entitled to the *peirot*. The *mishnah* establishes that while Rachel is alive, she has full control — she may buy and sell freely — and both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree to this. The dispute arises only when she dies, at which point there is a question of who inherits: Lavan, her father, or Shimon, the *yavam*.

### Safek vs. Vadai

The question the *gemara* presses is this: if Beit Shammai holds that upon Rachel's death the estate is split between Shimon and Lavan — a ruling that appears to reflect Shimon's *safek* claim of quasi-marital status through *zika*, a doubtful *nisuin* — why does Shimon receive nothing while Rachel is alive? His potential entitlement to *peirot* exists regardless of whether she is alive or dead, yet during her lifetime Beit Shammai concedes entirely to her position. Why does his *safek* claim not entitle him to at least something?

### Ein Safek Motzi

The *gemara* resolves this by invoking the principle of *ein safek motzi midei vadai*: an uncertain claim cannot displace a certain one. While Rachel lives, she unquestionably holds title. Shimon's claim — whether or not *zika* gives him a quasi-marital status that would entitle him to *peirot* — is at most a *safek*. Since she is a *vadai* possessor of the property, even Beit Shammai concedes that his *safek* cannot dislodge her. When she dies, however, the question of who holds title to the estate becomes genuinely open, and that is where Beit Shammai says to divide.

### House Collapse Case

A difficulty arises, however, from another ruling associated with Beit Shammai: the case of a house collapsing on a minor and his father, where the question is whether creditors may claim a portion of the estate alongside the heirs. There, Beit Shammai appears to say that we divide despite someone being in presumptive possession — which would seem to contradict the principle just established, that a *safek* cannot displace a *vadai*.

### Shtar Ligvot Doctrine

The *gemara* resolves this by explaining that Beit Shammai holds *shtar ha-omed ligvot k'gavuy dami* — a document whose time for collection has arrived is treated as though collection has already taken place. In that case, therefore, it is not a matter of the creditors' *safek* claim attempting to extract money from heirs who are *vadai* possessors. Because the debt instrument was ripe for collection, both parties stand in an equal posture of possession. Neither party is more *muchzak* than the other. The two doctrines thus operate in tandem: Beit Shammai accepts *ein safek motzi midei vadai* as a general principle, but carves out an exception when the *safek* claimant holds a mature *shtar*, which grants them a co-equal standing rather than the position of an outsider.

---

## Sotah & Ketubah

### Sotah Mishnah

The *gemara* now asks: from where do we know that Beit Shammai holds *shtar ha-omed ligvot k'gavuy dami*? It cites the *mishnah* in the laws of *sotah*: a woman who was warned by her husband and secluded with another man, and who therefore must drink the *sotah* waters — if her husband dies before she is able to drink, what is the status of her *ketubah*? The *mishnah* records a dispute. Beit Shammai says: *notlot ketuvatam ve-ein shosot* — they collect their *ketubah* in full. Beit Hillel says: *o shosot o lo notlot ketuvatam* — either they drink, or they do not collect. The *gemara* clarifies that Beit Hillel cannot literally mean they should drink, since the verse states the husband must bring his wife to drink — and if the husband is dead, that is impossible. Rather, Beit Hillel means: *mitoch she-lo shosot, lo notlot ketuvatam* — since they cannot drink, they cannot collect.

### Sotah Safek Status

The *sotah*'s status is genuinely doubtful. She may have committed adultery, or she may not have — that is precisely why the entire *sotah* procedure exists. Her *ketubah* entitlement is therefore a *safek*. The heirs of the deceased husband, meanwhile, are in presumptive possession of the estate. A woman coming to collect her *ketubah* is, in the ordinary framing, a creditor seeking to extract money from people who hold title. Beit Hillel's position is therefore perfectly consistent with *ein safek motzi midei vadai*: her doubtful right cannot override the heirs' certain possession, so she collects nothing. Beit Shammai's position, however, requires explanation. Why does he allow collection despite her *safek* status?

### Shtar Proves Doctrine

The *gemara* answers: *shma mina shtar ha-omed ligvot k'gavuy dami*. A *ketubah* is a *shtar* — a legal instrument — and since it was ripe for collection at the moment of the husband's death, it is treated as though collection has already occurred. The *sotah* is not to be understood as a *safek* claimant reaching into the heirs' certain possession. Rather, both she and the heirs stand in an equal posture: her *ketubah* instrument grants her standing co-equal to the heirs, not subordinate to them. This is why Beit Shammai allows collection.

A further subtlety demands attention here. In the house collapse case, Beit Shammai splits the disputed property between the heirs and the creditors. But in the *sotah* case, Beit Shammai allows the woman to collect the *entire* *ketubah*, not merely half. Why the asymmetry?

Several distinctions apply. In the house collapse case, there is a pure epistemic vacuum: no one knows in which order the deaths occurred, and neither party has any prior claim to certainty. In the *sotah* case, the heirs are asserting that she committed adultery, but they have no actual knowledge of this — she, by contrast, is in a position to know whether she was faithful and is asserting her entitlement from a position of personal knowledge. Beyond that, the *ketubah* debt pre-existed in a fully established form: at an earlier point she was unquestionably entitled to it. That certain, prior entitlement distinguishes her claim from that of a creditor in the collapse case, where one cannot say the debt obligation ever attached beyond doubt. These distinctions must be worked through on a case-by-case basis, but the governing principle is clear: when both parties hold equal standing by virtue of the *shtar* doctrine, it is not a case of *safek motzi midei vadai*, and the particulars of each situation determine whether one party collects entirely or the two divide.

### Why House Case?

One might ask: given that the *sotah* case also demonstrates Beit Shammai's position on *shtar ha-omed ligvot k'gavuy dami*, why did the *gemara* not derive the principle from there in the first place? Since we are already in the legal domain of women and *ketubot*, why was it necessary to invoke the case of a collapsing house?

### Chinah Exception

The *gemara* answers: *dilma kesuvas isha shani mishum china*. One cannot necessarily generalize from the *ketubah* to all *shtarot*, because the Rabbis may have accorded special legal strength to a woman's *ketubah* that they would not extend to an ordinary debt instrument. The reason is *china* — a concept of attractiveness or desirability, reflecting the Rabbis' interest in strengthening the *ketubah*'s enforceability in order to make marriage an attractive and secure institution for women. Since the *ketubah* might occupy a uniquely privileged category, one cannot draw a general rule from it about *shtarot* as a whole. The case of the collapsing house, by contrast, involves ordinary creditors and ordinary debt instruments, making it the proper vehicle for establishing the general principle. And there, the answer is that a ripe *shtar* of any kind grants co-equal standing — not merely a *ketubah*.

---

## Ketubah Split Debate

### Mishnah Silence

With the framework of Beit Shammai's positions now established, the *gemara* turns to a tension internal to the *mishnah* itself. The *mishnah* addresses the scenario in which Rachel dies as a *shomeret yavam*, and it raises the question: *mah ya'aseh biktuvatah u-va-nekhasim ha-nikhnasim ve-ha-yotzim imah* — what should be done with her *ketubah* and with her property? The focus of the preceding discussion has been on the *nekhasim* — the *nichsei milug* — and the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel over how to divide that estate. But what about the *ketubah* — the 200 *zuz* Rachel held against Reuven, which by operation of *yibum* now effectively rests against Shimon's estate? The *mishnah* appears to say that Beit Shammai divides everything down the middle. Yet if Shimon is clearly *muchzak* in the estate he inherited from Reuven, why would Beit Shammai say that a *safek* claim to the *ketubah* can extract any portion from him?

### Rava's Reading

Rava resolves this by offering a bold re-reading of the *mishnah*: *lo palig* — Beit Shammai does not in fact disagree regarding the *ketubah*. Beit Shammai concedes that Shimon retains the *ketubah* money in full. The *mishnah*'s question — *mah ya'aseh biktuvatah* — is not answered by the subsequent ruling; it stands as an unanswered question, followed by a period. What follows — *nekhasim ha-nikhnasim ve-ha-yotzim imah* — is a separate statement about the property alone, and it is only regarding the property that Beit Shammai says *yachloku*. The *mishnah*, on this reading, rules explicitly only on the *nekhasim*, leaving the *ketubah* without a stated ruling from Beit Shammai — because Beit Shammai concedes the *ketubah* to Shimon entirely. This is admittedly a strained reading of the *mishnah*, and the *gemara* acknowledges as much, but it then attempts to find support from the *mishnah*'s own language.

### Language Proof

Rav Ashi observes that the *mishnah*'s language can itself be read as supporting this interpretation. The *mishnah* says *yachloku yorshei ha-ba'al im yorshei ha-av* — the heirs of the husband come and divide with the heirs of the father. The framing is that the husband's heirs — Shimon's side — are the ones who come to divide *with* the father's heirs. This implies that the father's family is already in possession, and Shimon is entitled to come and take his portion from them. That formulation naturally describes the *nekhasim*, where the father's family holds the default position. Had the *mishnah* also intended to address the *ketubah*, the language would have been reversed: the father's heirs come and take their portion from the husband's estate. Since the language is oriented in only one direction, it appears that only the *nekhasim* are being discussed, and the *ketubah* was never part of Beit Shammai's ruling of *yachloku* at all.

### Conclusion Admits

The upshot of Rava's analysis is that Beit Shammai is in full agreement with *ein safek motzi midei vadai* across the board. Beit Shammai concedes that when Rachel is alive, her certain possession of the *nichsei milug* cannot be overridden by Shimon's *safek* claim to *peirot*. And Beit Shammai likewise concedes that when Rachel dies, Shimon's certain possession of the estate cannot be disturbed by a *safek* claim to the *ketubah* on behalf of her heirs. The dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel concerns only the *nichsei milug* upon Rachel's death, where the question of title itself becomes genuinely uncertain — and there Beit Shammai says to divide, because at that point neither side is more *vadai* than the other.

---

## Abaye's Timing

### When Inherited

Abaye offers an alternative explanation of the *mishnah* that shifts the axis of analysis entirely. Rather than locating the critical variable in whether Rachel is alive or dead, Abaye proposes that the real distinction is *when* she came to own the property. The *reisha* of the *mishnah* — the case in which Beit Shammai agrees that Rachel retains full control — concerns property that fell to Rachel *after* Reuven had already died, that is, while she was already a *shomeret yavam*. The *seifa* — the case in which Beit Shammai says to divide — concerns property that fell to Rachel *while she was still married to Reuven*.

### Ownership Strength

This distinction carries significant legal weight. When Rachel inherits property after Reuven's death, there is no real husband in the picture. Her *zika* to Shimon is at most a quasi-relationship. In this posture, Rachel establishes herself as the undisputed, uncompromised owner of the property. Her title is clean. Shimon's quasi-claim through *zika* is not strong enough to cloud what is, in effect, sole ownership. Beit Shammai therefore concedes she retains full control — while she lives, and presumably also in terms of her family's inheritance claim.

When, however, Rachel acquired the property while she was still married to Reuven, the situation is fundamentally different. At that moment, Reuven — as her real, full husband — had a recognized and substantial position in the property by virtue of his entitlement to *peirot*, which carries a quasi-proprietary character (*k'kinyan haguf*). Her title was never clean in the way it is in the first case; from the moment of acquisition, she and Reuven stood in a kind of co-ownership. When Reuven dies and Shimon steps in through *zika*, Shimon steps into a relationship with property that never belonged exclusively to Rachel. Since she never fully established herself as sole owner, Shimon's position — though weaker than Reuven's had been — is sufficient to generate a genuine dispute, and Beit Shammai therefore says to divide.

### Co-Equal Partner

A key question in Abaye's framework is precisely how to characterize the shift from Reuven's position to Shimon's. If Reuven had a strong position in the property — and his entitlement to *peirot* gives him at least a quasi-proprietary claim — and Shimon's position through *zika* is admittedly weaker, then why does Shimon's weaker position suffice to generate a *yachloku*? Abaye's answer is that while Shimon's claim is indeed weaker than Reuven's was, the key point is that Rachel's title had already been compromised before Reuven's death. She never fully owned the property in an unencumbered sense. When Reuven leaves the picture and Shimon enters at a somewhat lower level of entitlement, the result is that Shimon's claim and Rachel's claim are now roughly co-equal — neither clearly superior — which is precisely the condition under which Beit Shammai says *yachloku*.

Beit Hillel disagrees with this analysis. Beit Hillel holds that Reuven's position in the property, though significant, was co-equal to Rachel's rather than superior. Under that view, when Reuven dies and Shimon steps in at the lower level of *zika*, Rachel's title effectively reasserts itself as the dominant one, and it is her heirs — Lavan's family — who receive the property. The dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, on Abaye's reading, thus turns on whether a husband's position in his wife's *nichsei milug* is stronger than, or merely equal to, hers.

### Yadav Keyidah

Abaye's formulation of Beit Hillel's position invokes the phrase *yado k'yidah* — his hand is as her hand, meaning the husband and wife occupy equal positions in relation to the property. It is precisely because Beit Hillel holds *yado k'yidah* that they do not say *yachloku* in the *seifa*. When Reuven — who was merely co-equal — exits the picture, and Shimon — who is at the still-lower level of *zika* — enters, Rachel's position is now unambiguously superior, and Beit Hillel therefore awards the property to her family.

---

## Rava's Rejoinder

### Husband Stronger

Rava now engages with Abaye's framework, accepting the basic structural insight — that the timing of Rachel's acquisition is the relevant variable — but disagreeing sharply on the characterization of the husband's position. Rava holds that there is no debate: *dechulei alma lo pligi deyado adifa miyidah* — everyone agrees that the husband's position in *nichsei milug* property is stronger than the wife's, not merely equal. The husband's entitlement to *peirot*, understood at the level of *kinyan ha-guf* or reinforced by rabbinic enactment, makes him the senior property partner. This is not a disputed premise; it is a baseline legal reality that even Beit Hillel would accept.

If this is true, then Abaye's proposed distinction between the two cases — one where she inherited while a *shomeret yavam* versus one where she inherited while fully married — would actually yield the wrong result for Beit Hillel. If the husband was the senior partner and Shimon steps in at a co-equal level, even Beit Hillel ought to say *yachloku*. There would be no case in which Beit Hillel grants Rachel's family the full property under Abaye's framework.

### Maamar Difference

Rava therefore proposes a different variable to distinguish the *reisha* from the *seifa*: whether or not Shimon performed *maamar* with Rachel. The *reisha* — where Beit Shammai concedes that Rachel retains full control, and by extension that Lavan retains the estate upon her death — is the case in which no *maamar* was performed. In this scenario, Shimon's connection to Rachel remains at the level of *zika* alone — a purely halakhic, quasi-marital bond that is real but limited. Beit Shammai concedes that this is insufficient to generate a competing claim to the property while Rachel lives, and that upon her death her family takes the estate.

The *seifa* — where Beit Shammai says *yachloku* — is the case in which Shimon did perform *maamar*. The *maamar* introduces a new and significant factor, elevating Shimon's relationship with Rachel beyond the baseline *zika*.

### Maamar Effect

According to Rava, *maamar* for Beit Shammai accomplishes the following: *oseh vaday arusah ve-safek nisu'ah* — it renders Rachel a definite *arusah* and a doubtful *nisu'ah* vis-à-vis Shimon. The status of definite *arusah* has implications for *erva* and *tzarat erva* cases — it is enough to push away co-wives in the context of *yibum* eligibility. But the status of *safek nisu'ah* has implications for property: as a doubtful *nisu'ah*, Shimon acquires a *safek* claim to the *nichsei milug*. When Rachel then dies, her family's claim to the property is a *vadai* in one sense, but Shimon's *safek nisu'ah* status generates a competing claim that is not simply a *safek* coming to displace a *vadai* from the outside. Rather, both claims are now of a character that justifies division — and Beit Shammai accordingly says *yachloku*.

---

## Maamar Dispute

### Attribution

The *gemara* notes that the two *amoraim* of the earlier generation map onto the positions of Rava and Abaye: the tradition in the name of Rabbi Elazar follows Rava's position, while the tradition in the name of Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Chanina follows Abaye's position.

### Challenge

A challenge is immediately raised against the attribution to Rabbi Elazar: did Rabbi Elazar not himself say that *maamar* for Beit Shammai only operates *lidchos b'tzarah bilvad* — that its sole halakhic effect is to push away co-wives in the context of *erva* and *tzarat erva*, implying that it has no relevance to property claims? If so, how can Rabbi Elazar be aligned with Rava, who holds that *maamar* generates a *safek nisu'ah* status with direct property implications?

### Clarification

The *gemara* resolves this apparent contradiction by clarifying what Rabbi Elazar's statement actually meant. Rabbi Elazar can maintain that *maamar* creates both an *arusa* status and a *safek nisu'ah* status — including for property purposes — consistent with Rava's position. What his earlier statement was saying is something different: that *maamar* does not fully replace the woman's status as a *yevamah*. Even after *maamar*, she remains in some sense a *shomeret yavam*, and therefore if Shimon subsequently wishes to separate from her, a *get* alone is insufficient — *chalitzah* is also required. The *chiddush* of Beit Shammai on Rabbi Elazar's account is not that *maamar* is legally weak, but rather that it adds a layer of status without eliminating the pre-existing *yevamah* relationship. Shimon has done *kiddushin* through *maamar*, and she may even acquire a quasi-*nisu'ah* status for monetary purposes — but since *yibum* was never performed, the *yevamah* relationship remains simultaneously in force, and *chalitzah* is still needed to sever it. Both statuses coexist; *maamar* adds without displacing.

---

## Mishnah Language

### Rav Papa Proof

Rav Papa now offers linguistic support from the *mishnah* itself for Abaye's reading. The *mishnah* refers to the disputed property as *nekhasim ha-nikhnasim ve-ha-yotzim imah* — property that "comes in and goes out with her." This phrase demands explanation: where is this property going? Rav Papa argues that it must mean: property that entered into the domain of the husband — *nikhnasim le-reshut ha-ba'al* — and went out with her from the husband's domain — *yotzim mi-reshut ha-ba'al le-reshut ha-av* — at his death. In other words, the *mishnah* is describing property that Rachel acquired *while she was married to Reuven*, such that it entered into the marital estate and then reverted when Reuven died. This phrasing appears only in the *seifa* of the *mishnah*, and Rav Papa argues that it therefore indicates that the *seifa* is specifically discussing property acquired during the marriage to Reuven — precisely the scenario Abaye identified as the relevant distinction.

### Death Emphasis

This support is real, but a difficulty remains. The plain reading of the *mishnah* structures its two cases around whether Rachel is alive or dead: in the *reisha* she is alive, in the *seifa* she is dead and they are dividing the estate. If, as Abaye holds, the real distinction is when she acquired the property rather than whether she is alive or dead, why does the *mishnah* frame the *seifa* around her death at all? One could have discussed the implications of having acquired property during the marriage even while Rachel is still alive — for instance, in terms of *peirot* rights. The fact that the *mishnah* introduces the case by telling us she died and asks what to do with the estate suggests, on its face, that the critical variable is her death, not the timing of acquisition.

### Support Despite

Despite this problem, the *gemara* concludes that the linguistic evidence from *nikhnasim ve-ha-yotzim imah* lends meaningful support to Abaye's reading. Rashi's comment at this point is precise: *ein lahashiv al kach, devadai dika kavatei, ve-kashya le-meiti* — there is nothing to refute the linguistic support for Abaye, yet the emphasis on death in the *seifa* remains a genuine difficulty against him. The *mishnah* thus offers simultaneous support and challenge to Abaye's framework, and the *gemara* leaves the matter with a *ve-tulo midai*, noting that there is nothing more to resolve the tension definitively.

---

## After Yibum

### Full Wife

The *mishnah* now addresses what happens after Shimon performs *yibum* with Rachel. The ruling is straightforward in principle: once *yibum* is accomplished, Rachel becomes Shimon's full wife in every respect.

### Get Divorce

The first practical consequence is that if Shimon subsequently wishes to separate from Rachel, he must give her a *get*. The mechanism of *chalitzah* — which was the operative mode of separation while Rachel was a *yevamah* — is no longer available or relevant. She is no longer a *yevamah*; she is simply a wife.

### Remarry

The second consequence is that if Shimon divorces Rachel and she subsequently marries another man and is widowed or divorced from him, Shimon may remarry Rachel through ordinary *kiddushin*. The relationship has been entirely normalized.

### Challenge

The *gemara* challenges the apparent obviousness of the first ruling. Surely it goes without saying that after *yibum* one gives a *get* rather than performs *chalitzah*? The *gemara* responds that this needed to be stated. One might have thought — *salka de-atach amina* — that since the Torah says "take her for a wife and perform *yibum*," the act of *yibum* initiates the relationship but does not fully extinguish her *yevamah* status. Perhaps she retains the status of sister-in-law throughout the marriage, such that separating from her would require both a *get* and *chalitzah*.

### Complete Change

The *mishnah* therefore teaches that this is not so. Once *yibum* is performed, *amar kra u-lakachah lo l'ishah* — the Torah describes the act as taking her as a wife. *Keivan she-lakachah, harei hi k'ishto le-chol davar* — once he has taken her, she is fully his wife in every respect. All prior statuses — sister-in-law, *yevamah*, *shomeret yavam* — are entirely dissolved. The act of *yibum* is not merely a marital act that coexists with her former status; it transforms her status completely.

The same principle resolves the concern about remarriage. One might have thought that if Shimon divorces Rachel and she marries another man, she cannot return to Shimon — not because of any general prohibition, but because the act of *yibum* functioned as a divinely mandated override of the normal prohibition of a brother's wife, and that override applied only within the specific context of the *mitzvah*. Once divorced, a remarriage would not be a continuation of *yibum* but a new marriage — and a new marriage to a brother's wife would reinstantiate the original prohibition. The *mishnah* teaches that this concern is unfounded. The *yibum* act comprehensively changes her status, and she is simply his wife; the prohibition of *eishet ach* has no further purchase.

### Ketubah Collection

One qualification attaches to this full-wife status in the domain of *ketubah*. If Shimon dies after *yibum*, Rachel collects her *ketubah* primarily from Reuven's estate — because the *ketubah* obligation originated with Reuven, and Shimon effectively stepped into Reuven's position along with Reuven's estate. The *gemara* notes: *ishah hiknu lo min ha-shamayim* — a wife was given to him by Heaven, meaning that the *ketubah* obligation tracks the estate that was transferred to Shimon from Reuven, and thus remains anchored there. However, if Reuven's estate is insufficient to satisfy the *ketubah*, Rachel may collect from Shimon's own estate — *tiknu lah mi-sheini* — because without recourse to Shimon's estate she would be left without protection, and the Rabbis were concerned that absent such protection a husband might be too quick to divorce his wife: *kedei she-lo tehei kalah be-einav le-hotzi'ah*. As Tosafot observes, since Shimon in any event now possesses Reuven's property, the practical question of which estate she collects from involves careful analysis of what the distinction amounts to — but the *halakha* establishes a clear ordering of primary and secondary sources of collection.

---

## Mitzvah Begadol

### Oldest Obligated

The *mishnah* now turns to a topic that, the *gemara* suggests, probably should have appeared at the very opening of the *masechet*: the primary obligation to perform *yibum* falls on the oldest brother. *Mitzvah begadol leyabem* — the *mitzvah* of *yibum* is incumbent first and foremost upon the eldest brother. This principle carries two implications: first, that *yibum* is preferred over *chalitzah*; and second, that among the brothers, the eldest bears the primary obligation.

### Go to Others

If the oldest brother is unwilling to perform *yibum*, the *mishnah* directs that one should go to the other brothers — not necessarily in order of age — to see whether any of them is prepared to perform *yibum*. The preference for *yibum* over *chalitzah* means that a younger brother's willingness to do *yibum* is worth pursuing even at the cost of bypassing the older brother's readiness to do *chalitzah*. Notably, the *mishnah* frames this entire process from the perspective of the brothers; the woman's preference is not foregrounded, a point to which the discussion will return.

### Force Oldest

If none of the brothers wish to perform *yibum*, one returns to the oldest brother and tells him directly: *alecha mitzvah* — the obligation is yours. He must either perform *yibum* or perform *chalitzah*; the obligation cannot remain unresolved. He is the one to be pressured and, if necessary, compelled.

### No Waiting

The *mishnah* further specifies that there are cases in which one might be tempted to delay: if there is a younger brother who is a minor and might grow up and wish to perform *yibum*; if the oldest brother is overseas and one might wait for his return; or if one of the brothers is a *cheresh* or *shoteh* who might conceivably recover. In all these cases, *ein shom'in lo* — we do not listen to arguments for delay. The response is: *alecha mitzvah, o chalotz o yabem* — you are the one obligated, act now. The *mishnah* emphasizes that the present situation, with the brothers who are present and capable, is what determines the obligation. One does not suspend action in hopes that a better outcome might materialize.

---

## Yibum vs. Chalitzah

### Case Setup

The *gemara* now poses a specific case that tests the priorities established by the *mishnah*: a younger brother wishes to perform *yibum*, while the older brother is prepared to perform *chalitzah*. The question is which takes precedence. Based on the *mishnah*'s plain reading — which sends us to the younger brothers only when the oldest refuses to do anything — one might think the answer is obvious. But the *gemara* shows that the matter is in fact disputed.

### Yibum Priority

Rabbi Yochanan holds *biat katan adifa* — the act of *yibum* by the younger brother is preferable. His reasoning: *yibum* is a greater *mitzvah* than *chalitzah*, and therefore if *yibum* can be achieved through any brother, that outcome is to be preferred over *chalitzah* even by the oldest.

### Obligation Priority

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds *chalitzat gadol adifa* — the action of the oldest brother takes precedence. His reasoning does not deny that *yibum* is the more significant *mitzvah*. Rather, he argues that *b'makom gadol, biat katan lav klum hu* — when the oldest brother is present and prepared to act, the younger brother's act is of no legal significance. The oldest brother is the one upon whom the obligation devolves; his willingness to do *something* means that he is the relevant actor, and one does not look past him to the other brothers.

### Logic

The underlying disagreement, then, is between two frameworks. Rabbi Yochanan focuses on the quality of the *mitzvah* being performed: if *yibum* is better, find the best person to do it. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi focuses on the identity of the obligated party: once the oldest brother is ready to fulfill his obligation in any manner, he is the man, and the question of which *mitzvah* is greater is secondary.

---

## Mishnah Interpretation

### First Reading

The *gemara* attempts to read the *mishnah* as settling this dispute. The *mishnah* says that if the oldest brother *lo ratza* — did not want — one goes to the other brothers. A natural reading of *lo ratza* is that he refused to perform *yibum* but was prepared to perform *chalitzah*. If so, the *mishnah* is teaching that even though the oldest brother is willing to do *chalitzah*, one still goes to the other brothers to seek *yibum* — proving that *yibum* of a younger brother takes precedence over *chalitzah* of the oldest, in accordance with Rabbi Yochanan.

### Lo Ratza Both

The *gemara* rejects this reading. *Lo ratza* must mean that the oldest brother refused to do anything — neither *yibum* nor *chalitzah*. It is this total refusal that prompts the *mishnah* to send us to the other brothers.

### Force Issue

This corrected reading creates its own difficulty. If all the brothers ultimately refuse to do anything — neither *yibum* nor *chalitzah* — and compulsion becomes necessary, why does the *mishnah* direct us to compel the oldest brother specifically? Once we are in the realm of compulsion, the question of who bears the primary obligation seems less relevant. We simply need someone to act — so why not compel a younger brother?

### Mitzvah Priority

The *gemara* answers without hesitation: *keivan de-mitzvah le-didei ramya, le-didei kafnan* — since the *mitzvah* is primarily incumbent upon the oldest brother, he is the one we compel. Even when force is necessary, the legal structure of obligation has not changed. The oldest bears the primary responsibility, and that responsibility means he is the one subjected to compulsion.

---

## Waiting Cases

### Wait for Young

Having established that *lo ratza* means refusing both *yibum* and *chalitzah*, the *gemara* presses a further question. According to Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that *yibum* is always preferable even when performed by a younger brother — why does the *mishnah* say we do not wait for a minor brother to grow up? If we could obtain *yibum* by waiting for the younger brother to come of age, should we not do so?

### Wait for Old

The same challenge can be posed in the opposite direction, now aimed at Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who holds that the oldest brother's action takes precedence. If so, why does the *mishnah* say we do not wait for the oldest brother to return from overseas? If the oldest brother is the obligated party and his action is what we prefer, we should be willing to wait for him.

### No Delay

The *gemara* answers that neither challenge lands, because both rest on the same false premise — that our hierarchy of preferences justifies delay. The *gemara* states: *ella kol she-hu mitzvah lo mashinan* — wherever there is a *mitzvah* to be done, we do not postpone it. No matter what one's priorities are regarding who should perform the *mitzvah* or in what form, the overriding imperative is that the *mitzvah* be discharged promptly with the people who are present and capable right now.

### Act Now

The two questions thus cancel each other out, and the answer is the same in both directions: it is not a question of which preference takes precedence, but of the principle that a *mitzvah* cannot be held in abeyance while we hope for a more optimal actor to become available. Whatever our series of preferences — *yibum* over *chalitzah*, oldest over youngest — those preferences operate among present options, not as grounds for indefinite delay.

---

## Chalitzah Preference

### Chalitzah Dispute

A second version of the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi now emerges, one that sharpens the question. In the first version, the debate concerned *yibum* by a younger brother versus *chalitzah* by the older brother. Now the question is narrower: if *yibum* is entirely off the table and the only available outcome is *chalitzah*, does the principle of *mitzvah begadol* still apply? That is, when choosing between *chalitzat katan* and *chalitzat gadol*, is there a preference for the older brother to perform *chalitzah*?

### Mitzvah Applies

One opinion holds *chalitzat gadol adifa* — the *mitzvah begadol* principle extends even to *chalitzah*, and therefore the older brother should be the one to perform it.

### Equivalent

The other opinion holds *ke-hadadi ninhu* — once we are operating in the *chalitzah* domain, the brothers are equivalent. The reasoning behind the *mitzvah begadol* principle was connected to the role of *yibum* in perpetuating the dead brother's name and legacy, an act for which the oldest brother's position is especially meaningful. *Chalitzah*, however, is simply an act of severing the levirate bond, with no such resonance — and for a mere act of severance, age confers no special significance.

### Mishnah Proof

The *gemara* attempts again to resolve the dispute from the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* says *lo ratzu, chozrin eitzel gadol* — if the brothers did not want to act, one returns to the oldest brother. The *gemara* reads *lo ratzu* as meaning the younger brothers refused to do *yibum* but were prepared to do *chalitzah*. If so, we now have a situation where multiple brothers are prepared to do *chalitzah*, and the *mishnah* directs us to return to the oldest — proving that even in the *chalitzah* domain the older brother's action is preferred.

### No Proof Yet

Once again, however, the *gemara* corrects this reading: *lo ratzu* means the brothers refused to do anything at all — neither *yibum* nor *chalitzah*. The same logic as before applies: we go to the oldest because the *mitzvah* obligation remains on him, and we compel him because he is the obligated party. But this tells us nothing about whether, when *chalitzah* is the only option and the brothers are cooperating, there is a preference for the oldest to perform it. The *mishnah* provides no resolution to this question, and the dispute remains unresolved.

---

---

# Yevamot 40

## Yibum vs Chalitzah

### Mishna Setup

The daf begins in the middle of 39b, picking up from a *mishna* cited from tractate *Kesubos* that establishes the basic halakhic ordering: *mitzvas yibum kodemes lemitzvas chalitzah* — the commandment of *yibum* takes precedence over the commandment of *chalitzah*. This was the original arrangement, operating under the assumption that men performed *yibum* for the right reasons: *barishona shehayu miskavnim leshem mitzvah* — originally, they had proper intent, acting for the sake of the *mitzvah* itself.

### Intent Changes Priority

The *mishna* then introduces a striking reversal. Once the situation changed — *achshav she'ein miskavnim leshem mitzvah*, now that men no longer perform *yibum* for the sake of the *mitzvah* — the ruling shifts: *mitzvas chalitzah kodemes lemitzvas yibum*, the *mitzvah* of *chalitzah* now comes first. The most obvious ulterior motive, as the very next *mishna* will make clear, is the inheritance: a man who performs *yibum* acquires his deceased brother's entire estate. Once financial gain rather than religious purpose drives the act, the Sages reversed the priority.

This raises a profound question: what exactly constitutes acting *shelo leshem mitzvah*, without proper intent? And what is the practical consequence of that reversal — does it mean *chalitzah* is now strictly mandated, or merely preferred? These questions animate the entire subsequent *sugya*.

### Rashi's Approach

*Rav* addresses the question with the ruling *ein kofin* — we do not compel. *Rashi* explains this to mean that we do not force a couple to perform *chalitzah* when both parties wish to perform *yibum*. On *Rashi*'s reading, while we may now prefer *chalitzah*, we do not prevent *yibum* when both sides genuinely want it. The preference for *chalitzah* is real, but it does not translate into outright prohibition of *yibum* when there is mutual consent.

### Woman's Consent

At this point *Rashi* introduces a critically important dimension that the *sugya* had until now entirely ignored: the woman's voice. *Rashi* writes that if the *yabam* wishes to perform *yibum* but the woman says *lo ba'ina lei* — she does not want him — and she offers *devarim nikarim*, a reasonable explanation for her refusal, then the court intervenes. The first step is essentially a form of financial inducement: the court encourages the *yabam* to perform *chalitzah* by offering him compensation on her behalf, up to two hundred *zuz*. If that fails, *kafnan lei v'chalatz* — the court compels him to perform *chalitzah*.

*Rashi* goes further, clarifying that the standard is not limited to extreme cases of physical repulsion — the example given is a *yabam* afflicted with *mukei shechin*, a severe skin disease — but extends to *kol amasa shetitan lidevareha*, any reasonable grounds she articulates. This is a remarkable insertion, because the entire preceding discussion had been framed entirely around the brothers and their preferences. *Rashi* here establishes that the woman's reasoned refusal is legally determinative: if she does not consent, *yibum* will not take place, whether through persuasion or coercion of the *yabam*.

### Rav's Position

When couples actually came before *Rav*, his practice illustrates the tension vividly. He would say: *iba'is chalot iba'is yabem* — do you wish to perform *chalitzah*, or do you wish to perform *yibum*? He presented both as genuine options. True, he listed *chalitzah* first, and that ordering reflects the preference — but the framing otherwise treats them as equivalent choices. He then cited the verse: *ve'im lo yachpotz ha'ish*, if the man does not wish to do *yibum* he performs *chalitzah*, but *ha im chafetz* — if he does wish to — the choice is his, *bedidach tala rachmana*, the Torah leaves it in his hands.

This practice goes even further than merely not preventing *yibum*: *Rav* is actively presenting it as a legitimate option. The only concession to the preference for *chalitzah* is the order in which he raises the possibilities. The Torah's own prioritization of *yibum* makes it difficult to do more than that: one can acknowledge the problems with *yibum* performed for ulterior motives and still recognize that the Torah itself frames *yibum* as the primary act.

### Torah Priority

*Rav Yehuda* likewise held *ein kofin*, as demonstrated by the document he established for *chalitzah* proceedings — the *get* of *chalitzah*. In that document, the court offers the *yabam* the option of performing *yibum* even as he stands before the court to perform *chalitzah*. This detail will be explored in full in the next section, but its relevance here is clear: even in the formal procedure for *chalitzah*, the option of *yibum* is explicitly preserved. And *Rav Yehuda* explicitly grounded his position in the verse *ve'im lo yachpotz ha'ish* — the Torah's own framing, which treats the man's willingness as the deciding factor and implies that if he does wish to perform *yibum*, that remains a legitimate path.

---

## Chalitzah Document

### Get of Chalitzah

*Rav Yehuda* established the precise language for the formal court record of a *chalitzah* proceeding — called the *get* of *chalitzah*, a usage worth pausing on. The term *get* does not mean divorce specifically; it means a writ or document. This document is the *beis din*'s official record that the *chalitzah* took place, and the woman could produce it subsequently to establish that she was free to remarry. *Rav Yehuda* fixed the language of this document, and it opens with the words *anan sahadei* — we testify.

### Brother Identification

The document begins by identifying the woman: *plonis bas ploni*, so-and-so daughter of so-and-so. It then records that she, the *yevamah*, brought her *yabam* before the court — the Torah frames the woman as the active party who brings the *yabam* to the *beis din*. The court then attests: *ve'ishtemod'einu hu de-achua de-misna me'abba nihu* — we recognized him to be a paternal brother of the deceased.

### Shoe Removal

The document continues: the court said to him, if you wish to perform *yibum* do so, and if not, extend your right leg toward her. He extended his right leg, and she removed the shoe from his leg.

### Spitting & Verse

She then spat before him — *roka d'miskhazi leBeis Dina*, a spitting that was visible to the *beis din*, directed toward the ground in front of him rather than literally at his face. *Rav Chiya bar Avya* adds, in the name of *Rav Yehuda*, an additional element: the court had him recite the relevant verse from the Torah, *lo chafatzti lekachtah*, "I do not wish to take her," with the communal response *kacha ye'aseh la'ish asher lo yivneh es beis achiv*.

One might note what is conspicuous about the first version of the document: it omits those verses. This is likely deliberate. Since we now wish to hold out *chalitzah* as a dignified option — and since we are trying to make *chalitzah* function without the stigma of the *yabam* being publicly shamed — emphasizing the *pesukim* that frame the *yabam* as shirking his familial responsibility would be counterproductive. The *gemara* has effectively transformed *chalitzah* into a technical legal procedure, stripped of the element of social reproach that the Torah seems to have built into it.

It is also worth noting the structural point that throughout this entire procedure, the woman is the initiating actor: she brings the *yabam* to court, she removes the shoe, she spits. When *yibum* is the act, the man is the primary agent; in *chalitzah*, the woman is.

### Rav Achai/Ravina

One phrase in the document requires further analysis: *ve'ishtemod'einu hu* — "we recognized him" to be a paternal brother. This raises a practical question: how does the court establish that identification? *Rav Achai* and *Ravina* debate the matter. One holds that formal witnesses are required to testify that he is a paternal brother. The other holds that even a relative or a woman — people ordinarily ineligible to serve as formal witnesses — suffice.

The *halacha* follows the latter view: *giluy milsa b'alma hu*, this is merely a matter of publicly known information, not formal testimony. Since the fact of someone being a brother is typically known to the community, the ordinary rules of testimony do not apply, and we may rely on whatever evidence establishes the fact — even a single relative or woman.

The practical reason this identification matters is that without it, there could be abuse of the procedure. If a woman's *yabam* is refusing to act, or is threatening to perform *yibum* against her wishes, she might conceivably bring a stranger to *beis din* and claim he is the *yabam*, thereby fraudulently obtaining a *chalitzah*. The identification requirement prevents this. But since the fact is generally in the realm of common knowledge rather than disputed legal fact, the standard of proof is correspondingly relaxed.

The *sugya* notes that this detail also reinforces the earlier point: even in the formal document for *chalitzah*, the man is told he may still perform *yibum* if he chooses. This is the ongoing demonstration that even as we say *mitzvas chalitzah kodemes*, we are not eliminating *yibum* as an option.

---

## Intent Dispute

### Later Reversion

The *gemara* now reports a further development. *Rami bar Chama* says in the name of *Rav Yitzchak*: *chazru lomar mitzvas yibum kodemes lemitzvas chalitzah* — they went back to saying that the *mitzvah* of *yibum* comes first. This appears to undo the entire premise of the preceding discussion, reverting to the original formulation of the *mishna*.

### Spiritual Capacity

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* challenges this immediately: *achshar daray*? Have the generations suddenly improved? If the reason for reversing the priority was that people were no longer performing *yibum leshem mitzvah*, and *yeridat hadorot* — the general decline across generations — is a familiar assumption, on what basis could a later generation simply revert to the original practice?

### Shift in Views

The answer is not that the generations improved morally or spiritually. Rather, the shift reflects a change in which *tannaitic* position is being followed. *Me'ikara savri lah ke'Abba Shaul* — originally they held in accordance with *Abba Shaul*, who says that *kavana*, intent, is determinative. *Ulevasof savri lah keRabbanan* — later they reverted to holding like the *Rabbanan*, who say that intent is legally irrelevant to the validity of *yibum*. The reversal was not demographic; it was doctrinal.

### Abba Shaul

The *gemara* now presents the fundamental dispute directly. *Abba Shaul* says: one who takes his *yevamah leshem noi*, for her physical attractiveness, *leshum ishut*, for the social status of marriage — *Tosafos* explains this as a desire for the standing that comes with being a married man — or *leshum davar acher*, for any other ulterior motive, most obviously the inheritance of the brother's estate: *ke'ilu pogea be'ervah*, it is as if he is engaging in a forbidden sexual relationship. And *Abba Shaul* adds: *vekarov ani be'einai lihyot havlad mamzer* — I would consider the child close to being a *mamzer*.

This is a striking position, and notably non-technical in character. *Abba Shaul* is not arguing that the formal categories of *yibum* were not met. He is arguing from the logic of what makes *yibum* permissible in the first place. The relationship between a man and his brother's wife is ordinarily an *ervah*, one of the gravest sexual prohibitions. What overrides that prohibition is the *mitzvah* of *yibum* — specifically the imperative *lehakim shem achiv*, to perpetuate his brother's name and legacy. When a man performs *yibum* not for that purpose but for his own desires or financial gain, *Abba Shaul* holds that the overriding consideration is effectively absent, and therefore the underlying prohibition reasserts itself. The technical category of *yibum* is present, but its validating rationale is not.

One might observe that even on *Abba Shaul*'s view, one could argue that regardless of the man's subjective intent, if a child results, *lehakim shem achiv* is objectively achieved. *Abba Shaul* seems to respond that when the act is not subjectively framed in terms of religious purpose, it cannot function at the societal level as an act of perpetuating the brother's name — whatever the metaphysical outcome. The reasoning is admittedly elusive, but the moral seriousness of *Abba Shaul*'s position is unmistakable.

### Rabbis' Position

*Vachachamim omrim* — the *Rabbanan* disagree entirely. *Yevamah yavo aleiha mikol makom* — the Torah says he shall have relations with her, full stop. The halakhic permission established by the *mitzvah* of *yibum* does not depend on the actor's internal religious motivation. The Torah established an act; when that act is performed, the permission applies, regardless of whether the man's *kavana* was *leshem shamayim* or otherwise. Intent may be a religious desideratum, but it is not a halakhic condition for the validity of *yibum* according to the *Rabbanan*.

### Braita Source

The *gemara* now asks: *man tanna leha detanu Rabbanan*? Which *tanna* is the source of the *Rabbanan*'s position? It then cites a *braita* that formulates the issue in structural terms: the *yevamah* was originally *mutar* to the *yabam* before she married his brother; then she became *assur*; then upon the brother's death she became *mutar* again. The *braita* asks: does she revert to her original status of full *heter*? The answer is: *talmud lomar yevamah yavo aleiha mitzvah* — the Torah says the *yabam* shall come to her as a *mitzvah*, indicating that the current *heter* is not identical to the original one.

*Yitzchak bar Avdimi* reads this *braita* as representing *Abba Shaul*'s position. The *braita* is saying that returning to *heter* after the brother's death does not restore the original unconditioned permission: now the act must be done *lemitzvah*, for the sake of the *mitzvah*, as *Abba Shaul* requires.

*Rava*, however, reads the *braita* as consistent with the *Rabbanan*'s position. His reading reframes the *hava amina* entirely. Originally, before she married the brother, the man had no obligation toward this woman: *ratza konsah, ratza eino konsah* — if he wished to marry her he could, if not he need not. After the brother's death, *zika* — the bond of *yibum* — attaches. One cannot imagine that he might simply walk away; she is *agida bei*, bound to him. So the *hava amina* is not that he can walk away altogether, but rather that perhaps *yibum* and *chalitzah* are fully equivalent options, as unconditioned as his original relationship to her. The Torah answers: no, *yibum* is the primary *mitzvah*. This is *Rava*'s reading for the *Rabbanan* — the verse prioritizes *yibum* over *chalitzah*, not as a condition of intent, but as a statement of halakhic hierarchy.

---

## Parallel Examples

### Rava's Reading

Having established *Rava*'s reading of the *braita* in favor of the *Rabbanan*, the *gemara* tests this reading against the parallel case the *braita* employs: the *mincha* offering eaten by the *kohanim* as *matzot* in a sacred place. The *braita* applies the identical logical structure — original *heter*, then *issur*, then return to *heter* — asking whether the flour reverts to its original unconditioned status. The verse answers: *matzot teiachel b'makom kadosh mitzvah* — it shall be eaten as *matzot* in a sacred place, as a *mitzvah*. On *Rava*'s reading, this is a structural parallel: just as *yibum* is the prioritized option over *chalitzah*, here there is a prioritized manner of eating the *mincha*, with a second-grade alternative that is still valid.

### Matza Case

How does this parallel work in practice? The *gemara* works through several possibilities for what the two "grades" of eating might be. The initial *heter* was that the flour, before being sanctified, could be eaten by anyone, in any manner, for any reason — *ratza ochla ratza eino ochla*, one could eat it or not eat it. After sanctification it becomes *assur*. After the *kometz* is brought, it becomes *mutar* again for the *kohanim*. The *hava amina* that it might revert to the original equivalence of options is dismissed by the *gemara*: how could one imagine that the *kohen* might simply choose not to eat it? The verse *ve'achlu otam asher kuppar bahem* — "they shall eat those through which atonement was achieved" — establishes that the *kohanim*'s eating is obligatory, as it is through their eating that the owner's atonement is effected, *hakohanim ochlim ube'alim mitchaprin*.

So the *hava amina* is reframed: perhaps the specific *kohen* who performed the *avoda* and brought the *kometz* could choose to have a different *kohen* eat the *mincha* instead. The verse answers that there is a *mitzvah davka* with him — he should eat it himself, in priority over another *kohen*. This parallels the *yibum* case: just as *yibum* is preferred over *chalitzah*, this *kohen* eating is preferred over another *kohen* eating. Both options are valid; one is prioritized.

### False Alternatives

Having established the structural shape of the parallel, the *gemara* must now identify the actual two grades in the *matza* case that correspond to *yibum* and *chalitzah* in *Abba Shaul*'s reading — since *Rava* reads it for the *Rabbanan*, but the *braita* itself needs to make sense on *Abba Shaul*'s account as well. On *Abba Shaul*'s reading, the two variations are *yibum leshem mitzvah* (the higher grade) and *yibum shelo leshem mitzvah* (the lower but still technically valid grade). What is the parallel in the *mincha* case?

The *gemara* first considers: perhaps eating *achilah gassah* — eating when completely sated and forcing oneself — is the lower grade. This is rejected: *achilah gassah mi shma achilah*? Forced eating is not eating at all. *Resh Lakish* rules that one who eats *achilah gassah* on *Yom Kippur* is *patur*, since the Torah prohibits *inui*, affliction, which presupposes that normal eating would provide genuine satisfaction. *Tosafos* notes that there are degrees of *achilah gassah*: mild overeating ("oh, perhaps just a bit of dessert") does not reach the level that is halakhically exempt on *Yom Kippur*; only eating when truly unable to experience any satisfaction does. But either way, the most extreme form of *achilah gassah* cannot serve as a lower grade of eating, because it is not eating at all.

The *gemara* then considers: perhaps the two grades are eating it as *matza* versus eating it as *chametz*. This too is dismissed: eating the *mincha* as *chametz* is simply forbidden. *Resh Lakish* derives from the verse *lo te'afeh chametz chelkam* that even the priestly portion of a *mincha* may not be baked as *chametz*. Since *chametz* is not a permitted option at all, it cannot be the lower-grade alternative.

### Scalded Matza

The *gemara* arrives at the correct answer: the two grades are *matza* baked in the ordinary fashion versus *chalut* — flour that has been scalded prior to baking. *Chalita* is a process that alters the texture of the dough without necessarily rendering it *chametz*. If after scalding the dough is baked, does the result still qualify as *matza*? The *gemara* raises the question: *im matzah hi hamatzah hi* — if it still counts as *matza*, then why is it a second-grade option? And if it does not count as *matza*, then one is not *yotzei* the obligation and the Torah would not permit it at all.

The resolution is: *lo, le'olam eima lach matzah hi* — it is indeed *matza*, but of a lesser grade. The verse *matzot ye'achel* specifies this to teach that there are two tiers of *matza*: ideal *matza* and *matza* that is technically valid but halakhically inferior. This is structurally parallel to *yibum leshem mitzvah* and *yibum shelo leshem mitzvah* on *Abba Shaul*'s reading.

### Halacha Purpose

Having established that scalded *matza* is valid but second-grade for the *mincha*, the *gemara* asks *l'mai hilchata*? — beyond the structural parallel, what is the practical halakhic implication of declaring *chalut matza*? The answer: *lomar she'yotzei bo yedei chovato bePesach* — one may use such scalded *matza* to fulfill the obligation of eating *matza* on Pesach. Even though it is a second-grade option for the *mincha*, for other contexts requiring *matza* it is fully adequate: *af al pi d'chalitah mei'ikara*, even if the grain was scalded at the outset, *keivan d'hadar afyeih batenur*, since it was subsequently baked in an oven, *lechem oni karina bei*, we call it "poor person's bread," and one fulfills one's Pesach obligation with it.

In sum, the *braita* operates on two levels simultaneously. On *Rava*'s reading it speaks for the *Rabbanan*, establishing that *yibum* is the prioritized option over *chalitzah*, parallel to the specific *kohen* eating being prioritized over another *kohen* eating. On the reading of *Yitzchak bar Avdimi* it speaks for *Abba Shaul*, establishing that *yibum leshem mitzvah* is the higher grade and *yibum shelo leshem mitzvah* is a lower but technically valid grade, parallel to ideal *matza* and scalded *matza*.

The *gemara*'s conclusion is significant: after introducing the reversal — that *mitzvas chalitzah kodemes* — and then showing how extensively even the Amoraim preserved *yibum* as a live option, the discussion ends by reporting that later authorities reverted to saying *mitzvas yibum kodemes*, because they followed the *Rabbanan* over *Abba Shaul*. This appears to be the conclusion of the *Bavli*.

---

## Geography Factor

### Babylonian Polygamy

The *Bavli*'s conclusion — reverting to *mitzvas yibum kodemes* — stands in contrast to the *Yerushalmi*, which maintains the earlier position that *mitzvas chalitzah kodemes*. This divergence is not arbitrary; it reflects the radically different social realities in which each Talmud developed. *Bavel* was a polygamous society, situated within a Zoroastrian and later Islamic cultural world in which a man having multiple wives was entirely normative. In such a context, performing *yibum* even when already married posed no legal or social difficulty. Prioritizing *yibum* as the ideal was therefore practically feasible.

### Eretz Yisrael Monogamy

*Eretz Yisrael*, by contrast, came under the influence of Rome, which was moving toward monogamy — and Rome's cultural trajectory was followed by Christianity, under which monogamy became a religious requirement. In a monogamous society, *yibum* is frequently not a practical option: if the *yabam* is already married, he cannot simply take a second wife. To hold *yibum* out as the halakhic ideal in such a society would create systematic problems. The *Yerushalmi* therefore maintained that *mitzvas chalitzah kodemes*, which functions as the workable norm across a wide range of circumstances.

### Sefardic Tradition

This geographic and cultural divide maps directly onto the division among the *Rishonim*. The *Sefardic* tradition, as the inheritors of the Babylonian halakhic culture and living within Islamic societies that permitted polygamy, continued to hold that *mitzvas yibum kodemes*. Even in more recent generations, as formal polygamy became less common even in *Sefardic* communities, the tradition of treating *yibum* as the preferred option persisted.

### Ashkenazi Tradition

The *Ashkenazic* tradition, living in Christian lands under conditions of strict monogamy and the *Cherem de-Rabbeinu Gershom* — the rabbinic prohibition of polygamy accepted across Ashkenaz — reached the opposite conclusion: *mitzvas chalitzah kodemes*. In a society where a married man absolutely cannot take a second wife, consistently prioritizing *yibum* would be untenable.

### Tosafot Reinterpret

*Rashi*, writing within the *Ashkenazic* world, reads the *gemara* straightforwardly without signaling any divergence from what the *gemara* seems to conclude. This is perhaps because *Rashi*'s reading of *ein kofin* — that we allow *yibum* when both parties consent — is already somewhat of a mitigation, and the *gemara*'s final position as read by *Rashi* is not entirely irreconcilable with practical *Ashkenazic* preference for *chalitzah*. *Tosafos*, however, goes further and explicitly reinterprets the *Bavli* to align with *Ashkenazic* practice.

*Tosafos* offers a sophisticated reading of the passage where *Rav* offered both options to the couple and *Rav Yehuda*'s document invited the *yabam* to perform *yibum*. *Tosafos* argues that these cases were exceptional: *ve-chi havru atu l'kamei de-Rav* — those were people who came to *Rav* already intending to perform *yibum leshem mitzvah*, and it was precisely because their intent was pure that *Rav* validated *yibum* as an option. Similarly, the person in *Rav Yehuda*'s document who was offered the choice was someone who had originally come to perform *chalitzah*: since he had come for *chalitzah*, he clearly had no ulterior motives for *yibum*, and therefore, if he changed his mind and chose *yibum*, his intent would by definition be *leshem mitzvah*.

The result is a near-perfect logical catch: a man who wants to perform *yibum* may be suspected of ulterior motives and is therefore not permitted to do so. A man who wants to perform *chalitzah*, and is therefore free of suspicion, is then offered the option of *yibum* — but if he takes it and appears eager, the suspicion reattaches. *Tosafos* concludes that *Rabbeinu Tam* ruled in accordance with *Abba Shaul*, as reflected in an apparently uncontested *mishna* in *Bechoros*, and that the *halacha* therefore follows *mitzvas chalitzah kodemes*. *Rabbeinu Chananel* initially ruled that *mitzvas yibum kodemes*, but subsequently retracted and ruled *mitzvas chalitzah kodemes*. The *machloket* between the *Bavli* and the *Yerushalmi*, and between *Ashkenazim* and *Sefardim*, is thus a principled disagreement rooted in divergent social and legal contexts as much as in divergent readings of the Talmudic text.

---

## Inheritance

### Chalitzah Share

The next *mishna* addresses the property implications of *chalitzah* and *yibum*. When a brother performs *chalitzah* with his *yevamah*, *harei hu ke'echad min ha'achim linachal* — he retains an equal share of the deceased brother's estate, the same as any other surviving brother. One might have thought otherwise: having rejected the *yevamah*, perhaps he also forfeits any claim to his brother's property, analogous to the episode in *Megillas Rus* where the *goel* who initially wished to redeem the land withdrew when he learned that Ruth came with the transaction. Here, the *mishna* rules that rejecting the woman does not mean rejecting the estate.

*Ve'im yesh sham av* — however, if the father is still alive, *nichasim shel av*, the estate goes to the father. This is simply the ordinary rule of inheritance: when a son dies, the father precedes the brothers in the line of heirs.

### Yibum Estate

For *yibum* the situation is dramatically different: *hakones es yevamto zacha benichasim shel achiv* — one who performs *yibum* acquires the entirety of his deceased brother's estate. This is the financial incentive *Abba Shaul* found so troubling. The verse *yakum al shem achiv* — he shall stand up on his brother's name — is understood to link the act of *yibum* to the acquisition of the brother's name and, with it, his property.
