*Rabbi Yehuda* disagrees: *bein kach uvein kach im yesh sham av nichasim shel av* — in both cases, whether *chalitzah* or *yibum*, if the father is alive the property goes to the father. *Rabbi Yehuda* reads *yakum al shem achiv* as establishing no independent property right; it speaks to something metaphysical or relational — the *yabam* perpetuates the brother's legacy in some sense that does not necessarily translate into estate acquisition, at least not when a prior heir such as the father is present.

### Father Precedence

The *gemara* establishes *Rabbi Yehuda*'s reasoning through an analogy to the *bechor*, the firstborn son. The verse *vehayah habechor* is read earlier in the *masechta* as a reference to the *yabam* performing the act of *yibum*, with *k'bechor* implying that he is treated like a firstborn. A firstborn son receives a double portion — but crucially, *mah bechor ein lo bechayei av*, a firstborn has no portion while the father is still alive. His enhanced share materializes only after the father's death. *Af hai nami ein lo bechayei av* — similarly, the *yabam*'s claim to the brother's estate does not materialize if the father is alive.

The *gemara* raises the possibility that this analogy implies even more: just as the *bechor* eventually receives his double portion after the father dies, so too perhaps the *yabam* should eventually receive the estate after the father dies. The *gemara* rejects this: the verse says *yakum al shem achiv*, he stands on his brother's name, not his father's. If at the moment of the brother's death he did not step into the brother's estate — because the father was alive and took it — then his connection to that estate is severed permanently. *Yakum al shem achiv velo al shem aviv*.

One might then ask: if the father is alive and takes the property, in what sense does the *yabam* perpetuate his brother's name at all? The *gemara* does not pursue a financial answer here. The *Ramban* suggests something more metaphysical — an allusion to *gilgul neshamot*, transmigration of souls — but beyond that, caring for the widow, providing her with a home and continuity, is itself the fulfillment of *yakum al shem achiv* regardless of property.

### Yibum vs Estate

The *gemara* then raises a further implication of *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position. If the *yabam* and the estate are conditionally linked — he gets the estate only when there is no father — one might argue that the *mitzvah* of *yibum* itself is similarly conditional: perhaps where there is a father who will take the estate, there is no *mitzvah* of *yibum* at all, since *yibum* and *nachalah* go together as a package. The *gemara* dismisses this emphatically: *midi yibum benachalah talah rachmana*? Does *yibum* depend on the *nachalah*? The causality runs in the opposite direction. *Yibumei miyatney* — *yibum* comes first; it is the act of *yibum* that, when performed, carries the *nachalah* with it as a consequence. If there is no *nachalah* — either because the brother had no property or because the father takes it — the *mitzvah* of *yibum* is unaffected. The *nachalah* follows *yibum*; *yibum* does not follow *nachalah*.

### Text Correction

*Ulla* and *Rabbi Yitzchak Napcha* both rule *halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda*. This is then complicated by a fascinating episode of textual transmission. *Rav Chanina Kara*, a Torah reader who sat before *Rabbi Yannai*, stated *halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda*. *Rabbi Yannai* told him: *puk kari karich l'bara* — go teach your readings outside. He rejected the ruling, saying the correct formulation is *ein halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda*.

Similarly, a *tanna* — a reciter of *baraisos* rather than a reader of *pesukim* — sat before *Rav Nachman* and recited *ein halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda*. *Rav Nachman* challenged him: if that is the *halacha*, that we do not rule like *Rabbi Yehuda*, why is a *braisa* needed to say so? The principle *yachid verabim halacha kerabim* — the majority position prevails over the individual — should make it obvious without any formal teaching that we reject *Rabbi Yehuda*'s minority view.

*Rav Nachman* then reconstructs what must have happened. The original tradition was *halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda* — we do rule like *Rabbi Yehuda*. This was a case where we follow the minority, an unusual but not unprecedented ruling. The *tanna* who transmitted this was troubled by it: how could we rule like a *daas yachid*, a solitary opinion? His discomfort led him unconsciously to invert the text, remembering it as *ein halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda*. *Rav Nachman* says: your fix, though born of misunderstanding, happens to be correct — *shappir afachit*, you corrected it correctly — because in fact the *halacha* does not follow *Rabbi Yehuda*. The original *braisa* was corrupted, but the corruption produced the right result. We therefore preserve *ein halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda* as the authoritative formulation, even though the path by which it arrived was through an unconscious scribal correction.

---

## Chalutzah Status

### Man's Relatives

The *mishna* now addresses the web of prohibited relationships that flows from *chalitzah*. The act of *chalitzah* creates a relationship that is treated, for purposes of prohibited relatives, as analogous to a dissolved marriage. The woman who underwent *chalitzah* — the *chalutzah* — is treated in certain respects as the man's divorced wife. As a consequence, *hu assur bikrovoteha vehi assurah bikrovov* — he is forbidden to her relatives and she is forbidden to his relatives.

Specifically, the man who performed *chalitzah* is forbidden to: her mother, her maternal grandmother, her paternal grandmother — since these fall under the prohibition of a woman and her daughter's line, the virtual "wife's grandmother"; her daughter; her granddaughter through a daughter; her granddaughter through a son. He is also forbidden to her sister, *bizman shehi kayyamet* — as long as the *chalutzah* herself is still alive. This mirrors exactly the prohibition of wife's sister, which lapses only upon the wife's death.

*Vehachim mutarin* — the other brothers, who did not perform *chalitzah*, are permitted to all these women. The restrictions attach only to the specific brother who performed the act, not to the entire family.

### Woman's Relatives

The *chalutzah* is in turn forbidden to certain relatives of the man who performed *chalitzah*: his father and his paternal grandfather; his son and his grandson; his brother's son. The reasoning for each runs as follows. His father: from the father's perspective, this woman is his daughter-in-law — a biblical prohibition. His grandfather: from the grandfather's perspective, this woman is his son's daughter-in-law — a rabbinic prohibition, since the biblical categories extend only one generation in that direction. Nonetheless, the *mishna* includes rabbinic prohibitions within this framework. His son: from the son's perspective, this woman is his father's wife or ex-wife — a biblical prohibition. His grandson: she would be the grandfather's wife, again a rabbinic prohibition. His brother's son: from the nephew's perspective, this woman is his father's brother's wife, i.e., his aunt by marriage — a biblical prohibition.

### Tzara Rules

The *mishna* closes with a more complex case involving the *tzara*, the co-wife. *Mutar adam bikrovat tzarat chalutzato* — a man is permitted to marry a relative of the *tzara* of his *chalutzah*. *Ve'assur betzarat krovat chalutzato* — but he is forbidden to the *tzara* of a relative of his *chalutzah*. This distinction requires illustration.

Take *Shimon*, who performs *chalitzah* with *Rachel*. *Rachel* is his *chalutzah*. *Rachel* had a co-wife, *Leah*, who was simultaneously married to the same deceased *Reuven*. *Leah* goes free as a result of the *chalitzah* — she no longer has any *yibum* obligation — but she did not herself undergo *chalitzah*, so she is not a *chalutzah* and does not bear the status of *Shimon*'s virtual divorced wife. Therefore, *Shimon* is permitted to marry *Leah*'s relatives — for instance, *Leah*'s daughter *Dinah* — because *Leah* carries no prohibited status vis-à-vis *Shimon*. That is the case of *krovos tzarat chalutzato*: relative of the co-wife is permitted.

The reverse case is more puzzling. Suppose *Baruch* was married to both *Leah* and *Devorah*. *Leah* is *Rachel*'s sister — a relative of *Shimon*'s *chalutzah*. *Baruch* then dies or divorces *Devorah*, leaving *Devorah* free. Why would *Shimon* be forbidden to *Devorah*? *Devorah* is the *tzara* of *Leah*, and *Leah* is a relative of *Rachel*, *Shimon*'s *chalutzah*. The case of *tzarat krovat chalutzato* — the co-wife of a relative of the *chalutzah* — is apparently *assur*. The reason *Shimon* cannot marry *Leah* is clear: *Leah* is his *chalutzah*'s sister, and a man is forbidden to his virtual divorced wife's sister while she lives. But why *Devorah* is also *assur* is less obvious — and the *gemara* will address that question in the following *sugya*.

---

---

# Yevamot 41

## Shniyot B'Chalutza

### Shniyot Application

The Gemara on 41b opens with a focused question: *gazru shniyot b'chalutza o lo?* When the *chalutza* is treated like a *gerusha* and the relatives of the woman with whom *chalitza* was performed become forbidden to him, does that prohibition extend beyond the biblical *arayot* to include the rabbinic secondary prohibitions — the *shniyot l'arayot* — as well? The *mishna* sounds as though it does, but the Gemara subjects that assumption to careful scrutiny.

### D'Oraisa vs. D'Rabbanan

The Gemara's initial answer draws a principled distinction: *d'oraisa gazru rabbanan shniyot; b'chalutza lo gazru rabbanan shniyot.* The secondary prohibitions are applied where the man was actually married to the woman — a biblical relationship — but not in the case of the *chalutza*, whose status as a quasi-wife is itself only rabbinic. Before proceeding, it is worth noting a broader point: the *chalutza* is treated as a *gerusha* for the purposes of a *kohen*, and there is some evidence in tannaic literature that this status was understood as *d'oraisa*, though the Gemara insists it is rabbinic. In any event, the prohibition on a *kohen* marrying a *chalutza* is a distinct question from whether the *arayot* framework — with all its secondary extensions — applies to the *zika* relationship created by *chalitza*.

### Ima v'Eim Ima

To test this principle, the Gemara turns to the *mishna*'s specific examples. The *mishna* states that the man who performed *chalitza* is forbidden in his *chalutza*'s mother and grandmother — *ima u'veim ima* — but does not mention the great-grandmother. Since the great-grandmother would represent a rabbinic *shniya*, the omission seems to prove that *shniyot* do not apply to the *chalutza*. The Gemara deflects: perhaps the reason the great-grandmother is not mentioned is simply that the *mishna* then goes on to teach the leniency that the brothers are permitted with all these relatives, and had the *mishna* mentioned the great-grandmother, a reader might mistakenly think the brothers are permitted only with the great-grandmother but not with the grandmother and mother. By stopping at grandmother, the *mishna* prevents that misreading. The Gemara counters: but why not simply state explicitly that both the man is forbidden in the great-grandmother *and* the brothers are permitted with all of them? *Kashya* — this is difficult. So there remains a strong suggestion that the *mishna* stops at grandmother because *shniyot* are not applied to the *chalutza*.

### Aviv v'Avi Aviv

The Gemara tries a different case: the *mishna* states the *chalutza* is forbidden with his father and his grandfather — *aviv u'vavi aviv*. This becomes more interesting when analyzed carefully. Why cannot she marry the father? Because from the man's perspective, she is his daughter-in-law — an explicit biblical *erva*. But the grandfather? She would be his son's daughter-in-law — a *shniya l'arayot*, a second-degree rabbinic prohibition. So it seems the *mishna* applies *shniyot* to the *chalutza* status.

The Gemara replies: *lo mishum mishna* — this is not because of the *chalitz* himself (the man who performed *chalitza*, here called *Shimon*), but rather *mishum mes* — because of the deceased brother (*Reuven*). In other words, the grandfather is also Reuven's grandfather, and she is his son's daughter-in-law through the biblical relationship with Reuven, not through the rabbinic *chalutza* relationship with Shimon. It is a *shniya l'arayot*, yes, but generated by the *d'oraisa* relationship with Reuven, not by the *d'rabbanan* relationship with Shimon.

### Reuven vs. Shimon

This logic drives the entire analysis of the subsequent cases in the *mishna*, and it is worth pausing to appreciate its structure. Throughout these cases, what looks like *shniyot* applied to the *chalutza* relationship turns out, on examination, to be *shniyot* applied to the underlying biblical relationship with the deceased husband. The prohibition attaches because of Reuven, not because of Shimon.

To illustrate: if Shimon performed *chalitza* with Rachel, and the question is whether she may marry Shimon's grandfather Yitzchak, the answer is no — but the reason is not that Yitzchak's relationship to Rachel through Shimon's *chalutza* status generates a *shniya*. The reason is that Yitzchak is also Reuven's grandfather, and Rachel is Reuven's daughter-in-law through the biblical marriage, making this a *shniya* derived from the *d'oraisa* relationship, not the *d'rabbanan* one.

This framing — that all these prohibitions trace to Reuven and not to Shimon — is how the Gemara defends the position that *shniyot* do not apply to the *chalutza* relationship per se.

### Rabi Chiya Arba

This analysis receives its most explicit formulation in a *beraita* of Rabbi Chiyya: *d'tani Rabbi Chiyya arba midivrei Torah v'arba midivrei Soferim.* Among those forbidden to the *chalutza*, four categories are forbidden based on biblical relationships and four based on rabbinic ones. The four biblical categories are his father, his son, his brother, and his brother's son — all of whom, when analyzed from the perspective of the relative in question, stand in a relationship of biblical *erva* to Rachel through their connection to Reuven. For example, why is Shimon's brother's son forbidden? Because from that son's perspective, Rachel is his father's brother's wife — aunt — which is biblical.

The four rabbinic categories — grandfather (*avi aviv*), maternal grandfather (*avi imo*), grandson (*ben bno*), and daughter's son (*ben bito*) — are *midivrei Soferim*, and it is explicit that they represent *shniyot*. The Gemara then goes through each of these, attempting to demonstrate that even these four could be explained through the biblical Reuven relationship rather than the rabbinic Shimon relationship.

### Avi Imo Case

Take the case of *avi imo*, the maternal grandfather — in our terms, Lavan, the father of Rachel's mother Leah. The Gemara asks: is this forbidden because of Shimon's relationship to Rachel (*mishum choletz*), making this his daughter's daughter-in-law, a *shniya l'arayot*? Or is it because of Reuven (*mishum migareish*), making it Reuven's daughter's daughter-in-law? The Gemara gives the same answer — it is because of Reuven. But this requires a slight digression. The natural extension of *shniyot* follows within the same gender — a son-in-law is biblical, so a son's son-in-law is rabbinic. The extension to daughter's son-in-law, crossing genders, is less obvious but nevertheless how the system operates. The answer remains the same in structure: yes, it is a *shniya*, but it derives from the biblical relationship with Reuven, not from the rabbinic *chalutza* relationship with Shimon.

### Ben Beno Proof

The Gemara then turns to the case of *ben bno* — Shimon's grandson. From the grandson's perspective, Rachel would be his grandfather's wife — *eshes avi aviv* — a rabbinic *shniya*. The Gemara asks whether this prohibition flows from the *chalutza* status (*mishum choletz*). The Gemara replies: *lo mishum mifna* — no, because through Reuven's relationship, Rachel is the great-uncle's wife (*eshes achi avi aviv*), which is itself a *shniya l'arayot* derived from the biblical concept of uncle's wife.

### Ameimar Machshir

At this point the Gemara introduces a critical complication. *Ameimar machshir b'eshes achi avi aviv* — Ameimar holds that a great-uncle's wife is not subject to *shniyot* at all, and therefore the Reuven-based explanation is unavailable for the *ben bno* case. The Gemara acknowledges that Ameimar's position cannot be rescued by pushing things up a generation, as was done in earlier cases, when working within Rabbi Chiyya's *beraita*. Therefore the Gemara concludes: *Ameimar mokim lah mishum choletz* — Ameimar is forced to ground the prohibition in Shimon's *chalutza* relationship to Rachel, *v'kasavar gazru shniyot b'chalutza* — and Ameimar would have to concede that *shniyot* do apply to the *chalutza* relationship. This proves the point for Ameimar's position, at least.

The Gemara presses further with the case of *ben bito* — the daughter's son. From the perspective of this descendant, Rachel would be his mother's father's wife. The Gemara attempts the same Reuven-based explanation: she is the wife of his mother's father's brother (*eshes achi avi imo*). But the Gemara then recognizes that a mother's father's brother's wife is simply not recognized as a *shniya l'arayot* — *shniyot de'erva lo gazru* for that relationship. Therefore the Reuven-based explanation fails entirely, and the prohibition can only be grounded in the *chalutza* relationship with Shimon. *Shema mina gazru shniyot b'chalutza shema mina* — this establishes definitively that *shniyot* do apply to the *chalutza* relationship.

---

## Tzaras Krovat Chalutza

### Mutar vs. Assur

The *mishna* concludes with the rule: *mutar adam b'krovos tzaras chalutzaso* — a man is permitted to marry the relatives of the co-wife (*tzara*) of his *chalutza*. To understand this, consider the setup: Reuven was married to both Rachel and Devorah. Reuven dies. Shimon performs *chalitza* with Rachel. Rachel thereby acquires *chalutza* status with respect to Shimon, making her relatives forbidden to him. But Devorah, the co-wife, never underwent *chalitza* — the act of *chalitza* was performed only with Rachel. Since the *chalutza* status attaches only to the woman with whom the act was performed, Devorah is not Shimon's *chalutza*, and her relatives remain permissible to him.

### Haba al Tzarat

Against this background, Rav Tuvi bar Kisna citing Shmuel teaches: *haba al tzarat chalutza, havlad mamzer* — if Shimon goes ahead and has sexual relations with Devorah, the child is a *mamzer*. The reason: *be'issura kaima* — she retains her original forbidden status. Devorah was Reuven's wife. She would have been permitted to Shimon only through the act of *yibbum*. Since no act of *yibbum* was performed — and *chalitza* was performed to Rachel, not to Devorah — Devorah remains forbidden as a brother's wife, and relations with her produce a *mamzer*.

### Rav Yosef

Rav Yosef infers from the *mishna*'s ruling that the *chalutza* status applies exclusively to the woman who was party to the act. The *mishna* says he is permitted to marry Devorah's relatives. If Devorah herself were considered a *chalutza*, one could not explain why her relatives are permissible — they would be the relatives of a *chalutza* and therefore forbidden. It must be, then, that Devorah has no *chalutza* status whatsoever. This explains simultaneously two things: why he may marry Devorah's relatives (she is not his *chalutza*), and why relations with Devorah produce a *mamzer* (her status as brother's wife was never altered by the *chalitza* performed to Rachel).

### Rabbi Yochanan

A tension arises when the Gemara considers the position of Rabbi Yochanan. Rabbi Yochanan holds that neither the man nor his brothers incur *karet* for relations with either the *chalutza* herself or with her co-wife — *ein chayavin lo al hachalutza karet v'lo al tzarata karet*. This implies that Devorah's status *does* change as a consequence of the *chalitza* performed to Rachel — she is no longer considered a biblical *eshet ach* — yet the *mishna* still permits the man to marry Devorah's relatives. This seems contradictory: if her status changes enough to remove *karet*, why does she not acquire *chalutza* status sufficient to forbid her relatives?

### D'Oraisa vs. D'Rabbanan

Rabbi Yochanan's response is instructive: *v'chi tisbara? achot chalutza d'oraita?* Does anyone think the relative of a *chalutza* is a biblical prohibition? Reish Lakish already stated — *kan shana Rabbi: achot gerusha midivrei Torah, achot chalutza midivrei Soferim* — the sister of a *gerusha* is a biblical prohibition, whereas the sister of a *chalutza* is only rabbinic. This resolution hinges on distinguishing the *d'oraisa* plane from the *d'rabbanan* plane. On the biblical level, the *chalitza* performed to Rachel transforms the status of both Rachel and Devorah — neither is any longer *eshet ach* in the full biblical sense, and *karet* no longer applies. But the rabbinic enactment that forbids the relatives of a *chalutza* is a separate layer, and that rabbinic enactment is applied only to the woman who was actually party to the act, not to Devorah who was affected incidentally.

### Mai Shna Hai

The Gemara then addresses the final line of the *mishna*: not only is the man permitted with the relatives of his *chalutza*'s co-wife (*krovos tzaras chalutzaso*), but he is also forbidden with the co-wife of his *chalutza*'s relative (*tzara* of *krovat chalutzato*). The question is: *mai shna hai u'mai shna hai?* — why the asymmetry? One case is permitted, the other forbidden.

### Two Brothers

This is where Tosafot offers a fundamentally different reading of the *mishna*'s scenario. According to Rashi, the *mishna* is discussing a situation where Barak — a completely external party — was married to both Leah (the *chalutza*'s relative) and some second wife Devorah. But Tosafot finds this logically unsatisfying and the Gemara's answer strained under Rashi's reading. Tosafot instead reads the *mishna* as dealing with a case of two brothers married to two sisters — Levi, another brother of Shimon and Reuven, who was married to Leah. Under this reading, the scenario makes immediate sense.

### Tzarat Ervah

Once Shimon performed *chalitza* with Rachel, Rachel becomes like his ex-wife — *achos chalutza*, which carries the status of a quasi-*erva*. Leah, as Rachel's sister, is therefore a quasi-*erva* to Shimon as well. If Levi then dies, Leah falls before Shimon for *yibbum*. But Leah is a *tzarat erva* — the co-wife of a quasi-*erva* — and just as *tzarat erva* is exempt from *yibbum* on the biblical level, this rabbinic analog creates the same exemption. The answer to *mai shna hai u'mai shna hai* is therefore self-evident under Tosafot's reading: the woman who underwent the act of *chalitza* is the source of the *chalutza* status; *hach d'azla behada l'vei dina* — she who was brought to court and had the act performed with her acquires the full *chalutza* status, from which all subsequent prohibitions derive. The co-wife who never came to court, *d'lo azla behada l'vei dina*, acquires no *chalutza* status, so her relatives remain permissible — and yet, on the *d'oraisa* plane, her own status changes such that relations with her are no longer an *issur karet*.

---

## Shomeres Yavam

### Setup

The next *mishna* opens a new scenario that follows naturally from the Tosafot reading just discussed. *Hacholeitz l'yevimto v'nasa achiv et achoto* — a man performed *chalitza* with his *yevama*, and his brother then married her sister. So Shimon performed *chalitza* with Rachel, and Levi comes along and marries Leah, Rachel's sister. This is precisely the scenario that Tosafot identified in the previous *mishna*'s final case. Leah is forbidden to Shimon because she is his *chalutza*'s sister — a rabbinic *erva*. But Leah is permissible to Levi, because the *chalutza* status created by the *chalitza* act applies only between Shimon and Rachel, not between Levi and Rachel. Levi's ability to marry Leah is thus unaffected.

### Hamten

The complication arises when the *mishna* introduces the scenario of *shomeres yavam* — a woman awaiting *yibbum*. Here, Rachel was not yet a *chalutza* but a *shomeres yavam*, waiting for one of the brothers to act, while Levi went ahead and performed *kiddushin* with Leah. The problem: if Levi consummates with Leah, he will be having relations with *achot zikukato* — the sister of the woman to whom he has a *zika* (levirate bond). The ruling, in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, is *hamten* — wait. Levi must wait until Shimon performs either *yibbum* or *chalitza* with Rachel. Only once Shimon has done something to sever Levi's *zika* to Rachel may Levi proceed to consummate with Leah.

### Death Scenarios

Once Shimon performs *chalitza* or *yibbum* with Rachel, or if Rachel herself dies, Levi's relationship to Rachel is terminated and he may consummate with Leah. These are the uncomplicated resolutions. *Chalatz l'achiv o kinsah — yichnos et ishto; metah hayevama — yichnos et ishto.*

### Met Hayavam

The tragic scenario is when Shimon himself dies. Now Levi is stuck. Rachel falls before him as a second *yevama* through the now-deceased Shimon. What can Levi do? He cannot perform *yibbum*, because that would mean having relations with his wife's sister. He cannot do *chalitza* freely and then marry Rachel, because Rachel would then be his *chalutza* and Leah is Rachel's sister — he would be in the same trap. The ruling: *yotzi et ishto b'get v'eshet achiv b'chalitza* — he must divorce Leah and perform *chalitza* with Rachel. Both relationships must be dissolved; he cannot be with either woman.

### Wording

The Gemara notes a textual issue with the *mishna*'s transition. When the *mishna* moves from the *chalutza* case to the case of a genuine *gerusha*, it uses the language *v'chen* — "and similarly." But the cases are not similar at all: if Reuven genuinely divorced Rachel (making her a *gerusha*), and Levi then married Leah, Leah would be a full biblical *erva* to Levi — a *d'oraisa* prohibition — and she would need no *chalitza* at all; she is entirely exempt. So *v'chen* is misleading. The Gemara says: read it as *aval* — "but" — indicating a contrast rather than a similarity.

### Divorcee vs. Chalutza

This is the occasion for Reish Lakish's statement, already cited in an earlier context: *kan shana Rabbi: achas gerusha midivrei Torah, achas chalutza midivrei Soferim.* The sister of a *gerusha* is forbidden on a biblical level, and therefore Leah in the *gerusha* case requires no *chalitza* and is entirely exempt. The sister of a *chalutza* is forbidden only rabbinically, and therefore even though she may not do *yibbum*, she must nonetheless perform *chalitza*.

---

## Mesa Ishto Status

### Mahu B'Yevimto

The Gemara now poses the key question arising from the *shomeres yavam* scenario: *mesa ishto mahu b'yevimto?* If, after Levi married Leah and created the forbidden status for Rachel, Leah then dies — what is the law regarding Rachel? We know that in the *mishna*'s case, Rachel was initially a *shomeres yavam* and therefore permissible to Levi before his marriage to Leah. Marriage to Leah then made Rachel forbidden. But now that Leah is dead, does Rachel revert to her originally permitted status, or does she remain permanently forbidden?

The case involves a sequence of three statuses: first permitted (as *shomeres yavam*), then forbidden (when Levi married Leah), then potentially permitted again (when Leah dies). The question is whether the intermediate period of prohibition permanently locks in her status.

### Rav Position

Rav and Rabbi Chanina both hold: *mesa ishto, mutar b'yevimto* — if his wife dies, he may once again consummate with his *yevama*. Rava explains the reasoning: *mishum d'hava yevama she'hutrah, v'ne'esra, v'chazra v'hutrah* — she was a *yevama* who was permitted, became forbidden, and then became permitted again; *tachzor l'heiteira harishon* — she returns to her original status. The foundational identity of a *yevama* is determined at the moment of the husband's death. When Reuven died, Rachel was in no way an *erva* to Levi, and that basic, original status can reassert itself once the intervening obstacle is removed.

### Shmuel Position

Shmuel and Rav Assi disagree: *mesa ishto, assur b'yevimto.* Once forbidden, she remains forbidden — even though she was initially permitted and only became forbidden subsequently.

### Gimmel Achim

Rav Hamnuna challenges Rav's position with the following case: three brothers — Reuven, Shimon, and Levi — where Reuven and Shimon are married to two sisters, Rachel and Leah respectively, and Levi is single. Reuven dies. Levi performs a *ma'amar* with Rachel (a quasi-betrothal in the *yibbum* context). Then Shimon dies. Now Levi has a *zika* to Leah as well, while being quasi-married to Rachel. He cannot consummate with either, as one is his wife's sister and the other creates the symmetric problem. Then — and here is the crucial question — Leah dies. May Levi now consummate *yibbum* with Rachel?

### Shomeres Yavam

One might argue, using Rav's logic, that Rachel was initially permitted when she became a *yevama* through Reuven's death, that she became forbidden only because of Leah, and that now that Leah is gone, she should revert to her permitted status. But closer examination reveals the cases are not parallel. In the original case, Rachel was a *shomeres yavam* and thus permissible to Levi *before* he married Leah. It was only Levi's act of marrying Leah that then made Rachel forbidden. There was a genuine prior permitted state from Levi's perspective. In Rav Hamnuna's case, by contrast, when Leah became a *yevama* through Shimon's death, Levi had already performed a *ma'amar* with Rachel. At the very moment Leah entered *yevama* status, she was already the sister of someone who was quasi-his-wife. She was *never* permissible from the moment she became a *yevama*. Therefore — *otah yevamah choletzet v'lo mityabemet* — she may only perform *chalitza*. This seems to prove that even Rav would agree: a *yevama* who was never permitted cannot revert to a permitted state, and here there is nothing to revert *to*.

### Rabbi Eliezer

After this exchange, Rav was silenced — *ishtik* — apparently conceding the point. But after leaving, he reflected and said: why didn't I invoke Rabbi Eliezer? *Amai lo amart lei, Rabbi Elazar hi* — that case in the *beraita* is the position of Rabbi Eliezer, who holds *keivan she-amdah alav sha'ah achat be-issur, ne'esrah alav le-olam* — once a woman stood before him in a forbidden status for even one moment, she is forbidden to him forever. He could have said: I do not rule like Rabbi Eliezer — I rule that she may revert to being permitted — and you have cited a *beraita* that follows Rabbi Eliezer's stringent position.

### Gerusha Case

Then he reconsidered further: could I actually have said it was Rabbi Eliezer? When does Rabbi Eliezer say once forbidden, always forbidden? The case of Rabbi Eliezer is as follows: Reuven married Rachel, then divorced her. At that point, Rachel became a biblical *erva* to Shimon — a divorced brother's wife, without any context of *yibbum* whatsoever. Reuven then remarried Rachel. Reuven dies. Does Rachel now come before Shimon as a *yevama*, or does her earlier status as his brother's *gerusha* — which occurred outside any *yibbum* framework — permanently bar her? Rabbi Eliezer says yes, once she was forbidden to him, she remains forever forbidden.

### Lo Chazya

The critical limiting principle is: *heicha d'lo chazya bi-she'at nefilah* — Rabbi Eliezer's stringency applies where the woman was never in a permissible *yevama* status at the moment she became a *yevama*. In the *gerusha* case, when Reuven died and she became a *yevama*, her prior history of having been a divorced brother's wife outside the *yibbum* context meant she entered *yevama* status already tainted. But in Rav's case — the case of the *mishna* — when Reuven died and Rachel became a *shomeres yavam*, she was entirely permissible. The question is only whether a subsequent intervening prohibition (Levi's marriage to Leah) can permanently bar her.

### When Status Locks

So Rav Hamnuna's challenge ultimately resolves differently from what it first appeared. In the three-brothers case, Leah was never permissible *from the moment of her entry into yevama status* — and even Rav might agree she remains forbidden. In the original case, Rachel *was* permissible at the moment of entry into *yevama* status, and once Leah dies the question is whether she can revert. Rav says yes; Shmuel and Rav Assi say no. The *beraita* of Rabbi Eliezer cannot resolve this debate because Rabbi Eliezer's principle is limited to women who never had a permissible *yevama* status to begin with.

---

## Shlosh Chodashim

### Yevama

The *mishna* introduces an entirely new topic: *ha-yevama lo tachlot v'lo tityabem ad she-yeish la shlosha chodashim* — the *yevama* may not perform *chalitza* nor may she consummate *yibbum* for three months after the death of the husband. The concern, in a world without pregnancy testing, is to establish who the father of any child will be.

### Kol Hanashim

This rule is extended to all women whose marriages have ended: *v'chen kol sh'ar nashim* — widows and divorcees alike must wait three months before entering any new marital relationship. *Lo ye'arsu v'lo yinasu ad she-yeish lahem shlosha chodashim* — they may neither perform *kiddushin* nor proceed to *nisuin* during this period.

### Lo Ye'arsu

The extension to *kiddushin* is notable, since *kiddushin* without *nisuin* involves no sexual relations and would seem to pose no risk of paternity confusion. This prohibition on *kiddushin* is a kind of *lo plug* — a blanket rule that does not differentiate — because once you permit *kiddushin* for some women immediately, you risk confusion about which women may and may not proceed.

### Lo Plug

The first *tanna* draws no distinctions among women: *echad betulot v'echad be'ulot, echad gerushos v'echad almanos, echad nesuas v'echad arusos* — whether a virgin or a non-virgin, whether divorced or widowed, whether the first marriage involved full *nisuin* or only *eirusin*, all must wait three months. Even a woman who was only an *arusa* to her first husband — with no sexual contact possible — and who is now only about to be an *arusa* to her second husband — still involving no sexual contact — must wait. This double extension to cases where the concern is entirely theoretical represents a deliberate *lo plug*.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda takes a more calibrated position. Women who had been *nesuous* to their first husbands — where sex was possible and the pregnancy concern is real — must wait before proceeding to *nisuin* with their second husbands, but they may at least enter *kiddushin* in the interim, since *kiddushin* alone does not permit sexual relations. Women who had only been *arusot* to their first husbands — where sex was not permitted — may proceed directly to *nisuin* with their second husbands, since there is no possibility they are pregnant. He does not accept the *lo plug* reasoning.

### Arusa B'Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda's single exception is the *arusa* from Yehuda — *mipnei shelibo gas bah* — because in Yehuda the practice was for the *arus* and *arusa* to spend private time together before *nisuin*, becoming comfortable with one another. This private time occasionally led to sexual relations, meaning *arusot* in Yehuda could in fact be pregnant. Therefore they must also wait, and may not even enter *kiddushin* with their next partner during the three-month period.

### Rabbi Yosi

Rabbi Yosi agrees with Rabbi Yehuda's general framework — that *kiddushin* is permissible for all women during the three months — but adds one exception for a different reason entirely: *chutz min ha'almana mipnei ha'eivul* — a widow must wait because of the *aveilus* mourning period. Even setting aside the pregnancy concern, Rabbi Yosi holds that propriety requires a widow to complete her mourning before taking a new partner, and therefore she may not even perform *kiddushin* until the *aveilus* has concluded.

---

## Shma Yehei Velad

### Ben Kayama

The Gemara now analyzes the *mishna*'s reasoning. The most obvious question is: why may the *yevama* not do either *chalitza* or *yibbum* for three months? The concern is *shema yehei velad ben kayama* — perhaps there is a viable child in utero. If there is, no action is necessary or appropriate.

### Eshet Ach

For *yibbum*, the concern is particularly weighty. If the woman is pregnant and the child is viable, there is no *mitzvah* of *yibbum*, and performing *yibbum* would constitute a violation of the biblical prohibition of *eshet ach* — *vekapaga be'issur eshet ach de'oraisa*.

### Karoz

But why should *chalitza* be delayed? Surely *chalitza* cannot violate a biblical prohibition even if a child exists. The *mishna* must be implying that *chalitzas me'uberes* — *chalitza* with a pregnant woman — does not take effect. This, indeed, was the subject of an earlier dispute, where Rabbi Yochanan held that *chalitzo me'uberes shema chalitza* — it does take effect. Our *mishna*'s prohibition on *chalitza* within three months would then seem to contradict Rabbi Yochanan's position. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan has already been challenged on this point before, and piles on this *mishna* as an additional proof against him.

The Gemara then offers Rabbi Yochanan a defense. Even if *chalitza* with a pregnant woman is technically valid, we still prohibit it *lechatchila* for a practical reason: *shema yehei velad ben kayama* — perhaps the child is viable, meaning *chalitza* was not needed at all — *venimtzesa ata matzricha karoz l'kehuna* — and then a retraction must be announced, correcting the public impression that she has become a *chalutza* (which would disqualify her from marrying a *kohen*). The Gemara proposes: just make the announcement. The Gemara responds: *dilma ika d'havai bachalitza v'lo havai bahachraza* — perhaps some who were present at the *chalitza* ceremony were not present at the retraction, and they will go about saying she is disqualified from marrying a *kohen* without having heard the correction. Like a retraction printed in small type the following day, the announcement does not reach everyone.

### Grusha

A further question: even granting that concern, why does the three-month waiting period apply to a *grusha*? If the woman had already been divorced from a previous marriage before marrying Reuven, she is already disqualified from marrying a *kohen* regardless of any *chalitza* status. The concern about an uncorrected *karoz* therefore does not apply. So why cannot Shimon proceed to *chalitza* with her immediately?

### Mezonos

The Gemara's answer reframes the entire rationale: *mishum d'mapslu lah mimezonos* — because performing *chalitza* prematurely would deprive the woman of her *mezonos*, the financial support she is entitled to receive from the deceased husband's estate during the waiting period. Before *chalitza* is performed, she is supported by the estate. Once *chalitza* is performed, that entitlement ends. The Gemara is therefore saying: regardless of the *kohen* concern, there is an independent reason not to perform *chalitza* too early — it removes her from the estate's support before the appropriate time.

The Gemara presses further: this works for a *nesu'ah* — a woman who was in full *nisuin* and therefore entitled to *mezonos* from the estate. But what about an *arusa* who had only *kiddushin* and is therefore not entitled to *mezonos*, and who was also a *gerusha* from a previous marriage? The *kohen* concern does not apply (already disqualified), and the *mezonos* concern does not apply (she has no entitlement). Why must she wait?

### Oleh Leyibum

The Gemara's final answer invokes the principle of Rabbi Yosi: *ella mishum d'Rabbi Yosi* — because of Rabbi Yosi's teaching. A *ma'aseh* is cited in which someone came before Rabbi Yosi and asked whether he could perform *chalitza* within the three months. Rabbi Yosi said no. The petitioner pressed: *v'sachloz umah bekach?* — what would be the harm? Rabbi Yosi responded by citing the verse — *im lo yachpotz*, "if he does not wish" — implying that the alternative of *yibbum* must be a genuine option: *ha im chafetz, yabem*. This leads to the principle: *kol ha'oleh leyibum oleh lechaltiza v'kol she'eino oleh leyibum eino oleh lechaltiza* — whoever is eligible for *yibbum* is eligible for *chalitza*, and whoever is ineligible for *yibbum* is ineligible for *chalitza*. We perform *chalitza* only where *yibbum* would also have been a valid option. Since during the first three months, *yibbum* is not a valid option — the child may be viable — *chalitza* is likewise not performed. Rabbi Yosi's principle thus provides a conceptual ground for the three-month restriction that applies even where the *mezonos* and *kohen* concerns are absent. As Rashi observes, this principle holds even in cases where *yibbum* is ultimately forbidden rabbinically, so long as *chalitza* is performed only when *yibbum* could theoretically be an option — that is, *lechatchila*, we confine *chalitza* to contexts where the *yibbum* option genuinely exists.

---

---

# Yevamot 42

## Three-Month Wait

### Three-Month Wait Intro

The daf opens on 42b, picking up approximately five lines from the top, with the Mishnah's statement *achas besulos v'achas beulos* — whether the woman is a virgin or a non-virgin, whether her first marriage was *eirusin* or *nissuin*, she must wait three months before remarrying. The rationale is the familiar principle of *lo plug*: even in cases where logic would seem to confirm that pregnancy is impossible, we do not make distinctions. The Gemara then opens by asking why the Mishnah needed to list both categories of virgin/*arusa* and non-virgin/*nesuah* separately, since they appear to overlap entirely.

### Virgin/Non-Virgin Distin…

The Gemara resolves this: *hachi ka'amar* — what the Mishnah is saying is that the categories of virgin and non-virgin simply map onto the categories of *eirusin* and *nissuin*, respectively. They are not independent variables but rather explanatory: women widowed or divorced from *eirusin* and women widowed or divorced from *nissuin*. The two terms elaborate the same two categories rather than introducing additional ones.

Following this, we are told that *Rabbi Eliezer* did not come to the *beis medrash* on a particular occasion. He later encountered *Rabbi Assi* and inquired what had been taught. Rabbi Assi reported: *hachi amar Rabbi Yochanan, halacha k'Rabbi Yossi* — Rabbi Yochanan ruled that we follow Rabbi Yossi, who holds that we do *not* apply *lo plug*. Both Rabbi Yossi and Rabbi Yehuda agree that the three-month wait is only necessary when the first marriage involved *nissuin* and the new marriage will also be *nissuin* — i.e., when there was an opportunity for marital relations at both ends. If either stage is merely *eirusin*, there is no concern, and Rabbi Yossi adds a separate point regarding *aveilus* that we will address later.

### Lo Plug as Daas Yachid

This ruling prompts the Gemara to observe: *mikhlal d'yechida pligi alei* — does this imply that the *stam* voice in the Mishnah, which demands the three-month wait universally and thus represents the position of *lo plug*, is in fact not the consensus but a *daas yachid*, a single minority opinion? The Gemara answers: *in* — yes, and it can be demonstrated from a *braisa*.

### Pregnancy-Impossible Cas…

The *braisa* enumerates a long series of cases in which we can effectively presume that the woman is not pregnant, yet the requirement to wait three months nonetheless applies. Among these: a woman who was always running off to her father's house during the marriage (*redufa l'beis aviha*), a woman who was in open conflict with her husband (*katata im ba'ala*), a woman whose husband was imprisoned, or was elderly, or was sick, or who was herself ill. Additionally: a woman who suffered a miscarriage after her husband's death, a woman who was infertile (*akara*), a woman who was post-menopausal (*zkeina*), a woman who was too young, a woman born incapable of bearing children (*ailonis*), or any woman for whatever reason incapable of giving birth. In all of these cases, *Rabbi Meir* says she must wait three months.

Then Rabbi Yehuda — and some have the variant reading *Rabbi Yossi*, since both make a similar distinction — says: *matir l'areis v'linasei miyad*, she may perform *eirusin* immediately, and in these specific cases where pregnancy is impossible, she may even proceed to *nissuin* immediately. The *lo plug* position is thus identified as the view of *Rabbi Meir* alone — a *daas yachid* — which is why Rabbi Yochanan was able to rule against it, following Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Yossi, who permit immediate *nissuin* in circumstances where pregnancy is demonstrably impossible.

---

## R. Yochanan Reversal

### Chazar Bo Ruling

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba then reports: *chazar bo Rabbi Yochanan* — Rabbi Yochanan reversed himself. He now reverts to *lo plug* and holds that the three-month wait is always required. Rav Yosef explains the reason for this reversal: *mi-misneisa d'karma hadar bei* — he reversed himself on account of the *braisa* from *Kerem B'Yavne*. As the *braisa* records, Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka testified: I heard from the sages gathered in *Kerem B'Yavne* — the seat of rabbinic authority established after the destruction of the Temple, so called because the sages sat in rows like a vineyard — *kulam tzrichin l'hamtin shlosha chodashim*, all women, without exception, must wait three months. No distinction is made based on the possibility or impossibility of pregnancy.

### Stam Mishna Challenge

Rabbi Yirmiya then instructs Rabbi Zeira: when you appear before *Rabbi Abbahu*, present him with the following contradiction. On one hand, Rabbi Yochanan ruled *halacha k'Rabbi Yossi*, following the opinion that we do not apply *lo plug*. On the other hand, Rabbi Yochanan is the one who established the principle that *halacha k'stam mishna* — we rule in accordance with the anonymous, unattributed Mishnah. And our Mishnah states *stam*, without attribution, that all women must wait three months regardless of whether they are virgins or not. How could Rabbi Yochanan have originally ruled against that *stam*?

Rabbi Abbahu's response is sharp: *lo chash l'kimchei* — the one who raised that question has not ground his flour properly; it is an unworthy question. The case before us is not a simple *stam mishna* — it is a case of *stam v'acharav machlokes*: the Mishnah first presents an anonymous ruling and then immediately records a dispute. Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yossi disagree right there in the very same Mishnah. When Rabbi Yochanan says we rule according to the *stam mishna*, that principle applies only when the *stam* stands uncontested in its own context, while dissenting opinions are found elsewhere — in other *mishnayos* or in a *braisa*. But when the Mishnah itself voices the disagreement immediately after the *stam*, that is a case of *stam v'acharav machlokes*, and that configuration carries different weight.

### Stam V'Achar Machloket

The governing rule is stated explicitly: *machlokes v'acharakav stam, halacha k'stam* — if a dispute appears first and is then followed by a *stam*, we rule according to the *stam*. But *stam v'acharakav machlokes, ein halacha k'stam* — if the *stam* comes first and is then followed by a dispute, we do not necessarily rule according to the *stam*. This does not necessarily mean we rule against the *stam*, but it does mean we are not obligated to follow it in the way we would follow an unchallenged *stam*. This is why Rabbi Yochanan was initially free to rule like Rabbi Yossi, notwithstanding the *stam* in the Mishnah. When he subsequently reversed himself, it was due to the independent authority of the *braisa* from *Kerem B'Yavne*, not because of the *stam*.

This principle — that *stam* followed by *machlokes* does not carry binding force — has broad significance well beyond our *sugya*. The same hermeneutic logic applies to the interpretation of the *Shulchan Aruch*: when the *Shulchan Aruch* states a ruling anonymously and then introduces *v'yesh omrim*, there is a developed jurisprudence around which opinion is operative, parallel to the Talmudic questions of *stam v'yesh omrim* and *yesh omrim v'stam*.

It is worth noting that the Gemara had earlier identified the *stam* voice in this Mishnah as representing *Rabbi Meir*. This observation is appropriate, since *stam mishna aliba d'Rabbi Meir* — the anonymous Mishnah generally reflects Rabbi Meir's position. The Gemara's point that the *stam* is really a *daas yachid* carries extra weight here, since every *stam* is in some sense traceable to Rabbi Meir rather than to a genuine consensus.

### Stam/Machloket Configs

Rabbi Abbahu's attendant (*shammash*) uses their time together — as Rabbi Abbahu was being supported on the attendant's shoulders and the attendant was gathering *halachos* from him — to work through several configurations of *stam* and *machlokes* across different sources. The attendant asks: *machlokes v'achar kach stam, mai?* — if the dispute appears first and the *stam* follows, what do we say? Rabbi Abbahu answers: *halacha k'stam*, we rule according to the *stam*. And if the *stam* appears first and the *machlokes* follows? *Ein halacha k'stam*.

Then the question of cross-source configurations: *stam* in the Mishnah, *machlokes* in a *braisa* — what is the rule? *Halacha k'stam*, still follow the *stam*. If anything, this is even clearer than the case where the debate is embedded within the Mishnah itself. What about the reverse — *machlokes* in the Mishnah and *stam* in a *braisa*? Rabbi Abbahu answers: *v'chi Rabbi lo shna'ah, Rabbi Chiya m'na lei* — if Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi chose not to codify that position as a *stam* in the Mishnah, on what basis would Rabbi Chiya's transmission of it as a *stam* in the *braisa* override that? The Mishnah carries supreme authority; the compiler's editorial choices are themselves normative signals. The fact that Rabbi chose not to present a given opinion as an uncontested ruling in the Mishnah cannot simply be overridden by Rabbi Chiya's different editorial decision in the *braisa*.

---

## Combs Digression

### Flax/Wool Combs

The attendant now challenges Rabbi Abbahu's principle by producing a *stam mishna* that everyone knows is not ruled upon in practice. The Mishnah in question concerns combs — specifically, flax combs and wool combs — and whether they remain susceptible to *tumah* when their teeth have been broken off.

The relevant Mishnah teaches: regarding a flax comb (*masreika shel pishtan*) whose teeth have been removed — if two teeth remain together (*nishtayaru vo shtayim*), the comb is *tamei*, meaning it retains its status as a functional vessel and can become *tamei*. If only one tooth remains (*achas*), it is *tehorah*, since a comb with a single tooth is no longer functionally a comb and loses its *kli* status. As for the individual teeth themselves that break off one by one, they are *temeios* — susceptible to *tumah* — because a single tooth can be repurposed as something like a toothpick.

The Mishnah then turns to a wool comb (*shel tzemer*): if teeth are missing such that there is a gap of one between every two remaining teeth (*achas mibein shtayim*), it is *tehorah*. If three teeth remain in one place (*nishtayaru vo gimel bemakom echad*), it is *tamei*. If the outermost tooth is one of those three, it is *tehorah*, since the outer teeth are less functionally significant than the inner ones. If two teeth broke off together and can serve as a tweezer-like implement, they are *temeios*. If a single tooth was fashioned into a lamp cleaner or thread-stretcher (*tikkena l'ner o l'misuach*), it is *tamei*.

The point of invoking this Mishnah is this: *dekayma lan de'ein halacha k'zos hamishna* — we know that the *halacha* is not like this Mishnah. Here is an apparently uncontested *stam mishna* that is nonetheless not followed. How then can one maintain that we always rule according to a *stam mishna*?

The Gemara does not immediately accept the attendant's challenge at face value, however, and instead probes whether the Mishnah is internally consistent at all. The section on the wool comb appears contradictory: one clause implies that two teeth together render the comb *tamei*, while the concluding clause states that only three together do so. The Gemara asks: *umai kashya* — is this truly a contradiction? Perhaps the two clauses refer to different types of teeth — inner teeth versus outer teeth (*gavyaysa* vs. *varaysa*), as Rashi explains in terms of a two-tiered comb structure where the outer teeth scrape and the inner teeth collect. The outer teeth require three in one place to constitute a functional configuration; the inner teeth require only two.

The Gemara then pursues a different internal contradiction between the flax and wool sections. By the flax comb, individual broken teeth are *temeios* without any modification — it is assumed they can naturally serve as toothpicks. By the wool comb, a single tooth is *tamei* only *if* it was modified and fashioned into a usable instrument. That appears contradictory. The Gemara proposes: perhaps one speaks of a tooth that broke off with a piece of the base still attached (*b'kataya*) and one of a tooth that broke off cleanly without the base (*b'lo kataya*) — the tooth with a base-piece has a natural handle and needs no modification, while the bare tooth requires fashioning. Rav Papa offers yet another resolution: perhaps the difference is between thin teeth and thick teeth (*katinta* vs. *alimta*), where the thinner ones naturally lend themselves to reuse while the thicker ones do not.

### Comb Mishna Attribution

After exhausting these resolutions, the Gemara concedes that the internal contradictions can in fact be resolved — the Mishnah may not be genuinely problematic at all. But then the Gemara discloses the true reason we do not rule like this Mishnah: *mishum demasaymi bei dokanay, zu divrei Rabbi Shimon* — those who are precise about the text (*dokanai*) conclude the Mishnah with the words *zu divrei Rabbi Shimon*: "these are the words of Rabbi Shimon." It is therefore not a true *stam mishna* in the first place. Other textual versions attribute the ruling explicitly to Rabbi Shimon, and once the opinion carries an attribution, the rule of following the *stam* does not apply. The attendant's challenge thus collapses: this is not a case where a genuine *stam mishna* is overridden — it is a case where the *stam* is more apparent than real. Certain manuscripts and precise transmitters record it with explicit attribution, and that suffices to classify it as a named opinion.

This entire digression — remarkable in how many distinct sub-questions it generates about combs and tumah — is in the end a vehicle for clarifying the limits and the reliability of the principle of *halacha k'stam mishna*.

---

## Day 90 vs. Day 91

### Eirusin Within 3 Months

Returning to the main topic of the three-month wait, the Gemara records a ruling transmitted by *Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avin*: *ma'arsin toch gimel* — one may perform *eirusin* within the three-month period. This reflects the approach of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that *eirusin* does not place the woman in a context where she could become pregnant, and therefore does not trigger the waiting requirement. Furthermore, *v'chein osin ma'aseh* — this is the operative practice. Rabbi Elazar is also cited as having taught similarly in the name of *Rabbi Chanina hagadol*.

Associated with this position is the teaching that *rubo shel rishon, v'emtza'i mishalem, v'ruvo shel shelishi* — the majority of the first month, the entirety of the middle month, and the majority of the third month would suffice as the requisite waiting period. This formulation is striking, and neither Rashi nor Tosafot engage with it directly in the context of the Gemara's discussion. One possible reading is that this opinion does not accept the Gemara's earlier principle that a viable birth can occur after six months and two days of gestation — perhaps this view requires a full seven months. If so, then waiting two months plus a portion of a third would be sufficient to rule out the earliest possible birth being attributed to the deceased husband. This remains somewhat unclear from the Gemara's framing. Tosafot suggests this lenient calculation applies only to the case of an *arusah* — it represents not a complete waiver of the three-month period but a more flexible definition of how those three months are measured.

### Amimar vs. Rav Ashi

*Ameimar* went further and ruled that one may even perform *eirusin* on day ninety itself — the ninetieth day counting from the husband's death. This reflects a measure of leniency in defining the conclusion of the three-month period, stopping short of requiring a full ninety-one days. Rav Ashi challenged this position.

### Rav/Shmuel Exclusion Rule

Rav Ashi invoked the joint ruling of *Rav and Shmuel*, who both stated: *tzricha l'hamtin gimel chodashim, chutz mi'yom she'meis bo v'chutz mi'yom she'nis'arsah bo* — the woman must wait three months, not including the day of the husband's death and not including the day of the *eirusin*. The practical implication is that the *eirusin* must be performed on day ninety-one, not day ninety. Ameimar attempted to deflect this: he argued that the citation from Rav and Shmuel was not about the three-month wait at all, but about the twenty-four-month nursing period — the rule that a nursing mother must wait twenty-four months before remarrying, *chutz mi'yom she'nolad bo v'chutz mi'yom she'nis'arsah bo*, not counting the day of the birth and not counting the day of the *eirusin*, so that the wedding takes place on the twenty-fifth month. Rav Ashi rejected this reading: the formulation applies to both contexts.

### Final: 3 Months Always

The Gemara then records a case involving someone who made a *seudat erusin* — a betrothal feast — on the ninetieth day; *Rava* voided the event and required them to wait until the following day. The Gemara notes that this case was actually a *seudat nissuin*, a full marriage feast, not merely *eirusin* — and naturally, for *nissuin*, day ninety-one is unambiguously required.

The *hilchata* — the authoritative conclusion — is stated: for the nursing mother's twenty-four-month wait, not counting the day of the birth and not counting the day of *kiddushin*, so the wedding falls on the twenty-fifth month. For the three-month remarriage wait, not counting the day of death and not counting the day of *eirusin*, so *eirusin* falls on day ninety-one.

The most significant point of the conclusion, beyond the day-ninety versus day-ninety-one question, is that *lo plug* is fully in force: even *eirusin* requires a complete three-month wait. The discussions of leniency — whether to permit *eirusin* within three months, or to count day ninety as sufficient — are consistently ruled against. The final position is unequivocal: three months are required across the board, including for *eirusin*.

---

## Pregnancy Testing

### Pregnancy Test Validity

One might conclude from the *lo plug* ruling that modern pregnancy tests cannot satisfy the requirement — that we always demand three months regardless. But this may not follow. The Gemara itself, in earlier portions of the *sugya*, entertained the possibility of physical tests to establish the woman's status. That suggests the underlying concern is not three months for its own sake, but rather a reliable determination of whether she is pregnant.

Understood this way, there are two distinct questions. The first is whether we require *some* means of determination in all cases. The second is whether the only valid means is the three-month wait, or whether an alternative means — such as a modern pregnancy test — would be equally acceptable. There is a coherent argument that *lo plug* operates on the first question, not necessarily on the second. The rationale of *lo plug* is not that we genuinely believe a post-menopausal woman might be pregnant; rather, we do not wish to create distinctions between cases, lest some genuine cases of potential pregnancy slip through undetected. If that is the concern, then *lo plug* demands that we require *a* determination in all cases — but the determination itself need not be limited to the passage of three months. A reliable pregnancy test, even for a woman where pregnancy is biologically impossible, might satisfy the requirement under this logic: we require the test universally, but we allow the test to substitute for the three-month wait. Whether *poskim* in fact permit this is a *machlokes haposkim*, and the question is live.

---

## Eirusin/Aveilus Issue

### R. Yossi Widow Exception

We now turn to the second dimension of Rabbi Yossi's position: his exception for widows. As the Mishnah records, even if *eirusin* is otherwise permissible within the three-month period — because *eirusin* does not place the woman in a context of marital relations — a widow (*almanah*) may not enter into *eirusin* during the first month, because she is still in *aveilus* for her deceased husband. The paradigmatic case involves a woman who was *nesuah* to her first husband, who died; she is in *aveilus* for him. She is now going to perform *eirusin* with a second man. Since the new relationship is only *eirusin* — not yet *nissuin* — there is no concern of pregnancy attribution. But the first month of *aveilus* for the deceased husband still applies, and during that period, the *eirusin* cannot take place.

The complication that the Gemara will work through is this: the assumption that there is no *aveilus* for a relationship that was merely *eirusin* is universal and undisputed. If the deceased husband and this woman were only *arusim* — never *nesuim* — she would not be in *aveilus* at all. So Rabbi Yossi's exception must be addressing a case where the first marriage was *nissuin*, meaning she genuinely is in *aveilus*, and the new relationship is going to be *eirusin*, which is why there is no pregnancy concern — but the *aveilus* concern remains.

### Kal V'Chomer Argument

*Rav Chisda* challenges this by means of a *kal vachomer*: if during a period when laundering is forbidden — such as the first week of *shiva* — *eirusin* is nonetheless permitted, then certainly during the rest of the month of *aveilus*, when laundering *is* permitted, *eirusin* should be permitted. The *kal vachomer* rests on the premise that *eirusin* does not constitute the kind of *simcha* that is prohibited during *aveilus* — only *nissuin* does. It is well established, after all, that one may perform *kiddushin* even on *Tisha B'Av* itself, as *Shmuel* rules based on the concern *shema yekadmena acher* — lest someone else preempt him in betrothing the woman. If *kiddushin* is permitted on *Tisha B'Av*, how can it be restricted during the less stringent later period of personal *aveilus*?

### Tisha B'Av Kiddushin

The Gemara probes the sources underlying this *kal vachomer*. A Mishnah teaches that during the week in which *Tisha B'Av* falls (*shavua she'chal bo Tisha B'Av*), one may not get a haircut or do laundry. A *braisa* then states that beginning from *Rosh Chodesh Av*, the public limits its commerce, building, and planting — but *ma'arsin*, *kiddushin* may be performed. One may not, however, bring the woman into the home (*lo konsin*) — *nissuin* is prohibited. Nor may one hold a *seudat erusin*, a betrothal feast, though the act of *kiddushin* itself is permitted.

The Gemara then complicates the *kal vachomer*: perhaps the *braisa*'s phrase "before this time" (*kodem hazman hazeh*) does not mean during *Rosh Chodesh Av* in anticipation of *Tisha B'Av*, but rather before the week of *Tisha B'Av* itself — and during the actual week of *Tisha B'Av*, even *kiddushin* is forbidden. Rava responds: *v'kodem d'kodem nami kal v'chomer* — even if *kiddushin* is forbidden during the week of *Tisha B'Av*, I can reconstruct the *kal vachomer* using the earlier period. During the nine days when business is restricted (*mishenikhnas Av mema'atin b'simcha*), *kiddushin* is still permitted. Certainly then, during the month of personal *aveilus* when business is *not* restricted, *kiddushin* should be permitted.

### Case Flip Strategy

At this point the Gemara shifts strategy. The *kal vachomer* appears compelling — *eirusin* seems like it should always be permitted during *aveilus*. The Gemara therefore concludes that it must reread Rabbi Yossi's position entirely. Rather than accepting the plain reading of the Mishnah — that Rabbi Yossi says *all women may do eirusin* except for the *almanah* who is in *aveilus* — the Gemara proposes: *lo teima d'Rabbi Yossi omer kol hanashim ye'arsu; ella eima kol hanashim yinashu* — do not read it as saying all women may do *eirusin*; read it instead as saying all women may do *nissuin*, except for the *almanah* due to her *aveilus*. On this reading, *eirusin* is entirely unmentioned and unproblematic; it is *nissuin* that Rabbi Yossi is discussing.

The Gemara immediately asks: but *nissuin* is a problem for all women during the three-month waiting period — why would the *almanah* be singled out? The answer: *leit lei l'Rabbi Yossi l'havchana* — Rabbi Yossi is not concerned with establishing paternity. He does not require the three-month wait in principle. So for Rabbi Yossi, *nissuin* is generally permitted immediately after widowhood or divorce; the only constraint is *aveilus*.

An alternative formulation is then proposed: perhaps Rabbi Yossi is saying that *all arusot grushot* — women who were *arusot* and are now *grushot* (divorcees), not *almanos* — may proceed to *nissuin*. The case is inverted: the first marriage was *eirusin* (hence no pregnancy concern), and the question is whether the woman may proceed to *nissuin* in the new marriage. The *almanah* from *eirusin* cannot, because — but now the Gemara will question even that, since it is precisely the case of an *almanah from eirusin* that raises the problem: does she have *aveilus* at all?

### Braita Reinterpretation

The Gemara continues to work through this reinterpretation in a *braisa*. The *braisa* states: *Rabbi Yossi omer kol hanashim yit-arsu chutz m'almanah min ha-eibol* — all women may perform *eirusin* except for the *almanah* due to *aveilus*, and the period of her *aveilus* is thirty days. Furthermore, all women may not do *nissuin* until three months have passed.

The plain reading of this *braisa* corresponds to the plain reading of the Mishnah: *neshuot* may do *eirusin*, with the only exception being the *almanah* during her month of *aveilus*. The Gemara had earlier resolved the Mishnah by inverting its terms; it now attempts the same with the *braisa*. *Okmina b'arusot* — we interpret the Mishnah's references not to *neshuot* doing *eirusin*, but to *arusot grushot* doing *nissuin*. And *hachi nami kol arusot grushot yinase'u* — the *braisa* similarly is reread: all *arusot grushot* may proceed to *nissuin*.

The end of the *braisa* — *v'kulan lo yinase'u ad sheyihiye lahem gimel chodashim* — yields a further inference: *ha arusah shapir dami* — if the woman started as an *arusah*, she may presumably perform *eirusin* and even proceed to *nissuin* immediately. This would imply that Rabbi Yossi permits a *nesuah* to perform *eirusin* freely. Rava intervenes: *tartzei v'eima hachi* — reread the end of the *braisa* as well. Rabbi Yossi's ruling is now to be read as: all *arusot grushot* may do *nissuin*, except for the *almanah* who is in *aveilus* for thirty days. And in the reverse case: *nesuos lo yisarsu ad she'yehu lahem shlosha chodashim* — women who were *nesuot* may not do *eirusin* until three months have passed.

This rewriting is acknowledged as extremely complex. What is not fully explained in the Gemara is why Rabbi Yossi, once his case is flipped to be about an *arusah* doing *nissuin*, should thereby be committed to prohibiting a *nesuah* from doing *eirusin* in all circumstances. Why could he not hold, like Rabbi Yehuda, that as long as one of the two stages is *eirusin*, there is no pregnancy concern? The Gemara does not fully resolve this, but the result of the entire textual reworking is to demonstrate that the Gemara is bothered by any reading of Rabbi Yossi under which *eirusin* would be restricted during *aveilus*, and it therefore inverts his case so that only *nissuin* is at stake.

### No Aveilus Eirusin

The fundamental premise underlying all of this is now made explicit: does a woman who was only *arusa* — never *nesua* — to a man have *aveilus* if he dies? A *braisa* transmitted by *Rabbi Chiya bar Ami* is unequivocal: if a man's wife was only his *arusa*, he is not an *onen* for her if she dies, and if he is a *kohen*, he does not become *tamei* for her. Similarly, if the husband dies, she is not an *onenet* and has no burial obligations toward him. If she dies, he does not inherit her. If he dies, she is entitled to collect her *kesubah* — the basic sum of two hundred *zuz* is owed from the time of *eirusin* — but she has no *aveilus* obligations. There is thus no *aveilus* whatsoever in an *eirusin* relationship, neither for the man nor the woman.

This brings the Gemara back to where it began. No one disputes that there is no *aveilus* for an *eirusin* relationship. Therefore, if the case involves a woman who was only *arusa* to her first husband and he died, she is in no *aveilus* at all and could in principle do *kiddushin* immediately. If the case involves a woman who was *nesuah* to her first husband, she is in *aveilus*, but in order to remove the three-month pregnancy concern, the new relationship must be *eirusin* — and that raises the question of why *eirusin* would be problematic during *aveilus*.

### Tannaim Debate

The Gemara resolves the tension: *ella tanai hi* — the question of whether *eirusin* is prohibited during personal *aveilus* is itself a *machlokes tannaim*. A *braisa* records: from *Rosh Chodesh Av* until the fast, one limits business and also refrains from *me'ares u'milisa* — from *eirusin* and *nissuin*. Then, during the week in which *Tisha B'Av* falls, haircuts and laundry are also prohibited. Some say the haircut and laundry restrictions extend through the entire month.

According to one opinion in this *braisa*, then, even *eirusin* is prohibited during the nine days preceding *Tisha B'Av*. It is that position which Rabbi Yossi follows when he prohibits *eirusin* during personal *aveilus*.

Rav Ashi then raises a careful question: when the *braisa* prohibits *eirusin* before *Tisha B'Av*, does it really mean the formal act of *kiddushin*, or does it mean only the *seudat erusin* — the betrothal feast? Perhaps the act of *kiddushin* itself is always permitted, and only the feast is restricted. The Gemara pushes back: by the same token, when the *braisa* prohibits *nissuin*, would we say only the *seudat nissuin* is forbidden but the actual bringing-in of the bride is permitted? Obviously not — *nissuin* without a feast still constitutes the full *simcha* of marriage. But *eirusin* without a feast is a different matter: *erusin belo seuda mi ika simcha?* — is there any *simcha* at all in *eirusin* without a feast? The answer is that there is not. Therefore, the *braisa*'s prohibition of *eirusin* must refer only to the feast, and the act of *kiddushin* itself is always permitted.

We are thus back to the original question: if *kiddushin* itself is always permitted even during the *Tisha B'Av* period, what is Rabbi Yossi's basis for restricting it during personal *aveilus*?

### Aveilus Chadasha

*Rav Ashi* resolves this definitively: *shani aveilus chadasha m'aveilus yeshana* — a fresh, new *aveilus* differs from an old, commemorative one. *Tisha B'Av* is an *aveilus yeshana*, an ancient collective mourning; its demands are real but not of the same intimate, personal character as fresh personal mourning. Additionally: *shani aveilus d'rabbim m'aveilus d'yachid* — communal *aveilus* differs from individual *aveilus*. While one might argue that communal *aveilus* is more weighty in some respects — it affects the entire people — it is also less personally intimate than the acute grief of an individual mourner. Any evidence drawn from the *Tisha B'Av* laws is therefore inapplicable to the case of personal, fresh *aveilus*. Rabbi Yossi is entitled to hold — and Rabbi Yehuda may disagree — that in a personal, newly occurring *aveilus*, there is an *issur* of *kiddushin*. And with that resolution, we return to the simple reading of the Mishnah: Rabbi Yossi says *eirusin* is restricted during the first month of personal *aveilus*.

---

## Four Brothers Setup

### Mishna: 4 Brothers

The daf concludes with the opening of a new Mishnah. *Arba'ah achim nesuim arba nashim u'metu* — four brothers were married to four women, and all four brothers died. The Mishnah does not specify that the four wives are sisters; it is simply presenting a scenario in which a single surviving fifth brother is faced with multiple *yibum* obligations simultaneously, from the wives of four of his brothers. The question is how he may and should proceed. *Im ratza hagadol shebahem l'yavem et kullan, hareshut b'yado* — if the oldest brother wishes to perform *yibum* with all four of them, the prerogative is his. The responsibility devolves upon the eldest surviving brother, and he may choose to perform *yibum* with any or all of the *yevamos*.

### Chalitzah Disqualifies

A related rule is introduced: *mi she-hayah nasui l'shtei nashim u-meit* — if a man was married to two women and died, and *chalitzah* was performed with one of them, or marital relations were established with one of them, the co-wife (*tzarah*) is automatically released. Either *chalitzah* or *biah* with one of the *yevamos* exempts all the others.

### Preference Strategy

A practical principle follows: *hayetah achas k'sheirah v'achas p'sulah* — if one of the two wives was *k'sheirah* and the other was already *p'sulah l'kehunah* — for instance, she was a *grushah* from a prior marriage, and performing *chalitzah* with her would not add to her *pesulah* status since she already bears it — then if the *yavam* intends to perform *chalitzah*, he should perform *chalitzah* with the *p'sulah*, thereby not rendering the *k'sheirah* wife *p'sulah* to a *kohen* by virtue of *chalitzah*. Conversely, if the *yavam* intends to perform *yibum*, he should perform *yibum* with the *k'sheirah* — the more strategically and halachically preferable match. Whether this means he should exclusively do *yibum* with the *k'sheirah*, or merely that it is preferable, will be clarified by the Gemara in subsequent discussion.

---

---

# Yevamot 42b

## Lo Pelug Principle

### Virgins vs Non-Virgins

The *daf* begins in the middle of a discussion about the three-month waiting period that a woman must observe before remarrying, so that it can be determined whether she is pregnant from her previous husband. The *mishna* states that this requirement applies equally whether the woman is a *betula* — a virgin whose first marriage was her only marriage — or a *be'ula*, a non-virgin, and regardless of whether either the prior or the forthcoming relationship is *erusin* or *nissuin*. The logic behind applying the wait even where pregnancy is clearly impossible is *lo pelug*: the Rabbis did not wish to introduce distinctions that might lead to confusion or abuse. However, the *mishna* then records that both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yossi disagree, holding that if either the prior marriage or the new relationship is merely *erusin* — a stage that has not yet involved marital relations — there is no need to impose the three-month wait.

The *Gemara* opens with a textual question: since virgins are by definition women whose only prior relationship was *erusin*, why does the *mishna* list "virgins" and "those who were only *arusa*" as if they were two separate categories? Similarly, being a *be'ula* is equivalent to having been *nesua*. The *Gemara* answers through *Rav Yehuda*, who explains that the *mishna* is not presenting two independent categories but rather is clarifying a single one: women who were either divorced or widowed whether from *erusin* or *nissuin*. The mention of *erusin* and *nissuin* is therefore explanatory of the earlier distinction between *betulot* and *be'ulot*, not an additional case.

### Divorced/Widowed Categor…

With this reading established, the discussion moves to a practical ruling. Rabbi Eliezer had missed the session in the *beis medrash* and sought out Rabbi Assi to learn what had been said. Rabbi Assi reported that Rabbi Yochanan had ruled: *halacha k'Rabbi Yossi* — the law follows Rabbi Yossi. Rabbi Yossi's position, shared in substance with Rabbi Yehuda, is that the three-month wait is necessary only when the woman was *nesua* to her prior husband and is entering *nissuin* with the new one, meaning there was opportunity for marital relations at both ends. If either the prior or the new relationship is only *erusin*, no such wait is required.

### R. Yochanan's Ruling

This ruling immediately raises a methodological problem. Rabbi Yochanan is known for the principle that *halacha k'stam mishna* — the law follows the anonymous, unattributed position in the *Mishna*. But our *mishna* opens with an anonymous *stam* voice demanding the three-month wait in all cases. How, then, can Rabbi Yochanan rule against that *stam*? The *Gemara* responds that the *stam* voice in this case should not be treated as the standard authoritative *stam*, because it is *yachid* — it reflects only a single opinion — as the *Gemara* is about to demonstrate from a *braisa*.

### Non-Pregnant Cases

The *braisa* presents a series of circumstances in which the woman is presumptively not pregnant: she had been habitually at her father's house away from her husband (*redufa levei aviha*); there had been ongoing conflict (*ka'as*) between the spouses, making relations unlikely; the husband had been imprisoned; he was elderly to the point of near-infertility; he was ill; she herself was ill; she miscarried after the husband's death; she was infertile (*akara*); she was postmenopausal (*zekeina*); she was a minor (*ketana*); she was an *ailonis*, a woman constitutionally incapable of bearing children; or for any other reason she could not carry a pregnancy. In all of these cases, Rabbi Meir rules that she still must wait three months. The *lo pelug* of our *mishna* is therefore the position of Rabbi Meir alone.

Rabbi Yehuda — or in some versions, Rabbi Yossi, as both draw distinctions based on the circumstances — permits *erusin* immediately even following a prior *nissuin*, and in these demonstrably non-pregnant cases permits even *nissuin* immediately.
