This confirms that the anonymous *stam* voice is effectively *Rabbi Meir's* individual opinion, and therefore Rabbi Yochanan was entitled to rule against it in favor of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yossi.

### R. Yochanan Reversal

However, Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba then reports that Rabbi Yochanan subsequently reversed himself — *chazru bo Rabbi Yochanan* — and returned to demanding the three-month wait in all cases without distinction. Rav Yosef clarifies that the reversal was prompted by the *braisa* of the *Kerem b'Yavneh*, the tradition preserved from the sages who gathered at Yavneh following the destruction of the Temple. Rabbi Yishmael, the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, testified: *shamati mipi chachamim b'Kerem b'Yavneh* — "I heard from the sages in the *Kerem b'Yavneh* that all women must wait three months." No distinctions are made, regardless of whether pregnancy was possible. This *Kerem b'Yavneh* tradition evidently carried sufficient weight to cause Rabbi Yochanan to reverse his earlier ruling.

---

## Stam vs Machloket

### Contradiction Raised

Rabbi Yirmiya then sends Rabbi Zerika to raise the following contradiction before Rabbi Abbahu: on the one hand, Rabbi Yochanan ruled *halacha k'Rabbi Yossi*; on the other, Rabbi Yochanan is the very authority behind the principle of *halacha k'stam mishna*. And our *mishna* states explicitly, in anonymous voice, that *kol hanashim lo yinaseu v'lo yisarsu* — all women may neither marry nor become betrothed — until the three-month waiting period has elapsed, whether they are virgins or non-virgins.

Rabbi Abbahu's response is pointed: the one who posed this question *lo chash l'kimchei* — is not careful about the quality of his thinking. This is not a standard *stam mishna*. A *stam mishna* that obligates us is one where the anonymous position stands uncontested within the *mishna* itself. Here, the *mishna* immediately follows the *stam* with a recorded debate — Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yossi disagree. This configuration is called *stam v'achar kach machlokes*, and in such a case, *ein halacha k'stam* — we are not obligated to rule according to the *stam*. One may note that this does not necessarily mean we rule *against* the *stam*, only that we are not bound by it.

### Stam Then Machloket

The *Gemara* then articulates the general principle through the name of Rav Papa, with some attributing it to Rabbi Yochanan himself: *machlokes v'achar kach stam — halacha k'stam*. If the debate appears first in the *Mishna* and the anonymous position follows it, we rule according to the *stam*. But *stam v'achar kach machlokes — ein halacha k'stam*. When the *stam* comes first and the debate follows, we do not rule according to the *stam*.

This hermeneutical framework has broad applications. It is worth noting that comparable interpretive questions arise in the *Shulchan Aruch* as well — when the *Shulchan Aruch* states a ruling and then records *v'yeish omrim*, there is an entire developed methodology for determining which view carries practical weight depending on the order and structure of the presentation.

One might observe that, as the *Gemara* already noted, the *stam* of our *mishna* represents the opinion of Rabbi Meir — since the anonymous voice in the *Mishna* is generally attributed to Rabbi Meir. This makes it no surprise that it stands in tension with the views of other *tanna'im*. That said, even the principle of *stam mishna* does not typically concern itself with who authored the *stam* but with whether it is formally presented as uncontested — and here it clearly is not.

### R. Abbahu's Cases

Rabbi Abbahu expands the discussion to enumerate four configurations. His attendant Rabbi Nachum posed a series of questions while accompanying him, and Rabbi Abbahu addressed each in turn. First: *machlokes v'achar stam* — *halacha k'stam*, we follow the *stam*. Second: *stam v'achar machlokes* — *ein halacha k'stam*, we do not follow the *stam*. Third: *stam b'masnisin, machlokes b'braisa* — the *Mishna* presents it anonymously but a *braisa* records it as a debate. Rabbi Abbahu rules *halacha k'stam*: since the anonymous position stands uncontested in the *Mishna*, the *braisa's* recording of a debate does not dislodge it. Fourth: *machlokes b'masnisin, stam b'braisa* — the *Mishna* records a debate, but a *braisa* presents the matter anonymously. Here Rabbi Abbahu replies: *v'chi Rebbi lo shna'ah, Rebbi Chiyya minalo* — if Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi did not include this as a *stam* in the *Mishna*, on what authority does Rabbi Chiyya present it as one? The *Mishna* carries ultimate authority, and the *braisa's* anonymous formulation does not override the *Mishna's* explicit recording of a dispute.

The overall logic of these cases is intuitive: the *stam* carries authority when it represents the formal, uncontested position in the highest-level source. Any configuration that diminishes either the formality or the source level weakens its claim to be the definitive ruling.

### Combs Mishna

At this point Rabbi Abbahu's questioner challenges the principle with a *mishna* that is taught as *stam* yet, as everyone knows, is not followed in practice. The *mishna* in question concerns combs used for processing fiber. A flax comb (*masreik shel pishtan*) whose teeth have been removed: if two teeth remain adjacent to one another, the implement is *tamei* because it retains functional utility; if only one tooth remains, it is *tahor* since a single tooth is useless for combing. As for the individual teeth that break off one by one, they are themselves *tamei* because a single tooth can serve as a toothpick. Now regarding a wool comb (*shel tzemer*): if every other tooth has been removed such that no two remain adjacent, the comb is *tahor*. If three teeth remain together in one location, it is *tamei*. Further, if the outer tooth is one of a cluster of three, it is *tahor* — the outer teeth being less functionally critical. If two adjacent teeth broke off still connected at their base, they can serve as tweezers and are *tamei*. If one tooth broke off and was modified to serve as a lamp-wick cleaner or for stretching material, it is *tamei*.

This final ruling — that a single modified tooth is *tamei* — is presented in the *Mishna* as a *stam*. Yet Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish are known to both declare *zu einah mishna* — this ruling is not authoritative and we do not decide the law accordingly.

The question is pressing: here is a *stam mishna* that established authorities explicitly set aside. How can one maintain that *halacha k'stam mishna* as a binding principle?

### Combs Resolution

Rabbi Abbahu answers: *bar minei d'hi* — put that case aside entirely. It is a known exception, and both Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish explicitly identified it as one. The *Gemara* then proceeds to explain *why* this *mishna* is treated as an exception, and the answer turns on internal problems within the *mishna* itself. Rav Huna bar Minyumi in the name of Rav Idi reports that the *reisha* contradicts the *seifa*: the opening of the *mishna* dealing with the wool comb states that when teeth are missing with a gap between remaining ones (*achas mi-beino*), the comb is *tahor*, implying that two adjacent teeth (*shtayim b'makom echad*) would render it *tamei* — yet the later clause specifies *three* together (*shalosh tamei*), implying that two alone would not suffice. The *Gemara* raises several possible resolutions of this apparent internal contradiction — perhaps the cases involve outer versus inner teeth, or teeth that break off with the base of the comb attached versus those that break off cleanly, or thick teeth versus thin teeth — and concludes that none of these distinctions are entirely forced. The *mishna* is not demonstrably self-contradictory.

The final answer is therefore textual rather than logical: those who are precise about the *girsa* — the exact text — note that their manuscripts conclude the *mishna* with the phrase *zu divrei Rabbi Shimon*, identifying the final ruling as specifically the opinion of Rabbi Shimon rather than an anonymous *stam*. There is therefore no *stam* ruling here to begin with, and the challenge to the principle dissolves. As the *Gemara* acknowledges, this was a rather extraordinary digression — the example chosen to challenge the principle of *stam mishna* turns out to involve the textual apparatus of combs, a matter of limited practical consequence. Whether the ruling about the modified tooth affects any of the other cases in the *mishna* is left unexplored.

---

## Three Months & Erusin

### Day Ninety Question

The *Gemara* returns to the three-month waiting period and records a series of practical rulings. Rabbi Yoshiyah bar Avin sent a ruling that *me'arsin toch gimel* — one may perform *erusin* within the three months — following the lenient view of Rabbi Yehuda that *erusin* is not problematic because it does not yet place the woman in a context of marital relations. He adds that this was also the practice and teaching of Rabbi Elazar. Additionally, a tradition in the name of Rabbi Chanina HaGadol holds that *rubo shel rishon, v'rubo shel shlishi, v'emtza'i v'hashalem* — the majority of the first month, the majority of the third month, and the entirety of the middle month would be sufficient. This formulation is striking, as it implies that something less than three complete months may suffice — perhaps reflecting a view that seven full months are required to establish paternity, in which case slightly more than two months of waiting would be adequate. Neither *Rashi* nor *Tosafot* address this point directly.

*Tosafot* suggests that this leniency in counting applies only when the waiting woman is an *arusa*, not a *nesua*. On that reading, the ruling is less radical: it is not that such a woman need not wait at all, only that the three months may be calculated with some flexibility.

*Ameimar* went further and permitted performing *erusin* on day ninety itself, without requiring the couple to wait until day ninety-one. Rav Ashi challenges this from a ruling attributed to both Rava and Shmuel, who state that the three-month wait requires a full three months, exclusive of the day of the husband's death and exclusive of the day of the *erusin* itself — meaning the *erusin* must take place on day ninety-one at the earliest.

### Nursing Women Case

The *Gemara* resolves this challenge by clarifying that the ruling of Rava and Shmuel was not stated in the context of the three-month wait at all. It was stated regarding the waiting period before remarriage for a woman who is nursing her infant — *l'inyan meneket*. Rava and Shmuel had said that a nursing mother must wait twenty-four months before remarrying, exclusive of the day the child was born and exclusive of the day of the *erusin*, placing the *erusin* on the day after the twenty-four months conclude. The version cited by Rav Ashi had confused the two contexts: it was not three months and day ninety-one, but twenty-four months and the day following.

A subsequent case reinforces this: there is a report that a man arranged a *seudas erusin* on day ninety and Rava compelled him to cancel the feast and postpone. The *Gemara* clarifies that this too involved *seudas nissuin*, not *seudas erusin* — and for *nissuin*, the stricter count indeed applies.

### Lo Pelug Conclusion

The final ruling (*hilchasa*) is that a nursing woman must wait twenty-four months, exclusive of the day of birth and the day of *erusin*. For the three-month wait applicable to all other remarrying women, it is likewise exclusive of the day of death and exclusive of the day of *erusin*. The more significant conclusion, however, is substantive: the *halacha* follows *lo pelug*, and even *erusin* requires the full three-month wait. This represents Rabbi Yochanan's final position following his reversal based on the *Kerem b'Yavneh* tradition.

This conclusion raises a broader question about the applicability of *lo pelug* in the contemporary context. The *lo pelug* rationale does not express a genuine belief that a postmenopausal woman or a minor might be pregnant. Rather, it reflects a concern that if we begin introducing distinctions, borderline cases will escape the necessary scrutiny. But if that is the logic, then the underlying concern — which is determining pregnancy status — could in principle be satisfied by a modern pregnancy test. On this analysis, *lo pelug* requires *some* form of determination in all cases; it does not necessarily require that the determination take the form of waiting three months. That said, whether pregnancy tests may substitute for the three-month wait is a *machlokes haposkim*, and on the strict reading, one would require even an elderly woman to demonstrate non-pregnancy before proceeding.

---

## Widow's Aveilus Issue

### R. Yossi Exception

The *mishna* records that Rabbi Yossi permits women to perform *erusin* immediately — *chutz min ha'almanah mipnei ha'eibul* — except for a widow who is in *aveilus*. The logic is straightforward: if the woman was *nesua* to her first husband and he died, she is in *aveilus* for the first month. Even though the new relationship involves only *erusin*, and therefore poses no concern about determining paternity, she is still mourning the prior husband and may not yet enter even a betrothal relationship.

The background assumption is that a woman who was *nesua* to her first husband and is now entering *erusin* with a new partner does not need the three-month wait — because the new relationship is only *erusin*, which involves no marital relations. Yet she cannot proceed even with this limited step during the first month, because she is in personal *aveilus*.

### Rav Chisda Challenge

Rav Chisda challenges this on *kal v'chomer* grounds. He argues: during the period when it is forbidden to launder one's garments — that is, during the first week of personal *aveilus*, when the laws of mourning are most severe — it is still permitted to perform *erusin*. How much more so during the subsequent weeks of the month, when laundering is again permitted, should *erusin* certainly be allowed? If the severity of the prohibition does not extend to blocking *erusin* even at its most stringent point, how can Rabbi Yossi claim there is any prohibition at all?

### Tisha B'Av Precedent

The *kal v'chomer* draws on a *Mishna* and *braisa* relating to the nine-day period preceding *Tisha B'Av*. The *Mishna* states that during the week in which *Tisha B'Av* falls (*shavua she'chal bo Tisha B'Av*), it is forbidden to take a haircut or launder clothing. A *braisa* records that during the period before this week, the people limit business dealings, building, and planting — yet they may still perform *kiddushin*, though not *nissuin*, and may not hold a *seudas erusin*. The *Gemara* understands *Shmuel's* principle — that one may perform *kiddushin* even close to *Tisha B'Av* lest another man get there first (*shema yekadmenu acher*) — as the basis for this leniency.

The preliminary *braisa* seems to speak of the period before the *shavua she'chal bo*, meaning even before the most restricted week. The *Gemara* considers whether the permission to perform *kiddushin* extends into the *shavua she'chal bo* itself, when laundering is forbidden. Rava constructs a *kal v'chomer*: if during the nine days when business dealings are restricted one may still perform *kiddushin*, how much more so during the less restricted days of personal *aveilus* when business dealings are permitted should *kiddushin* be allowed?

### Reinterpreting R. Yossi

In order to accommodate the evident logic that *erusin* should not be prohibited during personal *aveilus*, the *Gemara* undertakes a significant reinterpretation of Rabbi Yossi's ruling. Rather than reading him as saying *kol hanashim yisarsu chutz min ha'almanah* — all women may perform *erusin* except for the widow — the *Gemara* proposes reading: *kol hanashim yinaseu* — all women may perform *nissuin*. What Rabbi Yossi objects to is not *erusin* during *aveilus*, but *nissuin* during *aveilus*. *Erusin*, he agrees, is unproblematic.

On this revised reading, the structure of the case changes entirely. The prior relationship was *erusin* — which is why there is no concern about determining pregnancy — and the new step being contemplated is *nissuin*. Rabbi Yossi says: ordinarily this *nissuin* is fine (since the prior stage was only *erusin*, there is no issue of confusing lineage), but if the woman is an *almanah*, her first month of *aveilus* blocks even *nissuin*.

The *Gemara* immediately asks: but if Rabbi Yossi is talking about a woman whose prior relationship was *erusin*, and she is now proceeding to *nissuin* — why should there be any concern about determining pregnancy at all? Since the prior stage was *erusin*, there were no marital relations, and she cannot be pregnant. The *Gemara* answers: *lais lei* — Rabbi Yossi is simply not concerned about determining pregnancy in this case. He does not hold the position of *lo pelug* in this context.

Alternatively, the *Gemara* considers: perhaps Rabbi Yossi does accept the concern about pregnancy but is dealing with a different configuration — specifically, women who were previously *arusot* and are now divorced (*arusot gerushot*) and wish to proceed to *nissuin*. In this reading, there is no *aveilus* concern because a *gerusha* is not a widow; the exception is only an *almanah* — a woman who was previously *arusa* and whose *arus* died. In that case, one might ask: does such a woman have *aveilus* at all?

The *Gemara* then asks: if Rabbi Yossi is now only talking about an *arusa* who became an *almanah* proceeding to *nissuin* — what is the difference between his position and Rabbi Yehuda's? The *Gemara* answers: the distinction lies in the case of a *nesua* seeking to perform *erusin*. Rabbi Yehuda permits *erusin* as well — as long as *one* of the two stages is *erusin*, the waiting period is unnecessary. Rabbi Yossi, on the revised reading, addresses only the case where the *first* stage is *erusin* and the *second* step is *nissuin*; he does not explicitly permit *erusin* for a woman who was already *nesua*.

### Almanah Question

This generates the next question. According to the revised reading of Rabbi Yossi — where he is discussing an *arusa* who is an *almanah* proceeding to *nissuin* — does such a woman even have *aveilus*? The *Gemara* cites a *braisa* taught by Rabbi Chiyya bar Ami: a man's wife who is only his *arusa* — they have not yet begun living together — *lo onen*, he is not an *onen* for her if she dies; *v'lo mitame lah*, if he is a *kohen* he does not become *tamei* on her account; *v'chen hi*, and similarly she is not an *onenes* for him and does not defile herself for him; *mes hu — govah kesuvashah*, if he dies she is still entitled to collect her *kesuvah*, since the basic obligation of the *kesuvah* attaches from the time of *erusin* even though the ongoing marital obligations do not yet apply; *meitah — eino yorshah*, but if she dies he does not inherit her. The clear implication of this *braisa* is that there is no *aveilus* obligation for an *arusa*.

This brings the discussion full circle. Everyone agrees there is no *aveilus* for an *arusa* relationship. If the deceased was the woman's husband in a full *nissuin* relationship, then there is *aveilus*, but then in order to remove the three-month concern, the *new* relationship must be only *erusin* — and we are back to the original question: why should *erusin* be prohibited during *aveilus*?

The *Gemara* concludes that this question reflects a genuine *machlokes tanna'im*. A *braisa* addressing the nine-day period states: from *Rosh Chodesh Av* until *Tisha B'Av*, people limit business dealings, building, planting, *erusin*, and *nissuin*. This represents a *tanna* who holds that *erusin* is indeed restricted during mourning-adjacent periods. The same *braisa* then states that during the *shavua she'chal bo Tisha B'Av* it is forbidden to launder and to take a haircut, with one opinion extending these restrictions to the entire month. Rabbi Yossi may be following this stricter *tanna* who restricts *erusin*.

### New vs Old Aveilus

Rav Ashi raises one final challenge. How do we know that the *braisa*'s prohibition of *le'ares* during the nine days refers to the actual act of *kiddushin* rather than merely to holding a *seudas erusin*? The *Gemara* answers: the same question could be raised regarding *nissuin* — and we know that the prohibition on *nissuin* during this period refers to the act itself, not merely to the feast. The distinction is: *nissuin* without a feast still constitutes a full marriage and carries its own inherent *simcha*; but *erusin* without a feast carries no *simcha* at all. Therefore, if there is any prohibition of *erusin* in such a context, it must apply to the act itself.

This brings us back to the starting point without resolution through the *Tisha B'Av* material alone. The final answer given by Rav Ashi is conceptual: *shani aveilus chadasha me'aveilus yeshana* — a fresh personal *aveilus* is categorically different from the ancient, commemorative mourning of *Tisha B'Av*. And *shani aveilus derabbim me'aveilus deyachid* — the communal mourning of *Tisha B'Av* is different from the individual's personal *aveilus*. Whatever evidence one brings from the *Tisha B'Av* period — whether permissive or restrictive — is not directly transferable to personal *aveilus*. Rabbi Yossi is therefore entirely entitled to hold that in a fresh, personal *aveilus*, even the act of *kiddushin* is prohibited, regardless of what one rules about the analogous period before *Tisha B'Av*. And if Rabbi Yehuda disagrees, the dispute is rooted in precisely this question: whether the communal, commemorative mourning of *Tisha B'Av* is strict enough to serve as a relevant precedent for individual personal *aveilus*. On the simple reading, the *mishna* is restored: Rabbi Yossi prohibits *erusin* for a widow during the month of *aveilus*, and the permissive cases discussed throughout the *sugya* do not override this.

---

## Next Mishna Preview

### Four Brothers Case

The *daf* concludes with a preview of the next *mishna*. Four brothers are married to four women, and all four brothers die, leaving a fifth surviving brother. The *mishna* states that if the eldest brother wishes to perform *yibum* with all four widows, the prerogative is his — the responsibility for *yibum* devolves primarily upon the eldest, and he may choose to marry all four.

### Two Brothers Case

The *mishna* then turns to a man who was married to two women and dies. Performing either *bi'ah* or *chalitzah* with one of them automatically exempts the other — as has been established from the beginning of the tractate.

### Kasher/Pasul Mix

Finally, the *mishna* addresses the case where of the two wives, one is *kashera* — eligible for marriage to a *kohen* — and one is *pesulah*, already disqualified by virtue of a prior divorce. If the surviving brother intends to perform *chalitzah*, he should do so with the *pesulah*, so as not to add a further disqualification to the *kashera*. If he intends to perform *yibum*, he should do *yibum* with the *kashera*. Whether this means he performs *yibum* exclusively with the *kashera*, or whether after performing *yibum* with the *kashera* he may also marry the *pesulah*, will be taken up in the *Gemara*.

---

---

# Yevamot 44

## Yibum Rights & Exemption

### Mishnah Clarification

The daf opens with a corrective gloss on the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* speaks of four brothers, and the *gemara* immediately notes that the formulation "four brothers" raises an obvious difficulty: if they all died, who remains to perform *yibum*? The *gemara* therefore emends the reading — *ela eima arba me-achim*, say rather that four of the brothers died, leaving four widows, while other brothers survive. This is, as the lecturer observes, one of those *mishnayot* in this *masechet* that would have made an excellent opening for the tractate had it appeared earlier.

### Oldest Brother Priority

With the corrected reading in place, the *mishnah* establishes that the oldest surviving brother holds the right — *ha-reshut beyado* — to perform *yibum* with all four widows before any other brother may act. He is not limited to one; if he wishes, he may marry all of them before the younger brothers have any opportunity to intervene.

### One Exempts All

The *mishnah* then addresses the exemption principle that has underlain the entire tractate from its opening: *chalitzah* or *yibum* performed with any one wife exempts all the others from further obligation. Though this has been assumed throughout, the *gemara* now derives it explicitly from scriptural sources, which are examined in detail in the following section.

---

## Four Wives Limit

### Elders' Advice

The *gemara* raises a challenge: would we simply allow this brother to marry four women simultaneously? Surely that is an extraordinary domestic situation. The *gemara* invokes a *baraita* on the verse *ve-karu lo ziknei iro* — "and the elders of his city shall call to him." The *gemara* understands *ve-dibru eilav*, "and they shall speak to him," as mandating substantive guidance, not mere ritual formality. *Melamed she-masiin lo eitzah hogenes lo* — they give him advice that is appropriate and fitting for him specifically. Crucially, the elders must address him directly, *hen ve-lo sheluchan*, not through an intermediary.

### Age Matching

The content of that guidance is elaborated: if he is young and the *yevamah* is elderly, or he is elderly and she is young, the elders say to him — *mah lecha etzel yaldah*, what do you want with such a young woman, or *mah lecha etzel zekeinah*, what do you want with such an old woman? *Kelech etzel she-kamotecha*, go and find someone of your own age, *ve-al tasim ketatah be-veitecha* — do not bring strife into your house. The advice is non-binding; he is free to reject it. And notably, the woman's own voice is not heard in this passage, a theme that recurs throughout the tractate.

### Math of Conjugal Rights

The immediate question is why the *mishnah* limits the brother to four wives. If he is a man of means who can support multiple wives — the *gemara* answers *lo tzericha de-efshar lei*, this is indeed a case where he has the resources — why not permit ten or twenty? The *gemara* answers: *eitzah tovah ka mashma lan*, this is good advice even for a wealthy man. *Arba in, tfeih lo* — four wives yes, more no. The reasoning is mathematical: *ki heichi de-timtei onah be-chodesh*, the *mitzvah* of *onah* for a *talmid chacham* is once per week. With four wives rotating, each wife receives conjugal attention once a month. Any more than four wives and a woman would receive her *onah* less than once a month, which is an unacceptable diminishment of her rights. Four, therefore, is both the maximum permitted and the outer limit of practical wisdom.

### Senegal Digression

It is an interesting coincidence that Islamic law similarly limits a man to four wives, a number said to reflect the personal practice of Muhammad. The parallel with the Talmud's reasoning is worth noting, though the justifications differ. By way of illustration: on a rabbinic mission to Senegal — a society in which the overwhelming majority of the population practices polygamy, with only a small Christian minority living monogamously — the lecturer had occasion to observe a kind of living parallel to the world of *Avraham, Yitzchak, ve-Yaakov*: village compounds in which co-wives occupied separate quarters, maintained their own domestic rotations, and shared child-rearing responsibilities. A question from one of the visiting rabbinical students — "what is it like living in a polygamous society?" — met with understandable puzzlement from the Senegalese women, who might equally have asked what it is like to be monogamous. The tension was dissolved with a joke: asked what the penalty for polygamy is, the answer was — two mothers-in-law. The laughter that followed confirmed that mother-in-law humor requires no translation across cultures.

---

## Yibum vs. Chalitzah

### Bayis Echad Proofs

Having addressed the practical question of how many wives a *yavam* may take in *yibum*, the *gemara* now establishes the scriptural basis for the principle that *yibum* or *chalitzah* with one wife exempts all the others — and that it must be one or the other, not both. *Amar Rabbi Chama berabi Chanina amar Rabbi Yochanan amar kra*: the verse reads *asher lo yivneh et beit achiv*, describing the man who will not build his brother's house. The *gemara* derives: *bayis echad hu boneh, v'ein boneh shenei batim* — he builds one house, not two. And since *beito zu ishto* — "his house" is his wife — this limits *yibum* to a single wife. The equation of *bayis* and *ishah* is a well-established trope in the *gemara*.

### Chalitzah Exclusivity

The same principle is derived for *chalitzah* from a different verse. *Amar Mar Zutra bar Tuvia amar kra*: the verse *beit chalutz ha-na'al*, "the house of the withdrawn shoe," similarly uses the singular — *bayis echad hu choletz, v'ein choletz shenei batim* — he performs *chalitzah* with one house, not two.

### Mixed Option Question

The *gemara* now raises a question that it acknowledges is somewhat unusual: if one cannot perform *yibum* with two wives and cannot perform *chalitzah* with two wives, perhaps he should do *yibum* with one and *chalitzah* with the other? After all, neither verse individually prohibits this combination. Why assume the obligation is purely either/or?

### Either/Or Resolution

The *gemara* resolves this from a third verse: *im lo yachpotz* — if he does not wish to perform *yibum*, he does *chalitzah*. The implication is: *ha im chafetz, yavam* — if he wants to, he performs *yibum* and does not perform *chalitzah*. The governing principle follows: *kol ha-oleh l'yibbum oleh l'chalitzah, v'chol she-eino oleh l'yibbum eino oleh l'chalitzah* — whoever is eligible for *yibum* is eligible for *chalitzah*, and whoever is ineligible for *yibum* is equally ineligible for *chalitzah*. Once *yibum* has been performed with one wife, the others are no longer candidates for *yibum*; they are therefore also not candidates for *chalitzah*.

The *gemara* then adds a rabbinic rationale as well: *she-lo yomru bayis miktzaso banuy u-miktzaso chalutz* — lest people say that one may build half a house through *yibum* and release the other half through *chalitzah*. This seems circular at first — why should we care if people say that? — but the concern is practical: if it were permitted to do *yibum* first and then *chalitzah*, people might attempt the reverse, performing *chalitzah* first and then *yibum*. That sequence is forbidden, because *keivan shelo banah shuv lo yivneh* — once he has declined to build, he may not build again. The prohibition of *asher lo yivneh* applies retroactively.

### Tzarat Ervah Issue

The *gemara* entertains a further *hava amina*: perhaps the entire *yibum* obligation applies only when there is a single *yevamah*, since all the relevant verses are phrased in the singular — *bayis echad*, one house. When there are two *yevamot*, perhaps there is no *yibum* obligation at all. The *gemara* dismisses this forcefully: *im kein tzaras ervah d'asar rachmana lamah li*? If the obligation simply dissolves whenever there are two *yevamot*, the entire first chapter's discussion of *tzaras ervah* — the co-wife of a forbidden relative — would be superfluous. If two wives already eliminate the *yibum* obligation, there is no need to specify that it is eliminated when one of the two is an *ervah*.

The *gemara* pushes back: perhaps *tzaras ervah* is still necessary. One might have thought that since the *ervah* herself is outside the *yibum* framework — *ervah abara'i kaima* — her co-wife should still be subject to *yibum*. The verse therefore tells us that even the co-wife of an *ervah* is forbidden. This remains a meaningful ruling even within the framework of the *hava amina*.

### Multiple Wives Apply

The *gemara* resolves the question of how *yibum* can apply at all when there are multiple *yevamot* by invoking the doubled formulation of *yevimto yevimto* — the word *yevimto* appears more than once in the Torah, teaching by way of expansion (*ribuy*) that the *yibum* framework applies even when there are multiple *yevamot*. Only one wife need perform *yibum* or *chalitzah*, but the obligation is real and the exemption is comprehensive.

---

## Preferential Choice

### Valid vs. Invalid Wife

The *gemara* addresses a refinement: what if among the *yevamot* one woman is *kesheirah* — of full valid status — and another is *pesulah*, disqualified in some way (not an *ervah*, but perhaps already a *grushah* from a previous marriage)? The *halacha* differentiates based on whether *chalitzah* or *yibum* is being performed. If the *yavam* intends to perform *chalitzah*, he should do so with the woman who is already *pesulah*. If he intends *yibum*, he should do so with the *kesheirah* — or at minimum, the *Rambam* understands, he may do *yibum* with whichever he wishes, but the preference is for the *kesheirah*.

### Don't Waste Wells

The rationale for performing *chalitzah* specifically with the *pesulah* is articulated by *Rav Yosef*: *amar Rav Yosef kan shanah Rebbi* — here the *Rebbi* taught the principle of *lo yishpoch adam mei boro v'acherim tzrichim lahem* — a person should not pour out the water of his well when others need it. In other words, do not casually disqualify someone when the act of doing so serves no purpose. If *chalitzah* is to be performed anyway, and it will disqualify a woman from marrying a *kohen* by conferring upon her the status of *chalutzah*, perform it with the woman who already cannot marry a *kohen*. Do not needlessly foreclose the options of the *almanah* who retains her full status.

---

## Personal Status Issues

### Three Cases Intro

Following the conclusion of the *yibum* discussions, the *mishnah* pivots to questions of personal status and *mamzer*. These topics — *geirusin*, *mamzer*, and *psul l'kehunah* — are deeply connected to *Masechet Yevamot*, which serves as a natural home for these fundamental questions of Jewish identity and status.

### Machzir Gerushah

The first case is *hamachzir grushaso* — a man who remarries a woman he previously divorced, after she had in the interim married another man. This is a violation of a negative prohibition in the Torah, but it is not categorized as one of the *arayot* — the cardinal sexual prohibitions. It is an *issur lav*, a simple negative commandment.

### Chalutzah Marriage

The second case is *ve-honosei chalutzaso* — a man who marries a woman with whom he performed *chalitzah*. This too is a simple negative prohibition, grounded in the principle of *keivan she-banah shuv lo yivneh*: once the bond of *yibum* has been formally dissolved, it cannot be rebuilt. This prohibition applies even if the woman subsequently married and divorced another man entirely.

### Relative of Chalutzah

The third case is *ve-honosei kerovas chalutzaso* — a man who marries the relative of his *chalutzah*, for example her sister or her mother. This prohibition appears on its face to be purely rabbinic in character: just as a man may not marry his divorced wife's sister while that prohibition persists, so too the rabbis extended that restriction to the relative of a woman with whom he performed *chalitzah*, treating the *chalutzah* as if she were his divorced wife. The *gemara* will subject this assumption to considerable scrutiny.

---

## Mamzer Debate

### Rabbi Akiva Strict

The *mishnah* records the dispute regarding the offspring of these unions. *Divrei Rabbi Akiva* — Rabbi Akiva holds that the child is a *mamzer*. His position is striking in its severity: any offspring of any prohibited relationship, even a violation of a simple *lav*, even a case as remote from incest as a man remarrying his own ex-wife, renders the child a *mamzer*. Equally, the child of a man who married his *chalutzah* or the relative of his *chalutzah* is a *mamzer* according to Rabbi Akiva.

### Sages' Standard

The *chachamim* disagree. *Chachamim omrim ein ha-vlad mamzer* — the child is not a *mamzer*. In the Sages' view, the *mamzer* status arises only from the offspring of a relationship that carries *issur kares*, not from a mere *issur lav*. This is the authoritative ruling.

### Divorcée Relatives

Nevertheless, the *chachamim* concede one case: *u-modim be-nosei kerovas gerushaso she-ha-vlad mamzer* — they agree that if a man marries the relative of his actual *grushah*, his divorced wife — her sister, daughter, or mother — the child is a *mamzer*. The prohibitions that attach to relatives of one's wife are not dissolved by divorce (with the single exception of the wife's sister, whose prohibition lapses upon the wife's death). All other prohibited relatives remain forbidden even after divorce, and those prohibitions carry the weight of *ervah* and *kares*. It is therefore a genuine *ervah* violation, and the Sages accordingly agree that a *mamzer* results.

---

## Text Emendation

### Chalutzah Problem

A sharp textual question now emerges: does Rabbi Akiva really hold that marrying the *relative* of a *chalutzah* produces a *mamzer*? That prohibition, as established in an earlier *mishnah*, is only rabbinic. *Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish* had already stated explicitly: *achot gerushah midivrei Torah, achot chalutzah midivrei sofrim* — the sister of a *grushah* is a biblical prohibition, while the sister of a *chalutzah* is only rabbinic. Surely Rabbi Akiva would not generate a biblical *mamzer* status from a rabbinic prohibition.

### RSBL's Solution

Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's formulation thus creates a difficulty for reading the *mishnah* at face value. If the prohibition of marrying a *chalutzah*'s relative is only rabbinic, Rabbi Akiva cannot have intended to declare such a child a *mamzer* in the full biblical sense.

### Text Amendment

The *gemara*'s response is to propose an emendation: *tani kerovas gerushaso* — the text of Rabbi Akiva's ruling should be corrected to read "relative of his *grushah*," not "relative of his *chalutzah*." On this reading, Rabbi Akiva's third case is the relative of a woman he genuinely divorced — a biblical prohibition — and the Sages, while disagreeing with his first two cases, concede this third one.

### Akiva's Intent

The *gemara* marshals an argument in favor of this emendation. The *mishnah* closes with the concession of the *chachamim*: *u-modim be-nosei kerovas gerushaso she-ha-vlad mamzer*. One asks: why do the Sages frame their concession specifically around the case of the relative of a *grushah*, rather than simply stating in the abstract that *mamzer* status applies wherever there is *issur kares*? That latter formulation would appear in a later *mishnah* in any case. If all the Sages wished to convey was the principle that *kares* produces a *mamzer*, there was no need to single out this particular case. *Ela shema mina airy bah* — it must be that Rabbi Akiva himself mentioned this case, and the Sages responded to it specifically, conceding it while rejecting his other claims. This strongly implies that Rabbi Akiva's three cases were: remarrying a *grushah*, marrying a *chalutzah*, and marrying the relative of a *grushah* — not the relative of a *chalutzah*.

### Counter Argument

Yet the *gemara* acknowledges that this inference is not airtight. The Sages might have chosen the case of the relative of a *grushah* not because Rabbi Akiva mentioned it, but because Rabbi Akiva *did* mention the relative of a *chalutzah*, and the Sages wished to contrast that case — which they reject — with the stronger case of the relative of a *grushah*, which they accept. On this reading, the *mishnah* text stands as written: Rabbi Akiva genuinely spoke of *kerovas chalutzaso*, and the Sages replied by conceding only *kerovas gerushaso*. The *gemara* concludes: *ve-dilma le-olam lo airy bah* — perhaps Rabbi Akiva was never discussing the case of the *grushah*'s relative at all, and the plain reading of the *mishnah* — that Rabbi Akiva's three cases include the relative of a *chalutzah* — is in fact the correct one.

---

## Chalutzah Status

### Beit Chalutz

If the *mishnah* is taken at face value — that Rabbi Akiva genuinely holds the relative of a *chalutzah* produces a *mamzer* — one must explain the basis for treating a *chalutzah*'s relatives as biblically forbidden. *Amar Rabbi Chiya bar Avin amar Rabbi Yochanan hayinu ta'ama de-Rabbi Akiva*: the reason for Rabbi Akiva's position is derived from the very verse that describes the *chalitzah* ceremony. The Torah calls the result *beit chalutz ha-na'al* — "the house of the withdrawn shoe." *Ha-kasuv kera'o bayis* — the verse itself designates the *chalutzah*'s household as his *bayis*, his house. This is the same word used to denote his wife. Rabbi Akiva therefore understands the *chalutzah* as possessing a biblically grounded equivalence to a divorced wife.

### Biblical Equivalence

The implication is significant and marks a genuine departure from the assumed framework: although *Rebbi* (Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi) taught that the prohibition of marrying a *chalutzah*'s relative is rabbinic — and this has been the operating assumption throughout — Rabbi Akiva holds it to be biblical. In Rabbi Akiva's reading, *beit chalutz ha-na'al* creates a full scriptural equivalence between a *chalutzah* and a *grushah*, making the relatives of a *chalutzah* as forbidden as those of an ex-wife at the level of *de-Oraisa*. As the *gemara* notes: *ein hachi nami kerovas chalutzaso de-Oraisa* — and that is indeed Rabbi Akiva's view.

---

## Lav vs. Kares

### Machzir Consensus

The *gemara* now turns to the specific question of what status attaches to the *offspring* of these forbidden unions. *Amar Rav Shimon bar Rebbe: ha-kol modim be-machzir grushaso she-ha-vlad pagum li-kehunah* — everyone agrees that in the case of *machzir grushaso*, even though the child is not a *mamzer*, the child is *pagum li-kehunah*, disqualified for priestly purposes. For a female child, this means she may not marry a *kohen*. The question, then, is whether the offspring of a simple *issur lav* — a union that produces no *mamzer* — nonetheless carries a taint of *psul l'kehunah*.

This is not an abstract question. Its most practically significant application, as the *gemara* will make clear, is the case of a non-Jewish father and a Jewish mother.

### Almana Counterpoint

To establish that the offspring of an *issur lav* carries *pagum* status for *kehunah*, the *gemara* constructs a *kal v'chomer* from the case of *almana l'kohen gadol* — a widow who marries a *kohen gadol*. That union is a violation of a narrowly scoped *lav*, applying only to the *kohen gadol*, not to all priests. Yet the offspring of such a union is *pagum*. If so narrow a prohibition produces *pagum* offspring, how much more so should a universal *issur lav* — like *machzir grushaso*, which applies to all Jewish men — produce *pagum* offspring?

### Almana Unique

The *gemara* rejects this *kal v'chomer*: *mah le-almana she-kein hi atzmah mischaleles* — the *almana* case is unique in that the woman herself becomes a *chalalah* through that act of union. It is specifically because the act of sex constitutes a violation of a *kohen*-specific prohibition that the woman acquires a changed status, and it is that changed status which transmits *psul* to the offspring. This dynamic does not apply in the case of *machzir grushaso*.

### Woman's Status Proof

The *gemara* elaborates on this distinction. A woman's status is affected by an act of prohibited sex only when that act is a prohibition specific to *kehunah* — for example, a *kohen gadol* marrying a widow, or an ordinary *kohen* marrying a *grushah*. In such cases, the woman becomes a *chalalah* and is barred from *kehunah* benefits even if the *kohen* subsequently dies. By contrast, *machzir grushaso* is not a prohibition rooted in *kehunah*. The woman in that case is already a *grushah* and already disqualified from marrying a *kohen*; the act of remarriage does not further diminish her status — she does not, for example, lose her entitlement to eat *terumah* if she is a *bat kohen* (as *Rashi* and *Tosafot* note). Since the woman's status is unchanged by the act, there is no basis for arguing that the child's status is affected.

### To'evah Proof

An additional proof had been raised from the verse *hi to'eivah* — the Torah describes the act of remarriage as "an abomination." A *derashah* reads: *hi to'evah, v'ein baneha to'evim* — she is the abomination, but her children bear no problematic status. This verse seems to explicitly exempt the children of this prohibition from any stigma. The *gemara*, however, notes that this *derashah* can be redirected: *hi to'evah, v'ein tzaratah to'evah* — she is the abomination but not her co-wife. The verse excludes the co-wife from the taint of the prohibition, but says nothing about the children. The *phat* in the verse thus does not definitively resolve the question of the offspring's status.

### Three Cases Baraita

A *baraita* revisits all three cases from the *mishnah* in light of this framework. Rabbi Akiva holds that in each of these *issur lav* cases — *machzir grushaso*, *nosei chalutzaso*, and *nosei kerovas chalutzaso* — *ein lo bakiddushin*, the *kiddushin* is not binding, no *get* is required, the woman becomes invalid, and the child is *pasul*. The *chachamim* take the opposite position on every point: *kiddushin* is binding, a *get* is required if she wishes to leave, *hi kesheirah* — the woman's status is unchanged — and *vlada kasher* — the child is *kasher*.

---

## Context Specificity

### Akiva vs. Sages

The debate between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages on these three points — the validity of *kiddushin*, the woman's status, and the child's status — is now examined carefully. When the Sages say *vlada kasher*, how comprehensive is that *kashrut*? Does it mean the child is fully valid, including for *kehunah* purposes? Or does it mean only that the child is not a *mamzer*, while still being *pagum li-kehunah*?

### Grammatical Parsing

The *gemara* parses the language precisely. According to Rabbi Akiva, the baraita states *hi pesulah* — she is disqualified. To whom is she disqualified? It cannot mean disqualified from marrying other Jews, since no act of forbidden sex can render the woman herself a *mamzer* — that category applies only to offspring. The only meaningful disqualification the woman could acquire is disqualification from *kehunah* — either from marrying a *kohen* or from eating *terumah* as a *bat kohen*. So when Rabbi Akiva says *hi pesulah*, he means: this *issur lav* is so weighty that it retroactively makes the woman invalid for *kehunah* purposes. When he then says *vlada pasul*, the *gemara* notes that we know from elsewhere that Rabbi Akiva declares such a child a *mamzer*; therefore *pesul* here means *mamzer* status, disqualified from the congregation of Israel.

Turning to the Sages' parallel formulation — *hi kesheirah, vlada kasher* — the *gemara* applies the same logic. *Hi kesheirah* cannot mean that the woman is *kasher* to marry other Jews in the general sense, since that would never have been in doubt; forbidden sex does not create *mamzer* status in the woman herself. Therefore *hi kesheirah* must mean she remains *kesheirah li-kehunah* — the act of sex with an *issur lav* did not alter her *kehunah* eligibility. And since the woman's status remains unchanged by the act, the parallel reading of *vlada kasher* must mean the child too is *kasher li-kehunah*.

Yet the *gemara* resists this inference. *Midi irya? Ha kide'ita, ve-ha kide'ita* — each statement exists in its own context. When the Sages say *hi kesheirah*, they address her particular vulnerability: could she have become a *chalalah*? No, she remains *kesheirah*. When they say *vlada kasher*, they address the child's particular vulnerability: could the child be a *mamzer* as Rabbi Akiva claims? No, the child is *kasher* — meaning, not a *mamzer*. It does not follow that the child is also *kasher li-kehunah*, since that question was never the focus of the Sages' statement about the child.

### No Almana Proof

The *gemara* thus concludes that the *kal v'chomer* from *almana li-kohen gadol* provides no valid proof, and the linguistic analysis of the *baraita* also provides no proof. The underlying question — whether the offspring of a simple *issur lav* is *pagum li-kehunah* — remains genuinely unresolved on the basis of these sources. The *gemara* acknowledges: *almanah kashya* — the attempted proof from *almanah* is problematic — and the entire structure built upon it collapses. In the case of *machzir grushaso*, a simple *issur lav* in which the woman's *kehunah* status is not altered by the act, there is no demonstrated basis for saying the child is *pagum li-kehunah*.

---

## Kares Only Pagum

### Kares Pagum

The *gemara* now shifts the framework. *Amar Rav Yosef bar Shimon bar Rebbe: ha-kol modim be-ba al chayavei kerisos she-ha-vlad pagum* — everyone agrees that if a man had relations with a woman whose prohibition carries *issur kares*, the child is *pagum*. Having abandoned the claim that an *issur lav* makes a child *pagum*, the *gemara* asks instead about *issur kares*.

### Teimani Concession

Who is the "everyone" who concedes this point? The *gemara* identifies the concession as belonging to Rabbi Yehoshua. Rabbi Yehoshua holds an even narrower definition of *mamzer* than the *chachamim* — he requires not merely *kares* but *chayavei misos beis din* (capital offenses by a court, such as adultery) to produce a *mamzer*. Even he concedes that the offspring of an *issur kares* is at minimum *pagum*, even if not a full *mamzer*.

### Kal V'Chomer

This concession is again derived via *kal v'chomer* from *almana l'kohen gadol*: if the offspring of that narrow, *kohen*-specific *lav* is *pagum*, then certainly the offspring of a universal *issur kares* should be *pagum*. This time, the *gemara* does not dismiss the argument.

### Zonah Transfer

The reason the *kal v'chomer* succeeds here, where it failed for *issur lav*, is that a woman who engages in a sexually prohibited act carrying *issur kares* is rendered a *zonah* — a category explicitly disqualified from *kehunah* marriage. *Keivan she-ba'alah, asa'ah zonah* — the act of union itself confers *zonah* status upon the woman. Since the woman herself becomes disqualified, that disqualification flows to the child as well. The mechanism thus mirrors that of the *almana*-*kohen gadol* case: it is always the woman's changed status that serves as the conduit for the child's *psul*. When the woman's status does not change — as in a simple *issur lav* — the child is unaffected. When the woman becomes a *zonah* through *issur kares*, that status transmits to the offspring.

---

## Non-Jew Father

### Consensus Claim

*Amar Rabbah bar bar Chana amar Rabbi Yochanan: ha-kol modim she-eved ve-oved kochavim ha-ba al bas Yisrael she-ha-vlad mamzer* — everyone agrees that a slave or a non-Jew who has relations with a Jewish woman produces a *mamzer*. This is a striking claim, and the *gemara* immediately asks: who is the "everyone" here? The answer is *Shimon Ha-Teimani* — even he who insists that *mamzer* status requires *issur kares* concedes this case.

### Lav But No Kiddushin

The concession is puzzling, because relations with a non-Jew are only an *issur lav*, not an *issur kares*. On Shimon Ha-Teimani's own framework, there should be no *mamzer*. The *gemara* resolves the apparent inconsistency: *hani mili* — the rule that *issur lav* does not produce a *mamzer* applies specifically to *lav*-prohibitions where *kiddushin* is nonetheless valid and binding. In ordinary *issur lav* cases, the man could in principle marry the woman through *kiddushin*, and if he does, a *get* is required to dissolve the marriage. It is within that framework of potential marital bindingness that we say the child is not a *mamzer*.

### Kiddushin Theory

But in the case of a non-Jew or a slave, *kiddushin* is categorically impossible — *keivan d'lo tafsi bu kiddushin, k'chayavei krisos dami* — since marriage cannot be binding, the case is treated as if it were *issur kares*. This raises a broader theoretical question: perhaps the operative criterion for *mamzer* is not *lav* versus *kares* at all, but rather whether *kiddushin* could be binding. When *kiddushin* is binding, the union carries a marital framework, and even a severe prohibition like *kares* does not produce a *mamzer* (for this we shall see the *niddah* counterexample shortly). When *kiddushin* cannot be binding, the offspring lacks any legitimate familial framework, and *mamzer* status results.

### Niddah Comparison

The *niddah* case presents itself as a powerful illustration. Relations with a *niddah* carry *issur kares*, yet the offspring of a husband and wife during a period of *niddah* is universally held not to be a *mamzer*. Why? Because *kiddushin* is fully binding in that marriage — the couple is validly married. The *kares*-level prohibition is severe, but it occurs within the context of a legally recognized marriage, and therefore the *mamzer* criterion is not triggered. This inverts the logic: it is not the *kares* per se that creates a *mamzer*, it may be the absence of bindable *kiddushin*. And if so, the non-Jew case — where *kiddushin* can never bind — would produce a *mamzer* even though it is only a *lav*. This is, the *gemara* acknowledges, a coherent and reasonable argument — though we shall see that the *halacha* does not follow it.

---

## Non-Jew Non-Mamzer

### RSBY Baraita

The *gemara* raises a challenge from a *baraita*: *Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda omer ein mamzer ela mi-she-issuro issur ervah ve-onush kares* — a *mamzer* results only from a union that is both a sexual prohibition (*issur ervah*) and punishable by *kares*. Intercourse with a non-Jew, being only an *issur lav*, would not produce a *mamzer* on this view. The *baraita* thus directly contradicts the claim that "everyone" agrees a non-Jew-fathered child is a *mamzer*.

### Rabbi's Possible Excepti…

*Rav Yosef* responds: *Ella amar Rav Yosef man d'chula modei Rabbi* — the "everyone" who concedes this point is *Rebbi*, Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi himself. Although *Rebbi* in another context says the lenient positions apply only according to Rabbi Akiva, and his own ruling aligns with the view that *mamzer* requires *issur kares* — nevertheless, in the specific case of a non-Jewish or slave father, *Rebbi* may concede that the child is a *mamzer*. The rationale is that even one who normally reserves *mamzer* status for *issur kares* might make an exception when *kiddushin* is categorically impossible, treating the non-Jew case as functionally equivalent to an *issur kares* situation in terms of its legal consequences. This remains the position being tested.

---

## Captive Woman Case

### Ami's Consultation

A narrative is now introduced. *Rabbi Acha Sar Ha-Birah* and *Rabbi Tanchum* the son of *Rabbi Chiya* of *Kfar Akko* redeemed a group of captive women traveling from Armon to Tiberias. One of these captive women had become pregnant through a non-Jew. The practical question of the child's status was brought before *Rabbi Ami*.

### Three Say Mamzer

*Rabbi Ami* reported the opinions he had received: *Rabbi Yochanan, Rabbi Elazar*, and *Rabbi Chanina* all held that a non-Jewish or slave father together with a Jewish mother produces a *mamzer*. These are three of the most authoritative voices in the generation of Palestinian *amoraim*.

### Four Say Kasher

*Rav Yosef* is unimpressed with the weight of three authorities and responds in kind: *ravusa le-mechashev gavrei* — is it such an achievement to count up names? He provides a counter-list of four: *Rav* and *Shmuel* in Bavel, and *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* and *Bar Kappara* in Eretz Yisrael — or, in an alternative formulation, *Bar Kappara* is replaced by the *ziknei darom*, the elders of the south. All four (or this variant group of four) hold that the child of a non-Jewish father and Jewish mother is *kasher*.

### Rabbi's Mamzer

The *gemara* does not resolve the standoff by simple head-counting. Instead, *Rav Yosef* himself declares: *ella amar Rav Yosef: Rebbe hi* — it is *Rebbi*'s position that is operative. The basis is the tradition brought by *Rav Dimi* in the name of *Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi* in the name of *Rabbeinu* — *Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi* — that *oved kochavim ve-eved ha-ba al bas Yisrael, ha-vlad mamzer*. So we have an explicit ruling attributed to *Rebbi* himself: the child born of a non-Jewish father and a Jewish mother is a *mamzer*.

### Kehunah Status TBD

The daf closes with this contested ruling standing unresolved in terms of final *pesak*. The *gemara* notes, and leaves for the following daf, the second question that flows from this discussion: even granting that we ultimately rule the child is *not* a *mamzer* — as the majority of *poskim* conclude — what is the child's status for *kehunah*? May a daughter born of a non-Jewish father marry a *kohen*? That question, deeply relevant in practice and tightly connected to everything that has been established in today's analysis, will be taken up on the next *amud*.

---

---

# Yevamot 51

## Framework: Acts After Ac…

### Mishna Overview

The Mishna on daf 51 works through an intricate series of permutations involving four distinct acts in the context of *yibum*: *maimar*, *get*, *biah*, and *chalitzah*. The governing question is what happens when one act follows another — whether performed by the same *yavam* with the same *yevama*, or across different brothers-in-law and different co-wives. Before entering the *Gemara*'s analysis, it is worth fixing the basic framework in mind.

### Rabbinic vs. Torah Acts

The four acts divide into two categories based on their legal standing. *Maimar* and *get* are rabbinic in this context. *Maimar* is an act of *kidushin* — literally *harei at mekudeshet li* — performed in the proper form, and *get* is a standard bill of divorce, executed properly in every technical respect. The critical point is that because these acts take place within the framework of *yibum*, their operative force is only *derabbanan*, not *d'oraisa*. *Biah* and *chalitzah*, by contrast, are *d'oraisa*: they constitute the Torah-mandated mechanisms for either completing or releasing the *yibum* bond. This distinction between rabbinic and Torah-level acts is the fulcrum on which the entire Mishnaic debate turns.

### Debate Structure

With that framework in place, the dispute between Rabban Gamliel and the *chachamim* can be stated precisely. Rabban Gamliel holds: *ein get achar get v'lo maimar achar maimar* — once a *get* or *maimar* has been given, no subsequent act of the same kind carries any consequence, even though those acts operate only rabbinically. And of course, *biah* after *biah* and *chalitzah* after *chalitzah* are similarly without effect, since the Torah-level act has already been completed. The *chachamim* agree regarding *biah* and *chalitzah*, but disagree regarding *get* and *maimar*: *yesh get achar get v'yesh maimar achar maimar* — because these acts are only rabbinic, they do not fully terminate the situation, and a second act of the same or a different type may still carry halakhic import. The debate thus focuses on a single axis: how absolute is a first rabbinic act against anything that comes afterwards?

---

## Foundational Principles

### Mehani Concept

Before entering the dispute itself, the *Gemara* at the bottom of 51b steps back to establish the conceptual foundations. The opening question is: *mahani mai ta'ama* — on what basis did the Rabbis institute the concept that a *get* or *maimar* has any effect at all in the *yibum* context? The term *mehani* here does not mean that these acts accomplish everything. A *get* given to a *yevama* does not function as a *chalitzah*, which is required *d'oraisa*; a *maimar* does not constitute *yibum*, which requires actual *biah*. What *mehani* means is that these acts carry halakhic implications. A *get* given to a *yevama*, for instance, closes off the possibility of *yibum* — *pasla kol ha'achim*; the other brothers can no longer perform *yibum* with her, and she takes on a status analogous to a divorced wife, prohibiting marriage to the *yavam*'s relatives. A *maimar* similarly creates a quasi-marital relationship, implicating the prohibitions involving relatives of the *yevama* and affecting the ability to perform *yibum* with another co-wife.

### Public Confusion Risk

The *Gemara* then explains why the Rabbis could not simply declare these acts meaningless. The argument is one of public confusion: *get l'hotzi v'chalitzah l'hotzi* — a *get* normally functions to release a full wife, and *chalitzah* functions to release a *yevama*. Were the Rabbis to say that a *get* given to a *yevama* is entirely meaningless, people would observe such a *get* being given and then watch as the *yavam* proceeds to perform *yibum* nonetheless. They would conclude that *chalitzah* is similarly meaningless — *chalitzah nami lo mahani* — and would come to believe that only *yibum* itself counts. The result would be that after a *chalitzah* they might still permit *biah* — *v'atei l'miba'al achar chalitzah* — which would be a severe violation. The same logic applies to *maimar*: were it declared null, people would conclude from parallel reasoning that *biah* in this context is also ineffective, leading to the possibility of *biah* after *biah* — violating the principle of *bayis echad hu boneh*.

### Rabbinic Necessity

The practical upshot is that the Rabbis needed these institutions to carry some weight in order to prevent the entire halakhic structure of *yibum* and *chalitzah* from becoming unintelligible to the public. Whether this represents a purely reactive rabbinic response to existing popular practice or a more proactive rabbinic design is a nuanced question — the *Gemara*'s framing here sounds reactive, as though people were already performing these acts and the Rabbis could not simply negate them. Other sources may present a more deliberately constructive picture of the institution of *maimar* in particular. In any case, the conclusion is firm: *get* and *maimar* in the *yibum* context must carry *some* halakhic meaning — *mehani* — even if not the full force of the Torah-level acts they parallel.

---

## Biah Pesulah Doctrin (II)

### Biah After Get

The *Gemara* continues: *u'mai ta'ama amru rabanan bi'ah pesulah yesh achareiha klum* — why did the Rabbis say that after an invalid *biah* (*biah pesulah*), subsequent acts remain meaningful? To answer this, one must understand what *biah pesulah* actually is. The Mishna at the close of the preceding discussion states: *bizman she'hi b'techilah ein achareiha klum* — when *biah* comes at the outset of the *yibum* process, the act of *yibum* is complete and nothing afterward counts. But *ba'emtza uv'sof* — when *biah* comes after something else has already transpired — things that follow it can still be meaningful.

The paradigmatic case of *biah pesulah* involves a scenario where the *yavam* gave a *get* to one *yevama* and then performed *biah* with another. The *Gemara* reasons: *gezeirah bi'ah achar get mishum bi'ah achar chalitzah* — the Rabbis treat *biah* following a *get* as problematic by analogy to *biah* following *chalitzah*. The logic is as follows. Suppose, instead of giving a *get* to the first *yevama*, the *yavam* had performed *chalitzah* with her — then *biah* with the second would be entirely forbidden, as *chalitzah* definitively closes the process. Since *get* and *chalitzah* are easily confused, and since permitting *biah* after *get* risks being confused with the forbidden *biah* after *chalitzah*, the Rabbis characterize *biah* after *get* as *biah pesulah* as well. The consequence is that although *d'oraisa* the *biah* constitutes valid *yibum* with the second *yevama*, the Rabbis do not allow the *yavam* to remain in that relationship; he must give her a *get* and she requires *chalitzah* to be fully released.

### Gezeirah Logic

A parallel case of *biah pesulah* arises when *biah* follows a *maimar*. If the *yavam* performed *maimar* with one *yevama* and then *biah* with another, the principle *bayis echad hu boneh v'eino boneh shnei batim* — that a man builds one household, not two — means that had the first act been full *yibum* rather than *maimar*, the *biah* with the second would be impermissible. Since *maimar* is a quasi-*yibum*, the *Gemara* treats *biah* after *maimar* as *biah pesulah* by a *gezeirah*: *gezeirah bi'ah achar ma'amar mishum bi'ah achar biah*.

The crucial consequence of *biah pesulah* is that the relationship is not considered fully consummated. Something remains unresolved, and therefore subsequent acts — giving a *get*, performing *maimar*, or doing *chalitzah* — can still carry halakhic meaning. The *Gemara* designates this with the phrase *yesh achareiha klum* — there is still something after it.

### Chalitzah vs. Biah

At this point one might ask: if *biah* after *get* is rendered *pesulah* because of its similarity to the forbidden *biah* after *chalitzah*, why does *chalitzah* after *get* not similarly become *chalitzah pesulah*? The *Gemara* addresses this directly: *mai nigzar* — what decree should we make? If we were to treat *chalitzah* after *get* as *pesulah* because it resembles *chalitzah* after *chalitzah*, the consequence would only be that we demand further *chalitzahs* — *kol ki hani tachlots v'teitzei* — and since *chalitzah* is not a forbidden act, requiring additional *chalitzahs* carries no grave consequence. It does affect the woman's status as a *chalutzah* and her prohibition to a *kohen*, but it does not generate the kind of severe *arayot* violation that motivates the *gezeirah* regarding *biah*. *Biah* with a woman one is forbidden to is a fundamentally different order of problem from performing an extra *chalitzah*. Therefore the *gezeirah* applies to *biah pesulah* but not to *chalitzah*: a *chalitzah* that follows a *get* or a *maimar* remains fully valid and ends the process — *ein achar chalitzah klum*.

---

## Rabban Gamliel's Model

### All-or-Nothing Logic

The *Gemara* now turns to explain Rabban Gamliel's position in depth. *Mai ta'ama d'Rabban Gamliel* — what is Rabban Gamliel's reasoning that even *get* after *get* and *maimar* after *maimar* are without effect? The *Gemara* answers: *demispeka lei get ee dachi ee lo dachi, maimar ee kani ee lo kani* — Rabban Gamliel is uncertain whether a *get* in the *yibum* context fully "pushes off" (*dachi*) all the *yevamot*, or does nothing at all; and similarly whether *maimar* fully "acquires" (*kani*) the *yevama* in a quasi-marital bond, or accomplishes nothing.

The binary nature of this uncertainty is what drives his ruling. If the *get* fully pushes off — *ee ka madchi* — then the first *get* has already resolved the situation with respect to all the *yevamot*, and the second *get* finds nothing left to accomplish: *basar mai ka avid*. If the *get* accomplishes nothing — *v'ee kama lo dachi* — then even the first *get* did nothing, and the second certainly does not: *basar nami lo dachi*. Either the first fully worked or neither works. The same analysis applies to *maimar*: if the first *maimar* fully acquired the *yevama*, the second is superfluous; if the first acquired nothing, the second is no better. The only meaningful act is therefore always the first one — which *might* be fully effective — while every subsequent act of the same kind is certainly without consequence.

### Consistency Argument

This binary model has a striking implication that Tosafot and Rashi both highlight. Rabban Gamliel says *ein get achar get v'ein maimar achar maimar* — but he appears to concede that a *get* after a *maimar*, or a *maimar* after a *get*, *can* be meaningful. If he truly held that these rabbinic acts function at full force, why would mixing them matter? The binary model explains this elegantly. The uncertainty about *get* and the uncertainty about *maimar* are independent of one another: *get* might be effective or might not; *maimar* might acquire or might not. They need not share the same outcome. Therefore, if *maimar* was effective and *get* was not, the *get* after *maimar* does something previously unaddressed, and vice versa. Two acts of the same type, however, necessarily target the same outcome — either the first worked and the second is redundant, or the first failed and the second will likewise fail.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye raises a sharp difficulty against Rabban Gamliel's binary model. The Mishna acknowledges that Rabban Gamliel concedes the existence of *biah pesulah* — that *biah* following *get* or *maimar* remains problematic and subsequent acts carry meaning. Abaye asks: *v'ee salka da'atach d'Rabban Gamliel havyah k'viah d'lechatchilah v'tikni* — if the *maimar* is either fully effective or fully zero, as Rabban Gamliel maintains, how does *biah pesulah* arise at all? If the *maimar* with the first *yevama* was fully effective, then the subsequent *biah* with the second is like *biah* that comes *b'techilah* — at the outset — and nothing afterward counts: *ein achareiha klum*. If the *maimar* was zero, then the subsequent *biah* is a clean *biah* not preceded by anything, and again nothing afterward would count. On either prong of the binary, there is no room for *biah pesulah*. Yet Rabban Gamliel concedes the category. The binary model, taken strictly, cannot account for it.

---

## Fifty-Percent Model

### Two Halves Concept

Abaye's challenge dissolves Rabban Gamliel's pure binary framework and compels a different account of how *get* and *maimar* function. *Ella amar Abaye* — rather, Abaye says, the correct understanding is that the Rabbis established *get* and *maimar* in the *yibum* context not as all-or-nothing propositions, but as acts that each address exactly one half of the *zikah* bond. The *zikah* — the quasi-spousal connection that ties the *yevama* to the *yavam* — is not a single undifferentiated legal relationship but is conceptually composed of two distinct components.

### Slot Division

One half of the *zikah* is the *kinyan* component — the aspect of acquisition and quasi-marital attachment. This is the half that *maimar* addresses. The other half is the *dechiyah* component — the aspect of release and severance. This is the half that *get* addresses. *Maimar* fills the *kinyan* slot; *get* fills the *dechiyah* slot. Each act operates on its own distinct portion of the *zikah*: *bechad tzad mahani bah get uvechad tzad mahani bah maimar*.

### Same vs. Different Acts

This fifty-percent model explains the full pattern of what does and does not carry effect. *Get achar get lo dachi* — a second *get* cannot do anything because the first *get* already addressed the *dechiyah* half; there is nothing remaining in that slot for the second to work on. *Maimar achar maimar lo kani* — a second *maimar* similarly finds the *kinyan* half already addressed. But *get achar maimar* and *maimar achar get* do carry meaning, because each act addresses the half that the other left untouched. The cross-combination works precisely because the two acts target distinct halves of the *zikah*.

### Partial Connection Effect

The fifty-percent model also explains *biah pesulah* in a way the binary model could not. When a *maimar* was performed with one *yevama*, the *yavam* has forged a half-connection to her — the *kinyan* half of the *zikah* has been engaged. When he then performs *biah* with a second *yevama*, this is not a *biah* that comes against the backdrop of either zero or a full prior relationship. There is a genuine, if partial, prior bond to the first *yevama* — the released half of the *zikah* remains unreleased. This unresolved partial connection makes the *biah* with the second *yevama* a *biah pesulah*: it is not the clean, first-in-time *biah* of a complete *yibum* situation. The relationship is therefore not treated as concluded, and subsequent acts retain halakhic significance. The intermediate state is not a conceptual fiction born of doubt — it is a real halakhic condition arising from the structure of the *zikah* itself.

The *Gemara* elaborates further: *biah pesulah* occupies an intermediate position — stronger than *maimar* in some respects, weaker in others. *Adifa mi'maimar* — stronger than *maimar* — in that if a second *maimar* follows the first, it is meaningless because it tries to fill an already-occupied slot; but *biah* after *maimar* does carry force because the *biah*, being *d'oraisa*, effectively dominates and causes us to view the situation as *biah* followed by *maimar* — a different pairing that can still be operative. *Gri'ah mi'maimar* — weaker than *maimar* — in that if *maimar* had filled its half of the *zikah*, a second *maimar* that follows would find nothing left; but because *biah* fills that slot in a weaker mode, the *maimar* that follows it remains operative rather than being treated as a redundant overlay.

---

## Biah Pesulah Doctrin (II)

### Chalitzah Efficacy

The fifty-percent model also clarifies why *chalitzah* that follows *maimar* or *get* remains fully valid and terminates the process. *Chalitzah* is not an act that targets one half of the *zikah* to the exclusion of the other; it is a Torah-level act of release that cuts through the entire bond. Whether the *kinyan* half or the *dechiyah* half has or has not been previously addressed at the rabbinic level, *chalitzah d'oraisa* dissolves whatever remains. There is therefore no basis for treating it as *chalitzah pesulah* — it accomplishes its full work regardless of what preceded it. The consequence is that once *chalitzah* has been performed, the process is genuinely complete: *ein achar chalitzah klum*. The *yavam* may need to address whatever rabbinic acts were done beforehand — for example, giving a *get* to the *yevama* with whom *maimar* was performed — but the *chalitzah* itself is unimpaired and conclusive.

---

## Chachamim's Response

### Individual Slots

The *chachamim* accept the basic architecture of the fifty-percent model — that every relationship between a *yavam* and a *yevama* contains a *kinyan* slot addressable by *maimar* and a *dechiyah* slot addressable by *get* — but they contest Rabban Gamliel's premise that these slots are shared across the entire class of *yevamot* and *yevamim*. The *chachamim* hold: *kol chad v'chad tikinu lei Rabbanan get u'maimar b'yevama* — the Rabbis established a *get* and a *maimar* for each individual brother-in-law with each individual *yevama*. Every *yavam*–*yevama* pairing has its own independent set of slots.

### Problematic Efficacy

This individualization means that even when one *yavam* has performed *maimar* with a particular *yevama* — filling the *kinyan* slot in their relationship — a second *yavam* can come and perform *maimar* with that same *yevama*, addressing *his* *kinyan* slot in *their* pairing, which is distinct. Similarly, a second *maimar* with a different *yevama* addresses that pairing's independent slot. The result is that what Rabban Gamliel treats as exhausted — because the class-wide slot has been filled — the *chachamim* treat as potentially still operative, because each pairing maintains its own capacity. This does not mean that subsequent acts confer rights or privileges upon the second *yavam*; rather, it means they generate halakhic complications, obligations, and prohibitions — the need for additional *gitin*, *chalitzot*, and so forth. Once these entanglements accumulate, the practical result is a complex web of relationships that must each be individually resolved. The *chachamim*'s disagreement with Rabban Gamliel is therefore not about whether the fifty-percent model is correct, but about whether the slots are pooled or individuated.

---

## Two Sisters, One Brother

### RG: Two Gets Rule

The *Gemara* now presents the practical cases from the *baraita* that illustrate the dispute. The case of two *yevamot* and one *yavam*: he gave a *get* to one and a *get* to the other — *natan get l'zo v'get l'zo*. Rabban Gamliel rules: *choletz l'rishonah v'asur b'krovoteha u'mutar b'krovot shniyah* — he does *chalitzah* with the first *yevama*, since the second *get* was entirely without effect, and he is forbidden to her relatives. With the second *yevama*, the *get* was meaningless and she carries no *grusha* status; he is therefore permitted to her relatives.

### Chachamim: Both Divorced

The *chachamim* rule differently: *natan get l'zo v'get l'zo asur b'krovot shteihen* — the second *get* also carries meaning, rendering her a quasi-*gerushah*, and he is forbidden to the relatives of both. Moreover, since both carry *grusha* status, *chalitzah l'achat mehen* — a *chalitzah* to either one suffices, as neither has a halakhic advantage over the other.

### Parallel: Two Brothers

The *baraita* notes the symmetric case: *v'chen ata omer b'shnei yevamim v'yevamah achat* — the same principles apply when two brothers-in-law each give a *get* to the same *yevama*. According to Rabban Gamliel, only the first *yavam*'s *get* carries effect; he is forbidden to her relatives. The second *yavam*'s *get* is without consequence; he remains permitted to her relatives. The *chachamim* hold that the second *yavam*'s *get* also carries effect, and he too is forbidden to her relatives.

### RG: Two Maimars Rule

Turning to the *maimar* cases: two *yevamot* and one *yavam*, and he performed *maimar* with both — *asa ma'amar b'zo u'ma'amar b'zo*. Rabban Gamliel rules: *noten get l'rishonah v'choletz lah v'asur b'krovoteha u'mutar b'krovot shniyah* — only the first *maimar* was operative, so he must give a *get* for the *maimar* and perform *chalitzah* with the first *yevama*, and *chalitzah* should not be done with the second so as not to impose *chalutzah* status upon her unnecessarily, since the second *maimar* was meaningless. He is forbidden to the first's relatives and permitted to the second's.

### Chachamim: Both Need Get

The *chachamim* rule: *noten get l'shteihen* — the second *maimar* was also operative, so both *yevamot* require a *get*. Because both carry quasi-*gerushah* status, he is forbidden to the relatives of both — *asur b'krovot shteihen* — and *chalitzah l'achat mehen* is sufficient. Again, the symmetric case of two brothers-in-law performing *maimar* with a single *yevama* follows the same logic in both directions.

---

## Chalitzah After Get

### Contradiction Setup

The *Gemara* raises a challenge from Shmuel's earlier ruling. Rabban Gamliel has said that in the case of two *gets* and two *yevamot*, one need only do *chalitzah* with the first *yevama* — *choletz l'rishonah* — and that is sufficient. But Shmuel had stated: *chalatz l'ba'alas haget lo nifterah tzarah* — if the *yavam* did *chalitzah* with the *yevama* who had received a *get*, the co-wife is *not* thereby released.
