Shmuel's position is that *chalitzah* following a *get* is a weakened *chalitzah* — something like *chalitzah pesulah* — because the *get* already diminished the *zikah* bond, and therefore this *chalitzah* does not exempt the co-wife; all co-wives must receive individual *chalitzahs*. This appears to flatly contradict Rabban Gamliel's ruling that one *chalitzah* to the first *yevama* suffices.

### Shmuel's Ruling

The *Gemara* resolves this by placing Shmuel's ruling in its proper doctrinal context. Shmuel himself explains: *ki amina ana aliba d'man d'amar yeish zikah* — when I said that *chalitzah* after *get* is weakened and requires multiple *chalitzahs*, I was speaking according to the view that there is a *zikah*, a genuine quasi-spousal bond connecting the *yevama* to the *yavam*. On that view, the *get* has already eroded the *zikah*, and the *chalitzah* that follows it is correspondingly diminished in force.

### RG: No Zikah

Rabban Gamliel, however, holds *ein zikah* — there is no *zikah*. While there is a *mitzvah* of *chalitzah* binding the *yevama* to the process, Rabban Gamliel does not recognize the category of a quasi-marital bond called *zikah* as such.

### Consequence: One Chalitz…

If there is no *zikah* to be weakened, then a *get* given to a *yevama* cannot diminish what does not exist. The *chalitzah* that follows the *get* is therefore not a weakened *chalitzah* — it is as full and effective as any other *chalitzah*. Consequently, Rabban Gamliel can consistently hold that one *chalitzah* with the first *yevama* suffices, with no need to repeat the process for the second. Shmuel's ruling of multiple *chalitzahs* and Rabban Gamliel's ruling of a single *chalitzah* reflect not a contradiction but the application of each position to its own foundational premise — *yeish zikah* versus *ein zikah* — and the two rulings are entirely coherent with one another.

---

---

# Yevamot 52

## Ma'amar/Get debate

### Opening context

Today's daf is 52. We pick up on 51b, in the middle of the extended discussion concerning *ma'amar* after *ma'amar* and *get* after *get*. The most technically demanding portions of that analysis are largely behind us. What the *gemara* is doing now is clarifying how these principles interact with related questions raised earlier in the sugya.

### Rabban Gamliel's rule

When Rabban Gamliel says *ein ma'amar achar ma'amar v'ein get achar get*, the *gemara* considers a specific scenario: the *yavam* gave a *get* to two *yevamot*, and according to Rabban Gamliel he may ignore the second co-wife and proceed to perform *chalitzah* with the first. The *gemara*'s question is how this squares with Shmuel, who holds that a *chalitzah* following a *get* is a weakened *chalitzah pesulah* — because the *get* has already attenuated the *zika* — and in such a case the *chalitzah* must be extended to the other co-wife as well. Yet Rabban Gamliel rules that even in the case of *chalitzah* after *get*, the other woman is completely released. The *gemara* resolves this by attributing to Shmuel the position of *yesh zika*: the *get* weakens the *zika*, thereby weakening the *chalitzah* that follows. Rabban Gamliel, by contrast, holds *ein zika*, so the *get* has no such attenuating effect on the *chalitzah*.

### Zika disagreement

The *gemara* then suggests that the *rabbanan* who disagree with Rabban Gamliel hold *yesh zika*, and examines the end of the relevant *mishnah* — the case of two *yevamin* and one *yevamah*, where both brothers gave her a *get* and the *chalitzah* is performed by only one. If the *rabbanan* hold *yesh zika*, the *chalitzah* following the *get* would be a *chalitzah pesulah*, and by the principle stated in the name of Rav Abba bar Avina in the name of Rav — that a *chalitzah pesulah* requires going back to all the brothers — each brother should have to perform *chalitzah* separately. Yet the *mishnah* indicates that one *chalitzah* suffices, which would seem to contradict Rav Abba bar Avina's ruling if the *rabbanan* hold *yesh zika*.

### Ein Zika consensus

Rav Abba bar Avina resolves this by stating that both Rabban Gamliel and the *rabbanan* in fact hold *ein zika*. The entire framework of a weakened *chalitzah* requiring repetition across all brothers and co-wives depends on the position of *yesh zika*, whereby the *get* drains strength from the *zika* and consequently from the *chalitzah* that follows. Since both Rabban Gamliel and the *rabbanan* reject this — they hold *ein zika* — the *get* has no impact on the *chalitzah*, the *chalitzah* is not weakened, and it is therefore not a challenge to Rav Abba bar Avina's principle. Their dispute is confined to the question of *ma'amar achar ma'amar* and *get achar get*, not to the consequences of *zika*.

---

## Gezeirah concern

### Amar Mar setup

The *gemara* now returns to examine a previously cited statement more closely. The case: a *yavam* performed *ma'amar* with each of two co-wives. Rabban Gamliel rules: ignore the second *ma'amar* as meaningless, and treat only the first as operative. To extricate himself from the first, he gives her a *get* to dissolve the *ma'amar* and then performs *chalitzah*. He is then permitted to marry the relatives of the second woman, since the second *ma'amar* was legally void and created no relationship. He does not perform *chalitzah* with the second woman, since doing so would damage her status unnecessarily; the relevant legal relationship exists only with the first.

### Why break first?

This generates an obvious difficulty. If the second *ma'amar* was entirely meaningless — as Rabban Gamliel explicitly holds — then the first *ma'amar* remains uncompromised. Why must he break off from the first wife with a *get* and *chalitzah* at all? He should simply be permitted to proceed directly to *yibum* with her, since the second *ma'amar* never affected their relationship.

### Gezeirah rationale

The *gemara* answers: *gezeira*. Even though the *yibum* with the first wife would be entirely permitted in this case, we are concerned that observers will draw an incorrect inference. They will see that a *ma'amar* was followed by *yibum* and reason that the same logic applies to the second *ma'amar* — thus permitting *yibum* after the second *ma'amar* in some future case, which would be forbidden because one cannot establish two households simultaneously (*bayis echad hu boneh v'eino boneh shenei batim*). Once two co-wives are implicated, we require complete dissolution even according to Rabban Gamliel — not because the first relationship is legally compromised, but to preserve clarity and prevent confusion in analogous cases. The *gezeira* is admittedly somewhat far-fetched, since the present case itself presents no problem once the *yibum* is performed with one. Nevertheless, the rabbis preferred to keep the rules clean rather than risk someone drawing the wrong conclusion in a structurally similar situation.

---

## Ma'amar opinions

### Rabban Gamliel

Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabban Gamliel, Beit Shammai, Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai, and Rabbi Nechemiah all hold, in varying formulations, that *ma'amar koneh kinyan gamur* — *ma'amar* effects a complete *kinyan*. It is important to note, as Tosafot emphasizes repeatedly, that saying all these *tannaim* hold the same position means they share a family resemblance of approach, not an identical ruling. Beginning with Rabban Gamliel: his position, as already established, is *ein ma'amar achar ma'amar*. Once a *ma'amar* has been performed, no second *ma'amar* can take hold. Within the *ma'amar* slot, the first act fills it completely and leaves no room for a subsequent one — demonstrating that *ma'amar* is a full *kinyan*.

### Beit Shammai

The case for Beit Shammai involves three brothers: two married to two sisters and one *mufneh* (unmarried). One of the married brothers dies. The single brother performs *ma'amar* with that brother's widow, Rachel. Then the second married brother dies, leaving his widow Leah. At this point the *yavam* has a *zika* to both women — who are sisters. Normally, since he is bound to both, he would need to perform *chalitzah* with each, since consummating with one would render the other *achos zikukaso*, a prohibited relation under *arayot*.

Beit Shammai rules: since he has already performed *ma'amar* with Rachel, it is as if he has already consummated the *yibum*. The *ma'amar* operates at a *d'oraita* level for Beit Shammai, reframing the relationship as though Rachel is already his wife. Leah therefore walks away entirely as an *ervah* — she requires no *chalitzah*. This is the paradigmatic expression of *ma'amar koneh kinyan gamur*: the *ma'amar* is treated as equivalent to consummation itself, with full *d'oraita* consequence.

### Rabbi Shimon

The case for Rabbi Shimon involves two brothers who are both under the age of Bar Mitzvah — nine years old and a day — who each had relations with a *yevamah*. The *halacha* establishes that *bias katan* (intercourse by a minor) is treated by the rabbis as equivalent to *ma'amar*: it is not a full act of *yibum*, since the boy has not reached adulthood, but it carries sufficient legal significance to be treated as a rabbinic *ma'amar*.

If both underage brothers had relations with the same *yevamah*, this constitutes the analog of *ma'amar achar ma'amar*. The *chachamim* hold that both must give a *get*. Rabbi Shimon disagrees: *im bias rishon bia, bias sheni einah bia* — if the first act was legally meaningful, the second is not. And *v'im bias rishon einah bia, bias sheni nami einah bia* — if the first is not meaningful at all, neither is the second. Either way, there is no need to address the second brother's act. This is the direct parallel to Rabban Gamliel's *ein ma'amar achar ma'amar*, applied to the domain of *bias katan*.

### Ben Azzai

Ben Azzai's position is more nuanced. He holds *yesh ma'amar achar ma'amar bishnei yevamin v'yevamah achas* — if there are two brothers-in-law and one *yevamah*, the second *ma'amar* (from the second brother) is meaningful. However, *ein ma'amar achar ma'amar bishtei yevamot v'yavam echad* — if there is one *yavam* and two *yevamot*, once he has used his *ma'amar* on one woman, he cannot perform a valid *ma'amar* on the other. There is a dispute between Rashi and Tosafot over whether the *girsa* should be read in the opposite direction. The underlying question is which configuration better fits the *kiddushin* model: intuitively, it makes more sense that a woman who is already *mekudeshes* cannot be the object of a second *ma'amar* from another man, but the *girsa* and its reversal are debated. Whichever reading one accepts, Ben Azzai agrees with Rabban Gamliel in at least one configuration of *ein ma'amar achar ma'amar*.

### Rabbi Nechemiah

Rabbi Nechemiah states: *achas bia v'achas chalitza bein batchila bein ba-emtza bein basof, ein achareiha klum* — whether it is *bia* or *chalitza*, whether performed at the beginning, middle, or end of the process, nothing counts afterward. This is more sweeping than what we have established elsewhere. We have generally said that *bia pesulah* (defective intercourse) is treated rabinically as equivalent to *ma'amar*, and that something may still be done afterward. Rabbi Nechemiah disagrees: even a *bia pesulah* in the middle of the process terminates it entirely. The *gemara* notes that this position presupposes *ein ma'amar achar ma'amar*, since *bia pesulah* has been assimilated to *ma'amar*, and Rabbi Nechemiah holds that once that has occurred, nothing further can follow. It should be noted that Rabbi Nechemiah's view is not identical to Rabban Gamliel's — these *tannaim* share the general orientation that *ma'amar* or its equivalent forecloses what follows, but the specific applications differ.

---

## Ma'amar mechanics

### Keitzad meaning

The *mishnah* now turns to the question *keitzad asa ma'amar* — how is *ma'amar* performed? But before the *gemara* can address the mechanics, it must clarify what the *mishnah* is doing. The section proceeds to discuss hybrid cases — *ma'amar* followed by *get*, *get* followed by *chalitzah*, and so forth — rather than the pairings of *ma'amar* after *ma'amar* or *get* after *get* that dominated the preceding discussion. The *gemara* notes the apparent incongruity: the *mishnah* says *keitzad* as though elaborating on *get achar get*, yet it goes on to discuss different acts combined with each other. Rav Yehuda clarifies: the debate between Rabban Gamliel and the *chachamim* regarding *get achar get* and *ma'amar achar ma'amar* is what was already stated. *Keitzad* introduces the hybrid cases — one *yavam* and one *yevamah* — where two qualitatively different acts are combined, and asks what the implications of each sequence are.

### Basic sequences

In all hybrid cases, both Rabban Gamliel and the *chachamim* agree that the second act remains meaningful, since it is of a different type than the first. The *mishnah* then proceeds through the various combinations. *Asa ma'amar v'natan lah get, tzricha heimenu chalitzah* — if he began with *ma'amar* and then gave a *get*, he has not concluded the process and she still requires *chalitzah* from him. This is the standard incomplete-release scenario. The *mishnah* also addresses *ma'amar* followed by *yibum*: *asa ma'amar u'va'al harei zu kemitzvatah* — if he performed *ma'amar* and then consummated the *yibum*, this is the proper procedure. Just as *kiddushin* precedes *nisuin* in ordinary marriage, here the *ma'amar* precedes and frames the act of *yibum*.

### Rav Huna

The *gemara* asks whether the phrase *harei zu kemitzvatah* supports Rav Huna's ruling. Rav Huna states: *mitzvat yavam mekadesh v'achar kach bo'el* — the ideal manner of performing *yibum* is first to perform *ma'amar* (the rabbinic analog of *kiddushin*) and only then to have intercourse, mirroring the structure of normal marriage in which *kiddushin* precedes *nisuin*. The logic is compelling not only formally but substantively: one should not begin the relationship with the physical act. The relationship ought to be framed legally and relationally before the intimacy follows — even where the *d'oraita* act is the intercourse itself and the *ma'amar* is purely rabbinic.

### Reframing question

The *gemara* raises a concern: when *ma'amar* precedes *yibum*, does this not reframe the entire relationship such that it no longer looks like *yibum* at all? Once the *ma'amar* is performed, the *gemara* reasons, *parchah himenu zikat yavam v'chalah aleha zikat eirusin* — the *yibum* bond falls away and is replaced by an *erusin* bond. The woman is no longer treated as a *yevamah* but as an *arusah* in the ordinary sense. If that is so, perhaps the ideal procedure should avoid *ma'amar* before *yibum*, lest it transform the relationship into something that loses its character as *yibum*.

### Acceptable answer

The *gemara* dismisses this concern: *af zo kemitzvatah* — even this is an acceptable, indeed praiseworthy, manner of performing the *mitzvah*. The reframing is not a problem; it is in fact the preferred result. Remarkably, the Rambam rules (*Mishneh Torah, Hilchot Yibum*) that when a *yavam* does *ma'amar* with his *yevamah*, he recites *birkat nisuin* — *sheva brachot* — with ten men present, and writes a *ketubah*. The act is treated in every external respect exactly like a normal marriage. The underlying *d'oraita* category remains *yibum*, but the rabbinic overlay of *ma'amar* causes the relationship to present itself in precisely the form of ordinary *kiddushin* and *nisuin*, and according to the Rambam this is entirely the point.

---

## Rav's lashes

### Lashes question

The *gemara* cites Rav Huna's full statement: *mekadesh v'achar kach bo'el* is the ideal; however, *sheim ba v'lo asah ma'amar kanah* — if he had intercourse without having performed *ma'amar* at all, the *yibum* is nonetheless valid. The *gemara* immediately questions this: *peshita*, of course the *yibum* takes effect — *kaniah be'via*. The question is therefore refined: the point is that even if he reversed the order entirely, having intercourse without ever performing *ma'amar*, it still works. But the *gemara* counters with a *baraita*: such a person receives *makat mardut* — rabbinic lashes for defying the rabbinic norm.

### Makat Mardut

The lashes are not because the *yibum* is invalid. The *yibum* is entirely valid *d'oraita*. Rather, the lashes are *makat mardut midrabbanan* — punishment for contravening the rabbinic preference for *ma'amar* to precede intercourse. The institution of *ma'amar* was created precisely so that *yibum* not be inaugurated purely by the physical act, mirroring the rabbinic insistence in ordinary marriage that *kiddushin* precede *nisuin*. Bypassing this framework violates the rabbinic expectation, even though it does not invalidate the underlying transaction.

### Broader principle

This connects to a broader principle of Rav's, who would administer rabbinic lashes in several analogous situations. Rav would give *malkut* to one who performed *kiddushin* by means of *bia* — using intercourse as the act of *kiddushin* rather than *kesef* or *shtar*. This is striking, since *kiddushei bia* is itself a biblical institution — the first *mishnah* of *Kiddushin* lists *kesef, shtar, v'via* as the three modes of *kiddushin*. Yet Rav held this to be morally and socially unacceptable, regardless of its legal validity *d'oraita*. His principle: sex should not inaugurate the relationship; the legal commitment should precede the physical one. Similarly, Rav would give lashes for one who performed *kiddushin be-shuka* — giving *kesef kiddushin* in a public marketplace. Whatever the precise objection (whether it is the lack of intimacy in the setting, the impulsiveness it suggests, or the objectifying nature of a public transaction), the act is deemed improper. And likewise for one who performed *kiddushin belo shidukhei* — without any prior courtship or engagement process. Just as the physical relationship should be preceded by the legal commitment, the legal commitment (*kiddushin*) should itself be preceded by a considered process of *shidukhim*. One should not leap directly into *kiddushin* without having built a relationship first.

Rav extends these lashes further: to one who effects *bittul* of a *get* when the *shaliach* is not present (causing the woman to believe she is divorced when she is not); to one who submits a *moda'a* before signing a *get* (a prior declaration that the document he is about to sign is given under duress and therefore invalid — Tosafot notes that even where these acts may technically fail on legal grounds, the mere doing of them casts doubt on the woman's status and constitutes *motzi la'az* on the *get*); to one who behaves contemptuously toward a rabbinic messenger; and to one who has had a *niduy* placed on him for thirty days without appearing before the court to resolve it. Finally, Rav addresses one who lives in his father-in-law's house, where the concern is proximity to his mother-in-law in her husband's absence. The *gemara* qualifies: *dedayer in, dechalif lau* — only one who actually resides there, not one who merely passes by. The case of Rav Sheshet, who administered lashes to someone who was merely passing the door of his father-in-law's house, is explained differently: that individual was already under suspicion of an improper relationship, and the frequent appearances made the concern concrete.

### Nahardai limits

The *nahardeai* qualify Rav's practice significantly: in none of these cases would Rav actually administer lashes except when two factors converged — *kiddushin* performed via *bia* and the complete absence of *shidukhim*. Only when the intercourse was the very first act, with no prior courtship whatsoever, did Rav act. A dissenting view among the *nahardeai* holds that even when *shidukhim* did precede, if the *kiddushin* were effected via *bia* it is still *mishum pritzuta* — licentious — and lashes are appropriate. This latter view coheres with the general orientation noted earlier: the insistence that *ma'amar* precede *yibum*, the parallel insistence that *kiddushin* precede marital intercourse, and the further insistence that *shidukhim* precede *kiddushin* — all reflect a consistent rabbinic concern that relationships be built in ordered stages, each stage providing the framework within which the next properly occurs.

---

## Ma'amar wording

### Cash/Shtar method

A *baraita* now addresses the mechanics of *ma'amar*: *natan lah kesef o shaveh kesef* — he gives her money or something worth money, precisely as in regular *kiddushin*. Rashi understands that accompanying words are required — something like *hitkadshi li* or *hitkadshi li b'ma'amar yevamin* — though the *gemara* itself focuses on the act of giving rather than specifying the formula. The *gemara* proceeds to ask about *ma'amar* by *shtar*: if a *get* of a *yevamah* is rabbinic, is the *shtar* of *ma'amar* analogous to a normal *shtar kiddushin*? The answer given is *ki-de-amran* — yes, like a standard *shtar kiddushin*, written on paper or pottery, worth less than a *perutah*, bearing the formula *harei at mekudeshet li*. The *gemara* does not posit different language for *ma'amar* in this context.

### Shtar wording

Abaye reframes the question: the *mishnah*'s inquiry about *shtar* is actually asking how one writes a *ketubah* for *yibum* — *shtar ketuvas yevamin keitzad*? The *ketubah* obligation has now transferred to the *yavam*, and a new document must be written. The formula: *ana ploni bar ploni kabbaleit yat plonit yevamti alai la-zun u-le-farnesah ke-ra'uy* — I, so-and-so son of so-and-so, accept so-and-so, my *yevamah*, upon me, to sustain and support her as is fitting. This constitutes the ongoing *tenai ketubah*. The *gemara* adds: the lien for collecting the *ketubah* falls on the estate of the first husband — the *ketubah* obligation follows the original matrimonial bond. If the first estate lacks sufficient assets, the *rabbanan* established that she may collect from the second husband, *kedei she-lo tehei kallah b'einav le-hotzi'ah* — so that it should not be easy for him to dismiss her without financial consequence.

### Get wording test

Abaye poses a question to Rabba: if the *yavam* said to the *yevamah*, *harei at megureshet mimmeni v'i at muteret le-chol adam* — "you are divorced from me, but not permitted to anyone else" — does this constitute a valid *get* for the purposes of *yibum*? This formulation would be meaningless in an ordinary marital *get*, since a *get* that fails to render the woman *muteret le-chol adam* does not fully dissolve the marriage for all purposes. But the *get* of a *yevamah* is rabbinic in nature, and its function is specific: it operates to prevent *yibum*, to *pasul* her from the other brothers, and to implicate the co-wives. The question is whether this half-formulated expression carries enough *get*-like character to trigger those consequences.

### Reiach HaGet

Rabba bar Chanan objects: if we say that anything resembling a *get* carries its consequences, one could argue that handing over a blank piece of paper while saying *harei zeh gittech* would equally *pasul* her. Surely there must be some minimum standard.

The *gemara* distinguishes: *hatam lo pasil bekhuna, hacha ka pasil bekhuna*. The relevant criterion is whether the act is sufficient to render the woman a *gerusha* with respect to *kehuna*. The *gemara* cites the *baraita*: *v'isha gerusha meisha, lo yikachu* — the prohibition on a *kohen* marrying a divorced woman applies to one who is *gerusha me'isha*, divorced from her husband, even if not *muteret le-chol adam*. The Talmudic derivation — *afilu lo nitgareshah ela meisha* — indicates that the one-sided formula *harei at megureshet mimmeni* is sufficient to confer the status of *gerusha* at a rabbinic level for purposes of *kehuna*, even though *d'oraita* the marriage remains intact.

This is the concept of *reiach ha-get* — the "smell of a *get*." A document or act that shares enough of the characteristics of a *get*, even if technically invalid, may carry sufficient *get*-like quality to produce certain rabbinic consequences: rendering a woman a *gerusha* for *kehuna* purposes, and — as the present discussion shows — having real legal effect in the domain of *hilchos yibum*. Not all *gittin psulim* possess *reiach ha-get*; determining which defective *getin* have sufficient formal integrity to be treated as carrying this "smell" is a question that will recur throughout *masechet Gittin*. What this passage establishes is that *reiach ha-get* operates in two distinct areas simultaneously: *issur kehuna* and the laws of *yibum*.

---

## Future Get questions

### Get for Arusah

Rami bar Chama introduces a series of questions by first laying out established rules of *hilchos gittin*. If a man told a scribe to write a *get* for his *arusah* — a woman to whom he had already performed *kiddushin* — with the intention of divorcing her after *nisuin*, the *get* is valid even though written before *nisuin*. The reasoning: *mipnei she-beyado le-garshah* — he could have given it to her immediately, since one may divorce an *arusah*. The fact that he intended to wait does not affect the validity of the writing. By contrast, if he instructed a scribe to write a *get* for a woman with whom he had no current marital relationship — merely intending to betroth her in the future — the *get* is invalid: *mipnei she-ein beyado le-garshah* — he has no current power to divorce her, and a *get* requires a present relationship to which it is addressed.

### Get for stranger

These two cases establish the principle: the validity of a *get* written before the marital bond it is intended to dissolve depends on whether the relationship exists at the time of writing. A *get* written for an *arusah* is valid because the bond of *kiddushin* is already in place; a *get* written for a woman with whom no relationship yet exists is not.

### Yevama Get

Rami bar Chama now poses his question: *le-yevamto mahu*? A man's brother has died; he has a *yevamah* bound to him by *zika*. May he instruct a scribe to write a *get* now, planning to give it after performing *ma'amar*? Is the *zika* sufficient to treat her as analogous to an *arusah*, such that a *get* written at the stage of *zika* is valid for use after *ma'amar*? Or is the *zika* alone insufficient — no *get* can be written because she is not yet truly his in any legally actionable sense?

Rashi suggests the question may alternatively concern whether a *get* can be written at the stage of *zika* for use after *yibum* itself has been performed, but the more straightforward reading keeps the discussion within the rabbinic plane of *zika*, *ma'amar*, and *get*.

### Yevama status

Two positions emerge. On one view: *keivan de-agidah bei ka-arusato damya* — since she is bound and knotted to him via *zika*, she is comparable to an *arusah* and the *get* written now would be valid. On the other view: *keivan de-lo avad bah ma'amar*, since he has not yet performed *ma'amar*, there is no real relationship yet, and the *get* is meaningless. The *gemara* leaves this unresolved: *teiku*.

---

## Partial Get

### Divided Get

Rav Chanina raises a further question: *katav get le-zikato v'lo le-ma'amaro, le-ma'amaro v'lo le-zikato* — after a *ma'amar* has been performed, the *yavam* writes a *get* and declares that it is intended to sever only the *ma'amar* component of his relationship, not the *zika*. Or alternatively, only the *zika* but not the *ma'amar*. Is such a targeted *get* legally effective?

To understand the stakes: if the *get* attacks only the *zika*, it would in principle prevent *yibum* entirely (since *yibum* depends on *zika*) and perhaps affect the co-wives, even though the *ma'amar* remains nominally in place. If the *get* attacks only the *ma'amar*, it restores the situation to pre-*ma'amar* *zika* — the woman remains a *yevamah* but the rabbinic *ma'amar* layer is peeled away.

### Half-divorce

The initial analysis frames this as analogous to divorcing half a woman: *v'havay lei ke-migaresh chatzi isha, ha-migaresh chatzi isha lo asa v'lo klum* — the woman carries a double-layered status (*zika* and *ma'amar*), and trying to dissolve only one stratum while leaving the other intact is like divorcing half a wife — a legal nullity. The *get* would have no effect whatsoever, leaving intact both the *zika* and the *ma'amar*, and theoretically leaving open the possibility of *yibum* afterward.

### Independence theory

The counterposition: *o dilma hai lachud v'hai lachud* — perhaps *zika* and *ma'amar* are independent legal statuses. They were created by distinct acts and occupy distinct legal registers. If so, a *get* directed at one could validly sever that one, even without addressing the other.

### Rava precedent

The *gemara* suggests that Rava's ruling offers support. Rava states: *natan get le-ma'amaro hutra tzarata* — if after performing *ma'amar* with one co-wife, the *yavam* gives a *get* addressed to the *ma'amar*, it frees the co-wife and returns the situation to its prior state. This shows that a *get* can operate exclusively against the *ma'amar* layer, without simultaneously addressing the *zika*. That the *ma'amar*-targeted *get* is effective is thus established.

### Conclusion

For Rava, the question of whether a *get* can target only the *ma'amar* (*peshita lei*) — obviously yes. What remains genuinely uncertain is whether a *get* can be directed exclusively at the *zika* layer without addressing the *ma'amar* built upon it — attacking the foundation while leaving the superstructure. Rav Chanina's question precisely concerns this more difficult case. The *gemara* concludes: *teiku*.

---

## Chalitzah Ma'amar

### Setup

The *gemara* now turns to the case of *chalatz v'achar kach ma'amar*. The *yavam*'s brother has died, leaving two *yevamot*, call them Sarah and Rivkah. He performs *chalitzah* with Sarah. He then attempts to perform *ma'amar* — either with Sarah or with Rivkah. What is the status of this *ma'amar*?

When the *yavam* performs *ma'amar* after *chalitzah*, he is attempting to effect *kiddushin* with a woman who is now his *chalutza*. This raises an immediate question about the nature of his prohibition toward her.

### Issur Lav

The prohibition on a *yavam* remarrying his *chalutza* is not *arayot* — it is not *kareit*-level. Rather, it derives from the *lav* of *keivan she-lo bana, shuv lo yivneh* — since he failed to "build" with her via *yibum* and instead performed *chalitzah*, he may not build with her again. It is a simple *issur lav*. The question is therefore: does *kiddushin* — or its rabbinic analog *ma'amar* — take hold on a woman who is subject to an *issur lav*? This is the general principle of whether *kiddushin tossin b'chayei lavin* — whether *kiddushin* is binding when the woman is prohibited to the man via a *lav* rather than an *ervah*.

### Rabbi Akiva

According to Rav Yehuda citing Rav, the ruling that *ma'amar* after *chalitzah* is entirely void (*ein achar chalitzah klum*) follows Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Akiva holds *ein kiddushin tossin b'chayei lavin* — *kiddushin* does not bind when the woman is prohibited to the man by a *lav*. Since the *chalutza* is forbidden to him by *lav* (*shuv lo yivneh*), neither *ma'amar* nor regular *kiddushin* can take hold.

### Chachamim

The *chachamim* disagree: *yesh achar chalitzah* — even after *chalitzah*, a subsequent *ma'amar* creates binding *kiddushin*. The *chachamim* do not subscribe to Rabbi Akiva's blanket rule that *kiddushin* cannot attach when the woman is subject to a *lav*. In their view, *kiddushin* is a sufficiently robust legal act that it binds even in the presence of a *lav* prohibition, leaving the man in a position where he has violated a *lav* but the *kiddushin* is nonetheless valid.

The *gemara* now raises a difficulty: the *mishnah* states that if the *yavam* gave a *get* to the *yevamah* and then performed *ma'amar*, the *ma'amar* is effective and she requires a *get* to dissolve it. But if Rabbi Akiva holds *ein kiddushin tossin b'chayei lavin*, and if a *get* of a *yevamah* creates the same prohibition as *chalitzah* — namely that she becomes forbidden to him — then the *ma'amar* after *get* should equally fail. Why does the *mishnah* treat *ma'amar* after *get* as effective? Rabbi Akiva even derives from the verse *lo yuchal ba'alah ha-rishon asher shilchah* — *achar shiluach* alone is sufficient to create a permanent prohibition — suggesting the *get* of a *yevamah* is *d'oraita*. If so, the prohibition created by the *get* should be at least as strong as that created by *chalitzah*, and *ma'amar* should equally fail afterward.

### Abiyi resolution

Abaye resolves this: *get yavni mi-de'rabbanan* — the *get* of a *yevamah* is rabbinic, not *d'oraita*. The verse (*lo yuchal ba'alah ha-rishon asher shilchah*) is merely an *asmachta* — a rabbinic support text, not the source of a biblical prohibition. After a *get*, therefore, she is forbidden to him only at the rabbinic level, not the *d'oraita* level. Since Rabbi Akiva's principle (*ein kiddushin tossin b'chayei lavin*) operates only with respect to *d'oraita* prohibitions, a rabbinic-level prohibition does not block *kiddushin* from taking hold. *Ma'amar* after *get* therefore works. By contrast, after *chalitzah* the prohibition is *d'oraita*, and under Rabbi Akiva's rule, *kiddushin* — including *ma'amar* — cannot bind.

---

## Framing matters

### Yibum framing

A *baraita* introduces a further distinction, attributed to Rabbi (Rebbi). Rabbi holds that the effectiveness of *kiddushin* performed after *chalitzah* depends on how the *kiddushin* was framed. If the *yavam* said *hitkadshi li b'ma'amar yevamin* — framing the act explicitly as a *ma'amar* of *yibum* — then it does not take effect. The reasoning is that *ma'amar* is structurally built upon *zika*: it is the rabbinic *kiddushin* that operates within and atop the *yibum* framework. Once *chalitzah* has severed the *zika*, the foundation upon which *ma'amar* rests no longer exists. An act framed as *ma'amar yevamin* thus reaches for a foundation that has been dissolved.

### Regular framing

However, if after *chalitzah* the *yavam* said simply *harei at mekudeshet li* — the ordinary formula of *kiddushin* — without invoking the *yibum* context, Rabbi holds this should in principle bind as regular *kiddushin*. Regular *kiddushin* does not depend on *zika* as its foundation; it stands on its own. The prohibition she carries toward him is a *lav*, and the question of whether *kiddushin tossin b'chayei lavin* is debated — but Rabbi does not necessarily accept Rabbi Akiva's position on that question.

### Baraita

The *baraita* formalizes Rabbi's distinction: *im kidshah le-shum ishus tzricha heimenu get* — if he betrothed her framed as ordinary marriage (*ishus*), she requires a *get* to be released; *le-shum yevamus ein tzricha heimenu get* — if framed as *yevamus* (as an act of *yibum*), she does not require a *get*, because the *kiddushin* did not take hold.

### Chachamim

The *chachamim* reject this distinction entirely: *bein she-kidshah le-shum ishus bein she-kidshah le-shum yevamus tzricha heimenu get* — regardless of how the *kiddushin* was framed, if he said *harei at mekudeshet li*, she requires a *get*. The *chachamim* hold that the words *harei at mekudeshet li* are operative regardless of the speaker's framing intent.

### Ger analogy

Rav Yosef defends Rabbi's position with an analogy: one who plows in the field of a *ger* (a convert whose estate is ownerless upon death, claimable by the first person who works it) without knowing it belongs to a *ger* — thinking it is his own field — does not acquire it. *Lo kavan le-mikni* — he had no intent to perform a *kinyan*. The acquisition fails not because the act was wrong but because the specific *kinyan*-intent was absent. Similarly, one who says *harei at mekudeshet li b'ma'amar yevamin* did not intend to perform regular *kiddushin*; his intent was directed at a *yibum*-framed act, and since that frame is no longer available (the *zika* having been severed by *chalitzah*), the *kiddushin* fails.

### Counter analogy

Abaye counters: the analogy does not hold. *Hatam lo kavan le-mikni* — in the *ger* case, the person truly had no *kinyan*-intent at all; he thought he was working his own property. *Hacha kavan le-mikni* — in the *kiddushin* case, the *yavam* fully intends to acquire this woman; he is simply operating under a mistaken classification of the type of acquisition he is effecting. A better analogy: one who plows in the field of one *ger*, thinking it belongs to a different *ger* who died — both fields being ownerless, both eligible for acquisition by *chazakah*. In that case, the *kinyan* succeeds: the person has full *kinyan*-intent directed at this field, even if his identification of the deceased owner is mistaken. Similarly, here the *yavam* has full intent to acquire this woman via *kiddushin*; his characterization of the *kiddushin* as *yibum*-framed is immaterial to the operative intent.

### Resolution

Abaye resolves the difficulty by clarifying the precise scope of Rabbi's ruling. Rabbi does not hold that background intent — thinking one is doing *kiddushin yevamin* rather than regular *kiddushin* — suffices to defeat the *kiddushin*. Rather, Rabbi's ruling applies only where the actual words spoken framed the act as *ma'amar yevamin*. When the formula itself invokes *yevamin*, the act is constituted as a *ma'amar* — an act that by definition builds on the *zika*. Since the *chalitzah* severed the *zika*, there is no foundation left for the *ma'amar* to rest on, and the act is void. The *rabbanan*, by contrast, hold *hai lachud v'hai lachud* — *zika* and *ma'amar* are independent, and even without *zika*, the words *harei at mekudeshet li* — even with the appended *b'ma'amar yevamin* — carry their own *kiddushin* force and bind the woman. The dispute thus turns on whether *ma'amar* is so intrinsically constituted by its dependence on *zika* that an explicit invocation of *ma'amar yevamin* renders it a structural nullity once *chalitzah* has dissolved the *zika*, or whether the *kiddushin* language stands independently regardless of the framing.

---

---

# Yevamot 57

## Forbidden Marriage S (II)

### Daf Overview

The present *daf* takes up from the bottom of 56b, at the *mishnah* there. The preceding *gemaras* addressed significant questions: the halachic definition of the act of *bi'ah*, and the status of a *kohen*'s wife who is raped and thereby forbidden to her husband — a *halacha* with profound and tragic consequences. The sugya now turns to the next *mishnah*, which continues the theme of personal status as it intersects with *kehuna*.

### Mishnah Introduction

The *mishnah* opens by enumerating cases of forbidden relationships involving *kohanim*: an *almanah* with a *kohen gadol*, or a *gerushah* or *chalutzah* with a *kohen hedyot* — all situations we know are forbidden at the stage of *nisuin*, when the couple has actually gone under the *chuppah* and consummated the marriage. Through that forbidden act of *bi'ah*, the woman not only transgresses a negative prohibition but also becomes a *chalalah*.

Why does *chalalah* status matter if she is already forbidden to a *kohen*? For an *almanah* forbidden to a *kohen gadol*, the consequence is that she becomes lost even to a *kohen hedyot*. And for a *gerushah* or *chalutzah* with a *kohen hedyot*, it matters in a different way: if she was a *bat kohen*, she would ordinarily be entitled to return to her father's household and continue eating *terumah* after her husband's death — provided she has no children and meets the other conditions. But if she has become a *chalalah*, she is disqualified even from eating *terumah* from her father's household, just as a male *kohen* who is a *chalal* loses his *kedushas kehunah*.

## Erusin vs Nisuin

### Rebbi Meir Position

All of the above consequences attach after the act of *bi'ah*. But the *mishnah* raises the case of *erusin* alone — *erusin* with a *kohen* in circumstances where the eventual *nisuin* would constitute an *issur*. The *tanna kamma* of the *mishnah*, whom the *gemara* will identify as Rebbi Meir, rules: *min ha-erusin lo yokhelu bi-trumah* — even during *erusin*, she may not eat *terumah*. Since *erusin* is but one step removed from *nisuin*, and there is no purpose to *erusin* unless one intends to proceed to *chuppah* and *nisuin*, Rebbi Meir treats the situation as though *bi'ah* is already imminent. She is therefore regarded as quasi-*chalalah* — at least rabbinically — and she cannot eat *terumah*.

## Forbidden Marriage S (II)

### Chalalah Status

Before proceeding to the opposing positions, the case requires clarification. There is a debate among the *rishonim* — reflecting a disagreement between Rashi and Tosafot — as to whether the *mishnah* speaks of a *yisraelit* married to a *kohen*, or of a *bat kohen* married to a *kohen*. If the subject is a *yisraelit*, one confronts a double difficulty: normally, a *yisraelit* cannot eat *terumah* until *nisuin*, not merely *erusin*, and furthermore, this is an *erusin* leading toward an *issur bi'ah*. It is difficult to see how anyone could permit her to eat *terumah* in such circumstances. Rashi nevertheless defends that reading, though we will not develop it here.

The more straightforward approach — that of Tosafot — reads the case as one involving a *bat kohen* married to a *kohen*. She is already entitled to eat *terumah* by virtue of her father's household. The question, therefore, is not what entitles her to eat, but whether something now disqualifies her. Does the *erusin* to a *kohen* — when it would eventually ripen into a forbidden *nisuin* — strip her of her existing entitlement to eat *terumah*?

## Erusin vs Nisuin (II)

### R. Eliezer & Shimon

Rebbi Eliezer and Rebbi Shimon disagree with Rebbi Meir and rule *makhshirin* — they permit her to eat. Their reasoning is that until *nisuin* actually occurs, until *bi'ah* actually takes place, she has not become a *chalalah*. She was eating *terumah* by virtue of her father, and that entitlement continues. The *kiddushin* is not *nisuin*; there has been no *chuppah*, no *bi'ah*, and therefore no disqualification.

### Bat Kohen Case

The *gemara* then addresses the transitions in this woman's status across the different stages of the relationship. The positions of Rebbi Eliezer and Rebbi Shimon hold that she may continue eating by virtue of her father. Rebbi Meir holds she cannot. The husband's *kohen* status, it bears noting, is not at issue — *terumah* entitlements are not a punishment; the question concerns how her own status has been affected.

### Position Analysis

Proceeding from *erusin* to *nisuin* clarifies matters further. *Nis'almanah o nisgareshah min hanisuin pesulah min haterumah* — if she becomes an *almanah* or *gerushah* after *nisuin*, she is fully disqualified. Once they have actually gone under the *chuppah* and consummated the marriage, she truly becomes a *chalalah*. Even if the husband dies the next moment, she remains a *chalalah* and cannot eat *terumah*. This is the universal position; everyone agrees to it.

## Gittin Status

### Post-Nisuin Chalalah

Once the relationship has reached the stage of *nisuin* — actual *chuppah* and *bi'ah* — the woman's disqualification as a *chalalah* is complete and permanent. The *gemara* will later discuss what happens in the case of *chuppah* without *bi'ah*, but in the standard case of *nisuin* with consummation, the *chalalah* status is irrevocable. Even subsequent death or divorce of the *kohen* does not restore her.

### Erusin Only Reversal

However, *min ha-erusin kesherot* — if the *kohen* dies during *erusin* alone, before *nisuin* has taken place, the women are *kesherot*, their status is restored. Presumably this holds even according to Rebbi Meir, who disqualifies her during *erusin*. His reasoning was that *kiddushin* places her on the cusp of forbidden *bi'ah* — but if that *bi'ah* never materializes, the anticipated disqualification never crystallizes, and she reverts to her prior acceptable status.

## Kal Vachomer Debate

### Meir's Argument

A *baraita* records Rebbi Meir's *kal vachomer* argument. He reasons: *u'mah kiddushei reshut ein ma'achilin, kiddushei averah lo kol sheken?* — if *kiddushei reshut*, the case of a *bat kohen* who marries a *yisrael*, removes her from her father's household and disqualifies her from eating *terumah*, then *kiddushei averah* — a betrothal leading toward a forbidden *bi'ah* — should certainly do so. When a *bat kohen* marries a *yisrael*, she is immediately pulled out of her father's category; she cannot eat *terumah* as a result of those *kiddushin*. How much more so, argues Rebbi Meir, should *kiddushin* to a *kohen* in a context of *issur* pull her out.

### Refutation Logic

The response to Rebbi Meir's *kal vachomer* is striking. The refutation is: *im amarta b'kiddushei reshut sheken ein lo lehachil b'makom acher* — in the case of *kiddushei reshut*, the *yisrael* cannot enable anyone to eat *terumah* on his account under any circumstances. *Tomar b'kiddushei averah sheken yesh lo lehachil b'makom acher?* — but in the case of *kiddushei averah*, this *kohen*, if he were married to another woman permissibly, she would eat *terumah* on his account. Being married to a *kohen* — even in a context of *issur* — is categorically different from being married to a *yisrael*.

### Middle Zone

The logic of the refutation reflects a subtle and counterintuitive principle: although this marriage, if consummated, would produce a full *issur* and make her a *chalalah*, the fact that she is betrothed to a *kohen* rather than a *yisrael* keeps her within the *kehuna* realm during *erusin*. She has not yet had *bi'ah*, and so has not yet become a *chalalah*; and she has not married a *yisrael*, so she has not been pulled out of her father's household. She exists in a middle zone — within the *kohen* realm but not yet disqualified by *bi'ah*.

The underlying structure is this: normally, *erusin* — even to a *yisrael* — is enough to pull a *bat kohen* away from her father's household, even though *nisuin* has not yet occurred. She does not yet eat on her husband's account, but she can no longer eat on her father's account either. And yet, Rebbi Eliezer and Rebbi Shimon maintain that being betrothed to a *kohen* — however forbidden the ultimate *nisuin* would be — keeps her within the *terumah* realm. Marriage to a *kohen*, even a forbidden marriage, is better than marriage to a *yisrael* for purposes of eating *terumah*. The *chalalah* status has not occurred, and she remains, during this middle zone, able to eat *terumah* by virtue of her father.

## Ptzua Daka Case

### Oshaya's Position

The *gemara* then extends this framework. Rebbi Elazar reports in the name of Rebbi Oshaya: if a *kohen* who is a *ptzua daka* — one with crushed testicles, forbidden to marry — betroths a *bat kohen* (reading the *girsa* with Tosafot, not *bat yisrael* as Rashi had it), the same three-way *machloket* between Rebbi Meir, Rebbi Eliezer, and Rebbi Shimon applies. The *ptzua daka kohen*, if the relationship were to become *nisuin* and were consummated, would make her a *chalalah*. The parallel to our *mishnah*'s case is exact: the problem is not her status but his, yet the consequences of consummation are identical.

### Problem Distinction

The *gemara* immediately interrogates this parallelism. Perhaps Rebbi Eliezer and Rebbi Shimon said what they said in the original case only because *yesh lo lehachil b'makom acher* — in that case, the *kohen* is the sort of person whose wife, in a permissible marriage, would eat *terumah* on his account. That quality — the capacity of this type of *kohen* to cause someone to eat *terumah* through marriage — is what keeps her within the *terumah* realm even during the forbidden *erusin*. But a *ptzua daka* is one who, by definition, cannot legally have a wife who eats *terumah* on his account. Is he not therefore equivalent to a *yisrael* from this perspective? And if marriage to a *yisrael* removes her from her father's *terumah* category, should not *erusin* to a *ptzua daka kohen* do the same?

### Support Criterion

The *gemara* then asks: but can we not say *yesh lo lehachil* even for a *ptzua daka kohen*? Perhaps there exists a woman he could marry such that she would eat *terumah* on his account — specifically, a *bat gerim*. The question of whether a *ptzua daka kohen* marrying a *bat gerim* can enable her to eat *terumah* is, as the *gemara* records, precisely the question that Rebbi Yochanan posed to Rebbi Oshaya — and to which Rebbi Oshaya gave no answer. Therefore, Rebbi Oshaya's own assumption that the case of a *ptzua daka kohen* maps cleanly onto the three-way *machloket* is itself unresolved: we do not know whether this *kohen* is *yesh lo lehachil b'makom acher*, because we do not know the answer to Rebbi Yochanan's unanswered question.

## Abaye vs Rava

### Abaye Position

The *gemara* now records a dispute between Abaye and Rava. The specific scenario, as Rashi explains it, is a *kohen* who married a woman while he was still fully fit, and subsequently became a *ptzua daka*. He has not had *bi'ah* with her since becoming a *ptzua daka*. The question is whether she continues to eat *terumah* on his account.

### Rashi Explanation

Rashi's explanation of the case is that the *nisuin* was entirely valid at the time it was performed — the *kohen* was not yet a *ptzua daka* — and she therefore became a full *eshet kohen* and was eating *terumah*. Now that he has become a *ptzua daka*, if he were to have *bi'ah* with her he would make her a *chalalah*. But as long as he has not done so, she has not become a *chalalah*, and the marriage remains valid because it was contracted when he was still permitted. Abaye therefore rules: *ho'il u'machilah belo bi'ah* — he can cause her to eat even without having now had *bi'ah* with her. The relationship is legitimate and she continues to eat.

### Continuity Proof

Abaye's proof: one cannot simply say that what happened earlier dictates ongoing status. The *gemara* puts it this way — *v'i lo tema hachi*, if you say that an earlier state alone justifies the continuation, then a *bat yisrael* who was married to a *kohen* and the *kohen* died should continue to eat *terumah* on the logic that she was already eating it. Obviously we do not say that. This demonstrates that ongoing eating is not justified merely by prior status. There must therefore be something currently active in the relationship between a *bat kohen* and her *ptzua daka* husband that supports her eating — and Abaye identifies that as the fact that the *kinyan* of *ishut* between them remains intact.

### Rava Response

Rava responds by distinguishing the two cases. When the *kohen* dies, the relationship is severed entirely — *paka kinyano*, his bond lapses — and that is why she stops eating. Here, by contrast, the *kohen* has become a *ptzua daka* but has not died; the relationship, the *kinyan*, has not been severed — *lo paka kinyano*. She therefore continues to eat not merely on the basis of the past but because the ongoing *kinyan* remains in force. Abaye's rejoinder to Rava is that one should derive the law about the *kinyan* of *ishut* from another case of *kinyan* of *ishut*, not from the *kinyan* of slaves — *kinyan d'ishut mikinyan d'ishut yalfinan v'lo yalfinan kinyan d'ishut mikinyan d'avadim* — since Rava had proposed that the *ptzua daka kohen*'s *avadim* eating *terumah* demonstrates that he is *yesh lo lehachil b'makom acher*. Rava's response is that in the case where the *kohen* married before becoming a *ptzua daka*, she is eating on the basis of the continuation of the earlier relationship, and this does not demonstrate that a *ptzua daka* can newly enable his wife to eat.

## Bat Gerim Question

### Unresolved Question

Against this background the *gemara* returns to the question Rebbi Yochanan posed: *ptzua daka kohen she-nasa bat gerim mahu she-yachilenah bi-trumah?* — a *kohen* who is a *ptzua daka* and who married a *bat gerim* in a straightforward way (she is not herself a *giyoret*, and there is no *issur* from the *ptzua daka* side if she is indeed permitted to him) — can he enable her to eat *terumah*? This question remained unresolved.

### Oshaya's Silence

Rebbi Oshaya gave Rebbi Yochanan no answer. Sometime afterward, another great scholar — the *gemara* suggests this was Resh Lakish — came and posed a different question, and Rebbi Oshaya resolved it. This contrast prompted a rebuke from Rebbi Yehuda Nesia.

### Rebuke & Explanation

Rebbi Yehuda Nesia — the grandson of Rebbi Yehuda HaNasi, not Rebbi Yehuda HaNasi himself — said to Rebbi Oshaya: is Rebbi Yochanan not also a great person? Why did you answer Resh Lakish and not Rebbi Yochanan? Rebbi Oshaya responded: *de-ka bei minai milta de-lav pshita li* — Rebbi Yochanan asked me something I did not know the answer to. My silence was not a slight on his stature; it was because the question has no clear resolution. The *gemara* now examines why.

## Gerim Status Analysis

### Yehuda Position

The difficulty lies in what position one takes on several intersecting questions. The *gemara* frames it by examining the two major opinions — those of Rebbi Yehuda and Rebbi Yossi — and then a third, that of Rebbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

The *gemara* begins: *ei Rebbi Yehuda bein bi-kdushateih kaei bein be-lav bi-kdushateih kaei lo achlah* — according to Rebbi Yehuda, whether the *ptzua daka kohen* retains his *kedushas kehunah* (meaning, whether the marriage restrictions of *kehunah* still apply to him) or not, the woman cannot eat.

There are two sub-questions embedded in the phrase *bi-kdushateih kaei*: first, whether a *kohen* who is a *ptzua daka* retains the *issurim* that govern whom a *kohen* may marry; and second, the *machloket* between Rebbi Yehuda and Rebbi Yossi regarding whether descendants of *gerim* — *kehal gerim* — are themselves still considered *kahal* for purposes of the restriction of *ptzua daka*.

If the *ptzua daka kohen* retains his *kedushas kehunah* in full, then one cannot solve the problem by having him marry a *bat ger*, because Rebbi Yehuda rules *bat ger ke-vat chalal zachar* — the daughter of a male *ger* is like the daughter of a *chalal*, and a *kohen* may not marry her, just as he may not marry a *gerushah* or *chalalah*. This is not the *halacha* as we rule, and one can only note what enormous implications such a ruling would have — a *kohen* would have to investigate any trace of a *ger* in a woman's lineage, through the father's line as well as the mother's, for all generations. But according to Rebbi Yehuda, it is so.

### Bat Ger Status

Thus, if the *kohen*'s *kedushas kehunah* remains operative, there is no one this *ptzua daka kohen* can marry who would be permitted by the *kohen* rules and yet would be permitted by the *ptzua daka* rules — at least not among the natural candidates.

### Yossi Position

Rebbi Yossi takes the opposite position: *bein bi-kdushateih kaei bein be-lav bi-kdushateih kaei achla* — either way she can eat. His reasoning on both flanks is the mirror image of Rebbi Yehuda's. As to the *kehuna* restriction: *ger she-nitgayer bito keshera li-kehuna* — a convert's daughter is fully *keshera* to marry a *kohen*. A *kohen* is forbidden to a *giyoret* herself, but her children, born after conversion, have no such restriction. And as to the *ptzua daka* restriction: *kehal gerim lo ikrei kahal* — the descendants of *gerim* are not considered *kahal Hashem* for purposes of the *ptzua daka* prohibition. A *ptzua daka* may marry into the second generation of converts.

### Status Paradox

The paradox Rebbi Yossi's position generates is notable. He holds that a *bat giyoret* is sufficiently a full Jew that a *kohen* may marry her — no residual *ger* status clings to her in that context. Yet simultaneously, she retains enough of a non-native status that she falls outside *kehal Hashem* and may marry a *ptzua daka*. Rebbi Yehuda's position produces the mirror-image paradox: a *bat ger* is still enough of a *ger* that a *kohen* cannot marry her — but she is enough of a *yisrael* that a *ptzua daka* cannot marry her either. Both *tanna'im* end up in an internally asymmetric position, though each in the opposite direction. According to Rebbi Yossi, the question posed by Rebbi Yochanan poses no difficulty — either way she can eat. According to Rebbi Yehuda, either way she cannot. The question is therefore answerable according to both — which only deepens the puzzle of why Rebbi Oshaya said he had no answer.

## Eliezer b. Yaakov

### Conditional Status

The resolution lies with the position of Rebbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. He occupies a middle position: *isha bat gerim lo tinase li-kehuna ad she-tei imah mi-Yisrael* — a woman of *gerim* descent may not marry a *kohen* unless her mother is a *yisraelit*. In other words, Rebbi Eliezer ben Yaakov distinguishes between the *bat ger* — whose father is a *ger* but mother is a *yisraelit* — and the *bat giyoret*, whose mother is a convert. The former may marry a *kohen*; the latter may not.

### Implication Question

Now, if Rebbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's rule is that a *yisraelit* mother enables the daughter to marry a *kohen*, the question becomes: what does that *yisraelit* mother add? Does it add *kashrut* in the sense of *kashrus li-kehunah* — fitness to marry a *kohen* — but nothing else? Or does it add *kedushah* — a higher level of *kehal Hashem* status — which would simultaneously make her *assur* to a *ptzua daka*? According to Rebbi Yehuda and Rebbi Yossi, the two categories (permitted to *kohen* / forbidden to *ptzua daka*) always move in tandem: what is forbidden to one is permitted to the other. But perhaps Rebbi Eliezer ben Yaakov contemplates a third category: a woman who, by virtue of her *yisraelit* mother, has been elevated to *kashrus* for *kehunah* — but not so elevated in *kedushah* as to become *assur* to a *ptzua daka*. This is the question Rebbi Oshaya could not resolve.

### Baraita Proof

The *gemara* then adduces a *baraita* brought by Rav Aha bar Katinah from the south. The *baraita* asks: *minayin le-ptzua daka kohen she-nasa bat gerim she-ma'achilah bi-trumah?* — how do we know that a *ptzua daka kohen* who married a *bat gerim* may enable her to eat *terumah*? It derives this from the verse *ve-kohen ki yikneh nefesh kinyan kaspo hi yokhal bo*. The *gemara* immediately asks: according to whose opinion is this *baraita* needed? According to Rebbi Yehuda — it contradicts his position, since he holds she cannot eat. According to Rebbi Yossi — no verse is needed, since either way she may eat. It must therefore be according to Rebbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, whose position left open the question of the *ptzua daka*'s case. And from the *baraita* we learn: *kashira hi ve-tosaf bah acher* — she is *kashira*, more fit to marry a *kohen*, but no additional *kedushah* is added to place her in the *kehal Hashem* category. Therefore the *ptzua daka kohen* can marry her and enable her to eat *terumah*.

## Eliezer b. Yaakov (II)

### Kashrah vs Kedushah

The upshot, then, is a three-way taxonomy. According to Rebbi Yehuda and Rebbi Yossi, the two axes — permitted to *kohen* / forbidden to *ptzua daka* — are perfectly correlated. What is *assur* on one side is *muttar* on the other. But Rebbi Eliezer ben Yaakov introduces a conceptual split: *kashrut* for *kehunah* and *kedushah* for the *ptzua daka* restriction are not identical measures. The *yisraelit* mother adds *kashrut* to the daughter — making her eligible to marry a *kohen* — without adding enough *kedushah* to remove her from the set of women a *ptzua daka* may marry. The *baraita* confirms this: the *ptzua daka kohen* who married a *bat gerim* (with *yisraelit* mother) enables her to eat *terumah*. *Shema mina.*

## Chuppah Pesulot

### Rav vs Shmuel

The *gemara* now turns to a new dispute. Rav holds *yesh chuppah le-pesulot* — there is a meaningful act of *chuppah* even for *pesulot*, women in forbidden marriages. Shmuel holds *ein chuppah le-pesulot* — the act of *chuppah* has no halachic significance in a forbidden relationship.

The question being asked requires some framing. There is a well-known debate among the *rishonim* about *chuppas niddah* — whether a *chuppah* performed when the woman is a *niddah* is halachically valid for purposes of *nisuin*, *sheva berachot*, and so on. Sefardim, following the Rambam, hold one may not; Ashkenazim hold one may. But that debate concerns whether *chuppah* in such circumstances is meaningful enough to constitute *nisuin*. The present dispute is effectively the reverse: given a situation where the parties are forbidden to ever consummate the marriage — an *almanah* to a *kohen gadol*, a *gerushah* to a *kohen hedyot*, a *ptzua daka* with a woman, and so on — does the act of *chuppah* without *bi'ah* carry any significance? Specifically: does it operate as though they have had *bi'ah*, so as to make her a *chalalah* and disqualify her from eating *terumah* from her father?

This is a ratcheted version of Rebbi Meir's *mishnah* position: Rebbi Meir held that mere *kiddushin* operates quasi-like *bi'ah*. Now we ask — even according to those who rejected Rebbi Meir, what about *chuppah* itself, which is more advanced than *erusin* but still without actual *bi'ah*?

### Rav Agrees Exception

Shmuel notes that Rav — whom Shmuel refers to as *Abba* (Tosafot notes, against Rashi's reading of this as an honorific, that *Abba* was simply Rav's actual name, as the *Aruch* explains) — agrees with him in one specific case: *betinoket p'chuta mi-bas shalosh shanim ve-yom echad* — a girl under three years old and one day. *Ho'il ve-ein lah bi'ah ein lah chuppah* — since an act of *bi'ah* with such a girl has no halachic standing, an act of *chuppah* similarly has no standing. Even Rav concedes this exception.

### Sex Possible Rule

The corollary is also spelled out: once a girl is three years old and one day — the threshold at which *bi'ah* has halachic effect — the act of *chuppah* does carry significance.

### Consequences List

Rava confirms this from the *mishnah*: *bat shalosh shanim ve-yom echad mitkadeshet be-vi'ah* — *kiddushei bi'ah* takes effect from this age. *Ve-im ba aleha yavam kana'ah* — an act of *yibbum* is effective at this age. *Ve-chayavin aleha mishum eshet ish* — if she was betrothed and someone has *bi'ah* with her, the laws of *eshet ish* apply. *U-metamah et bo'alah* — if she is a *niddah*, her *tumah* transfers to the man who has *bi'ah* with her, rendering the bedding beneath and above subject to *mishkav* and *moshav tumah*. *Niset le-kohen ochelet bi-trumah* — if she is married to a *kohen* in the context of valid *nisuin*, she eats *terumah*, because *nisuin* is only meaningful in a context where *bi'ah* is halachically possible. *Ba aleha echad mi-kol ha-pesulim paslah* — if one of the *pesulim* has *bi'ah* with her, he disqualifies her, rendering her a *chalalah*.

### Final Conclusion

The *baraita* draws the conclusion: *bat shalosh shanim ve-yom echad hu de-mipsala be-vi'ah mipsala be-chuppah* — it is at the age of three years and one day that *bi'ah* disqualifies her, and *chuppah* likewise disqualifies her at that age. *Ha-p'chuta mi-bas shalosh shanim ve-yom echad de-la mipsala be-vi'ah lo mipsala nami be-chuppah* — below that threshold, since *bi'ah* itself would not disqualify her, *chuppah* similarly does not disqualify her. *Shema mina.* The principle is clear: *chuppah* for *pesulot* carries halachic weight — it operates as *bi'ah* for purposes of *chalalah* status — but only where *bi'ah* itself would be halachically significant, i.e., where the girl is at least three years and one day old.

---

---

# Yevamot 58

## Chuppah for Psulot

### Intro: Chuppah Status

The daf under discussion opens with a debate introduced by Rami bar Chama concerning whether *chuppah* is halakhically meaningful for women who are *psulot* — women disqualified from marrying a *kohen*, such as a *grushah*. The question of *yesh chuppah li-psulot* has been framed as whether the act of *chuppah* carries legal weight when the woman is forbidden to the husband.

Before engaging the Gemara's argument directly, it is worth clarifying what "meaningful" means in this context. The question is not whether one fulfills the *mitzvah* of *chuppah* for the purposes of *sheva brachot* — a separate issue that arises, for instance, in the case of a *niddah*, who is a woman in a temporary forbidden status that will eventually be permitted. Here we are speaking of a *psulah* in a substantive sense: a *grushah* to a *kohen*, for example, a woman who is categorically disqualified. The halakhic question is whether the act of *chuppah* carries any legal consequence — specifically, whether it is treated as equivalent to *biah*.

The relevance of this question is not primarily whether such a woman may now marry the *kohen*, since she is already disqualified. Rather, the concern is whether she has been invalidated from eating *terumah*. If she is the daughter of a *kohen*, she eats *terumah* by virtue of her father. An act of forbidden intercourse of the kind that concerns *kehunah* would render her a *chalalah*, permanently stripped of that right. The prior discussion in the Gemara established that we speak only of a *bat shalosh shanim v'yom echad* — the halachically significant threshold age — and the question is whether *chuppah* functions like *biah* in that regard.

### Rashi: Chuppah Alone

Rashi's reading of the Gemara is that the entire debate concerns *chuppah* that occurred without any prior *kiddushin*. The couple proceeded directly to *chuppah* without having performed *kiddushin*. This creates two opposing arguments simultaneously.

On one hand, one might be more lenient than in a case of *kiddushin* alone: even if Rabbi Meir holds that *kiddushin* by a *kohen* to a *psulah* disqualifies her from *terumah*, he might agree that *chuppah* without *kiddushin* has no halakhic standing whatsoever and therefore creates no consequence. *Chuppah* that arrives without *kiddushin* perhaps means nothing at all.

On the other hand, one might be stricter than in a case of mere *kiddushin*: even if Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon hold that *kiddushin* alone does not disqualify her — since *kiddushin* is still distant from actual *biah* — they might agree that *chuppah* is different. *Chuppah* is fundamentally about *nisuin* and cohabitation; it exists in the very context of sexual union. Therefore, even those who are lenient about *kiddushin* might concede that *chuppah* disqualifies her, treating it as functionally equivalent to *biah*.

### Tosafot: Chuppah Act

Tosafot finds Rashi's framing difficult. It seems strange, Tosafot argues, to treat *chuppah* completely devoid of *kiddushin* as though it carries any independent halakhic significance. If the act has no halakhic grounding whatsoever, why would it create legal consequences? A couple who entered a room together without any prior *kiddushin* — why should that be treated as tantamount to forbidden *biah*?

Tosafot therefore turns to a Talmudic debate in tractate Kiddushin that considers whether *chuppah* can itself constitute an act of *kiddushin*, parallel to the standard modes of *kesef*, *shtar*, and *biah*. On Tosafot's reading, the Gemara here presupposes this possibility: the *chuppah* is being discussed as itself an act of *kiddushin*, and the question is whether that kind of *kiddushin* — effected through *chuppah* — disqualifies the woman.

Tosafot acknowledges that this reading creates its own circularity. If *chuppah* functions as *kiddushin*, then one is back to the question of *kiddushin* itself, and it is not immediately clear how this advances the debate beyond where Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer already stand. Tosafot also offers an alternative reading according to which the Gemara is asking about a case where there was *kiddushin* followed by *chuppah* but no actual *biah*, and then the husband died or divorced her. The question becomes whether the *chuppah*, having occurred without *biah*, has permanently altered her status — rendering her a *chalalah* — or whether it is only the act of *biah* that causes permanent invalidation.

### Baraita: No Sex Yet

The Gemara now introduces a *baraita* in support of the discussion. The *tanna kamma* teaches that women — whether *kesherot* or *psulot* — who married *kohanim*, or who entered *chuppah* without having had sexual relations, eat from the husband's table and eat *terumah*.

The Gemara questions this reading. When the *baraita* says "*nisu*" — they married — surely that implies actual marriage including consummation. How, then, could these *psulot* be eating *terumah*? If they have had actual *biah* that is forbidden from a *kehunah* perspective, they should be disqualified as *chalalot* and permanently barred from *terumah* even from the father's house.

The Gemara resolves this by reading the two phrases — *nisu* and *nichnesu l'chuppah v'lo niv'alu* — as parallel descriptions of the same scenario rather than two distinct categories. The *baraita* must be speaking of women who entered *chuppah* but did not have intercourse. In that case, *psulot* who had *chuppah* without *biah* are still permitted to eat *terumah*. The *tanna kamma* holds *ein chuppah li-psulot*: *chuppah* without *biah* is not treated as equivalent to *biah*, and her status remains unchanged.

### R. Yishmael: Parallel Ac…

Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka, takes the opposing position and articulates it by drawing a direct parallel between *chuppah* and *biah*: whatever *biah* would entitle a woman to eat — *chuppah* also entitles her to eat. Whatever *biah* would not entitle her to eat — *chuppah* also does not. In a case where the woman is a *psulah* and the *biah* would not only fail to entitle her to eat *terumah* but would affirmatively disqualify her by making her a *chalalah*, Rashi understands Rabbi Yishmael as saying that *chuppah* operates the same way: it is not merely that she is not entitled to eat in this state, but that the *chuppah* itself has rendered her permanently a *chalalah*.

This represents *yesh chuppah li-psulot* at its most sweeping: even without *biah*, the act of *chuppah* with a *psulah* creates the same permanent disqualification that actual forbidden intercourse would.

The Gemara then asks whether this dispute between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Yishmael simply maps onto the existing debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon. It concludes that the mapping is not straightforward. Rabbi Meir might be lenient specifically about *chuppah* without *kiddushin* — since without *kiddushin* there is no halakhic *kinyan* at all — even though he is strict about *kiddushin* alone. And Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon might be stricter about *chuppah* than about *kiddushin* alone — since *chuppah* is, by its very nature, oriented toward *biah* in a way that *kiddushin* is not. The *baraita*'s emphasis on *chuppah* rather than *kiddushin* or *kesef* points toward the *chuppah* itself as the operative legal act, which supports reading the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Yishmael as staking out independent positions rather than merely echoing the tannaitic dispute.

Rav Pappa then reports that Rav Sheshet illuminated this very question from a *mishnah*, declaring *yesh chuppah li-psulot*, and promising to demonstrate that this position is already embedded in an existing *mishnah*. This brings the discussion to the *mishnah* in tractate *Sotah*, which will reframe the question in far broader terms.

---

## Sotah Investigation

### Sotah Prerequisites

The Gemara turns to the *mishnah* in *Sotah* to support the position of *yesh chuppah li-psulot*. That *mishnah* explains the double *amen* spoken by the suspected woman: *amen she-lo satisi arusa v'nesuah, shomeret yavam u-knusah* — I did not stray when I was an *arusah*, when I was a *nesuah*, when I was a *shomeret yavam*, or after *yibum* was performed. The *mishnah* thus indicates that the *kinui* — the formal jealousy warning — and the *stirah* — the seclusion — can operate even in the context of *arusah* and *shomeret yavam*, not only in the standard case of full *nisuin*.

The Gemara immediately asks: what exactly is the case of *arusah* here? If the *kinui* was issued while she was an *arusah* and the *hashkayah* — making her drink the *sotah* water — also occurred while she was an *arusah*, this cannot work. The *mishnah* in *Sotah* itself establishes that an *arusah* and a *shomeret yavam* do not drink and do not collect their *ketubah*. The *sotah* water is administered only when the verse *tachat ishech* — under your husband — applies, meaning the woman must be a full *nesuah*. An *arusah* has not yet reached that status.

### Chuppah No Consummation

The Gemara therefore reconstructs the case: the *kinui* was issued when she was an *arusah*, the *stirah* occurred, and then they proceeded to *chuppah* without having had intercourse — *nichnesah l'chuppah v'lo niv'alah*. The husband can now administer the *sotah* water for what she did during the *erusin* period, because she is now considered a *nesuah* by virtue of the *chuppah*.

But — and here lies the broader legal significance — this is only possible if the *chuppah* itself is meaningful. She was a *sotah* during *erusin*, forbidden to her husband after the *stirah*. The *chuppah* therefore occurred while she was a *psulah* — forbidden to him. If *chuppah* for a *psulah* has no halakhic standing, then she never became a *nesuah* at all, and the *sotah* procedure cannot be performed. The very structure of the *mishnah* thus implies *yesh chuppah li-psulot*.

This is a striking broadening of the question. Earlier the discussion was confined to a narrow question: does *chuppah* create the equivalent of *biah* to invalidate a woman for *terumah*? Now the question has become general: is *chuppah* with a woman who is forbidden to the husband a meaningful act of *nisuin* at all? The *sotah* case demonstrates that *chuppah* in the presence of *issur* can be halakhically operative in the full sense — not merely creating an analogue to *biah*, but conferring the complete status of *nesuah*.

### Sex Requirement Issue

The Gemara now raises a further difficulty from a *baraita* brought by Rav Acha bar Chanina, who came from the south bearing a teaching: *mibal'adei ishech* — the verse "aside from your husband" — applies only when *shechivat ba'al* preceded *shechivat bo'el*: the husband must have had intercourse with the woman before the suspected adulterer. If the adulterer had intercourse with her first, the *sotah* water does not apply. This is derived from the plain sense of the verse — your husband has already been with you, and now another man has been with you as well.

This creates a serious problem for our constructed case. We said the *stirah* and suspected sin occurred when she was an *arusah*. How, then, did they ever proceed to *chuppah*? After *stirah*, the husband is forbidden to have intercourse with a suspected *sotah*. If they had *chuppah* without *biah*, then the condition of *shechivat ba'al* preceding *shechivat bo'el* is never satisfied, and the *sotah* water would not work.

Rami bar Chama proposes: the *arus* had intercourse with her while she was still in her father's house — an act of intimacy during the *erusin* period, before the *kinui* and *stirah* took place. He then performed *kinui*, she had the *stirah*, and now — after *chuppah* but without *biah* — he can make her drink, because the prior *biah* satisfies the condition of *shechivat ba'al*, and his current abstinence ensures he is *menukah me'avon*.

This resolves the case of *arusah*. But the *sotah mishnah* also includes *shomeret yavam*. The Gemara asks: how can one construct a case of *shomeret yavam* in which there has already been *shechivat ba'al*? Once the brother-in-law has intercourse with the *yevamah*, she is no longer a *shomeret yavam* — she is fully his wife.

### Rav: Intent Irrelevant

The Gemara recalls the earlier debate between Rav and Shmuel. Rav holds *kanah l'chol mili* — an act of *biah* with a *yevamah*, even if performed with no intent to fulfill the *mitzvah* of *yibum*, with no intent to create a marital bond, but purely for the sake of gratification, nevertheless acquires her completely and makes her his full wife in every respect. Shmuel disagrees: without the proper intent to effect *yibum*, such intercourse acquires her only for those matters explicitly enumerated in the *parshah* of *yibum* — exempting co-wives, exempting other brothers from *yibum*, creating inheritance rights — but does not confer the full status of *ishto* that we speak of in general *halacha*.

If so, one might think: according to Shmuel, the *yavam* could have had intercourse with the *yevamah* purely for gratification, and since that intercourse does not confer full wife-status, she could still be called a *shomeret yavam* in a meaningful sense. But then the *sotah* water would not work on her either, since for *sotah* purposes one needs the full status of *nesuah*. The circle cannot be squared using Shmuel's position alone.

The Gemara therefore notes that this entire line of reasoning is being advanced in support of Rav — who is the one who holds *yesh chuppah li-psulot*. It is Rav's position we are trying to demonstrate from the *mishnah*. But the *shomeret yavam* case cannot be explained satisfactorily according to Rav, because Rav holds that any act of *biah* with a *yevamah* makes her completely his wife, leaving no room for the category of *shomeret yavam who has already had relations with the yavam*.

### Maamar Changes Status

The Gemara now introduces an answer of remarkable conceptual audacity. According to Beit Shammai, *maamar* — the formal levitical declaration analogous to *kiddushin* — acquires the *yevamah* with the force of a complete *kinyan* and effects a full *arusah* status. More than that, it completely displaces (*hefriach*) the *zikat yibum*. Once *maamar* is performed, she is no longer in the category of *shomeret yavam*; she is now in the category of a standard *arusah*.

The consequence is striking: subsequent intercourse — if performed not for the purpose of *nisuin* or *yibum* but simply as an act of intimacy — does not have the normal halakhic effect that *biah* with a *yevamah* would have. In a standard *yibum* case, any *biah* automatically elevates the woman to *nesuah* status. But according to Beit Shammai, once *maamar* was performed, the *zika* is removed, and the subsequent intercourse is more analogous to *biah* with an *arusah* — meaningful but insufficient to create *nisuin* without the proper intent.

This means the *yavam* can have had intercourse with her while she was still classified as an *arusah*, satisfying the condition of *shechivat ba'al*, and yet she remains in an *arusah*-like status — parallel to the category of *shomeret yavam* — without having been elevated to *nesuah* through that act.
