Rabbi Eliezer is manifestly unconcerned with the minority possibility that she might become an *ailonit*. This eliminates the first leg of Rabba's combination.

The *gemara* then proceeds to show that Rabbi Eliezer also does not hold like Rabbi Yehuda, by quoting a *baraita* that presents a full range of *tanna'ic* positions on the definition of *zonah*.

### Zonah Definitions

The *baraita* records a fascinating and consequential dispute among the *Tannaim* about the biblical category of *zonah* that renders a woman forbidden to a *kohen*, conducted with almost no subsequent *gemara* analysis despite its weighty halakhic implications. The positions are as follows:

The first opinion says simply: *zona kishmah* — a *zonah* as her name implies. This is the position of Rabbi Eliezer. Rashi explains that *zona kishmah* in Rabbi Eliezer's usage refers to a woman who committed adultery — she strayed from beneath her husband to others — and that for Rabbi Eliezer, the category of *zonah* is limited to a married woman who engaged in such an act.

Rabbi Akiva says: *zona* refers to a *mufkeret* — a promiscuous woman who has indiscriminate relations, even if not for payment.

Rabbi Matya ben Charash says: even a woman whose husband went to administer the *sotah* waters to her and a man had relations with her along the way — even that forbidden act within the very context of marriage renders her a *zonah*. This is a striking position: an isolated act of forbidden intercourse occurring within an otherwise completely legitimate marriage suffices to confer the status of *zonah*.

Rabbi Yehuda says: *zonah* refers to an *ailonit* — which is precisely the view we encountered in the *mishnah*.

The *Chachamim* say: *zonah* applies only to a female convert or a freed slave woman who had relations in the manner of *zenut*. This position is more limiting than that of Rabbi Matya ben Charash, since the *beilat zenut* in question would need to be an act forbidden under penalty of *kares* or an *issur kehunah*, and the concern extends either to having had relations with a non-Jew or to a more foundational view of how to regard the non-Jewish world. The implications for *kohanim* today — particularly regarding the question of a woman who has had relations with a non-Jew — are real and not infrequent.

One further opinion deserves attention: Rabbi Elazar says that any act of extramarital sex — even between two unmarried, unattached individuals, even in a committed relationship — renders the woman a *zonah*. He goes even further than Rabbi Akiva, who required promiscuity. Notably, a brief *Tosafot* on *panuy ha-ba al penuyah* adds that the prohibition applies *a fortiori* if the man is himself married, since then he is being *mezanneh al ishto* — unfaithful to his wife. What is fascinating here is that *Tosafot* is invoking a concept of marital fidelity as incumbent on both partners, even within a halakhic framework that historically permitted polygamy. This likely reflects the normative reality of Ashkenazic life after *Rabbeinu Gershom*, where monogamy had become the communal standard, and *Tosafot* appears to incorporate that sensibility into its reading.

### Rabbi Eliezer's View

For the purposes of the *gemara*'s question, the critical point is that Rabbi Eliezer — the one who prohibits a *kohen* from marrying a *ketana* — holds *zona kishmah*, which in Rashi's reading means a woman who committed adultery. This is emphatically not the category of *ailonit*. The combination Rabba attempted — Rabbi Yehuda's view that an *ailonit* is a *zonah* together with Rabbi Meir's principle of *chaishinan lemiut* — cannot be attributed to Rabbi Eliezer, since Rabbi Eliezer holds neither position. Both legs of the combination collapse.

## Alternative Reasons

### Kohen Gadol Case

The *gemara* must now find an alternative explanation for why Rabbi Eliezer prohibits a *kohen* from marrying a *ketana*. Rava proposes: perhaps the case concerns a *kohen gadol*. A *kohen gadol*, it is widely held, may not marry a *bogeret* — a fully mature woman past *na'arus*. Now consider the situation: if a *ketana* betroths herself to a *kohen gadol*, when will the marriage take legal effect? Only when she reaches adulthood. By that time, she will already be a *be'ulah* — a non-virgin — because intercourse will have occurred between betrothal and the moment the *kiddushin* is legally binding. On this reasoning, the prohibition would not be unique to Rabbi Eliezer at all.

### Seduction Concern

Rava himself immediately dismisses this suggestion — calling it *mi-blei lev*, a thought offered without sufficient consideration. He notes: if the father betrothed her, the marriage takes effect immediately and there is no problem. If she betrothed herself, the difficulty that would arise — she would be a *be'ulah* at the moment the *kiddushin* becomes binding — would be a problem for every *posek*, not only Rabbi Eliezer.

Rava therefore returns to the case of a *kohen hedyot* and offers a different rationale: we are concerned that she might be seduced by another man, rendering her forbidden to her *kohen* husband. One might object that this concern should apply equally to a non-*kohen* — why should any man marry a *ketana* if she is vulnerable to seduction? The answer is that *pittuy ketana ones hu* — seduction of a minor is legally equivalent to rape. Therefore, if a man has relations with a *ketana*, it is considered *ones*, non-volitional on her part, and she remains permitted to a non-*kohen* husband. But if she is married to a *kohen*, it makes no difference whether the act was volitional or not — she is forbidden to him regardless. This asymmetry is what makes the *ketana* specifically problematic for a *kohen*.

### Naara Age Limit

Rav Pappa returns to the case of a *kohen gadol* and offers a different resolution, citing a specific *tanna*. The *baraita* reads: one might think a *kohen gadol* may marry a *ketana* — the *talmud lomar* teaches *isha*, a woman. And one might think he may marry a *bogeret* — the *talmud lomar* teaches *betula*. Since *betula* in this context means one whose *betulim* are fully intact — which is not the case with a *bogeret* — and *isha* excludes a *ketana*, the *kohen gadol* is restricted to the narrow window between the two: a girl who is *yatz'ah mi-klal ketana u-le-klal bagrut lo ba'at* — who has left the category of *ketana* but has not yet entered full maturity. That is precisely a *na'ara*, a girl between twelve and twelve-and-a-half years of age.

### Betula Definition

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds another version of the same conclusion, citing a *tanna* who derives it differently: *ein betula ela na'ara* — *betula* means only a *na'ara*. The proof text is the verse describing Rivkah: *ve-ha-na'ara tovat mareh me'od betula ve-ish lo yeda'ah* — the two terms are presented together, indicating that they describe the same status. The conclusion is identical: a *kohen gadol* may only marry a *na'ara*, the intermediate stage. All of these are distinct answers to a single question, and the *sugya* presents them as alternative approaches rather than a single resolved position.

## Halachic Ruling

### Rav Amram Ruling

At the close of this *sugya*, the *gemara* records: *amar Rav Amram ein halacha k'Rabbi Elazar* — we do not rule like Rabbi Elazar's position that any act of extramarital sex between two unmarried individuals renders the woman a *zonah* forbidden to a *kohen*. This ruling carries significant practical weight. Nowadays, when questions arise about whether a woman's prior sexual history disqualifies her from marrying a *kohen*, it is the position of the *Chachamim* — limiting *zonah* to a convert or freed slave who had relations in the manner of *zenut* — that governs, not Rabbi Elazar's sweeping definition. The ruling *ein halacha k'Rabbi Elazar* ensures that we do not extend the prohibition to every case of premarital relations.

As for whether an *ailonit* is forbidden to a *kohen*, since we rule like the *Chachamim* who restrict *zonah* to specific categories, the *ailonit* would not be included. The broader and more fraught questions — such as the *kohen* whose prospective wife has had relations with a non-Jew — belong to the category the *Chachamim* address, and those situations arise with some regularity in contemporary *psak*.

## Pru U'Revu Basics

### Mishnah Intro

The preceding discussion of an *ailonit* forbidden to a *kohen*, and the broader question of whether non-procreative marital sex constitutes *zenut*, forms a natural bridge to the *mishnah* that now opens on the primary *gemara* discussion of the *mitzvah* of *pru u'revu*. It is worth noting that the central *sugyot* on *pru u'revu* are found here in Yevamot rather than in Kiddushin or Kesuvos — which is fitting, since Yevamot addresses questions of personal status and the legal dimensions of sexual relations, and *pru u'revu* belongs naturally in that conversation.

The *mishnah* frames the obligation not as "when have you fulfilled *pru u'revu*?" but rather as "do not cease from *pru u'revu* until you have children." This framing is deliberate. Unlike taking a *lulav* and *esrog*, *pru u'revu* is not a single, discrete act of fulfillment. People may try for many years without success. Moreover, in cases such as a man whose wife of twenty years has died — the very scenario at the heart of *yibbum* — the framing of "do not stop" is apt: the *mitzvah* of *pru u'revu* remains incumbent upon him and should motivate remarriage.

### Shammai/Hillel

The *mishnah* presents the dispute between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* on the minimum required to fulfill *pru u'revu*. *Beit Shammai* says: two males. *Beit Hillel* says: a male and a female, as the verse states *zachar u-nekevah bera'am* — male and female He created them.

### Hillel's Purpose

The verse *Beit Hillel* cites — *zachar u-nekevah bera'am* — is not itself the verse of *pru u'revu*. Its invocation requires explanation. *Beit Hillel*'s reasoning appears to be twofold. First, there is the practical concern of continuing to populate the world: a son and a daughter leave behind both male and female contributors to the next generation. Second, and perhaps more profoundly, the verse gestures toward *imitatio Dei* — replicating the original divine act of creation by bringing forth male and female into the world. The *mitzvah* of *pru u'revu* is thus not merely instrumental but participates in the ongoing work of creation inaugurated when God fashioned *adam* and *chavah*.

A practical dimension of *Beit Hillel*'s position also deserves attention. Because the requirement is a boy *and* a girl, couples who have two children of the same sex must continue. This means that the actual average number of children produced under *Beit Hillel*'s standard will exceed two: roughly half of couples will stop at two — those who happen to have a boy and a girl — while the other half will continue until they achieve the required combination. The expected birth rate under *Beit Hillel* is therefore something in the range of two-and-a-half children per couple, not exactly two, which has its own demographic interest.

The *gemara* also raises the question of what it means for a man who already has children to be *batel* — released — from *pru u'revu*, but who is still not released from the obligation to be married. This is derived from the statement of Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel: *af al pi she-yesh lo le-adam kama banim, assur la'amod belo isha* — even if a man has several children, he may not remain without a wife. The proof text is *lo tov heyot ha-adam levado* — it is not good for a person to be alone. Marriage is thus an intrinsic good, not merely an instrument for procreation. This is an important clarification: elsewhere the value of marriage is framed instrumentally, as a safeguard against transgression, but this *gemara* grounds it in the inherent worth of human companionship.

The *gemara* then considers how the *mishnah* might be read in the opposite direction — that once *pru u'revu* is fulfilled, one is also released from any obligation to marry. The *gemara* resolves the tension: the *mishnah* means only that after fulfilling *pru u'revu*, one need not specifically marry a fertile woman, nor need one go so far as to sell a *Sefer Torah* to fund a marriage. But the intrinsic obligation to be married remains. The statement *batel mi-pru u'revu* does not mean *batel mi-isha*.

### Shammai Logic

Returning to the *mishnah*, the *gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama de-Beit Shammai?* What is the reasoning of *Beit Shammai* for requiring two males? The answer is: *yalfina mi-Moshe* — we learn from Moshe Rabbeinu, who had two sons: Gershom and Eliezer. This is presented not as a logical argument about the purpose of *pru u'revu* but as a proof of its minimum threshold.

The *gemara* immediately asks why *Beit Shammai* does not instead learn from the creation of the world — *beri'ato shel olam* — as *Beit Hillel* does, which would point toward a son and a daughter. And conversely, why does *Beit Hillel* not learn from Moshe? The *gemara* answers both questions together.

*Beit Shammai* responds to the argument from creation: *ein danin mi-efshar mi-she'i efshar* — one cannot derive a rule from a case of necessity. The world could not have been populated unless Adam and Chava had both male and female children; that was a structural requirement of the beginning of creation, not a model for individual obligation. The fact that God commanded *pru u'revu* for the first pair necessarily implied both sexes, but that tells us nothing about what is required today when the world is already populated.

*Beit Hillel* responds to the argument from Moshe: *Moshe mi-da'atei hu de'avid* — Moshe acted on his own understanding, and his behavior is not a normative model. His case belongs to the three things Moshe decided on his own initiative and in which his judgment was confirmed by God — *ve-hiskima da'ato le-da'at ha-Makom*.

## Moshe's Exception

### Wife Separation

The first of the three decisions attributed to Moshe's independent judgment is *perash min ha-isha* — he separated from his wife after the revelation at Sinai. The *gemara* reconstructs Moshe's reasoning: if the entire Jewish people, who received the divine communication only for a brief, defined moment — and were told not to approach a woman in preparation for it — how much more so does Moshe, who communes with God at any time without advance notice, need to remain in a constant state of readiness? Moshe could never know when God would speak to him, and therefore he could not maintain a marital relationship. The confirmation that God approved this decision comes from the verse: *lech emor lahem shuvu lachem le-oholeichem* — go tell them to return to their tents — followed immediately by *ve-ata po amod imadi* — but you, stand here with Me. The instruction for Israel to return to their wives is paired with an instruction for Moshe to remain permanently in divine attendance. This is read not as a temporary arrangement but as an ongoing existential state.

### Broken Tablets

The second decision is *shiber ha-luchot* — Moshe broke the tablets. The *gemara* reconstructs his reasoning: if *Pesach*, which is only one of 613 *mitzvot*, excludes one who has become *mechuyyav* — estranged from God through his deeds — from participation, then how much more so should a people who have become *mumarim* in some sense be excluded from receiving the entire Torah in its totality? On this reasoning, Moshe concluded that presenting the tablets to Israel in its current state would be wrong, and he broke them.

The divine confirmation is the verse: *asher shibarta* — which you broke — and Reish Lakish reads this with a characteristic wordplay: *yishar kochacha asher shibarta* — well done, *shkoyach*, that you broke them. The phrase *asher*, understood here almost in the sense of *ashrei*, becomes an expression of divine endorsement.

One further point arises: the underlying *kal va-homer* from *Pesach* is itself noted as imperfect — *Tosafot* observes that *ein zeh kal va-chomer gamur*, since *Pesach* involves a *korban kodashim* and the *korban* dimension may make it more exclusive, whereas the entire Torah has a dimension of outreach and *teshuvah*. Nevertheless, this was Moshe's reasoning, and it was confirmed.

### Extra Day

The third decision is *hosif yom echad mi-da'ato* — Moshe added one extra day of separation before the revelation at Sinai. The Torah instructed: *ve-kidashtam ha-yom u-machar* — prepare them today and tomorrow. Moshe calculated that *machar leilo imo* — tomorrow includes the night before it. If the command was issued at some point during the day, then "today" had already partially elapsed; to count two full days starting from the night, Moshe had to push the beginning of the period back. The math therefore required beginning the count from the previous evening, adding what amounted to a third day. The divine confirmation is derived from the same structural reading: God's intent corresponded to Moshe's conclusion.

The *gemara*'s point in presenting all three cases is to establish that Moshe's behavior — including his having had only two sons and apparently not having more children — cannot serve as a normative halakhic model. *Moshe mi-da'atei hu de'avid ve-hiskima da'ato le-da'at ha-Makom*: he acted uniquely, under unique circumstances, and his judgment was uniquely confirmed. *Beit Hillel* is therefore correct not to derive the minimum of *pru u'revu* from Moshe's family.

## Baraita Variants

### Two Males/Females

After establishing the basic positions of *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel*, the *gemara* presents alternative versions of their dispute recorded by Rabbi Natan. The first *baraita* has Rabbi Natan reporting that *Beit Shammai* requires two males and two females. This version essentially combines both the *imitatio dei* logic — one of each sex — and the *pru/revu* structure, perhaps reading *pru* as generating one pair and *revu* as doubling it to two pairs.

Ravina asks: what is the reasoning of Rabbi Natan according to *Beit Shammai*? The proof is from the verse describing Chava's births: *va-tosef laledet et achiv et Hevel* — and she continued to give birth to his brother Hevel. The word *et* is understood as indicating a sister who was born alongside each male child — Kayin was born with a twin sister, and Hevel with a twin sister. Subsequently, when Kayin killed Hevel, Chava had Shet — with the verse explaining: *ki shat li Elohim zera acher tachat Hevel ki harago Kayin* — God has given me another seed in place of Hevel, whom Kayin slew. This implies that by Hevel's death, the fulfillment of *pru u'revu* was incomplete, requiring replacement. The *Hagahot ha-Bach* reads this as indicating that *pru u'revu* requires two males and two females, since Hevel's death left a deficit that Shet came to fill. The Rabbis, however, reject this derivation: Chava's words were simply an expression of gratitude — *hoda'aya de-ka moda* — not a statement about the requirements of *pru u'revu*.

### Male & Female

The second *baraita* attributed to Rabbi Natan presents an even more striking version: here, *Beit Shammai* requires a male and a female — what we had previously understood to be the *Beit Hillel* position — while *Beit Hillel* requires only one child of either sex. Rava explains *Beit Hillel*'s position in this version from the verse in Yeshayahu: *lo tohu bera'ah la-shevet yetzarah* — God did not create the world to be desolate but to settle it. Even contributing one additional person to the settled world is a fulfillment of *la-shevet*. This is a notably minimalist reading of the *mitzvah*, and it places the entire weight of *pru u'revu* on the concept of *yishuv ha-olam* — settling the world — rather than on any particular numerical threshold.

It is striking that across these *baraitot*, the rationale of *la-shevet yetzarah* plays a decisive role not only in determining the minimum number of children required, but also, as we will see, in shaping the question of what happens when those children predecease the parent.

## Non-Jews & Converts

### Convert's Children

The *gemara* next addresses a case that sits at the intersection of the legal question of *pru u'revu* and the broader question of a convert's legal continuity: what of a person who had children as a non-Jew and then converted? He has biological children who were legally recognized as his children under the laws governing non-Jews. Does this count toward the fulfillment of *pru u'revu*?

Two considerations are in tension. On one hand, as a non-Jew he did not bear the *mitzvah* of *pru u'revu* in the same sense as a Jew. On the other hand, as is well established, *ger she-nitgayer ke-katan she-nolad dami* — a convert is like a newborn child — which means his prior legal relationships may no longer be recognized after conversion.

### Conversion Debate

Rabbi Yochanan says: he has fulfilled *pru u'revu* — *kiyam pru u'revu* — because he has children. Reish Lakish says: he has not — *lo kiyam pru u'revu* — because as a convert he is like a newborn, and those children are no longer legally considered his.

The *gemara* notes that this dispute tracks a parallel one: the same two *amora'im* dispute whether the first child born to this man after his conversion has the status of *bechor* for purposes of inheritance. Rabbi Yochanan says the first post-conversion child is not a *bechor le-nachala*, because the man's biological firstborn preceded the conversion and is considered *reishit ono* — the first of his strength — in a biological sense. Reish Lakish says the post-conversion child is a *bechor*, because the convert starts fresh. The *gemara* notes that both disputes are necessary, as the reasoning in each case might not entail the conclusion in the other.

### Inheritance/Bechor

The *gemara* spells out why both cases must be stated explicitly. With respect to *pru u'revu*, one might have argued that Rabbi Yochanan acknowledges the biological children because even as non-Jews, those individuals were *bnei pru u'revu* — they were born within a normative framework where *pru u'revu* applies to all of humanity. The verse supports this: God commanded *pru u'revu* first to Adam and Chava, and then again to Noach, making it a universal obligation. This is not a major *chiddush* — it is the plain sense of the Torah's universal address. Nevertheless, the question of whether non-Jews are formally *metzuveh* in *pru u'revu* is debated among *rishonim*, and its practical implications are real: is it a *mitzvah* to arrange a *shidduch* between two non-Jewish individuals as part of *milu et ha-aretz*?

In the inheritance case, by contrast, one might have thought that Rabbi Yochanan would concede to Reish Lakish, since inheritance operates according to strictly halakhic categories of legal parentage rather than the broad biological framework that underlies *pru u'revu*. And correspondingly, one might have thought that in the *pru u'revu* case, Reish Lakish might concede to Rabbi Yochanan. Since each case has a distinct internal logic, both disputes must be stated.

Rashi confirms: *bnei Noach bnei pru u'revu ninhu*, derived from the verse *va-yomer lahem pru u'revu* — the universal command establishes that all of humanity is included in the *mitzvah*.

The *gemara* then records a direct exchange between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish. Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse describing the Babylonian king as *Ben Hadad ben Tavrimon ben Hezyon* — a chain of paternal lineage across generations — demonstrating that non-Jews legally recognize paternal descent. Reish Lakish concedes this point for non-Jews who remain non-Jews, but maintains that upon conversion, *leit lehu chayyus* — the legal parentage is dissolved. One might ask why the establishment of legal parentage in a non-Jewish framework should dissolve upon conversion if it was genuine legal recognition while it existed. Reish Lakish's position is that the convert's new legal identity as a Jew is so thoroughgoing that prior legal relationships are entirely superseded.

### Slaves vs. Non-Jews

Rav Ami states a point on which all agree: with respect to a slave, even the initial legal recognition of parentage was absent. A slave's children are not legally his children in any halakhically recognized sense, and therefore even Rabbi Yochanan would concede that a freed slave who had children during his enslavement cannot fulfill *pru u'revu* through those children. The verse *shvu lachem po im ha-chamor* — remain here with the donkey — is read as *im ha-domeh la-chamor*, those who are similar to donkeys, understood as a reference to a slave among those accompanying Avraham to the *akeida*, illustrating that a slave lacks the legal standing of a full person in this regard.

The *gemara* then asks: if non-Jewish parentage is merely biological, why do we assume it is legal? The answer is that the biblical text explicitly traces paternal descent — *ben so-and-so ben so-and-so* — in the case of non-Jews, while no such genealogical recognition appears in contexts involving slaves. Moreover, in some cases non-Jewish parentage is traced across multiple generations — grandfather and great-grandfather — indicating not merely biological reproduction but a recognized family structure. This distinguishes the non-Jewish case from the slave case and supports the initial recognition of legal parentage for non-Jews, even if that recognition dissolves upon conversion according to Reish Lakish.

## Children's Longevity

### Death of Children

The final question the *gemara* raises on this daf is whether *pru u'revu* is fulfilled if a person's children predecease him. This question connects to the earlier material about Chava's having Shet in place of Hevel — which the *gemara* initially read as suggesting that the death of a child can undo the fulfillment of *pru u'revu* — and it also connects to the purpose-driven analysis of *la-shevet yetzarah*. The case is stated clearly: *hayu lo banim u-mesu* — he had children and they died.

### Huna's View

Rav Huna rules: *m'kayem pru u'revu* — he has fulfilled *pru u'revu*. The children were born; the biological event of birth suffices.

### Messiah Theory

Rav Huna grounds his position in the view of Rabbi Assi, who states: *ein ben David ba ad she-yichlu kol ha-neshamot she-ba-guf* — the son of David, the *Mashiach*, will not come until all the souls stored in the heavenly repository known as *guf* have been brought into the world. On this understanding, the *mitzvah* of *pru u'revu* functions as the mechanism for drawing down souls and thereby hastening the coming of *Mashiach*. Each birth depletes the store; each soul that enters the world brings redemption closer. If this is the purpose of *pru u'revu*, then even if a child dies, the soul has been brought into the world and the goal has been advanced. The birth itself is the *kiyum*, regardless of how long the child lives.

### Living Settlement

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *lo kiyam pru u'revu* — he has not fulfilled the *mitzvah*. His reasoning draws again on *la-shevet yetzarah*: the purpose of procreation is to settle the world, and settling the world requires living people who actually contribute to it. A child who has died is no longer settling the world. The fulfillment of *pru u'revu* thus requires not only that the children be born, but that they survive and inhabit the world.

This raises a further question about the practical scope of Rabbi Yochanan's position. If a man has children and they live for decades — and then, at the age of, say, seventy, predecease their ninety-year-old father — does he retroactively lose his *kiyum*? The *gemara* does not fully resolve this, but the underlying principle of *la-shevet* suggests that there is a threshold of lived contribution to the world, not merely the fact of birth.

### Raising Children

Rabbi Yochanan's position, that *la-shevet* requires living children who actually inhabit and contribute to the world, opens a broader conceptual window. If *pru u'revu* is not simply about the biological event of birth but about bringing people into the world who then settle and sustain it, then the *mitzvah* encompasses not just the having of children but their raising. This understanding carries significant halakhic implications for couples who face infertility. If part of the *mitzvah* of *pru u'revu* is raising children rather than merely birthing them, adoption may constitute at least a partial *kiyum* of *pru u'revu*. Some *poskim* have indeed understood it this way — that bringing children to adulthood and contributing to their formation as people who will settle the world is itself a dimension of *pru u'revu*, not merely a worthy act adjacent to it.

# Yevamot 61b

## Aylonit & Zonah (III)

### Aylonit Zonah

We open at the top of 61b with the position of Rabbi Yehuda, who rules that an *aylonit* — a woman who is not merely infertile but whose very physical development places her categorically outside the realm of childbearing — is forbidden to a *kohen* on the grounds that she falls into the category of *zonah*. The underlying principle is that sexual relations in a context entirely removed from procreation, even in the broadest theoretical sense, constitutes an act of *zenut*. This is a significant and particular rabbinic attitude; it is certainly not the only such attitude toward marital sex, and it will bear heavily on the discussions that follow.

The *gemara* then cites Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that a *kohen* may not marry a *ketanah*. Notably, the *gemara* does not suggest that a *ketanah* is herself a *zonah*, nor does it characterize relations with her as *bi'as zenut* — presumably because the larger context of procreation remains theoretically within the picture. So the prohibition cannot rest on the same logic Rabbi Yehuda applied to an *aylonit*.

## Ketanah Prohibition

### Rabba: Minority Risk

Rabba offers the first explanation: the prohibition is constructed from a combination of two Tannaitic positions — Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that an *aylonit* is forbidden to a *kohen*, and Rabbi Meir's principle of *chayesh l'miyuta*, concern for minority likelihoods. Put together: a *kohen* should not marry a *ketanah* because she might grow up to become an *aylonit*.

## Aylonit & Zonah (III)

### Rabbi Eliezer & Meir

The *gemara* immediately challenges this construction. Does Rabbi Eliezer actually hold like Rabbi Meir? The challenge comes from a *baraita*: *katan v'ketanah lo choltzin v'lo meyabmin divrei Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Meir rules that a minor, whether boy or girl, cannot perform *chalitzah* or *yibum*. When challenged on the *yibum* ruling — since *yibum* does not require intent and the *gemara* has established that relations with a girl over three years old and a boy over nine years old constitute a halachic act of intercourse — Rabbi Meir responds: *katan shema yimtza saris*, perhaps the minor will turn out to be a *saris*, and *ketanah shema timtza aylonit*, perhaps the girl will turn out to be an *aylonit*. In such a case, if either party is categorically excluded from the realm of procreation, there is no *mitzvah* of *yibum* — and without a *mitzvah* of *yibum*, the act retroactively becomes a forbidden relation with a sister-in-law, an *isur* of *arayos*.

It is worth pausing here to note what Rabbi Meir does and does not say. He does not invoke the worry *shema timtza akarah* — perhaps she will turn out to be simply infertile. The concern is specifically the categorical status of *aylonit* and *saris*, which implies something more fundamental than merely practical inability to conceive. This connects directly to why, in the earlier discussion, an *aylonit* is considered a *zonah*: the exclusion is categorical and essential, not merely contingent.

The *gemara* now adduces a further *baraita* to show that Rabbi Elazar (the authority whose prohibition of a *kohen* marrying a *ketanah* we are trying to explain) does not hold like Rabbi Meir: *ketanah me'ana bo be-emet ve-eina choletzet divrei Rabbi Elazar* — Rabbi Elazar holds that a *ketanah* can perform *yibum* but not *chalitzah*, the latter being excluded because the Torah specifies *ish*, an adult male, and the woman is *hukshah* to him. Rabbi Elazar's willingness to allow *yibum* by a *ketanah* demonstrates that he is not concerned with the minority possibility of her becoming an *aylonit*. This disposes of Rabba's construction at the first step: Rabbi Elazar clearly does not hold like Rabbi Meir.

The *gemara* then continues to show that Rabbi Elazar also does not hold like Rabbi Yehuda — which brings us to the *baraita* cataloguing the debate over the definition of *zonah*.

### Definitions of Zonah

The *baraita* presents a striking range of Tannaitic opinions on the biblical category of *zonah* as it applies to a *kohen*, with almost no *gemara* analysis to sort through them — and yet with enormous practical implications for *kohanim* today.

The first opinion: *zona zona k'shma* — "a *zonah* is as her name implies" — stated by Rabbi Eliezer. The second: *zona zu mufkeret*, said by Rabbi Akiva — a *zonah* is a woman who has sex indiscriminately, not necessarily for pay but promiscuously. Rabbi Matya ben Charash says: even if a husband is on his way to administer the *sotah* waters to his wife and another man has relations with her along the way — even this act of forbidden sex, occurring within the marital context and technically prohibited only on account of *safek* (suspicion), renders her a *zonah*. Rabbi Yehuda says: *zona zu aylonit* — as we saw in the *mishnah*. And the Sages say: *ein zona ela giyoret u'meshuchreret v'shenib'ala beilat zenut* — a *zonah* is only a convert, a freed slave, or a woman who has had a forbidden sexual encounter.

### Rashi on Zonah

Rashi's comment on the phrase *zona zona k'shma* — Rabbi Eliezer's position — is quite unexpected. Rather than reading it as a reference to a prostitute, Rashi explains: *lashon to'eh she-to'eh mi-tachat ba'alah la-acherim de-le-Rabbi Eliezer ein zona ela eshet ish* — a *zonah* is a woman who has strayed from her husband to other men; according to Rabbi Eliezer, *zona* means specifically a married woman who committed adultery. This is a strikingly narrow definition and not the reading one would naturally assume from the phrase *zona k'shma*.

The Sages' category of *beilat zenut* is narrower than Rabbi Matya ben Charash's formulation in one respect: while Rabbi Matya includes violations that are prohibited only rabbinicly or by reason of doubt, the Sages appear to require either an *isur kares* or an *isur kehunah*-level violation. (Though one might note that if she has already violated an *isur kehunah*, the *kohen* question is moot, so that prong may better be understood as pertaining to *chalalah*.) The *giyoret u'meshuchreret* category reflects concerns either about sexual history with non-Jews or a more fundamental perspective on the non-Jewish world.

### Eliezer: Non-Marital Sex

Turning now to Rabbi Elazar's own position in the *baraita*: *panui haba al pnuyah shelo leshem ishut as'ah zona* — any act of extra-marital intercourse, even between two unattached individuals and even in the context of a committed relationship, renders the woman a *zonah* forbidden to a *kohen*. This is in one sense even more expansive than Rabbi Akiva's *mufkeret*, which requires promiscuity; Rabbi Elazar requires only that the sex occur outside of marriage.

This is important for resolving the *gemara*'s investigation. Rabbi Eliezer — whose position we are trying to explain — states *zona zona k'shma*, which, as Rashi reads it, means a woman who committed adultery. That definition does not encompass an *aylonit* at all. We have now established both prongs: Rabbi Elazar does not hold like Rabbi Meir (from the *yibum* case), and Rabbi Eliezer does not hold like Rabbi Yehuda (from the definition of *zonah*). Rabba's combined construction is therefore doubly disproven.

### Tosafot: Cheating Znut

*Tosafot* adds a pointed observation on Rabbi Elazar's formulation of *panui haba al pnuyah*. The *Tosafot* notes: *lav davka nakat panui v'chol shekein nasui* — the word *panui* (single man) is not precise; the ruling applies all the more forcefully if the man is married. The reason: *shemizanneh al ishto d'chashuva zona* — because he is being unfaithful to his wife, which makes the act of *zenut* even more severe.

What is striking here is that *Tosafot* introduces the moral concept of marital fidelity as a category that intensifies the character of the forbidden act — and this in a halachic framework that, in principle, did not prohibit polygamy and in which the prohibitions on sexual relations were asymmetrical between husband and wife. The notion that a man is *mizanneh al ishto* by having sex with another woman almost certainly reflects the reality of *Ashkenaz* after *Cherem de-Rabbeinu Gershom* and the internalization of monogamous norms, such that extramarital sex by a married man is characterized as a betrayal of his wife.

## Ketanah Prohibition (II)

### Kohen Gadol Timing

Having exhausted Rabba's construction, the *gemara* turns to a second explanation. Rav Adda bar Ahava suggests: *hacha b'kohen gadol askinan* — we are dealing with a *kohen gadol*. A *kohen gadol* may not marry a *bogeret* (a fully mature woman past *na'arut*). The concern is the timing of *kiddushin*: if a *ketanah* were to arrange her own marriage to a *kohen gadol* (without her father's involvement), *kiddushin* would not take legal effect until she reaches adulthood — at which point she is already a *be'ulah* (no longer a virgin), disqualifying her for a *kohen gadol*.

### Fituy & Ones

Rava rejects this immediately: *michlei lev* — this was said without thinking. If her father arranged the marriage, there is no issue at all; and if she arranged it herself, that would be a universal problem, not specific to Rabbi Eliezer's ruling. Rava then offers his own explanation: *l'olam b'kohen hedyot askinan* — we return to an ordinary *kohen*. The concern is *de-chayshinan shema tispateh alav* — we worry that she will be seduced by another man, thus rendering her an *eshet ish* who committed adultery, making her a *zonah* and therefore forbidden to her *kohen* husband.

The *gemara* objects: if so, why shouldn't even a non-*kohen* avoid marrying a *ketanah*? The answer is: *pituyei ketanah ones hu* — seduction of a minor is legally equivalent to rape (*ones*), non-volitional. And *ones b'Yisrael mishra shari* — if the wife of a non-*kohen* is raped, she remains permitted to her husband. But if she is the wife of a *kohen*, it makes no difference whether the intercourse was voluntary or coerced; she becomes forbidden to him. Hence the prohibition applies specifically to a *kohen*.

### Kohen Gadol Na'arah

Rav Papa returns to the *kohen gadol* explanation but with a different source. He cites a *baraita* that derives from the verse *ve-hu ishah be-visuleha* that a *kohen gadol* must marry a *be-sulah* who is an *ishah* — an adult. *Yachol ketanah?* Could she be a minor? No — *talmud lomar ishah*. *Yachol bogeret?* Could she be fully mature? No — *talmud lomar be-sulah*, which implies intact *betulim*, characteristic of a *na'arah* rather than a *bogeret*. The result: *ha ketzad? yatza mikhlal katnut ve-lo ba le-khlal bagrus* — she must be in the intermediate stage, neither *ketanah* nor *bogeret*, which is a *na'arah* between twelve and twelve and a half years of age. According to this Tanna, the *kohen gadol* may only marry a woman during that narrow window.

## Aylonit & Zonah (III)…

### Ruling Rejected

The *sugiyah* concludes with Rav Amram's ruling: *ein halacha k'Rabbi Elazar* — we do not rule like Rabbi Elazar's position that a woman who has had any non-marital sexual encounter is a *zonah* forbidden to a *kohen*. This is practically significant: questions about whether a *kohen* may marry a woman who has had premarital relations do arise, and Rabbi Elazar's formulation would forbid such a marriage categorically. We do not rule that way. We rule, rather, like the *chachamim* that *zona* means only a *giyoret*, a freed slave, or a woman who has engaged in *beilat zenut* in the more restricted sense.

The question of whether an *aylonit* remains forbidden to a *kohen* as a *zona* is left somewhat open: since we rule like the *chachamim* and not like Rabbi Yehuda, and an *aylonit* does not appear in the *chachamim*'s definition, she would presumably not be prohibited on grounds of *zona*.

This entire discussion — the definition of *zenut*, sex in a non-procreative context, and the *aylonit* — serves as a natural bridge into the *mishnah* before us, which takes up the *mitzvah* of *pru urvu* in earnest. It is worth noting that the primary *gemara* on *pru urvu* is found here in Yevamot rather than in Kiddushin or Ketubot, which makes a certain sense: Yevamot deals extensively with personal status and with the legal dimensions of sexual relations, and it is within that frame that the *mitzvah* of having children is most fully analyzed.

## Pru Urvu Basics

### Obligation & Cessation

The *mishnah* opens: *lo yivatel adam mi-piryah ve-rivyah* — a man must not cease from the *mitzvah* of having children *ela im kein yesh lo banim* — unless he already has children. The phrasing is notable. Rather than stating the threshold at which one has *yatza* the *mitzvah*, the *mishnah* frames it as a prohibition on stopping — which captures something important. *Pru urvu* is not a discrete act like taking a *lulav*; it is an ongoing obligation that some people pursue for years without success. The *mishnah* may therefore be addressing the phase of continued effort: do not abandon the endeavor until you have fulfilled the obligation.

### Shammai vs. Hillel

How many children constitute fulfillment? *Beit Shammai omrim shnei zecharim* — two males. *Beit Hillel omrim zachar u-nekeva* — a male and a female, *she-ne'emar zachar u-nekeva bera'am* — as it is said, "male and female He created them."

### Hillel: Imitatio Dei

Beit Hillel's reasoning, grounded in the verse *zachar u-nekeva bera'am*, points to two distinct rationales simultaneously. On a straightforward level, having one son and one daughter ensures that the world continues to be populated — each child represents a gender necessary for future generations. But the citation of the verse from creation suggests something deeper: the fulfillment of *pru urvu* is not only about achieving a demographic goal but about replicating the original divine act of creation. To bring a male and a female into the world is, in some sense, an act of *imitatio dei*, a participation in the creative act by which God populated the world with *zachar u-nekeva*.

Beit Shammai, by requiring two males, clearly has a different conception of the *mitzvah*'s purpose. One might ask: doesn't requiring only sons skew the population? In practice, the birth rate implied by Beit Hillel's ruling is also above two per couple, since those who have two daughters or two sons must continue. But Beit Shammai appears unconcerned with population balance, suggesting their conception of the *mitzvah* is not fundamentally about the continued settlement of the world in the way Beit Hillel understands it.

## Marriage Intrinsic Value

### Rav Adda: Must Stay Marr…

The *gemara* infers from the *mishnah* that once a man has children — *batel mi-pru urvu* — his obligation regarding *pru urvu* is fulfilled; however, *mi-ishah lo batel* — he does not cease his obligation to remain married. This inference is said to support the position of Rav Nachman bar Shmuel: *af al pi she-yesh lo le-adam kama banim, assur la'amod belo ishah* — even a man who already has several children is forbidden to remain without a wife if his wife dies or they divorce.

### Lo Tov Levado

The source for this obligation is the verse *lo tov heyot ha-adam levado* — "it is not good for man to be alone." This framing is important. One might argue that a man should remarry simply to manage his own drives and avoid transgression. But Rav Adda's formulation grounds the obligation to be married not in an instrumental concern but in an intrinsic one: the state of marriage is a human good in itself, independent of its procreative function. This is a significant *gemara* for thinking about marriage and companionship as values in their own right.

### Alternative Reading

The *gemara* then offers an alternative reading of the *mishnah*: *ika de-amri*, some say the *mishnah* implies both that the obligation regarding *pru urvu* ceases *and* that the obligation to remain married ceases — *batel mi-pru urvu u-vatel min ha-ishah*. Under this reading, the *mishnah* would be a challenge to Rav Nachman bar Shmuel's position.

The logic underlying this alternative reading rests on the practical reality of a society without effective contraception. How does a married man stop having children? The only plausible mechanism is by not being married. So the *mishnah*'s statement that one may stop once the *mitzvah* is fulfilled is implicitly a statement about not having to remarry.

### Infertile Partner OK

The *gemara* rejects this challenge: *lo* — it is not a contradiction. The distinction is as follows. A man who has not yet fulfilled *pru urvu* must marry a woman capable of bearing children. Once he has fulfilled *pru urvu*, the *mishnah* is telling him that he need not restrict his choice of wife to a fertile woman — *nosei ishah delav bat banim* — he may marry a woman without fertility potential. He must still marry, but the fertility requirement no longer constrains his choice.

*Tosafot* adds a further *nafka mina*: the *gemara* elsewhere teaches that the *mitzvah* of *pru urvu* is so weighty that one would even sell a *sefer Torah* to obtain the funds necessary to marry and fulfill it. That extreme measure applies only before one has fulfilled the *mitzvah*. After *yatza hamitzvah*, the *mishnah*'s declaration that one is *batel mi-piryah ve-rivyah* means he need not take such measures — but it does not mean he is exempt from marriage altogether.

## Pru Urvu Basics (II)

### Shammai's Logic

The *gemara* returns to the debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. *Mai ta'ama de-Beit Shammai?* — What is Beit Shammai's reasoning? *Yalfina mi-Moshe* — they derive it from Moshe, who had two sons, Gershom and Eliezer. Presumably Moshe would not have stopped had he not been *yatza* the *mitzvah*, and since he stopped with two boys, the fulfillment requires two males.

But why does Beit Shammai not learn from creation — *beri'ato shel olam* — as Beit Hillel does? The *gemara* answers: *ein danin efshar mi-she-iy efshar* — one cannot derive a ruling for the possible from the impossible. God's creation required both male and female for the world to begin; there was no alternative. That extraordinary situation cannot serve as a normative model for individual obligation in an ongoing populated world.

### Hillel & Moshe

Conversely, why does Beit Hillel not derive the requirement from Moshe's two sons? The *gemara* answers: *Moshe mi-da'atei hu de-avad* — Moshe acted on his own judgment in ways that were exceptional and unrepeatable. He may not have been *mekayem pru urvu* in the conventional sense at all; *ve-hiskim da'ato le-da'at ha-Makom* — his reasoning aligned with God's will, but it was not a model for others.

### Moshe's 3 Acts

The *gemara* elaborates on three things Moshe did independently — *shlosha devarim asa Moshe mi-da'ato ve-hiskim da'ato le-da'at ha-Makom*:

The first is *pirash min ha-isha* — he separated permanently from his wife after *Matan Torah*. His reasoning: the Jewish people were told to abstain from relations only for the brief period before God spoke to them at Sinai, and the Torah says *al tikrevu el isha* for that duration. Moshe, however, was always potentially available for divine communication — God could speak to him at any moment, without advance notice. Therefore he concluded he must remain in a constant state of readiness, which required permanent separation from his wife. How do we know God ratified this? From the verse *lechu imru lahem shuvu lachem le-oholeichem* — go tell them to return to their tents (i.e., resume marital relations) — *ve-attah poh amod imadi* — but you, stand here with Me, implying an ongoing, not merely temporary, condition.

The second is *ve-shiber ha-luchot* — he broke the *luchot*. His reasoning: *u-mah Pesach she-hu echad mi-shesh me'ot u-shlosh esreh mitzvos* — the Pesach offering, which is merely one of 613 commandments, is restricted so that *kol ben nechar lo yochal bo* — a foreigner may not eat from it, and this is understood halachically as referring to one who has distanced himself from God. How much more so, he reasoned, should the entire Torah — represented by the *luchot* — not be given to a people who have become *mumarim*? God's ratification is indicated by the verse *asher shibarta* — Reish Lakish reads this as *yishar kochacha she-shibarta*, an expression of divine approval for the breaking.

The third is *ve-hosif yom echad mi-da'ato* — he added one day of separation before *Matan Torah*. The verse says *ve-kiddashtam hayom u-machar* — prepare today and tomorrow. Moshe reasoned: just as tomorrow is a full day beginning from its preceding night, so too must today be a full day from its preceding night — but that night had already passed. Therefore two complete days were required from that point forward. God's approval is evident from the fact that the schedule proceeded without correction.

## Variant Baraitas

### Shammai: 2M 2F

A *baraita* attributed to Rabbi Natan presents a variant reading of Beit Shammai: *Beit Shammai omrim shenei zecharim u-shtei nekevot* — two males and two females. In this version, Beit Shammai agrees that gender parity matters for the purpose of *pru urvu*, but doubles the requirement: *peru* generates one boy and one girl; *revu* doubles it.

### Shammai/Hillel Variants

A second *baraita* attributed to Rabbi Natan presents yet another version: *Beit Shammai omrim zachar u-nekeva* (what we had known as the Beit Hillel position), and *Beit Hillel omrim o zachar o nekeva* — even one child of either sex suffices.

### Hevel & Sister

Rav Huna explains Rabbi Natan's version of Beit Shammai — two males and two females — from the verse *va-tosef laledet et achiv et Hevel*. The word *et* implies an accompanying sister; so Kayin had a sister and Hevel had a sister. When the *gemara* then reads *ki shat li Elohim zera acher tachat Hevel ki harago Kayin* — that God gave Chava another child to replace Hevel — it understands this as indicating she needed to restore the full complement: if *pru urvu* had been fulfilled with Hevel and his sister and Kayin and his sister, then losing Hevel meant the *mitzvah* was no longer fulfilled, and she needed to replace him. This implies the minimum is two boys and two girls.

The *gemara* objects: perhaps Chava simply wanted to mourn and replace Hevel as a human being she loved, not because she was no longer *mekayem* the *mitzvah*. The *rabbanan* respond: *oduyei hu de-kamodei* — she was simply thanking God for a new child. The verse need not be read as evidence about the parameters of *pru urvu* at all.

### Settlement World

Rava explains Rabbi Natan's version of Beit Hillel — even one child suffices — from the verse *lo tohu vera'ah lashevet yetzarah*: God did not create the world to be desolate but to be settled. The *mitzvah* of *pru urvu* is oriented toward *yishuv ha-olam* — the settling of the world — and even one child constitutes a contribution to that end. *Ve-ha avdei lah shevet* — having even one child is an act of settling the world.

What is striking about this *gemara* is that the *mitzvah* of *pru urvu* is being analyzed almost entirely through the lens of its purpose rather than through the technical requirements one might expect. And the verse from *Yeshayahu* — *lo tohu vera'ah lashevet yetzarah* — appears to carry more weight in shaping these parameters than one might have anticipated. This approach of deriving halachic parameters from the purpose of a *mitzvah* is relatively uncommon; here it is the dominant mode of analysis.

## Pre-Conversion Children

### Case Setup

The *gemara* now takes up a new case: *hayu lo banim biyoto oveid kochavim ve-nitgayer* — a man who had children while he was a non-Jew and subsequently converted. The question is twofold: first, is he *mekayem pru urvu* through those children? Second — which turns out to require a separate analysis — does his first child born after conversion carry the status of *bechor* for purposes of inheritance?

### Yochanan: Yes

Rabbi Yochanan rules: *kiyam pru urvu* — yes, he has fulfilled the *mitzvah*. His reasoning encompasses two components: the children are biologically his, and even as a non-Jew he was within the framework of *pru urvu*.

### Reish Lakish: No

Reish Lakish disagrees: *lo kiyam pru urvu de-keivan she-nitgayer k'katan she-nolad dami* — upon conversion a person is like a newborn child; his prior legal relationships — including parenthood — are severed, and his pre-conversion children do not count.

### Two Cases

The *gemara* establishes that both cases — *pru urvu* and *bechor* for inheritance — are necessary to state the dispute. If only the *pru urvu* case were stated, one might have thought Rabbi Yochanan rules as he does because non-Jews are themselves within the *parshah* of *pru urvu*, so the act of having children was already a fulfillment of the *mitzvah* even before conversion, and that fulfillment carries over. But in matters of inheritance — where the pre-conversion children have no halachic standing as legal heirs at all — one might have thought Rabbi Yochanan would concede to Reish Lakish. Conversely, if only the inheritance case were stated, one might have thought Reish Lakish concedes on *pru urvu* since it is ultimately about biological children. Stating both cases makes clear that they maintain their respective positions across both contexts.

### Non-Jews Obligated

This discussion carries an important implication: non-Jews are themselves obligated in *pru urvu*. This should not be surprising — God commands *pru urvu* first to Adam and Chava, then to Noach, making it a universal command. And yet there is a genuine *machlokes rishonim* on this question, partly because *pru urvu* does not appear explicitly among the *sheva mitzvos benei Noach*. Rashi here affirms the position clearly: *bnei Noach bnei pru urvu ninhu de-chtiv vayomer lahem pru urvu* — the sons of Noach are in the category of *pru urvu*, as it is written that God commanded them to be fruitful and multiply.

### Parentage Recognition

The *gemara* establishes a further distinction: non-Jews have legally recognized parentage — the example being *Berodach Baladan ben Baladan melech Bavel*, where a non-Jewish king is identified by his father's name, indicating halachic recognition of the parent-child relationship. Slaves, however, have no legally recognized parentage at all — only biological children, with no halachic *chiyus*. The source cited is *shvu lachem po im ha-chamor*, and the famous *drasha*: *am ha-domeh la-chamor* — those who are like donkeys. The point is not about all non-Jews but about the slave Avraham brought with him, indicating that a slave's children carry no legal relationship to him whatsoever.

An additional proof is drawn from the fact that non-Jewish parentage is traced not only one generation back but several: *vayishlach ha-melech Asa ben Hadad ben Tavrimon ben Chezyon melech Aram*, where three generations of ancestry are recorded for a non-Jewish king. This multi-generational tracing indicates a genuine, legally recognized family structure — distinct from the purely biological description that applies to a slave's offspring.

The practical upshot: when it comes to the question of whether a converted man's pre-conversion children count for *pru urvu*, they did at least exist within a halachically recognized legal family relationship as non-Jews. The dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish is therefore not about whether there was any prior status at all, but about whether conversion severs that prior status for purposes of the Jewish legal framework going forward.

## Children Predecease

### Huna: Fulfilled

The *gemara* turns to a final question: *hayu lo banim u-metu* — a man had children who subsequently died. Is he *mekayem pru urvu*? Rav Huna says yes — *kiyem piryah u-rivyah* — because he had the children.

### Assi: Mashiach Purpose

Rav Huna's position rests on the view of Rabbi Assi: *ein Ben David ba ad she-yichlu kol ha-neshamot she-ba-guf* — the Mashiach will not come until all the souls stored in the heavenly *guf* (the divine repository of souls) have been used up, as the verse says *ki ruach mi-lefanai ya'atof*. Under this understanding, the *mitzvah* of *pru urvu* is oriented toward bringing about the conditions for *mashiach* — each child born depletes the heavenly reservoir of souls. From this perspective, the child need not survive; the act of birth already accomplishes the purpose of the *mitzvah*.

### Yochanan: Settlement

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *lo kiyem piryah u-rivyah*. He grounds his position in the verse *lashevet yetzarah* — the purpose of *pru urvu* is to settle the world, and settling the world requires that the children actually be present to do so. If they have died, the goal of *yishuv ha-olam* has not been achieved, and the *mitzvah* remains unfulfilled.

### Raising Children

This is a striking position with significant implications. If the purpose of *pru urvu* is *lashevet* — settlement — then not only must children be born, they must live and contribute to the world's settlement. The *mitzvah* is not merely about birth but about the entire arc of bringing children into productive existence.

### Adoption & Pru Urvu

This understanding opens the door to a discussion that has very real relevance for couples challenged by infertility. If part of *pru urvu* is the raising of children — not just their biological production — then adoption can be understood as at least a partial *kiyum* of the *mitzvah*. Indeed, a number of *poskim* take exactly this view: that raising children, even if not one's biological offspring, fulfills a genuine dimension of *piryah u-rivyah*. This remains an active area of halachic discussion, and the *gemara*'s grounding of *pru urvu* in *lashevet yetzarah* provides the conceptual foundation for such a position.

# Yevamot 63

## Marriage & Wife's Value

### Context & Review

Today's daf is 63, and we pick up at the very bottom of 62b. Before doing so, a brief recap is in order. Yesterday's discussion covered the *mitzvah* of *pru u'revu* and specifically Rabbi Yehoshua's position about not stopping at two children — along with the broader question of how much of that represents a formal obligation versus *minhag derech eretz*. The *gemara* is now in the middle of a discussion about the importance of marriage, presented from a man's perspective. We have already seen two schools attributed to Bavel and Eretz Yisrael respectively: the Babylonian position frames marriage as an intrinsic good — a source of *simcha*, wholeness, and blessing — while what is attributed to Eretz Yisrael is more instrumental, focusing on the prevention of sin and the husband's ability to learn Torah. It is worth noting the irony that most other sources suggest the actual schools were reversed, with the differing attitudes relating to leaving home to study Torah in Bavel versus Eretz Yisrael, and to questions of polygamy and monogamy.

### Tanu Rabbanan

The *gemara* opens with a *tanu rabbanan*: one who loves his wife as himself — *ha'ohev et ishto k'gufo* — and respects her even more than himself — *u'mechabda yoter m'gufo* — where "respect" here is understood similarly to how *kibbud em* is understood: attending to the person's physical needs such as clothing, feeding, and care, though it appears to carry a broader meaning as well. The *baraita* continues: one who instructs his sons and daughters to walk on the right path — *ve'hamadrich banav u'venotav b'derech yeshara* — and who marries them off close to their age of maturity — *ve'hamassian samuch l'pirkan* — regarding him the verse says: *v'yadata ki shalom ohalecha u'fakadta navecha v'lo techeta*, "you will know that your tent is at peace, and you will see that your dwelling is without sin." What is added here beyond the earlier discussion is the dimension of children: educating them on the right moral path and marrying them off while young, so that once they are sexually mature they are already married and protected from sin. This includes even the notion of marrying off a young son while he is quite young.

### Neighbors & Charity

The *gemara* then continues with further obligations: one who loves his neighbors — *ha'ohev et shechenav* — one who draws his relatives close — *ve'hamakarev et kerovav*, a nicely phrased formulation acknowledging that relatives are not always actually close — one who marries his niece (*ve'hanosei et bat achoto*, though there is some discussion as to whether this refers specifically to his sister's daughter or also his brother's daughter), and one who lends money to a poor person in a moment of particular distress — *ve'hamalveh sela l'ani b'shat dochko* — regarding all of these the verse says: *az tikra v'Hashem ya'aneh tishva v'yomar hineni*, "then you will call out and God will answer, you will cry out and He will say: here I am." As Rashi points out, this verse follows the passage *ki tireh arom v'chisito u'mibesarcha lo titalam* — seeing a naked person and dressing him — where covering the naked corresponds to lending to the poor in their distress, and "not hiding from your own flesh" corresponds to taking care of relatives, marrying one's niece, and so forth.

### Marriage Essential

Rabbi Elazar offers a striking teaching: *kol adam she'ein lo isha eino adam* — any man without a wife is not a man — as it is written, *zachar u'nekeva bera'am vayikra shemam Adam*: only when they were both male and female together was the name "Adam" applied to them. This clearly reflects the message of Bereishit — the sense of wholeness and oneness that is created through marriage.

Rabbi Elazar then adds: *kol adam she'ein lo karka eino adam* — any person without land is likewise not a real man. The introduction of land into the discussion is surprising, and one is prompted to reconsider what he means with the earlier statement about a wife. The scholar Satlow, in his study of marriage in Jewish antiquity, argues that Rabbi Elazar's point is primarily about a person's social standing — that having a home and being married is what it takes to be recognized as a person within society. Seen this way, the two statements complement each other: they are not existential claims about human completeness in a philosophical sense, but rather a description of what constitutes full membership in the community. This reading is supported by the sociological reality that in many Jewish communities, even now, unmarried individuals are sometimes not viewed as fully integrated members — a reality that may not be ideal but is nonetheless real.

### Helper Interpretations

The *gemara* continues with Rabbi Elazar: *mai d'chtiv e'eseh lo ezer k'negdo* — what is the meaning of the verse "I will make him a helpmate opposite him"? *Zacha* — if he merits — *ozarto*, she will be his help. *Lo zacha* — if he does not merit — *k'negdo*, she will be against him. A second tradition presents the same idea through a textual discrepancy: the word is written *k'negdo* but read *k'nigdo*. The homiletical reading derives: if he merits — *k'negdo*, meet for him, appropriate for him; if he does not merit — *minagdato*, from the Aramaic for "lashing" — she lashes him.

### Wife's Support

Rabbi Yossi found Elijah and asked him: the verse says "I will make him a helpmate" — in what way does a woman help a man? Elijah responded: when a man brings wheat home from the field, does he chew wheat directly? When he brings home flax, does he wear raw flax? Rather, the wife grinds the wheat into flour and bakes bread from it; she beats the flax and fashions it into linen and clothing. Thus: *nimtzeit me'ira einav u'ma'amidato al raglav* — she lights up his eyes and makes him stand on his legs. This is, admittedly, a very concrete, material understanding of the wife's contribution — placing her in what we might call the kitchen or the workroom — and it must be acknowledged that not all of these framings reflect modern sensibilities.

### Bone & Flesh

Rabbi Elazar then addresses the verse *zot hapa'am etzem me'atzami u'vasar mibsari* — "this time, bone of my bone, flesh of my flesh." He reads it as teaching that Adam had relations with every animal and creature — *melamed sheba adam al kol behema v'chaya* — but *lo nitkarera da'ato*, his mind was not put at ease, until he came to Chava. Only then did he recognize, "this is my own species." The reading is motivated by the interpretive question: what exactly prompted Adam's declaration? Merely seeing her did not seem sufficient to explain the force of the words.

### Abraham's Blessing

Rabbi Elazar continues: what is the meaning of *v'nivrechu becha kol mishpachot ha'adamah* — "and through you all the families of the earth will be blessed"? God said to Avraham: I have two graftings to graft onto you — *shtei brachot tovot yesh li l'havrich becha*. The word *l'havrich* carries a double meaning: not only "blessing" (*berachah*) but also *havrachah*, the grafting of a branch from one tree onto another. The two graftings are Ruth the Moabite and Na'amah the Ammonite. From Ruth will come David; Na'amah, too, produces children who enter the royal lineage. This is a particularly significant statement within the context of Yevamot, where questions of lineage and the status of converts have been and will continue to be central themes. Here the *gemara* is emphasizing, rather pointedly, the wonderful blessing that comes specifically from outside one's own gene pool.

### Israel's Centrality

The *gemara* continues: *kol mishpachot ha'adamah* — all the families of the earth — *afilu mishpachot hadarot ba'adamah*, even the families dwelling out in the countryside, far from cities — *ein berachah ela bishvil Yisrael*, all their blessing derives from Israel. *Kol goyei ha'aretz* — all the nations of the earth — even the ships sailing from Gaul to Spain, entirely remote from the land of Israel and not even on solid ground but on the sea — *einan mitbarechot ela bishvil Yisrael*, all their blessing is by virtue of Israel. Interestingly, there is actually a rabbi from Gaul mentioned in the Yerushalmi, suggesting that the Jewish world extended even to that distant region.

---

## Labor Professions

### Future Agriculture

Rabbi Elazar continues with a series of statements. He teaches: *atidin kol ba'alei umanut sheya'amdu al hakarka* — in the future, all craftspeople will stand upon the land, meaning they will ultimately turn to farming. The verse cited is *veyardu me'oniyotayhem kol tofsei mashot malachim kol chovlei hayam al ha'aretz ya'amdu* — all those who work the sails, all the mariners, will descend to the land.

### Agriculture Lowly

Rabbi Elazar then immediately declares: *ein lecha umanut pechutah min hakarka* — there is no craft more lowly than working the land. This is striking: if in the future all craftspeople will leave their trades and turn to the land, one might expect that to be presented as a positive development. Yet here Rabbi Elazar seems to be saying the opposite. One possible resolution is that the vision of the future involves the non-Jews becoming the farmers, freeing others — perhaps, to learn Torah — but the tension remains worth noting. The verse cited is *veyardu* — they will descend — understood as a downward movement, not merely from their boats but from their station.

### Against Farming

The *gemara* then offers two anecdotes illustrating this attitude. Rabbi Elazar saw a particular plot of land in which a furrow — or, in another reading, a head of cabbage — was being planted widthwise. He said to it: even if you were planted lengthwise, it would be better to be involved in business than to worry about working you. Rav walked between stalks of grain and saw them swaying in the wind. He said to them: wave all you like — it is still far better to be involved in business than to farm.

### Business Economics

Rava offers an economic analysis. If one invests a hundred *zuz* in business — *me'ah zuzei be'iska* — every day one eats meat and drinks wine. If one invests the same hundred *zuz* in farming — *me'ah zuzei be'ara* — one eats vegetables with salt. Moreover, one has to sleep on the land to guard the crops — *maganya leh a'ara* — and gets into disputes with neighbors — *uramya leh tigrei*. The conclusion is that it is better to be a businessman.

### Plant vs. Purchase

Rav Papa, however, offers a counter-position: *zara velo tazbin* — plant rather than purchase. Even if the cost works out the same, the work of one's own hands is blessed, so one should produce one's own food rather than go buy it in the market. Then he adds: *zabin velo tazor* — purchase rather than weave. The precise interpretation of this second clause is disputed. Rashi reads it as: sell your property before you become impoverished, though with the caveat that this applies to certain objects like mats; for a cloak, one would not sell it — *lo mistramlei* — out of concern that one would not be able to find another that fits as well. Tosafot, working from a variant text, reads the contrast differently: while one should grow one's own food, one should purchase one's own clothes rather than weave them — except that for a garment like a cloak, custom tailoring may be preferable. This raises the natural question of how Rav Papa's endorsement of personally working the land sits alongside the earlier denigration of farming — a tension the *gemara* leaves in place.

---

## Suffering & Justice

### Punishment Purpose

Rabbi Elazar bar Avina teaches: *ein puraniyot ba'ot la'olam ella bishvil Yisrael* — bad things happen to the world for the sake of Israel. The verse cited is *hikratti goyim nashammu pinnotam, hecherevti chutzotam* — I have cut off nations, their corners are desolate, I have laid waste their courtyards — followed by: *amarti ach tir'i oti tikchi musar*, "I said: perhaps you will fear Me and take heed." The implication is that all the devastation visited upon the entire world is ultimately so that Israel should take heed and return.

### Rav's Wife

The *gemara* introduces a transition. Rav was departing from Rabbi Chiyya, and Rabbi Chiyya said to him: *rachamana litzlan mimmidi de-kashi mimota* — may God save us from something that is worse than death. Rav wondered to himself: is there anything worse than death? He went and searched and found the verse: *u-motze ani mar mimmavet et ha-ishah* — I find more bitter than death the woman. We now enter a section of the *gemara* that is, it must be acknowledged, written entirely by men discussing wives. What came before was also from the male perspective — the value of a wife for the husband, whether intrinsically or instrumentally, the husband's obligations — but now the *gemara* turns to a frank and mixed assessment of marriage from the man's vantage point. The question of when we get to hear how wives feel about their husbands is a pointed one, and we will return to it.

The *gemara* reports: *Rav hava ka metzatra leih devitehu* — Rav's wife was causing him a great deal of anguish. When he would ask her to make *tluphi* — lentils — she would make *chimtzi* — a type of pickled or brined dish, not radically different but not what he asked for. When he asked for *chimtzi*, she would make *tluphi*. She would invert his requests.

### Food Requests

When his son Chiyya grew up, he began relaying his father's requests to his mother — but inverting them, so that Rav ultimately received what he actually wanted. When Rav noticed that his meals were now matching his requests, he said to his son: your mother has improved! The son replied: no — *ana hu de-ka-afichna lah* — I was the one inverting her responses so that you got what you wanted. Rav then said to him: that is exactly what people mean when they say *de-nafik minach ta'ama malfach* — the one who comes from you will teach you. You learn wisdom from your children. Nevertheless, Rav continued, *at lo ta'avid hachi* — do not do this — citing the verse: *limdu leshonam daber sheker* — "they have taught their tongues to speak falsehood." Do not teach deception, even for a worthy end.

### Wife's Perspective

At this point it is worth pausing to read a contemporary *midrash* by Rivkah Lubitch, who wrote the wife's perspective on this story. Her account asks: why did Rav's wife do this? Not, she writes, because Rav would sometimes tell her he was coming home early from the *beit midrash* and would arrive only after dark — leaving her sitting in distress, waiting, until anger and resentment finally overtook her. Not because he would sometimes say he was coming home late and would arrive early, leaving her scrambling to prepare the meal. Not because he would sometimes signal that they would dine together privately — only for him to arrive from the *beit midrash* with many students, all of whom would sit, eat, and enjoy themselves in Torah discussion while she labored to serve them all. Not because he would sometimes say he was bringing guests and then come home alone.

Rather, Lubitch writes, it was because when Rav knew she had cooked *chimtzi*, he would ask for *tluphi*; and when she had cooked *tluphi*, he would ask for *chimtzi*. And she — she was silent. She said nothing. She simply served him what she had already prepared in the pot. And he never knew why she was doing this. And she, this poor woman, did not know why her husband was treating her this way — he who was her entire world and everything she worked for. And so she was bitter all her days, and nearly longed for death. And it is for this that the verse says: *u-motze ani mar mimmavet et ha-ishah*.

This rendering gives a profound sense of what the same story looks like from a very different vantage point, and it is with this in mind that we turn to the rest of the *gemara*.

---

## Marriage Complexity

### Rabbi Chiyya

The *gemara* now turns to Rabbi Chiyya. His wife, too, caused him much anguish — *Rabbi Chiya havah ka metzaara lei devitehu*. Yet when he found a nice thing in the marketplace, he would wrap it in his handkerchief and bring it to her as a small gift. Rav asked him: but she causes you such suffering! Rabbi Chiyya responded: *dayeinu* — it is enough for us — *she-megadlot baneinu u-matziylot otanu min ha-chet*: that they raise our children and save us from sexual sin. Even through all the difficulty, one must remain appreciative.

### First Wife

The *gemara* then presents what appears to be a contradiction. Rav Yehuda was teaching his son Rav Yitzchak the verse *u-motze ani mar mimmavet et ha-ishah* — I find bitterer than death the woman. Rav Yitzchak asked: who is an example of such a woman? Rav Yehuda replied: your mother. But elsewhere Rav Yehuda taught his son the verse *yehi mekorecha baruch u'smach me-eshet neurecha* — "may your source be blessed and rejoice with the wife of your youth" — with the interpretation *ein adam motze korat ruach ela me-ishto rishona*, a man finds true satisfaction of spirit only with his first wife. And when asked for an example of this, he again said: your mother.

One wonders about the wisdom of these conversations with one's children about their other parent. But the *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *matkif takifa ve-avurei mi-avurei be-milei* — she would get very angry but could also be calmed down and pacified with words. In other words, the marriage was genuinely mixed — at times very difficult, at times a source of deep satisfaction. This is, of course, true of many marriages. It is neither all one thing nor all another.

### Good vs. Bad Wife

The *gemara* asks: *heichi dami isha ra'ah* — what would be an example of a bad wife? Abaye says: *mekashta lei taka u-mekashta lei puma* — she prepares the dish and at the same time prepares her mouth — she makes his meals while simultaneously getting ready to berate him during the meal. Rava says: *mekashta lei taka u-mahadra lei gava* — she prepares the dish and turns her back to him. She feeds him while shunning him.

Rabbi Chama bar Chanina then offers a more positive teaching: *keivan she-nasa adam isha, avonotav mitpakkekim* — when a man marries a woman, his sins are sealed up or covered over, as derived from the verse *matza isha matza tov ve-yafek ratzon me-Hashem* — "one who finds a wife finds good and draws favor from God," where *vayafek* is understood as related to *pitpuk*, closing or sealing. And in Eretz Yisrael, when a man would marry a woman, they would ask him: *matza o motze?* — is your wife a *matza* or a *motze*? A *matza*, as in *matza isha matza tov* — one who finds good — or a *motze*, as in *u-motze ani mar mimmavet et ha-ishah* — one who is bitterer than death? This was an ingenious way of asking how the marriage was working out, while simultaneously acknowledging that marriages exist on a wide spectrum — sometimes good, sometimes mixed, sometimes genuinely difficult.

A beautiful *drasha* on this exchange suggests that the question was not about the woman at all but about the man: *matza o motze* — what kind of person are you? Are you a *matza*, someone who, having found something, is content — who has a *metzia* and stops searching? Then *matza isha matza tov*. Or are you a *motze* — someone who, even after finding, keeps looking around, wondering if something better is out there? Then *u-motze ani mar mimmavet et ha-ishah* — you will never be satisfied.

### Divorce Obligation

Rava teaches: *isha ra'ah mitzvah le-garsha* — if a man has a bad wife, it is a *mitzvah* to divorce her, as derived from the verse *garesh letz ve-yeitzei madon ve-yishbot din ve-kalon* — "drive out the mocker and strife departs, quarreling and disgrace will cease." This is a significant ruling in light of a tendency in some *batei din* to resist any action toward divorce under the blanket assumption — invoked under the name of *shalom bayit* — that it is always better to remain married. Rava's position pushes back clearly against that assumption.

### Bad Marriage Remedies

Rava adds: if the wife is bad but her *ketubah* is large and the husband cannot afford to divorce her, the remedy is to marry another wife — the presence of a competitor will change the dynamic. The popular saying is invoked: *be-chavarta v'lo b'silta* — better to change someone's behavior through a friend (i.e., a rival) than with a thorn.

### Wife Comparisons

Rava then elaborates: *kasheh isha ra'ah k'yom sagrir* — a bad wife is as terrible as a stormy, relentless day, as the verse equates: *delef tored b'yom sagrir v'eshes midyanim nishtaveh* — a dripping leak on a stormy day and a contentious woman are the same.

Rava then offers a comparative hermeneutic: *bo u're'ei kamah tovah isha tovah v'kamah ra'ah isha ra'ah* — come and see how good is a good wife and how bad is a bad wife.
