If the verse *matza isha matza tov* is read literally, then the simple meaning testifies to the goodness of a good wife. If it is read metaphorically — as *isha* referring to Torah or wisdom, as is common in Mishlei — then how good is a good wife that the Torah itself is likened to her. Either way, the goodness of a good wife is established. Conversely, if *u-motze ani mar mimmavet et ha-ishah* is read literally, it testifies to how terrible a bad wife is. If it is read metaphorically — *isha* as a reference to *Gehinnom* — then how bad is a bad wife that *Gehinnom* itself is compared to her.

### Escape Verses

The *gemara* continues with several verses interpreted through the lens of the bad wife with a large *ketubah*. *Hineni meivi ra'ah she-lo yuchlu latzes mimena* — "behold I bring an evil from which they cannot escape" — Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha says: this refers to a bad wife with a large *ketubah*. *Nesannani Hashem b'yadei lo uchal kum* — "God has delivered me into the hands of those before whom I cannot stand" — this too, say Rav Chisda quoting Mar Ukva bar Chiyya, refers to the same situation. In Eretz Yisrael, the reading is: *zo she-mezonoseha teluyim b'chaspa* — one whose food supply depends entirely on purchasing, who cannot grow her own food, always uncertain whether what she needs will be available in the market. This also echoes the earlier passage about the wife who makes her husband *stand on his feet* and *lights up his eyes* — *me'iras eineinu u'mekimas ragleinu* — suggesting that the counterimage is the wife whose household cannot function without her.

The *gemara* then reads *banecha u'venotav nesunim l'am acher* — "your sons and daughters shall be given to another people" — as referring to a stepmother: one's children are under the authority of someone who is not their parent. And *b'goy naval ach'isaim* — "I will anger them with a degenerate nation" — is interpreted by Rav Chanan bar Rava in the name of Rav as again referring to a bad wife with a large *ketubah*, though the precise connection to *naval* is not spelled out. Rabbi Eliezer (with the correct reading being *eilu ha-minim* rather than *Tzedukim*, as found in the Steinsaltz edition) says: these are the *minim*, the heretics. The connection may relate to the pattern of verbal argumentation and debate associated with the *minim* — and thus the verse *amar naval belibo, ein Elokim* — "the fool has said in his heart: there is no God." A *beraita* adds: *elu anshei Barbarya ve-anshei Martanai* — these are the Barbarians and the people of Mauritania — *she-mehalchin arumim ba-shuk*, who walk mostly unclothed in the marketplace — *she-ein lecha meshukatz u-metoav lifnei ha-Makom yoter mimi she-mahalech ba-shuk arum* — for there is none so disgusting and abhorrent before God as one who walks naked in the marketplace. Here *naval* points not to speech but to degenerate conduct.

---

## Chabarim Persecution

### Denying God

Rabbi Yochanan says: *eilu Chaverin* — these are the *Chabarim*. Now *chaver* can refer to the class of people in the Second Temple period who ate *chulin be-tahara*, but here it refers to a specific group in Babylonia — Zoroastrian priests who came to Bavel in the time of Rav and later and were notably oppressive, showing no deference to *talmidei chachamim* as other Babylonian authorities had.

### Three Decrees

When Rabbi Yochanan was told that *Chabarai le-Bavel* — the *Chabarim* had come to Babylonia — *shaga ve-nafal*, he collapsed in distress, recognizing what this would mean for the rabbis there. When told that they could be bribed, *taritz ve-yativ* — he straightened up and recovered, understanding that as long as they were susceptible to bribery, matters were not hopeless.

The *Chabarim* issued three decrees against the Jews of Bavel corresponding to three sins. First: *al bisra mipnei ha-matanot* — they prohibited eating kosher meat, understood as punishment for the Jews' failure to give the priestly gifts — *matanot* — from slaughtered animals, a discussion with implications for whether those obligations apply outside Eretz Yisrael. Second: *gazru al ha-merchatza'ot mipnei ha-tevila* — they shut down the bathhouses, understood as punishment for laxity in attending the *mikveh*. Third: *ve-ka-machtati shichvei* — they exhumed the dead. The Zoroastrian theological position held that burying bodies in the earth defiles the ground; their practice was to expose the body in a covered outdoor structure where birds of prey would strip the flesh from the bones.

### Body Exhumation

The penalty of exhumation brings with it a theological difficulty. The verse says *vahayta yad Hashem bachem uv'avoteichem* — "the hand of God will be against you and against your fathers." How can punishment reach one's fathers? The *gemara* answers: only in the case of exhumation of the bodies — *davar ze, chitutei shichvi*. Rabbah bar Shmuel explains: *ba'avon chayim metim mitchatetin* — because of the sins of the living, the dead are exhumed. The *gemara* continues with an exchange between Rabbah and Rav Mari about two apparently contradictory verses on the subject of burial: one says the dead *lo ye'asfu velo yikaveru, ledomen al pnei ha'adamah yihiyu* — will not be gathered or buried, left like dung on the earth — while the other says *venivchar mavet mechayim* — death will be preferred to life. The resolution offered is that the second verse applies to the *resha'im*: for the wicked, it is better that they die than that they continue to live in this world, sin further, and fall into *Gehinnom*.

### Ben Sira

The *gemara* now turns to the book of Ben Sira, citing it with the word *katuv* — "it is written" — as though it carries scriptural weight, despite Ben Sira being classified among the *sefarim chitzoniyim*. A selection of passages is quoted. *Isha tova matana tova leva'alah* — a good wife is a good gift to her husband — *becheik yerei Elokim tinaten* — she will be given into the bosom of one who fears God. *Isha ra'ah tzara'at leva'alah* — a bad wife is like leprosy to her husband — and what is the remedy? *Yegareshena miyad vetitraper mitzara'ato* — divorce her immediately and be healed.

*Isha yafa ashrei ba'alah* — a beautiful woman: happy is her husband — *mispar yamav kiflayim*, the number of his days will be doubled. But: *he'alem eineicha me'ishet chen* — hide your eyes from a charming woman who belongs to another — *pen tilached bimtzudatah*, lest you be caught in her net. Do not incline toward her husband — *al tetei etzel ba'alah limsoch imo yayin veshichar* — do not join him in drinking wine and mead. For in the beauty of another man's wife, *rabbim hushchatu* — many have been destroyed — *va'atzumim kol harugeiha* — and great are the numbers of those she has killed. *Rabbim hayu pitzei rochel* — great are the wounds of the spice merchant, the seller of fragrances — *ha-margilim lidvar aveira* — who habituate people to transgression, since the fragrances lead people to sin — *kenitzotz mav'ir gachelet* — like a spark upon a coal. *Kechluv malei of ken bateihem mele'im mirma* — as a bird trap full of birds, so their houses are filled with deceit.

The selection then pivots away from the subject of women: *al tetzar tzarat machar* — do not grieve over tomorrow's troubles — *ki lo teda mah yeled yom* — for you do not know what the day will bring — *shema machar ba ve'einenu* — perhaps tomorrow will come and none of your fears will have materialized — *nimtza mitzta'er al olam she'eino shelo* — and you will have been suffering over a world that was never yours to begin with. Finally: *mine'a rabbim mitoch beitecha* — keep many people out of your home — *velo hakol tavi leveitecha* — do not bring everyone in — *rabbim yihiyu dorshei shelomecha* — many will present themselves as seeking your welfare — *vegale sod leachad me'alef* — but reveal your secrets to only one in a thousand.

---

## Procreation Mitzvah

### Mashiach Condition

Rabbi Assi teaches: *ein Ben David ba ad sheyichlu kol neshamot shebaguf* — Ben David does not come until all the souls stored in the heavenly repository have been sent into the world — as the verse says: *ki ruach milifnai ya'atof uneshamot ani asiti* — "for the spirit that passes before Me, and the souls that I have made." The coming of *Mashiach* is thus linked to the exhaustion of the reservoir of souls, which in turn depends on the fulfillment of *pru u'revu*.

### Three Views

A *tanna* teaches: Rabbi Eliezer says: whoever does not engage in *firya verivya* — procreation — it is as though he has spilled blood — *ke'ilu shofech damim* — as derived from the juxtaposition of *shofech dam ha'adam ba'adam damo yishafach* with *ve'atem pru urevu*. The one who takes life and the one who fails to create life are placed side by side. Rabbi Yaakov says: it is as though he has diminished the divine image — *ke'ilu mema'et hadmut* — since *ki betzelem Elokim asa et ha'adam*, humans are made in the image of God; not bringing human beings into the world therefore diminishes God's presence in the world, not merely in biological terms but in terms of the person as a bearer of *tzelem Elokim*. Ben Azzai combines both: *ke'ilu shofech damim umema'et hadmut* — as though he has both spilled blood and diminished the divine image.

They said to Ben Azzai: *yesh na'eh doresh vena'eh mekayem* — some expound well and fulfill well; *na'eh mekayem ve'ein na'eh doresh* — some fulfill even without eloquence. But you — *ata na'eh doresh ve'ein na'eh mekayem* — you speak beautifully but do not practice what you preach. You are not married. Ben Azzai replied: *uma e'ese shenafshi chashka baTorah* — what can I do? My soul is bound up in Torah. *Efshar la'olam sheyitkayem al yedei acherim* — let others fulfill the obligation. This raises a fascinating question that generates much subsequent discussion: can one who devotes himself entirely to Torah study be exempt from *pru u'revu*? And is there a sense in which Torah study serves as some kind of analog or substitute?

### Torah Priority

The *gemara* records a second *beraita* with the same essential structure — Rabbi Eliezer: *shofech damim*; Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya: *mema'et hadmut*; Ben Azzai: both — followed again by the challenge to Ben Azzai and his reply. The repetition prompts a closer look at what is really at stake in the debate between *shofech damim* and *mema'et hadmut*. Are these not both ultimately saying the same thing — that failing to bring life into the world is a grave failure?

A possible reading is that the distinction tracks the debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on the minimum requirement for *pru u'revu*. Beit Shammai requires two boys; Beit Hillel requires a boy and a girl. The logic behind Beit Shammai's position — why boys specifically? — has never been fully explained, and the usual answer that boys were simply more valued in rabbinic culture, while sociologically accurate, does not resolve the internal halakhic logic. But if the emphasis falls on *betzelem Elokim* — on bringing into the world beings who will bear and enact the divine image through Torah and *mitzvot* — and if in the halakhic framework of the *gemara* men are the primary bearers of Torah obligation, then one could argue that Beit Shammai's preference for boys flows directly from the *mema'et hadmut* framework. The point of procreation, on that view, is not merely biological perpetuation of life — that would be captured by *shofech damim* — but the amplification of God's presence in the world through Torah-observant persons. That framing might genuinely favor boys over girls in Beit Shammai's understanding. Whether or not one accepts this reasoning normatively, it offers a coherent internal logic for an otherwise puzzling position.

### Divine Presence

A *tanu rabbanan* is cited: *uvenucho yomar shuva Hashem rivvot alfei Yisrael* — "and when it rested, he said: return, O God, to the myriads of thousands of Israel." This teaches that the *Shechina* does not rest on fewer than two thousand and two myriads — twenty-two thousand — of Israel. Suppose Israel numbered exactly one fewer than that — 21,999. And suppose one person among them had not engaged in *pru u'revu* — *nimtza ze gorem la-Shechina shetistalek mi-Yisrael*: that one person's failure to bring the missing child into the world is what caused the *Shechina* to depart from Israel. This is the fullest expression of *mema'et hadmut*: not an abstract diminishment but a direct causal link between one individual's failure to procreate and the withdrawal of divine presence.

### Lineage Continuity

Others say: *gorem la-Shechina shetistalek mi-Yisrael*, derived from the verse *lihyot lecha l'Elokim u'l'zaracha acharecha* — "to be your God and the God of your offspring after you." *Bi-zman she-zaracha acharecha, ha-Shechina shorah* — when you have offspring after you, the *Shechina* rests. *Ein zaracha acharecha* — if there is no offspring — *al mi shorah? al ha-eitzim v'al ha-avanim* — upon whom will it rest? Upon the sticks and stones?

It is worth noting that the phrase *al ha-eitzim v'al ha-avanim* likely carries an additional resonance. There is a *gemara* elsewhere that speaks of wasting seed *al ha-eitzim v'al ha-avanim* — upon the sticks and the stones — in the context of improper emission of seed. The echo here seems intentional: if one's seed does not produce children and thereby provide a vessel for the *Shechina*, the implicit question is where exactly that seed was going, and where the divine presence could possibly be expected to reside. The emphasis in both passages on *Yisrael* — that the *Shechina* requires Israel specifically, not humanity in general — also connects to the earlier point about *betzelem Elokim* and the patrilineal continuity of *zaracha acharecha*, which in a patriarchal framework focuses on the male line: Avraham, Yitzchak, Yaakov. This in turn further illuminates the Beit Shammai position: the continuity of *Yisrael* as the bearer of God's presence in the world depends on sons.

---

---

# Yevamot 64

## Ten-Year Rule & Divorce

### Mishnah Setup

The daf opens with a *mishnah* addressing a man who has been married for ten years without his wife giving birth: *nasa isha ve'shaha imah eser shanim velo yalda* — he married a woman and dwelt with her ten years and she did not give birth. The immediate question the *mishnah* raises, though without resolving it explicitly, is whether the absence of children is attributable to her or to him. What is clear from the outset is that the *mishnah* is building on the language of the previous *mishnah*, which discussed when a man may cease pursuing the obligation of *pru u'rvu* once he has a son and a daughter. Here the *mishnah* rules: *eino rashai levatel* — he cannot simply nullify his obligation. Even after ten childless years, he cannot declare the matter closed and allow the situation to remain as it is. He must do something.

### Cannot Nullify Obligation

What, precisely, must he do? The *mishnah* contemplates two possibilities: he may marry a second wife while remaining married to the first — for in a society where multiple wives were permitted, this was legally available — or he may divorce her. The *mishnah* proceeds to note that if he did divorce her, *muteret le'hinasay le'acher* — she is permitted to marry another man. The implication is significant: the other man need not have yet fulfilled *pru u'rvu* himself, because we do not presume that the inability to have children was rooted in her. She may therefore marry another man who hopes to fulfill the *mitzvah* through this marriage. And that second husband, the *mishnah* adds, is similarly entitled to a waiting period: *ve'rashai ha'sheni lishhos imah eser shanim* — the second husband may remain with her for up to ten years before he too must act. The language *rashai* again implies that after ten years the man has no further discretion; he will be required either to divorce her or to take an additional wife.

One further provision: if she miscarried, the count of ten years restarts from the moment of the miscarriage, *moneh mi'sha'ah she'hipila*. A miscarriage is not treated as confirmation of infertility — quite the contrary, it is taken as evidence of potential fertility, of an ability to conceive even if not to carry to term, and so the clock begins anew from that point.

### Divorce & Ketubah

A *baraita* cited immediately afterward makes the *mishnah*'s ruling more explicit: *nasa isha ve'shaha imah eser shanim velo yalda yotzi ve'yitein kesubah* — he must divorce her and pay her *kesubah*. The requirement to pay the *kesubah* carries its own legal weight. This is a society in which divorce has a fault structure: whether the woman receives her *kesubah* depends in part on whether the fault for the dissolution lies with her or not. By requiring payment of the *kesubah*, the *baraita* is declaring that we do not presume the infertility to be her fault. As the *gemara* phrases it: *shema lo zachah le'hibanot mimenah* — perhaps it is he who has not merited to have children from her. The fault, if any, is assigned to him, and she collects her *kesubah*.

This leads directly to the question of whether the language *yotzi* — he must divorce her — implies actual compulsion. The *Tosafot* addresses this immediately, noting that at the end of tractate *Hamadir* there is a dispute among *amoraim* about whether a husband in this situation is actually forced to divorce or not, and concludes that even verbal compulsion may not apply. The word *yotzi* should be understood as expressing what he ought to do, not necessarily what *beit din* physically compels. This ties into a ruling of the *Rema* in *Shulchan Aruch* that in contemporary circumstances we do not in general compel divorce in cases of this nature, particularly given that Jewish communities no longer wield the autonomous coercive power they once did.

### Abraham & Ten Years

The *baraita* derives the ten-year principle from the episode of *Avraham* and *Hagar*: *mi'ketz eser shanim le'sheves Avram be'eretz Kena'an* — after ten years of Avram's dwelling in the land of Canaan, Sarai gave him Hagar. The plain reading is that ten years had passed and something had to be done. This is taken as the textual basis — *zecher la'davar* rather than a full *ra'aya* — for the ten-year rule of our *mishnah*.

### Exclusions from Count

A further inference is drawn from this source: since the *pasuk* specifies *Avram's dwelling in the land of Canaan*, time spent outside *Eretz Yisrael* does not count toward the ten years. *Rashi* explains that dwelling in *chutz la'aretz* itself may have been a cause preventing them from having children, and so years spent there cannot be used to measure a couple's fertility. The *gemara* generalizes this principle: *lefikach chalah hu o she'chalsa hi* — therefore, if he was ill during some period, or she was ill, or if both were imprisoned — *chavushim be'veis ha'asurim* — those periods do not count toward the ten years, since the absence of children can be attributed to an independent cause. This principle of excluding periods where external factors may explain the childlessness considerably narrows the practical application of the rule. One might extend the principle to other circumstances, such as periods of significant stress, though the *gemara* specifies only illness and imprisonment explicitly.

---

## Patriarchs' Sterility

### Isaac vs Abraham

The *gemara* raises a pointed question: why derive the ten-year rule specifically from *Avraham*? Could we not equally derive it from *Yitzchak*? As the *pasuk* records, *Yitzchak* was forty years old when he married *Rivka*, and sixty years old when she gave birth — a gap of twenty years. Since he appears to have prayed for children only shortly before the birth, it seems he waited twenty years before taking any action. Why not learn from *Yitzchak* that twenty years is the relevant threshold?

*Tosafot* notes that according to the *midrash*, *Rivka* was only three years old at the time of the marriage, which would mean that *Yitzchak* naturally had to wait until she was of childbearing age — perhaps around twelve — and from that point the twenty years reduce to something closer to eight or nine, which fits comfortably within the ten-year framework. However, the *gemara* itself does not rely on that *midrash*.

Instead, the *gemara* offers a different answer: *Yitzchak akar hayah* — *Yitzchak* himself was sterile. Since the problem was with him, there was no remedial action he could take — he could not simply marry another woman and hope for children from her. His situation was categorically different from the *mishnah*'s case, in which we are uncertain whose fertility is compromised. This raises an important question that the *gemara* will address later: if a husband is himself the *akar*, does that relieve him of all obligation? The answer will involve the question of whether women are themselves obligated in *pru u'rvu* and whether a wife has an independent right to demand children.

But the *gemara* continues: if that objection applies to *Yitzchak*, does it not equally apply to *Avraham*? *Avraham nami akar hayah* — *Avraham* too was sterile, as the *gemara* will demonstrate. Why then can we learn the ten-year principle from *Avraham*? The answer is that the twenty years associated with *Yitzchak* is mentioned in the *Torah* not to teach a halachic principle at all, but to provide chronological data needed for an entirely different purpose. *Chizkiyah bar Abba* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan* taught: why does the *Torah* enumerate *Yishmael*'s years? In order to establish the chronology of *Yaakov*'s life — to calculate how old *Yaakov* was when he fled from home and when he returned, and to track the broader family history. The *psukim* that list *Yitzchak*'s age at marriage and at the birth of his children exist to enable those calculations, not to teach anything about a waiting period. By *Avraham*, however, there is no parallel chronological need; the only reason to highlight that *Hagar* was introduced specifically after ten years of dwelling in *Eretz Yisrael* is to teach the halachic principle itself.

### Isaac's Sterility

The *gemara* establishes *Yitzchak*'s sterility from the language of the *pasuk*: *vaye'etar Yitzchak l'Hashem lenochach ishto* — *Yitzchak* importuned God *lenochach* his wife. Why does the *pasuk* say *lenochach* rather than simply *al ishto*, for his wife? The *Maharsha* explains this beautifully. The word *lenochach* implies a parallel or facing position — suggesting that both *Yitzchak* and *Rivka* were sterile, *melamed she'shneihem akurim hayu*.

The *gemara* then asks: if both were sterile, why does it say *vaye'etar lo Hashem* — God responded to him — rather than *vaye'etar lahem*, to them? If *Yitzchak* too was sterile, then *Rivka* was also praying for him, and God should have responded to both of them. The *Maharsha* resolves this with an elegant reading. The *gemara* invokes the principle that *kol hamitpallel al chavero hu ne'eneh techilah* — one who prays for another is answered first. *Yitzchak* was praying for *Rivka*, and so he would be answered. But if *Yitzchak* is also sterile, then *Rivka* must also be praying for him — and then the response should address both. The fact that it says only *lo*, to him, requires explanation.

The *gemara* answers: *lefi she'eino domeh tefilat tzaddik ben tzaddik litefilat tzaddik ben rasha* — the prayer of a *tzaddik* who is the son of a *tzaddik* is not equivalent to the prayer of a *tzaddik* who is the son of a *rasha*. *Yitzchak* was the son of *Avraham*; *Rivka* was the daughter of *Betuel*. Both prayed, but it was *Yitzchak*'s prayer that was primarily answered, because of the greater potency of his lineage. This gives rise to a curious stylistic observation: the standard Aramaic idiom *eino domeh X le-Y* typically presents the second term as the more important or potent — as in the famous teaching that in the place where *ba'alei teshuvah* stand, *tzaddikim gemurim* cannot stand, where the *ba'al teshuvah* is the second term. Here, however, the more potent prayer is clearly that of the *tzaddik ben tzaddik*, who is mentioned first. This is a striking inversion of the usual rhetorical structure, and it remains difficult to resolve satisfactorily.

### Why Sterility

*Rabbi Yitzchak* asks: *mipnei mah hayu avoteinu akurim* — why were our forefathers sterile? The answer: *mipnei she'Hakadosh Baruch Hu mit'aveh l'tefilatan shel tzadikim* — because God desires the prayers of the righteous. The pattern is strikingly consistent throughout the narratives of the *avot* and *imahot*: in each generation, those whose fertility flows easily — *Nachor* with his twelve sons, *Yishmael* with his twelve princes, *Esav* with his multitude of descendants — are peripheral figures. Those at the center of the covenant struggle intensely. The *gemara* frames this as God's deliberate desire to draw forth prayer, though the theme clearly invites deeper reflection: the covenantal path is not one of effortless blessing but of hard-won closeness.

### Prayer as Pitchfork

*Rabbi Yitzchak* extends this idea with a *mashal*: *lamah nimshelah tefilatan shel tzadikim ke'atar* — why is the prayer of the righteous compared to a pitchfork? Because *Yitzchak* importuned God using the root *vaye'etar*, which shares its root with *atar*, a pitchfork. Just as a pitchfork turns grain from one place to another, so the prayers of the righteous turn God's attributes from *middat rogez* — the attribute of anger — to *middat rachamim* — the attribute of compassion. Prayer is not a plea into a fixed order; it is a force that reorients the divine stance entirely.

### Abraham & Sarah Tumtumim

The *gemara* now substantiates *Avraham*'s sterility. *Rabbi Ami* teaches: *Avraham ve'Sarah tumtumim hayu* — *Avraham* and *Sarah* were originally *tumtumim*, individuals whose genitalia were initially undifferentiated or concealed beneath a membrane, rendering their sex anatomically indeterminate at birth. Even after the condition is resolved, such individuals are presumed to face ongoing challenges with fertility. This is derived from the *psukim* in *Yeshayahu*: *habitu el tzur chutzavtem ve'el makevet bor nukartem* — look to the rock from which you were hewn and the hollow from which you were chiseled — followed immediately by *habitu el Avraham avichem ve'el Sarah techolelchem* — look to *Avraham* your father and *Sarah* who gave birth to you. The language of chiseling and hollowing is read as describing a process of physical completion, of forms not yet fully expressed requiring further formation.

*Rava bar Avuha* adds a further dimension: *Sarah Imeinu ayalonit hayata* — our matriarch *Sarah* was an *ayalonit*, a category of woman distinguished from a simple *akara* (infertile woman) by specific physical characteristics indicating a congenitally different physical constitution. The *pasuk* states: *vatehi Sarai akara ein lah valad* — *Sarai* was barren, she had no child. The apparent redundancy — if she was barren, obviously she had no child — is read as adding something: *afilu beit valad ein lah* — she did not even have a uterus. This goes beyond ordinary infertility and places her in the category of *ayalonit*. And all of this, of course, magnifies the *nes*: that from two individuals with such profound physical challenges, a child was ultimately born.

---

## Generational Adjustments

### Earlier Generations

Having anchored the ten-year rule in *Avraham*'s experience, the *gemara* immediately confronts an obvious tension: *Avraham* lived 175 years; the fertility window of his generation was proportionally vast. Does the ten-year standard derived from him apply without modification to generations with dramatically shorter lifespans? *Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Rav* rules: *lo shanu ela bedorot harishonim*, the ten-year standard was stated only for earlier generations whose years were many — *sheshnoteihem merubot*.

### Modern Timeline

For later generations, with shorter lifespans and narrower windows of fertility, the obligation comes much sooner: *shtei shanim u'mechtza* — two and a half years. The rationale is *keneged shelosha iburim* — corresponding to three pregnancy cycles. Three pregnancies of nine months each yields twenty-seven months, plus time between pregnancies, approximating thirty months or two and a half years. The underlying logic is that three cycles without a successful pregnancy is enough to trigger concern and action. The number of years is contextually determined by the lifespan and fertility window of the generation; the structure of the obligation — that after a sufficient period without children, something must be done — remains constant.

### Three-Year View

*Rava* in the name of *Rav Nachman* dissents: the threshold for later generations is *shalosh shanim* — three full years — *keneged shalosh pekidot*, corresponding to three divine visitations. The *gemara* invokes the teaching that *berosh Hashanah nifkedu Sarah Rachel ve'Channah* — on Rosh Hashanah, *Sarah*, *Rachel*, and *Channah* were remembered by God and their fertility was granted. The three-year figure gives a couple three Rosh Hashanahs — three full cycles of divine remembrance and potential intervention — before concluding that conception is not forthcoming.

### Ten Years Standard

*Rava* then dismisses both of these modifications with a decisive argument: *leis lehu lehani klalei* — neither of those principles applies. Who authored our *mishnah*? *Rabbi*. And *Rabbi* himself lived at a time when people's years were already few — as the *pasuk* says, *yemei shnoteinu bahem shiv'im shanah*, our years are seventy. Yet *Rabbi* codified ten years in the *mishnah*, not two and a half and not three. Therefore, *Rabbi*'s ruling in our *mishnah* is authoritative and stands as the standard for all subsequent generations: ten years is the threshold. The attempted revision based on generational lifespan is rejected, because *Rabbi* himself bridged the gap by writing ten years into the *mishnah* for people of shorter lifespan.

---

## Fault & Ketubah

### Uncertainty of Cause

The *gemara* returns to the question of why the husband must pay the *kesubah* upon divorcing his wife after ten childless years. One might argue that since at least one of them is clearly not fertile — the absence of children proves that — the woman should bear the burden of proof that it was his problem rather than hers, in accordance with the principle *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'ayah*, the one seeking to collect from another must prove the claim. Why do we default to protecting her *kesubah* without requiring her to establish that the fault lies with him?

### Woman & Pru U'Rvu

The *gemara* answers: *kivan d'lo amifkada a pru u'rvu lo m'ancha* — since she is not commanded in *pru u'rvu*, she is not punished through it. If we view the absence of children as a form of divine punishment — an inability to fulfill one's obligation — and she bears no such obligation, then we look to see who is being penalized by this absence. That must be the man, who does bear the obligation. Therefore we assign the inability to have children to him rather than to her, and she collects her *kesubah*.

This reasoning is admittedly difficult to receive simply, since women are the ones who conceive, carry, and give birth — the entire physical experience of fertility and its absence falls on them in the most immediate way. To say they are not suffering through it because it was not their *mitzvah* seems jarring. One possible reading, offered in the course of discussion, is not that we are making an objective metaphysical claim that she suffers no consequence — but that *halachically* we choose to assign the fault to him, in a way that works entirely in her favor: she can remarry, the new husband can hope to fulfill *pru u'rvu*, and she retains her *kesubah*. Whether or not that is precisely the *gemara*'s intent, it reflects a legal structure that consistently protects her interests.

### Rabbi Abba Bar Zavda

The *gemara* cites a challenge to this framework. The rabbis had said to *Rabbi Abba bar Zavda*: you have had one child, but now your wife is presumably past the point of bearing children — why not remarry and attempt to have more? He replied: *zakai havah li mikamaita* — had I merited it, I would have had children with my first wife. Since I did not, I will not have children with a second wife either.

What does this prove? If he is saying that the infertility lies with him definitively, that seems to undermine the *gemara*'s framework, which holds that perhaps a different pairing will work. The *gemara* responds: *hasam de-chovah ka medachi lehu de-rabbanan* — there he was merely deflecting the rabbis. His case was in fact unique: *Rav Abba bar Zavdi* had become sterile as a direct result of remaining in *Rav Huna*'s *shiur* without excusing himself to relieve himself, a situation that caused him physical damage. The sterility was therefore clearly traceable to him as the cause, unlike the ordinary case of a couple who have not had children and where attribution remains uncertain. In that unusual case there was no sense in remarrying; the problem was entirely and unambiguously his.

### Middle Ground Position

The *gemara*'s full framework is thus revealed as occupying a carefully constructed middle space. On one side: she is entitled to her *kesubah*, because we cannot say with certainty that it was her problem. On the other side: he is still obligated to try to have children, so he must divorce her (or marry another woman), because we cannot say with certainty that it was his problem. The two inferences run simultaneously and in tension: *lo zachah l'hibanot mimenah* — it did not work out between them — a formulation that assigns no blame to either party individually, but maintains the imperative of *pru u'rvu* on the man while protecting the woman financially.

It is a strikingly sophisticated legal position. It protects her right to remarry without the stigma of presumed infertility; it protects her financial entitlement; and simultaneously it preserves his religious obligation and requires him to continue pursuing it. The situation is not that she is at fault, and it is not that he is definitively at fault — it is that together they have not succeeded, and he must try again.

---

## Two vs Three Times

### Mishnah Position

The *mishnah* adds that while she may marry a second husband after the first marriage ends childlessly, a third man who has not yet fulfilled *pru u'rvu* should not marry her: *sheni in, shelishi lo* — the second is permitted, the third is not. After two marriages without children, we begin to presume that the infertility may lie with her. The *gemara* notes that this position belongs to *Rabbi* — *matnitin mani Rabbi hi* — and a dispute between *Rabbi* and *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* about precisely this question is embedded in the broader *sugya* to follow.

### Brit Milah Dispute

The *baraita* introduces the dispute in the context of *brit milah*: if a family's first son died following circumcision, and the second son also died following circumcision, *Rabbi* rules that the third son should not be circumcised — *shelishi lo simol*. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* rules that the third son should still be circumcised, and it is only if that child too dies that the fourth — *revi'i lo simol* — should not be. A complicating *baraita* appears to reverse the attributions, and the *gemara* cannot readily resolve which position belongs to whom from the text alone.

It is worth noting at the outset why this is not simply a debate about what constitutes a *chazakah*. A *chazakah* means something is definitively established as a pattern. Here the question is more nuanced: at what point must one act out of concern — not certainty — that a pattern exists? After one death from circumcision, no one is suggesting we abandon the *mitzvah* entirely, even though the evidence of danger is already present. The question is when the threshold of concern becomes actionable.

### Four Sisters Case

To help resolve the dispute over attribution, the *gemara* cites a *ma'aseh* reported by *Rabbi Chiya bar Abba* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*. In the city of *Tzipori* there were four sisters. The first gave birth to a son, circumcised him, and the boy died. The second and third did likewise, with the same fatal result. When the fourth sister came before *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*, he told her: *al tamoli* — do not circumcise your son. This establishes that *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* required three occurrences before ruling against the *brit milah* — and accordingly, he holds three is the operative number.

The *gemara* objects: perhaps *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* was only responding to the situation as presented. Maybe if the third sister had come to him after only two deaths, he would have ruled against circumcision even then. The *gemara* responds that if so, there would be nothing at all to learn from *Rabbi Chiya bar Abba*'s story — it would communicate no principle. Therefore, the story must be teaching something — and that teaching is the content of the next segment.

### Genetic Teaching

What *Rabbi Chiya bar Abba*'s story does teach is this: *achayos machazkos* — sisters establish a *chazakah* for one another. Information about what happened in one sister's family is halachically relevant when evaluating risk for another sister. The reason is immediately evident: hemophilia — which is transmitted through females and expressed in males — runs through the maternal line exactly in this fashion. The sisters are carriers; their sons are at risk. The *gemara*'s teaching that one draws inferences from sister to sister maps precisely onto the genetics of hemophilia, and it is almost universally understood that this is the medical reality underpinning these *gemarot*.

This is no small *chiddush*. It means that evidence need not be derived from the individual alone; family medical patterns are legally cognizable in halachic decision-making.

### Family Conditions

*Rava* extends the principle: *lo yissa adam isha lo mi-mishpachas nichpin ve-lo mi-mishpachas metzora'in* — a man should not marry a woman from a family with epilepsy or from a family with leprosy — *ve-hu de-itchazek tlata zimni*, provided the condition has occurred three times in that family. Even if the woman herself has not manifested the condition, what has occurred in her relatives is relevant to the assessment.

This teaching opens onto a painful contemporary reality. The stigmatization of families in certain communities because of known or rumored health conditions — epilepsy in particular — creates enormous social pressure and suffering. The fact that people in these communities sometimes travel to distant hospitals so that no one from their own community will recognize them in the same ward reflects both the weight the community places on this information and the devastation that exposure can cause. The institution of *Dor Yeshorim* — genetic testing for compatibility — was designed precisely to address this: results are never reported to individuals directly; couples are only told whether they are or are not compatible with each other, so that no individual or family is labeled or stigmatized. The *gemara*'s framework provides the halachic foundation, even as its contemporary application requires enormous sensitivity.

---

## Abaye & Choma

### Yom Kippur Incident

The *gemara* now presents a dramatic episode. A story occurred before *Rabbi Yochanan* in the synagogue of *Ma'on* — and it was Yom Kippur that fell on Shabbat. In that setting, circumcisions were being performed, and one after another, children died following their *brit milah*. *Be-yoma di-kippura she-chal lihyos be-Shabbos* — the stakes could hardly have been higher. The first child died, the second died, and the third case was brought before *Rabbi Yochanan*. He ruled: *lechi u'moli* — go ahead and circumcise.

### Abaye's Challenge

*Abaye* challenged the reporter of this ruling, *Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef*: *chazi de'kashris issura ve'sakanta* — notice that on your testimony you are permitting both *issur* and *sakana*. The *issur* is performing *brit milah* on Shabbat and Yom Kippur when, if the circumcision is medically contraindicated due to risk to life, it constitutes *chilul Shabbat*. The *sakana* is exposing the infant himself to a potentially life-threatening procedure. This is not a trivial ruling; it carries enormous consequences either way.

*Abaye* nevertheless noted that this ruling follows *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*'s position — that three cases are required before stopping, not two. He then added, *samach alei Abaye* — he relied on this ruling.

### Abaye Marries Choma

The reliance takes a personal and startling turn. *Abaye* went and married a woman named *Choma*, described as the daughter of *Issi* the son of *Rav Yitzchak* the son of *Rav Yehuda*. What was *Choma*'s history? *Rechava of Pumbedisa* had married her and died. *Rav Yitzchak* the son of *Rabbah bar bar Chana* had married her and also died. Two previous husbands had died after marrying her.

*Abaye* proceeded to marry her anyway, and he too died — *ve'shachiv*. *Rava* responded with the observation: *umi ika de'avid uvda be'nafshei ki hai* — where do you find someone who experiments on himself like this? One does not use oneself as the test case for a ruling of this nature.

The episode thus raises the question of the credibility of the evidence *Abaye* relied upon. The *gemara* points out that *Abaye* had based himself on a report from *Yitzchak Sumcha* about what *Rabbi Yochanan* had ruled — and *Abaye* himself had said that *Avin* is reliable when reporting in *Rabbi Yochanan*'s name because *Avin yeshno be'chazarah* — he reviews his learning or goes back to check whether *Rabbi Yochanan* has revised his view. *Yitzchak Sumcha eino be'chazarah* — *Yitzchak Sumcha* does not do this, and so his reports of *Rabbi Yochanan*'s rulings are unreliable. *Abaye*'s reliance on *Yitzchak Sumcha*'s version of this ruling was therefore questionable from the start.

Moreover, the *gemara* asks: even granting the authenticity of the ruling, *Rabbi* and *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* disagree specifically *be'inyan milah* — in the context of circumcision. Does that debate extend to *nisuin*, to marriage? Presumably the causal mechanism in the two cases differs entirely. The *gemara* resolves this: yes, they do in fact debate the marriage case as well. A *baraita* states: if a woman's first husband died, and her second husband died, *Rabbi* rules she should not be married to a third man — *lo sinasei*. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* rules the third may marry her; it is only the fourth who should not.

### Causation Debate

The *gemara* then asks what makes sense as the causal mechanism in each case. By *brit milah*, the explanation is clear: *ika mishpacha de'rafi dama ve'ika mishpacha de'kamit dama* — some families have loose, free-flowing blood, others have more viscous blood. A bleeding disorder running in the family — precisely hemophilia — explains why circumcision proves fatal for the children of this family. The cause-and-effect relationship is medically coherent.

But what explains the case of the woman whose husbands die? *Rav Mordechai* in the name of *Bibi of Agronya* in the name of *Rav Huna* offers one answer: *mayan gorem* — the sexual union itself is somehow the cause, suggesting perhaps some form of transmissible disease through intimacy. *Rav Ashi* offers a different answer: *mazal gorem* — it is simply her *mazal*, her fate, that causes harm to those who are bound to her, with no medical mechanism required.

The practical difference between these two positions: if a fiancé died during *erusin*, before any physical union occurred, the *mazal* theory would treat that death as equally significant — being betrothed to her is enough to be subject to her *mazal*. But if the cause is the sexual union itself, a death before consummation would be irrelevant. Similarly, if a husband fell from a tree and died — an obvious accident — that would count toward the pattern under the *mazal* theory, since bad fate could manifest in any form of death, but would not count under the *mayan* theory, since the death had no connection to the physical relationship. The example of the man who fell from a tree is a vivid illustration that two occurrences of something do not by themselves establish causation — the cause may be entirely independent of what they appear to have in common.

---

## Differentiated Rulings

### Rav Yosef's View

The *gemara* has been circling the question of what the operative *halacha* is. *Rava* reports having asked *Rav Yosef*: do we rule like *Rabbi*? *Rav Yosef* said yes. Do we rule like *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*? *Rav Yosef* again said yes. *Rava* thought he was being mocked — *achyuchei achyuch bi* — but *Rav Yosef* clarified: *stamei hi* — it is a *stam* ruling, and the correct answer is that we rule like each of them in different domains.

### Marriage & Lashing

For *nisuin* — marriage — and for *malkiyos* — lashes — we rule like *Rabbi*: two occurrences are sufficient to require action. By marriage, this means that if a woman has been married twice and both husbands died, a third man who has not yet fulfilled *pru u'rvu* should not marry her. By lashes, the *mishnah* rules that if someone received *malkos* for a transgression and repeated the same transgression a second time, *beit din* does not simply administer another round of lashes and release him — it places him in the *kippah* and feeds him barley until he dies. This is already triggered after the second offense. The language there — *beit din konasin oso la-kippah u-ma'achilin oso seorin ad she-tibaka kreiso ve-yumas* — is arresting. *Tosafot* suggests that the phrase about the stomach bursting is hyperbolic, meaning merely that they confine him and give him coarse barley rations; but in either reading, drastic action follows the second offense.

### Menstrual & Ox

For *vestos* — menstrual patterns — and for *shor ha-muad* — the habitually goring ox — we rule like *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*: three occurrences are required. Regarding *vestos*, the *mishnah* rules that *ein ishah kova'as lah veses ad she-tikba'enah shalosh pe'amim* — a woman does not establish a fixed menstrual cycle until it has occurred three times. Similarly, *einah mitaheres min ha-veses ad she-ta'akrenah shalosh pe'amim* — once a regular cycle is established, it is not considered changed until three consecutive cycles have diverged from it. The halachic implications are significant: if a woman has a fixed *veset* and the time of her expected period arrives, she is treated as if she has become a *niddah* even without a physical check. That presumption requires a three-time foundation. Similarly, a *shor ha-muad* — an ox whose owner is liable for full damages rather than half — attains that status only after *sheyeidu bo shalosh pe'amim*, three witnessed gorings.

### Two vs Three Synthesis

The best resolution of this apparent contradiction — ruling like *Rabbi* in some areas and *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* in others — is that the two thresholds address two categorically different questions. Two occurrences are enough to generate concern and require a response. They establish that we cannot dismiss what has happened as a pure coincidence, and they obligate action. Three occurrences, however, establish something stronger: that the pattern is fixed, regular, and essentially certain. This is the difference between *choshesh* — being apprehensive — and *chazakah* — a legally established presumption.

The *Pnei Yehoshua* and other *achronim* articulate this distinction clearly. For *vestos*, we are not merely saying a woman should be concerned about bleeding on a certain day — we presume she has bled. That is a full legal presumption, requiring three-time establishment. For the *shor ha-muad*, the ox is not merely one to watch carefully — his legal identity changes; he becomes a definitively dangerous animal whose owner bears full liability. That too requires three. But for marriage and for punishing a repeat offender, two times is enough to act: the evidence of danger or habitual wrongdoing is sufficient to respond, even before the pattern is definitively established. This is analogous to the *Chofetz Chaim*'s distinction in *hilchos lashon hara* between believing a report and being *choshesh* for it — between accepting information as true and treating it as warranting concern.

Returning to the *mishnah*'s case: a woman who has gone through two marriages of ten years each without children may not be married by a third man who has not yet fulfilled *pru u'rvu*. Yet the second husband who divorced her must still pay her *kesubah*, because we have not definitively established that the infertility lies with her. These two rulings, taken together, define precisely the space between two-time concern and three-time certainty: there is enough evidence to prohibit the third marriage, but not enough to deprive her of her *kesubah*. That is exactly the distinction between ruling like *Rabbi* in matters of marriage — where two times suffices to require action — and what it would mean to have established her infertility with the certainty of a *chazakah*.

The question of how these principles apply today — particularly in the case of a woman whose multiple husbands have died, where the causal theories of *mayan gorem* and *mazal gorem* are both medically elusive — remains open and, as the *gemara* itself demonstrates through the case of *Abaye*, requires considerable care.

---

---

# Yevamot 65

## Three Marriages

### Marriage Setup

The daf under discussion is 65, and we pick up where the previous discussion left off. The sugya concerns a woman who has been married to a man for ten years without bearing children and is subsequently divorced. The situation carries an interesting internal tension: on one hand, there is a presumption that the infertility is not necessarily her fault, such that she may remarry a man who still needs to fulfill *peru u'revu*; on the other hand, there is a countervailing assumption that she may be a contributing factor, which is why the first husband is permitted — indeed encouraged — to take another wife.

### Tanu Rabbanan

The *Gemara* cites a *baraita* beginning *tanu rabbanan*, found four lines from the top of 65a. The case runs as follows: she married the first man and had no children, married the second man and still had no children — that is two marriages without children, which, as we have seen, is the subject of the dispute between *Rebbe* and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel regarding how many instances are required to establish a *chazakah*. The *baraita* then rules: *vishlishi lo tinasei ela lemi sheyeish lo banim* — she should not marry a third man unless that man has already fulfilled the *mitzvah* of *peru u'revu*. Following *Rebbe*'s position, after two such marriages we must at minimum be concerned that the problem lies with her. Therefore, if she does marry a man who has no children, *taitzei belo kesubah* — she is divorced without receiving her *kesubah*, since it has effectively been established that the infertility is her problem, and that husband must now pursue having children elsewhere.

### Third Marriage Query

An *ibaya* is then posed: suppose she proceeds to marry the third man, waits the requisite ten years, and still has no children. At this point, after three successive childless marriages, the case that the infertility lies with her seems firmly established. The question is whether the first two husbands — who did pay her *kesubah* at the time of their divorces, since the fault had not yet been conclusively identified as hers — may now return to her and demand the *kesubah* money back: *mahu delitve'u hanach kamaei, mi matzu amru lah, iglai milta de'at hu digramat* — it has now been revealed that you were the cause.

### Ketubah Return Claim

The thrust of this question is really about the burden of proof. Throughout these cases, the woman appears to be presumed entitled to her *kesubah*, placing the burden on the husband to establish otherwise. The question is whether newly available evidence — the failure of the third marriage — retroactively shifts that burden and allows the first two husbands to recover what they paid.

### Body Weakened Defense

The *Gemara* answers: *mistavra matzi amrah lehu hashta hu de'achash* — the more reasonable conclusion is that she can respond to them, "It is only now that my body has grown weaker." Perhaps twenty years have passed since the first marriage, ten since the second. Even if she was a partial cause earlier, or no cause at all, the passage of time and the weakening of her constitution may explain the current pattern. The *Gemara* accepts this defense: *mistavra matzi amrah lehu hashta hu de'achash*. She may say this to them, and they cannot recover the *kesubah*.

---

## Fourth Marriage

### Fertile Fourth

A second *ibaya* follows: suppose she marries a fourth man and now, with him, she does have children. So she was fertile all along. The question is now the mirror image of the previous one.

### Demand Third

May she go back to the third husband — who, recall, did not pay her *kesubah* precisely because by that point there was sufficient grounds to presume the infertility was hers — and demand her *kesubah* now that her fertility has been demonstrated?

### Shtikosayich Yafah

The *Gemara* answers with a striking formulation: *shtikosayich yafah midibura'yich* — your silence is better than your speech. The reason is that if she presses her claim against husband number three, asserting that she was always fertile and that the failure of that marriage was his fault, he can turn around and say: *ana ada'ata de'hachi lo garashtich* — had I known you were fertile, I never would have divorced you. If that argument succeeds, it would mean the *get* was given in error, invalidating it retroactively. And if the *get* is invalid, then the child she bore with husband number four is a *mamzer*. The stakes of pressing this claim are therefore catastrophic.

### Rav Pappa Raises

Rav Pappa objects: *ee ishtaka ishtakin? anan mi shatkinan? nimtza get batel u'vanim mamzerim* — if the concern about the *get*'s validity is real, how can we simply stay silent? We ourselves — the *beit din*, the *Gemara*, everyone — cannot simply keep quiet if there is a genuine question about whether the divorce was valid and the children are legitimate.

### Status Changed

The *Gemara* responds: *ella amrinan hashta hu d'avraya* — we say that it is only now that her condition has improved. That is, we adopt the position that her fertility is a new development, not a revealed truth about her condition at the time of the third marriage. This is consistent with the earlier principle that she could claim her body weakened over time; the converse applies here as well — we will say her body strengthened or her circumstances changed, and we will not revisit the factual premise of the original divorce.

### No Retroactive

The underlying principle is that we do not retroactively revise legal determinations based on later-emerging evidence. The divorce was valid on the facts as they were understood at the time, and we judge the case as it stood then. Subsequent developments are treated as changes in status, not revelations of hidden prior truth. This principle operates in everyone's best interest: the woman avoids the catastrophic outcome of her children being declared *mamzerim*, and the legal system avoids the destabilizing effect of constantly re-litigating settled matters whenever new evidence surfaces.

One might ask whether this principle extends to business or damages contexts — whether claims could be revisited whenever a counter-assumption cannot be articulated. The broader answer is grounded in the concept of *dvarim she-balev einam dvarim* and the general rule that legal determinations are made on the basis of the best available assumptions at the time, without regularly revising them based on facts that emerge only later.

---

## Infertility Source

### Mutual Blame

The *Gemara* now turns to the classic scenario: *hu amar minei, v'hi amra mineh* — he says the infertility problem is hers, and she says it is his. This is presumably the standard case underlying the entire discussion, and the *halacha* would seem to be that she receives her *kesubah* since the fault is not established. Tosafot raises a number of complicated questions about what precisely distinguishes this scenario from earlier cases, but the *Gemara* here takes a specific direction.

### Yora K'chetz

Rabbi Ami rules: *dvarim she-beino l'veina ne'emenes* — in matters that are between the two of them privately, she is believed. The *Gemara* then explains the mechanism: *hi kama leh b'yora k'chetz, hu lo kama leh b'yora k'chetz* — she is in a better position to know whether he ejaculates with the force of an arrow, *yora k'chetz*, than he is during the act itself. If she is claiming that the cause of the infertility is a weakness in his ejaculation, we credit her testimony because she has better access to that information than he does. This raises a natural question: why must this be the specific claim? Why isn't a general assertion that it may be his problem sufficient? We have already said that since it may be his problem, she receives her *kesubah* — the language *lo zachah l'hibanos mimenah* suggests the possibility is always open. This is a question that Tosafot grapples with, though the discussion there is complicated enough not to pursue here in full.

### Fertility Test

The husband then proposes: *eizal insiv iteta v'ivdok nafshai* — I will go ahead and marry another woman and see if I have children with her. If I do, that will prove the problem is hers and she should not receive her *kesubah*.

### Divorce First

Rabbi Ami responds: *be-zo yotzi ve-yitein ketubah* — if he wishes to pursue that course, he must first divorce his wife and give her the *kesubah* before marrying another woman. The *Gemara* frames this in terms of a broader principle: *she'ani omer kol hanosei isha al ishto yotzi v'yiten ketubah* — anyone who marries another woman while still married to his first wife, at least if the first wife protests, must give the first wife a *get* and pay her *kesubah*. The first wife has the right to object to a second marriage, and if the husband insists on proceeding, that objection entitles her to a compelled divorce with *kesubah*.

---

## Polygamy Debate

### Rabbi Ami Monogamy

Rabbi Ami's position thus treats the first wife's protest as legally effective: if she does not want him to take another wife, he cannot do so while remaining married to her. If he insists, he must divorce her with her *kesubah* first. This is not merely a moral preference but a legal entitlement.

### Rava Polygamy OK

Rava disagrees: *nosei adam kama nashim al ishto ve-hu d'is lei l'mizan ninhu* — a man is entitled to marry multiple women even alongside his existing wife, provided he has the means to support them all. On Rava's view, the first wife's protest does not carry legal force sufficient to prevent a second marriage; the only operative constraint is economic capacity.

### Bavli-Yerushalmi

This disagreement is not merely a technical *halachic* dispute but reflects a deeper question about whether polygamy is regarded as fundamentally incompatible with the first wife's rights or as a permissible institution subject only to practical constraints. As noted, this maps quite neatly onto the broader divide between *Bavel* and *Eretz Yisrael*, and historically between Sephardic and Ashkenazic practice, which in turn tracks whether these communities were embedded in polygamous or monogamous surrounding cultures. It is worth noting that even in polygamous cultures, multiple wives were practically possible only for wealthy men who could support them — which is precisely the limiting condition Rava articulates.

The *aguna* question hovers in the background here as well: in cases where the husband refuses to give a *get* while pursuing or maintaining another relationship, the question of whether *beit din* has the authority and will to actually compel the divorce and *kesubah* payment is distinct from what *halacha* says ought to happen. It is also worth noting — and this was confirmed in the course of discussion — that Rabbi Ami was from *Eretz Yisrael*, which tracks perfectly: Rabbi Ami's more restrictive view of polygamy aligns with the *Eretz Yisrael* tradition, while Rava's permissive view aligns with the Babylonian tradition.

---

## Women Sue Divorce

### Miscarriage Dispute

The *Gemara* turns to a new set of cases in which it is the woman who is suing for divorce. *Hu amar apalta b'go eser ve'hi amra lo apaliti* — he claims that she had a miscarriage during the ten-year period, such that he is not yet obligated to divorce her, since the ten-year clock has not run uninterrupted by any pregnancy. She denies having had a miscarriage and demands her divorce and *kesubah*. Note the curious posture here: she is the one pressing for divorce, presumably because she wishes to have the opportunity to remarry and have children.

Rabbi Ami rules: *af b'zu hi ne'emenes* — here too she is believed. The reason: *d'ei issa d'hapila nafshah b'akarta lo machzaka* — if it were true that she had not miscarried, she would not be claiming that she went the full ten years without even a miscarriage. By claiming there was no miscarriage, she is effectively establishing herself as infertile, which is *halachically* not a definitive ruling — she can still remarry — but practically is damaging to her prospects. As one participant noted with some wry understatement, it is not good for a *shidduch*. She would not fabricate a claim that stigmatizes her in this way if it were not true, and therefore we believe her even though the claim serves her interest in the immediate legal context by entitling her to a divorce with *kesubah*.

### Chazaka Miscarry

*Hapila v'chazra v'hapila v'chazra v'hapila* — what if she miscarried three times? In that case she does not have a *chazakah* of being unable to conceive, but she may well have a *chazakah* of being unable to carry to term. The *Gemara* rules: *huchzaka l'nefalim* — she has established a *chazakah* of miscarrying. Rashi explains: *yotzi v'yiten ketubah shema lo zachah libanos mimena* — he divorces her and gives the *kesubah*, because perhaps he has not been granted the merit of having children through her. The *kesubah* is still paid, because even with this established pattern it is not conclusively proven that the problem lies exclusively with her — it might be some combination — and so the *lo zachah l'hibanos mimena* framing keeps the possibility open that it is not solely her deficiency.

### Count Miscarriage

A dispute then arises: *hu amar hapila terei ve'hi amra telasa* — he claims she miscarried twice, not yet reaching the threshold for a *chazakah*, while she claims it was three times. This matters because three miscarriages triggers the *chazakah* and with it the obligation to divorce her and pay the *kesubah*.

### Negates Self

Rabbi Yochanan bar Elazar reports: *uvda hava b'bei midrasha de'amru hi mehemana* — a case came before the *beit midrash* and they ruled she is believed. The reasoning is the same as before: *d'ee issa d'lo aplah nafshah b'nefalim lo machzeka* — if it were false, she would not be willing to establish herself as a woman who regularly miscarries. The *beit midrash* credits her precisely because the claim, while advantageous to her in the immediate dispute, carries a broader self-stigmatizing dimension that she would not invoke falsely. Underlying all of these cases is a consistent pattern: she is believed over him across the full range of disputes, in each instance because her claim contains an element that works against her broader interests. This functions as something like a *migo* or an analogous credibility-enhancing consideration.

What is particularly striking is the uniformity of this pattern across such varied scenarios — the source of the infertility, the occurrence of a miscarriage, the count of miscarriages — and the interesting question this raises about what distinguishes these cases from earlier *mishnayot* in which the husband's claim was credited. Tosafot engages this question, though the details are sufficiently complicated as to require separate treatment.

---

## Peru u'Revu

### Mishnah Setup

The *Gemara* now transitions to the *mishnah* that concludes this *perek*: *haish metzuveh al peru u'revu aval lo haisha* — the man is commanded on *peru u'revu* and not the woman. This ruling is striking on its face, given that it is the woman who bears children.

### Both Commanded

Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka dissents, arguing that both are commanded, deriving this from the verse: *vayivarech osam Elokim vayomer lahem Elokim peru u'revu* — God blessed them and said to them, to both of them, be fruitful and multiply. This is a reasonable textual argument, and one that carries additional intuitive force given that it is the woman who carries and births children.

### Man Conquers

Rav Illa, in the name of Rabbi Elazar the son of Rabbi Shimon, derives the limitation to the man from the continuation of the same verse: *u'milu et ha'aretz v'chivshuha* — fill the land and conquer it. *Ish darko lichvosh v'ein isha darkah lichvosh* — it is the way of the man to conquer and not the way of the woman. Since the verse concludes with an act — conquest — that characterizes the man, the rabbis conclude that even the earlier command was addressed to the man alone.

### Plural Objection

An objection is raised: *adderaba, v'chivshuha tarti mashma* — on the contrary, the word *v'chivshuha* is in the plural form, implying *atem tichvishu osah* — you, in the plural, shall conquer it. How then can the verse be read as addressing only the man?

### Kri u'Kesiv

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves this: *v'chivshah ksiv* — the word is actually written in the text without the *vav*, making it singular rather than plural. The *kri* — the traditional reading — has it in the plural, but the *kesiv* — the written spelling — renders it singular. On the basis of this *kri u'chesiv*, the verse is read as addressing the man alone. It is quite striking that a verse which in its plain reading appears to address both husband and wife is restricted to the man alone on the basis of a defective spelling — but that is how the *Gemara* proceeds.

---

## Woman Exempt Why

### Lashevet

The *Gemara* having established the textual derivation, the question remains: what is the theological or conceptual rationale? One approach, grounded in the *Gemara* itself, connects *peru u'revu* to the broader principle of *lashevet* — settling and populating the world — derived from the verse *lo tohu b'ra'ah lashevet yetzarah*, God did not create the world to be void but to be inhabited. On this reading, *peru u'revu* is not merely about biological reproduction but about the larger project of *yishuv ha'olam*, building and sustaining civilization. That project, on a traditional division of roles, falls to the man as the one who goes out into the world to build society, while the woman remains in the domestic sphere. If this framing is correct, the *mitzvah* of *peru u'revu* as an aspect of settling the world naturally devolves upon the man. This is probably the most straightforward reading of the *Gemara*'s own logic in context, even if it carries its own set of assumptions.

### Patriarchy

A second explanation, noted by several *acharonim*, focuses on the verb *v'chivshuha* and reads it not as conquering the land but as the man's conquest, so to speak, in the act of sexual intercourse — connecting it to the *Gemara*'s broader framing of the man as the initiator and active party in relations, with the woman cast in a more passive role (*karka olam*). On this reading, since children come through the man's active role in the sexual act, the *mitzvah* is assigned to him as the agent. More broadly, the patriarchal structure of the family as understood throughout *Yevamot* — where children belong to the father's household, not the mother's — renders the father the primary party in the act of having children. This is reflected in the very language of *Tanach*: *Avraham holid et Yitzchak* — Abraham sired Isaac — where the woman, Sarah, is invisible in the formulation even though she is the one who gave birth. Within a social structure where children are born into and named for the father's household, it follows that the *mitzvah* of having them is primarily attributed to him.

### Feminist View

This dimension of the sugya raises what one might call the feminist critique: the woman is simultaneously burdened with the physical reality of pregnancy, labor, and childbirth, and excluded from receiving credit — *mitzvah* credit — for the very act she alone performs. She is assigned the traditional role of child-bearer by societal expectation, and then rendered invisible in the legal framework that assigns the corresponding *mitzvah* to the man. It is, as one might put it, the worst of both worlds: socially defined by her child-bearing role but not recognized *halachically* as the one obligated — or credited — in that act.

### Berman Freedom

Rabbi Saul Berman, in a well-known essay written approximately thirty years ago, proposed a reading that inverts this critique. On his account, the *halacha*'s exemption of the woman from *peru u'revu* is not a denial of her role but a liberation from a compelled one. By not obligating her in *peru u'revu*, the *halacha* leaves open the possibility that a woman may choose not to marry, or choose not to have children, and pursue a more independent path without violating a Torah obligation. The exemption thus functions as a grant of freedom rather than an erasure. Readers may evaluate which of these readings they find more persuasive — or reject both — but the question itself is one the sugya genuinely invites.

---

## Rule Like Broka

### Yochanan Dispute

The *Gemara* now turns to the *amoraic* dispute over the *halacha*: *itmar, Rabbi Yochanan v'Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* — there is a recorded dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, one of whom says we rule like Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka that the woman is also commanded, and one of whom says we do not rule like him.

### Don't Rule Broka

The *Gemara* seeks to determine which *amora* held which position: *tistayayeim d'Rabbi Yochanan hu d'amar ein halacha* — let us conclude that it is Rabbi Yochanan who says we do not rule like Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka. The basis for this conclusion is discussed in the next segment.

---

## Practical Diff

### Stay Single

Before examining the evidence for how Rabbi Yochanan ruled, it is worth pausing to consider what practical difference this dispute makes — because beyond the abstract question of who receives *mitzvah* credit, the *halacha* has substantial real-world implications. If a woman is not commanded on *peru u'revu*, can she choose to remain unmarried without violating any Torah obligation? On the view that she is not commanded, the answer would appear to be yes.

### Demand Divorce

A second practical difference: suppose a man has already had children from a previous wife but his current wife has not. If the woman is commanded, she has the basis to demand a divorce so that she may remarry and attempt to have children with another man. If she is not commanded, it is less clear what legal standing she has to compel such a divorce, as we will see in the stories below.

### Birth Control

A third and particularly significant contemporary implication: if a woman is not commanded on *peru u'revu*, may she use contraception freely? Rav Moshe Feinstein raised precisely this question — if a woman is not commanded, perhaps she may use hormonal contraception without *halachic* objection, since she bears no obligation regarding *peru u'revu*. Of course, the residual question then becomes whether she is permitted to do so if it prevents her husband from fulfilling *his* obligation, since the context in which he can fulfill it is dependent on her. But the question is genuinely opened by the exemption, and the story of Yehudit later in this sugya is one of the primary *Talmudic* sources engaged in that discussion.

---

## Peru u'Revu (II)

### U'Milu

The *Gemara* cites a further source for the derivation: *u'milu et ha'aretz v'chivshuha* — the verse from which the gendered reading of *peru u'revu* is established, as discussed above.

---

## Rule Like Broka (II)

### Abbahu/Chiya

Returning to the question of how Rabbi Yochanan ruled: *d'yativ Rabbi Abbahu v'ka'amar mishmeih d'Rabbi Yochanan: halacha* — Rabbi Abbahu sat and declared in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka, meaning the woman is also commanded. There is then a textual variant: some say it was not Rabbi Abbahu but Rabbi Chiya bar Abba who transmitted this ruling in Rabbi Yochanan's name.

### Face Away

In either version: *hadreinh Rabbi Ami v'Rav Assi l'apeihu* — Rabbi Ami and Rav Assi turned their faces away from the speaker. They did not openly contradict him, but their gesture of disapproval made clear that they believed this ruling was incorrect and did not represent Rabbi Yochanan's actual position.

### Rav Pappa Why

Rav Pappa raises a question about the textual variant: *bishlama* if it was Rabbi Abbahu who said it, then one can understand why Rabbi Ami and Rav Assi merely turned away rather than explicitly contradicting him — *mishum kevod beit Keisar*, because Rabbi Abbahu had a close relationship with the imperial court and they did not want to publicly contradict someone of his standing; hence their silent expression of displeasure rather than open refutation. But *ella l'man d'amar* that it was Rabbi Chiya bar Abba who said it — who is Rabbi Chiya bar Abba that they could not simply tell him directly that Rabbi Yochanan did not rule this way? Why would they resort to turning their faces rather than saying *leimru lei lama amar Rabbi Yochanan hachi* — just tell him explicitly that Rabbi Yochanan did not say this?

The conclusion that emerges is that Rabbi Ami and Rav Assi clearly believed Rabbi Yochanan held that we do *not* rule like Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka, and that the *halacha* is therefore that the *mitzvah* of *peru u'revu* falls on the man alone.

---

## Not Commanded Cases

### Rabbi Ami

The *Gemara* now presents narrative episodes illustrating the practical stakes. *Ki ha de'asa l'kamei d'Rabbi Ami* — a woman came before Rabbi Ami. From the context, the man in question apparently already had children from another woman, so the case is not one where he is being compelled to divorce in order to fulfill *peru u'revu* himself. She, on the other hand, has not had children and wishes to be divorced so she can remarry. He wants to remain married. She demands a divorce with *kesubah*. Rabbi Ami says to her: *zil lo mifkadat* — go, you are not commanded on *peru u'revu*, and therefore you have no legal basis for compelling a divorce with *kesubah*. Without a commanded obligation, there is no cause of action, and a divorce without cause would not entitle her to the *kesubah*.

### Old Age Need

The woman responds: *l'siva d'la mai tehvei alah* — but what about her old age? Who will take care of her? The implicit claim is that regardless of any formal *mitzvah*, she has a fundamental human need and desire to have children — people who will support her in old age — and that this constitutes sufficient cause to compel a divorce with *kesubah*.

Rabbi Ami accepts the argument: *hi vadai kafinan* — in that case, we will certainly compel it. The woman's basic human interest in having children, quite apart from any *mitzvah* obligation, is recognized as legitimate cause. The practical import is significant: even without a formal *mitzvah*, the desire to have children — grounded in the very human need for support and continuity — gives her standing to sue for divorce with *kesubah*.

### Rav Nachman

The same argument plays out again before Rav Nachman. He too initially tells the woman she is not commanded and therefore cannot demand a *kesubah*.

### Grave Need

She responds: *lo ba'ya hach iteta chutra l'yadah u'mara l'kvurah* — does this woman not need a staff for her hand and a shovel for her grave? She needs someone to support her in old age and to bury her when she dies. Rav Nachman accepts this: *ki ha vadai kafinan* — in that case we will certainly compel the divorce. The story carries a wry edge: one might wonder why *beit din* should have to wait for the woman to articulate this claim herself, rather than assuming it from the outset. The fact that the judges do wait reveals something about how automatic or invisible these basic human needs were in the context of the legal discourse of the time.

---

## Yehudit

### Twin Birth

The *Gemara* introduces the story of Yehudit, the wife of Rabbi Chiya. *Yehudah v'Chizkiyah te'omei havu* — Yehudah and Chizkiyah were twins, one whose formation was completed after nine months and one after seven. This unusual pregnancy — two children forming at different intervals within the womb — caused their mother, Yehudit, *tza'ara d'leidah*, severe pain in childbirth.

### Disguise Query

*Shinatah manah* — she disguised herself, changing her clothes, and came before her husband Rabbi Chiya as if she were a different woman. *Amrah lei: iteta mifkeda apirya v'rivya?* — she asked him: is a woman commanded on *peru u'revu*?

### Chiya Answers No

*Amar lah: lo* — he answered: no, she is not.

### Sterilize

*Azlah ashtaya sama d'akrta* — she went and drank a sterilizing potion, a medical preparation that rendered her infertile, because she could not endure the prospect of more pregnancies like the last one, and her *posek* had told her she was not obligated to do so.

### Matter Revealed

*U'l'sof igli milta* — eventually the matter came to light. Rabbi Chiya discovered what she had done. He said to her: *eichu yaladt li chada karsa achriti* — I wish you had waited to give us one more brood of children. He was, apparently, already *yotzei peru u'revu* twice over: *d'amar mar, Yehudah v'Chizkiyah achi* — Yehudah and Chizkiyah, his sons, were his; and *Pazi v'Tavi achvata* — Pazi and Tavi, his daughters, were also his, apparently another pair of twins. So he had already fulfilled his obligation with two boys and two girls, even according to Beit Shammai's standard. His lament was not that she had deprived him of his *mitzvah* but that they could have had one more cohort of children.

The *halachic* question this story raises is whether it constitutes evidence that a woman who is not commanded on *peru u'revu* may use sterilizing contraception without restriction, leaving the consequences for the husband's fulfillment of his *mitzvah* as his concern alone. The complicating factor here is that the husband was already *yotzei*, so the story cannot straightforwardly be extended to cases where he has not yet fulfilled his obligation. Nevertheless, it is one of the central *Talmudic* sources in discussions of women and birth control.

---

## Half Slave

### Half Free Freed
