*V'amar Rav Acha bar Katina amar Rabbi Yitzchak: ma'aseh b'ishah achat she-chatziyah shifchah v'chatziyah bat chorin v'kafu et rabah v'asa'ah bat chorin* — a case is cited in which a woman who was half slave and half free was compelled by *beit din* to be fully freed. The parallel case involving a man in this status has appeared earlier in *Yevamot*. One might infer from this ruling that the woman must be freed in order to be able to have children, which would in turn suggest she bears some form of obligation regarding *peru u'revu* — otherwise why compel her master to free her?

### Sex Protection

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rejects this inference: *minhag hefker nahagu bah* — the compulsion was not because she had an obligation to have children, but because her intermediate status exposed her to sexual exploitation. A woman who can neither marry a free man nor a slave is left with no legitimate marital option, and as a result was vulnerable to being taken advantage of sexually. *Beit din* intervened to protect her from that situation, not to vindicate a *mitzvah* obligation. One cannot therefore derive from this case that the woman is commanded on *peru u'revu*.

---

## Conclusion

### Bavli View

The consistent weight of the *Bavli* is that the *mitzvah* of *peru u'revu* is not incumbent upon the woman. Case after case — the ruling of Rabbi Ami, the turning away of Rabbi Ami and Rav Assi from the claim that Rabbi Yochanan ruled otherwise, the resolution of the half-slave case by Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak — all point in the same direction.

### Yerushalmi

It should be noted, however, that the *Yerushalmi* treats this question in a more open way, and at least creates the impression that there is a genuine ongoing debate over the woman's obligation, or that the ruling may actually go in the direction of obligating her. The *Bavli* arrives at a firm conclusion; the *Yerushalmi* does not appear to foreclose the question in the same way.

---

## Woman Exempt Why (II)

### Childbirth Risk

One final explanatory approach to the woman's exemption is worth noting, even though it cannot be found in the *Gemara* itself: the *Meshech Chochma*, writing approximately 150 years ago, proposed that since childbirth involves genuine physical risk to the woman's life, the *Torah* could not impose it as a *mitzvah* obligation upon her. A *mitzvah* that mandates a person to undertake life-threatening danger as a positive obligation would be problematic, and therefore the *Torah* leaves *peru u'revu* as a free choice for the woman rather than a commanded act. This explanation resonates with many people, and one hears it cited frequently as though it were a traditional *Talmudic* position; in fact, as best one can determine, it originates with the *Meshech Chochma* and has no earlier source. Whether it captures the *Gemara*'s reasoning is another question entirely.

---

## Conclusion (II)

### Tosafot

Tosafot raises an interesting position that also deserves mention in this context: even if a woman is not technically commanded in *peru u'revu* in its formal sense, she may nonetheless be included in the broader mandate of *lashevet* — settling and populating the world, derived from *lo tohu b'ra'ah lashevet yetzarah*. This is one opinion in one Tosafot, and it is not codified in the *Shulchan Aruch*, but it receives serious attention in *halachic* discussion. The implication is that even without the technical form of the *mitzvah*, the woman partakes in its underlying value — not through strict obligation but through a kind of mandated orientation toward the project of *yishuv ha'olam*. Whether this constitutes *psak halacha* is genuinely debated, but it is an important position to be aware of.

---

## New Topic

### Perek Start

With the conclusion of this *perek* — *hadran alach HaBa Yevimto* — the *Gemara* opens the following chapter, which returns to the domain of *kehunah* and forbidden marriages. The opening *mishnah* establishes the cases: *almana l'Kohen Gadol, gerusha v'chalutza l'Kohen Hedyot* — a widow married to a *Kohen Gadol*, or a divorcée or *chalutza* married to a regular *kohen*. These are marriages that are *halachically* forbidden yet legally binding — the child is not a *mamzer*, but the woman, through the forbidden act of sexual intercourse with a *kohen*, becomes a *chalala*, disqualified from the benefits she would otherwise enjoy by virtue of being a *kohen*'s wife.

### Servants Brought

The *mishnah* addresses a specific scenario within these forbidden marriages: *hechnisa lo avdei melog v'avdei tzon barzel* — the woman brings into the marriage servants who belong to two different legal categories, *nichsei melog* or *nichsei tzon barzel*. The status of those servants with respect to eating *terumah* will turn on which category they belong to, and that in turn depends on how ownership and title are structured in each type.

---

## Property Types

### Tzon Barzel

*Nichsei tzon barzel* — literally "iron sheep property" — refers to property she brings into the marriage where title transfers entirely to the husband. Upon bringing in, say, a parcel of real estate, the deed is effectively signed over to him; he becomes the full legal owner. However, the value of that property is assessed at the time of entry into the marriage, and that assessed value constitutes a debt he owes her: if they divorce or if he predeceases her, she is entitled to recover that sum. This is precisely what is reflected in the standard *ketubah* text, where the groom accepts responsibility for all the property she brings in — *bein b'manei d'levusha bein b'manei d'arsa* — at an assessed value. The groom acquires full title but is liable for the value. With respect to slaves classified as *nichsei tzon barzel*, they thus become his slaves entirely during the marriage.

### Melog

*Nichsei melog* operates differently. The wife retains title to the property — it remains hers — but the husband enjoys the *kinyan peiros*, the right to benefit from the property's fruits, its *usufruct*, during the marriage. Rental income from her land, produce from her fields, the labor of her slaves — all of this goes to him during the marriage. Correspondingly, he bears the obligation to maintain those assets: *af al pi she-hu chayav b'mzonoson* — even though he is responsible for feeding her *melog* slaves. But the title remains hers. If the slaves die, the loss is hers; if they increase in value or produce children, the gain is hers. He has rights over the benefit but not the ownership.

---

## Terumah Rights

### Normal Both

In a normal, permitted marriage between a *kohen* and a woman he may marry — say, a *bat Yisrael* or *bat kohen* — both categories of servants eat *terumah*. The servants classified as *tzon barzel* eat by virtue of him, since title has passed to him and they are his slaves. The servants classified as *melog* eat by virtue of her, since she, as the wife of a *kohen*, is herself entitled to eat *terumah*, and her slaves eat through her.

### Chalala Block

Now the complication: when the marriage is a forbidden one and the woman thereby becomes a *chalala*, she loses her entitlement to eat *terumah*. She cannot eat it because she is now disqualified from the priestly benefits she would otherwise enjoy as a *kohen*'s wife. This disqualification flows from the forbidden union itself.

The question is what happens to her *melog* slaves. The *tzon barzel* slaves are straightforward: title passed to him, they are his slaves, they eat *terumah* through him, and his priestly status is unaffected — a *kohen* never loses his own priestly standing through a forbidden marriage, only the woman is degraded. So the *tzon barzel* slaves eat. But the *melog* slaves are still *her* slaves. Their right to eat *terumah* would have to flow through her, and since she herself cannot eat, the question arises whether they can.

A diagram may help clarify the issue. In a normal case, the *kohen* is at the top, his wife — whether *bat Yisrael* or *bat kohen* — eats *terumah* by virtue of the marriage, the *tzon barzel* slaves eat by virtue of him directly, and the *melog* slaves eat by virtue of her, which is legitimate because she herself is entitled. But when she becomes a *chalala*, she is cut off from *terumah*: she cannot eat it, and therefore the *melog* slaves, whose eating must flow through her, cannot eat either. The *tzon barzel* slaves, eating directly through him, are unaffected.

### Mishnah Rule

The *mishnah* states the rule explicitly: *v'avdei milug lo yochlu bitrumah v'avdei tzon barzel yochlu bitrumah* — the *melog* servants do not eat *terumah* and the *tzon barzel* servants do eat. The *mishnah* then defines each category: *melog* slaves are those for whom *im meisu meisu lah* — if they die, the loss is hers — and *im hosiru hosiru lah* — if they increase in value, the gain is hers — even though *af al pi she-hu chayav b'mzonoson*, he must feed them. *Tzon barzel* slaves are those for whom *im meisu meisu lo* — if they die, the loss is his — and *im hosiru hosiru lo* — if they appreciate, the gain is his — *ho'il v'hu chayav b'achrayusan*, since he bears full responsibility for them. In the normal case of a *bat Yisrael* married to a *kohen*, both types eat *terumah*; in the case of a *bat kohen* married to a *Yisrael*, neither type eats, since she has lost her entitlement upon marrying a non-*kohen* and he never had it.

---

## Why Not Eat

### Indirect Query

The *Gemara* now asks: why should the *melog* slaves not eat *terumah*? The *kohen* does own something in relation to those slaves — he owns the *kinyan peiros*, the right of usufruct. Let the wife be regarded as *his* acquisition in some sense, and the slaves as her acquisition, so that we view the *melog* slaves as an indirect acquisition of his own: *lahavei kekinyano shekana kinyan* — let it be treated as his acquired property that itself has acquired additional property. If the *Gemara* elsewhere extends *terumah* eating rights through indirect ownership chains, why not here?

### Scripture

The *Gemara* answers from the verse: *v'Kohen ki yikneh nefesh kinyan kaspo hu yochal bo* — when a *kohen* acquires a soul through his money, that soul shall eat of it. From this the *Gemara* derives the right of a *kohen*'s wife and slaves to eat *terumah*, and extends it: *kinyano shekana kinyan* — if the *kohen*'s acquisition itself acquires another being, that being may also eat. So a wife can eat, her slaves can eat, his slaves' slaves can eat. The chain of indirect ownership can support *terumah* rights.

### Ochel Principle

But the *Gemara* then formulates a limiting principle: *kol ha'ochel ma'achil, kol she'eino ochel eino ma'achil* — whoever can eat herself enables her dependents to eat; whoever cannot eat herself cannot enable her dependents to eat. The *melog* slaves eat by virtue of the wife. If she can eat — if she is a legitimate *eishes kohen* entitled to *terumah* — then she enables them. If she cannot eat because she has become a *chalala*, the enabling link is broken, and they cannot eat through her.

### Areil Exception

An apparent exception is raised: what about a *kohen* who is an *areil* — uncircumcised, whether due to medical necessity or other reason — or who is *tamei*, ritually impure? Such a *kohen* may not eat *terumah* himself, yet his wife and slaves may still eat. If the principle is that only one who can eat enables others to eat, this seems to be a counterexample: here is one who cannot eat, yet he enables others to eat.

### Temporary vs Permanent

The *Gemara* resolves this by drawing a distinction based on the nature of the disqualification: *hasam pumayu ka'iv lehu* — there, their mouth is hurting them, meaning the impediment is a personal, temporary incapacity, not a fundamental change in status. An *areil* could in principle become circumcised — whatever the practical obstacles — and a *tamei* person can always become *tahor*. The disqualification is situational and reversible. A *chalala*, by contrast, is in a permanent state: the forbidden sexual union has categorically changed her status, and there is no mechanism by which she reverts. A permanent status-change severs the enabling link entirely; a temporary personal incapacity does not.

---

---

# Yevamot 66

## Slaves of Chalalah

### Mishnah Setup

The *mishnah* at the opening of our discussion addresses the status of slaves belonging to a woman married to a *kohen*. Two categories of property are relevant here. *Nichsei milug* refers to property over which the wife retains title, though the husband enjoys its use; *nichsei tzon barzel* refers to property that has been assessed and formally transferred to the husband's ownership, leaving the wife with only a monetary claim. The *mishnah* focuses on the more interesting case — the slaves she owns through *nichsei milug* — and introduces a complicating factor: if she is an *almanah*, a *gerushah*, a *chalutzah*, or an *almanah l'kohen gadol*, she becomes a *chalalah* through the marriage. As a *chalalah*, she cannot eat *terumah* even by virtue of being married to the *kohen*. The question then becomes: what is the status of her slaves? Can they eat *terumah*?

The *mishnah* rules that they cannot. The *gemara* explains that this follows from the principle governing *kinyano she-kanah kinyan* — that is, the wife herself, who is his *kinyan* of a kind and who owns these slaves, is the conduit through which they eat. If she herself cannot eat *terumah*, the question is whether she can nonetheless enable her slaves to eat.

### Eating Through Whom

The *gemara* raises an apparent challenge to the principle that those who eat do so through her. The case involves a *mamzer* — and the word *mamzer* is used here to make the example as extreme as possible, though the core case could involve any non-*kohen*. Suppose a *kohen* has a daughter who marries a *mamzer* or a *yisrael*, and they have a child. That child is not a *kohen* — the father being a non-*kohen* — and would never himself eat *terumah*. Yet if the *kohen* dies and there remains such a grandchild descended from the marriage, the widow may continue eating *terumah* for as long as that grandchild is alive, even after she has collected her *ketubah*. The grandchild enables her to eat even though the grandchild itself cannot eat and is, in an extreme case, even a *mamzer*.

This seems to challenge the rule that only one who eats can enable others to eat. The *gemara* cites this case with the phrase *va-harei mamzer she-ein ochel u-maachil* — "behold, the *mamzer* who does not eat yet enables." Should this not demonstrate that someone who cannot eat can still enable others to?

### Kinyan Ochel

Ravina responds sharply: *kinyan ochel ka'amar* — the relevant principle concerns specifically a *kinyan* that eats. The case of the grandchild enabling the grandmother to eat is categorically different: the grandmother eats not because the grandchild "enables" her in the technical sense relevant to property ownership, but because the grandchild's existence keeps her connected to the *kohen*'s family. That is a distinct mechanism entirely. The operative principle for our *mishnah* remains: *kinyan ochel ma'achil, kinyan she'eino ochel eino ma'achil* — only a *kinyan* that itself eats can feed others. Since the wife is called a *kinyan* in this context, and since she cannot eat *terumah* as a *chalalah*, her slaves cannot eat through her. This is the first explanation of the *mishnah*.

### Rava's Gezerah

Rava offers a second explanation. He acknowledges that in principle, the slaves of the *chalalah* ought to be entitled to eat *terumah*, because indirectly they are connected to the *kohen* and their eating flows through him rather than purely through her. *Mide'oraisa me'achlei* — by Torah law they would be permitted to eat. However, *verabbanan hu de-gazru behu* — the Rabbis enacted a prohibition against their eating in this case, as an incentive to dissolution of the forbidden marriage.

The logic is as follows: because the *kohen* is married to a *gerushah*, *chalutza*, or the *kohen gadol* to an *almanah*, a situation the Rabbis find deeply objectionable, they sought to create pressure toward divorce. The wife can be expected to say: *ani eini ochelet* — I myself cannot eat *terumah*; *avadai einam ochlim* — my slaves cannot eat *terumah*. She is, as it were, like a *zonah* to him, *zonah hi etzlo* — not fully a wife in the sense of enjoying the privileges of wifehood. This sense of exclusion and non-belonging, says Rava, was designed by the Rabbis — *va'ati lefuka* — to bring about a divorce. The slaves could in principle eat; the Rabbis withheld that entitlement as a form of social and legal pressure.

### Rav Ashi's Concern

Rav Ashi agrees with the premise that the slaves could in principle eat, but offers a different reason for the rabbinic prohibition: *gezerah shema ta'achilah achar misah* — a decree lest she continue feeding them *terumah* even after the *kohen* dies. Her entitlement to feed them *terumah* is entirely contingent on her husband's status; once he dies, that entitlement ceases. If we permit her to feed them during the marriage, we fear she will continue the practice after his death.

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: that concern should apply universally. Every Jewish woman married to a *kohen* might continue feeding her slaves *terumah* after his death — should we therefore prohibit all such wives from feeding their slaves? Rav Ashi withdraws that formulation and offers a refined version.

### Rav Ashi's Concern

*Ela amar Rav Ashi: be-almanah kohenes* — the particular case that generates a real risk is when the woman married to the *kohen gadol* is herself a *bas kohen*, a daughter of a *kohen*. Here is the chain of reasoning she might follow after her husband dies: *me'ikara achli bi-terumah debei nasha* — originally, my slaves ate *terumah* because of my father's house, by virtue of the fact that I was a *bas kohen*. Then *inseiva le-hai kohen* — I married this *kohen*, *achli bi-terumah de-gavrai* — and they continued eating *terumah* by virtue of my husband. Now that my husband has died, she may reason, *hadri leh milsa ke-me'ikara* — things return to their original state and my slaves may continue eating *terumah* as they did before.

The flaw in this reasoning is that she may be unaware — *delo yade'a* — that in the course of this marriage she became a *chalalah*. *De-me'ikara lo shavisah le-nafshah chalalah* — originally, when the slaves ate by virtue of her father's house, she was not yet a *chalalah*. *Hashta shavisah nafshah chalalah* — but now, by virtue of this forbidden marriage, she is a *chalalah*, and therefore her slaves cannot eat even after her husband dies. The concern, then, is not general but specific: she will assume she may revert to her original entitlement without recognizing that the marriage itself permanently altered her status.

### Almanah Kohenes

The *gemara* asks: this reasoning accounts for the case of the *almanah kohenes*, the *bas kohen* who married the *kohen gadol*. But what of the *almanah bas yisrael* — the woman who is not a *bas kohen*? She has no prior entitlement from her father's house; why should the same prohibition apply to her? The *gemara* answers: *be-manusa lo pligi rabbanan* — where there is a specific case that genuinely warrants the decree, the Rabbis did not distinguish among cases. *O lo plug* — they enacted a uniform prohibition across all these situations rather than creating distinctions that might be confused in practice.

The upshot is that we have two general approaches. The first, associated with Ravina, is that the slaves eat only through the wife, and since she cannot eat, they cannot either — this is the *de'oraisa* position. The second, associated with Rava and Rav Ashi, acknowledges that in principle the slaves eat through the *kohen*, but a rabbinic *gezerah* was imposed for the reasons described. In either case the practical ruling is that the slaves of a *chalalah* do not eat *terumah*.

---

## Tzon Barzel Debate

### Property Assessment

The *gemara* introduces a new topic with the word *itmar* — "it was stated" — signaling an *amoraic* dispute. The subject is *nichsei tzon barzel*: property a woman brings into the marriage whose value is formally assessed — *shum* — and recorded in the *ketubah*. The *ketubah* lists the items and assigns them a total monetary value, and the husband accepts full financial responsibility for that amount. If the property appreciates, he benefits; if it depreciates or is lost, he bears the loss. What the wife is guaranteed is the return of the assessed monetary value.

The practical question arises when the husband dies or the marriage is dissolved and the actual property is still available — the original field, the original slaves, the original vessels. Can the wife demand the return of the specific items? Or has the husband taken absolute title, leaving her only a monetary claim against the estate?

### Title vs. Debt

This is precisely the dispute between Rav Yehuda and Rav Ami. Rav Yehuda rules *hadin immah* — the law is with her; she may demand the return of the specific property. Rav Ami rules *hadin immo* — the law is with him; she holds only a monetary debt and cannot compel return of the items themselves.

Rav Yehuda's reasoning is formulated as *mishum shevach beis aviha* — on account of the benefit of her father's house. This is the property that came with her from her father as a dowry; she ought to be entitled to reclaim it. Rav Ami reasons from the *mishnah* itself, which states explicitly regarding *nichsei tzon barzel*: *im mesu mesu lo, ve-im hokiru hokiru lo* — if they die, it is his loss; if they appreciate, it is his gain. This language, he argues, demonstrates that the property entered his possession absolutely, *bi-rshusei kayami* — it stands in his domain, *u-ch'didei damu* — and is treated as fully his.

### Rental Comparison

The *gemara* attempts to test whether formal liability (*chiyuv achrayus*) alone is sufficient to give a person such a relationship to property that the property's slaves could eat *terumah* on his account — without necessarily establishing outright ownership. If we take seriously the claim that *chayav be-achrayusan* establishes this relationship without full title, we should be able to find a parallel. The *gemara* brings a *mishnah*: a *yisrael* who rents a cow from a *kohen* may feed it *terumah* fodder, because the cow remains the *kohen*'s and he has the relevant interest in it. But a *kohen* who rents a cow from a *yisrael* — even though *mezonoseha alav*, he is responsible for feeding it and bears liability for certain losses — nevertheless *lo ya'achilennah karshinei terumah*, he may not feed it *terumah* fodder. The cow is still the *yisrael*'s. Rental liability is simply insufficient to confer the kind of interest that enables feeding *terumah*.

### Middle Zone

The *gemara* responds that the husband's relationship to the *tzon barzel* property is not comparable to a renter's. A renter bears liability only for theft and loss; he is not responsible for depreciation due to market changes, normal wear, or reduction in market value. The *tzon barzel* relationship is categorically different: no matter what happens — whether the market changes, whether the property deteriorates through ordinary use, whether the decrease is anyone's fault or not — the husband must restore the full assessed value. Conversely, any increase in value belongs entirely to him.

This sliding scale of liability raises the question acutely. The *gemara* is exploring whether there exists a legal middle zone: the wife retains formal title, but the husband has such comprehensive rights and obligations with respect to the property — all gains his, all losses his regardless of fault — that the slaves can eat *terumah* through his relationship to them, even without his having acquired outright ownership. The *gemara* presses: *v'chol heicha de-chayav be-achrayusan achli bi-terumah?* — does any degree of comprehensive liability trigger the right to eat? The rental cases show low-level liability is insufficient. The question is whether this uniquely intensive relationship suffices to permit *terumah* eating without constituting full ownership.

### Two Braitot

Rava and Rav Yosef were sitting together at the conclusion of Rav Nachman's *drasha*, and in their discussion they noted that the sources appear to point in both directions. One *braita* supports Rav Ami: *avdei tzon barzel yotzin be-shen va-ayin la-ish, aval lo la-ishah* — slaves brought in as *tzon barzel* go free if the husband knocks out their eye or tooth, but not if the wife does the same. This strongly implies the husband is considered their master — he is the one whose act of violence triggers the law of *shen va-ayin*. If she retained genuine title, why would her striking not also trigger their release?

The second *braita* supports Rav Yehuda: *ha-machneses shum le-ba'alah im ratza ba'al limkor lo yimkor* — if a wife brings in assessed property and the husband wishes to sell it, he may not do so. If he held absolute title, he would plainly be entitled to sell his own property. The fact that he cannot sell it — and that the *ma'aseh* before Rabban Gamliel affirmed that any such sale is void and the husband must retrieve the property from the purchasers — demonstrates that she retains rights in the objects themselves, not merely a monetary claim.

---

## Rava's Ruling

### She Retrieves

Rava, citing Rav Nachman, rules: *halacha ke-Rav Yehuda* — the law follows Rav Yehuda. The wife is entitled to retrieve the specific property she brought in. The *braita* showing that the husband cannot sell the property without her consent was evidently persuasive.

### Shen V'Ayin

Rava acknowledges the counter-*braita*, which seemed to prove Rav Ami's position by stating that only the husband's violence triggers the slave's freedom. He addresses this directly: *af al gav de-tanya ke-vassa de-Rabbi Ami, mistabra ta'ama de-Rav Yehuda mishum shevach beis aviha* — even though the *braita* appears to favor Rav Ami, the underlying rationale of Rav Yehuda's position is more compelling, because this property came from her father's house and she ought to be entitled to reclaim it. Tosafot, for their part, find the *shen va-ayin braita* less than a decisive proof for Rav Ami in any case: just as the slaves eat *terumah* by virtue of the husband's comprehensive relationship to them, so too the *shen va-ayin* law might operate through him without that implying full title.

### Cloak Story

A *ma'aseh* illustrates the practical limits of Rav Yehuda's ruling. A woman brought into her marriage a fine wool cloak as part of her *nichsei tzon barzel*, recorded in her *ketubah*. Her husband died. Before she had the opportunity to claim the cloak, the orphans seized it and spread it over the dead body, using it as a shroud. Once an object is designated and used as a shroud for a deceased, it becomes *assur be-hana'ah* — prohibited from benefit.

Rava ruled: *kanya misna* — the dead body acquires it. The cloak has changed its identity and she loses any right to that specific object, though she remains entitled to its monetary value from the estate. A grandson of Rava challenged: do we not rule like Rav Yehuda, that the property is hers? If so, the orphans had no right to use her property as a shroud, and their doing so should not affect its status. The response is decisive.

### Requires Collection

The reply: *mi lo modeh Rabbi Yehuda de-mechusar gubyanya?* — even Rav Yehuda concedes that the property requires active collection before it reverts to her control. Rav Yehuda's ruling does not mean that the property is automatically, at every moment, fully under her title and control. He holds that she has a right to reclaim it — but that right must be exercised; it must be collected. *De-kivun de-mechusar gubyanya bi-rshusei kai* — since it still requires collection, it remains under the control of the husband's heirs.

The conceptual picture that emerges is subtle: she may hold some form of title, or she may hold only a superior claim of retrieval, but in neither case does the property automatically revert to her domain upon the husband's death. Until she acts to collect it, it remains under the heirs' effective control. And because of that, the heirs were in a position to use it as a shroud, triggering *asur be-hana'ah* and extinguishing her specific rights in that object.

Rava's reasoning invokes his broader principle: *hekdesh, chametz, u-shichrur motzi'in mi-yedei shibud* — that sanctification of property (*hekdesh*), the transformation of *chametz* during Passover into something *assur be-hana'ah*, and the emancipation of a slave all operate to dissolve existing liens or encumbrances upon property by fundamentally transforming the identity of the object. Here, using the cloak as a shroud similarly transforms its identity — just as *chametz* that becomes forbidden during Passover loses its character as encumbered property, so too this cloak, once assigned to the dead, loses whatever lien or claim she held over it.

---

## Appreciation Cases

### Two Vessels

Rav Yehuda presents the following scenario at the top of 67a: a wife brings into the marriage two vessels assessed at one thousand *zuz*. By the time of divorce or the husband's death, they have appreciated and are now worth two thousand.

### Shevach Rule

The ruling is: *echad notalah bi-chtuvtasah* — she takes one vessel back as part of her *ketubah* entitlement. *Ve-echad nosenet damim ve-notalah mipnei shevach beis aviha* — and the second vessel she is also entitled to demand, paying the difference in value, on account of *shevach beis aviha*, the benefit of her father's house.

The *gemara* asks: what is the novelty here? Didn't Rav Yehuda already establish that she can retrieve her property? The answer: one might have thought that her right to retrieve extends only up to the original assessed value — that is, she can demand the vessels back insofar as they satisfy her monetary entitlement, but not insofar as they have appreciated beyond that value. Perhaps she should be entitled to only one of the two vessels, since one is now worth the full original thousand. The ruling teaches that *mipnei shevach beis aviha* she is entitled to retrieve both the objects she brought in and to pay the appreciated difference — not merely to receive the monetary equivalent. The same logic applies in reverse: if the property has lost value, she retrieves all of it and the estate compensates her for the shortfall.

---

## Fetus & Eating

### Mishnah Setup

The *mishnah* turns to a related but distinct problem. A *bas yisrael* — a non-*kohen* woman — was married to a *kohen*, and the *kohen* dies leaving her pregnant. When a *kohen* dies, the general rule is that if he leaves behind a child from that marriage, the widow continues to eat *terumah* through the child. But here the child is not yet born. What is the status of the slaves?

The *mishnah* rules *lo yokhlu avadeha bi-terumah mipnei chelko shel ubar* — the slaves may not eat *terumah* on account of the portion of the *ubar* (the fetus). The reasoning requires unpacking. The *kohen* died leaving his estate to his heirs. If he left sons, those sons are the heirs and are co-owners of the slaves; the slaves eat *terumah* by virtue of those sons. But here, the *ubar* is among the heirs — indeed, if the child is born and is male, he will inherit a portion. The *ubar* is thus a partial owner of the slaves. Since the *ubar* cannot yet cause the slaves to eat *terumah* — he is unborn — his partial ownership prevents the slaves from eating, because that portion of the slaves that is owned by him is not entitled to eat. Ten percent owned by the *ubar* is not entitled; and since the slaves are partially owned by one who cannot enable their eating, none of them may eat.

Furthermore, the *mishnah* notes that the *ubar* also does not enable his mother to eat: she too cannot eat *terumah* on account of an unborn child. This produces the striking result that the *ubar* *posel* — he disqualifies — and yet *eino ma'achil* — he does not feed. He is the worst of both legal worlds: his existence as a partial owner creates a disqualification, but his unborn status prevents him from conferring any entitlement.

### Rabbi Yosi

*Divrei Rabbi Yosi* — this is the ruling of Rabbi Yosi. Rabbi Yosi formulates the principle: *ha-ubar posel ve-eino ma'achil* — the fetus invalidates and does not feed. He prevents the slaves from eating by virtue of his partial ownership, while himself being unable to enable anyone to eat.

### Kohenes Challenge

The Sages pose a challenge to Rabbi Yosi: *me'achar she-eidasta lanu al bas yisrael le-kohen, af bas kohen le-kohen* — if this is true when the mother is a *bas yisrael* married to a *kohen*, the same logic should apply equally when the mother is a *bas kohen* married to a *kohen*. Why would the mother's lineage matter? The fetus still holds a portion of the estate and is still unborn. The Sages appear to be making the point that according to Rabbi Yosi's reasoning, the same ruling should hold in both cases.

### Two Theories

The *gemara* raises a fundamental question about what Rabbi Yosi's reasoning actually is. Two possible explanations are offered. The first — associated with Rabba — is: *ta'ama de-Rabbi Yosi mishum de-kasavar ubar be-mei zarah zar hu* — Rabbi Yosi's reason is that the fetus, while still in the womb of a non-*kohen* mother, is considered a *zar*, a non-*kohen*. He has a portion of the estate, but because his mother is not a *kohen* and he has not yet achieved independent identity, he is classified as a *zar*. The slaves thus have a partial *zar*-owner, and therefore cannot eat. On this reading, the critical variable is the mother's status, not the fact of being unborn.

The second explanation — associated with Rav Yosef — is: *yalud ma'achil, she-eino yalud eino ma'achil* — one who is born enables feeding; one who is not yet born does not enable feeding. On this reading, it has nothing to do with the mother being a non-*kohen*. Even if the mother were a *bas kohen*, the result would be identical: being unborn is itself the disqualifying factor.

### No Ruling

The *nafka mina* between these two theories is precisely the case of an *ubar* whose mother is a *bas kohen*. On Rabba's reading, since the mother is a *kohen*, the *ubar* is not a *zar*, and therefore his partial ownership creates no problem — the slaves could eat. On Rav Yosef's reading, being unborn is categorically disqualifying regardless of the mother's identity, so the result would be identical: the slaves cannot eat.

The *braita* presses Rabbi Yosi directly on this: *zo shamati ve-zo lo shamati* — this I have received as a tradition, and that I have not. He has a tradition that a *bas yisrael*'s slaves cannot eat on account of the *ubar*; whether the same applies when the mother is a *bas kohen*, he declines to rule. If his reasoning were simply that an unborn person cannot enable feeding regardless of the mother's identity, then the Sages' challenge would be unanswerable and he would have had to respond in kind. His silence on the *bas kohen* case suggests that his actual reasoning was the first — that the relevant factor is the *ubar*'s status as a *zar* by virtue of his mother being a *bas yisrael*. But this is not resolved definitively, and the *gemara* leaves the ambiguity in place.

---

## Fetus Inheritance

### Fetus Title

The *gemara* now examines the deeper theoretical issue beneath the surface of the *mishnah*: does a fetus acquire title to an inheritance before birth? Rabbi Yosi's ruling in the *mishnah* rests on the premise that the *ubar* already holds a portion of the estate — that he is, in some sense, already a partial heir from the moment of his father's death. This is assumption number one. Assumption number two is that the *ubar*, despite holding this partial title, cannot cause slaves to eat *terumah* because he is unborn.

The *chachamim* who challenge Rabbi Yosi appear to reject assumption number one entirely. Their position is that *yesh lo banim, okhlin mishum banim* — if the deceased left sons, the slaves eat through those sons; *ein lo banim, okhlin mishum achim* — if there are no sons, the slaves eat through the brothers. In other words, the *ubar* is simply not counted until he is born. Before birth, the existing relatives — sons, brothers, or any *mishpachah* — are treated as the heirs for purposes of determining who can enable *terumah* eating. The *ubar* creates no disruption because he has, in the view of the *chachamim*, no present title to the estate.

This produces a sharp disagreement: Rabbi Yosi holds that the *ubar* acquires a portion of the inheritance immediately upon his father's death, even before birth. The *chachamim* hold that no such acquisition occurs until birth. The *gemara* asks whether Shmuel, who reports Rabbi Yosi's position, personally agrees with it or merely reports it neutrally.

### Shmuel's Rule

The answer emerges from Shmuel's dramatic declaration to Rav Chana Bagdata — identified by Rashi as either a master of *aggadah* or, more likely given the name, a resident of Baghdad in Babylonia: *puk ayti li bei asara* — go and bring me a group of ten people — *ve-eima lach be-anpaihu* — and I will declare publicly before them: *ha-mezakeh le-ubar kanah* — one who transfers title to a fetus, the fetus acquires it. This is not a quiet, tentative ruling; Shmuel wants to make a public declaration of principle. A fetus can receive a transfer of title — *da'at acheret makneh oto*, through the mechanism of another person acting on its behalf — and presumably, if it can receive a transfer, it also inherits by operation of law while still unborn. This aligns Shmuel clearly with Rabbi Yosi on assumption number one.

### Shmuel vs. Sages

The *gemara* then revisits the phrase *zu divrei Rabbi Yosi* — "this is the position of Rabbi Yosi" — which might have implied that Shmuel was merely reporting a minority view without endorsing it. In light of Shmuel's public declaration, the *gemara* corrects course: *ela zu u-sevira lei* — it means both "this is Rabbi Yosi's position" and "this is how Shmuel himself holds." Shmuel endorses Rabbi Yosi's first principle that the *ubar* acquires a portion of the inheritance before birth. He notes, however, that *chachamim* disagree with this, so students of the tradition should be aware that the matter is not uncontested.

### Shemaya Testimony

The *gemara* introduces a report: Rabbi Zakai testified that Rabbi Yosi transmitted this ruling *mipi Shemaya ve-Avtalyon* — in the name of Shemaya and Avtalyon. This clarifies an apparent anachronism: Rabbi Yosi did not testify *before* the *tanna'im* of earlier generations but rather passed on a tradition *in their name*. The question then becomes whether this transmission constitutes a definitive ruling. *Ve-hodu lo* — and they conceded to him, or agreed that his reasoning made sense.

Rav Ashi clarifies the force of that concession: *mi katani de-kiblu?* — the text does not say they *accepted* his position. *Ve-hodu lo katani* — it says they *conceded* or acknowledged that the reasoning was compelling. *De-mistabra ta'ameih* — it made great sense to them. But acknowledging that an argument is compelling is not the same as issuing a formal ruling in its favor. The *chachamim* were impressed but did not formally commit to the position. This leaves the debate in a nuanced state: Shmuel holds like Rabbi Yosi; the *chachamim* of the *mishnah* appear to disagree; and even the great authorities of earlier generations, while finding the argument persuasive, stopped short of a definitive acceptance.

---

## Eating Scenarios

### Sons Present

The *gemara* now presents a systematic *braita* working through the various scenarios. The first case: *heniah banim* — the *kohen* dies leaving sons. *Elu va-elu okhlin* — both these slaves and those slaves eat *terumah*. The *nichsei tzon barzel* slaves eat because they are part of the estate now inherited by the sons. The *nichsei milug* slaves eat because the wife herself is entitled to eat *terumah* — there are living children from the marriage who keep her connected to the *kohen*'s family, and through her the slaves eat.

### Only Pregnancy

The second case: *heniah meuberet* — he leaves her pregnant, with no born children. *Elu va-elu einan okhlin* — neither set of slaves may eat. This is the teaching of the *mishnah* itself, following Rabbi Yosi. The wife cannot eat *terumah* through an unborn child, so her *milug* slaves cannot eat through her. And the *tzon barzel* slaves are now partially owned by the *ubar*, who cannot enable them to eat. *Ubar posel ve-eino ma'achil*.

### Sons & Pregnancy

The third and most complex case: *heniah banim ve-heniah meuberet* — the *kohen* leaves both born sons and a pregnant wife. *Avdei melog okhlin ke-derekh she-hi okhelet* — the *milug* slaves eat, just as the wife herself eats. Since there are born children from the marriage, she is entitled to eat *terumah*, and they eat through her. *Avdei tzon barzel lo yokhlu mipnei chelko shel ubar* — but the *tzon barzel* slaves may not eat, because the *ubar*'s partial ownership of the estate prevents them. The *ubar* thus *posel* — he disqualifies the *tzon barzel* slaves — while the born sons enable the wife and through her the *milug* slaves. The *ubar* does not enable anything; he only disqualifies. *Divrei Rabbi Yosi* — this is Rabbi Yosi's position.

### Daughter vs. Son

Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yosi reports a position *mishum aviv* — in his father's name: *ha-bat ma'achelet, ha-ben eino ma'achil* — the daughter enables feeding but the son does not. The *gemara* leaves this to be unpacked further.

### Shimon View

Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai offers a further position: *zekharim yokhlu kullan, nekeivot lo yokhlu, shema yimatzei ubar zeh* — males eat, all of them, but females do not, out of concern that this *ubar* may turn out to be male. The discussion of these positions and their underlying reasoning extends into the following *daf*, where we will continue the analysis tomorrow.

---

---

# Yevamot 66b

## Slaves & Chalalah

### Setup: Property Types

The *mishnah* on this *daf* addresses the question of what happens to the slaves of a woman married to a *kohen* with respect to the eating of *terumah*. Two categories of property require distinction from the outset. The first is *nichsei milug*: property that the wife retains legal title to, though the husband enjoys its use. The second is *nichsei tzon barzel*: property whose title transfers to the husband, in exchange for which he bears all losses and retains all gains, while remaining obligated to return the assessed value upon divorce or death.

The *mishnah* focuses on the more conceptually interesting category, *nichsei milug*, the slaves she owns. The case involves a woman who, by virtue of her marriage to a *kohen* — whether as a *gerusha* or *chalutzah* married to an ordinary *kohen*, or as an *almanah* married to a *kohen gadol* — becomes a *chalalah*. The very act of marital relations in a forbidden union renders her a *chalalah*, disqualified from eating *terumah*. The question is: what about her slaves? They are, in some sense, connected to the *kohen* household. May they eat *terumah*?

The *mishnah* rules that they may not. The *gemara* explains by invoking the principle *kinyano shekanah kinyan* — a formulation that, while uncomfortable in its description of the wife as a *kinyan*, refers to the husband's legal relationship to her and through her to what she owns. The slaves, in turn, are eating by virtue of her, and if she cannot eat — being a *chalalah* — then she cannot, as it were, confer that right upon her slaves.

### Kinyan Ochel Maachil

The *gemara* challenges this straightforward explanation. If the reason the slaves can eat *terumah* is traced back through the wife, consider the case of a *mamzer* who cannot himself eat *terumah* yet can enable his grandmother to eat. The scenario is this: a *kohen* dies leaving a daughter, who has since married a *mamzer* or even an ordinary *Yisrael*. Their child, not being a *kohen*, cannot eat *terumah*. Yet as long as that grandchild is alive, the grandmother — the original wife of the *kohen* — may continue eating *terumah* by virtue of the connection maintained through her child or grandchild, even if that descendant could never eat *terumah* himself. Here, then, is someone who cannot eat yet enables another to eat. Does the same logic not apply to the wife's slaves?

Ravina replies that these two cases are categorically different. The grandmother eats by virtue of a descendant who traces back to the *kohen* lineage — a separate and independent principle. The question in the *mishnah* concerns eating by virtue of a *kinyan*, specifically the rule *kinyan ochel maachil*: only a *kinyan* that eats can feed. A *kinyan* that cannot itself eat — here, the wife who is a *chalalah* — cannot enable those she owns to eat. That is the first explanation of the *mishnah*.

### Rava's Gezeira

Rava offers a second approach. In truth, *mid'raisa* — on the level of Torah law — the slaves could eat. They are connected to the *kohen* and, independent of the wife's personal disqualification, they retain a basis for eating *terumah* through him. However, the rabbis instituted a *gezeira* preventing the slaves from eating in this case. The reasoning is social and corrective: the *kohen* finds himself in a forbidden union, married to a woman who should not have entered into this marriage with him. By disallowing the slaves from eating, the rabbis create pressure. The wife says: I cannot eat *terumah*, my slaves cannot eat *terumah* — *zona hi etzlo*, I am like a stranger to him, excluded from the very benefits of his priestly status. This discontent, the rabbis reasoned, would motivate the couple to dissolve the marriage.

### Rav Ashi: Gezeira

Rav Ashi also agrees in principle that the slaves could eat, but offers a different rationale for the rabbinic prohibition. The *gezeira* is *shema ta'achil achar misa* — lest she continue feeding the slaves *terumah* even after the *kohen* dies. Having become accustomed to feeding them during the marriage, she might simply continue the practice after his death, when she is no longer entitled to do so.

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: by that logic, why should any *bat Yisrael* married to a *kohen* be permitted to feed her slaves *terumah*? She, too, might continue after his death. Should we not decree against her as well? This objection effectively forces Rav Ashi to refine his position.

### Almanah Kohenet Case

The concern, says Rav Ashi, is specific to the case of an *almanah* married to a *kohen gadol* who is herself a *bat kohen*. Here is where the *gezeira* finds its most compelling foothold. Such a woman, upon the *kohen gadol*'s death, could reason as follows: *me'ikara achli bitruma devei nasha* — originally, my slaves ate *terumah* by virtue of my father's household, because I was a *bat kohen*. Then, when I married this *kohen gadol*, they continued eating by virtue of my husband. Now that he has died, they should revert to their original status and continue eating on account of my being a *bat kohen*.

What she fails to realize is that by entering into the forbidden union — as an *almanah* who had relations with a *kohen gadol* — she became a *chalalah*. She is no longer a *bat kohen* in the relevant legal sense. Her slaves cannot eat by virtue of her father's household anymore, because that status has been forfeited. The fear is that she will not appreciate this transformation and will permit the slaves to eat *terumah* erroneously after his death. The *gezeira* addresses precisely this case.

### Uniform Gezeira

The *gemara* then asks: very well, the concern makes sense when the wife is an *almanah kohenet*, but why does the *mishnah* apply this ruling even when she is a *bat Yisrael* — an ordinary Jewess who has no such parallel status to return to? The *gemara* answers with the principle *lo plug rabanan* — the rabbis did not differentiate within a single category. Since the *gezeira* was necessary for the case of the *almanah kohenet*, the rabbis applied it uniformly to all cases of *almanah*, without distinguishing between those who are daughters of *kohanim* and those who are not. This avoids confusion and ensures consistent application of the rule.

To summarize: two explanatory frameworks emerge. The first, Ravina's, holds that the slaves eat only by virtue of the wife, and since she is a *chalalah* and cannot eat, she cannot extend that right — *kinyan ochel maachil*. The second, shared by Rava and Rav Ashi, holds that in principle the slaves could eat through the *kohen*, but a rabbinic *gezeira* overrides this, whether to discourage the forbidden marriage or to prevent erroneous feeding after the husband's death.

---

## Tzon Barzel Ownership

### The Dispute

The *gemara* now takes up a distinct but related question about *nichsei tzon barzel*. When a woman brings assessed property into the marriage — the husband enters the value into the *ketubah*, accepting full financial responsibility — and the marriage subsequently ends through divorce or death, what exactly is she entitled to recover? She assessed, say, a set of vessels at one thousand *zuz*. Those vessels are still extant. Does she retrieve the vessels themselves, or only their assessed monetary value?

The wife says: *keli ani notelet* — I take my vessels. The husband says: *damim ani noten* — I owe you money, not objects. The dispute is whether title fundamentally transferred to the husband upon the bringing in of the dowry, leaving her only a creditor's claim, or whether she retained some form of ownership such that she may demand the objects back.

### Rav Yehuda Position

Rav Yehuda rules *hadin imah* — the law favors the wife. She is entitled to retrieve the actual objects. His reasoning is *mishum shevach beit aviha* — on account of the benefit, or honor, of her father's house. This is the property she received from her family, and she is entitled to reclaim it. It is admittedly not a purely technical legal argument — it is an appeal to equitable principle — but it is the position Rav Yehuda maintains.

### Rav Ami Position

Rav Ami rules *hadin imo* — the law favors the husband. His reasoning flows from the language of the *mishnah* itself: *im mesu mesu lo v'im hosiru hosiru lo* — if the property dies or is lost, the loss is his; if it increases in value, the gain is his. This, says Rav Ami, demonstrates conclusively that title has transferred. He bears all risk and receives all benefit. The property is therefore his, and she is merely a creditor for its assessed value.

### Renting Analogy Test

The *gemara* attempts to probe the logic by noting the *mishnah*'s further language: *v'hoil v'chayav b'achrayusan yochalu* — and since he is responsible for them, the slaves eat *terumah*. This seems to confirm both that the slaves belong to him and that his responsibility is characteristic of ownership. But does mere responsibility, *achrayus*, suffice to allow slaves to eat *terumah* even if they are not technically owned by the *kohen*?

A *baraita* is introduced: a *Yisrael* who rents a cow from a *kohen* — the cow remains the *kohen*'s, and the renter may feed it animal fodder of *terumah*. Conversely, a *kohen* who rents a cow from a *Yisrael*, even though he is responsible for feeding it and bears the liability of a renter, may not feed it *terumah*, because it remains the *Yisrael*'s cow. Mere *achrayus* of the renter's level does not confer the right to eat *terumah*.

The *gemara* responds: there are degrees of *achrayus*, and rental is a low degree. A renter is liable for theft and loss, but not for unavoidable accident, not for the animal becoming thinner through natural attrition, and not for a decline in market value. By contrast, the husband who takes in *nichsei tzon barzel* is responsible for the full assessed value regardless of fault, market changes, or any other cause. If the slaves were worth one thousand when they entered the marriage and the market drops so they are now worth five hundred at divorce, he must nonetheless restore the full thousand. This degree of *achrayus* is qualitatively different — it resembles ownership far more than rental does.

### Responsibility vs. Owner…

The *gemara* is therefore pressed: perhaps this extraordinary level of responsibility is tantamount to ownership after all, which would support Rav Ami. But it resists this conclusion. The *baraita* itself offers a parallel case that illuminates the middle ground. If a *Yisrael* assesses a cow from a *kohen* and takes full responsibility to return its assessed value regardless of circumstance, he may not feed it *terumah* — the cow remains the *kohen*'s. Conversely, if a *kohen* does the same from a *Yisrael* — undertakes full assessed-value responsibility — he may feed it *terumah*, even though technically speaking the cow has not been transferred in title. This suggests that a sufficiently high level of *achrayus* can ground the right to eat *terumah* without constituting full legal ownership. Applying this to the dowry slaves: the husband's extraordinary responsibility may suffice for the slaves to eat *terumah*, while the wife technically retains her entitlement to reclaim the objects themselves.

Rabbah and Rav Yosef were present at the end of one of Rav Nachman's public lectures and remarked that there exists *baraita* support for both positions. In favor of Rav Ami: *avdei tzon barzel yotzin b'shen v'ayin la'ish aval lo l'isha* — if the husband knocks out the eye or tooth of a *tzon barzel* slave, the slave goes free, because the husband is treated as the slave's master; but if the wife does the same, the slave does not go free, suggesting the husband holds full title. In favor of Rav Yehuda: if the husband wishes to sell the dowry property, he may not. This is a powerful indication that she retains rights over the property that transcend a mere creditor's claim. Indeed, even property that the husband himself contributed to her dowry cannot be sold by him unilaterally. This case came before Rabban Gamliel, who voided the sale and ordered restitution from the buyers.

### Baraita: No Sale Right

The force of this *baraita* — that neither party may sell the dowry property without mutual consent, and that Rabban Gamliel enforced this rule against buyers — strongly supports Rav Yehuda's position. If he held full title and merely owed a monetary debt, there would be no legal basis to void his sale.

### Rava's Ruling

Rava rules in accordance with Rav Yehuda: *halacha k'Rav Yehuda* — she is entitled to retrieve the actual property she brought in. The *baraita* concerning the prohibition on sale was evidently persuasive, and Rava adds that the reasoning *mishum shevach beit aviha* — the property of her father's house — supports giving her the right to reclaim what she brought in, even though the *baraita* supporting Rav Ami regarding *shen v'ayin* presented a counterweight. As Tosafot notes, even if the slaves technically belong to her, it is conceivable that the *kohen*'s extensive rights over them — rights sufficient for them to eat *terumah* on his account — could also ground the *shen v'ayin* rule without establishing full title in him. Rava thus dismisses that *baraita* as a conclusive proof for Rav Ami and rules for Rav Yehuda.

### Shroud Story

A practical story follows. A woman brought a fine wool cloak into her marriage as part of her *tzon barzel* dowry. The husband died. Before she had an opportunity to act, the orphans — the husband's heirs — took the cloak and used it as a shroud for the deceased. Something designated and used as a shroud for a corpse is *asur b'hana'ah* — forbidden for any benefit.

Rava rules: *kanye misna* — the dead body has, as it were, acquired it. Its status has been permanently transformed. While the wife retains her monetary claim against the estate for the assessed value of the cloak, she loses any right to reclaim this particular object.

### Collection Requirement

This ruling prompted a sharp question from Nemchi, the grandson of Rav Yosef the son of Rava, to Rav Kahana: but do we not rule like Rav Yehuda that she is entitled to retrieve the objects? If so, the cloak was hers. The orphans had no right to use her property as a shroud, and their doing so should not affect her claim.

Rav Kahana responded: *mi lo modei Rabbi Yehuda demchusar guvaina* — even Rav Yehuda concedes that her entitlement requires actual collection. The right to reclaim exists, but it has not yet been exercised. Until she actively retrieves the object, it remains under the husband's — or now the heirs' — control. *Dekeivan demchusar guvaina birshuseih kai* — since it has not yet been collected, it stands in his domain. The heirs are therefore in a position to use it, and their doing so — transforming it into a shroud, rendering it *asur b'hana'ah* — removes her practical rights in this object, even if she is technically owed its value.

This connects to a broader principle that Rava articulates: *hekdesh chametz veshichrur motzi'in miyedei shibbud* — sanctification, *chametz* on Passover, and manumission of a slave are three situations where a change in the object's essential identity dissolves an existing lien or claim. Here, the transformation of the cloak into a *tachrichim* — a burial shroud that is *asur b'hana'ah* — operates analogously to *chametz* becoming prohibited on Passover, severing the wife's rights in the object itself. This illustrates that even where Rav Yehuda's ruling grants her the right to retrieve, that right must be actively exercised; it does not automatically transfer control.

### Two Vessels Example

Rav Yehuda then presents a concrete scenario that bears on the practical implications of his own ruling. A woman brings two vessels worth a total of one thousand *zuz* into the marriage; by the time of divorce or the husband's death, they are worth two thousand *zuz*. What does she retrieve?

The ruling is: she takes one vessel as part of her *ketubah* entitlement — that is, within the original assessed value — and for the second vessel, she pays the difference in value and retrieves it as well, *mipnei shevach beit aviha*. Even though the vessels have doubled in value, she is entitled to take both back and simply compensate for the increase.

The *gemara* asks: is this ruling necessary? Has Rav Yehuda not already stated that she is entitled to retrieve the property? The answer is that one might have thought her entitlement to retrieve extends only up to the original assessed value — meaning she could take back property worth up to a thousand, but not beyond that threshold. The ruling teaches that even when the property has appreciated beyond its original value, she may still retrieve all of it by paying the increment. The principle *shevach beit aviha* — the special consideration given to property that she brought from her father's house — extends to allow her to reclaim the full quantity of objects she originally brought in, with the increase in value paid out to the estate.

---

## Fetus & Slave Terumah

### Ubar Posel

The *mishnah* now turns from the question of forbidden marriage and its effect on the wife's status to a different dynamic entirely: the role of an unborn fetus in determining whether the slaves of a deceased *kohen* may eat *terumah*. The case is as follows. A *bat Yisrael* marries a *kohen*, the *kohen* dies, and she is left pregnant. What is the status of the slaves?

As a general rule, when a *kohen* dies and leaves a child through his wife, that wife may continue eating *terumah* on account of her child's connection to the priestly lineage. But that applies to a born child. Here, only an unborn fetus remains. The *mishnah* rules: *lo yochlu avadeha biterumah mipnei chelko shel ubar* — the slaves may not eat *terumah* on account of the fetus's portion. That is, we assume the fetus will be a son and will therefore inherit a portion of the estate, including a portion of the slaves. Because he is a partial owner, the slaves cannot eat *terumah* by virtue of him — not yet, since he is unborn.

### Rabbi Yossi's Principle

The *mishnah* encapsulates the rule: *she'ha'ubar posel ve'eino ma'achil* — the fetus invalidates and does not feed. He is in the worst of both positions simultaneously. On the one hand, his partial ownership of the estate — specifically, of the slaves — invalidates them from eating *terumah* through that portion he owns. On the other hand, he is not yet sufficient of a person to enable his mother to eat *terumah*, and cannot cause his own portion of the slaves to eat through him. Were he fully nonexistent in legal terms, the other heirs' portions of the slaves would eat unimpeded. Were he fully born, his mother would eat and all the slaves would eat. In his intermediate state, he creates problems without providing any benefit. This is the position of Rabbi Yossi.

The sages in the *mishnah* respond by pointing out that this logic should apply equally when the mother is a *bat kohen* married to a *kohen*. If the *kohen* dies and she is pregnant, by the same reasoning the slaves should not eat on account of the fetus's portion. Rabbi Yossi's response, and whether the sages are genuinely disagreeing or merely drawing out the implications, remains to be developed in the *gemara*.

### Reason A: Non-Kohen

The *gemara* raises the question of what exactly underlies Rabbi Yossi's ruling. Two possible reasons are entertained, and the difference between them has a practical *nafka mina*. The first possibility: *ubar b'mei zara zar hu* — an unborn fetus takes on the legal identity of his mother. Before birth, the fetus is considered an extension of his mother — *ubar yerech imo*. Since his mother in the *mishnah*'s case is a *bat Yisrael*, a non-*kohen*, the fetus is also considered a non-*kohen*. If a partial owner of the slaves is a non-*kohen*, those slaves cannot eat *terumah* through that portion, because a *zar* — a non-priest — cannot confer the right to eat *terumah*.

### Reason B: Yalud Maachil

The second possibility: *yalud machil she'ein yalud eino machil* — only a born person can enable others to eat *terumah* through him; an unborn person cannot. On this reading, the fetus's *kohen* status is not in question — once born, he will be a *kohen* — but his being unborn disqualifies him from serving as the basis for others' eating of *terumah*. The incapacity is not about identity but about actualized legal personhood.

The *nafka mina* between these two reasons is stark: what if the mother is a *bat kohen*? If the reason is *ubar b'mei zara zar hu* — that the fetus takes on his mother's non-*kohen* identity — then when his mother is a *bat kohen*, that concern disappears. The fetus's mother is a *kohen*, and therefore the fetus is not a *zar*. In that case, the slaves would eat. But if the reason is *yalud machil she'ein yalud eino machil*, it makes no difference whether his mother is a *bat kohen* or a *bat Yisrael* — the problem is solely that he has not yet been born.

### Sages: No Fetus Share

Rabbah identifies reason A as Rabbi Yossi's actual position: *ubar b'mei zara zar hu* — the fetus, while still in a non-priestly mother, takes her identity and is therefore a *zar* whose portion of the slaves cannot eat *terumah*. Rav Yosef identifies reason B: *yalud machil she'ein yalud eino machil*, independent of the mother's status.

The *gemara* then presents the disagreement of the sages and unpacks it. The sages of the *mishnah* — the *chachamim* who respond to Rabbi Yossi — hold the following position. If there are born children of the deceased *kohen*, they eat *terumah* by virtue of those children. If there are no children, others eat *terumah* by virtue of the *kohen*'s brothers or by virtue of any other living member of the priestly family. The presence of the unborn fetus does not alter these arrangements.

### Two Assumptions

What drives the sages' disagreement? Rabbi Yossi's ruling rests on two assumptions. Assumption one: the fetus already acquires a portion of the estate, even before birth. Assumption two: since he is unborn, no one may eat *terumah* by virtue of that portion. The *chachamim* reject assumption one outright. Until the fetus is born, he has no title to the estate whatsoever. He is not a legal heir in the present moment. The other relatives — sons, brothers, or extended family — are the current heirs, and the slaves eat *terumah* through them without any interference from an unborn fetus who holds no current legal claim.

It is worth noting the important implication: even the *chachamim* do not necessarily deny that once born the child will inherit. Their claim is merely temporal — until birth, he holds nothing.

### Shmuel's Stance

Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel: *zo divrei Rabbi Yossi* — this, the ruling of the *mishnah*, is the position of Rabbi Yossi. The phrasing suggests that Shmuel is presenting Rabbi Yossi's ruling as a particular opinion, implying he himself may not hold it. This leads the *gemara* to question whether Shmuel actually rejects Rabbi Yossi's ruling.

The *gemara* challenges this impression: did Shmuel not say to Rav Chana Bagdatna — *puk aytei li bei asara ve-eima lachu be-anpaihu ha-mezakeh le-ubar kanah* — go gather me ten people, and I will declare publicly before them that one who transfers an asset to a fetus acquires it on the fetus's behalf? If Shmuel holds that a fetus can receive a transfer of title through someone acting on his behalf, then presumably he also holds that a fetus inherits from his father — which is precisely assumption one of Rabbi Yossi. How then can Shmuel be understood as rejecting Rabbi Yossi?

### Fetus Can Inherit

The *gemara* resolves this: *ela zu ve-sevira leh* — Shmuel is not dismissing Rabbi Yossi's ruling. He agrees with it, and by saying "this is the position of Rabbi Yossi," he is not distancing himself but rather identifying and affirming it. He is informing his audience that there is a competing opinion — that of the *chachamim* who deny assumption one — of which they should be aware. But Shmuel himself sides with Rabbi Yossi, consistent with his broader principle that a fetus can acquire title.

The *gemara* then asks: *mahu mashma lan* — what is the novelty in Shmuel's statement? The answer is that Shmuel is letting us know that the *chachamim* do in fact disagree with Rabbi Yossi, even though their formulation in the *mishnah* may have sounded like they were merely drawing out his logic rather than disputing him.

A further complication is introduced. Rabbi Zakai reports that Rabbi Yossi gave this testimony in the name of Shemaya and Avtalyon, and the sages conceded to him — *ve-hodu lo*. Does this mean the ruling achieved consensus? Rav Ashi responds: *mi katani ve-kibbelu* — it does not say they accepted it. *Ve-hodu lo katani* — they conceded, meaning *de-mistabar tameh* — they acknowledged the reasoning was cogent, but this falls short of a formal ruling that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yossi. The tradition from Shemaya and Avtalyon confers weight to Rabbi Yossi's position, but does not settle the dispute.

### All Scenarios

A *baraita* now plays out the full range of scenarios according to Rabbi Yossi's position. If the *kohen* dies leaving sons — and no pregnancy — then *elu va'elu ochlin*: all the slaves eat. The *nichsei tzon barzel* slaves eat because they form part of the estate now in the sons' possession. The *nichsei milug* slaves eat because, with living children from the marriage, the wife continues to eat *terumah* and therefore her slaves eat through her. If the *kohen* dies leaving his wife pregnant and no other children — *elu va'elu ein ochlin*: none of the slaves eat. She cannot eat on account of an unborn child, and both categories of slaves are blocked.

If he leaves both sons and a pregnant wife — a mixed case — then *avdei melog ochlin kederech shehi ochelet*: the *milug* slaves eat, because the presence of born children entitles the wife to eat, and therefore her slaves eat through her. But *avdei tzon barzel lo yochlu mipnei chelko shel ubar*: the estate's slaves cannot eat because the fetus holds a partial ownership in them, and that partial ownership — *she'ha'ubar posel ve'eino ma'achil* — invalidates their eating without itself enabling them to eat through the fetus. The born sons' portions would normally suffice, but the fetus's portion creates an insoluble impediment for that share of the slaves.

### R. Yishmael Position

Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yossi adds a ruling in his father's name: *ha'bat ma'achelet, ha'ben eino ma'achil* — a daughter enables the mother to eat, but a son does not. The precise meaning of this statement is not immediately clear and the *gemara* will unpack it in subsequent discussion.

### R. Shimon Position

Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai adds yet another nuance: *zecharim yochlu kulam, nekevot lo yochlu* — all males eat, but females do not. His reasoning appears to hinge on a concern about the possibility of finding a male fetus — *shema yimtza ubar zachar* — but the full elaboration of his position, along with the full analysis of Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yossi's ruling, will be taken up in the continuation of the *gemara*.

---

---

# Yevamot 67

## Pregnant Woman & Slaves

### Baraita Overview

The daf opens at the bottom of 67a, where the Gemara presents a *baraita* that elaborates on the positions already introduced in the *Mishnah*. The *baraita* examines a series of scenarios involving a woman married to a *kohen* whose husband has died, asking in each case whether her slaves may eat *terumah*. The three basic cases are: born children only, a fetus only, and a combination of born children alongside a current pregnancy.

### Born Children

In the first case — *hiniach banim*, where the husband left behind born sons — the ruling is *elu v'elu okhlim*: both the woman and all the slaves may eat *terumah*. The born child entitles the woman to eat, and the slaves, now fully owned by the *kohen*'s heirs, eat by virtue of that ownership. There is no complication.

### Fetus Alone

In the second case — *hiniach ubar*, where the only surviving connection is a fetus — the ruling reverses: *elu v'elu ein okhlim*, neither the woman nor the slaves may eat. The woman cannot eat on behalf of the fetus, since only a born child confers that right. And the slaves cannot eat because they are owned, at least in part, by the fetus — and the fetus cannot cause them to eat.

### Born + Pregnant

The third case — *hiniach banim v'hiniach uberet*, where there are born children and the woman is also pregnant — produces a split ruling. Her own slaves, the *avdei milug*, may eat, because she herself eats by virtue of the born children, and her slaves follow her status. However, his slaves — the *avdei tzon barzel*, which remain part of the estate — may not eat, *mipnei chelko shel ubar*, because the fetus holds a portion of what the born sons have inherited, thereby creating a problem. The principle articulated is *she'ubar posel v'eino ma'achil*: the fetus invalidates — enough to prevent the estate slaves from eating — but does not itself feed, meaning the woman cannot eat on its account. This is identified as the position of Rabbi Yose, consistent with what the *Mishnah* already established.

### R. Shimon Yochai

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai offers a different position. He rules that if the living children are male — *zekharim yokhlu kulam* — then all the slaves may eat despite the pregnancy. If the living children are female — *nekevot lo yokhlu* — the slaves may not eat, *shema yimatze ubar zakhar*, lest the fetus turn out to be male and thereby inherit the entire estate, leaving the daughters with nothing.

### Minority Principle

The obvious question on Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's position regarding male children is: why aren't we concerned that the fetus might be a boy and thereby hold a portion in the estate? The answer the Gemara provides is that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai holds *ein choshashin l'miuta* — one need not be concerned with a minority. Since there is only a 50% chance the fetus will be a boy, and since not every pregnancy results in a live birth, the probability that a live baby boy will emerge is less than 50% — call it something like 48%. That minority possibility does not generate enough concern to prevent the slaves from eating.

This is, it must be said, a striking position. In the realm of *issurim*, we generally are concerned even with much smaller minorities when there is a *miut hamatzuy* — a commonly occurring minority. *Tosafot* wrestles with precisely this tension. One possible distinction is the unique status of the *ubar*, something that is not yet *lefanenu*, not yet present before us — but the oddness of disregarding a near-50% possibility is not lost on the commentators.

As for the case of daughters only: the Gemara notes that there the problem is actually two-fold. If the fetus is a girl, she splits the estate with the daughters already alive. If the fetus is a boy, he displaces them entirely. So the *baraita*'s formulation — *shema yimatze ubar zakhar* — is not the exclusive reason. The Gemara explains: *chada v'od ka'amar* — the *baraita* states one reason and then an additional, stronger one. First, even a female fetus would create a problem for the existing daughters' portion. And furthermore, there is the additional concern that the fetus may be male and take everything.

### Two Reasons

Returning to the case of male children, the Gemara now asks: granted that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai holds we need not concern ourselves with the minority — but perhaps there is an alternative explanation that does not depend on the *miuta* principle at all. Perhaps Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai actually does hold *choshashin l'miuta*, that one is generally concerned with minorities, but holds that there is an independent mechanism that resolves the problem even if the fetus would be a boy.

### Apotropos Solution

That mechanism is the ruling of Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel: *yetomim sheba'u lachalok benichsei avihem* — when orphaned heirs, some adults and some minors, come to divide their father's estate, *beit din* appoints an *apotropos*, a guardian or steward, who selects a favorable portion on behalf of the minors. The question of whether the minors, upon reaching adulthood, can subsequently challenge and reverse that assignment is itself disputed: the ruling in the name of Shmuel suggests they can, while Rav Nachman himself holds *higdilu ein yekholim limchot* — once they come of age, the apportionment stands, because to allow reversal would undermine the authority and effectiveness of *beit din*.

The application to the *ubar* is as follows: rather than allowing the fetus to hold an undivided fractional share in every slave in the estate — which would prevent all of them from eating — *beit din* could appoint an *apotropos* for the fetus and carve out a specific portion of the estate on his behalf. If there are ten slaves, the *apotropos* might assign two of them to the fetus's account. Those two slaves cannot eat, since the fetus owns them and a *ubar* cannot cause slaves to eat. But the remaining eight, now wholly owned by the born brothers, can eat freely. The *apotropos* effectively transforms a fractional co-ownership of every slave into an exclusive ownership of specific slaves — freeing the majority for *terumah* consumption.

One might ask: what happens if the fetus is ultimately a girl? Then the entire premise of the assignment would need to be revisited. This solution was constructed on the assumption the fetus would be a boy. If a girl is born, the allocation would need to be redistributed. And in the case where the existing children are daughters, the *apotropos* solution is more complicated, since a male fetus would be entitled to everything, not just a fractional share.

### Apotropos Rejected

The Gemara then considers whether the underlying dispute between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai might itself reflect a dispute about the validity of the *apotropos* mechanism — i.e., whether *beit din* can in fact make such an assignment for an *ubar*. But the Gemara dismisses this: *lo*. Everyone can accept the ruling of Rav Nachman. The *apotropos* idea is set aside entirely. The dispute returns to its simpler formulation: the question is simply whether we are concerned with the minority possibility that the *ubar* will be born as a live male. The *tanna kamma* holds *choshashin l'miuta* and is therefore concerned; Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai holds *ein choshashin l'miuta* and is therefore not.

---

## R. Yishmael's Teaching

### Puzzle Stated

The *baraita* also records a teaching of Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yose, transmitted in his father's name: *ha-bat ma'akhila, ha-ben eino ma'akhil* — the daughter feeds, the son does not feed. This statement, on its face, is deeply puzzling. Everything we have seen until now suggested the opposite: a son in the estate is the mechanism that allows eating, while a daughter does not carry the same inheritance rights and therefore creates different dynamics. How can it be that daughters allow the slaves to eat but sons do not?

### Limited Estate

Abaye resolves this by positing that the case concerns a *nechasim mu'atim* — a small or limited estate. The relevant *halachah* is that when an estate is small, the daughters' claim to be supported takes priority over the sons' right to inherit. The daughters are entitled by rabbinic enactment to be maintained from the estate until they marry, and if the estate is small enough that fully supporting them leaves nothing for the sons, so be it — the sons may have to go without, while the daughters' support rights are fully honored. In such a case, the daughters' claim effectively controls the estate, even though technical title may still rest with the sons.

### Daughters' Priority

The case Rabbi Yishmael is describing, then, involves a living son, a living daughter, and a pregnant woman. The *baraita*'s teaching can be parsed as follows. *Ha-ben eino ma'akhil* — if there is only a son, the slaves cannot eat, because the fetus might also be a boy and would then hold an equal portion in the estate alongside the living son. *Ha-bat ma'akhila* — but if there is also a daughter, the slaves can eat. Why? Because in a *nechasim mu'atim* situation, the daughter's support rights consume the entire estate. The slaves are effectively at her disposal, and her entitlement is what governs whether they eat.

### Fetus & Daughters

This then raises a further question: even granting the daughter's priority, why doesn't the fetus disrupt her control of the estate? Consider the two possibilities. If the fetus is a boy, does he get a portion of this small estate alongside the daughter? In a *nechasim mu'atim* case, no — the daughter's support rights trump even a male heir's claim. If the fetus is a girl, should she not be entitled to a share of the daughters' support allocation?
