Here the *halachah* distinguishes sharply: the daughters' support rights established by rabbinic enactment apply only to born daughters. *Kama de-lo nafka la'avir ha'olam, lo takinu rabbanan* — until she emerges into the world as a born person, the Rabbis did not extend their enactment to cover her. The fetus, therefore, cannot diminish the living daughter's claim, whether the fetus would be male or female.

### Estate Challenge

The Gemara, however, challenges Abaye's reading. The end of the *baraita* — in Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's statement — says that if the fetus turns out to be male, the daughters get nothing, *v'ein la-banot bimkom ha-ben klum*. This implies that in the scenario Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is discussing, the son takes everything and the daughters have no claim. But that is precisely the opposite of a *nechasim mu'atim* case, where the daughters' rights would prevail. So the *baraita* appears to be addressing a *nechasim merubim* — a large estate — not a small one.

Abaye's response is that the two halves of the *baraita* need not address the same scenario: the statement of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai concerns a large estate, while Rabbi Yishmael's statement concerns a small one.

The Gemara then pushes further. Even granting that the daughters control a small estate in terms of support, the *halachah* established by Rabbi Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan is that if the sons of such an estate go ahead and sell it — *yetomim shekadmu u'makhru be-nechasim mu'atim, mah she-makhru makhru* — the sale is binding. This implies that the legal title to the property remains with the sons, not the daughters. The daughters have a *right* against the estate, something like a debt or lien, but title is the sons'. If so, the slaves are the sons' slaves, and the question of whether the daughters "control" the estate in a way that determines eating rights becomes considerably more complicated.

### Mother & Father

Faced with this difficulty, the Gemara proposes an entirely different reading of the *baraita*. The words *bat* and *ben* in Rabbi Yishmael's statement do not mean daughter and son at all — they mean *em* and *av*, mother and father. *Ha-bat ma'akhila* means the mother's property enables eating; *ha-ben eino ma'akhil* means the father's property does not. In other words, the statement is simply recapitulating what Rabbi Yose already established: when there are born children and a pregnant woman, her *avdei milug* eat because she eats, while his *avdei tzon barzel* do not eat because of the fetus's portion in the estate.

This reading is admittedly forced — *bat* and *ben* as stand-ins for mother and father is an unusual usage — but the Gemara accepts it: *kula Rabbi Yishmael beno shel Rabbi Yosi katani*. The entire teaching of Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yose was simply an elaboration and explanation of the ruling already stated in his father's name. It adds nothing substantively new.

---

## Gray Zone Cases

### Gray Zone Intro

The *sugya* now turns to a broader framework that extends well beyond the specific question of slaves and *terumah*. The underlying issue is a woman who stands in an intermediate relationship — partially connected to her husband's household, partially not. The practical consequence of this ambiguity plays out differently depending on the woman's lineage and her husband's status.

To appreciate the framework, consider two mirror-image scenarios. First: a *bat kohen* who married a *Yisrael*. If her husband dies and she has no children, she reverts to her father's household and may once again eat *terumah*. But if she has children, she remains connected to her deceased husband's household and does not revert; she cannot eat *terumah*. Second: a *bat Yisrael* who married a *kohen*. If her husband dies and she has children, she remains connected to his household and may continue eating *terumah*. But if there are no children, she reverts to her father's household and loses the right to eat *terumah*.

The gray zone arises when the connection to the husband is real but incomplete. Such a partial connection is strong enough to pull the woman out of her father's household — and thereby prevent a *bat kohen* who married a *Yisrael* from reverting and eating *terumah* — yet it is not strong enough to fully integrate her into the husband's household, and therefore does not entitle a *bat Yisrael* who married a *kohen* to eat *terumah* on the basis of that connection. In the language of the *Mishnah*: these cases *poslim v'lo ma'akhilim* — they invalidate but do not feed.

The *Mishnah* lists several such cases, each presenting its own variety of partial or ambiguous connection: the *ubar* (fetus), the *yavam* (brother-in-law awaiting *yibum*), *erusin* (betrothal without consummation), a *cheresh* (deaf-mute husband), and a nine-year-old in a specific context. Before unpacking each case, the *Mishnah* also mentions a *safek* variant: situations where it is uncertain whether the man is nine years old, or uncertain whether he has reached halachic adulthood through the appearance of two pubic hairs. Even these doubts are sufficient to invalidate.

The *Mishnah* includes a digression about a collapsed building that killed both a man and his niece — his wife — leaving unresolved which died first. This bears on whether the surviving co-wife undergoes *yibum* or *chalitzah*. The connection to the present context is the shared theme of *yavam* and *safek* cases; the Gemara notes it is a digression, explained by the fact that *yavam* was just mentioned and *safek* cases were at hand.

### Fetus Gray Zone

The Gemara now provides the sourcing for each case. Regarding the *ubar*: if the woman is a *bat kohen* married to a *Yisrael*, the fetus invalidates her from reverting to eat *terumah*, because the verse says *ki-neureiha* — she returns to her father's house as in her youth — and *perat l'muberet*, the case of pregnancy is excluded, as she is still too connected to be considered fully reverted. If she is a *bat Yisrael* married to a *kohen*, the fetus does not allow her to eat because of the principle *yalud ma'akhil she'ein yalud ma'akhil* — only a born child, not an unborn one, generates the right to eat. No verse is quoted for this latter point; it is treated as an established axiom.

### Yavam Gray Zone

The *yavam* — the brother-in-law awaiting *yibum* — presents the same dual dynamic. If the woman is a *bat kohen* and the brother-in-law is a *Yisrael*, he invalidates her from returning to eat *terumah*, because *v'shava el beit aviha* — she can only return to her father's house — and *perat l'shomeres yavam*, she cannot return while she is still bound to the *yavam* and requires *chalitzah* to free herself. If she is a *bat Yisrael* and the *yavam* is a *kohen*, the *zikah* relationship is not strong enough to entitle her to eat, because *kinyan kaspa amar Rachmana* — the Torah requires that she be his acquisition of money, i.e., properly betrothed — and at this stage she remains a woman his brother married, not yet his own acquisition.

### Erusin Gray Zone

The case of *erusin* — betrothal without consummation — is almost a *kal va-chomer* from the *yavam*: here there has been genuine *kiddushin*, yet the relationship remains in a gray zone. If the woman is a *bat kohen* and her betrothed is a *Yisrael*, the betrothal invalidates her, because *d'hakanya bahavaya* — the verse ובת כהן כי תהיה לאיש זר, "and a daughter of a *kohen* when she belongs to a foreign man," establishes that once there is any connection to another man, she is no longer entirely in her father's household. Even though conceptually the period of *erusin* is still the time when she lives in her father's house before moving to her husband's house at *nissu'in*, the connection to the other man is real and sufficient to disqualify her from eating on the basis of her father's household.

If she is a *bat Yisrael* and her betrothed is a *kohen*, the betrothal does not entitle her to eat. Here the Gemara invokes the ruling of Ulla. There is actually a dispute between the Bavli and the Yerushalmi on this point: the Bavli's logic would suggest that *kiddushin*, which is effected through money and constitutes a form of *kinyan*, should in principle entitle her to eat already at the stage of *erusin*. The Yerushalmi, by contrast, holds that the mechanism for a wife's eating is *beiso hem yokhlu b'lachmo* — being part of his household — which applies only after *nissu'in*. According to the Yerushalmi, it is actually a biblical prohibition for her to eat *terumah* before *nissu'in*. According to the Bavli, Ulla's rationale is practical and rabbinic: during *erusin* the woman still lives in her father's house, and if the *kohen* sends her *terumah*, she will end up sharing it with her father and brothers, who are not permitted to eat it. This concern provides the rabbinic basis for not allowing her to eat during this period.

### Deaf-Mute Marriage

A marriage to a *cheresh* — a deaf-mute — presents yet another gradient. The status of the *cheresh* in halachic discourse is significant: treated in the Talmudic period as lacking the legal competence of a fully cognizant adult, though recognized as occupying a considerably higher level than a *shoteh*, the Rabbis nonetheless instituted a form of rabbinic marriage for a *cheresh*. That rabbinic institution is sufficient to remove the woman from her father's household in the relevant halachic sense. Therefore, if she is a *bat kohen* married to a *Yisrael cheresh*, the rabbinic marriage invalidates her from eating *terumah*, *d'hakanya b'takanata d'rabbanan* — through rabbinic enactment she has been acquired. If she is a *bat Yisrael* married to a *kohen cheresh*, she cannot eat, because *kinyan kaspo amar Rachmana v'hai lav bar kinyanei* — the Torah requires a genuine biblical *kiddushin*, and the *cheresh* is not capable of effecting one biblically. The rabbinic institution of marriage, powerful enough to invalidate, is not powerful enough to entitle.

### Nine-Year-Old

The case of the nine-year-old is the most complex in this section. Initially, it might seem to refer to a *yibum* scenario: a woman waiting for *yibum* from a nine-year-old brother-in-law who consummates the relationship. The Gemara, however, works through the logic and finds this reading inadequate. If the concern is that the *yavam* prevents her return to her father's house — the *poslim* side — even a one-day-old infant would create that bond, since she is a *shomeres yavam* regardless of the *yavam*'s age. And if the concern is whether he entitles her to eat — the *ma'akhilim* side — then even an adult *yavam* does not entitle her to eat until consummation. So a nine-year-old *yavam* who has actually had relations would be an interesting case: Abaye initially suggests that the novelty is that although the act of *bi'ah* is biblically valid as an act of *yibum* — *de-mid'oraita kani lei* — the Rabbis treated the sexual act of a nine-year-old as equivalent only to *ma'amar*, the rabbinic act of betrothal, rather than full consummation. She might think she is entitled to eat since biblically the *yibum* is complete; the teaching comes to say she is not.

Rava rejects this reading, however, and points out that the subsequent clause of the *Mishnah* — *safek ben tesha shanim, safek eino* — becomes unintelligible under Abaye's interpretation. If a definite nine-year-old who has had relations does not entitle her to eat, it would be obvious that an uncertain nine-year-old also does not. But the *Mishnah* appears to teach it as a separate point, implying that in the case of certainty the answer would be different.

Rava therefore reframes the entire case. The nine-year-old here does not belong to the gray-zone section at all. Rather, it belongs to the following category: people whose sexual act *invalidates* the woman completely. The *Mishnah* is transitioning to a new list — people whose forbidden sexual contact renders the woman a *zonah* or *chalalah* and disqualifies her from marrying a *kohen* or eating *terumah*. Even a nine-year-old from such a category has this effect. And if it is uncertain whether he is nine years old, the doubt itself is sufficient to invalidate — which now makes perfect sense, because even certainty that he is younger would not help her if it is a *safek* whether the disqualifying act occurred.

---

## Forbidden Acts

### Invalidation Intro

With Rava's reframing established, the Gemara turns directly to the new topic: the category of sexual acts that completely invalidate a woman, removing her from the rights of *kehunah* — either the right to eat *terumah* if she is a *bat kohen*, or the right to marry a *kohen* if she is a *bat Yisrael* or *Leviyah*.

### Forbidden Partners

The *baraita* states: a nine-year-old and a day who is a *ger*, a convert of Ammonite or Moabite origin — forbidden by the verse *lo yavo Ammoni bikhal Hashem* — or an Egyptian, an Edomite (before the third generation of conversion), a *Kuti* (Samaritan, treated as not fully Jewish in this context), a *nasin* (of Gibeonite descent), a *chalal* (a *kohen* who has lost his sanctity through a disqualifying union), or a *mamzer* — any of these who engages in sexual relations with a *kohenet*, a *Leviyah*, or a *Yisraelit*, *pasluha*: they invalidate her. If she is a *bat kohen*, she is disqualified from eating *terumah*. If she is a *Yisraelit* or *Leviyah*, she is disqualified from marrying a *kohen*.

It is worth noting the structural diversity of this list. Some of these figures are forbidden to marry *any* Jew — a *mamzer* cannot marry into the community of Israel, nor can an Ammonite or Moabite convert. Others are specifically forbidden to *kohanim* — a *chalal*, for example, does not create a problem for marriage to a *Yisrael* but does affect the woman's *kehunah* status. The Gemara will distinguish between these two sub-categories, identifying the first group as *psulei kahal* — those barred from the general community — and the second group as *psulei kehunah* — those specifically barred in the context of priestly marriage. The *chalal* in particular occupies an unusual position: his act of sex is not itself a forbidden one in the ordinary sense, but it renders the woman a *chalalah*.

### R. Yossi View

Rabbi Yose qualifies the general rule: *kol she-zaro pasul, posel* — only one whose offspring would be disqualified invalidates the woman. *Kol she-ein zaro pasul, eino posel* — one whose offspring would not be disqualified does not invalidate her. The implication is that there are cases of forbidden sexual contact where the resulting child would not be halachically problematic. One such scenario might involve a man who is at the boundary of permissibility — for example, the third generation of Egyptian or Edomite converts, who are just crossing the threshold into full eligibility. In such edge cases, Rabbi Yose would hold that the act does not invalidate the woman.

### R. Shimon Rule

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel articulates his position as a memorable rule: *kol she-ata nosei bito, ata nosei almanato* — whoever's daughter you may marry, you may marry his widow (in the sense of the woman with whom he had relations). *V'kol she-ei ata nosei bito, ei ata nosei almanato* — whoever's daughter you may not marry, you may not marry the woman he has rendered a widow. The import is that the eligibility of the man's daughter to marry a *kohen* determines whether his sexual act invalidates the woman. At first glance this seems very close to Rabbi Yose's position — in both cases the determining factor is the status of offspring — and the Gemara will address the relationship between these views.

---

## Source & Scope

### Verse Source

Having laid out the rules, the Gemara asks: *mena hani mili*? Where do we derive the foundational principle that forbidden sexual intercourse invalidates a woman — specifically, that a *bat kohen* who has such relations loses her right to eat *terumah*? Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav cites the verse: *u-vat kohen ki tihyeh l'ish zar* — "and a daughter of a *kohen* when she belongs to a foreign man." In its simple reading, this refers to a *bat kohen* who marries a *Yisrael* and can no longer eat *terumah* during the marriage. But the Gemara derives from it a more far-reaching principle: *keivan she-niv'alah l'pasul lah* — once she has had relations with a *zar* in the sense of someone wholly forbidden to her, she is permanently invalidated from eating *terumah*, not merely during the marriage. The word *zar* is read not simply as "non-*kohen*" but as "someone completely foreign to her" — that is, halachically prohibited to her.

The Gemara then carefully accounts for every component of the verse's derivation. One might object that this verse is needed to teach the simple *pshat* — that a *bat kohen* married to a *Yisrael* cannot eat *terumah*. But that, the Gemara replies, can be derived from the continuation of the passage: *v'shava el beit aviha mi-lechem aviha tochel* — "she shall return to her father's house and eat of her father's bread" — implying that while married she does not eat. So the *ki tihyeh* clause is available for the new *derasha*.

One might then object that if we derive the prohibition of eating during marriage inferentially, it carries only the weight of a *mitzvat asei* — a positive commandment's implicit negative. We need the Torah to state a direct *lav*. But that too is addressed: the prohibition of a *Yisrael* eating *terumah* — and by extension, a woman connected to a *Yisrael* — is derived from *v'chol zar lo yochal kodesh*, "no stranger shall eat of sacred things," which appears twice in the relevant passages. One instance teaches that a non-*kohen* cannot eat *terumah*; the other teaches that a woman married to a non-*kohen* cannot eat. The word *v'chol* in the second instance further teaches, following Rabbi Yose the son of Rabbi Chanina, that it is specifically the status of *zarus* — foreignness — that disqualifies, and not *aninus* (the state of mourning before burial). An *onen* is forbidden to eat *korbanos* but not forbidden to eat *terumah*. All of this is accounted for, leaving *ki tihyeh l'ish zar* free to teach the invalidating effect of forbidden sexual relations.

The Gemara also notes another teaching derived from this passage. A *baraita* teaches that when a woman reverts to her father's household after her husband's death, *chozeret l'terumah v'einah chozeret la-chazeh v'shok* — she returns to eating *terumah* but does not return to eating the *chazeh v'shok*, the breast and thigh portions of certain offerings. The phrase *bi-trumat ha-kodashim lo tochal* is read as *bi-murum min ha-kodashim lo tochal* — she no longer partakes of what is lifted up from the *korbanos*. Once she has been married to a non-*kohen*, that permanent exclusion from *kodashim kalim* remains, even after she reverts and resumes *terumah*. The phrasing *bi-trumat ha-kodashim* rather than simply *ba-kodashim* signals that both *terumah* and *kodashim* are being addressed in a single formulation.

### Extra Vav

Having established the invalidation of a *bat kohen* from *terumah*, the Gemara asks how this extends to all women — *Leviyah* and *Yisraelit* as well. The answer, following Rabbi Abba in the name of Rav, is derived from the prefix ו in ובת כהן: *bat u-vat* — the extra ו extends the ruling beyond the *bat kohen* to include all women. Since the law of invalidation now applies to a *Leviyah* or *Yisraelit*, the relevant consequence cannot be the loss of *terumah* eating rights — those women never ate *terumah* to begin with. The implication must therefore be the prohibition of marriage to a *kohen*. The Gemara notes that this derivation follows even the *Rabbanan* who generally do not learn from extra letter forms, since here the entire phrase *u-vat kohen* is superfluous — the verse could have begun simply with *ki tihyeh l'ish zar*. The full prefix phrase is thus available as an extension to all women.

### Terumah Loss

At this point in the derivation, the Gemara has established from the verse that forbidden sexual relations invalidate a woman — specifically that a *bat kohen* is disqualified from eating *terumah*. This much follows from the direct reading of the verse about a *bat kohen* and *terumah*.

### Marriage Ban Q

What remains to be established is that the same act disqualifies all women from marriage to a *kohen*. As noted above, this is the implication of extending the ruling to a *Leviyah* or *Yisraelit* through the extra ו. But the derivation merits closer attention: once we say *bat u-vat* includes all women, and for those women the only relevant consequence is marriage prohibition, the *terumah* dimension and the marriage dimension are brought together under a single biblical source.

### Kal VeChomer

Could one not derive the marriage prohibition through a *kal va-chomer*? If forbidden sex invalidates a *bat kohen* — who has her own intrinsic sanctity, *kedushat ha-guf* — surely it should all the more so disqualify a *bat Yisrael* from marriage to a *kohen*. The Gemara rejects this argument with a sharp reversal: *hee ha-notenet* — it is precisely the opposite. A *bat kohen* eats *terumah* by virtue of her own personal sanctity, *kedushat gufah*, and forbidden sex impinges directly on that sanctity. But a *bat Yisrael* who eats *terumah* does so not by virtue of her own status but by virtue of her child — *bishvil benah*. If her eating is not based on her own sacred status but on an external connection, perhaps forbidden sex, which affects personal status, is simply irrelevant to her ability to eat. *Lo kadish gufah* — her body carries no inherent *kedushah* that the forbidden act can desecrate. The *kal va-chomer* thus fails: far from being more stringent for a *bat Yisrael*, the logic of personal sanctity would suggest she should be *less* affected. A verse is therefore necessary, and the verse provides it through the extension to all women.

The *sugya* thus concludes this daf with the question of invalidation from *terumah* fully resolved, and sets the stage for the following discussion: the derivation of the prohibition on marrying a *kohen* that applies to all women who have had forbidden sexual relations — which will be taken up on the following daf.

---

---

# Yevamot 67b

## Uber & Slave Status

### Braita Cases

The daf begins with a *braita* that elaborates upon the position of Rabbi Yose set out in the *mishna*, spelling out the various scenarios in which a pregnant woman married to a *kohen* has died and the question turns on which household members may eat *terumah*.

*Tanu rabbanan*: if the *kohen* left behind born sons and his wife was not pregnant, then both she and all the slaves may eat — the born child entitles the wife to remain connected to the *kohen*'s household, and all the slaves are fully owned by the heirs. If he left the wife pregnant but with no born children, then neither she nor the slaves may eat: she cannot eat on the basis of an unborn fetus, and the slaves cannot eat because they are owned, wholly or in part, by the fetus, who cannot confer upon them the right to eat *terumah*. If he left both born children and a pregnant wife, then her *nichsei melog* slaves — those she brought as her personal dowry property — may eat, because she herself eats by virtue of the born children, and *kederech she-hi ochelet* her slaves follow her status. The *nichsei tzon barzel* slaves, however — those she brought as the husband's property and which remain part of his estate — do not eat, *mipnei chelko shel uber*, because the fetus holds a partial share in what the born sons have inherited, and that share creates the problem. This is summarized as: the fetus *posel ve-eino ma'achil* — he invalidates but cannot feed. This is the ruling of Rabbi Yose, and the *braita* is simply an expansion of the *mishna*.

Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yose then states in his father's name: *ha-bat ma'achelet, ha-ben eino ma'achil* — the daughter feeds, the son does not feed. The *gemara* notes that this statement is initially opaque and proceeds to unpack it.

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai adds: *zecharim yochlu kulam, nekevot lo yochlu* — if there are only male children and the wife is pregnant, all the slaves may eat; if there are only daughters and the wife is pregnant, the slaves may not eat.

### Male Minority Risk

The *gemara* presses on Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's ruling: if there are born boys and a pregnant wife, why are the slaves permitted to eat? The fetus might itself be a boy and thereby hold a share in the estate, which should prevent the slaves from eating. The answer given is that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai holds *ein choshishin le-mi'uta* — one need not be concerned about a minority possibility. The chain of logic is this: there is a fifty percent chance the fetus will be female, in which case it holds no share in the estate (daughters do not inherit when sons are present). Even if the fetus is male, not every pregnancy results in a live birth. The combined probability that a live baby boy will be born from this pregnancy falls below fifty percent — a *mi'ut* — and one need not worry about a *mi'ut* in the majority of cases.

The *gemara* then asks why, when there are only daughters and the wife is pregnant, the slaves cannot eat. The answer, *chada ve-od*, is twofold: first, if the fetus is female, she too will share in the estate with the other daughters; second, even if the fetus is female and girls generally share in the estate only by rabbinic enactment, there remains the possibility the fetus is male and takes the entire estate — *ve-ein la-banot bi-makom ha-ben klum*, the daughters have no share in the presence of a son.

The *gemara* then raises a second possible reading of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's ruling. Perhaps he does hold *choshishin le-mi'uta* — he is indeed concerned about a forty-eight percent probability — but holds that there is a practical solution available via the ruling of Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel. Rav Nachman amar Shmuel teaches that when orphans come to divide their father's estate and some are minors, *beit din* appoints an *apotropus* — a guardian or steward — to choose a good portion on behalf of the minor heir. The *apotropus* can then carve out specific property for the fetus: instead of the fetus holding an undivided fractional interest in every slave, he holds full ownership of two specific slaves (for example), and the remaining eight slaves are fully owned by the born brothers and may eat *terumah*.

A further nuance of Rav Nachman's ruling concerns what happens when the minors come of age: in the name of Shmuel, the ruling states that they may reverse the division if it did not serve their interests, since the *apotropus* only acted on their behalf. Rav Nachman himself, however, rules that once they reach adulthood they *cannot* reverse it — *mah koach beit din yafeh?* For otherwise, what power does *beit din* have?

The *gemara* then steps back and rejects this entire approach, concluding *lo* — everyone can hold by Rav Nachman's principle, the *apotropus* idea is not the point at all, and the debate among the *tanna'im* is simply whether one is concerned about the *mi'ut* that a live boy will be born.

### Small Estate Rule

The *gemara* turns to the cryptic ruling of Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yose: *ha-bat ma'achelet, ha-ben eino ma'achil*. Abaye explains that the entire case concerns *nichsei mu'atim* — a small estate. When the estate is small, a well-known *halacha* applies: the daughters' right to be supported from the estate until marriage takes full precedence over the sons' inheritance. Even if meeting the daughters' maintenance costs consumes the entire estate and leaves the sons nothing, the daughters' rights come first.

The case, therefore, involves the presence of both a born son and a born daughter. *Mima nafshach* — either way: if the pregnant woman's fetus is a boy, he is no better positioned than the born boy who is already present. In a small estate, the daughter already owns the whole of the estate for purposes of support, so the fetus acquires nothing from it even if male. If the fetus is a girl, why do girls eat in this case at all? Because it is by virtue of a *takana d'rabbanan*, a rabbinic enactment — and the rabbis enacted that right only for a born girl, not for an unborn fetus. So when there is a daughter present, the slaves may eat — the daughter holds the estate by rabbinic enactment, and the fetus, whether male or female, does not disturb her hold on it.

The *gemara* then tests this reading: the end of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's statement spoke of boys getting everything if the fetus is male, which presupposes a large estate where sons inherit everything and daughters are left with nothing. The *gemara* concedes that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's statement applies to a large estate, while Rabbi Yishmael's teaching concerns the special small-estate case.

But a further challenge arises: if the estate is a *nichsei mu'atim*, can one truly say it belongs to the daughters? Rabbi Assi amar Rabbi Yochanan teaches that if orphans in a small estate go ahead and sell property, the sale is legally binding — which demonstrates that ultimate *title* remains with the sons, even if the daughters have a right to be fed. The daughters hold a right akin to a debt against the estate, not outright ownership.

The *gemara* therefore abandons the reading that *bat* and *ben* refer to literal daughter and son of the deceased, and proposes instead that the text uses *bat* to mean the mother — the wife — and *ben* to mean the father — the deceased husband. *Ha-bat ma'achelet* means: the mother's own property (*nichsei melog*) feeds her slaves; *ha-ben eino ma'achil* means: the father's property (*nichsei tzon barzel*) does not feed those slaves, because of the fetus's partial share. The *gemara* concludes: *hainu Rabbi Yose* — this is simply what Rabbi Yose already taught, and Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yose is merely restating his father's ruling with different terminology, which is admittedly an unusual reading of the *braita*.

---

## Gray Zone Status

### Gray Zone Intro

The discussion shifts to a broader framework: a list of cases in which a woman finds herself in a legal gray zone with respect to *terumah* consumption. The governing principle is as follows. When a *bat kohen* marries a *yisrael* and he dies, the presence or absence of children determines whether she remains connected to the *yisrael*'s household or reverts to her father's. If she has children, she remains connected to her dead husband's household and may not return to eating *terumah*. If she has no children, she reverts to her father's house — conceptually, not physically — and resumes eating *terumah*. The mirror image applies to a *bat yisrael* married to a *kohen*: with children she remains in his household and eats *terumah*; without children she reverts to her father's household and does not eat.

The *uber* — fetus — creates precisely the gray zone the *gemara* now catalogs. The fetus is enough of a connection to the dead husband that it prevents the woman from being considered fully reverted to her father's house, thereby *poseling* a *bat kohen* from eating *terumah*. But the fetus is not enough of a connection to the husband's house to entitle a *bat yisrael* married to a *kohen* to eat *terumah* in the first place. The fetus thus occupies both the *posel* function and the non-*ma'achil* function simultaneously.

The *mishna* presents a list of relationships that share this dual gray-zone character: the *uber*, the *yavam*, *erusin*, a *cheresh*, and a *ben tesha shanim ve-yom echad*. In all these cases: *poslin ve-lo ma'achilin* — they invalidate but they do not feed. And even a *safek* of such a relationship, whether it is uncertain if the man is nine years old and a day, or uncertain whether he has reached halachic maturity through two pubic hairs, is sufficient to invalidate.

The *mishna* also mentions, as an aside, a *nafal ha-bayit* case: a house collapsed upon a man and his brother's daughter (his wife), with no known order of death, and he had a co-wife. Since the *tzarah*'s obligation of *yibbum* depends on the order of death — if the niece-wife died first, the co-wife requires *yibbum*; if the husband died first, the co-wife is exempt because a niece cannot create the *yibbum* bond — the *halacha* is that the *tzarah* performs *chalitzah* and not *yibbum*.

### Fetus Case

The *gemara* unpacks the *uber* case. If the woman is a *bat kohen* married to a *yisrael*, the fetus *paslah* — invalidates her from returning to *terumah*. The derivation: the verse speaks of her returning to her father's house *ke-ne'ureha* — as in her youth — implying a full reversion; a pregnant woman has not fully reverted. If she is a *bat yisrael* married to a *kohen*, the fetus does not entitle her to eat, because *yalud ma'achil she-ein yalud ma'achil* — only a born child confers that right; an unborn fetus does not.

### Yavam Case

For the *yavam*, the *gemara* reasons as follows. If she is a *bat kohen* and the *yavam* is a *yisrael*, he *paslah*, because the verse says *ve-shavah el beit aviha* — she can return to her father's house — which implicitly excludes a *shomeret yavam*, who remains bound by the *zikah* bond and cannot return until *chalitzah* is performed. If she is a *bat yisrael* and the *yavam* is a *kohen*, she does not eat, because *kinyan kaspo amar rachamana* — the Torah requires that she be his acquisition through money (the paradigm of *kiddushin*), and this woman was acquired by his *brother*, not by him. Once *yibbum* is consummated the relationship is complete, but at the stage of *shomeret yavam* it is not sufficient.

### Erusin Case

For *erusin*, the case involves actual *kiddushin* without *nisuin*. If she is a *bat kohen* and the *arus* is a *yisrael*, he invalidates her: once there is some *kinyan* to another man, the verse *u-vat kohen ki tihyeh l'ish zar* applies and she is no longer considered fully within her father's house — or, more precisely, even if she remains physically in her father's house, her connection to another man is sufficient to sever her *terumah* entitlement based on her father. If she is a *bat yisrael* and the *arus* is a *kohen*, she does not eat — and here the *gemara* invokes the ruling of Ulla. Biblically, it would seem that *kiddushin* should suffice to allow her to eat *terumah*, since the verse speaks of *kinyan kaspo* — his monetary acquisition, encompassing both slaves and wife acquired through *kiddushin*. However, Ulla explains that the rabbis were concerned lest she share the *terumah* with her father and brothers while still residing in her father's house during the period between *erusin* and *nisuin*. Accordingly, the rabbis enacted that she does not eat until *nisuin*. The *gemara* notes that the Yerushalmi actually takes a stronger position: *terumah* entitlement is derived not from *kinyan kaspo* but from *beito hem yochlu belachmo* — the idea of his *bayit*, his household — which is only established at *nisuin*, making this a biblical, not merely rabbinic, exclusion during *erusin*.

### Cheresh Case

For the *cheresh* — a deaf-mute — the *gemara* notes that while a *cheresh* is not considered legally competent in the biblical sense and thus cannot effect a biblical *kiddushin*, the rabbis nonetheless instituted a form of rabbinic marriage for a *cheresh*, recognizing that he functions at a higher level than, for example, a *shoteh*. If she is a *bat kohen* and the *cheresh* is a *yisrael*, this rabbinic institution is sufficient to remove her from her father's house and *posel* her. If she is a *bat yisrael* and the *cheresh* is a *kohen*, she does not eat, because *kinyan kaspo amar rachamana*, the Torah requires a real biblical acquisition, and a *cheresh lav bar kinyan hu* — a deaf-mute is not capable of effecting a biblical acquisition. So the rabbinic marriage invalidates but does not feed.

### Nine Years Old Case

The *ben tesha shanim ve-yom echad* case requires further clarification. One might initially think this refers to a *yavam* who is nine years old and a day performing *bi'ah* for *yibbum* purposes. The *gemara* considers whether the intent is to show that the *yavam*'s minority status alone — even without any act of *bi'ah* — invalidates. But the *gemara* notes that even an infant *yavam* invalidates her as a *shomeret yavam*; and conversely, even an adult *yavam* does not *feed* her until *yibbum* is consummated. Abaye therefore proposes that the case involves a nine-year-old *yavam* who has actually had *bi'ah* with the *yevamah*. Since biblically this act of *bi'ah* is a valid act of *yibbum*, one might think she should be entitled to eat *terumah* if he is a *kohen*. The *chiddush* is that the rabbis treated the *bi'ah* of a nine-year-old not as a complete *yibbum* but as equivalent to *ma'amar* — a stronger but still incomplete form of the *yibbum* bond — and thus she remains in the gray zone and does not eat.

Rava objects to Abaye's reading: the *mishna* states that even a *safek* of nine years old invalidates. If a definite nine-year-old having consummated does not *feed* her, of course a doubtful nine-year-old does not feed her — there is no *chiddush* in the *safek* formulation. Rava therefore reinterprets: the *ben tesha shanim ve-yom echad* in this *mishna* is not about *yibbum* at all. It belongs to a different category — the category of forbidden sexual relations. Starting at age nine years and a day, an act of *bi'ah* with one of the persons listed in the following *braita* is considered a legally significant act of sex that invalidates the woman. That is the *chiddush*, and the *safek* formulation then makes perfect sense: even if it is uncertain whether he was nine years old and a day, the woman is still invalidated by the act.

---

## Forbidden Relations

### Braita Categories

The *gemara* now turns to the *braita* it has been previewing: a nine-year-old boy and a day who is a *ger Amoni o Mo'avi*, an Ammonite or Moabite convert, or a *Mitzri*, *Edomi* (within the first three generations), *Kuti*, *natin*, *chalal*, or *mamzer*, who has relations with a *kohenet*, a *Leviyah*, or a *Yisraelit* — all are *pasluha*, they invalidate her. If she is a *bat kohen*, she is prevented from eating *terumah*. If she is a *Yisraelit*, she is prevented from marrying a *kohen*.

The *gemara* notes a structural distinction in the *mishna*: the first section of the *mishna* addressed the *pesulei kahal* — those forbidden from entering the congregation of Israel altogether, not merely from *kehuna* — including Ammonites, Moabites, *mamzerim*, and the like. The subsequent *mishna* will address *pesulei kehuna* — those specifically forbidden to *kohanim*, such as a divorcée or widow married to a *kohen*. Though different in kind, both categories of forbidden relations invalidate the woman.

### Rabbi Yose View

Rabbi Yose states: *kol she-zar'o pasul posel* — anyone whose offspring from this woman would be *pasul* (invalid) invalidates the woman through this act of sex. *Ve-kol she-ein zar'o pasul eino posel* — anyone whose offspring would not be *pasul* does not invalidate her. This formulation raises the question of what kind of relationship might be forbidden yet produce valid offspring — for instance, a man who is forbidden to marry into the congregation only for a limited number of generations, where the offspring of the union would fall on the permitted side of that generational threshold.

### Rabban Shimon View

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel offers a parallel formulation: *kol she-ata nosei bito ata nosei almanato* — anyone whose daughter you (the *kohen*) could marry, you could also marry his widow (the woman he had relations with). *Ve-kol she-ei ata nosei bito ei ata nosei almanato* — anyone whose daughter you could not marry, you cannot marry his widow either. This sounds closely parallel to Rabbi Yose's position, and the *gemara* will explore the relationship between the two formulations.

### Parashat Emor Source

The *gemara* asks: *mena hanei milei* — what is the biblical source for the principle that forbidden sexual relations invalidate a woman from eating *terumah* or from marrying a *kohen*? Rav Yehuda amar Rav derives it from the verse *u-vat kohen ki tihyeh l'ish zar* (Parashat Emor). While the *peshat* of the verse is that a *bat kohen* married to a non-*kohen* (*zar*) may not eat *terumah* of her father's house, Rav reads it as follows: *zar* means someone totally foreign, completely forbidden to her. Once she has been *niv'ala* — had relations — with such a man, *paslah* — she is permanently invalidated from eating *terumah*, not merely suspended during the marriage. This reading converts a temporary status rule into a permanent invalidation based on an act of forbidden sex.

The *gemara* immediately challenges: we need this verse simply for its *peshat* — to teach that a *bat kohen* married to a non-*kohen* cannot eat *terumah* while married. The *gemara* replies that we could derive that rule from elsewhere: from the verse *ve-shavah el beit aviha* — when she returns to her father's house she may eat — we can infer by implication that while she is married she cannot eat. The *gemara* pushes back: that inference produces only a *lav ha-ba mi-klal aseh* — a negative prohibition inferred from a positive commandment, which carries only the weight of a positive *mitzvah*. We need the verse *ki tihyeh l'ish zar* to establish this as a full, black-letter negative prohibition.

The *gemara* counters that the negative prohibition can be derived from the verse *ve-chol zar lo yochal kodesh* — no non-*kohen* may eat *terumah*. By extension, a woman connected to a non-*kohen* may not eat. Then the *gemara* notes that *ve-chol zar lo yochal kodesh* appears twice in the Torah. One instance teaches that a non-*kohen* cannot eat *terumah*; the other, appearing in the section of a *bat kohen*, teaches that a woman married to a non-*kohen* cannot eat. And the word *ve-chol* in that context comes specifically to teach, as Rabbi Yose birabbi Chanina states: *zarut amarti lach ve-lo aninut* — only the disqualification of being a *zar* prevents eating *terumah*; being an *onen* (mourner on the day of burial) does not. An *onen* is forbidden to eat *korbanot* but not *terumah*.

The *gemara* then layers in yet another *halacha* that requires a verse: *Rami bar Avin amar Rav Ashi* teaches from the phrase *u-vat kohen ki tihyeh l'ish zar hi bi-trumat ha-kodashim lo tochel* — the specific phrase *trumat ha-kodashim* teaches that she cannot eat *be-muram min ha-kodashim*, the portions lifted from *korbanot* (i.e., the *chazeh ve-shok*, the breast and thigh of peace-offerings given to *kohanim*). Once a *bat kohen* has been married to a non-*kohen*, even after that husband's death and her return to her father's house, she can resume eating *terumah* but she does not resume eating the portions of *kodashim*. The *gemara* then asks: if the verse only wanted to prohibit *kodashim*, it should have simply said *lo tochel ba-kodashim* — why does it also mention *terumah*? The answer is *shma mina tarti* — the verse is doing double duty, teaching both rules. The full accounting of available verses thus yields: one *ve-chol zar* for the prohibition on a non-*kohen* eating *terumah*, one *ve-chol zar* (with *ve-chol*) for the prohibition on a *bat kohen* married to a non-*kohen*, the *ve-chol* particle specifically excluding *aninut*, and the phrase *ki tihyeh l'ish zar* for the permanent invalidation through forbidden sex.

### Non-Kohen Women

The analysis has established that forbidden sexual relations invalidate a *bat kohen* from eating *terumah*. But how do we know the rule extends to a *Leviyah* and a *Yisraelit* — for them, the relevant consequence is not *terumah* (which they do not eat in their own right) but prohibition from marrying a *kohen*? The *gemara* answers by invoking the ruling of Rabbi Abba in the name of Rav: *bat u-vat* — the extra *vav* in *u-vat kohen* is textually superfluous, since the verse could simply have stated *ki tihyeh l'ish zar* without specifying *bat kohen* at all. The additional *u-vat kohen* comes to include all women — *Leviyot* and *Yisraeliyot* as well. And once the rule applies to a *Leviyah* and *Yisraelit*, who have no connection to *terumah* in the first place, the only operative consequence must be the prohibition from marrying a *kohen*.

The *gemara* asks whether this derivation follows only the view of Rabbi Akiva, who characteristically derives law from extra *vavim*. It answers that even the *rabbanan* concede the point here, because the entire phrase *u-vat kohen* is textually excess — not just a single letter. The verse could have been written simply as *ki tihyeh l'ish zar*; the addition of *u-vat kohen* is therefore available to teach the extension to all women.

### Leviyah Status

Now that the rule has been extended to all women, the *gemara* asks: we have established the rule for *terumah* — but how do we know that forbidden sex prohibits a *Leviyah* or *Yisraelit* from marrying a *kohen*? At first glance, once we extend the verse to a *Leviyah* and *Yisraelit*, who do not eat *terumah*, the only possible implication is marriage — so it is self-evident. But the *gemara* entertains a counterargument: one could construct a *terumah* case for a *Yisraelit*. If she had previously been married to a *kohen* and bore him a son, she would be eating *terumah* by virtue of that son. Now she has forbidden sex with one of the listed men — she is invalidated and may no longer eat. Perhaps, then, even the extension to *Yisraelit* is still only about *terumah*, not about marriage to a *kohen*.

The *gemara* dismisses this with a *kal va-chomer*: if a *bat kohen*, whose personal status entitles her to eat *terumah*, is invalidated by forbidden sex — then a *Yisraelit*, who eats only on account of her son's status and not her own, would surely be invalidated as well. The *gemara* pushes back: *mah la-kohenet*, one can distinguish — a *bat kohen* has inherent *kedusha*, and her personal status is what is impaired by the forbidden act. A *Yisraelit* has no such inherent *kedusha*; her eating *terumah* is entirely derivative of her child, and perhaps her own status is irrelevant to the act. The *kal va-chomer* therefore fails.

The *gemara* leaves us at the threshold: we have now established, through the extension via *u-vat*, that forbidden sexual relations invalidate all women — *bat kohen*, *Leviyah*, and *Yisraelit* alike — and that for *Leviyot* and *Yisraeliyot* the operative consequence must be prohibition from marrying a *kohen*. The further analysis of exactly how that prohibition is derived for purposes of marriage, as distinct from *terumah*, will be taken up in the following session.

# Yevamot 72

## Northern Wind & Chatzot

### Wind Timing

The *sugya* of *he'arel* — the laws governing what an *arel* may and may not eat, and particularly the prohibition against eating *terumah* derived from the *Korban Pesach* — continues on 72a. The discussion has been anchored in the narrative from Yehoshua establishing that *Bnei Yisrael* were *areilim* throughout their years in the *midbar*, and the *Gemara* has attributed this to the danger of performing *brit milah* when the northern wind did not blow. Before returning to the *halacha*, the *Gemara* lingers on an *agadata* that creates an apparent tension.

A *tanu rabanan* teaches: *kol osan arba'im shana shehayu Yisrael bamidbar, lo haya yom shelo nashva bo ruach tzephonit* — throughout all forty years that Israel was in the wilderness, there was no day on which the northern wind did not blow. This seems to directly contradict the earlier teaching that the north wind was absent during those years. The resolution is that the wind did blow, but only *bachatzot halayla* — precisely at midnight. It did not blow during the day with sufficient force to make *brit milah* safe, yet it blew at midnight nonetheless.

### Chatzot Eis Ratzon

The *Gemara* derives this from the verse *vayehi bachatzot halayla v'Hashem hika kol bechor b'eretz Mitzrayim* — "And it was at midnight, and God smote every firstborn in the land of Egypt." The *Gemara* asks: *mai talmuda* — what is the lesson drawn from this verse? *De'eis ratzon milta hi* — we learn that *chatzot* is a time God regards with special favor, an *eis ratzon*.

This is a striking observation. One might have expected that the midnight plague of the firstborn — a catastrophic act of divine judgment — would mark *chatzot* as an *eis din*, a time of judgment. Yet it is interpreted as an *eis ratzon*, a time of divine favor. The logic is that even that fearsome event was ultimately an expression of redemption for Israel. And so even when the north wind could not blow during the day, the corresponding *eis ratzon* on high found its earthly expression in the wind blowing at midnight.

### Tikkun Chatzot

This connects directly to the practice of *Tikkun Chatzot*. The understanding that night is generally an *eis din* while *chatzot* itself is an *eis ratzon* provides its theological foundation. Rashi references the *Gemara* in Berachot, where the northern wind blowing at midnight caused David Hamelech's harp to play, awakening him at *chatzot* for his *slichot* — which is precisely the wind described in this passage.

The question of how people before the modern era managed to rise at midnight without alarm clocks is itself illuminating. One answer may simply be that without artificial lighting, *chatzot* was understood more loosely as the deep of night. A more compelling answer, however, emerges from recent studies on natural human sleep patterns. When subjects are removed from artificial light and modern time structures, they tend to fall asleep at nightfall, sleep approximately four hours, then experience a natural period of wakefulness lasting roughly two hours, before returning to sleep. The suggestion is that *Tikkun Chatzot* was organically aligned with this natural awakening — a period of wakefulness in the middle of the night that was, in pre-modern life, entirely normal and expected.

---

## Mashoch Status

### Rav Huna's Ruling

The *Gemara* returns to *halacha*. Rav Huna states: *devar Torah, mashoch ochel biterumah* — biblically speaking, a *mashoch* — someone who underwent *brit milah* but subsequently reversed it through a procedure that stretches the remaining skin to recreate the appearance of a foreskin — is permitted to eat *terumah*. The foreskin was removed; whatever it looks like, he has had a *brit milah*. *Midivreihem gazru alav mipnei shenireh ke'arel* — the Rabbis, however, enacted a decree forbidding him, because he appears to be an *arel*. The prohibition is therefore *derabbanan*, not *deoraita*.

### Braita Contradiction

A challenge is immediately raised: *meisiv* — a *braita* states that a *mashoch tzarich sheyimal*, a *mashoch* must have a *brit milah* performed. The *Gemara* notes that this says no more than *derabbanan* — it does not prove a biblical prohibition.

*De-ka-remi mai ka-remi lei* — the *Gemara* expresses surprise: why was this even presented as a challenge? The *braita* does not say the *mashoch* is *assur* in *terumah*; it merely says *tzarich*, he must. *Tzarich* is notably soft language, far from the categorical formulation one would expect for a biblical prohibition.

### Language Analysis

The *Gemara* explains that the challenge arose not from the opening clause but from the *seifa* — the end of the *braita* — which had made it sound as though the obligation was biblical. Rabbi Yehuda says in the *seifa*: *lo yimal mipnei shesacanah hi lo* — such a person should not have a *brit milah* because it is dangerous. Rashi explains that attempting to circumcise skin that has been stretched risks turning the person into a *kerus shofcha*, causing damage to his genitalia and rendering him unable to have children.

The *amru lo* — the response to Rabbi Yehuda — is that many men underwent this procedure during the days of Ben Koziva and subsequently had children, demonstrating it was not categorically dangerous. The *braita* then invokes the verse *himol yimol* — the doubled language — which is taken to mean the obligation repeats even if the *brit milah* must be performed again, up to *afilu me'ah pe'amim*, even one hundred times. A second verse, *et briti heifar* — "he has violated my covenant" — is cited *lerabbot es hamashoch*, to include someone who has reversed his circumcision as having violated the covenant and being obligated to correct it.

The *Gemara* asks: *mai ve-omer* — why was the second verse necessary? Because one might say that *himol yimol* addresses only *tzitzin sheme'akvin*, fragments of foreskin that prevent the *milah* from being complete — meaning the doubled language teaches that one must go back and finish the job, not that a reversed *brit milah* requires repetition. The verse *et briti heifar* is therefore needed separately to include the *mashoch*.

The *Gemara* concludes that the Tannaic author (*hashas*) — an unusual term here applying to the author of the *braita* rather than to the *Mishnah* or *Gemara* — quoted these verses, and this gave the impression of a biblical obligation. In reality, *ve-lav hi mi-derabbanan ve-kra asmachta be-alma* — the prohibition is Rabbinic and the verse serves only as an *asmachta*.

### Historical Context

What emerges incidentally from this passage is a window into historical reality. The reference to *bimei Ben Koziva* — the period of Bar Kokhba — establishes that reversal of circumcision was practiced in two distinct historical contexts: the Hellenistic period and the Bar Kokhba period.

In the Hellenistic period, Jewish men who wished to assimilate into Greek culture sometimes underwent this procedure because the Greeks regarded circumcision as a disfigurement of the body. The *gymnasia*, central to Hellenistic civic and religious life, were venues of athletic competition conducted in the nude, making circumcision visible and socially stigmatizing for those seeking to integrate. In the Bar Kokhba period, the motivations may have been different — sometimes external pressures rather than voluntary assimilation. The fact that the *braita* mentions that many who underwent the re-circumcision during that period subsequently had children suggests that the *braita* addresses both those who reversed the reversal willingly and possibly those for whom even the restoration of circumcision may not have been entirely an act of free choice.

---

## Tumtum Status

### Tumtum Eating

The *Gemara* raises a challenge against Rav Huna's ruling from a *braita*: *tumtum eino ochel biterumah, nashav va'avadav ochlin* — a *tumtum*, someone whose genitalia are covered and whose sex is therefore indeterminate, cannot eat *terumah*, but his wives and slaves can eat.

The reason the *tumtum* himself cannot eat *terumah* requires unpacking. If he is the child of a *kohen*, he should presumably be permitted to eat *terumah* regardless of sex. The answer is that if he is male, he is necessarily an *arel*, since his genitalia are covered and he cannot have had a *brit milah*. Therefore, because he might be male — and thus an *arel* — he cannot eat *terumah*.

The *braita* continues: *mashoch*, a *mashoch*, *venolad keshu maul*, or someone born already circumcised — *harei eilu ochlin*, these may eat *terumah*. This appears to be a direct challenge to Rav Huna, since a *mashoch* is declared simply permitted, not merely Rabbinically restricted. Rashi, apparently working with a variant text, suggests reading this not as a *tiyuvta* — a refutation — of Rav Huna, but as a support: the *braita* establishes that a *mashoch* is at least *biblically* permitted, which is precisely what Rav Huna said. In the text as standardly printed, however, the *Gemara* reads it as *tiyuvta deRav Huna tiyuvta*.

The *braita* also addresses: *androgynos ochel biterumah* — an *androgynos*, one who has both male and female genitalia, may eat *terumah*. Since he has had a *brit milah* performed on his male anatomy and is the child of a *kohen*, he is not an *arel* and may eat *terumah*. However, *ve'eino ochel bekodshim* — he may not eat *kodshei kodashim*, which are restricted to male *kohanim*, since he might be female or a third category. The *tumtum*, by contrast, cannot eat *terumah* or *kodshim* — he cannot eat *terumah* because he might be a male *arel*, and he cannot eat *kodshim* because he might be female.

The *Gemara* then focuses on the line that a *tumtum*'s wives eat. This raises an immediate difficulty: *nashav detumtum mena leh* — how does a *tumtum* have wives? If he performed an act of *kiddushin* with a woman, this leads to the question: *eileima dekideish itata* — if he married a woman. A *braita* teaches: *tumtum shekideish, kidushav kidushin* — if a *tumtum* performs *kiddushin*, it takes effect, because out of doubt we must be concerned that he is male. Similarly, *nitkadesh* — if a man gave a ring to a *tumtum*, it too has binding implications, since the *tumtum* might be female.

However, the *Gemara* objects: that stringency applies *lechumra*, to be strict about the consequences — implications for relatives, the need for a *get*, *mamzerut* and so forth. But *lekula mi amrinan* — can we rule leniently and assume the *tumtum* is male such that his "wife" is the wife of a *kohen* and therefore permitted to eat *terumah*? *Safek isha hi* — she might not actually be his wife if he is female, and *ein isha mekaddeshet isha* — a woman cannot marry a woman.

### Abaye vs. Rava

Abaye resolves the problem by proposing: *kiveitzav mibachutz* — the case in the *braita* involves a *tumtum* whose testicles have descended visibly. This is not a total *tumtum* in the classic sense of complete indeterminacy; his maleness is established through visible anatomy even though a *brit milah* cannot be performed. He is thus a definite male, a definite *arel*, and his wife's status is certain. According to Abaye, the *braita* thus presents two distinct cases: the *reisha* describes this unusual *tumtum* who is a *vadai arel*, while the *seifa* — which repeats that a *tumtum* cannot eat *terumah* or *kodshim* — refers to the ordinary *tumtum* who is a *safek arel*.

Rava disagrees and offers a different reading of *nashav*. *Mai nashav* — what does "his women" mean? *Imo* — his mother. The word *isha* can mean wife or woman, and Rava reads *nashav* as referring not to wives but to the mother of the *tumtum*, who is married to a *kohen* and may eat *terumah* as long as there is a surviving child, regardless of that child's sex.

The *Gemara* objects that this is obvious — *pshita* — and asks what novel point Rava would be making. The *Gemara* answers: *mahu deteima, ei ma hazera molid umachil, she'ein molid eino machil* — one might have thought that only a child capable of procreation enables the mother to eat *terumah*, whereas a child who cannot reproduce does not. Since a *tumtum* was presumed incapable of having children, one might have concluded the mother cannot eat. The *Gemara* teaches otherwise — *kamashma lan*, she may eat regardless. Rava's explanation, the *Gemara* acknowledges, is a stretch, and so is Abaye's; both are reconstructions that do not settle comfortably as *peshat*.

The *Gemara* then addresses the later passage of the *braita* — *tumtum eino ochel lo biterumah velo bekodshim* — which repeats that a *tumtum* cannot eat *terumah*. According to Abaye this is elegantly coherent: the *reisha* addressed an unusual *tumtum* who is a *vadai arel*, while the *seifa* addresses the ordinary *tumtum* who is a *safek arel*, demonstrating that even a doubtful case disqualifies. According to Rava, the repetition of *tumtum* serves to explain the *reisha*: why did it originally say a *tumtum* cannot eat *terumah*? Because he might be a *safek arel*, and *arel eino ochel lo biterumah velo bekodshim*.

### Tumtum Safek Arel

The *Gemara*'s final resolution of the *tumtum* discussion is that the *tumtum* is excluded from *terumah* because he is a *safek arel*. This also explains the relationship between the two parts of the *braita*: the opening statement that a *tumtum* cannot eat *terumah* and the closing statement that underscores this — both are expressions of the same concern that he might be male and therefore an *arel*.

The outstanding question about whether a *mashoch* is Biblically or Rabbinically forbidden remains: the *braita* either wholly contradicts Rav Huna or — per Rashi's reading — supports him. Either way, the *braita* treats *mashoch* as a distinct category, and the language of *tzarich* rather than *assur* continues to suggest Rabbinic rather than Biblical status.

### Transgender Discussion

One might ask whether the *Gemara*'s discussion of *tumtum* — and especially the ruling that *tumtum shekideish kidushav kidushin, nitkadesh kidushav kidushin* — has any bearing on contemporary questions of transgender and intersex identity in *halacha*.

The *androgynos* tends to generate more significant discussion in this context than the *tumtum*. The *androgynos* raises the possibility, contemplated in Tannaic literature, that the *androgynos* is a *biryah bifnei atzmah* — a category unto itself, neither male nor female — which speaks directly to intersex questions and the possibility of recognizing a third halakhic sex category. The *tumtum*, by contrast, is fundamentally a case of *safek* — the sex is one thing or the other, we simply do not know which.

As for the transgender question: the *Gemara*'s framework rests on the assumption that sex is determined by genitalia. Most contemporary *poskim* hold that *halachic* status is determined by birth sex. The more complex question arises when a child is born with ambiguous genitalia requiring surgical determination of sex in infancy — that is, where there is a genuine indeterminate status at birth. In that case there may be more basis to argue that a subsequent determination, through medical intervention, affects *halachic* status. When an individual has a clearly defined birth sex and later transitions, the overwhelming *halachic* consensus is that status is determined by what one is at birth.

---

## Brit Milah Timing

### Rabbi Elazar Debate

The *Gemara* now explores whether the dispute about a *mashoch*'s status — biblical or Rabbinic — corresponds to a known Tannaic debate. A *braita* lists: a *mashoch*, a convert who was already circumcised at the time of conversion, an infant whose *brit milah* was not performed on day 8, and all other non-standard cases of *milah* — *einam nimolin ela bayom*, all of these must be circumcised specifically during the day.

Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon dissents: *bizmano eno nimol ela bayom, shelo bizmano nimol bayom ubalayla* — the requirement of daytime applies only to the eighth-day *brit milah*; if it is performed later than the prescribed time, it may be done either by day or by night.

### Daytime Requirement

The *Gemara* proposes that the underlying dispute concerns whether a *mashoch*'s obligation is *deoraita* — in which case it follows the rules of the classic *brit milah* and must be performed during the day — or *derabbanan*, in which case it might be permitted at night.

The *Gemara* immediately rejects this framing. *Ve-tisbara* — does this make sense? An infant whose *brit milah* is performed after day 8 — *katan she'avar zamano* — is surely a biblical obligation. No one would say *derabbanan*. So the question of day versus night clearly does not track the biblical/Rabbinic distinction, since the list contains both clearly biblical cases and clearly Rabbinic ones.

### Vav Drashah

Rather, *dechulei alma mashoch derabbanan* — let us accept that the obligation to re-circumcise a *mashoch* is Rabbinic. And *katan she'avar zamano deoraita*, that the infant after day 8 is biblical. The list contains both, and nevertheless the same question applies to all: does the Torah's requirement of *bayom* apply only to day 8 itself, or does it extend to any later performance?

The debate is resolved to be specifically about a textual *drashah*. The verse states *bayom hashmini yimol basar orlato* — on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised. The word *uvayom* — with the extra *vav* — is read by one opinion as teaching that even if it is not the eighth day, it must still be *yom*, daytime. The other opinion does not read the *vav* of *uvayom* as bearing this extended meaning.

### Notar Parallel

Rabbi Yochanan was sitting and expounding a parallel from the laws of *notar*. The verse *vehanotar bayom hashlishi baesh yisaref* — "and the remainder on the third day shall be burnt in fire" — establishes that the burning of *notar* must begin by day, specifically day 3. Rabbi Yochanan taught: *nosar bizmano eno nisraf ela bayom, shelo bizmano nisraf bayom ubalayla* — when the time first arrives it must be by day, but once the obligation has begun and extends beyond its initial moment, it continues into the night and is not limited to daytime thereafter.

### Rabbi Yochanan Exchange

This parallel was taken to support the position that *brit milah*, too, begins with a daytime requirement on day 8 but may be performed at night if delayed — like the view of Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon.

Rabbi Elazar then challenged Rabbi Yochanan directly: *ein li ela nimol lishmini she'eno nimol ela bayom* — I know only that the eighth-day *brit milah* must be during the day. *Minayin lerabot letisha le'asara leachad asar velishnem asar* — from where do I know that even if performed on day 9, 10, 11, or 12, it must still be during the day? *Talmud lomar uvayom* — the extra *vav* teaches that even on a later date, it is exclusively daytime.

The days 9 through 12 correspond to real cases. A baby born on *erev Shabbat bein hashmashot* presents a safek, and one must assume the later possibility, pushing the *brit milah* to day 9. If Shabbat itself was *bein hashmashot*, it becomes day 10. A Shabbat followed by *Yom Tov* produces day 11, and two days of *Rosh Hashanah* yield day 12.

Rabbi Elazar added that even the opinion that does not read *uvayom* as extending the daytime requirement must acknowledge the *vav-heh* of *vehanotar* — the longer prefix — which teaches that even when the obligation extends beyond its starting point, it remains tied to daytime. Rabbi Yochanan, confronted with this argument, fell silent. Afterward, when Rabbi Elazar had left, Rabbi Yochanan turned to Resh Lakish and said: *ra'iti le-Ben Pedat she-yoshev ve-doresh ke-Moshe mi-pi ha-Gevurah* — I saw Ben Pedat sitting and expounding like Moshe from the mouth of the Almighty. Whether this was admiration or mild criticism — he was doing what I was doing, but perhaps with greater authority — is not entirely clear.

Resh Lakish replied: *dideih?* — Do you think Rabbi Elazar composed that *drashah* on his own authority? *Matnitin hi* — it is a *braita*; he was quoting established teaching, not originating it. Rabbi Yochanan asked: *heicha tana leih* — where is this *braita* found? Resh Lakish answered: *be-Toras Kohanim* — in the Sifra.

---

## Brit Milah Timing (II)

### Toras Kohanim Study

Upon hearing this, Rabbi Yochanan went and immersed himself in *Toras Kohanim*: *tanyah be-tlata yomei* — he mastered the text in three days, *ve-savrah be-tlata yarchei* — and spent three months working through its analysis. This raises a remarkable question: had Rabbi Yochanan truly not previously learned *Toras Kohanim* with sufficient depth? Or had he not appreciated it as he should have? The implication seems to be that until this moment he had not engaged with the Sifra adequately, and the encounter with Rabbi Elazar's precise citation of a *braita* he did not recognize prompted him to undertake that study.

This naturally raises the question of when *Toras Kohanim* was committed to writing. The general assumption has been that any written form of *Torah she-ba'al peh* belongs to the Geonic period or later. However, Shlomo Naeh published a study examining the various and overlapping division systems of *Toras Kohanim* — its dual organization by *prakim* and *parshiyyot*, whose boundaries frequently do not align and seem to have been laid atop one another — and proposed that the length of each unit, across all divisions, falls within a specific range. That range corresponds to the accepted dimensions of scrolls in the Greco-Roman world, where scroll length was governed by practical considerations: too short meant too many scrolls; too long meant too much winding. Naeh argued that these divisions reflect the original written organization of the text, and that *Toras Kohanim* may be the earliest component of *Torah she-ba'al peh* to have been set down in writing — plausibly because the dominance of *Beit HaMikdash* culture preceded the Tannaic era, and the practical requirements of *avodah* demanded written precision. Scholarly opinion on his conclusions is divided, but the argument is considered compelling.

---

## Arel & Parah

### Rabbi Elazar Ruling

The *Gemara* turns to a new ruling: *amar Rabbi Elazar, arel shehizah hazaso kesherah* — an *arel* who performed the *hazaah*, the sprinkling of the *parah adumah* waters, his sprinkling is valid. The question is whether there is any reason to think an *arel* should be disqualified from performing this service.

### Tvul Yom Comparison

Rabbi Elazar offers a comparison: *mi havei mi-tvul yom* — is an *arel* any worse than a *tvul yom*? The practice of using a *tvul yom* to perform the *parah adumah* service was deliberately instituted by the *chachamim* to refute the *tzedukim*, who insisted the *kohen* performing the *parah* service must have waited until nightfall after immersion. The *chachamim* ensured the service was performed by one who had immersed that day but nightfall had not yet come — demonstrating the *tzedukim* were wrong. A *tvul yom*, who retains some residual *tumah* until nightfall, is *asur biterumah* yet *kasher beparah* — forbidden from eating *terumah* yet valid for the *parah adumah* service.

The *Gemara* challenges this comparison: *mah litvul yom sheken mutar bemaaser* — a *tvul yom* is permitted to eat *maaser*, whereas an *arel* may not be. This will be discussed in subsequent *sugyot*. But the *Gemara* immediately deflects this objection: *atu anachilah kamina* — who said we are talking about eating? *Ana lenegiah kamina* — the relevant category for performing the service is the ability to handle and touch, not the rules of eating.

The proper comparison, then, is a *kal vachomer*: a *tvul yom* who is *asur binegiah biterumah* — forbidden from touching *terumah* — is *mutar beparah*, valid for the *parah adumah* service. An *arel*, who is *mutar binegiah* — permitted to handle *terumah* — surely should be permitted for the *parah adumah* service, *ain din shemutar beparah*. This argument is confirmed by a *braita*: *arel shehizah hazaso kesherah, umaaseh hayah vehichshiru chachamim hazaso* — an *arel* who performed the *hazaah* is valid, and this was actually practiced and the *chachamim* ruled it acceptable.

### Arel Cannot Mix

A challenge is immediately raised: *tumtum shekidesh kiddushav pasul* — here *kiddush* refers not to marriage but to the *kiddush* of the *parah adumah*, the mixing of the ashes with water — a *tumtum* who performed this mixing has rendered it invalid, *mipnei shesafek arel*, because he might be an *arel*, and *arel pasul lekadesh* — an *arel* is invalid for the *kiddush*. This *braita* explicitly states that an *arel* cannot perform the *kiddush*, directly contradicting the ruling that he may perform the *hazaah*. The *Gemara* accepts for the moment that these two acts — *kiddush* and *hazaah* — are treated equivalently.

The *braita* continues: *androgynos shekidesh kiddushav kasher* — an *androgynos* who performed the *kiddush* is valid, because the concern about an *androgynos* is that he might be female, not that he might be an *arel*. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *af androgynos shekidesh kiddushav psulin, mipnei shesafek isha hi, ve'isha psulah melekadesh* — an *androgynos* is also invalid, because he might be a woman and a woman is invalid for this service. This frames the debate between Rabbi Yehuda and the *Tanna Kamma* about whether women may perform the *parah adumah* service.

A further *braita* states explicitly: *arel vesafek arel pasul melekadesh* — both a definite and a doubtful *arel* are invalid for the *kiddush* of the *parah adumah*.

### Rav Yosef Akiva

Rav Yosef offers a resolution: *hai tanna tanna devei Rabbi Akiva hu, demarbei leh le'arel ketamei* — this *tanna* who invalidates the *arel* belongs to the school of Rabbi Akiva, who treats the *arel* as equivalent to a *tamei*.

Rav Yosef's reference is to the beginning of the *perek*, where the source of the prohibition against an *arel* eating *terumah* was disputed. Rabbi Akiva derived it from the double expression *ish ish* in a verse about *tmei'im* — *lerabbot es ha'arel*, to include the *arel* in that verse's prohibition. From this, Rav Yosef draws the stronger conclusion: Rabbi Akiva treated the *arel* not merely as analogous to a *tamei* for purposes of *terumah*, but as equivalent to a *tamei* in terms of personal status across the board. Wherever a *tamei* is personally excluded — not in the sense of transferring *tumah*, but in terms of his own disqualification — an *arel* would be similarly disqualified. That is why Rabbi Akiva's school would invalidate an *arel* from performing the *parah adumah* service.

### Rava's Objection

Rava objects strongly: *hevei yasivina kamei d'Rav Yosef ve-kashyei li* — I sat before Rav Yosef and this troubled me. If there were truly a position of Rabbi Akiva treating the *arel* as a *tamei* in all areas, we should have found some statement in *Shas* that said *ha'arel ve-hatamei* cannot do such-and-such, accompanied by the attribution to Rabbi Akiva. The absence of any such formulation across the entirety of *Shas* argues strongly against this being Rabbi Akiva's position. *Lo ishtami tanna ve-lisni ha'arel ve-hatamei ve-leima Rabbi Akiva hi* — it would not have escaped notice; some *tanna* would have formulated the rule in that way.

### Arel Tamei Mishna

The *Gemara* responds: *ve-haktani ha'arel ve-hatamei paturim min hare'iyah* — there is a *Mishna* stating that an *arel* and a *tamei* are both exempt from *olat re'iyah*, the pilgrimage offering. Here we have exactly the formulation Rava said was missing — *ha'arel ve-hatamei* — grouped together.

The *Gemara* counters: *chutz mishum d'mais* — an *arel* is excluded from the *Beit HaMikdash* not because he has the status of a *tamei*, but simply because it is unseemly for someone who is an *arel* to present himself in the Temple. The grouping with *tamei* in that *Mishna* is incidental and does not reflect a principled equation of the two categories.

The *Gemara* acknowledges that this response somewhat undercuts Rava's objection — after all, the *Mishna* does say *ha'arel ve-hatamei* together, and the reason given for excluding the *arel* could itself reflect an assumption of equivalence. What remains is the fascinating Tannaic possibility — preserved in the school of Rabbi Akiva — that in terms of personal status, wherever a *tamei* is excluded, an *arel* is excluded as well. Rava's objection does not fully resolve the matter, and the question of whether this was Rabbi Akiva's position continues to resonate through the *sugya*.

---

## Parah Service Debate

### Disqualified List

The *Gemara* continues with the broader dispute about who may perform the various functions of the *parah adumah* service, following the principle *ve-azdu le-taimeihu* — Rabbi Yehuda and the *Rabbanan* proceed according to their respective reasoning.

A *braita* states: *hakol keshairin lekadesh* — anyone is eligible to perform the *kiddush* of the *parah adumah*, mixing the ashes with water, *chutz mi-cheresh shoteh ve-katan* — with the exception of a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor.

### Androgynos Status

Rabbi Yehuda differs: *machshir be-katan u-fosel be-ishah* — he validates the *katan* but invalidates the *ishah*, and by extension an *androgynos* who might be female. The *Rabbanan*, conversely, invalidate the *katan* but validate the *ishah*. An *androgynos* according to the *Rabbanan* is valid — he is excluded only if he might be female, and if his male nature is established his participation is permitted.

### Verses Asifah Kiddush

The debate between the *Rabbanan* and Rabbi Yehuda is rooted in the interpretation of two adjacent verses. One verse states *ve-asaf ish tahor* — "and a pure man shall gather" the ashes. The next verse states *ve-lakhu latamei me'afar sereifat hachatat* — "and they shall take for the *tamei* person from the ashes" — and place it with water. The principle derived is: *hanakh de-pasli be-asifah psulin be-kiddush* — those who are invalid for the gathering of the ashes are invalid for the mixing of the water; *hanakh de-keshairin be-asifah keshairin be-kiddush* — those valid for gathering are valid for mixing.

### Women Included

The *Rabbanan* argue as follows. The word *tahor* in *ve-asaf ish tahor* is understood to include women — there is a *drashah* elsewhere establishing this. Therefore, the *asifah* can be performed by any adult of sound mind, male or female, but not by a *katan* who lacks *da'at*. Since the same persons valid for *asifah* are valid for *kiddush*, a woman is valid for *kiddush* as well. A *katan* is excluded from both.

### Rabbi Yehuda Counter

Rabbi Yehuda counters: *amar lach* — if the intent of *ve-lakhu* were simply to preserve the same eligibility as *ve-asaf*, the verse should have said *ve-lakach* in the singular, parallel to *ve-asaf*. *Mai ve-laku* — why does the verse shift to the plural? This teaches that the category for *kiddush* is actually *broader* than for *asifah*: *de-afilu hanakh de-psulin hatam keshairin hacha* — even those invalid for *asifah*, such as a *katan*, are valid for *kiddush*. Rabbi Yehuda therefore holds that a *katan* may perform *kiddush*.

*Ei hachi, ishah nami?* — But if the plural *ve-laku* expands eligibility to include even those excluded from *asifah*, why is a woman still invalid? The answer comes from the verse continuing: *ve-nasan alav mayim chayim el keli* — "and he shall place living water into a vessel." The verse says *ve-nasan* in the masculine singular, not *ve-nasnah*, implicitly excluding a woman.

### Plural Laku Analysis

The *Rabbanan* respond to Rabbi Yehuda's grammatical argument. Had the verse said *ve-lakach ve-nasan* in the singular throughout, one might have concluded that the identical person who gathers must be the one who mixes, and that only one person may perform the entire act. The plural *ve-laku* teaches that multiple people may be involved in the gathering — or that different people may perform different stages. Had it continued *ve-lakhu ve-nasnu*, one might have required two people for the mixing as well. *Ve-lakhu ve-nasan* — the shift from plural to singular — teaches that even if multiple people gathered, a single person may perform the mixing. The grammatical movement from plural to singular is not meant to exclude women but to clarify the flexibility of personnel for each stage.

### Hizah Verse
