The *Gemara* concludes with the verse that grounds the initial argument about the *tvul yom* and the *hazaah*: *ve-hizah ha-tahor al ha-tamei* — "and the pure one shall sprinkle upon the impure one." *Tahor miklal she-hu tamei* — this is a remarkable *drashah*: the word *tahor*, pure, implies by contrast that this person had previously been *tamei* and went through a process of *taharah*. Yet the verse's qualification of *tahor* — rather than calling him simply pure — suggests that his *taharah* is not entirely complete. From here we derive that a *tvul yom*, who has immersed but whose *taharah* is not yet concluded until nightfall, is valid for performing the *hazaah* of the *parah adumah*. And from this teaching about the *tvul yom*, the *Gemara* earlier sought to establish that an *arel* could likewise perform the *hazaah* — though that proposal encountered the challenge of the *braita* invalidating an *arel*, attributed to the school of Rabbi Akiva, who equates the personal status of an *arel* with that of a *tamei*.

---

---

# Yevamot 73

## Arel & Maaser Intro

### Question Posed

The sugya opens with a new question posed to Rav Sheshet: *arel mahu bema'aser* — can an *arel*, an uncircumcised person, eat *ma'aser*? This question arises in the midst of the chapter of *Ha'Arel*, which deals broadly with the legal disabilities of an uncircumcised man. Just before this, the *gemara* had been discussing whether an *arel* can perform the sprinkling of the ashes of the *parah adumah*, a question in which two opinions were recorded. One view, attributed to Rabbi Akiva, held that wherever a *tamei* person is disqualified on account of personal status rather than the transmission of *tuma*, an *arel* is likewise disqualified. Rava disagreed, but the position remained significant. Now the discussion shifts to a new and somewhat more obscure question: can an *arel* eat *ma'aser*?

### Maaser Sheni Status

The *ma'aser* at issue is specifically *ma'aser sheni*, the second tithe, for a straightforward reason. *Ma'aser rishon* goes to the *Levi*, and *ma'aser ani* is a gift distributed to the poor — neither of these carries any inherent *kedusha*. They are simply agricultural gifts, and the produce itself has no sanctified status.

### Types of Maaser

*Ma'aser rishon* is given to the *Levi* and *ma'aser ani* to the *ani*; neither imposes restrictions on the produce itself. The only *ma'aser* that possesses a quality of *kedusha* is *ma'aser sheni*, and it is therefore the only one that could plausibly be subject to the same restrictions as *terumah*. We will also encounter, later in the discussion, the anomalous position of Rabbi Meir regarding *ma'aser rishon*, but the default assumption is that *ma'aser sheni* alone carries sanctity.

### Maaser Sheni Laws

What is the nature of *ma'aser sheni*'s *kedusha*? It must be eaten in Yerushalayim. If one does not wish to bring the produce itself to Yerushalayim, it may be redeemed — its sanctity is transferred onto coins, which are then brought to Yerushalayim and spent on food, drink, or anointing, that is, on things that are directly consumed or used by the body. According to Rashi, *ma'aser sheni* may only be used for these direct bodily benefits. It cannot be used in commercial transactions; it is not at the owner's disposal in the way ordinary property is.

### Kal Vachomer Analysis

Given this *kedusha*, the question takes shape. We already know that an *arel* cannot eat *terumah* — that is the very subject of this chapter, derived from a *pasuk*. The questioners now ask: do we extend this to *ma'aser sheni*? The *gemara* frames the question around a potential inference. We know that an *onen* — a mourner in the immediate period following a relative's death — cannot eat *ma'aser*, derived from the phrase *lo achalti be'oni mimenu* in the *viduy ma'aser*. From that, the *gemara* elsewhere learned that an *onen* cannot eat the *korban Pesach*. The logic moves from the lighter (*ma'aser*) to the weightier (*Pesach*): if even *ma'aser* bars an *onen*, certainly the *korban Pesach* does. Can we run this logic in reverse and say: since an *arel* cannot eat *Pesach*, therefore an *arel* cannot eat *ma'aser*?

The *gemara* raises the objection: *chamir mikal yalif, kal michamir lo yalif* — an inference from the lighter to the weightier works, but you cannot necessarily reverse it and infer from the weightier to the lighter. The *korban Pesach* is *kodshim*; it is far more weighty than *ma'aser sheni*. The fact that an *arel* is forbidden from *Pesach* does not by itself establish that he is forbidden from the lighter *ma'aser sheni*. Tosafot notes that the question may turn on whether the link between *Pesach* and *ma'aser* is a *kal vachomer* or a *hekesh* — a formal textual equation — since a *hekesh* is not directional in the same way.

### Rav Sheshet Answers

Rav Sheshet responds to those who asked him: *tenituha* — we have already learned the answer. He directs them to a *mishna* in *Bikkurim*.

---

## Mishna Distinctions

### Mishna Introduction

The *mishna* in *Bikkurim* lists the ways in which *terumah* and *bikkurim* share laws that do not apply to *ma'aser sheni*. Everything enumerated in this first list is a stringency or a property that *terumah* and *bikkurim* share and that *ma'aser sheni* does not.

### Bikkurim Hybridity

Before proceeding, it is worth noting the somewhat surprising structure of this *mishna*. Intuitively, one might have expected *bikkurim* to be grouped with *ma'aser sheni* rather than with *terumah*. Both *bikkurim* and *ma'aser sheni* involve bringing produce to a central location — *ma'aser sheni* to Yerushalayim, *bikkurim* to the *Beit HaMikdash* — and both involve a formal declaration. Yet the first list groups *bikkurim* with *terumah*. The reason is that *bikkurim*, like *terumah*, is given to the *kohen* and may only be eaten by *kohanim*; a non-*kohen* who eats it is liable. So *bikkurim* is genuinely a hybrid: it shares properties with *terumah* by virtue of its priestly ownership and restriction, and it shares properties with *ma'aser sheni* by virtue of being brought to Yerushalayim and requiring a declaration. This duality explains why both lists exist.

### Mita & Chomesh

*Haterumah vehabikkurim chayavim aleihem mita vechomesh.* Both *terumah* and *bikkurim* carry the penalty of *mita* — death at divine hands — for a non-*kohen* who eats them, as derived from *umetu vo ki yechalelehu*. *Bikkurim* derives this law from the linkage to *terumah* through the phrase *terumat yadecha*. Alongside *mita*, there is the *chomesh*: if a non-*kohen* eats *terumah* or *bikkurim* unintentionally, he must return the principal to the *kohen* plus an additional fifth. These penalties obviously have no application to *ma'aser sheni*, since non-*kohanim* eat *ma'aser sheni* routinely.

### Property Rights

The *mishna* continues: *shehen nichsei kohen* — they are the property of the *kohen*. This may seem self-evident given that one gives them to the *kohen*, but it carries a meaningful legal consequence that is actually a leniency of *terumah* and *bikkurim* relative to *ma'aser sheni*. Because *terumah* is the *kohen*'s property, he may dispose of it as he sees fit within the constraints of its sanctity. He can, for example, use it as a medium of exchange — bringing it to a shopkeeper and purchasing goods with it. The shopkeeper, a non-*kohen*, may not eat the *terumah*, but he can trade it onward to another *kohen* or otherwise realize its value. The *terumah* has a diminished market value because of its restrictions — it can only be consumed by *kohanim*, must be kept *tahor*, and so forth — but it is nonetheless treated as genuine transferable property. A *kohen* could even use *terumah* to effect *kiddushin* with a woman, telling her *harei at mekudeshet li b'terumah zo*, and once she is fully married and eats *terumah* as a *kohen*'s wife, that is valid.

### Maaser Restriction

*Ma'aser sheni* is fundamentally different. It cannot be used in *sechorah* — commercial transactions — at all. It may only be directly consumed: eaten, drunk, or used for anointing. The owner has no freedom to trade it or use it as a medium of exchange. There is a further, deeper question about *ma'aser sheni*'s legal status: Rabbi Meir holds that *ma'aser sheni* is *mammon gavoha* — it belongs to the divine realm — while the *Chachamim* hold it is *mammon hedyot* — the owner's property, albeit with *kedusha* and attendant restrictions. This debate has practical consequences for questions of ownership such as liability when an animal purchased with *ma'aser sheni* money causes damage. The point for our purposes is that whatever one holds about ultimate ownership, the prohibition against using *ma'aser sheni* in transactions is clear.

### Bittul Ratios

A further distinction: *v'erev echad bemeah* — *terumah* and *bikkurim* are only *batel*, nullified, when mixed with other produce if the other produce constitutes at least one hundred times their volume. This is a special stringency the Rabbis applied to *terumah* — and extended to *bikkurim* — as well as to *orlah* and *kilayim*. The rationale that Rashi implies is that *terumah* is so potent in concept, since even a tiny amount of *terumah* can exempt an enormous pile of grain from the obligation, that it does not become *batel* at normal proportions. One needs a hundred-to-one ratio. *Ma'aser sheni*, by contrast, follows the ordinary rule, which according to Rashi is *rov* — a simple majority — though perhaps *shishim* might apply as well.

### Hand Washing

*Teunim rechitzat yadayim* — eating *terumah* and *bikkurim* requires prior washing of hands. This is because the Rabbis declared hands to be at the level of *sheni letumah* — a secondary source of impurity — and since *terumah* can be made *tamei* by a *sheni*, one must wash before handling it. *Ma'aser sheni* does not carry this requirement, reflecting its lower level of *kedusha*.

### Tumah Levels

*Ve-ha'arev shemesh* — the requirement of waiting until nightfall after immersion. A person who was *tamei* and immersed in a *mikveh* is not fully *tahor* until sunset. In the interval — after immersion but before nightfall — he has the status of a *sheni letumah*. He may therefore not touch *terumah* or *bikkurim*, but he may touch *ma'aser sheni*.

The broader *halakhic* picture here is worth sketching. A primary source of *tuma* — an *av hatuma*, such as a dead animal — can make a person, food, or a vessel *tamei*. A person so made *tamei* becomes a *rishon letumah* and can in turn make food *tamei*. That food becomes a *sheni*, and a *sheni* can make *terumah tamei*, rendering it a *shlishi*. A *shlishi* in *terumah* can then make *kodshim tamei*. This chain of *tuma* transmission operates precisely because *terumah* has a higher level of *kedusha* — it is restricted to *kohanim*, and violating it carries *mita*. *Ma'aser sheni* does not have this elevated *kedusha*, and therefore a *sheni letumah* cannot make *ma'aser sheni tamei* in the same way. The hand-washing and *ha'arev shemesh* requirements follow from this: since one's hands have the status of *sheni*, and since a *sheni* can make *terumah* into a *shlishi*, one washes before touching *terumah*. This does not apply to *ma'aser sheni*.

### Burning When Tamei

The final distinction in this first list, and one that will receive extensive analysis later: when *terumah* becomes *tamei*, the correct procedure is to burn it and derive benefit from it as fuel — the classic case discussed in the *mishna* of *Bameh Madlikin* involving *shemen sereifa*. By contrast, when *ma'aser sheni* or *bikkurim* becomes *tamei*, one may not burn it for fuel and benefit from it. Similarly, eating *tamei* *ma'aser* incurs *malkot*, lashes, since it violates a *lo ta'aseh*, whereas eating *tamei* *terumah* does not incur lashes.

---

## Non-Exhaustive Lists

### Arel Absence

The *gemara* now attempts to draw a proof from this *mishna*. If an *arel* is permitted to eat *ma'aser sheni*, then the prohibition against an *arel* eating *terumah* and *bikkurim* — which is the subject of this entire chapter — would constitute another point of distinction between *terumah*/*bikkurim* on the one hand and *ma'aser sheni* on the other. The *mishna* could have said: *arel assur bahem*, an *arel* is forbidden in *terumah* and *bikkurim*, *mah she'ein kein bema'aser*, but not in *ma'aser sheni*. Since the *mishna* did not include this as a point of difference, the implication seems to be that an *arel* cannot eat *ma'aser sheni* either — otherwise it would have been mentioned as a distinction. This appears to be a strong proof.

The *gemara*'s response: *tana veshayar* — the list is not exhaustive; things were left off. One cannot infer anything from an absence in an incomplete list. But this requires substantiation. *Uma'i shayar de-hai shayar* — what else was left off, such that we can say this too was left off? The *gemara* needs to identify at least two omissions to establish that the list is genuinely non-exhaustive, since if only one item were missing, one should simply have included it.

### Second List

The *gemara* points to the *seifa* — the second half of the *mishna*, which lists the ways in which *ma'aser sheni* and *bikkurim* are similar to each other and different from *terumah*. This second list includes: the requirement to bring them to a specific place — *ma'aser sheni* to Yerushalayim, *bikkurim* to the *Beit HaMikdash*; the requirement of *viduy*, a formal declaration — the *bikkurim* declaration of *Arami oved avi*, and the *ma'aser sheni* declaration including *lo achalti be'oni mimenu*; the prohibition against an *onen* eating them, derived from *lo achalti be'oni mimenu*; and the requirement of *biur* — clearing them out at the end of the three-year cycle.

Regarding the last two items, the *mishna* records a dispute. The *tanna kamma* holds that the *onen* and *biur* restrictions, which clearly apply to *ma'aser sheni*, also apply to *bikkurim*, since the *pasuk lo tuchal le'echol bish'arecha* links *ma'aser sheni* and *bikkurim* together. Rabbi Shimon disagrees and exempts *bikkurim* from both, holding that *bikkurim*'s fundamental identity is that of *terumah*, not *ma'aser*.

### Omitted Items

The *gemara* observes that this second list also left things off — and not just one thing. Two items that belong on this list, in that they apply to *ma'aser sheni* (and arguably to *bikkurim*) but not to *terumah*, are missing. First: *assur leva'er mehem betumah* — when *ma'aser sheni* becomes *tamei*, one may not burn it for fuel, whereas *terumah* that becomes *tamei* is burned. Second: *ve'ochlan betumat atzman lokeh* — if one eats *tamei* *ma'aser sheni*, one receives *malkot*, lashes, since the prohibition derives from *lo tuchal le'echol bish'arecha*, a *lo ta'aseh*, whereas the prohibition on eating *tamei* *terumah* is derived from a positive commandment and therefore does not carry lashes.

Both of these omissions are rooted in the same *pasuk* — *lo bi'arti mimennu betamei*, from the *viduy ma'aser*. That verse teaches: do not consume it in a state of *tuma*, whether you were *tamei* and the *ma'aser* was *tahor*, or you were *tahor* and the *ma'aser* was *tamei*. The word *bi'arti* encompasses both burning for fuel and eating. Neither applies to *tamei* *ma'aser sheni*, in stark contrast to *terumah*.

### Inference Prevention

The demonstration that the second list is also non-exhaustive establishes the general point: these are not complete enumerations. Both the first list (*terumah* and *bikkurim* against *ma'aser sheni*) and the second list (*ma'aser sheni* and *bikkurim* against *terumah*) leave things off. One may therefore not infer from the absence of a distinction that no such distinction exists. The failure to mention the *arel* as a point of difference between *terumah*/*bikkurim* and *ma'aser sheni* proves nothing. Perhaps an *arel* can eat *ma'aser sheni*, and the *mishna* simply left that distinction off an incomplete list.

To make this vivid: the entire thrust of the attempted proof was that since the *mishna* did not say "an *arel* cannot eat *terumah* and *bikkurim* but can eat *ma'aser sheni*," this must mean the *arel* is treated the same way by *ma'aser sheni*. The *gemara* dismantles this inference by showing that both lists are admittedly truncated, and therefore silences cannot bear the weight of legal conclusions.

---

## Onen & Biur

### Pasuk Linkage

The *gemara* now returns to examine the debates embedded in the *mishna*'s second list. It asks: what is the source for the *tanna kamma*'s view that the *onen* and *biur* rules apply to *bikkurim* as well as to *ma'aser sheni*? The answer is the *pasuk*: *lo tuchal le'echol bish'arecha ma'aser deganecha tiroshcha veyitzharecha u'terumat yadecha*. This verse prohibits eating certain things "in your gates" — meaning outside Yerushalayim. Taken at face value the verse is puzzling, since *ma'aser rishon* is given to the *Levi* in one's own city and *terumah* is eaten by *kohanim* throughout the land. The *gemara* therefore clarifies: the *ma'aser* that cannot be eaten "in your gates" is *ma'aser sheni*, which must be eaten in Yerushalayim. And the *terumat yadecha* refers to *bikkurim*, as the tradition has it: *terumat yadecha elu bikkurim*. The verse thus links *ma'aser sheni* and *bikkurim* together.

### Tanna Kamma Onen

From this linkage, the *tanna kamma* derives: just as an *onen* cannot eat *ma'aser* — as stated explicitly in the *viduy* declaration *lo achalti be'oni mimennu* — so too an *onen* cannot eat *bikkurim*, since they are joined in the same *pasuk*.

### Rabbi Shimon Onen

Rabbi Shimon rejects this extension. His argument is that *bikkurim*'s identity is fundamentally that of *terumah* — *terumah karinah Rachmana*. Although *bikkurim* appears in the same verse as *ma'aser sheni*, that linkage reflects the coincidence of both being brought to Yerushalayim, not a substantive equation of their *kedusha*. The basic character of *bikkurim* — given to the *kohen*, eaten only by *kohanim*, carrying *mita* and *chomesh* — aligns it with *terumah*. And *terumah* is permitted to an *onen*. Therefore *bikkurim* is also permitted to an *onen*. It is worth noting that Rabbi Shimon's position is the more intuitively compelling one: since every substantive legal property of *bikkurim* tracks *terumah*, it is difficult to uproot it from that identity on the basis of a single verse that places it in proximity to *ma'aser sheni*.

### Biur Debate

The same logical structure governs the *biur* dispute. The *tanna kamma* holds that just as *ma'aser sheni* must be cleared from the house in the third year of the *shemita* cycle — derived from *bi'arti hakodesh min habayit* — so too must *bikkurim*, on the basis of the same *pasuk* linkage. Rabbi Shimon exempts *bikkurim* from *biur*, for the same reason: *bikkurim*'s identity is *terumah*, and *terumah* has no such *biur* requirement. Rabbi Shimon adopts a minimalist stance throughout — he will link *bikkurim* to *ma'aser sheni* only where the connection is entirely obvious, and in all other respects he insists on *bikkurim*'s identity as *terumah*.

---

## Lo Ba'er Baraita

### Lo Ba'arti Meaning

The *gemara* now examines the source for the two items omitted from the second list — the prohibition on burning *tamei* *ma'aser sheni* and the prohibition (with attendant *malkot*) on eating it when *tamei*. A *baraita* is cited in which Rabbi Shimon expounds: *lo bi'arti mimennu betamei* — I did not consume it in a state of *tuma*. This covers two scenarios: *bein she-ani tamei v'hu tahor*, whether I was *tamei* and the *ma'aser* was *tahor*, or *bein she-ani tahor v'hu tamei*, whether I was *tahor* and the *ma'aser* itself had become *tamei*. The word *bi'arti* is understood to include both burning for fuel and eating. Therefore: if the *ma'aser* became *tamei*, one may not burn it for fuel and may not eat it. One must simply set it aside and allow it to decompose.

### Tumah Types

The *baraita* then proceeds to address the prohibition on eating *ma'aser* when *tamei*, and at this point the *gemara* interrupts. The *baraita* poses the question *va'hiecha muzhar al achilato* — how do we know eating *tamei* *ma'aser* is prohibited? — and answers *eini yodea*, I do not know, before citing the *pasuk* as the source. The *gemara* interjects: what do you mean you don't know? The case where a person is *tamei* and the *ma'aser* is *tahor* is written explicitly in the Torah — *nefesh asher tiga bo vetame'ah ad ha'erev velo yokhal min hakodashim* — a *tamei* person may not eat *kodashim*, and *ma'aser sheni* is clearly included in *kodashim*.

The *gemara* then clarifies the *baraita*'s actual question: *tumat atzmo minalan* — what the *baraita* was asking about is not the case where the person is *tamei* but the *ma'aser* is *tahor*; that is well established. The question is: how do we know that one may not eat *ma'aser sheni* that is itself *tamei*, when the person is *tahor*? This is a different and subtler question, since when an object becomes *tamei* it has lost its pristine state and one might have thought the prohibition is less severe.

### Eating Restriction

The answer comes from the *pasuk* *lo tuchal le'echol bish'arecha ma'aser deganecha* — you may not eat your *ma'aser* in your gates. This is then read in light of another verse: *bish'arecha tochelenu* — you shall eat it in your gates — which appears in the context of *kodashim* that became *pasul* and were redeemed. The Torah says that once redeemed, such *kodashim* may be eaten in your gates, *hatamei vehatahur yachdav*, by the *tamei* person and the *tahor* person together, just as one eats a deer or an ibex — animals that can never be *korbanot* and hence carry none of the restrictions of *kodashim*. The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught this explicitly: even a *tamei* and *tahor* person can eat this redeemed *kodshim* from the same plate without concern.

The logic of the derivation is elegant. Eating "in your gates" in the Torah represents a mode of unrestricted consumption: outside Yerushalayim, without the limitations of *kedusha*, including the ability to eat even in a state of *tuma*. When the Torah says about *ma'aser sheni* *lo tuchal le'echol bish'arecha*, it is not merely saying "don't eat it outside Yerushalayim." It is also saying: do not eat your *ma'aser sheni* in the manner of eating "in your gates" — do not eat it as you eat things that carry no *kedusha*, do not eat it *betumah*. Therefore *ma'aser sheni* that has itself become *tamei* may not be eaten by a *tahor* person.

### Terumah Contrast

This rule — do not burn *tamei* *ma'aser sheni* for fuel, do not eat it when it is *tamei* — stands in contrast to *terumah*. When *terumah* becomes *tamei*, the established practice is precisely to burn it and benefit from it as fuel. How do we know this? The *gemara* cites Rabbi Abahu citing Rabbi Yochanan, who derives it from *mimennu* in the verse *lo bi'arti mimennu betamei*: the word *mimennu* — "from it" — implies a limitation, indicating that while you cannot burn *ma'aser sheni* when it is *tamei*, you can burn oil of *terumah* that has become *tamei*.

---

## Kal Vachomer

### KV Objection

This ruling raises an immediate difficulty. *Ma'aser sheni* is the lighter item, and yet one cannot burn it when it is *tamei*. *Terumah* is weightier — restricted to *kohanim*, carrying *mita* and *chomesh* — and yet one may burn it. Is this not backwards? Someone raises the *kal vachomer*: if *ma'aser*, which is the lighter item (*ma'aser hakal*), may not be burned when *tamei* because the Torah says *lo bi'arti mimennu betamei*, how much more so should *kodshim* — which is weightier — not be burnable when *tamei*?

### Counter KV

But if *kodshim* cannot be burned, then *terumah* should also be caught in the same *kal vachomer*: if *ma'aser* cannot be burned, *terumah* cannot either, since *terumah* is more weighty than *ma'aser*.

### Mimenu Exclusion

The response: *haktiv mimennu* — the Torah writes *mimennu*, "from it," which must be limiting something. The word implies that while you cannot burn *ma'aser* when *tamei*, something else can be burned. The question is then *uma ra'ita* — given that the *kal vachomer* would extend to everything more weighty than *ma'aser*, and given that *mimennu* must exclude something, what justifies excluding *terumah* and permitting its burning while leaving *kodshim* subject to the prohibition?

### Weighting Logic

The *gemara* answers: it makes sense not to exclude *kodshim* from the prohibition because *kodshim* is the weightier item overall, and we do not extend leniencies to weightier items. *Terumah*, though weightier than *ma'aser sheni*, is lighter than *kodshim*, so it is *terumah* that receives the leniency of being burnable when *tamei*.

### Kodashim Weights

How do we know *kodshim* is weightier than *terumah*? The *gemara* uses the mnemonic *pinkhas* — spelling out the stringencies of *kodshim*: *pigul* (improper intent during the *avodah* renders it forbidden), *nosar* (leaving it past its time), the fact that it is brought within the *Beit HaMikdash* itself, *meila* (misuse of *kodshim* is a distinct prohibition), *kares* (eating *tamei* *kodshim* incurs *kares*), and it is *assur le'onein* — forbidden to an *onen*.

### Terumah Weights

The *gemara* then entertains the counterargument: *terumah* has its own stringencies. The mnemonic *machpaz*: *mita* — a non-*kohen* who eats *terumah* is liable to death at divine hands; *chomesh* — he must add a fifth if he ate it unintentionally; *ein lah pidyon* — *terumah* cannot be redeemed, whereas consecrated animals that acquire a *mum* can be redeemed; *asurah lezarim* — while some *korbanot* such as *shelamim* may be eaten by non-*kohanim*, *terumah* may never be eaten by a non-*kohen*. These are genuine stringencies of *terumah* that *kodshim* does not share.

### Kares Priority

The *gemara* resolves the tension in two ways. First, quantitatively: *hanech nefishan* — the stringencies of *kodshim* are more numerous, six to four. Second, and more incisively: *kares adifa* — *kares* is a more severe punishment than *mita biyedei shamayim*. The fact that eating *tamei* *kodshim* incurs *kares*, while eating *terumah* incurs only *mita biyedei shamayim*, decisively tips the scales in favor of *kodshim* being weightier overall. Therefore, the leniency to burn when *tamei* is given to *terumah* — which is the intermediate item, less weighty than *kodshim* but more weighty than *ma'aser sheni* — and not to *kodshim*.

---

## Non-Exhaustive Lists (II)

### Rav Ashi's Proof

Rav Ashi now offers a more economical solution to the earlier proof attempt. Recall that the entire discussion of the second list and its omissions was mobilized to show that the first list is non-exhaustive — that the absence of *arel* from the list of distinctions between *terumah*/*bikkurim* and *ma'aser sheni* cannot be taken as proof that an *arel* may eat *ma'aser sheni*. Rav Ashi points out that one need not look to the second list at all. Even from the beginning of the first list — *mereisha* — one can see that things were left off. *Midelo katani venohagin bish'ar shenei shavua* — the *mishna* did not say that *terumah* and *bikkurim* apply in all years of the *shemita* cycle while *ma'aser sheni* applies only in the third and sixth years. That is a major point of difference and it was not listed. *Ve'ein lahem pidyon* — nor did the *mishna* say that *terumah* and *bikkurim* cannot be redeemed, while *ma'aser sheni* can be redeemed by transferring its *kedusha* to coins. Both of these are prominent distinctions between *terumah*/*bikkurim* and *ma'aser sheni*, and neither appears on the list. *Shema mina* — one learns from this, already from the beginning of the *mishna*, that the list is non-exhaustive. The entire detour through the second list, while illuminating, was unnecessary for this specific point.

---

## Baraita on Arel

### Baraita Text

The *gemara* now brings a stronger challenge. *Ta shema* — come and hear. A *baraita* teaches that in the case of *nishtayeru tzitzin hame'akvin et hamilah* — pieces of flesh that should have been removed in the *brit mila* were left in place — the person is still considered an *arel*. And the *baraita* then enumerates what this person may not eat: *harei zeh eino ochel lo bitrumah velo bePesach velo bekodshim velo bema'aser*. He may not eat *terumah*, he may not eat *Pesach*, he may not eat *kodshim*, and he may not eat *ma'aser*. This is an apparently explicit source that an *arel* cannot eat *ma'aser*. The *gemara* asks: does this not mean *ma'aser* of grain, i.e., *ma'aser sheni*?

### Maaser Behema

The *gemara* offers a first deflection: *ma'aser behemah* — the *ma'aser* referred to is the animal tithe, which is a *korban*. When an animal is designated as *ma'aser behemah*, it has the status of *kodshim*. So the *baraita* is not adding a new category at all; it is simply another way of saying the *arel* cannot eat *kodshim*. The *gemara* makes this explicit: *ma'aser behemah hainu kodshim* — the animal tithe is *kodshim* and was already covered.

### Maaser Rishon

But this explanation is strained. If *ma'aser behemah* is already subsumed under *kodshim*, why mention it separately? The *gemara* points out that this problem mirrors an analogous one in the *baraita* itself: *mi lo tenan Pesach vetani kodshim* — the *baraita* already mentions *Pesach* and also mentions *kodshim*. Isn't *Pesach* already subsumed under *kodshim*? The *gemara* answers that both are necessary: had the *baraita* mentioned only *Pesach*, one might have thought the prohibition on an *arel* applies only to *Pesach* specifically, where the *pasuk* states *kol arel lo yokhal bo*; had it mentioned only *kodshim*, one might have thought the word *kodshim* refers specifically to *Pesach*. Mentioning both clarifies that *kodshim* means all *korbanot* and that *Pesach* is merely one instance. But this analysis makes the redundancy of *ma'aser behemah* all the more glaring.

### Rabbi Meir View

The *gemara* therefore offers a second explanation: the *ma'aser* in the *baraita* refers to *ma'aser rishon* according to the position of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Meir holds the anomalous view that just as *terumah* is forbidden to non-*kohanim*, *ma'aser rishon* is forbidden to non-*Leviyim*. Under this view, *ma'aser rishon* carries a restriction analogous to that of *terumah*, confining its consumption to the *Levi* just as *terumah* is confined to the *kohen*. The *gemara* suggests that the *baraita* may be invoking this position: an *arel* cannot eat *ma'aser rishon* according to Rabbi Meir, for the same reason he cannot eat *terumah* — these are items restricted to a particular class of people and the *arel*'s status creates an additional disqualification.

### Inconclusive

The *gemara*'s conclusion is notably tentative. Even with the *baraita* in hand — which states explicitly that an *arel* may not eat *ma'aser* — it has not been definitively established that an *arel* cannot eat *ma'aser sheni*. The *baraita* can be explained as referring either to *ma'aser behemah* (a form of *kodshim*) or to *ma'aser rishon* according to Rabbi Meir's distinctive position that treats it similarly to *terumah*. Neither of these is *ma'aser sheni*. The original question — *arel mahu bema'aser* — thus remains unresolved, and the *gemara* leaves it so.

---

---

# Yevamot 74

## Arel & Maaser Sheni

### Two Maasrot

The question before the *gemara* is whether an *arel* — an uncircumcised man — is permitted to eat *maaser sheni*. A *braita* had already been cited stating that an *arel* is forbidden in *maaser*, and the *gemara* attempted to reinterpret this as referring to *maaser behema* — the tithe of animals — rather than the grain tithe. That reading was clearly strained. The *gemara* then fell back on a second escape: the *braita* might be referring to *maaser rishon* according to the position of Rabbi Meir, who holds that *maaser rishon* is forbidden to *zarim* and is thus treated analogously to *teruma*. This is admittedly a radical position of Rabbi Meir, but it is the vehicle the *gemara* uses to avoid conceding that an *arel* is forbidden in *maaser sheni*.

### Chiya Bar Rav

The *gemara* presses further: come and hear. Rabbi Chiya bar Rav of Difti teaches a *braita*: an *arel* is forbidden in two *maasrot* — *shtei maasrot*. The natural reading is that one of these is *maaser dagan*, the grain tithe, and the other is *maaser behema*, the animal tithe — the latter being *kodshim* and thus clearly forbidden. If so, the prohibition on the grain tithe establishes that an *arel* is forbidden in *maaser sheni*.

### Maaser Rishon Defense

The *gemara* deflects once more: here too, the reference is to *maaser rishon* and *maaser behema*, invoking Rabbi Meir's position. The *braita* still does not compel the conclusion that *maaser sheni* is forbidden to an *arel*.

### Maaser Rishon Again

The same move is made a second time: whenever a *braita* appears to establish the prohibition of an *arel* in the grain tithe, the *gemara* reasserts that the reference is to *maaser rishon* according to Rabbi Meir. Each iteration of this defense holds off the proof but is clearly makeshift.

### Onen Pattern

The *gemara* now introduces a structurally elegant *braita* that compares three categories of persons — *onen*, *tvul yom*, and *mechusar kippurim* — against three categories of sanctity: *maaser* (which, as will become clear from the cases, can only mean *maaser sheni*), *teruma*, and *para aduma*. The pattern is a rotating one: each of the three persons is forbidden in exactly one of the three categories and permitted in the other two, and the forbidden category differs for each. This creates a kind of three-way matrix in which every combination is covered.

### Onen Rules

An *onen* — a mourner before the burial of his close relative — is forbidden in *maaser*, as the verse states *lo achalti be'oni mimenu*, and permitted in *teruma* and *para aduma*. The permission to eat *teruma* was established earlier in the *sugya*. The permission to perform the *avoda* of the *para aduma* — including the burning and the sprinkling — follows from the fact that, although an *onen* cannot eat *kodshim*, the *para aduma* is not technically a *korban*; it belongs to the category of *bedek habayit* and is not treated as a sacrificial offering in the usual sense.

### Tosafot Onen

Rashi notes parenthetically that the permission of an *onen* to perform the *para aduma* follows by *kal vachomer*: if a *tvul yom* can do so, certainly an *onen* can. Tosafot pushes back on the logic of this inference: it does not always follow that leniency in one area implies leniency in another, given that the *onen* is actually more restricted than the *tvul yom* regarding *maaser*, while the *tvul yom* is more restricted than the *onen* regarding *teruma*. Tosafot therefore clarifies that the only prohibition on an *onen* in the context of *maaser sheni* is eating it — *le'achilah* — whereas touching *maaser sheni* is permitted for both; the *onen*'s permission to perform the *para aduma* speaks to physical involvement, not consumption, and the two categories therefore cannot be simply compared.

### Onen Logic

Why should an *onen* be more restricted regarding *maaser sheni* than *teruma*, given that *teruma* is generally the more stringent category? The answer lies in the character of *maaser sheni*: it must be brought to Jerusalem and consumed there, making it structurally analogous to a *korban*. Just as an *onen* is forbidden in a *korban*, he is forbidden in *maaser sheni*. *Teruma*, by contrast — though possessing greater *kedusha* — is eaten anywhere, and thus lacks the *korban*-like quality that triggers the *onen*'s restriction.

### Tvul Yom Rules

A *tvul yom* — one who has immersed in a *mikvah* but for whom nightfall has not yet arrived — is forbidden in *teruma*, because a *tvul yom* has the status of a *sheni* and would render *teruma* a *shlishi*, disqualifying it. He is, however, permitted to perform the *avoda* of the *para aduma* — this is in fact the famous *halakha* that the *para aduma* was specifically performed by a *tvul yom*, demonstrating that *tahor min hakhlal de'ika tamei*. He may also eat *maaser sheni*.

### Mechusar Kippurim

A *mechusar kippurim* — one who has immersed and for whom nightfall has passed, but who has yet to bring the required *korban* — represents a weaker degree of residual impurity than the *tvul yom*. He is forbidden in *para aduma* but permitted in *teruma* and *maaser sheni*. This requires explanation: if the *tvul yom* — who is more restricted than the *mechusar kippurim* in most respects — can perform the *para aduma*, why can the *mechusar kippurim* not?

### Tvul Yom Para

The resolution is that the *tvul yom* who may perform the *para aduma* is one whose remaining purification process consists entirely of waiting — no additional action, no *korban*, is pending. For instance, someone who touched a carcass, immersed, and need only wait for nightfall: that person may perform the *para aduma*. But a *tvul yom* who still has a *korban* to bring — someone in a longer purification process such as a *zavah* — cannot perform the *para aduma* even after immersion, and cannot do so even after nightfall until the *korban* is brought. When we say the *tvul yom* can perform the *para aduma*, we mean specifically the person whose entire remaining process will resolve on its own within a matter of hours.

### Missing Pattern

Now the *gemara* turns to use this *braita* as a proof regarding the *arel*. If it were true that an *arel* can eat *maaser sheni*, the *braita*'s rotating pattern would have included a fourth configuration: an *arel* is forbidden in *teruma* — which we know — permitted in *para aduma* — since there is no reason to exclude him — and permitted in *maaser sheni*. This configuration would have fit perfectly into the pattern being elaborated, yet it is conspicuously absent. The omission implies that an *arel* cannot be described as forbidden in *teruma* but permitted in *maaser sheni*, because in fact he is forbidden in *maaser sheni* as well.

### Rabbi Akiva Defense

The *gemara* deflects once more: this *braita* might reflect the position of Rabbi Akiva, who — as will be elaborated — treats an *arel* as equivalent to a *tamei* person in all matters where personal status creates a prohibition. According to Rabbi Akiva, an *arel* would also be forbidden in *para aduma*, since the verse states *ve'asaf ish tahor*, and the *arel* is equated to one who is not *tahor*. If so, the configuration of *arel* being permitted in *para aduma* and *maaser sheni* but forbidden only in *teruma* was never available to the *braita* — and its absence therefore proves nothing about *maaser sheni*.

## Rabbi Akiva Arel

### Ish Ish

With Rabbi Akiva's position now brought into focus, the *gemara* cites his derivation explicitly: *Rabbi Akiva omer, ish ish le'rabos es ha'arel* — the doubled language of *ish ish* in the verse about the *tamei* person who may not eat *teruma* is used by Rabbi Akiva to include the *arel* in that prohibition. The broader implication drawn from this is that wherever a *tamei* person is forbidden due to his personal status — not merely because of the risk of contaminating food, but because of who he is — an *arel* is likewise forbidden.

### Yosef HaBavli

The *gemara* now asks: who is the *tanna* who disagrees with Rabbi Akiva and holds that an *arel* is not equivalent to a *tamei*? The answer is the *tanna kamma* of the *braita* of Rabbi Yosef haBavli.

### Para Srifa

The relevant *braita* states: *sreifat onen u'mechusar kippurim kesheira* — the *tanna kamma* holds that both the *onen* and the *mechusar kippurim* are valid performers of the burning of the *para aduma*. Rabbi Yosef haBavli, however, distinguishes: an *onen* is valid (*kesheira*), but a *mechusar kippurim* is invalid (*pesulah*). Both positions concern which residual-impurity categories are excluded from the *para aduma* by the verse's requirement of *ish tahor*.

### Rashi Inference

Rashi infers from this debate a parallel controversy about the *arel*: just as the *tannaim* disagree about whether a *mechusar kippurim* may perform the *para aduma*, so too they would disagree about whether an *arel* — given his contested equivalence to a *tamei* — may perform it.

### Tosafot Object

Tosafot objects to Rashi's inference on logical grounds: the dispute over *mechusar kippurim* concerns the extent of his residual impurity, while the dispute over the *arel* concerns a categorically different question — whether he is classified as *tamei* at all. These are independent considerations, and one does not follow from the other. Indeed, Tosafot appears to have had a different text of the *braita* that explicitly mentioned *arel* rather than leaving it to inference by analogy. Our standard text does not mention *arel* directly, and Rashi's inference by analogy is what fills the gap — but it is an inference Tosafot explicitly rejects.

## Gezeira Shava

### Mimenu Link

Beyond the series of *braitot*, Rabbi Yitzchak independently establishes that an *arel* is forbidden in *maaser*. He derives this through a *gezeirah shavah* on the word *mimenu*: in *maaser* the verse states *lo achalti be'oni mimenu*, and in *pesach* the Torah states *al tochlu mimenu na* and *lo totiru mimenu ad boker*. Just as *mimenu* at *pesach* implies an *arel* is forbidden — since he may not eat the *korban pesach* — so too *mimenu* at *maaser* implies an *arel* is forbidden there as well.

### Weight Challenge

The *gemara* immediately raises a challenge: if the word is not free — *mufneh* — at both ends of the *gezeirah shavah*, the analogy is vulnerable to a logical rebuttal. In this case, the rebuttal is compelling: *pesach* is weightier than *maaser*, since one is liable for *pesach* meat on account of *pigul*, *notar*, and *tumah* — none of which apply to *maaser sheni*. If the *gezeirah shavah* is not ironclad — because the word is not free — one could argue that the severity of *pesach* accounts for the restriction and it cannot be extended to the lighter *maaser*.

### Free Words

The resolution lies in establishing that the word *mimenu* appears three times at *pesach*, and at least one of those appearances is free — not required by the grammatical or legal demands of the verse. It is the *mufneh* — free — word that enables a valid *gezeirah shavah*.

### Tochlu Use

The first occurrence of *mimenu* at *pesach* is in the phrase *al tochlu mimenu na* — do not eat of it raw. This is grammatically required; the verse cannot function without *mimenu* and it therefore does no independent legal work beyond what the verse demands.

### Free for Gezeira

The second occurrence is the word free to anchor the *gezeirah shavah*, available precisely because the first was required by plain grammar and the third is dealt with separately.

### Notar Clause

The third occurrence of *mimenu* at *pesach* appears in the clause *ve'hanotar mimenu ad boker ba'esh tisrofu* — what remains of it until morning you shall burn with fire. The question is whether this *mimenu* is itself doing independent legal work, or whether it is merely incidental to the larger phrase.

### Notar Purpose

There is a dispute about what this third clause accomplishes. One view holds that the phrase *ba'esh tisrofu* following *lo totiru mimenu* creates a *mitzvat asei* linked to the *lo ta'aseh* of not leaving the *pesach* overnight — making the prohibition *nitak la'asei* — and thus the word *mimenu* was simply carried along for linguistic flow, doing no independent work. Another view holds that the purpose of this verse is to establish that if *notar* remains, one does not burn it on the morning of the 15th of Nisan — which is *yom tov* — but waits for the morning of the 16th. Either way, the *mimenu* in this third clause is not doing independent legal work; it was written along with the phrase that was needed, whether for *nitak la'asei* or for the teaching about a second morning of burning. The conclusion is the same: the *mimenu* at the end is written only because the larger phrase was needed, and is therefore genuinely free, available to serve as one node of the *gezeirah shavah*.

### Maaser Mimenu

The *gemara* turns to the three appearances of *mimenu* in the *maaser* context: *lo vi'arti mimenu be'oni*, *velo vi'arti mimenu be'tamei*, and *velo natati mimenu le'met*.

### Maaser Grammar

The first *mimenu* in the *maaser vidui* passage is grammatically required — it is the natural mode of expression and does no more than what the text demands.

### Abbahu Teaching

The second *mimenu* — *velo vi'arti mimenu be'tamei* — is the source for the teaching of Rabbi Abbahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: this prohibition of burning *tamei maaser sheni* applies specifically to *maaser sheni*, whereas *teruma* that has become *tamei* may indeed be burned. The *mimenu* at *maaser* thus derives a specific law about *maaser sheni*, and is not free.

### Anointing Tamei

The third *mimenu* — *velo natati mimenu le'met* — is the source for Reish Lakish's teaching, cited in the name of Rabbi Samya: how do we know that *maaser sheni* which has become *tamei* may be used for *sichah* — anointing the body — even though it may not be eaten? From the word *mimenu*: I did not give *of it* to the dead. The inference is that what I did not do for the dead — anoint them — I may do for the living. What is something equally relevant to both the living and the dead? Anointing. The living person may therefore use *tamei maaser sheni* for *sichah*. This is a striking *halakha*: even though you cannot burn *tamei maaser sheni* for fuel or light, you may anoint your body with it, because *sichah* is a form of bodily consumption that does not constitute eating or drinking and therefore remains legitimate even in a state of *tumah*.

### Sichah Debate

The *gemara* challenges this derivation. Mar Zutra asks: perhaps the verse means that one should not use the proceeds of selling the *maaser sheni* to buy a coffin or shrouds for the dead — implying that one may sell it and buy clothes or other items for the living? Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua responds: *mimenu migufo* — *of it* means direct use of the item itself. You do not make shrouds from produce; therefore, the verse must be speaking of direct bodily application, not indirect commercial use. Rav Ashi adds a parallel argument: *lo natati* is analogous to *lo achalti* — just as eating is a direct consumption of the object itself, so too the giving spoken of here must be a direct use of the *maaser sheni* itself on the body.

### One Side Free

The analysis reveals an asymmetry: at *pesach*, one of the three *mimenu* words is genuinely free. At *maaser*, however, all three words are occupied — none is free. The *gezeirah shavah* therefore has only one free node, at *pesach*, and is technically a *gezeirah shavah mitzad echad* — free on only one side. According to the view that such a one-sided *gezeirah shavah* can be challenged, the weight-of-*pesach* argument remains a valid rebuttal and the proof is not ironclad.

### Abaye Free Sides

Abaye resolves the problem by drawing on a teaching of Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha. If the teaching that *tamei teruma* may be burned — which Rabbi Abbahu derived from the second *maaser mimenu* — can actually be derived from a different source entirely, then that second *mimenu* is genuinely free after all, and we have *mimenu* free on both sides of the *gezeirah shavah*.

### Teruma Burning

The alternative source is Rav Nachman's teaching in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha: the verse states *va'ani hineh natati lecha et mishmeret terumotai* — I have given you the guardianship of my *terumot*, in the plural. The Torah speaks of two *terumot* — one *tehorah* and one *teme'ah*. Even *tamei teruma* has a use: *lehasikah tachat tavshilcha* — you may burn it to fuel your cooking fire. Since the permission to burn *tamei teruma* can be derived from this verse about *teruma* directly, the second *mimenu* at *maaser* — which Rabbah bar Avuha used for the same teaching — is freed from that obligation. With the second *maaser mimenu* now available as a free word, both sides of the *gezeirah shavah* are free, and the analogy between *pesach* and *maaser sheni* regarding the *arel* is established on firm ground.

## Conclusion & Tamei

### Summary Arel

The *gemara*'s sustained treatment of the *arel* and *maaser sheni* draws to a close. Multiple *braitot* — each of which the *gemara* attempted to neutralize through various reinterpretations — consistently pointed toward the same conclusion: an *arel* is forbidden in *maaser sheni*. Rabbi Yitzchak then provided an independent derivation via *gezeirah shavah* linking *pesach* and *maaser* through the word *mimenu*, and Abaye secured both sides of that *gezeirah shavah* by showing that the relevant *maaser* word is genuinely free. The overall conclusion is that an *arel* is forbidden in *pesach*, forbidden in *teruma*, and likewise forbidden in *maaser sheni*.

### All Tamei

With the *arel* question resolved, the *mishnah* moves on to what would seem to be the more self-evident clause: *ve'chol ha'tmei'im* — all *tamei* persons are likewise forbidden in *teruma*. This transition shifts the discussion from a category defined by a physical status (*arel*) to the broader world of ritual impurity.

## Tamei Teruma

### Yochanan Source

The *gemara* asks: where is the source that all *tamei* persons are forbidden in *teruma*? Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Yishmael, identifies the verse: *ish ish mi'zera aharon ve'hu tzaru'a o zav ba'kodashim lo yochal ad asher yithar* — any man of the seed of Aharon who is afflicted with *tzara'at* or is a *zav* shall not eat of the holy things until he becomes *tahor*. The verse continues with additional categories of *tamei* persons. The operative question is: what do *kodashim* — holy things — refer to here?

### Zera Aharon

The key to the identification lies in the phrase *mi'zera aharon* — of the seed of Aharon. The *gemara* asks: what holy thing is shared equally by all members of the seed of Aharon? *Kodshei kodashim* cannot be the answer, because those may only be eaten by male *kohanim* — women of priestly lineage cannot eat them. *Teruma*, on the other hand, may be eaten by both male and female members of a *kohen*'s household. The *gemara* therefore identifies *kodashim* in this verse as *teruma*: *havei omer zo terumah*.

### Women Exclusion

A possible alternative is raised: perhaps the reference is to *chazeh ve'shok* — the breast and thigh of the *shelamim* offering, which are *kodshim kalim* that women of priestly families may eat. The *gemara* rejects this: a *bat kohen* who marries an *Yisrael* and is subsequently widowed without children returns to eating *teruma*, but cannot return to eating *kodshim kalim* of her father's house — this is derived from a separate verse. So *kodshim kalim* is not equally accessible to all *zera aharon* once they enter various marital situations. *Teruma* remains the most universally shared form of *kodesh* for all of *zera aharon*.

One might further argue that even *teruma* is not truly universal: a *chalalah* — a woman born of a disqualified priestly union — cannot eat *teruma*. The *gemara* resolves this: a *chalalah* is not considered *zera aharon* in the relevant halachic sense. Although she is obviously his biological descendant and carries all obligations of *kibbud av va'em*, her lineage is no longer considered *meyuchas* in the priestly sense; a male in her position would not be a *kohen*. The phrase *zera aharon* therefore points precisely to *teruma*.

### Ad Asher Yithar

The verse states these *tamei* persons may not eat *kodashim* — now established as *teruma* — *ad asher yithar*, until they become *tahor*. A question arises: how do we know this phrase means specifically until nightfall following immersion — which would exclude a *tvul yom* but permit a *mechusar kippurim*? Perhaps *ad asher yithar* means until one has completed the entire purification process, including bringing a *korban*? If so, even a *mechusar kippurim* would be forbidden in *teruma*.

### Tanna Kamma

The *gemara* cites the school of Rabbi Yishmael: the verse is speaking specifically of a *zav ba'al shtei re'iyot* — a *zav* who experienced only two sightings — and a *metzora musgar* — a leper in the confined stage but not the declared stage. These two cases are cited as parallel to the case of one who becomes *tamei* through contact with a corpse (*tmei nefesh*).

### Sunset Meaning

The logic is that one who is *tamei* through corpse contact does not bring a *korban* at all. Since the verse draws these cases together, when we read *ad asher yithar* in this context, we read it as applicable to persons who likewise are not in a *korban*-bearing process. A *zav* with only two sightings does not bring a *korban*; a *metzora musgar* does not bring a *korban*. For such people, *tahor* means: go to the *mikvah* and wait for nightfall. Hence *ad asher yithar* signifies sunset alone.

### Korban Extension

The *gemara* resists the inference: perhaps this means only that those without a *korban* obligation need wait only for nightfall — but those who are obligated to bring a *korban* must wait until they have done so, even for *teruma*. This is a reasonable position and is not automatically refuted by the reading of the verse. The *gemara* presses: what then is the source that permits a *mechusar kippurim* to eat *teruma* the night before bringing the *korban*?

### Mishna Hierarchy

The *gemara* brings the *mishna*: one who immerses and emerges may eat *maaser*; once the sun sets (*he'erev shemesh*), one may eat *teruma*; once the *korban* is brought, one may eat *kodshim*. This neatly establishes three ascending levels of purity required for three ascending levels of sanctity.

### Mechusar Position

The *gemara* asks: where is the proof that specifically the *mechusar kippurim* — one who still needs to bring a *korban* — is permitted in *teruma* the night before? The source for this precise ruling requires its own derivation.

## Three Psukim (IV)

### Rava Teaching

Rava, citing Rav Chisda, explains that three verses underlie this three-tier hierarchy, each corresponding to one level of sanctity.

### Mikvah Pesach

The first verse states *lo yochal min ha'kodashim ki im rachatz besaro ba'mayim* — he shall not eat of the holy things unless he has bathed his flesh in water. This establishes that immersion in a *mikvah* alone is sufficient to permit eating something. This is the lightest level, corresponding to *maaser*.

### Korban Kodshim

The third verse states *ve'chipper aleiha ha'kohen ve'tahera* — the *kohen* shall atone for her and she shall be *tahor*. This establishes that bringing a *korban* is required to achieve the fullest *tahara*, corresponding to *kodshim*.

### Sunset Teruma

The second verse — *uva ha'shemesh ve'taher ve'achar yochal min ha'kodashim* — establishes that sunset marks the purity threshold for the intermediate level, corresponding to *teruma*.

### Teruma Weight

How do we know *teruma* is heavier than *maaser* and lighter than *kodshim*? A mnemonic is employed: *mechpaz*. *Mem* stands for *mita bidei shamayim* — one who eats *teruma* in a state of impurity incurs death at the hands of Heaven; *chet* is *chomesh* — one who eats *teruma* accidentally must add a fifth; *peh* is the absence of *pidyon* — *teruma* has no redemption, whereas *maaser sheni* does; *zayin* is *zar* — *teruma* is forbidden to non-*kohanim*. Against this, one might argue that *maaser* is weightier, represented by the mnemonic *hadastav*: *hei* is *hava'as makom* — *maaser sheni* must be brought to Jerusalem; *dalet* is *vidui* — a declaration is required; *samech* represents that an *onen* is forbidden in it; *tet* is *tumah* — *tamei maaser sheni* may not be burned for benefit; and *bet* is *biur* — one must eliminate *maaser* from the house every three years. The *gemara* resolves the question: *mita bidei shamayim* tips the balance — the consequence of death at the hands of Heaven makes *teruma* demonstrably weightier. Rava adds that even without invoking *mita*, the first verse — which speaks of *nefesh* — itself points to *maaser* as the lightest category.

### Nefesh Logic

The verse that requires only immersion reads: *nefesh asher tiga bo ve'tame'ah, ki im rachatz besaro ba'mayim*. The word *nefesh* — person — implies something available to every person. *Teruma* is restricted to *kohanim* and their households; it is not *shaveh bechol nefesh* — equal for all people. The only form of *kodesh* that all people may eat is *maaser sheni*. Therefore the verse permitting eating after immersion alone must be speaking of *maaser sheni*.

## Yoledet Case (III)

### Yoledet Status

The remaining question — whether a *mechusar kippurim* who is obligated to bring a *korban* may nevertheless eat *teruma* before bringing it — is answered through the case of a *yoledet*, a woman who has given birth. Her purification process spans forty days for a boy (and eighty for a girl). At the end of seven days she immerses in the *mikvah*. From that point, any blood she produces is *dam tohar* and does not render her *tamei*. However, she is not fully *tehorah* until she brings her *korban* on day forty.

### Long Tvul Yom

After her immersion on day seven, she enters a prolonged *tvul yom* status — she has immersed but her effective nightfall does not arrive until the night before day forty. During these thirty-three intermediate days she is called a *tvulas yom aroch* — a *tvul yom* of extended duration. In that period she may eat *maaser* but not *teruma*.

### Night Before

On the night before day forty — the evening preceding the morning on which she brings her *korban* — she transitions to *mechusar kippurim* status. She is now permitted to eat *teruma*, even though she has not yet brought her *korban*. The following morning, when she brings the *korban*, she may eat *kodshim* as well.

## Three Psukim (IV) (II)

### Kodshim Weight

*Kodshim* is weightier than *teruma*. The mnemonic is *pinkakas*: *peh* is *pigul*, *nun* is *notar*, *kaf* is *karet*, *ayin* is *meila*, and *samech* is the general prohibition of *assur*. None of these — with the exception of some overlap — apply to *teruma*, which instead carries *mita bidei shamayim* rather than *karet*. While one might object that *teruma*'s features from *mechpaz* are more numerous, the *gemara*'s conclusion is that the *kodshim* characteristics as a collection outweigh those of *teruma*.

## Yoledet Case (III)

### Milos Yamim

Abaye demonstrates the two-stage purity of the *yoledet* from two verses. The first verse states *ad milos yemei tahara* — until the completion of the days of purity. This verse establishes that once the days of purity are complete — that is, when nightfall arrives on the night before day forty — she is in some sense *tehorah*.

## Three Psukim (IV) (III)……

### Rabba Language

Rabba offers an alternative derivation: even without counting features, the language of the verse *ve'chipper aleiha ha'kohen ve'tahera* itself establishes that *kodshim* is weightier. The language of *kapparah* — atonement — is uniquely associated with *korban*-bearing, and the fact that the verse uses this formulation to mark the point of *tahara* for *kodshim* demonstrates that *kodshim* occupies a categorically higher level of sanctity.

## Yoledet Case (III)…

### Vechiper

The second verse states *ve'chipper aleiha ha'kohen ve'tahera* — after the *kohen* brings the atonement-*korban* for her, she becomes *tehorah* for *kodshim*. This verse marks the moment of full *tahara*.

### Resolution

Two verses therefore govern the *yoledet*'s purity: the first — *ad milos yemei tahara* — applies to *teruma*, marking the night before the *korban* as her point of *tahara* for purposes of eating *teruma*; the second — *ve'chipper aleiha* — applies to *kodshim*, marking the bringing of the *korban* as her point of *tahara* for eating sanctified offerings.

### Inference

From this we draw the critical inference: a woman who is *mechusar kippurim* — who still has a pending *korban* obligation — is nonetheless *tahor* for *teruma* from the night before the *korban* is brought. This is the halachic proof that a *mechusar kippurim* is not forbidden in *teruma* even when a *korban* is required.

## Three Psukim (IV) (III)……

### Tamei Status

The second verse's formulation — *ve'chipper aleiha ha'kohen ve'tahera*, signaling that she becomes *tehorah* only through the *korban* — implies that before the *korban* is brought, she retains a personal status of *teme'ah* with respect to *kodshim*. The verse *ve'habasar asher yiga bechol tamei lo ye'achel* is explicit: one with a personal *tamei* status may not eat the meat of *kodshim*. Therefore, even after nightfall and even after becoming permitted in *teruma*, she remains forbidden in *kodshim* until the *korban* is brought. It would be untenable to say that one still considered *teme'ah* in any degree could eat *kodshim* — the prohibition is categorical.

## Sheshet Challenge

### Non-Priestly

Rav Sheshet, son of Rav Idi, raises a powerful challenge against the entire framework. He notes that a *braita* on the laws of *yoledet* cites the verse *daber el bnei Yisrael*, and asks: I know only that Jewish women by birth are subject to *tumas leida* — how do I know a *giueres* and a *shifcha meshucheres* are also subject to it? The answer given in the *braita* is that the verse *isha ki tazria* — when a woman conceives — comes to include any woman. The *braita* therefore explicitly establishes that the *tahara* laws of the *yoledet* apply even to a *giueres* and a freed slave woman.

### Contradiction

Rav Sheshet presses: if the verses we have been using to derive the hierarchy of *maaser*, *teruma*, and *kodshim* are speaking about *teruma* — as the *gemara* has concluded — how can they apply to a *giueres* or a *shifcha meshucheres*? These women cannot eat *teruma*. Paradoxically, a *giueres* may eat *shelamim* — she can eat *kodshim kalim* if she wishes, as a full member of the Jewish people — but she has no access to *teruma*, which is restricted to priestly households. If the verses regarding her purity are about *teruma*, the *braita*'s inclusion of a *giueres* is incoherent.

### Multiple Segments

Rava responds that the verse operates in distinct segments — *kra milei milei kachashiv* — different parts of the verse address different matters and different audiences. It is not the case that every clause of the passage speaks to every person mentioned. The *braita*'s inclusion of a *giueres* establishes only that she is subject to *tumas leida* as such, not that every specific law derived from the passage applies to her.

### Inclusion Logic

The *tahara* laws regarding *teruma* — derived from the same verses — continue to apply to *kohen* women who are the primary subjects of the passage. The fact that the *braita* also applies *tumas leida* to a *giueres* does not transform the purity thresholds for *teruma* into laws for non-priestly women. The two teachings coexist within the same passage without conflict: one clause teaches universality of *tumas leida*, while another teaches the specific *teruma*-based purity thresholds applicable to those who can eat *teruma*.

## Teruma Purity

### Three Needed

The *gemara* now asks why three separate verses are required to establish the *teruma* hierarchy. Could we not have derived everything from one or two?

### Process Req

The first verse — *ad asher yithar* — establishes that there is some purification process required before eating *teruma*. Without it, we would not know that any formal *tahara* step is necessary at all.

### Sunset Spec

The second verse — *uva ha'shemesh ve'taher* — specifies that the relevant moment of *tahara* is sunset. Without this verse, knowing only that *tahara* is required, we would not know when that threshold is crossed.

### Ambiguity

Even with both of these verses, an ambiguity would remain: perhaps the sunset rule applies only when no *korban* is pending, but for a *bar kapparah* — one who must bring a *korban* — perhaps the requirement extends until the *korban* is brought, even for *teruma*. Without a third verse, this question would remain unresolved.

### Yoledet Proof

The third verse — the *yoledet* passage with *ad milos yemei tahara* — resolves this ambiguity. It demonstrates that even a woman in the *korban*-bearing process becomes *tehorah* for *teruma* once nightfall arrives before the day of her offering. The *mechusar kippurim* status, even when a *korban* is required, does not extend the *teruma* restriction beyond nightfall.

### Why Yoledet

Had we had only the *yoledet* verse — *ad milos* — without the intermediate sunset verse, we might have concluded that the completion of the purification *days* is the determinative factor, and that immersion in a *mikvah* alone, without waiting for nightfall, would suffice. It is the second verse (*uva ha'shemesh ve'taher*) that corrects this, insisting that nightfall is necessary. The *yoledet* verse alone would have been insufficient to teach that.

### Summary Three

Together, the three verses establish the complete framework: *ad asher yithar* teaches that a purification process is required; *uva ha'shemesh ve'taher* specifies that nightfall is the critical moment; and the *yoledet* verses demonstrate that even in the presence of a pending *korban* obligation, nightfall suffices to permit *teruma*, while full *tahara* for *kodshim* awaits the bringing of the *korban* itself. This three-verse architecture corresponds precisely to the three-tier hierarchy of *maaser*, *teruma*, and *kodshim* — each requiring a progressively more complete form of *tahara*.

# Yevamot 75

## Mechussar Kipurim

### Intro: Mechussar Kipurim

The daf opens at approximately ten lines down on 75a, at the words *asher yithar*. We are completing the discussion of how we know that a *mechussar kipurim* — one who has undergone immersion and waited until nightfall but has not yet brought the required *korban* — may eat *terumah* but may not eat *kodshim*. The preceding analysis established three progressive stages of purification, derived primarily from the case of the *yoledes*: after immersion in the *mikvah* one may eat *maaser*; after nightfall one may eat *terumah*; and only after bringing one's *korban* does one attain full *tahara* permitting the eating of *kodshim*. A key point in learning from the *yoledes* was demonstrating that even a person still in the process of completing the *korban* obligation is already permitted to eat *terumah* once nightfall has passed.

### Dissenting Tana View

The *gemara* now addresses an alternative reading. The *tana de-bei Rabbi Yishmael* had read the verse *ad asher yithar* as referring to a *zav* who had seen a flow only twice and a *metzora* who was at the final stage of purification — individuals who do not require a *korban* — so that the phrase means only "until nightfall." But the dissenting *tana* reads the verse as referring to a classic *zav* with three episodes of flux (*zav ba'al gimel re'iyot*) and a fully quarantined *metzora muchlat*, who do require a *korban*. According to this view, *ad asher yithar* means "until he brings his *kapparah*," and the prohibition against eating *kodshim* (*u-vakodshim lo yokhal*) refers to actual *korbanot* — meaning one may not eat one's own sacrificial portions until one has completed the atonement process.

### Two Pesukim Analysis

This raises the question: according to the dissenting *tana*, why do we need two verses — the verse in Leviticus governing the *zav* and *metzora*, and the verse by the *yoledes* (*ve-chiper alav ha-kohen ve-taherah*) — both teaching that one may eat *korbanot* only after bringing the *korban*? The *gemara* answers that both are necessary. Had the Torah written only the verse regarding the *yoledes*, one might have thought the requirement is specific to her case because her *tum'a* is so extensive — spanning forty days for a boy and eighty for a girl — and therefore one might reason more leniently about the *zav* whose process is shorter. Conversely, had the Torah written only the verse regarding the *zav*, one might have said that his *tum'a* is strict precisely because it admits of no exceptions (*lo hutchal mikelalo*), whereas the *yoledes*, whose flow during the thirty-three or sixty-six days of *dam tohar* does not increase her *tum'a*, might be treated more leniently even before bringing her *korban*. Both verses are therefore needed, and in either case the conclusion is the same: a *mechussar kipurim* may eat *terumah* but not *kodshim*.

---

## Tvul Yom & Contact

### Vessels & Tvul Yom

The *gemara* now cites the verse *bamayim yuva ve-tamei ad ha-erev ve-taher*, which appears in the context of non-kosher animals and their carcasses, and which addresses the case of a vessel that has become *tamei* through contact with such a carcass. The verse prescribes that the vessel be immersed in water and remains *tamei* until nightfall — the same principle of *tvul yom* applies to vessels. One might ask: what is the *chidush* of this verse if the principle of *tvul yom* is already known? The answer points to something deeper than the application to vessels.

### Rav Zeira's Insight

Rav Zeira explains: the verse comes to teach us the law of *negi'ah* — contact. Until now the entire discussion has been framed in terms of eating: after immersion, when may one eat *maaser*? After nightfall, when may one eat *terumah*? But the question of what a *tvul yom* may touch is a separate matter entirely. A *tvul yom* holds the status of a *sheini le-tum'a*. A *sheini* does not transmit *tum'a* to *chullin* or *maaser*, but does render *terumah tamei* by contact. The verse, by speaking of the vessel — which cannot eat anything — teaches that the category of *tvul yom* is a problem not only for eating *terumah* but for coming into contact with *terumah*. These are not the same prohibition, and one cannot automatically derive the latter from the former.

A *Baraita* elaborates: the phrase *ve-tamei ad ha-erev ve-taher* creates a tension between *ve-tamei* ("it is still *tamei*") and *ve-taher* ("it becomes *tahor*"). The *drasha* notes that *ve-taher* is written in a form that implies an already-present degree of *tahara*, not purely a future state. The *gemara* resolves the tension: *kan le-ma'aser, kan le-terumah* — relative to *maaser* it is already *tahor*, but relative to *terumah* it remains *tamei*. This establishes a two-tiered status for the *tvul yom*.

### Kal Vachomer

Could one reverse the hierarchy — treating *maaser* as the more stringent category? The *gemara* rejects this: it is straightforward that eating *terumah* is more stringent than eating *maaser* — this we have already established — and therefore the parallel holds that touching *terumah* is more stringent than touching *maaser*. The argument proceeds with its own internal logic: since a *tvul yom* is prohibited from eating *terumah*, it follows naturally that this same status makes contact with *terumah* problematic.

### Yoledes & Tamei Status

The *gemara* then offers an alternative source: *bechol kodesh lo tiga ve-el ha-mikdash lo tavo*, the verse describing the *yoledes* during her thirty-three or sixty-six days of *dam tohar*. Her status during this period is that of a *tvul yom shel yom aroch* — a long-day *tvul yom* — since she has immersed but is still awaiting the night before her *korban*. The verse says she may not "touch" anything holy (*kodesh*). One might suppose this directly prohibits contact. However, the *gemara* demonstrates that *bechol kodesh lo tiga* means "do not eat *terumah*," not "do not physically touch." The analogy is drawn between *kodesh* and *mikdash*: just as entering the *mikdash* while *tamei* carries the penalty of *karet* — a punishment involving *netilat neshamah* — so too the prohibition of *kodesh* must refer to something that carries such a penalty. Since one is never liable to *karet* for merely touching *terumah*, only for eating it while *tamei*, the verse must be speaking of eating, not touching.

Yet the verse uses the language of *tiga* — touching — rather than *achila* — eating. The *gemara* explains: *negi'ah ke-achilah* — touching is being compared to eating, teaching that the same prohibition applies to contact as applies to eating. Just as the *tvul yom* cannot eat *terumah*, she cannot touch it either. The same parallel hierarchy applies: a *tvul yom* may eat *maaser* but not *terumah*, and similarly may touch *maaser* but may not touch *terumah*; a *mechussar kipurim* may eat *terumah* but not *kodshim*, and the same follows for contact.

---

## Ptzua Daka Marriage

### Intro: Ptzua Daka

The *gemara* now shifts to a new section of the *mishnah*, turning to the laws of *ptzua daka* and *krus shofcha* — those whose reproductive injury prohibits them from marrying a naturally born Jewish woman, as derived from the verse *lo yavo bi-khal Hashem*. The *mishnah* notes that a *ptzua daka* who is a *kohen* retains his ability to eat *terumah* — his own status is not compromised — but his wife loses the ability to eat *terumah* because by having relations with a man forbidden to her she becomes a *chalalah*, and a *chalalah* is excluded from eating *terumah*. This asymmetry is striking: the verse speaks primarily to him, yet his *terumah* status is unaffected while hers is transformed.

### Wife's Status Change

An interesting case arises at the end of the *mishnah*: what if the man's condition developed after they were already married but before they had consummated the marriage? The woman has not yet had relations with him, has not yet become a *chalalah*, and therefore has not yet been invalidated. The question is whether she should nonetheless be prohibited from eating *terumah* on the grounds that consummation — and thus her invalidation — is inevitable. The *mishnah* rules that she may continue eating *terumah* until she has actually had relations with him under these circumstances.

### Rabbi Elazar Debate

The *gemara* asks: whose position does this *mishnah* reflect? *Mishtameret le-vi'ah pesulah de-Oraita achla?* Who holds that a woman "watching" for a *bi'ah* that is forbidden and that will surely come — yet has not happened — may still eat *terumah*? Rabbi Elazar identifies this as the position of Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon in an earlier dispute, which addressed the analogous case of a widow (*almanah*) betrothed to a *Kohen Gadol*, or a divorcée betrothed to a regular *kohen*, where *erusin* has taken place but the marriage has not yet been consummated. In those cases as well, the question is whether the anticipated — but not yet actualized — *bi'ah psulab* disqualifies her from *terumah*. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon said she may still eat, and our *mishnah* follows that ruling.

### Rabbi Yochanan Reply

Rabbi Yochanan offers a broader reading: even according to Rabbi Meir — who in the *erusin* case prohibits eating *terumah* because the anticipated invalidation is so clear — here the *mishnah* would be different. Why? *She-kvar achlah* — she has already been eating *terumah* throughout the marriage. Under these circumstances, one does not force her to stop eating based on something that has not yet happened. The ruling is not to initiate eating when invalidation is on the horizon, but where she has already been eating validly, she is not told to stop until her status actually changes.

Rabbi Elazar pushes back: *she-kvar achlah lo amrinan* — the fact that one has been eating is not in itself a halakhically relevant consideration. He offers a proof: a *bat Yisrael* married to a *kohen* who was eating *terumah* during the marriage certainly cannot continue eating after her husband dies, even though *she-kvar achlah*. Rabbi Yochanan responds: *hasam pasak kinyana* — there the marriage bond has ceased entirely. But here the relationship has not ended; she is still married. The only reason to stop her would be anticipation of a future event that has not yet occurred, and so long as her actual status has not changed, and she has been eating legitimately, she may continue.

---

## Ptzua Daka Definition

### Testicle Injuries

The *gemara* now turns to a detailed and practically significant discussion of what physically constitutes *ptzua daka*. The *mishnah* states: *eizu p'suah dakah — kol she-niftzu ha-beitzim shelo*, any case in which the testicles have been *niftzu*. Rashi understands *niftzu* as deriving from the word *petza* — a wound, specifically a cutting-type injury, such as one made with a knife. Rashi's reading should be kept in mind when other translations are considered.

### Three Injury Types

The *Baraita* elaborates further: the injuries include *niftzu* (wounded), *nikbu* (punctured, i.e., a hole has been made), and *nimoku* (withered or shrunken). Rashi explains *nimoku* as *machamas makkah nimoku ufachtu lahem mei'aleihem* — they shrank as a result of an injury. This is significant: Rashi specifies that it was *machamas makkah*, due to a blow, because the entire discussion — as becomes explicit shortly — pertains only to injuries caused through human agency (*bidei adam*). Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka adds: *ve-afillu chasru* — even if a small portion is simply cut away. He reports this ruling in the name of the sages of *Kerem Beyavneh*.

The *gemara* also derives from the word *dakah* a third injury type — crushing — alongside cutting and severing.

### Three Body Parts

Rava then teaches that all three injury types are interchangeable across all three relevant body parts: the *gid* (penis), the *beitzim* (testicles), and the *chutei beitzim* (the ducts, analogous to the vas deferens, that connect the testicles to the penis). The full formulation is: *ptzua* (wounded/punctured) in any of them, *dach* (crushed) in any of them, *karus* (severed) in any of them — whether the injury occurred to the *gid*, the *beitzim*, or the *chutei beitzim*.

---

## One Testicle Status

### Rabbi Yishmael Teaching

Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka reported from the sages of *Kerem Beyavneh*: *kol she-ein lo ella beitzah achas eino ella saris chamah* — whoever has only one testicle is like a *saris chamah*, and is *kasher*. This teaching is immediately surprising. We have just established that even a wound to a single testicle is disqualifying, so surely the complete absence of one testicle should be even more severe. And the comparison to a *saris chamah* — a man rendered sterile naturally, typically through illness or fever — raises its own complications, since we are not necessarily speaking of sterility.

### Saris Chama Clarified

The *gemara* presses: is he literally a *saris chamah*? That cannot be, since a *saris chamah* is someone rendered sterile through a natural process such as illness, whereas missing one testicle may be a birth defect with no such connection.
