The *gemara* clarifies: *ela harei hu ke-saris chamah* — he is not a *saris chamah*, but he is *like* a *saris chamah*, and just as a *saris chamah* is *kasher*, so too is he.

### Bidei Shamayim

Rashi's explanation is that the case involves a birth defect — the person was born with only one testicle — and the ruling follows from the principle that *bidei shamayim* conditions do not disqualify. The comparison to *saris chamah* fits perfectly on Rashi's reading: just as a *saris chamah* is naturally sterile and yet *kasher* because it is *bidei shamayim*, so too someone born with one testicle is *kasher* by the same principle. Tosafot, however, reads the case differently and says we are dealing with *bidei adam* — a case where one testicle was removed through human action. On Tosafot's reading, the ruling would represent a disagreement with the earlier position, or alternatively, an ironic inversion: a complete removal of a testicle may be *less* problematic than an injury to it, because an injury to the testicle may cause infertility whereas removal of a complete testicle — as Tosafot observes from practical experience — need not.

### Tosafot Surgical Evidence

Tosafot's evidence is remarkable. At the bottom of 75a, and continuing onto 75b, Tosafot writes: *ve-od de-bidei adam nami hachazinan kama bnei adam she-gomemim mehen beitza achat u-molidin* — and furthermore, even when done through human agency, we see a number of people from whom one testicle has been removed who nonetheless father children. Tosafot adds that we cannot simply respond by saying *d'lo mistavra lomar tzei ve-chakur bneihem me'eimat* — that all these men's children are suspected of being *mamzerim* and their wives have been unfaithful. That would be absurd given the scale of the phenomenon. So Tosafot concludes that removal of a single testicle does not render a person infertile and therefore does not create the status of *ptzua daka*.

This raises a further question about what precisely Tosafot is observing historically. He appears to be referring to surgical removal of a testicle as a common practice in his time. He even notes, toward the end of that *tosafot*, that since there is a *Yerushalmi* opinion that the right testicle may be treated differently from the left, *ve-tov le-hazhir la-refuim la-chtoch shel smol im efshar* — it is advisable to instruct physicians, if they are removing one, to remove the left one if possible. The medical and halachic engagement here is striking.

### Rav Moshe Reassessment

This leads to a significant responsum by Rav Moshe Feinstein. A man had undergone a testicular biopsy — a small portion of tissue was removed from a testicle — in order to assist with fertility treatments. The earlier *Baraita* had explicitly stated *ve-afillu chasru* — even if a small portion is cut away, it is disqualifying. On a straightforward reading, a biopsy would seem to fall under this category, since it is *bidei adam* and involves the removal of even a small portion. Rav Moshe argues, however, that the *gemara's* entire framework ties the disqualification to infertility. Since modern medicine demonstrates that such a biopsy does not cause infertility — indeed, the very purpose of the procedure was to enable fertility — the *gemara's* criterion of *chasru* must be understood as referring only to cases where infertility results. When it does not, the *din* of *ptzua daka* does not apply. This is a striking example of the interplay between halachic categories and empirical medical knowledge.

---

## Fertility & Causation

### Case: Man in Palm Tree

The *gemara* now asks directly: *ve-nekev lo molid?* — is it truly the case that a person with a puncture cannot father children? A case is cited: a man climbed a palm tree (*salikal'dikla*) and a thorn punctured his testicle (*charzeia silu be-beitzim*). A viscous stream then emerged from his penis (*ve-nafak minei ke-chut de-mugla*), and he subsequently fathered children. This would seem to prove that *nekev* — puncture — does not necessarily cause infertility.

### Rav's Skeptical Reply

Shmuel transmitted this story to Rav. Rav's response was dismissive: *tzei u-vtzor bivnav mei'ayin heim* — go and investigate the origins of his children. Rav was not prepared to accept the empirical evidence at face value and instead suggested that the children might not actually be his. This response represents one pole in the ongoing tension between empirical observation and established *halachic* categories: rather than revising the *halakha*, Rav preferred to question the apparent facts.

### Natural Causes Kosher

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *ptzua daka bidei shamayim kasher* — if the condition arose through natural causes, the person is *kasher*. The category of *bidei shamayim* includes birth defects, illness, and conditions arising from the natural functioning of the body. The question of whether a physical trauma caused by an external but non-human event — such as a falling tree branch struck by lightning — would be considered *bidei shamayim* is left open, but standard *bidei shamayim* cases such as illness and congenital conditions are clearly excluded from the prohibition.

### Ptzua vs. Haptzua

Rava derives this distinction from the language of the verse itself: the Torah writes *ptzua* and not *ha-ptzua*. *Ha-ptzua* would suggest a permanent, pre-existing state — how one was born. *Ptzua* indicates that this occurred to the person as an event, implying that the disqualification requires an act of injury, not a natural condition.

### Mamzer Comparison

A *Baraita* reinforces this: *ne'emar lo yavo ptzua daka ve-ne'emar lo yavo mamzer* — the Torah employs the same language of *lo yavo* for both *ptzua daka* and *mamzer*. Just as *mamzeirus* arises only through a human act — a forbidden sexual union — *ma le-halan bidei adam, af kan bidei adam* — so too *ptzua daka* applies only when the injury resulted from human agency. Where the condition is entirely natural, there is no disqualification.

### Rav Herzog Principle

A further and quite radical extension of the *bidei shamayim* category is proposed in a responsum by Rav Herzog. He addresses a case where a person had a natural condition — such as cancer — which required surgery, and the surgery itself constituted one of the physical injuries that would ordinarily create the status of *ptzua daka*. One would initially classify this as *bidei adam*, since a surgeon performed the procedure. Rav Herzog argues otherwise by analogy to the *mamzer* case. With *mamzeirus*, the human act (*bidei adam*) occurs at the beginning of the process — the forbidden union — while the rest of the process, the gestation and birth of the child, is *bidei shamayim*. What makes something *bidei adam* is that the initiating cause was a human act. By parallel reasoning, where the initiating cause — the underlying condition — was *bidei shamayim*, the fact that a surgeon then treated it does not transform the entire sequence into *bidei adam*. The initial cause governs the classification. Therefore, surgery performed to treat a naturally occurring condition remains in the *bidei shamayim* category, and the resulting state does not disqualify the person.

---

## Injuries Interchangeable

### Rava's Rule

Rava's teaching, noted above, is that all three injury types (*ptzua*, *dach*, *karus*) apply to all three body parts (*gid*, *beitzim*, *chutei beitzim*). The *gemara* spells this out fully: whether the *gid* is wounded, whether the *beitzim* are wounded, whether the *chutei beitzim* are wounded; whether the *gid* is crushed, whether the *beitzim* are crushed, whether the *chutei beitzim* are crushed; whether the *gid* is severed, whether the *beitzim* are severed, whether the *chutei beitzim* are severed — in all cases the *din* of *ptzua daka* or *krus shofcha* applies.

### Bar Hamduri Challenge

Bar Hamduri challenged Rava: *mimai de-hai ptzua daka be-oto makom?* — how do we know that *ptzua daka* refers specifically to the genitals? Perhaps *ptzua* (wounded) and *dakah* (crushed) describe any kind of bodily wound, such as a head injury?

### Future Generations Test

Rava responds: from the fact that the verse does not enumerate *dorot* — future generations — as it does by *Ammoni u-Mitzri* (*dor shlishi yavo lahem*) or *mamzer* (*lo yavo ad dor asiri*). The absence of any generational qualifier implies that we are discussing an injury the very nature of which precludes future generations — i.e., an injury affecting fertility, which necessarily points to the genitals.

### Alternative Explanation

Bar Hamduri counters: perhaps the verse mentions no future generations simply because only the man himself is forbidden — *ihu hu de-assur, brei u-bar brei kashrei* — only he is disqualified, not his descendants. On this reading the absence of generational language proves nothing about the nature or location of the injury.

### Krus Shofcha Parallel

The *gemara* therefore turns to the companion term: *ptzua daka* is juxtaposed with *krus shofcha*. The word *shofcha* — from *lishpoch*, to pour out — evokes a pouring or spilling of fluid. *Krus shofcha* thus means a severing that causes a flow, rather than a stream. This makes plain that we are speaking of the genitals, since the *shofcha* terminology describes what ordinarily emerges as a stream now emerging as a flood because of the injury. Thus by analogy, *ptzua daka* must also be speaking of the same bodily location.

### Stream vs. Flow

But the *gemara* then asks: how do we know that *krus shofcha* itself refers to the genitals? Perhaps *shofcha* refers to a wound on the lip, causing profuse bleeding? The *gemara* responds: *shafcha ketiv bi-mkom she-shofech* — the word *shafcha* indicates a place where fluid ordinarily flows, but now, as a result of the cutting (*krus*), it pours out as a flood rather than a stream. *Mi she-al yedei krita shofech* — it must be a part of the body that, because of the injury, now pours where it formerly streamed. *She-lo al yedei krita eino shofech ela mekale'ach* — without the injury, the fluid from that location would emerge only as a stream, not a flow. This excludes the nose and mouth, where fluids flow freely regardless of injury. The combination of "a place where fluid ordinarily exits as a stream" and "only as a result of the cutting does it now pour" identifies the genitals unambiguously.

---

## Corona Cases

### Through-Piercing Case

The *mishnah* had stated: *ve-im nishtayer me-ha'atara afillu ke-chut ha-sa'arah kasher* — if even a hair-thin strip of the *atara* (corona) remains toward the body, the man is *kasher*. The implication is that the disqualifying injury to the penis (*krus*) must extend from the corona toward the body; an injury affecting only the portion from the corona toward the tip is not disqualifying.

A specific case is now posed: *nikav le-mata me-atara she-kenegdo le-mala me-atara* — what if a puncture begins below the *atara* (i.e., on the side of the tip) but passes entirely through the thickness of the penis and emerges on the other side above the *atara* (i.e., on the side toward the body)? Does the point of entry — which would not be disqualifying — determine the status, or does the point of exit — which is toward the body — disqualify?

### Corona Debate

Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba was inclined to rule *le-achshurei* — that such a case is *kasher*, since the puncture originates from below the *atara*. Rabbi Assi corrected him, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *atara kol she-hi me'akevet* — even a minimal amount of the *atara* is decisive. As long as any portion of the puncture emerges from the side of the corona toward the body, it is disqualifying. The fact that part of the puncture originates from the other side does not save the case.

### Hair-Thin Strip Rule

Returning to the ruling about the severed penis: if even a hair-thin strip of the corona remains toward the body, the person is *kasher*. This rule requires clarification.

### Circumference Question

Ravina raised the following question: when the Sages say that a hair-thin strip (*ke-chut ha-sa'arah*) of the *atara* suffices — must this strip extend across the full circumference of the *atara*, or does a *rov* (majority) of the circumference suffice?

### Majority Answer

Rabba Tospa'a answered Ravina: a hair-thin strip across the majority (*rov*) of the circumference, toward the body (*ve-chelapi reisha*), is sufficient. The *Gra* notes that there is an *alef* indicating a variant reading of *kula* (the entire circumference) rather than *ruba* (majority), and so the precise textual tradition here is a matter of some question. But on the version of the text as cited, Rabba Tospa'a's answer is that majority suffices.

---

## Thickness Removal

### Quill Case

Rav Huna rules on two cases involving partial removal of the penis's thickness rather than complete severance. The first is *ke-kulmus* — like a quill. When scribes prepared quills, they would shave down the thickness of the shaft to create a tapered tip. Similarly, if the thickness of the penis was cut away on one side, creating a tapered appearance without puncturing all the way through, Rav Huna rules this is *kesherah* — valid.

### Drain Pipe Case

The second case is *ke-marzav* — like a drain pipe. Here the exterior remains intact but the interior flesh has been hollowed out, leaving the internal piping (*gid*) in place but removing the surrounding tissue. Rav Huna rules this is *pesulah* — disqualifying.

### Air Exposure Test

What is Rav Huna's reasoning? *Hai sholet ba-avira, ve-hai lo sholet ba-avira* — in the case of the pipe, the interior workings of the penis are exposed to air, which somehow leads to infertility. In the case of the quill, only the external thickness is affected; the interior remains protected and unexposed to air. This is Rav Huna's determinative criterion.

### Rav Chisda Opposite

Rav Chisda rules precisely the opposite: *ke-marzav kesherah, ke-kulmus pesulah* — the pipe is valid, the quill is disqualifying.

### Friction Theory

Rav Chisda's reasoning is different: *hai garid ve-hai lo garid* — one case draws out semen effectively during intercourse and the other does not. Rashi explains: if the outer thickness of the penis is cut away, friction during intercourse is reduced, and this impairs the ejaculation of semen, thus affecting fertility. In the case where the interior is hollowed out but the thickness remains, friction is preserved and ejaculation is normal. The criterion for Rav Chisda is not air exposure but the mechanics of fertilization.

### Rava Agrees

Rava sides with Rav Huna: *ke-vatei de-Rav Huna mistavra* — Rav Huna's reasoning is persuasive. The air-exposure criterion is the more compelling one.

### Faucet Analogy

Rava addresses Rav Chisda's friction argument directly: even if the outer thickness is reduced, this need not impair fertility, because *midi de-havah a-barza de-chavita* — it is like the faucet inserted into a barrel. Rashi explains that such a spout, though it may be wide at one end, narrows as it enters the barrel; similarly, even if the exterior of the penis is thinned, during deeper penetration the surrounding tissue narrows and provides friction at that point. Therefore, reduction in outer thickness does not necessarily impair the drawing out of semen, and Rav Chisda's concern about *gridusa* — the friction mechanism — is answered.

### Final Ruling

Ravina reported to Mareimar: *hachi amar Mar Zutra mishemei de-Rav Pappa, hilchasa bein ke-kulmus bein ke-marzav kesherah* — the *halakha* is that in both the quill case and the drain pipe case, the ruling is *kasher*. The *gemara* then notes a further question — *mihu miba'ei lei le-mata me-heter le-mala* — regarding the precise location of the injury relative to the permissible and prohibited zones, which carries over into the continuation of the *gemara*.

---

---

# Yevamot 76

## Penile injuries

### Prior interpretations

Today's daf is 76, and we continue the important discussion surrounding the halachic definition of *patzua daka u'krut shofcha*. Yesterday we noted how some of these definitions were changed radically — or interpreted in a radically narrow way — after the time of the Gemara, in order to permit men with these conditions to marry. Tosafot addresses the distinction between injury and complete removal, suggesting that the latter may not fall under the prohibition. Rav Moshe takes the position that even conditions explicitly mentioned in the Gemara are not disqualifying if we now know that they do not lead to infertility, since the Gemara's physical descriptions assumed infertility as their operative concern. Rav Herzog goes further, arguing that if a medical procedure was performed to treat a pre-existing medical condition, the entire situation is considered *b'yedei shamayim* and therefore excluded from the prohibition. With that context established, we continue in the Gemara at the bottom of 75b.

### Komus and Mardik cases

Mar Zutra, in the name of Rav Papa, states the *halacha*: whether the penis was thinned and tapered like a quill (*kekomus*) or hollowed out like a drainpipe (*kemardik*), either way it is *kashera* — valid. Presumably, neither condition constitutes a sufficiently serious wound, likely because neither necessarily leads to infertility, which is the Gemara's central concern.

Ravina then transmitted a question to Mareimar in the name of Mar Zutra: when we say these injuries are *kashera*, are we referring to injuries above the corona — meaning toward the body — or below the corona, toward the tip? The Gemara immediately answers: obviously we are discussing injuries above the corona, toward the body. Injuries below the corona, toward the tip, are not a problem even if the organ is completely severed at that point. As the Gemara remarks, *pshita d'l'mata me'hatara* — it is self-evident that such injuries would not be a concern. The Gemara then adds that Ravina's purpose in posing the question to Mareimar was not truly to resolve a doubt, but to test him.

There follows a case from Masa M'chasya: Mar Bar Rav Ashi performed a procedure on a man whose condition resembled the *mardik* case, and surgically converted it into what resembled the *komus* case, thereby rendering it valid. Rashi explains that this was the nature of the intervention — transforming one configuration into the other — though the Gemara moves forward without elaborating further.

### Blocked semen passage

The Gemara then introduces a case from Pumbedita. The pathway of the semen had become blocked (*istatam*), and the semen was emerging from the urinary tract rather than through its natural channel. Rav Bibi bar Abaye initially ruled that the man was still valid — after all, the semen was still emerging, so what difference did the pathway make? Rav Papa rebuked him, and Rashi notes that his formulation alludes to Abaye's lineage from the house of Eli, which carried a divine curse — the implication being that Rav Bibi spoke carelessly. Rav Papa's substantive point is: *bimkomo mevashelah shelo bimkomo lo mevashelah* — when semen travels through its natural passage, it is properly warmed by the body and is capable of causing conception; when it travels through the urinary tract, this does not occur, and the man is therefore infertile.

What is striking about this case is that there is no obvious physical injury of the kind the Gemara elsewhere describes — no severing, no crushing. The passage was simply *istatam*, blocked or clogged. One might ask: since when does a blocked duct fall into the category of *kerus shofcha* or *patzua daka*? The Gemara seems to imply that any physical condition causing infertility in this manner is disqualifying, even without a classic wound. One possibility, raised in discussion, is that the blockage may itself have resulted from a physical injury rather than occurring *b'yedei shamayim* — which would explain both why it is disqualifying and why the *b'yedei shamayim* exemption does not apply here.

### Corona hole test

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: if a hole existed in the penis — the classic case of *nikaiv* — and it subsequently became sealed (*nistam*), the determining criterion is *kol she'ilu nikri v'nikra pasul* — if, at the moment of seminal emission (*keri*), the hole would reopen, then the man is invalid. The reasoning is presumably that a hole that reopens upon ejaculation demonstrates that the channel has not truly healed, with direct implications for fertility. If it does not reopen, he is *kasher*.

Rava then raised the question: where exactly is this hole located? If it is below the corona — toward the tip — even complete severance would be permissible, so that cannot be the scenario. It must therefore be speaking of a hole in the corona itself. A parallel statement is then cited in the name of Shmuel through Rav Mari bar Mar citing Mar Ukva, specifying explicitly that we are discussing a hole *in the corona itself* (*nikaiv ba'atarah atzmah*), with the same rule applying: if it would reopen upon ejaculation, *pasul*; if not, *kasher*.

Rabbah bar Brei d'Rabba then sent an inquiry to Rav Yosef: *heichi avdinan* — how do we actually determine this in practice? The problem is circular: one cannot simply instruct the man to examine himself after relations with his wife, because the entire question is whether he is permitted to have relations with his wife in the first place. Some procedure for inducing ejaculation in a controlled way is needed.

### Ejaculation methods

Rav Yosef replied: bring hot barley bread, place it near the anus, and this will induce ejaculation (*mikrei*), after which the organ can be inspected. Abaye objected: does one assume that everyone is as righteous as Yaakov Avinu? The Gemara understands *kochi v'reishit oni* — Reuven is described as the first of his father's strength — to mean that the conception of Reuven was Yaakov's first seminal emission ever; he was so scrupulous that he had never experienced one prior to his first conjugal act with Leah. Most men, Abaye observed, require far less inducement. Instead, Abaye suggested: pass brightly colored women's garments before him (*bigdei tzvonin*), and for most men that will be sufficient stimulation to cause ejaculation.

Rava countered in the opposite direction: does one assume that everyone is as licentious as Barzillai the Gileadite, who the Gemara elsewhere describes as *shatuf b'zimah* — immersed in licentiousness? Colored garments may not be sufficient for everyone; many men require more. Since no satisfactory middle ground could be identified between the colored garments and the more invasive medical procedure, the Gemara concludes *mechvarta k'dishninan me'ikara* — the original method, the barley bread procedure, stands.

What is noteworthy here is that the Gemara has no apparent concern about *zera l'vatala* or *hirhurim* in this context. The barley procedure, being purely physiological, may not involve *hirhurim* at all. But the *bigdei tzvonin* presumably do. The Gemara's silence suggests that when ejaculation is induced for a legitimate medical or halachic purpose, neither concern applies. This has obvious relevance to the contemporary responsa literature on procuring semen from a husband for fertility treatment involving that same couple — a topic for which this *sugya* serves as a foundational model.

## Healing defects

### Hole closure

The Gemara now presents a *Baraita*: *nikaiv pasul mipnei shehu shotet* — if there is a hole, it is invalid because the semen dribbles rather than flowing in a proper stream. This is a restatement and formalization of what was discussed previously. *Nistam kasher mipnei shemolid* — if it becomes sealed, it is valid because the man can now father children. *Ve-zehu pasul she-chozer l'hechsheiro* — and this is a case of invalidity that can revert to validity through healing. The man was in the category of *kerus shofchah*, but if the hole closes, he is restored to fitness.

### Scab coverage issue

The Gemara then asks: *zehu l'mautei mai* — what does the word *zehu* ("this is") come to exclude? The answer: it excludes a case where what appears to be closure is in fact only a *kerum she'alah machamas makah* — a membrane or scab that has grown over a wound. In the laws of *treifot* pertaining to the lung, such a covering is not considered a genuine seal; the lung is still regarded as perforated, and the animal remains *treifah*. The analogy here is that a mere scab over a hole in the relevant organ does not constitute true closure. The hole remains, and the man's status is unchanged.

This connects to the broader halachic question of *glatt* — literally "smooth." The entire debate around the smoothness of the lung turns on whether abrasions, *sirchos*, or membranous growths are indicative of an underlying perforation or are independently problematic. A *kerum*, properly understood, is not a scab but a membrane — the *sircha* is closer to what one would call a scab in common usage. In any case, the principle is clear: genuine physical closure restores validity; superficial coverage does not.

### Wound healing methods

Rav Idi bar Avin sent an inquiry to Abaye: *heichi avdinan* — if there is a hole and we want the body to close it, what do we do to facilitate that healing? Abaye replied with the following protocol. Take a barley kernel and scratch the area around the hole, drawing some blood and stimulating the body's healing response. Then apply fat to the area, rubbing it in, to promote scabbing and filling. Finally, obtain a large ant — *gamla*, camel-sized — place it at the wound site, allow it to bite the area, and then sever its head, leaving the head embedded. As the head decomposes, it may serve as raw material for the body to seal the wound.

An important clarification: one must scratch specifically with barley and not with iron, because *de-mizraf zarif* — iron causes inflammation rather than the beneficial scabbing one wants. This reflects a practical awareness that metal contact with a wound produces a different physiological response than a gentler abrasion. And all of this applies only to a small hole (*katana*); for a large one, any such closure will ultimately peel away and prove ineffective.

### Dual urination

Rava bar Rav Huna ruled: if a man urinates from two places — apparently from some opening in the penis in addition to its normal tip, possibly indicating that the urine is passing through two internal channels — he is *pasul*. The same underlying puzzle applies here as in the case of the blocked semen passage: why does a condition that is not obviously a classic physical wound fall under these categories? Unless, again, the presumption is that such a condition results from some form of physical injury rather than arising *b'yedei shamayim*.

Rava then ruled: *leit hilcheta* — the halacha does not follow Rava bar Rav Huna in either of his rulings. Neither regarding the son's statement about urination from two places, nor regarding the father Rav Huna's statement, which held that women who engage in sexual contact with one another (*nashim hamisolelot zo b'zo*) are *psulot l'kehuna*, disqualified from marrying a *kohen*. Rashi understands the disqualification to affect eligibility for a *kohen gadol*, implicating the requirement that he marry a *betulah*. Tosafot suggests it relates to the category of *zona* for an ordinary *kohen*. The Gemara rules that neither position is accepted as *halacha*.

The discussion here opens onto a range of fascinating contemporary questions. The Gemara's treatment of female same-sex contact as *pritzuta b'alma* — licentiousness but not halachically constituted sexual intercourse — reflects the principle that *halacha* defines sexual intercourse as requiring penile penetration, whether vaginal or anal. Without that element, there can be no *halachic* act of sex, and consequently no *zona*, no loss of *betulah* status in the operative halachic sense, and arguably no *zera l'vatala* and no *hirhurim* in the same way that male sexual activity generates those concerns. The Gemara confirms this by invoking even Rabbi Elazar's stringent position — that extramarital relations between an unmarried man and an unmarried woman constitute *znut* — and limiting it explicitly: *hatam mili ish*, that applies when there is a man, meaning an act of halachically defined intercourse. *Aval isha* — when only women are involved, it cannot rise to that level.

## Ptzua marriage

### Marriage restrictions

Having worked through the physical definitions, the Gemara turns to the halachic consequences for marriage. A *patzua daka* or *krut shofcha* is *mutar b'giyoret u'meshuchreret* — permitted to marry a convert or a freed slave, women who were not born into the Jewish people. The basis is *de'eino assur ella m'lavo b'kahal* — the prohibition is specifically against entering the *kahal*, meaning against marrying those who are natural-born members of the community. A *giyoret* is not included in that category. The verse is: *lo yavo patzua daka u'krut shofcha b'kehal Hashem*.

This leniency, while welcome, does prompt discomfort. The Torah's principle of *k'ger k'ezrach* implies that a convert stands fully equal to a born Jew, yet in several halachic contexts — including the law of *tum'at yoledet* which required a separate derivation to include a *giyoret*, and here — converts are treated as outside the primary *kahal*. This tension between the ideal of full conversion and the practical halachic categorizations is a recurring theme.

### Priestly status

The question is then posed to Rav Sheshet: a *patzua daka* who is also a *kohen* — what is his status regarding marriage to a *giyoret* or *meshuchreret*? We already know from an earlier *mishnah* that a *patzua daka kohen* retains his priestly status and may eat *terumah*. His *kedushat kehuna* is intact. Given that, should the ordinary restrictions on whom a *kohen* may marry still apply to him? Or, since he is now excluded from the *kahal* with respect to marriage, does that exclusion open up categories of women who would ordinarily be forbidden to a *kohen*?

This is a genuine tension: on one side, his *kedushah* remains in every domain where a physical injury is irrelevant; on the other, the very fact that he is now categorized as outside the *kahal* for marriage purposes may simultaneously remove certain barriers. As was clarified in discussion: the question is not about a *gerushah*, whom a *patzua daka kohen* still cannot marry regardless, but specifically about a *giyoret* — a woman who is excluded from the *kahal* but would otherwise be permissible to a *yisrael*.

### Excluded status benefit

Rav Sheshet responded: *tanituha* — the answer has already been taught. The parallel case involves a *patzua daka yisrael* and a *netina* — a woman descended from the Gibeonites, members of the seven Canaanite nations who converted in the time of Yehoshua by subterfuge. Ordinarily a *yisrael* may not marry someone from the *shivat amamim*, just as a *kohen* may not marry a *giyoret*. Yet a *patzua daka yisrael* is permitted to marry a *netina*. If he still retained his full *kedushah* — including the prohibition *lo titchaten bam* — this should be forbidden. Since it is permitted, it must be that exclusion from the *kahal* opens up marriage to those who are themselves outside that category.

Rava, however, raised a complication. The prohibition of *lo titchaten bam* for the *shivat amamim* is not straightforwardly biblical once they convert. When they are still non-Jews, the verse *lo titchaten bam* cannot mean prohibiting marriage in the halachic sense, since their *kiddushin* would not take effect. The prohibition must therefore be speaking of after conversion. But Rava then suggests that the rabbinic extension of this prohibition — covering converts from the *shivat amamim* — was enacted only where children are in the equation, since the Torah's concern (*ki yasir et bincha me'acharai*) is about children being led astray. A *patzua daka* who cannot have children was never included in that rabbinic decree. So the leniency regarding the *netina* may be rabbinic in character and cannot be used to prove the case of a *kohen* and a *giyoret*.

## Mamzer and Netin

### Excluded analogy

But this argument is then challenged by Rava himself. If the *netina* case is merely rabbinic, consider: a *mamzer* can certainly have children, and yet the *mishnah* teaches *mamzerim u'nesinim mutarim lavo zeh b'zeh* — a *mamzer* and a *netin* may marry one another. If the criterion were about fertility, a *mamzer* should be forbidden to a *netina*. Evidently the principle is different: *ki gazru Rabbanan b'ksherim, b'psulim lo gazru* — when the Rabbis enacted the prohibition against marrying *nesinim*, they only applied it to those who are halachically *kasher*. Those who are themselves in a category of *pesul* — like *mamzer* and *patzua daka* — were not included. So the leniency has a different basis than fertility.

### Biblical vs rabbinic

Rava then reconsidered his own earlier position entirely: *lav milsa hi d'amri* — what I said was not correct. He had claimed that the biblical prohibition of *lo titchaten bam* applies only to the *shivat amamim* while they are non-Jews, and that the prohibition post-conversion is rabbinic. But in fact, when the nations are non-Jews, their *kiddushin* has no binding effect — *leis lehu chasnus*. The very concept of marriage (*chasnus*) only becomes relevant after conversion. Therefore, the Torah's *lo titchaten bam* must be speaking of the prohibition even after conversion — which means it is a *d'oraisa* prohibition. And yet, despite this being biblical, a *patzua daka* and a *mamzer* are permitted to marry *nesinim*. This demonstrates the principle clearly: once someone is excluded from *kahal Hashem*, they are freed from certain restrictions vis-à-vis others who are similarly outside that category. And this principle applies equally to a *kohen* who is a *patzua daka* — despite his *kedushat kehuna*, his exclusion from *kahal Hashem* for marriage purposes opens the door to marry a *giyoret*. This is indeed the ruling recorded in the *Shulchan Aruch*, Even HaEzer, siman 5, se'if 1, which states explicitly that even a *kohen* who is a *patzua daka* is permitted to marry a *giyoret* or *meshuchreret*, since he is no longer within his [full marital] *kedushah* in that domain.

### Shlomo and Egypt

Rav Yosef challenged the position that the biblical *lo titchaten bam* applies only after conversion. If that were so, he asked, how could the verse say *vayitchaten Shlomo es bat Paroh melech Mitzrayim* — that Shlomo married the daughter of Pharaoh? The Gemara responds that she converted (*digayara*). But one might raise an obvious objection: was it not a rule that converts were not accepted in the times of David and Shlomo due to suspicion of ulterior motives — joining the king's household for material benefit? The Gemara answers: the concern about *shulchan melachim* does not apply to bat Paroh herself, since she already came from a royal table; she had nothing to gain materially from conversion. So she was accepted.

But the Gemara presses further: even if she converted, she was a *mitzrit* of the first generation. The verse states *lo tita'ev mitzri ki ger hayita b'artzo*, and then *banim asher yivaldu lahem dor shelishi yavo lahem bikhal Hashem* — only the third generation of a Mitzri convert may enter the *kahal*. A first-generation *mitzrit* converting would not be eligible to marry into the *kahal* for two more generations. So how was Shlomo permitted to marry her?

To illustrate that the Mitzri prohibition was still operative in that era, the Gemara cites a *Baraita* in which Rabbi Yehuda reports: "I had a colleague, Minyamin the Mitzri convert, from among the students of Rabbi Akiva. He told me: I am a first-generation Mitzri convert, and I married a first-generation Mitzrit. I intend to have my son marry a second-generation Mitzrit, so that my grandson will be a third-generation [convert of Mitzri descent] and permitted to enter the *kahal*." This shows that even in the time of Rabbi Akiva — well after Sancheriv had displaced populations — the *halacha* still treated the Mitzri prohibition as operative. The governing principle is *holchin achar hapesul*: if a first-generation marries a second-generation, the child's status follows the more disqualified line and is counted as second-generation; only when a second-generation marries a second-generation does the child achieve third-generation status and full eligibility.

Since the Mitzri prohibition was still in effect in the era of the Talmudic Sages, it must have been in effect in Shlomo's time as well, making bat Paroh's status highly problematic. How then did Shlomo marry her?

Rav Papa answered: *anan miShlomo leika d'lisof* — are we really going to ask questions from Shlomo? The implication is that Shlomo transgressed. But the Gemara then revisits this and suggests: *Shlomo lo nasiv midi* — Shlomo did not actually marry them. The verse says: *min hagoyim asher amar Hashem el bnei Yisrael lo tavo'u bahem... bahem davak Shlomo l'ahava* — unto them Shlomo cleaved for love. The word *davak*, cleaved, indicates passionate attachment, not formal marriage. He was bound to them deeply, but did not legally marry them.

The Gemara then acknowledges the residual difficulty: but the verse explicitly says *vayitchaten* — he married. The answer: *mitoch ahava yeseirah she'ahava, ma'alah alav ke'ilu yitchaten bah* — because of the exceptional love he bore her, it was as though he had married her, but technically he had not. This is, the Gemara acknowledges, a somewhat forced reading.

Tosafot raises an important related point: after Sancheriv displaced the nations, shouldn't we simply say that the people living in Egypt are no longer the halachic *mitzrim* of the Torah? Tosafot quotes a *Tosefta* in which Rabbi Akiva told Minyamin directly: *ta'isa* — you made a mistake. You think you are a *mitzri*, but Sancheriv already came and scrambled all the nations (*bilbel kol ha'olam*), and therefore no one living now can be considered a halachic *mitzri*. The Gemara itself, however, maintains that the identification persisted — not just in Shlomo's time but even in the era of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Akiva.

One broader halachic point emerges from this entire discussion. The prohibitions we have been examining — *patzua daka*, *mamzer*, *mitzri*, *amoni* — concern the formal institution of *nisu'in*, marriage. The question of whether the prohibition is violated by sexual relations outside the framework of marriage is a distinct and nuanced question. As the Gemara implies here, the *lo titchaten* formulation presupposes a formal act of marriage. By contrast, prohibitions that involve *kares* — the severe biblical penalties for incestuous or adulterous relations — are entirely about the act of intercourse, and marriage is not even a relevant concept in those contexts since *kiddushin* would not take effect.

## Intermarriage rules

### Amoni/Moavi rules

The *mishnah* now turns to the generational restrictions on various nations joining the *kahal*. *Amoni u'Moavi asurin v'isuran issur olam* — an Ammonite and a Moabite are forbidden forever. Even *gam dor asiri* — a tenth generation — may not enter the *kahal* of Hashem. Their females, however, are *mutarot miyad* — immediately permissible upon conversion.

### Mitzri/Edom rules

A Mitzri or an Edomite is forbidden only *ad shelosha dorot* — for three generations, after which *dor shelishi yavo lahem bikhal Hashem*. Here the *mishnah* specifies *echad zecharim v'echad nekivot* — both males and females must wait three generations. This is notable: the more severe prohibition of *amoni u'moavi*, which is permanent for males, is actually more lenient for females. The less severe prohibition of *mitzri* and *edomi* applies equally to both genders.

### Shimon's logic

Rabbi Shimon rules that females of Egyptian and Edomite descent should be *mutarot miyad*, just as female Ammonites and Moabites are. He advances a *kal vachomer*: if in the case where males are permanently forbidden — *amoni u'moavi* — the females are immediately permitted, then certainly in the case where males are forbidden only for three generations — *mitzri v'edomi* — the females should be permitted immediately. The Sages responded: if you have a tradition (*halacha*) we will accept it, but if you are arguing by logic (*ledin*), we have a refutation of your *kal vachomer*. Rabbi Shimon replied: I am not relying solely on logic; I am stating this as a received *halacha*. Whether that tradition was ultimately accepted will emerge from the Gemara's continued discussion.

## David and Ruth

### Saul's inquiry

The Gemara now grounds the rule that a female Ammonite or Moabite is *muteret miyad* in a narrative from *Navi*. Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse: *v'chirot Shaul et David yotzei likrat haplishti* — when Shaul saw David going out to confront the Philistine, Goliath, *amar el Avner sar hatzava* — he said to Avner, his general — *ben mi zeh hana'ar* — whose son is this young man?

This seems puzzling. Surely Shaul knew who David was — David had been his personal armor-bearer, and the verse itself records *vayeehavehu me'od vayehi lo nosei keilim* — Shaul loved him greatly and David bore his weapons. Furthermore, Yishai was not an obscure figure: the verse describes him as *zaken ba b'anashim*, a man of great stature in the time of Shaul, and the Gemara cites Rav (and some say Rabbi Abba): *zeh Yishai avi David shenichnas b'uchlusa v'yatza b'uchlusa* — whenever Yishai entered or departed, he was accompanied by tens of thousands. Rashi notes that Yishai commanded 600,000. How could Avner not have known him?

The Gemara resolves: Shaul was not asking about David's identity or about Yishai. *Ei mi'Peretz asi ei mi'Zerach asi* — what he wanted to know was: does David descend from Perez or from Zerach, the two lineages of Yehuda? *Ei mi'Peretz asi, malka havei* — if from Perez, Shaul had reason for concern. The king is said to *poretz*, to burst through boundaries without restraint — that is the nature of royal power. Descent from Perez would indicate David was destined for kingship. *Ei mi'Zerach asi, chashiva b'alma havei* — if from Zerach, the shining one, David would have prestige but not threaten the throne.

What provoked Shaul's anxiety at precisely this moment? The verse records that Shaul dressed David in his own garments — *madav kemidoto* — and David wore them to measure, fitting him as perfectly as they fit Shaul, who was *mishichmo vamala gavoah mikol ha'am*, a head taller than all the people. David matched Shaul physically, and Shaul, seeing before him a young man of equal stature and evident charisma, felt genuinely threatened.

### Doeg's objection

At this point, *Doeg ha'Edomi* intervened. He said to Shaul: *ad she'ata mash'il alav im hagun hu l'malchus im lav* — before you worry whether he is of royal lineage, ask a more fundamental question: *sha'al alav im ra'uy lavo b'kahal im lav* — is he even eligible to be part of the *kahal*? *Mai ta'ama deka'asi me'Rus haMoaviyah* — because he descends from Ruth the Moabitess.

Avner responded: *tanina, Amoni velo Amonit, Moavi velo Moavit* — we have a tradition: the prohibition is *Amoni*, not *Amonit*; *Moavi*, not *Moavit*. A female Moabitess is immediately permitted. Doeg challenged Avner's silence with a counter-argument: very well, but then say *Mitzri velo Mitzrit* — why don't we apply the same logic to Egypt and permit female Egyptian converts immediately?

## Intermarriage rules (II)

### Greeting logic

The Gemara explains the textual basis for distinguishing between male and female Ammonites and Moabites, and thereby answering Doeg's challenge about Egypt. The verse gives a specific reason for the prohibition: *al asher lo kidmu etchem balechem uvamayim* — because they did not come out to greet you with bread and water. This reason generates the limited application: *darko shel ish lekadem velo darko shel isha lekadem* — it is the way of a man to go out and greet, not the way of a woman. Therefore, only the men can be held culpable for the failure to extend hospitality; the women cannot. This is the basis for reading *Amoni* and not *Amonit*, *Moavi* and not *Moavit*.

## David and Ruth (II)

### Beis HaMedrash

Doeg was not satisfied. He pressed: if men should have gone out to greet the men and women should have gone out to greet the women — *anashim likrat anashim venashim likrat nashim* — then the women of Moab were equally remiss for not greeting the women of Israel. Why should they be exempt? Avner fell silent. He had no ready answer.

Shaul then directed: *tze ushal b'veis hamedrash* — go and pose this question in the *Beis HaMedrash*. The Gemara notes the wordplay: Shaul called David an *elem* in this verse rather than a *na'ar* as he did earlier, and the Gemara reads this as Shaul saying *halacha nit'almah mimcha* — the *halacha* has been hidden from you; Avner does not know the answer. Go to the *Beis HaMedrash* and find out.

When they arrived at the *Beis HaMedrash*, the ruling was the same as Avner had stated: *Amoni velo Amonit, Moavi velo Moavit*. But Doeg was there in the *Beis HaMedrash* and challenged everyone with all the same objections. *Ba'i le'achruzei alei* — he sought to make a public proclamation disqualifying David. The entire *Beis HaMedrash* fell silent before his challenge. How David's lineage was ultimately vindicated and his legitimacy as king of Israel established — that we will take up tomorrow.

---

---

# Yevamot 78

## Rabbi Shimon vs. Rabbanan

### Shimon's Kal Vachomer

We pick up toward the very bottom of 77b, in the midst of the debate concerning Rabbi Shimon's position in the Mishnah. Rabbi Shimon maintains that *Mitzri* and *Adomi* women should be permitted immediately — that is, from the first generation — reasoning by way of a *kal vachomer*: just as *Ammoni* and *Moavi*, where the prohibition is far stricter (applying to all generations), is limited to males — *Ammoni v'lo Ammonit* — then certainly *Mitzri* and *Adomi*, whose prohibition extends only two generations, should similarly not apply to the women.

### Rabbanan's Challal Prece…

The Rabbis respond by adducing the cases of *mamzer* and *arayot* as precedent: in those contexts, the prohibition falls upon both men and women, demonstrating that a prohibition need not be limited to males even where other asymmetries exist. Rabbi Shimon would rejoin that *arayot* and *mamzer* are different in a crucial respect: *mamzer* is conceived through an act carrying *karet*, and *arayot* themselves are *karet* offenses. By contrast, the prohibition against marrying *Mitzri* or *Adomi* does not even rise to the level of a *lav* — it is merely an *issur asei*. Given that lighter status, the *kal vachomer* in favor of permitting the women should hold.

### Shimon's Kareis Distinct…

The Gemara then asks: what would the Rabbis answer to this? Seven lines from the bottom of the page, we read *rabbanan* — the Rabbis would cite the case of the *challal* who is produced through a violation of an *issur asei*, in accordance with Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov. For example, a *Kohen Gadol* who marries a non-*besulah* violates only an *issur asei*, yet according to Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov the child of that union is a *challal*, and *challal* status applies to both males and females immediately. This parallel, the Rabbis argue, shows that even an *issur asei* can yield a prohibition that applies equally to both sexes.

### Rabbanan's Asei Argument

Of course, the analogy is imperfect in one respect — the *challal* case is a *issur kehunah*, not an *issur kahal* — but the point stands nonetheless: there do exist cases where a person's status, derived from an *issur asei*, applies equally and immediately to both men and women.

### Halakha Ani Omer

Six lines from the bottom of 77b, the Gemara asks what Rabbi Shimon means when he concludes the Mishnah debate with the formulation *halacha ani omer* — "I have a tradition." The Gemara clarifies: *hachi ka'amar lehu* — here is what he is actually saying to them. *Ledidi lo svira li de'Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov* — I personally do not hold like Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov; I maintain that an *issur asei* does not create *challal* status. Therefore, *ledidchu de'svira lechu ke'Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov* — you, who do hold like Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov, think you can draw the parallel to *Mitzri* and *Adomi*. But even so, *halacha ani omer* — I still have a received tradition, and therefore even if my logical argument cannot be pressed to a definitive conclusion, the tradition itself is determinative. It is worth noting, as an aside, that the logical argument is in fact on Rabbi Shimon's side as well, even if the Rabbis have a technical basis for pushing back.

### Tosafot on Tradition

An interesting point emerges from *Tosafot* here. *Tosafot* notes: *lav halacha le'Moshe mi'Sinai ka'amar* — Rabbi Shimon is not claiming a *halacha le'Moshe mi'Sinai* in the technical sense. For if he were, why would the Rabbis continue to debate him? Rather, *ella hachi ka'amar halacha ani omer kach kibalti mei'rabosai* — he is saying, "This is my tradition: I received it from my teachers."

This point resonates with the broader position of the Rambam, who argued that genuine *halachot le'Moshe mi'Sinai* are never subject to rabbinic debate. This was the Rambam's response to the Karaite critique that the very existence of Talmudic disputes undermines the claim to an authentic *mesorah*. The Rambam's answer is that all rabbinic debates concern human minds engaging with the sacred text, reaching different conclusions through reasoning — not a broken chain of tradition. Where there was an actual transmitted tradition, there is no dispute. While the Rambam's position is itself subject to challenge — there are in fact disputes recorded about matters described as *halacha le'Moshe mi'Sinai* — *Tosafot*'s point here is more specific: in this Mishnah, the Rabbis do not appear to be advancing a competing tradition of their own. They are simply arguing from logic. That being the case, why do they not simply concede to Rabbi Shimon's tradition? The answer, says *Tosafot*, is that he does not have a *halacha le'Moshe mi'Sinai* — he has something more limited, a ruling or understanding received from his *Rebbi*, perhaps based on earlier *pesak* or on argument, and thus the Rabbis feel entitled to contest it.

---

## Baraita on Women

### Barim Pasuk Support

A *baraita* now addresses the same dispute. *Tanu rabbanan*: Rabbi Shimon said to them, *halacha ani omer* — I have a received tradition — *v'od mikra mesay'ani* — and moreover the verse itself supports me. And this support is arguably even stronger than the inference from *Ammoni v'lo Ammonit*. The verse reads: *banim asher yivaldu lahem dor shelishi yavo'u lahem b'kahal Hashem* — "the children that will be born to them, the third generation, shall enter the congregation of Hashem." Rabbi Shimon reads *banim* — "sons" — as excluding daughters: the sons will be permitted in the third generation, implying the daughters were never restricted in the first place.

### Yehuda's Yuladu Reading

Rabbi Yehuda offers an alternative reading of the same verse. The verse says *banim asher yivaldu lahem dor shelishi* — "the children that will be born to them, the third generation." Rabbi Yehuda observes: *hakatuv telayan b'leida* — the verse has made the matter dependent upon birth, upon the act of giving birth. The one who gives birth is the mother, and the mother is a woman. This suggests that the mothers themselves — that is, women of the first and second generation *Mitzri* or *Adomi* — are also forbidden. The verse is concerned with when they will give birth, implying those women are themselves subject to the prohibition until the third generation.

### Yochanan's Evaluation

Rabbi Yochanan's assessment of this exchange is striking. He says: *ilmalei d'amar Rabbi Yehuda hakatuv telayan b'leida* — if Rabbi Yehuda had not made his point about the verse focusing on birthing and thereby demonstrating that women too are forbidden, *lo matza yadav v'raglav b'beit hamidrash* — he would have had no standing in the study hall, meaning his overall position would have been logically incoherent. The reason will now become clear.

---

## Marriage Possibility Iss…

### Gerim Are Kahal

Rabbi Yochanan's remark points to a fundamental problem with Rabbi Yehuda's position that had not yet been articulated. The issue stems from another ruling associated with Rabbi Yehuda: *kahal gerim ikrei kahal* — converts are considered part of *kahal*, that is, the term *kahal Hashem* encompasses converts as well. This means that those who are forbidden from marrying into *kahal Hashem* may not marry *gerim* either. The standard assumption in this entire sugya had been that *Ammoni*, *Moavi*, *Mitzri*, and *Adomi* converts could at least marry other *gerim*. But Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on *kahal gerim* closes that door.

### Marital Impasse

This creates a severe problem: *Mitzri sheni bameh yit-har?* — how does a second-generation *Mitzri* ever come to have a third-generation child who is permitted? He cannot marry a *Yisraelit* — she is in the *kahal*. He cannot marry a *giyores* — she too is now *kahal* according to Rabbi Yehuda. Who remains for him to marry?

One might suggest he could marry a *mamzeret* — but then the children would themselves be *mamzerim* and could never enter *kahal Hashem* regardless. Another suggestion: perhaps he could marry a *Mitzrit* convert. But if, following Rabbi Shimon, *Mitzrit* women are permitted to all of Israel — that is, they are included in *kahal Hashem* like ordinary *gerim* — then they too would be forbidden to him. So if one holds both that *gerim* are *kahal* and that *Mitzrit* women are unrestricted, there is simply no permissible path by which a male *Mitzri* convert can ever produce a third generation that enters *kahal Hashem*.

### Mutar Pathway

The resolution must be, then, that *Mitzrit* women are themselves forbidden — that is, they are not included in *kahal Hashem*, their status is restricted just like the men, and therefore a male *Mitzri* can marry a female *Mitzrit*. That union provides the *mutar* pathway through which the third generation can ultimately come about.

### Torah Doesn't Speak B'di…

The Gemara suggests an alternative: perhaps we are talking about *b'di'avad* — a second-generation *Mitzri* who transgresses and marries someone he should not, and whose child similarly transgresses, thereby producing a third generation through prohibited unions. But the Gemara rejects this: *d'i lo katav kra* — the Torah does not write a verse addressing what happens when people have been sinning for two generations. The Torah would not frame a *hetter* — a permission to enter *kahal Hashem* — around the premise that transgressions were committed to get there.

### Mamzer Precedent

The Gemara challenges this principle with the case of *mamzer*: is not *mamzer* status itself created only through a transgression, and yet the Torah writes about it? So the Torah does speak of *b'di'avad* scenarios.

### Negative vs. Positive

The Gemara answers: *d'ei l'issura ktiv* — that verse addresses *b'di'avad* in order to impose negative consequences. If someone transgresses and a child is born from a forbidden union, the Torah tells you the negative outcome: the child is a *mamzer*. That is fundamentally different from a verse that would, *de'ei lehateira*, come to teach a *hetter* — a positive permission — that results from transgression. The Torah will tell you the negative consequences of sin; it will not frame a *hetter* as something achieved through sin.

### Mechzir Grushato Case

But is that really true? The Gemara raises the case of *machzir grushato* — the prohibition against a man remarrying a woman he divorced after she had married another man. From the verse dealing with that prohibition, a *drasha* teaches *hi toeivah ve'ein baneha toeivim* — she is forbidden but her children from the second marriage do not acquire a degraded status. That is a *hetter* derived from a context of prohibition. So the Torah does teach *heteirim* arising from problematic situations.

### Primary vs. Secondary

The Gemara resolves the difficulty: *hasam mishum ikar issura hu dekatveih* — the primary purpose of that verse is to teach the *issur*, to say that this man may not remarry her. The *hetter* regarding the children is incidental, secondary to the main point. A verse whose primary purpose is to establish a prohibition may include, in passing, a *hetter*. But a verse would not be written *primarily* to teach a *hetter* that is only accessible through transgression.

### Women Forbidden Necessary

The conclusion stands: for the Torah to have written that the third generation *Mitzri* may enter *kahal Hashem*, there must be a *mutar* path to reach that third generation. Given Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that *kahal gerim ikrei kahal*, the only available *mutar* path is for *Mitzri* men to marry *Mitzrit* women. And for that to be permissible, the *Mitzrit* women must themselves be in a restricted status — forbidden to ordinary Israel, and therefore available to marry *Mitzri* men. This is Rabbi Yochanan's point: without Rabbi Yehuda's observation that the verse focuses on birthing — thereby establishing that women too are subject to the prohibition — Rabbi Yehuda would have been unable to defend any coherent position. His ruling about *kahal gerim* would render the entire mechanism of the three-generation process impossible.

---

## Textual Parsing

### Banim vs. Dorot

The Gemara now turns to close textual analysis of the verse *banim asher yivaldu lahem dor shelishi yavo'u lahem b'kahal Hashem*. The verse contains apparent redundancy: it uses both *banim* (children) and *dor* (generation). Why are both necessary? If the Torah wished to say "the third generation may enter," why not simply say *ben shelishi* or *dor shelishi*?

### Banim Meaning

*Im ne'emar banim lama ne'emar dorot* — if it had only said *banim* (sons or children), without specifying *dorot* (generations), one might have thought the count is based on children, not generations. That is, the third child born to the convert — even if that child is a sibling of the first and second child — would already be permitted. This would mean you need only a third child, not a third generation. Therefore *lekach ne'emar dorot* — the term "generations" is necessary to establish that it is the third generational descent that is required, not merely the third child.

### Dorot Meaning

Conversely, *im ne'emar dorot lama ne'emar banim* — had it said only *dorot* without *banim*, one might have read the three generations as counting from Har Sinai, or from the time the Torah was given, rather than from the moment of conversion. This would be a reasonable reading: these were the nations that wronged Israel, and so three generations from the revelation — from a fixed historical point — they will be permitted. Therefore *lekach ne'emar banim* — the word *banim* is needed to anchor the count to when they begin having children, that is, from the time of conversion and the onset of their progeny. Both terms are thus indispensable.

### First Lahem

The verse also contains the word *lahem* twice: *banim asher yivaldu lahem dor shelishi yavo'u lahem b'kahal Hashem*. Each appearance teaches something distinct. The first *lahem* — *mehem meneh*, count from them — establishes that the generational count begins with the converts themselves, not from Har Sinai, and not from the children. The *lahem* fixes the starting point as the converts themselves. Without this, one might have read *asher yivaldu* (that will be born) as making the children generation one, so that the "third generation" would in fact be the great-grandchildren of the convert. *Lahem* corrects this: the convert is generation one, the children are generation two, and the grandchildren are the third generation permitted to enter *kahal Hashem*.

This is confirmed by the following consideration: one might have thought that a pregnant *Mitzrit* who converted, she and her fetus count as one — the fetus, having been converted as a fetus, remains generation one along with the mother. Therefore *katav rachamana asher yivaldu* — "that will be born" — to teach that once the child is actually born, that birth already advances the count to the next generation, even though the fetus was converted in utero.

### Second Lahem - Psul

The second *lahem* teaches *halech achar psulan* — go after their disqualification, whichever parent bears the *Mitzri* or *Adomi* status, the child inherits that status, regardless of whether it is the father or the mother. One might have assumed that status follows only the father — given the general patrilineal principle in matters of tribal and national identity — or conversely only the mother. The second *lahem* establishes that whenever a *Mitzri* or *Adomi* is in the parentage, the *psul* follows.

A practical example: if a first-generation *Mitzri* marries a second-generation *Mitzrit*, or vice versa, the child is counted as second generation rather than third — because the child goes after the more severe of the two statuses. Similarly, if a *Mitzri* marries a *Yisraelit*, the child does not simply become a full *Yisrael* by following the father; the *lahem* ensures the *Mitzri psul* continues.

### Mamzer Parallel

A parallel derivation exists by *mamzer*. The verse regarding *mamzer* says *lo yavo mamzer b'kehal Hashem*. From the word *lo* — corresponding to the *lahem* by *Mitzri* — the Gemara derives that wherever the *mamzer* is in the parentage, the *psul* follows that parent, whether the *mamzer* is the father or the mother. The same principle applies: the child of a *mamzer* father or a *mamzeret* mother is a *mamzer*.

One might ask: why state this principle separately for both *mamzer* and *Mitzri*? State it once and derive the other by analogy. The Gemara explains that each is necessary. Had the principle been written only by *Mitzri*, one might have said it is so because the *Mitzri* comes from a *tipah pesulah* — he was born outside the Jewish people, and therefore there is a profound invalidity to either parental line. But a *mamzer*, who was born Jewish albeit through a forbidden union, might be different — perhaps the *psul* would not follow from either parent. Therefore *lo* is written by *mamzer* as well.

And conversely, had it been written only by *mamzer* — whose prohibition is absolute and eternal — one might have concluded that this severe, permanent *psul* is what generates the rule that either parent transmits it. But by *Mitzri*, whose prohibition is only two generations and lighter in character, perhaps the *psul* follows only one parent. Therefore *lahem* is needed by *Mitzri* as well. Both formulations are indispensable: *tzericha*.

---

## Paternity vs. Maternity

### Yochanan - Follow Father

The Gemara now addresses whether the *psul* in practice follows the father, the mother, or simply the weightier of the two statuses. Rabba bar bar Chana cites Rabbi Yochanan: *Mitzri sheni she'natal Mitzrit rishona bnah shelishi havei* — a second-generation *Mitzri* man who marries a first-generation *Mitzrit* woman, their child is a third generation and therefore permitted. This is a significant statement: it means that what matters is the father's status, not the mother's. Since the father is second generation, the child is third, regardless of the mother being first generation.

### Patrilineal Status

The implication, as the Gemara draws it: *alma kasavar basar didei shadina lei* — Rabbi Yochanan holds that we follow the father. This is, after all, the intuitively natural position in a patrilineal system. Yet the Gemara does not simply accept this inference and moves on to interrogate it.

### Rav Yosef Challenge

Rav Yosef challenges this with a *baraita*. Rabbi Tarfon says: *yecholim mamzerim litaher* — it is possible to purify *mamzerim* from their status. How? If a *mamzer* marries a *shifcha* (a Canaanite slave woman), the child is an *eved* — a slave — and the *mamzer* status is overridden or displaced by the slave status. If that child is subsequently freed, the person is a free Jew with no *mamzer* status. This practice was in fact suggested as a practical ruling by Rav Moshe Feinstein.

The Gemara then notes that from the *shifcha* case it might appear that the child follows the mother exclusively — the child of a slave woman is a slave, which seems to say you go by the mother.

### Minymin Example

Rav Yosef's challenge is further developed by a *baraita* about Minymin, a first-generation *Mitzri* convert who was a student of Rabbi Akiva. Minymin said: "I am a first-generation *Mitzri*, and I married a first-generation *Mitzrit*. I intend to have my son marry a second-generation *Mitzrit*, so that my grandson will be fit to enter *kahal*." The critical element here is that Minymin planned for his son — who as the child of two first-generation *Mitzrim* is himself second generation — to marry a second-generation *Mitzrit*. The assumption is that the child of a second-generation father and a second-generation mother would be third generation, and therefore permitted. But this only works if both parents' status matters. If you simply followed the father, Minymin's son could marry even a first-generation *Mitzrit* — the child would still be third generation by the father's reckoning. The fact that Minymin insists on a second-generation mother demonstrates that you do not simply follow the father.

### Yochanan Emends

Rabbi Yochanan responds to this challenge by amending the text: *l'tana tani rishona* — emend the *baraita* to read that Minymin said his son could marry even a first-generation *Mitzrit*, consistent with the view that you always follow the father. Rabbi Yochanan is revising the wording of the *baraita* to conform to his own ruling, rather than taking the *baraita* as evidence against his position.

### Dimi - Follow Mother?

When Rav Dimi arrived from Eretz Yisrael, he transmitted a different version of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: *Mitzri sheni shenassa Mitzrit rishona beno sheni* — a second-generation *Mitzri* man who married a first-generation *Mitzrit* woman, the son is second generation. This is the opposite conclusion from what Rabba bar bar Chana cited in Rabbi Yochanan's name. In this version, the child is second generation — apparently because the mother is first generation, which is the more severe status. The Gemara reads this as implying that you follow the mother: *alma basar imeh shadinan lei*.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye challenges Rav Dimi: if Rabbi Yochanan truly holds that you go by the mother, this contradicts another ruling of Rabbi Yochanan concerning a *chatas* that was pregnant when sanctified.

### Chatas Precedent

The ruling is this: if one set aside a female animal as a *chatas* while it was pregnant, and it subsequently gave birth, one may use either the mother or the offspring as the *chatas*. Rabbi Yochanan holds that this works because *ubar lav yerech imo hu* — the fetus is not considered a limb of the mother; it has an independent identity even while in the womb. Therefore when the pregnant animal was sanctified, there were effectively two animals sanctified: the mother and the fetus as an independent entity. This is like sanctifying two animals *le'achrayut* — as mutual backups — in which case one may use either one, and the other grazes until it acquires a blemish and is redeemed. Rabbi Oshaya rules that if two *chataot* are designated as backups for each other, one may atone with one of them and the other grazes until it is redeemed.

### Ubar Yerech Imo

The principle *ubar lav yerech imo hu* — the fetus is not a limb or extension of the mother but has its own independent identity — is what enables this ruling. If, by contrast, *ubar yerech imo hu* — the fetus were merely part of the mother's body — then the fetus would be in the status of *velad chatas*, a child born to a sanctified animal, and *velad chatas lemissa azil* — such an offspring must be left to die and may not be used as a *korban*. The fact that Rabbi Yochanan permits using the offspring shows he holds *ubar lav yerech imo*.

### Abaye's Logic

Abaye's argument is as follows: if the fetus has an independent identity — separate from the mother even while in the womb — then its personal status should not follow the mother. The independent entity of the fetus ought to follow the father, consistent with the general patrilineal principle. How, then, can Rabbi Yochanan simultaneously hold *ubar lav yerech imo* and also that the *psul* follows the mother?

It must be said that this is a striking association. The principle of *ubar yerech imo* concerns whether a fetus is viewed as a separate legal entity for purposes of sanctification, ritual status of *kodshim*, and similar matters. Why would the same concept govern whether a child's national or ethnic *psul* follows the father or the mother? The application seems genuinely difficult to understand. Yet the Gemara draws precisely this connection — and it is worth flagging that the Gemara itself, in debates about abortion and other *peshat* applications of *ubar yerech imo*, does not typically invoke this principle in the same framework. Here, the Gemara is forcing an association that, as the Gemara itself seems aware, requires explanation. Nevertheless, that is the argument Abaye presents.

### Dimi's Pasuk Response

After the challenge, Abaye himself suggests the resolution: *dilma shani hasam dichtiv asher yivaldu* — perhaps by *Mitzri* it is different, because the verse says *asher yivaldu*, "that will be born," and *hakatuv talao b'leida* — the Torah has made the matter dependent on the act of birth. Since the verse focuses on the birthing, perhaps the Torah is specifically indicating that here, uniquely, the status follows the mother — she is the one who gives birth — even though in general *ubar lav yerech imo* would seem to point the other way.

### Normally Father

Rav Dimi responds with warm acknowledgment: *karkafna chaziti lreishach beini amudei* — I saw your head among the pillars of the study hall, meaning: you were there with Rabbi Yochanan when this was taught. And indeed, *ki amar Rav Yochanan lha shmata* — when Rabbi Yochanan taught this ruling, *taama dichtiv asher yivaldu* — the reason he gave was precisely the verse *asher yivaldu*, the focus on birthing. And he explicitly added: *ha be'alma basar avuh shadinan lei* — in all other cases, you follow the father. The rule here is a local exception derived from the specific formulation of the verse, not a general principle.

It is worth noting that the Gemara's entire discussion oscillates between three apparent positions: always following the father, always following the mother, and following the more severe of the two *psulim*. The resolution, as the Gemara will ultimately frame it, is that in general you do indeed follow the *psul* — the more severe of the two parental statuses — but by *Mitzri* and *Adomi* there is the additional local rule derived from *asher yivaldu* that anchors the status particularly in the birth, and thus the mother. The discussion of the *chatas* and *ubar yerech imo* in this connection, though logically puzzling, is the Gemara's vehicle for arriving at this conclusion.

---

## Non-Jews Follow Father

### Males Determine

When Ravin arrived from Eretz Yisrael, he cited a third version of Rabbi Yochanan's teaching, one that synthesizes the various strands: *ba'umot halech achar hazachar* — among non-Jews, before conversion, you follow the male. When two individuals of different national backgrounds — say, a *Mitzri* and an *Ammonit*, or any two nationalities — have a child, and neither parent is Jewish, the child's national identity follows the father. This is the straightforward expression of the patrilineal principle in a context of non-Jewish nationality.

### Canaanite Case

This is derived from a *baraita*: *minayin le'achad min ha'umot sheba al hakena'anit veholid ben* — from where do we know that a man of another nation who had relations with a Canaanite woman and produced a child — that child is not Canaanite and you may purchase him as a slave? The verse states: *vegam mibnei hatoshavim hagerim imachem mehem tiknu* — from the settlers and sojourners who dwell among you, from them you may purchase. These are men of other nations settling among the Canaanites and having children with Canaanite women. Those children are not Canaanite, and may be acquired as slaves — whereas a Canaanite would have to be killed. This demonstrates that among the nations, identity follows the father: the child of a non-Canaanite father is not Canaanite even if born of a Canaanite mother.

Conversely, one might have thought the reverse — that a Canaanite man who had children with a woman of another nation would produce Canaanite children. The verse *asher holidu b'artzechem* — that were born in your land — implies that the children are born where the mothers are from, and those born in the land of another nation (through a Canaanite father with a foreign mother) are not of the same national status as Canaanites born locally. This reinforces: among non-Jews, identity follows the father.

### Worse Status

Once they have converted, however, the rule changes: *nitgeiru halech achar pagum she'bishneihem* — after conversion, you follow the worse status of the two parents. Whatever *psul* is weightier between the two parents is the one that determines the child's status.

### Gender-Dependent

The Gemara clarifies this with a concrete example. Suppose it is an *Amoni* man who married a *Mitzrit* woman. What is the worse status? The answer depends on the sex of the child, and this is where the analysis becomes nuanced. If the child is male, then being *Amoni* is the worse outcome — an *Amoni* male is forbidden to *kahal Hashem* for all generations. Being *Mitzri* is better since it is only two generations. So for a male child, the worse status is *Amoni*, and the child is classified as *Amoni* and forbidden entirely. If the child is female, however, then being *Amoni* is in a sense not a *psul* at all — *Ammonit* women are entirely permitted. Being *Mitzrit* is actually worse for a female, because she carries the two-generation restriction. So a female child of this union would be classified as a second-generation *Mitzrit*.

In other words, both parental identities are present in the child, and the one that generates the greater actual disability in that particular case — given the child's sex — is the one that governs. The conclusion, *halach achar ha'psul*, is thus not a simple mechanical rule but must be applied with attention to the specific configuration of both parents and the sex of the child.

---

## Mamzer Discussion

### Mishna Rule

We now turn to the final sugya of the daf. The Mishnah states: *mamzerim u-netinim asurim be-issur olam echad zecharim ve-echad nekevot* — *mamzerim* and *netinim* are forbidden forever, and this applies equally to males and females. The *netinim* are the Gibeonites who converted; their precise status — whether the prohibition against them is biblical or rabbinic — is a matter for subsequent discussion. The *mamzer* prohibition, of course, is well established.

### Resh Lakish

Against this Mishnah, Resh Lakish advances a startling position: *mamzeret le-achar asarah dorot muteret* — a female *mamzer* becomes permitted after ten generations. This is undeniably a bold claim given the explicit language of the Mishnah, and it demands careful examination.

### Gezeira Shavah

Resh Lakish learns this through a *gezeira shavah* connecting *mamzer* to *Ammoni* and *Moavi*. The verse concerning *Ammoni* and *Moavi* reads: *lo yavo Ammoni u-Moavi b'kahal Hashem gam dor asiri lo yavo lahem b'kahal Hashem ad olam* — they shall not enter the congregation of Hashem; even the tenth generation shall not enter the congregation of Hashem forever. Here, *dor asiri* (tenth generation) functions as a gloss on *ad olam* (forever): what "ten generations" means is "forever." By *mamzer*, the verse says: *lo yavo mamzer b'kahal Hashem gam dor asiri lo yavo lo b'kahal Hashem* — the same formulation of *dor asiri* appears, but without *ad olam*. Resh Lakish proposes to borrow the *ad olam* from *Ammoni* and *Moavi* and apply it to *mamzer* via this *gezeira shavah*. But — and this is the crux — the *ad olam* of *Ammoni* and *Moavi* applies only to the males of those nations: *Ammoni v'lo Ammonit*. Women of *Ammon* and *Moav* are permitted. Therefore, when we extend *mamzer* to *ad olam* via this *gezeira shavah*, we can only extend the male *mamzer*. Female *mamzerim*, after the tenth generation, are no longer covered by the *ad olam* and become permitted.

### Gezeira Shavah Method

The Gemara reconciles Resh Lakish's position with the Mishnah, which states that males and females are equally forbidden *ad olam*, by reference to a classical dispute about the methodology of *gezeira shavah*. There are two approaches: *don minah u-minah* — you take the learned principle together with its original context — and *don minah ve-okei be-atrah* — you derive the principle from the *gezeira shavah* but then anchor it in the new context. If you follow *don minah u-minah*, you take the *ad olam* of *Ammoni* and *Moavi* along with its original restriction to males, and apply that to *mamzer*: males are forbidden forever, females are not. If you follow *don minah ve-okei be-atrah*, you take the *ad olam* from *Ammoni* and *Moavi*, but plant it in the soil of *mamzer* — where the context is males and females equally — and then *ad olam* applies equally to both sexes.

### Compromise Resolution

The Mishnah, then, follows *don minah ve-okei be-atrah*, and Resh Lakish follows *don minah u-minah*. The *gezeira shavah* itself operates on the word *asiri*: both verses contain *dor asiri*, and from this shared term the *ad olam* is extended to *mamzer*. The practical upshot of Resh Lakish's position is that the first ten generations of both male and female *mamzerim* are explicitly forbidden by the verse; beyond ten generations, the *ad olam* extension applies only to males.

### Eliezer Cryptic

The Gemara then cites an enigmatic exchange: *sha'alu et Rabbi Eliezer* — they asked Rabbi Eliezer, what is the status of a *mamzer* after ten generations? He answered: *mi yiten li dor shelishi va-ataharenu* — if I had a third generation in hand, I would purify them, make them permissible.

### Mamzerim Don't Live

The Gemara explains: *amar kasavar mamzera lo chaya* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that *mamzerim* simply do not live long enough to reach many generations. This is a metaphysical proposition: God, as it were, would never allow a situation in which unwitting Jews might transgress by marrying *mamzerim* whose status has been forgotten. Therefore divine providence ensures that *mamzerim* do not survive beyond a small number of generations. When Rabbi Eliezer says "if I had a third generation I would purify them," he means: you are asking me about ten generations — but they won't even reach three. And Rav Huna similarly holds: *mamzera lo chaya*.
