But if so, why does the Mishnah speak of *mamzerim* being forbidden *ad olam*? Presumably the Mishnah implies they do in fact persist. The Mishnah's language of eternal prohibition must be addressing the normative rule, even if in practice the situation is mitigated by providence.

### Zeira's Nuance

Rabbi Zeira offers a more precise formulation of this principle, transmitted from Rav Yehuda. The rule is not absolute: *d'yedya chaya* — a *mamzer* who is publicly known does live, because there is no danger of unwitting transgression. The community is aware of his status and will not intermarry with him. *D'lo yedya lo chaya* — a *mamzer* who is unknown to the community dies, because the danger of inadvertent transgression is immediate. *D'yedya v'd'lo yedya* — one who is somewhat known, where there is uncertainty, *ad telata dara chaya* — lives up to three generations, because for one or two generations the memory of his status will keep people wary, but by the third generation the memory will have faded entirely, and at that point he will die.

### Rav Ami Story

The Gemara concludes this section with a striking story. There was a *mamzer* who lived in the neighborhood of Rav Ami. Rav Ami investigated and determined that this person was indeed a *mamzer*, and he made a public announcement to that effect. The man wept: what have you done to me by announcing my status to all? Rav Ami said to him: *chayim natati lach* — I have given you life. Had your status remained unknown, you would have died — God's providence would have ensured it, to prevent the community from inadvertently transgressing. Now that everyone knows you are a *mamzer*, you will live. The announcement of his *mamzer* status was itself an act of kindness, preserving his life by transforming him from an unknown *mamzer* into a known one.

We will pick up tomorrow with the discussion of *netinim*.

---

---

# Yevamot 79

## Givonim & David

### Intro: Netinim

The daf begins in the middle of 78b, following a relatively brief discussion in the Gemara concerning *mamzer* status. The Mishnah now turns to the *netinim* — the designation applied to the *givonim*, the Gibeonites, who are forbidden in marriage. The *givonim* were members of one of the *shivat ha-amamim*, the seven Canaanite nations, who had deceived Yehoshua into making a pact with them. They are assumed to have converted at some point — otherwise they would simply be non-Jews — and so the question becomes one of their status as a distinct group even after conversion.

### Lo Titchaten Bam

One might suggest that the source of the prohibition is the biblical verse *lo titchaten bam* — the prohibition against intermarrying with the seven Canaanite nations. There is an earlier discussion in the tractate regarding whether this prohibition applies even after the *shivat ha-amamim* have converted. That debate bears on the *givonim* as well, but the Gemara now proceeds to explore an additional basis for the prohibition, rooted in a later episode in the narrative of Tanakh.

### David's Gezeirah

The Gemara introduces the following teaching: *Amar Rabbi Chana bar Adda: netinim David gazar aleihem* — it was David who issued a decree concerning the *netinim*, presumably prohibiting intermarriage with them. The proof-text is drawn from Shmuel, where the narrative of a famine in David's time opens: *vayikra hamelech lagivonim vayomer aleihem* — the king called the Gibeonites and spoke to them. The verse also notes, *veha-givonim lo mibnei Yisrael heim* — they were not of the Jewish people. The question the Gemara then pursues is: *mai ta'ama gazar aleihem* — why did David enact this decree?

### Three-Year Famine

The basis for the decree emerges from the account of a three-year famine during David's reign: *vayehi ra'av bimei David shalosh shanim shana acharei shana* — there was a famine, year after year, for three consecutive years. The Gemara understands that David actively investigated the cause each of those years.

In the first year, David told the people: *shema ovdei avodah zarah yesh bachem* — perhaps there are idolaters among you. The scriptural basis is the verse warning that serving other gods will cause God to close the heavens and withhold rain. They investigated — *badku velo matzu* — and found nothing.

In the second year, he said: *shema ovrei aveirah yesh bachem* — perhaps there are sexual sinners among you. The verse cited describes God withholding the rains and invokes the imagery of the brazen forehead of a wayward woman — a punishment associated with sexual sin. Again they investigated and found nothing.

In the third year, he said: *shema porskei tzedakah b'rabim yesh bachem ve'einam notnim* — perhaps there are those who make public pledges at an appeal and do not fulfill them. The verse speaks of clouds and wind that promise rain but deliver none, analogous to the person who praises himself with a false donation. They investigated and again found nothing.

### Divine Inquiry

At this point David declared, *ein hadavar taluy ela bi* — it must be up to me to determine the cause — and immediately sought God directly: *vayevakesh David et pnei Hashem*. The Gemara asks how David sought God in this manner, and Resh Lakish answers: *she-sha'al ba-Urim veTummim* — he inquired through the Urim and Thummim. Rabbi Elazar confirms this through a *gezerah shavah* on the word *pnei*: the verse here says *vayevakesh David et pnei Hashem*, and elsewhere the Torah says regarding the Urim and Thummim, *vesha'alu lo b'mishpat ha-Urim lifnei Hashem* — the shared word *pnei* / *lifnei* connects the two passages.

God's response was: *Vayomer Hashem sha'ul v'el beit hadamim* — it is on account of Shaul and the house of blood, *al asher hemit hagivonim* — because he killed the Gibeonites. The Gemara then identifies two causes implicit in this divine response: (1) *al Shaul shelo nispas ke-halacha* — Shaul was not properly eulogized, and (2) the killing of the Gibeonites. The motivation to read a secondary theme of the eulogy into this passage comes from the end of the narrative in Shmuel, where David retrieves and reinters the bones of Shaul and Yehonatan alongside those of the executed sons — indicating that the proper treatment of Shaul's remains was part of what this entire episode addressed.

### Saul's Culpability

The Gemara then asks: *ve-chi heichan matzinu b'Shaul shehemit et hagivonim* — where do we ever find explicitly that Shaul killed the Gibeonites? The verse in this story is the first such mention. The Gemara answers: *ela mitoch sheharag Nov ir Kohanim* — because Shaul destroyed Nov, the city of priests. The Gibeonites, who served the priests as hewers of wood and drawers of water — a role assigned to them by Yehoshua and later connected to the altar — were thereby deprived of their livelihood and sustenance. *Ma'aleh alav ha-katuv k'ilu haragam* — Scripture accounts it to Shaul as though he had killed them outright. This reading notably softens what the plain reading of the Shmuel narrative implies — that Shaul had actually attempted to decimate the Gibeonites — reducing it to an indirect harm caused by the destruction of those they depended upon.

### Dual Punishment

This raises an apparent difficulty: the text assigns punishment for two things simultaneously — Shaul's lack of proper eulogy, and the harm done to the Gibeonites. How can both be true together? Is Shaul a victim in one sense and a perpetrator in another? Resh Lakish resolves this through a verse: *bikshu et Hashem kol anvei ha-aretz asher mishpato sham pa'alu* — seek God, all the humble of the earth, where God's justice is, there too are God's righteous deeds. The same point where justice is exacted is also where the person's due is rendered. David reflected that Shaul had gone twelve months — indeed thirty years — without a proper *hesped*, and that while the formal mourning period had long passed and it was no longer the ideal time for a eulogy, *velo dacha le-mispedei* — he had not pressed to make it happen. His more immediate task was to address the Gibeonites: *nikrina u-nepaysinu* — let us call them and attempt to appease them.

### Givonim Demand

The king called the Gibeonites and asked: *mah e'eseh lachem u-bamah achaper* — what shall I do for you and how can atonement be made? The Gibeonites responded that they wanted neither silver nor gold, nor any claim against the broader Jewish people — only seven of Shaul's sons: *yutan lanu shiv'ah anashim mibanav ve-hokanum le-Hashem* — give us seven of his sons, and we will impale them before God. David attempted to negotiate some other form of appeasement — *mifas lo faysinu* — but they would not be moved.

### Jewish Virtues

Confronted with this display of implacable cruelty, David reflected on the defining characteristics of the Jewish people. He declared: *shloshah simanim yesh b'umah zu* — the Jewish nation has three identifying marks: *ha-rachmanim* — they are compassionate, *ha-bayshanim* — they are capable of shame and embarrassment, and *gomlei chasadim* — they perform acts of loving-kindness.

Each characteristic is grounded in a scriptural source. Compassion: *ve-nasan lecha rachamim ve-richamcha* — God will instill compassion in you. Shame: *ba-avur tihyeh yir'aso al pneichem le-vilti techetau* — God's awe should be upon your faces so that you do not sin, implying a non-brazen, humble bearing. Kindness: *le-ma'an asher yetzaveh et banav ve-et beiso acharav ve-shamru derech Hashem la'asos tzedakah u-mishpat* — to walk in God's ways and do righteousness and justice.

The principle then follows: *kol she-yesh bo shloshah simanim elalu ra'uy le-hidabek b'umah zu* — whoever possesses these three traits is fit to attach themselves to the Jewish people. For a nation that lacks them, intermarriage is not appropriate even if they have converted and are technically Jewish.

### Conclusion: Unfit

This observation — made in the context of the Gibeonites' heartless demand — is what leads David to his conclusion. Having seen their cruelty firsthand, David determined that they were unfit to intermarry with Israel, and *gazar aleihem* — he issued his decree. Some derive the prohibition from the very verse introducing the Gibeonites in this narrative, *ve-ha-givonim lo mibnei Yisrael heim* — not merely that they were not originally of Israel, but that they were never to be integrated into the people through marriage.

Tosafos identifies three possible understandings of what David's *gezeirah* actually entailed. One view holds that the biblical prohibition of *lo titchaten bam* ceases to apply after the *shivat ha-amamim* convert, and David's *gezeirah* was a rabbinic or extra-legal decree filling that gap — prohibiting intermarriage even post-conversion. A second view suggests that David's contribution was to extend Yehoshua's designation of the Gibeonites as servants beyond the specific conditions Yehoshua had set, and since slaves cannot be married into the congregation, the marriage prohibition follows indirectly from their servitude. A third view, that the biblical prohibition applies even after conversion, would leave David's decree focused purely on the question of servitude rather than intermarriage directly.

The plain sense of the Gemara here, it should be noted, concerns only marriage — there is no hint in this passage of the servitude question. The discussion is entirely embedded in a tractate about who may or may not marry whom. The servitude dimension will enter later.

## Execution & Kiddush

### Selection Process

The seven descendants of Shaul were identified through a specific selection process. The verse specifies that David took the two sons of Ritzpah daughter of Ayah — Armoni and Mephiboshes — as well as five sons of Michal daughter of Shaul whom she bore to Adriel ben Barzillai ha-Mecholasi. This Mephiboshes is not the son of Yehonasan, as the verse immediately prior notes that David had compassion on Yehonasan's son Mephiboshes on account of the oath he had sworn to Yehonasan — there were two individuals of that name.

Rav Huna teaches that the selection of which seven to hand over was determined by passing them before the *aron*: *kol she-ha-aron kolto le-misah* — whoever was drawn in by the Ark was designated for death; *kol she-ein ha-aron kolto le-chayim* — whoever was not drawn in was spared. This parallels a similar methodology used in another episode. The Gemara then raises a difficulty from the verse *vayachmol ha-melech al Mephiboshes ben Yehonasan* — the king had compassion on Mephiboshes son of Yehonasan — which implies that it was David's personal discretion rather than an objective test that determined his fate.

The Gemara resolves this in stages. First it is suggested that the compassion was simply that David did not submit Yehonasan's Mephiboshes to the test at all — that was the act of mercy. But then it is objected: *ve-chi maso panim yesh badavar* — is it permissible to show favoritism in capital matters? One ought to let God decide. The Gemara then revises: Mephiboshes was in fact submitted to the test, but David prayed that he not be drawn in — *bikaesh alav rachamim shelo yikletenu ha-aron* — and he was spared.

But the objection resurfaces: *ve-achti maso panim yesh badavar* — even that involves favoritism, since sparing one through prayer effectively sends another in his place. Rashi articulates this point with striking force: by praying that Mephiboshes be released, David was implicitly assigning someone else to death in his stead. The Gemara ultimately resolves this by clarifying that David's prayer preceded the test entirely — he prayed from the outset that Mephiboshes would not be drawn in, rather than praying for his release after the Ark had already claimed him, meaning no other individual was displaced.

### Children Punished

The Gemara asks the obvious question: *ve-haktiv lo yumtu avot al banim* — does the Torah not prohibit putting children to death for the sins of their fathers? These seven sons were being executed for what Shaul had done. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *mutav she-te'aker ot achat min ha-Torah u-val yitchalel Shem Shamayim be-farhesya* — it is better that one letter of the Torah be uprooted than that the divine name be publicly desecrated.

One might have supposed that executing innocent people is itself a desecration of the divine name — but Rashi explains the calculus differently. The concern was what the nations would say: *she-yehu ha-umot omrim ein umah zo re-uyah le-hidabek bah* — this is not a nation worthy of joining, because they allowed these converts to be killed without their food being provided and without any vengeance being taken on their behalf. The perception of Israel as a nation that abandoned vulnerable converts in their midst would constitute a *chilul Hashem*. To prevent that, even a violation of the prohibition against punishing children for their fathers' sins was permitted — a genuinely radical application of the concern for how Israel presents itself to the outside world, and one where the concern extends specifically to non-Jewish perception.

### Ritzpah's Vigil

After the execution, Ritzpah daughter of Ayah, the mother of two of the executed sons, took sackcloth and spread it by the rock, keeping vigil from the beginning of the harvest season until rain finally fell: *lo natnah of ha-shamayim lanoach aleihem yomam ve-chayat ha-sadeh laylah* — she did not let the birds of the heaven rest on the bodies by day, nor the beasts of the field approach them by night.

This raises another halakhic problem: *ve-haktiv lo talin nivlato al ha-etz* — does the Torah not prohibit leaving a body hanging on a tree overnight? Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak answers with the same formulation: *mutav she-te'aker ot achat min ha-Torah ve-yitkadesh Shem Shamayim be-farhesya* — it is better that one letter of the Torah be uprooted than that the divine name be desecrated in public. Here the argument inverts: what is gained by leaving the bodies exposed is not the avoidance of *chilul Hashem* but the active achievement of *kiddush Hashem*.

### Kiddush Hashem

The mechanism of *kiddush Hashem* is spelled out explicitly. Passersby would stop and ask: *mah tivan shel elu* — who are these people? Why are they hanging here? And they would be told: *hallalu b'nei melachim hem* — these are the sons of kings, princes. *U-mah asu* — and what did they do? *Pashtu yadeihem be-geirim gerurim* — they acted against lowly converts. The word *gerurim* here refers to their status as converts who had entered under deception — not the most sincere or prestigious of converts, yet still the objects of such punitive concern.

The conclusion drawn by the onlookers: *ein le-cha umah she-re-uyah le-hidabek bah ke-zo* — there is no nation as worthy of joining as this one. *U-mah b'nei melachim kach* — if that is what they do to princes for harming such people, *b'nei hedyotot al achat kamah ve-chamah* — how much more would they demand of ordinary citizens who harm the vulnerable.

The narrative is striking in how it inverts the moral positions established earlier. Shaul had committed a terrible act against the Gibeonites. Yet ultimately, it is the Gibeonites themselves who are shown to be heartless — demanding the lives of seven men — while Israel emerges as the nation of exceptional ethical standards. Tosafos notes a beautiful *midrash* on the phrase *va-tatehu lah el ha-tzur*: the word *ha-tzur* alludes to the *tzidduk ha-din*, the acceptance of divine judgment — *Ha-Tzur Tamim Pe'alo* — suggesting that Ritzpah, in her grief, affirmed the justice of what had occurred.

### Converts Arrive

As a direct result of this demonstration of Israel's moral standards, 150,000 people converted: *nisvasfu Yisrael me'ah va-chamishim elef*. The scriptural basis is drawn from the account of Shlomo's workforce: *vayihi li-Shlomo shiv'im elef nosei saval u-shmonim elef chotzeiv ba-har* — 70,000 burden-bearers and 80,000 hewers in the mountain, for the construction of the Beit HaMikdash.

The Gemara questions whether these might simply have been native-born Israelites. The objection is raised: *u-mibnei Yisrael lo nasan Shlomo eved* — Shlomo did not impose servitude on the children of Israel — yet this workforce was engaged in labor that resembles servitude, so they must have come from the gentile nations. A further verse makes this explicit: *vayispor Shlomo kol ha-anashim ha-geirim asher be-eretz Yisrael vayimmatze'u me'ah va-chamishim elef* — Shlomo counted all the resident aliens in the land of Israel and found 150,000, placing 70,000 as burden-bearers and 80,000 as hewers.

## Netinim Status

### Yehoshua's Decree

The Gemara now turns to the legal status of the *netinim* in terms of servitude, tracing its origins back to Yehoshua. The verse records: *vayitneim Yehoshua ba-yom ha-hu chotevei eitzim ve-sho'avei mayim la-eidah u-le-mizbeach Hashem* — Yehoshua designated them on that day as hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of God. This is the foundational act that established the Gibeonites as servants in relation to the Beit HaMikdash.

### Moshe vs. Yehoshua

The Gemara then asks whether Moshe might have preceded Yehoshua in this designation, citing the verse *mi-chotev eitzecha ad sho'ev meimecha* — from the hewer of your wood to the drawer of your water — which appears in the Torah itself. The Gemara thus suggests that Moshe had already in some sense identified a people for this role, even before the conquest of Canaan and before the episode with the Gibeonites. The question of how this works precisely — since the Gibeonites had not yet made their pact with Yehoshua in Moshe's time — is left somewhat open. The conclusion is: *Moshe gazar le-hu dara* — Moshe's decree was for that generation only; *David gazar le-chulei dara* — David extended it to all future generations.

### David's Extension

Yehoshua's decree, the Gemara explains, was conditioned on the existence of the Temple: *Yehoshua gazar bi-zman she-Beit HaMikdash kayam* — the verse says *le-mizbeach Hashem*, "for the altar of God," tying the servitude to the Temple's operation. Since there was no Temple in David's time — only David extended their status to periods when there is no Temple: *David gazar bi-zman she-ein Beit HaMikdash kayam*. This extension is what David added beyond Yehoshua's designation.

The question of what exactly David was extending — the servitude status, or the prohibition of intermarriage — becomes complicated here. The Gemara seems to intertwine the two, and Tosafos proposes that the intermarriage prohibition may follow naturally from slave status, since one cannot marry a slave. The simpler reading of the earlier Gemara, however, would suggest that David's decree was directly about intermarriage, with no dependence on the slave question.

### Repeal Attempt

In the time of Rabbi, an attempt was made to rescind the *netinim* status: *bikshu le-hatir nesinim* — they sought to permit the *netinim*, at least by releasing them from servitude. Rabbi responded: *chelkeinu natia* — we can release our portion, the claim the Jewish people hold over them, through the principle of *hefker beit din hefker*. But *chelek mizbe'ach mi yatish* — who are we to release the Temple's portion? The Temple's share in their servitude is not ours to annul.

### Shares Doctrine

This position is in tension with a view of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *chelek adam le-olam assur* — the people's portion is forever forbidden unless released; *chelek mizbe'ach bi-zman she-Beit HaMikdash kayam assur* — the Temple's portion is forbidden when the Temple stands, *ein Beit HaMikdash kayam shari* — but when there is no Temple, the Temple's portion is no longer binding. According to this view, the people could in theory release their portion, and the Temple's portion would lapse in the absence of the Beit HaMikdash, potentially opening the door for the *netinim* to be freed from their status entirely — and perhaps, by extension, permitted for intermarriage. The Gemara remains somewhat ambiguous about whether the ultimate focus is on servitude or on the marriage prohibition, with the two questions running through each other throughout this passage.

## Saris & Ailonit

### Saris Traditions

The Mishnah now shifts to a discussion of *chalitzah* and *yibum* as they apply to a *saris* — a eunuch — and to an *ailonit*, a woman who cannot bear children. Rabbi Yehoshua opens with a declaration: *shamati she-saris choletz* — I have heard that a *saris* performs *chalitzah*, and *choltzin le-ishto* — that one performs *chalitzah* with the wife of a *saris* who dies. This runs against intuition: if a man cannot have children, why should he or his wife be relevant to *yibum* and *chalitzah*, whose entire purpose is *le-hakim shem achiv* — to perpetuate the name of the deceased brother?

Rabbi Yehoshua then adds: *ve-saris lo choletz ve-lo choltzin le-ishto* — I also heard the opposite, that a *saris* neither performs *chalitzah* nor is *chalitzah* performed with his wife. He acknowledges he cannot reconcile the two traditions.

### Akiva's Distinction

Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Yehoshua's student, offers to resolve the contradiction: *ani afareish* — I will explain. *Saris adam choletz ve-choltzin le-ishto* — a man who became a *saris* through human agency performs *chalitzah* and one performs *chalitzah* with his wife. *Saris chamah lo choletz ve-lo choltzin le-ishto* — a man who is a *saris* by nature does not perform *chalitzah* and one does not perform *chalitzah* with his wife.

### Sha'at Kosher

The basis for Rabbi Akiva's distinction is the concept of *sha'at kosher* — a prior moment of valid capacity. A *saris adam* — one whose condition was caused by a later physical event, analogous to *ptzua daka* or *khrut shofcha* — at least began life with the capacity to father children. Even if that capacity has been entirely and permanently eliminated, his personal identity is not intrinsically that of someone excluded from the category of procreation. He had *sha'at kosher*, and so in terms of his halakhic *gavra* status he remains within the *parshah* of *yibum* and *chalitzah* — even though fathering children is currently and permanently impossible.

A *saris chamah*, by contrast — one born with the condition, whose entire life has been that of someone incapable of reproduction — never had *sha'at kosher*. His personal identity is intrinsically that of someone excluded from the category, and therefore *yibum* and *chalitzah* do not apply.

### Eliezer's View

Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua's colleague and a fellow teacher of Rabbi Akiva, disagrees and inverts the ruling. *Saris chamah choletz ve-choltzin le-ishto* — a natural *saris* performs *chalitzah* and one performs *chalitzah* with his wife, *mipnei she-yesh lo refua* — because his condition may be curable. If the incapacity arose from natural circumstances — a condition one was born into — perhaps it is something that could yet resolve itself. *Saris adam lo choletz ve-lo choltzin le-ishto mipnei she-ein lo refua* — a *saris adam* cannot perform *chalitzah* and one does not perform it with his wife, because when something anatomically decisive has been done through human agency — severed, as in *khrut shofcha*, or damaged, as in *ptzua daka* — it is permanent and admits of no remedy.

The underlying logic of the two positions is thus symmetrical but opposite. Rabbi Akiva focuses on prior personal identity: was there ever a moment when this person stood in the category of one who can have children? Rabbi Eliezer focuses on present and future reality: is there any possibility, however remote, that this condition is reversible? Both agree that the immediate practical impossibility of conception is not the operative question — the *saris* who cannot have children right now and never will again can nonetheless, under the right analytical framework, remain within the halakhic category. What differs is what places one inside or outside that category.

### Ben Magusas Case

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Betira testified regarding a certain Ben Magusas who lived in Jerusalem: he was a *saris adam*, and when he died, *yibum* was performed with his wife — *veyibemu et ishto le-kayem divrei Rabbi Akiva*. The testimony was not issued in order to affirm Rabbi Akiva's position, but it functions as corroboration. Here was an actual case of a *saris adam* where *yibum* — not merely *chalitzah* — was performed with the deceased's wife, consistent with Rabbi Akiva's ruling that *saris adam* retains full standing in the laws of *yibum* and *chalitzah*.

### Final Ruling

The Mishnah then presents what appears to be a later, independent formulation: *ha-saris lo choletz ve-lo meyabem* — the *saris* does not perform *chalitzah* and does not perform *yibum*. And similarly: *ve-chen ailonit lo choletzet ve-lo mityabemet* — an *ailonit* does not perform *chalitzah* and is not subject to *yibum*. This categorical statement makes no distinction between types of *saris* and seems to ignore the entire preceding debate among Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Eliezer. The most natural reading is that this was an earlier, undifferentiated *stam* teaching, upon which the later *tannaim* built their distinctions — similar to other cases in *Shas* where an early undifferentiated Mishnah is followed by a debate that constitutes the various *tannaim*'s interpretations of its terms.

### Sex vs. Chalitzah

Regarding the *saris* who nevertheless goes ahead and performs *chalitzah* with his *yevamah*: *lo pasla* — it does not invalidate her for a *kohen*. The act is halakhically meaningless; it accomplished nothing. But if he had sexual relations with her — *pasla* — he has invalidated her. Since there is no *mitzvat yibum* with a *saris*, the act is one of *arayot* — it constitutes *eshet ach* in a context where the *mitzvah* does not apply — and she is therefore rendered a *chalalah*, *mipnei she-hi be'ilat zenut*. It is more precise to say *be'ilat arayot* — an act of forbidden relations.

The distinction is thus clear: meaningless *chalitzah* leaves her status unchanged, while sexual relations in the absence of a valid *mitzvat yibum* renders the act prohibited and invalidates her.

### Ailonit Rules

The same framework applies to an *ailonit*. If one of the brothers performed *chalitzah* with her: *lo pasluha* — they did not invalidate her for a *kohen*, since the act was halakhically meaningless in the absence of any *mitzvat yibum* or *mitzvat chalitzah*. If they had sexual relations with her — *pasluha* — they invalidated her, since without *mitzvat yibum* the act is one of *arayot*, *mipnei she-be'ilatah be'ilat zenut*.

An *ailonit* is not simply a woman who is currently infertile or who has not yet conceived. The parallel to the *saris* is instructive: just as the relevant question for the *saris* is not whether conception is practically possible at this moment but whether his personal identity places him within the category, so too the *ailonit* must be someone whose identity is intrinsically that of a woman outside the category — not an *akara*, a woman who happens not to be bearing children, but an *ailonit*, defined by specific physical characteristics that place her categorically elsewhere.

## Gemara Problem

### Prohibition Paradox

The Gemara now raises a striking analytical problem with Rabbi Akiva's position. We know that Rabbi Akiva holds *chayavei lavin ke-chayavei keritot dami* — those who violate a *lav* are treated as those who violate an *issur karet*. This means, among other consequences, that the offspring of such unions is a *mamzer*, that *kiddushin* is ineffective, and — crucially for our context — that the *mitzvah* of *yibum* and *chalitzah* is entirely excluded, just as it is excluded in cases of *arayot*. The very first Mishnah in the tractate established that if a woman is forbidden to her *yavam* by an *issur karet*, she is exempt from *yibum* and *chalitzah* altogether.

But a *saris adam* — the category in which Rabbi Akiva says *chalitzah* and *yibum* apply — is presumably someone in the category of *ptzua daka u-khrut shofcha*, who is forbidden by a *lav* to marry a Jewish woman. If Rabbi Akiva treats a *lav* like an *issur karet*, then the *saris adam*'s wife should be entirely excluded from *yibum* and *chalitzah*, not included. The contradiction is direct: *ve-chayvei keritot lav benei chalitzah ve-yibum ninhu* — those subject to *issur karet* are not within the category of *yibum* and *chalitzah* at all.

### Convert Resolution

Rabbi Ammi resolves the problem: *hakha be-mai askinan ke-gon she-nasa achiv giyoret* — we are discussing a case where the deceased brother's wife is a convert. There is no prohibition of *ptzua daka* applying to a *giyoret* — the *lav* of *lo yavo ptzua daka be-kehal Hashem* does not prohibit marriage with a convert.

### Kahal Gerim

Rabbi Akiva follows the position of Rabbi Yossi, who holds *kehal gerim lo ikrei kehal* — the congregation of converts is not considered *kehal* for this purpose. Therefore, the prohibition does not apply to the *saris adam* who married a convert, there is no *lav*, and consequently the relationship is not treated as *chayvei keritot* by Rabbi Akiva — leaving *chalitzah* and *yibum* applicable.

### Yibum Question

A follow-up question arises: if the prohibition is entirely absent in the case of a *giyoret*, why does the Mishnah speak only of *chalitzah* rather than *yibum* as well? If there is no *lav*, why not simply perform *yibum*?

### Restriction Scope

The Gemara answers: Rabbi Yehoshua, who reported the two traditions in the first place, would hold that the prohibition of *ptzua daka* applies even to *geirim* — he does not accept Rabbi Yossi's position that *kehal gerim* is not *kehal*. Therefore, Rabbi Yehoshua had to frame the teaching as *chalitzah* only, since in his view there remains a prohibition even vis-à-vis a convert. Rabbi Akiva, by contrast, would have no objection in principle to *yibum* as well in this case. When Rabbi Akiva stated *choletz* — he used the language of Rabbi Yehoshua's formulation, but in principle according to his own view, *yibum* could also be performed.

### Testimony Inference

This is confirmed by the testimony regarding Ben Magusas: when Ben Magusas, a *saris adam*, died, *yibum* was performed with his wife — not merely *chalitzah*. The Gemara infers: *shema mina* — this is evidence that even *yibum* was considered possible for a *saris adam*, supporting the Gemara's conclusion that the case involves a *giyoret* and that there is no operative prohibition preventing *yibum*.

## Saris Obligations

### Permission Principle

The Gemara now presents a *baraita* that lays out the full application of the laws of *yibum* and *chalitzah* for those with physical defects or advanced age. *Ptzua daka u-khrut shofcha*, as well as an elderly man who is no longer capable of reproduction — whether such a person died leaving a wife, or whether he is the surviving brother obligated in *yibum* — the ruling is: *o chaltzin o meyabmin* — either *chalitzah* or *yibum* may be performed. These men are not categorically excluded from the framework of *yibum* and *chalitzah*.

### Valid Acts

The *baraita* elaborates: whether it is the *saris adam* or elderly man who died and left a *yevamah* behind for his brothers, or whether he is the living brother, all legal acts are fully valid. *Maamar*, *get*, *chalitzah* — and *yibum* itself — are all binding and effective: *mah she-asu asui*. The Gemara stresses this applies regardless of whether the deceased was in this condition or the surviving brother is.

### Prohibition Remains

Yet the *baraita* adds: *ve-assur le-kayanam* — they are nevertheless forbidden to remain married. Even though *yibum* is valid and effective, the husband cannot maintain the marriage, because the prohibition of *lo yavo ptzua daka u-khrut shofcha be-kehal Hashem* still applies. The Gemara notes that here we are dealing with a case where the wives are not converts — the prohibition does apply — which raises anew the question of how Rabbi Akiva can permit *yibum* and *chalitzah* in the presence of a *lav* that he treats as equivalent to an *issur karet*.

## Later Defects

### Rava's Question

Rava proposes a resolution. The scenario described in the *baraita* — where *yibum* and *chalitzah* apply despite the *lav* of *ptzua daka* — is one where the physical condition arose after the husband's death: *ke-gon she-naflo lo be-sof niftzu* — the condition occurred at the end, meaning after the original obligation of *yibum* was already established. At the moment the brother died and the *mitzvah* of *yibum* attached, everything was normal. The *saris* condition of the surviving brother arose only afterward.

### Rava's Proposal

Rava's reasoning is that if the *issur* came after the *mitzvah* had already taken hold, it does not retroactively dissolve the obligation. The *yevamah* was already fully obligated in *yibum* or *chalitzah* at the moment of the brother's death; a condition that subsequently afflicts the surviving brother should not undo what had already been established.

### Abaye's Objection

Abaye challenges this reasoning: *ve-dachi issur ptzua ve-nidchei issur asei de-yibum* — why should the newly arising prohibition of *ptzua daka* not override and displace the positive obligation of *yibum*, even if it came later? He brings proof from an established teaching: *min lo tanan Rabban Gamliel omer im mianah mianah* — Rabban Gamliel ruled regarding a man married to an underage girl whose sister fell before him for *yibum*. Rabban Gamliel said that if the underage wife performs *mi'un* — refusal — the *yibum* obligation with her sister can proceed.

### Underage Wife Case

The mechanics of Abaye's proof: when the brother died, his wife's sister was only rabbinically married to the surviving brother, not yet a full halakhic *ishah*. The prohibition of *achot isha* — a man's wife's sister — had not yet fully crystallized. At that moment, the *mitzvah* of *yibum* applied to the deceased's wife. But if the surviving brother waits until the underage girl matures, she becomes his full halakhic wife, and her sister — the *yevamah* — becomes his *achot isha*, canceling the obligation of *yibum*. Rabban Gamliel rules: *tamtin ad she-tagdil ve-tetzei halazu mishum achot isha* — wait until she grows up, and the *yevamah* must leave on account of the prohibition of a wife's sister.

### Prohibition Cancellation

This case demonstrates that even when the *mitzvah* of *yibum* was established at the moment of death, a prohibition that arises afterward — here *achot isha* — can come along and override the obligation. *Alema ati issur achot isha ve-dachi* — we see that a later *issur* can displace an earlier *mitzvah* of *yibum*. Therefore, says Abaye, the same should be true here: even if the *saris* condition arose after the brother's death, the resulting prohibition of *ptzua daka* should be sufficient to cancel the *mitzvah* of *yibum*. Rava's proposed resolution is therefore inadequate.

## Simple Lav

### Rav Yosef Answer

Rav Yosef provides the definitive answer: *hai tanna d'vei Rabbi Akiva hi de-amar me-chayavei lavin d'she'er havei mamzer, me-chayavei lavin geridei lo havei mamzer* — this teaching follows the position of the school of Rabbi Akiva, which distinguishes between two types of *lavin*.

### Simple Lav Category

When Rabbi Akiva says that *chayavei lavin* are treated like *chayavei keritot* — producing *mamzer* status and being excluded from *yibum* and *chalitzah* — he does not apply this to every *lav* universally. The prohibition of *ptzua daka* is a *lav gerei* — a simple, freestanding prohibition — that has nothing to do with kinship or relational categories. Rabbi Akiva's equation of *lavin* with *keritot* applies only in a more limited domain.

### Kinship Lavim

The category of *lavin* that Rabbi Akiva treats as equivalent to *issur karet* — producing *mamzer* status and excluding the relationship from *yibum* — is specifically *chayavei lavin d'she'er*: prohibitions rooted in the relational category of *she'er*, kinship. These are the prohibitions that neighbor the domain of *arayot* — unions forbidden because of who the parties are to one another, not merely because of some personal defect or disability. *Ptzua daka* is not in this category. It is a prohibition about the man's physical status, entirely unrelated to kinship between the parties. Therefore, even Rabbi Akiva does not treat it as producing *mamzer* status or as excluding the couple from the framework of *yibum* and *chalitzah*. The *lav* remains — they may not stay married — but it does not rise to the level of an *issur karet* analog that would dissolve the *yibum* obligation entirely.

---

---

# Yevamot 80

## Saris Adam Status

### R. Akiva: Saris Adam

The daf opens by returning to Rabbi Akiva's ruling regarding the *saris adam* — a man who was born fertile and subsequently became infertile through some human act or accident. Rabbi Akiva holds that such a person remains within the halakhic category of *yibum* and *chalitzah*, whether as the deceased husband or as the surviving brother, because his having been born fertile places him fundamentally in that category even if he can no longer produce children.

### Issur Lav & Mamzer

The Gemara raises a difficulty with this position. A *saris adam* who is a *ptzua daka u'krot shofcha* is subject to an *issur lav*. Rabbi Akiva famously treats an *issur lav* similarly to an *issur kares* with regard to the offspring being a *mamzer* — which would seemingly exclude such a person from the *parsha* of *yibum* entirely.

### Rav Yosef: School Source

Several answers are offered, and the last of them is introduced at the bottom of 79b: *ela amar Rav Yosef — hai tana, tana de-bei Rabbi Akiva hi*. The *tanna* of our *mishnah*, who holds that a *ptzua daka* is nonetheless included in the category of *yibum* and *chalitzah* according to Rabbi Akiva, belongs to Rabbi Akiva's own school.

### Issur Kinship Types

The key to understanding this answer lies in a distinction within Rabbi Akiva's own position. When Rabbi Akiva says an *issur lav* produces a *mamzer*, he means specifically an *issur lav* that falls under the category of *she'er* — a kinship-based prohibition, one rooted in a familial or quasi-familial relationship. The school of Rabbi Akiva holds: *mi-chayvei lavin de-she'er havei mamzer, mi-chayvei lavin geridei lo havei mamzer* — a plain *issur lav* unrelated to kinship does not produce a *mamzer*. Rashi on an earlier daf cites two examples of *issur lav* prohibitions that would qualify as *she'er*: a woman with whom one's father had relations (*lo yigaleh knaf aviv*), and a woman with whom one performed *chalitzah* (*keivan she-lo banah shuv lo yivneh*). By contrast, a *kohen* with a *gerushah* or our case of a *ptzua daka* is a plain *issur lav* with no kinship dimension — and therefore would not produce a *mamzer* and would not exclude the person from the *parsha* of *yibum*. This is a clean and straightforward resolution.

---

## Rava's Objection

### No Children Possible

With the *saris adam* question settled, the Gemara turns to a broader and more fundamental challenge. Whatever the *saris adam*'s formal status, practically speaking he cannot have children. The verse speaks of *le-hakim l'achiv shem* — establishing a name for his brother — and this person is not capable of doing so. The Gemara thus asks: *ikri kan le-hakim l'achiv shem v'ha lav bar hachi hu* — how can there be a *mitzvah* of *yibum* or *chalitzah* when producing children is simply not possible?

### Death Moment Proof

Rava responds with a striking argument: *im ken, ein lecha isha she-keshera le-yabem* — if practical fertility at the moment is the determining criterion, then there will never be a woman who is subject to *yibum*. Why? *She-lo na'aseh ba'alah saris chamah sha'ah achat kodem le-mitato* — because a man who dies naturally, whether from old age or illness, is in all likelihood not fertile in the final moments before his death. If we required actual capacity to produce children, *yibum* would never apply to any normal death. Rava's proof thus establishes that we do not measure eligibility by the last moment of incapacity; we look at the person's status more broadly. A man who was once fertile and capable of having children remains categorially within the *parsha*, even if that capacity has since ceased.

### R. Eliezer vs Rava

The Gemara notes that for Rabbi Eliezer, Rava's argument is actually a question rather than a proof: *peruka de-Rava pircha hi*. Rabbi Eliezer does not rely on the principle of *sha'at ha-kosher* — the fact that earlier in life the person was capable. Rabbi Eliezer grounds his position in the theoretical possibility of recovery. A *saris chama* may potentially heal; it is that reversibility, not prior fertility, that places him in the category.

### Temporary vs Permanent

Given Rabbi Eliezer's framework, one might ask: how does he respond to Rava's scenario of a man dying — since by Rabbi Eliezer's logic, a dying man is not in a theoretical state of recovery either? The Gemara answers: *hatam kichishuta de'atchala bei* — in a dying man, it is not that the reproductive capacity is truly broken; it is a weakening that has overtaken him. The equipment, as it were, is not itself defective, even if the person cannot in practice exercise it. The moment the physical apparatus actually breaks down, however — as with a *saris adam* — that is a different matter entirely. 

What emerges is a highly formalistic ruling: as long as people fall within the category of those who were at some stage capable of producing children — or, in Rabbi Eliezer's view, theoretically capable of recovery — the *mitzvah* of *yibum* applies, even if children are practically impossible at the time, even if the marriage itself produced no children, and even if the surviving brother is currently incapable. Conceptual membership in the category is what drives the obligation.

---

## Saris Chama Defined

### Never Fertile Once

Having established the theoretical framework, the Gemara turns to defining *saris chama* in practical terms. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rabbi Yochanan defines it precisely: *kol shelo ra'ah sha'ah achat be-chashruto* — someone who never had even one moment of fertility. This definition is the hinge of Rabbi Akiva's position: such a person was never in the category, and therefore Rabbi Akiva excludes him from *yibum* and *chalitzah* entirely.

### Urination Arc Test

The Gemara then asks: how does one identify someone who has never had that moment of fertility? Abaye offers a diagnostic: *kol ha-matil mayim ve-ein oseh kipa* — anyone whose urination does not form an arc. If this condition was observable even in early childhood, it indicates a permanent, congenital state rather than something acquired later in life.

### Birth Defect Causes

The Gemara then asks what causes this condition to develop in utero. Two maternal factors during pregnancy are identified: *de-afya imei be-tihara* — the mother baked bread in the noonday sun, so that both the heat of the oven and the heat of the midday sun acted upon her while pregnant — and *ve-shashtya shikra* — she drank strong or heavily mixed intoxicating drink. These are the causes of this particular birth defect.

### Smitten from Womb

Rav Yosef adds: this is what I had heard Rav Ami teaching when he said *kol she-mi-me'ei imo laki* — whoever was smitten from his mother's womb — and I did not know what he was referring to. Now I understand: he was identifying the *saris chama*, someone whose condition traces back to the womb itself.

### No Recovery Presumed

The Gemara raises a further concern: even if we observed this urination pattern when the child was six years old, perhaps at some point between that early observation and the present he recovered — even briefly — which would, according to Rabbi Akiva, place him in the category. The Gemara resolves this: *keivan de-tichilaso ve-sofo laki, lo chashinan* — since we see the condition at the beginning and at the end, we do not concern ourselves with the possibility of an intermediate recovery. A consistent beginning and end permit a reasonable presumption of continuity.

### Bechor Limb Distinction

Rav Mari challenges this reasoning from a *braita* concerning a *bechor* animal with a certain eye condition. Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos rules there that one must examine the animal three times within eighty days — beginning, middle, and end — before concluding that the condition has persisted continuously. Why is a two-endpoint check sufficient here but not there? The Gemara answers: *le-chad evar chashinan, le-chula gufa lo chashinan* — for a condition affecting a single limb, we worry about possible intermediate recovery; for a systemic condition affecting the whole body, we do not. The *saris chama* condition, even though it manifests in a particular way, is understood as something systemic rather than a localized physical defect, and therefore the two-endpoint check suffices.

---

## Saris Adam Distinction

### Age 20 Indicator

The Gemara now introduces a *braita* that addresses how one identifies a *saris* and when that status becomes operative. The case: *ben esrim shana ve-lo heivi shtei se'aros* — a man who has reached the age of twenty without having grown two pubic hairs. Such a person must bring proof that he is indeed twenty years old, and he is then classified as a *saris*. The underlying reasoning is that a *saris chama* — someone with this systemic condition — never reaches sexual maturity, never develops secondary sex characteristics, and therefore will not grow pubic hair. Ordinarily, halakhic adulthood requires reaching thirteen years of age and having two pubic hairs. When someone reaches twenty without pubic hair, it is not a case of delayed puberty but of an absence of natural maturation altogether, and the person is classified as a *saris* — an adult by virtue of age alone.

### No Chalitzah/Yibum

The *braita* then states the *nafka mina*: *lo choletz ve-lo meyabem* — such a person does not perform *chalitzah* and does not perform *yibum*. The parallel ruling applies to a woman: *bas esrim ve-lo hevia shtei se'aros* — a woman of twenty without two pubic hairs is classified as an *ailonit*, the female counterpart, *lo choletzet ve-lo misyabemes* — she neither performs nor receives *chalitzah* or *yibum*. This is *divrei Beis Hillel*, who set the threshold at twenty. Beis Shammai says eighteen for both. Rabbi Eliezer says: follow Beis Hillel for males (twenty) and Beis Shammai for females (eighteen), since women mature earlier and their status can therefore be determined at a younger age.

It is worth noting what the *saris* category actually represents here. This is not merely a person who is infertile — an *akara* (a barren woman) would still be subject to *yibum* and *chalitzah*. The *saris chama* and *ailonit* are people whose entire physical development has not followed the normal trajectory; it is a systemic condition, not simply the absence of offspring.

### R. Eliezer Contradiction

This creates an apparent contradiction. Rabbi Eliezer, in participating in the *braita*'s debate about whether the threshold is eighteen or twenty, seems to accept its *nafka mina* — namely, that a *saris* does not perform *chalitzah* or *yibum*. Yet in our *mishnah*, Rabbi Eliezer explicitly says that a *saris chama* does perform *chalitzah*, because people with this condition can be healed in Alexandria in Egypt.

### Retraction Debate

Rami bar Dikuli in the name of Shmuel says: *chazar bo Rabbi Eliezer* — Rabbi Eliezer retracted one of these positions. The question then becomes: which one did he abandon? A further *braita* is cited in which Rabbi Eliezer explicitly states that a *saris chama* performs *chalitzah* and *chalitzah* is performed with his wife, because *she-ken be-minan misrapin be-Alexandria shel Mitzrayim* — those with this condition are healed in Alexandria in Egypt. This *braita* thus aligns with the *mishnah*. Rashi explains that the concreteness of Rabbi Eliezer's knowledge — that healing is actually available in Alexandria — indicates that this was his considered and final position, and that it was the statement in the *braita* excluding the *saris* from *chalitzah* that he abandoned.

### Not About Chalitzah

Rabbi Elazar (not to be confused with Rabbi Eliezer) offers a different resolution: *le-olam lo hadar bei* — Rabbi Eliezer never retracted at all. *Ve-chi tnan ha-hi le-onshin itmar* — when Rabbi Eliezer participated in the discussion about eighteen versus twenty, he was not endorsing the *nafka mina* of exclusion from *chalitzah* and *yibum*. That *braita* is concerned with a different question entirely: the *onshin* — the question of when a *saris* or *ailonit* becomes halakhically adult for purposes of liability and punishment. Rabbi Eliezer disagrees with the other positions about the *nafka mina* of *chalitzah* and *yibum*, but agrees that there is a distinct question of when the person is considered a *gadol* for other legal purposes, and it is only on that question that he offers the eighteen-versus-twenty ruling. In Rabbi Elazar's reading, Rabbi Eliezer consistently holds throughout that a *saris chama* does perform *chalitzah* and *yibum*; both the *mishnah* and the *braita* about Alexandria reflect his unretracted view.

---

## Adult Status at 20

### Forbidden Fat Case

Having established that Rabbi Eliezer did not retract, the Gemara now explores the practical implications of the age-twenty determination for *onshin*. The case: a person ate *chelev* (forbidden fat) from the age of twelve years and one day — the age of halakhic maturity for a girl, had she had pubic hair — through the age of eighteen, without ever developing pubic hair. At eighteen (or twenty, depending on the authority), the *simanei saris* or *ailonit* manifest, and the person is categorized accordingly. Then, afterward — *le-achar mikan* — pubic hair does appear. The question is when, exactly, this person became a halakhic adult, and whether the sins committed between twelve and eighteen carry liability.

### Rav: Retroactive

*Rav amar na'aseh saris le-mafreia* — Rav holds that once we identify a person as a *saris* at the age of eighteen or twenty, that status applies retroactively to age twelve or thirteen. The person was, in hindsight, a *saris* from the point of *bar* or *bas mitzvah* — they are therefore liable for the *aveiros* committed during that period, since retroactively they were an adult at the time.

### Shmuel: Forward

Shmuel disagrees: *katan haya be-osa sha'a* — at the time of those transgressions the person was still a minor. Adult status is conferred only from the moment the *saris* classification is established — at eighteen or twenty.

### Later Hair Appears

The *le-achar mikan* clause — the appearance of pubic hair after the *saris* classification — adds a further complication. One might think that subsequent pubic hair growth is evidence of delayed rather than absent puberty, suggesting that adult status should be assigned even later. Yet Rav maintains his retroactive position even in this case: once classified as a *saris* at eighteen or twenty, the person is retroactively an adult from twelve or thirteen, regardless of later pubic hair. The *nafka mina* here extends beyond questions of sin and punishment; it applies equally to financial transactions undertaken during that period, which would be binding retroactively according to Rav but not according to Shmuel.

### Ailonit Knas Proof

Rav Yosef challenges Rav from the laws of *knas* in *Kesubos*. Rabbi Meir holds that *knas* — the fifty-shekel payment for rape or seduction — applies only to a *na'arah*, not to a *ketanah*. An *ailonit*, having no pubic hair, remains a *ketanah* and therefore has no *na'arus* period. According to Rav's retroactive logic, however, since an *ailonit* is retroactively an adult from age twelve, she should have a *na'arus* period from twelve to twelve-and-a-half — and should therefore be entitled to *knas* during that window.

### No Na'arus Period

Abaye resolves the difficulty: *mi-katnusa nafka le-voger* — she goes directly from *ketanah* to *bogeres*. The period of *na'arus* — the transitional stage of physical maturation between twelve and twelve-and-a-half — presupposes a naturally maturing body. *Na'arus* is constituted by the process of puberty itself; it is the stage during which the body is actively developing the secondary sex characteristics. An *ailonit* undergoes no such process. Even according to Rav, who says that retroactively she became an adult at twelve, she became a *bogeres* directly — there is no *na'arus* interlude. This is equally true according to Shmuel: whether the transition to adulthood occurred at twelve or at eighteen, in neither case does the *ailonit* pass through a stage of *na'arus*. A supporting *braita* confirms: *ein saris nidon ke-ven sorer u-moreh* — a *saris* cannot be a *ben sorer u-moreh*, because a *ben sorer u-moreh* requires the presence of lower pubic hair, which a *saris* will never have. *Ve-ein ailonit nidonis ke-na'arah me'orasah* — an *ailonit* is not in the category of *na'arah me'orasah*, with its associated capital punishment for adultery, *she-mi-katnusah yatz'ah le-darga* — she leapfrogs directly from *ketanah* to *gedolah*, bypassing the *na'arah* status entirely.

---

## Physical Simanim

### Waiting Until 20

Rabbi Abbahu states: *simanei saris ve-ailonit u-ven shemonah ein osim bahem ma'aseh ad she-yihyu ben esrim* — for someone who displays the indicators of *saris* or *ailonit*, and for someone born in the eighth month of pregnancy, no halakhic determination is made until they reach the age of twenty. Even if at nineteen a person presents all the indicators of *saris* or *ailonit*, the formal classification cannot be finalized until twenty. The eighth-month baby (*ben shemonah*) is grouped here because the Gemara assumes such a child cannot survive, and therefore the child has no presumption of viability (*chazakas chayah*) until the twentieth year.

### Eighth Month Baby

This prompts an immediate question: *u-ven shemonah mi chayei?* — does an eighth-month baby actually survive? A *braita* is cited: *ben shemonah harei hu ke-even* — an eighth-month baby is like a stone; it is *muktzah* on *Shabbos* and one may not handle it. The implication is stark: such a child is presumed to be non-viable, essentially already dead. How, then, is it possible to speak of waiting until this child reaches twenty?

### Held-Over Theory

The Gemara resolves this: *kesha-gamru simanav* — the case is one where the physical characteristics at birth are those of a complete child. Hair, fingernails, and other markers are developed. In such a case, the Gemara concludes, *amina hai bar sheva hu ve-ishtahui de-ishtahi* — this is really a seven-month baby that was held over in the womb beyond its term. The standard view is that a seventh-month baby is viable while an eighth-month baby is not. A baby born in what appears to be the eighth month, but whose physical markers are those of a full-term child, is presumed to be a seven-month baby born late. The *chiddush* of Rabbi Abbahu is that even such a child — whose physical development looks normal — requires waiting until twenty before the full *chazakas chayah* is established. Conversely, even a person with all the *simanei saris* must wait until twenty before that status is formally confirmed.

### Twelve Month Birth

This idea of in-utero delay gives rise to a striking practical ruling: *ha de-avad Rava Tosfaah* — Rava Tosfaah issued a ruling in a case of a woman whose husband had traveled overseas and who gave birth twelve months after his departure. Rava Tosfaah declared the child *kasher* — not a *mamzer*. The reasoning: following Rabbi's view that babies can be held over in the womb, a nine-month fetus that was retained for three additional months would still be the husband's child.

### 30 Day Survival

The Gemara adds that Rava Tosfaah's ruling was not merely a lone opinion: *keivan de-ika Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel de-amar mishtahai* — since Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel also holds that babies can be held over in the womb, the ruling reflects a broader consensus. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's relevant teaching: *kol she-shaha sheloshim yom ba-adam eino nefel* — any infant who survives thirty days is no longer classified as a *nefel*. A child born in the eighth month who survives a full month is no longer treated as a stillborn; the thirty-day survival is itself evidence that the child was a viable holdover. This supports the broader framework: even an apparent eighth-month birth may represent a held-over seven-month fetus, and survival confirms that presumption.

---

## Saris Signs Listed

### No Beard/Hair

The Gemara now presents the full enumeration of the physical signs of *saris chama*. A *baraisa* teaches: *eizehu saris chama? Kol she-ben esrim ve-lo heivi shtei se'aros* — anyone who reaches twenty without two pubic hairs. *Ve-afilu heivi le-achar mikan, harei hu ke-saris le-chol devarav* — even if pubic hair appears afterward, this does not lead to a reassessment of status. Once classified as a *saris* at twenty, that classification is final.

### Smooth Skin

Additional signs follow: *kol she-ein lo zakan* — anyone without a beard; *ve-sa'aro lakui* — whose hair is affected (seemingly sparse, soft, or insufficiently developed); *u-vesaro machlik* — and whose skin is smooth. These are characteristics that reflect the absence of normal male physical development and are understood as more feminine-type traits.

### Urination & Heat

Several further traditions are cited. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Yair: *kol she-ein meimav ma'alin retichu* — anyone whose urine does not produce foam (or, according to another reading, steam) upon urination. Another view: *kol ha-matil mayim ve-ein oseh kipah* — one whose urine does not form an arc (as noted earlier by Abaye). Another: *kol she-shichvat zaro dacha* — one whose semen is watery rather than viscous. Another: *kol she-mei raglav machmitzim* — one whose urine does not become malodorous. And yet another: *kol she-rocheitz bi-ymot ha-geshamim ve-ein besaro ma'aleh hevel* — one who bathes in winter and whose body produces no steam. All of these indicators point in the same direction: a systemic absence of the bodily heat and physical characteristics associated with normal male development.

### Voice Quality

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds: *kol she-kolo lakui, ve-ein nikar bein ish le-isha* — anyone whose voice is affected such that one cannot distinguish whether it is a man's or a woman's voice. This is the male counterpart of the corresponding sign for an *ailonit*, where Rabban Shimon ben Elazar notes that a deep voice indistinguishable from a man's is a sign of that condition. The parallel list of *simanei ailonit* includes: absence of breasts, difficulty during intercourse, absence of the Mons pubis (*shipulei me'ayim*), and a low voice indistinguishable from a man's.

---

## All vs One Sign

### Rav Huna: All

With the full list of *simanim* before us, the Gemara takes up the question of how many are required. *Simanei saris* — *Rav Huna amar: ad she-yihyu kulam* — Rav Huna holds that a person is classified as a *saris* only if all the *simanim* are present.

### R. Yochanan: One

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *afilu be-echad mehen* — even one of these signs suffices to establish *saris* status.

### Hair Present: All

The Gemara clarifies the scope of the dispute. *Heicha de-heivi shtei se'aros ba-zakan* — where a person has two hairs of the beard (or, per the *Gra*'s reading, two pubic hairs), everyone agrees that all the *simanim* together would be required to overcome the evidence of that hair growth. *Ki pligi be-shelo heivi* — the dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan applies specifically where the person has neither pubic hair nor facial hair (depending on the reading). In that case: does the presence of even one of the listed signs establish *saris* status (Rabbi Yochanan), or must all signs be present (Rav Huna)?

### Rav Nachman Case

The Gemara cites a remarkable incident. Rava bar Rav Huna instructed the rabbis to observe Rav Nachman: *inu bei Rav Nachman* — if when bathing his body produced steam, *i besaro ma'aleh havel*, then *asiv lei brat* — you could go ahead and give your daughter in marriage to him, knowing that he was not a *saris*. The implication is that Rava bar Rav Huna was looking to rule out *saris* status on the basis of a single *siman* — consistent with Rabbi Yochanan's position.

### Hair Likely Present

The Gemara, however, offers a different reading of this incident. *Rav Nachman sichei dikna havu leh* — Rav Nachman in fact had some stubble of beard, or some small amount of pubic hair. In that case — where some hair is present — everyone agrees that all the *simanim* are required for *saris* classification. Since Rav Nachman had that hair, checking for even one counter-indicator was sufficient to rule out *saris* status: if he had steam from his body, there was at least one *siman* working against *saris* classification, and in a case where all *simanim* are required, failing even one test means he is not a *saris*. The incident therefore does not compel the conclusion that Rava bar Rav Huna held like Rabbi Yochanan; it is compatible with Rav Huna's position as well.

---

## No Chalitzah/Yibum

### Mishnah Rule

The Gemara returns to the concluding ruling of the *mishnah*: *ha-saris she-chalatz le-yivamto* — the *saris* who performs *chalitzah* and *yibum*, and similarly the *ailonit*.

### Saris Chama Only

The Gemara observes: *katani saris dumya de-ailonit* — since the *mishnah* groups *saris* and *ailonit* together, they must be parallel categories. An *ailonit* is unambiguously a natural condition — *bidei Shamayim*. Therefore the *saris* referred to in the *mishnah* is also *bidei Shamayim* — a *saris chama*, not a *saris adam* who acquired his condition through human action or injury.

### R. Akiva Rule

*Ve-stama ke-Rabbi Akiva* — the *stam mishnah* ruling here reflects Rabbi Akiva's position. Rabbi Akiva holds: *bidei adam* — a *saris adam* — is included in the category of *chalitzah* and *yibum*; *bidei Shamayim* — a *saris chama* — is not.

### Yibum Invalidates

If the *saris* nonetheless performs *yibum* with his *yevamah*, he invalidates her — *pesulah le-kehunah*. The reason: he has engaged in a forbidden sexual union with his sister-in-law outside the context of *mitzvah*, an *issur arayot*, and this makes her prohibited for marriage to a *kohen*. If, on the other hand, he performed *chalitzah*, she is not invalidated, since a non-meaningful *chalitzah* carries no such consequence.

One might have thought that any man's sexual relations with the *yevamah* — not just the *saris* brother-in-law — would invalidate her, given that she is a *shomeret yavam* and her *zikah* bond constitutes a quasi-marital relationship. The Gemara indeed confirms this: *hu ha-din afilu le-acher nami* — even if another man had relations with her while she was a *shomeret yavam*, she would likewise be invalidated for the remaining brothers. The reason the *mishnah* frames the ruling in terms of the *saris* himself is literary: since the opening of the clause discusses what happens when *he* performs *chalitzah*, the *mishnah* naturally continues by discussing what happens when *he* performs *yibum*.

### Ailonit Rule

The same rules apply to an *ailonit*: if the brothers perform *chalitzah* with her, she is not invalidated; if they perform *yibum* — sexual relations with her outside of *mitzvah* — she is invalidated, because it constitutes relations with an *eishet ach* in the absence of the *mitzvah* of *yibum*.

### Ailonit Permitted

The Gemara notes the implicit assumption: *ta'ama de-ba'aluha* — it is specifically the sexual act that creates the invalidation. If no such act occurred, she would not be invalidated merely by virtue of being an *ailonit*. This ruling stands in contrast to Rabbi Yehuda's position, which holds that an *ailonit* is inherently a *zonah* — since she can never conceive, every sexual act she engages in is considered fornication outside the context of procreation. The *mishnah* here does not follow Rabbi Yehuda. According to the *mishnah*, an *ailonit* is not a *zonah* by nature, remains permitted to a *kohen*, and is only invalidated by the specific prohibited sexual act of *yibum* performed without the force of *mitzvah*.

---

---

# Yevamot 81

## Saris & Androgynos

### Saris Wife Terumah

The mishnah on this daf returns us to the question of the *saris* — one who is incapable of procreation — and its implications for *chalitzah* and *yibum*. Having established in earlier discussion that a *saris chama* (one whose condition is congenital, from the sun, as it were) cannot perform *yibum* or *chalitzah* according to Rabbi Akiva — whereas a *saris adam* (one castrated by human intervention) had at one point been capable and is therefore not categorically excluded — the mishnah now turns to a distinct question: the *saris chama*'s wife and her eligibility to eat *terumah*.

The mishnah states: a *kohen* who is a *saris chama* and who married a *bat Yisrael* — she may eat *terumah* on his behalf. The distinction is critical. A *saris adam* is a *patzua daka*, whose marriage is forbidden, rendering the woman a *chalalah*. But a *saris chama* has committed no *issur* in marrying her; the marriage is fully valid, and she accordingly enjoys the rights of a *kohen*'s wife, including eating *terumah*.

### Androgynos Categories

Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon introduce the case of an *androgynos* — a person with both male and female genitalia — who is a *kohen* and has married a *bat Yisrael*. They rule that she may eat *terumah* on his behalf. Before examining the ruling itself, it is worth considering the three possible halakhic frameworks for understanding an *androgynos*. The intuitive assumption might be *safek* — perhaps we simply do not know whether to categorize this person as male or female. But there are two other possibilities as well. One is that the *androgynos* is a *berya bifnei atzmo*, a creature of a third category entirely, neither male nor female but something unto itself — a recognition that the binary division of the world into male and female may not be exhaustive. The third possibility is that the *androgynos* is definitively male, on the reasoning that maleness is defined by the presence of male genitalia, and since this person possesses male genitalia, he is male regardless of any other characteristics present.

### Androgynos Marriage

The ruling of Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon — that an *androgynos kohen*'s wife may eat *terumah* — presupposes that the *androgynos* is halakhically male. For the marriage to confer *terumah* rights upon his wife, he must be definitively her husband, which requires him to be definitively male. Were he a *safek* or a *berya bifnei atzmo*, it is difficult to see how the marriage would unambiguously transfer *terumah* eligibility.

The mishnah further states that an *androgynos* can marry a woman but cannot be married by a man — again consistent with the position that he is definitively male. Rabbi Eliezer goes further, ruling that if an *androgynos* marries a man, the act is treated as an act of male homosexuality and carries the penalty of *sekilah*, again treating him as fully male. Whether the earlier positions in the mishnah require us to view the *androgynos* as definitively male, or whether they are compatible with a *safek* reading, remains to be examined in the *gemara*.

### Tumtum Chalitzah

Rabbi Yehuda adds that a *tumtum* — a person whose genitalia were covered and whose sex was initially indeterminate — who was later found upon tearing of the skin covering to be male, may nonetheless not perform *chalitzah*, because he is considered like a *saris*. The presumption is that someone born in this condition will be unable to father children, rendering him a *saris chama* from birth and thus excluded from the entire framework of *yibum* and *chalitzah*.

---

## Yochanan vs Lakish

### Saris Wife Terumah

The *gemara* opens by questioning whether the first ruling — that a *saris chama*'s wife may eat *terumah* — is even in need of stating. *Peshita* — it seems obvious. He is a valid *kohen*, the marriage is valid, she is not *pesulah* in any way. Why would we think otherwise? The *gemara* answers: one might have thought that the verse *yelid beito hem yochlu belachmo* — members of his household eat of his bread — is tied specifically to the context of a marriage that produces progeny. One might reason that only *molid ma'achil*, one who can have children causes his wife to eat *terumah*, and one who cannot, *she'eino molid*, does not. The mishnah teaches us that we do not apply this reasoning; the wife of a *saris chama* is his wife in every sense, and she eats *terumah*.

A related question arises as to whether the *saris chama* and the *tumtum she-nikra* — the *tumtum* who was found to be male — are treated identically. In both cases, the person is male but incapable of procreation; the mishnah simply addressed each in the context of a different *halakha* — *terumah* for the former, *chalitzah* for the latter. But these are not contradictory rulings; both *halakhot* apply to both cases. The distinction that does emerge from earlier discussions is between a *saris* and an ordinary *akar* — a man who is simply infertile. An *akar* does perform *chalitzah*, while a *saris* does not, and it is the *saris*'s categorical status, not merely his infertility, that excludes him.

### Lakish Safek View

The *gemara* now turns to the case of the *androgynos*. Reish Lakish states: the wife of an *androgynos kohen* may eat *terumah*, but she may not eat *chazeh v'shok* — the breast and thigh portions of *kodashim* that a *kohen*'s wife is entitled to receive. Rabbi Yochanan disagrees and holds that she may even eat *chazeh v'shok*.

The logic of Reish Lakish's position flows from his view that an *androgynos* is a *safek* — possibly male, possibly not. If there is genuine doubt as to whether this woman is legally married to a *kohen*, then she cannot eat *chazeh v'shok*, which is biblical. Why then can she eat *terumah*? Because, the *gemara* explains, the *gemara* is speaking of *terumah bizman hazeh* — *terumah* in our times, which is only rabbinic in force, presumably because following the destruction of the *Beis HaMikdash* the land lost its sanctification for purposes of *terumah* and *ma'asros*. In a case of *safek*, we are lenient in matters of rabbinic law, and so she may eat *terumah* even though the marriage is uncertain.

### Yochanan Male View

Rabbi Yochanan, by contrast, holds that the *androgynos* is definitively male, the marriage is fully valid, and the woman may eat *terumah* and *kodashim* alike, with no restriction.

### Terumah Status

At this point the *gemara* shifts from the primary dispute — the status of the *androgynos* — to challenge the secondary premise underlying Reish Lakish's position, namely that *terumah* today is rabbinic. Rabbi Yochanan presses: do you really hold that *terumah bizman hazeh* is *derabbanan*?

Reish Lakish confirms this and offers a proof: he teaches a *baraita* in which an *igul* — a round of pressed figs — of *terumah* that becomes mixed with ordinary rounds of pressed figs is *oleh b'echad u'me'ah*, nullified in a ratio of one to a hundred. Now, an *igul* is a *davar she-biminyan* — an item sold by count — and the general rule is that things counted individually are *chashuv* and cannot be subject to *bittul*. The fact that *bittul* works here, Reish Lakish argues, must be because *terumah* nowadays is only rabbinic, and in rabbinic matters we are lenient enough to allow *bittul* even for a *davar she-biminyan*.

The *gemara* raises the obvious objection: *terumah* is itself a biblical prohibition. Reish Lakish acknowledges this but maintains the distinction between *terumah* in Temple times and *terumah* today, given the absence of the *Beis HaMikdash*.

The *gemara* then points out: if Reish Lakish wishes to contrast *terumah* as rabbinic with *chazeh v'shok* as biblical, he need not reach for *chazeh v'shok* at all. He could simply distinguish within *terumah* itself — rabbinic *terumah* today versus biblical *terumah* at the time of the *Beis HaMikdash*. The *gemara* accepts that this is indeed Reish Lakish's intent. When he says she eats *terumah* but not *chazeh v'shok*, he means: she eats today's *terumah*, which is rabbinic. And at a time when the *Beis HaMikdash* stood and *terumah* was biblical, she would not eat even that. Moreover, even rabbinic *terumah* — such as *terumah* of fruit, which is rabbinic even in Temple times — would be prohibited to her at the time of the *Beis HaMikdash*, because *dilma asi l'ochla b'terumah d'oraisa*: one might come to eat from the biblical *terumah* as well, and we are strict across the board when biblical *terumah* coexists with rabbinic *terumah*. In our times, however, when there is no biblical *terumah* at all, there is no such concern, and she may eat rabbinic *terumah*.

---

## Bittul Evidence

### Igul Batel Proof

Reish Lakish's proof that *terumah* today is rabbinic rests on the *igul* case: a round of pressed figs of *terumah* that becomes mixed with other rounds is *batel* in a hundred, despite being a *davar she-biminyan*. This requires some background on the principles of *bittul*.

The mechanism of *bittul* — halakhic nullification — operates on the logic that when a prohibited item is mixed into a much larger quantity of permitted items, the prohibited item loses its independent identity and becomes absorbed into the whole. This works when the items are undifferentiated and can be viewed collectively. When, however, items are individually significant — *chashuv* — each one retains its independent identity and cannot simply be dissolved into the collective. Such items are not subject to *bittul*.

One basis for this individual significance is the principle of *davar she-biminyan* — items sold by count. Things one counts by number, rather than by weight or volume, are treated as individually significant, and they are therefore generally not *batel*. The intuition is straightforward: a chair, a house, a barrel of wine — these are things one counts individually, each retaining its separate existence. They are not viewed as an undifferentiated mass.

Now, Reish Lakish argues that an *igul* — sold by count — should not be *batel* under this principle. Yet the *baraita* says it is *batel*. This can only be because, Reish Lakish reasons, *terumah* today is rabbinic, and in rabbinic domains we relax the strictures of *bittul* sufficiently to allow *bittul* even of a *davar she-biminyan*.

### Et vs Kol

Rabbi Yochanan rejects this inference entirely. The proof fails, he says, because Reish Lakish has misread the *baraita* about *davar she-biminyan*. Reish Lakish understood the rule to be *kol she-darko limanot* — everything that is ever sold by count — is not *batel*. Rabbi Yochanan corrects him: the proper text of the *baraita* is *et she-darko limanot* — only that which is sold *exclusively* by count is not *batel*. The word *et* rather than *kol* narrows the category considerably.

The distinction is meaningful. Some items are *sometimes* sold by count and *sometimes* sold by weight or volume. Eggs, for instance, may be purchased individually or by the basket. Under Reish Lakish's reading, anything that is ever counted — even if it is also sometimes sold otherwise — would be *chashuv* and thus not *batel*. Under Rabbi Yochanan's reading, only that which is *exclusively* counted — always and only sold by number, never by weight or volume — is considered sufficiently individuated to resist *bittul*.

An *igul* of pressed figs, Rabbi Yochanan explains, is sometimes sold by count and sometimes not. It therefore falls outside the narrow category of *et she-darko limanot*, and accordingly it *can* be *batel*. This has nothing whatsoever to do with *terumah* being rabbinic. The *igul* is *batel* simply because it is not a *davar she-biminyan* in the strict sense Rabbi Yochanan defines. Reish Lakish's inference collapses.

### Kilaim Baraita

The underlying dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish — *et she-darko limanot* versus *kol she-darko limanot* — finds its source in a *baraita* about *kilaim*. The *mishnah* teaches: one who possesses bundles of fenugreek (*tiltan*) that are *kilei hakerem* — produce that grew intermixed with a vineyard and is therefore forbidden — must burn them. If these bundles become mixed with other bundles of ordinary fenugreek, Rabbi Meir says all of them must be burned, because the forbidden bundles are not *batel*. The *chachamim*, however, say they are *batel* in one part in two hundred.

The basis of Rabbi Meir's stringency is his rule that a *davar she-biminyan* is not *batel* — and the text attributed to Rabbi Meir is *kol she-darko limanot*, everything that is counted.
