It is also worth noting that Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah was himself a *kohen*.

### 24 Places Doctrine

The *gemara* explains that Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah's position follows the principle articulated by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *b'esrim v'arba'ah mekomos nikra'u kohanim Levi'im* — in twenty-four places in the Torah and *Nevi'im*, *kohanim* are called *Levi'im*. This is one of those places. The verse governing the distribution of *ma'aser* addresses *ha-Levi'im*, and since *kohanim* are themselves called *Levi'im* in Scripture, the *kohen* too falls within the category of those to whom *ma'aser rishon* may be given. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi himself likely made this observation as a standalone *midrashic* point — that the *kohanim* are consistently referred to as *Levi'im* in twenty-four places — without necessarily knowing he was providing the conceptual basis for Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah's position.

### Cemetery Argument

Rabbi Akiva's counter-argument is based on a different verse. The Torah states *achaltem oto bechol makom* — "you shall eat it in every place." Rabbi Akiva reads this to mean that only someone who can eat *ma'aser* in every place is entitled to receive it. A *kohen*, however, cannot eat in a cemetery — he is forbidden from contracting corpse-impurity in a graveyard. Therefore a *kohen* does not qualify as someone who can eat it *bechol makom*, and he is excluded from the class of recipients.

### Garden Collection

There is a historical incident that illuminates this dispute. Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah — himself a *kohen* — was in the habit of collecting *ma'aser rishon* from a certain garden. This was his practice in accordance with his own ruling that a *kohen* is entitled to receive *ma'aser*.

### Cemetery Blockade

Rabbi Akiva responded to this practice. The *gemara* initially appears to describe him leading Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah to the entrance of a cemetery, as if to say: you think you can eat *ma'aser* — go ahead and enter. But a more careful reading of the *gemara*'s language suggests something more pointed: Rabbi Akiva arranged that the only entrance to the storage area of that garden ran through a cemetery, effectively blocking all *kohanim* from accessing it. When the *gemara* asks why Rabbi Akiva would do this if even according to one opinion the *ma'aser* was to be redistributed to *kohanim*, the answer is that Rabbi Akiva was sending a message to Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah: if you are taking this as a legal entitlement (*torat chalukah*), that is unacceptable; if you understand it only as an emergency measure flowing from the historical *knas* on the *Levi'im*, that is another matter. Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah reportedly responded: "Akiva with his shepherd's sack — and I shall live." The wry remark reflects that Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah was wealthy, and he was speaking not for himself but for *kohanim* in general who have no fields of their own: where are we *kohanim* supposed to get our food?

---

## Levites' Punishment

### The Punishment Q.

The *gemara* now asks a foundational question: *mifnei mah kinsu Levi'im b'ma'aser?* — Why were the *Levi'im* punished by having *ma'aser rishon* taken away from them? The historical premise is that at some point, the *Levi'im* lost their statutory right to *ma'aser rishon*, and the *gemara* seeks to understand why this occurred and what became of it.

### Two Explanations

There is a dispute between Rabbi Yonatan and the *sav'ya* — the elders. One view holds that the *Levi'im* were punished because they did not make *aliyah* in the time of Ezra, when the Jewish people returned to the Land of Israel from Babylon. The other view holds that the redistribution of *ma'aser* was instituted so that *kohanim* would have something to rely upon during the periods when they were *teme'im* and therefore unable to eat *terumah*.

### Consensus Reached

The *gemara* challenges the second explanation. If the only reason the *Levi'im* lost their *ma'aser* was in order to feed *kohanim* when they were *teme'im*, why should the *Levi'im* bear this burden? The *gemara* concludes that in fact *kulei alma* — all opinions agree — that the *knas* was imposed because the *Levi'im* did not make *aliyah* in the time of Ezra. That is the core punishment; the *Levi'im* chose not to return to the Land, and so they forfeited the privilege that was theirs within the Land.

### Secondary Dispute

Having established that the punishment was for failing to make *aliyah*, the *gemara* identifies the actual point of dispute more precisely: the two opinions disagree about where the confiscated *ma'aser* was redirected. One opinion holds that it was distributed to the *ani'im* — the poor. If the *Levi'im* forfeited their *ma'aser*, it should simply go to those most in need. The other opinion holds that it was redirected to *kohanim* — specifically because *kohanim bimei tum'atan ani'im ninhu*: when *kohanim* become *teme'im* and lose access to *terumah*, they suddenly find themselves with nothing to eat, since unlike ordinary *Yisrael'im* they have no fields of their own. In their state of impurity they are effectively destitute, and the former *ma'aser* of the *Levi'im* was redirected to address their need.

This secondary dispute also illuminates Rabbi Akiva's behavior. According to the opinion that the *ma'aser* was redirected to the *ani'im*, Rabbi Akiva's blocking of Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah's collection is entirely comprehensible — the *kohen* has no legitimate claim to that *ma'aser* at all. But according to the opinion that it was redirected to *kohanim*, Rabbi Akiva's message was more nuanced: you may collect it, but understand that you do so only as a consequence of the *knas* against the *Levi'im*, not as an expression of your inherent legal entitlement.

### Scriptural Evidence

The *gemara* asks: how do we know that the *Levi'im* in fact failed to make *aliyah* in Ezra's time? The answer comes from a *pasuk meforash* in the book of Ezra: *va'akbetzem el ha-nahar ha-ba el Ahava va-nachaneh sham yamim sheloshah va-avinan ba-am u-va-kohanim u-mibnei Levi lo matzati sham* — "And I gathered them at the river that flows to Ahava, and we camped there for three days, and I looked among the people and the *kohanim*, and I found none of the sons of Levi there." The verse is explicit: when Ezra assembled the returnees, no *Levi'im* were to be found among them.

### Rav Chisda's History

Rav Chisda adds a historical observation that flows from this situation: *batchilah lo hayu ma'amidim shotrim ela min ha-Levi'im* — originally, communal officials (*shotrim*) were drawn exclusively from the *Levi'im*, as indicated by the verse *ve-shotrim ha-Levi'im lifneichem*. But now, following the *Levi'im*'s failure to return in Ezra's time, officials are drawn from *Yisrael* instead. Rav Chisda cites a verse for this latter point, though the *Masoret ha-Shas* notes that the verse he cites does not appear verbatim in *Tanach*. The commentators suggest he may be loosely paraphrasing the verse in Devarim 1:13 — *havu lachem anashim chachamim u-nevonim vi-yedu'im le-shivteichem va-ashimem be-rasheichem* — though the correspondence is imprecise.

---

## Woman's Status Shifts

### Bat Yisrael Path

The second mishnah of the *daf* sets out the full range of possible status shifts for a woman over the course of multiple marriages. A *bat Yisrael* who marries a *kohen* eats *terumah*. If her husband dies and she has a son from him, she continues to eat *terumah* by virtue of that son. If she then marries a *Levi*, she eats *ma'aser*. If he too dies and she has a son from him, she can eat *ma'aser* by virtue of that son — but she has lost her access to *terumah*, since the *levi* son does not restore that privilege. If she then marries a *Yisrael*, she eats neither *terumah* nor *ma'aser*. If he dies and she has a son from him, she remains excluded from both.

### Sons' Effect

But the status conferred by a son persists even after the relevant marriage ends. If the son from the *Yisrael* dies, she regains her status from the *Levi* son — she may again eat *ma'aser*. If the son from the *Levi* dies, she regains her status from the *kohen* son — she may eat *terumah*. The sons function as status-anchors that outlast the marriages which produced them, and their deaths can restore her to progressively earlier entitlements. It is worth noting that this applies to a son of any age — even a minor child functions to determine the mother's eligibility.

### Bat Kohen Path

The mishnah then traces the corresponding path for a *bat kohen*. A *bat kohen* who marries a *Yisrael* does not eat *terumah*. If he dies with no son from him, she still does not eat *terumah*. If she then marries a *Levi*, she eats *ma'aser*. If he dies with no son from him, she continues to eat *ma'aser*. If she then marries a *kohen*, she eats *terumah*. The mishnah implies that her final marital connection carries priority: if her last husband was a *kohen*, and she has a son from that *kohen* as well as sons from earlier marriages, she eats *terumah* — the highest status — even though she also has a *ben Yisrael*.

### Reversion to Origins

As sons die, the woman's status reverts. If her *kohen* son dies, she can no longer eat *terumah*. If her *Levi* son dies, she can no longer eat *ma'aser*. If her *Yisrael* son dies, *chozeret le-veit aviha* — she returns to her father's house. *Beit aviha* here is understood as her tribal identity, not necessarily the physical home of her biological father; the term *beit av* refers broadly to her collective family and original tribal affiliation. Once all her sons from all her marriages have died, she reverts entirely to her original status as a *bat kohen*, and may again partake of the privileges of that station — eating as though she had never left her father's house. As was observed at the close of the shiur, this entire complex of shifting entitlements is the reason why the daughters of *kohanim* ideally marry *kohanim* — so that they never face these complications at all.

---

---

# Yevamot 88

## Single Witness Testimony

### Mishna Setup

The perek of *Ha-Ishah Rabbah* is one of the most perplexing and challenging *perakim* in all of Shas — not only analytically, but in terms of *rabbinic* justice. The central difficulty is understanding how a woman who appears to have done everything right ends up in such severe legal jeopardy: she must leave both husbands, and she loses her rights from each of them.

The *Talmud* begins by identifying the precise situation described in the *Mishnah*. A single witness came and told the woman that her husband was dead. She went to the *beit din*, received permission to remarry, and did so. Because the remarriage was predicated on the testimony of a single witness, all of these harsh consequences follow. Had two witnesses come and told her that her husband was dead, the picture would be entirely different — she could return to her first husband, the second marriage would be treated as a nullity, and so on. What the *Mishnah*'s structure implies, then, is that a single witness is in fact *believed* in such a case.

### Korban Chatas Source

This leads the *Gemara* to a further implication. It is established that if one witness comes and says *achalta chelev* — "you ate forbidden fat" — and the accused responds *lo achalti chelev*, he is *patur* from bringing a *korban*. But if he remains silent, he would be *chayav*. This means that on the basis of a single witness, one is obligated to bring a *korban chatas* — not merely an *asham talui*, the offering brought in cases of genuine doubt, but the *chatas* itself, which implies that the sin is treated as established. This in turn implies that the single witness has been believed *m'doraisa* — a striking conclusion.

The *Gemara* asks: *minalan* — from where do we derive that a single witness can be believed at the Torah level? The source is a *baraita* interpreting the verse *o hoda eilav chataso*: his sin must become known *to him*, and not through others informing him. The *baraita* raises the possibility that even if he fails to contradict someone who accuses him, he might still be *patur* — since another person informed him, perhaps that does not satisfy the requirement of *o hoda eilav*. The verse is therefore read broadly: *mikol makom*, from any situation, he can come to know of his sin.

### Ne'emanut vs. Shtika

The *Gemara* now asks: *heichi dami* — what exactly is this case? If two witnesses came and the accused failed to contradict them, why would we need a verse at all? Two witnesses establish a fact; the *korban* obligation would be obvious. It must therefore be that the *baraita* is discussing a single witness — *chad* — and the inference is that if one fails to contradict a single witness, one is *chayav*. This would mean that the single witness is actually believed, *shema mina eid echad ne'eman*.

The *Gemara* immediately pushes back: *umimai demishum de'meiman*? Perhaps this has nothing to do with the reliability of the witness at all. Perhaps the reason for the *chiyuv* is *mishum de'kashtik* — because the accused was silent. And *shtika ke'hoda'ah damya* — silence functions as a form of admission. This is confirmed by the *seifa* of the *baraita*.

### Two Witnesses Problem

The end of the *baraita* states: if two witnesses say *achalta chelev* and the accused says *lo achalti*, he is *patur* — even against two witnesses. *Rabbi Meir* disagrees and holds him *chayav*. This is a striking passage. Our initial assumption was that two witnesses obviously should be believed — *lama li kra*, why would we need a verse to establish what is self-evident? But the *seifa* reveals that the *Rabbanan* do not convict even on the basis of two witnesses if the accused denies it. This suggests that the *Rabbanan* are not operating in the realm of *ne'emanut* — of witness reliability — at all.

### Shtika K'Hoda'ah

*Rabbi Meir* argues by way of a *kal vachomer*: if two witnesses can bring a person to the death penalty, surely they should be sufficient to obligate a *korban*, which is far less severe. The *Rabbanan* respond: the accused is not without recourse even against two witnesses, because he could always say *mezid hayiti* — I acted intentionally — in which case no *korban* would be due. This is a form of *migo*: since he has available to him a more extreme claim that would exempt him, we credit his denial as well. The deeper point is that a *korban chatas* depends not on whether a person sinned, but on whether they *know* they sinned. No external testimony can substitute for a person's own internal certainty about what occurred and what their intentions were.

### Rabbi Meir's Kal Vachomer

Returning to the opening of the *baraita*, the *Gemara* asks: *reisha mai ta'ama kemachayvei Rabbanan* — why do the *Rabbanan* hold that silence in the face of a single witness creates *chiyuv*? If it were because the single witness is *ne'eman*, then we would be back to a contradiction — here are two witnesses who are *ne'eman* in all circumstances, yet the *Rabbanan* exempt the accused even against their testimony. The answer must be that the *Rabbanan* are not working within the framework of *ne'emanut* at all. Rather, *ela lav mishum de'ishtik* — it is entirely because the accused was silent. *Shtika ke'hoda'ah damya*: silence is treated as an admission.

### Internal Knowledge Model

The *Gemara* therefore proposes to abandon the verse entirely and seek a *sevara* — a logical basis. It cites the known case of *safek chelev safek shuman*: a piece of meat that might be *chelev* or might be permitted fat, where a single witness comes and declares *bari li d'shuman hu* — I am certain it is permitted — and is believed. A brief aside is warranted here: it is striking that the *Talmud* reaches for the analogy of the piece of meat to describe the legal status of a wife. Feminist scholars of the *Talmud* have noted this kind of comparison, as the *din* of the woman in this case is treated as formally identical to the *din* of a cut of meat.

### Chelev Analogy

Can this analogy actually sustain the case of the woman? The *Gemara* objects: *hatam lo itchazek issura* — in the meat case, the prohibition was never established; we simply did not know what category the piece fell into. *Hacha itchazek issura d'eshet ish* — here we know for certain that this woman was married. Furthermore, *ein davar she-be'erva pachot mishnayim* — in cases that touch on sexual prohibitions, we require no fewer than two witnesses. These two objections are related: once we say *itchazek issura d'eshet ish*, we are in the domain of *arayot*, and therefore we cannot rely on a single witness.

The objection can be sharpened further. Our case does not resemble *safek chelev safek shuman* at all. It more closely resembles a case of *vadai chelev* — a piece of fat that is definitely forbidden — where a single witness comes and says it is actually permitted. In that case, *d'lo meheiman* — the single witness is not believed.

One might ask: is it not the case that even where *itchazek issura* applies, a single witness would be ineffective? Yes — and this is precisely the point. Even the case of *safek chelev* allows a single witness only because there is no established prohibition. The moment something is *vadai chelev* or *itchazek issura*, no number of witnesses can overturn the established fact through testimony alone. The only exception would be personal knowledge — if you yourself saw a piece of meat cut from the animal's kidney, no hundred witnesses can tell you otherwise, because it is your direct knowledge, not testimony at all, that establishes the *issur*.

This leads to a further observation from the *Gemara*: *hatam afilu bei mea lo meheimni* — in the case of *vadai chelev*, even a hundred witnesses cannot permit it. But *hacha keivan d'ki atu bei trei meheimni* — in the case of the woman, if two witnesses came and said her husband is dead, we would believe them. Therefore, *chad nami meheiman* — perhaps we should believe a single witness as well, just as we do in the analogous cases of *tevel*, *hekdesh*, and *konamot*.

### Tevel, Hekdesh, Konamot

The *Gemara* now examines each of these three parallel cases in detail to see if any of them can actually serve as the source or model for the woman's case.

Regarding *tevel* — grain from which tithes have not yet been separated — suppose we have a basket that may not have been tithed, and a single witness comes and says it has been properly separated. The *Gemara* asks: *ei dideih* — if the witness is the owner himself, then we understand why he is believed: *mishum d'beyado l'takno* — it is within his power to fix it at any moment, and since he could always tithe it, we treat his assertion that he already did so as credible. But the case that actually resembles ours must involve a witness speaking about *someone else's* property. In that case, the analysis depends on a *machloket*: can one tithe on behalf of another person using one's own grain, without the owner's consent? If so, then *mishum d'beyado l'takno* — this witness himself could effect the remedy at any moment, and so he has a degree of standing analogous to ownership. But if the owner's knowledge is required, then the witness is simply making an assertion about a fact he did not himself create — and we are back to the question of where we get the authority to believe him.

The same difficulty recurs with *hekdesh*. If something has been consecrated to the Temple and a witness says it has been redeemed, we can explain the case of *kedushat damim* — monetary consecration — by saying *mishum deyadei liftoto*: the owner can always effect a redemption. And even for *kedushat haguf* — where the animal itself has been consecrated for a *korban* — if it is the owner's own animal, *mishum deyadei leishalei alei*, he can always go to a *talmid chacham* and have the *hekdesh* annulled. But once again, the case that resembles ours is where a third party comes and says the owner went to a *talmid chacham* and cleared the animal of its consecrated status. And *hi gufa minlan* — from where do we derive that such a witness is believed?

The same pattern plays out with *konamot*. A *konam* can operate in two ways: it can render something forbidden to oneself, or it can render one's own property forbidden to others. In either case, if it is one's own *konam*, the owner can seek annulment at any time, which explains why a single witness who happens to be the owner is credited. But the moment we move to a witness testifying about someone else's *konam* — that the owner has already sought annulment — we once again reach *hi gufa minlan*. Each time the analysis is brought to the point that actually resembles our case, the underlying logic collapses.

It is notable that all of this reasoning has been *stama d'Talmuda* — anonymous throughout. Every one of these exchanges represents the back-and-forth of the *Gemara*'s own anonymous layer of analysis, and no solution has been found.

### Agunah Prevention

Now, for the first time, a named *amora* steps forward with a direct answer. *Amar Rabbi Zeira: mitoch chomer she'hichmarta aleha besofah hekaltah aleha betechilah.* Because the consequences at the end are so severe — because she must leave both husbands, forfeit her *ketubah*, and face all the attendant penalties — the rabbis did not need to make life so difficult for her at the beginning. Knowing full well that she stands to lose everything if she acts precipitously, she can be trusted to wait until she is genuinely certain that her husband is dead before proceeding to remarry. Therefore the rabbis permitted reliance on a single witness.

The *Gemara* responds tartly: *lo tachmir velo takal* — do not make it harder at the end and thereby justify making it easier at the beginning. Leave well enough alone; the cost is too high.

But the final answer is: *mishum aguna ikilu bah rabanan*. Ultimately, the rabbis were lenient with her out of concern for the *agunah*. Without this leniency, a woman whose husband disappears and is presumed dead would have no legal recourse and would remain chained for the rest of her life. It is important to note that this type of *igun* — where a husband has actually died or disappeared — is categorically different from the *agunah* crisis of the modern era, which involves husbands who are known to be alive yet refuse to deliver a *get*. The halakhic solutions that have been developed for the former have far less application to the latter.

---

## Husband Returns

### Rav's Position

The *Mishnah* continues: if the husband returns after she has remarried, *tetze mizeh umizeh* — she must leave both the second husband and the first. At this point, *Rav* makes a striking statement: *lo shanu ela she'niset be'ed echad, aval niset al pi shenei edim lo tetze.* Rav holds that the rule of *tzet mizeh umizeh* applies only when she remarried on the basis of a single witness. But if two witnesses came and testified that her husband was dead, and she married on that basis — she does not have to leave her second husband.

In *Eretz Yisrael*, they laughed at this: *machku aleha bema'arava.* The man is standing right in front of you, and you are telling her she may remain with the second husband?

### Gemara's Objection

The *Gemara* formulates the objection directly: *ata gavra veka'i* — the man has come and is standing before you. *Ve'at amart lo tetze?* And you are saying she does not need to leave?

### Identity Recognition

The *Gemara* answers: *lo tzericha* — Rav's ruling is still necessary. The case is one of *d'la yad'ina leh* — we do not recognize this person. Someone is claiming to be the long-lost husband, but there is no positive identification. The *Gemara* presses: if we do not recognize him at all, why would she even need to leave her second husband in the case where she married on the basis of a single witness? It answers: the ruling is needed for the case where two witnesses come and say, *anan havainan bahadei mikai nafak v'ad hashta* — "We have been with him continuously from the time he left until this very moment; it is you who fail to recognize him."

The *Gemara* supports this with the verse describing Yosef's reunion with his brothers: *vayaker Yosef et echav ve-hem lo hikiruhu* — Yosef recognized his brothers but they did not recognize him. *Rav Hisda* explains: he left before the seal of a beard had formed on his face, and he returned with it. The broader point is clear: it is entirely plausible that a person could return after a long absence and not be recognized, whether because of physical changes, the passage of time, or the disappearance of those who originally knew him.

### Conflicting Testimony

The *Gemara* then raises a further difficulty. Even granting all of this — even accepting that the two witnesses who accompany the returning husband are credible — we now have *trei v'trei ninhu*: two witnesses who said the husband was dead against two witnesses who say he is alive and present. This creates a *safek*, and anyone who now sleeps with this woman would be obligated in an *asham talui* — the conditional guilt offering for uncertain sin. How then can Rav say *lo tetze*, that she remains with the second husband, when every act of marital relations generates a *safek* requiring an *asham talui*?

### Rav Sheshet's Solution

*Rav Sheshet* offers a solution: *kegon she-nisset l'achad me-adeha* — the case is one where the woman married one of the original witnesses who testified to her husband's death. This is relevant because an *asham talui* is not an offering that comes from external legal pressure; it reflects a person's own internal doubt about whether they have sinned. If she married the very witness who established the fact of the husband's death, that witness himself has no doubt whatsoever — he was there. He does not feel any uncertainty, and therefore an *asham talui* simply does not apply to him.

The *Gemara* pushes further: even if the man does not have a doubt, *hi gufa be'asham talui* — what about her? Does she not still feel uncertain? The answer is: *be'omeret bari li* — she herself says, "I am certain that he is dead." Rashi explains that the witnesses produced convincing signs — an item that only the husband would have had, for example — that left her with no personal doubt.

### Temporal Sequence

The *Gemara* then raises the question of *novelty*: if the case requires both that she married one of her witnesses and that she herself is certain the husband is dead, what is the *chiddush* of Rav's ruling? Even *Rabbi Menachem Berabbi Yosi* — who takes the strictest position — confines his ruling to a specific scenario. *Afilu Rabbi Menachem Berabbi Yosi lo ka'amar ela sheba'u eidim ve'achar kach niset* — even he only rules strictly when both sets of witnesses appeared *before* she married. But if she married first and only then did contradicting witnesses emerge, *Rabbi Menachem Berabbi Yosi* would also not require her to leave.

### Baraita Dispute

The *Gemara* cites a *baraita* to clarify this. Two witnesses say the husband is dead; two witnesses say he is not. Two witnesses say she was divorced; two witnesses say she was not. *Harei zo lo tinasei* — she should not marry, since she is a *safek*. *Ve'im niset, lo tetze* — but if she did marry, she need not leave, say the *Rabbanan*. *Rabbi Menachem Berabbi Yosi omer tetzei* — Rabbi Menachem Berabbi Yosi says she must leave.

*Rabbi Menachem Berabbi Yosi* clarifies his own position: *eimatai ani omer tetzei? Bizman sheba'u eidim ve'achar kach niset.* He requires her to leave only when both sets of contradicting witnesses appeared *before* she married. If she knew going in that the situation was a *safek*, and she married anyway, she cannot now claim the protection of *lo tetze*. But if she married first and only afterward did contradicting witnesses arrive, even he would agree she need not leave.

Rav's ruling is therefore not merely a restatement of what all *Tannaim* agree on. There are two ways to read Rav. According to the first reading (*yesh omrim*), Rav's case is one where she married *after* the contradicting witnesses appeared, and he rules *lo tetze* — unlike *Rabbi Menachem Berabbi Yosi*. On this reading, Rav is announcing that the *halacha* does not follow *Rabbi Menachem Berabbi Yosi*. According to the second reading, Rav's ruling applies to the case where she married *before* the contradicting witnesses appeared, meaning Rav actually holds *like* Rabbi Menachem Berabbi Yosi — his *chiddush* being simply that the *halacha* follows that position.

### Kohen Case Challenge

*Rava* raises an objection to Rav from a different *baraita*. The case is a *kohen* who has married a woman forbidden to him — a *gerushah*, for example. The *baraita* asks: from where do we know that if he refuses to divorce her, we compel him? The verse says *ve-kidashto* — "you shall sanctify him": he is made holy whether he wishes it or not. Now, *heichi dami* — what is the scenario of this *baraita*? If it is the simple case without the complications of contradicting witnesses and personal certainty, the *kohen*'s obligation to divorce is obvious; no *baraita* is needed. It must therefore be referring to the more complex case — one where she did marry one of her witnesses and she herself declared certainty about her husband's death. And yet the *baraita* says we compel him. This seems to be a direct challenge to Rav, who said *lo tetze*.

### Kohen Exception

The *Gemara* offers several possible resolutions. First: *issur kehunah shani* — the *kohen* case is categorically different. A *kohen* faces additional prohibitions that do not apply to a regular *Yisrael*, and therefore even a doubt that would not require dissolution of an ordinary marriage is sufficient to require dissolution of a *kohen*'s marriage.

Second: *mai dafnu? Dafnu be-eidim.* What does it mean to "compel" him in the *baraita*? Rashi explains that this refers not to forcing him to give a *get* after the fact, but rather to preventing the marriage in the first place — by producing witnesses who will complicate the situation and demonstrate that she may in fact still be married, thereby deterring him from marrying her at all. But once the marriage has occurred, we would not necessarily dissolve it.

Third: *kasheba'u eidim ve'achar kach niset ve-Rabbi Menachem Berabbi Yosi hi* — perhaps this *baraita* represents the position of *Rabbi Menachem Berabbi Yosi* specifically, in the scenario where the contradicting witnesses appeared before she married. Rav may simply hold differently.

---

## Rav Ashi & Shmuel

### Rav Ashi's Reinterpretat…

*Rav Ashi* now offers a fundamentally different reading of Rav's original ruling. *Mai lo tetze deka'amar Rav? Lo tetze meheterah harishon.* When Rav said *lo tetze*, he did not mean she stays with the second husband. He meant she does not lose her permitted status with respect to the *first* husband. In other words, when two witnesses testified that her husband was dead and she married on that basis, and the husband subsequently returns — she is not *asurah* to the first husband. She may go back to him. She is *asurah* to the second husband, whose marriage has been nullified, but her original marriage is very much intact.

### Mishna's Case

The *Gemara* then asks: but Rav already said this once — why does he need to say it a second time? *Detnan: niset shelo birshut muteret lachzor lo* — the *Mishnah* states that if she married *shelo bi-reshut* (understood here to mean on the basis of two witnesses, without needing the permission of *beit din*), she is permitted to return to the first husband. And *Rav Huna* reported that Rav ruled that the *halacha* follows this *Mishnah*. So Rav has already told us she can return to the first husband. Why restate it?

The answer is: *chada miklala de-chavreita itmar* — one ruling was derived from the other. Once we know the *halacha* follows the end of the *Mishnah* — that she can return to her first husband — it follows as a corollary that she does not forfeit her original *heter*.

### Shmuel's Condition

*Shmuel* now enters with his own formulation: *lo shanu ela shelo machchishto, aval machchishto lo tetze.* What we have been discussing applies only when the woman does *not* contradict the returning man. If the husband returns and she contradicts him — she says, "You are not my husband; I do not know you" — then she does not have to leave her second husband and may remain with him.

### One vs. One Witness

The *Gemara* asks: *bemai askinan* — what is the scenario? If two witnesses come and say the husband is alive, then her denial is irrelevant; two witnesses cannot be contradicted by one person's claim. It must therefore be that a *single* witness comes and says the husband is alive. So the *Gemara* concludes: *ta'ama demachishatei* — the reason she stays with the second husband is that she contradicted the single witness. *Ha shetaka teitzei* — but if she had been silent, she would have had to leave, even on the basis of this single witness.

### Ulla's Principle

This prompts the *Gemara* to invoke *Ulla*'s principle: *kol makom she-he'emina Torah ed echad harei kan shnayim, ve-ein devarav shel echad bimkom shnayim.* Anywhere that the Torah has granted the reliability of a single witness, the Torah has not simply lowered the bar — it has elevated that witness to the status of two. So when the original single witness said the husband was dead and the woman was permitted to remarry on that basis, that witness now carries the weight of two. A single witness who subsequently says the husband is alive cannot override that, because one witness cannot stand against two.

One might ask: the *Gemara* earlier concluded that it was the *rabbis* who permitted reliance on a single witness, out of concern for the *agunah* — not the Torah itself. How then can *Ulla* invoke the language of *he'emina Torah*? The force of the objection is real, and the *Gemara* does not resolve it fully here. What seems to be operating is the understanding that even the rabbinic permission was grounded in a Torah-level framework, and that the leniency — once granted — confers the full status that the Torah accords to a single witness in contexts where it is permitted.

### Disqualified Witnesses

The *Gemara* then asks: what exactly is the case where someone comes after the fact and says the husband is alive? If it is a *kosher* single witness against the original *kosher* single witness who now has the status of two — the later witness can obviously not override. So the *Gemara* answers: *bipsulei edut* — the case is where two disqualified witnesses, such as two women or two relatives, come and say the husband is alive. *Ucherabbi Nechemiah* — and this is in accordance with the view of *Rabbi Nechemia*.

### Rabbi Nechemia's Rule

*Rabbi Nechemia* holds: *kol makom she-he'emina Torah ed echad halach achar rov de'ot* — in all cases where the Torah accepts a single witness, one follows the majority of opinions. Since the original single witness has the status of two, and the two disqualified witnesses also count as two opinions, one follows the larger number. *Ve-asu shtei nashim ke-ish echad* — and by this principle, two women count like one man in terms of testimony.

But this rule applies symmetrically only when the original witness was also a woman. *Aval shtei nashim be-ish echad — ke-palga u-palga dami* — if two women testify against a single male witness (who has the Torah-granted status of two), the result is half against half — a standoff. On the alternative reading proposed by the *Gemara*, the case is that the original witness was a woman from the outset, and the principle of *Rabbi Nechemia* is applied accordingly: two women testifying against one woman is treated like two men against one man.

---

---

# Yevamot 89

## Husband Returns Alive

### Setup: Single Witness

The sugya opens on 88b at the bottom, still discussing the case of a woman whose husband departed to a distant land, whereafter a single witness testified that he had died. Acting on this testimony — and with the permission of *beit din* — she remarried, only for her first husband to return alive. The ruling is that she must leave both husbands. The *gemara* now takes up the question of *get*: the *mishnah* states *tzericha get mizeh umizeh* — she requires a *get* from each husband.

### Rav Huna Gezeira

The *gemara* begins with a *bishlama*: it is straightforward that she needs a *get* from the first husband, since she was legally married to him and, if she ever wishes to remarry, she must be formally divorced. But why does she require a *get* from the second husband? Her union with him was *zenut b'alma* — mere adultery. She was still a married woman when she entered that relationship; no marriage was ever contracted. Why should a *get* be necessary?

Rav Huna answers: it is a *gezeira*. The Rabbis were concerned that observers would say: the first husband divorced her, she then married the second, and now she is leaving the second — all without a *get*. This perception would create the impression that a married woman can exit a marriage without a *get*, which is intolerable.

### Kiddushin Only Case

The *gemara* then raises a challenge from the continuation of the *mishnah*: if she was told her husband died and she accepted only *kiddushin* — betrothal — but did not proceed to *nisuin*, she is permitted to return to her first husband. The *gemara* asks: should we not also be concerned in that case that people will say the first husband divorced her, she became betrothed to a second man, and now she is leaving him without a *get*?

### Public Perception Issue

If we apply the same logic, we would say that even in the *kiddushin*-only case she should need a *get* from the second man — *le'olam ba'ei get*, she always requires a *get*. But this leads to a further difficulty.

### Mechzir Gerushato

If she must obtain a *get* from the second man (her *mekudeshet*, her betrothed), then her first husband — having "divorced" her in the eyes of observers who believe she received a *get* — would be re-taking a woman who had been "divorced" and then betrothed to another. This implicates the prohibition of *mechzir gerushato*, the prohibition against a man remarrying his divorced wife after she has been married to another.

### R. Yose ben Kipur

One might argue this is only a problem according to Rabbi Yose ben Kipur, who holds that *mechzir gerushato* applies even from *eirusin* alone — *min hanisuin asurah, min ha'eirusin muteret*, that only after full *nisuin* is she forbidden to return, but from *eirusin* she may return. Since Rabbi Yose ben Kipur's view is a *da'at yachid* not accepted as *halacha*, one could argue that public confusion about his position is itself undesirable, which would make the entire scenario problematic.

### Get Doesn't Matter

The *gemara* now adduces evidence from the *mishnah* itself: *af al pi she-natan ha-acharon get, lo pasla min hakehunah* — even if the second husband gave her a *get*, she is not disqualified from *kehunah*. This tells us something important: a *get* from the second husband does not carry the halachic force of a real *get*. For if it were a genuine *get*, it would render her a *gerushah* and disqualify her from marrying a *kohen*. The fact that it does not disqualify her proves the *get* in this case is essentially meaningless — it is given only for the purpose of appearances, not as a real act of divorce.

### Kiddushei Ta'ut

The resolution is *amrei kiddushei ta'ut havu*: in the *kiddushin*-only case, people will naturally understand that the betrothal was a mistake — she accepted *kiddushin* without knowing her first husband was still alive. Therefore, when she exits the situation without a *get*, no one concludes that a married woman can leave without a *get*; everyone understands it as a nullification of a betrothal entered under false pretenses. This is what people will think.

### Kensu Rabbanan

If that is so — that in the *kiddushin* case people will say *kiddushei ta'ut havu* — why don't we say the same in the first case, where she actually married and lived with the second man? There too, was it not a marriage entered in error?

The answer is *kensu rabanan* — the Rabbis penalized her. In the first case, an actual act of prohibition took place: she cohabited with a man while still legally married. The Rabbis therefore imposed a penalty. In the second case, *delo avda issura* — she did not actually commit any prohibited act; she merely accepted some tokens of betrothal without knowing the full picture. Where no genuine transgression occurred, *lo kensu rabanan* — the Rabbis did not impose the penalty.

---

## Woman's Consequences

### No Ketubah

The *mishnah* states *ein lah ketubah* — she receives no *ketubah* from either husband. The *gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama tiknu lah rabanan ketubah?* What was the entire purpose of the rabbinic enactment of the *ketubah*? *Kedei shelo tehei kalah be'einav lehotzi'ah* — so that divorcing her would not be a trivial matter in the husband's eyes; the financial burden of the *ketubah* payment was meant to deter hasty divorce. In the present case, however, we actively want the husband to divorce her. Creating any obstacle to that divorce by requiring a *ketubah* payment would be counterproductive. Therefore, the Rabbis do not require it.

### Ketubah Nature

A question arises here: is not at least some component of the *ketubah de'oraita*? The answer is that the *ketubah* — the obligation to pay a sum upon divorce — is entirely *takanat derabbanan*. What is *de'oraita* is the clause of *she'er, kesus, v'onah*: the husband's obligations to provide food, clothing, and conjugal rights. The monetary payment upon divorce is purely a rabbinic institution.

This raises a more refined question: if the *ketubah* is a contractual document that has already been entered into, does one not need to honor the terms of a contract? Two approaches suggest themselves. One could argue that the *ketubah* is not a fully voluntary contract — it is a mandated condition of marriage — and therefore the assumption underlying the contract is that the rabbinic mandate for it remains in force. Once the reason for the *ketubah* is void — as in this case, where divorce is required — the *ketubah* itself is also void. Alternatively, and relatedly, the principle of *hefker beit din hefker* — which the *gemara* will develop at length later — gives *beit din* the authority to dissolve obligations of this kind. The final clause of the *ketubah* document supports this reading: *v'kibel alav chasan den kichomer kol shtarei ketubot v'toseftos de-nahagin bivnot Yisrael hatzni'ot ketikkun chachameinu zichronam livrachah* — the groom accepts the terms "according to the enactment of our Sages of blessed memory," which means the contract operates within the rabbinic framework that established it, and that same framework can dissolve it.

### No Support Benefits

Beyond the *ketubah* itself, the *mishnah* states *ein lah peiros, v'lo mezonot, v'lo blaot* — she is entitled to neither *peiros* nor *mezonot* nor *blaot*. To explain briefly: *nichsei milog* are properties a wife brings into the marriage that she retakes upon divorce, while the husband enjoys the profits — the *peiros* — during the marriage. In cases where the marriage is found to have been invalid (such as an *almanah l'kohen gadol*), the husband must retroactively return those profits. In our case, she does not even receive that restitution. *Mezonot* — her food support — likewise does not apply, nor do the *blaot* — the worn garments that ordinarily belong to the wife.

The *gemara* explains: *tenai ketubah ke-ketubah dami* — the conditions and appurtenances of the *ketubah* share the same status as the *ketubah* itself. Since she forfeits the *ketubah*, she forfeits everything that comes along with it.

### Competing Values

This ruling raises a genuine moral tension. The Rabbis were lenient with this woman at the outset — they permitted her to remarry on the basis of a single witness — precisely because they did not want her to become an *agunah*. As the *gemara* stated elsewhere, *mishum agunah akeilu bah rabanan*: to prevent the tragedy of a chained woman, the Rabbis eased the standard of evidence. And yet, when things go wrong through no real fault of her own, the full weight of the consequences falls on her alone.

One might argue that at minimum she should receive her *ketubah*: it is not her fault this happened, and she now finds herself with nothing. The *gemara's* response to this, implicitly, is that the Rabbis view the *ketubah* instrumentally — as a mechanism for regulating the husband's motivation, not as a social welfare provision for the wife. Since the goal here is to ensure the husband divorces her promptly and without financial hesitation, the *ketubah* serves no purpose and is withheld. Compelling as this logic is from a purely formal standpoint, it leaves the woman in a precarious position that is difficult not to find troubling. The *gemara* itself, back on an earlier *daf* (around daf 8), acknowledged the tension: *shappir avdu Rabbanan de'avdu hachi* — the Rabbis structured it correctly — though it also acknowledged the ulterior motive of preventing *iggun*.

### Return Property

*Natlah mizeh umizeh* — if she actually took anything from either husband, she must return it. One might think this is *peshita* — obvious. The *gemara* clarifies: it is necessary to state this because one might have thought that *keivan detafsa, lo mafkinan minah* — since she has already taken possession, we do not wrest it from her. In many cases of disputed property, once someone has gotten hold of something, we do not remove it. This ruling teaches that in our case we do: she must return it. This makes the ruling even more stringent from the woman's perspective — not only does she receive nothing, but whatever she may have already received must be given back.

---

## Mamzerim Status

### Mamzerim Both Sides

The *mishnah* further states: *v'havlad mamzer mizu umizu* — children she bears are *mamzerim* from either husband. The *gemara* will now examine exactly what the nature of this *mamzer* status is: when is it *de'oraita* and when *de'rabbanan*? Counterintuitively, as will become apparent, the one whose *mamzeirus* is *de'rabbanan* is actually in a worse position than the one whose status is *de'oraita*.

To address this, the *gemara* pivots entirely to *Seder Zeraim*, specifically *Masechet Terumot*, and stays there for a substantial discussion.

### Terumah Analogy

*Tenan hatam* — a *mishnah* in *Masechet Terumot* states: *ein tormin min ha-tamei al ha-tahor* — one may not separate *terumah* from *tamei* produce on behalf of *tahor* produce. If one does so *b'shogeg* — accidentally — *terumato terumah*, it counts as *terumah*. If one does so *b'meizid* — intentionally — *lo asa v'lo klum*, one has accomplished nothing.

### Bad Terumah

Before analyzing this *mishnah*, the *gemara* introduces a parallel case from *Masechet Terumot*: if one sets aside a cucumber (*kishut*) as *terumah* and it turns out to be bitter, or a melon and it turns out to be rotten — the ruling is *terumah v'yachzor v'yitrom*: it counts as *terumah* (and must be treated accordingly) but one must go back and separate *terumah* a second time from valid produce.

### Chisda vs. Natan

The *gemara* now presents a dispute between Rav Chisda and Rav Natan bar Rav Yehoshua regarding the precise meaning of *lo asa v'lo klum* when *tamei terumah* is separated on *tahor* produce intentionally.

Rav Chisda interprets it maximally: *lo asa v'lo klum kol ikar* — he has done absolutely nothing whatsoever. Even the *se'ah* of produce that was physically separated as *terumah* from the *tamei* pile reverts to *tevel* status; it is as if no *terumah* was ever separated from either the *tamei* pile or the *tahor* pile.

Rav Natan bar Rav Yehoshua takes a narrower view: *lo asa v'lo klum letaken et ha-shirayim* — he has accomplished nothing with respect to permitting the *tahor* remainder for consumption. The *tahor* produce still requires valid *terumah* to be separated from it. However, the produce that was physically taken as *terumah* from the *tamei* pile does have the status of *terumah* — it is *tamei terumah* that must be burned.

The reason Rav Chisda rejects Rav Natan's position is a practical concern: *gezeira dilma pasha v'lo mafrish* — if we tell the person that the *tamei* stuff he separated really is *terumah*, he may become negligent and fail to separate valid *terumah* a second time. He will reason: "I already separated *terumah* — the fact that it must be burned is irrelevant, I fulfilled my obligation." To prevent this negligence, Rav Chisda holds that nothing the person did has any *terumah* status whatsoever, and he must start from scratch.

The *gemara* then challenges Rav Chisda from the *mishnah* about the bad cucumber: there, even though the *terumah* was invalid, we say *terumah v'yachzor v'yitrom* — it has *terumah* status and he goes back to separate more. Why does the same logic of negligence not apply there? The *gemara* answers: *shogeg ameizid karamis* — you are comparing an accidental case to an intentional one. In the *shogeg* case, the person is fundamentally trustworthy and genuinely attempting to fulfill the obligation; we can rely on him to separate *terumah* again when told to do so. The *meizid* case involves someone who is already acting improperly, and we cannot trust him to do anything correctly thereafter. Therefore the concern about negligence applies only to the *meizid* case, justifying Rav Chisda's ruling.

A further question is raised: *v'rami shogeg ashogeg* — let us compare a *shogeg* case to another *shogeg* case. In our *mishnah*, *b'shogeg terumato terumah* — accidentally separating *tamei* on *tahor* results in *terumah* status without requiring a second separation. But in the case of the bad cucumber, it says *terumah v'yachzor v'yitrom* — it is *terumah* and one must separate again. Why the difference?

The answer: *shogeg karov lemeizid* — the *shogeg* in the case of the bad cucumber is closer to *meizid*. *Ibai lei l'mitamei* — he really should have tasted the produce before designating it as *terumah*. Since he failed to take that simple precaution, his negligence is borderline intentional. The *Tosfos* raise the obvious question: how is one supposed to taste *tevel* produce before the separation? Their answer is that one should first separate *terumah* from a small piece that one then tastes for quality; having confirmed it is fit, one gives the remainder to the *kohen* as *terumah*.

A further comparison is raised: *v'rami meizid ameizid* — comparing intentional cases to intentional cases. In our *mishnah*, intentional separation of *tamei* on *tahor* is *lo asa klum*. But another *mishnah* in *Masechet Terumot* discusses taking *terumah* from a flowerpot without drainage holes (which is not obligated in *terumah*, being treated as detached from the ground) on behalf of a flowerpot with holes (which is obligated). There the ruling is *terumah v'yachzor v'yitrom* — it counts as *terumah* and one separates again. Why is that not also *lo asa klum*?

The *gemara* answers: *bitrei mani tza'at, uvechad mana la tza'at* — when dealing with two different types of vessels (one with holes, one without), the distinction is visually apparent and the person will understand when told to separate again. When dealing with a single vessel (as in the *tamei/tahor* case — two piles of identical-looking produce), the person will protest: "What difference does it make? This is *tevel* and that is *tevel*, they look the same to me." He will not comply with a second separation, and therefore we must tell him upfront that his action accomplished nothing at all.

Returning to Rav Natan bar Rav Yehoshua's position, the *gemara* poses the parallel challenge: a *mishnah* states that if one separates *terumah* from a flowerpot *with* holes on a flowerpot *without* holes — taking from the obligated on behalf of the exempt — *terumato terumah*, it has *terumah* status, and *velo tochal ad she-yotzi aleha terumah u-ma'aser mi-makom acher*, she may not eat from it until additional *terumah* and *ma'aser* are taken from elsewhere. Rashi explains: the separation has removed a portion from the obligated pile and treated it as *tevel*, so one cannot eat it or give it to a *kohen* until *terumah* is properly taken for it from another source. The question to Rav Natan bar Rav Yehoshua is: why in *his* case do we say the separated portion retains *terumah* status (and must be burned), while in this case we treat it as *tevel*?

The *gemara* answers: *shani hacha de-mi-d'oraita terumah me'alyata hi* — our case is different, because the *tamei* *terumah* that was intentionally separated is in fact genuine *terumah de'oraita*. This is the position of Rabbi Ilai.

### Invalid Terumah

The *gemara* works through several configurations of valid and invalid *terumah* separation to clarify the positions of Rav Chisda and Rav Natan bar Rav Yehoshua and where the respective concerns about negligence and *terumah* status apply. The critical variable throughout is whether we are dealing with a *shogeg* or *meizid*, and whether the two types of produce involved are visually distinguishable.

### Rabbi Ilai Source

Rav Natan bar Rav Yehoshua's position that *tamei terumah* intentionally separated still has genuine *terumah* status is grounded in Rabbi Ilai's teaching. Rabbi Ilai asks: *minayin li-trom min ha-ra'ah al ha-yafah she-terumato terumah* — how do we know that if one separates *terumah* from low-quality produce on behalf of high-quality produce, it nonetheless counts as *terumah*? He derives it from the *pasuk*: *v'lo tisu alav cheit ba-harimechem et chelbo mimenu* — "you shall not carry a sin upon it when you take the best of it." The *gemara* reasons: *v'ee ein kodesh, nesi'at cheit lama* — if separating from low-quality produce were not *terumah* at all, there would be no legal implication to the act, and therefore no *cheit* to speak of. The very fact that the *pasuk* speaks of a *cheit* for failing to take the *chelev* — the best — proves that when one does separate from inferior produce, the separation is legally effective as *terumah*. Otherwise, the person has done nothing at all and there is nothing to have a *cheit* about.

The *pasuk* itself, when read contextually, is an exhortation to remember to give *terumah* and to give it from the best. But Rabbi Ilai reads it to yield a specific *halachic* derivation: the obligation to give the best implies that giving the worst still constitutes a valid act of *terumah* — *mikan she'ha-toram min ha-ra'ah al ha-yafah, terumato terumah*.

---

## Beit Din Authority

### Challenge to Authority

Rabbah now turns to Rav Chisda with a sharp challenge: according to Rav Chisda, who holds that intentionally separating *tamei terumah* on *tahor* produce accomplishes absolutely nothing — even the portion physically removed reverts to *tevel* — the reason is a *gezeira* against negligence: we worry that if we call it *terumah*, the person will not separate again.

But this is a remarkable claim. *Mi ika midi de-mide'oraita havi trumah, u-mishum dilma pasha, afkuha rabanan l'chulin?* — Can it be that something which is *terumah de'oraita* is retroactively stripped of that status and converted back into *chulin* by the Rabbis, simply because they are worried the person might not act properly? *V'chi beit din matnin la'akor davar min ha-Torah?* — Can *beit din* make a ruling that uproots something from the Torah?

### Mamzer Restriction

Before Rav Chisda responds, Rabbah himself presents the *mamzer* case as an instance of exactly this problem. *V'hatnan, havlad mamzer mizeh umizeh* — the *mishnah* declares the children *mamzerim* from both husbands. With respect to the second husband, this is straightforward: she was still legally married to the first husband when she cohabited with the second, and so the child is a genuine *mamzer de'oraita*.

But what of a child from the first husband? *Ishto hi* — she is his legal wife. *V'Yisroel ma'alya hu* — and he is a perfectly kosher Jew. How can their child be a *mamzer*? And this is not a mere stringency we can treat lightly: *v'kashrina lei b'mamzeret* — by declaring him a *mamzer*, we are binding him to a status that restricts whom he may marry. He cannot marry a *bat Yisroel*, and he cannot marry a *mamzeret* either.

Indeed, the *gemara* brings in the ruling of Shmuel — confirmed by Rabbi Yochanan when Ravin came from *Eretz Yisroel* — that this child is *assur b'mamzeret*, forbidden even to a *mamzeret*. This is a *mamzer l'chumra* in the most stringent sense: he cannot marry a *bat Yisroel* (because the Rabbis call him a *mamzer*) and cannot marry a *mamzeret* (because *de'oraita* he is a perfectly kosher Jew, and the Rabbis did not create a positive permission for him to marry a *mamzeret* — only the real prohibition). The *gemara* states explicitly: *v'amai karay lei mamzer? L'osro b'vat Yisroel* — why do we call him a *mamzer*? Specifically in order to prevent him from marrying a *bat Yisroel*. He can, however, apparently marry another *mamzer derabbanan*. This is the painful architecture of *mamzeirus derabbanan*: the child is the vehicle through which the mother is punished, and he is caught in a status that makes him, in one sense, worse off than a *mamzer de'oraita*.

### Chisda's Examples

Rav Chisda responds to Rabbah's challenge — *v'at lo tisbera?* You yourself don't think *beit din* has that power? — by marshaling examples of cases where Chazal undeniably do uproot Torah obligations. The *mamzer* case just discussed is itself such an example: a child of a perfectly valid marriage is declared a *mamzer* by rabbinic decree.

### Minor Daughters

Rav Chisda sends Rabbah further proof via Rav Acha bar Rav Huna: the *baraita* dealing with the marriage of a minor girl (*ketanah*). When a father dies, the mother and brothers may arrange the marriage of a daughter who has not yet reached majority. Such a marriage is only *de'rabbanan*; the girl retains the right, upon reaching majority, to exercise *mi'un* — refusal — and leave without a *get*, with no blemish to her status. The *baraita* states that this husband can inherit her, can become *tamei* for her if he is a *kohen*, and she can eat *terumah* by virtue of his household. The dispute is about the precise timing.

### When Inherit

*Beit Shammai* holds the husband can inherit her *mishe'ta'amod be-komatah* — from when she reaches physical maturity (in years and signs). *Beit Hillel* holds it is *mishetikanes le-chuppah* — from when she enters the *chuppah*. *Rabbi Eliezer* holds it is *mishetiba'el* — from when the marriage is consummated.

The *gemara* then clarifies *Beit Shammai's* position. One might have read them as requiring *both* maturity *and* the *chuppah*. The *gemara* explains that this is actually Beit Shammai's critique of Beit Hillel: Beit Shammai is saying to Beit Hillel — when does the *chuppah* actually take legal effect? Only if she has already reached majority. If she is too young, the *chuppah* is legally meaningless. Conversely, Beit Shammai holds that once she is of age, *chuppah* alone is sufficient — even without a second ceremony.

### Rabbi Eliezer

The *gemara* then notes a tension with Rabbi Eliezer's own position: *v'ha amar Rabbi Eliezer ein ma'aseh ketanah klum* — Rabbi Eliezer himself holds that the acts of a *ketanah* are legally null. If so, how can consummation of the marriage while she is still a minor establish his right to inherit her? The resolution is *eima mishe-tagdil ve-tibaeil* — Rabbi Eliezer must mean from when she has reached majority *and then* the marriage is consummated. This aligns him with the thrust of Beit Shammai's position.

### Hefker Beit Din

Returning to the central question: the *baraita* states *yorshah* — he inherits her. But *d'midoraita* her family inherits her property, since the marriage is only *derabbanan*. The Rabbis are therefore taking property that belongs *de'oraita* to her family and transferring it to the husband. This is a direct application of *hefker beit din hefker* — the principle that *beit din* has the authority to declare property ownerless and redistribute it. Rav Chisda is using this as proof that rabbinic authorities can indeed override Torah-level property rights.

### Ezra Precedent

The *gemara* asks: *minayin she-hefker beit din hayah hefker* — what is the source for this principle? Rabbi Yitzchak cites the verse in Ezra: *kol asher lo yavo li-shloshet ha-yamim ba-atzat ha-sarim ve-ha-zekenim, yachoram kol rechusho* — whoever fails to appear within three days at the order of the princes and elders will have all his property confiscated and he will be separated from the community. The *gemara* notes that this proof is not quite a textual derivation in the classical sense — it is not using the verse to establish what God intended as law. Rather, Ezra's authoritative precedent demonstrates that *beit din* possesses this power; the assumption is that Ezra was acting within the framework of *halacha*, and therefore his action is evidence that *halacha* permits it.

### Joshua Source

Rabbi Elazar cites a different source, from Yehoshua: *eleh ha-nechalot asher nichalu Elazar ha-Kohen v'Yehoshua bin Nun v'rashei ha-avot l'matot Bnei Yisrael* — these are the inheritances that Elazar the Kohen, Yehoshua bin Nun, and the heads of the fathers of the tribes of Israel distributed. Rabbi Elazar asks: what is the connection between *rashim* (leaders) and *avot* (fathers)? He derives: just as fathers apportion inheritance to their children however they wish, so too the *rashim* — the *beit din* — can distribute the people's property however they choose. Here, unlike the Ezra source, there is a genuine textual derivation being offered.

### Tamei Authority

The *baraita* also states *u-metame lah* — if the minor wife dies, her husband (if he is a *kohen*) may become *tamei* for her. But *de'oraita*, only her father may become *tamei* for her — the husband's right to do so comes from the rabbinic recognition of the marriage. The Rabbis are therefore overriding a *de'oraita* restriction on a *kohen's* becoming *tamei*.

### Met Mitzvah

The justification offered is *mishum de-havya lah met mitzvah* — she is treated as a *met mitzvah*, a corpse with no one to bury it. The *baraita* defines *met mitzvah* as *kol she'ein lo kovrim* — one for whom there are no available mourners. *Korei v'achereim onim oto, ein zeh met mitzvah* — if one calls out and others respond that they will attend to the burial, that is not a *met mitzvah*. How does this girl become a *met mitzvah*? Because the Rabbis, through *hefker beit din hefker*, have transferred her property to the husband. Her family therefore says: since we receive no inheritance from her, we decline to bury her — let the one who inherits her take care of the burial. When the husband calls out for the family to bury their daughter and they refuse, she becomes a *met mitzvah* and he, as her husband and heir, must attend to her. This is admittedly a stark picture of the rabbinic reconstruction of incentives.

### Terumah D'Rabbanan

Finally, the *baraita* states *v'ochelet bigino terumah* — she eats *terumah* by virtue of being part of his household. The *gemara* specifies: *biterumah derabbanan* — she eats only *terumah derabbanan*, since the marriage itself is *derabbanan*. A marriage that exists only by rabbinic enactment confers only rabbinic-level rights, and therefore *terumah de'oraita* is not available to her through this marriage.

---

---

# Yevamot 90

## Woman Remarries

### Perek Overview

Daf 90 falls within the *perek* of *Ha'isha Raba*, one of the more challenging *perakim* in Yevamot — challenging both because the logic of the first *mishna* is genuinely difficult to follow, and because the *sugyot* themselves are dense and complicated. The *perek* introduces the sweeping idea of *yesh koach l'chachamim la'akor davar min ha-Torah*, as well as the whole framework of believing an *ed echad*. It is also, notably, one of the *perakim* of the *masechet* most intensively studied in the *yeshivot*.

### Mishna's Logic

The *halacha* in the *mishna* is as follows: a woman receives a report that her husband has died and she proceeds to remarry. If she does so *birshut beit din* — with the permission of the court — and the husband subsequently reappears alive, she suffers a cascade of negative consequences: she must receive a *get* from both husbands, any child born is a *mamzer*, and she forfeits all of her financial rights. However, if she remarried *shelo birshut beit din* — without court authorization, operating unilaterally — she simply returns to her first husband without suffering any of these consequences.

This boggles the mind on two fronts. First, why the negative consequences at all? And second, why is her situation worse when she acted *birshut* — with official backing — than when she acted *shelo birshut*, which would seem to be the more reckless course?

### One vs. Two Witnesses

The very first line of the *gemara* — spoken in the voice of the *stam*, not a specific *amora* — resolves the distinction by reinterpreting the terms. *Birshut beit din*, it proposes, refers to a case in which she remarried on the basis of a single witness, and it was the *beit din* that granted permission to do so on that thin evidence. *Shelo birshut beit din*, the case without negative consequences, refers to a situation in which there were actually two witnesses — no special *heter* was even necessary, and therefore there was no court involvement. So what initially appears to be a harsher case (*shelo birshut*) is actually grounded in stronger evidence.

### Consequences as Mechanism

This reframing still leaves the underlying question unresolved: even granting that there was only a single witness, why do all these consequences follow? If *beit din* gave her permission, why should she bear such severe penalties?

The *stam* of the *gemara* introduces the principle of *dayka u-mintsva*: we permit a woman to remarry on the strength of a single witness only because we rely on the assumption that she will thoroughly investigate the matter before proceeding. She knows, in other words, that if the husband returns, devastating consequences await her — and it is precisely this knowledge of those consequences that motivates her to investigate carefully. The negative consequences are thus framed not as punishments but as the mechanism that underwrites and legitimates the radical leniency of allowing remarriage on the basis of *ed echad* in the first place.

This explanation is difficult on its own terms. One wonders how a woman stranded in distant *Bavel* is supposed to conduct such an investigation, and indeed some *acharonim* argue that she should therefore be formally warned of the consequences before remarrying — something the *gemara* never actually requires. The explanation strains, but it is the *stam*'s answer.

## Friedman's Reading

### Stripping Stam

The scholarly reading offered by Shamma Friedman of Bar-Ilan University proposes a different approach. His method involves stripping away the *stam* layer of the *gemara* to recover what the *amoraim* themselves understood — a methodology associated with the academic study of Talmud. When one does this, he argues, there is no trace whatsoever among the *amoraim* of the radical reinterpretation that *birshut* means one witness and *shelo birshut* means two witnesses. That reading appears to be a *stam* innovation with no amoraic foundation. The *mishna* should instead be read *k'pshuto*.

### Reinterpreting Terms

On this reading, *birshut* and *shelo birshut* mean precisely what they say: in both cases the woman may have acted on the same quality of evidence (whether one witness or two is not the operative distinction), but in the *birshut* case she brought the evidence before *beit din* and received an official ruling, while in the *shelo birshut* case she acted on her own without seeking a *psak*. The question then remains: why the vastly more severe consequences when she operated through the court?

### Natural Consequences

Friedman's answer is that the consequences are not a *knas* — not a punishment — at all. The *pshat* of the *mishna* is that when she acts *birshut beit din*, the court officially recognizes the second marriage. That is the *chiddush* of *chachamim*: in the name of *mishum agunah akilu bah rabanan*, the rabbis validate a second marriage on grounds that would ordinarily be insufficient. Having done so, if the first husband reappears, the woman's *halachic* status is not that she has committed adultery — she acted with full *beit din* authorization — but rather that she is now, in an unprecedented situation, legally married to two men simultaneously.

### Married to Two

All of the consequences that follow are not punishments but the natural *halachic* fallout of this unprecedented status. She needs a *get* from each husband because she is married to both. She forfeits financial rights from each because the entitlements of one marriage are incompatible with a simultaneous second marriage. *Halacha* has simply never encountered this creature before, and the consequences are the necessary result of working out what it means.

### No Recognition

When she acted *shelo birshut beit din*, by contrast, the second marriage was never officially recognized. She slept with another man believing her husband to be dead, and in that sense she is something of an *anusah* — she did not willfully commit adultery. But since the court never validated the second marriage, it remains legally invisible; she returns to her first husband, and there is nothing to undo. The second man's *kiddushin* was never acknowledged as a marriage in the eyes of *halacha*.

This reading preserves the plain meaning of *birshut* and *shelo birshut*, and renders the consequences comprehensible as logical rather than punitive. It also arguably reflects better on the institution: the rabbis were not designing a punitive apparatus to intimidate women into investigating carefully; they were simply confronting the *halachic* reality generated by their own leniency on behalf of *agunot*.

### Audience Q&A

Several questions arise naturally from Friedman's reading. One might ask: the first marriage was also just two witnesses without court involvement — why should the court's validation of the second marriage create a categorically different status? The answer is that the second marriage requires court permission because a woman cannot simply acquire a second husband while still legally married to a first; it is the *beit din*'s ruling that creates the recognition, not the act of *kiddushin* alone.

A deeper question concerns incentive structures: does Friedman's reading not create a strong incentive to avoid the *beit din* altogether, since operating *shelo birshut* produces none of these consequences? The *mishna* itself addresses this, at least partially, by noting that the woman who acted *birshut beit din* does not bring a *korban* and is not considered to have sinned, whereas the woman who acted unilaterally would still owe a *korban*. And practically, social pressure to have marriages recognized by the court remains powerful — people do not typically wish to enter marriages that society will not acknowledge.

As for the status of a child born in the *shelo birshut* scenario: a child born to the first husband would not be a *mamzer*, since she returns to that marriage; a child born from the unrecognized second union, however, would still be a *mamzer*, since that was an act of adultery, however unintentional.

One might finally ask why, if this is the better reading, the *stam* of the *gemara* did not adopt it. That question is difficult to answer definitively; at some point, reconstruction of editorial motivations becomes speculation. What can be said is that the *stam* consistently pushes toward a stricter, more punitive reading throughout this *perek*, treating the consequences as a *knas*, and reads both the *mishna* and the statements of the *amoraim* through that lens.

## Why Ed Echad?

### Three Approaches

Setting aside the question of how to read the *mishna*, the deeper issue lurking behind the entire discussion is: on what basis do we believe an *ed echad* in this context at all? Torah law requires two witnesses for matters of consequence, yet the entire architecture of this *perek* rests on permitting remarriage on the testimony of one. This is a major question, and the *rishonim* offer three distinct answers.

The first is *yesh koach l'chachamim la'akor davar min ha-Torah* — the rabbis simply have the power to uproot a Torah rule. This is the position associated with Tosafot, and it helps explain why the *sugya* on *yesh koach* appears here: not merely to address the *mamzer* question raised by the *gemara*, but to justify the entire framework of *ed echad* in this context.

The second approach, associated with Rashi, is *hafka'as kiddushin*: the rabbis have a particular power in the domain of marriage to uproot *kiddushin* retroactively. This is not a sweeping power to override Torah law in general, but a targeted capacity tied to the institution of marriage itself.

The third approach, offered by the Ra'ah (and rejected by Tosafot), is that once there is sufficient circumstantial evidence, it rises to the level of *anan sa'adi* — something so self-evident that it operates on a *d'Oraisa* level without any rabbinic override at all. The combination of *ed echad* and the woman's theoretical capacity to investigate, the Ra'ah argues, creates that threshold. Tosafot rejects this: it is simply not a genuine *anan sa'adi*, and to claim otherwise is to stretch the category beyond recognition.

There is also a *Sifrei* that attempts to anchor *ed echad* directly in a biblical verse: *lo yakum ed echad b'ish l'chol avon u'l'chol chatas* — one witness shall not stand against a man for any sin or transgression. The *Sifrei* reads *l'chol avon u'l'chol chatas* as limiting: one witness does not suffice for those matters, but it does suffice for testimony about a woman's marital status. This would give a biblical basis for the *ed echad* leniency here. But the question of why we believe *ed echad* remains genuinely difficult, and *yesh koach la'akor davar* is one serious answer — all the more striking given that the very *sugya* we are in the middle of cannot definitively establish that principle.

## Limiting the Mishna

### Rav's Position

Against the background of the *stam*'s sweeping and stringent reading of the *mishna*, the *amoraim* themselves attempt to limit its scope. Rav's position is perhaps the most radical: where there were two witnesses who testified to the husband's death, even if the husband subsequently reappears alive, she may remain married to the second husband. The *gemara* cannot straightforwardly accept this, since the husband is standing there in front of everyone, so it qualifies Rav's statement by framing it as a case of competing testimonies — two witnesses say he is dead, others say this man before them is the husband — and adjudicates between them.

But the Yerushalmi, as Tosafot notes, reads Rav's statement more simply. It accepts the apparent legal fiction: two witnesses have testified he is dead, and even if the man appears before us and every person in town recognizes him, we create a legal fiction and say he is not the man. Two witnesses are as authoritative as a hundred, and patently obvious reality cannot simply override their testimony. The implication is stunning: once she has remarried on the basis of two witnesses, even if he returns, she stays with the second husband, and none of the *mishna*'s negative consequences apply.

### Shmuel's Position

Shmuel offers a different limiting principle: when she herself contradicts the witnesses — when she denies that this man is her husband, or makes some claim against the testimony — she also does not suffer the full consequences of the *mishna*. The *gemara* reads this in a similar frame to Rav's position, involving competing testimonies about identity. But read straightforwardly, Shmuel may simply be saying that when the woman herself disputes the matter, whether by claiming the returnee is not her husband or in some broader sense denying the situation, her position carries weight sufficient to change the outcome. Together, Rav and Shmuel chart two paths for limiting the *mishna*'s harsh sweep.

### Stam Rejects Limits

The *stam* of the *gemara*, however, consistently resists these limiting moves. Rather than accepting Rav's or Shmuel's positions as valid limitations on the *mishna*, the *stam* repeatedly narrows the scope of those amoraic statements themselves, so that the *mishna*'s consequences remain applicable in nearly all cases. The dynamic is a recurring one throughout this *perek*: the *amoraim* try to limit the *mishna*, and the *stam* pushes back, insisting on a broader, more stringent application of the *mishna*'s rule. The *stam* thus consistently presents itself as more *machmir* than the *amoraim*, reading the case as a *knas* and treating the sweep of the consequences as essentially unqualified.

## Why Ed Echad? (II)

### Tosafot's View

Returning to the question of why *ed echad* is believed here, Tosafot's approach, noted above as *yesh koach la'akor davar min ha-Torah*, carries an important nuance. Tosafot does not simply say the rabbis can uproot Torah law whenever they wish. Rather, Tosafot's position is that when an innovation has some logical support behind it — when it *appears* to operate within Torah categories even if technically it does not — then the rabbis may effectuate it without it constituting a genuine *akira d'Oraisa*.

The paradigm case is the discussion elsewhere in this *perek* about a *kohen* being *metamei* to a minor wife (*ketana*) whose *kiddushin* is rabbinically dissoluble. The *gemara* justifies this by analogy to *meis mitzvah*. Tosafot objects: she is not really a *meis mitzvah* — a *kohen* cannot be *metamei* to every relative who happens to have no other heirs simply by invoking that category. But Tosafot explains that because it is *sort of like* a *meis mitzvah*, because there is a logical basis to the parallel, it does not constitute a clear *akira d'Oraisa*. The same logic applies to *ed echad*: because the woman is assumed to investigate (*dayka u-mintsva*), and because there is therefore some rational basis for treating the testimony as sufficient, the act of relying on it is not a naked uprooting of Torah law. There is enough of a fig leaf to place the innovation in a category short of outright *akira*.

### Rashi's View

Rashi's approach points in a similar direction but rests on a distinct mechanism. Rashi's explanation of why *ed echad* suffices here is *afkinu rabbanan l'kiddushin minei* — the rabbis have the power of *hafka'as kiddushin*, the uprooting of the marital bond. Critically, Rashi does not regard this as an unlimited power. The rabbis exercise *hafka'as kiddushin* only when there is, in the phrase used to describe it, a fig leaf — some mechanism that makes it appear as though something legitimate is happening.
