Until *chalitzah* is performed, the *kiddushin* has no effect; once *chalitzah* is performed, it takes effect at that future time.

### Rabbi Yannai Sharecrop

Rabbi Yannai's case follows: *de-Rabbi Yannai hava lei arisa de-hava maytei lei kinta de-peirei kol ma'alei shabta* — Rabbi Yannai had a sharecropper who would bring him a basket of fruit every *erev Shabbos*. On one occasion the sharecropper was delayed and *Shabbos* was approaching. Rabbi Yannai wished to eat the fruit on *Shabbos* but could not separate *tithes* on *Shabbos* itself, and the fruit had not yet arrived. He therefore took *ma'aser* from fruit in his own house *on behalf of* the fruit that would arrive — fruit not yet in his possession. This is parallel to *adam makneh davar shelo ba la'olam*: he is designating *ma'aser* for produce that is not yet in his control and perhaps not even legally his.

### Rabbi Hiyya Dream

Rabbi Yannai was uncertain whether his action was valid and went to ask Rabbi Hiyya. Rabbi Hiyya said to him: *shapir avadt* — you did well. The *gemara* cites a *braita*: the verse *lema'an tilmad leyira es Hashem Elokecha kol ha-yamim* — "in order that you shall learn to fear Hashem your God all the days" — teaches that even on *Shabbatot* and *Yamim Tovim* one takes *ma'aser*. The question is what practical ruling this verse comes to allow on *Shabbos*, since separating *ma'aser* is in any case only a rabbinic prohibition and a scriptural verse would not be needed to override a rabbinic ruling. The *gemara* concludes that the verse comes to validate a case precisely like Rabbi Yannai's: one who takes *ma'aser she-lo min ha-mukaf* — not with all the produce physically present in one location — because circumstances compelled it. Despite the technical deficiency that the designated *ma'aser* and the produce it covers were not in the same place, the designation is valid.

Rabbi Yannai then tells Rabbi Hiyya: but in a dream they showed me the verse *kaneh ratzutz* — a weak reed — suggesting that what I did was unreliable, like resting one's weight on a broken reed (*hinei vatachta lecha al mish'enet ha-kaneh ha-ratzutz ha-zeh*). Rabbi Hiyya responds: they were citing you a different verse with the same phrase — *kaneh ratzutz lo yishbor, u-fishtah kehah lo yichebenah* — a bent reed shall not be broken, and a dimly burning wick shall not be extinguished. In other words, the heavenly message was one of reassurance, not rebuke: something that appears fragile and questionable is in fact sound and will not break.

This little narrative carries a significant implicit message about *halachic* methodology. The image of the flexible reed that does not snap — as opposed to something rigid and brittle — points toward a posture of finding valid grounds for leniency rather than mechanically rejecting what is imperfect. One is reminded of the well-known principle of *hanach lahem le-Yisrael im einam nevi'im hem b'nei nevi'im hem* — if they are not prophets, they are the children of prophets — where the question among later *acharonim* is whether a certain *rishon* was invoking the principle of *mutav sheyihyu shogegim* (tolerated inadvertent transgression) or the principle that the Jewish people intuited correctly. The *kaneh ratzutz* image here functions similarly: it can be read in either direction, and the proper reading depends on where the verse ends.

### Rebbe Slave Freedom

Rebbe's position is derived from a *braita* interpreting the verse *lo tasgir eved el adonav* — do not hand over a slave to his master. Rebbe reads this as referring to one who purchases a slave from another master on the condition of freeing him. Rebbe's reading implies that the act of manumission — the *shichrur* — takes effect at the moment of purchase. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak specifies the mechanism: *de-chtav lei lich'she'ekachecha harei atzmecha kanuy lach me'achshav* — the purchaser wrote a writ of manumission stating "when I purchase you, you own yourself as of now." Here again the *me'achshav* formulation is used, and the act of freedom takes effect upon acquisition even though the document was written when the seller had no ownership.

### Rabbi Meir Conditional

Rabbi Meir's position is drawn from the *mishnah* already cited above: *ha'omer le'isha harei at mekudeshet li le'achar she'agayer* etc. — where he rules *mekudeshet*, in contrast to the *tanna kamma* who rules *einah mekudeshet*. Rabbi Meir holds that where the condition (*le'achar she-yachalotz yevamayich*, for instance) is later fulfilled, the *kiddushin* that was performed before those conditions were satisfied retroactively or prospectively takes effect. This is the direct application of *adam makneh davar shelo ba la'olam* to *kiddushin*.

### Rabbi Elazar Terumah

Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov is cited from a *braita*: *afilu amar peirot arugah zu tlushin yihyu terumah al peirot arugah mechubarim* — even if one says that the picked fruit of this row shall be *terumah* on the attached fruit of the row, or conversely that the attached fruit shall be *terumah* on the picked fruit — to take effect when the attached fruit has ripened to a third and been picked — *devarav kayamim*, his words stand. One performs an act of designation for produce that does not yet meet the conditions required for *terumah*, and when those conditions are met, the designation takes effect. This is another variant of the broad principle.

### Rabbi Akiva Earnings

Finally, Rabbi Akiva's case returns us to the *mishnah* about *konam she'ani osa leficha* — the woman who makes her future earnings *assur* to her husband. Rabbi Akiva holds *yafer* — the husband must annul the *neder* — because she may produce in excess of what belongs to him, and a *neder* on non-existent future labor is valid. This is the *adam makneh davar shelo ba la'olam* in the domain of *nedarim*. (Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua's interpretation — that she is actually consecrating her existing hands and not the non-existent fruit — was flagged earlier as creating tension with this chain, since Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explicitly includes Rav Huna in the list of those who affirm *adam makneh davar shelo ba la'olam*.)

---

## One Witness Yibum

### Why Believe Ed Echad

The *gemara* opens a new inquiry: Rav Sheshet asks *ed echad b'yevamah mahu* — what is the *halacha* regarding one witness testifying for the purpose of *yibum*? That is, if a single witness testifies that a woman's husband has died, thereby allowing her to perform *yibum* with her *yavam*, do we accept that testimony? This question forces an explicit articulation of the foundations upon which we credit the testimony of a single witness (*ed echad*) in matters of marital status — a question central to the entire *perek*.

Two theories are advanced. The first: *ta'ama d'ed echad mishum d'milta d'avida l'igluye lo meshaker* — the reason we believe a single witness is that such matters have a way of coming to light. Because the truth about a husband's death will eventually emerge, the witness will not risk the disgrace of being exposed as a liar. This rationale operates independently of the woman; it is a feature of the social and epistemic environment. If this is the *ta'am*, it should apply equally to testimony enabling *yibum*: what is known will come to light, and the witness will not lie.

### Woman Loves Brother

The second theory: *ta'ama d'ed echad mishum d'hi daika u-minsva* — the reason we believe a single witness is that the woman herself will investigate the claim before proceeding to marry. Her personal stake in not unwittingly marrying a man whose first husband is alive motivates her to verify the testimony independently. If *this* is the *ta'am*, a question arises for the *yibum* scenario: *ve-hacha kivvan d'zimnin d'rachamah lei, lo daika u-minsva* — since she may have feelings for the *yavam*, her motivation to investigate might be compromised. She might not investigate as thoroughly as she ought to, precisely because she is eager to proceed with *yibum*.

### Mishnah Evidence

Rav Sheshet answers his own question: *tanitu'a* — we have already learned this. He points to the *mishnah*: *amru lah mes banayich ve'achar kach mes ba'alayich ve-nisyabma* — they told her your sons died and then your husband died, and she performed *yibum*; and then *amru lah chiluf ha-devarim* — they said it was the reverse — and the *mishnah* rules that she must leave the *yavam* and the children are *mamzerim*.

The *gemara* asks: what is the scenario? If the first testimony was two witnesses and the second testimony was also two witnesses, why would the second override the first? And furthermore, the ruling of *mamzer* would then be problematic — since there are conflicting testimonies, the child should at most be a *safek mamzer*. Yet the *mishnah* rules *mamzer* definitively and is precise about which children are *mamzerim* and which are not. Therefore, the *mishnah* must be describing a case where the first testimony that permitted *yibum* was given by a *single* witness, which was then contradicted by two witnesses. *Ve-ta'ama de-asu betrei akachshuha* — the reason the second report prevailed was only that two witnesses contradicted the single one. *Ha lav hachi ne'eman* — had there been no such contradiction, the testimony of the single witness would have been sufficient to permit *yibum*.

### Conclusion Ed Echad

The proof is thus established: a single witness is believed to permit *yibum*, even in circumstances where the woman might have an incentive to remarry her *yavam* and therefore might not investigate with full diligence. Whether this follows because *milta d'avida l'igluye* operates independently of the woman's investigation, or whether we simply do not treat the possibility of emotional attachment to the *yavam* as a sufficient reason to distrust her investigation — the practical conclusion is unambiguous. An *ed echad* is believed for *yibum* just as he is believed for ordinary remarriage.

The *gemara* will continue this discussion in the next *daf*, where it bears directly on the broader question — central to the entire *perek* — of why we credit a single witness at all in matters of marital status.

---

---

# Yevamot 94

## Eid Echad Foundation

### Single Witness Yibum

The daf opens in the midst of a question that has been developing across several folios: can the principles governing *eid echad* — the credibility extended to a single witness — be applied to the domain of *yibum*? The standard scenario for *eid echad* is familiar: a single witness testifies that a woman's husband has died, and on the basis of that testimony she is permitted to remarry. The question now is whether the same credibility operates when, instead of marrying a stranger, the woman is to perform *yibum* with her brother-in-law.

Why might this case differ? Because the stranger is someone toward whom she has no particular prior relationship or incentive to cut corners, whereas the brother-in-law is a man who has been part of the family. She knows him. Perhaps she is even more fond of him than of her husband. The concern, then, is whether that familiarity might lead her to do inadequate investigation — to accept thin evidence of her husband's death because the result would be a marriage she actually desires.

### Two Explanations

The Gemara frames the question by articulating two alternative explanations for why we believe an *eid echad* in the first place. The first is *milta d'avida l'igluyei* — the principle that matters of life and death naturally come to light. A man is either alive or dead; that fact will eventually be known. Because the truth will surface on its own, the single witness has no motive to lie, and that alone is sufficient to render his testimony credible. Under this reading, her own investigation is irrelevant, and whether she wants the outcome or not makes no difference to the reliability of the *eid*.

The second explanation is *dayka u'minsva* — that the woman herself investigates carefully before acting on the testimony. It is her own due diligence that bolsters the single witness's credibility, providing an independent check on his report. Under this reading, the reliability of the *eid echad* is not self-contained but is intertwined with the quality of her investigation. And if her investigation might be compromised by self-interest — whether through love of the brother-in-law or, as we will see, through hatred of him — then the credibility of the *eid echad* is correspondingly weakened.

### Tosafot's Concern

Tosafot raises a pointed difficulty. If the Rishonim had all along assumed that the credibility of *eid echad* rests on her investigation, how can the Gemara now present these two explanations as genuine alternatives? Tosafot resolves this by distinguishing between degrees of reliance on her investigation: one can say the earlier discussions assumed *some* role for her investigation without committing to its being the *primary* or *exclusive* basis. Tosafot therefore reads the Gemara as positing that her investigation contributes meaningfully but need not bear the full weight alone. This is an important resolution, though one must acknowledge that the Gemara's own framing presents the two explanations as a genuine opposition.

---

## Husband vs Brother

### Overwritten Testimony

The Gemara had previously sought proof that *eid echad* is believed even for purposes of *yibum* from a case in the Mishnah where testimony about the order of deaths was subsequently reversed. The Mishnah discusses a scenario in which a woman is told that her husband died first and her son died afterward — an order in which she is *not* obligated in *yibum*, since her son was alive when her husband died and thus there is no surviving brother-in-law without offspring. She then remarries. Subsequently she is told *chiluf hayu ha-devarim* — the facts were reversed — that the son died first and then the husband, meaning she *was* obligated in *yibum*. The Mishnah rules that she must leave her new husband and that her children are *mamzerim*.

The question the Gemara raises is: why does the second report overturn the first? If both consisted of two witnesses each, there is no obvious reason to prefer the second over the first. The Gemara therefore infers that the first report must have been a single witness and the second consisted of two, and the two outweighed the one. This would demonstrate that in principle an *eid echad* can be credited with testifying about the order of deaths — effectively permitting her to escape the obligation of *yibum*.

### Critical Question

Now a further question is posed: the student body asks Rav Sheshet that the real question is not whether we believe an *eid echad* that the *husband* is dead and permits *yibum* — even the woman herself is believed to say her husband died, as a Mishnah teaches: *ha'isha she'amra met ba'ali tinasei*, a woman who says her husband died may remarry; and *met ba'ali tisyabem*, she may perform *yibum* on the strength of her own word. If she is believed in all this, certainly an *eid echad* is believed.

The real question is *lemishra yevama le'alma* — whether one can believe an *eid echad* in order to permit the *yevama* to marry someone outside the family altogether, thereby releasing her entirely from the *yibum* obligation.

### Woman's Testimony

There are two obvious scenarios in which this question arises. One: the husband is already known to be dead, there is a *yavam* waiting, and a single witness reports that the *yavam* has died in a foreign country — may she now remarry freely? The second scenario emerges from the Mishnah itself: the testimony about the order of deaths, which, if believed, releases her from *yibum* entirely.

The woman's own testimony provides the baseline. She is believed to say *met ba'ali* — her husband died — and on that basis she may remarry or perform *yibum*. But she is *not* believed to say *met yivami she'inasei* — my *yavam* has died so that I may marry another man. Nor is she believed to say *meta achoti* — my sister died so that I may marry her husband. These cases differ from testimony about the husband's death, and the parallel question follows naturally: if she herself is not believed in these cases, does the same limitation apply to an *eid echad*?

---

## Incentive Problem

### Hatred vs Love

Tosafot provides a penetrating analysis of why the concern about improper investigation is more acute when the woman hates the *yavam* than when she loves him. The Gemara had already raised the possibility that if she loves the brother-in-law she might not investigate sufficiently because she wants to marry him. But that concern was the original question — and we had in some sense decided that her own credibility regarding the husband's death was not undermined even then. Why should hatred be worse?

Tosafot explains with a principle both psychologically astute and Talmudically grounded: *shegedola sinas hasone me'ahavas ha'ohev* — the hatred of an enemy is a more powerful force than the love of one who loves. Those motivated by strong negative feeling act with greater urgency and force than those motivated by positive attachment. The hater is more likely to neglect due diligence than the lover. Tosafot adds that it is even more common for a woman to hate her *yavam* than to love him, as is stated elsewhere in the tractate.

### Trapped Marriage

Tosafot presses further and articulates what is perhaps the more decisive point: the consequences are asymmetric. If she loves the *yavam* and yet fails to investigate properly, the worst outcome is that *yibum* takes place — she winds up married to a man she favored. But she might not have been particularly invested, because perhaps he will do *chalitzah* instead, or perhaps she would have been equally happy marrying any number of other men. The upside is modest. By contrast, if she hates the *yavam*, the worst-case scenario is catastrophic: she is trapped in a marriage to a man she despises. She has no legal recourse, and if *yibum* is performed she cannot unilaterally escape it. *Einah yecholah linatzel mimenu linasei le'acher* — she cannot escape him to marry another. Her only alternative is perpetual *iggun*, never receiving *chalitzah*, never being free to move on.

The asymmetry is stark. Not marrying the man you love still leaves you free. Being married to the man you hate leaves you with no options. That is the most powerful of all the negative forces we have catalogued, and it is precisely why the Gemara is more troubled by the case of hatred than by the case of love.

---

## Rav Sheshet

### Woman Cannot Testify

Rav Sheshet responds to the students' formulation of the question by saying *tenisuah* — we have already learned this in the Mishnah. He cites the Mishnah: *amru lah meis ba'alaich ve'achar kach meis binaiach* — they said to her that her husband died and afterward her son died. She remarried. Then they said *chiluf hayu ha-devarim* — the order was reversed. The Mishnah rules *teitzei* — she must leave — *ve'havlad rishon ve'acharon mamzer* — and the children from her first and last relationships are *mamzerim*. This is the view of Rabbi Akiva, who holds that even a violation of an *issur lav* can produce a *mamzer*.

The force of Rav Sheshet's point is the following: the Mishnah overturns the first report in favor of the second. But why? If both consisted of two witnesses, there is no obvious basis for preferring one over the other. Furthermore, if both had equal standing, the child's status should be *safeik mamzer* — a doubtful *mamzer* — not a definite one. But the Mishnah does not say *safeik mamzer*; a later clause of the same Mishnah carefully distinguishes which child is a *mamzer* and which is not, demonstrating that the Mishnah is being quite precise. A *safeik mamzer* would not be called simply *mamzer*. Therefore, the Mishnah must be working with the assumption that the second report definitively outweighs the first — which can only be because the first was an *eid echad* and the second was two witnesses.

### Two vs One Witness

The Gemara rebuts Rav Sheshet. It says *le'olam trei ve-trei* — perhaps the Mishnah is discussing two witnesses against two witnesses throughout, and that does not preclude it being a valid proof of anything about *eid echad*.

### Eidei Hazama

The Gemara continues: according to Rav Acha bar Minyumi, the reason we credit the second set of witnesses over the first is that the second set are not merely offering contrary factual testimony, but are *eidei hazama* — witnesses who testify that the first witnesses were not present at the events they claimed to have witnessed, which is the formal Talmudic mechanism for invalidating testimony entirely. On this reading, the second witnesses first disqualified the first witnesses as *eidei hazama* and then provided their own account of the reversed order.

The Mishnah, however, does not say anything about *eidei hazama*; it says *chiluf hayu ha-devarim* — the facts were reversed. The Gemara is reading the *eidei hazama* dynamic into the Mishnah. This reading is possible, and if it is adopted, then the Mishnah cannot serve as proof that we believe a single witness at all: the Mishnah might be describing a scenario where two witnesses trumped two others for the specific reason of *eidei hazama*, not because one of the original reports was an *eid echad*. The hoped-for proof therefore collapses.

---

## Agunah Principle

### Trapped Status

The Gemara now draws on a broader principle to frame when *eid echad* is believed at all: the rabbinic leniency of *eid echad* is specifically extended in cases where a person's status is trapped and in need of relief. The clearest such case is the *agunah* — a woman whose husband may or may not be alive and who cannot remarry until his death is established.

### Man Not Trapped

With this principle in view, the Gemara examines the parallel Mishnah's cases about what a man is not believed to testify. The Mishnah states: a man is not believed to say that his brother died so that he may perform *yibum* with his brother's wife, nor is he believed to say that his wife died so that he may marry her sister. The Gemara asks: should we infer from this that while the man is not believed, an *eid echad* would be believed?

The answer is no — because the principle of *mishum igguna akeilu bah rabbanan* applies only where someone is genuinely trapped. A man is never truly trapped in the way a woman is. Even before Rabbeinu Gershom's enactment, a man could marry additional wives; he is never locked into an inescapable marital limbo. The worst a man faces is that there is a particular woman he cannot marry — but he is free. A woman, by contrast, may be completely unable to remarry and has no recourse. Therefore, the entire framework of leniency for *eid echad* is targeted at her situation, not his. One cannot infer from a Mishnah dealing with both a man and a woman anything definitive about whether an *eid echad* would be believed in cases where no one is truly trapped. The Mishnah's purpose is simply to state that she — and he — are not believed; it carries no implication about a third-party *eid echad*.

The Gemara adds that the reason the Mishnah even needed to state this about her — given that according to Rabbi Akiva, if she were lying the child would be a *mamzer* and she herself would face all the severe consequences catalogued in earlier Mishnayos — is precisely that we might have thought: *chaysa al kilkula d'zar'ah u'dayka* — she would be scrupulously careful because she would never risk producing a *mamzer*. She would not even risk not doing due diligence. Therefore, the Mishnah teaches us that even so, we do not believe her, because the force of hatred toward the *yavam* is powerful enough to override even the fear of producing a *mamzer*-status child. That is how deeply the Gemara takes that psychological dynamic.

### Kal Vachomer

Rava cuts through the accumulated complexity with a *kal vachomer*. If we believe an *eid echad* to permit an *issur karet* — the grave transgression of a married woman remarrying, or performing *yibum* with a *yavam* — how can we fail to believe an *eid echad* for the comparatively lighter *issur lav* of a *yevama* marrying someone outside the family before receiving *chalitzah*? Surely if we extend credibility for the heavier matter, the lighter follows automatically.

---

## Woman's Credibility

### Objection to Rava

One of the rabbis responds to Rava's *kal vachomer* with a pointed counter-argument: look at the woman herself as a proof. She herself is believed regarding the *issur karet* — the testimony that her husband died, which permits her to remarry or perform *yibum*, both of which involve *issur karet*. Yet she is *not* believed to say that the *yavam* died, even though that involves only an *issur lav*. So it is demonstrably not the case that lighter stringency automatically follows from heavier — we see a case where she is believed for the heavier but not the lighter.

### No Due Diligence

Why is she not believed about the *yavam*'s death? *De-kivan de-zimnin de-sanya lei, lo daika u'minsva* — because there are cases in which she hates the *yavam* and will not perform due diligence. She may not consciously lie, but she will accept insufficient evidence, she will not push hard enough to confirm that he is truly dead, because she desperately wants to escape the prospect of marrying him. That motivational failure renders her testimony unreliable — not because she is dishonest but because she may be self-deceived or insufficiently rigorous.

### Witness Bolstered

The implication for *eid echad* then follows directly. If the credibility of a single witness rests in part on *dayka u'minsva* — on her investigation bolstering his testimony — then in a case where we cannot trust her investigation, the *eid echad* loses that bolstering as well. We cannot believe the *eid echad* about the *yavam*'s death for the same reason we cannot believe her: because her investigation, which props up his testimony, may have been compromised by the powerful force of hatred.

The Gemara does not formally resolve whether we do or do not believe the *eid echad* in this case. The argument hangs on how deeply the credibility of the *eid* depends on her own reliability. What the *Shulchan Aruch* (*Even Ha-Ezer* 158, section 3) does rule is: *neeman eid echad lehahid leyevama shemet baalah umityabemet al piv, o shemet yevamah shetinasei lashuk* — a single witness is believed to testify that the *yevama*'s husband died and she performs *yibum* on his word, or that the *yavam* died and she may marry another man. So the practical ruling follows Rava leniently — we do believe the *eid echad* even for releasing her from *yibum*. But the Gemara leaves the theoretical underpinning unresolved, and it touches on the core question that has run through this entire chapter: is the *eid echad* believed because of his own inherent reliability, or because of the investigation she performs?

---

## Mishna Cases

### Husband Reappears

The Gemara now transitions to the Mishnah. The final case of the preceding Mishnah involved a woman who, based on testimony that her husband had died, performed *kiddushin* — betrothal — with another man, and then the husband reappeared alive. Since she had only done *kiddushin* and not yet *nisuin* — had not yet begun living with the second man — she simply returns to her husband. There is no harm and no foul. Furthermore, if the second man nonetheless gives her a *get*, that *get* does not render her a *grushah* — a divorcee — for purposes of marrying a *Kohen*, because he was never truly her husband.

### Grushah Drasha

The Mishnah attributes a *drasha* on this point to Rabbi Elazar ben Mattia, who derived it from the verse *ve-ishah grushah me-ishah* — a woman divorced from *her husband*. Since this man never achieved the status of her husband, the *get* he gives her carries no force and does not make her a *grushah*.

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav observes that Rabbi Elazar could have derived a much more illuminating ruling — a pearl — from that verse, and instead used it for something relatively obvious — a piece of pottery. The pearl would have been: *afilu lo nitgarsha ela me-ishah* — even if she was divorced only from her husband, meaning even a *get* that says "you are divorced from me but remain forbidden to everyone else," which is not a valid *get* that permits remarriage — even such a document renders her *pesulah le-kehuna*, invalid for marriage to a *Kohen*. This is the concept of *reiach ha-get ha-posel bi-kehuna* — the "scent" of a *get* that disqualifies for *kehuna* even without fully releasing from the marriage. That is a genuine *chiddush*. By contrast, using the verse to teach that a *get* from someone who was never truly a husband has no effect is, to put it plainly, not much of a teaching.

### Sister Marriage

The next Mishnah introduces a new scenario. A man's wife goes to a distant country. Others come and tell him she has died. He then marries her sister. Subsequently his wife returns, alive. The Mishnah rules that the wife is *muteret lachazor lo* — permitted to return to him. The marriage to the sister is treated as entirely without consequence: the sister walks away without needing a *get* from him, he is *mutar bi-krovot shniyah* — permitted to the sister's relatives — and *ha-shniyah muteret bi-krovav* — the sister is permitted to his relatives. It is as though the marriage to the sister never existed.

Why is this so different from the parallel case where the woman remarries based on false testimony about her husband's death? The answer lies in how the situation appears to onlookers. When a woman marries a second man while her husband may still be alive, people might reasonably think: perhaps the husband gave her a *get*; perhaps the marriage was dissolved legitimately. The second marriage therefore appears plausible and carries real legal weight — it must be undone with a *get* and produces all the negative consequences. But when a man marries his wife's sister and it turns out his wife is alive, everyone understands immediately that even if he had divorced his wife, he could not have been validly married to the sister while his wife was alive. There is no scenario, however one arranges the facts, in which this marriage could have been legitimate. Therefore it is not treated as a marriage at all, requires no *get*, and carries no consequences.

The Gemara adds that this holds *even* if he is *mutar* to remain with the wife — it is the woman whose legal status is affected by certain forbidden sexual relations, not the man. His sleeping with the sister does not alter his wife's status, because she was not a party to what occurred.

### Wife Actually Dies

A further case: suppose the man was told his wife had died, married the sister, and then — after this had already occurred — the wife actually does die. He is now *mutar bi-shniyah* — permitted to remain with the sister. Whatever occurred in the interim, the eventual death of the first wife removes all barriers. Furthermore, the Mishnah specifies: if it subsequently becomes clear that the wife was in fact still alive when he married the sister, *havlad rishon mamzer* — the child born during the period the first wife was alive is a *mamzer* — *ve'ha'acharon eino mamzer* — but the child born after the first wife genuinely died is not.

### Rabbi Yosi

Rabbi Yosi states a general principle: *kol she'posel al yedei acherim posel al yedei atzmo* — whoever disqualifies through others disqualifies through himself; *ve'chol she'ein posel al yedei acherim eino posel al yedei atzmo* — and whoever does not disqualify through others does not disqualify through himself. This statement, as the Gemara will clarify, requires considerable unpacking.

---

## Wife and Brother

### Both Dead Reports

The Gemara extends the discussion to an additional scenario. Suppose both the wife and the brother-in-law go to a distant country and witnesses report that both of them have died. To use the names introduced in the shiur: Reuven is married to Rachel, and Baruch is married to Leah. Rachel and Baruch go overseas. Reports come back that both have died. Now Reuven, believing Rachel is dead, is free to marry Leah — his wife's sister is no longer forbidden now that the wife has died, and Leah, believing Baruch is dead, is free to marry Reuven. They marry.

Then both Rachel and Baruch return alive. What are the consequences?

### Irony Unveiled

From Leah's perspective, she received testimony that her husband Baruch was dead, remarried Reuven, and it turned out the testimony was false. All the devastating consequences of the earlier Mishnah fall upon her: she must leave both men — *tetzei mizeh umizeh* — she receives *gettin* from both, she is forbidden to both, her children's statuses are affected. She bears the full weight.

But what of Rachel? One might think: if we say it *looked like* Reuven was married to Leah — seriously enough that Leah suffers all these consequences — then perhaps it *also* looks like Reuven was married to another woman, which should affect Rachel's ability to return to him. Yet the Gemara rules: *afilu hachi, eshet giso asira agiso, ishto sharya* — even so, the brother-in-law's wife is forbidden to the brother-in-law, but his own wife remains permitted to him. The two consequences do not run in parallel. *Ve'lo amrinan Rachel u'mitoch shenesra eshet giso agiso te'aser ishto alav* — we do not say that because Leah is now forbidden to Baruch, therefore Rachel should be forbidden to Reuven.

The irony is considerable. The Gemara acknowledges it directly: the very fact that the marriage looked real enough to heap consequences on Leah does not, by some form of symmetry, impose consequences on Rachel. The Gemara explains this partly on the grounds that it is the woman's status that is affected by forbidden relationships — Rachel was not involved — and partly on the grounds that with Rachel alive and known to have been alive the whole time, no observer could plausibly conclude that the marriage to Leah was ever legitimate. There is no scenario that makes it work, so it is not treated as a marriage with respect to Rachel, even as it is treated as consequential enough with respect to Leah to impose all the negative ramifications upon her.

### Marriage Reality

The proof that the marriage was real enough in some sense is that Leah requires a *get* from both Reuven and from Baruch — she is bound to divorce proceedings with two husbands. Why does she need a *get* from Reuven? Because it looked like they were married. Yet this same "it looked like they were married" reasoning does not extend to forbid Rachel to Reuven. This asymmetry — which the Gemara accepts without fully resolving the apparent tension — reflects the broader principle that a man's forbidden relationship does not alter his wife's personal status, which is determined by her own actions, not his.

---

## Rabbi Akiva

### Wife Consequence

The Gemara now raises a challenge from Rabbi Akiva's position. If the Mishnah says Leah needs a *get* from Reuven — and it does — then according to Rabbi Akiva, shouldn't that trigger consequences for Rachel as well? Once Leah needs a *get*, she is legally treated, at least nominally, as Reuven's divorcee. And if she is his divorcee, then Rachel — her sister — becomes his divorcee's sister, which is a category of *arayot* that a *Kohen* may not marry, and which, if treated seriously, could make Rachel forbidden to Reuven entirely.

This presents a real problem for the Mishnah's ruling that Rachel remains permitted. If Rabbi Akiva is the author of the Mishnah — or if we are ruling according to Rabbi Akiva — how does the Mishnah conclude that Rachel is *muteret*?

### Baraita Proof

The Gemara brings a *baraita* to resolve this. The *baraita* states: *kol elu she-ba-Torah ein tzerichos mimennu get* — all the forbidden relationships enumerated in the Torah: if a man began living with his sister, his father's wife, or any of the *arayot*, no *get* is required to separate them, because the relationship is understood by all to be legally meaningless. The one exception is: *chutz me-eshet ish she-niset al pi beit din* — a married woman who remarried based on testimony accepted by a *beit din*. That case, as we have seen, looks enough like a legitimate marriage — because it is conceivable the husband had given her a *get* — that it requires a *get* to formally undo it.

### Akiva Adds Cases

Rabbi Akiva then adds two further cases where a *get* is required: *af eshet ach ve-achot isha* — even the brother's wife and the wife's sister. What makes these two different from blood-relation *arayot*, and why would Rabbi Akiva demand a *get* in these cases?

The answer lies in two features unique to these two relationships. First, they are not blood relatives — there is no automatic universal recognition that such a relationship is forbidden by nature. Second — and more importantly — both of these relationships have circumstances under which they become entirely permitted: the brother's wife becomes permitted through *yibum* if the brother died childless; the wife's sister becomes permitted after the wife dies. The existence of a legitimate pathway to this marriage means that observers might actually believe the marriage was permissible, and therefore it looks real enough to require a formal *get*.

All other *arayot* are forever forbidden without exception — there is no scenario in which marrying one's mother or one's sister becomes permitted. Therefore no observer will mistake such a union for a legitimate marriage. But with brother's wife and wife's sister, one can imagine a legitimate pathway, and therefore the illicit union takes on the appearance of a real marriage, requiring a *get* to dissolve.

---

## Limiting Akiva

### Only Kiddushin

The Gemara immediately qualifies Rabbi Akiva's position significantly. Rav Yehuda, citing Rav Chiya bar Yosef citing Rav, asks: what exactly is the case in which Rabbi Akiva says the brother's wife needs a *get*? The answer: *kegon she-kiddesh achiv et ha-isha* — it is specifically where the brother had done only *kiddushin* with the woman, without *nisuin* — and then went to a distant country, and the other man heard he had died and married the brother's wife.

### Tnai Logic

Why does the stage of the first marriage matter? Because *de-amri inshi* — people will say — *tenai hava lei be-kiddushin* — perhaps the brother's *kiddushin* was subject to a stipulation that was never fulfilled, meaning the *kiddushin* never actually took effect. And therefore, *shappir nasa* — the second man genuinely and legitimately married her. Once people believe the second marriage was valid, it looks real, and it requires a *get* to undo.

This logic applies precisely because *kiddushin* without *nisuin* is subject to the possibility of conditions: it is known and understood that betrothal can be contingent on stipulations that may fail to be met. Therefore, the mere fact of *kiddushin* does not definitively settle the matter in the eyes of the public.

### Sister Kiddushin

The same reasoning governs the case of the wife's sister. If the man had done only *kiddushin* with his first wife Rachel and not *nisuin*, and she went abroad and he heard she had died and he married Leah, people might say: *tenai hava lei be-kiddushin* — the *kiddushin* to Rachel was conditional and never took effect — *ve-shappir nasiv* — and therefore the marriage to Leah was perfectly valid. Because the marriage to Leah thus appears real, it requires a *get*, and once it requires a *get*, the sister of his apparent divorcee becomes forbidden to him.

### After Nisuin

But after *nisuin*, even Rabbi Akiva agrees that no *get* is required. The principle *ein tnai be-nisuin* — stipulations do not apply after *nisuin* has taken place — means that no one will entertain the possibility that the first marriage fell through. Once a couple has lived together as husband and wife, the marriage is treated as complete and unconditional. Therefore, no observer will think the second marriage was legitimate, it will not be treated as a real marriage, and no *get* is required.

The practical outcome is significant. If a man had *nisuin* with his first wife — as is the standard case — and she goes overseas and is reported dead and he marries her sister, and then the first wife returns, no *get* is needed to separate him from the sister. The marriage to the sister is simply dissolved, without formal proceedings, without lingering consequences for status. Rachel remains permitted to Reuven, and Leah walks away as though the marriage never was — because, in the eyes of anyone who knows that *nisuin* had taken place, it effectively never was.

---

---

# Yevamot 95

## Wife Dead Report

### Case Setup

The daf begins toward the bottom of 94b. The case under discussion is not the more familiar scenario of a woman whose husband is reported dead and who then remarries — that case occupied much of the preceding material — but rather its mirror image: a husband whose wife is reported dead, who then marries her sister, and whose wife subsequently returns alive. The Gemara had already addressed certain preliminary complications arising from this scenario, particularly whether the marriage to the sister creates ongoing obligations. Specifically, it considered whether, according to Rabbi Akiva, the sister would require a *get*, which would in turn render the original wife forbidden to him as the sister of his divorcée (*achos grushaso*). That possibility was ultimately rejected, and even according to Rabbi Akiva, it is assumed that the husband may return to his first wife.

### Rabbi Akiva Position

At this point, Rav Ashi poses a question to Rav Kahana, beginning with the word *Akiva* approximately twelve lines from the bottom of 94b: if the *mishnah* can even be in accordance with Rabbi Akiva — since the man is not required to give a *get* to the sister — then why does the *mishnah* present only the case of the sister as the scenario in which the report of the wife's death would be relevant to his marrying someone new?

For most forbidden relationships (*arayot*), the prohibition does not dissolve upon the death of the relevant party. The sister, however, is the paradigmatic exception: the prohibition of *achos isha* is tied explicitly to the wife's lifetime, as the verse states that it is forbidden to take a woman alongside her sister *in her lifetime* (*bechayeha*). That is presumably why the sister is the only such case addressed in the *mishnah* — she is the only *ervah* who could become permitted once the wife dies. But one might ask: what about the mother-in-law (*chamuto*)? The general assumption is that the prohibition of marrying a woman and her mother applies even after the wife has died. Yet according to Rabbi Akiva, perhaps it does not. If so, then the *mishnah* should also have presented the case where the wife is reported dead and the husband marries the mother-in-law.

### Woman & Mother

To understand why this is relevant, the Gemara cites a *baraisa* on the verse *ki yikach ish es isha ve'imah* — "if a man takes a woman and her mother, you shall burn him and them (*oso ves-hen*)." The question arises: what did the wife do that she too should be executed? The debate between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva turns on the reading of *ves-hen*. Rabbi Yishmael reads it as referring to only one of them — the mother — *oso ves achas meihen*. Rabbi Akiva reads it as both — *oso ves shteihen* — meaning both the mother and the grandmother, or some other combination involving multiple generations, not the original wife.

### Abaye vs. Rava

Abaye and Rava disagree about how to interpret this tannaitic dispute. According to Abaye, Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva are not debating any practical *halakha* at all; they are debating only how to read the verse (*mashma'us dorshin ika beina'ihu*). Rabbi Yishmael understands the verse as describing one configuration of the prohibited relationship; Rabbi Akiva understands it as describing two distinct configurations. No one debates the underlying *din*. This reading, as Abaye acknowledges, is fine (*bishlama le-Abaye*).

According to Rava, however, there is a genuine halakhic dispute — namely, whether the prohibition of the mother-in-law persists after the wife's death (*chamosto le'achar misah ika beina'ihu*). On Rava's reading, Rabbi Akiva's phrase *oso ves shteihen* is interpreted to mean that the death penalty applies only when both women — the wife and the mother — are still alive. If the wife had already died, the man who then marries the mother would not be executed.

This reading creates the logical opening for Rav Ashi's question: if the *mishnah* can accord with Rabbi Akiva, and if Rabbi Akiva holds that the mother-in-law prohibition dissolves after the wife's death, then the *mishnah* should include the case of the mother-in-law as a second scenario in which hearing of the wife's death opens up a new permitted marriage. The Gemara's response, formulated by Abaye, is that even if Rabbi Akiva exempts from the *sreifah* (burning), one cannot conclude that he removes the prohibition entirely. As Tosafos makes explicit: the phrase *me'issura mi mietei rachmana* — "did the Torah exempt it from prohibition?" — refers not to some minor rabbinic *issur* but to the full weight of a negative commandment and *kares*. The man simply would not be executed; the *issur* remains. Therefore, it would not be relevant to include this scenario in the *mishnah*.

---

## Sleeping Sister

### Hava Amina

Returning to the case at hand — Reuven is married to Rachel, she travels to *medinat hayam*, word arrives that she has died, and Reuven marries her sister Leah — the Gemara now raises the following question: granted that we do not treat this as a genuine marriage, and Leah requires no *get*, should we not at least say that the very act of Reuven sleeping with Leah ought to render Rachel forbidden to him?

The intuition behind this suggestion is a kind of symmetry with the laws of adultery: if a woman sleeps with another man, that act renders her forbidden to her husband, even if she acted entirely unknowingly (*shogeg*). The Rabbis extended the biblical prohibition to cases of *shogeg* as a rabbinic decree (*gazru bah rabanan*). Should the same not apply here in reverse?

### No Prohibition

The Gemara rejects the comparison — *lo damya*. When a wife commits adultery, even inadvertently, the Rabbis decreed she becomes forbidden because the underlying biblical prohibition is severe: intentional adultery (*bemezid*) renders her forbidden *mid'Oraisa*. The rabbinic extension to *shogeg* is therefore grounded in a pre-existing biblical framework. But in the case of *achos isha*: sleeping with the wife's sister, even intentionally (*bemezid*), does not render the wife *Rachel* forbidden to Reuven under any biblical provision. There is no *issur d'Oraisa* establishing that intercourse with the sister causes the wife to become forbidden. Consequently, there is no basis for a rabbinic decree extending such a consequence to cases of *shogeg* either. (*Bishogeg lo gazru bah rabanan.*)

### Otah Drasha

The Gemara then cites a *baraisa* that grounds this principle in a textual source. From the verse in the *parsha* of *sotah* — *ve'shachav ish osah shichvas zera* — the Rabbis derive: *otah* — specifically *her* act of sleeping with another man renders her forbidden (*shichvasah osartah*), but the act of her sister sleeping with her husband does not render her forbidden (*ve'ein shichvas achosah osartah*).

But why did the Torah need to state this? Surely this is self-evident. The *baraisa* therefore presents the logical argument that might have led us astray — the *hava amina* requiring refutation.

### Kal Vachomer

The *hava amina* is a *kal vachomer*. In a case where a man has intercourse with a woman who is an *issur kal* — adultery is here called a "light prohibition" — the one who defines her status (*ha'oser*) becomes forbidden. Specifically: Reuven sleeps with Dvora while she is married to Barak. Reuven has committed adultery, the *issur kal*. The consequence: Barak — who is the *oser*, the one whose existence creates her forbidden status as a married woman — now finds his wife forbidden to him. That is the effect of *ba al issur kal ne'esar ha'oser*. By *kal vachomer*: if Reuven were instead to sleep with Leah, his own wife's sister, which is called *issur chamur*, then Rachel — the one who defines Leah's forbidden status as her sister — should certainly become forbidden as well.

The reasoning here is admittedly strained. The *baraisa* itself acknowledges that we need a verse to correct the *kal vachomer*, and the verse (*otah*) does so: only *her* act — the wife's own act of infidelity — can render her forbidden. Not the act of her sister.

---

## Beit Shammai Debate

### Rav Yehuda Opinion

Rav Yehuda now introduces a statement clarifying what Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel actually debate. According to Rav Yehuda, Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not disagree about the case where a man has intercourse with his wife's mother: in that case, all agree that the wife becomes forbidden (*posel*) as a result. The source for this position is the very verse we handled earlier — *ves-hen* — which, even if not interpreted to mandate execution of the wife, establishes that the wife's status is affected when a man sleeps with her mother. The debate of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, according to Rav Yehuda, concerns only the case of *boel achos ishto* — intercourse with the wife's sister. There, Beit Shammai says that the wife does become forbidden (*posel*), while Beit Hillel says she does not (*lo posel*).

### Rabbi Yosi Challenge

Rabbi Yosi disagrees with this framing entirely. He states that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not debate the case of the wife's sister at all — everyone agrees that sleeping with the sister does not render the wife forbidden. This follows directly from the *drasha* on *otah*: *otah* — *her* sleeping with another man makes her forbidden; the sleeping of her sister does not.

### Mother Debate

What then is the debate of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel? According to Rabbi Yosi, the debate is only in the case of *boel chamoso* — intercourse with the mother-in-law. Beit Shammai holds that this does render the wife forbidden (*posel*); Beit Hillel holds that it does not (*lo posel*). The ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel is stated explicitly: *ein halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda* — we do not rule like Rabbi Yehuda's position, which extended the prohibition to the mother-in-law even according to Beit Hillel. The law follows Beit Hillel, and thus sleeping with the mother-in-law does not render the wife forbidden. This ruling is illustrated with a practical case: a man who committed the transgression of sleeping with his mother-in-law was brought before Rav Yehuda and given lashes, but Rav Yehuda explicitly told him: had Shmuel not ruled otherwise, I would have declared you permanently forbidden to your wife — but since Shmuel ruled *ein halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda*, you may return to your wife.

---

## Beit Shammai Debate (II)

### Asymmetry Logic

The *baraisa* cited in this context articulates the logical basis for the *hava amina* that had suggested the wife's sister ought to render the wife forbidden. The argument proceeds by observing a fundamental asymmetry between the husband's and wife's respective prohibitions upon marriage.

Before marriage, he was permitted to any woman in the world and she was permitted to any man in the world (*hu mutar bechol hanashim shebaolam vehi muteret bechol ha-anashim shebaolam*). Upon marriage, he makes her forbidden to all other men, and she makes him forbidden only to her relatives. The asymmetry is therefore striking: his prohibition upon her is total — every other man in the world is now off-limits — while her prohibition upon him is narrow — only her immediate relatives (her mother, her sister, etc.) are now forbidden.

---

## Sleeping Sister (II)

### Wife vs. Husband

This asymmetry generates a *kal vachomer*. If we consider the wife's situation: he makes her forbidden to the entire world, and yet if she unintentionally (*shogeg*) sleeps with one of those men, that does not render her additionally forbidden to the one man she is permitted to, namely her husband — since as established, *shogeg* adultery renders her forbidden only by rabbinic decree in view of the underlying biblical prohibition. How much more so should the husband, whose prohibition created by her is far narrower, limited only to her relatives, not find that his act of *shogeg* intercourse with one of those relatives renders his wife forbidden to him?

The *kal vachomer*, properly formulated: the wife, whose prohibition is vastly more extensive and whose status is far more globally redefined by marriage, does not lose her permitted status vis-à-vis her husband when she unintentionally transgresses one of the men she is forbidden to. Certainly then the husband, whose prohibitions are far more limited — only her relatives — should not find that his unintentional intercourse with one of those relatives renders his wife forbidden.

This disposes of the *shogeg* case. But what of *bemezid*? After all, intentional adultery does render the wife forbidden to her husband. Perhaps intentional intercourse with the sister should similarly render the wife forbidden. The *baraisa* then addresses this: *v'zo adim l'shogeg* — the above reasoning is effective for *shogeg*, but *lamezid minayin*? How do we know that even intentional intercourse with the sister does not render the wife forbidden? The answer: *talmud lomar otah* — the verse says *otah*. Her own sexual act renders her forbidden; the sexual act of her sister does not, under any circumstances, render her forbidden.

---

## Issur Kal

### Rav Chisda Case

The Gemara now returns to examine the *kal vachomer* that drove the *hava amina* — the argument that sleeping with the wife's sister (*issur chamur*) should render the wife forbidden, since sleeping with a married woman (*issur kal*) renders her husband forbidden to her. The phrase *issur kal* in this context requires clarification. What precisely counts as an *issur kal*?

Rav Chisda proposes: *machzir grushato misheniset* — the case of a man who remarries his divorced wife after she had married another man. The structure of the case runs as follows. Reuven marries Rachel; he divorces her; she marries Barak. Now Barak divorces Rachel and Reuven remarries her. Reuven has committed the prohibition of *machzir grushato misheniset*. But what has happened to Barak's status vis-à-vis Rachel? Because Rachel remarried Reuven, she is now forbidden to Barak — he cannot take her back. So: Barak's prior marriage to Rachel is what made her forbidden to Reuven in stage two, making Barak the *oser*; and then Reuven's act of remarriage — the *issur kal* — renders the *oser* (Barak) forbidden to the woman. *Ba la-hai asra a-hai, ba la-idach asrah l'hai.* This, says Rav Chisda, is the paradigm of *bemakom she'ba issur kal ne'esar ha'oser*.

The Gemara rejects this as a basis for comparison, on two grounds. First: *nitma'ah haguf* — in that case the woman's own body was directly involved in the act that changed her status; she herself married Reuven. Second: *ve'issur olam* — the prohibition that results is permanent; she will always be forbidden to Barak. By contrast, the prohibition of *achos isha* dissolves if the wife dies. Therefore this is not a genuine *issur kal* — in the relevant respects, it is in fact more severe than the sister prohibition.

### Yevama Case

Reish Lakish proposes the case of a *yevama* — a woman awaiting *yibum*. The *issur kal* would be intercourse with another man, violating the prohibition of *lo tihyeh eishes hameis hachutza l'ish zar*, a simple *lav*. Per the ruling of Rav Hamnuna, a *shomeres yavam* who commits *zenus* becomes forbidden to the brother-in-law (*yavam*), who is the one who made her status as a *yevama* defined. This appears to be a cleaner parallel: a simple *lav* is violated, and the result is that the *oser* — the *yavam* who defined her status — becomes forbidden to her.

The Gemara again objects: *nitma'ah haguf* — it was her own person, her own act, that generated the consequence. And additionally, *issura berov* — the prohibition she now carries extends broadly: she is forbidden to the entire world, not just to one person, as would be the case for the wife whose husband sleeps with her sister. The parallel therefore fails on the same grounds.

The Gemara then considers whether the *yevama* case can be reformulated as one involving the *brothers* rather than a stranger — specifically, a case where one brother performed *ma'amar* with the *yevama* and a second brother then violated that by engaging in *yibum*, thereby rendering her forbidden to the first brother. The Gemara notes that it is not the sexual act per se that generates the prohibition; even a *get* or *chalitza* by the second brother would produce the same effect, making the act of intercourse irrelevant as the operative cause. This proposed parallel thus fails as well.

### Sotah Case

Rabbi Yochanan proposes *sotah* as the *issur kal*. The idea requires clarification, because the *sotah* case has two possible readings. One reading: the husband has intercourse with the *sotah*, and this makes her forbidden to the adulterer — *ba al ha-baal asar lah le-boel*. But the Gemara objects: the wife becomes forbidden to the adulterer from the moment she commits adultery, regardless of whether the husband subsequently has intercourse with her; even a *get* from the husband would seal her prohibition from the adulterer. The husband's intercourse is therefore not the operative cause.

The alternative reading, therefore, must be: the *sotah* as a paradigm for the prohibition of a married woman (*eshet ish*) sleeping with any man other than her husband — the fundamental prohibition of adultery itself. That act renders her forbidden to her husband. This would be the *issur kal*.

### Rava Conclusion

But can adultery really be called an *issur kal*? The Gemara itself raises the objection: *issur chamur hu, dehainu eshet ish* — it is a grave prohibition, carrying the death penalty. Rava's response, and simultaneously that of Ravin citing Rabbi Yochanan, is to simply own the comparison directly: yes, the *issur kal* we are discussing is *eshet ish* — adultery. Why does it merit the label *issur kal*? Because the prohibition is not permanent. A married woman could in principle become permitted to any given man — including the adulterer — if she were to receive a *get*. By contrast, the wife's sister is forbidden so long as the wife is alive, with no mechanism for permissibility. *She-eina ossra kol yamav* — she does not always remain forbidden to him. That is the tenuous distinction that allows us to call adultery *issur kal* relative to the prohibition of *achos isha*.

The *baraisa* cited by Abba Chanan in the name of Abba Elazar confirms this reading. *U-mah bimkom ha-baal issur kal she-eina ossra kol yamav ne'esar ha-oseh* — when a man comes upon a married woman (*issur kal*, since she could become permitted via divorce), the act makes her forbidden to the one who defined her status. *Ha-ba al issur chamur she-ossra kol yamav* — one who sleeps with the wife's sister, the more severe prohibition, applicable for the wife's entire lifetime — should render the one who defined her status (*ha-oseh*) forbidden as well, by a *kal vachomer*. The answer: *talmud lomar otah* — only her own act of forbidden intercourse renders her forbidden. *Otah shchivasah poseltah, ve-ein shchivat achotah poseltah.*

Tosafos notes a residual difficulty. Even granting that adultery is called *issur kal*, the earlier objection remains: in the adultery case, the woman's own body was the locus of the violation (*nitma'ah haguf*). That objection still applies and was never fully answered. Tosafos remarks with understated reserve — *aval kzat kashya* — that it remains somewhat difficult. The honest assessment is that the *hava amina* that sleeping with the sister should render the wife forbidden is not a particularly strong one; the *otah* verse is still needed, but the logical underpinnings of the argument being refuted are acknowledged to be strained.

---

## Rabbi Yosi Principle

### Tanna Kamma

The *mishnah* contains the following enigmatic ruling attributed to Rabbi Yosi: *kol sheposel al yedei acherim posel al yedei atzmo* — whoever invalidates others also invalidates himself; *v'chol she'eino posel al yedei acherim eino posel al yedei atzmo* — and whoever does not invalidate others does not invalidate himself. The Gemara asks: *mai ka'amar Rabbi Yosi* — what exactly is Rabbi Yosi saying?

The Gemara first considers whether Rabbi Yosi is responding to the case described by the *Tanna Kamma*, which the Gemara (following Tosafos) reads as the background scenario for this debate. That case is: both Reuven's wife Rachel and his brother-in-law Barak travel to a distant country (*medinat hayam*). Word arrives that both died. Reuven, hearing that Rachel is dead and Barak is dead, marries Leah (Barak's wife). It then turns out that both Rachel and Barak are alive.

### Lack of Parallel

What is Leah's status? She believed her husband Barak was dead, remarried Reuven, and now it turns out Barak is alive. She suffers all the negative consequences: *asura mizeh umizeh*, forbidden to both men and required to leave. What is Rachel's status? Rachel's husband Reuven married her sister Leah — as we have established, this does not constitute a genuine marriage, Leah requires no *get*, and Reuven may return to Rachel.

The striking asymmetry: Leah, the one who triggered the question about whether she was "really" married to Reuven, bears all the consequences of that quasi-marriage. Yet Reuven, who was on the other side of that same quasi-marriage, bears none of them and may freely return to Rachel. The *Tanna Kamma* accepts this asymmetry. Rabbi Yosi apparently does not.

### Consistency Principle

The Gemara explores how Rabbi Yosi would formulate his consistency principle. One possibility is that he argues *le-kula*: since Reuven is permitted to return to Rachel, showing that his marriage to Leah was not genuine, then by the same logic Leah should be permitted to return to Barak. If this is Rabbi Yosi's intent, then the formulation *kol she'eino posel al yedei acherim eino posel al yedei atzmo* — if you don't invalidate others, you don't invalidate yourself — fits this reading, starting with the *kula* and deriving leniency in both directions.

The alternative reading is that Rabbi Yosi argues *le-chumra*: just as Leah is forbidden to Barak, so Rachel should be forbidden to Reuven. This fits the other half of the formulation: *kol sheposel al yedei acherim posel al yedei atzmo* — whoever invalidates others also invalidates himself.

To properly situate Rabbi Yosi's position, the Gemara introduces the distinction between cases involving *eid echad* (one witness) and *shenei eidim* (two witnesses). The rule established earlier in the tractate is that all the negative consequences of a mistaken remarriage — the requirement to leave both men, the loss of the *ketubah*, etc. — apply only when the remarriage was based on a single witness (*al pi eid echad*), because only then does the Rabbinic leniency (*mishum iguna hikilu bah rabanan*) apply and the woman is expected to act on insufficient testimony. When two witnesses testified to the husband's death, the remarriage was fully permissible, and if the husband returns alive, she may return to him with no negative consequences.

Armed with this distinction, the *Tanna Kamma*'s position becomes: it does not matter whether the remarriage was based on one witness (such that Leah cannot return to Barak) or two witnesses (such that she can). Either way, Reuven may return to Rachel. Rabbi Yosi's response, as now understood, is: you cannot split the ruling this way. When it was *al pi beis din* (i.e., a single witness — *eid echad* — which is what relying on *beis din*'s authorization means in this context), and Leah is therefore forbidden to Barak, Rachel is also forbidden to Reuven — *poseil al yedei acherim, posel al yedei atzmo*. When it was *al pi shenei eidim*, such that Leah is not forbidden to Barak, Rachel is also not forbidden to Reuven — *eino posel al yedei acherim, eino posel al yedei atzmo*. You must be consistent.

A related question arises from this discussion: what standard of testimony does Reuven himself need in order to remarry in the first place — to marry Leah — upon hearing that Rachel has died? May he rely on a single witness? Tosafos on 94b (*af al gav*) addresses this directly, concluding that for Reuven to marry the sister specifically, two witnesses are required. The rationale for the general leniency of *eid echad* is *mishum iguna* — to spare a woman the suffering of remaining an *agunah*. A man does not face that predicament; he can always marry another woman. Therefore the same leniency does not apply, and he would need two witnesses to the wife's death before marrying her sister.

### Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha

Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha offers an alternative framing of the scenario. Rather than the one-witness versus two-witness distinction, he focuses on whether Rachel was fully married to Reuven (*nisuin*) or only betrothed (*eirusin*/*arusin*) at the time she traveled away with Barak.

This distinction matters for the following reason. The reason Reuven is generally permitted to return to Rachel — and the reason Leah is not viewed as his genuine wife — is that everyone understands that Leah's sister was alive and that Reuven was married to her. With *nisuin*, no one entertains the possibility that the marriage to Rachel somehow never materialized. With *eirusin* only, however, people might speculate that perhaps a condition (*tenai*) in the betrothal was never fulfilled, or that the *nisuin* simply never occurred, and therefore Reuven's marriage to Leah might be seen as more plausible. That perception matters enormously for how the community understands whether this was a genuine marriage or a complete mistake.

### Rav Yosef Reading

Rav Yosef's reading of Rabbi Yosi takes this even further, introducing a scenario where Rabbi Yosi is actually *lenient* — going even further than the *Tanna Kamma* in one respect. The *Tanna Kamma* says that in the case of *ishto ve-giso* (Rachel and Barak both went away), *eshet giso asura ve-ishto sharya* — Leah is forbidden to Barak and Rachel is permitted to Reuven. Rav Yosef's reading of Rabbi Yosi is: when Rachel was fully married to Reuven (*nisuin*), everyone in hindsight knows that it was simply impossible for him to have been genuinely married to Leah. Since everyone will understand this retroactively, the marriage to Leah will not even carry the appearance of a marriage — it will be seen universally as a mistake, indeed as *shogeg* if at all, but certainly not a genuine *kinyan*. In that case, not only can Reuven return to Rachel — Leah can return to Barak as well. There is no semblance of a real marriage to Reuven, and therefore Leah's status is not compromised. Rabbi Yosi, in the case of *nisuin*, is *meikel* in both directions.

In the case of *eirusin*, however — where Rachel was only betrothed to Reuven — people might genuinely wonder whether the first marriage ever fully took effect. In that case, the marriage to Leah does carry some semblance of a real marriage. Leah is forbidden to Barak (*posel al yedei acherim*), and therefore Rachel is also forbidden to Reuven (*posel al yedei atzmo*). Rabbi Yosi is *machmir* in both directions.

The elegance of Rav Yosef's reading is that Rabbi Yosi is entirely consistent: never splitting the ruling, going *le-kula* in both directions when *nisuin* makes the mistake transparent, and *le-chumra* in both directions when *eirusin* creates ambiguity.

### Final Ruling

Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules: *halacha k'Rabbi Yosi* — the *halakha* follows Rabbi Yosi, with his principle of consistency between the treatment of the two couples. The daf concludes here with Rav Yosef raising a challenge to this ruling — *metiv Rav Yosef, u-mi amar Shmuel hachi* — which will be taken up in the next session.

---

---

# Yevamot 96

## Rabbi Yossi & Shmuel

### Mishnah: Rabbi Yossi

The daf picks up at the bottom of 95b. The *mishnah* there contains a somewhat cryptic statement attributed to Rabbi Yossi, to the effect that whoever causes a prohibition to fall upon others causes the same prohibition to fall upon himself, and conversely, if no prohibition falls upon others, none falls upon him either. The *gemara* has been explaining this in terms of a case of consistency: a man's wife and his brother-in-law both travel to a distant country (*medinat hayam*), both are reported dead, and it subsequently emerges that both are alive. The man had, in the interim, married his wife's sister — believing his wife to be dead — and his wife's sister had married the brother-in-law, believing her husband to be dead. Rabbi Yossi's principle demands consistency: the question of whether that intermediate marriage is perceived as having been binding or not must be applied uniformly to both parties. Either both will be *muttar* or both will be *assur*, depending on whether that marriage was understood by onlookers as having actually taken effect.

### Shmuel's Ruling

Continuing from this point, the *gemara* records: *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel, halacha k'Rabbi Yosei* — Rav Yehuda rules in the name of Shmuel that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yossi. However, as the *gemara* will immediately make clear, there are different versions and interpretations of Rabbi Yossi's position, so it is not immediately obvious which formulation Shmuel intends to validate.

### Rashi's Reading

Rashi explains that Shmuel's statement is meant to apply to the entirety of Rabbi Yossi's ruling. The concern animating Rabbi Yossi's principle, according to Rashi, is whether people would perceive the intermediate marriage as having been binding — the same concern that underlies other restrictions, such as prohibiting a woman who remarried after a mistaken report of her husband's death from returning to her first husband, lest people conclude that her first husband had divorced her and she had legitimately remarried. The critical variable, Rashi notes, is whether the original marriage between Reuven and Rachel had been consummated through full *nissuin* or only *kiddushin*. If Rachel and Reuven had only reached the stage of *kiddushin*, it is conceivable that people might have perceived Reuven's subsequent marriage to Leah as valid — reasoning, perhaps, that the *kiddushin* with Rachel had fallen through. If, however, they had completed *nissuin*, no one could plausibly have viewed his marriage to Leah as binding, since a fully married man cannot take his wife's sister. Only if it had been *kiddushin* with Leah would there be no problem whatsoever.

---

## Rav Yosef Challenges

### Rav Yosef's Challenge

Rav Yosef raises a sharp question on Shmuel's ruling: *Umi amar Shmuel hachi* — did Shmuel really say this? *D'Shmuel l'taamei* — for Shmuel himself is on record elsewhere with a seemingly contradictory position.

### Rav vs. Shmuel Debate

The *gemara* cites a well-known dispute: *Yevamah — Rav amar harei hi k'eishesh ish*, Rav holds that a *yevamah* — a woman awaiting *yibum* or *chalitza* — is to be treated like a married woman. *U'Shmuel amar einah k'eishesh ish*, Shmuel holds she is not treated like a married woman. The bare formulation of this debate leaves its context obscure, and the *gemara* now turns to Rav Huna's interpretation to explain what exactly is at stake.

### Rav Huna's Context

Rav Huna proposes the following as the context of the Rav-Shmuel dispute: a man's brother performed *kiddushin* with a woman and then traveled to a distant country (*medinat hayam*), whereupon it was reported that the brother had died. The surviving brother, believing he was performing *yibum*, proceeded to perform *kiddushin* with the widow — his *yevamah*. Then the brother turned out to be alive. This case differs from a standard case of a woman who remarries after a mistaken report of her husband's death. In that ordinary case, even in hindsight, observers might still believe the second marriage was valid — reasoning, for instance, that the first husband had sent a *get* from afar. Here, however, once the brother emerges alive, it becomes retroactively impossible for anyone to have regarded the second marriage as binding, since a man's sister-in-law is forbidden to him even after divorce so long as the brother lives. In hindsight, no one could have perceived that *kiddushin* as a genuine marriage.

### Kiddushin & Perception

Yet the complication, as Rav Huna's reading highlights, is that the original marriage between the brother and the woman was only *kiddushin* — not full *nissuin*. This creates a potential avenue for people to think that perhaps the first *kiddushin* had not taken full effect, and therefore the second *kiddushin* — performed by the surviving brother thinking he was doing *yibum* — might have been perceived as valid. Rav holds that this concern is live: since the original marriage was only *kiddushin*, people in hindsight might plausibly imagine it had been conditional or defective, making the brother's subsequent *kiddushin* appear binding. Hence the *yevamah* is treated like a married woman, with all the attendant stringencies. 

---

## Shmuel's Leniency

### Gemara Resolves

Shmuel, however, rules *einah k'eishesh ish* — even the fact that the first marriage was only *kiddushin* does not lead us to fear that people will perceive the second act as a genuine marriage. Once the first brother appears alive, it is obvious to all that the surviving brother could never have validly married her, regardless of what stage the first marriage had reached. The *gemara* now returns to Rav Yosef's challenge: if Shmuel is lenient even when the first marriage was only *kiddushin* in the case of the *yevamah* and her brother-in-law, how can Shmuel also rule like Rabbi Yossi, who appears to impose a stringency specifically when the first marriage was only *kiddushin*?

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye presses the question further: *Memai d'chi amar Shmuel halacha k'Rabbi Yosei, ad Rabbi Yitzchak Napcha ka'amar* — how do we know which version of Rabbi Yossi Shmuel intended to validate? Perhaps when Shmuel said *halacha k'Rabbi Yosei*, he meant to endorse only the interpretation of Rabbi Ami, not that of Rabbi Yitzchak Napcha. And even granting that he meant Rabbi Yitzchak Napcha's version, perhaps he was endorsing only Rabbi Yossi's lenient ruling — not the stringent case involving *kiddushin*. That is: perhaps Shmuel's declaration that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yossi was intended to convey that, just as the husband may return to his original wife Rachel, so too Leah may return to her original husband Barak — in all cases, *l'kula*. Perhaps Shmuel was never endorsing any stringency at all.

### Hindsight Principle

The underlying logic that the *gemara* is developing is essential to appreciate in full. The usual stringencies applied to a woman who remarries after a mistaken report of her husband's death — which function not merely as a punitive fine but as a consequence of the fact that her union with the second man genuinely appeared, to observers, to be a valid marriage — depend on a factual predicate: that people actually could have perceived the second marriage as binding. There are cases, however, in which that predicate fails. When it subsequently emerges that the first husband's brother is alive, or that the first husband's wife's sister is alive, no one in hindsight could conceivably have viewed the second union as a legitimate marriage. The bond of the *yevamah* relationship, or the prohibition of marrying one's wife's sister, is absolute and applies even post-divorce. In hindsight, then, it is impossible that anyone would have perceived the intermediate marriage as valid, and therefore the entire foundation for the stringencies collapses.

### Special Cases

This insight applies distinctly in the cases of wife's sister and husband's brother. In an ordinary case of a husband returning alive after being reported dead, observers could still in hindsight theorize that the husband had sent a *get* from *medinat hayam*, and so the second marriage still appears potentially legitimate even after the fact. But in the special cases at issue here — where it is the wife's sister or the brother who reappears alive — such a theory is impossible, since the prohibition on marrying one's wife's sister, or a woman to her husband's brother, applies even after divorce and even after *get*. Hindsight therefore conclusively forecloses any perception of validity. And the question on the table reduces to this: can we be lenient even when the first marriage was only *kiddushin*, since even then people would in hindsight realize that the second union could not have been binding? Shmuel, on this reading, answers yes — even *kiddushin* at the beginning does not give us reason to fear that the second marriage was perceived as valid, and leniency applies across the board.

---

## Alt. Interpretations

### Rav Huna's Reading

The *gemara* then considers whether Rav Huna's framing of the Rav-Shmuel debate is even the correct one. *Dilma leita l'd'Rav Huna klal* — perhaps Rav Huna's interpretation is entirely off the mark. Perhaps the debate between Rav and Shmuel over whether a *yevamah* is *k'eishesh ish* concerns something altogether different.

### Zina Case

One alternative: perhaps the debate concerns the ruling of Rav Hamnuna, who teaches that *shomeret yavam she'zinta asura l'yivama* — a woman awaiting *yibum* who engages in illicit relations (*zina*) with another man becomes forbidden to her brother-in-law. On this reading, Rav holds that a *yevamah* is sufficiently like a married woman that her *zina* disqualifies her from *yibum*, while Shmuel holds she is not treated as a married woman and therefore is not disqualified.

### Kiddushin & Yevama

A third possibility: the debate between Rav and Shmuel concerns whether *kiddushin* from another man can take effect with a *yevamah* while she still awaits *yibum*. Rav holds that her *zika* to the brother-in-law renders her sufficiently like a married woman that *kiddushin* from an outside man cannot bind her. Shmuel holds she is not treated as a married woman, and therefore *kiddushin* from another man would be effective.

### One Debate, Multiple Fra…

The *gemara* notes that Rav and Shmuel are recorded as having debated the *yevamah*'s status using various formulations on multiple occasions, and raises the question of why the same dispute would be articulated twice. The answer: *chada miklal chaverta itmar* — the debate was actually stated only once, and the second formulation was derived inferentially from the first. The two framings are not independent disputes but different expressions of a single underlying *machlokes*.
