The last two cases — whether *zina* disqualifies and whether outside *kiddushin* can bind — fit together especially naturally, since both ask how thoroughly the *yevamah*'s bond to her brother-in-law resembles the bond of marriage.

The larger *chiddush* emerging from the entire extended discussion is worth pausing to appreciate. While the question of whether a husband can return to his wife after he mistakenly married her sister is relatively straightforward, the more striking case is whether the woman herself — having remarried, even if only on account of a mistaken report of her husband's death — can return to her first husband. The *gemara* has been exploring the narrow set of circumstances in which hindsight removes the very foundation of the stringencies: cases of wife's sister or husband's brother, where the reappearance of the "dead" party conclusively demonstrates, for all observers, that the intermediate marriage never could have been valid.

---

## Sequential Sisters

### Three Wives Setup

The *mishnah* now presents a striking scenario. A man is told that his wife died; he marries her sister from their shared father (that is, a paternal half-sister of his first wife). He is then told that the second wife died; he marries her sister from their shared mother (a maternal half-sister of the second). And so on: each wife is reported dead, he marries the next, and ultimately all of them turn out to be alive. The women form a chain: wives one and two share a father but not a mother; wives two and three share a mother but not a father; and so the chain continues through a fifth wife.

### Ruling on Validity

The *mishnah* rules: he may remain married to wives one, three, and five; he is forbidden to wives two and four. The logic follows directly. Wife one is a valid marriage. When he married wife two — who is the paternal sister of wife one — his first wife being still alive meant the marriage to wife two was invalid: one may not marry one's wife's sister. Wife three, however, shares no prohibited relationship with wife one (she is related only to wife two, through their mother), so the marriage to wife three was valid. Wife four, the sister of wife three through their mother, was therefore an invalid marriage. Wife five, bearing no prohibited relationship to wife three, was valid.

### Yibum Consequences

Since wives one, three, and five are his legitimate wives, they and their *tzaros* (co-wives) interact normally for purposes of *yibum*. Should he die, an act of *yibum* or *chalitza* with one of the valid wives would exempt the co-wives as well. Wives two and four, however, are not his wives, and an act with them by a brother would carry no exempting power.

### First Wife Truly Dead

The *mishnah* adds a case: what if the report about the first wife's death was actually true — she genuinely died? In that case, his marriage to wife two was valid (his first wife being truly dead, the marriage to her sister was permitted). Wife three, then, is the sister of his living wife two and is therefore forbidden to him. The pattern inverts: he is married to wives two and four and forbidden to wives one (dead), three, and five. And correspondingly, valid acts of *yibum* with wives two and four would exempt their *tzaros*, while acts involving wives three and five would not.

---

## Minor & Yibum

### Nine-Year-Old Status

The *mishnah* now transitions back squarely to the laws of *yibum*, introducing the case of a surviving brother who is nine years old and one day. At this age, an act of sexual intercourse (*bi'ah*) is legally cognizable — it is treated as a genuine act of *bi'ah* — yet because the boy is not yet an adult, it cannot constitute a fully consummated act of *yibum*. The question is what legal consequences flow from such an act.

### Disqualification Power

The *mishnah* rules: *Ben tesha shanim veyom echad hu posel al yedei achim* — the minor's *bi'ah* with the *yevamah* disqualifies the adult brothers from performing *yibum* with her thereafter. This act is treated as analogous to *maamar* — one of the quasi-acts that, while not completing *yibum*, is nevertheless legally consequential enough to remove others from the picture. Conversely, *ve'achim poslim al yado* — if the adult brothers act first, whether by *bi'ah*, *chalitza*, *maamar*, or *get*, that act will disqualify the minor from later completing a full act of *yibum* when he comes of age. The *mishnah* then specifies the asymmetry: *ela hu posel techilla ve'achim poslim techilla ve'sof* — his acts disqualify only if he goes first, whereas the brothers' acts disqualify him whether they act first or second.

### Maamar Question

The *gemara* pauses on a question implicit in this ruling: does a minor actually have a legally cognizable *maamar* at all? The *mishnah*, having established that the minor's *bi'ah* functions like *maamar* of an adult, and having then suggested that even other acts by the minor (such as *maamar* itself) are meaningful if performed first — prompts the question of whether the *mishnah* has now overstated the minor's legal capacity.

---

## Bia vs. Maamar

### Baraita on Bia

A *baraita* from the school of Rabbi Oshaya poses a direct challenge. The *baraita* teaches: if an adult brother performed *maamar* with the *yevamah*, and thereafter a minor brother — nine years old and one day — had *bi'ah* with her, that *bi'ah* disqualifies her to the first (adult) brother, even though the minor came second. This appears to contradict the *mishnah*, which stated that the minor's acts are only effective when he acts first.

### Mishnah Reinterpreted

To resolve the contradiction, the *gemara* proposes a revised reading of the *mishnah*: *bi'ah paslah afilu besof* — the minor's act of *bi'ah* disqualifies even when it comes second. The *mishnah*'s statement that the minor only creates a problem at the beginning (*techilla*) must therefore be referring not to *bi'ah* but to lesser acts such as *maamar* — quasi-acts that are effective only if the minor acts first. *Maamar techilla posel, besof lo posel* — *maamar* by the minor disqualifies only if it precedes the brothers' acts; *bi'ah* by the minor disqualifies regardless of order.

This is admittedly a strained reading of the *mishnah*, which appears to use the example of *bi'ah* when saying the minor is effective only first. But the *gemara* accepts this reinterpretation in order to maintain consistency with the *baraita*.

### Gemara Probes: Does a Minor Even Have Maamar or Get?

Having now said that the minor's *bi'ah* is powerful even at the end, while *maamar* is only effective at the beginning, the *gemara* probes further: does a minor have a legally recognized *maamar* at all? And does he have a legally recognized *get*? This question challenges the newly expanded picture of the minor's legal capacities.

### Bia Always Works

A *baraita* addresses the matter directly: *ben tesha shanim veyom echad hu posel bedavar echad, ve'achim poslin al yado bearba'ah devarim* — the minor can disqualify the brothers with one act, while the brothers can disqualify him with four. *Hu posel al yedei achim bevia* — his disqualifying act is exclusively *bi'ah*. *Ve'achim poslin al yado bevia, be'maamar, beget, uvechalitza* — the brothers can disqualify him through any of the four acts: *bi'ah*, *maamar*, *get*, or *chalitza*. This *baraita* seems to say that the minor has only *bi'ah*, not *maamar* or *get*. The *gemara* responds: the *baraita* lists only those acts that are always effective — *bi'ah* for the minor is always effective regardless of order, and therefore it is listed as his single act. *Maamar*, which is only effective when it comes first and not when it comes later, is not listed — not because it is meaningless, but because it is not *pesika*, not uniformly reliable. The *gemara* has thus, through this chain of reasoning, arrived at a richer account of the minor's legal capacities than either the *mishnah* or the *baraita* alone would suggest: *bi'ah* is always effective; *maamar* (and potentially other acts) are effective when performed first.

---

## Minor's Four Acts

### Minor Has Get

Additional *amoraic* statements now confirm and extend this picture. Rav Yehuda rules in the name of Shmuel: *yesh lo get* — the minor does have a legally meaningful *get*.

### Minor Has Maamar

Similarly, Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi rules: *yesh lo maamar* — the minor has a legally meaningful *maamar* as well.

### Rabbi Meir's View

A *baraita* then records that these positions align with the view of Rabbi Meir: *yesh lo get, yesh lo maamar, divrei Rabbi Meir*. The *gemara* then probes Rabbi Meir's position more carefully. The *baraita* had earlier taught: *asu biat ben tesha k'maamar begadol* — the Sages equated the minor's act of *bi'ah* with the *maamar* of an adult. The analogy is precise: just as an adult's *maamar* does not fully consummate *yibum* but does disqualify the other brothers, so too the minor's *bi'ah* does not fully consummate *yibum* but does disqualify the other brothers. Rabbi Meir then adds: *asu chalitzat ben tesha k'get begadol* — the Sages equated the minor's *chalitza* with an adult's *get*. One might ask: if Rabbi Meir also holds that the minor has a *get* of his own, why would one need to compare his *chalitza* to an adult's *get*? Why not compare it to his own *get*? The implication seems to be that the minor's *get*, while extant, is weaker than an adult's *get* — and therefore the comparison is made to the adult's *get*, to convey that the minor's *chalitza* rises to the level of an adult's *get*, even if the minor's own *get* does not.

### Chalitza Equals Get

Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua resolves this: *ait lei vezutar* — the minor does have a *get*, but it is weaker than an adult's *get*. The relevance of this distinction becomes clear in the context of Rabban Gamliel's ruling that a second *get* after a first *get* carries no legal effect (*ein get achar get*). According to Rabban Gamliel, this rule applies symmetrically — adult after adult, minor after minor — but an adult's *get* following a minor's *get* would be effective, since they are not equivalent. Conversely, among the Rabbis who hold that a second *get* after a first *get* is effective, this too applies symmetrically — adult after adult, minor after minor — but a minor's *get* after an adult's is not effective, since the minor's act is weaker.

### Acts Correspondence

The underlying logic can now be articulated cleanly. *Bi'ah* and *chalitza* are the two biblical acts pertaining to *yibum*; *maamar* and *get* are their rabbinic counterparts. For a minor, the biblical acts — when performed by the minor — carry the legal weight of the corresponding rabbinic acts performed by an adult. Hence, the minor's *bi'ah* is equated to an adult's *maamar*, and the minor's *chalitza* is equated to an adult's *get*. This is what it means to say that a minor's *chalitza* is like an adult's *get*: it is not comparing his *chalitza* to his own *get* (which would be weaker), but to the full strength of an adult's *get*. The logic preserves the parallel structure of biblical and rabbinic acts while accounting for the diminished legal capacity of the minor.

---

## Second Minor's Bia

### Second Minor Question

The *mishnah* now addresses a further case: if a first minor has *bi'ah* with the *yevamah*, and then a second minor — also nine years old and one day — likewise has *bi'ah* with her, does the second minor's act disqualify the first? The question is whether the logic that allows one minor's *bi'ah* to disqualify an adult brother (as established above) applies equally when both parties are minors.

### Self-Disqualification

A related case: the same minor who had *bi'ah* with the *yevamah* then also has *bi'ah* with her *tzarah* (co-wife). If his first act was quasi-effective (analogous to *maamar*), then his second act with the co-wife should, by the same logic, disqualify himself from completing *yibum* with the first — since one can build only one household (*bayit echad hu boneh*) and cannot do *yibum* with two wives. The *mishnah* indicates that in this case, *posel al yedei atzmo* — he disqualifies himself.

### Rabbi Shimon View

Rabbi Shimon disagrees with both cases. His position, explained in the *baraita*, is: *im biah rishonah biah, biah sheniyah einah biah* — if the first act was a full, binding *bi'ah*, then the second act is simply not a *bi'ah* at all (since the matter is already settled). And *v'im biah rishonah einah biah, biah sheniyah nami einah biah* — if the first act was not a full, binding *bi'ah*, then the second act is likewise not a *bi'ah*. Rabbi Shimon rejects the intermediate, fifty-percent position entirely. For him, the minor's act is either one hundred percent effective or zero percent effective — there is no quasi-status.

### All-or-Nothing Logic

This all-or-nothing position has decisive implications. When two minors each perform *bi'ah*, or when the same minor performs *bi'ah* with both co-wives, Rabbi Shimon reasons that the second act cannot do anything the first act did not already do. If the first act was fully effective, it is already settled and the second act is irrelevant. If the first act was not effective, the second act is equally ineffective — one cannot accumulate two zero-percent acts into a meaningful result. Therefore, Rabbi Shimon rules that neither a second minor's *bi'ah* nor the same minor's *bi'ah* with the co-wife creates any additional disqualification.

The *gemara* notes: *matnitin de'lo k'Ben Azzai* — the *mishnah*'s ruling (against Rabbi Shimon) is not in accordance with Ben Azzai. Ben Azzai teaches that *maamar* after *maamar* by two different brothers (*yevamim*) is effective — the second brother's *maamar* disqualifies the first — but *maamar* after *maamar* by the same brother with two different *yevamot* is not effective: having done *maamar* with one co-wife does not disqualify him from the other. Translating to the present case: the minor's *bi'ah* with one wife followed by *bi'ah* with the co-wife should, according to Ben Azzai's logic, not disqualify him from the first wife. The *mishnah*'s ruling that he does disqualify himself therefore runs contrary to Ben Azzai's principle.

---

## Minor Dies & Yevama

### Complex Case Setup

The next *mishnah* presents a more intricate scenario. The minor — nine years old and one day — performs *bi'ah* with his *yevamah*. Thereafter, once he has grown to adulthood, he marries another woman. He then dies without having consummated *yibum* with the *yevamah* as an adult (he had only the act as a minor, which was equivalent to *maamar*, not full *yibum*).

### Zikat Shnei Yevamim

This creates the unusual situation of *zikat shnei yevamim* — a dual *zika* (brother-in-law connection) encumbering the first woman. The surviving brothers are bound to the *yevamah* through two separate obligations: the original biblical obligation arising from her first husband (say, Er), and a rabbinic obligation arising from the minor's quasi-*maamar*-level *bi'ah* (say, Onan). These two *zikot* are of different legal grades — one *d'oraisa*, one *d'rabbanan* — and they coexist because the minor's act, being only rabbinic in weight, never displaced the underlying biblical *zika* of the first husband. This situation would never arise when a full adult performs *yibum*, since a fully consummated act of *yibum* is entirely *d'oraisa* and completely absorbs and resolves the original *zika*. It is the uniquely intermediate character of the minor's *bi'ah* that creates this dual-*zika* situation.

The surviving brother (Shelah, in this illustration) therefore faces obligations to two women: the *yevamah* from the first husband (Tamar, from Er), carrying *zikat shnei yevamim*, and the second wife the minor married as an adult (say, Devorah), to whom he has a straightforward *d'oraisa yibum* obligation.

### First Woman Chalitza

The *mishnah* rules: *harishona choletzet v'lo mityabemet* — with respect to the first woman (who carries the dual *zika*), the surviving brother may only perform *chalitza*, not *yibum*. This is because her status is complicated by the dual obligation: she stands in the *yibum* relationship to him both through the biblical *zika* of her original husband and through the rabbinic *zika* of the minor. Performing *yibum* with a woman in this doubly encumbered state is not permissible; only *chalitza* will suffice. *Ve'shniya o choletzet o mityabemet* — with the second wife (who has a straightforward *yibum* obligation), the brother may choose either *yibum* or *chalitza*.

### Rabbi Shimon's Option

Rabbi Shimon, consistent with his all-or-nothing position, rules differently: *miyabem eizo sheyirtze, v'choletz lashniya* — he may perform *yibum* with whichever woman he chooses and then *chalitza* with the other. According to Rabbi Shimon, the minor's act is either fully effective or entirely null. If it was null, then Tamar stands only in the *zika* of Er, and there is no complicating dual encumbrance; she is no different from any other *yevamah*. If the minor's act was fully effective, then Tamar was fully Onan's wife, and the surviving brothers face two distinct and independent *yibum* obligations — one per wife — and must perform *yibum* with one and *chalitza* with the other, but there is no reason *yibum* cannot be done with either. The one thing Rabbi Shimon concedes is that *yibum* cannot be performed with both women, since it is possible that the minor's act was fully effective (meaning Onan had two full wives), and one may perform *yibum* with only one of them. Therefore he must do *yibum* with one and *chalitza* with the other — but he has free choice as to which.

---

## Adult Without Puberty

### Pubic Hair Requirement

The *mishnah* closes with a brief but significant ruling: *echad shehu ben tesha shanim veyom echad, v'echad shehu ben esrim shelo hevi shtei sa'arot* — both the nine-year-old and a twenty-year-old who has not yet developed two pubic hairs are governed by the same *halacha*. The physiological sign of adulthood — the presence of two pubic hairs — is the operative criterion, not chronological age alone. An individual who has reached twenty years of age but lacks this sign of physical maturity retains the same *halachic* status as a minor of nine years and one day, with all the attendant consequences for the laws of *yibum* discussed throughout this *daf*.

---

---

# Yevamot 97

## Underage Kiddushin

### Bi'ah of Minor

The daf begins at the middle of 97b. The preceding *Mishnah* had established a case involving a young man who is nine years and a day old or more — past the threshold of *bi'ah* taking legal effect, yet still before *bar mitzvah* — whose act of intercourse with his sister-in-law functions as a kind of *ma'amar* but does not constitute *yibum* in the full halachic sense. The scenario that follows is this: if such an underage man performs *bi'ah* with his sister-in-law and subsequently dies, the next surviving brother faces what the *Mishnah* calls *zekat shnei yevamim* — an obligation to two sisters-in-law simultaneously. The first *mitzvah* of *yibum*, deriving from the original marriage that was never actualized through proper *yibum*, remains outstanding; and a second, *derabbanan* obligation to the deceased minor's quasi-wife also attaches. The result is that the surviving brother is not permitted to perform *yibum* at all, and instead *chalitzah* is required.

### No Co-Wife Case

The *Gemara* opens its analysis with Rabbah's clarification: *Amar Rabbah: Hada amar rabbanan zekat shnei yevamim mechelatz chaletz yevamim lo meyabbem* — the rabbinic rule that a woman bearing two *zekot* from two brothers-in-law requires *chalitzah* and not *yibum*. Rabbah stresses that one should not think this ruling is limited to cases where there is a co-wife. The prior discussions in an earlier *perek* had involved a co-wife scenario, and one might have supposed that the restriction was tied specifically to that concern. Rabbah therefore insists: *lo teima heicha de'ika tzara*, do not say it applies only where there is a co-wife. In our case — *leka tzara*, there is no co-wife — and the rule of *chalitzah* rather than *yibum* still applies.

To make the case concrete: using the paradigm of Er, Onan, and Shelah — if Onan, as an underage *kattan*, performed *bi'ah* with Tamar, this creates a *derabbanan* quasi-marriage but not a *de'oraita yibum*. When Onan then dies, Shelah's obligation to Tamar has two dimensions: a *de'oraita* obligation stemming from Er's genuine marriage to her, which was never resolved through *yibum* or *chalitzah*; and a *derabbanan* obligation stemming from Onan's quasi-marriage. Because Onan's *bi'ah* was not *de'oraita*, it did not displace Er from the picture. Tamar therefore stands under two *zekot*, and the *halacha* is *chalitzah*, not *yibum*. In this version of the case there is no co-wife at all — that is Rabbah's point.

### Appearance Concern

What then is the rationale for the restriction in the co-wife case that Rabbah is distinguishing from? In that scenario, where husband number two had done *ma'amar* and was also married to another woman, the concern is one of appearances. If the surviving brother performs *yibum* with the first woman — legitimately, on account of the *de'oraita* obligation from husband number one — it will appear as though he has performed *yibum* with two wives of the same deceased husband. People will not understand that one *yibum* is being done on account of Er and the other would have been on account of Onan. The obvious resolution of doing *yibum* with one and *chalitzah* with the other is itself rejected, because regardless of which direction one goes, the appearance of *yibum* with two women of the same deceased man will arise. The restriction on *yibum* in the co-wife case is therefore driven by this appearance concern. Rabbah's contribution is to establish that even in the absence of a co-wife — where that concern does not apply — the rule of *chalitzah* rather than *yibum* holds.

### Regular Marriage Rules

The *Gemara* then adds a brief but important note: if this *kattan* had simply contracted a normal marriage — *kiddushin* and *nisuin* — with a woman, and then died, that marriage carries no legal weight and the woman has no obligation of *chalitzah* or *yibum* with his brothers whatsoever.

## Capacity & Status

### Shotim Exemption

This point is underscored by a *tannaic* teaching: *shoteh* — a person of unsound mind — and *katan* — a minor — who contracted marriage and died: *neshoteihem peturot min hachalitzah umin hayibum*, their wives are entirely exempt from both *chalitzah* and *yibum*. The marriage of a *shoteh* or *katan* carries no halachic recognition. The *Gemara* notes that the classic triad of those lacking legal capacity — *shoteh*, *katan*, and *cheresh* — is only partially represented here, since the Rabbis did institute *kiddushin* and *nisuin* for a *cheresh* at least on a rabbinic level, which is why the *cheresh* is treated differently and not mentioned in this context.

## Underage Kiddushin (II)

### Rav Ashi vs. Shmuel

The *Gemara* now takes up a case where the underage Onan did *bi'ah* with Tamar but was also married to Devorah. If he subsequently comes of age and consummates his relationship with Tamar as an adult, she becomes a genuine wife alongside Devorah. But if he did not consummate the relationship with Tamar as an adult and then dies — Devorah is a real wife, and Shelah may perform *yibum* with her; Tamar, however, was only rabbinically acquired, and Shelah must do *chalitzah* with her. The reason Tamar's *chalitzah* cannot be replaced by *yibum* with Devorah alone — the normal resolution in a *zekat shnei yevamim* scenario — is that the *de'oraita* obligation stemming from Er has never been resolved.

This prompts the *Gemara* to ask from an earlier passage: if the *bi'ah* of a *kattan* functions like a *ma'amar begadol*, then by analogy to the *ma'amar* case, shouldn't the surviving brother be required to do *chalitzah* with both Tamar and Devorah, not *yibum* with Devorah and *chalitzah* with Tamar?

*Amar Rav Ashi: Lo asu biat ben tesha kemamar begadol* — Rav Ashi says that the Sages did not equate the *bi'ah* of a nine-year-old fully with a *ma'amar* by an adult. It carries legal weight in various respects — enough to disqualify the brothers and produce other halachic consequences — but it is weaker than a full *ma'amar*, and therefore Devorah is not displaced from the picture. Shelah can still perform *yibum* with Devorah. Shmuel disagrees: *Ushemuel amar asu va'asu* — the *bi'ah* of the *kattan* is fully equivalent to a *ma'amar begadol*. Rabbi Yochanan likewise: *vechan amar Rabbi Yochanan asu va'asu*.

### Tannaitic Dispute

The *Gemara* then reframes the apparent contradiction between two *mishnayot* — one requiring *chalitzah* with both women, the other permitting *yibum* with the co-wife — not as a question about the strength of the minor's *bi'ah* relative to an adult's *ma'amar*, but as a *machloket tanna'im*.

The *tanna* of the *Perek Arba Achim*, who rules that the co-wife also requires *chalitzah*, made a *gezeirah* on account of the co-wife scenario: *gazar mishum tzara*. He ruled that *yibum* is entirely prohibited in order to prevent the appearance of *yibum* being performed with two women simultaneously. This *tanna* would say the same *halacha* whether the deceased second husband had performed a *ma'amar* as an adult or was a *kattan* whose *bi'ah* is the equivalent — the *gezeirah* applies equally. The *tanna* of our *Mishnah*, by contrast, does not make this *gezeirah* at all. He permits *yibum* with the co-wife Devorah even while requiring *chalitzah* with Tamar. This *tanna* would similarly permit *yibum* with a co-wife even in the adult *ma'amar* case.

The upshot is striking: the real dispute between the two *mishnayot* is not whether *bi'ah* of a *kattan* equals *ma'amar begadol* — both *tanna'im* would treat them identically — but whether one makes a *gezeirah* to prevent *yibum* entirely when there is a co-wife. Each *tanna* applies his view equally to both *kattan* and *gadol* cases; the apparent difference in the *mishnayot* arises only because each *tanna* chose the example most directly relevant to his discussion.

## Attribution Dispute

### Teaching Without Name

Rabbi Elazar, the student of Rabbi Yochanan, went and presented this entire analysis — the framing of the contradiction as a *machloket tanna'im* — in the *beit midrash*. However, *v'lo amrah mishmei d'Rabbi Yochanan* — he did not attribute the teaching to Rabbi Yochanan. When Rabbi Yochanan learned of this, *v'ikpad* — he was deeply offended that his *Torah* was being transmitted without his name.

### Tiberias Synagogue

Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi came to calm Rabbi Yochanan down. They invoked the famous episode of the synagogue in Tiberias. A dispute had arisen there between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yose concerning a bolt — *nagar sheyesh b'rosho glustra* — a door-bolt that has a rounded bulb at its end, making it usable for grinding and thus more of a *kli*, which would reduce concerns of *binyan* and *muktzah*. The question was whether one may insert it to lock a door on *Shabbat*. The debate between the two Sages became so heated that, while it was not intentional, a *sefer Torah* was torn in the tumult — *shenikra sefer Torah b'chamatan*. Rabbi Yose ben Kisma, who was present, declared: *temei'ani im lo yihyeh beit haknesset zu avodah zarah* — I would be utterly astonished if this synagogue does not ultimately become a house of idolatry. *V'chein havah* — and so it came to pass.

The point was plain: it is not worth allowing a dispute to escalate to such destructive ends. But when Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi made this comparison, it only made matters worse. *Hadar ikpeid zina achrina* — Rabbi Yochanan became still more angry, asking: *chavruta nami?* — are you comparing me to their situation, as if Rabbi Elazar is my colleague and peer? That dispute was between equals. Rabbi Elazar is my student. I have every right to be treated differently.

### Yehoshua Analogy

Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi then came to try his hand at the matter. He cited the verse from Yehoshua: *Ka'asher tzivah Hashem et Moshe avdo kein tzivah Moshe et Yehoshua vecheyn asah Yehoshua, lo hesir davar mikol asher tzivah Hashem et Moshe*. The verse emphasizes how scrupulously Yehoshua carried out everything Moshe commanded. But, Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi asked: do you imagine that every time Yehoshua taught, he explicitly declared, "Here is what Moshe told me"? *Ela Yehoshua yoshev vedoresh stam* — Yehoshua would simply teach *Torah* without constant attribution. *Vehakol yod'im sheToraso shel Moshe hi* — everyone understood that everything he taught came from Moshe. The verse's very emphasis on his fidelity to Moshe demonstrated precisely that he did not need to label each teaching explicitly, because his role as the faithful channel of Moshe's *Torah* was self-evident.

*Af Rabbi Elazar talmidcha yoshev vedoresh stam* — similarly, your student Rabbi Elazar teaches without attribution, *vehakol yod'im sheshelcha hi* — and everyone knows that his *Torah* is yours.

This argument succeeded where the earlier attempt had failed. Rabbi Yochanan said to Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi: *mipnei mah ein atem yod'in lepayeis keven Idi chaveireinu* — why did you not know how to appease me as Ben Idi does?

### Immortality via Torah

The *Gemara* then explains what lay at the root of Rabbi Yochanan's concern — and it was not mere pride. *De'amar Rabbi Yehuda amar Rav*: what does David mean when he says *agurah be'aholcha olamim* — I will dwell in Your tent in two worlds? Can a person actually dwell in two worlds? Rather, David was praying: *sheyomru davar shemuah mipi ba'olam hazeh* — that even after his death, people in this world would transmit his teachings in his name.

The source for why this matters: *De'amar Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: kol talmid chacham she'omrim davar shemuah mipi ba'olam hazeh siftosav dovvot bakever* — any *talmid chacham* whose *Torah* is transmitted in his name in this world, his lips continue to murmur in the grave. The continuity of attribution is not about honor; it is about a form of continued presence in this world, a way of remaining alive while dwelling in the world to come. *Amar Rabbi Yitzchak ben Zeira* — and what is the verse? *Vecheichech kayayin hatov holeich ledodi lemeisharim doveiv sifsei yeshenim* — and your palate is like fine wine, going straight to my beloved, causing the lips of those who sleep to murmur. *Kechomer shel anavim* — like a press of grapes: the moment one lays a finger upon pressed grapes, they immediately flow. So too with the *Torah* of *talmidei chachamim* — the moment it is spoken in their name, their lips begin to murmur in the grave.

Rabbi Yochanan's concern was not vanity but this: the transmission of *Torah* in a teacher's name is the mechanism by which a *talmid chacham* remains present in this world even after death. When his student taught his insight without attribution, Rabbi Yochanan felt that something vital had been severed — not his reputation, but his continued living connection to this world. The *Gemara* notes that the *pasuk* in *Shir Hashirim* invoked here is also from Shlomo, making it in some sense an apt citation in this context.

## Capacity & Status (II)

### Saris Definition

The *Gemara* returns to the question of the *kattan* who reaches the age of twenty without having developed pubic hair. The *Mishnah* treats such a person as still legally a *kattan*, still somewhat within the categories of *yibum* and *chalitzah*. But a *baraita* seems to say otherwise: *ben esrim shana shelo hevi shtei searot* — if a twenty-year-old has not produced two pubic hairs, *yaviu reaya shehu ben esrim vehu hasaris* — bring proof of his age, and once it is established that he is twenty and lacks the hair, he is classified as the *saris* of whom the Rabbis spoke — *lo choletz velo meyabem* — exempt entirely from *chalitzah* and *yibum*. This would apparently undercut the *Mishnah*'s premise that a twenty-year-old without pubic hair still functions as a *kattan* in these matters.

The resolution: *Amar Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak amar Rav: vehu shenoldu lo simanei saris* — it is not sufficient that the person be twenty and lack pubic hair; he must also manifest specific physiological signs of being a *saris*, which were discussed in earlier passages. *Amar Rava: deika nami d'katani vehu hasaris* — Rava notes that the *baraita* itself says "and he is the *saris*," implying that additional identifying characteristics are required beyond age alone. The *Mishnah* therefore governs the case of a twenty-year-old who lacks pubic hair but does not display those other signs — such a person is still treated as a *kattan* who may yet reach maturity.

### Rava's Ruling

The *Gemara* then asks: if a person never develops those other signs of a *saris*, at what point must we conclude that he will never achieve biological maturity? *Tani d'vei Rebbi Chiya: ad rov shnotav* — until the majority of his years. Since seventy years is assumed to be the typical lifespan, once a person passes approximately thirty-six, he is presumed a *saris* even without the other specific indicators.

A practical dimension follows. When such cases were brought before Rava, he would not immediately declare the man a *saris*. If the person appeared lean and underfed, *amar lehu zilu avriyuhu* — Rava would say: go and feed him properly first. Malnutrition can prevent the development of pubic hair just as it prevents menstruation in women who are severely undernourished. Conversely, if the man was overweight, *amar lehu zilu acchishuhu* — Rava would prescribe an exercise regimen to reduce his weight. *D'hanei simanei zimnin d'nafli machamat kachishuta vezimnin d'nafli machamat briyuta* — these signs sometimes fail to appear due to being underfed, and sometimes due to being overfed. Only after addressing those external factors could a proper determination be made.

### Ha-Isha Rabba End

*Hadran alach Ha'isha Rabba* — and with that, the *perek* known as *Ha'isha Rabba* comes to its conclusion. It is called *Ha'isha Rabba* — the "great" *Ha'isha* — to distinguish it from a later chapter also beginning with *Ha'isha*, which is called *Ha'isha Shalom*. It was a rich and challenging *perek*, covering the case of the husband who returned from afar, then pivoting to the wife in the analogous situation, and ultimately returning to the core discussions of *yibum* centered on the underage young man whose *bi'ah* generates such complex legal consequences.

## Oneis & Mefutah

### Non-Marital Relations

With the opening of the new *perek*, the discussion shifts from *yibum* to the subject of familial prohibitions arising from non-marital sexual relations. The *Mishnah* opens: *nosein al ha-anusa ve'al ha-mefuta* — one may marry a woman who is related to him only through an act of rape or seduction, meaning through a sexual relationship that was not a marriage.

The underlying principle is this: the prohibitions of wife's sister, wife's mother, and wife's daughter are predicated on the existence of a *wife* — on there having been a marriage. These prohibited relationships are defined by the man's marriage to the first woman. If no marriage took place, if the man merely had sexual relations with a woman outside of marriage — labeled by the *Mishnah* using the legal categories of *anusa* or *mefuta*, rape or seduction, since these are the two cases the Torah explicitly addresses involving non-marital intercourse — then the relational prohibitions that attach through wifehood do not apply. He may marry her sister, mother, or daughter. This is the rule of *nosein al ha-anusa*: when the first relationship was not a marriage, the subsequent relationship with the relative is permitted *de'oraita*.

### Father's Exception

The *Mishnah* then considers cases involving not the man's own wife but his father's or son's relationships. The *Tanna Kamma* holds: *nosei adam anusat aviv u-mefutat aviv* — a man may marry a woman his father merely slept with, since she was never the father's wife. Similarly, *anusat beno u-mefutat beno* — he may marry a woman his son merely slept with, since she was never the son's wife. The prohibition of stepmother and daughter-in-law requires an actual marriage; without marriage, the relationship does not generate the prohibition.

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees in one specific case: *Rabbi Yehuda oser be-anusat aviv u-mefutat aviv* — Rabbi Yehuda prohibits a man from marrying a woman his father had sexual relations with, even outside of marriage. This exception for the father's partner, while not shared by the *Tanna Kamma*, has some resonance with the prophetic condemnation in Amos, where father and son going to the same woman is condemned as a profound moral degradation — even if it does not rise to the level of a formal *issur* of *arayot*.

### Daughter Prohibition

A *baraita* makes the principle more explicit: *oneis isha mutar liseis bita* — if a man had forced sexual relations with a woman, he is permitted to marry her daughter. The lack of marriage means that the woman-daughter chain of relationship never became a prohibited chain of *she'erah* — biological or marital kinship of the relevant type.

### Suspected Affair

The *Gemara* then raises an apparent challenge from a different *baraita*: *ha-nichshad min ha-isha assur be-imah u-ve-vitah ve-achotah* — a man suspected of having an affair with a woman is prohibited from marrying her mother, daughter, or sister. This seems to contradict the principle just stated. If a man who actually slept with a woman may marry her relatives, why should a man *suspected* of an affair be *more* restricted?

The answer is that this prohibition is *mi-derabbanan* — rabbinic, not biblical. And the rationale is not difficult to see: if the suspicion has some basis, and the man proceeds to marry the woman's mother or daughter, it is likely that he will continue his relationship with the original woman after the marriage. At that point, he will be guilty of a biblical prohibition — sleeping with his wife's mother or daughter. The Rabbis therefore prohibited the marriage preemptively to prevent it from leading to a *de'oraita* violation.

But would the *Mishnah* then use the language of *nosein l'chatchilah* — permitted outright — in a case where there is at least a rabbinic concern? The *Gemara* resolves this: *ki tnan matnisin le-achar misah* — our *Mishnah* is speaking of a case where the first woman has already died. Once she is dead, the concern that the man will continue sleeping with her no longer applies, and the rabbinic prohibition accordingly falls away. He may freely marry her mother, daughter, or sister.

### Death Removes Ties

This leads to a clarification of the overall structure. The fundamental biblical scheme is: first there is a marriage to woman one, and then an act of sex with woman two — the wife's sister, mother, or daughter — is what is prohibited. The *Mishnah* establishes that the reverse — first sex with woman one, then marriage with woman two — generates no *de'oraita* prohibition, since the relational chain begins with sex rather than marriage. The *baraita* about suspected affairs then adds that even this permitted path is rabbinically restricted during the first woman's lifetime, lest it lead to the prohibited reverse scenario. Once the first woman dies, however, even the rabbinic concern dissolves entirely, and the marriage is fully permitted.

The *Mishnah* employs the legal terminology of *anusa* and *mefuta* because those are the two categories through which the Torah addresses non-marital intercourse. In practice, for the purposes of this *halacha*, the distinction between them is irrelevant — both simply denote sexual relations outside of marriage.

## Kichah vs. Shichvah

### Terminology Pattern

The *Gemara* now investigates the textual basis for the entire framework: why does the prohibition depend on whether the first relationship was a marriage? *De-tanu rabbanan: be-chulhu ne'emar shichivah* — by all the *arayot*, the Torah uses the language of *shichivah* — lying with, i.e., sexual intercourse. *Ve-khan ne'emar kichah* — but in the specific cases of wife, mother, and daughter-in-law (and sister), the Torah uses the language of *kichah* — taking, i.e., marriage. Rashi points to the verse *ish ki yikach et ishah ve-et imah* — a man who *takes* a woman and her mother — and to *ve-achoto lo tikach* — his sister he shall not *take*. The Rabbis derive from this terminological distinction: *derech likuchin asra Torah* — the Torah's prohibition operates through the framework of marriage. Where the text says *kichah*, the operative relationship is a marital one; only once marriage is in place do the prohibited acts of *shichivah* with the relatives come into force.

### Rava Challenges

Rava then poses a sharp question to Abaye: if the use of *kichah* in these passages means the prohibition is triggered only through marriage, consider the prohibition of a man's sister, where the verse reads *ish asher yikach et achoto bat aviv o vat imo* — a man who *takes* his sister. Would one say, by the same logic, that it is only prohibited to *marry* one's sister, but sexual relations with her outside of marriage — *derech shichivah* — would be permitted? Clearly not. So how can *kichah* be the operative trigger?

### Context Determines

The resolution: *likuchin ketivah be-Torah stam* — the word *kichah* in the Torah is generic; it can mean marriage or, depending on context, simply an act of sexual taking. *Ra'uy likichah* — where the woman in question is one who could in principle be married, *kichah* means marriage in the full sense. This applies to the cases of wife, mother, and daughter-in-law, where a prior legitimate marriage is what establishes the relational framework. *Ra'uy lishchivah* — where the woman is one who could never be married — as with one's sister, where marriage is simply impossible halachically — then *kichah* in that context means *shichivah*, sexual intercourse. The prohibition against one's sister attaches to any act of intercourse, not to a marital act that can never occur.

The approach is admittedly not perfectly clean — *kichah* does not always mean what it most naturally means — but the distinction is workable: in cases where marriage is a meaningful legal possibility, *kichah* means marriage; where it is not, *kichah* is read as referring to sexual relations.

## Granddaughter Rules

### Conflicting Verses

The *Gemara* now examines the case of a granddaughter through two apparently contradictory verses. The verse in Vayikra reads: *ervat bat bincha o vat bitcha lo tegaleh* — do not expose the nakedness of your son's daughter or your daughter's daughter. The plain sense seems to refer to one's own biological granddaughter. A separate verse reads: *ervat ishah u-vitah lo tegaleh et bat benah ve-et bat bitah lo tikach* — you may not expose the nakedness of a woman and her daughter, and you shall not take her son's daughter or her daughter's daughter. This second verse refers to *the wife's* granddaughter — a step-granddaughter who is not biologically the man's own.

*Ha ketsad? Kan be-onsin kan be-nisuin* — how do we reconcile these? The first verse prohibits one's own biological granddaughter, and that prohibition exists regardless of marriage — it is a bond of *she'er*, of flesh and biological kinship. The second verse prohibits the *wife's* granddaughter — but only when there is a marriage to the grandmother. If the relationship with the grandmother was only sexual and not marital, the wife's granddaughter is not a step-granddaughter in any meaningful sense and is therefore permitted.

One might ask whether to read the verses in reverse — prohibiting the wife's granddaughter in cases of non-marital relations and perhaps permitting the step-granddaughter in cases of marriage. But the *Gemara* rejects this: the prohibitions of *arayot* use the term *she'er* — *she'erah henah*, the flesh of one's flesh. *Be-nisuin ika she'er* — in marriage, a step-relationship carries a degree of *she'er*, even if it is relational rather than biological. *U-ve-onsin leka she'er* — in a purely sexual relationship outside of marriage, the granddaughter of that woman is not one's biological granddaughter, is not one's step-granddaughter, and cannot be described as *she'er* in any meaningful sense.

### Sheir Concept

The concept of *she'er* thus does the decisive work in this analysis. Biological kinship always carries *she'er*; marital kinship generates a kind of derivative *she'er* through the step-relationship; but a purely sexual relationship, absent marriage, generates no *she'er* at all. The entire framework of what is prohibited and what is permitted in cases of non-marital relations flows from this principle.

## Father & Son

### Shomeret Yavam

The *Gemara* records that Rabbi Yose prohibits a man from marrying a woman his father had sexual relations with — *asar be-anusat aviv* — a position aligned with Rabbi Yehuda's view in the *Mishnah*.

### Knaf Aviv

Rav Gidel cites Rav in explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's position: *de-chtiv lo yikach ish et eshet aviv ve-lo yigaleh knaf aviv* — the verse in Devarim first prohibits marrying one's stepmother, and then adds the prohibition of *lo yigaleh knaf aviv* — do not uncover the hem of the father. The *knaf ha-av* — the father's hem — refers to the nakedness that the father himself saw: the woman with whom the father had sexual relations. *Lo yigaleh* — this man may not have sexual relations with that woman, even if she was never formally the father's wife. This is Rabbi Yehuda's source for his stricter position.

### Rabbanan Counter

The Rabbis, however, reject this reading. *Ei hava samich leh kedekamarat* — if the prohibition of *knaf aviv* were directly juxtaposed to the earlier passage dealing with rape and payment to the father — *venatan ha'ish hashochev imah la'avi ha-na'ara chamishim kasef* — one could concede that the context establishes that *knaf aviv* refers to a woman the father merely had sexual relations with. But *hashta d'lo samich leh* — since those passages appear much earlier in the text and are not immediately adjacent, the juxtaposition argument fails. Instead, the Rabbis read the verse in accordance with *Rav Anan* in the name of Shmuel: *beshomeret yavam shel aviv hakatuv medaber* — the verse is speaking of a *shomeret yavam*, a woman who stands in a quasi-marital *zekah* relationship with the father, awaiting *yibum* or *chalitzah*. The prohibition of *lo yigaleh knaf aviv* refers to this woman — the father's *shomeret yavam* — not to a woman with whom the father merely had casual sexual relations. *Knaf harauya l'aviv* — the hem appropriate to the father refers to the woman who is fit to be, in some legal sense, the father's wife.

### Aunt Status

The *Gemara* immediately raises an objection: if the *shomeret yavam* of the father is the father's brother's wife, then she is already the man's *dodah* — his aunt — and as such she is already prohibited under the *de'oraita* prohibition of *arayot*, which carries *karet*. Why would one need an additional verse to establish a prohibition that is already in place? *La'avor alav bishnei lavin* — to add a second *lav* to the transgression, yielding two counts of prohibition.

Furthermore, this woman is also forbidden as *yevama lashuk* — any woman who is a *shomeret yavam* is prohibited to other men until the *yibum* or *chalitzah* is completed. *La'avor alav bishloshav lavin* — that gives three *lavin* simultaneously.

### Post-Death

The *Gemara* offers a final possible resolution: *ve-iba'it eima le-achar mita* — or one could say the verse is addressing the case after the father's death. Once the father has died, she is no longer a *yevama lashuk* — if there was only one brother with the obligation and he has now died, the *zekah* lapses. She remains, however, a *dodah*, an aunt, and the *knaf aviv* prohibition adds a third *lav* even at that stage. *La'avor alav bishloshav lavin* — three counts of prohibition are nonetheless established.

## Relationship Riddles

### Stepdaughter Case

Having concluded the legal analysis, the *Gemara* turns to a remarkable series of family-relationship riddles — puzzles about how a single person can bear multiple overlapping legal relationships to another. These were likely posed as intellectual exercises among *talmidei chachamim*, testing their ability to reconstruct unusual genealogical scenarios. As one observer once put it, this is what the Rabbis did before television.

The first riddle: *achi me'av velo me'em, vehu ba'ala de'em, va'ana barta de'ittateih* — he is my half-brother on my father's side but not on my mother's, he is the husband of my mother, and I am the daughter of his wife. Rashi explains: my father's son — my half-brother — married my mother. He is therefore my half-brother (through the father) and simultaneously my stepfather (through his marriage to my mother). I am his wife's daughter — his stepdaughter. And crucially, Rami bar Chama notes that this scenario is only possible *d'lo k'Rabbi Yehuda d'matnitin* — if we do not follow Rabbi Yehuda's position in our *Mishnah*. Because the father must have had sexual relations with this man's mother without marrying her — otherwise the son could never have married his own stepmother. That makes her *anusat aviv*, and according to Rabbi Yehuda, this son would be prohibited from marrying her. Only the *Tanna Kamma*, who permits *anusat aviv*, allows the scenario to work.

### Son-Brother

The second riddle: *achi v'breih hu, achateih ana, d'hai d'darina aktephai* — he is my brother and my son; I am his sister; I am the sister of the one I am carrying on my shoulders. In other words: my son is my brother. How? *Mishkachat lah be-oved kochavim haba al bito* — the scenario involves a non-Jew who had sexual relations with his own daughter. Since the discussion of forbidden relations among non-Jews in this context does not carry the same formal prohibitions, the *Gemara* constructs these riddles using non-Jewish actors to avoid any implication that a Jew engaged in such conduct. The child born of this union is the mother's son and simultaneously her sibling, since both share the same father. She is thus the sister of the one she carries.

### Aunt Case

The third riddle: *shalom lach chavri, bat achatech ana* — greetings, my friend; I am the daughter of your sister. Meaning, this person's daughter is his sister's daughter — his niece through his sister. *Mishkachat lah be-oved kochavim haba al bat bito* — a non-Jew who had sexual relations with his granddaughter. The child born of this union is simultaneously the grandfather's daughter — and therefore the father's sister — and the mother's daughter. The daughter of the mother is therefore the father's sister's daughter — his niece on his sister's side. The child's own child stands in the relationship of "daughter of your sister" to the grandfather-father.

### Multi-Relation

The fourth riddle is the most elaborate. *Baia baia wo wo me'ach hu av v'hu ba'al v'hu bar ba'al v'hu ba'ala d'imei va'ana barta d'ittei v'lo yeihiv pita l'achoi yasmei b'nei bartei* — woe, woe, he is a brother and he is a father and he is a husband and he is the son of a husband and he is a stepfather, and I am his wife's daughter, and yet he will not feed the orphaned brothers who are the sons of his daughter.

*Mishkachat lah be-ovdei kochavim haba al imo, v'holid minah bat, v'chazar uva'al oto bat, v'chazar zakein uva'alah v'holid minah banim* — a non-Jew had sexual relations with his mother and produced a daughter. He then had sexual relations with that daughter and had children with her. From the perspective of the daughter: this man is her biological father and brother (since he was born of his mother, and she shares the same mother); he is her husband (since he had sexual relations with her); and since his father also had sexual relations with her, he is the son of her husband as well. He is thus simultaneously her brother, father, husband, and husband's son. And he withholds food from the orphaned sons — who are at once his children and the sons of his daughter.

### Cousins Case

The fifth riddle: *ana ve'at achin, ana ve'avuch achin, ana ve'imach achin* — you and I are siblings; you and your father are siblings; you and your mother are siblings — meaning, I and your mother are siblings. *Mishkachat lah be-ovdei kochavim haba al imo v'holid minah shetei banot, v'chazar uva'al achat meihen v'holid minah ben* — a non-Jew had sexual relations with his mother and produced two daughters. He then had sexual relations with one of the daughters and had a son. The other daughter says to the son: you and I are siblings — we share the same father. I and your father are siblings — we also share the same father. I and your mother are siblings — your mother and I are sisters, born of the same mother.

### First Cousins

The sixth riddle is, by comparison, almost refreshingly simple: *ana ve'at benei achi, ana ve'avuch benei achi, ana ve'imach benei achi* — you and I are the children of siblings (i.e., first cousins); I and your father are first cousins; I and your mother are first cousins. The *Gemara* notes that this case does not require any incest scenario at all — *habita nami mishkachat lah* — you can construct it from entirely regular marriages. For instance, *Reuven sheyesh lo shetei banot* — Reuven has two daughters. Shimon marries one of them. Levi's son marries the other. Then Shimon's son says to Levi's grandson: you and I are first cousins (our mothers are sisters); I and your father are first cousins (he is Levi's son and I am Shimon's son, whose mothers were sisters); and I and your mother are first cousins (your mother is Reuven's daughter, and so is my mother).

### I Am My Grandpa

The *Gemara*'s series of riddles calls to mind a famous American novelty song — *I Am My Own Grandpa* — which presents a superficially similar tangle of relationships arising from perfectly legal marriages:

> When I was 23, I was married to a widow who was pretty as can be. This widow had a grown-up daughter who had hair of red. My father fell in love with her and soon they, too, were wed. This made my dad my son-in-law and changed my very life. My daughter was my mother 'cause she was my father's wife. To complicate the matters, even though it brought me joy, I soon became the father of a bouncing baby boy. My little baby then became a brother-in-law to dad, and so became my uncle, though it made me very sad. For if he was my uncle, then that also made him brother of the widow's grown-up daughter who of course was my stepmother. Father's wife then had a son, kept him on the run, and he became my grandchild, for he was my daughter's son. My wife is now my mother's mother, and it makes me blue, because although she is my wife, she's my grandmother too. If my wife is my grandmother, then I'm her grandchild, and every time I think of it, it nearly drives me wild. For now I have become the strangest case you ever saw. As husband of my grandmother, I am my own grandpa!

The crucial distinction, of course, is that the *Gemara*'s riddles required incest — conducted, in its framing, by non-Jews — to generate the overlapping relationships, whereas the song achieves its tangle entirely through regular and entirely permitted marriages. *Beheter* — all above board. Though, as is worth noting, in most jurisdictions at present, not all of the marriages involved would be legally permitted.

---

---

# Yevamot 99

## Brother's Wife After Con…

### Ger & Brother's Wife

The daf opens with a question that has occupied the preceding discussion: may a *ger* marry the wife of his biological brother after both have converted? The Gemara has been bringing various proofs, each of which it finds ways to deflect. The current attempt to resolve the matter comes from a *baraita* introduced with the formula *ta shema*.

The *baraita* opens with the case of *ger she-haysa lidato bi-kedushah ve-horato she-lo bi-kedushah* — a convert whose conception occurred before his mother's conversion but whose birth occurred after it. The ruling: *yesh lo she'ar ha-em, ve-ein lo she'ar ha-av* — there remains a prohibited-relative relationship on the mother's side, but not on the father's side. The practical illustration given is *nasa achoto min ha-em, yotzi* — if he marries a woman who is his maternal half-sister (biologically, though not legally, since she was born before their mother converted and the legal bond of kinship was severed), he must divorce her. But if she is only his paternal half-sister, *yekayem* — he may maintain the marriage. What is striking here is that despite the obvious biological incest, the paternal relation does not trouble us. The reason, as the preceding discussion has established, is that relationships on the mother's side are far more evidently perceived by others as genuine familial bonds, whereas paternal relationships among non-Jews are not perceived in the same way.

### Maternal vs. Paternal Si…

The *baraita* continues with a further distinction. *Achot ha-av min ha-em, yotzi* — if his father's sister is a maternal sibling of his father's (i.e., the father and the aunt share a mother), he must divorce her. But if the father and his sister are only paternal siblings, *yekayem* — the marriage stands. The same logic operating on the sibling level is extended one generation upward: whether the relation is problematic depends on whether the sibling bond runs through the mother or through the father.

Similarly, *achot ha-em min ha-em, yotzi* — a mother's maternal sister clearly falls under the prohibition. Then comes the interesting mirror case: *achot ha-em min ha-av* — a mother's sister who is related to his mother only through their shared father (a paternal sister). Here the mother is one link in the chain, but the sibling bond itself is paternal. *Rabbi Meir omer yotzi* — Rabbi Meir says he must still divorce, on the grounds that *kol ervah she-mishum she'ar ha-em yotzi, mishum ha-av yekayem*: any prohibited relation that involves the maternal line at any point requires dissolution. *Chachamim omrim yekayem* — the Sages, however, hold that what matters is the nature of the sibling bond, and a paternal sibling bond is not treated as a prohibited maternal relationship even when one generation removed through the mother.

### Rashi vs. Tosafot Debate

The underlying rationale for why the maternal side generates this prohibition while the paternal side does not is debated by *Rashi* and *Tosafot*. *Rashi* frames it as a *gezeirah*: if we allow this person to maintain a marriage to a woman who was his sister before conversion, we will come to allow him to marry a sister who was born after conversion — a woman who is legally his sister under Jewish law. *Tosafot* rejects the *gezeirah* framing and instead argues that the concern is one of appearance (*mar'it ayin*): because the maternal relationship is perceived by onlookers as a genuine sibling bond, allowing such a marriage looks inherently improper. According to *Tosafot*, there is no fear of a mistaken legal conclusion, merely of a disturbing social appearance. *Tosafot* notes that the practical implications of these two positions differ in certain cases, and takes the appearance-based rationale as more fundamental. The critical point for both opinions is that the concern is triggered specifically by the maternal relation, which is the one that registers publicly as a family bond.

### Father's Sibling Relatio…

The extension to the father's sibling relationship warrants brief clarification. Even though the case of *achot ha-av min ha-em* runs through the father — the ger's relation to this woman is via his father's sibling bond — *Rashi* explains that since the category remains one of sibling, and the sibling bond in question runs through a mother (the father and his sister share a mother), the same sensitivity applies. The logic is that we are still operating within the framework of maternal siblinghood, even if the pathway to the ger runs through his father. This is why Rabbi Meir's sweeping rule captures it: any *ervah* that reaches the convert through a maternal-sibling link requires divorce.

### Brother & Uncle's Wife P…

The *baraita* now turns directly to the very question the Gemara has been investigating. *U-mutar be-eshet achiv me-imo* — he is permitted to marry his maternal brother's wife. This is exactly our question, and the *baraita* answers it affirmatively. Even though he may not marry his maternal sister herself, he may marry his maternal brother's wife — the reasoning being that while the blood relation on the maternal side is perceived as genuine, the marital extension (his brother's wife) is one further degree removed, and we are correspondingly more lenient. *U-ve-eshet achi aviv* — he is likewise permitted to marry his uncle's wife, since again the bond is through marriage rather than blood. *Ve-she'ar kol arayot mutarot lo* — and all other formerly prohibited relations are now permitted to him. The Gemara specifies that *le-atuyei eshet ha-av* — this includes, for example, his father's wife, who is no longer legally related to him since his father was a non-Jew.

### Mother-Daughter Marriage…

A striking case follows: *nasa isha u-vittah* — if before his conversion he had been married to both a woman and her daughter, upon converting *kones achat u-motzi achat* — he may keep one of them but must divorce the other. This might seem puzzling: if both women converted along with him, they are no longer legally mother and daughter — *ger she-nitgayyer ke-katan she-nolad dami*, a convert is like a newborn with no prior legal relations. So why can he not keep both? The answer is that this is a case of blood relation — a biological mother and daughter — and the perception of that bond is so powerful that we do not permit him to remain married to both simultaneously, even after conversion. The *baraita* adds *lechatchila lo yichnos* — he should not enter such an arrangement even initially.

### Baraita on Brother's Wife

The Gemara now zeroes in on the section of the *baraita* relevant to its inquiry: *katani mihat u-mutar be-eshet achiv* — the *baraita* taught that he is permitted to marry his brother's wife. The Gemara asks: *mai lav de-nasvu ke-shehu ger* — does this not refer to the obvious case where his brother married this woman after the *ger* had already converted, making her legally his brother's wife while the *ger* and his brother share a genuine legal bond of siblinghood? If so, this *baraita* would directly answer our question in the permissive direction.

### Non-Jew Marriage Resolut…

The Gemara deflects: *lo, de-nasvu ke-shehu akum* — no, the *baraita* speaks of a woman his brother had married while still a non-Jew. In that case, the brother's conversion dissolves the marriage, meaning the woman was never legally his brother's wife under Jewish law. The Gemara has now deployed the same escape it used in every prior case: the *baraita* speaks only of a pre-conversion marriage.

### No Gezerah Concern

But then the Gemara adds: *mahu de-teima, ligzor ke-shehu akum atu ke-shehu ger* — one might have thought we should issue a decree prohibiting even a pre-conversion brother's-wife relationship lest it lead to permitting the post-conversion scenario. *Kamashma lan* — the *baraita* teaches us that we make no such decree. The practical upshot of the Gemara's entire discussion is thus: the evidence from all these cases, when taken together, clearly points to the conclusion that a *ger* marrying his biological brother's wife is permitted at least *mi-de-oraita*, and the evidence strongly suggests it is permitted *mi-de-rabbanan* as well — though the Gemara has not arrived at a definitive resolution.

### Lechatchila Restrictions

The Gemara returns to the *lechatchila* ruling in the *baraita*: *nasa isha u-vittah, kones achat u-motzi achat, lechatchila lo yichnos*. The Gemara objects: *hashtah mafik mafik, lechatchila mibaya?* — if he must divorce one of them even after the fact, is it necessary to add that he shouldn't do it *lechatchila*? The Gemara resolves this: the *lechatchila* clause does not refer to the mother-daughter case immediately preceding it, but rather to the earlier rulings — those cases where the Rabbis said he may maintain a marriage *bedi'avad*. On those, the *baraita* now adds: even though *bedi'avad* the marriage stands, one should not enter into such a situation *lechatchila*, even in something like a paternal sister case.

### Wife's Death & Mother-in…

The *baraita* concludes with: *metah ishto mutar be-chamato* — after his wife dies, he may marry her mother (the biological mother, now a convert and hence legally no longer his mother-in-law). *Ve-ika de-amrei asur be-chamato* — some versions state that even after the wife's death he may not marry her. The Gemara identifies these two positions: *chada ke-Rabbi Yishmael ve-chada ke-Rabbi Akiva*.

The stringent view follows Rabbi Yishmael, who holds that a man's mother-in-law remains fully prohibited even after his wife's death — *chamato le-achar mitah be-isura kayma*, the prohibition does not weaken. Accordingly, *le-gabei ger, gazru bei Rabbanan* — the Rabbis imposed the same rule on the *ger*, making no distinction for the post-death scenario. The lenient view follows Rabbi Akiva, who holds that after the wife's death the prohibition against the mother-in-law weakens — *kalash lei isura*. *Tosafot* notes that "weakened" for Rabbi Akiva still means a biblical prohibition carrying *karet*, but it is no longer a capital offense. Since there is some degree of weakening, and the prohibition applicable to the *ger* in any event is only *mi-de-rabbanan*, the Rabbis did not extend their decree to the post-death scenario according to this view. *Tosafot* concedes that the reasoning is not entirely obvious — why a non-capital prohibition should generate a more lenient rabbinic stance toward the *ger* — but accepts this as the Gemara's framework.

---

## Mixed Children Scenarios

### Five Women Setup

The Mishnah now introduces what is one of the more involved practical constructions in the tractate. *Chamesh nashim she-nisarvu vildoseihen* — five women whose newborn children became mixed up with one another. The scenario is that the women were all in the same location — a cave, or as one might modernize it, a darkened ward — and gave birth simultaneously, after which it became impossible to determine whose child was whose. The critical detail is that each of these five women also has an older child whose identity is certain. Thus there are two groups of sons: five young men of known identity, one per mother, and five young men of completely uncertain identity, any one of whom could be the son of any of the five mothers.

All five of the uncertain-identity sons grow up, marry women, and then die childless. This triggers the laws of *yibum* and *chalitzah*: the widows require either levirate marriage or release. The known brothers — one per mother — must step forward, but the problem is that nobody knows which of the five mixed sons is his brother.

### Rotation & Yibum

The Mishnah's ruling: *arba'ah choltzin le-achat ve-echad meyabbemet* — for each widow, four of the known brothers perform *chalitzah* and one performs *yibum*. The rotation proceeds so that for each successive widow, a different known brother is the one who performs *yibum*. The Gemara clarifies that this is not the only valid arrangement — one could in principle have a single man perform *yibum* with all five widows — but the Mishnah teaches that the rotating arrangement is also permitted and perhaps preferable, as each man may thereby happen to perform *yibum* with his own sister-in-law.

The Gemara makes explicit why the rotation is preferable: *dilma mistarmia le-didei* — perhaps by this arrangement each man's rightful sister-in-law will fall to him, maximizing the chance that each act of *yibum* is halakhically optimal. From a purely combinatorial standpoint, if one man performs *yibum* with all five, exactly one of the five acts of *yibum* will be with his genuine sister-in-law, while the remaining four are simply permitted marriages to unrelated women. With the rotation, one could in a favorable case have all five *yibum* acts performed by the correct men — though one could equally have none done correctly.

Regarding the widows' situation: it is worth noting that the Mishnah does not simply require all five known brothers to perform *chalitzah* and leave the women as *chalutzohs*. Rather, it actively structures a rotation to ensure each woman receives *yibum* as well, reflecting a concern either for the woman's interests or for the performance of the *mitzvah* of *yibum* itself.

### Chalitzah Before Yibum

The Gemara adds an important procedural requirement: *vedavka machlatz ve-hadar yibbumei* — specifically, the *chalitzah* from the four must precede the *yibum* by the fifth. One may not begin with *yibum*: *aval yibumei be-reisha la, de-kapaga bi-yevamah la-shuk* — because if *yibum* is performed first, the man might be having relations with a woman who is in fact not his sister-in-law but still requires *chalitzah* from someone else to be released. To cohabit with such a woman would constitute *yevamah la-shuk*, a violation of her *yibbum*-bond without proper resolution.

### Partial Brothers' Chalit…

The Mishnah continues: *miktzatan achin u-miktzatan she-ein achin* — some of the known brothers are full brothers to some of the mixed sons and mere maternal half-brothers to others. The ruling seems strange at first: *ha-achin choltzin ve-she-ein achin meyabbemin* — the brothers do *chalitzah* and the non-brothers do *yibum*. The Gemara asks: *mai ka-amar* — what could this possibly mean? A maternal half-brother has no obligation of *yibum* or *chalitzah* whatsoever.

### Paternal-Maternal Mix

Rav Safra explains: *miktzat achin min ha-av u-miktzat achin min ha-em* — the case is where some of the known brothers are only paternal half-brothers and some are only maternal half-brothers to the mixed sons. *Achin min ha-em choltzin ve-achin min ha-av meyabbemin* — the maternal half-brothers perform *chalitzah* and the paternal half-brothers perform *yibum*?

This too seems backwards. *Rashi* clarifies the underlying situation: suppose one of the known brothers is a paternal half-brother to one of the mixed sons and a maternal half-brother to another. He cannot perform *yibum*, because one of the widows might be the wife of his maternal half-brother — and cohabiting with his maternal half-brother's wife would constitute an *issur arayot* with no *mitzvah* of *yibum* attached. He must, however, perform *chalitzah* with all the widows, because he needs to free the wife of his paternal half-brother. The combined effect is: *chalitzah* for all, and no *yibum*.

### Kohanim Restrictions

*Miktzatan kohanim u-miktzatan she-ein kohanim* — some of the known brothers are *kohanim* and some are not. A *kohen* may not marry a *chalutzah*, but *chalitzah* must precede *yibum*. Therefore, once a widow has received *chalitzah* from others, the *kohen* may no longer perform *yibum* with her — she has become a *chalutzah*. Accordingly: *kohanim choltzin ve-she-ein kohanim meyabbemin* — the *kohanim* can only perform *chalitzah*, while the non-*kohanim* perform *yibum*. In this arrangement, a single non-*kohen* may end up performing *yibum* with more than one widow, since the equal one-to-one rotation of the Mishnah's first scenario no longer holds.

### All Chalitzah Cases

The Mishnah then presents the most restrictive configuration: *miktzatan kohanim u-miktzatan achin min ha-em* — some have the *kohen* restriction and others have the maternal-half-brother restriction, with no one in the group who has neither limitation. In such a case, *elu va-elu choltzin ve-lo meyabbemin* — every one of the known brothers can only perform *chalitzah*, and no *yibum* is performed at all. Neither category of men can perform *yibum*: those with a maternal half-brother among the mixed sons cannot, lest they commit an *issur arayot*, and the *kohanim* cannot, lest they marry a *chalutzah*.

---

## Doubtful Incest Relations

### Mother & Other Woman

The Gemara now presents a series of cases where a person may be obligated to perform *chalitzah* with a woman who is possibly his own close relative. These scenarios emerge from the same framework of mixed-up children.

*Yesh choletz le-imo mi-safek la-achoto mi-safek le-vito mi-safek* — there are cases in which someone may be required to perform *chalitzah* with his mother under uncertainty, with his sister under uncertainty, or with his daughter under uncertainty.

The case of the mother: *imo ve-ishah acheret, ve-lahen shenei zecharim, ve-chazru ve-yaldu shenei zecharim be-me'arah* — his mother and another woman each have sons whose identity is known, and then both women give birth to two sons in a cave, with the identities mixed. *U-va benah shel zo ve-nasa imah shel zo u-meitu* — one of the known sons married the other woman, and then both men die childless. Now the widow requires *yibum* or *chalitzah*. The obligation falls on the deceased husband's brother — but one of the mixed-identity sons is certainly the deceased's brother, while the other is the widow's son. Neither can perform *yibum*. But who does *chalitzah*? Since we do not know which of the two mixed-identity men is the brother, both must perform *chalitzah*. The result is *nimtza kol echad ve-echad choletz le-imo mi-safek* — at least one of the men is definitively performing *chalitzah* with his own mother, though under uncertainty.

### Brother-Sister Mix

The case of the sister: *imo ve-ishah acheret she-yaldu shtei nekevot be-machba* — his mother and another woman gave birth to two daughters in hiding, with identities mixed. *U-va'u acheihem shelo mi-ota ha-em ve-nasa'um* — their paternal half-brothers (sharing the same father but different mothers) came and married these two daughters. This is permitted: since the brothers share only a father and not a mother with these daughters, and the daughters' identities are entirely unknown, these men may marry them. The husbands then die childless.

Now the paternal half-brothers of the deceased must perform *chalitzah*. But two women must receive *chalitzah*, and one of the two women is the surviving brother's sister — the daughter born to his mother. He cannot perform *yibum* and must perform *chalitzah* with both. He is therefore definitively performing *chalitzah* with his sister, albeit under uncertainty as to which one she is. *Nimtza choletz achoto mi-safek*.

### Paternal Brothers & Daug…

The case of the daughter: *isha ve-ishah acheret she-yaldu shtei nekevot be-machba* — his wife and another woman gave birth to two daughters in a cave, identities mixed. *U-va'u acheihem ve-nasa'um* — the man's brothers came and married these daughters. A man is permitted to marry his niece, so no prohibition applies at the time of the marriages. The brothers then die childless. The surviving brother — the father of one of the girls — must now perform *chalitzah* with both widows, since one of them is his daughter. *Choletz le-vito mi-safek*.

*Rashi* works to make each of these cases as precise and structurally parallel as possible, so that in each scenario the person performing *chalitzah* is certainly doing so with his close relative — not merely possibly doing so — while the uncertainty lies only in *which* of the women that relative is. The Gemara confirms this reading and notes that the parallel constructions for each sub-case can be built either with one brother performing *chalitzah* to both women or with two brothers on either side, the result in each case being the same.

### Niece & Daughter

The subsection of the daughter case draws the section to a close. The Gemara confirms that in the scenario of *isha ve-ishah acheret*, his wife and another woman giving birth to daughters whose identities are mixed, and his brothers marrying those daughters — both daughters must receive *chalitzah* from the surviving brother. *Zeh choletz le-vito mi-safek ve-zeh choletz le-vito mi-safek* — each of the relevant men is performing *chalitzah* with his own possible daughter.

---

## Five Categories Scenario

### Slave Conversion Setup

The Gemara now introduces a celebrated *baraita* attributed to Rabbi Meir: *pe'amim she-molidin chamesh umot* — sometimes a man and a woman can produce children belonging to five distinct national-halachic categories. *Yisrael she-lakach eved ve-shifcha min ha-shuk* — a Jew purchased a male and female non-Jewish slave from the marketplace. *Ve-lahem shenei vanim* — they already had two biological children. These children are not themselves slaves: either because children of non-Jewish slaves owned by non-Jews were not automatically considered the property of a new Jewish owner, or — as *Rashi* discusses — because the parents were enslaved only after the children had already been born.

*Ve-nitgayyer echad mehem* — one of those two children converted. The result: *nimtza echad geir ve-echad oved kochavim* — one child is a *ger* and one is a non-Jew. *Hitbilu le-shem avdut* — the two parents were then immersed in a *mikveh* to become *avdei Kena'ani* of the Jewish owner. *Ve-nizkak zeh la-zeh* — they then cohabited. A child born at this point is a slave. So now there are three children: a *ger*, a non-Jew, and a slave.

### Mamzer from Eved

*Shichrar et ha-shifcha* — the master then freed the female slave. *U-va aleha ha-eved* — the male slave continued to cohabit with her. The child of a slave and a free woman, following the position of Rabbi Meir (who defines a *mamzer* broadly to include such a union), is a *mamzer*. Thus the fourth category is added: *harei kan geir ve-oved kochavim ve-eved u-mamzer*. The Gemara confirms this is specifically the *chiddush* of the case: *oved kochavim ve-eved ha-ba al bat Yisrael havei mamzer* — an *eved* who cohabits with a free woman produces a *mamzer*, at least according to this *baraita* and its underlying authority.

### Israeli-born Status

*Shichrar shenehem ve-hisiam zeh la-zeh* — the master then freed both the male slave and the woman and caused them to marry one another. The child born of a freed male slave and a freed female slave who are now legally married is a full-fledged Jew born in Israel — a *Yisrael*. Thus: *harei kan geir ve-oved kochavim ve-eved u-mamzer ve-Yisrael* — five distinct categories from one couple.

---

## Selling Father for Ketub…

### Mother's Ketubah Lien

Another playful *baraita*: *yesh mocher et aviv le-hagbot et ketuvas immo* — there is a case in which a man sells his own father in order to pay his mother's *ketubah*. *Keitzad?* — how?

*Yisrael she-lakach eved ve-shifcha min ha-shuk, ve-lahem ben* — a Jew bought a male and female slave who had a son. *Ve-shichrar et ha-shifcha ve-nesa'ah* — the master freed the female slave and married her. He now owns his new wife's former husband as a slave. *Ve-amar ve-chasav kol nechasai le-vni* — after marrying this woman, the master transferred all his property to her son — the son she had had with the slave.
