When the master dies, his wife (the freed slave, now his widow) wishes to collect her *ketubah*. The lien for the *ketubah* falls on her son, who now owns all the property — including his own biological father, who remains a slave. In order to pay off his mother's *ketubah*, the son sells his father.

### Slave Lien Chiddush

*Ma kamashma lan?* — what is the *chiddush*? *Kula Rabbi Meir hi* — this *baraita* follows Rabbi Meir throughout. *Ve-avda ke-metalteli, u-metalteli mishtabdi li-ketuvah* — the legal novelty is that Rabbi Meir holds that an *eved* has the status of movable property (*metalteli*), and Rabbi Meir further holds that movable property is subject to the lien of a *ketubah*. Alternatively, *ve-i ba'it eima, avda ke-mikarkei dami* — one might say the *chiddush* is that Rabbi Meir treats an *eved* as real property (*mikarka'i*), which is obviously subject to a *ketubah* lien. The point in either reading is a legal principle about *eved* and *ketubah* liens — not a moral lesson about selling one's father.

---

## Uncle-Nephew Mix

### Uncle-Nephew Setup

The Mishnah now presents a variation: *ha-isha she-nitarev valdah be-vlad kallatah* — a woman whose newborn child was mixed up with her daughter-in-law's newborn child. The result is a man and his nephew of uncertain identity — neither the uncle nor the nephew knows who he is. Both men grow up, marry, and die childless.

### Other Brothers Chalitzah

The Mishnah distinguishes between different categories of brothers who must now respond. *Bnei ha-kalah choltzin ve-lo meyabbemin* — the other sons of the daughter-in-law (i.e., the additional brothers of the mixed sons from that side) may only perform *chalitzah*, not *yibum*. The reason: *safek eshet achiv safek eshet achei aviv* — each widow might be a brother's wife (requiring *yibum*) or might be an uncle's wife (an *ervah*). Since the *ervah* possibility exists, *yibum* is prohibited.

### Flexible Chalitzah or Yi…

*Bnei ha-zekenah* — the other sons of the older woman (from the grandmother's line, so to speak) are in a more favorable position. For them, *o choltzin o meyabbemin* — they may perform either *chalitzah* or *yibum*. The reason: *safek eshet achiv ve-eshet ben achiv* — each widow is either a brother's wife or a nephew's wife. Both possibilities permit *yibum* or *chalitzah* without any *ervah* concern.

### Role Reversal

*Meitu ha-kesherim* — the Gemara specifies that when "the kosher ones" die, the reference is not that the others are disqualified (*pesulim*) in some way, but simply that those of certain identity (*ha-vadayim*) have now died. Rav Pappa accordingly emends the reading: *eima u-meitu ha-vadayim* — read it as "those of certain identity died." The situation then reverses: *ha-ta'arovot li-vnei ha-zekenah choltzin ve-lo meyabbemin*, while *li-vnei ha-kalah echad choletz ve-echad meyabem* — the analysis mirrors what was laid out above, with the widow categories flipped. As before, the Gemara emphasizes: *vedavka be-reisha chalitzah ve-hadar yibum, aval yibum be-reisha la* — the mandatory order is *chalitzah* first, then *yibum*, never the reverse.

---

## Kohen & Slave Child Mix

### Terumah Sharing

The final Mishnah of the daf introduces the case of *kohenet she-nitarev valdah be-vlad shifchatah* — a *kohen*'s wife whose newborn child was mixed up with her slave's newborn child. One of the two mixed children is a *kohen* and one is a *kohen*'s slave. Since the slave of a *kohen* eats *terumah*, both children may eat *terumah* — whichever one is the slave eats by virtue of his status as the slave of a *kohen*, and the other eats as the *kohen* himself. *Chelkei ke-echad ba-goren* — at the threshing floor they receive one combined portion, since regardless of which is which, together they are entitled to only a single family portion.

### Restrictions While Mixed

*Ve-einam mitam'im le-meitim* — they may not contract corpse-*tumah*, since one of them is a *kohen*. *Ve-einam nosim nashim* — they may not marry, since the *kohen* among them may only marry certain categories of women while the slave may not marry at all; the two categories of permitted women are mutually exclusive. *Bein kesherot bein pesulot* — this restriction holds regardless of whether the prospective wife is of fully valid lineage or not.

### After Mutual Freedom

*Higdilu ha-ta'arovot ve-shichreru zeh et zeh* — when they grew up, they freed one another: each declared that if the other is the slave and he himself is the master, he frees him. Now both are free men. *Nosim nashim re'uyot li-khunah* — they may now marry women who are fit to marry *kohanim*, since whoever the *kohen* among them is, he must marry appropriately, and the freed slave may also marry such women. *Ve-einam mitam'im le-meitim* — they still may not contract corpse-*tumah*, as one remains a *kohen*. *Ve-im nitme'u einam sofgin et ha-arba'im* — if they did contract *tumah*, they do not receive lashes, because lashes require certainty as to which man is the definite *kohen*.

### Terumah Selling Solution

*Ve-einam ochlim bi-terumah* — they may no longer eat *terumah*. Previously, even the slave was permitted because a *kohen*'s slave eats *terumah*. Now that both are free, neither can be presumed to be the *kohen*'s slave, and the uncertainty means neither may eat. *Ve-im achlu einam meshalmin keren ve-chomesh* — if they did eat *terumah*, they need not pay the principal and the fifth that a non-*kohen* who eats *terumah* must pay, since either of them might in fact be a *kohen* eating his own *terumah*.

*Ve-einam cholkim al ha-goren* — they cannot receive *terumah* at the threshing floor, since neither is certainly a *kohen* or a *kohen*'s slave. *U-mochrin et ha-terumah ve-ha-damim shelahen* — however, the *terumah* they separate from their own produce they need not give to anyone else. They may sell it and keep the money. The rationale is *ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-ra'ayah*: the claimant bears the burden of proof. Anyone seeking to take their *terumah* would need to prove that they are not *kohanim*, and this cannot be established. They themselves, however, may not eat it, since they might equally not be *kohanim*.

*Ve-einam cholkim be-kodshei ha-mikdash* — they do not receive a share in the *kodshim* of the *Beit Hamikdash*, since one may not be a *kohen*. *Ve-ein notnim lahem kodshim* — one does not give them *korbanot* to sacrifice, nor — as will be seen — does one give them a *bechor*.

### Bechor Waiting for Mum

The Mishnah addresses *bechor*: if one of them has a firstborn animal, *yireh ad she-yista'ev* — it is allowed to graze until it develops a *mum* (a blemish). Once the *bechor* has a *mum*, the *kohen* may eat it outside the *Beit Hamikdash* without the act of *korban* being brought. Since one of the two men is a *kohen*, and since neither needs to hand the animal to another *kohen* (by virtue of *ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-ra'ayah*), they wait out the *bechor*'s life until it is blemished and then eat it.

Regarding their own *korbanot*: *Rashi* addresses two possibilities. If they have a *bechor*, the procedure is as above. If they have an *olah* or *chatat* to bring, they may designate a *kohen* to perform the *avodah* on their behalf and declare that if they themselves are the *kohen*, they retain the right to the *or* (hide) or equivalent, since it may belong to them — but they cannot personally perform the *avodah* or eat from the *kodshim* portions.

### Double Stringencies

*Ve-notnim alav chomrei kohanim ve-chomrei Yisraelim* — they are treated with the stringencies of both *kohanim* and *Yisraelim*. This formulation encapsulates the entire preceding discussion: any stringency that attaches to *kohanim* applies because one of them may be the *kohen*, and any stringency that attaches to ordinary Israelites applies because one of them may be the non-*kohen*. The leniences of either status are unavailable to either man in their mixed condition.

---

## Terumah & Kohen Percepti…

### Rabbi Yehudah's Rule

The Mishnah's ruling that the two mixed children must go to the threshing floor together — *chelek ke-echad* — is now explained in light of a *machlokes* between Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Yossi. *Ein cholkin terumah le-eved ela im kein rabo imo, divrei Rabbi Yehudah* — Rabbi Yehudah holds that one does not distribute *terumah* to a slave unless his master is present with him. The *baraita* requires the two of them to come together: *chelek ke-echad* means they must appear together to collect.

### Rabbi Yossi's Allowance

*Rabbi Yossi omer yachol she-yomar: im kohen ani, tnu li bishvil atzmi; ve-im eved le-kohen ani, tnu li bishvil rabbi* — Rabbi Yossi says the slave may appear alone and state: "If I am a *kohen*, give it to me on my own account; if I am a slave of a *kohen*, give it to me on behalf of my master." Under this reasoning, the slave's presence alone is sufficient, and there is no need for the master to accompany him.

### Perception-Based Halacha

The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehudah's position: *bi-mkomo shel Rabbi Yehudah hayu ma'alin mi-terumah le-yuchasin* — in Rabbi Yehudah's locale, the practice of collecting *terumah* was treated as evidence of *kohen* lineage. If a man came to the threshing floor and collected *terumah*, people would assume he was a *kohen* and would arrange marriages for him accordingly — marrying him off to women appropriate for *kohanim*.

Given this communal expectation, if a slave were to go alone to collect *terumah*, bystanders would assume he was a *kohen* and treat him as such in matters of marriage and lineage. Therefore, in Rabbi Yehudah's locale, the rule is that a slave may only collect *terumah* in the presence of his master, making the nature of the arrangement evident. The logic is circular in an instructive way: because only *kohanim* collect *terumah*, people infer that *kohen* status from *terumah* collection; and because people draw that inference, the halacha must protect against it by ensuring no slave collects alone. *Bi-mkomo shel Rabbi Yossi lo hayu ma'alin mi-terumah le-yuchasin* — in Rabbi Yossi's locale, no such assumption was made. People understood that one who collected *terumah* might be a slave doing so on his master's behalf, so no presumption of *kohen* lineage attached, and the slave could collect independently.

### Elazar's Testimony

A *baraita* relates: *amar Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok, miyamai lo he'edeti ela eidut achat* — Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok said that in his entire life he gave only one testimony, and that testimony led to a result in which *he'elu eved li-khunah al pi* — a slave was elevated to *kohen* status on the basis of his words. He had testified that a certain man collected *terumah*, and on that basis the community treated the man as a *kohen* and arranged a marriage for him accordingly — only for it to emerge that the man was in fact a slave.

### Prevented Error

The Gemara objects: *ve-he'elu salka da'atak?* — could we truly think that such an error actually occurred and was consummated, particularly through the testimony of a *tzaddik* of Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok's stature? *Hash-ta bi-vehemtan shel tzaddikim ein ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu meivi takala al yadam; tzaddikim atzmam lo kol she-kein* — if the Holy One does not allow even the animals of the righteous to stumble into transgression (as illustrated by the donkey of Pinchas ben Yair, which would not eat *tevel*), how much more would He not allow a *tzaddik* himself to cause such an outcome. Therefore: *ela eima, bikshu le-ha'alot eved li-khunah al pi* — emend the text to say that they were *about* to elevate a slave to *kohen* status on the basis of his testimony, but were prevented before the error was finalized.

### Locale Customs Difference

The Gemara then explains how such a near-error came about. *Chaza be-asrei de-Rabbi Yossi* — Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok witnessed the event in Rabbi Yossi's locale, where slaves routinely collected *terumah* at the threshing floor without their masters present, and where no inference of *kohen* lineage was drawn from such collection. He then testified about what he had seen — "I saw this man collect *terumah*" — but he gave this testimony in Rabbi Yehudah's locale, where the same act of collecting *terumah* was taken as definitive evidence of *kohen* status. The testimony was accurate as a description of events, but its halachic implications were entirely different depending on the locale's custom. In Rabbi Yehudah's locale, his truthful testimony nearly caused a slave to be enrolled as a *kohen* — and the Gemara's emendation ensures that the *tzaddik* was spared from having his words actually produce that outcome.

---

---

# Yevamot 100

## Ten Categories

### Initial List

The *gemara* opens a *baraita* that emerges directly from the preceding discussion about the *kohen* and the slave of a *kohen* whose identities became confused — specifically, the question of whether one may distribute *terumah* to a slave in the absence of a *kohen* without creating the misleading impression that the slave is himself a *kohen*. With that context in mind, *tanu rabbanan*: there are ten categories of people who, although they possess a right to *terumah*, are not given their portion at the threshing floor. The *baraita* then proceeds to enumerate them: the *cheresh*, the *shoteh*, and the *katan*; the *tumtum* and the *androgynos*; the slave; the woman; the *arel* and the *tamei kohen*; and finally, a *kohen* who has married a woman he is forbidden to marry — for instance, a *gerushah*.

The *baraita* then adds that for all of these individuals, one does send the *terumah* to their homes, since they are in fact entitled to *terumah* and permitted to eat it. The exceptions are the *tamei* and the *kohen* married to an unsuitable woman, who are excluded even from home delivery. The reasons behind each category require the *gemara*'s elaboration, since it is not immediately obvious why people who are fully entitled to *terumah* should be denied it at the threshing floor.

### Cheresh, Shoteh, Katan

The *gemara* begins its analysis with the first group: *bishlama cheresh shoteh ve-katan* — understandable. *Lav benei dei'a inhu*, they are not people of mature intellect. But what exactly follows from that? Rashi explains that it is a matter of *ziluta de-terumah le-chalek lahem be-goren le-ein kol* — it is undignified for *terumah* to be distributed to them publicly at the threshing floor. The *goren* is a setting where all can observe who is receiving *terumah*, and handing it over to people whom society does not regard with full respect is seen as disrespectful to the sanctity of *terumah* itself. This is, of course, a striking basis for the ruling, since the concern is less about the legal standing of these individuals and more about how their receipt of *terumah* would be perceived by onlookers.

Tosafot raises a different concern. If the *cheresh* and *shoteh* lack mental competence, perhaps they will fail to guard the *terumah* in a state of *taharah* — which would seem to be the real problem. Yet the *baraita* itself establishes that you do send *terumah* to their homes, which seems to undercut that concern entirely. Tosafot resolves this by noting that presumably such individuals have an *apitropas* — a guardian — overseeing them at home. Even so, says Tosafot, you do not distribute to them at the *gronot* because there may be occasions when they arrive without their guardian. According to Tosafot, then, the *gronot* concern cannot primarily be about their inability to preserve the *terumah*'s *taharah*, since that concern applies at home as well. The reasoning that ultimately prevails in the *gronot* setting must be something else — and here Tosafot presumably would concur with Rashi's account of *ziluta*.

### Tumtum, Androgynous

Regarding the *tumtum* and the *androgynos*, the *gemara* explains: *biryah bifnei atzmo hinhu* — they are their own distinct category of creature, falling outside the standard gender binary. Rashi frames this again as *ziluta de-kodshim* — the same principle of unseemly public distribution. People perceive these individuals as unusual, and because they do not fit neatly into the recognized social categories, distributing *terumah* to them publicly at the *goren* is not regarded as befitting the sanctity of *terumah*.

This is a recurring theme in *hilchos kodshim* more broadly — the *kohanim* with physical blemishes are excluded from Temple service; everything associated with the *Beis Hamikdash* must conform to an aesthetic ideal of wholeness and dignity. There is a real tension here, since *kedushah* is presumably about internal quality, yet the *halacha* here accommodates prevailing social perceptions rather than correcting them. The *gemara* proceeds without pausing to resolve this tension; it simply legislates within the reality of how society actually functions.

### Slaves

The *eved* presents no difficulty: *dilma ati le-asuki mi-terumah le-yuchsin* — people will observe a slave receiving *terumah* at the threshing floor and conclude that he must be a free *kohen*, with the potential that they will then consider marrying him off as such. This is precisely the concern that gave rise to the *baraita* in the first place.

### Arel, Tamei

Regarding the *arel* and the *tamei*, the *gemara* offers a different explanation: *mishum de-me'isi* — there is something abhorrent about it. These individuals are not in a condition that permits them to eat *terumah* at this moment, and handing *terumah* to someone who cannot eat it creates an inherently discordant situation. There is a meaningful distinction between this category and the earlier ones. *Ziluta* is a matter of social perception — how the act of distribution appears to onlookers. *Me'isi*, by contrast, may carry something more objective: it is the essential incompatibility of the transaction itself, giving *terumah* to someone for whom it is currently prohibited, regardless of whether anyone is watching. One might observe that *ziluta* concerns what people see, while *me'isi* concerns what the thing itself is — even if the status of the *arel* is known only to himself.

This distinction also illuminates why the *arel* receives his *terumah* at home even though the *tamei* does not. The *arel* is *anus* — his condition is entirely beyond his control; if his brothers died in *bris milah* he is a hemophiliac and bears no responsibility for his status. Why should he be penalized? You therefore send it to his home, where he can distribute it to his wife, children, and slaves who are permitted to eat it. The *tamei*, one might think, deserves the same treatment — he too may have become *tamei* in the course of fulfilling a *mitzvah*, such as burying a relative. Yet the *gemara* answers: *hai nafush unsei ve-hai lo nafush unsei* — the degree to which the *arel*'s condition is beyond his control is absolute and permanent, whereas the *tamei* can, in principle, immerse in a *mikvah*. As a general communal statement underscoring how important it is for *kohanim* to be zealous about maintaining *taharah*, there is value in not sending *terumah* to the *tamei* even at home — not necessarily as a condemnation of every individual case, but as a collective posture conveying that the community takes *tumah* seriously.

### Women

The remaining category is the woman, and the *gemara* notes that she does not fit any of the obvious explanations. She occupies a recognized place within the social order, she is fully *bat dei'a*, and she falls squarely within the standard gender binary. So *isha mai ta'ama lo*?

*Pligi bah Rav Pappa ve-Rav Huna breih de-Rav Yehoshua*. One says the concern is *mishum gerushah*: if you begin distributing *terumah* at the threshing floor to the wife or daughter of a *kohen*, people may continue to give it to her even after she has been divorced and lost her entitlement — either because they don't realize she has been divorced, or simply because the habit of giving has formed. The other says the concern is *mishum yichud*: a woman should not be going out to the threshing floor, an isolated location, in the manner that Boaz and Ruth illustrates — it is simply improper.

The *gemara* identifies a practical difference between these two positions. Consider a threshing floor that is *de-makrav le-mata* — located close to the city — *ve-lo shchichi bah inshi* — but where there is not much foot traffic at the site itself. If the concern is *gerushah*, there is no problem: because the floor is close to the city, the woman is known there, people are aware of her marital status, and no one will mistakenly give her *terumah* after she is divorced. But because the site itself is quiet, there remains a *yichud* concern. Conversely, a floor that is distant from the city — so people do not know the woman's status — but has heavy traffic, presents no *yichud* concern while retaining a *gerushah* concern.

## Distribution Methods

### Tamei Exception

Returning to the rule that all ten categories receive their *terumah* at home — except the *tamei* and the *kohen* married to an unsuitable woman — the *gemara* presses on the *tamei*. The *kohen* married to a forbidden woman is comprehensible: withholding even home delivery functions as a communal sanction, signaling societal disapproval and applying pressure for him to address the situation. But the *tamei*? Unlike the case of *tumah* being a permanent or semi-permanent state, a *tamei kohen* may well be able to immerse today and become *tahor* by nightfall.

The *gemara*'s answer — *hai nafush unsei ve-hai lo nafush unsei* — draws the line between a condition that is categorically beyond one's control (the *arel*) and one that, however understandable in any given instance, admits at least theoretically of remedy. The withholding of home delivery from the *tamei* is not so much a judgment of each individual case as it is a collective statement of communal seriousness about *tahara* among *kohanim*.

### General Rule

The *gemara* then introduces a second *baraita*: *ha-eved ve-ha-isha ein cholkin lahem terumah be-veit ha-granot* — the slave and the woman do not receive *terumah* at the threshing floor, for the reasons already discussed. This much is simply a restatement. What follows, however, is more complex.

### Women, Ma'aser Ani

The *baraita* continues: *u-ve-makom she-cholkin, notnim la-isha techila u-potrin otam mi-yad* — in a place where they do distribute, they give it to the woman first and send her off immediately. The *gemara* pauses: surely the *baraita* just said you don't give it to women at the threshing floor — so what does it mean to say "in a place where they do give"?

*Hachi kamar*: the reference is not to *terumah* at all. The *baraita* means: in a case where one distributes *ma'aser ani*, you give it to the woman first. *Ma'aser ani* — the poor tithe of the third and sixth years — is owed to impoverished women just as to men, and the concern about *gerushah* simply does not apply, since a woman's entitlement to *ma'aser ani* has nothing to do with her marital status. If the concern driving the *terumah* restriction was *gerushah*, that concern drops away entirely here.

What about *yichud*? Here too, *ma'aser ani* is different: Rashi explains that *ma'aser ani* is distributed not at the threshing floor but *be-toch ha-bayit ba-ir* — within the city — as derived from the verse *ve-achlu vish'arecha ve-save'u*, "they shall eat within your gates," meaning in the city rather than out in the fields. In the city, people are present, the setting is populated, and there is no *yichud* concern. Rashi adds a further reason: *mishum de-lo lichsefu aniyim* — so that the poor are not embarrassed. The precise sense of this last point is not entirely transparent; one might suggest that it means the poor should not have to journey out to the fields and thereby advertise their poverty to the broader public, though Rashi's formulation leaves room for further interpretation.

### Women Priority

Once it is established that women do receive *ma'aser ani* in the city, the *baraita* specifies that they receive it first. *Mah ta'ama mishum ziluta* — because it is unseemly for a woman to be made to stand and wait among a crowd of men. Having established that there is no *yichud* and no *gerushah* concern in this context, propriety requires that the distribution be handled quickly and the woman sent on her way.

Rava adds a striking personal observation. He says: *merish ki havu atu gavra ve-itata le-dina kamei, hava sharina tigra de-gavra be-reisha* — initially, when a man and a woman would come before him for a court case, he would attend to the man's case first, reasoning that the man's greater obligation in *mitzvot* confers a kind of priority status. *Keivan de-shamana lah le-ha* — once he heard this ruling about giving priority to women in the distribution of *ma'aser ani* — *sharina tigra de-itata be-reisha*, he changed his practice and began hearing the woman's case first. *Mah ta'ama mishum ziluta* — because making a woman stand and wait in such a public setting is itself a form of disrespect. Men are more habituated to the public sphere and to waiting in such contexts; women are not, and the norms of society make their prolonged presence in such settings uncomfortable for all. Rava draws a direct halachic inference from a procedural rule about agricultural distribution and applies it to judicial practice — a remarkable illustration of how sensitivity to *kavod ha-briot* can migrate across domains.

## Kohen-Slave Mix

### Forced Release

The *gemara* now returns to the central case that has run through this section: two infants — one the son of a *kohen* and one the slave of that *kohen* — who were mixed up, so that neither can be identified with certainty. The *mishnah* had discussed the scenario in which these two men, now grown, might free one another. The *gemara* probes the language: the *mishnah* says *she-yesh la-hem*, which might suggest that freeing one another is optional. But *amar Rava*: *eima kofin otan u-mishachrin zeh es zeh* — read it as compulsory. The *mishnah* means they are compelled to free one another. The rationale is that neither one can currently marry: he cannot marry a slave woman because he might be a *kohen*, and he cannot marry a free woman because he might be a slave. Such an intolerable state of affairs compels the master to free the slave, as is the rule in analogous cases throughout the *gemara*. The mechanism is a *tenai* — whichever of the two is actually the slave is freed by the other.

### Mincha Rules

After the manumission, the *gemara* establishes that both men are treated with the stringencies of *kohanim* and the stringencies of *Yisrael*. The *gemara* asks: *le-mai hilchasa* — to what practical *halachah* does this double stringency apply, beyond what has already been spelled out?

*Amar Pappa*: *le-minchasam nikmetzes ke-minchas Yisrael, ve-einan ne'echeles ke-minchas kohanim* — regarding their *minchah* offering. When a *Yisrael* brings a *minchah*, the *kohen* takes the *kometz* — the handful — and burns it on the *mizbe'ach*, while the remainder (*shiyarayim*) is eaten by the *kohanim*. When a *kohen* brings a *minchah*, the entire offering is burned: *ve-chol minchas kohen kalil tihyeh, lo te'achel*. What, then, is done with the *minchah* of a person who is uncertain whether he is a *kohen* or a *Yisrael*?

If you perform the *kemitzah* and then eat the remainder, you may have treated as a *minchas Yisrael* something that is actually a *minchas kohen* and should have been fully burned. If you burn the entire thing, you may have burned the remainder of what is actually a *minchas Yisrael*, in which case the remainder ought to have been eaten by *kohanim* rather than burned. The *gemara* proposes: *ha keitzad* — how is it done? The *kometz* is burned first, by itself. The *shiyarayim* is then burned separately. But immediately the *gemara* raises an objection: *kol she-mimenu le-ishim harei hu be-val taktirun* — once any part of an offering has been placed on the altar fire, the remainder is prohibited from being burned on the altar. Burning the *shiyarayim* on the *mizbe'ach* would thus appear to violate this prohibition.

*Amar Rav Yehuda breih de-Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi*: the solution is *de-masik leihu le-shem eitzim* — one places the *shiyarayim* on the altar not as a sacrificial offering but as fuel. By stipulating that the act is one of fueling the altar fire rather than offering a *korban*, the *halakhic* character of the act changes, and the prohibition of *val taktirun* is not violated. This is, as noted, a powerful illustration of how *kavanah* — intention — defines the nature of an act on the *mizbe'ach*.

The *gemara* raises a further complication: this solution works according to Rabbi Eliezer, who accepts the principle of designating remnants as fuel in cases of uncertainty. But what of the Rabbis, who reject that principle? *Avid lei ke-Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon* — the *gemara* invokes a related ruling by Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon, which concerns the *minchas chotei* of a *kohen* — a *minchah* brought as a *chattas*. The question there is whether the entire offering must be burned, as with an ordinary *minchas kohen*, or whether a *kemitzah* is taken. Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon holds that the *kemitzah* is taken but the *shiyarayim* are neither burned on the altar nor eaten; instead, they are scattered on the *beis ha-deshen* — the ash pile located beside the ramp of the altar — which is where disqualified *korbanos* are disposed of.

### Sacrificial Remnants

The *gemara* concludes that even the Rabbis would agree in our case of the *safek kohen safek Yisrael*. Their dispute with Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon concerns only the particulars of the *minchas chotei* of an actual *kohen* — where they hold that the *shiyarayim* should in fact be offered on the altar because it is a *bas hakrava*, a fully offered sacrifice. But in the present case, where one is genuinely uncertain and it is conceded that the *shiyarayim* cannot be eaten (lest the person be a *kohen*) and cannot be offered as a sacrificial remnant on the altar (due to *val taktirun*), even the Rabbis would concede that the *shiyarayim* are scattered on the *beis ha-deshen*, as is done with *pasul korbanos*.

## Paternity Unknown

### Scenario Setup

The *gemara* turns to a fresh category of cases: *mi she-lo shahasa achar ba'alah shloshah chodashim* — a woman who did not wait the required three months after separating from her first husband before remarrying. The concern is that she may have been pregnant when she remarried, so that a child born within an ambiguous window — potentially nine months from the first husband or seven months from the second — has an uncertain paternity. The *mishnah* stipulates that she *nisas ve-yalda* — she remarried and gave birth — and *ein yadu'a ben tesha la-rishon im ben sheva la-acharon* — it cannot be determined whether the child is a nine-month child from the first or a seven-month child from the second.

The *mishnah* further specifies that she also had unambiguous children from both husbands — establishing a clear sibling relationship between the child of uncertain paternity and children from each household, on the maternal side.

### Both Chalitza

When this son of uncertain paternity grows up, marries, and dies without children, the *mishnah* rules: *choltzin ve-lo meyabmin* — both sets of brothers must perform *chalitza*; none may perform *yibum*. This requires explanation. Why can one set not perform *chalitza* while the other performs *yibum*?

Consider the scenario: the brothers from husband one's household are definitely the maternal brothers of the deceased. The brothers from husband two's household are also definitely his maternal brothers. Neither set knows with certainty that they are also his paternal brothers. If one set were to perform *yibum* — even conditionally, reasoning that if they are not the paternal brother, the other set has already released the widow through *chalitza* — there is a fatal flaw: the one who performs *yibum* may be the maternal brother and not the paternal brother. Marrying one's maternal brother's wife falls under the category of *arayos* — incestuous unions. Since maternal brotherhood is certain and paternal brotherhood is uncertain, none of them may risk performing *yibum*. Both sets of brothers must therefore perform *chalitza*.

### Arayos Risk

The *mishnah* continues: *ve-chein hu lahem, choleitz ve-lo meyabem* — and symmetrically, if one of the brothers from either household dies, the son of uncertain paternity himself performs only *chalitza* and not *yibum* with the widow. The reason is the same: he is certainly the maternal brother of that deceased man, and since he cannot be certain he is also the paternal brother, *yibum* would expose him to the *issur arayos* of marrying his maternal brother's wife. Only certainty of paternal brotherhood, which would also establish the obligation of *yibum*, could override the prohibition, and that certainty is absent.

## Multiple Siblings

### Different Mothers

The *mishnah* now introduces a variation: *hayu lo achim min ha-rishon ve-achim min ha-sheini she-lo me'osah ha-eim* — the first and second husbands each had children from *different* mothers. These half-brothers of the child of uncertain paternity are thus not his maternal brothers at all — they share only a possible paternal connection with him.

This changes the analysis entirely. Take, for example, a son of husband one born from a different woman. His relation to the child of uncertain paternity is: possibly his paternal brother (if husband one was the father), but definitely not his maternal brother. If he is not the paternal brother, he is simply an unrelated man. There is therefore no *arayos* concern if he were to marry the widow: either he is the paternal brother and performs a proper *mitzvah* of *yibum*, or he is entirely unrelated to the deceased and the widow is simply a permitted woman to him.

### One Each Option

The *mishnah* rules accordingly: *hu choleitz u-meyabem* — the individual in question may perform either *chalitza* or *yibum*. And when it comes to the brothers collectively: *echad choleitz ve-echad meyabem* — one may perform *chalitza* and another may perform *yibum*. Crucially, the order matters: *chalitza* must come first, and only then may *yibum* follow. If the one who performs *chalitza* is in fact the true paternal brother, the widow is thereby released from the *yibum* obligation entirely and may remarry freely; the second man then simply marries her as any other woman. If the one who performs *chalitza* is not the paternal brother, his *chalitza* was meaningless, and the second man — who is the true paternal brother — performs *yibum* properly. Either way, the outcome is halachically sound.

## Kohen-Unsuitable

### Diet, Purity, Marriage

The *mishnah* turns to the child of uncertain paternity whose two possible fathers are, respectively, a *kohen* and a *Yisrael*. Since he might be a *kohen*, he is required to marry only a woman who is suitable for a *kohen* — *nosei ishah re'uyah le-kohen*. Similarly, he may not become *tamei le-meitim*, since he might be a *kohen* who is Biblically prohibited from corpse *tumah*. Yet if he does become *tamei*, he does not receive lashes — *eino sofeg et ha-arba'im* — because he might be a *Yisrael* to whom that prohibition does not apply, and in the absence of certainty there can be no punitive lashes.

### Terumah Sale, Kodshim

He may not eat *terumah* — *eino ochel bi-trumah* — because he might be a *Yisrael*. Yet if he does eat it, he does not pay the *keren ve-chomesh* — the principal plus a fifth — that a non-*kohen* who eats *terumah* inadvertently is required to pay, because he might be a *kohen* who was entitled to eat it. He does not receive a portion at the threshing floor — *eino cholek al ha-goren* — for the reasons established earlier. However, *terumah* that he himself separates from his own produce belongs to him in the sense that one cannot prove he is not a *kohen*; since he may not eat it but owns it, he sells it and retains the proceeds — *ve-ha-damim shelo*. He does not receive a portion in *kodshei kodashim* — *eino cholek be-kodshei kodashim* — since he cannot prove entitlement, nor is he given priestly gifts.

### Bechor Rules

If someone gives him a *bechor* — a firstborn animal — it is not taken away from him, since he might be a *kohen* who is entitled to it. But since he might not be a *kohen*, he may not eat it while it is unblemished. The *mishnah* rules: *ye-hei ro'eh ad she-yista'ev* — it grazes until it develops a blemish, at which point a *kohen* of certain status may eat it. He is also exempt from the priestly gifts of *zero'a*, *lechayayim*, and *keivah* when he slaughters an animal — since he might be a *kohen* and *kohanim* do not give these gifts to themselves — and he may eat those portions himself, as they are not *kodshim*. The *mishnah* concludes, as with the earlier case: *ve-notnim lo chumrei kohanim ve-chumrei Yisra-elim*.

## Both Kohanim

### Onen, Inheritance

If both possible fathers are *kohanim*, then the child is certainly a *kohen*, since the only circumstance in which a woman could legitimately have been married to a second *kohen* while the first was still alive would be that the first had divorced her — but if she is a *gerushah*, any child from the second *kohen* would be a *chalal*. For both possible sons to be valid *kohanim*, the first husband must have died and the woman remarried as a *widow*, not a *divorcée*. Certainty of *kohen* status is therefore established; what remains at issue is whose son he is.

When either of his two possible fathers dies, he is an *onen* — in the acute mourning status of the day of death — *mi-safek*, out of doubt, and therefore refrains from Temple service. Similarly, when he himself dies, both possible fathers must observe *onen* status, since for each of them he might be their son. Despite all this, he does not become *tamei* to either of them upon death — he might not be that man's son — and they do not become *tamei* to him, for the same reason.

Regarding inheritance: *hu eino yoresh otan* — he cannot inherit from either of them, because the heirs of each household tell him he cannot prove he is their father's son. *Ve-hem yorshim oto* — but if he dies without children, both potential fathers inherit from him, since one of them is certainly his father, and no third party has a superior claim. They divide the estate between them. If he strikes or curses either of his potential fathers, he is exempt from the Biblical prohibitions against striking or cursing one's father, since the paternity cannot be established.

### Temple Service

*Oleh be-mishmaro shel zeh ve-shel zeh* — he may perform Temple service during the *mishmar* week of either family, since one of them is certainly his, and no one can stop him from working. However, *ve-eino cholek* — he does not receive a portion of the *korbanos* distributed to that *mishmar*, since he cannot prove that this particular week is his. If, however, both potential fathers happened to be from the same *mishmar*, then he receives one portion — not two — since he has only one father, whoever that father is, and that father is certainly of this *mishmar*.

## Shtuki

### Shtuki Definition

The *gemara* now introduces the case of the *shtuki* in Shmuel's formulation. *Asarah kohanim omdim u-peirash echad meihen u-va'al* — ten *kohanim* were standing together, one of them went and had relations with a woman, and it is unknown which one. *Ve-ha-valad shtuki* — the child born of this encounter is a *shtuki*. The word itself carries the sense of being silenced or shut down: when the child asks "who is my father?" the answer is, in effect, "we don't know — be quiet."

The mere fact of uncertain paternity might seem to be a question only of inheritance or personal identification, not of fundamental status, since we know with certainty that the child is the son of some *kohen*. Why should the term *shtuki* carry the weight of a significant legal category?

### Genealogy Req.

The *gemara* clarifies: *ilima de-mashtakinan lei mi-nechasei de-aviv* — if it merely means he is deprived of his father's estate, that is obvious and needs no special ruling. The real *chiddush* of *shtuki* is *de-mashtakinan lei mi-dinei kehunah* — he is excluded from the privileges of *kehunah* proper, specifically from serving in the *Beis HaMikdash*, even though we know he is a *kohen* by blood.

The *gemara* derives this from the verse: *ve-hayesa lo u-le-zaro acharav bris kehunas olam* — "and it shall be to him and to his seed after him a covenant of eternal priesthood." *Ba'inan zaro meyuchas acharav* — we require that his lineage be traceable *after him*, meaning that a *kohen*'s descendant must be able to identify his father in order to serve. *Ve-leika* — and in the case of the *shtuki*, that identification is absent.

### Rishon Objection

The *gemara* raises a challenge from an earlier *mishnah*. In the case discussed above — the child born during the ambiguous window whose mother married a second *kohen* after the first — the *mishnah* ruled that *rishon ra'ui lihayos Kohen Gadol* — even the first child, whose paternity between the two *kohanim* is uncertain, is considered fit to serve as *Kohen Gadol*. But if we require *zaro meyuchas acharav* for Temple service, how can someone who does not know which *kohen* was his father serve at all, let alone as *Kohen Gadol*? This appears to be a direct refutation of Shmuel's ruling.

### Znus Distinction

The *gemara* resolves the tension: *zera meyuchas acharav derabbanan u-kra asmachta be'alma* — the requirement of traceable genealogy for Temple service is rabbinic in origin, with the verse serving merely as an *asmachta*. The Rabbinic decree, however, was enacted only in cases involving *znus* — illicit sexual relations. *Ve-chi gazar rabbanan bi-znus?* — the question becomes: when the Rabbis enacted this disqualification, did they intend it to apply to cases of *znus* specifically, or more broadly?

The *gemara* asserts that the Rabbinic sanction applies specifically *bi-znus*: a child born of relations that were inherently illicit and outside the framework of marriage carries a more deeply compromised social and personal status, and it is there that the Rabbis imposed the disqualification from Temple service. *Be-nisu'in lo gazar rabbanan* — in cases of legitimate marriage, the Rabbis did not enact the disqualification. The child from the *mishnah*'s case was born to a woman who was legitimately married — first to husband one, then to husband two — without any *znus* involved. His uncertain paternity is a product of circumstances, not of illegitimacy. That child, therefore, can serve in the *Beis HaMikdash*.

### Legit Marriage

This resolution, however, creates a new problem. The *gemara* challenges: *u-vi-znus mi gazar rabbanan?* — is it actually true that the Rabbis imposed this disqualification in cases of *znus*? Consider our very *mishnah*: *mi she-lo shahasa achar ba'alah shloshah chodashim* — and the case is parsed carefully. The *mishnah* mentions *onen* status for both potential fathers when the child dies, implying that both are alive. If the first husband died, the wife is an *almana* and there is no *znus* at all. For both to be alive and for the child still to be a valid *kohen* on either side, the woman must not have been a *gerushah* — for if she were, the child from the second union would be a *chalal*. The only scenario in which both fathers are alive, the child is a *kohen* on either account, and she has not been divorced is if there was no prior marriage at all — meaning the first relationship was indeed *znus*.

Yet that *mishnah* rules that *oleh be-mishmaro shel zeh ve-shel zeh* — the child of uncertain paternity works in the Temple during the *mishmar* of either family. This appears to be a direct refutation: here is a child born of *znus* who is permitted to serve in the *Beis HaMikdash*, contradicting Shmuel's position.

### Kidushi Taus

The *gemara* offers one resolution: *amar Rav Shemaya be-mema'enes* — perhaps we are dealing with a case of *mi'un*, where the woman had been married to husband one as a minor, in a marriage contracted by her father or brothers, and she exercised her rabbinic right to repudiate it without a *get*. In that case, husband one is alive, she is not a *gerushah*, there was no *znus*, and yet both fathers could be alive. The difficulty with this answer is that a *mema'enes* — a minor girl young enough to exercise *mi'un* — is presumably too young to carry a pregnancy to term safely. As *Rav Bibi* taught before *Rav Nachman*: a *ketana* between the ages of eleven and twelve who becomes pregnant faces mortal danger, and younger than eleven she will not become pregnant at all. A child born of a marriage dissolved by *mi'un* would require the mother to have been a minor, making it nearly impossible for her to have also produced a viable child.

The *gemara* therefore concludes: *mishtakcha lah be-kidushi taus* — the scenario involves a case of *kidushi taus*, a marriage contracted under false pretenses or based on an erroneous assumption, which is dissolved without a *get* when the error comes to light. Such a marriage is rabbinic in nature; its dissolution leaves the woman neither a *gerushah* nor an *almana*, and any child born within that union was not born of *znus* but of a legitimately constituted (if ultimately invalid) marriage. The *gemara* supports this with the ruling of *Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Shmuel*, citing *Rabbi Yishmael*: a woman who was not taken by force is forbidden to her husband if she committed adultery, but a woman who was raped is permitted. And there is yet another case — a woman who lay with a man even without compulsion and is nonetheless permitted: this is the case of *kidushi taus*, where the original marriage is voided retroactively, rendering her subsequent relations outside that marriage not adultery at all. *Sheafilu benah murkav al kesefah, mema'enes ve-holechet lah* — even if the child is already perched on her shoulder, she walks away from the marriage. The child of that union was born within the framework of a marriage, however flawed; there was no *znus*. And therefore Shmuel's disqualification — which applies only *bi-znus* — does not apply, and the child may serve in the *Beis HaMikdash*.

---

---

# Yevamot 101

## Two Fathers: Smiting

### Two Fathers Setup

The daf opens in the middle of a case involving a child who does not know which of two men is his father — a situation arising when his mother remarried after leaving her first husband. Whatever the precise circumstances, it is certain that his father is a *kohen*; the uncertainty is only as to which of the two men that is. The Gemara on 101a explores the legal consequences of this ambiguity across several domains, beginning with the laws of smiting and cursing a parent.

### Exemption Principle

If such a child strikes or curses either of the two potential fathers, he is exempt from liability. The reason is straightforward: since it is unknown which man is actually his father, one cannot say with certainty that the particular individual he is striking or cursing is the one to whom he bears the filial obligation. The act, taken in isolation, lacks the definitive quality that the prohibition requires.

### Simultaneous Acts

A *baraita* then distinguishes cases based on how the acts are performed. If he cursed both men simultaneously — *killel shneihem bebat achat* — or struck them both in one act, he is liable. This case is actually the more intuitive of the two: in a single act targeting both men, he is definitively striking his father, even if he cannot identify which of the two that is. The larger *chiddush* is the sequential case: if he cursed one and then went back and cursed the other, or struck one and then struck the other, he is also liable according to the first opinion.

### Doubtful Warning

The sequential ruling turns on the principle of *hatra'at safek shemah hatra'ah* — that a doubtful warning counts as a valid warning for purposes of criminal liability. The scenario unfolds as follows: before the first act, witnesses warn him that this man might be his father. He disregards the warning and proceeds. Before the second act, they warn him again. He again disregards and proceeds. At that point, having completed both acts, he is liable, even though neither individual warning was directed at a certain transgression. The principle holds that the cumulative effect of two doubtful warnings — each acknowledged and disregarded — is sufficient to render him liable for the act that definitively constitutes the violation.

It is worth being precise about what *hatra'at safek* means here. The doubt is not about what the person will do next — every warning involves some uncertainty about that. Rather, the doubt is whether, even if he proceeds, his act will constitute a definite violation. The first opinion holds that such doubtful warnings, when combined to cover both potential fathers, are sufficient.

### Yehuda's View

*Rabbi Yehuda* takes a more restrictive position: *bebat achat chayav, bezeh achar zeh patur* — if he performed both acts simultaneously he is liable, but if he acted sequentially he is exempt. According to Rabbi Yehuda, *hatra'at safek* does not suffice. A sequential warning — "do not strike that man, he might be your father" — targets a single act that, at the moment of its commission, remains doubtfully a violation. The warning cannot aggregate across two separate acts to create retroactive certainty.

### Baraita Debate

The Gemara then raises a *baraita* suggesting that Rabbi Yehuda takes an even more lenient position — that even the simultaneous case renders him exempt. This creates an apparent contradiction with the view just attributed to him. The Gemara resolves this by invoking *trei tannai aliba de'Rabbi Yehuda*: there is a tannaitic dispute about what Rabbi Yehuda's actual position is, with some authorities reporting that he exempts even the simultaneous case.

### God/Father Analogy

To explain the reasoning of the more lenient version of Rabbi Yehuda's position, the Gemara cites *Rabbi Chanina*, who derives it from a textual analogy. The Torah uses the term *berachah* — a euphemism for cursing — in two contexts: cursing God (*ish ish ki yekallel elohav*) and cursing one's father (*umkallel aviv ve'imo mot yumat*). Just as in the case of cursing God there is no ambiguity about the object of the curse — there is only one God, and no question of which divine being is being cursed — so too by cursing one's father, there must be no ambiguity about who the father is. This requirement of clarity applies not merely to avoiding dual targets, but to the very identification of who the father is. Where that identification is genuinely uncertain, even a simultaneous act targeting both candidates fails to satisfy the standard established by the analogy to cursing God.

### Smiting-Cursing Link

The Gemara notes that *hukshah haka'ah liklalah* — smiting is compared to cursing. Therefore, the same requirement of clarity that applies to cursing applies equally to smiting. If the act of cursing requires unambiguous identification of the father as its object, so does the act of striking. This connection ensures that the analogy drawn by Rabbi Chanina governs both prohibitions.

---

## Kohanim Mishmarot

### Kohanim Setup

The Gemara now turns to the consequences when both potential fathers are *kohanim*. The *mishnah* establishes that the child in such a case goes up and performs the *avodah* in whichever *mishmar* he appears in, but does not receive a portion of the *korbanot*. The *mishmarot* are the rotating priestly watches that serve in the *Beit HaMikdash* by week; each *mishmar* will refuse to give him a *korban* portion on the grounds that he may belong to the other *mishmar*.

### Work Without Pay

This immediately raises a question: *lama oleh* — why would he bother performing the *avodah* if he receives no portion? The Gemara offers one answer: he is not working for pay. He works because he wants the privilege and the *mitzvah* of performing the *avodah* in the *Beit HaMikdash*. That said, this answer does not fully address the force of the question, because the language of the *mishnah* — *oleh*, he goes up — sounds not merely permissive but compulsory. It sounds as though he is being compelled.

### Family Honor Concern

The Gemara therefore reads the term *oleh* as indicating forced participation: *be'al korcho*, he is made to go up against his will. The reasoning is attributed in a long chain — *Rav Acha bar Chanina* said that *Abaye* said that *Rav Assi* said that *Rabbi Yochanan* — to the concern of *pgam mishpacha*, family disgrace.

The dynamic works as follows. Both potential paternal families are *kohanim*. When it is their *mishmar*'s week to serve, each family faces the same concern: if this young man is not seen performing the *avodah* alongside the rest of the *mishmar*, observers may assume he belongs to that family but is disqualified — a *pasul kohen*. Neither family wants the public to associate them with an unfit member. Each family therefore insists that he perform the *avodah* during their week, lest his absence create suspicion that falls on them. The result is that he ends up performing *avodah* in both *mishmarot*, even though he receives no *korban* portion from either.

### Tosafot Alternative

*Tosafot* raises a pointed objection to this reading, noting — with characteristic understatement, *teima ktzat*, one might wonder a bit — that it is not the straightforward reading of the word *oleh*. If you focus on the language carefully, the more natural reading is not that he is forced to go up, but that he has the right to compel them to allow him to go up: *be'al korcham de-vnei mishmeret*. Even if the *mishmar* refuses to give him a *korban* portion, they cannot legitimately bar him from performing the *avodah* itself. He is entitled to insist on participation. This reading inverts the direction of the compulsion — it is not the families forcing him, but he insisting on his right against the families.

### Beit Av Problem

The Gemara then complicates the picture further. Even granting that both potential fathers are from the same *mishmar* — the same weekly rotation — this does not resolve his inability to receive a *korban* portion. Within each *mishmar*, there are six *batei av*, each of which serves on a different day of the week, with all of them serving together on *Shabbat*. The *korban* portions are distributed daily based on which *beit av* is serving that day. If he does not know which *beit av* his father belongs to, he faces the same problem at a smaller scale: he goes to one *beit av* and they push him away, saying his father may be from the other one serving on a different day.

### Rav Papa's Fix

*Rav Papa* resolves this by rereading the *mishnah*'s condition. It is not sufficient that both potential fathers are from the same *mishmar*; for him to actually receive a *korban* portion, they must be from the same *mishmar* and the same *beit av*. Only then — *notel chelek echad* — does he work on that specific day and receive a definite entitlement to his portion. This significantly narrows the scope of the *mishnah*'s ruling, but it makes the internal logic precise.

---

## Chalitzah Overview

### Chapter Transition

The daf now moves into the next *perek*, which turns from the theoretical discussions of the preceding chapter to the practical mechanics of *chalitzah* — the ceremony in which the *yavam* who declines to perform *yibum* removes his sandal, enabling the *yevamah* to go free. The *perek* begins with the *mishnah*: *mitzvat chalitzah bishloshad dayanim* — the *mitzvah* of *chalitzah* requires three judges.

### Three Judges Rule

The source for three judges is the Torah's requirement that she come *l'einei hazkeinim* — before the elders. The word *zekeinim* implies a *beit din*. The *mishnah* adds: *v'afilu shlosha hedyotot* — even three commoners suffice. They need not hold *semikhah* or be formally ordained; they need not be *mumchin*, experts in the technical sense.

The Gemara asks: if even *hedyotot* suffice, why does the *mishnah* use the term *dayanim* at all? The answer is: *de'beinan shlosha she'yode'im lehakrot ke'ein dayanim* — we require three people who are literate enough to lead the recitation of the verses, functioning in the role of judges even if not possessing their formal qualifications. The practical need is clear: during the *chalitzah* ceremony, the *yavam* and *yevamah* must recite specified Biblical verses. Since many people were not literate, the judges would recite the text and have them repeat it. Accordingly, the judges must themselves be able to read and recite — they must be capable of *lehakrot*, of leading the recitation. The title *dayanim* in the *mishnah* thus sets a functional bar of literacy rather than a technical bar of ordination, reflecting the role these three individuals are serving rather than any personal credential they must possess.

### Shoe Requirements

The *mishnah* then addresses the type of shoe used in the ceremony. The ideal instrument is a *sandal* — a hard leather base with straps — which *Rashi* describes as cooked leather fashioned to be rigid. If she performed *chalitzah* with a regular shoe (*minal*), it is valid. If she used a soft slipper or sock (*anpilya*), it is invalid, since such a covering does not qualify as a shoe even after the fact. As for the *sandal* specifically: *besandal sheyesh lo akeiv kasher* — a sandal with a heel is valid; *veshein lo akeiv psula* — one without a heel is invalid.

### Leg Location Rule

The *mishnah* further specifies that the location on the leg matters: *min ha'arkuva ulemata chalitzah kesheirah* — from the knee downward the *chalitzah* is valid; *min ha'arkuva ulema'alah chalitzah psula* — from the knee upward it is invalid. *Rashi* understands this as addressing a case where the man has a partially amputated leg. The shoe must be worn on a portion of the limb that falls below the knee. If what remains of his leg is only above the knee, and the shoe is placed on that portion, it does not qualify as a shoe in the relevant sense. The *chalitzah* must involve the removal of a shoe from a part of the body that functions as the lower leg or foot.

### Shoe Variations

The *mishnah* continues with a series of cases. If the sandal does not belong to the *yavam* — *shein shelo* — or if it is made of wood rather than leather, or if it is his left sandal worn on his right foot, the *chalitzah* is nonetheless valid after the fact. If the sandal is oversized but he can still walk in it, or if it is undersized but covers the majority of his foot, it is likewise valid. These cases represent situations where the shoe is not ideal but remains sufficient to constitute the shoe that the Torah requires.

### Literacy Requirement

The Gemara's discussion of why the *mishnah* calls the participants *dayanim* leads, as noted above, to the conclusion that the essential qualification is the ability to lead the recitation of verses. This literacy requirement distinguishes the role from a purely passive one: the three individuals are not merely witnesses but active participants who enable the *yavam* and *yevamah* to fulfill their verbal obligations within the ceremony. The Gemara confirms this by reading the *mishnah*'s use of *dayanim* as shorthand for those who are *ke'ein dayanim* — functioning in the manner of judges — which carries with it this minimal literacy expectation.

---

## Three vs Five Debate

### Three Judges View

A *baraita* is then cited that articulates the standard position more explicitly: *mitzvat chalitzah bishloshad sheyodim lehakrot ke'ein dayanim* — the *mitzvah* of *chalitzah* requires three who know how to lead the recitation, functioning like judges. The *baraita* presents this as the normative rule, understood as a *lechatchila* standard that does not demand formally ordained judges.

### Five Judges View

*Rabbi Yehuda* dissents: *bachamisha* — five judges are required. This is a notably uncommon requirement; while the first *perek* of *Sanhedrin* does discuss courts of various sizes, a *beit din* of five is not a common or familiar institution.

### Word Count Analysis

The *baraita* derives the required numbers through a counting of the word *zekenim* in the relevant *pesukim*. *Zekenim* — elders — appears in the plural, indicating at minimum two. *Zekenim* without the definite article implies two; the additional occurrence of *ziknei* adds another two, bringing the total to four. Since a *beit din* cannot have an even number of judges — *ein beit din shakul* — one more is added.

### Odd Numbers Rule

The prohibition against an even-numbered court underlies the logic of both positions. The *tanna kamma* counts two occurrences of *zekenim* yielding two, adds one to avoid an even number, and arrives at three. *Rabbi Yehuda* counts additional occurrences yielding four, adds one to avoid an even number, and arrives at five. In both cases, the derivation is a counting exercise rather than a direct invocation of *beit din* as a formal legal institution — a point that carries significant implications, as we will see.

---

## Textual Derivations

### Zekenim Counts

The Gemara now examines what each *tanna* does with the words left over once the numerical derivation is complete. Since both positions use some occurrences of *zekenim* to count up their required number, the question arises: what does each position do with the remaining textual details? This produces a set of independent *derashot* from the *pesukim* of *chalitzah*.

### Hedyotot Allowed

According to the *tanna kamma*, one occurrence of *zekenim* is used not for counting but as a source permitting non-expert judges: it broadens the class of eligible participants to include *hedyotot*. Even though *zekenim* implies something like a *beit din*, the additional usage signals that the category is wider than formally ordained judges.

### Yisrael Derivation

*Rabbi Yehuda* derives the permission to use non-experts from a different source: the word *b'Yisrael* in the phrase *veyikarei shemo b'Yisrael*. Since it says "among Israel" without further qualification, this includes any member of Israel — even one without *semikhah*. For Rabbi Yehuda, the *zekenim* occurrences are thus entirely consumed by the numerical derivation, and the permission for *hedyotot* must come from elsewhere.

### Sight Requirement

The Gemara then addresses the requirement that the judges have sight. This is derived from the word *l'einei* — "before their eyes" — in the phrase *l'einei hazkenim*: *prat lesumim*, this excludes blind judges. The Gemara adds an important inference: the very fact that the Torah found it necessary to exclude the blind implies that these judges are not required to be *semuchim*. If they were required to be formally ordained members of a *sanhedrin*, blind individuals would already be excluded by the general rules governing ordained courts — the special exclusion in *chalitzah* would be superfluous. The necessity of the exclusion thus demonstrates that *chalitzah* does not require ordained judges, who are already disqualified from being blind.

### Direct Witness Rule

*Rava* offers an additional and more specific interpretation of *l'einei*: *tzrichei dayani lemichzi roka dekanfik mipuma deyevama* — the judges must actually see the spit exit from the mouth of the *yevamah*. This goes beyond merely possessing the faculty of sight; it demands that the judges directly witness the act of spitting at the moment it occurs. The source is the verse *veyorka befanav* — "and she shall spit before him" — which is governed by the earlier phrase *l'einei hazkenim*, meaning the *zekenim* themselves must witness the spitting as it happens.

This creates a textual accounting problem: if *l'einei* is used to teach Rava's requirement of directly witnessing the spit, it cannot simultaneously serve as the source for excluding blind judges. And if *l'einei* teaches the exclusion of the blind, where does Rava's requirement come from? The Gemara works through this tension carefully. The resolution is that *Rabbi Yehuda* uses *l'einei* exclusively for Rava's requirement — the judges must witness the spit — and derives the permission for *hedyotot* instead from *b'Yisrael*, as noted above. The *tanna kamma*, by contrast, uses one occurrence of *zekenim* to permit *hedyotot* and relies on *l'einei* for Rava's requirement as well, with the exclusion of the blind following as a natural implication.

### Non-Convert Requirement

Another derivation from *b'Yisrael*: *b'Beis Din shel Yisrael velo b'Beis Din shel geirim* — the *beit din* for *chalitzah* must consist of native-born Jews, not converts. This is taught in a *braita* attributed to *Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda*, whose ruling will become practically relevant later in the daf.

### Proclamation Duty

Finally, the phrase *veyikarei shemo b'Yisrael beis chalutz hana'al* — "and his name shall be called in Israel, the house of the one whose sandal was removed" — is read not merely as a future description but as an active directive. *Rabbi Tarfon* is cited as an example: when a *yevamah* came to perform *chalitzah* before him and those assembled with him, he instructed everyone present, *enu kulchem chalutz hana'al* — all of you should respond and say "the one whose sandal was removed." This proclamation is part of the role of those constituting the *beit din*: they represent *Yisrael* in publicly calling him by this designation. The verse is thus not merely a passive prediction but a mandate for active declaration.

---

## Halakhic Ruling

### Three Judges Ruling

*Rava* quotes *Rav Nachman*: the *halakhah* is *chalitzah bishloshad* — three judges. The basis for this ruling is that the *mishnah* in our tractate, which is a *stam mishna*, reflects the view of the *tanna kamma*. When a *stam mishna* exists, we follow it as the established *halakhah*.

### Mi'un Comparison

*Rava* then presses *Rav Nachman* with a question: if we rule three for *chalitzah* on the basis of a *stam mishna*, should we not likewise rule three for *mi'un* — the procedure by which a minor girl refuses a marriage arranged by her mother or brothers? There is a *stam mishna* in *Sanhedrin* that lists both *mi'un* and *chalitzah* together as requiring three. On the same logic, *mi'un* should also require three.

### Mi'un Debate

This is complicated by a *baraita* concerning *mi'un*. *Beit Shammai* holds that *mi'un* requires a *beit din* of *mumchin* — experts. The reasoning is intuitive: *mi'un* effectively dissolves what is treated as a marriage, and dissolving a marriage might be thought to require a court of greater authority. *Beit Hillel* disagrees: *mi'un* may be performed with or without a formal *beit din*. Yet both *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* agree — *v'eilu v'eilu modim she'tzrichim shlosha* — that three are still required. Thus the *baraita* seems to confirm three.

### Mi'un: Two Judges

Nevertheless, a further teaching — *Rav Yosef bar Minyumi* said in the name of *Rav Nachman* — rules that the *halakhah* follows the pair of *Rabbi Yehuda ben Yehuda* and *Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosi*, who hold that even two suffice for *mi'un*. This appears to contradict the *stam mishna* pairing *mi'un* with *chalitzah* at three.

### Source Count Method

The Gemara attempts to justify this asymmetry through a counting of *stam* sources. For *chalitzah*, there are two independent *stam* sources requiring three: the *mishnah* in our tractate and the *mishnah* in *Sanhedrin*. For *mi'un*, there is only one — the *mishnah* in *Sanhedrin*. Therefore, the ruling for *chalitzah* is more firmly established. The Gemara, however, immediately pushes back: since when do we count *stam mishnayot* and give greater weight to two over one? A single *stam mishna* should suffice to establish the *halakhah*. Having two does not logically add force.

The Gemara then proposes a further count: even for *mi'un* there are two *stam* sources — the *mishnah* in *Sanhedrin* and a separate *mishnah* that discusses whether a judge who witnessed a *mi'un* may subsequently marry the woman, ruling that he may because he acted *b'Beis Din*, implying a court of three. For *chalitzah*, one might then count three *stam* sources. But again, the Gemara objects: why should three count for more than two? The differential between two and three sources does not explain why one *halakhah* overrides its *stam* and the other does not.

### Yehuda Concedes

The Gemara ultimately resolves the matter through a different argument. *Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* explains: the reason we are confident that *chalitzah* is definitively three is because the *stam* ruling follows a *machloket* in which one party — *Rabbi Yehuda* — implicitly conceded.

The evidence comes from the *mishnah* in *Sanhedrin*. That *mishnah* lists *semichat zekenim* and *egla arufa* as requiring three, and attributes the alternative view of five to *Rabbi Yehuda*. The same *mishnah* then continues and rules that *chalitzah* and *mi'un* require three — and notably, *Rabbi Yehuda does not dispute this*. Since Rabbi Yehuda explicitly argued for five by *chalitzah* in the *baraita* we quoted earlier, his silence in the *mishnah* in *Sanhedrin* indicates that he retracted his position — *hadar bei Rabbi Yehuda*. He abandoned the view of five specifically with respect to *chalitzah*. This concession by the dissenting voice makes the ruling of three especially solid. No such concession exists for *mi'un*, which is why that ruling remains more open to challenge.

---

## Chalitzah Procedures

### Location Designation

*Rava* introduces a procedural requirement: *tzrichei dayani l'mikva duchtah* — the judges must designate a specific location for the *chalitzah* proceeding. They cannot conduct it in an ad hoc manner, convening wherever they happen to be. The source is the verse *v'altah yevamto hasha'arah el hazkeinim* — "and his sister-in-law shall go up to the gate, to the elders." The *sha'ar ha'ir*, the city gate, was historically where elders would sit in judgment. Even in times when there is no such physical gate serving that function, the requirement that she "come to" the judges implies that the judges must have a designated and established place.

### Five Judges Practice

The Gemara then brings examples of Amoraim who, in practice, assembled five judges for a *chalitzah*. *Avtolas* and *Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua* performed a *chalitzah* with five. The Gemara asks: like whom? Is this following *Rabbi Yehuda*? But we established that Rabbi Yehuda himself retracted his position. How can they be acting on a view he abandoned?

### Five for Publicity

The Gemara answers: *l'firsumei milta* — they assembled five not because of a technical halakhic requirement but in order to publicize the matter. The *chalitzah* has real consequences for the woman's status: a *chalutza* may not marry a *kohen*, and potential suitors should know she is now available. Assembling five rather than three serves the purpose of making the proceedings more public and well-known — a larger gathering ensures broader awareness. This is reinforced by the verse *veyikarei shemo b'Yisrael*: there is a built-in publicizing function to the ceremony. *Rashi* notes both dimensions: ensuring a *kohen* does not inadvertently marry her, and ensuring that eligible men know she is now free to remarry.

### Publicity Examples

*Rav Ashi* once arrived at the *yeshiva* of *Rav Kahana*. Rav Kahana said to him: *salik mar l'gaban l'miluyei bei chamisha* — master, come join us to complete our number of five. Here too the purpose was *pirsumei milsa*: Rav Kahana wanted five specifically to publicize the *chalitzah* proceeding, not because the law demanded it.

### Yehuda's Explicit

In a separate account, *Rav Kahana* recalled standing before *Rav Yehuda*, who told him to come stand on a particular woodpile — *sak l'tzikli d'kani* — to be counted among five, for the purpose of *l'firsumei milta*. This detail about the woodpile is also relevant to the *duchta* requirement: the "designated place" need not be a permanent or formal courtroom. Designating any specific spot — even a pile of wood — appears to satisfy the requirement. The designation itself is what matters, not the permanence or formality of the location. When those around him asked *Rav Yehuda* why he needed five, he replied explicitly: *ki heichi d'lifarsim milsa* — to publicize the matter. His reason was entirely one of publicity and not of legal necessity.

---

## Ger Status Issue

### Ger Exclusion

The Gemara records that *Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda* was in the presence of *Rav Yehuda* when the same invitation was extended — come stand on the woodpile and be counted among five, for the purpose of publicizing the *chalitzah*. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda declined, citing the rule that he had studied: *b'Beis Din shel Yisrael velo b'Beis Din shel geirim* — the *beit din* for *chalitzah* must consist of native-born Jews, not converts.

### Textual Source

His refusal was grounded in the *pasuk*: *veyikarei shemo b'Yisrael* — the phrase *b'Yisrael* is read to require a *beit din shel Yisrael*, excluding a court composed of *geirim*. Since he himself was a *ger*, he could not participate. *V'ana geira ana* — and I am a convert. The *braita* that Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda himself taught had excluded *geirim* from the *beit din* of *chalitzah*, and he applied it scrupulously to himself.

### Praised Stringency

*Rav Yehuda* responded with high praise: *k'gon Shmuel bar Yehuda* — someone like Shmuel bar Yehuda, who is so meticulous and *frum* that he disqualifies himself even when invited to participate in an honor — such a person I would trust so implicitly that I would treat his testimony as determinative enough to extract money. In other words, Rav Yehuda held Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's integrity and scrupulousness in such esteem that he considered his word effectively equivalent to full testimonial proof.

### Witness Reliability

The Gemara does not accept Rav Yehuda's hyperbole at face value. *Mafkina salka deitach?* — would you really extract money on his testimony alone? The Torah requires two witnesses: *hasvei shnei eidim amar Rachmana*. The Gemara therefore reinterprets: *mar'ana shtara apumei* — rather, what Rav Yehuda meant is that if Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda testified that a particular document was forged or invalid, Rav Yehuda would trust him sufficiently to disqualify the document on that basis. That is a narrower but still meaningful expression of trust.

### Ger Bar Remains

The final observation the Gemara draws from this exchange is striking. Recall that the assembled group already had its three valid judges — the technical requirement of *chalitzah* was already satisfied. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda was being invited only to complete the number to five, which served merely the purpose of *pirsumei milta*. Yet he still declined. Even within the non-technical, publicity-oriented framework of adding a fourth or fifth person, he held that the *din* of *b'Yisrael* — which bars converts — applied. The conceptual framework of "five for publicity" did not operate in a legal vacuum; it was still understood as constituting a *beit din*, and a *beit din* requires non-*ger* status even for its non-essential members. The daf closes on this note, with the promise that tomorrow's discussion will continue exploring the role of a *ger* on a *beit din*.

---

---

# Yevamot 102

## Ger Serving on Beit Din

### Chalitzah & Beit Din

The daf begins at the very bottom of 101b, with two words — *amar Rava* — that carry us into 102a. The immediate context is *chalitzah* and the question of whether it requires a *beit din* of three or five. The *gemara*'s conclusion had been that three suffices halachically, yet we find stories of *rabbanim* who nonetheless ensured that five were present for the purpose of *lefirsumei milsa* — to make the matter more public. This concern for publicity may have been what led Rabbi Meir to require five as a matter of *halacha*, since part of the role of the *beit din* is not merely to adjudicate but to represent *klal Yisrael*. This is what the *gemara* expressed when it said that the *beit din* itself recites *chalutz ha-na'al*, because they are, in that moment, representing the community.

The *gemara* concluded the previous discussion with a story in which a *ger* who was invited to participate in a *chalitzah* declined, citing the requirement of *b'Yisrael* — that the *beit din* must represent naturally born Jews. What is striking is that he was only being asked to serve as one of the additional two members beyond the core three. The three essential members were already in place, and his role was purely for the sake of *lefirsumei milsa*. Nevertheless, since the entire group of five was being conceived as an expanded *beit din*, he did not wish to be part of even positions four or five. The *gemara* now pauses from the *yibum* material to examine the question of a *ger* serving on a *beit din* more carefully.

### Ger Dan Chaveiro

*Amar Rava*: a *ger*, though excluded in the ordinary case from sitting on a *beit din*, may judge a fellow *ger* — *devar Torah*, biblically speaking. The source is the verse in Deuteronomy: *som tasim alecha melech asher yivchar Hashem Elokecha bo mikerev achecha tasim alecha melech lo tuchal lases alecha ish nochri asher lo achecha hu*. The phrase *mikerev achecha* — from among your brothers — is understood to refer to those naturally born as Jews, and this requirement is extended beyond the institution of monarchy to encompass positions of appointed authority generally, including membership on a *beit din*.

Rashi offers two explanations for why the *melech* passage applies to a *dayan*. The first is based on the verse *melech b'mishpat ya'amid aretz* — the king establishes the land through justice — and from this we learn that judges participate in that very system; like a king, a judge must be independent, beholden to no one, and free from outside influence. The second explanation, which Rashi says flows more naturally from the broader *sugya*, is that every position of appointed authority — every *simah* — is included in the requirement of *mikerev achecha*. This is the formulation: *kol simot she'atah mesim lo yehei ela mikerev achecha*.

### Rav Moshe & Authority

The question of what constitutes a position of authority has broad practical implications. Rav Moshe Feinstein was asked whether a *ger* could serve as *rosh yeshiva* — a position that clearly carries with it significant authority: the power to admit or expel students, to impose disciplinary measures, and to govern institutional life. The question is not trivial.

Rav Moshe's approach begins from a fascinating premise: there is a *mitzvah* of *ahavas hager*, and that *mitzvah* creates a halachic pressure to read the restriction on positions of authority as narrowly as possible. The *mitzvah* does not dissolve the restriction, but it shapes the interpretive posture.
