From there, Rav Moshe develops a conceptual distinction that has become central to this entire area of *halacha*: the difference between *imposed* authority and *contractual* authority.

In a context where authority is genuinely imposed — where someone can be compelled, against their will, to submit to another's power — that is the paradigmatic case of *malchut*, of the kind of authority for which the Torah requires *mikerev achecha*. A king in an authoritarian society exercises precisely this kind of unilateral power over people who have not chosen it. By contrast, in modern democratic and institutional settings, most authority relationships are entered into voluntarily. When a student chooses to attend a yeshiva, he accepts, contractually, the authority of the *rosh yeshiva* over certain aspects of his conduct. That is a fundamentally different relationship. It is not *alecha* in the sense the Torah intends.

This reasoning naturally invites further examination. A *dayan* sitting in judgment is one of the few genuinely contemporary examples of imposed authority in the classic sense — a litigant can be summoned to court whether he consents or not. That kind of compelled submission to authority is precisely the scenario *mikerev achecha* addresses, and therefore the exclusion of a *ger* from serving as *dayan* retains its full force.

The contrast with voluntary arbitration is telling. As Rav Moshe's analysis implies, if both parties freely choose to bring their dispute before a particular *dayan* or *beit din* — even one that includes a *ger* — that is a contractual relationship, and the prohibition would not apply. The authority is not being imposed; it has been accepted.

One might raise the example of a shul president. The Young Israel organization once issued a letter asserting, among other things, that neither women nor *geirim* may serve as shul presidents, citing the *issur* of *she'im alecha ish nochri* and the parallel concern about women in positions of authority. This caused considerable consternation when the letter circulated among shul presidents, some of whom had not known this restriction existed. For Rav Moshe, however, the very idea that a shul presidency constitutes a position of *malchut*-level authority would be difficult to sustain. Paradoxically, given his framework, treating a *ger* as categorically barred from a purely elective, voluntary position might itself be a form of oppression — a violation of the very *mitzvah* of *ahavas hager* that animates his analysis.

The question was also raised about the Herodian dynasty, whose members were *geirim* of a sort and who wielded authority over the Jewish people by arrangement with Rome. Rav Moshe's framework cuts through that comparison: what matters is not the origin of the authority relationship but its character vis-à-vis those who are subject to it. The people over whom Herod ruled did not choose him; his power was imposed. That is the operative criterion.

### Chalitzah Parentage

The *gemara* now introduces an additional and quite striking requirement specific to *chalitzah*. The general rule, as developed, is: *ger dan et chaveiro* — a *ger* may judge a fellow *ger*. And further: *v'im hayesa imo miyisrael dan afilu Yisrael* — if his mother was from Jewish stock, he may judge even naturally born Jews. One might expect this to resolve the matter entirely: if someone has a Jewish mother, he is, by every standard we employ, fully Jewish — not a *ger* at all. Yet the *gemara* apparently treats such a person as occupying something of a liminal status if his father was a convert, and it feels the need to specify that yes, this person may serve on a *beit din*.

But then the *gemara* adds: *u'le'inyan chalitzah ad she'aviv v'imo miyisrael* — for *chalitzah* specifically, the requirement is more demanding still. It is not enough that the *dayan* himself not be a *ger*. His parents must also not be *geirim*. The derivation comes from the phrase *v'nikra shemo b'Yisrael* — the word *b'Yisrael* in the *chalitzah* passage imposes a heightened standard of natural Jewish lineage, beyond what is required for an ordinary *beit din*.

This is a remarkable *halacha*, and it generates several observations worth pausing over. The first is almost paradoxical: the scenario of a *ger* being judged by a *beit din* that includes a fellow *ger* — the *ger dan et chaveiro* case — does not in practice arise in *chalitzah*. How would a *ger* have a paternal brother? Only if their father was a *ger* who had multiple sons. But if a son of a *ger* had a Jewish mother, then *horaso v'lidaso bikdusha* — he was born in holiness — and he would be considered fully *Yisrael*, not a *ger* at all. The very scenario the *gemara* might seem to be protecting against — a *ger* serving on the *chalitzah beit din* for another *ger* — may be practically impossible to construct.

### Rashi vs. Tosafot

A second important issue concerns the scope of the *ger's* exclusion from *beit din* entirely, independent of the *chalitzah* special case. Rashi, in the entry beginning *hager afilu chaveiro*, explains that the exclusion of a *ger* from judging naturally born Jews applies specifically to *dinei nefashot* — capital cases, and presumably cases of lashes. For *dinei mamonot*, Rashi reads the *mishnah*'s language of *hakol kesherim la-don* — everyone is eligible to judge monetary cases — as explicitly including a *ger*.

Tosafot disagrees. Elsewhere in *Shas*, Tosafot argues at length that a *ger* is excluded even from a *dinei mamonot beit din* over naturally born *Yisrael* when the authority is imposed. The conceptual rationale offered by Rashi — that imposed authority over a person's life and body is the core concern — would limit the restriction to capital and corporeal punishment. Tosafot's broader reading sees the imposition of any binding judgment as falling within *mikerev achecha*.

Both Rashi and Tosafot, however, agree that if the parties have freely chosen to accept the *ger's* authority — if it is genuinely contractual — then the restriction does not apply. This is the point where Tosafot's analysis converges with the logic Rav Moshe would later develop so fully.

To summarize the framework: a *ger* may judge a fellow *ger*. A *ger* may not judge naturally born *Yisrael* in a case of imposed authority. According to Rashi, this restriction is limited to *dinei nefashot*; according to Tosafot, it extends to *dinei mamonot* as well. But in cases of freely accepted arbitration — *peshara* or voluntary submission to the *beit din*'s authority — both agree the restriction falls away. And then, as a category unto itself: *chalitzah* requires not merely a *dayan* who is not a *ger*, but one whose very parents were naturally born Jews.

---

## Sandals & Minhag

### Eliyahu & Minhag

The *gemara* now turns to the type of footwear used in *chalitzah*, and introduces a teaching that is, on reflection, among the more theologically charged statements in this entire passage. *Amar Rav Kahana amar Rav*: if Eliyahu HaNavi were to come and declare that one may perform *chalitzah* with a *minal* — a shoe — we would listen to him. But if he were to come and declare that one may *not* perform *chalitzah* with a sandal, we would not listen to him — *she-kevar nahagu ha-am be-sandal*, for the people have already established the practice of using a sandal.

Rav Yosef quotes essentially the same teaching with a subtle but revealing difference. According to his version, if Eliyahu were to say that one *cannot* use a shoe, we would listen — since there is no established practice one way or the other regarding shoes. But if he were to say one cannot use a sandal, we would not listen, again because the practice is fixed.

The difference between the two versions is the *ikka beineihu*: whether a shoe may be used *lechatchila*. One version assumes that shoes are already permissible *lechatchila* and that Eliyahu's possible contribution would be to tell us otherwise; the other assumes shoes are only *bedi'avad* and that Eliyahu might permit them outright. Both agree, however, that no voice — not even Eliyahu's — could overturn the established practice of using a sandal.

The *gemara* itself passes over the theological dimension of this statement without comment and moves on to the shoe-versus-sandal discussion. But it would be a mistake to let that dimension pass unexamined. This statement is sometimes placed alongside the principle of *lo bashamayim hi* — the Torah is not in heaven — as an expression of the autonomy of rabbinic legal process. But it is worth noting that what is actually being asserted here is somewhat different, and in one respect more modest and in another more pointed. More modest, because the classic *lo bashamayim hi* claim would be that we do not listen to Eliyahu about *any* halachic question — that a prophet carries no special authority in a halachic debate, that he would need to argue his position like any *amora* or *tanna*, and that his being a *navi* confers nothing. That would be a more absolute statement.

What this passage asserts is something narrower but in its own way more powerful: the reason we would not listen to Eliyahu is not that prophetic authority is irrelevant to *halacha* in general, but that established practice carries a weight that even a heavenly voice cannot overturn. The authority here is not the text against the prophet — it is *minhag* against the prophet. And that says something remarkable about the role of practice in the halachic system: that what the community has actually been doing, supervised by and in the presence of rabbis, acquires a standing that is not easily dislodged by theoretical authority of any kind.

An important nuance deserves emphasis: this is not folk custom in the ordinary sense. *Chalitzah* is performed before a *beit din*. The sandal has been used in the presence of rabbis, in a formal halachic setting, over many generations. The practice is not merely tolerated; it is rabbinically endorsed and overseen. That gives it the weight of established *halacha*, not merely popular habit. It sits, in effect, at the authoritative end of the spectrum of *divrei rabanan*.

### Shoe vs. Sandal

The *gemara* now examines the tanna'itic debate about shoes. The *mishnah* states *chaltza be-min'al, chalitzatah kesheirah* — if she performed *chalitzah* with a shoe, it is valid. The language sounds *bedi'avad*. But the *gemara* argues that even *lechatchila* a shoe would be fine according to one view: the *mishnah*'s phrasing is explained as a function of the parallel structure of the clause — since the *mishnah*'s second case (*anpalya*, a sock or slipper) is invalid even *bedi'avad*, the *reisha* mirrors that phrasing, even though the *din* of a shoe is fully valid even *lechatchila* according to this opinion.

The *gemara* then frames the question as a debate among *tannaim* and brings a *baraita* in which Rabbi Yosi recounts a journey to Netzivin. There he encountered an elderly man who reported that Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, a regular Shabbat guest at his home, had performed *chalitzah* many times. Rabbi Yosi asked: did he use a shoe or a sandal? The man's response was incredulous — *ve-chi choltzin be-minal?* — as if the question barely warranted an answer. Of course a sandal.

### R. Yehuda B. Beteira

Rabbi Yaakov, citing Rabbi Meir, states explicitly that one may perform *chalitzah* with a shoe *lechatchila*. The *gemara* then asks: according to the view that a shoe may *not* be used *lechatchila*, what is the reason?

The first possibility raised is the structural concern of *me'al de-me'al*: when removing a laced shoe, one first undoes the laces — which sit atop the leather upper — and then removes the leather upper itself. The Torah says *me-al raglo*, from upon his foot, and not *me-al de-me'al*, from upon the thing that is upon his foot. If the straps are *me'al de-me'al*, perhaps there is a *derashah* problem. The *gemara* rejects this: if that were truly a concern, it would invalidate a shoe *bedi'avad* as well, not merely *lechatchila*.

The *gemara* instead offers a *gezeirah mishum minal merupat* — a rabbinic precaution against using a torn or structurally compromised shoe. A shoe, unlike a sandal, provides substantial enclosure and support, such that even if it is torn beyond the point of halachic qualification, it can still be kept on the foot. Because it is difficult to evaluate on the spot whether a shoe in hand meets the standard, the rabbis ruled that shoes should not be used *lechatchila* — one should not create the risk of using a deficient shoe in the first place. A sandal, by contrast, is so minimally structured that if it is genuinely broken, it simply cannot be worn. The problem thus polices itself. An additional variation on this concern is the case of *chatzi minal* — half a shoe — which raises similar questions about what remains a valid *chalitzah* implement.

The *gemara* then presents a statement of Rav Kahana — here the Rav Kahana who was a student of Rav — that had he not personally witnessed Rabbi Chiya perform *chalitzah* with a sandal that had *shnatzin* (straps), he would have thought the proper implement was the sandal of a nomadic tribesman, which binds tighter to the foot. Since *chalitzah* is the act of removing something from the foot, the more securely the sandal is fastened, the more complete and deliberate the act of removal. The current practice, he reports, is to fasten the sandal with straps tied in a knot, not merely a simple knot without wrapping. The reason: *ki heichi de-tehavi chalitzah me-alya* — so that the *chalitzah* should be a well-executed, fully valid act. This progression of reasoning — from the choice of sandal over shoe, to the preference for a tight sandal over a loose one, to the development of dedicated *chalitzah* sandals used by communities today — reflects how halachic requirements, once articulated, generate a corresponding set of practical tools.

---

## Shoe Removal Mechanics

### Heel vs. Foot

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: the *yevamah* is released to remarry upon the removal of the majority of the heel — *bi-shmitat rov ha-akeiv*. That is, once the heel clears the sandal, even if the foot has not fully slipped out, the *chalitzah* is complete.

A *meitivei* challenges this: the *mishnah* teaches that if the straps undid themselves, or the sandal slipped off on its own — *shamat rov ha-regel* — the *chalitzah* is invalid. This formulation speaks of the majority of the *regel* — the foot — not the *akeiv*, the heel. The implication is that we require the majority of the *regel*, and mere removal of the majority of the heel is insufficient.

The *gemara* resolves the tension by identifying the two: *hainu rov ha-regel hainu rov ha-akeiv* — when we say "majority of the foot," we mean the heel. The reason: *d'kula cheila d'char'a a-leideh dachis* — the entire weight of the leg and body rests upon the heel. Since the heel bears the weight, it constitutes the functionally defining part of the foot for this purpose. When the heel is free, the foot is, in the halachically operative sense, removed.

### Process vs. Result

This discussion supports a teaching of Rav Yannai. *Bein she-hitir hu ve-shamatah hi* — whether he undid the straps and she removed the shoe, *bein she-hitirah hi ve-shamat hu* — or she undid the straps and he slipped his foot out — either way, the *chalitzah* is invalid. Validity requires that she both undo the straps and remove the shoe: *ad she-tatir hi ve-tishmot hi*. She must perform the entire act.

From this, Rav Yannai poses a further question: *kera'atehu mahu* — what if she did not remove the shoe by the ordinary act of undoing and sliding it off, but rather tore it off his foot? And *sraftehu mahu* — what if she burned it off? The underlying question is a classic *chakira*: *gilui kar'a ba'inan ve-ika, o dilma chalitzah ba'inan ve-leika* — do we require the end result of an exposed foot (achieved in either case), or do we require a specific *act* of *chalitzah* — removal in the formal sense — which would presuppose keeping the implement whole and drawing it off? This is the same question in two forms: one where the shoe is destroyed but the foot is exposed, and one — the double-shoe case below — where the shoe is removed without exposing the foot.

The question remains *teiku*, unresolved.

### Double Shoes

*Ba'ei Rav Nechemiah me-Rabba*: the double-shoe scenario. Suppose a person wears two shoes, one on top of the other. If she removes the top shoe while the bottom remains — that is straightforwardly invalid: *me-al amar rachmana, ve-lo me-al de-me'al* — the Torah says from upon his foot, not from upon the thing upon his foot. She removed something that was not directly on the foot.

But the more interesting case is: she tears open the top shoe and then removes the bottom one, while the top shoe remains in place on his foot. The bottom shoe has been removed; the top shoe remains. So: *chalitzah be'inan ve-ika* — was the shoe removed? Yes. *O dilma gilluya de-khar'a be'inan ve-leika* — but was the foot exposed? No, the top shoe remains over it. This is the mirror image of the process-versus-result question: there, the foot was exposed without the shoe being removed; here, the shoe was removed without the foot being exposed. The *gemara* confirms that this scenario is not merely theoretical — the *gemara* notes that Rav Yehuda was observed going out into the marketplace wearing five pairs of shoes layered one atop the other.

### Informal Removal

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: a *yevamah* who grew up in the household of the brothers — waiting, as a young girl, until she reached halachic maturity — and then *yibum* falls to one of them: we are not concerned that perhaps at some point during those years she had removed the sandal of one of the brothers. The concern being: if she had, that might have constituted a *chalitzah*, which would preclude *yibum*.

The *gemara* probes the implication. If the reason we are unconcerned is simply that we never witnessed it, then had we witnessed it, we might be concerned. But the *gemara* notes that a *beraita* teaches: *bein she-nitkaven hu ve-lo nitkavna hi, o she-nitkavna hi ve-lo nitkaven hu, chalitzatah psulah, ad she-yitkavnu shneihem* — unless both parties have *kavanah*, the *chalitzah* is not valid.

### Intent Requirement

Tosafot extends the *kavanah* requirement beyond mere interior intention. The *kavanah* must be evident — it must be contextually clear that what is happening is *chalitzah*. A child casually helping her brother-in-law remove his sandal after a long day, with no formal setting and no evident intent on either side, would not constitute *chalitzah* even if technically she removed the shoe.

The *gemara* offers two responses to the question of why we are unconcerned. The first: even if we had witnessed the removal, we would not be concerned — *ein chosheshin shema kivnu* — because we would not assume the requisite intent was present, and moreover, following Tosafot's reading, the context would not have manifested the intent that *chalitzah* requires. The second, more stringent position: *davka ta'ama d'lo chazinan* — the only reason we are unconcerned is that we did not see it. Had we seen it, we would be concerned. This second opinion then resolves the *kavanah* requirement by distinguishing between levels of *chalitzah*: a fully valid *chalitzah* — one that releases her to marry anyone — requires evident, bilateral intent. But a middling, defective *chalitzah* — one where the formal conditions are questionable — may still be sufficient to disqualify the brothers from performing *yibum*, even if it does not fully release her. She would need a second, valid *chalitzah* to remarry. The *gemara* thus allows for the possibility of a *chalitzah* that is *poseles* for the brothers without being *matir* for the world.

---

## Shoe Materials

### Tachash Leather

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: a sandal sewn with flax — *sandal ha-tafur be-pishtan* — may not be used for *chalitzah*. Rashi offers two readings of what this means: either the threads used to sew the sandal are made of flax, or a flax insert has been sewn into the sandal as a cushioning sole. In either case, the sandal is disqualified.

The source is the verse in Ezekiel: *va-eneilech tachash* — I will shoe you with *tachash*. The *tachash* is understood to be an animal, and therefore the verse is read as establishing that the material of footwear must be of animal origin — leather. This is consistent with broader discussions of *chalitzah* footwear that emphasize leather as the primary material, and it connects to the related *halacha* of Yom Kippur and the prohibition of leather shoes.

The *gemara* pushes further. *Teima tachash, in midi achrini lo* — perhaps only *tachash* skin may be used, to the exclusion of all other materials? The *gemara* rejects this: the verse also uses the word *na'al* (*na'al na'al ribba*), and the repetition implies a broader category. Yet the mention of *tachash* is not superfluous: it limits the category to leather, excluding plant-derived materials like flax entirely. *Im ken tachash mai ahani* — if all materials were permitted, the *tachash* reference would contribute nothing. The *tachash* therefore draws the line: the shoe must be leather.

### Hair Straps

*Ba'ei minei Rav Elazar meRav*: what about a shoe whose body is leather but whose straps (*trisiotav*) are made of hair? Rav responds: *u-mi lo karina beih ve-analach tachash* — does not such a shoe still fall within the description of the *tachash* verse? Hair is, after all, a product of the animal kingdom, consistent with the category the verse establishes. Rav therefore permits hair straps on a leather shoe.

The *gemara* then asks: if hair straps are permitted, why not make the entire shoe of hair? The answer: a shoe made entirely of hair is called *karka* — which Rashi and the translation both render as a slipper — something so minimally protective and structurally insubstantial that it does not qualify as a proper shoe for *chalitzah* purposes. The principle that emerges is that the *ikar*, the primary substance of the shoe, must be leather; secondary components, such as straps, may include other animal-derived materials. What precisely falls within the permissible range of non-leather animal materials — wool, goat hair, or otherwise — is not spelled out with full precision, but the basic framework is clear: leather for the body of the shoe, and for the straps, something from the animal kingdom may suffice.

---

## Chalitzah Etymology

### Remove Definition

*Amar Rav Kahana leShmuel*: how do we know that the word *chalatz* in the verse *ve-chaltzah na'alo me-al raglo* means to remove, rather than to strengthen or arm? After all, *chalatz* appears elsewhere with the latter sense: *hechalitzu me-it-chem anashim la-tzava* — arm yourselves, men for battle. Perhaps the verse in *chalitzah* means something like: help him put on his shoe, prepare him for the road?

Rav Kahana brings proof from the verse in Leviticus regarding *tzara'at* of a house: *ve-chiltzu et ha-avanim asher ba-hen ha-naga* — they shall remove the stones in which the affliction appears. There, *chalatz* unambiguously means to remove.

But Shmuel pushes back: even in the military context, perhaps *chalatz* means to remove — specifically to remove men from their homes and send them out to war: *shalufi mi-beisa le-karba*. The word may be rooted in the concept of extraction, of drawing out, in both senses.

The *gemara* examines further verses. *Yachallaitz ani be-onyo* — will God strengthen the poor in his poverty? The *gemara* reads this as: because of his suffering, he will be removed from the judgment of *Gehennom* — *yechaltzu me-dina shel Gehennom*. Similarly, *choneh mal'ach Hashem saviv li-reyav vi-yachaltzem* — the angel of God encamps around those who fear Him and arms them — is read: because of their fear of God, they are removed from the judgment of *Gehennom*. And *ve-atzmotecha yachalitz* — God will strengthen your bones — which Rav Elazar calls the greatest of all blessings, *me'ula sheba-berachot* — is explained by Rava as *ziruzei garmei*, the invigorating of the bones.

The *gemara* concedes: *mashma hacha u-mashma hacha* — the word *chalatz* carries both meanings, removal and strengthening, and context determines which applies. But in the *chalitzah* verse, the *gemara* demonstrates that removal must be the intended meaning through a *derashah* on the preposition *me-al*. If *chalatz* meant to strengthen or to put on, the Torah would have written *be-raglo* — on his foot. Had it written *be-raglo*, one might have thought that only the foot proper is included and not the calf. So the Torah wrote *me-al raglo* — from upon his foot. But *me-al* already implies removal; if the meaning were to put on, the verse would have said *b'me-al raglo* — on the part above his foot. Since *me-al raglo* is used, *shema mina mishlaf hu* — it must mean to remove.

### Heretic's Polemic

The *gemara* closes with a remarkable exchange. A *min* — a heretic, in this context typically understood as a Jewish Christian — approached Rabban Gamliel with a provocative claim: *ama de-chalatz marei minei* — you are a people whose Master has done *chalitzah* to you, has abandoned you. The proof text: *be-tzonam u-ve-vekaram yelchu le-vakesh et Hashem ve-lo yimtza'u, chalatz me-hem* — they will go with their flocks and herds to seek God and will not find Him; He has removed Himself from them.

Rabban Gamliel responded sharply: *shoteh* — fool. *Mi ksiv chalatz la-hem* — it does not say He performed *chalitzah to* them. *Chalatz me-hem ksiv* — it says He removed Himself *from* them. And who performs *chalitzah* in the ceremony? The woman removes the shoe of the man. If God is cast as the man in this scenario, then for God to have done *chalitzah* — which is the woman's act — would be meaningless. *Ve-ilu yevamah de-chalatz la achi midei mashasha it bah* — and if a brother were to do the *chalitzah* to the *yevamah*, that would accomplish nothing.

The force of the response operates on two levels. Formally, the *min*'s grammatical reading is challenged: the verse says *chalatz me-hem*, not *chalatz la-hem*. But the deeper point is about who acts and who receives. The polemic sought to cast God as having turned away from the Jewish people. The response reframes the relationship: if anything, the verse describes *Bnei Yisrael* as having turned away from God — they sought and did not find because the withdrawal came from their side. The one who performs *chalitzah* is the one who chooses to walk away. And a *chalitzah* performed by the wrong party — by the man rather than the woman — carries no legal force whatsoever.

---

---

# Yevamot 103

## Chalitza & Leather

### Slipper Invalidity

The daf opens in the middle of the bottom of 102b, approximately fifteen lines from the end, at a new paragraph. The *Mishnah* establishes: *ba'anpalya chalitzatah pesulah* — if the *yevamah* performed *chalitza* using a slipper, the *chalitza* is invalid. It is worth recalling the earlier ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, which required the shoe used for *chalitza* to be made of leather, derived from a *pasuk*. That requirement, however, is by no means straightforwardly established from the *tannaitic* material. The *Gemara* will work to reconcile everything into a consistent requirement of leather, but as the discussion unfolds it becomes clear that multiple sources complicate, rather than confirm, that position.

### Slipper Not a Shoe

From the *Mishnah*'s ruling, the *Gemara* infers: *danpalya lav min'al hu* — a slipper is not legally classified as a shoe. This inference sets up the broader discussion of what, precisely, constitutes a *min'al* for purposes of *chalitza* and related laws.

### Shekalim Parallel

The *Gemara* supports this inference by citing a parallel from *Shekalim*. When a person brings his *trumat halishka* — the annual contribution to the *Beit HaMikdash* — and goes in person to deposit it in the *pushka*, the *Mishnah* in *Shekalim* specifies: *ein hatorim nichnas* — the one who separates the funds may not enter *Har HaBayit* or the *Beit HaMikdash* with a cloak that has a hem (*lo bepargout chafut*), out of concern that he might conceal money in the hem, thereby appearing suspect (*nishchad*). Equally, he may not enter *v'lo b'anpalya* — with slippers — presumably, as Rashi explains, because slippers similarly create the appearance that money might be concealed within them.

### Temple Shoe Distinctions

The *Mishnah* in *Shekalim* then adds: *v'ein tzarich lomar bemin'al vesandal* — and needless to say, not with a shoe or sandal. The reason here is entirely different: not the suspicion of hiding money, but the prohibition against entering the *azarah* in an ordinary shoe. This derives from the verse *shal ne'alecha me'al raglecha* — remove your sandal from upon your foot — and from the *pasuk*, *lamma zeh lachem remos chatzerai* — why do you trample My courtyards. Entering the Temple precinct while wearing regular shoes is considered disrespectful, a different category of concern than the slipper issue. Thus the *Mishnah* in *Shekalim* places *anpalya* in a legally distinct category from *min'al vesandal*: the slipper is addressed separately and for a separate reason, reflecting its distinct *halachic* status. The *Gemara* then raises a contradiction (*reminihu*): another *braita* groups *min'al*, *sandal*, and *anpalya* together in the prohibition of walking in them on *Yom Kippur* — *lo yitayel adam bahen lo mibayit lebayit velo mimita lemita*. If the slipper is in a separate legal category from shoes, why does this *braita* lump them together?

---

## Yom Kippur Debate

### YK Braita

The *braita* states that one may not walk about — not from house to house and not from couch to couch — whether wearing a shoe, sandal, or slipper. This is the *Yom Kippur* context. The difficulty is immediate: if a slipper is not a shoe, why should it be forbidden on *Yom Kippur*, where the prohibition is specifically against wearing shoes?

### Abaye: Pleasure

Abaye offers an initial resolution: the *braita* is speaking of a slipper that contains *ketiti* — small stuffed pieces of cloth — giving it a pleasant, cushioned feel. The prohibition in this case, he suggests, is *mishum ta'anug* — because of the pleasure it provides, which is inappropriate on *Yom Kippur*.

### Rava Rejects

Rava immediately dismisses this reasoning. Since when, he asks, is pleasure that does not fall within one of the five formally prohibited categories of *Yom Kippur* a *halachic* problem? The *Yom Kippur* prohibition concerns wearing shoes, not deriving comfort for one's feet in general. To illustrate, Rava cites the well-known example: *v'ha Rabbah bar bar Chana karchis sudra akarei* — Rabbah bar bar Chana would wrap a cloth around his leg and go out on *Yom Kippur*. This cloth served the function of a shoe and provided comfort, yet it was entirely permissible, because halachically it was not a shoe. The point is clear: if it is not a shoe, it is not a shoe, regardless of the pleasure involved.

### Bar Chana Example

The case of Rabbah bar bar Chana's cloth wrapping serves as a compelling proof that the formal category matters, not the experiential comfort. Functional similarity to a shoe does not make something a shoe.

### Rava's Solution

Rava therefore resolves the apparent contradiction differently: *kan be'anpileya shel or, kan be'anpileya shel beged* — here we are speaking of a leather slipper, there of a cloth slipper. The *braita* that forbids a slipper on *Yom Kippur* is referring to a leather slipper, which does count as a shoe; the *Mishnah* that renders *chalitza* with a slipper invalid is referring to a non-leather slipper, which is not a shoe at all. This solution reintroduces the leather criterion — not only as a *chalitza*-specific requirement derived from a *pasuk*, but as a general definitional principle in *halachah*: leather is what makes a slipper cross the threshold into being legally classified as a shoe.

---

## Leather: Form vs. Functi…

### Modern Shoes

This distinction carries direct practical implications. The question of whether one may wear a well-made, highly supportive non-leather shoe on *Yom Kippur* turns on precisely this issue. Is the requirement of leather a purely formal, definitional *halachah* — in which case even the most supportive canvas sneaker would be permitted — or does it reflect a functional criterion, leather being the material that most effectively protects and supports the foot? If it is purely formal, non-leather shoes of any quality remain permitted on *Yom Kippur* and the question is closed. If it is functional, the analysis may shift as materials and norms evolve.

The *Gemara* keeps returning to leather as though it is the dispositive criterion, which can certainly give the impression of a formal requirement. On the other hand, one might argue the other way: that the distinction between leather and non-leather maps onto the distinction between what does and does not provide meaningful protection, and that the *halachah* tracks the function rather than the material itself. The lecturer notes his personal practice not to wear even comfortable cloth slippers on *Yom Kippur* or *Tisha B'Av*, wearing only thin socks with minimal rubber traction, because experientially such an arrangement does not feel like it honors the spirit of the prohibition. Others hold that non-leather is simply not a shoe — pure formalism — and have no hesitation. Still others might argue that even Rava's formal leather distinction is less relevant in a time when non-leather shoes can be as protective and shoe-like as leather ones, though this approach would not apply to *chalitza*, where the *pasuk* anchors the requirement more firmly.

### Rashi: No Protection

Rashi's commentary on the *Shekalim* case illuminates his position. In the margin between Rashi and the *Gemara*, Rashi explains: *matnitin de'terumat halishka be'anpileya shel beged* — the *Mishnah* concerning the *trumat halishka* is speaking of a cloth slipper. *Delav magen hu* — because it is not protective. *Delo havei min'al* — it is not classified as a shoe. And: *u'legabei azara nami leka bizayon* — nor does it constitute a disrespect relative to the *azarah*. He adds: *ve'ein derech lehachnisah betit* — and it is not the normal way to enter with mud underneath, which seems to refer to the lack of a ridged sole that would trap dirt. The crucial phrase is Rashi's *delav magen hu*: the slipper fails the definitional threshold not because it is categorically non-leather, but because it does not protect. By contrast, Rashi explains of the *Yom Kippur* case: *dehai d'kippurim beshel or* — that prohibition concerns a leather slipper.

### Form or Function?

What emerges is a significant question: by *chalitza*, where a *pasuk* mandates the use of a shoe, the leather requirement appears to be an absolute formal criterion. But when the same distinction between leather and non-leather governs the laws of *Yom Kippur* and the *Beit HaMikdash*, is that too a formal definition — or is it grounded in the functional capacity of leather to protect and cover the foot, as Rashi's language of *magen* suggests? Rashi does not say that a non-leather slipper is definitionally not a shoe; he says it does not protect, and therefore is not a shoe. This functional reading has real consequences: if leather's relevance is protective function, then materials that provide equivalent protection might carry equivalent *halachic* weight, at least in non-*chalitza* contexts.

---

## Braita: Valid Objects

### Torn & Broken

The *Gemara* now presents a *braita* enumerating cases of *chalitza* that are valid, at minimum *b'dieved*. The list begins: *chalitza b'min'al hanifram shechofeh rov haregel* — if she performed *chalitza* with a torn shoe, provided it covers most of the foot. Similarly, *basandal hanifchat she'mekabbel rov haregel* — a broken sandal that still supports most of the foot is valid. The structural integrity required is that the object cover or support the majority of the foot; so long as that threshold is met, damage does not invalidate it.

### Cork & Fiber

The *braita* continues: *u'v'sandal shel sha'am v'shel siv* — a sandal made of cork (*sha'am*) or of fiber (rush or bass, *siv*). These are self-evidently non-leather materials. This is significant: the *braita* is validating *chalitza* performed with sandals that are not made of leather. This stands in apparent tension with Rav Yehuda's statement in the name of Rav that leather is required. The *Gemara* will have to reckon with this.

### Prosthetic Shoe

The *braita* then introduces the case of *v'kav hakite'ah* — the prosthetic used by an amputee. This is the wooden peg-leg used by someone whose leg has been severed. According to Rashi's reading of the *Mishnah*, if the amputation is below the knee, the prosthetic functions as the person's shoe and its removal constitutes valid *chalitza*; if the amputation is above the knee, it does not. In Rashi's framework, the reasoning is that when the leg is amputated below the knee, the remaining stump of the *shok* — the calf — is considered the foot for *halachic* purposes, and the prosthetic that covers and protects it is classified as a shoe upon that foot.

The *braita* also mentions *b'mook* — using a felt covering. Rashi explains that *mook* denotes a hard felt, which does provide protection. So here we have another non-leather material being validated, this time even in the context of the prosthetic. This reinforces the growing picture that the list of valid *chalitza* objects includes numerous non-leather items.

The *braita* then mentions *u'v'smichat haraglayim* — the supports for the feet. Rashi describes this as the situation of a person whose legs are not functional and who moves by dragging himself along the ground, propelling with his arms, with a protective mat or covering on his feet to prevent them from being scraped. This object, worn on the dragging legs, is also included in the list of valid *chalitza* objects.

Finally, the list includes *u'v'anpilaya shel or* — a leather slipper. This confirms that for the slipper specifically, leather is the operative distinction.

### Invalid Cases

The *braita* then turns to invalid cases. A torn shoe that does not cover most of the foot (*she'ein chofeh rov haregel*) is invalid. A broken sandal that does not support most of the foot is invalid. *U'vsmichat hayadayim* — the protective covering for the *hands* of the same person who drags himself — even though his hands are functionally his means of locomotion, we do not classify hand-coverings as shoes. *U'v'anpilya shel beged* — a cloth slipper is invalid. *V'choletzet min hakatan* — *chalitza* performed with a minor is invalid. *Chalitzatah pesulah* — all of these are invalid.

What this *braita* makes vividly clear is that the requirement of leather, while operative for the slipper, does not apply universally. Cork, fiber, felt, and wood all appear in the valid column without any qualification. This substantially complicates any claim that leather is a formal universal requirement for *chalitza* footwear. It appears that leather matters specifically — and perhaps only — in the case of the *anpilya*, where without leather the object functions more like a sock than a shoe. For genuinely shoe-like objects — sandals of cork or fiber, a prosthetic, a protective mat for dragging legs — leather is not demanded.

A question naturally arises regarding straps: the *Gemara* earlier mentioned undoing the straps as part of the *chalitza* act, and the *braita* there stated that if he undoes the straps and she removes the shoe, it is invalid — she must do both. But this should be read as: if the shoe happens to have straps, she must perform every component of the removal. It does not appear that straps are a mandatory feature of the *chalitza* shoe. The many cases in this *braita* that clearly involve no straps — a broken sandal, a prosthetic, a felt covering — bear this out. The *Gemara* never explicitly states that straps are required.

---

## Leather Contradiction

### Abaye: All Leather

Having identified that the *braita*'s valid cases include non-leather materials alongside the leather requirement for the slipper, the *Gemara* asks: *kav kita mani?* — who is the *tanna* behind the prosthetic ruling? The answer is Rabbi Meir, based on the *Mishnah* in *Shabbat*: *hakita yotzei b'kav shelo divrei Rabbi Meir* — an amputee may go out on *Shabbat* with his prosthetic, for Rabbi Meir classifies it as a shoe. Rabbi Yossi forbids it, considering the prosthetic an external object rather than a shoe.

Thus the ruling that a prosthetic validates *chalitza* reflects Rabbi Meir's position — and implicitly, Rabbi Meir's position that leather is not required. The end of the *braita*, however, distinguishes between leather and non-leather slippers, which sounds like the position of the *Rabbanan*. How can the beginning of the *braita* follow Rabbi Meir (no leather requirement) while the end follows the *Rabbanan* (leather required)?

Abaye resolves this by insisting that the *braita* follows the *Rabbanan* throughout: *mide-seifa rabbanan, reisha nami rabbanan*. Since the end requires leather for the slipper, the beginning must also be read as requiring leather throughout. Accordingly, the prosthetic case must involve a prosthetic covered in leather — *v'reisha b'mechuppeh or*. The *braita* is not validating a plain wooden prosthetic; it is validating one that has been covered with a leather surface.

### Rava: Functional

Rava challenges this reading. If we are going to require a leather-covered prosthetic, the *braita* should have said so explicitly — it should have distinguished between a leather-covered prosthetic and a non-leather one, just as it distinguished between a leather slipper and a cloth slipper. The fact that the *braita* draws no such distinction for the prosthetic undermines Abaye's interpretation.

Rava therefore inverts the approach: *mide-reisha Rabbi Meir, seifa nami Rabbi Meir* — both the beginning and the end of the *braita* follow Rabbi Meir. And Rabbi Meir does not require leather as a formal criterion. How, then, does Rava explain the distinction between a leather slipper (valid) and a cloth slipper (invalid)? The answer is functional: *hai magein ve-hai lo magein* — one protects and one does not.

### Protective Function

Rava's position, which Rashi's language in the *Shekalim* context foreshadowed, is that leather is never a formal, definitional requirement in its own right. It is a proxy for protection. When a non-leather material is genuinely protective — a cork sandal, a fiber sandal, a felt prosthetic covering, a wooden peg-leg — it qualifies as a shoe and validates *chalitza*. When a non-leather material is not protective — a cloth slipper, which functions more like a sock — it does not qualify. The cloth slipper requires leather precisely because without leather it fails the protective function entirely; with leather, even the slipper becomes sufficiently shoe-like.

This has significant *halachic* implications. If Rava's functional reading is correct, the leather requirement for *Yom Kippur* is likewise not a formal rule but a reflection of leather's historically superior protective and shoe-defining qualities. A non-leather shoe that genuinely protects and supports the foot might, on this reading, be considered a shoe for *Yom Kippur* purposes — though for *chalitza*, the *pasuk* may impose a more fixed formal standard regardless.

---

## Chalitza Requirements

### Planted Feet

Ameimar introduces a further requirement: *hai man de-chalitz tzarich le-midchasei le-char'ei* — the man performing *chalitza* must push his foot firmly to the ground. The reasoning, while not fully explicit, seems to be that the act of *chalitza* involves a transition — from foot firmly planted to foot unplanted as the shoe is removed. The moment of removal is defined against the prior state of the foot being fully planted.

### Position Flexibility

Rav Ashi challenges Ameimar from the *braita*: *bein omed bein yoshev bein mutteh* — whether standing, sitting, or leaning, the *chalitza* is valid. If firm planting were essential, how could a reclining position qualify? Ameimar's response, as the *Gemara* understands it, is that these positions are not in conflict: whether sitting, standing, or leaning, the requirement is that the foot be firmly planted on the ground. Even someone reclining — much like sitting in a recliner — must have his feet pressing down on the ground. The position of the body is flexible; the grounding of the foot is not.

### Foot Disability

Ameimar adds a second ruling: *hai man de-masgei al lachusta de-char'ei lo chalitz* — a person who walks on the front of his foot — whose foot is twisted such that the upper part of the foot drags along the ground rather than the sole — cannot perform *chalitza*. Even if such a person is wearing a shoe, it is not functioning as a shoe for him: the sole of the shoe is not what protects his foot in contact with the ground; rather, it is the upper portion of the shoe. Since the shoe does not functionally serve the purpose of a shoe for this individual, its removal does not constitute valid *chalitza*.

This connects to a famous incident in *Moed Katan*: two eulogizers who said something Rav Ashi found inappropriate received the evil eye from him, rendering them lame. Rav Ashi applies Ameimar's ruling to say that these individuals — *lav bar chalitz ve-lav bar kifaf chalitz* — cannot perform *chalitza* because their lameness prevents them from wearing shoes in a normal, functional way.

---

## Prosthetic Debate

### Support Objects

Rav Ashi raises a question against Ameimar's ruling about the person who walks on the front of his foot. The *braita* listed *smichat haraglayim* — the supports for the feet of the person who drags himself — as a valid *chalitza* object. In that case, the person's feet are also not contacting the ground through their soles; they are dragging. Is that not precisely the same functional situation?

The *Gemara* clarifies: no. The *braita* is not saying that this person himself uses those foot-supports for *chalitza*. Rather, *de-yahvi lei le-achrini ve-chalatz* — someone else wears those supports. The supports are valid *chalitza* objects, but only when used by a person whose feet function normally. The person who actually drags himself cannot perform *chalitza* with those supports, because for him they are not functioning as shoes on his feet. For a person with normal feet who wears the same object, it counts as a shoe and *chalitza* is valid.

### Rashi: Shok

Rashi addresses an apparent difficulty: if the person who walks on the front of his foot cannot perform *chalitza* because the shoe is not protecting the sole of his foot, why does the amputee below the knee fare differently? After all, the prosthetic is not covering the sole of a foot either — the foot is gone.

Rashi explains by invoking the principle that emerges from the *Mishnah*'s ruling: *uve'af al gav de-tenan min ha-arkuvah u-le-mata kesherah* — the *Mishnah* validates *chalitza* from below the knee. Rashi's reading: *chi nachis raglo kamei lei shok* — when the leg descends, what is there is the *shok*, the calf. *De-rachmana amar me-al raglo de-hainu shoko* — the Torah says *me-al raglo*, "above his foot," meaning above what now serves as his foot, which is the *shok*. The prosthetic that covers and protects the base of the *shok* is therefore protecting what is halachically considered the foot. This is fundamentally different from the person who walks on the front of his foot: that person's actual foot exists and is present, but the shoe does not protect its sole.

### Tosafot View

Tosafot takes a different approach entirely. Rather than distinguishing between the amputee and the front-foot walker on the grounds of what counts as the foot, Tosafot reads the prosthetic case in the *braita* identically to the dragging-foot case: in both instances, the *braita* is describing the object being used by someone other than the person who actually has the condition. The prosthetic, on this reading, is valid *chalitza* only when used by a person who does not have an amputated leg — perhaps by bending the leg underneath somehow. The amputee himself, just as the person who drags himself, cannot perform *chalitza* using his prosthetic.

This is a striking position and creates significant practical consequences. On Tosafot's reading, an amputee below the knee cannot perform *chalitza* with his own prosthetic, just as someone who walks on the front of his foot cannot perform *chalitza*. Tosafot supports this by explicitly citing the *Gemara*'s ruling about *smichat haraglayim* as the model: *yahvi le-achrini ve-chalatz, ke-de-amar somchos ha-reglayim*.

### Above Knee

Both Rashi and Tosafot agree that if the amputation is above the knee, *chalitza* is impossible. The *Gemara*'s distinction — *min ha-arkuvah u-le-mata kesherah* — limits validity to below-the-knee amputation. Beyond that, the only debate between the *rishonim* is about below-the-knee amputation: can the amputee himself use his prosthetic (*Rashi*), or only a non-amputee wearing that same prosthetic (*Tosafot*)?

This raises a profound and sobering question. Suppose a man has no brothers other than one who is severely lame — unable to wear shoes normally — or whose leg is amputated above the knee. The *yevamah* cannot obtain *chalitza*. Everyone wants to do the right thing, everything is known, and yet there is no halachic solution. This is categorically different from the *agunah* cases where the problem is evidentiary uncertainty. Here, the facts are clear, all parties are willing, and still *chalitza* may be legally unavailable. What the *poskim* say about such a case would require separate investigation.

---

## Regel: Foot or Leg

### Regel Definition

The *Gemara* now addresses a foundational linguistic question that underlies all the above: does *regel* in the relevant *pasuk* — *v'chaltzah na'alo me'al raglo* — mean *foot* specifically, or does it mean *leg*? This matters enormously. If *regel* means leg, then amputation above the knee should still leave enough of the leg to satisfy *me-al raglo*, and *chalitza* should remain possible. If *regel* means only foot, then we must work our way up from the foot and the knee joint becomes the outer limit.

Rav Kahana raises a challenge: *beshelia yetzei mibein ragleha* — a miscarried fetus that comes out from between her *reglayim*. The *regel* in question here clearly refers to the thigh region, not the foot. This suggests *regel* can mean leg — even the upper leg.

### Euphemistic Usage

Abaye responds to Rav Kahana's challenge: *bisha'a she'kar'a lileid, no'etzet ekeveha beyarcheha* — when a woman crouches to give birth, she digs her heels into her sides. At that moment, what comes out literally comes out from between her feet. Abaye is reading *ragleha* as feet, not thighs, because of the crouching posture.

The *Gemara* then marshals further proofs. *Lo asa raglav velo asa sefamo* — he did not do his *raglav* and did not trim his mustache. The *Gemara* understands this as referring to pubic grooming, where *raglav* is used as a euphemism for the private area. Similarly, *vayavo Shaul lehasech et raglav* — Saul went to relieve himself — where *raglav* again euphemistically refers to the area between the thighs, not to the feet themselves. And *ach masi'ach hu et raglav* — he is relieving himself in an inner chamber.

In each of these cases the *Gemara* gives the same answer: *lishna me'alya* — refined language. The word *regel* is being used euphemistically to avoid direct mention of the thighs or private areas. The underlying denotation of *regel* remains *foot*; it is only deployed as indirect speech when referring to intimate areas. The fact that it is pressed into service as a euphemism does not mean it actually denotes the entire leg.

### Foot Conclusion

After working through all these cases — including *bein ragleha kara shachav* from the episode of Yael and Sisera, which the *Gemara* also answers with *lishna me'alya* — the conclusion is firm: *regel* means foot. The *Gemara* consistently deflects every apparent counterexample as euphemistic usage rather than evidence of a broader denotation. The consequence is maintained: *chalitza* requires the shoe to be removed from what is legally the foot, and amputation above the knee removes any possibility of meeting that requirement.

---

## Sisera & Yael

### Seven Times

Having cited the *pasuk* from Yael and Sisera in the linguistic discussion, the *Gemara* pivots to an extended *aggadic* passage. Rabbi Yochanan states: *sheva be'ilot ba'al oto rasha be'oto hayom* — that wicked man had relations with Yael seven times that day. The source is a close reading of the *pesukim* in *Shoftim*: *bein ragleha kara nafal shachav, bein ragleha kara nafal, ba'asher kara sham nafal shadud*. Counting the verbs — *kara, nafal, shachav, kara, nafal, kara, nafal* — yields seven acts.

### Pleasure Problem

The *Gemara* immediately raises a serious theological and moral difficulty: *v'ha kamistanya mei'aveira?* — but was Yael not deriving pleasure from a transgression? This question would seem to undermine the moral heroism for which she is celebrated. If she experienced physical pleasure in the course of her sin, even if the sin was committed for a righteous purpose, how does the tradition valorize her act? The concern is not merely whether she *could* do it — the concept of *aveirah lishmah* addresses that — but whether an act from which one derives pleasure can be celebrated as self-sacrifice.

### Zuhama Solution

Rabbi Yochanan resolves the question in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: *kol tovasan shel resha'im ra'ah hi etzel tzaddikim* — any good that the wicked have to offer is, from the perspective of the righteous, only evil. The verse cited is God's warning to Lavan: *hishamer lecha pen tedaber im Yaakov mitov ad ra'* — take care not to speak to Yaakov from good to bad. The *Gemara* understands: not speaking bad to Yaakov is obvious; why also not speak good? This demonstrates that whatever good a *rasha* would offer is experienced by the righteous only as harm.

But the *Gemara* does not accept this as a bare metaphysical principle and probes further: in Lavan's case, the explanation is clear — any blessing he would pronounce would invoke the name of his god (*Elohei Nachor*, etc.), which Yaakov would not want. But what is the harm in Sisera's case, where the concern seems to be purely physical pleasure? The *Gemara* answers: *de-ka shadei bah zuhama* — because Sisera cast into her a *zuhama*, a spiritual stench or contamination.

### Theology

This leads to a broader theological statement from Rabbi Yochanan: *besha'ah sheba nachash al Chava hitil bah zuhama* — when the snake had relations with Chava, he instilled in her a *zuhama*. *Yisrael she'amdu al Har Sinai, paska zuhamatan* — when Israel stood at Sinai, their *zuhama* ceased. *Ovdei kochavim shelo amdu al Har Sinai, lo paska zuhamatan* — the idolaters, who did not stand at Sinai, retain their *zuhama* to this day.

The implied polemical context is worth noting. This tradition appears to be a Jewish response to the Pauline Christian doctrine of original sin, reversing its terms entirely: the Jews are not burdened with original sin — they were cleansed of it at Sinai. It is the nations who never received the Torah who retain the primordial contamination of the snake's encounter with Chava. Far from sex being intrinsically sinful, as early Christian theology would have it, the Jewish people were specifically liberated from the condition that makes it so. Hence, when Sisera — a non-Jew carrying the full *zuhama* of the unredeemed nations — had relations with Yael, whatever physical sensation she experienced was accompanied by a deep spiritual contamination that entirely negated any pleasure. The good that a *rasha* offers the righteous is not merely neutral; it actively does harm.

Tosafot's engagement with this *aggadah* focuses on the *aveirah lishmah* dimension. Even granting that what Yael did was halachically justified as a great act done for the sake of *Klal Yisrael*, the *pesukim* celebrate her with a heroism that implies self-sacrifice. If she were experiencing genuine pleasure throughout, the celebration would be misplaced — there is no sacrifice in an act one enjoys. The answer, then, is not to deny the *aveirah lishmah* justification but to explain why it was also a genuine sacrifice: the *zuhama* ensured that what appeared to be pleasure was in fact causing her harm.

---

## Shoe Ownership

### Fit Requirement

The *Gemara* turns to the question of whether *chalitza* may be performed using a shoe that belongs to someone else. The *braita* derives from the word *na'alo* — his shoe — that the shoe must be *ra'ui lo*, appropriate for him.

### Borrowed Allowed

The derivation proceeds through *gezeirah shavah* or *ribbui*: the word *na'al* appears multiple times in the *pasuk*, and from the repetition the *braita* learns *na'al na'al mikol makom* — the word *shoe* in any context, meaning even a borrowed shoe is valid. The term *na'alo* thus does not require ownership but suitability.

### Shoe Exclusions

From *na'alo hara'ui lo* — a shoe appropriate for him — the *braita* derives several exclusions. A shoe too large, such that he cannot walk in it normally (*perat legadol she'eino yachol lahaloch bah*), is invalid. A shoe too small, such that it does not cover most of his foot (*perat lekatan she'eino chofeh rov raglo*), is invalid. And *u'perat lesandal hamasulayin she'ein lo akeiv* — a sandal of the type that has no heel is excluded. This last exclusion shifts from a personal fitness requirement to an objective structural standard: regardless of fit, a heelless sandal does not qualify.

### Abaye Story

The *Gemara* relates an incident involving Abaye and Rav Yosef. Abaye was standing before Rav Yosef when a *yevamah* came to perform *chalitza*. Rav Yosef instructed Abaye: *hav lei sandalach* — give the *yavam* your sandal. Perhaps the *yavam* had only a non-leather slipper or otherwise unsuitable footwear. Abaye, apparently wishing to make a point, deliberately gave the *yavam* his left sandal — knowing that the right sandal is the *lechatchila* requirement. Rav Yosef rebuked him: when did the rabbis say a left sandal is acceptable? Only *b'dieved*. They never said *lechatchila*.

Abaye responded with equal sharpness: and when did you tell me to give him my sandal? When did the rabbis say a borrowed sandal is acceptable? Only *b'dieved*. So why are you asking me to give him a borrowed sandal *lechatchila* in the first place? My use of the left sandal is no more problematic than your instruction to lend him mine.

### Transfer Rule

Rav Yosef clarified his original intent: *hav lei v'aknei lei* — give it to him and transfer possession to him. The instruction was not to lend the sandal but to make the *yavam* the owner of it for the duration of the *chalitza*, after which it would be returned. Since the sandal would be legally his at the moment of *chalitza*, the concern of borrowed footwear is entirely resolved.

---

## Wood & Disease

### Wooden Sandals

The *Gemara* now asks about wooden sandals: *sandal shel etz, man tanna?* — who is the *tanna* that holds a wooden sandal is valid for *chalitza*? The question circles back to the leather issue. If wood is valid, that is in tension with any formal leather requirement.

Shmuel answers: it is Rabbi Meir, based on the same *Mishnah* — *hakiteia yotzei b'kav shelo divrei Rabbi Meir* — where Rabbi Meir classifies a wooden prosthetic as a shoe for purposes of *Shabbat*. Attributing the wooden sandal ruling to Rabbi Meir places this leniency in the same camp: Rabbi Meir does not require leather. Rabbi Yossi disagrees and forbids the prosthetic on *Shabbat* — for him, it is not a shoe.

### Shmuel: Covered

Shmuel then offers an alternative reading: *b'mechupah or divrei hakol* — the wooden sandal case is universally valid, because it is speaking of a wooden sandal covered in leather. On this reading, the permissibility of the wooden sandal is not evidence against a leather requirement; rather, the leather covering satisfies the requirement. This mirrors Abaye's earlier attempt to read leather covering into the prosthetic case, which Rava rejected. Here, though, it is Shmuel advancing the position, and the *Gemara* does not immediately challenge it.

### Tzara'at Issue

The *Gemara* then presents the rulings of Rav Papa in the name of Rava regarding sandals afflicted with *nega tzara'at* — signs of ritual leprosy that appear in leather objects. The case of *sandal hamusgar* is a sandal that has been sealed (*musgar*) — placed in quarantine pending inspection after the first week, not yet definitively determined to be *tamei*. The case of *sandal hamuchlat* is a sandal definitively ruled to be *metzora* and therefore subject to destruction.

### Rav Papa Strict

According to one version of Rav Papa's ruling in the name of Rava: a *musgar* sandal — *lo tachlotz bo* — should not be used for *chalitza lechatchila*, but *v'im chaltza chalitzatah kesherah* — if she did, the *chalitza* is valid *b'dieved*. A *muchlat* sandal, however — *lo tachlotz bo, v'im chaltza chalitzatah pesulah* — must not be used, and if she did, the *chalitza* is invalid even *b'dieved*. The reason for this stricter position is the principle of *kitutei michtat shiurei* — an object that is going to be destroyed is considered as if already destroyed, or at minimum has its legally relevant thresholds undermined. A sandal that has been definitively ruled *metzora* and is headed for destruction cannot be considered a shoe in the full legal sense.

### Lenient View

A second version of the ruling, attributed again to Rav Papa in the name of Rava, takes a more lenient position: *echad sandal hamusgar v'echad sandal hamuchlat* — both the sealed and the definitively afflicted sandal — *lo tachlotz bo lechatchila* — should not be used *lechatchila*; *v'im chaltza chalitzatah kesherah* — but if she did, the *chalitza* is valid in both cases. This view rejects the application of *kitutei michtat shiurei* to the *muchlat* sandal, holding that however undesirable its use, the sandal retains its status as a shoe sufficiently to validate *chalitza b'dieved*. The discussion of *kitutei michtat shiurei* and the resolution between these two positions will continue in the next *daf*.

---

---

# Yevamot 104

## Sandal & Tzara'at

### Bayit Hamusgar

Today's daf is 104, and we pick up somewhere in the middle of 103b, where the *gemara* raises a challenge — *meitivei* — concerning the status of a *bayit hamusgar*, a sealed house whose *tzara'at* status is being determined. The broader question under discussion is whether a sandal that has been afflicted with *tzara'at* may be used for *chalitza*. The relevant distinction is between *musgar* — a house or object whose status is being evaluated but has not yet been finalized — and *muchlat* — one whose status has been finalized and which is destined for destruction.

The question is whether something destined for destruction can still function as a meaningful halachic object. There is no per se quantitative *shiur* at stake, but the concern is whether the sandal retains its identity as a shoe. Can it be considered a significant shoe if it is slated for destruction?

### Kitutei Mechatat

This brings us to the principle of *kitutei mechatat shiurei* — the idea that something destined for destruction has already, in a conceptual sense, lost its identity as a functional object. It is not merely that a quantitative measure has been diminished, but that the very status of the object as a coherent, purposeful thing has been undermined. The *gemara* will use this principle repeatedly, and it is important to keep it clearly in view.

### Rav Pappi/Pappa

The practical question is framed through two competing traditions in the name of *Rava*. *Rav Pappi* said in *Rava*'s name that a *sandal muchlat* is not valid for *chalitza*, while *Rav Pappa* said in *Rava*'s name that it is valid. The *gemara* then attempts to challenge and resolve these positions through a series of cases from the laws of *tzara'at*.

The *gemara* challenges: a *bayit hamusgar*, once sealed, is *tamei* from the inside; a *bayit muchlat*, once its status is finalized and it is destined for demolition, conveys *tumah* from both inside and outside, and even causes *tumah* simply by entering — as the *pasuk* says *haba el habayit*, one who enters the house. If we apply *kitutei mechatat shiurei* — if the house scheduled for destruction is as if already ground up — how can it still function as a house for the purpose of the *tumah* of entry? Should it not lose its identity as a house, just as we are suggesting it loses its identity as a shoe?

### House Identity

The *gemara* answers: *shani hacha damar kra* — here the verse itself is different, because it says *venatatz et habayit*, "you shall demolish the house." The *Torah* teaches that even in the act of demolition, the structure is still called a *bayit*. The *Torah* explicitly preserves the object's identity within the framework of *tzara'at* law, even as it is being destroyed. This, however, is an internal ruling confined to the laws of *tzara'at*. When one wishes to apply the object's identity to some other *halachic* context — such as using it for *chalitza* — that is an entirely different matter.

---

## Matlit & Kezayit

### Matlit Garment

The *gemara* then says *tashma* — come and hear a further challenge. If a piece of cloth (*matlit*) is three finger-widths by three finger-widths — the minimum size that defines it as a *beged* — and it is a garment afflicted with *tzara'at*, it conveys *tumah* to a pure house when brought inside. Crucially, this holds even if the garment does not have the volume of a *kezayit*, a detail that will become significant momentarily.

### Majority Entry

The operative rule: *keivan shenichnas rubo leveit tahor tim'ahu* — once the majority of the garment has entered a pure house, it has rendered that house *tamei*. The majority entering is treated as if the whole object entered. This implies that the garment retains its identity as a unified *beged*. As *Rashi* explains, the *gemara* is not suggesting that a *muchlat* object loses its *shiur* and therefore fails to cause *tumah* — obviously, if that were true, nothing with *tzara'at* could ever cause *tumah*, since we would always say it has no *shiur*. Rather, the argument is about *coherence of identity* as a unified object: we said that something whose *shiur* is compromised loses its identity as a coherent object. Yet here, even a fractional majority is treated as representing the whole.

### Muchlat Question

The *gemara* asks: are we not discussing a *muchletet* — a garment that is *muchlat* and destined for destruction? And yet it retains sufficient identity to cause *tumah*? The *gemara* answers: *lo* — *musgeret*. No, we are actually discussing a *musgar* garment, one whose status is still being evaluated, not yet finalized for destruction. So this does not prove anything about a *muchlat* object.

*If* that is so, says the *gemara*, *eima seifa* — let us look at the end of this *braita*.

### Seifa Analysis

The *seifa* discusses a thick garment whose volume amounts to several *zeitim* of material. The ruling there is: *keivan shenichnas mimenu kezayit* — once a *kezayit* worth of the garment enters the house, even if it is not a three-by-three piece, it renders the house *tamei*. Why would a *kezayit* be the operative measure for a garment? Normally, *kezayit* is not a relevant measure for cloth at all.

### Meit Parallel

The *gemara* explains: *ei amrat bishlama muchletet* — if we are indeed discussing a *muchlat* garment, this makes sense. *Hainu de-itkash le-meit* — it is because a *metzora* is compared to a dead person, as Moshe prayed for Miriam: *al na tehi ke-meit asher bezeito me-rechem imo*. The comparison to a *meit* brings the measure of *kezayit* into play, since a *kezayit* of a corpse conveys *tumah*. But this *itkash la-meit* — this comparison to a *meit* — only applies in the *muchlat* state. If we were discussing a *musgar* garment, there would be no basis for the *kezayit* measure. Therefore, the *seifa* must be discussing a *muchlat* garment.

And yet, even in the *muchlat* state, the garment retains a coherent identity such that a majority entering is treated as the whole entering. So the challenge to *kitutei mechatat shiurei* remains.

---

## Object Identity

### Shani Hataim

The *gemara* responds with the same logic it used for the house: *shani hatam de-amar kra ve-saraf et habeged* — the *Torah* says "and he shall burn the garment," teaching that *afilu bish'at sreifa karui beged* — even in the moment of its burning, it is still called a *beged*. Just as the *Torah* explicitly preserves the house's identity as a house throughout the process of its destruction, it preserves the garment's identity as a *beged* throughout the process of its destruction. This preservation of identity, however, operates within the laws of *tzara'at* internally — it does not follow that the object carries its identity into other domains of *halacha*.

### Issur Tumah

The *gemara* then raises an obvious question: *ve-nigmor mineh* — why not derive from this that the *sandal muchlat* retains its identity for *chalitza* as well? Since within *tzara'at* we see the object is still called by its name even when destined for destruction, let us apply that to *chalitza*!

The *gemara* answers: *issur mi-tumah lo gamrinan* — we do not derive *issur* rulings from *tumah* laws. As *Rashi* explains, the entire category of *hilchot tumah* is a *chidush* — it operates by its own internal logic, which is somewhat arbitrary and not necessarily generalizable to other *halachic* domains. The preservation of identity within *tzara'at* is internal to those laws; it does not flow outward into other categories.

### Rava Hilchasa

This gives us the framework for the two versions of *Rava*. The position that *bedieved* the *sandal muchlat* is not valid — *Rav Pappi*'s version — holds that we do not learn *issur* from *tumah*, and therefore the preservation of identity within *tzara'at* cannot be applied to *chalitza*. The position that *bedieved* it is valid — *Rav Pappa*'s version — holds that once we see the object retains its identity within *tzara'at*, it retains its identity for other *halachic* purposes as well.

What is striking is that the *gemara* now quotes *Rava* directly: *amar Rava hilchasa* — the ruling is that both a sandal that is *muskav* (set aside) and one that is *muklat* (afflicted with *tzara'at* and destined for destruction) are valid for *chalitza*. This corresponds to *Rav Pappa*'s version. One cannot help but note the irony: if *Rava* himself ruled explicitly, why did we need two competing traditions transmitted in his name?

---

## Avodah Zarah

### AZ Distinctions

*Rava* continues: *ve'echad sandal hamuklat ve'echad sandal shel avodat kochavim* — and even a sandal used as an object of idolatrous worship, *lo tachlotz* — one should not use it *lechatchila*, but *ve'im chaltzah chalitzatah kesherah* — if one did use it *bedieved*, the *chalitza* is valid.

### Ir Nidachas

However, *she-teikroves avodat kochavim* — if the sandal was offered as a sacrifice to an idol rather than being worshipped directly — or if it belonged to an *ir nidachas*, a city condemned to complete destruction — *lo tachlotz*, and *ve'im chaltzah chalitzatah pesulah* — even *bedieved* it is invalid. For an *ir nidachas*, this is because *Rava* acknowledges that *kitutei mechatat shiurei* applies when something is genuinely destined for total destruction outside the special framework of *tzara'at*.

### Zakein Issue

The *gemara* then introduces the case of *zakein asui lichvodo* — a euphemism for a shroud shoe, a shoe prepared specifically to be placed on a corpse and not made for actual walking. Such a shoe, *Rava* rules, is invalid even *bedieved*. Why? The obvious answer: *delav lehilocha avid* — it is not made for walking. It does not qualify as a shoe in the functional sense required for *chalitza*.

Before proceeding to the challenge this ruling raises, it is worth pausing to appreciate a remarkable detail that emerges here. It becomes clear that already in the *talmudic* era, the *beit din* maintained a dedicated *chalitza* shoe — a special shoe set aside specifically for performing *chalitza*. This is far from the straightforward scenario in which two people simply appear before a court wearing their ordinary shoes. The existence of a communal *beit din* shoe already reflects an institutional practice of considerable sophistication.

What is the difference between *avodat kochavim* and *tikroves avodat kochavim* — why is one valid *bedieved* and the other not? *Rava* offers no explicit distinction in the text, so *Rashi* supplies one: a sandal used as an object of *avodah zarah* by a non-Jew could potentially have its status annulled — a non-Jew can be *mevatel* it by renouncing belief in it, after which it ceases to be *avodah zarah*. Because it has the potential of not being destroyed, we do not fully apply the principle of *kitutei mechatat shiurei*. *Tosafot* disagrees, understanding the case as referring to *avodah zarah* that has already been annulled, and argues on the basis of a related *sugya*. *Tosafot* further raises the question of whether using an object associated with *avodah zarah* is problematic for a *mitzvah* object — drawing a comparison to the *shofar* of *avodah zarah* — and treats the *chalitza* shoe in a similar conceptual category.

*Rashi*, by contrast, invokes the principle of *mitzvot lav leihanos nitnu* — the fulfillment of *mitzvot* does not constitute *hana'ah* — to explain why using an *avodah zarah* sandal for *chalitza* would not violate the prohibition against deriving benefit from *avodah zarah*. This framing is itself significant: *Rashi* is conceptualizing *chalitza* primarily as a *kiyum mitzvah*, a ritual act, rather than as a quasi-transactional act of releasing the woman. Whether *chalitza* is more like a *mitzvah* or more like a legal transaction — analogous to *get* — has real *halachic* implications, and *Rashi*'s deployment of *mitzvot lav leihanos nitnu* reveals his position clearly.

### Rav Papa Q

*Rav Papa* poses a challenge to *Abaye*: what distinguishes the shroud shoe? Even granting that *delav lehilocha avid* — it is not made for walking — the same would seem to be true of the *beit din*'s *chalitza* shoe. Who walks around in the *beit din*'s special *chalitza* shoe? It too is kept exclusively for the performance of *chalitza* and is never used for ordinary walking.

### Beit Din Shoe

The *gemara* responds: *ilu mash'il lei shulcha debei dina mi kapid alei dayana?* — if the court's attendant wanted to borrow the *chalitza* shoe, would the judges object? Of course not. The *beit din* shoe is available in principle for ordinary use; it simply is not used that way in practice. The shroud shoe, by contrast, is intrinsically defined by its purpose of accompanying a corpse — it is not made for walking by design, not merely by convention. The answer is logically coherent, though one cannot help noting the irony: the *gemara* is essentially defending the validity of the *beit din*'s *chalitza* shoe on the grounds that, in theory, anyone could borrow it for a stroll.

---

## Mishna Chalitza

### Night & Left

The *Mishna* teaches: *chaltzah balaylah* — if she performed *chalitza* at night, *chalitzatah kesheira* — it is valid. *Rabbi Eliezer posul* — Rabbi Eliezer rules it invalid. Similarly, if the *chalitza* was performed on his left foot, *chalitzatah pesulah* — it is invalid; *Rabbi Eliezer machshir* — Rabbi Eliezer rules it valid.

The *gemara* proposes that the dispute about whether *chalitza* may be performed at night turns on the question of whether we link court proceedings to the laws of *negaim*. The *pasuk* says *al pihem yihyeh kol riv vechol nega* — on their word shall be every litigation and every *nega*. Since *tzara'at* declarations by the *kohen* must be made by day — *bayom hira'os bo hakohen yitma* — one might extend this requirement to court proceedings as well.

The *gemara* immediately rejects a sweeping application of this link: *d'chulei alma lo makshinan rivim lenegaim* — everyone agrees we do not make a global equation between litigation and *negaim*. Were we to do so fully, we could not even conclude a court case at night, which contradicts established *halacha*: while *dinei nefashot* must begin and be conducted entirely in the daytime, *dinei mamonot* may continue into the night once proceedings have begun.

The debate is then reframed: *mar savar chalitza k'techilas din damya* — one holds that *chalitza* is analogous to the beginning of a court proceeding, while *umar savar chalitza k'gmar din damya* — the other holds it is analogous to the conclusion of proceedings. The *gemara* itself provides no explanation of this distinction. One might suggest that viewing *chalitza* as the *gmar din* is natural because, like a verdict, it is the moment at which the legal change of status is effected — it is simultaneously the beginning and end of the proceeding, and the act itself produces the definitive outcome.

The question of whether *chalitza* is more like a *mitzvah* or more like a *din* proves directly relevant here. *Rashi* notes that *chalitza* has a *din* element because the woman collects her *ketubah* as a result. More broadly, framing *chalitza* as a *din* explains why it would be placed in the category of *riv* at all, and the *machloket* over whether it is the beginning or end of that *din* flows naturally from there.

One might have thought to derive the requirement of daytime from the word *le-einei*, since the witnesses must see the act — but this cannot be the source, as we have seen that even a *suma* poses complications, and the *gemara* does not pursue that derivation.

The narrative then introduces *Rabba bar Chiya Katuspa'ah*, who performed a *chalitza* using a *mok* — a hard felt shoe, previously established as technically valid though not ideal — alone (*bi-yechidi*), without a *beit din*, and at night. *Shmuel* responded with what *Rashi* reads as sarcasm: "How great is this man," meaning: look how freely he relies on minority opinions. The *gemara* analyzes which element actually troubled *Shmuel*. The *mok* was established as valid by an anonymous *braita*, not a minority view. The nighttime *chalitza* corresponds to the *stam* position of our *Mishna*, which overrides *Rabbi Eliezer*'s lone dissent. The genuinely troubling element, says the *gemara*, is the absence of a *beit din* — *yechidai katani lah* — that position is sourced in a minority opinion.

The *Mishna* on the following *amud* records that *chalitza* performed before only two judges, or before three where one turned out to be a relative or otherwise disqualified — effectively making it two — is invalid. *Rabbi Shimon* and *Rabbi Yochanan ha-Sandlar* validate it.
