And there is the famous case of one who performed *chalitza* privately in prison, before no court at all, which *Rabbi Akiva* nonetheless upheld. This is the *da'as yachid* upon which *Rabba bar Chiya* relied.

*Rav Yosef bar Minyumi* quoted *Rav Nachman*: *ein halacha ke-osah ha-zug* — we do not rule like *Rabbi Shimon* and *Rabbi Yochanan ha-Sandlar*, the pair who validated two-judge *chalitza*. Thus *Rabba bar Chiya* was going even further, relying on the even more isolated view of *Rabbi Akiva*. The *gemara* adds: and if you prefer, you could say that even all three leniencies — the *mok*, the nighttime, and the absence of a *beit din* — ultimately trace back to a single chain of minority tradition, as recorded in a *braita* reporting that *Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha* himself once performed *chalitza* using felt, alone, and at night. *Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosi* reports this — characteristically, as he is consistently the tradent of eyewitness accounts throughout *hazal*. Whether this means the other two leniencies should now be revisited is a separate question for the *poskim*.

### Metzora Source

The *Mishna* teaches that *chalitza* performed on the left foot is invalid, and the *gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama d'rabbanan?* What is the Rabbis' source for requiring the right foot when the *Torah* does not say "right" anywhere in the *chalitza* passage? *Ulla* answers: *yalfinan regel regel mimitzora* — we derive "foot" from "foot" by the *metzora*. In the purification ritual of the *metzora*, the text specifies the right foot explicitly. We learn from there to here: *mah lehalan yamin af kan yamin*.

### Position Reversal

*Rabbi Eliezer*, who validates left-foot *chalitza*, does not accept this *gezeira shava* from *metzora*. Yet a *braita* reports *Rabbi Eliezer* himself deriving "right ear" for the case of ear-piercing of a slave from the *metzora* — *ne'emar kan ozen ve-ne'emar lehallan ozen*, a *gezeira shava* of "ear" to "ear." If he accepts that *gezeira shava*, he might as well accept the one from *metzora* to *chalitza*. *Rabbi Yosef bar Yosef* said in the name of *Yochanan*: *muchlefet hashita* — reverse the positions, and restore consistency to *Rabbi Eliezer*.

### Rava Gezeira

*Rava* says: *le'olam lo tehipach* — do not reverse the positions. There is no need to. *Ozen ozen mufni* — the word "ear" appears redundantly in the slave passage, which makes it available to serve as one end of a *gezeira shava*. *Regel regel lo mufni* — the word "foot" does not appear redundantly in the *chalitza* passage, so *Rabbi Eliezer* has no available endpoint to anchor the *gezeira shava* from *metzora* to *chalitza*. Hence there is no inconsistency in *Rabbi Eliezer* accepting one *gezeira shava* but not the other.

### No Redundancy Q

The *gemara* presses further: *ve-chi lo mufni mai pircha ika?* — even granting that "foot" is not redundant by *chalitza*, what specific logical challenge would defeat the *gezeira shava*? After all, a *gezeira shava* need not have redundancy at both endpoints to function; the presence or absence of redundancy affects only whether it can withstand a challenge, not whether it can be made at all.

The answer: *mah le-metzora sheken ta'un erez eitz erez ve-eizov ve-shani tola'as* — *metzora* involves an elaborate ritual with cedar wood, hyssop, and crimson thread. Precisely because *metzora* is accompanied by such a detailed and demanding set of ritual criteria, its requirement of the right foot is contextually justified. *Chalitza* lacks these elaborate requirements, so one cannot assume its rules must mirror those of *metzora* in this respect. This challenge cannot be refuted, and therefore the *gezeira shava* from *metzora* to *chalitza* remains unavailable to *Rabbi Eliezer*.

This allows us to articulate a taxonomy of *gezeira shava* strength: the most robust form has redundancy at both endpoints and is immune to challenge; a somewhat weaker form has redundancy at one endpoint; the weakest has redundancy at neither endpoint, which means it may still be proposed but can be defeated by any contextual objection. This is precisely the structure the *gemara* is working with here.

---

## Components

### Chaltzah Verakeka

The *Mishna* now turns to the three components of *chalitza*: removal of the shoe, spitting, and recitation of the verses. *Chaltzah verakeka aval lo kara* — she removed the shoe and spat but did not recite — *chalitzatah kesheira*, it is valid. Recitation is not *me'akev*.

### No Removal

*Kara verakeka aval lo chaltza* — she recited and spat but did not remove the shoe — *chalitzatah pesulah*, it is invalid. The act of removal is the core of the entire proceeding; there is a reason it is called *chalitza*.

### No Spitting

*Chaltza vekara aval lo rakeka* — she removed the shoe and recited but did not spit — *Rabbi Eliezer omer chalitzatah pesulah*, invalid; *Rabbi Akiva omer chalitzatah kesheira*, valid. The debate concerns whether spitting is *me'akev*.

### Acts Essential

*Rabbi Eliezer*'s reasoning: *kkah yeaseh* — "thus shall be done" — means *kol davar shehu maaseh me'akev*, anything that is an act is indispensable. Spitting is an act; therefore it is *me'akev*. By the same logic, recitation is not an act in the operative sense, and therefore is not *me'akev*. This raises the philosophically rich question of whether *dibbur* constitutes *maaseh* — a question *Tosafot* engages with at length.

### To the Man

*Rabbi Akiva* responds: *misham raya?* — you want to bring proof from there? Read the verse carefully: *kacha yeaseh la-ish* — this shall be done *to the man*. *Kol davar shenaaseh ba-ish* — only what is done *to* the man is *me'akev*. Removal of the shoe is done to him. Spitting in front of him is not done to him — she spits before him, not upon him. Therefore spitting is not *me'akev*.

---

## Disqualified

### Cheresh

*Hacheresh she-nichlatz veha-chereshet she-chaltzah* — if a deaf-mute man had the *chalitza* performed, or a deaf-mute woman performed it, *chalitzatah pesulah* — it is invalid.

### Ketanah

*Ketanah she-chaltzah* — a minor girl who performed *chalitza* — *tachlotz mishetagdil*, she must redo it when she reaches adulthood. *Ve'im lo chaltzah chalitzatah pesulah* — if she does not redo it, it remains invalid.

### Court Size

*Chaltza bishnayim o bishloshoh ve-nimtza echad mehem karov o pasul* — if she performed *chalitza* before two, or before three where one proved to be a relative or otherwise disqualified, *chalitzatah pesulah* — it is invalid. *Rabbi Shimon* and *Rabbi Yochanan ha-Sandlar* validate such a *chalitza* after the fact.

### Private Case

*U-ma'aseh be-echad she-chalatz beino le-veinah be-veis ha-asurim* — there was an incident of a man who performed *chalitza* privately in prison, with no *beit din* present whatsoever — *va ma'aseh lifnei Rabbi Akiva ve-hichshir* — and when it came before *Rabbi Akiva*, he declared it valid. This is a striking ruling. The *psukim* repeatedly emphasize *le-einei ha-zekeinim* — in the presence of the elders — yet *Rabbi Akiva* validates *chalitza* with literally no court at all. *Rav Nachman* rules we do not follow this *da'as yachid*.

The situation of the *chereshet* raises a deeply troubling practical question. If the *yavam* is a *cheresh* and cannot have *chalitza* performed with him, and cannot do *yibum* properly either, what becomes of the *yevamah*? *Rashi* acknowledges explicitly that a *chereshet* who needs *chalitza* has no remedy through *chalitza* — *ein la takana* — and her only possible relief is *yibum*, and if they subsequently wish to separate, he may give her a *get*. The *halacha* does contemplate situations in which *chalitza* is simply impossible and *yibum* is the only path, even when that outcome is profoundly difficult. This follows from the structure of the *Torah*'s framework: because *yibum* remains an alternative, the impossibility of *chalitza* does not automatically release the woman from the *levirate* bond.

---

## Cheresh Analysis

### Ileim Intellect

The *gemara* now probes the grounds for the *cheresh*'s disqualification. *Rava* opens with the observation: since the *Mishna* unanimously agreed that *kriyah* — recitation — is not *me'akev*, the *cheresh*'s disability need not be the cause of disqualification. Therefore *Rava* reasons that a mute person — *ileim* — who is fully hearing and of full intellect, merely unable to speak, should be perfectly valid for *chalitza*. *Hashta de-amarta kri'ah lo me'akva, lefichach ileim ve-ilemet she-chaltzah chalitzatam kesherah* — since recitation is not *me'akev*, a mute person may perform *chalitza* and it is valid.

### Intellect Challenge

The *gemara* challenges: but then what is the reason the *cheresh* and *chereshet* are disqualified? *Mai ta'ama?* If it is because they cannot recite — *lav mishum delav benei kri'ah ninhu* — then a mute person would be equally disqualified by the same reasoning, since a mute person also cannot recite. So is the *cheresh*'s disqualification on account of the inability to recite, or on account of lacking full *da'at*?

The *gemara* answers: the *cheresh* is disqualified *mishum delav benei da'ah ninhu* — because they are not of full intellect, not because of the inability to speak. The category of *cheresh* in *halachic* discourse reflects the reality that, in a society without schools for the deaf, an individual who could neither hear nor speak often developed without acquiring the conceptual framework of normal social and legal life. This is distinct from a mute person who can hear — who processes language, understands the world, and simply cannot produce speech. *Ufumaihu hu de-che'av lehu* — their mouth causes them difficulty, not their minds.

### Recitation Ability

However, the *gemara* then raises a further challenge from the school of *Rabbi Yannai*: *lefi she-eino be-omar ve-omrah* — the *cheresh* and *chereshet* are disqualified precisely because they are not in the category of "he says and she says," meaning the inability to recite is itself the disqualifying factor, not the lack of *da'at*. This reading is actually more favorable to the dignity of the *cheresh* — it treats them as intellectually capable — but it has the practical consequence of excluding the *ileim* as well.

The *gemara* concedes the point: *ela ki itmar de-Rava aseifa itmar* — *Rava*'s statement must actually have been directed at the end of the *Mishna*, and his ruling is reversed. A mute person cannot perform valid *chalitza*, because although recitation is not *me'akev* as an act that must be performed, the person performing *chalitza* must at least have the capacity to recite. Even if the act is not required, the potential must exist.

### Potential Test

This brings us to the principle articulated by *Rabbi Zeira*: *kol ha-ra'uy le-bilah ein bilah me'akevet bo, ve-chol she-eino ra'uy le-bilah bilah me'akevet bo.* By the case of the *mincha*, the *Torah* describes the flour as *belulah ba-shemen* — mixed with oil. If one fails to mix it, *bedieved* the *mincha* is valid. But if it was impossible to mix — because the volume of flour was too great — the *mincha* is entirely invalid. The principle: one does not actually have to perform the act, but the act must be performable in principle.

### Mincha Parallel

*Tosafot* illuminates the conceptual basis: where the *Torah* frames a requirement as a descriptor — *belulah ba-shemen*, "mixed with oil," an adjective rather than a verbal command — we read it as characterizing the nature of the object rather than mandating a specific act. Therefore, it suffices that the object has the *potential* to exhibit that characteristic, even if the act is not performed. By contrast, where the *Torah* says *ve-amar ve-omrah* — "and he shall say and she shall say" — one might think this demands actual performance. *Rava* resolves this by reading the verbal form as a characterization of the *gavra*, the person: the participants must be of the type of person who can say — they must have the capacity, even if the act is waived. A mute person, lacking that capacity, is therefore excluded, even though the act of recitation itself is not *me'akev*.

---

## Spitting Power

### Spitting Alone

The *gemara* records a ruling sent to the father of *Shmuel*: *yevamah she-rakakah tachlotz* — a *yevamah* who spat alone, without performing any other component of *chalitza*, must subsequently perform full *chalitza*. The implication is that the mere spitting alone is enough to disqualify her from *yibum* with any of the brothers, leaving *chalitza* as her only path.

### Akiva Question

This raises an immediate question: whose opinion does this reflect? If it is *Rabbi Akiva*, who rules that spitting is not *me'akev* even when one is in the midst of performing *chalitza*, then spitting alone — performed outside the context of *chalitza* entirely — should carry even less weight. *Rabbi Akiva* does not even require spitting when everything else is being done properly. How then could spitting alone, stripped of any further act, be sufficient to disqualify her from *yibum*? Surely spitting should be entirely trivial for *Rabbi Akiva*.

### Two Acts

The *gemara* resolves: this must be *Rabbi Eliezer*'s view, for whom spitting is *me'akev*. But then a further difficulty arises: *Rabbi Eliezer* requires two acts — removal of the shoe and spitting. The principle of *shenei devarim ha-matirin* is that when two elements are jointly required to produce a permitted status, neither element alone carries any legal weight. If you have not done both, you have done nothing. How then does spitting alone carry enough weight to disqualify her?

### Eimurim

The *gemara* draws an analogy to the *emurim* — the internal sacrificial parts that must be burned on the altar before the rest of the animal may be consumed. If the *emurim* are lost or become *tamei* and cannot be burned, the meat may nonetheless be eaten. But if the *emurim* are present, the meat may not be eaten until they are burned. This suggests a nuanced position: when an element that would otherwise be *me'akev* is unavailable, its absence does not block the permitted act; but when it is present and available, it must be performed. By analogy, one might say that spitting, when present and possible, is *me'akev* within *chalitza* — yet its lone occurrence outside *chalitza* should still carry no weight, since the removal of the shoe has not been performed.

### Half Status

The *gemara*'s resolution invokes *Rabbi*'s position in an unrelated case of *kivsei atzeret* — the lambs brought on *Shavuot*. Sanctification of the accompanying loaves requires both the *shechita* and the *zerakat hadam* of the lambs, performed with proper intent. If the *shechita* was proper but the *zerakat hadam* was not, *Rabbi* rules *kadosh ve-eino kadosh* — it is half-consecrated. There exists an intermediate state of partial sanctification. *Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon* disagrees: it is either fully sanctified or not at all; there is no halfway.

Applied to our case: according to *Rabbi Eliezer*, *chalitza* requires two acts. By analogy to *Rabbi*'s view, if only one of the two required acts has been performed, the result is not zero — it is a partial state. The woman has done enough to be in an intermediate status: she has not completed *chalitza*, but she has done enough to sever the *yibum* bond. It is, in *Rabbi*'s terms, a kind of fifty percent — enough to block *yibum* even though full *chalitza* has not been achieved. This is a genuinely striking *gemara*: the halachic consequence of spitting alone, for *Rabbi Eliezer*, flows from the recognition that a partially performed multi-element act can produce a real, if incomplete, legal effect.

---

---

# Yevamot 106

## Private Chalitza Story

### Mishna Overview

The daf opens at the bottom of 105b, with the conclusion of the *mishna*'s treatment of *chalitza* performed outside the formal framework of a *beit din*. The *mishna* had cited a range of views regarding the minimum requirements for a valid *chalitza*, culminating in the opinion that perhaps even two witnesses — or fewer — suffice. Rabbi Shimon ben Yochanan HaSandlar is among those who held that a *beit din* is not strictly necessary. The practical ruling, however, is that *bedi'avad* one does need a *beit din*, and *lechatchila* three judges is sufficient — indeed, even *lechatchila* one need not convene five, though the *Gemara* from the previous daf established that doing it with five is preferable for the sake of greater publicization.

### Proof of Event

The *mishna* then records a story: *ma'aseh b'echad she'chalatz beino l'veinah b'veit ha'asurim* — a man performed *chalitza* with his *yevama* privately, in prison, and the matter came before Rabbi Akiva, who declared it *kasher*. On this the *Gemara* asks: *beino l'veinah mi yadeinan* — if the act was entirely private, how do we know it occurred? Even if the parties themselves report it, on what basis can a *beit din* rule accordingly?

### Eidim Mibachutz

Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers: *b'eidim ra'uhu she-tzofin mibachutz* — there were witnesses who observed the proceedings from the outside. They were not themselves a *beit din* and were not physically present as part of the ceremony, but they provided sufficient evidence that the event had in fact taken place.

### Types of Witnesses

This raises a deeper distinction. Witnesses in halachic contexts serve two distinct functions. *Eidei kiyum* are witnesses whose presence actually effectuates and validates the legal act — as in *kiddushin*, where even certainty that the act occurred is insufficient without witnesses who legally constitute the act. *Eidei birur*, by contrast, serve only the evidentiary function of establishing that something happened. Here, the witnesses observing from outside operated only as *eidei birur*. They were certainly not a *beit din*, and likely did not even fulfill the role of *eidei kiyum* for the *chalitza* itself. In principle the act was done entirely privately; there is simply sufficient evidence that it occurred.

### Location Dispute

A further question is then raised: when the *mishna* says the story occurred in *beit ha'asurim* and came before Rabbi Akiva — who exactly was in prison? Did the *chalitza* take place outside, with the case subsequently brought to Rabbi Akiva who was imprisoned by the Romans? Or did the *chalitza* itself occur inside the prison, and was then reported to Rabbi Akiva who was elsewhere? Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav resolves it: *b'veit ha'asurim haya ma'aseh ul'veit ha'asurim ba ma'aseh* — the event happened in prison, and it was brought to Rabbi Akiva in prison as well.

### Tosafot Analysis

Tosafot notes that this question is somewhat puzzling, since the *mishna*'s own language appears unambiguous. The text reads: *ma'aseh b'echad she'chalatz beino l'veinah b'veit ha'asurim u'va ma'aseh lifnei Rabbi Akiva v'hichshir* — clearly placing the event in prison and the reporting to Rabbi Akiva thereafter. Tosafot explains that the ambiguity only arises if one removes the *vav* of *u'va ma'aseh*, yielding a reading where *b'veit ha'asurim* modifies the arrival before Rabbi Akiva rather than the event itself — though even that reading is a stretch. The reason Tosafot pursues this is that the *Yerushalmi* preserves an explicit tradition that this question was brought to Rabbi Akiva while he was incarcerated, and the *Gemara* Bavli is attempting to read that tradition into the *mishna* as well.

### Secret Message

Tosafot cites the *Yerushalmi*'s colorful account of how the question reached Rabbi Akiva in prison. Yochanan HaSandlar — himself mentioned in the *mishna* as one who ruled that a *beit din* is not required — passed by the prison of Rabbi Akiva. Posing as a peddler, he called out: *man ba'ei nach'tin, man ba'ei tzinon* — who needs needles, who needs pins — as cover for delivering a covert halachic message. Slipped into his peddler's cry was the question: *chalitza beno uveinah, mahu* — what is the law if *chalitza* was performed privately? Rabbi Akiva, understanding, thrust his head through the prison bars and replied in kind, using the word *kushin* — some type of pin or implement — whose sound evokes the word *kasher*: it is *kasher*.

## Mutat & Muafit

### Chalitza Mutat

The *Gemara* moves to the top of 106a with a *baraita*: *chalitza mutat keshera* — a *chalitza* performed under deception or trickery is valid. The *baraita* then asks: what constitutes *chalitza mutat*?

### Reish Lakish's View

Reish Lakish defines it as a case where the *yavam* wished to perform *yibum* but was told: *chalot uv'chach konesah* — go through this *chalitza* ceremony and through it you will acquire her as your wife. In other words, he was misled into believing that the *chalitza* ceremony was itself a form of *yibum*. Since he may have been unaware of what the ceremony entailed, and since *bedi'avad* the recitation of the verses is not indispensable, the *chalitza* might be considered valid despite his misunderstanding.

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan objects sharply. He cites a teaching: whether he had intent and she did not, or she had intent and he did not, or neither of them had intent — *chalitzatah pesulah*. Both parties must intend for the act to take effect as a *chalitza*. How then can Reish Lakish say this is valid? If the man believed he was performing an act of *yibum*, his *kavanah* was for its very opposite — he cannot be said to have intended an effective *chalitza*.

### Money Condition

Rabbi Yochanan therefore reframes the definition of valid *chalitza mutat*: *kol she'omrim lo chalot lamah she'titein lach matayim zuz* — they tell him to perform *chalitza* and in exchange she will give him two hundred *zuz*, but she never actually intends to pay, and in the end does not. In this case, the man fully understood he was performing *chalitza*; he simply expected compensation that never materialized. Since he intended the act as *chalitza*, it is valid — the unkept promise is the *mutat*, the deception, but it does not undermine the *chalitza* itself.

### Woman's Story

A corroborating *baraita* is then cited. *Ma'aseh b'isha achas she'nafelah lifnei yavam she'einah haguna lo* — a woman fell before a *yavam* who was not appropriate for her. They told him: perform *chalitza* and she will give you two hundred *zuz*. The case came before Rabbi Akiva, who validated it even though the money was never paid.

### Conditions Logic

This raises an obvious question: if the *chalitza* was made *al menat* — on the condition that she pay him two hundred *zuz* — why is the *chalitza* valid when the condition was not fulfilled? A condition that is not met should render the act void. The answer lies in a principle cited by Rashi from the *Gemara* in Ketubot: any act that cannot be delegated to a *shaliach* cannot be made conditional. Agency is possible only where a person holds the legal power to effect a transaction and can therefore transfer that power. Where agency is impossible, conditions too cannot bind.

### Rav Chaim

This leads to a fundamental conceptual point developed by Rav Chaim. He asks why it is that *chalitza* performed by a minor woman is, according to a serious opinion, nonetheless valid, when ordinarily a minor cannot perform legally binding acts. His answer addresses the very structure of *chalitza* and *yibum*. The *Torah* does not invest the *yavam* or the *yevama* with power to effect a change of status. Rather, the *Torah* itself severs or creates the bond when the prescribed ritual is performed. The parties are not empowered actors — they are participants in a ritual whose legal consequence the *Torah* draws automatically. This is why *yibum* can take effect even through an inadvertent act of intercourse: the *Torah* creates the bond upon the act occurring, regardless of *da'at*. Similarly, *chalitza* does not require the parties to "do" something in the sense of exercising legal capacity — they go through the motions and the *Torah* effects the change.

This understanding explains why agency is impossible: you can appoint a *shaliach* to exercise a power you hold, but if you hold no power — if it is the *Torah* that does the effecting — there is nothing to transfer. And since conditions are structurally linked to agency, the same reasoning applies: you cannot condition whether the *Torah* will or will not sever a bond upon the ritual's completion. Therefore, even if the money is not paid, the *chalitza* is fully valid.

## Rabbi Chiya Case

### Setup

The *Gemara* now introduces a case involving Rabbi Chiya bar Abba. A woman had fallen before a *yavam* who was inappropriate for her. Her mother indicated to Rabbi Chiya bar Abba that the man was interested not in the woman but in her money — he intended to perform *yibum*, take her assets, and then divorce her.

### First Trick

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba attempted to induce the *yavam* to perform *chalitza* by telling him: *chalot lah betachat hakonsa* — perform *chalitza* and through it you will be married to her. This is precisely the maneuver that Reish Lakish had proposed and that Rabbi Yochanan had rejected.

### Invalid Chalitza

Indeed, the first *chalitza* was not a valid one, since the man's intent was for *yibum*, not *chalitza*. However, Rabbi Chiya bar Abba then confronted him after the fact: while the *chalitza* did not achieve what you thought it would — it does not make her your wife — it nonetheless constitutes a *chalitza pesulah*, a defective *chalitza*. And the *halacha* is that after a *chalitza pesulah*, *yibum* is no longer permitted. Since *yibum* is now foreclosed in any case, Rabbi Chiya bar Abba urged him: *chalotz lah chalitza ma'alyasa* — you might as well now perform a proper *chalitza* to free her entirely. Of course, this placed him in a precarious situation, since the man, feeling deceived, might well refuse the second *chalitza* out of spite.

## Rav Papa Case

### Money-Seeker

A parallel case is then introduced. The daughter of the father-in-law of Rav Papa — apparently a sister-in-law or close female relative — fell before a *yavam* who was not suitable for her. His motivation, too, was purely financial: he was interested only in consuming her money. Rav Papa, concerned for her welfare, came before Abaye.

## Rabbi Chiya Case (II)

### Money Trick

Returning briefly to the Rabbi Chiya bar Abba narrative, the better resolution — and the one relevant to the Rav Papa case — is to promise the *yavam* money as inducement for the *chalitza*, without intending to pay. Since, as established above, conditions cannot attach to *chalitza*, the *chalitza* is valid regardless of whether the money is delivered.

## Rav Papa Case (II)

### Abaye's Trick

Abaye, addressing the *yavam* in the Rav Papa case, initially proposed the same approach that Rabbi Chiya bar Abba had tried: *chalot lah betachat hakonsa* — perform *chalitza* and you will thereby be married to her. Rav Papa immediately challenged Abaye: does the master not hold the ruling of Rabbi Yochanan, that this form of deception invalidates the *chalitza*?

### Rav Papa

Abaye conceded and asked: so what should I tell him? Rav Papa replied: tell him *chalot lah al menat she'titein lach matayim zuz* — perform *chalitza* and she will give you two hundred *zuz*. This is the valid form of *chalitza mutat*. The *yavam* proceeded to perform *chalitza*.

### Payment Dispute

After the *chalitza* was completed, Abaye told the woman she should pay the man the two hundred *zuz* — not because the *chalitza* required it to be valid, but because she had made a promise, and one ought to honor one's word. Rav Papa objected: she can say *meshata ni bach* — I was only joking with you, I never really intended to pay.

Here the *Gemara* enters territory of *Choshen Mishpat* rather than *Even HaEzer*. Even granting that the *chalitza* is valid regardless, why should she be free of the monetary obligation? Rashi notes the distinction between a gratuitous promise — which is not legally binding — and *sechirus*, a fee for services rendered. If she agreed to pay him two hundred *zuz* for performing *chalitza*, that looks like a contracted fee, and ordinarily one is bound by a contracted fee.

### River Story

Rav Papa's answer draws on a *baraita*: a person fleeing from prison came to a river crossing and said to the boatman, *tol dinar v'ha'avireini* — take a *dinar* and ferry me across. He is obligated only to pay the normal going rate, not the inflated sum — because the boatman took advantage of the man's desperate circumstances, and in such situations the claim of *meshata ni bach* is available: the agreed price is not binding beyond what the service actually warrants. *Chalitza* is a *mitzvah*, not a commercial transaction. No one is normally paid for performing it. Any agreement to pay is therefore not a genuine commercial arrangement, and the woman may invoke *meshata ni bach* to be released from the obligation.

### Death Curse

Abaye, apparently frustrated, asked Rav Papa: where is your father? In the city. Where is your mother? In the city. Abaye then cast his gaze upon them, and they died. The reason for Abaye's anger is not immediately apparent, since both he and Rav Papa were working toward the same goal. One explanation, cited in the name of the Ravyatz, is that Abaye did not intend to harm Rav Papa's parents; rather, by contemplating Rav Papa's good fortune in having his parents nearby, Abaye inadvertently caused divine scrutiny to fall upon them, with tragic results.

### Fee Conditions

Tosafot adds an important qualification to the principle of *meshata ni bach*. The claim is available specifically in a case where an exorbitant sum was demanded far in excess of the normal rate — as with the boatman exploiting a fugitive's desperation. Where the agreed fee actually reflects the going rate, or where the person agreeing to perform the service bears genuine risk or cost, the claim of *meshata ni bach* is unavailable and the obligation stands.

## Get vs Chalitza

### Tricked Status

A *baraita* now draws the contrast systematically. *Chalitza mutat keshera* — a *chalitza* performed under financial inducement that is never paid is valid. *Get mutat pasul* — a *get* obtained under a broken promise of payment is invalid. The reason follows directly from the earlier analysis: a *get* is a legal act that can be given through a *shaliach*, and therefore conditions can attach to it. If the *get* was given *al menat* that she pay him a sum of money, and the money is not paid, the condition is not fulfilled and the *get* is void. *Chalitza*, by contrast, cannot be made conditional, and therefore the unkept promise does not affect its validity.

### Conditional Acts

This distinction — that *chalitza* cannot be conditioned because it cannot be delegated to an agent — has already been fully developed above, and the *baraita* confirms it.

### Forced Acts

The *baraita* continues: *chalitza muafit pesulah* — a *chalitza* that was outright compelled, with no pretense of the *yavam*'s agreement, is invalid. *Get meuaseh kasher* — a *get* that was forced by a *beit din* is valid, as will be learned in *Gittin*.

### Difference

The *Gemara* presses: what is the principled distinction? If the *yavam* says *rotzeh ani* — I am now willing — after being compelled, then surely *chalitza* too should be valid; and if he does not say *rotzeh ani*, then the *get* too should be invalid. On simple analysis there seems to be no asymmetry between them. The *Gemara* resolves this: *hachi ka'amar* — the *baraita* must be read as distinguishing cases. *Chalitza mutat* is always valid; *get mutat* is always invalid. *Chalitza muafit* and *get meuaseh* are each sometimes valid and sometimes not — and the determinative factor is whether the party ultimately says *rotzeh ani*.

### Korban Parallel

A *baraita* about *korbanot* anchors the principle: *yakriv oto* — he shall offer it — teaches that *beit din* compels a person who refuses to bring an obligatory *korban*. *Yachol al korcho* — might this mean against his will entirely? *Talmud lomar lirtzono* — the verse says it must be with his will. The resolution: *kofin oto ad she'yomar rotzeh ani* — one compels him until he says he wishes to do it.

### Willingness Principle

The same principle applies to *gittin*: *kofin oto ad she'yomar rotzeh ani*. And the *baraita* draws the parallel explicitly. The forced act is validated not by the compulsion but by the eventual expression of willingness.

### Motivation vs Desire

This reflects a striking philosophical distinction the *Gemara* draws between motivation and desire. The *Gemara* even permits, in a number of contexts, transactions entered into under extreme duress — on the theory that whenever someone sells property, it is because economic necessity forced them to, and external compulsion operates no differently. What matters is not the source of motivation but the present state of will. If the *yavam* now says *rotzeh ani*, his motivation for reaching that point is irrelevant — he presently desires it, and the act is valid. The distinction between external compulsion and internal desire, the *Gemara* teaches, is less sharp than one might assume.

## Beit Din & Docs

### Rav's View

The *Gemara* turns to a ruling transmitted through a chain: Rav said in the name of Rava who said in the name of Rav Sechora who said in the name of Rav Huna — *choltzin af al pi she'ein makirim*, a *beit din* may conduct a *chalitza* ceremony even if they do not personally know who the parties are. Similarly, they may conduct a *mi'un* ceremony without knowing the parties.

### Document Rules

The consequence follows directly: *lefikach ein kotvim get chalitza ela im ken makirim* — witnesses cannot write the documentary record of the *chalitza* unless they personally know who the parties are. The reasoning is that since the *beit din* performs the ceremony without verifying identity, there is a real possibility that the man was not in fact the *yavam* — a woman might arrange for a stranger to go through the ceremony. If the witnesses write the document without knowing the man, they would be attesting to something they cannot verify.

### Future Courts

The concern is specifically for *beit din* to'eh — a later *beit din* that receives the document and assumes it was properly conducted, not realizing that the original *beit din* may have been misled about who the *yavam* was. Therefore the witnesses, who do have the capacity to know the parties, bear the responsibility of verification before committing anything to writing.

### Rava's View

Rava, on his own account, takes a stricter position on the front end: *ein choltzin ela im ken makirim* — a *beit din* may not conduct the ceremony at all unless they know the parties. This is the straightforward rule, and it is difficult to argue otherwise.

### Safe Documents

The consequence of Rava's view for the documentary question is the inverse: *v'lefikach kotvim get chalitza af al pi she'ein makirim* — the witnesses may write the document even if they themselves do not know the man. Since the *beit din* has already established the identity of the parties before proceeding, the witnesses need not independently verify. The first *beit din* has done its due diligence, and no later *beit din* will be misled.

## Chalitza Ceremony

### Initial Advice

The final *mishna* of the *perek* describes the complete *chalitza* ceremony step by step. He and his *yevama* come before the *beit din*, and the *beit din* gives them appropriate guidance — *eitzah ha'hogenet lo* — advice suitable to his situation, counseling whether *yibum* or *chalitza* is the proper course.

### Woman Declares

Once the decision for *chalitza* is made, the woman recites: *me'ein yivmi l'hakim l'achiv shem b'Yisrael lo avah yivmi* — my *yavam* does not wish to establish his brother's name in Israel; he does not desire to do *yibum*.

### Man Declares

The man then recites: *lo chafatzti lekachtah* — I do not desire to take her. The *mishna* notes that this recitation is not strictly *me'akev* but constitutes the proper procedure. Both declarations are made *b'lashon hakodesh*, in Hebrew — as the *mishna* in *Sotah* enumerates among the acts that must be performed in the original Hebrew.

### Shoe Removal

*V'nigshah yevimto eilav l'einei hazekenim v'chaltzah na'alo me'al raglo* — the *yevama* approaches him before the elders and removes his shoe from his foot, following the verse.

### Spitting

*V'yarkah b'fanav* — and she spits before him. The *mishna* inserts: *rok ha'nireh la'dayanim* — the spit must be visible to the judges. Whether spitting is strictly *me'akev* has been debated, but the requirement that it be visible to the judges is essential.

### Final Verses

She then recites: *kachah ye'aseh la'ish asher lo yivneh et beit achiv* — thus shall be done to the man who does not build his brother's house.

### Horkanus

Until this point, the *beit din* would prompt her to recite each phrase after them, and the ceremony concluded with that verse. But *u'cheshe'hikri Rabbi Horkanus tachas ha'elah b'Kfar Eitam v'gamar kol haparasha* — when Rabbi Horkanus officiated under the *elah* tree in Kfar Eitam, he had her continue to the end of the verse: *v'nikra shemo b'Yisrael beit chalutz hana'al* — and his name shall be called in Israel: the house of the removed shoe. After Rabbi Horkanus instituted this, the practice spread and it became standard to have her recite the full verse through to that concluding phrase.

### Who Declares

The *mishna* then states: *mitzvah b'dayanim v'lo mitzvah b'talmidim* — the obligation to make the declaration *beit chalutz hana'al* rests with the judges, not the students observing the proceedings. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: the verse says *b'Yisrael* — before Israel — implying that all those present at the ceremony should call out *chalutz hana'al*.

## Verse Recitation

### Woman's Recitation

Abaye rules that the person conducting the *chalitza* ceremony — the member of the *beit din* who is having the parties recite their lines — must be careful not to have her recite the words with pauses that break the verse into misleading segments.

### Lo Aba Yibmi

Specifically: do not have her say *lo* alone and then pause before *aba yibmi*. The verse is *lo aba yibmi* — my *yavam* does not wish — but if she says *lo* and pauses, the phrase *aba yibmi* standing alone means "my *yavam* does wish." She must say the full phrase *lo aba yibmi* in one breath.

### Lo Chafatzti

Similarly, do not have him say *lo* and then pause before *chafatzti lekachtah*. That creates the impression *chafatzti lekachtah* — I do desire to take her. He must say *lo chafatzti lekachtah* as one continuous phrase.

### Rava Lenient

Rava takes a more lenient position: *pesukei milta* — making a pause is simply a matter of completing one's sentence. The context makes clear what is meant, and a brief pause between *lo* and the rest of the phrase does not create a genuine misunderstanding.

### Exception

Nevertheless, Rava agrees that for the specific phrase *lo aba yibmi* there is no room for leniency, and it must be said as a single phrase. Rashi explains: unlike *lo chafatzti lekachtah*, which begins the verse and has nothing preceding it to create ambiguity, the phrase *lo aba yibmi* appears mid-verse, following *me'ein yibmi l'hakim shem l'achiv b'Yisrael*. In that context, a pause after *lo* is far more likely to be heard as a denial of what preceded: "that's not right — *aba yibmi*, actually he does want to." Therefore this particular phrase must be delivered without interruption.

### Care Story

The *Gemara* illustrates the importance of this ruling. Rav Papa and Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua once observed Rav Kahana going to great lengths to have the *yevama* recite the words *lo aba yibmi* all as one phrase. They asked: does the master not hold like Rava's lenient view? Rav Kahana replied: Rava concedes regarding *lo aba yibmi*. Even Rava agrees that for that specific phrase, pauses are not acceptable.

## Get Writing

### Fragment Rule

Abaye rules regarding the writing of the *get chalitza* — the documentary record of the ceremony. One should not write out the complete biblical verses. Rather: *akrinuhu l'didah min me'ein yibmi ad lo aba yibmi* — we had her recite from *me'ein yibmi* until *lo aba yibmi*, citing the opening and closing words but not writing out the full text. Similarly: *akrinuhu l'dideih min lo ad lekachtah* — we had him recite from *lo* until *lekachtah*, deliberately omitting the middle word *chafatzti*. And for her subsequent verse: from *kacha* until *vuchalutz hana'al*.

### Sirtuv Issue

The reason for these deliberate gaps is the prohibition against writing biblical passages without *sirtut* — the scored lines that must accompany Torah writing. If one were to write out the full verses, three or more consecutive words of scripture would appear in the document without the requisite scoring, raising a concern about treating biblical text improperly outside the context of a sacred scroll. By dropping a word in the middle, the document avoids transcribing a complete biblical phrase.

### Man's Verse

For the man's verse, the document records: from *lo* until *lekachtah* — with *chafatzti* omitted so that no three consecutive biblical words appear in sequence.

### Woman's Verses

For the woman's verse at the conclusion of the ceremony, the document records: from *kacha* until *vuchalutz hana'al*, similarly structured to avoid a complete biblical phrase.

### Mar Zutra

Mar Zutra followed a different practice: *mesartet v'chatav lechulah parasha* — he scored the document with *sirtut* and wrote out the entire *parasha*. He evidently held that with proper scoring the concern is resolved.

### Objection

Rav Papa bar Idi challenged this: *veha lo nitenu lichtov* — one is not permitted to write out individual sections of the Torah as standalone passages. The *Gemara* in *Gittin*, Perek Hanizukin, teaches that one does not write a *megillah* — a miniature scroll of select passages — for a child to learn from, precisely because Torah must be written as a complete unit.

### Resolution

The *Gemara* rules: *v'hilchata k'Mar Zutra* — the law follows Mar Zutra. The prohibition against writing isolated Torah passages applies where one is writing it *ada'ata d'parasha* — as a small self-contained excerpt intended to function as a standalone Torah text. The *get chalitza* is different: *v'lo lekdusha hu* — it is not written as a sacred text but as a legal document, to record what was recited during the ceremony. Since the intent is documentary rather than scriptural, writing the full passage with *sirtut* is permitted.

## Spitting Details

### Wind Effect

Abaye rules: if the woman spat and the wind carried the spit away — *lo asa velo klum* — it counts for nothing. The *Torah* requires *v'yarkah b'fanav* — she shall spit *before him*, meaning the spit must arrive in his presence.

### Presence

The requirement is not that the spit physically strike him, but that it land in front of him in a way that constitutes spitting *before* him.

### Height Factor

Height differences between the parties affect whether this requirement is met. If he is tall and she is short, then even if the wind blows the spit away after it leaves her mouth, it was already *b'fanav* — before his face — the moment it emerged, since he was towering above her as she spit in his direction. In that case the *chalitza* is valid even if the spit is carried off.

### Front of Face

If she is tall and he is short, the spit leaves her mouth at a height above his face. The requirement — *ba'inan ad demati lahadi apeih* — is that the spit must actually descend to the level of his face before any dispersion occurs. If the wind catches it before it reaches his face level, the requirement has not been met and the *chalitza* is compromised.

### Eating Effect

Rava adds: if the woman ate garlic, or ate clay, and then spat — *lo asa velo klum* — it does not count.

### Own Accord

The reason: *v'yarkah me'atzma ba'inan* — the spitting must come from her own initiative and from her natural saliva. If she ate something that induced her to spit, or that altered the character of what she produced, the act is not genuinely *her* spitting but something caused by the food. This fails the requirement.

### Judge Witness

Rava further rules: *tzrichi dayanei lemichzi roka ki nafik mipuma d'yevama* — the judges must see the spit at the moment it leaves the *yevama*'s mouth. The verse states *l'einei hazekenim v'yarkah* — to the eyes of the elders and she shall spit — meaning the act of spitting itself must be directly witnessed by the judges, not merely inferred from its result.

## Final Proclamation

### Name Change

*V'nikra shemo b'Yisrael beit chalutz hana'al* — and his name shall be called in Israel: the house of the one whose shoe was removed. This declaration concludes the ceremony and formally fixes his new status.

### Declaration Role

The *mishna* rules: *mitzvah b'dayanim velo b'talmidim* — the obligation of this declaration falls upon the judges, not upon students or observers. Rabbi Yehuda holds, as noted above, that *b'Yisrael* implies all those present.

### Tarfon Story

A *baraita* records: Rabbi Yehuda said — once we were sitting before Rabbi Tarfon and a *yevama* came to perform *chalitza*. Rabbi Tarfon said to all of us: say *chalutza na, chalutza na, chalutza na* — three times in succession, in a manner similar to other rabbinic proclamations of permitted status (*mutar lach, mutar lach, mutar lach*). This triple declaration publicly and ceremonially marks the finality of the *chalitza* and the new status of the *chalutzah*.

### Perek End

*Hadran alach mitzvas chalitza* — with the conclusion of this *baraita*, the *perek* of *mitzvas chalitza* formally ends.

# Yevamot 107

## Mi'un Overview

### Perek Intro

Today's daf opens a new *perek* — *Perek Beit Shammai* — which, despite its name, is not exclusively focused on *Beit Shammai* but rather opens with a series of debates between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel*, returning us to the world of *yibum*.

### Mi'un Definition

The *perek* centers on the institution of *mi'un* — refusal by a minor girl. The background is as follows: a girl whose father has died may be married off by her mother and brothers. Even though the marriage is of rabbinic force only, and even though she actually assents to it (*mi-da'atah*), she retains the right to be *mema'enet* — to refuse her husband — until she reaches adulthood. The critical and defining feature of *mi'un* is its retroactive effect: unlike a *get*, which dissolves a marriage that existed, *mi'un* renders the marriage as though it never took place at all. She is considered to have never been married. This distinction carries significant practical implications, not least for matters of *kehunah* status.

### Marriage Stages

The *perek* raises questions about precisely at which stages of the marriage process *mi'un* may or may not be exercised, and what its implications are for *yibum* when a husband dies and a brother-in-law enters the picture.

---

## Arusot/Nesuot Debate

### Shammai Position

The *Mishnah* opens: *Beit Shammai omrim, ein mema'anin ela arusot* — only girls who are still in the *arusah* stage, the stage of betrothal, may perform *mi'un*. Once the girl has become a *nesuah* — once she has begun actually living with her husband and the marriage has become a lived reality — *Beit Shammai* holds that *mi'un* is no longer available to her. The marriage has reached a qualitatively different level when it has moved beyond the purely legal and technical into the genuinely lived.

### Hillel Position

*Beit Hillel* disagrees: *arusot u-nesuot* — at either stage, whether she is an *arusah* or a *nesuah*, she retains the right to perform *mi'un*. The *Mishnah* continues with additional disputes. *Beit Shammai* holds that *mi'un* is effective only against the husband (*b'ba'al*) but not against the *yabam*. *Beit Hillel* holds it applies *be-ba'al u-ve-yabam* — against both the husband and the brother-in-law. *Beit Shammai* further requires that the *mi'un* be performed in the presence of the husband and before a *Beit Din*; *Beit Hillel* permits it even not in his presence and even outside of a formal court setting.

The *Mishnah* then notes that *Beit Hillel* observes that a girl may be *mema'enet* as a minor even four or five times — her mother and brothers remarry her, she refuses again, and the cycle repeats. While this is stated as a legal observation, *Beit Shammai* responds with a sharp principle.

### Hefker Concern

*Beit Shammai* declares: *ein benot Yisrael hefker* — daughters of Israel must not be treated as ownerless or unprotected. Even if the mechanism is technically her choice, allowing a girl to be serially married off and to repeatedly refuse reduces her to an object passed from one man to the next in a manner fundamentally at odds with her dignity and the protections she deserves. Therefore *Beit Shammai* rules: she may perform *mi'un* with the first husband, but thereafter she must wait until she reaches adulthood — *mamtenet ad shetagdil* — and only then marry again. The concern of *lo yehei Bnot Yisrael hefker* translates into a legal restriction: we prevent the second rabbinic marriage from being eligible for *mi'un* at all.

### Discussion

A closer look reveals that this injunction is directed not purely at her but at the institution itself. While the girl assents to each marriage — the *Gemara* will later make clear that *kiddushei ketanah* by mother and brothers requires her *da'at* — the concern of *lo yehei Bnot Yisrael hefker* operates at the structural level. The rabbis are not simply protecting her freedom; they are preventing a pattern that, however voluntary in form, compromises her standing. The *Mishnah*'s curious insertion of the word *tema'en* a second time — even in the instruction to wait until adulthood — is something the *Gemara* will address.

---

## Ein Tenai Principle

### Stipulations Fail

The *Gemara* now turns to explain *Beit Shammai*'s position. *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel*: *mai ta'ama de-Beit Shammai? Lefi she-ein tenai be-nisu'in* — because there are no effective stipulations at the stage of *nisu'in*. The underlying assumption is that in a standard marriage, while stipulations (*tenaim*) might theoretically function at the stage of *kiddushin*, once the couple reaches *nisu'in* such conditions become inoperative. And therefore, in a normal marriage, there would be no mechanism by which the marriage could be retroactively dissolved after *nisu'in* through an external stipulation.

### Tnai vs Ta'ut

This principle requires some precision. *Ein tenai be-nisu'in* is not an absolute statement that stipulations are legally impossible at the *nisu'in* stage. The *Gemara* elsewhere explains that the reason *tenaim* are considered waived at *nisu'in* is *ein adam oseh beilato beilat zenut* — a man does not want his acts of marital intimacy to be conditional, such that if the condition is not met, the sex retroactively becomes extramarital. Therefore, as a general presumption, any stipulation he might have made is considered voluntarily waived once the couple begins living together. This is distinct from *kiddushei ta'ut* — a case of fundamental error — which can retroactively nullify even a *nisu'in*-stage marriage, since it is not an external stipulation but a basic mistake about the nature of the transaction itself.

### Public Misconception

Given this background, *Beit Shammai*'s concern becomes clear: if we allow a *nesuah* to perform *mi'un* and simply walk away without a *get*, observers who see a couple who have been living together for years suddenly separate will assume there must have been a *tenai* — a stipulation — that was activated. And from that they will draw the dangerous and false inference that *tenaim* are operative at the stage of *nisu'in*. The consequence would be that people would believe they can construct conditional marriages that dissolve retroactively even in full adult marriages, leading to the erosion of the entire institution of *nisu'in*. This concern for public misconception — *ati l-meimar yesh tenai be-nisu'in* — is the driving force behind *Beit Shammai*'s position according to this explanation.

This principle of *ein tenai benisuin* became historically significant: it is the very title of a famous *sefer* compiled from the rabbinic responsa that opposed the mid-nineteenth-century proposal by French rabbis to use conditional marriage as a solution to the *agunah* problem.

### Tosafot Caveat

*Tosafot* here raises a pointed difficulty. The same *Shmuel* who formulates the reasoning of *Beit Shammai* as based on *ein tenai benisuin* appears elsewhere — in the context of *Perek HaMadir* — to hold that if a man betrothed a woman with a condition and then cohabited with her without repeating the condition (*kidshah al tenai ve-khansah stam*), she does not require a *get*, a ruling that *Abaye* and *Rava* explain according to *Beit Shammai*'s own reasoning of *ein adam oseh beilato beilat zenut*. But this implies that even according to *Beit Shammai*, in *Shmuel*'s view, *yesh tenai benisuin* under certain circumstances. *Tosafot* works through the resolution, and the essential point is that *ein tenai benisuin* is not an absolute legal impossibility — it is a presumptive rule that may yield under specific conditions, and the principle is less categorical than the polemical use of its name might suggest.

---

## When Mi'un Ceases

### Chuppah Stage

The *Gemara* probes the precise boundary of *Beit Shammai*'s position. Since *Beit Shammai* says only an *arusah* can perform *mi'un*, this means anyone who is no longer an *arusah* cannot — even if she has not yet become a full *nesuah*. *Rashi* highlights the logical asymmetry: *Beit Shammai* does not say "a *nesuah* cannot perform *mi'un*" — they say "only an *arusah* can." These are not equivalent. The excluded middle matters. Someone who is no longer an *arusah* but not yet a *nesuah* is also excluded.

Who occupies this intermediate status? The *Gemara* considers the case of *nichnesah lechuppah velo niv'alah* — a girl who has entered the *chuppah* but has not yet had sexual relations. She is beyond *erusin* but not yet fully *nesuah* in the sense of consummated cohabitation. Perhaps *mi'un* should work here, since the reasoning that *tenaim* fail at *nisu'in* is grounded in the concern about *beilat zenut*, and there has been no *beilah* yet?

### Chuppat Issura

The *Gemara* responds: *lefi she-ein tenai be-chuppah* — stipulations do not work even at the *chuppah* stage. The reasoning is that just as a man would not want his act of *beilah* to be retroactively recontextualized as *beilat zenut*, so too he would not want his *chuppah* — which is entirely suggestive of and oriented toward marital intimacy and cohabitation — to be retroactively rendered *chuppat issura*, a *chuppah* in a non-marital context. The *chuppah* is not merely a ceremony; it represents the crossing of the threshold into marital life, and one would not want it to have taken place under conditions that would render it as though the couple were never married. Therefore, *lo nicha lei d'teihavei chuppat issura* — he would never have allowed his *chuppah* to stand on conditional terms, meaning any *tenai* is considered waived there as well. Consequently, since there is no *tenai* operative at *chuppah*, there is also no *mi'un* after *chuppah*.

### Transfer to Agents

The *Gemara* pushes further. Even before *chuppah*, there is a stage at which the girl has left the domain of her father — or in this case her mother and brothers — and been handed over to the husband's representatives for escort to his home: *masar av li-shluchei ha-ba'al*. At this point she is no longer a pure *arusah*, but she has not yet entered *chuppah*. Here there should be no concern of *beilat zenut* or *chuppat issura* — nothing intimate has occurred or been initiated. If *tenai* could work here, why not *mi'un*?

### No Distinction

The *Gemara* answers with the principle of *lo plug rabanan* — the rabbis did not draw fine distinctions between these intermediate stages. One might be right that, technically, *tenai* could be operative in this transitional state between *erusin* and *chuppah*. But once the rabbis established that *mi'un* does not apply once a girl is no longer an *arusah*, they did not distinguish between the subtle gradations between *arusah* and *nesuah*. All of those intermediate stages are treated as connected to the concerns of *nisu'in*, and allowing *mi'un* in any of them would create precisely the false impression of *tenai be-nisu'in* that *Beit Shammai* sought to prevent.

---

## Bei'at Zenut Logic

### Husband Consent

*Rabba* and *Rav Yosef* offer an alternative explanation for *Beit Shammai*'s position that moves away from the concern about public misconception and engages instead with the reality of the marital relationship itself. Their reasoning: *ta'ama de-Beit Shammai lefi she-ein adam oseh beilato beilat zenut* — a man will not allow his acts of marital intimacy to be categorized as fornication.

### Sex Sanctity

The concern here is practical and relational. If we tell a man that even after *nisu'in* this young girl can at any moment perform *mi'un* and walk away — retroactively declaring that she was never his wife — then he will be unwilling to consummate the marriage at all. He does not want to be in the position of having had sexual relations with a girl who is not and never was his wife. The very integrity of the marital relationship demands that it not be subject to retroactive nullification through *mi'un*. This is not a concern about what observers will think; it is a concern about the husband's own experience of the relationship and his unwillingness to participate if its legitimacy is perpetually in abeyance.

The *Gemara* again applies this reasoning through the stages of *chuppah* and the transfer to the husband's agents, yielding the same *lo plug rabanan* conclusion — once the rabbis established the rule, they did not subdivide it by stage.

### Institution Context

*Beit Hillel* responds: *keivan d'ika kiddushin v'ketubah, lo atu l-meimar d'biato biat zenut* — since everything that happened took place within the framework of *kiddushin* and *ketubah*, no one will categorize the marital relations as *beilat zenut*. Even if *mi'un* is later performed and retroactively the marriage is dissolved, that does not recast the nature of the sex that occurred. It took place within a rabbinic institution, preceded by an act of *kiddushin* and a *ketubah*. It was not two people taking a hotel room — it was a structured, legally recognized framework. And therefore, even after *mi'un*, the sex that occurred within that framework will never be redefined as extramarital.

### Kehunah Status

This point carries significant implications. If retroactively the marriage never existed, one might ask: is the girl considered to have had sex outside of marriage, with all the *halachic* consequences that might entail? For instance, some *rishonim* hold that *zonah* status for a *kohen* applies to any woman who has had sex outside of marriage. The answer here is no — even though legally, in retrospect, there was no marriage, the sex that occurred within the rabbinic institution of *kiddushei ketanah* will never carry the stigma of extramarital relations.

This also bears on the broader question raised by the *Rambam*, who holds that any sex outside of marriage constitutes a *lav de-oraita* of *lo tihyeh kedeishah*. One might ask: how did the rabbis ever permit rabbinic marriages that are not *de-oraita* marriages, if all such sex is technically extramarital according to the *Rambam*? The answer is precisely this — even a rabbinic marriage, taking place within the legal and social institution of marriage with its formal acts of *kiddushin* and *ketubah*, redefines the nature of the sex. It is no longer *zenut* because the institution within which it occurs transforms its character.

This line of reasoning has been extended in modern discussions of *agunah* solutions. If *ein tenai benisuin* is grounded in *ein adam oseh beilato beilat zenut*, some contemporary *poskim* have asked whether a couple who remain in a secular legal marriage — even if the *halachic* bond is contested — would similarly not be considered to have engaged in *beilat zenut*, since they remain within an institutional framework of marriage. The analogy to *kiddushei ketanah* with subsequent *mi'un* is real, though extending it further — to a couple cohabiting without any legal framework whatsoever — raises distinct concerns.

---

## Financial Incentives

### Strip-Mining Property

*Rav Pappa* offers an entirely different rationale for both *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel*, anchored not in marital intimacy or public perception but in financial considerations. Both sides, he says, are reasoning from the same economic concern — *nichsei milug*, the wife's property over which the husband holds usufruct rights (*peiri*) — but reaching opposite conclusions.

*Beit Shammai*'s concern: *shama d'achil lehu minei, d'sof sof l-mafka ka-atya* — if the girl can perform *mi'un* at any time and walk away with her property, the husband will reason that his hold on the property is temporary and precarious. He will therefore strip-mine it — cut down the trees, extract what he can immediately — rather than tend to it, invest in it, and maintain it over time. The threat of *mi'un* thus creates a perverse incentive for destructive short-term exploitation of the wife's estate.

### Investment Incentive

*Beit Hillel* inverts the argument entirely: *adaraba* — quite the contrary. *Kivan d'amart tema'en, ashvochei mashvach lehu* — because she *can* perform *mi'un*, the husband will take excellent care of the property. He knows that if he mismanages it, her relatives will advise her to leave him — *yatz'u lah kroveha* — and she will take her property back. The threat of *mi'un* thus functions as a disciplining mechanism, incentivizing the husband to be a responsible steward of her estate.

### Wedding Expenses

*Rava* adds yet another dimension to *Beit Shammai*'s reasoning: *she-ein adam tore'ach be-seudah u-mafsidah* — a man will not go to the trouble and expense of a wedding celebration if he knows it may retroactively be rendered meaningless. The concern is not merely financial in the abstract; it points to the social reality that the progression from *kiddushin* to *nisu'in* involves real investment — the wedding feast, the communal celebration — and a husband unwilling to commit will avoid making that investment. Since the rabbis created *kiddushei ketanah* as an institution serving genuine economic and social needs of the time, they wanted it to actually progress to *nisu'in*; creating conditions that discourage the move to *nisu'in* undermines the entire institution.

### Celebration Value

*Tosafot* responds to *Rava*'s concern with a telling observation: *tara-vaihu nicha lehu* — both parties actually *want* the wedding celebration, even if it may later be retroactively dissolved. Why? *Kedei le-guzlei kalah kayetzei ishah* — people desire the social standing that comes with being publicly married. Even a young girl benefits from having had a wedding, from having this status in the community, regardless of what eventually happens. The desire for the celebration exists independently of the permanence of the marriage.

---

## Mi'un & Yibum

### Shammai: Ba'al Only

The *Mishnah* states: *Beit Shammai omrim b'ba'al* — she can perform *mi'un* only against her husband, not the *yabam*. The scenario is readily imagined: the girl was given in this rabbinic *kiddushei ketanah*, her husband died before she performed *mi'un*, and now she stands before the brother-in-law with the *mitzvah* of *yibum* or *chalitzah*. Can the *mi'un* she failed to perform against her husband now be exercised against the brother-in-law? *Beit Shammai* says no; *Beit Hillel* says yes — *be-ba'al u-ve-yabam*.

### Oshaya: Ma'amar Only

The *Gemara* cites *Rabbi Oshaya*'s interpretation: *mema'enet le-ma'amaro v'einah mema'enet le-zikato* — she may perform *mi'un* in response to his *ma'amar*, but not in response to the *zikah*. To understand this, recall what *ma'amar* is: it is an act by the brother-in-law in which he formally gives her *kiddushin* — *harei at mekudeshet li be-taba'at zo* — a ring and declaration. From the outside it resembles normal *kiddushin*, and the reason it does not constitute full *de-oraita* binding *kiddushin* is only because she is a *yevamah* whose relationship is governed by *yibum* or *chalitzah*. The rabbis encouraged this step of *ma'amar* before actual *yibum*.

So the scenario *Rabbi Oshaya* envisions is this: the husband died, the brother-in-law performed *ma'amar* with this minor girl — entering into what amounts to a new act of *kiddushei ketanah* — and now she wishes to perform *mi'un*. Her *mi'un* can reverse the *ma'amar*, undoing that new relationship. But it gets her only back to square one: she still has a *zikah* to the brother-in-law inherited from her deceased husband, and that *zikah* requires *chalitzah*. The *mi'un* cannot uproot the *zikah* — *einah mema'enet le-zikato*.

### Rav Chisda Distinction

*Rav Chisda* explains the reasoning behind *Rabbi Oshaya*'s distinction: *dim-da'atah matzi akra* — the *ma'amar*, like *kiddushei ketanah* itself when performed by mother and brothers, requires her willing acceptance. Since she entered into this relationship with her own *da'at*, she is empowered to uproot it through *mi'un*. The *zikah*, by contrast, is *de'al korchah* — it was imposed on her. She did not willingly enter into a relationship with the brother-in-law; the bond arose automatically through the death of her husband and the operation of the laws of *yibum*. Since she never willingly entered into it, she cannot unilaterally unilaterally undo it. *Lo matzi akra.*

### Bi'ah Challenge

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this reasoning. The brother-in-law can also perform *bi'ah* with the *ketanah*, and when he does so, because she is a minor, the *bi'ah* does not create full *de-oraita yibum* — it has the same rabbinic status as a *ma'amar*. Moreover, she may be *oker* — she may undo it through *mi'un*. But *Rav Chisda*'s reasoning was that *mi'un* applies where she willingly entered the relationship. Yet in the case of *bi'ah*, she did not necessarily do so willingly in the relevant sense. The *Gemara* therefore must refine the principle: it is not precisely about her *da'at* in entering the relationship; rather, the distinction is that the *ma'amar* and *bi'as ketanah* represent new acts undertaken by the brother-in-law — new relationships entered into with her as a *ketanah* — and for those, because they mirror *kiddushei ketanah*, the rabbis granted her the power of *mi'un*. The *zikah*, by contrast, flowed to her from her original husband ראובן — it is not a new relationship initiated with the brother-in-law but something inherited through the first marriage. That inherited bond cannot be severed through *mi'un*, since the proper moment to sever the bond to ראובן was while ראובן was alive.

---

## Ulla's Position

### Ulla Allows Zikah

*Ulla* takes a far more expansive position: *mena'enet af le-zikato* — she may indeed perform *mi'un* even to sever the *zikah*. On *Ulla*'s view, the *mi'un* she performs vis-à-vis the brother-in-law actually uproots the original marriage — *nisu'ei kammai ka-akra* — she is retroactively undoing the first marriage to ראובן, and therefore she is entirely free, without need of *chalitzah*.

### Tzarat Ervah

*Rava* challenges *Ulla* from the *baraita*: *kol she-yecholah le-ma'en ve-lo me'anah, tzarasah choletzet ve-lo mityabbemet* — any woman who could have performed *mi'un* and did not is a woman whose co-wife (*tzarah*) performs *chalitzah* with the brother-in-law and not *yibum*. The scenario: the deceased husband was also married to a second woman who happens to be the brother-in-law's daughter — a case of *tzarat ervah*. If the first wife (*mema'enet*) could truly perform *mi'un* and make the entire first marriage disappear, why not instruct her to do so, thereby freeing the brother-in-law to perform *yibum* with the co-wife rather than merely *chalitzah*? The fact that the *halacha* does not permit this implies that *mi'un* cannot fully erase the status that crystallized at the moment of the husband's death.

### Rami's Source

*Rami bar Yechezkel* provides a source that clarifies the underlying principle: *mi'un be-ba'al muteret le-aviv; bi-yabam asurah le-aviv* — if a girl performs *mi'un* against her husband (ראובן), she is permitted to marry his father (יעקב), since the marriage is retroactively dissolved. But if she performs *mi'un* against the brother-in-law (שמעון), she remains forbidden to his father (יעקב). What accounts for the difference? In both cases *mi'un* was performed. The answer lies in what transpired at the moment of ראובן's death.

---

## Death Instantiates

### Moment of Death

The principle the *Gemara* derives is: *bi-sh'at nefilah nirit ke-khallato* — at the moment of the husband's death, she is already viewed as his daughter-in-law in a meaningful sense, because that moment immediately generates demands: something must be done about her relationship with שמעון. That demand — that she must either do *yibum*, *chalitzah*, or *mi'un* — concretizes her status as ראובן's wife in a way that cannot be fully undone retroactively.

### Tzarat Ervah Effect

The consequence: *hacha nami bi-sh'at nefilah nirit ke-tzarat bito* — when the husband died, דבורה's status as *tzarat ervah* was already instantiated. Even if the first wife later performs *mi'un* and retroactively dissolves the marriage, that act of dissolution does not fully remove the *tzarat ervah* status that was created at the moment of death. The rabbinic prohibition on *yibum* with the co-wife therefore remains.

### Retroactive Limits

The general principle is therefore this: retroactive dissolution through *mi'un* does not undo the statuses that were created at the moment of the husband's death. At that moment, before any *mi'un* was performed, the world looked a certain way — she was his wife, there was a need for the brother-in-law to act, certain prohibitions crystallized. A subsequent *mi'un* can address the ongoing relationship and prevent further obligations, but it cannot reach back and erase what became real at that critical moment. This is why *mi'un* against the *yabam* leaves her forbidden to his father: her status as daughter-in-law to יעקב became a reality the moment ראובן died, and no retroactive act can fully dissolve it.

---

## Multiple Brothers

### Rav: All Disqualified

*Rav* rules: *mi'un b'zeh asurah le-zeh* — if she performs *mi'un* against one brother (שמעון), she is thereby forbidden to the other brothers (לוי, etc.) as well. The *mi'un* operates on the *zikah* as a whole.

### Get Analogy

*Rav*'s reasoning draws on the analogy of *baalas ha-get*: just as if the brother-in-law gives her a *get* — which in the *yibum* context dissolves his rabbinic *zikah* — she becomes forbidden to all the brothers, so too *mi'un* against one has the effect of foreclosing the *yibum* option with all of them. *Lav kivan d'it'asrah le-chad, it'asrah le-kulhu?* — once she becomes forbidden to one through this mechanism, she becomes forbidden to all.

### Shmuel: Individual

*Shmuel* disagrees: *mi'un b'zeh muteres le-zeh* — even after performing *mi'un* against שמעון, she may still enter into *yibum* with לוי. The key distinction *Shmuel* draws is the identity of the actor. In the case of *baalas ha-get*, it is the man whose act changes her status, and his act can be said to represent or implicate all the brothers. But in *mi'un*, it is she who is acting. And she is not saying something general about all men — she is saying something specific: *lo ravine bech, lo tzevine bech* — I do not want *you*, שמעון, specifically. *Ha becha u-ve'acharina* — as for שמעון, I reject him; as for לוי, she may well be interested. The act of *mi'un* is directed at a specific individual, and it changes only her relationship with that individual, not her status in the world at large.

### Her Action Only

This distinction — that in *mi'un* it is *hee d'ka avdah beih*, she is the one acting upon him — is not merely technical. It reflects a genuine conceptual difference in how *mi'un* functions. Normally, the legal acts that define a woman's status — *get*, *chalitzah*, and so on — are acts performed upon her or for her. *Mi'un* is unique in that she is the agent, and her agency is directed at a specific person. *Shmuel* therefore holds that it affects only that specific person.

### Rav Ashi: Collective

*Rav Ashi* goes further: *mi'un b'zeh muteres afilu lo* — if she performs *mi'un* against שמעון while לוי and other brothers remain, the *mi'un* is entirely meaningless, and she can even subsequently perform *yibum* with שמעון himself. The reason will emerge from the *Gemara*'s final analysis.

---

## All-or-Nothing

### Yochanan

When *Ravin* returned from Eretz Yisrael, he transmitted in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: *mi'un b'zeh muteres le-achim* — if she performs *mi'un* against one brother, she remains permitted to the other brothers. This accords with *Shmuel*'s view that *mi'un* is individual and directed.

### Abaye's ID

*Abaye* identifies who among the previously cited authorities would disagree with *Rabbi Yochanan*: it is *Rav*, because *Rav* holds that *mi'un b'zeh asurah le-zeh* — refused of one, forbidden to all. *Rav*'s position that *mi'un* operates wholesale on the relationship to all brothers is directly in conflict with *Rabbi Yochanan*'s ruling that she remains permitted to the other brothers.

### Rava's ID

*Rava* identifies a different dissenter: *Rabbi Oshaya*. *Rabbi Oshaya* holds that there is no *mi'un* operative against the *zikah* at all — *mi'un* can only address a new *ma'amar* or *bi'as ketanah* entered into by the brother-in-law, not the underlying *zikah* inherited from the first husband. *Rabbi Yochanan*'s ruling, read carefully, implies that *mi'un* against one brother would have been meaningful for the *zikah* to that brother while preserving the *zikah* to the others — precisely what *Rabbi Oshaya* denies.

### Indivisible Zikah

*Rav Ashi*'s position now becomes clear. The *Gemara* articulates the principle: *ein mi'un le-chatzi zikah* — one cannot sever half a *zikah*. The *zikah* that the brothers hold is not a collection of independent relationships, each severable on its own. It is a single *zikah* inherited from the original husband ראובן, transmitted collectively to all the brothers as a unit. If she wishes to use *mi'un* to sever the *zikah*, she must sever the whole of it — directing her refusal at all brothers collectively. Attempting to sever the *zikah* to one brother while leaving it intact as to the others is an attempt at *mi'un le-chatzi zikah*, and that is legally incoherent. The partial *mi'un* accomplishes nothing — *muteres afilu lo*, she can even subsequently perform *yibum* with the very brother she attempted to refuse, because the refusal had no legal effect.

### Conclusion

The full range of positions thus emerges. *Rabbi Oshaya* holds that *mi'un* never touches the *zikah* at all — it can only address the new relationship created by the brother-in-law's *ma'amar* or *bi'as ketanah*. *Rav* holds that *mi'un* does operate on the *zikah* but, analogous to the *get* case, operates wholesale — refuse one brother and all are foreclosed. *Shmuel* holds that *mi'un* operates individually — she can refuse one brother and remain available to others, because her act is specifically directed. And *Rav Ashi*, as the *Gemara* finally clarifies, holds that the *zikah* is indivisible — it comes as a single inherited unit from the first husband — and therefore any *mi'un* must address the whole *zikah* or it is void. She must either reject all the brothers collectively or her *mi'un* is meaningless. The *Gemara* continues into the next *daf*.

---

---

# Yevamot 108

## Miun: Beis Shammai vs. B…

### Dispute Framework

The daf opens at the first wide line of 107b. *Beis Shammai* holds that *miun* — the right of a minor girl married off without her father to refuse the marriage — is valid only when performed in the husband's presence and before a *beis din*. *Beis Hillel*, by contrast, holds that *miun* is effective whether or not it is performed in his presence, and whether or not it takes place before a *beis din*.

### Camel Driver Example

A *braita* records *Beis Hillel*'s counter-proof to *Beis Shammai*: the case of Pishon the camel driver, whose wife performed *miun* in his absence. Given that camel drivers are away for extended periods — a year at a time — it would be exceedingly difficult to insist that *miun* occur in the husband's presence. *Beis Shammai* responds that Pishon measured with a *mida kefusha* — an overturned or upended measure, an idiomatic expression for dealing improperly — and therefore was measured back against him in kind. He had mistreated her property, so they treated him in kind.

### Proportional Response

The phrase *mida kefusha*, as Rashi explains, conveys something like the bottom of the barrel — a reversal, an upending. The specific impropriety, the *gemara* clarifies, is *mi-deka achal perei*: he consumed the produce of her *nichsei milug*, essentially strip-mining her property out of concern that she might perform *miun* and walk away. The rabbis responded by making it easier for her to do precisely that.

### Two Violations Analysis

This raises an immediate difficulty. If he was eating the *peirot*, that implies the marriage had already reached the stage of *nisuin*. But *Beis Shammai* itself holds that a *nisuah* cannot perform *miun* — so there are in fact two violations present: the *miun* was performed outside his presence (*shelo befanav*), and it was performed after *nisuin*. The *gemara* responds: *trei kuteiri avdu bah* — they did him two knots, meaning they penalized him on both counts simultaneously, allowing her *miun* despite its violating both of *Beis Shammai*'s normal conditions.

This is a striking passage. *Tosafot* notes that the *Yerushalmi* asks pointedly: can it really be that simply because someone acts improperly we dissolve his marriage? *Tosafot* responds that since *kiddushei ketanah* is entirely rabbinic in origin, the rabbis retain the authority to uproot those *kiddushin* — *afkinu rabbanan l'kiddushei minei*. Yet even *Tosafot* acknowledges this is somewhat different from the standard cases of *hafka'at kiddushin*, where the *kiddushin* themselves were invalid from the outset. Here, *Beis Shammai* is granting special *miun* rights on a case-by-case basis in response to his improper conduct — a genuinely unusual application of rabbinic authority.
