One participant raised an intriguing alternative reading of the *befanav* requirement: perhaps his presence is not a formal condition of the *miun* act itself — the way, say, the *get* must reach the woman or the *kiddushin* money must reach her hand — but rather a procedural protection of his rights, analogous to how testimony is not given in someone's absence. On this reading, the *befanav* requirement is less about the mechanics of the act and more about safeguarding his interests. This framing, however, would not resolve the separate problem the *gemara* raises about *nisuin*, though it offers an interesting way of conceptualizing the first requirement.

---

## Chalitza & Miun: Three W…

### Three-Witness Rule

The *gemara* transitions to a *mishna* from *Sanhedrin*: *ha-chalitza veha-miun bi-shlosha* — both *chalitza* and *miun* require three. The *gemara* asks: who is the author of this *mishna*? Its ascription of a three-member panel to *miun* reflects the position of *Beis Shammai*. Accordingly, Rabbah identifies the *mishna* as authored according to *Beis Shammai*.

### Abaye's Position

Abaye disagrees. He maintains that the *mishna* can even be attributed to *Beis Hillel*. When *Beis Hillel* says *miun* does not require a *beis din*, that means it does not require *mumchin* — ordained, expert judges — but three witnesses are still needed. A *braita* makes this explicit: *Beis Shammai* requires a *beis din*; *Beis Hillel* permits *miun* before or without a formal *beis din*; yet both houses agree (*ve-elu ve-elu modim*) that three are required.

### Two-Witness Minority

Against this consensus, Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon hold that *miun* with only two suffices. And the ruling follows them: Rav Nachman, cited by Yosef bar Minyumi, states that the *halacha* is in accordance with that pair — in contrast to *chalitza*, where the view of fewer than three was explicitly rejected.

---

## Miun Eligibility Standar…

### Multiple Miun Debate

The *mishna* asks whether a *ketana* can perform *miun* repeatedly. *Beis Hillel* permits it; *Beis Shammai* objects that allowing a minor to marry, perform *miun*, marry again, and perform *miun* again renders *benot Yisrael hefker* — treats Jewish women as disposable. The language of the *mishna* on this point is somewhat ambiguous: it speaks of her performing *miun*, then waiting until she grows up, or alternatively performing *miun* and then marrying immediately. This led to two readings.

### Reaffirmation Upon Matur…

Shmuel reads the *mishna* as requiring that after performing *miun* as a minor, the girl must, upon reaching adulthood, reaffirm her *miun* — she must say *rotzah ani be-miyvunin ha-rishonim*, "I affirm my earlier refusal." This is a striking idea with no prior parallel: a kind of confirmation, ensuring that the act of *miun* performed during minority is endorsed by the adult woman. The *gemara* objects that the *mishna*'s language does not express this clearly — it should have said she "reaffirms" rather than she "does *miun*" — and acknowledges this as a difficulty (*kashya*).

Ulla offers an alternative reading: the *mishna* is presenting two options (*tarte katani*). Either she performs *miun* and waits until she becomes an adult before marrying again, or she performs *miun* and marries again immediately — but only on condition that this second marriage includes *nisuin* straightaway. Why would *Beis Shammai* require immediate *nisuin* in the second scenario? Because according to *Beis Shammai*, once *nisuin* has taken place, *miun* is no longer available. So if she wants to remarry as a minor, *Beis Shammai* insists that the marriage be consummated immediately with *nisuin*, thereby foreclosing the possibility of a second *miun*. The ו in the *mishna* is thus read as "or," presenting two alternatives — a reading also supported by a *braita* that phrases them disjunctively.

### Minor's Consent Requirem…

The next *mishna* asks: which minor must perform *miun*? The answer: one whose mother and brothers married her off *l'da'atah* — with her knowledge and consent. This is a remarkable requirement. When a father marries off his daughter, her personal awareness and consent are irrelevant — she could be an infant. Here, by contrast, the entire rabbinic institution is conditioned on her participation. The *Rambam*, it should be noted, largely drops the reference to the mother and brothers in his formulation, framing this institution more directly as the girl marrying herself off, with the mother and brothers acting alongside her rather than independently.

The inverse case is likewise stated: if the mother and brothers married her off *shelo l'da'atah*, without her knowledge, she does not require *miun* — the marriage carries no binding force even at the rabbinic level.

### Capacity to Protect

Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos adds a further threshold: any girl who is too young to be able to watch over (*lishmor*) her *kiddushin* does not require *miun*. If she is so young that she would simply drop or lose the token of *kiddushin* — unable to grasp its value or preserve it — then the *kiddushin* cannot take effect even rabbinically. This parallels a similar principle found in the law of *get*, where the recipient must have sufficient awareness to protect her *get*. The conceptual thrust is striking: the minor is being configured not merely as a passive recipient of the marriage act but as an active participant in it — almost as an agent.

### Rabbi Eliezer's Rejection

Rabbi Eliezer takes a radical position: *ein ma'aseh ketanah klum* — the acts of a minor are legally void. He does not deny that something occurs when a minor is married off by her mother and brothers with her consent, but he refuses to characterize it as *kiddushin d'rabbanan*. Instead, he likens her status to that of a *mefutah* — a seduced woman. The rabbis tolerate the couple living together, but they do not recognize the arrangement as any form of rabbinic marriage.

This position has a pointed internal logic. The *mishna* has been moving steadily toward treating the minor as the operative agent of her own marriage — her consent, her receipt of *kiddushin*, her capacity to protect it. Rabbi Eliezer accepts that trajectory and draws its conclusion: if she is the operative agent, her act cannot create binding *kiddushin*, because a *ketanah* has no legal capacity to perform binding acts. Therefore, what exists between them is not quasi-marriage but an unrecognized cohabitation. The practical consequences are total: the husband is not entitled to her earnings (*metziatah*), the produce of her property (*peirot*), or the annulment of her vows (*hafrasat nedarim*); he does not inherit her; and if he is a *kohen*, he does not become *tamei* for her. She is not his wife in any sense — except that if she wishes to terminate the arrangement, she requires *miun*. As for *trumah*: if she is a *bat Yisrael* married to a *kohen*, she may not eat *trumah*; if she is a *bat kohen* married to a *Yisrael*, she continues to eat *trumah*. In neither case is she treated as a married woman.

---

## Miun: Documentation (II)

### Document Reform

Rav Yehuda, and a *braita* corroborates this, reports that originally the document recording an act of *miun* was written in an elaborate formula: *lo ra'ina beih* — I do not desire him; *v'lo tzavina beih* — I do not want him; *v'leis ana beih l'hitnasva leih* — I do not wish to marry him. This lengthy formulation was ultimately shortened. The reason: *ati l'chlufi b'gita* — scribes would confuse it with a *get*. Both Rashi and *Tosafot* explain this not as a fear that onlookers would mistake the woman for a *gerushah*, but rather that an ignorant *sofer*, having been called to write a *get miun* in its long form, would later be called to write a *get gerushin* and, remembering only the length and formality of the first document, would write the wrong type. This explanation is admittedly puzzling — a *get* is typically a far longer and more formalized document — but that is how the *rishonim* read it.

---

## Miun: Documentation (II)

### Standard Formula

The shortened standard form retained only the essential: on such-and-such a day, *mi'anah plonit bat ploni* — so-and-so the daughter of so-and-so performed *miun* — *b'apana*, in our presence. Nothing more.

---

## Valid Miun Contexts

### Absence & Informality

A *braita* then defines what constitutes an act of *miun*. The girl says either *ee efshi b'ploni ba'ali* — I do not want so-and-so my husband — or *ee efshi b'kiddushin she'kiddushuni imi va'achai* — I do not want the marriage that my mother and brothers put me into. Beyond this, Rabbi Yehuda adds a series of expanding cases demonstrating just how informally *miun* can be expressed.

### Carriage Statement

Even if she is sitting in the wedding carriage (*apiryon*), being conveyed from her father's house to her husband's house, and while still in transit she says *ee efshi b'ploni ba'ali* — this constitutes *miun*. One might have thought: if she truly does not want this marriage, she should stop the procession and leave the carriage. The ruling is that even her statement from within the carriage, without halting the ceremony, is sufficient.

### Serving Guests Context

More striking: even if she is already in her husband's home, guests are gathered, and she is standing and serving them drinks — and in the midst of doing so she says *ee efshi b'ploni ba'ali* — this too is *miun*. Rashi identifies the *chiddush* here as the absence of any *beis din*. But the broader force of the case is that she is, at that moment, visibly performing the role of a wife, yet her verbal declaration suffices to dissolve the marriage. The question of whether she is expressing genuine legal will or merely marital frustration appears to be deliberately sidelined.

### Storekeeper Complaint

Further still: if her husband sends her to the storekeeper to collect something on his behalf, and while there she says *ee efshi* in reference to her husband — complaining, as it were, to the shopkeeper about the man who sent her on this errand — *ein lach miun gadol mizeh*: there is no greater *miun* than this. It qualifies.

### Will-Centered Principle

This is a genuinely striking series of rulings. The formal requirements appear to dissolve almost entirely: no *beis din*, no solemnity, no procedural acknowledgment that a legal act is taking place. The context in each case might easily be read as mere venting or frustration rather than a considered legal declaration. Yet the *gemara* insists each qualifies.

One participant raised the question of how this squares with the ruling, agreed upon even by *Beis Hillel*, that three witnesses are required. Rashi notes the tension. It may be that Rabbi Yehuda here represents a minority view that no *beis din* is required at all — not merely that *mumchin* are unnecessary, but that three are not required either. But part of the *chiddush* is conceptual, not merely technical: even where three witnesses happen to be present (guests, bystanders at the store), they are not constituted as a *beis din* and the statement is not framed as a legal act. Yet it counts.

Another participant offered an interesting perspective: perhaps these rulings are not about prospective *miun* but about retrospective identification. That is, if at a later point one needs to determine whether she had performed *miun* during her minority — say, she is now an adult and her husband refuses to give a *get*, and it is in her interest to establish that she had already performed *miun* while a *ketanah* — the *gemara* is teaching that these earlier statements, made in contexts that seemed informal or incidental, can be identified *ex post facto* as valid acts of *miun*. This reading would resolve some of the tension, though it is not how the *rishonim* generally frame these cases.

What the cases collectively express is the principle embedded in the *mishna*'s requirement of *l'da'atah*: the institution of *kiddushei ketanah* without a father was constructed as fundamentally grounded in her will, and therefore its dissolution is also anchored entirely in her will. All of her actions as wife may point in one direction; her words point the other way. The *gemara*'s formulation — *ein lach miun gadol mizeh*, there is no greater *miun* than this — is not ironic but precisely literal: the more embedded in the wifely role she appears, the more forceful her verbal rejection becomes as an expression of autonomous will.

---

## Miun Via Alternative Act…

### Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira

The *gemara* records that Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira holds: if a minor who was married without her father's involvement neither performs a formal *miun* but instead stands up and marries another man, her act of *nisuin* with the second man itself constitutes her *miun* from the first. The *mishna* states this regarding *nisuin*; a subsequent *braita* extends it to *kiddushin* as well: if she accepts *kiddushin* from a second man, that too is her *miun* from the first.

### Kiddushin vs. Nisuin

The *gemara* then poses a multi-layered question (*ibaya lehu*): Do the *rabbanan* dispute Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira at all? If they do, is their dispute limited to the *kiddushin* case, or does it extend even to *nisuin*? And if there is a dispute, do we rule like Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira — and if so, in which cases?

### Kiddushin as Miun

The resolution comes from Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: *halacha ke-Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira*. The word *halacha* itself implies that the *rabbanan* disagree — for one rules *halacha* against an opposing position. Both Rashi and *Tosafot* infer from context that this ruling covers both the *kiddushin* and *nisuin* scenarios: we rule like Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira in both directions, meaning that even mere *kiddushin* from a second man constitutes *miun* from the first, and we assume the *rabbanan* contest this in both cases.

A further question then arises: does it matter what the nature of her relationship with the first man was? Is the ruling that *kiddushin* from guy number two constitutes *miun* from guy number one applicable even where she had already reached *nisuin* with guy number one — a far more actualized form of marriage? The *gemara* seeks to resolve this from a specific case.

### Avdin's Daughters

The daughters-in-law of Avdin — the same Avdin, as one participant noted, who appears earlier in the *daf* in connection with the humiliation of Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yosi — had married Avdin's sons while minors, without paternal authorization. Both performed *miun* against their husbands. Rabbi sent a pair of *rabbanan* to investigate — likely either because he did not trust the report or because he wanted to assess whether the statements were genuine expressions of will or merely complaints.

When the two *rabbanan* approached, some women at the scene told the daughters-in-law that their husbands were coming. The girls, apparently confusing the approaching *rabbanan* for their husbands, responded: *le-havu gavreichu didchu lanan lav gavreinu* — let them be your husbands; we have no need of them. Rabbi ruled: *ein lecha miun gadol mi-zeh* — there is no greater *miun* than this.

The *gemara* attempts to use this case to resolve the earlier question: if we can identify these girls as having performed *miun* at the level of a mere verbal rejection addressed to bystanders, and if this occurred after *nisuin* with the first husband, it would demonstrate that even *nisuin* with guy number one does not require a more elevated form of *miun*. The *gemara* ultimately declines the proof, suggesting the marriages may have been at the stage of *kiddushin* only. The ruling, however, stands: *ve-halacha ke-Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira ve-afilu be-nisuin de-kama* — we rule like Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, and even if the relationship with the first man had reached *nisuin*, the standard for *miun* remains accessible and low. The *gemara* makes it very easy for a *ketanah* to exit this institution.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer's Model

### Consistency Problem

The *gemara* returns to Rabbi Eliezer's position. Shmuel, as transmitted by Rav Yehuda, articulates a pointed observation: *chozani kol tzaddei chachamim v'lo matzati adam she'hishveh midotav be-ketanah ke-Rabbi Eliezer* — I have examined all the angles of the sages' positions and found no one as internally consistent in his treatment of the *ketanah* as Rabbi Eliezer.

The consistency problem Rabbi Eliezer identified is this: the institution of *kiddushei ketanah* without a father has been progressively reconfigured so that the minor herself is the operative agent. Her consent, her receipt of *kiddushin*, her capacity to protect it — these are the conditions. If that is the case, then her act cannot create rabbinic *kiddushin*, because a *ketanah*'s legal acts are void. The institution therefore cannot be *kiddushin d'rabbanan*. Instead, Rabbi Eliezer characterizes the relationship as *k'mefutah*: the rabbis tolerate cohabitation without recognizing it as marriage.

### Non-Wife Status

The *gemara* then draws out the full range of legal consequences. The husband is not entitled to her earnings (*metziatah u-ma'aseh yadeha*), cannot annul her vows (*hafrasat nedarim*), does not inherit her (*eino yorshah*), and — if he is a *kohen* — does not become *tamei* for her (*eino mitamei lah*). The governing principle: *eino k'ishto le-chol davar* — she is not his wife in any regard. The one exception: *ella she-tzricha mi'un* — if she wishes to terminate the cohabitation, she still requires *miun*. This is described as being like someone taking a walk in a garden together, sharing a bed, with her thereafter going to the *mikvah* and eating *trumah* (if she is a *bat kohen*) — no marital status attaches, only a cohabitation that can be ended by a simple statement.

### Rabbi Yehoshua Position

Rabbi Yehoshua takes the diametrically opposite view. The husband is entitled to everything: her finds, her earnings, the right to annul her vows, inheritance rights, and if he is a *kohen*, he becomes *tamei* for her — the *gemara* earlier explained this is treated rabinnically like a *met mitzvah*, despite there being no *d'oraisa* basis. She is *k'ishto le-chol davar* — fully his wife in every respect. The one anomaly: *yotzah be-miun* — she can exit the marriage through *miun* alone, without requiring a *get*.

### Consistency Evaluation

Rabbi — referring here to Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi — evaluates the two positions: *nirein divrei Rabbi Eliezer mi-divrei Rabbi Yehoshua* — Rabbi Eliezer's position is more persuasive. The reason is precisely the consistency that Shmuel praised. Rabbi Eliezer *hishveh midotav be-ketanah*: he applied a uniform standard. If she is not a wife, she needs no *get* — and that is what he holds. Rabbi Yehoshua *chillek* — he made a distinction — treating her as a full wife in every respect yet exempting her from the requirement of a *get*. If she is truly his wife, *tibaye get* — she should need a *get*.

The *gemara* then probes Rabbi Eliezer's own consistency. If she is not his wife at all, why does she require *miun*? The *gemara* responds: *ella b'kadi teipuk* — should she simply walk out with nothing? Even a cohabiting couple that decides to separate requires some formal acknowledgment of the breakup. Rabbi Eliezer's *miun*, on this reading, is not the severing of *kiddushin* but the formal acknowledgment that a live-in relationship has ended. It is not *aishut* at all — not rabbinic marriage — merely a relationship that must be terminated by some act. This, the *gemara* suggests, is an internally consistent position. And it also explains why *miun* is so easy to perform: if there is no real marriage, the act dissolving it need not be a formal legal instrument.

The practical *halacha* does not follow Rabbi Eliezer. We rule that *kiddushei ketanah* without a father does create a form of rabbinic *kiddushin* — a pseudo-*kiddushin*, as it were — from which *miun* is the mechanism of exit.

---

## Miun vs. Get Status

### Refusal Signals Consent

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's statement in the *mishna* — that if she holds back because of the man it is as though she is his wife, and if not, it is not — is cryptic. *Tosafot* offers a reading that places this not in the context of *miun* at all but rather in the context of the *mishna*'s earlier condition: *l'da'atah* — that the *kiddushin* must have been performed with her knowledge and consent. How do we determine after the fact whether she consented?

The answer: if a second suitor approaches her and proposes, and she refuses him saying *machmat ploni ba'ali* — "I cannot marry you, I am already married to so-and-so" — that refusal signals that she regards herself as married to guy number one. She is being *held back* because of him (*akavta de-minei de-ish*). This demonstrates that she consented to the original marriage. Conversely, if she refuses the second suitor by saying *machmat b'nei adam she-einam mehuganim li* — "I would consider marrying someone suitable, but not you" — this indicates she does not regard herself as bound by the first marriage, and therefore she had never truly consented to it.

On *Tosafot*'s reading, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's statement is about identifying consent to *kiddushin* number one, not about the mechanics of *miun*. What she says to a potential second husband is a retrospective signal of her attitude toward the first.

### Consent Indicator

Abaye and Rav Chanina bar Avin both offer a different reading: *natan lah get* — if guy number one gave her a *get* — *zu hi akavta de-minei de-ish*: that shows he was holding her back. Conversely, if she performed *miun*, *zu hi akavta d'lav minei de-ish* — it was she who was determining the outcome, not him. The practical implication of this reading follows immediately.

### Miun After Get

If he gave her a *get* and then remarried her and she subsequently performed *miun*, the *miun* redefines her status retroactively. Even though she had been his *gerushah* after the first *get*, the *miun* following the second marriage erases that status — she is treated as though she was never his *gerushah* at all. Therefore, even after she marries a second man and that marriage dissolves, she may return to guy number one. There is no prohibition of *machzir gerushato*, because the *miun* has effectively rendered the *gerushin* status null.

How does this work conceptually? Rashi's explanation is that the *miun* — by its nature — underlines that she is a *ketanah* and this entire institution is rabbinic. Once she performs *miun* the second time, it retroactively recharacterizes the entire relationship: she was never truly married to him, not even rabbinically. The first *get* disappears along with the marriage it purported to dissolve.

It should be noted that on a *d'oraisa* level, none of this creates any real prohibition in any case, since there was never a *d'oraisa* marriage to begin with. The concerns about *machzir gerushato* and about *gerushin* status for *kehunah* are entirely *mi-derabbanan*.

### Get After Miun

The converse: if the sequence is reversed — she performed *miun* first, then he remarried her, and then he gave her a *get* — her most recent status with him is that of a *gerushah*. The *miun* is now in the past; the *get* is the more recent and defining act. She is forbidden to return to him after marrying another man, because she is his *gerushah* and the prohibition of *machzir gerushato* applies. The rule is stated concisely: *get achar miun* — *asura lachzor lo*. *Miun achar get* — *muteret lachzor lo*. Whichever act came last defines her status.

---

## Multiple Partners Cases

### Three-Partner Order

The *mishna* then presents a more complex scenario involving three successive husbands. She performs *miun* with guy number one; marries guy number two and receives a *get*; marries guy number three and performs *miun* with him. After all of this, can she return to any of them? The *gemara* works through the implications.

### Same-Partner Rule

The *gemara* at first seems to assume a contradiction between the cases: in the first scenario, *miun* following *get* with the same man redefines her as a non-*gerushah*; in the three-partner scenario, *miun* with guy number three does not redefine her status with guy number two. The *gemara* initially suggests (*amru*) that the two halves of the *mishna* reflect a genuine dispute — *mi she-shanah zo lo shanah zo*.

Rava dissolves the apparent contradiction: there is no dispute at all. *Miun dide mevattel get dide* — his own *miun* can retroactively undermine his own earlier *get* — because the *miun* redefines the entire relationship with that specific person. *Miun de-chavrei lo mevattel git dide* — a different man's *miun* cannot undermine a previous man's *get* — because the relationships are distinct. The *miun* with guy number three says nothing about the nature of her relationship with guy number two. This is the obvious answer, and Rava offers it as such.

### Leverage Problem

Yet the *gemara* presses further. In principle, the *gemara* argues, any act of *miun* — even with a different man — announces that she is a *ketanah* and therefore her entire history of rabbinic marriage is questionable. On pure principle, even another man's *miun* could redefine an earlier *get*. So there must be a positive reason why we do not allow it. The *gemara* provides one: *eidi d'makaras bi-remi'zosav u've-kitzotzav azil meshabesh u-meisei lah* — because she has been intimate with guy number one and knows his manner and his signals, he can go and manipulate her, inducing her to perform *miun* with guy number two or three, which would then free her to return to him. Allowing a different man's *miun* to override her *get* from guy number one would give guy number one leverage to destroy her subsequent marriages.

### Failed Attempt Exception

This raises a parallel question: why is the same concern not present in the case where the same man's *miun* is allowed to override his earlier *get*? If she performed *miun* from him the second time around and we let her return to him after her subsequent marriage dissolves — has he not also been given the leverage to signal her and bring her back?

The *gemara*'s answer: *hacha tiv sheiv velo meshabesh* — in this case, he already tried and it did not work. The *miun* the second time around was *her* act of rejection. She wanted out, and he could not keep her in the marriage. Given that history, we are not concerned that he will subsequently be able to manipulate her into returning, because she has already demonstrated that she is not under his influence. By contrast, when he was the one to give the *get* — perhaps she wished to remain married but he rejected her — and she then marries someone else, he may retain emotional leverage over her and use it to encourage her to perform *miun* and come back to him.

The *gemara*'s resolution operates on the level of practical social concern — identifying where leverage exists and where it has been negated by prior events. The more formalist explanation would simply observe that a *miun* redefines only the specific relationship in which it occurs. But the *gemara* prefers to ground the rule in the concrete reality of power dynamics between the parties, and to explain both the rule and its limits in those terms.

---

---

# Yevamot 109

## Me'un After Get

### Mishnah Contradiction

The daf opens in the middle of 108b, continuing the discussion of *me'un* following a *get*. The broader question is whether a *me'un* performed after a *get* redefines the woman's status — specifically, whether it undoes her classification as a *gerushah* and thereby permits what would otherwise be a violation of *machzir grushato*. The *mishnah* has already established that if the same man who gave the *get* subsequently remarried her and she then performed *me'un* against him, that *me'un* does redefine her status. But if a different man married her and she performed *me'un* against him, that does not redefine her status vis-à-vis the first husband.

The *gemara* had explained this distinction not on the intuitive ground that only the same man can redefine her status, but rather on a concern that the first husband will attempt to signal her — exploiting her recognition of his gestures — and thereby manipulate her into performing *me'un* with the second husband so she can return to him. With that resolved, the *gemara* moves to a new internal difficulty in the *mishnah*.

The *gemara* notes: *ika hashta dechavrei adechavrei kashya* — even setting aside the first problem, there remains a contradiction within the *mishnah*'s own treatment of a second man's *me'un*. The *mishnah* first describes a case in which the man performed *me'un* against her, then remarried her, then gave her a *get*, and she subsequently married someone else. The *mishnah* states that if that second man died or divorced her, she is forbidden from returning to the first husband on account of *machzir grushato*. The precise formulation — specifying death or divorce — implies that had the second man's dissolution of the marriage taken the form of *me'un* rather than death or divorce, she *would* be permitted to return to the first. This *diyuk* suggests that a second man's *me'un* does, in fact, redefine her status even vis-à-vis the first husband.

### Conclusion Dispute

Yet the concluding rule of the *mishnah* states explicitly: *kol sheyatzat mimeno beget asura lachazor lo* — anyone from whom she departed with a *get* may not take her back, even if she subsequently performed *me'un* with another husband. And anyone from whom she departed with *me'un* may return to her. This is as clear a statement as possible that a *me'un* performed with a different man does *not* undo the *gerushah* status vis-à-vis the first. So the two halves of the *mishnah* appear to contradict one another directly.

Rabbi Elazar's response is stark: *miy sheshana zu lo shana zu* — the two halves of the *mishnah* were authored by different *tanna'im* and reflect a genuine dispute. The first half operates under the assumption that a second man's *me'un* can redefine her status even vis-à-vis the first husband; the second half denies this. Two distinct positions, two *tanna'im*, and no resolution between them.

It is worth pausing here to appreciate just how seriously the *gemara* entertains the position that a second man's *me'un* should work. The intuitive assumption — that only the same man can redefine the status, not an entirely different party — is not the *gemara*'s operating premise. The *gemara* is genuinely prepared to accept that even a *me'un* performed with a second husband could, in principle, strip away the *gerushah* status the first husband created. The dispute is not about whether this is theoretically possible, but about whether we permit it in practice.

One must also keep in mind throughout this entire discussion that everything here exists in the *derabbanan* world: the *kiddushin* is *derabbanan*, the *get* is *derabbanan*, and the *me'un* operates within that framework. It is precisely because all of this is rabbinic that the question of redefining statuses is even coherent. Were we dealing with *de'oraisa* marriage and divorce, there would be no mechanism for retroactive redefinition of this kind.

### Ulla's Solution

Ulla offers an alternative resolution that avoids splitting the *mishnah* between two disputants. He argues that both halves can reflect the same *tanna* — but the final case of the *mishnah*, in which a second man's *me'un* does not redefine her status, is a specific scenario involving *shilsha begetin*: she had gone through a sequence of marriages and received three *getin* over the course of her history. After three *getin*, even if subsequent husbands performed *me'un*, the cumulative pattern of divorce documents has established her *gerushah* status so firmly — at least vis-à-vis the husbands from whom she received those *getin* — that it cannot be overridden.

The logic, as Ulla explains, is that *demichzi kegdola*: after three *getin*, she looks like an adult. Despite remaining a *ketanah* throughout, the repeated formal divorces create the appearance of full adult status, and that appearance fixes her *gerushah* identity at least with respect to those specific husbands. As a result, in this particular case, no subsequent *me'un* — even from a different man — can dislodge the *gerushah* classification.

This is a striking resolution. The ordinary rule, according to Ulla, is that a second man's *me'un* can indeed redefine her status vis-à-vis the first husband. The final case of the *mishnah* is a narrow exception: when there have been three *getin*, the accumulated weight of formal divorce creates an irreversible *gerushah* status. She may still return to husbands from whom she departed through *me'un*, but she cannot return to those from whom she received *getin*, because their *gerushah* status has become fixed and is no longer amenable to redefinition through a later *me'un*.

The counterintuitive element here is worth highlighting. One would expect the rule to be that another man's *me'un* never works to redefine her status with the first husband — that seems self-evidently correct. Instead, the *gemara* reasons in the opposite direction, treating a second man's *me'un* as ordinarily effective, with the three-*getin* scenario as the exception.

### Historical Testimony

The *gemara* now asks: according to the first answer, which treats the two halves of the *mishnah* as a *machlokes tanna'im*, where do we find this debate represented among the *tanna'im*? The answer comes through Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, introduced with a striking verse from *Eicha*: *meimenu bechesef shatinu ateinu bimchir yavo'u* — our water we had to purchase with silver, our wood we had to buy. The *gemara* applies this as a metaphor: just as water represents *Torah* and had to be acquired at great cost, so during the period of Hadrianic persecution, the following halachic question had to be pursued at enormous expense.

The question posed was: if a woman departed from the first husband with a *get* and from the second husband through *me'un*, may she return to the first? Scholars hired an intermediary for 400 *zuz* to smuggle the question into prison to Rabbi Akiva. He ruled: *ve'asar* — forbidden. A second man's *me'un* does not redefine her status. They then traveled to ask Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira in Nitzivin, who similarly ruled *ve'asar*.

### R. Yishmael Position

Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yose, however, takes sharp issue with this account. He insists the question itself was obvious — the answer could not possibly be in doubt — and that the actual question brought to Rabbi Akiva in prison was an entirely different one. His reasoning: *issur kares hitarta* — if *me'un* has the power to permit what would otherwise be an *issur kares* — since a *ketanah* who is betrothed is considered halachically married and *me'un* dissolves that betrothal, allowing her to go to another man who would otherwise be having relations with a married woman — then certainly *me'un* should be powerful enough to remove the much lesser prohibition of *machzir grushato*, which is merely an *issur lav*. An *a fortiori* argument: if *me'un* can eliminate a *karet* prohibition, it certainly eliminates a *lav* prohibition. Therefore, Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yose maintains that a second man's *me'un* obviously does redefine her status and permits her return to the first husband.

Rabbi Yishmael's objection is noted: the *me'un* dissolves the relationship with the man she is performing *me'un* against, not vis-à-vis a different man. There is a meaningful distinction between redefining her status with respect to husband number two versus redefining her *gerushah* status with respect to husband number one. Nevertheless, Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yose maintains that the power of *me'un* is broad enough to accomplish this.

The actual question, Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yose insists, involved a far more elaborate scenario: where a man's brother's wife — who was a *ketanah* and therefore an *issur derabbanan* to him as *eshet achi imo* — had been married by a different paternal half-brother (who was not related to her on the maternal side and could therefore marry her without violation), and that half-brother died. Could she perform *me'un* retroactively on her first marriage — even though the first husband had already died — in order to undo the prohibited relationship and enable *yibum* with the surviving brother? This would constitute *me'un le'achar mita bimkom mitzvah*: a posthumous *me'un* aimed at enabling the fulfillment of *yibum*. The *gemara* concludes that even in Rabbi Yishmael's framework, the answer here is *assur* — a posthumous *me'un* stretching back to an already-dissolved prior marriage goes too far.

## Divorce & Remarriage

### Me'un After Death

A related question arises in connection with retroactive *me'un* after death: specifically, whether *me'un* may be performed posthumously *bimkom mitzvah* — where performing it would enable *yibum* that would otherwise be impossible. Two scholars were dispatched at great cost to bring this question to Rabbi Akiva in prison, and both he and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira ruled it forbidden. The case involved the *zikah* relationship and whether *me'un* can operate retroactively once the first husband has already died, effectively reaching back in time to unwind a prior marriage that no longer exists in any tangible form. The conclusion here is that *me'un* cannot function in that posthumous mode, even for the worthy purpose of enabling *de'oraisa yibum*.

## Me'un After Get (II)

### Practical Resolution

Returning to the main discussion, Rav Yitzchak bar Ashian makes an important practical observation: *u'modeh Rav shemuteret le'achiv shel zeh sheniesra alav* — even Rav, who rules that the second man's *me'un* does not allow her to return to the first husband, would agree that the second man's *me'un* does permit her to marry the first husband's *brother*. This is a remarkable concession that reveals how the *gemara* conceptualizes what is happening when we forbid her return to the first husband.

The prohibition on returning to the first husband is not because the *me'un* failed to redefine her status as a non-*gerushah*. In principle, the *me'un* does work. The concern is specifically that the first husband, who is familiar with her personal signals — *d'makir be'mizatah u'v'kritzatah* — will manipulate her into performing *me'un* with the second husband in order to free her to return to him. We therefore forbid the return to the first husband as a precautionary measure. But since we genuinely view her as having had her *gerushah* status redefined — since the *me'un* is considered effective in principle — she is not a *gerushas achiv* at all, and the first husband's brother may marry her freely.

The *gemara* then raises a counterpoint: one might argue that since we have already forbidden her to the first husband, we should extend that prohibition by *gezeirah* to the first husband's brothers as well. Rav Yosef bar Ashian adopts exactly this position — *keshem she'asura lo kach asura le'achiv* — reasoning that once we have forbidden her to the first husband, a *gezeirah* should cover his brothers as well, lest they enable or facilitate the first husband's improper conduct. The first opinion disagrees: the concern is specific to the first husband himself, who knows her signals. There is no basis for extending the rabbinic fence to cover people who present no such risk.

The practical implication is striking and worth stating explicitly: the *gemara* is operating on the assumption that a second man's *me'un* is genuinely effective as a matter of principle. The entire edifice of what the *gemara* forbids or permits flows not from doubts about the *me'un*'s power but from precautionary concerns about the first husband's potential misconduct. And notably, the *gemara* leaves unexplored the question of whether she could thereby marry a *kohen* — since that too would seem to be answered in the affirmative if her *gerushah* status has genuinely been erased.

## Divorce & Remarriage (II)

### Simple Case Setup

The *mishnah* now introduces a new topic: *hamigaresh et ha'isha v'yachzirah* — a man who divorces his wife and then takes her back, without an intervening marriage to anyone else. The question for our purposes is whether her status as *grushas achiv* — the brother's divorcee — carries forward and prevents *yibum* when the husband subsequently dies, or whether the remarriage redefines her status so that she is once again simply *eshet achiv hamet*, the brother's wife, triggering the ordinary *mitzvah* of *yibum*.

The question has real conceptual depth: when she received the *get*, she became *grushas achiv* vis-à-vis the surviving brother. When the first husband then remarried her, did that second marriage erase the earlier status? Or does the *grushas achiv* designation persist latently, re-emerging with full force once the husband dies?

The plain ruling of the *mishnah* is *muteres leyavam* — she is permitted to *yibum*. The remarriage redefines her status and she is no longer *grushas achiv*. But Rabbi Eliezer disagrees and rules she is forbidden.

### Adult Remarriage

The *mishnah* then presents a parallel case involving a *yesomah* — a minor whose father has died, such that her original marriage was *kiddushin de'rabbanan*. He divorced her and then remarried her. Here too the *mishnah* rules *muteres leyavam*, and here too Rabbi Eliezer forbids *yibum*. At first glance this case seems identical in structure to the first, raising the question of why it is stated separately. The answer emerges only when we reach the third case.

### R. Eliezer Position

The third case illuminates everything: *ketanah she'hisi'ah aviha* — a minor who was married off by her father, making the original marriage *kiddushin de'oraisa*. He then divorced her, producing a *gerushin* of full *de'oraisa* force. After the divorce, she becomes *k'yesomah b'chayei ha'av* — like an orphan while the father is alive. She has left the father's household (since she was married and then returned), is no longer under her husband's control (since he divorced her), and is in a kind of emancipated status. If the same man then remarries her, this second marriage is only *kiddushin de'rabbanan*, because the father can no longer marry her off *de'oraisa* in this state. The *gemara* then rules *divrei hakol asurah leyavam* — everyone agrees that she is forbidden to *yibum*, because the *gerushin* was a full *de'oraisa* divorce, creating a genuine *grushas achiv de'oraisa* status, while the remarriage was only *de'rabbanan* and therefore cannot undo it.

This third case is the key to understanding Rabbi Eliezer's position throughout. The reason he forbids *yibum* even in the first two cases — the adult who remarried as an adult, and the *yesomah* who was at *de'rabbanan* level throughout — is to protect against confusion with this third case, where everyone agrees she is truly *grushas achiv*.

An interesting question arises from the structure of case three: if the father loses his *de'oraisa* authority to marry her off after the first marriage dissolves, who performs the second *kiddushin*? The *Rambam* does not mention the mother or brothers in this context, which might suggest she effectuates the *kiddushin* herself, or alternatively that the father retains *de'rabbanan* authority analogous to what the mother and brothers possess — but this remains an open question.

### Eliezer's Reasoning

The *gemara* (through Eifa) initially suggests Rabbi Eliezer's rationale is *ho'il ve'amdah lo sha'ah achas be'issura* — since she stood in a forbidden relationship for at least one moment (when she was *grushas achiv* following the *get*), that status persists even after remarriage. The rabbis challenge this: if so, she should not even require *chalitzah*, since she would simply be a full *grushas achiv de'oraisa*. But a *braisa* records that Rabbi Eliezer does require *chalitzah*, which demonstrates that he does not treat her as straightforwardly *grushas achiv de'oraisa*. He must be operating with some form of rabbinic prohibition or doubt.

Eifa then concedes: *Rabbi Eliezer lo yadan mai ta'amei* — I do not know Rabbi Eliezer's reason.

Abaye provides the answer: *misafka lei ee misah mapil ee nisuin rishonim mapilin* — Rabbi Eliezer is in doubt about what determines a woman's status for purposes of *yibum*. Is it the moment of the husband's death that triggers the assessment of her status? Or is it the moment of the original marriage — the *nisuin rishonim* — that determines all relevant classifications? If one assesses from the moment of the first marriage, then she was already *grushas achiv* at the time of the *get* and that status, once created, governs. If one assesses from the moment of death, then the relevant marriage is the second one, and she should be eligible for *yibum*. Since this is unresolved, Rabbi Eliezer requires *chalitzah* as a hedge.

Rava offers a different explanation: Rabbi Eliezer actually holds clearly that *misah mapil* — it is the death that triggers the assessment. In principle, then, she should be eligible for *yibum*. But a *de'rabbanan* concern prevents it: *hakol beki'in be'geirushin ve'ein hakol beki'in be'hazara* — everyone knows about a divorce (since the community witnessed the *get*), but not everyone knows about the remarriage (which may have been private). If the brother performs *yibum* with her, onlookers who know about the divorce but not the remarriage will think he is performing *yibum* with his brother's ex-wife, which is ordinarily forbidden. To forestall this misimpression, Rabbi Eliezer requires *chalitzah* but not *yibum*. The *gemara* challenges this on the grounds that remarriage, since they live together, tends to be publicly known — but responds that one could imagine scenarios where he remarried her at night and died the next morning, meaning the community never learned of the reconciliation.

### Father-Married Minor

Rav Ashi offers a third explanation that he argues is the most straightforward reading of the *mishnah*: *de'gazar hani mishum yesomah b'chayei aviha ve'hichzirah* — Rabbi Eliezer's prohibition in the first two cases is a *gezeirah* enacted to protect against confusion with the third case. The third case — father-married minor, full *de'oraisa* divorce, *de'rabbanan* remarriage — is a genuine, unanimous *grushas achiv* situation. To prevent people from mistakenly permitting *yibum* in that case by confusing it with the first two, Rabbi Eliezer extends the prohibition to all cases where the pattern of divorce-followed-by-remarriage exists, even when both stages were *de'oraisa* or both were *de'rabbanan*.

This is confirmed by a *braisa*: *modim chachamim le'Rabbi Elazar be'ketanah she'hisi'ah aviha ve'nisgarsha harei hi k'yesomah b'chayei ha'av* — the *chachamim* agree with Rabbi Eliezer that in the third case she is genuinely *grushas achiv*, since *geirusheiha geirushin gemurin* — her divorce was a complete *de'oraisa* divorce — *ve'ein chazarasah chazara gemura* — and her remarriage was not a full *de'oraisa* remarriage. The *gemara* notes that the very inclusion of this agreed-upon third case in the *mishnah* serves precisely to frame Rabbi Eliezer's positions in the first two cases as a *gezeirah* extending from it.

The *braisa* further clarifies: *bamei devarim amurim* — when does everyone agree she remains *grushas achiv*? When he divorced her as a minor and remarried her as a minor, so the remarriage was only *de'rabbanan*. But if he divorced her as a minor and remarried her as an adult (*ve'hichzirah k'she-hi gedolah*), or remarried her as a minor but she reached adulthood while still married to him (*gadla etzlo*), then the second marriage attains *de'oraisa* status — presumably because marital relations after she becomes an adult constitute *bi'as kiddushin* — and *o choletzet o misyabemes*, she may either perform *chalitzah* or *yibum*. Rabbi Eliezer, however, in his *gezeirah*, still requires *chalitzah* even in those latter cases.

The *gemara* then addresses a follow-up question from Rabbah to Rav Nachman: *tzarasah mahu* — what about the co-wife? If Rabbi Eliezer forbids *yibum* with this woman, can the brother perform *yibum* with the co-wife? If Rabbi Eliezer treats her as a *de'rabbanan erva*, then she would be a *tzaras erva* and the co-wife could not perform *yibum* either. But if Rabbi Eliezer's prohibition is purely a *gezeirah* — not a genuine *ervah* classification — then the co-wife remains eligible for *yibum*. Rav Nachman's initial instinct: the whole thing is a *gezeirah*, and one does not make a *gezeirah* atop a *gezeirah*, so the co-wife may perform *yibum*.

A *braisa* appears to contradict this, stating in the name of Rabbi Eliezer that both she *and* her co-wife perform *chalitzah*. The *gemara* resolves this by reading the conjunctive *vav* as disjunctive — meaning one or the other performs *chalitzah* — and then further revises: the woman herself performs *chalitzah*, while the co-wife may perform either *chalitzah* or *yibum*. This confirms that Rabbi Eliezer's prohibition, while real, does not generate full *tzaras erva* status, and the co-wife retains access to *yibum*.

## Me'un & Yibum Conflict

### Setup

The *mishnah* now introduces a new scenario that brings *me'un* and *yibum* into direct conflict: *shnei achim nesuim lishtei achayos ketanos* — two brothers married to two minor sisters. One of the brothers dies. Since both marriages are *de'rabbanan* (the *gemara* assumes the fathers are deceased, making these *yesomot ketanot*), all the relevant obligations — the *mitzvah* of *yibum* and the prohibition of *achos ishah* — exist at the same *de'rabbanan* level and therefore cancel one another out. She simply walks away without *chalitzah* or *yibum*, since there is no *de'oraisa* obligation that would require a formal release.

### Simple Scenarios

The *mishnah* then works through a series of graduated cases. If one of the women is an adult (*gedolah*) and the other is a minor (*ketanah*), the outcome depends on which husband dies. If the *ketanah*'s husband dies, the surviving brother has a *yibum de'rabbanan* obligation toward her, but she is his wife's sister at the *de'oraisa* level — *achos ishah de'oraisa*. The *de'oraisa erva* overrides the *de'rabbanan yibum*: she walks away. The *mishnah* states plainly: *teitzei ketanah mishum achos ishah*.

### The Dilemma

The genuinely difficult case arises when the *gedolah*'s husband dies. Now the surviving brother has a *de'oraisa* obligation of *yibum* — the deceased was fully and biblically married to a *gedolah* — but he is *de'rabbanan* married to the sister, creating a *de'rabbanan* prohibition of *achos ishah*. He cannot simply perform *yibum*, because he would then be perpetually violating a *de'rabbanan achos ishah* prohibition. He cannot simply perform *chalitzah* and remain married to his wife, because then she becomes *achos chalutzaso*. He cannot divorce his wife and perform *yibum*, because then she becomes *achos grushaso*. Every path creates a new forbidden relationship.

The problem cannot be resolved by invoking *be'makom mitzvah lo gazru rabbanan* — the principle that rabbinic decrees do not apply in the presence of a *mitzvah* — because *yibum* is not a momentary act that overrides the prohibition in passing. If he marries her, he will be living with her in an ongoing *de'rabbanan achos ishah* violation. This is not a situation of two competing momentary obligations; it is a structural incompatibility.

Additionally, even doing nothing creates a problem according to those authorities who hold that *zikah* — the legal bond that exists between the levir and the *yevamah* before he acts — is strong enough to create a prohibition of *achos zekukaso*. If *zikah* is real, then simply remaining married to his wife while the *zikah* to the sister-in-law persists is itself forbidden.

### R. Eliezer Solution

Rabbi Eliezer cuts the knot: *melamdin et haketanah shetime'en bo* — instruct the minor wife to perform *me'un* against her husband. If she performs *me'un*, the marriage is retroactively treated as never having taken place, she is no longer his wife, there is no *achos ishah* impediment, and he may proceed to *yibum de'oraisa* with the *gedolah*'s widow. The simplicity of the solution is elegant.

### Rabban Gamliel

Rabban Gamliel allows a middle path: *me'anah me'anah* — if the minor herself wishes to perform *me'un*, that resolves everything. But we do not instruct her to do so. If she does not wish to do *me'un*, she waits until she becomes an adult. Once she becomes an adult, the *kiddushin* attains *de'oraisa* force, and she then constitutes a genuine *achos ishah de'oraisa*, permitting her to exit without *chalitzah*. Rabban Gamliel's position presupposes that *zikah* is not strong enough to create a prohibition of *achos zekukaso*, so there is no problem with the brother remaining in his current marriages while waiting for the minor to come of age. The minor may, of course, be effectively an *agunah* for some period of years while this plays out.

### Rabbi Yehoshua

Rabbi Yehoshua rejects both solutions. He holds that one cannot instruct a woman to perform *me'un* — that is simply not a permissible intervention. And he holds that *zikah* is real enough to create *achos zekukaso*, so the brother cannot simply remain in his current marriage while the *zikah* to the sister-in-law persists. He therefore sees no exit that does not generate a new problem. His ruling: *motzi et ishto be'get ve'eshet achiv be'chalitzah* — he must both give his wife a *get* and perform *chalitzah* with the sister-in-law. He cannot do one without the other, because doing one first makes the other *achos chalutzaso* or *achos grushaso*. In theory both must happen simultaneously — and the result is that both women are released, and he ends up with neither. *Oy li al ishto oy li al eshet achiv* — woe to his wife, woe to his brother's wife.

### Teaching Me'un

The *gemara* raises the question that motivates Rabbi Yehoshua's position: is it permissible to instruct a woman to perform *me'un* at all? This challenge emerges from a teaching of Bar Kapparah, which introduces the next section.

## Rabbinic Values

### Bar Kapparah Teaching

Bar Kapparah taught: a person should cleave to three things and distance himself from three things. Cleave to: *chalitzah* over *yibum*, bringing *shalom*, and annulling vows (*haforas nedarim*). Distance from: *me'un*, accepting objects for safekeeping (*pikdonos*), and being a cosigner (*aravon*). It is from the first of these — that one should prefer *chalitzah* to *yibum* — that the *gemara* derives its answer to the question about Rabbi Eliezer's solution. The *gemara* concludes: *me'un de'mitzvah shanei* — ordinarily we do not instruct people to perform *me'un*, in keeping with Bar Kapparah's teaching. But when performing *me'un* enables a *de'oraisa* obligation of *yibum* to be fulfilled, it is an exceptional case. In that context, teaching the minor to perform *me'un* is not only permissible but appropriate.

### Abba Shaul Yibum

The preference for *chalitzah* that Bar Kapparah cites follows the position of Abba Shaul. A *braisa* records: *ha'kones et yevamto le'shem noy, le'shem ishus, le'shem davar acher* — one who takes his *yevamah* for reasons of her beauty, for the desire for marriage, or for any other motivation other than purely *le'hakim shem achiv*, establishing his brother's name — *ke'ilu poga be'erva*, it is as if he engaged in a prohibited relationship, since the ordinarily-forbidden status of *eshet achiv* is lifted only by the *mitzvah* of *yibum* performed with proper intent. When that proper intent is absent, the override does not fully function. Moreover, Abba Shaul states *ve'karov be'einai lihyos ha'vlad mamzer* — it is almost as though the child born from such a union is a *mamzer*. This harsh formulation reflects Abba Shaul's view that *yibum* performed without its proper *le'shem mitzvah* motivation is deeply compromised. Hence Bar Kapparah's teaching that one should incline toward *chalitzah*, which carries no such risk.

### Peace Imperative

The second thing one should cleave to is the pursuit of *shalom*. *Bakesh shalom ve'rodfehu* — seek peace and pursue it. Rabbi Abahu adds a *gezeirah shavah* connecting the language of *redifah* (running after) in this verse to a second verse: *rodef tzedakah va'chesed yimtza chayim tzedakah ve'chavod* — one who runs after righteousness and kindness will find life, righteousness, and honor. Life in this world, honor in the world to come. The active, relentless pursuit of peace is thus associated with the fullest range of divine reward.

### Vows & Institutions

The third positive practice is *haforas nedarim* — annulling vows. This follows Rabbi Natan, who taught: *ha'noder ke'ilu banah bamah* — one who takes a vow is like someone who built a *bamah* (a private altar), which is forbidden when there is a central *Beis Hamikdash*. And *ha'mekaymo ke'ilu hikriv alav korban* — one who fulfills that vow is like one who offered a sacrifice on that *bamah*.

The metaphor is illuminating. The underlying impulse to make a vow is a desire for personal religious expression beyond what the established system of *mitzvos* and *halacha* provides. One is not satisfied with communal religious institutions and seeks a private avenue for devotion. Rabbi Natan frames this as analogous to building a private altar: subjectively, the person believes they are performing a sacred act of dedication; objectively, from the perspective of those committed to centralized religious institutions, it represents an undermining of the communal framework. Vows therefore should not be made — and if made, they should be annulled.

### Cosigners & Judges

Turning to the three things from which one should distance: *me'un* is the first. Bar Kapparah's concern is *de'ma gadla u'micharta* — perhaps she will become an adult and regret it. *Pikdonos* is the second: accepting objects for safekeeping from a neighbor (*bar mata*), because *de'veiteih ke'veiteih dami* — his house is like your house; he will come and go freely, creating conditions under which he could take the object back and then claim you lost it.

The third is *aravon*, being a cosigner — specifically in the mode of *arvei shel Tzion*, where creditors would pursue the cosigner before even turning to the actual debtor. Rabbi Yitzchak explains via a verse: *ra yero'a ki arav zar* — evil after evil because one has entangled oneself as a guarantor for an outsider. The verse yields two further readings.

### Gerim Concerns

One reading: *ra'ah achar ra'ah tavo le'mekablei gerim* — evil after evil should come to those who accept converts. This is, taken at face value, a strikingly negative statement about accepting *gerim*. It reads *arav zar* as referring to involving an outsider in one's religious community. Rav Chelbo's teaching is cited in support: *kashim gerim le'Yisrael ke'sapachat ba'or* — converts are as difficult for Israel as a skin affliction, based on a wordplay between *ve'nispechu* (they will attach) and *sapachat* (an affliction).

This is the most negative statement in the *gemara* about accepting converts, and it must be read carefully. *Tosafot* immediately contextualizes and mitigates: the negative statement applies specifically in two circumstances — where one is proactively proselytizing and persuading people to convert, or where one accepts a prospective convert without adequate process. But if they themselves are pressing insistently to convert, *yesh lanu le'kablam* — we should accept them, and doing so is not merely permitted but meritorious. As proof, *Tosafot* cites the *midrash* that Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov were punished for failing to accept Timna when she sought to convert, with the consequence that *Amalek* descended from her.

### Learning to Action

The second reading of *arvei shel Tzion* concerns *tokeia atzmo lidvar halacha* — one who sticks himself onto a matter of *halacha*. This phrase requires unpacking.

A *braisa* records Rabbi Yose teaching: *kol ha'omer ein lo Torah ein lo Torah* — one who says "I have no interest in Torah" receives no reward from Torah. This seems obvious and barely worth stating. The *gemara* clarifies: the real case is *kol ha'omer ein lo ela Torah ein lo ela Torah* — one who says "I have only Torah, nothing else" — meaning one who learns but does not act, who remains in the *beis medrash* but never translates learning into practice, receives only the reward for learning and not the reward of *mitzvah* performance. Still, the *gemara* pushes further: even that seems obvious.

The real *chiddush* is more radical: if one's learning never translates into action, *afillu Torah ein lo* — one does not even receive the reward for Torah study. The basis is the verse *u'lemadetem va'asitem* — learn and do. *Kol she'yeshno ba'asiyah yeshno ba'limidah* — only if one is embedded in a world of action does the learning have value. *Kol she'eino ba'asiyah eino ba'limidah* — if one is not in a world of doing, the learning itself yields no reward.

An extension of this: what if one stays in the *beis medrash*, teaches others, and through teaching sends others out to perform *mitzvos*? One might think this vicarious doing should count. The *gemara* says no: if the teacher himself never acts, the fact that students go out and act does not earn the teacher reward for their actions. The teacher gets credit for the Torah taught but not for the actions performed by others. Learning must translate into personal action to be credited as such.

### Judge's Weight

A final interpretation of *tokeia atzmo lidvar halacha* applies to a judge: a case comes before a *dayan* and he recognizes something vaguely analogous in what he has studied. He analogizes — *medami milsa le'milsa* — and renders a ruling based on that imperfect parallel, despite the fact that he has a *rebbe* he could consult and does not bother to do so. *Tokeia atzmo lidvar halacha*: he is stuck on the one thing he happens to know, applying it as if it were a hammer to every nail, never acknowledging the limits of his expertise. This is a grave failure.

Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rav Yonasan: *le'olam yehei dayan atzmo ke'ilu cherev munachas lo bein yarcheisav* — a judge should always regard himself as though a sword is placed between his thighs, *ve'Gehenom pesucha lo mitachtav* — and *Gehenom* is open beneath him. The weight of judgment demands complete seriousness and genuine *yiras shamayim*. A judge who overreaches, who applies a single learned rule without seeking guidance where guidance is needed, risks far more than a wrong ruling. The verse from *Shir Hashirim* about the sixty warriors guarding the bed of Shlomo, each with a sword on account of *pachad baleilos* — fear of nights — is read as *pachad shel Gehenom shedomeh le'layla*: the fear of *Gehenom*, which resembles the night.

---

---

# Yevamot 110

## Kiddushei Ketanah & Yibum

### Scenario Setup

The daf opens at the bottom of 109b, with the Mishnah's discussion of *Rabban Gamliel*'s ruling. The case involves a man who contracted *kiddushei ketanah* — a marriage to a minor girl that was effected not through her father, and therefore binding only *derabbanan* — and whose brother subsequently died, leaving him with an obligation of *yibum derabbanan* toward his sister-in-law. To make the scenario concrete: Reuven is married to Rachel through *kiddushei ketanah* (a *derabbanan* marriage), and his brother dies leaving Leah as the *yevamah*. The complication is that Leah is Rachel's sister — i.e., *achot ishto* — and is therefore an *ervah* who normally cannot be subject to *yibum*. But is this *ervah* relationship truly operative here, given that the marriage to Rachel is only *derabbanan*?

### Rabban Gamliel's View

*Rabbi Eliezer*'s position is that one should teach the minor girl to perform *mi'un* — the minor's right to refuse and exit the marriage — thereby dissolving the *derabbanan* bond and permitting *yibum* with Leah. *Rabban Gamliel* takes a more nuanced stance: if the girl does *mi'un*, well and good; if not, one should simply wait until she matures. Once she becomes an adult, she becomes his wife *de'oraita*, and at that point Leah, as her sister, becomes a genuine *ervah* and may walk away entirely — without *chalitzah*, and without *yibum*.

### The Core Problem

The difficulty with *Rabban Gamliel*'s position is immediate. The obligation of *yibum* begins at the moment the brother dies. At that moment, Rachel is only a *derabbanan* wife, and thus Leah is only a *derabbanan ervah* — not a *de'oraita ervah*. Given that the *mitzvah* of *yibum* had already taken hold when the *ervah* was merely *derabbanan*, how can Leah walk away entirely simply because Rachel later becomes an adult? Perhaps one should argue that since the *zikah* (the *yibum* bond) was already in force when the *ervah* was only rabbinic, the *mitzvah* should persist — and at minimum, *chalitzah* might be required.

### Rav Elazar Asks

*Rabbi Elazar* posed this question directly to *Rav*: what exactly is *Rabban Gamliel*'s reasoning?

### Suspended Kiddushin

The first possibility *Rav* considers is that *Rabban Gamliel* holds *kiddushei ketanah* are *teluyim* — suspended or held in abeyance. The Aramaic phrase used is evocative: *kiddusheha mitla talu*, and *chi gadlah gadli bahadah* — the *kiddushin* "grows up with her." According to this view, when she contracts *kiddushin* as a minor, the act is not simply a *derabbanan* institution with no *de'oraita* dimension. Rather, the *de'oraita* marriage is latent within the original act and automatically comes into force when she reaches adulthood. There is no new act of *kiddushin* required; the original act, held in suspension, simply activates. On this reading, even retroactively, Rachel was in some sense already his wife when the *yibum* obligation began — and therefore Leah was already an *ervah* in some meaningful sense from the outset.

### New Kiddushin Theory

The second possibility is that *Rabban Gamliel* holds an entirely different view: the original *kiddushei ketanah* carry no *de'oraita* weight whatsoever. When Rachel becomes an adult, it is not that the old *kiddushin* activates — rather, a new act of *kiddushin* is created. This raises a separate question within *yibum* law: if a man has a *mitzvah* of *yibum* with a woman and then, without having performed either *yibum* or *chalitzah*, proceeds to marry her sister, mother, or daughter — creating an *ervah* situation after the *zikah* has already begun — does that *ervah* status dissolve the *zikah*? Can one simply generate an *ervah* after the fact and thereby neutralize the *yibum* obligation? *Rabban Gamliel* apparently holds yes: even if the *ervah* is created after the *zikah* began, she walks away — *nifterah yevamah ve-halchah lah*. On this reading, the crucial question then becomes: when does the new *kiddushin* with Rachel take effect? Since there is no ring or document, only *bi'ah* (intercourse) could create a new act of *kiddushin*. Hence the formulation: *ei baal in, ei lo baal lo* — if they have had *bi'ah*, yes; if not, no.

Two distinct analytical threads thus emerge: a *yibum* question about whether an *ervah* created after the *zikah* began dissolves it, and a *ketanah* question about what precisely happens when a minor girl grows up — whether the original *kiddushin* automatically activates, or whether a new act of *kiddushin* is required. The *Gemara* proceeds to focus on the latter.

### Rav Sheshet Objects

*Rav Sheshet* dismisses *Rav*'s framing sharply, suggesting that *Rav* must have been dozing off when he said it — a turn of phrase *Rav Sheshet* apparently favored. His basis is a *baraita* that, in his view, settles the matter clearly.

### Baraita on Teluyim

The *baraita* states: *hamekadesh et ha-ketanah, kiddusheha teluyim* — one who betroths a minor, her *kiddushin* is suspended. *Rav Sheshet* reads this as unambiguous support for the position that once she grows up, the *kiddushin* automatically takes effect — *gadlah gadli bahadah* — without requiring any new act of *bi'ah*.

### Rav Avin's Response

*Rav Avin bar Rav Nachman* responds that *mitalyasa ve-kayma* — "in abeyance and pending" — does not necessarily mean the *kiddushin* will automatically crystallize upon adulthood. Rather, it means the situation remains unresolved: *ei baal in, ei lo baal lo*. The *kiddushin* will take effect only if *bi'ah* occurs.

### Woman's Rights

The reasoning offered is that the woman retains her own set of prerogatives parallel to his. He has advantages she lacks — the power to divorce her unilaterally — but she has advantages he lacks: the right to perform *mi'un* and exit the marriage on her own initiative. As long as she has not had relations with him as an adult, she has not yet relinquished that right, and the *kiddushin* has not yet resolved into something definitive.

### Core Question

The core question thus crystallizes: is *kiddushei ketanah* automatically operative upon her reaching adulthood, or is a new act of *bi'ah* required to effectuate it? This is not merely a technical question about the minor's marriage — it ramifies into major areas of practical *halacha*.

---

## Rav vs. Shmuel/Sheshet

### Rav's Position

*Rav* holds that a new act of *bi'ah* is required. When a *ketanah* grows up, the original *kiddushin* does not automatically become operative *de'oraita*; only if they subsequently have intercourse as adults does the marriage become fully binding at a Torah level. *Rav Sheshet* disagrees: the *kiddushin* activates automatically, without any new act.

### Challenge to Rav

The *Gemara* now challenges *Rav*'s position. A *ketanah* who did not perform *mi'un* grew up, and then accepted *kiddushin* from a second man. What is the ruling?

### Rav Implied

*Rav* rules that she does not need a *get* from the second man — the second *kiddushin* was ineffective. *Shmuel* rules that she does need a *get* from the second man. The implication of *Rav*'s ruling seems to be that when she becomes an adult she is already *mekudeshet* to the first husband — automatically, even without intercourse — which appears to contradict his stated position that *bi'ah* is required.

### Gemara's Resolution

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: the case where *Rav* says she does not need a *get* from the second man is specifically the case where she had already had *bi'ah* with the first husband after reaching adulthood. The second man's *kiddushin* failed because she was already fully *mekudeshet* *de'oraita* to the first husband — via that act of *bi'ah*. *Rav*'s position is therefore internally consistent: *bi'ah* is indeed required, and it had occurred in this case.

### Shmuel's Position

But the *Gemara* then presses: if she had *bi'ah* with the first husband as an adult, why does *Shmuel* say she still needs a *get* from the second man? How could the second *kiddushin* possibly be effective? *Shmuel*'s answer is the crucial formulation: *kol ha-bo'el al da'at kiddushin ha-rishonim hu bo'el* — anyone who has intercourse does so within the framework of the original *kiddushin*. According to *Shmuel*, even when the adult woman has intercourse with her husband, that act is not a new, independent *kiddushin*; it is a continuation of the original *kiddushei ketanah*. Since the original *kiddushin* was only *derabbanan*, the subsequent intercourse — framed entirely by that context — never creates a new *de'oraita kiddushin*. Therefore, there is no *de'oraita* marriage, and when the second man gives *kiddushin*, it could potentially take effect.

### Three-Way Debate

The three-way structure of the debate is now clear. *Rav Sheshet* holds that upon reaching adulthood, the *kiddushei ketanah* automatically activates *de'oraita* — no intercourse required. *Rav* holds that intercourse after adulthood creates a new act of *kiddushin de'oraita*, independent of and superseding the original rabbinic framework. *Shmuel* holds that even post-adolescent intercourse does not create a new *kiddushin*, because all intercourse is understood within the context of the original *kiddushin* — and since that original *kiddushin* was *derabbanan*, the couple never achieves a *de'oraita* marital status unless they explicitly reframe the relationship.

This three-way debate is not merely of theoretical interest. It bears directly on the practical reasoning of major twentieth-century *poskim*.

### Rav Moshe Approach

*Rav Moshe Feinstein*'s well-known approach to cases of *agunah* and potential *mamzerut* frequently relied on invalidating the original *kiddushin* — by identifying a *pesul* in the witnesses, for instance — and thereby establishing that no valid marriage ever took place. A standing objection to this approach is that even if the original *kiddushin* were defective, the couple lived together for years and had repeated intercourse: why would each act of intercourse not itself constitute a new *ma'aseh kiddushin*? *Rav Moshe* answered by invoking precisely *Shmuel*'s principle: *kol ha-bo'el al da'at kiddushin ha-rishonim hu bo'el*. The subsequent intercourse was not intended as an independent act of *kiddushin*; it was understood by both parties as occurring within the framework of what they believed was their already-established marriage. Since no one had in mind to create a new *kiddushin*, none was created. The difference from the *ketanah* case is that there the original *kiddushin* was merely *derabbanan*, while in *Rav Moshe*'s cases the original *kiddushin* was attempted *de'oraita* but was *pasul*; the principle, however, operates analogously.

### Henkin's Disagreement

*Rav Yosef Eliyahu Henkin* disagreed with *Rav Moshe*'s application of this principle. His argument was that *kiddushei bi'ah* — betrothal effected through intercourse — does not depend on subjective intent. The objective reality of sustained marital cohabitation, of a man and woman living together as husband and wife and engaging in intercourse within that context, itself creates *kiddushin*, regardless of whether either party consciously intends the act as a new *kinyan*. The *de'oraita* framework, in his view, is activated by the reality of the marital relationship, not merely by articulated intent. On this reading, *Rav Moshe*'s leniency would not hold, since the years of cohabitation would themselves constitute valid *kiddushin*. One can see this disagreement as corresponding, at a theoretical level, to the debate between *Rav* and *Shmuel*: *Rav* might hold that the objective act of *bi'ah* in a marital context creates *kiddushin* even without explicit intent, while *Shmuel* would say the act is always colored by the original framing.

---

## Tnai Case & Limits

### Kiddushin B'Tnai

The *Gemara* notes that *Rav* and *Shmuel* have already debated this same underlying question in a different context: *kidesh al tnai ve-chanas stam* — a man performed *kiddushin* with an explicit condition (*tnai*), and then the couple began living together without reiterating the condition. They continued to live as husband and wife and to have intercourse, but the *tnai* was never formally addressed again.

### Rav on Tnai

*Rav* rules that a *get* is required. Since the husband has moved forward into married life with her, he has implicitly waived (*achulei achlah*) his original *tnai*. The act of living together and having intercourse overrides the earlier conditional framework and creates a new, unconditional marital reality.

### Shmuel on Tnai

*Shmuel* rules that no *get* is needed. All subsequent intercourse is understood as occurring within the framework of the original *kiddushin* — including its *tnai*. *Kol ha-bo'el al da'at kiddushin ha-rishonim hu bo'el*. Since the *tnai* was never fulfilled or waived explicitly, it remains operative, and the marriage was never fully effectuated.

### Gemara's Reasoning

The *Gemara* then asks: if so, why does the debate need to be stated in both cases — the *ketanah* case and the *tnai* case? Perhaps one could derive the other. The *Gemara* explains that the two cases are not fully parallel. In the *tnai* case, the *tnai* is explicit and the husband is directly confronted with it; when he subsequently has intercourse, one can reasonably infer that he is consciously setting the *tnai* aside. Therefore, *Rav*'s position — that the *bi'ah* overrides the earlier context — is most naturally at home in the *tnai* case.

### Possible Agreement

By contrast, in the *ketanah* case, there is no explicit problem confronting the husband. He married a young girl, they grew up together, and nothing in his lived experience signals that a new act of *kiddushin* is needed. He simply does not perceive a problem. Therefore, *Rav* might in fact agree with *Shmuel* in the *ketanah* case — holding that since the husband has no awareness that a new *de'oraita* framework is called for, the *bi'ah* does not generate one. Conversely, in the *tnai* case, *Shmuel* might agree with *Rav* — since the problem is so explicit that the husband's continued *bi'ah* could be construed as a conscious act of waiver. Both cases need to be stated to prevent either such inference.

---

## Challenge & Bei Korsaia

### Objection to Rav

The *Gemara* raises a further challenge to *Rav*'s stated position: does *Rav* really hold that the *ketanah*'s *kiddushin* only becomes *de'oraita* upon subsequent *bi'ah*? A story from *Narash* appears to cut the other way.

### Abduction Story

The case: a girl who had been married as a *ketanah* grew up, and was being conveyed in the *bei korsaia* — a special seat or conveyance used to bring the bride to the *chuppah* — when another man appeared and abducted her, apparently accepting her *kiddushin* on the spot. In other words, she had become an adult, had not yet had *bi'ah* with the first husband, and the second man performed an act of *kiddushin* before the *chuppah* took place.

### Rav Huna/Chananel

*Rav Huna* and *Rav Chananel*, both students of *Rav*, were present in *Narash* at the time, and ruled that she does not need a *get* from the second man — the second *kiddushin* was simply ineffective.

### Implication

The apparent implication is that she was already fully *mekudeshet* to the first husband the moment she became an adult — automatically, without *bi'ah* — consistent with *Rav Sheshet*'s position, not *Rav*'s.

### Rav Papa's Explanation

*Rav Papa* resolves the difficulty by noting a local custom: in *Narash*, the couple has *bi'ah* before the ceremonial chariot ride, not after. The *chuppah* and consummation preceded the *bei korsaia* procession. Therefore the ruling of *Rav Huna* and *Rav Chananel* was issued in a case where *bi'ah* with the first husband had already occurred — fully consistent with *Rav*'s position.

### Rav Ashi's Approach
