Even when we have physical evidence — a charred body, a hand — we face the independent question of what conclusions we can reasonably draw from those facts. The woman may be reporting accurately what she observed, yet the question remains: do the facts she has accurately reported actually establish that the husband is dead? Cases of *agunah* arising from uncertainty about a husband's fate often turn not on doubting the witness's sincerity but on precisely this kind of evidentiary ambiguity. What does it mean to "see" someone die when what one observed were circumstances that strongly implied death without confirming it absolutely?

---

## Single Witness War

### Ed Echad Question

The *Gemara* now poses a new question: *ed echad b'milchama mahu* — what is the law if a third-party witness — not the woman herself — reports that the husband died in war? The question is somewhat surprising. If the concern is not intentional deception but rather the drawing of incorrect conclusions in chaotic circumstances, why would a third party be any more reliable than the woman herself? Both were presumably present in the same chaotic environment and subject to the same perceptual limitations.

One answer is that a third party, being less emotionally invested and not a direct subject of the events he is narrating, will be more careful and precise. When one presents oneself explicitly as a witness rather than as a party to the events, there is a greater awareness of the implications of testimony, a greater compunction about stating things as certain that are not fully verified.

### Why Believe Him

The *Gemara* presents the argument for believing the single witness. The ordinary basis for accepting *ed echad* in cases of a husband's death is *milta de'avida le'igloyei hu* — the matter is one that will eventually become known — *lo meshaker* — and therefore he will not lie, since truth will surface in any case. The argument applies here too: *hacha nami lo meshaker* — here too he will not lie. Furthermore, the general basis for accepting a single witness's report of a husband's death is reinforced by the assumption that the woman herself will investigate before remarrying, knowing the grave consequences if the husband is still alive.

### Why Not Believe

The argument against believing him in a war situation is as follows. If the ordinary basis for trusting a single witness is that she herself — *hi gufa daika uminisba* — will investigate and verify before remarrying, then in a war situation that backstop is undermined. The *Gemara* explains: *lo daika uminisba de'amra bidedamei* — she will not investigate carefully enough, because what the witness has told her coheres with what she herself perceived. She heard the witness say her husband died in war; this fits her own impressions; and so she proceeds to remarry without the careful independent investigation that normally underwrites the trust we extend to a single witness. The risk of drawing incorrect conclusions is therefore compounded: the witness may have made assumptions, and the woman may not independently verify because the witness's account confirms her own perceptions. Rashi similarly explains that the concern about *bidedamei* applies not just to the woman's testimony but to this entire chain of inference.

---

## Akiva's Report

### Nehardea Story

Rami bar Chama brings a *tanna'itic* account as a potential proof. Rabbi Akiva reports: when I went to Nehardea *le'aber shanah* — to intercalate the year — I found Nechemia, a man from the house of Beit Dali, who told me: I have heard that in the Land of Israel they do not allow a woman to remarry on the basis of one witness, except for Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava, who permits it alone. Rabbi Akiva confirmed this. Nechemia then said: go back and tell them in my name — *atem yode'im hamedina hazzo meshubeshet begayasot* — you know that this country is disrupted by army troops — and this is the tradition I have received from Rabban Gamliel the Elder: *shemashi'in et ha'isha al pi ed echad* — that a woman may be allowed to remarry on the basis of one witness.

### Troops Context

The question is how to understand the mention of troops. Does Nechemia mean to say: even though this country is in a state of war and troops are passing through, the tradition from Rabban Gamliel the Elder is that a single witness is believed even under such circumstances? If so, this would be a direct answer to our question — a single witness *is* accepted in a war situation. *Alma ed echad meheman* — one witness is believed.

### Rava Reinterprets

Rava rejects this reading. If the point were that one witness is accepted in time of war, he argues, Nechemia should have stated the rule in universal terms: *kol makom sheyesh gayasot* — wherever there are troops, a single witness is believed. Why would he refer specifically to *this* country? Moreover, the discussion was focused on the halakhic practice of *Eretz Yisrael* — Nechemia was delivering a tradition about what Rabban Gamliel the Elder ruled. The mention of troops, Rava explains, is entirely incidental. Nechemia was explaining why he could not go deliver this tradition to the authorities in *Eretz Yisrael* himself: *ve'i efshar li lemishbak inshi beiti umaytei kamei rabbanan* — it is impossible for him to travel, because the region is in chaos due to military activity. He was therefore asking Rabbi Akiva to carry the message back. The ruling itself — that a woman may remarry on the basis of one witness — has nothing to do with war. It is simply the general *halakha* according to Rabban Gamliel the Elder, and the mention of troops explains only why Nechemia could not convey it in person. The incident is therefore not a proof regarding *ed echad b'milchama*.

---

## Drowned Scholars

### Drowned Case

The *Gemara* presents another account. Two Torah sages were traveling with Abba Yossi ben Simai on a boat. *Ve-tavu* — they drowned. *Ve-hesi Rabbi nishoteihan al pi nashim* — Rabbi permitted their wives to remarry on the basis of women's testimony. Women who had been present or had witnessed the sinking reported the deaths, and Rabbi acted on those reports.

### Water = War

The *Gemara* observes: *mayim kemilchama dami* — water is treated like war in the relevant sense. In chaotic and dangerous circumstances on the water, those reporting what happened may be drawing conclusions based on perception rather than certainty. Furthermore, the testimony here is not that of two formal male witnesses. A hundred women, the *Gemara* notes, have the legal status of one witness — *bi'nashim afilu me'ah k'echad dami* — because women do not constitute formal *edut* in the technical sense. So Rabbi was relying on what is legally equivalent to *ed echad* testimony, in a situation analogous to war. This seems to be a strong proof that such testimony is accepted.

### Water Problem

But the *Gemara* immediately challenges this reading. *Mayim she'ein lahem sof ninhu* — this was open water without visible boundaries. And *mayim she'ein lahem sof isha asura* — in the case of water with no visible end, a woman may not remarry even if two formal witnesses testify that they saw her husband drown. The logic is counterintuitive: rather than reasoning that without a visible shore the man had nowhere to swim, the concern runs the other direction. If the water has no visible end, then somewhere beyond the witnesses' sight the man may have surfaced and survived. No testimony about drowning in such conditions is ever absolutely conclusive. If that is so, how could Rabbi have permitted remarriage at all? The case seems impossible to rely upon as a proof for anything.

### Simanim Required

The *Gemara* resolves this: *ela heichi dami* — what must the situation actually have been? The witnesses must have said *ashkachinhu kaman* — we found them before us, meaning the bodies were retrieved — *ve-chazinahu l'altar* — and we saw them immediately, before the water had time to completely disfigure the faces — *ve-amri simanim* — and they identified the bodies by specific bodily marks. Tosafot raises the question of why facial recognition alone would not suffice; the answer appears to be that even brief immersion can alter appearance enough that identification by *simanim* — distinctive physical marks such as a mole, a birthmark, or a physical abnormality — is needed to reinforce the identification. In that case, the *Gemara* concludes, *d'lav aleiyhu samchinan ela a'simanim* — we are not relying on the witnesses' general impression; we are relying on the concrete identifying marks they specified. There is therefore no concern of *amri bidedamei* — the testimony is grounded in specific, verifiable physical evidence, not in perception or assumption.

The *Gemara* has thus not definitively resolved whether *ed echad* is accepted in a war situation without additional grounding. The drowned scholars case, which seemed to offer a proof, turns out instead to rest on the presence of *simanim* rather than on the testimony of informal witnesses under chaotic conditions per se.

---

## Sesame Seeds

### Seeds Dispute

The *Gemara* shifts from the weighty terrain of death and remarriage to a *dinei mamonot* case involving sesame seeds — but the analogy it draws will illuminate the broader question of when we may connect circumstantial dots. A certain man had deposited a quantity of sesame seeds with his friend for safekeeping. When he later asked for them back, the friend said: you already took them back. The first man pointed to a barrel and said: I gave you exactly this measure, and here is the same measure of sesame seeds sitting in this barrel — *ha kaila ve-kaila havyan* — the amounts match precisely. The friend replied: those are mine; yours you already took.

### Chisda's Analogy

Rav Chisda sought to resolve the case by analogy to the drowned scholars. Just as in that case we matched two bodies to two men and assumed they were the same, so here — two matching quantities, same container, reasonable to assume it is the same deposit. The application from a case about remarrying widows to a property dispute over seeds raises immediate questions: do we apply different standards of proof in *dinei mamonot* versus cases of personal status? And how much circumstantial convergence is needed in each context to draw a confident conclusion?

### Rava Rejects

Rava rejected the analogy: *mi dami* — how can you compare? *Hatam ka'amar simanim* — in the drowned case, the witnesses identified specific bodily marks. That is what made the identification reliable. *Hacha shumshumei mai simanei it lehu* — here, sesame seeds have no identifying marks whatsoever. One measure of sesame seeds looks exactly like any other measure of sesame seeds. The analogy simply does not hold.

### Weight Not Enough

The *Gemara* then asks: is not the matching quantity itself a kind of identifying mark? *Ha kaila ve-kaila havyan* — they are the same measure. The *Gemara* answers: *chushbana itremi* — it may simply be a coincidence that the amounts match. Just as one cannot identify a person by height alone — many people share the same height — one cannot identify a deposit by quantity alone. Many quantities happen to be identical, and identical weight or volume does not constitute a meaningful *siman*. The claim fails.

---

## Labeled Vessels

### Vessel Labels

Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda raises a question to Rav Ashi: are we really concerned, in the sesame seeds case, that the borrower might have emptied the barrel and refilled it with different seeds? He cites a *mishnah*: if a vessel is found with the letter *kuf* written on it, one assumes it contains *korban* — something consecrated to the Temple; *mem* indicates *maaser*; *dalet* indicates *dimua* — a mixture of *chullin* and *terumah*; *tet* indicates *tevel* — untithed grain; and *tav* indicates *terumah*. The *mishnah* notes that in times of danger, people wrote *tav* in place of spelling out *terumah* in full. The principle behind all of this is that one assumes the vessel still contains what its label indicates — that is, we do not ordinarily suppose that a person emptied a labeled vessel and reused it for something else.

### Label Principle

The rationale is intuitive: the whole point of labeling a vessel is to maintain consistent use. A person who has gone to the trouble of marking a storage container with its contents is unlikely to repurpose that container while leaving the old label in place. From this, one might conclude that we never assume a vessel was emptied and reused, which would support the view that the sesame seeds in the barrel are the original deposit.

### Yosei Exception

But Ravina draws attention to the end of the *mishnah*: Rabbi Yosei says that even if one finds a whole barrel explicitly labeled *terumah*, one may still say that its current contents are *chullin*. His reasoning: *shani omer eshtakad havei meleiah terumah u-pina* — I can say that last year it was filled with *terumah*, it was then emptied, and now it is being used for ordinary produce. Rabbi Yosei explicitly entertains the possibility of emptying and reusing a vessel.

### Label Dispute

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction between Rabbi Yosei's view and the earlier assumption of consistency. The dispute turns on a specific question: *im issa de-panya michpar hava kafar* — if you were going to reuse the vessel for something else, would you not have erased the label? One position holds that no one would leave a misleading label on a vessel; therefore, the presence of the label proves continued consistent use. Rabbi Yosei, however, holds that there are two plausible ways the label could remain despite a change of contents: either the owner forgot the vessel was labeled — *ishtaluyei ishtali* — or he intentionally kept the *terumah* label as a deterrent, knowing that people will not touch something marked *terumah* and thus using the label to protect ordinary produce from being eaten.

### Seeds Application

The implication for the sesame seeds case: when it comes to explicitly labeled vessels, there is at least a basis for arguing that the label proves continuity of use — that is the majority position against which Rabbi Yosei dissents. But an unlabeled barrel of sesame seeds lacks even that basis. With no label, there is no reason to presume that the contents are original. It is entirely plausible that the barrel was emptied, the original seeds returned to their owner as the depositor claims, and then refilled with the friend's own seeds. The sesame seeds case therefore cannot be resolved on the basis of continuity of possession.

---

## Reish Galuta

### Death Report

The *Gemara* introduces a new story and a new question about identification. Yitzchak the *Reish Galuta* — the political head of the Jewish diaspora in Babylonia — who was the son of the sister of Rabbi Bibi, was traveling from Cordoba to Spain. *Ve-shakhiv* — he died en route. A message was sent back: Yitzchak the *Reish Galuta*, son of Rabbi Bibi's sister, was traveling from Cordoba to Spain and died.

### Name Worry

The question posed: *mi chayishinan le-trei Yitzchak o lo* — must we be concerned that there might be two people named Yitzchak who fit these identifying details? At first glance this seems almost absurd. How many people named Yitzchak could there be who simultaneously hold the position of *Reish Galuta*, are nephews of Rabbi Bibi, and were traveling on that same route? And yet the *Gemara* treats this as a live question, because the broader principle at stake is one of general importance: when we receive a report about a person identified by name and other particulars, how much specific identification is required before we may act on the assumption that we know who is meant?

### Abaye's View

Abaye holds: *chayishinan* — we are concerned. Even with multiple identifying details, one must verify that no other person fits the same description before relying on the report for a matter of consequence.

### Rava's View

Rava holds: *lo chayishinan* — we are not concerned. Once a person fits the specific identifying details provided, there is no need to investigate further for potential duplicates. Rava's position is that context and convergence of identifying information are, in principle, sufficient.

---

## Androlinai Get

### Get Found

Rava supports his position with the following proof. A *get* was found in Nehardea, written as follows: I, Androlinai, from Nehardea, hereby divorce and dismiss so-and-so my wife. The father of Shmuel sent this document to Rav Yehuda Nesi'ah — the grandson of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi — asking: we know a man in Nehardea named Androlinai whose wife is named Sarah. May we assume this *get* refers to him and allow his wife to remarry?

### Investigation Need

Rashi notes that the *get* contained not only the husband's unusual name but also the wife's name and the city — all three identifying details matching someone known to the community. And yet the question was raised: must we verify that no other person in Nehardea shares these same particulars?

### Investigation Order

Rav Yehuda Nesi'ah responded: *zil bedok bi-Nehardea kullah* — go and check the entire Nehardea — meaning the entire district — to determine whether anyone else has the same name as this husband and the same name as his wife. He thus apparently required active investigation before assuming that the *get* referred to the known Androlinai.

### Rava's Critique

Rava, however, argues that this cannot be the actual *halakhic* ruling. If we truly could not draw logical inferences from identifying information, then *yidbok kulei alma mibei leh* — one would have to search the entire world. The *get* says the man is from Nehardea, but Rashi notes that perhaps he was merely *in* Nehardea when he wrote it; perhaps he had since moved on; perhaps there was once another Androlinai who lived there and left. There would be no end to such concerns. Rava therefore concludes: *mishum kevodo de-avuh de-Shmuel hu de-shalach hakhi* — Rav Yehuda Nesi'ah's instruction to investigate was not a true halakhic ruling but a gesture of respect to the father of Shmuel, who had raised the question. Rather than dismissing it as unnecessary, he gave him work to do. In reality, Rava maintains, once the known Androlinai fits all the identifying details, we do not require a search for hypothetical duplicates.

---

## Mirror Names

### IOU Story

Rava offers an additional proof from a case in Mechoza. Two loan documents — IOUs — were found from Mechoza, and the names on them were *Chavi bar Nigai* and *Ninai bar Chavi*: almost mirror images of each other, each component of one name appearing inverted in the other. These were very common names in that city, making the prospect of confusion quite real.

### Collection Allowed

Rava bar Avuha nevertheless permitted collection on the basis of these IOUs, notwithstanding the similar names and the possibility of confusion about which document referred to which party.

### Context Works

Rashi and Rava's conclusion is that context and circumstances are sufficient to identify the correct parties. Despite the commonality of these names and despite the mirror-image similarity between them, the combination of circumstances surrounding who holds the document, who is being approached for payment, and what the overall situation is allows us to draw a reliable conclusion about which document refers to which transaction and which parties.

---

## IOU Safety

### Three Protections

Abaye frames his own understanding of why the creditor holding these IOUs may be trusted, offering three reasons not to worry that the wrong person is presenting the document. First, Abaye raises the possibility that the creditor might have *dropped* the IOU — *ei l'nefilla* — and someone else found it. But creditors are careful: *mizahar beh* — they safeguard such documents precisely because their entire claim rests on them. The concern about accidental loss is therefore negligible. Second, one might worry the creditor gave the IOU to someone else for *pikadon* — safekeeping — who now misuses it. But as Abaye explains, *keivan d'shmei k'shmei lo mafkad gabei* — no creditor would be so foolish as to entrust a document bearing his debtor's name to another person who happens to share that exact name, since that person could then fraudulently use it to collect. Third, one might argue the IOU was transferred — *mesar leh* — sold or assigned to another — but the transfer was not completed and therefore the holder has no valid claim. But this too fails: *osiyos niknos b'mesira* — the transfer of written documents is effected by the very act of handing them over. If the creditor gave the document to someone, that act itself completes the acquisition, and the holder has a valid claim.

### Creditor Logic

The logic threading through all three answers is that the circumstances themselves constrain the universe of plausible explanations. A creditor would not drop his IOU carelessly; a creditor would not entrust it to someone with an identical name; and if it was intentionally transferred, the transfer was legally complete. These considerations together mean that the person presenting the IOU is almost certainly the legitimate creditor, and we may rely on context to establish that identification without demanding additional proof.

---

## Context & Conclusions

### Spectrum

Stepping back, the cases discussed across 115a–b form a spectrum. At one extreme is the Yitzchak *Reish Galuta* situation — a case with an extraordinary concentration of identifying information, where Abaye nonetheless insists on concern that another individual might match all the same particulars. In the middle is the Androlinai *get* — a document with multiple identifying details including an unusual name, a wife's name, and a city, where the question of possible duplicates arises and Rava argues that practical logic forecloses the need for further investigation. At the near end is the mirror-name IOU case from Mechoza, where the names are common, the possibility of confusion is real, and yet collection is allowed based on the totality of circumstances.

### Connecting Dots

This spectrum is worth reading alongside the earlier discussion of *amra bidedamei*. The concern running through that entire section is that a woman — or any witness — might connect dots incorrectly, reasoning from circumstances to a conclusion that seems warranted but is not actually certain. The cases in this later section demonstrate that such dot-connecting is unavoidable. In the charred body case, in the drowned scholars case, and now in the name-identification cases, some inference from context is always required. The question is not whether we may ever reason from circumstances to conclusions — we must — but rather how many inferential steps we may take, what quality of identifying information we require, and how much weight we give to explanations that would undermine the most natural reading of the facts.

### Investigation Missing

What runs through all of this as a striking omission is the question of why the *Gemara* so consistently treats the woman's testimony as a fixed datum to be believed or disbelieved, rather than as a starting point for investigation. If the concern is that she is drawing incorrect conclusions — that she saw her husband shot in battle and assumed he died, or saw smoke and assumed he perished — the obvious response would be to ask her detailed questions: what exactly did you see, when, from what distance, what happened immediately after? A careful interrogation might well reveal whether her report reflects direct observation or inference. The *Gemara* does not explain why this kind of probing examination is not the standard response, and that absence remains a notable gap in the analysis.

---

---

# Yevamot 116

## Witness Testimony Review

### Impressions vs Facts

Yesterday's discussion centered on a fundamental problem in the law of witness testimony regarding a husband's death: when a woman reports facts that would permit her to remarry, we must ask whether she is conveying concrete knowledge or merely drawing conclusions from impressions. The Gemara uses the phrase *amar bedami* to capture this concern — she may be stating as fact something she perceived or inferred, perhaps without even being fully aware that she has done so. At the same time, the Gemara acknowledges that in many cases we simply will not have all the concrete facts available to us, and that we may nonetheless be entitled to draw certain conclusions from what we do know.

### Death Cases Overview

That tension — between requiring concrete facts and permitting reasoned inference — was the backdrop for the Gemara's discussion of cases such as a drowned man pulled from the water, a charred body, and reports of death delivered by messenger. The Gemara now turns to a case that sits precisely at the intersection of these two concerns: a message was sent that Yitzchak Reish Galuta, the son of the sister of Rav Bibi, had died. The question is whether we can act on that report — and underlying it is a question about whether knowing a person's name, and knowing someone who fits that name, is sufficient context for us to conclude that the report refers to the person we know.

## Yitzchak Reish Galuta

### Identity from Name

The case itself raises an immediate puzzle. The term *reish galuta* ordinarily refers to the Exilarch, a singular political office. How, then, could there be any question about which person named Yitzchak Reish Galuta died? It seems the term may have been used more broadly to refer to regional officials of some standing, or alternatively, the title here is secondary and the identifying detail is really "the son of the sister of Rav Bibi" — yet even that description raises the question of how many individuals might fit it. The Gemara's point is precisely this: we have a name and a identifying detail, and we know someone who matches. Is that enough to allow us to act?

### Abaye vs Rava

The Gemara introduces here the foundational debate between Abaye and Rava about what level of verification is required when we have a name — and possibly identifying details — that matches a known individual. Abaye holds that we must be concerned that another person might share the same name, and we are therefore obligated to investigate. Rava holds that if we are going to take that concern seriously, we would need to search the entire world, since a person who once lived in a given city might now reside elsewhere and still match the description. That standard would be impossible to meet, and so Rava concludes there is in practice no such requirement. As a gentle gesture toward Rav Bibi's father, who had asked the question, Rava suggests that when Rabbi Yehuda Nesiah told him to investigate all of Nehardea, he did not mean it as a formal legal requirement but as a courtesy response to an honorable inquiry.

## Found Get Case

### Neharda'a Get

Abaye cites his own proof-text for his position. He says: where do I derive that we are concerned about another person with the same name? From a *get* found in Nehardea. The *get* identified the husband as Andulinay of Nehardea and named his wife. The father of Shmuel sent this *get* to Rabbi Yehuda Nesiah, the grandson of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, asking whether we must investigate to confirm there is no one else matching that description, or whether the person we already know who fits it is sufficient. Rabbi Yehuda Nesiah ruled: *tivdu Neharda'a kula* — you must check all of Nehardea. Despite knowing someone who matched the name, city, and wife's name, that is not enough; you must confirm that no one else fits the same profile.

### Abaye: Check & Eliminate

Abaye's position is thus that while verification is required, it is not an infinite regress. If one checks and finds no other candidate, the investigation has done its job. The standard is not to canvass the whole world, but to make a reasonable and thorough inquiry within the relevant community. If after that inquiry there is no competing candidate, we may proceed.

## Rava: Common Names

### Mechuza Writs

Rava brings his own proof from practice. He reports that in Mechuza, his home city, two writs of debt circulated bearing the names *Chavi bar Nanai* and *Nanai bar Chavi* — clearly very common names in that locale. It is important to clarify a point about these cases: the common names belong to the *creditors*, not to both parties. The debtor's identity was presumably unambiguous. The question was whether the individuals presenting the writs and bearing those common names could be assumed to be the genuine creditors, given that many others shared those names. Rabba bar Avua — presumably a court authority in Mechuza — allowed collection on these documents. He was not deterred by the fact that many others in the city shared the creditors' names.

## Found Get Case (II)

### Rashi: Money vs Issur

Rashi draws an explicit analogy from this *dinei mamonot* case to the domain of *issur*. His reasoning runs as follows: here we have a monetary case where we concretely know that other people share the creditor's name — *shechichi tuva*, they are very common — and yet we do not require further verification beyond the fact that the person is presenting the document. If we do not demand exhaustive verification even under those conditions in money matters, then certainly in a case of *issur* — permitting a woman to remarry — where we do not actually know of anyone else with the same name, we should not be required to investigate the entire city. The analogy is admittedly imperfect, since one could distinguish in multiple directions, but the underlying principle is that not every circumstance of a shared name triggers an obligation to search and verify.

## Rava: Common Names (II)

### Document as Testimony

Abaye, however, does not simply concede. He distinguishes the *Mechuza* case by pointing to the supporting evidence inherent in the act of *presentation*. In a case where a person presents a document bearing their name, that act of presentation is itself meaningful. The Gemara considers and eliminates several alternative explanations for how the writ might have come into the wrong hands. If we worry that the original creditor dropped it, the Gemara responds that people are careful with their financial documents. If we worry that the real creditor deposited it with someone of the same name for safekeeping, the Gemara responds that no one would be foolish enough to entrust such a document to a person who shares their own name. If we worry that the sale of the debt to this person was not legally completed, the Gemara responds: *otiyot niknot bimesirah* — documents are acquired through physical transfer, so the moment it was handed over, the sale was complete.

### Possession vs Authority

This leads to a subtle but important conceptual point, one that Tosafot makes explicit. We have a general principle in *dinei mamonot* that *chazakah mah shetachas yad adam harei hu shelo* — what a person holds is presumed to be theirs. Why, then, do we need all of these elaborate arguments to justify Abaye's position? Tosafot answers: the presumption of physical ownership covers the piece of paper itself. But a document's legal force — its capacity to function as testimony, to speak as a writ — depends on something more. For a *shtar chov* or a *get* to operate as a legal instrument, it must not merely be owned but must be *presented by the right person*, by the one to whom it testifies. The document, in this sense, does not merely sit passively in one's possession; it actively testifies on behalf of the person presenting it. That is precisely why Abaye argues that a *get* found on the street raises questions that a *get* being actively presented does not. When someone produces a writ and their name matches it, the document is engaged in an act of testimony on their behalf, and the concern about mistaken identity is substantially diminished.

## Anan bar Chiya Get

### Get from Sura

The Gemara now presents a concrete case that brings the Abaye-Rava debate into sharp relief. A *get* was found in Sura. It read: "In the city of Sura, I, Anan bar Chiya of Nehardea, have divorced my wife" — and named her. The man identified himself as Anan bar Chiya, from Nehardea, and the *get* was physically written in Sura.

### Alternative Candidate

The Rabbis conducted an investigation from Sura to Nehardea and found only one other individual named Anan bar Chiya — a man originally from a place called Chagra, but who had been residing in Nehardea. His wife's name presumably also matched. So there did exist a second person who fit the description in the *get*: his name matched, his city of residence matched (Nehardea), and his wife's name matched. However, witnesses testified that on the very day the *get* was written in Sura, this second Anan bar Chiya — the one from Chagra — had been with them in Nehardea. He was demonstrably not in Sura on the day the *get* was executed.

### Abaye: Elimination

Abaye responds: even according to my view, which requires investigation, this case presents no problem. I said you must check — and you checked. You found one other candidate, and you were able to eliminate him. Witnesses confirm he was in Nehardea on the day in question. *Ma ba'ei b'Sura?* — what would he be doing in Sura on that day? The investigation was done properly, a potential competing candidate was identified and eliminated, and therefore we may proceed.

### Rava: Concrete Doubt

Rava, characteristically, takes the opposite position. Even according to his general view that we are not concerned about other people with the same name, here — where a concrete second candidate has actually been identified — the concern becomes real and cannot simply be waved away. The very fact of investigation has introduced a concrete doubt where none existed before. And as for the evidence that the second candidate was in Nehardea that day: *dilma begamla parcha azal* — perhaps he traveled by some extraordinarily fast means and arrived in Sura in time. The point seems almost deliberately absurd, and indeed Rashi and Tosafot note that this likely refers to some form of miraculous transport or *sheid*. The argument appears to be that once a concrete alternative exists, even logically implausible explanations cannot fully dispel the doubt.

### Mili Masar

The Gemara then offers a third and considerably more reasonable possibility for Rava's concern: *mili masar* — it is not necessary for the husband to be physically present in the place where the *get* is written. The *get* names the city in which it is being executed, not the city where the husband issued his instructions. Rav Safra and Rav Huna both taught this explicitly to scribes: if you are sitting in Shili writing a *get* but the husband gave you instructions while in Hini, you write Shili as the place of the *get*. And conversely, if you are in Hini when the husband spoke to you in Shili, you write Hini. The language of the *get* is in the first person — "I, so-and-so, divorce my wife" — but the place recorded is the scribe's location, not the husband's. Therefore, the fact that the *get* says it was written in Sura does not tell us anything about where Anan bar Chiya himself actually was. The second candidate need not have traveled to Sura at all — his instructions could have been transmitted to a scribe who happened to be writing in Sura. This makes Rava's concern not only plausible but quite rational.

## Sesame Seeds Recap

### Apply Standards

The Gemara then returns to a case that had been set aside — the case involving sesame seeds. Rav Yeimar rules *lo chaishinan* — we are not concerned. Rav Ashi rules *chaishinan* — we are concerned. And the *halachah* follows Rav Ashi: we are concerned. This conclusion is reached in what is effectively a *mammonot* context, one with perhaps fewer identifying marks than some of the other cases. The broader point is that all of these cases — the *get*, the death report, the drowned body, the writ of debt — are variations on a common set of questions about what level of identification is required, what kinds of evidence are sufficient, and at what point we may conclude that a report or document refers to a specific known individual. The cases are not necessarily governed by a single rule, and the standards likely vary depending on numerous factors: the number and specificity of identifying marks, whether there is supporting evidence, whether we concretely know of another candidate, and whether the domain is *mamonot* or *issur*.

### Sesame Seeds

One correction to what was said previously: the case at issue involves sesame seeds, not sunflower seeds. Sesame seeds are in any case likely the more valuable commodity.

## Ketata Quarreling

### Ketata Definition

The Mishnah had mentioned two scenarios in which a woman's report of her husband's death is not believed: when there is a state of war (*milchama*) in the world, and when there is *ketata* — fighting — between husband and wife. The war scenario raises concerns about the fog of war and misperception; the *ketata* scenario raises a different set of concerns. The Gemara now asks: *heichi dami ketata*? What constitutes *ketata* in practice? Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says: she tells her husband "divorce me" — *garsheni*. The Gemara objects: *kulan nami amru hachi* — all women say this in the heat of argument. Rashi explains that this is a common expression of frustration. The Gemara therefore clarifies: the operative case is not that she says "divorce me" but that she goes about telling people "*gerashtani*" — "my husband has already divorced me." She is publicly claiming to be divorced even though she has no *get* and even though we know it is not true.

At that point, the Gemara raises a further question: if she is publicly claiming to be divorced, why not simply believe her about the divorce itself, based on the ruling of Rav Hamnuna? Rav Hamnuna held that a woman who tells her husband to his face that he has already divorced her is believed, on the principle that *ein isha me'iza paneiha bifnei baalah* — a woman would not be so brazen as to say this to her husband's face unless it were true. The Gemara resolves this by establishing a more specific case: she said she was divorced in front of named witnesses — Reuven and Shimon — and when those witnesses were asked, they said it never happened. She is thus a confirmed fabricator of the divorce claim, yet she does not have a *get*. This very fact — that she is publicly asserting a fictional divorce — demonstrates that she has emotionally and psychologically exited the marriage, and it is this posture that disqualifies her subsequent report of his death from being credited.

### Lying vs Misinterpretati…

The Gemara presents two distinct rationales for why *ketata* undermines credibility. Rav Chanina says: *mishum de'meshakra* — because she will intentionally lie. Rav Shimi bar Ashi says: *mishum de'amra bedidami* — not because she is deliberately deceptive, but because her emotional state colors her perception. She would like her husband to be dead, and so she interprets ambiguous or incomplete evidence in that direction, unconsciously constructing a narrative of his death from vague impressions. Tosafot raises the obvious question: if the *ketata* case involves a woman who has already been proven to lie — she claimed a divorce that witnesses denied — why does the Gemara need a separate explanation about unconscious misinterpretation? She is already a confirmed liar.

### Blame Shifts Concern

The distinction between the two rationales becomes practically significant at the top of 27b, where the Gemara introduces the case in which *he* is to blame for the fighting — *adal hu ketata*. If it is clear that the husband's behavior is driving the conflict, that she is not seeking to leave the marriage but is being mistreated within it, then the concern about intentional lying is substantially reduced. She demonstrably wants to remain married and has no motive to fabricate his death. However, the concern about unconscious misinterpretation — *bedidami* — remains. Even if she would not deliberately lie, the ongoing difficulty and pain of the marriage might still unconsciously influence how she reads ambiguous information about his fate.

Tosafot addresses the apparent contradiction: if we know she has already lied — she made a false divorce claim — why don't we conclude she is a confirmed liar and disbelieve her regardless of who is to blame? Tosafot answers: lying about a divorce is one thing, but falsely claiming her husband is dead is another matter entirely. An earlier *perek* catalogued the severe consequences that fall upon a woman who claims her husband is dead, remarries, and is then confronted with his return. A woman would not be willing to expose herself to those consequences — losing both the first and second husband, and bearing children of uncertain status — merely to escape a marriage in which the husband is at fault. She would not go that far in her deception when she knows he bears the blame. So the concern narrows to unconscious misinterpretation, not intentional lying, in the case where he is responsible.

## Ed Echad Ketata

### Third Party Credibility

The Gemara now asks the parallel question it had asked regarding *milchama*: what if the report of the husband's death comes not from the wife herself but from an objective third-party witness — an *ed echad*? In the *milchama* context, the value of an outside witness was not obvious, since the fog of war affects everyone's perceptions. Here, by contrast, the concern about *ketata* is specifically tied to the wife's emotional state and her relationship with her husband. A third party has none of that emotional involvement. Should an *ed echad* be believed straightforwardly when there is a known *ketata*?

### Two Theories

The answer depends on which underlying theory explains why an *ed echad* is believed in the first place when testifying to a husband's death. The first theory: *milta de'avida le-igluya lo meshaker* — a person will not lie about something that will eventually come to light. If the husband is alive, he will show up, and the false testimony will be exposed. Under this theory, an outside witness in a *ketata* situation should indeed be believed; his concern about being found out is entirely independent of the state of the marriage. The second theory: *hi dayka u'minsava* — the reason we trust an *ed echad* is that we rely on the wife's own careful investigation before she acts on the testimony. She knows the consequences of remarrying incorrectly, and so she will rigorously verify the report before proceeding. The *ed echad*'s testimony is thus only valid in combination with the wife's backup diligence.

### Teiku Unresolved

Under the second theory, the case of *ketata* presents a real problem. *Ve-hacha keivan de-is lah ketata lo dayka* — since the marriage is in turmoil, she is not going to exercise careful, sober investigation. She is motivated, consciously or not, to accept the report and act on it without the diligent scrutiny that ordinarily backs up the *ed echad*'s testimony. The Gemara leaves this unresolved: *teiku*.

## Modern Applications

### War & Tragedy

The practical stakes of this unresolved question are significant. The concepts of *ketata* and *milchama* have very broad potential application. Many of the most devastating human catastrophes — wars, terrorist attacks, building collapses, plane disasters — fall into the category of *milchama*-type scenarios. And marriages, particularly under conditions of stress and tragedy, are not always in a state of tranquility. The *teiku* on *ed echad* in a *ketata* situation means that in precisely those circumstances where testimony is most urgently needed, its admissibility may be in doubt.

### Agunah Solutions

This directly affects the scope of the rabbinic solutions to the *agunah* problem. The leniencies that the Sages developed over centuries to permit women to remarry when their husbands' deaths cannot be formally established depend heavily on the credibility of *ed echad* testimony and on the woman's own report. If *ketata* limits even third-party testimony, and if *milchama* scenarios are broadly defined, then the practical availability of these solutions is substantially curtailed. There is an extensive literature of responsa dealing with precisely these questions — following the Holocaust, after 9/11, and in other mass-casualty events — and the *poskim* have had to navigate all of these considerations with enormous care.

## Rabbi Yehuda Stringent

### Mourning Signs

Against this backdrop, the Mishnah records the view of Rabbi Yehuda, who applies a more stringent standard across the board: *le'olam ein ne'emenet* — she is never believed without additional corroboration, regardless of whether it is wartime or peacetime and regardless of the state of the marriage. Specifically, Rabbi Yehuda requires that the woman exhibit visible signs of mourning — torn garments, weeping, and other outward expressions of grief — before her testimony about her husband's death will be credited.

### Smart vs Foolish

The Sages respond with a straightforward objection: *de'varecha pike'achas tinasei, shotah lo tinasei* — according to your position, a clever woman who knows how to perform grief convincingly will be permitted to remarry, while a simple woman who does not know to stage a display will not. That is an arbitrary and unjust standard. The Sages therefore conclude: *achas zu ve'achas zu tinasei* — whether she is shrewd or not, if the facts support her claim, she may remarry.

### Woman Coached Act

The Gemara then records an illustrative incident. A woman came before Rabbi Yehuda's court — which required these outward signs of mourning — and the people around her coached her in advance. They told her: before you walk in, eulogize your husband, rend your garments, loosen your hair, and then enter and tell Rabbi Yehuda what happened.

### Coaching Falsification

The Gemara asks: did they thereby teach her to falsify evidence — *afu'ei shikra*? The Gemara answers no. Those who coached her held like the Sages, not like Rabbi Yehuda: in their view, she was fully believable even without the dramatic display. Rabbi Yehuda's requirement was, in their opinion, an artificial condition not demanded by law. When they coached her to perform the display, they were not teaching her to lie but rather helping her satisfy what they considered to be an illegitimate technical hurdle in order to reach what they believed was the correct halachic outcome. The discomfort remains — there is something troubling about the entire episode, a kind of *limdu leshonam davar sheker* — but the Gemara accepts the explanation as technically exculpatory.

## Beis Hillel Principle

### Major Innovation

We now reach the foundational principle that underlies this entire *perek*: the rule that a woman is believed to report her husband's death and may on that basis remarry. This is a striking *chiddush* on multiple levels. Ordinarily, a woman's testimony is not accepted in the same way as a man's, and certainly one would not expect a *nogea badavar* — a party with a personal interest in the outcome — to be credited. Yet here the Sages introduced exactly that rule: the wife's own testimony about her husband's death suffices to permit remarriage. This principle had already been assumed in earlier *perakim* of the tractate, which discussed the consequences when a woman remarried on the basis of such testimony and the husband later appeared. But the principle itself is introduced and established here.

### Beis Hillel Limited

Interestingly, it is Beis Hillel who initially takes the more restrictive position. They rule: *lo shama'nu ela be-va min ha-katzir u've-otah medinah ke-ma'aseh she-hayah* — we have only heard this leniency as applying to the specific type of case that served as the original precedent. That precedent involved a woman returning from the grain harvest, reporting that her husband died, and the death occurring in the same locale — not in a distant country. Beis Hillel holds that the leniency cannot be extended beyond those parameters: the same type of agricultural work, the same local setting.

### Beis Shammai Object

Beis Shammai responds that this level of specificity is untenable. They ask: does it matter whether she came from the wheat harvest or the olive harvest or the grape harvest? Is the type of agricultural work actually relevant? And does it matter whether the death occurred locally or in a distant country? The principle behind the leniency, they argue, has nothing to do with those particulars; they appeared in the original case by historical accident. *Lo dibru chachamim ba-katzir ela ba-hoveh* — the Sages spoke of the harvest because that was the circumstance that happened, not because the harvest is legally significant.

## Generalize Case

### Reductio Ad Absurdum

Beis Shammai's argument is a *reductio ad absurdum*. If Beis Hillel insists on replicating the original case's details, then the leniency should apply only to wheat — *katzir chittim* — and not even to barley harvest. And should it extend only to grain and not to olive-picking, date-gathering, grape-harvesting, or any other form of agricultural work? Since Beis Hillel would surely agree that the type of crop is irrelevant, they must concede that at least *some* abstraction beyond the literal original case is required. And once that concession is made, Beis Shammai asks, why stop at the type of harvest? Why not also generalize with respect to geography?

### Local vs Distant

Beis Hillel, however, does not concede equally on both points. They hold that while the type of agricultural work is indeed irrelevant — that much they grant — the distinction between a local death and a distant one is substantive. When the death occurs locally — *be-otah medinah de-shchichi inshi* — people are present, people who know the husband and wife, and if the husband is alive, the lie will quickly be exposed. That social visibility is a real deterrent to false testimony. When the death is reported from a distant country — *de-la shchichi inshi* — no one there knows them, and the woman could plausibly lie without discovery. *Mirtata* — she is afraid to lie when she is locally known; *la mirtata* — she is not similarly afraid when the event occurred far away where no one recognizes them.

### Caravans Counter

Beis Shammai counters: *hachi nami shchichi shayarta* — there are caravans, there is regular travel and commerce between cities and countries, and the facts will surface regardless of distance. Word travels. The threat of exposure is not meaningfully diminished merely because the death occurred in a distant place.

### Hillel Concedes

Ultimately, Beis Hillel concedes and rules like Beis Shammai, accepting the broader generalization. This concession is significant — it is one of the relatively rare instances where Beis Hillel acknowledges that Beis Shammai's reasoning is compelling and reverses course.

## Original Case

### Snake Bite Case

The Gemara then identifies the original case that gave rise to this entire body of law. Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel reports: it was the end of the wheat harvest season, and ten men went out to harvest wheat. A snake bit one of them, and he died.

### Investigation Confirmed

His wife came and reported the death to the *beis din*. The court did not simply accept her word; *veshalchu umatzu kidvareha* — they investigated and found her account to be accurate. There was independent corroboration. What is notable, given that ten people were present at the scene, is that it was specifically the wife who came to report to the *beis din*. And it is equally notable that despite the availability of corroborating witnesses, the case led the Sages to establish a principle based on the wife's testimony.

### Remarriage Principle

One possible reading of the Gemara's thinking: the Sages found themselves asking what would have happened had the corroboration not been available. What if there had been no surviving witnesses, or they were inaccessible? Would the woman have been left without remedy? That hypothetical seems to have prompted the more general principle. Having confirmed through investigation that this woman told the truth, the Sages extrapolated to establish the rule: *ha-isha she-amrah meis ba'ali tinasei* — a woman who says her husband has died may remarry. And similarly, she may enter into *yibum*. The principle was crystallized from a concrete, verified case and then extended as a general rule.

## Parah Adumah

### Prohibition Rules

The Gemara introduces a parallel case from a seemingly unrelated area of law to analyze the question of when we generalize from a concrete case and when we confine a ruling to its original circumstances. The *Braisa* teaches a series of prohibitions relating to the transport of the ashes and water of the *parah adumah*: one may not carry *mei chatas* and *efer chatas* — the purification water and ashes — and take them across the Jordan River, whether by boat, by throwing them from one bank to the other, by floating them on a raft, or by carrying them on the back of an animal or a person who is not standing with feet on the ground. However, it is permitted to carry them over a bridge, since the bridge is connected to the earth. And this applies to the Jordan and to all other rivers alike.

### Narrow View

Rabbi Chanina ben Akiva disagrees. He rules: *lo amru ela Yarden u'vesfinah* — the prohibition was stated only regarding the Jordan River, and only in a boat. Not other rivers, and not other means of crossing. His principle is *ke-ma'aseh she-hayah* — like the case in which it occurred. The ruling is limited to the precise parameters of the original incident.

### Broad View

The *Rabbanan* take the broader view: once the prohibition is established for the Jordan and for boats, it extends to all rivers and all methods of crossing that share the relevant characteristics.

## Generalize vs Limit

### Logic Purpose

The Gemara now analyzes whether the debate of Rabbi Chanina ben Akiva and the *Rabbanan* maps onto the debate of Beis Hillel and Beis Shammai, and what principles govern when to generalize and when to limit. The *Rabbanan* could say: even we, who generalize here, would not necessarily generalize in all cases. In the case of the woman's testimony about her husband's death, Beis Hillel initially did limit the ruling. But there was a clear reason Beis Hillel ultimately conceded and expanded: the rationale for believing the woman is *mirtata* — she fears exposure, she fears the consequences — and that rationale applies equally in all circumstances. There is an identifiable logic underlying the leniency, and because that logic applies broadly, the rule can be extended broadly.

### No Logic Limits

Here, with the *parah adumah* transfer prohibition, there is no such clear logic. Why should carrying *mei chatas* over a river on a boat be prohibited? There is no obvious reason that such transport is inherently problematic for the sanctity or purity of the ashes. The prohibition exists because something went wrong once — it is a *gezerah*, a rabbinic response to an event. And since there is no clear underlying logic, there is no principled basis for extending it beyond the specific circumstances of that event. Rabbi Chanina ben Akiva's view that we confine it to *ke-ma'aseh she-hayah* reflects exactly this principle: without a rationale to drive abstraction, we stay with the concrete.

### Corpse Incident

The original incident was this: someone was transporting *mei chatas* and *efer chatas* across the Jordan in a boat, and *nimtza kezayis min ha-mes tachuv b'karkisa shel sefinah* — a piece of a human corpse, the size of an olive, was found lodged in the hull of the boat. That corpse piece rendered the contents of the boat *tamei*, contaminating the ashes. The Sages responded immediately — *b'otah sha'ah amru* — and prohibited this practice. But the prohibition was a reaction to a specific accident, not derived from a general principle.

### Woman vs Parah

Rabbi Chanina ben Akiva, conversely, could explain why he does not apply Beis Shammai's logic in the *parah adumah* case even while Beis Shammai generalizes in the woman's case. The reason Beis Shammai generalizes there is *dayka u'minsava* — there is always a structural logic at work: the woman will investigate carefully before acting, and the prospect of exposure will deter false testimony across all circumstances. That logic provides a principled basis for abstraction. In the *parah adumah* case, there is simply no equivalent logic. *Mishum ma'aseh she-hayah b'Yarden u'vesfinah d'hava ma'aseh gazru rabbanan* — the Rabbanan issued their prohibition because of that specific event. *B'she'ar naharos d'lo hava ma'aseh lo gazru rabbanan* — for other rivers, where no such event occurred, there is no basis for the *gezerah* to apply. The rule should therefore remain as narrow as its origin. In the case of the woman's testimony, there is a reason we want to extend the leniency broadly: we want her to be able to remarry, there is a rationale supporting the rule's application in all circumstances, and therefore we generalize. In the case of *parah adumah*, we have no such driving rationale and no logic compelling extension, and so we limit.

# Yevamot 117

## Shammai vs. Hillel

### Ketubah Collection

The daf opens in the middle of a running discussion about the foundational *chiddush* of *Chazal*: the willingness to believe a woman who testifies that her husband died, enabling her to remarry. This innovation arose from a specific historical scenario involving a husband who died during the wheat harvest, and it generated a remarkable debate in which *Beis Shammai* took the more lenient position. The *mishnah* on 117b records another such debate — again, with *Beis Shammai* on the side of leniency.

*Beis Shammai omrim tinasei v'sitol kesubasah*: once she is permitted to remarry, she may also collect her *kesubah* from her husband's estate. *Beis Hillel omrim tinasei v'lo tital kesubasah*: they are prepared to believe her testimony for purposes of personal status and remarriage, but not to allow her to collect from the estate. The concern is not only one of testimonial weight. There is a secondary worry that allowing monetary collection alongside remarriage makes the entire arrangement more attractive — not merely liberating her from the *agunah* situation, but providing a financial incentive that could color, whether consciously or unconsciously, the quality of her testimony.

### Shammai Package Deal

*Beis Shammai* presses back: *hishvitem ervah chamurah v'lo nakil mamon hakal?* You have already crossed the far more serious threshold — releasing her from the prohibition of *ervah*, treating her as no longer a married woman, permitting her to marry another man — and yet you refuse to cross what should be the easier threshold of monetary collection? *Beis Shammai*'s argument is that the permissive ruling on *ervah* and the permissive ruling on *mamon* are a package deal. If she is believed enough to remarry, she is believed enough to collect.

### Hillel Brothers Inherit

*Beis Hillel* responds with a striking argument: *matzinu she-ein ha-achim nichnasin lenachalah al piha* — we find that the brothers cannot enter into the inheritance on the basis of her testimony alone. This concession, made by *Beis Shammai* themselves, demonstrates that her belief is not across-the-board. If her testimony constituted genuine *eidus* in the full sense, the brothers — or father, or other heirs — would be entitled to divide the estate on that basis. But take that testimony to a court handling inheritance and they will demand proper witnesses; a single woman's testimony does not constitute the standard of proof required for probate. The fact that *Beis Shammai* agrees on this point shows that her believability is context-specific.

### Status vs. Monetary

What emerges is a clean distinction: her testimony is accepted in the context of the court adjudicating her personal status — whether she is a widow permitted to remarry — but not in a separate court case concerning the distribution of her husband's estate. *Beis Hillel* carries this logic further: if the testimony is not universal but court-specific, then even within the domain of personal status, one can distinguish between her status as a widow permitted to remarry and her status as a widow entitled to collect her *kesubah*. These are two different claims, even if they often travel together.

### Ketubah Text

*Beis Shammai* offers a textual counter: *v'lo mi-sefer kesubah nilmod?* Can we not learn the package-deal nature of the ruling from the *kesubah* document itself? The language of the *kesubah* as they understood it reads: *she-im tinasei le-acher titali mah she-kasuv lichi* — if you remarry someone else, you are entitled to collect what is written for you. The *kesubah* itself thus ties the permission to remarry to the right to collect, making them inseparable. When her testimony is accepted in family court, the *kesubah*'s own language makes the monetary entitlement a built-in consequence. The probate court is a separate matter — that testimony remains irrelevant there — but within the framework of her own status and remarriage, the *kesubah* creates the package.

### Hillel Concedes

*Ve'chozru Beis Hillel le'horot k'divrei Beis Shammai* — and *Beis Hillel* reversed their ruling and held in accordance with *Beis Shammai*. Even they ultimately acknowledged that once the *kesubah*'s own language creates this connection, the monetary collection follows from the permitted remarriage. The two cannot be separated when the very document at the center of the case binds them together.

The *Gemara* adds a related ruling from Rav Chisda: if the *yevamah* performs *yibum* with her brother-in-law, he enters into the inheritance on her account — *nichnas lenachalah al piha* — because the inheritance in that case is not a separate proceeding but flows directly from his status as one who has performed *yibum* and thereby stepped into his brother's role. The *Torah* itself says *yakum al shem achiv*: he shall stand in his brother's name, and with that comes the estate.

### Ketubah Derash

The *Gemara* then comments that *Beis Hillel* and *Beis Shammai* essentially treated the language of the *kesubah* as quasi-scriptural — *heim darshu midrash ketubah* — subjecting it to the same kind of textual analysis one applies to *pesukim*. The *Gemara* uses this as an occasion to note that we, too, can do *midrash pesukim*, and the *pasuk yakum al shem achiv* allows us to derive that the estate passes with the act of *yibum*.

A *Tosafos* cited in this context notes that the approach of doing *midrash ketubah* — treating the *kesubah*'s precise phrasing as determinative — is characterized in the *Gemara* in *Kesubot* as a *Beis Shammai* methodology. *Beis Hillel* does not generally engage in *midrash ketubah*. The broader question of what it means to treat a contractual document with the kind of textual weight one accords to Scripture — giving decisive weight to precise formulation rather than seeking intent or context — is a topic that will be developed extensively when the learning reaches *Maseches Kesubot*.

---

## Rav Nachman Intent

### Two Scenarios

Rav Nachman introduces a crucial procedural distinction. When a woman comes to *beit din* and says *meis ba'ali — hiteiruni lehinasay* — "my husband died, permit me to remarry" — the ruling follows naturally: *matirin osah lehinasay v'nosnim lah kesubasah*, we permit her to remarry and she receives her *kesubah*. The intent is clear, the case is framed in the domain of personal status, and the *kesubah* follows as a package.

But now suppose she comes to *beit din* and says *tenu li kesubasi* — give me my *kesubah* — without expressing any interest in remarriage. In that case, Rav Nachman rules: *af lehinasay ein matirin osah* — not only do we not give her the *kesubah*, we do not even permit her to remarry. The reason is *ada'ata de'kesubah asai* — she came with the intention of collecting the *kesubah*. She has framed her case as a monetary claim.

### Wrong Courtroom

Rashi's explanation is precise: *uva'afokei mamona sahadusa ba'inan* — when the case is about extracting money, we require formal *eidus*. This is not primarily a suspicion that she is lying or manipulating the system in order to collect. Rather, she has walked into the wrong courtroom. The door she entered is the door of *dinei mamonos*, and in that courtroom the standard of proof is full testimony. The special rabbinic dispensation that allows her single testimony to carry weight was created for the domain of personal status — the family-court door, so to speak — not the civil-court door of monetary claims.

### Locked In

This raises the obvious question: why can she not simply close that door and open the other one? The *sugya* strongly implies that she cannot — that once she has framed the case as a monetary claim, she is locked into that framing. The ruling does not suggest that we send her home, tell her to come back and say the right words, and then grant both permissions. She appears to be stuck. This is a striking and somewhat troubling feature of the analysis, given the lengths to which the rabbis went in creating the *agunah* dispensation in the first place. It is worth noting that the *Gemara* need not have gone down this path at all.

---

## Simultaneous Claims

### Both Together

The *Gemara* then raises the *ibaya*: what if she demands both simultaneously — *hiteiruni lehinasay v'tenu li ketubati*, "permit me to remarry and give me my *kesubah*"? Two possible readings present themselves. On one reading, the mere mention of *kesubah* signals that this is a *kesubah* case — *kivun de'amra ketubati, da'ata de'kesubah avda*. On the other reading, people simply put all their claims before the court at once — *kol milei de'is lei inshi amru lah le'beit dina* — and since she opened with the marriage claim, the case is framed accordingly.

### Order Matters

If the first formulation leaves some ambiguity, the *Gemara* then poses a starker scenario: she says *tenu li ketubati v'hiteiruni lehinasay* — she leads with the *kesubah* and follows with the request to remarry. Here, the *Gemara* suggests, she has *vadai* framed it as a *kesubah* case — *hecha vadai da'ata de'kesubah avda*.

### Ignorance Defense

Yet the *Gemara* raises a counterargument: *ho'il v'lo yad'a be-mai mistaryah* — perhaps she simply did not know through what mechanism she would be permitted to remarry. People commonly misunderstand procedure. Perhaps she mentioned the *kesubah* because she believed, based on popular misapprehension, that submitting the *kesubah* was part of the process of obtaining permission to remarry — *shem kasabra hu she-zo hatartah*. Her fundamental interest is in being freed to marry again, and her mention of the *kesubah* reflects a procedural misunderstanding, not an intention to frame the case as monetary.

---

## Rav Nachman Intent (II)

### Agunah Concern

This is where the *sugya* becomes genuinely troubling, and it deserves to be flagged directly. The entire enterprise of believing a woman's testimony about her husband's death was built on the extraordinary concern for the *agunah* — the rabbis went to remarkable lengths, departing from ordinary evidentiary standards, in order not to leave women bound and unable to remarry. And yet here, that entire protection becomes precarious based on how she phrases her opening words to *beit din*. If she says the wrong thing — if she mentions her *kesubah* first, or even mentions it alongside her request to remarry — the door may slam shut entirely, leaving her not merely without the *kesubah* but without permission to remarry at all.

One could have constructed the ruling differently and with far less severity. The *Gemara* could have said: if she frames it as a *kesubah* case, we deny the *kesubah* on those grounds but still permit her to remarry on the basis of her testimony. That would have been a coherent and far less punishing result. The *Gemara* instead makes it sound as if the wrong framing locks her out of everything. The practical implication — one the *Gemara* does not shy away from — is that she desperately needs good legal counsel before she ever opens her mouth in front of *beit din*. Indeed, the role of the *to'ein rabbani* in contemporary rabbinic courts exists in part precisely for this reason.

The *Gemara* does raise the possibility that a *drasha* on the *kesubah* language may be involved in all of this — a theme, as *Tosafos* notes, that connects to debates in *Maseches Kesubot* about whether *midrash kesubah* is a legitimate methodology and whose position it actually reflects.

---

## Who Testifies

### Seven Excluded

The *mishnah* now turns to a different dimension of the same subject: who may testify that a husband has died? The general rule, *hakol ne'emanim le'ha'idah*, is that all are believed to testify on her behalf. The exceptions, however, form a defined list: *chutz me'chamotah* — all are believed with the exception of her mother-in-law; and the mother-in-law's daughter (*bas chamotah*), meaning the husband's sister on the mother's side; her *tzarah* (co-wife); her *yevamah* (husband's brother's wife); and her *bas ba'alah* (stepdaughter). The *mishnah* also notes the distinction from the parallel ruling in *Gittin*: these same women are believed to deliver a *get* from the husband, because *she-ha-ksav mochiach* — the signed document itself provides the verification that makes their delivery reliable. Oral testimony about death is an entirely different matter.

The underlying logic of the exclusion list is that these are women who may have reason to hate the wife — and specifically, who might lie not out of a desire to help her but in order to set a trap. If she remarries on the strength of false testimony and the husband subsequently reappears, she suffers the devastating consequences that the earlier chapters of the tractate describe. The excluded witnesses, on this reading, are women whose animosity toward the wife makes them capable of engineering precisely that outcome.

### Mother-in-Law

The mother-in-law's hostility toward her daughter-in-law is easy to characterize in personal terms — no one is ever quite good enough for her son. But the *Gemara* locates a less personal and more economically grounded motive as well. Property that the wife brought into the marriage will pass to the husband and, upon his death, may ultimately leave the family entirely, enriching the daughter-in-law rather than remaining within the husband's family of origin. The mother-in-law thus has both emotional and financial reasons to bear the wife ill will.

### Co-Wife

The *tzarah*'s motive is the most direct: she is in direct competition with the wife. If she testifies that the husband died and the wife remarries on that basis, and the husband subsequently returns alive, the wife will be forced out of the marriage and the *tzarah* will remain as the sole wife. She has everything to gain from the wife's downfall and nothing to lose from testifying falsely.

### Brother's Wife

The *yevamah* — the wife of the husband's brother — presents a paradoxical situation. Her concern is that if the husband dies without children, her own husband will be obligated to perform *yibum* with the wife, making the wife a co-wife in her household. One might think she would therefore want to testify that the husband is alive and thus prevent the *yibum* scenario from ever arising. In fact, the *Gemara* suggests the opposite dynamic: she may reason that it is better to trigger the *yibum* now, on her own terms, in the hope that the husband will turn up alive shortly thereafter — at which point the *yibum* marriage would be invalidated and the threat would be permanently eliminated. There is thus an ironic quality to her testimony: she is hastening the very outcome she fears, gambling that it will be only temporary. Nevertheless, her interest is compromised, and she is excluded.

### Stepdaughter

The stepdaughter's exclusion requires little explanation. The animosity between a stepdaughter and her stepmother — the wife in question — is presumed and obvious. She has no motivation to assist the woman who has, in her view, taken her mother's place.

### Husband's Sister

The husband's sister on the mother's side (*bas chamotah*) is excluded because she absorbs her mother's animosity. The mother-in-law hates the daughter-in-law; the mother-in-law's daughter learns and adopts that attitude. *Hi nami sanyah lah* — she too comes to hate her. The animus is personal, inherited from the household atmosphere created by the mother.

### Father's Side Sister

The *Gemara* then raises a *ibaya*: what about the husband's sister on the *father's* side — *bas chamiv* — who has a different mother entirely? Here the mother-in-law's personal hatred does not enter the picture, since there is no shared mother to transmit it. Does the exclusion still apply?

Two possible reasons for the exclusion of the husband's sister are offered. The first grounds it entirely in the personal, matrilineal transmission of hatred: *mishum de'ika ima desanya lah* — it is because there is a mother who hates her, and *hi nami sanyah lah* — the daughter adopts it. On this reading, a sister with a different mother would *not* be excluded. The second grounds it in a financial concern that applies regardless of which side of the family: the sister feels that the wife is consuming the fruits of her family's labor — *ka'akhla li legeisana* — that property from her family is passing out through the marriage and will end up in the hands of this woman. On this reading, whether the family wealth at issue came from the mother or the father makes no difference; the animosity exists either way, and the exclusion applies to *bas chamiv* as well.

The *Gemara* notes in passing that the term *bei nasha* — which appears in the phrase *geisana de'bei nasha*, referring to the toil of the father's household in the *bas chamiv* scenario — is an interesting locution. Normally *bei nasha* refers to the mother's side of the family, the side that tends to be forgotten in a patriarchal system (related to the root of *nashani*, "He has caused me to forget"). It can also appear in the formulary of a *kesubah* when the property brought into the marriage comes from the mother's house rather than the father's. Its appearance here as a reference to the father's household is somewhat unusual and the precise usage remains worth examining more carefully.

The *sugya* does not resolve the question conclusively; it ends with the observation that once we understand the financial motive to be the operative concern, *lo shena bas chamotah v'lo shana bas chamiv* — it makes no difference which side the sister is from. The companion *braisa* that lists five excluded women (rather than the *mishnah*'s implicit listing) is reconciled by treating the two types of husband's sister as one category, since the underlying logic subsumes both.

---

## Yehudah Additions

### Implicit Reverses

The *Gemara* cites the view that a *braisa* reflects the position of Rabbi Yehudah: *Rabbi Yehuda mosif af eshet av v'ha-kallah* — Rabbi Yehudah adds the stepmother and the daughter-in-law to the list of those who may not testify. The Sages respond that these cases are already implied by the reverse relationships listed in the *mishnah*. If the *mishnah* already excludes the stepdaughter from testifying about her stepmother, then by symmetry the stepmother cannot testify about the stepdaughter. Similarly, if the mother-in-law cannot testify about the daughter-in-law, the daughter-in-law cannot testify about the mother-in-law. There is no need to enumerate them separately.

### Explicit Listing

Rabbi Yehudah maintains that the reverse relationships are not obvious and must be stated explicitly. In the case of the mother-in-law and daughter-in-law, *bishlama chamotah tanya* — we understand perfectly well why the mother-in-law hates the daughter-in-law: *d'amrah ka'achlah l'girsana'i* — she feels the daughter-in-law is consuming the fruits of her labor, or simply that nobody is good enough for her son. But *kallah mai ta'ama sanyah l'chamotah?* — what reason does the daughter-in-law have to hate her mother-in-law? That requires an explanation, and since the animosity runs in a less obvious direction, the exclusion must be stated independently.

Similarly, *bishlama bas ba'al d'sanyah l'eshet av* — we understand why a stepdaughter hates her stepmother: *d'amrah ka'achlah l'girsana'i d'immi* — she feels this woman is consuming the property her mother brought into the estate. But *eshet av mai ta'ama sanyah l'bat ba'al?* — what does the stepmother have against the stepdaughter? That too is not obvious, and therefore Rabbi Yehudah must list it explicitly rather than relying on an implied reverse.

### Secrets Exposed

The *Gemara* then provides Rabbi Yehudah's reasoning. Why does a daughter-in-law hate her mother-in-law? *D'megalya l'vnah kol d'avdah* — because the mother-in-law sees everything that goes on in the house and reports it to her son. The daughter-in-law feels that her private life is exposed, that her faults and failings are being narrated to her husband by his mother, and she therefore comes to bear the mother-in-law deep animosity. This is not a financial concern but an entirely domestic one — the fear of surveillance and of being badmouthed in one's own marriage.

### Stepmother Parallel

The same logic explains the stepmother's animosity toward the stepdaughter: *d'megalya l'aviah kol d'avdah* — the stepdaughter sees everything the stepmother does in the household and will report it to her father, the stepmother's husband. Just as the daughter-in-law fears being exposed to her husband through his mother, so the stepmother fears being exposed to her husband through his daughter. Once this dynamic is spelled out, Rabbi Yehudah's logic becomes clear: neither of these hostilities is intuitive, so both must be stated.

### Water Reflects

The Sages respond with a principle: *kamayim hapanim lapanim ken lev ha'adam la'adam* — as water reflects a face back to the one looking into it, so the heart of one person reflects back the feelings of another. The principle is that animosity is reciprocal by nature: if A bears animosity toward B, B will come to bear animosity toward A, even without a specific practical trigger. Once the *mishnah* establishes that the mother-in-law may not testify — thereby acknowledging that there is animosity running from mother-in-law to daughter-in-law — the reciprocal animosity is automatic, and no separate ruling is needed to establish that the daughter-in-law cannot testify either.

Rabbi Yehudah demurs: *hahu b'divrei Torah ketiv* — that verse is written about words of Torah, meaning that if you invest your heart in Torah you will receive back in kind. It does not describe the general psychology of interpersonal relationships, and one cannot derive from it a principle that all animosity is automatically reciprocal.

---

## Future Mother-in-Law

### Not Yet MIL
