A question was raised in *Eretz Yisrael* (*ba'u b'ma'arava*): what is the status of a *chamotah haba'ah l'achar mikan* — a future mother-in-law? How can there be such a thing? The scenario involves *yibum*: a woman's husband is absent or has died, and there exists a brother-in-law whose mother would, in the event of *yibum*, become the woman's mother-in-law. That brother-in-law's mother is thus a *potential* future mother-in-law. The question is whether such a woman is already in the category of those excluded from testifying, or whether since she has no actual present relationship of animosity, she may testify.

*Mi mapka da'atah d'nasva v'naflah kamei yavam v'sanyah lah?* — Is this future mother-in-law already anticipating the possibility that this woman will fall before her son for *yibum*, and has she begun to hate her preemptively? Is she, so to speak, getting a head start on the inevitable animosity?

### Both Die Case

The *Gemara* brings a *ta shema* from a related ruling. If a woman comes and says: "My husband died, and then my father-in-law died" — both men having been away together, say, in *medinat hayam* — the ruling is: *tinasei v'ticul kesubasah*, she may remarry and collect her *kesubah* based on her own testimony about her husband. But her mother-in-law is *asurah* — the mother-in-law may not remarry on the basis of this same testimony. Why?

The technical objection might seem easy to dismiss: once the husband died, the father-in-law was no longer her father-in-law, and the mother-in-law was no longer her mother-in-law, so she should be believed to testify about what happened to him. But the *Gemara* does not accept this reasoning.

### Ruse Theory

*Mahu d'amrinan? — Lo ba'alah meis v'lo chamotah meis.* The concern is that perhaps this entire narrative is a ruse — that neither the husband nor the father-in-law actually died, and the wife has constructed the entire account precisely in order to harm her mother-in-law. She knows that if she testified directly about her mother-in-law she would not be believed, so she testifies first about her husband's death (which benefits herself and which she knows will be accepted), and then appends testimony about the father-in-law's death (which enables the mother-in-law to remarry and thereby creates the trap — because if the husband turns up alive, the mother-in-law will have remarried on the strength of false testimony). The entire scheme is designed to destroy the mother-in-law.

*Savrah levatar de'asya sha'atah lo seisi v'sis'aran* — her reasoning, according to Rashi, is that she wants to ensure that in the future the mother-in-law will not come and continue to cause her trouble. Even though her husband is currently absent, she is acting now based on the animosity that already exists — animosity rooted in the fact that the mother-in-law has been badmouthing her to her husband. She is not acting out of an immediate threat but out of an accumulated resentment, and that resentment is real and pre-existing.

### Pre-existing Animosity

But the *Gemara* then draws the distinction that answers the original question about the future mother-in-law. *Dilma shani hasam de'mei-ikra de'asya sanyah lah* — the case of the existing mother-in-law is different because the animosity is already there, pre-existing and rooted in a real relationship. In the hypothetical above, the daughter-in-law's willingness to harm her mother-in-law through this elaborate scheme makes sense precisely because she already harbors deep animosity from the years of the marriage. The future mother-in-law, by contrast, has no relationship with this woman whatsoever. She has not yet become anyone's mother-in-law. There is no prior history, no accumulated grievance, no existing hostility. The concern about lying for the sake of a future animosity that has not yet taken root does not apply.

The upshot is: we do not extend the exclusion to those whose animosity is merely hypothetical or future. The rule applies only where there is a pre-existing relationship of actual animosity.

---

## Conflict Cases

### 1v2 Early

The *mishnah* now addresses cases of conflicting testimony. First: *ed echad omer meis venisat* — one witness says the husband died and she remarries on that basis, *uva acher v'amar lo meis* — and then a second comes and says he did not die. *Harei zu lo tetze* — she does not have to leave her new marriage. The principle is that once *beit din* has accepted the testimony and acted upon it, a subsequent conflicting testimony cannot unravel what has already been ruled upon and executed.

### 2v1

If two say he died and she married, but one says he did not die: *af al pi she-niset, tetze* — even having already remarried, she must leave. Two witnesses prevail over one, and the remarriage must be undone.

Conversely, if two say he died and one says he did not: *af al pi she-lo niset, tinasei* — even before she has remarried, the two witnesses establish his death and she is permitted to proceed. The implication of the *mishnah*, left implicit until the *Gemara* makes it explicit, is that if it is one against one before she has remarried, she may not remarry.

### 1v1 Later

This implication — that one against one before remarriage leaves her unable to proceed — creates the analytical problem that the *Gemara* addresses. If it is *ed echad* saying he died against *ed echad* saying he did not, why should she not be permitted? The answer involves the principle of *ed echad*'s special weight in this domain.

### Ulla Principle

*V'amar Ulla: kol makom she-he'emina Torah ed echad harei kan shnayim v'ein davar she-echad b'makom shnayim.* Ulla's principle is that wherever the Torah gave special weight to a single witness, that testimony is treated as equivalent to two witnesses — and a single subsequent witness cannot override it, since one cannot stand against two.

There is a broader set of cases where the Torah gives special weight to a single witness — *Sotah*, *Eglah Arufah*, and others. In those cases, the witness given special weight testifies to one side of the equation, and a single witness on the other side cannot override it. Here, the *Gemara* notes, the rabbis gave special believability to the testimony that the husband died; they gave no such special weight to testimony that he did not die. Therefore, even in a one-against-one scenario, the one who says he died should carry the weight of two.

But the *Gemara* reformulates Ulla's principle more precisely: *ed echad omer meis v'hityiruha linase* — it is not merely about the testimony being given; the testimony must be acted upon. *Ba echad v'amar lo meis lo tetze me-heteirah harishon* — once *beit din* has ruled on the basis of that first testimony, it acquires the weight of two, and a subsequent single witness cannot override it. Before *beit din* rules, the testimony does not yet carry that locked-in weight. This is why one-against-one before remarriage does not permit her to proceed: the first testimony has not yet been ruled upon, and so it has not yet acquired the weight of two.

---

## Ulla vs. Nechemiah

### Ulla Model

Ulla's model is fundamentally one of formal testimony. When the Torah or the rabbis give special weight to a single witness in a particular domain, they are placing that witness within the framework of *eidus* — formal testimony — and elevating it to the status of two. The consequence is that the world remains one of formal evidentiary standards: one becomes two, two beats one, and only two legitimate witnesses on the other side would override it. The count never involves informal assessments or quantities of opinions; it is always about the quality and formal weight of testimony.

### Nechemiah Model

Rabbi Nechemiah articulates an entirely different model: *kol makom she-he'emina Torah ed echad halach achar rov de'os* — wherever the Torah believed a single witness, the determination follows the majority of opinions. This is a fundamentally quantitative approach. Rabbi Nechemiah holds that when the standard of proof departs from formal two-witness *eidus*, one has left the world of formal testimony entirely and entered a world of counting opinions. There is no elevation of one to two, no locking in, no special weight accorded to any one testimony. Instead, all testimonies are placed on a scale and the heavier side wins.

### Two Women Count

The practical consequence of Rabbi Nechemiah's model is stark: *v'asu shtei nashim b'ish echad kishnei anashim b'ish echad* — two women testifying against one man count the same as two men testifying against one man. Ordinarily, two women do not constitute formal *eidus* and cannot override a single male witness. But in Rabbi Nechemiah's model, when we are in the domain of *ed echad* believability, we are no longer asking about formal *eidus* at all. We are simply counting: two against one, regardless of the gender or formal qualification of the testifiers.

This has severe implications for women in the *agunah* context. A woman remarries on the strength of a single permitted testimony that her husband died. If two women — even if they are *psulin*, formally disqualified — then testify that he did not die, Rabbi Nechemiah's model would require her to leave the remarriage, because two opinions now outweigh one. This is a far more precarious protection than Ulla's model offers.

### Reconciliation

The *Gemara* offers a reconciliation of the two positions that is worth examining carefully. *Kol heicha d'asa ed echad kasher mei-ikara* — wherever the first witness who came was a formally qualified (*kasher*) male witness, we are in Ulla's world. That single testimony, once ruled upon by *beit din*, is treated as two witnesses, is locked in, and can be overridden only by two formally qualified witnesses. *Afilu me'ah nashim k'ed echad damyan* — even a hundred women count as only one, and they cannot override the locked-in testimony of that *kasher* witness.

### Woman First

The domain of Rabbi Nechemiah applies when the first witness was not a formally qualified witness — *kigon d'asa isha mei-ikara*, such as when a woman testified first. In that case, we are not in the world of formal *eidus* from the outset, and Rabbi Nechemiah's quantitative principle governs. *V'asu shtei nashim b'isha achas kishnei anashim b'ish echad* — two women against one woman is like two men against one man. We count opinions rather than weigh formal testimony.

The reconciliation thus turns on the identity of the first witness. If a formally qualified witness initiated the testimony, the case enters Ulla's framework and the testimony is locked in formally. If an informally qualified witness (a woman, a relative, or another *pasul*) testified first, the case operates under Rabbi Nechemiah's quantitative model from the start.

This represents two genuinely distinct conceptual frameworks. Ulla's model maintains that even in the special domain of *ed echad* believability, we remain within the structure of formal testimony — one has simply been elevated to two. Rabbi Nechemiah's model holds that once you have departed from the ordinary standard of two witnesses, you have left *eidus* territory entirely and are now simply doing arithmetic.

### Majority Principle

The final line of the *mishnah* — *shnayim omrim meis, echad omer lo meis* — states that if two say he died and one says he did not die, she may remarry even before having done so. The *Gemara* asks: *pshita* — isn't that obvious? Two beats one. The answer is that the *chiddush* here operates under Rabbi Nechemiah's model: the two who say he died may be *psulei eidus* — formally disqualified witnesses — and yet their two opinions outweigh the single opposing opinion. This is the domain of *rov de'os*, the majority of opinions, and the ruling teaches that the majority principle applies even to leniency, not only to stringency.

One might have thought that when the quantitative model leads to a lenient outcome — permitting remarriage — we would refuse to apply it and instead require formal *eidus*. The *mishnah* teaches that this is not the case. Whether the majority of opinions points toward stringency or leniency, the principle is applied consistently: *halach achar rov de'os*. The *Gemara*'s synthesis of Ulla and Rabbi Nechemiah thus determines not only how to handle conflicting testimony but how to understand the very nature of *ed echad* believability — whether it is an elevation within the world of formal testimony or a departure from that world altogether.

---

---

# Yevamot 118

## Single Witness Testimony

### Rabbinic Innovation

Daf 118 is the last daf of the second-to-last *perek*, and we pick up with the *mishna* on the bottom of 117b. The broader context is the series of sugyot dealing with the specifics of believing testimony that a woman's husband has died. This represents a tremendous rabbinic innovation: the extension of legal credence to ordinarily disqualified testimony — from a single witness, and by extension from a woman — in order to permit a wife to remarry. As the preceding sugyot have established, this leniency applies not only to a single male witness but to a woman testifying about her own husband's death, and not to a woman testifying for her daughter-in-law, mother-in-law, or stepdaughter. The principle that emerges across all these cases is that any single qualified witness, including a woman, may testify to a husband's death and enable his wife to remarry.

### One vs. One/Two

The prior *mishna* addressed scenarios where testimony conflicts: one witness against one, or one against two. The *gemara* there gave greater weight to the testimony that the husband had died, such that even in the case of one against one, the side affirming death carries additional force — particularly when the testimony had already been accepted by *beit din* before it was contradicted. If it was accepted first and then contradicted, the contradiction cannot dislodge it. If the contradiction came simultaneously, or before formal acceptance, the competing claims may neutralize one another.

### Ulla vs. R. Nechemiah

Two underlying theoretical models govern how this weighting works. Ulla understands the rabbinic enactment as operating within the framework of actual *edut* — testimony proper — in which the single witness testifying to death is treated as if he or she were two witnesses, thereby achieving the weight of full legal testimony. Rabbi Nechemiah, by contrast, frames it not as testimony at all, but as a form of evidence, and accordingly the weight assigned on each side is assessed numerically. The *gemara* works to reconcile these two models throughout the preceding discussion.

---

## Co-wives Contradicti (II)

### Two Co-wives

The *mishna* at the bottom of 117b introduces the following case: *achat omeret met ve-achat omeret lo met* — one co-wife says the husband died, and the other says he did not die. The ruling is that the co-wife who says he died may remarry and collect her *ketubah*, while the co-wife who says he did not die may neither remarry nor collect her *ketubah*. The scenario is vivid: they were traveling together, one returns saying he fell and died, and the other says the whole thing never happened.

### Co-wife Excluded

There are two distinct reasons why the co-wife who says "he did not die" cannot remarry. The first is obvious: she herself has declared that her husband is still alive, and one cannot remarry a living husband. The second reason — which the *gemara* will elaborate — is that even had she remained silent, a woman is not believed to testify on behalf of her co-wife (*tzaratah*). The concern is that the natural rivalry and animosity between co-wives, who share a husband, creates a presumption of bias sufficient to disqualify the co-wife's testimony entirely.

This raises a question, however. The earlier *mishna* suggested that when testimony is contradicted before it has been accepted in *beit din*, the contradicting testimony neutralizes it. If so, why doesn't the co-wife's denial neutralize the first wife's claim that he died — and thereby prevent the first wife from remarrying? The *gemara* will address this below: the *chiddush* of the *mishna* is precisely that we completely dismiss the co-wife's denial. Since she cannot testify for her co-wife to say that the husband died, she equally cannot testify for her co-wife to say that he did not die. Her statement is simply disregarded in its entirety.

---

## Died vs. Killed

### Died vs. Murdered

The *mishna* continues with a related but distinct case: *achat omeret met ve-achat omeret neherag* — one co-wife says the husband died of natural causes, and the other says he was murdered. Both agree he is dead; they differ only on the manner of death.

### R. Meir Position

Rabbi Meir rules: *ho'il u-makchishot zo et zo harei elu lo yinase'u* — since they contradict one another, neither may remarry. This is a striking position. In the prior case, one wife said "he died" and the other said "he did not die" — and there, the second wife's claim was simply dismissed because a co-wife cannot testify against her co-wife. But here, Rabbi Meir treats the contradiction differently. Why?

Tosafot explains the distinction carefully. When one wife says "he did not die," that claim carries no independent weight — the rabbinic institution gave heightened credibility specifically to testimony that a husband *died*, not to testimony that he did not die. Therefore, the co-wife's denial cannot neutralize the first wife's affirmation. But when one wife says "he died" and the other says "he was murdered," both statements are in the affirmative about death — each co-wife is testifying about something she would herself be believed about under ordinary circumstances, namely, the death of her own husband. Each woman's testimony has a degree of independent weight, and precisely because they have weight, the fact that they describe the death in mutually incompatible ways creates a genuine contradiction sufficient to neutralize one another. That is Rabbi Meir's position.

### R. Yehuda & Shimon

Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon disagree. In their view, both wives agree on the central fact — the husband is dead — and therefore both may remarry. The discrepancy in the details does not rise to the level of mutual neutralization. If you split the decision, as in the first case, you accept one and reject the other. Here, because both are affirming death, you either accept both or reject both. Since there is no reason to reject them outright, both may remarry.

---

## Co-wives Contradicti (II)

### Shimshon Analogy

The *gemara* now probes the reasoning behind the *mishna*'s ruling in the first case — that the co-wife cannot remarry. The *gemara* opens with a *diyuk*: *ta'ama d'amrah lo meit* — the reason the co-wife cannot marry is specifically because she said "he did not die." But this implies that had she remained silent, she might have been able to marry on the strength of the first wife's testimony. The *gemara* challenges this immediately: *v'ha ein tzarah me'idah l'chavertah* — a co-wife cannot testify for her co-wife! How could the co-wife have benefited from the first wife's testimony even in silence?

The *gemara* answers with a surprising twist. One might have thought that when the co-wife says "he did not die," she should actually be *more* believed than if she remained silent — and should even be permitted to remarry. The logic would run as follows: the husband is in fact dead, the second wife knows this too, and the only reason she says "he did not die" is to spite her co-wife and prevent her from remarrying. She is, in other words, willing to hurt herself — sacrificing her own ability to remarry — in order to damage the other wife. The *gemara* gives this attitude a memorable name: *tamus nafshi im Plishtim* — "let me die with the Philistines," the dying words of Shimshon. Just as Shimshon pulled down the hall to kill himself along with his enemies, so too the co-wife might say: I will forgo remarriage if it means my rival cannot remarry either.

If so, the *gemara* reasons, perhaps we should interpret the co-wife's denial not as genuine testimony that he is alive, but as an expression of spite — which would reinforce our assumption that he is dead and might even allow the denying wife to remarry. The *gemara* rejects this: *lo meis itztrichah lah* — the *mishna* needed to tell us that even in this case we do not reason this way. We cannot be certain the denying wife is lying to spite her rival; she might also be lying to implicate the first wife in a false claim. In any event, we do not go ahead and allow either wife to benefit from this chain of speculation.

### First Wife Marries

The genuine *chiddush* of the *mishna*, as the *gemara* makes clear, operates in the other direction. If a stranger — a non-co-wife — had contradicted the first wife's testimony that the husband died, and this contradiction came before the testimony was accepted in *beit din*, the two claims would neutralize and the first wife could not remarry. But here, the *chiddush* is that we completely dismiss the co-wife's denial — not only may the co-wife not remarry based on the first wife's testimony, but the co-wife's counter-testimony does not prevent the first wife from remarrying either. The co-wife's word is disregarded in its entirety. Just as she is not believed when she says "he died" (to benefit her rival), she is equally not believed when she says "he did not die" (to harm her rival). Either way, the testimony of the co-wife, directed toward the status of her rival, is simply voided.

---

## Died vs. Killed (II)

### Elazar vs. Yochanan

The *gemara* now examines Rabbi Meir's position — that in the case of "died" versus "killed," the testimonies neutralize one another — and asks: why does Rabbi Meir not also say the same in the first case, where one says "died" and the other says "did not die"? The implication is that if Rabbi Meir rules stringently in the "died/killed" case, he should rule stringently in the more obvious "died/didn't die" case as well. *Rav Elazar* responds: *bemachloket shenuya* — the first part of the *mishna*, which allows the first wife to remarry even over the co-wife's objection, is actually the position of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, not Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Meir would in fact also prohibit the first wife from remarrying in that case. So Rabbi Meir's position is internally consistent: in both the "died/didn't die" case and the "died/killed" case, the testimonies neutralize one another.

Rabbi Yochanan reads the *mishna* differently: *afilu teima Rabbi Meir* — even according to Rabbi Meir, there is a meaningful distinction between "died/didn't die" and "died/killed." In the former case, even Rabbi Meir would agree that the testimonies do not neutralize, because the claim "he did not die" in the context of testimony about a husband's death is treated as legally worthless.

### Co-wife Claim Void

Rabbi Yochanan's principle requires careful qualification. It is not that any claim of "he did not die" is always ignored — the end of the *mishna* states plainly that when one witness says "he died" and another says "he did not die," they do neutralize one another. So it cannot be a categorical rule that denials of death are void. The precise rule is this: a *co-wife's* claim that the husband did not die is voided, because just as a co-wife is not believed to say "he died" for the benefit of her rival, she is equally not believed to say "he did not die" to the detriment of her rival. The reasoning is the same in both directions — we do not trust any testimony the co-wife offers about her rival's husband's death or survival.

By contrast, when each wife says "he died," but one says "naturally" and the other says "by murder," each woman's testimony is accepted *for herself*. It is at that point — once each woman's individual testimony has been admitted for her own case — that the contradiction between the two accounts, both of which carry independent weight, creates the neutralization that Rabbi Meir invokes.

The *gemara* attempts to reconcile this analysis with the end of the *mishna*, which, when it says one woman says "died" and another says "did not die," could appear to include co-wives. According to Rabbi Elazar, that case in the *mishna* indeed reflects Rabbi Meir's position that co-wives can neutralize one another. According to Rabbi Yochanan, this case does not involve co-wives at all — and the difficulty for Rabbi Yochanan (*kashya*) is acknowledged. The overall upshot is clear: the co-wife's testimony, in any direction, is completely disregarded with respect to her rival.

---

## Woman Returns Testifies

### Classic Case

The next *mishna* presents the archetypal case of overseas testimony: *ha-isha she-halcha hi u-va'alah limdinat ha-yam* — a woman who went with her husband overseas, and returned to testify that he died. The ruling is *tinasei ve-titol ketuvatah* — she may remarry and collect her *ketubah*. This is the foundational case of the entire rabbinic innovation.

### R. Tarfon & Akiva

The *mishna* then adds: *ve-tzaratah asurah* — the co-wife is forbidden to remarry, since a woman's testimony about the death of a husband is not believed on behalf of her co-wife. The *mishna* then asks a further question about the co-wife's status: if the co-wife had previously been married to a *kohen*, may she continue to eat *terumah*? Rabbi Tarfon rules that she may — since we completely reject the co-wife's testimony, we do not treat it even as a *safek*, a doubt, and therefore the co-wife retains her presumed status as the wife of a living husband, allowing her to continue eating *terumah*. Rabbi Akiva rules more stringently: *ein zo derech motzi mi-yedei aveirah* — this approach does not protect her from sin. Since the testimony creates at least enough uncertainty to prevent her from remarrying, it creates enough uncertainty about eating *terumah* as well, and she must abstain from both. Rabbi Akiva's position is a *machmir* one precisely because treating the matter as a *safek* obligates caution on all sides.

### Father-in-law Case

A parallel case follows: *amra meit ba'ali ve-achar kach meit chami* — a woman who says "my husband died and then my father-in-law died." Ordinarily, a woman is not believed to testify on behalf of her *chamotah* (mother-in-law) or father-in-law, because we suspect the lingering animus of the in-law relationship. However, the *gemara* notes that once her husband has died, her father-in-law is no longer halachically her father-in-law — the relationship has dissolved. And a woman is believed to testify on behalf of an *ex*-father-in-law. So she is claiming: accept my testimony about my husband's death first, and then — since he is now my former father-in-law — accept my testimony about his death as well.

The *mishna* rules: *tinasei ve-titol ketuvatah*, she may remarry and collect her *ketubah*, but *chamotah asurah* — the mother-in-law's status is not changed by this testimony. Why not? Because since the entire chain of reasoning rests on the woman's own testimony, we are concerned that she has constructed the whole account to harm her mother-in-law. Her motivation to do so is real: if the mother-in-law is married to a *kohen* and we accept the testimony that her husband died, she can no longer eat *terumah*. So even if the woman is lying about her husband's death — which the *mishna* says she is believed about — she still achieves something negative against her mother-in-law. That concern alone is sufficient to reject the mother-in-law's portion of the testimony.

The ruling for the mother-in-law therefore mirrors that of the co-wife: Rabbi Tarfon says the testimony is completely rejected and the mother-in-law may continue eating *terumah*, while Rabbi Akiva says it is not enough to protect her from sin and she must treat the matter as a *safek*, refraining from both remarriage and *terumah*.

A question worth raising is why the co-wife should suffer this liminal status when the testimony might be entirely true and she has done nothing wrong. This is a genuine difficulty, and it underscores the tension the rabbis created when they expanded the category of believed testimony: they recognized the leniency could be abused and therefore imposed limits, but those limits sometimes fall on an innocent party caught in the wrong formal relationship. Rabbi Tarfon's approach — completely rejecting the testimony and restoring the co-wife's unambiguous prior status — has real appeal precisely because it avoids leaving an innocent person in an undefined halachic limbo.

### Both Cases Needed

The *gemara* establishes that both cases — the co-wife and the mother-in-law — are necessary, and neither can be derived from the other. Had the *mishna* taught only the co-wife case, one might have thought Rabbi Tarfon completely rejects the testimony because *tzarat ha-gufa* — the co-wife's animosity is intensely personal, rooted in the intimate fact that the husband sleeps with her rival rather than with her. One might then think Rabbi Tarfon would concede to Rabbi Akiva in the case of the mother-in-law, where the animosity is of a more ordinary social variety — perhaps she badmouths her daughter-in-law to her son, a complaint common enough but far less visceral. Conversely, had the *mishna* taught only the mother-in-law case, one might think Rabbi Akiva concedes in the co-wife case, where the bias is so extreme that even he might agree we completely reject the testimony. By teaching both cases, the *mishna* makes clear that neither tanna modifies his position based on the type of animosity involved — each maintains his view across both scenarios.

The *gemara* then reports: *amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel, halacha ke-Rabbi Tarfon* — the *halacha* follows Rabbi Tarfon. The co-wife is not left in a state of ambiguity. The testimony is fully rejected, and she may go on living her life as before, without the paralysis of a *safek* she never created.

---

## One of Five Women

### Uncertainty Case

The *mishna* now takes up what the *gemara* presents as a digression occasioned by the debate between Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva. The case is: *kidesh achat mi-chamesh nashim ve-eino yodea eizo kidesh* — a man performed *kiddushin* with one of five women but does not know which one. Each woman claims he married her. This is not an impossible scenario given the realities of the time, when *kiddushin* and *nisuin* could be separated by years and the formal act of *kiddushin* might be the transfer of money to a father on behalf of a daughter, leaving uncertainty about which daughter was intended.

The *mishna* states that he must give a *get* to each one — since he cannot be certain which woman is his wife, he cannot simply live with any one of them or leave them all bound without resolution. As for the *ketubah*: *maniach ketubah beineihen u-mistalek* — he deposits the *ketubah* money among them and withdraws. He knows he is obligated to one of them but does not know which one, so he leaves the money for them to resolve.

### Hamotzi Framework

The underlying legal question is how to apply the principle of *hamotzi me-chavero alav ha-re'ayah* — the burden of proof lies on the one seeking to extract from another. Each woman presents herself to him with a definite claim: you owe me a *ketubah*. He responds that he is uncertain. This is not precisely the case where a lender says "I lent you money" and the borrower denies it — there the certainty and uncertainty are on opposite sides. Nor is it quite the case where one says "I lent you money and I am not sure if you paid me back" — there the debtor concedes the debt. Here it is an intermediate case: he concedes the existence of an obligation to one of them, but not necessarily to the particular woman standing before him. This framing of the *hamotzi* analysis shapes the subsequent debate.

### R. Tarfon Position

Rabbi Tarfon says: he places the *ketubah* money among them and withdraws. He has discharged his definite obligation — to one of them — by depositing the full amount. They must resolve the distribution among themselves.

### R. Akiva Position

Rabbi Akiva rules: *ein zo derech motzi mi-yedei aveirah* — the same phrase we encountered above — this does not protect him from sin. He must give a *get* and a *ketubah* to each woman individually. The question is whether Rabbi Akiva is speaking in strictly legal terms — that a court would compel him to pay each one — or whether he is articulating a moral obligation that, while not technically enforceable through *dinei mamonot*, nonetheless constitutes a real spiritual and ethical debt. The parallel the *gemara* raises elsewhere is illuminating: one who places poison before another's animal is exempt *be-dinei adam* but liable *be-dinei shamayim* — exempt in human courts but obligated before the heavenly court. The language *ein zo derech motzi mi-yedei aveirah* suggests Rabbi Akiva may be operating in that register: you have a specific, concrete moral obligation that a *beit din* will seek to enforce, even if strict *dinei mamonot* would not technically mandate it.

---

## Theft from Five

### Theft Scenario

A parallel case follows immediately: *gezel echad mi-chamishah ve-eini yodea me-eizeh gazal* — a man stole from one of five people and does not know which one. Each person claims he stole from them. Rabbi Tarfon rules that he deposits the stolen object among them and withdraws; Rabbi Akiva rules he must make full restitution to each one.

### Heightened Obligation

The obvious moral distinction between the two cases is that in the *kiddushin* scenario, the man did nothing inherently wrong — he entered into a marriage, lost track of which woman it was, and now must extract himself. In the theft scenario, he committed a transgression. One would therefore expect the obligation to make amends to be greater in the theft case. The *mishna* seems to present Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Tarfon as disagreeing in both scenarios equally — and it raises the question of whether the same analysis governs a morally neutral situation and a situation involving actual wrongdoing.

### R. Shimon b. Elazar

The *gemara* introduces a *braita* in which Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar clarifies the scope of the debate: *lo necheleku Rabbi Tarfon ve-Rabbi Akiva al she-kidesh achat mi-chamesh nashim ve-eino yodea eizo kidesh she-maniach ketubah beineihen u-mistalek* — Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva did not disagree at all in the case of simple *kiddushin* without a more heightened involvement. Both agree that he deposits the *ketubah* and withdraws. Similarly, they did not disagree in the case where someone purchased an item from one of five merchants and forgets which one — there, too, both agree he deposits the payment and withdraws. The debate, says Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, applies only in cases of heightened obligation: *kiddushin* accomplished through an act of intercourse (*kiddushei bi'ah*), and theft.

### Special Obligation

This creates a problem for how to read our *mishna*, which appears to present the debate in the cases of simple *kiddushin* (without *bi'ah*) and theft — one from each column. The *gemara* resolves: *le-olam Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar* — our *mishna* is in fact consistent with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view. When our *mishna* says *kidesh*, it means *kiddushei bi'ah* — *kiddushin* effected through intercourse, which carries a special moral weight because, regardless of whether *kiddushei bi'ah* was halachically proper (and the rabbis disapproved of it, though it is valid), having been intimate with a woman and then walking away without ensuring she receives her *ketubah* creates a particular obligation. The *mishna* thus presents the two cases of heightened obligation — *kiddushei bi'ah* and theft — as the arena of the dispute.

Within those cases, moreover, the *gemara* identifies a further gradation. *Kiddushei bi'ah* involves only a rabbinic prohibition (*issur d'Rabbanan*), whereas theft is an *issur d'Oraita*. The *mishna* therefore teaches Rabbi Akiva's ruling in the lighter case — *kiddushei bi'ah* — to demonstrate the strength of his position: even where the transgression was only rabbinic in character, he imposes the full obligation to pay each woman. Conversely, the *mishna* teaches Rabbi Tarfon's ruling in the heavier case — theft — to demonstrate the strength of his position: even where there was a genuine biblical transgression, he does not require full individual restitution to each claimant.

The *gemara*'s closing word on Rabbi Akiva's position is *kanis* — a fine. This framing clarifies what Rabbi Akiva means: not that strict *dinei mamonot* technically obligates him to pay each woman, but that we impose a *knas* to ensure he fully discharges his responsibility to the one he actually wronged, since we cannot know which one that is.

---

## Son & Yibum Status

### Husband Then Son

The last *mishna* of the *perek* presents a series of cases involving a woman's testimony about events overseas that affect her *yibum* status. The *mishna* opens with the case we touched on earlier: *ha-isha she-halcha hi u-va'alah limdinat ha-yam u-vnah imahem* — a woman who departed with her husband and her son. Since she left with a son, she would not be obligated in *yibum* if her husband died. She returns and testifies: my husband died, and then my son died. In this configuration, she is believed — the only thing she is specially credited to testify about is her husband's death, and the two statements about the son cancel each other out. We assumed she would not be obligated in *yibum* when she left, and nothing she says about her son changes that. She may act accordingly.

### Son First Claim

Now consider a variation: she left with no son — so we assumed she *would* be obligated in *yibum*. She returns and says: I had a son born to me overseas, and my husband died, and then my son died. She is neutralizing her own claim: yes I had a son, but he died after my husband, so I am still not obligated in *yibum*. Since she is not trying to change her status in an advantageous direction — she is not claiming *yibum* rights or *yibum* exemption beyond what we already assumed — and her credibility extends to the statement about her husband's death, she is believed.

But if she says instead: my husband died, and then my son died — and she had left without a son — she is now claiming she is *exempt* from *yibum* based on a son whose existence and death she alone asserts. She is not believed to change her status in this way, because her special credibility pertains to her husband's death, not to the existence or death of a son. Nevertheless, *chosheshin li-dvareha* — we take her words into account enough to require caution. Since she claims exemption from *yibum*, we cannot permit *yibum* to proceed. The ruling: *choletzet ve-lo mityabemet* — she performs *chalitzah* but does not perform *yibum*.

### Brother-in-law Overseas

The *mishna* then turns to cases involving a brother-in-law. If she left without any brother-in-law and says a brother-in-law was born to her in-laws overseas, and she then reports his death in either order relative to her husband, her statement neutralizes itself: I had a brother-in-law who is now dead. She is believed, since she is not claiming any change of status — she ends up in the same position she would be in had there never been a brother-in-law.

### Overseas Events

The more difficult case: she departed together with her husband and a known brother-in-law — *halchah hi u-va'alah ve-yavamah limdinat ha-yam* — meaning we know there is a *yibum* obligation should her husband die. She returns and testifies that both her husband and her brother-in-law have died — in either order. Since either order leads to the same result — no brother-in-law, no *yibum* — one might expect she is believed. But the *mishna* rules: *einah ne'emenet* — she is not believed.

### Scope Limited

The reason is that she is testifying about her brother-in-law's death, which falls outside the scope of the special rabbinic credibility accorded to a wife. That credibility extends only to testimony about her own husband's death. The *mishna* articulates the principle broadly: *she-ein ishah ne'emenet lomar meit yavmi she-tinasei* — a woman is not believed to say "my brother-in-law died" so that she may remarry freely. Similarly, *ve-lo meitah achotah she-tikaneis le-veiso* — a woman is not believed to say "my sister died" so that she may marry her sister's husband. And *ve-ein ha-ish ne'eman lomar meit achi she-yiyabem et ishto* — a man is not believed to say "my brother died" in order to perform *yibum* with the brother's wife.

This last case is worth examining carefully. If a man returns and says his brother died, that statement is actually a form of testimony that a husband died — and one might think the sister-in-law could rely on it to remarry if there are children, in which case there is no *yibum* obligation. And indeed, in that context she might be able to. But she cannot rely on it to permit *yibum*, because his testimony in that case would *matir* an *issur* — it would be removing the prohibition of *eshet ach*, a brother's wife, which is otherwise biblically forbidden. The rabbinic credibility granted to single witnesses and wives applies only to permitting a woman to remarry as a widow, not to enabling an otherwise prohibited relationship.

The practical consequence for the woman in the brother-in-law case is severe: she testified that the brother-in-law died, she is not believed, and yet there is no brother-in-law present to perform either *yibum* or *chalitzah*. She is effectively an *agunah* — bound by a *yibum* obligation to a man whose whereabouts cannot be confirmed.

---

## Get to Absent Wife

### Get via Agent

The *gemara* now introduces a question posed by Rava to Rav Nachman: *ha-mezakeh get le-ishto bimkom yavam mahu?* — if a husband wishes to give a *get* to his wife in a situation where there is a *yavam* (brother-in-law who would be obligated in *yibum*), but the wife is not present, can the husband appoint a third party to receive the *get* on the wife's behalf?

The scenario is one in which the husband wants to preempt the *yibum* obligation — perhaps he is terminally ill or departing for war and fears he will die, leaving his wife subject to *yibum* with a brother-in-law she does not want. He would like to give a *get* now so that upon his death the *yibum* obligation never arises. But the wife is not present to receive the *get* directly and has not appointed an agent to receive it. Can the husband effectively appoint a representative on his wife's behalf?

### Mezakeh Principle

The operative principle is *mezakeh* — one may acquire something on behalf of another person without their presence or knowledge, provided it is to that person's benefit (*zechus*). A husband can give his wife a *get* against her will, since once instituted, Cherem de-Rabbenu Gershom notwithstanding, *halacha* recognizes a unilateral *get*. But for the *get* to take effect, it must be received by the wife or her validly appointed agent. The question is whether the husband can himself appoint someone to represent the wife — treating this as an act of *mezakeh*, done on her behalf without her knowledge — given that a *get* would seemingly benefit her by freeing her from the *yibum* obligation.

### Benefit vs. Harm

The *gemara* frames the question as a genuine uncertainty. On one hand, *keivan d'sanya lah* — since we can assume she hates the brother-in-law, being freed from *yibum* is clearly to her benefit, and *zakin le-adam she-lo be-fanav* — one may acquire benefit for another without their presence. On the other hand, *dilma zimnin de-rachma lei* — perhaps there are times when a woman actually likes or loves her brother-in-law and would prefer *yibum* to remaining a widow. In that case, being divorced precludes the *yibum* she would have wanted, which makes the *get* a *chov* — a harm rather than a benefit. And *ein chavin le-adam she-lo be-fanav* — one cannot impose a harm on another person without their presence and consent.

The *gemara*'s framing is notable: it does not assume we can simply inquire about each woman's individual feelings. It is asking whether a general presumption can be established — can we rule categorically that a *get* in a *yibum* situation is always, or almost always, to the wife's benefit?

### Fighting Couple

The question is pressed further by Ravina, who asks Rava: *ha-mezakeh get le-ishah bimkom ketatah mahu?* — what if the husband and wife are in the midst of a serious conflict? They are fighting, tensions are high, perhaps legal proceedings have begun. Surely, one might argue, in that case the *get* is clearly to her benefit — she obviously wants out of the marriage. Or perhaps not: *nicha de-gufa adif lah* — even when a woman is fighting bitterly with her husband, the physical and emotional security of being married may still matter more to her than being free of him. Even in the midst of a quarrel, a woman may not want to be divorced.

### Two vs. Widow

The *gemara* invokes a famous statement of Reish Lakish: *tav lemetav tan du milemetav armalu* — better to sit as two than to sit as a widow. This is presented as a sociological assessment: women, as a general matter, prefer the state of being married — even to an imperfect husband — over the state of widowhood or singlehood. The statement carries enormous halachic weight and would later become the subject of a famous dispute between Rabbi Rackman and Rav Soloveitchik about whether changing social realities could alter this assumption. But in the *gemara* itself, it is offered as a presumption about women's preferences.

### Women Settle

Several *amoraim* elaborate on this theme with increasingly pointed formulations. Abaye states: *deshumshmana gavra* — my husband could be as small as an ant, but as long as *kursiyei be-charta rami* — my seat is set among people of standing — I am content. A woman will accept a negligible husband if it means having the social standing of being married. Rav Pappa states: *denafsa gavra* — my husband could be a flax comber, but *tikrei be-seifei bava ve-teitiv* — as long as I am called to the door and given a place to sit, the dignity of being married suffices. Rav Ashi states: *dekulsa gavra* — my husband could be a cabbage head, but *lo ba'ei talfei le-kedira* — as long as I do not need to worry about putting food on the table myself, I will manage. The repeated motif is that women are willing to settle for husbands of very modest character and capacity rather than remain unmarried.

### Adultery Reversal

The *gemara*, however, does not end on that note. A *braita* is cited that dramatically reverses the valence of all that has been said: *ve-kullan mezanot ve-tolot be-ba'aleihen* — all of them commit adultery and attribute the resulting pregnancies to their husbands. What began as a description of women's willingness to endure and settle within marriage ends as an indictment: the very willingness to remain with inadequate husbands generates unfaithfulness, because the unhappiness they suppress does not simply disappear.

### Modern Issues

The *gemara*'s conclusion — that we cannot give a *get* to a wife without her presence even when she is fighting with her husband, because we cannot assume she would want it — flows from the assumption encoded in *tav lemetav tan du milemetav armalu*. And this has real and troubling contemporary consequences. The presumption that women prefer marriage to its absence, that they will endure rather than leave, has been invoked by *batei dinim* — particularly those identified as deeply committed to *shalom bayit* — to resist granting a *get* even in situations involving documented physical, emotional, or sexual abuse. "Try to work it out" becomes a halachic default rooted in this Talmudic assessment of women's preferences. What began as a sociological generalization in the *gemara* functions in practice as a structurally powerful obstacle for women seeking to leave dangerous or degrading marriages. Reading this *gemara* in full — ending not with the neat statement of Reish Lakish but with the *braita*'s unsettling reversal — should at minimum prompt honest reflection on how these assumptions shape rabbinic decision-making today.

---

---

# Yevamot 120

## Two Sisters-in-Law

### Mishna Review

The daf opens with a brief review of the mishna on 119b. The case involves two women each married to one of two brothers. Each woman comes and reports that her own husband has died, and each is believed — a woman's testimony about her husband's death is accepted in order to permit her to remarry. The complication, however, is that each woman also has a *yavam*: her deceased husband's brother. And the testimony of one co-wife about her sister-in-law's husband carries no legal weight for purposes of releasing the sister-in-law from the obligation of *yibum*.

To map out the case concretely: Reuven and Shimon are brothers. Rachel is married to Reuven and Sarah is married to Shimon. Rachel testifies that Reuven is dead — she is believed, and in principle could remarry, but she cannot, because Shimon is still alive and she requires either *yibum* or *chalitza* from him. Sarah testifies that Shimon is dead — again, believed for her own purposes, but she cannot act on it because Reuven may still be alive, and his status has only been established by Rachel's testimony, which does not function as admissible testimony vis-à-vis releasing Sarah from her *yibum* obligation. The mishna concludes that both women are stuck.

### Reb Eliezer Position

Rabbi Eliezer introduces a leniency. If these women went ahead and performed *yibum* with the surviving brothers — that is, if Rachel performed *yibum* with Levi (Reuven's brother) and Sarah performed *yibum* with Yehuda (Shimon's brother) — and those *yevamim* subsequently died, then Rabbi Eliezer holds that both women are free to remarry anyone they wish. They need not worry that one of the original husbands may still be alive.

### Acting on Testimony

The final line of the mishna articulates Rabbi Eliezer's rationale: *ho'il vehutru leyevamim hutru lechol adam* — since they have been permitted to the *yevamim*, they are permitted to all men. The key move is that by allowing Rachel to perform *yibum* with Levi, the legal system has not merely accepted Rachel's testimony in the abstract — it has acted upon it. The death of Reuven has been established as a legal fact. Correspondingly, Sarah's *yibum* with Yehuda establishes the death of Shimon as a legal fact. Once both deaths have been legally acted upon in this way, each woman can rely on the other's established fact, and both are free to remarry after the *yevamim* themselves die.

---

## Rava's Question

### Rava Inquiry

The Gemara opens with Rava's inquiry: *mai ta'ama deRabbi Eliezer?* — what is the underlying rationale of Rabbi Eliezer's ruling? Two possible explanations are offered. The first: *mishum dekasavar tzara me'ida lachavirtah* — perhaps Rabbi Eliezer holds that in general, a co-wife may testify on behalf of her competing co-wife. This would be a sweeping position, and both Rashi and Tosafot reject it as inconsistent with the language of the mishna. The mishna uses the formulation *hutru leyevamim*, not the language of testimony being accepted. Moreover, the entire prior discussion has established that co-wives, mothers-in-law, and daughters-in-law are precisely the category of women whose testimony is *not* accepted.

The more plausible explanation, suggested by Tosafot explicitly and Rashi implicitly, is that Rachel is fundamentally testifying about herself — about her own husband's death, for her own purposes of remarriage. The testimony is, at its core, testimony *for herself*. Rabbi Eliezer may be saying that once testimony is accepted as fundamentally self-directed, it carries weight even for the competing co-wife, even though that co-wife would normally fall outside the scope of acceptable testimony.

### Two Interpretations

This leads to a second layer of Rava's question. Even granting that Rabbi Eliezer extends the effect of self-directed testimony to the co-wife, *when* does that extension take effect? Two possibilities emerge: either the testimony alone suffices — the very act of testifying for oneself automatically confers permissibility on the co-wife (*tzara me'ida lachavirtah*) — or the extension only operates once the testifying woman has actually *acted* on her own testimony. Under the second reading, the operative factor is not the testimony per se but the willingness to personally stake one's own status on the truth of the claim: *mishum dehi lo mekalkela nafsha* — because she would not ruin herself.

### Co-Wife Case

The practical difference between these two interpretations is precisely the question of *le'insuvei letzara mikamei didah* — whether the co-wife may remarry before the testifying woman has herself acted. In a simpler case involving two co-wives whose joint husband went overseas: Sarah says the husband died. That testimony is accepted for Sarah's own purposes of remarriage. May Rachel immediately rely on that testimony to remarry as well, even before Sarah has herself taken any action?

If Rabbi Eliezer's principle is that self-directed testimony automatically extends to the co-wife, then Rachel can act immediately — *af agav dela insava mansavinan lah letzara*, even before Sarah herself has married, we permit the co-wife to marry. But if the operative principle requires action — that Sarah must demonstrate her own genuine conviction by actually remarrying — then *ei lo insava lo mansavinan lah*: until Sarah acts, Rachel cannot rely on it.

---

## Textual Analysis

### Language Analysis

The Gemara attempts to resolve Rava's question from the language of Rabbi Eliezer's ruling in the mishna. The phrase is *ho'il vehutru leyevamim hutru lechol adam* — "since they have been *permitted* to the *yevamim*, they are permitted to all men." The operative word is *hutru*, "permitted," not "married." The mishna does not say "since they *married* the *yevamim*." This linguistic observation becomes the pivot of the Gemara's analysis.

### Automatic vs. Conditional

The Gemara argues: if Rabbi Eliezer's rationale requires action — that is, he only extends the testimony's effect once the woman has *married* her *yavam* — then the language *vehutru leyevamim* makes perfect sense, because *hainu dechi insav manzveina lah* — only because they married the *yevamim* does the permission flow to the co-wife. But if Rabbi Eliezer's principle is that the testimony alone automatically works for the co-wife even without any subsequent action, the mishna's wording becomes puzzling: it should have simply said *ho'il vehutru hutru*, without specifically tying it to the *yibum* having occurred. The fact that it anchors the permission in the *yibum* itself seems to indicate that action is required.

The Gemara, however, deflects this reading. *Rabbi Eliezer lidvreihem ka'amar* — Rabbi Eliezer is arguing within the framework of the Rabbis' position, not necessarily expressing his own full view. According to his own reasoning, Rabbi Eliezer may well hold that the co-wife is automatically permitted once testimony is given for oneself, even without any subsequent action. But addressing the Rabbis on their own terms, he argues: at least concede that once she has performed *yibum* and thereby staked her own status on the truth of her testimony — *lo mekalkela nafsha* — surely you must agree the co-wife should be permitted. To this the Rabbis respond with the principle of *tamus nafshi im pelishtim* — she is willing to bring the stadium down on her own head if she can take down her co-wife in the process.

### Baraita Case

A *baraita* is then introduced: a woman and her husband went overseas. She returned and declared that her husband had died. She may remarry and collect her *ketuva*. Her co-wife, however, is forbidden. This is the classic formulation — believed for herself, not for the co-wife. Rabbi Eliezer says: *ho'il vehutra hi hutra nami tzarata* — since she has been permitted, her co-wife is also permitted. Crucially, the baraita uses the language of *hutra* — "she has been permitted" — rather than saying she actually married. This seems to vindicate the reading that Rabbi Eliezer does not require prior action; the mere permissibility itself extends to the co-wife.

The Gemara attempts to read the baraita as implying *ho'il vehutra veniseit* — "permitted and then married" — so that action is still required. But the plain reading clearly supports the automatic interpretation.

---

## Hidden Divorce Problem

### Secret Get Concern

If Rabbi Eliezer's principle requires the woman to act on her own testimony before her co-wife can benefit, a serious objection arises: even when she acts, her action may not reliably demonstrate the truth of her testimony. The Gemara raises the concern of *veleichush shema begita asai* — what if she is coming with a *get*? That is, what if her husband had secretly sent her a *get* that no one else knows about? In that case, she is already divorced and not bound by her own claim that he died. She goes ahead and remarries, ostensibly "acting on" her testimony — but in reality she knows she is safe because of the hidden *get*. Her entire purpose is to ruin her co-wife by inducing the co-wife to remarry while the husband is, in fact, still alive. In this scenario, her act of remarriage proves nothing.

### Kohen Exception

The Gemara resolves this difficulty by limiting the applicability of Rabbi Eliezer's leniency to a specific circumstance: *de'insva l'Kohen* — she must have married a *kohen*. If there is a hidden *get*, then when the husband eventually returns alive, the truth will emerge, and at that point she will also be ruined — she will be divorced from the *kohen* because a *kohenet* who was previously divorced or who came through improper circumstances is *assura* to remain married to a *kohen*. Since she faces this additional exposure, she would not have concocted the *get* scheme in the first place. Marrying a ישראל, by contrast, does not eliminate the hidden *get* scenario: her risk there is limited, and the concern remains.

### Legal vs. Factual Truth

This exchange opens a broader question about the nature of halachic truth. When a *beit din* rules that a woman may remarry, is it establishing a legal fact or merely permitting action under uncertainty? One might think the ruling functions like a judicial determination of fact, binding on subsequent proceedings. Indeed, that might be Rabbi Eliezer's point — particularly under the reading that does not require prior action: once testimony is accepted for one party, it is accepted as established fact, and others may rely on it.

But the Gemara's willingness to entertain the hidden *get* scenario reveals that *beit din*'s acceptance of testimony does not constitute a universal determination of fact. It is a permission granted within a particular legal context, for particular parties, and it does not automatically extend as a factual determination to all related questions. This parallels the concept of *palginan dibura* found in tractate Sanhedrin — the same statement can be believed in one direction and disbelieved in another. Halacha regularly operates within a framework of legal truth that does not always correspond to objective, verifiable fact, in the same way that legal systems employ constructs like *rov* and *chazaka* not because they guarantee factual accuracy but because they provide workable presumptions for adjudication.

---

## Identifying the Dead

### Face with Nose

The daf now shifts to a new mishna addressing the *content* of valid testimony — specifically, how one establishes that the body one has seen is indeed the person in question. *Ein me'idin ela al partzuf panim im hachotem* — one may only testify based on having seen the face together with the nose. *Af al pi she'yesh simanim b'gufo uvkhelav* — even if there are identifying marks on the body or on the clothing, that is not sufficient. The standard requires direct facial identification.

### Three-Day Limit

An additional limitation: *ein me'idin ela ad gimmel yamim* — one may only testify within three days of the death. Beyond three days, the decomposition of the body alters the appearance to such a degree that reliable identification is no longer possible.

### Context-Dependent

Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava dissents from the three-day rule. He argues that no uniform rule can be applied: *lo kol ha'adam velo kol hamakom velo kol hasha'ot shavin* — not every person is the same, not every place is the same, and not every time is the same. Body decomposition varies by individual constitution, climate, and circumstance, and a rigid three-day cutoff fails to account for this variability.

---

## Facial Recognition

### Forehead & Nose

A *baraita* elaborates on the mishna's requirement: *padachat velo partzuf panim, partzuf panim velo padachat — ein me'idin* — neither a forehead alone without a face, nor a face without a forehead, is sufficient for testimony. One requires both together, along with the nose: *ad she'yihyu shneihem im hachotem*. A full, head-on view of the face is necessary.

### Scriptural Source

Abaye — and some attribute it to Rav Kahana — derives this from the verse *hakarat pneihem antah bam* — "the recognition of their face answered against them." Rashi reads the verse as establishing the face, rather than any other part of the body, as the locus of reliable identification. Tosafot notes that the word *hakarat* — "recognition" — implies not merely that a face was seen, but that a full identification of the face was achieved.

### Wax Disguise

The Gemara illustrates the sensitivity of facial recognition with a story about Abba bar Marta, also known as Abba bar Minyumi, who owed money to the house of the *Reish Galuta*. He took wax (*kira*), smeared it onto his forehead, and walked past their guards — *velo baskruha* — and they did not recognize him. The episode demonstrates that even minor alterations to the forehead and nose can defeat reliable identification, reinforcing why the requirement for a complete, unobstructed view of the face is necessary.

---

## Tosafot Reinterpretation

### Whole Body Recognition

Rabbeinu Tam, at the top of Tosafot on this daf, offers a significant reinterpretation of the mishna's requirements. He argues: *hainu davka keshein sham ela hapartzuf* — the requirement of face-with-nose applies only when all one has seen is the face. But *aval kol gufo shalem* — if the entire body is intact and has been seen — *afilu ein kan padachat vechotem nikar hu heitev al yedei simanei haguf* — even without the forehead and nose, the body is clearly identifiable through its physical characteristics.

### Recognition vs. Marks

Rabbeinu Tam draws a further distinction. He suggests that when the mishna says *simanim* on the body are insufficient, that ruling applies only to a case where the witness is relying on specific *marks* — pointing to particular features and saying, "I see a mole here, therefore this is him." That is fundamentally different from *tevi'as ayin* — genuine recognition, where the totality of what one sees produces confident identification. If the witness truly *recognizes* the person — not by pointing to individual marks but through the holistic experience of recognition — that may be perfectly valid even without the specific facial requirements.

### Extended Timeframes

Rabbeinu Tam extends this reasoning further: *va'afilu achar kama yamim* — even after many days, if the body is complete and the witness genuinely recognizes it, testimony may be valid. The three-day limit and the facial requirements, on this reading, apply specifically to the case of *simanim* — where one is relying on particular identifying marks rather than direct recognition. The creative thrust of this position is unmistakable: Rabbeinu Tam is deliberately reframing stringent Talmudic requirements as applying only to a narrower category of cases, opening the door to much more flexible standards of identification. Given the practical reality that these standards could leave many women unable to remarry, it is clear what pastoral and halakhic need is driving the reinterpretation.

---

## Marks: Biblical or R (II)

### Simanim Status

The Gemara returns to the mishna's statement that *simanim* on the body are insufficient for testimony. *Lemeimra desimanim lav de'oraita* — does this establish that identifying marks have no biblical validity? If so, that would be a significant and far-reaching ruling.

### Get Case

The Gemara challenges this inference from a ruling in *Gittin*. If a *get* was found tied to a pouch, wallet, or signet ring (*matza kashur bekis uve'arnaki uvetaba'as*), or found among the owner's possessions, it may be returned to its owner and used to divorce his wife — even after a considerable time has passed. The *get* is valid even for the weighty matter of *eishes ish*. The identification of the *get* as belonging to a particular person rests entirely on the *simanim* — the associated objects. This seems to demonstrate that *simanim* do have biblical validity, since the stakes here are clearly *de'oraita* in nature.

---

## Rava's Resolution

### Everyone Accepts Simanim

Rava proposes a resolution: *dechuli alma simanim d'oraita* — everyone agrees that identifying marks have biblical validity. The debate elsewhere — specifically the *baraita* involving testimony based on a *shuma* (mole) — is not about whether *simanim* work in principle, but about a more specific question.

---

## Marks: Biblical or R (II)

### Mole Case

The *baraita* records a debate: *ein me'idin al hashuma* — one may not testify to a man's death based on a mole. Rabbi Elazar ben Mahavai disagrees: *me'idin* — one may. Abaye initially suggests this debate reflects a disagreement about whether *simanim* are *de'oraita* or *derabbanan*. But Rava's resolution — that everyone agrees *simanim* are *de'oraita* — redirects the question: if so, what exactly are Rabbi Elazar ben Mahavai and the Rabbis debating?

---

## Rava's Resolution (II)

### Qualifying Marks

Rava explains that the debate about the mole concerns *shuma metzuya beven gilo* — whether a mole of that type is commonly found among people born under the same astrological influence (*ben gilo*), i.e., whether it constitutes a sufficiently distinctive identifying mark. One opinion holds that such moles are common enough to other individuals that they do not meet the threshold of a valid *siman*; the other holds they are uncommon enough to qualify. The underlying principle is that even if everyone agrees *simanim* are *de'oraita*, not every proposed *siman* actually meets the threshold. There is a spectrum: at the top is the *siman muvhak* — the distinctively unique mark, analogous to a fingerprint — about which there is no dispute. At the bottom is something so generic (tall, short) that no one calls it a *siman*. The debate about the mole lies somewhere in the middle.

### Change or Common

Tosafot introduces two additional considerations that bear on the validity of a *siman*: first, whether it may *change after death* — certain bodily marks shift in appearance following death, and if so, they cannot serve as reliable *simanim*; second, whether the mark is simply too common to be identifying. The Gemara presents a second version of this debate — *shuma ha'asuya lehishtanos le'achar misa* — where the dispute is specifically about whether moles of this kind change after death. One opinion holds they do; the other that they do not. This version does not require invoking the *ben gilo* framework at all.

---

## Generic vs. Specific

### Generic Characteristics

With the principle that *simanim de'oraita* established — at least according to one significant position — a new question arises: why does the mishna exclude *simanim* on the body from valid identification? The Gemara answers that the mishna's case is not one involving genuine *simanim* at all. *Gufo — d'arich vegutz*: the "identifying marks" referenced are nothing more than height — tall or short. Such characteristics are far too generic to count as a *siman*. They do not rise to the level of an identifying mark in any meaningful sense.

Regarding clothing — *keilav* — the Gemara raises the concern of *she'ila*: people lend their clothes to others, so clothing cannot serve as a reliable identifier. This concern, however, generates a counter-challenge: if we are worried about objects being lent, how do we return lost items (*hashavas aveida*) based on *simanim* such as the saddle (*uchaf*) of a donkey, as is done in tractate Bava Metzia? The Gemara replies: *lo sheili inshi uchfa demaska lei lechara* — people do not lend out saddles, because a saddle not fitted to a particular donkey will irritate its back. The same concern that produces the rule also supplies its exception.

### Ketubot Standard

A parallel challenge is raised regarding the *get* case: how can a *get* be returned based on its attachment to a pouch or signet ring if people lend such items? The Gemara answers: *taba'as chashinan leziyufa* — one does not lend out a signet ring for fear of forgery; *menachshi inshi velo moshli* — people treat their personal pouches and wallets as highly personal objects, associated with personal identity to such a degree that they will not lend them. The Gemara thus accounts for each category individually rather than resolving the lending concern universally.

An alternative resolution — *iba'is eima keilav d'chivri vesumki* — proposes that we are not concerned about lending of this kind in general, and that the mishna's exclusion of clothing applies only because the description was wholly generic: "he was wearing a white jacket" is too common to identify anyone.

### Final Ruling

The Gemara's conclusion, at least according to one strand of analysis, is that *simanim de'oraita*: identifying marks have biblical validity. The mishna's rejection of body characteristics is because those characteristics fell below the threshold of *simanim* entirely — they were generic descriptions, not identifying marks. A genuine *siman*, and certainly a *siman muvhak*, would in principle suffice even without seeing the face. This ruling substantially expands the halakhic basis for Rabbeinu Tam's more flexible approach, which now appears less as a creative departure and more as a logical extension of the Gemara's own framework.

---

## Wounded vs. Dead

### Wounds Alone

The mishna now addresses a second dimension of the testimony requirement: it is not enough to identify who the person was — one must also establish that he is actually dead. *Ein me'idin ela ad she'teitzei nafsho* — one may only testify once the soul has actually departed. *V'afilu ra'uhu meguyad* — even if witnesses saw him with severed arteries (*meguyad*, which Rashi explains as referring to severed *gidim*, and Jastrow renders as cut arteries, apparently a mode of execution in some places), *o tzaluv* — crucified, *o chayah ochelet bo* — or being consumed by a wild animal: none of these observations suffices. The man was still alive, however improbably he might have survived, and testimony of his death requires witnessing actual death.

### Severed Artery Debate

This ruling seems to imply that a *meguyad* — someone with severed arteries — can in fact survive. The Gemara challenges this from a mishna elsewhere stating that a person does not cause corpse-*tumah* until he has literally expired: *afilu meguyad ve'afilu goses*, even someone with cut arteries or someone in his final death throes. The implication, the Gemara observes, is that while such a person has not yet died, it is clear he will die — *hamachya lo chaya*. If so, how can our mishna say we cannot testify to his death?

Abaye resolves the contradiction: *ha Rabi Shimon ben Elazar veha rabbanan* — the two sources reflect a *tannaitic* dispute. A *baraita* records that one *may* testify about a *meguyad* but may *not* testify about someone crucified — but Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says *af al hameguyad ein me'idin*, even about a *meguyad* one may not testify, *mipnei sheyakhol lachvot velichyot* — because the wound might be stanched and the person might survive. Our mishna follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar; the *baraita*'s first position reflects the view of the Rabbis who hold that a *meguyad* will definitely die.

### Asia Case

The Gemara raises a further difficulty: if our mishna follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, it seems to contradict itself. The later portion of the mishna (to be discussed in full on the following daf) records a case from Asia in which a man was lowered into the sea and when the rope was pulled back up only his leg remained — *velo alta beyadam ela raglo*. The *chachamim* ruled: *min harkuva ulemala tinasei* — if the leg was severed from above the knee, his wife may remarry; *min harkuva ulemata lo tinasei* — below the knee, she may not. Severing a leg above the knee necessarily involves severing major arteries, making this essentially a case of *meguyad*. Yet the *chachamim* permit remarriage in that case. How can the mishna simultaneously follow Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and permit testimony in the Asia case?

---

## Fatal Wounds

### Water Irritation

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction: *shani mayim demirzaz maka* — water is different, because water irritates the wound. When a man is submerged in the ocean with a severed leg, the seawater irritates and aggravates the wound in a way that makes survival impossible. This is unlike a standard case of *meguyad* on dry land, where cauterization or stanching might allow survival. The Asia case is therefore a special category where death is certain even according to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

### Camel Example

The Gemara then addresses a related challenge from a story told by Rabba bar bar Chana: *ledidi chazi li hahu taya* — "I myself saw a certain Arab nomad who took his sword and severed part of a camel, *velo afsiktiah line'urasei*" — and it did not cease its moaning." Rashi explains this as meaning the camel moaned continuously until it died. The story seems to prove that a *meguyad* dies — which supports the Rabbis against Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who says survival is possible. But of course the fact that a camel died in one instance does not establish that all *meguyad* cases are fatal; it merely shows death is possible, not inevitable.

The alternative and more workable reading of the story is that the camel survived despite the severing — the moaning continued because it was still alive — which would prove that a *meguyad* can indeed live, supporting Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's position. The Gemara then confronts the challenge: if the camel *lived*, how does this coexist with the Rabbis' view that a *meguyad* certainly dies?

### Special Circumstances

Two answers are offered. Abaye says: *haki kachisha havya* — it was a thin, sickly camel, and some particular feature of its weakened constitution explains the outcome. Rava offers a more satisfying resolution: *besakin meluvenet divrei hakol* — the sword was white-hot, and everyone would agree that in such a case the cauterizing effect of the heated blade would allow survival. The case of the Arab nomad was a special circumstance — a cauterizing wound — and proves nothing about ordinary *meguyad* cases. Both answers accept that the camel survived, and explain why the case is exceptional rather than representative.

---

## Gittin Get Case

### Two Simanim

Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel: *shachat bo shnayim o rov shnayim uvarach me'idin* — if the trachea and esophagus (the two *simanim* of *shechita*) or the majority of them were severed and the man fled, one may testify to his death. This ruling is consistent with the earlier discussion: just as an animal being consumed at the neck would permit testimony (since the vital site is directly involved), so too the severing of the two *simanim* at the throat establishes that death is certain.

Rav Yehuda further cites Shmuel in the *Gittin* context: *shachat bo shnayim o rov shnayim veramaz ve'amar kitvu get le'ishti harei elu yichtevu veyitnu* — if a man with his trachea and esophagus severed signals that a *get* should be written for his wife, it may be written and delivered. This is a striking ruling. Why would a man want his wife to receive a *get* at the moment of death? The answer — consistent with the *masechta* being studied — is to release her from *yibum*: she will receive the *get*, become a divorcée rather than a widow, and not require *yibum* from the surviving brothers.

### Alive Until Dead

The Gemara notes an apparent tension: if the man with severed *simanim* will certainly die, how can a *get* be valid? A *get* requires the husband to be alive at the time of delivery. The Gemara resolves it simply: *chai hu vesofo lamut* — he is alive right now; his death is coming, but he has not yet died. The *get* is valid because he is halachically alive at the moment of delivery. This point carries significant weight for broader halakhic discussions of the definition of death. Even a person whose trachea and esophagus are both severed is halachically alive — capable of giving a *get*, presumably capable of other halachic acts — until actual death supervenes. This understanding has direct implications for contemporary discussions of brain death, a topic the Gemara here deliberately sidesteps by focusing on the biological threshold as understood in its own framework.

### No Galut

The Gemara raises a difficulty: if severing the two *simanim* will certainly result in death, why does a *baraita* rule *harei ze eino goleh* — that someone who accidentally severs the trachea and esophagus of another person does not go into exile (*galut*)? Accidental killing normally requires exile. If death is certain from this wound, exile should follow.

---

## Multiple Causation

### Wind or Self-Action

Rav Hoshaya resolves the difficulty: *chayshinan shema haruach bilbelato* — we are concerned that perhaps the wind contributed to the person's death after the initial wounding. Or alternatively: *shema hu kirev mitato* — perhaps the victim himself hastened his own death, by convulsing or agitating the wound. The principle is one of multiple causation: when factors beyond the initial act may have contributed to death, the standard for *galut* is not met, because *galut* requires that the death be entirely and unambiguously attributable to the perpetrator's act.

### Marble vs. Outdoors

The Gemara distinguishes between the two possibilities raised by Rav Hoshaya. *Deshachte beveisa deshisha uperches* — if the severing occurred in a marble house (completely enclosed, no wind) but the victim convulsed (*parches*), wind is not a factor but self-action may be. *Deshachte bevara velo parches* — if it occurred outdoors (wind possible) but the victim did not convulse, then wind is a factor but self-action is not. The Gemara explores how these scenarios map onto the two distinct explanations offered by Rav Hoshaya.

### Intentional Acts Standard

Tosafot observes that the principle of multiple causation and the *galut* exemption are specific to the laws of *galut*, which have uniquely demanding standards for establishing causation.
