The analogy to the contemporary case of a person who was wounded decades ago and recently died from those wounds is instructive: in such a case, even if other factors over the intervening years contributed to the eventual death, the original wound remains the foundational cause. For *galut*, however, the halakha demands a much higher degree of exclusive causal attribution — if *any* other factor may have contributed, the exemption applies. If the severing had been intentional rather than accidental, there would be no question: the perpetrator would be liable, regardless of whether wind or other factors may have marginally accelerated death. The *galut* exemption is a function of the narrow and highly technical standards that govern that specific *din*, not a general principle about causation in homicide.

---

---

# Yevamot 121

## Body ID & 3-Day Rule

### Rabbi Yehuda's Position

The daf opens with a *mishna* near the top of 121 in which the question of identifying a drowned man's body is governed by a three-day standard: after three days the body may bloat beyond recognition, so the window for valid identification closes. Rabbi Yehuda dissents, arguing that not all people are the same and not all conditions are the same — no fixed rule can be applied uniformly across every case.

### Lenient or Strict?

The *gemara* asks: *Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava, likula pligi o lechumra pligi?* — Is Rabbi Yehuda being lenient or strict relative to the *chachamim*? Tosafos notes that the obvious answer is neither, or rather both: his position is that there is no fixed rule. He is strict in the sense that sometimes even fewer than three days may be insufficient, and lenient in the sense that sometimes more than three days may still allow valid identification. The point is that circumstance determines the outcome, not an arbitrary standard.

### Proof Sources

The *gemara* then brings two cases to demonstrate that Rabbi Yehuda's position at minimum permits leniency beyond the three-day limit. In the first, a man drowned in a place called Charmi, his body was recovered in a location called Chadya, and Rav Dimi of Nehardea permitted his wife to remarry — after three days. In the second, a man drowned in the Tigris, his body was recovered at the bridge of Shavistana, and Rava permitted his wife to remarry based on the testimony of the deceased's *shushvini* — his close companions — after five days. The *gemara* argues: if Rabbi Yehuda is being lenient, these rulings make sense as following his position. But if he is only being strict — tightening the standard so that even fewer than three days may be insufficient — then who are Rav Dimi and Rava following?

### Water Shrinkage

The *gemara* deflects: *shani maye d'tsamtei* — water is different, because it shrivels the body. Therefore, in drowning cases specifically, there is more time within which identification remains possible. This means Rav Dimi and Rava may actually be following the *chachamim* who maintain the three-day standard, while applying a recognized extension for the category of drowning — distinct from Rabbi Yehuda's case-by-case approach. The irony is not lost: Rabbi Yehuda's whole point is that you cannot make categorical rules, yet the *gemara* proposes that drowning constitutes its own formal category warranting extended time.

There is an apparent tension with a principle discussed previously — that *maya marzu maka*, water exacerbates a wound and makes even non-fatal injuries lethal. The *gemara* resolves this: that principle applies where there is an existing wound. Where there is no wound, *mitsmat tsamit* — the water will shrivel the body, permitting identification over a longer period.

### Timing of Exam

A further qualification follows: this extended window applies only *dehachi aska chazi besha'atei* — if, when the body was brought out of the water, it was examined immediately. But *aval ishtahi*, if they waited before examining it, *mitpach tapach* — it will bloat once removed from the water and will no longer be recognizable. The *gemara* does not reach a firm conclusion about the precise scope of Rabbi Yehuda's disagreement, but it is clear that even the *chachamim's* three-day standard should not be read as an absolutely rigid rule.

---

## Edges of Water

### Definition of Edges

The *mishna* now introduces one of the central distinctions in this chapter: *mayim she-yesh lahem sof* versus *mayim she-ein lahem sof* — water that has a visible edge versus water that does not. The formulation, *nafal lemayim bein she-yesh lahem sof bein she-ein lahem sof*, sets up the question of whether the wife of a drowning victim may remarry. The principle that emerges is counterintuitive at first glance: if the shores of the water are visible on all sides, the wife may remarry even without a body; if the shores cannot be seen, she may not. One might have thought that visible shores would give the man a better chance of escape and survival — which is precisely why the rule makes sense. If the shores are visible and he did not emerge, we can be confident he did not survive. If the water is boundless and the far edges cannot be seen, he may have emerged somewhere beyond sight.

A student raises a sharp point: a river would always seem to qualify as *ein lahem sof*, since one can never see its terminus. The *gemara* will bear this out.

### Rabbi Meir Position

The *mishna* opens with the position of Rabbi Meir, clarified by a *baraita*: *nafal lemayim bein she-yesh lahem sof bein she-ein lahem sof ishto asurah divrei Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Meir holds that in either case, without a body, the wife is forbidden. He supports this with a case: *ma'aseh be-echad she-nafal le-vor gadol ve-alah le-achar sheloshah yamim* — a certain person fell into a deep pit and emerged alive after three days. As long as there is no confirmed body, the man might have survived. Rabbi Meir's position is therefore absolute: no body, no testimony, no remarriage, regardless of the water's extent.

### Rabbi Yosi's Cases

Rabbi Yosi disagrees, though characteristically he does not state a legal principle directly — he responds with stories. First, a blind man descended into a cave to immerse; another person apparently followed him down. The sages waited the time estimated to be sufficient for both men to die from lack of air or sustenance, and then permitted their wives to remarry. Second, in Asia, a man was lowered into the sea for deep-sea diving and only his leg was recovered.

### Severed Limb Rule

Regarding the recovered limb, the sages ruled: *min ha-arkuvah ule-ma'lah tinasei* — if the leg was severed above the knee, the wife may remarry, since a wound of that severity is certainly fatal. *Min ha-arkuvah ule-matah lo tinasei* — if it was severed below the knee, she may not. This case is somewhat distinct from the broader debate, since here physical evidence of a fatal wound exists; the question is merely whether the partial body is sufficient proof of death. The deeper disagreement between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosi concerns whether one can declare death without any body at all, based solely on lethal circumstances.

### Baraita Rule

The *gemara* presents a *baraita* that makes the positions explicit: *nafal lemayim bein she-yesh lahem sof bein she-ein lahem sof ishto asurah divrei Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Meir forbids in all cases. *Ve-chachamim omrim, mayim she-yesh lahem sof ishto muteret* — the *chachamim* permit the wife to remarry if the water has a visible edge. *Ve-she-ein lahem sof, ishto asurah* — if the water has no visible edge, she is forbidden, since the man might have emerged somewhere beyond the observer's sight.

### 4-Direction Test

The *gemara* asks: what exactly constitutes *mayim she-yesh lahem sof*? Abaye defines it: *kol she-omed vero-eh me-arba ruchotav* — any body of water where one can stand and see its shores in all four directions. If even one direction is unobserved, one cannot rule out that the man emerged there.

---

## Rav Shila Story

### Wife Married

The *gemara* presents a case: a man drowned in the swamp of Samki. Rav Shila permitted the man's wife to remarry. Upon learning this, Rav said to Shmuel: *ta nishmateih* — let us excommunicate him, placing him in *shamta*, since this swamp appears to be a case of *ein lahem sof*, and Rav Shila had no authority to permit the wife.

### Shmuel's Advice

Shmuel counseled restraint: *nishlach lei bereisha* — let us first send him a message and investigate before acting. They sent Rav Shila two questions. First: in water that has no visible edge, is the wife permitted or forbidden? He responded: *ishto asurah* — she is forbidden. Second: is the swamp of Samki considered *yesh lahem sof* or *ein lahem sof*? Pressed, he acknowledged it was *ein lahem sof*. They then asked him directly: given these concessions, why did you permit her to remarry?

### Rav's Admission

Rav Shila admitted: *mita te'ina* — I made a mistake. *Ana savri, kivan d'ka-i v'kaimi k'mayim she-yesh lahem sof dami* — I assumed that since this is standing water — a swamp, with no moving current — even though the edges cannot be seen, it functions like *mayim she-yesh lahem sof*. My reasoning was that if the water is still, a person who survived would have surfaced near where he went under. There would be no current to carry him elsewhere.

This was, on its face, a very reasonable assumption. Indeed, the puzzle in the story is how exactly Rav Shila came to reverse himself. When asked whether the swamp was *yesh lahem sof* or *ein lahem sof*, he presumably should have answered *yesh lahem sof* — since that was his original reasoning. Somewhere in the questioning he recognized that his interlocutors did not approve of his ruling, and he adjusted his position accordingly.

### Waves Theory

The *gemara* explains why the reasoning fails: *kivan d'ika gali, eimar gali ashpluhu* — since there are waves, or currents, in the swamp, perhaps the currents carried him beneath the surface. Even in seemingly still water, wind alone acting on the surface can generate waves sufficient to carry a body. Therefore, even standing water without visible shores remains categorically *ein lahem sof*.

### No Shamta

Once it became clear that Rav Shila had acted in good faith, making an honest legal error rather than willfully defying accepted practice, the question of *shamta* fell away. *Shamta* is reserved for one who brazenly violates established bounds, not for a *posek* who reasons carefully and errs. Accordingly, Shmuel applied to Rav the verse *lo ye-uneh la-tzadik kol aven* — no harm comes to the righteous man — since Rav was spared from the improper act of excommunicating someone who had made an honest mistake. And Rav applied to Shmuel the verse *ve-teshuah b'rov yo-etz* — salvation comes from good counsel — crediting Shmuel's prudent advice for saving him from that error. Regarding the woman herself, the *gemara* will address this shortly: even in a case of *ein lahem sof* without a body, if the wife was in fact permitted and married, she may remain married *bedi'avad*.

---

## Against Rabbi Meir

### Rejected Meir

By this point in the sugya it has become clear that the *halacha* follows the *chachamim* against Rabbi Meir. In cases of *mayim she-yesh lahem sof*, even without a body, one may testify to the husband's death and the wife may remarry.

### Torah Sages

Rav Ashi introduces a further extension: *hada amru rabanan mayim she-ein lahem sof ishto asurah, hani mili be-inish de-alma* — when the *rabbanan* say that in boundless water the wife is forbidden, that applies to an ordinary person. *Aval tzurba me-rabanan* — but if the deceased was a Torah sage, then even in *ein lahem sof*, one may assume he is dead. The reasoning is: *e d'salik, kala is lei* — if he had survived and emerged somewhere, word would have spread, since he is a person of consequence. The absence of any such report is itself evidence of his death.

### No Fame Rule

The *gemara* rejects this: *velo hi, lo shna inish de-alma velo shna tzurba me-rabanan* — this distinction does not hold. Fame does not create a legal category that transforms the evidentiary standard. The underlying concern about boundless water applies equally to sages and ordinary men.

### Bedi'avad Rule

However, the *gemara* now introduces, without extensive discussion, a principle that is not apparent in the *mishna* at all and is something of a surprise: *bedi'avad*, if the woman already remarried — even in a case of *ein lahem sof* without a recovered body — *le-chatchila lo*, she cannot be permitted to remarry at the outset, but if she did, she may remain with her new husband. This is a significant ruling that the *gemara* drops almost in passing, and it will resurface explicitly in the later discussion of the Chassa case.

---

## Shipwreck Stories

### Rav Dimi Case

The *gemara* cites a *baraita* in which Rabbi — Rebbe Yehuda HaNasi — reports a story of two fishermen casting nets in the Jordan. One entered an underwater tunnel where fish were found and became trapped when night fell and he could no longer see the exit. His companion waited long enough to conclude the man had died and informed his household. The next morning, when light returned, the trapped fisherman found the opening and returned home to find a *hesped gadol* — a great eulogy — already underway in his house. Rashi explains that there were air pockets within the cavern that allowed him to survive.

### Gamliel's Praise

Rabbi concludes this account with the words *kamah gedolim divrei chachamim* — how great are the words of the sages. The *gemara* will explain his precise intent in what follows.

### Gamliel Shipwreck

The *gemara* raises an objection: if this cavern-survival is possible, should we not also be concerned about it even in cases of *yesh lahem sof*? The *gemara* responds: *mayim she-yesh lahem sof, mechila shel dagin lo shchichi* — in smaller, bounded bodies of water, such underwater caverns with air pockets are uncommon. The rule for *ein lahem sof* is thus justified by the greater range of unusual possibilities that vast bodies of water present, including both distance of emergence and subterranean air pockets.

A *baraita* records Rabban Gamliel's testimony: he was once sailing and saw another ship wrecked at sea. He was distressed in particular for the Torah sage aboard — Rabbi Akiva. When he later docked and Rabbi Akiva appeared before him to discuss *halacha*, Rabban Gamliel asked how he had survived. Rabbi Akiva told him that a plank from the shipwreck had come his way, and he had clung to it. Regarding each wave that approached, *naaneti lo roshi* — he bent his head so the wave passed over him rather than knocking him off.

### Akiva's Survival

From this experience Rabbi Akiva derived a *mashal*: *im yavo-u resha-im al adam, yenane-a lo rosho* — when wicked people come against a person, bow the head, let the force pass. Discretion is preferable to a futile stand. Rabban Gamliel concluded: *kamah gedolim divrei chachamim she-amru mayim she-yesh lahem sof muteret mayim she-ein lahem sof asurah* — how great is the ruling that in boundless water the wife is forbidden, because he himself had witnessed a shipwreck in open ocean and yet the man survived, carried to safety on a plank, invisible to any observer.

### Akiva's 2nd

A second *baraita* then presents the parallel account from Rabbi Akiva's own perspective. Rabbi Akiva reports that he was once at sea and saw another ship in distress, aboard which was a Torah sage — Rabbi Meir. When Rabbi Akiva later arrived at Cappadocia (*Kaftor*, identified with modern-day Turkey), Rabbi Meir appeared and wished to discuss *halacha*. Rabbi Akiva asked how he had survived. Rabbi Meir replied: *gal tardani le-chavero ve-chavero le-chavero, ad she-hikiani la-yabasha* — one wave cast me to the next, and the next to the next, until I was thrown ashore. Rabbi Akiva likewise concluded: *kamah gedolim divrei chachamim she-amru mayim she-yesh lahem sof isha muteret mayim she-ein lahem sof isha asurah* — since a person can survive in open water by being swept from wave to wave to a shore beyond sight, therefore we must forbid remarriage in *ein lahem sof*.

It is worth noting that this shipwreck — an event presumably of great consequence in Rabbi Akiva's life — appears here only as an aside. And as one might note, the stories have a somewhat formulaic quality: in each account, the teacher witnesses his student's ship in distress, the student survives through a remarkable means, and the teacher draws the same legal conclusion. Nevertheless, the Talmudic point they illustrate remains clear and vivid.

---

## Non-Water Cases

### Lions Pit

The *gemara* turns to cases that do not involve water. *Nafal le-gov arayot, ein me-idim alav* — if a man fell into a pit of lions, one cannot testify to his death, because we cannot be certain the lions attacked him. Rashi suggests the lions may not have been hungry, and indeed observation from wildlife contexts suggests that lions do not attack simply out of proximity.

### Snakes/Scorpions

*Le-chafura me-le-a nechashim va-akrabim, me-idim alav* — if he fell into a pit full of snakes and scorpions, the *tanna kamma* holds that one can testify to his death, since in such crowded conditions they will certainly attack him. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira disagrees: *af le-chafura me-le-a nechashim va-akrabim ein me-idim alav* — even there one cannot testify, since we must consider the possibility that *shema chaver hu* — perhaps the man is a snake charmer who knows how to handle them. The *tanna kamma* responds: *agav itzam mat-ke-lei* — even a snake charmer, if he is being pressed and crowded by them, will be bitten.

### Fiery Furnace

*Nafal le-toch kivshan ha-esh, me-idim alav* — if thrown into a fiery furnace, one can testify to his death. This scenario recalls the story of Chananya, Mishael, and Azaryah, and it is understood that survival in such circumstances would require open miracle.

### Boiling Liquids

If a man fell into a large vat, *yora*, filled with boiling wine or oil, a distinction is drawn. In the name of Rabbi Akiva: *shemen me-idim alav mipnei she-hu maveer* — in boiling oil one can testify to his death, since when he falls in, the oil splashes onto the fire and intensifies it. *Shel yayin, ein me-idim alav mipnei she-hu mechabeh* — but in boiling wine, one cannot testify to his death, since the wine splashes onto the fire and extinguishes it, potentially allowing escape. The sages respond to this: *techila hu mechabeh ve-sofo maveer* — it may initially douse the flame but the fire will reignite, so ultimately death can be assumed.

### Well Miracle

Rabbi Meir reasserts his position: *ma-aseh be-echad she-nafal le-vor gadol* — a man fell into a large well and survived for three days. Therefore, absent a confirmed body, one can never testify to death. The *baraita* records the sages' response: *ein mazkirin ma-aseh nissim* — one cannot cite miracles as legal precedent. Halachic standards must be calibrated to normal circumstances.

### Sleep & Ledges

The *gemara* asks what the miraculous element of the survival was. If it was merely that he went without food and water for three days — *tzomu alai ve-al tochlu ve-al tishtu shloshet yamim* — we know people can survive that long. Rather, the *gemara* suggests, the miracle is that he did not sleep. Rabbi Yochanan rules that a vow not to sleep for three days is a *shvuat shav* — an oath that cannot be kept — and the person is immediately lashed and permitted to sleep. Staying awake for three days is considered physiologically impossible and therefore miraculous.

Rabbi Meir's counter: Rav Kahana suggests that perhaps *kifin al gabi kifin havu* — there were ledges within the well on which he could have positioned himself and slept. The Rabbis respond that *de-shisha havu* — the ledges were smooth marble, offering no secure foothold for sleep. Rabbi Meir maintains it is conceivable to lean against a small indentation and rest. The discussion leaves unresolved exactly how any of this maps onto the water-survival question, but the broader point stands: miracles cannot serve as the basis for legal standards.

---

## Nechunya Story

### Daughter Saved

The *gemara* presents a well-known *aggadic* account: the daughter of Nechunya the well-digger — whose great *mitzvah* to the public was digging wells for the *olei regel*, those who ascended to Jerusalem for the pilgrims' festivals — fell into a large well. The people came and informed Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa. After the first hour he told them: *shalom*, she is fine. After the second hour: *shalom*. After the third hour — the point at which survival was considered no longer possible — he said: *alta*, she has been saved, she has come up.

### Ram & Old Man

When asked how she survived, she reported: *zachar shel rachelim nizdamen li, ve-zaken manhigo* — a ram appeared for her, and an old man was leading it. Rashi identifies the old man as Avraham Avinu, and the ram as the ram of the Akeidah.

### Tzadik Logic

When people came to Rabbi Chanina and said *navi ata* — you must be a prophet, to have known she was saved — he replied: *lo navi anochi velo ben navi anochi*. His reasoning was not prophecy but inference: *ela davar she-ha-tzadik mit-asek bo, yikashel bo zar-o?* — could it be that the very thing this righteous man devoted his life to would be the instrument of his child's death? His whole life was spent ensuring the public had water. That his daughter would perish in a well was inconceivable to Rabbi Chanina. A *tzadik's* life's work cannot end in the undoing of his own household through that very work.

### Son's Thirst

Rabbi Abba then introduces the jarring counterpoint: *af al pi chen, met b'no ba-tzama* — nevertheless, his son died of thirst. The man who spent his life making water available died having a son who perished for lack of it.

### Harsh Justice

The verse cited is *u-svivav nis-ara me-od* — around Him there is great storm — interpreted as *melamed she-ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu medakdek im svivav ke-chut ha-se-ara* — God exacts from those close to Him with the precision of a hair's breadth. Tosafos attempts to soften the juxtaposition, noting that at least it was not the same well Nechunya dug from which his son died. But the *gemara* does not allow the narrative to rest comfortably on the idea that the world is simply just or that *tzadikim* are shielded from tragedy. The juxtaposition is deliberate: yes, the daughter was saved, and yes, the son died. The world is not simply ordered by reward and punishment in predictable ways, and even those close to God are held to an exacting standard that brings suffering alongside blessing.

---

## Hearsay Evidence

### Women's Hearsay

The *mishna* now broadens the categories of acceptable testimony in agunah cases in a striking direction: *afilu shama min ha-nashim omrot met ish ploni dayo* — even if one merely heard from women saying that so-and-so has died, that suffices. While earlier *mishnayot* had already indicated that women could testify in these contexts, the novelty here is not the gender of the witness but the informality of the communication. This is not a formal act of testimony — it is hearsay.

### Children Testify

Rabbi Yehuda goes further: *afilu shama min ha-tinokot omrim harei anu holchim lispod u-likbor et ish ploni* — even if one hears from children saying, "we are going to eulogize and bury so-and-so," that suffices. Here the witness lacks legal standing on two grounds: children are not formal witnesses, and the statement is not presented as testimony.

### Intent Question

The *mishna* continues: *bein she-nitkaven bein she-eino mitkaven* — whether the speaker intended to testify or not. This raises the question of whether intentionality, which typically strengthens testimony, is here a factor at all.

### Jew vs. Non-Jew

Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava distinguishes between Jews and non-Jews. Regarding a non-Jew: *u-v'ovdei kochavim im haya mitkaven ein eduto edut* — if a non-Jew intentionally testified, it is not valid testimony. The concern is that an intentional non-Jewish declaration may be motivated by a desire to cause harm. Only when a non-Jew speaks innocently — *mesiach lefi tumo* — do we trust him, since there is no suspicion of an ulterior motive. Regarding a Jew, there are two variant readings in the text: one holds that even intentional testimony by a Jew is acceptable; the other, the inverse — that a Jew must testify formally and intentionally for his statement to carry weight, while mere passing remarks are insufficient.

---

## Intention Narrowed

### Rav Yehuda

The *gemara* now works to narrow the category of *nitkaven* — intentional testimony — to a very thin slice. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules: *lo shanu ela she-nitkaven le-hatir* — the disqualification of a non-Jew's intentional testimony applies only if his explicit intent was to permit the woman to remarry. *Aval nitkaven le-ha-id, eduto edut* — if he came merely to testify, stating the fact of the man's death without specifically invoking the wife's status, his testimony is valid. The practical result is that *nitkaven le-hatir* — explicitly coming to court to say "permit this woman to remarry" — becomes an extremely narrow category. How often does someone phrase his testimony that way? In almost every realistic case the man will simply say that the husband is dead, and that is accepted.

The *gemara* asks: how would we even know which intent he had? Rav Yosef clarifies: *ba le-veit din ve-amar ish ploni met, hasi-u et ishto, zehu nitkaven le-hatir* — if he came to court and said, "so-and-so has died; you should permit his wife to remarry," that is *nitkaven le-hatir*, and it is rejected. *Meit stam* — if he simply said "so-and-so is dead" without mentioning the wife, that is *nitkaven le-ha-id*, and it is accepted.

### Reish vs. Yochanan

Reish Lakish states the same principle: only explicit intent to permit her remarriage disqualifies the testimony. Rabbi Yochanan objects, citing a tradition that this very position — "only *nitkaven le-hatir* is disqualified, but *nitkaven le-ha-id* is valid" — was contested by eighty-five elders, who rejected it. According to Rabbi Yochanan, any intentional testimony by a non-Jew is disqualified, regardless of how he frames it. The *gemara* then presses Rabbi Yochanan: if any intentional statement is invalid, what does *mesiach lefi tumo* look like? The answer: *bemesiach lefi tumo* — a person simply speaking without any formal purpose. The subsequent cases illustrate this.

---

## Intention Narrowed (II)

### Innocent Speech

The *gemara* presents examples of *mesiach lefi tumo*. In one case, a man was walking about lamenting: *vai lah le-parshata de-zeriza dahavei be-Pumbedita de-shachiv* — woe to the zealous soldier from Pumbedita who has died. He was simply bewailing someone's death. On the basis of this, Rav Yosef — or according to another version, Rava — permitted the dead man's wife to remarry.

### Chassa Case

In another case, someone was going about asking: *man ika bei Chassa? tava Chassa* — who is from the family of Chassa? Chassa drowned. Rav Nachman, upon hearing this, exclaimed: *achlu kavrei le-Chassa* — the fish have eaten Chassa. What is striking here is that Rav Nachman's exclamation itself constitutes an implicit ruling: by saying the fish ate Chassa, he was accepting the testimony of this non-Jew speaking innocently, and implicitly ruling that Chassa should be presumed dead — without apparent concern that Chassa might have emerged on another shore. From this it follows that Rav Nachman was treating this as a case he was willing to rule upon.

---

## Bedi'avad Remarriage

### Stays Married

The *gemara* uses the Chassa case to crystallize the *bedi'avad* principle. When the *rabbanan* say *mayim she-ein lahem sof isha asurah* — that in boundless water the wife is forbidden — this refers to *lechatchila*: at the outset, a *beit din* may not permit her to remarry in such circumstances. But that prohibition is not absolute.

### Self-Marriage

Upon hearing Rav Nachman's remark that the fish had eaten Chassa, Chassa's wife took matters into her own hands: *azlah devinhu de-Chassa ve-insava* — she went and remarried on her own, without rabbinic sanction. She had not received a formal ruling; she overheard a scholar make a loose remark and acted unilaterally.

### No Divorce

Nevertheless, *velo amru lah velo midi* — no one said anything to her, before or after. The *gemara* did not require her to divorce her new husband. This is a powerful illustration of the *bedi'avad* principle: even where remarriage was not permitted prospectively, after the fact she is not compelled to undo it.

### Rav Nachman's Role

Some say (*ika de-amri*) that Rav Nachman actually did formally permit her: *ansivah Rav Nachman lidevinhu* — Rav Nachman permitted his wife to remarry. His reasoning would then parallel Rav Ashi's earlier suggestion: *Chassa gavra rabba isei, im issa de-salik kala is lei le-milsa* — Chassa was a man of great stature, and had he survived and emerged elsewhere, word would have reached us. The *gemara* rejects this reasoning: *velo hi, lo shna gavra rabba velo shna lo gavra rabba* — fame creates no legal distinction. This is not a valid basis for a *lechatchila* ruling, neither for the famous nor for the ordinary man.

### Lechatchila/Bedi'avad

The final distinction stands: *lechatchila*, a *beit din* may not permit remarriage in *ein lahem sof* without a body. *Bedi'avad* — if she remarried, she remains married. This principle, barely hinted at in the *mishna*, emerges through the case of Chassa's wife as one of the significant practical *chiddushim* of the entire sugya. The *gemara's* sustained drive throughout the daf has been to expand the conditions under which a woman can be freed from her *agunah* status, not by overriding the rules but by carefully defining their contours and by establishing that post-facto remarriage, even in borderline cases, is not undone.

# Yevamot 122

## Non-Jew Testimony

### Non-Jew Threat Case

The final daf of Masechet Yevamot picks up three lines from the bottom of 121b, in the midst of the broad question of who may be believed to testify that a man has died. The mishnah had already introduced the categories of women, children, and even incidental statements — *mesiach lefi tumo* — made in passing without deliberate intent to testify. The Gemara now turns to a specific case that tests the limits of accepting such testimony from a non-Jew.

A certain non-Jew told a Jew: cut down this fodder and throw it to my animals on Shabbat. And if you refuse, I will kill you just as I killed a certain other Jew — Reuven ben Shimon — who refused to cook for me on Shabbat. The non-Jew's threat was overheard by the wife of the man he claimed to have killed. She came before Abaye, reasoning that the statement sounded like *mesiach lefi tumo*: the non-Jew was not trying to testify but was simply invoking the killing as a point of intimidation, incidentally revealing what had happened. Could she assume her husband was dead and remarry?

Abaye kept her waiting through three *regalim*. Rashi offers two explanations for this delay. The first is that the *regalim* — the pilgrimage festivals — were occasions when Torah scholars gathered to hear discourses on the laws of each *chag*, and Abaye was using those assemblies to consult colleagues. The second reading comes from a responsum of the Geonim: that *regalim* as used by Amoraim does not refer to the pilgrimage festivals at all, but to the annual yahrzeit commemorations of great sages. According to this reading, Abaye waited three years. The Geonim describe the yahrzeit of a major *talmid chacham* as an occasion when scholars from the surrounding area would gather at his grave and hold a day of Torah study in his memory — essentially a yahrzeit lecture and commemorative gathering. This is fascinating not because the Gemara explicitly says any of this, but because the Geonim read the practice into it, revealing that such commemorations were already established by their time.

In any event, Abaye remained unresolved after all three consultations. Rav Adda bar Ahava told the woman she should go to Rav Yosef, Abaye's own teacher, who has a sharp knife — *deharif sakhina* — meaning he can cut through ambiguous questions decisively. She went, and Rav Yosef resolved the matter from a *braita* about a non-Jew selling fruit in the marketplace who said: these fruits are from a tree only in its second year, or from the place called Azaka, or from a fourth-year planting — *neta revai*. The Gemara rules that such a statement carries no weight — *lo amar klum* — because the seller was not speaking incidentally but with an ulterior motive: to make his wares sound more appealing. He was not *mesiach lefi tumo*; he had a reason to say what he said.

A brief but significant digression arises regarding the term *azaka*. Rashi prefers the reading that it refers to a place in Eretz Yisrael, raising questions of *tevel* when the fruit is sold in *chutz la'aretz*. He rejects the alternative reading — that the fruit came from a field that had been guarded during *shmita* — because he sees no reason why guarding a field during the sabbatical year would render its fruit forbidden. However, Tosafot cites Rabbeinu Tam, who brings the *Torat Kohanim* explicitly: "Do not harvest your grapes from the guarded" — *min hamshumar*; one may only harvest from produce that has been declared *hefker*. The act of guarding the field — exerting ownership over it — renders the fruit forbidden for harvest and likely forbidden altogether. It is striking that so central a question of *shmita* law finds its primary textual basis in the *Torat Kohanim* alone, with neither the mishnah nor the Yerushalmi addressing it directly.

Returning to the main thread: how is the fruit-seller case relevant to the woman whose husband may have been killed? Because in that case too, the non-Jew had a reason to say what he said — not to inform, but to threaten. He was coercing the Jew into violating Shabbat by claiming to have already killed someone who refused him. That is not *mesiach lefi tumo*. There is good reason to think he was lying, or at minimum not speaking as a disinterested party. The answer Rav Yosef gave was therefore that the woman could not remarry — not a useful result for her, though one might speculate that Abaye, who kept delaying, sensed this conclusion and was searching for a way to permit her rather than to forbid.

One might push back: the non-Jew was extremely specific — he named Reuven ben Shimon — and the man had not been seen for three years. That specificity might have been a reason to credit the testimony. But the Gemara is unpersuaded, because the motivation to threaten overrides the specificity. The principle that emerges is that *mesiach lefi tumo* is qualified: it does not operate when there is affirmative reason to think the speaker may be fabricating or exaggerating.

## Witnessing Standard (III)

### Geonic Responsum

As noted above, within the discussion of Abaye's extended deliberation, Rashi introduces a Geonic responsum identifying the *regalim* mentioned in the Gemara not as pilgrimage festivals but as the yearly yahrzeit gatherings held at the graves of major sages. The Geonim describe a practice in which, *midei shanah be-shanah*, scholars from the surrounding region would convene at the sage's burial site each year on the anniversary of his death, together with the broader community, to conduct a *yeshivah* — a day of Torah study — in his honor. This represents the earliest known reference to something resembling the yahrzeit lecture as an institution, though the Gemara itself says nothing of the kind. It is the Geonim who read this practice into the text, revealing both their interpretive creativity and the antiquity of the commemoration as a living custom by their era.

## Non-Jew Testimony (II)

### Fruit Seller Example

The analysis of the fruit-seller case establishes the controlling principle for when non-Jewish testimony is rejected: not because of a categorical rule against non-Jews, but because in that instance there was an identifiable motive for the speaker to say what he said that was independent of its truth. When the non-Jew in the market claimed his fruit came from a young tree or a protected field or from Eretz Yisrael, he was doing so to enhance the perceived value of his merchandise. His statement was therefore not a genuine *mesiach lefi tumo* — it was not an incidental, unmotivated disclosure, but a sales pitch. If we do not treat such a statement as reliable enough to be *machmir* — to create a *halakhic* concern about *orla* or *tevel* — then certainly we cannot treat it as reliable enough to be *meikel* — to permit a woman to remarry. The asymmetry is significant: even the lenient application of non-Jewish testimony requires the baseline of *mesiach lefi tumo*, which is absent when the speaker has an ulterior motive.

### Accepted Testimonies

In contrast, the Gemara proceeds to a series of cases in which non-Jewish testimony was fully accepted. Abba Yudan Ish Tzaidan reports: a Jew and a non-Jew were traveling together. The non-Jew returned alone and said, *chaval al Yehudi she-hayah imi baderech* — woe to the Jew who was traveling with me — he died on the way and I buried him. On that basis, his wife was permitted to remarry. This is a straightforward case of *mesiach lefi tumo*: the non-Jew was not being questioned, not trying to establish a legal fact, simply lamenting out loud.

A second story involves a group of people, described as a *kolar shel bnei adam*, who were traveling to Antioch. A non-Jew who had come from the same direction — not even a member of their party — arrived and said: woe to that group of people, they all died and I buried them. Their wives were married off on this basis. A third story: sixty people traveling toward the besieged city of *Karkom Beitar* — where *karkom* means besieged, not a place name — and a non-Jew who reported that they had all died and he had buried them. Their wives too were permitted to remarry.

It is worth pausing on the context of these final two cases. If *kolar* means that the first group were prisoners shackled with collars, then there was already an elevated likelihood that something terrible had happened to them. And people traveling toward a city under siege face obvious danger. It is not entirely clear how much the surrounding context of likely peril contributed to the credibility of the non-Jew's report, but the Gemara does not explicitly make that a condition. The principle appears to be that *mesiach lefi tumo* — the incidental statement without identifiable motive — is sufficient, and the Gemara is willing to be quite broad in applying it.

One might note that in none of these cases does the Gemara describe any attempt to verify the facts — to locate the grave, to find corroborating witnesses, to identify the body. The question the Gemara addresses is purely one of whose testimony is admitted, not of evidentiary sufficiency in the modern sense. These *halakhot*, it is worth noting, have found real application in tragic historical circumstances, including in *responsa* literature dealing with mass casualties where identifying individual deaths was impossible.

## Witnessing Standard (III)

### Light Requirements

The next mishnah shifts from the question of *who* may testify to the question of *how* clearly the death must have been witnessed. The mishnah rules: one may testify — and on that basis a woman may remarry — even if the witnessing occurred by candlelight or by moonlight. The requirement that the witness see the deceased's face does not mean he must have seen it under ideal conditions; limited illumination suffices.

### Bat Kol Testimony

The mishnah adds a remarkable ruling: *umasin al pi bat kol* — a woman may even be remarried based on a *bat kol*. This term, so common in the Bavli in the sense of a heavenly voice, carries a different and more primary meaning here. Rashi explains: *bat kol* means a disembodied voice — a voice whose source is not visible to the hearer. The witness heard someone announce that so-and-so had died, but did not see who was speaking. The *bat kol* is not a supernatural phenomenon; it is simply unattributed testimony heard without visual identification of the speaker. And since the Gemara has already extended acceptance to any category of testimony in this context, the identity of the speaker becomes irrelevant — which is precisely why even a *bat kol* is sufficient.

### Mountain Voice Case

The mishnah records: a person heard from the top of a mountain a voice declaring that so-and-so the son of so-and-so, from such-and-such a place, had died. They went to investigate who had spoken — and found no one. Even so, the wife was permitted to remarry. This case illustrates both the broad acceptance of unattributed testimony and also an important procedural instinct: when the source of testimony is unclear, one makes an effort to investigate further. Here the effort was made and came to nothing, yet that did not undermine the ruling. There was an attempt to verify; the attempt was inconclusive; the *bat kol* remained sufficient.

### Snake Bite Case

A parallel story from the town of Tsalmon: a man declared — *ani Ish Ploni ben Ish Ploni nashchani nachash* — I, so-and-so the son of so-and-so, have been bitten by a poisonous snake, and I am dying. By the time people arrived, they could not identify him — his features had apparently changed due to the venom. Nevertheless, his wife was permitted to remarry. The combination of self-identification and the plausible mechanism of death was deemed sufficient, even without a confirmable corpse. Once again, the effort to gather more information was made; once again it was frustrated; once again the testimony stood.

What emerges across these cases is a pattern: the Gemara expects an attempt to investigate further when the source of testimony is unknown or unclear, but it does not require that the attempt succeed. And the standard for what constitutes testimony acceptable enough to permit remarriage is, by this point, remarkably permissive.

## Beit Shammai/Hillel

### Bat Kol Dispute

Rabba bar Shmuel cites a *braita*: Beit Shammai says a woman may not be remarried on the basis of a *bat kol*; Beit Hillel says she may. The Gemara immediately asks: given that we have a *stam mishnah* — an anonymous mishnah — ruling in accordance with Beit Hillel, why does it matter that the *braita* records Beit Shammai's position? The Gemara answers: to tell us that if one finds another *stam* source appearing to say that a woman may not remarry on the basis of a *bat kol*, one should not conclude that the *halakha* is undecided. Rather, recognize it as the position of Beit Shammai and set it aside accordingly.

### Recording Minority Views

This answer surfaces a well-known question from Masechet Eduyot: why record a minority opinion if we do not rule in accordance with it? Two quite opposite answers are offered there. The first is inclusive: minority opinions are recorded so that they remain available for future use in cases of pressing need — *sha'at hadechak*. The second is exclusionary and is the one the Gemara invokes here: minority opinions are recorded precisely so that if anyone ever advocates for that position, it can be identified and dismissed. Recording Beit Shammai's view on *bat kol* is not an invitation to reconsider it; it is a taxonomic act, filing it away so that it can never be mistaken for mainstream *halakha*. These two rationales are not complementary; they represent genuinely opposite approaches to the status of rejected legal positions within the tradition.

There is an additional irony worth noting. The celebrated dispute between Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai over which school's rulings we follow was itself famously resolved by a *bat kol* that declared the *halakha* to follow Beit Hillel. Here it is Beit Shammai who rejects the evidentiary weight of a *bat kol*, and Beit Hillel who accepts it — which lends a certain poetic consistency to each school's position across these two quite different contexts.

## Witnessing Standard (III)

### Demon/Co-wife Question

The Gemara raises an obvious challenge to the mountain-voice case: perhaps the voice came not from a human being at all, but from a demon. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav responds that the figure appeared to have the *dmus adam* — the form of a human being. The Gemara presses: but demons can appear in human form. What if a shadow was seen? Demons too can cast shadows. What if a shadow of a shadow was observed? Rav Chanina cites Rabbi Yonasan, who reports having been told by a demon directly: demons have shadows, but they do not have shadows of shadows. Seeing a shadow of a shadow is thus the identifying mark of a genuine human presence.

A further concern is raised: perhaps the voice belonged to a *tzarah* — a co-wife — who has a clear motive to lie about her rival's husband's death and is explicitly excluded from this type of testimony. The Gemara invokes a parallel teaching from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: in a time of danger, one may write and deliver a *get* even without knowing the person, relying entirely on their self-identification, because the alternative is that the woman will be left without recourse. Similarly here — *kasha'at sakana damya* — if we cannot determine who spoke, and the only alternative is leaving the woman as an *agunah*, we proceed on the reasonable assumption that the speaker was not one of the five excluded categories.

It is admittedly difficult to know exactly where the threshold of *mesiach lefi tumo* lies — the Gemara elsewhere counted as *mesiach lefi tumo* a person who came specifically intending to inform the wife, without being questioned at all. Yet that same Gemara did not consider it *nitkavein l'haid* — deliberate testimony. The category seems to resist clean definition. What is clear is that the further from a formal testimonial context, the more comfortable the Gemara is in accepting what is said.

## Halacha Development

### Akiva in Nehardea

The Gemara now delivers one of its most historically remarkable passages — a window into how a sweeping *halakhic* innovation actually developed. Rabbi Akiva says: when I went down to Nehardea — the phrase *yaradti* reflecting the geographical and perhaps spiritual descent from Eretz Yisrael to the diaspora — I went to intercalate the year, which itself is striking, since the authority for *ibbur hashanah* ordinarily resided in Eretz Yisrael. There I found a certain Nechemya from Beit Deli, who told me: I have heard that in Eretz Yisrael a woman is not permitted to remarry on the basis of a single witness — *ed echad* — except according to Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava. Only he holds that position; no one else does.

This statement stops the reader cold. Everything the Gemara had seemed to take for granted — that *ed echad* is broadly accepted — turns out to have been the solitary position of one sage. The broad acceptance of testimony that has been the assumed framework throughout this *masechet* was not established practice at all; it was a contested minority view. Nechemya reported this to Rabbi Akiva and confirmed it was accurate. Nechemya then added: I cannot travel to testify myself because the country is *meshubbeshet begaysot* — riddled with military forces — but tell them in my name: *mekublani me-Rabban Gamliel Hazaken* — I have a tradition going back to Rabban Gamliel the Elder — that a woman may be remarried based on a single witness.

### Tel Arza Incident

Rabbi Akiva returned and reported this tradition to Rabban Gamliel the Younger — Rabban Gamliel of his own generation, not the Zaken. Rabban Gamliel rejoiced, saying: we have found a *chaver* — a supporting authority — for Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava. And in the midst of this conversation, Rabban Gamliel recalled that there had been a group of people killed at Tel Arza, and that their widows had not been permitted to remarry because the reports of their deaths rested only on *ed echad*, which had not been established practice. Armed now with the tradition from Rabban Gamliel Hazaken, Rabban Gamliel the Younger acted: he married off the wives of those killed at Tel Arza based on *ed echad*. The *halakha* moved from contested theory to executed practice.

And once it became established through practice — *ve-huchzeku* — the expansion did not stop there.

### Expansion of Testimony

The Gemara reports: once the practice was consolidated, they went further and permitted remarriage based on *ed mipi ed* — hearsay testimony, where the witness did not personally observe the death — and based on the testimony of a slave, a woman, and a female slave. Until this point, slaves had not been mentioned as a distinct category; the Gemara does not assume that because non-Jews are believed, slaves are believed automatically. And the category of hearsay testimony is itself a major *chidush* — one may remarry based on testimony from someone who did not witness the death firsthand but merely heard it reported.

### Tannaim Positions

The final line of the mishnah then reveals that this entire developmental history has a *tannaitic* antecedent. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua — who were Rabbi Akiva's own teachers — held that a woman may not be remarried based on *ed echad*; only two qualified witnesses or the wife's own testimony sufficed. Rabbi Akiva, in his earlier position before the Nehardea episode, agreed to accept *ed echad* but insisted it must be a qualified male witness — not a woman, not a slave, not a relative. The Gemara asks: but does Rabbi Akiva truly hold that a woman's testimony is insufficient? And it cites a *braita* in which Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reports in Rabbi Akiva's name that a woman is believed to bring her own *get* based on a *kal vachomer*.

### Women's Credibility

The *kal vachomer* runs as follows: the women whom the Sages said are *not* believed to testify that a husband has died — the co-wife, the mother-in-law, and the others in that category — are nonetheless believed to bring a *get* for a woman and attest that it was properly executed, since the physical document supports their word. If even those disqualified women are trusted in that context, how much more so should a woman who *is* believed to testify about death be trusted to bring her own *get*? The implication is that the five excluded women are the exception, and ordinary women are assumed to be reliable. Rabbi Akiva clearly held this.

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction between Rabbi Akiva's general principle of women's credibility and his specific ruling against accepting women's testimony in *eidut isha* cases as follows: *lo kashya* — the early position of Rabbi Akiva excluding women was *kodem she-hecheziku* — before the practice was consolidated by the Nehardea report and Rabban Gamliel's action. His later position accepting women was *me-acharei she-hecheziku* — after that consolidation.

The picture that emerges is breathtaking in its historical specificity. At the earliest stratum — the Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai debate — all that had been established was that a *wife* could testify about her own husband's death in a narrow set of circumstances. The acceptance of any other category of witness — *ed echad*, women, non-Jews, slaves, hearsay — was not a natural outgrowth of that ruling but a subsequent and contested development. The last line of the mishnah preserves the early, pre-consolidation positions as a kind of archaeological stratum within the text, a reminder of a moment when the *halakha* could have taken an entirely different path.

## Innkeeper Story

### Levites/Innkeeper

The next and final mishnah of the *masechet* presents a challenge to the pre-consolidation position of Rabbi Akiva. They said to him — to the early Rabbi Akiva who rejected women's testimony in *eidut isha* — there is a story about people called *Bnei Levi* who went to Tzo'a, the city of date palms. One of them fell ill, and they left him at an inn while they continued their journey. On their return, they asked the innkeeper: where is our companion? She said to them: he died and I buried him. On the basis of this testimony, his wife was permitted to remarry. If you can believe the word of this innkeeper, Rabbi Akiva, can you really maintain that women are not believed?

### Akiva's Challenge

Rabbi Akiva's response, in his early position: *le-she-tihiye ke-fundakit ne'emenet* — if women in general were to be like this innkeeper, they would indeed be believed. What distinguished this innkeeper?

### Physical Evidence

The innkeeper did not merely make a verbal report. She produced his effects: his staff, his traveling sack, and the *Sefer Torah* he had carried. *Mesiach lefi tumo* alone was not what made her credible in the early Rabbi Akiva's view — it was the physical evidence she brought forward that corroborated her statement. *Ze maklo ve-ze tarmilo ve-ze kever she-kevartiv bo* — this is his staff, this is his sack, and here is the grave where I buried him.

The Gemara then confirms, via Rav Kahana, that the innkeeper was in fact a non-Jewish woman — *pundakis ovedes kochavim hayasah* — which means the *kal vachomer* being pressed on Rabbi Akiva was even sharper than it had appeared. Not only was she a woman; she was a non-Jew. And she was believed — implicitly establishing that non-Jewish testimony was already a matter of *tannaitic* debate even at this early pre-consolidation stage, woven into the fabric of the dispute before Rabban Gamliel's decisive action.

The Gemara then raises a technical challenge: the innkeeper's testimony was not truly *mesiach lefi tumo*, because she was being directly asked — *aychan chaveirenu* — where is our friend? A direct question would seem to elicit deliberate testimony rather than an incidental remark. The Gemara resolves this: *keivan de-chazatinhu bachya* — because she saw them return and began to cry before they questioned her, the emotional response came first, naturally, and only then did the questioning follow. The crying established the spontaneous, unguarded quality of the disclosure — and then the verbal statement, though prompted, rode on that foundation of *mesiach lefi tumo*. The operative principle seems to be that testimony ceases to be *mesiach lefi tumo* when the speaker is being formally drilled for information in a context that resembles examination — but a natural emotional response, even if followed by direct questioning, preserves the character of an incidental statement.

## Cross-Exam Cases

### Spontaneous ID

The Gemara presents a case in which a man came to testify about a woman's status before Rabbi Tarfon. Rabbi Tarfon asked him: how do you know this testimony? The witness explained: I was traveling with this man when a military troop — *gayas* — pursued us. My companion grabbed the branch of an olive tree, tore it off, and used it to beat the pursuers back. Impressed, I called out: *Aryeh, yishar kochacha!* — Lion, may your strength be straight! He turned to me and said: how did you know my name was Aryeh? That is indeed what they call me in my city — Yochanan ben Yehonasan, Aryeh, from Kfar Shichayah. The name had come out spontaneously — it was a metaphor the witness offered, and it turned out to be the man's actual nickname. Some time later the man fell ill and died. Rabbi Tarfon accepted this testimony and permitted the wife to remarry.

This case presents a striking feature: the identifying information emerged through coincidence, through the witness's use of a metaphorical epithet that happened to match the subject's actual name. The detail is concrete, the self-identification was unrehearsed, and the testimony was sufficiently specific.

### Rigorous Questioning

A second *braita* tells what appears to be the same story with a crucial difference. In this version, after the witness delivered his account — this time involving a fig tree rather than an olive tree — Rabban Gamliel, not Rabbi Tarfon, put the witness through a rigorous consistency check. He said to him: wait — didn't you tell me his name was arranged differently? Was it not Yochanan ben Yehonasan from Kfar Shichayah, Aryeh — in a different order than you just gave? The witness pushed back: no, I said it exactly as I said it now. Rabban Gamliel pressed him two and three times — *dikdek oto b'shtayim u-beshalosh pe'amim* — trying to find any inconsistency, any shift in how the details were presented. The witness remained consistent throughout, and only then was the wife permitted to remarry.

This is a very different posture toward testimony. Rather than accepting what the witness said at face value, Rabban Gamliel was actively trying to induce an inconsistency — the kind of technique one might recognize from interrogations designed to detect unreliable accounts by repeatedly asking the subject to repeat their story and looking for variation. Had the witness altered even an apparently insignificant detail, one senses the testimony would have been rejected. The fact that he did not, and was then believed, shows that the rigor was real.

### Drisha/Chakirah

The two versions of the story — one before Rabbi Tarfon accepting the testimony without such review, the other before Rabban Gamliel with elaborate consistency-checking — prompt the Gemara to ask: did Rabbi Tarfon really not require *drisha vechakirah*? And a *braita* is cited: the debate is explicitly a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Tarfon. Rabbi Akiva says *ein bodkin edei nashim b'drisha vechakirah* — witnesses in *eidut isha* cases are not subjected to *drisha vechakirah*. Rabbi Tarfon says they are. Some versions of the text read the lenient position as anonymous and Rabbi Tarfon as the stricter one; the implication is similar.

### Monetary vs. Capital

The underlying dispute is traced to a principle stated by Rabbi Chanina: biblically, both monetary cases and capital cases require *drisha vechakirah* — the formal inquiry into time and place that is the classic tool of witness examination — as derived from the verse *mishpat echad yihye lachem*, one law for all proceedings. The Sages relaxed this requirement for monetary cases to avoid *neilas delet bifnei lovin* — locking the door before borrowers, meaning that if creditors had to subject their claims to full *drisha vechakirah* before recovering debts, lenders would simply stop lending.

The question then is how to categorize *eidut isha*. One view holds that since collecting the *ketubah* is involved, the case resembles a monetary case and *drisha vechakirah* is not required. The other view holds that since we are binding or releasing a woman from *isur eshet ish* — a prohibition of the severity of capital law — it resembles *dinei nefashot* and *drisha vechakirah* is required.

### Takkanat Agunah

The Gemara does not leave the tension unresolved. Tosafot, citing *Chad Mi-Kamai*, states explicitly: since we have already extended *eidut isha* to include testimony from men, women, slaves, non-Jews, children, and even *ed mipi ed*, and we have done all of this *mishum takanat agunah* — on account of the enactment to free chained wives — we have so fundamentally reshaped the evidentiary framework here that it cannot be made to conform to the rules of either *dinei mamonot* or *dinei nefashot*. The Rambam rules accordingly, as does Rabbeinu Tam in Tosafot Yeshanim: *drisha vechakirah* is not required. The framing of the case as *dinei mamonot* by virtue of the *ketubah* is thus best understood not as a genuine classification but as a legal hook — a way of reaching the conclusion the *halakha* demands once the *takkanat agunah* lens is applied. The entire evidentiary edifice for *eidut isha* is its own category, shaped not by the standard rules of testimony but by the overriding imperative of preventing women from being trapped as *agunot* for life.

## Conclusion/Aggada

### Scholars & Peace

The Gemara closes with the statement of Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina: *talmidei chachamim marbim shalom ba'olam* — Torah scholars increase peace in the world — as it is written, *ve-chol banayich limudei Hashem ve-rav shalom banayich* — and all your children will be students of God, and great will be the peace of your children. The choice to end Masechet Yevamot with this *aggadic* statement is not incidental. The final daf has shown, in remarkable historical detail, how the Sages expanded and reshaped the *halakha* of *eidut isha* — from narrow spousal testimony to the acceptance of any witness, in any form, under any ordinary circumstances — in order to free women from the trap of *iggun*. The peace the Sages increased was the peace of women whose lives were otherwise suspended indefinitely.

### Maharsha Exegesis

The Maharsha, commenting on this closing *aggadata*, addresses the obvious tension directly. One might object that the entire final section of Yevamot — indeed, the final several chapters — appears to be a systematic setting aside of Torah evidentiary requirements: the rules of *shnei eidim*, the rules of *eidut*, the prohibition of *eshet ish*. Is this not *akiras davar min ha-Torah* — a uprooting of biblical law?

The Maharsha answers: *ain zeh akirah ela mi-midat shalom* — this is not an uprooting but an expression of the quality of peace. The Torah itself declares *deracheha darchei no'am ve-chol nesivoteha shalom* — its ways are ways of pleasantness and all its paths are peace. A woman left permanently *me'ugenet* — chained — is incompatible with the Torah's own stated character. The Sages did not override the Torah; they read it through the lens the Torah itself provided. And the acceptance of *ed echad*, of women, of non-Jews, of *ed mipi ed*, of slaves — all of it flows from that same lens. *Mishum takanat agunah* is not a departure from Torah; it is Torah's way of peace made concrete in *halakha*.

The note that *banayich* may also be read as an acronym is left, appropriately, as the final word of the masechet's discourse — *hadran alach Ha'Ishah Basra ve-salikah lah Masechet Yevamot*.

---

---

# Ketubot 2

## Intro to Ketubot

### Opening & Context

We begin a new *masechta*. There is a well-known saying in the *yeshiva* world that three *masechtot* will, as it were, wipe you out — and the acronym for them is *Ani*, meaning poverty: *Eruvin*, *Niddah*, and *Yevamos*. Having just completed *Yevamos* — which was particularly challenging at the outset, though the middle and end proved highly relevant and engaging — we turn now to *Ketubot*. *Niddah* remains for the very end.

*Ketubot* carries its own famous reputation in the *yeshiva* world: it is known as the *Shas Katan*, the mini-*Shas*, because so many diverse concepts from across *Shas* arise in the course of its discussions.

### Nisuin vs. Kiddushin

The primary topic of *Ketubot* is, one might say, the *ketubah* — but more precisely, it is the legal and practical state of *nisuin*, as distinct from *kiddushin*. *Kiddushin* is the formal legal act of marriage: the giving of the ring in contemporary practice, which renders the woman fully and legally married such that any subsequent infidelity would constitute adultery. Yet at this stage, the couple has not begun living together. That actualization — the setting up of a shared home and life — is *chuppah*, the moment of *nisuin*.

In ancient practice, *kiddushin* could take place when a woman was still a minor, arranged between the prospective husband and her father, and might precede *nisuin* by many years. *Chuppah* was thus the moment when the marriage became real, not merely legal. As a result, it is *chuppah* that is the great communal event — the *simcha* with the large *seudah*, the *sheva brachot* requiring a *minyan* and representing the blessing of the community upon the *chatan* and *kallah*. The *bracha* of *eirusin*, by contrast, does not require a *minyan* and is far more private in character. It is worth noting that while one certainly requires *edim* for *kiddushin*, it is not entirely clear that formal *edim* are required for *chuppah* itself, since *nisuin* may be understood simply as the actualization of the *kiddushin* that had already taken place — potentially years earlier.

### Three Parts Ketubah

Once *nisuin* begins, a range of reciprocal obligations take effect. The husband becomes obligated to provide food, lodging, and *mitzvat onah* — conjugal relations at prescribed intervals. The wife takes on obligations toward the husband as well, including the rabbinic institution that her earnings belong to him. These ongoing mutual obligations are referred to as *tnai ketubah*, the stipulations of the *ketubah* — not "conditions" in the technical sense, but rather the ongoing terms that govern the marriage.

The *ketubah* itself, then, has three major components. The first is this body of ongoing reciprocal obligations. The second is the lump-sum payment — 200 *zuz* for a virgin bride, 100 *zuz* for a widow or divorcee — which would be collected by the wife either upon her husband's death or upon divorce. Although the Torah does not provide for a wife to inherit her husband, the rabbis instituted that she may draw this sum from the estate. The third component is the documentation of whatever property, the *nedunyah*, the bride brings into the marriage as a dowry, which she is entitled to take back upon death or divorce.

These three elements together constitute the subject matter of *Masechet Ketubot*. Crucially, these obligations are legally binding whether or not any document was actually written. The reciprocal obligations exist; the lump-sum liability exists — the document records them, but they do not depend on it. In a deeper sense, *Ketubot* is a tractate about the legal texture of *nisuin* itself.

One might ask about the modern *ketubah*, in which the dowry property is not specifically enumerated. The phrase *bein b'chesef bein b'zahav bein b'tachshitin* functions as a pro forma statement encompassing all property brought into the marriage at a stated valuation, without itemizing it in detail.

It should also be noted that the ordering of the tractates may seem counterintuitive. *Kiddushin* — the legal act of betrothal — comes later in the order of *Seder Nashim*, and *Gittin* precedes it, simply because *masechtot* are ordered by length as measured in chapters. *Ketubot*, as the longest, comes first.

### Broader Themes

Beyond these central themes, *Ketubot* earns its reputation as *Shas Katan* through the many broader halakhic discussions it occasions. One major area is the law of *kam lei b'derabba minei*: since part of the *ketubah* payment derives historically from the fine imposed upon a man who rapes or seduces an unmarried woman — a fine calibrated to the *ketubah* sum she might otherwise have expected — the tractate engages extensively with the cases of rape and seduction from the Torah's relevant *parshiyot*. This in turn generates discussions of when a more severe transgression incurred through a given act displaces a financial obligation, which is the principle of *kam lei b'derabba minei*. Another broad *Shas* theme introduced by this tractate concerns *edim*: questions of when witnesses can retract testimony on a signed document, whether because they were compelled to sign, were minors at the time, or for other reasons. Since *Ketubot* deals centrally with a signed legal document, such questions arise naturally — and their implications extend far beyond the *ketubah* itself.

### Student Q: Dowry

As noted above, the listing of dowry property in the modern *ketubah* takes a pro forma form: the text encompasses all property brought by the bride without specific enumeration, ascribing it a stated value. The detailed itemization that characterized the classical *ketubah* is no longer the practice.

---

## Wedding Days

### Mishnah Text

The *masechta* opens with the *mishnah*: *betulah niset l'yom ha-revi'i* — a virgin would have her *nisuin* on Wednesday. *V'almanah l'yom hachamishi* — a widow or divorcee on Thursday. The *mishnah* then explains: *shepaamayim b'shabbat batei dinin yoshvin ba'ayarot* — because the courts would convene in the villages twice each week, on Monday and Thursday. Therefore, *she'im haya lo ta'anat betulim haya mashkim l'veit din* — if the groom had a *ta'anat betulim*, a claim regarding his bride's virginity, he could appear in court the very next morning.

It is worth being precise about what is meant here. The *nisuin* referred to is *chuppah*, not *kiddushin*. The *kiddushin* could have taken place at any time — even years earlier, even when the bride was a minor. The *chuppah*, the communal *simcha* with the *seudah*, the *sheva brachot* before a *minyan*: that is the event the *mishnah* is discussing.

### Ta'anat Betulim

*Ta'anat betulim* — the claim that one's bride was not a virgin — carries significant halakhic weight and will dominate the entire first *perek*. Two distinct consequences flow from it. The first is financial: the *ketubah* of a *betulah* is 200 *zuz*, while that of a non-virgin is 100 *zuz*, and the groom's claim that she was not a virgin therefore affects his payment obligations. The second and weightier consequence is the suspicion of adultery. Since *kiddushin* may have taken place years before *nisuin*, a bride who is found not to be a virgin on her wedding night raises the concern that she may have been with another man during the intervening period — that is, after the legal marriage of *kiddushin* — which would constitute adultery and render her forbidden to her husband.

### Wednesday Purpose

The logic of the *mishnah* is therefore clear. By scheduling the *nisuin* on Wednesday, the groom who discovers grounds for a *ta'anat betulim* on that night can appear before *beit din* the very next morning, Thursday, when the court is in session. The underlying concern is that if he waits, he may calm down, reconcile himself to the situation, and ultimately decide not to pursue the matter — while the halakhic problem, if she did in fact commit adultery, would remain unresolved.

### Why Not Sunday?

An obvious question presents itself immediately: why not have the *nisuin* on Sunday, allowing the groom to appear before *beit din* on Monday, when the court also convenes? This question is one the *gemara* will address, and it fundamentally changes the nature of the explanation offered by the *mishnah*.

The *mishnah* might be understood as describing a common social practice that developed organically — men found it convenient to marry on Wednesdays so that the courts would be available the next day. Alternatively, as the *gemara* will develop, it may represent a *takanat chachamim*, a formal rabbinic enactment requiring that *nisuin* take place on Wednesday. This distinction, seemingly technical, carries significant practical consequences, as will become clear.

### Rashi vs. Tosafot

A major debate between Rashi and *Tosafot* concerns the mechanism by which *ta'anat betulim* operates. Rashi, in the very first line of his commentary, explains: *im hayu ta'anat betulim yashiv l'veit din b'od ka'aso alav* — while he is still angry; *shema yitpayes v'titkarer da'ato v'yikayemnah* — lest he cool down and they remain married; *v'shema hiznah tachtav v'ne'esra alav* — and perhaps she committed adultery and is forbidden to him; and therefore *mitoch she-yavo l'veit din yitbarer ha-davar kshe-yeitze ha-kol shemma yavo'u edim* — by bringing the claim before the court, word will spread and witnesses may come forward to clarify the matter. For Rashi, then, the groom's claim alone does not determine anything; it is the publicity generated by the court proceeding that may produce witnesses and objective clarification.

*Tosafot* disagrees. Based on the *gemara*, *Tosafot* understands that the groom's claim alone already carries consequences, through the principle of *shavyeh anafsheh chaticha d'issura*: by claiming that his wife was not a virgin — and thereby implying that she may have committed adultery — the groom renders her forbidden to himself by the force of his own declaration. He is bound by his own statement. This is a principle familiar from the laws of *kashrut*, here applied — as one might well note, rather strikingly — to a human being.

Yet according to *Tosafot*'s position, a difficulty arises. If the groom's declaration alone already creates the halakhic consequence, why is there a rabbinic interest in ensuring that he brings the matter to *beit din*? The objective clarification of witnesses, which was Rashi's answer, is not *Tosafot*'s mechanism — and *Tosafot* does not appear to directly address this difficulty.

There is also a separate question regarding why this situation does not generate a *sotah* proceeding, given the operative concern about adultery. The *sotah* process requires prior warning and testimony of seclusion. *Shavyeh anafsheh chaticha d'issura* is a different mechanism — it is the personal binding force of one's own claim, not an objective establishment of fact — and the two operate on distinct grounds.

Despite their disagreement on mechanism, both Rashi and *Tosafot* agree, based on the *gemara*, that the point is not merely to describe a communal practice but to ensure that the claim reaches the court rather than being abandoned.

---

## Mezonot Application

### Higia Zman

The *gemara* now introduces a chain of tradition: *amar Rav Yosef amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel* — Rav Yosef transmitting in the name of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel. The question posed is not why the *mishnah* ordained Wednesday — *mipnei ma amru*, as the phrase is used here, means something more like: what is the practical significance of this teaching? Why do we care? And the answer offered is: *lefi sheshaninu*, because of what we taught in a later *mishnah*: *higia zman v'lo nisu* — the designated wedding date arrived and they did not marry.

This later *mishnah* requires a word of explanation. The "year" referenced here is not a year from *kiddushin* — which might have taken place decades earlier. Rather, from the moment the groom declares his intention to proceed with *nisuin*, the bride is granted one year to prepare — to assemble her dowry, make her arrangements, and ready herself mentally, financially, and in all other respects. The wedding date is thus a year from that declaration of intent, not from the original *kiddushin*.

The later *mishnah* rules: *ocheles mishelo v'ocheles b'trumah* — once that date arrives, even if the *chuppah* has not yet taken place, the husband must begin providing food and support for his bride. His marital obligations commence on the appointed date. Furthermore, if he is a *kohen*, she may even eat his *terumah*, despite the fact that ordinarily eating *terumah* requires full *nisuin* rather than merely *kiddushin*. The rabbis suspended that requirement because by this date she ought already to have been *nesu'ah*. It is in any case practically convenient: if he is obligated to feed her, it is simpler if the food may consist of *terumah*.

### Sunday Case

The practical question that Rav Yosef is raising is this: suppose the year expires on a Sunday. Is the groom now obligated to pay *mezonot* from Sunday onward — even though Wednesday has not yet arrived? One might think so, since a year has passed.

### Wednesday Date

The answer is no. *L'kach shaninu besulah niset l'yom ha-revi'i* — that is precisely why the *mishnah* taught that virgins marry on Wednesday. The wedding date was never simply "one year from today." The wedding date is the first Wednesday that falls a year after the declaration of intent. If the year expires on a Sunday, the groom has no obligation to pay *mezonot* for those intervening days — Sunday through Tuesday — because the actual wedding date had always been Wednesday, not Sunday. The three days are not a delay; they were never part of the obligation.

---

## Mezonot Application (II)

### Dependency Issue

Rav Yosef, however, is troubled by the formulation he received from his teachers. *Mari d'Avraham* — God of Avraham! — he exclaims: *tali tanya bidla tanya?* You are making a *mishnah* that provides its own explicit reason dependent upon a different *mishnah* that gives no reason? The *gemara* challenges this immediately: *hai tanya v'hai tanya* — both are indeed *mishnayot*. To which Rav Yosef refines the objection: *ella tali tanya demefaresh ta'ama b'tanya d'lo mefaresh ta'ama* — you are making the *mishnah* whose reason is stated explicitly dependent, in terms of its practical import, upon a *mishnah* that states no reason. The explicit stated reason of the first *mishnah* is so that the groom can come to *beit din* the next morning. If you wish to derive an additional halakhic implication from it regarding *mezonot*, that is fine — but you cannot say that this implication is the point of teaching the *mishnah*.

---

## Why Wednesday

### Rav Yosef Objection

Rav Yosef's objection, then, is not merely formal but conceptual. The *mishnah* about *nisuin* on Wednesday states its own rationale: the groom should be able to appear in *beit din* on Thursday. To then say that the deeper reason for teaching this *mishnah* is to clarify the *mezonot* obligation — which depends on a second *mishnah* that offers no stated rationale — is to misread the teaching. Rav Yosef is not denying that both are *mishnayot*, but insisting that a *mishnah* with an explicit rationale should not be read as serving the purposes of a *mishnah* without one.

### Gemarah Response

The *gemara* responds: *ella ei itmar hachi itmar* — if the tradition was indeed transmitted, here is how it should have been formulated. The chain of transmission (*Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel*) should have framed the question differently: *mipnei mah amru besulah niset l'yom ha-revi'i she'im haya lo ta'anat betulim haya mashkim l'veit din* — why did they ordain that a virgin marries on Wednesday? So that if the groom had a *ta'anat betulim* he could appear in *beit din* the next morning. This formulation cleanly raises the purpose question without subordinating it to the *mezonot* *mishnah*. And immediately the obvious challenge follows: *v'tinasai b'echad b'shabbat she'im haya lo ta'anat betulim haya mashkim l'veit din* — let her marry on Sunday, so he could appear in *beit din* on Monday?

### Takanat Reason

The answer the *gemara* provides is entirely different from what one might have expected: *shakdu chachamim al takanas bnot Yisrael sheyehe tore'ach b'seudah shlosha yamim* — the rabbis were solicitous of the wellbeing of Jewish women, and they instituted that the groom should exert himself in preparing the *seudah* for three days. The *takanat chachamim* was designed not primarily around the question of *ta'anat betulim* and court access, but around ensuring adequate preparation for the wedding feast.

### Three-Day Preparation

The specific logic is this: the bride had a full year to prepare, while men, proverbially, tend to address such things at the last moment. If the *nisuin* were scheduled for Sunday, the groom might begin his preparations only from *Motzaei Shabbat*. By requiring Wednesday, the rabbis ensured that the groom would spend Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday — three full days — in active preparation for the *seudah*, and only on Wednesday would the *chuppah* take place.
