The groom's family is, of course, responsible for the wedding celebration, and the rabbis wished to ensure a genuinely festive and properly prepared event.

### Rabbinic Demand

The implicit consequence of this reframing is significant. The *gemara* has now treated the *mishnah*'s ruling not as a description of communal practice but as a rabbinic enactment — a *takanah* — that the wedding must take place on Wednesday. If it is a mere practice, then one might ask: what halakhic force does it carry, and what practical difference does it make? But if it is a *takanat chachamim* that the wedding shall not be held before Wednesday, then from the outset the wedding date was always the first Wednesday following the year of preparation. Sunday was never the date. The date was never postponed; it was always Wednesday. This is what allows the *gemara* to rule, in the context of the *mezonot* obligation, that the groom does not owe payment for the days between Sunday and Wednesday: those days were not a delay at all.

---

## Ones Exception

### Blame vs. Date

The *gemara* now draws a broader principle from this framework. Having established that when it is a *takanat chachamim* that prevents the wedding from occurring on an earlier day, the groom bears no *mezonot* obligation for those days — the *gemara* asks whether the same reasoning extends to other situations where the wedding is postponed through no one's fault. The underlying question is: does the obligation to pay *mezonot* commence automatically on the wedding date, regardless of why it was not observed, or does it only engage when there is someone to blame for the delay?

### Groom Illness

*Lefikach chala hu* — therefore, if the groom became ill and the wedding was postponed, does he pay *mezonot* from the appointed date or not? One view within the *gemara* frames it as a question of *ones*: *hatam ta'ama mai mishum d'ones* — the reason he did not owe for the Sunday-to-Wednesday period was that it was beyond his control, a product of the rabbinic institution. *Hacha nami ones* — here too it is beyond his control; therefore he should not pay. Alternatively: *hatam ones b'takantah d'takinu leh rabanan* — there, the reason it was beyond his control was built into the rabbinic institution itself, such that the date was never Sunday to begin with. Here, by contrast, the date actually arrived — it was Wednesday, and the wedding did not happen. Perhaps once the actual date arrives, the obligation begins regardless of why it was not fulfilled.

The distinction is sharp. When the rabbis say Wednesday, the pre-Wednesday period was never the wedding date. But when illness prevents a Wednesday wedding, the Wednesday date did arrive and was missed. These are halakhically different situations, and the question of whether *ones* constitutes an exemption in the latter case remains open.

### Bride Illness

The uncertainty cascades further. *V'im timtzi lomar chala hu ma'aleh lah mezonot* — if you rule that when the groom falls ill he does pay *mezonot*, then *chaltsah hi mah* — what if she is the one who falls ill? Here the groom might argue: *ana kaina* — I am ready to marry; it is you who cannot proceed. Should he then be exempt from payment since the delay originates with her? Or does she respond: *nistachfah sadehu* — it is your field that flooded? The underlying logic of this latter phrase, as *Tosafot* on 2b explains, reflects a view that within the patriarchal framework of the marriage relationship, misfortune that befalls the marriage is seen as the husband's misfortune — he is the one bringing a wife into his domain, and if that is disrupted, the loss is categorized as his. Rashi on 2a suggests a parallel formulation: *mazlacha garam ki mehayom ani mutal alecha lazon* — your fortune has brought it about that from this day I am your responsibility to sustain. One might read this either as the wife's argument that luck cuts against him, or more simply as the position that once the date arrives, the obligation of support begins regardless of fault — as long as the postponement was not willful.

### Niddah Case

A third scenario: *pirsah niddah* — what if the bride becomes a *niddah* on the wedding day? There are well-known differences between *Sephardim* and *Ashkenazim* as to whether a *chuppah* is legally valid when the bride is a *niddah*, since cohabitation would not be possible immediately. But regardless of the legal question, in practice no one wished to hold a *chuppah* when the couple could not begin their married life together. The question is therefore whether the *niddah* situation creates an exemption from *mezonot* for the groom.

### Rav Achai

Rav Achai attempts to resolve these open questions from the language of the later *mishnah* itself. The *mishnah* reads *higia zman v'lo nisu* — the time came and they were not married. Critically, the verb is *nistu*, passive: the women were not married by the men — not *nasu*, active, meaning the men did not marry. Rav Achai infers from this: *lo nasu lo katani, ella lo nistu* — it does not say the men did not marry; it says the women were not married. This implies that the women were somehow involved in the reason for the non-marriage — yet the *mishnah* still rules that he pays. Were it a case of the women willfully refusing — *d'kamakvan inu hi* — it would be obvious he should not pay. So it must be speaking of a case where the women were the involuntary cause of the delay — illness, or perhaps *niddah* — and yet the *mishnah* rules he pays. Rav Achai concludes that whenever the delay is involuntary on the woman's side, the man pays.

### Rav Ashi

Rav Ashi rejects this reading. *L'olam eima lach, kol ones lo achla* — any situation of *ones*, anything beyond anyone's control, exempts the man from payment. The man pays only when he willfully delays. *V'd'kamaachvi inhu* — the triggering case for payment is the man deliberately postponing the wedding. Grammatically, Rav Ashi notes, the *mishnah* should indeed have said *lo nasu* — the men did not marry; it uses the passive form only because the beginning of that *mishnah* speaks from the woman's perspective, and the end follows suit stylistically. It is not a substantive implication.

The *gemara* thus leaves us with two fundamental positions. One holds that the obligation begins automatically on the wedding date — as long as the woman is not herself willfully postponing, the man must pay from that date regardless of circumstances. The other holds that the man pays only when he is personally and willfully responsible for the delay; any genuine *ones*, on either side, exempts him from payment.

---

## Prenup Digression

### Historical Parallel

*Tosafot* raises a question that illuminates a dimension of this entire discussion: why did the rabbis stipulate that the *chuppah* must be held on Wednesday specifically during the day, rather than on Wednesday night — which is halakhically already Thursday? *Tosafot* answers that in Talmudic times there were frequently significant disputes surrounding the terms of the *ketubah*, and beginning the *chuppah* early on Wednesday allowed time for those disputes to be negotiated and resolved before the event proceeded. When the *ketubah* was a genuine financial document with real stakes — the specification of dowry property, the exact amount of the *ikar ketubah*, the various conditions — there was ample room for disagreement between the families, and the rabbis wished to ensure that such disputes did not derail the wedding at the last moment.

### Prenup Anecdote

This principle resonates powerfully in contemporary halakhic practice. A prenuptial agreement is today's functional analogue to those *ketubah* negotiations. The dangers of leaving such discussions to the last moment are very real. There are cases where a groom, coming from a family that had experienced a particularly acrimonious divorce, arrived at his own wedding refusing to sign the prenuptial agreement — raising objections that could and should have been addressed weeks earlier.

### Prenup Practice

The practical lesson is clear: a prenuptial agreement should be signed and notarized no later than two weeks before the wedding. The signing can certainly be acknowledged and celebrated at the *tish* if one wishes, but the document must not be left to the night of the wedding itself. Just as the Talmudic rabbis ensured that disputes over the *ketubah* would not disrupt the *chuppah* by building in lead time, so too contemporary practice should ensure that all such documents are fully in order well before the event.

---

## Ones in Gittin

### Ein Ones Gittin

Rava now introduces a striking contrast. *Ul'inyan gittin eino kein* — regarding *gittin*, this principle of *ones* does not apply in the same way. *Alma kasavar Rava ein ones b'gittin* — Rava holds that the fact that something occurred beyond one's control is not a relevant factor in the laws of *gittin*. Where we have just seen that *ones* can be a factor in the *mezonot* discussion — according to Rav Ashi's position, any *ones* exempts the man from payment — in the realm of *gittin*, *ones* carries no weight.

### Conditional Gittin

The source for Rava's principle is sought in a *mishnah* in *Gittin*: a man says to his wife, *harei zeh gittech im lo basi mikan ad shneim asar chodesh* — here is your *get*; if I do not return from here within twelve months, the *get* takes effect. The scenario is familiar: the man is traveling overseas, perhaps to war or distant business, and fears he may not return. To protect his wife from becoming an *agunah* — permanently bound and unable to remarry — he gives a conditional *get*. *U'meis betoch shneim asar chodesh* — and he died within those twelve months.

At the end of twelve months, the condition appears to have been met: he did not return. Is this a valid *get*?

### Ein Get Achar Misah

The *mishnah* rules: *eino get* — it is not a valid *get*. The reason Rashi articulates is *ein hameisim megarshin* — the dead cannot divorce; a *get* cannot take effect *l'achar misah*, after death. The *kiddushin* has in any event been dissolved by death, and one might ask why Rashi finds it necessary to invoke this principle rather than simply noting that widowhood has already dissolved the marriage. The *yeshiva* world enjoys posing this question, though in practice the principle of *ein get l'achar misah* stands on its own terms. The condition was technically met — he did not return — but the *get* fails because one cannot divorce a wife posthumously.

### Ones Factor?

The *gemara* now probes a deeper question. *Meiso de'eino get* — death prevents the *get*; that much is clear. But what if *chala* — what if he fell ill and was unable to return? In that case, the twelve months would also have passed without his return. Does the fact that his failure to return was due to *ones* — circumstances entirely beyond his control — mean that the condition is treated as if it were not met? That is: perhaps when he was prevented by force of circumstance, it is halakhically "as if he returned," and therefore the condition was not fulfilled and the *get* is not valid. Or is *ones* entirely irrelevant — the condition was not met regardless of why, and the *get* is therefore valid?

If *ones* is not a factor, then the *mishnah* teaches us only that death prevents the *get* via the principle of *ein get l'achar misah* — and nothing can be inferred about what would happen if he merely fell ill. The *get* in the illness case might well be valid. If *ones* is a factor, then even in the illness case the condition would be treated as unmet, and the *get* would be invalid — but then the *mishnah* about death is simply one application of the broader rule that *ones* negates condition-fulfillment.

### Social Policy

The *gemara* anticipates where this leads. If *ones* were a relevant factor in determining whether a condition was met, the consequences for practical halakha would be severe: we could never know with confidence whether conditions in *gittin* had been fulfilled or not, because we would always need to investigate whether any circumstance beyond the party's control had intervened. Such a regime would be unworkable. This social policy concern — that one cannot run a halakhic system if conditions can always be retroactively analyzed for possible *ones* — is precisely what Rava's principle is designed to prevent.

### Gemarah Resolution

The *gemara*'s conclusion is that the *mishnah* teaches one thing and one thing only: a *get* does not take effect after the groom's death, by virtue of the principle of *ein get l'achar misah*. The *mishnah* is not making any statement about the illness case, and nothing can be inferred from it regarding whether *ones* would affect the determination of condition-fulfillment. That question — whether *ones* serves to treat a condition as unmet — remains a separate discussion, and the resolution of Rava's principle *ein ones b'gittin* must be derived from elsewhere.

---

---

# Ketubot 3

## Ones BeGittin

### Ones Concept Intro

The *gemara* on the bottom of 3b takes up the question of *yesh ones begitin* — whether the claim of *ones*, an act of God or circumstance beyond one's control, is a relevant factor when a *get* has been given conditionally. If someone stipulates that a *get* should take effect under certain conditions, and those conditions are met only because of something entirely outside the husband's control — he became ill, was detained, or died — do we look at the situation as though the condition was not truly met in the sense he intended? The *gemara*'s first position is *ein ones begitin*: we do not factor that in. As was already noted, if we were to factor it in, things would become very complicated, since one could never know with certainty whether the conditions had truly been met.

### Get After Death

The *gemara* attempts to prove this from a *mishna* dealing with a case where a man says "This is your *get* if I die." This would seem to be an example of *ones*, and the question is whether we can infer something about what happens if he said "This will be your *get* if I don't return," and he then died — the condition being met only because of *ones*. However, the *gemara* concludes that the real point of that *mishna* is not to address the question of *ones* at all, but rather to establish the principle of *ein get achar misa* — that a *get* cannot take effect after a person has already died.

The *mishna* itself states: *harei zeh gitich im mati* — "This is your *get* if I die"; *harei zeh gitich mecholi zeh* — "This is your *get* if I don't recover from this illness"; *harei zeh gitich achar misa* — "This is your *get* after I die" — in all such cases, *lo amar klum*, it amounts to nothing. In each of these formulations, the husband is not merely imposing a stipulation; he is specifying the moment the *get* takes effect — when he dies, when he never rises from his sickbed. Since a *get* cannot take effect once the husband is dead, all these formulations fail. We thus already know the principle of *ein get achar misa* from the opening of that *mishna*.

### Dating Documents

Since the principle of *ein get achar misa* is already established by the beginning of the *mishna*, why does the *gemara* need to teach it again through the case of one who says "If I don't return in twelve months"? The *gemara* answers: *dilma l'apokei merabboseinu* — perhaps the second teaching is necessary to exclude the position of *Rabboseinu*. As a *braita* teaches, *Rabboseinu hitiru lenasei* — those authorities permitted the woman to remarry even when the husband said "This is your *get* after I die." How could they permit this given *ein get achar misa*?

The *gemara* asks: who is this *Rabboseinu*? The answer is *Bei Dina Desharu Mishcha* — the *beis din* that permitted non-Jewish oil. This is the *beis din* of *Rabbi Yossi*, or more precisely, a *beis din* that held like *Rabbi Yossi*, and they have become identified by their most famous leniency. Their position follows from the principle *zmano shel shetar mochiach alav* — that the date written in a legal document demonstrates something. If a *get* is dated from the day it was written, even when it contains a condition that it take effect upon death, the date in the document signals that it retroactively takes effect from the time of writing. According to *Rabbi Yossi*, then, there could in principle be a *get achar misa* as long as the document is dated.

This is precisely why the *mishna* must teach the principle of *ein get achar misa* twice: once as a general rule, and once to make clear that this holds even when the document bears a date — to reject *Rabbi Yossi*'s view. The case in the *mishna* of one who says "If I don't return in twelve months" and then dies is therefore not relevant to the question of *ones* at all. Its purpose is solely to reiterate *ein get achar misa* and to specify that a date in the document does not change this.

### Conditional Get Case

Having established that the earlier sources do not speak to the question of *ones*, the *gemara* turns to the end of that *mishna*. The case is: *me'achshav im lo basi mikan v'ad shenem asar chodesh* — if a man says explicitly that the *get* should take effect as of now if he does not return within twelve months. One can readily understand why a husband would phrase it this way — so that his wife would not be left as an *agunah* if he fails to return and she has no way of knowing what happened to him. *Umes b'soch shenem asar chodesh* — and he dies within the twelve months. The condition has been met: he did not return within the year. It is not a case of *get achar misa* because he explicitly said "from now." The *gemara* states: *harei zeh get* — it is a valid *get*. The fact that the condition was met only because of *ones*, because he died and could not control his return, is immaterial. *Ones* is not a factor.

### Dying vs. Sickness

The *gemara* immediately raises a qualification. *Mes v'hu hadin l'chola* — one might assume that the same would apply whether he died or merely became ill. But the *gemara* resists this inference. *Dilma mes davka* — perhaps dying is categorically different. *D'lo nicha lei d'tipal kamei yavam* — one of the main reasons a man might give his wife a conditional *get* in the first place, especially if he fears he might die, is so that she will not be subject to *yibum*, which was the entire subject of the previous tractate. If a man anticipates the possibility of death, that is perhaps precisely the kind of *ones* he had in mind when he formulated the condition. Death may well have been the very scenario he was thinking about. Getting sick, by contrast, is something he may never have anticipated — it represents a situation he would have wished he could have negated by returning, and therefore perhaps it should not be held against him.

This is the real conceptual heart of the issue. The question of *ones* in *gittin* is not primarily about blame or legal culpability in the usual sense. The governing principle of *ones rachmana patrei* — that the Torah does not hold a person liable for what is beyond their control — does not translate neatly here, since the issue is not one of fault but of whether the conditions stipulated were truly met. Nor does that principle distinguish between dying and becoming ill, since both are objectively outside one's control. The deeper question, as the *gemara* frames it, is really one of *da'as*: under what circumstances did the husband actually intend the *get* to take effect? The premise is that the husband's intention governs, and *ones* matters — or doesn't — depending on whether the particular event was one he would have included in his intent.

Of course, the difficulty is that one cannot run a legal system trying to reconstruct what was going on inside someone's mind. The general principle is *devarim shebalev einam devarim* — what is in one's heart is not legally operative. There is, however, an important nuance: the *Rambam* and the *Tosafos Rid* explain that *devarim shebalev einam devarim* applies with full force primarily in bilateral transactions — a sale, for instance, where money and goods change hands and only what is accessible to both parties can be legally relevant. But in a unilateral transaction — a gift, or a *get*, where the other party has no real say — what is in the giver's mind may carry more legal weight. So the question the *gemara* is working through is not a categorical principle about *ones*, but a question about intent: did I intend the *get* to take effect in these circumstances?

## River Case Analysis

### River Blockage

Having established the conceptual framework, the *gemara* attempts to derive a clear ruling from a concrete case. *De-hu de-amar le-hu* — a man said to witnesses: *i lo asina mi-kan ve-ad tlasin yomin, le-havei gitta* — if I don't return within thirty days, let it be a *get*. *Asa be-sof tlasin yomin* — he came at the end of thirty days, *u-paska mabra* — but a river blocked his path. He could not cross in time. *Amar le-hu chazu de-asai chazu de-asai* — he called out across the river: "Look, I am coming, I am coming!" His *ratzon* was evident: he wanted to negate the condition of the *get*. But he could not cross in time. *Amar Shmuel: lav shemei masia* — it is very well that he announced his arrival, says *Shmuel*, but he did not come. And therefore the *get* takes effect. *Ones* is irrelevant.

### Anticipated Ones

The *gemara* does not accept this as a conclusive proof, however. *Ve-dilma unsa de-shiyach shani* — perhaps a common type of *ones* is categorically different. Perhaps when the *ones* is something foreseeable, it simply cannot operate to negate the condition.

### Foreseeability

*De-keivan de-ibayei lei le-asnu-ei ve-lo asni* — since he could have stipulated otherwise and did not, he is responsible for the gap. He should have said: this will be a *get* if I do not return, unless I am held up by circumstances beyond my control. A river blocking one's path is a perfectly ordinary and foreseeable occurrence. Since he did not exclude it, we assume he intended the *get* to take effect regardless. *Ihu de-afsidei nafshiyei* — he has brought this upon himself.

This is again consistent with the *da'as*-centered reading of the issue. Something foreseeable is assumed to have been included in the husband's intent even if unstated, because any reasonable person would have thought of it. The remaining question is what happens with a truly extraordinary *ones* — something no normal person would ever anticipate, like being struck by lightning. Is that also assumed to be within the husband's intent, or do we say it was so far outside normal expectation that it genuinely was never part of what he envisioned? The *gemara* cannot resolve this from the river case alone, and concedes there is no clear proof.

## Raba's Position

### Raba's Reasoning

Rather than simply articulating *ein ones begitin* as a legal principle — which one might derive straightforwardly from *devarim shebalev einam devarim* — *Rava* formulates his position as a policy ruling, based on *sevara d'nafshei*, his own independent reasoning. He has no definitive source to cite. But the *gemara* then makes a critical move: it argues that the policy itself demands this position.

### Policy Problems

The *gemara* explains: *mishum tznuos u-mishum prutzos* — because of women who are overly cautious and because of women who are overly ready. If we were to say that *ones* matters and can negate the *get*, we would create an impossible social situation. On the one hand, *mishum tznuos* — there will be times when there is no *ones* at all, the condition was met straightforwardly, and yet the woman will worry: perhaps there was some act of God I have no knowledge of, perhaps he was struck by lightning, perhaps something beyond his control occurred. *U-me'aguna v'yasva* — she will sit and remain an *agunah* when she has every right to remarry.

On the other hand, *mishum prutzos* — there will be women too eager to move on. Even when there is genuine reason to believe there was an *ones*, *v'azla u-minsva* — she will say it was not an *ones* and proceed to remarry, *v'nimtza get batel u-vaneha mamzerim* — and it will turn out the *get* was never valid and her children will be *mamzerim*. You simply cannot run a society in which the validity of every *get* depends on an invisible and unknowable question of whether some unforeseeable act of God occurred in a distant place.

### Hafka'as Kiddushin

The *gemara* presses back sharply: are you saying that merely for policy reasons — *mishum tznuos u-mishum prutzos* — we would declare a married woman permitted to the world? *Sharinan eshes ish l'alma?* We would say it is always a valid *get*, ignoring *ones*, even when legally *ones* should have negated it?

The *gemara* answers: *in, kol d'mekadesh ada'ata d'rabanan mekadesh* — yes, because anyone who marries does so on the terms set by the rabbis. We do not live in a world of pure biblical Judaism alone; every legal act is performed within the framework that the rabbis have constructed and defined. *V'afkinhu rabanan l'kidushin minei* — and the rabbis can retroactively uproot the *kiddushin*. Under these circumstances, even though the *get* is technically defective because *ones* should have negated the condition, the rabbis retroactively declare the *kiddushin* void, so that the *get* — whatever its legal infirmity — is treated as effective.

This is one of the classic *sugyos* of *hafka'as kiddushin*, the retroactive uprooting of marriage, and it has obvious resonance in contemporary discussions about the *agunah* problem. Two important points about how it operates here deserve emphasis. First, this is not a case-by-case intervention. It is a general systemic rule, operative from the very moment of marriage. The *kiddushin* was contracted with this rule already in place: *ada'ata d'rabanan mekadesh* — the marriage was entered into on the rabbis' terms, which include the possibility of retroactive uprooting in defined circumstances. Second, even within this mechanism, a *get* is still required — even if defective. *Rashi* consistently emphasizes this point throughout the *sugya*: the rabbis uproot the *kiddushin* specifically *al yedei gittin she-hikshiru chachamim* — through *gittin* that the rabbis have validated in this manner. The *Rashba* elaborates on this principle, explaining that *hafka'as kiddushin* is not a bold direct exercise of rabbinic power. It operates as a hidden mechanism behind the scenes. The *Rashba* calls what is required a *srach get* — a semblance of a *get*, what one might call a fig leaf. The *get* may not function on its own terms, but it provides the formal occasion for the hidden mechanism of *hafka'as kiddushin* to operate. We do not walk in and announce that we are nullifying the *kiddushin* directly; rather, the *get* stands upfront, and the *hafka'as kiddushin* works silently behind it.

This same logic, the *Rashba* notes, operates in the *sugyos* of *Yevamos* involving *ed echad* — a single witness to the husband's death. There the "fig leaf" is not a *get* but the reliance on the single witness's testimony, however legally insufficient on its own. Behind that reliance, the *hafka'as kiddushin* provides the ultimate mechanism.

A small but illuminating point from *Tosafot*: the practice of reciting *kedas Moshe ve-Yisrael* at the moment of *kiddushin*, though nowhere explicitly mandated in the *gemara*, encodes this principle. *Moshe* represents *Torah de-oraisa*; *Yisrael*, the Jewish people as represented by the rabbis, signals *ada'ata d'rabanan mekadesh* — that the marriage is entered into on the rabbis' terms.

## Hafka'as Kiddushin

### Fig Leaf Get

The question then arises of exactly how the mechanism of *hafka'as kiddushin* operates in this case. The *get* here is technically defective — the condition was ostensibly not met in a legally valid sense, since *ones* arguably should have negated it. Yet the *get* stands as the fig leaf behind which *hafka'as kiddushin* operates. *Rashi*'s language throughout this *sugya* is precise: *afkinu rabbanan le-kiddushin kshe-yavo get kazeh achareihen* — the rabbis uproot the *kiddushin* when a *get* like this follows. The *get* need not be fully valid on its own; what it provides is the formal occasion for the rabbinic mechanism to operate. The *Rashba* reinforces this: direct, unadorned exercise of *hafka'as kiddushin* without any *get* would undermine the institutions of Jewish marriage altogether. The power exists, but it must operate through proper legal form, however attenuated.

### Money vs. Sex

*Ravina* poses a pointed question to *Rav Ashi*: *teynach de-kadesh be-chaspa* — this works well enough if the *kiddushin* was performed with money. In that case, the mechanism of *hefker beis din hefker* — the court's power to declare property ownerless — explains how the rabbis can retroactively undo the monetary *kiddushin*. They declare the money that effected the *kiddushin* to have been ownerless from the start, thus voiding the transaction. But *kadesh be-via mai ika le-meimar* — what happens if the *kiddushin* was *kiddushei biah*, effected through marital relations? The physical reality of the sexual act has occurred. How can the rabbis change that? How can they retroactively declare it not to have been an act of *kiddushin*?

### Redefining Acts

The *gemara* answers: *shavyuha rabbanan le-veilaso veilas zenus* — the rabbis can redefine the context. Not every act of sex is *kiddushin*. Most sexual relations between people have no legal status of *kiddushin* at all; they are *zenus*, non-marital relations. What makes a sexual act into *kiddushin* is the legal and social context in which it occurs — and the rabbis are the ones who determine what that context means. Retroactively, they declare that this particular act, which appeared to be marital, is to be regarded as *zenus* — legally unrecognized as a marriage-effecting act.

This is admittedly a striking *chiddush*. We might be dealing with a couple who have lived together for years, raised children, participated in communal life as a married couple — and retroactively we say no, that was all *beilas zenus*. One might ask: if witnesses were present who explicitly heard the man declare his intent to effect *kiddushei biah*, does the rabbinic recharacterization override even their testimony? The answer would have to be yes — the rabbis' framework for what constitutes *kiddushin* supersedes even how the witnesses understood the act they observed.

### Alternate View

There is a famous alternative interpretation of this passage, cited by *Rashi* though firmly rejected by him. According to this reading — which *Rashi* notes is reflected in some *rishonim* — the reason *kiddushei kesef* is easier to retroactively undo is not *hefker beis din hefker*, but rather because *kiddushei kesef* is itself only *derabbanan*. On this view, the only form of *kiddushin* that is *de-oraisa* is *biah*. *Kiddushei kesef* and *kiddushei shtar* are rabbinic constructs, and the rabbis can therefore undo what they created. As for *kiddushei biah*, which would be *de-oraisa*, this reading says the rabbis never recognized it as valid *kiddushin* in the first place — it was always treated as *beilas zenus* from the outset, given that the *gemara* elsewhere records that lashes were administered to one who effected *kiddushin* through *biah* because it was *pritzus*.

The implication of this view would be that the only form of *kiddushin* truly beyond rabbinic power to undo is *kiddushei shtar*. *Kiddushei kesef* is *derabbanan* and can be controlled; *kiddushei biah* is never recognized. *Rashi*, however, is sharply critical of this reading. He calls it *ta'us gomur* — a complete error — and points out that accepting it would mean that a woman who underwent *kiddushei biah* could simply walk away without a *get* on the basis of this reasoning alone, and *lo matzinu zos batalmud* — we find no such ruling anywhere in the Talmud. *Rashi* firmly rejects the entire construct.

## Alternative Position

### Ones Matters

The *gemara* now presents a second version of *Rava*'s position: *ikha de-amri, amar Rava ve-chein l'inyan gittin* — there are those who say that *Rava* actually ruled that *ones does* matter in practice, not merely in theory. On this reading, *Rava* held *yesh ones begitin* — we genuinely factor in *ones*, not just in principle but as a practical legal ruling.

### Mishna Challenge

The *gemara* immediately challenges this position from the *mishna*. The case of *me'achshav im lo basi mikan v'ad shenem asar chodesh*, where the husband said "from now if I do not return in twelve months" and he died within the twelve months — the *mishna* rules *harei zeh get*, it is a valid *get*. If *ones* mattered and could negate the *get*, then the fact that he died — surely an *ones* — should have invalidated it.

### Death Anticipated

The *gemara* responds: *lo, meis davka* — only dying is different. *D'lo nicha lei d'tipal kamei yavam* — death is not treated as a disqualifying *ones* because that may well have been precisely the contingency the husband had in mind when giving the *get*. He wanted the *get* to protect her from *yibum* in the event of his death; he intended the *get* to take effect in that scenario. Getting sick, however, is different — that may have been something he never anticipated and would never have intended to include within his condition. So on this version of *Rava*'s position, *ones* does matter, but dying is not classified as an *ones* in this context because the husband can be presumed to have intended that very outcome.

The *gemara* revisits the river case as well — *Shmuel*'s ruling that the man who was blocked by the river and called out "I am coming" has not fulfilled the condition — but notes that this too can be explained as a case of *unsa de-shchiach*, a foreseeable *ones* the husband should have anticipated and excluded explicitly.

### Final Conclusion

*Tosafot* works through the competing positions at length and concludes that we must adopt *ain ones begitin* — the ruling that *ones* does not negate a conditional *get* — as the operative position. The societal stakes are simply too high. With *yesh ones begitin*, the *tznuos* will become unnecessarily chained and the *prutzos* will remarry in situations they should not, producing *mamzerim*. The conclusion is thus driven not by pure legal logic but by the existential requirements of communal stability.

*Tosafot* does note, however, that even at the end of the matter, a residual question remains: there may be extreme cases of *ones* — something so extraordinary that no one could ever have anticipated it — where even those who rule *ain ones begitin* as a matter of policy might concede that the *ones* is operative. The *gemara* does not arrive at a fully clean resolution, and that ambiguity in the extreme case persists.

## Wednesday Wedding

### Three-Day Prep

Having concluded the discussion of *ones*, the *gemara* returns to the basic premise of the *mishna* that opens the tractate: virgins marry on Wednesday, so that if the husband has a *ta'anas besulim* — a complaint that she was not a virgin — he can go to court on Thursday morning. The choice of Wednesday rather than, say, Sunday was deliberate: the groom needed three days to prepare the wedding feast, so Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday were preparation days, with Wednesday as the wedding.

### Court Schedule

*Amar Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak*: *lo shanu ela mi-takanas Ezra v'eilach* — this rule applies only from the *takana* of *Ezra* onward. *Ezra* instituted regular courts that convened specifically on Mondays and Thursdays. Since Thursday was the fixed court day, Wednesday was the optimal wedding night — the husband could appear in court the very next morning. But before *Ezra*'s *takana*, when courts sat every day, *ishah nisas b'chol yom* — a woman could marry on any day, since no single day had any special relationship to the court schedule.

*Tosafot* raises a difficulty here: did *Ezra*'s *takana* actually *reduce* the frequency of court sittings? Before *Ezra*, courts apparently sat daily; afterward, only on Monday and Thursday. *Tosafot* offers two resolutions. The first: before *Ezra*, courts sat daily but only in the cities; *Ezra* decreed that courts should sit less frequently but extend their reach to the villages as well. The second: before *Ezra*, courts were convened on an ad hoc basis whenever the need arose; *Ezra* instituted fixed, regular courts with set hours and set days, replacing the ad hoc system with a structured institution.

### Variable Courts

The *gemara* makes clear that the historical question about pre-*Ezra* practice is not the point. *Hachi ka'amar* — what the *gemara* is actually saying is: *ei ika batei dinin di-kvu-in idna* — if today you had regular courts sitting every day, or conversely if today there were no fixed court schedule at all, then *k'kodem takanas Ezra* — the situation would resemble the pre-*Ezra* era, and *ishah nisas b'chol yom* — a woman could marry on any day. The connection between Wednesday and Thursday courts is entirely instrumental: it was never about the day itself but about ensuring the husband had recourse to the court immediately after the wedding night.

*Tosafot* notes an apparent problem with this reasoning: what about Friday? Even if courts are in session on every other day, a *beis din* cannot convene on *Shabbat*. How could marrying on Friday ever be permitted? *Tosafot* responds with two points. First, in practice the formal procedure that would be required — producing witnesses, conducting a full trial — is not what is needed today. All that is required is registering a complaint, which can be done informally before three people even on *Shabbat*. Second, *Rashi*'s understanding of the court's role in the original *takana* was about gathering witnesses for a potential capital prosecution, which is not at all the legal landscape of later generations. The concerns we now face regarding *ta'anas besulim* can be addressed without the same formal *beis din* structure.

### Core Requirement

The *gemara* then asks: even if there is no fixed Thursday court, does the three-day preparation requirement not still apply? *Ha ba'inan shakdu* — don't we still need the rabbis' conscientious provision that the groom spend three days preparing? The *gemara* answers: *tarach lei* — he can get married on any day, provided he has spent three days preparing. The *takana* imposes a minimum investment in wedding preparation, not a fixed calendar day. The day is entirely instrumental; the preparation is the substance.

## Takana Source

### Shakdu Source

The *gemara* asks: *mai shakdu* — where does this concept of *shakdu* — the rabbis' solicitude — come from? A *braita* provides the answer. *Mipnei ma amru besula nises l'yom ha-revi'i?* — Why did the rabbis say that a virgin marries on the fourth day of the week? *She'im haya lo ta'anas besulim, haya mashkim l'beis din* — so that if the husband has a complaint about her virginity, he can go to court first thing the next morning. And why not Sunday? *Shakdu chachamim al takanas bnos Yisrael* — the rabbis were conscientious, they took special care for the welfare of Jewish women, ensuring that the groom would invest in the wedding: *she-yehei torech b'seuda shlosha yamim* — that he should busy himself with preparing the feast for three days.

### Three-Day Pattern

The three-day pattern that results is: *echad b'shabbos, sheni b'shabbos, shlishi b'shabbos* — Sunday, Monday, Tuesday are the days of preparation; *u-v'revi'i konesah* — and on Wednesday he marries her. This is the full structure of the *takana*.

### Wednesday to Tuesday

The *baraita* continues: *u-mei-hasakana v'eilach, nahagu lichnos b'shlishi* — once a certain danger emerged, the practice shifted to marrying on Tuesday. *Ve-lo miku beyadam chachamim* — and the rabbis did not object to this departure from the original *takana*.

### Monday Exception

As for Monday: *u-v'sheni lo yichanes* — as a general rule one should not marry on Monday. There is a dispute between *Rashi* and *Tosafot* about how to read this — whether it refers to the danger scenario or to ordinary circumstances — but *ve'i machmat ha'ones*, if there were special extenuating circumstances, getting married on Monday is nonetheless permitted. So the *takana* maintained its formal structure even as practical circumstances drove the actual custom toward Tuesday, with Monday available as a further fallback in cases of pressing need.

## Sakana Definition

### Ruler's Right

What was this *sakana* that caused the shift from Wednesday to Tuesday? The *gemara* considers and rejects the most direct possibility — that the non-Jewish authorities were persecuting the practice of Wednesday weddings as a religious observance, threatening death to those who continued it. If that were the case, the *gemara* notes, why not uproot the *takana* entirely rather than simply shift to Tuesday? A persecuting government that targeted Wednesday weddings would simply target Tuesday weddings next.

*Rava* therefore offers a different account of the danger: *betulah niseit beyom revi'i tiba'el le-hegmon techilah* — when a virgin married on Wednesday, the local ruler or governor would claim the right to sexual relations with the bride before the groom. This was the *droit de seigneur*, a real practice in medieval contexts where local nobles claimed first access to brides on their wedding night. The danger was thus not religious persecution of the *takana* as such, but a specific and predictable abuse that would reliably occur whenever a wedding took place on a fixed, known day. By shifting to Tuesday — a day the governor would not anticipate — the community could avoid the problem, since the ruler simply would not know when to show up.

### Tznuot Resistance

The *gemara* asks: *hai sakana* — why do you call this a *sakana*, a danger to life? *Ones hu* — it is an act of forced sex, an *ones*, but not a life-threatening situation. The woman is not being killed; she is being raped. Why frame it as a *sakana*?

The answer is: *mishum de'ika tznuos de-masran nafshaihu le-katla* — because there are women, the *tznuos*, so deeply modest and principled, that rather than submit they would actually resist unto death. For these women, the situation would genuinely become a *sakana*. *Ve-asyan lidei sakana* — they would come to risk their lives. The *tznuos* here are clearly acting *lifnim mishurat ha-din*, beyond the letter of the law; their resistance, though admirable, is not legally required.

### Submission Permitted

This leads the *gemara* to an important halakhic ruling: *ve-lidrosh lehu de-ones shari* — why not simply teach these women that submission is permitted? One might expect that since the woman is married — already having undergone *kiddushin* — this would fall under *giluy arayos*, which is one of the three cardinal sins subject to the rule of *yehareg ve-al ya'avor*, dying rather than transgressing. Why does the *gemara* assume she may simply submit?

This is a critical *gemara* for the discussion of *yehareg ve-al ya'avor* as it applies to *giluy arayos*. *Tosafot* addresses the question with two answers. The first, advanced by *Rabbeinu Tam*, is that sex with a non-Jew belongs to a categorically different legal domain and does not constitute *giluy arayos* for purposes of *yehareg ve-al ya'avor*. *Tosafot* ultimately rejects this approach, though *Rabbeinu Tam* appears to have advanced it to deal with a specific practical case — a Jewish woman who had lived with a non-Jewish man and then sought to return to a Jewish husband after that man converted; *Rabbeinu Tam* argued that her relationship with the non-Jew did not trigger *asura le-bo'el* or the *yehareg ve-al ya'avor* prohibition.

The second answer, which is generally taken as the operative explanation, draws on the principle found in *Sanhedrin*: *isha karka olam* — a woman in the act of rape is categorically passive, and the rule of *yehareg ve-al ya'avor* applies only to acts one actively performs. If someone threatens to use a person as an instrument of killing — throwing them onto an infant — the person need not give up their life if they are entirely passive. The question is whether we genuinely conceive of the woman as performing no act in the context of rape.

The *Ramban* offers what is perhaps the most persuasive resolution. He argues that the very nature of rape makes the choice of *yehareg ve-al ya'avor* a false one. Even if a woman were to say "kill me rather than rape me," the rapist could choose to rape her anyway. The anatomy and physics of the situation mean that she cannot truly choose martyrdom over the act in the way that a man could, for instance, refuse to perform an idolatrous ritual. It is therefore not genuinely a situation where the rule of *yehareg ve-al ya'avor* can be applied, since the act can be imposed on her regardless of her choice. This explains why a married woman may legally submit rather than give up her life.

### Education Risk

The *gemara* asks: if submission is permitted, why not simply educate the women? Why allow the situation to remain one of *sakana* when the *tznuos* could be told that halakha does not require them to die? The *gemara* answers: *ika prutzos ve-ika nami kohanos* — because of two distinct concerns.

The first is the problem of the *prutzos*: a little knowledge in the wrong hands is dangerous. If women are broadly taught that in such circumstances submission is permitted, some will use this information to rationalize submission in cases where it is *not* truly an *ones* — where there is no real compulsion at all. They will claim *ones* retroactively to justify conduct that cannot be justified.

The second is the particular problem of *kohanos* — women married to *kohanim*. Even though submission is legally permitted in a genuine *ones* scenario, the halakhic consequence for a *kohenes* is irreversible: she becomes forbidden to her *kohen* husband. For such women, the calculus is entirely different. They may rationally conclude that the irreversible halakhic consequence of submission — the permanent destruction of their marriage — is worse than the alternative. For them, the situation genuinely remains a *sakana*, and teaching them broadly that submission is permitted would not help them; it might actually harm them by obscuring the specific and severe consequence they face.

The *gemara* therefore maintains the framing of *sakana* rather than *ones*, and explains why public education was not the solution. One might find it deeply troubling that the *tznuos* were left exposed to lethal risk rather than being taught a ruling that would save their lives — all because of concern about the *prutzot* misusing the information. The better reading of the *gemara*, and the one that avoids the alternative implication that the rabbis were prepared to tolerate actual deaths in order to preserve the *takana* of Wednesday weddings, is that the *gemara*'s question is not about whether to move away from Wednesday. Of course the community moved to Tuesday. The *gemara*'s question is only about the framing: why describe the situation as *sakana* rather than *ones*? And the answer is that even with all the education in the world, there would still be *kohanos* for whom it remained a genuine life-threatening situation, and there would still be *prutzos* who would misuse the ruling.

## Takana Preservation

### Gezeira vs. Takana

The question remains: given all of this difficulty, why did the rabbis not simply uproot the *takana* of Wednesday weddings altogether? If the fixed Wednesday date was the source of the danger, why not abolish the fixed day entirely and permit marriage on any day? The *gemara* answers with a foundational principle: *gezeira avidah de-batlah* — a governmental edict will eventually pass away. But *takkanata de-rabbanan mi-kamei gezeira lo akrinan* — we do not uproot a rabbinic ordinance in the face of a governmental edict.

This reflects a deep institutional orientation. The rabbis took a long view. Legal systems and religious frameworks must be built to outlast the particular political pressures of any given era. To dismantle a *takana* every time history presents a threat would be to have no enduring legal structure at all. The *takana* of Wednesday weddings was not abolished; the community adapted around it, found a workaround, and waited for the edict to pass.

### Shift to Tuesday

The adaptation was the shift to Tuesday. The *takana* remained formally in place — Wednesday was still the halakhically ideal day for a virgin to marry — but the custom shifted to Tuesday without the rabbis objecting. The *takana* was not repealed; it was preserved in its theoretical integrity while practical necessity drove behavior in a different direction.

### Tuesday Strategy

The *gemara* asks the obvious question: *ee hachi, beshlishi nami atei u-va'eil* — if they start marrying on Tuesday, won't the governor simply show up on Tuesdays instead? The *gemara* answers: *misfeka lo akar nafshei* — out of uncertainty, he will not uproot himself and come. Once there is no fixed and predictable day — once weddings occur on whatever Tuesday or other day they happen to fall on, with no reliable pattern — the governor cannot know in advance when to appear. He would have to be present every day in every village, which is simply not practical. The uncertainty itself becomes the protective mechanism. The number of successful interceptions drops dramatically. Whereas a fixed Wednesday schedule turned every wedding into a predictable target, the shift to a variable day — theoretically any day, in practice often Tuesday — introduced enough unpredictability to make the abuse far less systematic.

This is how the *takana* was preserved: not by upending it, not by surrendering to the pressure, but by a careful and principled adaptation that maintained the legal framework while rendering the specific vulnerability much harder to exploit.

---

---

# Ketubot 4

## Ones & Early Marriage

### Sakana vs. Ones

The daf picks up near the bottom of 3b, where a *braita* — essentially a *Tosefta* — discusses the established practice of getting married on Wednesdays. The *braita* records that during a period of *sakana*, a genuine risk to life, the community shifted weddings to Tuesday. The Gemara explains this as a response to a local ruler who was forcing brides to sleep with him on their wedding night, so that making the wedding day less predictable offered some protection. The *braita* then states that in a time of *ones* — a circumstance beyond one's control, but short of a life-threatening *sakana* — one may marry on another day, using Monday as the example.

The Gemara immediately distinguishes between these two terms. If the prior case was already called a *sakana*, why is this one now called an *ones*? The change in terminology signals that we are dealing with an altogether different kind of circumstance. Rashi adds a further nuance: the earlier formulation described a communal *minhag* that developed organically, whereas here the language *mutar* — it is permitted — carries the flavor of a formal, proactive rabbinic allowance, perhaps even a *l'chatchila* ruling for an individual case.

### Military Threat

Rava identifies the *ones* in question: word spreads that a military commander — a *sar tzava* — is coming to the city with his troops, who will requisition all available food and supplies. Since the wedding feast has already been prepared and will be seized if left for Wednesday, the couple has grounds to move the wedding earlier. The financial disruption of having all the food confiscated constitutes a sufficient *ones* to justify departing from the standard Wednesday date.

### Duration of Threat

The Gemara raises a challenge: *heichi dami* — what exactly is the case? If the commander is simply passing through and will leave after a short time, Rashi reads the Gemara's response as: just wait, and hold the wedding the following Wednesday or the one after. There is no need to act early if the disruption is temporary. Tosafos reads the case differently, suggesting that if the commander is leaving on that same Wednesday, one should simply schedule the feast for later in the day — but this reading is difficult, since the problem is that once the food is gathered it will be seized regardless of timing. The Gemara accordingly sets the case as *de-ati ve-kava*: the commander is arriving and settling in indefinitely. Under those circumstances, there is no later Wednesday to wait for, and moving the wedding earlier is warranted.

### Advanced Retinue

This raises a follow-up question: if the commander is arriving on Wednesday, why not simply hold the wedding on Tuesday? The answer is that in this case, there would be no *chiddush* — no novel ruling — since one is merely moving back one day to avoid the exact day of the disruption. The Gemara therefore frames the case more pointedly: the commander's *asafrava* — his advance retinue — is arriving on Tuesday, ahead of his own arrival on Wednesday. This means the food could be seized even earlier, justifying moving the wedding all the way back to Monday. That is the genuine novelty: the disruption threatens not merely Wednesday but the days leading up to it, and we permit the wedding as early as necessary to avoid the loss.

---

## Death & Wedding

### Setup: Food & Death

Having outlined the *ones* of military requisition, the Gemara now turns to what may have been the original referent of the word *ones* in the first *braita*, or at minimum a distinct and important case that several *braisos* address in their own right. The scenario: *harei she-haya pito afui* — the bread has been baked, fresh; *u-tivcho tavuach* — the meat has been slaughtered, freshly; *ve-yaino mazug* — the wine has been mixed; everything is prepared for the wedding feast and will spoil if not consumed imminently. And at that moment, *u-mais aviv shel choson o imah shel kallah* — the father of the *chosson* or the mother of the *kallah* dies.

This is not merely a theoretical case. It combines two pressing concerns: the catastrophic financial loss of irreplaceable prepared food, and the death of the very parent who was instrumental in preparing for the wedding. If they wait a month until after *shiv'ah* and *shloshim*, not only will the food be lost, but the father will not be there to oversee the *chosson*'s preparations, nor will the mother be there to prepare the *kallah* — the people uniquely responsible for making this wedding what it is. That combination drives the entire *halacha* that follows.

### Postponing Burial

The practical opportunity created by this moment is that the body has not yet been buried. *Avelus* does not begin until burial — and that creates room to maneuver. The *braita* prescribes: *machnisin es ha-meis la-cheder* — bring the corpse into a room — *ve-es ha-chosson ve-es ha-kallah la-chuppah* — and bring the *chosson* and *kallah* to the *chuppah*. The wedding proceeds while the body remains unburied and before *avelus* has begun, while the couple are still technically *onanim*.

What *chuppah* means in this context deserves attention. It may refer to a *yichud* room, in which case the act of *bi'ah* would follow immediately within it; or it may refer to the formal wedding canopy, with the act of *bi'ah* occurring afterward. Since *kiddushin* has already been performed, there is no question about *bircas erusin*, and the *sheva brachos* are recited by the *tzibbur*. The precise mechanics of what constitutes *chuppah* here can be addressed separately.

### Why Sex Needed

The *braita* continues: *u-vo'el bi'as mitzvah u-foresh* — he has relations once, the act of *mitzvah*, and then separates. Why is this required? Two explanations present themselves. One is a kind of *rachmanus*: they have prepared for this night, they anticipated it, and it would be deeply cruel to deny it entirely. The second, and perhaps more structural, reason is that the act of *bi'ah* concretizes and actualizes the status of *chosson va-kallah* — it makes the marriage genuinely real, not merely formal. Since the entire enterprise depends on establishing that the *shivas yemei ha-mishteh* status of *chosson va-kallah* precedes the onset of *avelus*, having the *bi'ah* makes that status more robust and unambiguous.

### Celebration Before Mourn…

Having had *bi'as mitzvah*, the *braita* continues: *ve-nohag shivas yemei ha-mishteh, ve-achar kach nohag shivas yemei avelus* — the full seven days of the wedding feast are observed, and only afterward does the week of mourning begin.

This is the crux of the entire arrangement, and it is worth dwelling on. The logic parallels the laws of *avelus* during a *regel*. Ordinarily, if a burial occurs before a festival, the *regel* cancels the remaining days of *shiv'ah*, because the public joy of the *regel* cannot coexist with the public mourning of *avelus*. Here, the *shivas yemei ha-mishteh* of *chosson va-kallah* functions as a kind of *regel*: because it began before the *avelus* — because the burial takes place after the *chuppah* — the status of the wedding week precedes and displaces the onset of *avelus* during that entire week. The *avelus* does not kick in until the wedding week concludes.

This is a more significant leniency than it might first appear. Had *avelus* already begun, perhaps we would have permitted a single wedding night — but we would not have allowed the *shivas yemei ha-mishteh* to run its full course. By manipulating the timing to ensure that *avelus* had not yet commenced, the couple gains not just the first night but the entire week of celebration. The *avelus* then follows in full.

Several practical advantages flow from acting before burial: first, the status of *onen* may be less restrictive than that of *avel* regarding *nissuin* and regarding *bi'ah* — since there is a *machlokes* whether sex is even prohibited for an *onen*, making it less severe than the explicit prohibition during *avelus*; second, and more fundamentally, the *chuppah* itself and the *simcha* associated with *nissuin* are deeply bound up with that status of *chosson va-kallah*, and it is far less problematic to initiate *nissuin* during *aninus* than during *avelus*.

Tosafos raises a striking point: the Gemara is in effect being more lenient regarding *aninus d'oraisa* — since *aninus* has a Torah root, at least with respect to *korbanot* — than it is regarding *avelus d'rabbanan*. Tosafos explains that although *aninus* may have a *d'oraisa* anchor, the practical obligations and restrictions of an *onen* are structured very differently from those of an *avel*: an *onen* does not sit on the ground, does not rend garments, does not observe the other symbolic mourning practices. The status of *onen* is simply a different kind of status, and within that status, the space for *nissuin* and even *bi'ah* is greater.

### Sleeping Separate

Although the *shivas yemei ha-mishteh* precedes *avelus*, the Gemara is clear that once the burial takes place — which occurs after the *bi'as mitzvah* — *avelus* begins. Even while the wedding week is in full swing, the private dimension of *avelus* obtains. The principle is that *devarim she-be-tzina* — private matters — apply even when *avelus* is otherwise suspended, just as they apply when a burial occurs during a *regel*. The most classic example of *devarim she-be-tzina* is the prohibition on marital relations. Accordingly, although the public celebrations of the week continue, the couple may not continue to have sex.

To enforce this, the *braita* prescribes: *hu yashen bein ha-anashim ve-hi yeshena bein ha-nashim* — he sleeps among the men and she sleeps among the women. This is stronger than merely sleeping in separate beds; they are placed in entirely separate company to prevent them from acting on the very powerful impulse to be together — having just gotten married — in violation of the *issur* that is now in effect. The reason this extreme measure is required, as the Gemara will explain through Rav Ashi, is that the rabbis were so lenient in enabling all of this manipulation in the first place that the couple might not take the residual *avelus* obligations seriously. Since the *avelus* has been pushed aside and only the *devarim she-be-tzina* remain, the sole live prohibition is the most invisible one. Extra measures are needed to ensure it is honored.

One might observe, as an interesting point, that requiring the couple to sleep in conspicuously separate quarters — surrounded by others of the same gender — turns what was meant to be a private matter into a very public one. The very act of enforcing the private prohibition makes it publicly visible. This tension remains unresolved in the Gemara.

### Bride's Beautification

The *braita* adds: *ve-ein monin tachshitin min ha-kallah kol shloshim yom* — one does not prevent the *kallah* from wearing jewelry and beautifying herself throughout the first thirty days, even though she is an *aveilah* and even though *shloshim* normally restricts such beautification. The rationale is clear: this is the first month of marriage, and doing everything possible to encourage mutual attraction between the new couple takes precedence over the standard requirements of *avelus* in this context.

### Father/Mother Restriction

The *braita* specifies: *ve-davka aviv shel chosson o imah shel kallah* — specifically the *chosson*'s father or the *kallah*'s mother, not the reverse. The reason is *d'ika inish d'tarach lehu*: these are the people who were actively engaged in preparing for the wedding. The father oversaw and coordinated his son's preparations; the mother prepared her daughter. If we were to say simply postpone the wedding until after the *avelus*, the argument that "it can be replicated later" fails — because what cannot be replicated is the preparation that parent performed. The *kallah*'s mother prepared her for this wedding, and then died moments before it took place. The emotional and practical dimensions of that are real; it is that irreplaceability that drives the ruling. *Aval ipcha lo* — the reverse configuration does not qualify, because that presumption of active personal preparation does not apply.

Contemporary *poskim* have at times been less strict about insisting on the exact formulation of *aviv shel chosson*, particularly given the enormous financial losses involved in modern weddings — deposits, caterers, halls — that are also irretrievable. The Gemara does say *ve-davka*, which implies the specification is meaningful. Whether the financial loss alone suffices, or whether it requires both the financial factor and the irreplaceable-preparation factor together, is a genuine question. One could read the Gemara as requiring both: a purely financial loss, however large, may not be sufficient without the specific circumstance of the irreplaceable parental role.

### Food Spoilage Rules

Rav Chisda introduces a qualification: *lo shanu ela she-natan mayim agabi basar* — this leniency applies only when water has been applied to the meat, i.e., the meat has been rinsed in preparation for *melichah* to remove the blood. In that state, it cannot be preserved or resold; if not consumed immediately it is lost. But if the meat has not yet been rinsed and is still in a more preserved state, it can be sold and the financial loss can be recouped — and therefore the wedding should be postponed.

Rava qualifies this further: in a large city, *u-va-krach*, even rinsed meat can be sold quickly — enough buyers exist that one can set up and sell it all within hours. The financial loss is therefore recoverable, and the wedding should be postponed. Rav Pappa offers the counter-qualification: in a village, *u-vi-chfar*, even unrinsed meat cannot be sold, because the population is too small to absorb it. So the wedding should always proceed in a village, and never needs to be postponed in one on account of rinsed versus unrinsed meat.

This leaves Rav Chisda's original distinction — rinsed versus unrinsed — without an apparent case. Rav Ashi resolves it: Rav Chisda's case is a medium-sized city, like *Masa Machasya*, which is neither a full metropolitan center nor a village. In such a town, rinsed meat cannot be sold fast enough to prevent loss, but unrinsed meat can still be preserved and sold. The *tosefta kevasei de-Rav Chisda* — the *braita* that accords with Rav Chisda — then repeats the full scenario, including the condition *ve-natan mayim agabi basar*, confirming that the operative halacha requires the meat to have been rinsed. The remainder of the *braita*'s formulation is essentially identical to what we have already seen: the corpse into the room, the couple to the *chuppah*, *bi'as mitzvah*, the seven days of wedding feast, then seven days of *avelus*, and the sleeping-separate requirement for all those days.

---

## Chuppat Niddah

### Niddah Sleeping Rules

The *braita* continues with a second scenario: *ve-chen mi she-pirsa ishto niddah* — similarly, a man whose wife becomes a *niddah* on the wedding night — *hu yashen bein ha-anashim ve-hi yeshena bein ha-nashim*, he sleeps among the men and she among the women. At first glance, this is startling, since the Gemara elsewhere is quite clear that a husband and wife share a room even when she is a *niddah*; isolating the woman to a separate dwelling is associated with practices of ancient cultures that maintained strict menstrual taboos, not with *halacha*. The key is context: the entire *braita* is addressing the wedding night specifically. Here, the couple has not yet had relations. When a *chuppat niddah* occurs — when the wife becomes a *niddah* before *bi'ah* on the wedding night — there has been no established marital intimacy, the desire is at its most intense, and the concern that they will not be able to withstand the temptation is acute. The requirement to sleep in separate company therefore applies specifically in this pre-*bi'ah* context. This is in fact a real and practically significant *halacha*, and the question of how to implement the requirement of sleeping *bein ha-anashim* and *bein ha-nashim* in contemporary circumstances is one that *poskim* address.

### Devarim Shebetzina

The Gemara notes that this *braita* — specifically the requirement of sleeping separate even after the *bi'as mitzvah* in the death case — provides strong support for Rabbi Yochanan's position: *af al pi she-amru ein avelus ba-moed, aval devarim she-be-tzina noheg* — even though *avelus* does not apply during the *regel*, the private dimensions of *avelus* are nonetheless observed. Here, the *shivas yemei ha-mishteh* functions as the *regel*, and yet they must sleep separate — demonstrating that the *devarim she-be-tzina* prohibition of *bi'ah* applies even within that week. The sleeping-separate requirement is precisely the *braita*'s way of enforcing that private prohibition.

### Before vs. After

Rav Yosef the son of Rav Ami in the name of Rava then introduces a distinction: *lo shanu ela she-lo ba'al, aval ba'al, ishto yeshena imo* — this separation requirement applies only where they have not yet had *bi'ah*; once they have had *bi'ah*, the wife sleeps with him normally.

The Gemara immediately challenges this: in the death case, the whole point is that they did have *bi'ah* — *bi'as mitzvah* — and still they are required to sleep separate. So how can Rava say that *bi'ah* removes the separation requirement? The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by re-reading the *braita*: the *ve-chen* — "similarly" — introducing the *niddah* case does not indicate identical circumstances. Rather, it indicates that the same *halacha* of sleeping separate applies. The *niddah* case itself, however, is specifically one where *bi'ah* has not occurred; it is *mi she-pirsa ishto niddah ve-lo ba'al* — she became a *niddah* and they never had *bi'ah*. In that situation — *chuppat niddah* before any *bi'ah* — the separation requirement applies. Once *bi'ah* has taken place and the woman subsequently becomes a *niddah* in the normal course of marriage, the couple continues to share a room.

---

## Avelus vs. Niddah

### Niddah Duties

The Gemara now turns to a broader comparison, framing it as a question: does *avelus* exhibit greater stringency than *niddah* in this regard, such that the sleeping-separate requirement would make sense as a routine feature of any case of *avelus*? The Gemara cites Rabbi Yitzchak bar Chanina in the name of Rav Huna: *kol melachot she-ha-ishah osah le-va'alah, niddah osah le-va'alah* — all the domestic duties that a wife performs for her husband, a *niddah* continues to perform. The extensive list of domestic responsibilities that will be enumerated later in the tractate applies equally during *niddah*.

### Three Harchakot

The exceptions are three specific acts designated as intimate: *chutz mi-mezigat ha-kos* — she does not mix his drink, which is seen as an act of personal and affectionate service; *ve-hatza'as ha-mitah* — she does not make his bed in the final decorative, presentational sense (Tosafos clarifies this refers specifically to the finishing touches, not the basic spreading of sheets); *ve-harchatzat panav yadav ve-raglav* — she does not wash his face, hands, and feet. These constitute the *harchakot*, the specific intimate acts that a *niddah* refrains from performing for her husband as a form of distancing.

### Avelus Leniency

By contrast, when a woman is an *aveilah*, a *braita* teaches: *af al pi she-amru ein adam rashai lichof ishto lihyot kochelet lihyot pokeset* — a husband cannot compel his *aveilah* wife to beautify herself; he cannot insist she apply eye makeup (*kochelet*, which Rashi may read as rouge) or braid her hair (*pokeset*). Even so, *be-emet amru* — the halakhic truth is — she still performs all the intimate domestic acts, including mixing his drink, making his bed, and washing his face, hands, and feet. The *harchakot* that apply by *niddah* do not apply by *avelus*. An *aveilah* may perform all of these acts.

### Beautification Prohibiti…

The asymmetry is noteworthy. During *niddah*, certain intimate domestic acts are prohibited to preserve appropriate boundaries; during *avelus*, those same acts are permitted — the restriction runs the other way: the husband cannot compel the *aveilah* wife to beautify herself against her will. Her state of mourning is hers to observe, and he may not override it by demanding she present herself in a way that contradicts her *avelus*.

---

## Avel Sleeping Rules

### General Avel Rule

Having established that *avelus* is in fact *more lenient* than *niddah* when it comes to intimate acts, the Gemara confronts its earlier assumption. It had been reading the *braita*'s sleeping-separate requirement as a general feature of any *avelus* situation. But if *avelus* is less stringent than *niddah* in terms of *harchakot*, why would we impose a more severe sleeping arrangement — separate rooms, sleeping among members of the same gender — in any ordinary case of *avelus*? This requires explanation. The Gemara's initial answer: *yetzer hara*. A man is assumed to be less in control of his sexual impulses, more capable of pressuring his wife even if she is reluctant, and more likely to override even his own *avelus* obligation. Therefore, when *he* is the *avel*, more protective measures are required.

### Husband vs. Wife

This leads the Gemara to distinguish between two configurations: *kan be-avelus didei, kan be-avelus didah* — in one case he is the *avel*, in the other she is the *aveilah*. When he is the *avel*, his *yetzer hara* may lead him to violate the prohibition on marital relations — and to bring his wife along, whether she wants to or not. When she is the *aveilah*, the same dynamic does not hold: she is in mourning, she will resist, and he will be unable to override her refusal. The Gemara therefore proposes that the sleeping-separate requirement applies specifically when the husband is the *avel*, and not when only the wife is the *aveilah*.

### Amended Braita

The Gemara faces an objection: the original *braita* specifies *aviv shel chosson o imah shel kallah* — either his father or her mother. That means both cases — he as *avel* and she as *aveilah* — result in the same sleeping-separate arrangement. How then can we say the requirement applies only when he is the *avel*? The Gemara resolves this by proposing that the *braita* be read differently: the *ve-davka* formulation of the father-of-the-*chosson* / mother-of-the-*kallah* applies to most of the *halachos* discussed, but the specific sleeping-separate rule should be understood as inserted only for the case where he is the *avel*. The *braita* is to be read — *teni* — with that clarification built in.

### Spouse Respect

The discussion of who is the *avel* raises a further question from a second *braita*: when a man's father-in-law or mother-in-law dies — his wife's parent, not his own — he cannot compel his wife to beautify herself, and moreover, *kofeh mitaso ve-noheg imah avelus* — he overturns his own couch and himself observes *avelus* together with her. The same applies in reverse: if his parents die, she cannot beautify herself and she too turns over her couch and observes *avelus* with him. Neither of those *braisos* mentions any sleeping-separate requirement in its description of the spousal-respect dimension of *avelus*. This seems to undermine the Gemara's claim that sleeping separate is a feature of *avelus* when the husband is the *avel*.

The Gemara's response is to amend the *braita* once more — *teni be-avelus didei hu yashen bein ha-anashim ve-ishto yeshena bein ha-nashim* — inserting the sleeping-separate rule into the *braita* where the husband is the *avel*. The Gemara also resolves the phrase *kofeh mitaso ve-noheg imo avelus* — "observing *avelus* with him" — not as meaning sharing his bed, but rather as meaning that in his presence she too practices *avelus* out of respect. This is grounded by the tradition in Rav's name to his son Chiya: when in your wife's presence during her *shiv'ah*, observe *avelus*; when not in her presence, you need not. The word *imo* — "with him" — refers not to physical proximity in bed but to observing *avelus* when together in the house.

---

## Special Avelus

### Normal Avelus Serious

Rav Ashi then intervenes with a resolution that reframes the entire discussion: *mi kamadmis avelus de-hacha le-avelus de-alma*? How can you compare the *avelus* in this specific case to ordinary *avelus*? The two are fundamentally different situations, and the sleeping-separate requirement in the *braita* does not indicate anything about routine *avelus*. *Avelus de-alma chamir* — ordinary *avelus* is treated seriously. People do not take it lightly, do not disparage it, and do not need additional safeguards to ensure the prohibitions are respected.

### This Avelus Lenient

*Avelus de-hacha*, however — this particular *avelus* — is a completely different matter. *Keivan d'akilu rabbanan* — since the rabbis themselves were so lenient in this case, enabling the entire arrangement to proceed — *asu lizilzuli bei* — the person may come to treat it lightly. When the *avelus* has been pushed aside and manipulated so that the wedding week could come first, the psychological weight of the mourning obligation is diminished. The person may not feel fully bound by even what remains of the *avelus* during the wedding week.

### Leniency Explained

The Gemara then clarifies what the specific leniency was. It was not the act of *bi'ah* itself — the Gemara states *hatam mishum de-lo chala alei avelus*: *avelus* had not yet begun when they had *bi'ah*, because the *meis* was still unburied. According to Rabbi Eliezer, *avelus* begins when the body is removed from the house on the way to burial; according to Rabbi Yehoshua, it begins when the *golel* — either the tombstone or, according to Rashi, the cover of the *aron* — is put in place. Either way, at the time of *bi'as mitzvah*, *avelus* had not yet commenced, and so permitting *bi'ah* then was no leniency at all. The leniency — *mai kula* — is precisely what the *braita* states: *nohag shivas yemei ha-mishteh ve-achar kach noheg shivas yemei avelus* — that the entire week of wedding celebration is permitted to precede the entire week of mourning. That is the rabbinic manipulation, the pushing-aside of *avelus* to enable the *simcha* to run its course first. And it is because of that extraordinary leniency — not a violation of *halacha*, but a deliberate restructuring of its onset — that the person may come to treat the residual obligations lightly.

### Private Laws Only

The upshot is this: once the burial occurs, *avelus* begins; but since the *shivas yemei ha-mishteh* has already started and that status came first, most of the outward and public dimensions of *avelus* are suspended during that week. The only operative dimension of *avelus* during the week is *devarim she-be-tzina* — the private prohibition on marital relations. That prohibition is, by its very nature, invisible to others. And since the entire frame has been one of leniency — you were allowed to have your *bi'as mitzvah*, the wedding week is proceeding — there is a real concern that this one remaining, private prohibition will be taken lightly or ignored. It is precisely because *devarim she-be-tzina* is all that remains that we must go to the extreme of having him sleep among the men and her among the women, making the enforcement of a private prohibition through very public means.

---

---

# Ketubot 6

## Ketubot Overview

### Topics Survey

The daf we take up today — 6a — finds us in the middle of a challenging *sugya* concerning first-time intercourse on *Shabbat*. Before proceeding, it is worth pausing to appreciate just how much ground has been covered in the opening pages of this *masechet*. Beginning with the question of when a *besulah* gets married and whether the groom must pay support when the marriage is delayed, the *masechet* quickly moved far afield of its core theme. On 2b we encountered the laws of conditions in a *get* and whether an unfulfillable condition is nonetheless considered fulfilled — a major question in contract law and *gittin*. On daf 3 came the topic of *hafka'as kiddushin*, the rabbinic power to retroactively dissolve a marriage. Then, on 3b, a case of a woman compelled to submit to intercourse with a local ruler under threat of death, bringing in questions of *yaharog v'al ya'avor*. From there the *masechet* turned to *aveilus* and *aninus* — whether a funeral may be postponed to permit a scheduled wedding, the laws of *devarim she'betzina noheg*, and related questions. On daf 5 came the question of what types of matters may be discussed on *Shabbat* and the permissibility of doing *cheshbonos* on *Shabbat*, before returning to the themes of *ketubot* proper: the date of the wedding, the *beracha she'ne'emra bo l'adam*, the *beracha she'ne'emra bo l'dagim*, and an *agadata* about why one should not listen to *lashon hara*.

### Mini-Shas Structure
