The range of topics traversed in four *daf* — *niddah*, *aveilus*, *gittin*, *Shabbat*, and more — is precisely why *Ketubot* is famously described as a *Shas Katan*, a mini-tractate of the entire Talmud. And it is not merely the breadth of subject matter that earns it this title. The *sugyot* in *Ketubot* tend to arrive at the very heart of each conceptual question rather than working around its periphery for many sessions. Each discussion reaches the core of a central halakhic principle, which is one reason why this *masechet* is studied so extensively in *yeshivos*.

### Pedagogy Issues

That said, a word must be said about the pedagogical difficulties this particular *sugya* presents. The questions being analyzed here concern first-time intercourse, whether the act creates a wound, whether it creates an opening, what the groom's intent is, whether he wishes to see blood to confirm his bride's virginity, whether making her a non-virgin is seen as an act of desire or as damaging something pristine — all of this is typically taught to teenage boys in *yeshiva*. The difficulty is not the explicitness of the discussion per se; frank conversation about the body is appropriate. The deeper challenge is the orientation of the entire discussion: it is conducted entirely from the man's perspective. The woman's body is analyzed as an object of halakhic scrutiny. Nobody in the *gemara* asks whether the woman is permitted to have intercourse on *Shabbat*. That question is treated as simply irrelevant. This framing — focused on what the man is doing, what the man intends, what the man sees — and the way it objectifies the woman's body and renders her something of a passive subject in the analysis, creates real challenges for how this material ought to be taught. Those challenges, in the experience of most *yeshivos*, are never actually raised.

---

## First-Time Sex Issue

### Prohibitions

To distill the halakhic structure: there are two potential prohibitions associated with first intercourse on *Shabbat*. The first is *chaburah* — the act of wounding — depending on how the *gemara* understands the underlying physiology. If the blood emerges because the hymenal tissue tears away from the wall and blood is released from vessels within that tissue, that constitutes wounding. The second possible prohibition is *petach* — making an opening — which would presumably fall under the category of *binyan*, an interesting application of the concept of building to a human body, though we do encounter that elsewhere in the *gemarot*. With these two possible prohibitions established, the *gemara* then asks about the groom's intent: is he *mechaven* for this outcome, or is he *eino mechaven*? Does his intent matter, and does the principle of *mekalkel* apply — the notion that since wounding is inherently a somewhat destructive act, perhaps there is a special *halakha* regarding *chaburot* such that even a *mekalkel* is *chayav*?

### Mekalkel

*Tosafot* raises a sharp conceptual question about the category of *chaburah* and its relationship to *melachehet machshevet*. *Chaburah* is categorized under *netilat neshamah* — the same prohibition that forbids *shechting* an animal. Making a wound is like a miniature act of taking life. But how precisely is it a taking of life? *Tosafot* suggests two possibilities: either wounding weakens the living being and thus represents a step toward death, or the very extraction of blood is itself the halakhic act, since blood represents life regardless of the physical harm caused. *Tosafot* argues that it must be the latter. If wounding were prohibited because it harms or weakens the person, there would be no basis for the *gemara* to consider it an intentional *melacha* in this context, since no one desires to wound the woman or cause her pain or weakness. The only way the *gemara* can speak of the groom being *mechaven* is if the blood itself — as a symbol of life — is the object of his intention: he wants to see the blood to know that his bride is a *besulah*. This frames *netilat neshamah* in an almost symbolic sense, independent of physical harm.

### Shabbat Criteria

*Tosafot* then presses a further question. If *mekalkel bechabura chayav* — if even a destructive act of wounding incurs *chiyuv* — then why does the *gemara* treat *kavanah* as relevant at all? If *Rabbi Shimon* holds you are *chayav* for *mekalkel bechabura*, why would *eino mitkaven* provide an exemption according to *Rabbi Shimon*? *Tosafot* answers with an important conceptual distinction: *mechaven* — having intent — is not a uniquely *Shabbat* requirement. It is a general requirement applicable to all prohibitions. What *Rabbi Shimon* is saying when he rules *chayav* by *mekalkel bechabura* is that he waives the special *Shabbat* criterion of *melachehet machshevet* — the requirement that a prohibited act be constructive — in the context of wounding. But the general principle that a person must intend the prohibited act in order to be liable is not a *Shabbat* criterion; it applies universally. Accordingly, *eino mitkaven* remains an exemption even by *chaburah* according to *Rabbi Shimon*, because that exemption derives not from the *Shabbat* requirement of *melachehet machshevet* but from a general principle of halakhic liability.

*Tosafot* makes this point explicitly at the top of 6a. He writes that the reason both *mekalkel* and *misasek* are exempt in other *melachos Shabbat* is: *detam sheneihem depeturin beshaar melachos Shabbos havei mishum debe'inan meleches machsheves* — because we require *meleches machsheves*, and that is the specifically *Shabbat* criterion. But *aval she-eino miskavein klal le-melachah* — if one is not intending to perform the prohibited act at all — *lo mishum debe'inan meleches machsheves mister* — that exemption does not derive from the *Shabbat* requirement of *meleches machsheves* — *deshaar mekomos nami piter aino miskavein* — because *eino miskavein* is an exemption in other prohibitions as well, such as *kilayim*, where those who sell garments may do so in their normal manner provided they do not intend a violation, and similarly a *nazir* may comb his hair even if strands may come out. *Hilkach be-chaburah nami shari* — therefore, *eino miskavein* remains an exemption by wounding as well, even where *mekalkel* does not.

This distinction is not merely relevant to the present *sugya*. It applies practically wherever *mekalkel bechabura* might come up — for example, in the context of an injection on *Shabbat* that draws blood. Does *eino miskavein* still exempt in such a case even if *mekalkel bechabura* is *chayav*? *Tosafot* establishes clearly from this *gemara* that yes, *eino miskavein* remains an exemption, because it is a general halakhic principle, not a specifically *Shabbat* criterion.

---

## Rav vs. Shmuel

### Dispute Versions

The *gemara* now presents the central *amoraic* dispute. In the *yeshiva* of Rav, the tradition was: *Rav shari ve-Shmuel assur* — Rav permits first intercourse on *Shabbat* and Shmuel forbids it. In *Neharde'a*, the city of Shmuel, the tradition was reversed: Rav forbids it and Shmuel permits it. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak provides a *siman* — a mnemonic — to remember the correct version: *eilu mikilin le-atzman ve-eilu mikilin le-atzman* — each *yeshiva* attributed the lenient position to their own master.

### Wine Rag Proof

The *gemara* then challenges Rav's permissive position. Does Rav truly permit first intercourse on *Shabbat*? But Rav Shimi bar Chizkiya transmitted in the name of Rav that a *mesukhraya d'nazeita* — a rag stuffed into the bunghole of a wine barrel — is forbidden to be tightened on *Yom Tov*. The implicit reasoning, as Rashi explains, is that tightening the rag wrings out wine absorbed in it, constituting *sechita*. And this ruling, the *gemara* assumes, indicates that Rav holds *eino miskavein* is *assur* — since the wine being squeezed is unintended — which would in turn make first intercourse on *Shabbat* far more likely to be forbidden.

---

## First-Time Sex Issue (II)

### Tosafot Analysis

A major *Tosafot* engages this passage and raises a series of layered difficulties. If the prohibition of tightening the rag is rooted in *sechita*, the nature of that *sechita* must be clarified. If the *issur* of *sechita* is like laundering — where one soaks a garment and wrings it out — then, *Tosafot* argues, the prohibition would apply only to water, since the wringing of water is part of the laundering process. It would not extend to wine, which does not belong to that category. *Tosafot* therefore identifies a second category of *sechita*, analogous to *dash* — threshing. Just as threshing removes grain from its husk, squeezing a lemon removes juice from its natural container. When wine has been absorbed into a cloth, wringing it out would similarly constitute removing liquid from its place of containment. This would be *d'Oraisa*.

However, *Tosafot* immediately raises a further difficulty: even granting this second category of *sechita*, the wine being squeezed out in this case is *holeich le-ibud* — it falls to the ground and is lost. An act that is *holeich le-ibud* is at least *mekalkel*, if not even less than *mekalkel* from the standpoint of halakhic liability, since there is no constructive purpose achieved even in the most basic sense. Why then is it prohibited?

But before reaching this difficulty, *Tosafot* raises another that is arguably more fundamental: even if we say this is a *pesik reisha* — something that will inevitably occur — if the person derives no benefit from the result, it is a *pesik reisha d'lo nicha lei*. Is such a case *mutar lechatchila* or *assur lechatchila*? This question, which is central to *hilchos Shabbat*, receives its primary treatment in this very *Tosafot*. *Rabbeinu Tam* argues that the act should be prohibited by virtue of *mefarek* — the *dash*-like *sechita* — even in a case of *lo nicha lei*. *Tosafot* then cites the *Aruch*, who writes: *dechol psik reisha d'lo nicha lei shari* — any *pesik reisha d'lo nicha lei* is permitted. The *Ri* disagrees and maintains that *psik reisha d'lo nicha lei* remains *assur*. This debate among the *rishonim* — whether *psik reisha d'lo nicha lei* is *mutar lechatchila* or forbidden at least *m'derabbanan* — is one of the most consequential discussions in practical *hilchos Shabbat*, and it is this *Tosafot* that is the primary locus of that question.

One further note from *Tosafot*: the distinction between *mekalkel* and *misasek* on one side, and *eino miskavein* on the other, clarifies why *psik reisha* matters. The *gemara*'s discussion of *eino miskavein* as permissible according to *Rabbi Shimon* refers to cases where the prohibited outcome is not inevitable. Once the outcome is inevitable — *pesik reisha* — *eino miskavein* no longer exempts, as *Abaye* and *Rava* both rule: *modei Rabbi Shimon be-pesik reisha ve-lo yamut* — even *Rabbi Shimon* concedes that if one chops off an animal's head one cannot claim not to have intended its death. The exemption of *eino miskavein* is suspended by *pesik reisha*. The further question, introduced here by the *Aruch* and the *Ri*, is whether *pesik reisha d'lo nicha lei* — where the outcome is inevitable but unwanted — restores the exemption at the level of *d'Oraisa*, and whether it remains forbidden *m'derabbanan*.

---

## Rav vs. Shmuel (II)

### Rav's Resolution

The *gemara* returns to the challenge against Rav from the case of the wine rag. Rav Chiya bar Ashi transmitted in the name of Rav that the *halakha* follows *Rabbi Yehuda* — that *eino miskavein* is *assur*. Rav Chanan bar Ami transmitted in the name of Shmuel that the *halakha* follows *Rabbi Shimon* — that *eino miskavein* is permitted. And Rav Chiya bar Avin teaches the same positions without the chain of transmission, stating directly: Rav rules like *Rabbi Yehuda*, Shmuel rules like *Rabbi Shimon*. So the very same dispute between Rav and Shmuel on *eino miskavein* maps precisely onto their positions on first intercourse on *Shabbat*.

But this creates an apparent contradiction: if Rav rules like *Rabbi Yehuda* that *eino miskavein* is *assur*, how can Rav permit first intercourse on *Shabbat*, given that the allowances discussed in the preceding analysis were largely predicated on *eino miskavein*?

The *gemara* resolves this: *l'olam Rav ke-Rabbi Yehuda sevira lei* — Rav indeed holds like *Rabbi Yehuda* that *eino miskavein* is *assur*. His permissive ruling on first intercourse, however, does not depend on *eino miskavein*. According to the position that *dam mizkar pakid* — that the blood is pooled behind the hymen and its release does not constitute a wound — the relevant prohibition is *petach*, making an opening. And here, *mekalkel hu etzel pesach* — it is *mekalkel* with respect to the opening, since from one perspective the husband regards his wife's prior virginal state as something to be preserved, and its transformation is therefore a form of destruction. According to the other position, *dam chiburei miptar* — that there is indeed a wound involved — *mekalkel bachabura hu* — it is similarly a *mekalkel* act of wounding, in the sense that causing the wound is not constructive from his perspective. In both cases the exemption rests on *mekalkel*, not on *eino miskavein*. *Tosafot* adds the observation that being *mekalkel* does not make the act *mutar lechatchila*; there are other considerations at play, namely that this is a *mitzvah* — but that is a separate question.

---

## Tinokes Case

### Beis Shammai vs. Hillel

Rav Chisda raises a challenge from a *Mishnah* in *hilchos niddah* concerning the case of a *tinokes she-lo higia zemana liros* — an underage girl who has not yet reached the age of menstruation — who is married and has intercourse. The *Mishnah* operates on the principle that *dam besulim* — hymenal blood — exempts from concern about *dam niddah*; bleeding in the days following the wedding night is attributed to the hymen rather than to menstruation. The question is how long this exemption extends.

*Beis Shammai omrim nosna lo arba leilos* — Beis Shammai holds that the first four nights are covered; any bleeding within those four nights is not treated as *niddah*. *U-Veis Hillel omrim ad she-tiyeh hamakah* — Beis Hillel holds that the exemption is indefinite, until one is confident the wound has healed.

Where the girl has reached the age of menstruation, *Beis Shammai omrim nosna lo laila harishon* — Beis Shammai limits the exemption to the first night only. *U-Veis Hillel omrim ad motzei Shabbos arba leilos* — Beis Hillel says until *motzei Shabbat*, four nights — reflecting the institution that virgins marry on Wednesday, so that Wednesday night, Thursday night, Friday night, and Saturday night constitute the four nights, after which *motzei Shabbat* arrives.

### Four Nights Implication

The mention of *motzei Shabbat* and four nights implies that the couple is having intercourse on Friday night — *Shabbat* eve — and that the resulting bleeding is not a concern. This seems to bear directly on the question of whether first intercourse is permitted on *Shabbat*. Even if by the third or fourth night the hymen has already been ruptured, the *gemara* understands that continued intercourse can still produce hymenal bleeding, so the scenario remains analogous to the central question.

### Rava vs. Abaye

The *gemara* asks: *mai lav de-ilu bo'al matzi bo'al* — does this not mean that if he has not yet completed intercourse he is permitted to do so, implying even on *Shabbat*? *Amar Rava: lo, levar mi-Shabbos* — Rava says no; the four nights extend until *motzei Shabbat* but exclude *Shabbat* itself; they are not having intercourse on Friday night. *Amar lei Abaye: veha ad motzei Shabbos arba leilos katani* — but the *Mishnah* explicitly states four nights until *motzei Shabbat*, which implies every one of those nights, including Friday. *Ella amar Rava keshe-baal* — Rava responds: the case is that he has already had intercourse. By that rereading, the *chiddush* is not that they are having first intercourse on *Shabbat* but rather something else. *Veki ba'al mai ka mashma lan?* — but then what is the *chiddush* in mentioning *motzei Shabbat* and four nights at all? The *gemara* answers: *ka mashma lan deshary lemiv'al beShabbos kedishmuel* — it teaches that intercourse on *Shabbat* is permitted even where it might entail some continued bleeding, in accordance with Shmuel's teaching. *De'amar Shmuel pirtzah dechukah mutteres likannes bah beShabbos ve'af al pi shemeshir tzeroros* — Shmuel taught with the image of a narrow breach in a stone wall: one may pass through it on *Shabbat* even if a few stones fall away in the process. The ongoing friction of intercourse that produces some residual bleeding is analogous. However, this does not straightforwardly prove permissibility of first intercourse on *Shabbat*, since the situation after the hymen has already been ruptured is meaningfully different.

---

## Chatan Shema

### RY Question

Rav Yosef raises a further challenge. The question is whether the four-night framework in the context of the *chatan*'s exemption from *Shema* includes *Shabbat* night — and what this might imply about the permissibility of first intercourse on *Shabbat*.

### Chatan Exemption

The *Mishnah* states: *chassan patur mikrias shema laylah harishon* — a groom is exempt from reciting *Shema* on the first wedding night, because his mind is occupied by the fact that he is going to have intercourse. This exemption extends *ad motzei Shabbos* — until *motzei Shabbat* — *im lo asa ma'aseh* — if he has not yet had intercourse. The structure here differs from the earlier *Mishnah*: there, bleeding continued for four nights after intercourse had occurred; here, the exemption applies for four nights because he is still in the process of attempting first intercourse. If they did not succeed the first night, they will be trying again; the second night he is still planning it; and so on for four nights, after which a certain *ye'ush* — a giving up — may set in. That intercourse may not have been consummated even after several attempts is a real phenomenon, with causes that may be psychological, physiological, or medical, and the *gemara* acknowledges it here matter-of-factly.

The *gemara* generally understands the *chatan*'s exemption in one of two ways. The plain reading of the *Mishnayos* is that someone who is distracted — particularly by sexual anticipation, but perhaps more broadly — is exempt from *davening* and from *Shema*. The *gemara* in *Sukkah*, and the present sugya as well, frames it in terms of *osek bemitzvah* — being occupied with a *mitzvah*. Since the groom is mentally engaged in planning to fulfill the *mitzvah* of first intercourse, he is considered involved in the *mitzvah* and therefore exempt. This is an unusual form of *osek bemitzvah*, since the engagement is purely mental rather than active, but the *gemara* treats it as sufficient.

### Rava Proof

Rava argues that the four-night exemption — which explicitly includes Friday night — proves that the groom intends to have first intercourse on *Shabbat* night. If first intercourse were forbidden on *Shabbat*, there would be no reason to extend the exemption to Friday night; the *chatan* would know he cannot have intercourse that night and his mind would not be occupied with it. The exemption on Friday night is thus evidence that first intercourse on *Shabbat* is permitted.

### Abaye Counter

Abaye counters: *lo de-tarid de-lo ba'al* — the groom is not planning to have intercourse on Friday night; he remains distracted nonetheless because he is anguished over not having succeeded the previous two nights. His mind cannot focus on *Shema* not because he is about to engage in a *mitzvah* that night but because the distress of not having accomplished it yet has not left him.

---

## Osek Distinction

### Abaye Reframe

Abaye's counter reframes the entire discussion. He is not arguing about whether first intercourse on *Shabbat* is permitted. He is arguing that the Tannaitic debate about the *chatan*'s exemption from *Shema* concerns the grounds for that exemption — not whether intercourse on *Shabbat* is allowed. One view holds that the exemption is grounded in *osek bemitzvah* — active involvement in a *mitzvah* that one is about to perform — and on Friday night, if he cannot have intercourse, there is no such *osek*. The other view holds that the exemption is rooted in distraction, and even without intercourse planned for that night, his ongoing distress about not having yet succeeded is sufficient to exempt him.

### Avel Problem

Rava challenges Abaye's position: *u-mishum tirda patur?* — does mere distraction exempt someone from *Shema*? If so, a person whose boat sank in the sea, or who suffered a catastrophic financial loss, would also be exempt from *Shema* due to his inability to concentrate. *Hachi nami de-patur?* The implications would be far-reaching. And if you were to say yes — that such a person is also exempt — *ve-ha amar Rabbi Abba bar Zavda amar Rav: avel chayav be-chol ha-mitzvot ha-amurot ba-Torah chutz min ha-tefillin* — an *avel* is obligated in all *mitzvot* enumerated in the Torah except for *tefillin*, because *tefillin* are called *pe'er* and it is not fitting for a mourner to adorn himself with glory during *shiva*. But the *avel* is obligated in *Shema*. Yet surely an *avel* is profoundly distracted by grief and anguish over the deceased. If distraction exempts, why is an *avel* obligated?

### Rashi Solution

Rashi addresses this problem at a point further along in the *gemara* and his answer is instructive. He explains: *amar lach hacha nami betirda pligi* — and the *Tanna* who exempts does so for the following reason: *lav mishum deshurei lemeyal* — it is not because he is going to have intercourse that night, *ella kasavar mista'er tza'ar shel mitzvah patur mikriyas shema* — but rather because one who is suffering a *tza'ar shel mitzvah* — a distress that is rooted in a *mitzvah* — is exempt from *Shema*. The groom on Friday night, even if not having intercourse, is anguished because he has failed for two nights to fulfill a *mitzvah*. That *mitzvah*-rooted anguish is a *tza'ar shel mitzvah*, and it is that specific category of distress — not generalized distraction — that exempts him.

This explains why the *avel* is not exempt. Rashi writes: *velo dami le-ovel detarid tirda d'reshus* — it is not similar to an *avel*, whose distraction is not *mitzvah*-related. *She'ein tza'aro mitzvah* — his anguish is not itself a *mitzvah* — *af al pi she'aveiluso mitzvah* — even though his *aveilut* is a *mitzvah*. This is a striking claim. Rashi appears to be distinguishing between the *mitzvah* of *aveilut* — its external observances — and the internal experience of grief itself. The *mitzvah* of *aveilut* consists of behavioral expressions of mourning; the anguish one feels, while natural and perhaps even appropriate, is not itself commanded. The groom's distress, by contrast, is directly caused by his not yet having fulfilled the *mitzvah* of *beilat mitzvah*; his suffering is a consequence of an unperformed *mitzvah*, and that renders it a *tza'ar shel mitzvah*. This is genuinely difficult: even granting Rashi's distinction between *aveilut* as a *mitzvah* and grief as an emotional state, it is not clear why the *avel*'s very real distress would be any less of a legitimate exemption than the groom's frustration. The reason the *gemara* favors the *osek bemitzvah* framing over the distraction framework is precisely this: once you allow distraction to exempt, you have to explain why only certain distractions qualify, and that boundary is difficult to draw cleanly.

---

## Original Sugya

### Baraita Debate

The *gemara* now arrives at what is likely the original *sugya* underlying the entire discussion. A *baraita* states explicitly: *ha-koneh et ha-besulah lo yavo betchilah be-Shabbat* — one who marries a virgin may not have intercourse for the first time on *Shabbat*. *Ve-chachamim matirin* — and the *chachamim* permit it. Here at last is a direct Tannaitic dispute on the question that has occupied the entire passage.

### Chachamim ID

Rava identifies the *chachamim*: *amar Rava Rabbi Shimon hi* — it is *Rabbi Shimon*, *de'amar davar she-eino mitkaven mutar* — who holds that an unintended act is permitted. This *baraita* is almost certainly the original *sugya*. The elaborate logical framework constructed over the preceding pages — the decision tree of different scenarios and their *issur* or *heter* — is the work of the *stam*, the later anonymous redactional layer. The underlying Tannaitic source is this single *baraita*, a debate attributed to *Rabbi Shimon* on the permissibility of first intercourse on *Shabbat* based on the principle of *eino mitkaven*.

---

## Baki Argument

### Pesik Reisha

Abaye immediately presses: *ve-modeh Rabbi Shimon be-pesik reisha ve-lo yamut* — and *Rabbi Shimon* concedes that *eino miskavein* does not exempt in a case of *pesik reisha*. If the hymen will inevitably rupture during intercourse, how can the *chachamim* permit it on the basis of *eino miskavein*? Is this not a *pesik reisha* — an inevitable consequence — and therefore no different from chopping off a chicken's head while claiming not to have intended its death?

### Baki Can Avoid

Rava responds: *lo ka-elu Bavlayim she-ein beki'in be-hataya* — unlike those Babylonians who do not know how to incline, *ela yesh beki'in be-hataya* — there are those who know how to incline, meaning it is possible to engage in intercourse in a manner — at a more horizontal or angled approach — that does not rupture the hymen. If such a technique exists, then rupture is not inevitable, and the case is not a *pesik reisha*. The exemption of *eino miskavein* therefore remains applicable.

### Baki Tensions

This answer generates its own difficulties. *Im kein tarud lamah* — if men are capable of having intercourse without rupturing the hymen, why is the *chatan* so distracted? The whole basis of the exemption from *Shema* is that his mind is consumed by the difficulty of what he is attempting. If the *baki* performs it smoothly without rupture, why is there such distress? Conversely, if he is distracted because he is *she-eino baki* — not an expert — how can we permit the act on *Shabbat* on the grounds that it is not a *pesik reisha*? The permission rests on the assumption that a *baki* can avoid rupture; but the distraction argument seems to assume the person is *she-eino baki*. These cannot both apply to the same person. The *gemara* responds: *tarud lamah l'she-eino baki* — the distraction applies to the non-expert. But this generates yet another difficulty: *yomru baki mutar she-eino baki assur* — are we going to rule that an expert may have intercourse on *Shabbat* and a non-expert may not? This seems practically untenable, and conceptually bizarre. The *gemara* responds: *rov baki'in hen* — the majority of men are in fact *baki'in*. Yet this answer is deeply puzzling. How do most men, expected to arrive at the wedding night without prior sexual experience, come to possess such expertise? And even granting that the majority are *baki'in*, one would expect the rule to follow the *individual* before us rather than the statistical majority. The *gemara* here is genuinely difficult, and *Tosafot*'s attempt to reconcile the tensions is strained.

### Groomsmen Custom

Rava bar Rav Chanan raises a final challenge to Abaye: if men can and typically do have intercourse without rupturing the hymen, *shushbinin lamah mapah lamah* — why do the groomsmen wait outside the room and why is a pre-verified sheet prepared? The practice of *parsu hasimlah lifnei ziknei ha'ir* — spreading the sheet before the elders of the city — is described in the *Torah* itself as a means of verifying the bride's virginity through evidence of hymenal blood. Why establish an elaborate verification system if rupture is not reliably expected? The answer given is: *hasam shema yireh ve-yoveid* — the concern is not that rupture will fail to occur but that the evidence, once produced, may be lost before the groomsmen can confirm it. The custom of the *shushbinin* and the pre-checked *mapah* exists to ensure that if there is blood it is found and preserved, not to verify that rupture occurred. Rashi adds that if rupture did not occur and there is therefore no blood, the wife simply says the hymen has not yet been ruptured and they will repeat the act — and this time evidence will be present. The larger concern driving the institution is thus the preservation of evidence, not the occurrence of rupture.

---

---

# Ketubot 7

## Blister Case

### Intro: Sex on Shabbat

The sugya on daf 7b continues the discussion of *bi'ah rishonah* — first-time sexual relations — on Shabbat, focusing on the concern that breaking the hymen may constitute a prohibited act. The Gemara picks up toward the bottom of 6b with the case of *hamefis mursa b'Shabbos*: one who lances a blister on Shabbat.

### Blister Halakha

The ruling is as follows: *im la'asos lah peh* — if the person's intent is to create an opening in the blister — *chayav*, he is liable. But *im l'hotzi mimenu leicha* — if his intent is merely to extract the pus — *patur*, he is exempt. The question that naturally arises is: for what exactly is one liable when making an opening? This is not an act of wounding in the conventional sense.

### Rashi: Opening = Boneh

Rashi explains: *im niskavin la'asos lah peh, shemiskayvein l'yafosah, lihayos lah pesach zeh l'yom achar, chayav shehu mesakein pesach, v'chayav mishum boneh* — if one intends to create an opening so that the blister will have a fixed aperture going forward, this constitutes fixing an opening, and he is liable on account of *boneh*, the prohibited labor of building. Rashi cites the verse describing the creation of Chava — *vayiven es hatzela* — as the prototype for this category, the same source he invoked earlier in the discussion about first-time intercourse. The parallel is noted, though it remains conceptually curious why creating a small drainage opening in a blister should rise to the level of *boneh*.

### Pakid vs. Akir

The Gemara then turns to the second half of the ruling — the exemption when one intends only to extract the pus — and considers how this relates to the earlier discussion about blood released during first intercourse. The Gemara's answer is: *hasam pakid v'akir, hacha pakid v'lo akir* — in the blister case, the pus is both stored and already fully uprooted from the flesh, contained entirely outside the skin. In the case of the hymen, the blood may be stored behind it, but it is not yet uprooted from within the skin. When the hymen breaks, blood is still being released from within the skin — it is bleeding in the full sense.

This answer is somewhat puzzling. One might have expected the Gemara simply to say that the blister case involves pus, not blood, and that the prohibition of *chavala* — wounding — is fundamentally defined by the extraction of blood. The Gemara's distinction between *pakid v'akir* and *pakid v'lo akir* seems to assume that the pus in the blister may contain some blood, which is why the answer focuses on degrees of uprootedness rather than on the substance itself. One might also ask what the Gemara's question was in the first place: the physical question of whether hymenal blood is truly comparable to blood drawn through a wound is not obviously answered by a case about pus in a blister. The Gemara's conclusion is simply that the blister case involves material already fully outside the skin, while the hymenal case does not.

### Pattur Aval Mutar

A further point arises regarding the category of *patur* in the blister case. As established at the beginning of Maseches Shabbos, *patur* on Shabbat ordinarily means *patur aval assur* — exempt from liability but still forbidden. There are, however, three exceptions where *patur* means *patur aval mutar* — exempt and actually permitted. This blister case is one of them, on account of the element of *tza'ar*, physical suffering, involved. Rashi confirms this reading.

---

## Amoraim Debate

### Rav Ami Permits

With that digression resolved, the Gemara returns to the central question of first-time intercourse on Shabbat. *Rav Ami sharah l'meiva batchilah b'Shabbos* — Rav Ami permitted *bi'ah rishonah* on Shabbat. The debate among the *Tannaim* and earlier *Amoraim* on this question evidently continued into later generations. Upon hearing Rav Ami's ruling, the rabbis of the academy challenged him: *ha lo kesiva kesuva* — but the *ketuva* has not yet been written! The assumption behind this objection is that if the wedding took place on Friday afternoon or Friday night, there would not have been time to write the *ketuva* before Shabbat. And a husband and wife are not permitted to live together without a *ketuva* — indeed, the Gemara will later characterize such an arrangement as resembling *be'as znus*, because without the protections of the *ketuva* the wife lacks the commitment and security that sanctify the relationship and guard against capricious divorce.

### Ketuva & Collateral

Rav Ami's response was: *atfuso matalten* — in the case under discussion, the woman had been given movable property as collateral to hold until the *ketuva* could be formally written. This ensures that even before the document is drawn up, she has concrete security for her eventual collection in the event of divorce. This exchange signals a broader theme of Maseches Ketubot: it is not merely the act of *nisuin* itself — the *chuppah*, the *sheva brachot* — that constitutes a fully sanctioned marriage. The protections of the *ketuva* are themselves a constitutive element of a committed marital relationship, providing reciprocal obligations and security for both parties.

### Other Authorities

The Gemara then records additional authorities who permitted *bi'ah rishonah* in similar circumstances. *Rav Zvid sharah l'meiva betechila b'Shabbos* — Rav Zvid likewise permitted it, and some report that he personally did so at his own wedding. *Rav Yehuda sharah l'meiva betechila b'Yom Tov* — Rav Yehuda permitted it on Yom Tov.

### Rav Pappi vs. Pappa

At this point the Gemara records a significant dispute between two authorities, each transmitting a ruling in the name of Rava. Rav Pappi in the name of Rava held: *lo teima b'Yom Tov desharei ha b'Shabbos assur* — do not suppose that Rava made a distinction between Yom Tov and Shabbat. Rather, *hu hadin d'afilu b'Shabbos nami sharei* — the same ruling applies even on Shabbat. The case simply happened to arise on Yom Tov. Rav Pappa in the name of Rava, however, held precisely the opposite: *b'Yom Tov sharei b'Shabbos assur* — Rava specifically permitted *bi'ah rishonah* on Yom Tov but not on Shabbat. The question is immediately apparent: whether the issue is *petach* or *chavala*, the physical concern is identical on Yom Tov and Shabbat. What could be the basis for a distinction?

### Mitoch & Shaveh

Rav Pappa explains to Rav Pappi: *mitoch shehutra chabura letzorech hutra nami shelo letzorech* — since wounding (*chavala*) is permitted on Yom Tov for a purpose, namely *shechitah* for food as taught at the beginning of Maseches Beitzah, it is therefore permitted even in a context that is not directly related to food preparation. The concern about *bi'ah rishonah*, on this view, is primarily a concern of *chavala* rather than *petach*, and on Yom Tov a specific leniency applies through the principle of *mitoch*.

Rav Pappa then challenges this reasoning: *aval ela me'ata mutar la'asos mugmar b'Yom Tov* — if *mitoch* works that broadly, one should similarly be permitted to burn incense on Yom Tov, since fire (*havara*) is permitted on Yom Tov for cooking, and by *mitoch shehutra havara letzorech hutra nami shelo letzorech*, burning for any purpose should follow. The implicit premise of the objection is that burning incense is in fact *assur* on Yom Tov. The answer given is: *alecha amar kra, ach asher ye'achel lechol nefesh* — the verse says "only that which shall be eaten by every soul," indicating that only something that is *davar hashaveh lechol nefesh* — universally beneficial, something that every person appreciates — may be performed on Yom Tov outside of direct food preparation. Burning incense benefits some people and repels others; it does not meet this threshold.

This Gemara is a central *sugya* for understanding the two distinct models of Yom Tov leniency. One model, the blanket *mitoch*, tends to apply to fire-making and carrying — two *melachot* that are somewhat conceptually marginal: carrying is described by the *Rishonim* as a *melacha geru'a* because it is not inherently creative, and fire, though the one *melacha* explicitly mentioned in the Torah (*lo teva'aru bechol moshvoteichem beyom haShabbat*), has an opinion among the *Tannaim* that one is not *chayav misa* for it on Shabbat. By contrast, other *melachot* require something analogous to the permitted act of eating — something *shaveh lechol nefesh*, a pleasure or need that is both universal and bodily. This Gemara insists on this second model. Under this model, the distinction between sex and burning incense is clear: sexual relations are a basic human need and pleasure, universal in scope, whereas burning incense is not.

### Sex vs. Incense

Tosafot elaborates on the *mitoch* principle, explaining: *perush l'tzorecho shel nefesh, ubilvad sheyihiyeh tzorech hana'at hayom o tzorech kiyum mitzva b'Yom Tov kigone hotza'at katan u'l'molo v'Sefer Torah likros bo* — it must serve some legitimate purpose, whether for personal enjoyment or for fulfilling a *mitzva* on Yom Tov, such as carrying a child to circumcise him or carrying a *Sefer Torah* for reading. Tosafot does not require *shaveh lechol nefesh* for the *mitoch* of carrying. This reinforces the point that the two models operate differently.

The Gemara's resolution — that *bi'ah rishonah* on Yom Tov is permitted because *chavala* in that context is *shaveh lechol nefesh* while incense-burning is not — is itself worth examining. It is true that sexual relations in general are a universal human pleasure. One might raise the point that first-time intercourse, from the woman's perspective particularly, is not the pleasurable experience the category implies, and that the *chavala* component is not itself pleasurable at all. The Gemara, it must be said, is approaching this entirely from the man's perspective. Nevertheless, the principle being invoked is that within the context of a pleasure that is universally *shaveh lechol nefesh*, a *chavala* that is necessary to enable that pleasure is subsumed under the leniency.

### Deer Case

The Gemara then presents a further challenge: *nizdamen lo tzvi b'Yom Tov, ho'il v'eino shaveh lechol nefesh, hachi nami d'assur l'mishchatei* — would you say one is forbidden to slaughter a deer on Yom Tov because venison is a rare delicacy, not something universally enjoyed? The response is: *ana davar hatzarich lekhol nefesh ka'amina* — the rule of *shaveh lechol nefesh* applies to things that are *necessary* for all people, not merely enjoyed by all. The underlying logic seems to be that since deer is food, it falls under the general category of eating, and the leniency for food preparation on Yom Tov does not require that every individual enjoy that particular food. The *shaveh lechol nefesh* requirement operates to extend Yom Tov leniency to things that are *not* food-related, by analogy to food; once something is food, the ordinary rules of Yom Tov cooking apply regardless of the specific delicacy involved.

---

## R. Yochanan & Lore

### Hora'ah Halakha

The Gemara records: *hora Rabbi Yochanan b'Tzaidan, assur lavo betechila b'Shabbat* — Rabbi Yochanan ruled in Tzidon that *bi'ah rishonah* on Shabbat is forbidden. The Gemara immediately questions whether a ruling to forbid can properly be called a *hora'ah* at all. *Umi ika hora'ah le'issur* — is there such a thing as authoritative adjudication in the direction of prohibition?

### Matir Authority

Rashi's explanation is illuminating. He writes: *mi kari issur hora'ah mishum dechol adam matzi lehachmir, she'afilu min hasafek she'ein lo barur lo hu ba ve'oser* — calling something forbidden does not demonstrate rabbinic authority because anyone can be strict, and even one who is uncertain about the law can simply declare something forbidden without any real knowledge or tradition behind the ruling. *Aval hamatir somech al shmu'ato o sevara chochmato vehi hora'ah* — but one who rules permissively must be relying either on a received tradition or on the strength of his own scholarly judgment, and that is what constitutes genuine *hora'ah*. The ability to say *mutar* is the true mark of judicial authority.

This principle is illustrated by a famous anecdote involving the Noda BiYehuda. A *shochet* from a neighboring town would make the long journey to ask his *treifa* questions, but eventually stopped coming. When he resumed, he explained that he had found a simpler method: upon reading the verse *uvasar basadeh treifa lo socheilu lakelev tashlichun oto*, he realized he could simply throw questionable meat to the dog — if the dog ate it, it was *treifa*; if not, it was kosher. The Noda BiYehuda asked why he had then returned. The *shochet* replied: "The dog was too much of a *machmir*." The point is well taken: being strict requires no expertise.

### Rebbe Examples

The Gemara offers two examples of *hora'ah le'issur* to complicate this principle. First: *horu Beis Hillel shetei nezirut sheva shanim acherot* — Beis Hillel ruled that Heleni HaMalka, having fulfilled her vow of *nezirut* in *chutz l'aretz*, had to repeat the full seven years upon entering Eretz Yisrael. While this ruling is strict, it is a genuine *chiddush* — the ruling that her vow did not count requires real knowledge. Second: *chut hashidra shenifsak berubo, divrei Rabbi; Rabbi Yaakov omer afilu nikev; hora Rebbe ke-Rabbi Yaakov* — Rebbe first ruled that the spinal cord must be severed in its majority to render an animal a *treifa*, then reversed himself and ruled, like Rabbi Yaakov, that even perforation suffices. The latter case is more directly relevant because Rebbe's reversal could be understood as mere stringency rather than authoritative ruling. The Gemara accepts that such language can be used even for a strict ruling. *Amar Rav Huna: ein halacha ke-Rabbi Yaakov* — and in fact we do not rule like Rabbi Yaakov; the cord must be severed in its majority.

### R. Yochanan Forbidden

The Gemara then presents the full account. Rabbi Abbahu reports: *sha'al Rabbi Yishmael ben Yaakov d'min Tzur et Rabbi Yochanan b'Tzaidan, ve-ana shemi'ah* — Rabbi Yishmael the son of Yaakov from Tzur asked Rabbi Yochanan in Tzidon whether *bi'ah rishonah* on Shabbat is permitted, and Rabbi Abbahu overheard the response. *Ve-amar lei assur* — Rabbi Yochanan ruled it forbidden. Nevertheless: *ve-hilchata b'tzlachot mutar liv'ol bitchilah b'Shabbat* — the final *halakha* is that it is permitted.

It is worth noting, as Tosafot observes, that Rabbi Yochanan is an *Amora* of Eretz Yisrael, while most of the *Amoraim* who ruled permissively throughout this *sugya* appear to be Babylonian. The *hilcheta* here follows the Babylonian *Amoraim*. Tosafot at the end of this passage adds: *ve-hilchata mutar liv'ol bitchilah b'Shabbat, v'lo chayshinan shema yishchot ben of* — we do not also worry that the groom will come to perform *shechitah* for the wedding meal and accidentally violate another *melacha* in the process. *V'aha samchinan l'me'evad seuda b'Shabbat* — and it is on this basis that the Ashkenazic custom developed to marry on Friday afternoon and hold the wedding *seuda* on Shabbat, a practice that also had the practical benefit of allowing the costs of Shabbat hospitality to serve double duty as the wedding meal.

---

## Sheva Brachot

### Rav Huna Teaching

The *sugya* now transitions from *bi'ah rishonah* to the laws of *birchat chatanim* — the wedding blessings. *Amar Rabbi Chelbo amar Rav Huna amar Rabbi Abba bar Zavda amar Rav: achas betulah v'achas almanah, te'unah bracha* — whether the bride is a *betulah* or an *almanah* (meaning a woman marrying for the second time), a *bracha* is required. The term *birchat chatanim* is the language the Gemara uses throughout; it does not use the phrase *sheva brachot*, in part because the Geonic period later added the *borei pri hagefen* to bring the count to seven, and the Gemara's set consists of six blessings. The *Mishnah* in Megillah establishes that *birchat chatanim* requires a *minyan* of ten: *ein birchat chatanim pachot m'asarah*.

The teaching uses the striking formulation *te'unah bracha* — she requires a *bracha*, literally, the *bracha* is incumbent upon her. This language, centering the woman as the subject to whom the blessing attaches, will become conceptually significant as the discussion develops.

### Duration Rules

The Gemara challenges Rav Huna's ruling by citing a contradictory statement attributed to him: *almanah einah te'unah bracha* — for a widow, no *bracha* is required. The Gemara resolves this with the distinction: *kan b'bachur shenasa almanah, kan b'alman shenasa almanah* — in one case a bachelor married a widow, in the other a widower married a widow. The principle that emerges is that if for either member of the couple this is a first marriage, the full seven days of *sheva brachot* are observed; if for both it is a second marriage, only one day is required.

It is also important to note the conceptual distinction between the *brachot* recited under the *chuppah* and the *brachot* recited at the meals during the week. The *Rambam* rules that if the *sheva brachot* were not recited at the time of *nisuin*, they may be recited many days later — but one cannot make up for *sheva brachot* missed at the meal by reciting them at a different time within the week. The *brachot* under the *chuppah* are attached to the act of *nisuin* itself, while the meal *brachot* belong to the ongoing celebration.

The Gemara further addresses a *braita* that teaches: *she'kedu chachamim al takanas benos Yisrael she'yesame'ach imah gimel yamim* — the Sages enacted that a husband should rejoice with his wife for three days, which was achieved by the practice of marrying an *almanah* on Thursday, yielding Thursday, Friday, and Shabbat together. The Gemara asks: if it is a first marriage for him, do you not say seven days of *sheva brachot*? And if it is a second marriage for him, do you not say only one day? What then is the meaning of "three days"? The Gemara offers two resolutions: either it is a case of a second marriage for both, where the *bracha* requirement is one day but *simcha* continues for three; or it is a first marriage for him, where *brachot* extend for seven days but the three days refers to a separate rabbinic expectation of sustained *simcha* and companionship.

### Gemara Resolution

The Gemara then raises a further challenge from a *braita*: *mevarchin b'betulah sheva ule'almanah yom echad* — we bless for seven days for a *betulah* and one day for an *almanah*. The *braita* makes no mention of the man's status. Does this not imply that the distinction is entirely based on the woman's status — a widow who marries a bachelor would still receive only one day?

The Gemara rejects this: *lo, kan b'alman shenasa almanah* — the *braita* refers only to the case where the man is also a widower. If a bachelor marries a widow, the ruling would be seven days. The *braita*'s formulation is *milta psikta katani* — it states things in absolute terms: a *betulah* never has fewer than seven days, and an *almanah* never has fewer than one day, but sometimes an *almanah* also receives seven. The Gemara's answer is admittedly not entirely satisfying, as the *braita* does seem to ground the distinction entirely in the woman's status.

### Status Shift

This observation leads to an important conceptual observation. The original framing of these laws — much like the *ketuva* system itself — orients entirely around the woman's status: is she a *betulah* or not, is her *ketuva* 200 *zuz* or 100 *zuz*? In that framework, the degree of communal celebration is entirely a function of what type of woman is being married. The Gemara's reframing, by introducing the man's prior marital status as the determining variable, represents a significant shift: the duration of *sheva brachot* now reflects the *simcha* of the couple as a couple — the degree to which this is a new beginning for either of them — rather than the personal status of the bride alone.

This distinction carries conceptual weight. The *sheva brachot* are a communal celebration, which is why a *minyan* is required. The extent to which the community continues to celebrate corresponds to the degree of novelty and joy for both parties. If for both it is a second marriage, the communal celebration is more abbreviated. If for either it is a first, the full week of celebration is warranted. The three days of *simcha* in the *braita*, by contrast, belong to the couple themselves — a period of time spent together at the outset of their shared life, regardless of prior marital history.

---

## Minyan Requirement

### Minyan Sources

Having established that *birchat chatanim* requires a *minyan*, the Gemara now examines the sources for this requirement. The *Mishnah* in Megillah states it as a rule alongside other rabbinic acts requiring ten men, but what is the textual or exegetical basis?

### Ruth 4 Source

*Amar Rav Nachman amar lei Huna bar Nasan: tana, minayin l'virchat chatanim b'asarah? Shene'emar, vayikach asarah anashim mizeknei ha'ir vayomer shevu po vayeisheivu* — Rav Nachman, citing a tradition from Huna bar Nasan, grounds the requirement in Ruth 4:2, where Boaz took ten elders of the city and said, "Sit here," and they sat. The blessings given to Boaz and Ruth by the assembled elders and people at the gate serve as the prototype for *birchat chatanim*.

### Makor Imagery

Rabbi Abbahu derives the *minyan* requirement from a different verse: *Bemakhelos barchu Elokim Hashem mimakor Yisrael* — "In the assemblies, bless God, the Lord, from the *makor* of Israel" (Psalms 68:27). *Makor* here points to matters connected with marriage and reproduction, and *bemakhelos* implies a gathering — hence a *minyan* of ten.

### Makor Meaning

The Gemara asks what each authority does with the verse cited by the other. Rav Nachman uses the verse from Psalms for a different *drasha* altogether, as cited in a *braita*: *haya Rabbi Meir omer minayin she'afilu ubarim she-bimei imanim amru shira al ha-yam* — Rabbi Meir asks how we know that even fetuses in their mothers' wombs burst forth in *shira* at the crossing of the *Yam Suf*. The answer is from this very verse: *Hashem mimakor Yisrael* — praise arose from the *makor*, the womb, meaning from within the bodies of the Israelite women. On this reading, *makor* means womb, the source of fetal life.

Rabbi Abbahu responds: *im ken limra kra mibeten* — if the verse meant only to indicate the womb, it should have used the word *beten*. The use of *makor* instead points to something more specific: *al iskei makor* — related to matters of the *makor* itself. And *makor*, as is clear from the verse *es mekora hera* used in the context of marital law, refers not to the womb but to the genitals themselves.

This is a striking and theologically significant point. If *birchat chatanim* finds its scriptural anchor in the verse *Hashem mimakor Yisrael*, and *makor* there refers to the genitals rather than the womb, then the blessings are oriented toward the sexual union of husband and wife rather than toward fertility and children. Indeed, a close reading of the text of the *sheva brachot* bears this out: there is no explicit reference to children in the blessings themselves. The *brachot* speak of the creation of *Adam* and *Chava*, of the joining of *chatan* and *kallah*, of the joy each finds with the other — but not explicitly of procreation. The implicit theme of *birchat chatanim*, understood in light of this *drasha*, is the sanctification of the sexual union itself, set in the context of creation and covenant. The *bracha* of *birchat eirusin* makes this even more explicit: *assar lanu es ha-arusos ve-hittir lanu es ha-nessuos* — He forbade for us the *arusos* and permitted for us the *nessuos* — the blessing is directly about the permissibility of marital sex.

### Pirsum Requirement

The Gemara then returns to the question of what Rav Nachman does with the verse in Ruth 4. On the surface, the ten elders there were needed to formalize the legal transaction — the redemption and the *chalitzah*-like proceeding — not to recite *brachot*. Rabbi Abbahu therefore says that what Rav Nachman needs the verse for is a different *drasha* entirely: *lemidrash amoni velo amonit moavi velo moavit* — to publicize the ruling that the prohibition on Moabites and Ammonites applies only to males, not females, and this is why Boaz needed elders present before he could marry Ruth.

The Gemara then asks: if the ten were needed for the *drasha*, why specifically elders rather than any ten people? And if needed for the *bracha*, why elders rather than any *minyan*? The Gemara's answer is: *lefirsumei milta* — to publicize the matter. The *zekeinim* serve as a *beis din* for the legal ruling; the ten are needed for *pirsum*, public announcement. This is illustrated by the story of Shmuel who told Rav Chanan: *puk veaisi li bei asarah, ve-ima lach b'anpaihu: hamizakeh le'ubar kanah* — go gather ten people, and I will declare in their presence that a transfer of property to a fetus is legally effective. The need for ten here is specifically to publicize an innovative ruling. (The Gemara adds parenthetically: *ve-hilchata hamizakeh le'ubar lo kanah* — the final ruling does not, in fact, follow this view.)

---

## Brachot Location

### Chatanim Brachot

A *braita* teaches: *mevarchin birchat chatanim beveis chatanim* — the *birchat chatanim* is recited in the house of the *chatanim*, meaning at the wedding venue or in the context of the *nisuin* itself.

### R. Yehuda Eirusin

Rabbi Yehuda, however, says: *af beveis ha'irusin mevarchin osah* — one also recites the blessings at the *eirusin*, the betrothal. This is not merely a question of physical location but of timing: Rabbi Yehuda holds that *birchat chatanim* — what we would understand as the blessings associated with *nisuin* — is recited not only at the time of *nisuin* but already at *kidushin*, which could precede the *nisuin* by months or years.

### Abaye Explanation

Abaye explains: *uviYehuda shanu, mipnei shemisyached imah* — this applies specifically in Yehuda, where the practice was that after *kidushin*, even before *nisuin*, the couple would spend time alone together in the bride's father's house in order to grow comfortable with one another. Since seclusion could lead to sexual relations — not as an explicit intention but as a natural result — special rules applied there.

### Rashi: Kallah Forbidden

Rashi explains the necessity for *birchat chatanim* at this stage as follows: *kallah belo beracha asurah le-ba'alah keniddah* — a bride without having had *birchat chatanim* is forbidden to her husband like a *niddah*. On this view, the *sheva brachot* function as a *matir* — they are what renders marital sex permissible. Without them, the sexual act is forbidden. Therefore, if the couple in Yehuda might have sexual relations during the period of *eirusin*, the blessings must be recited beforehand to avoid a forbidden act.

### Tosafot Nuance

Tosafot's explanation differs somewhat. Tosafot writes: *u-lefi she-pe'amim ba aleha shelo leshem chuppah, osim beracha kedei shetehei kallah be-beracha* — since on occasion the husband would come to her not in the context of the formal *chuppah*, they recite the *bracha* so that the *kallah* should have the *bracha* in place. Tosafot does not go so far as Rashi in saying she is forbidden like a *niddah* without it; the concern is simply that there should be a *bracha* before any sexual act occurs.

### Sex vs. Joy

This discussion raises a deeper conceptual question about the nature of *sheva brachot*. The blessings speak of *simcha*, of *chatan* and *kallah* rejoicing together, of *menucha* and *bayit ne'eman* — the language is that of marital joy and communal celebration. Yet here, the Gemara seems to root the necessity of the blessings specifically in the potential for sexual relations. The language of *te'unah bracha* — she requires a *bracha* — and the comparison to *niddah* point toward an understanding of *birchat chatanim* as a *matir*, a ritual permission-granting act, rather than simply a communal celebration. A parallel might be drawn to *birchat hanehnin* — blessings recited before deriving physical pleasure — where the act of blessing frames and sanctifies a physical experience rather than merely marking a social occasion. Whether *birchat chatanim* functions primarily as such a *matir* for marital sex, or primarily as a celebration of the couple's new life together, is a question the Gemara gestures toward without fully resolving.

### Two Brachot

A final *braita* clarifies: *mevarchin birchat chatanim b'veis chatanim u'virchat eirusin b'veis ha'eirusin* — the *birchat chatanim* is recited at the *nisuin*, and a separate *birchat eirusin* is recited at the *eirusin*. This is striking, because while *birchat chatanim* appears in the *Mishnah* in Megillah and has clear Tannaitic grounding, the idea of a distinct *birchat eirusin* has no explicit earlier source. The *Gemara* will open tomorrow's discussion with precisely this question — what is the *birchat eirusin*, and where does it come from?
