# Ketubot 8

## Sheva Brachos Intro

### Previous Review

The daf begins embedded in the classic *sugya* concerning *birchas chasanim* — what we commonly call *sheva brachos* — and *birchas erusin*. The previous day's discussion had centered on the language of *te'una bracha*, the sense in which the *kalla* requires a *bracha*. Rashi and Tosafos, quoting Maseches Kalla, introduced the formulation *kalla blo bracha asura le'ba'ala* — that the *kalla* is in some sense forbidden and the *bracha* effects her permissibility. The *bracha* can thus be reframed as a sanctification of the act of marital relations, though the language also focuses quite specifically on the woman as the object being rendered permissible.

### Ruth & Boaz Source

The *gemara* also raised the question of whether the requirement of a *minyan* derives from the *pasuk* concerning Ruth and Boaz — a blessing of their union by the assembled people — or from the verse *bemakhelos barchu Hashem mi'mekor Yisrael*, where *mekor* appears from the *gemara* to refer specifically to the sexual dimension rather than merely fertility. What emerges clearly is that this is a blessing given by the community to the couple for their union, with the sanctification of the sexual act as a central element. The *bracha* functions as a *matir* of sorts — not necessarily in a strictly technical sense, but as a framing that sanctifies and thereby enables the couple's union.

Tosafos also quotes a passage from Maseches Kalla concerning the blessing that Rivka's mother and brother gave her — a *bracha* recited before only two people, not a *minyan*, and directed to the *kalla* alone rather than the couple. As one participant astutely noted, that blessing — *achoseinu at hayi l'alfei revava* — is also a blessing of fertility rather than of the sexual union. Whether it constitutes a serious *makor* for *birchas chasanim* or for *birchas erusin* is therefore uncertain. Tosafos raises the possibility that it may serve as a source for *birchas erusin*, though that too seems somewhat tangential.

### Nisuin vs Erusin

What the *gemara* has established so far about *sheva brachos* is that it concerns *birchas nisuin* — the blessing of the couple's union, related to the sanctification of their shared life together. That the *minyan* is required for *birchas chasanim* makes sense precisely because this is a *bracha* of the *tzibur* to the *chasan* and *kalla*. The *gemara* had also noted the case of Yehuda, where the possibility of relations before *nisuin* — following *erusin* alone — might also require a *bracha*, which is somewhat ironic given that the text of the blessing clearly envisions the beginning of married life together. Yet that case focuses the mind on the sexual act as such, which is precisely what the blessing addresses. With that context established, the *gemara* now turns its attention to *birchas erusin*, a concept not found in any *mishna* — this is the first we hear of it.

## Birchat Erusin

### Tanya Idach Formula

The *gemara* introduces this with a *baraisa*: *mevarchin birchas chasanim be'beis chasan u'virchas erusin be'beis erusin* — we recite *birchas chasanim* in the home of the *chasan* and *birchas erusin* in the home of the *erusin*. What is the text of *birchas erusin*? Ravin bar Rav Adda and Rabba bar Rav Adda both say in the name of Rav Yehuda: *Baruch atta Hashem Elokeinu melech ha'olam asher kideshanu be'mitzvosav ve'tzivanu al ha'arayos ve'assar lanu es ha'arusos ve'hitir lanu es ha'nesuos*. Rabbeinu Tam added the word *lanu* to clarify that the only *nesua* with whom a man is permitted to have relations is the one married to him — *al yedei chupa ve'kiddushin*. Rav Acha the son of Rava concludes it in the name of Rav Yehuda with the *chasima*: *Baruch atta Hashem mekadesh Yisrael* — some versions have *amo Yisrael* — *al yedei chupa ve'kiddushin*.

### Asur/Hitir Language

What is immediately striking about this formulation is what it does *not* say. It could have said *asher kideshanu be'mitzvosav ve'tzivanu al ha'kiddushin* or *al ha'erusin*, yet instead it chooses to frame the entire blessing around the language of *isur* and *heter*: *ve'assar lanu es ha'arusos ve'hitir lanu es ha'nesuos al yedei chupa ve'kiddushin*. Once again, the focus falls squarely on marital relations.

What is notable is that the *bracha* does not say *assar lanu penuyos* — it does not address the general prohibition of relations outside of marriage. What it says is that the *arusa* specifically is forbidden to us at this stage, and that she will become permitted when we proceed to *nisuin*. In a remarkable way, then, this is a *bracha* that openly acknowledges the present incompleteness of the marriage: we are not there yet. The *kiddushin* is a preparatory stage, and this blessing frames it as pointing forward toward the *nisuin* when the full married life will begin. The institution is described as one that operates in stages, and the *bracha* itself is constructed around that staging.

### Rambam 2 Stages

This is an appropriate place to note what the Rambam writes at the opening of Hilchos Ishus. Before *matan Torah*, he explains, the practice for a man and woman who wished to marry was simply to begin living together — marriage was a single, immediate act. This remains the structure for a non-Jew. The Torah introduced the innovation of two distinct stages: first *kiddushin*, then *nisuin*, after which they commence their shared life. The Torah divided into two what had previously been one.

### Kiddushin Contract

What is the profound significance of this two-stage structure? If marriage begins entirely with the reality of living together, then the marriage is defined by that lived reality at any given moment. And reality fluctuates — there will be periods of tension, distance, and estrangement, times when the couple is not living as a married couple in any practical sense. Without something that precedes and transcends that lived reality, such moments would simply unravel the marriage itself.

*Kiddushin* is best understood as a binding contractual commitment that precedes the reality of married life precisely because there will be times when that reality falters. It establishes a legal and spiritual framework — not one that cannot be dissolved, but one that creates a genuine obligation to work through difficult periods. The binding nature of *kiddushin* is not contingent on the day-to-day happiness of the couple. It precedes that happiness and persists even when it is absent. That is the point of separating the two stages.

### Geonic Variants

Returning to the text of the *bracha*: the formulation *mekadesh Yisrael al yedei chupa ve'kiddushin* raises an obvious question. We say *mekadesh Yisrael ve'hazmanim* in *kiddush*, but we do not ordinarily say *mekadesh Yisrael al yedei X* for any particular *mitzvah* — we do not say *mekadesh Yisrael al yedei tzitzis* and so on. The *geonim* therefore proposed an alternative reading: the *chasima* is simply *mekadesh Yisrael*, without the *al yedei*. That is a powerful statement on its own — that this *mitzvah* in particular is connected to *kedushas Yisrael*. Marriage and family life taking place within a framework of *kedusha* is what defines and hallows the people.

As for the phrase *al yedei chupa ve'kiddushin* — in which *chupa* precedes *kiddushin* despite *kiddushin* coming first chronologically — the *geonim* offer an ingenious explanation. Originally, they suggest, the text read *be'kiddushin* with a *bet* rather than *ve'kiddushin* with a *vav*. Due to the phonological rules of *dagesh* following a *hey*, the *bet* loses its *dagesh* and becomes a *vet*, which was subsequently misread as a *vav*. The original meaning would therefore have been *chupa bi'kiddushin* — the *chupa* effected through the act of *kiddushin*. Regardless of whether one accepts that reading, the ordering does accomplish something important. By naming *chupa* first, the *bracha* points toward the ultimate destination of married life. And by concluding with *kiddushin*, the *bracha* ends on the word that describes what is actually happening now. Had it read *al yedei kiddushin ve'chupa*, a *birchas erusin* would have ended on the word *chupa* — and that would have been incongruous.

### Chasima Question

The *gemara* addresses the question of whether *birchas erusin* requires a *chasima* — a closing *baruch atta* at the end. Two positions emerge: *man de'lo chasim* holds that it is like *birchas hapeiros* and *birchas hamitzvos*, which are short *brachot* that do not require a *chasima*. *Man de'chasim* holds that it is like *kiddush*, which does conclude with a *chasima*.

### Rashi Kedusha

Tosafos frames the question as purely technical: the *bracha* is longer than a standard *birchas hamitzvah* but shorter than *kiddush*, so it is genuinely unclear which category applies. Rashi, by contrast, begins from the position that the *bracha* belongs in the short category — it does not introduce multiple themes the way *kiddush* does — but explains why one might nonetheless treat it like *kiddush*. His answer: *keivan de'vilashon kedusha hu ke'kiddush hayom chasminan beih* — since it employs the language of *kedusha*, with *kiddushin* and *mekadesh* throughout, it is structured like *kiddush* and therefore takes a *chasima*. For Rashi, then, the issue is not merely a matter of length but of the nature of the *bracha* itself.

### 3 Models Erusin

This discussion opens up three genuinely distinct ways of understanding the function of *birchas erusin*.

The first is that it is a *birchas hamitzvah* — a *bracha* recited before performing a *mitzvah*, specifically the act of *kiddushin*. This is the most straightforward reading: *asher kideshanu be'mitzvosav ve'tzivanu*, just as one recites before taking a *lulav* or immersing in a *mikveh*. This raises an immediate question among the *rishonim*: is there actually a *mitzvah* of *kiddushin* per se, distinct from *peru urevu*? That is a major debate. If it is a *birchas hamitzvah*, the *bracha* should be recited by the *chasan* himself and should precede the act — consistent with our practice of reciting it before the *mesiras tabaas*. However, our actual practice is a hybrid: the *bracha* is recited by the rabbi, which reflects not a *birchas hamitzvah* but a *birchas hashevach* — a praise of God for the institution of marriage, recited by one who witnesses the act rather than performs it. A *birchas hashevach* need not be recited before the act; indeed, it would typically be recited afterwards, in response to what one has witnessed. Some *rishonim* do hold that *birchas erusin* is recited after the *mesiras tabaas*. At a wedding where the rabbi forgot to recite it beforehand, one can rely on those *rishonim* and have it recited afterwards, precisely because it can be understood as a *birchas hashevach*.

The third model draws the comparison to *kiddush*. *Kiddush* involves not merely acknowledging that *Shabbos* is holy but actively participating in declaring it so. By reciting *kiddush*, one adds a human layer of sanctification. Similarly, one might understand *birchas erusin* not only as praise for a holy institution but as the act by which one sanctifies the union — the human element that consecrates the couple's shared life and their intimacy. That is the *kiddush* dimension.

The comparison to *birchas hapeiros*, finally, connects to the previous day's discussion: it frames the sexual dimension of marriage as an act of pleasure that is elevated by directing it toward God through a *bracha*, just as one elevates physical enjoyment of food. Each of these models carries different *nafka minos*, and taken together they reflect a richly layered understanding of what *birchas erusin* is doing.

## Birchat Chasanim

### Week Practice

The *gemara* states: *mevarachin birchas chasanim be'asara kol shiva* — we recite *birchas chasanim* with ten people throughout the seven days. Note that *birchas erusin* carries no requirement of *borei peri hagafen*. The *sheva brachos*, by contrast, do eventually incorporate wine — though this addition comes from the *geonic* period rather than the *gemara* itself. The reason *borei peri hagafen* became so intrinsic to *sheva brachos*, while the same is not true of *birchas erusin*, is likely because *sheva brachos* is anchored in the context of meals, and wine is the natural accompaniment of a *seudah*.

Rav Yehuda adds: *v'hu shebo panim chadashos* — this applies when new guests have arrived. Tosafos explains that *panim chadashos* refers specifically to people whose presence genuinely adds to the *simcha* — those whose arrival generates a qualitatively greater joy. The underlying logic is that the *brachos* are an expression of joy: either they are a continuation of the existing *simcha*, or they reflect something new. The presence of new guests who increase the *simcha* provides that new element.

### Shehakol/Yotzer

Rav Yehuda then transmits the text of the *brachos* themselves. The first is *shehakol bara lichvodo* — God created everything for His honor. The second is *yotzer ha'adam* — You have created the human being.

### Divine Image

The third is *asher yatzar es ha'adam betzalmo betzelem demus tavniso ve'hisin lo mimenu binyan adei ad* — who formed the human in His image, in the image of His likeness, and fashioned from him an everlasting structure. The *binyan adei ad* points to the woman, created from man, and the *adei ad* indicates human continuity — children and generations proceeding from that original creation.

### Sos Tasis

The next *bracha* shifts register: *sos tasis ve'tagel ha'akara bekibbutz baneha le'socha be'simcha* — the barren one will greatly rejoice and exult as her children are gathered joyfully within her. This is *Yerushalayim*. The *chasima* is *Baruch atta Hashem mesameach Tzion bivneha*.

### National Themes

This is a notable pivot. We have moved from the creation of the human being and the fashioning of woman from man, and now — before returning to the couple themselves — we introduce the national dimension. This does not strike the note of mourning (*Im eshkachech*), but rather the positive one: the gathering of the children of Israel to Jerusalem will be cause for joy. This presages the redemption and frames the couple's joy within a larger messianic horizon. The reference to the *akara* carries the suggestion of fertility as well, though this remains implicit.

### Gan Eden

The *bracha* of *sameach tesamach re'im ha'ahuvim ke'samechacha yetzircha be'Gan Eden mikedem* returns to the couple directly. The language is striking: may this couple rejoice as their Creator rejoiced with them — or rejoiced for them — in the Garden of Eden. *Gan Eden mikedem* may mean Eden in the east or Eden in the primordial past. In either case, the image is of the original union of man and woman, *zot hapa'am etzem me'atzami uvasar mibsari* — the moment of recognition and joy at coming together. The *chasima* is *Baruch atta Hashem mesameach chatan ve'kallah*.

### Sasson Brachos

The next *bracha* is *Baruch atta Hashem Elokeinu melech ha'olam asher bara sasson ve'simcha chatan ve'kallah gilah rinah ditzah ve'chedvah ahavah ve'achvah shalom ve're'us* — who created all these forms of rejoicing: joy and gladness, groom and bride, delight, song, mirth, and exultation, love, brotherhood, peace, and companionship. This is then followed by: *mehera Hashem Elokeinu yishama be'arei Yehuda u've'chutzos Yerushalayim kol sasson ve'kol simcha kol chatan ve'kol kallah* — may there soon be heard in the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the groom and the voice of the bride, concluding with *Baruch atta Hashem mesameach chatan im hakallah*.

The structure here is chiastic. We moved from the creation of man and woman, to the national-messianic theme of Zion and her children, back to the couple rejoicing in Gan Eden. Now the final *bracha* unifies both themes: the joy God created — *sasson ve'simcha chatan ve'kallah* — is the same joy that will ring out in the streets of Yerushalayim at the time of redemption, echoing the *pesukim* in Yirmiyahu. The couple's wedding joy and the national redemptive joy are woven together. This is one reason the *brachos* carry such power when recited *be'asara* — as a communal act. The blessing declares that this is not merely a private *simcha*. It is a *simcha* of the entire community, intertwined with national hope, and the presence of ten is what gives it that communal dimension.

Rashi notes the distinction between the *chasima* of the penultimate *bracha* — *mesameach chatan ve'kallah* — and the final one — *mesameach chatan im hakallah*. The former, he says, expresses the wish that each of them individually should have success and blessing — *besipuk mezonos ve'chol tuv*. The latter, *chatan im hakallah*, refers specifically to the joy they find *with one another* — that the *couplehood* itself should be a source of joy. Both dimensions matter, but they are distinct.

### Baruch Opening

A technical question arises: why do some of the *brachos* open with *Baruch atta* while others do not? Tosafos provides a clear answer. The general rule is that a *bracha* which follows immediately upon another — *samuch la'chavertah* — does not require its own opening *Baruch atta*. However, when two consecutive *brachos* are very short, they must each open with *Baruch atta* or they will simply sound like a single continuous *bracha*. If one were to say *Baruch atta Hashem Elokeinu melech ha'olam shehakol bara lichvodo yotzer ha'adam*, without a new *Baruch atta* at *yotzer ha'adam*, the listener would take it for one strange undifferentiated *bracha*. Similarly, if *asher yatzar es ha'adam betzalmo* did not open with *Baruch atta*, one would hear *Baruch atta Hashem yotzer ha'adam asher yatzar* as a single unit. The brevity of those *brachos* requires the explicit opening to signal that a new *bracha* has begun.

Once *asher yatzar es ha'adam* is clearly a distinct, somewhat longer *bracha*, the shift to *sos tasis* with its entirely new theme is obviously a different *bracha*, and therefore *sos tasis* does not require its own *Baruch atta*.

As for the final *bracha* — *asher bara sasson ve'simcha chatan ve'kallah* — it does open with *Baruch atta*, and Tosafos explains why: because this *bracha* may sometimes be recited independently, without the preceding *brachos*. Since it can stand alone — as we will see below in the discussion of the week following the wedding — it must be formulated as a self-contained *bracha* and therefore opens with *Baruch atta*. Rav Moshe Feinstein rules that once the *nusach* was established in this form, the opening *Baruch atta* or its absence is fixed regardless of how the *brachos* are distributed among different participants.

### Community Simcha

The *brachos* as a whole intertwine the joy of the couple with the joy of the community and the joy of national redemption. The making of these *brachos be'asara* is not incidental — the community is not merely an audience. The assembled ten are participants in a *simcha* that transcends the private moment of the wedding.

### Rashi Am Assembled

Rashi's reading of *shehakol bara lichvodo* is particularly striking. Rashi says — and the text reads *einah min haseder ela asifas ha'am hane'esafim sham ligmol chesed, zecher chasdei haMakom she'nahag im Adam HaRishon shena'asu lo shoshvinin ve'nit'asek bo, ve'asifah zo mihu kevod haMakom* — that *shehakol bara lichvodo* is not primarily a cosmological statement but a *bracha* for the assembled people themselves. All who have gathered here to gladden the *chasan ve'kallah* are performing an act of *chesed*, following in the ways of God, who Himself attended to Adam HaRishon and was *mesameach chatan ve'kallah*. The gathering itself is *kevod haMakom* — an honor to God — because the assembled are imitating God's own conduct. Whether this is *peshat* in the *bracha* is debatable — *shehakol bara lichvodo* most naturally reads as a statement about creation and God's purpose — but Rashi's reading gives the opening *bracha* a remarkable social and ethical valence, framing the entire ceremony as a communal act of *chesed* modeled on the divine.

On the question of whether the six *brachos* include *borei peri hagafen*: the *gemara* records only six. The *borei peri hagafen* was added in the *geonic* period and is not part of the *talmudic* text. For *birchas erusin*, the addition of a cup of wine is clearly later and universally recognized as not intrinsic. The *borei peri hagafen* of *sheva brachos*, while also *geonic*, came to be seen as far more integral to the *brachos* — likely, as noted, because *sheva brachos* is so thoroughly anchored in the context of the meal.

## Count & Creation

### Levi/Rav Ashi

The *gemara* records two incidents. Levi visited the household of Rebbi at the wedding celebration of Rav Shimon, Rebbi's son, and recited five *brachos*. Rav Ashi visited the household of Rav Ashi at the wedding celebration of Mar, his son — Mar bar Rav Ashi — and recited six. The *gemara* proposes that this reflects a *machlokes*:

### Chad vs Shtei

*Leima b'hai kamifligi: de'mar savar chada yetzira havai u'mar savar shtei yetziros havai* — one holds that *yotzer ha'adam* and *asher yatzar es ha'adam betzalmo* describe a single act of creation and should be collapsed into one *bracha*, while the other holds that they describe two distinct acts and therefore require two *brachos*. What is the basis for this question?

### Together/Separate

Rashi connects this to the familiar reconciliation of Bereishis 1 and Bereishis 2. In Bereishis 1, the human is created male and female simultaneously — *zachar u'nekeva bara osam*. One reading of this, familiar from the *midrash*, is that the first human was created as a single being comprising both male and female, joined back-to-back, subsequently divided into two. Under this reading, *chada yetzira havai* — it was always one creation, always male-and-female, and the separation was not a conceptually distinct second act but merely the division of what was already present. The two *brachos* can therefore be collapsed into one.

### Plan vs Execution

The *gemara* rejects the premise of this *machlokes*. *De'kulei alma chada yetzira havai* — everyone agrees there was one creation. The real question is *mar savar basar machshava azlinan u'mar savar basar ma'aseh azlinan* — do we follow the original intention or the actual execution? And this is *ki ha d'Rav Yehuda*, who raised a contradiction: it says *vayivra Elokim es ha'adam betzalmo betzelem Elokim bara oso*, a single male figure, and elsewhere *zachar u'nekeva bara am* — male and female. *Ha keitzad? Bet'chila ala be'machshava lehivaros shnayim — the original plan was to create two — u'le'vasof nivra echad* — but ultimately they were created as one, then divided.

The conclusion that *chada yetzira havai* — reflecting the reading that male and female were already present together from the outset — carries a theological resonance that commends it to our contemporary sensibilities: woman is not an afterthought or appendage of man, but part of the original and complete creation. The two accounts of creation read together convey something profound: the individual human being bears *tzelem Elokim* and full dignity, while simultaneously being incomplete without the other. The original human comprised both; division into two created not lack but the possibility of wholeness through reunion. And there is something to the observation that the *machshava* envisioned two distinct beings while the *ma'aseh* began with one — the separation itself grounds a kind of autonomy and individual wholeness that is distinct from the wholeness of union.

## Week Conditions

### Day 1 Rules

Having established the *brachos* themselves, the *gemara* now turns to the conditions under which they are recited throughout the seven days. Rav Ashi came to the home of Rav Kahana. On the first day — *yoma kama barech kulhu* — he recited all of the *brachos*. From that point forward: *ei ika panim chadashot barech kulhu* — if there are *panim chadashot*, new guests, he recited all of them. If not — *afushei simcha be'alma hu* — it is simply more of the same *simcha*, not a qualitatively new one.

### Shehasimcha

In that case, *mivarech she'hasimcha bimono* — one recites the addition of *she'hasimcha bimono* in the *zimmun*, the opening of *birchas hamazon*: *Baruch Elokeinu she'hasimcha bimono ve'she'achalnu mishelo*. And together with that, *asher bara* — the final *bracha* of the *sheva brachos* — is recited on its own. This is precisely why *asher bara sasson ve'simcha* opens with *Baruch atta*: it can be recited independently, as it is in this situation during the week when *panim chadashot* are absent. The fact that *she'hasimcha bimono* functions as an insertion in the *zimmun* anchors the whole structure in the context of the meal, and makes explicit what the *gemara* had previously left implicit: *sheva brachos* is a practice of the meal.

### Week 2 Month

*Mishiva ve'ad shloshim* — from after the first week until thirty days: *bein amruhu machmat hilula bein lo amruhu machmat hilula* — whether or not one specifies that the meal is in honor of the wedding, one adds *she'hasimcha bimono* in the *zimmun*. There is no *asher bara* recited independently during this period — at most, the *zimmun* addition. It is worth noting the parallel structure with *aveilus*: the stages of seven days, thirty days, and twelve months mirror the structure of mourning. Whether this reflects a general pattern of how significant life events recede over time, or whether the parallels are more pointed, the *gemara* will make explicit by comparing *birchas chasanim* and *birchas aveilim* directly.

### Twelve Months

After the first month: *ei amar lehu machmat hilula* — if one explicitly frames the meal as being in honor of the *chasan ve'kallah*, as when celebrating with guests who were unable to attend the wedding, *mivarech she'hasimcha bimono*. If not — one does not. And to what point can one still frame a meal as *machmat hilula*? Rav Papa says in the name of Rava: *treisar yarchei shata* — twelve months, the first year.

### Early Erusin

The *gemara* then asks: from the earlier side, what is the earliest point from which one may begin reciting *she'hasimcha bimono*? The *gemara* considers whether it can be said even before the wedding, in anticipation of it. Rav Papa married off Abba Mar his son, and he recited *she'hasimcha bimono* from the time of *erusin* — at the engagement celebration, which was explicitly *leshem chatan ve'kallah*. The *gemara* responds: *shani Rav Papa de'hava tari'ach lei* — Rav Papa was different because he was wealthy and had people to manage all the preparations; there was no perceived obstacle between *erusin* and *nisuin*, and he was therefore genuinely already in the mode of *simcha*. Similarly, Ravina married off his son to the daughter of Rav Chaviva, and he too recited *she'hasimcha bimono* from the time of *erusin*, saying *kim li be'gavaihu de'la hadri behu* — I know they will not back out. As long as no obstacle is perceived, one is already in the mindset of *simcha* and may say *she'hasimcha bimono*. The *gemara* then adds with wry economy: *le'vasof lo istai'a milsa ve'hadru vehu* — in the end it did not work out and they did back out. The lesson: do not be overconfident.

### Bris Milah Limit

Rav Chaviva came to a *bris milah* and added *she'hasimcha bimono* in the *zimmun*, reasoning that any *seudas mitzvah* might warrant the addition. *Ve'leis hilchasa ke'vosei* — we do not rule that way — *mishum de'tridi, de'is tza'ara le'yanuka* — because the participants are disturbed: the baby is in pain. This *gemara* is the source for the *Ashkenazi minhag* of not reciting *shehecheyanu* at a *bris milah*. Though a *bris* is undeniably a *simcha*, the baby's suffering introduces a dimension of distress that is incompatible with the full declaration of joy that *she'hasimcha bimono* — or *shehecheyanu* — would represent. *Sefardim* do recite *shehecheyanu* at a *bris*, treating it primarily as a *bracha* on a new *mitzvah*, but the *gemara* here reflects a more ambivalent assessment.

## Minyan Rules

### Groom Counts

Rav Nachman says in the name of Rav: *chassanim min haminyan* — the *chasan* counts toward the ten required for *birchas chasanim*. This may seem obvious, but it is not. If the *minyan* is conceptualized as a *tzibur* giving a blessing to the couple, one might argue that the recipients of the blessing cannot simultaneously constitute the quorum of blessers. The answer is that at a wedding, everyone present is part of the *simcha* — there is no division between the one who rejoices and those who cause his rejoicing. The *chasan* is not a passive recipient; he too is part of the *kehilla* assembled in joy, and therefore counts.

### Aveilim Intro

The *gemara* introduces a parallel: *ve'ein aveilim min haminyan* — but for *birchas aveilim*, the *avel* does not count toward the required ten. Here the logic is the inverse: at a house of mourning, there are clearly distinct roles — the *avel* is the mourner, and everyone else is there to console. The *menachamim* constitute the quorum; the *avel* is its recipient.

### Rav vs Braisa

The *gemara* raises an objection: a *baraisa* states *chassanim ve'aveilim min haminyan* — that even the *avel* counts. The *gemara* resolves this by invoking the principle that *Rav tanna u'palig* — Rav, who belongs to the transitional generation between *tannaim* and *amoraim*, may dispute a *baraisa*.

### Yitzchak/Yochanan

The same positions are then attributed to Rav Yitzchak in the name of Rav Yochanan: *chassanim min haminyan ve'ein aveilim min haminyan*. Here too the *gemara* raises the *baraisa* stating that *aveilim* count. But since Rav Yochanan is an *amora*, the solution of *tanna u'palig* is less available, and the *gemara* must find another resolution.

### Shurah Context

The *gemara* distinguishes between two contexts. The *baraisa* that counts *aveilim* in the *minyan* refers to *birchas hamazon* — there is a form of *birchas aveilim* that occurs in the context of *birchas hamazon* at the meals during the week of *aveilus*, and there the *avel* does count. When Rav Yochanan says the *avel* does not count, he refers to the *shurah* — the two lines formed by the consolers when the mourners return from the graveside, through which the *avel* passes to receive words of *nichum*. In the *shurah*, the *avel* is clearly distinct from the participants and cannot count.

### First vs Later

The *gemara* then asks: but the *baraisa* that excludes *aveilim* from the *minyan* specifically in the context of *birchas aveilim* — if *birchas aveilim* occurs at *birchas hamazon* and *aveilim* count there, where does this exclusion apply? The *gemara* answers: *ki ka'amar Rabbi Yochanan be'rachava* — Rav Yochanan refers to the *rachava*, the open space or street where the first meal is served to the mourners upon returning from the cemetery. At that first meal, the roles are maximally differentiated — those who feed and console on one side, the *avel* on the other — and therefore the *avel* does not count toward the ten. This is a distinct *bracha* associated with that initial meal, not the *birchas aveilim* of later meals during the week.

### Mourner Panim

The *gemara* then asks: can there really be a *birchas rachava* throughout all seven days? The *baraisa* says *ein aveilim min haminyan* for *birchas aveilim kol shiva* — all seven days. But the *rachava* is only the first meal. The *gemara* answers: *meshkachas la be'panim chadashot* — you find it through *panim chadashot*. Just as *sheva brachos* continues throughout the week when new guests arrive to augment the *simcha*, so too *birchas aveilim* can recur throughout the week when new *menachamim* arrive — new consolers who were not present before. Their arrival creates a new instance of the *mitzvah* of *nichum aveilim*, and a new occasion for the *bracha*. In those cases, the *avel* does not count toward the ten, for the same reason as always: the *avel* and the *menachamim* occupy fundamentally distinct roles, and the quorum must consist of those performing the *mitzvah* of consolation, not its recipient.

# Ketubot 9

## Brachot Aveilim & Shiva

### Intro Aveilim

The Gemara on 8b introduces the institution of *birchat aveilim*, the special blessing recited for mourners, which likewise requires a *minyan* — with the important distinction that the *aveilim* themselves do not count toward that *minyan*. The Gemara also discusses the *rechava*, the practice of the mourners walking back from the burial while the community forms two rows to offer *nechama*, and the *seudat havra'ah*, the meal of comfort served to the mourner immediately upon returning. Whether the *minyan* requirement for that *seudat rechava* differs from the *minyan* required for the *birchat hamazon* at subsequent meals is not entirely clear from the Gemara, but what does emerge plainly is that *birchat aveilim* forms a recognized component of *birchat hamazon* in the house of mourning.

The Gemara then asks: the statement of Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that *birchat chatanim* is recited with ten throughout the entire seven days, with the *chatanim* counting toward the *minyan*, parallels a teaching that *birchat aveilim* is recited with ten throughout the entire seven days, but with the *aveilim* excluded from the *minyan* — since the roles of *menachamim* and *aveilim* are fundamentally distinct. The Gemara asks: where do we find *birchat rechava* repeated throughout the week? And it answers: *meshkachat lah bipanim chadashot* — just as *panim chadashot*, new faces, arriving during the week generate renewed *simcha* and therefore occasion the recitation of *sheva berachot* anew, so too when new *menachamim* arrive there is a fresh opportunity for *nechama*, and *birchat aveilim* would be recited again.

It is worth noting that the Rambam, in his discussion of *hilchot berachot*, records the *nusach* of *sheva berachot* in full but offers only a simplified version of *birchat aveilim*, which likely reflects the fact that by his time this practice had largely fallen into disuse. The Rambam's formulation adds to the fourth *beracha*, *hatov vehametiv*, language of *dayan emet* — affirming divine truth and judgment — and then provides an opportunity to add one's own words of *nechama* for the *avel* before the *harachamanim*, which function as a kind of appendage to the four main *berachot*. Whether this captures the full original *nusach* as the Gemara presents it is, as we shall see, an open question.

### Rabbi Chiya Bar Abba

The Gemara relates the following story. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba served as the *mikrei b'nei* — the *cheder* teacher — of Resh Lakish's sons. A child of his died. On the first day Resh Lakish did not go to pay a *shiva* call, and on the second day he went, bringing with him Yehuda bar Nachmani, his *meturgeman*. A *meturgeman* was a kind of public announcer who would receive the Sage's words and then proclaim them to the assembled students or community; he was sometimes given a degree of latitude to elaborate. Resh Lakish instructed Yehuda bar Nachmani: *kum eima miltha kaveil yanuka* — rise and say some words in commemoration of the child who had passed away.

Yehuda bar Nachmani stood and opened with the verse *vayar Hashem vayina'atz mikas banav uvnotav* — "God saw and was provoked by the anger of His sons and daughters." He interpreted this to mean: in a generation whose fathers provoke God, God's anger is directed at their children, and the children die young. He went on to cite a second possibility — that the deceased was a young adult, not an infant — and quoted another verse: *al kein al bachurav lo yismach Hashem v'et yetomav v'et almanotav lo yerachem*, "therefore God will not rejoice over his young men, nor will He show compassion to their orphans and widows, for all of them are faithless and evildoers, and every mouth speaks *nevala*." The Gemara takes up this last phrase in a related digression. Rav Chana bar Abba teaches that *hakol yod'im kalla lama nichnesa l'chuppa* — everyone knows why the bride enters the *chuppa* — and yet whoever commits *nival peh*, who speaks of such matters explicitly, even if seventy years of good fortune were decreed for him, it will be reversed for evil. It is a striking formulation, particularly because the statement is framed entirely around the *kalla* rather than the groom — an unusual focus given the Gemara's general tendency to address male sexual consciousness.

The Gemara itself voices the obvious critique: *ata lenichumei tzo'arei ka metza'er lei* — he came to offer consolation and instead caused anguish. The Gemara then offers an exculpatory reading: what Yehuda bar Nachmani meant to say was that Rabbi Chiya bar Abba was so important a figure that he bore the suffering of an entire generation — it was the generation's sin, but a person of such high *madrega* is the one who bears its consequences. Even granting that interpretation, however, the statement remained a painful one to deliver, and it stands as a vivid illustration of how people say hurtful things at a *shiva* call even with the best of intentions.

### Seven Brachot

Resh Lakish then turned to Yehuda bar Nachmani and gave successive instructions, each producing a distinct *beracha*. The first instruction: *kum eima milta keneged shivcho shel Hakadosh Baruch Hu* — rise and say words in praise of God. Yehuda bar Nachmani proclaimed:

> *el gadol berov godlo adir vechazak berov nora'ot mechaye metim bema'amaro ose gedolot ad ein cheker venifla'ot ad ein mispar — baruch ata Hashem mechaye hametim.*

This is a full *baruch ata Hashem* blessing, framed as praise of God, but unmistakably resonant in the setting of a *beit avel*: God who revives the dead.

Resh Lakish then said: *kum eima milta keneged avelim* — now say something directed toward the mourners. This is different in character from the preceding blessing, which praised God. The *birchat aveilim* proper follows:

> *acheinu hameyuga'im hameduka'im ba'avel haze — tnu levavkhem lachkor et zot: zot omedet la'ad, nativ hu misheshet yimei Bereshit. Rabim shatu verabim yishtu — kemishte rishonim kach mishte acharonim. Acheinu ba'al nechamot yenachem etkhem — baruch menachem avelim.*

The message is one of consolation through universal human experience: this is the way of the world since the six days of creation, many have drunk from these waters before you, and many will drink after — the Master of consolations should comfort you. The blessing concludes: *baruch menachem avelim*.

Abaye comments that one should not say *rabim yishtu* — "many will drink" — referring to future deaths, so as not to invoke future suffering. And one should not say *kemishte acharonim* — "like the drinking of those who come after" — because, as Resh Lakish himself taught, and so too it is taught in the name of Rabbi Yosi: *le'olam al yiftach adam piv l'Satan* — one should never open one's mouth to the Satan by invoking the possibility of future misfortune. Rav Yosef adds a proof-text: when Israel said *k'Sdom hayinu l'Amora daminu* — "we have become like Sodom, we resemble Amora" — the very next verse addresses them as rulers of Sodom, fulfilling the feared comparison.

Resh Lakish then directed Yehuda bar Nachmani: *kum eima milta keneged menachmei avelim* — now say a blessing for the *menachamim*, for those who have come to comfort the mourners. This blessing celebrates the comforters as *gomlei chasadim bnei gomlei chasadim*, practitioners of *chesed* in the tradition of Abraham our father, and concludes: *baruch ata Hashem meshalem hagemul* — blessed is God who repays acts of kindness.

Finally: *kum eima milta keneged kol Yisrael* — say a blessing on behalf of all of Israel. The text is a plea for divine protection:

> *Ribbono shel olam — pedeh ve'hatzel, malet ve'hosha amcha Yisrael min hadever u'min hacherev u'min habizah, u'min hashidafon u'min hayarkon, u'mikol minei puranyot hamitragshot u'va'ot la'olam. Terem nikra ve'atah ta'aneh — baruch ata otzer hamagefah.*

What emerges from this extended passage is that *birchat aveilim* had a defined structure — one blessing for the deceased, one for God (*mechaye hametim*), one for the mourners (*menachem avelim*), one for the *menachamim*, and one for the community at large — while the precise wording within each blessing appears to have been more flexible. The *meturgeman* was given latitude to compose the content, provided the themes and conclusions (*siumim*) were honored. This stands in some contrast to the fixed text of *birchat chatanim* presented on the preceding *daf*. Whether these blessings were formally tied to *birchat hamazon* or could stand independently is not entirely resolved — the Gemara did not foreground a *minyan* requirement in this passage, though that may simply be because it had already been established.

### Ten Cups Wine

Ulla taught — and some say this was a *Baraita* — that the Sages instituted ten cups of wine to be drunk in the house of mourning: three before the meal, to open the appetite; three during the meal, to settle the food; and four after the meal, corresponding to the four blessings of *birchat hamazon* — *hazan*, *birkat ha'aretz*, *boneh Yerushalayim*, and *hatov vehametiv*. The logic of drinking wine in a house of mourning presumably reflects its role in dulling grief, echoing the imagery of *mishte* — the drinking party — that runs through the passage, and consistent with the halachic distinction between an *onen*, who does not drink wine before burial, and an *avel*, for whom wine was permitted as a way of bearing grief.

The Sages later added four more cups: one in honor of the *chazanei ha'ir*, the communal functionaries; one for the *parnasei ha'ir*, the community leaders who supported the mourners; one *keneged beit hamikdash*; and one in memory of Rabban Gamliel. The first two reflect the communal support structure around the mourning family. The one *keneged beit hamikdash*, Rashi explains, is not merely a messianic gesture but an acknowledgment of communal *avelut* over the *churban* — we are all *aveilim* on the destruction of the Temple, and God should also console us and rebuild it.

The cup *keneged* Rabban Gamliel is explained by a *Baraita*: in earlier times, the cost of burial was so crushing to a family that relatives would abandon their dead rather than bear the expense. *Barishona hayu hotza'at hamet kashah likrovav yoter mimitato* — the funeral was harder for the family than the death itself. Rabban Gamliel — the *Nasi*, a man of great wealth — commanded that when he died he be buried in simple linen shrouds, and all the people followed his lead. In memory of this act of compassion, a cup was drunk in his honor. Rav Papa adds that in his own day the practice had become even simpler, with the most minimal burial garments costing almost nothing. It is worth emphasizing the deliberate message of Rabban Gamliel's choice: precisely because he was the most prominent figure of his generation, his insistence on a simple funeral carried maximum force as a statement of principle.

However, once the count reached fourteen cups, people were drinking to excess and becoming drunk. The Sages therefore reversed course — *hechziru davar l'yoshno* — and reverted to the original ten.

It is striking that both the *birchat aveilim* and the *asara cosot* have largely disappeared from contemporary practice. The *daf* as a whole has a clear thematic unity: just as 8a presented the *birchat chatanim* for the wedding setting, 8b presents the *birchat aveilim* for mourning — a beautiful structural pairing of the liturgies that accompany life's two great threshold moments.

---

## Non-Virginity Claim

### Pesach Patuach Claim

The Gemara now turns to the central legal concern of the *daf*: the husband who, the morning after the wedding, claims his wife was not a virgin. There are two distinct ways he might make this claim. The first is the absence of blood — a relatively concrete form of evidence, especially given that the practices described later in the *perek* involved guards at the door and a special sheet to be inspected. The second is what the Gemara calls *tainas pesach patuach* — the claim that during the act of intercourse itself he experienced no obstruction, no hymen, and thereby concluded experientially that she was not a virgin. This second claim carries an additional layer of uncertainty: not only is it without external evidence, but one might argue that even in his own mind he does not actually know what he is talking about — his subjective experience may simply be an error.

Rabbi Elazar states: *ha'omer pesach patuach matzati ne'eman l'osrah alav* — one who says "I found the door already open" is believed to the extent that she becomes forbidden to him. The principle at work is *shavya anafshei chaticha d'issura* — a person who declares something forbidden binds himself by that declaration, as when one declares a piece of meat to be *chazir*: even without objective confirmation, he is bound by his own characterization of reality. The effect here is that, given his claim that she is not a virgin and therefore may have committed adultery, a married woman who commits adultery being forbidden to her husband, he cannot continue living with her. The ruling contains two *chiddushim*: first, that *petach patuach* is a recognized claim and not dismissed as the speculation of someone who simply does not know what he is talking about; and second, that *shavya anafshei chaticha d'issura* can operate even where the forbidden status results not from a direct assertion ("this is forbidden") but from a factual claim whose halachic consequence is a *safek* of forbidden status.

### Safek Sefeika Analysis

The Gemara immediately raises an objection: *ve'eima sfeik sfeika hu* — even granting his claim at face value, this is a case of double doubt, and a *sfek sefeika* should be permissive. The analysis runs as follows. The first *safek*: perhaps she had sexual relations *tachtav* — after the *kiddushin*, which would constitute adultery — or perhaps it was before the *kiddushin*, in which case she was unchaste but did not commit adultery against him and would not be forbidden. The second *safek*: even if we assume it occurred after *kiddushin*, perhaps it was *b'ones* — rape — in which case she did nothing wrong and is not forbidden to her husband — or perhaps it was willful. For both conditions to render her forbidden, the encounter must have been after *kiddushin* and consensual. A *sfek sefeika* in the direction of leniency should therefore permit her to remain with her husband.

The Gemara answers: *lo tzricha* — the ruling is needed specifically in cases that reduce the double doubt to a single doubt. One such case is *eshet kohen*: the wife of a *kohen* is forbidden even if the violation was through rape, so the second *safek* disappears. The other case is where the father betrothed her before she was three years old: since the Gemara assumes that penetration before age three leaves no lasting physical effect (*biah* under three causes the hymen to regenerate), the absence of a hymen can only reflect an encounter after she turned three — at which point she was already betrothed — thus eliminating the first *safek* regarding timing.

Tosafot raises an additional question: what about a case where the act occurred willingly but she was under twelve? Such an act would be treated as *ones* under the principle of *pituy ketanah ones* — the seduction of a minor is legally equivalent to rape — and would not render her forbidden. Is this not yet another branch of *sfek sefeika*? Tosafot resolves this by observing that this scenario collapses into the same category as *ones*, since statutory incapacity and physical coercion are both subsumed under *ones*. For a *sfek sefeika* to function, the two doubts must be genuinely distinct questions; where they merge into the same legal category, they do not multiply into a *sfek sefeika*. The upshot is: in the ordinary case, the double doubt insulates the wife from being rendered forbidden. Only where the *sfek sefeika* is dismantled — through *eshet kohen* or *pachot mibat shalosh* — does the husband's claim take effect.

### Sotah Contradiction

The Gemara now raises a sharp internal contradiction. Rabbi Elazar himself elsewhere stated: *ein isha ne'eset al ba'ala ela al iskei kinu v'stira* — a woman is not rendered forbidden to her husband except through the process of *kinui v'stira*, the formal warning-and-seclusion procedure that initiates the *sotah* process. How can Rabbi Elazar simultaneously hold that a husband's subjective claim of *pesach patuach* is sufficient to forbid the wife? The one statement seems to demand the full *sotah* mechanism; the other allows a bare assertion to suffice.

The Gemara first considers whether the *ma'aseh shehaya* — the story invoked to support the *sotah* principle — refers to David and Batsheva, and immediately questions this: was there any *kinui v'stira* in that story? And furthermore, why was Batsheva not rendered forbidden to David if adultery had clearly occurred? These questions stand as difficulties that the Gemara must address.

The Gemara begins by untangling the statement itself. The correct reading is: *ein isha ne'eset al ba'ala ela al iskei kinu v'stira mi'ma'aseh shehaya* — we learn that the only mechanism is *kinui v'stira* from the case of David and Batsheva precisely because there was no *kinui v'stira* there, and therefore she was not rendered forbidden. The argument is: from the fact that she was not forbidden despite the adultery having demonstrably occurred, we infer that without the *sotah* process, no prohibition attaches.

The Gemara presses: *uto v'tisbara* — does this reasoning make sense? She clearly committed adultery; why should the absence of a formal procedure matter when the act is known? And more pointedly, a straightforward objection: *kinui v'stira in edim lo* — according to you, does the prohibition apply only through *kinui v'stira* and never through witnesses? Of course if there are two witnesses it applies. So the statement cannot be excluding all other mechanisms. Rather, it addresses cases below the threshold of two witnesses: absent *edim*, the only other operative mechanism is the *sotah* process. The question then remains: does a husband's lone assertion constitute a mechanism below or at the level of two witnesses?

### Self-Testimony Weights

The Gemara's resolution is as follows: *petach patuach k'shnei edim dami* — a claim of *pesach patuach* carries the evidentiary weight of two witnesses. Why? Because *ne'eman adam al atzmo k'mea edim* — a person is believed against himself like a hundred witnesses. When a person makes a self-incriminating claim, it carries maximal credibility precisely because no one would voluntarily accept a disadvantageous ruling without good reason.

The Gemara is aware that the question is sharper than the answer. The original statement was that a woman is forbidden only through *kinui v'stira* — meaning that anything less than two witnesses is insufficient, and only the *sotah* process fills the gap. Now we are told that the husband's own claim counts as two witnesses. But this seems to undercut the entire force of the restriction: if I say my wife committed adultery and that statement alone counts as two witnesses, then the restriction adds little. The Gemara accepts this tension because both rulings are attributed to Rabbi Elazar and must be reconciled; the resolution is that the husband's self-testimony operates as a special mechanism, analogous to — but not the same as — objective testimony from outsiders.

It should be noted that *ne'eman adam al atzmo* operates in the monetary sphere in a straightforward way — if one says "I owe a thousand *zuz*" one is bound. But in matters of prohibition and, critically, in criminal matters, no person can testify against himself to generate an objective criminal sanction. What the Gemara describes here is not criminal self-incrimination but a form of personal restriction: based on your own stated understanding of reality, you are bound to conduct yourself accordingly, even though it will have indirect consequences for the wife.

### David Batsheva

The Gemara returns to the question of David and Batsheva directly. Tosafot frames the difficulty sharply: if the principle of *shavya anafshei chaticha d'issura* means that when a husband claims his wife committed adultery he is bound by that claim and cannot continue living with her, then why did David continue living with Batsheva? He knew he had committed adultery with her. Why was he not compelled to separate?

The Gemara offers two answers. The first: *hasam ones havei* — in that case it was *ones*. David did not use physical violence, but what genuine choice did Batsheva have when the king summoned her? The Gemara is working with a broader conception of *ones* that encompasses situations of severe social coercion. The halachic consequence is significant and, as the Gemara notes, somewhat ironic: the prohibition on a woman who commits adultery applies only when the act was willful. If she was raped, she committed no wrong and is not forbidden to her husband — nor to the man who violated her. Since Batsheva was compelled, she did not commit willful adultery, and therefore no prohibition attached to David's living with her.

### Uriah Get

The second answer the Gemara offers is attributed to Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *kol hayotzei l'milchemes beis David get krisus kosev l'ishto* — anyone who went out to fight in the wars of the house of David first wrote a *get* for his wife. The practice of writing a conditional *get* before going to war is explained in two ways: Rashi says it was to spare the wife from the *yibbum* obligation if the husband died childless; Tosafot objects that *kol hayotzei* implies universal practice, not just men with brothers, and argues instead that the concern was *agunah* — a woman whose husband's fate is unknown. The *get* was written on the condition that it would take effect if the husband did not return within a specified period after the war's end.

Uriah had therefore given Batsheva such a conditional *get* before going to war. When David ensured that Uriah did not return — as the narrative of Tanach makes plain — the *tenai* was fulfilled retroactively. The *get* took effect retroactively, Batsheva was divorced from Uriah, and technically the act between David and Batsheva did not constitute adultery, since she was no longer Uriah's wife in halachic terms from the moment the condition was fulfilled. The proof-text: *v'es arubasam tikach* — the word *aruvah* (bond/pledge) is interpreted by Rav Yosef as a reference to the instruments of the husband-wife bond, i.e., the *getin*, that David was to collect from the soldiers before they marched.

This resolution is cited alongside the *ones* resolution as an alternative (*v'iba'is eima*), and both stand in the Gemara.

---

## Wed Wedding Court

### Wednesday Takana

The Gemara returns to the *takana* of the fourth-*amud* mishnah: *b'sula niseis l'yom harevi'i* — a virgin marries on the fourth day of the week, i.e., Wednesday. The Gemara has been assuming throughout that this is not mere custom but an enacted *takana* in which there is a communal interest. The specific mechanism identified is *icrurei da'ata* — the concern that if one waits too long, the husband will cool off and not pursue the matter.

### Takana Purpose

One might ask: why should the community care whether the husband cools off? The Gemara poses this directly: *ul'mai* — for what purpose do we want him to bring his claim to court the next morning? If the purpose is merely to allow him to deprive her of her *ketuva* — to protect his own financial interests — then this is purely his concern. If he cools off and decides not to pursue it, that is his prerogative. There is no communal interest in helping a husband reduce his wife's *ketuva*.

The answer must therefore be: *ela l'osra alav* — the concern is that she may have committed adultery and therefore be forbidden to him. In that case, the community has a genuine interest in ensuring the matter is adjudicated promptly, because we do not want a husband and wife living together when they may be halachically forbidden to each other. This is the only rationale that justifies a *takana* to ensure the husband can appear in court the following morning.

### Blood vs Door

With that purpose established, a closer look reveals which type of claim the *perek* is primarily addressing. The Gemara asks: *v'dekhatani ta'anah mai* — what claim is the husband making when he comes to court the next morning? Is it the claim of *pesach patuach* — based on his subjective experience during intercourse — or the claim of *tainas damim* — the absence of blood on the sheet?

The Gemara concludes: *lo dekhatani tainas damim* — the *perek* is dealing with the claim of absence of blood. This is the more concrete and objectively assessable claim: there were witnesses positioned at the door, there was a special sheet, and its inspection either confirmed or did not confirm blood. The *perek*'s central scenario is therefore this evidentiary framework. The *pesach patuach* claim — that of subjective experiential inference — is Rabbi Elazar's ruling and stands as a significant *chiddush*, but it is not necessarily the baseline case that the whole structure of Wednesday weddings and next-morning court appearances was designed to address.

### Judah Galilee

The Gemara introduces a regional distinction. A *baraita* teaches that one who ate in the home of his father-in-law in Judah without witnesses — alluding to the known practice in Judah where a betrothed couple might be permitted to be alone together during the *erusin* period — cannot thereafter claim that his wife was not a virgin, because the obvious retort is that any non-virginity may be attributable to premarital relations with him. By contrast, in Galilee, where such seclusion was not permitted, the husband's claim retains validity.

The Gemara then sharpens the question: in Judah, the husband cannot make the claim — for what purpose? If it is merely to make her forbidden to him based on his own say-so (*l'osrah alav*), then even in Judah this should apply, because the principle of *shavya anafshei chaticha d'issura* operates on his own consciousness regardless of external suspicion. The fact that in Judah his claim is undermined only makes sense if what he is trying to do is to hurt her — specifically, to deprive her of her *ketuva*. And that is the claim the regional distinction addresses: in Judah, where prior seclusion was possible, his claim that she was not a virgin is not accepted for the purpose of causing her monetary loss. In Galilee, it is.

### Rashi Credibility

This brings the Gemara to a foundational question that will animate the entire remainder of the *perek*: on what basis is the husband believed at all, given that he has no witnesses and no objective supporting evidence, to cause his wife to lose her *ketuva*?

Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states: *ha'omer pesach patuach matzati ne'eman l'hafsidah kesubasah* — a man who says "I found the door already open" is believed to cause her to forfeit her *ketuva*. Rashi provides the foundational rationale, and it is significant: *de'amrinan ee lav dekushta hu, lo hayah mafsid se'udaso* — we reason that if his claim were false, he would not have wasted all the money he spent on the wedding feast. He threw a *se'udat nisuin*, invited guests, incurred great expense — and all that to make one night of marriage and then claim she was not a virgin? Moreover, if he hated her from the start, he would simply have divorced her without going to all this trouble.

Rashi's reasoning is essentially one of implausibility: the claim made the morning after the wedding carries a built-in credibility that a claim made years later would never enjoy. A husband who has just spent a fortune on a wedding celebration and who comes to court the next morning with this complaint is presumed to be telling the truth, because no one would construct such an elaborate scenario merely to avoid paying a full *ketuva*. The moment he makes this claim, moreover, he faces real consequences — not just a reduced *ketuva* obligation, but potential forced divorce. A man who genuinely wanted out of the marriage without this claim could have found simpler means. Thus the timing and context lend the claim a degree of credibility that the law recognizes.

This ruling, and Rashi's explanation of it, will be central to the rest of the *perek*, which unfolds the full picture of what happens in court the morning after a Wednesday wedding: what claim the husband makes, how it is evaluated, and what its halachic consequences are both for him and for his wife.

---

---

# Ketubot 10

## Petach Patuach & Ketubah…

### Petach Patuach Claim

The *gemara* opens with a case that had been discussed at length: whether a husband is believed when he claims *petach patuach* — that upon consummating the marriage, he experienced what felt like an already-open entrance, as opposed to finding no *dam betulim* whatsoever. The stakes of this claim are significant. One consequence is that, in certain configurations — such as where the wife is the wife of a *kohen* — the claim effectively translates into an allegation of prior adultery, rendering her forbidden to him by operation of the principle *shavya anafshei ḥaticha de-issura*: he has bound himself by his own words. But the more immediately surprising consequence is that he is believed to cause her to forfeit her *kesuva*. The *gemara* now addresses both the mechanism by which he is believed and the deeper question of what the *kesuva* itself actually is.

### Rabbinic Institution

*Itmar* — it was taught. Rav Naḥman said in the name of Shmuel in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: *ḥachamim tiknu lahem livnot yisrael masayim u-le-almanah maneh* — the rabbis instituted that a virgin receives a *kesuva* of 200 *zuz*, and an *almanah* — a widow, or more broadly, a woman who is not a virgin — receives 100 *zuz*. The entire institution, in other words, is rabbinic in origin. And since it is rabbinic, *ve-hem hem eminu'hu*: the very same rabbinic authority that created the institution chose to believe the husband when he claims *petach patuach matzasi* and to rule accordingly that she does not receive her *kesuva*.

The *gemara* immediately raises the obvious challenge: *im kein mah ho'ilu ḥachamim betakkanatam*? If the rabbis created an obligation and simultaneously gave the husband an easy exit from it, what exactly did their enactment accomplish? A man need only say *petach patuach* and he avoids payment entirely. The *gemara* responds with Rava's principle: *ḥazakah ein adam tore'aḥ bise'udah u-mafsidah* — we may assume that a person does not go to the trouble of making a wedding feast only to destroy it. The expense and effort of a wedding creates a strong presumption that the husband is not fabricating this claim, because making it up would mean throwing away everything he invested. This presumption is sufficient to render the enactment functionally effective: cases of false claims will be rare enough that the *takkanah* retains its protective force.

### Tosafot Qualification

*Tosafot* raises a pointed objection. The logic of *ein adam tore'aḥ bise'udah u-mafsidah* presupposes that the husband is sacrificing something by making the claim. But what if he is not? *Tosafot* notes that there is a later dispute in the *gemara* about the consequences of a husband discovering that his wife was not a virgin as he had expected: is this a *mekaḥ ta'os* — a transaction conducted on false premises — in which case the marriage is annulled and she receives no *kesuva* at all? Or does it merely warrant an adjustment of the *kesuva* downward from 200 to 100 *zuz*, leaving the marriage intact?

This distinction is critical. If the claim of *petach patuach* results in something drastic — she is forbidden to him because adultery is implied, or the entire marriage is void as a *mekaḥ ta'os* — then indeed one would not fabricate such a claim after investing in a wedding, because the consequence is losing one's wife entirely. *Tosafot* states this explicitly: *tinaḥ be-eshes kohen o bifḥut mibas gimmel* — in a case involving a *kohen*'s wife or a girl married under the age of three, where the claim implies forbidden relations, *keivan d'mifsada*, since he loses his wife, we believe him. Similarly, according to the view that the result is *mekaḥ ta'os* and she gets nothing, the drastic nature of the consequences again supports his credibility.

But *Tosafot* continues: *aval le-man d'amar yeish lah kesuva maneh* — according to the opinion that the only result is reducing her *kesuva* from 200 to 100, *lo mafsid midei* — he loses nothing. He remains married, keeps the wedding gifts, and simply pays less. In that scenario, *amai meheiman*? Why should he be believed at all? *Ve-yeish lomar de-lo meheiman* — and one may answer that indeed he would not be believed. This is an important qualification on the *gemara*'s blanket statement: the husband's credibility when claiming *petach patuach* applies only in contexts where his claim carries sufficiently drastic personal consequences for him.

---

## Mohar to Kesubah

### Rabbinic Fine & Land

Having established that the *kesuva* is a rabbinic institution, the *gemara* now cites a *beraita*: *havi knas ḥachamim hu lo tigbeh ella min ha-ziburis* — since the *kesuva* is a rabbinic fine, she may collect only from *ziburis*. Land in rabbinic law is categorized into three grades: *idis* is Grade A, *beinonis* is Grade B, and *ziburis* is Grade C — the lowest quality. Ordinarily, a creditor collecting a debt is entitled to land of equivalent value, but the location and quality of that land matters enormously. The *beraita* reasons that since the *kesuva* is not a conventional debt arising from a prior obligation but rather a rabbinic creation, collection is limited to the least desirable category of land.

The *gemara* notes that the word *knas* — fine — requires explanation: what wrong did the husband commit that we are fining him? The *gemara* emends the framing: *ho'il ve-takkanat ḥachamim hu* — since it is a rabbinic institution, it is simply of lesser legal weight than a biblical or naturally arising obligation, and therefore collection is restricted accordingly. Underlying this ruling is also the rabbis' persistent concern for social equilibrium: the protective obligations upon the husband must be calibrated so as not to be so burdensome that men become reluctant to marry. The limitation to *ziburis* reflects that balance.

### Biblical Mohar Basis

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel omer: kesubas isha min ha-Torah* — the *kesuva* is biblical in origin. The *gemara* challenges this immediately: did Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel actually say this? A *beraita* is cited in which he appears to say the opposite — that the *kesuva* is purely rabbinic.

The *gemara* first discusses the biblical foundation itself. The verse *kesef yishkol ke-mohar ha-betulos* — he shall weigh out silver according to the *mohar* of virgins — appears in the context of a man who seduces a virgin. Because she is no longer a virgin, she loses her *mohar*, the traditional payment given by the groom to the bride's father when contracting a marriage. Accordingly, the seducer must compensate the father for that loss. The *pshat* of the Torah, and the position of biblical scholars as well, is that the *mohar* was a genuine bridal price, paid up front and given to the father — not a symbolic token like a ring or a *perutah*, but a substantial sum.

By combining this passage with the case of the rapist in *Devarim*, who pays fifty units of silver, and identifying the currency as *shekel* — itself derived from the word *yishkol* — the Sages establish that the standard *mohar ha-betulos* was 50 *shekel*, which equals 200 *zuz*. *Mikan samchu ḥachamim le-kesubas isha min ha-Torah* — from here the rabbis found a biblical basis for the institution of a woman's *kesuva*. The 200 *zuz* that was once the *mohar* paid at the beginning of a marriage became the 200 *zuz* of the *kesuva* payable at the end, in cases of death or divorce. The rabbis transformed an upfront biblical payment into a deferred rabbinic institution.

### Reconciling Positions

The *gemara* now faces the contradiction: in one source Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the *kesuva* is biblical, in another he says it is rabbinic. The *gemara*'s first solution is *ipoch* — reverse the attribution in the *beraita* — assigning the position of biblical origin to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the rabbinic position to the *ḥachamim*. But why reverse the *beraita* rather than the earlier statement? Because we have independent evidence that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel treats the *kesuva* as a serious, binding obligation: *de-tenan, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel omer noten lah mi-me'os Kapotkia*.

A later *mishnah* addresses a case where a man married in Kapotkia and divorced in Eretz Yisrael, or vice versa. The *shekel* of Kapotkia was worth more than the *shekel* of Eretz Yisrael — comparable to the relationship between US and Canadian dollars. The *ḥachamim* say one always pays in the local Israeli currency, the lesser amount, reasoning that since the *kesuva* is rabbinic we go easy on the husband. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: if you contracted the obligation in Kapotkia, you pay in Kapotkia currency. This position — that the obligation is binding according to where and how it was contracted — reflects treating the *kesuva* as a weighty, serious obligation rather than a lenient rabbinic creation. The *gemara* therefore finds it consistent to attribute to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel the position that the *kesuva* is biblical.

The *gemara* then offers a second resolution: *ve-iba'it eima, kulei Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel hi* — perhaps the entire *beraita* reflects only Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view, and it is missing a crucial distinction. *Ve-ḥisurei meḥsera ve-hachi tanni*: the *beraita* is incomplete and must be read as follows. The *kesuva* of a *betulah* — a virgin — has a biblical basis in the *mohar ha-betulos*. The *kesuva* of an *almanah*, however, *eina mi-divrei Torah ela mi-divrei Sofrim* — is purely rabbinic — because the Torah never assigns any *mohar* for non-virgins. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement that the *kesuva* is rabbinic referred only to the *kesuva* of a widow, not to the *kesuva* of a virgin. The contradiction is resolved.

### Dual Nature Analysis

It is worth pausing to note something striking even in the position that the *kesuva* is *de-Oraita*: the language is *samchu ḥachamim*, they found support — not that the obligation flows directly from biblical law. The Torah's *mohar* was paid up front, at the initiation of the marriage; the *kesuva* is paid at the end. The rabbis took a biblical phenomenon and transformed it into a different institution. So even according to the *de-Oraita* position, the *kesuva* as we have it is a rabbinic re-application of a biblical prototype, not a direct biblical mandate.

This dual nature resolves a well-known difficulty raised by *Tosafot* in their first comment on the *daf*. The anonymous *stam* of the *gemara* throughout *Shas* assumes the *kesuva* is *de-rabbanan* — the *gemara* in *Isha Rabbah*, for instance, gives the reason for the institution as *she-lo te'hei kalla be-einav le-hotzi'ah*, so that divorce should not be easy, which is a classic *de-rabbanan* rationale. Yet Ashkenazic *ketubot* include the language *mohar besulayichi de-ḥazi lichi mi-de-Oraita* — the 200 *zuz* of your virginal *mohar* that is fitting to you biblically. Sephardic *ketubot* use *de-ḥazi lichi* without the word *mi-de-Oraita*, but still employ the term *mohar*. How can we write *mi-de-Oraita* if the accepted ruling is *de-rabbanan*?

The *Rosh* offers one answer: the obligation is rabbinic, but the method of calculating the amount — the coinage, the specific figure of 200 *zuz* — is derived from biblical standards. *Tosafot* offers another approach, arguing that we do in fact rule it is *de-Oraita*. But perhaps the clearest answer is simply that both are true simultaneously. The *kesuva* is *de-rabbanan* in the form we have it — a deferred payment at the end of marriage — and it is *de-ḥazi lichi mi-de-Oraita* in that it ultimately originates in, and draws its weight from, the biblical obligation of *mohar ha-betulos*. The *gemara*'s phrase *mikan samchu ḥachamim le-kesubas isha min ha-Torah* captures precisely this: it originates in the Torah but its current form is a rabbinic institution.

---

## Testing Non-Virginity

### Rav Naḥman's Case

The *gemara* returns to practical cases of *petach patuach*. A man came before Rav Naḥman and said *petach patuach matzasi* — he claimed that his experience of consummation indicated his wife had not been a virgin. Rav Naḥman's response was striking: *asvuhi kufrei* — go beat him with palm branches, the barbed kind that cut as well as strike.

The *gemara* explains: *mavrachta ḥaviva lei* — he must have had prostitutes available to him. In other words, the only way he would know the difference between a virgin and a non-virgin from physical experience alone is if he had been sexually active beforehand. Two interpretations follow. Rashi reads Rav Naḥman as ordering the beating on account of the man's prior promiscuity — he has no standing to complain about his wife when he himself has been involved with prostitutes. *Tosafot* reads it in the opposite direction: precisely because only a promiscuous man would know the difference, and we cannot assume he is promiscuous, we must conclude he is lying — and so he is beaten for *motzi shem ra*, for slandering his wife.

The *gemara* then raises the obvious tension: but Rav Naḥman himself is the authority who said the husband is believed in such a case! The resolution is that he is indeed believed — *meheiman* — and we also beat him. The belief and the beating coexist: his *petach patuach* claim is accepted as evidence regarding his wife's status, but the claim simultaneously serves as evidence of his own prior sexual activity, for which lashes are appropriate. The practical effect of this approach is that very few men will come to *beit din* with such a claim once word spreads that making it results in a beating.

One might ask whether the man could simply say that he never experienced *petach patuach* but found no blood — *lo matzati dam betulim*. That would indeed be a different matter, and the answer is yes, that would be a different claim.

### First vs. Remarriage

Rav Aḥai draws a further distinction: *kan bevachur kan benasui* — it matters whether this is the man's first marriage or whether he has been married before. If he has been previously married, he has legitimate basis for comparison and would be believed when he claims *petach patuach*. If this is his first marriage, he would not be believed — and in that case, rather than lashes for promiscuity, he would receive lashes for *motzi shem ra*, for slandering his wife without any possible basis for the claim. This distinction significantly qualifies the earlier principle: the husband's general credibility regarding *petach patuach* applies only when he has had prior marital experience from which to draw a legitimate comparison.

### Door in Darkness

A man came before Rabban Gamliel with the claim *petach patuach matzasi*. Rabban Gamliel responded: *shema hitita* — perhaps you approached at an angle. He then offered a *mashal*: a man walking in the dead of night and in total darkness approaches the door of his house. If he comes in at an angle, he may find it appears open — he slips through a crack without realizing that the door had in fact been closed. But had he come straight on, at a perpendicular, he would have discovered that the door was indeed locked. Because he did not know what he was doing, he came in at an angle and experienced it as open when it was in fact closed.

The parable maps onto the situation of a first-time husband who genuinely does not know what he is doing in consummating a marriage. His experience of *petach patuach* may be the result of his own inexperience rather than any prior breach on his wife's part.

A second version of the story — *ika d'amri* — offers a related but distinct explanation: *shema be-mazid hitatso va'akarta le-dasha ve-avra* — perhaps you pushed through so forcefully that you ripped out the door and its bolt. That is, if the husband came with such force that he broke through without feeling the obstruction, he would falsely conclude that there had been nothing there. This version maps onto a different kind of inexperience — not going in at the wrong angle, but going in with such force that the presence of an intact barrier was not registered. In either case, the conclusion is the same: a man who has not been married before has no reliable basis for such a claim.

---

## Blood Evidence Cases

### Dirty Sheet Case

A man came before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi — the son of Rabbi — and said *ba'alti ve-lo matzati dam*: I had relations with my wife on the wedding night and found no blood. This claim — the absence of blood on the sheet — is more objective than *petach patuach*; the couple had been supervised and the sheet was present for inspection. His wife, speaking for the first time in these cases, said: *Rabbi, betulah hayiti* — I was a virgin. She does not deny that no blood was found; she asserts nonetheless that she had been a virgin.

Rabban Gamliel told them to bring him the sheet. He immersed it in water, cleaned it, and found several drops of blood. The sheet had been so grimy and dusty — conditions of the time — that the blood had been invisible against the general dirtiness. Once cleaned sufficiently to remove the surface dirt, the drops of blood became apparent. He told the husband: *lech zechei be-mikḥacha* — go, take good possession of your purchase. The wife was vindicated. One cannot help but notice the language throughout these cases: the woman is consistently framed as an object of purchase — *mekach*, *mikchacha* — which relates directly to the legal framework being applied. The *kesuva* of 200 *zuz* reflects what he expected to be acquiring; if she is not a virgin, it is analogous to *mekaḥ ta'os*, a transaction on false premises.

### Cleaning Concern

Huna the son of Rava of Parzika raised a question to Rav Ashi: why can we not simply employ this same technique today — clean the sheet when there is a claim of *lo matzati dam* and look for blood?

Rav Ashi replied: *gihutz shelanu ke-kibus shelahem* — what counts as a simple laundering for them required only immersion in water, which was sufficient to remove the surface dirt without disturbing the blood. For us, basic laundering already involves the level of scrubbing and soap that they would call *gihutz* — a deep cleanse involving rubbing against a stone and the use of cleansing agents.
