And if we were to perform *gihutz* in order to remove the dirt, *ma'aver lei ḥumra* — the stone used in *gihutz* would also remove the blood. There is no method available to us that removes the dirt without also removing the blood, and therefore the test cannot be replicated today.

### Wine Barrel Test

Another man came before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi with the same claim: *ba'alti ve-lo matzati dam*. His wife responded differently this time: *Rabbi, adayin betulah ani* — I am still a virgin. Her claim is not that she was a virgin who produced no blood, but that the consummation never actually succeeded; the husband had not achieved full penetration and was falsely attributing the absence of blood to her prior non-virginity.

Rabban Gamliel said: bring me two maidservants, *achat betulah ve-achat be'ulah* — one who is a virgin and one who is not. They were brought. He had each of them sit on top of an open barrel of wine. *Be'ulah reicha nodef* — from the non-virgin, a smell of wine became detectable; *betulah ein reicha nodef* — from the virgin, it did not. Rashi explains: for a woman who is no longer a virgin, the fumes rising from the wine barrel travel upward through her body and emerge through her mouth, where the scent is detectable. For a virgin, the physical barrier prevents this from occurring.

Having confirmed through the controlled experiment that the test worked as he understood it should — the virgin and non-virgin responding exactly as his tradition described — Rabban Gamliel then applied the same test to the woman in question. *Ve-lo haya reicha nodef* — no smell was detectable from her. She was indeed still a virgin, and her husband had not achieved penetration. *Amar lo lech zechei be-mikḥacha* — go, your wife is still yours, and still a virgin; go try again.

The *gemara* asks: why did he first test the maidservants before applying the test to the woman in question? The answer: *gemara hava shemia lei, ma'aseh lo hava chazi* — he had received the tradition that this test works, but he had never actually carried it out. One can know a technique in principle without knowing whether one is able to execute it correctly in practice. He therefore first ran the experiment on women whose status he knew, to confirm that he was administering the test competently. Only once that was established did he apply it where it mattered. Additionally, *ve-lav oraḥ ar'a le-zalzulei bivnot Yisrael* — it would not be respectful to subject a Jewish woman to this test if there were any doubt that it would yield reliable results. As to why we do not use this test today: we simply no longer know how to administer it correctly.

---

## Special Cases

### Durkani Family Case

A man came before Rabban Gamliel ha-Zaken — the elder Rabban Gamliel, at the time of the *Beis Hamikdash* — with the claim: *ba'alti ve-lo matzati dam*. His wife responded: *Rabbi, mi-mishpaḥat Durkani ani* — I am from the Durkani family, *she-ein lahem lo dam niddah ve-lo dam besulim* — who have neither menstrual blood nor hymenal blood. She is asserting a hereditary physiological condition.

Rabban Gamliel investigated her relatives — *badak Rabban Gamliel bi-krovoseha* — and found that her account was accurate. He told the husband: *lech zaḥei be-mikḥacha* — go, take good possession of your purchase. He added: *ashrecha she-zaḥita le-mishpaḥat Durkani* — praised are you that you merited a woman from the Durkani family.

This last remark is challenged by Rav Ḥanina: *tanḥumin shel hevel niḥamo Rabban Gamliel le-oso ha'ish* — Rabban Gamliel offered that man empty consolation. The reason is stated by Rav Ḥiyya: *keshem she-has'or yafeh la-isah, kach damim yafim le-ishah* — just as yeast is beneficial for dough, blood is beneficial for a woman. Menstrual blood is a sign of fertility. A woman without such blood is, in a meaningful sense, like unleavened dough — the capacity for growth and new life is impaired. *Ve-harei zeh ke-nodos* — it is like an empty wineskin.

Furthermore, *tana mishum Rabbi Meir: kol ishah she-dameha merubim, baneha merubim* — any woman whose menstrual flow is abundant will have many children; she is highly fertile. The Durkani woman's condition thus raises serious questions about childbearing, making *ashrecha* a hollow blessing. Whether the phrase the *gemara* attributes to Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba — *zachei be-mikḥacha* — or the one attributed to Rabbi Yosef and Rabbi Avin — *niṣ-ḥayeiv be-mikḥacha* — you are stuck with your purchase — the tone differs markedly. The *gemara* resolves this by noting one genuine advantage: *de-lo asi lidei sefek niddah* — since she has no menstrual blood, there is never any question of *niddah* or doubt-*niddah* status. That is the grain of truth in Rabban Gamliel's blessing, though it is a thin consolation.

### Famine Case

A man came before Rabbi — Rabban Gamliel's era having passed — with the same claim. The wife said she was still a virgin. Rabbi, however, observed that *sheni batzorot havei* — these were years of famine, and *ra'ah Rabbi she-pneihem sheḥorim* — he saw that their faces were blackened from malnutrition. He had them bathe, and then fed and gave them drink. Once they had recovered somewhat, he had them return to the bedroom, and this time *matzu dam* — blood was found. The verse Rabbi applied to them was *tzafad oram al atzmam, yavesh haya ka-etz* — their skin cleaved to their bones, it was as dry as wood.

Whether the absence of blood in the original consummation was due to the hymen failing to bleed because of extreme dehydration and malnourishment, or due to insufficient physical capacity for full penetration under conditions of severe physical debilitation, the *gemara* does not specify precisely. What is clear is the pastoral lesson: *lo matzati dam* in such circumstances reflects bodily conditions, not prior unchastity.

This sequence of cases — *petach patuach* dismissed as inexperience or promiscuity, the dirty sheet revealing hidden blood, the failed penetration exposed by the wine barrel test, and now famine undermining the very physical evidence — creates a cumulative picture. The theoretical framework giving the husband credibility is maintained in the books, but in practice rabbis worked carefully and creatively to arrive at just outcomes, and the *halacha*'s bark turns out to be considerably worse than its bite.

---

## Mishnah Categories

### Betulah vs. Almanah

The *mishnah* now states the foundational categories: *betulah kesuvatah masayim* — a virgin receives a *kesuva* of 200 *zuz*; *ve-almanah maneh* — a widow, or more broadly a non-virgin, receives only 100 *zuz*. The biblical basis for the figure of 200 *zuz* has already been laid out in the preceding *gemara*: it derives from the *mohar ha-betulos*, the standard bridal payment for virgins in the Torah, which was 50 *shekel* or 200 *zuz*. For the *almanah*, as established above, there is no biblical *mohar* equivalent, and the 100 *zuz* is purely a rabbinic institution.

### Widow from Erusin

The *mishnah* adds that a woman who is an *almanah*, *gerushah*, or *ḥalutzah* — widow, divorcée, or one who has undergone *ḥalitza* — but whose prior marriage consisted only of *eirusin* (betrothal) and never reached *nisuin* (the consummated marriage stage), receives a *kesuva* of 200 *zuz* for her next marriage, not 100. This produces a seeming paradox: a woman who has been married before yet whose *kesuva* is 200. The rule is that *eirusin* alone, absent *nisuin*, does not change the presumption of virginity. Since *eirusin* in standard practice did not involve cohabitation — unlike in Yehuda where couples sometimes had relations after *kiddushin* — a woman who was betrothed and then separated before *nisuin* is still treated as a *betulah* and receives the full *kesuva* of 200 *zuz*.

### Ta'anas Betulim

The same logic that entitles her to 200 *zuz* also exposes her to *ta'anat betulim*: the husband's claim that she was not a virgin. The two sides of this coin are inseparable. Because the presumption is that she is a virgin — sufficient to grant her the full 200 *zuz kesuva* — the husband has a legitimate expectation of virginity. If on the morning after he claims either *petach patuach* or *lo matzati dam*, he cannot be told that he should have expected otherwise given her prior marital history, because *eirusin* alone does not change that presumption. He is therefore entitled to raise *ta'anat betulim* in such a case, with all the consequences that entails.

---

## Almanah Etymology

### Maneh Etymology

*Mai almanah?* — What is the origin of the word *almanah*? Rav Ḥana Bagdata'ah — possibly from Baghdad, though that city is typically dated somewhat later — offers an etymology: *almanah al shem maneh* — the word *almanah* derives from *maneh*, the hundred-*zuz* sum she receives. It is a functional etymology: she is called *almanah* because her *kesuva* is a *maneh*.

### Biblical Anticipation

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: a woman who is an *almanah* from *eirusin* receives 200 *zuz*, not 100 — so the etymology cannot apply to her. The response is that because the standard *almanah* from *nisuin* is called *almanah* on account of her *maneh*, the same term is extended to the *almanah* from *eirusin* by association, even though her *kesuva* is 200.

But a deeper objection follows: *almanah di-chtiv be-Oraita mai ika lemeimar?* The word *almanah* appears throughout the Torah — long before any rabbinic institution of a 100-*zuz kesuva* existed. How can the Torah's use of the word be explained by a rabbinic institution that would not be created for a thousand years? The *gemara* answers: *de-atidin rabbanan de-matkenei lah maneh* — the Torah used the term *almanah* in anticipation of the future rabbinic enactment. And yes, the Torah does write with reference to future events: *ve-shem ha-nahar ha-shlishi Ḥidekel hu ha-holech kidmat Ashur* — the third river is the Ḥidekel, going east of Ashur. Rav Yosef teaches that *Ashur* here refers to Selika, a city that did not yet exist at the time of *Gan Eden*, when this verse was set. Thus the Torah names a future reality. Here too, the Torah called the widow *almanah* in anticipation of a future rabbinic institution.

---

## Aggadic Wordplay

### Rain Drashah

Since Rav Ḥana Bagdata'ah has been cited, the *gemara* brings several additional teachings in his name. On the word *matar* — rain — he offers an alliterative *drasha* on the letter *mem*: rain *mashkeh* — waters the ground; *meraveh* — sates it; *mezabel* — fertilizes it; *me'aden* — moistens it; and *mamshich* — draws out the fruit from the trees. Rava bar Yishmael, and some say Rav Yeimar bar Shelamya, identifies the scriptural basis in the verse *telameha raveh, naḥat gedudeha bi-rvivim, temogegenah bi-rviv, tzimḥah tevarech* — you will sate its furrows, bring down its banks with raindrops, make it fertile with drops, bless its sprouting.

### Altar Drashah

Rabbi Elazar offers a similar alliterative treatment of the word *mizbe'aḥ* — altar. It *mazi'aḥ* — repels; *mazin* — sustains; *meḥabev* — makes Israel dear; and *meḥaper* — atones. The *gemara* asks whether *mazi'aḥ* and *meḥaper* are not simply the same thing — both suggesting the removal of sin. The *gemara* distinguishes them: *mazi'aḥ* refers to *mazi'aḥ gezeirot* — casting off evil decrees — while *meḥaper avonot* refers to atoning for sins themselves. Two distinct functions of the *mizbe'aḥ* are thus identified.

### Dates Discussion

Rav Ḥana Bagdata'ah then expounds on *tamrei* — dates. They *meshachnan* — warm the body; *mesav'an* — sate it; *meshalshelan* — act as a laxative; *me'ashran* — cause contentment; and *lo mefantan* — do not make one overly fastidious or spoiled.

Rav rules: *ekhol tamrei al yoreh* — if one has eaten dates, one should not issue *halachic* rulings, since they were thought to cloud thinking somewhat. The *gemara* challenges this from a teaching that dates in the morning and evening are beneficial, at midday they are unparalleled, and only at *Mincha* time — on an empty stomach in the afternoon — are they inadvisable. But clearly dates have many benefits; why should they impair judgment?

The resolution is that the goodness of dates for the body — *ilu'ei ma'alu* — is not in question, but *le-fi sha'ata tarda* — at the moment of eating, they temporarily cloud one's thinking. They are analogous to wine in this respect: wine is beneficial, yet *ha-shoteh revi'it yayin al yoreh* — one who has drunk even three fluid ounces of wine should not issue rulings. A further resolution notes that the timing relative to a meal is decisive: *ha mikamai nahama, ha batar nahama* — the concern applies before bread, not after. Abaye's nursemaid taught him: *tamrei mikamai nahama ke-narga le-dikula* — dates before a meal are like a hatchet to a palm tree, destructive; *batar nahama ke-avra le-dasha* — after a meal they are like a bolt on a door, strengthening and beneficial.

### Final Wordplay

The *gemara* concludes with a series of wordplays. *Dasha* — a door — Rava explains as *derekh sham*, the path in. *Darga* — a step — is *derekh gag*, the way to the roof. *Puraiya* — a bed — Rav Papa explains as the place where *parin ve-ravin*, one procreates and multiplies. Finally, Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak adds: *af anan nami neima* — let us similarly expound — *ilonit*, the term for a woman who has not physically matured and cannot bear children, is *dukhranita de-lo yadla* — like a male ram that cannot give birth. The *gemara* thus concludes this aggadic interlude with a series of playful but pointed observations about language, physiology, and the vocabulary through which the Sages described human life and its conditions.

---

---

# Ketubot 11

## Status Transitions

### Ketubah Amounts

Daf 11 opens with a new *mishnah*. The previous *mishnah* had established the basic distinction in *ketubah* amounts between a *besulah* and a non-*besulah* — the difference between 200 and 100 *zuz* — grounded in the biblical verses, where the Torah recognizes only a *mohar*, an upfront payment, for a *besulah*. This *mohar* is not itself a *ketubah*, but it serves as its foundation. *Chachamim* subsequently instituted a transformation: they converted the upfront *mohar* into a deferred *ketubah* payment, and they further instituted a *ketubah* for a widow (*almanah*) as well.

One might ask whether the *ketubah* is accurately described as alimony. The answer is that it is only partially analogous. In a case of divorce, the *ketubah* is indeed a lump-sum payment — but it is also collected upon the husband's death, functioning simultaneously as a substitute for inheritance, since by Torah law the wife does not inherit from her husband.

### Mishnah: Three Categories

The remaining *mishnayot* of this section address cases that fall somewhere in between the clear categories of *besulah* and *almanah* — cases where it is not immediately obvious whether the woman's *ketubah* is 200 or 100. One such case was already addressed: a woman who is a *besulah* but had been married at the stage of *kiddushin* without *nisuin*, and therefore retains her status as a *besulah*.

The *mishnah* at the top of 11a introduces three new categories: *hagiyores vehashvuyah vehashifchah* — a female convert, a woman taken captive, and a maidservant who was a non-Jewish slave. In the first and third cases, the assumption is that as non-Jews, these women were presumed to be sexually promiscuous. In the case of the captive woman, sexual assault is assumed. If these women underwent their respective transitions — redemption, conversion, or manumission — while still under three years and one day old, then *ketuvasan masayim*, their *ketubah* is 200. The *mishnah* further states *veyesh lahen ta'anas besulim* — the husband retains a legitimate claim if, on the wedding night, she is discovered not to be a virgin.

### Under Three: Virginity

Why does being under three years old at the time of these transitions guarantee a *ketubah* of 200? The *gemara* operates with two interlocking assumptions. First, an act of intercourse with a girl under three years old is not halachically defined as an act of intercourse at all. Second, even if such an act occurred, the hymen regenerates — it does not remain ruptured. These two assumptions will be unpacked further in the following *mishnah*, which explores precisely what the definition of *besulah* requires: is it the absence of any act of intercourse, or is it the physical integrity of the hymen? As we will see, a girl under three satisfies both conditions: the act is legally a nullity, and the hymen is presumed to have restored itself.

---

## Ger Katan

### Rav Huna's Rule

The *gemara* does not immediately focus on the *ketubah* aspects of the *mishnah*. Instead, it pivots to the topic of *ger katan* — converting someone who is still a minor. This *sugya* dominates the remainder of the *amud*.

*Amar Rav Huna*: *ger katan matbilin oso al da'as beis din* — a minor who is converted is immersed on the understanding and with the approval of *beis din*. What is the underlying case? It could be an adopted infant, or it could be a situation in which someone wishes to convert a child born of a mixed marriage. The case *Rashi* describes, however, is somewhat different: the father is absent (*ein lo av*), and the mother — presumably herself a recent convert — brings the child to convert. The emphasis *Rashi* places on the father's absence is halachically significant, as we will discuss shortly.

### Zachin Principle

The *gemara* asks: *mai ka mashma lan* — what is the novel teaching here? The answer is: *dezchus hu lo*, that becoming Jewish is a benefit for the child, *vezachin l'adam shelo befanav*, and one may perform a meritorious act on behalf of another person even without their presence. The minor is not considered "present" in the legally operative sense because he lacks the full adult capacity to give meaningful consent. The principle of *zachin l'adam shelo befanav* therefore applies — *beis din* can act on his behalf precisely because this is considered to his benefit.

### Benefit Question

Yet the *gemara* immediately questions whether this is in fact the obvious application of *zachin*. One might have thought, *oveid kochavim be-hefkira nicha lei* — that a non-Jew prefers the unrestrained life of *hefker*, the freedom from the obligations that come with Jewish identity. If so, we could not objectively say that it is better for this infant to be Jewish. The *gemara* raises this further by noting the rule regarding a slave: *de-eved vadai be-hefkira nicha lei* — for a slave, we certainly assume he would prefer to remain a slave and live a life of *hefkerus*, rather than be freed and thereby become subject to Jewish obligations. The assumption is that the slave's life is even less constrained than that of a standard non-Jew, since the Sages assumed that slaves, lacking the structure of married life, lived with even fewer social constraints. If that is so for the slave, perhaps we should say the same for a non-Jewish infant: his subjective preference might be for a life without halachic obligation, and therefore we cannot assume that conversion constitutes a *zechus* for him.

### Taste of Forbidden

The *gemara* resolves this: *kamashma lan* — the teaching is specifically telling us that we do consider it his benefit. The distinction is: *hani milei gadol*, this concern about subjective preference applies to an adult, *de-taim taim de-issura* — who has already tasted the forbidden fruit, who knows what that unrestrained life feels like and may be reluctant to give it up. *Aval katan*, for a minor, *zechus hu lo* — he has never had that experience. When you assess what is subjectively in his best interest, you assess it based on his current psychological reality and life experience, and from that vantage point conversion is unambiguously to his benefit.

### Beit Din's Role

This establishes the underlying structure: we have a principle that one may act on another's behalf if it is to that person's benefit; we assert that conversion is objectively and even subjectively to the minor's benefit; and therefore *beis din* may proceed even though no adult is present representing the child's interests. The role of *beis din* here is to function as the adult in the room — to stand in for the minor and provide the legal acquiescence that makes the conversion effective. Just as parents make consequential decisions for their children all the time, legally authorized to act on their behalf and in their best interest, *beis din* is legally entitled to represent the interests of the minor and grant the necessary approval to proceed.

### Rashi's Case

This explains *Rashi*'s position. *Rashi* specifies that the case involves a child *ein lo av* — without a biological father — and that the mother brings the child to convert. If the biological father is Jewish, he can make this decision for the child himself. Parents always make decisions for their children, and the father, as the legal head of the family in this patriarchal framework, can substitute for *beis din*. This is why *Rashi* specifically points to the absence of the father — it is precisely what necessitates *beis din*'s involvement.

One might ask: if the father's role can substitute for *beis din*, why not the mother's role as well? It is a legitimate question, and the reality of the patriarchal legal structure means that the mother's role receives less legal recognition in this context. The practical upshot is that *Rashi*'s case is describing a less common scenario — most cases of *ger katan* involve either an absent father or a Jewish father, and *Rashi* chose to illustrate the case where *beis din* is most clearly necessary.

### Three Positions

This foundational *gemara* sets the stage for what becomes in practice a three-way debate among later authorities regarding the standards for *geyrus katan*, particularly in the context of converting children in intermarried families. Some *achronim* argue that *beis din*'s role is not merely to provide acquiescence as described above, but to perform the act of *kabbalas mitzvos* on behalf of the minor — since the minor himself cannot accept the commandments. This reading, it must be said, is not *pshat* in the *gemara* at all; this *gemara* does not mention *kabbalas mitzvos* even in passing, and most *rishonim* either say that *kabbalas mitzvos* is not required for a minor, or that the minor's subsequent adult life of Jewish observance constitutes a quasi-*kabbalas mitzvos*.

These different readings of *beis din*'s role generate three distinct practical camps:

The first camp holds that no *kabbalas mitzvos* is required at all. The only question is whether the conversion is a *zechus* for the minor. Even if the child is being raised in a non-observant home, this camp would argue that objectively it is still a *zechus* to be Jewish — the *mitzvos bein adam l'chaveiro* alone constitute a benefit, and the principle of *kol Yisrael yesh lahem chelek l'olam haba* may confer an objective advantage to Jewish status regardless of the level of observance in the home.

The second camp — the mainstream middle position — holds that while full observance need not be guaranteed, the conversion must put the child on a reasonably likely path toward Jewish life. The family does not need to be *shomer Shabbos* or fully *shomrei kashrus*, but there must be some meaningful Jewish engagement — sending the child to Jewish day school, having a Jewish home environment, some connection to *shul*. This position attempts to make *zechus* a concrete and reasonable prediction rather than a pure abstraction.

The third camp, drawing on those *achronim* who understand *beis din* as performing *kabbalas mitzvos* on the minor's behalf, holds that *beis din* can only legitimately stand in for the minor and perform that *kabbalas mitzvos* if the child will in fact live a life of *shemiras mitzvos*. On this view, conversion is valid only when the child is being raised in a fully observant home.

### Father Converts Too

The *gemara* attempts to bring a proof for *Rav Huna*'s ruling from our very *mishnah* — a woman who converted under three years old must have done so with *beis din* approval. The *gemara* rejects this proof: *lo, hacha bemai askinan*, we are dealing here with a case of a convert who came with his children, *shenisgayer hu uvanav uvenosav imo*, where the father himself converted simultaneously with his children. In that case, *denicha lehu bemai de'avid avuhon* — because any child would naturally want what his father wants, the children's implicit will can be assumed, and there is no need to invoke the full mechanism of *beis din* acting through *zachin*. Therefore, this case provides no proof for the principle *Rav Huna* articulated, which addresses the more complex situation where no such assumption is available.

---

## Objection Rights

### Rav Yosef Rule

*Amar Rav Yosef: higdilu yecholim limchos* — once minor converts reach adulthood, they can object and reverse their status. Since the conversion was done through the mechanism of *zachin l'adam shelo befanav* — acting on behalf of the minor because it was deemed to be his benefit — the logic of that principle implies that when the minor actually becomes an adult and can speak for himself, he has the standing to say: this was not done for my benefit, and I reject it. The analogy is apt: if someone accepts a gift on my behalf while I am absent, that is valid through *zachin*. But the moment I am informed of the transaction and say I do not want it — invoking the principle of *soneh matanos yichye* — it is as though the acquisition never took place. We do not say I acquired it and must now divest myself of it; rather, the act retroactively loses its force. So too here: when the convert reaches adulthood, it is as though he is now present. If he objects, the conversion never fully took hold. If he does not object, it is sealed.

### Ketubah Timing

*Eitivei Abaye*: Abaye challenges *Rav Yosef* from the *mishnah* itself. The *mishnah* states that a woman who converted under three years old has a *ketubah* of 200 *zuz*. If *higdilu yecholim limchos* — if she can reverse the conversion upon reaching adulthood — then how can we pay out her *ketubah*? *Yahavinan lah ktuva de'azla ve'achla begiyuta* — we would be giving money to a woman who will retroactively turn out to have been a non-Jew! The *gemara* answers: *lechi gadla* — we wait to pay the *ketubah* until she becomes an adult. If she reaches adulthood and does not object, her Jewish status is sealed, and only then do we make the payment.

### Sha'ah Achat

Abaye's challenge is then pressed further: *lechi gadla nami mimcha ve'afka* — even when she becomes an adult, she can still object and leave. Why does becoming an adult resolve anything? The *gemara* answers: *kivan she'gadla sha'ah achas velo michasa, shuv einah yechola limchos* — once she reached adulthood for even one moment and did not object, from that point forward she can no longer do so. The moment of reaching adulthood is the operative window. If at that first moment, upon being apprised of her situation, she does not protest, then it is as though she affirmed the transaction. After that, there is no reversal. Just as accepting a gift in the moment forecloses a later claim that you never wanted it, failing to object at the first moment of legal adulthood forecloses the possibility of later protest.

*Rava* poses an analogous challenge regarding the *knas* — the fifty-*kesef* penalty for rape that applies to a *naarah* who is a virgin. The same problem arises: if we might pay this *knas* and she later objects to her conversion, the money would retroactively have gone to a non-Jew. The *gemara* gives the same structural answer, but the two *Amoraim* frame the concern differently. *Abaye* was not bothered by the *knas* case because, as the *gemara* explains, *she-lo ye-hei chotei niskar* — we do not want to benefit the sinner. Even if the money winds up going to someone who turns out to have been a non-Jew, the more pressing concern is that the rapist pays. *Rava*, for his part, was not bothered by the *ketubah* case because *she-lo te-hei kallah b'einav l'hotzi'ah* — the institution of *ketubah* exists to protect women in marriage, and that concern outweighs the possibility that in some cases the payment might go to someone who retroactively loses her Jewish status.

### Tosafot Position

What precisely constitutes the *sha'ah achas* — the critical moment in which the failure to object becomes irreversible? *Tosafos Yeshanim* addresses this directly, asking: *masai teida sha'as hamacha'ah* — how does one even identify the moment of objection? One answer given is that if, in the days immediately surrounding her *bat mitzvah*, she began behaving as a non-Jew — both shortly before and after — that constitutes a *micha'ah*.

*Tosafos* adds a further point in the context of the *knas* discussion. The *gemara* asks why we would pay out the *knas* when she might yet object upon becoming an adult. *Tosafos* (*Ri*) explains: *likhshe-t'gdal v'nahaga minhag yehudis* — we wait until she has grown up and conducted herself in the manner of a Jewish woman. This implies that it is not sufficient merely to refrain from objecting; the young woman must also have done something that affirmatively demonstrates Jewish conduct, even if only briefly, in the period immediately following her *bat mitzvah*.

This raises the broader question: does the *micha'ah* require a formal act in front of witnesses, or can it be any behavior that demonstrates rejection of Jewish identity? And from the other side, does affirmation require a specific positive act? The *gemara* itself only speaks of the *absence* of *micha'ah* — it never demands a positive affirmation. Therefore, the standard is one of *i-michui*, not affirmative confirmation. What constitutes *michui* then becomes context-dependent: going for a cheeseburger in an observant household would likely constitute a *micha'ah*, while the same act in a non-observant household that nevertheless identifies as Jewish might not.

In practice, many poskim hold that the rabbi performing the conversion should speak with the child before or at the time of *bar* or *bat mitzvah*, inform them of their status, and give them the opportunity to affirm or reject it. The child's continued Jewish conduct in the period immediately following *bar* or *bat mitzvah* — even if not explicitly articulated as an affirmation — would then constitute the operative non-*micha'ah*. These questions carry enormous practical weight in contemporary *gerut*, and the *sugya* of *ger katan* here is one of the central sources for navigating them.

---

## Besulah Definition

### Mishnah Cases

The following *mishnah* takes up the fundamental question underlying the entire discussion: what does it mean to be a *besulah*? Is virginity defined by the absence of any halachic act of intercourse, or by the physical intactness of the hymen?

The *mishnah* presents three cases. First, *ha-gadol she-ba al ha-ktana* — an adult man who had intercourse with a minor girl under three years old. Second, *v'katan she-ba al ha-gedolah* — a minor boy under nine who had intercourse with an adult woman. Third, *u'mukas eitz* — a woman whose hymen was ruptured by an external object rather than through intercourse. In all three cases, *Rabbi Meir* rules: *ketuvasan masayim*, they receive a *ketubah* of 200. Rabbi Meir's position is internally consistent: virginity is defined as never having had an act of intercourse. In all three cases, there was no halachically recognized act of intercourse, and therefore they remain *besulos*.

### Chachamim View

*Vachachamim omrim*: the *Chachamim* disagree specifically regarding *mukas eitz*, ruling *kesuvosah maneh* — she receives only 100. For the *Chachamim*, the physical intactness of the hymen is part of the definition of *besulah*. A woman whose hymen has been ruptured, even not through intercourse, is not fully in the *besulah* category and therefore receives only a *maneh*.

### Post-Chuppah

The *mishnah* then addresses the case of a woman who was a *besulah* but had proceeded to *nisuin* — not merely *kiddushin* but *chuppah*, living in her husband's home — before being divorced or widowed without actually having had intercourse. Such a woman, *besulah almonah gerushah vechalutzah min ha-nisuin*, receives a *ketubah* of only 100, and there is no *ta'anas besulim* available to a subsequent husband. The rationale is formalistic: once a woman has entered into a state of *nisuin*, even if she never actually had intercourse, the legal presumption is that she has. We do not investigate every individual case; *lo plug*, the rule applies uniformly to all women who have been through *nisuin*. Correspondingly, since the *ketubah* is set at 100 on the assumption that she is not a virgin, a subsequent husband cannot complain that she was not a virgin — the two go together as a package. One cannot receive the reduced *ketubah* while simultaneously maintaining the expectation of physical virginity.

### Minor Boy Case

The *mishnah* also addresses the converse of the first two categories: a convert, captive, or maidservant who underwent her status transition after three years and one day. In such cases, it is assumed that intercourse during that period would have constituted a halachic act and would not have allowed the hymen to regenerate. Therefore, *ketuvasan maneh ve'ein lahen ta'anas besulim* — the *ketubah* is 100 and there is no *ta'anas besulim*.

### Rav vs. Shmuel

The *gemara* now takes up the case of *katan haba al ha-gedolah* — the minor boy who had intercourse with an adult woman. *Amar Rav Yehudah amar Rav: katan haba al hagedolah asaah mukas eitz* — this act, while not a halachic *biah* because the boy is under nine, nonetheless renders the woman a *mukas eitz*. The hymen has been physically ruptured, and that physical rupture has consequences regardless of whether the act is classified as *biah*.

*Ki amriseh kamei de-Shmuel*, but when this was reported before *Shmuel*, he responded: *ein mukas eitz be-basar* — one cannot create the status of *mukas eitz* through an act of flesh. If the rupture occurred through what was, even if not legally recognized as *biah*, nonetheless an act of intercourse, then the woman is neither a *mukas eitz* nor someone who has had a halachic act of sex, and she remains a *besulah*.

### Tosafot Critique

This position of *Rav* is deeply counterintuitive, and *Tosafos* does not accept it. *Tosafos* argues that *Shmuel*'s statement *ein mukas eitz be-basar* must be describing a scenario where the hymen was in fact not ruptured — *b'lo hipshir besulim*. If the hymen were ruptured, *Tosafos* cannot comprehend how the woman could be in a worse position than a *mukas eitz*: *lama yesh la lihyos p'chusa mi-mukas eitz?* — why should she be treated as less protected than a woman who experienced a traumatic external rupture? On the *Rav*'s reading, a completely formalistic framework applies: the act was not *biah*, but it ruptured the hymen, and yet she is still a *besulah* in some fully valid sense. *Tosafos* finds this untenable. If the hymen is intact — which is what *Tosafos* argues *Shmuel* must be describing — then of course she remains a *besulah* and there is no issue. The debate of *Rav* and *Shmuel* therefore, on *Tosafos*' reading, is not about whether physical rupture creates the status of *mukas eitz*, but rather whether this particular kind of non-*biah* act can rupture the hymen at all.

---

## Mukat Eitz

### With Knowledge

*Amar Rami bar Chama*: the debate between *Rabbi Meir* and the *Chachamim* regarding whether *mukas eitz* receives 200 or 100 is specifically in the case of *keshehikker bah* — when the husband knew about the woman's condition before marriage. He was aware that her hymen was not intact due to an external injury rather than intercourse, and he married her nonetheless. Even in that case, *Rabbi Meir* says 200 and *Chachamim* say 100. The entire debate therefore concerns the formal categorical question of which legal category she belongs to — not a question of mismatch between expectation and reality.

### Rabbi Meir Logic

Why does *Rabbi Meir* classify her as a *besulah* and award 200? *Rabi Meir medamme lah l'bogeres* — he analogizes her to a physically mature woman (*bogeres*) whose hymen has naturally thinned with age but who is still considered a *besulah* because she has never had intercourse. The key distinction in *Rabbi Meir*'s logic: *beulah asvid bah ma'aseh bidei adam* — a non-virgin is defined by the fact that a human act of intercourse took place. *Ha lo asvid bah ma'aseh bidei adam* — in the case of *mukas eitz*, no such act occurred. Without an act of intercourse, she remains in the *besulah* category, regardless of the physical state of the hymen.

### Chachamim Logic

*Chachamim*, by contrast, analogize her to a *beulah* — a woman who has had intercourse. Why not classify her as a *bogeres*? *Bogeres lo asvid bah ma'aseh klal* — in the case of a *bogeres*, nothing external happened to her at all; the natural thinning of the hymen with physical maturity is not comparable to an external rupture. *Ha asvid bah ma'aseh* — here, something did happen. An external event ruptured the hymen, and that rupture places her in the same functional category as a woman who has had intercourse, even if it was not an act of intercourse. The *Chachamim* therefore rule that she receives only 100.

### No Knowledge Case

*Aval lo hikker bah divrei hakol velo klum* — but if the husband did not know about the *mukas eitz* condition, then by unanimous agreement she receives nothing. In that case, the husband can claim *mekach taus* — a mistaken transaction. He was not merely asking whether she had had intercourse; he was expecting her to have an intact hymen, and she did not. When the reality diverges from what he was led to expect, the entire transaction is treated as entered into on false premises, and the *ketubah* obligation falls away entirely.

### Two Frameworks

The *gemara* thus sets up two competing analytical frameworks. One centers on the question of formal halachic category: regardless of what the husband expected, what legal classification does this woman belong to? *Rabbi Meir* says she belongs in the *besulah* category; *Chachamim* say she belongs in the *beulah* category. This debate operates when the husband had full knowledge — expectation plays no role, and the question is purely formal.

The other framework is built around the expectation mismatch: when the husband did not know, the issue is not categorical but contractual. He entered the marriage with a certain expectation, that expectation was not met, and therefore the entire transaction is void. On this reading, the question of *mukas eitz*'s formal category becomes irrelevant — what matters is whether there was a *mekach taus*.

The *gemara* continues by opening the possibility that the entire debate between *Rabbi Meir* and *Chachamim* might in fact be structured the other way around: perhaps the disagreement concerns specifically the case where the husband did *not* know, and the question is how far the logic of *mekach taus* extends — whereas when the husband did know, perhaps all would agree that she receives the full 200. That alternative reading will be developed as the daf proceeds.

---

---

# Ketubot 13

## Virginity Dispute

### Claims Setup

The Mishnah that opens our discussion on 12b is the culmination of a theme that has run through the tractate from its very first pages. From the outset, Ketubot has been concerned with the day of the wedding and the morning appearance in court, with the varying amounts of the *kesubah* depending on the woman's status. Now we finally arrive at the scenario that makes all of that relevant: the morning after the wedding, when a dispute erupts.

The case is introduced as follows: *hanoise es ha'isha velo matza lah besulim* — he married a woman and found no evidence of virginity. Notably, in this case the wife does not dispute the underlying fact; she does not claim she was a virgin at the time of the wedding. Instead, the debate is over the interpretation of events. She says, *mishe'erastani ne'enasti* — "After our *kiddushin*, I was raped." In the striking idiom of the Mishnah: *venistachfa sadehu* — "his field was flooded." The imagery is vivid if jarring; the point is that something happened to him, an event that befell his property after he had already acquired it, and therefore she is still entitled to the full *kesubah* of 200.

The husband's counter-claim is equally direct: *lo ki ela ad shelo erastich* — "No, you were not a virgin even before the *kiddushin*." And with that he invokes the concept of *mekach taus* — the entire transaction was entered into under a misapprehension. The precise implications of *mekach taus* for the validity of the *kiddushin* itself remain complex, but at the very least the husband is arguing that he owes nothing close to 200, and perhaps owes nothing at all.

### Tannaim Debate

The Mishnah records a three-way Tannaitic debate. *Rabban Gamliel ve'Rabbi Eliezer omrim ne'emenes* — Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer say she is believed. Rabbi Yehoshua demurs sharply: *lo mipiha anu chayim* — "We do not live from her mouth, from her words alone." In his view, *harei zu bechezkas be'ula ad shelo tisarast* — she carries the presumption of having been a *be'ulah* before the *kiddushin*, and she has deceived him. Until she brings actual proof of her claim, that presumption stands against her.

### Monetary Framework

One natural way to frame this dispute is through the lens of *dinei mamonos*. She holds a *shtar* — her *kesubah* — which she claims is worth 200. He disputes that valuation and contends it is worth 100 or perhaps zero. When there is a monetary dispute of this kind and no clear evidence, the governing principle should be *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'aya*: the party seeking to extract money from another's possession bears the burden of proof. The Gemara's initial approach to our Mishnah is precisely this — to apply that rule and determine who, on that basis, should prevail.

---

## Bari vs. Shema

### Definite vs. Doubtful

The Gemara now introduces a parallel case to sharpen the analysis. *Maneh li beyadcha vehalla omer eini yodea* — one person says to another, "You owe me a hundred," and the other responds, "I don't know." This is to be distinguished from the case where the second party concedes the debt but claims he may have repaid it; there, everyone agrees he must pay, since he acknowledges the obligation without being able to affirm its discharge. Here, however, the claimant has a *bari* — a definite, certain claim — while the respondent holds a *shema* — a position of genuine uncertainty.

### Definite Prevails

Rav Yehuda and Rav Huna rule: *chayiv* — the respondent must pay. Their principle is *bari ve'shema bari adif*: when a definite claim confronts an uncertain one, the definite claim prevails.

### Possession Rule

Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan rule: *patur* — the respondent is exempt. Their principle is *oki mamona bechezkas mara* — money remains in the possession of the one currently holding it, and to extract it requires concrete proof. The *hamotzi mechavero* rule stands.

### Shmuel's Position

At this point, Abaye reports to Rav Yosef a tradition in the name of Shmuel: the ruling of Rav Yehuda and Rav Huna — that the *bari* claim prevails — is in fact the position of Shmuel. The proof is from the very Mishnah we will be examining on 13a.

The Mishnah there presents a case of a single woman who is pregnant. She is asked *ma tivo shel ubar zeh* — what is the nature of this fetus, meaning: is there any concern that this child is a *mamzer* or otherwise *pasul*? She responds: *me'ish ploni ve'kohen hu* — the father is so-and-so, and he is a *kohen*, meaning a man of unblemished status. Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer say she is believed, both regarding her own personal status and presumably the fetus's. Rabbi Yehoshua says she is not believed.

And Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *halacha ke'Rabban Gamliel* — we rule like Rabban Gamliel. Then Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda pressed Rav Yehuda further, calling him *Shinena* — "sharp one" — and reminded him that Shmuel had said *halacha ke'Rabban Gamliel af berishona*, meaning: Shmuel rules like Rabban Gamliel not only in the case of personal status, but even in the *first* Mishnah — the monetary dispute about the *kesubah* value. And what makes that first case a larger *chiddush*? Because there, one could have said *okim mamona bechezkas marei* — keep the money where it is. Despite that, Shmuel rules for her.

This gives us the conclusion: *amar Rabban Gamliel bari adif* — even against the *chezkas mamona* of the husband, her *bari* claim carries the day.

The Gemara then asks directly: perhaps the dispute between Rav Yehuda and Rav Huna on one side and Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan on the other is simply a reprise of the Tannaitic dispute in our Mishnah — Rabban Gamliel versus Rabbi Yehoshua? To this question, Rav Nachman himself responds: the positions need not collapse into one another, and he can agree with Rabban Gamliel in our Mishnah even while maintaining his general rule. This is the burden of the next section.

---

## Reconciling Positions

### Migo & Chazakah

Rav Nachman explains: *ad kan lo ka'amar Rabban Gamliel hatam ela d'ika migo* — Rabban Gamliel's ruling in the Mishnah is not simply about *bari adif* in the abstract. It is grounded in additional considerations that are particular to this case. Specifically, the woman has a *migo*. A *migo* is the principle that if a party could have made a stronger or more favorable claim, the fact that she chose a lesser or more vulnerable one gives that claim additional credibility.

### Could Lie Better

What is her *migo* here? As we shall see, the next Mishnah involves the claim of *mukas etz* — that a woman's non-virginal state results not from intercourse but from a physical injury. In the first Mishnah, the wife is not claiming *mukas etz*; she is conceding she was raped. Had she wanted to lie in a more self-serving way, she could have claimed *mukas etz*, which would have affected her status less adversely. The fact that she volunteered the more damaging claim — that she was raped — lends her words greater credibility. She had a better lie available and chose not to tell it.

Alternatively — or additionally — she holds a *chazakah*. Every person is born with the presumption of whatever status they began with. A woman is born a virgin, and therefore we maintain that presumption until the last possible moment. If we are uncertain when her virginity was lost, we push that event as late as we can — meaning after the *kiddushin*, which supports her claim.

Neither of these factors operates in the simple *maneh li beyadcha* case. The person demanding money has no *migo* — there is no "better lie" he declined to tell — and he has no *chazakah* of a previous debt. Hence Rav Nachman can say: by the clean *bari ve'shema* case, I maintain *okim mamona bechezkas mara*; but in our Mishnah, there are the additional supports of *migo* and *chazakah*, which justify the ruling of Rabban Gamliel independently of any general *bari adif* principle.

It is worth noting that Tosafos develops an even more textured analysis here by distinguishing between a *bari tov* and a *bari garu'a*, and between a *shema tov* and a *shema garu'a*. Not all *bari* claims are of equal strength, and not all *shema* positions are of equal weakness. In our Mishnah, the wife's *bari* is in one sense weak — she is the only one who knows the truth and faces no real check on her ability to lie — while the husband's *shema* is also correspondingly weak, since he really should have some independent knowledge of the situation. Tosafos notes that this actually makes our Mishnah a *bigger chiddush* than the simple *maneh li beyadcha* case, rather than a smaller one. But that analysis belongs to a deeper level of the discussion.

### Resolution

The Gemara confirms that this answer is sound: *hach nami mistabra kidimishaninan* — it makes good sense the way we have answered. The proof is structural: we rule like Rav Nachman in monetary cases, which means our baseline *psak* is *lav bari adif*. Yet we also rule like Rabban Gamliel in our Mishnah, as Shmuel established. The only way to hold both positions without contradiction is to say that our Mishnah is a special case — that it is the *migo* or the *chazakah* (or both) that tips the scales for the woman here, not a general *bari adif* rule. *Shema mina* — this is a sound proof of that resolution.

The Gemara concludes by noting the practical ruling: *hilchesa* — the law — follows this structure, holding like Rav Nachman in general monetary disputes while affirming Rabban Gamliel's ruling in the specific context of our Mishnah.

---

## Mukat Etz Case

### Competing Claims

The Mishnah now introduces its second case, which runs in parallel to the first but with a significant shift in the nature of the competing claims. Again, both parties agree that the wife was not a virgin at the time of the wedding. The wife, however, says: *mukas etz ani* — I was injured by a piece of wood; my non-virginal state results from a physical injury, not from sexual intercourse. The husband counters: *lo ki ela drusas ish at* — no, you had intercourse with a man before the *kiddushin*. The same debate among the Tannaim follows: Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer believe her; Rabbi Yehoshua does not, maintaining her presumptive status as *drusas ish* until she proves otherwise.

### Rabbi Meir Frame

The Gemara now asks: what exactly are the monetary stakes in this second Mishnah, and how do the opinions of Rabbi Meir and the Rabbanan determine the structure of the dispute? Rabbi Yochanan reads the Mishnah as a debate conducted within the framework of Rabbi Meir. She is claiming 200, and he is countering that she deserves only 100. Why? Rabbi Meir holds that *bein hikkir bah bein lo hikkir bah masayim* — whether or not the husband was aware that the woman was a *mukas etz*, her *kesubah* is the full 200. Hence, she claims: I am a *mukas etz*, and under Rabbi Meir's ruling I deserve 200. He responds: you are in fact a *be'ulah*, not a *mukas etz*, and a *be'ulah* deserves only 100. The dispute is between 200 and 100, situated entirely within Rabbi Meir's position.

### Rabbanan Frame

Rabbi Elazar reads the Mishnah differently — as a debate conducted within the framework of the Rabbanan, with the stakes being 100 or zero. The Rabbanan hold that a *mukas etz* receives 100 regardless of whether the husband knew. She claims she is a *mukas etz* and therefore entitled to 100. He counters that she is a *be'ulah* — and since he entered the marriage under the presumption that she was a *besulah* and discovered otherwise, she receives nothing. This is the *kinsa bechezkas besulah venimtzes be'ulah* scenario, which yields zero under his reading.

The Gemara explains why Rabbi Yochanan cannot read the Mishnah within the framework of the Rabbanan: under the Rabbanan's position, and with Rabbi Yochanan's own view that *kinsa bechezkas besulah venimtzes be'ulah yesh lah kesubah maneh* — even if she was discovered to be a *be'ulah*, she still receives 100 — the husband's claim and the wife's claim would yield identical amounts. If she says *mukas etz* she gets 100, and if he says *be'ulah* she also gets 100. There would be no dispute to adjudicate, no *nafka minah*. Hence Rabbi Yochanan must situate the Mishnah within Rabbi Meir.

### Two Cases Purpose

The Gemara then asks: given that Rabbi Elazar reads both Mishnayot within the framework of the Rabbanan, we can readily explain why two separate Mishnayot are needed, since each one delivers a distinct *chiddush*. But what is the purpose of having two cases according to Rabbi Yochanan?

According to Rabbi Elazar, the first Mishnah — where the wife claims she was raped after *kiddushin* — establishes that *kinsa bechezkas besulah venimtzes be'ulah* yields zero. This rejects the position embraced by Rabbi Chiya bar Avin, who held that even when a woman enters as a presumed *besulah* and is found to be a *be'ulah*, she retains 100. The second Mishnah — the *mukas etz* case — establishes that *kinsa bechezkas besulah venimtzes mukas etz* still entitles her to 100. This rejects the position of Rami bar Chama, who held that any misrepresentation, even a *mukas etz* situation, results in zero. Each Mishnah is thus targeting a different mistaken view.

According to Rabbi Yochanan, however, who situates the second Mishnah within Rabbi Meir, the *chiddush* about *mukas etz* not yielding zero is obviously present there. And since Rabbi Yochanan himself holds that *nimtzes be'ulah* still yields 100, the first Mishnah under the Rabbanan's framework would also not yield zero. So what is the second Mishnah adding?

The Gemara's answer, attributed to Rav Sheshet, is that the two Mishnayot are needed to demonstrate the full extent of the opposing Tannaitic positions. The first Mishnah reveals the strength of Rabbi Yehoshua's position: *af al gav de'ika le'meimar migo lo mehemena* — even though the wife has a *migo* in that case (she could have claimed *mukas etz* rather than rape, a less self-incriminating claim), Rabbi Yehoshua still does not believe her. The second Mishnah reveals the strength of Rabban Gamliel's position: *af al gav de'leka le'meimar migo ne'emenes* — even though in the *mukas etz* case the wife has no *migo* (she is already making the best possible claim; *mukas etz* does not diminish her status), Rabban Gamliel believes her and she receives the full 200. The two cases are thus needed to trace the full arc of the disagreement between the Tannaim.

---

## Seen with Man

### Status Question

The Mishnah now shifts from monetary disputes to questions of personal status. *Ra'uah medaberes im echad* — a woman was seen speaking with a man. The Mishnah will ask what we are to make of this, and in particular whether we believe her account of who that man was. The question is not merely abstract; it bears directly on the woman's fitness to marry a *kohen* and on the status of any child she might have. If she had relations with a *mamzer* or a non-Jew, she would become *pasul* to a *kohen*, and the child's lineage would be compromised.

It is worth noting in passing that elsewhere in Ketubot, a wife who *medaberes im kol adam bashuk* — who speaks to strangers in the marketplace — is grounds for divorce without payment of the *kesubah*. This was a highly segregated society, and a woman's speaking to a strange man was not taken as an innocuous act.

She is asked: *ma tivo shel ish zeh* — what is the story of this man? She responds: *ish ploni ve'kohen hu* — it was so-and-so, and he is a *kohen*. The mention of *kohen* is not strictly necessary; the point is that the man is of valid Jewish lineage and that nothing about the encounter could have compromised her status.

### Tannaim Again

The same Tannaitic debate recurs with the same formulations. Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer say she is believed. Rabbi Yehoshua says *lo mipiha anu chayim* — we do not live from her words. He holds that she carries the presumption of having had relations with a *nasin* or a *mamzer*, rendering her *pasul* to a *kohen*, until she can prove otherwise.

---

## Seen with Man (II)

### Medaberet Definition

Before we can analyze the Tannaitic debate, we must establish what the Mishnah's first case actually involves. The Mishnah says she was *medaberes im echad* — "speaking with someone." But does this mean she merely conversed with a man, possibly in seclusion, or does it mean something more?

---

## Seclusion vs. Sex

### Zeiri: Seclusion

Zeiri says: *medaberes* means *nistera* — she went into seclusion with a man. The term is a description of private contact, not of sexual intercourse per se. Under this reading, the Mishnah is saying that even in a case where we only know she was alone with a man — without any direct knowledge of sexual activity — Rabbi Yehoshua holds that her status is in suspicion.

### Rav Assi: Sex

Rav Assi says: *medaberes* means *niv'ala* — she actually had sexual relations. The word *medaberes* is used because it is *lishana me'alya* — a euphemism, a refined term. The Mishnah employs indirect language to describe what is in fact a known sexual encounter.

### Mouth Euphemism

The Gemara brings a proof for Rav Assi's reading from the verse in Proverbs that describes the way of an adulterous woman: *achla umachta pi'a* — she eats and wipes her mouth. The "mouth" language is itself a euphemism for sexual activity. The Gemara connects this to the *medaberes* formulation in our Mishnah, suggesting that speech and mouth language function as established biblical idioms for sexual conduct.

This reading has significant practical consequences. If Zeiri is correct and the Mishnah's first case is merely seclusion, then Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling is extraordinarily stringent: even without knowing that any intercourse occurred, a woman's status becomes suspect based solely on private contact. This would seem to clash with the ruling of Rav, who holds that *malkin al ha-yichud ve-ein osrin al ha-yichud* — we administer rabbinic lashes for seclusion of a married woman with a stranger, but we do not thereby forbid her to her husband. If even a married woman does not lose her status from mere seclusion, why would a single woman's lineage-related status be compromised? The Gemara addresses this tension, suggesting that when it comes to *yuchasin* — questions of lineage and fitness to marry a *kohen* — a special stringency applies: *ma'ala asu be-yuchasin*.

### Two Cases Explained

The Gemara asks: according to Zeiri, why does the Mishnah need two separate cases — the case where she is *medaberes* and the case where she is pregnant? Each case adds a distinct dimension. The first — seclusion — tests how far Rabbi Yehoshua's stringency extends (even without knowing she had sex). The second — pregnancy, where we know beyond doubt that she had sex — tests how far Rabban Gamliel's leniency extends (even when the fact of intercourse is established).

According to Rav Assi, however, since the first case already involves known sexual relations, the two cases could seem redundant. The Gemara answers: *chada lehachsher ba ve'chada lehachsher be'vita* — one case establishes her own status as valid, and the other establishes that the fetus's status is also valid. Why might the fetus's status be treated differently? Because the woman herself has a *chazakah* — she started life with a presumptively valid status, and we are reluctant to undermine it. But the fetus has no prior status; its lineage is entirely unknown. One might therefore have said that even if we trust her account of her own status, we remain doubtful about the fetus. The second case teaches that Rabban Gamliel believes her even with respect to the child.

This analysis holds, the Gemara notes, according to the position that *le'divrei ha-machsher ba machsher be'vita* — according to those who validate her, they validate the child as well. But there is a competing view that *le'divrei ha-machsher ba posel be'vita* — even those who accept her own status would still consider the child of doubtful status. Under that view, both cases in the Mishnah are about her status only, and if the first case already establishes that point, the second adds nothing. The Gemara resolves this by concluding that Rav Assi held the former position — that validating the mother means validating the child — so that the two cases are indeed each necessary.

---

## Location Analysis

### Ruins Distinction

A *baraita* is now introduced to further elaborate the Mishnah's cases. The *baraita* speaks of a woman who went into a *churba* — a ruin — with a man. Rashi notes that a *churba* carries a stronger presumption of sexual activity than mere seclusion; ruins are places where people go specifically for trysts, away from public view, making the assumption of intercourse more reasonable than in a simple case of seclusion. The *baraita* then presents two sub-cases: *churba de'mata* — a ruin within the city — and *churba de'dabra* — a ruin in the field.

The Gemara asks: if the word *medaberes* in the Mishnah is understood in one way, we can explain why these two ruin cases are needed. But according to Rav Assi, who already interprets *medaberes* as actual intercourse, what is the point of distinguishing two kinds of ruins? The Gemara initially suggests that perhaps *seter* and *churba* describe a single scenario — the privacy of a ruin. But this is quickly rejected, since the text explicitly says *o le'churba* — "or a ruin" — implying two distinct situations. The Gemara then commits to the reading that there are genuinely two different cases of *churba*, distinguished by their location.

### Kosher Majority

*De'i ashmeinan churba de'mata* — had the *baraita* mentioned only the ruin in the city, we might have understood Rabban Gamliel's ruling narrowly. In that case, *rov ksheirim etzlah* — the majority of the people in the city who might have been her partner are halachically valid Jews; non-Jews and *mamzerim* are rare. Rabban Gamliel's willingness to believe her in that context would be unsurprising.

### Invalid Majority

Conversely, *churba de'dabra* — a ruin in the field — presents a different demographic reality. In the open countryside, *rov psulim etzlah* — the majority of men she might have encountered are non-Jews, who would render her *pasul* to a *kohen* if she had relations with them. One might have thought that even Rabban Gamliel would concede to Rabbi Yehoshua in that case, since the statistical likelihood cuts against her.

### Yichus Severity

Conversely, had the *baraita* mentioned only the field case, we might have understood Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling as limited to that scenario, where the majority are *psulim*. We might then have thought that in the city — where most are *kasher* — Rabbi Yehoshua would concede to Rabban Gamliel. By including both cases, the *baraita* teaches that Rabbi Yehoshua maintains his stringency *afilu be'rov ksheirim* — even where the majority are valid. His position is grounded not in statistics but in the categorical principle of *ma'ala asu be'yuchasin*: when it comes to questions of lineage and fitness for priestly marriage, we apply an elevated standard of scrutiny regardless of the demographic majority.

The Gemara confirms this analysis by citing a statement of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *mi'divrei ha-machsher machsher afilu be'rov psulim, u'mi'divrei ha-posel posel afilu be'rov ksheirim* — those who validate her do so even where most are *psulim*, and those who invalidate her do so even where most are *ksheirim*. The positions are absolute in both directions, which explains why the comparison to the captive woman could be introduced without those who defend her immediately objecting that the cases are statistically incomparable.

---

## Baraita Stringency

### Captive Comparison

Rabbi Yehoshua now challenges Rabban Gamliel with a comparison: *i atem modim bishvuya she'nishbet ve'yesh lah edim she'nishbet ve'hi omeret tehora ani she'eina ne'emenes* — do you not concede that if a woman has been taken captive by non-Jews, and there are witnesses to that captivity, she is not believed when she claims she was not violated? That case is one where you accept that a woman's assurances about her own sexual history cannot be credited. How, then, can you believe this woman when she identifies the man she was with?

Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer concede the captive case: *aval* — yes, that is true.

### Non-Jews Difference

They then press back: *mah hefresh bein zo l'zo?* — what difference is there between the captive and this woman? The answer is: *l'zo yesh edim u'l'zo ein edim* — in the case of the captive, there are witnesses to the captivity itself, establishing that she was in the hands of non-Jews who we presume would violate her. Here, in the case of seclusion or private contact, there are no such witnesses establishing that she was with a man who would be *pasul*. The cases are therefore not comparable.

### No Guardian

Rabbi Yehoshua counters: *af l'zo yesh edim she'harei k'reisa bein sheineiha* — but in the pregnant case, there is visible evidence; her pregnancy is itself the proof that she has had relations. So why is the pregnant woman more trustworthy than the captive?

They respond: *rov ovdei kochavim prutzim ba'arayot hem* — non-Jews are presumed to be sexually aggressive; when a woman is in their captivity, we assume violation occurred with non-Jews specifically, which is what renders her *pasul*. But when a Jewish woman goes into private with an unidentified man, we do not presume that the man was one who would disqualify her.

Rabbi Yehoshua's rejoinder is the principle that has become one of the most cited phrases in this area of halacha: *ein apotropus la'arayot* — there is no guardian over sexual urges. The impulse toward forbidden relations does not discriminate by nationality. If we are going to assume that non-Jewish captors will violate a woman, we must equally assume that when a man and woman are in private, relations occur. The argument from the captive therefore applies to the seclusion case as well.

### Status & Shtuki

The *baraita* concludes on a notably stringent note. When does the *ne'emanus* principle — that she is believed about her own status — apply? Only when *bata hee gufa* — she herself comes forward and testifies. But when the question is about the child — *aval he'idah isha be'vita* — the *baraita* rules *divrei ha'kol ha'velad shtuki*: everyone agrees that the child is a *shtuki*, a person of doubtful paternity whose claim of "who is my father?" is met with silence. This is a striking and severe conclusion. Even according to Rabban Gamliel, who validates the woman's own status, the child's status cannot be established on the basis of her testimony alone.

The Gemara at this point draws together the threads of the debate, noting that the exchange between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua moves through several shifting positions — the seclusion case, the pregnancy case, the captive comparison — each party advancing and retreating depending on which sub-case is under discussion. The *baraita* also confirms the reading of Zeiri that *medaberes* means seclusion rather than known intercourse, since the whole discussion about the captive comparison only makes sense if the first case involves doubt about whether intercourse occurred at all.

The discussion of Rabbi Yochanan's statement — *le'divrei ha-machsher bah machsher be'vita, u'le'divrei ha-posel bah posel be'vita* — and the question of whether those who validate her necessarily validate the daughter, will be taken up at the start of the next session.

# Ketubot 14

## Seclusion & Status

### Woman & Fetus

The *gemara* opens by picking up toward the bottom of 13b, in the context of the *mishnah*'s dispute between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding a woman who went into seclusion with a man of questionable status. What has already been established is that Rabbi Yehoshua's stringency applies even to mere seclusion — not only to cases where intercourse is known to have occurred.

Against this backdrop, Rabbi Yochanan formulates a sweeping principle: *le-divrei ha-machshir bah machshir be-vittah* — the authority who validates the woman validates the fetus as well; and correspondingly, *le-divrei ha-posel bah posel be-vittah* — the authority who invalidates the woman invalidates the fetus. The larger *chiddush* is the first half of the statement. The woman herself had a *chezkat kashrut* — a presumptive status of being permitted — before the encounter in question, and there is therefore a stronger basis to argue that a single doubtful incident should not strip her of that presumption. The fetus, by contrast, enters the world with no prior presumed status at all. Its very existence is bound up in the doubtful union. And yet Rabbi Yochanan maintains that according to Rabban Gamliel — who accepts her claim and rules her status unimpaired — the same leniency extends to the fetus. The specific concern is the daughter: if the woman slept with a man she was forbidden to, the resulting daughter would become a *chalala*, disqualified from marrying a *kohen*.

### Rabbi Elazar's Challenge

Rabbi Elazar disagrees. Even Rabban Gamliel, who validates the woman herself, would concede that her daughter born from this union is disqualified. The suspicion that she might be a *chalala* — or carry some other form of disqualification relevant to *kehunah* — is sufficient to render the child's status problematic.

### Chezakat Kashrut

Rava articulates the underlying rationale for Rabbi Elazar's distinction. *Bishlama hi it lah chezakah de-kashrut* — it is understandable that the woman herself is protected, because she possessed an established presumption of valid status before this event ever occurred. *Bittah leit lah chezakah de-kashrut* — the daughter, however, never had any such presumption. She may have been conceived in a forbidden union from the very outset, and in the absence of a prior *chezakah* to fall back on, the doubt attaches to her fully.

## Shetuki Status

### Beraitah Challenge

Rabbi Elazar then presses his challenge against Rabbi Yochanan's position by citing a *beraita*: *bameh devarim amurim be-edut ishah be-gufah* — when is a woman's testimony credited? Only with respect to her own personal status. But *edut ishah be-vittah* — when it comes to her daughter — *divrei ha-kol ha-valad shetuki*: all authorities agree that the child is a *shetuki*. The word derives from *shetok* — silence, or "be quiet" — conveying the idea that when the child asks who its father is, the answer is, in effect, withheld. The term denotes a recognized status of doubtful paternity, and the presumption is that such a child cannot marry a *kohen*.

### Shetuki Definition

Rabbi Yochanan, however, refuses to concede the point. *Mai lav shetuki u-pasul?* — does the *beraita* not mean that the child is a *shetuki* and therefore disqualified? *Lo*, he replies: *shetuki ve-kasher* — the child is a *shetuki* but is nonetheless *kasher*. The *gemara* presses back: *u-mi ika shetuki kasher?* Is there any recognized case in which a child is designated a *shetuki* and yet remains in good standing?

The answer is yes — and the proof is from Shmuel: if ten *kohanim* are standing together and one steps away, has relations with a woman, and returns to the group, the resulting child is a *shetuki*. The mother did not sleep with anyone of disqualifying status — she is a single woman, the father was undoubtedly a *kohen* — and so the child's personal status is entirely *kasher*. There is simply no way to establish paternity. Why then is the child called a *shetuki*?

The *gemara* first considers whether the term means the child is silenced from the father's estate — i.e., cannot claim inheritance from any of the ten *kohanim* should one die. But this is *pshita*, self-evident: since paternity is entirely unknown, of course no inheritance claim can be established. That cannot be the *chiddush*.

The operative meaning, the *gemara* concludes, is *ela she-mashtikin oto mi-din kehunah* — the child is silenced from the rights of *kehunah*. The verse states: *ve-hayta lo u-le-zaro acharav brit kehunat olam* — the covenant of *kehunah* shall be for him and for his seed after him. The Talmud derives from this that only *mi she-zaro meyuchas acharav* — one whose lineage is traced and attributed to him — may serve as a *kohen*. Since this child cannot identify his father, he is barred from performing the *avodah* of *kehunah*, even though there is no question that his father was a *kohen*.

### Shetuki vs. Pasul

This distinction is critical. Rabbi Yochanan is insisting that the *shetuki* designation in the *beraita* must be understood narrowly. The child's personal status — including the question of whether a daughter born of this situation may marry a *kohen* — remains entirely valid. The only consequence of *shetuki* status, in this case, is that a male child cannot serve in the *kehunah* because his specific patrilineal identity is unverified.

The contrast between the positions is thus quite stark. At one extreme, Rabbi Yehoshua is stringent even where the woman merely went into seclusion without confirmed intercourse; even if the majority of men she might have encountered would not have disqualified her, her status — and that of the child — is suspect. Rabban Gamliel occupies the opposite pole: even in a case where we know she had intercourse, even if it occurred in a field where the majority of men are non-Jews and would therefore disqualify her, her credible claim as to the identity of the man is sufficient to permit her. And according to Rabbi Yochanan, this leniency extends not only to the woman but to the fetus — though Rabbi Elazar disputes this on the grounds that the fetus lacks its own *chezakah de-kashrut*.

## Betrothed Pair Case

### Mutual Admission

The *gemara* presents a case that falls at the top of 14a. A betrothed man and woman — *arus ve-arusato* — came before Rav Yosef. The woman was pregnant. She said: *minei hu* — it is his child. And he said: *in minai* — yes, it is mine. Both parties thus affirm the same paternity. In the region of Yehuda, it was not unheard of for betrothed couples to cohabit before the formal *nisuin*, but the situation still raised questions about the child's status. Rav Yosef, however, expressed confidence in ruling leniently, citing two grounds: first, *chada de-ha kamodeh* — the man himself admits paternity, which is the more significant concession; and second, citing the principle established by Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel — *halacha ke-Rabban Gamliel* — that we rule in accordance with Rabban Gamliel's lenient position.

### Rov Kasherim Requirement

Abaye challenges this reasoning. He asks: are you suggesting that even had the husband *not* admitted paternity, Rabban Gamliel's ruling would apply? He recalls that Shmuel, when communicating this ruling to Rav Yehuda, added a crucial qualification: *ve-at lo ta'avid uvda ad de-ika rov kisherim* — and you, in practice, should not act on this ruling unless the majority of the men she might have had relations with are *kasher* and would not disqualify her status.

The application here is important. For a single woman, very few men would disqualify her from marrying a *kohen* — only a non-Jew, a *mamzer*, a *chalal*, and the like. In a Jewish town, the great majority would be unobjectionable. But a betrothed woman is in an entirely different situation: every man other than her designated husband would disqualify her, since intercourse with any other man constitutes *zenut* in this context. *Ve-hakha rov psulim etzlah* — in this case, the majority of men are *psulim* relative to her. How, then, can one invoke Rabban Gamliel's ruling without the condition of *rov kasherim* being met?

### Halacha vs. Practice

This raises a deeper question that the *gemara* confronts directly. If we say the *halacha* follows Rabban Gamliel, why does it follow that one should not act on it in practice? If it is the *halacha*, one should rule accordingly. The *gemara* resolves this by distinguishing between *lechatchila* and *bedieved*. When Shmuel cautions against acting on the ruling in practice, he means *lechatchila* — before the fact. Where the majority of men are *psulim*, we will not proactively permit the woman to marry a *kohen*. But when we say the *halacha* is like Rabban Gamliel even in such a case, we mean *bedieved* — after the fact. If she has already married a *kohen* without having sought guidance, or the situation has already occurred, we will not require them to separate.

The practical implication is as follows. If the majority of men are *kasherim* — for instance, the woman is single and the encounter occurred in a Jewish city — we will even *lechatchila* credit her claim and allow her to marry a *kohen*. If the majority are *psulim* — as in a non-Jewish city, or as in the case of a betrothed woman where every other man disqualifies her — we will not permit the marriage *lechatchila*, but *bedieved*, once the marriage has already taken place, we will rule like Rabban Gamliel and allow them to remain together.

In the case of the betrothed couple, then, the situation is already *bedieved* — the question before Rav Yosef is what to do now that the child exists and paternity is disputed. Since this is a *bedieved* scenario, the ruling of Rabban Gamliel applies even though the majority of men would have disqualified her, and the child's status is validated — all the more so given that both parties in this case openly affirm paternity.

## Eduyos Contradiction

### Almanas Issa

The *gemara* now introduces a new challenge. Abaye poses a difficulty to Rava: is it truly the case that Rabbi Yehoshua holds that a woman is never believed regarding the identity of the man she slept with? This appears to be contradicted by a *mishnah* in Eduyos. There, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira testify on behalf of an *almanas issa* — literally, a "widow of dough" — that she is permitted to marry a *kohen*. The image of dough (*issa*) conveys a mixture of uncertain composition, indicating a lineage in which some element of doubtful status has been blended in.

Rashi explains the scenario as follows. A woman received a *get* from her husband, but it was unclear whether the *get* took effect — for instance, it was uncertain whether the document landed within her domain. The next day the husband died. She is therefore a *safek gerusha*, a *safek almana*. She then married a *kohen*. If she was indeed a *gerusha*, then by having relations with a *kohen* she became a *challala*, and the son born of that union became a *challal*. That son then married a woman. The son is a *safek challal*, his wife thereby becomes a *safek challala*, and she is now an *almanas issa* — a widow carrying an uncertain taint of *challal* status.

Rashi also outlines a scenario that constitutes a genuine *safek sfeika*. Suppose, in addition to the doubt about the *get*, the woman also remarried within three months of her first husband's death and conceived a child shortly thereafter. Now there are two independent doubts: first, was the child conceived from the second man at all, or from the first husband? And second, even if conceived from the second union, was the mother a *gerusha* or an *almana* at the time? The child would be a *challal* only if both conditions obtain.

Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira testify that such an *almanas issa* is *ksheira li-kehuna* — she may marry a *kohen*. This appears to stand in direct tension with Rabbi Yehoshua's position in the *mishnah*, where he insists that a woman's claim about who she slept with is simply not credited. Here, apparently, he rules leniently in a case of acknowledged uncertainty. How are these positions to be reconciled?

The *gemara*'s initial answer is that the cases are structurally different. In the *mishnah*, the woman is *mezanah* — she engaged willingly in an act of *zenut*.
