One cannot assume that she investigated the status of her partner before acting. *Hatam isha nises bodeket ve-nises* — there, with a woman who is about to marry, we assume she looks into the man's status before doing so. But *hacha isha mezana bodeket u-mezana* — does a woman stop to verify a man's lineage before a casual liaison? The presumption simply does not apply.

### Definite vs. Doubtful Cl…

Rava then raises a further complication. Not only does Rabbi Yehoshua seem to contradict himself — Rabban Gamliel does too. In the *mishnah* in Eduyos, following the testimony of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira, Rabban Gamliel says: *kibalnu edutchem* — I accept your testimony — *aval ma na'aseh*, but what can we do? Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai enacted that a *beit din* should not rule leniently in such cases, because while *kohanim* will heed a stringency (*shom'im lachem le-rachek*), they will not accept a leniency (*aval lo le-karev*). The *gemara* reads this as Rabban Gamliel effectively declining to rule leniently in this case — yet in the *mishnah* he is prepared to credit a woman's claim about her own doubtful status and permit her to marry a *kohen*. How is that consistent?

Rava resolves both contradictions with a single principle: *hatam bari hacha shema*. In the *mishnah*, the woman makes a definite claim — she says she knows who the man was. Rabban Gamliel accepts that *bari* claim and rules accordingly. That is a case in which someone is actually asserting knowledge, and Rabban Gamliel's willingness to credit the claim is strong enough that he is even prepared to go against prevailing practice and tell the *kohanim* to trust the ruling. But in the *almanas issa* case, nobody is making a definite claim. The doubt arose from circumstances no one directly witnessed or can speak to with certainty; the woman's status is uncertain in an objective, external sense. With no *bari* claim to anchor the leniency, Rabban Gamliel is not prepared to stand behind a ruling the *kohanim* will refuse to follow anyway.

Once this is established, the *gemara* revisits Rabbi Yehoshua's apparent contradiction. The initial answer — that we assume a married woman investigates her prospective husband's status while a woman engaged in *zenut* does not — is now supplemented. *Hatam chad sefeika* — in the *mishnah*, there is a single, direct doubt: who did this woman sleep with, and was that man *kasher*? Even if she claims to know, Rabbi Yehoshua says *lo mipi anu chayim* — we do not live by her mouth — and he disregards the claim. A single doubt is weighty, and her statement does not overcome it. *Hacha trei sefeika* — in the *almanas issa* case, however, the doubt is either twofold, or it is a doubt that has attenuated across two generations. That is objectively weaker, and Rabbi Yehoshua, who weighs the strength of the doubt on its merits rather than relying on the woman's claim, will accordingly rule leniently.

### Rabban Gamliel vs. Yehos…

The *gemara* now sets out the two positions with clarity and precision.

*Hilkach le-Rabban Gamliel alim lei bari* — for Rabban Gamliel, the woman's definite claim is everything. It is so weighty that *afilu be-chad sefeika nami machshir* — even with a single, direct doubt, and even in a case of *rov psulim*, he is prepared to rule that she is *kasher*, because she has made a definite, credible assertion. *Ve-kil lei shema* — but when there is no definite claim, even if the doubt is objectively vague and attenuated — as in the *safek sfeika* of the *almanas issa* — he will not rule leniently. Without a *bari* claim to back the ruling, Rabban Gamliel is unwilling to permit what the *kohanim* will reject.

Rabbi Yehoshua's position is the precise inverse. *Alim lei chad sefeika* — a single doubt is weighty for him, and *afilu be-bari nami posel* — even a definite claim by the woman does not move him. He ignores her testimony and looks at the objective facts. *Ve-kil lei safek sfeika* — but a double doubt, or a doubt one generation removed, is objectively thin enough that *afilu be-shema nami machshir* — even absent any claim on the woman's part, he will rule that she is *kasher*.

This is a precise and elegant distillation of the underlying *machlokes*. Rabban Gamliel's entire system is anchored in the force of a *ne'emenes* claim: when there is a *bari*, he will go far in backing her; when there is not, he will not. Rabbi Yehoshua entirely discounts her statement and simply calibrates his ruling to the objective weight of the doubt itself.

## Silence Doctrine

### Beraitah Unpacked

The *gemara* now introduces a *beraita* that provides the legal definition of *almanas issa* and, in the process, opens a sustained discussion of how silence functions as a form of status admission.

*Eizu hi almanas issa?* — What constitutes an *almanas issa*? *Kol she-ein bah lo mishum mamzerus, ve-lo mishum nesinus, ve-lo mishum avdei melachim* — any woman in whose background there is no question of *mamzerut*, no question of *nesinus* (descent from the *netinim*), and no question of slave lineage. The *avdei melachim* — servants of kings — are mentioned because figures like the servants of Shlomo, or Hordus who was himself seen in some traditions as of slave origin, wielded sufficient power that their relations with women might have occurred under duress.

Implicitly, then, the *almanas issa* is characterized specifically by the presence of a *safek challal* doubt — the one form of doubtful status that does *not* appear on this list of disqualifying concerns. But this raises an immediate question: *mai shena hanei de-oraisa, challal nami de-oraisa* — why distinguish? A *mamzer*, a *netin*, and a *challal* all derive their status ultimately from biblically prohibited unions. A *challala* — a woman who results from a *kohen* having relations with a *gerusha*, for instance — emerges from a Biblically prohibited act just as surely as a *mamzer* does. Why should the doubt about a *challal* be treated differently from the doubt about any of the others?

The answer, as the *gemara* will develop, lies not in the formal biblical category but in the social and practical dynamics of how these statuses are known and contested.

The *beraita* continues. Rabbi Meir says: *shamati kol she-ein bah echad mi-kol elu, masi'in li-khehunah* — I have heard that when none of these factors is present, the woman may be married off to a *kohen*. This seems to simply repeat what the *tanna kamma* already said, and the *gemara* notes the apparent redundancy: *hainu tanna kamma*. Similarly, what Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says in the name of Rabbi Meir — that an *almanas issa* is characterized by *kol she-nitma bah safek challal*, anyone in whom a doubtful *challal* status has been intermixed — also seems to restate the same point, since the *tanna kamma*'s list excluded everything except the *challal* question. And the final line — *makkirin Yisrael mamzeirim she-beineihem, ve-ein makkirin challalim she-beineihem*, the Jewish people know who the *mamzerim* among them are and do not know who the *challalim* are — appears not only to not add anything but to actively contradict what immediately preceded it. If we do not know who the *challalim* are, why would a *safek challal* be *less* problematic than a *safek mamzer*? It should be *more* so.

To resolve this tangle, Rabbi Yochanan introduces an entirely new consideration: *mamzer tzove'ach ve-challal shotek ika beiniyahu* — the difference between these opinions turns on a case where a man is called a *mamzer* and protests, whereas when a man is called a *challal* he remains silent. In other words, the *beraita* is not merely classifying types of doubt in the abstract; it is addressing the evidentiary weight of a person's silence when he is identified by a particular status name. The *gemara* now reinterprets the entire *beraita* in this light.

The *tanna kamma*, properly understood, is saying: an *almanas issa* is valid as long as neither she nor the man she married was in a situation where any of these names — *mamzer*, *nesin*, slave, or *challal* — was called out against him and he remained silent. The *tanna kamma* holds that any silence in the face of such a designation is an admission. He did not single out *challal* as categorically different; *challal* silence, like any other silence, counts as an admission.

### Mamzer Silence

Rabbi Meir disputes this with regard to *challal* specifically. *Aval shetuk challal, kasher* — if a man is called a *challal* and does not respond, that silence is not an admission and he remains *kasher*. Why? *Mishum de-lo ikhpat lei* — because he does not care. A *challal* is barred from serving as a *kohen* and his daughters are barred from marrying *kohanim*, but his personal ability to marry any other woman is entirely unaffected. There is no compelling urgency to protest. His silence thus carries no probative weight. The *tanna kamma*'s error, according to Rabbi Meir, is treating *challal* silence the same as silence in response to a designation that would severely curtail one's personal status.

### Chalal Silence

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, transmitting a different tradition in the name of Rabbi Meir, reverses the logic entirely. It is *challal* silence that is an admission, and *mamzer* silence that is not. Why is a man silent when called a *mamzer*? *Savar mamzer kala it lei* — he reasons: everyone knows who the *mamzerim* are. Why should I bother responding? The public record speaks for itself, and there is nothing for him to clarify. His silence therefore does not indicate concession.

But why would a man be silent when called a *challal*? *Mistayid de-lo mafkei lei mi-kahal* — he calculates: if I respond and protest, they may investigate further and establish my status definitively. Better to let it remain a doubt. Remaining in a state of *safek challal* keeps him within the communal fold in ways that confirmed *challal* status would not. His silence is therefore strategic, not indifferent, and precisely because people do not maintain lists of *challalim* the way they maintain awareness of *mamzerim*, his silence cannot be explained away by reference to public knowledge. It therefore constitutes an admission.

The statement *makkirin Yisrael mamzeirim she-beineihem ve-ein makkirin challalim she-beineihem* — which seemed to contradict the earlier leniency regarding *challal* doubt — now makes perfect sense as the foundation of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view. Because everyone knows who the *mamzerim* are, silence in the face of that accusation is meaningless. Because no one keeps track of the *challalim*, silence in the face of that designation is telling.

This is admittedly a counterintuitive position. One might have expected that if everyone knows who the *mamzerim* are, then a false accusation of *mamzerus* would provoke vigorous protest, while a *challal* accusation — which carries no devastating personal consequence — would be greeted with indifference. That is precisely the logic of the first view attributed to Rabbi Meir. The reversal offered by Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar is striking, and the *gemara* acknowledges the tension by observing that a *mamzer* who actually does protest may in some sense be drawing more attention to his status than his silence would have.

### Dispute Resolution

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction between the two *beraitot* straightforwardly. One *beraita* states: silence in response to *mamzer* is *kasher*, silence in response to *challal* is *pasul*. Another states the opposite. *La kashya* — there is no contradiction. *Ha tanna kamma aliba de-Rabbi Meir, ha Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar aliba de-Rabbi Meir* — the first *beraita* reflects the position of the *tanna kamma* citing Rabbi Meir (in which *challal* silence is not an admission), and the second *beraita* reflects the view of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in the name of Rabbi Meir (in which *challal* silence is an admission and *mamzer* silence is not). These are simply the two sides of the internal dispute within the name of Rabbi Meir, as transmitted through different tradents.

What is significant for the broader discussion is the conceptual apparatus now established: silence, in the halachic assessment of personal status, can function as a form of admission — but whether a given silence is probative depends on why a reasonable person in that position might be silent. The debate between the traditions attributed to Rabbi Meir is precisely about which psychological assumptions one applies: does a person not bother responding because the accusation is beneath notice, or does a person stay quiet for strategic reasons? That determination is what distinguishes *kasher* silence from *pasul* silence. And the reinterpretation of the entire *beraita* on *almanas issa* through this lens — mapping the three seemingly redundant statements onto the *tanna kamma*'s view, Rabbi Meir's exception, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's reversal — organizes what initially appeared to be a series of near-identical statements into a coherent three-way *machlokes*.

This maps back as well onto the broader framework of Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua. Rabban Gamliel's reliance on the woman's *bari* claim stands in structural parallel to the use of subjective statements as halachically operative; Rabbi Yehoshua's focus on the objective weight of the doubt parallels the external evidentiary analysis that the silence doctrine employs.

## Raped Girl Case

### Rov Standard

The final *mishnah* on this *daf* introduces a new scenario. Rabbi Yossi relates a case of a young woman who went to draw water from a well and was raped (*ne'ensa*). Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri rules: *im rov anshei ha-ir masi'in li-kehunah, harei zu tinasei li-kehunah* — if the majority of the men in the city are such that women who slept with them may marry a *kohen* — that is, they are Jewish, not *mamzerim*, not *chalalim*, not *netinim* — then this woman too may marry a *kohen*.

This case differs critically from the *mishnah*'s dispute in one key respect: the woman has no ability to claim knowledge of her attacker's identity. The entire mechanism of *ne'emenes* — whether Rabban Gamliel's reliance on her definite claim or Rabbi Yehoshua's dismissal of it — is simply unavailable. No one is asserting anything. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri therefore rules purely on the basis of *rov*, the halachic principle of following the majority. Since the majority of men in the city are *kasher*, we attribute the attack to a member of that majority and rule accordingly.

### Position Identification

Rava raises the question to Rav Nachman: *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri de-amar ke-man?* — whose position does Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri follow? The difficulty is as follows. If he follows Rabban Gamliel, the result should be even more expansive: Rabban Gamliel rules leniently *even* when the majority are *psulim*, provided the woman makes a definite claim. But here, with no claim at all, Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri requires a *rov kasherim*. And if he follows Rabbi Yehoshua, the result should be stricter: Rabbi Yehoshua is *machmir* even when the majority are *kasherim*, since he does not rely on the woman's claim at all, regardless of the percentages.

Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri thus seems to occupy a middle position — one that neither Rabban Gamliel nor Rabbi Yehoshua clearly maps onto. The *gemara* cites Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: *be-karonot shel Tzippori haya ma'aseh*, this case involved wagons of Tzippori, *u-ke-Rav Ami* — and the ruling was in accordance with Rav Ami's position. The full unpacking of this citation and how it resolves the question of which tannaitic position Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri represents — along with the precise conditions under which *rov* suffices and under which a definite claim is required — will be taken up at the beginning of the next *daf*.

---

---

# Ketubot 15

## Rape & Rov in Yichus

### Mishnah Setup

The Mishnah presents the case of a young girl who was raped. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri rules that if most of the people in the city are those whose intercourse with the woman would leave her *ksheira l'kehunah* — that is, they are Jewish and not *mamzeirim* or *chalalim* — then she remains *ksheira* for marriage to a *kohen*. With this ruling, the Mishnah introduces the principle of *rov* (majority) into questions of *yichus*.

### Rov & Earlier Debate

The Gemara immediately raises a difficulty. Until now, the tractate has been preoccupied with the debate between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua, a dispute centered entirely on the woman's claim and her credibility — the percentage composition of the surrounding population played no role. Rava therefore poses the question to Rav Nachman: according to whom does Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri rule? If he follows Rabban Gamliel, then Rabban Gamliel permits her even when the majority of the neighborhood consists of *psulin* — non-Jews or those otherwise disqualifying — provided she identifies the man and attests to his fitness. If he follows Rabbi Yehoshua, then even when the majority are *ksheirim*, she is *pesulah*, because Rabbi Yehoshua does not accept her unilateral claim. Tosafot works through this tension and suggests that perhaps the Gemara assumes the woman did identify her attacker; Rashi, however, reads the entire discussion as proceeding according to Rabbi Yehoshua — a reading that will become significant as the *sugya* develops.

### Caravans of Tzipori

The Gemara's answer comes in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Rav: the story in the Mishnah involved the caravans (*kronot*) of Tzippori. Rabbi Ami qualifies the Mishnah accordingly — it applies only when a group of *ksheirim* was passing through the area. Rabbi Yannai adds that if she had intercourse at the time when the caravans were passing through, she is *ksheira l'kehunah*. The Gemara then introduces a complication: if, on the other hand, one man separated from Tzippori and had intercourse with her — even though the majority of Tzippori's residents are *ksheirim* — the child is a *shtuki*, a foundling of uncertain paternal lineage, whose status is therefore suspect. The question is: why should the presence of caravans make any difference at all?

## Kavuah vs. Parush

### Caravans Always Parush

The answer arrives when Rav Dimi brings a tradition from Eretz Yisrael in the name of Zeiri citing Rabbi Chanina: we follow the majority of the city (*rov ha-ir*), not the majority of the caravan (*rov siya*). This seems to contradict what was just said — the caravan is supposed to help! The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction: *hani naydi v'hani kvi v'kaimi* — the caravan is moving, while the townspeople are fixed in place. The actual ruling is that one follows the majority of the city *combined with* the majority of the caravan. Both majorities are required simultaneously.

### Gezeirah Risk

The reason a double *rov* is necessary is rooted in a *gezeirah* — a protective decree. If one were permitted to rely solely on the majority of the caravan (which is always *parush*, separated, because the travelers are not in their home location), one might come to permit reliance on the majority of the city even in circumstances where the encounter took place in someone's home — a case of *kavuah*. Conversely, if one relied solely on the majority of the city, one might permit the case even when the woman went to the man's home rather than meeting him in the field, which transforms the situation from *parush* to *kavuah*. The requirement for both *rov ha-ir* and *rov siya* together prevents any such slide.

### Kol d'Parish & Kavuah

This is the occasion for the Gemara to articulate the foundational principles at stake: *kol d'kavuah k'mechtza al mechtza dami* — anything in a fixed location must be treated as a fifty-fifty doubt — and *kol d'parish me-rubah parish* — anything that has separated from a group is judged by the majority. These principles are formally strange; they resist simple probabilistic logic. The intuition behind *kavuah*, however imperfect, seems to be that when one confronts a bounded, fixed set of objects — among which one is definitively problematic — and asks about the identity of a particular member of that set, one cannot simply ignore the definite presence of the problematic element. One is forced to acknowledge a genuine fifty-fifty doubt, as opposed to the case of *parush*, where one approaches an object of unknown provenance and asks what the majority would indicate about its identity.

### Meat Analogy

The classic paradigm is the case of meat. If one finds a piece of meat lying in the street and wishes to know its status, and in the city there are nine *kosher* butchers and one non-*kosher* butcher, one follows the majority: the meat is *kosher*. The meat has *parish* — it has separated from its source — and the inquiry is about its status, not about which fixed location it came from. However, if one returns home and finds meat there without remembering where it was purchased, the question becomes: which store did I enter? Those stores are fixed in their locations. The inquiry is now directed at a fixed set of objects, and therefore the ruling is *safek asur* — a doubtful prohibition — even though nine out of ten stores are *kosher*. That is *kavuah*: *kol d'kavuah k'mechtza al mechtza dami*.

### Rape Case Application

Applying these principles to the rape case: if the man left Tzippori and encountered the woman in the field, he is *parush* — he has separated from his fixed location — and we therefore follow *rov*, which in Tzippori is *ksheirim*. But if the woman went to the man's home, that is *kavuah*: she is asking, in effect, which of these fixed domiciles did I enter? In that case, even a ninety-percent majority cannot help her; we treat it as fifty-fifty. The caravan is always *parush* by definition, because travelers are never in their fixed home location. The genius of requiring both *rov ha-ir* and *rov siya* together is that the caravan component guarantees a *parush* framework, preventing any confusion with a *kavuah* scenario. In principle, a single *rov* of the city would suffice when the encounter is genuinely *parush*, but because the circumstances can blur — sometimes she comes to him, sometimes he comes to her — the Rabbis required the additional safeguard of the passing caravan, ensuring the case always carries the character of *parush*. This is the *gezeirah*: insist on both majorities so no one mistakenly permits a *kavuah* case.

## Kol D'Kavuah Principle

### Nine Stores Case

The Gemara now turns to examine the principle of *kol d'kavuah k'mechtza al mechtza* more rigorously. It opens with the classic *baraita*: nine stores all sell *shechutah* (properly slaughtered meat) and one sells *neveilah* (non-slaughtered meat). One purchased from one of the stores but cannot remember which. The ruling is *safek asur* — forbidden, because the doubt is framed around which store was entered, and the stores are fixed (*kavuah*). If, on the other hand, meat is found in the street, one follows *rov* — the question is about the meat's status, not the store's identity, and so it is *parush*.

This paradigm, the Gemara notes, only demonstrates the principle operating *le-chumra* — to generate stringency. Even though nine out of ten stores are *kosher*, if the doubt is *kavuah*, we treat it as fifty-fifty and forbid. But the formulation cited earlier in the name of Rabbi Zeira was *bein le-kula bein le-chumra* — the principle of *kol d'kavuah k'mechtza al mechtza* applies whether toward leniency or stringency. Where does Rabbi Zeira get this? The nine-stores case only shows stringency.

### Single vs. Double Rov

The question that drives the entire inquiry is whether the meat case — the classic paradigm of *parush* — requires a single *rov* or a double *rov*. The Gemara suggests: perhaps we should reconstruct the meat case as involving a double *rov*, on the grounds that the gates of the city were open, meaning meat might have arrived from travelers passing through, just as in the caravan case. But Rabbi Zeira explicitly ruled that even when the gates of the city are locked — guaranteeing the meat came from one of the city's stores and nowhere else — one still follows *rov*. The meat case, therefore, operates on a single *rov*. This stands in contrast to the rape case, where a double *rov* was required.

### Yichus Stringency

The Gemara resolves the disparity with a single phrase: *ma'alah asu be-yuchsin* — the Rabbis enacted an extra stringency in matters of *yichus*, fitness for marriage to a *kohen*. Under ordinary *halakhic* principles, when the situation is one of *parush*, a single *rov* suffices. In the domain of *yichus*, however, the Rabbis demanded the additional layer of a second *rov*. This accounts for why the rape case requires both *rov ha-ir* and *rov siya*, while the meat case does not. The normal rules of *rov* — *kol d'parish me-rubah parish* — would have resolved even the rape case with a single majority, but the elevated standard of *yichus* necessitates more.

### Rodents/Frog Case

Returning to Rabbi Zeira's claim that *kol d'kavuah k'mechtza al mechtza* applies even *le-kula*, the Gemara works through the candidates. The nine-stores case shows stringency: *kavuah* overrides a nine-to-one majority in the direction of leniency. The case of nine frogs and one *sheretz* (a dead rodent that conveys *tumah*, while frogs do not), where one touches one of the ten without knowing which, is also *le-chumra*: even though nine of the ten are harmless, the doubt is *kavuah* and the ruling is *safek tamei*. Neither case demonstrates leniency.

The Gemara then cites a *Tosefta* in Taharot with the reverse configuration: nine dead *sheratzim* and one frog. One touches one of the ten without knowing which. Now ninety percent of the set conveys *tumah*. Under ordinary probability, one would expect a ruling of *vadai tamei* — certain impurity. Yet because the doubt is *kavuah*, the principle *kol d'kavuah k'mechtza al mechtza* converts it into a fifty-fifty *safek*. And once it is a *safek*, the general rule of *safek tumah bi-reshut ha-rabbim tahor* applies: a doubt of *tumah* arising in a public domain leaves one *tahor*. Here, then, is the *le-kula* application — the *kavuah* principle generates leniency even when the majority would point toward impurity.

### Reshus Ha-Yachid/Rabbim

The ruling that *safek tumah bi-reshut ha-yachid tamei* and *safek tumah bi-reshut ha-rabbim tahor* is itself one of the striking features of this *sugya*. The distinction between private and public domain for doubts of *tumah* is not intuitively obvious, and the Gemara acknowledges it by tracing the rule to its source: the Torah describes a *sotah* — a woman suspected of infidelity — with the language *ve-hi nitma'ah*, she became *temeiah*. The moment of suspected *tumah* for a *sotah* is her act of seclusion with the man, which occurs in a private space. From this the rule is derived: a doubt of *tumah* that arises in a private domain (analogous to the secluded space of the *sotah*) is treated as *tamei*; a doubt arising in a public domain is treated as *tahor*. This framework then interacts with *kol d'kavuah k'mechtza al mechtza*: by converting a ninety-percent likelihood into a fifty-fifty *safek*, *kavuah* places the case within the category of *safek*, which then triggers the *reshut ha-rabbim / reshut ha-yachid* distinction.

### Biblical Source

The Gemara then asks for a biblical source for *kol d'kavuah k'mechtza al mechtza* as a Torah-level principle. The verse adduced is from the laws of murder: *ve-arav lo ve-kam alav* — he lay in wait for him and rose against him. This phrase teaches, according to Rabbi Shimon in Sanhedrin, that criminal liability for murder requires that one kill the specific individual one intended to kill. If one aimed at Reuven and killed Shimon, Rabbi Shimon holds this is *shogeg*, not *meizid*. The Rabbis disagree: intention to kill Reuven and killing Shimon is still murder. But what does the phrase *ve-arav lo* exclude, according to the Rabbis? The school of Rabbi Yannai answers: it excludes one who throws a stone into a group (*lego*) — that is, fires randomly into a crowd.

The Gemara works through the case. If the group consists of nine non-Jews and one Jew and one shoots randomly, one is obviously not liable — the majority are non-Jews, and even at fifty-fifty, the principle of *safek nefashot le-hakel* (leniency in capital matters) would apply. The novel case, the *chiddush*, is nine Jews and one non-Jew. One might think that shooting into such a group constitutes an act directed against a Jew, and that whoever was killed — even if it turned out to be the non-Jew — should generate liability on the analogy of intending to kill Reuven and killing Shimon. The Torah excludes this: the non-Jew is fixed within the group (*kavuah*), and *kol d'kavuah k'mechtza al mechtza dami* — the act is therefore treated as fifty-fifty, not as definitively aimed at a Jew. The shooter is exempt. This is the biblical derivation of the principle.

## Mishnah Reconciliation

### Horat Sha'ah View

Having established the principle of *kol d'kavuah k'mechtza al mechtza* and its implications for *yichus*, the Gemara now returns to the Mishnah. Two *amoraim* take different positions. Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi in the name of Rav rules *le-halakha* in accordance with the Mishnah — one does follow *rov* in the rape case. Rav Chanan bar Rava, by contrast, says *hora'at sha'ah hayta* — that ruling was a special circumstance, not a normative *halakhic* precedent.

### Yirmiya's Challenge

Rabbi Yirmiya challenges the first position. If Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi rules in accordance with the Mishnah, he is saying that for *yichus* a single *rov* suffices. But the entire preceding *sugya* has been premised on the assumption that *yichus* demands a double *rov*. How can one rely on a single *rov* for something as consequential as permitting a woman to marry a *kohen*?

### Foundling Infant Case

To sharpen the point, Rabbi Yirmiya cites the Mishnah at the top of 15b: if a foundling infant (*tinok mushlach*) is discovered and the majority of the city's residents are non-Jewish, the infant is presumed non-Jewish; if the majority are Jewish, the infant is presumed Jewish; and if the population is evenly split, the infant is still presumed Jewish. Rav qualifies this ruling: the presumption of Jewish status operates only *le-hachyoto* — in order to fulfill our obligation to sustain and care for him (*ve-chai achicha imach*) — but not for purposes of *yichus*. For *yichus*, even a majority of Jews in the city is insufficient. This shows that the Gemara is consistent: *yichus* demands more than a single *rov*, and therefore one cannot rule like the Mishnah as if a single *rov* were enough.

### Resolution

The Gemara resolves the tension by noting: *ishtamitei'eihu* — whoever was ruling in accordance with the Mishnah had simply forgotten the tradition of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, that the Mishnah's case specifically involved the caravans of Tzippori — a double *rov* situation. Once reminded, the apparent contradiction dissolves.

The Gemara then addresses a further difficulty: according to Rav Chanan bar Rava, who says *hora'at sha'ah hayta*, what is the meaning of calling it a special circumstance if in fact the case involved a double *rov*? Should a double *rov* not suffice as a matter of normal *halakha*? The Gemara's answer is clean: *man d'matni ha lo matni ha* — the two traditions are not held by the same authority. The one who says the Mishnah is ruled *le-halakha* because it was a double *rov* case (the caravans of Tzippori) would not say it was *hora'at sha'ah*. The one who says it was *hora'at sha'ah* holds that it was only a single *rov* — and precisely because it was only a single *rov*, it cannot serve as a normative precedent for *yichus*. Either way, the conclusion is the same: do not draw from this Mishnah the inference that a single *rov* suffices for *yichus*. Whether the case was ruled permissibly because of a double *rov*, or whether the ruling was an unrepeatable special circumstance, the general principle stands — *yichus* demands a double *rov*.

## Foundling Infant

### Mishnah Ruling

The Gemara now turns in full to the *gufah* — the body of the Mishnah about the foundling infant. If the majority of the city's residents are non-Jewish, the infant is treated as a non-Jew. If the majority are Jewish, the infant is treated as a Jew. If the population is evenly divided, the infant is treated as a Jew.

### Rav's Limits

Rav qualifies the Mishnah: *lo shanu ela le-hachyoto* — the assumption of Jewish status operates only for purposes of sustaining the infant's life, fulfilling the obligation of *ve-chai achicha imach*. For *yichus* — whether this child may marry a *kohen*, whether there is concern for *mamzerut* — a single *rov* is not enough. The Mishnah's ruling does not extend to genealogical status determinations.

### Shmuel & Pikuach Nefesh

Shmuel goes further in a different direction: *le-fake'ach alav et ha-gal* — the basis for treating the infant as Jewish is not merely the general obligation of *hachyasah* but the imperative of *pikuach nefesh*, saving life on *Shabbat*. Shmuel's broader principle, transmitted by Rav Yosef in the name of Rav Yehuda, is this: *ein holchin be-pikuach nefesh achar ha-rov* — when it comes to saving a life, we do not follow majority reasoning. Even if there is only a small likelihood that the person is Jewish, one violates *Shabbat* to save them. Shmuel's qualification therefore applies not to the case where the majority is Jewish, but to the opening case of the Mishnah — where the majority is non-Jewish. Even there, *Shmuel* says, we do not withhold life-saving on *Shabbat*.

This is a striking position. The Gemara's implication is that even if for years one has treated this individual as a non-Jew for every other purpose — using him as a *Shabbat goy*, feeding him *treifot* — the original uncertainty of his birth is never fully extinguished. When the building collapses and he may be underneath, we remember that his parentage was never conclusively established, and we violate *Shabbat* to save him.

### Long-term Doubt

This has a counterintuitive quality that the Gemara itself highlights. Normally, once a *halakhic* status has been determined and acted upon, subsequent doubts do not revive the old uncertainty. The *safek* does not survive across generations of rulings. Yet in this case, the Gemara is prepared to say: even after twenty years of treating this person as a non-Jew in every practical sense, we remember for the purposes of *pikuach nefesh* that his identity was never resolved. The *safek* of his birth remains live — but only for that one purpose. This is precisely Shmuel's position: when the majority is non-Jewish and we have treated the infant accordingly, we have nonetheless never truly closed the file on his Jewish identity, and that open file obligates us to violate *Shabbat* on his behalf.

### Dinei Mamonot

Rav Papa then enumerates the practical applications of these distinctions. When the majority of the city is non-Jewish and the infant is presumed non-Jewish: *le-ha'achilo neveilot* — one may feed him non-*kosher* meat, use him as a *Shabbat goy*, and treat him in every active sense as a non-Jew. When the majority is Jewish and the infant is presumed Jewish: *le-hachazir lo aveidah* — one must return lost objects to him. The *nafka mina* between the fifty-fifty case (where one already treats him as *safek Yisrael* for *hachyasah*) and the clear majority case emerges specifically in monetary law. At fifty-fifty, the principle of *hamotzi me-chavero alav hara'aya* applies: since the claim to Jewish status has not been established by majority, one may say to him, "bring proof that you are Jewish," and in the absence of such proof, one is not obligated to return the lost object. Once there is a majority of Jews, however, no such demand is necessary.

### Ox Goring

Rav Papa's further illustration involves the laws of *nezikin*. The *halakha* assumes different rules for an ox goring depending on whether owner and victim are Jewish or non-Jewish. The Gemara works through the case: if our ox gored his ox and his status is uncertain (fifty-fifty), we can tell him, "bring proof that you are a Jew and then collect." If, however, his ox gored our ox — a *tam* (first-time gorer) — he pays *palga*, half damages, which is what he would owe under the assumption he is Jewish. But if we then demand he pay more (as we would if he were non-Jewish and therefore always liable in full), he can respond: "bring proof that I am not Jewish, and I will pay you more." The burden of proof operates symmetrically, cutting in both directions, always governed by the principle of *hamotzi me-chavero alav hara'aya*. The general rule holds throughout: we follow *rov* in all matters except *yichus*, where a double *rov* is demanded.

## Next Mishna Intro

### Marriage Status

With *hadran alach Betula Nisat* — the conclusion of the chapter — the Gemara introduces the opening Mishnah of the next *perek*. The shift is significant. The previous chapter dealt with *ta'anat betulim* — the claim regarding virginity on the wedding night. The new Mishnah addresses a different question entirely: not whether the woman was a virgin when married, but whether the marriage was a first marriage or a second marriage, a distinction that determines whether her *ketubah* is two hundred *zuz* or one hundred. Suppose the couple is divorcing or the woman is widowed twenty years after the wedding, and neither party has preserved the original *ketubah*. She claims it was a first marriage (two hundred); he claims she was already a widow at the time of marriage (one hundred). How is this resolved?

### First Marriage Signs

The Mishnah identifies the evidentiary markers of a first wedding. If there are witnesses that she went out *be-hinuma* — in a wedding carriage — and that her head was uncovered (*rosho parua*), with her hair flowing down on her shoulders as Rashi describes, these are recognized signs that it was a first marriage. When such evidence exists, her *ketubah* is two hundred.

### Parched Grain Sign

Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka adds a further sign: *af chiluk kalyot raya* — even the distribution of roasted or parched grain to the guests is sufficient evidence of a first wedding. This was a custom specific to first marriages, analogous perhaps to other celebratory practices that distinguish the first wedding from subsequent ones.

### Peh She'asar

The Mishnah concludes with the ruling of Rabbi Yehoshua — presumably the same Rabbi Yehoshua from the previous *perek*, who consistently required external corroboration and refused to accept unilateral claims. Here, however, Rabbi Yehoshua concedes. The principle he invokes is *peh she'asar hu peh she'hitir* — the same mouth that created the prohibition is the mouth that permits it. The illustration is from monetary law: if one says to another, "this field was your father's and I purchased it from him," he is believed, because without his own statement we would have had no grounds to question his title to the field. The very mouth that introduced the claim of the other's father's ownership is the mouth that asserts the subsequent purchase — and therefore that mouth is trusted. This is the limiting principle: Rabbi Yehoshua does not believe a woman who makes a claim *stam* to extract money. But when the claimant's own statement is what generates the doubt in the first place, the same statement can resolve it. If witnesses establish that the field originally belonged to the father, however, then the man who admits ownership and claims to have purchased it is no longer in a *peh she'asar peh she'hitir* position — external evidence has created the doubt, and he is not believed. The Gemara will explore in the next session how *peh she'asar peh she'hitir* applies to the woman's claim in this new Mishnah.

---

---

# Ketubot 16

## First/Second Wedding

### Mishnah Overview

The second *perek* opens with a *mishnah* describing a dispute that arises not over the woman's physical state on the wedding night, but over the nature of the wedding itself — decades later, when she is being divorced and there is no *ketubah* to produce. The debate is not "why wasn't she a virgin?" but rather "was this a first or second wedding?" The *gemara* teaches that in such a case, the woman requires witnesses who can testify to the indicators of a first wedding: that she left her father's home with a full wedding procession, that roasted grain was distributed, that three hundred guests attended, or similar markers of a *nisu'in besulah*. Without those indicators, she would not be believed, because the operative principle is *ha-motzi mei-chaveiro alav ha-re'ayah* — the burden of proof rests on the one seeking to extract payment.

The *gemara* opens on 16a by asking: since witnesses are required, does this mean the *mishnah* does not follow Rabban Gamliel? After all, Rabban Gamliel consistently rules that the woman is believed. The *gemara* responds: *afillu teima Rabban Gamliel* — one can say even this *mishnah* follows Rabban Gamliel.

### Bari v'Bari Analysis

The *gemara* distinguishes the case of the first *perek* from this one. In the earlier cases, the dispute was *bari v'shema* — she makes a definite claim and he responds only with uncertainty. Here, both parties make definite claims: she says with certainty that it was a first wedding, and he says with equal certainty that it was a second. This is *bari u'bari* — two equally firm competing claims — and that is a qualitatively different situation. The principle of *ha-motzi mei-chaveiro alav ha-re'ayah* applies with full force.

### Rabban Gamliel Concedes

The *gemara* proceeds to establish that Rabban Gamliel concedes this case. The logical structure of the *mishnah* supports this: the *mishnah* closes with the statement *u'modeh Rabbi Yehoshua* — Rabbi Yehoshua concedes a certain case. The *gemara* argues that this concession only makes sense if the earlier portion of the *mishnah* represents Rabban Gamliel's concession in the *bari u'bari* scenario. If the entire *mishnah* were authored from Rabbi Yehoshua's perspective, then to whom is Rabbi Yehoshua conceding? The structure implies a mutual yielding: Rabban Gamliel concedes that in a *bari u'bari* dispute she does not win, and Rabbi Yehoshua in turn concedes a different point — the case of *ha-peh she'asar hu ha-peh she'hitir*.

### Rov Nashim Betulot

One might ask: even in a *bari u'bari* scenario, why not simply apply *rov nashim betulot nisos* — the statistical majority that most women marry for the first time? Since most weddings are first weddings, her claim is probabilistically more likely to be true. The *gemara* acknowledges this consideration and notes that this is precisely what might lead one to think Rabban Gamliel would still rule in her favor even in a *bari u'bari* case, treating her *bari* as somewhat stronger by virtue of the *rov*. The *gemara* will return to the question of *holchin b'mammon achar ha-rov* — whether a statistical majority is sufficient to extract money from someone — but signals here that this is not sufficient. A definite competing claim cannot simply be overridden by probability alone.

---

## Migo vs. Peh She'Asar

### R. Yehoshua Concedes

The *gemara* now pivots. It explains that Rabbi Yehoshua's concession — *u'modeh Rabbi Yehoshua* — need not be read as a response to a concession by Rabban Gamliel in the current *mishnah* at all. Rather, *amigo ka'i v'pirka kamma ka'i*: Rabbi Yehoshua is going back to a *migo* that was raised in the first *perek*. In that earlier *perek*, Rabban Gamliel argued that the woman should be believed, at least in part because she had a *migo* — a more advantageous claim she could have made but did not. Rabbi Yehoshua rejected that *migo*. Now, in this *mishnah*, Rabbi Yehoshua declares that while he rejected that *migo*, he will concede a case that is *stronger* than a *migo* — namely, *ha-peh she'asar hu ha-peh she'hitir*.

The case in question is the closing clause of the *mishnah*, where a man says: "This field that I have been occupying was originally your father's — and I bought it from him." He is the one who introduces the entire scenario. The other party had no idea a claim was even forthcoming. Rabbi Yehoshua concedes that in such a case the man is believed. Rabbi Yehoshua is thus not conceding to anything Rabban Gamliel said in this *mishnah*; he is drawing a contrast with his own earlier position rejecting *migo*.

### Four Migo Cases

To understand exactly what *migo* Rabbi Yehoshua rejected, the *gemara* works backward through all the *mishnayot* of the first *perek*, asking in each case whether there was indeed a *migo* that Rabban Gamliel relied upon.

The first case reviewed is *hi she'muberet* — she is visibly pregnant, and she identifies the father as a *kohen* of unimpeachable lineage. The *gemara* asks: what *migo* does she have? *Harei kreisa bein shineha* — her pregnancy is manifest; everyone already knows she had relations with some man. She is already making the best claim she could. There is no *migo* here at all.

The second case is *hi m'daberet im echad* — she was seen in conversation (or in seclusion) with a man, and she identifies him as a *kohen*. The *gemara* notes that this case depends on how one reads the language. According to Zeiri, who understands *m'daberet* as referring to *nistera* — seclusion — there is indeed a *migo*: she could have denied that any relations occurred (*migo d'i ba'i amra lo nistarti*), yet she concedes they did. That concession, under circumstances where she did not need to make it, gives her claim credibility. This is a *migo* that Rabbi Yehoshua refuses to accept. According to Rav Ashi, however, *m'daberet* means she actually had relations and that is already established — in which case there is no *migo*, and Rabbi Yehoshua's rejection of her claim is unremarkable.

The third case is *hi omeret mukat etz ani* — she claims her lack of *betulim* is due to a physical injury, and he claims she had relations. Here too the *gemara* examines whether there is a *migo*. According to Rabbi Eliezer, who rules that if she was *be'ulah* she receives nothing, a *migo* exists: she could have claimed *mukat etz tachteich* — the injury occurred after the *kiddushin* — and thereby claimed the full 200. Instead she claims the injury preceded the *kiddushin*, reducing her claim to 100. That self-reduction is a powerful *migo*. But according to Rabbi Yochanan, who rules that even a *mukat etz* from before the wedding receives 200, she is already making the maximum possible claim and there is no *migo*.

### Rape Case Migo

The fourth and earliest *mishnah* — *ha-nosei et ha'isha v'lo matza lah betulim* — is the one where the *migo* is beyond dispute. She claims she was raped after the *kiddushin*; he claims she had relations before. Here she clearly possesses a stronger claim she did not make: she could have said *mukat etz ani tachteich*, an injury after the *kiddushin*, which would have entitled her to 200 and would not have disqualified her from marrying a *kohen*. Instead she claims rape, which entitles her to 200 but *does* disqualify her from a *kohen* — *d'lo pasla nafsha mi-kehuna*. By making the more damaging claim, she shows that she is not trying to maximize her position, which is the essence of a *migo*. Rabban Gamliel believes her, and the *gemara* explains that this is because she has a *bari* claim reinforced by a *migo*. Rashi adds that even in cases where there is no *migo*, Rabban Gamliel has another basis for belief: *chezkat ha-guf* — the presumption that she has not transgressed, that she did not sleep with a man who would have rendered her unfit. So Rabban Gamliel always has her *bari* claim, sometimes plus a *migo*, and always plus a *chazaka*.

Rabbi Yehoshua's position, by contrast, is stated in its full force: even a *bari* against a *shema*, even a *bari* reinforced by a *migo*, is not sufficient for him to believe her. He responds: *behai migo d'hacha modina lach, behahu migo d'hatam peligina alach* — the *migo* in this second *perek*'s field case I concede; the *migo* back there in the first *perek* I rejected. This elegantly reviews the entire earlier debate while advancing the analysis.

### Field Example

The *gemara* now asks: *mai shena hai migo me-hai migo* — what distinguishes the *migo* that Rabbi Yehoshua accepts from the one he rejects? The *gemara's* answer is: *hacha ein shor shachut lefanecha, hatam harei shor shachut lefanecha* — here there is no slaughtered ox before you; there, there is a slaughtered ox before you.

The image requires explanation. When a woman's lack of *betulim* is established — when the sheets have been examined, or the fact is simply not in dispute — that is a concrete, undeniable datum that demands an explanation. Like a slaughtered ox lying in the road, the fact is before you and you must account for it. Under those circumstances, the choice between alternative explanations is not the same as introducing a claim out of nowhere. Even if she chooses the more self-damaging explanation, she is still operating under the constraint of having to explain observable evidence. That is what Rabbi Yehoshua does not find convincing as a *migo*.

### Rashi/Tosfos Debate

Rashi and Tosafot understand this point differently, and the difference is significant.

Rashi explains that the superiority of *ha-peh she'asar* lies in the fact that the claimant was not even being challenged. Nobody approached Reuven; nobody sued him or asked him about the field. He simply volunteers: "This field used to belong to your father — and I bought it from him." He could have remained completely silent. *Migo d'i ba'i shatik* — since he could have said nothing at all, the fact that he makes this admission is the strongest possible form of trustworthiness. When, by contrast, a woman must explain an established fact about her body, she cannot say "I'm making nothing up," because the datum is there and demands explanation.

Tosafot does not accept this framing. According to Tosafot, the field case in the *mishnah* does involve a *ta'ana* against him — the other party is indeed claiming the field. The difference, Tosafot argues, is not about whether the person is being challenged, but about whether there is concrete evidence that must be answered. In the field case, the opposing party claims the field was his father's, but there is no evidence that forces an explanation. The defendant could simply say *lo hayu devarim me'olam* — I don't know what you are talking about, I never saw your father in my life. Since he could deny everything, his *migo* is powerful: he has the option of total denial. But when the evidence is already before the court — the *shor shachut* — no such total denial is available, and the range of alternative claims is constrained to explanations, not denials. That is what Tosafot means by *shor shachut lefanecha*: there is a dead animal in front of you; you cannot claim it is alive; you can only offer competing accounts of how it died.

This debate between Rashi and Tosafot has concrete implications: according to Rashi, Rabbi Yehoshua accepts *ha-peh she'asar* only when the claimant was not being challenged at all. According to Tosafot, Rabbi Yehoshua would accept it even when challenged, provided the alternative available to the claimant was a complete denial rather than merely a different explanation of established facts.

---

## Rov Presumption

### Qol Counteracts Rov

With the structure of the debate clarified — Rabban Gamliel concedes the *bari u'bari* case, Rabbi Yehoshua concedes the *ha-peh she'asar* case — the *gemara* returns to the question left open earlier. If *rov nashim betulot nisos*, if the statistical majority of women are married for the first time, why does the absence of witnesses leave her without recourse? Why not let the *rov* itself carry her claim, at least according to Rabban Gamliel?

Ravina answers: *mishum de-ika le-meimar rov nashim betulot nisos u'mi'ut almanot, v'chol ha-nisos betula yesh lah kol* — it is true that most women's weddings are first weddings, but there is a countervailing consideration. Every first wedding generates *kol* — public knowledge, communal awareness, memory. A first wedding is announced; three hundred guests are invited; people remember. Therefore, when twenty years later no one can be found who remembers this as a first wedding, that absence of *kol* undermines the force of the *rov*. The statistical likelihood is balanced — and neutralized — by the inference that had it truly been a first wedding, people would have remembered.

### Balance of Rov/Qol

The *gemara* presses this reasoning. If every first wedding produces *kol*, then even the testimony of witnesses should be unnecessary — we would simply ask whether there is communal memory. And conversely, if the absence of *kol* is so telling, should we not distrust even witnesses who come forward, on the grounds that the absence of broad awareness is suspicious?

The *gemara* refines Ravina's statement: *rov ha-nisos betulot yesh lahen kol* — most, but not all, first weddings generate persistent *kol*. The *rov* and the expected *kol* together create a presumption, but since neither is absolute, they balance one another. The result is that without witnesses, we have neither a strong presumption for her nor conclusive evidence against her — a genuine equilibrium that leaves the burden of proof on her. When witnesses do come, they provide the concrete evidence that tips the balance. And since the concern is not about *kol* in isolation but about the interplay between statistical likelihood and communal memory, witnesses testifying to concrete acts at the wedding override the abstract inference from the absence of general awareness.

---

## Rov: Witnesses

### Witness Evidence

Having established that witnesses can overcome the absence of *kol*, the *gemara* specifies what those witnesses must testify to. The case at hand is witnesses who testify that she went out in *behinuma* — the bedecked wedding procession indicative of a first marriage. This is the kind of direct, concrete testimony about a specific act that constitutes genuine evidence rather than an inference from probability or the presence or absence of communal memory.

---

## Receipts/Shover

### Double Collection Risk

With witnesses established as sufficient to allow collection, a new problem emerges. If she collects her *ketubah* on the basis of witnesses in one *beit din*, what prevents her from going to another *beit din* in another city — where nothing is known of the first proceeding — producing a different set of witnesses from the same wedding, and collecting a second time? A first wedding would have had many guests; there is no shortage of potential witnesses. The *gemara* articulates this concern clearly: *dilma mafka edim be-hai bei dina ve-gavya, ve-hadar mafka le-kesuvatah be-hai bei dina ve-gavya* — perhaps she will produce witnesses in one court and collect, then produce her *ketubah* (or more witnesses) in another court and collect again. If the husband has no protection against this, the system is exposed to abuse.

### Shovar Solution

Rabbi Abba's response is direct: *zos omeres kotvin shovar* — this case teaches that we write a receipt. The husband, having paid out the *ketubah*, holds a *shovar* — a written receipt — that protects him against a subsequent claim. The conceptual challenge underlying this is significant. The normal principle in financial law is that a creditor holds the document, and once a debt is paid, it is the creditor's responsibility to return or destroy the document. Demanding that the debtor hold a receipt forever is a burden. One view in the Talmud elsewhere resolves this by simply refusing to allow collection without producing the original document: if you have lost your *shtar*, you cannot collect, regardless of whether you can prove the debt. Under that view, there is no need for receipts — but the cost falls entirely on the creditor who has lost documentation.

### Rav Pappa Position

Rav Pappa takes a more nuanced position. He does not simply accept the conclusion that receipts are written. Rather, he argues: *bi-makom she'ein kotvin ketubah askinan* — the entire discussion concerns a place where *ketubot* are not normally written at all. The *ketubah* obligation derives from rabbinic enactment and does not require a written document; some communities relied entirely on witnesses without producing a written *shtar*. In such a place, there is no document to return or destroy, so a system of receipts is necessary. But in a place where *ketubot* are normally written, Rav Pappa maintains that no receipts are written: the responsibility lies with the document, and if the document cannot be produced, collection cannot proceed.

This position has a stark implication. If a woman loses her *ketubah*, or if it is destroyed, in a community where *ketubot* are written — according to Rav Pappa she cannot collect at all, unless she can prove the document was definitively destroyed. The inability to produce the document is her problem, not the court's, and the court will not fashion an alternative mechanism.

### Baraita Reinterpretation

The *gemara* notes that this same debate between Rabbi Abba and Rav Pappa appears not only in connection with the *mishnah* but also in connection with a *baraita*, and the *baraita* version is more explicit and therefore more revealing.

The *baraita* lists three scenarios: *avda kesuvatah* — she lost her *ketubah*; *hitmina kesuvatah* — she secreted it away; *nisrefa kesuvatah* — it was burned. In all three cases, the *baraita* says, she may produce witnesses to the wedding ceremonies — dancing before her, *kos shel besora*, the *mappa shel betulim* — and collect. The *baraita* then concludes: *kesuvatah masayim*, she collects 200.

Since the *baraita* clearly began with a case where a *ketubah* existed — it was lost, hidden, or burned — and yet allows collection on the basis of witnesses, this appears to be direct evidence that even in a place where *ketubot* are written, there is a mechanism for collecting without the document, which supports Rabbi Abba's position that receipts are written.

The *gemara* presses Rav Pappa: how can you maintain your position given that the *baraita* explicitly says the *ketubah* was lost and she can still collect? Rav Pappa responds with a forced but internally consistent reading. *Avda*, he says, means she claims it was lost — but claiming a loss is treated like hiding it: *ki hitmina bifneinu dami*. If she says "I lost it," the court suspects she is hiding it somewhere to use later. Therefore, Rav Pappa reads the *baraita* as a dialogue: when she says *avda*, we say *hitmina* — we suspect concealment — and we do not let her collect. The only case where she may collect is *nisrefa* — the *ketubah* was burned and we have evidence of the destruction.

Under this reading, the three terms in the *baraita* are not three parallel cases each permitting collection. Rather, *avda* is the opening claim, *hitmina* is the court's response expressing suspicion, and only *nisrefa* is the scenario where collection is actually permitted. This is a significant *chiddush* to extract from a *baraita* whose plain meaning seems to permit collection in all three cases.

### Final Shovar Rule

The *gemara* then turns to the situation we have been circling: even where witnesses to the wedding can be produced, the double-collection risk remains. The *gemara* closes this discussion with a clear principle: *bi-makom d'lo efshar vadai kasvinan shovar* — where there is no alternative, a *shovar* is certainly written. This is the position that I had previewed earlier in the discussion, and the *gemara* arrives at it here as a *svara* that even Rav Pappa must acknowledge.

The practical upshot is as follows. According to Rav Pappa: in a community where *ketubot* are written, no receipts — the document governs, and if it cannot be produced (other than in a case of proven destruction), collection is impossible. In a community where *ketubot* are not written, or where the document was proven destroyed, there is no alternative, and a *shovar* must be written to prevent double collection. The more permissive view — that of Rabbi Abba — would write a *shovar* even in communities where *ketubot* are normally produced, thereby allowing collection whenever witnesses can testify to the nature of the wedding, with the husband protected by his receipt.

---

## Wedding Practices

### Kos Shel Besora

Having established that witnesses can testify to wedding ceremonies as proof of a first marriage, the *gemara* — and the *baraita* cited earlier — enumerates those ceremonies. The first is *kos shel besora*, the cup of good tidings. Rav Adda bar Ahava explains: *kos yayin shel terumah mevi'in lefaneha* — they would bring before her a cup filled with *terumah* wine. The symbolism, he says, is *re'uya hayta zu le'echol bi-terumah* — she is fit to eat *terumah*, meaning that if she is marrying a *kohen*, her status as a woman who has never had relations with a man forbidden to a *kohen* is being publicly affirmed.

Rav Pappa objects: *atu almana mi lo achla bi-terumah?* — Does a widow not also eat *terumah* if she marries a *kohen*? Her being a non-virgin does not disqualify her from *terumah*, so this symbolism does not track the *betulah/be'ulah* distinction at all. Rav Pappa therefore offers his own explanation: *zu reishit ke-terumah* — this cup is like *terumah* in its quality of being *reishit*, a first. Just as *terumah* is the first portion separated, this night is her first, and the cup symbolizes that *rishonah*, that primacy.

### Wine Barrel Symbolism

A *baraita* cites Rabbi Yehuda's view that they would bring before her a barrel of wine. Rav Adda bar Ahava again supplies the interpretive key: *besulah mevi'in lefaneha setumah* — for a *besulah* they would bring a sealed cask; *be'ulah mevi'in lefaneha petucha* — for a *be'ulah* they would bring an open one. The symbolism is entirely transparent, and the wine barrel — sealed or open — would serve as direct concrete evidence of the woman's status at the time of her wedding.

### Concrete vs. Absence

The *gemara* asks: why not simply use the sealed barrel as an indicator, and the *absence* of any barrel as the indicator for a *be'ulah*? Why go through the effort of displaying an open barrel?

The answer returns to the principle established earlier in the discussion of *shor shachut*: we need concrete positive evidence, not merely the absence of evidence. *Zimnin di-tafsa masayim* — sometimes she will have already seized her husband's property and will claim 200, forcing him to bear the burden under *ha-motzi mei-chaveiro alav ha-re'ayah*. If she claims *besulah havina* and the only counter-evidence is that no sealed barrel was displayed, she can readily explain: *itnusi hu di-itnusu* — they were too caught up in the celebration, or too drunk, and simply never got around to the barrel ceremony. The absence of the practice proves nothing in the face of that ready excuse. But if an open barrel was explicitly brought before her, that is a concrete act — a *shor shachut* — that cannot be explained away, and that will serve as definitive evidence of her *be'ulah* status at the time of the wedding.

---

---

# Ketubot 17

## Praise the Bride Debate

### Shammai vs. Hillel

The daf opens two lines from the bottom of 16b, in the midst of a broader discussion about the practices that served as evidence of a first wedding — relevant decades later when a couple might divorce and the amount of the *ketubah* is disputed. Against that backdrop, the Gemara transitions to one of the more famous debates between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, introduced by the formula *tanu rabbanan*: How does one dance before the *kallah*? What does one say while performing this *rikud*?

### Kallah Kemoshechi

Beit Shammai says: *kallah k'moshechi* — you praise her according to what she actually is. You tell it straight, you are honest about her. Beit Hillel says: *kallah na'ah vechasudah* — you say that she is beautiful and charming, regardless of the particulars.

### Kallah Na'ah Vechasudah

Beit Shammai challenges Beit Hillel directly: What if she was lame or blind — *chigeret o sumah*? Would you still say *kallah na'ah vechasudah*? It is worth pausing over the fact that Beit Shammai hones in specifically on physical disability as its test case. The Torah itself says *midvar sheker tirchak* — distance yourself from falsehood. How can Beit Hillel countenance saying something demonstrably untrue?

### Mikach Ra Debate

Beit Hillel responds with an analogy: If someone made a bad purchase in the marketplace and comes to you and says, "What do you think of what I bought?" — *yishabchenu be'einav o yiganenu be'einav* — do you praise it in his eyes or disparage it? The obvious answer is *yishabchenu be'einav* — of course you say something nice. From here, the *chachamim* derive a broader principle: *le'olam tehei da'ato shel adam me'urevet im habriyot* — a person should always conduct himself in a way that is amenable to other people, sensitive to what they want and need to hear.

It is worth noting what Beit Hillel is *not* saying. They are not claiming that the praise is objectively true. Rather, the rationale is rooted in human sensitivity — in attending to what a person actually wants. Rashi captures this with the phrase *la'asot le-ish ve-ish kirtzono*: to do for each person according to his desire. The bride's husband is the one marrying her; the question is what will serve him and her at this moment. This dynamic, in many ways, captures something essential about the broader Beit Shammai–Beit Hillel divide: does one orient primarily toward some objective truth that human beings must accommodate themselves to, or does one begin with human realities and work outward from there? One way to frame that debate is the question of *mah nivra techilah* — whether *shamayim* or *aretz* was created first. Beit Shammai prioritizes the objective and transcendent; Beit Hillel begins with the human and the earthly.

### Finding Nice Words

Rashi's reading of *kallah k'moshechi* is that you emphasize what is genuinely beautiful about her, what is praiseworthy — *l'fi yofyah vachashivutah m'kalsim otah*. But this immediately raises a difficulty: what if there is simply nothing nice to say?

Tosafot addresses this directly. If she has a blemish — *im yesh bah mum* — then one should be silent, *yishtaku*. As the saying goes, if you have nothing nice to say, don't say anything at all. Alternatively, Tosafot says, *yishabchu b'davar na'eh sheyesh bah* — find something nice to say: perhaps her eyes, perhaps her hands, perhaps some other quality. But Beit Hillel, on Tosafot's reading, says you praise her *l'gamri* — in general terms, *kallah na'ah vechasudah*. And therein lies the difficulty: if for everyone else you say the full formula, but for *this* bride you mention her lovely eyes — people can read between the lines. The selective praise becomes an implicit critique.

Tosafot's reading also illuminates Beit Hillel's position in a different way. *Kallah na'ah vechasudah* is to some extent a formulaic expression, and formulaic language operates differently from a literal claim. Everyone understands that it is a convention; no one hears it as a precise assessment. Furthermore, beauty is subjective — and in the eyes of her husband, she may indeed be all of that.

### Maharsha Reconciles

The Maharsha goes further and tries to tone down the apparent harshness of Beit Shammai's position. When Beit Shammai says *kallah k'moshechi*, he argues, it does not mean that each wedding requires a fresh individual assessment of the bride's qualities. Rather, it means that however this *kallah* is — whoever she is — she is beautiful for *her* husband. She is *k'moshechi* in the sense that she is exactly what he wants and needs. On this reading, Beit Shammai is also making a formulaic statement, just one that more explicitly underscores the subjective dimension: she is beautiful *as she is*, meaning in his eyes. The difference between the two schools, then, is simply that Beit Shammai calls attention to the subjective frame while Beit Hillel does not.

Tosafot makes a related point about the Beit Shammai position elsewhere in the discussion. Even Beit Shammai would not instruct one to disparage a new purchase. Everyone understands that social sensitivity requires saying something kind when someone asks your opinion. Beit Shammai's objection is narrower: one should not establish a rabbinic *takkanah* requiring a formulaic falsehood. *Ain lahem l'chachamim l'saken v'yizakku l'mar sheker* — the sages should not be institutionalizing the practice of saying something that is not true, given that the Torah says *midvar sheker tirchak*. Beit Shammai acknowledges social grace; they simply resist encoding it as law.

---

## Wedding Practices

### Lo Kchal v'lo Srak

When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he reported what they would sing before the bride in the west: *lo kchal v'lo srak v'lo pirchus v'ya'alat chen* — no eyeshadow, no rouge, no elaborate hairdo, and yet she radiates charm. The song celebrates natural, unadorned beauty — an inner grace that requires no embellishment.

### Smicha Celebration

Strikingly, the Gemara then reports that when the rabbis gave *smicha* to Rabbi Zeira, they sang this same song. They had a full celebration — singing and dancing at the ordination — and the song they chose for the *kallah* was the one they sang for the newly ordained *talmid chacham*. This is at once arresting and profound. The comparison of Torah scholarship to a bride, and of the *talmid chacham* to the beloved, runs deep in rabbinic culture. The relationship between the scholar and the Torah is, in certain registers, an intimate and even erotic one — husbands leaving their wives to go and learn, scholars described as married to the Torah. Here, the honoree of the *smicha* celebration is cast, in the song, in the role of the bride: naturally beautiful, requiring no adornment.

### Ami and Assi Songs

When *smicha* was conferred upon Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi, the song was different. The rabbis sang: *kol mindein v'kol mindein s'muchu lana* — anyone like this one and this one, we should ordain from among us. And: *lo t'samchu lana lo min sarmisin v'lo min sarmitin* — do not ordain for us from among the *sarmisin* and the *sarmitin*.

Rashi explains: the *sarmisin* are those who distort the Torah, from the root *lesares* — to twist. The *sarmitin*, Rashi says, connotes rags, something worthless. There is an alternate version: *lo min chamisin v'lo min turmisim* — not from those who deliver only a fifth of the reasoning, and not from the empty or worthless ones. The Maharsha adds a pointed observation here: that in his own day, many rabbis had fallen into precisely these failings — *ki ba-avonoteinu rabbim me-ha-rabbanim she-nichshalim be-zeh ba-dor ha-zeh* — and that the matter deserved remedy at the hands of the communal and civic leadership. Whoever unpacks the full context of that Maharsha's complaint will find it worth studying.

It is somewhat deflating, of course, to be celebrated at your *smicha* with a song that says, in essence, at least you are not a corrupt distorter of the Torah. The song for Rabbi Zeira — natural beauty, no adornment needed — is rather more flattering.

### Abbahu's Prestige

The Gemara then describes Rabbi Abbahu: when he would come from the *metivta* to the house of the Caesar, the maidservants of Caesar's household would come out to greet him and sing: *rabba de-ameih u-madbarna de-umteih botzina de-nehora baruch matyeich le-shalom* — teacher of his people, leader of his nation, candle of light, blessed be your coming in peace. Presumably he would arrive radiating something from his learning, and even the non-Jewish servants of the imperial household recognized it. The Maharsha notes this context.

What is striking throughout this passage is the persistent way in which discussions of weddings and brides fold into discussions of Torah learning and scholars. The woman as purchase, the *kallah* as beloved, and the *talmid chacham* as one who is himself like a bride — these images keep circling back on one another.

### Dancing with Hadassim

They said about Rabbi Yehuda be-Rabbi Ilai that he would take a branch of myrtle — *bad shel hadas* — and dance before the bride, *merakked lifnei ha-kallah*. And as he danced, he would sing: *kallah na'ah vechasudah*. So he enacted the practice fully — physical dancing with the *hadas*, combined with the Beit Hillel formula. This is the same Rabbi Yehuda be-Rabbi Ilai we will encounter again shortly, and his conduct here is entirely consistent with what we will find there: a person who was *mochel* on his own dignity in order to bring joy to others.

### Three-Fold Dancing

Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak would dance *a-tlat* — by threes. Rashi understood this to mean he would juggle three branches of myrtle, though the Maharsha objects on both textual and practical grounds: the Aramaic would be *bi-tlat* rather than *a-tlat* for that meaning, and in any case, myrtle branches do not make for good juggling implements. The Maharsha prefers to read it as meaning he danced with three times the vigor of anyone else — he threw himself into the *rikud* with an abandon that put everyone around him to shame.

Rabbi Zeira, watching, said: *ka-machsif lan sabba* — the elder is embarrassing us. On Rashi's reading, Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak was simply undignified, carrying on in a way unbefitting a scholar. On the Maharsha's reading, he was embarrassing the younger scholars by outpacing them entirely — they were young, and the old man was dancing three times as hard.

### Pillar of Fire

When Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak died, *afsik amuda de-nura bein dideih le-chulei alma* — a pillar of fire separated between him and all the rest of the world. And it is transmitted that a pillar of fire only appears for someone who is singular in the generation, or perhaps one of two people — *le-chad be-dara ei le-trei be-dara* — because it marks them as set apart, in a class unto themselves.

The same Rabbi Zeira who had said the elder was embarrassing them now said: *ahani leih shutita de-sabba* — it was the branch of the elder that helped him. Or, in the alternate versions: his *shtus* — his wildness — or his *shita* — his approach — that was what elevated him. The one who was *mochel* on his own *kavod* to bring *simcha* to the *chatan* was the one who merited this singular distinction. There is an unmistakable echo here of David dancing before the Ark and Michal's critique, and while the Gemara does not make that comparison explicitly, the structural parallel — dignity versus abandon in the service of something sacred — is very much present.

### Bride on Shoulders

Rav Acha would carry the *kallah* on his shoulders and dance. The rabbis asked him: are we permitted to do the same? He replied: *ei damya aleichu k'kashura l'chai* — if she is to you like a beam of wood, if there is no sexual dimension to it whatsoever, then yes, go ahead. *V'ei lo, lo* — but if it will arouse improper thoughts, then no. The ruling is entirely subjective. This opens onto a broader discussion among the *Rishonim* about which categories of male-female interaction are governed by subjective assessment and which by objective prohibition — a question with real practical implications.

---

## Bride vs. Dead

### Looking All Week

Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: *mutar le-histakel bifnei kallah kol shiva* — one is permitted to gaze admiringly at the *kallah* all seven days of the wedding celebrations. The purpose is *kedei le-chabevah al ba'alah* — to make her beloved in her husband's eyes: if everyone is looking at her admiringly, the husband will feel that she is genuinely beautiful and desirable. However, the Gemara notes: *leit hilcheta ke-vatei* — the law does not follow this ruling. That is simply asking for trouble.

### Ma'avirin Hamet

The Gemara now turns to other expressions of communal participation in the life-cycle moments of marriage and death. Just as there is *merakdin bifnei ha-kallah* — the community dancing before the bride — there is a broader principle of communal obligation at both weddings and burials. And just as there is a week of *shiva brachot* when the community participates in the joy, there is a week of *shivah* when the community participates in the mourning. These are not private affairs; they are communal experiences.

So the Gemara teaches: *ma'avirin et ha-met milifnei ha-kallah* — you move the funeral procession aside to make way for the wedding party. When the two groups converge in the street, the *kallah* has the right of way. This is a striking ruling. A reader of *Kohelet* might expect the opposite — *tov la-lekhet el beit avel milalechet el beit mishteh* — it is better to go to a house of mourning than a house of feasting. Yet the rabbis make a strikingly life-affirming ruling: attending to joy, to the next generation, to *simchat chatan ve-kallah*, takes precedence over the funeral. Both groups, in turn, yield to the king, who always has priority.

### Agrippas's Humility

The Gemara recounts that Agrippas the king stepped aside before the *kallah*, and the sages praised him for this. *Shibchu chachamim* — they commended him. But the Gemara immediately puzzles over this: if the sages praised him, does that mean it was the right thing to do?

### Royal Honor Doctrine

Rav Ashi weighs in: even according to the view that a *nasi* — a prince or governor — who waives his honor has waived it legitimately (*nasi she-machal al kvodo, kvodo machul*), a *melech* who waives his honor has *not* waived it (*melech she-machal al kvodo, ein kvodo machul*). The verse says *som tasim alecha melech* — the double language of *som tasim* indicates that the king's authority must remain perpetual and inviolable. *She-tehei emato alecha* — his awe must remain upon the people. The Maharsha adds that royal honor is also an expression of *chalak michvodo le-vasar ve-dam* — it reflects a dimension of divine kingship that cannot simply be set aside by the king's personal choice.

So how was Agrippas praised for doing something that seems halachically impermissible? The Gemara answers: *parashat derachim havai* — it was a crossroads. The two parties encountered each other at an intersection, and the king's entourage made a turn that happened to open the way for the wedding party. It was not an explicit act of stepping aside; there was no obvious *mechilah* on the king's *kavod*. The praise was real, but the mechanism was subtle enough not to constitute a formal waiver of royal dignity.

---

## Suspending Torah Study

### Mevatlin Talmud Torah

The Gemara now turns to the relationship between *talmud Torah* and the communal obligations of burial and wedding celebration. *Mevatlin Talmud Torah le-hotza'at ha-met ule-hachnasat kallah* — one sets aside Torah study for the procession of the dead and for bringing in the bride.
