This ruling reflects something deeper than a formal principle of *osek be-mitzvah patur min ha-mitzvah*. It captures something about the relationship between the scholar and the community, between the *beit midrash* and the lived realities of the people around it.

### Leaving Beit Midrash

They said about Rabbi Yehuda be-Rabbi Ilai — the same one who danced with the *hadas* — that he would leave the *beit midrash* for both occasions. This is deeply consistent with everything we know about him. He was *mochel* on his *kevod ha-Torah* to be genuinely present with people in their *simchas* and their losses. There is something powerful here. The *Yerushalmi* formulation captures the underlying principle: *kol ha-lomed she-lo al menat la-asot, mutav lo she-lo lamad* — one who studies without the intention to act would have been better off not learning at all. Torah must translate into the real world, into how one actually shows up for people.

The parallel to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai emerging from the cave is worth noting. There too the question is whether the scholar, at his elevated level of Torah, can connect to and participate in ordinary human life and joy. The image of the man running with two *hadassim* to honor *Shabbat* — that mundane, earthy expression of love for a mitzvah — is what opens Rabbi Shimon's eyes. Here, Rabbi Yehuda be-Rabbi Ilai models the same orientation from the outset.

### Enough People Condition

But the Gemara qualifies this: *bameh devarim amurim beshein imo kol tzorko* — when is Torah study suspended? Only when there are not enough people for the occasion. *Aval yesh imo kol tzorko, ein mevatlin* — if there are already enough, there is no obligation to leave the *beit midrash*. The question then becomes: what counts as enough?

### Required Numbers

*Amar Rabbi Shmuel bar Ini mishmeih de-Rav*: twelve thousand men, and six thousand *shofarot* — trumpeters or horn-blowers who would either call people to attend or simply be part of the procession. An alternate version gives thirteen thousand men, with six thousand of those blowing *shofarot*. Ulla offers a different and more visual measure: that there are enough men to form a wall from the gate of the city all the way to the cemetery.

### Natilatah Kentinatah

Rav Sheshet — and some attribute it to Rabbi Yochanan — offers the most demanding standard: *netilatah kentinatah* — the taking away of Torah is like the giving of Torah. Just as the Torah was given with 600,000 people present, so too, for the death of a *talmid chacham*, there are "enough people" only when 600,000 are present. This makes clear what had perhaps not been obvious: these enormous numbers are not about any ordinary deceased person. They are about the death of a *talmid chacham*, and the obligation is rooted in *kevod ha-Torah*, not merely *kevod ha-met*. You leave your *beit midrash* to show honor to the Torah that is being taken from the world. This shifts the calculus significantly: the *beit midrash* is not competing with *chesed* to the dead; it is itself engaged in *kevod ha-Torah*, which is why it requires a demonstration of *kevod ha-Torah* on the other side to dislodge it.

This also raises a question about the *kallah* case: there, there is no threshold tied to the stature of the *chatan* or *kallah* — one simply goes. The asymmetry is worth sitting with.

### Teachers Exception

The Gemara adds a final, remarkable qualification. *Ve-hanie milei le-man de-kari ve-tani* — these thresholds apply for someone who read Scripture and learned Mishnah but never taught. *Aval le-man de-matni, leit lei shiura* — for one who taught Torah, there is no measure; everyone must attend, and no number is sufficient to say there are already enough.

Rashi draws the implication in the other direction as well: *shemeinan de-le-man de-la kari ve-la tani* — for someone who was entirely outside the world of Torah learning, the measure is purely pragmatic. If there are enough people present to accomplish the burial, you are not obligated to leave the *beit midrash* to make the crowd larger. For an ordinary deceased person, ten people may well be enough. The gap between the thresholds is vast. This further confirms that the entire framework is not primarily about dignity for the dead, but about *kevod ha-Torah* — and only *kevod ha-Torah* is weighty enough to pull one out of the *beit midrash*.

---

## First Marriage Evide (II)

### Hinuma Practice

Returning to the evidential practices that distinguish first weddings from second, the Gemara asks: *ei yesh edim she-yatzah be-hinuma* — if there are witnesses that she went out with a *hinuma*, that establishes that it was a first wedding. But what is a *hinuma*?

### Myrtle Dome

Surhav bar Pappa in the name of Ziri says: *tanura d'asa* — literally, an oven of myrtle, understood by Rashi as a kind of dome constructed from myrtle branches, perhaps something like a canopy or archway for the bride to walk beneath.

### Veil Practice

Rabbi Yochanan says: *kviyasta d'mnamnu bah kallah* — a covering in which the *kallah* would doze off. Rashi understands this as a kind of veil covering her eyes, something that shielded her so thoroughly she could even catch a brief sleep. Both descriptions point toward practices that parallel, in one way or another, what we still recognize as the *chuppah* and the veil — two of the most ancient and enduring features of a Jewish wedding.

### Roasted Grain

Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka holds that the distribution of roasted grain is sufficient as evidence. A *Baraita* confirms that in *Yehudah*, the distribution of roasted grain was indeed the recognized sign of a first wedding.

### Oil on Rabbis

But in Babylonia? The Gemara asks: *B'Bavel mai?* Rav answers: *dardugei d'mishcha areisha d'rabbanan* — the dripping of oil on the heads of the rabbis. At a first wedding, they would go to the rabbis' table and pour oil over the heads of the scholars present. Once again, the intersection of the rabbinic world and the wedding celebration is striking.

### Oil Ritual Challenge

Rav Pappa challenged this: *mishcha d'chafifusa ka'amar mar* — are you saying they would take hair-washing oil and pour it over people's heads? Rashi suggests he was offended by the image — as though the rabbis needed a grooming treatment or something unseemly was being implied.

### Abaye's Reminder

Abaye responded pointedly. He called Rav Pappa *yatma* — orphan — which is remarkable, since it is Abaye who was himself orphaned. Whether this is ironic or whether he is speaking loosely, the force of his reply is clear: *v'lo avda lach immach dardugei mishcha areisha d'rabbanan b'sha'as ma'aseh* — did your own mother not do this at your wedding? Are you really going to take offense at a practice that was performed for you? The word *yatma* carries additional poignancy in Abaye's mouth given his own biography.

### Rabbinical Practice

The Gemara then records a concrete historical account: one of the rabbis married his son into the household of Rabbah bar Rav Ulla — or in the alternate version, Rabbah bar Rav Ulla married his son into another rabbinic family — and at the time of the wedding, *dardig mishcha areisha d'rabbanan b'sha'as ma'aseh*, oil was dripped on the heads of the rabbis. The practice is thus attested in actual rabbinic family life.

---

## First Marriage Evide (II)

### Widow Weddings

The Gemara asks: *almanusa mai* — what about a widow? If the evidential practices mark a first wedding, is there a corresponding practice that marks a second? The Gemara does not provide an affirmative answer. Rav Yosef teaches: *almanusa leisa kisnai* — for a widow, the roasted grain is not distributed. The evidence for a first wedding is thus largely defined by the presence of these practices, and for a second wedding by their absence. Tosafot notes the gap: one might have hoped for a more active marker of the second wedding, but the Gemara does not supply one.

---

## Ha-Peh She-Asar

### Field Admission Case

The Gemara now returns to the principle of *ha-peh she-asar hu ha-peh she-hitir* — the mouth that bound is the mouth that permits, also called *modeh bi-miktzat* or, in this context, *ha-peh she-asar*. The case is: a man is found on a field and says to the person who challenges him, "This field belonged to your father, and I purchased it from him." By admitting that it once belonged to the other party's father, he opens himself to that claim — but having made that admission, he is believed when he adds that he purchased it, because he could have remained silent.

### Rashi and Tosafot

There is a fundamental debate between Rashi and Tosafot about what "he could have remained silent" means. Rashi holds that the other party — the one challenging him — was entirely oblivious. He had no awareness that this person was on the field, no complaint, no suspicion. In that situation, the occupant had nothing to answer; his voluntary admission and explanation together constitute a *ha-peh she-asar*. Tosafot argues that this is too narrow and that the actual case involves a genuine challenge: the other party says, "That's my field, what are you doing there?" There is, however, no *evidence* that needs answering — it is *stam kala*, an unsubstantiated claim. The occupant could have simply said *lo hayu devarim me-olam* — it is completely false — and the challenger would have had nothing. Instead, he concedes the historical ownership and claims a purchase. That concession, volunteered when it was not required, creates the *ha-peh she-asar*. This is already more of a *chiddush*.

### Father Mentioned

One asks: why does the *Mishnah* frame the case as "I purchased it from your *father*" rather than "I purchased it from you"? On Rashi's reading, asking why the man doesn't say he bought it directly from the challenger is almost incongruous — if the challenger is oblivious, how could he have been the one who sold it? But on Tosafot's reading, the question is sharper: the challenger himself is present, claiming the field is his. Why not have the occupant say, "I bought it from you"? That would be an even stronger case of *bari u-bari* — both parties making certain claims — and yet Rabbi Yehoshua would still believe the occupant.

The Gemara explains: *mishum de-ka-ba'ei le-mitni seifa* — it is because of the need to teach the *seifa*. The end of the *Mishnah* states: if there are witnesses that the field belonged to the challenger, the occupant is not believed. And the Gemara asks — what is the *chiddush* of the *seifa*?

### Three Year Chazakah

If the occupant had three full years of uncontested residence — *achal shenei chazakah* — he should win regardless of witnesses to original ownership. If he did not have three years, of course he is not believed; that is obvious. So where is the novelty?

### Katan Property

The answer: *bishlama gabei aviv* — with the father framing, we can construct a genuine *chiddush*. The case is *mashkachat lah de-achal shtayim be-chayei ha-av ve-achat be-chayei beno* — the occupant was on the field for two years during the father's lifetime and one year during the son's. That gives him three years of residence. Yet he is not believed, because of Rav Huna's principle: *ein machzikin be-nichsei katan* — one cannot establish *chazakah* over the property of a minor.

The reason *chazakah* works at all is that three years of uncontested residence is taken as evidence that the original owner waived his claim — he saw you on his field, knew about it, and said nothing. But a minor cannot be expected to register the presence of someone on his field and formulate a protest. His silence is therefore meaningless; it creates no presumption.

### Afilu Higdil

The larger *chiddush* of Rav Huna is *afilu higdil* — even once the minor becomes an adult, the years that began during his minority do not retroactively become valid years of *chazakah*. If someone was on that field during the child's minority, and the child grows up and says nothing for another nine years, those nine years of adult silence are tainted by the original period. The occupant would need to leave and return — or obtain a *shtar* — to establish a valid *chazakah* from scratch.

### Father's Role

So the *Mishnah* needed the father precisely to give the *seifa* a meaningful *chiddush*: you have three years of residence, witnesses confirm the field once belonged to the other party, and yet you are still not believed — because two of those years were during the son's minority, and *ein machzikin be-nichsei katan afilu higdil*.

### Shelo Befanav

The Gemara then asks: could the *Mishnah* not have achieved the same *chiddush* without introducing the father, by using the scenario of *shelo befanav* — years of residence when the owner was not present? *Chazakah* requires that the owner could have protested; if he was absent, his silence is not meaningful, and the *chazakah* does not take hold. One year's absence could thus undercut an otherwise complete three-year *chazakah*.

### Judea and Galilee

The Gemara invokes the *Mishnah* in *Bava Batra*: *shalosh aratzot le-chazakah* — there are three regions with respect to *chazakah*: *Yehudah*, *Ever HaYarden*, and *ha-Galil*. If the owner was in *Yehudah* and the occupant was on his field in the *Galil* — or the reverse — it is not a valid *chazakah* until they are in the same region. The Gemara probes this: if a protest not in the owner's presence — *mecha'ah shelo befanav* — is legally effective, then news travels across regions and *chazakah* should work regardless of which region each party is in. And if such a protest is *not* effective, then even within the same region, so long as the parties are in different cities, *chazakah* should not work. What is the principled distinction that makes region matter?

### Emergency Situation

Abba bar Memel resolves this: *le'olam kasavar mecha'ah shelo befanav havya mecha'ah* — in principle, a protest not in the owner's presence is valid, and news is presumed to travel. *U-matnitin b'sha'at cheirum shanoy* — but our *Mishnah* is dealing with a time of emergency, when an edict restricts travel. In such circumstances, the normal presumption that news crosses borders does not hold.

Why specifically *Yehudah* and *Galil*? *D'stam Yehudah ve-Galil ke-sha'at cheirum damu* — because as a general rule, the border between *Yehudah* and the *Galil* functioned like a time of emergency: crossing it was difficult and politically fraught. News did not flow freely between them. The ruling thus reflects not an abstract theoretical position, but an observed social reality — that information travels within a country's borders far more reliably than it crosses political and geographic boundaries, especially when those crossings are contested or restricted.

The Gemara concludes that the *shelo befanav* scenario could in principle have served to explain the *Mishnah's seifa* — a case where *chazakah* fails despite three years of residence — but it would have been a less striking *chiddush* than the case of the father and the minor son. Hence the *Mishnah* chose the father formulation, precisely because the *chiddush* of Rav Huna — that *chazakah* begun during a minor's infancy remains invalid even after he reaches majority — is less intuitive and more genuinely novel.

---

---

# Ketubot 18

## Field vs. Loan Example

### Introduction & Overview

The daf opens by returning to a question left hanging from the previous discussion: why did Rabbi Yehoshua, when illustrating the principle of *peh she-asar hu peh she-hitir*, choose the example of a field — "this field belonged to your father, and I purchased it from him" — rather than some other example? The remainder of this section of the *gemara*, and indeed a substantial portion of the rest of this *perek*, will feel at times like a digression into the territory of Bava Metzia, exploring *to'en v'nitan*, *modeh b'miktzat*, and related principles of monetary law. But this is not a digression. The *mishnayot* that follow in this *perek* are built around the principle of *peh she-asar* as it applies across a range of cases, many of them far removed from the original *ketubot* context. *Peh she-asar* in *dinei mamonos* is precisely the subject, and the *gemara* is using the question about Rabbi Yehoshua's choice of example as a gateway into that broader discussion.

### Loan Case Doesn't Fit

The *gemara* asks: why not frame the case as a loan? Why not say that Rabbi Yehoshua's example of *peh she-asar* is a person who tells his friend, "I borrowed a hundred dollars from you and I paid it back," where no external evidence exists? That too would be a clean *peh she-asar* — the same mouth that admitted the debt also claimed repayment. The answer the *gemara* gives is that such a case would not work for the *mishnah*'s structure. The *mishnah* is structured in two halves: when the person freely offers up all the information, *peh she-asar*, he is believed; but when witnesses independently establish the first part of his claim, he is not believed regarding the second. Applied to a loan, the *seifa* would have to say: if there are witnesses that he borrowed the money, and he now claims repayment, he is not believed. But that is simply not true.

### Repayment Without Witnesses

The *gemara* has already established the principle: *ha-malveh et chaveiro b'edim eino tzarich l'poreo b'edim* — if someone lends money to another with only witnesses (as opposed to a written *shtar*), the borrower is not required to produce witnesses at the time of repayment. He may simply pay back the money, and his claim that he did so is believed. This is the established *halacha*. And if that is the case, then even where witnesses testify to the original loan, the borrower's unilateral claim of repayment remains credible. The *seifa* the *gemara* would have constructed — that witnesses to the borrowing render the repayment claim unbelievable — would therefore be halachically false. Hence, the loan scenario cannot serve as Rabbi Yehoshua's example.

### Business & Policy Impact

This *halacha* is striking from a practical standpoint. One might reasonably worry about its societal effects. If a borrower can simply claim repayment without any corroboration even when witnesses exist to the original debt, that creates a significant disincentive for lenders. On the other hand, the ruling may function as a quiet push toward writing a *shtar* for every transaction, which has its own advantages in terms of documentation and clarity. But then again, the burdens of formalizing every loan also carry costs — they make lending more cumbersome, and history has shown that anything which makes lending more difficult tends to disadvantage those who most need credit. The tension here is real, even if the *halacha* is clear.

### Audacity Presumption

The underlying logic of this ruling is a *chazakah* that will recur throughout the *gemara*: *ein adam meiz panav bifnei ba'al chovo* — no one has the audacity to look the person who did them the favor of lending money straight in the eye and brazenly deny repayment if they never actually paid. This *chazakah* is weighty enough, in the *gemara*'s view, to counteract the evidentiary force of witnesses to the original loan. The logic is reinforced by the nature of a loan itself: unlike a disputed ownership claim, a loan is by its very nature meant to be repaid. Witnesses to a loan are witnesses to a transaction whose next natural step is repayment. Testifying to the existence of the loan does not foreclose the obvious possibility that the expected repayment followed. The *chazakah* then adds that a person would not lie about that repayment to the very creditor who helped him. The *halacha* stands, and consequently, the loan example cannot fit the *mishnah*'s structure.

---

## Loan to Father, Claim by…

### Case: Half Consumed

Having explained why the loan example fails, the *gemara* presses further: why not use a different case? Specifically, why not have Rabbi Yehoshua's example be a person who says to a friend, *maneh l'avicha b'yadi v'he'achalti pras* — "a hundred dollars of your father's is in my hands, and I consumed half of it"? In other words, the father lent me a hundred dollars, I still owe fifty, and I am now voluntarily disclosing this to you, the son. This too appears to be a clean *peh she-asar* scenario: the same mouth that disclosed the debt also limits it. And structurally, it seems like it could parallel the *mishnah*'s two-part structure — free disclosure leads to belief, while witnesses to the borrowing would lead to a different result.

### Modeh B'Miktzat Concept

Before analyzing why this case cannot serve as Rabbi Yehoshua's example, the *gemara* introduces a necessary background concept: *modeh b'miktzat*. If someone is confronted with a claim — "you owe me a hundred dollars" — and responds, "I only owe you fifty," that partial admission creates a legal obligation to take an oath regarding the disputed remainder. This is a Torah-level rule. And the obvious question, already anticipated by the *gemara*, is why this person does not simply have a *miggo* — a logical argument from a stronger position. If he were truly lying, he could have denied the entire claim. By admitting half, he is actually weakening his own position. So why should his partial concession not be treated as fully credible on the strength of the *miggo* that he could have denied everything?

The answer, as the *gemara* will spell out through *Rabba*'s principle, is precisely that he does not have a *miggo*, because the *chazakah* of *ein adam meiz panav bifnei ba'al chovo* forecloses the option he supposedly "could have" taken. He could not, psychologically and socially speaking, have denied everything to the very person who lent him the money. And therefore the "stronger position" from which the *miggo* would be drawn — complete denial — was never actually available to him. Since he could not have denied the whole debt, partially admitting it earns him no evidentiary credit, and he must swear about the remainder.

Now, what happens when there is no formal *ta'anah* — no active claim being pressed? What if the son has made no demand, and the borrower simply volunteers the information? Is this person still a *modeh b'miktzat* with an obligation to swear? Or is the absence of a formal claim dispositive?

### Rabbis: Meshiv Aveida

The *gemara* explains that this case cannot be used as Rabbi Yehoshua's example because it does not work according to either of the two positions among the *tana'im*. According to the *Chachamim*, the borrower in this scenario is always treated as a *meshiv aveida* — someone who returns a lost object. The logic, as *Tosafot* frames it, is essentially a *miggo*: when dealing with the son rather than the father himself, the borrower is fully prepared to deny the entire debt. The son does not know his father's business dealings; there would be no social or psychological pressure preventing a complete denial. Therefore, any admission at all is entirely voluntary, an act of pure good faith, analogous to returning a found wallet. Just as we cannot demand an oath from someone who returns a found object — doing so would destroy the incentive to ever return anything — so too we do not impose an oath here.

This logic holds even when witnesses independently establish the first part — that the father made the loan. After all, we have already established that even with witnesses to a loan, the borrower is believed to claim repayment. If even full repayment could be claimed credibly in the face of witnesses, then a partial repayment claim to the son, where the borrower could have denied everything, is all the more clearly a *meshiv aveida*. The *Chachamim* therefore hold that in all variants of this case — whether or not there are witnesses to the original loan — the borrower is exempt from an oath. This means the *mishnah*'s structure cannot be reproduced: there is no scenario where witnesses to the first half of the claim render the second half unbelievable.

### R. Eliezer: Oath Required

At the other extreme, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that even when the borrower volunteers the information entirely on his own, he is still obligated to take an oath. This emerges from a *beraita*: *pe'amim she'adam nishba al ta'anat atzmo* — sometimes a person takes an oath even on a claim that he himself raised, not in response to any demand from the other party. The example given is precisely this case: if someone says "I borrowed a hundred dollars from your father and consumed half," he must take an oath. The *Chachamim* respond that he is no different from a *meshiv aveida* and is exempt.

So at first glance, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position seems to be that *peh she-asar* does not even work here to produce an exemption. The *gemara* questions this: does Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov not accept the *meshiv aveida* principle at all? The *gemara* introduces *Rav*'s answer: the *beraita*'s language of *ta'anat atzmo* is not to be taken literally. There is in fact a *ta'anah* — a claim — being pressed. It is just that the one pressing it appears to be a *katan*, a minor, whose claim would ordinarily carry no legal weight, and so it is described as if no claim were being made at all.

### Son's Claim Weight Debate

The *gemara* immediately questions this: but we know that one does not take an oath in response to a claim from a *cheresh*, *shoteh*, or *katan*! And so the *gemara* clarifies: *mai katan? gadol* — "what is meant by minor? A full adult." He is called *katan* only in the metaphorical sense that he is uninformed regarding his father's affairs — a junior figure who lacks access to the information of his father's business dealings.

This clarification then exposes the real heart of the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the *Chachamim*, as *Tosafot* elegantly formulates it. The two sides are not really arguing about whether *meshiv aveida* is a valid principle. They are arguing about whether the son's claim carries the same psychological weight as the father's own claim. The *Chachamim* hold that a borrower is fully prepared to deny everything when facing the son — the son's claim, in the borrower's mind, carries no weight, and therefore any admission is purely voluntary, a genuine *meshiv aveida*. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that the son's claim does carry weight — just as one would not be prepared to completely deny a debt to the creditor himself, one is equally unprepared to completely deny it to the creditor's heir. Therefore the admission of half is not freely voluntary; it is the same *modeh b'miktzat* dynamic as dealing with the father directly, and an oath is required.

The reason the *beraita* phrases it as *ta'anat atzmo* is not because Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov considers it literally a self-generated claim. Rather, the *Chachamim* consider the son's claim to have no weight — from their perspective it is *as if* no claim were being made. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov is correcting that premise, insisting that what the *Chachamim* call *ta'anat atzmo* is in fact a real *ta'anah*, and that he treats the son's position the same as the father's.

### No Chutzpah to Creditor

The *gemara* now invokes *Rabba*'s principle to spell out the underlying logic more fully. *Rabba* asks: why does the Torah require a *modeh b'miktzat* to take an oath at all? Why is there no *miggo* — I could have denied everything, so why not believe me when I concede half? The answer is the *chazakah*: *ein adam meiz panav bifnei ba'al chovo*. A person simply will not deny an entire debt to the very face of the creditor who helped him. And if he could not have taken the "stronger position" of complete denial — because human psychology forecloses it — then there is no *miggo*. He was never able to claim the whole thing, so admitting half earns him no credit. We therefore suspect him of lying about the other half, and the Torah imposes the oath to pressure a full admission.

The *gemara* then completes the psychological portrait: if this person is not prepared to lie completely, then one might ask — why is he lying at all? Why not just admit the whole debt? The answer is that he genuinely intends to pay eventually, but does not have the funds right now. He is buying time — *lishtamit* — rationalizing his partial denial as a delay tactic rather than outright theft. He has not psychologically committed to stealing; he is deferring. This explains both why the oath is effective (he is not a committed thief who would simply take a false oath) and why the partial denial occurs in the first place.

### Oath Compels Admission

This framework then maps directly onto the debate about the son. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds *lo shna bo v'lo shna b'vno* — there is no difference between the father and the son. The borrower is not prepared to baldly deny the entire debt even to the son, and therefore any admission is not a free *meshiv aveida* but a constrained *modeh b'miktzat*. The *Chachamim* hold *bo hu d'eino me'iz, aval b'vno me'iz* — he is not brazen enough to deny the whole thing to the creditor himself, but toward the son he is fully prepared to deny everything. Therefore any admission to the son is entirely voluntary, making him a genuine *meshiv aveida*, and he is exempt from an oath even where there are independent witnesses to the original loan.

The conclusion is clear: according to the *Chachamim*, this case cannot illustrate the *mishnah*'s structure because the borrower is always exempt regardless of whether witnesses exist. According to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, this case cannot illustrate the *mishnah*'s structure because the borrower is always obligated to swear regardless of whether he volunteers the information. Neither position produces the bifurcation the *mishnah* requires — free disclosure yields exemption; witnesses to the first part yield obligation. Hence, the field example remains the uniquely appropriate illustration, and Rabbi Yehoshua's choice is vindicated.

---

## Document Validation & Re…

### Witness Self-Validation…

The *mishnah* now pivots to a new class of *peh she-asar* cases involving the authentication of documents. The scenario is as follows: a *shtar* is produced in court but has not yet been independently verified. The process of *kiyum shtarot* — validating a document's signatures — normally requires either bringing the signatories themselves to affirm their signatures, producing witnesses who recognize those signatures, or comparing them against a previously certified document. Until this process is complete, the *shtar* does not have the standing of formally delivered testimony.

In the *mishnah*'s case, the witnesses themselves come forward and affirm: yes, that is our signature. But in the very same statement they add a disqualifying claim — we were minors when we signed it, or we were relatives of one of the parties, or we were coerced into signing a document we knew to be false. In the first two instances, the underlying transaction may well have occurred, but the testimony is invalid because the witnesses were legally disqualified. In the third instance — coercion — the transaction itself allegedly never occurred; the witnesses were forced at gunpoint, so to speak, to sign a fabricated document.

The *mishnah* rules *harei elu ne'emanim* — they are believed. This is a *peh she-asar*: the same mouth that validated the document also neutralized it. However, if other witnesses independently verify the signatures, or if a previously authenticated document with matching signatures establishes their validity, then the signatories are no longer believed to add the disqualifying claim. At that point, the first half of their statement is no longer theirs to give — it has been established independently — and *peh she-asar* does not apply.

### Peh She-Asar in Documents

Before proceeding, it is worth pausing to examine what *peh she-asar* actually means in this context, because there are two possible understandings, and they lead to different legal consequences. One understanding is that *peh she-asar hu peh she-hitir* means we accept both halves of the statement: we believe both that it is their signature and that the disqualifying circumstance is true. The alternative understanding is that the two halves of the statement cancel each other out entirely — as if nothing was said, and the document remains in its prior unvalidated state.

The practical difference emerges in a case where accepting the first half of the statement would trigger some independent legal consequence. If, for example, the witnesses say "it is our signature, but we were minors," and we treat the first half as believed and thus the *shtar* as validated, then we have effectively admitted live testimony into evidence. At that point, can the second half of the statement undo what the first half set in motion? Or has the first half already triggered an independent effect that the second half cannot reverse?

*Tosafot* addresses this and indicates that in the *mishnah*'s framework, the *peh she-asar* logic functions more like neutralization — the witnesses are treated as having said nothing. It is not that we validated the *shtar* and then un-validated it; rather, the entire combined statement never constituted a *kiyum* of the *shtar* at all. The two halves are so intertwined — indeed, *Rashi* even characterizes it as delivered *toch kedei dibbur*, as a single uninterrupted utterance — that they function as a unit that leaves the *shtar* exactly where it was.

### Rami bar Chama's Distinc…

*Rami bar Chama* introduces an important qualification that applies to the first part of the *mishnah* — the case where the witnesses themselves are the ones affirming their signatures, before any independent verification. He distinguishes between two types of claimed coercion. When the witnesses say *anusim hayinu machmat nefashot* — we were coerced under mortal threat, a gun was held to our heads — they are believed. But when they say *anusim hayinu machmat mamon* — we were coerced by financial threat, the man threatened to destroy our property unless we signed — they are not believed as to the disqualifying claim.

The reason for this distinction is the principle of *ein adam meisim atzmo rasha*. When witnesses claim that they signed a false document under threat of financial loss, they are admitting to having committed the biblical prohibition of *edut sheker* — bearing false testimony — for a reason that halachah does not recognize as sufficient justification. A threat to one's property does not permit transgressing a Torah prohibition; only a mortal threat creates that exemption. Therefore, by saying "we signed falsely because he threatened our finances," they are declaring themselves *resha'im* — wicked, in the technical legal sense of having violated a biblical law. And the rule is that a court does not admit self-incriminating testimony of this kind. The statement is therefore inadmissible insofar as it declares them wicked, and we are left with only the first part of their combined statement: the validation of the *shtar*.

This is a revealing illustration of how *peh she-asar* operates. The *gemara* here is not treating the two halves as mutually canceling. Rather, it is saying: we are prepared in principle to believe both halves — but sometimes, after accepting the first half, a legal rule prevents us from accepting the second. *Ein adam meisim atzmo rasha* is precisely such a rule. The court accepts the validation of the *shtar* and is then legally barred from registering the self-incriminating second half of the statement. The result is that the *shtar* stands.

By contrast, when the claimed coercion was mortal — *machmat nefashot* — no transgression occurred. Signing a false document to save one's life is halachically permitted. Therefore there is no self-incrimination, no *rasha*, no bar to accepting the second half of the statement, and *peh she-asar* operates in its full form: both halves are believed, and the document is neutralized.

The case of minors and relatives stands differently again. Claiming to have been a minor or a relative when signing does not constitute a claim of having borne false testimony at all. The witnesses in those cases are not saying the underlying transaction was fabricated — only that their testimony was legally invalid. They are not *resha'im*; they are simply disqualified witnesses. There is therefore no bar from *ein adam meisim atzmo rasha* to accepting the second half of their statement, and *peh she-asar* functions straightforwardly.

The *gemara* then considers a further objection raised by *Rava*. Even granting that two witnesses speaking together constitute testimony — so that their combined declaration that they were coerced under mortal threat should be treated as live, valid testimony against the document — there is a fundamental problem: *keivan shehigid, shuv eino chozer umagid*. Once a person has testified, he cannot retract his testimony. This principle, rooted in the language of the verse *ve'im lo yagid venasa avono*, establishes that the moment testimony is delivered and is no longer within *toch kedei dibbur*, it is irrevocable. How, then, can these witnesses now contradict what they effectively testified to when they signed the document?

### Testimony Non-Retraction

The principle of *keivan shehigid shuv eino chozer umagid* is absolute once testimony has been delivered. *Rava* raises this as a challenge to *Rami bar Chama*'s ruling: even in the case of mortal coercion, once the document has been validated independently, the witnesses' subsequent oral declaration that it was all fabricated amounts to a retraction of their prior testimony, and such a retraction is legally ineffective. One might have thought that the retraction should be accepted because the original testimony was not delivered orally in court but was embodied in a signed document — perhaps a document does not carry the same weight as live courtroom testimony. But this is precisely where *Reish Lakish*'s ruling intervenes.

### Reish Lakish on Document…

*Reish Lakish* holds: *edim ha-chatumim al ha-shtar na'asu ke-mi she-nichkera edutam be-veit din* — witnesses who sign a document have the same legal standing as witnesses whose oral testimony has been formally cross-examined in court. The signature on a validated *shtar* is equivalent in evidentiary weight to direct courtroom testimony. Once the *shtar* has been independently validated, the witnesses cannot retract. The earlier part of the *mishnah* — where the witnesses themselves are the source of validation and are therefore believed to add the qualifying claim — accordingly applies only to that first scenario, before independent validation. Once the *seifa*'s condition is met and the signatures are established through external means, no subsequent claim by the witnesses can dislodge the document.

### Ein Adam Meisim Atzmo Ra…

The principle of *ein adam meisim atzmo rasha* — that a person is not believed, and indeed that the court will not give legal force to testimony, when it would require treating the speaker as a *rasha* — applies specifically to the case of financial coercion. In that case, the witnesses have admitted to having committed *edut sheker* for an insufficient reason. Their self-incriminating declaration is inadmissible. The *shtar* stands, and the second half of their statement — the part that would have voided it — cannot be entered into evidence. This is the structure *Rami bar Chama* describes, and it holds for the *reisha* of the *mishnah* where independent validation has not yet occurred. The combined effect of *ein adam meisim atzmo rasha* and the rule of *keivan shehigid* means that in the *seifa* — where the document has been externally validated — the witnesses are never believed to retract their testimony under any circumstances.

---

## Rabbi Meir's Strict View

### Meir: No Self-Disqualifi…

The *gemara* now introduces a *beraita* that records a further stringency. *Tanu Rabbanan*: *ein ne'emanim le-foslo* — they are not believed to disqualify the document — *divrei Rabbi Meir*. The *Chachamim* say they are believed. This applies to the *reisha* of the *mishnah* — the case where the witnesses themselves are the ones validating the *shtar* and simultaneously claiming disqualification. The *Chachamim* hold that this is a classic *peh she-asar*: the same mouth that validated, disqualified. Rabbi Meir does not accept the disqualifying claim even here.

### Presumptions Override Cl…

Rabbi Meir's position requires explanation, since on the surface the two halves of the statement appear perfectly matched: the mouth that bound also released. The *gemara*'s answer distinguishes between accepting the *peh she-asar* logic in principle and recognizing that the first half of the statement, once accepted, can trigger presumptions strong enough to override the second half. For Rabbi Meir, *peh she-asar* does not mean the two halves automatically neutralize each other. Rather, the first half is accepted on its own terms, and the second half must be weighed against whatever it stands against — including firm halachic presumptions.

### Chazaka: Valid Witnesses…

In the case where the witnesses claim to have been relatives of a party, the *gemara* explains Rabbi Meir's ruling through the following reasoning: *malveh gufeih meidak dayyek u-michtav* — a creditor who goes to the trouble of having a document written takes care to ensure that the witnesses he uses are valid witnesses. A person protecting his financial interests will not carelessly use relatives as signatories. This is a *chazakah*: an established pattern of human behavior. The witnesses' claim that they were relatives therefore runs directly against this presumption, and the presumption wins.

Similarly, *Reish Lakish* provides the parallel *chazakah* regarding minors: *ein ha-edim chotmim al ha-shtar ella im ken na'asa be-gadol* — witnesses do not sign a document unless it was executed when they were adults. Minors simply do not appear as signatories on formal legal documents. Once we have accepted the first half of the witnesses' statement — that the signatures are genuine — the *chazakah* kicks in and tells us that genuine adult signatories means the transaction was executed with adult witnesses. Their subsequent claim that they were minors is overridden by this presumption. The *peh she-asar* logic gives the second half of the statement a degree of credibility, but that credibility is not sufficient to overcome an established presumption operating in the other direction.

### Coercion Claim Status

The *gemara* then asks about the case of claimed coercion. In the cases of relatives and minors, Rabbi Meir is able to invoke *chazakot* — it simply does not happen that creditors use relatives or minors as witnesses. But coercion is different. Sadly, coercion does happen. People do find themselves forced to sign documents at threat. There is no equivalent *chazakah* that coerced signatures are vanishingly rare. So why does Rabbi Meir not believe them when they claim coercion? The answer to this will be taken up in the next discussion — the *gemara* closes here, leaving that thread open for continuation.

What the overall structure of Rabbi Meir's position reveals, however, is a particular understanding of *peh she-asar*: it does not operate as an automatic mutual cancellation. It means that we grant the second half of the statement a claim to credibility — and in ordinary circumstances, that credibility is sufficient, which is why the *Chachamim* accept it. But Rabbi Meir holds that wherever the second half runs against a strong presumption — a *chazakah* that the disqualifying circumstance simply does not occur — the presumption takes precedence, and only the first half of the statement is accepted. The document stands.

---

---

# Ketubot 22

## Kiyum Shtarot & Judges

### Peh She'Asar Intro

The daf opens three lines from the bottom of 21b, with a teaching transmitted in the name of Rabbi Abba, who said it in the name of Rav Huna, who said it in the name of Rav. Before turning to that teaching directly, it is worth noting the broader context. The overarching theme of this section of *Ketubot* is *peh she-asar hu ha-peh she-hitir* — the principle that the same mouth which creates a prohibition is believed to remove it. One of the central examples in the *mishnah* we have been working through involves witnesses who testify that a signature on a document is their own, but then introduce circumstances that would effectively invalidate it. That discussion has led us into a broader treatment of *kiyum shtaros* — the formal validation of documents by a *beis din* — and the rules governing contradictory testimony. The material we are about to address continues squarely within that world.

Before proceeding, it is worth briefly revisiting a question that arose in the previous session: whether it matters that a text is written before it is accurate, provided the signatories wait until it becomes accurate before signing. The concern is one of *me-chazi ke-mezuyaf* — the appearance of forgery. If the document declares "the three of us recognize this signature" but at the time of writing there are not yet three who have concurred, can it be pre-written in anticipation of the eventual signing? One practical echo of this question involves the *kesubah*, where some have the custom not to complete the *kuf* of *ve-kanina* until after the *kinyan* has been made, so that the text should not assert something as done that has not yet occurred. And yet, as was pointed out, the rest of the *kesubah* is also not yet true at the time of writing — it attests to a marriage that has not yet taken place, since *Ashkenazim* sign before the wedding. What makes the document valid is ultimately its signing, not its writing, and so the preoccupation with that single letter is puzzling. But this is an interesting tension and was the issue left at the end of the previous session.

### Three Judges, Challenge

The teaching of Rabbi Abba in the name of Rav Huna in the name of Rav runs as follows: when three judges convene to validate a document — *sheloshah she-yashvu le-kayem es ha-shtar* — and a challenge (*irer*) arises against one of them questioning his validity, the following distinction applies. *Ad she-lo chasmu* — before they have signed the document — the other two may testify on behalf of the third. The reasoning is that at this stage they are not *nogeia badavar*, not a party to the matter. Their own standing has not yet been formally committed to the document, and so if the third turns out to be invalid, they can simply ask him to step down and bring in a replacement. There is no self-interest compelling their testimony. *Vechasim* — they may then go ahead and sign. But *mishechasmu* — if they have already signed the document — they can no longer testify on his behalf. At that point, their testimony in support of the third judge is tantamount to testifying in support of their own document, and they are considered *nogeia be-eidus*, partial witnesses whose testimony cannot be credited.

### Challenge Types

The *gemara* now asks: what type of challenge are we dealing with? *Ei irur de-gazlanusa* — if the challenge is one of *gazlanusa*, meaning that two witnesses are asserting that this third judge is a *gazlan*, a thief, and therefore disqualified as a witness and a *dayan* — then the situation is *trei u-verei ninhu*, two against two. If two are saying he is a *gazlan* and the other two members of the *beis din* are countering that he is not, that would ordinarily be a standoff of equal testimony. Why would the second two be credited?

One might ask whether the word *irer* here implies formal testimony at all, or merely a rumor. Other *gemaros* assume that *irer* refers to actual testimony by two people, and that is the assumption adopted here.

### Giluy Milta Doctrine

The *gemara* therefore turns to a second type of challenge: *irur de-pgam mishpacha*, a challenge to his personal status — for example, a claim that he is a slave, which would disqualify him. In such a case, the *gemara* says: *giluy milsa be-alma hu*. This is not true testimony in the conventional sense; it is merely disclosure of a matter. The reasoning, as *Rashi* explains, is that a person's lineage and personal status are facts that are ultimately going to become known. They are not the kind of thing that is exclusively within the knowledge of two individuals. Other people know, there are records, the matter will be discovered. Because of this, the two *beis din* members who declare him valid are not regarded as offering formal *eidus* — they are merely providing information that is itself susceptible to public corroboration.

*Rashi* articulates this clearly: even after they have signed the document — *mishechasmu* — why can they not testify that he is not a slave? The concern would be *nogeia be-eidus*. But here, he writes, this is a matter that requires investigation and is of the type that will come to light on its own. They are not truly testifying; they are *megalei davar be-alma* — merely disclosing a fact. And therefore the concern about partiality does not apply in the same way.

There is, however, a difficulty worth noting. The principle of *giluy milsa be-alma* seems to work symmetrically. Those who are claiming he is a slave are also disclosing a matter of public record — their claim is equally subject to the logic that it will become known. It is not immediately obvious why this logic tilts the scale in favor of those declaring him valid rather than those declaring him disqualified. *Rashi*'s formulation does not fully resolve this asymmetry, and one is left wondering why the doctrine of *giluy milsa* gives greater weight to the validators rather than the challengers. The point that emerges from *Rashi* is perhaps more modest: the concern of *nogeia be-eidus* does not bar their testimony in either direction, since the whole inquiry is not truly *eidus* in the formal sense. Whether that fully resolves the asymmetry is less certain.

A further question was raised: if *giluy milsa* applies to claims about personal status, why did the *gemara* earlier not apply the same logic to witnesses whose signatures appear on a document but who were claimed to be *ketanim* at the time of signing? That too is a question of personal status — how old were they then? — and one might think it is equally a *giluy milsa*. The answer offered is that at the time the document was signed, the question of whether they were of age is a historical question that may no longer be determinable. Now they may be middle-aged; their parents may be gone; the evidence may simply not exist. The *giluy milsa* doctrine presupposes that the matter can indeed be disclosed and investigated. If the facts are no longer recoverable, the doctrine loses its force.

### Thief vs. Repentance

The *gemara* resolves the case differently. *Le-olam eima lach irur de-gazlanusa* — in fact, the challenge is one of *gazlanusa*, theft. The reason the other two are credited is that they are not contradicting the challengers. Rather, they are saying: *yadeinan bei de-avad teshuvah* — we know that he performed *teshuvah*. They concede that he stole, but they add that he has since repented, and therefore his *kashrus* as a *dayan* has been restored.

This opens an important and, sadly, recurring discussion. There are two distinct types of *teshuvah*. One is *teshuvah* between a person and God — an internal process of regret and resolve, which may be fully sincere and which one hopes God will accept. But that is not the *teshuvah* relevant to restoring a person's communal standing or halakhic *kashrus* as a witness or *dayan*. For that, a far more concrete standard applies, as developed at length in *Sanhedrin*: restitution of what was taken, and concrete, observable evidence that the person has genuinely changed. Expressions of regret, or returning to public religious observance, are not sufficient. This distinction has obvious relevance whenever questions arise about whether a figure who has acted improperly may be rehabilitated and trusted with a position of authority.

In the present case, the second two witnesses are not contradicting the first two — they affirm the theft — but they add the critical fact of *aved teshuvah*. The testimonies are therefore not in direct conflict.

### Before vs. After Signing

The overall principle is restated: *ad she-lo chasmu*, before signing, testimony about the third judge's validity may be heard; *mishechasmu*, after signing, it may not, because by then the two signing judges are *nogeia be-eidus* in an unambiguous sense.

---

## Judge Dies Before Signing

### Declaration of Three

Rabbi Zeira introduces the next ruling, noting that he had heard it from Rabbi Abba — and that had Rabbi Abba of Akko not reminded him, he would have forgotten it. The teaching itself echoes the theme we encountered in an earlier *sugya* about a witness who had forgotten testimony and was reminded of what he had always known.

The case is as follows: *gimmel she-yashvu le-kayem es ha-shtar* — three sat together as a *beis din* to validate a document — *u-meis echad meihem* — and one of them died before they signed. The three had already deliberated and reached their conclusion, but only two now remain to sign. The ruling is that they must write explicitly on the document: *be-moshav tlasa havina* — we were a sitting of three — *ve-chad laytohei* — and one of us is no longer present. The echo of *ve-echad einenu* — "and one is not" — the brothers speaking of Joseph — is deliberate and striking. The surviving two must note that the third has died, explaining why only two signatures appear. This is necessary because otherwise observers will assume that only two judges validated the document — which would undermine the requirement that a *kiyum ha-shtar* rest on a *beis din* of three.

### Official Authority

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers an alternative formulation. If the document contains the phrase *shtar denan nafak le-kadmana bei dina* — "this document was brought before us, the *beis din*" — followed by their signatures, that is sufficient. The statement that they were a *beis din* is understood to imply they were three, and so no explicit mention of the number is required.

### Chatzuf Beit Din

The *gemara* challenges this: perhaps it was a *beis din de-Chatzpa* — a brazen *beis din* of only two? The reference is to Shmuel's ruling that *shnayim she-danu dineihem din* — if two sat in judgment, their ruling stands after the fact — except that they are called a *beis din chatzuf*, an insolent court. So if Shmuel's view is that two can validate in principle, perhaps the term *beis din* on the document does not guarantee three were present. The mere use of the title may not be enough.

The *gemara* responds: the document does not merely say *beis din*; it says *bei dina de-Rabbana Ashi* — the *beis din* of Rav Ashi, the *rav* of Mata Mechasya. That institutional affiliation implies that all proper procedures were observed, and no one would imagine that the official court of Rav Ashi would operate with only two judges.

### Technical Language

But the *gemara* presses further: perhaps even the rabbis of Rav Ashi's court followed Shmuel's view and were comfortable with two? The *gemara* resolves this by noting that the document contains yet a further phrase: *ve-amar lana Rabbana Ashi* — "and Rav Ashi commanded us" to sit as a *beis din*. Rav Ashi himself would never have directed a *beis din* to sit with fewer than three, and therefore this phrase conclusively establishes that three were present.

There is an irony worth noting: the discussion began by saying that if you write *beis din* you need not specify the number three explicitly. By the time it concludes, the required language is quite elaborate — the institutional affiliation, the invocation of Rav Ashi's authority, his specific directive — which, as the *gemara* essentially concedes, amounts to proving three were present in a roundabout way. One might as well have simply written that there were three. But this elaborate language reflects what appears to be the actual technical formulation that was in use in the Geonic courts.

---

## Peh She'Asar Principle

### Personal Statements

Having completed the discussion of *kiyum shtaros* and the rules of documentary validation, the *gemara* now returns to the broader principle of *peh she-asar* and its intersection with matters of personal status. The *mishnah* presents two cases in which a woman's own statements determine whether she is permitted or forbidden.

### Woman's Marital Status

The first case: *ha-ishah she-amra eshet ish hayiti, u-gerushah ani* — a woman who declared that she was married, and then stated that she is now divorced. She is believed — *ne'emenes* — since *ha-peh she-asar hu ha-peh she-hitir*: the same mouth that made her forbidden to all other men by declaring she was married is the mouth that is now saying she is divorced. However, *ve-im yesh eidim she-haitah eshet ish* — if there are independent witnesses who established that she was married — *ve-hi omeret gerushah ani* — and she merely claims to be divorced — *einah ne'emenes*, she is not believed. Once her married status is independently attested, her own word alone cannot dissolve it.

### Captive Woman Case

The second case involves a woman taken captive. The general presumption is that a captive woman was violated, which would render a *kohen*'s wife forbidden to her husband. Yet if the woman herself says *shiviti ve-tehorah ani* — I was taken captive but was not raped — she is believed, again on the basis of *peh she-asar*: we only know of her captivity through her own words, and therefore her own words are also credited regarding the conditions of that captivity. Again, if there are independent witnesses to the captivity, *einah ne'emenes* — she is no longer believed about the consequences.

The *mishnah* then adds: *ve-im mi-she-nises bau eidim* — if, after she married a second man, witnesses came and established that she had been married previously — *harei zu lo tetzei*, she does not have to divorce her current husband. This is a significant ruling, and one that extends the discussion of *peh she-asar* into territory with real consequences for an established marriage.

One might ask whether the captivity case can properly be governed by *peh she-asar* at all. After all, the *gemara* elsewhere raises the possibility that when there is a strong countervailing presumption — as there is that a captive woman was violated — we might not credit the second part of the statement. *Rabbi Meir*'s position regarding witnesses who claim they were *ketanim* at the time of signing was understood by some as reflecting exactly that: even granting *peh she-asar* in principle, a counter-presumption can override the second half of the statement. But the *mishnah* here does not adopt that stringency for the captive woman case. The distinction, as *Rashi* explains *peh she-asar*, is between a case where the person volunteers the information without any prompting — which is the core of *peh she-asar* — versus *migo*, where a person has a strategic alternative available. *Tosafot* disagrees and maintains that *peh she-asar* can apply even when the person is responding to a challenge, but distinguishes it from *migo* in that there is no concrete piece of evidence — no *shor shachut lefanecha* — that must be explained away. These distinctions matter for determining when a counter-presumption can override the mechanism.

### Source of Principle

After several *daf* of applying *peh she-asar* to a range of cases, the *gemara* now finally raises the foundational question: *minayin le-ha-peh she-asar hu ha-peh she-hitir* — what is the source of this principle? Perhaps particularly in a case of personal status, where the stakes are an *issur* rather than merely a monetary question, we require a stronger basis than mere logic.

Rabbi Assi cites a *pasuk*: *es biti natati la-ish ha-zeh le-isha* — I gave my daughter to this man as a wife. The reading is: *la-ish* — "to a man" — the father creates a prohibition on his daughter vis-à-vis all other men; *ha-zeh* — "this man" — he then specifies who is permitted. So the same mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted.

### Sevara Over Scripture

The *gemara* immediately pushes back: *lamah li kra? sevara hu* — why do you need a *pasuk* for this? It is simple logic. *Hu asar, hu hetir* — he is the one who created the prohibition, he is the one who removes it. If you are going to believe one part of a person's statement, you should believe the whole of it.

There is a point worth noting about the *derashah* itself. In the *pasuk* about *motzi shem ra*, nobody is actually debating whether the daughter was married — that is conceded. The father is there to defend her honor, not to establish the fact of her marriage. Using this *pasuk* to derive that a father's testimony creates a marital bond is a significant inferential leap from the context in which those words appear.

Ultimately, the *gemara* accepts that *peh she-asar* rests on *sevara* — logical reasoning — not on scriptural necessity. Everything that has been discussed for the past several sessions regarding *peh she-asar* is thus grounded in *sevara*, which is in keeping with how it has largely been understood throughout.

### Biblical Derivation

If *peh she-asar* does not require the *pasuk*, the *gemara* asks: *lamah li kra?* What then does the verse teach? *Ki itzterich le-chide-Rav Huna* — it is needed for a separate teaching of Rav Huna. For Rav Huna said in the name of Rav: *minayin le-av she-ne'eman le-esor es bito min ha-Torah* — how do we know from the Torah that a father is believed to establish that he has married off his daughter, such that she would be treated as an *eshet ish* as a result? The answer: *shene'emar, es biti natati la-ish ha-zeh* — as it says, "I gave my daughter to this man." This, the *gemara* holds, establishes that the father's declaration carries legal weight to create her marital status, quite apart from the *peh she-asar* principle itself.

The *gemara* then asks: *ha-zeh lamah li?* — why is the word *hazeh* needed? Now that the *pasuk* is used to establish the father's credibility and not to derive *peh she-asar*, what work does *hazeh* do? The answer comes from what Rabbi Yona teaches in a *baraisa*: *es biti natati la-ish ha-zeh* — to this man, *ve-lo le-yavam* — and not to the brother-in-law. In the context of *motzi shem ra*, if it is the brother-in-law who spreads the false report about the woman's virginity, he is not subject to the laws of *motzi shem ra*, because those laws apply specifically to the husband. *Hazeh* — this specific man — is what distinguishes the husband from others, including the *yavam*.

---

## Retracting Statements

### Marriage Retraction

The *gemara* now turns from *peh she-asar* to a related but distinct question: can a person retract an earlier statement about personal status if they provide a reasonable explanation? The starting point is a *baraisa*: *ha-ishah she-amra eshet ish ani ve-chazra ve-amra penuyah ani* — a woman who went around saying she was married and then changed her statement and said she is single. In principle, *einah ne'emenes* — she is not believed. But *im nasna amatla le-devareha* — if she provides a reasonable explanation for why she originally said she was married — *ne'emenes* — she is believed.

### Forbidden Status

The *gemara* challenges the very idea that she could be believed to retract. *Ve-shavya le-nafshah chaticha de-issura* — she has made herself a forbidden object. The principle of *shavya le-nafshah chaticha de-issura* holds that when someone makes a declaration that renders themselves forbidden, we accept that declaration as binding against them. We accept statements that restrict a person — we do not accept statements that benefit them — and therefore she would seem to be locked into her earlier declaration that she was married.

### Amtla Explanation

The resolution comes from Rav, as transmitted by Rav Huna: the key is *k'gon she-nasna amatla le-devareha* — when she provides a reasonable explanation for her original claim. A person is believed to retract an earlier statement, even a statement that bound them in terms of personal status, if they can explain coherently why they said what they said initially. This is confirmed by a *baraisa* that restates the same rule and immediately follows it with a concrete historical illustration.

### Woman's Strategy

The story is told of a woman *gedolah be-noi* — a woman of exceptional beauty — who had suitors constantly pressing her for marriage. She began telling them *mekudeshes ani* — I am married. *Li-yamim* — after some time — *amda ve-kidshah atzmah* — she went ahead and contracted a proper marriage. The *chachamim* asked her: what made you do this — first you said you were married, and now you have married? She replied: *be-tchilah she-ba-u elai anashim she-einam hagunim, amarti mekudeshes ani* — at first, when men who were unsuitable were pressing their suits, I said I was married to deter them. *Achshav she-ba-u elai anashim hagunim, kidashti es atzmi* — now that suitable men came forward, I went ahead and married.

One might wonder why the proper suitors would even approach a woman who had been telling everyone she was married. Perhaps she had moved, or the right suitors came from elsewhere. In any case, the *gemara* does not censure her behavior in the slightest. The *halacha* of *midvar sheker tirchak* applies in the context of *beis din*, not to ordinary interpersonal dealings, and *muter lishanot mipnei ha-shalom* is well established. What matters halakhically is whether her explanation is reasonable, and here it clearly is. She is believed. This ruling was presented by Rav Acha Sar Ha-Bira before the *chachamim* in Usha, who affirmed: *im nasna amatla le-devareha, ne'emenes*.

### Niddah Retraction

Shmuel asked Rav the following: *amra temei-ah ani ve-chazra ve-amra tehorah ani* — a woman told her husband she is a *niddah*, and then she retracted and said she is actually *tehorah*. What is the law? Rav replied: *af be-zo, im nasna amatla le-devareha ne'emenes* — even in this case, if she provides a reasonable explanation, she is believed. Shmuel reportedly asked this forty times and received the same answer forty times.

*Ve-afilu hachi lo avad Shmuel uvda be-nafshei* — and yet, despite this, Shmuel was not prepared to rule on this for himself. *Tosafot* quotes a *Yerushalmi* that gives the backstory: Shmuel sought to be intimate with his wife, who told him she was a *niddah*. The next day she said she was *tehorah*. Shmuel pointed out that one cannot change from *niddah* to *tehorah* in a single day. She explained: *etmol lo havi bi cheila ki ha-hi sha-ata* — yesterday I did not have the strength at that moment. Shmuel then went and asked Rav, who confirmed that with a reasonable explanation she is believed.

This case is a greater *chiddush* than the marriage case in several respects. First, the *amatla* here — exhaustion, not wanting to have relations at that particular time — requires the woman to have essentially fabricated a *niddah* status, which carries significant consequences extending well beyond a single night. Second, the possibility that she genuinely became a *niddah* is real — women sometimes have unexpected breakthrough bleeding — which introduces grounds for suspicion about the retraction rather than the original declaration. Third, this arises in an ongoing marital context, not a one-time social claim, and so its implications play out differently over time. One can understand why Shmuel resisted applying the ruling to himself, even after hearing it confirmed repeatedly.

Some sociologists who have studied the practice of *hilchos niddah* in traditional communities have noted that the laws can function in an empowering way for women, providing a halakhic basis for saying no to a husband at times when social dynamics would otherwise make refusal very difficult. The *sugya* here makes that dimension explicit in a striking way: the *gemara* records, without censure, that a woman may use the declaration of *niddah* status for that purpose and then retract it the next day if she provides a reasonable explanation. The question of what then happens to the credibility of future *niddah* declarations — and whether that is part of why Shmuel resisted — is left implicit but is clearly in the background of the discussion.

---

## Contradictory Witnesses

### Death Testimony Rule

The *gemara* now moves to a series of cases involving contradictory testimony about a woman's status — specifically, whether her husband has died or whether she has been divorced — and what the consequences are when witnesses are in conflict. A *baraisa* teaches: *shnayim omrim meis ve-shnayim omrim lo meis* — two witnesses say the husband died and two witnesses say he did not die. *Harei zu lo tinasei* — the woman may not marry another man. With contradictory testimony canceling out, she retains her status as a married woman. *Ve-im nises, lo tetzei* — but if she went ahead and married, she does not have to divorce from the second marriage. This is the position of the *tanna kamma*.

### Divorce Testimony Rule

Rabbi Menachem bar Rabbi Yossi adds a parallel case with a different outcome: *shnayim omrim nitgarshah ve-shnayim omrim lo nitgarshah* — two say she was divorced, two say she was not. *Harei zu lo tinasei* — again, she may not marry. But *ve-im nises, tetzei* — if she married, she must divorce from the second marriage. Rabbi Menachem bar Rabbi Yossi himself then clarifies the timing: when he rules that she must leave, he means specifically when the witnesses came and contradicted each other *before* she married the second man. If she married first and the contradicting witnesses came afterward, *lo tetzei* — even he would agree she need not divorce.

### Marrying Witness

The *gemara* asks how the *tanna kamma* can rule that if she married she need not divorce, given that the testimony is neutralized and she retains a *chezkas eshet ish*. Any man who had relations with her under such circumstances would be liable for an *asham talui* — the suspensive guilt-offering brought for doubtful violations of *issur kares* — and yet we are tolerating the marriage after the fact?

Rav Sheshet resolves this: the case is specifically where she married one of the witnesses who testified that the husband had died — *nises le-echad me-eideha*. That witness is saying, in effect: I personally know the husband is dead. From the perspective of the broader community and *beis din*, there is a contradiction and a *safek*. But from his own perspective, there is no *safek*. He knows what he saw.

### Beit Din Authority

This leads to a broader observation about the limits of *beis din* authority. We tend to think of *beis din* as overseeing all halakhic matters — but there is a meaningful distinction here. *Beis din* cannot impose *malkot* in a case of *safek*, and bringing a *korban asham* or *korban chatat* for personal *kapara* is not something *beis din* can compel. If the individual says "I know I am not sinning" and *beis din* cannot demonstrate otherwise — if all *beis din* has is a *safek*, not a *vaday* to the contrary — then the matter is between that person and God. *Beis din* will not force a divorce in such a case. This stands in contrast to other situations — such as where a wife has committed adultery and wishes to remain with her husband — where *beis din* does intervene actively to break up the marriage, because there the *issur* is objectively established.

### One vs. One Rule

Abaye offers a different resolution of the entire *baraisa*. He says: *targema be-eid echad* — read the case not as two against two but as one against one. One witness says the husband died; one witness says he did not. Now, by the special rule of *Yevamos*, when one witness testifies that a husband died, the *rabbonim* gave that witness the weight of two — *heimnuhu rabbanan ke-vei trei*. This is based on the rule of Rabbi Ulla: whenever the Torah or the rabbis believe one witness, that witness is treated as two. So the one who says the husband died carries the weight of two, while the one who says he did not die carries only the weight of one. *Ein devarav shel echad bi-mekom shenayim* — one cannot override two. So, in the death case, one against one effectively becomes two against one in favor of death, and she is believed.

If so, asks the *gemara*, why can she not marry *le-chatchila*? If the testimony in favor of death prevails, she should simply be permitted to remarry outright. The *gemara* answers by invoking Rabbi Assi's principle: *haser mimcha ikshus peh ve-lazus sefasayim harchek mimcha* — remove from yourself perversion of speech and keep scandalous rumor far from you. Even if halakhically the testimony resolves in her favor, the appearance of the situation — one witness against another — is such that it will generate *lashon ha-ra* and suspicion. Therefore, *le-chatchila* she should not marry, but *bedi-avad* she need not divorce.

In the parallel case of *gerushin*, however — one witness says she was divorced, one says she was not — both witnesses are conceding that she was a married woman. The one who says she was divorced is then just a single witness to the act of divorce, and *ein devarav shel echad bi-mekom shenayim*. There is effectively no valid testimony of divorce. In that case, even *bedi-avad*, if she married, she must divorce.

### Two vs. Two Analysis

Rava disagrees with Abaye and maintains that the case is indeed two against two — *terei ve-terei ninhu* — in both the death case and the divorce case. The difference in outcome must therefore be explained differently. Rava says that Rabbi Menachem bar Rabbi Yossi was persuaded by the argument that *bedi-avad* she must leave only in the case of *gerushin*, but not in the case of *misah*.

### Death vs. Divorce

The distinction Rava draws is as follows: *misah einah yecholah le-hachchishot* — death cannot be contradicted. If witnesses say the husband died and the woman remarries on that basis, and the husband then appears alive, she cannot simply say "I knew he was alive all along." The risk she took was total and irreversible. A woman therefore takes tremendous care before acting on testimony of death, and if she does act, we may credit that she had genuine certainty. In the death case, therefore, the *tanna kamma* rules that *bedi-avad lo tetzei* — she need not divorce.

But *gerushin yecholah le-hachchishot* — divorce can always be contradicted. If the husband appears and says he never gave a *get*, she could claim he is wrong. The risk is far smaller, and so the inclination to act on possibly insufficient testimony is much greater. We therefore do not extend the same degree of trust to her judgment in the *gerushin* case, and even *bedi-avad*, she must divorce.

### Conclusion

The *gemara* asks: but would she really be so *chatzuf* — so brazen — as to falsely claim she was divorced with the husband potentially able to deny it? The answer is provided by Rav Hamnuna's ruling: *ha-ishah she-amerah le-va-alah gerashtani, ne'emenes* — a woman who says to her own husband "you divorced me" is believed. Why? *Chazakah ein ishah me-izah paneha bifnei ba-alah* — a woman would not be so brazen as to say this to her husband's face without it being true. Should this not mean we trust her in the *gerushin* case as well?

The *gemara* responds: *hani mili heicha de-leika sahadei* — that principle applies only where there are no witnesses at all. *Aval heicha de-ika sahadei de-kamsayiah lah* — but where there are witnesses supporting her claim — *me-aza u-me-aza*, she is quite willing to be brazen. The presence of supporting witnesses is itself what emboldens her, removing the deterrent effect that would otherwise make us trust her. Therefore, when there are two witnesses saying she was divorced alongside two saying she was not, the logic of Rav Hamnuna does not apply, and even *bedi-avad* she must divorce.

In sum: the *machlokes* between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Menachem bar Rabbi Yossi, and the further split between *misah* and *gerushin*, resolves as follows. When it is two against two and the testimony concerns death, *bedi-avad* she may remain married, because the very gravity of the situation ensures she acted with sufficient confidence. When the testimony concerns a *get*, even *bedi-avad* she must divorce, because the softness of the risk makes her willingness to act an insufficient guarantee of the truth of her claim.

---

---

# Ketubot 23

## Death vs. Divorce

### Rav Yochanan

The daf opens by completing a discussion carried over from the bottom of 22b. Rav Yochanan had distinguished between contradictory witnesses in cases of divorce and cases of death: when witnesses contradict one another regarding whether a woman's husband died, she may remain in a second marriage contracted in reliance on the original testimony, whereas if the contradictory testimony concerned whether she received a *get*, she would be required to leave. The *gemara* had been working through several explanations for this asymmetry.

### Rav Asi

One of those explanations involved the notion that in divorce cases, the woman would not have been sufficiently careful before remarrying, because she could always counter her husband's appearance with a direct claim of having been divorced. Now the *gemara* delivers its final answer to close the *sugya*. Rav Asi says: *kegon de'amri edim achshav met, achshav gershah* — the case is where the witnesses specified that the event happened just now, yesterday, this very day. One set says the husband died just now; another set says he was seen alive just now. Or: one set says she was just divorced; another says she was not.

In the death case, *mita lo salka l'verurah* — if the witnesses are wrong about the death, there is no further means of verification that specifically undermines their testimony. There is nothing structurally suspicious about the contradiction, and therefore *bedi'eved* — after the fact, if she has already remarried — she need not leave. But in the divorce case, *gerushin ika l'verurah*: if she claims she was just divorced yesterday, the obvious question arises — where is the *get*? You haven't had the *get* long enough to lose it. If you claim you lost it since yesterday, that alone raises serious doubts.

### Missing Get

The *gemara* makes this explicit: *de'amrinan lah, i ita dehachi hava, achvi lan gitach* — we say to her, if this really happened, show us your *get*. The inability to produce a very recent *get* creates an additional layer of suspicion beyond the bare contradiction, and it is this additional factor — not present in the death case — that justifies the stricter ruling *bedi'eved* in divorce cases.

---

## Marriage vs. Divorce

### Mishnah Cases

A new *braita* is introduced. *Shenayim omrim nitkadesha u-shenayim omrim lo nitkadesha* — two witnesses say she was betrothed, two witnesses say she was not. *Harei zo lo tinasei* — she may not marry another man *lechatchila*; *ve'im nisset lo tetzei* — but if she did remarry, she need not leave.
