Tosafot, however, has a lengthy discussion explaining that Rabbi Chiyya in principle accepts that graduated framework; his objection is specific to this particular case of family testimony, for reasons Tosafot develops at length.

### Father's Control

Rabbi — Rebbi — responds to Rabbi Chiyya's challenge with a new and distinct reasoning: *she-beyado le'hachilo bitrumah* — because it is within the father's own power to feed the son *terumah* regardless of our ruling. The father is a *kohen*, the *terumah* is his, and he could give it to this person claiming to be his son even without any formal recognition from the *beit din*. Since the father could accomplish the *terumah* outcome on his own, we accept his testimony at that level. But marriage to a *meyuchas* family is not something the father can arrange unilaterally; it requires the community's recognition of the son's status. Therefore, the father's testimony is insufficient for *yuchsin*. This represents a meaningfully different conceptual basis from the earlier discussions: it is not merely that *terumah* is a lesser obligation, but that the father's control over the *terumah* outcome makes his testimony reliable at that level in a way it simply is not for marriage.

### Brother vs Father

The Gemara then asks: Rabbi Chiyya challenged Rebbi's acceptance of the father's testimony for the son. Yet Rabbi Chiyya himself appears to have accepted a brother's testimony that another person is his brother and a *levi*. Why is brother testimony different from father testimony? Both are *karov* — close relatives — and both are *eid echad*. If the *karov* problem bars the father, it should equally bar the brother.

The Gemara's answer introduces the concept of *mesiach lefi tumo* — speaking in all innocence. The distinction is not really between father-son and brother-brother relationships as such. The distinction is between formal testimony, where the witness is conscious of the *halachic* consequences and is deliberately trying to establish a status, versus casual speech, where a person mentions something in passing without any awareness that it carries legal weight. When someone speaks *lefi tumo* — innocently, without understanding the implications — there is a strong presumption that he is telling the truth, precisely because he has no ulterior motive and no awareness of the consequences. Formal testimony, even from a perfectly valid witness, carries the risk that the witness is consciously trying to achieve a particular outcome.

### Yochanan Story

The Gemara illustrates *mesiach lefi tumo* with a story. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: there was a person who was speaking casually and said — *zachurni keshe'ani tinok umurkav al ktefav shel Abba* — I remember when I was a small child, riding on my father's shoulders, *vehotzi'uni mibeit hasefer* — and they took me out of *cheder*, *vehipshituni et ktunti* — and they removed my cloak, *vehitbiluni* — and they immersed me in a *mikveh*, *le'echol bitrumah la'erev* — so that I could eat *terumah* that night. The person recounted this as a simple childhood memory, with no awareness that it served as evidence of anything.

### Innocent Speech

Rabbi Chiyya himself completes the story: *vechaveirai bedilin mimeni* — and my friends would keep their distance from me — *vehayu korin oti Yochanan ochel chalot* — and they called me Yochanan the *challah*-eater, because they had to maintain distance from a *kohen* eating *terumah*. And based on this innocent, casual recollection — this *mesiach lefi tumo* — *ve'he'eluhu Rebbe likhunah al piv* — Rebbi was prepared to recognize his *kehuna* based on his testimony. The child Yochanan, now an adult, recalled these events without understanding their *halachic* significance. It was precisely that innocence — the absence of strategic intent — that made the testimony compelling and led Rebbi to act on it.

---

---

# Ketubot 27

## Besieged City

### Context & Overview

Daf 27 continues the tractate's sustained focus on questions of personal status (*ishus*), and specifically on the status of women. The preceding daf addressed the case of a woman taken as collateral for a loan and under what circumstances she might be assumed to have been raped or to have consented willingly — a discussion with deep resonances in the stories of Esther and Achashveirosh. Today we turn to a more overtly violent scenario: a city under siege, and the status of the women found within it when the besieging army breaks through.

### Mishna Text

The *mishna* opens with the phrase *ir she'kevashuha karkom* — a city that has been besieged and finally breached, with the invading army now inside. The word *karkom* itself is a subject of some interest; Rashi traces it to an Aramaic root, and it connotes a siege in which no one can escape.

### Kohanic Status

*Kol kohanot shenimtzu betochah psulot* — all wives of *kohanim* found in the city are invalidated to their husbands, on the presumption that they have been raped. The relevant concern here is specific to women who are married to, or who might wish to marry, a *kohen*: a woman who has had intercourse with a non-Jew, whether willingly or by force, is forbidden to a *kohen*. (She would still be permitted to eat *terumah* from her father's household if she is a *kohenet* by birth, and an Israelite woman who is raped does not become forbidden to her Israelite husband — but she is permanently disqualified from marrying a *kohen*.) The *mishna* therefore addresses precisely this population.

### Witness Exception

The *mishna* continues: *ve'im yesh lahen eidim* — but if there are witnesses that they were not raped, even normally invalid witnesses are believed. *Afilu eved afilu shifchah harei elu ne'emanim* — even a slave or slave woman. This echoes leniencies we have seen elsewhere in *Yevamot* regarding testimony about a potentially deceased husband, where a single witness, or even a normally disqualified witness, suffices.

The *mishna* closes with the statement *ve'ein ne'eman adam al yedei atzmo* — a person is not believed about himself. The shift to the masculine form is notable; the *gemara* will show that this applies not only to the woman testifying about herself, but also to a husband testifying on behalf of his wife — since his testimony in her favor is effectively testimony in his own interest.

One earlier *mishna* had already gone further, permitting two women to testify on behalf of each other even where reciprocity might be suspected. The *chiddush* there was the basic acceptance of women as valid witnesses in captivity cases — and the rule that when one witness says she was raped and another says she was not, we always follow the lenient position, even if that witness would normally be disqualified.

---

## Wine Question

### Contradiction Raised

The *gemara* opens with a *rominhu* — a challenge from a contradiction. A *baraita* discusses a marauding troop (*baleshet*) that enters a city. *Bishat shalom*, in peacetime, open barrels of wine (*chaviyot ptuchot*) are forbidden — we fear the soldiers helped themselves and their contact rendered the wine *stam yeinam* — while sealed barrels are permitted. But *bishat milchama*, in wartime, *eilu va'eilu mutarot* — even the open barrels are permitted, because *ein pnai l'nasech* — the soldiers do not have time for libation. The concern about deliberate idolatrous contact is set aside when troops are in the midst of active combat.

The difficulty is apparent: if soldiers at war have no time to attend to wine, how can the *mishna* assume they do have time to rape the women of a conquered city? The two rulings seem to pull in opposite directions.

### Priority Answer

Rav Mari offers the first resolution: *l'iba'el yesh pnai, l'nasech ein pnai* — for sexual violence there is always time; for wine libation there is not. Rape is a priority that soldiers will pursue even under combat conditions; attending to wine is not. This answer, while blunt, has considerable pragmatic truth to it.

### Country Distinction

Rabbi Yitzchak bar Eleazar in the name of Chizkiya offers a second answer: *kan b'charkom shel otah malchut, kan b'charkom shel malchut acheret* — it depends whether the city belongs to the same kingdom or to a different one. The question is how to understand this distinction.

Rashi reads it as follows: when fighting within one's own country — say, suppressing a provincial rebellion — the army exercises greater restraint, since the city is ultimately their own. They will neither plunder the wine nor rape the women. Against a foreign enemy, no such restraint applies, and both concerns come into force.

### Tosafot Reading

Tosafot reads the distinction in precisely the opposite direction, and this reading integrates more naturally with the *gemara*'s subsequent development. According to Tosafot, when fighting in enemy territory, the army is operating under urgent pressure — surrounded by hostile forces, unable to linger — and so there is no time even for rape, let alone wine. But when the fighting is within one's own country, where the army is secure, unhurried, and in command of the surrounding territory, there is ample time for both. The *issur* on the women therefore applies specifically when the city is *shel otah malchut* — one's own country — while in enemy territory, neither concern is operative.

Tosafot's reading is to be preferred because it better fits the *gemara*'s broader thrust, which is to progressively narrow the circumstances under which the *mishna*'s prohibition actually applies — a point that will become increasingly clear as we proceed.

---

## Escape Routes

### All Women Raped?

Even accepting that the prohibition applies in one's own country, the *gemara* raises a further challenge: *iy efshar d'lo arak chada minayhu* — is it really impossible that even one woman escaped? Why should we assume that every single woman in the city was raped? Given any realistic scenario, some women must have found a way out.

### Guards Prevent Escape

The *gemara* responds with the answer of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: *keshe'mishmarot ro'ot zo et zo* — when the conquering army has set up overlapping patrols within the city, each watching the others, so that there is truly no avenue of escape.

### Guards Must Sleep

But the *gemara* presses further: *efshar de'lo naima porta* — is it truly impossible that even one guard dozed off? Surely at least one person on patrol must sleep at some point. Perfect surveillance is not humanly achievable.

### Alarm System

Rabbi Levi provides the definitive answer: *kigun de'mahaderah le'mata shushilta ve'kalba ve'gaza ve'avza* — they have ringed the city with chains, dogs, loose debris that rattles underfoot, and geese. The combination creates an alarm system so comprehensive that no one can slip through undetected even when a guard is momentarily inattentive. It is only under such extreme circumstances — total physical enclosure reinforced by an active alarm network — that the *mishna*'s presumption of rape holds.

The *gemara* has now done something remarkable: it has essentially made the *mishna* moot in any ordinary scenario. We begin with a presumption that all the women have been violated, and then the *gemara* immediately begins dismantling the conditions under which that presumption could ever actually apply.

### Tannaim Debate

Rabbi Abba bar Zavda reports a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah and the Rabbis on precisely this question. One position resolves the wine-and-rape contradiction purely through the distinction between one's own country and a foreign one — and, having made that distinction, does not require any further narrowing. In that country where the prohibition applies, we simply assume all the women were raped, full stop, without entertaining further questions about possible escape. *Ve'lo kashya lei ve'lo midi* — he is not troubled by the objection at all.

The other position, however, is genuinely troubled by the possibility of escape and can only sustain the *mishna*'s presumption in the extremely narrow case where the city has been completely sealed with the alarm system described by Rabbi Levi — chains, dogs, debris, and geese. Short of that, the concern is always alive that a given woman may have managed to escape or hide, and this possibility is sufficient to suspend the blanket prohibition.

---

## One Tunnel Rule

### One Tunnel Permits

Rav Idi bar Avin in the name of Rav Yitzchak bar Ashian states: *im yesh sham machvoah achas, matzelas al ha'kohanot kulan* — if there is even a single tunnel or hiding place in the city, it permits all the *kohanot*, all the wives of *kohanim*, even if the city is otherwise perfectly sealed. The reasoning is that since any particular woman might have been the one who used that hiding place, no individual woman can be presumed with certainty to have been among those violated.

### One Hiding Place

Rabbi Yirmiya — who had a characteristic fondness for probing borderline cases, testing the precise limits of legal principles — poses the obvious follow-up question: *eina machzekes ela achas, mahu* — what if the hiding place can only conceal one person? Is it still true that all the women are permitted, on the theory that each one might have been that single individual?

### Two Paths Analogy

The *gemara* draws a comparison to the classic case of the two paths (*shtei shevilin*): one path has a corpse buried across its width, rendering anyone who walks it *tamei meis*, while the other is *tahor* — but no one remembers which is which. Two people each walked one of the paths and then handled *tahor* food. Rabbi Yehuda rules: if each comes to the *beis din* separately to ask his ruling, *tahorot* — each is declared *tahor* individually, because each has a *safek* and, in certain domains, *safek tumah birshut ha'rabbim* is always *tahor*. But *sheneihem ke'achas* — if both arrive together and present the question as a unit, they are *tmeim*, because we cannot simultaneously declare both *tahor* when we know with certainty that one of them is *tamei*. Rabbi Yossi rules *tmeim* in both cases.

Rava (and some say Rabbi Yochanan) clarifies: when they come *be'vat achas*, at the same time, everyone agrees they are *tmeim*; when they come *be'zeh achar zeh*, truly sequentially, everyone agrees they are *tahorim*. The dispute concerns only the intermediate case: someone who comes and asks about both himself and his companion in one presentation — is that treated as simultaneous or sequential?

Tosafot's reading of the dispute is sharper: the intermediate case is where a person came on one day and received a ruling for himself, then returned the next day to ask about his companion. Can the *beis din* issue a second, contradictory ruling knowing what they already told this person? That is the question the *tannaim* debate.

### Rava's Resolution

The parallel to our case is then stated: *keivan d'shara lehu le'chulhu, ke'vat achas dami* — if we issue a ruling permitting all the women at once, it is as if they all came before us simultaneously. Can we give a blanket ruling that every woman is permitted when we know that not all of them could physically have been in that one hiding place?

### Suspicion vs. Certainty

The *gemara* rejects the analogy: *hachi hashta* — how can you compare the cases? *Hatam vadai ika tumah* — in the paths case, there is definite *tumah*; it is certain that one of the two walked across the buried corpse. *Hacha mi yeimar de'itmei* — here, who says any woman was actually raped? It is only a concern, a *chashasha* — we do not know for certain that every woman, or even most women, was violated. And since it is only suspicion rather than certainty that grounds the *issur*, we can freely apply the *machvoah* as a basis for leniency across the board, even if it cannot physically accommodate everyone. This is the principle of *bishvuya hekilu* — in captivity cases, the rabbis were lenient — operating through the recognition that the entire prohibition rests on doubt, not established fact.

---

## Woman's Statement

### Rav Ashi's Question

Rav Ashi poses a further question: a woman says *lo nechbeisi ve'lo nitmeisi* — I did not hide in a cellar, and I was not raped. She is neither claiming to have used the one tunnel nor to have escaped the city. She simply says nothing happened to her. Do we believe her?

The issue is whether she has a valid *migo*: since she could have said she was the one who hid in the tunnel — a claim we would have accepted — she is instead saying something weaker (she was not raped, without any explanation), and we ask whether that weaker claim is believed because she could have made the stronger one.

### Donkey Case

The *gemara* draws a parallel to the case of a man who rented a donkey and was told explicitly not to travel by the road of Nahar Pekod because of the water there, but to go instead by the road of Narsh. He went by Nahar Pekod anyway, and the donkey died. When he came before Rava, he admitted the path he had taken but claimed there was no water that day. Rava applied *mah li leshaker* — he had no reason to lie, since he could have said he traveled the permitted route and no one would have known otherwise. Since he could have made the more advantageous false claim and did not, we believe the admission he did make along with the exculpatory detail. This is the operative logic of *migo*.

### Abaye's Limit

Abaye, however, challenges the application of *migo* in a famous limitation: *mah li leshaker be'makom eidim lo amrinan* — we do not apply *migo* against what is effectively established fact, something so widely known that it functions like witness testimony (*anan sahadei*). In the donkey case, everyone knows there is always water on the Nahar Pekod road; to claim otherwise is not simply an alternative version of events but a claim against general knowledge. Accordingly, the *migo* cannot save him in Abaye's view.

### Migo Applies

The *gemara* then applies this distinction to our case: *hatam vadai ika eidim de'ika maya* — in the Nahar Pekod case there is definite, established knowledge that water is present on that road; the claim to the contrary runs against certainty. *Hacha vadai itmei* — but here, is it certain that this woman was raped? It is not. It is only a *chashasha*. And *be'makom chashasha amrinan* — where there is only suspicion, not established fact, the *migo* does apply. The woman is believed when she says she was not raped, because she could have said she was in the cellar and we would have believed that too.

The progressive effect of the *gemara*'s reasoning is now fully visible. Not only does the entire *mishna* depend on extreme and rarely occurring physical conditions — total enclosure with chains, dogs, debris, and geese, and no hiding place anywhere in the city — but even in those rare conditions, a woman's own statement, backed by *migo*, is sufficient to permit her. The *mishna*'s prohibition is all but eliminated in practice.

---

## Witness Credibility

### Slaves Believed

Having established that the concern rarely applies and that women can free themselves from it easily, the *gemara* turns to the *mishna*'s provision that even a slave or slave woman (*eved* or *shifchah*) can serve as a valid witness. The *mishna* states: *afilu eved afilu shifchah harei elu ne'emanim*.

### Contradiction

The *gemara* immediately raises a contradiction (*u'rominhu*) from another *baraita* that limits the validity of a slave woman's testimony — and specifically singles out her own slave woman (*shifchasa*) as not believed. How are we to reconcile the two sources?

---

## Get & Seclusion

### Get Seclusion Rule

The *baraita* in question addresses a different context: a woman who has received a *get* (or whose *get* has been written but has not yet taken effect, or is to take effect at a later time — the precise scenario is the subject of a *machlokes* between Rashi and Tosafot). In any of these situations, if the woman enters into seclusion (*yichud*) with her soon-to-be or recently former husband, there is concern that they may have intercourse, which would invalidate or complicate the *get*. She will then circulate as a divorced woman when her status is in fact uncertain.

### Witness Requirement

To prevent this, witnesses are required who can attest that no *yichud* took place. The *baraita* rules that even a slave or a slave woman can serve in this capacity — by testifying, in effect, "I was present with her throughout," their presence eliminates the concern of seclusion.

### Her Own Slave Excluded

The one exception is *shifchasa* — her own slave woman. *Mipnei she'liba gas be'shifchasa* — because a woman feels completely uninhibited in the presence of her own slave woman, she will engage in intimate behavior even when the slave is present. The slave is treated as invisible, as furniture. This being so, the slave woman's presence does not constitute a real interruption of *yichud*, because the woman of the house does not modify her behavior on account of her slave's observation. From this it follows — or at least appears to follow — that we should not believe her own slave woman in captivity cases either.

---

## Witness Credibility (II)

### Whose Slave?

Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between whose slave woman is testifying. When the *mishna* says slaves are believed in captivity cases, it refers to the husband's slave woman. The wife's own slave woman (*shifcha didah*) is the one who cannot be trusted.

The *gemara* challenges this: a *baraita* states explicitly that *ein adam meid al atzmo* — a person cannot testify about herself — but that everyone else can testify for her. Surely that "everyone else" includes even her own slave woman? The *gemara* answers: *shifchasa ke'atzma dami* — her own slave woman is treated as equivalent to herself and falls within the same prohibition. Just as the woman cannot testify on her own behalf, neither can her slave testify as if she were the woman herself.

### No Active Lies

Rav Ashi offers a more refined resolution that does not depend on *bishvuya hekilu* at all. He argues that the two sources address different types of conduct. A slave woman *meichazi chazya ve'shaski* — sees what she sees and stays silent. That is, in the *get* context, she was present while her mistress had relations with the husband and said nothing, because her mistress acts with complete freedom before her. This silence, or this withholding of information, is one thing. But when she comes to court and must make an affirmative statement — that too might involve simply saying "I was with her," without actively vouching for something she knows to be false.

### Silence vs. Testimony

The key distinction is as follows. In the *get* case, where her silence makes her mistress more permissible, the slave woman may simply not disclose damaging information. But in the captivity case, *de'shikuta osarta* — where silence would render her mistress forbidden, the only way to help her mistress is to actively testify that she was not raped. And that, Rav Ashi argues, she will do honestly. *Tartei lo avda* — she will not do two things wrong simultaneously. She may withhold; she will not lie outright. Therefore, when she does come forward and testify affirmatively that her mistress was not raped, she is believed — not as a special leniency for captivity cases, but because we are simply not concerned that she is fabricating testimony.

---

## Mari Bar Isak Case

### Brother Inheritance

The *gemara* now introduces a parallel case that illuminates the same principle. Mari bar Isak (some say Chana bar Isak) had a long-lost brother appear from Bei Chozai claiming a share of their late father's estate. Mari replied that he did not recognize this person as his brother. When the matter came before Rav Chisda, Rav Chisda initially sided with Mari: *shapir ka'amar lach* — he is saying well to you. As proof that non-recognition does not imply bad faith, the *gemara* cites the verse *vayakker Yosef et echav ve'heim lo hikkiruhu* — Yosef recognized his brothers but they did not recognize him — and explains that Yosef had left without a beard and returned with one, making recognition genuinely difficult after many years. Mari's failure to recognize a brother he had not seen for two decades cannot be taken as evidence of fraud.

### Fear Shifts Burden

Rav Chisda then told the claimant to bring witnesses to establish his identity. The claimant said he had witnesses, but *mistafu minei degavra alma hu* — they were afraid of Mari, who was a man of force, a powerful and intimidating figure. According to Tosafot, what actually happened is that the witnesses were brought and then refused to testify at all — neither confirming nor denying the claim. This conspicuous silence was itself suspicious; why would witnesses refuse to speak unless they were being intimidated into silence? Rav Chisda therefore took the striking step of reversing the burden of proof and instructing Mari to go bring witnesses that the claimant was *not* his brother — an essentially impossible evidentiary demand, but one that Rav Chisda justified by saying: *hachi danina lach u'le'chulhu amei chaverach* — this is how I deal with you and with all men of your kind. Where a party's intimidation of witnesses is evident, the ordinary rules of who bears the burden of proof can be adjusted accordingly.

### Fear & False Testimony

The *gemara* then asks: but if this man is so terrifying, will witnesses not be induced to testify *falsely* on his behalf as well? The answer is the same principle stated earlier: *tartei lo avdi* — people do not do two things. They may be intimidated into silence; they will not be frightened into outright false testimony. The case of Mari bar Isak and the case of the slave woman both illustrate this single principle from different angles. The degree of suborning required to induce active false testimony is categorically different from the pressure required to induce silence or omission.

---

## Many Witnesses

### All Can Testify

A *baraita* states that testimony about a woman's non-rape is accepted from the broadest possible range of witnesses: men, women, children, parents, siblings — virtually anyone.

### Own Children Excluded

The one exception noted in this *baraita* is her own son and daughter — presumably because children are so closely identified with their mother's interests that their testimony is not considered independent.

### Except Self & Husband

A second *baraita* takes a different approach: *hakol ne'emanim le'ha'id*, everyone is believed to testify, *chutz mi'heimeina u'va'alah* — except for herself and her husband. This *baraita* does not mention the exclusion of her children but does explicitly add the husband.

### Tannaim Views

The *gemara* observes that the positions of Rav Pappa and Rav Ashi — who disagree about her own slave woman — reflect this underlying *tannaitic* dispute. The first *baraita* (excluding her children and slaves) corresponds to one *tanna*'s position; the second *baraita* (excluding only herself and her husband) corresponds to another's. The debate among the *Amoraim* is anchored in a genuine disagreement among the *tannaim* about precisely which witnesses are too closely identified with the woman's interests to be credited.

---

## Innocent Speech

### Masiach Definition

*Masiach lefi tumo* — innocent speech, or testimony offered without awareness of its legal implications — is a recognized category in which we accord credibility even to normally disqualified witnesses or parties. When a person relates facts casually, as part of ordinary conversation, without realizing they are making a legally consequential claim, their account is treated as more reliable precisely because they have no strategic motive to shape it.

### Mother Captivity

Rav Dimi, upon returning from Eretz Yisrael, reported in the name of Rav Chanan of Carthage (*Kartagina*) a case that came before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi (some say before Rabbi himself): a certain man was relating his experience of captivity among non-Jews. He said — apparently as part of a general account of what captivity was like — *ani ve'imi nishveinu levein ovdei kochavim* — my mother and I were taken captive together. *Yatzati lishov mayim, da'ati al imi* — when I went to draw water, my thoughts were always on my mother. *Le'laket eitzim, da'ati al imi* — when I gathered wood, my thoughts were always on her. The implication of his story was that he was constantly watching over her, never leaving her unguarded.

### Mother Permitted

*Ve'hishiah Rabbi le'khunah al piv* — Rabbi ruled, on the basis of this account, that the mother was permitted to marry a *kohen*. The son had not come to offer testimony; he was simply telling the story of their captivity. Yet his innocent account contained within it all the elements needed to establish that his mother had not been violated. This is *masiach lefi tumo* at its most striking — credibility derived precisely from the absence of testimonial intent.

---

## Mishna Moot

### Leniency Summary

The *gemara* has now layered leniency upon leniency in a way that all but eliminates the practical reach of the *mishna*. The first leniency: the prohibition only applies in one's own country (per Tosafot's reading), not in enemy territory. The second: even in one's own country, it only applies if the city was sealed with a complete alarm system — chains, dogs, debris, geese. The third: even in that extreme case, if there is so much as one hiding place anywhere in the city, every woman may be presumed to have used it. The fourth: even if there is no hiding place, a woman who says she was not raped is believed by virtue of *migo*, since she could have claimed to have been in the hiding place. The fifth: even a slave woman's affirmative testimony is accepted, because *tartei lo avdi* — people do not both withhold information and testify falsely. The sixth: even casual, innocent speech (*masiach lefi tumo*) suffices to establish non-rape.

### Practical Rarity

The cumulative effect is that it is nearly impossible to construct a realistic scenario in which a woman would actually be rendered forbidden to her *kohen* husband. The *mishna*'s presumption of violation was always a *chashasha*, a concern rather than a certainty, and the *gemara* has systematically provided tools to overcome it at every stage. In practical terms, almost no actual case will result in forbiddance.

---

## Husband Testimony

### Rabbi Zechariah

The next *mishna* opens with a striking historical account. Rabbi Zechariah ben HaKatzav — Rabbi Zechariah son of the butcher — invokes an oath by the *Beis HaMikdash* and declares that from the moment the enemy entered Jerusalem until they departed, his wife's hand never left his hand. He was with her constantly, and she was not harmed.

### Self-Testimony Banned

The response from the Sages is immediate: *ein adam meid al atzmo* — a person cannot testify about himself. The phrase is in the masculine because, as the *gemara* makes clear, a husband testifying on behalf of his wife is, in effect, testifying about himself — his ability to remain married to her depends on the outcome, and he is therefore a directly interested party whose testimony cannot be received.

### Husband Can't Permit

The practical implication is stark: even a *kohen* husband who was physically present with his wife throughout the siege, never separated from her for a moment, cannot by his own testimony render her permitted to him. His testimony, however honest and however corroborated by circumstance, is categorically excluded. This ruling reminds us that the *mishna*'s framework, for all the *gemara*'s leniencies, still has a floor: the husband's word alone will never suffice.

---

## Protective Arrangement

### Separate Housing

A *baraita* describes the practical arrangement that Rabbi Zechariah ben HaKatzav put in place given his legal situation. Since he could not testify on his wife's behalf and therefore could not simply continue their marriage as before, he arranged for her to have her own house (*bayit*) within the family compound (*chatzeiro*). They remained married, but they would no longer share quarters.

### Seclusion Prevention

The challenge was to ensure that they were never in *yichud* together, which would itself raise concerns and complicate her status further. The solution was carefully choreographed around the movements of their children. *U'che'she'yotza, yotza be'rosh baneha* — when she left the compound, she would walk at the head of the group of children, so that the husband would never be left alone with her. *U'che'she'nichnesa, nichnesa be'sof baneha* — when they returned, she would enter last, after the children had already gone in.

### Marriage Maintained

In this way, Rabbi Zechariah ben HaKatzav managed to maintain the marriage legally — keeping his wife within the family compound, within reach of the children, and part of the household — while ensuring that no opportunity for *yichud* ever arose that could further compromise her status or his. It is an arrangement that reflects both legal ingenuity and personal devotion: a *kohen* who could not testify for his wife found a way, through scrupulous arrangement of daily life, to keep the marriage intact within the law's constraints.

---

---

# Ketubot 28

## Zechariah ben HaKatzav

### Non-Jews Enter City

The daf opens by returning to the *mishna* at the bottom of 27b, which deals with the question of whether women's marital status is compromised when enemy troops enter a city. Although the *mishna* appears to treat the concern broadly — that any woman married to a *kohen* may be suspected of having been violated — the *gemara* effectively narrows the circumstances to the point where the rule would rarely apply. The *mishna* already establishes that a single witness is believed in such a case, though there is debate about a maidservant or the husband himself. Working within the framework of the *mishna*, which does not credit the husband's testimony, we arrive at the case of Zechariah ben HaKatzav.

### Zechariah Testimony

The *mishna* records: *Amar Zechariah ben HaKatzav: hamaon hazeh* — by this Temple, he swore, *lo zaza yada mitoch yadi mishesha nichnesu ovdei kochavim li'Yerushalayim v'ad sheyatzu* — from the time the non-Jews entered Jerusalem until they left, her hand never left my hand. Whether this refers to the destruction of the Temple or a later episode such as the time of Bar Kochba is uncertain. The claim is clear: he was with her the entire time, so she could not have been violated. Yet the Rabbis respond: *ein adam me'id al atzmo* — a person cannot testify on his own behalf. Because his testimony bears directly on his wife's permissibility to him, it is considered self-interested and therefore inadmissible. What is striking here is that both he and she presumably know the true facts — and yet the rabbinic posture is that they cannot simply continue their lives together on the basis of their own knowledge.

### Living Arrangements

A *tanna* adds: *v'af al pi chen yiched lah bayit bechatzeiro* — even so, he set aside a house for her within his courtyard. They did not — or could not — simply resume cohabitation, yet she remained within the family compound. The arrangement was carefully managed: *uch'she'hi yotza yotza berosh b'nei uch'she'hi nichneset nichneset besof b'nei* — when she left she went at the head of the children, and when she entered she came in at the rear of the group, so that she would never be left alone with him in the courtyard. Whether they divorced formally or simply ceased living as husband and wife is not entirely clear from the text, but the living arrangement itself was structured to prevent *yichud*.

## Gerusha Restrictions

### Abaye's Question

This case prompts Abaye to pose a question: *mahu la'asot begerusha kein?* — what about arranging a similar arrangement for a *gerusha*, a divorced woman? That is, if a *kohen* divorces his wife and she wishes to continue living within the same courtyard — perhaps to continue raising the children — can that arrangement be structured so as to prevent *yichud* and thereby be permissible?

### Shvuyah vs. Gerusha

The *gemara* distinguishes the cases. In the earlier scenario, the leniency derives from the fact that we are dealing with a *shvuyah* — or a woman in analogous circumstances — where there is doubt about what actually occurred. *Hatam hu debishvuyah hikilu* — there they were lenient because it was not established that she was actually forbidden. *Aval hacha lo* — but here, in the case of a *gerusha*, there is no doubt: she is definitively forbidden to her former husband who is a *kohen*. The question remains whether this distinction is determinative: *o dilma lo shna* — or perhaps it makes no difference?

### Baraita Shchunah

*Ta shema, ditanya* — come and hear what was taught in a *baraita*: *Hamgaresh ishto lo tinnasei bishchunutah* — if a man divorces his wife, she should not remarry and settle within the same *shchunah*, the same neighborhood. Rashi explains the concern: this previously married couple, who now belong to others, know each other's body language and habits well, and proximity will make it dangerously easy for them to fall into an illicit relationship. *V'im haya kohen lo tadur immo bemavui* — and if the divorcing husband was a *kohen*, she cannot even live with him in the same *mavui*, even if she has not remarried at all.

### Shchunah/Mavui Defined

It is worth clarifying the spatial terminology. A *shchunah* refers to a neighborhood in the general sense — Tosafot defines it as within three houses. A *mavui* is an alley or passage into which multiple courtyards open, making it a larger area than the *chatzer*, the courtyard, where individual homes face each other. The earlier case of Zechariah ben HaKatzav involved housing within a single *chatzer* — *bayit bechatzeiro*. The *baraita* here speaks of a *kohen* and his *gerusha* needing to be separated by an even greater distance, namely the entire *mavui*, precisely because when she is not remarried the concern for renewed intimacy is even more acute.

Tosafot notes that the distinction maps onto the level of concern: when she has remarried another man, keeping them out of the same *shchunah* suffices. But when she is unmarried and forbidden to him as his *gerusha*, they must be entirely out of the same *mavui*. If the town is a small village, the *baraita* treats it as equivalent to a *shchunah*, though the Bach emends this to read *kemavui*.

### Who Must Move

This raises a practical question: *Mi nidche mipnei mi?* — who must actually leave? The language of the *baraita* — *lo tadur*, *lo tinnasei* — places the obligation on her. A further *baraita* confirms: *hi nidcheit mipanav, veino nidche mipaneha* — she is the one displaced by his presence; he need not move on account of her. The underlying logic is that upon divorce she leaves the household — *veyatza mibeito* — and so the question of where she resettles is hers to manage, not his.

However, this changes if she owns the property: *veim hayta chatzer shelah, hu nidche mipaneha* — if the courtyard was hers, he is the one who must move.

### Joint Ownership

A question is then raised: *hayta chatzer shel shneihem mahu?* — what if the courtyard was jointly owned? Both have a legal claim to remain. The *gemara* attempts to resolve this by examining the source of the rule that she is displaced: *hi nidcheit mipanav* — the initial statement assumed his courtyard. If it were hers, he moves. The joint case is left ambiguous, and the *gemara* considers the possibility that the ruling applies only when one party is a renter with no real ownership stake — *dilma de'oger miger* — in which case she, as the departing party, would be the one to go. But when there is true joint title, who prevails is genuinely unclear.

### Rav's Statement

The *gemara* resolves the case of joint ownership by appeal to a verse and a ruling of Rav. The verse, *Hinei Hashem metaltelcha taltela gever*, speaks of divine exile as a punishment — *taltela gever*, the exile of a man. From this Rav derives: *taltulei de'gavra kashi mede'itata* — it is harder for a man to be uprooted than for a woman. Since this was framed as a curse, the inference is that displacement is more burdensome for a man. Therefore, even in a case of joint ownership, she is the one required to move, as her uprooting causes relatively less hardship.

One might note the irony: the woman is called the *bayit*, the home; she is the one who raises the children and provides domestic stability. And yet the societal structure — the assumption that the household belongs to the man — leads to this conclusion. The practical reality in many divorce situations today, of course, runs in the opposite direction, precisely because the woman's stability is recognized as essential for the children.

## Legal Proceedings

### Loan Repayment

The *gemara* continues in this vein, addressing further contact between a *kohen* and his divorced wife. *Tanu Rabbanan*: if when they were married he took out a loan from her — Rashi explains this refers to property she brought into the marriage, the *nichsei milog* — and now they are divorced, *ela einah nifraat ela al yedei acher* — she may only collect repayment through an intermediary. The concern is that having them meet privately for the purpose of a financial transaction will lead to intimacy. Similarly, she should not personally press the claim; she too should send a representative.

### Rav Sheshet

Rav Sheshet goes considerably further: *de'atu lekaman ledina, lo mizdakkinnan lehu* — if they come before us for a court case, we refuse to hear it. This is a striking and puzzling position. Any two people involved in a legal dispute must be able to bring their matter before a *beit din*. The concern, as Rav Pappa explains, is that litigation between a *kohen* and his *gerusha* will involve repeated meetings — at the courthouse, over discussions of the case — and familiarity will breed opportunity. One might ask: is the alternative really better? Refusing to adjudicate hardly eliminates the tension; if anything, it forces them to deal with their dispute without any structure at all.

### Shamta/Lashes

The alternatives offered are even more puzzling. Rav Pappa says *shamutei mishamttinan lehu* — we place them under *shamta*, a minor form of excommunication. Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua adds *nagudei nami menagdinan lehu* — we even administer lashes. What this is meant to accomplish in practical terms is difficult to understand. It does not resolve their dispute or give either party a remedy.

### Rav Nachman Source

Rav Nachman cites a Tannaitic source: *Tana d'vei Abba Rabbati*, meaning the tractate known as *Masechet Semachot* (also called *Avel Rabbati*), a collection of Tannaitic and Amoraic statements. Though associated with mourning law, the passage here is not about *aveilut* at all.

### Nisuin vs. Eirussin

The source clarifies: *bamei devarim amurim* — when do these restrictions apply? *Shenitgarsha min hanisuinn* — when they had actually lived together as husband and wife, having had full *nisuinn*. *Aval nitgarsha min haeirussin* — but if they had only been *mekudeshet* and the marriage was dissolved before *nisuinn*, with no prior sexual relationship, then *nifraat al yedei atzmah* — she may herself be present to collect the loan, *she'ein libo gas bah* — because he does not feel so comfortable with her that contact will lead to intimacy.

### Rava's Intermediary

A case then comes before Rava: a man and woman who had been betrothed — *eirusin* without *nisuinn* — came to him for a court case. Rav Adda bar Matna was sitting before him. Rava placed a third party between them — *oki Rava shlucha beinaihu* — so that they could each present their positions through a representative rather than address each other directly. This is the practical solution the *gemara* has been moving toward.

Rav Adda bar Matna challenges Rava: we have just learned from Rav Nachman that in the case of *eirusin* alone, no such precaution is necessary. Rava responds: *k'chazina d'kagaissi b'hadadi* — I can see from their body language that they are very comfortable with one another, and so I am being appropriately cautious.

### Implementation Dispute

An alternative version of the exchange presents the case in reverse. According to *ika d'amri* — some say — Rava did *not* initially put an intermediary in place. Rav Adda bar Matna suggested he should, citing Rav Nachman's leniency for *eirusin* cases. Rava replied that in this particular instance the couple's ease with one another was evident — *k'chazina d'ka gaissi b'hadadi* — and therefore caution was warranted. The two versions converge on the same outcome: the intermediary is required when the couple demonstrates a level of comfort that creates genuine risk, regardless of whether they had experienced *nisuinn*.

One student's observation sheds light on the earlier puzzle of refusing to hear cases or imposing *shamta* and lashes: perhaps those rulings apply only where no intermediary arrangement has been established. Once the *gemara* arrives at Rava's solution, it retroactively supplies the practical mechanism that makes the other restrictions coherent.

## Childhood Testimony

### Mishna Categories

The *mishna* — the final *mishna* of the chapter — introduces a new set of rules: *v'eilu ne'emanim l'ha'id b'godlan mah she'ra'u b'kotnan* — the following are believed to testify as adults about what they saw when they were children. The underlying principle requires explanation. The *gemara* will establish that for standard testimony, a person must be a *kosher eid* — a valid witness — not only at the moment of testifying but at the moment of witnessing. A child, like a slave or non-Jew, is not a valid witness. Therefore, observations made in childhood would ordinarily be inadmissible. The *mishna* lists the exceptions, and the *gemara* will explain each one.

This *mishna* serves as a fitting conclusion to the chapter. The chapter began with the question of whether a woman was a *besulah* at the time of her first marriage — relevant to her *kesubah* of 200. That led to discussions of testimony about personal status, about weddings and witnesses, about women suspected of violation. Now the chapter closes by addressing how certain kinds of testimony about such matters — observed in childhood — may nonetheless be accepted.

### Signature Recognition

The first category: *ne'eman adam lomar zeh ktav yado shel abba, v'zeh ktav yado shel rebbi, v'zeh ktav yado shel achi* — a person may testify that he recognizes the signature of his father, his teacher, or his brother, having seen it as a child. This is relevant to *kiyum shtaros*, the rabbinic requirement to validate the signatures on a document before it may be enforced in court.

The second category: *zachur hayiti b'ploni sheyatza behinuma verosha parua* — I remember that so-and-so went out in that bridal procession with her hair uncovered, meaning it was a first wedding, with all the ceremony and display that that entails. This ties directly back to the first *mishna* of the chapter, about whether a woman was a virgin at the time of her marriage, which determines whether her *kesubah* is 200 or 100.

### Establishing Kohen

The third and fourth categories involve testimony establishing someone as a *kohen*. One may testify: *v'shayah ish ploni yotzei mibeit hasefer litvol leechol bitrumah* — I remember that a certain man would leave our school, go to the *mikvah*, and eat *terumah*. Or: *v'shayah cholek immanu al hagoren* — he would come with us and receive a portion at the granary. Both are forms of childhood observation that can establish someone's priestly status.

### Beit Hapras

One may also testify: *vehamakom hazeh beit hapras* — this area is a *beit hapras*, a field in which a grave has been plowed over and is therefore off-limits to *kohanim* due to *tumah* concerns. At first glance this seems puzzling, since such testimony restricts rather than permits. Tosafot explains that the leniency runs in the opposite direction: when a *beit hapras* cannot be precisely located within a large plot of land, *kohanim* are barred from the entire area. A childhood witness who can pinpoint the location of the grave thereby *permits* access to the rest of the field. The testimony, properly understood, is a *kulah*.

### Techumim

A further category: *vead kan hayinu ba'im b'shabbat* — we would come only this far on *Shabbat*, or we would go as far as this point, establishing the *techum*, the Sabbath boundary for the town. Since it is laborious to verify the precise location of the last inhabited structure and measure 2,000 *amot* from it, the testimony of someone who recalls the boundary from childhood carries practical weight.

### Not Believed Cases

The *mishna* then draws a sharp contrast. One is *not* believed to say *derech hayah l'ploni bemakom hazeh* — that a certain person had a right-of-way through this field — or *ma'amad umisped hayah l'ploni bemakom hazeh* — that a funeral procession with its attendant gathering of mourners would take place on this patch of land belonging to another. Both of these claims would effectively transfer property rights from one party to another. These are strict *dinei mamonot* cases, requiring formal *edut*. Childhood observation cannot supply it.

The contrast is instructive: matters of personal status, priestly standing, Sabbath boundaries, and document validation are all areas where the *mishna* makes exceptions. But the moment the testimony would result in taking property from one person and assigning rights to another, the full rigor of evidentiary law applies without exception.

## Gemara Analysis

### Kiyum Shtarot

The *gemara* now works through each category in the *mishna* to explain why the exception is warranted. Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua opens with a general qualification: *vehu sheyesh gadol immo* — the child is believed only when testifying together with an adult witness. This qualification applies at minimum to the first case of signature recognition, where two witnesses are always required to validate a document. Whether it applies to some of the other cases as well is a matter of debate among the *rishonim*.

The *gemara* also notes that all three examples of signature recognition — father, brother, and teacher — are necessary and cannot be derived from any two. If only the father's signature were mentioned, one might say the child was believed *mishum d'shchiach gabei* — because he spent so much time with his father and saw the signature frequently. But one might not extend this to the teacher. Conversely, if only the teacher's signature were mentioned, one would say the child was believed *mishum d'isa emteh d'rabbo* — because fear of the teacher made the child pay particularly careful attention, and he would never claim to recognize the signature unless he was certain. But one might exclude the father on that basis. And neither consideration applies to a brother, who is neither so constantly present as the father nor so awe-inspiring as the teacher — *d'lais lei lo hai velo hai*. Hence all three must be stated.

The underlying reason the *mishna* accepts this testimony at all: *keivan d'kiyum shtaros m'drabbanan, heimnu rabbanan b'drabbanan* — since the validation of documents is itself only a rabbinic requirement, the rabbis were willing to be lenient in accepting this testimony for a rabbinic matter.

### First Wedding

For the case of testimony that a woman was married with the full ceremony of a first wedding — *gilluy milsa b'alma hu* — the *gemara* explains that this is not really testimony in the formal sense at all. *Keivan d'rov nashim besulos nisas* — since most women who marry do so as virgins, in a first wedding, we are already operating from a strong presumption. The testimony of the childhood witness merely confirms what we would assume in any event. Rashi explains: *ein hadavar tzarich edus ela l'farseim sheyeitzei hadin l'or belo gimgum* — we do not truly need the testimony; it is only required so that the ruling can be issued with clarity and without hesitation. Since it is not substantive testimony so much as confirmation of an existing presumption, we are more lenient about its source.

### Slave Distinction

For the testimony establishing someone as a *kohen* — that he would leave school, go to the *mikvah*, and eat *terumah* — the *gemara* raises an objection: *v'dilma eved kohen hu?* — perhaps he was a slave belonging to a *kohen* rather than a *kohen* himself? Slaves of *kohanim* are permitted to eat *terumah*, so the mere fact of eating *terumah* does not prove priestly lineage.

The *gemara* answers by invoking the principle of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *asur l'adam sheyelameid avdo Torah* — it is forbidden to give one's slave a formal Torah education. If the person in question was attending school — *beit hasefer* — he cannot have been a slave, since slaves were not sent for formal Jewish schooling. One might ask: what kind of slave is this? It is an *eved Kena'ani*, a non-Jewish slave, who is on a trajectory toward partial observance but is not sent to *cheder*. The Talmud notes that such a slave might acquire some self-taught knowledge and might even read *pesukim* on his own — and a *baraita* confirms that even one who reads three *pesukim* in the synagogue, wears *tefillin* before his master, or serves as an *apitropos* over his master's estate does not thereby achieve freedom (*harei zeh lo yatza l'cheirus*). The *gemara* distinguishes between self-acquired knowledge and formal schooling: *d'kanoi bei minhag banim* — it is specifically sending a slave to school in the manner of sons that is forbidden. Since the person in question was being formally educated, he was clearly not a slave.

### Terumah D'rabbanan

Having established that the person was a *kohen* and not a slave, the *gemara* turns to why we believe the childhood witness on this point. The answer: *b'terumah d'rabbanan* — we believe him only to the extent of permitting the person to eat *terumah d'rabbanan*, rabbinic *terumah*. We are not establishing his priestly status for more consequential matters — such as questions of lineage or marriage — on the basis of childhood observation alone. Again, the pattern holds: childhood testimony is accepted for rabbinic matters or for things where formal testimony is not strictly required, but not for biblical-level determinations or for the transfer of property.

### Terumah Distribution

The *gemara* then asks about the second proof of *kehuna* — that the person would come to the granary and receive a portion — and raises the same concern: *v'dilma eved kohen hu?* — perhaps he was a slave of a *kohen*? Here the answer is different. A *baraita* is cited: *ein cholkin terumah l'eved ela im ken rabbo immo* — according to Rabbi Yehuda, you do not distribute *terumah* to a slave unless his master is present. The reason is that in a community where people draw an inference from receiving *terumah* to priestly status — *maalin mi-terumah le-yichusin* — giving *terumah* to a slave in the absence of his master would cause observers to wrongly conclude that the slave is himself a *kohen*. Therefore, if someone is receiving *terumah* independently, we may assume he is actually a *kohen*.

Rabbi Yose disagrees, permitting a slave to go on his own and state: *im kohen ani tnu li bishvil atzmi, v'im eved kohen ani tnu li bishvil rabi* — if I am the *kohen*, give it to me for myself; if I am the slave of a *kohen*, give it to me on behalf of my master. This arises in a case where a free woman and a slave woman both gave birth simultaneously and the infants were mixed up, so that neither boy knows whether he is the master or the slave. Rabbi Yose permits one to go independently in this fashion.

The *gemara* notes that the positions of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yose are perfectly correlated: in the place of Rabbi Yehuda, where receiving *terumah* serves as an indicator of priestly status for purposes of *yichusin*, one does not give to a slave without the master present. In the place of Rabbi Yose, where no such inference is drawn, one may give to a slave independently. The two rulings are logically interdependent.

### Rabbi Elazar Tale

A *baraita* concludes with a cautionary tale from Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yose. He states: *mi-yamai lo he'edati* — throughout my life I was scrupulous about not giving testimony, out of fear of causing harm through error. But *paam achas he'edati* — once I did testify — *he'alu eved le-kehuna al pi* — and based on my testimony they nearly elevated a slave to priestly status.

The *gemara* immediately asks: can we really say that happened? *Ve-hashta ma-behemtan shel tzadikim ein Hakadosh Baruch Hu mevi takala al yadam* — if God does not bring about stumbling even through the animals of the righteous (alluding to the famous story of the donkey of Pinchas ben Yair, which refused to eat food that was *tevel*), how much more so would God not allow the righteous themselves to sin? Therefore the *gemara* amends the account: *ela bikshu le-haalos eved le-kehuna al pi* — they were on the verge of doing so, and the mistake was caught at the last moment.

What happened? Rabbi Elazar had seen someone receive *terumah* independently in the locale of Rabbi Yose — where such practice is permitted even for a slave. He then went and testified about it in the locale of Rabbi Yehuda — where independent receipt of *terumah* is taken as proof of priestly status. The observation was accurate; the inference drawn from it was wrong, because the evidentiary standard was different in the two communities.

Tosafot, in several places, notes that the principle *ein Hakadosh Baruch Hu mevi takala* — that God does not cause the righteous to stumble — applies specifically to matters of forbidden food. The connection here is not exact, since it is about priestly status rather than directly about eating. But the *gemara* invokes the principle nonetheless. Whatever its precise scope, the tale is a vivid illustration of why testimony must be evaluated not only for its factual accuracy but for the interpretive framework within which it is being offered.

## Additional Categories

### Family Status

The *gemara* turns to the remaining categories of the *mishna* and the *baraita* that supplements it. The *baraita* states that a child is believed to testify: *kach amar li abba, mishpachah zu tehorah, mishpachah zu tmeiah* — my father told me that this family is *tehorah* and this family is *tmeiah*. The *gemara* immediately flags the language: *tehorah u'tmeiah salka da'atach?* — can you really have families classified as ritually pure or impure in the relevant sense? The *gemara* clarifies that this is a euphemism — or more precisely, a substitution — and the actual content is: *mishpachah zu ksheirah, mishpachah zu psulah* — this family is of fit lineage (*ksheira*), this family is of disqualified lineage (*psulah*), meaning perhaps there are *challalim* or *mamzerim* among them.

This is a considerably more sweeping claim than the other categories. Here the child is being believed not merely for the purpose of *terumah d'rabbanan* but apparently for personal status and lineage — *yichusin* — itself. The *gemara* does not dwell on this tension, moving on to the *ketzatzah* case.

### Akum/Eved

The *baraita* then addresses cases analogous to childhood: *im hayah akum v'nisgayer, eved v'nishtachrer, ein ne'emanim* — if a person was a non-Jew when he witnessed something and has since converted, or was a slave when he witnessed it and has since been freed, he is not believed. This is the default position. The question is whether such a person is in a position structurally parallel to a child — someone not yet a *kosher eid* who has now attained that status — or whether the gap is more fundamental.

The *baraita* also reiterates that in neither the case of a convert nor a freed slave is the person believed to testify about rights of way or funeral procession rights — those remain strictly in the category of *dinei mamonot* requiring formal testimony.

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka dissents: *ne'emanim* — they are believed. His position is that a former non-Jew or slave who observed certain matters is believed to testify about them now.

### Attention Debate

The *gemara* analyzes the debate between the anonymous first opinion and Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka in psychological terms. *Tanna Kama savar kivan d'akum hu lo hava dayik* — the first *tanna* holds that since the person was a non-Jew or slave at the time of witnessing, he was not paying careful attention. The events of the Jewish world were not his concern; he lacked the context to understand what he was seeing. *Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka savar kivan d'daiteih l'igiyurei mah daik yifei* — Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka holds that since the person intended to convert, he was paying close attention. The debate is thus not formal but psychological: was this person in a position to register what he witnessed with the care and comprehension that valid testimony requires?

One might note the difficulty with this framing: the *tanna kama*'s position is understandable for someone with no connection to conversion at all, but Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's leniency seems to assume the person was already on the path to conversion at the moment of witnessing — which may not always have been the case. For a freed slave, the question of whether he "intended" freedom at the time of witnessing is even more complex. The Talmud also suggests that this could be a case of *masiach l'fi tumo* — offhand, unselfconscious testimony — which carries its own evidentiary weight.

### Ketzatzah Case

The *gemara* finally turns to the *ketzatzah* case: *mai ketzatzah?* — what is this *ketzatzah* ceremony? The Rabbis taught: *Keitzad ketzatzah? Echad min ha'achim shenasa isha she'eina hogenes lo* — what is *ketzatzah*? If one of the brothers married a woman beneath his family's standing, *ba'in bnei mishpacha u'mevi'in chavit m'leia peiros, v'shovrin osa b'emtza rechova* — members of the family would come, bring a barrel filled with fruit, and smash it in the middle of the street. *V'omerim: acheinu beit Yisrael, shim'u — ploni nasa isha she'eina hogenes lo* — they would declare publicly: our brothers, the Jewish people, hear us — this man has married a woman unbefitting to him. *U'misyar'im anu shema yisarev zaro b'zareinu* — and we fear lest his offspring intermarry with ours, since by this marriage his children's *yichus* has been diminished. *V'kachu lachem dugma l'doros shelo yisarev zaro b'zareinu* — take this as a lesson for generations: his seed shall not mix with ours.

This is the ceremony that a child may testify he witnessed. What he learns from it — and what he transmits — is *yichus* information: this family's status, and by extension the standing of those who marry into it or out of it. The weight placed on lineage throughout this chapter is nowhere more dramatically illustrated than here, where a family stages a public shaming of one of its own members rather than allow the perception that his descendants carry their name and their status.

The *gemara* closes the chapter by noting the symbolic resonance of the barrel. At a first wedding, the barrel of wine — associated with the imagery of the bride — was a sign of joy and wholeness. Here, the barrel is filled with fruit, and it is smashed. If wine in the wedding context evokes the bride herself, and children are the fruit of the union, then the smashing of a barrel of fruit in the public square is a declaration that the fruit of *this* union will not be grafted onto the family tree. The imagery with which the *perek* began — the status of a bride, the question of her first wedding, the *kesubah* she is owed — closes with this public reckoning with the consequences of a marriage made without regard for *yichus*.

# Ketubot 29

## Intro & Kim Lei

### Perek Overview

The fourth *perek* of Ketubot is a chapter studied extensively in *yeshivos*, though it connects only loosely to the earlier two *perakim*. Its subject matter is more theoretical in character, dealing with cases in the Torah concerning a woman who is raped or seduced, the fines imposed, and the *mitzvah* incumbent upon the violator to marry the woman. These laws were already largely theoretical in the time of the Gemara, and certainly in our own day no one is *paskening* them practically. Nevertheless, the *perek* is rich in *lamdus* and in conceptual issues that reverberate throughout *Shas*. There is also a considerable body of *Rishonim* and Tosafot on these pages, which means that each daf will contain a relatively modest amount of actual Gemara text.

### Kim Lei Concept

One of the major theoretical issues running through the *perek* is *kim lei b'derabbah minei* — the principle that when a person is liable for two punishments simultaneously, only the more severe one is applied. This becomes directly relevant here because, in many of the cases to be discussed, the man who raped a woman was also violating an additional prohibition — for example, she is a relative — and the question arises whether that weightier punishment of *kares* or *misah* overrides the financial penalty the Torah imposes. These are among the central questions the *perek* addresses.

## Na'arah Definition

### Na'arah vs. Bogeres

The *mishnah* opens: *elu na'aros sheyesh lahem knas* — the following young women have a *knas*. A *na'arah* is a young woman who has reached *bas mitzvah* but has not yet become a *bogeres*. Halachically, *na'arah* is defined as a girl who is twelve years and one day old and has produced two pubic hairs, indicating the onset of puberty. Six months after that stage she is presumed to have reached *bagrut* and become a *bogeres* — fully physically mature, and legally independent. There are discussions in the Gemara suggesting that the transition may depend not solely on age but on additional physical indicators signaling the completion of puberty; biologically, of course, puberty takes considerably longer than six months. But halachically the framework is fixed: twelve years and one day with two pubic hairs marks the *na'arah*, and six months later the *bogeres*.

### Bogeres Exclusion

It is universally agreed upon that when the Torah describes the case of a *na'arah betulah* who is seduced or raped and imposes various fines and consequences, the word *na'arah* serves to exclude the *bogeres* — the woman who has completed puberty and is legally independent. Once she is a legal adult who stands on her own, no longer under her father's authority, the Torah's framework does not apply to her. The fine and the accompanying obligations are structured around a woman who remains under her father's control; the father, as we will see, is the recipient of the payments. This will also raise the question of what happens with a *ketannah* — a girl younger than *na'arah* — a matter the Gemara takes up in due course.

## Forbidden Women

### Mamzeres & Knas

The *mishnah* begins its list with the more marginal cases — those where one might have supposed the *knas* would not apply — in order to teach explicitly that it does. *Haba al hamamzeres* — if he raped a woman who is a *mamzeres* — one might have thought that since the Torah bundles the fine together with the *mitzvah* to marry the woman, and since it is impossible to legally marry a *mamzeres* (unless one is also a *mamzer*), perhaps none of the *halachos* would apply at all. The *mishnah* therefore teaches that this is not so: even where he cannot marry her, he must still pay the *knas*.

## Rape & Ethics

### Shechem & Dinah

To understand the Torah's framework here, some orientation to the scenario the Torah is envisioning is essential, and it is genuinely difficult for a contemporary reader. The *mohar* — the fifty *shekel* of silver that the rapist pays — and its later transformation into the *kesuvah* exist to protect the woman. In the social world the Torah addresses, a woman who had been raped or seduced would face severe difficulty in finding a husband, since she was no longer a virgin. The *mohar* was the sum that would normally pass to the father upon her marriage; the *knas* ensures that money is available to protect her when the normal path to marriage becomes difficult. And in the most extreme case — that of the rapist — the Torah goes further and requires him to marry her and prohibits him from ever divorcing her, because in that social context marriage to him may represent the most reliable form of protection available to her.

For a modern reader, the notion that the rapist must marry his victim is deeply troubling, and it is important to think carefully about what the Torah is imagining. The *Shechem v'Dinah* narrative is instructive. The text says *vayishkav otah vayan'ah* — he lay with her and violated her — but it also describes Shechem's profound attachment to Dinah afterward: *vatidbak nafsho*, his soul cleaved to her, and he sought to marry her. The Torah seems to be imagining cases that, while unambiguously constituting rape, involve a man who was deeply attracted to a woman, had no legitimate avenue to pursue her in a tightly controlled society with no courtship culture, and acted on impulse — while not necessarily being someone who would be characterized as a predatory rapist in the way that term is understood today. The Torah apparently envisions scenarios in which, if the woman acquiesces, a viable marriage might follow. This does not excuse the act, and there is a spectrum, but it helps explain why the Torah could conceive of marriage as a possible outcome.

### Ethical Problem

A serious pedagogical problem attends the study of this *perek*, and it deserves to be named. Because the chapter is studied so widely in *yeshivos* as a vehicle for abstract legal analysis, the actual human reality that underlies it tends to disappear entirely from view. The words *ones* and *mefateh* — rapist and seducer — become technical legal categories, not descriptions of real acts committed against real women. Nobody uses the word "rape" in the learning, which would be deeply disturbing and would force a confrontation with the real world. The entire *perek* can be traversed as a set of interesting conceptual problems in *Shas* while the human situation that generated those laws remains completely bracketed. This is particularly acute in contexts where the Hebrew vocabulary does not carry the immediate emotional register it would carry for a native Hebrew speaker, and the Aramaic terminology of the Gemara adds another layer of abstraction. It is a real problem in how this material is transmitted, and it is worth pausing to acknowledge it before proceeding.

## Forbidden Women (II)

### Netinah Category

The *mishnah* continues: *v'al hanetinah* — and also if he raped a woman who is a *netinah*. There is a significant dispute between Rashi and Tosafot regarding the identity of the *netinim*. Rashi holds that the *netinim* are the Gibeonites — the *Givonim* — who made peace with Yehoshua. When Yehoshua realized they had deceived him, he made them into slaves to serve the *Beis HaMikdash*, as woodchoppers and water-drawers (*chotevei etzim*). According to Rashi, the prohibition against marrying a *netinah* stems from their slave status. This is somewhat difficult, however, because the relevant prohibition against marrying a slave would normally apply only to a non-Jewish slave, not a *shifcha Kena'anit* or an *eved Ivri* — categories that can in various ways involve marriage. Tosafot therefore offers a different explanation: the *netinim* are forbidden not because of slave status but because they are descendants of the *shiv'at amamim*, the seven Canaanite nations, and the prohibition of *lo titchaten bam* — do not intermarry with them — continues to apply even after they converted.

### Kutit/Samaritans

The *mishnah* then adds: *v'al ha-Kutit* — and also a Samaritan woman. The question of what is problematic about marrying a Samaritan turns on a dispute about the validity of their conversion. According to Rashi, the *mishnah* is operating on the assumption that the Samaritans' conversion during the period of the *Bayit Sheini* was not considered valid — that they were *gerei arayot*, converts who adopted the religion of the land only because lions came and frightened them, not *gerei emet*, genuine converts. On that reading they would be non-Jews, which immediately creates a difficulty: a *knas* is paid only to a Jewish woman, as is clear from the earlier Gemara. If they are non-Jewish, there should be no *knas* at all.

Tosafot addresses this by assuming that the Samaritans did undergo a valid conversion and are considered Jewish. Why then might one have thought there would be no *knas*? Because the *Chachamim* were deeply concerned about maintaining separation between normative rabbinic Jews and the Samaritans. The Samaritans had their own place of worship on *Har Gerizim*, their own interpretations of law, and their own communal identity — they were essentially a separate sect, almost a separate religion, even if technically Jewish. The rabbis therefore worked hard to maintain firm communal boundaries. One might have thought: do not pay a *knas* to a Samaritan woman, because doing so might blur those boundaries and encourage the very intermingling that rabbinic policy sought to prevent. The *mishnah* teaches that even so, the *knas* is paid. To summarize the first three cases: a *mamzeres*, prohibited to marry but *knas* still applies; a *netinah*, prohibited to marry either because of the *shiv'at amamim* or slave status, but *knas* still applies; and a *Kutit*, where policy considerations might have militated against the *knas* but do not.

## Non-Virgin Cases

### Pre-3-Year-Old Rule

The *mishnah* continues: *haba al ha-giyores v'al ha-shevuyah v'al ha-shifchah* — if he raped a convert, a captive woman, or a freed slave woman. These three constitute a second category, distinct from the first. The issue here is not a prohibition against marriage, but rather the presumption that these women may not be virgins. A woman who converted from non-Jewish status, or who was taken captive, or who had been a slave, may have had prior sexual experience — in which case she would not be a *betulah* and the *knas*, which is tied to virginity, would not apply.

The *mishnah* specifies: *shenifdu v'shenisgayru v'shenishtachreru pachos mibnos shalosh shanim v'yom echad* — if they were redeemed, converted, or freed before the age of three years and one day, then they do have a *knas*. The Gemara operates on the assumption that intercourse with a girl under the age of three is not halachically considered an act of *biah*, and moreover, that physiologically the *besulim* would have grown back. Therefore, even if something had occurred before that age, she would still be considered a *betulah* for these purposes. If these events — conversion, redemption, or freedom — occurred after the age of three, there is concern that virginity may have been lost and the presumption of *betulah* status cannot be maintained.

## Karat Relatives

### Karat List

The *mishnah* presents a third category: *v'haba al achoso v'al achas aviv v'al achas imo v'al achas ishto v'al eshes achiv v'al eshes achi aviv* — if he raped his sister, his father's sister, his mother's sister, his wife's sister, his brother's wife, or his father's brother's wife. These are all cases of *chayavei krisos* — violations subject to *kares*. Several conditions must be met in each case for the *knas* to apply. In the case of the brother's wife, the brother must have either divorced her or died, since if the brother is still married to her she is a fully married woman, a different category entirely. And the woman must never have had intercourse with the brother, because she must still be a *betulah*. Similarly with the father's brother's wife: the uncle must have died or divorced her, and she must never have had relations with him.

### Niddah & Knas

The *mishnah* adds: *v'al ha-niddah* — and also a woman who is a *niddah*. This too carries an *issur kares*, and nevertheless there is a *knas*.

### Karat vs. Knas

The *mishnah* concludes: *af al pi shehen b'hikhares ein bahen misat beis din* — although these women carry the punishment of *kares*, there is no *mitat beis din* — no court-imposed death penalty — and therefore in all these cases there is still a *knas*. This is the key distinction. The first category — *issur lav* — is notable because even though there is a negative prohibition, the *knas* applies, and moreover, while the marriage would be prohibited, it would be binding *bedi'eved*. The third category — *issur kares* — is more striking, because marriage would not be binding even after the fact, and one might have argued that the weightier punishment of *kares* overrides the monetary obligation through *kim lei b'derabbah minei*. The *mishnah* teaches that neither of these considerations eliminates the *knas*, provided the woman is still a *betulah* in each case.

## Meir vs. Chachamim

### Rabbi Meir View

The Gemara notes that the *mishnah* speaks of a *na'arah* and infers that a *ketannah* is excluded. The Gemara asks: whose position is this? *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav* — Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav — *Rabbi Meir hi*, it is the position of Rabbi Meir, as taught in a *braisa*. The *braisa* states: *ketannah mi-bat yom echad v'ad she-tavi shtei searot yesh lah mecher v'ein lah knas* — from the day she is born until she produces two pubic hairs and reaches twelve years old, the father may sell her as a slave (*shifchah*), as we read in Parshas Mishpatim, and during this period there is no *knas*. *U-mi-she-tavi shtei searot v'ad she-tivgar yesh lah knas v'ein lah mecher* — once she has the two hairs until she reaches full maturity as a *bogeres*, she has a *knas* and can no longer be sold. These are mutually exclusive categories according to Rabbi Meir: *kol makom she-yesh mecher ein knas v'chol makom she-yesh knas ein mecher* — wherever there is *mecher* there is no *knas*, and wherever there is *knas* there is no *mecher*.

### Chachamim View

The *Chachamim* disagree. They say: *ktana mi-bat shalosh shanim v'yom echad v'ad she-tivgar yesh lah knas* — from age three years and one day until she reaches full maturity, there is a *knas*. This creates an overlap with the period of *mecher*: from age three until twelve, the father can still sell her, since she is a *ketannah* under full paternal control, but at the same time the *knas* already applies because she is old enough for the act to be considered a halachic *biah*.

### Gemara Resolution

The Gemara clarifies the positions. According to Rabbi Meir, *mecher* and *knas* are strictly exclusive: from zero to twelve there is *mecher* and no *knas*, from twelve to twelve-and-a-half there is *knas* and no *mecher*. According to the *Chachamim*, *mecher* applies from birth until twelve (since she is a *ketannah*), while *knas* begins at age three and continues until *bagrut*, creating an overlap between ages three and twelve.
