Everyone agrees that *mecher* applies only while she is a *ketannah*, and everyone agrees that acts of *biah* with a girl under three are not halachically considered *biah* for these purposes. The debate between Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* comes down to whether the *knas* applies to a *ketannah* at all.

## Marriage Requirement

### Fitness to Marry

Having established this debate, the Gemara returns to the main point of the *mishnah*: that even these women who cannot be married by the rapist still receive a *knas*. The Gemara asks: *ve-hanei bnei knasa ninhu?* — are these women really subject to the *knas*? *Ve-amai?* — why? The Torah says *v'lo tihiyeh l'ishah* — she shall be to him as a wife — which implies, *isha ha-rauyah lo*, a woman who is fitting for him, someone he could in theory marry. Should not all these forbidden women be excluded? The reason the *knas* is not simply identical to a requirement of actual marriage is that the woman could refuse, or he might not be able to marry her for other reasons, and the *knas* is still paid. But at minimum she ought to be someone who *could* in principle be married.

## Textual Redundancy

### Reish Lakish

Reish Lakish answers that the Torah uses the word *na'arah* in redundant ways that allow for additional *drashos*. The *pasuk* says *ki yimtza ish na'arah betulah* — once — and then says *v'natan le-avi ha-na'arah* — to the father of the *na'arah*. That second mention, *ha-na'arah*, is understood as extra: the Torah could have said *le-aviha*, to her father. By saying *le-avi ha-na'arah*, the definite form counts as two words — *na'arah* and *ha-na'arah* — since it could have said simply *na'arah* without the definite article. *Chad legufei* — one usage is needed simply to establish that the victim must be a *na'arah* and not a *bogeres*. *V'chad le-atuyei chayavei lavin* — the extra word teaches that even women for whom there is a negative prohibition to marry are included. *V'chad le-atuyei chayavei krisos* — and the further extra word teaches that even women carrying an *issur kares* are included.

### Rav Pappa

Rav Pappa derives the same provisions from a different source: *betulah betulah ha-betulos*. In the case of the seducer (*mefateh*), the Torah says *v'ki yefateh ish betulah asher lo orasa v'shachav imah* — if a man seduces a *betulah* who is not betrothed — which is needed for its own sake. It then says *ke-mohar ha-betulos* — like the *mohar* of virgins — where it could have simply said *ke-mohar* or *ke-mohar ha-betulah*. The plural *ha-betulos* is treated as contributing two words. *Chad legufei*, one for its own sake; *v'chad le-atuyei chayavei lavin*, one to include those with a negative prohibition; *v'chad le-atuyei chayavei krisos*, one to include those with *kares*.

### Abaye's Rule

The Gemara then asks why Rav Pappa did not simply use Reish Lakish's *drasha* from *na'arah*. The answer is that Rav Pappa needed the word *na'arah* to derive what Abaye teaches. *De-amar Abaye: ba'ah le-ha'amadah patur* — if the girl died before the time came to pay the fine, the rapist is exempt. The source for this ruling is *v'natan le-avi ha-na'arah* — and he shall give to the father of the *na'arah* — not *le-aviha*, to her father in the abstract. The definite form *ha-na'arah* implies that at the moment of payment she must be identifiable and present as a *na'arah*, meaning she must still be alive. *Le-avi ha-na'arah v'lo le-avi mesah* — to the father of the *na'arah*, not to the father of a dead woman.

This ruling opens a deeper conceptual question: when the father receives the *knas*, is he receiving it directly in his own right, or is he collecting on behalf of the daughter? The ruling of *ba'ah le-ha'amadah patur* suggests the latter — that the payment flows through her, which is why her absence at the time of payment exempts the payer. One could argue it is simply *gzeiras ha-kasuv*, but the question will generate a broader discussion about the nature of the *knas* payment that the Gemara will pursue.

### Six Words Rule

The Gemara then observes that both Reish Lakish and Rav Pappa need their respective words for different purposes, and asks how either of them can derive the inclusion of *chayavei lavin* and *chayavei krisos* if each extra word is already spoken for. The resolution is that there are in fact six words combined: *na'arah, na'arah, ha-na'arah* (from the *pasuk* dealing with the rapist) and *betulah, betulot, ha-betulos* (from the *pasuk* dealing with the seducer). *Trei l'gufeih* — two are needed for the plain sense of the *pesukim*, one *na'arah* and one *betulah*. *Chad l'chid'Abaye* — one of the *na'arah* forms teaches Abaye's rule that she must be alive at the time of payment. *V'chad l'gezeirah shavah* — one of the *betulah* forms is needed for the *gezeirah shavah* linking the two cases. And the remaining two — one extra *na'arah* and one extra *betulah* — serve to include *chayavei lavin* and *chayavei krisos* respectively. *Yasiri lehu trei, chad l'atuyei chayvei lavin v'chad l'atuyei chayvei keritot.*

It is worth pausing to note what the *gezeirah shavah* accomplishes. The *pasuk* by the *mefateh* says *kesef yishkol ke-mohar ha-betulos* — he shall pay money like the *mohar* of virgins — without specifying a quantity. The *pasuk* by the *ones* says *v'natan le-avi ha-na'arah chamishim kesef* — fifty *kesef* — without specifying the denomination. From the seducer's case we know a number but not the coin; from the rapist's case we know the coin is *shekel* from context, but not which number applies to the seducer. The *gezeirah shavah* linking *betulos* here to the fifty over there allows us to derive: fifty *shekel* in both cases.

## Shimeon Positions

### Hatimni View

The Gemara turns to alternative positions that the *mishnah* is implicitly rejecting. A *braisa* teaches the view of Shimon Hatimni: *v'lo tihiyeh l'ishah* — she shall be to him as a wife — this means only a woman for whom the *havayah* of marriage would be binding: *isha she'yesh bah havayah*. Since *kiddushin* does not take effect with *chayavei krisos*, those women would be excluded from the *knas* according to Shimon Hatimni. Women subject only to an *issur lav* would still be included, because marriage to them, while prohibited, would be binding *bedi'eved*.

### Ben Azai View

Rabbi Shimon ben Azai goes further, deriving from *v'lo tihiyeh* — with emphasis on *lo*, for him — that the woman must be *isha ha-re'uyah lekayma*, a woman fitting for him to remain married to. This means she must be completely permitted (*mutar*), not merely capable of a binding marriage. On this reading, even *chayavei lavin* — where marriage is prohibited but would be binding — would be excluded from the *knas*.

### Rav Zeira

Rav Zeira identifies the practical difference between these two positions: *mamzeres u'nesina ika beinaihu*. A *mamzeres* or a *netinah* — their marriages are prohibited, but marriage with them would be binding *bedi'eved*. According to Shimon Hatimni, who requires only that the marriage be binding (*havayah*), a *mamzeres* and a *netinah* would be included in the *knas*: *hai nami yesh bah havayah*. According to Rabbi Shimon ben Azai, who requires that the woman actually be fitting to remain married to (*re'uyah lekayma*), a *mamzeres* and a *netinah* would be excluded: *ha einah re'uyah lekayma*. Our *mishnah* rejects both positions and rules that the *knas* applies regardless — whether *issur lav* or *issur kares*, the fine is paid.

## Rabbi Akiva

### Akiva Rule

The Gemara digresses to explore an adjacent question. According to Rabbi Akiva, *ein kiddushin tofsim b'chayavei lavin* — betrothal does not take effect with women subject to a negative prohibition. If that is so, then for Rabbi Akiva the distinction between the two positions above collapses: whether you require binding marriage or permitted marriage, the result is the same, since even *chayavei lavin* cannot be married bindingly according to Rabbi Akiva. What then would be the *nafka mina* between those two positions for Rabbi Akiva? The Gemara answers: *ika beinaihu almanah le-kohen gadol* — the case of a widow married to a *kohen gadol*. This is an *issur lav*, yet a unique *braisa* teaches: *detanya Rabbi Simai omer min ha-kol osir Rabbi Akiva mamzerim* — Rabbi Akiva would declare children *mamzerim* from all forbidden unions, *chutz me'almanah le-kohen gadol*, except for the case of a widow with a *kohen gadol*.

### Mamzer & Binding

The assumption underlying the entire discussion is that these two principles — whether *kiddushin* is binding and whether the child is a *mamzer* — are two expressions of the same underlying rule. If Rabbi Akiva holds that *kiddushin* does not take effect by *chayavei lavin*, then the child born of such a union would be a *mamzer*; and conversely, the statement that he would make *mamzerim* from *chayavei lavin* implies that *kiddushin* is not binding in those cases. The standard ruling (*halacha*) is that *mamzer* status results only from an *issur kares*, and correspondingly, *kiddushin* is not binding only in *issur kares* cases. Rabbi Akiva extends both principles to *issur lav* as well.

The reason the *almanah le-kohen gadol* case is different, the Gemara explains, is the *pasuk*: *lo yikach v'lo yechalel* — he shall not marry her and shall not desecrate his seed. *Chilui hu oseh v'ein oseh mamzer* — if the *kohen gadol* marries a widow, he produces a *chalal* (a desecrated *kohen*) but not a *mamzer*. This is because the prohibition of *almanah le-kohen gadol* is a prohibition that applies only to *kohanim*, not to all Jews (*asurah lakol*). When a prohibition pertains only to *kehuna*, it affects the *kehuna* status of the child — producing a *chalal* — but does not affect the validity of the *kiddushin* or generate *mamzer* status. This means that even within Rabbi Akiva's system there remains a gap between "not binding" and "not permitted": a *gerushah le-kohen hedyot*, for example, is prohibited to that *kohen* yet the *kiddushin* would remain binding — the child would be a *chalal*, not a *mamzer*.

## Yeshevav Position

### Yeshevav All Case

The Gemara continues: *u'le-Rabbi Yeshevav* — and according to Rabbi Yeshevav, *d'amar bo v'nitztavei'ach al Akiva ben Yosef* — who said: come, let us cry out against Akiva the son of Yosef — *she-haya omer kol she'ein bo biah b'Yisrael ha-vlad mamzer* — who taught that any forbidden act of intercourse whatsoever produces a *mamzer*. The expression of outrage built into the way Rabbi Yeshevav formulates his criticism is itself significant: it reflects the enormity of the category he is attributing to Rabbi Akiva. If literally every forbidden union produced a *mamzer*, the number of *mamzerim* would be staggering. The Gemara is interested in whether *kol* — all — truly means all, or whether Rabbi Yeshevav is only pushing back against one specific position.

### Yeshevav Limited

The Gemara considers two readings of Rabbi Yeshevav's statement. If he is responding specifically to Rabbi Simai — who said that *almanah le-kohen gadol* does not produce a *mamzer* — then Rabbi Yeshevav's *kol* might only mean: even that case produces a *mamzer*, not necessarily every conceivable case including *chayavei asei*. In that reading, *kol* is rhetorically expansive but not literally all-inclusive. However, if Rabbi Yeshevav is issuing a free-standing statement on his own authority, then *kol she'ein bo biah b'Yisrael* should be understood literally — any forbidden intercourse produces a *mamzer*, including cases of *issur asei*. In that case, the Gemara asks, *mai beinaihu* — what would be the difference — between the two formulations (binding versus permitted) for Rabbi Akiva according to Rabbi Yeshevav? And it answers: there would still be one case remaining where even Rabbi Akiva, according to Rabbi Yeshevav's broadest reading, might concede that *kiddushin* is binding — *be'ulah le-kohen gadol*, a non-virgin woman with a *kohen gadol*. This is an *issur asei*, and moreover it is an *asei she'eino shaveh ba-kol* — an obligation that does not apply equally to all Jews, only to *kohanim*. The combination of these two features — that it is merely an *asei* and that it applies only to *kohanim* — makes this the one case where even on the broadest possible reading of Rabbi Akiva's position, marriage might still be binding.

## Beulah L'Kohen

### Kohen Exception

This brings the Gemara to a final, unresolved ambiguity. The case of *be'ulah le-kohen gadol* has been identified as a potential exception — the one category where even the most expansive reading of Rabbi Akiva's principle does not dissolve the binding nature of *kiddushin*. But this raises a difficulty in the context of the *knas*: how can the case of *be'ulah le-kohen gadol* be cited at all in a discussion of *knas* liability, given that the fundamental requirement for a *knas* is that the victim be a *na'arah betulah*? If she is a *be'ulah*, a non-virgin, she cannot receive a *knas* regardless of her relationship to a *kohen gadol*.

### Rashi/Tosafot

Rashi addresses this difficulty by suggesting that the case involves *biah shelo k'darkah* — anal intercourse — which does not rupture the hymen. On this reading, the woman is a *be'ulah* in the sense relevant to *kehuna* law (she has had intercourse), yet remains technically a *betulah* for the purposes of the *knas* because her physical *besulim* are intact. The same type of question arose earlier in the discussion of the *kesuvah* of 200 versus 100 *zuz*. Tosafot, however, rejects this bifurcated analysis and argues that the case is more straightforwardly understood: she was a *betulah* when the rape occurred — the rapist himself deflowered her — and the *knas* is owed because she was a virgin at the moment of the violation. After the rape she is indeed a *be'ulah*, but the *knas* crystallized at the moment of the act. The question then becomes whether a *kohen gadol* can marry a woman made non-virgin by his own act — *beulat atzmo* — and the Gemara leaves this as a continuing discussion to be taken up in the next session.

---

---

# Ketubot 30

## Knas & Prohibited Status

### Knas Prohibited Women

The sugya opens with a statement of Rav Chisda, found approximately seven or eight lines into the daf. The background issue concerns the *knas* — the statutory fine imposed upon a man who rapes or seduces a young, unmarried girl — specifically in cases where the woman is someone he is prohibited from marrying, whether due to an *issur kares* or an *issur lav*. The *mishnah* has already stated that even in such cases a *knas* is owed. Yet the upcoming *mishnah* will rule that when the act entails a *chiyuv misah* — when the woman is forbidden to him under penalty of court execution — no *knas* is paid. The reasoning behind that latter ruling will become clearer as the discussion unfolds.

### Niddah Exception

Before engaging the broader debate, Rav Chisda introduces a point of consensus: *hakol modim bevo'al haniddah meshalem knas* — everyone agrees that a man who has relations with a *niddah* does pay the fine, even though the act constitutes an *issur kares*. The question is why this case is uncontroversial.

### Niddah Status

The *Gemara* addresses this from two angles, corresponding to the two opinions about what qualifies a woman for *knas*. According to the view that the woman must be someone to whom *kiddushin* is binding (*yesh bah havayah*), this too is unproblematic — *kiddushin* is perfectly valid when performed with a *niddah*. There is a separate and interesting question regarding *nisu'in*: can *chuppah* take place when the woman is a *niddah*? Ashkenazim permit it; Sephardim as a matter of principle do not, since *nisu'in* is bound up with the initiation of shared marital life, which presupposes the possibility of conjugal relations. But *kiddushin* unambiguously takes effect even when the woman is a *niddah*. According to the other view — that the question is whether the man is *permitted* to remain married to this woman (*re'uyah lekayyema*) — the answer is equally clear: a man is permitted to be married to a *niddah*, even though he may not currently have relations with her. Her status as a *niddah* is a transitory condition, not a permanent disqualification from marriage.

This analysis reveals a crucial conceptual distinction that runs throughout the entire discussion. Until now, the debate about *knas* when there is a prohibition has focused on the *woman's personal status* — whether she is someone to whom marriage can bind, or whom the man may lawfully keep as a wife. The *niddah* case raises something different: there is nothing wrong with her personal status, yet the *act itself* — the act of intercourse — was an *issur kares*. The same applies to any of the cases in our *mishnah* where the man engages in an act that is prohibited under penalty of *kares*, independent of any issue with her personal status. The question then becomes: should that *issur kares* of the act itself — not of the person — override the *knas* through the principle of *kim lei bidrabba minei*?

This is precisely the tension the *mishnah* seems to navigate. When there is a *chiyuv misah*, the next *mishnah* exempts from payment — and that is readily understood as an application of *kim lei*: the court cannot simultaneously prosecute for a capital crime and impose a monetary fine. But our *mishnah* assumes that an *issur kares* does *not* trigger *kim lei*. It is against this assumption that the *Gemara* now introduces a dissenting opinion.

---

## R. Nechunya Kim Lei

### R. Nechunya Position

The *Gemara* introduces the phrase *ul'afokei mid'Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah* — the ruling that *knas* is paid even in the case of an *issur kares* comes to exclude, to reject, the position of Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah. For Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah holds that even in a case of *kares* we apply *kim lei bidrabba minei*, and the weightier prohibition overrides the monetary liability.

### Haystack Yom Kippur

This position is expressed in a *baraita*: *Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah hayah oseh Yom HaKippurim ke-Shabbos le-tashlumin* — Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah treated Yom Kippur like Shabbat with respect to payment obligations. The reference point is the classic case of burning down someone's haystack on Shabbat: the perpetrator is exempt from damages, because the very act that caused the loss — the burning — was simultaneously an act of *chilul Shabbos*, which carries capital liability. This is the principle of *kim lei*: the court must choose how to prosecute the matter, and the capital crime overshadows the civil one. Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah extends this: if one burned down a friend's haystack on Yom Kippur, even though that transgression is punishable by *kares* rather than court execution, it would equally exempt from payment. *Mah Shabbos mitchayev benafsho patur min hatashlumin, af Yom HaKippurim mitchayev benafsho patur min hatashlumin* — just as one who becomes liable with his very life on Shabbat is exempt from monetary payment, so too one who becomes liable "with his life" on Yom Kippur — understood as the excision of the soul — is likewise exempt.

This position is, as the *Gemara* signals, a significant *chiddush* on multiple levels. First, *kares* is objectively a less severe penalty than court-imposed execution. Second — and more fundamentally — *kim lei* is typically understood as a principle operating within the framework of the *beit din*. The court cannot prosecute a person simultaneously for a capital crime and for civil damages; it must, as it were, choose its docket. But *kares* is entirely a matter between the person and God. It is not a court sanction at all. Why should the *beit din*, adjudicating a civil claim for property damage, be deflected by a divine punishment that is not within the court's purview? One can understand why an act deserving of execution — even if technically unprosecutable due to lack of witnesses, lack of *hasra'ah*, or because the act was done *beshogeg* — still exempts from payment, since the *nature* of the act was a capital offense. But to say the same about something that is categorically and exclusively a *chiyuv* toward Heaven, never an issue for the court — that is the considerable *chiddush* of Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah.

---

## Ason Tragedy Basis

### Abaye Ason

The *Gemara* now asks: *mai ta'ama d'Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah?* — what is the underlying source for this position? Abaye derives it from the concept of *ason* in Scripture. The relevant passage describes two men fighting, and one of them strikes a pregnant woman standing nearby, causing a miscarriage. The Torah states: *im ason yihyeh venasata nefesh tachas nafesh* — if there is a tragedy, you give a life for a life — and by implication, *lo yihyeh ason*, if there is no tragedy, you pay the monetary fine for the miscarriage. The rabbinic reading is that *ason* refers to the death of an already-born person in the incident. If such a death occurs, the perpetrator faces the capital charge of murder and does not pay the fine for the miscarriage. This is the scriptural basis for *kim lei* itself: when a death arises from the same act, monetary liability is displaced.

The significance for Abaye's derivation lies in the additional usage of the word *ason* — this time in the story of Yaakov and Binyamin, where Yaakov fears that if he sends Binyamin down to Egypt, *ason* will befall him on the way. This *ason* at the hands of Yaakov is understood as a divinely-ordained misfortune — *ason bid'ei shamayim*. The *ason* in the earlier passage, by contrast, is one caused through human agency — *ason bid'ei adam*. Abaye draws the *gezerah shavah*: just as the human-caused *ason* exempts from monetary payment, so too a divinely-ordained *ason* — death or excision brought about by God — similarly exempts. And *kares*, the divinely imposed cutting-off of the soul, falls within the category of *ason bid'ei shamayim*.

Admittedly, the analogy is not seamless. In the original case of *im ason yihyeh*, the tragedy strikes a *victim* — the perpetrator's act caused someone else's death, and *that* death displaces the fine. Here, the *kares* falls upon the *perpetrator* himself. The two situations are structurally distinct. Nevertheless, this is Abaye's derivation.

### Challenge Yaakov

Rav Abba bar Abba challenges the derivation. The question is: how do we know that the *ason* Yaakov feared for Binyamin refers specifically to a divine punishment — the kind of providential misfortune (*tzinin u'pachim*, cold and heat, understood as God's direct intervention) — as opposed to something caused through human agency, such as lions and thieves (*arya u'ganavei d'viyedei adam ninhu*)? The *Gemara* is operating here with a specific understanding of *bid'ei shamayim*: it does not simply mean "natural causes" (i.e., anything not done by a person), but specifically means *divinely directed* punishment — something God actively brings about as a consequence of sin. By contrast, *bid'ei adam* encompasses not only human acts but random or negligent occurrences that God did not specifically ordain. On this understanding, lions and thieves might not qualify as *bid'ei shamayim* in the relevant sense, since their actions are not necessarily a divine decree. The challenge, then, is that Yaakov's *ason* might refer to non-divinely-directed tragedies — and if so, it cannot serve as the source for *kares* being an exempting *ason bid'ei shamayim*.

### All Tragedies

The *Gemara* dismisses the challenge directly: *Yaakov ha mi-kuleihu azhir* — Yaakov was warning about all types of tragedies. When Yaakov says "lest an *ason* occur," he encompasses the entire spectrum of possible misfortune, whether divinely directed, humanly caused, or naturally random. Since his usage of *ason* includes divinely ordained punishment, it suffices to establish the principle — even if it also includes other categories.

### Heat Cold Divine

The *Gemara* then indulges a delightful digression prompted by the mention of *tzinin u'pachim* (cold and heat). A *baraita* states: *hakol bid'ei shamayim chutz mi-tzinin u'pachim* — everything is in divine hands except for cold and heat. The verse cited is *tzinim pachim b'derech itkesh; shomer nafsho yirchak me-hem* — cold and traps are in the path of the crooked; one who guards his life keeps away from them. Rashi and Tosafot read this as referring to hot and cold weather. The implication is striking: of all the misfortunes that might befall a person, extreme weather is the one that lies within human control — bundle up, seek shade, stay hydrated — and therefore God does not deploy it as an instrument of directed punishment.

But this creates an apparent contradiction. If cold and heat are *bid'ei adam* — within one's own hands to prevent — and lions and thieves are *bid'ei shamayim* — divinely directed — then the earlier challenge would be fully resolved. Yet wait: are lions and thieves really divinely directed? The *Gemara* then cites Rav Yosef, and so too the school of Rabbi Chiyya taught it, that since the destruction of the *Beit HaMikdash* and the cessation of the *Sanhedrin*, the four modes of execution were not abolished — *arba misos lo batlu* — meaning that divine providence ensures analogous fates befall those who deserve them. Someone liable to *sekilah* (stoning) will either fall from a roof or be trampled by an animal. Someone liable to *sereifah* (burning) will either perish in a fire or be bitten by a venomous serpent. Someone liable to *harigah* (the sword) will be handed over to the Roman authorities or attacked by bandits. Someone liable to *chenek* (strangulation) will drown or die of a respiratory ailment (*srunki*). The *Gemara* thus confirms that lions and thieves are indeed instruments of divine punishment — *bid'ei shamayim* in the fullest sense — while cold and heat are categorically in one's own hands.

Tosafot, noting this, explains that while in principle any misfortune can serve as a vehicle for divinely ordained punishment, cold and heat are the one category God specifically does not use, because the relevant verse teaches that a person can always take preventive measures against them, and God does not override those measures. Everything else — including bandits and wild animals — can be the vehicle through which God exacts what is deserved.

The *Gemara* therefore reverses the terms of the *baraita*: *chaya v'ganavei bid'ei shamayim; tzinin u'pachim bid'ei adam* — lions and thieves are divinely directed; cold and heat are in human hands. And either way, the point stands: when Yaakov says *v'karah ason*, he is speaking about the full range of misfortune, including those that are divinely ordained. It follows that divinely imposed *ason bid'ei shamayim* — and by extension *kares* — belongs in the same category as the court-imposed death that exempts from monetary payment.

Tosafot raises at this juncture what is, frankly, an ancient theological question: if divine punishment invariably catches up with sinners, why do we observe so many sinners dying peacefully in their beds? The question receives a characteristically concise answer — the possibility of *teshuvah* entirely removes the punishment, or a meritorious deed is being repaid in this world, or the reckoning is deferred to the next. The brevity of the treatment is itself telling. As a legal tradition, the *Gemara* allots this question of theodicy two lines in Tosafot and moves on.

### Four Executions

The passage about divine execution also touches on the principle of collective responsibility implicit in the phrase *ba'ish ha'hu u'v'mishpachto* — "that man and his family." Rashi explains that the family is included because no sinner operates without some degree of enablement from those around him. Onkelos, by contrast, translates *mishpachto* as *u'v'sa'adohi* — his supporters — avoiding the presumption that biological family members are necessarily complicit, and instead understanding the term figuratively as referring to those who actively enable him.

---

## Rava Kim Lei

### Korban Molech

Rava offers an alternative derivation for Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah's position. The proof text he adduces is from the passage concerning one who gives his child to *Molech*: if the people of the land avert their eyes and fail to execute him, God declares *v'samti ani et panai ba'ish ha'hu u'v'mishpachto, v'hichratti oto mikerev ammo* — I will direct My attention toward that man and his family and will cut him off from his people. This is a far more direct source: the Torah explicitly equates God's *kares* with the court's execution. Where the court fails to execute, God steps in with *kares* as the substitute. This establishes the equivalence of the two punishments as a general principle.

### Rava vs Abaye

The *Gemara* asks: *mai ikka bein Rava l'Abaye* — what practical difference exists between deriving the principle from Abaye's *ason* source versus Rava's *Molech* source? The answer is the case of *zar she'achal terumah* — a non-*Kohen* who eats *terumah* belonging to a *Kohen*. In doing so, he simultaneously steals (a civil wrong entailing payment) and commits a transgression that is *chayav misah bid'ei shamayim*. The question is whether *kim lei* applies here to exempt him from payment.

It is worth pausing to note that *misah bid'ei shamayim*, despite containing the word *misah*, is understood by the *Rishonim* as actually less severe than *kares*. Rashi holds that *kares* additionally entails the premature death of one's children, while Tosafot disagrees about the precise details; but either way, the halakhic consensus treats *misah bid'ei shamayim* as a lesser category than *kares*.

According to Abaye — who derives *kim lei* from *ason*, encompassing all forms of divinely ordained punishment regardless of degree — even *misah bid'ei shamayim* would suffice to trigger the exemption. *Abaye patur*: the non-*Kohen* who eats the *terumah* is exempt from payment. According to Rava — who derives it from the *Molech* passage specifically equating *kares* with court execution — only *kares*, as the direct divine analogue of *mitat beit din*, qualifies. Anything less severe, such as *misah bid'ei shamayim*, does not. *Rava chayav*: the non-*Kohen* is liable to pay.

---

## Kares vs Mita

### Terumah Eating

With the dispute between Abaye and Rava established, the *Gemara* turns back to scrutinize Abaye's position more carefully. *Vha'amar Rav Chisda: modeh Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah begonev chelvo shel chaveiro v'achalo shehu chayav* — Rav Chisda stated that even Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah concedes that one who steals another's *chelev* (forbidden fat) and then eats it is liable to pay. The reason: *shekevar nitchayev bigniva kodem sheba lidei issur chelev* — the obligation to pay arose at the moment of theft, *before* the transgression of eating the forbidden fat occurred. The moment he lifted the *chelev*, he acquired it through the act of theft and became liable for payment. The *chiyuv nefesh* — the liability that might trigger *kim lei* — only arose later, when he ate it. Since the two liabilities arose at separate points in time, one cannot overshadow the other.

---

## One Act Temporal

### Theft Separate

This principle — that temporal separation between the civil and the religious liability prevents *kim lei* from applying — now becomes the central analytical focus. All the cases considered until now involved the civil and religious dimensions of the *same act*: the burning of the haystack was simultaneously the *chilul Shabbos* and the property damage; the sexual act was simultaneously the *kares* violation and the basis for the *knas*. But if the theft and the eating are separated even by a split second, they are two distinct events and each is prosecuted independently.

### Forced Food

The *Gemara* therefore constructs increasingly precise hypotheticals to create scenarios in which the two liabilities genuinely coincide. *Hacha bemai askinan? Kegon she'dachvo chaveiro letoch piv* — what is the case we are discussing? It is where one's friend forcibly thrust the *terumah* into his mouth. If that happened, the person never lifted the food himself and therefore never committed the act of *gneivah* through lifting. The act of eating might then simultaneously be the act of acquiring (and thus the theft) and the act of consuming *terumah* (the religious violation). But the *Gemara* objects: *sof sof, keivan dile'asei kanyei* — in the end, when he chews it, he acquires it. And *nitchayev benafsho lo havai ad de'balyei* — the religious prohibition of eating *terumah* is only transgressed at swallowing, not chewing. So even here, the civil liability (at chewing) and the religious liability (at swallowing) are still temporally distinct.

### Spitting Out

The *Gemara* refines the scenario further: *kegon she'dachvo lo letoch beit habli'ah* — the friend thrust it directly into the throat. Now, swallowing is the act in question, and swallowing would simultaneously be the act of eating *terumah* and the act of civil liability. But the *Gemara* challenges: *heichi dami* — what exactly is the case? *Ei dematzi le'ahadura, nahadar* — if he can spit it back out, let him do so. *Ei lo matzi le'ahadura, amai chayav* — if he cannot, why is he liable at all, since everything was compelled?

Rashi's resolution is illuminating: if he *can* spit it out but chooses not to, it is that very choice — the decision not to return it — that constitutes the act of *gneivah*. And the subsequent swallowing, which is the act that triggers the religious prohibition, comes *after* the theft is already complete. So they are still not simultaneous. The *Gemara* therefore specifies: *lo tzricha dematzi le'ahadura adei d'chak* — the case is where he can spit it out, but only with great difficulty. Rashi explains that by this point the food has become revolting, such that spitting it out would return nothing of value — it is already effectively destroyed. Consequently, the friend who initially thrust it in is the one who caused the *nezek*, and our person cannot be said to have stolen anything by not spitting it out (since the object is already ruined). Yet when he swallows, he derives benefit from something that belonged to another.

### Stomach Benefit

This brings in the concept of *hana'as meiav* — the benefit of one's stomach. Even when no act of *mazik* or *gneivah* can be clearly attributed to a person, if he derived tangible benefit from another's property, he owes restitution for the value of that benefit. The benefit is concretized precisely at the moment of swallowing, when the food enters and nourishes the body. And it is at that same moment that the religious violation of eating *terumah* is completed. The two liabilities thus converge at a single point, and the question of *kim lei* becomes applicable.

### Liquids Terumah

Rav Pappa applies the same framework to a parallel case: *kegon shetachvo lo chaveiro mashkin shel terumah letoch piv* — where one's friend thrust liquids of *terumah* into his mouth. Rashi explains that liquids become immediately revolting when placed in someone else's mouth, so the same analysis applies: the friend has already caused the initial damage, the person faces only a liability of *hana'as meiav* upon swallowing, and this coincides with the consumption of *terumah* — such that the two arise simultaneously.

### Simultaneous Acts

Rav Ashi takes a completely different approach: *bezar she'achal terumah mishelo v'kara shirayin shel chaveiro* — a non-*Kohen* who eats his own *terumah* (legitimately owned *terumah*, say given to him) and at the same time tears his friend's fine silk garment. Here, there is no connection whatsoever between the two acts — one is the eating of *terumah* and the other is a separate act of *nezek* to an entirely different object. Yet they happen to occur at the exact same moment. Rav Ashi holds that temporal simultaneity is itself sufficient to trigger *kim lei*, regardless of whether the two acts are part of the same process or even related to one another.

This is a striking and counterintuitive position. If anything, one might expect the principle to apply more naturally in cases where the two acts are part of a single integrated process — like chewing and swallowing — even if separated in time. Rav Ashi seems to hold the opposite: only the fact of occurring at the same moment matters, not the relationship between the acts. On Rav Ashi's view, if a person happens to be eating *terumah* with one hand and tearing a garment with the other, the *kim lei* of the eating exempts him from payment for the garment. The conceptual difficulty is plain: the logic of *kim lei* has generally been understood as the court being unable to simultaneously prosecute the same act under two different legal categories. Applying it to two entirely unrelated acts that happen to coincide in time is a very different — and considerably more expansive — claim.

### Timeline Separate

Rav Chisda's foundational principle, then, is that liability attaches at the distinct moment of each act. When theft and eating are separated on the timeline, even if one leads naturally to the other, they generate independent obligations that do not cancel each other out.

---

## Arrow Shabbat

### Arrow Four Amos

The *Gemara* now asks whether this ruling of Rav Chisda conflicts with a position of Rabbi Avin. Rabbi Avin states: *hazorek chetz mitchilat arba l'sof arba* — one who shoots an arrow from the beginning of four *amos* to the end of four *amos* in *reshut harabim* on Shabbat, *v'kara shirayin bahalichata* — and in the course of its flight the arrow tears through someone's fine garment — the ruling is *patur*: *kim lei* applies and the *chiyuv* of *chilul Shabbos* overrides the civil liability. The *chiyuv* for *chilul Shabbos*, strictly speaking, is only complete when the arrow lands — yet the tearing of the garment occurred mid-flight, *before* the *chiyuv Shabbos* was finalized. How, then, can one say *kim lei*?

### Akira Hanachah

The answer lies in the principle *she'akira tzorech hanacha hi* — the picking up (*akira*) is a necessary part of the putting down (*hanacha*). In the laws of *Shabbos*, the prohibited act of carrying (*hotza'ah*) requires three components: *akira* (lifting the object), traversal of four *amos* in *reshut harabim*, and *hanacha* (setting it down). The entire sequence constitutes a single *ma'aseh aveirah*. Since the *akira* is legally part of the *aveirah*, the whole process — from the moment the arrow was launched to the moment it landed — is treated as one continuous act. The garment was torn in the middle of this legal act, and therefore it is within the compass of the *aveirah*.

### Eating No Pickup

The *Gemara* distinguishes this from the case of theft and eating. One might think: just as the picking up of the arrow was part of the process that led to its landing, so too picking up the food was part of the process that led to eating it — and therefore we should say *hagbahah tzorech achilah hi* and treat them as one process. The *Gemara* rejects this: *hasam ee efshar l'hanacha b'lo akira* — there, it is physically impossible to put the arrow down without first having picked it up. You cannot complete the act of carrying without the *akira*. *Hacha efshar l'achilah b'lo hagbahah* — here, you can eat without picking up, since *de-ba'ei gachin v'achil* — one can crouch down and eat directly off the ground.

### Interrupt Criterion

The second, and likely stronger, answer: *hasam ee ba'ei l'ahadorei lo matzi mehadar lei* — there, if one wanted to interrupt the process and retrieve the arrow, one could not — once shot, the arrow cannot be recalled mid-flight. *Hacha matzi mehadar lei* — here, after picking up the food, one can always stop and put it back. The interruptibility of the process is decisive. When a process cannot be interrupted once begun, it is treated as a single continuous act and *kim lei* may apply to everything occurring within it. When a process *can* be interrupted — when at any moment the actor could choose to stop — then distinct stages on the timeline remain legally distinct, and each generates its own independent liability.

The *Gemara* here is notably bracketing the strictly legal definition of the *aveirah* and focusing on a physical criterion of continuity: either the practical necessity of the earlier stage for the later stage, or the impossibility of interruption once begun. One might argue — and there is something to this — that the principle of *akira tzorech hanacha* is properly a legal point: it is because the *akira* is legally constitutive of the *ma'aseh aveirah* of *hotza'ah* that the entire process is treated as one act. On this reading, anything that is part of the *halachically* defined act would be encompassed by *kim lei*, and the physical criteria the *Gemara* invokes are approximations of that legal definition rather than independent factors.

### Knife Reshus

The *Gemara* notes the practical difference between the two formulations by means of a test case: *maavir sakin b'reshut harabim v'kara shirayin b'halichato* — one who carries a knife through *reshut harabim* on Shabbat and in the course of walking it tears someone's garment. According to the first formulation — that the criterion is whether the beginning of the process is physically necessary for the end — here too *ee efshar l'hanacha b'lo akira*: you cannot transport the knife four *amos* without first having picked it up. The *kim lei* of *chilul Shabbos* would apply and exempt from payment. According to the second formulation — that the criterion is whether the process can be interrupted — here *matzi mehadar lei*: one could stop walking at any moment, set the knife down, and reverse the act. The process is interruptible, and therefore the garment-tearing and the *chilul Shabbos* are not sufficiently fused to trigger *kim lei*; the civil liability stands independently.

---

---

# Ketubot 31

## Kiyma Lei Intro

### Opening

We pick up in the middle of 31a, approximately ten lines before the lines widen, beginning with the words *lo hachi matnina hadola*. The word *gufa* signals that the Gemara is now returning to analyze a previously cited source in full.

### Kiyma Lei Concept

The broader context has already introduced the principle that if someone performs an act that renders them liable to execution by *beis din* — or, according to Rabbi Nechunia ben HaKanah, even liable to *kares* — that capital liability overrides any concurrent monetary payment or fine. The question driving the discussion is: what precisely constitutes the relevant "overlap"? In what sense must the capital and monetary obligations coincide in order for the capital one to override?

### Single Act Scenarios

The earlier discussion began with cases in which a single act simultaneously generated both liabilities — for instance, burning a haystack on *Shabbos* or *Yom Kippur*. That is the clearest instance: one action, two consequences. But the Gemara has since moved to more complex territory, examining situations involving two distinct acts that either occur sequentially or appear to occur at the same time. An extreme formulation held that timing alone is dispositive: if someone is simultaneously eating *chelev* and, with his feet, destroying property, the two obligations coincide in time and the monetary one is overridden.

### Multiple Acts Timing

We now return to a different framing: rather than focusing purely on the clock, the Gemara considers whether a series of actions can be understood as constituting a single unified *process*. If the act that makes a person deserving of the death penalty is defined as a process — with a beginning, a middle, and an end — then any monetary damage or fine incurred at any point within that process would be overridden. This is the conceptual lens through which the Gemara proceeds.

---

## Arrow Case

### Arrow Setup

The Gemara opens with a teaching of Rabbi Avin: *hazorek chetz mit-techilas arba l'sof arba* — one who shoots an arrow from the beginning of four *amos* in *reshus harabim* to the end, and in its flight it tears fine silk garments, is *patur* — exempt from paying for the damage. The technical violation of *Shabbos* is not completed until the arrow lands — that is, until the end of its trajectory — yet the shooter is exempt from the monetary damages incurred along the way.

### Carrying Process

The reason given is: *she-akira tzarach hanacha hi* — the *akira*, the picking up, is necessary for the *hanacha*, the putting down. One might understand this physically: once the arrow is in flight, the archer cannot retrieve it, so the entire arc of motion is one indivisible event. But the deeper and more compelling reading is a halachic one.

### Carrying Definition

The act of carrying is not defined merely by the moment of *hanacha*. One does not carry by depositing an object in *reshus harabim*; one carries by picking it up, traversing the domain, and setting it down. The entire sequence — from the initial *akira* through the traversal to the final *hanacha* — constitutes a single, unified act of carrying. Since liability is incurred at the end of this process, but the process itself began at the moment of pickup, any damage occurring anywhere within that process is subsumed under the same act. The exemption from monetary liability follows, not from some physical impossibility of interruption, but from the halachic conception of carrying as an integral whole.

One might ask: is the *patur* here referring to exemption from the monetary damages for the silk? It is. The archer remains fully *chayav* for *chillul Shabbos*. The exemption is solely monetary, not religious.

---

## Theft & Shabbat

### Wallet Theft

The Gemara now introduces a challenge from Rabbi Bibi bar Abaye. The *braisa* teaches: *hagonev kis b'Shabbos chayav* — one who steals a wallet on *Shabbos* is still liable to pay, because the obligation of *geneiva* was incurred before the *issur* of *sekila* (execution) came into play. The act of theft is completed the moment the thief picks up the wallet — that is the act of *kinyan* by *hagba'ah* — while the violation of *Shabbos* occurs only later, when the object is carried four *amos* or transferred from the owner's *reshus hayachid* to a *reshus harabim*. The two obligations arise from distinct acts at distinct moments, so the later capital liability does not retroactively override the earlier monetary one.

### Dragging Property

The *braisa* continues: *ha im megorer v'yotzei, megorer v'yotzei, patur* — but if the thief was dragging it and going, dragging it and going, he is *patur*, because the *issur Shabbos* and the act of *geneiva* arrive simultaneously. To understand this, consider the following. If the thief drags the wallet along the ground rather than lifting it, he has not yet performed *hagba'ah*, and thus has not yet acquired it through a recognized act of *kinyan*. He drags it through the owner's domain — still not stolen — and then crosses the threshold into some other domain. That crossing is where both the *issur Shabbos* and the act of *geneiva* are completed at the same moment, and therefore they coincide.

### Domains Explained

This raises an immediate structural question: what counts as an act of *geneiva* in the first place? The general assumption is that theft is consummated through the same type of act by which property is legitimately transferred — that is, through an act of *kinyan*. Picking the object up (*hagba'ah*) in the owner's domain would accomplish this. But if one does not lift it, then *geneiva* can only be accomplished by moving it into a domain where one has some degree of control — one's own property, or at minimum some semi-private space in which one can be considered to have possession. That space is not *reshus harabim*. Meanwhile, *chillul Shabbos* requires precisely the transfer from *reshus hayachid* to *reshus harabim*. These two requirements seem at first to be mutually exclusive: the act that triggers *chillul Shabbos* is not the act that triggers *geneiva*, and vice versa. Much of the remainder of the Gemara's discussion will resolve this tension.

---

## Why Dragging?

### Comparison

The Gemara now asks a pointed question. The arrow case established the principle that the entire process of carrying — from the moment of *akira* — counts as a single act. If so, why does the *braisa* require the unusual case of dragging at all? In the normal case of picking up a wallet and walking it out of the house, the theft by *hagba'ah* occurs first, and then the *Shabbos* violation follows when the carrier crosses into *reshus harabim*. The arrow principle would seem to apply here as well: the *akira* — the picking up that constituted the theft — is the beginning of the process of carrying, and therefore the two offenses should be considered part of the same act, rendering the thief *patur*. Why then does the *braisa* not simply state: if you picked it up and walked it out, you are *patur*?

### Process Challenge

The Gemara answers: *kegon shehigbiha al menas lehatznio* — the case in the *braisa* is one where the thief picked up the wallet intending not to carry it out to *reshus harabim*, but to hide it somewhere else within the house. He then changed his mind and walked it out. In such a case, the theft by *hagba'ah* and the beginning of the carrying process are not the same act, because the act of *akira* that commences carrying must include the intent to carry it out. If he picked it up with intent to rehide it indoors, that picking up was an act of *geneiva* but not the beginning of the carrying process. When he subsequently decided to walk it out, that is when the carrying process began — but he did not pick it up again, so there is no *akira* at that moment.

Yet this immediately generates a further difficulty: if he is now walking toward the door with no fresh act of picking up, how can there be a valid *akira* for *Shabbos* purposes at all? The Gemara invokes the ruling of Rav Simon in the name of Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: one who moves objects from corner to corner within his house without intending to take them outside, and then changes his mind and carries them out, is *patur* — *she-lo hayetah akirah mi-sha'ah rishonah le-kach* — because the original picking up was not directed toward that purpose, and there was no subsequent valid *akira*.

### Rest vs Adjust

The Gemara then discards the "intent to hide" scenario and reformulates: *ela eima al menat le-hotzi* — say instead that he picked it up intending to carry it out. Still, the *braisa* describes him as pausing. The Gemara asks: *amad le-mai?* For what purpose did he stop? If he stopped *le-chateif* — to shift the object from one shoulder to the other, or to adjust his grip — *orcheih hu*, that is simply the normal manner of carrying, and such an adjustment does not constitute an interruption. It does not end one process and begin another. But if he stopped *be-omed la-fush* — to take a genuine rest — that is a meaningful pause. In that case, the object has "settled" in its current location, and when he resumes walking, that resumption functions as a new *akira*. Thus the theft, which occurred at the original *hagba'ah*, is temporally separated from the beginning of the carrying process, and the two offenses are distinct. He would then be liable for the monetary penalty.

The insight here is precise: *akiras gufo ke-akiras chafetz* — when a person who has been stationary begins to move, that is treated as the object being lifted from its resting place. If he truly paused for rest, the object effectively settled; his subsequent movement constitutes a new *akira*. If he only adjusted without pausing, no such resetting occurred.

### Ben Azzai

Having established that one who picks up the wallet, pauses, and then carries it out would be *chayav* — because the theft and the carrying process are separated — the Gemara asks again why the *braisa* chose the unusual case of dragging rather than formulating a simpler distinction within the normal pickup case. Specifically, *niflog venisni bedidei* — let the *braisa* draw the distinction internally: one who picks it up and carries it straight out without stopping is *patur* (subsumed in one process), but one who pauses for rest is *chayav* (two distinct acts). Why introduce the strange case of dragging?

The Gemara answers: *ben Azzai hi* — this *braisa* follows the view of Ben Azzai, who holds *mehalach keomed dami* — that walking is like standing. According to Ben Azzai, every step a person takes constitutes a momentary pause. Each footfall is a brief settling, so continuous walking is a series of micro-stops rather than one unbroken motion. This means that the only act truly qualifying as *akira* from *reshus hayachid* to *reshus harabim* is the single step crossing the threshold — the step just before the line is the *akira*, and the step over the line is the *hanacha*. There is no extended unified process that begins at the original pickup; each step resets. Consequently, picking up the wallet inside the house and walking it out is never a case where the theft and the *Shabbos* violation form part of the same continuous process, because every step effectively interrupts the process.

The natural question follows: if walking is like standing under Ben Azzai's principle, how does one ever become liable for carrying *arba amos* in *reshus harabim*, since every step would reset the process? The *Yerushalmi* addresses this, suggesting that according to Ben Azzai, liability for the *arba amos* carrying would require actually jumping the four *amos* in one motion. Alternatively, for the *reshus hayachid*-to-*reshus harabim* transfer, only that single crossing step is the act — and it is enough.

Under Ben Azzai's framework, then, in the normal case of picking up a wallet inside the house and walking it out, the theft (the *hagba'ah*) and the *Shabbos* violation (the final crossing step) are never part of the same unified act. They are invariably separate events, and the thief is always *chayav* for the monetary penalty. The *braisa* needed a case where they genuinely coincide — and that case is dragging, or alternatively, throwing it out. Yet the *braisa* chose dragging rather than throwing, and the Gemara explains why.

The Gemara briefly raises the possibility of formulating the novel case as throwing rather than dragging — *aval zorek, patur* — since throwing, like the arrow, constitutes a unified process from the moment of release. But the Gemara deflects: *megarer deika itztaricha lei* — the case of dragging was specifically needed as a teaching in its own right. One might have thought that dragging an object along the ground is a *shinui*, an unusual mode of carrying, and that one would therefore be exempt from *Shabbos* liability. The *braisa* comes to teach that depending on the size of the object, dragging can be a perfectly normal mode of transport. If the object is large, dragging is obviously normal; if tiny, it is obviously abnormal. The *braisa* addresses the intermediate case — *b'mitziei* — where the object is medium-sized and dragging is just barely within the range of normal handling, sufficient to constitute *hotza'ah* for *Shabbos* purposes.

---

## Dragging Details

### Destinations

Having established why dragging is the case of choice, the Gemara now asks the central structural question: *u'd'afkeih l'heicha?* — where exactly did the thief drag the wallet? This is not a casual question. As established above, *chillul Shabbos* requires transfer from *reshus hayachid* to *reshus harabim*, while *geneiva* — without *hagba'ah* — requires bringing the object into a space where the thief exercises some measure of control. These requirements seem to pull in opposite directions.

If the thief dragged it straight into the major public thoroughfare: *issur Shabbos ika, issur geneiva leika* — there is a *Shabbos* violation, but no *geneiva*, because the public thoroughfare is not a space over which the thief has any personal control. If he dragged it into his own *reshus hayachid*: *issur geneiva ika, issur Shabbos leika* — there is *geneiva*, but no *Shabbos* violation. And if he dragged it from one *reshus hayachid* into another adjacent *reshus hayachid*, there is neither.

### Thoroughfare Sides

The Gemara then proposes: *d'afkeih l'tzidei reshus harabim* — he dragged it onto the sides of the public thoroughfare, the edges or shoulders flanking the main road. But this immediately raises the question of which authority governs. *K'man?* Like whom?

According to Rabbi Eliezer, the sides of *reshus harabim* are legally equivalent to *reshus harabim* itself. Under that view, *issur Shabbos ika* — there is a *Shabbos* violation — but *issur geneiva leika* — still no *geneiva*, since it remains *reshus harabim*. According to the Rabbis, the sides are not equivalent to *reshus harabim*, in which case *issur geneiva ika* — one can acquire there — but *issur Shabbos leika* — no *Shabbos* violation. So the problem appears equally intractable under either authority.

The Gemara resolves this elegantly: *l'olam k'Rabbi Eliezer* — the *braisa* follows Rabbi Eliezer. But Rabbi Eliezer's equation of the sides with *reshus harabim* applies only for purposes of *chillul Shabbos* — *hani mili l'chiyuva d'Shabbos* — because *d'zimnin d'dachki rabim v'asu l'hatam*, sometimes the press of the crowd overflows from the thoroughfare onto the shoulders, and the public uses them. This makes the sides sufficiently connected to, and occasionally part of, the main public artery that they count as *reshus harabim* for *Shabbos* purposes. However, *aval l'inyan mikna* — for purposes of acquisition — *d'la shechichi rabim* — since most of the time the public is not crowding those edges, the space is quiet enough that a person standing there has a measure of personal control over his immediate surroundings. He can therefore effect a *kinyan* there.

This creates the solution: a space that simultaneously satisfies the *Shabbos* requirement (it is treated as *reshus harabim* for *chillul Shabbos*) and the *geneiva* requirement (it affords enough private control to effect acquisition). The thief drags the wallet from the owner's house across the threshold into this border space — the *simta*, in Rashi's terminology — and at that single moment both the *chillul Shabbos* and the *geneiva* are complete.

### Hand Acquisition

Rav Ashi offers an alternative resolution: *k'gon shetziref yado l'mata mishlosha v'kiblo* — the case is one where the thief, as the wallet crosses into *reshus harabim*, reaches down with his hand and catches it. The legal principle underlying this is *kinyan yad* — if an object is on one's person, in one's hand, it is as though it is in one's own domain. Just as I can acquire an object by bringing it into my yard, I can acquire an object that comes to rest upon my person.

The key specification is that the hand must be kept below three *tefachim* from the ground. If the thief were to raise the wallet higher than three *tefachim* in order to catch it in his hand, that lifting would itself constitute *hagba'ah*, and the *geneiva* would be complete before the crossing into *reshus harabim* — which is the *Shabbos* violation — meaning the two offenses would once again be sequential rather than simultaneous. By keeping the hand below three *tefachim*, no *hagba'ah* occurs, and the moment the object lands in the thief's hand in *reshus harabim* is the moment both offenses are consummated together.

### Rava's Hand Rule

This solution draws on a principle of Rava: *yado shel adam chashuva lo k'arba al arba* — a person's hand is considered equivalent to a four-by-four *tefachim* space for *Shabbos* purposes. An object resting in one's hand is legally treated as though it has been set down on the ground, satisfying the *hanacha* requirement. Simultaneously, by virtue of *kinyan yad*, the object is acquired. So catching the wallet in one's hand in *reshus harabim* accomplishes both *geneiva* and *chillul Shabbos* at once.

### Ravina Position

Ravina takes a more radical position. None of these special mechanisms — *tzidei reshus harabim* or catching in the hand — are necessary. *L'olam d'afkeih l'reshus harabim* — the simple case is that the thief dragged it straight into *reshus harabim*. And *u'v'reshus harabim nami kana* — one can actually effect acquisition even in *reshus harabim*. This challenges everything assumed up to this point.

---

## Geneiva vs Kinyan

### Animal Mishna

Ravina and Rav Acha debate how to read this position, and both ground their dispute in a *mishna*. The *mishna* discusses a case of someone stealing an animal: *haya moshcho ve'yotze*, he was dragging it out of the owner's property. The animal then dies. If it died *b'reshus ba'alin* — while still in the owner's domain — the thief is *patur*, exempt. If he already performed *hagba'ah*, lifting it, or *she'hotzi'o* — took it out — and it then died, he is *chayav*.

The question driving the debate between Ravina and Rav Acha is: what does it mean to have "taken it out" so as to become *chayav*? Where must the animal end up?

### Ravina Read

*Ravina deyiek me'reisha* — Ravina derives his interpretation from the opening clause of the *mishna*. The *mishna* says: if it died *b'reshus ba'alin*, in the owner's domain, *patur*. The implication of this phrasing, as Ravina reads it, is: *ta'ama d'meis b'reshus ba'alin* — the only reason for exemption is that it died while still in the owner's domain. *Ha hotzio me'reshus ba'alin, u'meis chayav* — as soon as it is removed from the owner's domain, even if it enters *reshus harabim*, the thief becomes *chayav*. The emphasis falls entirely on removal from the victim's domain. Where the object goes next is irrelevant.

### Rav Acha Read

*Rav Acha deyiek me'seifa* — Rav Acha derives from the closing clause. The *mishna* states: *higbi'o o shehotzio* — he lifted it or he took it out. Rav Acha reads this as *hotza'ah dumiya d'hagba'ah* — the act of "taking out" must be analogous to *hagba'ah*. Just as *hagba'ah* means bringing the object fully into one's own control, so too *hotza'ah* — removal — must result in the object coming into the thief's control. It is insufficient merely to remove the object from the owner's sphere; the thief must bring it into his own sphere. Therefore, dragging it into *reshus harabim* alone does not constitute *geneiva*, because *reshus harabim* is nobody's controlled domain.

### Debate Resolution

This debate is subtle and important. It would be a mistake to read this as a disagreement about *kinyan* in the ordinary sense. The assumption throughout *Shas* is that one cannot acquire an object in *reshus harabim* without *hagba'ah* or *yad*. Neither Ravina nor Rav Acha is challenging that general principle of property law. The dispute is specifically about the *definition of geneiva*. Does committing *geneiva* require an act structurally equivalent to a *kinyan* — taking the object out of the victim's control and into the thief's control? Or is *geneiva* defined solely from the victim's perspective: once the object is removed from the victim's domain, the theft is complete, regardless of where it goes?

Ravina holds the latter: the act of *geneiva* is the deprivation of the owner's possession. The moment the object exits the owner's *reshus*, the theft is complete. This is a perfectly coherent reading — from the victim's standpoint, what matters is that they no longer have control, not that the thief has assumed it. Under this view, dragging the wallet straight into *reshus harabim* causes *geneiva* and *chillul Shabbos* to coincide immediately.

Rav Acha holds the former: *geneiva* must mirror *kinyan*, requiring that the thief bring the object into his own control. Taking it out and leaving it in *reshus harabim* — where no one controls it — is not yet a completed act of theft.

The Gemara then resolves how each Amora handles the textual difficulty posed by the other's preferred clause. The beginning of the *mishna* is not difficult for Rav Acha: he reads "owner's domain" expansively — *kama d'lo asyei l'reshusei, reshus ba'alin karinan beih* — as long as the object has not entered the thief's domain, it is still considered as though it remains in the owner's. And the end of the *mishna* is not difficult for Ravina: *hotza'ah dumiya d'hagba'ah lo aminan* — he simply does not accept the analogy between *hotza'ah* and *hagba'ah*. *Hagba'ah* is one method of theft effected within the owner's domain; *hotza'ah* is another method — removal from the owner's domain — and the two need not be structurally identical.

It is worth pausing to note that this entire extended *sugya* — the arrow case, the wallet dragging, the analysis of *tzidei reshus harabim*, the debate between Rav Acha and Ravina — is a construction of the *stam*, the anonymous editorial voice of the Gemara. There is almost no case where an Amora steps forward to make a direct statement in his own right. The entire analysis is the *stam* weaving together statements made by various authorities in other contexts, forming a unified *sugya* around the concept of *kiymah lei* and the question of what it means for two prohibitions to arise "at the same time" or as part of "the same process." Notably, the phrase *kiymah lei* itself never actually appears in this entire discussion — the concept has been explored throughout without the term ever being invoked.

---

## Incest & Lashes

### Incest Acts

The Gemara now transitions to a new application of the same underlying principle. The case is one who engages in sexual relations with his sister or his father's sister — an *issur kares*. Despite the severity of the prohibition, the Gemara records that such a person nonetheless pays the *knas*, the statutory fine associated with forbidden relations. The reason is that *kares* is a heavenly punishment; it does not on its own preclude a court-imposed monetary penalty. This is consistent with the framework established earlier in the *sugya*.

### Ain Lokeh

But the Gemara now raises a different and sharper challenge. A *braisa* enumerates a series of forbidden sexual relationships whose violation is punishable by *malkus* — lashes administered by the court. These include relations with one's sister, father's sister, mother's sister, wife's sister, brother's wife, uncle's wife, and a *niddah*. And the Gemara states the established principle: *de'eino lokeh umishalem* — one who receives lashes does not also pay. This is *ain lokeh u'meshalem*.

### Challenge

The challenge is immediate. If a man who has relations with his sister is subject to *malkus* — a real, court-administered punishment — then by the principle of *ain lokeh u'meshalem*, he should not also pay the monetary fine. Yet the *mishna* appears to say he does pay. This is a genuine tension.

It is important to note a distinction that clarifies the structure of the question. The *kiymah lei* principle discussed throughout this *sugya* — the capital crime overriding monetary liability — operates even when the court never actually administers the punishment. The act is of sufficient gravity that one is considered "already situated in" the greater punishment, and the monetary obligation falls away. The principle of *ain lokeh u'meshalem*, by contrast, seems to be triggered specifically by actual administration of *malkus*: if the court actually gives you lashes, it will not also make you pay. But even that distinction may be too simple, and the Gemara is pressing the question.

### Ulla Answer

Ulla begins to provide an answer. *Amar Ulla lo kashya* — Ulla says there is no difficulty. *Kan be'achoto na—* The Gemara cuts off at that point. Ulla appears to be drawing a distinction between different sub-cases within the list — perhaps between his sister as a *na'arah* (a minor girl subject to the fine) and other configurations. The full development of Ulla's answer will be taken up in the next session.

---

---

# Ketubot 32

## Lashes vs. Payment

### Incest/Rape Case

The *sugya* opens by picking up from the bottom of 31b and the beginning of 32a, in the context of a broader discussion that has been unfolding across the preceding pages. The *mishna* has established that one who rapes a woman to whom he is forbidden under penalty of *kares* — such as his sister or his father's sister — still owes the monetary fine (*knas*) applicable in cases of rape of a *na'arah*. The *gemara* has already wrestled with the position of Rabbi Nechunya ben Ha-kanah, who holds that liability for *kares* overrides monetary liability, just as liability for court-administered execution does. That discussion occupied the preceding *sugya*. Now a new dimension of the problem comes into focus.

The *gemara* introduces a *tannaitic* source from the tractate dealing with those who receive lashes: *elu hen ha-lokin* — the following people receive lashes — and proceeds to list precisely the cases of forbidden relationships that the *mishna* in Ketubot addresses: one who has relations with his sister, his father's sister, his mother's sister, his wife's sister, his brother's wife, his father's brother's wife, and a woman in a state of *niddah*. All of these carry the punishment of *kares*, and when prosecuted by the court, that punishment takes the form of lashes.

### Both Lashes & Payment

The difficulty is now apparent. The *mishna* in Ketubot says these individuals pay the monetary fine. The other *mishna* says they receive lashes. And we have an established principle — *ein lokeh u-meshalem* — that the court does not administer both lashes and monetary payment to the same person for the same act. So which is it?

It is important to distinguish this problem from the one treated earlier. The principle of *kim lei bidravah minei* — the override of a lesser liability by a greater one — operates on the level of intrinsic severity: an act deserving of execution or *kares* is weighty enough to negate the concurrent monetary liability altogether, regardless of whether the court actually administers any punishment. That was Rabbi Nechunya ben Ha-kanah's position. The present question is different in character. It concerns the *actual administration* of punishment by the court: the court simply will not do both things to the same person. But this raises the question of which one yields. The easiest answer — and one the *gemara* will indeed offer — is that in our *mishna*'s case, warning (*hatra'ah*) was never given, so lashes cannot be administered, and the monetary obligation therefore stands uncontested.

### Ein Lokeh u-Meshalem

But the *gemara* presses harder: even if we assume a case where the court *was* prepared to administer lashes — where all procedural requirements including *hatra'ah* were met — how does the *mishna* justify requiring payment? Once we have a case deserving of lashes, does the rule of *ein lokeh u-meshalem* not eliminate the monetary obligation? This is the core tension the *sugya* will now explore.

---

## Ulla's Position

### Na'arah vs. Bogeret

Ulla offers the first resolution. The apparent contradiction between the two *mishnayot* dissolves once we distinguish between two different scenarios. When does one pay the fine? In the case of *achoto na'arah* — his sister who is a *na'arah*, a girl between twelve and twelve-and-a-half, to whom the special *knas* of the Torah applies. When does one receive lashes? In the case of *achoto bogeret* — his adult sister, who is past the age of *na'arah*, for whom no *knas* exists. Since there is no monetary obligation in that case, lashes can be administered without conflict.

This resolution, however, implicitly reflects a significant position on Ulla's part: when both lashes and payment apply, it is the *payment* that takes precedence, not the lashes. The *mishna* that speaks of payment is teaching that even where lashes are in principle warranted — even where warning was given — the monetary obligation overrides and the lashes are not administered. Lashes appear only where there is no monetary obligation at all.

### Boshet u-Pegam

The *gemara* immediately challenges this. Even in the case of a *bogeret*, where the special *knas* of fifty *shekel* does not apply, there remain other monetary obligations. Under *halacha*, rape is treated as an act of physical violence against a person, subject to the same framework of compensatory payments as any such act. Even without the special fine of the *na'arah betula*, the rapist still owes *boshet* — compensation for embarrassment — and *pegam* — compensation for the injury to the victim's dignity and diminished value, assessed analogously to the way one evaluates physical damage. This *pegam* is calculated as the difference between the market value of a slave woman who is a virgin and one who is not, an admittedly imperfect but legally operative measure of the harm inflicted. Beyond these two, there is also *tza'ar* — payment for pain and suffering.

If all of these payments remain due even in the case of a *bogeret*, then even there the conflict between lashes and monetary obligation persists, and Ulla's distinction collapses.

### Consensual Sex

The *gemara* resolves this by narrowing the case further: *b'shotah* — in the case of a woman who is mentally incapacitated. Such a person would not experience embarrassment in the legally cognizable sense and therefore *boshet* would not apply. The *gemara* then anticipates the follow-up: even a *shotah* experiences physical pain, so *tza'ar* would remain. The answer: *bimfutah* — in a case where the act was consensual, not rape. In that case there is no *tza'ar* owed, and indeed no compelled harm at all.

Once the *gemara* arrives at the scenario of consensual relations, it draws a further conclusion. *Hashta d'atit l'hachi* — now that we have established that it must be a consensual case — the woman need not even be a *bogeret*. She could be a *na'arah*, provided she is a *yetomah u-mfutah* — an orphan who acts willingly. An orphan girl, even if she is only twelve years old, is legally emancipated from paternal authority since her father is deceased, and her own consent therefore governs. In such a case there is no *knas*, no *boshet*, no *tza'ar* — no monetary liability of any kind — and so lashes can be administered without conflict.

The upshot of Ulla's position is now fully articulated: *kol heicha de'ika mammon u-malkus, mammona meshalem malka lo laki* — wherever there is both monetary liability and liability for lashes, one pays the money and does not receive lashes. The *mishna* that speaks of payment reflects cases where money is owed; the *mishna* that speaks of lashes reflects cases where no money is owed. This is the rule according to Ulla: money overrides lashes.

### Money Overrides

The *gemara* asks: what is Ulla's source for this principle? The answer is that he derives it by analogy from the case of *chovel b'chaveiro* — one who physically injures another person. That case is paradigmatic: there is a negative prohibition against striking another person, derived by a *kal va-chomer* from the verse *lo yosif lehakkoto* which limits the lashes administered by the court, and yet the *halacha* requires monetary payment rather than lashes. This is taken as a model for the general rule that monetary obligation takes precedence over lashes.

---

## Chovel b'Chaveiro

### Five Payments

The *gemara* now examines the paradigm of *chovel b'chaveiro* more carefully. One who injures another person is liable for up to five distinct categories of payment: *nezek* (damages, assessed by the difference in the injured person's value as a slave before and after the injury), *tza'ar* (pain and suffering), *boshet* (embarrassment), *ripuy* (medical expenses), and *shevet* (lost income during the period of recuperation). These five payments make the monetary obligation in cases of injury particularly weighty. At the same time, the prohibition against striking carries a potential lashes-based sanction. The *halacha*, however, requires payment rather than lashes.

### Why Money?

The *gemara* challenges Ulla's use of this case as a general paradigm. The argument from *chovel b'chaveiro* can be read in two opposite ways, depending on how one ranks lashes against monetary payment in terms of severity.

If monetary payment is considered the *more severe* punishment, then the rule that one pays rather than receives lashes in cases of injury could reflect the exceptional weightiness of the injury case — five separate payments make it an unusually heavy monetary liability — and one might therefore conclude that in less weighty cases, lashes would apply rather than payment.

Conversely, if monetary payment is the *more lenient* option, then the injury case might be exceptional for a different reason: *shekein hutrah mikhlalah b'veit din* — the prohibition against striking is not absolute, since the court itself is permitted to administer lashes. Because the prohibition is not categorical, it is not as severe a transgression, and therefore the Torah imposes the lighter sanction of monetary payment in this context. But other prohibitions — like that of incest — are absolute, and one might say the Torah would insist on the heavier sanction of lashes there.

Either way, the injury case cannot serve as a clean paradigm from which to derive a universal rule.

### Edim Zomemin

The *gemara* then proposes a second paradigm: *edim zomemin*, false witnesses. When witnesses are found to have testified falsely, they are subject to the sanction of *ka'asher zamam* — do to them what they intended to do to the accused — which in a monetary case means paying the sum of money they sought to extract from the accused. They also transgress the prohibition of *lo sa'aneh b'rei'acha eid shaker*, which carries lashes. Yet the *halacha* requires monetary payment under *ka'asher zamam* and not lashes. Here too, then, we have a case where money overrides lashes.

If monetary payment is considered more severe, one might argue that *edim zomemin* are an exceptional case because they do not require *hatra'ah* — warning is not needed for the sanction of *ka'asher zamam* to apply. The absence of a warning requirement is itself a marker of the heightened severity of this category, and therefore it is not surprising that they receive the harsher sanction of monetary payment.

If monetary payment is considered more lenient, one might argue that *edim zomemin* are exceptional because *lo asu ma'aseh* — they committed no physical act, only speech — and therefore the Torah goes easy on them, requiring only the lighter sanction of monetary payment. But this leniency would not extend to someone who commits a physical act such as incest.

### Common Denominator

Anticipating these objections to each individual case, the *gemara* proposes a *tzad hashaveh* — a common-denominator argument. Even if each of the two paradigms has its own special features, the one thing they share is precisely the relevant feature: each involves both monetary liability and lashes, and in each case the outcome is monetary payment rather than lashes. That common denominator should therefore yield the general rule: *kol heicha de'ika mamona u-malkus, mamona meshalem u-malka lo laki*.

---

## Special Features
