### Chovel Exceptions

The *gemara* rejects the *tzad hashaveh* argument as well. When constructing a common-denominator argument, one must eliminate all features that distinguish the cases from each other and from the general rule one seeks to derive. But here, each case retains a distinctive feature that can explain the outcome independently. In the case of *chovel b'chaveiro*, one can point to the five payments as a distinguishing feature — whether as a marker of weightiness (if money is more severe) or as a leniency trigger (the prohibition having exceptions in the context of court-administered lashes).

### Edim Zomemin Features

In the case of *edim zomemin*, one can point either to the absence of a *hatra'ah* requirement (a marker of severity) or to the purely verbal nature of the transgression (a marker of leniency). Each case, in other words, has a feature that explains why *that* case results in monetary payment rather than lashes.

### Not a General Rule

Because each case can be explained by its own special feature, the *tzad hashaveh* fails to establish a general rule. As Tosafot notes, taken to its logical conclusion this objection would seem to undermine the *tzad hashaveh* as a tool of derivation entirely, since one could always point to some distinctive feature of each case. Tosafot addresses this difficulty in their commentary. In any case, the *gemara* concludes here that neither paradigm individually nor their combination is sufficient to establish a universal rule. The question of where Ulla derives his position thus remains open, and the *gemara* now turns to a different type of derivation.

---

## Gezeirah Shavah

### Tachat Connection

Ulla in fact derives his rule through a *gezeirah shavah* — a verbal analogy between two verses that share a common term. The verse describing the rapist's monetary obligation reads *tachat asher innah* — because he afflicted her — using the word *tachat*. The verse establishing the principle of monetary compensation for physical injury reads *ayin tachat ayin* — an eye for an eye — also using the word *tachat*. By this *gezeirah shavah*, Ulla links the two contexts: just as *ayin tachat ayin* is interpreted by *chazal* to mean monetary payment rather than literal retaliation, and just as that monetary payment takes precedence over any lashes-based sanction, so too in the case of rape — *ayin tachat ayin* being the locus classicus for monetary payment overriding lashes — the monetary obligation of the rapist takes precedence over the lashes he would otherwise receive for the associated prohibition.

### Tosafot on Rape

Tosafot offer an important interpretive observation here. It would be a striking and counterintuitive position to hold, as a universal principle across all of Torah, that monetary payment always overrides lashes whenever both apply. The evidence for such a sweeping rule is thin. Tosafot therefore suggest that at this point in the *sugya*, the *gemara* is shifting to a more limited claim: Ulla's *gezeirah shavah* from *tachat* to *tachat* is not establishing a general principle at all. Rather, it is a derivation specific to the case of rape. When rape coincides with a prohibition that would otherwise carry lashes — such as rape of a sister — Ulla holds that the monetary obligation for the rape takes precedence and the lashes are not administered. This is analogous to the case of *chovel b'chaveiro*, where the logic is that compensating the victim takes priority over punishing the perpetrator through lashes. Ulla extends this logic to rape by means of the *gezeirah shavah*.

On this reading, Ulla may well concede the general rule that lashes override monetary payment; his claim is confined to the specific case of rape and incest occurring together. In that case alone, the monetary obligation of the rape is treated like the monetary obligation of *chovel b'chaveiro* — it takes precedence, and the lashes are not administered.

---

## Rabbi Yochanan

### Warning Requirement

Rabbi Yochanan takes a fundamentally different position. His resolution of the conflict between the two *mishnayot* does not require distinguishing between *na'arah* and *bogeret* at all. He says: *afilu tima achoto na'arah* — even if we are dealing with his sister who is a *na'arah*, the classic case where both the *knas* and the lashes theoretically apply, there is no contradiction. *Kan she-hitru bo, kan she-lo hitru bo* — in one case warning was given, in the other it was not. When warning was given and lashes can be administered, lashes are given and money is not paid. When warning was not given and lashes cannot be administered, money is paid.

This means Rabbi Yochanan holds the opposite of Ulla's general rule: *kol heicha de'ika mamona u-malkuta ve-atru bei, milka laki mamona lo meshalem* — wherever there is both monetary liability and liability for lashes and warning was given, lashes are administered and money is not paid. Lashes override monetary payment, not the reverse.

### Lashes Primary

The practical disagreement between Ulla and Rabbi Yochanan comes into sharp focus in the case of rape combined with incest where warning was given. For Ulla, even in that case the monetary obligation takes precedence and the man pays rather than receiving lashes. For Rabbi Yochanan, once warning was given, lashes are the operative sanction and no monetary payment is made.

---

## Rabbi Yochanan's Source

### Kedei Rishato

The *gemara* asks: what is Rabbi Yochanan's source for the principle that lashes override monetary payment? He derives it from the verse *kedei rishato* — according to his wickedness — which appears in the context of lashes. The verse says to administer lashes commensurate with his wickedness.

### One Wickedness

The *gemara* derives: *mishum rish'ah achat atah mechayvo* — you make him liable on account of one act of wickedness, *ve-i atah mechayvo mishum shtei rishayot* — but not for two acts of wickedness arising from the same transgression. The verse singles out *his* wickedness — *rish'ato*, in the singular — indicating that for any single act, only one form of punishment is administered. And then, immediately adjacent in the text, the verse continues with the instruction to administer lashes. The juxtaposition teaches that when a choice must be made, lashes is the punishment imposed — lashes being identified as the primary punishment for a single act of wickedness.

### Multiple Lashes

One might note an apparent tension: the *gemara* in Makkot discusses cases where a single act triggers liability for multiple prohibitions, resulting in multiple sets of lashes — if one eats a certain insect, one might be liable under several overlapping prohibitions simultaneously. So multiple lashes are possible. The principle here is narrower: it is specifically the combination of lashes and *monetary payment* that cannot coexist. Two separate lashes-based sanctions, each arising from a distinct prohibition, can both be administered. What cannot happen is lashes for one dimension of the act and monetary payment for another dimension of the same act. The verse *kedei rishato* teaches that these two distinct modalities of punishment cannot be combined.

---

## Personal Injury

### Perutah Case

If Rabbi Yochanan's general rule is that lashes take precedence over monetary payment, how does he explain the exception of *chovel b'chaveiro*, where the *halacha* clearly requires monetary payment and not lashes? One might suggest that this exception applies only where *hatra'ah* was not given — in which case lashes cannot be administered and monetary payment simply fills the vacuum. But if *hatra'ah* was given, perhaps even in a case of personal injury, one would give lashes and not require payment.

### Any Payment

This suggestion is foreclosed by a teaching transmitted by Rav Ami in the name of Rabbi Yochanan himself: *haka'ah she'ein bah shaveh perutah lokeh* — if one struck another person in a manner that inflicted a wound of less than a *perutah*'s worth of damage, the perpetrator receives lashes. This ruling is striking in its irony: the most trivial act of physical aggression, one that caused essentially no quantifiable harm whatsoever — no *nezek*, no *tza'ar*, no *shevet*, no *ripuy*, no *boshet* of any monetary significance — results in forty lashes. Meanwhile, cutting off a person's arm results in monetary payment with no lashes. The more serious the injury, the more certain one is to pay rather than be lashed.

The ruling necessarily implies that the case involves *hatra'ah* — if there were no warning, lashes could not be imposed for any reason. And yet lashes are imposed. This means that even *with* warning, the general rule in cases of personal injury is monetary payment — but in the singular edge case where no monetary obligation whatsoever exists, not even a *perutah*'s worth, lashes apply. The moment there is any monetary obligation — even the smallest amount — monetary payment takes over and lashes are not administered.

### Torah Explicit

This brings Rabbi Yochanan back to his overarching position. His general rule is lashes over payment. The case of *chovel b'chaveiro* is an exception, but it requires a textual basis — the Torah must explicitly identify it as such. And indeed, as Rabi Ila states, *bifiresh ribtah Torah eidim zomemim l'tashlumin* — the Torah explicitly includes *edim zomemin* in the category of monetary payment — and the same principle applies to *chovel b'chaveiro*: *bifiresh ribtah Torah chovel b'chaveiro l'tashlumin* — the Torah explicitly mandates monetary payment in cases of personal injury, making it an explicit exception to the general rule.

---

## Edim Zomemin Source

### False Witness Verse

The *gemara* now examines where exactly the Torah makes this explicit statement regarding *edim zomemin*. The relevant verse reads: *ve-asitem lo ka'asher zamam la'asot le'achiv* — do to him as he plotted to do to his fellow. This already establishes the principle of *ka'asher zamam*. Why then does the verse continue with the phrase *yad beyad* — hand for hand?

The case of *edim zomemin* involves a range of possible sanctions, since the witnesses may have sought to impose upon the accused any manner of punishment — death, lashes, or monetary liability. The continuation of the verse, *yad beyad regel beregel ayin be'ayin*, might be read as a list of retaliatory penalties to be imposed literally. Rabi Meir indeed holds that false witnesses who sought to have the accused executed receive lashes (for the prohibition of *eidut shaker*) *and* pay monetary compensation as separate sanctions arising from distinct legal categories, since the prohibition of false testimony and the sanction of *ka'asher zamam* are legally independent of one another: one can transgress the prohibition of *lo sa'aneh* without being subject to the sanction of *ka'asher zamam* (e.g., if the procedural requirements for *hazamah* are not met), and the *ka'asher zamam* penalty is not a punishment for the personal transgression but a broader institutional mechanism for protecting the integrity of judicial proceedings. The rabbis, however — the position the *gemara* adopts — hold that one pays and does not receive lashes.

### Hand for Hand

The textual basis for the rabbinic position is derived from the phrase *yad beyad* itself. The *gemara* asks: given that the verse has already established the principle of *ka'asher zamam*, what additional meaning does *yad beyad* contribute? The answer: *davar hanitan miyad leyad* — something transferred from hand to hand, evoking the image of handing over money. The Torah thereby signals explicitly that the sanction of *edim zomemin* in monetary cases takes the form of monetary payment. And since the Torah has explicitly categorized this as a monetary obligation, and one cannot impose both lashes and monetary payment, the monetary obligation prevails and lashes are not administered.

---

## Chovel Source

### Injury Verse

Having established the textual basis for *edim zomemin*'s exception, the *gemara* turns to *chovel b'chaveiro*. The relevant verse reads: *ka'asher asa ken ye'aseh lo* — as he has done, so shall be done to him. This appears to mandate literal retaliation for physical injury. Why, then, does the verse then add a further phrase?

### Yinaten Means Money

The verse continues: *ken yinaten bo* — so shall it be *given* in him. The *gemara* asks: given that the verse already stated *ke'asher asa ken ye'aseh lo*, why add *ken yinaten bo*? The answer derives from the word *yinaten* — *given*: *davar sheyesh bo netina*, u-*mai nihu mamon* — something that is given over, and what is that? Money. The word *yinaten*, evoking the act of handing something over, signals that the compensation for physical injury takes the form of monetary payment. This is the explicit textual basis — identified through *chazal*'s reading — for the exception of *chovel b'chaveiro*: the Torah itself has explicitly designated this as a case of monetary obligation, thereby establishing it as an exception to the general rule that lashes take precedence.

---

## Defending Lashes

### Gemara Challenge

With Rabbi Yochanan's general principle and its two explicit exceptions now established, the *gemara* presses a different challenge. Rabbi Yochanan holds that in the case of rape combined with incest, lashes take precedence — to pay money rather than administer lashes would, in his view, undermine the weight of the prohibition of incest, *bataltah ervat achoto lo tigaleh*. If money replaces lashes, the prohibition loses its deterrent force and its appropriate gravity as a sanction.

But this reasoning creates a difficulty with the very exceptions Rabbi Yochanan acknowledges. If paying money rather than lashing undermines the weight of a prohibition, why does he accept the exceptions of *chovel b'chaveiro* and *edim zomemin*? Does permitting monetary payment in those cases not equally undermine the weight of those prohibitions?

What lies beneath this exchange is significant. The technical disagreements between Ulla and Rabbi Yochanan about how to read certain verses are not occurring in a vacuum. Rabbi Yochanan's preference for lashes reflects a substantive jurisprudential commitment: serious sins require serious punishment, and monetary payment — whatever its practical benefits — is not an adequate substitute for the punitive weight of lashes when a genuine prohibition has been violated. This underlying philosophy shapes how he reads the relevant verses.

### Ben Gerusha Case

Rabbi Yochanan responds to the challenge regarding *edim zomemin* as follows: *efshar lekiyumah b'ven gerusha u'ven chalutza* — it is possible to fulfill the prohibition's lashes-based sanction in the case of a *ben gerusha* or a *ben chalutza*. If the false witnesses testified that a certain *kohen* was a *ben gerusha* or *ben chalutza* — that is, born of a union that disqualifies priestly lineage — the sanction of *ka'asher zamam* cannot be applied in the normal way, because one cannot impose a status-based disqualification on witnesses who are themselves not *kohanim* or who already bear that disqualification. When *ka'asher zamam* is inapplicable, no monetary payment is due, and the witnesses instead receive lashes for the prohibition of bearing false witness. Thus the prohibition of *eidut sheker* remains one for which lashes can and do apply in certain configurations; the fact that monetary payment takes over in other configurations does not strip the prohibition of its lashes-based dimension. The underlying force of the prohibition is not undermined.

### Perutah Edge Case

Similarly, regarding *chovel b'chaveiro*: the edge case of *haka'ah she'ein bah shaveh perutah* — a wound of less than a *perutah*'s worth — demonstrates that the prohibition against striking another person retains its lashes-based sanction. In the rare theoretical scenario where no monetary obligation whatsoever arises from the act, lashes are administered. One can therefore say that the prohibition is not undermined: it remains, at least in principle and in rare practice, a prohibition that carries the sanction of lashes. The fact that in most cases monetary payment takes over does not negate the underlying lashes-based character of the prohibition.

### Incest Lashes

Rabbi Yochanan now turns the argument back in his own favor. If the logic for maintaining lashes as the appropriate sanction for those two categories is that there exist configurations in which lashes do apply — and this is considered sufficient to preserve the weight of the prohibition — then the same reasoning actually *strengthens* his position regarding incest. In the case of incest, the *majority* of cases will result in lashes: whenever the act is consensual, or whenever the woman is a *bogeret*, there is no monetary obligation and lashes are administered. The configuration where both rape and incest coincide — the scenario Ulla would resolve in favor of monetary payment — is a minority of cases. The prohibition of incest is overwhelmingly a lashes-based prohibition. To say that in this particular configuration money should replace lashes undermines a prohibition that in most of its applications carries lashes. Rabbi Yochanan therefore insists that even in the rape-and-incest case, lashes must prevail.

---

## Conclusion

### Tachat Already Used

The *gemara* concludes by addressing why Rabbi Yochanan does not adopt Ulla's *gezeirah shavah* from *tachat* to *tachat*. Rabbi Yochanan would say: *hai tachat asher innah* — the word *tachat* in the rape verse — *mibaya lei lekhed'Abaye*, I need that word to teach something else entirely, as Abaye derives from it a different *halacha* altogether.

### Ulla's Deduction

Abaye derives from the phrase *tachat asher innah* that the fifty *shekel* fine paid by the rapist constitutes payment specifically for the act of sexual violation itself — and that this very specification implies, *michlal de'ika boshet u-pegam*, that there are additional payments owed beyond the fifty *shekel*, namely *boshet* and *pegam*, which remain as independent obligations. Since Rabbi Yochanan uses the word *tachat* for this derivation, he cannot simultaneously use it for Ulla's *gezeirah shavah*. Ulla, for his part, derives the same teaching about additional payments from a different verse, attributed to Rava: *venatan ha'ish hashochev imah la'avi ha-na'arah chamishim kasef* — the man who lay with her shall give fifty silver pieces to the father of the young woman. The phrase *hanat shechiva chamishim* — the fifty is for the pleasure of the act itself — indicates by implication that *boshet* and *pegam* are paid separately. With this derivation available to him, Ulla does not need *tachat asher innah* for that purpose and is therefore free to use it for the *gezeirah shavah*.

### Bottom Line

The final picture is this. The general rule, as Rabbi Yochanan establishes from *kedei rishato*, is that when one must choose between lashes and monetary payment, lashes take precedence. The court administers lashes and does not collect monetary payment. There are two explicit exceptions — *chovel b'chaveiro* and *edim zomemin* — where the Torah itself mandates monetary payment through textual signals (*yinaten* and *yad beyad* respectively), making these deliberate exceptions to the general rule. In the case of rape combined with incest, Rabbi Yochanan holds that the general rule applies: lashes are administered and monetary payment is not collected. Ulla disagrees, holding — through a *gezeirah shavah* of *tachat* to *tachat* — that in the specific case of rape, as in *chovel b'chaveiro*, the monetary obligation takes precedence. On Tosafot's reading, this is Ulla's limited claim: not a universal principle, but a rule confined to the rape case alone, derived through the verbal analogy and justified by the same logic that protects the victim's interests in cases of personal injury.

---

---

# Ketubot 35

## Mechitzah Overview

### Opening Remarks

The topic of *mechitzah* opens onto a wide range of questions: What is its source? What are its requirements — how high must it be, must it be transparent or opaque, and when exactly is one required? These are practical, technical questions that demand careful attention. But underlying all of them is a deeper philosophical question about how we understand women's place within the synagogue. Does the *mechitzah* define the synagogue as a fundamentally male space, one in which women do not truly belong? Or is there another way to understand *mechitzah* that is not exclusionary and does not relegate women to the margins of the worship community?

### Philosophy of Space

This is not merely an abstract philosophical debate — it carries real consequences for how we structure our communal spaces and how we speak about them. The question, at its core, is whether women are understood as part of the *tzibbur* or as guests within a male domain.

### Related Issues

Related questions flow naturally from this central one. Consider, for instance, the question of architectural changes to a synagogue: if a congregation wishes to expand one section at the expense of another, can the women's section be converted into men's space and vice versa? A number of *poskim* have ruled that converting the women's section into the men's section is permissible because it constitutes an elevation in sanctity, but that the reverse conversion — men's space into women's space — is forbidden because it represents a diminishment. Others disagree. But the very existence of that position reveals how some authorities conceptualize not merely the physical arrangement of the synagogue but the nature of women's presence within it.

### Women & Minyan

A related question concerns *davening be-tzibbur*. It is actually the ruling of almost all *poskim* that there is no individual obligation to *daven* with a *minyan* — the community as a whole has an obligation to maintain a regular *minyan*, and it is certainly preferred for individuals to *daven* with one, but it is not strictly obligatory on each person. The community's obligation to maintain a *minyan* is real and serious, particularly in a close-knit community where each person's participation is felt. But the individual *chet* for *davening* at home does not rise to the level of a formal prohibition. The more interesting question, however, is whether we say the same thing about women — that it is preferable and valuable for a woman to come to shul, to *daven* there, to answer *Kaddish* and *Kedushah* and hear *Kriat HaTorah*. Or do we say that for a woman it makes no difference whether she comes at all? On each of these questions — the sanctity of the women's section, women's encouraged attendance, and the nature of *mechitzah* — there is a clear division between those *poskim* who treat the synagogue as a fundamentally male space and those who do not.

---

## Historical Sources

### Gaonic Period

Strikingly, in the *Gemara* itself there is no explicit source for the requirement of a *mechitzah* for *davening*. The first explicit references to men and women *davening* separately appear in the Gaonic period — roughly the sixth through eighth centuries — and even there, the mentions are incidental. For example, a discussion about whether one may accept women's testimony in the absence of men arises in the context of disputes over synagogue seating. The passage does not speak of a women's *section* but of a *Beit Knesset l'nashim* — evidently a separate structure entirely. The reference tells us that women were *davening* apart from men by the Gaonic period, but it tells us this only in passing. The *Gemara* contains no explicit ruling one way or the other on the question.

### Archaeology

Archaeological evidence is equally indeterminate. For many years, archaeologists discovering ancient synagogues would identify certain rooms as "women's sections" — only for later scholars to point out that this identification was entirely assumed. An additional room is simply an additional room; the label "women's section" was projected onto it based on contemporary practice rather than established from the evidence itself. What we can say is that separate *davening* for men and women is attested at least from the Gaonic period and possibly earlier, but the *Gemara* offers no explicit reference in either direction.

### Modern Context

It only became necessary to articulate a halachic basis for *mechitzah* in the modern period, when the practice came under scrutiny. The *Chatam Sofer* — the great late-eighteenth and early-nineteenth century Hungarian authority — was one of the first to reach back into *Talmudic* sources and articulate a reasoned justification. He did so in the context of a responsum concerning a mixed choir that was proposed to perform for the Tsar in the main synagogue of Saint Petersburg, and in that *teshuvah* he discussed why men and women do not sit together in the synagogue in the first place. What had been an unquestioned practice for perhaps fifteen hundred years was now being asked to justify itself.

---

## Temple Model

### Ezrat Nashim Role

One major basis that was offered for the *mechitzah* requirement — particularly in response to the legal and social pressures of twentieth-century American Jewish life — was the model of the Temple. The argument runs as follows: the synagogue is a *mikdash me'at*, a temple in miniature, and therefore its architecture should mirror the Temple's arrangement of separate sections for men and women.

A closer look at the Temple's structure, however, complicates this argument considerably. The *Ezrat Nashim* — the so-called "women's courtyard" — was in fact enormous. This size does not reflect a proportionally larger female attendance at sacrificial worship. Rather, the *Ezrat Nashim* functioned as a social hall. It was the gathering space where men and women mingled freely until it was time to proceed to the worship area proper. As will be discussed further, it was also the site of the *Simchat Beit Hasho'eiva*, the great celebration on *Sukkot*. The actual *Beit HaMikdash* — the sacred precinct defined halachically as the temple — begins only at the wall separating the *Ezrat Nashim* from the *Ezrat Yisrael*. Everything to the east of that line was, functionally, a lobby.

---

## Mount Clemens Case

### Charter & Battle

The legal and communal battle that most forcefully drove Orthodox authorities to articulate explicit halachic justifications for *mechitzah* was the famous Mount Clemens case in Michigan. This synagogue had a charter provision stipulating that no change inconsistent with *halacha* could be made if at least ten members in good standing objected. In the 1950s or 1960s, as the congregation moved toward removing the *mechitzah* — a move that effectively marked the transition from Orthodox to Conservative affiliation — ten members invoked that clause. The question that reached the American civil courts was whether a *mechitzah* was in fact a halachic requirement.

### Orthodox Identity

This legal battle played out against a backdrop in which the *mechitzah* had become the single most visible marker distinguishing Orthodox from Conservative synagogues in mid-twentieth century American Jewish life. Many congregations of that era had memberships and rabbis of similar backgrounds and education; the *mechitzah* — its presence or absence — was what defined a synagogue's denominational identity. The stakes were therefore enormous, and both sides sought the most authoritative responsa they could obtain.

### Responsa Collections

The Conservative side assembled responsa from the faculty and leadership of JTS, collected in an issue of *Conservative Judaism*. The Orthodox side gathered *teshuvot* from Rav Soloveitchik, Rav Moshe Feinstein, and other leading authorities of the day; these were published in a volume called *Sanctity of the Synagogue*, which for many years was actually distributed at one rabbinical school's *semichah* ceremony — a telling illustration of how central the *mechitzah* question had become to the definition of Orthodox rabbinic identity.

---

## Temple Model (II)

### Worship as Male Space

Returning now to what the Temple model actually implies: if the *Ezrat Nashim* was not the sanctuary but the lobby — the space where mixed mingling was normal — and if the genuine worship space begins only at the *Ezrat Yisrael*, then using the Temple as the model for synagogue *mechitzah* is effectively saying that worship is a male space. Women's designated area was not the *Mikdash*; it was the antechamber. And the message imported into the synagogue by this model is correspondingly stark: the *Beit HaKnesset* is fundamentally male space, and women are present at its margins.

There is a further, troubling detail. The section that men occupied in the Temple was not called the *Ezrat Gevarim* — the men's courtyard — but the *Ezrat Yisrael*, the Israelites' section. The name *Yisrael* functions in contrast to *Kohanim* on one level, denoting the non-priestly Israelite males; but it also implicitly contrasts with *Ezrat Nashim*, suggesting that it is the men who constitute *Klal Yisrael* in the primary sense, while women occupy a secondary or peripheral category. Even setting aside the question of whether the Temple model carries halachic weight as a normative source for synagogue architecture — and it does not, since the *Talmud* contains no such requirement — the model raises profound philosophical concerns about the nature of the worship space and who is understood to belong there.

There are also practical implications. When the *mechitzah* is placed at the back of the synagogue — rather than down the middle or along the sides — on the explicit grounds that this mirrors the Temple arrangement, women are pushed entirely to the periphery, effectively outside the congregation.

### Kiddushin 52b

A striking *Gemara* in *Kiddushin* 52b illustrates the underlying assumption that the *Ezrat Yisrael* was a male space into which women entered only in exceptional circumstances. The passage begins with a halachic question: can a man effect *kiddushin* — betrothal — by giving a woman meat from his sacrifice, since he has a right to eat the meat but does not technically own it in a proprietary sense? The ruling is that such *kiddushin* does not take effect.

The context is established through a small drama. After the death of Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda told his students not to admit Rabbi Meir's disciples to their *Beit Midrash*, saying they were disputatious and came not to learn but to overwhelm him with questions. Nevertheless, Sumchus — one of Rabbi Meir's prize students — *dachak ve-nikhnas*, forced his way in, and transmitted a teaching in his master's name: if one betroths a woman using his portion of sacrificial meat — whether *kodshei kodashim* or *kodashim kalim* — the betrothal is invalid, since the meat is not truly his property.

Rabbi Yehuda was furious and repeated his warning. But then a logical problem arose: the case of betrothal with *kodshei kodashim* is particularly vexing, since those sacrifices cannot be taken out of the *Ezrat Yisrael* — and what would a woman be doing in the *Ezrat Yisrael*? Surely this is merely a theoretical puzzle, not a practical scenario. Rabbi Yosi, unwilling to remain silent while a genuine Torah teaching of Rabbi Meir went undefended, offered several solutions. Perhaps the father accepted the *kiddushin* on his minor daughter's behalf — a transaction between men, requiring no woman's presence at all. Or perhaps the woman had appointed a male agent to receive the *kiddushin* on her behalf — again, no woman need be physically present. And then the final answer: *v'od dachaka ve-nichnasa shema* — perhaps she simply forced her way in, just as Sumchus had forced his way into the *Beit Midrash*.

The echo is deliberate and the point is clear: the *Gemara* treats a woman's presence in the *Azara* as something so anomalous that it requires a battery of explanations, the last of which is that she simply pushed through. Women were not the expected population of that space. Their presence required justification; their absence was the default. One might observe, as was noted in discussion, that Rabbi Yosi ultimately concedes the possibility — implying that if a woman forced her way in, she could not simply be expelled, and that she had some legitimate standing to be there for the purpose for which she came. That is true, and worth noting. But it does not alter the fundamental characterization: the space was defined as male, and female presence was the exception that proved the rule.

### Rav Kook

This is precisely the model that Rav Kook invokes in one of the responsa collected in *Sanctity of the Synagogue*. He writes: "According to the Talmud, the synagogues are to be looked on as the sacred temple in miniature. It is therefore our duty to exalt them to the same level of holiness as our holy temple, may it be rebuilt in our day. Our fathers in establishing two separate divisions for men and women, thereby continuing the system inaugurated in the temple and using that as the model." That is the argument in its most direct form.

---

## Simchat Beit Hasho'eva

### Sukkah 51b

The second major Talmudic source adduced for *mechitzah* is also Temple-derived but addresses a different concern. The passage is found in *Sukkah* 51b, and it describes the arrangements made for the *Simchat Beit Hasho'eiva* — the great nighttime celebration on *Chol HaMoed Sukkot* preceding the water-drawing ceremony. The *Gemara* asks what the *tikkun gadol* — the great arrangement — was that they would set up when *Yom Tov* ended. Rabbi Elazar explains: the *Ezrat Nashim* had originally been flat, and they surrounded it with a *gezustra* — apparently a balcony or elevated gallery — so that the women were above and the men below.

A *baraita* then elaborates the historical development. Originally, women were on the inside and men on the outside. This arrangement led to *kalus rosh* — improper levity and mixing — because a woman making her way to her section would have to pass through the men's area. So they reversed it: men inside, women outside. But this too led to *kalus rosh*, since now men had to pass through the women's area. The final solution was to place women above and men below, eliminating the problem of crossing through each other's space.

The Gemara then asks: how could they make a structural change to the Temple? The verse in *Divrei HaYamim* states that David declared the entire plan of the Temple was given to him by God — implying it cannot be altered. The answer is that they found a verse in *Zechariah* that prophesies the end of days: *ve-safda ha'aretz mishpachot mishpachot l'vad* — "the land shall mourn, family by family, apart" — and it specifies, *mishpachat beit David l'vad u-nesheihem l'vad*, the family of the house of David separately, and their wives separately.

### Kal Vachomer

From this verse the *Gemara* derives a *kal va-chomer*: in the future, at the time of the mourning for *Mashiach ben Yosef*, people will be engaged in a eulogy — a solemn occasion — and moreover, the *yetzer ha-ra* will not dominate them as it does in this world. Yet the Torah still requires men and women to be separate. Now (*achshav*), when people are engaged in *simcha* — great joy and festivity — and the *yetzer ha-ra* does exert its pull: *al achat kama ve-kama*, how much more so must men and women be kept separate. This *kal va-chomer* becomes the basis for the separation enforced during the *Simchat Beit Hasho'eiva*.

### Scope Problem

This source is genuinely useful, but it presents a challenge: it is either too narrow or too broad as a basis for a general *mechitzah* requirement. If one focuses on the party context — the *Simchat Beit Hasho'eiva* — all one can establish is that mixed celebrations of that kind require separation. That tells us something important about mixed dancing and festive gatherings, but it does not straightforwardly extend to *davening*. If, on the other hand, one focuses on the *kal va-chomer* from the funeral context — the eulogies for *Mashiach ben Yosef* — then one seems forced to conclude that men and women must be separate at all times and in all serious contexts, a position that some *Haredi* communities do in fact adopt, extending the requirement even to lectures and study sessions. So the passage proves both too much and too little, depending on where one places the emphasis.

---

## Chatam Sofer Bridge

### Directing Thoughts to God

The *Chatam Sofer* bridges the gap between the *Simchat Beit Hasho'eiva* source and *davening* by identifying a common denominator. He argues that the requirement of separation applies whenever one is engaged in directing words or thoughts toward God — a religious activity in which the mind must be focused upward and not distracted. Prayer clearly qualifies. So does the *Simchat Beit Hasho'eiva*, since *Sukkot* joy is explicitly described in the Torah as *usmachtem lifnei Hashem Elokeichem* — rejoicing *before God* — making it a form of divine service rather than mere festivity. And a eulogy, too, carries a dimension of prayer. The *Chatam Sofer* thus argues that what these cases share is the directedness of the act toward God, and that in all such contexts the concern for distracted thought requires separation between men and women.

### Women Made Invisible

The specific concern the *Chatam Sofer* identifies is that men will see women and have sexual thoughts, thereby disrupting their *davening*. This framing has a significant implication: the concern is entirely about the men. It is men's prayer, men's mental purity, and men's concentration that is at stake. Women are cast as the source of distraction. Since seeing women creates the problem for men, the solution is to make women invisible — to ensure that men cannot see the women's section at all. Whether women's prayer is disrupted by seeing men is a question the *Chatam Sofer* does not raise, reflecting a broader set of assumptions in the *Talmud* about whose sexual thoughts are considered a halachic concern.

### Full-Height Requirement

The practical consequence of this reasoning is that the *mechitzah* must be full-height — ceiling to floor — so that women are completely invisible to the men. The *Chatam Sofer* was the dominant authority for Hungarian Jewry, and in Hungarian communities this was taken seriously enough that some refused to *daven* in a synagogue that had only a balcony, since a balcony actually maximizes visibility rather than eliminating it. From the perspective of the *Chatam Sofer's* reasoning, a balcony is among the worst possible arrangements.

---

## Rav Moshe Alternative

### Single-Sex Space

Rav Moshe Feinstein offers a fundamentally different analysis. He argues that the requirement of *mechitzah* is not about preventing men from having sexual thoughts (*hirhur*) about women. The concern, he says, is not *hirhur* at all but *kalus rosh* — the qualitative difference between a single-sex environment and a co-ed environment. A co-ed space has a different social character than a single-sex space, and that difference is what is at stake.

### Education Analogy

One way to understand what Rav Moshe means is through an analogy to single-sex versus co-ed education. The evidence in educational research tends to show that single-sex settings benefit girls while co-ed settings benefit boys — though the dynamic is more nuanced than any simple summary. The underlying mechanism seems to be that co-ed environments heighten self-consciousness: in a mixed setting, people become more attuned to how they are perceived by others of the opposite sex. For boys, the presence of girls tends to be moderating and self-regulating; for girls, it tends to be inhibiting — socialized patterns of deference and quietness are activated. When girls are in an all-female environment, they are less self-conscious in that particular way and more free to assert themselves intellectually.

### Vertical Experience

Translating this into the context of *davening*: Rav Soloveitchik, in a related context, spoke of wanting *davening* to be a vertical experience rather than a horizontal one — a turning upward toward God rather than a social awareness of those around us. The reality, of course, is that *shul* is often deeply horizontal — a place of reunion, conversation, and social reinforcement. But the aspiration is to create a space in which one can focus on God rather than on how one appears to others. The argument, following Rav Moshe's logic, is that a single-sex environment better enables that kind of vertical focus, for men and women alike — not because the opposite sex is a source of illicit thoughts, but because a co-ed environment is structurally more social and self-conscious.

One might of course push back: perhaps for some people a co-ed space is entirely natural and their *davening* is not enhanced by single-sex separation. Perhaps a men's section without women becomes more of a social club. These are legitimate observations, and no claim is being made that the argument is empirically airtight. But the crucial point is that Rav Moshe's framework does not define the synagogue as a male space or cast women as a problem to be managed. It says: we want single-sex prayer spaces, not co-ed ones, and that applies symmetrically to men and women.

### Practical Criteria

This philosophical difference translates directly into practical requirements. Since the concern is not visibility but the nature of the space, Rav Moshe rules that the *mechitzah* need not be full-height. Shoulder height — eighteen *tefachim*, translating to somewhere between fifty-four and seventy-two inches depending on the measurement of a *tefach*, with Rav Soloveitchik specifying fifty inches — is sufficient to create a meaningfully separate space. A balcony, far from being problematic as in the Hungarian tradition, is in Rav Moshe's view an excellent arrangement, since it clearly demarcates separate spaces even while permitting visual connection. Similarly, the *mechitzah* need not be opaque; transparency is not a problem because the issue is not seeing but the designation of separate spaces.

---

## Mechitzah Specificat (II)

### Height Measurements

To recapitulate the technical parameters: Rav Moshe Feinstein specifies eighteen *tefachim* as the minimum *mechitzah* height, which translates to between fifty-four and seventy-two inches. Rav Soloveitchik set fifty inches. These figures reflect the principle that the *mechitzah* must be high enough to function as a genuine spatial designation — not merely a token marker — while not being required to eliminate all visual contact between sections.

### Ma'akeh Status

Underlying these rulings is an important conceptual point: the *mechitzah* functions as a *ma'akeh* — a protective fence, a prophylactic measure — rather than as an absolute biblical prohibition. This means that while *davening* in a mixed space is not ideal and is contrary to established practice, it does not technically render one's prayer invalid. The distinction is between the character of the space one ideally creates and the validity of *tefillah* in imperfect circumstances. A person *davening* at home while men and women are present in the room is not in the same category as a congregation that has abandoned *mechitzah* in its synagogue.

### Context Variation

This distinction helps explain why *mechitzah* requirements are applied differently in different contexts. When a group *davens Mincha* on a field trip, one creates separate spaces but does not erect a *mechitzah* in the full halachic sense. At a *shiva* house, if possible men and women will be on different levels or in different rooms, but if not, *davening* can proceed. At a wedding, similarly, one tries to arrange separate areas without necessarily requiring a formal *mechitzah*. None of this is inconsistent, because *mechitzah* in the synagogue is about the identity and character of the *shul* as a designated prayer space, and that is the context in which the full requirement applies. In all other contexts, the concern for appropriate separation remains, but it is calibrated to the setting. As was accurately observed in discussion, even a person *davening* alone in an airport, surrounded by men and women going about their business, is in a categorically different situation from a congregation *davening* together in a mixed setting.

---

## Egalitarian Paradox (III)

### Sisterhood Comment

A striking observation came from a woman who noted that in certain social environments — particularly family-focused congregations organized around couples and children — she had felt excluded and peripheral. What she found, paradoxically, was that the *mechitzah* created a kind of *sisterhood* in which her marital status, family configuration, and social standing became irrelevant. Within the women's section she was simply one of the *tzibbur*, neither marked nor judged by the categories that structured the rest of congregational social life.

---

## Mechitzah Specificat (II)

### Placement Models

Beyond height and opacity, the question of placement is also significant. A *mechitzah* running straight down the middle of the sanctuary sends a very different message from one that confines women to the back or sides. The Hebrew Institute of Riverdale, under Rabbi Weiss, aimed for an arrangement in which, when *davening* is not in session, a visitor cannot tell which is the men's side and which is the women's side. The *mechitzah* runs straight down the center; the *bimah* stands on an island surrounded by its own *mechitzah*; the two sections are visually parallel. This is not always architecturally achievable, but it represents an important aspiration.

---

## Egalitarian Paradox (III)

### Leadership Challenge

The acknowledgment of this egalitarian structure carries with it an honest reckoning: even if the *mechitzah* runs down the middle and the physical space is divided equally, if men are the ones leading all of the *davening* and holding all of the participatory roles, it becomes very difficult for the *mechitzah* not to be perceived as a marker of differential status. The physical equality does not by itself resolve the deeper question of women's role within the prayer community.

---

## Cultural Definitions

### Wide Aisle Option

One might ask whether a cultural marker or a wide aisle could substitute for a physical *mechitzah* — whether the *de facto* separation of spaces could be achieved without a physical partition. This is indeed a live question among *poskim*.

### Aisle Examples

Rav Yehuda Herzl Henkin maintains that ten *tefachim* — roughly three feet, which in other areas of *halacha* is considered sufficient to designate separate domains — would suffice to define distinct prayer spaces. A small number of Orthodox synagogues have in fact operated on this basis, some with aisles as wide as thirty feet serving as the separation. Rav Moshe Feinstein, however, while agreeing that the concern is about the nature of the space rather than visibility, holds that a very low or narrow divider fails to actually create the distinct single-sex spaces that the requirement demands; the practical feeling of the space must reflect the separation.

### Inconsistency

It must be acknowledged frankly that actual practice in this area is not always logically consistent with any single underlying argument. The way *mechitzah* rulings developed — starting from a well-established communal practice and working backward to find Talmudic sources and conceptual foundations — means that the application of the rule does not flow neatly from one coherent principle. The result is an amalgam, and it can be difficult to *pasken* these questions in the way one would normally derive rulings: from the *Gemara* outward through the commentaries to practical application.

---

## Egalitarian Paradox (III)

### Variable Heights

Even setting aside the theoretical questions, the practical reality is that people have different sensibilities. In one setting, when asked whether people would object to lowering an unusually high *mechitzah* at a *Limmud* *minyan*, the silence broke only when one woman said, plainly: "Please." Yet in another setting, a woman expressed that she specifically did not want a lower *mechitzah* — she wanted to be able to *daven* without being conscious of men watching her, to focus inward, to connect to God without the self-consciousness that a low partition introduces. This is itself an expression of Rav Moshe's logic: the point is the environment, and different people may need different environments to achieve the vertical focus that *davening* demands. Accommodating this sometimes means having sections of the *mechitzah* at different heights, allowing people to sit where they feel most comfortable.

---

## Cultural Definitions (II)

### Lower Mechitzah Limits

A lower *mechitzah* is not therefore simply and universally "more inclusive." Inclusivity means taking seriously what different people need to *daven* well, and for some that means a higher barrier. The goal is not to impose a particular aesthetic or comfort level but to create a space in which all members of the congregation can genuinely engage in prayer.

---

## Sefardic/Ashkenazi

### Rav Ovadia Yosef

An ironic and illuminating contrast emerges when one compares Ashkenazi and Sefardi *halachic* responses to questions about women's participation. One might expect, given that women in Ashkenazi communities have historically played more active public roles in broader society, that Ashkenazi *psak* would be more inclusive. Sometimes it is — an Ashkenazi woman who takes a *lulav* makes a *bracha*, while a Sefardi woman who takes a *lulav* does not, which is not a minor distinction: the *bracha* is what transforms the act into a *mitzvah*. But on many questions of women's participation in synagogue life, Rav Ovadia Yosef is actually more permissive than his Ashkenazi counterparts, and the reason is instructive: he was not responding to Reform Judaism or to the feminist movement. He was not looking over his shoulder at what the non-Orthodox denominations were doing. When the question of a *Bat Mitzvah* ceremony was raised, Rav Ovadia said straightforwardly: of course one can have a *Bat Mitzvah* ceremony — in what way is it different from a *Bar Mitzvah*? It will increase people's involvement in Judaism; why would one not do it?

### Women's Participation

Similarly, on the question of whether a woman may recite *Birkat HaGomel* in *shul*, Rav Ovadia's answer was direct: of course she may — why should she not? The elaborate considerations that occupied Ashkenazi *poskim* on this question were simply not operative for him. Because he was not engaged in a defensive posture against the challenge of Reform and feminism, he could assess each question on its merits and arrive at inclusive conclusions without the baggage of ideological boundary-drawing.

### Historical Context

There is also a historical dimension to this comparison. In some communities — whether Hungarian Ashkenazi or certain Sefardi communities — women simply did not come to *shul* regularly. In those contexts, the question of *mechitzah* was largely moot: if women are not present, the *mechitzah* question does not arise in a practical sense. This may explain why the *mechitzah* did not become a live issue in those communities in the way it did in settings where women's attendance was more common.

---

## Women in Congregation

### Home vs. Shul

A responsum from Rav Henkin directly addresses the question of whether women should be discouraged from attending synagogue, and it is worth reading carefully. The question presented to him concerned women who wished to come to *shul* and *daven* but brought their young children with them, creating noise and disruption. The questioner suggested that since the Torah exempted women from time-bound positive commandments precisely so that they could focus on child-rearing, women should be told to stay home with the children rather than come to *shul* and disrupt the *davening*. Rav Henkin responds sharply: *ta'ut hi ba-din* — this is a halachic error. Women are not exempt from *tefillah* as such, and the broader attitude that women's place is at home and not in the synagogue is not grounded in *halacha*.

### Modern Reality

Rav Henkin then makes a pointed observation about the contemporary reality: since women today go out of the house for countless reasons — work, socializing, errands — it would be far better if among those reasons were attending *shul*. *Halevai* — if only they would come to *batei kneisiyot* and places of *kedushah*. The exemption from time-bound *mitzvot* was not intended to strand women at home in a general sense; in a world where women are active participants in public life, that rationale for keeping them away from *shul* collapses entirely. On the contrary, women should be actively encouraged to attend.

### Childcare Rotation

As for the practical problem of children creating disruption, Rav Henkin proposes a rotation: a system of *toranut shmirat ha-tinokot* — a childcare schedule — so that mothers can take turns attending *shul* while others remain with the children. He notes that when many women attend *shul* and only a few must remain outside to watch the children, those few feel marginalized and excluded, week after week bearing the burden so that others may participate. A rotation addresses this inequity.

### Childcare Funding

The further step — which flows from Rav Henkin's logic even if he does not himself state it — is that the *shul* itself should fund organized childcare, freeing all members of the community, women and men alike, to attend *davening* on equal terms.

---

## Conclusion

### Ingrained Assumptions

These issues are not merely matters of sources and legal analysis. They require a profound sensitivity to how deeply ingrained certain assumptions about the synagogue as male space have become — assumptions so embedded that they often operate invisibly, below the level of conscious reflection.

### Practical Steps

Practical steps follow from this sensitivity. Adjusting childcare timing so that women feel fully included rather than treated as spectators. Using language that actually reflects who is present. Protecting women's space within the synagogue as genuinely equal, not as borrowed or conditional.

---

## Subtle Exclusion

### Etched Text

A student once shared an observation from his wife after they stopped to *daven Mincha* in an unfamiliar *shul*. As they left, she said to him: "You never have to *daven* where the Hebrew writing is reversed on your side of the *mechitzah*." The etched text on the glass *mechitzah* faced the men's side. Its orientation communicated silently but unmistakably: this space is for you. You are here at our leave.

### Prayer Inscription

A related example concerns the phrase *Da Lifnei Mi Atah Omed* — "Know before Whom you stand" — commonly inscribed in large letters at the front of the *aron kodesh*. A student once gave an extended presentation on the history and sources of this inscription. Only afterward was it pointed out to him that he had spoken for seven minutes without once noting that the phrase is written in the masculine. *Atah*, *omed* — addressed to a man, not a person. Whether or not it registers consciously, the subconscious message of that inscription to a woman is that she is not the one being addressed; the primary audience is the men. An easy alternative is to use *Shiviti Hashem Lenegdi Tamid* — "I have set the Lord before me always" — a phrase written in the first person that addresses every worshipper equally, without grammatical gendering.

---

## Conclusion (II)

### Communal Involvement

What these examples converge on is the importance of involving the entire community in these conversations rather than relying on rabbinical pronouncements alone. A rabbi who is genuinely trying to be sensitive can still miss things that congregants — particularly women — see and feel every day. The process of creating a genuinely inclusive *davening* community requires ongoing conversation, not a single corrective ruling issued from above. Sensitivity grows through dialogue, and the goal is to create a community in which all members feel that they belong — fully, not conditionally.

---

## Subtle Exclusion (II)

### Language Choices

A further, subtle example of exclusionary language: a rabbi announces before the end of *davening* that "everyone" should put away their *tallit* and *tefillin*. "Everyone," of course, means the men — but using the word "everyone" to mean a subset of those present invisibly redefines the actual audience. The women in the room are not "everyone." Noticing this requires no special effort; it requires only the willingness to attend to how language constructs who the real community is.

---

## Equal Space Protection

### Men's Spillover

A concrete and consequential expression of the male-space assumption is the common practice of men spilling over into the women's section during weekday *davening* when women are absent. Men put on their *tallit* and *tefillin* on the women's side, occupy those seats, use that space. If a woman then arrives, the men graciously make room for her. But the message this practice sends is unmistakable: fundamentally, all of this is our space. We will cede some of it when necessary. The women's section is conditional space — theirs only when they show up to claim it.

### Yeshiva Practice

A different practice reflects a different philosophy. In one *yeshiva*, before any *davening* begins — even though the *yeshiva* is composed entirely of men and perhaps only one or two women ever attend — the *mechitzah* is put straight down the middle, and it is completely forbidden for any man to cross to the women's side. It does not matter if he needs a *sefer* from that side. It does not matter if the other door is more convenient. The women's side is off-limits to men, period. The space belongs to the women; it is not borrowed from the men.

### Equal Portion

The principle that underlies this practice is simple and important: women must always feel that they have an equal portion as part of the *davening* community — not a contingent portion, not a graciously granted portion, but an equal one. The *mechitzah* going down the middle before *davening* begins, not after most people have already settled, is a structural statement that the women's space is as primary and inviolable as the men's. This principle — ensuring that women always feel genuinely included in the *davening* community — is the practical, communal expression of everything that the philosophical and halachic discussion has been working toward.

---

---

# Ketubot 36

## Kim Lei Review

### Kim Lei Summary

Today's daf is 36, and we pick up roughly two-thirds of the way down the page, at the words *ilanit ein lah knas*. We have, for the time being, finished with the extraordinary seven-*daf* *sugya* on *kim lei b'deraba minei*. By way of brief review: the *gemara* ultimately phrased the range of opinions as follows. Where the transgression carries a penalty of *misa beis din*, a biblical death sentence, the *gemara* at minimum implies — though *Tosfos* questions whether this is truly universal — that everyone would agree the death penalty overrides any monetary obligation, even in a case of *shogeg*. Where the penalty is *kares*, that was the position of Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah and was subject to debate. Where the penalty is *malkus*, the debate was widest: Rabbi Meir held that both punishments could be administered simultaneously; Ulla held that the offender pays rather than receives *malkus* (or, according to *Tosfos*, this may have applied only to the specific *knas* of *ones umefate*); and the standard position was that *malkus* is administered and no monetary payment follows — within which there was a further dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish, Rabbi Yochanan maintaining that this principle applies only when *malkus* was actually administered, and Resh Lakish holding it applies even in cases of *shogeg*, without *hatara*, even when *malkus* was never carried out.

### Ilanit & Age Status

The *gemara* now turns back to the categories of women who do or do not receive a *knas*, not from the perspective of *kim lei* but from the perspective of their personal status. The *mishna* had established that even women in certain *arayos* relationships — as long as the offense is not in the category of *chayav misa* — can still give rise to a *knas*, though a *beraisa* reflecting the positions of either Rabbi Shimon Hatimani or Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya restricted the *knas* to cases where marriage to the woman is at least theoretically binding, or even more restrictively, where marriage is actually permitted.

The *gemara* now returns to the question of whether the *knas* applies only to a *na'arah* or even to a *ketana*. Rabbi Meir holds it is limited to a *na'arah*; the *chachamim* extend it to a *ketana* as well. One practical application of this dispute involves the *ilanit* — a woman who never achieves physical maturity and therefore transitions directly from the status of *ketana* at age twenty to *bogeret*, never passing through the stage of *na'arah*. A *beraisa* stated that she receives no *knas*, presumably because she is never a *na'arah*.

### Besula Status

Beyond the *na'arah* question and the *arayos* question, a third axis of analysis concerns whether the woman can be presumed to be a *besula*. This issue was touched upon in connection with the *mema'enet* — a girl who is rabbinically but not biblically married and has been living with another man, and who therefore cannot be presumed a *besula*. The *gemara* now proceeds to examine other cases where the *besula* dimension of the definition is at stake.

---

## Ilanit Ein Lah Knas

### Ilanit Case

The *gemara* cites a *beraisa* stating: *ilanit ein lah knas* — an *ilanit* has no *knas* — and likewise no *knas* in the case of seduction involving her. This is consistent with what was established previously: she is never a *na'arah*.

### Ilanit Contradiction

The *gemara* immediately introduces a contradiction: *u-remihu* — and we raise a difficulty — for another *beraisa* lists the *chereshet*, the *shota*, and the *ilanit* together and declares *yesh lahem knas* — they do have a *knas*. Moreover, that same *beraisa* adds *ve-yesh lahem ta'anat betulim*: the husband has grounds to raise a claim of non-virginity the morning after the wedding night. This *ta'anat betulim* is, of course, no advantage to the wife; it means the husband has a legitimate basis to challenge her presumed *besula* status and seek to reduce her *kesuvah* from two hundred to one hundred or eliminate it entirely. The *chereshet* and the *shota* are new information here and will be addressed in a moment. As for the *ilanit*: one *beraisa* says she has a *knas* and the other says she does not — an apparent contradiction.

### Meir vs Rabbanan

The *gemara* immediately resolves this: *ve-hai mai rumiya?* — what kind of contradiction is this at all? *Ha Rabbi Meir, ha Rabanan.* We already established that the entire debate about the *ilanit* traces directly to the *tanna'im* dispute about whether a *ketana* has a *knas*. The *beraisa* that denies her a *knas* reflects Rabbi Meir's position that only a *na'arah* is entitled, while the *beraisa* that grants her one reflects the *Rabanan*'s view that even a *ketana* qualifies. There is no contradiction at all. The *gemara* therefore asks: *ve-ka'arei lei mai ka'arei lei?* — why did you even think to raise this as a difficulty, given that this is transparently a *machlokes* between *tanna'im*? The *gemara* answers: *mishum de-is lei de-mir me-achrisi aloyei* — he knew full well the *ilanit* question was answerable; he introduced it only to lay the groundwork for bringing a second *beraisa* that poses a genuine difficulty, one he truly wanted to examine.

---

## Chereshet & Shotah

### Have Knas & Betulim

The more serious challenge involves the *chereshet* and *shota*. The *beraisa* just cited declares that a deaf-mute woman and a mentally ill woman — neither of whom is considered a *bar da'at* — are presumed virgins, have a *knas*, and are subject to *ta'anat betulim*. This is itself a striking *chiddush*: these are women that people might readily take advantage of, and yet the *beraisa* presumes they remain virgins, entitling them to the full protections of a *besula*.

### No Ta'anat Betulim

A contradictory *beraisa*, however, lists *ha-chereshet ve-ha-shota ve-ha-bogeret u-mukat eitz ein lahem ta'anat betulim* — a deaf-mute, a mentally ill woman, a *bogeret*, and a *mukat eitz* are not subject to *ta'anat betulim*. The *mukat eitz* is a woman who has sustained a physical injury that has ruptured the hymen; she obviously cannot be presumed a *besula* in the physical sense. The *bogeret* will be addressed separately. But the *chereshet* and *shota* are the live contradiction: one *beraisa* says the husband can raise a *ta'anat betulim*, the other says he cannot. One might have assumed this reflects a dispute about whether we presume these women are virgins — and if we do not, then there would similarly be a debate about whether they are entitled to a *knas*. But the *gemara* rejects this framing.

### Gamliel vs Yehoshua

Rav Sheshet resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya — ha Rabban Gamliel, ha Rabbi Yehoshua.* This answer is elegant. The question of *ta'anat betulim* is not simply a function of whether we presume the woman to be a virgin. Even if we universally presume she is a virgin — and the *gemara* maintains that everyone agrees a *chereshet* and *shota* are presumed virgins, so that everyone agrees they are entitled to a *knas* — the husband's *ta'anat betulim* claim may or may not succeed for entirely separate reasons. Recall the dispute in the first *perek* between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding the defenses available to a wife when her husband raises a claim of non-virginity. Rabban Gamliel accepts certain counter-claims — for instance, that she was violated after the *kiddushin*, or that she is a *mukat eitz* — and if she makes such a claim, the husband's assertion does not prevail. Rabbi Yehoshua, by contrast, holds *lo mipi anu chayim*: no defense she can offer will save her. Accordingly, the *beraisa* that says the husband has a valid *ta'anat betulim* follows Rabbi Yehoshua — since she cannot rebut him successfully, his claim stands. The *beraisa* that says there is no *ta'anat betulim* follows Rabban Gamliel — not because we presume her not to be a virgin, but because there is always a counter-claim available that will defeat the husband's assertion.

### Beis Din Representation

The *gemara* presses further: granted that Rabban Gamliel validates such defenses — but Rabban Gamliel's validation was predicated on *her* making the claim. What if she cannot speak for herself? Does Rabban Gamliel's leniency apply when the wife never personally lodges any particular defense? The *gemara* answers affirmatively: *kivan de-amar Rabban Gamliel mehemana, she-kegon zeh ptach picha l'ilem hu* — since Rabban Gamliel established that a wife is believed when she offers such explanations, the principle of "open your mouth for the mute" applies, and *beis din* steps in to present the most advantageous position on her behalf. These women, as non-*bnei da'at*, cannot represent themselves, and so *beis din* assumes the role, arguing for them — whether the defense is that she was violated after the *kiddushin*, as *Rashi* suggests, or that she became a *mukat eitz*, as *Tosfos* prefers.

It is worth noting the underlying tension here: some of Rabban Gamliel's defenses derive their persuasive force from the woman's *nes* — the brazenness required to lie in her husband's presence — or from the definite (*bari*) character of her own claim. When *beis din* makes the argument on her behalf, those considerations weaken. Nevertheless, the principle of *beis din* representing those without legal competence extends to cases of *ketanim* and others lacking *da'at*, and the *gemara* accepts that this representation can suffice to defeat the husband's claim.

The upshot is significant: the contradiction in the *baraitot* about *chereshet* and *shota* has nothing to do with whether they are presumed virgins. Universally, we assume they are virgins, and universally they are entitled to a *knas*. The contradiction concerns only whether the husband's *ta'anat betulim* succeeds — and that turns on the Rabban Gamliel–Rabbi Yehoshua debate about available defenses.

---

## Bogeret & Suma Cases

### Bogeret Layla Rishona

The *gemara* now turns to the *bogeret*, who the *beraisa* listed as one who has no *ta'anat betulim*. What is the basis for this? The *gemara* cites Rav: *bogeret nosnin lah layla rishona* — for a *bogeret*, all hymenal bleeding during the first night of marriage is attributed to the hymen rather than to *dam niddah*. This refers back to the *niddah* discussion in the earlier *perekm* where the question was how long after the wedding night a woman's bleeding could be attributed to the hymen and therefore not treated as *niddah*. For a younger woman or one who has not yet established a regular cycle, more time is granted; for a *bogeret*, who has been regularly menstruating, only the first night qualifies. The critical point is that this ruling presupposes that a *bogeret* does have a hymen that bleeds. We assume the hymen is intact. So if the husband maintains the hymen was not intact on the wedding night, why can he not make a *ta'anat betulim*?

### Blood vs Petach

The *gemara* clarifies the distinction between two possible claims. The discussion is at the top of 36b. If the husband claims *ta'anat damim* — that there was no blood on the wedding night — then *hacha nami*, he would have a valid claim, because we assume a *bogeret* does have an intact hymen and there will be blood; the absence of blood is meaningful evidence. But the case of *bogeret ein lah ta'anat betulim* is where he makes not a claim about blood but a claim of *petach patuach* — that physically the experience did not feel as it would with a virgin. This claim fails for a *bogeret*, because the *gemara* says her more developed physiology means the situation will feel different regardless, and no inference can be drawn from that sensation. As *Rashi* explains, *bo'el kama be'ilos* — the first night includes multiple acts, and all the bleeding throughout that night is attributed to hymenal rupture, which is why the analysis focuses on the night as a whole. But once we shift to the *petach patuach* claim rather than the blood claim, the *bogeret*'s physical maturity renders that claim meaningless, and the husband loses.

### Suma Accident Theory

The *beraisa* cited earlier included a position from Sumchos, in the name of Rabbi Meir: *suma ein lah ta'anat betulim* — a blind woman cannot be subject to a *ta'anat betulim*, meaning the husband has no valid claim even if he finds evidence of non-virginity. The reasoning offered by Rav Zeira on behalf of Sumchos is that a blind woman is prone to stumbling and falling — *mipnei she-nichbetes al gabei karka* — and such a fall might cause a physical injury that ruptures the hymen, effectively making her a *mukat eitz*. Since one cannot rule out such an accident, the husband should not have assumed that an intact hymen was guaranteed, and his claim therefore carries no weight.

### All Women Have Accidents

The *gemara* challenges this immediately: *kulan nami chabutei michabtan* — all women trip and have accidents, not only blind women. Sighted women sustain physical injuries too. Notably, the *gemara* does not respond by arguing that blind women are statistically more accident-prone. That is not the *gemara*'s answer.

### Blind Woman Unawareness

Instead, the *gemara* offers a distinct principle: *kulan ro'ot u-mar'ot l'iman* — a sighted girl who has an accident and notices blood or some other indication will tell her mother what happened, and her mother will explain that the hymen has been affected. *Zo eina ro'a ve-eina mar'a l'ima* — this woman does not see what happened, and therefore she does not inform her mother, and she remains unaware that she has effectively become a *mukat eitz*. Accordingly, when she marries, she does not disclose anything to her husband — not out of concealment, but out of genuine ignorance. He, having had no reason to suspect an injury, enters the marriage assuming she is a *besula* in the full physical sense. According to Sumchos and Rabbi Meir, this is sufficient to deny the husband a valid *ta'anat betulim*: since she might have sustained such an injury without knowing it, he cannot now claim he was deceived.

One might note — and this was acknowledged — that this reasoning sits uncomfortably with what a woman's own physical senses would detect. The *gemara*'s formulation rests on the visual dimension of the experience, and the logic is somewhat strained when applied to a woman without sight. Nevertheless, the operative ruling according to Sumchos is that we place the blind woman in the category of one who might unknowingly be a *mukat eitz*, and the husband's claim is therefore not actionable.

---

## Shem Ra & Promiscuity

### Shem Ra Divorce

The *gemara* now returns to the first *beraisa* with which this section began, which listed another category of women who do not receive a *knas*: *ha-yotzet mishum shem ra ein lah knas v'lo pitu'i* — a woman who has been sent away on account of *shem ra* has neither a *knas* nor a claim arising from seduction. The *shem ra* referenced by the *Torah* in the case of *ve-hotzi aleha shem ra* is the husband's allegation of adultery that, if substantiated, results in the wife's execution. That is a woman who has already been married; what does this have to do with the laws of a *na'arah betulah*?

The *gemara* raises the obvious question: *b'skila hi* — she is subject to stoning. *Tosfos* addresses this with two lines of analysis. First, if she committed adultery she is definitively a *be'ulah* and self-evidently not a candidate for *knas*, which is limited to a *besula*. Second, one might have thought the issue is *kim lei b'deraba minei* — that the perpetrator's capital liability overrides the monetary *knas* — but *Tosfos* points out this is not the right framing here, because it is not the same individual facing both punishments in the usual sense of *kim lei*.

### Rumor vs Proof

Rav Sheshet therefore reinterprets the case entirely: *mi she-yatza lah shem ra be-yaldutah ein lah knas* — we are not speaking of the biblical *shem ra* case of proven adultery. Rather, *yotzet mishum shem ra* means that a rumor has circulated in the community that this woman is promiscuous — not proven adultery, not judicial procedure, but public gossip suggesting she has been sexually active. On that basis, she is presumed to be a *be'ulah* and loses her entitlement to a *knas*.

### Rumor Insufficient

Rav Pappa then draws an inference: *shma mina* — we can learn from this case that if there is only an unsubstantiated rumor, that alone is not legally sufficient. He analogizes to a *shtar* with a disputed validity: if people are merely gossiping that a document is a forgery — *nefik kala* — we do not refuse to enforce the document on that basis alone. The parallel would suggest that mere gossip about a woman's promiscuity is similarly insufficient to deny her a *knas*. And indeed, Rava states explicitly: *yatza lah shem mezana ba-ir ein chosheshin lah* — if a rumor circulates in a town that a woman is promiscuous, we give it no halachic weight whatsoever.

### Witnesses & Behavior

If so, what level of evidence does suffice? *De-atu bei terei ve-amri* — two people come and give firsthand testimony. But what exactly do they testify to? Not that they personally witnessed her engage in intercourse — that would not be mere *shem ra* at all. Rather, in the parallel case of the *shtar*: two witnesses come and testify that the claimant personally approached them and asked them to forge a document on his behalf. They refused, but the fact that he solicited forgery creates concrete suspicion about the document now before the court.

Analogously, by the woman: two men come and testify that she approached them and solicited intercourse. They declined, but the act of solicitation itself — firsthand knowledge of actual conduct, not mere rumor — creates a presumption that she has been *ba'alas* with someone, since such overtures, if repeated, will eventually find a willing recipient.

### Document vs Woman

The *gemara* pauses to question whether these two cases are truly analogous. *Bishlama hasam shechichi prutzim* — in the case of the woman, it is entirely credible to assume that if she repeatedly propositioning men, eventually someone will say yes, because promiscuous men are not uncommon. *Ela hacha* — but in the document case, if someone is looking for a forger and has not found one yet, should we not assume that people generally have a *chezkas kashrus* and will refuse? Perhaps even with money offered, no one agreed to forge.

The *gemara* rejects this distinction: *kevan de-mahader a-ziyufa, eimar zeiyuphi zeiyeiph* — since he was actively searching for someone to forge the document, even if he found no partner, he likely forged it himself. So in both cases — the woman who propositioned witnesses, and the man who sought a forger — concrete evidence of actual behavior (not mere rumor) creates a sufficient presumption to change the legal outcome. In neither case does bare gossip suffice; in both, firsthand testimony about specific conduct does. The *gemara* notes, with some irony, that we are apparently more willing to assume a man will ultimately say yes to a sexual proposition than to assume he will agree to forge a document, even when financial inducement is involved.

---

## Mishna: No Knas

### Convert/Captive/Slave

The *gemara* now arrives at the next *mishna*, which mirrors the first and makes explicit what the preceding week's discussion had been assuming. *Ve-eilu she-ein lahem knas* — the following women are not entitled to a *knas*. The first group consists of women presumed to be a *be'ulah* by virtue of their prior status. *Ha-ba al ha-giyores ve-al ha-shvuya ve-al ha-shifcha* — a woman who is a convert, a woman who was taken captive, or a woman who is a non-Jewish slave — *she-nifdU ve-she-nitgeiyeru ve-she-nishtachreru* — and who have since been redeemed, converted, or freed — are presumed *be'ulot* if their transition out of that status occurred when they were older than three years of age. The reasoning is that in their prior condition — as non-Jews, slaves, or captives — we assume they engaged in or were subject to intercourse, and since this occurred after age three, it constitutes a legally cognizable act that ruptures the hymen permanently.

### Yehuda: Captive Virgin

Rabbi Yehuda dissents regarding the captive woman: *shvuya she-nifdas harei hi be-kedushata* — a redeemed captive retains her sanctity, and we presume she was not raped, *af al pi she-gedolah* — even if she was an adult when captured. Accordingly, even an adult captive woman receives the *knas* and retains the full presumption of virginity.
