Two approaches exist: one holds that since the eating is abnormal it is simply re-categorized as *keren*; the other holds that even if it remains under *shein*, just as the *tam* pays only half damages because the goring was unexpected and the owner was not negligent, so too an animal that eats in a totally unexpected way pays only half damages and that half-payment is a *knas*. Either way, the practical outcome is the same. If the dog or cat eats small animals — *zutrei* — that is normal behavior (*orcheih hu*) and the owner pays full damages, collectible in any court.

### Collection Outside Israel

The classification of *meshuneh* behavior as *knas* carries an important jurisdictional consequence. A *knas* requires not merely any court, but a court possessing *smicha* — the ordination chain tracing back to Moshe Rabbeinu — which confers on the court the authority designated in the Torah by the term *Elohim*. Such courts are empowered only within *Eretz Yisrael*, where *smicha* is granted. Consequently, *knas* payments — including half damages for unusual animal behavior — cannot be collected in Babylonia (*lo magbinan be-Vavel*). This rule applies not only to *al pi atzmo* but to the entire process: without the properly ordained court, the *knas* simply cannot be imposed.

### Shaming Remedies

Despite this jurisdictional limitation, the injured party is not entirely without remedy outside Israel. The Gemara offers three practical tools. First, if the damagee has physically seized property equivalent to his loss (*tafas*), the court will not compel him to return it — though a court proceeding may still be needed to determine the precise amount seized. Second, if the damagee wishes to pursue the matter formally, he may petition the Babylonian court to schedule a hearing for him in *Eretz Yisrael*, and if the damager refuses to appear, the court will place him under *cherem* (excommunication) until he complies. Third — and this applies regardless of whether a court date has been set — the court will declare the damager under *cherem* until he removes his dangerous animal, invoking the principle of *de'amrinan lei silik hezeikach*, "we tell him: eliminate your hazard." This last principle is attributed to Rabbi Nosson, who derives from the verse *velo sasim damim beveisecha* that one may not maintain a dangerous dog or a rickety ladder in one's home.

---

## Rape/Seduction Payments

### Three/Four Payments

The *mishnah* establishes the basic framework: a seducer (*mefateh*) pays three things — *boshes* (embarrassment), *pegam* (physical injury devaluing her marriage prospects), and *knas* (the fifty-*shekel* fine) — while a rapist (*ones*) pays four, adding *tza'ar* (pain and suffering). All of these go to the father.

### Paternal Rights

The father's right to collect is not absolute; it is conditioned on his being alive and the daughter not yet having reached majority (*bogeret*) at the time the court case is adjudicated. The *mishnah* walks through the permutations: if the case came before the court while the father was alive and the daughter was still a *na'ara* or *ktana*, the payments belong to the father. If the father dies after the court has ruled in his favor (*amda bedin*), the debt — now a monetary obligation owed to him — passes to his sons as heirs.

### Daughter's Rights

Two scenarios transfer the right to collect directly to the daughter. First, if the father died before the court case was held (*lo hispika la'amod bedin ad shemes ha'av*), she is the litigant when the case is finally adjudicated and she herself receives the payment. The underlying logic is that the obligation fundamentally runs to the daughter — the wrong was done to her — and the father collects through her. Once he is no longer alive when the case is decided, there is no channel transferring the payment to him, and it remains with her. Second, if by the time of the court case she has become a *bogeret*, she has been emancipated from her father's authority, and the payment similarly goes to her. A daughter reaching majority is treated equivalently to paternal death for these purposes: in both situations, the conduit through which the father would have collected has closed.

### Rabbi Shimon's View

Rabbi Shimon holds a more stringent position regarding the father's rights: even after *gmar din* — after the court has issued its ruling — the obligation is not yet considered a direct debt to the father. It continues to travel through the daughter to the father. Therefore, if the father dies after the court case but before the money has actually been paid out, it still goes to the daughter rather than to the brothers. The *Chachamim*, by contrast, hold that *gmar din* converts the obligation into a direct debt to the father, such that his death after *gmar din* transfers it to his sons as part of his estate. The *mishnah* notes an important contrast: with respect to her earnings (*ma'aseh yadeha*) and found objects, even Rabbi Shimon agrees that the debt vests in the father as soon as it is earned, regardless of collection. It is specifically the *knas* payment for rape or seduction that — according to Rabbi Shimon — retains its character of flowing through the daughter rather than being directly owed to the father, even after the court has ruled.

---

## False Oaths & Korban

### Braita on False Oaths

The Gemara now introduces a *mishnah* from *Shevuot*. The relevant law is that one who falsely swears to deny a financial obligation — invoking God's name to avoid paying — incurs liability to pay the principal plus a fifth, and to bring a special *korban* (*korban shvuah*). This liability is triggered only when the underlying claim is *mammon*: were the claimant to admit the obligation, he would be required to pay. When the underlying claim is *knas*, however, no such oath liability exists, because even an admission would not create a binding obligation.

The *mishnah* in *Shevuot* presents the scenario: a father says to someone, "you raped or seduced my daughter" (*onasta u'fitita es biti*), the accused denies it, swears to that denial, and then admits. The question is whether he is liable for the false oath. Rabbi Shimon exempts him, reasoning that since one would not be obligated to pay a *knas* upon admission, there is no mechanism by which denial under oath can create a *korban* obligation. The *Chachamim* respond: even if the *knas* itself is not payable *al pi atzmo*, the *boshes* and *pegam* components are ordinary *mammon* and are payable by admission. One who denies having raped or seduced is implicitly denying the *mammon* components as well, and is therefore liable for the false oath on that basis.

### Qnes vs. Mammon

The analysis reveals that the underlying dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the *Chachamim* is not about the legal categories themselves — both sides agree that *knas* does not generate oath liability while *mammon* does — but rather about what the claimant is primarily demanding when he says "you raped my daughter." Is the demand centered on the *knas*, in which case the denial relates to a non-obligating admission? Or does it encompass the *boshes* and *pegam*, in which case denial does generate oath liability? Everyone agrees one is not liable for swearing falsely about a pure *knas*, and everyone agrees one is liable for swearing falsely about *mammon*. The question is which component of the compound claim this particular denial is addressing.

### Abaye's Question

A sharper question is now raised. Abaye asked Rabbah: suppose the father says not merely "you raped my daughter," but "you raped my daughter, and we took the case to court (*ve-amadtinu ba-din*), and the court ruled you owe me money (*ve-nischayavta li mamon*)." The accused denies the entire claim — no rape, no court case, no ruling — swears to that denial, and then admits. What is the law according to Rabbi Shimon?

The thrust of the question is whether *amad bedin* — the issuance of a court judgment — converts a *knas* into *mammon*. When the *knas* was first incurred, it could not generate oath liability because an admission would not have been obligating: there was no debt without a court imposing it. But after a court has already imposed the debt, the accused is no longer merely admitting to an act; he is admitting to the existence of a judicially imposed obligation. At that point, one might argue, the origin of the obligation as a *knas* is irrelevant — what exists now is a court-imposed debt, and denying a court-imposed debt is exactly the kind of denial that generates *korban shvuah* liability. Does the fact that it originated as a *knas* permanently color its identity, or does the court judgment transform it into *mammon*?

### Rava's Response

Rava answered: it is *mammon* — after *amad bedin*, the obligation is monetary, and therefore if one swears falsely about it one is liable to bring a *korban shvuah*.

---

## Braita & Rabbi Shimon

### Korban Cases

The Gemara now examines this claim against a *braita*. The *braita* enumerates the cases that generate *korban shvuah* liability: the *Chachamim* ask, from where do we know that even cases of double payment (*kefel*), fourfold and fivefold payment, and *ones u'mefateh* and *motsi shem ra* — all of which are *knas* — require a *korban shvuah*? The answer is derived from the verse's additional language *u'ma'alah ma'al* (a trespass), which extends the obligation beyond purely *mammon* cases.

### Rabbi Shimon Exempts

Rabbi Shimon then states his position in this *braita*: cases of rape and seduction, the goring of a slave, and a master knocking out a slave's tooth or blinding his eye — all instances of *knas* — do not generate *korban shvuah* liability even if denied under oath. The derivation is from the verse *vekichesh ba'amito b'fikadon o viteshumat yad o vegazel* etc., which describes purely monetary wrongs; actions that began as *knas* are excluded.

### Court Judgment Proof

The Gemara now advances a critical argument against Rava's original position. If Rabbi Shimon's exemption applied only before *amad bedin*, there would be no need for the *braita* to use a *pasuk* to prove the exemption. The logic is as follows: if denying the *knas* before *amad bedin* carries no *korban* liability, that is self-evidently because an admission at that stage would not be obligating either — there is nothing to deny oath-worthy. A *pasuk* would only be necessary to exempt someone who is denying something that — had he admitted it — would have obligated him. Rava initially responded that perhaps the *braita*'s exemption speaks of a case before *amad bedin*, and the *muad*-like cases where the *Chachamim* impose liability speak of after *amad bedin*. The two positions within the *braita* would then represent the same speaker — Rabbi Shimon — at different stages of the proceedings.

Rava rejects this reading himself, noting that the structure of the *braita* does not support it. Rabbi Shimon's name appears only at the point of exemption; if he were also the author of the liability ruling, his name would appear there as well, or the entire *braita* would be labeled his. The natural reading is that the *Chachamim* assert liability and Rabbi Shimon dissents. And since the *Chachamim* — in asserting liability — cannot be speaking of a denial that would have been entirely non-obligating even by admission, they must be speaking of the case after *amad bedin*. And since Rabbi Shimon is responding to the *Chachamim*'s case, his exemption also applies after *amad bedin*. This is a powerful demonstration that Rabbi Shimon holds the *knas* retains its identity even after *amad bedin*, at least for the purposes of *korban shvuah*.

### Rava's Concession

Rava concedes this point specifically regarding *korban shvuah*: *u'modinu lach l'inyan korban shvuah d'Rachmana patrei* — regarding the *korban shvuah*, I concede that the Torah specifically exempts a *knas* from this obligation, even after *amad bedin*. The verse *vekichesh ba'amito* establishes that only what began its life as pure *mammon* generates *korban shvuah* liability. A *knas* — even one that has been adjudicated by *beis din* — retains its character as *knas* for this specific purpose and remains exempt.

However, Rava maintains that for other areas of *halacha*, the court judgment does convert *knas* to *mammon*. His primary example is *lehorish le-vanav* — bequeathal: if the claimant dies after *amad bedin*, the judicially imposed debt should pass to his sons as part of his estate, because at that stage it exists as a *mammon* obligation. The *korban shvuah* exemption is understood as a special *halacha* with its own textual basis, not as evidence that the *knas* retains its identity across the board.

---

## Contradiction & Resoluti…

### Mishna's Bequeathal Rule

The Gemara now confronts Rava's position with the very *mishnah* under study. Rabbi Shimon explicitly rules: *im lo hispika ligbot ad shemes ha'av harei hen shel atzmah* — if the money was not collected before the father died, it goes to the daughter. This is directly in tension with Rava's claim that after *amad bedin*, the *knas* is converted to *mammon* for purposes of bequeathal. If it were indeed *mammon* at that point, the brothers — as the father's heirs — should inherit the debt, not the daughter. Yet Rabbi Shimon says the daughter collects. This seems to prove that for Rabbi Shimon, *knas* remains *knas* even after *amad bedin*, across the board and not merely for *korban shvuah*.

### 22-Year Puzzle

This contradiction apparently troubled Rabba and Rav Yosef for twenty-two years (*hai milsa kashya beh le-Rabba u-le-Rav Yosef esrin v'sartin shanin*). Tosafot raises an obvious question: why not simply retract the position? If all evidence points to Rabbi Shimon maintaining *knas* status throughout, why remain committed to the tradition that it converts to *mammon* after *amad bedin*? Tosafot answers that they possessed a firm tradition — not merely a logical inference — that according to Rabbi Shimon, *knas* does convert to *mammon* after *amad bedin*. Yet the evidence from both the *korban shvuah* laws and the *mishnah*'s bequeathal rule contradicted this at every turn. They could not reconcile the tradition with the texts, and the difficulty stood unresolved for twenty-two years.

### Rav Yosef's Solution

The resolution came when Rav Yosef became *rosh yeshiva* after Rabba's passing. Rashi notes beautifully that it was precisely to honor Rav Yosef — known as the greater *baki* though Rabba had been the sharper analyst — that heaven assisted him in resolving what his predecessor could not. Rav Yosef's answer: *shani hatam de'amar kra* — the case of *ones u'mefateh* is itself an exception, because the Torah itself specifies: *v'nasan ha-ish ha-shochev imah l'avi ha-na'arah chamishim kasef* — "the man who lay with her shall give to the father of the girl fifty pieces of silver." The verb *v'nasan* — "he shall give" or "he has given" — implies that the father's entitlement is activated only at the moment of actual payment (*mishea's nesina*). Until the money physically changes hands, the Torah has not vested the right in the father; the obligation fundamentally belongs to the daughter, and the father receives only through her. Therefore even after *amad bedin*, in a case of *ones u'mefateh*, the father has not yet acquired a direct *mammon* claim — he would only acquire it upon actual receipt. If he dies before receiving it, the daughter collects.

### Rule of Natan

The general principle articulated by Rabba regarding other *knasot* — that after *amad bedin* the *knas* converts to *mammon* and can be bequeathed to the sons — thus stands for all *knasot* other than *ones u'mefateh*. Two exceptions have now been established. In the laws of *korban shvuah*, there is a Scriptural exclusion: anything that originated as a *knas* is exempt from oath-offering liability even after *amad bedin*, since the verse conditions that obligation on an underlying *mammon* obligation. In *ones u'mefateh*, the verse *v'nasan* conditions the father's right entirely on the act of giving, meaning the father's claim never becomes a direct *mammon* debt independent of the daughter until payment is actually made. In all other *knasot*, Rabbi Shimon would agree that *amad bedin* converts *knas* to *mammon* — the debt vests in the claimant, passes to his heirs upon death, and is treated as a standard monetary obligation.

---

---

# Ketubot 43

## 50 Shekel Fine Status

### Knas Identity After Court

The sugya before us concludes a sustained discussion that properly belongs to tractate *Shavuot*, yet bears directly on our *mishnah* in Ketubot. The underlying question is whether the fifty *shekel* fine paid in cases of rape retains its identity as *knas* even after *ha'amadah be-din* — that is, after court proceedings have been initiated — or whether *ha'amadah be-din* converts it into ordinary *mamon*. The practical stakes are considerable: if it remains *knas*, the defendant cannot be obligated through his own admission, it cannot be bequeathed to the father's sons if the father dies before collection, and there is no liability for a *korban shavuah* if one falsely denied it under oath.

### Rabbi Shimon Exception

*Rabbi Shimon*'s position, as it emerges both from our *mishnah* and from the parallel *mishnah* in *Shavuot*, is that the fifty *shekel* fine retains its identity as *knas* throughout — even after *ha'amadah be-din*. This is the source of his ruling in our *mishnah* that if the father dies before collecting the fine, it passes not to the brothers but to the daughter herself. Were it *mamon* once *ha'amadah be-din* occurred, it would pass to the sons like any other monetary debt.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava, however, maintains that *ha'amadah be-din* does in fact convert *knas* into *mamon* — with one notable exception. By the law of *korban shavuah*, even after the conversion, a special verse — *ve-kichesh* — teaches that if the obligation began its life as *knas*, no *korban* is ever incurred for a false denial, even once it has become *mamon*. So for *Rabbi Shimon*, the fifty *shekel* fine is categorically different: it remains *knas* across the board. For the *rabbanan* and for Rava's reading of *Rabbi Shimon*, only the *korban shavuah* exemption is categorically preserved, while the *mamon* conversion is otherwise standard.

The *gemara* arrives at this picture by parsing a detail: if *Rabbi Shimon* holds the fifty *shekel* is fundamentally *knas* in all respects, why does the *mishnah* in *Shavuot* need to cite the verse *ve-kichesh* to exempt it from *korban shavuah*? The verse *ve-natan* — which grounds the daughter's right to collect upon the father's death — should have sufficed to establish the *knas* identity of the fifty *shekel* for all purposes, including exemption from *korban*. The *gemara* answers that the verse *ve-kichesh* is needed for a specific and unusual scenario.

### Bogeret Exception

The scenario is: *kegon she-amdah be-din u-vagrah* — a case in which the girl first underwent *ha'amadah be-din* and then became a *bogeret*, an emancipated adult. Once she matures, the obligation is no longer directed to the father under the verse *ve-natan le-avi ha-na'arah* but shifts to her. This combination of *ha'amadah be-din* and her subsequent maturation together converts the fifty *shekel* into *mamon*, even according to *Rabbi Shimon*. The father may then inherit it back from the daughter — but he does so as *mamon*, not *knas*. In this scenario, then, even *Rabbi Shimon* concedes the conversion.

The *gemara* therefore explains: *de-hasam ki ka-yaris aviha mina didah ka-yaris* — when the father inherits it, he inherits it as her property. Why, then, is there still no *korban shavuah*? Here the verse *ve-kichesh* is essential: it teaches that even when the obligation has been fully converted into *mamon* in every other respect, if it originated as *knas*, the *korban shavuah* exemption persists permanently.

### Knas Origin Rule

The *gemara* presses further: if even *Rabbi Shimon* agrees this is now *mamon*, how can we call it *knas* and thereby exempt it from *korban shavuah*? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves this with the principle: *yatzu eilu she-ikaran knas* — "excluded are those whose very origin is *knas*." It is not necessary that the obligation currently retain its *knas* character; it is sufficient that it began as *knas*. The *korban shavuah* exemption, in *Rabbi Shimon*'s view, is categorical and permanent, anchored in the origin of the obligation rather than in its present legal status.

To summarize the layered structure: *Rabbi Shimon* holds (a) that generally the fifty *shekel* remains *knas* even after *ha'amadah be-din*, unlike other fines; (b) that in the specific *bogeret* scenario it does become *mamon* even for *Rabbi Shimon*; and (c) that in all cases where the obligation originated as *knas*, *ve-kichesh* permanently exempts it from *korban shavuah*, whether or not it has since been converted into *mamon*.

---

## Father's Implicit Demand

### Implicit Demand Debate

The *gemara* now returns to the surface-level dispute between *Rabbi Shimon* and the *rabbanan*. A *beraita* cites *Rabbi Shimon* as exempting from *korban shavuah* in the case where the father demands payment for the rape of his daughter, apparently because the demand is for *knas*, and one who admits to *knas* is exempt — *modeh be-knas patur*. The *gemara* notes that this implies it is still genuinely *knas* rather than merely a case where the original *knas* survives by force of verse. If *ha'amadah be-din* had converted it to *mamon*, the exemption would need to be explained differently — not simply as "it is *knas*."

The *gemara* resolves this by explaining that *Rabbi Shimon* is speaking *le-divreichem de-rabbanan* — framing his argument in terms his opponents will accept. His reasoning runs as follows: according to you, *rabbanan*, who hold that once it becomes *mamon* one incurs *korban shavuah*, you should at least concede that where there has been no *ha'amadah be-din*, it is still purely *knas*, and *modeh be-knas patur* — so there should be no *korban shavuah* even on your own terms. As for Rav's own position, *ve-kichesh* tells him there is never a *korban shavuah* on anything that began as *knas*, regardless.

### Torah Exemption

The top of our *daf* — 43a — introduces the *rabbanan*'s response and the analytical underpinning of the dispute. The *gemara* asks: *be-mai kamiplagei* — what exactly is the interpretive disagreement? When a father says to someone "you raped my daughter, pay me," what is he implicitly demanding — the fixed fifty *shekel knas*, or the indeterminate *boshet* and *pagam*, the shame payment and the diminishment in her value? Rav Pappa frames the dispute in these terms.

### Fixed vs. Amorphous

*Rabbi Shimon* holds: *lo shavik inish midi de-kaitz ve-tava midi de-lo kaitz* — a person does not abandon a claim with a fixed, determinate amount in order to demand something amorphous and indeterminate. The fifty *shekel* is concrete; *boshet* and *pagam* are subject to court assessment and could be anything. Therefore, the father is presumed to be demanding the *knas*.

### Escape vs. No Escape

The *rabbanan* hold the opposite: *lo shavik inish midi de-chi modi bei lo miftar* — a person does not abandon a claim from which the defendant cannot escape by confessing. If the demand is for *mamon*, an admission by the defendant obligates him to pay immediately, with no exit. By contrast, if the demand is for *knas*, an admission paradoxically exempts the defendant — *modeh be-knas patur* — and the father gains nothing from forcing a confession. The *rabbanan* therefore reason that the father is implicitly demanding *boshet* and *pagam*, not the *knas*, because that is the demand that can be enforced through admission.

This is ultimately an argument about human psychology and litigation strategy rather than a principled legal distinction. Interestingly, the *gemara* seems to assume these are mutually exclusive demands — it does not consider why the father would not be presumed to be demanding both simultaneously.

What remains clear as the halachic bottom line for our *mishnah* is *Rabbi Shimon*'s position that the fifty *shekel* retains its *knas* identity even after *ha'amadah be-din*, and therefore if the father dies before it is collected, the daughter — not the brothers — is entitled to collect it. That is the *chidush* of *Rabbi Shimon* that is directly relevant to our discussion in Ketubot.

---

## Daughter's Earnings Righ…

### Earnings Question

With the foregoing *sugya* concluded, the *gemara* transitions to a new but related topic raised by Rabbi Avina to Rav Sheshet: *bat ha-nizonet min ha-achin* — a daughter who is being supported by the brothers from the estate after her father's death. What are the brothers' rights, if any, to her *maaseh yadayim*, her earnings?

Some background is necessary. When a man dies, his estate passes to his sons. The daughters do not inherit. To protect the daughters, a standard *tenai ketubah* — indeed, one that applies even if not explicitly written — requires the estate to support any daughters until they marry. This is the case of *bat ha-nizonet min ha-achin*: the brothers have no discretion; the conditions of the *ketubah* bind the estate to provide for her.

The question is whether the estate, in exchange for this support, acquires rights to the daughter's earnings. On the surface, this resembles the *ketubot* arrangement between husband and wife, where the husband's support obligation corresponds reciprocally to his right to his wife's earnings — a rabbinic exchange of *maaseh yadayim* for *mezonot*. One might extend the same logic here: since the estate is providing her sustenance, perhaps the estate should receive her earnings.

### Reciprocity Principle

The difficulty is that the husband-wife exchange is explicitly a rabbinic reciprocal institution, created precisely because neither spouse has an entirely unilateral legal claim over the other. The father's relationship to his daughter's earnings, by contrast, is unilateral and biblical. The *gemara* grounds this in the fact that a father may sell his daughter as an *amah ivriyah* — a Hebrew maidservant — which is essentially a transfer of the right to her labor and earnings. This right is not conditional on his supporting her; it is a status right rooted in his paternal authority.

This is reinforced by an important distinction: *hatam mididei mizna* — in the father's case, he feeds the daughter from his own pocket and at his own initiative, since the Torah does not actually obligate him to support her. The *rabbanan* instituted that he is entitled to her *maaseh yadayim* in part to avoid the resentment (*eivah*) that would arise if he were feeding her voluntarily while she pocketed everything she earned or found. By contrast, the brothers are not feeding her from their own earnings; they are disbursing funds from the inherited estate. Moreover, they have no choice — the estate is legally obligated to support her as a condition of the *ketubah*. The volitional, unilateral character of the father's support is entirely absent.

### Widow vs. Daughter

Rav Sheshet attempted to answer the question from a *mishnah* regarding the *almana* — the widow. The *mishnah* states that a widow supported by the estate's heirs (*nizonet min nichsei yetomim*) surrenders her earnings to the estate in exchange. By analogy, the daughter supported by the estate should similarly surrender her earnings.

The *gemara* rejects the comparison: *mi dami?* The situations are not parallel, because the deceased husband's concern for his widow and his concern for his daughter are not equivalent — at least not along every axis.

### Father's Priorities

The *gemara* distinguishes between two dimensions: *ziluta* (shame and degradation) and *harvacha* (profit and financial gain). The principle it advances is: *le-inyan ziluta*, when it comes to avoiding degradation, the father demonstrated greater concern for his widow than for his daughter — as evidenced by the rule in *Bava Batra* that in a small estate (*nichsim mu'atim*), if there is not enough to support both the widow and the daughters, the widow takes precedence and the daughters must go begging. Yet *le-inyan harvacha*, when it comes to retaining financial upside, the father is more concerned that his daughter pocket her earnings than that his wife do so.

One might initially find this distinction arbitrary — the *gemara* could seemingly have argued the reverse. But one compelling explanation offered in discussion is that the father has an interest in his daughter accumulating a dowry in order to marry her off advantageously. He would therefore want her to keep whatever she earns. His wife's financial accumulation beyond what is needed for her maintenance is less of a priority in his thinking.

The *gemara* challenges this distinction by citing Rabbi Abba quoting Rabbi Yosei: *asu almana etzel ha-bat ke-vat etzel ha-achin* — they treated the widow vis-à-vis the daughter as the daughter vis-à-vis the brothers. This means the widow takes precedence over the daughter in a small estate, just as the daughter takes precedence over the brothers. Doesn't this prove the husband was more concerned with his wife than with his daughter? The *gemara* responds that this holds true only for the *ziluta* dimension — it is more degrading for a widow to beg than for a daughter. In terms of *harvacha*, the opposite priorities apply, and the father's posthumous concern for his daughter's financial gain exceeds his concern for his wife's.

---

## Mishna Implication

### Earnings During Life

The *gemara* now turns to our *mishnah* itself to attempt a proof about the daughter's entitlement to her own earnings. The *mishnah* states: *maaseh yadeha u-metziatah* — her earnings and her found objects — *af al pi she-lo gavtah*, even if she has not yet collected them, once earned during the father's lifetime, pass to the brothers upon the father's death. The *gemara* infers from this framing: *ta'ama de-ve-chayei ha-av* — the reason it goes to the brothers is specifically that she earned it while the father was alive; but *ha le-achar mitat ha-av le-atzmah* — had she earned it after the father's death, she would keep it herself. The *mishnah* thus implies strongly that earnings after the father's death remain hers.

### All or Excess?

The *gemara* immediately tests this inference: *mai lav bi-mezonot* — is this not speaking even in a case where the estate is supporting her? The attempted response is to say *lo*, perhaps the *mishnah* refers only to a case where she is *not* being supported by the estate — and if she is unsupported, of course she keeps her earnings, so nothing has been proved about the case of *bat ha-nizonet min ha-achin*.

The *gemara* pushes back: if it were referring to the unsupported case, the *mishnah*'s implication would be obvious and thus no *chiddush* at all. Even according to the opinion that a master may say to a non-Jewish slave *aseh imi ve-eineni zoncha* — work for me without my feeding you — this does not apply to a Jewish slave, regarding whom the Torah writes *imcha*, "with you," implying an obligation of care. Certainly the daughter is no worse than a Jewish slave in this regard. So if the estate is not supporting her, it is trivially obvious she keeps her earnings. The *mishnah* must therefore be speaking about the supported case and still teaching she keeps her earnings — which would be the *chiddush*.

### Hadafah Theory

Rava bar Ula offers a way to preserve the *gemara*'s resistance. Even granting that the *mishnah* concerns a supported daughter, perhaps she does not keep *all* her earnings. Perhaps she only keeps the *hadafah* — the additional earnings beyond the cost of her upkeep. On this reading: if her weekly food and lodging costs one hundred units and she earns one hundred and fifty, she keeps only fifty, using the first hundred to repay the estate for her support. The *mishnah*'s implication that she keeps earnings after the father's death would then prove only entitlement to the *hadafah*, not to the full amount.

---

## Earnings & Found Objects

### Found Object Problem

Rav Yosef dismisses this proposal and argues that the *mishnah* itself contains a stronger proof — one that cannot be deflected by the *hadafah* reading. The *mishnah* packages earnings together with *metziatah* — found objects. When the *mishnah* says that earnings not yet collected (*af al pi she-lo gavtah*) become debts to the father that pass to the brothers upon his death, it makes the same statement about found objects not yet collected. But this raises an obvious difficulty: *metziatah me-man gavya?* How does one "collect" a found object? A found object, the moment it is acquired, is in the finder's possession. There is no prior stage at which it is "owed" to her and then collected later. The formulation makes no sense as applied to found objects in isolation.

### Earnings=Found Objects

The *gemara* therefore concludes: *ella lav hachi ka'amar — maaseh yadeha ke-metziatah* — the *mishnah* is not making two parallel statements; it is equating earnings to found objects. Just as found objects: *mah metziatah be-chayei av le-av, le-achar mitat av le-atzmah* — found objects during the father's lifetime go to the father, but after the father's death they go to her — so too earnings: during the father's lifetime they go to him, but after his death they go to her. And crucially, when it comes to found objects, everyone agrees she keeps them entirely, not merely the *hadafah*. By packaging earnings together with found objects, the *mishnah* teaches that she keeps her earnings entirely as well, even when supported by the estate.

This is Rav Yosef's decisive argument: the *hadafah* theory cannot survive the equation with found objects, because no one ever suggested the daughter owes the estate for found objects found after the father's death. The full amount is hers.

### Volitional Support

Why is it taken for granted that she keeps found objects after the father's death? Rashi explains: *de-metziatah peshita lan de-le-atzmah* — even during the father's lifetime, the father's entitlement to his daughter's found objects was contingent on his actually supporting her — *semucha al shulchano*, eating at his table. The *gemara* in Bava Metzia establishes this. And why was it instituted that the father gets her found objects in the first place? Because of *eivah* — resentment. Since the father is not *legally* obligated to support his daughter yet is doing so volitionally, we worried that he would stop feeding her if she pocketed everything she found. So we gave him the found objects as an incentive.

### Mandatory Obligation

Once the father is dead, however, the entire rationale evaporates. The estate is *obligated* to support the daughter — it is a condition of the *ketubah*, not a voluntary act. There is no volitional benevolence to protect and no *eivah* to worry about. Therefore she unambiguously keeps her found objects. And since the *mishnah* equates earnings to found objects, the conclusion extends equally: she keeps all her earnings after the father's death, even the portion that would cover the cost of her upkeep.

---

## Brothers Don't Inherit

### Rav Yehuda's Ruling

The *gemara* reinforces this conclusion with a direct *amoraic* statement. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *bat ha-nizonet min ha-achin maaseh yadeha le-atzmah* — a daughter supported by the brothers keeps her earnings. The brothers do not inherit the father's entitlement to her *maaseh yadayim*.

### Scripture Proof

Rav Kahana asks: what is the reason? The *gemara* cites the verse in the context of non-Jewish slaves: *ve-hitnachaltem otam li-vneichem achareichem* — "you shall bequeath them to your sons after you." *Otam li-vneichem* — your slaves you bequeath to your sons; *ve-lo benoteichem li-vneichem* — but not your daughters to your sons. The verse teaches that the paternal rights a father held over his daughter's labor and earnings are not heritable. Just as one bequeaths non-Jewish slaves to one's children — because the master's rights over a slave are a transferable ownership — by contrast, the father's rights in his daughter are not of that nature and do not pass to the sons.

### Rabba Objects

Rabba objects: perhaps the verse is speaking only about extraordinary payments — *fitzuyei ha-bat, kinsatah ve-chavalatah* — the damages, fines, and injury payments the father would collect on his daughter's behalf. These are by their nature more intrinsically the daughter's, since they compensate for wrongs done to her person, and they are less common. Perhaps it is specifically these that do not pass to the sons, while ordinary *maaseh yadayim* — regular earnings — does pass, since the father's biblical entitlement to earnings was more like a property right that should be inheritable.

Rabbi Chanina indeed reads the verse this way: *be-fitzuyei ha-bat u-knasatah ve-chavalatah ha-katuv medaber* — the verse is specifically speaking about injury, seduction, and fine payments, not ordinary earnings.

### Injury Distinction

The *gemara* questions this reading by noting that *chavalos* — injuries — present their own complication. Even during the father's lifetime, injury payments (*tza'ara de-gufa*) are not simply pocketed by the father; they are held in a form of escrow for the daughter, since it is her body that was harmed. So the verse cannot be referring to injury payments as something the father would have claimed and now cannot bequeath, since he never had full claim to them in the first place.

Rabbi Yose bar Chanina resolves this: *she-patza'ah be-faneha* — the reference is to a blow to her face, a non-permanent injury. The distinction between permanent and non-permanent injury is what determines who collects. For a permanent injury — something that will diminish her for life, well beyond her period as a *ketanah* and *na'arah* — the payment is for the daughter, not the father, because it is fundamentally her loss. For a non-permanent injury, or one that affects only the period during which the father could have sold her or married her off, the father absorbs the loss and collects the payment.

Tosafot develops this logic further: an injury that heals before the daughter reaches adulthood — before she becomes a *bogeret* — is the father's loss, because it diminished the value of his asset during the period he controlled it. An injury that persists beyond that point is her loss, and she collects accordingly.

The distinction between *Rabbi Shimon* and the *rabbanan* as to what the verse excludes — whether regular earnings or only fines and injury payments — thus remains analytically live. But the *gemara* has already demonstrated from the *mishnah* and from the Rav Yehuda/Rav tradition that ordinary earnings also remain hers.

### Final Halacha

The *gemara* closes with competing traditions. Ami bar Maimra told Rav Ashi that in Nehardea the tradition was *hilchesa ke-vateih de-Rav Sheshet* — we rule like Rav Sheshet, meaning the daughter's earnings go to the estate. Rav Ashi himself ruled *hilchesa ke-vateih de-Rav* — we rule like Rav: the daughter keeps her earnings; the brothers do not inherit the father's rights over them. And this is the accepted *halacha*: *ve-hilchesa ke-vateih de-Rav*.

---

## Ketubah Rights (Betr (II)

### Eirusin Divorce

The *mishnah* now turns to the question of *ketubah* collection rights when a father betrothes his daughter and the marriage subsequently dissolves. The relevant legal background is that after *eirusin* but before *nissu'in*, the daughter remains under her father's authority. If the *eirusin*-stage marriage ends — whether through divorce or the death of the husband — she reverts entirely to paternal control.

The first case: *ham'ares et bito ve-gerashah* — the father betrothes his daughter and she is then divorced. The question is who collects the *ketubah*. Since she never reached *nissu'in* and therefore never left her father's control, the *ketubah* collection right belongs to the father. This ruling assumes, incidentally, that the *ketubah* obligation attaches already at *eirusin*, a position that is itself debated.

### Eirusin Widowed

The same result obtains in the parallel case: *iresah ve-nit'almanah* — the father betrothed her and the husband died. Since she was still an *arusah* and had not yet undergone *nissu'in*, she remained under the father's authority. Therefore the father again collects the *ketubah*.

### Nissu'in Collection

The scenario shifts dramatically once *nissu'in* takes place. *Hisi'ah ve-gerashah* — the marriage was consummated and she was then divorced; *hisi'ah ve-nit'almanah* — consummated and she became widowed. In both cases: *kesuvatah shelah* — she collects her own *ketubah*. Indeed she may have a *ketubah* from two marriages, and she collects both. Once *nissu'in* occurs, the father loses all rights over her person and her monetary entitlements. She is in her own domain.

---

## Ketubah Rights (Betr (II)

### Rabbi Yehuda Position

*Rabbi Yehuda* introduces a refinement: *harishonah shel av* — even after *nissu'in*, the *ketubah* from the first marriage, the one the father initiated through *kidushei ketanah*, belongs to the father. His reasoning appears to be that since the father originated the *eirusin*, the financial obligations that arose from that *eirusin* remain directed to him even after the *nissu'in* converts her status.

### Gemara Rejects Yehuda

The *rabbanan* reject *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position categorically: *mi-she-hisi'ah ein av reshut bah* — once *nissu'in* has taken place, the father has no authority over her whatsoever, and any claim to her *ketubah* that might have existed before is extinguished. *Nissu'in* functions as a total legal break, severing all paternal rights regardless of whether the father originally arranged the match.

---

## Deaths vs. Divorces

### Two Deaths Avoidance

Before proceeding to the *gemara*'s analysis of the *mishnah*'s rulings, the *gemara* pauses to note a structural choice in how the *mishnah* composed its cases. The *mishnah* gives one scenario of divorce (*gerushah*) and one of widowhood (*almanah*) to illustrate a progression of two marriages. One might ask: why not give both scenarios as deaths — why not say she was widowed twice? Why the asymmetry of one divorce and one death?

### Husband Deaths Debate

The *gemara* answers: *aval nit'almanah trei zimnei lo chazya le-inasba* — if two husbands had died on her, she would no longer be fit to remarry. The *gemara* notes that there is an unresolved debate about a woman whose husbands keep dying: at what point does a pattern of deaths create a *chazakah* — a legal presumption — that she is in some way the cause, such that a third husband should not take her? Is it after two deaths, or after three?

### Rabbi's Two-Time Rule

The *gemara* notes *agav orcha* — incidentally, in passing — *kasavar tana ke-Rabbi* — our *mishnah* is following the position of *Rabbi* (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi). *Rabbi* holds *de-amar be-trei zimnei havei chazakah* — a presumption is established after two occurrences. Therefore, once two husbands have died on a woman, the presumption already applies and she may not remarry. By constructing its case as one divorce and one death rather than two deaths, the *mishnah* sidesteps this concern entirely, implicitly aligning itself with *Rabbi*'s two-occurrence rule. We will continue from here in the next session.

---

---

# Ketubot 44

## Ketuva Collection Rights

### Mishna Framework

The daf begins in the middle of 43b, approximately four lines after the new *gemara* begins. The *mishna* addresses the question of who collects a woman's *ketuva* depending on the stage of marriage at which she is divorced. If she is divorced from *erusin*, the father collects, because the daughter remains under his legal authority (*reshut av*) throughout *erusin*, and he retains the right to remarry her after such a divorce. If the divorce follows *nisuin*, she herself collects — with one important exception articulated by Rabbi Yehuda.

### R. Yehuda's Position

The *gemara* directs its attention to Rabbi Yehuda's position: *harishona shel av* — even the payment from the first *nisuin* goes to the father, provided the father arranged the *erusin* when his daughter was a *ketana*. The *gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama d'Rabbi Yehuda* — what is his reasoning?

### Rabba & Rav Yosef

Rabba and Rav Yosef both explain: *hoil u-mishe'as erusin zachah bahen ha-av* — since the *ketuva* obligations commenced at the time of *erusin*, and at that moment the father would have been the payee had a divorce occurred, those obligations remain payable to the father even after *nisuin*. The argument is straightforward: the *ketuva* debt originated at a time when the father was the entitled party, and therefore he remains so even once *nisuin* takes place. It is a reasonably coherent position — yet the *gemara* will challenge it.

## Bogeret Between Erusin

### Rava's Challenge

Rava raises a difficulty from the following *braita*: Rabbi Yehuda himself concedes that if the father arranged *erusin* when the daughter was a *ketana*, but she became a *bogeret* before *nisuin*, and then the *nisuin* took place — *she'ein l'aviha reshut bah* — the father no longer has any authority over her, and therefore the *ketuva* from this *nisuin* is not payable to him.

The challenge is sharp. If Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning is that *erusin* established the father as the payee and that status persists, then even her becoming a *bogeret* between *erusin* and *nisuin* should make no difference — he was the payee, and nothing should change that. Why, then, does Rabbi Yehuda concede this case?

To sharpen the point further: imagine the *erusin* occurs at a certain time, establishing the *ketuva* obligation with the father as payee. The daughter subsequently becomes a *bogeret*, exits her father's authority, and then *nisuin* takes place. According to Rabbi Yehuda's stated logic — that the obligation began under the father's authority and therefore remains his — her transition to *bogeret* status ought to be irrelevant. The original payee was the father; that should not change. Yet Rabbi Yehuda concedes it does.

### Unwritten vs Written

The resolution turns on a crucial distinction between the unwritten and written dimensions of the *ketuva* obligation. The obligation to pay a *ketuva* exists even before any document is written — it is a *takanas chachamim*, a Rabbinic enactment that takes effect from *erusin*. However, just before the *chuppah*, an actual *ketuva* document is written. This writing is not merely a record of the pre-existing obligation; it *redefines* and recreates the obligation. The written *ketuva* generates new obligations distinct from the earlier unwritten ones.

### Formalist Approach

With this distinction in hand, Rabba and Rav Yosef restate Rabbi Yehuda's position more precisely: *hoil u-vireshuso nichtavin* — the determining factor is not when the *erusin* occurred, but under whose authority the *ketuva* is written. If the *ketuva* is written while she is still a *ketana* under her father's control — as typically happens just before the *chuppah*, at the *tish* — then those written obligations are created while she is in his *reshut*, and accordingly the father becomes the payee. In the scenario where she becomes a *bogeret* before *nisuin*, the *ketuva* is written after she has already exited her father's authority. At that moment she is her own person, and the newly created written obligations belong to her.

This is a notably formalist approach. Rabbi Yehuda is saying: we can only define the obligation in terms of who holds legal authority at the time the *ketuva* is written. Whatever the social purpose of the *ketuva* — and it is admittedly strange, since the *ketuva*'s entire function is to protect her after divorce or widowhood, at a time when the father will no longer take her back — Rabbi Yehuda maps the payee onto the legal reality at the moment the document is created. If she is eleven years old and the *nisuin* occurs at a very young age, the *ketuva* gets paid to the father, even though the purpose of the *ketuva* is entirely oriented toward protecting her. It is a peculiar result, but Rabbi Yehuda's framework is a consistent one: the writing of the *ketuva* recreates and defines the obligation, and that definition is fixed by the legal authority in force at the moment of writing.

The broader implication, accepted even by Rabbi Yehuda, is that the writing of the *ketuva* before *nisuin* genuinely recreates the obligations rather than merely recording existing ones. This has direct consequences for the lien question the *gemara* is about to raise.

## Liens & Dating

### When Liens Exist

The *gemara* now poses the question *u-migba mei-eimat gavya* — from what date does the *ketuva* carry liens against the husband's estate? The *mishna* assumes that *ketuva* obligations are in force already from *erusin*. If *erusin* occurred in 2010 and *nisuin* — with the writing of the *ketuva* — occurred in 2015, and she comes to collect in 2030, against which properties does she have lien rights? Does her lien reach back to 2010 and encompass property the husband sold between 2010 and 2015, or does it begin only from 2015, when the *ketuva* was written?

This question is sharpened by the preceding discussion: if the writing of the *ketuva* at *nisuin* recreates and redefines the obligations, one might argue that the liens are equally reset — the old liens dissolved and new ones created at the time of writing. On the other hand, one could argue that the core obligation, which existed from *erusin* as an unwritten *takanas chachamim*, carries liens that were never interrupted.

### Rav Huna's Split

Rav Huna takes a middle position. He distinguishes between the *ikar ketuva* — the core *ketuva* of 200 *zuz* (or the standard amount), which is obligated even without being written — and the *tosefet*, the additional amount the husband voluntarily adds at the time of writing. The *ikar ketuva* exists from *erusin*, and so its liens continue from *erusin* as well. The *tosefet*, however, is something that arises only at the time of the written *ketuva* and is associated specifically with *nisuin*; therefore its liens begin only from *nisuin*. Rav Huna in effect says: even though the writing recreates the obligations in some sense, the lien attached to the underlying debt that existed from *erusin* survives.

### Rav Assi's Position

Rav Assi takes the more sweeping position: *echad zeh ve-echad zeh min ha-nisu'in* — both the *ikar ketuva* and the *tosefet* carry liens only from *nisuin*. Once we accept that the writing of the *ketuva* recreates the obligations, it follows naturally that all liens are reset and begin from the time of that writing. This is the more internally consistent view given the framework established earlier.

## Competing Ketubos

### Two Documents Case

The *gemara* now asks whether Rav Huna's position is self-consistent, by confronting it with another ruling attributed to him. The case: a woman who divorces produces two *ketubot* — one dated 2015 for 200 *zuz*, and one dated 2017 for 300 *zuz*. Rav Huna rules that if she wishes to collect the 200, she may do so using the earlier date, and her liens extend back to 2015; if she wishes to collect the 300, she may do so, but her liens run only from 2017.

### Addition Question

The *gemara* challenges this ruling. If Rav Huna is willing to split the *ketuva* obligations in the *erusin*/*nisuin* case — allowing the 200 *zuz* core to carry liens from *erusin* while the *tosefet* carries liens only from *nisuin* — why does he not apply the same logic here? The 300 *ketuva* should simply be read as the original 200 plus an additional 100. Under Rav Huna's own reasoning, the woman ought to be entitled to collect 200 from the earlier lien date and 100 from the later one. And pushing the logic further: why not even read it as a total of 500 — the full 200 from the first document and the full 300 from the second, each with its own lien date?

### Explicit Language Rule

The *gemara* provides its answer: *keivan d'lo kasav lah* — since he did not write in the second *ketuva* the explicit language, *z'visi v'osifis lach slas me'ah a-masayim* — "I have desired and I have added to you 300 upon the existing 200" — we cannot read the second document as an addition to the first. If he had intended to supplement the first, he had language available to say so clearly. Similarly, if the 300 were meant to represent the original 200 plus 100 more, he should have written: *osifis lach me'ah a-masayim* — "I am adding 100 to the 200." He did not write either of these formulations.

### Competing Alternatives

Since no such language appears, the two documents are read not as cumulative or as B incorporating A, but as separate and competing alternatives: *i mi-zman rishon gavis, gavis masayim; i mi-zman sheni gavis, gavis slas me'ah* — if you choose to collect from the first date, you collect 200; if you choose to collect from the second date, you collect 300. They are alternatives. She picks one. We do not aggregate them, and we do not read the later one as reinterpreting or supplementing the earlier one.

The rule that flows from this is that in the ordinary *ketuva* case — where the husband at *erusin* incurs an unwritten base obligation of 200, and then at *nisuin* writes a *ketuva* that explicitly adds a *tosefet* on top of the core amount — the structure is different. There the *ketuva* document explicitly layers the *tosefet* onto the *ikar*, so that we do treat them as a layered obligation: the 200 carries liens from *erusin*, the *tosefet* from *nisuin*. But where no such explicit language exists, competing documents are read as alternatives, not as cumulative obligations. Furthermore, the *gemara* notes — *acholi achlei l'shibuda kama* — if she chooses to use the later document, she has implicitly waived her earlier liens. The second *ketuva* represents an entirely new obligation of 300, not the first obligation reconstituted.

## Supersession Doctrine

### Rav Nachman's Rule

At this point the *gemara* introduces a broader principle through Rav Nachman. The case now shifts from two *ketubot* to two *shtarot* — documents of title transfer on the same piece of property. If Michael holds one document stating that a co-op was sold to him in 2012, and a second document stating the same co-op was sold to him in 2015, when did the sale occur? And more practically: from what date do Michael's liens on the seller's estate begin?

The reason the date matters is this: when a seller transfers property, he implicitly undertakes to reimburse the buyer if any creditor of the seller later takes the property away from the buyer by virtue of a pre-existing lien. The buyer therefore acquires lien rights on the seller's estate from the date of purchase — so that if a creditor seizes the property, the buyer can collect from the seller's remaining assets. An earlier date means broader access to those assets, because it extends the buyer's lien further back in time.

Rav Nachman rules: *bitel sheni es ha-rishon* — the second document supersedes the first. The buyer, by accepting the second document, has implicitly forfeited the earlier lien. His liens run only from 2015. The logic is that since the second document provides no additional benefit over the first — it is the same property, at a later date — the only thing the buyer could have been signaling by accepting it is a willingness to treat the first document as though it never happened. It is a worse deal at a later date with no compensating advantage. Accepting it therefore functions as a waiver of the rights established by the earlier document.

### Rav Pappa's Caveat

Rav Pappa qualifies Rav Nachman's rule: *u-modei Rav Nachman d'i hosif bah dikla l'tosefes kasveih* — Rav Nachman would concede that if the second document includes something additional — the classic example is a palm tree added to the property transferred — then supersession does not apply. When the later document conveys something the earlier one did not, the buyer is not simply accepting a worse version of the first; he has a genuine tradeoff. The later document carries a later lien date but confers an additional benefit. In that case, the two documents stand as competing alternatives, and the buyer may choose which to invoke.

### Sale vs Gift

The *gemara* extends the analysis: *pshita* — it is obvious — that if the first document framed the transfer as a sale and the second as a gift (*rishon be-mecher ve-sheni be-matanah*), the later document does provide a benefit, and choice is available. The benefit derives from *dina de-bar metzra* — the neighbor's right of first refusal. When property is sold, the neighboring owner has a halachic claim to be offered the property before a stranger is approached; but when property is given as a gift, no such claim applies. A person may give a gift to whomever he chooses. So if the second document frames the transfer as a gift, Michael acquires protection against the neighbor's claim under *dina de-bar metzra* — a distinct advantage not available under the first document. The two documents therefore offer different benefits, and Michael may choose between them.

(It is worth noting that in practice, the *dina de-bar metzra* has indeed been applied halachically in modern times: the Heschel School board, when selling its 89th Street building, offered B'nai Jeshurun on 88th Street — a former owner of the building and its neighbor — the right of first refusal, and B'nai Jeshurun ultimately acquired the property.)

The *gemara* adds *ve-chol she-ken* — certainly the reverse also holds: if the first document was a gift and the second was a sale (*rishon be-matanah ve-sheni be-mecher*), the sale document is also the more beneficial in its own way, because a buyer who paid money can claim reimbursement if a creditor seizes the property, whereas a recipient of a gift has no such recourse. In each permutation, the later document carries a distinct advantage, and so Michael retains the right to choose.

One might ask: if the property was already sold in 2012, how can a 2015 document frame it as a gift? The answer is that this is an acknowledged legal fiction, permissible because both parties consent. In theory, Michael could have returned the property to the seller and the seller could then have given it as a gift. Since both parties agree to the framing, halacha allows it to be treated as such. It is, as acknowledged, a somewhat extraordinary construction, but a permissible one within the framework of *mamon*.

### Implications

Where the second document adds no benefit — both documents are, say, bills of sale for the same property on the same terms — supersession applies in full: *bitel sheni es ha-rishon*. Rav Pappa explains the mechanism: *eimar oduye odi leih* — Rav Pappa attributes this to what functions as an implicit admission (*hoda'as ba'al din*) on Michael's part. By accepting the 2015 document, he is treated as admitting that the 2012 sale never really took effect — that the true date of transfer was 2015. The legal fiction of *hoda'as ba'al din k'me'ah edim dami* — an admission by a party in interest carries the weight of a hundred witnesses — creates this result even if it is factually inaccurate.

Rav Acha offers a narrower reading: Michael need not be read as denying that the 2012 transaction occurred. Rather, he has simply *waived his liens* — *acholi achlei l'shibudeh* — from the earlier date. The 2012 sale happened; he merely gives up the lien rights that attached from that date.

The practical difference between these two positions — *nafka mina* — is substantial. First, concerning witnesses: if we accept that Michael is effectively denying the 2012 event ever occurred, then he is implicitly treating those witnesses as false. As *Tosafot* explains, this would not impugn those witnesses in any general sense, but it would affect Michael's own rights under any other document he holds bearing the same witnesses' signatures — since he cannot selectively invalidate their testimony only when convenient. Second, concerning the fruits of the property (*lishlumei peiri*): if Michael is merely waiving liens, he retains the benefit of whatever he derived from the property during those three years — he owned it, he ate its fruit. If however the entire 2012 transaction is treated as a fiction that never happened, the seller could demand back-payment for three years of use. Third, regarding taxes (*arnona*): whoever is deemed to have owned the property during those years bears the tax liability for that period. Under the waiver reading, Michael owned it and owes the taxes; under the denial reading, the seller is deemed to have owned it and the tax falls on him.

The obviously more proportionate and factually honest reading is the narrower one — that Michael waives his earlier liens. To treat his acceptance of a later-dated document as a denial of the very witnesses who signed the earlier one, with cascading consequences for all his other documents bearing those signatures, is a remarkably far-reaching implication of what appears to be a relatively modest act.

## Ketuva Application

### Summary & Ruling

The *gemara* now returns to the original *ketuva* lien question and reaches its conclusion. *Tosafot* address the issue at this point. The position of Rav Huna — splitting between the *ikar ketuva* with liens from *erusin* and the *tosefet* with liens from *nisuin* — is contrasted with the position of the *chachamim*. The *chachamim* rule: *echad zeh ve-echad zeh min ha-nisu'in* — both the core *ketuva* and the *tosefet* carry liens only from *nisuin*. And the *halacha* follows the *chachamim*: when the *ketuva* is written at the time of *nisuin*, the old liens from *erusin* do not survive, and all lien rights are anchored to the moment of the *ketuva*'s writing. Whatever obligations existed at the time of *erusin* do not continue to generate liens into the period following *nisuin*.

## Motzi Shem Ra Intro

### Torah Case Overview

With the *ketuva* discussion concluded, the *gemara* pivots to the next *mishna*, which opens a new subject — *motzi shem ra*. It is worth appreciating how these topics connect. The *ketuva* as a Rabbinic institution traces its origins to the Torah's cases involving young girls and marriage-related payments. The *ones* and *mefateh* cases established the 50 *shekel* fine — itself rooted in the societal reality of *mohar*, the bride-price — and that fine became the template for the *ketuva*'s base amount. Now the *gemara* turns to the second Torah case in this constellation: the *motzi shem ra*, where after the wedding night a husband falsely claims his wife was not a virgin.

The Torah's framework for *motzi shem ra* is as follows. If a husband makes this claim and it proves true — if she in fact committed adultery as a *na'arah betulah me'orasah* — she is executed by *sekilah* at *petach beit aviha*, the entrance of her father's house. The Torah specifies: *ki astah nevalah b'Yisrael* — because she committed an outrage in Israel. The location — the father's house — and the mode of execution — *sekilah* rather than the *chenek* that normally applies to adultery — are the distinctive features of this case. If, on the other hand, the husband lied, he receives *malkus* and a fine of *me'ah kesef* — 100 silver pieces, double the standard *ketuva* amount of 50 — which is given *l'avi ha-na'arah*, to the girl's father. This doubling is no accident: he attempted to have her killed and to deprive her of her *ketuva* (equivalent to 50 *kesef*), and so he pays double. He also loses the right ever to divorce her.

### Giyoret Exception

Rather than beginning with the standard case, the *mishna* opens with an unusual exception: *hagiores she-nisgayra bita ima* — a convert woman who converted together with her daughter, whose daughter then committed adultery as a *na'arah me'orasah*.

### Conceived Pre-Conv

The first scenario: the daughter was conceived before the mother converted and was also born before the conversion. In this case none of the special laws of *motzi shem ra* apply to her at all. She did not begin life as a *bat Yisrael*; the Torah's formulation *ki astah nevalah b'Yisrael* excludes her.

### Born Post-Conv

The second scenario: the daughter was conceived before the mother converted, but was born after the conversion — *horasa shelo bi-kedusha ve-lidasa bi-kedusha*. In this case she is executed by *sekilah* — because she was born as a Jew, and *b'Yisrael* is satisfied — but *ein lah petach beit av*, there is no father's house to bring her to, and *ein lah me'ah sela*, there is no fine of one hundred *sela*. She has no legal father, so those elements of the *motzi shem ra* framework simply do not apply. She receives *sekilah*, but without the full ritual specified in the Torah.

### Full Status

The third scenario: both conception and birth occurred after the mother's conversion. In this case *harei hi ke-vat Yisrael le-chol devareha* — she is treated in every respect as a daughter of Israel, and all the normal laws apply.

### Father Deceased

The fourth case introduced by the *mishna*: a daughter who does have a legal father, but whose father has died — she is an orphan. The *mishna* states *harei zeh bi-sekilah* — she receives *sekilah*. The *mishna* notes that *lo ne'emar petach beit av ela l'mitzvah* — the requirement of the father's house is only a *mitzvah* (an ideal, not an absolute requirement), and so its absence does not block the execution. What the *mishna* does not clarify, however, is whether the *me'ah kesef* fine applies in the case of an orphan. That question is left open.

### Torah's Law

To summarize the Torah's law as it applies to the standard case: the subject is a *na'arah betulah me'orasah l'ish* — a young woman, a virgin, betrothed to a man. He claims *lo nimtze'u vetulim la-na'arah* — signs of virginity were not found in her. If the claim is true and she committed adultery during her *erusin*, *ve-hotzi'u et ha-na'arah el petach beit aviha u-sekaluha* — she is brought to the entrance of her father's house and stoned. The punishment is *sekilah* rather than *chenek* because the Torah treats this as a more severe form of adultery — she was still under her father's roof, still in the period of *erusin*. If the husband lied — *moti shem ra* — he receives *malkus* and pays *me'ah kesef*, double the *ketuva* value of fifty *kesef*, given to the girl's father.

The fine of *me'ah kesef* is explicitly structured as *kefel* — a doubling. He was trying both to kill her and to cause her to lose her *ketuva* entitlement of fifty *kesef*; therefore he pays double that amount in fine.

### Orphan's Fine

The *mishna* has told us that an orphan girl receives *sekilah* but has left us without a ruling on whether the *me'ah kesef* fine applies in her case. Since the Torah says the fine is given *l'avi ha-na'arah* — to the girl's father — and she has no father, it is unclear whether the fine exists at all, and if so to whom it would be paid. This open question — whether an orphaned daughter receives the *me'ah kesef* — is what the *gemara* will take up in the following discussion.

---

---

# Ketubot 44b

## Motzi Shem Ra Intro

### Overview & Ketubah

The *sugya* we now enter is that of *motzi shem ra* — the case in which a husband rises the morning after his wedding and claims his wife was not a virgin. This topic is one of two places in the Torah where the framework of *na'arah betulah* and virginity converges, and it connects directly to the very first *mishnah* of the tractate. The institution of the *ketubah* itself is rooted in this passage: if the husband is proven a liar, he pays one hundred *kessef*, which is double the fifty *kessef* of the *mohar* — the bride-price that serves as the basis for the Rabbinic institution of the *ketubah*. (To be precise, fifty *kessef* equals two hundred *zuz*, so one hundred *kessef* equals four hundred *zuz* — the relationship is one of *keifel*, doubling.)

### Mishnah Cases

The *mishnah* addressed several cases that bear on the application of these laws. One case involves a woman who converted — touching on the phrase *be-Yisrael* in the verse, since such a woman was not originally *Yisrael*. Another involves a woman whose mother converted while pregnant, meaning she was conceived before her mother's conversion and born after. This woman has no legal father in the relevant sense, implicating the phrase *beis aviha*. These cases raise the question of how much the special *halachos* of *na'arah betulah* depend on the full framing of the Torah's language.

### Special Halachos

The special *halachos* of *na'arah betulah me'orasah* are these: if she committed adultery, she receives *sekilah* rather than the ordinary *chenek* that applies to adultery in general; and if the husband is lying and spreading a false report, he pays one hundred *kessef* and receives *malkus*. The operative question throughout this *sugya* is which of these consequences depends on the full configuration of *na'arah betulah me'orasah*, and how much the surrounding phrases — *navala be-Yisrael*, *beis aviha* — affect each of these *dinim* individually.

---

## Sekilah Derivation

### Reish Lakish's Source

The *gemara* opens with the question *mina hani mili* — from where are all these laws derived? Reish Lakish answers: from the word *u-mesah* in the verse. The verse states *ve-sakluha kol anshei ira ba-avanim va-mesah* — they shall stone her and she shall die. Since stoning obviously results in death, the word *u-mesah* is redundant and therefore available for a *derasha*.

### Conception Non-Jewish

Reish Lakish uses this extra word *u-mesah* to include the case of *horasah she-lo bi-kdusha ve-liddasah bi-kdusha* — a woman conceived when her mother was not yet Jewish but born after her mother converted. To review the *mishnah*'s ruling: if a woman converted as an infant, she is entirely outside this *parshah* and receives *chenek* rather than *sekilah*. But if her mother converted while pregnant with her, the *mishnah* says she does receive *sekilah* despite having no legal father. The source for retaining *sekilah* in this intermediate case is the extra *u-mesah*.

### Limitation to Meisa

The *gemara* immediately challenges: *i hachi*, once we include this woman via *u-mesah*, why not include her for all the *halachos* — meaning, why shouldn't the husband also pay the hundred *kessef* and receive *malkus* if he is lying? The *gemara* answers: *le-misa israbsa ve-lo le-knas* — she was included only for the *din* of *misah*, not for the fine. The word *u-mesah* is the mechanism of inclusion, and it extends only to the punishment of death.

The *gemara* then asks: perhaps *u-mesah* is not including this intermediate case at all, but rather is simply including the ordinary case of a woman born after her mother's conversion — *horasah ve-liddasah bi-kdusha*? The *gemara* dismisses this: *hi Yisrael me-ikara hi* — such a woman is fully Jewish from the outset and requires no special inclusion.

### Exclusion Logic

A further possibility is raised: perhaps *u-mesah* includes even a woman who converted as an infant — *horasah ve-liddasah she-lo bi-kdusha*? The *gemara* rejects this as well: *be-Yisrael mai ahni lei* — if the extra *u-mesah* is doing that work, what purpose does the word *be-Yisrael* serve? Obviously *be-Yisrael* is not simply excluding non-Jews — that is self-evident. So *be-Yisrael* must be doing something, namely excluding someone who is in some sense not fully rooted in Jewish status from birth. That exclusion reaches the *halachos* of the hundred *kessef* and *malkus*, removing the husband from those obligations. Meanwhile, the extra *u-mesah* overrides that exclusion specifically with regard to *sekilah*, retaining her in the *parshah* for that punishment alone.

---

## Yesomah & Knas

### Rav Yose on Yesomah

Having established the case of the woman conceived as a non-Jew, the *gemara* turns to a second case — the *yesomah*, a woman whose father is dead. Rav Yose bar Chanina teaches: *hamotzi shem ra al ha-yesomah patur* — one who spreads an evil report against a fatherless woman is exempt from the special punishments. The *mishnah* had already indicated that such a woman still receives *sekilah* — that was not considered a great *chiddush*, since even the woman conceived as a non-Jew retained *sekilah*. What the *mishnah* did not address explicitly is whether the husband's obligations — the hundred *kessef* and *malkus* — still apply when there is no living father.

### Source Exclusion

Rav Yose bar Chanina's source is the verse *venatenu le-avi ha-na'arah* — the payment is given to the father of the *na'arah*. *Prat lezo she-ein lah av* — this excludes the case where she has no father. The payment of the hundred *kessef* is directed to the father, and without a father, the obligation does not attach.

### Challenge from Mefateh

Rav Yosef bar Avin — some say Rav Yosef bar Zvida — raises a challenge from a *braisa* discussing the case of *mefateh*, seduction. The verse there uses the double formulation *ma'en yema'en aviha*, which Rabbi Yose HaGlili interprets as including the *yesomah* — even if there is no father, the *knas* is still paid in a case of seduction. If the *knas* applies by *mefateh* without a father, why should it not apply equally in *motzi shem ra*?

### Obligation Timing

The *gemara* notes that the challenge and its resolution come from the same voice: *hu mosev lah ve-hu mifarek lah*. The distinction is *be-vallah ve-achar kach nis'asama* — the *braisa* about *mefateh* is discussing a case where the father was alive at the time of the act and died afterward. In that case the obligation had already crystallized, and it remains payable even after the father's death — to her, or to the brothers, as discussed elsewhere. But if there was no father at the time of the original act, the obligation never came into existence in the first place, since the *knas* is by its nature payable to the father. This reasoning applies equally to *ones*, *mefateh*, and *motzi shem ra*: if there was a father at the time of the act, the obligation exists and survives his subsequent death; if there was never a father, there is no obligation.

### Rava's Position

Rava, however, disagrees and rules *chayav* — the fine does apply even when there is no living father. Rava's position extends not only to *motzi shem ra* but presumably to *mefateh* and *ones* as well. His reasoning is drawn from the teaching of Ami.

### Betulat Yisrael

Ami teaches: *betulat Yisrael ve-lo betulat gerim* — the verse *ki motzi shem ra al betulat Yisrael* specifies a *betulat Yisrael*, excluding the convert. This exclusion of converts is meaningful only against a baseline in which the ordinary case — a naturally born Jewish woman whose father happens to have died — still obligates the *knas*.

### Reconciliation Logic

The *gemara* makes this explicit: *i amarta bishlama ki hai gavna be-Yisrael mechayev* — if in the standard case of a Jewish woman with no living father the *knas* still applies, then the exclusion of *betulat gerim* is meaningful, because it tells us that the woman who came through conversion is a special exclusion beyond the mere absence of a father. But *ela i amarta be-Yisrael ki hai gavna patur* — if a natural-born Jewish *yesomah* were also exempt, then the exclusion of the convert would be entirely superfluous, since the convert is obviously in a more attenuated position than a Jewish *yesomah*. The force of the exclusion *betulat gerim* therefore proves that the ordinary *yesomah* who is naturally born Jewish remains fully obligated in the *knas*. The payment in that case would be made to her directly.

---

## Motzi Shem Ra & Ketanah

### Reish Lakish on Ketanah

The *gemara* now shifts from the question of *yesomah* to the question of age. Reish Lakish teaches: *hamotzi shem ra al ha-ketanah patur* — one who spreads an evil report against a minor is exempt. While there was a debate between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding *ones u-mefateh* and whether a *ketanah* is included, Reish Lakish holds that in *motzi shem ra* everyone would agree the minor is excluded.

### Father-Based Exemption

Reish Lakish's initial source is the verse *venatenu le-avi ha-na'arah*, where *na'arah* is written in full — *na'arah malei diber ha-katuv* — with the letter *hey*, indicating a full *na'arah*, which the *derasha* reads as specifying an adult. Beyond the textual point, there is also a compelling logical basis: the act of *motzi shem ra* against a minor is not nearly as consequential as against an adult, because even if the husband's claim were believed, the minor could never be executed as a result — since *pituyas ketanah ones* is the law, sexual activity with a minor is always treated as statutory rape. The minor would never be found guilty of voluntary adultery and thus could never receive the capital punishment this *parshah* contemplates.

### Rav Acha's Objection

Rav Acha bar Abba challenges Reish Lakish's derivation. He argues: the mere presence of the letter *hey* in *na'arah* is not sufficient to derive that we are discussing an adult. Without the *hey*, *ta'ima de-ketav beh* — without that *hey*, I would have thought even a minor is included. But, he continues, the Torah itself makes clear that an adult is meant from context: *ha-ketiv ve-im emet hayah ha-davar ha-zeh lo nimtzu betulim la-na'arah ve-hotzi'u et ha-na'arah petach beit aviha u-skaluha* — the text explicitly involves execution. Since a minor cannot be executed, the *parshah* is obviously discussing an adult. The extra *hey* therefore seems unnecessary — the context already implies adulthood.

### Context & Execution

The *gemara* accepts the force of this observation. *Ve-ketanah lav bat onshin hi* — a minor is not subject to capital punishment. Therefore: *ela kan na'arah* — the starting point is the explicit context of the *parshah*, which clearly addresses an adult. It is not the letter *hey* that teaches us we require an adult; rather, the entire scenario of execution makes it self-evident.

### Linguistic Rule

Once we establish from context that this *parshah* discusses an adult, a general linguistic principle follows. *Ha-kol makom she-ne'emar na'arah* without the *hey* — written as *na'ar* — *afilu ketanah be-mashma* — even a minor is included. The derivation thus proceeds in stages: the context makes clear we are dealing with an adult, and once we know that, the presence or absence of the *hey* in other places becomes a systematic indicator of whether the reference is to an adult or potentially to a minor as well. By *motzi shem ra*, then, the woman must unambiguously be an adult *na'arah* — neither a *ketanah* nor, as will emerge, a *bogeret*.

---

## Three Cases Adultery

### Case 1: After Nisuin

The *gemara* presents a *braisa* from Shila: *shalosh middot be-na'arah* — there are three scenarios involving the *na'arah me'orasah* who committed adultery.
