The first is the classical case of the Torah: *ba'u lah eidim be-veit chamiha she-zineta be-veit aviha* — witnesses come when she is already in her father-in-law's house, meaning after *nisuin*, and testify that she committed adultery while she was still in her father's house, meaning during *erusin*. This is the paradigmatic case of *na'arah me'orasah*, and one notes that *chazal* understand the Torah's apparently evidentiary procedure — producing the bedsheet — as in fact a shorthand for witnesses whose testimony is subsequently tested and either confirmed or refuted by *eidim zomemim*. In this case: *soklin osah al pesach beis aviha* — she is stoned at the doorway of her father's house.

### Sekilah Location

The symbolism here is explicit in the *braisa*: *re'u gidulim she-gidalten* — look at what you have raised. The stoning at the father's doorway is an act of casting shame back upon the household that produced her. The case differs from the second scenario, where the adultery is discovered before *nisuin*, in which case execution takes place at the city gate — *al pesach sha'ar ha-ir* — in keeping with the verse in the *parshah* of *na'arah me'orasah* that says *ve-hotzeisem et sheneihem el sha'ar ha-ir ha-hi*. Why is the location different? When the matter is discovered after *nisuin*, the husband and his family are the injured party in a specific and intimate way; the symbolism of shame cast back on the father's house fits that context. When it is discovered before *nisuin*, the act is equally severe but the dynamic of injury is not yet framed in the same way, so the punishment is public but without that directed element of shame. The two locations thus reflect not just the legal stage of the relationship but the distinct moral and symbolic messaging each scenario conveys.

### Case 2: Becomes Bogerit

The third scenario introduced by Shila is the most striking: *sarcha u-vasof bagra* — she committed adultery as a *na'arah me'orasah*, but by the time the matter is discovered and adjudicated she has become a *bogeret*, an adult woman no longer in her father's domain. In this case, Shila rules: *tidon be-chenek* — she is judged by strangulation, not by *sekilah*.

### Shila's Position

This is a remarkable ruling. The sin was committed when she was a *na'arah me'orasah* and was therefore deserving of *sekilah*. Yet Shila holds that the applicable punishment is determined not by the time of the sin but by the woman's current status at the time of judgment. Were she to commit the same act now as a *bogeret*, the punishment would be *chenek*; therefore, even though she deserved *sekilah* when she sinned, she now receives only *chenek*. The principle Shila articulates is: *kol heika de-ishtani gufa ishtani ktala* — when the body changes, the punishment changes.

---

## Sin vs. Status Debate

### Braita Contradiction

The *gemara* immediately raises a contradiction from another *braisa*. That *braisa* discusses a case where a *na'arah me'orasah* committed adultery, and after she became a *bogeret* the husband spread the evil report — *u-mishe-bagra hotzi aleiha shem ra*. The *braisa* states: *hu eino lokeh ve-eino noten me'ah sela* — if he is lying, he does not receive *malkus* and does not pay the hundred *sela*, because the act of *motzi shem ra* occurred when she was already a *bogeret* and the category therefore does not apply to him. Up to this point, the ruling follows a logic consistent with Shila.

But the *braisa* continues: *hi ve-zomemeiha makdimim le-veit ha-sekilah* — she and the false witnesses go to be stoned. The *gemara* objects: *hi ve-zomemeiha salka da'atach* — it cannot be both! Either she did it and is stoned, or the witnesses lied and they are stoned; they cannot both be stoned. The *gemara* therefore emends: *ela o hi o zomemeiha makdimim le-veit ha-sekilah* — either she or the false witnesses are put to death by *sekilah*. The critical point follows: if it was true and she actually committed adultery as a *na'arah betulah*, even though it is now five years later and she is a *bogeret*, she receives *sekilah* — the punishment she deserved at the time of the sin. This is a direct contradiction of Shila, who said she should receive *chenek* based on her current status.

The *gemara* acknowledges this is apparently a *machloket tanna'im* and attempts to reconcile the sources before resorting to that conclusion.

### Rava's Resolution

Rava proposes a distinction: *motzi shem ra ka-amart* — are you speaking of the *motzi shem ra* scenario? *Shani motzi shem ra de-chidusho* — *motzi shem ra* is different because it is itself a *chiddush*. Normally, witnesses come and testify that a woman committed adultery; we judge her based on her current status. But the entire category of *motzi shem ra* is already exceptional.

The exceptional nature of *motzi shem ra* is illustrated by the following case. Consider a woman who entered the *chuppah* but the marriage was not yet consummated — *nichnesah le-chuppah ve-lo niv'alah*. She is technically a *nesu'ah*. If she were now to commit adultery, the punishment would be *chenek*, not *sekilah*, because the category of *na'arah me'orasah* no longer applies once she has entered the *chuppah*. Yet if this is the *motzi shem ra* scenario — if the husband makes his claim the morning after — and witnesses prove he is telling the truth, she receives *sekilah*. The fact that she is already a *nesu'ah* does not change the outcome; the *din* of *motzi shem ra* goes by the original act, not by her status at the moment of discovery. Rava thus argues: since *motzi shem ra* is already an exception in the case of the *nesu'ah*, one who holds Shila's position can say the same extends to the *bogeret* — *motzi shem ra* simply always follows the time of the original act, while for all other cases the principle of judging by current status remains intact.

### Why Exception

The *gemara* challenges this: why should *motzi shem ra* be treated as an exception to the current-status rule? The argument seems to use clear evidence against Shila's position as proof of an exception, rather than as a refutation. One who starts with Shila's assumption and then encounters the *nesu'ah* case could simply conclude that *motzi shem ra* is categorically different — it always reverts to the time of the original act — while other adultery cases continue to follow current status. But is this a principled distinction or merely a defensive maneuver?

### Body Change Criterion

The *gemara* pushes back through Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua. If Shila's rule is that when the *body changes* the punishment changes, then the *nesu'ah* case cannot establish *motzi shem ra* as an exception to that rule. Why? Because in the *nesu'ah* case the body has *not* changed — she is essentially the same person. Her status has shifted but her physical person has not. *Ki chidesh rachmana heicha de-lav ishtani gufa* — the Torah's novelty in that case operates where there is no significant change in the person. Therefore, one cannot infer from the *nesu'ah* case that *motzi shem ra* would similarly override the rule even when the body *has* changed, i.e., when she has become a *bogeret*. If Shila's premise is that a genuine change in the person demands current-status judgment, then the *nesu'ah* case does not dislodge that premise, and we are left with a genuine contradiction between Shila and the *braisa* that gives *sekilah* even when she is a *bogeret*.

---

## Tannaitic Status Debate

### Priest Korban Example

The *gemara* now invokes the solution of *machloket tanna'im*, supported by a *mishnah* that connects directly to this week's *parshah*. The *mishnah* in *Kodshim* discusses cases involving the *chatas* offering: a *nasi* brings a male goat and a *kohen gadol* brings a bull, whereas an ordinary *Yisrael* brings a female sheep or goat. The question is: if a person sinned before receiving a new appointment — as *nasi* or *kohen gadol* — and then was appointed before the obligation was discharged, by which standard is the obligation measured?

The *mishnah* states: *chatu ad she-lo nitmanu ve-nitmanu harei hen ke-hedyotot* — if they sinned before their appointment and then were appointed, they bring the *korban* of a lay person, since the obligation was incurred at the time of the sin.

### Rabbi Shimon vs. Tanna

Rabbi Shimon disagrees: *noda lahem ad she-lo nitmanu chayavim* — if they became aware of their sin before the appointment, they are obligated as lay persons. *Aval mishe-nitmanu pturim* — but if the awareness came only after they were appointed, they are exempt. Rabbi Shimon holds that there are two critical moments: the time of the sin and the time the obligation crystallizes (i.e., when the person becomes aware of the transgression). If those two moments straddle a change in status, the obligations do not align and the result is exemption. This parallels the debate about whether punishment follows the time of the sin or the time of execution: the *tanna kamma* holds that the time of sin is determinative throughout; Rabbi Shimon introduces the moment of crystallization as a second pivot.

### Gemara's Difficulty

The *gemara* raises a difficulty. If we accept Rabbi Shimon's logic — that both the time of the sin and the time of the obligation are relevant, and a discrepancy between them produces exemption — then one would expect the same logic to apply to capital cases. If a woman deserves *sekilah* at the time of the sin but *chenek* at the time of execution, why should the result be *chenek* rather than nothing? Apples and oranges cannot be combined; by *korban* the result is exemption, so perhaps by capital punishment it should also be exemption. The *gemara* presses: *im kein leitei korban ki de-hashtah* — by the same logic applied to *korban*, the result should be bring the *korban* appropriate to the current status, just as you propose giving *chenek* based on current status. But Rabbi Shimon says bring nothing at all. Why, then, in the capital case would you give the lesser punishment rather than no punishment?

It is worth noting that *Tosafot* points out an available answer that the *gemara* does not explicitly take up: unlike different types of *korbanot*, *sekilah* and *chenek* exist on a linear hierarchy, with *chenek* being the lesser. Indeed, elsewhere the *gemara* discusses a case where death-row inmates deserving different modes of execution are confused, and the ruling is to give them all *chenek* — demonstrating that *chenek* can legitimately discharge even a *sekilah* obligation. The common denominator of *sekilah* and *chenek* is *chenek*, and giving *chenek* to one who deserves *sekilah* is a legitimate mode of execution. *Tosafot* observes that this reasoning would resolve the *gemara*'s objection, but the *gemara* itself does not pursue it.

### Execution Parallel

Rather than resolving the *machloket tanna'im* approach, the *gemara* concludes that it cannot satisfactorily be sustained. The attempt to equate the capital-punishment question to the *korban* question — saying that if you follow current status you should impose the current punishment, and by parallel to *korban* where a discrepancy yields nothing, you should yield nothing here — leaves the *gemara* without a clean resolution.

### Rabbi Yochanan's Rewrite

Rabbi Yochanan, rather than continue developing these lines of reasoning, simply instructs the *tanna sefaina* — the reciter of *baraisos* — to amend the text: *tani tidon be-sekilah*. The *braisa* that Shila attributed to himself, which ruled *chenek*, should be rewritten to say *sekilah*. The ruling that punishment follows current status, giving the woman *chenek* because she is now a *bogeret*, is simply wrong and the text is to be corrected. Punishment follows the time of the sin, and she receives *sekilah*.

---

## Final Resolution

### Reconsideration

Even after the *braisa* is rewritten, the *gemara* raises one further question. The Torah specifies *na'arah ha-me'orasah* — perhaps this means the laws apply only when the woman is discovered *as* a *na'arah me'orasah*, i.e., she must still be in that status at the time of the court proceedings? On this reading, *sheila*'s original position might not have been wrong on its merits; rather, the Torah's language itself might confine the category to women who are currently *na'arah me'orasah* when brought before the court.

### Rabbi Ila's Interpretati…

Rabbi Ila addresses this from the verse itself: *amar kra ha-na'arah* — the definite article in *ha-na'arah* signals *zu ha-na'arah she-asata kvar* — this refers to the one who *was* the *na'arah* at the time of the sin. She is called *ha-na'arah* not because she is a *na'arah* now but because she was the *na'arah* in question. This resolves any reading of the verse as demanding current status and confirms that the punishment tracks the time of the sin.

### Rav Yitzchak Resolution

However, the final resolution turns on a different axis entirely, introduced by Rav Yitzchak bar Avin — some say Rav Yitzchak bar Abba. When Rabbi Chanina had pressed Rabbi Ila with the implication that if punishment follows the time of the sin, then the *motzi shem ra* case should likewise follow the time of the alleged sin — meaning even if the husband libels her when she is a *bogeret*, he should incur the full obligations — Rabbi Ila responded with incredulity (*rachmana litzlan mei-hai da'ata*), and Rabbi Chanina returned the sentiment in kind (*rachmana litzlan mi-da'ata didach*). The exchange is pointed; the *gemara* then resolves it cleanly.

### Person/Act Logic

*Ve-ta'ama mai* — why is the *motzi shem ra* case genuinely different? Rav Yitzchak bar Avin teaches: *zu ma'aseha garmu lah ve-zeh kimatz sefasav garmu lo* — for her, it was her own actions that brought the punishment upon her, *keshe-hi zanesa na'arah zanesa* — when she committed adultery she committed it as a *na'arah*, and it is that act which is the basis of judgment. For him, however, it is the movement of his lips — his libel — that brings the punishment upon him. *Ve-eimas kamichayev* — when does he become obligated? *Ha-hi sha'ta* — at the moment he commits the *motzi shem ra*. *Ve-ha-hi sha'ta bogeret haviah* — and at that moment she is a *bogeret*. Therefore his act of slander simply does not fall within the category of *motzi shem ra*, which requires that the slander be directed against a *na'arah me'orasah*. The two cases are thus entirely distinct in principle: her act and his act are different acts occurring at different times, and each is judged by the time at which the relevant act was committed.

---

## Stoning Locations

### Father's Doorway

The *gemara* turns to the practical rules governing where *sekilah* takes place in these cases. The standard ruling: *soklin osah al pesach beis aviha* — she is stoned at the doorway of her father's house. This applies in the paradigmatic case where the matter is discovered after *nisuin* and the adultery occurred during *erusin*.

### City Gate Alternative

If the father has no home — *ein lah pesach beis av* — then: *soklin osah al pesach sha'ar ha-ir ha-hi* — she is stoned at the gate of the city. This mirrors what the Torah prescribes in the general *na'arah me'orasah* case, and it also applies, as established earlier, when the discovery occurs before *nisuin*.

### Beis Din Alternative

If the city is majority non-Jewish — *ube-ir she-rubah ovdei kochavim* — the city gate carries no appropriate Jewish communal symbolism, and so: *soklin osah al pesach beis din* — she is stoned at the entrance of the *beis din*. The court itself then serves as the institutional expression of communal judgment. The same rule applies to the one who worships *avodah zarah*: *soklin oto be-sha'ar she-avad bo* — he is stoned at the gate of the city where the worship occurred, so that the consequence is visible to the community most affected by the idolatry. And if that city is predominantly non-Jewish: *soklin oto al pesach beis din*.

### Avodah Zarah Parallel

The *gemara* notes this parallel explicitly: *kayotze ba-davar atah omer* — and similarly you may say regarding *avodah zarah*. The motivation for stoning at the specific location of the idolatry is the concern about its pernicious communal effects; the statement must be made to the people in the place where the act occurred. This provides the structural parallel to the *na'arah me'orasah* case, and the two sets of laws illuminate each other.

### Textual Derivation

The *gemara* asks *mina hani mili* — from where are these rules derived? The *baraisa* cites *she'arecha* — "your gates" — appearing twice in the passage about *avodah zarah*: once describing where the sin was committed and once prescribing where the stoning takes place. *Ne'emar she'arecha le-malah ve-ne'emar she'arecha le-matah* — the word *she'arecha* appears above and below. *Mah she'arecha ha-amor le-malah sha'ar she-avad bo* — just as the upper occurrence refers to the gate of the city where the worship took place, *af she'arecha ha-amor le-matah sha'ar she-avad bo* — so too the lower occurrence, prescribing execution, refers to the same gate. Furthermore, *she'arecha* — "your gates" — excludes *sha'arei ovdei kochavim*, the gates of non-Jewish cities, which establishes the *beis din* alternative. The *gemara* notes that if *she'arecha* were already used solely to identify which city's gate is meant, one could simply have written *shaar* without the possessive; the full form *she'arecha* therefore teaches both things simultaneously. *Shema mina tartei* — derive two laws from it.

For the *na'arah me'orasah* case, the Torah does not use *she'arecha* but rather *petach beis aviha*. The derivation connecting the two cases is attributed to Rabbi Abbahu: *gamar petach mi-petach u-fetach mi-sha'ar ve-sha'ar mi-she'arecha* — a *gezerah shavah* or *hekesh* linking *petach* as it appears in the *na'arah* passage to *petach* as used in the context of the *mishkan*, and from there to *sha'ar*, and from *sha'ar* to *she'arecha* in the *avodah zarah* passage. Rashi characterizes this derivation as *asmachta* — a textual support rather than a strict *derasha*. The practical upshot is clear: the standard case is stoning at *petach beis aviha*; if there is no *petach beis av* or if the discovery preceded *nisuin*, it is at the *sha'ar* of the city; if the city is non-Jewish, it is at the entrance of *beis din*.

---

---

# Ketubot 46

## Motzi Shem Ra

### Context & Setup

Today's daf is 46, picking up from the bottom of 45b. We are wrapping up the *parsha* of *motzi shem ra* before transitioning, God willing, to what many consider the core subject matter of *masechet Ketubot* itself.

The immediate context involves the *pesukim* concerning *petach beit aviha* — the Torah's specification that the proceedings of *motzi shem ra* take place at the doorway of the father's house — which the Gemara had established applies specifically in the case of after *nisuin*. A separate *pasuk*, concerning the *naarah meurasah* who is stoned, uses the expression *petach*, understood as *shaar ha'ir*, and this applies in a case of *erusin* rather than *nisuin*. Even in the classic case of *nisuin*, if there is no *petach beit ha'av*, the stoning is carried out at *shaar ha'ir*, and if there is no *shaar ha'ir* — for instance, in a city of non-Jews — it is done at *shaar beit din*. This parallel is drawn from the case of one found committing idolatry, who is executed in the city where the idolatry occurred rather than where judgment was rendered, presumably as a lesson to the inhabitants of that city.

### Lashes & Payment

The Gemara now presents a *baraita*: *ha-motzi shem ra lokeh v'nosein me'ah sela* — one who spreads false evil repute against his wife receives lashes and pays one hundred *sela* (equivalent to four hundred *zuz*). This is the standard formulation of the dual penalty in *motzi shem ra*.

### R. Yehuda's View

Rabbi Yehuda qualifies this. As far as lashes are concerned, *lokeh mikol makom* — he receives lashes under any circumstances. However, with respect to the hundred *sela*, *baal nosein, lo baal eino nosein*: only if he had intercourse with his wife and then brings the false claim does he pay; if he did not have intercourse, he does not pay.

One might wonder how he spreads evil repute without having had intercourse. The answer lies in how *chazal* understand the entire *parsha*. The plain sense of the *pesukim* — *v'avo eleha v'lo matzasi lah betulim*, "I came to her and found no signs of virginity" — sounds like a straightforward claim the husband makes the morning after the wedding. The burden then appears to fall on the girl and her family to produce the bedsheets. *Chazal*, however, require a proper judicial proceeding. There must be witnesses, and not just any witnesses: the husband must have been the one who initiated, urged, or hired them. Furthermore, the father and the girl counter with *eidim zomemim*, witnesses who refute and invalidate the first set. The claim thus becomes entirely a matter of witness testimony, which means it is possible for a husband to manufacture such a proceeding without the wedding night ever having occurred — bringing false witnesses to claim she committed adultery after betrothal, without the physical predicate of their own intercourse. In that scenario, Rabbi Yehuda says, he still receives lashes but does not pay the hundred *sela*.

The logic underlying Rabbi Yehuda's distinction is instructive. Spreading false and damaging repute about a young woman — ruining her standing — is a moral wrong regardless of whether it fits neatly within the *parsha* of *motzi shem ra*. But the hundred *sela* payment functions more like a *keifel*, a double payment, because the husband was in effect trying to rob the girl of her *mohar*, her bride price of fifty *shekel*. If they never had intercourse and the slander is exposed, she is still free to marry someone else and receive the standard bride price. The monetary penalty, then, is specifically anchored to the situation in which sex has occurred and the wedding-night claim is relevant — which is why Rabbi Yehuda limits it to that case.

### Sex Requirement

The Gemara identifies the underlying dispute as that between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the *Rabbanan*. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that the entire *parsha* of *motzi shem ra* in the Torah speaks only of a case in which intercourse has occurred. The *Rabbanan* hold that the *parsha* applies even without intercourse.

How does this map onto the dispute in the *baraita*? On one reading, the *Tanna Kamma* reflects the *Rabbanan*: whether or not there was intercourse, both lashes and the monetary penalty apply, because the *parsha* is not limited to cases of intercourse. Rabbi Yehuda then emerges as reflecting Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position that the *parsha* is only operative after intercourse, but extends lashes independently of the *parsha* — based on the prohibition of *lo telech rachil b'amecha*, the general prohibition against talebearing and slander. On this reading, anyone who spreads damaging false report, at least in a sufficiently provable and weighty manner, receives lashes based on this *lav*, regardless of whether they are technically within the *parsha* of *motzi shem ra*. The hundred *sela*, however, belongs exclusively to that *parsha* and is therefore conditioned on intercourse having occurred.

There is a second reading of the *baraita* as well: *ika d'amri kulah k'Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* — perhaps the entire *baraita* assumes like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov that the *parsha* operates only after intercourse. The *Tanna Kamma* says that in that scenario — one in which they have had intercourse — both lashes and payment apply. Rabbi Yehuda then adds that lashes are given even without intercourse, based on the general *lav* of *lo telech rachil*, while agreeing that payment requires the context of intercourse.

### Lashes Explained

The Gemara then challenges: does Rabbi Yehuda really hold that lashes are given under all circumstances? A *baraita* is cited in which Rabbi Yehuda himself says *ba'al lokeh, lo ba'al eino lokeh* — only if there was intercourse does he receive lashes, not otherwise. This appears to be a direct contradiction of the position just attributed to him, creating a *machlokes Tannaim* within Rabbi Yehuda's own rulings.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves this: when the first formulation says the husband receives lashes *mikol makom*, it means only *makas mardus*, rabbinic lashes — not Torah-level *malkot*. Rabbi Yehuda does not maintain a general biblical liability for talebearing. He holds that Torah-level lashes require being within the *parsha* of *motzi shem ra*, which itself requires intercourse. The earlier statement that he always receives lashes refers merely to a rabbinic disciplinary penalty for spreading evil repute, reflecting a societal interest in deterring such conduct.

Rav Pappa offers a different resolution. He maintains the original reading: Rabbi Yehuda does hold that lashes apply under all circumstances in the broad sense. When the second *baraita* says *ba'al lokeh, lo ba'al eino lokeh*, the word *lokeh* there does not mean lashes at all — it means monetary liability. *V'kari lei mamon malkut* — can a monetary payment really be called *malkut*? The Gemara answers: yes. A *baraita* records a dispute regarding one who says *chatzi erchi alai*, "I obligate myself to pay half my assessed value." Rabbi Yose berabbi Yehuda says *lokeh v'nosein erech shalem* — he is "*struck*" with the full bill. Rav Pappa explains that *lokeh* there means he is assessed the full amount, not that he receives lashes. The reason is a rabbinic decree: *gezeira chatzi ercho atu erech chatziyo* — saying "half my *erech*" might be confused with saying "the *erech* of half of me," and since the *erech* of half of one's body encompasses a vital organ and therefore equals the *erech* of the whole, one pays the full amount in either case. The word *lokeh* in that passage simply means "he is hit with the full payment." So too in the second *baraita*: *ba'al lokeh* means the husband is "hit" with the monetary obligation if there was intercourse, *lo ba'al eino lokeh* means no monetary obligation without intercourse.

The Gemara then turns to the derivation of the lashes themselves. A *baraita* states: *v'anshu oso* — "they shall punish him" — refers to the monetary fine, as the Torah makes explicit: *v'anshu oso me'ah kesef v'nasnu la'avi hana'arah*. But *veyisru* — "they shall chastise him" — refers to *malkot*. How do we know *veyisru* means lashes? Rabbi Abbahu derives it through a chain: the word *yisru* is linked to a parallel *yisru* in the *parsha* of *ben sorer umoreh* — *veyisru oso v'lo yishma aleihem* — and through the word *ben* appearing there, it connects to the *parsha* of *vehaya im ben hakot harasha*, the classic Torah passage prescribing lashes. Once *veyisru* means lashes in the context of the *ben sorer umoreh*, it likewise means lashes in *motzi shem ra*.

The Gemara then asks: *azhara lemotzi shem ra minlan* — what is the prohibitory *lav* that must be transgressed before lashes can be administered? Rabbi Elazar says: from *lo telech rachil b'amecha*. Rabbi Natan says: from *venishmarta mikol davar ra* — "guard yourself from every evil thing," interpreting *davar* as *dibbur*, speech, so that it means one must guard against spreading harmful words.

Why does Rabbi Elazar not use *venishmarta mikol davar ra*? Because that verse is needed for a teaching of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair: *al yeharher adam bayom*, a person should not entertain improper thoughts during the day lest they lead to a seminal emission at night — a teaching rooted in the contextual juxtaposition of that verse with the *parsha* of *ki yihye vecha ish asher lo yihye tahor mikre laila*.

Why does Rabbi Natan not use *lo telech rachil b'amecha*? Because that verse is needed to instruct a *beit din* not to be *rach* — gentle — toward one litigant and harsh toward the other. Rashi notes that *rachil* may be read as a compound: *rach li*, soft to me. This is an explicit *pasuk* against judicial partiality in conduct, not merely in judgment. As one student aptly observed, the verse *lo telech rachil b'amecha* follows immediately upon *lo ta'asu avel bamishpat, lo tisa pnei dal v'lo tehedar pnei gadol*, providing the contextual basis for reading it as an instruction to the court.

### Witness Liability

The *baraita* continues. If the husband did not tell the witnesses to come and testify — *lo amar l'eidim bo v'heiduni* — and they testified on their own accord, then *hu eino lokeh v'eino nosein me'ah sela*: he receives no lashes and pays nothing. He is effectively a victim. In that case, *v'hi v'zomemeha makdimin l'beis ha-skila* — either she is stoned (if the witnesses are truthful) or the *eidim zomemim* are stoned (if they are refuted).

The Gemara notes the implication: if he did tell them to come testify, even without hiring them, he bears liability. This brings us to Rabbi Yehuda's dissenting view: *eino chayav ad she-yiskor edim* — he is not liable unless he actually hired the witnesses. The Gemara's question is sharp: why should persuasion alone be insufficient? The principle of *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah* — that there is no agency for transgression, since the agent should have heeded God rather than the sender — would seem to insulate the husband even if he hired them, let alone merely asked. The counter-intuition here is that by paying the witnesses, the husband transforms them into something closer to his employees and agents. The money concretizes his responsibility in a way that mere instigation does not.

Rabbi Abbahu derives Rabbi Yehuda's position through a *gezeira shava* of *sima sima*: the Torah uses the word *v'sam lah alilos devarim* — "and he placed upon her libelous words" — and elsewhere, *lo tasimun alav neshech* — "do not place interest upon him." Just as "placing" in the context of *neshech* involves monetary conduct, so too "placing" false words against her must be through money, through hiring. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a parallel teaching of Rabbi Yose the Sidonian in the school of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai making the identical *gezeira shava*.

The Gemara then records a series of unresolved questions posed by Rabbi Yirmeyah. If he hired the witnesses with land (*karka*) rather than money — does that qualify? What if he hired them for less than a *perutah*'s worth? What if two witnesses together were hired for a single *perutah*, so that each individually received less than a *perutah*? These questions revolve around how formally the *gezeira shava* from *neshech* must be applied — whether the hiring must meet the technical minimum of *mammon* as defined in monetary law, or whether any act that concretizes the agency-like relationship suffices. The Gemara leaves these questions unresolved.

### Edge Cases

Rav Ashi raises further questions about the scope of *motzi shem ra*. *Hotzi shem ra al nisuin harishonim mahu* — what if he is spreading false repute regarding the first marriage? The scenario is: he married her, divorced her, remarried her, and now — in the context of the second marriage — he is bringing false witnesses to claim she had committed adultery before the *nisuin* of the first marriage. The classic *motzi shem ra* is the morning after the wedding night, but surely the claim need not literally be made the next morning; the husband might simply explain that the witnesses only came to him now. Nevertheless, is a second marriage a separate enough context that the *parsha* no longer applies?

A related question: *al nisuei achiv mahu* — what if it is the brother making the claim? The entire *parsha* in the Torah is framed around the husband, and as the Gemara makes clear, if any other man did the identical thing — hired witnesses, spread evil repute — he would still be exempt from the penalties of *motzi shem ra*, even if the witnesses themselves would be *eidim zomemim*. What then of a *yavam*, a brother-in-law who inherits the marriage through *yibum*? If Reuven died and Shimon married Reuven's widow through *yibum*, and Shimon now claims that witnesses have told him she committed adultery prior to the *nisuin* with Reuven — is Shimon perhaps a continuation of Reuven's marriage, such that his claim falls within the *parsha*?

The tension here, as one student rightly noted, is fundamental. Once *chazal* have reconceived *motzi shem ra* as a judicial proceeding centered on witnesses rather than the concrete experience of the wedding night, the logic of limiting the *parsha* to the husband — and only to the original marriage — becomes less obvious. Why shouldn't any man who manufactures such a proceeding be equally liable? The Gemara is navigating the balance between reading the *parsha* as a normal judicial category capable of generalization and remaining tethered to the Torah's specific framing.

The Gemara resolves one of these questions. From the *baraita* taught by Rav Yona: *et biti nasati la'ish hazeh* — "I gave my daughter to this man" — *lazeh v'lo l'yavam*, to this one and not to the *yavam*. At least the case of the brother is excluded. The question of *nisuin harishonim* remains unresolved, and the Gemara notes *pashat mi'achada* — we can answer one question, not both.

### Pesuk Analysis

The Gemara now returns to the core dispute of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the *Rabbanan*, laying out the textual debate in detail. A *baraita* describes the procedure of *hotza'at shem ra*: the husband comes to *beit din* and says the daughter was not a virgin. If witnesses testify that she committed adultery *tachtav* — after betrothal, while under him — then she is stoned. The *baraita* first misstates this as her *ketubah* being reduced to a hundred, and the Gemara immediately corrects: she would be executed. The *baraita* is re-read: if witnesses confirm she committed adultery after betrothal, she faces *skila*; if it turns out she had intercourse before betrothal, then *nimtza shem ra eino shem ra* — the evil repute is not really evil repute, meaning the precise charge (post-betrothal adultery) was not substantiated — and he receives lashes and pays the hundred *sela*, *bein ba aleha bein lo ba aleha*, whether or not there was intercourse. This is the *Rabbanan*'s position.

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says: *lo ne'emru devarim halalu ela kesheba aleha* — the entire *parsha* applies only when intercourse has occurred.

The Gemara then walks through the *pesukim* systematically. According to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, *uba eleha v'kerav eleha* — "I came to her and drew near to her" — straightforwardly describes intercourse. According to the *Rabbanan*, *uba eleha* means he approached her with this charge, and *vekerav eleha* means he drew near her with words — a strained but not impossible reading of a verse that is somewhat redundant even on its surface. According to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, *v'lo matzasi lah betulim* plainly means he found no signs of virginity after intercourse. According to the *Rabbanan*, it means *lo matzasi lah kishrei betulim* — I did not find reliable vouchers for her virginity, i.e., I have no witnesses who can testify that she was a virgin, because the witnesses who appeared testified to her adultery. According to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, *ve'eleh betulei biti* — "and these are my daughter's tokens of virginity" — the father literally produces the bedsheet. According to the *Rabbanan*, *ve'eleh kishrei betulei biti* — these are those who validate my daughter's virginity, meaning the father produces counter-witnesses.

Rabbi Abbahu then derives the metaphorical reading for *ufarshu ha-simla* — "and they shall spread out the garment." He reads it as *pirshu mah she-samah* — they laid out and clarified the claim placed against her, a metaphor for the judicial clarification of competing testimonies. A *baraita* confirms: *melamed she-ba'in eidim shel zeh v'eidim shel zeh u-vorin es ha-davar ke-simla chadasha* — witnesses for one side and witnesses for the other come and clarify the matter like a brand-new cloak. Whether the metaphor derives from *simla chadasha* (a clean garment, white as clarity itself) or from *sam lah* (what was placed against her) is a point of minor debate: *Tosafot* argues it is not derived from the word *simla* at all, insisting it is not a wordplay on *simla*, while the reading that parses it as *pirshu mah she-samah* offers a more direct connection to the root *s-m* from *v'sam lah alilos devarim*.

What is striking here is that the Gemara's own presentation reveals that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov is not merely making a technical argument that intercourse is required while the rest of the *parsha* is about witnesses. He is reading *devarim kiksavam* — the *parsha* as written. He says *simla mamash* — a literal garment. The implication is that according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, what happens is literally what the Torah describes: the husband makes a claim about the wedding night, the parents produce the bedsheet, and that is what is being contested. It is the *Rabbanan* who have transformed the entire *parsha* into a metaphor for judicial witness proceedings. This is an important observation because it means the gap between the two positions is not merely about whether intercourse is technically required — it is a gap about whether the entire structure of the case is literal or metaphorical.

This realization has a profound halachic dimension. Reading the *parsha* literally — as Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov appears to do in its fullest sense — creates a deeply troubling legal situation: the husband's unilateral claim, backed by no witnesses at all, would suffice to put the woman in jeopardy, with the burden of proof on her. *Chazal*'s reinterpretation transforms it into a normal judicial proceeding, which is precisely why the *Rabbanan*'s metaphorical readings, however strained, are halachically necessary.

### Kedarkah

Rav Yitzchak bar Rabbi Yaakov bar Giyori sent a ruling from Eretz Yisrael in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: even though throughout the entire Torah, when it comes to prohibited sexual acts, the Torah does not distinguish between *biah kedarkah* (vaginal intercourse) and *biah shelo kedarkah* (anal intercourse) — both being equally actionable for the purposes of lashes and capital punishment — the case of *motzi shem ra* is different. *Eino chayav ad she-yivo shelo kedarkah v'yotzi shem ra kedarkah*: he is not liable unless the intercourse was *shelo kedarkah* and the false claim is framed as if it were *kedarkah*.

Rashi notes that the phrase *she-yivo shelo kedarkah* means *afilu shelo kedarkah* — even if the intercourse was not the usual way. The Gemara will now explain the precise logic. The substance of the challenge is immediately apparent: according to whom does this ruling hold? If it follows the *Rabbanan*, then the whole case is about witnesses and what they testify — it has nothing to do with hymenal blood or the mode of intercourse. If it follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, then by his own logic *idi va-idi kedarkah beinan* — since the entire discovery is predicated on the absence of hymenal blood on the wedding night, both the intercourse and the claim must be about vaginal intercourse *kedarkah*, and the case of *shelo kedarkah* would never arise.

The Gemara therefore corrects: Rav Kahana sent a ruling in the name of Rabbi Yochanan — *eino chayav ad she-yivo kedarkah v'yotzi shem ra kedarkah*. He is not liable unless both the intercourse and the false claim are *kedarkah*. This follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov consistently: since the mechanism by which the husband discovers the claim is the absence of hymenal bleeding, both the intercourse that would have caused such bleeding and the claim about the absence of it must be *kedarkah*. The case requires that they had vaginal intercourse, that there was no blood, and that the claim is that she previously had vaginal intercourse with another man. The entire evidentiary structure revolves around the hymen.

The Rambam in *Hilchos Naarah Bisulah* (chapter 3, *halacha* 6) rules accordingly: *keitzad motzi shem ra* — the case begins with the husband's own experience: "I came to her and found no signs of virginity," after which he investigated and was then informed by witnesses that she had committed adultery after betrothal, and he brings those witnesses to *beit din*. The Rambam thus requires both elements: the concrete reality of intercourse and the judicial proceeding with witnesses — a kind of hybrid. Furthermore, the Rambam rules: *ba'alah shelo kedarkah v'amar lo matzasi betulim patur u-makin oso makas mardus* — if he had non-vaginal intercourse and claims she was not a virgin, he is exempt from the *motzi shem ra* penalties but receives *makas mardus*. As for hiring witnesses, the Rambam rules that he must have *heivi* the witnesses himself, but does not require that he actually hired them for payment. This raises a noteworthy question: if all he needed to do was produce them, could he in theory still have been acting in good faith, believing their testimony? The answer is not entirely clear, but presumably *heivi* assumes a knowing and malicious initiation.

---

## Ketubah Intro

### Bookend

With the conclusion of *motzi shem ra*, it is worth pausing to note the structural significance of what we have just completed. The opening *perek* of *Ketubot* began with the question of when a woman gets married and what happens if the husband makes a claim the morning after regarding her virginity — a scenario directly rooted in the *parsha* of *motzi shem ra* in the Torah. The motivation for the practice of marrying on Wednesday, so that the husband could appear before *beit din* the following Thursday while still in the heat of the moment, is precisely to replicate the conditions under which the *parsha* operates. The intervening material — about the fifty *shekel* payment, the *mohar* — prefigures the foundational financial structures of marriage. The daf now turns decisively from that framework toward what is in some respects the true subject matter of the *masechta*: the financial and legal relationship between husband and wife, structured around the *ketubah*.

### Paternal Rights

The *Mishnah* states: *ha'av zakai bivito b'kiddusheha b'kesef b'shtar uv'viah* — the father has legal rights over his daughter, whether she is a *ketanah* or a *naarah*, to betroth her through money, through a written document, or through an act of intercourse. That is, the father has the authority to give her in marriage by whatever of the three modes of *kiddushin* he chooses.

### Father's Control

Beyond the right to betroth her, the father is also legally entitled to *metziatah uma'aseh yadeha* — anything she finds and her earnings. He may annul her vows (*hafarat nedarim*), and if she is divorced while still a *nesuah* while an *arusah*, her *get* is given to him as her representative. The one thing the father is not entitled to, the *Mishnah* notes, is *peiros* — the earnings or produce from her property. If, for example, she inherits from a maternal grandfather with no surviving sons, the father does not collect the income from that inheritance. Importantly, this contrasts with the husband's rights once *nisuin* occurs.

### Husband's Rights

The *Mishnah* continues: once she enters into *nisuin* and passes from her father's control to her husband's, *yeseir alav ha-baal she'ochel peiros b'chayyeha* — the husband has all the rights the father had, and additionally he collects the produce of her property during her lifetime. This is the institution of *nichsei milog*: property that remains hers in title and returns to her upon dissolution of the marriage, but whose produce belongs to the husband throughout the marriage.

The transition from father to husband here reflects a model in which a woman's life between roughly the ages of three and twelve and a half is governed by her father's authority, and from *nisuin* onward by her husband's. The Mishnah frames this explicitly as the husband having *more* than the father — *yeseir alav* — not a different kind of authority but an extension of it. It should be noted, however, that *Masechet Kiddushin* fully recognizes the category of a *bogeret*, a young woman past the age of twelve and a half, who can betroth herself independently — a reality that creates a substantial window of personal autonomy entirely unaddressed by this Mishnah's framework.

### Obligations

The Mishnah also enumerates the husband's obligations. In exchange for these rights, he is *chayav b'mzonoteha* — obligated to feed and support her — *b'firkonah* — obligated to redeem her if she is taken captive — and *b'kvuratah* — obligated to pay for her burial. Rabbi Yehuda adds that even the poorest man in Israel may not stint on his wife's funeral below a bare minimum: *lo yifchos mishnei chalilin u-mkonenet* — he must provide at least two flutes and one wailer, the conventional minimum expression of public mourning.

---

## Father Pockets Money

### Money Source

The Gemara now asks: *bechessef minalan* — from where do we derive that the father not only has the power to betroth his daughter but also pockets the money received? Rav Yehuda cites the verse *v'yatza chinam ein kesef* — when the father sells his daughter as a servant and the conditions of the sale are not fulfilled, she goes free without money. The analysis: *ein kesef la'adon zeh* — for this master, no money changes hands upon her release; *v'yesh kesef la'adon acher* — but there is another master who does receive money for her departure. *U-mano aviha* — and who is this other master? The father. The Gemara is explicit and unapologetic: the father's legal relationship to his daughter is described in terms parallel to a master's relationship to his servant. The Torah itself structures it that way, and the Gemara is simply making the implicit explicit.

### Father as Master

Having established that the father functions as a kind of "master" who receives money when the daughter leaves his domain, the Gemara anticipates an objection: *v'eima ledidah* — perhaps while the father has the power to betroth her, the money goes to the daughter herself, not the father? The Gemara responds: *hatam aviha mikabel kiddusheha* — the father is the one who receives the *kiddushin*, as derived from *et biti nasati la'ish hazeh* — "I gave my daughter to this man." The very framing of the verse, in which the father is the active agent giving the daughter, establishes that the transaction runs through him and that the money is received by him.

### Ketanah vs Naarah

The Gemara refines further. One might grant that this applies to a *ketanah*, a minor who has no independent legal agency at all. But what of a *naarah*, a girl who has reached the age of twelve and is to some degree her own person — perhaps she could both betroth herself and pocket the *kiddushin* money? The Gemara responds with a verse.

### Shevach Ne'urim

*Amar kra bine'ureiha beit aviha — kol shevach ne'urim la'aviha*: while she is in her youth in her father's house, all the benefit and value of her youth (*shevach ne'urim*) belongs to her father. The Gemara notes, however, that this derivation will be examined further, as it does not yet fully satisfy the question. The underlying assumption being tested is that as a *naarah* she might have sufficient independent standing to act on her own behalf and retain the proceeds — and the verse is brought to foreclose that possibility. The discussion will continue on the following daf, where the Gemara will work through precisely how we know not only that the father controls the betrothal but that he is entitled to all the financial benefits that flow from his daughter's youth.

---

---

# Ketubot 48

## Framework of Ketubot

### Women's Status & Transit…

The daf we take up today — picked up in the middle of 47b, roughly ten lines below the two dots — sits at the heart of *masechet Ketubot*, the section that deals with the *ketubah* proper: the reciprocal rights and responsibilities between husband and wife. Before arriving at those obligations, however, it is worth situating the *masechet* within a broader framework.

The earlier chapters of *Ketubot* focused on the father's rights over his daughter: his power to annul her vows, to marry her off, and to claim her earnings — most of which are biblical. Notably, the father bears almost no reciprocal responsibilities. He has no legal obligation even to feed his daughter; he could, in principle, send her out of the house to earn her own keep.

This reflects a portrait of women in the *Torah* that is striking to the modern reader: the woman never appears as a fully autonomous agent directing her own fate. She moves from one man's house to another — from her father's house to her husband's house. The *Torah*'s language bears this out explicitly; when a *kohen*'s daughter is widowed or divorced, the verse says *v'shava el beit aviha kine'ureha* — she returns to her father's house. It is the Rabbis who open up the space for a woman's legal independence, ruling that the father's authority ceases when she becomes a *bogeret* at twelve and a half, at which point she becomes her own legal agent. That emancipation is a rabbinic innovation, not a biblical one; the baseline framework of the *Torah* is the transit from father's house to husband's house, and that is precisely the framework *masechet Ketubot* addresses.

### Erusin vs. Nissuin

Within that framework, there is an important distinction between *erusin* — betrothal — and *nissuin* — the actual consummation of marriage and cohabitation. After *erusin*, the woman remains essentially in her father's domain. It is only with *nissuin*, when she begins living together with her husband, that the primary obligations and rights of the *ketubah* fully take effect. The base amount of the *ketubah* — 100 or 200 *zuz*, depending on whether she is a widow or a virgin — exists from the time of *erusin*, but whether the additional amounts, the *tosefes* and the *nedunya* (dowry), take effect before *nissuin* was a matter of debate, as was discussed in the preceding material.

### Three Main Obligations

The ongoing rights and responsibilities during marriage bear a distinct name: *t'nai ketubah* — the stipulations of the *ketubah*. This term refers not to conditions in the contractual sense, but to the ongoing obligations that govern the marriage itself, as distinct from the *ikar ketubah* (the base lump-sum payment of 100 or 200) and the *tosefes* (any additional amount the groom undertakes). The *ikar* and *tosefes* are payable at divorce or the husband's death, functioning essentially as alimony or, in the case of his death, as a substitute for inheritance — since a wife does not inherit her husband — protecting her when she is left without his support. The *t'nai ketubah*, by contrast, are the live, ongoing obligations.

Three primary reciprocal obligations structure this discussion: the husband's duty to provide *mezonot* (food and sustenance) in exchange for his wife's earnings; his duty to redeem her from captivity (*pirkyon*) in exchange for his right to the *peiros* — the fruits and earnings from her *nichsei milug* (property to which she retains title but whose income accrues to him); and his duty to bury her should she predecease him, in exchange for the *nedunya*, the dowry property she transfers to his estate at marriage (*nichsei tzon barzel*).

---

## Reciprocal Obligations

### Tanu Rabanan

The *Tanu rabanan* at 47b articulates these exchanges formally: *tiknu mezonoteha tachat maaseh yadeha* — they established his obligation to feed her in exchange for her earnings; *upirkona tachat perot* — his obligation to redeem her from captivity in exchange for his right to the *peiros*; and *ukvorata tachat ktuvata* — his obligation to bury her in exchange for the *ketubah*, which here means the *nedunya*, the dowry property.

### Whose Rights Matter?

The *Gemara* then asks a pointed question: *lefikach baal ochel perot* — "therefore the husband eats the fruit" — why is this stated with the word *lefikach* ("therefore"), as if it were the conclusion to be derived, when all three obligations have already been stated? The question exposes an important ambiguity in how the entire structure is framed: is the husband the entitled party — in which case he holds the rights and the obligations are what he concedes in exchange — or is the wife the entitled party, in which case her rights are primary and his benefits are what he receives in exchange?

This framing question matters enormously for practical *halakha*. If the husband is the entitled party — if we read the *braita* as saying, essentially, he has a right to her earnings, and in exchange he feeds her — then it is *he* who can opt out: he could say, keep your earnings, I will not feed you. If, on the contrary, the wife is the entitled party — she has a right to be supported, and in exchange he takes her earnings — then *she* is the one who can opt out: she could say, don't support me, and I will keep my own earnings.

### Fruit & Redemption

The *Gemara* resolves the specific question of the *lefikach* as follows. One might think that since the husband's right to the *peiros* exists specifically to ensure he will redeem his wife from captivity, we should place those earnings in escrow — a dedicated emergency fund — rather than allow him to spend them freely. If the money is segregated, the reasoning goes, he will feel his obligation is discharged once that fund is exhausted, and if the ransom demanded exceeds the amount saved, he will simply refuse to pay the difference. *Lefikach baal ochel perot* — therefore we let him eat the fruit freely, without strict accounting — because if he has used the earnings over the years without segregating them, no exact accounting is kept in either direction: he is not limited to a fixed sum when the time comes to redeem her, and he understands that the obligation to redeem her is open-ended. *Zimnin d'lo malu* — sometimes the accumulated earnings will not be sufficient — and precisely because he has enjoyed them without limit, he will reach into his own pocket to make up the difference and redeem her fully.

This exchange may be difficult for the modern reader to fully appreciate on two levels. First, it presupposes that capture and the need for ransom were not rare occurrences — the *masechet* returns to the topic repeatedly — though that reality is remote from contemporary experience. Second, the *Gemara*'s assumption that a husband might hesitate to redeem his wife is jarring. Yet the discussion notes a real concern: if a wife taken captive might have been raped, or might even willingly engage in sexual relations in order to secure her freedom, a husband might pause before paying the ransom. The *Gemara*'s frank acknowledgment of this dynamic is a striking window into the social and moral realities that shaped these laws.

### Modern Ketubah Reform

The framing question — whose rights are primary — is not merely academic. Returning to it: against the plain sound of the *braita*, which makes the husband appear to be the entitled party, the *halakhic* conclusion is that the wife is the protected party. She is the one entitled to support, and in exchange he receives her earnings. This means she is the one who can opt out of the exchange: she may declare that she will retain her own earnings and forego his support obligation.

This conclusion has direct modern application. *Kolech*, a women's Orthodox organization in Israel, has created a rider to the standard *ketubah* in which the wife first waives her right to be supported and retains her own earnings and the income from her property, thereby severing the exchange on which the standard *t'nai ketubah* rest. Having done so, both parties are then free to enter a new, mutual set of obligations — pooling their earnings and accepting joint responsibility for one another's financial well-being. This restructuring is only legally available to the wife, and only because *halakha* recognizes her, not the husband, as the fundamentally protected party in the original exchange.

Since the *ketubah* in Israel occupies a dual status — simultaneously a ritual document and a legally operative instrument before the rabbinical courts — *Kolech* issues this restructuring as a separate rider rather than altering the traditional *ketubah* text itself, preserving the ritual formula while achieving the legal goal.

---

## Common & Uncommon

### Abaye's Principle

Having established the three paired exchanges, the *Gemara* asks why specifically these obligations are matched to these rights — why *mezonot* for earnings, *pirkyon* for *peiros*, and burial for *nedunya*, and not some other pairing. *Abaye* supplies the organizing principle: *tiknu matzui l'matzui ve'she'eino matzui l'she'eino matzui* — common things are matched with common things, and uncommon things with uncommon things.

### Classification of Obliga…

The matching follows accordingly. *Mezonot* — the daily obligation to feed his wife — is an everyday, ongoing expense. It is matched against *maasei yadeha* — her earnings — which are likewise an ongoing, regular matter, whether from labor outside the home, or more commonly, from the domestic work she performs within it: cooking, sewing, running the household. Common is matched with common.

*Kevurah* — burial — is a one-time event, as is the *nedunya* the wife brings into the marriage: she brings it once, and it is transferred once. Uncommon is matched with uncommon.

*Pirkyon* — redemption from captivity — and *peiros* — the ongoing earnings from her property holdings — present a more complex case. The *peiros* are an ongoing accumulation, while the ransom may be a one-time and potentially very large demand. The *Gemara* already explained why the lack of exact accounting between these two serves both parties: the husband enjoys the earnings freely, and therefore is expected to redeem her without limit when the moment comes.

### Historical Context

*Rashi* notes a further dimension relevant to the matching of *pirkyon* with *peiros*: while a *nedunya*, a dowry of transferred property, was extremely common — virtually every woman brought one — property that the wife *already owned* at the time of marriage, to which she retained title and from whose income the husband benefited (*nichsei milug*, producing *peiros*), was less common in the *Gemara*'s world. In the contemporary context, by contrast, a professional woman is far more likely to bring personal assets and investments into a marriage than to bring a formal dowry, which inverts the historical frequency. This does not change the legal structure, but it does illuminate why *Rashi* treats *peiros* as the less common item in its pair.

---

## Ketubah Document

### Ketubah Formulas

It is worth pausing to examine the actual text of the *ketubah* document, which translates these abstract obligations into a formal written formula. The *ketubah* opens with the date — *b'echad b'shabbat*, on the first day of the week, in year such-and-such — and the groom's declaration: *amar lah l'hada betulta, havi li l'intu* — he said to this woman, be for me as a wife. This declaration corresponds to the moment of *kiddushin*; the *ketubah* obligations, however, take effect at *nissuin*.

The groom then undertakes the central obligations: *eflach v'okir ve'ezon ve'afarnes yatich ke'hilchat guvrin yehuda'in* — I will work, honor, sustain, and provide for you in the manner of Jewish husbands. *Eflach* — I will work — means that he commits to going out and earning a living for her benefit. *Okir* — I will honor — reflects the principle *chayav adam l'chaved es ishto yoser m'gufo*, a man must honor his wife more than himself; this is a personal rather than financial obligation. *Ezon* — I will feed — corresponds to *mezonot*. *Afarnes* — I will provide — likely refers to *ksus*, clothing. The phrase *ke'hilchat guvrin yehuda'in* — in the manner of Jewish husbands — signals that he commits to doing all of this properly, without cutting corners.

Later in the document comes the formula *u'me'ayel lavasayichi k'orach kol ar'a* — I will enter upon you in the way of all the earth — which refers to *bi'ah*, the sexual relation, the *mitzvah* of *onah*. The phrase *k'orach kol ar'a* may be read in parallel with *ke'hilchat guvrin yehuda'in* — not merely as a bare description of intercourse, but as a commitment to fulfill this obligation in the proper, respectful manner.

### Listed & Unlisted

The *ketubah* formula thus mentions *mezonot*, *ksus*, and *onah* — sustenance, clothing, and conjugal relations. What is conspicuously absent from the explicit text is *refuah* (the obligation to pay for his wife's medical care) and *kevurah* (burial). These obligations exist, but they are not spelled out in the formula, presumably because they do not require a fixed monetary amount to be stipulated in the document.

Similarly, the husband's corresponding *rights* — his entitlement to her earnings, the *peiros* of her *nichsei milug*, and so forth — are not enumerated in the *ketubah* text. The *ketubah* is primarily a document of his obligations to her, not a ledger of mutual exchanges.

### Fixed Amounts

The *ketubah* does specify the *nedunya* — the dowry — listing what she brings from her father's house and fixing a monetary value for it. It is this fixed value that the estate must return to her in the event of divorce or the husband's death. In practice, rather than enumerating the specific assets — two sheep, ten garments, one camel — the document fixes the amount as a round sum: *hakol kibel alav chasan dena b'me'ah zkukan kesef tzaruf* — the groom accepted upon himself the equivalent of one hundred *zekukim* of refined silver as the value of the *nedunya*.

Beyond the *nedunya*, the *ketubah* also specifies the *tosefes ketubah* — the additional amount the groom undertakes above the base *ikar ketubah*. These two amounts — the fixed *nedunya* and the *tosefes* — together constitute the sum the wife collects at the dissolution of the marriage.

### Zuz to Kesef Tzaruf

The historical background to these numbers deserves explanation. The biblical *ketubah* amount — *ikar ketubah* — is 200 *zuz* for a virgin and 100 for a widow. By the time of the *Rishonim*, however, the *zuz* had become so debased in value that 200 *zuz* offered virtually no protection to the woman. To remedy this, the *Rishonim* effectively replaced 200 *zuz* with 100 *kesef tzaruf* — refined silver coins — a sum of substantially greater real value. They accomplished this through two mechanisms.

First, the *nedunya* was fixed at 100 *kesef tzaruf*, even for a woman who brought nothing to the marriage — the document simply states that as the agreed valuation. Second, the *tosefes ketubah* was standardized at an additional 100 *kesef tzaruf*, making it a boilerplate requirement rather than a voluntary addition. The two amounts together — 100 for the *nedunya* and 100 for the *tosefes* — total 200 *kesef tzaruf*, and the document closes with *sach hakol mas'ayim zekukim kesef tzaruf*, the total being 200 *zekukim* of refined silver, effectively replacing the 200 *zuz* of the biblical standard with a figure of real monetary weight. The combination of a fixed *nedunya* and a fixed *tosefes* into a single total is admittedly an unusual conflation, but the purpose — protecting the wife — is transparent.

The *Kolech* *ketubah* rider, mentioned earlier, represents the most recent significant modification to this framework, though no formal communal fix has been enacted since the *Rishonim*'s standardization roughly six hundred years ago.

---

## Biblical & Rabbinic

### Rava's Question

Having outlined the structure of the reciprocal obligations, the *Gemara* turns to a fundamental question: which of these obligations are biblical (*m'deoraisa*) and which are rabbinic enactments (*m'derabanan*)? *Rava* raises the question: the earlier *braita* framed the husband's *mezonot* obligation as a rabbinic enactment — the Rabbis established his duty to feed her in exchange for her earnings, implying it was not a pre-existing biblical duty. But the following *braita* appears to treat *mezonot* as biblical. Which is correct?

### Three Torah Obligations

The *braita* invoked is derived from the verse in Exodus describing the case of a man who acquires a female slave with the intention of marrying her. If he subsequently takes a second, free-born wife of higher social standing, the *Torah* warns: *she'erah kesutah ve'onatah lo yigra* — he may not diminish the first wife's *she'er*, *kesut*, and *onah*. The concern is that the husband, preferring his second wife, will treat the first as a second-class wife in every dimension. The *Torah* prohibits this, and from this prohibition we derive the affirmative obligations owed to every wife.

The classic reading, familiar from *Rashi* on the *Chumash*, maps the three terms as follows: *she'erah elu mezonot* — *she'er* (flesh) refers to food, derived from the verse *va'asher achalu she'er ami*, "they ate the flesh of my people," meaning that flesh requires food to sustain it. *Kesutah k'mashma'an* — *kesut* means clothing, simply as the word implies. *Onatah zeh onah ha'amurah ba-Torah* — *onatah* refers to the regular conjugal times, derived from the verse *im ta'aneh benotai* — if you afflict my daughters — where withholding is the *inuy* and the obligation is its positive counterpart.

So according to this first reading, all three — food, clothing, and conjugal relations — are biblical obligations derived from the *Torah*.

### Rabbi Eliezer's View

*Rabbi Eliezer* disagrees with the assignment of terms. He reads *she'erah* not as food but as sexual relations: *she'er* in the *Torah* typically denotes flesh in the sense of bodily closeness — *ish ish el kol she'er besaro lo tikrevu l'galot ervah* — a man shall not draw close to any who is *she'er*, his close flesh, to uncover nakedness. Thus *she'erah* signals the fleshly, sexual relation.

In his reading, then, *she'erah* is *onah*, *kesutah* remains clothing, and *onatah* becomes *mezonot* — sustenance — derived from *vay'anecha vayarchivcha*, God caused Israel to suffer hunger (*inuy*) in the wilderness before feeding them with the *man*. The same root that denotes the withholding of sex also denotes the withholding of food, and from either withholding we derive an obligation to provide.

The conclusion is the same trio — food, clothing, sex — but the words from which each is derived are rearranged.

### Rabbi Eliezer b. Yaakov

*Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* offers a substantially different reading. He treats the verse not as a list of three separate obligations, but as two paired phrases: *she'er kesut* together, and *kesut ve'onah* together. *She'er* functions as an adjective qualifying *kesut*: *le'fum she'erah ten kesutah* — according to her flesh, give her clothing. That is, provide her with clothing appropriate to her body and stage of life. *Shelo yiten lo shel yaldah le'zekenah ve'lo shel zekenah le'yaldah* — do not give an old woman a young woman's garments or a young woman an old woman's garments. Similarly, *kesutah ve'onatah* — according to the season's time, give her clothing: *shelo yiten chadashim biyemot ha'chamah ve'lo shechakim biyemot ha'geshamim* — do not give new, thick garments in summer, nor worn, thin garments in winter.

According to *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov*, the entire verse speaks only of clothing, with two specifications: that the clothing be appropriate to her age and that it be appropriate to the season. This is a striking position. It would seem to leave *mezonot* and *onah* entirely without a biblical source, at least from this verse. Several *Rishonim* note that this need not mean those obligations are nonexistent or unimportant, but rather that they understand them differently: the sexual relationship is not merely one item among a list of obligations, but is constitutive of the very identity of marriage. A husband who cannot fulfill this dimension of the marriage is not simply failing one obligation among many — he is undermining what marriage fundamentally is. This has halakhic implications when, for example, a husband is physically incapable of conjugal relations: the question is whether the wife can sue for divorce not merely on the grounds that one obligation is unmet, but on the grounds that there is, in some sense, no marriage at all.

### Kiruv Basar

*Rav Yosef* cites yet another tradition: *she'erah zu kiruv basar* — *she'erah* means the coming-together of flesh. *Shelo yinhag bah minhag Parsiyim she'meshamshin mitosaihen belivushaihen* — he should not conduct himself with her as the Persians do, who have marital relations while clothed. This *braita* uses the exotic figure of the Persians — the *Gemara*'s analogue, apparently, of the various cultural stereotypes every society projects onto others — to make the point that conjugal relations must involve *kiruv basar*, actual bodily union, not merely the act of intercourse while remaining clothed.

This supports a ruling of *Rav Huna*: if a husband declares *ee efshi ela ani be'vigdi vehi be'vigdah* — I refuse to have relations unless we are both clothed — he must give a divorce and pay the *ketubah*. The intimacy of marriage requires nakedness; the *Gemara* assumes that a husband and wife share a bed unclothed. This is why the *Gemara* elsewhere considers whether, when a wife is a *niddah*, it suffices for the couple to wear nightclothes rather than having separate beds — since the assumption is that normally they are unclothed together, the wearing of clothes might itself constitute sufficient *hekker* (marking of separation). The *Gemara* ultimately rejects this and requires separate beds, but the very framing of the question reveals the baseline assumption.

### Halakhic Consensus

The consensus position among the *Rishonim*, notwithstanding *Rashi*'s well-known commentary on the *Chumash*, is that the only obligation that is definitively biblical (*m'deoraisa*) is *onah* — the conjugal relation. *Mezonot* and *ksus* — food and clothing — are rabbinic obligations. This is consistent with the plain language of the first *braita*, which framed *mezonot* as a rabbinic enactment in exchange for her earnings. What *Rashi*'s reading captures is the content of the three obligations, not their legal source; the *halakhic* derivation of which is biblical and which is rabbinic is a separate question.

### Ramban's Framework

The *Ramban*, in his *Torah* commentary, offers a reading that both accommodates the *halakhic* consensus and gives depth to all three terms. If the only biblical obligation is *onah*, and *she'erah* and *kesutah* cannot straightforwardly be read as food and clothing in this context, then what do all three words mean?

The *Ramban* proposes that the verse describes three dimensions of the *sexual* relationship between husband and wife — particularly with reference to the first wife whom the husband might be inclined to treat contemptuously. *She'erah* refers to *kiruv basar* — actual bodily union, the quality of the intimate act itself, not merely its occurrence. The husband may not treat the first wife as a purely instrumental sexual partner while reserving emotional and physical tenderness for the second; even with the first wife, the intimacy must be real. *Kesutah* — "her covering" — the *Ramban* reads as referring to the setting and environment: the marital bed, the linens, the physical context in which intimacy occurs. Relations must not be conducted in a degrading or perfunctory manner, as one might visit a prostitute, but with the full dignity of the marital environment. *Onatah* — "her times" — refers to the regularity and ongoing rhythm of conjugal life: it must occur at appropriate intervals and reflect a sustained connection, not a sporadic or arbitrary one.

On this reading, the three words all speak to *onah*, but they articulate its three necessary dimensions: the quality of bodily union, the dignity of the environment, and the regularity of the relationship. This also explains, the *Ramban* argues, why the *halakhic* conclusion places only *onah* in the biblical category — because all three terms are ultimately about *onah*, not about separate obligations of food and clothing.

One might observe that in the *ketubah* text itself, *onah* appears somewhat separately — *u'me'ayel lavasayichi k'orach kol ar'a* — and the formula *ke'hilchat guvrin yehuda'in* and *k'orach kol ar'a* may both carry the sense of the *Ramban*'s understanding: not merely that the act occurs, but that it is carried out in the proper, dignified, and fully human manner.

---

## Burial Standards

### Rabbi Yehuda's Minimum

The *Gemara* now returns to the *mishnah*, which addresses the standard for the husband's obligation to bury his wife when she predeceases him. *Rabbi Yehuda* rules that even the poorest man in Israel must provide his wife with a burial that includes no fewer than two flutes (*chalilim*) and a wailer (*mekonenes*) — professional mourners of a minimum standard.

### Family Practice vs. Mini…

The *Gemara* reads this ruling in contrast to the *Tanna Kamma*, who appears to accept a lower standard. The *Gemara* clarifies the precise case of dispute: everyone agrees that the husband must provide for the burial at *at least* the standard to which the wife's family is accustomed. The question is what happens when his family standard is higher than hers. In that case, does he owe her the higher standard?

The *Tanna Kamma* holds that he need only meet her family's customary standard. *Rabbi Yehuda* holds that he must provide whatever is the *higher* of the two standards — his or hers.

### Ascent & Non-Descent

This dispute reflects the broader principle of *olah immo ve'einah yoredes immo* — she ascends with him but does not descend with him. That is, if the husband is of higher social or economic standing than his wife, she is entitled to be maintained at *his* standard, not merely her own. Conversely, if he falls into poverty, he cannot reduce her maintenance to below what she was accustomed to before marriage. The principle governs his obligations of food, clothing, and housing during the marriage; the question here is whether it also governs the funeral.

### Living vs. Deceased

The *Gemara* frames this as follows: everyone may agree that *olah immo ve'einah yoredes immo* applies during the couple's shared life — while both are alive, she is maintained at the higher of the two standards. The question is whether it continues to apply *after death*, when there is no longer a shared life to speak of. *Rav Chisda* rules in the name of *Mar Ukva*: *halakha ke-Rabbi Yehuda* — we follow *Rabbi Yehuda*. Even after death, the burial must be conducted at the higher of the husband's and wife's family standards. The principle of *olah immo ve'einah yoredes immo* is not extinguished by her death.

---

## Absent/Incapacitated Hus…

### Deranged Husband

*Rav Chisda* further rules in the name of *Mar Ukva* regarding a husband who has become a *shoteh* — who is in a state of mental incapacity, unable to manage his own affairs or provide for his household. *Beit Din* intervenes actively: *Beit Din yordin l'nechasav v'zanin u'mefarnesin es ishto u'vanav u'vnosav* — *Beit Din* descends to his property, selling it off as necessary, and uses the proceeds to provide *mezonot* and *parnasah* for his wife, his sons, and his daughters, as well as for a *davar acher* — another matter — to be specified below.

### Conscious Abandonment

This is contrasted with a different *braita*: a man who has gone abroad — who left on his own initiative, consciously, without making arrangements for his family. His wife comes before *Beit Din* demanding *mezonot*. Here too *Beit Din yordin l'nechasav* and sells off property to sustain his wife — but *aval lo vanav u'vnosav*, not his sons and daughters — *v'lo davar acher*, nor for the other matter. The children and the additional obligations are not covered when the husband has consciously abandoned his responsibilities.

### Legal vs. Intent

*Ravina* raises the question to *Rav Ashi*: what is the operative distinction between these two cases? The answer lies in a difference between legal obligation and presumed intent. A husband has a legal obligation to support his wife; he has no such legal obligation to support his children. *Beit Din* can enforce legal obligations against his estate in any case. But when *Beit Din* acts on behalf of a *shoteh* — a man who is incapacitated and not consciously choosing to abandon his family — it acts not merely to discharge legal obligations but also to fulfill what the man himself would presumably have wanted: to care for his children, to provide the additional comforts for his wife that go beyond the strict legal minimum. We assume that a man who has not made a conscious choice to abandon his family would, if he could, continue to care for them fully.

When, however, a man has left consciously and deliberately — even if he may have expected to return — the fact that he did not provide for his children before leaving is read as a communication: he is not attending to those responsibilities. Since he is not legally obligated, *Beit Din* cannot override this. Only the wife's strict legal entitlement can be enforced against his estate.

### Additional Matters

The *davar acher* — the additional matter mentioned in both the case of the *shoteh* and the absent husband — is now identified. *Rav Chisda* says: *ze tachshit* — this refers to jewelry or personal adornments for the wife (or, according to *Rashi*, to perfume — something that is an ongoing personal expense but not within the strict legal category of *ksus*/clothing). *Rav Yosef* says: *tzedaka* — charitable donations that the husband regularly made.

The relationship between these two opinions: if one holds that even *tachshit* is provided for the wife even when the husband has consciously abandoned the family — because *delo nicha lei d'titnaval*, he does not want his wife to be degraded — then *tzedaka* would certainly be provided in the case of incapacity. But if one holds that *tachshit* is provided only in the case of incapacity, not conscious abandonment, then *tzedaka* would certainly not be provided in the case of conscious abandonment: if *Beit Din* will not even provide for his own family, it will surely not make charitable donations on his behalf. *Tzedaka* is provided only in the case of a *shoteh*, not when the husband has voluntarily left.

---

## Husband Predeceases

### Husband Abroad

*Rabbi Chiya bar Avin* cites *Rav Huna*: if a man has gone abroad and his wife dies during his absence, *Beit Din* again descends to his property and buries her — *lefi kvodo*, according to his status.

### Higher Status Standard

The *Gemara* immediately asks: why *lefi kvodo* — his status — and not *lefi kvodah*, her status? What if her family's standard is higher than his? The *Gemara* corrects: read it as *af lefi kvodah* — even according to her status, meaning the *higher* of the two. This is the application of *olah immo ve'einah yoredes immo* even after death: *Beit Din* uses the estate to bury her at the higher of his and her family standards.
