The *gemara* immediately challenges this from a *baraita*: *bogeres harei hi ke-tavu'ah* — a *bogeres* is treated as if the husband had already demanded that the marriage proceed. *Tavu'ah* is the terminology for when one party says it is time for *nissuin*, which triggers the twelve-month clock for a *betulah*. The *baraita* seems to say that reaching *bagrus* automatically triggers that clock — and it is a twelve-month clock, not thirty days. This constitutes a direct *tiyuvta* of *Rav Huna*'s position. The *gemara* attempts to deflect this by suggesting that *ke-tavu'ah* here means like the demand-triggered clock for an *almanah*, which is thirty days — but this reading is rejected as too forced.

---

## Mishna Reconciled

### Tva'ah Eidun

A *baraita* clarifies the underlying mechanics: after *eirusin* has taken place, either party — husband or wife — may demand that *nissuin* proceed. *Bein she-tav'ah ha-ba'al ve-hi me'akeves* — whether the husband demanded and she sought to delay, *bein she-tav'ah hi u-va'al me'akev* — or she demanded and he sought to delay: in both cases, the clock for the preparation period is triggered and the other party is given time to prepare.

### Shas Tvuah

The *baraita* further specifies: *notnim lo shneim asar chodesh mi-shas tevi'ah* — twelve months are granted from the time of the demand, *aval lo mi-shas eirusin* — not from the time of *eirusin* itself. The *eirusin* may have taken place years before; the clock begins only when one of the parties actively presses for the transition to *nissuin*.

### Bogeret Ktavuah

The *baraita* then states: *u-vogeres harei hi ke-tavu'ah* — and a *bogeres* is treated as equivalent to having been demanded of. This means that the moment a woman attains *bagrus*, it is as if the demand for *nissuin* has been made, and her twelve-month preparation period begins automatically from that point. This directly contradicts *Rav Huna*'s ruling of thirty days and is declared *tiyuvta de-Rav Huna tiyuvta* — a definitive refutation of *Rav Huna*.

---

## Ein Poskin Ketana (II)

### Rav Papa Resolve

*Rav Pappa* resolves the tension by distinguishing between two scenarios involving a *bogeres*. The ruling that a *bogeres* gets twelve months — because her reaching *bagrus* functions as an automatic demand — refers to a woman who has just entered *bagrus* and whose *kiddushin* was contracted around that time. The ruling of thirty days, akin to an *almanah*, applies to a *bogeres* who has already been in *bagrus* for twelve months before entering into *kiddushin* — that is, a woman who is 13 and a half years old at the time of *kiddushin*. By that point, the automatic demand that came with *bagrus* has long since been triggered; she has already had the full benefit of the twelve-month window. When *kiddushin* is contracted now, after that window has elapsed, she receives only thirty days, like an *almanah*, since the delay is no longer attributable to preparation for an imminent marriage but to a situation that has been waiting far beyond the normal timeframe. *Rav Huna*'s ruling was therefore not refuted but rather correctly limited to this specific scenario.

---

## Mishna Reconciled (II)

### Tosafos Naara

*Tosafos* raises a structural difficulty with the entire framework. The *mishnah*'s twelve-month rule — triggered by a demand for *nissuin* — appears to apply to the paradigmatic case. But when we examine the cases on either end: if the woman is a *ketanah*, the right to delay extends beyond twelve months for the entire duration of her *ketanah* status; if she is a *bogeres*, the clock starts automatically without any demand. The case where the twelve-month clock triggered by a *tevi'ah* — a demand — is the operative rule is specifically when she is a *na'arah*, the period between twelve and twelve and a half years old.

This creates a complication: if she was a *na'arah* when the demand was made and the twelve-month clock began ticking, but she transitions to *bogeres* six months into that period, what happens? At the moment of *bagrus* the automatic demand kicks in independently — but she is already mid-way through a twelve-month period. *Tosafos* works through the implications of this timing, examining whether the clock that began during her *na'arah* status continues or is superseded by the automatic *tevi'ah* created by *bagrus*, and at what stage the various rules intersect. The *gemara*'s basic architecture, as *Tosafos* articulates it, reserves the twelve-month period for the *na'arah* stage specifically; the *ketanah* has more than twelve months and the *bogeres* has twelve months counted differently — from the moment of *bagrus* itself, without the need for any explicit demand.

---

---

# Ketubot 56b

## R. Meir: Ketubah Stipula…

### Yehuda vs. Meir on Waiver

The daf opens in the middle of a discussion about the respective positions of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir regarding whether the obligations of the *ketubah* can be modified. The prior context established that Rabbi Yehuda allows a woman to be *mochel* — to waive — part of the *ketubah*, so that effectively the operative amount falls below the standard 200 *zuz* for a *betulah* or 100 for an *almanah*. However, Rabbi Yehuda does not permit the amount to be stipulated as less than those figures from the outset. The *Gemara* had asked: why not? He could say that one is permitted to be *matneh al mah she-katuv ba-Torah* — to modify the parameters of the monetary aspects of biblical obligations of *kiddushin*, such as *shear* and *kesut* (though not *onah*). So why can he not modify a rabbinic one? Rabbi Yehuda's answer is that the rabbis wanted to strengthen the rabbinic institution of the *ketubah* — *asu chizuk l'divreihem yoter mishel Torah* — and therefore the base obligation must remain in place, even if the monetary obligations of the Torah could otherwise be modified. The woman must start with 200 or 100; only afterwards may she be *mochel*.

The *Gemara* then raises a challenge from the case of donkey drivers (*chamarin*): we were taught in the *Mishnah* that if merchants come to a city and one says *sheli chadash v'shel chaveirai yashan* — mine is new grain (and therefore inferior) and my friend's is old — or that his goods are untithed while his companion's are *metukan* with *terumos u'maasros* separated, they are not believed (*einam ne'emanin*). But Rabbi Yehuda says they are believed (*ne'emanin*). The issue concerns *demai* — the rabbinic concern that an *am ha'aretz* may not have separated *terumos u'maasros*. Why does Rabbi Yehuda not reinforce this rabbinic institution as he reinforces the *ketubah*?

Abaye answers: the rabbis reinforced only what was a definite (*vadai*) institution. The *ketubah* obligations are definite, and therefore the rabbis said they cannot be directly modified. The concern about *terumos u'maasros* in the case of *demai*, however, is inherently based on doubt — it is only a *safek* — and something that is fundamentally weaker in that way was not reinforced in the same fashion. Rava adds a further point: it is not merely that *demai* is based on doubt in general, but specifically *demai* has many leniencies because in principle we actually believe that *terumos u'maasros* were separated. Given that, the rabbis did not bother reinforcing it.

The bottom line of this section is that Rabbi Yehuda is less strict than Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Meir does not allow the woman to be *mochel* any part of the *ketubah* at all — the effective obligation for Rabbi Meir must be the full 200 or 100. Rabbi Yehuda allows a woman to be *mochel* after the fact but does not allow the amount to be modified at the outset, because even though he permits modification of the biblical monetary obligations of marriage, this rabbinic one he wishes to reinforce, and therefore the base obligation must stand.

### Stipulation Nullity Theo…

Turning to Rabbi Meir's position as it appears in the *Mishnah* — *kol hapocheis l'betulah mi'masayim u'l'almanah mi'maneh harei zu biat zenut* — one might initially have understood Rabbi Meir as saying that you cannot effectively make the obligation less, and that continuing to live in such a marital state constitutes something closer to *zenut* than to marriage. The whole weight of marriage — the *ketubah*, the reciprocal obligations and protections — is what gives *nissu'in* its character. So the simple reading of Rabbi Meir is that you may have lowered the amount but you transgress.

The *Gemara*, however, takes this one step further. From the word *hapocheis* — one who is *attempting* to reduce the amount — the *Gemara* infers *afilu b'tnai*, even if you explicitly stipulate that it should be less. *Alma kasavar tnai batel* — it seems that Rabbi Meir holds the stipulation itself is void. This is not a simple inference from the *Mishnah*, as the *Gemara* acknowledges and *Tosafos* addresses at length, but the *Gemara* assumes it as Rabbi Meir's position: the attempt to make the *ketubah* less does not succeed. The woman retains the full amount; *v'is lei* — she still has her 200.

### Biat Zenut Analysis

But if the stipulation is void and the woman still has the full amount in principle, how can the situation constitute *biat zenut*? The *Gemara* answers: *ve'cheivan de'amar lah leis lich ela maneh* — since the husband told her that she only has 100, *lo samcha daatah* — her sense of security is not established. Even though in truth and in law she has 200, her subjective sense that she is unprotected — because she believes she only has 100 — is sufficient to create *biat zenut*. *V'hava lah biatah biat zenut* — and therefore the relations take on the character of *zenut*. This is a striking position: even a legally full *ketubah* does not prevent the designation of *biat zenut* when the woman subjectively believes she lacks protection.

### Ketubah d'Oraisa

The *Gemara* then asks why the stipulation is void at all. It notes that we know Rabbi Meir holds that if you try to stipulate against a Torah obligation, even a financial one, the condition is *batel* — but *habderabbanan tnai kayyam* — specifically against a rabbinic obligation, an explicit stipulation would be binding. So why can you not stipulate against the *ketubah*? Could one not simply say that Rabbi Meir is reinforcing the *ketubah* institution in a special way, given that the stakes are marriage and *biat zenut*?

The *Gemara* does not take that route. Rather than treating the *ketubah* as uniquely protected among rabbinic enactments, the *Gemara* says: *kasavar Rabbi Meir ketubah de'Oraisa* — Rabbi Meir may actually hold that the *ketubah* is a biblical obligation. That debate appeared earlier in the *masechet*. And since it is biblical, one cannot stipulate against it — *matneh al mah she-katuv ba-Torah* — and therefore the stipulation is void. This is a significant *chiddush*. Rabbi Meir, who in the *Mishnah* seems merely to be saying that you transgress by effectively lowering the amount, is reinterpreted by the *Gemara* to mean that the attempt does not even succeed — because the *ketubah* is *d'Oraisa*, and it is impossible to stipulate against a biblical financial obligation. And even though the amount therefore remains in full, the situation is still *biat zenut* because the woman believes otherwise.

---

## Three Positions: Stipula…

### R. Yosi: Allowed

A *baraisa* now presents all three positions. Rabbi Meir says: *kol hapocheis l'besulah mi'masayim u'l'almanah mi'maneh harei zu biat zenut* — any attempt to lower the amount from the base is *biat zenut*. Rabbi Yosi says *rashai* — it is permitted. Rabbi Yosi goes one step further than Rabbi Yehuda: not only may the woman be *mochel* after starting with the base amount, but the parties may stipulate from the outset for a lesser amount.

### R. Yehuda: Waiver Method

Rabbi Yehuda occupies the middle position. *Rotzeh koseiv l'vesulah shtar shel masayim v'hi koseves lo hikkabalti mimcha maneh* — the husband writes a *ketubah* for 200 and she writes a receipt acknowledging she has received 100. For an *almanah*, he writes 100 and she writes that she received 50. So Rabbi Yehuda requires the full base amount to be the starting point, but then permits the woman to effectively reduce it through a receipt — an indirect *mechilah* rather than a direct stipulation.

### R. Meir: Stipulation Void

Rabbi Meir's position remains as analyzed above: the stipulation fails entirely, and even the attempt to lower the amount creates *biat zenut*. The *Gemara* now asks how Rabbi Yosi — who showed himself so protective of the woman's interests, as we are about to see — could permit a lesser amount from the outset.

---

## Chattel Designation Disp…

### Chattel Prohibition

The *Gemara* introduces a *braisa*: *ein osin kesubas ishah mitaltlin mipnei tikkun ha-olam* — you do not designate *metaltalim*, movable property — chattel — as the lien on which the *ketubah* will be collected, for the sake of the benefit of society (*tikkun ha-olam*). This is not a reduction of the woman's liens on real estate — the standard formulation *kol nichasai achrayin*, which is a *tenai beit din*, remains — but rather a prohibition on affirmatively designating specific movable property as the designated source of collection. The *tikkun ha-olam* reason: chattel can be destroyed, lose value, or be lost, whereas real estate cannot be stolen away. If you designate only the Wedgwood China and it breaks, the woman is left with nothing.

### R. Yosi: Liability Insuf…

Rabbi Yosi objects: *v'chi mah tikkun ha-olam yesh bazeh* — what societal benefit is served by this? *Vehalo ein kesuvos u'pochsin* — does not the value of such property diminish? At first glance this seems to simply restate what the *Tanna Kamma* already said. The *Gemara* observes: *Tanna Kamma nami ein osin ka'amar* — the *Tanna Kamma* also said you are not allowed to make such a designation. So what precisely is their dispute?

### Unilateral vs. Mutual

The *Gemara* resolves this: the *braisa* must be reread as follows. *Bamah devarim amurim* — when is the designation of chattel as *ketubah* lien prohibited? *Beshelo kibel alav achrayus* — when the husband does not accept liability for its value, meaning the woman can only collect from the chattel itself. In such a case, if it breaks she is left with nothing. But *aval kibel alav achrayus* — if the husband backs it up by accepting personal liability for its worth even if the chattel is destroyed — then *osin*, you are allowed to designate it.

Rabbi Yosi then comes along and says: that is not sufficient protection. *Ki kibel alav achrayus amai osin* — even if you accept liability for breakage, why should that solve the problem? *Vehalo ein kesuvos u'pochsin* — the chattel may depreciate in value without breaking. Even if the China is intact when she comes to collect, it may be worth far less than her *ketubah* amount. So Rabbi Yosi holds that accepting liability for breakage does not fully protect the woman's interests when the value of the chattel itself may have declined.

The *Gemara* then uses this to ask the obvious question: if Rabbi Yosi is so concerned to protect the woman's interests that he objects even to a scenario where the husband accepts liability for breakage, how can he permit an outright stipulation for a lesser amount? The *Gemara* answers: *hachi hashta* — what kind of comparison is that? In the chattel case, *hasam lo yade'ah detimchol* — the woman does not know she is conceding. She is demanding her full 200 and the husband is unilaterally setting up a scenario in which she might not be able to collect the full amount. That is one-sided and impermissible. But in our case, *yada'ah v'kamachla* — she knew about it and agreed to it. She was a party to the stipulation from the outset. Rabbi Yosi therefore holds that if she agrees, a lesser amount is permissible. His objection in the chattel case applies only to a unilateral arrangement that compromises her interests without her knowledge.

---

## Lost Ketubah Case

### Sister of Rami: Lost Doc

The *Gemara* now presents a practical case. The sister of Rami bar Chama was married to Rabbi Avya. *Irkas kesuvtasa* — her *ketubah* document was lost. Not a divorce situation — simply the physical document had been misplaced. This scenario, as a practical matter, arises not infrequently: a couple returns from a wedding and cannot locate the *ketubah*, or a couple married for twenty or thirty years moves and cannot find the document, or the signatures on a *ketubah* hanging on the wall have faded to illegibility. In such cases one must write a substitute *ketubah*, known as a *ketubah d'irkasa* — *irkas* being the Aramaic for "lost" — typically signed by the original witnesses, who testify that they originally signed a *ketubah*, that it was lost, and that this document reflects its contents.

### Rav Yosef's Citation

They came before Rav Yosef. He said to them: *hachi amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel — zu divrei Rebbi Meir* — the principle that it is *biat zenut* to live together without proper *ketubah* protection is the position of Rabbi Meir alone. *Aval Chachamim omrim* — but the sages say *masha adam im ishto shtayim v'shalosh shanim belo kesuvah* — one can live with his wife for two or three years without a written substitute *ketubah*. There is no great urgency.

One might ask: who ever said Rabbi Meir would prohibit remaining together when the document is merely lost? The full amount is still owed, since we have already taught that even without a physical document the obligation exists. But the *Gemara* reasonably understands that just as the woman's subjective belief that she has only 100 when in fact she has 200 is sufficient to create *biat zenut*, so too the absence of the physical document is enough to create in her a subjective sense of vulnerability — she feels unprotected, she lacks proof that the debt exists, she cannot prevent him from claiming it was already paid. That subjective unease is, for Rabbi Meir, enough to constitute *biat zenut*.

### Sages: No Rush

The sages, however, hold that the mere absence of a document does not rise to that level. The underlying obligation remains intact and the woman is protected in substance even without the paper, so there is no prohibition against continuing to live together. There is no great rush.

### Abaye: Rule Like R. Meir

Abaye then interjects: *v'ha'amar Rav Nachman amar Shmuel halacha k'Rebbi Meir bigzeirotav* — but we have a ruling that we follow Rabbi Meir in his *gezeirot*, his edicts. It is noteworthy that the *Gemara* describes this as a *gezeirah*. Normally *gezeirot* are safeguards against transgression of some other prohibition. Here the *Gemara* uses the term to describe Rabbi Meir's protective stance toward the institution of marriage — a *gezeirah* in the sense of safeguarding the integrity and proper protections of the marital relationship. Since we rule like Rabbi Meir in his *gezeirot*, Abaye concludes: *zil katuv la* — go write her a substitute *ketubah*. So it sounds as though we rule like Rabbi Meir in this case.

### Modern Practice

What is the practical *halacha*? In principle, the answer follows Rabbi Meir — one should write a substitute *ketubah* as quickly as possible. However, the Rema notes that in the present day, given *takanas Rabbeinu Gershom* — the enactment that a husband cannot divorce his wife against her will — the underlying concern that generates *biat zenut* in Rabbi Meir's framework is substantially mitigated. The *biat zenut* concern arises because the woman feels that she is not truly protected: she could be casually divorced at any moment, and without the document she cannot prevent that or prove her claim. But now that she cannot be divorced without her consent, she knows she is protected even without the physical *ketubah*. The Rema therefore holds it is not *biat zenut* in such a case today. Nevertheless, one should take care of writing the replacement *ketubah* as promptly as possible; we do not tell the couple to cease living together until it is produced.

A question arises regarding *Sefardim*, who in various ways have adopted the spirit of *takanas Rabbeinu Gershom*, though the precise application is a matter that requires further analysis.

A related question: if one is writing a substitute *ketubah* with the same original witnesses, why not simply write the identical document? The answer is that writing an identical document on the same date creates a concern that the woman may possess two equivalent documents and attempt to collect twice. The *ketubah d'irkasa* therefore uses a different formulation that explicitly records that the original was lost — thereby preventing double collection, since once the husband has paid and the document is surrendered, no second claim can be made.

---

## Techilla vs. Sof Dispute

### Rav Dimi: Debate Techilla

The *Gemara* now turns to a question about the scope of the three-way debate — in particular the debate between Rabbi Yosi, who allows a lesser amount, and Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir, who do not. When exactly does the debate apply?

When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he reported in the name of Rav Shimon ben Pazi, in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, in the name of Bar Kappara: *machlokes b'techilla* — the debate applies only at the outset of the wedding. *Aval besof divrei hakol eina mocheles* — but at the end, everyone agrees that the amount cannot be changed. The question of what "the beginning" and "the end" refer to will require clarification, but the initial formulation is: there is a *machlokes* before a certain point, and universal agreement after another point.

### R. Yochanan: Both Cases

Rabbi Yochanan says: *bein b'zo u'vein b'zo machlokes* — they debate in both cases, whether at the beginning or at the end.

### R. Abbahu: Harmonization

Rabbi Abbahu then clarifies: it was explained to him directly from Rabbi Yochanan that Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi are not actually disagreeing. When Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says the *machlokes* is *b'techilla* — at the beginning — he means *techillas chuppah*, before the *chuppah*. And when he says that everyone agrees at the end, he means *sof biah*, after they have actually had relations. And when Rabbi Yochanan says the *machlokes* applies to both cases — beginning and end — he means *techillas chuppah* (before the *chuppah*) and *sof chuppah* (at the *chuppah* but before *biah*). So both authorities agree that the *machlokes* spans everything up through the *chuppah*, and that once *biah* has occurred, everyone agrees the amount cannot be changed. On this reading, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yochanan are saying the same thing, simply using different terminology for adjacent points on the timeline.

### Ravin: Debate Sof

When Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael, he had the opposite version of the same tradition — transmitted in the same chain, Rav Shimon ben Pazi, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, Bar Kappara — but with inverted positions. According to Ravin's version, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said *machlokes l'vsof* — the debate is only at the end. *Aval b'techilla divrei hakol mocheles* — but at the outset, everyone agrees the amount can be changed. Rabbi Yochanan in this version still says *bein b'zo u'vein b'zo machlokes* — they debate in both cases.

Rabbi Abbahu again harmonizes the two: when Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says the *machlokes* is *l'vsof* he means *sof chuppah* — after the *chuppah* but before *biah*. And when he says everyone agrees at the beginning, he means *techillas chuppah*, before the *chuppah*. And when Rabbi Yochanan says they debate both, he means *techillas biah* — the beginning of *biah*, i.e., after the *chuppah* — and *sof biah*, after relations. So this version has everyone agreeing that before the *chuppah* the amount can be changed, and everyone agreeing that after *biah* it cannot — and the entire *machlokes* falling in the middle zone between *chuppah* and *biah*. This is the mirror image of the green version: there, the *machlokes* covered everything before *biah*; here, the *machlokes* is confined to the interval between *chuppah* and *biah*.

### Rav Pappa: Sevara Best

Rav Pappa concludes the sugya with a methodological observation. Had Rabbi Abbahu not told us that Rabbi Yochanan himself said that he and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi were not really disagreeing, Rav Pappa says he would have preferred to read it differently: he would have said that Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi genuinely disagree — each one staking out a different position about where the *machlokes* of the *Tannaim* logically belongs — while the two transmissions of Rav Dimi and Ravin do not actually conflict. In that alternative reading, *sof* in Ravin's version equals *sof chuppah* and *techilla* in Rav Dimi's version equals *techillas biah*, making the two transmissions equivalent.

The *Gemara* asks: what difference does it make which debate we collapse? Rav Pappa's preference rests on a principle: *d'pligi trei amorai ta'ama d'nafshaihu v'lo pligi trei amorai aliba d'chad amora* — it is preferable to say that two *Amoraim* are arguing based on their own reasoning and analysis rather than to say that two *Amoraim* are disputing what a third *Amora* actually said. When Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi debate where the *machlokes* logically occurs, they are disagreeing about *sevara* — about what makes sense, about in which domain the debate is most coherent. That is the natural stuff of the *Shas*. But if we instead say Rav Dimi and Ravin are reporting different versions of what Rabbi Yochanan said, we are implying that one of them got it wrong — that there is an error in transmission. It is always better, if we must reduce one dispute, to do so by harmonizing transmissions than by eliminating a genuine debate in *sevara*.

---

## Twelve-Month Waiting Per…

### Mishnah: 12 vs. 30 Days

A new *Mishnah* opens: *notnin l'betulah shneim asar chodesh mishetav'ah ha-ba'al l'farnos et atzmah* — we give a *betulah* twelve months from the time that the husband demands to begin living together to prepare herself for marriage. This is not twelve months from the time of *kiddushin*, but from the time the husband says he is ready to proceed to *nissu'in*. She is entitled to use that time to prepare her trousseau. Similarly, *u'keshem shenotnin l'ishah kach notnin l'ish* — just as she is given time to prepare, so too he is given time to prepare the home if he needs it. And *v'almanah shloshim yom* — for a second marriage, only thirty days are required, since a widow is more independent and the wedding would not involve the same elaborate preparation.

*Higi'a zman v'lo nisu* — once the period expires and they are not yet married, *ochelet mishelo* — he must now begin supporting her financially. Once *nissu'in* should have occurred and it has not, his obligation of *mezonot* begins.

### Support Begins

The onset of this financial obligation is tied directly to the expiration of the waiting period. From that point forward, she eats from his account, regardless of who bears responsibility for the delay — a question addressed at the beginning of the *masechet* but not the focus here.

### Terumah Eligibility

*V'ochelet b'terumah* — if he is a *kohen*, he may now feed her *terumah*, since the wife of a *kohen* is entitled to eat *terumah* even before *nissu'in*, even at the stage of *erusin*. This ruling conveys two things: first, from the laws of *terumah*, she is permitted to eat it even as a mere *arusah* to a *kohen*; and second, in satisfying his obligation of *mezonot*, he may discharge it by providing *terumah*, which is cheaper.

### Terumah Dispute

Rabbi Tarfon says he may give her the entire amount in *terumah*. Rabbi Akiva disagrees: *mechtzah chullin u'mechtzah terumah* — half must be ordinary *chullin*. The reason is that roughly half the month — and more, given *chumras Rabbi Zeira* — she is *tme'ah* as a *niddah* and therefore cannot eat *terumah*. It is therefore unfair to give her only *terumah* that she will have to sell at a loss to obtain *chullin* she can actually consume when she is *tme'ah*. He must provide at least half as *chullin*, food she can eat at all times.

### Yavam Exception

*Ha-yavam eino ma'achil b'terumah* — the case of the *yavam* is different. If a *kohen* was married and died, and now his brother the *kohen* stands as *yavam* and she is *shomeres yavam*, she cannot eat *terumah* even after twelve months of waiting. There is no twelve-month clock after which she gains *terumah* eligibility; as long as she is awaiting *yibbum*, she does not eat *terumah*.

### Split Service

The *Mishnah* then covers cases where the twelve-month period is split between time in front of the husband and time in front of the *yavam*. If she spent six months in front of the husband (after he said it was time to proceed) and six months awaiting the *yavam*, she does not eat *terumah*. Even if eleven months and twenty-nine days were in front of the husband and one day awaiting the *yavam*, or vice versa — in all such mixed cases, *einah ochelet b'terumah*. Rashi notes that the last scenario — almost all the time in front of the *yavam* — is in a sense obvious, since the *Mishnah* already indicated that even years of waiting for *yibbum* do not generate *terumah* eligibility. Tomorrow's daf will examine the *Tosafos* position on this.

---

## No Terumah Until Chuppah

### Original Teaching

*Zu mishnah rishonah* — that was the first, original teaching. The term *mishnah rishonah* is significant: it refers to earlier collections of *mishnayot* that, even when subsequently revised, were not discarded. The *Gemara*'s phrase *mishnah rishonah lo zazah mimkomah* — the original *Mishnah* has not moved from its place — reflects the principle that earlier texts are preserved, not silently replaced by later rulings.

### Later Restriction

*Beit din shel achareihem amru* — the later *beit din* then ruled: *ein ha'ishah ochelet b'terumah ad shetikanes l'chuppah* — a woman does not eat *terumah* until she has entered the *chuppah*, meaning until *nissu'in* has actually taken place. This is actually to the woman's detriment in terms of the husband's food bill — since he must now provide all *chullin* during the waiting period rather than satisfying his obligation with cheaper *terumah* — and it prevents the woman from giving *terumah* to her family. The source for the twelve-month right is derived from the verse in which the family of Rivkah says *teshev hana'arah itanu yamim o asor* — let the girl remain with us for "days" or ten. *Yamim* unqualified, as shown through a *gezeirah shavah* from *yamim tihyeh ge'ulato* (the year of redemption for a house in a walled city), means a full year. And "ten" — in context, ten months rather than ten days, paralleling the year reduced by two months. The *Gemara* thus derives that there is an established right to request a full year.

---

## Postponement Rights: Ket…

### Ketanah: Can Postpone

Rabbi Zeira cites a *baraisa*: *ketannah bein hi uvein aviha yecholim l'akeiv* — while the girl is still a *ketannah* — a minor — either she or her father can prevent the *nissu'in* from proceeding. This introduces a new principle: the twelve-month framework applies once the woman is past minority; as long as she is a *ketannah*, she and her father can in principle delay indefinitely.

### Father's Right Question

The *Gemara* asks: *bishlama hi matzi me'akeva* — it is understandable that she can postpone, since she is the one being married. *Ella aviha* — but the father: *ei hi nicha lah* — if she herself wants to proceed to *nissu'in* after *kiddushin* has already occurred, *mai nafka lei minnah* — what is the father's legitimate claim to stand in the way?

### Father's Concern Logic

The *Gemara* answers: *sevar* — the father reasons as follows. *Hashta lo yade'ah* — she is young, perhaps seven years old, and does not know what she is agreeing to. *Lemachar mimreda* — tomorrow, once married, she will be too young and will rebel against the marriage, reject her husband. *V'nafkah* — she will leave or be divorced. *V'asya v'nafala alavei* — and she will fall back on him, become his responsibility once again. This is a striking *Gemara*: the more obvious reason for the father's right to delay is that as long as she remains at home before *nissu'in*, he retains certain entitlements to her labor and earnings. The *Gemara*, however, deliberately grounds the father's right in a concern internal to the marriage itself — that he legitimately believes the *nissu'in* is premature and will ultimately fail, and that he will bear the consequences. The other reason — his financial interest in her remaining home — is not given standing here as a sufficient justification.

### R. Abba: No Nissuin

Rabbi Abba bar Levi states explicitly: *ein poskin al ha-ketannah lehasi'ah keshehi ketannah* — one does not make an arrangement to perform *nissu'in* with a *ketannah* while she is still a *ketannah*. This goes one step beyond the prior ruling. First, the *Gemara* established that she and her father have the right to prevent it — which already signals disapproval. Now it states affirmatively that one should not do it. *Aval poskin al ha-ketannah lehasi'ah keshehi gedolah* — one may, however, arrange while she is a *ketannah* that the *nissu'in* will take place once she reaches adulthood, once she is a *na'arah* after *Bat Mitzvah*.

This is worth pausing over. People are rightly troubled when confronted with *kiddushei ketannah* — the betrothal of a minor. It is worth noting that *kiddushin* alone does not involve cohabitation; the sexual dimension of marriage begins only with *nissu'in*. And the *Gemara* here is clearly discouraging *nissu'in* during minority. Once she reaches *Bat Mitzvah*, the situation is different — and while that too may strike modern sensibilities as troubling, the *Gemara* is at least insisting that *nissu'in* not precede that threshold.

### Psychological Concern

The *Gemara* then asks: is it not obvious that one may arrange while she is still a *ketannah* for *nissu'in* to take place after she grows up? What is the *chiddush*? The *Gemara* answers: one might have thought that even this should be prohibited — *dilma milai pachda mehashta v'chalsha* — that by telling an eleven-year-old that she will be married after her *Bat Mitzvah*, one fills her with fear now, and she grows despondent or psychologically burdened. The *Gemara* therefore had to teach that we are not concerned about this — *kamashma lan* — and such advance planning is permitted.

---

## Bogeret Timing: 12 Months

### Rav Huna: 30 Days

Rav Huna rules: *bogra yom echad veniskadsha notnin lah shloshim yom k'almanah* — if a woman hits *bagrus* — majority at twelve and a half — and then has *kiddushin*, she is given only thirty days, not twelve months, in which to prepare for *nissu'in*.

### Baraisa: 12 Months

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this from a *baraisa*: *bogeret harei hi k'tav'uha* — when a woman hits *bagrus*, it is as if one of the parties has made a *tvi'ah*, a demand to proceed to *nissu'in*. One might read this as: it is like the *tvi'ah* of a *betulah* — twelve months. *Mai lav k'tav'uha d'betulah* — does that not mean twelve months, as when a *betulah* is *tavu'ah*? The *Gemara* responds: *la, k'tav'uha d'almanah* — no, it is like the *tvi'ah* made of a widow, thirty days. But a further *baraisa* is cited: *bogeret sheshahata shneim asar chodesh* — a woman who has been a *bogeret* for twelve months. Rabbi Eliezer says that since the husband is now obligated in *mezonot*, he may annul her vows. Setting aside the question of vow annulment, the implication of this *baraisa* is clear: twelve months after *bagrus* he is obligated in *mezonot* — meaning the clock runs for twelve months, not thirty days. This directly contradicts Rav Huna.

The *Gemara* attempts to adjust the text: *eima bogeret v'sheshahata shneim asar chodesh* — read it as a case of a *bogeret* combined with a separate twelve-month period, not twelve months of *bagrus*. But this is acknowledged as far-fetched, *v'lo pshat*, and the *Gemara* moves on. A further *baraisa* settles the matter explicitly: *hama'ares et ha-betulah* — one who betroths a *betulah* — whether the husband demanded and she postponed, giving her twelve months, or whether she demanded and he postponed, giving him twelve months, *notnin lah shneim asar chodesh misha'as tvi'ah* — twelve months from the time of the demand. *Aval lo misha'as erusin* — not from the time of *erusin* itself, but from the moment one side says it is time to proceed. *U'vogeret harei hi k'tav'uha* — and a *bogeret* is treated as if there has been a *tvi'ah*. *Bogra yom echad veniskadsha notnin lah shneim asar chodesh* — she hit *bagrus* one day and then had *kiddushin*: she is given twelve months. This explicitly refutes Rav Huna. *Tyuvta d'Rav Huna tyuvta* — a full contradiction of Rav Huna's position.

### Rav Pappa Resolution

Rav Pappa then resolves the apparent tension: *bogeres she'avru aleha shneim asar chodesh b'vagrus v'niskadshah* — if a woman is already a year into *bagrus* before *kiddushin* — she is the ripe old age of thirteen and a half — and then has *kiddushin*, she is given only thirty days. At that point the clock has long been running and one cannot give her a full additional year. The scenario in which a full twelve months applies is when she hits *bagrus* and then promptly has *kiddushin*; but if *bagrus* predates *kiddushin* by a year, the thirty-day rule applies.

### Tosafot Synthesis

*Tosafos* observes a broader structural point about the timeline. If a *ketannah* can postpone indefinitely, and a *bogeret* triggers the clock at *bagrus* itself, then the twelve-month scenario of the *Mishnah* applies specifically to the period of *na'arus* — between twelve and twelve and a half. The *tvi'ah* and the twelve-month clock begin in that window. But this raises a complication: what if the twelve-month period begins while she is a *na'arah* and she becomes a *bogeret* six months into that period? *Tosafos* works through the stages — *ketannah*, *na'arah*, *bogeret* — and their interaction with the *tvi'ah* and waiting periods, a matter that requires careful analysis of when precisely she transitions between those stages relative to the demand to proceed with *nissu'in*.

---

---

# Ketubot 58

## 12-Month Wait & Terumah

### Nisuin Delay Context

The daf opens by picking up from the final sugya of 57b, which introduced the twelve-month postponement available to either party when the time arrives to move from *kiddushin* to *nisuin*. As we learned, a *katana* — a minor girl — along with her father could defer the *nisuin* throughout the period of her minority; the actual cohabitation was not meant to begin until she was at least a *naara*, twelve and a half years old. By contrast, once a woman becomes a *bogeres*, the clock begins running automatically, without any formal demand. The debate about who caused the delay — whether it was the husband's fault, the wife's fault, or no one's — was addressed on the opening daf of the tractate and is not the concern here.

What the *gemara* now addresses is this: once the twelve-month period has arrived and the parties have not yet proceeded to *nisuin*, the husband must begin paying the wife's food bills and may provide her with *terumah* as part of that support — if the husband is a *kohen*. The immediate question is on what basis she is permitted to eat *terumah* at all, given that she is still only an *arusah* and not yet a *nesu'ah*.

### Ulla: Kinyan Kaspo

Ulla teaches: *devar Torah arusah bas Yisrael ocheles biterumah* — biblically, a betrothed daughter of a *Yisrael* household is permitted to eat *terumah* from the moment of *erusin*. The source is the verse, *v'kohen ki yikneh nefesh kinyan kaspo* — "and a *kohen* who acquires a soul, the acquisition of his money" — which in its simple reading addresses a slave purchased by a *kohen*, who thereby becomes entitled to eat *terumah*. The *gemara* extends this: *v'hai nami kinyan kaspo hu* — a wife is likewise the acquisition of his money, since *kiddushin* is effected through a monetary transfer. This is the foundational teaching of the first *mishnah* in *Kiddushin*: a woman is *nikneis* through *kesef*. Accordingly, from the moment of *kiddushin*, she falls within the category of *kinyan kaspo* and is in principle entitled to eat *terumah*.

### Yerushalmi Debate

The *Yerushalmi* takes a different approach. Rather than deriving the wife's right from *kinyan kaspo*, it derives it from *beiso* — "his household." The verse speaks of the household of the *kohen* eating *terumah*, and *beiso zo ishto*, "his household — that is his wife." Since *bayis* ordinarily implies the context of *nisuin*, the *Yerushalmi* appears to hold that biblically one must wait until *nisuin*, or at least until a stage sufficiently close to it. According to this view, the arrival of the twelve-month mark — at which point there is a binding obligation to proceed with *nisuin* and the husband is already paying the food bills — constitutes a state close enough to *nisuin* to qualify as *beiso*.

The *Bavli*, by contrast, holds that even from the moment of *erusin* the wife is in principle permitted to eat *terumah* by virtue of *kinyan kaspo*. This reflects a genuine dispute between the two Talmuds: the *Bavli* requires no proximity to *nisuin* for the biblical entitlement to attach; the *Yerushalmi* does.

### Concern: Sharing

If the woman is biblically entitled to eat *terumah* from the time of *kiddushin*, why did the rabbis forbid it during that period? The *gemara* explains: *shema yimze'gu lah kos b'veit aviha v'tashkehu l'achia ul'achota* — lest they pour her a cup of *terumah* wine in her father's house and she go and give her brother and sister to drink. While she remains in her father's household, the practical danger of inadvertently sharing *terumah* with non-*kohanim* is too great, and the rabbis therefore prohibited it. Once the twelve months arrive, however, the prohibition is lifted.

The *gemara* immediately challenges: even when the twelve-month mark arrives and the wedding has been postponed, she is still not yet living with her husband — so why should we no longer be concerned that she will share with family members?

### Father's House Setup

The *gemara* answers: *hatam duchtam m'yached lah* — once the twelve-month deadline arrives, the husband will designate a separate place for her to live apart from her father's household. Even if the wedding itself has been delayed for some reason, he will set her up in a distinct residence. It is a striking assumption on the *gemara*'s part that this was so standard a social reality that it could be relied upon halachically — particularly when one considers that maintaining a third residence requires financial resources the groom may not always have.

The *gemara* then raises an analogous challenge: if a *kohen* is a hired laborer working for a non-*kohen*, should he not be permitted to bring his *terumah* food to work, lest he share it with his employer? The *gemara* dismisses the comparison: *hashta mididei safu leh* — there, the employer is the one providing the worker's food anyway; there is no realistic concern that the employer will reach for the *kohen*'s sandwich. The domestic situation of a woman still in her father's household, surrounded by family, is categorically different.

---

## Simpon & Defect

### Defect Concern

Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda offers a second, independent reason why the rabbis forbade an *arusah* from eating *terumah* even though she is biblically entitled: *mishum simpon* — because of the concern over a defect. The term *simpon*, apparently a Greek loanword, describes a material flaw in an acquisition that would render the entire transaction a *mekach ta'ut* — a sale based on a mistake. Transposing this concept from commercial law to marriage: once the couple begins to live together and becomes physically intimate, the husband may discover something about his wife that he did not know before, something so fundamental that it constitutes a *mekach ta'ut* and retroactively nullifies the *kiddushin* altogether. Were she eating *terumah* in the interim — from the time of *kiddushin* — she would have been doing so without legal basis. A contemporary example that *poskim* grapple with: if it emerges that the husband was gay and had concealed this, the entire *kiddushin* may be void from the outset as *kiddushei ta'ut*, in which case no *get* would be required. These situations have arisen in practice.

The *gemara* immediately presses: if the concern is *simpon*, how does anything change after twelve months? And more pointedly, how can we permit *terumah* after *chupah* — the actual wedding — if the couple has not yet been intimate? Perhaps we should wait until after *biah* before permitting *terumah*.

The *gemara* responds: *hatam mivdak badik lah v'hadar minasav* — before proceeding to the wedding itself, with its attendant expense and social commitment, the parties will have spent time together getting to know one another. Physical intimacy may not yet have occurred, but by the time of the *chupah*, there has been sufficient personal acquaintance that we are no longer meaningfully concerned about *bitul kiddushin*. The *gemara* concedes that this does not eliminate all risk — theoretically, something could still come to light after *biah* — but the remaining concern is diminished enough that providing for the woman outweighs it. The earlier stage, when the parties had barely met, was a categorically different situation.

### Slave Purchase Rules

The *gemara* then poses a parallel from the world of acquisition: *eved kohen she'lakacho mi'Yisrael lo yochal b'trumah mishum simpon* — should not a slave purchased by a *kohen* from a non-*kohen* be barred from eating *terumah* on account of *simpon*, lest the purchase turn out to be a *mekach ta'ut* and the slave will have eaten *terumah* retroactively without authorization?

The *gemara* answers: *simpon b'avadim leika* — the concern of *simpon* does not apply to slaves. Why not? Two principles dispose of the cases: if the alleged defect is external and visible — such as a limp or a broken limb — then *de'ee d'eilai ha kachazi leh*, the buyer could see it, and if he did not look carefully, that is his own failing; he cannot claim *ta'ut*. And if the defect is internal or not readily apparent — things that would only be visible when the slave is undressed, for instance — *l'mlacha kaba'ei*, the slave is acquired for labor; what does the buyer care about private physical characteristics that are irrelevant to the work?

### Visible vs Hidden

The *gemara* then asks: does it truly not matter what is hidden? Some hidden facts are certainly significant. For instance, if the slave turns out to be a thief, or — and here the *rishonim* disagree on the translation — a *kuvyustus*: Rashi understands this as a kidnapper; Tosafot argue that it means a dice player, a gambler. ArtScroll follows Rashi's reading. Are these not hidden defects that one could not have known about?

The *gemara* replies: *hachi hu* — these are on you. In the social reality in which the *gemara* operates, such attributes were considered something a buyer of a slave ought to anticipate. More precisely, as Rashi frames it, the buyer should have expected this; and Tosafot frames it even more squarely as a matter of buyer responsibility: these were things of public knowledge, and entering into a purchase without investigating them is the buyer's own problem. He cannot claim *mekach ta'ut* for failing to do due diligence.

### Known Defects

What then would constitute a genuine hidden defect that could undo a slave purchase? The *gemara* offers two examples: *listim mezuyan* — an armed bandit, not merely a petty thief or gambler, but a violent criminal — and *muchtav lamalchut* — one who was already registered for execution or designated as a felon by the government. These, however, also do not support a *mekach ta'ut* claim: *hanehu kala it lehu* — these are matters of public record. If the slave was wanted by the government or known to be a dangerous criminal, this was knowable information. Rashi's position is that the buyer effectively knew and accepted; Tosafot's position is that even if he did not personally know, the information was publicly available and it was his responsibility to investigate. Either way, one cannot claim to have been duped when the defect was a matter of common knowledge. The only genuine basis for *mekach ta'ut* in a slave purchase would be something that was truly unknowable and not of public record at all.

The *gemara* then draws together the two concerns — sharing with family, and *simpon* — and asks *mai beinaihu*, what practical case would depend on which rationale is operative? One such case: *kabal u'masar v'halach* — if the husband said explicitly that he accepts whatever turns out to be true about his wife, whatever condition she is in, he waives any *mekach ta'ut* claim. According to the *simpon* concern, once he has accepted the risk, she could eat *terumah* immediately from *kiddushin*. According to the concern about sharing with family, it would not help at all — she is still living in her father's house and the risk of sharing remains.

A second case: *masar v'halach* — the situation discussed earlier where the father transfers the bride to the groom's emissaries and she is in transit between the two households, no longer in her father's home but not yet in the groom's. According to the sharing concern, she can now eat *terumah* — she is out of her father's house. According to the *simpon* concern, she still cannot — the intimacy that would reveal any defect has not yet occurred.

---

## Terumah Proportions

### R. Tarfon: All

The *gemara* now turns to a different dimension of the same question: not whether the wife may eat *terumah*, but how much of her food allocation the husband may provide in the form of *terumah*. *Terumah* requires more careful handling than *chulin* — most critically, a woman in a state of *niddah* may not eat it, and *terumah* typically fetches less on the market than ordinary food. Rabbi Tarfon holds that the husband may give her *kol terumah* — her entire food allocation in the form of *terumah*.

One should note that at the time of the *mishnah*, a woman was *niddah* for approximately one week out of the month — a strict seven-day period from the onset of bleeding. The later practice of counting seven clean days, which became universal and extended the period of *niddah* to roughly one third of the month, came about only in the *gemara*'s era. At the time of the *mishnah*, then, a woman was a *niddah* for only about a quarter of the month — which makes the option of providing all *terumah* somewhat less extreme than it would later appear, though still a meaningful challenge.

Abaye clarifies the scope of the dispute: *machlokes be-vas kohen le-kohen* — the disagreement between Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva applies only when the wife comes from a *kohen* household. If she herself is a *bas kohen*, she has grown up handling *terumah*, knows its laws, understands when she must refrain from eating it and how to arrange for its conversion to *chulin* when necessary. Only in that case does Rabbi Tarfon say the husband may give her all *terumah*.

### Abaye's Limits

*Aval be-vas Yisrael le-kohen* — if the woman is a daughter of a *Yisrael* household marrying a *kohen*, then *divrei hakol mechtza chulin mechtza terumah* — everyone agrees it must be half *chulin* and half *terumah*. A woman with no prior experience of *terumah* cannot reasonably be expected to manage the full complexity of an all-*terumah* food supply — knowing when to refrain, arranging for its sale when she is *niddah*, ensuring that *terumah* temeiah is not consumed. Providing her with only half *terumah* is both more manageable and removes the *michshol* of giving her *terumah* at times when she must be eating *chulin*.

Abaye adds a second dimension: *machlokes be-arusa* — this entire dispute applies only to an *arusah* whose twelve-month deadline has arrived and whose husband is paying her food bills before the *nisuin* itself. *Aval be-nesu'ah* — if the *nisuin* has already taken place and she is living as a married woman — then again *divrei hakol mechtza chulin mechtza terumah*, everyone agrees it must be half and half.

The reason for this distinction, as Rashi explains, is tied to logistics: while she is still an *arusah* living in her father's house, the father is available to help her arrange the conversion of *terumah* to *chulin* when necessary. A *bas kohen* in her father's house has that practical infrastructure. But once she is a *nesu'ah* and is living separately from her husband — for instance, if he has gone on a business trip and is sending her food — she no longer has that support structure, and therefore even a *bas kohen* receives only half and half.

A question arises: during the weeks when she is *niddah* and cannot eat *terumah*, why should the husband be permitted to provide *terumah* at all? He has an obligation to feed her; during that period, the *terumah* is inedible. The answer implicit in these opinions is that she converts the *terumah* she cannot eat into *chulin* — selling it and purchasing ordinary food. The question of whether she can efficiently do so, and at what cost to her, drives the later opinions in the *mishnah*.

### Baraita Echo

A *baraita* is then cited — *tanya nami hachi* — and what follows is, word for word, what Abaye himself said. This raises a genuine methodological question: why was Abaye's statement needed? Why not simply quote the *baraita*?

This is part of a recognized phenomenon that scholars have noted: there exist *baraitot* in the *Bavli* that have no parallel in the *Yerushalmi* or anywhere else in *Shas*, and these *baraitot* are often word-for-word identical to the statements of an *amora*. The possibility worth considering is that either an *amora*'s statement was eventually preserved and transmitted as a *baraita*, or alternatively that the *amora* was quoting a *baraita* and the attribution shifted over time. Whatever the explanation, the phenomenon of an *amora*'s statement being immediately confirmed by a *baraita* in identical language — where that *baraita* has no independent attestation — is a recurring and noteworthy feature of the *Bavli*.

### R. Yehuda Views

Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira offers a different ratio: *shtei yadot shel terumah v'achat shel chulin* — two-thirds *terumah* and one-third *chulin*. This more closely tracks the actual calendar of her *niddah* status. At the time of the *mishnah*, a woman was *niddah* for one week out of the month — approximately one quarter. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira appears to reason that one third *chulin* provides an adequate buffer without giving her more *chulin* than strictly necessary.

Rabbi Yehuda takes yet another position: *notnin lah hakol terumah v'hi mocheret v'lokachat bi-dmei chulin* — one gives her all *terumah*, but she goes and sells it and uses the proceeds to purchase *chulin*. This sounds similar to Rabbi Tarfon's view, but Rashi identifies a crucial difference. *Terumah* does not sell at par; if *chulin* costs ten units and *terumah* sells for eight, then giving her the same nominal quantity of *terumah* as *chulin* leaves her unable to purchase the full *chulin* equivalent she needs. Rabbi Yehuda therefore holds that the husband must give her sufficient *terumah* — an augmented quantity — so that when she converts it to *chulin*, she receives the full equivalent of what she is entitled to eat. He must compensate her for the discount at which *terumah* trades.

### R.S. ben Gamliel

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel extends this logic further: *kol makom she'huzkera trumah noten lah kiflayim bachulin* — wherever *terumah* is mentioned as the currency of her food support, he gives her double the quantity in *terumah* compared to what he would give in *chulin*. The difference between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, the *gemara* explains, is *tircha* — the inconvenience and effort involved in converting *terumah* to *chulin*. Even if the monetary value could be recovered by patient dealing, the practical burden of arranging the sale, waiting for a buyer, and navigating the market must be compensated. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that the husband must give her enough of a surplus that she can convert the *terumah* quickly and without effort, rather than holding out for full market value.

---

## Yavam & Zika

### Yavam No Terumah

The *mishnah* states: *hayavam eino ma'achil b'trumah* — if the husband (a *kohen*) dies and the wife falls before the *yavam* for *yibum*, the *yavam* cannot feed her *terumah* during the period of *zika*. This applies whether the deceased husband was at the stage of *erusin* or *nisuin* — either way, the surviving brother has a *mitzvah* to perform *yibum*, and the *zika*, the legal bond that ties her to him, functions as a kind of quasi-*kiddushin*. One might have thought that since *zika* resembles *kiddushin* and since the *yavam* is in fact obligated to marry her, she should be permitted to eat *terumah* — perhaps even without waiting a further twelve months.

The *mishnah* rejects this. The *gemara* explains: *kinyan kaspo amar rachmana* — the Torah's basis for allowing a wife to eat *terumah* is *kinyan kaspo*, the acquisition through his money. The *kiddushin* of the original husband was an act of *kinyan kaspo*. The *zika* of the *yavam*, by contrast, is *kinyan d'achiv hu* — it is the *kinyan* of his brother, not his own. It does not carry the full legal force of his own *kiddushin* and therefore does not entitle her to eat *terumah* before the act of *yibum* itself.

### 6 Mo. Yavam

A further ruling: if the wife spent six months with the husband before his death and then six months with the *yavam* — or even eleven months and twenty-nine days with the husband and one additional day with the *yavam* — these periods do not combine to constitute the twelve-month threshold that would ordinarily permit *terumah* consumption.

The *gemara* notes a certain redundancy in the *mishnah*'s formulation. If eleven months and twenty-nine days with the husband himself does not suffice, it is obviously true that the same period partially spent with the *yavam* would not. The *gemara* answers: *zu v'zu v'ein tzarich lomar zu katani* — the *mishnah* employs the rhetorical device of stating both cases in ascending order, even when the second follows logically from the first.

There is a related question about the *kinyan kaspo* derivation. The verse reads *v'chol kohen ki yikneh nefesh kinyan kaspo* — and one might wonder why the *gemara* specifically emphasizes the language *kinyan kaspo* when *kiddushin* need not be performed through money; *kiddushei biah* or *kiddushei shtar* would seem equally applicable. Rashi (or Tosafot — the *shiur* notes some uncertainty in attribution) addresses this: the *gemara* highlights *kinyan kaspo* not to exclude other modes of *kiddushin*, but rather to avoid simply equating the wife with the slave under a single generic *kinyan* rule. The extra language of *kinyan kaspo* specifically addresses *kiddushin* as a distinct category of acquisition. Regardless of the mode of *kiddushin*, the underlying *halacha* would apply equally.

---

## Simpon & Defect (II)

### 12 Mo. vs Chupah

The *gemara* returns to the question of *simpon* in its broader structural context. The *mishnah* notes that there was an earlier ruling (*mishna rishona*) permitting the wife to eat *terumah* after twelve months, and a later teaching requiring her to wait until the actual *chupah*. The *gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama* — what was the reason for the later, more stringent ruling?

Ulla, or according to another version Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda, says: *mishum simpon* — the same concern over a defect leading to *bitul kiddushin* that was introduced earlier in the *sugya*. The *gemara* then asks the obvious structural question: if the concern is *simpon*, why did the earlier ruling permit *terumah* after twelve months at all? And why does the later ruling then change course and require waiting until *chupah*? The *simpon* concern is equally present at both stages.

The *gemara* now draws out the important distinction: *bishlama le-Ulla* — according to Ulla, the progression is internally coherent. Initially the only concern was that she would share *terumah* with family members. Once the twelve months arrived and he designated a separate residence for her, that concern fell away, and she was permitted to eat *terumah*. Only later did an additional concern surface — *mishum simpon* — which led to the more stringent ruling requiring her to wait until *chupah*. Two separate concerns, discovered at two separate stages, explain why the law tightened over time.

But for Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda, who said from the very beginning that the reason for withholding *terumah* was *simpon*, the question is sharp: *kemeikara mishum simpon ul'vasof mishum simpon* — the concern at the outset was *simpon*, and the concern at the end was *simpon*. What changed? Why was twelve months once considered sufficient, and then later declared insufficient?

The *gemara* answers: *ika beinaihu bdikat chutz* — the point of departure between the two rulings is the question of whether an external background check — investigating the other party through third parties and acquaintances — constitutes adequate due diligence. One sage held that *bdikat chutz shma bdika*: an external background check is a meaningful investigation, and after twelve months one could reasonably have conducted such an inquiry; we were therefore not concerned that *simpon* would follow. The other sage held that *bdikat chutz lo shma bdika*: external investigation, however thorough, cannot substitute for actually living with a person. True knowledge of a spouse only begins with cohabitation, and therefore twelve months of external investigation does not suffice to allay the *simpon* concern. Only once they have reached the stage of *chupah* — when they are on the verge of actual life together — can we say the background check has been meaningful enough.

This also explains, incidentally, why a post-discovery *simpon* claim is not defeated simply by the passage of time. The relevant question is not when the couple married but when the defect was discovered. If a husband concealed something and it came to light only years later, the *mekach ta'ut* analysis runs from the moment of discovery, not from the date of *kiddushin*. Where the husband himself was aware of the defect and concealed it, *savar v'kibel* — the principle that one who knew and said nothing implicitly accepted the condition — would not apply against the wife.

---

## Sanctify Labor

### Mishna Intro

The *gemara* now transitions to a new *mishnah*: *hamakdish ma'aseh yedei ishto* — a man declares that his wife's labor is *hekdesh*, consecrated to *hakodesh*. The *mishnah* rules: *harei zo osah v'ochelet* — she goes ahead and does her work, and eats. The consecration is ineffective. The *gemara* will now explain why.

To understand what is at stake, one must appreciate the underlying structure of the *ketubah* arrangement. The husband is obligated to provide *mezonot* — to cover his wife's food expenses. In exchange, he is entitled to *maaseh yadeha* — the proceeds of her labor. This reciprocal arrangement, however, raises the question of who is the fundamental rights-holder: is the entitlement to *mezonot* the primary right that generates the wife's obligation to hand over her earnings, or is the husband's entitlement to her labor primary, with *mezonot* established as the corresponding counterbalance?

Additionally, one must note the *mishnah*'s later teaching about *motar* — the surplus that a wife produces beyond the minimum defined work expectation. The *mishnah* will state that Rabbi Meir holds that the husband can effectively consecrate the *motar*, while Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar holds that it remains *chulin*. It is striking that the extra amount — the *motar* — is more susceptible to sanctification in Rabbi Meir's view than the core amount. The *gemara* will work out why.

The minimum expectation of *maaseh yadeha*, it should be noted, does not require the wife to hold an outside job. The later *mishnah* will spell out that work performed within the home — including household tasks and child-rearing — satisfies the obligation. There is a defined minimum output, but it is not necessarily commercial in nature.

### Rav: Woman's Right

Rav Huna says in the name of Rav: *yechola isha lomar le'ba'ala, eini nizonet v'eini osa* — a woman may say to her husband, "You need not pay my food bill, and I will not hand over the proceeds of my labor." She may, in other words, opt out of the entire reciprocal arrangement, retain her own earnings, and forgo the *mezonot* support.

This is a statement of considerable significance for how we understand the *ketubah* framework. If the husband were the primary rights-holder — the one whose entitlement to *maaseh yadeha* was the bedrock — one would expect that it is he who determines the terms and she who must comply. But Rav frames it the opposite way: she has the power to reverse the arrangement unilaterally. This strongly suggests that the *ketubah* is fundamentally constructed for her benefit, and its terms are hers to waive.

This principle has had practical legal application. In Israel, before the *Knesset* legislated in this area, organizations concerned with women's rights in the *beit din* system would arrange for the *ketubah* to include a rider — effectively an exercise of the woman's *eini nizonet v'eini osa* right — so that both spouses could then enter into a separate arrangement of shared or independently held financial interests on terms of their own choosing.

An important implication follows: since she retains the right to opt out at any time, she can equally reverse course at any time. If she loses employment and wishes to return to the *ketubah* arrangement, she may do so — because the entire framework exists in her interest, and she may invoke or waive it as her circumstances change.

### Mezonot Primary

The *gemara* explains the theoretical basis for Rav's ruling: *ki takinu rabanan mezoni, mezoni ikar* — when the rabbis established the *ketubah* arrangement, *mezonot* — the obligation to provide for her sustenance — was the primary *takana*. *U'maaseh yadeha mishum eiva* — her corresponding obligation to hand over her earnings was added only secondarily, to prevent resentment (*eiva*) from arising if he were supporting her without receiving anything in return. Since *mezonot* is primary and its purpose is her protection, she is the one who holds the power: *v'chi amra eini nizonet v'eini osa, ha'reshut b'yadah* — if she says she neither wants the sustenance nor will hand over her labor, the right is hers.

### Woman Owns Labor

The *gemara* attempts to draw support from the *mishnah* itself: *mai lav bimzonot* — the case of *hamakdish maaseh yedei ishto* must be a case where he is in fact paying the food bills, and even so, the consecration fails. Why? Because even though he is currently providing *mezonot* and receiving her labor, she retains the power to say no at any moment. Since she can at any time withdraw from the arrangement, she remains the true owner of her labor — and one cannot sanctify what one does not own. Even before she has exercised her right to withhold, the ongoing possibility of her doing so means that the earnings are fundamentally hers, not his.

The *gemara* deflects this proof: *lav bimzonot* — no, the *mishnah* may be speaking of a case where he is *not* paying the food bills. Since he is not fulfilling his *mezonot* obligation, she is under no obligation to hand over her earnings, and therefore it is entirely unsurprising that he cannot consecrate them.

### Resh Lakish View

Resh Lakish disputes the entire framework of Rav Huna citing Rav. Resh Lakish holds: *lo teima ta'amei de-Rabbi Meir mishum dekasavar adam makdish davar shelo ba l'olam* — do not say that Rabbi Meir permits sanctification of the *motar* because he holds, characteristically, that one may sanctify things that have not yet come into existence. Rather, says Resh Lakish, the reason is different and the underlying model is entirely different: *mi-tokh she-yakhol l'kofah l'maaseh yadeha* — since the husband can *compel* his wife to work, *na'aseh ke-omer lah yikdeshu yadekh l'oseihem* — it is as though he said, "Let your hands be consecrated to their Maker."

The implication is fundamental. In Resh Lakish's model, the husband is the *ba'al habayit* — he is in control. The wife *cannot* say no. Because he can coerce her labor, he has a present, real monetary ownership in her labor capacity — not merely in future earnings that do not yet exist, but in the very ownership interest in her hands, right now. When he declares *hekdesh*, he is not sanctifying something that does not exist (*davar shelo ba l'olam*); he is sanctifying a present ownership right that he already holds.

This stands in direct opposition to Rav's view. For Rav, she is the *ba'alat habayit*; for Resh Lakish, he is the *ba'al habayit*. For Rav, she can say no; for Resh Lakish, she cannot. And because Resh Lakish holds that the husband has a genuine present ownership in her labor, the act of *hekdesh* is legally coherent — it sanctifies something he truly owns right now.

### R. Meir: Motar

This still leaves open the question raised by the *mishnah* itself: why can Rabbi Meir consecrate the *motar* — the surplus — but not the core *maaseh yadeha*? The *gemara* explains the structure this way: the core amount of *maaseh yadeha* is tied to the *mezonot* arrangement. He is obligated to feed her; her obligation to produce the minimum is the quid pro quo. His right to the core amount is entirely contingent on his fulfilling the *mezonot* obligation, and that contingency makes it insufficiently "his" to consecrate with full legal effect. But the *motar* — what she produces beyond that minimum — is tied not to *mezonot* but to the pin money (*ma'ah sela*) he gives her as discretionary spending. That amount is genuinely and independently his — it is not conditioned on the primary *mezonot* exchange in the same way — and therefore he can consecrate it.

### Future Things

The *gemara* then notes that Resh Lakish's explanation — that Rabbi Meir sanctifies his present ownership in her hands rather than future earnings — carries an implicit assumption: that Rabbi Meir holds one cannot sanctify *davar shelo ba l'olam*. But this is surprising, because Rabbi Meir is elsewhere among the *tannaim* who are most permissive on this very issue.

The *gemara* proves the point from a *baraita*: *ha-omer le-ishah harei at mekudeshet li le-akhar she-etgayer* — if a man says to a woman, "You are betrothed to me after I convert," or "after you convert," or "after I am freed from slavery," or "after your husband dies," or "after your sister dies," or "after your *yavam* performs *chalitzah* for you" — *Rabbi Meir omer mekudeshet* — Rabbi Meir holds that such a conditional *kiddushin* is valid. This is structurally analogous to *davar shelo ba l'olam*, and Rabbi Meir accepts it.

The *gemara* resolves: *me-hahu in* — yes, from that *baraita* one can prove that Rabbi Meir holds one may sanctify things that do not yet exist, and that could theoretically be the explanation for the *mishnah* as well. *Me-ha leika le-mishma minnah* — but from our *mishnah* alone, one cannot draw that conclusion. The *mishnah* is equally explicable on Resh Lakish's model — that Rabbi Meir is sanctifying a present ownership right in the wife's hands, rather than future produce. The *mishnah* therefore remains ambiguous between the two positions, and the deeper dispute — whether she is the *ba'alat habayit* who can say no, or he is the *ba'al habayit* who can compel — remains the animating question underlying the entire chapter.

---

---

# Ketubot 59

## Wife's Labor Ownership

### Intro: Labor Ownership

The daf opens by returning to a discussion begun at the bottom of 58b. The *mishnah* establishes that if a husband attempts to sanctify the labor of his wife's hands, the act is void. The *gemara* explored two distinct reasons for this ruling, both of which turn on the foundational question: who is fundamentally the owner of the wife's labor?

### Rashi vs. Tosafot

Two approaches emerge. Rashi understands that since the wife retains the power to refuse her husband's support — opting out of the arrangement by which he feeds her in exchange for her labor — she is considered the fundamental owner, and his ownership never fully takes hold, even when she does not in fact refuse. Tosafot, by contrast, limits this reasoning: only when she actually refuses to accept support from him does ownership revert to her; so long as the arrangement is operative, he controls her labor. A second approach altogether frames the case differently — it is the husband who is in control, but who has chosen to forfeit his claim by failing to provide for her, and it is this forfeiture that strips him of entitlement.

### Motar: Meir vs. Yochanan

The closing section of the *mishnah* presents a dispute regarding the *motar* — the amount that the wife produces beyond the minimum she is obligated to provide. Rabbi Meir holds that if the husband sanctifies this excess, it is *kadosh*; Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar holds it is not. The *gemara* now turns to examine what precisely underlies this disagreement.

---

## Rav & Shmuel View

### After Death Kiddushin

Rav and Shmuel, speaking in tandem, offer a striking reading of Rabbi Meir's position. They interpret *motar le-achar misah kadosh*: the *kiddushin* takes effect only after the wife dies. Their reasoning reconstructs the case as one in which the husband is not, in fact, entitled to the *motar* during the wife's lifetime — the scenario being that he has failed to fulfill one of his obligations, thereby forfeiting his right to her excess labor. The husband will eventually come into possession of those earnings only when he inherits them after her death. At that point, the sanctification he declared during her lifetime finally takes effect, retroactively, once the property enters his domain.

This reading renders Rabbi Meir's position nearly vacuous as a statement about *motar* per se. The real issue is not who owns the excess labor but whether one can sanctify something before it comes into one's possession.

### Davar Shelo Ba L'olam

Under this framework, the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar reduces entirely to a question of *davar shelo ba l'olam* — whether a person can sanctify something that has not yet entered the world or entered his ownership. Rabbi Meir holds that such a sanctification can take effect retroactively; Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar holds it cannot. The question of who owns the *motar* is, on this reading, a side condition of the case rather than the core of the debate.

---

## Rav Adda: Alive Kiddushin

### Motar Sanctified Alive

Rav Adda bar Abba dissents: *motar mechayim kadosh* — the *motar* is sanctified even during the wife's lifetime. On his reading, the *mishnah* is dealing with a case where the husband is in fact entitled to the *motar*, and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar is genuinely about who owns the excess labor.

### Forfeiture Conditions

The *gemara* then asks: precisely in which scenario does the husband forfeit his right to the *motar*? It frames the question by examining the system of reciprocal obligations. He is paying the *mezonot* — the regular food bill — but not the *ma'ah kesef*, the fixed weekly pin money he is obligated to provide for her personal use. The question becomes whether, in that configuration, he retains rights to the *motar* or not, and this is what the Tannaitic dispute is about.

---

## Correspondence Debate

### Common-to-Common Logic

The *gemara* now articulates the underlying structural question: what exchange corresponds to what? One view holds *midi deshachich mimidi deshachich* — common things correspond to common things. The *mezonot*, the food bill, is a ubiquitous expense and a constant presence in every household; similarly, the wife's baseline labor — the minimum she is obligated to produce — is a regular, ever-present obligation. These two common quantities therefore correspond to one another: the food bill is the exchange for the minimum *ma'aseh yadeha*. Likewise, the *ma'ah kesef* — the pin money, less essential, more variable in its significance — corresponds to the *motar*, the excess labor that also varies and does not always arise. So on this view: regular food bill for regular labor, pin money for excess labor.

To understand what *ma'aseh yadeha* means concretely, the *gemara* later makes clear that it encompasses not only domestic chores — cooking, baking, laundry — which produce no separate income, but also productive work such as weaving and seamstress activity, through which the wife could earn money beyond household upkeep. Her minimum obligation in this latter category is quantified: the weight of five *sela'im* of warp thread in Judea, equivalent to ten *sela'im* in the Galilee, where coins were of a different weight. This is the minimum amount of productive spinning and weaving she is expected to contribute weekly.

### Fixed-to-Fixed Logic

The opposing view holds *midi dekaitz mimidi dekaitz* — fixed amounts correspond to fixed amounts. The pin money is a precisely specified sum, a fixed quantity. The minimum *ma'aseh yadeha* is also a fixed obligation — she must produce exactly a certain amount, neither more nor less. These two fixed quantities therefore pair with one another. What is unfixed — the *mezonot*, which can fluctuate depending on the week's needs and expenses, and the *motar*, which can vary enormously depending on how much extra work the wife takes on — these two variable quantities correspond to each other. On this reading: pin money for minimum labor, variable food bill for excess labor.

This second approach makes a compelling point. The *motar* in a given week might be trivial, or it might be enormous — a wife who is exceptionally productive could generate a sum vastly exceeding any minimum. The food bill, similarly, is not truly a constant; it rises and falls. So it is more natural to pair the fixed with the fixed and the fluctuating with the fluctuating.

### Practical Consequences

The *nafka mina* between these two positions becomes clear in the case of a refusal. If the husband stops paying one of his obligations, the question of what he loses access to depends on which view one adopts. If the common-to-common view is correct, refusing to pay the food bill costs him access to her minimum labor; refusing the pin money costs him the *motar*. If the fixed-to-fixed view is correct, the correspondences are reversed. The same logic applies symmetrically: if the wife refuses to perform a given category of labor, the husband is relieved of the corresponding obligation.

---

## Source Reconciliation

### Pin Money Baraita
