The *gemara* challenges one of these positions by citing a Tannaitic source — apparently a *mishnah* — that states: if the husband does not give her the *ma'ah kesef* for her personal needs, *ma'aseh yadeha shelah* — she retains her labor. This seems to support the view that the *ma'ah kesef* corresponds directly to the core *ma'aseh yadeha*, i.e., the fixed-to-fixed alignment: pin money in exchange for minimum labor. The *mishnah* then goes on to describe what that minimum labor consists of — the weight of five *sela'im* of warp — which seems to confirm that what she reclaims when he withholds the pin money is precisely her core minimum obligation.

### Gemara Reinterprets

The *gemara* resists this reading. *Eima motar ma'aseh yadeha shelah* — what she retains is not the core *ma'aseh yadeha* but the *motar*, the excess beyond the minimum. The description of the minimum, the *gemara* argues, is included only so that one can calculate what exceeds it: *ma'aseh yadeha kama havei, de-layeida motar didah kama* — it tells you what the minimum is precisely so that you know how much is above and beyond it. The *mishnah*, in other words, describes the baseline not to define what she keeps, but to define the threshold above which she keeps the surplus.

This is admittedly a reading that imposes something on the plain meaning of the text. The *gemara* acknowledges the tension: different Tannaitic formulations seem to pull in different directions on whether it is the *ma'ah kesef* that corresponds to the minimum labor or to the *motar*. The question of correspondence is genuinely unresolved across the sources.

---

## Shmuel's Ruling

### Shmuel's Position

The *gemara* now records Shmuel's ruling: *halacha ke-Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar* — we rule like Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar, who holds that the husband's sanctification of the *motar* does not take effect, i.e., it remains *chullin*. Under the framework of Rav and Shmuel — where the case is one in which the husband is not entitled to the *motar* until he inherits it — ruling like Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar means affirming that one cannot be *makdish* a *davar shelo ba l'olam*.

### Konam vs. Kiddushin

But the *gemara* immediately raises a contradiction. Shmuel also rules *halacha ke-Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri* in a different *mishnah*, which involves a woman who declares *konam she'ani oseh lefichah* — using the vow-formula *konam*, a shorthand for *korban*, she forbids the labor of her hands to her husband. The *Tanna kamma* holds that the husband need not annul this vow because it is inherently void: she does not own her labor, and one cannot forbid what one does not own. Rabbi Akiva holds he must annul it, lest she produce more than the minimum, in which case the excess — which is hers — would be caught by the vow. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds he must annul it because if he subsequently divorces her, the vow will take effect at the moment of divorce, and once operative, it cannot be retroactively annulled; it would then prevent them from remarrying.

Shmuel rules like Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, which implies the vow can take effect at the moment of divorce — i.e., that a *konam* declared now over something she does not yet own can take hold later when she acquires it. But this seems to contradict ruling like Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar, who denies that a *davar shelo ba l'olam* can be sanctified. Why should a *konam* succeed where *hekdesh* fails?

The *gemara* attempts to rescue the consistency of Shmuel's rulings by suggesting he only meant to rule like Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri regarding the concern about *hadafa* — the possibility she produces extra labor — effectively aligning him with Rabbi Akiva rather than with Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's reasoning about the delayed effect of the vow. But this answer is immediately rejected as strained: if that were Shmuel's meaning, he should simply have said the ruling follows Rabbi Akiva, or that it does not follow the *Tanna kamma*. The *gemara* therefore abandons this resolution and turns to Rav Yosef for a different approach.

---

## Woman's Vow Case

### Konam at Divorce

The underlying question is why the *konam* should be able to take effect at the moment of divorce. When the woman declares her labor forbidden to her husband, she does not own that labor — he is currently entitled to it. So how can her vow have any grip? The answer requires explaining what is distinctive about *konamot* relative to ordinary *hekdesh*.

### Motar Yedei Hadachak

One possibility raised by the *gemara* is that even while he is entitled to the standard *motar*, there exists an additional category — *motar yedei hadachak*, an extraordinary surplus produced when the woman pushes herself beyond all normal expectations, working late into the night. That extreme excess remains hers even during the marriage, and it is to that excess that Rabbi Akiva is referring when he says the vow may take hold.

### Divorce Trigger Rule

Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's position goes further. He argues that the vow's concern is not about what she produces during the marriage but about what happens afterward. Even if the vow is entirely inoperative while she is married, it is poised to take effect the moment the marriage ends. Once the *get* is given, she regains ownership of her labor, and the *konam* she declared at the outset snaps into effect. At that point, her labor is forbidden to her ex-husband. The problem is not the present but the future: if they then wish to remarry, it will be too late for him to annul the vow — a vow can only be annulled on the day it is made. Therefore, Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri rules that the husband must annul the vow now, before this scenario ever materializes.

---

## Konamot vs. Hekdesh

### Identity Change Power

Rav Yosef explains: *shani konamos* — *konamot* are different in kind from ordinary *hekdesh*. Normal *hekdesh* is *kedusha shel damim* — a transfer of ownership, where the Temple treasury becomes the owner of the sanctified object in the same way any other legal entity is an owner. One cannot transfer ownership of something one does not own, which is why *hekdesh* cannot work on a *davar shelo ba l'olam* or *davar shelo ba lirshuto*. But *konamot* operate through a different mechanism, comparable to *kedushat haguf* — they change the very identity of the object rather than merely reassigning its ownership.

### Identity Examples

This principle has wider ramifications, articulated by Rava: *hekdesh, chametz, ve-shichrur mafkin mi-yedei shibud* — sanctifying an object as a *korban*, rendering *chametz* forbidden on Passover, and freeing a slave all remove existing liens, because these acts do not merely change an object's owner but change its identity. A creditor who holds a lien on an animal cannot collect once the animal becomes a *korban*, because a *korban* is not simply property under different ownership — it has been taken out of the ordinary world of ownable things entirely. Similarly, a lien on *chametz* that becomes *assur b'hana'ah* on Passover is extinguished; and a lien on a slave evaporates upon manumission, because a free person cannot be the subject of a lien.

The power of *konamot* is that they operate through this identity-altering mechanism. A woman who declares *konam* on her hands is not merely transferring ownership of her labor; she is invoking the framework of *kedushat haguf*, which operates more fundamentally than a simple change in title.

---

## Abaye's Challenge

### Fruit Analogy

Rav Yosef's initial formulation of why *konamot* are more powerful than *hekdesh* draws on the following observation: *mitokh she-adam oser peirot chaveiro alav, adam makdish davar shelo ba lirshuto* — since a person can, by vow, forbid another's fruit to himself, it follows that *nedarim* can reach beyond what one owns. Therefore, the woman can forbid her future labor even though she does not currently own it, since *konamot* belong to the realm of *nedarim*.

### Abaye's Logic

Abaye objects with precision. He distinguishes two types of *neder*-formulas: I can forbid my fruit to you; I can also forbid your fruit to me. The common thread that makes both possible is that in each case, at least one party has some connection — either the owner forbids his own property, or the person becoming forbidden is the subject of the restriction. What one cannot do is forbid your fruit to you. That would require no connection whatsoever to either the owner or the one being restricted. Now apply this to the woman's case: her labor is his, and she is trying to make it forbidden to him. That is precisely the forbidden configuration — she is making his property forbidden to him, which has no parallel in the world of *nedarim*. The analogy to forbidding another's fruit therefore fails.

---

## Sanctify Hands Solution

### Hands Exist Now

Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua offers a different approach: *be-omeret yakdishu yadai le-oseihem* — what if the woman frames her declaration as sanctifying her hands themselves, not the labor they will produce? The hands already exist in the world. The problem with *davar shelo ba l'olam* is that the object of sanctification is not yet present; if what she is sanctifying is the hands themselves, which are physically present now, perhaps that resolves the *lo ba l'olam* difficulty. The *gemara* engages this idea: *d'yadayim isnhu b'olam* — indeed, the hands are present.

### Ownership Objection

But there is a second problem independent of whether the hands exist: she does not own them, in the relevant sense. While she owns her body in a fundamental way, the monetary rights in the work her hands produce currently belong to her husband. Even if we have resolved the *lo ba l'olam* issue by pointing to the physical existence of the hands, the ownership problem remains. He has the entitlement; she cannot sanctify what is his.

---

## Delayed Formula

### Future Ownership Trigger

The *gemara* therefore refines the formula: *d'amra lichshe'etgaresh* — she declares her hands sanctified *when she gets divorced*. By specifying the future moment of divorce, she is not trying to sanctify something she currently owns but rather the ownership she will regain once the marriage ends. This is more defensible: she does have a base, residual ownership in her own body and labor — an ownership that is currently suppressed by the husband's entitlement but that will resurface upon divorce. She is sanctifying specifically that latent, future-oriented ownership right now.

### Resurfacing Ownership

The analogy offered is to China's rights over Hong Kong during the lease period: the underlying ownership existed and was real, even though it could not be exercised for ninety-nine years. The reversionary right was a genuine legal interest that could be assigned or acted upon during the lease period. Similarly, this woman holds a genuine, if dormant, ownership interest in her own labor — the interest she will have when single — and that interest is what she is sanctifying now. This formulation appears promising, and it is precisely what Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's ruling presupposes: that the vow has no present effect but is primed to activate at the moment of divorce.

---

## Uncertainty Problem

### Death Before Divorce

The *gemara* poses a serious difficulty: *umi ika midi de-lo hashta lo kadish ul'kame kadish?* — is there really such a thing as a sanctification that does not work now but will work later? Rabbi Elai responds affirmatively and supplies an analogy. If someone says to his friend: "This field that I am selling you — when I repurchase it from you, it shall be sanctified," the *gemara* takes it as obvious that this would be effective. The seller has an interest in the field — the right to buy it back — and sanctifies that interest now for the moment it is exercised. Similarly, she has an interest that will resurface upon divorce, and she sanctifies it now.

### Field Repurchase

But Rabbi Yirmiyah immediately challenges the analogy. In the field case, the one making the declaration is the owner at the moment of speaking — he owns the field before he sells it, so his act of sanctification at that moment is grounded in real ownership. Moreover, he has the power to bring the sanctification about: he can choose to repurchase the field. The woman is in a fundamentally different position in both respects.

---

## No Control Objection

### Lack of Control

Rabbi Yirmiyah reformulates the field analogy in a way that strips out the favorable elements. The apt comparison, he says, is not to a field being sold with a repurchase clause declared before the sale, but to someone who has already sold the field and then declares, post-sale, that when he repurchases it, it shall be sanctified. There he has no current ownership, and no guaranteed ability to repurchase. That, Rabbi Yirmiyah argues, is void — and that is the woman's situation. She has no current ownership of her labor's monetary rights, and she has no power to bring about the divorce that would restore them. She could die before him; he could never choose to divorce her. The future ownership is genuinely uncertain, not merely delayed.

Rav Pappa pushes back by introducing a distinction: in the field case, the buyer owns both the *guf* — the body of the field — and the *peirot* — its produce. He owns everything. Here, the woman owns her own body — *gufa beyadah hu* — even while he owns the *peirot*, the entitlement to her labor. This is analogous, Rav Pappa suggests, to a field given as collateral for a loan: the borrower retains title while the lender holds and benefits from the field's produce. In such a case, the borrower can sanctify the field even now, because he retains title. So too the woman, who retains ownership of her body, might be able to sanctify her hands.

### Body Ownership

Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi further refines this: the better analogy is to a field given as collateral for a fixed term — say, ten years — during which the borrower cannot redeem it. After ten years, however, the right of redemption returns automatically. Even so, the *gemara* accepts, the borrower can sanctify the field for after the ten-year period, because he knows with certainty that the right will eventually return to him.

Rav Ashi then makes the decisive objection: *hatam le-achar eser shanim miha beyado lifdotah* — after ten years, the borrower will certainly regain control. The certainty of eventual repossession grounds the sanctification. But the woman has no such certainty: *ein beyado legaresh atzmah l'olam* — she has no ability to divorce herself, ever. If he lives and refuses to divorce her, she will never regain her labor rights. There is therefore no sufficiently grounded reversionary interest to anchor the sanctification.

---

## Rav Ashi Identity

### Identity vs. Ownership

Rav Ashi ultimately returns to and reformulates Rav Yosef's approach, applying it with greater precision. *Shani konamos dekedushat haguf ninhu* — *konamot* are different because they operate through *kedushat haguf*, identity-level sanctity, rather than *kedusha shel damim*, which is merely ownership-level sanctity. This is the principle underlying Rava's statement: *hekdesh, chametz, ve-shichrur mafkin mi-yedei shibud* — these three — consecration as a *korban*, *chametz* on Passover, and freeing a slave — dissolve all liens, because they alter the object's identity rather than merely transferring title. A lien is a right attached to an owner's property; when the property ceases to be ownable property in the ordinary sense, the lien has nothing to attach to.

The *konam* the woman declares operates through this mechanism. She is not trying to transfer ownership of her labor to some third party. She is, as it were, changing the identity of her hands — making them like a *korban*, not in a literal sense (her hands will not be used in the Temple), but in the legal-structural sense that the *neder* invokes *kedushat haguf*. This is more powerful than what the husband attempted in the *mishnah*'s original case, where he sought to sanctify the *motar* through *hekdesh* — a simple ownership transfer — which fails when the object is not in his possession.

### Husband's Lien Strengthe…

Yet even this more powerful mechanism has limits. The *gemara* asks: if *kedushat haguf* can overcome liens, why does the woman's *konam* not take effect immediately, dissolving the husband's rights on the spot? The answer: *amru rabanan le-shibuda de-ba'al ki heichi de-lo tikdesh me-hashtah* — the Rabbis strengthened the husband's lien specifically so that the *konam* cannot take effect during the marriage. This is a rabbinic reinforcement of the husband's entitlement, designed to prevent the identity-altering power of *konamot* from unraveling the marital arrangement mid-marriage. The result is a carefully constructed compromise: the *konam* is real and will take effect upon divorce, but the Rabbis ensured that during the marriage, the husband's lien is robust enough to suppress it.

The *gemara* acknowledges that the mechanics here are not fully transparent. A *konam* is not truly a *korban* — the woman's hands are not going to perform Temple service. The identity change is structural rather than literal. And the exact boundary between "the husband's lien is strong enough to suppress it now" and "it will take effect at divorce" is left somewhat inexact. Nonetheless, the conclusion holds: the husband cannot sanctify his wife's labor that he is not entitled to until she dies — following Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar — and the wife can use a *konam*-formula to forbid her labor to her husband in a way that takes effect upon divorce, through the mechanism of *kedushat haguf*, with the Rabbis' having ensured it does not unravel the marriage prematurely.

---

## Wife's Obligations

### Core Duties List

Having resolved the extended discussion of ownership and sanctification, the *gemara* at last arrives at the next *mishnah*, which enumerates the wife's actual domestic obligations. *Ve-eilu melachot she-ha-isha osa le-vaalah* — these are the labors the wife performs for her husband. The list is comprehensive and reflects a traditional household structure: she grinds the wheat (*tochenet*), bakes (*ofa*), does the laundry (*mechabbeset*), cooks (*mevashelet*), nurses the children (*meineika et benah*), makes the beds (*matzaat lo ha-mitah*), and works with wool (*osa ba-tzemer*). This last item — working with wool, weaving, and seamstress work — is particularly significant, as it represents the category of productive labor that generates actual income beyond mere household upkeep.

### Slaves Reduce Duties

The *mishnah* then introduces a sliding scale keyed to the number of *shefachot* — maidservants — the wife brings into the marriage as part of her dowry. If she brings one servant, she is relieved of the three most laborious tasks: grinding, baking, and laundry. Two servants relieve her also of cooking and nursing. Three servants relieve her of making the beds and the seamstress work as well.

### Four Slaves Freedom

If she brings four servants, *yoshevet be-katedra* — she sits on her throne. *Katedra* is the Roman-derived term for a formal seat of authority, the root from which "cathedral" derives. Rashi explains that sitting on the *katedra* means not merely that she has no formal obligations, but that she need not even perform the smallest incidental task — fetching something from another room, bringing an object at her husband's request. Every conceivable request falls to the fourth servant. She is entirely exempt.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer Spin

### Idleness Leads Zeimah

Rabbi Eliezer dissents. Even if a wife brings a hundred servants into the marriage, the husband may still compel her to do the seamstress work — spinning and weaving. His rationale: *she-ha-batalah mevi'ah lidei zimmah* — idleness leads to licentiousness. If she has nothing productive to occupy her, she will seek out trouble. The choice of seamstress work as the irreducible minimum is notable; it is purposeful labor that keeps the hands and mind engaged without being as physically strenuous as grinding or laundry.

---

## Rabban Shimon Shiamum

### Vow Against Labor

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel takes an entirely different perspective, and from a different direction. He addresses the case of a husband who takes a vow — *madir ishah milasot melachah* — forbidding his wife's labor to himself. If he cannot benefit from her work, then requiring her to do that work makes no sense.

### Divorce Consequence

Rabban Shimon rules: *yotzi ve-yiten ketubah* — he must divorce her and pay the *ketubah*. The reason he gives is arresting: *she-ha-batalah mevi'ah lidei shiamum* — idleness leads to *shiamum*, going out of one's mind, a kind of psychological disintegration. This is a notably different moral framework from Rabbi Eliezer's. Rabbi Eliezer is concerned that idleness will lead the wife to sin; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is concerned that idleness is itself harmful to the wife — that productive engagement is a basic human need, and that a situation in which she is barred from all meaningful work is intolerable for her wellbeing. The contrast between *zimmah* and *shiamum* captures two entirely different orientations: moral surveillance versus concern for the person.

---

## Gemara Interpretation

### Grinding Explained

The *gemara* raises an immediate question about the first item on the *mishnah*'s list: *tochenet salka deitach* — can you really mean she grinds wheat herself? Grinding grain was the province of millstones and water-wheels. The *gemara* resolves this with two options: *ela eima matchenet* — she causes it to be ground, meaning she brings the wheat to the mill, or alternatively, it refers to a case of *reichaya de-yada* — a hand mill, a scenario where hand-grinding is in fact expected.

### Not Like Rabbi Hiyya

The *gemara* then notes that the *mishnah*'s comprehensive list of domestic obligations does not accord with the view of Rabbi Hiyya. The *mishnah* assigns the wife significant labor responsibilities; Rabbi Hiyya's perspective implies a very different understanding of what a wife is primarily for.

---

## Rabbi Hiyya View

### Three Purposes

Rabbi Hiyya taught three formulations: *ein ishah ela le-yofi* — a woman is only for beauty; *ein ishah ela le-banim* — a woman is only for children; *ein ishah ela le-tachshitei ishah* — a woman is only for adornment. These are not presented as legal rulings in context but as statements of attitude — they echo the voice of the women who danced in the fields on Tu B'Av and Yom Kippur as recorded elsewhere, each group calling out what men ostensibly seek in a wife. Nevertheless, the *gemara* takes these statements seriously enough to note that if Rabbi Hiyya's view were adopted as a legal baseline, the wife would not be expected to perform work that might compromise her beauty or her ability to bear children, and the *mishnah*'s extensive catalog of obligations would not apply. Our *mishnah*, the *gemara* concludes, does not follow Rabbi Hiyya.

### Husbands' Duties

Rabbi Hiyya also taught practical guidance that flows from these premises. *Ha-rotzeh she-yadin et ishto* — if a husband wishes his wife to have a radiant complexion, *yalbishena klei pishtan* — he should clothe her in linen garments. And *ha-rotzeh she-yalbin et bito* — if a man wishes his daughter to have fair skin so that she will be attractive in marriage, *ya'achilenu efrochim ve-yashkenu chalav samuch le-pirkah* — he should feed her chicks and give her milk to drink near the time of her maturity. The *gemara* closes with these notes of practical domestic counsel, a fitting if somewhat surprising coda to a daf that began with the most intricate questions of ownership, sanctification, and identity.

---

---

# Ketubot 60

## Nursing Obligation

### Intro: Nursing & Vows

The daf begins approximately ten lines from the bottom of 59b, with the Mishnah's discussion of *umeneket beno* — a wife's obligation to nurse her husband's child. Among the various domestic tasks incumbent upon a wife, nursing is enumerated as one of her obligations to her husband. The Gemara immediately raises a challenge: is our Mishnah consistent with the position of Beit Shammai?

A Baraita is cited in which a woman takes a vow — *nadra shelo lehanik* — that prevents her from nursing the child. The Gemara clarifies what type of vow this could be. A vow functions by rendering something forbidden to a person. In this context, she might make the benefit of her nursing forbidden to her husband, who benefits indirectly because his child is being nursed. Alternatively, she might make the act itself forbidden to herself, given that the Gemara acknowledges that a woman derives a measure of pleasure from the act of nursing. Either way, the vow is structured so as to prohibit the nursing.

### Vow Mechanics

The question of what precisely is being forbidden by the vow — the benefit to the husband or the act itself — bears on the vow's validity and its interaction with her marital obligations. The Gemara's discussion implicitly recalls the earlier treatment of *maaseh yadayim*: just as a wife cannot render her labor forbidden to her husband because he holds a prior claim on it, so too there is a question of whether she can render her nursing forbidden when it is itself a marital obligation.

### Shammai vs Hillel

Beit Shammai rules: *shometet dad mi-pi* — she removes the breast from the child's mouth. Even if she is in the midst of nursing, she stops. The vow is binding and she has no legal compulsion to continue. Beit Hillel, by contrast, rules: *kofo umeneket oto* — her husband can compel her to nurse the child. The implication of Beit Hillel's position is that the vow was never binding in the first place, since she is not in a position to render forbidden a service that her husband already has a prior claim upon. Beit Shammai, it follows, holds that she bears no strict legal obligation to nurse her child, allowing the vow to take full effect.

### Divorce & Nursing

Once she is divorced, *einah kofah* — he can no longer compel her, since her obligation to him has ended. At that point, presumably, the vow takes effect. This touches on the earlier discussion about a vow taking effect at a postponed moment in time.

However, if the child already *recognized* the mother — and Rashi adds, though it is not explicit in the Gemara, that this means the child will not nurse from any other woman — then even in the post-divorce situation, the husband pays her a nursemaid's fee and can compel his ex-wife to nurse the child: *notin lah secharah ve-kofo umeneket oto*. The Gemara underscores the clinical importance of this: it is understood as a genuine *sakanah* — a danger to the child's life — if a child who will only nurse from his mother is denied her.

This raises a penetrating question: if the vow is binding, is the woman now violating it when compelled to nurse? One possibility is that this involves *pikuach nefesh*, overriding the vow entirely. Yet if so, one would expect the Gemara to discuss annulling the vow through a *heter neder* rather than simply compelling her. A more coherent reading may be that in any scenario where the husband retains the legal authority to compel nursing — even with payment — the vow never achieved binding status to begin with, since it could never take hold in a domain subject to that compulsion. The Gemara does not develop this explicitly, but it is the most internally consistent reading.

### Blame & Payment

The Gemara then entertains a reinterpretation of the entire Beit Shammai–Beit Hillel dispute. Perhaps neither side is debating whether the vow is binding or whether she can be compelled to nurse. Perhaps both agree the vow is binding, and the real dispute is about *who is to blame* — and therefore who bears the financial consequences. This reading is associated with Tosafot.

### Sakana Override

The Gemara notes explicitly: *mipnei hasakanah* — even where a vow might otherwise apply, the danger to the child represents an overriding concern. The recognition that a nursing mother's milk, and especially the act of nursing from one's own mother, constitutes a life-sustaining need for the infant is treated as a foundational *halakhic* principle.

### Affirmed Vow

The Gemara then frames a specific scenario: *shenadra hi vekiyam lah hu* — she made the vow and he not merely failed to annul it but actively *affirmed* it. Once a husband affirms the vow, he can no longer annul it even on the same day. Now the question becomes: who is culpable for the resulting situation?

Beit Shammai holds: *hu nosein etzba bein shineha* — he put his finger between her teeth. He is to blame; he is the one who affirmed the vow. Beit Hillel holds: *hi nosna etzba bein shineha* — she put her finger between her teeth. She made the vow; she bears responsibility.

On Tosafot's reading, what the two schools are debating is not whether she can be compelled to nurse but rather who must bear the financial cost of hiring a nursemaid. If he is to blame, she is exempt. If she is to blame, she must cover the expense. The Gemara, however, objects: if the debate were simply about blame and financial responsibility in cases where a wife's vow frustrates her *ketuva* obligations, the Tannaim could have framed the dispute in general terms about *ketuva* obligations — with the *nafka mina* being whether he must pay her *ketuva* upon divorce. Why single out the nursing case? Moreover, another Baraita states explicitly: *Beit Shammai omrim einah menikah* — Beit Shammai says she does not have to nurse. This makes clear that the dispute is indeed about the existence of the obligation itself. The Gemara concludes: *ela mehavarta kesimin d'lo ke-Beit Shammai* — the Mishnah simply does not follow Beit Shammai.

---

## Child Recognition

### Recognition Age

The Baraita we examined establishes that if the infant already *makkira* — recognizes — his mother, and according to Rashi will refuse to nurse from another woman, the ex-husband can compel even a divorced wife to nurse for pay. The Gemara now asks: from what age do we assume that a child will recognize the mother in this operative sense?

### Age Dispute

Three Amoraic opinions are given. Rava citing Rav Yirmiya bar Abba citing Rav: *shlosha chodashim* — three months. Shmuel: *shloshim yom* — thirty days. Rav Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan: *chamishim yom* — fifty days. Rav Shimi bar Chiya then rules: *halacha* follows the last-cited position of fifty days, in the name of Rabbi Yochanan.

The Gemara asks: the debate between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan — three months versus fifty days — is understandable, as it may reflect that different children develop recognition at different rates, each authority ruling according to the earlier or later range of typical cases. But Shmuel says the child recognizes the mother at thirty days — is such a thing possible at all?

The Gemara leaves this without definitive resolution. The practical question of what precisely "recognition" means is relevant here. Does it mean merely some inchoate awareness of the mother's presence, or specifically that the child refuses to nurse from anyone else — as Rashi's addition suggests? If it is the latter, testing would be more straightforward: simply offer the child another nursemaid and observe whether he accepts her.

### Case-by-Case

When Rav Dimi bar Yechezkel returned from Eretz Yisrael, he corrected the transmission. He said: do not follow these fixed rules that Yehuda my brother reported in the name of Shmuel. What Shmuel actually said is *kol zman shemakkira* — the determination is made case by case. Rather than applying a bright-line rule of thirty, fifty, or ninety days, one must examine the specific child to determine whether he recognizes his mother or not.

### Lineup Test

The Gemara then brings a story. A woman came before Shmuel: she had been divorced, and her husband sought to compel her to continue nursing. Shmuel instructed Rav Dimi bar Yosef: go and investigate whether the child recognizes her. Rav Dimi bar Yosef conducted a lineup — *dara d'neshei* — a row of women, and had the infant carried past them. When the child passed before his mother, *havat kemashfi le'apa* — he lit up, recognizing her face. She, seeking to avoid the obligation, averted her eyes — *kavashtanhu le'einei mineih*. Rav Dimi bar Yosef said to her: *netof einach kum dari brach* — lift your eyes, go carry your son. You must nurse him; he clearly recognizes you.

This story is notable precisely because the test was recognition, not refusal to nurse from another woman. The far simpler test — offering the child to a nursemaid and observing whether he nurses — was not employed. This suggests that the Gemara's operative criterion is recognition itself, and Rashi's addition about refusing to nurse from others may be his explanatory gloss rather than the Gemara's own requirement.

### Blind Child

One might ask: how would a blind child — *suma* — recognize his mother, given that the test used by the Gemara was visual? Rav Ashi answers: *be-reicha uve-ta'ama* — through smell and taste. The other senses are sufficient to enable identification even where sight is unavailable.

---

## Nursing Duration

### 24 Month Limit

The Gemara now transitions from the question of a wife's nursing obligation to a broader treatment of nursing in general, citing a Baraita: *yonek tinok ve-holech ad esrim ve-arba'ah chodesh* — a child may continue nursing until twenty-four months. Beyond that point, says the first opinion — that of Rabbi Eliezer — nursing is *ke-yonek sheket*, like nursing from something abominable.

The precise character of the prohibition is worth examining. The phrase *yonek sheket* suggests that the objection is not to the substance of human milk but to the *act* of nursing beyond a certain age. A nursing child beyond twenty-four months is described as nursing from something disgusting — the focus is on the act rather than the product. The *nafka mina* is significant: if a mother expresses her milk into a container and gives it to a child, would Rabbi Eliezer's objection apply? If the concern is the act of nursing, expressed milk would be unaffected; if the concern is the substance at that developmental stage, it would be equally problematic regardless of form of delivery.

### 4-5 Years Option

Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees sharply: *afilu arba va-chamisha shanim* — even four or five years old, nursing remains permissible. The Gemara considers whether Rabbi Yehoshua means literally up to five years as an upper bound, or whether he means there is no practical limit whatsoever. The Gemara's treatment suggests he does intend some upper boundary around five years.

Rabbi Yehoshua does, however, concede one point: *peiresh le-achar esrim ve-arba'ah chodesh ve-chazar* — if after the twenty-four-month mark the child ceased nursing for a period and then returned to it, then even Rabbi Yehoshua would agree this is *ke-yonek sheket*. Once the child has transitioned out of the nursing stage and entered the normal world of eating solid food, a return to nursing is considered inappropriate even according to the lenient view. How long a cessation constitutes *peiresh*? Rav Yehuda bar Chaviva cites Shmuel: three days of uninterrupted abstention from nursing suffices.

### Act vs Product

As noted, the central distinction being drawn throughout this passage is between the *act* of nursing and the *product* — expressed milk. The discussion of *yonek sheket* appears to target the act. This distinction will be reinforced momentarily by the analogy to blood.

### Kashrut Proof

The Gemara now marshals a proof from *kashrut* reasoning. A *kal va-chomer* might suggest that human milk should be non-kosher: if the milk of a non-kosher animal is forbidden even though that animal does not convey *tumah* through touch while alive, then surely human milk should be forbidden, since humans *do* convey *tumah* when alive. The Torah, however, teaches from the verse concerning the camel — *et ha-gamal* — that the milk of non-kosher animals is forbidden, but through the same derivation, the verse specifies only non-kosher animals: *hu tamei* — *it* is *tamei*, implying that human milk, by contrast, *ve-ein chalav meha-mehalech al shtayim tamei ela tahor* — is not non-kosher but is in fact permitted.

Similarly, one might think that human blood is forbidden: all animal blood is consistently forbidden, so human blood should be forbidden as well. The same verse teaches otherwise: the prohibition applies specifically to animal blood, not to human blood — *ve-ein dam meha-mehalech al shtayim tamei ela tahor*. Rashi and Tosafot work out the precise derivation from the verse, but the operative conclusion is clear: both blood and milk of human beings are not Biblically non-kosher. Rav Sheshet adds: *afilu mitzvat perishah ein bo* — there is not even a rabbinic prohibition against consuming human milk. It is entirely permitted.

### Blood Analogy

This raises a sharp question: if human milk is entirely permitted, how can the Gemara speak of *yonek sheket* — as though nursing beyond a certain age involves something disgusting? The Gemara answers: *lo kashya — ha de-parish, ha de-lo parish* — there is no difficulty. The cases are categorically different. When the milk has been separated from the mother — expressed into a cup — there is no halachic concern and no element of impropriety. When the child nurses directly from the mother, the *act* of nursing is what is considered inappropriate beyond a certain developmental stage.

Fascinatingly, the exact *converse* applies to blood. *Ve-chilufa be-dam* — the reverse principle governs blood. With blood, the concern runs in the opposite direction: if blood has been separated from the body and collected in a vessel, one may not drink it — not because human blood is itself non-kosher, but because an observer would assume the person is drinking animal blood and the appearance is impermissible. However, if a person's gums are bleeding and the blood remains *bein ha-shinayim* — between the teeth — or if one receives a cut and sucks the wound, *motzetzah ve-eino choshesh* — one may suck it out and need not be concerned. Here, an observer clearly understands that the person is ingesting blood from their own body, and there is no appearance of impropriety.

The contrast is structurally elegant: expressed human milk is unproblematic; direct nursing beyond a certain age is considered inappropriate. Expressed human blood presents an appearance concern; blood sucked directly from one's own wound is entirely permitted.

A practical question naturally arises in light of this analysis: human milk expressed and prepared as food — even as cheese — would be not only *kosher* but not even *milchig*. Tosafot also cites a *Torat Kohanim* to the effect that human flesh is likewise not Biblically forbidden, though there are significant discussions among *poskim* about whether it would be prohibited on other grounds, such as *bal tishaktzu*. The term *mehalechei shtayim* — two-legged beings — is used as a euphemism in these sources rather than specifying *adam* directly, possibly to avoid the discomfort of explicit discussion.

### Halakha Ruling

Rav Yosef rules: *halacha ke-Rabbi Yehoshua* — the law follows Rabbi Yehoshua, permitting nursing up to approximately four to five years. This is the operative *halakha*.

---

## Shabbat Suckling

### Sick Suckling

Rabbi Merinus taught: *gonei'ach yonek chalav be-Shabbos* — a person who is ill may directly suckle milk from an animal's udder on *Shabbat*.

### Shinui Leniency

The reason: *yonek mefarek ke-achar yad* — the act of suckling from the udder involves the forbidden labor of *mefarek*, a subdivision of *dash* — threshing — which means separating a substance from the medium in which it is bound. Normally one milks a cow with the hands; to suckle directly with the mouth is therefore a *shinui*, an unusual manner of performing the action, and constitutes *mefarek ke-lachar yad*. The Gemara adds: *u-vimkom tzara lo gazru rabbanan* — where there is genuine distress or pain, the rabbis did not extend their decree to prohibit even this modified form of the labor. The leniency is thus grounded in two factors: the *shinui* reduces the violation, and the *tzaar* of illness creates a threshold sufficient to permit a single Rabbinic-level prohibition.

It is worth noting that this Gemara does not treat direct suckling from an animal as *yonek sheket*. An ill adult suckling from a cow's udder is a *Shabbat* question, not one of propriety. This further supports the inference that the impropriety of *yonek sheket* in the nursing context is specifically tied to something about the mother-child relationship beyond a certain developmental stage — perhaps related to the intimate character of nursing from a human being rather than the act of suckling per se.

### Mother Expressing

This Gemara has critical implications for the question of a nursing mother expressing milk on *Shabbat*. Two preliminary issues arise. First, Tosafot notes that *dash* — from which the prohibition of milking derives — technically applies only to *gidulei karka*, things that grow from the ground. Human beings do not grow from the ground. Accordingly, Tosafot raises the possibility that expressing human milk may not be Biblically prohibited at all, but only Rabbinic — a position that, if accepted, significantly shifts the *Shabbat* analysis.

Second, even setting aside that question, one might ask whether expressing milk by hand constitutes a *shinui* for a human mother. By a cow, the *normal* method of extraction from the human perspective is hand-milking; suckling directly is the deviation. For a human mother, the natural mode of the milk's release is through the infant nursing; expressing by hand might itself be considered the deviation, and therefore a *shinui* already. Or one might argue that either method is equally natural for a human mother, making neither a *shinui*. This is not easily resolved.

Beyond the question of *shinui*, the *sakana* argument may apply: if failure to express milk threatens the mother's milk supply in a way that endangers the infant's nutrition, that *sakana* framework — which we have already seen the Gemara invoke prominently — would provide independent grounds for permitting expression. As a practical matter, an ideal solution is to attach an electric pump on a timer before *Shabbat* so that the device activates automatically, with the mother already connected; she then plays no active role in the expression itself.

### Drain Pipe Case

A parallel case is brought from Nachum Ish Galia: if a drain pipe on a roof has filled with debris and rainwater is backing up into the house, one may use one's foot to compress and push through the blockage on *Shabbat* — *memachan be-raglo be-tzina be-Shabbos*. The reason is the same structure: using one's foot rather than one's hand is a *shinui*, and *u-vimkom psida lo gazru rabbanan* — in a case of financial loss, the rabbis did not extend their decree. Rav Yosef rules: *halacha ke-Nachum Ish Galia zu* — we rule in accordance with Nachum Ish Galia in this matter.

Both of these rulings — the *gonei'ach* case and the drain pipe case — permit overriding a single Rabbinic prohibition on the basis of *tzaar* or *psida* combined with a *shinui*. This sits in some tension with other *sugyot* that appear to require a double Rabbinic qualifier before leniency applies, and the precise threshold of need that justifies which level of override remains a matter of ongoing discussion across the relevant *sugyot*.

---

## Nursing Post-Death

### Forbidden Betrothal

The Gemara presents a new Baraita: *meneket she-met ba'alah be-tokh esrim ve-arba'ah chodesh* — a nursing mother whose husband dies within twenty-four months. Since the obligation to nurse is framed as a marital duty to the husband, one might think that with his death her obligation dissolves. Why, then, can she not simply hand the child to the heirs, declare herself free of responsibility, and move on?

The Baraita's answer is that she may not: *harei zo lo t'ares ve-lo tinasei* — she may neither accept *kiddushin* nor enter *nissuin* for the duration of the twenty-four months. This reflects the concern that if she enters a new relationship, becomes pregnant, that pregnancy will compromise her milk supply and thereby harm the nursing child. Notably, the *Talmud* elsewhere acknowledges that active nursing itself typically functions as a natural contraceptive — it is generally understood that nursing suppresses fertility. Nevertheless, the *halakhic* framework addresses the reverse chain: not that nursing prevents pregnancy, but that a new pregnancy threatens nursing.

### Milk Supply Concern

The operative concern is the integrity of the milk supply. Even if actual conception is unlikely during active nursing, entering *kiddushin* sets in motion a path that could eventually lead to pregnancy. The concern is precautionary: once betrothal is permitted, *nissuin* follows, and with *nissuin* pregnancy becomes a realistic risk.

### Duration Dispute

Rabbi Meir holds that this restriction extends for the full twenty-four months. Rabbi Yehuda permits it after eighteen months, holding that the child's nursing needs diminish sufficiently by that point that the risk to the child no longer justifies continued restriction on the mother's freedom to remarry.

Rabbi Natan bar Yosef notes that this is effectively the same debate as that between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel: Beit Shammai holds twenty-four months and Beit Hillel holds eighteen months. This is somewhat surprising given that Beit Shammai earlier maintained that a mother has no enforceable obligation to her husband to nurse at all — yet here Beit Shammai holds to the longer restriction vis-à-vis the *child*. The reconciliation is that even Beit Shammai acknowledges an obligation where the infant recognizes the mother; in such circumstances, the twenty-four-month commitment to the child exists even without a living husband.

### Reconciliation

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel offers a clarification — not so much a compromise between the positions as a reframing of each one. According to the view of twenty-four months, *muteret le-innasei be-esrim ve-echad chodesh* — she may actually get married at twenty-one months, because the first three months of a new pregnancy do not yet compromise the milk supply. *Lefi she-ein ha-chalav ne'echar ella achar shlosha chadashim* — the milk is not affected until after three months of pregnancy. So "twenty-four months" effectively means the mother may not get married more than three months before the twenty-four-month mark. Similarly, according to the view of eighteen months, she may get married at fifteen months, because again the first trimester does not impact nursing. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is not adjudicating between the two positions but unpacking what each actually requires in practical terms.

### Amoraim Rulings

Ulla rules: *halacha ke-Rabbi Yehuda* — the law follows Rabbi Yehuda's eighteen-month position, though it is not entirely clear whether this means eighteen months as stated or fifteen months as reframed by Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Mar Ukva reports that Rabbi Chanina permitted him personally to marry a woman whose husband had died, once fifteen months had elapsed since the birth of the nursing child — confirming that the operative ruling is fifteen months.

### Sharecropper Case

Abaye's sharecropper came before Abaye with a case: his prospective wife was a nursing mother whose husband had died fifteen months earlier — may he now proceed with *kiddushin*? Abaye responded with confidence: the matter is completely clear. We rule like Rabbi Yehuda — eighteen months meaning fifteen. Beit Hillel, with whom we rule, also holds eighteen months meaning fifteen. Ulla ruled accordingly. And Rabbi Chanina permitted Mar Ukva's own case at fifteen months. With four independent convergent indications, and since this is *kiddushin* and not yet *nissuin*, the answer is obviously yes.

When Abaye reported this exchange to Rav Yosef, however, Rav Yosef corrected him sharply. Rav and Shmuel had both ruled: *tzricha le-hamtin arba'ah ve-esrim chodesh* — she must wait the full twenty-four months. Furthermore, the count does not even begin on the day of the birth — the clock starts the following day — and the day of the *kiddushin* itself does not count as the last day of the period. This is the most stringent possible reading, and it represents the ruling of Rav and Shmuel.

Abaye immediately ran after the sharecropper to stop the wedding — *ratz basei tlasa parsei*, three *parsangs*, and some say one *parsang* through sand — but could not catch him in time.

### Rebbe Authority

Abaye's own conclusion from this episode is striking: *ha milsa de-amru rabbanan afilu ke-beitza be-kutcha* — even a question as obvious as whether one may eat an egg with a dairy dip — *lo lishri inish be-makom rabei* — one should not issue a ruling in the place of one's *rebbe*. The reason is not merely one of respect or deference, which would be waived if the *rebbe* grants permission. Rather, *mishum de-lo mistayeim milta* — such a ruling will not succeed, will not be confirmed by heavenly assistance. A student who presumes to rule in his *rebbe*'s domain, even on an ostensibly clear matter, loses the *siyatta di-shemaya* that would otherwise guide him to the correct conclusion. In Abaye's own case: *deha ana hava gmirna leih la-hade de-Rav u-Shmuel* — I actually knew the ruling of Rav and Shmuel requiring twenty-four months. Yet even so, it slipped my mind at the critical moment. The impetuousness of confident self-sufficiency, even when the *rebbe* is present and available, is precisely what the episode illustrates.

---

## 24-Month Exceptions

### Exceptions Listed

A Baraita states: *natna bnah le-menekes* — if the mother gave the child over to a nursemaid, *o gemalto* — or weaned him, *o met* — or the child died, *mutteret le-hinnase miyad* — she may remarry immediately, within the twenty-four months. These are the three exceptions that remove the basis for the restriction: in each case, the infant is either being nursed by another or no longer nursing at all.

### Attempted Ruling

Rav Pappa and Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua wished to rule in practice according to this Baraita. An elderly woman corrected them: this very case happened to me, and Rav Nachman forbade it even though I had satisfied one of these criteria. Rav Nachman did not permit me to remarry before the twenty-four months.

### Resh Galuta Exception

The Gemara asks: but did not Rav Nachman himself permit the women of the house of the *Resh Galuta* to remarry earlier, once they had weaned their children or made other arrangements? The Gemara answers: *shani bei Resh Galuta de-lo hadru behu* — the household of the *Resh Galuta* is different, because those women will not reverse themselves. Once a decision is made in the *Resh Galuta*'s household — whether to give the child to a nursemaid or to wean — the new husband and the authority of that household ensure the decision will not be revisited. The fear that motivates the general restriction is that a woman who has weaned her child or arranged a nursemaid may have a change of heart, resume nursing, and then, having conceived with a new husband, find that the pregnancy compromises her milk. In the *Resh Galuta*'s household, that reversal is simply not going to happen. Ordinary women are subject to the more stringent standard.

### Paternity Analogy

Rav Pappi raises a further challenge. Rather than relying on the elderly woman's testimony, the ruling against the Baraita's leniency should have been derivable from an independent source. This leads to a discussion of the three-month waiting period before remarriage — a completely separate institution designed to prevent uncertainty about the paternity of a future child.

### 3-Month Cases

A Baraita lists women who must wait three months before remarrying even when there is no realistic concern that they are pregnant: a woman who is *redufah le-lech le-beit aviha* — always running to her father's house and presumably not having relations with her husband; a woman with severe marital discord in the home; a woman whose husband was imprisoned; a woman whose husband went overseas; a woman whose husband was elderly or infirm; and women who are clearly incapable of conception — sterile, elderly, *aylonit*, minor, or a woman who miscarried after her husband's death. In all these cases Rabbi Meir rules they must nonetheless wait three months.

### 3-Month Halakha

Rabbi Yosi permits immediate remarriage when there is no realistic concern of pregnancy. The ruling: *halacha ke-Rabbi Meir bi-gzeirosuav* — we rule like Rabbi Meir in his categorical decree. We do not make case-by-case exceptions even when the underlying concern is clearly inapplicable.

### Consistent 24-Month

The Gemara draws a structural parallel: just as we apply Rabbi Meir's categorical approach to the three-month waiting period and refuse to grant exceptions even where we know there is no pregnancy, the same categorical logic should govern the twenty-four-month restriction. Even if the child has been weaned or given to a nursemaid, we refuse to grant an exception. The *halakha* that emerges: *ve-hilkheta ve-halakha hi met* — the one case where we do permit remarriage within twenty-four months is where the child has died. *Gemaltathu* — if she weaned him — *asur*, she may not yet remarry, because we fear she may change her mind and resume nursing. All other exceptions fail for the same reason. Only the death of the child removes the concern entirely.

### Infanticide Fear

Mar bar Rav Ashi goes further: *afilu met nami asur* — even if the child has died, she may not remarry within twenty-four months. The fear: *dilma katla lei* — we are afraid that a woman desperately eager to remarry might kill her infant child in order to clear the way. An actual case is cited in which a woman strangled her child — *hahi uvda ve-chanaktia* — apparently driven by the desire to be free to remarry.

### Rejection

The Gemara rejects this stringency: *ve-lo hi* — that is not the correct ruling. *Hahi shota havat* — that woman was mentally ill. *Ve-lo avdi inshi de-chanki be-naihu* — normal women do not kill their own children. The extreme case cannot generate a categorical rule. The operative *halakha* therefore stands: the one recognized exception to the twenty-four-month restriction is the death of the child. All other putative exceptions — nursemaid, weaning — do not permit early remarriage.

A related question concerns the three-month waiting period in the context of conversion: if a woman converts together with her husband, must they wait three months to continue living together, in order to clarify whether any child conceived around that time was conceived before or after her conversion? Some *poskim* have permitted pregnancy tests to resolve this question, arguing that modern diagnostic tools create a factual certainty that moves the case outside the framework of the Gemara's categorical decree — though others maintain that the *lo plug* logic of Rabbi Meir's position admits no exceptions regardless of what can be empirically verified today.

---

---

# Ketubot 62

## Onah & Domestic Duties

### Maaseh Yadayim Review

The previous discussion addressed *maaseh yadayim* and a wife's domestic duties. The Mishnah now turns to the husband's corresponding obligation: *onah*, the conjugal duty. The Mishnah had first dealt with a man who takes a vow not to have relations with his wife, giving him one or two weeks. It then addresses a list of circumstances in which a husband may be absent from home for extended periods without his wife's express permission — Torah students for a month, workers for a week. Even though a husband's *onah* obligation may be more frequent, occasional travel for business or to visit one's *rebbe* is permitted within certain limits. The Mishnah then enumerates the frequency of *onah* based on a man's profession, concluding with the phrase *divrei Rabbi Eliezer* — a formulation that signals an implicit dispute, to which the Gemara will return.

### Onah Frequency Overview

The Gemara at the opening of 62a — roughly ten lines down at the asterisk — takes up the *orcha d'milsa* passage from earlier: even where a husband has obtained his wife's permission for extended absence, what conduct is appropriate? This question is itself striking, because one might assume that legal permission settles the matter entirely. The Gemara insists otherwise.

### Rashi on Permission

The first *Rashi* on 62a is indispensable here. On the phrase *orcha d'milsa*, Rashi writes: *derech eretz shelo yisa alav cheit, v'afilu hu yachol l'pattosa shetitein lo reshut* — proper conduct demands that he not bear the burden of a sin, even if he is capable of persuading his wife to grant permission. There is permission and there is permission. The husband may be able to talk his wife into consenting to something she would not truly have chosen. Rashi's language — *lo yisa alav cheit* — is powerful: this is not merely a matter of sensitivity or etiquette, but carries the weight of sin. It is an important reminder that *halakha* and morality do not always fully overlap, and that legal entitlement does not exhaust one's moral responsibility.

### Talmud Torah vs Home

The Gemara had already quoted two opinions: Rav's view that a man may be away one month and home one month, and Rabbi Yochanan's view that he may be away one month but must remain home two months. These positions are supported by respective *psukim*. What will emerge across today's *daf* is an ongoing reflection on the tension between a man's obligations at home — whether specifically *onah* or simply his presence and availability to his wife — and his obligation toward *talmud torah*. This tension has contemporary resonance wherever people are consumed by their work or their religious pursuits at the expense of their domestic responsibilities. In the Gemara's context, however, the competing obligations are both religiously freighted, which makes the tension sharper and more interesting. The dynamic will recur throughout the *daf* in different registers, with different voices landing differently on the question of where the balance lies.

---

## Sighing Breaking the Body

### Rav: Half the Body

Just as we had the dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan regarding how long a man may be absent, we now encounter a parallel dispute between the same two authorities on a different matter. Rav states: *anachah shever chatzi gufo shel adam* — sighing breaks half of a person's body. The proof-text is from Yechezkel, where God instructs the prophet: *he'anach beshivron motnayim* — moan with the breaking of the loins. Since the verse specifies the loins — the middle of the body — Rav infers that sighing breaks only half.

### Rabbi Yochanan: Full Body

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *af kol gufo shel adam* — sighing breaks the entire body. His proof-text continues from the same prophetic context: *venamas kol lev, verafu kol yadayim, vechahatah kol ruach, vechol birkayim telechnah mayim* — all hearts melt, all hands weaken, all spirit dims, all knees dissolve into water. The imagery encompasses the whole person.

### Reconciliation

The Gemara presses: how does Rabbi Yochanan handle the verse about the loins, which seems to specify only half the body? He answers: *hahi de'chi matchala mimotnayim matchala* — that is the starting point; the breakdown begins in the loins but spreads to destroy the whole body. And how does Rav handle the more encompassing verse? He says: *shani shemuat Beis HaMikdash detakifa tuva* — the destruction of the Temple is exceptional in its power to devastate. Ordinary sighing does not have that extreme effect.

### Traveler Story

The Gemara then offers a story to illustrate the distinction between acute and habituated grief. A Jew and a non-Jew were walking together. The non-Jew could not keep pace with the Jew, who was walking quickly. The non-Jew then reminded his companion of the destruction of the Temple. The Jew sighed and slowed — yet even so, the non-Jew still could not keep up. The non-Jew said: didn't you just learn in *Gemara Kesuvos* that a sigh breaks half a person's body? The Jew replied: *hanei milei milta chadeta* — that is when the report is new, something freshly devastating. *Aval ha de'dashnan bah* — but this, which we have heard again and again, we have become inured to. People say: a woman who has suffered many miscarriages does not feel the same terror at the next one, because experience has numbed the initial shock. So too, the accumulated suffering visited upon Jews by non-Jews means that revisiting ancient tragedies no longer carries the same physiological impact.

### Sighing & Absence

This parallel dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan seems at first glance to be an independent literary unit, but there is a clear thematic connection to the earlier debate. Rav, who permits a man to be away from home for half the time, effectively says: your wife is sighing and distressed at home — *chatzi gufo*, she will survive it. Rabbi Yochanan, who insists the man be home two months out of three, says: no, *kol gufo shel adam* — the impact of your absence can be entirely destructive, and you cannot permit that. How one assesses the impact of one's absence on a spouse is inevitably filtered through prior assumptions about marriage and *talmud torah*. And the closing note of the story — once you are used to it, it is not so devastating — could plausibly be read as a Babylonian response to the critique of Eretz Yisrael: here in Bavel, our wives are used to it.

---

## EY vs Bavel Dispute

### Monogamy vs Polygamy

The divergence between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan connects to a broader and deeper dispute between Eretz Yisrael and Bavel — one that touches on the very nature of marriage. Eretz Yisrael was already a monogamous society; Bavel permitted polygamy.

### Marriage Intrinsic Value

This institutional difference reflects a difference in how marriage itself was understood. In Eretz Yisrael, marriage appears to have been valued intrinsically. Statements like *kol adam she'eino shari belo isha shari belo tova* — anyone who dwells without a wife dwells without goodness — and the biblical *lo tov heyos ha'adam levado* reflect a sense that marriage is essential to human flourishing for its own sake. In Bavel, by contrast, marriage was understood more instrumentally: a man marries so that he has a legitimate outlet for his desires, which then frees him to devote himself to *talmud torah* without improper thoughts.

### Marriage Before/After To…

This difference manifests directly in the famous dispute in Kiddushin about whether a man should first marry and then learn *torah*, or first learn and then marry. In Bavel, the ruling is to marry first — once you have a wife, your desires are channeled appropriately, and you can go learn. In Eretz Yisrael, the ruling is to learn first, because once you are married — *reichaim betzavaro* — you have domestic responsibilities that you cannot simply set aside. You had better finish your learning before you take on those obligations.

### Rabbi Yochanan EY Positi…

It is therefore entirely unsurprising that Rabbi Yochanan — the great Amora of Eretz Yisrael — insists on two months home and one month away, while Rav, working within the Babylonian framework, permits equal time. The sighing debate is not peripheral; it reflects the same underlying disagreement about what marriage demands and how seriously the husband's absence weighs on the wife. This is a real dispute between two civilizational orientations toward the relationship between marriage and *talmud torah*, not merely a technical disagreement about frequency.

---

## Occupational Classificat…

### Tayalim Daily

The Mishnah states: *hatayalin bechol yom* — the *tayalin*, whoever they are, have a daily *mitzvat onah* when the wife is not in a state of *niddah*. There is an important background consideration here: in the era of the Gemara, *niddah* lasted approximately one week per month, whereas today it extends to nearly two weeks, which proportionally reduces the applicable *onah* obligation.

The Gemara asks: *mai tayalin*? Rava answers: *bnei pirkei* — those who come and study at a local *yeshiva* and return home each day. Because they are not worn out by physical labor and are at home each night, their *mitzvat onah* is daily, assuming the wife is interested.

### Wives Torah Students

Abaye objects. He cites the verse *shav lachem mashkimei kum, me'acharei shevet, ochlei lechem ha'atzavim* — it is vain for you to rise early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of toil — and the continuation: *ken yitein liyidido shena* — God will provide for His beloved in sleep. Rav Yitzchak applies this to the wives of Torah scholars: *eilu neshoteihem shel talmidei chachamim shemenadedot shena me'eineihem* — these are the wives of Torah scholars who chase sleep from their eyes in this world and thereby merit the life of the world to come. These women are working through the night to support their husbands' learning. If the wives are losing sleep because of their domestic labors and the husbands are returning home only late at night, how can one describe the daily frequency as the norm? Abaye therefore concludes that the *tayalin* must refer to something else — specifically to people like Rav Shmuel bar Shilat, as Rav taught.

### Wealthy Independents

The correct referent for *tayalin* is the independently wealthy person who lives modestly off his own means. *Kegon Rav Shmuel bar Shilat de'achal midideih* — he eats and drinks from his own resources and sleeps in the shade of his own home, *velo chalif peristaka demalka avaveih* — and the king's tax collector does not pass his door, because he conducts himself inconspicuously and thus avoids the attention of the government. This person has no need to labor strenuously, no financial obligations to others, and no demands on his time and energy. For such a person, the *mitzvat onah* applies daily.

### Ravin on Pampered

When Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael, he offered a parallel formulation: *kegon mefankei dema'arava* — like the pampered ones of the West, meaning Eretz Yisrael. The term *mefunack* suggests not spoiled in a pejorative sense, but independently sustained — wealthy individuals who do not work for a living, consistent with the category described above.

### Bathhouse Stories

At this point the Gemara provides two vivid anecdotes that illustrate what it means to be among the *mefankei dema'arava*. Rabbi Abbahu was in a bathhouse being supported by two servants — presumably because of his considerable physical bulk, which, as has been noted in scholarship on Babylonian imaginings of the sages of Eretz Yisrael, may reflect an orientalist projection of what wealthy and prominent figures looked like. The floor of the bathhouse collapsed beneath him, but he managed to catch himself on one of the supporting pillars — the kind visible at sites like Metzada, where the floor of the bathing area was suspended above the heated space below. Not only did he save himself, but he pulled both servants up as well. Similarly, Rabbi Yochanan was ascending steps, supported by Rav Ami and Rav Assi, when a step broke beneath him. He too pulled himself up and brought his attendants with him. When the rabbis asked why, if they were so strong, they needed to be supported in the first place, the reply was: *im ken ma ani mani'ach lezikna* — if I use my strength now, what will I preserve for old age?

These stories are presented in connection with the discussion of *mefankei dema'arava*, but they carry an additional resonance worth noting. Later in the *daf* we will encounter a story in which a roof collapses beneath a husband who has neglected his wife — a collapse that results in his death. Here, by contrast, things breaking underneath carries no such moral weight; the rabbis escape, even saving others. The contrast matters. The rabbis of Eretz Yisrael — Rabbi Yochanan, Rabbi Abbahu — are not the ones abandoning their wives. Their world is one of greater attentiveness to domestic obligation, which is precisely why the same image of collapse means something entirely different in their stories.

---

## Workers & Onah

### Workers Local vs Travel

The Mishnah states *v'hapolim shtayim bashabbat* — workers twice a week. But a *Braita* teaches *poel achas bashabbat* — once a week. Rabbi Yosi berabbi Chanina resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya kan be'osei melacha b'irono kan be'osei melacha b'ir acheres* — there is no difficulty; it depends on whether they are working in their own town or in a different town. Workers employed locally have more energy, return home each night, and thus fulfill *onah* twice weekly. Workers who commute to another town, even if they return the same day, are more worn out and are reduced to once a week. The *Braita* then confirms this distinction explicitly.

### Donkey Drivers

*Hachamorim achas bashabbat* — donkey drivers are obligated once a week.

---

## Neder & Divorce

### One Week Neder Q

Rabba bar Rav Chanan raises a question to Abaye. The Mishnah teaches that if a man takes a *neder* not to have relations with his wife, he must divorce her after one week according to Beis Hillel. But looking at the Mishnah's own classification of *onah* frequencies, very few men had an obligation more frequent than once a week — only the independently wealthy (daily) and local workers (twice weekly). Most men were obligated once a week or less. So if a man takes a *neder* for one week, what has he really withheld? For someone obligated once a week, he has missed exactly one *onah*. And for camel drivers or sailors, whose obligation falls far less frequently, a one-week *neder* withholds nothing at all. Why should such a *neder* compel divorce?

### Bread in Basket

Abaye replies: *eino domeh mi sheyesh lo pas besalo l'mi she'ein lo pas besalo* — one who has bread in his basket is not comparable to one who does not. The operative factor is not the frequency of actual relations, but the wife's knowledge that her husband is *legally available* to her at any moment. When he is merely traveling for work or absent for legitimate reasons, there is no barrier in principle — he could return, the opportunity exists. But a *neder* creates an actual legal prohibition. Even for someone whose normal *onah* frequency is once every six months, the existence of a formal *neder* — which forecloses the possibility of intimacy — constitutes a sufficient rupture of the marital bond to warrant divorce after one week. The absence of the bread from the basket, not merely its infrequency, is what matters.

---

## Job Change

### Occupation Switch

Rabba bar Rav Chanan poses a further question to Abaye: *chamor vena'aseh gamal mai* — what if a donkey driver wishes to become a camel driver? Moving from donkey driving to camel driving means longer journeys, greater absence from home, and a corresponding reduction in *onah* frequency. May he make this change without his wife's permission?

### Wife's Preference

The answer: *rotzah ishah be-kav ve-tiflut me-asarah kabin u-frishut* — a woman prefers one measure with *tiflut* over ten measures with abstinence. The word *tiflut* is somewhat loaded — it connotes something trivial or insubstantial, not a fully dignified expression of marital intimacy. The Gemara could have stated the principle in a more straightforward way: a man has a primary obligation to his wife and may not unilaterally reduce his presence. Instead, it frames the point through a somewhat unflattering characterization of women's preferences. The underlying *halakhic* conclusion is nonetheless clear: the husband may not unilaterally switch to an occupation that diminishes his availability to his wife without her consent.

### Rosh Exception

The Rosh adds an important qualification to this principle: if the proposed change is not a different occupation but a commitment to *talmud torah*, the husband does not require his wife's permission. The obligation and value of *talmud torah* stands apart from the ordinary calculus of occupational change, and a husband is entitled to pursue it even if it increases his absence, without seeking her approval for that specific transition.

---

## Sailors & Rabbi Eliezer

### Sailors Six Months

*Ha-sapanim achat le-shishah chodashim — divrei Rabbi Eliezer* — sailors, once every six months — this is the position of Rabbi Eliezer. Rav Bruna said in the name of Rav: *halakhah ke-Rabbi Eliezer* — we rule in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer.

### 2-3 Year Absence

Rav Adda bar Ahava said in the name of Rav: *zu divrei Rabbi Eliezer* — this is the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer specifically. But the Sages say: *ha-talmidim yotzin le-Talmud Torah be' ve-gimel shanim shelo bi-reshut* — Torah students may go out for two or three years to study without express permission from their wives. This reveals that the debate implicit in the phrase *divrei Rabbi Eliezer* at the end of the Mishnah is not primarily about the general classification of occupational *onah* frequencies. It is specifically about how long a Torah student may be absent from home. Rabbi Eliezer's position, as understood by the Gemara, is that the framework of the Mishnah applies — a month away without permission. The opposing Sages permit two or three years.

It should be noted in passing that there is another possible axis of dispute with Rabbi Eliezer that the Gemara does not pursue here but which is developed elsewhere: how to conceptualize the fundamental nature of *onah* itself. Rabbi Eliezer understands *onah* as a calendar-based frequency. An alternative understanding — and there are *poskim* who hold this represents the *de-Oraita* obligation — is that *onah* is contextual and demand-based: a man is obligated to be available to his wife whenever she wishes. This reading may be reflected in Rabbi Yehoshua's position. But the Gemara here directs the debate toward the question of extended absence for *talmud torah*, and that is where it proceeds.

### Students' Self-Reliance

Rava states: *samchu Rabanan ad'Rav Adda bar Ahava va'avdu uvda benafshayhu* — the rabbinic students relied on Rav Adda bar Ahava's articulation of the Sages' position and ruled for themselves accordingly, permitting themselves extended absence from home. Rashi presses the phrase *benafshayhu* — "with their own souls" — beyond the ordinary sense of ruling for oneself. He reads it as: they acted, but in doing so they were risking their own lives. The story that follows demonstrates exactly this.

---

## Rav Rechumi Story

### Rashi Risk Interpretation

The Ra'avad reads *va'avdu uvda benafshayhu* differently — not as risking one's life, but simply as ruling for themselves in a self-determined way. On the Ra'avad's reading, the position of the Sages permitting two to three years represents the operative *halakha*, and the students were entitled to rely on it. Rashi, by contrast, injects a note of moral caution: you may have the legal right, but you are playing with fire.

### Annual Return Delayed

*Ki ha de'Rav Rechumi* — like the story of Rav Rechumi. The name itself — *Rechumi*, cognate with *rachamim*, compassion — is resonant. He would regularly study with Rava in Mechuza. His practice was to return home once a year, on *Erev Yom Kippur*. One year, *yoma chad mashchateih shema'ta* — he became absorbed in a particularly engaging topic of learning and the learning stretched on.

### Wife's Tear Collapses

His wife was waiting at home, looking out repeatedly: *hashta ati, hashta ati* — now he will come, now he will come. He did not come. *Chalash da'ata* — she despaired. *Achit dima'ta me'eina* — a single tear fell from her eye. He was sitting on the roof. *Ifchit igra mituteih* — the roof collapsed beneath him, and *venach nafsheih* — he died.

Here again we have something collapsing beneath a rabbi — but this collapse is entirely different from the bathhouse stories above. There the collapse was incidental, almost comic, and the rabbis emerged stronger. Here a single tear causes the roof to give way and the scholar dies. The juxtaposition is stark, and the connection to the earlier discussion of sighing — *anacha shoveret gufo shel adam* — is unmistakable. Something did break; it was not the wife's body, but the roof, and the husband beneath it.

### Ra'avad vs Rashi

The Ra'avad, consistent with his more permissive reading, largely sets aside the cautionary implications of this story. He acknowledges that in principle the *halakha* permits two to three years of absence, but draws a practical lesson from the narrative: even if you are legally entitled to be away, make every effort to keep the one commitment you have made — come home on *Erev Yom Kippur* if that is what you promised. The Rif does not bring Rav Adda bar Ahava's ruling at all, holding that the *halakha* follows Rabbi Eliezer — which limits permissible unauthorized absence to one month, not two or three years. The Ramah rules like Rav Adda bar Ahava, based on the fact that the Gemara reports that the students *relied* on his ruling, treating it as the operative position. And the Ra'avad attempts to reintegrate both the legal entitlement and the moral responsibility: yes, we *pasken* like the Sages for two or three years — but let the story of the collapsing roof temper how you exercise that entitlement.

---

## Torah Scholars Onah

### Friday to Friday

The Mishnah discussed the *onah* for Torah scholars in terms of how long they may be absent without permission, but it does not specify the actual frequency of their *onah* obligation. The Gemara addresses this directly. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *me'erev Shabbos l'erev Shabbos* — from Shabbat eve to Shabbat eve, meaning Friday night.

### Oneg Shabbat

Rashi explains: *shehu leil ta'anug u'shvita ve'hana'at haguf* — Friday night is a night of pleasure, rest, and bodily enjoyment, making it the appropriate and natural time for *onah* as part of *oneg Shabbos*. This is also significant in light of certain sectarian positions of the *Bayit Sheni* period that prohibited marital relations on Shabbat. The Gemara here affirms not only that Shabbat night is permitted, but that it is the designated *onah* time for Torah scholars. Rav Yehuda — and this is also cited in the names of Rav Huna and Rav Nachman — adds: *ze hamishamesh mitaso me'erev Shabbos l'erev Shabbos* — one who maintains relations on a weekly Friday-night cycle fulfills the verse *asher piryo yiten be'ito*, the fruit given in its proper time, which also implies that children conceived in this manner and at this time will be born well.

---

## Yehuda Bar Chiya

### Weekly Returns

Yehuda the son of Rabbi Chiya — and son-in-law of Rabbi Yanai — would go and sit in the house of his *rebbe*. Every *Erev Shabbat*, at nightfall — as Tosafot notes, *bei shimshai* refers to the *bein hashmashos* of Friday evening — he would return home. And when he would return, *hava kachazi amuda d'nura* — a pillar of fire would be seen preceding him, marking his arrival.

### Missed Sign

One Friday, *yoma chad mashcheih shema'ta* — he became absorbed in his learning and did not return.
