When the members of the household did not see the usual sign — the pillar of fire — Rabbi Yanai, his father-in-law, said to the household: *kifu mitasu* — overturn the bed, the sign of mourning and *aveilus*. His reasoning: *she'ilmalei Yehuda kayam, lo bital onaso* — if Yehuda were still alive, he would never have shirked his obligation and missed coming home. Therefore, his failure to appear could only mean that he had died.

### Death from Word

*Hava kishgaga sheyotzei milifnei hashalit* — it was like an error that goes out from the presence of a ruler, words spoken by an important person that take on the force of reality. And indeed, *venach nafsheih* — Rav Yehuda died.

### Duty Message

This story is striking in its severity. The wife is not described as weeping; there is no tear, no visible suffering. The mere fact that the husband failed to fulfill his *onah* obligation — that he was not home on *Erev Shabbat* as he always had been — was itself treated as proof of death and triggered a verbal decree that became reality. The message is unambiguous: the *onah* of Torah scholars is not optional or subject to casual revision, even for a single week. This stands in sharp contrast to the earlier stories about twelve-year absences, and the range of stories presented in this *daf* reflects genuinely different valuations of how far *talmud torah* may impinge on domestic responsibility.

---

## Rabbi Judah's Son

### Bride Dies

The Gemara now records that Rebbi — Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi — arranged a match for his son with the family of Rabbi Chiya, to one of Rabbi Chiya's daughters. When they came to write the *kesuvah*, the bride died.

### Yichus Problem

Rebbi was disturbed: *chas v'shalom, psulei ika* — is there perhaps some disqualification, some problem with this union, that caused it to be prevented? They sat and examined the lineages. Rebbi descended from Shefatya ben Avital — Avital being one of David's wives — establishing his descent from the royal house of David. Rabbi Chiya descended from Shimi, David's brother — an honorable lineage, but not the royal line itself. This mismatch of *yichus* was identified as the source of the problem, and the bride's death was understood as a providential intervention preventing an unsuitable match.

### Second Marriage

Rebbi then arranged a match for his son with the family of Rabbi Yossi ben Zimra.

---

## 12 Years Pre-Marriage

### Bride Walks Forward

The agreement reached with Rabbi Yossi ben Zimra's family was that Rebbi's son would be supported for twelve years of study in *yeshiva* before the marriage. This reflects the Eretz Yisrael approach: learn first, then marry, so that you are not compelled to abandon your new wife for the *beis medrash*. However, the *kallah*'s family moved to accelerate matters. They had the bride walk before him — a pointed reminder of what was waiting for him — as if to ask: are you certain you want to wait?

### Marry Then Learn

He responded: *nava shish shanin* — perhaps six years would suffice. They had her walk before him again. At that point he said, *ichnis v'hadar eizil* — I will marry now, and then go to learn. This represents a capitulation to the Babylonian model: marry first, then pursue *talmud torah*. He was embarrassed before his father, who had envisioned twelve years of unencumbered study.

### Biblical Timeline

His father reassured him: *beni, da'as koncha yesh becha* — my son, you think like your Creator. He drew an analogy from the *Shirat HaYam*: the verse first says *t'vi'eimo v'sita'eimo behar nachalatcha* — bring them and plant them on the mountain of Your inheritance — meaning the people would enter the land and only then build the Temple. Yet God was so eager that He immediately said *v'asu li mikdash v'shachanti b'tocham* — make Me a sanctuary and I will dwell among them — advancing the union. So too, the son should not feel that his choice was wrong.

### Return Wife Sterile

He went and studied for twelve years in *yeshiva*. When he returned — *ad d'ata itkar d'vattayhu* — his wife had become sterile. Apparently he had not been present to fulfill his marital obligations; the marriage, though contracted, had been effectively abandoned during those twelve years. He had sought the best of both models and wound up satisfying neither: he married, but then behaved as if he had not.

### Rav Solutions

Rav considered the options: *nigrisha* — should he divorce her and marry another woman to have children? But then people would say: *ani azo l'shav shimra* — this poor woman waited in vain for twelve years. Should he take a second wife to have children, as was possible in Babylonian practice? Then people would say: *zu ishto v'zu zonoso* — this is his wife and this is his mistress. Neither option was acceptable.

### Prayer & Cure

So *ba'ei lei rachamei v'isis* — Rav prayed on her behalf, and she was healed. The problem was resolved through prayer. This reflects a distinctively Babylonian sensibility: yes, things went wrong, real harm was done — but the *Eibishter* can help, and solutions exist. The story does not minimize the consequences of neglecting domestic obligation, but neither does it leave the situation as irreparable tragedy.

---

## Rabbi Chanina Story

### Rabbi Shimeon Delay

Rabbi Chanina ben Chachinai was preparing to travel to his *rebbe*'s *yeshiva*. He was departing *b'shilhei hillula d'Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai* — at the conclusion of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's wedding celebrations. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai asked him to wait until the wedding week was over so they could travel to the *yeshiva* together. This request itself gestures toward the Eretz Yisrael sensibility: even one committed to *talmud torah* is expected to complete his week of marriage before departing.

### Chanina Proceeds

Rabbi Chanina did not wait. He went immediately and sat in the *yeshiva* for twelve years. We hear nothing further of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai — presumably he spent more time at home before eventually departing, which the story implies was the appropriate path.

### Lost Roads

After twelve years, Rabbi Chanina returned — but *ishtannu shivilei d'massa* — all the roads of the city had changed and he could not find his way home. He sat by the riverbank, disoriented, like someone waking after a very long absence from a world that had moved on without him.

### Hears Daughter

He overheard people calling out to a young woman: *bas Chachinai, bas Chachinai, malli kulskha v'sa nizil* — daughter of Chachinai, fill your basket and let's go. He said: I can infer from this that this girl is ours — she is my daughter. He followed her home.

### Wife Dies Shock

His wife was sitting inside, working with flour. She lifted her eyes, saw her husband who had been gone for twelve years — and *savyei libba* — her heart seized. *Parach rucha* — her spirit departed. She died from the shock of his sudden reappearance.

### Prayer Revives

He cried out: *Ribbono Shel Olam, aniya zo, zeh secharah* — Master of the Universe, is this her reward? He prayed for her, and she was revived. And here an important observation must be made: whereas in the story of the Rav Rechumi the husband died as a consequence of his neglect, in this story of Rabbi Chanina ben Chachinai it is the wife who suffers — and even then, she is revived through prayer. The husband does not bear the ultimate consequence. The asymmetry is significant: even in a story that is ostensibly cautionary, the man who abandons his wife for twelve years is not the one who pays with his life.

---

## Rabbi Chama Story

### Advance Notice

Rabbi Chama bar Bissa went and studied in the *beis medrash* for twelve years. When it was time to return, he said to himself: *lo e'evid ke-Rabbi Chanina ben Chachinai* — I will not do what Rabbi Chanina ben Chachinai did. He would not simply appear at home after twelve years and risk killing his wife with shock. Instead, he settled in the *yeshiva* at the edge of his hometown and sent word to his household that he was returning, giving his wife time to prepare herself emotionally.

### Son Recognition

His son Rabbi Oshaya came to the local *beis medrash* — not knowing, of course, that the scholar who had arrived was his father — and began studying with him. Rabbi Chama was immediately struck by the young man's sharpness and depth. *Chalash da'ateih* — he despaired and grew despondent, thinking: *i havai hacha, havai li zara ki hai* — had I stayed at home, I could have raised and educated a son as sharp as this. Of course, it was his son. He came into his home, and his son followed him inside — Rabbi Chama still did not recognize him, and rose to honor the distinguished visitor.

### Three-Bound Cord

His wife said to him: *mi ika abba d'kai mikmei bera* — is there a father who stands up for his own son? At that moment he realized who the young man was. He cited the verse about him: *hachut hameshulash lo bimehera yinatek* — a three-ply cord is not easily broken — for here was a chain of Torah scholarship: Rav Bissa, his father Rabbi Chama bar Bissa, and now his son Rabbi Oshaya, each a great *talmid chacham*. The Torah had passed through the generations despite — or perhaps alongside — the extended absences.

The message of this story, like the one before it, is genuinely mixed. There is a poignancy to the moment: Rabbi Chama did not know his own son. He had missed twelve years of his son's development and formation. Yet the ending does not dwell on that loss. The *hachut hameshulash* passage frames the outcome triumphantly. The Torah continuity is intact, the son is remarkable, and the family is reunited. The Gemara is not pretending there are no costs to twelve years of absence — the estrangement, the strangeness of not recognizing one's own child — but the overall arc of these stories, told through a Babylonian lens, tends toward resolution and even vindication.

---

## Rabbi Akiva Story

### Akiva Marriage

We now come to the most famous story of the *daf*, which extends the twelve-year framework to twenty-four. Rabbi Akiva was the shepherd of Kalba Savua, one of the wealthiest men in Jerusalem. Kalba Savua's daughter perceived that he was *tznia u-mali* — modest and of fine character. She said to him: if I agree to marry you, will you go and study in *yeshiva*? He agreed. *Ikdashalah betzina* — he married her in secret. *Ve-shadrateih* — she sent him off to learn. When the father heard, he expelled her from his home and took a vow forbidding her from deriving any benefit from his considerable wealth, furious that his daughter had married this ignoramus.

### First 12 Years

Rabbi Akiva went and learned in *yeshiva* for twelve years. When he was about to return, he overheard an old man speaking to his wife: *ad kama kamitbartat almanut chayut* — how long will you live the life of a living widow? She replied: *i ledidi tzaias, yativ treisar shani achrinei* — if my husband would listen to me, he should stay there another twelve years. At that, Rabbi Akiva said: *bi-reshut ka-avadna* — I am acting with her permission. And he turned back.

This moment is worth pausing over. Tosafot notes that this marks a significant shift in the Gemara's overall arc. Near the beginning of the *daf*, the concern was precisely that a husband might pressure his wife into granting permission she did not truly wish to give. Here, the wife is the one actively urging the husband to continue learning. The difference between the stories is not only one of different legal opinions or cultural frameworks, but also of different types of wives and different types of marriages — ones in which the wife is a genuine, enthusiastic partner in the enterprise of *talmud torah*, not merely a reluctant or resigned participant. Many *kollel* wives today inhabit exactly this kind of partnership — though how much is intrinsic and how much is shaped by the surrounding culture is a question the Gemara does not answer.

### Return with Students

Rabbi Akiva returned after another twelve years — twenty-four in total — bringing with him twenty-four thousand students. His wife heard and came out to greet him.

### Wife Knows Soul

Her neighbors urged her: *shili mani levushei ve-ichasi* — borrow some fine clothes and dress properly to greet your husband. She replied: *yodea tzaddik nefesh behemto* — the righteous man knows the soul of his animal. She was describing herself through this verse, which carries a somewhat discordant note — she speaks of herself as a beast, in a very self-effacing way, though one recalls that her name was Rachel, which is itself the word for ewe. The language is striking in its degree of submission, whatever the underlying intention.

### Wife Partnership

When she reached him and fell at his feet — *nafla al apa, ka-menashka* — kissing his feet, his attendant moved to push her away, as it was unseemly. Rabbi Akiva stopped him: *shabkuna, sheli ve-shelachem shelah hu* — leave her; everything that is mine and yours is hers. The partnership he articulates is complete. All the Torah, all the students, all the achievement — she shares in it equally.

### Father Reconciles

Kalba Savua heard that a great *talmid chacham* had arrived in the city and went to seek an annulment of the vow he had made years earlier forbidding his daughter from his wealth. He did not yet know that this great scholar was his son-in-law. Rabbi Akiva asked him: when you made that vow, would you have made it even if you had known that she would marry a great Torah scholar? Kalba Savua replied: *afilu perek echad afilu halacha achas* — even if he had known one chapter, one *halacha* of Torah, I would never have made the vow. Rabbi Akiva then revealed: *ana hu* — I am the man. Kalba Savua fell on his face, kissed his feet — mirroring his daughter's gesture — and gave him half his wealth. The story that began with exile from wealth ends with its restoration, and more. Twelve plus twelve years of *talmud torah*, a wife's genuine consent, and the outcome is students, wealth, and reconciliation.

### Daughter & Ben Azai

*Barteih de-Rabbi Akiva avdah lei le-Ben Azai hachi* — Rabbi Akiva's daughter made the same arrangement with Ben Azai, who is elsewhere known as one whose *toraso umnasao* — his Torah was his entire occupation, such that he famously did not marry. Here his daughter of Rabbi Akiva made a similar pact with him. *Ve-hainu d'amrei inshi, racheila basar racheila azla* — that is what people say: one sheep follows another. The name *Rachel* is the word for ewe, and Rabbi Akiva's wife was named Rachel. *Ke-ovdei ima kach ovdei barta* — as the mother did, so the daughter.

---

## Rav Yosef Story

### Early Return

Rav Yosef the son of Rava was sent by his father to learn in the *yeshiva* of Rav Yosef. They agreed on six years — not twelve. After three years, it was *Erev Yom Kippur*, and he thought to return home for a visit before completing his six years. He got up and came home early.

### Father Attacks

His father heard that his son was returning before the agreed six years were up. He took a weapon — *shakol mana* — and went out to confront him. He said: *zonachta nizkarta* — you remembered your prostitute? The implication: you were so consumed by your desire to see your wife that you broke your commitment to learning. An alternative version: *yonachta nizkarta* — you remembered your dove — which is less harsh but still dismissive, still insisting the son should not have returned early.

### Yom Kippur Fast

In the confrontation that ensued, *itrid* — they became so agitated and absorbed that *lo mar ifsach ve-lo mar ifsach* — neither the father nor the son managed to eat their *seudah mafsekes*, the final meal before the *Yom Kippur* fast. The *Yom Kippur* connection recurs pointedly throughout the *daf*: Rav Rechumi came home once a year on *Erev Yom Kippur* and died when he failed to do so; Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiya came home every *Erev Shabbat*; here the son is coming home after three years and is met with anger for returning too early.

### Concluding Message

The *daf* ends with this confrontation. And the implicit final message is one that the *yeshivot* in Eretz Yisrael sometimes invoke — but which the Gemara itself uses to draw a different conclusion. The stories of Rabbi Akiva involve twelve years and then another twelve years. Those in the *yeshiva* world who cite such stories to justify extended unbroken absence sometimes present twelve-plus-twelve as equivalent to twenty-four. But they are not the same. Rabbi Akiva *returned* after the first twelve years — he came home, heard his wife's voice urging him to go back, and only then went back. He did not simply disappear for twenty-four years without contact. The final story of Rav Yosef's son makes the same point in reverse: a son who tries to come home after three of six years is prevented from doing so — but a six-year agreement is a six-year agreement, not a twelve-year one. The structures and the commitments matter, and the Gemara's rich and sometimes contradictory collection of stories does not resolve easily into a single ruling, but it leaves the attentive reader with a sense that both poles — the obligations of *talmud torah* and the obligations of marriage — demand to be taken with full seriousness, and that collapsing one into the other comes at a cost.

---

---

# Ketubot 63

## Moredet Overview

### Onah to Moredet

Today's daf begins towards the bottom of 63a, where the Mishnah transitions from the topic of *onah* — the husband's obligation to have marital relations at regular intervals — into the subject of the *moredet*, a wife who is not living up to her responsibilities in the marriage. The earlier Mishnah had framed *onah* in terms of frequency, and the preceding Gemara had explored the tension between *talmud Torah* and a man's obligations at home. Now the Mishnah turns to examine the range of mutual responsibilities between husband and wife, and what happens when one party fails to meet them.

The term *moredet* — "one who rebels" — is the central concept here, along with its less common counterpart, *mored*, referring to a husband who similarly fails his obligations. This passage carries enormous practical weight, both for questions of *agunah* and for broader questions about how rabbinic courts should approach a marriage that is no longer functioning as it should.

### Mishna Penalties

The Mishnah states: *hamoredet al ba'alah* — a woman who rebels against her husband — *pofsin lach mi-ktuvatah*, we reduce the value of her *ketubah*. The mechanism is a progressive monetary fine: for each week that she remains in a state of rebellion, the total value of her *ketubah* is reduced. The *ketubah*'s total value encompasses the base amount — 100 or 200 *zuz* — plus whatever *tosefet* the husband added, plus the value of the dowry she brought into the marriage. All of this is slowly diminished on a weekly basis, so that even if she subsequently reconciles herself to her obligations, she will be unable to collect the full value of the *ketubah* upon divorce or the husband's death.

The Mishnah specifies the rate of reduction: *shiva dinarim b'shabbos*, seven *dinar* per week. Rabbi Yehudah says the rate is seven *tarpeikin*. The Gemara will clarify the precise monetary values involved and what they represent relative to the 200 *zuz* base amount. As to how long this process continues: *ad keneged ktuvatah*, until the total *ketubah* is reduced to zero. Rabbi Yosei disagrees and says *le'olam hu pofes v'holech* — one continues to reduce even into negative territory, so that she actually incurs a debt to her husband. The practical significance of this is that *she'im tipol lah yerusha mimakom acher* — if she ever comes into money from another source — *goveh mimena*, he can collect from her.

### Mored Reciprocal

The Mishnah then turns to the reciprocal case: *v'chein hamored al ishto*, a husband who rebels against his wife. Here the remedy runs in the opposite direction: *mosifin al kesuvatah*, we increase the amount of her *ketubah*. The practical impact, however, is similarly deferred — it is only felt when the *ketubah* becomes payable. The rate of increase is *sheloshah dinarim b'shabbos*, three *dinar* per week — less than half the rate applied to the wife. Rabbi Yehudah sets his rate at three *tarpeikin*. Why the disparity between the fine imposed on her and the one imposed on him? The Gemara will address this, but the asymmetry is already striking.

---

## Sex vs. Labor Debate

### Rav Huna: Sex

Before the Gemara addresses the monetary mechanics, it raises a prior question: *moredet mimah* — in what domain is the wife rebelling? Rav Huna says: *mi-tashmish hamitah* — she is refusing sexual relations. This is noteworthy, because the earlier Mishnah never explicitly stated that she has an obligation to have sex with her husband; it was simply assumed. If the Mishnah already detailed his obligation to have sex with her at regular intervals, it implicitly took her reciprocal obligation for granted. What she is now refusing, on Rav Huna's reading, is precisely that.

### R. Yose bar Chanina: Lab…

Rabbi Yose bar Chanina says: *mim'lachah* — she is refusing to perform her domestic duties, the very obligations detailed at length in the preceding Mishnah, such as cooking, baking, and laundry.

### Tosafot Analysis

Tosafot raises an important question: why not simply say that she can be a *moredet* with respect to either responsibility? The answer, Tosafot suggests, may lie in a position encountered earlier: *yacholah ishah shetomar l'baalah eini nizonas v'eini osah* — a woman is entitled to say to her husband, "I will not be supported by you, and I will not perform domestic labor for you." If that is her right, then refusing her *ma'aseh yadayim* is not a rebellion at all — she is simply exercising a recognized option. On this reading, Rav Huna holds that the only thing she can genuinely rebel against is sex, since refusing *melacha* while waiving *mezonot* is a legitimate choice, not a transgression. Rabbi Yose bar Chanina, by contrast, holds that this option belongs to the husband, not the wife — it is his right to say he will not feed her and she need not work, but she cannot unilaterally declare that arrangement. Even if she offers to waive her *mezonot*, she is still obligated to perform her domestic duties, and refusing them constitutes a genuine *moredet*.

---

## Mored Parallel Case

### If Sex: Parallel Sex

The Gemara now asks how the reciprocal case — the *mored* husband — fits into each position. *Bishlama l'man d'amar mi-tashmish* — if we are speaking about sex refusal, the parallel case is straightforward: the husband is refusing to have sex with his wife. That makes perfect sense as a mirror image.

### If Labor: Parallel Suppo…

*Ela l'man d'amar mimelocha* — if the *moredet* is one who refuses domestic labor, what is the parallel for the husband? He has no comparable domestic labor obligation to her. The Gemara answers: *be-omer eini zan v'eini mefarnes* — the case is one where he says he will refuse to feed her and support her. What does she receive in exchange for her *ma'aseh yadayim*? His *mezonot*. So if she rebels by withholding her labor, the parallel is his withholding her sustenance.

### Rav: Immediate Divorce

At this point the Gemara cites Rav: *ha-omer eini zan v'eini mefarnes yotzi v'yitein kesuvah* — a husband who says he will refuse to provide food and support must immediately divorce his wife and pay the *ketubah*. If that is so, there would seem to be no room for a drawn-out process of weekly increases to the *ketubah* — the obligation is immediate.

### Gemara Resolution

The Gemara responds: *lo l'mimluchi beih bayinan* — we still need to discuss the matter with him. Even if the goal is for him to give a *get*, the practical process of bringing that about may take some weeks. During that period, while the beit din is working toward compelling the divorce, the *ketubah* amount continues to increase. If he changes his behavior in the interim, all the better, but the orientation is not to invest a year or two hoping he will reform — it is to move toward the *get* expeditiously, while leaving a short window during which his behavior might change.

This question — how quickly a rabbinic court should move to dissolve a troubled marriage versus how long it should work to preserve it — is not merely an academic one. It maps directly onto contemporary disputes about the proper role of *batei din* when one party is clearly not meeting their obligations. Too often, courts invoke the rubric of *shalom bayit* to delay resolution in situations that are plainly untenable, when a more direct reading of the Gemara would counsel moving promptly toward the *get*.

One might also ask what exactly is meant by *eini zan v'eini mefarnes*. Rashi understands it to mean the husband is refusing to pay the food bills. Tosafot raises the question of whether it might also mean he refuses to go out and earn a living at all. Tosafot cites Rabbeinu Eliyahu, who argues that a husband is indeed obligated to hire himself out — even to work as a schoolteacher, which was considered a low-prestige occupation — in order to provide his wife's *mezonot*: *mikan mochi'ach Rabbeinu Eliyahu shechayav adam l'haskir atzmo u'l'lamed tinokos o la'asos melacha acheres kedei lazon es ishto*. Rashi, however, understands the obligation only as paying the bills from whatever resources he has. Tosafot then cites Rabbeinu Tam, who limits the work obligation to farming one's own land — *avodas hakarka*, *eflach* as in plowing and tending fields — but stops short of requiring a man to hire himself out to someone else: *aval l'haskir atzmo eino chayav*. The distinction reflects a society in which working one's own land and hiring oneself out for labor were understood as categorically different in terms of dignity and social standing. The underlying question — whether a wife can demand that her husband stop being a deadbeat and go find employment — is very much embedded in the language of the *ketubah* contract itself, with its phrase *v'ana eflach*, "and I will work."

---

## Rabbis' Enactment

### Four-Week Process

The Gemara now introduces a later ruling by the Sages. *Raboseinu chazru v'nimnu* — the rabbis reconsidered and voted — to replace the gradual week-by-week reduction of the *ketubah* with a different mechanism: *machrizin aleiha arba shabbatot zu achar zu*, they make public announcements for four consecutive weeks. At the end of that process, the woman loses the entire *ketubah* at once, however large it may be. The beit din sends her a formal notification: *hevei yoda'at she'afilu kesuvatech me'ah maneh hafsadta* — know that even if your *ketubah* is worth a hundred *maneh*, you have forfeited it. The ברייתא, *braita*, quoted here applies this ruling to a *moredet* who is an *arusah*, a *nesua*, even a *niddah*, even one who is ill, and even a *shomeret yavam*.

This shift from the Mishnah's gradual process to the four-week announcement reflects a decisional judgment — whether strategic, role-based, or diagnostic — that a drawn-out progressive fine is not the right tool. Whether the reasoning is that the rabbis do not see marriage counseling as their function, or that they believe a sufficiently severe and time-limited ultimatum is more effective, or that a marriage which has reached this point is unlikely to recover in any case, the result is a binary choice: change within four weeks, or lose everything and the *get* follows.

The announcements are made in public — *ein machrizin aleha ella bebatei knesiyot uvebatei midrashot* — in synagogues and study halls, plainly using social pressure and public shame as part of the mechanism. One notes the asymmetry: it is not clear from the sources that equivalent public announcements are made when the husband is the *mored*. As Rav Ameimar bar Chama notes, the choice of synagogues is deliberate: since the announcements are to be made on four consecutive *Shabbatot*, and *Shabbos* is when the public is gathered in those spaces, the two facts cohere — the four *shabbatot* of the *braita* are actual Sabbaths, not merely weeks, precisely because that is when the communities assemble.

### When to Engage

A dispute arises regarding when during this four-week process the beit din should directly engage the woman. Rav Ami bar Chama teaches that the beit din sends her two notifications: *achas kodem hachraza v'achas achar hachraza* — one before the announcement process begins, and one after it concludes. This represents a middle position: the court is not merely making passive public announcements and waiting; it actively reaches out to her at both ends of the process. Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda publicly declared that the *halacha* follows *raboseinu* — which, on Tosafot's reading, means we reach out only at the end, not at the beginning.

### Rava's Position

Rava objects to Rav Nachman's ruling, calling it *burcha* — foolish. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak responds that the ruling was not original to Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda but was transmitted from Rabbi Yose bar Chanina, a figure of considerable standing. The underlying dispute is then clarified through a further citation: *Rava amar Rav Sheshet, halacha nimlachim bah* — the *halacha* is that we do engage her, that we actively deliberate with her during the process. *Rav Huna bar Yehuda amar Rav Sheshet, halacha ein nimlachim bah* — no, we do not engage her at all; we make the public announcements, give her fair warning through those announcements, and then the *get* is given. There is no direct conversation with her from the beit din.

The result is three distinct positions along a spectrum: the Mishnah's drawn-out progressive fine over potentially many months or years; the four-week process with active engagement from the beit din at the start; and the four-week process with no direct engagement at all — announcements only, followed by loss of *ketubah* and *get*. Each reflects a different understanding of the court's role and its assessment of whether behavioral change in such cases is achievable.

---

## Ma'is Alai Case

### Ameimark Distinction

Having established the various procedural approaches to the *moredet*, the Gemara now introduces a critical distinction made by Ameimar. The cases discussed so far all involve a woman who is refusing relations or domestic labor but who has not said that the marriage itself is intolerable — she is using refusal as leverage, whether out of anger or some marital dispute. Ameimar describes this as *de-amra be'ina lei u-metza'arna lei* — she is saying, in effect, "I do want to be with him, but I am making him suffer." In such a case, there is reason to believe that her behavior can change — she is angry, she has not abandoned the marriage in principle, and therefore the processes described above make sense.

### Rav Sheshet vs. Mar Zutra

Ameimar distinguishes this from the case of *ma'is alai* — where the woman says she finds her husband repulsive and will never be able to live with him again. In this case, *lo kaifinan lah* — we do not employ financial penalties to try to force a change in her behavior. Mar Zutra, however, disagrees: *amar Mar Zutra, kaifinan lah* — even in the case of *ma'is alai*, we impose financial penalties and attempt to compel her to continue the marriage.

It is worth pausing to appreciate how disturbing Mar Zutra's position is. We are speaking of a woman who has declared that she finds her husband completely intolerable, that she cannot live with him, that she will never have sexual relations with him again. Mar Zutra's position is that we should apply financial pressure to coerce her back into the marriage — and into the marital bed — simply because sufficient financial threat might break her refusal. Even granting the most charitable interpretation — that Mar Zutra believes her attitude, not merely her behavior, might genuinely change — the posture of compelling a woman to have sexual relations with a man she explicitly finds repulsive is profoundly troubling. The language of Rashi's understanding of *lo kaifinan lah* is telling: *lo kaifinan lah lish'osei ela notnin lah get ve-yotzei be-lo ketubah* — we do not force her to remain with him; rather, the *get* is given and she leaves without her *ketubah*. That is the position the Gemara ultimately accepts.

### Mar Zutra Case

The Gemara records that Mar Zutra actually acted on his ruling: *hava uvda ve-achfa Mar Zutra* — there was a case and Mar Zutra compelled the woman to remain with her husband even in the case of *ma'is alai*. The outcome was that *ve-nafik minei Rabbi Chanina mi-Sura* — the great Rabbi Chanina from Sura was born from her having been compelled to continue that marriage. The implication is that perhaps we should always force couples to remain together in such cases, since great things can emerge from it.

The Gemara immediately dismisses this: *ve-lav hi, hatam siyata di-shmaya hava* — that cannot be used as proof; what happened there was a specially ordained divine intervention. The Gemara's rejection is striking in its reasoning. Whether one reads a case as evidence for a general rule or as a miraculous exception depends entirely on one's prior orientation. If one begins from the premise that we should keep marriages together at all costs, the story of Rabbi Chanina from Sura looks like compelling evidence. If one begins from the premise that a woman who says *ma'is alai* is describing an intolerable situation, the same story is read as an inexplicable exception from which no normative conclusions may be drawn. The Gemara chooses the latter reading.

### Agunah Implications

The more consequential question that the *ma'is alai* discussion opens up is not merely whether we impose financial penalties on the woman, but whether, once beit din declares *lo kaifinan lah*, we also compel the husband to give a *get*. The Gemara itself does not address this directly. The situation it describes — we will not try to force her to change, you are entitled to divorce her without paying the *ketubah* — leaves open the scenario in which the husband responds: I do not want to divorce her. I am content to remain married even without sexual relations. I know she will lose her *ketubah* if I eventually choose to give the *get*, but I choose not to.

Tosafot addresses this gap directly. One opinion holds that *kofin oto lehotzi* — we compel him to give the *get*. Rabbeinu Tam rejects this: *denichos shema einah nassan b'acherin* — perhaps she is only claiming *ma'is alai* because she has her eye on someone else. Allowing her declaration alone to trigger compelled divorce would fundamentally shift the balance of marital power, enabling a woman to exit any marriage she chose simply by declaring it intolerable, forfeiting the *ketubah* but gaining freedom. Rabbeinu Tam views this as an unacceptable result.

The Rambam, however, rules that if a woman says *ma'is alai*, we do compel the husband to give a *get*. The Rambam employs the formulation drawn from the Gemara: *ein adam dar bekhfifah im hanachash* — one cannot be forced to live under the same roof as a serpent. If a person finds their partner genuinely impossible to live with, beit din does not force cohabitation. On the Rambam's ruling, the woman's declaration of *ma'is alai* therefore generates a compellable obligation on the husband to divorce her.

The *Rishonei Ashkenaz*, led by Rabbeinu Tam, disagree, and in Ashkenazic practice the Rambam's position has not been accepted. The practical consequences are enormous: the rejection of the Rambam's ruling is one of the pillars of the contemporary *agunah* crisis. If a woman could say *ma'is alai* and thereby trigger a beit din's compulsion of the *get*, the *agunah* problem — in which a husband refuses indefinitely to give a *get* — would be substantially resolved. The Ashkenazic response invokes *shalom bayit* and the concern of *shema natna eineha b'acher*, that she may simply want out of the marriage for her own reasons, as grounds for withholding that power from the woman.

Some historians have argued that the Rambam's ruling was partly shaped by the social reality he faced: women in his milieu were converting to Islam in order to escape intolerable marriages, since the Muslim legal system did not recognize their prior marriage and allowed them to remarry. Faced with women resorting to apostasy as the only practical exit, the Rambam may have been additionally motivated to establish a legitimate halakhic solution. If a beit din would actually compel the *get* upon a declaration of *ma'is alai*, conversion would be unnecessary. The observation connects the medieval context to a perennial question about rabbinic jurisprudence: how much does the practical urgency of the situation on the ground inform the willingness to employ halakhic tools that are formally available but rarely used?

What is clear from the Gemara itself is that the entire range of questions — how long to work with the *moredet*, how quickly to move toward *get*, whether to engage her directly or only through announcements, and what to do when she declares the marriage intolerable — reflects a deep and unresolved tension between the court's protective role, its interest in preserving marriages, and its responsibility to the individuals trapped in untenable situations.

---

## Ketubah Loss Details

### Clothes & Property

The Gemara now turns to a practical question arising from the case of Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law, who rebelled against her husband and was in possession of a garment at the time. Ameimar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi were convened as a beit din, with Rav Gamda sitting among them. The question before them: when a *moredet* loses her entire *ketubah*, does that include the worn garments that are in her possession — *belosei ha-kayamim*, literally the existing worn clothes? On one version of the text, they ruled that she does lose even those. On an alternate version, they ruled she does not lose the worn clothes in her closet. In both versions, Rav Gamda challenges the panel, suggesting in the first that they are ruling too harshly against her out of deference to the eminence of Rav Zevid, and in the second that they are ruling too leniently in his favor for the same reason.

The underlying question — whether the worn clothes in her closet are part of the *ketubah* settlement she forfeits — was one that Rava raised but did not resolve. The practical consequence of that unresolved question: *tafsa lo mafkinan minah* — if she has those clothes in her possession, we do not take them from her, since she may be entitled to them; *lo tafsa lo yahavinan lah* — if she does not have them in hand, we do not give them to her. The default is determined by the status quo of physical possession.

The background to this dispute involves the nature of the dowry clothes. Rashi explains that these are garments she brought into the marriage as part of her trousseau, the value of which was recorded in the *ketubah*. He takes possession of them upon marriage, but she is entitled to their residual value upon dissolution. If she loses the entire *ketubah*, she loses that claim as well.

### Alternative Timelines

A further variant ruling is recorded: *umashinan lah tresar yarchei shata agita* — we actually extend the process for twelve months rather than four weeks. During those twelve months, however, *leis lah mezoni miba'al* — she receives no *mezonot* from her husband. This represents yet another point on the spectrum of possible approaches: a longer time horizon to allow for change, but with an additional financial disincentive layered on, removing her food support for the duration.

### Post-Talmud Practice

Tosafot, at the beginning of 63b, records a significant post-Talmudic development. Rabbeinu Yehudah found in the writings of Rav Sherira Gaon that the Geonim enacted *shetekenu beyamav latet get le'ishah la'altar* — they ruled in his time to give the *get* to the woman immediately, without waiting four weeks or twelve months. This mirrors what was said earlier about the husband who is *mored* — immediate *get* without extended process. Tosafot further records that the *Rabbanan Savorai* — the transitional authorities between the Talmudic period and the Geonic era — enacted that we also reclaim whatever clothing she had taken from her closet and give her the *get* at once.

The comparison raises an interesting question about which approach is ultimately more favorable to the woman. The drawn-out process of the Mishnah or the four-week Talmudic process, especially if she is engaged at the beginning, gives her time to reconsider and an opportunity to preserve the marriage if she chooses. The immediate *get* of the Geonic enactment is faster, but it also means she exits with nothing, no *ketubah*, no clothes, no transitional period. The four-week process with beit din engagement — particularly where she is reached out to at the start — may in fact represent the most balanced of the available approaches.

---

## Arusah & Yavam

### Arusah vs. Yavam

Rav Tuvi bar Kisna, citing Shmuel, rules: *kotevin iggeret mered al arusah ve-ein kotevin iggeret mered al shomeret yavam* — we write a writ of rebellion against an *arusah* but not against a *shomeret yavam*. The reasoning is that an *arusah*, even though she is not yet in a stage where she would be obligated to have sexual relations, has made a declaration that she will refuse to do so — or refuse to proceed to *nisuim* — when the time comes, and this is sufficient to trigger the process. A *shomeret yavam*, by contrast, is not yet in a stage where these obligations apply, and we therefore do not initiate the process against her.

### Braitah Challenge

The Gemara raises a challenge: the *braita* cited earlier specifically listed the *shomeret yavam* as one of the cases to which the *moredet* process applies — *achat le-arusah u-le-nesuah va-afilu niddah va-afilu cholah va-afilu shomeret yavam*. That seems to contradict Shmuel's ruling.

### Who Demands?

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya, kan she-tava hu, kan she-tav'ah hi* — there is no difficulty; the cases differ based on who is making the demand. When the man is the one asserting his right and the woman refuses, that is the case of the *braita* — we write the writ against the *shomeret yavam*. When she is the one demanding and he is refusing, that is Shmuel's case — we do not write the writ on her behalf.

This is confirmed by Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi citing Shmuel: *tava hu, nizkakim lo* — if he demands and she refuses, beit din attends to him and applies financial pressure on her; *tav'ah hi, ein nizkakim lo* — if she demands and he refuses, we do not attend to her demand. The Gemara's adjustment of Shmuel's formulation — reading *le-arusah* in the sense of the *braita* being written for her rather than against her — resolves the textual difficulty while preserving the substantive ruling.

---

## Yibum vs. Chalitzah

### No Yibum Compulsion

Having established that the question of who is making the demand determines whether beit din intervenes, the Gemara turns to the broader question of *yibum* versus *chalitzah*. The Gemara asks: why do we not compel a *shomeret yavam* to accept *yibum* when the *yavam* demands it? The answer: *de-amrinan lah, zil lo mifkadet* — we tell her, go, you are not commanded in *peru u-revu*. He has a *mitzvah* she does not share, and therefore his claim to compel her cooperation is stronger than hers would be in the reverse situation. She, for her part, can simply allow the relationship to remain unresolved or proceed to *chalitzah*.

### Chalitzah Claim

But if a woman cannot compel *yibum*, can she at least compel *chalitzah* when she demands it and he refuses? Here the Gemara introduces a striking argument: *de-amra, ba'ina chutra leyada u-mara likvura* — she says, "I want a staff for my hand and a shovel for my grave," meaning she wants children to care for her in old age and to bury her when she dies. She does not need to be commanded in *peru u-revu* to have a legitimate claim to children. This gives her standing to demand resolution of her situation — whether through *yibum* or *chalitzah* — even without the formal obligation that applies to him. The Gemara affirms that this same claim applies to the *shomeret yavam*: *hachi nami shomeret yavam de-ba machmas ta'ana* — when she comes with a legitimate claim, we do attend to her.

### Historical Preference Sh…

The Gemara then introduces a crucial historical distinction, cited from Rav Pada in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *tava lachalotz nizkakim lo* — if the *yavam* demands *chalitzah* and she refuses, beit din compels her; *tava le-yabbem, ein nizkakim lo* — if he demands *yibum* and she refuses, beit din does not compel her. The reason for preferring *chalitzah* and not compelling *yibum* is given through the teaching of the Mishnah: *mitzvas yibum kodemes lemitzvas chalitzah* — originally, *yibum* took precedence over *chalitzah*, because *be-rishona she-hayu miskavnim leshum mitzvah* — in earlier times, *yibum* was performed for the sake of the *mitzvah* itself. *Achshav she-ein miskavnim leshum mitzvah, amru mitzvas chalitzah kodemes* — now that it is no longer performed with that sincere motivation, we rule that *chalitzah* takes precedence. And since we favor *chalitzah*, when he demands *yibum* against her will, we do not compel her compliance.

### Enforcement Measures

The Gemara addresses the apparent inconsistency: if she can refuse *yibum* and he is told to go marry someone else, why can she not similarly refuse *chalitzah* and he be told the same thing? He responds: *kivan de-agida bi, lo ka yahvi li achriti* — since she is bound to him, no one will agree to marry him; the unresolved status of the *shomeret yavam* effectively bars him from remarriage. The same argument should apply whether she refuses *yibum* or *chalitzah*. The Gemara ultimately resolves this by distinguishing between the earlier and later Mishnah positions on which is preferred: under the initial ruling, *yibum* was favored and we would have compelled her; under the later ruling, we prefer *chalitzah* and therefore we do not compel *yibum* even when he demands it, while we do compel *chalitzah* when he demands it.

The final *Tosafot* of the sugya draws the parallel explicitly: just as the discussion of *ma'is alai* raised the question of what measures beit din may use to compel a husband to give a *get* when the wife declares the marriage intolerable, the analogous question here is what measures may be used to compel a *yavam* to give *chalitzah* when the woman demands it and he refuses — or worse, when he refuses both *yibum* and *chalitzah* and simply leaves her in limbo. The woman is then precisely in the position of an *agunah*: bound to him, unable to remarry, with no resolution in sight. The tools available to the court in both scenarios — and the willingness to deploy them — remain very much an open and contested question.

---

---

# Ketubot 64

## Overview & Setup

### Opening

We begin near the bottom of 64a, picking up five lines from the end at the words *ad masai hu pocheit* — "until when does he reduce it."

### Marriage Troubles Review

The preceding *sugya* dealt with the situation in which a marriage has broken down and one of the partners is failing to fulfill his or her obligations. The discussion centered on whether the goal is to achieve compliance over time or to move directly toward a *get*, and what is done in the interim. Two significant issues emerged from that discussion. First, whether the husband can actually be compelled to go out and find work — he has an obligation to pay the bills, but does the principle of *v'ana aflach* mean he can be forced to seek employment? Second, and more consequential for *agunah* concerns, when the wife declares the marriage intolerable, does the court move immediately to compel a *get*, or does the woman at once forfeit her *ketubbah*? The *sugya* also touched on *Tosafot*'s discussion of whether a husband who refuses *chalitzah* can in some fashion be compelled or induced to grant it.

### Financial Penalties

The *Mishnah* established financial penalties for marital defiance in either direction. When the wife is a *moredes* — refusing to fulfill her obligations — the *ketubbah* is reduced by seven *dinarin* per week. When the husband is a *mored*, the *ketubbah* is increased by three *dinarin* per week for the wife's benefit. A parallel opinion substitutes *tarpeikin* for *dinarin* in both amounts.

## Currency & Math

### Dinar/Zuz/Sela

To understand these figures, one must first establish the currency equivalencies. A *dinar* equals a *zuz*, and four *zuz* equal a *sela*. The significance of the *sela* here is that the *Torah*'s *mohar* of fifty *shekel* equals 200 *zuz* — which is why the base *ketubbah* for a *betulah* is 200 *zuz*.

### Depletion Calculations

If the *ketubbah* stands at 200 *zuz* and is reduced at seven *zuz* per week, it will be exhausted in roughly 28 weeks. If instead it is increased for the husband at three *zuz* per week, that three-*zuz* increment would take approximately 67 weeks to accumulate an equivalent sum — though of course a *ketubbah* typically includes *tosefet*, a dowry, and other additions beyond the base 200.

The *Gemara* then asks: *mai tarpeikin* — what are *tarpeikin*? Rav Sheshet answers: an *astira*, which is *palga d'zuza* — half a *zuz*. This is confirmed by a *baraita*: Rabbi Yehudah says three *tarpeikin* equal nine *ma'in*, which works out to a *ma'ah* and a half per day (excluding Shabbat). The practical consequence is significant: seven *tarpeikin* per week equals three and a half *zuz*, so the second opinion in the *Mishnah* represents a rate half as severe as the first. At three and a half *zuz* per week, the base 200-*zuz ketubbah* would be depleted in roughly 56 weeks — twice as long as under the first opinion.

## Tarpeikin & Meals

### Tarpeikin Definition

To summarize the coinage: a *tarpeikin* is an *astira*, which equals half a *zuz*.

### Rabbi Yehudah Opinion

Rabbi Yehudah specifies that three *tarpeikin* equal nine *ma'in*, yielding a daily rate of a *ma'ah* and a half when Shabbat is excluded from the count.

### Penalty Comparison

Setting aside the *tarpeikin*-versus-*zuz* question, the structural differences between the two penalties can be stated clearly. For the *moredes* — the wife who refuses her obligations — the *ketubbah* is reduced by one unit per day, including Shabbat, for a total of seven per week. For the *mored* — the husband who refuses his — the *ketubbah* is increased by only half a unit per day, and Shabbat is not counted, yielding three units per week. These two asymmetries — full versus half, and Shabbat included versus excluded — are the focus of the *Gemara*'s next inquiry.

## Mored vs Moredes

### Half vs Full Fine

Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef poses the question to Shmuel: *mah bein mored l'moredes* — why is there a difference between the *mored* and the *moredes*? Why is her penalty double his, and why is Shabbat counted against her but not against him?

### Shabbat Fining Logic

The *Gemara* addresses the Shabbat question first. When the wife is the defiant party and the *ketubbah* is being reduced, the fact that Shabbat is included does not create an appearance of payment for Shabbat labor — *lo michzi k'schar Shabbat* — because one is merely reducing a debt, not paying out wages. When the husband is the defiant party and the *ketubbah* is being increased, however, including Shabbat in the count would mean that the wife is effectively earning half a *zuz* on Shabbat — *michzi k'schar Shabbat* — which does create that problematic appearance. Hence Shabbat is excluded from his calculation.

A question was raised about *Yom Tov*: if there is concern about the appearance of *schar Shabbat*, why is *Yom Tov* not similarly excluded? *Tosafot* raises the related question of *havla'ah* — the practice of including Shabbat payment within a broader weekly wage so that it is not singled out — and whether that principle might apply here. The matter is left unresolved.

### Prostitute Market Evidence

On the question of why the wife's penalty is double the husband's, Shmuel tells Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef: *tzei u'lemad mi-shuk shel zonos* — go and learn from the marketplace of prostitutes, *mi socher es mi* — who hires whom? It is men who hire women. The market for female prostitution is vastly larger than that for male prostitution. This is taken as empirical evidence that men experience greater sexual desire, and therefore the husband is the more aggrieved party when conjugal relations are withheld. Since the *mored* and *moredes* framework is understood primarily in terms of withholding sexual relations, the wife who withholds is penalized more heavily, because she is inflicting greater harm.

### Biological Arguments

A second argument follows: *davar acher* — *zeh yitzro mi-bachutz v'zeh yitzrah mi-bifnim* — one's genitalia is external, the other's internal. Rashi explains this in two ways. Symbolically, it reflects who harbors the greater innate desire. More concretely, *kishuyo nikar u-misganeh*: the husband's arousal is visible and thus more conspicuous in its frustration, whereas the wife's is not. Together, these two arguments — the evidence from the marketplace and the biological argument — establish that the husband is regarded as the more injured party when sexual relations are denied, which is why the penalty for the *moredes* is double that of the *mored*.

It bears noting that even though the husband has a positive obligation of *onah*, he is nonetheless regarded as the party more harmed by deprivation. The overall asymmetry — double penalty, plus Shabbat — compounds a broader imbalance already present in the framework, since the husband retains the unilateral power to initiate a *get*, which the wife does not. As for the timeline: whether one follows the seven-*zuz* or seven-*tarpeikin* rate, the process of depleting the base *ketubbah* runs between roughly half a year and a full year — far longer than the more rapid resolution the *Gemara* elsewhere envisions, where one wants to move quickly toward the *get* rather than drag out the proceedings.

## Food Minimums

### Hamshrah Setup

The *Mishnah* now turns to the counterpart of the *moredes* and *mored* discussion: the husband's affirmative obligation to support his wife. The particular case treated here is one of *hamshrah* — the husband is providing for his wife through an intermediary, meaning they are not sharing a domicile. Whether he is away on a business trip, or they are separated pending resolution of their situation, or for whatever other reason, she is not in his house and he is having someone pay her food costs. The *Mishnah* therefore specifies the minimum she must receive.

### Grain Allowance

He may not give her less than two *kav* of wheat per week, or, if she prefers barley, four *kav* of barley. The *kav* is a volumetric measurement; barley was considered a less desirable grain, which is why it requires double the quantity.

### Barley Exception

Rabbi Yosi objects: the only authority who said barley is permitted as an alternative was Rabbi Yishmael, who lived near Edom — *she-hayah samuch le-Edom*. The *Gemara* clarifies that Rabbi Yosi's objection is not that barley is never eaten elsewhere, but specifically that the rule requiring double the quantity of barley compared to wheat was particular to Rabbi Yishmael's region. The Edomite barley was of notoriously poor quality — *se'oreihen Adomiyot ra'ot hen* — so twice the wheat measure was required to produce equivalent sustenance. Elsewhere, the ratio between barley and wheat would differ.

### Legumes & Fruits

In addition to the grain, the husband must provide a half-*kav* of *kitnis* — legumes — weekly, along with a half-*log* of oil (a *log* is four *revi'iyot*, so a half-*log* is approximately seven ounces), and a *kav* of *grogeros* — dried figs — or, alternatively, a *maneh* (a weight measure) of pressed dates, *deveilah*. If none of these fruits are locally available, he substitutes an equivalent measure of whatever fruit is at hand.

### Durables

Beyond the weekly consumables, the *Mishnah* enumerates durable goods: a bed, a *mapatz* (mat), and a *machatzeles* (a form of cushion or mat). These items are presumably provided once at the outset rather than weekly. He also gives her a head-covering (*kippah le-roshah*), a belt for her waist (*chagor le-mosneha*), and shoes.

### Clothing Allowance

Shoes are replaced *mi-mo'ed le-mo'ed* — once each *regel*, three times a year. For clothing, he provides fifty *zuz* worth annually. There is, however, an important specification about timing: new clothing — which is heavier and warmer, not yet worn thin — should not be purchased in summer, and worn, thinned clothing should not be given in winter. Rather, the fifty *zuz* of new clothing should be bought in winter. She wears them throughout the cold months and, as they wear out, the thinned garments serve her well in summer. At the end of the year, when new clothing is purchased, she keeps the old worn garments — *ha-shechakim shelah*.

### Pin Money & Meals

She also receives a *ma'ah kesef* each week — a small personal stipend for incidental needs, what we might call pin money. And even when they are living apart, the husband is obligated to eat at least one meal together with his wife every Friday night: *ochelet immo mi-leilei Shabbat le-leilei Shabbat*. This is striking. The law already mandates *onah* — conjugal relations at regular intervals — and here extends the same logic to the shared meal: even when circumstances have separated them, the weekly Friday-night meal together is enforceable. The Friday night Shabbat table functions as a minimum unit of shared domestic life, a requirement of presence and not merely of financial provision.

If the husband fails to give the *ma'ah kesef* stipend, then *ma'aseh yadeha shelah* — whatever work she produces belongs to her rather than to him.

### Ma'aseh Yadayim

The *Mishnah* then asks: *u-mah hi osah lo* — and what work does she do for him? The *Gemara* earlier debated whether *ma'aseh yadayim* refers to the entirety of her domestic labor or only the surplus she earns beyond her basic obligations, *motar ma'aseh yadayim*. The plain sense of the *Mishnah* here, however, seems to single out a specific, quantifiable category of work — the weaving that she can actually earn income from outside the house. This is distinguished from the standard domestic duties (baking, laundry, cooking, etc.) enumerated earlier. Whether the *Gemara*'s two opinions on this question fully account for this distinction is not spelled out there; nonetheless, the *Mishnah*'s framing points toward the income-generating weaving as the primary content of *ma'aseh yadayim* in the strict sense.

### Weaving Amounts

The specific amounts are given by region. She must produce the equivalent of five *sla'im* of warp — *sheti* — as measured in Judah, which equals ten *sla'im* by Galilean weights (since Galilean weights were half the value of Judean ones). Alternatively, she must produce ten *sla'im* of woof — *erev* — by Judean measure, which equals twenty *sla'im* in Galilee. The woof is the easier of the two to prepare, which is why its required quantity is double.

### Nursing Adjustments

If she is nursing, her required work output is reduced — *pochtin lah mi-ma'aseh yadeha* — both because nursing itself constitutes significant labor and, more importantly, because excessive physical exertion could compromise her capacity to nurse well. Correspondingly, her food allowance is increased — *mosifin lah al mezonoteha* — since she is eating for two.

### Status Adjustments

All of these minimums apply specifically to the poor — *ba-ani she-be-Yisrael*. If the husband is of higher social standing, then *hakol le-fi kvodo* — everything is calibrated to his status. The minimums are a floor, not a universal standard.

## Meal Measures

### Eruv Techumin Reference

The *Gemara* now questions which Tanna authored this *Mishnah*, and concludes it can be neither Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka nor Rabbi Shimon. The basis for this analysis is a *Mishnah* in *eruv techumin*: the minimum *eruv* contribution is the amount of food constituting two meals — *mazon shtei se'udot* — per person.

### Meir vs Yehudah

Rabbi Meir says the reference meal is a weekday meal, not a Shabbat meal; Rabbi Yehudah says it is the Shabbat meal, not the weekday meal. The *Gemara* notes that each is being lenient — *zeh ve-zeh mitkavnim le-hakel* — but in opposite directions. Rabbi Meir holds that one eats more bread on Shabbat, so the weekday meal represents a smaller bread portion. Rabbi Yehudah holds that on Shabbat one eats more varied dishes and consequently less bread, so the Shabbat bread portion is smaller. Both are defining two meals by the smaller of the two bread quantities.

### R. Yochanan b. Broka

Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka defines the size of a two-meal loaf as the bread purchased for a *pundiyon* when four *se'ah* of grain are sold for a *sela*. Working through the arithmetic: a *sela* equals 48 *pundiyon*, and a *se'ah* equals six *kav*, so four *se'ah* equal 24 *kav*. This means 24 *kav* cost 48 *pundiyon*, which is one *kav* per two *pundiyon*, or half a *kav* per *pundiyon*. A loaf costing one *pundiyon* is therefore made from half a *kav* of wheat, and that loaf constitutes two meals.

### Rabbi Shimon

Rabbi Shimon takes a different measure: two-thirds of a loaf — *shtei yadot be-kikar* — when three loaves are made from one *kav*. If three loaves come from one *kav*, each loaf represents a third of a *kav*. Two-thirds of a loaf is therefore two-thirds of one-third of a *kav*, which equals two-ninths of a *kav* for two meals. This is considerably less than Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's half-*kav*.

### Achilat Pras

Half of a two-meal loaf — that is, one meal's worth of bread — is called a *pras*, from the Aramaic for "half." Hence *kedei achilat pras* denotes the amount of time required to eat one meal's worth of bread, i.e., the time it takes to eat half a two-meal loaf. This becomes the standard measurement in a much broader range of halachic contexts. The *Gemara* notes related applications: *chatzi ha-pras* is the amount one must remain in a house afflicted with *tzara'at* to contract *tum'ah*; half of that is the amount of *tamei* food whose consumption renders one *tamei*; and half again — one-eighth of the full loaf — is *lekabbel tum'at ochlin*, the minimum food quantity susceptible to *tum'ah*, which Rashi identifies as a *beitzah*. These applications are noted but not pursued at length here.

## Two Kav Calculation

### Eight vs Eighteen

The *Gemara* now applies these two opinions to the *Mishnah*'s allowance of two *kav* of wheat. According to Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, half a *kav* yields two meals, so two *kav* yield eight meals. According to Rabbi Shimon, two-ninths of a *kav* yield two meals, meaning one *kav* yields nine meals, and two *kav* yield eighteen meals.

### Weekly Meal Mismatch

Neither figure matches the expected weekly meal count. A week contains fourteen meals — two per day, seven days — or fifteen if one counts *seudah shlishit* on Shabbat. Eight is far too few; eighteen is too many. This is the *Gemara*'s problem.

### Baker's Profit

Rav Chisda resolves the discrepancy for Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's position by pointing out that the latter was not specifying the actual flour content of the loaf but rather its market price. The storekeeper-baker does not convert the entire purchase price into flour; he keeps a portion as profit. Rav Chisda says to subtract a third for the storekeeper — *tzei me-hen shelish la-chanvani* — meaning that only two-thirds of the money paid goes toward the wheat itself, while the baker pockets a third. Conversely, if one starts with the raw wheat — as the *Mishnah* does when it gives the wife two *kav* — one must add back the profit margin to calculate how many meals the raw grain represents. Adding a third to the eight meals derived from the market-price calculation yields twelve meals, not eight.

### Adjusted Totals

Twelve meals is still not fourteen. The *Gemara* resolves this by noting that the *Mishnah* specifies the wife eats one meal together with her husband on Friday night — *ochelet immo la-leil Shabbat* — bringing the total to thirteen. The *Gemara* then reconsiders: some interpret *achila* in the *Mishnah* not as literal eating but as a euphemism for *tashmish*, conjugal relations. If so, that Friday night provision adds no meal, and even with the literal interpretation one only reaches thirteen. The *Gemara* therefore adopts Rav Chisda's second formulation: the baker's profit is not a third but a half. Half of the purchase price goes to the wheat, half is the baker's profit. Applying the reverse: two *kav* of raw wheat, with a 100% markup factored in, yields sixteen meals. Sixteen exceeds fourteen — but now a different problem arises.

### Shabbat Meals

The *Gemara* asks: is this calculation aligned with Rabbi Chidka, who holds that one is obligated to eat four meals on Shabbat rather than three? With four Shabbat meals, the week contains sixteen meals total, and sixteen matches perfectly. The *Gemara* replies that one can maintain the Rabbinic view of three Shabbat meals as well: the extra portion — one meal's worth of bread — is set aside *le-orchei u-farchei*, for guests who might arrive unexpectedly. Hence the two *kav* covers fourteen regular meals plus one for Shabbat's Friday night meal together (whether literal or euphemistic) plus one extra for hospitality, reaching sixteen. Returning then to Rabbi Shimon's eighteen: under the Rabbinic view of three Shabbat meals (fifteen total), three portions are reserved for guests; under Rabbi Chidka's four Shabbat meals (sixteen total), two portions go toward hospitality.

## Missing Items

### No Protein/Veg

One striking feature of this minimum allowance is what it omits. The wife receives grain (wheat or barley), legumes, oil, and dried fruit or dates. What is entirely absent is protein — no meat, no fish, no eggs, no milk, no cheese. Equally absent are vegetables. This is characterized explicitly as the minimum for the poor — *ani she-be-Yisrael* — yet even granting that qualifier, the diet described is extremely bare: essentially starch supplemented by a small quantity of fruit. The *Gemara* is not troubled by the absence of protein or vegetables; as we will see, what the *Gemara* focuses on instead is the absence of wine.

## Wine Restrictions

### No Wine Rule

The *Mishnah*'s list of provisions includes no wine, and the *Gemara* takes this as support for the position of Rabbi Elazar, who states: *ein poskin yeinot le-ishah* — wine is not allocated to a woman living apart from her husband. Whether *beit din* is directing provision from a living but absent husband's assets or from a deceased husband's estate (since the obligation of *mezonot* for the widow from the estate follows the same framework as for the living separated wife), the same rule applies: wine is not part of the court-ordered food allocation.

### Hosea Derashah

Rabbi Yehudah of Kfar Nevirya (or, in another version, Kfar Nafor Chayya) offers a scriptural basis for this rule, deriving it from the verse in Hosea (2:7): *elchah acharei me'ahavai notnei lachmi u-maymai tzamri u-fishti shamni ve-shikuyai* — "I will go after my lovers who give me my bread and my water, my wool and my linen, my oil and my drink." The verse lists what a woman seeks from her lovers. The *Gemara* explains: *shikuyai* in this context does not mean wine but rather *devarim she-ha-ishah mishtokeket aleihen* — things a woman desires — namely jewelry and adornments. The verse, on this reading, implies that wine is emphatically not what should be provided for a woman from outside.

A further *derashah* is built on the narrative of Hannah at Shiloh. The verse reads: *va-takam Chanah acharei ochlo ve-Shilo ve-acharei shato* — "and Hannah arose after he ate in Shiloh and after he drank." The *drasha* notes *shato* — his drinking — but not *shatetah*, her drinking; the implication is that she did not drink wine. The *Gemara* challenges this: should *ochlo* similarly be read as his eating alone, implying she did not eat? The *Gemara* responds: *anan be-shinui kera be-dibura ka-amrinan* — the *drasha* rests on the deviation in language. The verse is speaking about Hannah in the third person throughout; when it shifts to speak of *shato* — his drinking — without a corresponding form for her drinking, that deviation is the exegetical point. The eating is stated in a form that encompasses her as well, but the drinking is stated only for him.

### Accustomed Exception

A *baraita* qualifies Rabbi Elazar's rule: *regila nosnin lah* — if a woman is accustomed to drinking wine, wine is allocated for her. *Regila shani* — an accustomed woman is treated differently, on the theory that she has developed a tolerance and the concern for licentious behavior is diminished. Rabbi Chanina bar Kahana in the name of Shmuel specifies: if she is accustomed, she receives one cup; if she is not accustomed, she receives two cups — a formulation that on its face seems counterintuitive and requires Abaye's clarification.

### Abaye Refinement

Abaye explains that Shmuel's statement must be read comparatively, distinguishing between her situation *bifnei ba'alah* (when living with her husband) and *she-lo bifnei ba'alah* (when living apart). The full structure is: if she customarily drinks two cups when with her husband, she receives one cup when apart from him; if she customarily drinks only one cup when with her husband, she receives nothing when apart from him. The reasoning is that even for a woman accustomed to wine, the absence of her husband removes a check on her behavior — both because her marital desires may go unfulfilled and because her husband is not present to moderate her conduct — so the allocation is reduced by one full cup. And if she was already at the minimum of one cup with her husband, there is no further reduction available, so she receives nothing.

### Cooking Wine

An alternative resolution is offered: even when drinking wine is prohibited, wine for cooking — *le-tsikei kdera* — is permitted. The concern about licentious behavior attaches to drinking; using wine as a cooking ingredient does not implicate that concern.

### Nakdimon Story

This principle is illustrated by the story of the daughter-in-law of Nakdimon ben Guryon. The Rabbis allocated for her two *se'ah* of wine per week — *me-erev Shabbat le-erev Shabbat* — specifically for cooking. She responded, "May you merit to apportion the same for your own daughters" — whether sincerely or ironically is unclear. The narrator adds: she was a *shomeret yavam*, awaiting *yibbum*, and the Sages did not respond *amen* to her blessing, lest it be read as an ill omen for their own daughters to be left widowed awaiting *yibbum*. The detail about *yibbum* also illuminates why it is *beit din* rather than a living husband allocating her food: she is a widow drawing sustenance from the deceased husband's estate, which is precisely the situation in which the *Mishnah*'s minimum provisions become most practically important for the *almanah*.

## Wine & Behavior

### One to Three Cups

The *Gemara* now states the *tanna*'s teaching that underlies all these restrictions. One cup of wine is beneficial for a woman — *kos echad yafeh le-ishah*. Two cups is unseemly — *nival hu*. Three cups, and she will verbally proposition men for sex — *tova'at be-peh*.

### Four Cups

Four cups, and she will solicit even a donkey in the marketplace without shame — *afilu chamor tova'at ba-shuk ve-eina ikpat lah*. This is, manifestly, a teaching composed from a male perspective, and reflects the assumption — already encountered in the *mored/moredes* discussion — that women's sexual self-control is more vulnerable to alcohol than men's. The social context is also relevant: women in this society had far less habitual exposure to wine, which would indeed have lowered their tolerance. Even granting all this, the extreme escalation is notable.

### Rava Clarification

Rava limits the entire teaching: *lo shanu ela she-ein ba'alah imah* — all of this applies only when the husband is not present. When the husband is with her — *ba'alah imah leit lan bah* — there is no restriction. This confirms the framework of the whole discussion: these wine-allocation rules operate only when *beit din* is the one providing food and wine, i.e., when she is living apart from her husband. When she is with her husband, what the two of them choose to drink together is their own business, and we assume the husband's presence serves as a sufficient check.

### Guest Exception

The *Gemara* raises a challenge from the story of Hannah, who was with her husband Elkanah at Shiloh, yet did not drink — and we derived from this that wine is restricted even when the husband is present. Rava's ruling seems to contradict this. The *Gemara* resolves it: *achsanai shani* — guests are different. Rav Huna teaches: how do we know that a guest couple should not engage in marital relations while staying in someone else's home? From the verse describing Elkanah and Hannah: *va-yashkimu ba-boker va-yishtachavu lifnei Hashem va-yashuvu va-yavo'u el beitam ha-Ramatah va-yeida Elkanah et Chana ishto* — they rose in the morning, bowed before God, returned to their home in Ramah, and *only then* Elkanah knew Hannah. The sequence implies that the marital intimacy occurred only after they returned home, not while guests at Shiloh. The same principle governs wine: when one is a guest in another's home, the usual latitude that applies between husband and wife in their own home does not apply. Greater decorum is required.

## Allocation Stories

### Homa's Request

Homa, who was Abaye's wife and apparently a woman of notable beauty, came before Rava. She requested that he allocate food for her — *psok li mezoni* — presumably either because Abaye was absent or, as later details suggest, possibly because he had died. Rava made the allocation.

### Private Wine Use

She then asked him to also allocate wine — *psok li chamra*. Rava replied: I know Nachmani — Abaye's other name — and he would not drink wine. She responded: by your life, he would drink wine in a *shufrizi* — a long horn-shaped cup — *this* big, and she extended her arms to demonstrate the size. This exchange itself illustrates a point made earlier in the *sugya*: people behave privately in ways they do not display publicly. Rava was under the impression that Abaye never drank wine; his wife knew otherwise.

### Rava's Response

As she extended her arms to demonstrate the size of the cup, her sleeve fell back and her arm became exposed. The *Gemara* describes it: *nafal nehora be-vei dina* — light filled the *beit din*, meaning her arm was of such luminous beauty that it illuminated the courtroom. Rava was profoundly stirred. He rose, went home, and immediately propositioned his wife — the daughter of Rav Chisda — seeking to be intimate with her in the middle of the day.

### Wife's Pursuit

When his wife asked what had happened in court, Rava told her that Homa, Abaye's wife, had appeared before him. His wife immediately ran after Homa and struck her with the strap from a chest — *be-kofei de-shida* — chasing her from the entire city of Mechuza. She shouted at Homa: *katlat leh* — you have already killed one man (meaning her husband), and now you want to kill another? The background is that Homa had been married three times, each husband having died, and Rava's wife feared that Homa's beauty would lead yet another husband — her own — to his ruin. Whether Abaye was indeed among the three deceased husbands is not entirely clear from the text; the narrative leaves open whether he was dead or merely absent, which is why Homa was seeking a food allocation in the first place.

### Rav Yosef's Wife

A parallel story follows. The wife of Rav Yosef the son of Rava came before Rav Nechemia the son of Rav Yosef. She too requested a food allocation — *psok li mezoni* — and he provided it. She then requested a wine allocation — *psok li chamra* — and he provided that as well. He explained his reasoning: *yadana behu bi-venei Mechuza de-shatu chamra* — I know the people of Mechuza, that they drink wine regularly. Because wine is a routine part of daily life in Mechuza — much as it would be in regions where wine accompanies every meal as a matter of course — allocating wine to a woman from that city does not implicate the concerns that motivated the restriction. Custom and local practice determine what counts as ordinary consumption and what constitutes dangerous excess.

# Ketubot 64b

## Penalties & Reduction

### Marital Disputes Intro

The present *sugya* continues the discussion of marital dysfunction — specifically, the mechanisms by which we encourage compliance when a marriage is in trouble. The issues at stake include whether the husband can be compelled to go out and find work in order to meet his financial obligations (since his obligation is to pay the bills, but the question of whether he can be forced to find employment — *ve'ana eflach* — is debated), and, more significantly for *agunah* concerns, the degree to which we compel a husband to give a *get* when the wife declares the marriage intolerable. Related to that, *Tosafos* addresses the question of whether we may even "encourage" a husband to perform *chalitzah* when he refuses. The *daf* now turns to the financial penalties and why they differ between husband and wife.

### Penalty Structure

The *mishnah* established the following asymmetric penalty framework: when the wife is not fulfilling her responsibilities, we reduce her *kesuvah* by seven *dinarin* per week; when the husband is not fulfilling his responsibilities, we increase the *kesuvah* (for the wife's benefit) by three *dinarin*. A second opinion substitutes *tarpikin* for *dinarin* in both cases — seven *tarpikin* per week for her and three *tarpikin* per week for him.

### Currency Conversions

To understand the penalty's practical significance, one must first be oriented in the relevant currency equivalences. A *dinar* equals a *zuz*, and four *zuz* equals a *sela*, which is equivalent to a biblical *shekel*. The Torah's fifty-*shekel* bride price (*mohar*) accordingly equals two hundred *zuz* — which is precisely the basis of the standard *kesuvah* of two hundred *zuz*.

### Penalty Duration Math

If the *kesuvah* stands at two hundred *zuz* and is reduced by seven *zuz* per week, the base amount will be exhausted in approximately twenty-eight weeks. If the rate is instead three *zuz* per week — as is the case when the husband is being penalized — the base amount would last approximately sixty-seven weeks. These calculations apply only to the base *kesuvah* of two hundred *zuz*; the *tosefes* (additional sum) and *nidunya* (dowry) would extend the process considerably.

### Tarpikin Definition

The *gemara* asks: *mai tarpikin* — what exactly is a *tarpikin*? Rav Sheishes answers: *asteira*, a half-*zuz*.
