The implication is that domestic matters of this nature, which fall short of true *innuy nefesh*, are things people can manage within a marriage; they won't be destroyed by them. Tosafot clarifies that this is not a debate about whether the husband can annul *beino l'veinah* vows — that principle is taken as axiomatic — but rather a debate internal to Rabbi Yossi's position: when he said these things are not *innuy nefesh*, did he mean they are entirely beneath the threshold of any annulment, or merely that they fall into the lesser *beino l'veinah* category?

If one takes the stricter view — that according to Rabbi Yossi these vows cannot be annulled at all — then Shmuel's reading of the Mishnah collapses, because it assumes the husband had the power to annul and chose not to.

### Rav Kahana Sex

The Gemara therefore pivots to yet another reading. The Gemara cites the statement of Rav Kahana: *hana'at tashmishi alecha* — if the wife says "the pleasure of my marital relations is forbidden to you," *kopeh u'meshamasht'o* — we compel her to be with him, or at least the vow is unenforceable, because she cannot forbid him what he is entitled to. But if she says *hana'at tashmishcha alai* — "the pleasure of your marital relations is forbidden to me" — that is an indirect formulation, and the vow does bind. In that case, *yeifer* — he must annul it — because the alternative is either they transgress by having relations while forbidden, or they refrain from relations, neither of which is acceptable. This vow clearly falls under both *innuy nefesh* and *beino l'veinah*.

---

## Reframe Case

### Vow Structure

With Rav Kahana's principle established, the Gemara introduces a new and final reading of the Mishnah that resolves the remaining difficulties. The case is not really about perfume or fruit at all — not directly. What the Mishnah is describing is a vow structured as follows: *ye'aser hana'at tashmishcha alai im etkashat* — "the benefit of having sex with you will be forbidden to me if I adorn myself with jewelry." The adornment is merely the condition; the substance of the vow is about marital relations. This is precisely the type of vow Rav Kahana discusses: an indirect but effective prohibition on *tashmish*.

This reading resolves all the difficulties simultaneously. It explains why they must divorce — because the vow puts marital relations at risk, not merely a luxury food item. It explains why the husband can annul the vow — because it is unambiguously *innuy nefesh* and *beino l'veinah* when the ultimate subject is *tashmish*. And it explains why getting divorced actually helps — because the vow is structured to be triggered by something that is inevitable in normal life. The Gemara notes: if she does not adorn herself, she will be publicly embarrassed — *karu lah menuveles* — and the social pressure makes it inevitable that eventually she will put on the jewelry and the prohibition will take effect.

### Calm Affirmation

But one difficulty remains: why is there no waiting period? Even once the vow takes effect on *tashmish*, why not give them a week or two, as the Mishnah's earlier section suggests?

### Emotional Dynamics

The Gemara answers: *hani milei heicha d'adrah ihu* — the waiting period applies when he made the vow. In that case, she reasons: *mirtach rasach alai* — he was furious at me; he'll calm down. She can tolerate a week or two because she understands it as an episode of anger that will pass. But in our case: *aval hacha d'nadrah ihi, ve-shtik lah* — here she made the vow and he was silent. He calmly affirmed it. The subject of the vow is marital relations, and he — silently, without anger — let it stand. Her conclusion: *savrah mid'ishtik, misna hu d'sani li* — from the fact that he was quiet, she infers he must hate her. The emotional distance created by his calm acquiescence is far more damaging than the heat of an angry vow. It creates an immediate and unbridgeable rupture — and therefore the Mishnah demands immediate action rather than a waiting period.

### Rav Shmuel Reconcile

At this stage, the approaches of Rav and Shmuel can be fully reconciled within the Mishnah's framework. According to Rav, the husband made the conditional vow — indirectly, about sex — and since it was made without a specified duration, divorce is required immediately. According to Shmuel, she made the vow about sex, he affirmed it calmly and without anger, and the emotional dynamics of that scenario make waiting impossible. Both positions, through different paths, arrive at the same outcome: immediate divorce with full payment of the *ketubah*.

---

## Duration Thresholds

### Mishnah Rule

The Mishnah concludes with Rabbi Yossi's distinction between poor women and wealthy women with respect to the perfume case. For poor women, the vow is intolerable only if it has no stated limit at all; if a duration was specified, even a long one, we tolerate it. For wealthy women — *isha chashuvah* — even a month is intolerable.

### Limit Debate

The Gemara immediately asks: what exactly does "no stated limit" mean? Surely a vow made for twenty years has a stated limit, yet no one would say it is tolerable. At what point does a stated but very long duration become the equivalent of having no limit?

### Time Standards

Three *amoraim* offer their standards. Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel: twelve months. More than a year is considered tantamount to having no limit. Rabbah bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: ten years — a dramatically more lenient threshold. Rav Chisda in the name of Avimi: *regel* — until the next festival. His reasoning: *sheken bnot Yisrael miskashetos ba-regel* — Jewish women adorn themselves for *Yom Tov*. To deprive a woman of the ability to adorn herself even for the festival is intolerable even for the poor, and therefore if the vow extends beyond the nearest *regel*, it is effectively without limit.

### 30-Day Threshold

The Gemara then turns to the wealthy woman's one-month threshold. Why specifically thirty days? The Gemara asks: *peshita* — is this not obvious? And responds: *mai shana l'shloshim yom* — what is it about thirty days? Abaye explains: *sheken isha chashuvah nehenes me-rei'ach kishuteiha l'shloshim yom* — a woman of means still enjoys the residual fragrance of her perfume for up to thirty days. Beyond thirty days, even the lingering scent has dissipated. The Gemara thus makes explicit that the subject here is indeed perfume, and the thirty-day threshold corresponds precisely to the point at which even the most generous residual benefit of the perfume has been fully exhausted.

---

---

# Ketubot 72

## Father's House Vow

### Mishnah Intro

The *mishnah* on 71b introduces a case in which a man takes a vow preventing his wife from visiting her father's house. The mechanism by which he does so is worth pausing on: since a husband cannot directly obligate his wife through a vow, the operative structure is a conditional arrangement — something along the lines of "the pleasure of intimacy with you is forbidden to me if you go to your father's house." The effect is that the condition makes it impossible for her to go without triggering the vow. The scenario has an obvious domestic resonance: whether he simply does not wish to visit his in-laws, or feels that his wife has not fully acclimated to her new home, the *mishnah* treats this as a recognizable, if problematic, marital situation.

### Same City Rule

The *mishnah* distinguishes between cases based on where the wife's parents live. If the father's house is in the same city — where more frequent visits would be the natural expectation — then *chodesh echad yakayem, shnayim yotzi*: a vow lasting one month is tolerable and the marriage may continue, but beyond that he must divorce her. The question of whether the vow itself specifies "one month" or is indefinite with the *beit din* determining how long to allow it to stand is left open, but the practical threshold is clear.

### Different City Rule

When the parents live in a different city, the *mishnah* measures tolerance in *regalim* — pilgrimage festivals. *Regel echad yakayem, shelosha yotzi v'yiten ktubah*: up to one *regel* is sustainable; three consecutive *regalim* during which she cannot visit her father is unreasonable, and he must divorce her and pay her *ktubah*. This immediately raises the obvious question: what about two *regalim*?

### Internal Contradiction

The *gemara* presses on the internal tension: the opening clause implies that two *regalim* is the point of intolerability (since one is tolerable, *ha shnayim yotzi*), yet the closing clause implies that two is still manageable (*ha shnayim yakayem*, since three is the threshold). These cannot both be right.

### Abaye's Resolution

Abaye resolves this by distinguishing between two types of wives: *birdufa* — a woman who is prone to frequent visits, who constantly wants to return to her parents' home — and *she'eina redufa*, one who visits only occasionally. For the woman who constantly runs to her parents, two *regalim* is already intolerable; for the woman who visits only occasionally, the threshold is three. The distinction carries an additional layer of social reality. Given how young these women often were when they married, one can understand both why a husband might grow frustrated with a wife who never seems settled in her new home, and why the restriction on her visits is correspondingly more oppressive for such a woman.

Abaye's colleague Rava bar Ulla offers an alternative resolution: the difference between two and three *regalim* corresponds to a distinction drawn by Rabbi Yehuda between a woman married to a *yisrael* and one married to a *kohen*. Since divorce from a *kohen* is irreversible — a *kohen* may not remarry a divorcée — the rabbis are more reluctant to compel divorce in that case and therefore extend the tolerance to three *regalim*.

### Midrash Interlude

At this point the *gemara* introduces a *midrashic* interlude citing the verse from *Shir HaShirim*: *az hayisi b'einav k'motzet shalom* — "then I was in his eyes like one who found favor." Rabbi Yochanan interprets this as describing a bride who is at peace in her father-in-law's household — meaning her husband's home — and yet still feels drawn to return and share her happiness with her family: *redufa leilech lehagid shivchah b'veit aviha*. This may be setting up a contrast with the previous case: not every wife who wishes to visit her parents is doing so because she has failed to settle into married life. A woman can be genuinely content with her husband and still feel a strong, legitimate pull toward her parents. The *gemara* here acknowledges that longing as real and natural.

---

## Ish vs. Ba'al

### Hosea Prophecy

From this *midrashic* passage the *gemara* transitions to a verse in Hosea: *v'haya bayom hahu ne'um Hashem tikre'i ishi v'lo tikre'i li od ba'ali* — "On that day, says God, you will call Me 'my man' and you will no longer call Me 'my master.'" The plain meaning of the verse's conclusion, *vahasiroti et shem hab'alim mipihah* — "I will remove the name of the *ba'alim* from your mouth" — refers to the elimination of idolatrous associations, since the *ba'alim* were Canaanite deities. The prophetic vision is of a purified worship of God, free from any echo of idolatry.

### Ba'al Mastery

But the verse also says something about the nature of marriage. The word *ba'al* carries a double valence: it means master, and it is also the term for sexual possession — *bo'alaich osaich*, "He who possesses you made you." The relationship structured around *ba'al* is one of male dominance in which even sexuality can be an expression of mastery. *Ish* and *ishah*, by contrast, suggest equality — man and woman — in the same register.

### Feminist Reading

The verse's call to say *ishi* rather than *ba'ali* speaks directly to how one conceptualizes the marital relationship. Contemporary readers attuned to questions of gender equality find in this verse a powerful expression of partnership — *ish* and *ishah* standing on equal footing rather than the asymmetry of master and wife. The contrast is not merely linguistic but structural: saying "my man" rather than "my master" reflects an entirely different understanding of what marriage is.

### Rashi on Union

Rabbi Yochanan articulates the verse's application as follows: *kekallah b'veit chamia v'lo kekallah b'veit aviha* — like a bride who is at home in her husband's household, not one who is perpetually drawn back to her father's house. The connection to *ishi* rather than *ba'ali* is not entirely transparent, but Rashi clarifies: the language of *ishut* and *nisu'in* evokes the model in *Bereishit* of *al kein ya'azov ish et aviv v'et imo v'davak b'ishto* — a man leaves his father and mother and cleaves to his wife, the two becoming one unit. *Ba'al* may connote mastery and sexual possession, but it does not capture that idea of genuine union. Rashi adds: the bride who has already married feels at ease with her husband and is no longer embarrassed before him. That ease, that sense of being genuinely at home, is what *ish* and *ishah* point toward.

---

## Weddings & Funerals

### Mishnah Statement

The *mishnah* continues: *hamadir ishto shelo telech l'veit ha'evel o l'veit hamishte* — a man who vows to prevent his wife from attending a house of mourning or a house of festivity, which is understood to mean a wedding. In either case, *yotzi v'yiten ktubah* — he must divorce her and pay her *ktubah*. No grace period is specified, presumably because the occasion of a funeral is unpredictable: one never knows when it will arise, and the vow is therefore immediately intolerable. The *mishnah* provides the reason: *mipnei sheno'el bifaneha* — he is locking the door in her face, cutting her off from normal social and communal life.

### Locking Door Issue

The *gemara* accepts this reasoning without difficulty regarding the wedding: clearly, preventing a woman from attending celebrations closes off a dimension of normal social pleasure. But the *gemara* presses on the case of the house of mourning: *mai ne'ul bifaneha ika* — what "locking of the door" is involved in preventing her from attending a *beit ha'evel*? Going to a house of mourning is not a pleasure; in what sense is she being deprived?

### Reciprocal Obligation

A *braita* responds: *lemachar hi meita v'ein kol beryah sofedatah* — tomorrow she will die and no one will eulogize her. There is a reciprocal social fabric involved in attending funerals. The woman who is prevented from being present for others will find, when her own time comes, that no one comes for her. And some say the consequence is even starker: not merely that no one will eulogize her, but that no one will want to bury her. The harm, in other words, is not only spiritual but concretely social: it damages her standing in the community and severs the bonds of mutual obligation on which communal life depends.

### Rabbi Meir Teaching

A *braita* then cites Rabbi Meir interpreting the verse in *Kohelet*: *tov lalechet el beit ha'evel milalechet el beit hamishte ba'asher hu sof kol ha'adam v'hachai yitein el libo* — "Better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of rejoicing, for that is the end of all people, and the living should take it to heart." What should one take to heart while at the house of mourning?

### Funeral Consequences

Rabbi Meir spells out the reciprocal calculus in stark terms: *desapad yesafdunihu* — one who eulogizes will be eulogized; *dekavar yikvrunihu* — one who buries will be buried; *de'adli yadlunihu* — one who wails will be wailed over; *delavay yalvunuhu* — one who accompanies a coffin will be accompanied; *detaan yiteanunihu* — one who serves as a pallbearer will have pallbearers at his own burial. The deeper meaning of *v'hachai yitein el libo* is not merely memento mori — though certainly the verse means that too — but an instruction about the obligations of communal solidarity. Attending to the dead is not sentiment; it is the fabric of mutual responsibility without which no community can function.

---

## Legitimate Exception

### Exception Clause

The *mishnah* includes an important qualification: *v'im haya toen mishum davar acher rashay* — if he has another legitimate reason for the vow, it is permissible. This is a striking move: *chazal* are not simply adjudicating tolerability but making a more nuanced judgment about whether the harm to the wife is justified by competing considerations. The implication is that sometimes restrictions that would otherwise be intolerable can become acceptable when there is genuine cause.

### Promiscuity Reason

Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel identifies what counts as a legitimate other reason: *mishum benei adam perutzim she-metzuyim sham* — because there are people of promiscuous or morally loose character present at those gatherings. The husband's concern is not that he suspects his wife of anything specific, but that he objects to the environment and the company to which she would be exposed. Even granting that concern, the question remains: how much weight does his claim carry?

### Rav Ashi Standard

Rav Ashi sets a threshold: *lo amran ela de'itchazek* — this is only valid if the presence of such people at those gatherings has been objectively established. *Aval lo itchazek lo kol kemineih* — if it has not been established, his claim carries no weight. He cannot simply assert that the crowd is morally compromised; there must be some external, objective basis for that claim. This standard is important precisely because it prevents a jealous or controlling husband from manufacturing a pretext to isolate his wife. The distinction between tolerability and justifiability is thus not simply a matter of his subjective feeling, but is subject to some degree of communal verification.

---

## Silence & Absurd Vows

### Secrets Vow

The *mishnah* lists two further cases requiring divorce with *ktubah*. The first: *al menat shetomri l'ploni mah she'amart li o mah she'amarti lach* — a vow conditioned on her revealing to a third party either what she said to her husband or what he told her in private. Whatever she said to him privately, she must now disclose to someone else, or else remain bound by the vow's consequences. This too requires divorce.

### Shame Principle

Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel explains: *devarim shel kalon* — these are shameful matters, things that ought not to be disclosed. At minimum, the disclosure brings shame upon the one who originally spoke those words. Private marital communication has an inherent dignity that is violated when one spouse is compelled to broadcast it.

### Meaningless Labor

The second case: *o shetehei memale'ah um'arah l'ashpah* — or that she should fill things and spill them into the *ashpah*, the dunghill. This too requires *yotzi v'yiten ktubah*. But what does it mean? The plain reading suggests some absurd, repetitive labor. However, the *gemara*'s understanding is more specific.

### Shmuel Interpretation

Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel explains: *shetimaleh v'nofetzet* — the filling and spilling refers to intercourse: the husband ejaculates, her body is "filled," and she then washes out the semen, preventing pregnancy. This is the *gemara*'s primary reading: the husband is compelling his wife to ensure she cannot conceive. Even if a woman is not technically obligated in the commandment of *pru u'rvu*, she possesses the right to have children. Forcing her to prevent her own pregnancy — especially if she desires children — is an intolerable invasion. The phrase *memale'ah um'arah* is thus understood as a euphemistic description of this practice.

A *beraita*, however, presents a different version: *shetimaleh asarah kadei mayim v'saara l'ashpah* — fill ten jugs of water and pour them out into the dunghill. Pure, pointless labor. No preventative function, just meaningless repetition.

### Foolish Appearance

Against this second reading, the *gemara* asks: *v'sa'avid* — so let her do it. What is so catastrophic about having to perform useless work? The first reading is clearly worse because of its impact on the possibility of pregnancy. But the second — filling and spilling water — seems merely tedious. Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan answers: *mipnei shenira'it k'shotah* — because it makes her appear to be a crazy woman. The public dimension matters: she is made to look foolish in the eyes of the community, and this is sufficient grounds for divorce.

### Domestic Control

It is worth noting what the *gemara* does not quite say but what the phenomenon clearly implies. The pattern of compelling a wife to perform absurd, meaningless tasks — completely at the husband's whim, simply because he demands it — is a recognizable structure of domestic control. Those familiar with patterns of marital abuse will recognize that hyper-controlling behavior of this kind — making a spouse perform arbitrary, demeaning acts — is not merely a question of appearances. It reflects a dynamic of domination that often precedes or accompanies other forms of abuse. The *gemara*'s reasoning focuses on the public aspect, *nira'it k'shotah*, but the underlying reality it addresses is something more troubling.

---

## Borrowing & Lending

### Vessel Vow

Rav Kahana introduces a further case: *hamadir ishto shelo tishal v'shelo tash'il* — a man who makes a vow (or, as *Tosafot* notes, perhaps here a direct vow may function) preventing his wife from borrowing certain vessels or from lending them out. The vessels specified are a *nafa* (sieve), a *kivra* (a different type of sieve), a *reikayim* (millstone), and a *tanur* (oven) — all portable household implements of the kind regularly exchanged between neighbors. This too requires *yotzi v'yiten ktubah*.

### Bad Reputation

The reason: *mishum she-mashi shem ra bishcheinosha* — because it gives her a bad reputation among her neighbors. A woman who never lends the cup of flour, who never lets anyone use her sieve, is seen as unfriendly, selfish, closed off from the normal give-and-take of communal life. This social standing matters, and the husband who creates that situation through his vow is the one at fault.

### Wife's Vow

A *braita* teaches the same principle in the mirror case: *hamadir ishto shelo tash'il v'shelo tishal* — even preventing her from borrowing creates a bad reputation. One might think that never asking neighbors for anything is neutral or even virtuous — not imposing on others. But the *braita* rejects this: borrowing is itself part of community life. The woman who never asks her neighbors for anything is perceived as distant, and that too damages her standing.

### Clothing Vow

The *braita* extends this further: *v'shelo ta'arog begadim na'im livaneha* — if the wife herself vowed not to weave fine clothes for his children from a previous marriage. Weaving fine clothes for stepchildren is not among the wife's formal legal obligations. Yet the *braita* rules *teitzei shelo b'ketuva* — she leaves without her *ktubah*, because *mipnei she-mashi'aso shem ra bishcheinav* — she has given him a bad reputation among his neighbors. People ask: why don't your children have nice new clothes for *Yom Tov*? How comes your wife won't weave for them? His social standing suffers because of what his wife is — or is not — doing.

### Shared Standing

The broader principle is clear: community standing is not simply an individual matter. A husband's reputation and a wife's reputation are intertwined through their shared social relations. This is captured well in the vision of *eishet chayil* — *noda bashe'arim ba'alah*, her husband is known at the gates — where the wife's behavior reflects on and shapes the husband's standing in the community. Reputation, the ability to borrow and lend, the quality of one's participation in the routines of communal exchange: all of these are part of what makes a marriage viable or not. And it is worth noting in this context that the parallel from *darchei shalom* applies here as well: the same *braita* that records that we give *tzedakah* to the poor of non-Jews also records that we collect *tzedakah* from non-Jews. The reason: *mipnei darchei shalom*. The relationship of giving and receiving is itself constitutive of community. A woman — or man — who is cut off from that reciprocity is cut off from something essential.

---

## Transgressions Moshe

### Mishnah Intro

The *mishnah* now pivots significantly. Until this point, virtually all the cases we have examined involved the husband as the source of the problem — it was *yotzi v'yiten ktubah*, he must divorce her and pay her *ktubah*, he was at fault. Here the *mishnah* shifts: *v'eilu yotzot shelo b'ktubah* — these are the women who leave without a *ktubah*. The emphasis falls on her behavior. She is transgressing — and because she is at fault, she forfeits her *ktubah*. That said, one should note that *yotzot* itself raises the same interpretive question we have seen throughout: does the *beit din* compel the divorce, or does it merely determine that if a divorce happens, she is not entitled to *ktubah*?

The categories of transgression are: *da'overet al dat Moshe v'Yehudit* — she is transgressing the Law of Moshe or the practices of Jewish women. "Law of Moshe" refers to biblical law; "Jewish women" refers to accepted norms of conduct among Jewish women. Importantly, the *mishnah* is not saying that any transgression — smoking on *Shabbat*, say, or some sin that is entirely between her and God — constitutes grounds for divorce without *ktubah*. The *mishnah* is quite specific, and the *gemara* will clarify why: what is at issue is transgression that directly impacts the husband and makes the marriage untenable.

### Food Without Tithes

The first transgression under *dat Moshe*: *ma'achilato she'eino me'ushur* — she feeds him food that has not had *terumot* and *ma'aserot* properly separated from it, rendering it *tevel*, which is prohibited for consumption. This directly causes him to transgress, not merely a minor prohibition but a serious one — indeed, the class of transgressions listed here all carry severe consequences, many of them *karet*.

It is worth pausing on why the *mishnah* focuses on *tevel* rather than, say, feeding him *chazir*. At one level this reflects practical reality: feeding one's husband obviously non-kosher food was presumably rare and easily prevented, whereas the question of whether *terumot* and *ma'aserot* had been taken — especially from produce that passed through the household in various stages — was a live and common concern in the *mishnaic* period. The category of *am ha'aretz* — the ordinary Jew who was not scrupulous about *ma'aserot* — was a real social phenomenon. Moreover, the *mishnah* places this under *dat Moshe*, which raises a question noted by the students: much of this could be rabbinic obligation depending on the period. Yet the *mishnah* treats it as *dat Moshe*.

### Knowledge Problem

The *gemara* presses immediately: *heichi dami* — what exactly is the case? *Ei yada, nifrosh* — if he knows she is feeding him *tevel*, then don't eat it. The situation seems entirely within his control. *Ei lo yada, mena yada* — and if he doesn't know, how does he ever find out? If he trusts her, he trusts her, and if the transgression never surfaces, how does it become grounds for divorce?

### Indirect Evidence

The *gemara* answers: *lo tzricha d'amra leih ploni Kohen tiken li et hakari* — the case is one where she told him that such-and-such a *Kohen* came and helped her separate *terumot* and *ma'aserot* from the pile of produce. *V'azal v'shaleih v'ishtakach shikra* — he went and asked, and it emerged that she had been lying. He trusted her — that is the foundation of the relationship — and evidence surfaced through a third party that her assurance was false. The transgression was committed and the lie compounded it.

### Niddah Relations

The second transgression: *u'meshamshashu niddah* — she has sexual relations with him while she is a *niddah*. Again the *gemara* asks: if he knows she is a *niddah*, he should simply refrain. If he doesn't know, how does it emerge?

### Reliance Counting

The *gemara* begins from an established principle: Rav Chinana bar Kahana states that a man may rely on his wife in these matters. Shmuel derives this from the verse *v'safra lah shivat yamim* — she counts for herself — meaning the *niddah* herself determines her count and her own purity status. The husband trusts her completely; this is the normative expectation. How, then, could the husband ever come to know that she was lying?

The case is one where she told him she had asked a *chacham* about a blood stain and he had ruled it permissible — *ploni chacham tihar li et hadam*. The husband then went and asked that same *chacham*, and discovered that she had never brought such a question. The lie surfaced through a third party, exactly as in the *tevel* case. A variant offered by the *gemara*: the case of *huchzeka niddah bishcheinosha* — her *niddah* status had been established through her neighbors. In the absence of modern conveniences, a woman who was *niddah* would wear distinctive clothing to protect her regular garments from soiling. If neighbors observed her wearing *niddah* clothing, that was sufficient indirect evidence of her status, such that if she then had relations with her husband — inferred from the pattern of those clothes being worn before and after — the husband could even receive lashes on the basis of that indirect evidence. The broader point is that external evidence can establish what the husband, relying on her word, did not know.

This *gemara* occasions a notable *Tosafot* excursus. The *tosafot* observes that the counting described here is technically associated not with the *niddah* but with the *zavah*, who counts seven clean days. Since contemporary women treat themselves as both *niddah* and *zavah* and count seven clean days accordingly, the *tosafot* asks: why do we not recite a *bracha* on this counting, just as we recite a *bracha* on *sefiras ha'omer*? The answer offered is that a *bracha* presupposes a stable, completable act of counting. *Sefiras ha'omer* runs for forty-nine days without interruption. The *zavah*'s counting, by contrast, is liable to restart at any point if bleeding resumes during those seven days — meaning any individual day's count may turn out to have been invalidated. This makes it structurally different from the *omer*, which proceeds to completion. Most *poskim* resolve the *tosafot*'s question differently, reasoning that the seven-day count is not a formal act of counting at all but simply a process of noting the passage of time; it is not a *mitzvah* in the same sense as *sefiras ha'omer* and therefore does not carry a *bracha*.

### Challah Separation

The third transgression under *dat Moshe*: *v'lo kotza la challah* — she fails to separate *challah* from the dough. The *gemara* applies the same analysis: if he knew, he should not eat it; if he did not know, the case is one where she told him she had brought the dough to a kneader — *ploni gaval tiken li et ha'isa* — who had separated *challah* for her. He went and asked, and found she was lying.

### Unfulfilled Vows

The fourth transgression: *v'noderet v'eina mekayemet* — she makes vows and does not fulfill them. This one is less immediately obvious in its connection to the marriage. The first three transgressions directly cause the husband to eat forbidden food or engage in forbidden relations. What does her failure to fulfill her own vows have to do with him?

### Children's Death

The *gemara* explains via a teaching of the Sages: *ba'avon nedarim banim metim* — for the sin of unfulfilled vows, children die. The source is the verse *al titein et picha lachati et b'sarecha* — do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin — with the end of the verse: *v'chibbel et ma'asei yadecha*. The "work of your hands" is understood as *banav u'vnotav* — one's sons and daughters. Rav Nachman adds a parallel from Jeremiah: *lashav hikeiti et b'neichem* — for nothing have I smitten your children — where *lashav* is understood as relating to *shav*, unfulfilled vows. Whatever one's theological response to the idea that children bear consequences for their parents' failures, this is clearly the understanding that drives the halachic concern. The transgression affects not only the woman but the household, and the children are at risk. That is why unfulfilled vows are placed alongside the other three transgressions: in each case, the wife's conduct creates a consequence that falls upon the husband and the family.

### Meir Provocation

A *braita* cites Rabbi Meir: *kol hayodeia b'ishto shenoderet v'eina mekayemet* — a man who knows his wife takes vows and does not fulfill them. Rabbi Meir's advice: get her to take vows in your presence and then annul them. The *gemara* asks — *yadirna b'mai matkein lah* — how would making a vow on her help? The answer is: *ela yachzir v'yaknitena* — provoke her, make her angry, so that she will take a vow in front of him, and then he can be *mefer* it, annul it. Several problems with this approach are immediately apparent. Even if he manages to provoke her into taking a vow in his presence, what about the vows she takes when he is not there? Moreover, even if he is *mefer* at the end of the day, what happens to the period between when the vow was taken and when he annulled it — could she have transgressed in the interim? And whether the husband must actually hear the vow in order to annul it is itself a question.

### Snake Basket

The response to Rabbi Meir's suggestion — and apparently also to the parallel suggestion about *challah* — is decisive: *ein adam dar im nachash b'chfifah* — a person cannot be expected to live with a snake in a basket. The point is not technical; it is existential. Even if there is a mechanism by which the problem can theoretically be managed — don't eat it, provoke her to take vows in front of you — it is not a viable response. The constant vigilance required, the ongoing need to be on guard against one's own spouse, is itself the problem. A marriage in which one must perpetually protect oneself against the other partner is not a tenable marriage. Rabbi Yehuda similarly says regarding *challah*: go back and separate it yourself. The answer is the same: *ein adam dar im nachash b'chfifah*.

The image here is powerful, and its applications extend beyond this *gemara*. The *Rambam* famously invokes this very principle — *ein adam dar im nachash b'chfifah* — in the context of a wife who declares that she finds her husband physically repugnant and cannot bear intimacy with him. Even though she is the one making the claim, and even though she therefore forfeits her *ktubah*, the *Rambam* holds that the husband must be compelled to give a *get* — because she too cannot be forced to live with a snake. One cannot require a person to cohabit with someone she finds impossible to be with.

---

## Transgressions Jewish

### Mishnah Intro

The *mishnah* now enumerates the transgressions that fall under *dat Yehudit* — the practices of Jewish women — as opposed to *dat Moshe*, biblical law. Four examples are given. Before the *gemara* addresses each one, it is worth noting what the category of *dat Yehudit* represents. These are not biblical prohibitions; they are norms of conduct observed among Jewish women. The concern, as will become apparent, is less about her sinning per se and more about the social and relational signals that certain behaviors send — particularly signals that could attract the attention of other men or compromise the exclusivity and dignity of the marriage.

### Uncovered Head

The first example of *dat Yehudit*: *yotzah v'roshah parua* — going out in public with her head uncovered. The term *parua* connotes more than simply bare; it suggests disheveled, loose, free-flowing. This is the behavior that the *mishnah* categorizes as a violation of Jewish women's practice, making her liable to lose her *ktubah* in divorce.

### Sotah Source

The *gemara* immediately presses: if *roshah parua* is *dat Yehudit* — a norm, not a biblical law — why is it sourced in the *Torah*? The verse cited is *u'phara rosh ha'isha* from the *sotah* passage in *Bamidbar*, where the *kohen* uncovers the suspected adulteress's head. The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives from here *azhara livnot Yisrael shelo yetzu b'farua rosh d'Oraita* — a prohibition for Jewish women against going out with an uncovered head, which is of biblical force.

### Norm vs. Prohibition

Rashi, however, reads this differently. Rather than deriving a prohibition from the *sotah* ritual, Rashi understands the inference as follows: *mi-klal de-chtiv u'phara, mi-klal de-hahi sha'ata lav perua'h hi* — the fact that the *kohen* uncovers her head implies that, at that moment, it was covered. From this we can infer the norm: *ein derech b'not Yisrael latzeit b'farua rosh* — it was simply not the practice of Jewish women to go out with their heads uncovered. This is not a prohibition; it is a recorded norm. Rashi adds *v'chein ikar* — and this is the more accurate reading. A significant number of *rishonim* and *poskim* follow this position, treating the *Torah*'s reference as no more than *asmachta* or a record of existing practice, rather than a binding *d'Oraita* prohibition.

### Law vs. Practice

The *gemara* resolves the question of category by distinguishing between the biblical requirement and the *dat Yehudit* demand. Biblically — *d'Oraita* — a *kalta*, a simple basket-like head covering, is sufficient. The practice of Jewish women, *dat Yehudit*, demands more: *afilu kalta nami assur* — even a basket is insufficient. The exact content of this additional requirement is not fully specified — whether it concerns how much of the head is covered, the opacity of the covering, or some other quality — but the principle is clear: there are two thresholds, biblical and normative, and they differ.

### Context Question

Rabbi Zeira then asks a clarifying question: *heicha*? Where is the context in which this minimal covering — the *kalta* — satisfies requirements? The *gemara* has just established that in the marketplace, *dat Yehudit* demands more than a *kalta*, so it cannot be referring to the public marketplace. Perhaps it refers to her own courtyard? But that introduces a problem.

### Abaye Answer

Abaye (and some say Rav Kahana) answers: *me-chatzer le-chatzer derech mavoi* — the minimal *kalta* is required and sufficient when moving from one courtyard to another by way of the *mavoi*, the alleyway. This is the intermediate zone between the privacy of one's own space and the full publicness of the marketplace.

### Physical Layout

To understand this answer, one must picture the physical layout of the ancient Jewish residential neighborhood. Each household had its own *chatzer* — a courtyard — opening off the main house. Multiple *chatzeirot* opened into a shared, semi-communal space, and those in turn opened into the *mavoi*, the alleyway, which connected to the broader *shuk*, the marketplace. So the *chatzer* itself, while not fully private — other houses open onto it, and other men may be present — is not a genuinely public space either. The *mavoi* is more public, the *shuk* most public of all.

### Public Space Focus

The conclusion the *gemara* reaches is important: in her own *chatzer*, even with other people around, a woman need not cover her head at all. The absence of any head covering becomes a problem only as one moves into more genuinely public space. And in the marketplace, a simple *kalta* is not enough — *dat Yehudit* requires a fuller covering. The intermediate case — crossing briefly through the *mavoi* between courtyards — requires at least the *kalta*.

This emphasis on public space as the operative context has significant implications for contemporary discussions of *kisui rosh*. The concern is not hair as *ervah* in the manner of the *gemara* in *Berachot* — *se'ar b'isha ervah* — which appears to treat exposed hair as categorically problematic. Here the concern is contextual and tied to norms of visibility to strangers. If the governing principle is about public presentation and signals sent to unknown men, then the relevant questions become: what counts as public space, what counts as an accepted norm, and how those norms can evolve. These are live questions for *poskim* across traditions, and different communities have reached very different conclusions depending on which *gemara* they emphasize and how they understand the category of *dat Yehudit*.

### Knitting Arms

The second example: *v'tova ba-shuk* — she knits in the marketplace. Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel explains: *b'mar'eh zero'oteha livnei adam* — the problem is that knitting exposes her arms to men in public. The motion of knitting draws attention to the arms and makes them visible in a way that is considered immodest. It is striking that this particular behavior — which might seem innocuous in other cultural contexts — is listed as grounds for divorce without *ktubah*.

### Red Thread

Rav Chisda in the name of Avimi offers an alternative explanation: *bitova b'vrad k'neged paneha* — the issue is that she knits with a red thread positioned in front of her face. *Tosafot* reads this literally: a red thread (*vered*) catches the eye, draws attention to her face, and causes men to look at her. Rashi reads *paneha* as a euphemism, suggesting that the thread hangs down in front of her pubic area, attracting attention in a more directly suggestive way. Either reading points to the same underlying concern: the knitting creates an occasion for the eyes of strange men to rest on her in a way that the husband finds unacceptable.

### Flirtation

The third example: *u'medaberet im kol adam* — she speaks with every man. On its face this might simply mean conversing with strangers. But Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel specifies: *b'misacheket im bachurim* — she is joking around, being overly familiar, flirting with young men. The problem is not occasional conversation but a pattern of actively seeking flirtatious interaction with men.

### Joking Young Men

The application is not limited to an explicitly sexual or romantic overture; it describes a woman who is *misacheket*, playful and familiar, in a way that signals an inappropriate openness to male attention. *Al tarbeh sicha im ha-isha* from *Pirkei Avot* may similarly be understood in this light — not a prohibition on conversation per se, but on the kind of excessive, flirtatious familiarity described here.

### Arab Woman

A vivid illustrative anecdote: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan recounts that he was once walking behind Rav Ukva when he noticed an Arab woman sitting and throwing a spindle while weaving, with the thread positioned in front of her — whether in front of her face or lower, per the dispute above. When she noticed them approaching, she deliberately snapped the thread and threw the spindle down in front of him — the gesture of dropping an object for a man to retrieve, a classic invitation to interaction. She then said to him: *hav li pilcha* — young man, give me back my spindle. The flirtatious intent was transparent. Rav Ukva applied to her a ruling from our *mishnah*. The *gemara* debates which case: Ravina says Rav Ukva was citing *tova ba-shuk* — she was knitting in the marketplace in the problematic manner. The Rabbis say he cited *medaberet im kol adam* — she was proactively engaging strange men. On the second reading, *medaberet im kol adam* is understood not as casual conversation but as actively seeking flirtatious contact.

### Cursing Parents

Abba Shaul adds a fourth category that stands apart from the theme of female modesty and male attention: *af ha-m'kalelet yeladav b'fanav* — even a woman who curses her husband's parents in his presence. Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel extends this: *b'm'kalelet yeladav bifnei molidav* — she curses his children in the presence of their grandparents. The mnemonic offered is *Efraim u'Menashe k'Reuven v'Shimon yihyu li* — grandsons are like sons — so insulting a grandfather in the presence of the grandchildren is equivalent to insulting a father before his children. The example given is the wife who says to her children, *neichlei arya l'sabba* — "let a lion eat your grandfather." Whether said directly to the husband or in the presence of their children, this is placed in the category of conduct that makes the marriage untenable.

### Loud Voice

Rabbi Tarfon adds: *af ha-kolanit* — also the *kolanit*, the woman with the excessively loud voice. The *mishnah* then provides a definition: *likshehi medaberet b'toch beisah u'shcheneha shom'in kolah* — when she speaks inside her house and her neighbors can hear her voice. The plain reading is that she argues so loudly that the neighbors overhear their quarrels and private conversations — both embarrassing and invasive.

### Loud Sexual

Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel, however, interprets this very differently: *b'mashma'at kolah al iskei tashmish* — her voice can be heard regarding matters of sexual relations. The issue is not domestic arguments but sounds during intercourse that carry beyond the walls of the bedroom.

### Rashi Pleasure

Rashi offers two readings of this phenomenon: either she cries out because sex is painful to her — a genuinely sad interpretation — or she is expressing pleasure loudly. Either way, the *gemara* treats this as a matter of privacy that, when violated, damages the husband's sense of dignity.

### Defect Question

The *gemara* raises an objection to this second reading: if the issue with the *kolanit* is that she cannot control the sounds she makes during intimacy, then this seems like an intrinsic physical characteristic — a *mum*, a defect — rather than a behavioral choice. It should therefore belong in the category of *mumim* addressed in a separate *mishnah*, not among the behavioral transgressions listed here.

### Controllable Behavior

The *gemara* resolves this by preferring the first interpretation: *ela mechvarta kedishanin me'ikara* — the correct reading is the earlier one, that *kolanit* refers to a woman who speaks so loudly inside her house that the neighbors can hear her conversations. This is controllable behavior, a matter of how one conducts oneself, and therefore appropriately categorized among behavioral transgressions of *dat Yehudit* rather than among physical defects. The *mishnah* is about choices and conduct — things the wife can and should control — and the *kolanit* belongs there only if her loudness is understood as a behavioral pattern rather than an involuntary physical trait.

---

---

# Ketubot 73

## Intro & Head Covering

### Opening & Context

Today's learning is dedicated to the memory of those murdered in the *Shoah*. We transition from a *sugya* that dealt with the norms of married women's behavior — specifically the question of head covering — to the next *mishnah*, which opens a discussion of enormous contemporary relevance to *agunah* solutions and conditional marriage.

### Head Covering Review

The previous *mishnah*'s treatment of head covering was notably distinct from the discussion in *Berachot*, which addresses hair as a form of *ervah*. In the *mishnah* under that discussion, the concern is not absolute: it applies specifically to married women, only in public contexts, and bears on the question of whether a woman is drawing undue attention to herself. The *mishnah* emphasizes the head rather than the hair per se, and the *gemara* there raises whether the operative standard is *dat Yehudit* — the norms of Jewish women, which might be subject to change as societal norms evolve — or *dat Moshe*, which may carry biblical weight and may or may not be similarly amenable to change. These remain live and important questions.

### Cond. Marriage Intro

We now turn to the *mishnah* at the bottom of 73b, which addresses *kiddushin al tnai* — conditional betrothal — and which will draw us into one of the most significant *sugyot* for discussions of *agunah* and possible *agunah* solutions in contemporary *halachah*.

### No Vows Condition

The *mishnah* begins: *HaMekadesh et haIsha al menat she'ein aleha nedarim* — a man betroths a woman on the condition that she has no binding vows upon her. *V'nimtze'u aleha nedarim* — and it is subsequently discovered that she does in fact have vows. *Eina mekudeshet* — the betrothal is void. Since the *kiddushin* was made conditional and the condition was not met, the *kiddushin* never took effect. This is straightforward: he verbalized the condition explicitly.

### No Condition, Vows

The *mishnah* then continues with a second clause: *kinusah stam* — he brought her in, meaning he performed *nisu'in*, the stage of full marriage that is the focus of our *masechet*, without articulating any condition. *V'nimtze'u aleha nedarim* — and vows are discovered. *Teitze shelo biKetuvah* — she is divorced without receiving her *ketubah*.

The *gemara* will debate how to read this second clause. The most natural reading of the *mishnah* as a whole seems to be that the second clause builds on the first: the man had already stipulated at the time of *kiddushin* that he does not want a wife with vows, and then he proceeded to the *nisu'in* without re-articulating that condition. Because he had verbalized the *tnai* earlier, it is evident he cares about the matter — hence he may divorce her without a *ketubah*. Yet she may still require a *get*, since the *nisu'in* itself was performed without the condition being reiterated. Alternatively, one could read the second clause as entirely independent: a man simply married a woman with no condition stated at any stage, and the discovery of *nedarim* is, by itself, a sufficient basis for divorce without *ketubah*. This ambiguity is precisely what drives the subsequent *gemara*.

### Blemishes Parallel

The *mishnah* continues with a parallel case: *al menat she'ein ba mumin* — he marries on the condition that she has no blemishes. The condition is not met. Again, *kiddushin al tnai*, condition unmet, *kiddushin* void. Then *kinusah stam* — the *nisu'in* proceeds without re-articulation — and blemishes are discovered. *Teitze shelo biKetuvah*. The structure precisely parallels the vows case.

### Define Mumim

The *mishnah* adds: *kol haMumim haposlim baKohanim poslim baNashim* — whatever blemishes disqualify a *kohen* from Temple service disqualify a woman in this context. This is the operative standard if the husband did not specify which kind of blemish he had in mind. The *gemara* notes that the same *mishnah* appears in *masechet Kiddushin*, where its purpose is to establish the laws of conditional *kiddushin*, while here in *masechet Ketubot* the teaching is needed to address the *ketubah* consequences — specifically that she may be divorced without receiving one. The *mishnah* is thus needed in each tractate for a different focal point: *kiddushin* is the subject there; *ketubah* is the subject here.

---

## Which Vows Matter

### Inui Nefesh Vows

The *gemara* turns to define which category of vows is meant by the *mishnah*. *Amar Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Yosi ben Yehotzadak*: *be'elu nedarim amru* — when the *mishnah* speaks of vows, it is not referring to all vows indiscriminately. Only certain categories are meant. A *baraita* confirms this: *be'elu nedarim amru — dvarim sheyesh bahen inui nefesh* — the *mishnah* refers specifically to vows that involve affliction of the person, *inui nefesh*.

### Affliction Examples

The examples given are: *shelo tochal basar* — that she may not eat meat; *shelo tishteh yayin* — that she may not drink wine; *shelo titkashet bivigdei tzevonin* — that she may not adorn herself with colored garments. These are the same categories the *gemara* earlier identified as constituting *inui nefesh* according to one *tanna*. The implication is that lesser, more trivial vows would not rise to the threshold of being a disqualifying factor.

### Explicit vs Implied

*Ba'ei mineih Rav Pappa*: on which clause of the *mishnah* does Rabbi Yochanan's limitation apply? *Ilima areisha* — if it applies to the first clause, where the man explicitly stipulated "on condition of no vows," then since he expressed an explicit concern, surely any vow, however trivial, ought to matter. The threshold of *inui nefesh* seems out of place there. *Ela asifa* — it must therefore apply to the second clause, where no condition was stated. In that case, since nothing was articulated, the *mishnah* can only be referring to vows of meaningful consequence.

### Reasonable Concern

*Rav Ashi amar*: Rav Ashi disagrees with this framing and applies the limitation even to the first clause — even where the man explicitly said "no vows." *Mihu d'kafid inshi havei kfeida* — what counts as a legitimate concern is determined by what people normally care about. If he said "no vows" without further specification, we interpret that statement to encompass only vows that normal people would genuinely object to. *Mihu d'la kafdi inshi* — things that people ordinarily disregard are not included, even if the man used broad language. Of course, if he is explicit and specific — "I don't want any vow whatsoever, no matter how trivial" — then he may indeed make such a condition binding. A person may set any stipulation he chooses. But where he speaks in general terms, we do not read the condition to extend beyond what a person would reasonably mean. One might ask why *inui nefesh* is the relevant measure here, since the concept designates an affliction of *her* body — why should that be the operative criterion for *his* concern? The most natural answer is that what significantly affects her wellbeing and daily life also shapes the texture of the shared marital relationship in ways that matter to him as well.

---

## Rav v. Shmuel

### Condition Persistence

*Itmar*: the *gemara* now introduces the central dispute that emerges from this *mishnah*, and which has profound ramifications for *halachah*. The case: *kidsha al tnai* — the *kiddushin* was made with an explicit condition — *v'kansah stam* — and the *nisu'in* was performed without reiterating that condition. What is the *halachah*? Does the *tnai* made at the time of *kiddushin* continue to operate at the time of *nisu'in*, even though it was not repeated?

### Rav's Position

*Rav amar*: *tzricha heimenu get*. She requires a *get* from him. Once the *nisu'in* has taken place — even though the *tnai* was not repeated — she is considered married. The *tnai* made at the time of *kiddushin* does not persist through the *nisu'in* to void the marriage.

### Shmuel's Position

*Shmuel amar*: *eina tzricha heimenu get*. She does not require a *get*. Since the *tnai* was articulated at the time of *kiddushin*, if the *kiddushin* never took effect because the condition was not satisfied, then the subsequent act of *nisu'in* and cohabitation does not create a marriage. In Shmuel's view, marital relations are meaningful only insofar as they rest upon an antecedent valid *kiddushin*. Without a binding *kiddushin* as the foundation, the act of *be'ilah* is simply *be'ilah* — it is not an independent act of *kiddushin*.

### Ain Adam Oseh

*Amar Abaye*: Abaye clarifies that Rav's reasoning is not, as one might suppose, that by proceeding to *nisu'in* without reiterating the *tnai*, the husband implicitly waived it — thereby retroactively validating the original act of *kiddushin*. That would be a remarkable notion: that a waiver occurring a year later could retroactively render the original giving of the ring binding. Abaye dismisses that reading. *Ela ta'ama deRav* — Rav's reason is *she'ein adam oseh beilato beilat zenut* — because a person does not wish his act of marital intercourse to be an act of fornication. The original *kiddushin* was not binding because the *tnai* was unmet. But the act of *be'ilah* itself is one of the recognized modes of effecting *kiddushin*, and we presume that within the context of a *chuppah* and the entire marital framework, the man intends this act to be a marital one. Because he would not want it to be an illicit act, we conclude that he wishes the intercourse itself to constitute *kiddushei bi'ah*.

### Marital Intent

This reasoning raises a deeper question: does the principle of *ein adam oseh beilato beilat zenut* mean that the man actively intends the act of *be'ilah* to be an act of *kiddushin* — in which case *kavvanah* would be necessary — or does it mean that in a marital context *kiddushei bi'ah* operates automatically, irrespective of explicit intent? Some *Acharonim* take the latter position, that *kiddushei bi'ah* within a marital context requires no specific *kavvanah*. The practical concern with such a reading is significant, however: it would mean that any couple living together in an established marital arrangement, even without having contracted a halachically valid *kiddushin*, would be considered married and would require a *get* — a result with potentially sweeping implications for *agunah* cases and the like.

The *gemara* proceeds: once the *nisu'in* is performed and the couple cohabits, Rav holds they are married not because the original *kiddushin* has been retroactively validated, but because the act of *be'ilah* itself constitutes a new, independent act of *kiddushei bi'ah*. There is accordingly a *nafka mina* between these two theories: when precisely is the marriage considered to have taken effect? If it is from the time of the original *kiddushin*, one set of consequences follows; if from the time of *be'ilah*, another set applies. For example, if the woman had relations with another man between the *kiddushin* and the *nisu'in*, the question of when they are deemed married is directly material. In the *gemara*'s framing, *kiddushei bi'ah* and *nisu'in* here occur together at the time of *be'ilah*, with the earlier *kiddushin* not having been the operative act.

---

## Minor Girl Case

### Ktanah Growing Up

The *gemara* observes that Rav and Shmuel have already disputed this issue once before in an analogous context. *Ktanah shemi'anah v'higdilah*: the case of a minor girl who was married off by her mother or brothers — as is permitted when she has no father — and who did not exercise her right of *mi'un* (refusal) while she was still a minor. She then became an adult and continued to live with her husband. The original *kiddushin* effected by her mother or brothers had only rabbinic force; it was not a fully binding *kiddushin deOraita*.

### Rav on Intercourse

*Amda venisset* — suppose she then goes and marries a second man. Rav holds: *ein tzricha get misheini* — she does not require a *get* from the second man. Why? Because by continuing to cohabit with the first husband after reaching adulthood, she effected a new, binding *kiddushei bi'ah* with him. The continued marital intercourse in an established marital context is itself a valid act of *kiddushin*. Her subsequent "marriage" to the second man was therefore invalid from the outset, since she was already married. Consequently, the second *kiddushin* simply does not take effect and no *get* is required from that man.

### Shmuel on Original

Shmuel, by contrast, holds: *tzricha get misheini*. In his view, the continued marital cohabitation does not independently create *kiddushin* where none previously existed. Since the original *kiddushin* by her mother and brothers was not fully binding, and she never executed a new, independent act of *kiddushin* with her first husband as an adult, she was not halachically married to him when she contracted the second marriage. The second *kiddushin* is therefore valid, and if she now wishes to leave the second man she requires a *get* from him.

The parallel to the *tnai* case is evident. In both cases, the original *kiddushin* was deficient — in the *tnai* case because the condition was unmet; in the *ktanah* case because her original *kiddushin* lacked full *deOraita* force. The question in both cases is whether continued cohabitation independently generates a binding marriage. Rav says yes; Shmuel says no, everything depends on whether the foundational *kiddushin* was valid.

### Two Cases Needed

The *gemara* asks: since it is the same underlying dispute, why must it be stated in both cases? The *gemara* answers: *tzricha*. Each case is needed because it presents a scenario where one might have thought that even Rav would concede to Shmuel.

Had we only the *tnai* case, one might have said: that is where Rav says continued cohabitation is binding — *because* there is no explicit *tnai* in force at the time of *nisu'in*. But in the *tnai* case, where the man explicitly articulated "only on condition of no vows," one might think that even Rav concedes that the explicit *tnai* continues to frame the relationship, and that continued cohabitation does not override it. We therefore need the *tnai* case to show that even there, Rav holds the *be'ilah* creates *kiddushin*. This, in fact, is a larger *chiddush* on Rav's part: where a *tnai* was explicitly stated, there is greater reason to think it should persist and frame all subsequent relations, and yet Rav holds that the continued marital *be'ilah* nonetheless creates *kiddushin* unconditionally.

Conversely, had we only the *ktanah* case — where no *tnai* was ever articulated — one might have thought that Shmuel, who says continued cohabitation is not binding, agrees only there because nothing at all was ever said. But in the *tnai* case, where at least something was verbalized (even if the condition ultimately was not met), perhaps Shmuel would agree with Rav that continued living together creates *kiddushin*. We therefore need both cases to fully establish the scope of their dispute.

---

## Agunah Solutions

### Ein Tnai Principle

Our *amud* is brief, owing in part to the substantial *Tosafot* that occupies much of the page. The *Tosafot* engages with a statement found in another *gemara*: *ein tnai benis'uin* — conditions cannot operate at the *nisu'in* stage. This principle is of great moment for understanding whether conditional marriage can ever serve as a solution to the *agunah* problem.

From our *gemara* itself, the conclusion seems to be that it is specifically because the *tnai* was not reiterated at the time of *nisu'in* that Rav holds the *be'ilah* creates *kiddushin* unconditionally. One might reason, accordingly, that had he explicitly reiterated the *tnai* before the *chuppah* — "everything that follows, including our living together, remains conditional on her having no *nedarim*" — then perhaps even Rav would agree the *tnai* remains operative. But this other *gemara*, with its categorical *ein tnai benis'uin*, suggests that in principle, no matter what is said, once the couple begins living together they are married. There is no room for conditions at the *nisu'in* stage.

### Tosafot on Agunah

*Tosafot* directly engages this issue in the context of the *agunah* problem. The prospect of a solution through conditional *kiddushin* — making the original betrothal conditional on circumstances that would prevent an *agunah* situation — has been debated by *poskim* going back some 150 years, notably among the rabbis of France. The idea is straightforward: if the *kiddushin* is made conditional at the outset — for example, on condition that the husband will always give a *get* if the marriage breaks down, or on condition that some future circumstance does or does not come to pass — then if those conditions are not met, the *kiddushin* is retroactively void and no *get* is required.

### Explicit Tnai Option

One approach discussed by *Tosafot* is whether a sufficiently explicit and carefully framed *tnai* at the time of *kiddushin* might nonetheless operate effectively. From our *gemara*, the limiting factor appears to be the *be'ilah* at the time of *nisu'in*, which in Rav's view creates an unconditional *kiddushin* regardless of what came before — grounded in *ein adam oseh beilato beilat zenut*. But as *Tosafot* notes, the principle of *ein adam oseh beilato beilat zenut* operates *mistama* — as a default assumption in the absence of explicit statement. If the parties explicitly and unambiguously declare that their living together and cohabiting is itself still conditional, one could argue they have effectively acknowledged the possibility of *beilat zenut* and are consenting to the arrangement. In that case, perhaps the assumption no longer applies and the *tnai* could remain operative. The question then becomes whether the categorical *ein tnai benis'uin* from the other *gemara* would foreclose even this.

### Secular Marriage Impact

A further avenue discussed by later *poskim* is that the principle of *ein adam oseh beilato beilat zenut* was formulated in a social context where religious marriage was the only form of recognized marriage. In contemporary reality, where civil marriage exists and is recognized by the state and by society at large, the couple may not perceive their cohabitation as *beilat zenut* even if the halachic *kiddushin* were conditional or void. If there is civil marriage in place, the marital setting is defined not only by the religious *kiddushin*, and therefore the presumption that the man would not want his *be'ilah* to be *zenut* may operate differently. This provides an additional basis to argue that a properly structured *tnai* might remain effective in contemporary circumstances — at least as a matter of theoretical *lamdanut*, even if the *halachah lema'aseh* remains contested.

---

## Mishnah Reconcile

### Two Clauses Link

The *gemara* now examines how our *mishnah* relates to the debate of Rav and Shmuel. The second clause of the *mishnah* — *kinusah stam v'nimtze'u aleha nedarim, teitze shelo biKetuvah* — appears on its simple reading to be building on the first clause. That is, the *kiddushin* was already conditional, the *nisu'in* was done without repeating the *tnai*, vows are discovered, and she must be divorced. *Teitze* implies she requires a *get*. *Mai lav bid'katrei tnai* — is this not then explicitly a case where the *tnai* was stated at *kiddushin* and she still requires a *get* after *nisu'in*? That would be a clear contradiction of Shmuel.

### Rav Reads Stam

Rav resolves this by insisting that the second clause is an entirely independent case. When the *mishnah* says *kinusah stam* — he brought her in without condition — it means that nothing was said at either the *kiddushin* or the *nisu'in* stage. It is a simple case: a man married a woman, and after *nisu'in* vows are discovered. In that case, a woman with *nedarim* constitutes grounds for divorce, and though no *tnai* was ever stated, the man is not required to pay the *ketubah* — a woman with binding vows is precisely the kind of situation he cannot have been expected to knowingly accept. She requires a *get* because of course there was *nisu'in*, but the *ketubah* is forfeited.

### Shmuel Expects Chiddush

Shmuel's interpretation of the *mishnah* proceeds differently. He argues that the *mishnah* would be more instructive if it presented the case where the *tnai* was made at *kiddushin* and was followed by *nisu'in*. After all, the obvious *chiddush* from Shmuel's position would be: even if there was *nisu'in* after the conditional *kiddushin*, she is still not married if the condition went unmet — *eina mekudeshet*. Why does the *mishnah* tell us only what happens before *nisu'in*, the obvious case? It should have told us the more striking ruling: that even after *nisu'in*, the original *tnai* renders her *lo mekudeshet* with no *get* required. The *gemara* responds on Shmuel's behalf.

### Resolution: Any Stage

The *gemara* resolves: *hachi nami ka'amar* — that is indeed what the *mishnah* is saying. The *mishnah*'s first clause, which states that where *kiddushin* was conditional and the condition was not met she is *eina mekudeshet*, is not limited to the case where *nisu'in* has not yet taken place. The *mishnah* speaks to the general principle: if the *kiddushin* was made conditional and the condition was not satisfied, she is not *mekudeshet* — regardless of whether *nisu'in* subsequently occurred. The second clause then addresses an independent scenario: where no *tnai* was ever articulated, she requires a *get* but forfeits her *ketubah*.

---

## Vows Without Tnai

### Why Reject Vows

The *gemara* presses further on the second clause — the case where no *tnai* was stated. If the man never said anything, why should we assume he objects to vows sufficiently to justify his withholding the *ketubah*?

### Taos Analysis

This raises the possibility that a woman with vows should be regarded as *kiddushei ta'os* — a mistaken betrothal. If men universally object to vowed wives, then perhaps the *kiddushin* itself is void from the outset, and she should not even need a *get*. *D'amar* — since we say *ee efshi b'isha nadranit*, I cannot accept a wife who takes vows, why does this not void the marriage entirely? *Get nami lo tiba'ei* — why should a *get* be required at all if it is a clear case of *kiddushei ta'os*?

### Safek Position

*Amar Rabba*: it is not a clear-cut *kiddushei ta'os*. Rather, it is a *safek* — a genuine uncertainty as to whether the *kiddushin* was valid. We are not certain whether a man's objection to *nedarim* is so universal and absolute that we can declare the *kiddushin* void without any prior stipulation. *Sfuki maspka lei*. *V'chen amar Rav Chisda tzricha get midivrehem.* Rabba and Rav Chisda both rule that a *get* is required, though the nature of that requirement is now qualified by the *safek*.

### Issura-Mamona Split

The practical consequence of this *safek* is a well-known halachic split between *mamona* and *issura*. *Lgabei mamona l'kula* — on the monetary question of whether the *ketubah* must be paid, we rule leniently: since we are uncertain whether the *kiddushin* was binding, she bears the burden of proof, and *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'ayah* — the one seeking to extract money must prove entitlement. She cannot collect the *ketubah*. *Gabi issura lachumra* — on the question of personal status, however, where the concern is *safek eshet ish*, we are stringent: she requires a *get* because the *kiddushin* may have been fully valid.

---

## Intermediate Position

### No Middle Ground

What is striking here — and the *gemara* does not resolve it — is that the *gemara* does not recognize an intermediate category of *hakpadah*. One might have thought there exists a middle ground: not quite *kiddushei ta'os* (which would void the *kiddushin* entirely), but enough of an objection that the man is entitled to divorce her without paying the *ketubah*. The *kiddushin* would be valid and binding, yet her failing to disclose the *nedarim* would constitute a kind of fault on her part sufficient to justify divorcing her without *ketubah*.

### Warranty Analogy

Consider a parallel from commerce: if a person purchases a car and discovers a major defect, we might say it is a *mekach ta'os* — the entire transaction is void. But if the defect is minor — the CD player does not work — it is not a *mekach ta'os*, yet the buyer is still entitled to compensation or repair. There is a middle tier. By analogy, one could have imagined a case of *nedarim* where the man cannot say "we were never married," yet can legitimately say "this was not what I agreed to, and I am entitled to end the marriage without paying the *ketubah*."

### Gemara's Limits

The *gemara* does not pursue this middle path. Instead, it limits itself to two options: either it is a *safek kiddushei ta'os* — in which case we split the ruling between *mamona* and *issura* — or it is a *get midivrehem*, a rabbinically required *get*, without entitlement to *ketubah*. Notably, earlier in the *masechet*, the *gemara* did grapple with an analogous middle category: the case where a man married a woman believing her to be a *betulah* and discovering she was not. There, the *gemara* entertained the possibility of a binding *kiddushin* combined with reduced *ketubah* entitlement. It is therefore genuinely puzzling that here the *gemara* does not deploy similar reasoning, and no explicit resolution is offered for this apparent gap in the analysis.

---

## Rava Limits Debate

### Two Women Scenario

*Amar Rava*: the *gemara* now presents Rava's attempt to narrow the scope of the Rav-Shmuel debate. *Machlokes b'ta'os shtei nashim* — the dispute applies only in the case of two women. That is: a man made a *tnai* with one woman, that *tnai* was not met or the *kiddushin* was invalid, and he then went ahead and married a different woman without stating any condition. The question is whether the *tnai* he made with the first woman is somehow presumed to apply to his marriage with the second woman as well. In that peculiar scenario, Rav and Shmuel disagree.

### One Woman Consensus

*Aval b'isha achat divrei hakol eina tzricha heimenu get* — but in the straightforward case of one woman, where he made a *tnai* with her at *kiddushin* and proceeded to *nisu'in* with her, everyone agrees the *tnai* remains operative. If the condition was not met, she does not need a *get*, because the *tnai* at *kiddushin* naturally carries through to the *nisu'in* stage. Rava's reading thus fundamentally limits Rav's position: Rav agrees that a properly framed *tnai* at *kiddushin* binds the entire subsequent relationship, including the *be'ilah*.

### Abaye Challenges

*Amar Abaye*: Abaye challenges this immediately. *V'ha matnisin b'isha achas hi* — our *mishnah* deals with one woman, and we have just used it to challenge Shmuel's position. This presupposes that Rav and Shmuel's debate is relevant to the single-woman case. If Rava is correct that both Rav and Shmuel agree in the one-woman case, why would the *mishnah* be cited as a challenge to Shmuel at all? Rashi notes that an implicit consensus seems to have formed in the course of the *gemara* that the debate is indeed applicable to the one-woman case, precisely because we challenged Shmuel from our *mishnah* — which involves only one woman.

### Rava Refines

Rava accordingly refines his position: *machlokes b'isha achas k'ein shtei nashim* — the debate applies even in the case of one woman, but only when the circumstances resemble those of two women. The case Rava now envisions, according to Rashi, is something like this: a man betrothed a woman with a *tnai*, they had a troubled relationship, he then divorced her before *nisu'in*, and subsequently they reconciled and contracted a new *kiddushin* and *nisu'in* without re-stating the *tnai*. Does the *tnai* from the first *kiddushin* carry over into the second? Rav says it does not — the new *nisu'in* without re-articulation is a fresh, unconditional marriage. Shmuel says the *tnai* from the first round persists.

It is admittedly a strange reading of Rav and Shmuel, and Rava is clearly pressing to say that in an ordinary case — one woman, one *kiddushin*, one *nisu'in* — a *tnai* at *kiddushin* remains operative through *nisu'in* and the *be'ilah*, and this is universally agreed. The extraordinary *chiddush* of Rav, in Rava's reading, is limited to these peculiar edge cases.

---

## Invalid K. + Sex

### Baraita Setup

*Aisaivei Abaye* — Abaye challenges from a *baraita*: if a man performed *kiddushin* with a woman in error — *b'ta'us* — or with an object worth less than a *perutah*, such that the *kiddushin* was invalid; or a minor who betrothed — all cases where the *kiddushin* was not binding. *Af al pi sheshalach sivlonos l'achar mikan* — even if after these events he sent gifts (*sivlonos*) to her and her family in the customary manner between *kiddushin* and *nisu'in*, this does not constitute a new act of *kiddushin*. *Shemachmat kiddushin harishon shalach* — because the gifts were sent in the framework of the original (invalid) *kiddushin* and the social custom surrounding it, not with intent to effect a new *kiddushin*.

### Tannaim Dispute

*V'im ba'alu* — but if they subsequently had intercourse (after, for example, the minor became an adult): *kanu* — they are now married, according to one opinion. *Mishum Rabbi Yishmael omer*: *im ba'alu lo kanu* — the act of intercourse does not render them married. This is, the *gemara* observes, the precise dispute of Rav and Shmuel transposed to the level of *Tannaim*: an original *kiddushin* that was not binding, followed by cohabitation — does the *be'ilah* independently create *kiddushin*?

### Same as Rav-Shmuel

*Abaye* identifies this *baraita* dispute as identical in structure to the Rav-Shmuel debate. The case in the *baraita* is one of a deficient *kiddushin* followed by *be'ilah*; the question of whether *be'ilah* independently creates *kiddushin* is exactly what Rav and Shmuel argue about.

### Taos v. Tnai

*Rabba* objects: there is a meaningful distinction between *ta'us* and *tnai*. The *baraita* is dealing with a case of genuine error — *ta'us* — where the parties did not realize the original *kiddushin* was invalid. But a case of *tnai*, an explicit condition, is different. When there is an explicit *tnai*, the parties know exactly why the *kiddushin* might not be binding. That explicit framing arguably shapes all subsequent relations as well. Rabba thus maintains that even Rav, who holds that *be'ilah* creates *kiddushin* in a *ta'us* case, would agree that an explicit *tnai* frames all subsequent cohabitation — and that therefore the *baraita* deals with something different from our central case.

---

## Taos Definition

### Knowledge Approach

The *gemara* proceeds to clarify the internal logic of the *baraita*'s dispute. One view: *adam yodeia she'ein kiddushin tofsin b'pachot mishaveh pruta* — a person knows that *kiddushin* effected with less than a *perutah* (or by a minor) is invalid. Therefore, when they subsequently have intercourse, *v'gamar u'ba'al l'shem kiddushin* — they do so with conscious intent to create a new, valid *kiddushin*. On this reading, the *be'ilah* is an intentional, knowing act of *kiddushin*. Hence it is binding.

### Ignorance Approach

The opposing view: *ein adam yodeia she'ein kiddushin tofsin b'pachot mishaveh pruta* — people are generally not aware that *kiddushin* with less than a *perutah* is legally defective. They believe themselves to be already validly married. *V'chi ka ba'al adaata d'kiddushin harishonim ba'al* — and when they subsequently cohabit, they do so entirely in reliance on and within the framework of the original *kiddushin*. Since the original *kiddushin* was invalid, the *be'ilah* does not constitute a new act of *kiddushin* — it is framed by the original (defective) *kiddushin* and has no independent effect.

### Condition Frames All

The conceptual distinction Rabba draws between *ta'us* and *tnai* now becomes clearer: in the *ta'us* case, the question is one of knowledge — did the parties know or not know the original *kiddushin* was invalid? In the *tnai* case, that question is irrelevant. When a man explicitly says "I am marrying you only on condition of X," that explicit condition announces itself as the frame for everything that follows, regardless of knowledge. All subsequent cohabitation is colored by that declaration.
