Since she is effectively always in some *apitropya* relationship, the oath right always applies.

### Snake Proverb

The Sages respond: *ein adam dar im nachash bi-kfifa* — a person cannot live under the same roof with a snake. Allowing the husband to demand an oath at any time, over the grocery money or the dough, creates an intolerable atmosphere of suspicion. The *Gemara* works through the logical implications: if Rabbi Eliezer means the husband may do this entirely *le-chatchila* — that is, without any pre-existing oath context — then the Sages' response is apt and forceful. If he means it only as *gilgul* — the bundling doctrine — then one might ask why the wife should care.

### Gilgul Bundling

The *Gemara* answers: she cares even about the *gilgul* case. *Gilgul* means that once a party is already required to take an oath about one matter, additional obligations may be packaged into that same oath. Even this limited application of Rabbi Eliezer's position is psychologically devastating: *keivan de-daikat batrai kulei hai* — you are so exacting with me — *lo matzina le-meidar bahadach* — I cannot continue to live with you. It is one thing to be subject to oath-compulsion in the context of running your million-dollar business. It is another to have the same distrust extended to the few coins spent on groceries. The *ta shema* from the *baraita* confirms that Rabbi Eliezer does indeed mean the husband may act *le-chatchila*, and *shema mina* — we learn accordingly — that this is his explicit position.

---

## Oath Waiver Mechanics

### Wife Exemption

The new *mishnah* introduces the mechanism by which the husband may waive his oath rights entirely. *Katav lah neder u-shvu'a ein li alayich* — if he writes to her that he has no right to impose a *neder* or *shvu'a* upon her — *eino yachol le-hashbia* — he can no longer compel her to swear. A *neder* would take the form: "If I stole anything from you, let the fruits of the world be forbidden to me." A *shvu'a* is a direct oath: "I swear I did not steal from you." By writing this waiver — whether in the *ketubah* or as a separate document — he relinquishes the right to demand either.

### Heir Limitations

However, the waiver is limited to what was in his power to waive. *Aval mashbia hu et yoresheha ve-et ha-ba'im bi-rshuta* — but he may still compel her heirs and those who come through her authority to take an oath. When the heirs come to collect the *ketubah*, for instance, he may make them swear they have not already been paid. The exemption he granted runs only to her personally, not automatically to all who derive rights through her. This closely parallels the earlier *mishnah*'s discussion of *mechilah*: just as a seller cannot fully transfer a debt because the obligation runs to him and not to the buyer, so too a waiver of oath rights is interpreted narrowly unless its language is explicitly expansive.

### Explicit Language Rule

The *Gemara* establishes that the narrowest interpretation governs by default. A general waiver of the husband's own oath rights does not, without explicit language, extend to his heirs or to those to whom the wife sells her *ketubah*. The language must be spelled out.

### Complete Waiver

To foreclose all avenues, the husband must state: *neder u-shvu'a ein li alayich ve-al yoreshaich ve-al ha-ba'im bi-rshutaich* — I have no oath right over you, your heirs, or those who come through your authority — and further, *ve-lo ani ve-lo yorshai ve-chol ha-ba'im bi-rshuti* — neither I, nor my heirs, nor anyone acting through my rights. *Eino yachol le-hashbia* — in that case, none of these parties can compel an oath — *lo hu ve-lo yorshav ve-lo ha-ba'im bi-rshuto* — not from her, her heirs, or those who come through her.

### Post-Mortem Status

What happens after the husband's death? *Halcha mikever ba'alah le-beit aviha* — she went from her husband's grave back to her father's house — or she returned to live in the home of her father-in-law — *ve-lo na'asit apitropya* — and no new stewardship arrangement was established. In that case, *ein ha-yorshim mashbi'in otah* — the heirs cannot compel her to take an oath — because Reuven, the husband, had waived all oath rights in his lifetime, and her current role involves nothing beyond what was covered by that prior waiver.

### New Stewardship

But *ve-im na'asit apitropya* — if after her husband's death the heirs actively appoint her to continue managing the estate — *ha-yorshim mashbi'in otah al ha-atid lavo, ve-ein mashbi'in otah al ma she-avar* — the heirs may make her swear regarding future dealings but not past ones. The new appointment creates a fresh legal relationship with fresh oath rights; it is entirely unaffected by the deceased husband's prior waiver, which pertained only to obligations arising from her relationship with him. What he waived was his own authority and that of those acting through him — once that relationship ends and a new independent arrangement begins, the waiver does not reach it.

The general principle running through all of these cases is consistent: a person may waive only what is within his authority to waive. Additional parties, additional relationships, and future obligations require explicit language and cannot be assumed from a general grant. Absent such explicit language, the most restrictive interpretation prevails.

---

---

# Ketubot 87

## Oaths & Husbands' Author…

### Review of Ketubot 86b

The present daf, 87, opens as a golden continuation of the previous discussion. We pick up with the *gemara* at the very last line of 86b. The preceding material dealt with the idea that a husband whose wife manages his store may require her to take an oath that she has not misappropriated any funds. The *gemara* then turned to the next *mishnah*, which states that a husband may write for his wife — presumably at the time of their marriage — an exemption relieving her from ever having to take a *neder* or a *shevuah*.

### Exemption from Oaths

The *mishnah* thus contemplates a situation in which the husband anticipates future disputes and, at the outset of their marriage, formally waives any right he or his heirs might have to impose an oath upon her. This exemption covers the wife herself and, depending on the language employed, may extend to her heirs and his heirs as well — a question the *mishnah* explores in some detail. The discussion on 86b left open the precise meaning and scope of this exemption.

### Neder vs. Shevu'ah

To clarify the terminology at stake: a *shevuah* is a direct oath — "I did not steal any money." A *neder* operates differently; it is a vow of the form "If I misappropriated anything, let all the fruit in the world be forbidden to me." These are two distinct mechanisms by which a person might be bound to affirm the truthfulness of an account, and the *mishnah*'s exemption addresses both.

---

## Rav Yehuda vs. Rav Nachm…

### Apotropaya Interpretation

The *gemara* opens with the question: *shevuah mai avidatei* — what type of *shevuah* are we talking about, and in what context would the husband be exempting his wife from it? Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav answers: *al apitropaya shenasit bechayei ba'ala* — the exemption refers to the wife's role as administrator (*apitropaya*) of the husband's business during his lifetime. In this reading, the husband, anticipating that his wife will manage his affairs, preemptively exempts her from any oath she might otherwise be required to take as a business manager.

### Pogemet Ketubah

Rav Nachman in the name of Rabba bar Avuha disagrees. He holds that the *mishnah* is not referencing the previous *mishnah* about the storekeeper but rather the following one, which begins: *hapogemes kesuvasah lo tipara ela bishvua* — a woman who "injures" her *ketubah* may not collect except by oath. What does *pogemes* mean? The word *pogem* means to cut into or injure. The case is one where the woman comes to collect her *ketubah* and the husband claims he has already paid it. She, however, need not admit anything — she holds the *shetar*. Yet if she herself concedes that part of the *ketubah* has been paid — say, a hundred out of a thousand — she has voluntarily reduced her own claim. Once she makes such a concession, a *shevuah* is required that the remainder is still outstanding.

One might ask: doesn't she have a *migo* — an argument from the stronger position she could have taken? Had she said nothing, she would have been entitled to collect the full amount. The fact that she conceded more than she needed to might itself lend credibility to her claim. This question is noted here but deferred; it will be addressed as the *mishnah* is analyzed further.

According to Rav Nachman, then, what the husband writes in the *ketubah* is a preemptive waiver of this *shevuah* obligation — the obligation that arises precisely from the wife's own partial concession. He anticipates that at some point during the marriage she might need to draw on the *ketubah* as an advance, and he wishes to spare her the burden of a *shevuah* when the time comes to collect. As Rashi notes, the stakes of this debate are halachic: if the husband's waiver applies to the *apitropaya* case but not the *pogemet* case, then a woman relying on such language to avoid the *shevuah* of *pogemet* might find herself mistaken. The *shevuah* of *pogemet* is triggered not by the husband's demand but by the woman's own concession and, in a sense, by the court — which may mean it falls outside the scope of what the husband's waiver can reach.

### Rav Ashi's Clarification

Rav Mordechai brought this debate before Rav Ashi. The question he laid before him was: given these two positions, which of them correctly explains the *mishnah*, and are they truly in debate with one another about the opening of the *mishnah*?

---

## Resolving the Debate

### Why Not Apotropaya?

Rav Ashi responded with a striking reframing: *atun haha masnisula* — "you apply this statement of Rav Yehuda to the *mishnah*" — and then are puzzled that it yields an unusual scenario. The *gemara* indeed presses this point: *ela man d'amar apitropsha shenasis bechayei ba'ala, ee hava yad'a demoseiv apitropsha* — if the husband made his wife an administrator, why would it have occurred to her, at the time of the marriage, to preemptively request that he write an exemption from an oath arising out of business management? That is not the typical scenario one contemplates when drafting a *ketubah*.

Tosafot attempts a defense of this reading, suggesting that perhaps the woman was already serving as the husband's administrator before the marriage — they met through business, or he knew he would want her to continue in that role. There are indeed plausible scenarios: a husband who plans to travel and expects his wife to run the store, or one who had employed her previously. Nevertheless, the *gemara* concludes that this is not the *pshat* — the plain, standard reading of the *mishnah*. It is not impossible, but it is not the ordinary case that a *mishnah* would be expected to address.

### Pogemet as Plain Sense

Rav Ashi therefore establishes that Rav Nachman's position — that the *mishnah*'s opening refers to *pogemet ketubah* — represents the plain sense, and in fact reflects a consensus. Everyone agrees that the husband's waiver, written at the time of the *ketubah*, anticipates the future scenario of *pogemet*: the wife may one day take an advance on her *ketubah* and, when she later comes to collect, will concede that part has been paid. The husband, wishing to spare her the burden of a *shevuah* even in that circumstance — even though it is triggered by her own concession — writes the exemption in advance. This is the *reisha* of the *mishnah*, and Rav Yehuda's statement about *apitropaya* was never intended to address it.

### Apotropaya in Seifa

Rather, Rav Ashi explains, Rav Yehuda's statement belongs to the *seifa* — the end of the *mishnah* — not the beginning. The *seifa* of the *mishnah* reads: *halcha mikever ba'ala leveit aviha o shechazra leveit chamia* — she went from burying her husband to her father's house or returned to her father-in-law's house. If she was not appointed as administrator after his death, *ein hayorshin mashbi'in osah* — the heirs cannot make her swear regarding past business dealings, because the husband had already exempted her. But *ve'im nasis apitropsha* — if she does continue as administrator now for the heirs — *yoresh mashbi'in osah al ha'atid lavo* — they can make her swear regarding future dealings, *aval ein mashbi'in osah al she'avar* — but not regarding what is past.

It is on this clause — "what is past" — that Rav Yehuda's statement is addressed. His formulation, *al apitropaya shenasit bechayei habaal*, underscores that the heirs may not impose a *shevuah* for any business conducted when the husband was alive. That much the *seifa* makes clear. What remains to be asked is: what about the brief period between death and burial?

This resolution is, in itself, a remarkable moment. Rav Ashi is explaining to Rav Mordechai that two statements which appeared to be competing explanations for the *mishnah*'s opening were, in fact, never in dialogue with one another. Rav Nachman's statement belongs to the *reisha*, Rav Yehuda's to the *seifa*, and each addresses an entirely different question. The fact that they were juxtaposed and taken as competing readings reflects an understandable confusion about the context of each ruling — and Rav Ashi's correction illustrates how the original context of a statement could be obscured over time.

---

## Between Death & Burial

### Mishnah on Heirs' Rights

The *mishnah* in its *seifa* draws a clear line: past activities (those conducted during the husband's lifetime) are exempt from any oath the heirs might seek to impose, while future activities (those conducted by her for the heirs after his death) are subject to such an oath. But the precise boundary of "the past" is what now occupies the *gemara*: what about the period between death and burial?

### Rav Yehuda's Ruling

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states: the exemption from the heirs' oath covers all business dealings conducted *bechayei habaal* — when the husband was alive. The husband who exempted her shielded her completely from any oath regarding the decade or more she may have managed his affairs. The heirs cannot say that they know she was cheating for years and demand she swear otherwise. The exemption stands.

### Oath Between Mita-Kevura

But Rav Yehuda then adds: *aval bein mita likvura mashpinan lah* — between death and burial, they can impose an oath on her. The reasoning is that once the husband has died, the estate has technically passed to the heirs. If she sells property or handles funds during the period of *aninus* — the state between death and burial — she is now, in legal terms, handling the heirs' assets, not her husband's. That period constitutes *atid lavo* relative to the heirs' estate, and they may therefore demand accountability for it.

The scenario is not as strange as it might seem. Consider: the husband has been running a business, or she has been running it for him, for many years. He dies. Before burial, there may be urgent financial needs — the burial itself must be funded, the household must be provisioned, and so on. She continues managing the affairs. The *gemara* acknowledges that technically this is now the heirs' business, and the heirs can therefore make her swear regarding the propriety of those transactions. That is Rav Yehuda's position.

### Rav Matna's Position

Rav Matna disagrees: *afilu bein mita likvura lo mashpinan lah* — even between death and burial, no oath may be imposed on her. Despite the technical legal analysis that assigns those dealings to the heirs' estate, the practical reality demands protection for the woman managing affairs under extremely difficult circumstances.

### Urgent Sales Doctrine

To support this, the *gemara* cites the teaching of the scholars of Nehardea: *lekarga u'lemezonei u'lekvura, mazbininan belo achrazta* — for the payment of a poll tax, for the provision of food, or for burial, one may sell property from an estate without going through the normal process of public announcement. Ordinarily, when property of an estate must be sold to pay debts, a formal announcement must be made so that the market is informed and a fair price may be obtained. But in these three pressing cases — government tax obligations that carry serious consequences if delayed, the immediate food needs of the widow or heirs, and the necessity of burying the deceased without delay — we dispense with the announcement process and sell immediately.

The relevance to our question is that this doctrine establishes a recognized category of urgent, potentially imperfect transactions made under the pressure of death. The normal standards of careful stewardship cannot be applied to decisions made in this period.

### Rashi's Rationale

Rashi explains the connection as follows: the woman managing the estate in the brief window between death and burial may have been compelled to sell assets quickly and perhaps not at the best terms in order to raise funds for the burial. It would be unjust to then subject her to an oath in which she must account for every decision made under that pressure. The *halakha* accepts that such decisions will inevitably be somewhat imperfect, and therefore declines to impose an oath for the dealings of that period.

### Tosafot's Fear

Tosafot, however, takes a different approach. One might ask: even granting Rashi's point, why can't the heirs at least make her swear that she did not personally pocket any money — that she did not steal — even if they cannot demand she justify every business decision made under duress? Tosafot answers that the real concern is entirely practical. The woman has been willing to manage the business and the estate throughout precisely because she has not been subject to oath obligations. If the heirs tell her that any dealings she conducts during this period will be subject to a *shevuah*, she will simply refuse. She will say: I am not handling the burial arrangements and the estate under those conditions. You manage it yourselves. The heirs, suddenly confronted with an estate they have never administered and with the urgent demands of burial bearing down on them, will be left stranded. To prevent this outcome, the *halakha* grants her a blanket exemption even from a *shevuah* about personal misconduct during this period — because threatening her with any oath at all creates an unacceptable risk that she will abandon her post at the worst possible moment.

---

## Language of Exemption

### Dela vs. Naki

The *gemara* now turns to a separate question: what happens when the husband, rather than using the precise language of the *mishnah* (*neder ushevuah ein li alaich* — "I have no *neder* or *shevuah* against you"), uses more passive formulations? The *mishnah* explored whether the husband's language included his heirs and hers. Here the discussion concerns two alternative phrasings: *dela neder, dela shevuah* — "without a *neder*, without a *shevuah*" — and *naki neder, naki shevuah* — "clean from a *neder*, clean from a *shevuah*."

### Rabba's Interpretation

Rabba in the name of Rav Chiya rules as follows. If the husband uses the language *dela neder, dela shevuah* — without a *neder*, without a *shevuah* — *hu eino yachol l'hashbia, aval yorshin mashbi'in osah* — he himself cannot make her take an oath, but his heirs can. The language is narrow and applies only to him. By contrast, if he uses the stronger formulation *naki neder, naki shevuah* — clean from a *neder*, clean from a *shevuah* — *bein hu bein yorshav ein mashbi'in osah* — neither he nor his heirs can make her take an oath. The word *naki*, clean, conveys a total absolution: *minakish mishvuasa* — I have cleansed you from any need of a *shevuah* whatsoever. That language is expansive enough to bind the heirs as well.

### Rav Yosef's Counter

Rav Yosef in the name of Rav Chiya reaches a surprising and much harsher conclusion. He agrees with Rabba on the *dela* formulation: *dela neder, dela shevuah* — the husband cannot impose an oath, but the heirs can. On the *naki* formulation, however, he goes in the opposite direction from Rabba. Rav Yosef reads *naki neder, naki shevuah* to mean not exemption but affirmation of the obligation: *lah naki nafshach b'shvuasa* — "you will have to prove your own innocence through a *shevuah*." On this reading, both he and his heirs can make her swear.

This is a striking position. The practical implication is troubling: if the husband is writing language that merely restates the existing status quo — that she is required to make a *shevuah* — why would he write anything at all? As the *gemara* itself notes, *ein adam motzi d'varav livatalah* — a person does not issue statements for no purpose. If the *naki* language changes nothing, what was the point of writing it? The answer, apparently, is that a husband must be extremely careful about the language he uses; an ambiguous formulation may be read against the woman in ways that serve no one.

### Rav Zakai's Resolution

Rav Zakai sent a ruling to Mar Ukva that cuts through the terminological debate entirely. Whether one says *dela shevuah* or *naki shevuah*, whether *dela neder* or *naki neder* — none of these linguistic distinctions determines whether the heirs are bound. The only distinction that matters is possessive language. If the husband writes *b'nichsai* — "from my property" — then *hu eino yachol l'hashbia, aval yorshin mashbi'in osah* — he cannot impose the oath but his heirs can. The possessive "my" limits the exemption to assets that are his; once those assets pass to the heirs and are no longer "his," the exemption does not follow them. But if he writes *minichsaya ilin* — "from this property," using a demonstrative rather than a possessive — *bein hu bein yorshin ein mashbi'in osah* — neither he nor his heirs can impose an oath. The property is defined by reference to the thing itself, not the person who owns it, and the exemption travels with the property regardless of who holds it.

---

## Abba Shaul's Teaching

### Complete Exemption

Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel in the name of Abba Shaul ben Ima Miriam — a *tanna*, and notably identified here through his mother's name — rules with maximum breadth in the woman's favor. Regardless of which language the husband uses — *dela shevuah, naki shevuah, dela neder, naki neder, b'nichsai, nichsai ihu* — in every case, *bein hu bein yorshav ein mashbi'in osah*: neither he nor his heirs can impose an oath on her. Every formulation, however narrow or passive, is interpreted in the most expansive way possible to protect the woman from being subjected to a *shevuah*. This ruling is subsequently cited as *halacha* by Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel: *halachah k'ven Ima Miriam* — we rule like the son of Ima Miriam.

### Creditor Exception

There is, however, a crucial caveat. Abba Shaul himself acknowledges it: *aval mah e'eseh, sheharei amru chachamim haba lifra minichsei yesomim lo yifra ela b'shvuah* — "but what can I do, for the Sages have ruled that anyone who comes to collect from the property of orphans may not collect except by oath." This is a general rule of *halakha* applying to all creditors, entirely independent of any arrangement between husband and wife. Whoever comes to the heirs to collect a debt must swear that the debt has not been paid — because the heirs have no firsthand knowledge of the father's transactions and cannot be expected to know what was or was not settled during his lifetime.

### Two Types of Oaths

The result is that there are two distinct categories of *shevuah* in play here. The first is the oath of the *apitropaya* — the oath a business manager or administrator might be required to take to account for her stewardship. This is the oath the husband waives, and his heirs are bound by that waiver in all cases per Abba Shaul's ruling. The second is the oath of the general creditor — the oath required of anyone collecting a debt from heirs. This oath has nothing to do with the husband's trust of his wife or the specific relationship between them; it is a structural feature of the law of inheritance and debt collection. The husband cannot preemptively waive this obligation, because it is not an obligation owed to him — it is an obligation owed to the heirs, arising from their own ignorance of the prior state of accounts.

This distinction applies with equal force to the *pogemet ketubah* scenario. If the husband exempted her from the *shevuah* of *pogemet*, she need not swear when collecting from him that the remainder of the *ketubah* is unpaid. But if she is collecting from the heirs after his death, the ordinary exemption from *pogemet* is covered — yet she must nonetheless swear as a creditor collecting from an estate. The one exemption covers the oath owed to the father; it does not cover the oath owed to those who now hold his estate.

---

## Pogemet Ketubah Intro

### Mishnah Cases

Having completed the discussion of the oath exemption, the *gemara* now turns to the *mishnah* that Rav Nachman identified as the primary subject of that exemption — the *mishnah* of *pogemet ketubah*. The *mishnah* opens: *hapogemes kesuvasah lo tipara ela bishvua* — a woman who "injures" her *ketubah* by admitting that part of it has been paid may not collect the remainder except by oath. The *mishnah* then identifies a second case: *ed echad meidah sheparuah* — a single witness testifies that the *ketubah* has been paid in full — and rules that she likewise may not collect except by oath. These are the first two scenarios in which the oath requirement applies.

### Meshubadim & Absent Part…

The *mishnah* continues with additional cases: *minichsei meshubadim* — collecting from liened property — and *shelo b'fanav* — collecting in the debtor's absence. In the first of these, the husband has sold his property to others and the wife comes to execute her lien against those purchasers. The purchasers naturally cannot know whether the *ketubah* debt has been settled between husband and wife, and so she must swear that it has not. In the second case, the husband has gone abroad — to a distant land, as the *mishnah* puts it — and under certain circumstances collection may proceed without him present. There too, since he cannot speak for himself, she must swear that the debt remains outstanding.

### Case-by-Case Analysis

The *mishnah* then spells out each of these cases with unusual explicitness, almost as if anticipating confusion. For *pogemet*: the *ketubah* is a thousand, he says it has been paid in full, she says she received only a hundred — she must swear that the nine hundred remains unpaid. For the single witness: the *ketubah* is a thousand, he says it has been paid, she says she received nothing, and a single witness corroborates that it was paid — she must swear to collect. For *meshubadim*: he sold his property, she comes against the purchasers — she must swear. For the heirs: he died and left his estate to his heirs, she comes against them — she must swear. For the absent debtor: he has gone abroad, she collects without him present — she must swear. The *mishnah* finally records a view of Rabbi Shimon that as long as she is actively seeking her *ketubah*, the heirs may make her swear, and if she is not seeking it, they may not — a position whose elaboration is deferred to the next session.

---

## Biblical vs. Rabbinic

### Rami Bar Chama

With the *mishnah* now before us, the *gemara* raises the foundational analytical question: is the *shevuah* of *pogemet ketubah* a *shevuah de'oraita* — a biblically mandated oath — or is it a rabbinic enactment? Rami bar Chama initially proposes that it is biblical. His reasoning: the case of *pogemet* resembles a classic instance of *modeh bemiktzat* — a partial concession to a claim. The rule of *modeh bemiktzat* is biblical: if someone claims two hundred from you and you concede a hundred while denying the other hundred, you take a biblical oath and are exempted from paying the disputed amount. Here, he argues, the woman's concession that a hundred has been paid is analogous to a *modeh bemiktzat*, and the resulting *shevuah* should therefore be biblical.

### Rava's Refutation I

Rava offers two responses, both decisive. The first: *kol hanishba'in shebaTorah nishba'in velo meshalmin* — all those who swear biblical oaths do so and are thereby exempted from payment. In the classic *modeh bemiktzat* case, the debtor swears and does not have to pay the disputed portion. The *shevuah* functions to protect the swearer from payment. But here the situation is inverted: *vehi nishba'as venoteles* — she takes the oath and she collects. The *shevuah* enables her to extract money from the other party. No biblical oath operates in this direction. Biblical oaths protect the swearer from paying; they do not empower the swearer to collect.

It is worth dwelling on how this distinction works structurally. In a standard *modeh bemiktzat*, there is no *shetar* — no written instrument establishing the debt. The claimant says "you owe me two hundred," the respondent concedes a hundred and denies the rest, takes an oath, and pays only what he conceded. Without the *shetar*, the claimant's uncorroborated insistence on the additional hundred cannot extract payment. The oath resolves the dispute in favor of the swearer. In the *pogemet* case, however, the woman has a *shetar* — the *ketubah* document establishing the full debt. Even without any concession on her part, she would be entitled to collect the full amount. The *shetar* itself is her proof. Her concession that a hundred has been paid does not eliminate her entitlement to the remainder; it only raises a question, and the *shevuah* resolves that question in her favor and allows her to proceed to collect. The *shevuah* thus functions as a collection mechanism, not an exemption from payment — which is structurally incompatible with the biblical oath.

### Rava's Refutation II

Rava's second response: *ein nishba'in al kfirat shibud karka'os* — no biblical oath is administered in connection with a denial regarding a lien on land. Since the *ketubah* operates as a lien on real property, and the biblical oath does not apply in disputes involving land, this case simply cannot be a *shevuah de'oraita* on that basis alone.

### Rabbinic Purpose

Rava therefore concludes: *miderabbanan* — this is a rabbinic *shevuah*. The Sages enacted it for a specific purpose. Their reasoning is rooted in a realistic assessment of human psychology and attention.

### Psychology of Memory

*Depara dayek* — the one who is paying is careful and attentive. *Demifra lo dayek* — the one who is being paid is not necessarily so attentive. When a person is paying off a debt, that act of payment is significant and memorable; he knows precisely what he has paid and is motivated to keep accurate track. But the person receiving payment may not be equally attentive — she may not register with the same precision what she has and has not received, particularly if she is not the one initiating or controlling the transaction.

The Sages therefore concluded that when a woman concedes that part of her *ketubah* has been paid, this creates a real possibility — not an accusation of conscious dishonesty, but a recognition of differential attention — that perhaps more has been paid than she recalls. *Urami rabanan shvuah alah, ki heichi detidok* — the Sages imposed an oath on her so that she should pay close attention. The act of swearing forces careful reflection; it compels her to go back through her recollections with full seriousness before asserting that the remainder is unpaid.

This framework is notable because it deliberately avoids the implication that the woman is lying. If we assumed she was consciously lying, the oath would be of questionable value — a familiar principle established at the beginning of tractate *Bava Metzia*: one who is suspected of financial dishonesty (*chashud al ha'mamonah*) may also be suspected of swearing falsely (*chashud al hashevuah*). The rabbinic rationale for the *shevuah* of *pogemet* specifically avoids this inference. The woman is presumed honest; the *shevuah* is there to calibrate her memory to the same level of precision as the one who paid her.

---

## Clarifying Mishnah Cases

### Witnesses Question

The *gemara* now poses a series of questions about variations on the *pogemet* case. The first: *pogemes kesuvasah b'eidim mahu* — what if the partial payment that she concedes was witnessed? That is, there are witnesses who saw that a hundred was paid. Does she still need to swear that the remaining nine hundred is outstanding, or does the presence of witnesses on the partial payment actually strengthen her position?

The argument for exempting her from the oath runs as follows: if we observe that when he paid the first hundred, he ensured witnesses were present, then the inference is that this person is careful to document his payments. Had he paid the remaining nine hundred, he would likewise have secured witnesses or a receipt. Since there are no witnesses to any further payment, the absence of evidence is itself evidence of absence — and she should be able to collect without a *shevuah*. This is a version of the *migo* reasoning raised earlier.

### Oath Categories

The *gemara* seeks to resolve this by citing the *mishnah* that enumerates who takes oaths and collects: *kol hanishba'in shebaTorah nishba'in velo meshalmin* — all who swear in the Torah swear and do not pay. The *mishnah* then lists the exceptional categories where one swears and collects: the hired laborer (*sachir*), the person who was robbed (*nigzal*), the person who was injured (*nechbal*), the one against whom the opposing party is suspected of swearing falsely, and the storekeeper swearing by his ledger. Among these is also: *vehapogemet shtaro shelo v'edim* — one who injures a *shetar* without witnesses. The crucial qualifier is *shelo v'edim* — in the case where the partial concession was made without witnesses to the payment.

The *gemara* initially reads this as implying that when there are witnesses (*be'edim*), she does not need to swear. But the *gemara* then reverses this reading: *lo mibaya ka'amar* — the *mishnah* speaks in the form of "it goes without saying." The obvious case — where there are witnesses to the partial payment — she certainly needs a *shevuah*, because there is concrete corroboration that part was paid, making it all the more plausible that the rest was paid too. The *mishnah* specifies the less obvious case: even *shelo v'edim*, even when there are no witnesses to the first payment and she could have said nothing (the *migo* argument), she still needs a *shevuah*. Because if there were witnesses, the case for a *shevuah* is all the stronger. The question about what happens *be'edim* is thus left genuinely unresolved.

### Precise Accounting

The second question: *hapogemet ketubasah pachos pachos mishtei prutos mahu* — what if the woman's concession of partial payment is rendered in extremely precise terms, down to fractions of pennies? Rashi explains that the scenario envisions a woman who has kept careful, detailed records — she accounts for every payment with specificity, listing dates and exact amounts down to the last cent. Given this level of precision, one might argue that she is clearly on top of the accounting and is obviously truthful: *keivun dekadaika kulei hai, kushta ka'amrah* — since she is so precise in every detail, she must be telling the truth.

### Precision Paradox

But there is a countervailing possibility: *arumei kama'arimah* — she may be a sophisticated deceiver. By producing an elaborate and precise accounting, she hopes to project such an air of meticulous honesty that no *shevuah* will be required of her. The very precision may be a stratagem. After all, if she truly wanted to lie, she could claim nothing was paid at all — the *migo* runs in her favor on the fact of her concession regardless. But by combining a partial concession with extreme precision, she might achieve both the appearance of honesty and the avoidance of the oath. The *gemara* leaves this question unresolved: *teiku*.

### Reduced Amount

The third question: *pocheshes kesuvasah mahu* — what if the woman does not concede that part of the *ketubah* has been paid, but instead concedes that the original *ketubah* amount was less than what the document states? She is not saying "you paid me a hundred"; she is saying "we agreed from the outset that the real *ketubah* was only two hundred, not a thousand, even though a thousand is written." Is this a case of *pogemet*, requiring an oath?

### Conceding Lesser Amount

The argument is that *pogemet* involves a concession of partial payment, creating the concern that perhaps full payment has been made. But here there is no partial payment at all. She simply says the amount was always lower. Since the underlying concern — that he may have paid the full claimed amount and she has forgotten — does not apply when she is not claiming any payment has been made, she should be able to collect the lesser amount without a *shevuah*.

The *gemara* confirms this: *pocheshes tifrah shelo bishvuah* — one who concedes to a lesser original amount collects without a *shevuah*. The *mishnah* spells this out explicitly: the *ketubah* says a thousand, he claims it has all been paid, she says she was never paid a penny but the real *ketubah* was only a hundred — *tifrah shelo bishvuah*, she collects the hundred without an oath. This is structurally different from *pogemet*: she is not a *modeh bemiktzat* in any sense because she is conceding nothing about payments having been made.

### False Document Resolution

A natural difficulty arises: if the *ketubah* document says a thousand and she is conceding it should only be a hundred, she is effectively admitting the document is not accurate. How can she then use the document to collect anything? If the *shetar* is false, it is, as the *gemara* vividly puts it, *chispa be'alma* — a mere piece of pottery, worth nothing.

Rava the son of Rava resolves this: *be'omeres amanah haisah li beini leveino* — she is saying that there was an understanding of trust between them. The couple agreed at the time of the marriage that they would write the larger number — perhaps to honor the expectations of parents, or to make a certain impression at the wedding ceremony — but with a mutual understanding that she would only ever collect the lesser amount. The *shetar* itself was validly executed, the witnesses signed a genuine document, and he was genuinely obligated. She simply agreed, by virtue of their private understanding, not to collect the full face value. The document is therefore not false; it is a valid instrument against which she has voluntarily agreed to collect less. On that basis, she may use the *shetar* to collect the agreed-upon lesser amount, and since she is not conceding any partial payment but only a lesser original obligation, she collects it without a *shevuah*.

---

---

# Ketubot 88

## Modeh B'Miktzat

### Oath Cases Overview

The daf begins in the middle of 87b, amid a discussion of the various circumstances in which a woman must take an oath in order to collect her *ketubah*. The Gemara enumerates several distinct cases, each generating its own type of *shvua*, and it is worth pausing to understand what is at stake before working through them one by one.

### Partial Payment Concession

The first case is where the woman herself concedes that part of the *ketubah* has already been paid. This might seem like a straightforward instance of *modeh b'miktzat* — the well-known biblical rule that one who partially admits a claim must take an oath — but it is not quite that. The classical *modeh b'miktzat* applies to the party from whom money is being extracted, whereas here it is the collecting party — the woman — who is making the partial admission. The technical conditions for the biblical oath therefore do not apply.

### D'Rabbanan Oath Rationale

The oath imposed in this case is accordingly a *shvua d'rabbanan*. The concern driving it is that she may have forgotten: the fact that part of the debt has been paid creates a real possibility that she has lost track of the full account. The oath functions as a mechanism to force her to review the matter carefully and be doubly certain before collecting. The rabbis instituted this *shvua* precisely because the partial payment introduces reasonable doubt, and the gravity of the oath is meant to prompt genuine recollection.

---

## Ed Echad & Shvua

### One Witness Testifies

The second case shifts the dynamic considerably. Here, the woman comes to collect, the husband claims he has paid, and she denies it. Ordinarily she would prevail: she holds a *shtar*, and he has no receipt. But suppose the husband produces a single witness — an *ed echad* — who testifies that the *ketubah* has in fact been paid. She must now take a *shvua* to contradict that witness. This too has the structural feel of an oath rooted in biblical law.

### Rami Bar Chama Position

Rami Bar Chama indeed argued that this constitutes a *shvua d'oraita* — a biblical oath. His reasoning proceeds from the verse in Deuteronomy.

### Deut. Source & Ed Echad

The verse states: *lo yakum ed echad b'ish l'chol avon u'l'chol chatat* — one witness shall not rise up against a person for any sin or transgression. The Gemara derives from this that while an *ed echad* cannot prevail outright in court and impose liability, he does have the legal force to compel an oath from the opposing party. This interpretation is the foundation of the entire institution of the *ed echad* demanding a *shvua*.

### Witness Demands Oath

The operative principle is that an *ed echad* does not win the case — he cannot substitute for the two witnesses required to obligate payment — but he destabilizes the status quo enough that the other party cannot simply ignore him. Without any witness, the default rule of *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'ayah* governs: the one seeking payment bears the burden of proof. An *ed echad* disrupts that default, and the only way to neutralize him and restore the status quo is to take an oath. The oath does not itself create a new obligation; it dissolves the threat posed by the single witness, returning the parties to where they would have stood without him.

### Shnayim/Echad Rule

This logic is crystallized in a general principle: *kol makom she-shnayim m'chayvin oto mamon, echad m'chaivo shvua* — wherever two witnesses would obligate payment, one witness obligates an oath. It bears noting that this principle applies specifically in monetary matters. In the domain of *issurim*, a single witness is regarded as entirely without legal weight. But in monetary disputes, a lone witness has real, if limited, force: not to compel payment, but to compel an oath.

Applying this to the *ketubah* case: she holds a *shtar* — which functions as two testimonies — and he has one witness who says it is paid. Two witnesses would have cancelled her *shtar* entirely. One witness demands that she take an oath to neutralize his testimony, after which the *shtar* reasserts itself and she collects. The structure is symmetrical with the classical *ed echad* scenario. Rami Bar Chama's position that this is a biblical oath therefore appears quite reasonable.

---

## Rava's Two Reasons

### Oath Taker Benefits

Rava, however, rejects this analysis and offers two distinct reasons why the oath imposed here cannot be biblical. His first objection goes to the heart of how biblical oaths function: *kol hanishba'in she-ba-Torah nishba'in v'lo m'shalmin* — every biblical oath in the Torah is one where the oath-taker swears and thereby avoids paying. The paradigm of the biblical *shvua* is defensive: I am accused of owing you money, you have an *ed echad* backing your claim, and I take an oath to neutralize that witness and establish that I owe nothing. The oath is a shield.

### She Swears & Collects

In the *ketubah* case, however, the structure is inverted. The woman is not defending herself against a demand for payment; she is the one seeking to collect. She swears, and then she *takes* money — *nishba'at v'notlet*. That is the opposite of the biblical pattern. The oath here is a sword, not a shield, and the Torah's framework for the *shvua d'oraita* simply does not encompass this configuration. To be sure, the underlying logic is structurally similar: the *ed echad* creates a complication that must be neutralized, and the oath restores the status quo — but the status quo here is that the *shtar* entitles her to collect, not that she is exempt from paying. Biblically, one takes an oath to avoid paying; one does not take an oath in order to collect.

### Karka Lien Issue

Rava's second reason is equally dispositive. A *shtar* with a *ketubah* carries *shibbud karka'ot* — liens on land. When the dispute concerns a document that creates encumbrances on real property, there is a general rule that oaths are not taken with respect to the denial of *shibud karka'ot*. Since the *ketubah* is precisely such a document, the oath cannot be biblical on this ground as well.

### D'Rabbanan to Appease

With both biblical rationales eliminated, Rava concludes: this oath is purely rabbinic, instituted *kedei le-hafis da'ato shel ba'al* — in order to appease the husband. The husband is agitated; he has a witness who he believes confirms that he paid. The *shvua* is designed to calm him. One might fairly ask how an oath she takes really calms a husband who is convinced he is telling the truth and has a witness to back him up — the oath might strike him as just another layer of her alleged deception. The question is a real one, and the Gemara's choice of this rationale over more obvious alternatives deserves attention.

### Oath & Truthfulness

The more obvious explanation would be that the *ed echad* creates an objective concern that she may not be telling the truth, and the oath addresses that concern by making her formally accountable before God. But the Gemara pointedly does not say this. The reason, it seems, connects to a deep structural tension in the institution of the oath: if someone is willing to steal, will they really hesitate to swear falsely? The Gemara in Bava Metzia raises precisely this question — *chashud al mammon chashud al shvuasah* — and if the answer is that a person who steals will also swear falsely, then the oath does not actually address the concern that she is lying. It only functions as a deterrent if we assume that she is not an outright thief, perhaps that she has rationalized her position or made an honest error.

In the first case — where she conceded partial payment — that assumption was entirely plausible: maybe she forgot, maybe she lost track of the account. The oath prompts recollection. But in this case, where the dispute is total — he says he paid everything, she says he paid nothing — it is not plausible that she simply forgot the entire payment. So the honest-error explanation does not work here. And since the Gemara is implicitly reluctant to say that an oath deters an outright liar, it reaches instead for the relational explanation: it appeases the husband. The function of the oath, on this reading, is not evidentiary but social — it is designed to manage the interpersonal tension rather than to resolve a factual question.

---

## Biblical Oath Strategy

### Husband's Clever Move

The Gemara now introduces a striking practical turn. Rav Pappa observes: *i pike'ach hu, mati lah liydei shvuah d'oraita* — if the husband is clever, he can maneuver the situation so that she ends up taking a biblical oath rather than a rabbinic one.

### Rashi on Weightiness

Before examining the strategy, the Gemara implicitly raises the question of why this matters. Rashi explains: a *shvua d'oraita* is qualitatively different from a *shvua d'rabbanan*. The biblical oath is pronounced using God's name — or at minimum a divine epithet such as *Elokim* or *Shaddai* — and is administered while the swearer physically holds a *Sefer Torah*. The verse *lo yenakeh Hashem es asher yisa shemo la-shav* — God will not absolve one who takes His name in vain — gives the biblical oath a metaphysical weight that a rabbinic oath lacks.

### Curse vs. Oath

A *shvua d'rabbanan*, by contrast, is in essence *klala b'alma* — merely a curse, an invocation of ill fortune upon oneself if one is lying. The psychological and spiritual weight is considerably diminished. The husband, who is convinced he is in the right, has a strong incentive to force the more solemn form of the oath, which may either prompt her to recant or — should she proceed — carry far graver consequences.

### Double Payment Tactic

The husband's strategy, as the Gemara describes it, proceeds as follows: since he will likely have to pay out the *ketubah* anyway once she takes the rabbinic oath and collects, he should go ahead and pay her now — in front of a different witness, call him *Shimon* — even though he already paid her earlier (in front of the original witness, *Reuven*). He is paying her a second time, but calculating that the expenditure is worth the legal position it creates.

### Combining Witnesses

Having now paid her twice, he brings the two witnesses together — *Reuven* and *Shimon* — and confronts her: I have paid you the *ketubah*, I have two witnesses. She cannot deny the May payment because it is proven by both witnesses. Now he turns around and says: but what about the money I gave you in January? That was a loan. You owe me that money back. She denies the loan. He produces *Reuven*, who witnessed the January payment. Now the situation has been restructured: he is the one seeking to recover money, she is the one denying it, and he has an *ed echad* — the classic configuration of the biblical oath. She must swear a *shvua d'oraita* to get out of paying him.

### Combining Witnesses

The challenge with this scheme, however, is the problem of combining *Reuven* and *Shimon*: they witnessed different events at different times. Using *Reuven* first to establish that the *ketubah* was paid in January, and then turning around and using *Reuven* to claim that the January payment was actually a loan, creates an internal contradiction. The same hundred dollars cannot simultaneously be *ketubah* payment and a loan, and the same witness cannot serve both characterizations.

### Rav Sheshes Fix

Rav Sheshes, son of Rav Idi, therefore simplifies the scheme: in May, before making the second payment, bring both *Reuven* and *Shimon* together to witness it. The husband says to *Reuven*: come with *Shimon* and watch me pay her now. Now the May payment is unambiguously proven by two witnesses, and it stands on its own without any need to import *Reuven*'s January testimony into the question of whether the *ketubah* was discharged. The January payment, witnessed by *Reuven* alone, can then be characterized purely as a loan, and *Reuven* is not being asked to play contradictory roles.

### Two Ketubos Defense

Rav Ashi, however, raises a further objection: she can simply claim *bei kesuvos havai* — that there were two separate *ketubot*. She argues: you loved me so much that you wrote me one *ketubah* for a certain sum and another *ketubah* for the same sum. You paid off the first *ketubah* in January and the second in May. There was no loan; both payments discharged *ketubah* obligations. And since *Reuven* acknowledges that the January payment occurred in a *ketubah* context, he effectively corroborates her version: when asked whether there was any discussion of what the January money was for, *Reuven* will confirm it was a *ketubah* payment. She therefore owes the husband nothing and need not swear.

Crucially, she need not produce documentation of two *ketubot*. The evidentiary burden remains on him: he is the one seeking to extract money from her, and absent a *shtar* evidencing the loan, his only leverage is the *ed echad*. If that *ed echad* acknowledges that the January payment was presented in a *ketubah* context, it no longer functions as testimony of a loan, and his entire scheme collapses.

### Witness Confidence

The Gemara's resolution is that before bringing *Reuven* to witness the May payment, the husband takes *Reuven* into his confidence. He explains: look, you and I both know the January payment was the genuine *ketubah* payment. I am being forced to pay her again in May solely because she is denying the first payment and I do not have sufficient witnesses to prove it. This May payment is not a second *ketubah*; it is a forced repayment of the original one. *Reuven* now understands the full picture, and when the question of two *ketubot* arises, *Reuven* is in a position to clarify what he actually witnessed and understood.

### Rarity Assumption

What gives this resolution its legal traction is the sheer rarity of two *ketubot*. It is an extraordinary circumstance for a husband to write two separate *ketubot* for the same wife. Given that rarity, and given that *Reuven* — armed with the husband's explanation — can testify to his understanding of the January payment's purpose, the bet din has ample basis to be skeptical of the two-*ketubah* defense. The implausibility of the claim, combined with *Reuven*'s informed testimony, is sufficient to recharacterize the January payment as a debt and proceed to the *shvua d'oraita*.

The calculus for the husband is ultimately sound: if she would have taken the *shvua d'rabbanan* and collected anyway, he loses the *ketubah* sum regardless. The double-payment scheme costs him the same amount in the worst case, but in the best case — if she refuses to swear the more solemn *shvua d'oraita* — she repays the January sum and he breaks even. He stands to gain and cannot lose more than he already would have.

---

## Collecting from Heirs

### Dead Husband Case

The third scenario in which a woman must take an oath to collect her *ketubah* is where the husband has died and she is collecting from his heirs. The underlying logic is consistent with what has already been established: the husband is no longer present to assert a counterclaim, to produce a receipt, or to defend himself against her demand. In his absence — now permanent — she must take an oath that the *ketubah* has not already been paid.

### Shvuot Mishnah

The Gemara adduces a parallel from a *mishnah* in Shvuot: *v'chen hayetomim lo yifre'u ella bishvuah* — heirs of a creditor may likewise only collect on a debt by means of an oath. This provides a structural precedent: when the collecting party is not the original claimant, or when the debtor is no longer present to contest the claim, an oath is required.

### Why Heirs Swear

The Gemara immediately raises a difficulty. If the creditor himself could collect the debt without taking any oath — simply by producing the *shtar* and asserting that it has not been paid — why should his heirs, who have inherited that same *shtar*, be required to swear? They are in the same position he was; let them simply assert, as he would have, that to the best of their knowledge the debt has not been discharged, and collect.

### Debtor Dead Principle

The answer is that the *mishnah* in Shvuot is not discussing heirs collecting from the living debtor; it is discussing heirs collecting from *the debtor's heirs*. When the debtor is alive, he can defend himself — produce evidence of payment, dispute the amount, or make any other argument. The creditor's claim stands against the debtor's rebuttal, and no oath is needed. But when the debtor is dead and his heirs are the respondents, the debtor can no longer defend himself. In that circumstance, whoever is collecting — whether the original creditor or his heirs — must swear. The oath fills the void left by the debtor's absence and ensures that the claim is not collected without the check of a solemn affirmation.

### Heirs' Statement Test

Rav Zerika, citing Rav Yehuda, adds an important qualification. The oath requirement applies specifically when the heirs of the deceased debtor say: our father told us that he borrowed the money and paid it back. In that case — where they make a positive claim that the debt was discharged — the collecting party must indeed swear. Alternatively, if the heirs say nothing and simply do not know the status of the debt, the oath still applies, because the debtor is unavailable to confirm or deny.

### Complete Denial Rule

But what if the heirs claim: our father told us he never borrowed this money at all? In that case, one might think that the creditor cannot collect even with an oath, since the heirs are denying the existence of the debt entirely — and the creditor has no one to contradict. The Gemara presents this as one possible reading: if they deny the debt wholesale, perhaps even the *shtar* cannot overcome a complete denial.

### Rav Ashi Objection

Rav Ashi objects that this is precisely backwards. If the heirs say their father never borrowed the money, that very claim implies he never paid it back either — *kol omer lo lovisi k'omer lo parati dami*, one who says "I never borrowed" is in the same position as one who says "I never repaid." And the creditor has a *shtar* proving the loan took place. The heirs' denial of the loan does not override the documentary evidence.

### Heirs Say Father Paid

The Gemara accordingly inverts the ruling. Rav Zerika's statement must be read as follows: the oath requirement applies when the heirs say their father told them he *paid* — in that case, the creditor or his heirs must swear before collecting. But if the heirs claim their father denied ever having borrowed in the first place, the creditor may collect *without* an oath — because the heirs have effectively conceded non-payment by denying the loan, and the *shtar* is not contradicted by their denial in any meaningful sense. *Shekol omer lo lovisi k'omer lo parati dami.*

---

## Husband Absent & Women

### Husband in Hawaii

The fourth scenario brings us to the case of *shelo befanav* — the husband is alive but absent, having gone to a distant land. She wishes to collect her *ketubah* — either because he divorced her before departing, or because she needs to collect *mezonot* from his estate while they remain married — but he is not present in court to contest or confirm the claim.

### Oath for Absent Husband

Here too, the rule is: *v'nifra'at shelo befanav lo tipara ela bishvua* — if she is collecting while he is not present, she may only do so by taking an oath. Again, the oath serves the same structural function: it substitutes for the debtor's absence, providing the bet din with a solemn assurance before allowing collection to proceed.

### Mishum China Rationale

Rav Acha Sar HaBirah reports a ruling of Rabbi Yitzchak in Antioch that introduces an important distinction: *lo shanu ela kesubas isha mishum china* — this dispensation to collect *shelo befanav* was granted specifically for a woman collecting her *ketubah*, and the rationale is *mishum china*.

### Woman's Standing

*Mishum china* is the Gemara's compressed way of referring to concern for the woman's position in society. A divorced or widowed woman who cannot collect her *ketubah* is left in a precarious state — financially vulnerable and disadvantaged in her ability to rebuild her life. The institution of the *ketubah* exists precisely to protect her from this outcome. Allowing her to collect even in the husband's absence, provided she takes an oath, reflects the law's particular solicitude for her circumstances. To withhold collection until the husband could be physically brought before the court would expose her to prolonged hardship that the rabbis were unwilling to countenance.

### Creditor Different

Rav Acha Sar HaBirah's ruling implies that an ordinary creditor whose debtor has gone abroad would *not* enjoy the same dispensation — he would have to wait until the debtor could be brought to court.

### Rava's Broad Rule

Rava, however, citing Rav Nachman, disagrees and extends the rule broadly: *afilu baal chov* — even an ordinary creditor may collect from an absent debtor. The rationale is direct and practical.

### Absconding Risk

*Shelo yehei kol echad v'echad notel maosav shel chaveiro v'holech v'yoshev b'mdinas hayam* — we cannot allow a situation where any person can take another's money and simply relocate to a distant country with impunity. If the law provided no recourse against an absent debtor, it would create a standing invitation to defraud creditors by fleeing jurisdiction.

### Creditor Protection

One might think that this concern primarily protects wealthy lenders. In fact the opposite is true. If the legal framework fails to protect creditors, no rational person will lend money, and it is ultimately borrowers — particularly poor ones with no other source of funds — who suffer. The protective instinct here runs in both directions. The *pruzbul* of Hillel illustrates the same logic: rules that seem to favor creditors are often essential for maintaining the lending market that borrowers depend on.

### Tosafot Dispute

This is a striking passage. The Gemara's conclusion, backed by Rava and Rav Nachman and apparently confirmed by the *stam* of the Gemara in *Erchin* as well, is that even a *baal chov* may collect from an absent debtor. Yet Tosafot notes that the actual practice was exactly the opposite: *maasin b'chol yom she'ein nifrin shelo b'fanav l'baal chov* — the daily practice was not to collect for an ordinary creditor in the debtor's absence. Rabbeinu Chananel ruled accordingly.

### Yerushalmi Compromise

How does Tosafot justify a practice that contradicts the plain reading of the Bavli? The answer given is remarkable: *samchu amman d'dachi lei b'Yerushalmi* — they relied on a counter-position found in the Yerushalmi. The Yerushalmi articulates what amounts to a procedural compromise: three letters of summons are sent to the absent debtor. If he appears in response — good; the matter proceeds normally. If after three summons he fails to appear, then the court seizes his property and executes the judgment without him. This graduated approach acknowledges both the creditor's legitimate claim and the absent party's right to be heard, while foreclosing the abuse of indefinite delay. The practice on the ground apparently aligned with this Yerushalmi position despite the Bavli pointing in the other direction — a genuinely unusual case of received practice overriding the *peshat* of our Gemara.

---

## Rabbi Shimon Limits

### Only Ketubah

The *mishnah* records a cryptic ruling of Rabbi Shimon: *kol zman she-tova'as ketubatah, yorshin mashbi'in otah* — as long as she is demanding her *ketubah*, the heirs can make her swear; when she is not demanding her *ketubah*, they cannot. Taken at face value this seems almost tautological — of course the heirs would only seek an oath when she is demanding her *ketubah*. What is Rabbi Shimon adding?

### Context Identified

Rabbi Yirmiyah identifies the context: Rabbi Shimon is addressing the *shelo befanav* case — the husband alive but absent in a distant land.

### Maintenance & Ketubah

That case in fact encompasses two distinct scenarios. In one, they remain married and she needs to put food on the table — she requires *mezonot* from his estate while he is abroad. In the other, he divorced her and she is collecting her *ketubah*. The *mishnah*'s unqualified formulation of *shelo befanav* appeared to require an oath in both scenarios. Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between them: only when she is demanding her *ketubah* — in the divorce scenario — can the oath be required. When she is seeking *mezonot* for ongoing subsistence, we do not impose an oath. The woman must be able to put food on the table without first undergoing a formal swearing procedure.

### Chanan's Rule

This distinction maps precisely onto a debate recorded in an earlier *mishnah*, involving Chanan. In the case of a man who went to a distant land while still married, and his wife sought *mezonot* from his estate, Chanan ruled: *tishava basof v'lo tishava bitchila* — she swears at the end, not at the beginning. She may collect *mezonot* now without an oath; later, when she comes to collect her *ketubah* at the conclusion of the marriage, the bet din may then make her swear regarding any funds that may have been prepaid during the husband's absence. The oath is deferred, not waived.

### Bnei Kohanim View

*Bnei Kohanim Gedolim* — a group apparently identified by this title — disputed Chanan's position and said: *tishava bitchila u'vasof* — she swears at the beginning as well, both when collecting *mezonot* and when collecting the *ketubah*. On their view, any collection from the husband's estate in his absence triggers the oath requirement, without exception.

### Shimon = Chanan

Rabbi Shimon's position aligns with Chanan: he holds that the oath is required only when she is demanding her *ketubah*, not when she is seeking *mezonot*. The urgency of subsistence, on this view, overrides the procedural requirement of the oath.

### Rabbis = Bnei Kohanim

The Rabbis who dispute Rabbi Shimon align with *Bnei Kohanim Gedolim*: they require an oath in both scenarios, treating the *shelo befanav* dispensation uniformly across all collection contexts.

### Heirs Problem

Rav Sheshes raises a difficulty with this entire reading: Rabbi Shimon's statement uses the word *yorshin* — heirs. If the context is simply that the husband is alive and merely abroad, there are no heirs in the picture at all. Why does Rabbi Shimon say "the heirs can make her swear" when the husband is still living?

---

## Apotropos Role

### Apotropos Context

Rav Sheshes therefore proposes a different context entirely. Rabbi Shimon is addressing the scenario of the woman as *apotropos* — the manager of her late husband's estate on behalf of his underage heirs.

### After Husband's Death

The *mishnah* earlier described two paths a woman might take after her husband's death: she might return to her father's house, or she might continue living in her father-in-law's household. In either case, she may or may not have assumed a formal managerial role over the estate left behind for the orphaned heirs.

### No Oath Without Role

If she returned to her father's house and did not become *apotropos*, the heirs have no basis to make her swear at all. The husband had exempted her from oaths relating to past dealings, and if she played no ongoing managerial role, there is nothing about which she could be made to account.

### Future vs. Past

If, however, she did assume the role of *apotropos*, the *mishnah* ruled that the heirs may make her swear regarding *future* dealings — that is, regarding the ongoing management of the estate going forward — but they may not make her swear regarding *past* dealings, since the husband had exempted her from such oaths retrospectively.

### Abba Shaul Debate

The question of whether and when an *apotropos* can be compelled to swear is itself the subject of a separate Tannaitic dispute between Abba Shaul and the Rabbis.

### Abba Shaul Position

Abba Shaul holds: an *apotropos* appointed by the father of the orphans — appointed, that is, before the father's death — is exempt from swearing, because the father trusted him implicitly. Someone appointed by the court, however, must swear. The reasoning is that a court appointment carries institutional prestige; the appointee accepts the role willingly, knowing an oath may be required, precisely because the honor of a court appointment makes the responsibility worthwhile.

### Rabbis Position

The Rabbis take exactly the opposite view: one appointed by the father must swear, because that appointment was a private arrangement that does not carry the force of a court order. One appointed by the court, however, is exempt — because to require an oath of someone the court has publicly entrusted with this responsibility would deter capable people from accepting court appointments. The exemption is an institutional incentive.

### Shimon = Abba Shaul

Rabbi Shimon aligns with Abba Shaul. On this reading, when Rabbi Shimon says that the heirs cannot make the woman swear in her role as *apotropos*, it is because she was appointed by the father — and, following Abba Shaul, such an appointee is exempt. But when she comes to collect her *ketubah* from the orphans' estate, that is a different matter entirely: there, the general principle that one who collects from an orphans' estate must always swear applies, regardless of any exemption from oath in her capacity as *apotropos*.

---

## Waiver Exception

### Husband's Waiver

The Gemara turns to yet another context: the husband who explicitly wrote in his wife's *ketubah*: *neder ushvuah ein li alaich* — I have no vow and no oath authority over you. He has preemptively waived his right to impose an oath on her.

### Broad Waiver

The waiver could be formulated even more expansively: *neder ushvuah ein li, v'lo l'yorshay, v'lo l'ba'im birshuti alaich, v'lo l'yorshaich, v'lo l'ba'im birshusah* — not I, nor my heirs, nor anyone acting with my authority have any oath authority over you, nor over your heirs, nor over those acting with your authority. In its fullest form, this waiver extends to all successors on both sides. The question becomes: can even this sweeping waiver be circumvented?

### Cannot Waive Heirs

Abba Shaul ben Imma Miriam held that the waiver, however broadly written, is ineffective in one specific context. The husband can waive oaths that belong to him to waive — oaths that would have been demanded in his name, relating to claims he himself could have pressed. But there is a principle that stands independent of anything the husband can grant or withhold: *haba lipara minichsei yesomim lo yipara ella bishvuah* — one who comes to collect from an orphans' estate may only do so by means of an oath. This rule protects the orphans, who cannot protect themselves, and it belongs to no party in the dispute to waive it. The husband cannot prospectively extinguish a protection that exists for the benefit of heirs who have not yet lost their father.

### Heirs Oath Rule

The principle, then, is categorical: collecting from an orphans' estate always requires an oath, regardless of any prior waiver.

### Rav Papa's Question

Rav Papa raises a question about the second half of Rabbi Shimon's formulation. The first half — that she must swear whenever she collects her *ketubah*, notwithstanding any waiver — makes sense in light of the foregoing analysis. But Rabbi Shimon also says that when she is *not* demanding her *ketubah*, the heirs cannot make her swear. Is this not obvious? If she has a broad waiver and is not even seeking to collect the *ketubah*, why would anyone imagine she could be made to swear?

### Excludes R. Eliezer

Rav Pappa answers: the second clause of Rabbi Shimon's ruling is not addressing an obvious case — it is explicitly excluding the stricter position of Rabbi Eliezer. Without this second clause, one might have thought that Rabbi Eliezer's view governs: that a husband can compel his wife to swear even during the course of the marriage, regarding her management of household affairs.

### R. Eliezer Strict

Rabbi Eliezer's position is that the husband may impose an oath on his wife about any matter relating to household management — even something as granular as the dough she handled. On this view, a husband's authority to demand an accounting from his wife is quite broad, and it would extend well beyond *ketubah* collection.

### Chachamim Middle

The *Chachamim* occupy a middle position: the husband may compel an oath if his wife runs the shop — that is, a business in which she handles money and accounts on his behalf — but he may not impose an oath regarding purely domestic matters like the preparation of dough.

### Shimon Balanced

Rabbi Shimon takes a position that is simultaneously more stringent and more lenient than both alternatives. He is more stringent than Chanan regarding the *ketubah*: he insists that the oath is always required when she comes to collect it, no matter what was waived. But he is more lenient than the *Chachamim* and far more lenient than Rabbi Eliezer regarding everything else: during the marriage, whatever she does, she may not be compelled to swear. The two halves of his ruling are complementary — absolute accountability at the moment of final collection, and complete freedom from oath-pressure during the ongoing marriage.

---

## Rabbeinu Tam Ruling

### Ashkenazi Women

Tosafot brings this discussion to bear on a concrete contemporary situation — concrete, at least, in the world of medieval Ashkenaz. Women in that community frequently functioned as businesswomen, running shops and managing accounts, often serving as the commercial face of a household enterprise.

### Husband Suspects Wife

In one such case before Rabbeinu Tam, a husband had installed his wife as the manager of their shop — a *chanunis* — and she handled large sums of money in and out of the household. A dispute arose in which the husband suspected her of financial impropriety, or at least sought an accounting of her stewardship, and he wished to compel her to swear.

### No Oath in Marriage

Rabbeinu Tam refused to permit it. Even in this situation — a wife running the family business with full access to its funds — the husband could not force an oath during the marriage.

### Woman Empowerment

The legal basis is the final *halakha* as it emerges from the Gemara: we rule in accordance with Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Shimon holds that outside the context of *ketubah* collection, the husband has no authority to impose an oath. This applies even to a woman running a business enterprise on his behalf. The second half of Rabbi Shimon's ruling — that when she is not demanding her *ketubah* the heirs cannot make her swear — translates in practice into a prohibition on the husband making her swear during the course of the marriage, whatever the scope of her commercial activity.

### Practical Conclusion

The ruling of Rabbeinu Tam is not merely a technical application of Rabbi Shimon's position. It reflects a recognition that women who functioned as businesswomen in Ashkenaz needed legal protection from a mechanism — the compelled oath — that could be weaponized to harass or undermine them in their commercial roles. The *halakhic* conclusion, arrived at through a chain running from Abba Shaul ben Imma Miriam through Rabbi Shimon through the final redaction of the *sugya*, thus lands in a place that is both doctrinally grounded and practically protective of women's economic agency.

---

---

# Ketubot 90

## Multiple Documents

### Two Gets, Two Ketubos

The final *mishnah* of the ninth *perek* opens with a case involving multiple documents: *shnei gittin u-shtei ketubot* — a woman produces two *gittin* and two *ketubot*, staggered in sequence. The pattern is a *ketubah* from one date, a *get* from a later date, then a second *ketubah* and a second *get*, indicating two marriages followed by two divorces with the same husband. In such a case, the *mishnah* rules *gova shtei ketubot* — she may collect two *ketubot*.

### Remarriage & New Ketubah

This ruling requires explanation, because as we have seen in earlier discussion, remarriage to the same husband does not automatically generate a new *ketubah* obligation. The default assumption is that the original *ketubah* continues as the basis of the second marriage. However, if the husband proactively chose to write a new *ketubah*, he has created a distinct, second obligation — and in that case, both are binding. The staggered pattern of the documents, with two *ketubot* and two *gittin*, demonstrates precisely that he did so.

### Two Ketubos, One Get

The *mishnah* then addresses three additional configurations, each of which limits her to collecting only a single *ketubah*. The cases are: two *ketubot* and one *get*; one *ketubah* and two *gittin*; and one *ketubah*, a *get*, and the husband's subsequent death. The last case is self-evident — she was divorced, then her husband died, and she cannot collect again as a widow. The case of one *ketubah* and two *gittin* illustrates the default principle most clearly: even though the second *get* is evidence that he remarried her, the absence of a second *ketubah* means the remarriage was conducted *al menas ketubah ha-rishonah* — on the basis of the original *ketubah* — and no new obligation was created.

The case of two *ketubot* and one *get* is the one the *mishnah* identifies as needing explanation. One might have thought that both documents are simultaneously binding — perhaps the husband intended to accumulate additional obligations. Indeed, a reader familiar with earlier discussion will recall a scenario in which a woman possessed two *ketubot* and was permitted to collect from both. The present *mishnah* rules *eino gova ela ketubah achas* — she may collect only one — because the presumption is that the second *ketubah* was written in anticipation of a remarriage following a divorce that may or may not be documented here. But the question immediately arises: which *ketubah* may she use? The earlier one carries earlier liens and therefore broader collection rights; the later one might carry a higher monetary amount. The *mishnah*'s silence on which one suggests that the choice belongs to her — a point the *Gemara* will address directly.

### Sequential Documents

The *Gemara* raises the possibility that this choice contradicts the ruling of Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel: *shnei shtaros ha-yotzin zeh achar zeh, bitel sheni es ha-rishon* — when two documents emerge sequentially and clearly refer to the same underlying transaction, the second voids the first. The clearest example is two bills of sale for the same plot of land. Since one cannot purchase the same property twice, the later document supplants the earlier one, and the buyer may not rely on the earlier dating. The practical significance of the earlier date lies in the scope of liens: because the seller accepts responsibility if a prior creditor forecloses on the property, the buyer with earlier liens can recover from the seller's property of that earlier period. A later document narrows that window. Similarly, if a disputed claim of ownership arises, proof of an earlier acquisition date carries independent value.

The apparent contradiction with our *mishnah* is thus: if a woman possesses two *ketubot* for the same marriage, the second should void the first, leaving her only the second. Yet the *mishnah* implies she may choose between the two.

### Waiver Theory

Rashi explains the underlying logic of Rav Nachman's principle: no one compelled the holder to accept the second document. A second bill of sale generally weakens the buyer's position — it establishes ownership from a later date, with correspondingly later liens. By voluntarily accepting it, the buyer implicitly declares that he waives whatever rights and protections he had under the earlier document. The acceptance of the later, less advantageous document constitutes a form of *mechilah* — waiver — of the benefits conferred by the earlier one.

### Added Benefits
