Rav Papa then states the critical qualification: *umodu Abaye v'Rava d'ei hosif bah dikla l'tosefes kesavah* — Abaye and Rava concede that if the second document added even one additional palm tree, one additional parcel, or any incremental benefit beyond what the first document included, then acceptance of the second document does not constitute a waiver of the first. The reasoning is direct: if the second document is clearly and entirely inferior to the first in every respect, then accepting it can only be explained as a willing surrender of the first. But if the second document contains any dimension in which it exceeds the first, then the holder has a rational basis for accepting it that does not imply waiver — he is preserving his freedom to choose whichever instrument better serves his interests in a given situation. Acceptance of the second document under those circumstances signals choice, not surrender.

### Choice of Ketubos

The application to our *mishnah* follows directly. Rav Papa concludes: *hacha nami bid'osif lah* — here too, the second *ketubah* must have included some added amount, even a single additional monetary unit, beyond the first. This is what allows the woman to retain the option of choosing between the two. When the second *ketubah* is not uniformly inferior — because it carries a higher face value, even if it comes with later liens — she is not presumed to have waived the first by accepting it, and she retains the ability to elect whichever is more advantageous in the circumstances. The *Gemara* notes that a double, cumulative obligation — both *ketubot* simultaneously binding — would require explicit language in the second document expressing precisely that intent. Absent such language, the result is an *or*, not an *and*: she collects from one or the other, at her election.

### Get vs. Ketubah Dating

A related *braita* addresses the case in which a woman produces a *get*, a *ketubah*, and relies on the husband's subsequent death to claim as a widow. The rule is as follows: *im get kodem l'kesuvah, gova shtei ketubot* — if the *get* is dated before the *ketubah*, she collects two *ketubot*, because the later *ketubah* proves that he chose to obligate himself anew in a second marriage. If, however, the *ketubah* is dated before the *get* — *eina gova ela ketubah achas* — she collects only one, because even with clear evidence of divorce and remarriage, the absence of a new *ketubah* means the remarriage was on the basis of the original document alone.

## Minor's Ketubah

### Katan Marriage

The *mishnah* now introduces a new case: *katan she-hisio aviv* — a minor boy who was married off by his father. This is noteworthy because the earlier discussion throughout the tractate has focused predominantly on the father arranging the marriage of a minor girl. The *mishnah* contemplates actual *nisuim* — full cohabitation — even when the boy is a *katan*. It is worth reiterating what the *Gemara* elsewhere makes clear: even in the context of *kiddushei ketanah*, the *Gemara* stated that actual *nisuim* — the couple living together — would not occur until the girl was at least a *na'arah*, twelve and a half years of age. Nevertheless, the case of a minor boy is presented here as a recognized, if unusual, reality.

### Ketubah Continuity

The rule is *kesubasah kayamet* — her *ketubah* remains in force. Although the minor boy lacked the legal capacity to obligate himself in a *ketubah* at the time it was written, once he reaches adulthood and continues to maintain the marriage, it is understood that he does so *she-al menas kein kiymah* — on the basis of that original commitment — and the *ketubah* accordingly becomes binding upon him. The continuation of the marriage as an adult is itself the act that ratifies and assumes the earlier obligation.

## Ger & Conversion

### Non-Jewish Ketubah

The final *mishnah* of the *perek* presents a case of striking historical interest buried within a legal ruling: *ger she-nisgayerah ishto imo* — a man and his wife who both convert to Judaism together. Before their conversion, they had a marriage document drawn up according to the practices of their non-Jewish society. The *mishnah* notes, almost in passing, that non-Jews did indeed produce documents at marriage that functioned similarly to a *ketubah* — recording the dowry brought by the wife, and specifying the lump sum she would be entitled to in the event of divorce or the husband's death. This is not described as *pasak lah ketubah kedas Moshe v'Yisrael*, but the parallel institution is evident.

After their conversion, the couple remains married without rewriting a *ketubah*. When the husband later dies, the *mishnah* rules *kesubasah kayamet* — her *ketubah* obligation continues — because by remaining married after conversion the husband implicitly maintained the terms of the original agreement, based on the understanding that their earlier obligations carry forward.

### Base Amount Only

Rav Huna offers a reading of the *mishnah* that, as the *Gemara* notes, departs substantially from the plain meaning: *lo shanu ela maneh u-matayim* — the ruling applies only to the base *ketubah* amount. His position is that whatever additional amount (*tosefes*) appeared in the pre-conversion document does not carry over into a binding Jewish *ketubah* obligation. Only the standard statutory amounts — two hundred *zuz* for a *besulah*, one hundred for an *almanah* — remain in effect.

### Full Amount

Rav Yehuda disagrees: *afilu tosefes yesh lah* — even the additional amount she was promised continues to be binding. This appears to be the straightforward reading of the *mishnah*, which uses the unqualified language *kesubasah kayamet* — her *ketubah* stands — without any limitation to the base amount.

### Braita Contradiction

A *braita* is then cited as a challenge to Rav Yehuda. The *braita* states: *chidshu* — if after conversion or after the minor boy came of age they *innovated*, meaning they added a new amount to the *ketubah* — *noteles mah she-chidshu*, she is entitled to collect what they newly added. The *Gemara* initially attempts to read this as meaning she receives both the additional amount and the original full amount from before. But the *braita* continues explicitly: *lo chidshu — besulah gova matayim ve-almanah maneh* — if they did not add a new amount, she receives only the base statutory amount. This is unambiguous: the *braita* contradicts Rav Yehuda directly. *Tiyuvta de-Rav Yehuda tiyuvta* — it is a complete refutation of his position.

The *Gemara* explains that Rav Yehuda was misled by the language of the *mishnah* itself: *hu savar ketubatah kayamet akula milta* — he read *kesubasah kayamet* as meaning the entirety of the *ketubah* stands. In fact, as the *Gemara* clarifies, it means only that the base *ketubah* obligation stands: *akula milta* refers merely to the base amount.

### Tosafos Innovation

*Tosafos* presses the question further: if the ruling is only that she receives the base statutory amount, what is the *chiddush* of the *mishnah*? Any Jewish wife, even without a prior document of any kind, is entitled to the base amount by Rabbinic enactment. Why do we need the *mishnah* to tell us that a convert whose wife converted with him gets the standard hundred or two hundred *zuz*?

*Tosafos* offers a brilliant resolution. The *chiddush*, they explain, lies in the determination of which base amount she is entitled to. The *mishnah* is teaching: *de-ashmianu heicha de-nisa besulah, af al gav de-chasha gadla ve-nitgayera ke-she-hi be'ulah, afilu hachi yesh lah ketubah matayim* — we are taught about a case where they married when she was a *besulah*, and now after conversion she is a *be'ulah*. The question is whether she receives two hundred *zuz* as a *besulah* or one hundred as an *almanah*. The *mishnah* teaches that since they were first married when she was a *besulah*, that original context defines the marriage, and she therefore receives the full two hundred *zuz* — even though by the time of conversion she is no longer a *besulah*. The same logic applies in the case of the *katan*: the woman might now be a *be'ulah* at the time the obligation becomes binding, yet because the original marriage was to a *besulah*, that classification governs.

One sharp-eyed observer noted that *Tosafos*' reading carries a significant subtext: by assuming that the woman is still characterized as a *besulah* based on the context of the original non-Jewish marriage, the *mishnah* is implicitly attributing to that non-Jewish couple a standard of *tzniut* that one might not readily assume. The *chiddush* cuts against any casual assumption about the moral comportment of non-Jewish society.

The *Gemara* concludes: *Hadran alach kotev le-ishto* — and with that, the ninth *perek* comes to a close.

## Estate Claims

### Wife Priority

The tenth *perek* opens with a new *mishnah*: *mi she-hayah nasui shtei nashim* — a man married to two wives who then died. The *mishnah* addresses the competing claims against the estate. *Ha-rishonah kodemes la-shniyah* — the first wife has priority over the second. The two wives are positioned as creditors against the estate, and the earlier creditor has the right to collect first. If the estate is insufficient, the second wife receives only what remains.

### Creditor Priority

The same principle extends to the heirs: *ve-yorshei ha-rishonah kodmin le-yorshei ha-shniyah* — the heirs of the first wife take priority over the heirs of the second. The *mishnah* then describes a more complex scenario: *nasa es ha-rishonah u-mesah, nasa shniyah u-mes hu* — he married the first wife and she died; he then married the second wife and he died. In this case, *shniyah ve-yorsheha kodmin le-yorshei rishonah* — the second wife and her heirs come first, before the heirs of the first wife.

The reasoning reflects the distinction between debt and inheritance. The second wife (*Leah*, in our example) is a creditor of the estate: her husband died before her, and her *ketubah* obligation — say ten thousand and two hundred *zuz* — was never discharged. She or her heirs come to collect that sum as a debt owed to her. The heirs of the first wife (*Rachel*), by contrast, are not creditors; they are coming by virtue of the principle of *kesubas benin dichrin* — the rabbinic institution by which the male sons of a wife who predeceased their father take out their mother's *ketubah* amount from the estate as an inheritance before the estate is divided generally. Since creditors take precedence over heirs, Leah and her heirs collect first, and only thereafter do Rachel's heirs receive their special inheritance.

### Seizure Question

The *Gemara* examines the precise language of the *mishnah* — *ha-rishonah kodemes la-shniyah*, the first comes before the second — and asks whether this phrasing carries implications about what happens when the second wife does not wait her turn. The *Gemara* draws an inference: since the *mishnah* uses the language of *priority* rather than saying outright that the second wife has no claim at all, it may be implying that if the second wife seized the property before the first, she is permitted to keep it. From this the *Gemara* formulates a broader principle: *ba'al chov me'uchar she-kadam ve-gava, mah she-gava gava* — a later creditor who jumped ahead and seized property is entitled to retain what was seized.

### Tosafos Objection

*Tosafos* raises a powerful objection to this principle: *teima mah sevara hi zo, di-lo yehei ba'al chov ela ke-loke'ah* — what is the logic here? Let the later creditor be treated no differently than a purchaser. And we know that if someone purchased property *after* the earlier creditor's lien was established, the earlier creditor may foreclose on that property and take it even from the buyer who paid full value. If a creditor with earlier liens can take property from a bona fide purchaser, why should he not be able to take it from a later creditor who seized it? The later creditor's claim is, if anything, weaker than that of an innocent purchaser.

### Social Policy

*Tosafos* quotes the *Rashbam*'s answer: *ba'al chov me'uchar adif mi-loke'ah* — in this specific context, the later creditor who seizes actually has a stronger position than a purchaser would, because of a social policy consideration. The principle is *shelo tin'ol delet bifnei lovin* — we must not close the door before borrowers. If we were to hold that a later creditor who seizes property must always yield to an earlier creditor regardless of circumstances, the result would be that no one would lend money to a person who already has outstanding debts. By preserving at least the possibility that a later creditor who acts quickly may retain what he seizes, we keep open the incentive for continued lending.

*Tosafos* then grapples with whether this answer is fully satisfying: if a later creditor can seize and keep, would that not instead discourage the *earlier* creditor from lending, knowing that someone behind him in line might race ahead? The response is that each potential lender assumes he will be the one to act first. But *Tosafos* acknowledges the underlying tension honestly: the policy involves a genuine unfairness, and the question of where to draw the line — between protecting prior lienholders and keeping credit markets functioning — is genuinely difficult. What is notable is that the *Rashbam* explicitly adds *kesubas isha mishum china* — the wife's *ketubah* is included in this policy — indicating that the same principle extends to the competing claims of two wives against a single estate.

### No Permanent Rights

The *Gemara* ultimately declines to resolve the question from the language of the *mishnah* in either direction. One reading argues that *kodemes* — comes first — means fully excludes, and the second wife has no claim at all; if she were to seize property first, it would be taken from her. Another reading argues from the same word that she merely has a lower priority but is not entirely excluded, and seizure by the later party is valid. Each direction of inference is tested and found inconclusive, as the *Gemara* shows that the *mishnah*'s language can be explained away in both readings. The question of whether *mah she-gava gava* is resolved one way or the other thus remains without a definitive proof from this *mishnah*.

## Benin Dichrin

### Classic Scenario

The *mishnah* then sets out the classic scenario: *nasa es ha-rishonah u-mesah, nasa shniyah u-mes hu* — he married the first wife (*Rachel*) and she died; he married the second wife (*Leah*) and then he died. To give the facts concrete form: Rachel brought a large dowry and received a *tosefes* commensurate with her family's wealth, so that her *ketubah* totaled twenty thousand *zuz* (the base amount plus fifteen thousand in dowry plus an additional *tosefes* sum). Leah's *ketubah* totaled ten thousand and two hundred *zuz*.

### Principle Defined

When Rachel died, her husband inherited her estate. But when Reuven subsequently died, Rachel's sons by him come forward not as ordinary heirs but under the principle of *kesubas benin dichrin*: the male heirs of a wife who predeceased her husband are entitled to take out the full amount of their mother's *ketubah* from the estate as their inheritance, before the remainder of the estate is divided equally among all heirs. This ensures that the sons of the wife with the larger dowry receive the benefit of what their mother brought into the marriage, rather than seeing it absorbed into an undifferentiated pool to be shared with the children of another wife.

At the same time, Leah — or, if she has since died, her heirs — comes to collect her *ketubah* of ten thousand and two hundred *zuz* as a *creditor*. She was widowed when Reuven died, and her *ketubah* is an unpaid debt against the estate. As a creditor, Leah's claim is satisfied before any portion of the estate passes to heirs. Rachel's children, by contrast, are receiving their mother's share as an *inheritance*, not as a debt.

The *mishnah*'s ruling — that Leah's heirs come before Rachel's heirs — thus reflects the fundamental rule that a creditor's claim is satisfied prior to any division among heirs.

### Three Inferences

The *Gemara* proceeds to draw three inferences from this *mishnah*: *shema mina telat*.

### Inference One

The first inference: *shema mina achas be-chayav ve-achas be-moso, ve-yesh lahen kesubas benin dichrin* — even when one set of heirs derives their claim from a wife who died during the husband's lifetime and the other set derives their claim from a death that occurred at or after his death, *kesubas benin dichrin* still applies to the former group, and we are not concerned about fights — *velo chaishinan le-intzuyei*.

This inference requires explanation. In the *classic* formulation of *kesubas benin dichrin*, both wives predeceased the husband, and all heirs are on an equal footing: Rachel's boys take their mother's chunk, Leah's boys take their mother's chunk, and whatever remains is divided. In that symmetric case, while one set may receive more than the other, both are operating under the same institutional framework and neither has grounds to object in principle.

Here the situation is asymmetric. Leah is coming as a *creditor* — her ten thousand *zuz* is a debt. Rachel's children, by contrast, are coming as *heirs* under a *rabbinic* institution. Leah's children might credibly object: our mother collected her debt, which is fine — but why do you get a special Rabbinic inheritance before the rest of the estate is divided? Our mother didn't die before father, so we don't get *kesubas benin dichrin*; you get a special chunk and we get nothing extra. That seems unfair, and one might fear that this perceived unfairness would generate conflict and litigation — *intzuyei* — severe enough that the Rabbis would have declined to apply *kesubas benin dichrin* in such a case.

The *Gemara* rules that we do not have that concern. Rachel's children receive their *kesubas benin dichrin* even when Leah's heirs are coming as creditors. The asymmetry in the basis of the respective claims does not deprive the *benin dichrin* of their entitlement.

### Ketubah as Leftover

The second inference: *kesubah na'asis mosar le-chaverta* — a *ketubah* collection is considered as though it were the "leftover" (*mosar*) for the other *ketubah*. This requires context.

### Mosar Dinar Rule

The standard rule of *kesubas benin dichrin* includes a critical limitation: the institution applies only when there remains in the estate at least one *dinar* (*mosar dinar*) beyond what is disbursed under *benin dichrin*, available for division according to the ordinary rules of Biblical inheritance. This *mosar dinar* need not be large — a symbolic amount above a *perutah* suffices — but it must exist. The rationale is that *kesubas benin dichrin* is a Rabbinic enactment, and the Rabbis did not intend to override *yerusha de-Oraisa* entirely: if applying the Rabbinic institution would leave nothing whatsoever for a division according to Biblical rules, the Rabbinic institution is set aside and the estate is divided equally among all heirs. Rachel's children, who had a large *ketubah* behind them, would in that case receive far less — but the Biblical entitlement to an undivided inheritance takes precedence.

### Creditor as Mosar

The question the second inference addresses is this: suppose the entire estate is, say, twenty thousand *zuz*. Rachel's children want their twenty thousand as *benin dichrin*, and Leah's heirs come and take ten thousand as creditors. After Leah's heirs collect, only ten thousand remains. Is there a *mosar dinar* to support *kesubas benin dichrin* for Rachel's children, or have they been left with nothing for Biblical division?

The *Gemara* reasons that the very payment of Leah's *ketubah* debt *is* the functional equivalent of the *mosar dinar*. When a creditor holds a lien against an estate, the estate's assets conceptually include whatever is needed to satisfy that debt. Even if after the creditor is paid there is nothing left for equal division, the estate *had* money that was deployed to pay the creditor — and that payment is as if the money existed as surplus, was used to discharge a legitimate obligation of the estate, and thus satisfies the requirement that something existed beyond the *benin dichrin* entitlements. The critical formulation is: if, absent any creditors, the estate would have had just slightly more than the *benin dichrin* claims, then the fact that a creditor absorbed that surplus does not deprive Rachel's children of *kesubas benin dichrin*, because the surplus was there — it simply went to pay a legitimate debt.

The *Gemara* supports this by noting that the *mishnah* does not condition its ruling on the presence of a *mosar dinar* beyond the *benin dichrin* distributions. Since it does not mention this requirement, it must be that the creditor payment itself satisfies it.

### Inference Three

The third inference: *kesubas benin dichrin lo tarfei mi-meshabdei* — heirs collecting under *kesubas benin dichrin* do not collect from encumbered property, i.e., property that had already been sold or pledged. This distinguishes their status from that of creditors, who *do* hold liens against the debtor's prior encumbered assets and may foreclose on property sold after the lien was established.

The *Gemara* derives this from the structure of the *mishnah*. If Rachel's children were collecting as creditors — as the delayed collection of their mother's unpaid *ketubah* — then, because Rachel's *ketubah* predates Leah's *ketubah* in time, Rachel's children would have first priority even over Leah's children. A creditor with earlier liens collects before a creditor with later liens. But the *mishnah* rules that Leah's children come *first*. The only way to reconcile this is to conclude that Rachel's children are not creditors at all — they are *heirs*, receiving under the Rabbinic institution of *kesubas benin dichrin*. Since they are heirs rather than creditors, they cannot reach encumbered property, and when creditors (like Leah's heirs) compete with heirs, the creditors win.

### Rav Ashi Challenge

Rav Ashi challenges all three inferences. His opening point: *dilma l'olam eima lach, achas be-chayav ve-achas be-moso, ein kan kesubas benin dichrin* — perhaps I would say that in a case where one wife's claim arises from events during the husband's lifetime and the other's arises from events at his death, there is in fact *no* application of *kesubas benin dichrin* at all. The first inference would then be invalid.

### Alternative Reading

And if so, *u-mai kodmin, l'nachala katani* — what does the *mishnah*'s statement that Leah's heirs "come first" mean? Perhaps it means only that they come first in terms of the *nachala*, the inheritance — i.e., they collect their creditor's share first, and then the remaining estate is divided equally among all heirs. Rachel's children would receive their proportional share of what remains, but not any special *kesubas benin dichrin* entitlement above and beyond that. The word *yorshei rishonah* — the heirs of the first wife — appears in the *mishnah* only because the earlier clause mentioned Leah's heirs (*shniyah ve-yorsheha*), and the *mishnah* used parallel language for Rachel's children without meaning to indicate that they have any special status.

### Mosar After Creditor

Rav Ashi then challenges the second inference as well. The claim was that a creditor payment counts as the *mosar dinar* to support *kesubas benin dichrin*. Rav Ashi says: *dilma l'olam eima lach, ein kesubah na'asis mosar le-chaverta* — perhaps the *ketubah* payment to one wife does not serve as the *mosar* for the other's *benin dichrin* entitlement. You would need a genuine *mosar dinar* — an actual dollar remaining in the estate after all *benin dichrin* entitlements are distributed — and if that dollar was consumed by the creditor, it is gone. Perhaps the *mishnah* is simply operating in a case where there *was* a *mosar dinar* remaining after Leah collected and Rachel's children received their share — and the *mishnah* simply did not spell this out because it was assumed to be present in the background facts.

In sum, Rav Ashi argues that the two inferences that strengthen Rachel's children's position — that *kesubas benin dichrin* applies even in this asymmetric scenario, and that a creditor payment counts as the *mosar dinar* — are not compelled by the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* could be read as assuming, without stating explicitly, that the conditions for those inferences are met, rather than proving that those conditions are unnecessary. The *peshut* of the *mishnah* still favors the first reading, but Rav Ashi's point is that neither inference is *muchrach* — forced by the text — and the matter will require further analysis.

# Ketubot 91

## Achas B'chayav

### Case Setup

The sugya before us involves a case of competing claims from two sets of children whose mothers were married to the same husband, Reuven. Reuven first married Rachel, whose *ketubah* was worth twenty thousand dollars. Rachel died during Reuven's lifetime, meaning he retained the funds he would otherwise have paid her. Under the rabbinic enactment known as *ketubat benin dichrin*, however, Rachel's sons are entitled, upon Reuven's death, to extract the value of their mother's *ketubah* from his estate before the remainder is divided equally among all his heirs. Reuven subsequently married Leah, who survived him. When Reuven dies, Leah's children come to collect their mother's *ketubah* as a debt owed by the estate.

The structural asymmetry is significant. Rachel's children come as heirs — they are invoking a special inheritance right to their mother's *ketubah* amount. Leah's children come as creditors — they are collecting a monetary obligation the estate owes their still-living mother. The Mishnah's basic ruling for this scenario, called *achas b'chayav v'achas b'moso* — one wife died while the husband was alive, one died after him — is straightforward: debt takes priority over inheritance. Leah's children first collect their mother's *ketubah*, and then Rachel's children take their special portion, with whatever remains distributed equally.

### Mishnah Ruling

The Mishnah's resolution follows the general principle that a creditor's claim precedes an heir's claim. Once Leah's children, acting in the capacity of creditors, have collected their mother's *ketubah*, the remaining estate is available for the application of *ketubat benin dichrin*. Rachel's sons then extract the value of their mother's *ketubah* from that remainder, and only what is left after that is divided equally among all heirs. This ordering — debt first, then the special inheritance, then equal division — reflects the hierarchy that governs estates in *halacha*.

### Initial Question

The Gemara, however, is not satisfied with simply establishing the order of collection. It probes a deeper question: in a scenario where Leah's children are coming as creditors rather than as co-beneficiaries of *ketubat benin dichrin*, are Rachel's children still entitled to their special status at all? When both wives predeceased the husband, each set of children holds equivalent standing — both are special heirs under *ketubat benin dichrin*, each taking their mother's *ketubah* amount before the equal division. But here, Leah's children are not invoking *ketubat benin dichrin*; they are simply collecting a debt. Why, Leah's children might argue, should Rachel's children enjoy a privileged position that we are not receiving ourselves?

### Ben Nannas/R. Akiva

The Gemara establishes that this very question is the subject of a *tannaitic* dispute, introduced by the phrase *detanya* — as taught in a *baraita*. The case in the *baraita* is precisely *achas b'chayav v'achas b'moso*: Rachel died during Reuven's lifetime, Leah died after him. Ben Nannas rules that Rachel's children may say to Leah's children: *b'nei ba'alat chov attem* — you are the children of a creditor. Take your mother's *ketubah* and leave. The implication is that Rachel's children retain their full entitlement to *ketubat benin dichrin*, undisturbed by the asymmetry of positions.

Rabbi Akiva disagrees. He uses the vivid phrase *kvar kaftza nachalah lifnei bnei rishona v'nafla lifnei bnei shniya* — the inheritance has already leapt away from Rachel's children and fallen before Leah's children. The colorful language conveys that Rachel's sons, who seemed poised to take their special portion, have lost their grip on it. The Gemara initially reads this as a debate over a fundamental principle: does *ketubat benin dichrin* apply when the two sets of heirs come from different legal positions — one as special heirs, one as creditors? Ben Nannas says yes; Rabbi Akiva says no.

### Rava's Resolution

Rava, however, intervenes with a startling interpretive move. He reports that he encountered the Rabbis of the academy of Rav debating this very passage, and he challenged their reading. Their assumption had been that Rabbi Akiva and Ben Nannas dispute the fundamental question of whether *ketubat benin dichrin* applies in *achas b'chayav v'achas b'moso*. Rava argues otherwise: *d'kulei alma achas b'chayav v'achas b'moso yesh lahen ketubat benin dichrin* — everyone agrees that in principle Rachel's children are entitled to their special inheritance. The dispute, he insists, is not about whether the right exists but about a separate technical requirement: whether the conditions for activating that right have been met.

### Motar Dina Question

That separate technical requirement is the rule of *motar dina* — there must be leftover money in the estate beyond the amounts extracted by the special heirs. *Ketubat benin dichrin* cannot consume the entire estate; there must remain some residual amount subject to the ordinary rules of inheritance. The debate between Ben Nannas and Rabbi Akiva, on Rava's reading, is about whether paying out a *ketubah* debt counts as satisfying that requirement.

Consider the arithmetic: Reuven dies leaving an estate of thirty thousand dollars. Leah's children come and collect their ten thousand dollar *ketubah* debt. Twenty thousand dollars remains — precisely the amount of Rachel's *ketubah*. If Rachel's children take their twenty thousand dollars, nothing is left for equal division. Has the requirement of leftover money been met? Ben Nannas says yes: the money used to pay Leah's children counts as the portion of the estate that was subject to ordinary inheritance rules. All the heirs equally bore the obligation to pay that debt, and in discharging it, the estate effectively underwent a normal process of inheritance — then Rachel's children may step forward and take their special portion. Rabbi Akiva says no: that arrangement does not constitute genuine leftover money in the estate.

Rava sharpens the argument further. In the case of an ordinary third-party creditor — some stranger who had a claim against the estate — everyone would agree that paying that claim constitutes a *motar*, a leftover, sufficient to enable *ketubat benin dichrin*. The heirs collectively bore the debt, discharged it from the estate as a normal inheritance transaction, and Rachel's children may then take their portion. The dispute arises specifically when the creditor is Leah's children themselves. There, Leah's children might object: we are not first inheriting equally and then paying ourselves — we are simply being paid first, and the inheritance discussion begins only afterward. The payment to us is not a *motar*; it is merely the discharge of a prior claim. That is the crux of the debate.

Two related but distinct concerns thus animate the entire discussion. First, is it objectionable in principle that Rachel's children receive a special inheritance status that Leah's children do not? Second — and this is the concern Rava centers — even granting that Rachel's children are entitled in principle, has the *motar dina* requirement been satisfied when the only available funds were consumed in paying the debt to Leah's children?

### Rav Yosef Challenge

Rav Yosef challenges Rava's entire interpretive framework. If, as Rava claims, Rabbi Akiva agrees in principle that Rachel's children are entitled and disputes only the circumstantial question of whether there was sufficient *motar* in this case, then Rabbi Akiva should have expressed himself very differently. Instead of the dramatic phrase about the inheritance "leaping away" from Rachel's children, he should have said simply: *im yesh mosar dinar mibaei lei* — if there is leftover money, Rachel's children may collect; if not, they may not. The language Rabbi Akiva actually uses — the inheritance leapt away and they lost it — sounds like an absolute disqualification, not a circumstantial one. It sounds like Rabbi Akiva is saying that in *achas b'chayav v'achas b'moso*, Rachel's children categorically lose their special status.

Rav Yosef therefore concludes: *ela amar Rav Yosef, be'achas b'chayav ube'achas b'moso kamiflagi* — the dispute between Ben Nannas and Rabbi Akiva is genuinely about the fundamental principle. Rabbi Akiva holds that *ketubat benin dichrin* can only operate when both sets of children stand in the same position — both as special heirs simultaneously. When one set comes as creditors and the other as heirs, the mechanism breaks down entirely for the heirs. Ben Nannas holds that Rachel's children retain their special status regardless of the position from which Leah's children collect.

The Gemara then extends this analysis to a parallel *baraita* involving Rabbi Shimon and the *Tanna Kamma*, whose positions map onto the same underlying debate. In that *baraita*, the *Tanna Kamma* states only that Leah's children come and collect their mother's *ketubah*, conspicuously omitting any special treatment for Rachel's children — which appears to parallel Rabbi Akiva's categorical disqualification. Rabbi Shimon then states: if there is an extra *dinar* beyond the *ketubah* amounts, each set of children collects their mother's *ketubah* through *ketubat benin dichrin*; if not, they divide equally — which appears to parallel Ben Nannas's position that Rachel's children remain entitled in principle, subject to the *motar dinar* requirement.

The Gemara, however, resists accepting this straightforward alignment. It proposes alternative readings in which both the *Tanna Kamma* and Rabbi Shimon agree that Rachel's children are entitled in principle, while debating only the technical question of what constitutes a sufficient *motar*. The Gemara explores whether the dispute concerns the type of property that counts as leftover — specifically, whether *karka* (land) alone qualifies, or whether *metaltelin* (movable property, chattel) suffices — and whether encumbered property (*meshubadei*) can count, or only unencumbered property (*bnei chorin*). Each of these readings, however, runs into difficulties with the precise language of Rabbi Shimon's formulation, which, on close inspection, appears to be imposing a stricter standard rather than a more lenient one. The Gemara ultimately concludes — *ela ki hanech terei lishnei kamma'ei v'ipoch* — that we should revert to the first two structural explanations but reverse who is being lenient and who is being strict. On this reading, the *Tanna Kamma* is actually lenient: whenever any *motar dinar* exists, Rachel's children collect. Rabbi Shimon is being strict: he requires that the *motar dinar* consist specifically of land or of unencumbered property. The *Tanna Kamma*'s silence about Rachel's children in the opening clause reflects only the circumstance that in the case he described there was no *motar dinar* at all — not that Rachel's children lack entitlement in principle.

## Three Wives Case

### Hilchata Conclusion

After this extended analytical journey, the Gemara delivers its *halachic* conclusion through Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa: *hilchata, achas b'chayav v'achas b'moso yesh lahen ketuvat bnei dichrin* — the law is that even in *achas b'chayav v'achas b'moso*, Rachel's children are entitled to *ketubat benin dichrin*. This ruling vindicates the persistent interpretive instinct of the discussion, which kept trying to read every tannaitic position as agreeing in principle that Rachel's children are entitled. The social rationale is compelling: a father will give a generous dowry to his daughter only if he can be confident that those funds will remain within his grandchildren's inheritance, regardless of the circumstances surrounding the other wife's death or her children's legal posture at the time of collection.

The *hilchata* further establishes: *v'ketuvah na'asit motir l'chavertah* — a *ketubah* payment made to Leah's children counts as the *motar*, the leftover amount required to activate Rachel's entitlement. The logic is that all heirs equally bore the obligation to discharge Leah's *ketubah* debt, and the portion of the estate applied to that debt represents a legitimate predicate for the subsequent inheritance process. Concretely: if Reuven died leaving twenty thousand dollars and one additional dollar, and Leah's children collected their ten thousand dollar *ketubah* from that estate, that payment counts as establishing a *motar*. The remaining twenty thousand and one dollars is not fully consumed by Rachel's *ketubah*, because a real portion of the estate — even a single dollar — was independently inherited and paid out. Rachel's children may now take their special portion.

One might ask why the *hilchata* needs to state both principles explicitly — first that Rachel's children are always entitled, and second that paying Leah's *ketubah* counts as *motar*. If you only knew the first, you might have thought that Rachel's children are entitled only when there is genuine leftover money remaining *after* both *ketubah* payments, not money used to pay Leah's claim. If you only knew the second, you might have thought the rule about payment counting as *motar* applies only when both sets of children share equal standing as *ketubat benin dichrin* heirs — not when one set comes as creditors. Each principle is independently necessary.

### Three Wives Setup

The Gemara demonstrates why both principles require explicit statement through the case of three wives. Reuven married three women. Rachel and Leah both died during his lifetime, so their children are both entitled to *ketubat benin dichrin* on equal footing — this is the standard case with no asymmetry of standing. The third wife survived Reuven and has only daughters. When Rachel's and Leah's sons come to divide the estate, they discover that after their two *ketubah* extractions, the only remaining money in the estate is needed to pay the third wife's *ketubah* debt. Her daughters, as females, are not heirs under biblical law and will not claim *ketubat benin dichrin*.

### Why Both Rules

In this three-wife scenario, the second principle — that a *ketubah* payment counts as *motar* — is essential and would need to be stated even if one had never heard of *achas b'chayav v'achas b'moso*. The two boys (from Rachel and Leah) are on an equal playing field; their entitlement is not in question. What is in question is whether the money used to pay the third wife's *ketubah* qualifies as the *motar dinar*. Without the second ruling, one might think that only genuinely surplus funds — money left after all obligations are met — qualify, not money deployed to pay a creditor. The second principle answers this.

Conversely, in the *achas b'chayav v'achas b'moso* scenario, one might have thought that even if a payment to a third-party creditor counts as *motar*, the payment specifically to Leah's own children does not — because Leah's children might say we were never part of the inheritance, we were just getting paid first. Or one might have thought that since Leah's children are coming as creditors and Rachel's children as heirs, the asymmetry in standing disqualifies Rachel's children from *ketubat benin dichrin* entirely. The first principle — *achas b'chayav v'achas b'moso yesh lahen ketubat benin dichrin* — directly rules out that concern. Both rulings together ensure that the system functions even in the most complex configurations of wives, deaths, and creditor relationships.

## Motar Dinar Rules

### Two Wives Equal

The Mishnah now articulates the foundational mechanics of *ketubat benin dichrin* in the standard two-wife case. A man was married to two wives, both of whom predeceased him. He then died. The orphans — Rachel's sons and Leah's sons — each seek to extract their mother's *ketubah* from the estate as special heirs. If the estate contains exactly the combined total of the two *ketubah* amounts and nothing more, the rule of *ketubat benin dichrin* cannot operate. There is no *motar dinar* — no leftover amount for the ordinary laws of inheritance to govern. In such a case, *cholkin b'shaveh* — they divide the estate equally, without any special priority. The desire to activate *ketubat benin dichrin* is understandable: the children with the larger *ketubah*, or even those with fewer siblings (since a single son with a ten-thousand-dollar *ketubah* walks away with the full amount while ten sons sharing the same *ketubah* receive a thousand each), have a strong incentive to establish the *motar*. But absent that extra amount, no special extraction is permitted.

### With Extra Money

If, however, there is a *motar dinar* — a single *dinar*'s worth of value beyond the combined *ketubah* totals — then *elu notlin kesubas iman v'elu notlin kesubas iman*: each set of children extracts their mother's *ketubah* amount, and the residual estate, however modest, is then divided equally by the ordinary rules of inheritance. The extra *dinar* is what makes the entire mechanism operable.

### No Self-Assessment

A natural temptation arises: if the estate falls slightly short of having a *motar dinar*, can the heirs who want *ketubat benin dichrin* to apply simply declare that they will add money to the estate to create the needed surplus? The Mishnah answers emphatically: *ein shomin lahem* — we do not listen to them. Nor may they inflate the assessed value of estate property, claiming that a piece of land worth eight thousand dollars should be counted as ten thousand, thereby appearing to leave a surplus. The assessment of what the estate is actually worth is not in the hands of the interested heirs. *Ella shamin es hanechasim beit din* — rather, the court assesses the value of the assets. The *beit din* conducts an objective appraisal, and the legal outcome follows from that appraisal alone.

### What Counts

The Mishnah also addresses the question of anticipated but not yet received funds. If there is money that should be coming to the estate — whether because the estate expects to receive an inheritance from someone who has not yet died, or because there are outstanding receivables not yet collected — this does not count toward the *motar dinar*. *Einan kemuchzak* — such funds are not considered within the estate's current control. Only assets actually in hand at the time of assessment establish whether the *motar dinar* requirement has been met.

### R. Shimon Land Only

Rabbi Shimon adds a further stringency. Even if there is leftover money beyond the *ketubah* amounts, that money counts toward the *motar dinar* only if it consists of land — *karka*. Movable property, *metaltelin* — even valuable cattle or other chattel — does not satisfy the requirement. As Rabbi Shimon formulates it: *afilu yesh sham nechasim she-ein lahem achrayut einam klum* — even if there is property that carries no lien obligation (meaning it is technically free and clear but happens to be chattel), it counts for nothing. The extra *dinar* must be in real property, *nechasim she-yesh lahen achrayut*, encumberable land, in an amount exceeding the two *ketubah* obligations. The symbolic significance of land as the carrier of genuine ancestral inheritance — rooted in the biblical conception of the estate as a portion in the land — underpins Rabbi Shimon's position. The *Tanna Kamma*, by contrast, accepts chattel as a qualifying *motar*. The Gemara earlier sought to read the dispute between the *Tanna Kamma* and Rabbi Shimon as bearing on exactly this question — whether *karka* alone qualifies or whether *metaltelin* suffices — and the Mishnah now confirms that Rabbi Shimon indeed holds the more stringent position.

### Unequal Amounts

A *baraita* supplements the Mishnah with the case of unequal *ketubah* amounts: one wife's *ketubah* is a thousand *zuz*, the other's is five hundred. The children of the wife with the larger *ketubah* have a particularly strong incentive to activate *ketubat benin dichrin*. The rule, however, is identical: if there is a *motar dinar* — in this case, any amount beyond fifteen hundred and one *zuz* — each set of children extracts their mother's *ketubah* amount and the remainder is divided equally. If not, they divide the total estate equally. The *baraita* adds no new principle; it simply confirms that the mechanics apply regardless of whether the two *ketubah* amounts are equal or disparate.

## Property Appreciation

### Depreciation Case

The Gemara turns to cases in which the value of the estate changes between the time of the husband's death and the time of collection. The straightforward case is depreciation: the estate was worth fifteen hundred and one *zuz* at the moment of death — sufficient to satisfy both *ketubah* amounts with a *motar dinar* to spare — but by the time the heirs come to collect, the value has fallen to fourteen hundred. The Gemara treats this as self-evident: *kevar zachu bahen yorshin* — the heirs already acquired their rights at the moment of death. The status of the estate is determined as of the date of death, and a subsequent decline in value does not retroactively strip the children of their entitlement. The *motar dinar* requirement was satisfied when it needed to be satisfied.

### Bar Tsartsur Case

More complex is the reverse: the property of the house of Bar Tsartsur presented the mirror image — at the time of death the estate was insufficient (*mu'atin*), but afterward it increased in value (*v'nisrabu*). The heirs came before Rav Ami seeking a ruling on whether the appreciation should trigger the application of *ketubat benin dichrin*.

### Rav Ami Opinion

Rav Ami did not issue a clear ruling. Instead, he instructed the parties to negotiate among themselves — specifically suggesting to those with the smaller *ketubah* that they try to reach a settlement (*zilu paysuhu*) with those who held the larger claim. The implication of his direction was that the children with the larger *ketubah* might have the stronger argument in principle, since the property now had sufficient value. When the parties refused to negotiate, Rav Ami threatened rabbinic sanctions — the painful but non-physical sanction of excommunication — to compel a settlement. The inability to reach resolution led the matter to be referred to Rav Nachman.

### Rav Nachman Ruling

Rav Nachman ruled with apparent symmetry: just as when the estate begins large and depreciates — *zachu bahen yorshin*, the special heirs already acquired their rights — so too when it begins small and appreciates — *zachu bahen yorshin*, the heirs acquire their rights. But this formulation raises an immediate question: *which* heirs? In the depreciation case, the answer is clear — the heirs who needed the *motar dinar* already had it, and they keep their entitlement despite the later decrease. But in the appreciation case, if you say *zachu bahen yorshin*, it is ambiguous whether you mean the heirs who were being excluded (because at death there was no *motar*) now gain the right due to the appreciation, or whether you mean something else entirely.

### Rashi/Tosafot

Rashi and Tosafot dispute the import of Rav Nachman's ruling. Rashi understands it to mean that one always assesses as of the date of death. In the appreciation case, because there was no *motar dinar* at death, the heirs of the smaller *ketubah* wind up benefiting — the estate is divided equally, which favors them, and the later appreciation simply increases what each party receives from the equal division. The determining moment is fixed at death. Tosafot reads Rav Nachman's symmetrical language differently: just as in the depreciation case the rule of *ketubat benin dichrin* is applied because the *motar* existed at death, so in the appreciation case *ketubat benin dichrin* is also applied because the *motar* now exists at the time of collection. On Tosafot's reading, the principle is that one always resolves ambiguity in favor of applying *ketubat benin dichrin* — whether the qualifying *motar* appeared at death or at distribution. This disagreement reflects a fundamental question: is the determining moment fixed (Rashi) or does the system prefer, at any available snapshot in time, to activate the special inheritance mechanism (Tosafot)?

## Two Houses Case

### Setup

The final section of the *daf* introduces a case that initially appears to involve the rules of creditor collection but turns out to implicate broader principles about negotiation rights and asset valuation. A man owed a thousand *zuz* to a creditor. He had two houses — each worth five hundred — and sold them both to Michael for five hundred each. The seller then, presumably, dissipated the proceeds without paying his debt. The creditor now pursues Michael as the buyer of the encumbered properties. Michael acquired the houses subject to the seller's lien, so the creditor may collect from Michael's property.

### Michael's Offer

The creditor moved to seize the first house, and Michael saw that he was about to lose the second house as well. Michael approached the creditor with a thousand *zuz* and made the following proposal: I am prepared to tell you that the first house you already seized is worth a thousand *zuz* — that is, your full debt is satisfied. If you accept that valuation, consider your debt paid and leave me the second house. If you reject that valuation, then here — take the thousand *zuz* in cash and return the first house to me. Michael's gambit is elegant: he offers the creditor either a favorable valuation of one house covering the entire debt, or a cash payment of the full thousand *zuz*. Either way, Michael is trying to avoid losing both houses. What he is doing is effectively asserting his own assessment of the first house's value — claiming it is worth the full thousand — and daring the creditor to disagree.

### Mishnah Parallel

Rami bar Chama raised the possibility that this is analogous to the Mishnah's case of orphans who sought to inflate the value of estate property in order to create a *motar dinar*: *im amru yetomim harenu ma'alim al nichsei avinu yafeh dinar* — if the orphans say we will assess our father's property at a higher value to generate the required surplus — the Mishnah says we do not listen to them. Is Michael's self-serving valuation similarly inadmissible?

### Rava Distinction

Rava rejected the analogy. *Mi dami?* — are the cases really comparable? *Hatam ika pseida l'yatmi* — in the Mishnah's case, when one set of orphans inflates the property value, the other set of orphans suffers a real loss, because the inflated valuation distorts the equal division they are entitled to. *Hacha mai pseida?* — but here, what loss does the creditor actually suffer? *Alfa yahiv v'alfa shakil* — he put in a claim for a thousand and he is going to collect a thousand. His debt is fully discharged either way. If the creditor suffers no loss from Michael's proposed valuation, the Mishnah's prohibition — designed to protect parties who would be harmed by self-serving assessments — may not apply. Michael may well have the right to negotiate on precisely these terms.

### Mishnah Parallel

The Gemara leaves open the broader question of whether a purchaser of encumbered property generally has the right to pay the creditor in cash rather than surrendering the property — Tosafot notes and analyzes this as a potentially independent principle — but the immediate ruling flows from Rava's distinction: because the creditor is made whole either way, Michael's negotiating posture is not automatically disqualified by the Mishnah's rule against self-interested valuation.

### Rava Distinction

The Gemara thus proceeds on the assumption that Michael's offer is at least potentially legitimate, and the case is resolved in the creditor's favor in the following sense: the creditor, having now accepted one house in satisfaction of his full debt (whether because he agreed to the thousand-*zuz* valuation or because Michael paid cash and reclaimed the first house, retaining the second), has collected his thousand *zuz*.

### Ravina/Rav Ashi

A final question arises regarding Michael's claim against the original seller. Michael purchased two houses for five hundred each. One was seized by the creditor. Michael is now out one house and is entitled to compensation from the seller who sold him encumbered property. But how much? Ravina says Michael is entitled to a thousand *zuz* — because the house effectively discharged a thousand-*zuz* debt, and that is the measure of what it was worth in the transaction. Rav Ashi says five hundred *zuz* — because the house's actual purchase price was five hundred, the underlying value is five hundred, and Michael's loss is five hundred regardless of the debt it happened to satisfy. The *halacha* follows Rav Ashi: *hilchata b'chamesh me'ah* — Michael recovers only five hundred from the seller. The creditor received his full thousand, Michael retained one house and was compensated five hundred for the one he lost, and the seller — who generated this entire predicament by selling encumbered property and failing to pay his debt — bears the consequences of the shortfall.

---

---

# Ketubot 93

## Three Wives Case

### Mishna Setup

The daf opens with a *mishna* presenting one of the most analytically challenging division problems in all of rabbinic literature. The case: a man married three women and died. Rashi specifies that all three were married on the same day, a necessary condition for the problem to arise at all — if they had married on different days, the earlier *kesuvah* would hold a prior lien, and the division would simply proceed in chronological order of priority regardless of claim size. The three women hold *ketubot* of 100, 200, and 300 respectively. The question is how the estate is to be divided among them when its total value may be less than the sum of their claims.

### Estate = 100

When the estate is worth only 100, the *mishna* rules that the three women divide it equally — each receiving 33⅓. This is intuitive: all three women have an equal and total claim on that first 100. The woman owed 100 says "give me the 100," the woman owed 200 says "give me the 100," and the woman owed 300 says the same. Their claims are indistinguishable in their force against that amount, so equal division follows naturally.

### Estate = 200

The second case is where the difficulty begins. When the estate is worth 200, the *mishna* prescribes a distribution of 50 to the woman with the 100 *kesuvah*, and 75 each to the women with the 200 and 300 *ketubot*. This is deeply puzzling. One might attempt to apply the logic of the first case: on the first 100, all three have equal claims and divide it equally, yielding 33⅓ each. On the second 100, only the women with claims of 200 and 300 remain, and since both assert equal and total claims on that amount, they divide it equally — 50 each. That would yield 33⅓, 83⅓, and 83⅓. But the *mishna* gives 50, 75, 75. The problem is not merely that the numbers differ — it is that the *mishna*'s division does not transparently follow any single coherent principle. Why 50 as the threshold for the first division rather than 40 or 60? The *gemara* itself will note this difficulty explicitly, and Tosafot acknowledges that the rationale has not been satisfactorily explained.

### Estate = 300

The third case, where the estate equals 300, yields a distribution of 50, 100, and 150. Unlike the second case, this result follows cleanly from a straightforward model: proportional division according to claim size. The claims of 100, 200, and 300 stand in a ratio of 1:2:3, totaling 6 parts. One-sixth of 300 is 50, two-sixths is 100, and three-sixths is 150. This model works elegantly here. The difficulty is that it does not explain either of the earlier cases — applied to the estate of 200, proportional division would yield 33⅓, 66⅔, and 100, not 50, 75, 75.

### Two Models Explained

The *mishna* thus appears to employ at least two distinct models across its three cases, and possibly three. The first case follows a principle of equal division among all claimants with equal standing. The third case follows proportional division by claim size. The second case follows neither, at least not in any obvious way. The final line of the *mishna* — *v'chein gimel she'hitilu lakis*, "and so too with three who invested into a common purse" — reinforces the proportional model for the third case: if three partners invest 100, 200, and 300 respectively, the profits and losses are divided proportionally to their contributions. This makes good sense as a model for investment. It does not, however, explain the middle case, and the *mishna* presents all three rules as if they constitute a unified system.

---

## Aumann's Solution

### Aumann Introduction

It was the economist and mathematician Robert Aumann — Nobel laureate and game theorist — who, roughly 1,800 years after the *mishna* was written, published a paper demonstrating that all three cases follow a single, coherent, and mathematically unique principle. The paper appeared in the collected papers of Robert Aumann and was also printed in the Hebrew Torah journal *Moriah*. Once the principle is understood, the response is immediate: this must be the *pshat* of the *mishna*.

### Shnayim Ochzim Model

The foundation of Aumann's insight was already anticipated — at least partially — by the *Geonim* and by Rashi, who noted that the operative principle should be the one derived from the first *mishna* of Bava Metzia. In that famous case of *shnayim ochzim b'tallit* — two people grasping a garment — each claiming it entirely, the garment is divided equally. More precisely, what the *mishna* establishes is that what one side has already conceded to the other should be set aside, and only the contested portion is divided equally. If I claim half the garment and you claim all of it, I have implicitly conceded half to you. You receive that half outright; only the remaining half is in genuine dispute, and that is divided equally between us — yielding you three-quarters and me one-quarter. The principle, then, is: concede what is conceded, and divide equally only what is genuinely disputed.

### Pairwise Analysis

Aumann's critical insight — the step that eluded the *rishonim* — was that this principle must be applied not to all three women simultaneously as a group, but to every possible *pair* of claimants. In a three-claimant case, there are three such pairs: the 100 and 200 women, the 200 and 300 women, and the 100 and 300 women. Whatever amounts are assigned to any two of the claimants must satisfy the *shnayim ochzim* rule when those two are examined in isolation.

### Backwards Calculation

Working backwards from the *mishna*'s answer of 50, 75, 75 in the case of an estate worth 200, Aumann demonstrates that the numbers are consistent. The woman with the 100 *kesuvah* receives 50, and the woman with the 200 *kesuvah* receives 75 — a combined total of 125. Consider those two women alone: if 125 were being divided between a claimant of 100 and a claimant of 200, the first 100 is disputed equally between them (neither concedes anything within that range), yielding 50 each; the remaining 25 is conceded entirely by the 100-woman (whose claim is exhausted), so it goes entirely to the 200-woman. The result is exactly 50 and 75. The same analysis applies to every other pair.

### Pairwise Verification

The verification proceeds across all three pairs. The women with 200 and 300 *ketubot* receive 75 and 75, a combined total of 150. If 150 is divided between a claimant of 200 and a claimant of 300, neither concedes anything — both have claims exceeding 150 — so the entire amount is in dispute and is divided equally: 75 and 75. This matches. Now consider the women with 100 and 300 *ketubot*, who receive 50 and 75, totaling 125. Of that 125, the first 100 is in genuine dispute between them; they divide it equally (50 each). The remaining 25 is conceded by the 100-woman and goes entirely to the 300-woman, yielding 50 and 75. Again, this matches precisely. The solution works for every pairwise combination without exception.

For the case of the estate worth 300, the same verification holds. The 100 and 200 women receive 50 and 100, totaling 150. Dividing 150 between claims of 100 and 200: the first 100 is disputed equally (50 each), the remaining 50 is conceded by the 100-woman and goes to the 200-woman — giving 50 and 100. The 200 and 300 women receive 100 and 150, totaling 250. Dividing 250 between claims of 200 and 300: the first 200 is disputed equally (100 each), the remaining 50 is conceded by the 200-woman and goes to the 300-woman — giving 100 and 150. All pairs check out.

### Uniqueness Proof

What makes the result publishable — and what transforms it from an observation into a theorem — is Aumann's proof that for any number of claimants and any estate size, there is always exactly one and uniquely one division that satisfies the pairwise *shnayim ochzim* rule for every possible pair simultaneously. It is something like a Sudoku: there are constraints, and those constraints determine a unique solution. The *mishna*'s three cases, which appeared to follow unrelated rules, in fact all reflect this single underlying principle. One might add: it is striking that this explanation was apparently lost, that the *rishonim* could not reconstruct it, and that Tosafot itself acknowledges — in its laconic way — *lo ispareish shapir ta'ama d'hanei milta*: the rationale for these matters has not been well explained.

---

## Gemara Solutions

### Gemara Problem

The *gemara* focuses its critical attention on the second case, the one that resists obvious explanation. The *mishna* states that when the estate is worth 200, the woman with the 100 *kesuvah* receives 50. The *gemara* asks: why 50? She should receive only 33⅓. If we apply the principle of dividing equally what is disputed and conceding what is conceded, but we apply it to all three women together as a group, the reasoning would proceed as follows: on the first 100, all three have equal and total claims, so it is divided equally among them — 33⅓ each. On the second 100, the 100-woman has already staked her full claim; only the 200-woman and the 300-woman remain as claimants, and they divide it equally — 50 each. The result would be 33⅓, 83⅓, 83⅓ — not 50, 75, 75. The *gemara* thus implicitly accepts the principle of conceding what is conceded and dividing the remainder equally, but applies it group-wise rather than pairwise, and finds that the *mishna*'s answer does not follow.

### Shmuel's First Case

Shmuel offers an *okimta* — a contextualizing reinterpretation — to explain the second case. He says the *mishna* is dealing with a special situation: Mrs. 200 has written to Mrs. 100 a declaration that she waives any dispute with her (*din u'devarim ein li imach*) over the first 100. In other words, Mrs. 200 has removed herself from the contest with Mrs. 100 over that portion. With Mrs. 200 standing aside, Mrs. 100 is left dividing the first 100 with Mrs. 300 only. Those two divide it equally, and Mrs. 100 walks away with 50.

### Waiver Logic

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: if Mrs. 200 waived her claim against Mrs. 100 in the first 100, then when we get to the second 100, shouldn't Mrs. 300 be able to say to Mrs. 200 — you have already removed yourself from this *kesuvah*, so you have no standing here either? And if the two of them do compete on the second 100, why do they each get 75, not 66⅔ for Mrs. 300 and 83⅓ for Mrs. 200?

The *gemara* answers in Mrs. 200's voice: *mi'din u'devarim hu de'siliki nafshi* — "I only withdrew from the legal dispute; I did not give her a gift." The distinction is subtle. Mrs. 200's portion in the first 100 was 33⅓, representing her contested claim as one of three competing creditors. She conceded her claim *against* Mrs. 100 specifically, meaning she would not be counted as a competing force against Mrs. 100. The effect is that Mrs. 100 now faces only one competitor — Mrs. 300 — over that first 100, and they divide it equally, yielding 50 to Mrs. 100. Mrs. 200 has not transferred her claim to Mrs. 100 as a gift; she has simply stepped back from the contest. Now 50 remains. Mrs. 200 and Mrs. 300 stand in equal dispute over that remaining 50, dividing it 25 and 25 — giving 75 to each. This is the logic, though Tosafot itself notes, as mentioned earlier, that the rationale has not been fully and cleanly articulated within this framework.

### Shmuel's Second Case

For the third case — the estate of 300 — Shmuel offers a second, entirely separate *okimta*. Here, it is Mrs. 300 who has written to both Mrs. 100 and Mrs. 200 a declaration that she removes herself from dispute over the first 100 entirely. With Mrs. 300 absent from the first 100, Mrs. 100 and Mrs. 200 divide it equally — each receiving 50. Now for the second 100, Mrs. 300 has only waived her claim over the first 100; she re-enters for the second. All three divide the second 100 equally — another 33⅓ each, but since Mrs. 100 is already at her cap of 100, her claim is exhausted; in the contest over the second 100 between Mrs. 200 and Mrs. 300, they divide it equally — 50 to each. The final 100 is uncontested, going entirely to Mrs. 300. The result: 50, 100, 150. Shmuel's explanation works arithmetically, but is candidly arbitrary — it posits an ad hoc legal fiction for each case with no unifying principle connecting them.

### Staged Seizure Model

Rabbi Yaakov from Nehar Pekod, in the name of Ravina, proposes a different framework for both cases — one that does not rely on declarations of waiver but on the physical reality of when property is seized. He argues: *reisha bishtei tefisot ve-seifa bishtei tefisot* — both the second and third cases of the *mishna* involve two separate acts of seizure, two distinct moments at which property is grabbed, each of which must be adjudicated independently. The *mishna* is not describing a beit din sitting down with a full estate and dividing it in one stroke; it is describing a scenario in which property becomes available in stages, and each batch of property seized triggers its own independent division.

### Two Stages Analysis

In the case of the estate of 200, Rabbi Yaakov says the property was seized in two batches: first, 75 was seized simultaneously by all three women, and then 125 was seized simultaneously. When 75 is seized and all three women have equal and total claims on it, it is divided equally: 25 each. When 125 is then seized, we apply the *shnayim ochzim* analysis to this batch. The 100-woman still has 75 of her claim outstanding, so within the first 75 of this 125, all three compete equally — 25 each. The remaining 50 of this 125 exceeds the 100-woman's remaining claim; she has no stake there, leaving the 200-woman and 300-woman to divide it equally — 25 each. The result per person across both seizures: Mrs. 100 gets 25 + 25 = 50; Mrs. 200 gets 25 + 25 + 25 = 75; Mrs. 300 gets 25 + 25 + 25 = 75. This matches the *mishna*.

For the third case, the estate of 300, the property is again seized in two batches: first 75, then 225. The first 75 is divided equally — 25 each. Within the 225: the first 75 is in equal dispute among all three (25 each); of the next 150, Mrs. 100's claim is now exhausted (she has received 50), leaving Mrs. 200 and Mrs. 300. Rashi's treatment here is acknowledged to be descriptive rather than explanatory — he notes the outcome but does not fully derive why the 100 should come to be divided equally and the 50 given entirely to one party, and the underlying arithmetic of this final stage is difficult to reconstruct cleanly from first principles. Nonetheless, the conceptual thrust of the staged model is clear: the staged seizures force us to deal with the estate in segments, and each segment is governed by the *shnayim ochzim* principle applied to whoever retains an active claim at that moment.

The staged seizure model shares a structural intuition with Aumann's approach — both involve breaking the total amount into sub-units and identifying who has standing at each level — but Rabbi Yaakov's version is an *okimta* grounded in a specific physical scenario rather than a general mathematical theorem. The *mishna* according to this reading is not stating a universal rule but describing what happens when the circumstances on the ground happen to produce these particular seizure stages.

---

## Rabbi's Position

### Rabbi Rejects Natan

A *baraita* now informs us: *tanya zu mishnat Rabbi Natan* — this *mishna* is the teaching of Rabbi Natan. On this, Rabbi — the redactor of the *Mishnah* itself — says: *eini ro'eh divrei Rabbi Natan b'elu* — I do not see the logic of Rabbi Natan's words here, or perhaps: I do not accept them. In place of Rabbi Natan's complex graduated division, Rabbi says: *ela cholkim b'shaveh*.

### Mishna Authority Q

This raises a striking question: if Rabbi himself did not accept Rabbi Natan's ruling, why did he codify it as the *stam* — the anonymous, authoritative — *mishna*? It is a known phenomenon that Rabbi, as *mesader ha-mishna*, would sometimes record a minority or disputed opinion as the *stam mishna*, thereby lending it greater authority. But the question cuts the other way here: if the opinion is not his own, why give it that status? The text *tanya zu mishnat Rabbi Natan* might also suggest that this was a recognized independent collection — *mishnat Rabbi Natan* — perhaps connected to the tradition that Rabbi Natan's collection was characterized as *kav v'naki*, compact and precise. Whether Rabbi found the system conceptually valid but difficult to articulate, or simply chose to preserve an established tradition while registering his personal difficulty with it, remains genuinely unclear.

### Tosafot on Proportional

Tosafot addresses the question of what Rabbi's alternative — *cholkim b'shaveh* — actually means. Rabbeinu Chananel rules that the *halacha* follows Rabbi, so the entire elaboration of the Aumann solution, however brilliant, is *Torah lishmah* for practical purposes. As for the content of Rabbi's position: one reading of *cholkim b'shaveh* would be purely equal division — each woman receives an equal share regardless of her claim, up to the point her claim is satisfied. Tosafot rejects the implication that the larger claimant would receive no more than the smaller one, noting that *she'midat ha-din lo ken* — this does not conform to the measure of justice. Instead, Tosafot understands *cholkim b'shaveh* to mean proportional division in accordance with the size of each woman's claim — that is, the investment model applied universally. Each unit of *maneh* in the *kesuvah* entitles its holder to an equal share of that unit of the estate. Applied to the estate of 200: one-sixth of 200 is 33⅓, two-sixths is 66⅔, three-sixths is 100. Applied to the estate of 300: 50, 100, 150. This, according to Tosafot, is what Rabbi means, and it is the rule by which we rule.

---

## Investment Partnership

### Shmuel Investment

The *mishna* concludes with the parallel case of three partners who pool their money — *hitilu la-kis* — contributing 100, 200, and 300 respectively. Shmuel draws attention to a related rule: *shnayim she'hitilu la-kis zeh maneh v'zeh matayim ha-sachar l'emtza* — two partners who invest 100 and 200 respectively divide their earnings equally. Shmuel's language — *ha-sachar l'emtza*, "the earnings to the middle" — is deliberately chosen. The equal division applies to profits.

### Rava's Indivisible Asset

Rava qualifies Shmuel's ruling significantly: *mistavra milta de-Shmuel b'shor l'charisha v'omed l'charisha* — Shmuel's principle makes sense when we are dealing with an ox bought for plowing and used for plowing. The logic is that an ox engaged in agricultural labor is a single, indivisible asset. When it plows, it earns rental income as a whole unit. It is not the case that two-thirds of the plowing was done by Michael's two-thirds of the ox and one-third by my one-third — the ox plows as an ox. Therefore, while Michael has more capital at risk, the asset generating the return is indivisible, and the return it generates is treated as attributable equally to each partner's stake in that indivisible unit. This at least provides some conceptual grounding for Shmuel's otherwise counterintuitive rule, even if it remains economically strange.

However, Rava continues: *aval b'shor l'charisha v'omed l'tveicha* — but if the ox was bought for plowing and then the partners decided to slaughter it for meat, that is a different matter. Here, as Rashi explains, *omed* means not the original intention of the seller but the partners' own subsequent choice — they bought it for plowing but ultimately determined that slaughtering it was more profitable. Once slaughtered, the ox has been converted into a divisible asset: meat that can be parceled out, weighed, and sold in proportion. In that case, the division must follow each partner's proportional investment: *zeh notel l'fi ma'otav v'zeh notel l'fi ma'otav*.

### Hamnuna's Position

Rav Hamnuna disagrees: *afilu shor l'charisha v'omed l'tveicha ha-sachar l'emtza* — even if the ox was bought for plowing and later slaughtered, the proceeds are still divided equally. His reasoning is that the nature of the partnership was established at the outset — they entered as partners in an ox bought for plowing, and that original characterization defines the partnership terms regardless of what subsequently happens to the asset. The intent with which the joint acquisition was made governs the division of whatever it yields.

### Plowing vs. Slaughter

The *gemara* resolves the dispute between Rava and Rav Hamnuna by invoking a *tosefta*. The *tosefta* states that two partners who invest 100 and 200 divide the earnings equally — which initially seems to support Rav Hamnuna's broader position. The *gemara* asks: is this not dealing with a case of an ox bought for plowing that was then slaughtered, thereby supporting Rav Hamnuna against Rava? The *gemara* pushes back: no, the *tosefta* is referring only to the case of *shor l'charisha v'omed l'charisha* — bought for plowing and used for plowing. The question then becomes: if the *tosefta* intended to address the case of an ox bought for plowing and then slaughtered, it should have said so explicitly and stated that even in that case the division is equal. The *gemara* resolves this: the *tosefta* is in fact implicitly consistent with Rava. Its equal-division ruling applies only to the standard plowing case; for the slaughter case, the *tosefta* itself provides that *zeh notel l'fi ma'otav v'zeh notel l'fi ma'otav* — each takes proportionally. The final ruling is that when an ox is bought for plowing and remains in that use, the earnings are equal; if it was bought for plowing but was then slaughtered, the division is proportional.

### Tosafta Discrete Goods

The *tosefta* also addresses a further scenario: *lakach zeh b'shelo v'zeh b'shelo v'nitarevu* — each partner separately bought his own oxen with his share of the investment, and then the animals became mixed together so that it is no longer possible to identify which ox belongs to whom. In that case, even though the ownership is uncertain in fact, the proportional stakes are known — one partner owns a third, the other two-thirds — and the division follows accordingly: *zeh notel l'fi mamo v'zeh notel l'fi mamo*. Tosafot draws from this the broader principle that any investment structured around discrete, divisible goods is divided proportionally from the outset. The argument about equal division applies only where the partners genuinely entered a partnership in a single indivisible asset. Where the assets are inherently discrete and the investment is proportional in kind — whether it is livestock, goods, or money — all authorities agree that division follows the proportion of the investment.

---

## Investment & Wives Link

### Investment Profit Rule

The *mishna*'s final ruling on the investment case — *pichatu o hotiru kach hen cholkin*, if the investment lost or gained value they divide accordingly — is brought to bear on the *gemara*'s analysis. One might assume this refers simply to the normal case of a divisible investment that went up or down in value, with profits and losses divided proportionally in the obvious way. If so, it would be an unremarkable restatement. But the *gemara* raises the possibility that the *mishna* might be referring to something more unusual.

### Intrinsic Value Change

Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha explains: *lo*, this is not about normal market gains or losses. *Hotiru* — "they increased" — means *zuza chadtiti*, the coins themselves became newer and thus worth more intrinsically. *Pichatu* — "they decreased" — means *astira de-tzunita*, the coins deteriorated to the point of being used as metal tokens to place under the heel for some medicinal purpose, indicating they lost their monetary value entirely. In other words, the *mishna* is describing a change in the *intrinsic value of the currency itself*, not merely a return on an investment.

### Principal Value Impact

The implication is significant. If the partners had invested in an ox that earned rental income, and the question is how to divide that rental income, that is the case Shmuel addresses — and the division could be equal or proportional depending on the nature of the asset. But if what changed is the principal itself — the currency in which the investment was denominated went up or down in intrinsic value — then what is being divided is not profit from a jointly-owned indivisible asset, but a change in the value of what each partner actually contributed. In that case, since each partner owns his proportional share of the principal, any change in the value of that principal accrues or diminishes proportionally. The partner who invested 200 owns twice as much of the monetary principal as the partner who invested 100, and when the money itself changes in value, the gain or loss is distributed accordingly. This applies equally to the *mishna*'s wives case: when the underlying value of the estate fluctuates at the level of principal, each woman's proportional stake governs the division of gains and losses.

---

---

# Ketubot 94

## Four Wives & Oaths

### Four Wives Scenario

The *mishna* at the bottom of 93b introduces the case of *mi shehaya nasuy arba nashim umes* — a man who was married to four wives sequentially and then died.
