Unlike the preceding *mishna*, which dealt with the hypothetical scenario of a man who married multiple wives on the exact same date — so that all their liens were simultaneous — the present *mishna* addresses the normal, real-world situation in which the wives were married one after the other, creating sequential liens on the husband's estate. The governing rule is therefore straightforward: *harishona kodemes lashniya, veshniya lashlishit, veshlishit leriviit* — the first has priority over the second, the second over the third, and the third over the fourth.

### Oaths Between Wives

When each wife comes to collect, the *mishna* imposes an oath requirement. The general rule is that anyone collecting from orphans — whether a creditor or a widow — must swear that none of the debt has already been paid. The rationale is that the orphans, had the father been alive, might have contested the claim and asserted partial or full payment; the orphans, particularly if minors, are not positioned to investigate their father's papers and press that claim themselves. Rashi assumes that the *mishna* here is dealing with adult orphans, who are in principle capable of making their own claims and examining the father's records — and therefore would not ordinarily compel an oath from a claimant arriving with a signed *shtar*. Nevertheless, the *mishna* establishes a distinct obligation: wife one must swear to wives two, three, and four, because those later wives can say that by exercising her lien and seizing property, she may be impacting assets that would otherwise flow to them. If part of her *ketubah* had already been paid, she would be seizing property that should rightfully reach them.

Tosafot raises the natural question of whether this oath obligation applies equally whenever any creditor collects and thereby affects other creditors with later liens. The answer may well be no in general, but the unique dynamic here — all the wives are widows of the same man, all their claims were triggered simultaneously by his death, and they all appear before us as a collective group — creates a relational context that generates the mutual oath obligation among them.

### Fourth Wife Exempt

The *mishna* continues: *veriviit nifres shelo bishvua* — the fourth wife collects without any oath. Since she is last in line, no subsequent creditor is being harmed by her collection. The adult orphans, as noted, are in a position to press their own claims if they believe they have been wronged, so no oath is owed to them either. The fourth wife thus collects in peace, which might seem like a small consolation for receiving whatever is left at the end.

### Ben Nanas Disagrees

Ben Nanas disagrees. His position is that the mere fact of being last in line does not exempt wife four from taking an oath. The *gemara* will clarify precisely why — but his objection rests on the possibility that one of the fields seized by an earlier wife may turn out not to have belonged to the husband, leaving an earlier wife's debt still uncollected and potentially requiring her to look to the fourth wife's field for satisfaction.

### Same-Day Documents

The *mishna* addresses the scenario where all the *ketubot* bear the same date. Even where the marriages occurred on the same day, priority can still be established if the hour is known: *kol hakodemes l'chavertah afilu sha'ah achas zachsa* — even one hour's precedence is sufficient to establish priority. The *mishna* notes that in Jerusalem it was the practice to record the hour of the transaction in the document — *v'chach hayu kosvin b'Yerushalayim sha'os* — precisely to enable this kind of fine-grained determination. If, however, all the documents share the same hour with no further differentiation, and the estate is insufficient to satisfy all claims, then *cholekot b'shaveh* — they divide equally — with the detailed proportional rules of the previous *mishna* applying as needed.

---

## Oath Debate Analysis

### Shmuel's Framing

The *gemara* opens its analysis with the question *b'mai kamifligi* — what precisely is the dispute between the *Tana Kamma* and Ben Nanas regarding whether the fourth wife must take an oath? Shmuel's answer, which Tosafot's reading of the *gemara* makes most sense, is this: the case at issue is one where it emerges — or where there is reason to believe — that one of the fields seized by wife one, two, or three was not actually the husband's property. The husband may have sold it innocently after purchasing stolen goods, or there may have been some other defect in his title. In any event, one of the earlier wives has seized a field that turns out not to have been validly his, meaning she has not in fact collected her *ketubah* debt through that seizure and will need to look elsewhere for satisfaction.

Rashi reads the scenario as one where this has already been established as fact. Tosafot, whose reading the lecturer follows as more consistent with the flow of the *gemara*, understands the debate as a general one: in ordinary circumstances, whenever wives one through three have taken their fields, does wife four need to take an oath because of the *possibility* that one of those earlier fields may turn out to have been problematic? On that reading, the debate is about the structural obligation in a normal case, not about what happens after a defect has been proven.

The underlying legal question that drives the debate is framed by the *gemara* as *u-va'al chov me'uchar she-kadum v-gava kamifligi* — they dispute what happens when a later creditor jumped ahead and collected, and it subsequently turns out that an earlier creditor had a superior lien. Does the later creditor get to keep what she collected, or must she return it?

A vivid illustration: if a man died and two creditors both have liens on his estate — one lien dating back ten years, the other more recent — and the later creditor moved quickly and seized the only available field before the earlier one acted, can the earlier creditor come and demand the field back? Or does the later creditor's prior seizure give her a right to retain it?

### Tana Kamma Position

The *Tana Kamma* holds *mah she-gava lo gava* — what the later creditor took, she did not truly take. She cannot keep the field against an earlier creditor's superior claim. Applied to the wives: if wife four seized the last available field and it subsequently turns out that wife two, whose earlier field was defective, has an unsatisfied claim with an earlier lien, wife four must surrender her field to wife two. Given that outcome, there is no reason for wife four to swear to the earlier wives. She can never hurt their interests by holding her field, because if any of them ever need it, they are simply entitled to take it from her. An oath would serve no function.

### Ben Nanas Position

Ben Nanas holds *mah she-gava gava* — what wife four took, she may keep. If wife two comes and says her field was defective and she has an earlier lien, wife four can respond that she already collected her field and is entitled to retain it. In that case, wife four's retention of the field does affect the earlier wives' ability to satisfy their debts. It is therefore appropriate to require her to swear that her own *ketubah* has not already been paid — because her keeping the field while potentially owing a debt to an earlier wife creates real harm to that wife's interests, and the oath is designed to address exactly that harm.

### Strip-Mining Concern

Rav Nachman offers an entirely different framing of the dispute. He holds that *d'chulei alma mah she-gava lo gava* — in truth, everyone agrees that wife four cannot keep the field if an earlier wife's lien proves superior. The dispute is not about whether she keeps the field, but about whether she will *tachsif* — strip-mine or devastate — the field while it is in her possession. Knowing she will eventually have to surrender it, she has every incentive to extract maximum value from it in the interim: selling off timber, exhausting the soil, or otherwise depleting whatever she can while the field is under her control.

### Psychological Deterrent

This framing makes Ben Nanas's position both more surprising and more ingenious. According to Rav Nachman, the reason Ben Nanas wants wife four to take an oath is psychological: by requiring her to swear to the earlier wives that her *ketubah* has not been paid, we induce her to believe that she will be entitled to keep the field. After all, from her perspective, why would the court make her take an oath to the other wives unless she had some real claim to retain the field against their demands? She will reason that the oath is a precondition to keeping what she collected — and therefore she will handle the field responsibly, as a person who believes she will be its long-term owner, rather than strip-mining it as someone who knows she is a short-term custodian.

This is, as noted, a striking use of the oath mechanism. The oath is being imposed not because she is legally obligated to take it — everyone agrees she will have to return the field — but because making her take it creates a false impression that will deter destructive behavior. One might ask whether this involves a kind of deception. The response is that no real disservice is being done to the wife: all she is being asked to do is swear that she is entitled to collect what she is collecting. If along the way that oath causes her to believe she can keep the field, and if that belief in turn leads her to preserve the field's value, those are ancillary benefits. The oath itself is simply an affirmation of her legitimate claim to collect.

It is worth noting that Tosafot raises the broader question of why this kind of oath requirement — structured around the possibility of interconnected harm among multiple creditors — appears only in the context of a *ketubah* collection and not in ordinary creditor scenarios. The question does not receive a fully resolved answer, but the unique relational structure of the multiple-widow scenario, where all claims arise simultaneously from one death and all claimants are before us together, distinguishes it from the general creditor case.

---

## Partners & Representation

### Implicit Representation

The *gemara* cites a teaching by Rav Huna in the name of the elder Abaye — a *tanna* whose teaching frames the question of oaths to adult orphans — and then transitions to a related case. The teaching concerns *hanei trei achei vetrei shutfei* — two brothers who have inherited an undivided estate and are therefore effectively partners in it, or simply two partners in a jointly owned field. If a third party initiates a court case against the estate and only one of the partners appears to defend — *veazal chad mineihu bahadei ledina* — can the absent partner, upon learning of the outcome, say to the winning claimant: *at lav ba'al devarim didi at* — you never litigated against me, you only litigated against my partner's half, and I'm entitled to my own day in court?

Rav Huna's position is *shelichusei avad* — the partner who appeared was implicitly acting as the agent of the whole estate, and the absent partner cannot subsequently disavow the result. The one who appeared in court represented the entire jointly held property, not merely his own half.

### Why Not All Wives?

Rav Nachman, visiting Sura, was asked about this rule. He responded that it can be derived from the *mishna* itself. The *mishna* says wife one swears to wife two, wife two to wife three, wife three to wife four — but does not say that wife one must also swear directly to wife three and wife four, even though wife one's collection affects their interests as well. Why the omission? It would seem to be because wife two, when she receives wife one's oath, is implicitly representing the interests of wives three and four as well.

### One Oath Suffices

The *gemara* immediately questions this inference. Perhaps the reason wife one need not swear separately to wives three and four has nothing to do with representation at all — it may simply be that *shvua le-echad shvua le-me'ah*, an oath made once is effective for everyone. The oath, once sworn, functions as evidence: it demonstrates to any interested party that the swearer would not have taken God's name in vain if she were lying. That evidentiary value does not depend on who was in the room when the oath was taken. There is no need to repeat the same oath to multiple parties.

The *gemara* had initially explored the possibility that oaths operate more in the mode of personally satisfying the other party — giving them the subjective assurance of having received a direct commitment — in which case each wife would need her own oath. But the *gemara*'s resolution rejects this model: a single oath suffices for all, so the *mishna*'s structure tells us nothing about implicit representation.

### Context & Presence

Returning to the question of partners, the *gemara* refines Rav Huna's position. The rule that the appearing partner implicitly represents the whole is not categorical. Rather: *d'lo ite b'mata* — the rule applies when the absent partner was not in the city at the time of the court proceedings. *Aval ite b'mata, ibai leh l'meisei* — but if he was in the city, why didn't he show up? His presence in town and his failure to appear can be read as tacit authorization of his partner to represent the entire estate. The principle, then, is not a blanket presumption of representation, but a contextual one: one must look at the circumstances to determine whether the absent partner implicitly conferred authority on the one who appeared. If he was elsewhere and genuinely unaware, he may be entitled to his own proceeding. If he was present in town, the context suggests he acquiesced in the other's representation. As the *gemara* makes clear, these are not rigid categorical rules; context governs, and the de facto assumption is that each partner represents only his own share unless circumstances indicate otherwise.

---

## Same-Day Documents

### Rav: Split

The *gemara* now takes up a case structurally similar to the *mishna* — two claims on the same asset arising from the same date — but meaningfully different. In the *mishna*'s scenario, both wives' claims are fully valid; the problem is simply insufficient assets. Here the question is different: two people present deeds of sale for the same field, both dated on the same day. Only one of them can be the true owner — the seller could not have sold the same field twice. One of the documents, in some sense, reflects a genuine transaction and the other does not, even if we cannot determine which is which.

The question is how a court should adjudicate this. Rav rules *cholkin* — divide the field. This is striking, because unlike the *mishna*'s scenario, splitting here does not match any possible reconstruction of the facts. The field was sold either entirely to A or entirely to B; it was never half sold to each. Yet given that we have no way to determine the truth, Rav holds that division is the most judicious resolution available, even if it is guaranteed to be factually wrong.

### Shmuel: Guess

Shmuel rules *shuda de-dayni* — the judges should exercise their judgment and award the field to one party. Shmuel's basic point is that the court should try to match what actually happened, even if it cannot be certain of success. Rav's split guarantees being fifty percent wrong every time. Shmuel would rather aim for the full truth — knowing the attempt might fail entirely — than settle for a compromise that is always partially incorrect.

Rashi and Tosafot understand *shuda de-dayni* differently. Rashi holds that the judges should look at all available circumstances — whose story coheres better, who seems more credible, what other evidence can be assembled — and make their best informed guess. Tosafot, by contrast, understands *shuda de-dayni* as a genuinely arbitrary exercise of judicial authority: the judges simply award it to whomever they choose, without reference to any evidentiary considerations. On Tosafot's reading, the decision is essentially a crapshoot, and its legitimacy derives not from its accuracy but from the court's authority to resolve intractable disputes.

### Rav=Rabbi Meir

The *gemara* proposes that Rav's position aligns with that of Rabbi Meir, who holds *eidei chasima karsi* — it is the witnesses who sign the document who give it legal effect. The debate about *eidei chasima* versus *eidei mesira* originates in the law of *gittin*: is a *get* made effective by the witnesses who sign it, or by the witnesses who observe its delivery? Rabbi Meir holds it is the signatories. On that view, the operative legal reality of a document is entirely defined by its content — by what the signatures attest — not by when or to whom it was physically handed over. Since both documents in our case say the same thing and bear the same date, they carry identical legal weight. There is no extrinsic fact — such as which was delivered first — that could differentiate them. From Rabbi Meir's perspective, both documents took effect simultaneously and in contradiction to each other, so there is a genuine sense in which both parties acquired equal and simultaneous claims. Division is therefore not merely a fallback for uncertainty; it reflects an underlying legal reality in which neither party holds an unambiguous superior claim.

### Shmuel=R. Elazar

Shmuel's position aligns with Rabbi Elazar, who holds *eidei mesira karsi* — it is the witnesses of delivery who make the document legally effective. On this view, what matters is not what the document says but when it was actually handed over. One of the two buyers received his deed before the other, and that buyer is the true owner. The documents' identical dates are legally irrelevant; the truth lies in the sequence of delivery. Since there is one real owner and one who is not, the court should try to determine which is which, rather than split what is in principle an undivided whole.

The *gemara* confirms this alignment through a ruling of Rav Yehuda: Rav Yehuda reported that Rav stated *halacha k'Rabbi Eliezer b'gittin* — we rule like Rabbi Elazar in the laws of *gittin*. When Rav Yehuda reported this before Shmuel, Shmuel added *af b'shtaros* — not only in *gittin* but in all documents. This implies that Rav ruled like Rabbi Elazar only in *gittin*, not in documents generally — and therefore in the context of commercial deeds, Rav follows Rabbi Meir. The *gemara* concludes: *ela machvarta, Rav k'Rabbi Meir u'Shmuel k'Rabbi Elazar* — it is clear that Rav follows Rabbi Meir and Shmuel follows Rabbi Elazar.

### Braita Citation

The *gemara* raises a challenge from a *braita*: *shnei shtaros hayotzim b'yom echad, cholkin* — two documents issued on the same day, divide. This appears to directly contradict Shmuel. Shmuel responds that the *braita* follows Rabbi Meir. But the *gemara* presses: if the *braita* followed Rabbi Meir, why does its concluding clause rule that the one who received the document first acquires the field — *zeh shemasar lo kanah*? That ruling reflects Rabbi Elazar's principle that delivery determines acquisition, not Rabbi Meir's. And yet even while operating under Rabbi Elazar's framework — where there genuinely is one true owner determined by sequence of delivery — the *braita* still says to divide. This poses a problem for Shmuel's position that under Rabbi Elazar you try to identify the real owner rather than split.

Shmuel's ultimate response is that the question of whether to split or to exercise judicial discretion is itself a *tannaitic* dispute that runs independently of the Rabbi Meir / Rabbi Elazar debate. A further *braita* is cited involving a *shaliach* sent to deliver money to a party who had since died, whose sender had also died, leaving it unclear which estate the money belonged to. The sages say the agent should divide it between the two sets of heirs; the Babylonian tradition says the agent may do as he sees fit. This parallels the split-versus-decide question, demonstrating that both approaches have *tannaitic* support and that Shmuel can maintain his position as one legitimate opinion within that dispute.

---

## Rami & Ukva Case

### Competing Documents

The *gemara* now presents a concrete application. The mother of Rami bar Chama and Mar Ukva bar Chama — two brothers — wrote over her property to Rami bar Chama in the morning and then, the same halachic day toward evening, wrote it over again to Mar Ukva bar Chama. Each son presented his document to a different court: Rami bar Chama came before Rav Sheshet, who awarded him the estate; Mar Ukva came before Rav Nachman, who awarded it to him. Rav Sheshet then appeared before Rav Nachman to challenge his ruling.

### Written Date Priority

Rav Sheshet argued that Rami bar Chama's document came first — it was written and given to him in the morning — and therefore he should have priority. Rav Nachman rejected this: *atu be-Yerushalayim yasvinan de-kasvinan sha'os* — do we sit in Jerusalem where we write the hours into the document? Both documents bear the same date. We have no recorded indication in either document of when during the day the transaction took place. Since we do not record hours, we cannot go by who received it first; the two documents are on their face identical in date.

### Shuda De-Dayni Claim

Rav Nachman declared that he awarded the estate to Mar Ukva on the basis of *shuda de-dayni* — the judicial authority to decide between two equal claims. Rav Sheshet challenged this on two grounds. Rav Sheshet argued that he too had exercised *shuda de-dayni* when awarding the estate to Rami bar Chama, and therefore his prior ruling should stand. Rav Nachman responded with two counters. First: *ana dayana u'mar lav dayana* — I am a qualified judge and you are not. As Rashi explains, Rav Nachman was the supreme judicial authority of his generation, appointed and recognized by the relevant political and rabbinic institutions. The exercise of *shuda de-dayni* is not available to every judge.

### Tosafot Limitations

Tosafot articulates the tradition underlying this point with precision. The tradition, transmitted in the name of Rabbeinu Chananel, is that *shuda de-dayni* applies *davka be-mekarkei* — only with respect to land, not movable property. And it applies *davka dayan mumche ke-Rav Nachman be-doro* — only to the supreme expert judge of the generation, as Rav Nachman was in his time. Rav Sheshet, despite being an undeniably great authority, did not meet that standard. On Tosafot's reading, then, Rav Nachman's point is not merely that he outranks Rav Sheshet, but that Rav Sheshet fundamentally lacked the standing to invoke *shuda de-dayni* in the first place. The power is not a prerogative of any qualified judge; it is reserved exclusively for the singular supreme authority.

This dovetails with Tosafot's broader understanding that *shuda de-dayni* is a genuinely arbitrary exercise of judicial power — not a reasoned best-guess, but an authoritative pronouncement whose legitimacy flows from the judge's supreme standing. Precisely because such an unbound discretion would be dangerous in lesser hands, it is restricted to the one judge in each generation whose stature and experience make it trustworthy.

### Conscious Exercise

Rav Nachman's second response to Rav Sheshet's claim of having also exercised *shuda de-dayni* is equally important: *mei-ikara lav be-torat hachi asit lah* — when you awarded the estate to Rami bar Chama, you were not acting in the mode of *shuda de-dayni* at all. You gave it to him because you believed he deserved it — because his document came first, in the morning. You were attempting a normal legal adjudication, reasoning that prior receipt of the document confers priority. That was a mistaken judgment: since the hours were not recorded, we cannot go by the sequence of delivery. But it was an attempted legal ruling, not an exercise of *shuda de-dayni*. *Shuda de-dayni* requires a conscious, explicit invocation of judicial authority — the judge must be deliberately saying: I am empowered to award this to whomever I see fit, and I award it to X. That is not what Rav Sheshet did. One cannot retroactively reframe a failed legal ruling as an exercise of *shuda de-dayni*. The distinction matters: *shuda de-dayni* is a deliberate assertion of a judge's sovereign discretion, not a label applied after the fact to justify a decision that turned out to lack a proper legal basis.

---

## Ambiguous Dates

### Documents Compared

The *gemara* presents one final case. Two documents were brought before Rav Yosef. One bore the date *chamisha b'Nissan* — the fifth of Nissan — with full specificity. The other simply said *Nissan*, without specifying which day of the month.

### Specific Date Wins

Rav Yosef awarded the field to the holder of the specifically dated document — *ukmi Rav Yosef le-hahu de-chamsha be-Nissan be-nechasim*. The logic is that the ambiguous document leaves open the possibility that the transaction it records occurred anywhere from the first to the twenty-ninth of Nissan. The holder of the ambiguous document may well have a claim that predates the fifth of Nissan — but equally, he may have a claim that postdates it. Given this uncertainty, his document places him in the weaker position, *at yadcha al hatachtona* — he cannot prove that his date precedes the other's. Perhaps his document was executed on the twenty-ninth of Nissan. The specific document establishes its date clearly; the ambiguous one does not. The specific claimant prevails.

### Reimbursement Request

The claimant holding the ambiguous document accepted the ruling but then raised the question of reimbursement. He had paid for the field, and now the court had awarded it to someone else. He proposed to exercise liens on other fields that the original seller had sold to third parties, arguing that even in the worst-case interpretation of his document — that it was executed at the very end of Nissan — he had a lien predating the first of Iyar. He therefore asked the court to write him a *tirfa* — a court order authorizing collection — from the first of Iyar onward, so that he could pursue those other buyers for reimbursement.

### Buyer Response

Rav Yosef explained that those other buyers could turn this request against the claimant. They could say: *at bar Nissan at* — you are a Nissan person; that field was actually sold to you in Nissan, and it is therefore still yours. The fact that a court awarded it to someone else does not change the underlying reality, which they maintain is that the seller validly conveyed the field to the ambiguous-document claimant. Since the field is actually his, he has suffered no real loss and is not entitled to reimbursement from us. This is a strikingly counterintuitive result: a court determination that he does not own the field is apparently not conclusive against third-party buyers who claim to know the true facts and use that knowledge to defeat his reimbursement claim.

### Power of Attorney

The solution proposed by the *gemara* is *harsha'a*: the two claimants must grant each other power of attorney. Specifically, the holder of the specific-date document — who was awarded the field — must grant the other claimant his power of attorney to pursue reimbursement from the other buyers. Here is the logic: the buyers insist that the field truly belongs to the ambiguous-document claimant, not to the person the court awarded it to. If so, it is the court-awarded party — who "officially" holds the field as far as the legal record is concerned — who has a cognizable reimbursement claim against those buyers. The ambiguous-document claimant cannot collect from them in his own name, because they say the field was really his all along. But armed with the other party's power of attorney, he can present himself as collecting on that party's behalf — and since the buyers acknowledge the court's awardee as the one who "lost" the field to them, they cannot deny his representative's claim. Through *harsha'a*, the ambiguous-document claimant can thus recover the value of what was taken from him, channeling the reimbursement claim through the party whose standing the buyers are forced to recognize.

---

---

# Ketubot 97

## Widow Selling Fields

### Introduction to Selling

The daf opens with the word *keitzad* — "how does she sell?" — which signals that the Gemara is not merely continuing a narrative but is asking a structural question: what exactly is the mechanism by which a widow, dependent on her late husband's heirs for sustenance, goes about selling off their fields? This is daf 97a, and the scenario is one in which the heirs are failing to provide the widow with her *mezonot*, forcing her to take matters into her own hands by selling fields that belong to the estate — fields that could otherwise have been used to pay the *ikar ketubah* or to support the *yorshim* themselves.

The complication is immediate and practical. The moment she remarries, her right to *mezonot* from the estate vanishes. If she has already sold a field to a buyer, and then gets married the following month, the heirs will turn to that buyer and demand the field back, arguing that the widow had no right to convey what was not truly hers to give. The buyer, naturally, is left in an awkward position. So the question of *keitzad mocheret* — how exactly does this sale work — is not a theoretical one.

### Rav Huna's Position

Rav Daniel bar Rav Katina, a name that appears rarely in the Talmud, cites Rav Huna, the *Rosh Yeshiva* of Sura, as follows: *mocheret achat lishneim asar chodesh velokeach mefarnes achat lishloshim yom* — she sells enough to cover twelve months of sustenance, and the buyer pays her in monthly installments of one month at a time. The logic is structural rather than commercial. The buyer does not hand over the full value of the field at once, because doing so would immediately vest the property in him regardless of what happens to her *mezonot* rights. Instead, by paying month by month, the arrangement functions more like a rental with an option to purchase: each monthly payment covers one month's worth of *hana'ah* from the field, and the *yorshim* retain a lien on the property for as long as she remains entitled to *mezonot*. Should she remarry mid-course, the buyer returns whatever portion he has not yet paid, and the field reverts to the heirs.

Rashi's language makes this explicit: *she'im tinasei yachazir mah shebeyado leyorshim* — if she remarries, he returns what remains in his hand to the heirs. The total sum, *kol hama'os*, represents the full purchase price of the field outright; the reason the buyer does not simply pay that sum upfront is precisely to preserve the heirs' lien against the eventuality of her remarriage. Once the full price has been paid out, the *yorshim* lose their claim entirely.

### Rav Yehuda Position

Rav Yehuda takes a more conservative position: *mocheret lishisha chodashim velokeach mefarnes achat lishloshim yom* — she sells for only six months at a time, with the same monthly payment structure. Where Rav Huna permits her to sell up to a twelve-month horizon, Rav Yehuda limits her to six months. In both opinions, however, the monthly installment arrangement is the same.

### Baraitot & Ameimar

The Gemara presents a *baraita* in support of Rav Huna's twelve-month position, and separately a *baraita* supporting Rav Yehuda's six-month position: *tanya kavatei deRav Huna… tanya kavatei deRav Yehuda*. Having two *baraitot* supporting two contradictory opinions does not resolve the question of which is authoritative. Ameimar, however, rules: *hilcheta mocheret leshisha chodashim velokeach mefarnes achat lishloshim yom* — the *halacha* follows Rav Yehuda.

### Rav Ashi Challenge

Rav Ashi challenges Ameimar: *veRav Huna mai?* — what do you make of Rav Huna? Both Rav Huna, the *Rosh Yeshiva* of Sura, and Rav Yehuda, the *Rosh Yeshiva* of Pumbedita, are contemporaries of roughly equal authority, and we have a *baraita* behind each of them. Why rule definitively like one over the other?

Ameimar responds: *lo shemi'a lei* — I have not heard it. The Gemara clarifies that this expression should be understood as *kelomar lo sevira lei* — that is, not that Ameimar was simply unaware of Rav Huna's ruling, but rather that he does not accept it. This is a recognized idiom in *Chazal*: because everything is oral tradition, saying "I have not heard" functions the way we might say in English "I don't hear you" — meaning, I don't agree. Ameimar is registering a substantive disagreement with Rav Huna's position, not pleading ignorance, and therefore *paskens* like Rav Yehuda.

---

## Liens & Ketubah

### Rav Sheshet Query

The next question is addressed to Rav Sheshet, and it is a genuinely intricate one: *mocheret lemezonot mahu shetachzor vetitrof lekhetuvatah?* — if a widow sells estate property in order to fund her *mezonot*, can she later return and seize that same property to collect her *ketubah*?

### Liens Explained

To appreciate the difficulty, one must understand the mechanics of *shiabud* — the mortgage or lien that attaches to property in the context of debt. When a person takes a loan, all of his landed property becomes mortgaged to that debt. If he subsequently sells that property and then defaults, the creditor may approach the buyer and seize the land, leaving the buyer to seek reimbursement from the debtor. This is equally the case with a *ketubah*: when we write *ketubot*, we declare that everything the husband owns — even, as the formula puts it, the coat on his back — is mortgaged to the *ketubah*. If the husband dies insolvent, the widow may pursue property he sold during the marriage and seize it to satisfy her *ketubah*, leaving the purchaser to recover his money from the estate.

### Ketubah vs. Mezonot

The critical distinction here is that while the *ketubah* carries this power of *tereifah* — the ability to seize mortgaged property from a third-party purchaser — *mezonot* does not. A widow can sell property to fund her *mezonot*, but she cannot seize property as a lien for *mezonot*. The question is therefore whether this asymmetry creates a trap: she sells the field herself to obtain *mezonot*, the *yorshim* are bankrupt and cannot pay her *ketubah*, and she now wants to seize that very same field — the one she sold — to satisfy her *ketubah*. Is that permissible?

### Rav Yosef Ruling

The question is framed in terms of a ruling by Rav Yosef: *almanta dezabnah achrayut ayitmei* — when a widow sells land, the *achrayut* for that sale, meaning the obligation to make the buyer whole if the property is subsequently seized by a creditor, falls on the *yatmei*, the heirs of the original estate, not on her. The same applies to a *beit din* that sells property: the heirs bear the *achrayut*. This principle seems to suggest that she stands outside the transaction in a meaningful sense — she acted on their behalf, the responsibility rests with them, and therefore she should be free to step back in as a creditor in her own right and seize the property for her *ketubah*.

### Two Objections

The Gemara presents two possible lines of argument, pulling in opposite directions.

The first argument is that since the *achrayut* falls on the *yatmei* rather than on her, she is essentially acting as their agent in making the sale. Having not accepted responsibility herself, she remains a stranger to the transaction in the sense that matters, and she may therefore turn around and seize the property as a *ketubah* creditor.

The second argument, however, is the one the Gemara articulates with particular sharpness: *mineih de'achrayut de'alma lo kabalt alach, achrayut denafshach mi lo kabalt?* — You have not accepted responsibility for the general debts of the estate; but did you not accept responsibility for your own sales? The force of this objection is that the two transactions — selling the field for *mezonot* and then seeking to seize it for the *ketubah* — are both her doing. If she intended to preserve that field as collateral for her *ketubah*, she should not have sold it. Having sold it herself, she cannot now present herself as an innocent creditor exercising a lien. That is her business on both ends, and she should bear the consequences.

There is something intuitively compelling about the widow's counter-position. One might argue that from the beginning it was the heirs' obligation to provide her with *mezonot* and to honor her *ketubah*. If they failed in both, she was forced to act as their agent to feed herself, and she should not be penalized for having discharged their obligation on their behalf. The buyer, moreover, is not uninvolved in this calculus: anyone purchasing property that is known to be heavily mortgaged and sold under these circumstances is, in a sense, a venture capitalist — buying at a discount precisely because the title is uncertain, counting on the property eventually becoming fully his, and knowing that if it is seized he has a legal avenue to recover his funds from the party bearing *achrayut*.

### Sheshet's Answer

Rav Sheshet resolves the question by citing a *tanna* who taught: *mocheret veholechet ad kedei ketuvatah* — she may continue selling fields for *mezonot* until only enough property remains to cover her *ketubah*. *Vesamach lah sheteigbeh ketuvatah min hashe'ar* — and she relies on collecting her *ketubah* from what remains. The *tanna* thus envisions a self-limiting principle: she has the ongoing authority to sell, but she must preserve a residuum of property sufficient to satisfy her *ketubah*. The grammatical subject of *samach* — who exactly "relies" — is uncertain in the text; the masculine singular does not obviously refer to her, nor does it clearly refer to *beit din*, which would usually take a plural form.

### Eitza Tova or Din

The Gemara immediately raises the question of whether this *baraita* constitutes binding *din* or merely *eitza tova* — good practical advice. Perhaps the *tanna* is not establishing a legal rule but simply counseling wisdom: she ought to leave over enough property to cover her *ketubah* so that people will not call her unreliable, so that she will not acquire a reputation for doubling back on buyers. This echoes a theme from the prior day's learning, where *eitza tova derabnutah* was invoked in a similar context.

### Leaving Fields

The Gemara resists the *eitza tova* reading. If the *baraita* were merely advisory, it would have been sufficient to say "and she collects her *ketubah* from the remainder." The specific language — *vesamach lah sheteigbeh ketuvatah min hashe'ar*, with its implication of reliance rather than mere permission — suggests a binding legal rule. The inference drawn is: *shayra in, la shayra la* — if she leaves over sufficient property, she may collect her *ketubah*; if she does not, she may not.

---

## Rescission of Sale

### Rescission Query

The Gemara now broadens its inquiry: *zevnah delo itzterichah lei — zuzei hadrei zevini o lo hadrei zevini?* — If someone sells property and it turns out that they no longer need the money for which they sold it, can the sale be rescinded? This is framed as a general question arising in connection with the widow's situation, though it quickly takes on a life of its own as the Gemara canvasses concrete cases.

### Oxen Example

The first example: a man needed oxen to work his land. Without livestock — or, in modern terms, without machinery — land in the ancient world was of limited productive value. He therefore sold a portion of his property to Rav Pappa in order to raise funds to purchase oxen. *Lesof lo itzterichah lei* — ultimately, it turned out he did not need the money; the oxen were cheaper than he had anticipated, or he found another source of funds.

### Rav Pappa Piety

*Ahadrei nihalei Rav Pappa lara'ei* — Rav Pappa returned the land. The natural assumption might be that this is what the law requires, but the Gemara corrects that: *Rav Pappa lifnim mishurat hadin hu de'avad* — Rav Pappa acted beyond the letter of the law, out of personal piety. He recognized that the man had sold land he did not ultimately need to sell, and out of generosity returned it. This is therefore not a proof for or against the legal rule; it establishes only that Rav Pappa was a *tzaddik*, not that the law compels rescission.

### Famine Example

The second case is more instructive. There was a local famine in Nehardea. Rashi explains that the river rose, making it difficult for boats carrying grain to navigate, and the resulting shortage drove the price of wheat dramatically upward. In response, *zvinu kulei alma laafdanaihu* — everyone began selling off their *apadna*, their substantial homes, in order to purchase food. *Lesof atu chiti* — eventually, the grain boats did arrive, the artificial shortage collapsed, and wheat prices fell immediately.

### Nachman Ruling

Rav Nachman ruled: *dina hu dehadrei apadnei lemarihu* — it is the law that those mansions should be returned to their original owners.

### Mekach Taaut

The Gemara explains the basis for this ruling: *hatam nami zvinei beta'ut havu de'iglai milta de'arba bekilei havah kayma* — this too was a sale made in error, because it subsequently became clear that the boats were already stationed just around the bend, waiting for the river to subside. Had the sellers known the boats were nearby, they would not have sold their homes. The transaction was therefore predicated on a false factual premise, making it a *mekach ta'ut*.

### Rashi Clarification

Rashi draws a careful distinction here. The ruling applies specifically because the boats were nearby and discoverable — their presence was knowable, even if the sellers did not know it. This is a different situation from one in which grain arrived from a genuinely unexpected source: for example, if a merchant from a distant region with a wheat surplus happened to arrive in Nehardea, flooding the market in a way no one could have anticipated. In that case, Rashi indicates, there would be no *mekach ta'ut* and the sales would stand, because the change in circumstances was truly unforeseeable. The rule turns on the distinction between what was knowable and what was genuinely unknowable.

### Buyer Concern

Rami bar Shmuel raises a concern before Rav Nachman: *im ken nimtzeit machshilan le'atid lavo* — if you rule this way, you will end up creating obstacles for future transactions. Buyers, fearing that their purchases will be reversed whenever an artificial shortage dissipates, will decline to participate in such markets at all. In a time of famine, when people most need to convert assets into food, the very mechanism by which that conversion occurs will be paralyzed.

### Nachman Response

Rav Nachman responds: *atu kol yoma betzorta shchicha?* — does such an artificial shortage occur every day? Do we really encounter these conditions so frequently that buyers will be deterred from ordinary commerce by the possibility of rescission? The other party in the conversation replies, yes, in fact, in Nehardea it does occur with some regularity — something about Nehardea's geography makes it susceptible to these supply disruptions. But Rav Nachman's point stands: the ruling addresses a specific and unusual situation, and the concern about chilling future sales does not override the basic claim of justice on behalf of people who sold their homes under conditions of artificial and transient crisis.

### Final Hilcheta

The *hilcheta* is then stated: *zevin velo itzterichah lei zuzei hadar zevina* — if one sells property and it turns out that he did not need the money, the sale is reversed. This represents the standing law. The *hilcheta* formulas are, as is well known, the contributions of the *Rabanan Savorai*, the post-*Amoraic* scholars who edited the Talmud and appended definitive rulings to conclude *sugyot*; they carry full legal weight even if they arrive after the Amoraic discussion itself is concluded.

The underlying principle is one of legislated *rachmanus*: land was not mere commodity in the ancient world. To sell land was, in a sense, to give up a part of oneself, and the pain of that transaction did not disappear simply because the seller failed to announce his reasons at the time of sale. The fact that no explicit stipulation was made — that the sale appeared *stam*, without stated conditions — does not eliminate the equitable claim that a man who sold his land unnecessarily should be able to recover it upon returning the money.

---

## Widow Authority

### Tanna Kama Rule

The next *mishna* addresses the procedural requirements for a widow's sale of estate property. The *tanna kama* rules: *almana bein min ha'erusin bein min hanisu'in mocheret shelo b'veit din* — a widow, whether widowed from actual marriage or from *erusin* (engagement), may sell the heirs' property without the formal sanction of a *beit din*.

### Rabbi Shimon View

Rabbi Shimon disagrees and introduces a distinction: *min hanisu'in mocheret shelo b'veit din, min ha'erusin lo timkor ella b'veit din, mipnei she'ein la mezonot*. A widow from actual marriage may sell without *beit din*, but a widow from engagement may not — she must go through *beit din* — because she has no right to *mezonot*. The widow from marriage sells regularly because she has an ongoing need for sustenance, assuming the *yorshim* are failing to provide it. A woman widowed from engagement, however, has only a *ketubah* claim, not a *mezonot* claim; Rabbi Shimon therefore requires her to proceed through official channels.

### Question Setup

The Gemara asks: the case of the widow from marriage — we understand why the *tanna kama* permits her to sell without *beit din*, since she has an ongoing need for sustenance. But the widow from engagement — what is the reason that the *tanna kama* permits her to sell without *beit din* as well?

### Ulla/Chen Reason

Ulla answers: *mishum china* — because of *chen*. There is a *machloket* between Rashi and Tosafot as to exactly what *chen* means in this context, and the two interpretations yield meaningfully different analyses throughout the discussion.

### Rashi on Chen

Rashi explains *china* as follows: *sheyiheyu ba'aleihen lechen be'eineihen* — so that their husbands will be pleasant in their eyes, meaning so that the woman will retain a fond memory of the marriage. *Velo yimne'u nashim milinsa la'anashim* — and women will not be deterred from remarrying by the prospect of a cumbersome collection process. The idea is that if we make it burdensome for a widow to collect what she is owed, women may become averse to marriage altogether, knowing what awaits them if they are widowed. By streamlining the process, we make marriage a more attractive proposition and thereby serve a social interest. Rashi's reading has daughters in mind, one might say — a man ensuring that the women in his community do not face bureaucratic difficulty in their hour of need.

This interpretation becomes difficult in the continuation of the *sugya*, as will become clear.

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan offers a different rationale: *lefi she'ein adam rotze shetitbaze ishto b'veit din* — because no man wants his wife to be embarrassed by having to appear in *beit din*. The leniency is not for her future benefit but reflects the *kavod* a husband feels toward his wife even after his death: the social norms of the community are such that a woman appearing in *beit din* to wrangle over money is regarded as undignified, and the institution is designed to spare her that indignity. This connects to a broader theme running through *Masechet Ketubot*, where there is a recurring concern that daughters not be reduced to going *bichozrot al hapetachim* — going door to door begging — and that the honor of families not be compromised.

### Grushah Question

The Gemara identifies the practical difference between Ulla and Rabbi Yochanan: *ika beinaihu grushah* — the case of the *grushah*, the divorced woman. She too has a *ketubah* to collect, but she is neither a widow who needs to be encouraged toward remarriage nor a woman whose husband cares about her dignity in court.

### Chen Analysis

According to the view that the leniency exists *mishum china* — because of *chen* in Rashi's sense, to encourage remarriage — a *grushah* should also benefit, since she too may want to remarry and we similarly wish to make the process attractive for her.

### Embarrassment Analysis

According to the view that the leniency exists because a man does not want his wife embarrassed in *beit din*, the *grushah* should not benefit: *grushah mai ikpat leh?* — what does he care about her? Once she is divorced, his concern for her dignity dissolves. There is no longer a husband who would be pained by her public appearance in court.

### Grushah Mishna

The very next *mishna* in the tractate states explicitly: *vegrushah lo timkor ella b'veit din* — and a divorced woman may not sell except through *beit din*.

### Grushah Conclusion

The *mishna*'s ruling that a *grushah* requires *beit din* seems to confirm Rabbi Yochanan's position and to align with Rabbi Shimon's approach. However, the Gemara works through the implications carefully. If the *mishna* reflects the *chen* rationale, one would need to explain why a *grushah* does not need *chen*. The Gemara suggests: *almana min ha'erusin hu dela nafshuh lechen didah* — a widow from engagement has less *chen*, and it is for that reason that Rabbi Shimon requires her to go to *beit din*, while a *grushah* has more *chen* because she was involved in a real relationship — *aval grushah de'nafshuh chen didah*.

Here Rashi's interpretation begins to strain. Why would a widow from engagement have less *chen* in the sense of needing encouragement toward remarriage? Rashi suggests she was not as emotionally attached to her husband in the first place. This is acknowledged to be somewhat forced. Rabbeinu Chananel, cited in Tosafot, offers two alternative readings. First, that *nafish chen didah* in the case of the *grushah* means she has a larger *ketubah* because she typically receives the *tosefet* in addition to the *ikar ketubah*, and therefore has more at stake in the collection process — giving her more need for the facilitation that *chen* provides. Second, and more persuasively, that a *grushah* is in a more socially vulnerable and stigmatized position than a widow — *hi bzuya yoter min ha'almana* — and therefore she has a greater need for *chen* in the sense of assistance and social support, not that she has more of it inherently. The phrase *nafish chen didah* then means she needs more *chen* rather than that she possesses more of it.

---

## Heirs Selling

### Heirs Baraita

A *baraita* is cited: *keshem shemocheret shelo b'veit din, kach yorsheha yorshei ketubatah mocherin shelo b'veit din* — just as the widow herself may sell without *beit din*, so too those who inherit her *ketubah* may sell without *beit din*. This rule extends the widow's procedural leniency to whoever steps into her position as a creditor with a *ketubah* claim.

### Male Heirs Problem

This creates an immediate problem for the embarrassment rationale. If the reason a widow sells without *beit din* is that no man wants his wife to be embarrassed in court, why would the same exemption apply to her *yorshim*? One could argue that the concern extends to the *yorshim* as well — *ki heichi de'i'lei de'nicha lei de'titbazye yorshei nami de'nicha lei de'libazu* — just as he did not want his wife to appear in *beit din*, so too he did not want his *yorshim* subjected to the indignity of public litigation over money. On this reading, *bizayon* attaches to anyone — male or female — who has to go and haggle over an inheritance in court. It is simply beneath the dignity of the family.

### Grace Problem

The *chen* rationale, however, faces its own difficulty here. If the leniency exists to ease the widow's path toward remarriage or to maintain her favorable memory of the deceased, what does that have to do with male heirs? Sons who inherit their mother's *ketubah* claim have no need of the kind of *chen* being invoked on her behalf.

### Female Heirs

Ulla resolves the problem with a *targum* — a reinterpretation of the case: *tirgmah Ulla kegon sheyirshtah bitah o achotah* — the *baraita* is referring to a case where the widow's heirs are her daughter or her sister. These female heirs do have a need for *chen* in exactly the way the widow herself did. It is not *banin dichrin* — the usual case of sons inheriting through the *ketubot* provision — but rather female relatives who have stepped into the widow's position as creditors, and who similarly benefit from having the collection process made accessible and dignified. The daf concludes here.

---

---

# Ketubot 98

## Ketubah Payment & Mezonot

### Mishnah Overview

The daf opens with a *mishnah* found at the bottom of 97b. The *mishnah* addresses the situation of a widow whose husband's estate is obligated both to pay her *ketubah* and to provide her with *mezonot* — sustenance — for as long as she remains a widow. The underlying structure of this arrangement is that the widow is entitled to be fed from the estate during the period of her widowhood, and her collection of the *ketubah* effectively terminates that entitlement. The *mishnah* further concerns her ability to sell estate property in order to realize payment of what is owed to her, and whether doing so requires the involvement of a *beit din*.

The *mishnah* states: *makhra kesuvatah miktzatah* — if she sold her *ketubah* or even part of it; *mashkanah kesuvatah miktzatah* — if she collateralized her *ketubah* or a part of it; *nasanah kesuvatah le-acher o miktzatah* — or if she gave it as a gift, in whole or in part; then *lo timkor hash'ar ela beveit din* — she may not sell the remainder except through a court.

The *mishnah* here proceeds on the assumptions associated with Rabbi Shimon's position: first, that the only circumstance in which the widow may sell estate property without a *beit din* is when she is doing so to fund her *mezonot*, not to collect the base *ketubah* payment; and second, that once she begins to receive any payout toward the *ketubah* itself — even a partial payout — she loses her entitlement to *mezonot* entirely. With those two premises in place, the *mishnah*'s ruling follows logically: once she has begun collecting on the *ketubah*, any further sale is necessarily for the purpose of the *ketubah*, and that requires a *beit din*.

The *mishnah* may seem imprecise, because even the initial sale for the *ketubah* itself requires a *beit din* under Rabbi Shimon's view. What the *mishnah* is describing is a widow who has been selling property over time for her *mezonot*, and who has now crossed into the territory of receiving *ketubah* payment. From that point forward, two consequences follow: she no longer receives *mezonot*, and any further sale must proceed through the court.

### Rabbi Shimon's View

The *mishnah* then cites what appears to be a continuation of Rabbi Shimon's position. A *baraita* makes explicit what Rabbi Shimon holds: even if she only sold or collateralized half of her *ketubah* — *makhra v'lo mishkan kesuvatah ela machtzitah* — she has nonetheless *avdah mezonoteha*, lost her *mezonot* entirely. This is the essence of Rabbi Shimon's position regarding the relationship between partial collection of the *ketubah* and the ongoing right to *mezonot*.

### Chachamim's View

The *chachamim* reject both of Rabbi Shimon's positions. Their view is stated in the *mishnah* as follows: *mocheret hi afilu arbaah vachamishah peamim* — she may sell even four or five times. This reflects their ruling that even when collecting the *ketubah* itself, piecemeal and repeatedly, she does not require a *beit din*. Furthermore, *umocheret mezonot shelo beveit din* — she may continue to sell for *mezonot* without a *beit din* as well. The crucial addition of the *chachamim*'s position is that even after partial *ketubah* payment has begun, as long as the *ketubah* has not been fully paid out, she retains her right to *mezonot* and may continue selling for that purpose. She writes on the transaction record, as discussed in the previous daf, that the sale was for *mezonot* — *ha-kosevet limezonot machrati* — a formality whose purpose was analyzed there at length.

### Gerushah Rules

The *mishnah* concludes with a separate rule: *u-gerusha lo timkor ela beveit din* — a divorced woman may only sell through a *beit din*. The rationale is that the dispensation allowing the widow to sell without *beit din* — even according to the *chachamim* — is rooted in the concern that the husband would not have wished his widow to be subjected to the indignity of repeated court proceedings. That consideration applies to his widow, not to his divorced wife. Accordingly, the *gerushah* must transact through the *beit din*, and she does so only for collection of the base *ketubah*, as *mezonot* does not apply to a divorced woman.

---

## Miktzat Kesef Analysis

### Attribution & Baraita

The *gemara* opens by identifying the *mishnah*: *masnisin mani Rabbi Shimon hi* — our *mishnah* follows Rabbi Shimon — as demonstrated by the *baraita* which articulates the views of the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Shimon respectively. According to the *tanna kamma* (which may reflect the view of Rabbi Meir), once the entire *ketubah* is effectively collected — whether by sale, collateralization, or making it an *apotiki* — the widow loses her *mezonot*. Rabbi Shimon goes further: *af al pi she-lo machar v'lo mishkan kesuvatah ela machtzitah* — even if she only sold or collateralized half of it, *avdah mezonoteha* — she has lost her *mezonot*.

### Partial Payment Status

The *gemara* then draws out the conceptual underpinning of the dispute. It states: *le-meimra de-Rabbi Shimon savar delo amrinan miktzat kesef ke-chol kesef* — this seems to say that Rabbi Shimon holds we do not apply the principle that partial money is like all the money. This phrasing is initially counterintuitive, since Rabbi Shimon's ruling seems to equate partial receipt with full receipt. The resolution is that the phrase refers to what remains outstanding: *miktzat kesef ke-chol kesef* means that as long as some portion of the *ketubah* remains unpaid, it is as though the entire debt is still outstanding. Rabbi Shimon rejects this principle — once some of the *ketubah* has been received, the outstanding balance does not preserve her *mezonot* entitlement. The *chachamim*, by contrast, affirm the principle: *amrinan miktzat kesef ke-chol kesef* — as long as part of the debt remains, the full weight of the outstanding obligation continues, and she retains *mezonot*.

### Virginity Analogy

The *gemara* then raises an apparent contradiction from a different context. It notes: *ha-ipcha shaminun lehu* — we have heard them hold the exact opposite positions. The proof comes from a *baraita* concerning the verse *ve-hu ishah bi-vsuleha yikach* — the *kohen gadol* must marry a woman in her virginity. The *baraita* records a dispute: *prat le-voggeret she-kalu visuleha divrei Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Meir excludes a woman who has passed the age of majority, whose hymen has thinned with puberty. *Rabbi Eliezer ve-Rabbi Shimon makhshirin be-vogeret* — Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon permit the *kohen gadol* to marry her. This is a genuinely striking *gemara*, because the positions seem reversed: here it appears that Rabbi Meir holds that partial diminishment of the hymen is like total absence of it, while Rabbi Shimon holds that as long as some remains, it is considered fully present — the very opposite of their apparent positions in our *sugya* regarding the *ketubah*.

### Virginity Dispute

The details of the dispute are elaborated further in the *baraita*. Rabbi Meir interprets the verse *bi-vsuleha* — with its possessive and expanded form — to require that *kol bisuleha* be present, the full and complete hymen. Under his reading, *ke-darkah ein she-lo ke-darkah lo* — even if she had only non-vaginal relations, as long as the hymen itself has thinned due to puberty, she is disqualified. His focus is entirely on the physical intactness of the hymen, not on the question of sexual experience. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon interpret *besulah* in its base form to imply a complete virgin, while *bi-vsuleha* with its expanded construction means *afilu miktzat besulim* — even partial presence of the hymen suffices. Their interpretation shifts the disqualification to sexual activity itself: *bein ke-darkah bein she-lo ke-darkah* — whether vaginal or not, if she has had sexual relations she is disqualified regardless of puberty-related changes to the hymen.

### Why Analogy Works

The *gemara*'s introduction of this analogy may seem bizarre at first, but there is a genuine conceptual connection worth noting. The standard *ketubah* amount of two hundred *zuz* is traditionally associated with the *mohar* — the bride price for a *betulah*. The *ketubah* has its roots in the biblical institution of the bride price tied to virginity. There is thus an inherent connection between the intactness of the hymen and the amount of the *ketubah*: partial virginity maps, in a real sense, onto partial *ketubah*. The *gemara* may be reminding us of this deep structural echo — the transformation of an upfront bride price into a deferred insurance mechanism preserved the underlying logic that the *ketubah* reflects the status of *betulah* at the time of marriage.

### Clarifying the Analogy

Despite the apparent elegance of the analogy, the *gemara* ultimately rejects the cross-inference: *hasham bikra palgi* — there, in the case of *besulah*, the dispute is not about a general jurisprudential principle of whether partial presence equals full presence. It is a narrowly textual dispute about how to read the verse. According to Rabbi Meir, the base form *besulah* would have included even a partial *besulah*, and the expanded form *bi-vsuleha* signals that the full hymen is required. According to Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon, *besulah* in its base form implies a complete virgin, and *bi-vsuleha* expands eligibility to include partial intactness. The disagreement is entirely about the exegesis of the verse, and cannot be extrapolated into a general principle governing whether partial payment functions as full payment in other contexts. The positions of Rabbi Shimon and the *chachamim* in the *ketubah* dispute therefore stand independently of what may appear to be their inverse positions in the *besulah* context.

---

## Silver Cup Case

### The Story

The *gemara* now introduces a narrative. There was a certain woman — *hahi iteta* — who seized a cup of silver as partial payment toward her *ketubah*. This was not a *mezonot* transaction; she was beginning to collect the base *ketubah* itself. Having received this partial payment, she then came before the court seeking continued *mezonot*.

### Rava's Ruling

The case came before Rava. He ruled: *zilu havu lah mezonot* — go, continue to pay her *mezonot*. The partial receipt of *ketubah* does not sever her entitlement to ongoing sustenance.

### Halakhic Basis

Rava grounded his ruling explicitly: *leit dechash lah le-deRabbi Shimon* — nobody is concerned for the position of Rabbi Shimon. We rule in accordance with the *chachamim*: *amrinan miktzat kesef ke-chol kesef* — as long as a portion of the *ketubah* remains outstanding, the full debt is treated as outstanding, and *mezonot* continues. One might add that if the heirs wished to stop paying *mezonot*, the practical remedy was to pay out the full remaining *ketubah* balance — a choice they apparently preferred not to make.

---

## Shevuah Requirement

### The Question

The *gemara* records that Rava's son sent a question to Rav Yosef: *mocheret shelo be-veit din tzerikhah shevuah o einah tzerikhah shevuah* — when a widow sells estate property without going through the *beit din*, as she is entitled to do — certainly for *mezonot*, and possibly even for the base *ketubah* depending on which authority one follows — must she take an oath? The concern would be that she swears the debt has not already been paid, ensuring that she is not collecting twice. As *Tosafot* immediately notes, the requirement for a widow to take an oath before collecting from the orphans' estate is itself already established in an earlier *mishnah* in *perek ha-kones*: *ein almanah nifra'at mi-nechasei yetomim ela bi-shevuah* — a widow may not collect from the orphans' estate except by oath. The question here must therefore concern something beyond that basic oath — as *Tosafot* develops at length.

### Hachrazah Concern

The *gemara* challenges the framing of the question: *ve-tiba'ei leih hachrazah* — why not ask first about the requirement of public announcement? When property is sold under court supervision, a process of *hachrazah* — public advertisement and auction — is conducted to ensure the property fetches a fair price and protects the interests of the orphans. If the widow is selling without *beit din*, does she still need to conduct such a public process?

The questioner responds: *hachrazah lo kamiba'ya li* — I have no question about *hachrazah*. The reason is established by Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Nachman: *almanah she-shamah le-atzmah lo asata ve-lo kelum* — if a widow assessed the property for her own benefit, meaning she appraised it and then purchased it herself, the transaction is entirely void. The *gemara* asks: what are the circumstances? *Ei de'achriz* — if a proper process of public announcement had taken place, why should it matter that she was the winning bidder? If the auction was fair and open and she had the highest bid, who is harmed? The answer must therefore be that we are discussing a case where *no* public process occurred — *ela lav de-lo achriz*. And in that case, the rule is: *ha-la'acher mai de'avad avad* — if she sold to a third party without *hachrazah*, the sale stands. But she cannot sell to herself — *maan shamlich* — who was it that sold it to you? You cannot be both seller and buyer. *Lo yatzah karka me-reshut yetomim* — the land never left the orphans' domain. There must be two parties to a transaction.

The *gemara* is thus reading the law as follows: *hachrazah* is indeed required in the context of a court-supervised sale, but the widow selling on her own authority does not require it — and if she did require it, she could then legitimately participate as a bidder. The law that her self-sale is void is therefore on different grounds: the inherent structural requirement of a two-sided transaction. This is explicitly stated by Rashi: *mimi kabalt mechirah zo? Lo mi-veit din, ve-lo mi-yasmei* — from whom did you receive this transaction? Not from the court, and not from the orphans.

### Cannot Sell to Self

This raises a striking observation: the widow, selling without *beit din*, has enormous latitude. She may select which portion of the estate to sell, she may conduct a private transaction without public announcement, and she may sell for whatever price she negotiates. The only firm prohibition is self-purchase. This understandably prompts concern about the orphans' interests. If she is ignorant of the property's value, or indifferent to the orphans' welfare — for instance if they are not her own children — the estate could suffer significant loss without any obvious remedy. At the same time, the *sugya* suggests the law may be structured this way precisely to incentivize the heirs to take proactive steps: going to *beit din* preemptively and establishing a structured arrangement, perhaps setting aside funds in escrow, rather than leaving the widow with unrestricted access to the estate's *karka*.

### Self-Assessment Story

The *gemara* illustrates the prohibition on self-assessment with a narrative. A certain man was entrusted with an item belonging to orphans — whether a flask, some coral, or fodder, the precise nature being uncertain. He was serving in an *apotropus*-like capacity as estate administrator. He assessed the item himself at 400 *zuz* and purchased it for that amount, directing the proceeds to the estate. The value subsequently rose to 600 *zuz*. The case came before Rabbi Ami, who ruled: *maan shamlich* — who sold this to you? The property never legitimately left the orphans' domain. The transaction was void regardless of whether the price he paid was fair, because a person cannot serve simultaneously as both parties to a sale. The item belonged to the orphans.

### Tosafot's Analysis

*Tosafot* addresses the nature of the *shevuah* at stake. The *gemara*'s conclusion is *tzrikhah shevuah* — she must take an oath. *Tosafot* points out that one reading would be that the oath concerns whether she has already been partially paid — ensuring she is not collecting twice in the course of selling off the estate piecemeal. She might be required to swear that the *ketubah* has not already been collected to a greater degree than she claims.

However, *Tosafot* in the name of *Rabbi* (the *Ri*) argues that the *shevuah* is not about overpayment at all — *lo ke-ferush ha-kuntreis shelo gavtah yoter* — it is not the oath that she has not collected more than she states. Rather, *ela miba'ei lei im mashbi'in otah shelo zilzelah ba-nechasim* — the question is whether we require her to swear that she did not deal carelessly or irresponsibly with the estate property. This reading is supported by the structure of the *gemara*'s challenge about *hachrazah*: the connection between an oath and a public announcement process is not about prior payment but about the quality of the transaction itself. The *shevuah* and the *hachrazah* are both mechanisms for protecting the orphans against negligent or inadequate sale prices. The *gemara* concludes that *hachrazah* is not required, but an oath of responsible dealing is. Even so, the practical protection this affords the orphans is limited — an oath that one acted to the best of one's knowledge does not guarantee a competent or well-advised transaction.

---

## Oversell/Undersell Rules

### Undersell Case

The next *mishnah* addresses two scenarios of improperly calibrated sales. The first: *almanah she-hayetah ketuvatah matayim u-mocheret shaveh maneh be-matayim* — a widow whose *ketubah* was 200 sold a piece of estate property worth 100 for 200. In this case, *nigveta ketuvatah* — her *ketubah* is considered fully paid. She got 200; she was owed 200. The fact that the property was worth only half what she received is irrelevant — the debt is discharged.

The reverse is then stated: *o shavim matayim be-maneh* — or she sold property worth 200 for only 100. Again, *nigveta ketuvatah* — her *ketubah* is considered fully paid. Even though she undersold and received less cash than the property was worth, she is done. She sold a piece of the estate valued at the full amount of her *ketubah*, and the estate has discharged its obligation in the form of the property transferred, even if she made a bad deal in converting it to cash.

### Oversell Case

The second scenario is different in kind: *hayetah ketuvatah maneh ve-makhra shaveh maneh ve-dinar be-maneh* — her *ketubah* was 100, and she sold a piece of the estate worth 125 for 100. Here, *mekherah batel* — the sale is entirely void. She sold property worth more than her outstanding debt. She was authorized to sell in order to collect what was owed to her, not to sell estate property of greater value. And even if she offers to return the excess — *afilu hi omeret akhzir et ha-dinar la-yorshim* — to give back the 25 to the heirs, whether in cash or by purchasing replacement property for them, the *mishnah* still rules the sale void. She sold property she was not authorized to sell, and that invalidity is not cured by a subsequent offer of restitution.

### Rabban Shimon's View

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel qualifies this last ruling: *le-olam mekhra kayam ad she-tehe sham kedei she-tishtayer ba-sadeh bat tish'ah kabbin* — the sale is always valid unless the overage constitutes a separate and independently viable parcel of land — specifically, a field of nine *kav* (or, for a garden, a half *kav*, and per Rabbi Akiva, a quarter *kav*). His logic is that absolute precision in the size of property sold is not always possible. A seller cannot realistically draw a line through the middle of a field to sell exactly the square footage corresponding to her debt. Therefore, modest overage is acceptable — the law does not require impossible precision.

However, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel draws the line at overage large enough to constitute an independently subdivisible parcel. If the extra portion is sufficiently large that it *could* have been sold as a separate piece of land, then the seller had no excuse for not subdividing and should have done so. The criterion is not monetary value but physical acreage, for the reason that what determines whether a parcel is independently viable is its size, not its per-unit price. Notably, the principle regarding the quality of land (*ziburit*) is not at issue in this context.

### Multiple Sales

The *mishnah* then extends the analysis to a case involving sequential sales: *hayetah ketuvatah arba me'ah zuz u-machru la-zeh be-maneh, ula-zeh be-maneh, ula-acharon yafeh maneh ve-dinar be-maneh* — her *ketubah* was 400 *zuz*, and she sold to one buyer a field worth 100, to a second a field worth 100, to a third a field worth 100, and to a fourth, a field worth 125 for 100. The ruling is *acharon batel ve-shel kulan kayam* — only the last sale is void; all the prior sales are valid. She had a 400 *zuz* debt, she had collected 300 *zuz* worth of legitimate sales, and the final sale exceeded her remaining entitlement of 100 by 25. The invalidity attaches only to the transaction that overstepped her authority, while the preceding sales, which were within her rights, stand.

---

## Undersell/Oversell Analy…

### At Hifsadet Principle

The *gemara* analyzes the rulings of the *mishnah*. The first question is why, when she sells property worth 200 for only 100, her *ketubah* is considered discharged. The answer: *de-amri la at hifsadet* — they say to her, you suffered the loss. The estate delivered to her a piece of property valued at her full *ketubah*; whatever she received in cash for it is her business. She chose to undersell, and the estate has done its part by having property of the requisite value available for her to collect. This also provides a practical incentive: the widow has every reason to ensure she is not underselling. While she may not be motivated to drive the price higher than necessary, she certainly has reason not to be cheated.

### Reverse Question

The *gemara* then asks why the reverse does not apply symmetrically. When she sells property worth 100 for 200 — a genuinely good deal — why can she not argue *ana arvachna* — I only took a piece of the estate worth 100, and the extra 100 I received was the product of my own business acumen? If the standard for underselling is based on the size of the property transferred, why not apply the same logic to overselling, treating the surplus as a personal gain separate from the *ketubah* payment?

### Hakol Leba'al Hama'ot

Rav Nachman citing Rav bar Avuha answers: *kan shana Rabbi, hakol le-ba'al hama'ot* — here the rule is that everything goes to the one with the money. The principle is that when a transaction is conducted on someone else's behalf — when the money in question belongs to the person who sent you to the market — any surplus generated through that transaction accrues to the owner of the money, not to the one conducting the transaction. The widow is not selling her own property; she is selling estate property, collecting against a debt. The extra money she received above the property's value is part of the price realized for the estate's asset, and it goes toward payment of her *ketubah* debt. She cannot claim it as a personal windfall.

### Baraita: Fixed Amounts

A *baraita* is cited that complicates this picture. The case concerns an agent sent to purchase goods: *hosifu lo achat yeteirah* — if the seller added an extra item. Rabbi Yehuda says it belongs to the agent — *hakol la-shaliach* — it was a gift to him personally. Rabbi Yossi says they split it — *cholkin*. But a separate *baraita* records Rabbi Yossi as saying *hakol le-ba'al hama'ot* — all of it goes to the one who provided the money.

### Rami's Resolution

Rami bar Chama resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya — kan be-davar she-yesh lo kitzva, kan be-davar she-ein lo kitzva* — there is no difficulty. The cases differ. When there is a fixed, standard price for the item — a fixed quantity at a fixed rate — and the seller throws in an extra unit, that extra is a gift. It is not part of the agreed transaction; it is a bonus extended to the agent personally, and the agent may keep it or share it. But when the amount is not fixed — when the quantity or price is negotiable — then the extra is not a gift but part of the negotiated transaction, and it accrues to the person whose money funded the purchase.

### Land Sales Application

The application to the widow's case is then made explicit. The sale of land is always *ein lo kitzva* — there is no fixed price. Land is always subject to negotiation; there is no standard per-unit price at which real estate trades. Therefore, any surplus price she receives above the assessed value of the property is not a personal bonus to her — it is part of the negotiated price for that piece of land. The money all goes toward discharge of the *ketubah* debt. Accordingly, when she sells property worth 100 for 200, the entire 200 is treated as having been received by the estate against her *ketubah* claim, and her *ketubah* is discharged. Rav Pappa states the *halakha*: for items with a fixed price, they split the bonus between the agent and the owner; for items without a fixed price, *hakol le-ba'al hama'ot* — it all goes to the party who provided the money.

---

## Agent Excess Case

### Agent Excess Q

The *gemara* now poses a question that circles back to the *mishnah*'s case of the widow who oversold. The scenario: *amri lei zavin li litkha* — you instruct your agent to go purchase for you a *litkha*, half a *kor* of grain. *Ve-azil ve-zavin leh kura* — and he goes and purchases a full *kor*. What is the legal status of this transaction?

Two possibilities are presented: *mosif al devarav havei* — perhaps he is considered to have merely added to his instructions. On this reading, the first half of the purchase — the *litkha* — was conducted as a valid agent acting within his authority, and that half is a binding transaction. The second half he exceeded his mandate, and on that portion he acted on his own account. Alternatively, *ma'avir al devarav havei* — perhaps by buying more than he was told, he has completely disregarded his instructions, and is therefore considered to have acted entirely on his own initiative for the *entire* purchase. On this reading, even the first *litkha* is not a valid agency transaction, and *ve-litkha nami lo kani* — he has not even validly acquired the half he was authorized to acquire.

### Me'ilah Principle

To resolve this question, the *gemara* turns to the laws of *me'ilah* — misappropriation of consecrated property.
