The principle of *me'ilah* applies only *be-shogeg*, unwittingly; one who knowingly benefits from *hekdesh* property does not bring a *korban me'ilah* though other penalties may apply. One of the distinctive features of *me'ilah* is that it is among the few areas in which we apply *yeish shliach le-davar aveirah* — an agent's unwitting transgression on behalf of an equally unwitting principal is attributed to the principal. If both the one who sent the agent and the agent are *shogeg*, the *me'ilah* is treated as though committed by the sender.

### Meat Story

The relevant case from *me'ilah* law: *amar ba'al ha-bayit li-shlucho* — a homeowner says to his agent, *ten lahem chaticha la-orchim* — give each guest one piece of meat. The meat is *kodashim*. The agent instead says to the guests: *telu shtayim* — each take two. The guests then take three pieces each. The ruling: *kulam ma'alu* — all of them have committed *me'ilah*. The homeowner is liable for the first piece, since that was within his agency. The agent is liable for the second piece, since that was on his own initiative. The guests are liable for the third piece, since that exceeded even what the agent authorized.

### Attribution Distinction

The *gemara* then explains precisely when this apportionment applies. The case assumes that the agent explicitly distinguished between the two pieces: *telu achat mi-da'ato shel ba'al ha-bayit ve-achat mi-da'ati* — take one because the owner authorizes it, and take another because I say so. That explicit attribution is what creates the clean division of liability. If, by contrast, the agent simply said *telu shtayim* without any such distinction — presenting the double allocation as the owner's instruction — he would be treated as having completely overridden his agency, and the homeowner would bear no *me'ilah* liability at all, even for the first piece. The agent, by claiming to act for the owner while wildly exceeding his mandate, is considered to have been acting entirely on his own initiative. The *gemara* thus establishes: when an agent straightforwardly adds to what he was told, the first part remains valid agency and the excess is on his own account. But when the agent presents his excessive action as authorized — *ma'avir al devarav* — he has abandoned his agency entirely and acts solely for himself.

### Proof from Mishnah

The *gemara* now attempts to bring proof from our *mishnah* to resolve the original question. The case is: *hayetah ketuvatah maneh ve-makhra shaveh maneh ve-dinar be-maneh* — her *ketubah* was 100 and she sold property worth 125 for 100. The *mishnah* rules *mekherah batel* — the entire sale is void. The *gemara* reads this as: she actually sold the property worth 125 for 125 — the phrase *be-maneh* means she sold it in exchange for the discharge of her 100 *maneh* debt — and the question is why the sale is entirely void rather than valid for the first 100 worth of property.

The *gemara* suggests: *mai lav de-zavin shaveh maneh ve-dinar be-maneh ve-dinar* — is this not a case where she sold a property worth 125 for 125, and the only issue is that she sold 25 more than she was authorized to? If the principle were *mosif al devarav* — exceeding one's authority only invalidates the excess — then the sale of the first 100 should remain valid. Yet the *mishnah* rules the entire sale void. This would appear to prove that exceeding one's authority — *ma'avir al devarav* — invalidates the entire transaction, including the portion that was within the agent's authority.

### Rav Huna's Correction

Rav Huna son of Rav Natan rejects this proof. The *mishnah* is not discussing a case where she sold the property at fair value and simply took an oversized parcel. Rather, *be-doshaya* — the case in the *mishnah* is one of underselling: the property was worth 125 and she sold it for only 100. The reason the sale is void is not that she overreached her agency by taking too large a parcel at a fair price, but rather that she undersold a piece of property she was not fully authorized to sell, and the orphans are left worse off. The voiding of the sale is therefore a remedy for the loss caused to the orphans by the inadequate price, not a ruling about agency doctrine. Consequently, our *mishnah* provides no proof one way or the other about the question of whether *mosif al devarav* leaves the authorized portion intact.

### Unresolved Q

The *gemara* thus leaves the original question unresolved. If the widow sold a piece of property of appropriate size at a fair price, but the parcel happened to be slightly larger than the precise value of her outstanding *ketubah* — in a manner that exceeds her authorized mandate but does not prejudice the estate through underselling — it remains uncertain whether the portion she was authorized to sell is valid while only the overage is void, or whether the entire transaction is invalidated because she exceeded her authority from the outset. This question continues into the following daf.

---

---

# Ketubot 99

## Agency Boundaries

### Agent Mandate

The *gemara* on 99a opens with a question that sits at the heart of agency law: under what conditions is a *shaliach* considered to be operating within the terms of his mandate, and at what point has he gone rogue and acted independently? The practical stakes are significant. When an agent buys or sells property on behalf of the person who appointed him, the question of whether those transactions are binding depends entirely on whether he was acting as an agent or on his own account. If he was told to sell land worth a hundred and he sold land worth fifty, or conversely he was told to sell fifty and he sold a hundred, do we say there is at least a zone of overlap in which he was genuinely functioning as an agent? Or do we say that because he deviated from his instructions, the entire transaction is void and he was acting only for himself?

The question matters not only for the validity of commercial transactions but also for the parties' exposure to liability. The person who appointed the agent expects that what was done in his name is binding on him — but only to the extent he authorized it. The agent expects that his actions carry legal weight as an extension of his principal. When those expectations diverge, the *gemara* must draw lines.

It is worth noting that related discussions appear in tractate *Kiddushin*, where a *shaliach* is sent to betroth a woman for a specified sum of money and a dispute arises over whether the agent was authorized to act in a general or a precisely specified capacity. The underlying conceptual tension is the same, though the *sugyot* are scattered.

### Meila & Agency

The *gemara* draws in the laws of *meila* — misuse of *hekdesh*, sanctified property — as a productive test case for the limits of agency. Normally, the rule is *ein shaliach l'dvar aveira*, that an agent cannot be used to perform a transgression on one's behalf. But *meila* is an exception: the law of *yesh shaliach l'dvar aveira* applies here, at least in cases of unwitting misuse. If both the sender and the agent are unaware that the object is *hekdesh*, then the person who sent the agent is the one deemed to have committed *meila*.

This makes *meila* cases a particularly sharp testing ground: who bears the culpability depends directly on whose agency was operative at the moment of the misuse. If the agent deviated from his instructions, the question of whether he was still acting for the sender — or had stepped outside the bounds of agency entirely — determines which of them, or both, has transgressed.

### Overselling/Underselling

The concrete scenario that sets up the discussion involves an agent authorized to sell (or buy) a specific quantity or value and who either exceeds or falls short of that authorization. You tell your agent: sell a half-acre field. He sells an acre. Or: go buy fifty *dinar* worth of goods, and he buys a hundred. In each direction, the question is the same — is there a binding overlap, or is the deviation total? The *gemara* will work through these variations systematically, using both the case of the woman collecting her *ketuba* and the *meila* cases to probe the answer.

---

## Woman's Selling Power

### Woman as Agent

The *gemara* turns to the *mishna* of our *daf*, which concerns a woman who sells from the estate of her deceased husband's heirs in order to collect the outstanding balance of her *ketuba*. She was not formally appointed by anyone, yet she is treated as a kind of implicit agent — appointed, as it were, by rabbinic authority or by the logic of the *beit din* — acting on behalf of the orphans, even though they may not wish her to be doing so. The *mishna*'s case involves her selling property, and the question is whether her sale is binding.

One might ask why the *gemara* frames her role in terms of *shlichut* at all, since a creditor does not act as agent but simply seizes collateral through the court. The answer lies in the language the *mishna* uses: she sells *shelo b'beit din*, outside of court — language that is inapplicable to a creditor who exercises a lien through formal judicial process. Moreover, if she sells a piece of land worth two hundred for three hundred, the excess goes toward satisfying her debt. A creditor who seizes property and then sells it at a profit does not thereby reduce the underlying debt. The proceeds of her sale go to pay off what she is owed. That structure is characteristic of agency, not of simple debt-collection. The *gemara* therefore conceptualizes her as a *shaliach* of the heirs — a somewhat paradoxical framing, given that the heirs certainly did not appoint her — but that is the conceptual framework the *gemara* adopts.

This arrangement is particularly associated with *mezonot*, the ongoing obligation to provide for one's widow from the estate. Rather than going to court once to collect a fixed sum, she may periodically need to sell off small portions of the estate to cover her living expenses. This recurring character of the transaction explains why the *mishna* thinks in terms of agency rather than one-time judicial seizure.

### Overselling vs Underpric…

The *mishna* contains a case that the *gemara* initially understands as involving a sale of too much land: she was only authorized to sell enough to satisfy one hundred *maneh* of outstanding debt, yet she sold property worth one hundred and twenty-five for one hundred and twenty-five. The *mishna* declares this void. The *gemara*'s first reading is that this proves something about the rule for *shlichut*: that a *shaliach* who oversteps her mandate is treated as having acted entirely on her own — not merely for the excess, but for the whole transaction.

Rav Huna son of Rav Natan then reframes the case entirely. The *mishna* is not talking about overselling in terms of quantity; rather, she sold property worth one hundred and twenty-five for only one hundred. The problem is not that she sold too much — it is that she undersold. She had no right to sell at a loss that would be borne by the estate, and that is why the sale is void. This reading changes the evidentiary import of the case dramatically.

### Two Mishna Cases

Once the end of the *mishna* is read carefully, Rav Huna's reframing becomes not only plausible but necessary. The *mishna* closes with an explicit case: her *ketuba* was four hundred *zuz*; she sold to each of three buyers for one hundred *maneh* each; and to the last buyer she sold property worth one hundred and twenty-five for one hundred. The *mishna* declares: the last sale is void, the earlier ones are binding. That closing case is unambiguously a case of underselling. The *gemara* therefore reasons: *mid'seifa bid'ozil ha'rei reisha bid'lo ozil* — since the end of the *mishna* is clearly about underselling, the beginning need not be about underselling at all. The beginning must therefore be about a different problem: she sold more land than she was entitled to sell — namely, property worth one hundred and twenty-five when her outstanding debt was only one hundred. The two cases are thus distinguished: the first case is about exceeding the scope of her authorization by quantity, the second is about underselling at a price that shifts the loss onto the estate.

---

## Underpricing Principle

### Woman Takes Loss

Having established that the *mishna*'s first and last cases are distinct, the *gemara* now confronts an apparent difficulty. The first case of the *mishna* includes the scenario where her *ketuba* was two hundred and she sold property worth two hundred for one hundred — that is, she undersold it — and the *mishna* declares her *ketuba* satisfied. How can this be valid if, as the last case shows, underselling is void?

The answer is a fundamental distinction between who bears the loss. In the first case, the outstanding debt is two hundred, the land was worth two hundred, and she sold it for one hundred. She undersold, but there is no injustice to the estate: she simply takes the hit herself. The estate does not suffer. The property she sold was worth what she was owed, and the shortfall in the sale price is simply deducted from the debt as if she had been paid the full value. She pocketed one hundred but we consider her *ketuba* as having been fully paid. She hurt herself, not the heirs, and therefore the sale stands.

This principle works because there is no *ona'ah* by *karka* — no law of overcharging or undercharging that voids a land transaction on the basis of price discrepancy alone. Land has no fixed market price in the way that movable goods do, and therefore the normal *ona'ah* rules that can void a sale of chattel have no application here. If a sale of land is going to be voided, it must be for a different reason — such as the agent acting beyond the scope of her authority, or causing injury to a party who did not consent to the loss.

Here, no party is being injured against their will. The heirs receive what they would have received had she sold at full value: the debt is paid. The woman absorbs the difference. The sale is therefore binding.

### Estate Takes Loss

The last case of the *mishna* presents the contrast. Her *ketuba* was four hundred *zuz*. She has already sold three parcels at one hundred each, leaving one hundred outstanding. She then sells a parcel worth one hundred and twenty-five for one hundred. This is underselling — but now there is no room for her to absorb the loss. Her remaining debt is only one hundred; there is no excess debt against which the extra twenty-five can be offset. The estate — meaning the orphans and heirs — must take the loss. They receive property worth one hundred and twenty-five, and in exchange they have satisfied only one hundred of her debt. The remaining twenty-five in value has simply been taken from them.

Because the estate bears the loss rather than the woman, the sale is void. The heirs can say: you were empowered to act as our agent in selling property to satisfy your debt; you were not empowered to cause us financial injury in the process. That is the principle: *litkunei shidartich velo la'avutei* — I sent you for my benefit, not to harm me — a formulation the *gemara* will deploy again later in the context of a general agent. Since the estate takes the hit, the sale is void.

### Gezeira Explained

The *gemara* now pushes further and asks: why does the *mishna* need to tell us the last case separately? Is the principle not already implicit in the first case? The *gemara* answers that there is an important *chiddush* embedded in the *mishna*'s structure, and it involves a *gezeira* — a protective rabbinic safeguard.

Consider what would happen if the *mishna* only told us the first case and the last case, without implicitly authorizing the middle cases — that is, sales made when her *ketuba* is partially outstanding, say a parcel worth one hundred and twenty-five sold for one hundred, where she still has, say, two hundred in remaining debt. In that middle scenario, she could take the hit: the extra twenty-five would simply be deducted from her outstanding balance. The sale would be valid and she would absorb the shortfall.

One might have thought we should void even the middle sales, on the grounds that allowing them would *eventually* lead to the final scenario — where there is no longer any remaining debt against which to offset the loss. If we permit middle-case underselling on the theory that she will take the hit, buyers may come to rely on this principle; and when she finally reaches the last sale, where there is no hit for her to take, someone might mistakenly think that sale is valid too. To prevent that confusion, perhaps we should void all undersales uniformly.

The *gemara* rejects this reasoning: *nigzor mana rishon atu mana acharon* — do we make a *gezeira* voiding the first-hundred case because it might lead to the last-hundred case? No. The *chiddush* of the *mishna* is precisely that we do *not* make this *gezeira*. The middle sales are valid because in those cases she genuinely takes the loss, and the estate is not harmed. Only when the estate would bear the loss — in the final sale — does the transaction become void. The *mishna* is teaching us that we do not collapse all undersales into a single category; we assess each on its own terms.

---

## Mosif Doctrine

### Doing More

The *gemara* now abstracts to the general principle governing an agent who does *more* than he was authorized to do. The term is *mosif al devarav* — he adds beyond his mandate. The example: you told your agent to go sell a half-acre field, and he went and sold a full acre. In this case the *gemara* treats the agent's action as divisible: the half-acre that was within the scope of the mandate is a valid sale; the additional half-acre, which exceeded the mandate, was his own independent action. He was *mosif*, not *maavir* — adding on top of the authorized act, rather than going entirely rogue. The base transaction is therefore binding.

This is importantly different from *maavir al devarav*, where the agent steps entirely outside his authorization such that the entire act is his own and none of it is binding as agency. When he merely adds, there is genuine overlap between what was authorized and what he did; that overlap portion retains its status as *shlichut*.

Returning to the woman and her *ketuba*: if she sold one hundred and twenty-five for one hundred and twenty-five, the part of the sale up to her authorized one hundred would be valid under this *mosif* principle. It is only the extra twenty-five that was done on her own. The reason the first case of the *mishna* is void is not, therefore, that the *mosif* principle fails — it is that the *mishna* as Rav Huna reads it is not a *mosif* case at all, but an underselling case, as discussed above.

### Doing Less

The harder question is the reverse: what happens when the agent does *less* than he was asked? You told him to sell an acre and he sold a half-acre. There is no clean overlap in the sense of inclusion: he did not do part of what you asked and add something else. He simply did less. Is the half-acre sale binding as *shlichut* for that amount?

The *gemara* frames this as a genuine question with competing considerations. On one hand, the agent might say to the sender: I did you a favor. If you had needed all the cash right away, you would have needed to sell the whole acre; but by selling only half, I left you the option to come into funds another way and retain the rest of your land. Land, after all, is the primary source of wealth; no one sells it unless in genuine financial distress. To sell half is to preserve the other half against future necessity.

On the other hand, the sender might respond: *lo nicha li d'lifush shetarei ilavai* — I do not want to accumulate a history of multiple sales documents against me. To sell piecemeal is to create a record of repeated transactions, which in the context of this society signals a pattern of financial difficulty, a kind of bad credit history. The owner may well have preferred a single large transaction to multiple small ones — whether for reputational reasons, for the practical advantage of a better price on a larger parcel, or simply because he specified what he wanted and wants his instructions followed. The *gemara* leaves the tension explicit: when an agent does less than authorized, and there is a real consequential difference between what was done and what was asked — not merely a question of quantity — the question of whether the agent was acting within *shlichut* is genuinely unresolved.

---

## Shirt Purchase Case

### Meila Shirt Example

Rabbi Chanina of Sura introduces a *meila* case that places the question of underdoing in sharp relief. A man gives his *shaliach* a golden *dinar* and says: go buy me a shirt. Unbeknownst to either of them, the *dinar* was *hekdesh* — consecrated property. The agent takes the *dinar*, goes to the market, and with three *sela* — half the *dinar* — buys a shirt; with the other three *sela* he buys a *talit*, a cloak, on his own initiative.

The ruling: *shneihem ma'alu* — both of them committed *meila*. The sender committed *meila* in connection with the shirt, because the agent was acting on his behalf when he bought it. The agent committed *meila* in connection with the *talit*, because that purchase was entirely his own — the sender never authorized it. For the *talit*, the agent was operating outside *shlichut*, so the sender bears no culpability there; the agent does. For the shirt, the agent was operating within *shlichut*, so the sender is implicated.

But notice: the sender said to buy a shirt worth six *sela*, and the agent bought a shirt worth only three *sela*. He did less than he was asked. And yet he is still considered to have been acting as *shaliach* for that purchase. The *gemara* will now examine what exactly this case proves.

### Shirt Dispute

Reading the case straightforwardly: the sender asked for a six-*sela* shirt and received a three-*sela* shirt. Tanna Kamma holds that the agent was nevertheless acting within *shlichut* for the shirt purchase — the sender committed *meila*. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *chaluka di-veina lei sagi u-ma'alya ve-ayteit li chaluka katina ve-ra* — I wanted a large, superior garment and you brought me a small, inferior one. Since what was bought was categorically different from what was requested — not just a lesser quantity of the same thing, but an inferior object — Rabbi Yehuda holds the agent was not acting on behalf of the sender at all. The sender did not commit *meila*; only the agent did.

This maps directly onto the question of whether doing less constitutes valid *shlichut*. If I ask for a six-*sela* shirt and I receive a three-*sela* shirt, have I received what I asked for in diminished form, or have I received something different? Tanna Kamma says the former; Rabbi Yehuda says the latter.

### Sale vs Inferiority

The *gemara* then reframes the debate. Perhaps the dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda is not actually about whether a cheaper shirt counts as doing less of what you were asked. Perhaps everyone agrees that doing less of the same thing does not break *shlichut*. The actual scenario is: the shirt was on sale. The agent went to the market, found a six-*sela* shirt available for three *sela*, bought it at that bargain price, and then used the remaining three *sela* to buy a *talit* for himself.

Under this reading, Tanna Kamma says the agent did exactly what he was asked — he obtained the requested shirt — and did so efficiently, with funds left over. He was acting within *shlichut* for the shirt, and on his own for the *talit*. Rabbi Yehuda dissents: even if the shirt was on sale, the agent should not have pocketed the savings or spent them on a *talit*. Instead, he should have used the full six *sela* to obtain an even finer shirt — since if the shirt that cost three *sela* was worth six *sela* at full price, spending six *sela* could have obtained something worth twelve. The agent was therefore not fully operating as *shaliach* even for the shirt; he should have maximized the sender's benefit with the full sum entrusted to him.

Under this reframing, the underlying question about *doing less* — asking an agent to do one hundred and having him do fifty — is not actually resolved by this *beraita*. Both Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda might agree that when an agent does less of the same thing, the *shlichut* for the portion he did accomplish is binding. Their dispute is about a more specific scenario: whether buying a shirt at a bargain price and saving the rest (rather than spending the remainder on a better shirt) constitutes faithful execution of the mandate.

### Legumes Case

Rabbi Yehuda himself concedes the point in a different scenario: *modeh Rabbi Yehuda b'kitnit she-shneihem ma'alu* — Rabbi Yehuda agrees that both committed *meila* in the case of legumes. If the agent was told to buy legumes and bought half the quantity, he agrees the sender is implicated. Why? Because with legumes, it is purely a question of quantity. There is no question of inferior quality or missed opportunity to buy a better product. The agent bought legumes — the right commodity — just less of them. In that case, even Rabbi Yehuda concedes that the portion he did purchase was done within *shlichut*, and the sender therefore committed *meila* for that amount.

This distinction is then examined further. The *gemara* asks: what exactly is the case with the legumes? If produce is sold by rough estimate rather than by precise measure, then presumably buying more would have yielded a better deal — and one could ask why Rabbi Yehuda does not say here too that the agent should have spent the full sum to maximize the benefit. Rav Pappa answers: the case is in a place where legumes are sold by precise, individual measure — *de'amar leh kaneh kaneh b'peruta*, each unit costs a fixed *peruta*, with no bulk discount and no estimation. There is therefore no possible advantage to be gained by spending more, and no argument that the agent should have done otherwise. In that context, there is no ground for Rabbi Yehuda to dispute, and the half-purchase is clearly within *shlichut*.

The upshot of all this is: when the deviation from instructions is purely quantitative and there is no meaningful difference between the partial act and the full act (other than scale), *shlichut* applies to the portion accomplished. When the deviation is qualitative — a different object, a different grade, a different kind of transaction — the question is harder, and that is where the debate between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda, as the *gemara* ultimately understands it, is located.

---

## Agent Discretion

### One vs Many Buyers

The *gemara* raises a new scenario that shifts the focus from quantity and quality to the manner of executing a mandate. You tell your agent: sell this piece of land to someone. You do not specify *not* to sell it to multiple buyers — you simply say to find a buyer. The agent proceeds to sell it to two or even more buyers, dividing the parcel. Is the sale binding?

Rav Huna holds: *amar l'echad v'lo l'shnayim* — when I say "one," I mean one and not two. Saying "find someone to buy this" implicitly limits the agent to a single transaction. Rav Chisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna disagree: *afilu l'echad v'afilu l'me'ah* — even one hundred buyers would be acceptable. Saying "one" does not exclude others; it is simply an indefinite reference, not a restriction.

### Mistakes vs Latitude

When Rav Nachman visited Sura and Rav Chisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna came before him, they posed this very question. Rav Nachman responded in line with the more permissive position: *l'echad v'afilu l'shnayim, l'echad v'afilu l'me'ah* — one is not a limitation, and selling to multiple buyers is within the agent's discretion.

They then pressed him: so you are giving the agent broad latitude — would you therefore also say that if the agent made an outright mistake, such as underselling the land significantly, that too would be binding? Rav Nachman drew a sharp line: *d'b'ta'ei shaliach lo ka'amina* — I am not talking about mistakes. Discretion about the manner of execution — one buyer or several, a particular day or another — is one thing. An outright financial error that injures the sender is quite another. Latitude in execution does not extend to mistakes that fall outside any reasonable range of what the sender could have contemplated.

### Owner vs Agent

The questioners then note a seeming tension: you said that if the agent makes a mistake it is void — but we know that there is no *ona'ah* by *karka*! Real estate has no fixed price, and therefore the rules of *ona'ah* — which void a transaction when the price deviates by more than one-sixth from the fair market value — simply do not apply to land. If there is no fixed price, what does it mean for an agent to have made a "mistake"?

The *gemara* answers: *hani mili heicha de-ta'ah ba'al ha-bayit* — the *ona'ah* exemption applies when the *owner* himself buys or sells. Whatever price the owner accepts, that is a legitimate price for the land; there is nothing to void. But *aval shaliach* — an agent is different. When the owner sends a *shaliach*, he sends him with the instruction *litkunei shidartich velo la'avutei* — I sent you to benefit me, not to harm me. The *shaliach* therefore must operate within a reasonable range of the owner's intent. What the owner could do freely on his own account, the agent cannot do if it amounts to acting against the owner's interests.

### Trumah Range

The *gemara* now cites a proof from *trumah* — the priestly portion separated from grain — to demonstrate that acting within the owner's range is the standard of valid *shlichut*, while acting outside it is not. The principle is established in a *tanna'itic* source: if the owner tells his *shaliach* to separate *trumah* from his grain, the agent should ideally follow the owner's usual practice. If he does not know the owner's practice, he defaults to the middle standard of one in fifty — that is, two percent.

If the agent takes one in forty (slightly more generous) or one in sixty (slightly more conservative), his *trumah* is still valid — those figures represent the edges of the normal range: a generous person gives one in forty, a stingy person gives one in sixty. The agent has deviated somewhat from the middle, but he is still within the normal range of practice, and therefore the *trumah* is binding.

By contrast, if the *owner himself* separated *trumah* at one in ten — five percent, well above the normal range — his *trumah* is nevertheless valid: *taram ba'al ha-bayit afilu echad me'asara, trumato trumah*. The owner acting for himself is not constrained to the normal range; whatever he takes is a legitimate exercise of his ownership. There is no *ona'ah* standard that governs his own action.

This distinction is precisely the parallel to land sales: the owner acting on his own is not limited by a "normal range" of acceptable price; whatever he agrees to is binding. The *shaliach*, however, must operate within the range of what the owner would have sanctioned. Deviating beyond that range — whether in the context of *trumah* or in the context of land sales — takes the act outside the bounds of *shlichut* and renders it void.

### Conclusion

The *gemara* concludes by returning to the *mishna*'s scenario: the woman who sold four hundred *zuz* worth of land in pieces — three parcels for one hundred each and a final parcel worth one hundred and twenty-five for one hundred. The earlier sales are binding; the last is void. But one might ask: if she was supposed to sell on behalf of the estate, why is it permissible for her to sell in multiple transactions, piecemeal, when we have seen that multiple sales may not be in the interest of the seller?

Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi answers: *b'katinei* — these are small, scattered plots of land. There is no single large parcel to sell as a unit. Under those conditions, the only available method of collection is to sell the small plots as they come, and the concern about multiple sales documents and the cumulative record of transactions simply does not arise as a practical matter.

The broader principle that emerges from the *gemara*'s full discussion is this: agency requires operating within reasonable bounds of the owner's intent. An agent who does more than asked may still be valid for the overlapping portion of the mandate. An agent who does less raises a harder question — with the answer depending on whether the deviation is merely quantitative or qualitative, whether the agent's judgment can plausibly be said to serve the owner's interests, and whether the act falls within a normal range of what the owner would have countenanced. What the owner may do freely for himself, the agent may not do arbitrarily; the agent is always constrained by the implicit instruction: I sent you to benefit me, not to harm me.

---

---

# Ketubot 100

## Widow's Sale & Pricing

### Memorial Remarks

Before turning to the daf, we pause to note the passing of Belda Lindenbaum. Though her funeral was a small, family-only gathering — itself a testament to her values, as it could easily have drawn tens of thousands — her impact on *klal Yisrael* was enormous. Countless women have posted tributes describing how every Torah institution they benefited from was built through her vision and philanthropy. She demonstrated what guided, purposeful generosity can do to reshape the face of the Jewish community. She was 76. May her memory be a blessing.

### Dinar Correction

We pick up with the *mishnah* on 99b, which deals with a widow selling off estate property in order to collect her *ketubah*. Before proceeding, a correction is necessary regarding a point raised in the previous daf. When the *Gemara* spoke of a widow selling something worth a *maneh* and a *dinar* for only a *maneh*, the earlier discussion incorrectly assumed this referred to a golden *dinar* — worth 25 *zuz* — making the discrepancy roughly 20%. Rashi, both in the previous *sugya* and here, makes clear that we are dealing with a silver *dinar*, which is essentially a single *zuz* — representing a difference of approximately 1%. This correction is significant not only for today's daf but for all the preceding discussion about the widow over- or under-selling estate property. The two scenarios the *Gemara* addressed — selling something worth 101 for 100, or selling property worth 101 for 101 — reflect a trivially small, roughly 1% discrepancy. The question of how much latitude to grant a representative must be understood against that backdrop.

---

## Mishna on Court Sale

### Judges' Assessment

The *mishnah* introduces a new scenario: *shum ha-dayanim* — the judges themselves assess and sell the estate property. The *mishnah* states: *she-pichesu shtu'sh o hosifu shtu'sh* — if they were off by a *shtu'sh*, the sale is void, *mekhan batel*.

The *shtu'sh* (a sixth) is ordinarily the threshold for *ona'ah* — the laws of overcharging or undercharging that can void a commercial sale. However, there is no *ona'ah* for *karka'ot*, real property. So if an ordinary individual were selling his own land at a loss, the rules of *ona'ah* would simply not apply. The reason the court's sale can be voided is different: the court is not the owner selling on its own behalf, but a representative acting for the orphans. Just as the previous *mishnah* discussed the widow's role as a *shliach* of the orphans, here the court acts in that representative capacity. When a representative steps too far outside the bounds of proper valuation — selling at a discount of more than a sixth — they are understood to have exceeded their authority, and the sale does not stand.

The implicit logic of the *mishnah* is therefore that up to a sixth, the sale remains binding; beyond a sixth, the representatives have stepped outside their authorized role. This stands in notable contrast to the widow's case: given the correction noted above, even a 1% underprice voids her sale. The court, by contrast, is given considerably more latitude.

### Rabban Shimon's Position

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* disagrees: *mekhan kayam* — even if they are off by more than a sixth, the sale stands. His reasoning is captured in the phrase *she-im ken mah ko'ach beis din yafeh* — "if so, what power does the court have?" This can be read as a policy argument: if every court decision is subject to reassessment and reversal, the authority of the *beis din* is fundamentally undermined. Alternatively, one can invoke the principle of *hefker beis din hefker* — the court has the institutional authority to define legal realities through its rulings, and its acts are therefore binding by virtue of that authority alone.

A pointed question emerges from *Tosafos*: even if we accept *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*'s position that the sale is not reversed, must the excess be returned? In ordinary *ona'ah* cases, there are two distinct questions — whether the sale is void, and whether even a binding sale requires returning the overage. *Tosafos* asks the same question here: perhaps the court's action stands as a valid sale, yet the party who received the benefit of the mispricing must still repay the difference. Whether concern for undermining court authority extends even to requiring repayment of the overage is not resolved from the *mishnah* itself, though the plain reading appears to be that the sale is simply final.

### Igeret Bikoret

The *mishnah* concludes with an important addendum, attributed presumably to the *chachamim*: *im asu igeret bikoret beineihem* — if they produced a *writ of assessment* among themselves — then *afilu machru shaveh maneh be-masatayim*, even if they sold something worth 100 for 200, or 200 for 100, *mekhan kayam*, the sale is entirely binding. Even the *chachamim*, who ordinarily require voiding a sale that is off by more than a sixth, agree that when this document was produced, the sale stands regardless of the discrepancy.

The precise meaning of *beineihem* — literally "between them" — is somewhat puzzling. *Tosafos* suggests it might refer to a letter passing between courts, though that does not fit the context naturally. The phrase most likely refers to the members of the *beis din* producing an official written assessment among themselves. But what precisely is this *igeret bikoret*, and why should its existence render even a wildly mispriced sale binding?

### Rashi on Hachrazah

Rashi rejects the reading that the *igeret bikoret* simply means the court commissioned an assessor and wrote up a report. He explains: *u-leshon bikoret she-mevakrin oto bnei adam al yedei ha-hachrazah* — the *bikoret* refers to a process by which the public examines and evaluates the property through public announcement. In other words, the *igeret bikoret* does not mean a written appraisal but rather a public auction. Just as estates in later periods required advertisements and open bidding processes, the *hachrazah* ensures that the widest possible pool of buyers has had the opportunity to evaluate and bid on the property.

The logic follows naturally: if you have done everything humanly possible to achieve market price — made public announcement, held an open process, and let the market speak — then whatever price resulted *is* the market price by definition. Even if it deviates dramatically from a prior estimate, the process itself validates the outcome.

### Land Valuation Question

This raises a sharp question: if it is so difficult to establish an objective value for land, how can we meaningfully speak of a 1% underprice as rendering the widow's sale void? The gap between 100 and 101 *dinarim* seems impossible to detect with any precision, given that land valuation inherently involves a range. The answer, while not fully resolved by the *Gemara*, likely parallels what the *Gemara* will discuss regarding *terumah*: there is an accepted range of reasonable prices, and the widow's sale would only be void if it fell below even the lowest end of that range. This is admittedly speculative, but the need for some such framework is clear. Tellingly, the formal exclusion of land from *ona'ah* (*eino la-karka'ot*) itself reflects the impossibility of setting a precise value — which makes the standard applied to the widow's sale all the more noteworthy.

---

## Shaliach Classification

### Shaliach Category

The *Gemara* now pivots from the specific cases of the widow and the court to a broader question about the law of agency: *iba'ya lehu, shaliach ke-man?* — into which category does an ordinary *shaliach*, an agent, fall? We now have two clearly defined poles. The *almanah*, the widow, is held to a near-zero tolerance standard: even a 1% underprice voids her sale. The *beis din* is given substantially more room: up to a sixth off, the sale remains valid. When someone is simply appointed as an agent to sell property on another's behalf, which standard applies?

### Rava & R. Shmuel Dispute

The *Gemara* records a dispute in the name of Rav Nachman. *Rava amar Rav Nachman: shaliach ke-dayanim* — the *shaliach* is like the court. The parallel reasoning is: *ma dayanim lo le-didhu, af shaliach nami lo le-didei* — just as judges sell for the benefit of others with no personal stake in the outcome, so too an agent is acting for someone else's account with no vested interest of his own. That disinterested posture warrants the same latitude as the court: as long as the sale is not more than a sixth off, it stands.

*Rav Shmuel bar Bisna amar Rav Nachman: ke-almanah* — the *shaliach* is like the widow, and even a trivial underprice voids the sale. The reasoning here: *mah almanah yechidah, af shaliach yechidah* — the widow is an individual, and so is the *shaliach*. The strict standard applied to individuals is the baseline; it is only the *beis din*, as an institutional body of multiple judges — *de-rabbim ninhu* — that earns the relaxed standard. Whether the leniency derives from the collective nature of *beis din* or from its special institutional authority, a single individual acting as agent shares neither of those qualities and must be held to the individual standard.

There is another angle on the widow's case: one might suspect that she has a personal incentive to undersell, whether to conclude the sale quickly or even to arrange a side deal at the buyer's expense. The court has no such incentive. Does the *shaliach* resemble the court in that respect? One could argue he does — he has no personal stake in a lower price. But against that, he is enough self-motivated in accepting the agency that greater precision can be demanded of him. The *Gemara* does not fully adjudicate these competing intuitions, but they frame why the question is genuinely difficult.

### Shaliach Like Widow

*Ve-hilchasa: shaliach ke-almanah* — the ruling is that the *shaliach* is treated like the widow, and even a tiny underprice voids the sale.

### Paradox of Benefit

This ruling sounds harsh, but there is a striking irony embedded in it that works to the seller's advantage. Precisely because the *shaliach*'s sale is void at even the slightest underprice — and because there is no *ona'ah* for *karka'ot* when one sells for oneself — a seller who routes his land sale through an agent gains a protection unavailable to someone selling directly. If the agent gets even a dollar less than the property's value, the seller can void the transaction entirely. If you sell your own land, no *ona'ah* applies and you have no remedy at all for a below-market sale.

The asymmetry is interesting in the other direction too: if the *shaliach* oversells — gets more than the market value — there is no reason to void the transaction. There is no *ona'ah* for land, and the seller is perfectly happy to receive more. So the rule that the *shaliach* is like the *almanah* only cuts in favor of the seller when the price was too low; there is nothing in the sources suggesting it would void an oversale, which, as noted, may not be true when *beis din* oversells — since *beis din* represents all parties and cannot legitimately impose an unfair burden on the buyer either.

### Why Be a Shaliach?

One might reasonably wonder: given how easily a *shaliach*'s act can be invalidated, why would anyone agree to serve as an agent? And from the buyer's side, how does commerce function if a transaction can always be undone by the seller claiming the agent underpriced? The answer is partly pragmatic: in the ancient world of large landholders, managing every transaction personally was not possible, and agents — much like lawyers handling deals today — were a practical necessity. If a buyer wants security, he needs to deal with someone who genuinely holds full authorization; the law is simply clear about what that authorization entails. The business reality meant that agency relationships were understood and accepted as such.

---

## Terumah Comparison

### Terumah Range

The *Gemara* raises a comparison from a different *mishnah* to probe what it means to be "off." The *mishnah* states: if one tells his *shaliach* to go and separate *terumah* on his behalf, the *shaliach* does so according to what he estimates the owner would have wanted. If he does not know the owner's preference, he takes the average — one fiftieth, two percent. *Picheisu asarah o hosifu asarah* — if he took one sixtieth or one fortieth, his *terumah* is still valid. So here we see an individual *shaliach* operating with a recognized range — one fortieth to one sixtieth is all acceptable — rather than being held to an exact figure. How does this square with the ruling that a *shaliach* selling land is like the *almanah*, voided even by a tiny discrepancy?

### Range vs. Error

The *Gemara* answers: *ha-tam nami, kivan de-ika de-toreim be-ayin ra'ah ve-ika de-toreim be-ayin yaffah* — in the *terumah* case, there is a known range of legitimate practice. Some people are naturally generous in separating *terumah* and some are characteristically stingy, and both ends of that spectrum are recognized norms. The *shaliach* can be told: I estimated your practice falls at the generous or stingy end of this known range. *Aval hacha ta'usa hi* — but in the case of a sale, we are dealing with an objective error, not a range of practice.

### Market Context

This answer itself raises a challenge: if land valuation is so imprecise as to exclude it entirely from *ona'ah*, in what sense is a slight underprice an "objective error"? The resolution implicit in the *Gemara*'s logic is that one must work with an assessed range of market prices. If an appraiser would say that the property realistically could fetch anywhere between 110 and 140, then the sale is only a *ta'us* — an error — if it falls below the bottom of that range. This parallels the *terumah* case: it is not a question of a single precise number but of whether you have fallen outside any defensible range. The practical problem is that markets move: prices can be cut repeatedly below the assessor's estimate in a slow market, or surge well above it in a hot one. The *Gemara* seems to assume the existence of a relatively stable, determinable range, without which the entire framework becomes difficult to apply.

### Wheat Fields Pricing

The clearest scenario in which such a stable range exists is agricultural land with a clear, commodity-like character. Thousands of acres of wheat fields, for example, have a fairly objective per-unit price that does not fluctuate as wildly as residential or commercial property, where location and other idiosyncratic factors dominate. This probably represents the Talmudic default assumption — land value that, while not perfectly precise, is stable enough to support the notion of an objective error when the price falls sufficiently far outside the expected range.

---

## Halacha Ruling

### Halacha Ruling

*Amar Rav Huna bar Chinana amar Rav Nachman: halacha ke-divrei chachamim* — we rule like the *chachamim*, not like *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*. The court's sale is void when the price diverges from fair value by more than a sixth; it is not always binding simply by virtue of the court's authority.

### Orphans' Division

This ruling immediately generates a tension. Does Rav Nachman not hold the principle of *mah ko'ach beis din yafeh*? For he himself says in the name of *Shmuel*: when minor orphans come to divide their father's estate, *beis din* appoints a separate court-appointed representative — an *apitropus* — for each, and those representatives negotiate and divide the estate on behalf of their respective orphans. *Higdilu, yecholim limchos* — once they reach adulthood, Shmuel holds that they may object to the division.

### Challenge Division?

But Rav Nachman himself disagrees with Shmuel and rules: *higdilu, ein yecholim limchos, im ken mah ko'ach beis din yafeh* — they cannot object once they come of age, because the court-appointed division is binding. If the division could be unraveled years later simply because one of the orphans now prefers a different share, the entire institution of court-appointed guardianship collapses. How then does Rav Nachman simultaneously rule like the *chachamim* — voiding the court sale when it is off by more than a sixth — and insist that a court-appointed division of an estate is permanently binding?

---

## Error in Law

### Error vs. Preference

*Lo kashya* — there is no contradiction. *Ha d'ta'ah, ha d'lo ta'ah* — one case involves a genuine error, the other does not. When the court over- or under-assesses property by more than a sixth, that is an objective factual error of significant magnitude, and Rav Nachman would say it is not binding. But when the court appoints representatives to divide an estate and those representatives negotiate a division, there is no comparable objective error — there is at most a question of preference. One orphan might later wish he had received the plot closer to the city rather than the one closer to the river; another might prefer a parcel oriented differently. *B'ruchot* — matters of direction and preference — are not objective errors. For cases of preference, Rav Nachman says the division stands; for large objective errors in valuation, it does not.

The *chachamim*'s position is therefore internally coherent within Rav Nachman's framework: a court decision is binding when it falls within a reasonable range — even if not perfect — but becomes voidable when the error is sufficiently large and objectively demonstrable.

### Rabbi's Reversal

*Ki ata Rav Dimi amar*: when Rav Dimi came, he reported a relevant incident. *Ma'aseh va'asa Rebbe ke-divrei chachamim* — there was a case in which *Rebbe* (Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi) ruled like the *chachamim*, holding the court's sale void because it was off by more than a sixth. *Parta*, the son of Rabbi Elazar ben Parta and grandson of Rabbi Parta the Great, then said before him: *im ken mah ko'ach beis din yafeh* — if that is your ruling, where is the power of the court? *Ve-chazar Rebbe ve-asa ma'aseh* — Rebbe reversed his ruling and allowed the court's sale to stand.

### Two Story Versions

*Ika de'amri*, there is an alternate version. Rav Safra taught it differently: *uvikeish Rebbe la'asot ke-divrei chachamim* — Rebbe was *about* to rule like the *chachamim* when Parta interjected with the *mah ko'ach beis din yafeh* argument, and *lo asa Rebbe et ha-ma'aseh* — Rebbe never issued the ruling in the first place. In this version, there is no reversal, only a ruling withheld.

### Reversal Irony

The first version is particularly striking. The very principle that courts do not reverse their own rulings — *mah ko'ach beis din yafeh* — was invoked to cause Rebbe to reverse *his* ruling. He declined to reverse the court's sale, but he was perfectly willing to reverse his own *pesak*. The irony is impossible to miss.

### Law Always Reversed

*Lema bahai kamifligi?* — perhaps this is what the two versions of the story actually dispute. *Mar savar to'eh bidvar mishnah chozer, u-mar savar eino chozer* — one view holds that when a court errs in a matter of black-letter law, the ruling is reversed; the other holds it is not. The *Gemara* rejects this: *lo de-kuli alma to'eh bidvar mishnah chozer* — everyone agrees that an error in black-letter law (*to'eh bidvar mishnah*) requires reversal. The two versions of the story simply differ on what actually happened historically, not on the underlying *halacha*.

Here the *Gemara* draws out a deep structural parallel. There are two axes of error: error in fact and error in law. On the factual axis, the *mishnah* debates whether a court sale mispriced by more than a sixth must be reversed — the *chachamim* say yes, *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* says no. On the legal axis, there is a distinction between *to'eh be-shikul ha-da'at* — a judgment call where reasonable authorities might disagree, where the ruling stands even if the judgment was wrong — and *to'eh bidvar mishnah*, a clear error in established law, where everyone agrees reversal is required.

### Authority Concept

The parallel illuminates the conceptual framework underlying *mah ko'ach beis din yafeh*. An agent — whether a *shaliach* or the *beis din* itself — acts within their authority when they operate inside the law and within a reasonable range of factual judgment. The *mah ko'ach beis din yafeh* principle protects their acts within that zone: even mistakes of fact do not undo what they have done, because they were authorized. But when they act outside the law — when they are *to'eh bidvar mishnah* — they are no longer functioning as *beis din* at all. Their authorization extends only to lawful action; unlawful action is not protected by institutional authority.

This creates a precise parallel with the *shaliach* who undersells by a dollar: the moment he steps outside the authorized range, he is no longer acting within his *shlichus*. Correspondingly, *beis din* acts are binding when they stay within their lawful mandate — even with errors in fact — but not when they depart from it. The distinction is not about probability of error or quality of judgment; it is about whether one is acting within or outside the scope of one's authority.

---

## Widow's Warranty

### Estate Liability

Rav Yosef states: *almanah de-zabina, achrayus ayasmi* — when a widow sells estate property to collect her *ketubah*, the *achrayus* — the legal responsibility for warranty of title — falls on the estate, not on the widow personally. If the property turns out to have been improperly sold, if the original owner appears and reclaims it from the buyer, the buyer's claim for reimbursement goes against the orphans' estate, not against the widow who conducted the sale.

This is intuitive: the widow was selling the estate's property to satisfy the estate's debt to her. She was not selling something she owned. Similarly, *u-veis din de-zabni, achrayus ayasmi* — when *beis din* sells estate property, the warranty obligation likewise rests with the estate. The *Gemara* notes that while the widow's case is obvious, the court's case is not, since one might have thought that buying through a formal court process carries an implicit assurance. When property is sold by court order after extensive public announcement, every potential claimant has had ample opportunity to come forward. Perhaps the buyer implicitly waives his right to warranty by assuming no claim will arise. The *Gemara* rejects this: the buyer's assumption does not rise to an actual waiver, and if a title defect emerges, his claim against the estate stands.

### No Announcement

*Ameimar* then states in the name of Rav Yosef: *beis din she-machru belo hachrazah, na'asu ke-mi she-ta'u bidvar mishnah ve-chozrin* — if *beis din* sold estate property without going through the required public announcement process, the sale is treated as if the court committed an error in a matter of law (*to'eh bidvar mishnah*), and it is reversed.

Why is the failure to conduct a *hachrazah* classified as *to'eh bidvar mishnah* rather than as an error in fact? The answer is structural: the *hachrazah* is a procedural requirement, not a factual judgment. A court operating without it is not making a bad assessment of value — it is simply not following the procedure it is authorized to follow. It has stepped outside its lawful mandate, and actions outside that mandate are not protected by *mah ko'ach beis din yafeh*. This is precisely analogous to the principle established above: *beis din*'s authority covers errors within the law, not departures from it.

The *Gemara* notes that the *mishnah* itself states *shum ha-yetomim shloshim yom* — assessing orphans' estate requires a thirty-day public announcement process — and *shum ha-hekdesh shishim yom* — for *hekdesh* property, sixty days — with announcements morning and evening. This is not an optional enhancement but a required procedure. Selling without it is an error in law.

---

## Public Auction Rules

### Announcement Terms

The *mishnah* mandates two distinct announcement periods: thirty days for orphans' property and sixty days for *hekdesh*, with announcements morning and evening throughout. The logic of the thirty-day and sixty-day windows is to maximize exposure: the longer the window, the larger the pool of potential buyers who will hear of the sale and have the opportunity to evaluate and bid.

### Right Price Question

Rav Ashi poses a sharp question to Ameimar: the *mishnah* states that when *beis din* undersells or oversells by a sixth, *machran batel* — the sale is void. *Ha shaveh be-shaveh, machran kayam* — if they got the right price, the sale is valid. Now, if the failure to hold a public announcement renders the sale void regardless of the price achieved, then the *mishnah*'s discussion of correct pricing would be irrelevant — even a perfectly priced sale without a *hachrazah* should be void. Yet the *mishnah* makes clear that a correctly priced sale stands. This implies that the *mishnah* is discussing a case *without* a public announcement, which contradicts the claim that any sale without *hachrazah* is void.

The *Gemara*'s response: *lo, be-d'achriz* — the *mishnah* is actually discussing a case *with* a public announcement. We know this from the end of the *mishnah*, which says that if an *igeret bikoret* — which Rashi identifies with the *hachrazah* process — was conducted, the sale is binding regardless of the price. The *mishnah* thus discusses a situation where public auction was held: the beginning addresses the case where the right process was followed but the price was wrong; the end addresses the case where the right process was followed and the price was also drastically off. In both cases, the process was conducted.

### What Requires Announcement…

But this resolution creates its own problem: if the *mishnah* only addresses sales *with* a public announcement, how can it say that a correctly priced sale stands? The *Gemara* resolves this through a distinction among the categories of property being sold.

*Ela le-olam de-lo achruz* — fine, the *mishnah* may indeed address cases without a public announcement. The apparent contradiction disappears once one recognizes that the *hachrazah* requirement applies specifically to land. There are categories of property for which no public auction process is required at all: *ha-avadim ve-ha-metaltelin ve-ha-shtarot* — slaves, chattels, and documents of debt. For slaves, the reason is *shem'ei ve-arki* — they will hear they are about to be sold and flee. For chattels and documents, *shema yignavu* — during the extended public viewing period, items might be stolen. You cannot steal land. The *hachrazah* requirement therefore applies only to land, and the *mishnah*'s ruling that a correctly priced sale stands without formal announcement may simply be addressing a sale of these other categories — categories for which public auction is never required.

If so, why might the widow be collecting her *ketubah* through the sale of non-land property? Ordinarily, a *ketubah* lien applies only to real property. But the *Gemara* acknowledges this is a special case where the lien was extended to other property as well.

### Auction Exceptions

Beyond the distinction between property types, there are situational exceptions to the *hachrazah* requirement. The *Gemara* cites the practice articulated in Neharde'a: *le-kharga, u-le-mezonei, u-le-kevura* — when there is a need to pay government taxes immediately, when the widow needs funds for food support (*mezonot*), or when burial expenses must be met without delay. In these urgent circumstances, *mazbininan belo akhrazta* — one sells without public auction. Urgency overrides process. This also provides a natural reading of the main *mishnah*: the widow seeking to collect her *ketubah* for living expenses is a paradigmatic case of *mezonot*, and her sale can proceed without the thirty-day announcement, yet still remains binding as long as the price is within the acceptable range.

### Neharde'a Custom

Rav Nachman adds a third exception — one based not on property type or urgency, but on locale. *Me-olam lo asu igeret bikoret bi-Neharde'a* — they never conducted the public auction process in Neharde'a. One explanation offered is *de-vaki'ei bi-shuma* — the scholars and residents of Neharde'a were such expert assessors that no public bidding process was necessary to achieve a fair price; their expertise substituted for the market mechanism. A different explanation, attributed directly to Rav Nachman by Rav Yosef bar Minyumi, is more social in character: buyers at public auctions in Neharde'a were called *benei achli nichsei akhtekhasta* — "those who devour the property of the disadvantaged" — and the reputational stigma was severe enough that the practice was simply abandoned. The paradox is that the public announcement, designed to protect orphans by maximizing competition, ended up suppressing it because buyers were reluctant to participate. Neharde'a resolved this by foregoing the process altogether.

---

## Sales Timing Strategy

### Perishable Timing

The *Gemara* closes with a series of practical cases about how a court-appointed guardian should optimize the sale of orphans' property. *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel: metaltelin de-yatmi, shamminan le-hu u-mazbini le-hu altar* — chattel belonging to orphans should be assessed and sold immediately. The concern is that such goods are perishable: if value depreciates over time, delay works against the orphans' interests.

Rav Chisda says in the name of Avimi: *mazbininan le-hu le-yomei de-shuka* — you wait for market day. Even if the goods lose some freshness, selling on market day ensures a broader buyer pool, complete sales, and potentially better total returns than selling immediately to a thin local market. *Ve-lo peligi* — these two views do not actually disagree in principle. *Ha de-mikrav shuka, ha de-merachak shuka* — if market day is near, you wait; if it is far off and goods will significantly deteriorate in the interim, you sell at once. The principle in both cases is to maximize the orphans' return within the constraints of the situation.

### Holiday Timing

Rav Kahana had beer belonging to the orphan Rav Mesharshiya bar Chilkai in his care. He waited until the *regel* — the pilgrimage festival — to sell it. *Af gav de-nafal beih itzatza* — even though the beer had begun to turn slightly by the time of the festival, he reasoned *mai zuzei charifa* — at the *regel*, he would sell all of it immediately and collect payment in cash. Rashi adds that selling locally in the interim would have meant extended credit to buyers, whereas festival crowds pay on the spot. The small reduction in quality was therefore more than offset by the certainty and completeness of the cash sale.

### Shipping Risk

Ravina had in his possession wine belonging to his orphaned nephew. He was also transporting his own wine to Sichra by ship and asked Rav Ashi whether he should take the orphan's wine along. The concern was risk: if the ship sank, the orphan's wine would be lost. *Amar lei: zil, lo adif mi-didach* — Rav Ashi told him: go ahead, his wine is no different from yours. If you judge the profit opportunity to be worth the risk for your own wine, then it is a reasonable risk to take with his wine as well. The guardian is not required to be more conservative with the orphan's assets than he is with his own; he must simply exercise the same judgment he would apply to his own affairs.

### Discretion Balance

These cases close a full circle. The daf opened with a framework of sharply limited discretion — a *shaliach* who undersells by even a trivial amount has exceeded his authority and the sale is void. Yet the *Gemara* closes by recognizing that those responsible for orphans' assets must exercise real-world judgment: whether to sell immediately or wait for market day, whether to hold goods until a festival, whether to accept the risk of shipping. The tension between strict accountability and practical discretion defines the role of any fiduciary representative, whether *shaliach*, *apitropus*, or *beis din* itself.

---

---

# Ketubot 101

## Four Women, No Ketubah

### Mema'enes Definition

The *mishnah* at the bottom of 100b opens with the case of the *mema'enes* — the minor girl who refuses her husband. When a girl's father was absent, her mother and brothers were permitted by rabbinic enactment to marry her off while she was still underage. This institution, known as *kiddushei ketanah*, was established not as a financial arrangement but as a form of protection: the Rabbis were concerned that without a father present, a young girl would be vulnerable to exploitation. Crucially, the *kiddushin* in such a case is only rabbinic in force, not biblical, and the *nisuin* — the full consummation of the marriage — would ordinarily not take place until after she became a *bat mitzvah*. Since the marriage was not biblically binding, she retained the right to refuse at any point before she came of age. When she exercises that right of *mi'un* — refusal — the marriage is retroactively annulled, as though it had never taken place.

### Shniya Category

The second woman listed is the *shniya*, meaning a woman who is forbidden as a "secondary" relation — not a biblically defined relative, but one prohibited by rabbinic extension of the incest laws, as elaborated in Masechet Yevamos. She is not biblically forbidden; the prohibition is purely rabbinic, covering degrees of relationship removed enough that the Torah itself does not address them. Nevertheless, the Rabbis treated this category with seriousness, and the consequences for entering such a marriage are severe, as the *mishnah* goes on to describe.

### Ailonis Definition

The third case is the *ailonis* — a woman who not only is infertile but exhibits what the Rabbis understood to be physiologically male characteristics, indicating that she never developed normally as a female. The term itself derives from *ayil*, the ram, reflecting this association with maleness. The key halachic significance of this category is that it is treated as a *mekach ta'ut* — a mistaken transaction — on the theory that had the husband known she was an *ailonis*, he never would have agreed to marry her. There is therefore a presumption that the marriage was entered under a fundamental error.

### No Ketubah Rationale

In all three of these cases — the *mema'enes*, the *shniya*, and the *ailonis* — the *mishnah* rules that these women receive no *ketubah*. The reasoning differs by case. The *mema'enes* receives no *ketubah* because her *mi'un* retroactively erases the marriage entirely; there was never, in the end, a marriage at all, and therefore no *ketubah* obligation was ever created. The *ailonis*, similarly, exits through the logic of *mekach ta'ut* — the marriage was a transaction entered in error, and so likewise never legally materialized. The *shniya* is the most interesting case: the marriage was in fact binding, but the Rabbis, wishing to discourage such unions, strip her of her *ketubah* as a punitive measure. If the woman knows that there is no *ketubah* awaiting her when she leaves, the hope is that she will be less inclined to enter the forbidden marriage in the first place.

### Rashi: Peiros/Mezonos

The *mishnah* adds that not only do these women forfeit the *ketubah*, they also lose *peiros*, *mezonos*, and *bla'os*. Rashi explains that in this context *peiros* does not refer to the husband's right to enjoy the income from his wife's property — which is his benefit — but rather to what the wife is normally entitled to receive in exchange, namely the right to be redeemed if she is taken captive. *Mezonos* refers to her ongoing food support; she is not entitled to it, and indeed if she borrowed money to cover her food expenses during the marriage she cannot seek reimbursement. *Bla'os* — worn-out or consumed property — means either, as Tosafot reads it, that she cannot be reimbursed for property she brought into the marriage that was consumed during it, or, as Rashi reads it, that she cannot even take with her property that is still present but has become worn. The general thrust is that she walks away with nothing — an outcome even more severe than the departure of a freed slave.

### Biblical Prohibition Par…

The end of the *mishnah*, however, is striking. The *mishnah* lists cases of biblically forbidden marriages — a *kohen gadol* marrying a widow (*almanah*), an ordinary *kohen* marrying a divorcée or a woman who performed *chalitzah*, and a *mamzeret* or *nesinah* marrying a *yisrael* — and rules that in all these cases, even though the marriage is prohibited by the Torah itself, *yesh lahen ketubah*: these women do receive a *ketubah*. This is genuinely puzzling. One would think that the Rabbis' institution of the *ketubah*, designed to protect the wife and structure the marriage, would be the last thing one would apply to a biblically prohibited union. Extending the *ketubah* to such a marriage seems almost to confer on it a stamp of rabbinic recognition, even legitimacy.

### Rashi: Rabbinic vs. Bibl…

Rashi's explanation addresses this paradox directly, and it rests on a specific sociological assumption about who is the driving force behind each type of forbidden marriage. In the case of the *shniya*, a rabbinically forbidden marriage, Rashi reasons that the woman is unlikely to be deterred by the prohibition on her own, because the consequences fall lightly on her: her personal status is unaffected, she is not rendered forbidden to a *kohen*, and her children's status is not impaired. She therefore has an incentive to pursue the marriage and, in the Rabbis' framing, to seduce or persuade the man into it. The penalty of losing the *ketubah* is thus directed at her as a disincentive.

But in a biblically forbidden marriage — say, a *kohen gadol* marrying a widow — the woman faces real consequences. Rashi explains: *mipnei she-hi psulah v'valadah pasul al yedei nisuin* — the marriage renders her a *chalalah* and her children *chalalim*, which is a serious degradation of her and her offspring's status. She therefore has no reason to pursue such a marriage; the one with an incentive is the man, since his own status is not compromised. Thus the financial burden of the *ketubah* is placed on him — not as an endorsement of the marriage, but as a disincentive targeted at the party who might otherwise be inclined to enter it.

This explanation is elegant but not entirely satisfying. As the discussion in the shiur makes clear, not all the cases listed involve *kohanim*, so the status-change argument does not universally apply. More broadly, there is something genuinely strange about the Rabbis institutionalizing the *ketubah* within a biblically prohibited marriage. The *ketubah* is an ongoing legal instrument that sustains the structure of the marriage relationship. Attaching it to a biblically forbidden union does seem to implicitly recognize and reinforce that relationship in a way that sits uncomfortably alongside the prohibition. The contrast is almost ironic: the rabbinically forbidden marriage loses the *ketubah*, while the biblically forbidden one retains it. One might say the Rabbis were using the *ketubah* purely as a practical device to affect behavior, not as an expression of approval — but once one says the marriage is binding, the force of that logic becomes harder to maintain cleanly.

There is also a separate question, not resolved in this *mishnah*, of whether the husband in a biblically forbidden binding marriage has an ongoing obligation to pay *mezonot* during the marriage itself. It is possible that other *gemarot* would say he does not — since requiring him to sustain the marriage financially would be a much more direct form of support for it. The *mishnah*'s ruling about the *ketubah* on divorce is one thing; the question of ongoing obligations during the marriage is another.

---

## Rav vs. Shmuel Debate

### Rav: No Ketubah

The *gemara* now turns to a dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding the *ketanah* — the minor girl — who finds herself exiting a rabbinic marriage. Rav's version of the *mishnah* was more expansive than Shmuel's: Rav held that not only does the *mema'enes* — the girl who refuses — receive no *ketubah*, but even a *ketanah* who was divorced by her husband while still a minor receives no *ketubah* either. The reasoning is that Rav views the entire institution as so fundamentally not-a-marriage that even when the husband goes through the formal process of giving a *get*, the transaction is treated as having been essentially play-acting. If the marriage never rose to the level of a real marriage, the *get* cannot transform it into one retroactively. And since there was never a real marriage, there is no *ketubah*.

### Shmuel: Miaun vs. Get

Shmuel, by contrast, draws a sharp distinction. He teaches: *mema'enes ein lah ketubah* — the girl who refuses gets no *ketubah*, because her *mi'un* retroactively uproots the marriage. But *yotzei beget yesh lah ketubah* — if the husband gave her a *get* while she was still a *ketanah*, she does receive a *ketubah*. The reason is that in Shmuel's view, the *get* is not a nullification of the marriage — it is a termination of one. A *mi'un* says: there never was a marriage. A *get* says: there was a marriage, and now it is over. Even if the marriage was only rabbinic in origin, it was real while it lasted, and the *get* that ends it entitles the woman to the protections that normally accompany divorce.

Shmuel draws out the full implications of this distinction: after *mi'un*, the man is permitted to marry her relatives and she is permitted to marry his, since retroactively they were never husband and wife. She is also not *pesulah* — not disqualified from marrying a *kohen* — because *mi'un* leaves no trace of a prior marriage. But if he gave her a *get*: *paslah min ha-achim* — she may not marry his brothers — and *paslah min ha-kehunah* — she is halachically a divorcée and may not marry a *kohen*. Even though it was only a rabbinic marriage and a rabbinic divorce, Shmuel insists that these consequences follow as they would from any recognized marital dissolution.

### Shmuel: Three-Month Wait

Shmuel adds a further ruling: a *mema'enes* does not need to wait three months before remarrying, while a *ketanah* who received a *get* does. The three-month waiting period exists to prevent uncertainty about the paternity of a potential child. One might think the concern is irrelevant in the case of a *ketanah*, since we do not expect a minor girl to conceive. Rashi addresses this with a *lo plug* rationale — the Rabbis did not subdivide their enactment: wherever there was a genuine marriage and a genuine divorce, even a rabbinic one, the three-month waiting period applies, regardless of whether pregnancy is practically possible. The analogy is to a post-menopausal woman who converts together with her husband — the Rabbis still require the three-month separation even when conception is demonstrably impossible, because the rule was applied broadly across all cases of recognized marital dissolution. The *mema'enes*, by contrast, never had a recognized marriage at all, so no waiting period applies. This ruling — the three-month requirement for a *ketanah* who received a *get* — was the specific *chiddush* that Shmuel was adding beyond what was already known from earlier sources.

### Eliezer vs. Yehoshua

The *gemara* asks whether this dispute between Rav and Shmuel can be traced back to a *tanaitic* disagreement, and it finds one. A *baraita* records an explicit debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on exactly this question.

### Eliezer: No Effect

Rabbi Eliezer holds: *ein maaseh ketanah klum* — the legal acts of a *ketanah* are without effect. This sweeping statement encompasses the entire rabbinic institution of *kiddushei ketanah* when performed by the mother and brothers rather than the father. Because the father is absent and the marriage was not biblically authorized, Rabbi Eliezer treats it as non-marriage. The husband is not entitled to her found objects, her earnings, or the annulment of her vows; he does not inherit her; if he is a *kohen* he does not become *tamei* upon her death. *Klalo shel davar* — the summary principle — is that she is not his wife in any legal sense. The sole *halacha* that does apply is that she requires *mi'un* to exit: either she must affirmatively refuse before becoming a *bat mitzvah*, or else, if she remains with him past that point, she becomes his wife fully. But while she is a *ketanah*, nothing about the arrangement constitutes marriage.

### Yehoshua: Binding

Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees fundamentally: *maaseh ketanah klum* — the acts of a *ketanah* do mean something. He holds that this rabbinic marriage is a genuine marriage in every respect. The husband is entitled to her found objects, her earnings, and the annulment of her vows; he inherits her; he becomes *tamei* to her. *Harei hi k'ishto l'chol davar* — she is his wife in every legal dimension. The one difference between her status and that of a fully adult wife is that she can exit by *mi'un* alone, without requiring a *get*. For an adult woman, only a *get* terminates the marriage; for this *ketanah*, *mi'un* suffices. But absent *mi'un*, the marriage is fully in force.

### Amoraim Align with Tanna…

The *gemara* then maps the *amoraic* dispute onto the *tanaitic* one. Rav, who says that even a *get* does not give the *ketanah* any *ketubah*, follows Rabbi Eliezer: since the marriage was never real, giving a *get* changes nothing about its essential non-status, and no *ketubah* was ever owed. Shmuel, who distinguishes between *mi'un* and *get*, follows Rabbi Yehoshua: since the marriage was real — rabbinically binding and carrying all the normal marital consequences — a *get* is a genuine termination of a genuine marriage, and the *ketubah* is owed.

The *gemara* refines this, however. It notes that according to Rabbi Eliezer, there is no debate to be had: if the marriage was never real, obviously neither *mi'un* nor *get* changes that, and obviously there is no *ketubah*. The real dispute occurs *aliba deRabbi Yehoshua* — within the framework of Rabbi Yehoshua, who agrees the marriage was real.
