When she holds the *shtar*, everyone agrees she may collect forever. *Ve-halacha ke-divrei chachamim* — and the *halacha* follows the Sages, meaning that when she is in her father's house without a *shtar* and has been silent for 25 years, *mechila* is assumed, but when she is in her husband's household, her silence is never interpreted as *mechila* — the *kissufa* factor prevails and she retains her right to collect regardless.

---

## Base vs. Addition

### Base Only

*Ki ata Rav Dimi*: when Rav Dimi came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he transmitted a ruling in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, in the name of Bar Kappara: *lo shanu ela maneh matayim* — the entire framework of *mechila* after 25 years applies only to the base *ketubah* amounts of 100 and 200 *dinars*. *Aval tosefet yesh lah* — but the *tosefet*, the additional amounts voluntarily added by the husband, she retains in any event. The reasoning is that the *tosefet* is in the nature of a gift, and one does not assume *mechila* in the context of a gift the way one might in the context of a standard marital obligation.

### Tosafet Waiver

Rabbi Abbahu, however, citing Rabbi Yochanan, rules otherwise: *afilu tosefet ein lah* — even the *tosefet* is forfeited after 25 years. The support for this position comes from Rabbi Aibu citing Rabbi Yannai: *tnai ketubah ke-ketubah dami* — the conditions and additions of the *ketubah* are treated as equivalent to the base *ketubah* itself; the 25-year waiver rule applies to the whole.

### Abbahu View

The dispute between these positions thus turns on whether the *tosefet* retains the character of a gift — and is therefore never subject to *mechila* — or whether, once incorporated into the *ketubah* structure, it is treated identically to the base amount for all purposes including the 25-year waiver rule.

### Tosafet Disputes

*Itmar nami*: Rabbi Abba citing Rav Huna citing Rav rules that only the base 100 and 200 are subject to the waiver — the *tosefet* she retains. Rabbi Abba then challenged Rav Huna: *amar Rav hachi?* — did Rav really say this? Rav Huna replied: *ashtukin kaamart o ashkayin kaamart?* — when you challenge whether Rav said this, are you trying to silence me (*ashtukin*), meaning you disagree, or would you like to raise a drink to this ruling (*ashkayin*), meaning you approve and want to be sure of its attribution? *Amar lei: ashtukin kamina* — I want to silence you, Rav Huna replied; he did not accept the ruling as stated.

---

## Case Study

### Chiya Story

The *gemara* now presents a concrete case illustrating these principles. The mother-in-law of Rabbi Chiya Aricha — a different Rabbi Chiya — was the widow of his brother, who had died leaving Rabbi Chiya Aricha as the surviving heir and thus responsible for the estate. She had been living in her father's house — *be-vei nasha* — rather than in her deceased husband's household. *Ve-zana esrim ve-chamisha shanim* — Rabbi Chiya Aricha supported her for 25 years. He brought her food on his own shoulder, by his own account, taking great personal care of her provision.

### Heir Refusal

After 25 years she said to him: *hav li mezonei* — continue to pay my food bill. He replied: *leis lach mezonei* — you have no more right to *mezonot*, the 25-year period has elapsed. She then said: *hav li ktuvah* — give me my *ketubah*. He replied: *lo mezonei is lach ve-lo ktuvah is lach* — you have neither *mezonot* nor *ketubah*; you have waived everything.

### Judge Recognition

*Taviesay le-dina kamai d'Rabba bar Shila* — she brought him to judgment before Rabba bar Shila. The judge asked him to describe exactly what had occurred. Rabbi Chiya Aricha recounted that he had supported her for 25 years while she lived in her father's house, personally delivering the food with great care and dedication. Rabba bar Shila said: and this is precisely the point. *D'amrinan mishum kissufa hu d'lo tavah* — the reason she did not demand payment in 25 years is that she was *embarrassed* to ask, because you took such excellent care of her. The Sages' rule that living in the husband's household suspends *mechila* due to *kissufa* applies here as well: when a creditor is so attentive and generous that the widow feels she cannot press a demand, her silence is not waiver but *kissufa*.

### Payment Ordered

*Zil havlah* — go pay her. The judge ruled that the silence was not *mechila* and ordered continued payment.

### Escalation

*Ve-la ashgach* — he did not comply. *Katav lah adrachta anichsei* — the court then issued a written seizure order against his property, empowering her to collect from it. The case then came before Rava.

---

## Seizure Dispute

### Produce Claim

When the case came before Rava, Rabbi Chiya Aricha complained: *chazi mar heichi danyin* — do you see how they judged me? They issued a seizure of my property. Rava replied: *shappir duncha* — that was a sound judgment; you must continue to pay her.

The widow then pressed further. Since she now held the seizure document, she claimed: *neizil ve-neihadar lei peira mi-hahu yoma ad idna* — let him return to me the produce of that property from the time the seizure document was written until now. She had been entitled to that property, she argued, and he had withheld it; she should be compensated for the produce generated from it during that period.

### Document Defect

*Amar lah: achvi li adrachtich* — Rava said, show me the document. *Ve-lo hava katav bah: ve-ishtemodana de-nichsei de-misna inun* — and he found that the document did not contain the specification: and it is known to us that these properties belong to the deceased. A proper seizure order in this context must identify the specific property the widow has a right to seize — namely, the property that had belonged to her dead husband. The document lacked this specification.

### Wrong Property

*Adrachta la shappir ktiva* — the seizure document was not properly written, Rava ruled, because without proper identification, the widow might go and seize the wrong property entirely. If she were to seize the heir's own property rather than her deceased husband's estate, she might improve it, and meanwhile her deceased husband's property — the one she actually has rights to — might depreciate. Later, the heir would come to court and say: take your property and give me back mine. This creates potential for significant confusion and loss.

### Final Property Rule

Rava's ruling was therefore precise: she is entitled to seize and collect from her deceased husband's property for her support, not from the heir's own property. The defect in the seizure document, which failed to identify which property was subject to seizure, rendered the document invalid and prevented her from claiming produce from the time of its writing.

### Payment Remains

The widow then attempted a fallback position: even if not from the time of the document, she argued she should receive produce from the time the auction process had concluded and property had been assigned, prior to actual written seizure. *Amar lah: hani milei heicha de-lo ktiv tauta be-adrachta* — Rava ruled that this argument would hold only where there was no error in the seizure document itself. *Aval heicha de-ktiv tauta be-adrachta, leis lan bah* — where there is an error in the document, the entire process is voided, and actual possession is required before any rights in the produce can be claimed.

The heir argued that Rava himself held that *achrayut ta'us sofer hu* — an omission in a document is treated as a mere scribal error and does not invalidate the fundamental transaction. Rava responded: *beha lo matzi lemeimar ta'us sofer hu* — in this case, that principle cannot apply, *deha chazina de-veshivna ta'ei* — because this was a genuine error in judgment, not a scribal oversight. *Me'ikara hu savar ha ve-ha didei hu* — the court officer who drafted the document actually believed that all the property belonged to the heir, making it immaterial from which specific portion the widow collected. *Mai mehai u-mai mehai?* That was an error: she is not entitled to any of the heir's own property. *Zimnin de-azil u-meshabbach lehu ve-havu lehu nichsei* — if she were to take the heir's property, she might improve it, while her deceased husband's property simultaneously depreciates, and then the heir would come and demand: take yours and return mine — a result that would cast disrepute on the *beis din*. She is therefore limited to the property of her deceased husband for purposes of support collection, and the technical defects in the seizure document preclude any claim to produce from an earlier point.

Notwithstanding all these technical complexities, however, Rava's fundamental ruling that the heir must continue paying her support stands — the defects in the seizure document speak to which property may be seized, not to whether the underlying obligation to pay exists.

*Chazak u-varuch.*

---

---

# Ketubot 105

## Admon & Chanan

### Opening

We begin today the final *perek* of *Ketubot*, opening at the very bottom of 104b. The *daf* itself is 105.

### Two Judges Intro

The *mishnah* opens: *shne dayane gzerot hayu biYerushalayim* — two judges who made decrees were in Jerusalem: *Admon* and *Chanan ben Avishalom*. As Rashi explains, *Chanan* said two things — meaning two rulings for which he was known, rulings with which the Sages did not agree — and *Admon* said seven. The subsequent discussion in the *perek* will bring in all of the distinctive rulings of each, some tying directly into the themes of *Ketubot*, others less so. The hook is here in the opening of the *mishnah*, and the package of rulings follows from it.

### Wife's Support Case

The first case: *mi shehalach limdinat hayam veishto tova mezonot* — someone who went overseas and his wife demands her *mezonot*, her support. Obviously she must be able to put food on the table while her husband is away. The concern, however, is that he is not present to defend himself — perhaps he already prepaid her support, or there is some other outstanding question about what she has already collected.

### Chanan's Position

*Chanan* rules: *tishava basof velo tishava batchila* — she takes an oath at the end, not at the beginning. Rashi explains that "the end" means when the husband eventually dies and she comes to collect her full *ketubah*; at that point she takes the normal oath a woman takes when collecting a *ketubah*, and that oath will simultaneously cover any questions about what she collected during the period she was receiving her *mezonot*. If he does not die but eventually returns, the matter will presumably be dealt with at that point.

### Priests' Dispute

*Nechlaku alav bne kohanim gdolim* — the sons of the *Kohanim Gdolim* disputed this ruling. It is a notable fact that this group had a collective voice in *halacha*; during the period of *Bayit Sheni* there was indeed considerable turnover among the *Kohanim Gdolim* and presumably a large cohort of their sons. They maintained: *tishava batchila uvasof* — she must take an oath at the beginning when she comes to collect *mezonot*, and again at the end when collecting the *ketubah*. Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas ruled in accordance with their position.

### R. Yochanan Agrees

*Veamar Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai yafe amar Chanan* — Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai sides with *Chanan*: the oath should only be at the end. One might ask whether Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai is simply echoing *Chanan* without adding anything new. In general, when the *Gemara* records an opinion that appears merely to echo an earlier one, it seeks to understand the *chidush*. Here, however, it is clear that Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai is simply picking sides in an existing dispute, and the weight of his authority as a backing for *Chanan*'s position is itself significant, even without a novel ruling.

It should be noted that the *Gemara* today will not actually discuss this debate about *mezonot* and oaths at all. The discussion will focus entirely on the opening phrase — *shne dayane gzerot* — and use it as a platform for an extended treatment of the role, compensation, and integrity of judges.

### Tosafot on Name

Before turning to the *Gemara*, there is an interesting *Tosafot* on 104b worth noting. *Tosafot* states: *hachi gares Rabbeinu Tam* — Rabbeinu Tam's reading of the name is *Avishalom* rather than *Avshalom*. The reasoning: Rabbi Meir states in *Perek Chelek* that *Avshalom* — the son of David — has no portion in the *Olam Haba*. How then could anyone name their child after him? Therefore Rabbeinu Tam insists the name is the distinct form *Avishalom*, and pursues the discussion at some length. This, however, raises an obvious question that *Tosafot* elsewhere addresses: how do we have a *Tanna* named Rabbi Yishmael, if *Yishmael* in rabbinic literature is associated with wickedness? One could equally ask: who says the name was chosen after that particular person? Names recur without necessarily carrying reference to any specific historical bearer — just as modern Hebrew speakers use the name *Nimrod* without invoking the biblical figure. The observation stands, but the concern may be overstated.

---

## Two vs Three Judges

### Braita on Theft

The *Gemara* raises a contradiction from a *braita*: rather than *dayanei gezeirot* — judges who made decrees — the *braita* describes *dayanei gezeilot* — judges who ruled on matters of theft — and lists not two but three: *Admon ben Gadai*, *Chanan HaMitzri*, and *Chanan ben Avishalom*. So there are two difficulties: this source has three where the *mishnah* has two, and this source says *gezeilot* where the *mishnah* says *gezeirot*. As the *Gemara* puts it: *kashya tlata atrei, kashya gezeirot agezeilot*.

### Most Important Only

The first difficulty — three versus two — is resolved readily. *Dechashiv lei katani, delo chashiv lei lo katani*: the *mishnah* lists the most significant figures and omits the less prominent ones. The *mishnah* names *Admon* and *Chanan ben Avishalom* as the two most important, and leaves out *Chanan HaMitzri* as the third.

### Gezeirot & Gezeilot

The second difficulty — *gezeirot* versus *gezeilot* — is resolved by Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: *shehayu gozrim gezeirot al gezeilot* — they would issue edicts in connection with matters of theft. Hence, depending on one's angle of description, they could be referred to either as *dayanei gezeirot* or as *dayanei gezeilot*.

### R. Yosei Braita

A supporting *braita* is then cited: *kitema netiah* — if an animal enters a neighbor's property and nibbles at young plantings. Rabbi Yosei invokes *gozrei gezeirot she'biYerushalayim* — those who issue edicts in Jerusalem — and states that they would assign fixed values: a one-year-old planting is assessed at two silver coins, a two-year-old planting at four. This *braita* explicitly uses the phrase *gozrei gezeirot* in the context of what we might classify as *nezek* — tortious damage — rather than outright theft, which itself helps bridge the gap between *gezeirot* and *gezeilot*.

### Nature of Gezeirah

This passage opens an important conceptual point. We ordinarily think of a *gezeirah* in the rabbinic sense as a protective fence around the law — do not read by candlelight lest you tilt the flame, and similar safeguards. But here the term *gezeirah* is applied to something quite different: the act of judges establishing fixed parameters and guidelines for monetary liability. Why would these figures be called *dayanei gezeirot* rather than simply *dayanim*?

The answer seems to be that while an ordinary judge applies existing law to a given case, these judges had a specialized role: they were not merely adjudicating but actually setting down certain operative rules — fixing valuations for categories of damage, establishing procedures and frameworks — functioning in what we might call a legislative as well as a judicial capacity. In that sense, calling them *gozrei gezeirot* makes good sense: they were issuing binding rulings that set parameters for how the law would be applied. This also fits with the observation that later in the *perek* we will see a series of rulings attributed to *Admon*, some relating to *ketubot* and some not. The *mishnah* has collected this package around the hook of their identity as *gozrei gezeirot*.

### Nachum HaMadai

A second *braita* is then cited listing three *dayanei gezeirot* in Jerusalem: *Admon*, *Chanan*, and *Nachum* — with Nachum here being *Nachum HaMadai*, a figure familiar from the *Bameh Madlikin* chapter recited each *Shabbos* eve.

### Nachum Rejected

Rav Pappa identifies the source of this tradition: it is Rabbi Natan, as taught in a *braita* — *af Nachum HaMadai mi-gozrei gezerot she-biYerushalayim haya* — even Nachum HaMadai was among those who issued edicts in Jerusalem, *velo hodu lo Chachamim* — but the Sages did not agree with him. The debate appears to be not about whether he adjudicated cases at all — evidently he did — but whether he held the specific official status of *gozrei gezeirot*. That question the Sages resolved against him.

---

## Jerusalem Institutions

### 394 Numbers

The *Gemara* presses further: are we really saying there were only two or three such figures? Rav Pinchas cites Rav Oshaya: *shelosh me'ot tishim ve-arba'ah batei dinim she-hayu biYerushalayim* — there were 394 courts in Jerusalem. And correspondingly, 394 synagogues and 394 study halls — a remarkable claim. The number 300 is often a stylized large number in rabbinic literature, but the additional 94 makes this figure feel unexpectedly precise.

### Rashi Clarifies

Rashi notes that the *batei dinim* in question are *batei dinim shel esrim u-shelosha* — courts of 23, meaning major *batei dinim*, not the minor courts of three. Three hundred and ninety-four courts of 23 in Jerusalem is a striking number. Rashi also glosses — perhaps unnecessarily — that *batei knesiyot* are for prayer and *batei midrashot* for *mishnah* and *talmud*, and also that *batei sofrim* refers to elementary schools for children. That last clarification is useful; one might have read *batei sofrim* as houses of scribal work, but Rashi indicates these are what we would call *cheder*.

### Specific to Edicts

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent tension: *ve-chi ka-amrinan a-gozrei gezerot ka-amrinan* — when we were speaking of two or three, we were speaking specifically about those who held the distinctive role of *gozrei gezeirot*, not about the full complement of judges in the city. The 394 courts are a different category entirely; the two or three figures were specialists in a particular legislative-judicial function.

---

## Judge Compensation

### 99 Talents Payment

Rav Yehuda citing Rav Assi states: *gozrei gezerot she-biYerushalayim hayu notlin sacharam tishim ve-tisha maneh mi-trumat ha-lishka* — these figures who issued edicts in Jerusalem would receive their compensation of 99 *maneh* of silver from the *trumat ha-lishka*, the funds collected from the *machatzit ha-shekel* beyond what was needed for the *korbanot*. The surplus from those communal funds was directed toward ongoing Temple and communal needs, and the salary of these *gozrei gezeirot* was one such use.

### Payment Problem

This immediately raises a question: how could judges receive payment at all? The prohibition on *sachar la-dun* — taking a fee for rendering judgment — is well established, and the problem of *shochad* looms over any arrangement in which a judge receives money in connection with his judicial function. We will address this in detail shortly.

### Sustenance Requirement

*Lo ratzu* — if they did not want to accept that sum, *mosifin lahem* — the amount would be increased. The *Gemara* initially asks with some incredulity: *atu berishaye askinan* — are we dealing with wicked people who refuse their salary and need to be persuaded? The answer is: *ella lo safku* — it simply was not enough to cover their needs. The principle here is that the community must ensure these judges are provided for; if the fixed sum was insufficient, it would be increased. And even if the judges themselves were inclined to refuse the additional compensation, *mosifim aleihem* — you still increase it, because the obligation is to ensure their sustenance, not merely to offer what they are willing to accept.

---

## Karna's Case

### Karna Intro

Karna — a first-generation *Amora* — would accept a coin from each side when litigants came before him: *hava shakil istira mizakai veistira mechayav* — he would take an *istira* from the one who was ultimately exonerated and an *istira* from the one who was ultimately liable. He would do this before rendering judgment, and then *vedayan lehu dina* — he would adjudicate the case.

### Bribe Question

The *Gemara* asks: *veheichi avid hachi* — how could he do this? *Vehachtiv shochad lo tikach* — the Torah says, do not take a bribe.

### One Side Risk

The *Gemara* entertains a possible distinction: perhaps the prohibition is specifically *heicha deshakeil mechada gisa* — where one takes only from one side, because then *dilma ati leatzloyei dina* — one may come to tilt the judgment in favor of the side one took money from. But Karna, since he took equally from both sides, would not be drawn to tilt toward one over the other.

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this: *vechi lo ati leatzloyei dina mi sharei* — just because it will not lead to tilting the judgment, does that make it permitted? A *braita* is cited: *shochad lo tikach* — do not take a bribe. What does the Torah need to tell us? If the concern were only about perverting judgment, it would have been sufficient to say *lo tateh mishpat* — do not pervert justice. By adding the prohibition on bribery, the Torah is telling us something beyond the prohibition on corrupt verdicts. *Ella afilu lezakot et hazakai ulechayev et hachayav amrah Torah shochad lo tikach* — even if your intent is to acquit the innocent and convict the guilty, even if you plan to judge correctly and fairly, the Torah says you may not accept a bribe.

The *Gemara* is identifying a scenario in which someone pays a judge and says: I only ask you to judge me honestly; if I am innocent, find me innocent; I am not asking you to rule in my favor if I am guilty. Even that arrangement is prohibited, because money paid in connection with the final judgment — even a just one — falls within the category of *shochad*. Given this, taking equal fees from both sides would seem no better: the *Gemara* finds it difficult to see why that should be categorically different.

### Challenge Equal Fees

The *Gemara's* challenge stands: *vechi lo ati leatzloyei dina mi sharei* — even granting that equal fees from both sides remove the directional bias of a traditional bribe, how does that remove the underlying prohibition? The answer will turn on a different distinction entirely, developed in the following section.

---

## Sachar Batala

### Fee Voids Judgment

The *mishnah* states plainly: *hanoteil sachar ladun dinav betelim* — one who takes a fee for rendering judgment, his judgments are void. This goes beyond a simple prohibition; it is grounds for retroactive invalidation of the ruling itself.

### Sachar Batala Permitted

The *Gemara* resolves the question about Karna: *hani milei agar dina* — the voiding applies when you are paid for the act of judgment itself. *Hai tanna betorat agra hava shakeil* — but Karna was taking the money as a service fee, as compensation for his time, not as payment for the content of his ruling. This is the principle of *sachar batala* — compensation for lost opportunity, for the work one is not doing because one is sitting in judgment.

The principle has broad implications beyond the courtroom. The Torah states, in the phrase the *Gemara* invokes, *mah ani bechinam af atem bechinam* — just as I taught without charging a fee, so too you must teach the people without charge. This extends to teachers of Torah, doctors, and other roles where one might otherwise argue that payment is for a *mitzvah*. The conceptual problem is real: if rabbis and judges cannot be paid for their services, how do they support themselves?

The answer is *sachar batala*: we are not paying you for doing a *mitzvah*, we are paying you for the job you are not doing while you do the *mitzvah*. This is technically opportunity cost — compensation for the income foregone by spending time in a judicial or teaching role rather than in one's usual occupation. One might note, somewhat wryly, that taken strictly this would mean better-compensated judges are not the more skilled ones but the ones with higher market value in other fields; the person who left a lucrative law practice to become a rabbi would theoretically command a higher *sachar batala* than someone with no other marketable skill who happens to be an outstanding scholar. These complications are real, and the *Gemara* acknowledges that *sachar batala* as a practical mechanism involves a degree of legal fiction. Nevertheless, that is what permits it.

### Disgusting Fees

A *braita* complicates the picture: *mechoar hadayan shenotel schar ladun, ella shedino din* — it is disgusting for a judge to take fees for his judgment, yet his judgment nevertheless stands. The *Gemara* asks: what case is this describing? If it is *agar dina* — a fee for rendering judgment — how can the *braita* say the ruling stands, when the *mishnah* says *dinav betelim*? It must therefore be describing *agar batala* — compensation for lost work. Yet the *braita* calls it disgusting. So even *sachar batala* is considered *mechoar*?

### Obvious Loss Required

The resolution: *hani milei batala dela muchach* — that is when the lost opportunity is not obvious. If it is not apparent to onlookers that the judge is genuinely forgoing other income by sitting in court, the arrangement looks like being paid for the judgment itself, even if technically it is *sachar batala*. That situation is *mechoar* — disgraceful in appearance, even if technically permitted. *Karna batala demuchach havei shakil* — but Karna's situation was one of obvious, demonstrable lost opportunity.

### Wine Tasting

How was it obvious in Karna's case? *Dehavei tohei be'ambara dechamra* — he worked as a wine assessor, smelling in warehouse-style wine storage to determine which casks were approaching spoilage, and advising the owners accordingly. *Veyahavi lei zuza* — they would pay him for this service. When Karna left that work to sit in judgment, anyone could see that he was forgoing readily available income. The arrangement of collecting a fee from each litigant was therefore transparently a reimbursement for lost earnings, not a payment for the judgment.

### Rav Huna Story

A parallel story: Rav Huna, when a case came before him, would say to the litigants: *havu li gavra dedali li becharitai* — provide me a man to draw water in my place. He drew water for a living, and would not sit in judgment without someone covering his ordinary daily labor. *Ve'idun lechu dina* — and then I will judge your case. Again, the lost opportunity was concrete, visible, and undeniable.

---

## Tosafot Compensation

### R. Tam View

Returning to the question of how the *gozrei gezeirot* of Jerusalem were paid from *trumat ha-lishka* — public Temple funds — *Tosafot* offers two distinct approaches. Rabbeinu Tam's view: *mishum de-lo assur ela mi-ba'alei dinin* — the entire problem is when money comes from the litigants themselves, because that is where the risk of *shochad* arises. When payment comes from communal funds, it is outside that ambit entirely. The concerns about *sachar ladun* and *shochad* apply specifically to the money-for-judgment relationship between judge and litigant; public funding from *trumat ha-lishka* simply does not implicate those concerns, and no further legal fiction is required.

### Community Support

A second approach — attributed in this *Tosafot* to *Rebbi*, which, it should be noted, is the *Tosafot* of the school of Rabbeinu Shimshon, as stated at the opening of the tenth *perek* at 90a — offers a different framework. It is not that payment from public funds is simply permissible because it avoids the litigant relationship. Rather: these judges sat in court at all hours and engaged in no other occupation whatsoever; they had no means of support. The community had effectively required them to have no other source of income. Having placed them in that position, the community now bore a responsibility to sustain them — not as payment for services rendered, but as an obligation of *parnasah* toward people who are impoverished as a direct consequence of communal need.

This is a striking distinction. In the *sachar batala* model, one is compensated for a real alternative that one is forgoing. For a full-time judge with no alternative occupation, there is no such alternative — but the community has created the very condition of his poverty. The payment is therefore not for the *mitzvah* of judging; it is in fulfillment of a communal duty to support someone the community has rendered unable to support himself. The two models thus represent quite different understandings of the jurisprudential problem: one sidesteps it by removing the litigant relationship; the other works around it by recharacterizing the payment as communal welfare rather than compensation for services.

---

## Bribes Blind

### Eye Disease Analogy

Rabbi Abahu opens a striking reflection on the nature of *shochad*. He asks: come and see how blind are the eyes of those who accept bribes. A person who has a problem with his eye gives money to a doctor, and it is uncertain whether the doctor will heal it or not — he pays without any guarantee of benefit. Yet those who accept bribes take even a trivial sum and it blinds them. The asymmetry is the point: medical treatment cannot reliably heal a diseased eye even with payment, but bribery blinds infallibly even for a trifling amount.

---

## Bribes Blind (II)

### Exodus Verse

The *Gemara* cites the verse from Exodus 23:8: *ki hashochad ya'aver pikchim* — for bribery blinds the open-eyed. The phrase *pikchim* — the open-eyed, the perceptive — is precisely the target.

### Wise & Foolish

A *braita* extends this: *ki hashochad ya'aver einei chachamim* — bribery blinds the eyes of the wise; *kal v'chomer l'tipshim* — how much more so the foolish.

### Righteous & Wicked

And further: *v'isaleif divrei tzadikim* — it perverts the words of the righteous; *kal v'chomer l'rasha'im* — how much more so the wicked.

### Quality Judges

The *Gemara* raises an obvious difficulty: *atu tipshim u'rasha'im bnei dina ninhu* — would we appoint foolish and wicked people as judges in the first place? The very framing of the *kal v'chomer* seems to assume we are speaking about sitting judges. Why would the *braita* be warning about fools and wicked men on the bench?

### Righteous Corrupted

The resolution reframes the *kal v'chomer* entirely. The statement *ki hashochad ya'aver einei chachamim* means: even someone who is a great sage at the time he accepts a bribe, *eino niftar min ha'olam b'lo smiyut halev* — he does not leave the world without his heart becoming blinded. The first time he accepts *shochad* he is still a *chacham*; by the second time, the *shochad* has already made him into a *tipesh* — the *kal v'chomer* is thus a temporal progression, not a contrast between two different categories of judges. Similarly: *afilu tzadik gamur v'loke'ach shochad* — even a complete *tzadik* who accepts *shochad eino niftar min ha'olam b'lo tiruf hada'at* — does not leave the world without his mind being perverted, effectively becoming a *rasha*. The *kal v'chomer* again describes what the bribe does to him over time.

---

## King & Judge Self-Suffic…

### King Verse

Rav Dimi cites a teaching of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak on the verse: *melech b'mishpat ya'amid aretz* — a king through justice establishes the land, *v'ish trumot yeherseina* — and a man of *trumot* will destroy it. The word *trumot* is read not as donations but as related to neediness — one who is always extending his hand. The interpretation: *im domeh dayan l'melech she'eino tzarich l'klum* — if the judge is like a king who needs nothing from anyone, who is fully self-sufficient, *ya'amid aretz* — he will establish the land. *Aval im domeh l'kohen she'mechazer al hagranot* — but if he is like a *kohen* who goes from one threshing floor to the next seeking his *terumah*, who is needy, whose hand is perpetually out, *yeherseina* — that judge will destroy it.

### Needy Judge

The image of the *kohen* going from threshing floor to threshing floor is vivid: not corrupt in the obvious sense, perhaps, but dependent — always needing things from people, never approaching a case from a position of independence. That dependence, even without explicit bribery, creates the conditions for compromised judgment.

### Borrowing Judge

Rabba bar Rav Shila adds a practical ruling: *hai dayana d'shail she'ilta* — a judge who borrows objects, *pasul l'meidan dina* — is invalid to render judgment. The *she'ilta* here is literal borrowing of objects — asking a neighbor for a ladder, a few eggs, use of a car. Rashi clarifies: *d'ragil l'shail mivnei iro b'hemot v'kelim* — it must be a habitual pattern, not a one-time occurrence. Such a judge presents himself to the community as someone with needs, as someone dependent on others — and that dependence creates precisely the dynamic of the *kohen ha'mechazer al hagranot*. People who have lent him things may have their day in court; people who anticipate being able to do him favors may calculate accordingly.

### Reciprocal Borrowing

*V'lo aman ela d'leis lei l'oshulei* — and this applies only when the judge has nothing to lend others. *Aval is lei l'oshulei* — but if he also lends to others, then *leis lan bah* — it is not a problem. When there is genuine reciprocity — borrowing a cup of sugar and lending one in return, so to speak — the relationship is that of neighbors rather than that of petitioner and patron. The power dynamic disappears, and with it the concern.

### Rava & Bar Maryon

Yet the *Gemara* challenges this: *Rava shashilta midbei Bar Maryon* — Rava borrowed objects from the household of Bar Maryon, *af gav d'lo shailei minei* — even though they never borrowed from him in return, yet he remained willing to serve as their judge. The *Gemara* responds: *hasam lachshuvinhu hu d'baei* — there, Rava was not borrowing out of genuine need; he was doing it in order to honor them, to confer a sense of distinction upon them by having the great Rava come and borrow something from their household. One might still wonder whether the perception problem remains — whether those litigants, or observers, might think that Rava was now beholden to Bar Maryon — but the *Gemara* lets this stand as Rava's practice.

---

## Unconscious Bias

### Gift Identification

Rava offers what is perhaps the deepest analysis of why *shochad* corrupts. *Mai tama d'shochda* — what is the operative mechanism of bribery? *Keivan d'kablah shochda minei* — once a judge accepts a gift from someone, *ikrav leh daatei legabei* — his mind draws close to that person. *Vahavei k'gufei* — and the person becomes like himself to the judge.

### Self-Blindness

*V'ein adam roeh chov l'atzmo* — a person cannot see his own faults. This is not a character failing but a structural feature of human psychology: no one can be fully objective about oneself. Once a judge has accepted something from a litigant and that person has become, subconsciously, like an extension of the judge's own self, objectivity is structurally impossible — not because the judge is wicked or even negligent, but because the mechanism of self-perception precludes it. Even the most sincere attempt at fairness cannot fully overcome the identification created by the gift. This is why the Torah's prohibition applies even when the judge intends to rule correctly: the corruption is not in the intent but in the psychology.

### Shochad Etymology

*Mai shochad* — what does the word *shochad* itself mean? *Shehu k'chad* — that he becomes as one with the person from whom he received it. The word encodes the very dynamic it prohibits.

---

## Love & Hate

### Recusal Rule

Rav Pappa rules: *lo lidun inish dina l'man d'rachim leh* — a person should not judge a case involving someone he loves, *v'lo l'man d'sani leh* — nor someone he hates. This applies even to a mild positive or negative inclination, not only to the formally established categories of *ohev v'soneh* with which *halacha* is familiar.

### Love & Hate Effects

The reasoning follows directly from Rava's analysis: *d'rachim leh lo chazi leh chova* — one who loves the litigant will be unable to perceive any negative point against him; *d'sani leh lo chazi leh zachusa* — one who hates him will be unable to perceive any merit in his favor. The blindness is not necessarily willful; it is the natural consequence of a distorted lens.

---

## Community Love

### Beloved Rabbi

Abaye offers a sobering observation about communal dynamics: *hai tzurva meirabanan d'merachmin leh bnei masa* — a Torah scholar who is universally beloved by his community — *lav mishum d'maali tvei* — do not take this as evidence that he is exceptional. *Ella mishum d'lo mochech lhu b'milei d'shmaya* — rather, it likely reflects the fact that he is not doing his job: he is not rebuking them, not setting them straight, not challenging them in matters of heaven. They love him because he tells them what they want to hear.

### Rava's Realization

Rava offers a personal reflection. *Meireish havah amina hani bnei Mechuza kulhu rachmu li* — at first I thought that all the people of Mechuza loved me. We know that Rava had a complicated relationship with the cosmopolitan inhabitants of Mechuza. Once he became a judge and was forced to rule against some of them, he revised his assessment: *minaihu sanu li u'minaihu rachmu li* — some of them hate me and some of them love me. He had initially assumed that universal love reflected his personal qualities; he later understood that the moment one begins ruling against people, love becomes selective.

### Accept Both

The deeper realization: *d'man d'mechayev leh hai idna mazchei leh l'machar* — the one I ruled against today I may rule in favor of tomorrow. Since the same person who is ruled against in one case will be ruled for in another, the idea that one can calibrate one's rulings to achieve universal approval is simply false. Rava concluded: *im rachmu kulhu rachmu li v'im sanu kulhu sanu li* — whatever they feel about me, they feel. A judge who is trying to be universally liked is not a good judge; you cannot satisfy everyone, and eventually you must accept that some will love you and some will hate you depending on when they appear before you and what you are forced to rule. This is, as the *Gemara* presents it, a genuinely liberating insight for anyone who must render judgment or teach with integrity.

---

## Non-Monetary Bribes

### Verbal Bribes

A *braita* establishes: *eino tzarich lomar shochad mamon* — it goes without saying that monetary bribes are prohibited; *ela afilu shochad devarim nami assur* — even *shochad devarim*, which the *Gemara* will illustrate with actions and services rather than words, is also forbidden. The word *devarim* here may be read as "things" or "matters" rather than specifically "words," and the examples that follow make clear it encompasses non-verbal favors and services.

### Shmuel Bridge

Shmuel was crossing a bridge when a certain man came and gave him his hand to help him across. Shmuel asked: what brings you here? The man replied: I have a court case before you — I was coming to the city for the judgment, so I helped you along the way. *Psilna lach ledina* — Shmuel declared: you have disqualified me from judging your case.

### Ameimar Feather

Ameimar was seated in judgment when a feather fell on his head. A certain man came and removed it. Ameimar asked him what he was doing; the man replied that he had a case before him. *Psilna lach ledina* — you have disqualified me.

### Mar Ukva Spit

Mar Ukva spat in front of him. A certain man came and covered the spit. Again, the man said he had a judgment before him. *Psilna lach ledina*.

What is notable in all three cases is that in each instance the person explicitly mentions the upcoming court case. This raises the question of whether the problem is specifically the framing — the fact that the favor was articulated in connection with the judgment — or whether any unsolicited favor, even without such mention, would suffice to disqualify. If someone had helped Shmuel across a bridge and only appeared in his court three hours later without any explicit connection being drawn, would recusal be required? Perhaps; but the *Gemara's* examples all feature the explicit verbal linking of the favor to the judgment. Whether *shochad devarim* requires that conscious framing by the benefactor, or whether the mere receipt of the favor creates the disqualification, is a question the *Gemara* does not resolve explicitly here.

---

## Sharecropper Fruit

### Early Fruit

Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yossi had a sharecropper who, every Friday, would bring him a basket of produce — his share from the fields the sharecropper worked. One Thursday, the sharecropper brought the basket a day early. Rabbi Yishmael asked: why the change? The sharecropper explained that he had to come into the city early because he had a court case, and since he was passing by anyway, he thought he would bring the produce ahead of schedule.

### Recusal & Replacement

Rabbi Yishmael refused to accept the basket: *psilna lach ledina* — you have disqualified me from judging your case. He appointed two other rabbis to hear the case in his stead.

### Unconscious Arguments

While the two rabbis were deliberating and Rabbi Yishmael was walking about nearby, he found himself thinking: *ei ba'ei ta'in hachi, ve'ei ba'ei ta'in hachi* — if he wants to argue this way he should, if he wants to argue that way he should. He was spontaneously generating arguments in favor of the sharecropper.

### Subconscious Bias

He exclaimed: *tipach nafsham shel mekablei shochad* — blasted be the souls of those who accept bribes! And then he reflected on his own situation: I refused to take the produce. And even had I taken it, it was mine — it was my legitimate portion of the field that was merely being delivered one day early. Yet even so, that slight early delivery, that small favor never actually accepted, was already generating unconscious advocacy on his behalf in my mind. *Al achat kama vechama hamekablei shochad* — how much more so those who actually accept bribes, even with every intention of judging fairly.

---

## First Shearings

### Shearings Delivery

Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Elisha — a *kohen* — was entitled to receive *reishit hagez*, the first shearings of a flock, from anyone in his vicinity. A certain man traveled a considerable distance to bring him these shearings. Rabbi Yishmael asked where he was from; when told, he asked: was there truly no *kohen* anywhere between there and here to whom you could have given this? The man admitted: I have a court case before you, and since I was traveling to the city anyway, I thought I would bring the shearings to you.

### Second Recusal

Rabbi Yishmael declared: *psilna lach ledina* — you have disqualified me. *Lo kabil minei* — he declined to accept the shearings. He again appointed two other rabbis to hear the case.

### Arguments Again

And again, while the rabbis were deliberating, Rabbi Yishmael found himself pacing and thinking: *ei baisun hachi, ei baisun hachi* — if they argue this way, if they argue that way. Again, arguments in favor of the man who had been coming to bring him his due were forming in his mind unbidden.

### Entitled Benefit

His reflection again: *tipach nafsham shel mekablei shochad* — blasted be the souls of those who accept bribes. I did not accept the shearings. And even had I accepted them, I was legally entitled to them — they were literally mine by right. Yet even the entitlement, even the knowledge that this man had made a journey to bring me something I was owed, was enough to color my thinking subconsciously. *Mekablei shochad al achat kama vechama* — those who actually accept bribes, however certain they are of their own intentions, cannot escape the mechanism that Rava identified: the gift creates identification, the identification creates blindness, and the blindness is impervious to good intentions.

---

---

# Ketubot 106

## Rav Anan & Gifts

### Fish Gift Rejected

The daf opens with a story about *Rav Anan*. A certain man brought him a basket of small fish and, when asked what brought him there, openly stated that he had a case in judgment. *Rav Anan* refused the gift. *Lo kabil minei* — he did not accept it — and told the man: "You have invalidated me from serving as your judge." This mirrors the earlier stories on the daf, where the rabbis not only recused themselves from judgment but refused to receive the accompanying gifts as well, even though in principle one could imagine doing one without the other. The man responded that he was content to have his case heard elsewhere — *dina demar lo beina* — but asked that *Rav Anan* at least accept the gift as a *mitzvah*, independent of any judicial role, because he wished to perform the act of *kiruvei bikkurim*.

### Gifts as Bikkurim

The man's argument invokes a *braita*: the verse in the story of *Elisha* describes a man bringing bread of *bikkurim* — twenty loaves of barley bread and *karmel* — to the *ish ha'Elohim*. The *gemara* asks: did *Elisha* eat *bikkurim*? *Rashi* attempts to prove that *Elisha* was not a *kohen*; *Tosafot* notes the simpler answer that they were not in *Yerushalayim* and this was not being brought to the *Beit HaMikdash*. Rather, *ela lomar lach* — the verse comes to teach — that anyone who brings a gift to a *talmid chacham* is as if he brought *bikkurim*. That is the *mitzvah* the man wished to perform.

### Aliyah & Rebbe

This moment opens a broader reflection on how *Chazal* dealt with the absence of the *Beit HaMikdash* and created meaningful substitutes. Most striking in this regard is the idea that just as there is a *mitzvah* of *aliyah laregel*, so too the *gemara* teaches there is a *mitzvah* of *mekabel pnei rabo baregel* — presenting oneself before one's *rebbe* on the festivals. The *rebbe* in some sense takes the place of the *Beit HaMikdash* as the destination of spiritual pilgrimage. This is already hinted at in the *pesukim* themselves. The husband of the *Shunamit* says to her: *madua at holechet elav hayom lo chodesh velo Shabbat* — why are you going to him today, it is neither *Rosh Chodesh* nor *Shabbat*? — indicating that one of the practices of the time was to travel to the *ish Elohim* on *Shabbat* and spend the day in spiritual communion. And in *Yeshayahu* the vision of the end of days includes *umidei Shabbat beshabbato yavo kol basar lehishtachavot lefanai* — each *Shabbat* all flesh will come to prostrate before God. The *ish Elohim* in *Shmuel* and the eschatological vision in *Yeshayahu* share the same rhythm, and that pattern becomes the foundation for *mekabel pnei rav* as the post-*Beit HaMikdash* substitute for *aliyah laregel*.

### Gift Accepted

Returning to the story: the *gemara* concludes that *Rav Anan*, upon hearing the man's reasoning, accepted the gift. *Hashta d'amart li ta'ama* — now that you've given me a proper rationale — perhaps the explanation also freed the gift from any taint of *shochad* by reframing it entirely, *mikabelna*. He accepted it. But he would still not serve as the man's judge. And, as we will see, the story does not end there.

## Nachman & Bias

### Referral Letter

Because the man still needed his case heard, *Rav Anan* sent him before *Rav Nachman* and accompanied the referral with a letter: *dayneye l'mar l'hai gavra* — please hear this man's case — *d'ana Anan pasilna lei l'dina* — for I, *Anan*, am invalid to serve as his judge.

### Misinterpretation

There are multiple reasons one might be invalid as a judge. When *Rav Nachman* received this message, *mideshlach li hachi shma mina kriveye hu* — since he sent me this, it must be that this person is his relative — and that is why *Rav Anan* had to recuse himself.

### Two Mitzvot

At that moment, *Rav Nachman* had before him a case involving orphans. When the letter arrived requesting he hear this other man's case, he recognized that he faced two *mitzvot*: the obligation to adjudicate the orphans' case — a general *mitzvah* of *ushfatetem tzedek*, and as the *Maharsha* adds, also the *mitzvah* of *lo takiru panim bamishpat k'katon k'gadol tishm'un* with its particular application to vulnerable parties like orphans — and, on the other side, the *mitzvah* of *kavod Torah*, since hearing this man's case first would show honor to *Rav Anan* and thereby to *Torah* itself.

### Orphans Suspended

*Rav Nachman* resolved to set aside the orphans' case and hear this man's case first: *salik l'dina d'yasmei v'achtei l'dineye*.

### Silenced Party

The consequence was immediate and devastating. When the opposing litigant saw that *Rav Nachman* was setting aside the orphans' case to hear this man's — apparently because he had arrived with a letter from *Rav Anan* — it appeared to him as unambiguous favoritism. *Istatam tanateye* — he was silenced. He did not feel free to fully articulate his claim and position, because he perceived that the outcome was already determined.

### Bias & Perception

This story is striking in several respects. The earlier stories on the daf illustrated how a bribe, even when refused, exerts subconscious influence on the judge. Here, *Rav Nachman* received no bribe at all. He merely believed the man to be *Rav Anan*'s relative, and he was not even trying to favor the litigant himself — he was trying to honor *Rav Anan*. Yet even that action, taken for entirely legitimate reasons, was sufficient to silence the opposing party and potentially pervert the course of justice. The question is not only whether the judge will be impartial, but what messages his actions communicate and how those messages affect the people whose cases are being heard.

This dynamic appears in real-world settings as well. In cases heard before *batei din*, including those with strong reputations for fairness, similar dynamics can arise: a woman appearing before an all-male court may already feel inhibited from fully stating her case; if the *dayanim* happen to know the other party socially and exchange greetings with him at the outset, the effect on the opposing side can be immediate and silencing, regardless of whether any actual bias exists. The lesson is that it is not sufficient that the judge be impartial in his own mind; the culture, conduct, and visible signals within the courtroom must themselves be beyond reproach. *Kavod Torah* is a genuine consideration, but when it conflicts with the integrity of *din*, the *gemara* here suggests it must yield.

One might ask whether there is also an issue of *chalishut ha-da'at* — the harm caused to a party who has had their case interrupted mid-hearing. The *Maharsha* discusses this in connection with *Sanhedrin*. But the primary emphasis here is on the way in which even well-intentioned judicial conduct communicates bias and suppresses the speech of litigants.

## Anan & Eliyahu

### Eliyahu Visits

*Rav Anan* had a standing relationship with *Eliyahu HaNavi*: *Rav Anan havei ragil Eliyahu de-ati gabei* — *Eliyahu* would regularly come to visit him. During these visits, *Eliyahu* taught him *Seder de-Eliyahu*, that collection of stories and teachings associated with *Eliyahu HaNavi* — specifically *Seder Eliyahu Rabba* and *Seder Eliyahu Zuta*, as we will see in a moment.

### Eliyahu Withdrawn

*Keivan de-avad hachi* — once *Rav Anan* acted as he did — sending the letter, accepting the fish — *Eliyahu* withdrew. *Istalek*. This is a remarkable consequence, particularly because *Rav Anan* had not acted with malicious intent. Yet as noted, the problem is often not what one deliberately does, but what one fails to think through — the unintended consequences of one's actions.

### Fast & Fear

*Rav Anan* sat in a fast, *yativ be-ta'anita*, and prayed for mercy, *u-va'ei rachamei*, and *Eliyahu* returned. But when *Eliyahu* came back, *Rav Anan* was frightened of him — *havei miv-it lei be-vuta'ei* — perhaps in the wake of the withdrawal.

### Box Teaching

To manage his fear, *Rav Anan* constructed a box and sat inside it while *Eliyahu* continued to teach him — *ve-avad teivuta ve-yativ kamei* — until *Eliyahu* finished imparting the complete *seder* to him. This is the origin of the two versions: *Seder Eliyahu Rabba* and *Seder Eliyahu Zuta*.

### Rabba vs Zuta

*Rashi* explains that *Seder Eliyahu Rabba* is what was taught *outside* the box, and *Seder Eliyahu Zuta* is what was taught *inside* the box, without explaining why one is larger than the other. *Tosafot* explains: *Eliyahu* had already taught *Rav Anan* the majority of the material before the incident, and so the first, larger portion — taught before the disruption — is called *Rabba*, and the smaller remaining portion — taught within the box — is called *Zuta*. Perhaps, too, the teaching inside the box was of somewhat lesser quality or depth.

### Mida Kneged Mida

The *Maharsha* identifies a principle of *mida keneged mida* in the two aspects of *Rav Anan*'s response. The *ta'anit* served as atonement for having accepted the fish — even though his acceptance was grounded in a legitimate argument about *bikkurim*, he now acknowledged it was a mistake. The trembling before *Eliyahu* and the need to create a barrier — the box — corresponded to what *Rav Anan*'s actions had caused the opposing litigant to experience: the silencing, the pulling back, the fear to speak freely when one senses that the dynamic in the room is working against you. *Rav Anan* now experienced, in a different register, precisely what his conduct had imposed on another.

## Yosef & Famine

### Famine Prayer

The *gemara* shifts to a passage set in the years of *Rav Yosef*. There was *ritcha* — divine anger, meaning famine — and the rabbis asked *Rav Yosef* to pray for its removal.

### Elisha Precedent

*Rav Yosef* responded by pointing to the precedent of *Elisha*: in *Elisha*'s time there was also divine anger, *de-havi rabanan miftari mikamei* — when the rabbis would leave *Elisha*'s learning — *havei payshei trei alfein u'masan rabanan* — there would still be 2,200 rabbis remaining in the *beis medrash*. And even in a time of *ritcha*, *Elisha* did not pray to remove the divine anger — or at least there is no record in *Tanach* that he did. *Rav Yosef*'s implicit point: even at that level of Torah stature, prayer was not offered. How much more so should I not be expected to do so?

### 2200 Students

One might ask: how do we know that *Elisha* had 2,200 students? The source is the verse in which *Elisha*'s attendant says *u'mah eten zeh lifnei meah ish* — how shall I set this before 100 men? The verse refers back to the same *pasuk* that opened our discussion of *bikkurim*: the man from *Ba'al Shalishah* brought twenty loaves of barley bread and *karmel*.

### Bread Math

The calculation: if those 22 loaves were distributed, one per 100 men — each loaf set before 100 people — then 22 loaves times 100 people equals 2,200 people total. That is the size of the *talmidim* who remained in *Elisha*'s *beis medrash*.

## Yeshiva Decline

### Rav: 1,200

The *gemara* traces the decline of *yeshiva* enrollment across generations. When the rabbis would leave the *yeshiva* of *Rav*, there would remain *alfa u'masan rabanan* — 1,200 rabbis still in the *beis medrash*.

### Huna: 800

When the rabbis left the *yeshiva* of *Rav Huna*, there would remain 800 rabbis. *Rav Huna* taught with 13 *amoraim* — not *amoraim* in the sense of the rabbinic generation, but in the technical sense of the role: the *amora* was the *rav*'s loudspeaker, who would repeat and project the teacher's words to different sections of the large assembly hall. With 13 such figures distributed throughout the room, the scope of *Rav Huna*'s audience can be appreciated.

### Dust Covers Sun

When the rabbis would rise from *Rav Huna*'s *masivta* and shake out their garments, *havei salik avka* — dust would rise up — *ve'kasei leh leyoma* — and cover the sun, darkening the day. In *Eretz Yisrael* they would say: *kamu lehu mimasivta deRav Huna deBavel* — the Babylonian *yeshiva* of *Rav Huna* has finished.

### Rava & Yosef: 400

When the rabbis left the *yeshiva* of *Rava* and *Rav Yosef*, there remained 400 rabbis. *Ve-karu le-nafshaihu yasmei* — they called themselves orphans. Given the size of the previous generations — 2,200 under *Elisha*, 1,200 under *Rav*, 800 under *Rav Huna* — the descent to 400 felt like bereavement.

### Later: 200

When the rabbis left the *yeshiva* of *Abaye*, or according to others the *yeshiva* of *Rav Pappa*, or *Rav Ashi*, there remained only 200 rabbis. *Ve-karu le-nafshaihu yasmei de-yasmei* — orphans of orphans — so small a remnant compared to what had been.

## Temple Payments

### Blemish Inspectors

The *gemara* returns to the principal theme of the chapter, which emerged from the *Mishnah*'s reference to *shnei dayanei gezerot* and the question of their payment from communal funds. *Rav Yitzchak bar Redifa* said in the name of *Avani*: those in *Yerushalayim* whose role it was to inspect animals for blemishes — *mevakrim mumin she-be-Yerushalayim* — received their salary from *terumat ha-lishka*, the communal funds collected annually for the *korbanot*. When there were surplus funds from the *lishka*, they were also available for other Temple-related or communal services. The inspection of blemishes is clearly *tzorchei korban* — directly connected to the sacrificial service.

### Shechita Teachers

*Rav Yehuda* said in the name of *Shmuel*: the *talmidei chachamim* who taught the *kohanim* the *hilchot shechita* also received their pay from *terumat ha-lishka*, for this too falls under *tzorchei korban*. This calls to mind the stories at the beginning of *Yoma* about teaching the *Kohen Gadol* the laws of the *avoda*. The role of teaching the *halachot* is distinct from the physical transmission of practical skill — a *kohen* may receive the practical skill through tradition, but the legal framework governing each scenario had to be formally studied. Hence it is classified as a Temple service deserving communal support.

### Kemitza Teachers

*Rav Giddel* said in the name of *Rav*: those *talmidei chachamim* who taught the *kohanim* the *hilchot kemitza* similarly received their salary from *terumat ha-lishka*. The same principle applies: it is the legal dimension of the service — what constitutes a valid *kemitza*, what invalidates it — that requires instruction, and that instruction is considered integral to the *korban* service.

### Torah Proofers

*Rabba bar bar Chana* said in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: those who proofread *sifrei Torah* in *Yerushalayim* — *maggihei sefarim she-be-Yerushalayim* — also received their payment from *terumat ha-lishka*. This is more surprising, because proofreading *sifrei Torah* is not directly connected to the *korbanot*. As we will continue to see on this daf, *terumat ha-lishka* and particularly *shiyarei terumat ha-lishka* served as a broad catch-all for a range of Temple-related and communal needs. *Rashi* here notes the relevant justification: *lev beit din matne aleihem* — the *beit din* reserved the authority to reassign these funds as it saw fit. Anyone donating the *shekalim* understood that the ultimate disposition of the money lay with the *beit din*'s discretion, even if the primary purpose was the *korbanot*.

### Parochet Weavers

*Rav Nachman* said in the name of *Rabbah bar Avuha*: the women who wove the *parochet* — the curtain for the *Beit HaMikdash* — also received their payment from *terumat ha-lishka*. This immediately prompts a question: is the *parochet* related to the *korbanot* or is it really a structural element of the *Beit HaMikdash*, which would place it under *bedek ha-bayit*?

The *gemara* cites a dissenting view: *ve'ani omer mi-kodshei bedek ha-bayit* — I say it comes from *bedek ha-bayit* — *hu parochet tachat binyan asuyot* — because the *parochet* is made underneath the roofed structure. The logic is that something hanging within a roofed enclosure becomes part of the structure itself, not merely a suspended object. This distinction has a fascinating parallel in *hilchot Shabbat*: if one hangs a curtain across an open doorway, according to the *Chazon Ish* one is adding to the structure and not merely decorating it, making it more like installing a door than hanging a picture on a wall. The *parochet* hanging within the *heichal* functions similarly — it is integral to the architectural space.

The *gemara* then raises an objection from a *braita*: the women weaving the *parochet*, the *Beis Garmo* who taught the preparation of *lechem ha-panim*, and the *Beis Avtinas* who knew how to prepare the *ketoret* — all of them received their pay from *terumat ha-lishka*, not from *bedek ha-bayit*. The *gemara* resolves the contradiction: *hatam be-divavi* — that *braita* refers to the curtains hanging in the gates, which were in the open, unroofed areas of the Temple complex. Those would indeed be classified differently — more like a *kli* than part of the *binyan*.

### 13 Parochet

*Rav Zeira* said in the name of *Rav*: there were thirteen *parochet* curtains in the *Beit HaMikdash*. Seven corresponded to the seven gates. One was for the opening of the *heichal*, one for the opening of the *ulam*. Two were in the *dvir* — the *Kodesh HaKodashim* — and two corresponding ones above, since the *heichal* complex was a double-story structure. The curtains within the roofed structure — the *ulam*, *heichal*, and *dvir* — fall into the category of *bedek ha-bayit*; those at the gates in the open courtyards fall under *terumat ha-lishka*. Where a *parochet* does not come under *bedek ha-bayit*, it defaults to *terumat ha-lishka*, even though *terumat ha-lishka* is in principle designated for *korbanot* rather than all of these auxiliary purposes.

## Fund Sources

### Para Aduma

The *gemara* continues with another case. The women who raised their children for the *para aduma* service also received their support from *terumat ha-lishka*. The background: the *Tzadokim* maintained that the *kohen* performing the burning of the *para aduma* could never have been *tamei* at any point. The *Chachamim*, in a remarkable counter-move, deliberately arranged for the *kohen* to become *tamei* and then immerse in a *mikveh*, so that he would be a *tvul yom* at the time of the service — thereby demonstrating through practice that the law followed their understanding, not the *Tzadokim*'s. This very leniency on one end was balanced by extraordinary stringencies in other areas of *tahara* related to the *para aduma*. One of those stringencies involved raising children in conditions of guaranteed *tahara* from birth. Pregnant women would give birth in specially constructed spaces above caves, where the cave ceiling would block any potential *tumat ha-met* from bodies buried in the earth below. The children born there were raised entirely in those conditions, and they would assist in the preparatory stages of the *para aduma* service. The communal funds of *terumat ha-lishka* provided the financial support for the women maintaining these households.

*Abba Shaul* offers an alternative: the prominent women of *Yerushalayim* — *nashim yakirot she-be-Yerushalayim* — would voluntarily provide food, clothing, and other support for these women and children, so that the burden did not need to fall on *terumat ha-lishka* at all. *Rashi* specifies *levush u-chsut* as among the provisions — echoing the *zona u-mefarnes* language familiar from the laws of *ketuba*.

### Vessels Source

*Rav Huna* asked *Rav*: what is the source for the *klei shares*, the Temple service vessels? Do they come from *kodshei bedek ha-bayit*, or not? The framing of the question reflects what we have learned: *bedek ha-bayit* funds are for structural matters, while *terumat ha-lishka* is the catch-all for everything else. The vessels could be seen as *tzorech mizbe'ach* — connected to the altar, which is so large and fixed it functions almost as part of the structure itself, suggesting *bedek ha-bayit* — or as *tzorech korban* — used in the actual bringing of *korbanot*, suggesting *terumat ha-lishka*.

### Vessels Answer

*Rav* answered: they come from *terumat ha-lishka*.

### Proof Text

The *gemara* immediately challenges this from *Divrei HaYamim*: *vaya'asu keilim le-veis Hashem klei shares* — they made service vessels for the *Beit HaShem* — and the context is the leftover money from the *bedek ha-bayit* collection. This appears to show that the *klei shares* came from *bedek ha-bayit* funds.

### Melachim Version

The parallel account in *Melachim* resolves this: *ach lo ye'aseh beis Hashem safos kesef... hem le-melacha yisnehu* — the money collected for the *Beit HaShem* was not to be used for vessels, but was to be given to the craftsmen who would work on the structure. This directly contradicts the *Divrei HaYamim* passage.

### Lev Beis Din

The *gemara* resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya* — there is no difficulty. *Kan she-gavu ve-hosiru kan she-gavu ve-lo hosiru* — in one case they had collected and had a surplus; in the other they had collected and did not have a surplus. In principle, *bedek ha-bayit* funds are collected and designated specifically for structural purposes, not for *klei shares*. But if there were leftover funds, the *beit din* could reassign them. How is this reassignment legitimate? *Rabbi Abbahu* invokes the principle of *lev beis din matne aleihem*: the *beit din* stipulates in advance — *im hutzrechu hutzrechu, ve-im lav yehu le-klei shares* — if the money is needed for *bedek ha-bayit*, it will be used for that; if not, it will go to *klei shares*. Anyone contributing to the fund does so with the understanding that the *beit din* retains ultimate discretion over its use.

This principle consistently recurs in these discussions. The underlying assumption is that the *beit din* — conceived in the *gemara*'s framework as the rabbinic authority — holds ultimate oversight over Temple finances, an idealized picture that, historically, would have been complicated by the dominant role of the *kohanim* in actual Temple administration. As one might observe, the historical reality was that the *kohanim* ran the institution and the rabbis were largely outside its precincts, often in tension with the *Tzadokim* among the priestly class. The *gemara* retrospectively imagines an arrangement in which rabbinic authority supervises everything — *lev beit din matne aleihem*, not *lev kohanim matne aleihem* — a projection of rabbinic self-understanding onto the Temple era.

## Tannaim Debate

### Yishmael View

*Tana debei Rabbi Yishmael* states: *klei shares ba'in mi-terumat ha-lishka* — the Temple vessels come from *terumat ha-lishka*. The proof text is *es shear ha-kesef* — the remainder of the money. In context, this verse appears in the narrative about money collected for *bedek ha-bayit*, but *tana debei Rabbi Yishmael* understands *shear ha-kesef* as a reference to the *terumat ha-lishka*.

### Shirei Option

One might ask: perhaps *shear ha-kesef* means literally the *shirei terumat ha-lishka* — the leftover surplus — rather than the main body of the *terumat ha-lishka* fund? On that reading, the vessels would come not from the primary *terumat ha-lishka* but only from any unspent remainder.

### Kesef Rishon

The *gemara* rejects this. The word *hakesef* — with the definite article — focuses attention on the money itself, not on its remainder. Drawing on *Rava*'s interpretation of *zot torat ha-olah* — where the *heh* indicates the primary *olah*, the *olat ha-tamid*, which precedes all others — so too here: *hakesef* signals *kesef rishon*, the main fund. The vessels come from the primary *terumat ha-lishka*, not merely from its surplus.

### Main Items

The list of items that come from *terumat ha-lishka* thus includes: the *ketoret*, all communal *korbanot*, the golden altar, and the service vessels.

### Motar Nesachim

However, a competing *braita* presents a different source for the golden altar and the *klei shares*: they come from *motar nesachim* — the surplus of the libation funds. The practice was that when one donated funds for the *nesachim* accompanying a *korban*, one would intentionally provide slightly more than the required amount to ensure sufficiency; the *Beit HaMikdash* would level off the measure, and the small excess would be set aside for *hekdesh*. Over time, all these small surpluses accumulated into meaningful sums. According to this view, it was those accumulated funds — *motar nesachim* — that financed the *klei shares*, a somewhat counterintuitive assignment that may reflect the practical reality that the *klei shares* did not need frequent replacement and the accumulated *motar nesachim* was roughly equivalent in scale to what was needed.

### Building Funds

The outer altar — *mizbe'ach ha-olah* — together with the *lishkot* and the *azarot*, the chambers and the courtyards of the Temple complex, come from *bedek ha-bayit*. This is clear: these are the fundamental structural elements.

### City Needs

Any construction outside the walls of the *azara* — but still on the Temple Mount or in its vicinity — comes from *shiyarei ha-lishka*, the surplus of the *terumat ha-lishka* fund, which was regularly used for a broader range of communal purposes. The same source provides for the walls and towers of the city of *Yerushalayim* and all the *tzorchei ha-ir* — the general municipal needs of the city. The walls of *Yerushalayim* are not merely civil infrastructure; they are bound up with the *kedushah* of the *Beit HaMikdash* itself, since it is the wall of *Yerushalayim* that defines the *kedushah* of the *Mikdash*'s environs.

## Leftover Funds

### Kayitz Concept

The *gemara* addresses the *tannaitic* dispute over what to do with the leftover *truma* funds. The first opinion: *motar peirot l'kayitz ha-mizbe'ach* — the surplus was used to keep the *mizbe'ach* active, *kayitz ha-mizbe'ach*. The etymology is disputed: some derive it from *l'hakitz*, to awaken or rouse; others associate it with *kayitz*, the summer, as in something left idle — and just as one does not want fruit to sit unused in summer, so one does not want the *mizbe'ach* to stand idle. The concern was genuine: if there were periods — even within a single day — when no *korbanot* were being brought, the *mizbe'ach* would stand empty, an embarrassment to the institution. The solution was to ensure that communal *korbanot* would be offered during those intervals, funded by the surplus.

### Buy Low Sell High

The operational model under this first opinion: the *Beit HaMikdash* would purchase fruit cheaply and sell it at higher prices, and the profits would go toward the *kayitz ha-mizbe'ach*. The *Beit HaMikdash* was in a unique position to execute this — it had something approaching a monopoly and a captive market of pilgrims arriving for the *regalim*.

### Yishmael View

*Rabbi Yishmael* proposed a more targeted version of this business model: buy wines, oils, and fine flours — precisely the materials that pilgrims arriving at the *Beit HaMikdash* would need for their *nesachim* and *korbanot* — and use the profits from these sales to fund the operating expenses of the *Beit HaMikdash*. The strategic logic is clear: these were items in guaranteed demand, and the institutional position of the *Beit HaMikdash* made it uniquely positioned to profit from that demand.

### Akiva Objection

*Rabbi Akiva* objected on principle: *ein mishtakrin be-shel hekdesh* — one does not use *hekdesh* money for commercial profit. There is something fundamentally degrading about turning the funds of the *Beit HaMikdash* into business capital. *Ein aniyut bi-mkom ashirut* — there is no poverty where there is wealth — meaning that *hekdesh* ought to embody and project an image of transcendent abundance, and subjecting it to the contingencies and indignities of the marketplace undermines that dignity.

### Poor People

*Rabbi Akiva* pressed a second objection regarding the parallel case of charity funds: *af lo be-shel aniyim* — one also does not invest funds belonging to the poor. *Dilma mitrami lehu ani ve-leika le-mitav leh* — a poor person may need the money immediately, and if the funds are tied up in an investment, they will not be available when urgently needed. The principle extends naturally to institutional funds generally: an endowment may earn returns, but its primary obligation is to the constituency it serves, and availability matters as much as yield. The *gemara* here touches on a set of questions with obvious resonance for any institution that holds funds in trust for those who depend on them.

# Ketubot 107

## Rav vs. Shmuel

### Rav's Position

The daf begins at the very bottom of 106b, where the Gemara takes up the mishna concerning the *shnei dayanei gezerot* and the case of *Admon*. Among Admon's rulings was the scenario of someone who traveled overseas (*limdinat hayam*) and left his wife without provision. Admon holds that the wife takes an oath at the end of the process — presumably when it comes time to collect her full *ketuba* upon his death, at which point she swears that nothing had been prepaid and that her collection of *mezonot* was conducted properly. The *bnei kohanim gedolim*, by contrast, require an oath at the beginning as well, ensuring that before she draws on the estate she genuinely deserves the money. Admon's concern is the wife's immediate need: should the *shvua* stand in the way of her being provided for? The Gemara does not fully spell out what divides the two positions, but it opens, at the top of 107a, with the dispute between Rav and Shmuel, which frames the entire discussion.

The case is stated plainly: *mi shehalach limdinat hayam* — a husband has gone overseas. Rav rules *poskin mezonot l'eshet ish*: *beit din* assesses the situation and provides an allowance for the wife. As Rashi explains, *beit din yordin lenichsei mi shehalach limdinat hayam uposkin mezonot leishto* — the court descends to the husband's property and liquidates assets as necessary to feed his wife, since he carries a clear *ketuba* obligation to support her.

### Shmuel's Objection

Shmuel disagrees: *ein poskin mezonot l'eshet ish*. One should not do this. Shmuel himself, however, concedes that Rav would agree with him on one point: *bishlosha chadashim harishonim* — in the first three months, even Rav would not yet seize the property. The reason is *lefi she'ein adam maniach beito reikam*: we do not assume a person would be so irresponsible as to leave his household entirely unprovided for. This already signals the logic behind Shmuel's broader position — we simply do not know what arrangements may have been made, and we must give the husband some benefit of the doubt.

The Gemara then clarifies where agreement ends and dispute begins. If the husband has been heard to have died (*sheshamu bo shemet*), nobody disagrees: the wife is supported as a widow from the estate. The dispute concerns only the case where no such report has arrived and the husband is simply absent. Rav rules *poskin*, since he is obligated to support her and is merely not physically present. Shmuel rules *ein poskin*, and two explanations are offered for his position. One: *emma tzerorei atfsa* — perhaps he had already set aside money for her, a bundle of funds deposited on her behalf. The other, offered by Rav Pappa: *chaishinan shema amar lah tzei ma'aseh yadayich bimzonotayich* — perhaps he had told her that in his absence her own labor would substitute for his obligation to feed her, so that she would keep her earnings in lieu of receiving *mezonot* from him.

Rashi and Tosafot both address whether the husband could make such an arrangement unilaterally or whether her agreement was required, and both conclude — though this is not straightforward from the Gemara itself — that the case involves her having agreed to it. The underlying issue goes back to earlier discussions about whose interest is protected by the exchange of *mezonot* for *ma'aseh yadayim*. In any case, Shmuel's point is that we cannot know which of these arrangements was in place, and therefore we cannot move to seize the husband's property on the basis of her claim alone.

One might then ask: why not simply require her to take a *shvua* and resolve the doubt? The general rule of *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'aya* places the burden of proof on the one seeking to extract money. Here, no one is explicitly denying her claim; the husband is simply absent. Yet Shmuel apparently feels the doubt is serious enough that a *shvua* would not suffice to override it and justify seizing someone's property. That seems to be at least part of the reason why the debate between Admon and the *bnei kohanim gedolim* about the timing of the *shvua* is relevant, though the Gemara leaves this somewhat open.

The Gemara then asks why there is no dispute in the case where the husband has actually died. Even there, after all, he might have set aside money for her, or they might have made the arrangement about her labor. Rashi addresses the *tzerorei* concern by noting that when she eventually collects her *ketuba* she must take a *shvua* that she has not pre-collected, and that resolves the matter. As for the *ma'aseh yadayim* arrangement — that cannot apply to the heirs; whatever he agreed to during his lifetime does not automatically bind the estate, and any new arrangement would have to be contracted afresh. Tosafot takes a different approach: the presumption that the husband made some arrangement (*ein adam maniach beito reikam*) is only reasonable when he is alive and presumably acting responsibly. Death, however, is not something people arrange for, and therefore we cannot extend the presumption to a man who has actually died. That is why, once he is dead, the doubts Shmuel raises no longer apply, and everyone agrees to support the wife.

### Abaye's Distinction

Abaye points out a practical difference between the two explanations of Shmuel's position. The case to consider is either: an adult wife who does not earn enough to support herself (*gedola v'lo safka*) — perhaps she has no marketable skills, or as Rashi explains, it is a time of famine and food is prohibitively expensive — or: a minor wife who does earn enough to support herself (*ktana v'safka*). These two scenarios pull in opposite directions depending on which of Shmuel's rationales one adopts.

If the concern is *tzerorei* — that the husband set aside funds — that presumption applies only to an adult wife, someone capable of taking possession of money and managing it responsibly. A husband would not deposit a sum of money for a minor wife who cannot be entrusted with it. So if the case involves a minor, the *tzerorei* concern evaporates, and we might well go ahead and provide for her.
