But if she is an adult who cannot earn her own keep, then *tzerorei* remains a live concern and we would not provide. Conversely, the *ma'aseh yadayim* concern — that he told her to work for herself — is meaningful only when she can actually do so. If she is an adult who cannot earn enough to live on, that arrangement was never a real option, and therefore we would provide for her. But if she is a minor who can earn, we would say perhaps such an arrangement is operative here. These are the *ikei beinayhu*, the practical differences between the two explanations.

---

## Mishna & Death

### Admon & Priests

The Gemara now turns to the text of the mishna itself. *Mi shehalach limdinat hayam v'ishto tova'at mezonot* — a man goes overseas and his wife demands support. *Chanan omer tishava basof* — Chanan says she takes an oath at the end, not at the outset. The *bnei kohanim gedolim* disagree and say she must swear both at the beginning and at the end.

The Gemara immediately clarifies: *ad kan lo pligi ela l'inyan shevu'ah* — their dispute is only about the oath. But as for actually giving her *mezonot*, all agree that she receives them — *aval mezonei yahvinan lah*. This directly contradicts Shmuel, who holds that we do not provide *mezonot* when the husband is merely absent. The Gemara therefore reports that Shmuel interpreted the mishna — *targama Shmuel b'sheshamu bo shemet* — as referring to a case where the husband has been reported dead, and the woman is being supported as a presumed widow. Of course, this reading is strained: if the man is dead, why does the mishna introduce him as someone who went overseas? It should simply say *mi shemet*. Nevertheless, this is Shmuel's *tirutz*.

### He Set Aside Money

A *braita* is cited that appears to expand on the mishna. The husband goes overseas, the wife demands support, and the *bnei kohanim gedolim* say she must take an oath while Chanan says she need not. Then: *v'im ba v'amar pasakti lah mezonot ne'eman* — if the husband returns and says he had already made arrangements for her support, he is believed. The question is when this claim is being made: if he has returned and made the claim, why did the matter need to go to *beit din* in the first place? It seems the scenario is that *beit din* had already acted — selling off property to feed her — and only then did the husband return and protest that he had already made arrangements.

### Rashi & Tosafot

Rashi explains that the husband is saying he had set aside money for her — *af tafsa tzerori* — a box of funds she could have drawn from. He is believed, and she must return what *beit din* disbursed — *umachzeret mah shenatna lah beis din*. But why is he simply believed if she currently holds the money? Rashi resolves this by saying he must take a *shvua* in support of his claim.

Tosafot's Ri offers a different reading: *ne'eman l'hatrichah shvuah* — he is believed to the extent that she must now swear to him. That is, rather than forcing her to return the money, we impose an oath on her: she swears that he did not in fact make the arrangement he claims. She does not automatically pay back the money, but she must now substantiate her position under oath. These two readings leave the practical mechanics of the case somewhat unclear, but both agree that the original seizure of property — before any such claim was made — was legitimate, and this is precisely the kind of scenario where Shmuel has to intervene and explain things away.

### Rumors Exaggerated

The Gemara adds: *hacha nami b'sheshamu bo shemet* — this too, says Shmuel, is the case where the husband had been reported dead. But then how could he come back? *Im ba achar shemuah* — like Mark Twain, the rumors of his death were greatly exaggerated. We had heard that he died, we treated his wife as a widow and supported her from the estate, and it turned out he was alive all along. According to Shmuel, this actually makes the ending of the *braita* more intelligible: since Shmuel holds that one should never sell off the property of a living husband, the fact that we did so and then he returned to protest makes perfect sense — we shouldn't have done it at all, and now that he's back and saying he had set aside money, we'll believe him.

A second *braita* makes the same point. The husband is overseas, the wife demands support, and the text says: *im ba v'amar tzei ma'aseh yadayich bimzonotayich* — if he comes and says she should have provided for herself from her own labor, he is permitted to say so. Again, Rashi notes that if *beit din* had already acted and sold property — *ma shepasqu pasqu* — that stands. And again, this *braita* explicitly acknowledges the two scenarios Shmuel uses to explain his position: the possibility that money was set aside (*pasakti lah mezonot*) and the possibility that a *ma'aseh yadayim* arrangement was made (*tzei ma'aseh yadayich bimzonotayich*). From Shmuel's perspective, the *braisos* themselves show these are live possibilities, which is precisely why we should not assume they are absent and proceed to seize property. Yet the simple reading of all these *braisos* is that *beit din* does provide for the wife as a matter of course, and deals with any such claims by the husband only if and when he comes forward with them.

---

## Children Case

### Wife Not Children

A third *braita* is cited and proves to be the most powerful challenge to Shmuel. *Beit din yordin lenichsav vezonin umfarnisin l'ishto* — the court descends to the husband's property and provides for his wife — *aval lo banav uvenosav* — but not for his sons and daughters, and not for anything else. This is a decisive proof against Shmuel's reading that all these cases presume the husband to be dead. If we were presuming the husband dead, then his sons would inherit and his daughters would be supported as *yetomot* from the estate. The very fact that the sons and daughters are excluded demonstrates that we are presupposing the husband is *alive* — we are simply exacting his existing legal obligation to feed his wife. Sons and daughters are excluded because a father has no legal obligation to feed his children beyond a very young age; his wife is a different matter entirely.

### Trustee Appointed

Rav Sheshet responds: *b'mashlish et ishto bidei shalish* — this is the case where the husband had appointed a trustee to manage disbursements to his wife. That trustee has now either left for overseas himself or the funds in his care have been exhausted. So we are not acting in ignorance of what arrangement the husband made — we know precisely what arrangement he made, and we know it has lapsed. That is why we now descend to his property: the previously-known arrangement is gone, and the doubt Shmuel raises about possible alternative arrangements no longer applies.

The Gemara then asks: if so, why not also provide for the sons and daughters? Presumably if the husband was organized enough to appoint a trustee, he cared about his whole household. The Gemara answers: *kesheshlish lezu v'lo hishlish lezu* — he made the arrangement specifically for his wife, not for his sons and daughters. His legal obligation ran to his wife; it is entirely reasonable that he funded his legal obligation and not beyond. The Gemara then asks *mai piska* — what is the logical basis for splitting? Why assume he provided for one and not the other? Tosafot finds this question puzzling, noting that the distinction between legal obligation and voluntary generosity is obvious. Perhaps the Gemara is suggesting that if he cared enough to appoint a trustee at all, he would not have abandoned his family. In any case, this response narrows the *braita* considerably: it now addresses only a specific, unusual scenario.

### One Witness

Rav Pappa offers an alternative explanation of the *braita*. *Kesheshama bo shemet b'ed echad* — we heard that the husband died through the testimony of a single witness. This creative solution draws on the well-known principle from Yevamot: a woman is permitted to remarry on the basis of *ed echad* testifying to her husband's death, because she is trusted to take such a consequential step only when she is genuinely certain. The practical difference between wife and children follows directly. The wife, because of the special dispensation of *ed echad* regarding remarriage, is treated as if she can presume her husband dead. Since even when her husband is alive she would be entitled to support, and since *ed echad* allows her to treat him as dead, we provide *mezonot* for her. Her sons and daughters, however, have no comparable dispensation: *ed echad* does not allow them to treat their father as dead for purposes of inheritance. From their perspective, the father is still alive, and therefore they may not descend to his property. The result is a peculiar situation: from the wife's standpoint her husband is dead, from the children's standpoint their father is alive.

One might ask whether this is entirely coherent — in Yevamot, the reliability of *ed echad* was predicated on the wife's willingness to expose herself to severe consequences if she is wrong. Here she is only seeking *mezonot*, not remarriage; the stakes are lower. This is a fair question, and Tosafot addresses under what circumstances *ed echad* would suffice for various monetary claims related to the husband's presumed death. But the Gemara here uses this mechanism to preserve Shmuel's position: even this powerful *braita*, with its explicit exclusion of sons and daughters, can be explained without conceding that we support a wife whose husband is simply absent and alive.

The Gemara also addresses *mai davar acher* — the other things the *braita* excludes. Rav Chisda says we do not provide *tachshit* — jewelry or, as Rashi notes, perfume — from the estate. Rav Yosef says we do not draw from the estate for *tzedakah* contributions. The one who excludes *tachshit* would certainly exclude *tzedakah*, since that is not even for the wife's benefit. The one who excludes *tzedakah* would still provide *tachshit*, on the reasoning that *lo nicha lei detitgana v'detinval* — the husband would not want his wife going about in a degraded state simply because he is away. Some basic expenditures on her appearance and wellbeing are still covered.

---

## Sister-in-Law & Divorce

### Yevamah

The Gemara cites another *braita*: the *yevamah* — a sister-in-law awaiting *yibbum* or *chalitzah* — is supported from her deceased husband's estate for the first three months. During this period she cannot yet perform *yibbum* because she may be pregnant. *Mikan ve'eylach* — thereafter, she is supported neither by her dead husband's estate nor by the *yavam*'s. This leaves her in a difficult middle state: the obligation to perform *yibbum* is still pending, but as long as it is pending she is no longer simply a widow drawing on her late husband's estate, and since the marriage to the *yavam* has not occurred, she is not yet his responsibility.

The *braita* continues: *amda badin u-varach* — she brought him to *beit din* to compel him to act, and he fled. In this case, he is responsible to support her. The Gemara asks whether this applies specifically because he ran away — evading his legal responsibilities — or whether it applies more broadly whenever *beit din* has formally called upon him to act and his inaction, whether culpable or not, traps her in this state of *agunah*. In any case, once *beit din* has summoned him and he is not fulfilling his obligation, he must provide for her even in his absence. The Gemara asks: is this not exactly the same as a husband being absent overseas and *beit din* providing for his wife? Shmuel responds: *lemai neichush lah* — what are we really worried about here? The two concerns that Shmuel raises in the main case do not apply here. *Ai mishum tzerorei* — maybe he set aside money? *Lo mikrav daiteih legabah* — he has no closeness to her; they are not yet married, he has only this pending *mitzva* of *yibbum* and moreover he ran away from it, so obviously he would not have prepared a fund for her. *Ai mishum ma'aseh yadeha* — maybe he told her to work for herself? *Lo mishtabda lei* — she is not obligated to give her *ma'aseh yadayim* to him; in this middle state before *yibbum* is performed, her labor does not belong to him, though his obligation to support her exists. Since neither concern applies, we provide for her, but this tells us nothing about the case where those concerns are live.

### Claiming Divorce

A further *braita*: *ha'isha shehalcha hi uva'alah limdinat hayam* — she and her husband went overseas together, and she returned saying *met ba'ali* — my husband died. She is believed. She may either be supported from the estate as an *almana* or collect her *ketuba* in a lump sum. But: *im amra geirashani ba'ali* — if instead she says he divorced her, a different rule applies. *Mitparneset v'holekhet ad kedei kesuvatah* — she is supported incrementally until the total value of her *ketuba* is reached. This is because a woman is believed when she claims her husband died but not when she claims he divorced her. Since we do not fully accept her claim of divorce, we cannot give her the *ketuba* as a lump sum — perhaps she is still married. But *mi'man nafshach* — either way there is a liability: if still married, he owes her *mezonot*; if divorced, she has a *ketuba* claim. So we pay out *mezonot* until it reaches the value of the *ketuba* and then stop. The *chiddush* is that by saying *geirashani* rather than *met*, she has actually harmed herself: had she said nothing, we would have continued supporting her indefinitely as a presumed widow. By introducing the claim of divorce, she capped her own entitlement.

The Gemara raises this *braita* as evidence that we support a woman from the estate even though the husband's status is uncertain — precisely what Rav holds. Shmuel, predictably, replies *hacha nami deshamu bo shemet* — here too, it is a case where the husband had been reported dead.

---

## Minor Refused

### Mi'un Case

The Gemara cites a further *braita* on the theme of *mi'un*. *Keitzad amru mima'enet ein lah mezonot* — in what case is a girl who refuses (*mima'enet*) her minor marriage left without *mezonot*? It cannot be while she is still living together with the husband under normal marital arrangements, because *ba'alah chayav bimzonoteha* — as long as they are together, the husband is obligated to support her. The case must therefore be: *ella k'gon shehalach limdinat hayam* — the husband has gone overseas. *Lavta v'achalah* — she borrowed money and used it to feed herself. *V'amda u'mi'anah* — and then she performed *mi'un*, retroactively dissolving the marriage as though it had never existed.

The *chiddush* is not merely that from this point forward there is no marriage — that is obvious. The *chiddush* is the retroactive effect: since *mi'un* unwinds the marriage entirely, she is not in a position to collect from her ex-husband the borrowed money she had spent on *mezonot*, because retroactively she was never truly married and he never had that obligation. Importantly, however, the *braita* implies that *had she not done mi'un*, she would have been entitled to recover that borrowed money from the estate. The husband, even while overseas, had an obligation to support her, and her borrowed expenditures during that period would have been collectible. *Ta'ama d'mi'anah* — it is specifically because she did *mi'un* that she loses the claim; *ha lo mi'anah, yehavinan lah* — had she not done *mi'un*, we would have provided.

This is again strong evidence for Rav's position. Shmuel responds: *amar lach Shmuel hacha b'mai askinan* — the case here is a special one. *Ei mishum tzerorei, l'ktana lo masar* — the concern that the husband set aside money does not apply to a minor wife; one does not entrust funds to a minor. *V'ei mishum ma'aseh yadeha, l'ktana lo safka* — and the concern that she would earn her own keep does not apply as a general rule to a minor; minors typically cannot support themselves. So in this case, uniquely, both of Shmuel's concerns are absent, and therefore even Shmuel agrees that she should be supported — but this is a narrow exception that tells us nothing about adult wives.

A question arises about how a minor could have borrowed money in the first place. The Gemara presupposes transactions that minors can engage in, either under the rabbinic category of *pe'utot* — transactions by children of sufficient understanding — or perhaps the borrowing was done by the mother on her behalf.

---

## Rabbi Stories

### Rav Dimi's Story

After exhausting the textual evidence, the Gemara turns to recorded practice. *Ki ata Rav Dimi* — when Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he reported: *ma'aseh ba lifnei Rabbi b'Beit She'arim* — a case came before *Rabbi* (Rebbi Yehuda HaNasi) in Beit She'arim, and he *pasak lah mezonot* — ruled to provide *mezonot* for the wife whose husband had gone overseas. *Lifnei Rabbi Yishmael b'Tzippori, v'lo pasak lah mezonot* — a similar case came before Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yose in Tzippori and he refused to provide.

### Yochanan's Challenge

*Tamah Rabbi Yochanan* — Rabbi Yochanan was astonished, and asked: *v'chi mah ra'ah Rabbi Yishmael shelo pasak lah mezonot?* What could Rabbi Yishmael have seen to refuse support to this woman? After all, *halo nechelku Bnei Kohanim Gedolim v'Chanan ela l'inyan shvuah* — the only dispute in our mishna between Chanan and the *bnei kohanim gedolim* concerns the oath. *Aval mezonei yahvinan lah* — everyone agrees that *mezonot* is provided. How could Rabbi Yishmael simply refuse?

Rav Shemen bar Abba replied: *kvar tirgemah Rabbeinu Shmuel b'Bavel* — our master Shmuel already dealt with this mishna in Babylonia. His interpretation — *ksheshamu bo shemet* — explains the mishna as applying only to the case where the husband is presumed dead. Rabbi Yishmael presumably followed Shmuel's position and therefore refused to provide when the husband was merely absent. Rabbi Yochanan responded: *pastrisu bekulei hai?* — you are going to such lengths, twisting the plain meaning of the mishna by that much? Clearly that is not the *pshat*, and to do that to a woman who needs to eat is not a defensible *tirutz*.

### Ravin's Story

*Ki ata Ravin* — when Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael, he reported the same story in reverse: the case came before *Rabbi* in Beit She'arim and *he* refused to provide, while the case before Rabbi Yishmael in Tzippori resulted in an order to provide. The same exchange between Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Shemen bar Abba follows verbatim. The two reports from Eretz Yisrael — Rav Dimi's and Ravin's — simply contradict each other on who ruled which way, and the Gemara makes no effort to reconcile them.

### Final Ruling

*V'hilchesa kevasei d'Rav* — the *halakha* follows Rav. We provide *mezonot* for a married woman whose husband is away. The entire sustained effort by Shmuel to explain away every *braita* and every recorded practice ultimately fails to persuade, and the final ruling goes with the straightforward reading of the mishna and all the supporting *braisos*: *poskin mezonot l'eshet ish*.

---

## Final Rulings

### Mezonot Ruling

The Gemara summarizes three *hilchesos* as the masekhta draws to its close. The first follows directly from the foregoing discussion: *u-paskinan mezonot l'eshet ish* — we rule that *beit din* provides *mezonot* for a wife whose husband has gone overseas.

### Woman's Right

The second ruling: *v'hilchesa kevasei d'Rav Huna* — we rule in accordance with Rav Huna citing Rav, who said: *yechola isha she-tomar l'ba'alah eini nizonet v'eini osa* — a woman may unilaterally declare to her husband that she does not wish to receive *mezonot* from him and will not turn over her *ma'aseh yadayim* to him. The exchange of *mezonot* for labor was established to protect *her* interests, not his. She is therefore entitled to waive *mezonot* and retain her own earnings. This is not a decision reserved to the husband — she may invoke it herself.

### Kunia Vessels

The third ruling: *v'hilchesa kevasei d'Rav Zvid b'kunya* — we rule in accordance with Rav Zvid regarding *kunya*, which are glazed pottery vessels. The topic is included here apparently because the Gemara favors grouping *hilchesos* in threes. Rashi understands the glaze to be a metallic coating; Tosafot understands it as glass glaze.

Rav Zvid rules: *hanei mane d'kunya chivarei v'uchmei sharei* — white and black *kunya* vessels are permitted. *Yerokei, asirei* — green ones are forbidden. Rashi identifies the problematic substance in the green glaze as *alum*, a specific mineral compound (not the modern aluminum) that causes the glaze to absorb and then retain absorbed taste so that it cannot be extracted. The context is most likely wine of non-Jews (*stam yeinam*) stored cold — the question being whether the pottery absorbs enough of the wine's flavor that the taste cannot be expelled through normal *kashering*.

Even permissible white or black vessels must meet an additional condition: *ella d'reish bei kartufi* — there must be no ridges, cracks, or indentations. *Aval it beih kartufei, assur* — if there are such imperfections, the taste enters the crevices and cannot be expelled, rendering the vessel forbidden.

Tosafot, proceeding from the premise that the glaze is glass, adds an important observation. *Aval b'hataxas zechuchis nicha d'afilu konyah shel zechuchis einu ne'asar* — in principle, genuinely glass-glazed vessels would not absorb, *lefi shenisbashel heiteiv v'eino nivla* — because well-processed pure glass is non-porous. The problem with *kunya* is that the glass in question was not fully processed and contained metallic impurities or alloys that caused it to absorb. This sets up a broader question that Tosafot engages implicitly: does the non-porous character of true glass extend to hot liquids as well as cold, and what is the general *halakhic* status of glass vessels? These questions carry through into the wider *halakhic* literature on *kashering* glass, where there is significant debate about whether glass is entirely non-absorbent under all circumstances or only under specific conditions.

---

---

# Ketubot 108

## Chanan: Provisions

### Third-party provisions

The second ruling of Chanan — like the first — arises in the context of a husband who has traveled overseas and left no provisions for his wife. In the previous *mishnah*, the discussion centered on whether the wife must take a *shevuah* at the outset of receiving support from her husband's estate or only at the conclusion, with Chanan holding she swears only at the end. The present ruling addresses a related but distinct scenario: while the husband is abroad, a third party — perhaps a storekeeper, or simply a compassionate neighbor — notices the wife's predicament and, out of his own initiative and expense, provides her with food for the entire duration of her husband's absence.

### No reimbursement owed

When the husband returns, can this benefactor demand reimbursement? Chanan says: *ibad et me'otav* — he wasted his money. No contractual arrangement was ever made, no loan was extended, and therefore the husband owes him nothing. This is a striking ruling, given that the husband's obligation to feed his wife was entirely real, and the third party effectively discharged it. The obvious question is whether the objective reality of the benefit — that the wife was sustained — itself generates a legal debt.

### BKG: oath required

The *Bnei Kohanim Gedolim* disagree with Chanan, consistent with their stance in the previous *mishnah*. True to their characteristic approach, they require an oath: *yishava kama hotzi ve-yitol* — the third party takes a *shevuah* attesting to his expenditures and is then entitled to reimbursement.

### Dosa & Yochanan

The positions align precisely as they did in the prior dispute. Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas sides with the *Bnei Kohanim Gedolim*, while Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai endorses Chanan: *yafeh amar Chanan* — Chanan has spoken well. He adds the evocative phrase: *hinniach me'otav al keren hatzvi* — he placed his money on the horns of a gazelle, the Talmudic idiom for money irretrievably lost.

---

## Tosafot framework

### Michael's question

The pivotal question framing this entire discussion is: does an unsolicited act of benefit ever, by itself, create a legal obligation? Even absent any borrowing or hiring, is there a circumstance in which the objective improvement of my position gives you a cognizable claim against me?

### Lawn/field examples

Two illustrative scenarios clarify the range of possibilities. In one, a person is away and a neighbor mows his lawn. In the Talmudic idiom, the equivalent is someone planting another's field without permission. The question of whether this creates an obligation turns on whether we can imply a quasi-contractual arrangement — specifically, whether this is a *sadeh ha-asuya lita*, a field of the type that is typically planted, such that a reasonable owner would obviously desire the work done. Even absent explicit consent, the presumed desire to have the work done might approximate a constructive hire.

### Property vs. obligation

Even where there is no presumed consent, however, there is a second possible basis for liability: the actual, tangible increase in property value. If you fattened my cattle, I now possess fatter cattle — something of yours, as it were, is embedded in my property, and I am obligated to compensate you for it. This principle can be conceptualized as: where your effort has materially enhanced the value of my assets, you have in some sense transferred something of yours into my estate, and I must return it.

The crucial distinction in the case before us is that feeding the husband's wife does not increase the husband's property value. His estate has not grown; he has no more assets at the end than at the beginning. What occurred was the discharge of an obligation, not an enhancement of his holdings.

### Lion analogy

Tosafot raises an analogy that sharpens the analysis considerably. The Gemara elsewhere discusses *mavriach ari mi-nichsei chaveiro* — one who scares off a lion that is about to attack his neighbor's flock, incurring personal expense in the process. Here too there is no increase in property value — the owner ends up with exactly the sheep he had before. Yet the Gemara is clear that reimbursement is required. This appears parallel to our case: just as the lion-chaser prevented harm to the owner's assets, so too did the third party prevent the wife from seizing the husband's estate — a genuine benefit.

### Policy difference

Tosafot's resolution is grounded in public policy. In the case of the lion, we have an affirmative societal interest in encouraging individuals to come to one another's aid in emergencies, and it is therefore a *takanat chachamim* — a rabbinic enactment — that such a person be reimbursed, so that people will not hesitate to act. No parallel policy concern exists in our case. The wife already has a readily available remedy: she can simply appear before *Beit Din* and the court will authorize her to take food from her husband's property. There is no need to encourage third parties to pay off the husband's debt to his wife when she has a direct avenue of relief. The situation becomes even clearer according to Chanan's view in the previous *mishnah* — that the wife's access to the estate is uncomplicated and requires no oath at the outset — making any third-party intervention doubly unnecessary.

### Tosafot summary

Tosafot's conclusion is thus two-pronged. First, no direct benefit passed from the third party to the husband: the money went to the wife (effectively, the husband's creditor), and only indirectly and consequentially did the husband benefit from the removal of her claim. Second, there was no increase in the value of the husband's property. Both factors together — the indirect nature of the benefit (*grama be-alma*) and the absence of any *shevach nechasim* — explain why Chanan says the third party has no claim. The relevant lines from Tosafot make this explicit: *hatam ha-shevach b'ayin hu ve-din hu she-yitol* — in cases of actual property improvement, the enhanced value is tangibly present and reimbursement is appropriate — *aval hacha lo hishbi'ach lo shum shevach nechasim, ella she-hetzilo mi-geviyat ba'al chov, ve-lo midei yahiv lei, ve-havei ke-mavriach ari mi-nichsei chaveiro, ve-af al gav de-mithanno lo mitchayev* — but here no property value was enhanced; the third party merely protected the husband from his creditor's collection, gave him nothing tangible, and is therefore analogous to one who scared off a lion, who despite the benefit conferred creates no legal obligation.

The connection to the public policy point appears explicitly later in Tosafot: *takanat chachamim hatam she-yeshalmu lo kedei she-yashiv aveidato shel chaveiro* — the enactment requiring reimbursement in the lion case and in the case of returning lost objects exists to incentivize socially beneficial behavior. *Aval poreya chovo... lamah lanu la'asot takanah zo* — but for paying off another's debt, or for providing another's wife with food, why institute such a policy? Let the wife exercise her own legal rights. The husband is not a lion's prey.

---

## Nedarim vow cases

### Half-shekel case

The Gemara in *Nedarim* introduces a related set of cases involving *hanaah* — benefit — in a different but illuminating context. The scenario: one person is under a vow (*mudar hanaah*) prohibiting him from deriving benefit from his friend. Yet the friend wishes to assist him. What may the friend do?

### Three actions

The *mishnah* in *Nedarim* enumerates three actions the friend may perform without violating the vow: he may pay the person's *shekel* (the annual half-shekel contribution for the *korbanot*); he may pay off the person's debt to a creditor; and he may return the person's lost object. Each of these, despite conferring what would intuitively seem to be real benefit, is permitted.

The return of the lost object is perhaps the least surprising of the three. After all, the item already belongs to the person — he is merely receiving back his own property. Moreover, the one returning it is fulfilling a *mitzvah*, and *mitzvot lav le-hanot nitnu* — the commandments are not given for the purpose of benefit.

### Lost object payment

However, a complication arises: in places where it is customary to compensate the finder for his efforts in returning a lost object (*sechar batelah*), a new difficulty emerges. If the person under the vow is obligated to pay for the return, but the friend has also taken a vow against receiving benefit from him, then accepting payment would violate the friend's vow. Conversely, if the friend simply waives the payment — says "forget it, keep your money" — he has forgiven a debt the person owes him, which is itself a form of *hanaah* flowing to the person from the friend, in violation of the original vow.

### Hekdesh solution

The Gemara's solution is elegant: *tatil hanaah le-hekdesh* — the payment is dedicated to *hekdesh*. The person does not keep the money, the friend does not receive it, and neither party benefits from the other in a forbidden way. It is a well-established approach to such entanglements: when neither party may receive the value at stake, the funds are channeled to *hekdesh* as a neutral resolution.

### Rashi/Tosafot

Regarding the *shekel* payment, Rashi and Tosafot offer divergent explanations for why paying another's half-*shekel* does not constitute *hanaah*. The *mishnah* in *Shekalim* teaches *tormin al ha-avud, ve-al ha-gavuy, ve-al ha-atid ligbot* — the *terumah* taken from the *shekalim* chamber is brought on behalf even of those whose money was lost in transit, those whose money has been received but not yet brought to the *Beit Hamikdash*, and even those who have not yet paid at all. The *korbanot* purchased from the collected *shekalim* are thus brought on behalf of the entire community, even those who have yet to fulfill their obligation.

Rashi understands this broadly: since the *korbanot* are brought on behalf of everyone, including those who may never ultimately pay, the *shekel* obligation carries no real monetary consequence — the person would receive his share of the *korbanot* regardless. Paying his *shekel* therefore merely assists him in fulfilling a *mitzvah* obligation; it does not relieve him of any actual monetary debt. Under this reading, the *shekel* case is the weakest of the three in terms of *hanaah*, since the person was not truly obligated in any enforceable monetary sense.

Tosafot rejects this. In Tosafot's view, one who does not pay his *shekel* does genuinely forfeit his share in the *korbanot* — the text *al ha-atid ligbot* refers only to those who will eventually pay, not to permanent non-payers. Paying another's *shekel* therefore does discharge a real obligation and constitutes real benefit. To rescue the ruling that the friend may pay it, Tosafot narrows the case: the *mishnah* in *Nedarim* is describing a situation where the person has technically already fulfilled his obligation (for example, his money was sent but lost in transit before reaching Jerusalem, so he is halachically exempt), and the friend is merely paying a second time for his peace of mind. This is admittedly a *dachuk* reading of a case that the *mishnah* presents as standard. As Rashi would understand it, the straightforward reading is simply that the payment of a *shekel* for another person, under any normal circumstances, is permissible — because it only assists in performing a *mitzvah* and does not represent a transfer of substantial monetary benefit.

Ultimately, both Rashi and Tosafot agree that *hanaah* in this context refers to monetary benefit, not emotional satisfaction. They disagree on why the *shekel* case falls outside that category — whether because the obligation was illusory all along (Rashi) or because the particular case involves an already-exempt individual (Tosafot).

---

## Debt repayment grama

### Oshaya attribution

The Gemara now turns to the most conceptually significant of the three permitted actions: paying off another's debt. The Gemara asks: surely this is *kamesh-taresh lei* — a genuine and deeply rooted benefit? The person's net worth has increased; he is freed from a liability that burdened him. How can this not be *hanaah*?

Rav Oshaya resolves this: *ha mani Chanan hi* — this ruling reflects Chanan's position. Just as Chanan holds that discharging the husband's obligation to his wife creates no actionable debt in the husband's favor for the one who paid, so too here: paying off another's debt is not considered *hanaah* in the legally cognizable sense. The two rulings share the same conceptual foundation.

### Direct/indirect

Tosafot articulates the underlying principle in terms of the direct/indirect distinction. When I pay Michael's creditor, the money flows from me to the creditor — not from me to Michael. Michael's benefit is a consequence, a *grama be-alma*, an indirect downstream effect of my transaction with his creditor. He himself received nothing directly from me. Compare this to mowing Michael's lawn: in that case, the improvement flows directly from me to him, from my effort to his property. Even if I could not legally compel him to pay me for the lawn mowing, he has still received something *directly* from me. That is the line Tosafot draws: *de-hatam mi-didi le-didei ka-mitahni* — there, from me directly to him he derived benefit — whereas in the debt case, the money went to the creditor, and only consequently did Michael benefit.

### Storekeeper analogy

A parallel case reinforces this framework. The Gemara in *Nedarim* elsewhere discusses a scenario where a person under a vow of *hanaah* is starving: *yelech eitzel chanvani ha-ragil etzlo* — the friend goes to a storekeeper familiar with the person and arranges for food to be provided. Even though the friend's action ultimately results in Michael receiving food — concrete, measurable benefit — it is permitted, because the friend acted only as a *grama be-alma*, indirectly. The money went from the friend to the storekeeper; the storekeeper then gave food to Michael. At no point did anything pass directly from the friend to Michael.

Tosafot draws the explicit contrast: *de-lo avid ela grama be-alma... ve-dela dami le-oseh lo melachah* — because the friend did not act directly upon Michael, it is unlike performing labor for him directly. Performing labor directly for someone, even if you could not compel payment, still constitutes direct benefit and would be prohibited under the vow.

However, Tosafot notes an important nuance in the storekeeper case: unlike the debt-repayment case, Michael actually did receive something of tangible, increased value — food that he now has. The debt case is arguably stronger because there, there is not even an increase in property value, only the removal of a liability. Together, then, the two factors that insulate these actions from the category of *hanaah* are: (1) the indirect, *grama* character of the benefit, and (2) in the debt case specifically, the absence of any actual increase in the person's property.

### Rava challenge

Rava raises a challenge to Rav Oshaya's attribution of the debt-repayment rule to Chanan. Rava says: *afilu teima Rabbanan* — one could even reconcile the ruling with the majority position of the *Bnei Kohanim Gedolim*, without invoking Chanan at all. The explanation would be that the debt in question was borrowed *al menat she-lo lifroa* — on condition that it never had to be repaid, meaning the creditor could never bring the debtor to court to collect. Such a debt, though technically outstanding, does not truly burden the debtor's estate in a practical sense — it is a nominal obligation at best. Paying it off, therefore, barely qualifies as meaningful benefit.

The Gemara then asks why Rav Oshaya preferred the Chanan attribution rather than Rava's narrower reading. The answer: *nehi de-hana layt lei, kissufa mi layt lei?* — even if there is no monetary benefit from the debt payment (since the creditor could never sue), is there no benefit from the removal of embarrassment? Running into one's creditor and being reminded of an unpaid debt — even one that is legally unenforceable — is a source of genuine shame. Paying off that debt, under Rava's reading, would still confer real benefit by eliminating that embarrassment. Therefore, Rav Oshaya concluded that Rava's construction is untenable, and the only way to permit the debt repayment is through Chanan's broader conceptual framework of *grama*.

This also confirms that Chanan's approach carries significant practical weight, notwithstanding that the *Bnei Kohanim Gedolim* constitute the majority. The logic of *grama* — that indirect benefit, however substantial in practical terms, does not create direct legal liability — is the animating principle behind multiple rulings, and it is Chanan who gives that principle its clearest expression.

---

## Admon estate case

### Daughters/sons

The *mishnah* now transitions to the seven rulings of Admon. The first concerns the laws of inheritance in an estate too small to satisfy all claims. The general rule: when a man dies leaving both sons and daughters, in a large estate *ha-banim yirashu ve-ha-banot yizonu* — the sons inherit and the daughters are provided with food and maintenance from the estate. In a small estate, however, where there is not enough to both provide for the daughters' maintenance and leave a remainder for the sons to inherit, *ha-banot yizonu ve-ha-banim yechaizru al ha-pesachim* — the daughters are fed and the sons must go begging.

### Admon objects

Admon objects: *bishvil she-ani zachar hifsadeti*? Just because I am male I lose out? The implication is that the differential treatment is unjust — males are systematically privileged in inheritance law, yet when the estate is small, they bear the full loss.

### Abaye misreading

The Gemara struggles to identify the precise nature of Admon's complaint. Abaye offers one reading: *bishvil she-ani zachar ve-ra'ui la-asok ba-Torah hifsadeti* — because I am male and therefore the one who engages in Torah study, I have lost out? The suggestion seems to be that those who occupy themselves with the more important religious activity in society ought to be prioritized in financial matters.

### Rava response

Rava firmly rejects this: *man de-asik be-Torah hu de-yaris, man de-lo asik be-Torah lo yaris?* Would one who learns Torah inherit while one who does not, does not? Monetary rights and religious significance are entirely separate domains. An argument grounded in religious importance is irrelevant to questions of property entitlement.

Rava therefore reformulates Admon's complaint: *bishvil she-ani zachar ve-ra'ui liyarash bi-nechasim merubim hifsadeti bi-nechasim muatim?* — because I am a male and therefore the primary heir in a large estate, I should now, when the estate is small, be disadvantaged relative to the daughters? There is an internal inconsistency in a legal system that privileges males in large estates but places the entire burden of a small estate on them.

Rabban Gamliel endorses Admon's position: *ro'eh ani et divrei Admon* — I see the logic of Admon's argument.

### Tosafot reinterpret

The Gemara elsewhere rules that whenever Rabban Gamliel says *ro'eh ani et divrei Admon*, we rule accordingly. Yet Tosafot notes that other *sugyot* consistently maintain that in a small estate, the daughters are fed before the sons — a rule reaffirmed by Rav Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan with no hint of dissent. Rabbeinu Tam resolves the tension by reinterpreting the nature of the dispute: *Admon lav peligi a-milsa de-chachamim avdu* — Admon is not actually arguing against the established *halacha*. He concedes that the law gives priority to daughters in a small estate. Rather, *ella misma be-alma* — he is simply voicing outrage. His statement is a rhetorical expression of indignation, not a formal halachic challenge. And when Rabban Gamliel says *ro'eh ani et divrei Admon*, he too is not issuing a *psak din* — he is affirming: *mishum she-yesh bo kedei litmo'ah* — yes, I share his sense that this is astonishing. The established rule stands; Admon's statement registers a moral protest, not a legal position.

---

## Jugs of oil case

### Jugs claim

Admon's second ruling involves an application of *modeh be-miktzat* — partial admission. The case: Reuven claims that Shimon owes him jugs of oil. Shimon concedes that he owes the jugs but denies owing the oil. Can this constitute the partial admission (*hoda'at miktzat ha-ta'anah*) that triggers an obligation to take a *shevuah*?

### Admon: oath required

Admon holds that it does: *hu hodeh be-miktzat ha-ta'anah, yishava* — he has admitted to part of the claim, and therefore he must take an oath. The jugs are included in the claim of "jugs of oil," and conceding them while denying the oil is a classic partial admission.

### Chakhamim: no oath

The *chakhamim* disagree: *ein hoda'at miktzat mi-min ha-ta'anah* — this is not an admission of part of the actual claim. What was being demanded was the oil; the jugs were merely incidental. One who concedes something that was not truly the subject of the claim has not made a meaningful partial admission.

### Two vs. one claim

The Gemara initially attempts to locate the dispute within the broader question of *ta'ano chitin u-se'orin ve-hodeh be-se'orin* — if one claimed wheat and barley and the defendant conceded only the barley, is that *modeh be-miktzat*? This depends on whether we treat a single claim for two objects as one unified claim (conceding part of it = partial admission) or as two separate claims (conceding one entirely while denying the other = no partial admission at all). The Gemara initially suggests that the *chakhamim* hold that wheat and barley are two separate claims, and therefore there is no *modeh be-miktzat* here — the oil and the jugs likewise constitute two separate claims, and the full concession of jugs with full denial of oil is not a partial admission. This would conflict with the position of Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel, who holds that claiming two objects in a single demand is treated as one claim, such that conceding one part of it does create a *shevuah* obligation.

### Measurement language

Rav Yehuda resolves the apparent contradiction by introducing a critical distinction in language. If the claimant said *melo asarah kadei shemen yesh li be-vorch* — the fill of ten jugs of oil I have in your pit — then clearly he is measuring a quantity of oil; the jugs are purely a unit of measurement and are not themselves being claimed. In that formulation, there is obviously no claim for the jugs, and conceding jugs alone is entirely irrelevant. At the other extreme, if he said *asarah kadei shemen mele'in yesh li etzlecha* — ten jugs filled with oil I have with you — then he is explicitly claiming both: the physical jugs and the oil within them. Everyone would agree that in this case, conceding five jugs would constitute *modeh be-miktzat*, because both objects were clearly claimed together as one composite demand — consistent with Rav Nachman amar Shmuel that a combined claim for two objects is treated as unified.

The dispute of Admon and the *chakhamim* thus concerns only the intermediate formulation: *asarah kadei shemen yesh li etzlecha* — simply "ten jugs of oil I have with you." Is this phrasing understood to be a claim for the jugs themselves, or only for the oil?

### Ravina challenge

Rava had earlier suggested a different resolution, drawing on an analogy to *rimon bi-kelipato* — a pomegranate with its rind. Even those who would ordinarily treat wheat-and-barley as two separate claims would agree that a pomegranate and its rind are one indivisible thing; conceding the rind while denying the pomegranate flesh would therefore constitute *modeh be-miktzat*. Similarly, oil within jugs might be considered one thing, not two.

Ravina challenges this analogy: *rimon belo kelipato lo mintar* — a pomegranate cannot be preserved without its rind; the two are physically inseparable. *Shemen mintar belo kankanin* — oil, however, can be stored and preserved without any particular jug. The oil and the jugs are not intrinsically bound to one another. They are therefore more like wheat and barley — two separate objects — than like a pomegranate and its rind, and the analogy does not hold.

### Language inclusion

The Gemara ultimately resolves the entire discussion by anchoring the debate exactly where Rav Yehuda had located it: in the question of linguistic meaning. The final formulation: the claimant said *asarah kadei shemen yesh li etzlecha* — "ten jugs of oil I have with you" — and the defendant replied: as for the oil, *lo hayu devarim me-olam* — there was never any such thing; as for the jugs, *chamishah it lach ve-chamishah leit lach* — five I owe you, five I do not.

Admon's position — *yesh ba-lashon hazeh lashon kankanim* — is that the phrase "ten jugs of oil" intrinsically includes a claim for the jugs. Since the defendant conceded five jugs out of ten, he has admitted to part of a unified claim, and therefore takes a *shevuah*. Moreover, *u-migo de-kamishtava a-kankanin, mishtava nami a-shemen* — since he must take an oath regarding the jugs by force of partial admission, that oath is extended to the oil through *gilgul shevuah*: once an oath is obligated on one component of a claim, it rolls onto the related component as well.

The *chakhamim* hold — *ein ba-lashon hazeh lashon kankanin* — that when one says "jugs of oil," he is in ordinary usage referring only to the oil. The jugs are a colloquial measure, not an independent object of the claim. Since the jugs were never truly claimed, conceding them is conceding something that was never demanded — *mah she-ta'ano lo hodeh lo, u-mah she-hodeh lo lo ta'ano* — and no *shevuah* is triggered.

The debate thus reduces, at its core, to a question of ordinary linguistic convention: when a person says "jugs of oil," does that phrase carry within it a claim for the physical jugs, or does it refer exclusively to the oil measured in jug-units? Admon says yes, it includes the jugs; the *chakhamim* say no, it does not. That question of interpretive convention is, in the end, what determines whether a *shevuah* is required.

---

---

# Ketubot 109

## Father Reneges Deal

### Setup & Context

The daf opens at the very bottom of 108b, where the *mishna* introduces the first of *Admon*'s rulings. The case involves a father-in-law who made a financial agreement with his prospective son-in-law: marry my daughter and I will provide you with a sum of money in support. The Aramaic idiom *u'pashat lo es haregel* — literally, sticking out one's foot — captures the father-in-law's posture of reneging on the deal in a dismissive, almost contemptuous way. *Rashi* suggests the image may connote something like demanding that one clean the sole of his shoe, conveying disrespect, though the operative meaning is simply that the father-in-law is backing out.

A crucial detail: the couple had completed *kiddushin* but not *nisuin*. They are betrothed but not yet fully married. The son-in-law's response to being stiffed is stark — *teshev ad shetyalbin roshah*, let her sit until the hair on her head turns white. He will neither complete the marriage nor give her a *get*, leaving her in the position of an *agunah*. She cannot marry anyone else, and he exploits this leverage without paying what was promised.

*Tosfos* raises the question of whether the original financial agreement was legally binding at all. There is a principle — *hein hein ha-devarim ha-niknin ba-amira* — that an oral agreement can be binding when the marriage follows immediately upon it. *Tosfos* offers two readings: one, that the agreement here was not binding because some time elapsed between the agreement and the *kiddushin*, so the son-in-law cannot sue for the money; or two, that the agreement was indeed binding but would not take full effect until *nisuin* was consummated. Either way, the son-in-law finds himself unable or unwilling to pursue the money in court — perhaps the father-in-law has no assets, perhaps the litigation is not worth the trouble — and instead uses the *get* as a weapon. Whether or not the agreement was technically enforceable, the son-in-law's position is that his acquiescence to completing the marriage was conditioned on the support, and since that support is not forthcoming, he will not move forward. The result is a woman held hostage through no fault of her own.

### Admon's Position

*Admon* pushes back directly. The woman is permitted to say: *ilu ani pasakti l'atzmi* — if I had been the one who made this deal and I had reneged, then perhaps I would understand sitting here until my hair turns white, because the injury would have originated with me. But *abba pasak alai* — it was my father who made the agreement and my father who reneged. *Ma ani yechola la'asot* — what can I do about it? The conclusion is *o kenos o patur*: either complete the marriage or release me with a *get*. She cannot be made to suffer for her father's breach of contract.

This is a striking ruling. *Admon* is establishing that a woman cannot be held as an *agunah* as leverage for a financial grievance that is not her doing. The fact that the son-in-law was wronged by the father-in-law does not translate into a right to trap the daughter indefinitely.

### Wife's Own Deal

The *gemara* then raises a *beraita* attributed to Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda that reframes where the actual dispute lies. According to this *beraita*, *Admon* and the *chachamim* do not actually disagree in the case described by the *mishna*, where the father made the deal and reneged. In that scenario, everyone agrees the woman can say *abba pasak alai* — she bears no responsibility — and the husband cannot hold her hostage.

The debate, says Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda, is specifically *al she-paska hi al atzma* — when the woman herself made the financial commitment to the marriage. In that case, the *chachamim* hold that since she made the deal and she is the one who is reneging, the consequence falls on her and she may indeed sit until her hair turns white. *Admon*, however, says that even then she has a valid claim: *svura hayiti she-abba noten alai* — when I made that commitment, I assumed my father would be the one to write the check. Now that my father is not in fact providing the money, *ma ani yechola la'asot* — it is out of my hands. I made a promise I genuinely expected to keep; the non-fulfillment is beyond my control. Therefore, *o kenos o patur* — even in this case the husband must either marry her or release her.

### Rabban Gamliel's View

*Rabban Gamliel* weighs in: *ro'eh ani et divrei Admon* — I see the force of *Admon*'s position. The *gemara* then addresses a *beraita* that asks: when does all of this apply? The answer is *gdola* — when she is an adult. But *aval b'ktana*, if she was a minor when she made the commitment, *kofin* — we actually compel. The *gemara* asks: *kofin le-mi*, compel whom? If the answer is compel the father to pay, that makes little sense — a minor's commitment is less binding than an adult's, so it would be illogical to apply greater force in that case. Rather, says *Rava*, *kofin l'ba'al liten get* — in the case of a minor, the husband is actually compelled to give a *get*.

The logic is that the entire debate only arises when an adult woman made the agreement and backed out. Even in that case, *Admon* says she cannot be held hostage. But if she was a minor when she made the commitment, her agreement carries no binding weight whatsoever, and even the *chachamim* would agree that she cannot be held. In that case, the husband is compelled to act — either to complete the marriage or to release her.

---

## Halakhic Standard

### Affirmed Cases

Having concluded the first group of *Admon*'s rulings, the *gemara* turns to the question of practical *halacha*. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Elazar says in the name of Chizkiya: *kol makom she-amar Rabban Gamliel ro'eh ani et divrei Admon halacha kemoto* — wherever *Rabban Gamliel* says "I see *Admon*'s position," we rule like him. This establishes a clear halakhic standard: affirmation by *Rabban Gamliel* is the criterion for ruling in accordance with *Admon*.

*Rava* then asks *Rav Nachman*: does this apply even to the *beraita*'s version of the case — the scenario where the woman herself made the deal and is reneging, which is the terrain of the *beraita* rather than the *mishna*? *Rav Nachman* responds: I did not say "wherever *Rabban Gamliel* says this in the *mishna*." I said *wherever* he says it — *be-chol makom she-amar Rabban Gamliel ka-amina*. Since *Rabban Gamliel* affirms *Admon* in the *beraita* as well, we rule like *Admon* there too. Even when the woman herself made the commitment and is backing out, she cannot be held hostage.

### חנן vs Admon

The *gemara* then introduces a statement of Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rabbah bar Yirmeyah: regarding the two rulings of *Chanan*, *halacha kiyotzei vo* — we rule like him, and *kiyotzei vo*. The phrase *kiyotzei vo* is the subject of a dispute between *Rashi* and *Tosfos*. *Tosfos* understands it to mean that we not only rule like *Chanan* in the specific cases he addressed, but we extract the underlying principle and apply it to analogous cases. *Rashi*, by contrast, reads *kiyotzei vo* as referring to the one who affirmed the ruling — that is, since *Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai* affirmed *Chanan*'s two positions, we rule in accordance with that affirmation.

Regarding *Admon*'s seven rulings, Rabbi Zeira says *ein halacha kiyotzei vo*. On *Tosfos*'s reading, this means we do not extend *Admon*'s rulings to analogous cases. On *Rashi*'s reading, it means we do not rule in accordance with whoever affirmed him. The *gemara* immediately presses: if taken literally, this would seem to say we reject *Admon* entirely — but we know that cannot be right, since we just established from Rabbi Yitzchak bar Elazar that wherever *Rabban Gamliel* affirms *Admon* we rule like him.

### Partial Acceptance

The *gemara* works through the formulation carefully. An initial reading — *halacha kemoto u-kiyotzei vo* for *Chanan*, and *ein halacha kemoto* for *Admon* in all seven — is rejected because it contradicts the explicit ruling that we follow *Admon* in the cases where *Rabban Gamliel* affirmed him. Another reading — that *halacha kemoto* applies to all seven of *Admon*'s cases concretely, just not to analogous extensions — is also rejected for the same reason.

The *gemara* settles on the following resolution: by *Chanan*, we rule like him in both of his rulings and we apply his principles to analogous cases as well — *halacha kemoto u-kiyotzei vo*. By *Admon*, the picture is mixed — *yesh mehem she-halacha kemoto ve-hayotzei vo*, some of his rulings we rule like him and apply to similar cases, *ve-yesh mehem she-ein halacha kemoto ve-hayotzei bo*, and some we do not rule like him even in the concrete case. The determinant is straightforward: *ve-chol makom she-amar Rabban Gamliel ro'eh ani et divrei Admon halacha kemoto* — wherever *Rabban Gamliel* affirmed him, we rule like him and extend the principle; in the other four rulings of *Admon*, we rule neither like him in the specific case nor in analogous ones. This final formulation simply restates what was established earlier, resolving the apparent contradiction by making clear that Rabbi Zeira's statement referred to the non-affirmed cases.

On *Tosfos*'s reading, the point being made is that for *Chanan* we abstract a general principle, whereas for the unaffirmed *Admon* rulings we do not even do that much. On *Rashi*'s reading, the structure is about the voice of affirmation — we follow *Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai* who affirmed *Chanan* in both cases, and we follow *Rabban Gamliel* where he affirmed *Admon*, but we do not follow *Admon* where no affirmation was given.

---

## Field & Witness

### Witness Problem

The *gemara* now transitions to *Admon*'s second ruling, which concerns a different sort of case entirely — one involving a claim of stolen property and the complications that arise from having signed as a witness on a document. The case: Reuven claims that Shimon stole his field. Reuven has evidence that the field was originally his — Shimon cannot produce a bill of sale, and Shimon does not have three years of *chazaka*. The absence of those would normally be sufficient for Reuven to press his claim successfully. There is, however, one complication: *ha-over al ha-sadeh ve-chatam aleha be-ed* — Reuven himself signed as a witness on the document by which Shimon sold that very field to a third party, Levi.

How can Reuven now claim the field was his if he was a witness to Shimon's sale of it? The implicit logic is that by signing as a witness, Reuven appears to have conceded that the field belonged to Shimon — otherwise, why would he have signed?

### Admon Excuses

*Admon* holds that signing the document as a witness does not forfeit Reuven's claim to the field. The reasoning: *ha-sheni no'ach li ve-ha-rishon kasheh himenu* — it is easier to litigate against Levi, the buyer, than against Shimon, the original thief. Shimon is a dangerous or powerful figure; Reuven may have had good reason not to confront him directly. By signing the document facilitating the sale from Shimon to Levi, Reuven may simply have been positioning himself to retrieve the field more conveniently from Levi — allowing the field to change hands to someone less threatening, and then pursuing his claim against the new holder. This is a fully articulated rationale for why a signature on a document of sale does not necessarily constitute a concession of ownership.

### Chachamim Disagree

The *chachamim* reject this entirely. Their position is *ibad et zechuto* — he has forfeited his rights. If Reuven signed as a witness to a document in which Shimon presented himself as the owner selling the field to Levi, then Reuven has implicitly conceded that the field was Shimon's. The *halacha* follows the *chachamim* here, not *Admon* — this is one of the four rulings of *Admon* that *Rabban Gamliel* did not affirm.

### Judge Exception

*Abaye* introduces an important distinction: *lo shanu ela ed* — this dispute, and the implicit concession, applies only when one signed as a *witness* to the document. *Aval dayan* — but if one served not as a witness but as a judge validating the signatures on the document, the rule is different. *Abaye* derives this from a teaching of Rabbi Chiyya: *ein ha-eidim chotmim al ha-shtar ela im ken kerauhu* — witnesses may not sign a document unless they have read it, because they are attesting to its content and must know what they are attesting to. But *aval ha-dayanim* — judges who are validating signatures do not need to have read the document. *Chotmim af al pi shelo kerauhu* — they may validate the signatures even without reading the full contents.

The analogy to a notary public is apt: a notary attests that the signatures are genuine, not that the contents of the document are true. Since a judge validating signatures need not have read — and may not have read — what the document says, his signature carries no implicit endorsement of the document's claims. Therefore, *aval dayan lo ibad et zechuto* — if Reuven served as a validating judge rather than as a substantive witness, he does not forfeit his right to claim the field.

### Boundary Marker

A further distinction is introduced regarding a scenario where the field in question was not the field being sold but was mentioned only as a boundary marker. If Shimon sold Levi a neighboring field, Field B, and in that document described Field A — the field Reuven claims was stolen — as one of Field B's borders, then even *Admon* concedes that Reuven's signature on that document constitutes an implicit admission that Field A belongs to Shimon.

The reason is that in the original dispute — where Shimon was selling Field A itself to Levi — *Admon*'s rationale for Reuven's signature was that Reuven wanted the field to change to a less threatening holder. But here, Field A is not being transferred. It appears in the document only as a descriptive boundary marker. Reuven gains nothing from facilitating that transaction — there is no strategic reason for him to have signed a document that, in passing, describes Field A as belonging to Shimon. His signature therefore concedes Shimon's ownership, and *Abaye* rules *ibad et zechuto* — he has forfeited his claim.

---

## Coercion Defense

### Own Field Used

*Abaye* continues with another variation: *lo shanu ela le-achar* — the previous analysis applies when Shimon is selling the field to someone else. But *aval le-atzmo* — what if Shimon is selling a different field directly to Reuven himself, and in the document of that sale Shimon uses Field A — the field Reuven claims was stolen — as a boundary marker? In that case, *lo ibad et zechuto* — Reuven does not forfeit his right to claim Field A.

Why not? Because Reuven can say: *de-amar i lo avdi lei hachi, hava lo mazbin li* — if I had not agreed to let him write the document that way, he would not have sold me the other field. Reuven needed to acquire Field B from Shimon. Shimon, who already took Field A from him, was insisting on describing Field A as his in the document of sale. Reuven had no realistic option but to go along with it in order to complete the transaction. His acquiescence to that language does not constitute a concession; it reflects economic compulsion.

### Moda'a Objection

The *gemara* objects: if Reuven felt genuinely coerced, *ibai lei le-mimsar moda'a* — he should have issued a *moda'a*, a formal protestation made before witnesses. The institution of *moda'a* allows someone who anticipates being coerced into signing a document or entering a transaction to declare beforehand to witnesses: "Know that whatever I am about to sign or agree to, I am doing so under duress, and my apparent agreement should not be taken as genuine consent." Had Reuven issued such a *moda'a*, he could later produce those witnesses to challenge the document. Why did he not do so?

### Secrecy Problem

Reuven's response: *chavrach chavra is lei, ve-chavra de-chavrach chavra is lei* — your friend has a friend, and your friend's friend has a friend. The *gemara*'s formulation is its version of the principle that secrets cannot be reliably kept. If Reuven had issued a *moda'a* to witnesses, the word would inevitably have reached Shimon, who would then have refused to proceed with the sale of Field B at all — and Reuven would have lost his only leverage to acquire anything. The impossibility of keeping a *moda'a* secret is itself sufficient justification for why Reuven did not pursue that course.

This is therefore a reasonable explanation for Reuven's conduct: he allowed the document to proceed as written because he had no viable alternative, and the concern about secrecy adequately accounts for why he did not protect himself through a *moda'a*. Given that reasonable explanation, his signing cannot be read as a concession that Field A belonged to Shimon.

---

## Orphans Case

### Initial Ruling

The *gemara* now brings a *ma'aseh*, a concrete case, that illustrates these principles. A man who had claimed that a field had been stolen from him used that same field as a boundary marker in another transaction. He then died — *e'ar ve-shachiv* — before being able to press his claim in court. The court appointed an *apotropas*, a guardian, to represent the interests of the orphans, his heirs, with respect to the contested field. When the *apotropas* appeared before *Abaye* and presented evidence that the field had in fact belonged to the deceased father, *Abaye* ruled against him: *asa siman le-achar ve-ibeid zechuto* — by allowing the field to be used as a boundary marker in another document, the father had implicitly conceded ownership and forfeited the right to claim it. The orphans, as heirs to their father's claim, inherited that forfeiture.

### Guardian Argument

The *apotropas* was not finished. He argued: *i havi avuhon de-yasmei kayam, havi to'en ve-amar telem echad asiti lach* — had the father still been alive, here is what he would have claimed. He would have said: I conceded only one furrow's worth of land — a thin strip — not the entire field. The logic is that when the father's field was described as the boundary of another field in the document, the literal implication is only that a narrow strip at the edge of his field — the actual boundary — belongs to the other party. There is no reason to read the use of a field as a boundary marker as a concession of the entire plot. The father was conceding the furrow that formed the edge, no more.

This is a sophisticated argument for minimizing the scope of the implicit admission. The field appears in the document as a boundary, not as a subject of sale. A boundary, by definition, is an edge — a line, not a mass. To say that Field A's western edge borders Field B does not require that all of Field A belongs to Field B's owner; it requires only that the very edge of Field A — perhaps a furrow's width — does.

### Rabbi Yochanan

*Abaye* acknowledged the force of this argument and cited Rabbi Yochanan: *im ta'an ve-amar telem echad asiti lach, ne'eman* — if the claimant says that all he conceded was one furrow, he is believed. On this basis, *abaye* ruled to award the field to the orphans — *shakluha ve-havu lehu le-yasmei* — with the qualification that the narrow strip be returned to the other party. The *apotropas*, however, pressed further: that strip happened to contain a dense stand of palm trees, *richba de-diklei*, making it quite valuable. He was reluctant to hand it back.

So he argued again: *ee hava avun de-yasmei kayam, hava ta'in ve-amar chazarti ve-lakachtiha heimenu* — had the father been alive, he would also have claimed: yes, I once conceded that strip to you, but afterward I repurchased it from you. This is a startling claim — an admission followed immediately by a counter-claim of subsequent repurchase, with no bill of sale to show for it. *Tosfos* is troubled by why this should be believed and suggests that the answer lies in the fact that the document itself lacked properly validated witnesses, which undermined its evidentiary weight and gave additional latitude to reinterpret the scope of the concession. Rabbi Yochanan's ruling covers this as well: *ne'eman* — even the claim of repurchase is believed.

### Abaye's Praise

*Abaye* affirmed the *apotropas* on this second point as well, quoting Rabbi Yochanan both on the partial-concession argument and on the subsequent-repurchase argument. He then praised the *apotropas* directly: *hai man de-mokim apotropa, lokim ke-hai, de-yada le-hafocha bi-zchuta de-yasmei* — whoever appoints an *apotropas* should appoint someone like this one, who knows how to turn arguments in favor of the orphans.

*Tosfos* raises a pointed question: why was this adversarial advocacy necessary at all? A *beis din* is supposed to argue the best case for orphans without being prompted. Why did *Abaye* initially rule against the orphans rather than make these arguments himself? *Tosfos* answers honestly: *Abaye* had simply forgotten what Rabbi Yochanan had said. It was only when the *apotropas* made the argument that *Abaye* recalled the ruling and recognized that the *apotropas* had arrived at precisely the correct position.

---

## Lost Path

### Path Lost

The *gemara* moves to *Admon*'s third ruling, introduced in a new *mishna*. The scenario: *mi she-halach li-medinat ha-yam ve-avda derech sadehu* — a man went overseas, and while he was away, the path leading to his field was lost. The physical setting is important. Imagine a large agricultural district in which many fields are held by different owners. Nestled in the interior is Reuven's field, accessible only by passing through or alongside the surrounding fields. Reuven had an established right of access — a path — but after years away, no one can identify where it ran. Whether through genuine forgetting, neglect, or the self-interest of neighbors, the path has simply disappeared from collective memory.

### Admon Claims

*Admon omer yelech lo be-ketzara* — *Admon* rules that Reuven is entitled to be given the shortest available path through the surrounding property. The reasoning is that everyone knows Reuven is owed *some* path; the fact that the precise location has been forgotten does not extinguish the right. Since the right exists and the path must go somewhere, Reuven should receive the most efficient route — the shortest one. He cannot be asked to prove which specific path was his; it is enough that a path was his.

### Chachamim Harsh

The *chachamim* take a much harder line: *yikneh lo derech be-meah maneh, o yifrach ba-avir* — let him purchase a path for a hundred *maneh*, or fly through the air. In other words, if Reuven cannot identify which path was specifically his, he has no enforceable claim against any particular neighbor. Each neighbor can say "my field is not where your path was," and since Reuven cannot prove otherwise, he has no recourse. The neighbor is free to name any price for access, however exorbitant, and if Reuven cannot pay, he simply has no way in.

This is a striking ruling. As one listener in the shiur observed, it seems less like a legal principle and more like a neighbor squeezing a vulnerable party. And yet, the *gemara* takes it seriously as a *halachic* position.

### Ownership Analysis

The *gemara* seeks to understand the logical basis of the dispute. *Rav Yehuda* says in the name of *Rav*: the *chachamim*'s position makes sense in a case where *ke-gon she-hekifuha arba'ah b'nei adam me-arba ruchoteha* — four different individuals each own one of the four surrounding fields. In that scenario, any one of them brought to court can say: the path was never in my field — go prove it was. With four separate defendants each able to deflect responsibility to the others, Reuven has no effective legal recourse against any of them individually.

But then the *gemara* asks: *ei hachi, mai ta'ama de-Admon?* — if that's the scenario, then what is *Admon*'s basis for disagreeing? Even he should concede that Reuven cannot win. So the *gemara* concludes that the dispute must occupy a middle case.

### Rava's Rule

*Rava* identifies that middle case. The debate is not about four separate owners who were always separate (*arba'ah de-atu mi-koach arba'ah*) — in that scenario, everyone agrees Reuven cannot successfully sue anyone. Nor is it simply about four fields originally held by the same owner. The key case is *be-chad de-atu mi-koach arba'ah*: originally, each of the four surrounding fields belonged to a different farmer. Then a single entity — *Rava* describes it as one person who acquired from four — came and purchased all four fields. Now they all belong to one owner.

*Admon*'s position: *mikol makom darchai ika gabech* — regardless of how those fields were originally held, the path exists somewhere within property that now belongs to you. I can bring a single litigant to court and demand my path. *Rabban* (the *chachamim*) respond: *ai shatakt shatakt, ve-ai lo, mehadarna shtra le-marihu* — if you leave this alone, we can work something out quietly; but if you insist on litigating, I will simply transfer the fields back to the four original owners, and then you will be back to square one — four separate defendants, each able to deflect responsibility. Since your rights originated in a situation where you could not have successfully forced any one person to provide the path, you gain no additional rights now merely because I happened to consolidate those fields.

The *gemara* acknowledges the strangeness of this argument — it has the character of an economic threat rather than a principled legal defense. One would not expect the court to take seriously the claim "I will undo a commercial transaction to disadvantage you in litigation." And sympathies here rest naturally with *Admon*. Yet this is how the *gemara* frames the *chachamim*'s position.

---

## Palm Tree Legacy

### Bequest Ignored

The *gemara* concludes with a case that echoes the structure of the lost-path problem in a different context. A man on his deathbed said to his children: *dikla le-brat* — give a palm tree to my daughter. He did not specify which palm tree. He then died. The male heirs proceeded to divide up the entire estate among themselves without setting aside a palm tree for their sister. Now she comes to court demanding what her father bequeathed.

The *gemara* initially considers comparing this to the lost-path case: just as each surrounding field owner could deflect responsibility to the next, perhaps each brother can say "your palm tree was in the other brother's portion, not mine." *Rav Yosef* is inclined toward this comparison.

### Half vs Whole

*Abaye* rejects the comparison. *Mi dami* — the cases are not alike. In the lost-path case, *kol chad ve-chad matzi madchei lei* — each owner can genuinely deflect, because the path was originally located in a specific field and no one knows which one. But here, *dikla gabaihu* — there was never any question that the estate as a whole owed her a palm tree. The obligation ran against the estate, not against any particular plot. The division of the estate among the brothers does not discharge that obligation; it only complicates how it is fulfilled. The solution is *leihavu lah dikla* — give her a palm tree — and then *ve-hadar ve-lipalgu me-reisha* — re-divide the estate from the beginning, with the bequest having been satisfied first. If the brothers feel that one of them is bearing a disproportionate cost by giving up a palm tree, that is a matter to resolve among themselves; but the sister's right cannot be extinguished simply because they divided without her.

### Halves Equal Whole

The *gemara* then presents a related case. A man died with a similar bequest — *dikla le-brat*, a palm tree to his daughter — and it emerged that among the assets of the estate were two palm trees in which the deceased had a half-ownership interest in each. The heirs wished to discharge their obligation to the daughter by giving her the two half-interests — a full palm tree's worth, distributed across two trees — rather than one whole palm tree.

*Rav Ashi* was uncertain: *mi karu inshi le-trei palgei dikla dikla* — would people ordinarily refer to two half-palm-trees as "a palm tree"? The question is whether the deathbed bequest of *dikla* — a palm tree — can be satisfied by two partial interests, or whether the word *dikla* necessarily implies an undivided whole.

*Rav Mordechai* conveyed to *Rav Ashi* the ruling of *Abimi me-Hagronya* in the name of *Rava*: *karu inshi le-trei palgei dikla dikla* — yes, people do call two halves a palm tree. The ordinary usage of the term encompasses this configuration. Since the language of the bequest is not so precise as to demand a single, undivided tree, the heirs may satisfy the obligation with the two half-interests, and their obligation is thereby discharged.

---

---

# Nedarim 2

## Intro: Vows & Torah

### Neder vs. Shvuah

Masechet Nedarim concerns the laws of vows, and it is worth pausing at the outset to clarify what a *neder* is and how it differs from a *shvuah* before examining how the tractate understands these concepts.

In the Torah, there are two principal modes by which a person undertakes a binding verbal commitment: the *shvuah* and the *neder*. A *shvuah* is an oath. It involves calling upon God to witness a statement about something one has done or will do — whether a monetary claim, a past action, or a future undertaking. "I will give you a hundred dollars," "I will not eat bread tomorrow" — these are the kinds of statements that constitute a *shvuah*. Central to the concept of *shvuah* is the invocation of God's name: it is, at its core, a declaration made with God as witness, and swearing falsely in that context constitutes *lo tissa shem Hashem lashav* or *v'lo tishavu bishmi lashaker*.

A *neder*, on first reading of the biblical text, does not appear to be categorically distinct from a *shvuah*. Yaakov Avinu's famous vow — *vayidar Yaakov neder lemor im yihiyeh elohim imadi ushmarani baderech hazeh... v'chol asher titten li asser a'assrenu lach* — sounds very much like an oath about future conduct: if God does this for me, I will do such-and-such. The distinguishing feature might be the absence of direct invocation of God's name as a witness, since a *shvuah* classically entails calling upon God in precisely that way. But the difference is not sharply delineated in the *pesukim* themselves.

### Torah Examples

Several biblical contexts employ the word *neder*. In addition to Yaakov's vow, there is the vow of Israel before the battle with Canaan: *vayidar Yisrael neder lemor im nason titten es ha'am hazeh b'yadi v'hacharamti es areihem* — if You deliver this nation into my hand, I will dedicate their cities to God. That language of dedication, of giving something over to God, seems to be a common thread running through many Torah uses of *neder*.
