Similarly, the category of *korban* includes the possibility of a *neder* or a *nedavah*: *im neder o nedava zevach korbano* — the *neder* in that context is an obligation upon oneself to bring an offering.

Then there is Parshat Matos, which becomes the paradigmatic locus for this entire tractate. The verse reads: *ish ki yidor neder l'Hashem o hishava shvuah le'esor issar al nafsho lo yachel devaro* — a man who takes a *neder* or a *shvuah* to make something forbidden upon himself, he must not violate his word. Here the *neder* is explicitly about making something forbidden, and although the verse connects it to a *shvuah* as well, it is this formulation — the *neder* as an act that renders an object prohibited — that Chazal take as the defining model for the entire tractate.

### Chazal's Paradigm

What Chazal identify as the defining character of a *neder* is a focus on the *object* rather than on the *person*. A *shvuah* is person-oriented: "I swear that I will not eat this bread" — the person undertakes an obligation, and the object remains unchanged. A *neder*, by contrast, changes the status of the object itself: this bread becomes a forbidden object, much like other objects whose status is transformed by a verbal act. The object is the locus of the prohibition.

This understanding requires some reframing of the more prominent biblical examples. The cases of Yaakov and of Israel, where a *neder* sounds like a personal undertaking contingent on divine assistance, are reconceptualized by Chazal as *nidrei mitzvah* — vows to perform a *mitzvah* — a subcategory distinct from the standard *neder* discussed in this tractate. Similarly, the *neder* of a *korban*, while an obligation the person takes upon themselves, involves the verbal transformation of an object's status into the realm of the sacred. It is that element — the speech act that changes the object — which Chazal identify as the essential feature of a *neder*.

The question naturally arises: is there a unifying conceptual thread connecting all these cases? Even where the *neder* begins with a personal obligation, there is always an object whose status is being transformed. When Yaakov says he will give a *ma'aser*, he is verbally designating an object for God. When Israel vows to dedicate the cities as *cherem*, those objects are being given over through a declaration. When a *korban* is designated, the animal's status changes through words. The common denominator, then, is the power of verbal declaration to transform the identity and status of an object — *motzi b'peh* as the engine of change.

The contrast with a *shvuah* sharpens this point. In a *shvuah*, God's name is the key: you invoke God as witness to your action or commitment. In a *neder*, the key is not God's name but rather the object and your power — through your words — to alter its status. A *neder* draws upon a recognized domain in which human speech has transformative force.

### Korban Model

This leads to the concept of *ein nodrin ela bedavar hanadur* — one may only make a *neder* using the model of a *davar hanadur*, something whose forbidden status was itself produced by a human verbal act. If one says "this object should be like *chazir*," one has accomplished nothing, because the forbidden status of *chazir* derives from God's decree and its own nature, not from any human verbal transformation. One cannot, through speech, make something into *chazir*, because that domain is entirely outside the scope of human declarative power.

By contrast, if one says "this object should be like a *korban*," one is invoking a domain where human speech unambiguously transforms object-status. Just as one can make an animal a *korban*, or designate produce as *ma'aser*, or declare something *cherem*, one can render an object forbidden by likening it to these categories. The *korban* serves as the paradigmatic *davar hanadur* — the exemplary case of an object made forbidden through human declaration — and it is from this model that the standard vocabulary of *nedarim* is derived.

Importantly, a statement such as "this food is like *basar v'chalav*" or "like *chametz b'Pesach*" or "like *chelev*" would similarly accomplish nothing as a *neder*, even though those things are forbidden. The reason is the same: those prohibitions are divinely ordained categories, not the product of human verbal transformation. The valid model is exclusively the *davar hanadur* — something whose prohibited status flows from a human speech act of the same type.

### Konam

The classic term for this type of *neder* is *konam*, which is a variation — or euphemism — of the word *korban*. When one says *konam davar zeh alay* — "this thing should be like a *korban* to me" — one is drawing on that domain of human verbal transformation of object-status. *Konam* is thus not merely a substitute word; it is a word whose very form signals the conceptual underpinning of the *neder*: this object is to be treated like a sacrificial offering, whose status has been changed by my words.

It is worth noting in passing that even today, *bezman hazeh* when the *Beis HaMikdash* does not stand, one can still make a *neder* using this model. If something is declared like a *korban*, it becomes sanctified — it cannot be used, must be left to graze if it is an animal, and so forth — even without the possibility of actual sacrifice. The mechanism of declaring something like a *korban* remains operative.

### Speech Acts

All of this points to the broader category of *haplaa* — the speech act that transforms status. The Torah itself uses the root in *nazir ki yafli lindor neder nazir*, where *yaflia* means to enunciate or articulate, and in the rabbinic understanding it denotes specifically a speech act with transformative legal force. This is the category under which *nedarim*, *nezirut*, *ma'aser*, *hekdesh*, and *cherem* all fall: verbal declarations that change the ontological status of an object. A *shvuah* does not belong to this category in the same way — it does not change the status of an object but rather commits the person to a course of action or attests to a fact. The tractate before us is, at its heart, a sustained treatment of *haplaa* as applied to the domain of making objects forbidden.

---

## Masechet Nedarim

### Lashon Yerushalmi

Before beginning the *masechet* itself, it is worth noting several unusual features that set Masechet Nedarim apart from the rest of the Babylonian Talmud. The language of this tractate — its grammar, certain technical terms, and stylistic patterns — differs noticeably from the standard Babylonian Aramaic of the rest of the *Bavli*. This was already observed by Tosafot and the *rishonim* generally; Rashi designates this distinctive idiom in several places as *lashon Yerushalmi*, Palestinian Aramaic.

According to the scholarly literature, five tractates — Nedarim, Nazir, Meilah, Keritot, and Tamid — share a range of linguistic and grammatical peculiarities that distinguish them from the rest of the Babylonian Talmud. Notably, parts of Masechet Temurah exhibit the same phenomenon through what are labeled there as *lishna achrina* passages: one section of the text is in the familiar Babylonian Aramaic, and then an alternate version of the same passage appears written in this different idiom.

### Geonic Approach

Connected to this linguistic distinctiveness is a remarkable testimony concerning Geonic practice. The work *Otzar HaGeonim*, which collects and organizes Geonic responsa by tractate, records very little material on Nedarim. The reason given is telling: the *Geonim* who arose after the sealing of the Talmud and devoted themselves to clarifying its *halachot* — *hiziru atzmam mimasechet Nedarim* — they kept away from Masechet Nedarim. Within their *yeshivot* they formally announced: *de'anan la gersinan Nedarim* — "we do not study Nedarim." And further: *velo yediana le'asur ulehateir bah lo neder velo shevuah* — "we do not know how to prohibit or permit in this domain, neither by *neder* nor by *shevuah*." Consequently, they did not engage in *hataras nedarim* either on Rosh Hashanah or on Yom Kippur.

The text notes, however, that *be'Eretz Yisrael hayu nohagin bekach kol hayamim* — in the Land of Israel they maintained the practice throughout. One of the reasons cited for the Babylonian Geonic abstention is instructive: if *nedarim* are widely studied and discussed, people become aware of them as a readily available religious instrument and begin making them, sometimes inadvertently or inappropriately. Keeping the tractate out of the religious consciousness reduces the incidence of *nedarim*. This is analogous to the concern one might have about teaching certain sections of Masechet Kiddushin in a context where students might experiment with what they learn.

This warrants reflection. We tend not to appreciate how central the practice of making *nedarim* was to the religious lives of earlier generations. Vows were a standard mechanism for bringing God into one's daily world, for giving expression to one's religious impulses, for adding personal *chumrot* or taking on additional commitments. The *Gemara* elsewhere describes making a *neder* as analogous to building a *bamah* — with all the ambivalence that image carries. It can be an expression of genuine religious seriousness, but it also risks introducing a personal religiosity that operates outside communal norms, and the transgression risks involved in making and violating *nedarim* are considerable. The Geonic decision to deliberately abstain reflects a pastoral judgment about the balance of those risks.

### Pumbedita Theory

The question of the tractate's linguistic distinctiveness connects naturally to questions of provenance. Those who follow Rashi in calling the language *lashon Yerushalmi* have argued that the tractate ultimately reflects Palestinian usage and may be closer in origin to the *Yerushalmi* tradition than to the standard *Bavli*. This view is reinforced, they argue, by the fact that the Babylonian *Geonim* essentially did not engage with the tractate, while it remained part of living practice in Eretz Yisrael throughout the Geonic period.

However, this view is significantly contested in the scholarly literature. The more widely accepted position today is that the standard *Bavli* reflects the Babylonian usage of Sura — the academy where Rav Ashi edited the Talmud — while the distinctive idiom of Nedarim and the related tractates reflects the Babylonian usage of Pumbedita, the other great Babylonian academy, whose Aramaic differed in precisely these ways. On this account, there is no need to posit a Palestinian origin; the difference reflects a difference between the two great Babylonian centers of learning.

The further questions of relative dating — whether the Pumbeditan material is earlier, contemporaneous, or later than the Suran redaction, and whether it was re-worked or left in its original form — remain matters of scholarly debate, with multiple positions advanced. But the emerging consensus appears to favor the Pumbedita theory of origin rather than a Palestinian one.

### Textual Sources

Given the unusual character of the tractate, the question of which *rishonim* to rely on for commentary deserves attention. The commentary printed with the designation "Rashi" in standard editions of Nedarim is, by general scholarly acknowledgment, not actually Rashi's. The attribution is uncertain, and the commentary itself is considerably less rigorous and less precise than authentic Rashi — less consistent, less clear, and less analytically sharp. In many *yeshivot* that study this tractate, the pseudo-Rashi commentary is not treated as a primary learning resource.

The central commentary is instead the *Ran* — Rabbeinu Nissim of Gerona — who lived in the thirteenth century. The *Ran* is among the clearest of the *rishonim*, though not necessarily the most creatively innovative. He synthesizes the positions of earlier *rishonim*, presents the *Gemara*'s flow with admirable clarity, and brings in contradictions, difficulties, and resolutions in a manner that makes him function as something of a *rashi-tosafot* combined for this tractate. He is expansive, as the size of his commentary makes evident, but consistently lucid.

Tosafot and the Rosh are also present in the standard *Vilna* edition, appearing in their usual positions. The Tosafot here tend toward more straightforward commentary rather than the intensive *shakla vetarya* one finds in tractates like Bava Kamma or Gittin. Notably, despite the Geonic abstention, the *Rif* did write *Halachot* on Nedarim — his characteristic extraction of bottom-line *halachic* rulings — and the Ramban likewise composed *Hilchot HaRamban* on Nedarim, printed in the back of the *Gemara* parallel to the Rif. A range of *acharonim* have also written commentaries. The tractate is thus not without *rishonic* resources, even if they differ in character from those found in the more centrally studied *masechtot*.

---

## Kinuyim

### Kinuyim Rule

The first *mishna* of Masechet Nedarim opens with a broad principle: *kol kinnuyei nedarim kenedarim* — all *kinuyim* of *nedarim* have the status of *nedarim*. A *kinnuy* is a substitute word, a variation or euphemism — a term that is not exactly the standard vocabulary of a *neder* but is used in its place. The *mishna* establishes that such substitute language is legally effective and counts as if the standard term itself were used.

### Other Categories

The same principle is then extended in parallel formulations: *vacharamim kacharamim* — variations of *cherem* language carry the force of an actual *cherem*; and *ushvuot keshvuot* — variations of *shvuah* language are binding as a *shvuah*. The tractate also includes *nezirut kenezirut*: language that approximates or echoes the terminology of *nezirut* is binding as if one had formally declared oneself a *nazir*.

The *Ran* notes, in the context of *cherem*, that the tractate's treatment focuses on *cherem* understood primarily as a form of *neder* — that is, as a declaration making an object forbidden to oneself — rather than as the full category of dedicating objects to God or to the *kohanim*, which would belong more properly in the realm of *kodshim*.

### Konam Variations

The *mishna* does not immediately provide examples of these *kinuyim*; the examples appear only several *mishnayot* later, on daf 10. There the *mishna* states: *ha'omer konam konach konas harei elu kinnuyim l'korban* — one who says *konam*, *konach*, or *konas* has used a *kinnuy* for *korban*. One who says *cherek*, *cherech*, or *cheref* has used a *kinnuy* for *cherem*. One who says *nazik*, *naziach*, or *paziach* has used a *kinnuy* for *nezirut*. And terms like *shvuta* or *shkuka* are *kinuyim* for *shevua*. These words are recognizable echoes of their standard counterparts, with key letters altered or substituted.

### Purpose of Kinuyim

The *Gemara* addresses the origin and purpose of these invented terms. One possibility is that they derive from some other language — Aramaic or another Semitic tongue — that happens to sound similar to the Hebrew with slight variations. But the more straightforward explanation, and the one the *Gemara* endorses, is *lashon shebadu lahem chachamim* — it is a language the rabbis invented, a kind of technical terminology deliberately constructed to serve a purpose.

That purpose, as the *Gemara* explains, is to prevent the inadvertent utterance of *shem Hashem levatala*. If one uses the standard terms — *neder l'Hashem*, *korban l'Hashem*, *shvua l'Hashem* — one naturally appends God's name. By training people to use these unusual technical terms instead, the rabbis reduced the chance of God's name being used vainly. One might add that the strange and specialized nature of these terms also serves to make the speech act more conscious and deliberate — a person using *konam* knows they are engaging in a formal legal act, and the unfamiliarity of the word may introduce a moment of hesitation that the ordinary vocabulary would not.

Whatever the precise rationale, the *mishna* establishes that using these substitute terms is fully effective: *kol kinnuyei nedarim kenedarim*.

---

## Yadot

### Modrani Mimcha

The *mishna* then turns to a second concept, distinct from *kinuyim*: the *yad*. The *mishna* states: *ha'omer l'chavero modrani mimcha* — one who says to his fellow "I am vowed from you," *mufrashani mimcha* — "I am separated from you," or *meruchakani mimcha* — "I am distanced from you" — with respect to eating or tasting of his fellow's food, is *assur*, forbidden, from doing so. These formulations, though not standard *neder* vocabulary and not *kinuyim* in the sense of corrupted euphemisms, are nonetheless effective.

### Variations

The terms *mufrashani* and *meruchakani* are essentially translations or paraphrases of the concept of a *neder* — expressing the idea of separation or distance from the other person or their property. One might initially think these are additional *kinuyim*. The *Gemara*, however, distinguishes them: *kinuyim* are corrupted or variant phonetic forms of the standard words, while *modrani*, *mufrashani*, and *meruchakani* are ordinary, grammatically correct Hebrew expressions. The *Gemara* understands them instead as examples of *yadot* — abbreviated or elliptical statements.

There is also a textual question about whether the *mishna*'s language should be read as *she'ani ochel lach* — "those things that I eat of yours" — or *she'eini ochel lach* — "that I will not eat of yours." The distinction matters because a *neder* is object-focused: what becomes forbidden is the object, the food. If the formulation is "I will not eat," that sounds more like a *shvuah*, which is person-focused. The *Gemara* will engage with this question, and the precise text will bear on how we understand these abbreviated formulations.

### Menudeh Ani Lach

The *mishna* further records a case involving the phrase *menudeh ani lach* — "I am *menudeh* to you" — which borrows the language of *niduy*, Rabbinic excommunication. This usage is problematic as a *neder* formulation because it does not clearly invoke the model of a *davar hanadur*, nor does it straightforwardly transform the status of an object. Rabbi Akiva, as the *mishna* records, was inclined to rule stringently in such a case — not certain that it qualifies but not prepared to permit it — given the difficulty of fitting this language into the standard model of a *neder*.

### Yad Concept

The *Gemara* explains the concept underlying the cases of *modrani*, *mufrashani*, and *meruchakani*: these are examples of *yadot nedarim*, literally "handles" of *nedarim*. A *yad* is a handle in the sense of an abbreviated or elliptical statement — one that gestures toward a *neder* without articulating all of its required elements. The *Gemara* elsewhere discusses this concept in the context of *nezirut* as well: if someone is walking by and says "I will be" — stopping there — and the context makes clear that he meant "I will be like that *nazir*," the statement may be binding. The degree to which context must supply the missing elements distinguishes between *yadayim mochiachos* — handles that are self-evident from context — and *yadayim she'einam mochiachos* — handles where the intended meaning is not obvious and might be understood otherwise.

### Two Yad Models

The *Ran* explains precisely why *modrani mimcha* and similar formulations qualify as *yadot* rather than complete *nedarim*. He offers two distinct analyses. The first: *mishum delo masik diburei lemeimar kikorban* — the statement is abbreviated because the speaker did not complete it by saying "like a *korban*." On this understanding, the fundamental formulation of a *neder* requires the invocation of the *korban* model — *davar zeh assur kikorban* or *konam davar zeh alay* — and when that element is absent, the statement is only a *yad*, effective because we understand the *korban* reference to be the implicit completion of the sentence.

The second analysis: *i nami delo amar issura beheya* — alternatively, the statement is abbreviated because the speaker did not even say that something is *assur*, forbidden. A *neder* must change the status of an object; it must predicate *issur* of something. "I am separated from you" does not explicitly declare anything forbidden. Even setting aside the *korban* model, the very predication of prohibited status is missing. On this reading, the *yad* is effective because we understand the intent to create a prohibition, even though neither the language of prohibition nor the *korban* model was articulated.

These two analyses correspond to two different questions about what is strictly necessary for a complete *neder*: is explicit reference to the *korban* model required, or is an explicit statement of *issur* required? If one said *davar zeh assur alay beneder* — "this thing is forbidden to me as a *neder*" — without invoking the *korban* language, is that a complete *neder* or itself a *yad*? The two positions in the *Ran* reflect that underlying question.

---

## Object vs. Person

### Listing Order

The *Gemara* opens with an apparent discrepancy between our *mishna* and the opening *mishna* of Masechet Nazir. Our *mishna* provides a full list: *kol kinnuyei nedarim kenedarim, vacharamim kacharamim, ushvuot keshvuot, unezirut kenezirut* — all four categories. The opening *mishna* of Nazir, by contrast, states only *kol kinnuyei nezirut kenezirut* and lists nothing else. The *Gemara* asks: *mai shna gabei Nazir* — what is different about Nazir that it does not give the full list? And conversely, what is different about Nedarim that it does give the full list?

The *Gemara* answers: *neder* and *shvuah* appear together in the same *pasuk* — *ish ki yidor neder o hishavei shvua* — and therefore when discussing *neder*, one naturally includes *shvuah* as well. Once those two are mentioned together, one might as well fill out the complete list by adding *cherem* and *nezirut*. In Masechet Nazir, where the natural focus is *nezirut* alone, there is no comparable reason to list all the others.

### Heftzah vs. Nafsha

But this answer immediately generates a further question. If *neder* and *shvuah* are paired because they appear together in the *pasuk*, then the *mishna* should have listed them adjacently: *neder*, then *shvuah*, then the others. Instead, the *mishna* lists *neder*, then *cherem*, and only then *shvuah*. Why is *cherem* inserted between *neder* and *shvuah*?

Here the *Gemara* articulates one of the most fundamental conceptual distinctions of the tractate: *neder* and *cherem* both operate by making the *heftz* — the object — forbidden: *demis'ar heftza alei*. A *shvuah*, even when it concerns behavior toward an object, operates differently — *de'kasar nafshia min hacheftza* — it binds the person, not the object. Therefore, *neder* and *cherem* are grouped together as members of the same conceptual category, and *shvuah* is listed separately, after them. The Torah pairing of *neder* and *shvuah* explains why *shvuah* appears at all in this list; the conceptual distinction between *heftz*-focused and *nefesh*-focused prohibitions explains why *cherem* is placed between them. The *Gemara* thus uses this seemingly minor question of listing order to articulate what will prove to be the defining conceptual axis of the entire tractate.

### Kinuyim First

The *Gemara* raises a second structural question about the *mishna*: having established that the *mishna* discusses both *kinuyim* and *yadot*, why does it first mention the rule of *kinuyim* and then proceed directly to give examples of *yadot* — without first offering examples of *kinuyim*?

This is genuinely puzzling. The *mishna* opens with the general principle that *kinuyim* are effective. One would expect it then to illustrate that rule with examples of *kinuyim*, and only afterwards introduce the separate concept of *yadot* with its examples. Instead it introduces the rule of *kinuyim* and jumps immediately to examples of *yadot* — examples that won't be given until several *mishnayot* later.

### Rashi's Solution

Rashi's solution is that the *mishna* is a case of *chasorei mechasra* — the text is incomplete and must be supplemented. Reading the *mishna* as it stands is impossible without inserting a line that was implied but not written. The corrected reading should be: *kol kinnuyei nedarim kenedarim, v'yadot nedarim kenedarim* — all *kinuyim* of *nedarim* are like *nedarim*, and all *yadot* of *nedarim* are like *nedarim*. Once that missing line is understood to be present — at least implicitly — the *mishna* follows the chiastic ABBA structure: it states the rules for A (*kinuyim*) and B (*yadot*), and then provides examples beginning with B (the *yadot* examples, which follow immediately), returning to A (*kinuyim*) only in the later *mishna*. It chose to discuss B first in the examples because it had, in its implicit final clause, most recently mentioned *yadot*.

The irony that the *Gemara* acknowledges is that the entire argument for ABBA structure depends on an inserted line that was not actually there — it is a *yad*, one might say, in the *mishna* itself.

---

## Chiastic Patterns

### ABBA vs. ABAB

Following Rashi's invocation of the ABBA chiastic structure, the *Gemara* explores this pattern more broadly. It asks whether the rule is that a *mishna* always gives examples beginning with the item most recently mentioned — the ABBA pattern — or whether sometimes it begins with the first item mentioned, producing an ABAB structure. The *Gemara* brings a series of examples from across the *mishnah* to examine both patterns.

### Avot Examples

The three opening chapters of Masechet Shabbat provide the clearest examples of ABBA. *Bameh Madlikin u'vameh ein Madlikin* — with what may one light Shabbat candles and with what may one not? The *mishna* then begins its discussion with *ein madlikin*, the "may not" category — that is, B before A in the examples, having stated A then B in the rule. Similarly, *Bameh Tomnin u'vameh ein Tomnin* — with what may one insulate food and with what not? — followed by examples of what one may not use, again B first. And *Bameh isha yotzah u'vameh einah yotzah* — what may a woman wear in the public domain on Shabbat and what may she not — again followed by examples of what she may not wear, the second-mentioned category.

### Nochlim Example

Against these examples, the *Gemara* brings cases that follow the ABAB pattern. The *mishna* in Bava Batra: *yesh nochlin u'manchilim* — some inherit and bequeath — *nochlin velo manchilim* — some inherit but do not bequeath. The examples then begin with *v'elu nochlin u'manchilim* — those who both inherit and bequeath — the first-mentioned category. That is ABAB. An example of someone who inherits but does not bequeath would be a son relative to his mother: a son inherits from his mother, but the mother does not inherit from the son. Meanwhile a father and son illustrate the first category: a son inherits from his father, and if the son predeceases his father without other heirs, the father inherits from the son.

### Wife Examples

A parallel structure appears in Yevamot: *yesh mutarot l'va'aleihen va'asurot l'yivmeihen* — some wives are permitted to their husbands but forbidden to their brothers-in-law for *yibum* — *mutarot l'yivmeihen va'asurot l'va'aleihen* — and some are the reverse. A widow (*almanah*) married to a *kohen* whose husband's brother is a *kohen gadol* illustrates the first: she was permitted to her husband but the *kohen gadol* cannot perform *yibum*. A widow married to a *kohen gadol* illustrates the second: the marriage binds but she is forbidden to her husband (as a *kohen gadol* may not marry a widow), yet his ordinary-*kohen* brother can perform *yibum*. The *mishna* then begins its examples with the first category — again ABAB.

### Mincha Example

From the laws of *menachot*: *yesh te'unah shemen u'levonah* — some *menachot* require both oil and frankincense — *shemen v'lo levonah* — some require oil but not frankincense. The *mishna* then provides examples of those requiring both — ABAB again.

### Korban Example

Similarly, *yesh te'unah hagashah v'ein te'unah tenufah* — some offerings require *hagashah*, bringing them to the corner of the altar, but not *tenufah*, waving — *tenufah v'lo hagashah* — and some require waving but not *hagashah*. The examples begin with the first category — again ABAB.

### Bechor Example

From the laws of the firstborn: *yesh bechor l'nachala v'ein bechor l'Kohen* — some are considered firstborn for inheritance purposes but not for *pidyon haben* — *bechor l'Kohen v'ein bechor l'nachala* — and some are firstborn for *pidyon haben* but not for inheritance. A boy born after a miscarriage is the first viable son, so he receives the double inheritance portion, but since he did not breach his mother's womb he does not require *pidyon haben*. Conversely, a *kohen* who already has a firstborn son and then has another son by a different wife: that second son is the *peter rechem* of his mother and requires *pidyon haben*, but since he is not the firstborn of his father he does not receive a double portion. The *mishna* begins its examples with the first category — ABAB once more.

### Length-Based Rule

Facing this array of contradictory cases, the *Gemara* proposes a rule: *hanei mishum d'avshei lehu mefaresh hahu depatach berisha* — those that follow ABAB do so because the discussion of each category is long. In a chiastic ABBA structure, by the time you have given the rule for A, then B, and then a lengthy discussion of B examples, the reader will have lost track of what A was. The ABBA structure only works when the discussion is compact enough that the final return to A does not come so late as to be disorienting. When the treatment of B is going to be extensive, the *mishna* must restate A before going on to B, producing ABAB. The cases from Shabbat — the candles, the insulation, the woman's garments — are all relatively brief and thus can sustain the ABBA structure.

### No Fixed Rule

However, the *Gemara* notes a counterexample: the *mishna* regarding what animals may wear on Shabbat (*yotzei gamal* and similar) also follows ABAB despite involving only a brief list. This undermines the proposed rule, since brevity alone does not determine the choice of structure.

The *Gemara* concludes accordingly: *ella lav davka* — there is in fact no fixed rule. *Zimnin de-mafarash de-patach be-reisha* — sometimes the *mishna* gives examples beginning with the first-mentioned category, producing ABAB — *zimnin hahu de-sayeim mafarash be-reisha* — and sometimes it gives examples beginning with the last-mentioned category, producing ABBA. The *mishna* of Nedarim chose to present its examples in ABBA fashion, beginning with *yadot* before *kinuyim* — even though, as noted, the clause about *yadot* was implicit rather than explicit — and both patterns are legitimate. With that, the *Gemara*'s opening structural digression concludes, and the tractate will proceed to substantive analysis of *yadot* and *kinuyim* beginning tomorrow.

---

---

# Nedarim 3

## Shabbat Lamplight

### Reading by Lamplight

There is a *halacha* found in the *gemara* in *Masechet Shabbat* that a person is not permitted to read by the light of an oil lamp on *Shabbat*. The reason the *chachamim* gave for this is a *gezeirah* of *shema yiteh* — lest a person forget that it is *Shabbat* and tilt the lamp in order to bring the oil closer to the wick, which would constitute a violation of the *melacha* of *mavir*.

### Electric Lights Today

The question naturally arises as to whether this *halacha* applies nowadays when we have electric lights. The majority of *poskim* rule that it does not apply, both because there is no analogous way to tilt an electric lamp to make the light stronger, and because we are so accustomed to electric lights that the original concern simply does not obtain. Nevertheless, some are *machmir* and maintain that one should still exercise caution.

### Muktzeh Candles

Another important concept in this area concerns the *muktzeh* status of candles. If a candle was lit during *bein hashmashos* — the twilight period between Friday and *Shabbat* — it becomes *muktzeh* for the entire day. This follows from the principle of *migo d'itaktzai l'bein hashmashos itaktzai l'kuly yoma*: since the object was set aside at the onset of the holy day, that status persists through the whole of *Shabbat*. Accordingly, even if the candle goes out in the middle of the night, one still may not move the candlestick, because it was a *basis l'davar assur* — a base for a forbidden object — at the moment *Shabbat* began.

## Kinyan: Gold & Silve (II)

### Gold Acquires Silver

At the bottom of the preceding page — 46b — the *mishnah* states: *haZahav koneh et haKesef vehaKesef eino koneh et haZahav*, gold acquires silver, but silver does not acquire gold. According to the *mishnah*, gold is considered *peira* — a commodity — while silver is considered *matbeia*, currency. The governing rule of *kinyanim* is that the commodity acquires the currency: if one performs *meshichah* on the commodity, the currency is acquired by the seller wherever it may be. But if one pulls the currency, the commodity is not acquired to the buyer until the buyer separately performs *meshichah* on the commodity itself.

## Kinyan: Gold & Silve (II)

### Rav vs. Levi Debate

The *gemara* on 47a asks why gold should be classified as the commodity. A *machloket* emerges between Rav and Levi on this point. One holds that gold is *matbeia* — currency — because it is more valuable, while the other holds that silver is *matbeia* because it is more common. The *halacha* follows the view that silver is the currency.

### Meshichah Takana

The *gemara* further establishes that *mi-de'Oraita* — on the level of biblical law — *maot konot*: money itself constitutes a valid *kinyan*. However, the *chachamim* enacted a *takana* requiring *meshichah* to complete the transaction.

### Buyer Protection

This *takana* was enacted to protect the buyer in the event of a fire — a principle expressed by the phrase *nisrefu peirotecha ba'aliyah*. So long as the seller retains responsibility for the goods, he will exert himself to save them. If, however, a party retracts after having given money, the *beit din* subjects him to the curse of *Mi ShePara*, declaring that the One who punished the generations of the flood and the dispersion will punish one who does not keep his word.

## Taanis Tzibur

### Public Fasts

The *mishnah* in *Masechet Ta'anit* addresses the institution of *taanis tzibur*. When a *tzarah* befalls *Eretz Yisrael* — such as a drought — the *beit din* would declare a series of public fasts.

### Hissorerus Address

During these periods of communal crisis, the people would gather in the *rechovah shel ir*, the city square, where a *zaken* would deliver words of *hissorerus* to inspire the community to engage in genuine *teshuva*.

### Aron & Ashes

As part of this assembly, the *aron* would be brought out and *eifer* placed upon it, expressing the community's distress and *hachna'ah* before Hashem. The *sak* — sackcloth — was also part of this public display of submission.

### Tikun Ma'asim

The *gemara* emphasizes, however, that it is not the *sak* or the *taanis* itself that brings forgiveness, but rather the *tikun hama'asim* — the genuine improvement of one's actions. This is the true goal of any *taanis*: to move a person toward authentic *chazara b'teshuva*.

### Nineveh Example

This principle is illustrated from the story of Nineveh. The *posuk* does not say that *Elokim* saw their fasting; rather, it says *vayar Elokim es ma'aseihem* — He saw their deeds. The emphasis on actions over mere fasting is explicit and instructive.

### Between Man & God

We must examine our behavior and ensure we are conducting ourselves appropriately in *bein adam l'chavero* and *bein adam l'makom*. Through this dual rectification, we merit the *rachamim* of the *Borei Olam* and, ultimately, the *geulah sheleimah* speedily in our days.

## Sukkah & Ohel

### Rava's Question

Rava raises a pointed question against Rav: if Rav holds that even a *sukkah* higher than twenty *amot* can be valid when its *defanos* reach all the way up to the *sechach*, why is it that in the case of a bed one requires *asara tefachim*? Even if the bed stood less than *asara tefachim* high, it should already be considered an *ohel* — for according to Rav, a space of *asara tefachim* is not a prerequisite for *ohel* status.

### Intent of Walls

The *gemara* answers on Rav's behalf: *hasam defanos le'ohel avidi* — there, in the case of the *sukkah*, the *defanos* are constructed for the sake of the *ohel*. But in the case of the bed: *hacha karayei hamita lav le'ohel avidi* — the legs of the bed are not made for the sake of forming an *ohel*. Since they were not constructed with *ohel* intent, they can only confer *ohel* status under specific conditions.

### Asara Tefachim

When the bed legs reach a height of *asara tefachim*, the space beneath them is considered significant enough to constitute an *ohel* regardless of the original purpose for which the legs were made. But if the height falls short of *asara tefachim* and the structure was not constructed for *ohel* purposes, it does not attain *ohel* status. Consequently, it would not create a *chatzitzah*, and one would fulfill the relevant obligation. This is how Rav would answer Rava's challenge from the later *mishnah*.

## Elul & Rosh Hashanah

### Birkat HaChodesh

There is a well-established custom to recite a special prayer on the *Shabbat* before the beginning of each new month, petitioning Hashem to bless the coming month with life, peace, health, and prosperity. This prayer is known as *Birkat HaChodesh*. Yet one month each year is conspicuously absent from this practice: the month of *Tishrei*. On the *Shabbat* before *Rosh Hashanah*, we do not recite *Birkat HaChodesh*. Since *Rosh Hashanah* is *Rosh Chodesh* — the first day of *Tishrei* — the question demands an explanation.

### Elul as Blessing

The Rebbe, Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Rymanov, explains that we do not bless the month of *Tishrei* because the entire preceding month — the month of *Elul* — is itself one long blessing for *Tishrei*. *Elul* functions as the blessing; the month of preparation is the very vehicle through which *Tishrei* receives its sanctity.

### Elul Preparation

The month of *Elul* is a month of preparation, of introspection, and of *teshuva*. Through the work we undertake during *Elul*, we provide the blessing for the coming year. These days are designed for reflection: we look back at the year that has passed, consider the choices we have made, the actions we have taken, and the words we have spoken, and we ask ourselves where we can improve and how we can grow.

### Personal Reflection

This is the essence of *teshuva* — often translated as repentance, but more precisely meaning return: a return to our true selves and a return to our relationship with the Almighty. We look at the areas where we have fallen short and ask honestly how we can become more aligned with who we truly wish to be.

### Rambam Teshuva

The Rambam teaches that *teshuva* involves several distinct steps: *viduy* — verbalizing one's mistakes; *charata* — feeling sincere regret; and *kabbalah al ha-atid* — making a firm commitment to do better in the future. Yet the goal is not merely to repair the past; the goal is to genuinely transform oneself for the future.

### Blessing Year Ahead

As we draw closer to *Rosh Hashanah* and *Yom Kippur*, we should take full advantage of these final days of *Elul*. The coming year is blessed through our own efforts and growth. May we all be inscribed and sealed in the book of life for a good, healthy, and meaningful year — *ketiva v'chatima tova*.

## Neshama vs. Guf

### Neshama Tikkun

The *neshama* descends from a very elevated place specifically in order to perform its *tikkun*. We observe that different people are drawn to different *mitzvot* with greater intensity than others, and this is no accident — it reflects the particular *tikkun* that each *neshama* has come to accomplish. A person must recognize that the reason he is in this world is to fix something specific, and that this specificity is meaningful.

### Arizal Teaching

The Arizal HaKadosh teaches that certain *mitzvot* call to a person more powerfully than they do to others — not that they are easier, but that one finds oneself drawn to be especially careful and exacting in their performance. That particular *mitzvah* is very likely one's *tikkun*. And conversely, something that a person finds exceptionally difficult may also be part of what he must rectify — whether it manifests as a love for a *mitzvah* or as a struggle against a particular inclination.

## Neshama vs. Guf (II)

### Neshama as Royalty

The Chovos HaLevavos, in *Sha'ar HaBechina*, Rabbeinu Bachya describes the *neshama* as royalty — like a king or queen — that comes from a supremely elevated realm. When it is placed within the *guf*, it finds itself in a kind of prison: something lowly, physical, and coarse. The *guf* desires the physical and the mundane; the *neshama* yearns for the spiritual and the elevated.

### Soul-Body Battle

The result is a constant battle between *neshama* and *guf*. The *guf* pulls downward; the *neshama* reaches upward. The work of a person in this world is precisely to make the *guf* subservient to the *neshama* — to render the physical subordinate to the spiritual. This is the central task of human existence, and it is the reason the battle exists.

### Reward & Struggle

Nor should one be discouraged by the difficulty of this struggle, for the greater the struggle, the greater the reward: *lefum tza'ara agra* — according to the pain, so is the reward.

## Parshat Vayera

### Avraham's Guests

This week's *parsha* is *Parshat Vayera*. At its opening, the *posuk* states *Vayera Elav Hashem*. Rashi explains that it was the third day following the *brit milah* of Avraham Avinu, and despite the intense heat of the day — *k'chom hayom* — Avraham was actively searching for guests to welcome. When three *malachim* appeared in the guise of travelers, he ran to greet them. This exemplifies the *midah* of *chesed* and the practice of *hachnasat orchim* at its most exalted.

### Orchim Greatness

This is a striking *gemara*: the *gemara* in *Masechet Shabbat* states *gedolah hachnasat orchim mi'kabalat pnei hashechina* — welcoming guests is even greater than receiving the Divine Presence. Avraham's conduct in the opening of *Parshat Vayera* stands as the paradigmatic illustration of this teaching.

## Animals Shabbat

### Restraint Types

The fifth chapter of *Masechet Shabbat*, *Perek Bameh Behemah*, opens with the question: with what may an animal go out on *Shabbat*, and with what may it not go out? The *mishnah* enumerates: a camel may go out with a halter (*afsana*); a dromedary with a nose ring (*chotem*); a Libyan donkey with a bit (*farumbiya*); and a horse with a chain (*shir*).

### Chains Tumah

The *mishnah* further states: *ve-chol ba'alei ha-shir yotze'im be-shir ve-nimshachim be-shir* — all animals that have chains go out with a chain and are led by the chain. One may sprinkle on them or immerse them in their places (*u-mazin aleihen ve-tovlin bi-mekoman*) if they become *tamei*. This provision applies because the metal chains are susceptible to *tumah* by virtue of their status as a *kli* — a vessel — and yet the *mishnah* permits immersing them in a *mikvah* while they remain on the animal.

### Animal Rest

The underlying concern throughout is the prohibition against an animal carrying a burden on *Shabbat*. The *Torah* commands *lema'an yanuach shorecha va-chamorecha* — so that one's ox and donkey may rest — which means an animal may not perform *melacha* on *Shabbat*. Carrying a *masa*, a burden, in the *reshus ha-rabim* constitutes *melacha*.

### Burden Definition

However, if an animal is wearing something for its own protection or to prevent it from running away, that item is not a *masa* but a *tachshit* — an ornament, or necessary equipment. The distinction between a *masa* and a *tachshit* is critical: if more restraint is placed on an animal than it actually requires, the excess weight becomes a burden. A heavy halter placed on a small goat, for instance, is not necessary for restraint and therefore constitutes a prohibited *masa*; the same halter on a camel is indispensable and therefore permitted.

### Restraint Necessity

The *gemara* explains the specific restraints listed in the *mishnah* with reference to the nature of each animal. The *afsana* for a camel is a simple rope halter, sufficient for its control. A dromedary, however, is considerably more difficult to lead, and therefore requires the *chotem* — a ring passed through the nose — which provides the necessary degree of control. Each animal's permitted restraint is calibrated to what is genuinely required for its management.

## Rabbi Akiva

### Water & Stone

Rabbi Akiva and his wife Rachel chose to endure the most difficult conditions, understanding that they were building their foundation upon *Torah* and upon learning. Rabbi Akiva was not always a great scholar; for many years he was a simple shepherd who could not even read the *alef-bet*. One day, while tending his flock, he noticed a stone with a deep hole carved into it. Upon being told that the hole had been worn by water dripping on it day after day, Rabbi Akiva drew the lesson: if soft water can pierce hard stone through sheer persistence, then the words of *Torah* — which are like iron — can certainly penetrate his heart.

### Learning Begins

At the age of forty, Rabbi Akiva went to the schoolhouse with his young son and the two of them began to learn the *alef-bet* together, starting completely from the beginning.

### Study Success

He spent the next twenty-four years in intensive study until he became the leader of tens of thousands of *talmidim*. What began as an adult learning the *alef-bet* with his child culminated in one of the greatest rabbinic careers in Jewish history.

### Rachel's Role

When Rabbi Akiva finally returned home, he told his students that all of his *Torah* knowledge was only thanks to his wife Rachel. His words were direct and unambiguous: *sheli v'shelachem shela hu* — everything that I have and everything that you have belongs to her.

## Yosef Na'ar

### Yosef Grooming

The *posuk* describes Yosef as a *na'ar* — a young boy — in the phrase *v'hu na'ar et bnei Bilhah v'et bnei Zilpah*. Rashi explains that this refers to *na'arut*: Yosef would fix his eyes, tend to his hair, and conduct himself with the bearing of a young man conscious of his appearance. The question is striking — what was a *tzaddik* of Yosef's stature doing concerning himself with his grooming while enslaved in Egypt, while his father mourned him?

### Simcha Purpose

The answer is that Yosef understood, with great wisdom, that in order to survive his situation, he needed to maintain *simcha* and a sense of self-worth. Had he allowed himself to deteriorate, had he succumbed to depression and ceased to care about himself, he would never have been able to withstand the *nisayon* of *Eshet Potiphar*, and he would never have risen to become the ruler of *Mitzrayim*. He needed to keep himself together.

### Ben Melech

Yosef's self-presentation was not an expression of *ga'avah* — it was not vanity or self-absorption. It was a tool for survival. He reminded himself: I am a *ben melech*, a son of Yaakov Avinu; I am of worth; I matter. That sense of identity and dignity kept him going. This carries a vital lesson for us: when we find ourselves in difficult circumstances, in something of a *golus*, we must keep our heads high, remember that we are children of the King, and maintain that *simcha* — because *simcha* is the very means by which we overcome the challenges we face.

## Chanukah Identity

### Greek Threat

This theme connects directly to *Chanukah*. The Greeks sought to erase Jewish identity — to strip away our sense of self-worth and make us feel indistinct from everyone else. Their assault was not merely physical but existential: they wanted us to believe we were no different, no more special, no more connected to anything beyond the material world.

### Chashmonaim

The *Chashmonaim* refused. Their response was an unequivocal assertion: we are *kadosh*, we are different, and we have a connection to the *Ribbono Shel Olam* that cannot be severed. Their resistance was grounded not in politics but in identity.

### Chanukah Simcha

What we celebrate on *Chanukah* is precisely that sense of identity and that *simcha* — the joy of knowing who we are and refusing to relinquish it. Wishing everyone a *freilichen Chanukah* and a *gut Shabbos*.

## Aseret Yemei

### Judgment Sincerity

The *Mishnah Berurah* explains that during these days, when we stand before *HaKadosh Baruch Hu* in judgment, we wish to demonstrate that we are taking our *mitzvot* seriously — that our *teshuva* is genuine and not merely performative.

### Chumrot Days

One of the ways we express this sincerity is by adopting *chumrot* during the *Aseret Yemei Teshuva* — stringencies that go beyond our ordinary year-round practice.

### Pas Yisroel

A classic example is *pas Yisroel*. Many people rely all year on the more lenient position and eat *pas paltar* — bread baked by a non-Jewish baker. During the *Aseret Yemei Teshuva*, however, the practice is to be more careful to eat only *pas Yisroel*.

### Sincere Effort

This is a concrete way of showing Hashem that we are making an effort — that we wish to live more carefully and more holily. It is not about the bread itself; it is about the gesture of striving beyond the baseline requirement of *halacha*.

### Yesod Avodas

This is a fundamental *yesod* in the *avodas Hashem* of these days. We want to demonstrate that our *teshuva* is sincere and that we are willing to go beyond the minimal requirement in order to find greater *chen* in the eyes of the *Ribbono Shel Olam*.

# Nedarim 4

## Yad l'Nezirut

### Yad Framework

The daf opens approximately six lines down, with Rav Ashi's statement, picking up from the *baraita* that established the parallel between *yad l'nazir* and *yad l'nedarim* — that is, *l'hazir l'hazir*, the principle that an abbreviated statement counts as a full statement. This was the crucial point developed on the previous daf: the concept of *yad*, by which an incomplete verbal formulation is nonetheless legally effective as a *neder*.

### Thought & Speech

Underlying this discussion is the recognition that a valid *neder* requires two distinct components: correct thought and correct speech. One must say the right thing, and one must intend the right thing. The focus now shifts to what constitutes "the right thing to have said" — specifically, whether a complete verbal formulation is required or whether an abbreviated statement suffices. The principle of *yad* answers that an abbreviated statement can, under the right conditions, serve as a complete and binding declaration.

### Abbreviated Statement

The *Gemara* is equally concerned with establishing that just as there is *bal taachar* in the context of *nedarim* — the prohibition of postponing the fulfillment of a vow — so too does *bal taachar* apply to *nezirut*. The parallel drawn between *neder* and *nazir* thus operates on two axes simultaneously: the effectiveness of abbreviated speech, and the obligation to fulfill one's commitment without delay.

---

## Bal Taachar

### Link to Nezirut

Having established the *yad* framework, the *Gemara* turns to the application of *bal taachar* to *nezirut*. The prohibition of postponement, classically understood as the obligation not to delay bringing a *korban* past three *regalim*, is extended here to the domain of *nezirut*. The same way one transgresses *bal taachar* by delaying a vow of sacrifice, one transgresses it by improperly delaying the commencement or proper continuation of *nezirut*.

### Postponement Scenario

A question immediately arises: since accepting *nezirut* takes effect automatically upon utterance, how can there be a scenario in which one is obligated to be a *nazir* but has not yet become one — the very precondition for *bal taachar*? Two scenarios were proposed. First, if someone declared "I will become a *nazir* before I die," then every passing day on which he has not yet accepted *nezirut* constitutes a potential postponement, since he might die at any moment; each day of delay is thus a separate violation of *bal taachar*, even as the *nezirut* has not yet formally begun. Second, if one declared *nezirut* while standing inside a *beit hakevarot* (a cemetery), the *nezirut* may be delayed from taking proper effect by virtue of his remaining in that impure location.

### Cemetery Scenario

The *Gemara* went further in the cemetery case: even if the *nezirut* does take effect in the cemetery, by remaining there one delays the transition from *nezirut d'tumah* — the nazirite state under conditions of impurity — to *nezirut d'taharah*, the proper nazirite state of purity. The implication is striking: *bal taachar* is not merely about initiating *nezirut*, but about initiating *nezirut* in its proper form. It is insufficient to have technically begun; one must begin correctly, and delay in achieving that proper beginning is itself a violation.

### Rav Ashi's Chiddush

Rav Ashi extends this principle further with a significant *chiddush*. He rules that a *nazir* who intentionally renders himself *tamei* — impure — transgresses not only the prohibition against a *nazir* becoming *tamei*, but also the prohibition of *bal taachar d'nezirut d'taharah*. The reason is that intentional *tumah* forces the *nazir* to lose all days counted until that point — *hayomim harishonim yiplu ki tamei nizro* — and to restart the entire count from the beginning after completing a process of purification. Since the entire period of *nezirut d'taharah* must effectively begin anew, the gap between the original declaration of *harei ani nazir* and the eventual restart of the proper count constitutes a postponement of the beginning of *nezirut d'taharah*. The *chiddush* is that this applies even though the *nazir* did formally begin his *nezirut* weeks earlier — since the count must be entirely redone, the original start effectively did not count, and the substantial gap between declaration and the re-commencement of the proper *nezirut* is treated as *bal taachar*.

---

## Giluach & Bal Taachar

### Rav Acha Position

Rav Acha son of Rav Ika offers a different account of what constitutes *bal taachar* in the context of *nezirut*. In his view, the violation consists of postponing the *tighluach* — the shaving of the head that marks the conclusion of *nezirut*. Here, the concern is not with delaying the *beginning* of *nezirut* but with delaying its *end*. Once the period of *nezirut* is complete, the *nazir* is obligated to shave his head and bring his sacrifices, and postponing this ritual constitutes a violation of *bal taachar*.

### Nature of Giluach

The *Gemara* notes the conceptual ambiguity surrounding *giluach*. One might view the shaving as an essential ritual that itself terminates the *nezirut*; according to this view, delaying *giluach* directly delays the conclusion of *nezirut*. Alternatively, one might understand *giluach* not as constitutive of the ending but rather as an independent *mitzvah* performed in the *Beis HaMikdash* at the close of *nezirut*. According to this second view, *Abaye* and *Rava* each rule in accordance with their respective positions: the one who holds that *giluach* is indispensable (*me'akev*) for ending *nezirut* would naturally say that postponing it is *bal taachar* of *nezirut* itself; while even the one who holds that *giluach* is *not* indispensable agrees that one transgresses *bal taachar* of the *mitzvah* of shaving by delaying it.

### Giluach Problem

This remains a conceptually strange category of *bal taachar*. Classic *bal taachar* involves the postponement of something given or consecrated to God — a freely accepted obligation in the mold of a *korban*. The *nezirut* itself can be understood as giving oneself to God (*l'hazir l'Hashem*). But postponing the ritual of *giluach* — which is either the act of ending *nezirut* or an accompanying ritual in the *Beis HaMikdash* — sits uneasily within this framework. It is not an act of giving to God; it is, at most, a procedural rite that concludes a previously accepted state. The *Gemara* acknowledges this difficulty and proceeds to consider a more intuitively natural account of *bal taachar* in the context of *nezirut*: the postponement of the *korbanot*.

---

## Korbanot & Bal Taachar

### Mar Zutra

Mar Zutra son of Rav Ashi offers the most straightforward explanation: when we say that a *nazir* transgresses *bal taachar*, what we mean is that he has postponed bringing his *korbanot*. A *nazir* who has completed his *nezirut* is obligated to bring three sacrifices — an *olah*, a *chatat*, and a *shelamim* — and if he delays past three *regalim*, he violates *bal taachar*.

### Special vs. General

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this explanation: if *bal taachar* applies to all obligatory *korbanot* — a principle derivable from general *halacha* — why does the *Torah* need to link *nazir* to *neder* at all? The answer should already be obvious from the general rule. This pushes the *Gemara* to examine the textual derivation of *bal taachar* itself.

### Pesukim Source

The *Gemara* cites the relevant *pesukim*. The simple reading of the verse is *ki sidor neder l'Hashem Elokecha lo t'acher l'shalmo* — when you make a free-will vow to God, do not delay fulfilling it. The plain sense thus limits *bal taachar* to freely accepted obligations, *nedarim* and *nedavot*, not to *korbanot* that the *Torah* itself imposes as a consequence of sin or circumstance. However, the doubled language — *darosh yidreshenu* — extends the prohibition: God will *demand* it of you, implying that even *korbanot* that are demanded by the *Torah* (such as *chataot* and *ashamot*) fall under *bal taachar*. Once a *chiyuv korban* exists, whether arising from a freely accepted vow or from a Torah-imposed obligation, one who postpones it transgresses *bal taachar*. Given this general principle, of course there would be *bal taachar* for the *korbanot* of a *nazir* — no special derivation should be needed.

### Chatat Chelev

The *Gemara* reinforces this point by invoking the *chatat chelev* — the sin-offering brought by one who inadvertently ate forbidden fat, a paradigmatic sin carrying *chiyuv karet*. One cannot bring a *chatat chelev* through a *neder*; it is only possible if one has actually committed the relevant sin. And yet there is clearly *bal taachar* by a *chatat chelev*. This proves that *bal taachar* applies to obligatory *korbanot* entirely outside the category of *neder*. Thus, the *nazir's korbanot* — being Torah-mandated obligations — should self-evidently fall under *bal taachar*, and we still have not identified what *chiddush* the linking of *nazir* to *neder* was meant to teach.

---

## Nazir Korban Chiddush

### Hypothetical Objection

The *Gemara* now presses the question: what was the *chiddush* that the *Torah* needed to teach explicitly regarding *bal taachar* and the *korbanot* of a *nazir*? Two answers are proposed, each identifying a reason one might have thought that the *nazir's korbanot* specifically would *not* be subject to *bal taachar*.

### Package Nature

The first answer: *nezirut* is an unusual, package-like category. The *Gemara* cites the ruling that if someone declares *hareini nazir min hachartzan* — I am a *nazir* from [eating] the pits of the grapes — he becomes a *nazir* in the full sense, obligated in all the restrictions of *nezirut*, even though he articulated only one component. The Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon debate what happens in such a case: the *Chachamim* hold that he acquires the entire package, while Rabbi Shimon holds that since he did not accept all the obligations, he acquires nothing. Crucially, both agree that *nezirut* operates as an indivisible package — nobody holds that one can be a *nazir* with respect to grapes alone. The debate is only over whether a partial acceptance triggers the full package or triggers nothing. Given this all-or-nothing structure, one might have argued that because *nezirut* is such an anomalous category, *bal taachar* would not apply to its *korbanot* in the ordinary way. The *Gemara*, however, rejects the logical force of this reasoning: the strange, encompassing nature of *nezirut* is not a reason to conclude that one would not transgress *bal taachar* for postponing its *korbanot*.

### Weighting Question

The second and more compelling answer is introduced: *hanicha l'man d'amar i gilach al achat mi-shloshtan yatza* — since a *nazir* who performs the *giluach* in conjunction with any one of the three *korbanot* may be considered to have discharged the essential end of his *nezirut*, the remaining two *korbanot* have a diminished sense of urgency. Having in some sense already "finished," there is less felt pressure to bring the remaining *korbanot* promptly. One might therefore have thought that the obligation to bring these remaining sacrifices lacks sufficient weight to generate a *bal taachar* violation upon delay.

### Lack of Urgency

This line of reasoning is further sharpened by comparing the *nazir's korbanot* to other obligatory *korbanot*. When one sins and is obligated to bring a *chatat* for *kaparah* — atonement — there is an urgent underlying pressure: one is in a state of unremedied sin and needs *kaparah*. When one is *tamei* and needs to bring a *korban* to return to a state of *taharah*, there is again an urgent underlying pressure: the desire — at least conceptually — to be able to eat *kodashim* and enter the *Beis HaMikdash*. Both of these cases involve not merely a formal *chiyuv* but an existential pressure that makes the postponement genuinely weighty. The *nazir's* remaining *korbanot*, by contrast, involve no such urgency. There is no sin requiring atonement — even the *chatat nazir*, while it exists, is best understood (as the *Rambam* explains) not as atonement per se but as a change of personal status — and the *nezirut* has in some sense already concluded. One might therefore have thought that the obligation to bring the remaining *korbanot* is insufficiently weighty to generate *bal taachar*, since postponing them involves no deferred *kaparah* and no unresolved *tumah*. The *Torah's* linkage of *nazir* to *neder* therefore teaches — *kamashma lan* — that even these relatively "weightless" obligatory *korbanot* are subject to *bal taachar*.

A second formulation reinforces the same conclusion from a different angle: since the *korbanot* of a *nazir* cannot be created through a *neder* — one cannot say *harei zo alai chatat nazir* and thereby obligate oneself independently, since the *chatat nazir* is only available to one who is actually a *nazir* under *chiyuv* — one might have thought that since *bal taachar* is conceptually rooted in the domain of *neder*, it would not apply to a *korban* so entirely outside that domain. The *Gemara* responds that a *chatat chelev* similarly cannot arise through a *neder* and yet clearly carries *bal taachar*. The rejoinder, however, is that a *chatat chelev* carries *kaparah* as its purpose, and that urgency of *kaparah* is what grants it sufficient weight for *bal taachar*. The *chatat nazir*, which is about change of status rather than *kaparah*, lacks this urgency. The *chiddush* is thus that even such a *korban* — neither arising from *neder* nor serving *kaparah* — is subject to *bal taachar*.

### Chatat Yoledes

The *Gemara* raises a parallel case: the *chatat yoledes*, the sin-offering brought by a woman after childbirth. This *korban* involves no *neder*, no sin, and no *kaparah* in the conventional sense — it is a *korban* of status change, brought to return the *yoledes* from a state of *tumah* to *taharah*. Yet the *Gemara* affirms that there is *bal taachar* for the *chatat yoledes* — and explains this on the basis of Rabbi Yishmael's principle: there is an urgency to becoming *tahor*, because once one is *tahor* one regains the capacity to eat *korbanot* and to enter the *Beis HaMikdash*. Even if these practical privileges are rarely exercised, the conceptual importance of *tahara* — the potential to eat *kodashim*, the ability to access the *Beis HaMikdash* — creates a genuine pressure to resolve the *tumah* promptly. This urgency is sufficient to ground *bal taachar*, even without *neder* or *kaparah*. The *nazir's korbanot*, by contrast, carry no such urgency — not the urgency of *kaparah*, not the urgency of resolving *tumah* — and the *chiddush* that they nonetheless carry *bal taachar* is therefore genuinely novel. The *Gemara* thus arrives at a clear formulation of why a special derivation was necessary: the *korbanot* of a *nazir* are the weakest possible case of an obligatory *korban*, with the least urgency behind them, and the *Torah* teaches that *bal taachar* applies to them nonetheless.

---

## Annulment Powers

### Baraita Linkage

The *baraita* states the second principle derived from the linking of *nazir* to *neder*: just as a father may annul his daughter's vows and a husband may annul his wife's vows, so too a father may annul his daughter's *nezirut* and a husband may annul his wife's *nezirut*. The *Gemara* asks: why is an explicit textual linkage necessary? One might have derived this by analogy — *bemah matzinu* — directly from the laws of *nedarim*.

### Nezirut as Neder Type

The force of the question is this: *nezirut* is not a separate category parallel to *nedarim* — it is a *type* of *neder*. If that is so, there are not two independent categories (apples and oranges) between which a *gezeirah shavah* or textual link is needed. Rather, *nezirut* is a subset of *nedarim*, the way a specific variety is a subset of a broader category. If annulment applies to *nedarim*, it should self-evidently apply to this particular form of *neder* without requiring any additional derivation.

### Time Limit Defense

The *Gemara* responds: one might have thought to distinguish *nezirut* from ordinary *nedarim* on the following grounds. An ordinary *neder* has no intrinsic time limit; by default it is a permanent change of status, and therefore the *Torah* granted the father and husband the power to annul lest someone remain bound indefinitely. *Nezirut*, by contrast, has a built-in time limit — standard *nezirut* is thirty days — and might therefore have been excluded from the annulment power, on the reasoning that it will expire on its own shortly regardless. The textual linkage thus teaches that annulment applies to *nezirut* as well, despite its time-bounded nature.

### Neder Permanence

The *Gemara* briefly addresses the converse possibility: why not learn *in reverse* and say that since *nezirut* is thirty days, perhaps all *nedarim* default to thirty days? The answer lies in the conceptual model underlying *nedarim*. A *neder* operates on the paradigm of *hekdesh* — sanctification. When one consecrates an object as a *korban*, the change of status is permanent; there is no inherent clock on sanctification. Since a *neder* functions by changing the status of an object (rendering it forbidden as though it were sanctified), the default model of a *neder* is a permanent, open-ended change of status. The time-limited character of *nezirut* is thus a feature specific to that institution, not a general model for *nedarim*.

---

## Hamudar Hanaah

### Mishna Case

The *Gemara* now transitions to a new section of the *Mishnah*: the case of *hamudar hana'ah machaveiro* — one who has taken a vow prohibiting himself from deriving benefit from another person. This section of the *Mishnah* is understood by the *Gemara* as a presentation of *yadim* — abbreviated statements that function as effective vows.

### Statement Examples

The *Mishnah* lists several formulations that constitute effective prohibitions: *mudarani mimcha* ("I am vowed away from you"), *mofreshani mimcha* ("I am separated from you"), *she'ani ochel lach* ("the things I would eat of yours"), and *she'ani to'em lach* ("the things I would taste of yours"). Each of these is an abbreviated formulation — none states the full content of a *neder* — yet each is legally effective.

### Statement Components

To understand why these are *yadim*, it is useful to analyze the components of a complete *neder* formulation. A full statement would specify: the object (e.g., "your food"), the relationship of the speaker to the object (e.g., "to me"), and the legal status of the object (e.g., *assur* — forbidden — or *konam* — like a *korban*). A *neder* operates by changing the status of an object through a declaration modeled on *hekdesh*: "Your food is *konam* — like a *korban* — to me." This yields three elements: the object, the relationship, and the status. The formulations in the *Mishnah* each supply only one or two of these elements, leaving the remainder implicit. *Mudarani mimcha* indicates the relationship of separation but does not specify the object. *She'ani ochel lach* specifies the object class (food) but does not supply the status word. Neither supplies the word *assur* or *konam*, which explicitly establishes the forbidden status. Yet because these formulations occur within a recognizable context of *neder*-making, the missing elements are understood as implicit — and that is precisely the function of *yad*.

The *Ran* observes that the phrase *she'ani ochel lach* avoids ambiguity because the particle *she-* marks it as a definite reference — "that which I would eat of yours" — rather than an invitation. If someone meant to say "I would like to eat with you," he would say *ani ochel lach*, not *she'ani ochel lach*. The *she-* construction signals that the speaker is identifying an object class — the food he would eat — and intending to change its status. That is the *yad*: the object is indicated, and the context of *neder*-making supplies the rest.

---

## Shmuel's Position

### Shmuel's Rule

Shmuel states: *mudarani mimcha* alone accomplishes nothing — it is not even a *yad*. One must say *she'ani ochel lach* or *she'ani to'em lach*. By itself, *mudarani mimcha* is too vague to function as an abbreviated *neder*.

### Braitta Objection

The *Gemara* objects from a *baraita*: *mudarani mimcha*, *menudeh ani mimcha*, *mishamtani ani mimcha* — *harei zeh assur*. The *baraita* rules that even the "separation" formulation alone is sufficient to create a prohibition. Similarly, *she'ani ochel lach*, *she'ani to'em lach* — *harei zeh assur* — even just specifying the object class alone is forbidden. Either phrase alone, the *baraita* says, constitutes an effective *yad*. A second *baraita* that reverses the order of the phrases further forecloses the interpretation that the two phrases must be used together: it is clear that each phrase independently creates a prohibition.

### Reading Narrowly

After multiple attempts to harmonize Shmuel's statement with the *baraitot* — first by suggesting that the *baraita* describes the combination of both phrases, then by noting that the second *baraita* reverses the order, making such harmonization impossible — the *Gemara* ultimately reinterprets Shmuel. The *Gemara* reads Shmuel's statement not as ruling that *mudarani mimcha* alone is ineffective in all circumstances, but as addressing the differential legal effect of the phrases. Specifically: *she-k'var amar mudani* — when one has already said *mudarani mimcha* and then adds *she'ani ochel lach*. The reinterpretation shifts Shmuel from a ruling about validity to a ruling about scope.

---

## Shmuel's Distinction

### Both Phrases Effect

Once the *Gemara* has reinterpreted Shmuel, his actual ruling comes into focus. Shmuel holds that when someone says *both* phrases — *mudarani mimcha* together with *she'ani ochel lach* — the result is that only he himself is forbidden from eating the other's food: *hu d'assur v'chavero mutar*. He has specified the object (the food he would eat from the other) and indicated his separation from it; the vow is therefore directed and limited — his eating of the other's food is forbidden, but the other's eating of his food is not affected.

### One Phrase Effect

When, however, one says only *mudarani mimcha* — "I am separated from you" — without specifying the object, the result is different: *shneihem asurim*, both parties are forbidden to one another. This ruling is supported by Rav Yosef bar Chanina: *mudarani mimcha* — *shneihem asurim*.

### Filling Blanks Logic

The logic of this distinction is the logic of filling in blanks. When both phrases are used together, the second phrase (*she'ani ochel lach*) narrows and specifies the meaning of the first: the separation is with respect to "the food I would eat of yours," i.e., your food is forbidden to me. The *neder* is thus directed and unilateral. When only the first phrase is used — "I am separated from you" — no object is specified, and the court must fill in what "separation" means. Separation, in its unqualified sense, is bidirectional: I am separated from you and you from me. Since there is nothing to indicate that the speaker meant only one direction, the prohibition is interpreted to run both ways — your food is forbidden to me, and my food is forbidden to you. This is not the speaker imposing a *neder* on the other person; rather, the speaker is understood to have changed the status of all items relevant to the relationship of benefit between them, in both directions. Should the other party then take food from the speaker's table and eat it, it is primarily the speaker who has transgressed the *neder* by allowing the prohibited benefit to flow.

---

## Sheani Ochel Yad

### Girsa Question

A textual question arises regarding the phrase in the *Mishnah*: should the reading be *she'ani ochel lach* ("that which I eat of yours") or *she'eini ochel lach* ("I will not eat of yours")? The distinction carries significant legal weight.

### Reinterpretation

If the correct *girsa* is *she'eini ochel lach* — "I will not eat of yours" — then the *Ran* observes that one appears to have stated a complete sentence. There is ostensibly nothing missing. Yet the *Ran* argues that precisely *here* lies the *yad*: what the speaker has formulated is not a *neder* but a *shvuah*. A *neder* is object-based — it changes the status of an object — while a *shvuah* is action-based and person-based, restricting what the person will do. "I will not eat of yours" is formulated as an oath about the speaker's behavior, not as a declaration about the status of the food. The function of *yad* here is therefore not to supply a missing element of a *neder* formulation, but to *reinterpret* a statement that was phrased as a *shvuah* and treat it as though it were a *neder*. The abbreviated or hybrid nature of the statement — its blending of *shvuah*-language with *neder*-context — is what makes it a *yad*: we read "I will not eat of yours" as "the food of yours that I would eat is forbidden to me."

### Practical Application

This interpretive mechanism creates a noteworthy practical consequence. If *yad* can reinterpret an action-oriented statement as an object-oriented prohibition, then a person who uses *shvuah* language in a *neder* context cannot escape the *neder* simply by pointing out that he formulated it as an oath rather than a vow. The *yad* will do its work and convert the formulation into a *neder* regardless. This principle, taken to its logical conclusion, closes what might otherwise appear to be a convenient loophole: one who impulsively declares "I will never again drive on this road" cannot easily argue that since the formulation sounds like a *shvuah*, no *neder* was created. If the context is one of *neder*-making, the *yad* reinterprets accordingly — and the road itself becomes, in some sense, *assur alav*.

---

---

# Nedarim 5

## Shmuel's Position

### Reading the Mishnah

The Gemara on the previous daf had been working through a statement of Shmuel, who held that the Mishnah's language was obscure. The Mishnah had listed a series of formulations — *mudrani mimcha*, *mufrehani mimcha*, *she'ochal lcha*, *she'at'oam lcha* — each of which functions as a *yad*, an abbreviated or elliptical statement that attaches to a full *neder*. The question was how to read that Mishnah: does each formulation work independently, or does Shmuel require them in combination?

### Mudrani Mimcha

The Gemara demonstrated that each formulation works on its own, which forced a modification of Shmuel's position. As refined, Shmuel holds that when one says *mudrani mimcha* — a broad, generic statement of separation — without any qualifying predicate, the *neder* operates in both directions simultaneously. That is, not only is your property forbidden to me, but my property becomes forbidden to you as well. It is only when the speaker adds the phrase *she'ochal lcha* — specifying the things of yours that I would eat — that the prohibition is directionally limited: your property is forbidden to me, but mine remains permitted to you. The added qualifier thus narrows, rather than broadens, the scope of the *neder*.

### Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina

With this understanding in hand, the Gemara brings a statement of Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina, who teaches: *mudrani himcha shneihem assurin* — if one says "I am separated from you," both parties are forbidden. This parallels the revised reading of Shmuel. But the Gemara immediately raises a challenge from the Mishnah. The Mishnah states: *hareini alecha cherem* — behold, I am to you *cherem*, meaning my property bears the status of *cherem* relative to you. In that case, the Mishnah rules *hamudar assur* — the *mudar*, the person to whom the *neder* is directed, is forbidden to benefit from the *magdir*'s property — but the *magdir* himself remains permitted to benefit from the *mudar*'s property. The question is sharp: if we interpret *mudrani mimcha* as working in both directions, why does this formulation, *hareini alecha cherem*, operate only in one direction?

### Reconciling Views

The Gemara's resolution is that the cases in the Mishnah are not *stam*, not plain and unqualified. In each instance, the speaker went on to provide an explicit clarification. For instance, when the Mishnah says *hareini alecha cherem*, it turns out the speaker also said *ve'ani alecha lo* — "but I to you, no." And conversely, when the Mishnah says *ve'at alai cherem* — "you are to me *cherem*" — that is also qualified by the addition that the reverse does not apply. In both cases the outcome was already explicit.

The Gemara then asks: *aval stama mai* — but what if nothing explicit was added? The answer follows: in the unqualified case, *hu assur vechavero mutar* — only one direction applies. This appears to stand in direct tension with Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina, who said that *mudrani himcha* generates bilateral prohibition.
