How can the unqualified use of *cherem*-language operate unilaterally when *mudrani mimcha* operates bilaterally?

The Gemara resolves this through a careful restatement of Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina's position: *mudrani lcha shneihem assurin; mudrani mimcha hu assur vechavero mutar*. The critical distinction lies in the directional particle. *Mudrani lcha* — "I am separated to you" — is syntactically ambiguous. It can be read as "my property is forbidden to you," but it can equally be read, by supplying a *misha* prefix, as "I am removing myself from your property as well." Because *lcha* lacks a directional prefix that firmly fixes one reading, the phrase is genuinely open in both directions and therefore generates bilateral prohibition. *Mudrani mimcha*, by contrast — "I am separated from you" — contains the prefix *mimcha*, which unambiguously establishes the direction of removal: from your property. There is no legitimate grammatical way to read *mimcha* as simultaneously generating a prohibition running in the opposite direction. Hence it is unilateral.

### Lach vs. Mimcha

This resolution, however, circles back to the original difficulty with Shmuel's formulation. Shmuel had said that one needs to combine *mudrani mimcha* with *she'ani ochel lach* — the things of yours that I will eat. But if *mimcha* already operates in only one direction, what is the additional work being done by *she'ani ochel lach*? The need for that qualifier must mean something other than fixing directionality. The Gemara accordingly offers a reformulation: *hachi itmar* — here is what Shmuel actually meant. If one says *she'ani ochel lach*, the prohibition is limited to *achilah*, eating. *Mudrani mimcha* alone, without any qualifier, would be broader — potentially an *issur hana'ah*, a prohibition against all forms of benefit. The qualifying phrase *she'ani ochel lach* narrows the scope of the *neder* to the domain of eating rather than all benefit.

---

## Specificity Principle

### Scope of Prohibition

This leads to a general and important principle. If someone makes a *neder* using generic language — *cherem*, *konam*, *neder* — without specifying the nature of the prohibition, the default is *assur b'hana'ah*: any and all forms of benefit are forbidden. If one wishes to limit the *neder* to *achilah* alone, one must say so explicitly.

### Achilah vs. Hana'ah

The phrase *she'ani ochel lach v'she'ani toeim lach* — the things of yours that I will eat and that I will taste — establishes that the operative prohibition is one of eating. Since *te'imah*, tasting, is itself a subset of *achilah*, citing both narrows the *neder* to the category of consumption and excludes all other forms of benefit. Without that explicit narrowing, the prohibition stands at the broader level of *hana'ah*.

### Ambiguity Problem

A further issue emerges. One might assume that *mudrani mimcha*, stated alone, at least generates a *neder* — even if a maximally broad one. But the Gemara raises a more radical possibility: perhaps *mudrani mimcha* does not constitute a *neder* at all. The phrase may not even be referring to the forbidden status of objects. *Mudrani mimcha* could mean nothing more than: I am distancing myself from you. I do not want to conduct *masa u'matan*, business dealings, with you. I refuse to stand within your *arba amos*. I will not speak with you. All of these are modes of social and personal separation, and none of them necessarily involves the prohibition of an object under the framework of *neder*. The phrase is thus radically ambiguous — it might mean that your objects are *assur* to me for eating, or for benefit, or it might simply mean I want nothing to do with you personally. Given that ambiguity, who is to say that any *neder* was made at all? It is only when the speaker says *she'ani ochel lach* — the things of yours that I will eat — that we know unambiguously that the speaker intends to forbid objects in the domain of *achilah*.

---

## Yad Concept

### Three Levels of Yad

The Gemara now crystallizes a general conceptual framework. There are three distinct levels to consider when evaluating an elliptical speech act, a *yad*. The first is a *yad mochiach* — a statement where what the speaker means is entirely clear even without explicit articulation. An illustrative case: at a *chuppah*, when the *chosson* says *harei at mekudeshet* but fails to add *li* — to me — the omission does not necessarily invalidate the *kiddushin*. Since the entire ceremony is oriented around this man marrying this woman, the *li* is implicit; the *yad* is *mochiach*, clear from the entire context. The second level is a *yad she'einah mochiach*: the statement most likely means what we think it means, but there is some possibility it means something else. For instance, *harei at mekudeshet* said outside the context of a *chuppah* — in a world where men sometimes send agents — might refer to a *shaliach* acting on behalf of a third party. The meaning is probable but not unambiguous. The third level is no *yad* at all: the statement is so open-ended that no particular meaning can be ascribed to it.

### Ambiguous Yad Invalid

The Gemara now asks: does a *yad she'einah mochiach* — an ambiguous but probably-clear statement — constitute a valid *yad* or not? The formulation it proposes is: *leima kasavar Shmuel yadayim she'einan mochichot lo havyan yadayim* — perhaps Shmuel's entire position rests on the principle that handles which are not unambiguous do not count as handles at all. *Mudrani mimcha* falls into this category: most likely it is a *neder*, but it might mean nothing more than social distancing. That ambiguity, however slight, disqualifies it as a valid speech act, and without the clarifying phrase *she'ani ochel lach*, nothing takes effect.

### Get Parallel

The Gemara confirms this: *ein, Shmuel mokim lah matnitin k'Rabbi Yehuda* — yes, Shmuel is interpreting our Mishnah in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda's position. For the Mishnah in the laws of *gittin* teaches: *gufo shel get harei at muteret l'chol adam* — the core text of a *get* is "behold you are permitted to all men." Rabbi Yehuda, however, holds that one must add the phrase *v'den d'yehevei lichi minai sefer teiruchin v'igeret shevukin* — "and this shall be to you from me a writ of severance and a document of release." Without this addition, says Rabbi Yehuda, the statement *harei at muteret l'chol adam* is insufficient, because it does not unambiguously identify the document itself as the instrument effecting the divorce. Perhaps the man is merely making a verbal declaration of release, and the written text is simply that declaration recorded. Only when the text says explicitly "this document shall be to you from me" does it become clear that the document itself is the operative instrument. This is a direct application of *yadayim she'einan mochichot lo havyan yadayim*.

The Gemara asks: *amai dachik Shmuel l'ukma l'matnitin k'Rabbi Yehuda* — why did Shmuel strain to interpret our Mishnah according to Rabbi Yehuda, a minority opinion? We have *baraitot* that explicitly say *havyan yadayim* — ambiguous handles do work. Why not interpret the Mishnah according to the majority *Rabbanan*, who hold *havyan yadayim*? Rava answers: the language of the Mishnah itself forced Shmuel's hand. The Mishnah says *she'ani ochel lach v'she'ani toeim lach* — things of yours that I will eat, things of yours that I will taste — including the word *lach*, to you. But why is *lach* necessary? The speaker is already addressing the person directly and has already said *mimcha* — from you. The word *lach* is superfluous unless it is signaling a principle: when making a *neder*, the language must be maximally clear and unambiguous. The superfluous *lach* is itself evidence that the Mishnah demands *yadayim mochichot*, and that is why Shmuel read the Mishnah as he did.

### Ran's Explanation

The Gemara proceeds to state the *amora'ic* debate directly. *Abaye amar havyan yadayim* — Abaye holds that an ambiguous but probable *yad* is a valid speech act. *Rava amar lo havyan yadayim* — Rava holds that any ambiguity disqualifies the speech act entirely. Rava reports that Rav Ibi provided him with the proof from the verse *nazir l'hazir l'Hashem*. The word *l'hazir* teaches, through the principle of *hekkesh*, that *yadei nezirut* — elliptical statements indicating a *nazir* vow — must satisfy the same standard as *nezirut* itself. And *nezirut* requires *hafla'ah* — articulation and clarity. The *hafla'ah* requirement is derived from the root *l'hafli*, meaning to articulate distinctly and concretely. Just as the *neder* of *nezirut* must be made with complete clarity, so too must the *yad* of *nezirut* be unambiguous. And since we learn the *yad* of *neder* from the *yad* of *nazir*, the same standard applies across the board.

The Ran makes an important conceptual clarification regarding the *get* debate. When the Gemara says the *Rabbanan* do not require the text of the *get* to be explicit, this should not be misread as the *Rabbanan* accepting ambiguity. Rather, the *Rabbanan* hold that what renders the text clear is not the intrinsic language of the statement alone, but the surrounding context. There is a distinction between a *yad mochiach* — where the statement itself, read in isolation, is unambiguous — and a case where the statement is technically a *yad she'einah mochiach*, but the context supplies the clarity. In the latter case, according to the *Rabbanan*, the *yad* still works — not because ambiguity is acceptable, but because the context provides the *mochiach* that the language lacks. The implication is that even the *Rabbanan* may require some form of clarity; they simply allow context to supply it. The live debate between Abaye and Rava, then, is specifically about cases where even context does not resolve the ambiguity — whether that residual ambiguity disqualifies the speech act entirely.

---

## Rava's Argument

### Nazir L'hazir

Rava's proof rests on the verse *nazir l'hazir l'Hashem*. The word *l'hazir* — to vow as a *nazir* — is the source for the principle that elliptical statements (*yadayim*) are legally operative in the context of *nezirut*. The Gemara performs a *hekkesh*, a textual linkage: *makish yadei nezirut l'nezirut* — the *yad* of *nezirut* is compared to *nezirut* itself. From this comparison follows the principle: *mah nezirut b'hafla'ah af yadei nezirut b'hafla'ah* — just as full *nezirut* requires *hafla'ah*, so too must a *yad* of *nezirut* satisfy the standard of *hafla'ah*.

### Hafla'ah Requirement

*Hafla'ah* is a technical term in this context, derived from the root *l'hafli*, meaning to articulate or declare distinctly. The word appears in connection with speech acts — *neder* and *shevuah* — and it conveys the requirement that such acts be performed with concreteness and clarity. Things created through *hafla'ah* are, by definition, created through fully articulated speech acts. The *hafla'ah* standard thus requires not merely that the speaker had the intention to make a *neder*, but that the words themselves express that intention with sufficient clarity to constitute the operative act.

### Conditional Nazir

The practical implication of the *hafla'ah* requirement is illustrated through the case of *hareini nazir im zeh nazir* — "I will be a *nazir* if this person is a *nazir*." One opinion holds that such a vow is ineffective even if we subsequently discover that the person in question was indeed a *nazir*, because at the moment the vow was uttered there was genuine uncertainty whether it was taking effect. The concept of *hafla'ah* requires that the speech act be determinate at the moment of utterance. If the efficacy of the statement depends on a fact not yet known, the speech act lacks the requisite clarity — not merely because of the speaker's subjective uncertainty, but because the act itself is constitutively conditional and indeterminate. Whether one rules strictly on this question is a matter of some debate, but the conceptual point is clear: *hafla'ah* mandates that the speech act be unambiguous in its operation at the moment it occurs.

### Applying to Neder

From the *hafla'ah* requirement governing *nezirut* itself, the Gemara derives through *hekkesh* that the same standard governs a *yad* of *nezirut*. And since the *yad* of *neder* is learned from the *yad* of *nezirut*, the *hafla'ah* standard applies to *nedarim* as well. The consequence is Rava's position: a *yad she'einah mochiach* — a *yad* with any residual ambiguity — does not meet the *hafla'ah* standard and therefore cannot function as a valid speech act. The *neder* does not take effect.

---

## Abaye vs. Rava

### Abaye's View

Abaye holds *havyan yadayim*: even an ambiguous *yad*, one where the meaning is probable but not certain, constitutes a valid and operative speech act. A degree of ambiguity does not negate the *neder*.

### Rava's View

Rava holds *lo havyan yadayim*: any degree of ambiguity disqualifies the *yad* entirely. The speech act must be unambiguous in order to take legal effect. This is Rava's application of the *hafla'ah* principle derived through the *nazir* *hekkesh*.

### Get Connection

The Gemara asks whether Abaye and Rava are essentially replicating the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the *Rabbanan* in the Mishnah about the text of a *get*. The Mishnah rules that the core text of a *get* is *harei at muteret l'chol adam*. Rabbi Yehuda requires the addition *v'den d'yehevei lichi minai sefer teiruchin v'igeret shevukin* — "and this shall be to you from me a writ of severance and a document of release." The Gemara maps the positions: *Abaye de-amar k'Rabbanan* — Abaye rules like the *Rabbanan*, who do not require explicit articulation; *Rava de-amar k'Rabbi Yehuda* — Rava rules like Rabbi Yehuda, who does. The debate over *yadayim she'einan mochichot* thus appears to be the same debate, applied to different legal contexts.

### Kritut Distinction

Abaye, however, refuses this mapping of his position to the *Rabbanan*. He says: *ana de-amri afilu k'Rabbi Yehuda* — I rule even according to Rabbi Yehuda's position, and yet I still hold *havyan yadayim*. How? Because Rabbi Yehuda's stringency in the law of *get* derives from a special requirement unique to *gittin* — the Torah requirement of *kritut*, severance. *Kritut* demands that the divorce effect a complete and total rupture of the marital bond. Every ambiguity, every loose thread, every possible residual connection must be eliminated. Given that uniquely elevated standard, Rabbi Yehuda requires the text of the *get* to be explicitly unambiguous. But this is not a general statement about speech acts. In ordinary contexts — *nedarim*, *nezirut* and the like — Rabbi Yehuda might well accept an ambiguous *yad* as operative. The *kritut* requirement is a specifically heightened standard, and its demands cannot be extrapolated to areas outside the law of *get*. Therefore Abaye can hold *havyan yadayim* universally while simultaneously accepting Rabbi Yehuda's position regarding *gittin* as applying only in that specific context.

### Rava's Response

Rava in turn responds symmetrically: *ana de-amri afilu k'Rabbanan* — I hold even according to the *Rabbanan*, and yet I still hold *lo havyan yadayim*. The *Rabbanan* do not require explicit articulation in the text of the *get* — but this is not because they are tolerant of ambiguity. It is because in the context of a *get*, there is no ambiguity at all. *Ein adam megaresh ishet chaveiro* — a man does not divorce another man's wife. Given the entire context of a *get* proceeding, who is divorcing whom is perfectly clear, as is the fact that this document is the instrument of divorce. The *Rabbanan* say the text is sufficient not because they permit ambiguity, but because there is no ambiguity here. The context supplies the clarity that the intrinsic language might otherwise lack. In general, Rava still requires *yadayim mochichot* — the position that ambiguity nullifies the speech act — but contextual clarity can satisfy that requirement. The *Rabbanan*'s leniency in *gittin* is not a statement about accepting ambiguity; it is a statement that in this particular case there is none.

### Ran's Distinction

The Ran presses on this point and introduces a conceptual refinement. The Gemara states: *ad kan lo ka'palgei Rabbanan de-be-yadayim mochichot* — the *Rabbanan* say you do not need *yadayim mochichot* by *get*. But this seems to contradict the explanation just offered — that the *Rabbanan* do require *yadayim mochichot*, they just hold that the requirement is satisfied by context. The Ran resolves this by distinguishing between two different sources of clarity. A *yad mochiach* refers to a case where the statement itself — the intrinsic semantic content of the language, read apart from any context — is unambiguous. When it is the context, rather than the statement itself, that provides the clarity, this is not technically a *yad mochiach* at all; it is contextual *mochiach*. The text of a *get* as written — *harei at muteret l'chol adam* — is not, in isolation, a *yad mochiach*. It is a *yad she'einah mochiach* by its intrinsic language alone. What the *Rabbanan* hold is not that *yadayim she'einan mochichot* are valid in general, but rather that in the case of a *get*, contextual clarity — *ein adam megaresh ishet chaveiro* — is an independent and sufficient source of *mochiach* that operates entirely apart from the text. Therefore when the Gemara says the *Rabbanan* do not require *yadayim mochichot*, it means precisely that: the statement's intrinsic *yadayim* do not have to be *mochichot*, because context provides its own distinct form of clarity.

The upshot for the Abaye-Rava debate is this. Both agree that when there is clear context or a clear statement, the speech act is fully operative. The disagreement is confined to cases where even context does not eliminate the ambiguity — where the statement remains genuinely open to multiple interpretations and no external factor resolves it. In that situation, Abaye holds the speech act is still valid, while Rava holds it is not. This is the precise scope of *yadayim she'einan mochichot lo havyan yadayim* according to Rava, and the conceptual distinction the Ran draws makes clear why the *Rabbanan*'s position in *gittin* does not commit them to accepting ambiguity in general.

---

---

# Nedarim 7

## Yad Sheino Mochiach

### Definition of Yad

We pick up at the very top of daf 7, at the concept of *yesh yad*. We are in the middle of a discussion that began with a debate between Rav and Rav Yehuda over whether *yad sheino mochiach* qualifies as a *yad* or not. Tosafot raises a preliminary definitional question: what exactly is *yad sheino mochiach*? It must be distinguished from something that is not a *yad* at all — that is, a case where the speaker's meaning is completely uncertain and open-ended. *Yad sheino mochiach*, as we discussed yesterday, is best understood as a case where it is fairly clear what the person means, but not entirely so. There is some ambiguity, and if there is a concept of *yad*, we go by the most reasonable presumed meaning while acknowledging that some other meaning remains possible. This is distinct from a case where the statement is so open-ended that it could mean any number of things. *Yad sheino mochiach* involves one or two or three reasonable possibilities — not an infinite range of interpretations.

### Speech Acts vs Implicit

The broader question running through this section of the *gemara* is where the concept of *yad* applies at all. The fact that the *gemara* asks this question presupposes that in these domains, we are not merely interested in *da'at* — in subjective intent — but in the precise words used: in the *speech act* itself. With *kiddushin*, as Tosafot notes by drawing on the language of *hekdesh*, the declaration *harei at* functions as a formal *hekdesh*-like consecration, and therefore there is a genuine speech-act dimension: the question arises whether one must be entirely explicit or whether an abbreviated, slightly equivocal expression can still be effective. That is the question of *yad* in the context of *kiddushin*.

The case of *pe'ah* is even more striking, because the classical form of *pe'ah* involves no speech whatsoever — one simply refrains from cutting the corner of the field. But Tosafot's analysis requires us to envision a context where one does perform a speech act of designation: one says "this is *pe'ah*" rather than merely leaving the corner. In such a case, the question of *yad* becomes relevant.

### Complete Sentence Rule

Tosafot raises a subtle but important distinction. Why does it matter whether there is some ambiguity in the expression? After all, even if the meaning were completely unambiguous, if there is no concept of *yad*, the person never fully articulated what they meant, and the designation should be ineffective regardless. Tosafot's answer is this: there is a difference between a case where a full sentence was never begun and a case where a full sentence was already stated. If someone has already said *harei at mekudeshet li* to one woman, and then turns and says "and this one" — if that second expression is completely unambiguous, then *and this one* simply applies the entire first sentence to the second woman. It is like saying *amen* after hearing a *berachah*: it is as if you have said the full thing yourself. The Rambam makes this precise point — *ha'omer amen k'mevarech hu dami* — the one who says *amen* has, in a sense, said the entire *berachah*.

Since in such a case the second designation would be fully explicit by virtue of the first sentence, there would be no *yad* in play at all. The *gemara* therefore introduces a degree of ambiguity into these cases in order to ensure that the second expression cannot be read as a simple repetition of the first sentence. And once there is that ambiguity — once we cannot say with certainty that the second utterance was meant to extend the first — then the person has not said the thing explicitly, and the question of *yesh yad o lav* becomes relevant.

The upshot is this: the concept of *yad* addresses whether an inexplicit statement can be effective even when the meaning is clear. *Yesh yad* says yes — even without full articulation, if the meaning is discernible, it counts. *Ein yad* says no — you must say it explicitly, and knowing what you meant is not sufficient.

---

## Tzedakah & Yad

### Multiple Units Case

The *gemara* turns to the question of *yad* in the context of *tzedakah*. What is the case? If someone says, "This dollar is for *tzedakah*," and then says, "and this one also" — that is no question at all. The word "also" in this context is entirely explicit: it applies the first sentence to the second dollar without any ambiguity. The Rambam's formulation applies perfectly here: saying *v'hadein nami* when it is entirely clear what is meant is equivalent to restating the first sentence. No *yad* is involved.

The genuine *yad* question arises when someone says "this dollar is for *tzedakah*" and then simply says "and this" — *v'hadein* — without adding "also for *tzedakah*." What does *v'hadein* mean here? Perhaps he means, "and this one too is for *tzedakah*." Or perhaps he means, "and this one I'll use for something else entirely." There is just enough ambiguity that the second utterance cannot be read as a transparent repetition of the first full sentence. It is precisely to introduce that ambiguity that the *gemara* frames the case this way. Without it, as we said, there would be no *yad* question — the second expression would simply extend the first.

### Korbanot Connection

The *gemara* then asks: *mi amrinan keivan d'itkesh l'korbanot d'chtiv b'ficha zu tzedakah* — since *tzedakah* is compared to *korbanot* through the *pasuk* which teaches that "that which passes your lips" applies to *tzedakah*, and there is a prohibition of *bal te'acher* — of failing to fulfill a verbal commitment to give *tzedakah*, particularly when one pledges at a communal appeal — does the comparison to *korbanot* extend also to the concept of *yad*? Just as *korbanot* was the original domain from which *yad* was derived, does *tzedakah*'s linkage to *korbanot* carry that over as well? Or is the comparison limited: *bal te'acher* applies to *tzedakah*, but the structural category of *yad* does not?

### Tzedakah as Neder

It is striking that the *gemara* introduces *tzedakah* at this point in the discussion, placed after *kiddushin* and *pe'ah*, which are both quite distant from the *neder* category. *Tzedakah*, by contrast, is in many ways very close to it. When someone designates a specific sum as *tzedakah*, that money acquires a *tzedakah* status. It is not exactly *hekdesh*, but it is modeled on that structure — one cannot simply redirect those funds to a different purpose and replace them with a different donation later. The object itself becomes earmarked. Furthermore, when someone accepts upon themselves a *tzedakah* obligation through speech, there is the prohibition of *bal te'acher* if they fail to fulfill it. This combination — the designation affecting the status of an object, and the spoken commitment creating a personal obligation — makes *tzedakah* closely parallel to *nedarim* in structure.

It is therefore interesting that the *gemara* raises this question alongside *kiddushin* and *pe'ah*, because *tzedakah* is more naturally in the *neder* mold than either of those. Much of what applies to *tzedakah* reflects the *korban*-*neder* model directly, and one would expect the answer to be that *yesh yad* applies here more readily. Much of this, of course, is a question between a person and God — the courts may have limited jurisdiction over many of these verbal commitments — but the halachic effect is real.

---

## Tzedakah vs Hefker

### Hefker Comparison

The *gemara* then asks: *ma shehu l'hefker* — is there a concept of *yad* when someone declares property *hefker*? If I take my old possessions and place them outside, renouncing ownership so that anyone may take them, does that act of renunciation admit of a *yad* parallel? The *gemara*'s initial response is: *haynu tzedakah* — this is the same as *tzedakah*, since both involve making something available for others to take. The question is whether they operate through the same mechanism.

### Beneficiary Scope

The *gemara* then distinguishes: *shani tzedakah*, *tzedakah* is different, because *tzedakah lo chazya ela l'aniyim* — *tzedakah* goes only to the poor. *Hefker*, by contrast, *mi aniyim u'mi ashirim* — is available to rich and poor alike. This difference in the scope of beneficiaries may constitute a meaningful distinction. The logic is not entirely explicit — it is not immediately obvious why the fact that *hefker* can be taken by wealthy people should make it less susceptible to the *yad* principle — but the *gemara* raises this as a genuine differentiating factor.

### Mechanisms Differ

Beyond the question of who can benefit, there is a deeper structural difference. *Tzedakah* functions, as we have noted, somewhat like a *neder*: one designates an object with a *tzedakah* status, or accepts upon oneself a *tzedakah* obligation. In either case, the verbal act creates or defines a status. *Hefker*, by contrast, is not really about designating a status to an object. It is about renouncing ownership. When I declare something *hefker*, I am removing my control over it — severing my relationship to the property. The paradigm is *kol chamira vachamiya d'ika birshuti* — a declaration of non-ownership, of disavowal. Whether such a mechanism of renunciation is naturally susceptible to a concept of *yad*, which seems to operate through verbal acts of designation, is itself a genuine *chiddush* to consider. The inclusion of *hefker* in this list is, accordingly, quite striking.

---

## Hazmanah Designation

### Toilet Designation

Ravina now joins the discussion by asking a related question: *ve-yesh yad le-beit hakiseh o lo* — is there a concept of *yad* for a *beit hakiseh*? The *halakhic* relevance of designating a space as a toilet is that such a space acquires a status that forbids certain activities within it, such as Torah study or reciting *Kri'at Shema*. So what is the case? If someone says, "This house should be a *beit hakiseh*," and then says "and this one also" — that is fully explicit and presents no question. The question arises when he says "this house should be a *beit hakiseh*" and then simply says "and this" — *v'hadein* — leaving ambiguous whether he meant "this too should be a *beit hakiseh*" or "this one I'll use for something else."

### Hazmanah & Yad

The *gemara* notes that before Ravina can even get to the *yad* question, there is a prior issue: Ravina apparently takes for granted that *hazmanah* — verbal designation — gives a *beit hakiseh* its *halakhic* status even before the space has been used as such. But Ravina himself had asked elsewhere whether *hazmanah le-beit hakiseh mahu* and *hazmanah le-beit ha-merchatz mahu* — whether designating a space for use as a toilet or bathhouse, without yet having used it that way, confers the relevant status. Does *hazmanah milta hi o lav milta hi* — does designation create status or not?

The *gemara* resolves the apparent tension by explaining that Ravina asked one question because of the other: *chada migu chada ka mibaya lei*. First: does *hazmanah* work at all? And if you say it does, then second: is there a *yad* for *hazmanah*? The two questions are nested — the *yad* question is conditional on the *hazmanah* question.

### Teiku Conclusion

The *gemara* concludes: *tiba'ei lei* — let these questions stand, which is the formulation in *Masechet Nedarim* for what elsewhere appears as *teiku*. Tosafot notes this explicitly: *tiba'ei lei peirush k'mo teiku di-leshon Nedarim meshuneh* — *tiba'ei lei* means the same as *teiku*, but the language of *Masechet Nedarim* is distinctive, as we have noted before. All of these questions — *tzedakah*, *hefker*, *hazmanah*, *beit hakiseh* — are left unresolved.

---

## Ran's Framework

### Conditional Psak

What then is the *halakhah*? The Ran addresses this directly. He begins with a principle articulated by the Ramban: when the *gemara* poses a conditional question in the form of *im timtzei lomar* — "if you say A, then what about B?" — this structure implies that the *gemara* has already, implicitly, *pasak*'d the first premise. By building the question about *hefker* on the prior question about *tzedakah*, the *gemara* has effectively accepted that *yesh yad l'tzedakah*. One could argue that the conditional structure is merely a logical device for posing related questions and implies nothing about *psak*, but the Ramban maintains that *im timtzei lomar* carries an implicit resolution of the first issue.

### Safek Issurim

The second principle the Ramban invokes is the general rule that *kol heikha de-itamar teiku be-issurin le-chumra* — whenever a *teiku* arises in a matter of *issur*, we are *machmir*. Since the question of *yad* in *tzedakah* is left as a *teiku*, we treat it as binding.

But the Ran finds this startling. He notes that there is an explicit *sugya* at the end of *Perek Elu Metziot* that *safek mamona le-kula* — in doubtful monetary matters, we are lenient. And is not this precisely a monetary question? If it is uncertain whether these funds belong to the *aniyim*, then we should apply *hamotzi me-chavero alav ha-reayah* — the one claiming to take from another bears the burden of proof. The poor person cannot prove that the money belongs to them, so the owner would retain it.

This raises a broader conceptual question, discussed by Reb Shimon Shkop in his *Sha'arei Yosher*: why do we not apply *safek issur* logic to monetary disputes? If I genuinely do not know whether money belongs to me or to another person, should I not be *machmir* regarding the *issur* of *gezel* and simply hand it over? Reb Shimon's answer is that monetary questions are governed first by civil law — by how the law determines property rights — and the question of whether one violates *lo tignov* flows from that legal determination, not from an independent objective inquiry into who "really" owns the object. The civil law determines ownership, and only then does the *issur* question arise.

### Tzedakah Status

But the Ran's resolution is precisely the point we have been developing throughout: *tzedakah* is not simply a monetary dispute. When someone says *harei zo tzedakah*, the money acquires an actual *tzedakah* status — it is not merely that the *aniyim* now have a claim on those funds, as in a standard monetary dispute, but that the object itself has been designated, in a manner structurally similar to *hekdesh*, with a *tzedakah* identity. If one then uses those funds for something else, the violation is not simply one of stealing from the poor — it is a violation of the *tzedakah* status itself. That is why the Rambam and the Rashba are *machmir*: they treat this as *safek issur*, not *safek mamona*. The money is not simply owed to the poor the way a debt is owed; it has been invested with a quasi-sacred status through the act of verbal designation, parallel to a *neder*. And precisely because *tzedakah* functions in this *neder*-like capacity — affecting both the status of the object and creating a personal obligation — it belongs in the *safek issur* category, where we are *machmir* in a *teiku*.

---

## Menudeh Ani Lach

### Rabbi Akiva Position

We now move up to the top of 7a and into a new *mishnah*. The *mishnah* presents the expression *menudeh ani lach* — "I am distanced from you" — and records that Rabbi Akiva *chochech bezeh lehachmir*: he was conflicted but inclined toward stringency, treating this as a *lashon neder*. The question is why this expression should be treated any differently from clearly recognized *lashon neder* formulations such as *murchak mimcha*, *mechunak mimcha*, or *kanuy mimcha*, all of which are recognized as *lashon neder* without dispute.

The difficulty is that *menudeh* most naturally evokes *nidui* or *cherem* — excommunication — rather than the language of personal vow-making. *Cherem* is not exactly a *neder*: it is an objective status that a person acquires, not something done vis-à-vis a specific individual in the manner of a personal *neder*. That is why Rabbi Akiva does not rule with full confidence but rather is *chochech lehachmir* — he acknowledges the linguistic difficulty while leaning toward treating the expression as effective. And Abaye immediately concedes that even Rabbi Akiva agrees that one would not receive *malkot* for violating such a *neder*: it is at most a rabbinic *chumra* or a matter of *safek*.

### Nadina vs Mashmatena

Rav Pappa sharpens the analysis. He distinguishes between two formulations. If someone says *nadina minach* — "I am separated from you" — *kuli alma lo peligi de'asur*: all agree it is forbidden. The word *nadina* can be understood as "I am distancing myself from you," and this distancing — in the context of interpersonal relations — is the very mechanism of a *neder*: I am forbidding your possessions to me, thereby removing myself from you. *Minach* — "from you" — is the classic *lashon neder* of distancing. There is no dispute about this formulation.

By contrast, if someone says *mashmatena minach* — "I am in *cherem* from you" — *kuli alma sheru*: all agree it is permitted. The word *shamta* unambiguously means *cherem* in its technical sense. To say "I am in *cherem* from you" is meaningless as a *neder*: *cherem* is an objective communal status, not a relational prohibition between two individuals. It conveys nothing that functions as a *lashon neder*.

The debate between Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis, then, focuses on the intermediate case: *menudeh ani lach* — "I am *menudeh* to you." Rabbi Akiva holds that *lishna denidui hu* — the word *nidui* retains a connotation of distancing, akin to the root of separation. Even with the word *lach* ("to you"), it can be read as expressing a relational distancing from that person, which is the core of *lashon neder*. The Rabbis, by contrast, hold that *lishna deshamta hu* — the word *lach* transforms the meaning into something like "as far as you are concerned, I am in *cherem*," which is not *lashon neder* at all.

### Etymology Analysis

Why should *nidui* carry a connotation of separation distinct from *cherem*? Tosafot suggests, somewhat hesitantly, that the root *nidui* may be related to *niddah* — a term that itself connotes separation or removal. Some hold that *niddah* derives from *nad*, meaning "moved" or "displaced," evoking the image of someone separated from the community, as a menstruating woman was, in certain ancient societies, removed to a separate space. In that etymological reading, *menudeh* means simply "separated" or "distanced" — without the specific technical connotations of *cherem* and *shamta*. If so, saying *menudeh ani lach* could naturally be read as "I am separating myself from you," which is precisely the mechanism of a *neder*: forbidding your possessions to me and thereby creating distance.

Abaye thus concludes: *nadina minach* — using the verbal form that conveys relational distancing — is clearly *lashon neder*. *Mashmatena minach* — using the technical *cherem* language — is clearly not. *Menudeh ani lach* falls in between, and that is where Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis disagree.

### Rav Chisda Ruling

The *gemara* then notes that the ruling of the *mishnah* conflicts with the position of Rav Chisda. A certain man had said *mashlemna be-nichsei de-berei de-Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba* — expressing himself in explicit *cherem* language regarding the possessions of the son of Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba. He came before Rav Chisda asking whether he was now forbidden from those possessions. Rav Chisda ruled: *leit de-chash lah le-ha de-Rabbi Akiva* — nobody follows Rabbi Akiva on this point. You are permitted.

This ruling reveals something important about how Rav Chisda reads Rabbi Akiva's position. The fact that Rav Chisda said "we do not follow Rabbi Akiva" — in a case where explicit *cherem* language was used — implies that Rabbi Akiva would have said even explicit *shamta* language creates a *neder* obligation. Rav Chisda thus reads Rabbi Akiva as holding that *kasavar de-bi-mishamteina paligi* — even the explicit *cherem* formulation falls within Rabbi Akiva's view of *lashon neder*. This is indeed a far-reaching position: even if you say unambiguously "I am in *cherem*," Rabbi Akiva would treat that as generating a *neder* status. The practical *halakhah*, as stated by Rav Chisda and accepted by the *rishonim*, follows neither version of Rabbi Akiva — neither the one who says *menudeh ani lach* creates a *neder* nor certainly the one who says explicit *cherem* language does.

---

## Nidui Laws

### In-Person Rules

Having discussed *cherem* and *nidui* as linguistic categories, the *gemara* now pivots into a substantive discussion of the *halachot* governing *nidui* itself. Rav Ila reports in the name of Rav: *niduho be-fanav ein matirin lo ela be-fanav* — if someone was placed in *cherem* in his presence, the *cherem* can only be reversed in his presence as well. Conversely, if the *cherem* was imposed in his absence, it may be reversed either in his presence or not.

The *rishonim* debate the reason. One explanation holds that the act of removal must match the force of the act of imposition — if the *cherem* was imposed in full formal fashion with the person present, then the reversal must carry equivalent gravity. A *she'lo be-fanav* reversal would be insufficient to fully undo what was done *be-fanav*. A second, more interpersonal explanation holds that since the person was publicly humiliated by being brought before a *beit din* and placed in *cherem* in his presence, the restoration of his dignity requires an equally public acknowledgment — a reversal *be-fanav* — so that the community knows his status has changed. According to this second view, if the reversal was done *she'lo be-fanav*, it would be valid *bediavad*, since the concern is honor and public knowledge rather than the formal act itself.

### Shem Shamayim

Rav Chanan then teaches in the name of Rav: *hashome'a azkarat hashem mipi chaveiro* — one who hears a fellow Jew utter God's name unnecessarily, *shelo letzorech*, is obligated to place that person in *cherem*. And if he fails to do so, *hu atzmo yehei venidui* — he himself deserves to be placed in *cherem*. The underlying authority is broad: this is not a matter limited to formal *batei din*. The Rabbis have effectively authorized anyone who witnesses such an act to impose *cherem* as a form of communal censure — a kind of citizen's enforcement on behalf of the halachic order.

### Name & Poverty

The *gemara* grounds this in a striking chain of reasoning. *Shechol makom she'azkarat hashem metzuya, aniut hi metzuya* — wherever God's name is treated too casually, poverty is found in its wake. And *aniut kemita* — poverty is like death, as we learn from the *pasuk* in which God tells Moshe that all those who sought to kill him have died. Since Datan and Aviram were still alive at that point, the *gemara* concludes they must have become poor, which demonstrates that poverty is considered equivalent to death.

Some *rishonim* connect this to the *pasuk*: *bechol hamakom asher azkir et shemi avo eilecha uverachticha* — wherever My name is properly invoked, I will come and bless you. By implication, where My name is invoked improperly, the opposite of *uverachticha* follows — poverty rather than blessing.

The chain is then completed: *kol makom shenatnu chachamim eineihem, o mita o oni* — wherever the Rabbis directed their displeasure toward someone, the result was either death or poverty. *Nidui* and *cherem* are the instruments of that rabbinic censure. Someone who treats God's name carelessly is bringing poverty and virtual death upon the community; the Rabbis respond with *nidui*, which itself carries the consequence of poverty or death. The *mida keneged mida* symmetry is striking.

The connection to *Masechet Nedarim* is also worth noting. The prohibition of *lo tisa et shem Hashem Elokecha lashav* is primarily associated with *shevuot*, not *nedarim*. But since *nedarim* and *shevuot* are closely linked, and since carelessness with language — whether of *nedarim* or of God's name — represents the same broader failure to honor the weight of words, this discussion finds its appropriate home here. The power of speech runs through all of it.

---

## Immediate Reversal

### Story Example

Rabbi Abba relates: he was standing before Rav Huna when Rav Huna overheard a woman utter God's name without necessity. *Shamteh v'altar shara lah* — he immediately placed her in *cherem* and then immediately reversed it. He imposed the censure and undid it in the same moment, as a demonstrative act of rabbinic displeasure, with no intention of allowing it to take lasting effect.

### Three Inferences

The *gemara* draws three *halakhic* inferences from this episode. First: *hashome'a shem shamayim mipi chaveiro tzarich l'nadoto* — one who hears God's name uttered needlessly is obligated to place the offender in *cherem*, as Rav Huna demonstrated by acting immediately. Second: *mendeh befanav va'afillu mendeh shelo befanav* — one can reverse a *nidui* whether in the person's presence or not; Rav Huna made a point of reversing it *befaneha*, in her presence, which indicates that had he chosen to reverse it *she'lo befaneha*, that too would have been valid. Third: *ein bein niddui l'hafara v'lo kelum* — there is no required waiting period between the imposition of *nidui* and its reversal; it may be undone immediately.

This appears to contradict other *gemarot* that require a thirty-day wait. The resolution offered by the *rishonim* is that the thirty-day requirement applies to cases of genuine, serious violation — where someone persistently showed disrespect to halachic authority or to the Rabbis in a grave manner. For minor infractions, such as casual utterance of God's name, the *cherem* is purely expressive. It is a momentary act of censure, demonstrating that the community does not condone what occurred, without any intention to impose lasting social consequences. In such a case, immediate reversal is not only permitted but appropriate. 

It is also worth noting that the reversal of *cherem* is called *hafara* rather than *hattarah*. *Hattarah* is the process by which a *neder* is undone through a *chacham*, by establishing that the original intent never encompassed the present situation. *Hafara* is the annulment exercised by a husband over his wife's vow — an act of administrative power without reference to original intent. That the release from *cherem* is described as *hafara* underscores its nature: it is not a finding that the *cherem* was inapplicable or mistaken, but a simple exercise of authority to annul what authority had imposed.

---

## Self-Nidui Authority

### Self-Reversal Power

Rav Gidel teaches in the name of Rav: *talmid chacham menade l'atzmo u'meifer l'atzmo* — a *talmid chacham* can place himself in *cherem* and can also release himself from that *cherem*. The Ran qualifies this: the principle applies specifically in cases like those we have been discussing, where the person does not genuinely deserve the *cherem* — the self-imposed *nidui* is a formal or expressive gesture rather than a deserved sanction.

### Imprisonment Analogy

The *gemara* challenges this: *pshita* — is this not obvious? And the reply is: *ein chavush matir atzmo m'beit ha'asurim* — a prisoner cannot free himself from prison. If a *talmid chacham* truly deserves a *cherem* — if he has genuinely acted in a manner requiring rabbinic censure — then he cannot unilaterally reverse that *cherem* on his own authority. The act of reversal requires an external authority. The self-reversal power exists only where the self-imposed *cherem* was never deserved in the first place, or was imposed as an expressive or procedural act.

### Mar Zutra Story

The paradigm case is that of Mar Zutra the Pious. When a *yeshiva* student was required to be placed in *cherem* for some misconduct, Mar Zutra would first place himself in *cherem* — *mashmat nafshia b'reisha* — and only then place the student. Two explanations are offered for this practice. The first is that even when the *cherem* is necessary, it is a necessary evil — putting a *talmid chacham* in *cherem*, even for genuine misbehavior, carries a weight of gravity, and Mar Zutra felt that doing so required him to share in some of that gravity by subjecting himself to it as well, a form of solidarity or humility before the act. The second is practical and almost mnemonic: since someone in *cherem* may not reside normally with his household, when Mar Zutra returned home at the end of the day he would be reminded that he himself was in *cherem* — and thus prompted to reverse both his own *cherem* and then the student's. The sequence of reversal was also deliberate: *shari lei l'nafshia* first, placing himself back in a state of full standing, and only then *v'hadar shari lei*, reversing the student's *cherem* — paralleling the principle of the *Kohen Gadol* who first performs *kaparah* for himself before doing so for others. The student would thus remain in *cherem* for several hours, which was the intended period of censure.

---

---

# Nedarim 8

## Niddui & Cherem

### Previous Discussion

Daf 8 continues from the preceding discussion of *niddui* and *cherem*. The *mishnah*'s language of *mudrani mimcha* and *menudani mimcha* had drawn the *gemara* into an extended treatment of these forms of excommunication. On the one hand, there are clear parallels between *niddui* and *cherem* and the world of *nedarim* — the *gemara* had discussed performing *hatara* to annul a *cherem*, and there was a question whether certain formulations might constitute *lashon neder*, which is Rabbi Akiva's position. The *gemara*, however, rules that we do not *pasken* accordingly.

### Power of Speech

What lends this entire discussion its coherence within *Masechet Nedarim* is the centrality of speech. The preceding *daf* addressed the case of someone who uses God's name loosely — *levatala* — and is consequently placed in *cherem*, itself an act of speech, which is then released through another act of speech. This cycle of verbal creation, verbal sanction, and verbal release speaks directly to the animating theme of the *masechet*. It is in this context that the *gemara* now introduces another statement of Giddel in the name of Rav, one that bears even more directly on the concerns of *Masechet Nedarim*.

---

## Oath & Mitzvah

### Oath Source

At the top of 8a, Giddel in the name of Rav asks: *m'nayin she'nishba'im l'kayem et hamitzvah* — from where do we know that one may take a *shevuah*, an oath, to fulfill a *mitzvah*? The source is the verse *nishbati va'akayemah lishmor mishpatei tzidkecha* — "I have sworn and I will fulfill, to observe Your righteous edicts." The *gemara* understands this to mean either that it is a praiseworthy thing to do — not a concern of *shem shamayim levatala*, since the intent is to spur oneself to action — or that such a *shevuah* is actually binding. The *gemara* focuses on the second possibility.

### Double Oath Problem

The difficulty is immediately apparent: *v'halo mushba ve'omed meHar Sinai* — is the person not already foresworn from Sinai to observe the commandments? Two related principles apply. If one takes a *shevuah* to *batel* a *mitzvah* — saying, for instance, that he will not sit in the *sukkah* — it is non-binding because he is pre-foresworn to observe it. And conversely, if one takes a *shevuah* that he *will* sit in the *sukkah* and then fails to do so, he has not transgressed the violation of that *shevuah*, because *ein shevuah chala al shevuah* — a second oath cannot take effect upon an existing oath. The *gemara* is thus pressed to explain how an oath to perform a *mitzvah* could have any legal force at all.

### Oath as Zeruzon

The *gemara* resolves this by saying *lo* — technically it is not binding — but this teaches us *l'zeruzon*, *mishum l'ziruzei nafshei*: one is permitted to take such an oath even without binding force, because it serves as a powerful means of encouraging oneself to fulfill an existing obligation. The point is pragmatic: we know that having obligations does not guarantee their fulfillment, and finding ways to motivate ourselves to perform what we are already supposed to do is entirely legitimate.

### Ran's Position

The *Ran* is not satisfied with this simple reading and advances an alternative. He questions whether *ein shevuah chala al shevuah* necessarily means the second oath has no effect whatsoever. Perhaps, the *Ran* suggests, it only means one does not bring a *korban* for it — *de'ha lo mechayev korban* — but there may still be a transgression of *bal yachel*, the prohibition against violating one's oath, *afilu bedvar mitzvah*. He proceeds to argue from a comparison between *shevuah* and *neder* found elsewhere in the *gemara*, concluding that the principle of *ein shevuah chala al shevuah* pertains only to liability for a *korban*, while liability for the *lav* of *bal yachel* — and thus *malkos* — remains in force.

The *Ran*'s reading means that the *chiddush* of Giddel in the name of Rav is not to tell us that the oath takes effect — that is already assumed — but rather to tell us it is an affirmatively good thing to do as a way of encouraging fulfillment of one's obligations. The *Sifsei Avraham* at the bottom of the *daf* cites the *Ramban* in *Parshas Chukas* who takes the opposite position from the *Ran*: if one takes a *shevuah* to perform a *mitzvah* and then fails to do so, he incurs neither a *korban* nor *malkos* — the oath has no effect at all. On this reading, the point of Giddel's statement is simply that it is a legitimate and even meritorious practice to take such an oath to encourage oneself, even though it carries no halachic consequence.

---

## Neder Mitzva

### Ashne Perek Zeh

The *gemara* now introduces a second and closely related statement of Giddel in the name of Rav: *ha'omer eshne perek zeh* — one who says "I will study this *perek* today," or "I am studying this *masechet*" — *neder gadol nadar l'Elokei Yisrael*, he has made a great vow to the God of Israel. This is a striking *gemara*. The person used no *lashon neder* and no *lashon shevuah* — he simply said he was going to do something. How, then, does any form of *shevuah* or *neder* take effect?

### Binding Mechanism

The *gemara* treats the statement *eshne* — "I will study" — as *lashon shevuah*, as a verbal commitment to perform an act. That immediately raises the same problem as before: *v'halo mushba ve'omed hu*, is he not already foresworn from Sinai? *V'ein shevuah chala al shevuah* — how can a second oath take effect here? Nor can we say this is simply another formulation of the first principle, that it is permitted as an act of *zeruzon* to encourage oneself — if that were the whole point, it would be identical to what was already taught in the first statement of Giddel and would add nothing.

### Optional Learning

The *gemara* therefore resolves the difficulty differently here: *d'ei bei patar nafshei bikrias Shema shacharis ve'arvis* — a person can actually discharge his basic obligation of *Talmud Torah* through recitation of *Shema* morning and evening. The minimum threshold of *Talmud Torah* is derived from the verse *v'shinantam l'vanecha*, together with *uvshochbecha uvkumecha*, from which we learn that the explicit biblical mandate of *Talmud Torah* is fulfilled through *Krias Shema*. This is not a coincidence of formulation: the *psukim* from which we derive the *halacha* of *Krias Shema* are themselves, at the *pshat* level, *psukim* about *Talmud Torah* — which is why there are serious positions among the *Tannaim* that *Krias Shema* is itself only *m'derabanan*, since those *psukim* in their plain sense are about *Talmud Torah*, not about *Shema* as such. This also explains why the *brachos* of *Krias Shema* discharge the *brachos* of *Talmud Torah*: the recitation of *Shema* is understood as a fulfillment of *uvshochbecha uvkumecha*, which at the *pshat* level is the *mitzvah* of *Talmud Torah*.

Since the bare minimum of *Talmud Torah* can be discharged through *Krias Shema*, a person is not obligated to learn any particular *perek* or *masechet*. He could learn all day and satisfy his obligation by reviewing material he has already covered, without ever getting to this specific *perek*. Therefore, he is not *mushba ve'omed* with respect to this particular study, and a *shevuah* — or, as the *gemara* calls it, a *neder* — can take effect on it. *Mishum hachi chala shevuah aleiya.*

### Talmud Torah Scope

One might ask whether *Krias Shema* really constitutes *Talmud Torah* in the full sense, given that it functions primarily as *kabalas ol malchus shamayim*. The broader question of the extent of the *mitzvah* of *Talmud Torah* is significant: the plain sense of this *gemara* appears to be that the minimum is *Krias Shema shacharis ve'arvis*, which is consistent with a number of other *gemaras*. The *gemara*'s formulation here — that one can exempt oneself through *Krias Shema* — is the *pshat* of the passage, and has been used as a source for discussions about the scope of *mitzvas Talmud Torah* ever since, making it an apt text for a *shiur* on *Shavuos* night.

### Ran on Explicit

The *Ran*, however, is uncomfortable with the *gemara*'s apparent implication that a person is not obligated to learn *Torah* all day. In his view — citing the *gemara* in *Menachos*, *lo nitnu divrei Torah ella l'ochlei haman*, and the principle of *v'hagita bo yomam valayla* — every person is required to learn *Torah* to the maximum of his ability, *yomam valayla*, using every available moment. The *Ran* therefore resolves the *gemara* differently: *d'hacha d'mishtava l'kayeim mitzvah she'eina meforeshes b'hedya* — a *shevuah* to fulfill a *mitzvah* takes effect when the obligation is not stated explicitly in the *Torah*. Since the only *explicitly* stated obligation is *Krias Shema shacharis ve'arvis*, all learning beyond that — though obligatory — is not explicit, and therefore a *shevuah* does take effect upon it.

This alternative reading preserves both the *Ran*'s view of maximal *Talmud Torah* obligation and the *gemara*'s conclusion that the *shevuah* is effective. One could also propose a simpler resolution even granting maximal obligation: even if one is obligated to learn every available moment, one is not obligated to learn specifically *this masechet*. One could spend every moment in *chazara* on *Bava Kamma* and never arrive at *Bava Metzia*, and have discharged one's obligation entirely. Therefore there is no *mushba ve'omed* with respect to this specific *perek*.

---

## Neder Framework

### Shevuah vs Neder

Having established that a statement of intent to perform a *mitzvah* creates some form of binding obligation, the *gemara* calls it a *neder gadol* — a great *neder*. This creates two interrelated difficulties. First, the person used neither *lashon shevuah* nor *lashon neder* — he simply said he would do something. Second, and more conceptually significant, is the question of what the *gemara* means by calling this a *neder* at all, since the *gemara* simultaneously treats it as raising the problem of *ein shevuah chala al shevuah*, which is the language of *shevuah*.

The conceptual distinction between *shevuah* and *neder* is fundamental. A *shevuah* is a sworn declaration in the name of God: if one fails to fulfill it, one has violated an oath and has, in a sense, desecrated God's name by invoking Him as witness. A *neder*, by contrast, is not a promise in this sense — it is an act of creation. When one says *harei zeh asur*, one is not making a promise; one is bringing about a change in the metaphysical status of an object. The wrongness of violating a *neder* lies not in breaking a sworn promise but in failing to live up to the obligation one has constructed for oneself.

### Yaakov's Vow

The biblical model of this phenomenon is *vayidar Yaakov neder lemor* — and Jacob made a vow. Yet when one reads the actual words Jacob spoke — if God protects me and provides for me, then whatever You give me I will tithe to You — there is no formal invocation of an oath, no declaration in God's name. Jacob spoke with a quality of personal commitment and religious conviction, and the *Torah* characterizes the result as a *neder*. This is precisely the phenomenon the *gemara* is describing: a person who says *eshne perek zeh* with genuine commitment and the sense of creating an obligation is engaging in the same kind of act as Jacob's vow.

### Lashon Neder

This also clarifies why no particular formula is required for a *neder*. We have already seen in the *mishnah* that *harei zeh asur alai* — "this is forbidden to me" — constitutes *lashon neder* even without the word *konam* or any other technical term. Similarly, when one says "I am committed to learning this *perek*," that can function as an act of *kabbalah* — of accepting upon oneself an obligation — without any magic words. The line between an ordinary expression of intent and a genuine *neder* may not always be obvious, but the concept itself is entirely grounded in the *Torah*'s own use of the term: *vayidar Yaakov neder*.

What makes this a *neder* conceptually rather than a *shevuah* is precisely that it creates a metaphysical reality — a personal obligation — rather than merely invoking God's name as witness to a future act. When one says "I am accepting upon myself the obligation to do this," the wrong in failing to fulfill it lies in having failed to live up to the status one constructed for oneself, not in having violated a sworn oath. The *gemara*'s language of *neder gadol nadar l'Elokei Yisrael* thus captures something real: this is the Torah's own category of *neder mitzva*, a religious commitment to perform a specific act of divine service, modeled on the biblical narrative of Jacob's vow.

The question that then arises is where *Masechet Nedarim* has until now recognized anything of this kind. The entire *masechet* has been built around *nedarim* as a mechanism for forbidding objects — *konam*, *harei zeh asur*, objects rendered prohibited by one's declaration. Here we are encountering something different: a *neder* that creates a personal obligation to *do* something rather than making something forbidden. And notably, the *gemara* still raises the language of *ein shevuah chala al shevuah* in connection with this *neder*, suggesting that when a *neder* creates a personal obligation it is treated, for certain purposes, as equivalent to a *shevuah*.

### Rosh: Neder Tzedaka

The *Rosh* addresses this directly. In the first wide line of his commentary, he writes: *velav haynu neder mamash* — this is not a *neder* in the strict sense of *matfis bedavar hanadur*, making something forbidden by reference to a prohibited object. Rather, *ela mechashvinan lei ke'ilu nadar litzdaka* — we treat it as though one made a *neder tzedaka*. The source he invokes is *neder beficha zu tzedaka*: a commitment to give *tzedakah* creates a genuine binding obligation. The *Rosh* thus uses *neder tzedaka* as the halakhic model for *neder mitzva* — one can similarly obligate oneself to perform other *mitzvos* by adopting the same form of commitment.

The implication is that *neder tzedaka* itself represents a recognized halachic category in which one's words create a personal obligation, not merely a change in an object's status. Whether this category is *d'oraisa* or *d'rabbanan* is not entirely clear from the *Rosh*, but it functions as a real obligation with real consequences.

### Neder on Mitzvah

This raises an important question: can a *neder* take effect upon an existing *mitzvah* obligation? The *gemara* elsewhere — in the *perek* of *elu nedarim* — rules that a *neder* can indeed take effect on a *dvar mitzvah*, treating it like a *dvar hareshus*. A *shevuah* to not sit in the *sukkah* is ineffective because it directly countermands the *mitzvah*. But a *neder* that renders the *sukkah asur* is an indirect mechanism: the *sukkah* becomes forbidden and then when the *mitzvah* time arrives, there is a collision — this is treated differently, as the *neder* itself is effective even as it conflicts with the *mitzvah*.

However, the *Ran* draws a distinction. A regular *neder* — the classic *matfis bedavar assur* mechanism — is one thing. But a *neder* of the *tzedakah* type, which creates a personal obligation rather than forbidding an object, is effectively functioning like a *shevuah*: both obligate the person to do something. Therefore, the *Ran* argues, such a *neder* follows the rules of a *shevuah* with respect to existing obligations — it cannot take effect on something one is already obligated to perform. *V'gamrinan mishvua d'einah chala al devar mitzvah.* The *chiddush*, then, is precisely that it *can* take effect on a *mitzvah* one is not specifically obligated to fulfill in this particular form.

### Neder Obligations

This leads to a broader conceptual point. Until now the world of *nedarim* in the *masechet* has been the world of forbidden objects. Here we enter a different realm: the *neder* as a mechanism for creating personal religious obligations. This realm is rooted in the *Torah*'s own narratives — *vayidar Yaakov neder*, and the use of *neder* language in connection with *cherem* and *tzedakah* throughout *Tanach*. In all these cases, the underlying act is a commitment made to God in a religious context.

One might ask: why does *neder tzedakah* work at all, given that the standard *neder* mechanism operates on objects? A possible answer — one attributed to the *Ramban* — is that a *neder tzedakah* effectively creates a kind of lien on one's property, even if no specific property is identified. The money ultimately becomes a physical object upon which the *neder* rests, even if indirectly. If so, one might use *neder tzedakah* as a model for *neder mitzva* in other contexts: the *neder* to learn a specific *perek* is similarly treated as creating an object-like obligation in the sphere of religious life, modeled on the *tzedakah* paradigm.

Crucially, there is no suggestion in any of these discussions that one can use this form of *neder mitzva* to create an obligation for a purely secular act. The entire framework operates only in the religious sphere — *vayidar Yaakov neder*, one is *noder* to God. One cannot use a *neder* to obligate oneself to mow one's lawn. The category is specifically that of making a religious commitment to God, in the space where the act is not explicitly required in this specific form, and where one's words can construct a genuine personal obligation of divine service.

Also closely related is the well-known principle that performing a *davar tov* three times creates the equivalent of a *neder* — *ke'ilu kibel al atzmo beneder*. This again points to the same underlying category: through repeated action, one can implicitly construct a personal religious obligation, just as through explicit verbal commitment. This is also the framework invoked in *hatarat nedarim*, where one declares *lo mitzad shevuah velo mitzad neder* while seeking release from *chovoteinu* — the accumulated commitments, verbal or behavioral, that have created personal religious obligations. All of this is ultimately rooted in the same biblical *psukim*.

## Vow to Travel

### Nesak V'Niul

The *gemara* continues: *ha'omer lechavero neissak v'niul l'bei Tarmodei* — one who says to his friend, "Let's get up and go to such-and-such a place." Even if the friend does not comply, the one who made the statement is personally obligated to go. Moreover, the implication is that he must make sure to arrive before his friend — to be there first.

### Ezekiel Source

The source is God's command to Ezekiel: *kum tzei el habik'ah*, get up, go out to the valley, and there I will speak with you. When Ezekiel went out, the *kavod Hashem* was already there waiting for him. The one who initiates the arrangement has an obligation not only to follow through, but to be present and ready before those he has invited.

## Niddui Dreams

### Dream Niddui

The *gemara* returns to the topic of *niddui*. Rav Yosef teaches: if a person has a dream in which he is placed in *cherem*, he must take it seriously as a possible sign of divine displeasure — *kdeniddin min haMakom*. This concept, that a person can be *niduya l'Shamayim*, appears prominently in *Masechet Taanit* in the context of drought, where the community is called upon to act *kdeniddin min haMakom* in response to the apparent withdrawal of divine favor. A dream of being placed in *cherem* is treated as a potential signal of such heavenly censure.

### Ten People

To be released from such a *niddui*, the person requires ten people — *tzrichah asarah b'nei adam l'hatirah*. The *gemara* specifies further: *v'hu d'tani hilchata* — only if these ten have actually studied *halachos*, meaning Talmudic learning, not merely *Mishnah* alone. The reason ten specifically are needed is that ten constitute a *minyan*, in the presence of whom there is *Shechinah sheryuyah* — divine presence. If God's presence rests among ten people, they can act as divine representatives to release the person from the heavenly *niddui*.

### Crossroads Method

If ten people who have studied *halachos* cannot be assembled, the *gemara* offers an alternative: *neizil v'nisvei a'parashat drachim* — go sit at a crossroads, and keep offering *Shalom aleichem* to passersby until one has encountered ten people who have learned *halachos*. The *rishonim* debate the precise mechanism here. Some understand it to mean one continues greeting people until ten *talmidei chachamim* reciprocate and say *Shalom aleichem* back, and this somehow functions as a form of release. The majority of *rishonim*, however, incline toward reading this as a form of protection — greeting and being greeted by ten learned people provides some measure of divine protection until a proper *beis din* can be convened to effect a full release.

### Releaser Identity

Rav Acha posed a question to Rav Ashi: if one knows in real life who it was that placed him in *cherem* in the dream, can that person release him from it? Rav Ashi responds: *dilma shlicha hu d'shadruhu mishmeih d'Shamaya* — perhaps in the dream that person was acting as a divine agent, sent from Heaven to execute the *niddui*. If so, going to him in real life accomplishes nothing: he was authorized to impose the *niddui* on Heaven's behalf, but he has no authority to rescind what Heaven decreed.

### Dream Cancellation

A further question was posed: what if, within the same dream, the very same person who placed one in *niddui* subsequently released him from it? The dream would appear to cancel itself out, leaving no remaining obligation.

### Dream Nonsense

Rav Papa responds with a striking observation: *keshem she-ee efshar l'bar belo teven, kach ee efshar lachalom belo devarim betelim* — just as it is impossible for grain to exist without straw, so it is impossible for a dream to exist without some nonsense in it. Not every element of a dream carries prophetic weight. One must therefore remain *choshesh* that the part of the dream in which one was placed in *niddui* was the true, meaningful element — and the part in which one was released was the meaningless straw. The obligation to seek proper release therefore remains.

## Husband as Agent

### Wife's Neder

The *gemara* presents a case: Ravina had a *neder* that his wife had made upon herself — a *neder* of a type that was either beyond the window for a husband's unilateral annulment, or was not the kind that a husband can annul through *hafara* alone. He came before Rav Ashi seeking guidance.

### Representation Q

Ravina asked: *ba'al mahu she'ye'aseh shaliach l'charatat ishto* — can a husband serve as an agent representing his wife in the process of *charata*, the expression of regret that is the basis for *hatarat nedarim*? The scenario is that the wife has explained the circumstances to her husband, who would then present the grounds for *charata* before the *beis din* on her behalf.

### Already Gathered

Rav Ashi answered: *ee michnafim in, ee lav lav* — if the *beis din* is already assembled, yes; if not, no.

### Three Inferences

The *gemara* extracts three inferences from this exchange. First: *ba'al na'aseh shaliach l'charatat ishto* — a husband can indeed represent his wife. Second: *lo sharei l'mishrei nidra b'atra d'rabeih* — it is not appropriate to annul a *neder* in the location of one's *rebbe*, which explains why Ravina did not convene his own *beis din* and instead came to Rav Ashi — raising the larger question of whether a man can annul his own wife's vow, and the broader principle of deferring to one's *rebbe*'s authority. Third: *ki michnafim shapir dami* — if the *beis din* is already gathered, it is entirely proper to proceed.

### Rambam Tosafot

There is an important dispute among the *rishonim* about the underlying principles here. The *Rambam* understands the husband's representation of his wife as a unique exception grounded in *ishto k'gufo* — wife and husband are treated as a single legal unit in certain respects — and not as an instance of a general rule permitting representation before *beis din*. For the *Rambam*, the fundamental requirement is that every individual appear personally before the *beis din*. The condition that the *beis din* already be assembled is, on his reading, a further constraint on this already exceptional leniency: since we are permitting something inherently unusual, we do not extend it to cases where it would require specially convening a *beis din* for this purpose.

*Tosafot* disagrees sharply. *Tosafot* holds that representation before *beis din* is permissible as a general matter — one may even send a letter, and the *beis din* may annul a *neder* without the person's physical presence. The specific problem in the case of a husband representing his wife is not representation per se, but the husband's vested interest in obtaining the *hatara*. Because he benefits from his wife's release, he may unconsciously — or even consciously — present the circumstances in a slanted manner to make the case for *charata* seem stronger than it truly is. Therefore, the requirement that the *beis din* already be assembled serves as a check: if he is not going to all the effort and expense of specially convening a *beis din*, his investment in the outcome is less conspicuous and the concern about biased representation is accordingly reduced.

---

## Shamta in Rebbe

### Shamta Permitted

The *gemara* continues: *v'shamta afilu b'asrei d'rabbai* — in a case of *niddui*, even in the location of one's *rebbe*, one may release the person from the *shamta*. This is a surprising ruling. One would have thought the opposite: releasing someone from *cherem* is a more significant assertion of rabbinic authority than annulling a *neder*, since *hatarat cherem* involves representing communal standards and accepting someone back from a state of religious censure — it is more public, more institutional, more clearly an exercise of *rabbinic* power. It would therefore seem that performing *hatarat cherem* in one's *rebbe*'s presence would be a greater usurpation of authority than performing *hatarat nedarim*.

### Kavod HaRav

*Tosafot* addresses this tension directly. *Tosafot* explains: *shamta afilu b'asrei d'rabbai shapir dami lehatir hashamta d'pe'amim shelo yehei rav mzuman* — sometimes the *rebbe* is not available or is otherwise occupied, *v'ein l'akev heter hashamta* — and it is not fair to delay the release of a *shamta*. Leaving a person in a state of *niddui* is an ongoing harm that cannot simply wait for a more convenient moment. The principle is analogous to what the *gemara* says elsewhere — *b'makom sheyesh chilul Hashem ein cholkin kavod l'rav* — when the honor of Heaven demands action, the honor due to a *rebbe* yields. Here the pressing need of the person standing before you demands that one act immediately, even if doing so involves assuming an authority that would normally be deferred to one's *rebbe*.

### Yachid Mumche

Furthermore: *v'yachid mumche sharei shamta* — even an individual expert, without a full *beis din*, may release someone from a *shamta*. This principle applies even in the location of one's *rebbe*, combining both of the preceding points into a single halakhic ruling.

---

## Sun of Righteousness

### Fear of God

The *gemara* now offers a closing teaching on the theme that has run through this entire section. A chain of seven *Amoraim* — Rabbi Shimon ben Zavid citing Rabbi Yitzchak bar Tavla, citing Rabbi Chiya Aricha of Rabbi Acha's academy, citing Rabbi Zeira, citing Rabbi Elazar, citing Rabbi Chanina, citing Rabbi Mayasha in the name of Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai — transmit an interpretation of the verse *v'zarcha lachem yirei shmi shemesh tzedakah u'marpe*: to those who fear My name, the sun of righteousness will shine with healing. The *gemara* identifies *yirei shmi* as *bnei adam shehen yere'in l'hotzi shem shamayim l'vatala* — people who are careful not to pronounce God's name loosely. This circles back neatly to the discussion that preceded this *daf*, where a person who uses God's name *levatala* is placed in *cherem*: those who fear God's name precisely avoid that misuse of speech.

### Olam Haba

*Abaye* offers one reading of the verse: *shma mina charga d'yoma masi* — the *mefarshim*, including the *Ran* and *Tosafot*, explain *charga d'yoma* as the fine particles or motes visible in sunlight. On this reading the verse is taken straightforwardly: sunlight brings physical healing, and that is what the verse promises to those who fear God's name.

*Reish Lakish* reads the verse very differently, applying it to *olam haba*: *ein gehenom l'olam haba* — there is no *gehenom* in the world to come in the conventional sense. Instead, *hakadosh baruch hu motzi chamah m'nartika* — God will draw the sun out of its sheath, and the same sun will serve two opposite purposes simultaneously.

### Righteous Wicked

*Tzadikim mitrap'in bah u'rshaim nidonin bah* — the righteous will be healed by that sun, and the wicked will be judged and burned by it. Not only will the righteous be healed, but *shemitangin bah* — they will derive actual pleasure from it, as the verse continues: *v'yatzatem u'fishtem k'eglei marbek*, you will go forth and frolic like calves released from the stall. The wicked, by the same sun, will be punished. The same reality, the same light — experienced entirely differently depending on who one is.

## Mumche Requirements

### Smicha Question

The *gemara*'s ruling that *yachid mumche* may release from *shamta* raises an important halakhic question: what precisely qualifies one as a *yachid mumche* for this purpose? Does it require *smicha* in the classical sense — ordination traceable back to *Moshe Rabbeinu*?

### Taz View

The *Taz* addresses this question. He rules that *yachid mumche* for purposes of *shamta* does not necessarily require classical *smicha*. Rather, what is required is that the individual be a genuine *chacham* who is *baki b'hilchos nidduyin* — expert in the laws of *niddui*. Knowledge and expertise in the relevant halachic domain is the defining criterion, not formal ordination in the chain from Sinai.

### Neder Shamta Diff

There is, however, a meaningful distinction between the requirements for *hatarat nedarim* and the requirements for releasing from *shamta*. For *hatarat nedarim*, the *gemara* elsewhere and *Tosafot* raise the question of whether *parshas elohim* — the scriptural basis for the authority of those who annul *nedarim* — requires *semuchim*, formally ordained judges. The *Taz* discusses the difference between these two domains: the requirements for *hatarat nedarim* and the requirements for *shamta* may not be identical, and although both topics have been treated in parallel throughout this *daf*, they remain distinct areas with their own rules. This remains a matter of ongoing halakhic discussion.

---

---

# Nedarim 9

## Knidrei Reshaim

### Opening & Mishnah Text

The ninth daf of Nedarim opens with a new mishnah — one that is, from the outset, slightly peculiar. The mishnah introduces a category of vow phrased as *knidrei reshaim*, "like the vows of the wicked," and proceeds to establish whether such a formulation creates a binding *neder*, *nezirut*, or *shvuah*. The broader context is that of *yadot* — the continuation of the discussion about partial or indirect formulations that may or may not create binding vows. The question is always: when someone leaves part of the sentence unspoken, do we know how to fill in the blank, and is that incomplete formulation effective?
