The full range of the mishnah covers three categories: the person who says something *knidrei reshaim* may be intending *nezirut*, may be intending an obligation regarding a *korban*, or may be making a *shvuah*. The opening clause — *knidrei reshaim* — is what drives the entire analysis.

### Three Categories

The mishnah's statement is *nadar binazir u-vekorban u-vishvuah*: one who vows regarding *nazir*, *korban*, and *shvuah*. The basic scenario is that someone says *knidrei reshaim hareini* — "like the vows of the wicked, behold I am" — and leaves the end of the sentence incomplete. Depending on context, *hareini* might be followed by *nazir*; or one might say *alai* ("upon me"), suggesting a *korban*; or one might say *heimenu* ("from it"), gesturing toward a *shvuah* not to eat from something. In each case, part of the critical content of the statement is missing.

This is the standard *yad* problem: a *yad mochiach* — a probative indication — suffices, but a *yad she'einah mochiach* — an unclear indication — does not, and the question is always whether there is enough context to determine what was meant.

### Chiddush Analysis

The *chiddush* of the mishnah, however, lies not in the incomplete end of the sentence but in the opening qualifier. The mishnah tells us: *knidrei reshaim* works. *Knidrei kesherim lo amar klum* — if someone says "like the vows of *kesherim*," righteous people, they have said nothing, because *kesherim* do not make *nedarim*. *Knidvosam*, however — if someone says "like the *nedavah* of *kesherim*" — that does work. And by implication, *knidvos reshaim* would not work either.

There is also an item conspicuously absent from the end of the mishnah: *shvuah* does not appear in the closing formulation. The mishnah says *nadar binazir u-vekorban*, but does not add *u-vishvuah*. This asymmetry will require explanation.

What the mishnah is fundamentally communicating, then, is that *reshaim* make *nedarim* and *kesherim* make *nedavos* — and not vice versa. This sets up a crucial discussion about the intrinsic religious value, or disvalue, of making *nedarim* in the first place.

---

## Neder vs. Nedava

### Ran's Framework

The Ran explains that the word *nedava* — freely given donation — carries the connotation expressed in the verse *v'chol nediv lev asher yidvenu libo*: the generosity of the heart. A *nedava*, then, refers to an act performed out of sincere, uncomplicated religious motivation — a pure desire to serve God or to give something to God. A *neder*, by contrast, reflects a more complex motivational landscape. A person making a *neder* may have religious intentions, but there are other things operating in the background: guilt, shame, an impetuous desire to correct some failing, a wish to appear more *frum*, or simply complicated feelings that have been channeled into a religious act. The religious component is present, but it is not the clean, freely flowing, uncomplicated motivation that a *nedava* represents.

It follows, then, that calling someone who makes a *neder* a *rasha* does not mean they are wicked in all their ways. The Ran qualifies this as *bedavar zeh* — in this particular act. Within the narrow scope of making *nedarim* and *nedavos*, a *neder* reflects a lesser or at least more problematic act.

This distinction, it should be noted, is not a formal legal one. It is not about the mechanics of how you produce the *neder* or *nedava*. It is about describing the religious mindset and motivation of the person making it. Therefore: *nidrei reshaim* is a meaningful phrase — it refers to vows made from complicated motivation. *Nidrei kesherim* is not meaningful — *kesherim* simply do not operate that way. *Nidvos kesherim* is meaningful — that is precisely what a *kasher* person does. And *nidvos reshaim* is not meaningful — the *nedava* of a *rasha* is not a coherent category.

### Korban Analysis

The Ran then maps this distinction onto the technical language of *korban* vows. A classic *neder* of a *korban* is *harei alai* — "it is upon me," creating a personal obligation. A classic *nedava* of a *korban* is *harei zo* — "behold this [animal]," sanctifying the object itself rather than creating an obligation on the person. The Ran suggests that this technical legal distinction reflects the underlying motivational one: *harei alai* shows a certain hesitation — you are not yet giving it, you are promising to give it in the future. *Harei zo* is more wholehearted, because you are giving it over immediately. The act of *neder* thus maps onto the more complex, holding-back motivation, while *nedava* maps onto the fully generous one.

There is, however, a debate between the Ran and Tosafot about what *bekorban* means within the mishnah's context. The Ran understands it as a literal *korban* — a sacrificial offering, with the *neder/nedava* distinction playing out as just described. Tosafot reads *bekorban* as *konam* — the classic formulation of *nidrei issur* — meaning it is a standard prohibition vow, where the object is treated as though it were a *korban* and therefore forbidden. Tosafot's reading fits better with the three classic types of *hafla'ah* under discussion in this tractate: *neder*, *nazir*, and *shvuah* — with the *neder* category being the *konam* prohibition.

### Nazirut Analysis

The Ran then extends this framework to *nezirut*. Technically, there is only one way to become a *nazir* — you say *hareini nazir* — so there is no formal legal parallel to *harei alai* versus *harei zo*. Nevertheless, the Ran explains that someone whose *nezirut* flows from an uncomplicated, purely religious motivation — a true gift of the self to God — has made a *nezirut* of the *nedava* type. Someone whose *nezirut* flows from more complex, troubled, or impetuous motivations has made a *nezirut* of the *neder* type. This is not a legal distinction; it is a characterization of the act's religious character.

---

## Knidrei Reshaim (II)

### Shvuah Exclusion

Why does the mishnah omit *shvuah* from its closing list? The basic answer is that *kesherim* never take *shvuos* at all. The Ran states this directly. The underlying concern is the danger of *shem shamayim l'vatalah* — the non-weighty invocation of God's name. And we have already seen earlier in the tractate that someone who hears *shem shamayim l'vatalah* must put the offender in *cherem*.

There is a rich tradition on this point. Rashi on the *pasuk* *es Hashem Elokecha tira v'oso sa'avod u'vo sidbak u'vishmo tishaveia* says that only someone who possesses all of those qualities — fear of God, service, cleaving — is at the appropriate *madreiga* to take a *shvuah b'shem Hashem*. The Ramban there appears to disagree and reads *vishmo tishaveia* as meaning that if one is going to take a *shvuah* it must be in God's name, as opposed to the name of another deity — not that there is ever a positive circumstance for taking it.

Either way, the practical conclusion is clear. Since taking a *shvuah* in God's name is intrinsically fraught — *lo yenakeh Hashem es asher yisa es shemo lashav* — a *kasher* person would simply not do it. Therefore, one cannot invoke the concept of *knidvos kesherim* to validate a *shvuah*, because there is no such thing as a *shvuah* of the *kesherim*. Hence, *shvuah* is absent from the closing clause of the mishnah.

---

## Gemara Questions

### Shmuel's Three Ways

With the *chiddush* of the opening qualifier established, the Gemara turns to the question of the incomplete end of the sentence. *V'dilma hachi ka'amar* — perhaps what the speaker meant was "like the vows of *reshaim*, I will not vow" — in other words, they were disavowing *nedarim*, not making one. How do we know the speaker intended to become a *nazir*, or to obligate a *korban*, or to make a *shvuah*?

Shmuel answers: *b'omer k'nidrei reshaim hareini alai v'heimenu* — we are dealing with three distinct formulations. *Hareini*, behold I am, points toward *nezirut*. *Alai*, upon me, points toward a *korban* obligation. *Heimenu*, from it, points toward a *shvuah* not to eat. Each of these formulations provides a partial indication of what was meant, which is why the question of *yad* arises.

### Yad Sheeinah

The Gemara immediately presses: for *hareini* specifically, how does it point toward *nezirut*? *Dilma hareini betaanit ka'amar* — perhaps the speaker meant to be in a fast. Or any number of other things. At best this is a *yad she'einah mochiach*, an unclear indication, and Shmuel is on record holding that a *yad she'einah mochiach* is not effective. One might even say it is not a *yad* at all, since *hareini* is so vague that there is no way to determine what was intended.

### Okimta: Nazir Present

Shmuel's response is an *okimta* — a recontextualization: *keshehayah nazir over lefanav* — when there was a *nazir* walking in front of the speaker. In that context, when the speaker said *hareini*, it was obvious that he meant *hareini nazir*. The surrounding circumstance provided the necessary clarity.

This *okimta* reads a great deal into the mishnah — both the triggering word *hareini* and the contextual fact of the passing *nazir* — but the point is that these are not really where the mishnah's weight lies. The mishnah is not primarily interested in how we fill in the end of the sentence. The end of the sentence is assumed to be clear enough by whatever means — a *nazir* walking by, an explicit continuation, or some other contextual indicator. The *chiddush* of the mishnah is entirely concentrated in the opening qualifier.

### Ran vs. Tosafot

This is precisely where the Ran and Tosafot diverge. The Ran holds that the *chiddush* of the mishnah operates even if the end of the sentence is completely explicit. If someone says *knidrei reshaim kikar zeh alai konam* — "like the vows of *reshaim*, this loaf is forbidden to me as a *konam*" — the opening qualifier *knidrei reshaim* makes the vow effective, because that is a meaningful thing for a *rasha* to say. And if someone says *knidrei kesherim kikar zeh alai konam*, the opening qualifier *knidrei kesherim* prevents it from taking effect, because *kesherim* do not make *nedarim*, and therefore that qualifier signals that the vow is not seriously intended.

Tosafot disagrees. According to Tosafot, the qualifier at the beginning matters only because the end of the sentence is somewhat ambiguous — there is an element of *yad* in play. Given that ambiguity, if the opening qualifier is one that would not normally "work" — like *knidrei kesherim* — we do not resolve the ambiguity in favor of effectiveness. But if the end of the sentence were completely explicit, the opening qualifier would be irrelevant: *knidrei kesherim kikar zeh alai konam* would in that case be binding, because the commitment is unambiguous.

The Ran's reading, in a sense, is simpler. There was a *nazir* walking by; the speaker said *hareini*; we know what was meant. The entire force of the mishnah lies in the opening clause, regardless. One might ask why anyone would ever say *knidrei reshaim* when trying to create an effective vow — and this is genuinely curious. It may be that the mishnah is using this formulation to express a certain displeasure with the whole phenomenon of *nedarim* and *nezirut*, communicating that disapproval through the very *halacha* it is teaching. The phrase *knidrei kesherim*, for its part, has come down in popular usage precisely as that sort of hedge — an acknowledgment, very much like the contemporary *bli neder*, that the speaker is not fully committing.

### Raba: Hemenu

Turning to the third formulation — *heimenu*, "from it" — the Gemara asks: *dilma heimenu d'achila ka'amar*, perhaps the speaker meant "I will eat from it," not "I will not eat from it." There is simply no *shvuah* implied at all. Raba clarifies: the case is where the speaker said *heimenu shelo ochal* — "from it I will not eat." That makes the content explicit. The Gemara then asks: if so, what is the *chiddush*? The speaker said everything! The answer is: *kamah shmalan* — the speaker did not say the word *shvuah*. The *chiddush* is that even without explicitly pronouncing the word *shvuah*, saying "I will not eat from it" functions as a *yad lishvuah* and constitutes a binding *shvuah*. The significance of the end of the sentence, in other words, is also partly that it is incomplete — the keyword is absent — and nevertheless it is effective.

So the Gemara recognizes two layers of *chiddush* in the mishnah: the opening qualifier determines whether the statement is the kind of thing that would or would not take effect, and the remainder of the statement demonstrates that a *yad* without the explicit keyword is sufficient.

---

## Neder Values Debate

### Rabbi Meir's View

The Gemara now pivots to a broader question: who is the *tanna* of this mishnah that distinguishes between *neder* and *nedava*? The Gemara suggests it fits neither Rabbi Meir nor Rabbi Yehudah — and uses this as an entry point to discuss a fundamental *machlokes* about the religious value of making *nedarim*. *D'tanya*: the verse says *tov asher lo tidor mishetiddor v'lo tishalem* — better not to vow than to vow and not fulfill. *Tov mizeh umizeh she'eino noder kol ikar divrei Rabbi Meir*. Rabbi Meir says: best of all is simply not to vow at all.

### Risk & Non-Fulfillment

Rabbi Meir's position can be understood on two levels. The more pragmatic reading is that making a *neder* is inherently risky: you have now created a personal obligation, and if you fail to fulfill it — *ki tidor neder l'Hashem Elokecha lo te'acher l'shalmo* — you have transgressed. People may feel that the very act of raising their hand at a communal appeal has intrinsic religious value, but if they do not follow through, it would have been far better not to have made the commitment at all. The risk of non-fulfillment is simply too great.

But there is a deeper theological reading as well. One's *avodat Hashem* should consist of what God demands of a person. The obligations are divinely imposed — heteronomous, in the philosophical sense. When a person takes it upon themselves to create new religious obligations, they are in a sense serving their own religious impulses rather than the divine will. That is not true *avodat Hashem*. This may be the underlying concern: *kol hanoder k'ilu banah bamah v'chol hamkaymo k'ilu hikriv aleha korban* — every one who vows is as though he built a *bamah*, and one who fulfills it is as though he brought a *korban* upon it. A *bamah* may be a religious act, but unauthorized, individual religious construction is not self-evidently a positive phenomenon.

### Rabbi Yehudah View

Rabbi Yehudah takes a different position: *tov mizeh umizeh noder umshalem* — best of all is to vow and fulfill it. Rabbi Yehudah appears to regard the making of a *neder* as a genuine religious act, provided one sees it through. The vow, on this view, is not inherently problematic; it is the failure to fulfill it that is the danger.

### Mishnah & Meir

Returning to our mishnah: the mishnah seems to distinguish between *neder* (associated with *reshaim*) and *nedava* (associated with *kesherim*). This fits uncomfortably with Rabbi Yehudah, who seems to regard *nedarim* positively. But it also seems uncomfortable with Rabbi Meir — because Rabbi Meir, who says it is better not to vow at all, apparently allows for the positive phenomenon of a *nedava*, whereas the mishnah seems to treat *nedavos* as the clearly superior category.

### Meir Consistency

The Gemara resolves this: *afilu teima Rabbi Meir* — it can still be Rabbi Meir. *Ki ka'amar Rabbi Meir b'neder, b'nedava lo ka'amar* — when Rabbi Meir objects to vowing, he objects to the *neder*, not to the *nedava*. A *nedava* he does not include in his critique. This distinction has conceptual grounding beyond the risk of non-fulfillment: a *neder* creates a personal religious obligation that the person has imposed upon himself — something other than divinely mandated duty. A *nedava* merely sanctifies an object; it does not generate a personal obligation in the same way. One can thus argue that the concern about self-generated religious heteronomy applies to *neder* but not to *nedava*.

But the Gemara presses: a *nedava* also carries risks. *Dilma ati lidei takala* — what if the *nedava* also leads to stumbling? If you sanctify an animal and it wanders around your flock for months, you might come to misuse it, violating *meila*.

---

## Hillel Practice

### Hillel's Method

The Gemara answers with a historical precedent: *k'Hillel HaZaken* — like the practice of Hillel the Elder. *Amru alav al Hillel HaZaken shelo ma'al adam b'olato kol yamav* — they said of Hillel that no one ever committed *meila* with his *olah* throughout his lifetime. How did he accomplish this? *Meivi keshehei chulin la'azara, umakdisha, v'someich aleha, v'shochta* — he would bring his animal unsanctified to the outer precincts of the *azara*, sanctify it there and then, perform *semichah*, and immediately bring it for *shechita*. There was no window of time between sanctification and slaughter during which anything could go wrong.

### Nedava Safety

One might ask: why not do the same with a *neder*? Why not walk to the *beis hamikdash*, make a *neder* right at the entrance, and immediately bring the *korban*? The answer is that a *neder* creates a personal obligation — that step is simply unnecessary. Since you are going to be there and sanctify the animal anyway, why first take a *neder* that creates an obligation on your person? You can go straight to the *nedava*, sanctify the animal on the spot, and bring it immediately. The *nedava* allows a person to give a *korban* in a manner that involves no personal obligation, no window for *meila*, and no possibility of non-fulfillment. That is the paradigm of a *nedavat kesherim* — a *nedava* of the righteous.

### Tosafot Solution

This raises a question raised by both Tosafot and the Ran: does this mean that the mishnah's phrase *knidvat kesherim* can only take effect if the person is standing at the entrance to the *beis hamikdash*? That seems forced. Tosafot resolves this cleanly: the phrase *knidvat kesherim* works because the concept of a *nedavat kesherim* — a *nedava* in a fully unproblematic mode — genuinely exists. There is a real phenomenon that fits that description, even if it requires a particular set of circumstances. Because such a phenomenon exists, the phrase is meaningful and the vow takes effect. By contrast, there is no such thing as a *nidrei kesherim* — righteous people do not make *nedarim* — and therefore that phrase is not meaningful and the vow does not take effect. The mishnah is not requiring that one literally be at the gates of the *beis hamikdash*; it is simply invoking a concept that has a genuine referent.

---

## Reality of Nedava

### Nazir Nedava Q

Having established that *nedavat kesherim* is a real and achievable phenomenon when it comes to *korbanos*, the Gemara turns to *nezirut*: *nedava d'nezirus mai ika l'meimar?* Is there truly such a thing as an uncomplicated, purely motivated *nedavah*-type *nezirut*? The question is pressing precisely because the Gemara elsewhere associates *nezirut* with the expression *asher chata al hanefesh* — the *nazir* is said to have "sinned against the soul" — implying that something inherently problematic attaches to the *nazir*'s situation. Can *nezirut* ever truly be a pure religious gift?

The Gemara answers: *savar lah k'Shimon HaTzadik* — this view follows that of Shimon HaTzadik.

### Shimon HaTzadik

A *braisa* is introduced: *amar Shimon HaTzadik, miyamai lo achalti asham Nazir tamei* — Shimon HaTzadik said, "In all my days I never ate from the *asham* of an impure *nazir*." The *asham* of a *nazir tamei* is an offering brought when a *nazir* has become *tamei* and must begin the *nezirut* again. Shimon HaTzadik, who was the *kohen gadol* and entitled to eat from such offerings, consistently refused to do so in the case of a *nazir tamei*. Only one time did he consent to eat, and that occasion he describes in detail.

### Beautiful Nazir Story

*Ba adam echad Nazir min hadarom* — once a man came from the south, a *nazir*, and Shimon HaTzadik observed that he had beautiful eyes, was strikingly handsome, and had his hair arranged in flowing locks. Shimon asked him: what led you to accept upon yourself *nezirut* and thereby commit to shaving off this beautiful hair? The man replied: I was a shepherd for my father in my village. I went to draw water from the spring, and I saw my reflection. Suddenly my *yeitzer hara* seized me — *v'pachaz alai yitzri* — and it sought to take me away from this world, to lead me toward a life dominated by physical indulgence and vanity.

In response to his *yeitzer hara*, he said to himself: *lamah atah mitga'eh b'olam she'eino shelcha* — why do you glorify yourself in a world that is not yours? *B'mi she'asid lihayos rimah v'tole'ah* — in this body that will ultimately become food for worms. *She'agalechacha l'shamayim* — I will shave you for the sake of Heaven. Immediately he arose, kissed the young man on the head, and said: *bni, kamochah yirbu nozrei nezirus b'Yisrael* — my son, may those who take *nezirut* in Israel multiply like you. Regarding such a person the verse speaks: *ish ki yaifli lindor neder Nazir l'hazir l'Hashem* — the emphasis falls on *l'Hashem*, for God's sake.

---

## Nazir Motivation

### Tamei Nazir Issue

The Gemara now interrogates Shimon HaTzadik's practice more carefully. *Matkif leh Rav Mani: mai shna asham nazir tamei de-lo achal?* — Rav Mani presses: what is the particular reason Shimon HaTzadik refused to eat the *asham* of a *nazir tamei*? The stated rationale would seem to be that the offering comes as a result of sin — the *nazir* became *tamei*. But then *kol asham nami lo leachul* — he should refuse to eat any *asham* offering at all, since every *asham* comes to atone for some sin!

### Rav Yonah Regret

Rav Yonah responds: *hainu ta'ama* — this is the real reason. *Kishe'hen tohin, nozrin* — when people are in a state of being troubled or agitated about their own moral condition, filled with guilt and a desire to correct themselves, they impulsively accept *nezirut*. *Ukshe'hen mitamein, v'rabbim aleihem yemei nezirot, mitchartin bahen* — but when they then become *tamei* and the period of *nezirut* extends far longer than they had anticipated, they regret it. They wish they had never begun. *Venimtze'u mevi'in chullin la'azara* — and it turns out, in a sense, as though they are bringing *chullin* — non-sacred items — into the *azara*.

### Motivation Types

The insight here is significant. The *nazir tamei* reveals a person whose original motivation was impetuous rather than deeply rooted. The guilt or shame that drove them to accept *nezirut* was real, but it was not the product of a profound, settled conviction. When the *nezirut* becomes difficult — when it extends due to *tumah* — the depth of that commitment is exposed. They never had the endurance for it, because the conviction was never truly deep.

Shimon HaTzadik, seeing this dynamic, would not eat the *asham* of a *nazir tamei*, because such a person's *nezirut* was almost certainly of the *neder* type — complex, guilt-driven, impetuous — not the *nedava* type. The *nazir tahor*, whose period ended without interruption, remains at least formally in the category of someone who may have had genuine conviction. Perhaps the conviction was complicated, but there was no opportunity for regret to manifest. The *nazir tamei*, by contrast, had that opportunity, and the regret demonstrated what the conviction had really been.

The Gemara pushes: *i hachi afilu nazir tahor nami* — if the logic is impetuous motivation leading to eventual regret, should we not worry about even a *nazir tahor*? The answer is: *lo, de-amudei amei nafshia de-achul lemidor* — no, because the *nazir tahor* had assessed that he could endure the standard thirty days, and he did. The absence of demonstrated regret allows us to take his *nezirut* at face value, even if we remain somewhat skeptical. The *nazir tamei*'s regret, by contrast, has been publicly demonstrated.

---

## Yehudah Nedava

### Yehudah Reread

Having established all of this for Rabbi Meir's position, the Gemara now constructs a parallel reading for Rabbi Yehudah. *Afilu teima Rabbi Yehuda* — even according to Rabbi Yehudah, the mishnah can be explained consistently. *Ki amar Rabbi Yehuda* when he says it is best to vow and fulfill — *b'nedavah*, he really meant *nedavah*. His objection was only to *neder*, not to *nedavah*. The Gemara then reads back Rabbi Yehudah's statement in the *braisa* — *tov mizeh umizeh noder umekayeim* — and says we should actually read it as *tani nodev umekayeim* — he was speaking of *nedava*, not *neder*. This is explicitly not the plain sense of Rabbi Yehudah's words, but the Gemara is working to show that the mishnah can fit Rabbi Yehudah's view on this reinterpretation.

The Gemara then replicates the earlier analysis: *mai shna noder d'lo — dilma ati lidei takala*, same concern about stumbling. *Nedava nami dilma ati lidei takala* — so why is *nedava* any better? And here, unlike the case of Rabbi Meir where we needed to bring proofs from Hillel HaZaken, we have Rabbi Yehudah's own statements. *Rabbi Yehuda l'taameih — adam meivi kivshato l'azara, umakdisha, v'someich aleha v'shochta* — Rabbi Yehudah himself describes the practice of bringing one's animal unsanctified to the *azara*, sanctifying it there, performing *semichah*, and bringing it for *shechita* immediately. This is exactly what we said of Hillel, now attributed directly to Rabbi Yehudah's own teaching. And so the same analysis follows: *neder* is problematic because it creates a personal obligation at risk of non-fulfillment; *nedava* performed in this manner is entirely safe.

### Righteous Nazir

But the same question reemerges: *teinach nedava d'korbanos* — fine for *korbanos*, what about *nezirut*? Here Rabbi Yehudah also speaks from his own tradition. *Rabbi Yehuda omer: chasidim harishonim hayu mis'avim l'havi korban chatas* — the great righteous ones of earlier generations longed to bring a *korban chatas*, but they faced a fundamental obstacle: *lefi she'ein HaKadosh Baruch Hu meivi takala al yadeihem* — God would never bring them to unintentional sin, because that is the only circumstance under which a *chatas* may be brought. They could not sin intentionally — that would disqualify the offering — and God would not allow them to sin inadvertently. So how could they bring a *chatas*?

*Omdim umisnadbim nezirus l'Makom* — they would accept *nezirut* upon themselves, not for its own sake, but as a vehicle: *k'dei sheyischayeiv korban chatas l'Makom* — so that they would incur the obligation of a *korban chatas* for God. The *chatas* of a *nazir* who becomes *tamei* is the mechanism. They accepted *nezirut* knowing that they might become *tamei* and thereby be required to bring a *chatas*, which is what they ultimately sought to offer. This, according to Rabbi Yehudah, is the example of a genuinely righteous, purely motivated *nezirut* — a *nedavat nezirut* in the fullest sense.

---

## Shimon Objects

### Shimon Objection

Rabbi Shimon disagrees: *lo nadru b'nazir* — they would not have done this. They would not have accepted *nezirut* upon themselves even to obtain the ability to bring a *chatas*.

### Alternatives

Instead, Rabbi Shimon says, those who wished to bring *korbanos* freely would do so through other means. One who wanted to bring an *olah* would make a *nedava* of an *olah* and bring it. One who wished to bring *shlamim* would make a *nedava* of *shlamim*. One who wished to bring a *todah* with its four kinds of bread could do so as a *nedavah* as well. All of these could be freely offered as *nedavot* without *nezirut* being involved at all.

### Sinner Status

As for *nezirut*, *aval binezirus lo hisnadvu* — they would not accept *nezirut* even for this purpose. The reason: *k'dei shelo yikar'u chotim* — so that they not be called sinners. For even a *nazir* who has committed no wrong is described in the Torah's language as one who has *asher chata al hanefesh* — who sinned against the soul. The verse speaks in the context of a *nazir tamei*, and the Ran and others note that this refers specifically to that case, but Rabbi Shimon learns from it a broader principle about the nature of *nezirut* itself.

### Denial Problem

The *asher chata al hanefesh* points to the ascetic dimension of *nezirut*. A *nazir* separates himself from wine and certain aspects of ordinary life. He marks himself visibly as different from the rest of society. Rabbi Shimon sees this self-denial as intrinsically a form of sin — against the soul, against the self. *Nezirut* does not merely risk impure motivation from the outside; it contains within itself an element that is religiously problematic, regardless of motivation.

---

## Asceticism Debate

### Kadosh vs. Choteh

Rabbi Shimon's objection opens onto a profound theological question: is the ascetic a *kadosh* or a *choteh*? Is the person who sits in a *taanis* — a fast — holy, or a sinner? This is not merely a question of motivation, though motivation is certainly at issue. It is a question about the nature of religious life itself. Is the model of the religious ideal one who withdraws from the physical world, denies bodily pleasures, and focuses entirely on the spiritual? Or is that very withdrawal itself a kind of failure — a rejection of the world that God created and declared good?

### Embodied Religion

Judaism has, by and large, been understood as an embodied religion — one in which the physical world is not the enemy of the spirit but the medium through which God is served. We are not at war with the physical world. The pleasures of *Shabbos*, the joy of the *yom tov*, the *mitzvos* that engage the body and the senses — all of these reflect a fundamentally different orientation than that of a religion that sees the soul as imprisoned in the body, longing to escape. Yet the tension has always existed. Figures of *prishus* — separation from worldly pleasure — appear throughout the tradition, and the question of when separation is *kedushah* and when it is a betrayal of the world God made is genuinely unresolved.

### Rambam Critique

The Rambam addresses this tension directly in his *Peirush Mishnayos*. He criticizes at length the approach of the *Chasidei Ashkenaz* — the medieval German pietists — who practiced extensive self-denial and asceticism. The Rambam argues that this entire orientation was absorbed from Christian religious culture and has no authentic Jewish foundation. *Lo dayecha mah she'asra lacha Torah* — the prohibitions of the Torah are sufficient; one need not add to them by denying oneself what the Torah permits. To do so is not *kedushah* but a kind of unhealthy religious distortion.

Yet even acknowledging the Rambam's sharp critique, the tension remains. The debate between Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Shimon about whether the *chasidim harishonim* would have accepted *nezirut* in order to bring a *chatas* is one expression of that tension. Is *nezirut* a form of *nedavah* — a gift of the self — or is it always, by definition, a *chatas al hanefesh*, a sin against the soul? The question of whether a *nazir* is *kadosh* or *choteh*, and whether taking a *taanis* is holy or sinful, maps directly onto this larger question about the place of asceticism within Jewish religious life — a question that the Gemara introduces here and does not fully resolve.

---

---

# Nedarim 10

## Vows & Nazir Review

### Nidrei Reshaim

Today's daf is daf 10, and we find ourselves continuing from where we left off in the *gemara*. The *mishnah* that opened our discussion frames the fundamental tension of *masechet Nedarim* in stark terms: *nidrei reshaim* — the vows of the wicked — as opposed to *nidrei kesherim* and *nidvot kesherim*. The governing principle, put simply, is that *resha'im* make *nedarim* while *kesherim* make *nidavot*. It is worth pausing on the word *resha'im* here. The *Ran* explains the phrase as *resha'im badavar zeh* — wicked in this particular matter — and one should not read into it the full harshness that the term normally carries. And yet, however we soften it, it remains a striking characterization. Here we are in a tractate entirely devoted to *nedarim*, and the very opening move is to attach a disparaging label to those who take them. The implicit tension borders on the ironic: who, after all, would aspire to vow *as the resha'im do*? The *gemara*'s concern operates on at least two levels. First, there is the practical worry that a person who makes a *neder* may come to violate it. But second, and perhaps more fundamentally, there is something inherently questionable about the religious phenomenon itself — the idea that one must manufacture one's own religious realities, as though what God has commanded is insufficient, imposing upon oneself a self-styled spiritual regime rather than fulfilling what has actually been asked of us. Both concerns remain very much alive as the *gemara* develops.

### Nazir Nidavah

From there, the discussion turned naturally to the *nazir*, and the question of what it would even mean for *nezirut* to qualify as a *nidavah*. In this context, the distinction is not a technical legal one as it is for *korbanos* — a *korban* can formally be either a *neder* or a *nidavah*. Here the question is one of motivation: under what circumstances, if any, does a person's acceptance of *nezirut* reflect a genuinely worthy impulse?

### Shimon HaTzadik

This question brought the *gemara* to the celebrated position of Shimon HaTzadik, who declared that throughout his entire tenure he had never eaten from the *korban* of a *nazir tamei* — except for one singular instance. That exception involved a young man who had adopted *nezirut* for what amounts to a reverse-narcissism reason: confronting his own dangerous vanity, he chose to use his striking appearance as an occasion for sincere *avodas Hashem* rather than self-admiration. Shimon HaTzadik recognized this as a case of genuine *l'shem shamayim* and therefore ate from his *korban*.

### Rabbi Meir/Yehuda

The positions of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda were then brought into the picture. Rabbi Meir holds: *tov shelo yiddor mizeh u'mizeh she'eino noder kol ikkar* — better not to vow at all than to vow and not fulfill. Rabbi Yehuda initially appears to disagree, holding that *noder u'mekayem* is better than not vowing at all. But the *gemara* ultimately collapses the apparent dispute: Rabbi Yehuda is referring only to a *nidavah*, not a *neder*. Even Rabbi Yehuda agrees that a *neder* is problematic. The *gemara* further cites Rabbi Yehuda himself as offering a model of a legitimate *nazir*: one who becomes a *nazir* specifically in order to be able to bring a *korban chatas*. The analogy offered is to a person who, upon learning that it is a *mitzvah* to give a *get* to one's wife, deliberately goes out and divorces her in order to fulfill the obligation — using an ostensibly ordinary act as the vehicle for a genuine religious gesture. Similarly, someone who becomes a *nazir* in order to bring a *korban chatas* is treating the *nezirut* as a kind of *nidavah* vehicle for *korban*-giving.

### Nedarim vs Nidavot

The overall framework that emerges is thus: *nedarim* are something the *gemara* looks upon with suspicion and criticism, while *nidavot* are praiseworthy. The question of how to apply this framework to *nezirut* — which sits in an ambiguous middle position — generates multiple positions that will now be examined more closely.

---

## Rabbi Shimon Critique

### Lo Nadvu BeNazir

Picking up approximately fifteen lines into the relevant section, the *gemara* presents the position of Rabbi Shimon: *lo nadvu b'nazir* — people who genuinely wanted to give *korbanos* and to do so entirely *l'shem shamayim* would nonetheless not have accepted upon themselves to become a *nazir*. Instead, if one wished to bring an *olah*, one simply brought an *olah*; if one wished to bring *shelamim*, one brought *shelamim*; if a *todah* with its four types of bread, one brought that. *Aval b'nezirut lo hitnadvu* — even the most sincere and well-motivated individuals did not embrace *nezirut* as their vehicle.

### Vichiper Alav

The reason Rabbi Shimon gives is drawn from the *pasuk*: *vichiper alav asher chata al hanefesh* — the Torah says the *nazir* requires atonement for having sinned against the soul. And this is not being read here, in Rabbi Shimon's view, as referring specifically to the *nazir tamei*. Rather, Rabbi Shimon understands it as indicating that the very acceptance of *nezirut* constitutes a form of injury to oneself — specifically, *shetzier atzmo min hayayin*, that the person denied himself wine. A further *kal vachomer* is drawn: if one who denied himself merely wine is called a sinner, how much more so one who denies himself from everything. And from here the *gemara* extrapolates: *kol hayoshev b'taanis nikra chotei* — anyone who accepts upon himself a *taanis* is called a sinner. The counterpoint is also noted: an opposing opinion holds that *kol hayoshev b'taanis nikra kadosh* — such a person is called holy.

### Abaye's Synthesis

Abaye at this point performs one of his characteristic syntheses, collecting disparate Tannaitic opinions under a single organizing rubric. He declares: *Shimon HaTzadik v'Rabbi Shimon v'Rabbi Elazar Hakapar kulan shita achas hen* — all three hold essentially the same *shita*, or school of thought. It should be noted, as Abaye himself implies and the *rishonim* confirm, that this does not mean they said literally the same thing. The language here is *kulan shita achas hen* — they are of one orientation — not *kulan amru davar echad*. There is a recognized difference in formulation, perhaps even in the specific language associated with *nedarim*, but the underlying thrust is the same.

### Nazir Chotei

The common principle uniting all three: *denazir chotei havei* — that the *nazir* is to be considered a sinner. Shimon HaTzadik and Rabbi Shimon, the *gemara* notes, we have already addressed. Rabbi Elazar Hakapar beRabbi is cited from a *braita*: *vichiper alav asher chata al hanefesh — vichi be'eizo nefesh chata?* Against what soul did this person sin? His answer: *ella shetzier atzmo min hayayin* — he denied himself wine. The text could simply have said *asher chata*; the addition of *al hanefesh* implies a personal injury, a harm done to oneself. From there the *kal vachomer* proceeds as above, concluding with the sweeping principle about one who accepts a *taanis*.

---

## Chotei Interpretation

### Nazir Tamei Focus

The *rishonim* are careful to note that the three opinions gathered by Abaye are not identical in their emphases. Shimon HaTzadik's concern was focused specifically on the *nazir tamei*. His worry was essentially about the sincerity and depth of the *nazir*'s conviction: when a *nazir* becomes *tamei*, the vow extends, the count resets, and the person is forced to confront whether he really meant what he undertook. The *nazir tamei* is the test case for Shimon HaTzadik precisely because the impurity occasion reveals whether the commitment was genuine. His concern is thus primarily one of motivation and the quality of conviction behind the vow, not about *nezirut* as such.

### Pasuk Objection

The *gemara* raises a difficulty: the *pasuk* of *nikra chotei* is written in the context of a *nazir tamei* — so how can Rabbi Shimon apply it to *nezirut* in general, as though the problem is the very acceptance of *nezirut* regardless of *tumah*?

### Self-Denial Problem

Rabbi Shimon's emphasis, in contrast to Shimon HaTzadik, has nothing to do with *tumah*. His concern is with something intrinsically problematic about the phenomenon of self-denial — *shetzier atzmo min hayayin* — irrespective of what happens afterward.

### Repeated Sin

The *gemara* resolves the textual difficulty by noting: *mishum deshana b'cheit* — because this person has repeated the sin. Either the sin of self-denial is compounded when *tumah* occurs — in that the period is extended and the self-denial lengthened — or because the *nazir* has now piled upon the original sin of denying himself wine the additional sin of becoming *tamei*. One might object that becoming *tamei* is not always within the *nazir*'s control — the Torah itself uses the language of *b'feta pitom*, sudden, unexpected *tumah*. This is acknowledged; nonetheless, the situation of the *nazir tamei* is understood to be a particularly compounded and therefore particularly problematic case.

---

## Asceticism Philosophy

### Motivation Question

Before moving forward, it is worth stepping back and asking what precisely the source of the problem is — why is the motivation questioned at all in the first place? Shimon HaTzadik seemed to emphasize that the motivation behind *nezirut* is often impure. Consider: becoming a *nazir* is a highly visible, socially marked act. Long hair, abstention from wine, refusal to come in contact with the dead — these behaviors signal to everyone around you that you are trying to be holier, that you are among the spiritually elevated. This creates fertile ground for *yihra* — for a kind of spiritual vanity — even when the person is not consciously aware that this is driving them. There are serious questions about how pure somebody's motivation can really be when they adopt behaviors that so visibly separate them from ordinary society and signal membership among the *frum* elite. That, it seems, was Shimon HaTzadik's core concern: that when the *nazir* becomes *tamei* and faces the possibility of extending and restarting his *nezirut*, it emerges that the commitment was never deep enough to sustain itself. The conviction was not coming from a genuine place.

### Asceticism Trends

The latter opinions — Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Elazar Hakapar — seem to be pointing at something different: not a defect in the individual's motivation, but something intrinsically problematic about the phenomenon of self-denial as a religious ideal. And in any religion, one will always find ascetic tendencies, because the idea that religion is something spiritual, something beyond the physical, can easily shade into a form of mind-body dualism, in which the spiritual life is conceived as being at war with the body, and denying the body becomes the religious ideal. This is especially prominent in Christianity, though it is somewhat ironic there, given that the foundational Christian theological claim is of an embodied God. Nevertheless, the ascetic strand runs deep in that tradition.

### Jewish Embodiment

Judaism, by contrast, is a far more embodied religion. On *Shabbat* one is obligated in *oneg* — pleasure. There were sects in the Second Temple period that forbade marital relations on *Shabbat* out of an impulse toward the spiritual, but normative *halacha* holds the opposite: conjugal obligation is very much a feature of *Shabbat*. Judaism, in short, does not endorse the notion that freeing oneself from bodily desires is the path to holiness. And yet it is not surprising that the ascetic impulse would find its way into Jewish life as well — which is precisely why one finds both the opinion that *kol hayoshev b'taanis nikra chotei* and the competing opinion that *kol hayoshev b'taanis nikra kadosh*, and one finds both strands genuinely operative in the tradition.

### Rambam Critique

The Rambam addresses this directly. He argues that the trend toward asceticism found among *Chasidei Ashkenaz* in the medieval period — the extreme fasting, self-mortification, and bodily denial that characterized that movement — was a product of Christian influence, and he regarded it as a fundamentally anti-Jewish idea. And he is right that it represents a departure from the mainstream Jewish orientation, even if one can find textual support for some strain of it. The debate between *nikra chotei* and *nikra kadosh* shows that both positions are genuinely internal to the tradition.

### Wine Intent

There is one further point worth making before leaving this topic, and it is one that tends to be overlooked. We naturally think of *nezirut* in terms of asceticism and self-denial, but consider what the Torah actually prohibits: wine. That is the primary prohibition. Now, the prohibition of wine is not primarily about denying oneself a sensual pleasure. A *nazir* can eat a lavish meal every night, can enjoy all the pleasures of the table, can engage in marital relations — none of that is restricted. The prohibition on wine is about something specific to wine: it clouds the mind, it leads to inebriation, it diminishes one's mental clarity and judgment. The concern is not sensual indulgence per se but the loss of cognitive and moral clarity that comes with alcohol. So the *nazir*'s abstention from wine may be less about the denial of pleasure and more about the aspiration to maintain a certain sharpness of mind.

---

## Wine & Society

### Wine Symbol

This connects to a broader theme. Throughout *Tanach*, wine is indeed associated with *ta'anugei olam hazeh*, with the pleasures and temptations of this world — *yayin yesamach levav enosh*. But one should be careful here. The danger of wine in the tradition is not simply that it tastes good. It is that it pulls a person — *nimshachim acharei hayayin* — it draws one in through the mechanism of inebriation and addiction, leading one to want to return again and again. The power of wine is its particular capacity to compromise judgment and to perpetuate its own consumption. It is about becoming an alcoholic, about the progressive clouding of one's faculties, not merely about the enjoyment of a good beverage. So the label of asceticism does not quite capture what is happening. The *nazir*'s wine prohibition is specifically about clearing the head, keeping one's thinking unencumbered.

### Societal Separation

Still, the *nazir*'s regime as a whole does serve the function of keeping him separate from ordinary society. Not becoming *tamei* to the dead keeps him away from burial society and from the social obligations of mourning. The long hair marks him visibly. Together, these practices isolate the *nazir* and enforce a kind of *perisha*, a separation. It is possible to understand the wine prohibition in this light as well: not just clarity of mind in the abstract, but specifically keeping the *nazir* out of the social contexts in which wine is consumed — the dinner party, the symposium, the ordinary social gathering. In this sense, the prohibition on wine is as much about keeping the *nazir* separate from society as it is about any intrinsic harm of alcohol. Some traditions indeed use altered states — including intoxicants and other substances — as vehicles for spiritual elevation. *Chasidim* embrace a good *l'chayim*; various indigenous traditions use *peyote* or other plants in ritual contexts; certain Buddhist traditions have analogous practices. The point is that seeking a higher spiritual plane through such means is itself a recognizable phenomenon. The *nazir* is doing something different: he is seeking elevation precisely by refusing that path, maintaining sobriety in order to access a different kind of heightened awareness.

### Raisins Extension

One might note that the prohibitions extend even to raisins and grape products — which are not themselves intoxicating. These are extensions, safeguards on the core prohibition, which is itself centered on the wine and what wine does.

---

## Kinuyim Introduction

### Konam Substitutes

We now turn to a new topic, or rather to the topic that the *gemara* has been building toward all along: the subject of *kinuyim*, the substitute terms used in making vows. The *mishnah* presents these systematically. Someone who says *konam*, *konach*, or *konas* — *harei elu kinuyim l'korban* — these are recognized substitutes for the word *korban*. The structure is evident: the *kaf* and *nun* of *korban* are preserved, and the ending varies. *Konam* preserves the *nun*; *konach* substitutes a *chet*; *konas* a *samach*. These are the standard *kinuyim* for *korban*, and they serve as the operative language of a *korban neder*.

### Cherem Substitutes

Similarly, *cherek*, *cherech*, and *cheref* — *harei elu kinuyim l'cherem*. These preserve the root of *cherem* while substituting the final letter. The structure is parallel: the essential phonetic body of the word is maintained, but the last element is altered.

### Nezirut Substitutes

For *nezirut*, the substitutes are *nazik*, *naziach*, and *paziach* — *harei elu kinuyim l'nezirut*. The first two preserve the *nazi* beginning; *paziach* is the more striking entry, having altered both the first letter and the end. The *gemara* will address this.

### Oath Substitutes

For *shvuah*, the substitutes given are *shvuta* and *shkuka*. These carry the phonetic echo of *shvuah* in modified form and function as its recognized *kinuyim*.

### Bemosi/Bemohi

The last entry in the *mishnah* on this topic is the most interesting: *noder bemohi* — or in all the textual traditions of the *mishnah*, *noder bemosa*. The word *mosa* is simply the Aramaic for *shvuah*; one finds it in *Targum Onkelos*, rendered as *mumsah* or a related form. The word *noder* here is also striking, since we are dealing with what is technically a *shvuah*, not a *neder* — but this reflects a looser popular usage in which the two terms bled into each other, where one would say *noder* even when meaning to take a *shvuah*. A *neder belashon shvuah* and a *shvuah belashon neder* were realities of the vernacular.

Our textual version reads *bemohi*, and the *Yerushalmi* offers a remarkable reading: *mohi* is a *kinuy* for *Moshe* — that is, for *Moshe Rabbeinu* — and the phrase means that one is taking a *shvuah* in the manner of, or invoking, the *shvuah* that *Moshe* took. When did *Moshe* take such an oath? The *Yerushalmi* cites the *pasuk* *vayoel Moshe laveshes es ha'ish*, which is normally translated as "Moshe consented to dwell with the man," but the *Yerushalmi* reads *vayoel* from the root *alah* — a curse or oath — understanding it to mean that *Moshe* swore. *Bemohi*, on this reading, means: in the *shvuah* that *Moshe* swore.

---

## Kinuyim Debate

### Rabbi Yochanan

The *gemara* now records a dispute about the nature of these *kinuyim*. Rabbi Yochanan says: *lashon umos hein* — they are some form of foreign language. This presumably refers to a Semitic language with phonetic proximity to Hebrew, given how close the *kinuyim* sound to the original terms.

### Reish Lakish

Reish Lakish says: *lashon shebadu lahem chachamim veyihei noder bahem* — a language that the rabbis invented to serve as substitute terms, precisely to avoid using the actual official words. It is worth recalling that this dispute has halachic consequences: the *Ran* argues strongly that even on Reish Lakish's view — that these are invented terms — they are binding *deoraisa*. His reasoning is twofold. First, all language is ultimately convention, so the fact that the rabbis created these terms does not make them less real as language. Second, even if the *kinuy* is not technically the official word, it is at minimum a kind of *yad* — the speaker's intent is unmistakable — and *yad* is sufficient to create a binding *neder*. There is a minority view that *kinuyim* are only binding *derabbanan*, but the dominant position, and the *Ran*'s position, is that they are *deoraisa*.

### Badu Milibo

The *gemara* supports Reish Lakish's formulation by citing a *pasuk*: *bachodesh asher bada milibo* — the month that he invented from his heart. This is a somewhat puzzling proof-text to deploy. Why cite a verse about someone who invented a calendar month — apparently a criticism — to support the legitimacy of rabbinic linguistic invention? The *gemara* seems to be noting that *badu* is the operative word: it is used to mean "invented" or "created from nothing." But perhaps there is an interesting irony being invoked as well. The very phenomenon of *nedarim* is a kind of *badu milibo* — a person has invented a religious reality, transformed a permitted object into something forbidden through the sheer force of their declaration. The rabbis, in turn, create a language to go along with this invented phenomenon. And perhaps the reference to *asher badu milibo* carries a subtle signal: like the invented calendar month, this too is a created thing, a constructed reality. The *gemara* may be gently flagging the somewhat problematic character of the entire enterprise even as it regulates it.

### Why Kinuyim

Why did the rabbis establish *kinuyim* in the first place? This question is clearly most pressing according to Reish Lakish, but even according to Rabbi Yochanan, insofar as the rabbis endorse using these terms rather than the standard ones, the question of their rationale applies. The *gemara*'s answer: *delo leima korban* — so that people should not say the official word *korban*. But why not say *korban*? Because then the natural completion of that formulation would be *korban la'Hashem* — and once one says *korban*, it naturally triggers *la'Hashem* in the speaker's mind. And if one were to say *la'Hashem korban*, reversing the order, one would be invoking *shem shamayim* first, without having yet given it the proper context — which risks *levatala*.

---

## Shem Shamayim

### Korban Order

The relevant *braita* presents this concern precisely. Rabbi Shimon asks: from where do we know that one should not say *la'Hashem olah*, *la'Hashem mincha*, *la'Hashem toda*, *la'Hashem shelamim* — leading with *la'Hashem*? The Torah says *korban la'Hashem*: first *korban*, then *la'Hashem*. The divine name receives its proper context only after the subject matter has been established. To lead with *la'Hashem* is to invoke it without that grounding.

### Levatala

A *braita* is cited further: *ha-mazkir shem shamayim levatala* — one who mentions God's name *levatala* — *al achat kama v'chama*, how much more severely is this to be condemned. If even for a genuine *korban* the Torah insists on the ordering *korban la'Hashem* so as not to invoke the name without its proper framing, then someone who says *la'Hashem* in a loose or incomplete way — potentially without ever completing the phrase — has violated the name in vain.

### Kal Vachomer

The *kal vachomer* follows: if even for a genuine *korban* — where the intent is entirely appropriate, where one is doing something entirely sanctioned — the Torah still insists on care about how the divine name is introduced, then certainly one who mentions it *levatala*, in a context where the invocation adds nothing or is incomplete, has done something far worse.

### Dedication Irony

There is a further irony worth noting here. The paradigm of *neder* — *vayidor Yaakov neder*, vowing to give *ma'aser*, to bring a *korban* — is genuinely about dedicating something to God, which is why the formula *la'Hashem* is relevant in that context. But when a person makes a standard *neder* today — saying this loaf of bread is forbidden to me — the *la'Hashem* framing is actually not relevant at all. The person is not dedicating anything to God; he is simply imposing a personal prohibition on himself. To invoke *la'Hashem* in that context is therefore doubly inappropriate: it misrepresents the nature of what one is doing, and it risks invoking the divine name without genuine contextual grounding. The *gemara* just two dapim earlier had treated the concern of *mazkir shem shamayim l'vatala* at length, and that anxiety is very much alive here. There is a pervasive hesitancy around the entire phenomenon: the vow-maker may be a *rasha*, may be doing something religiously questionable, may be deploying the wrong language, and may now be pulling God's name into a context where it does not properly belong. The answer is *kinuyim* — a vocabulary that preserves the communicative function of the vow without triggering the cascade toward *shem shamayim*.

---

## Kinuyei Kinuyim

### Shammai Hillel

The *gemara* now asks whether the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish corresponds to a Tannaitic dispute. It finds a potential parallel: *Beis Shammai omrim kinuyei kinuyim asurim* — derivatives of *kinuyim* are binding — *u'Veis Hillel omrim kinuyei kinuyim mutarim* — derivatives of *kinuyim* are not binding. A *kinuy* of a *kinuy* means a further derivation from the already-substitute term: rather than *konam*, one might say something like *mekanamna* — a verbal, conjugated form derived from *konam* itself.

### Shammai Position

The *gemara*'s analysis: *man de-amar kinuyei kinuyim asurin kasavar kinuyim lashon umos hein* — the view that holds these derivatives binding presupposes that *kinuyim* are a real foreign language. And if they are a real language, then corruptions and dialectal variants of that language are still real speech, still legitimate expressions of the underlying concept.

### Hillel Position

*U-le-man de-amar mutarim kasavar lashon shebadu lahem chachamim* — the lenient view presupposes that *kinuyim* are an invented language. And if they are invented by the rabbis, then only what the rabbis actually invented carries validity; further derivations and conjugations that the rabbis did not specifically create do not participate in the original rabbinic enactment.

The *gemara* then entertains a second reading: *lo de-chulei alma kinuyim lashon umos hein* — perhaps everyone agrees they are a foreign language. On this reading, *Beis Shammai* holds that these further corruptions are still considered legitimate speech in that language — a recognizable dialect variant — while *Beis Hillel* holds that they are not *me-ikar ha-lashon*, not part of the genuine linguistic core; they are corruptions that no one actually speaks, not even as a dialect.

A third resolution is also offered: *Beis Shammai gazrinan kinuyei kinuyim mishum kinuyim* — even if these derivatives are not genuinely binding in their own right, Beis Shammai decrees that they are treated as binding as a safeguard for the *kinuyim* themselves. *Beis Hillel* declines to extend the rabbinic decree to this second level.

### Konam Examples

The *gemara* asks for concrete examples. Rav Yosef teaches: instead of *konam*, one says *mekanamna*; instead of *konach*, *mekanachna*; instead of *konas*, *mekanasna*. These are verbal, conjugated forms of the *kinuyim*, constructed as first-person verbal expressions — "I am making this a *konam*."

### Cherem Examples

For *cherem*: the *braita* gives *charkim* and *charchim* as the *kinuyei kinuyim*, which are effectively pluralizations of *cherekh* and *cherech*.

### Nezirut Examples

Rav Yosef also teaches the *nezirut* examples: from *naziach*, the derivative is *menazachna*; from *paziach*, it is *maphichna*; and there is *mechazakna* as well.

### Problematic Forms

The *gemara* then notes that certain further forms were brought as questions: *maphazna*, *methazna*, *metazna* — even more remote derivations. These apparently go beyond even *kinuyei kinuyim* in their distance from the original term, and Beis Shammai would presumably be uncertain how to categorize them.

---

## Ambiguous Cases

### Kinama Debate

Ravina said to Rav Ashi: *kinama mai?* — what is the status of someone who says *kinama*? The word sounds like *konam*, but *kinmon bosem* — cinnamon, the spice — is also called *kinamon* or *kinama*. Is the person invoking the vow language, or merely naming a spice? The ambiguity is genuine.

### Kina Debate

Rav Acha berei d'Rav Chiyya raised a parallel question to Rav Ashi: *kina mai?* — is *kina* a reference to *konam*, or is it *kina shel tarnegolim*, a chicken coop? The word appears in *Eicha* in other senses. The speaker's intent is unclear.

### Teiku Resolution

Both questions are left as *teiku* — unresolved. The practical difficulty this creates is particularly acute for Beis Hillel's position. If *kinuyei kinuyim* are not binding according to Beis Hillel, and we cannot determine whether a given word is a *kinuy* or a *kinuy* of a *kinuy*, we are left without a clear ruling. The *teiku* leaves the matter in the domain of unresolved uncertainty.

---

## Oath Kinuyim

### Oath Terms

The *gemara* turns to *kinuyei shvuah* — substitute terms for oaths. The forms given are *shvuel*, *shvutiel*, and *shkukiel*. These expand upon *shvuta* and *shkuka* from the *mishnah* by appending the divine name *El* — which is itself an interesting feature, suggesting that for *shvuah*, the invocation of a divine name is part of the linguistic structure even of the *kinuy*-level terms.

### Name Confusion

The *gemara* immediately questions *shvuel*: does it not simply sound like a proper name? *Shvuel ben Gershom* was indeed a person. The *gemara* therefore substitutes *shvuta-el* as the more clearly recognizable *kinuy* form for *shvuah*.

### Verbal Forms

Shmuel then rules: *amar ashishta lo amar klum* — if someone tries to make a verbal form out of these — *ashishta*, *ashkika*, *karinsa* — these are nothing, they are not effective declarations. The rabbinic construction of *kinuyim* does not extend to verbal conjugations of *kinuyei shvuah*.

### Hand Examples

The *Yerushalmi* adds what are probably the most intuitively natural examples of all: *ha-omer yamin harei zeh shvuah, ha-omer smol harei zeh shvuah* — if one says "my right hand" or "my left hand," that constitutes a *shvuah*. This is grounded in the biblical imagery of oath-taking by the upraised hand — *harimoti yadi el Hashem*, and *nishbati bi-ymini*. The right hand is entirely understandable as a form of oath-invocation. As for the left hand — perhaps for a left-handed person.

---

## Lieberman Context

### Gentile Practice

Saul Lieberman, in his essay "Oaths and Vows" in *Greek and Jewish Palestine*, provides extensive historical context for these phenomena. He demonstrates that among the non-Jewish population of the Greco-Roman world, oath-taking had become a ubiquitous and thoroughly debased practice. People would pile oaths one upon another, swear by absurd objects — by the dog, by the lettuce, by the fishnet, by the life of the fig picker — sometimes because they wished to avoid invoking the names of their gods, and so used these as a form of *kinuy*, and sometimes simply out of a kind of verbal prolificacy in which the oath had lost all weight through sheer repetition.

### Philo Critique

Philo of Alexandria describes the phenomenon in sharp terms. Writing about the Alexandrian Jewish community, he observes: "So highly impious are they, that on any chance matter the most tremendous titles are on their lips, and they do not blush to use name after name, one piled upon another, thinking that the continual repetition of a string of oaths will secure them their object." The oath has become a social lubricant, a verbal tic, entirely drained of the gravity that should attend it.

### Palestinian Usage

In Palestine the situation was similar. Lieberman documents how people swore on every occasion — in business, in everyday conversation, when accepting or declining invitations, when vouching for stories of questionable credibility. The rabbis consistently preached that it is better entirely to abstain from swearing, and held that one who swears unnecessarily is a sinner. The rabbis themselves swore, but they were understood to be in a position to assess whether the necessity genuinely warranted it. The ordinary person, by contrast, swore in houses, in the street, and in the market without discrimination.

### Rabbinical Regulation

Lieberman's central thesis is that the *kinuyim* in the *mishnah* are not purely rabbinic inventions — they are the product of a pre-existing popular practice that had already generated a welter of substitutes and near-substitutes for the formal vow words. People had been using these modified forms on their own, partly out of anxiety about invoking the sacred terms, partly simply out of the linguistic improvisation that characterizes popular speech. The rabbis' role was not to invent this vocabulary from scratch but to impose order on it — to determine which substitutes were close enough to the original to be genuinely binding, and which were so remote as to be meaningless. What looks like *lashon shebadu chachamim* may, in Lieberman's account, be better described as *lashon sheBireru lahem rishonim* — a language that earlier generations had selected and used, which the rabbis then ratified and regulated. The discussion of *kinuyei kinuyim* fits naturally into this picture: the masses had progressed from the reasonable substitute to the progressively more attenuated derivation, and the rabbis had to draw a line determining which level of derivation retained sufficient connection to the original to carry legal weight. The analogy to contemporary speech patterns is apt: just as certain expletives in English have spawned substitutes (*gosh*, *golly*, *gosh darn*) that everyone recognizes as proxies for the original — and which carry something of the original's social register — so too the *kinuyim* functioned in their cultural setting. The parallel also illuminates why the rabbis could not simply abolish the practice: it was too deeply embedded in the linguistic culture of the population. They could only regulate it.

---

## Sacred Objects

### Lachulin

The *mishnah* now turns to another category of vow language. *Ha-omer l'chulin she'ochel lach* — in Palestinian Aramaic, the prefix *la-* functions as a negation: *l'chulin* therefore means "not *chulin*" — not profane, not ordinary. And if something is declared not-*chulin*, the implication is that it is *kodesh*, sacred, like a *korban*. So the declaration *l'chulin she'ochel lach* — "what I eat of yours shall be un-profane" — functions as a *neder*, treating the object as though it were *hekdesh*.

### Kasher Terms

Similarly, *lo kasher* or *la'kasher* — "not kosher" or "un-kosher" — can function as vow language. *Lo dachi* and *lo tahor* — "not pure" — are parallel formulations. The *Ran*, based on the *Rambam*, understands that the correct reading of the *mishnah* is *la'tahor* for that final form as well, mirroring the pattern of the others.

### Tahor Terms

One might initially understand *lo kasher* and *lo tahor* as referring to ordinary ritual unfitness — like *chazir*, which is not *kasher*. But *chazir* is not a *davar hanadur*, not the sort of object one uses as a reference point for vowing. The *gemara* understands these terms as referring to forbidden states of a *korban* specifically — *notar* (leftover *korban* eaten beyond its permitted time), *pigul* (*korban* rendered invalid by improper intent), and *tamei* (a *korban* that has contracted ritual impurity). All of these are categories of forbidden consumption that belong to the world of *korbanos*, and are therefore legitimate *divrei hanadur*.

### Lechumra Principle

The *Ran* articulates the governing principle here explicitly. The case of *lo kasher* or *lo tahor* is one of genuine ambiguity: the speaker's words could be interpreted as referring to *chazir* or other ordinary forbidden foods, in which case no *neder* would be created; or they could be interpreted as referring to the forbidden states of *korbanos*, in which case a *neder* would be created. In cases of ambiguity — what we might call a *kinuy she'eino mochiach*, a *kinuy* whose reference is unclear — we go *lechumra*, we interpret strictly. This is distinct from a *yad she'eino mochiach*, where the issue is that a sentence is elliptical and we don't know what word to supply. Here the word is present but genuinely ambiguous between two meanings. And the principle of *stam nedarim le'hachmir* — that ambiguous vow language is interpreted stringently — dictates that we treat it as a *neder*.

### Sacred Objects

The *mishnah* then lists objects that, when invoked using the comparative *kaf* — like a sheep, like the pens for sheep, like wood, like fire-offerings, like the altar, like the *heichal*, like Jerusalem — constitute effective vow language. All of these belong to the world of *korbanos* and Temple service. One might have intended *imra* as someone's lamb, or the *etzim* as ordinary firewood; but these terms carry sufficient association with the Temple service that they are interpreted as *korban* references and treated accordingly.

### Kaf Necessity

The *Ran* raises the question: why does this latter group require the *kaf* — the word "like" — whereas *notar*, *pigul*, and *tamei* do not? His answer is illuminating. The words *notar*, *pigul*, and *tamei* are inherently defined by their forbidden status. The very identity of something as *notar* is inseparable from the fact that it is forbidden; the prohibitedness is constitutive of what *notar* means. Therefore, to say *harei zeh notar* is already to declare it forbidden — one does not need to say "let it be *like* notar" because the entire meaning of *notar* is its forbidden state. By contrast, Jerusalem or the altar or a sheep are not defined by being forbidden objects. A sheep is just a sheep. The altar is a holy place, but holiness is not the same as prohibition. Therefore, to make clear that one is invoking these objects as a *davar hanadur* — as the reference point for a vow — one must say *ke-imra*, *ke-mizbeach*, *ki-Yerushalayim*, making explicit through the *kaf* that one is declaring something to be forbidden *like* that object.

---

## Altar Appurtenances

### Mizbeach Items

The final *mishnah* of the daf states: if one takes a *neder* invoking any of the items that serve the altar — *meshamshei ha-mizbeach* — even if the word *korban* is not explicitly mentioned, *harei zeh nadar b'korban*, it is treated as a vow by a *korban*. The logic is that these items — the utensils, the vessels, all that directly serves the *mizbeach* — are so entirely bound up with the *korban* service that invoking them is effectively invoking the *korban* itself. They constitute a form of *kinuy* for *korban*, not because they are words that sound like *korban*, but because they are objects whose entire existence and identity is defined by their role in *korban*-service.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda enters with a dissenting opinion regarding Jerusalem specifically: *ha-omer Yerushalayim lo amar klum* — if one simply says "Jerusalem" without the *kaf*, it is meaningless. The question — whether the issue is the absence of the *kaf* in particular, or something more specific to Jerusalem as an object that does not qualify even with the *kaf* — will require further examination.

---

---

# Nedarim 11

## Kinnuyim Framework

### Kinnuyim Definition

The eleventh daf of Nedarim is brief in terms of raw text — as the lecturer observes, the entire daf amounts to only a handful of sentences — yet it demands close attention to the logic of vow-language. To orient ourselves, we return briefly to the *mishna* at the bottom of 10b, which introduces the category of *kinnuyim*. Unlike the concept of *yad*, which involves filling in a blank where part of a sentence has been left incomplete, *kinnuyim* operates differently: the sentence is formally complete, but we must determine what certain words mean — that is, what particular terms stand in for. The first category of *kinnuyim* explored earlier in the tractate involved phonetic variants of the word *konam* (*konas*, *konach*, and similar forms). Here we encounter a different type: words that are not variants of *konam* at all, but rather serve as stand-ins for the word *korban* itself.

### Mishna Categories

The *mishna* introduces the formula *ha'omer lachullin she'ochal lach* — "one who says: that which I eat of yours is *lachullin*." The word *lachullin* is a Palestinian Aramaic construction meaning "non-*chulin*," i.e., non-secular, and thus the statement is interpreted to mean that what he eats is *hekdesh*. The *mishna* continues: *lo kasher velo dachi* — "not *kasher*" or "not pure (*tahor*)" — noting that some have the variant reading *lo tahor*. These formulations are surprising: *kasher* and *tahor* are not inherently associated with *hekdesh*, and *tamei* does not exclusively describe *korban* status. Nevertheless, the principle of *stam nedarim l'hachmir* — that ambiguous vow-language is interpreted stringently — leads us to read these terms as invoking *korban* status. More directly, *tamei*, *notar*, and *pigul* are explicitly listed as forbidden formulas, since *notar* and *pigul* occur only in the context of *korbanot*, and even *tamei*, though applicable elsewhere, is understood here as invoking the *issur* status of a *korban*.

### Altar Associations

The *mishna* then lists a further set of expressions: *ke'imra* (like a sheep), *kedirim* (like the pens), *ke'etzim* (like the wood), *ke'ishim* (like the fires on the altar), *ke'mizbeach* (like the altar), *ke'heichal* (like the sanctuary), *ke'yerushalayim* (like Jerusalem). None of these objects is itself a *davar hanadur* in the primary sense — one does not vow the pens or Jerusalem itself — but all are associated with the *korbanot* and the *mizbeiach*, and thus the *mishna* rules that *neder be'achad mikol hameshamshim mizbeach*, a vow invoking any object that serves the altar, even without explicit mention of *korban*, constitutes a binding vow as if *korban* had been stated.

### Yerushalayim Debate

The *mishna* concludes with a named position: *Rabbi Yehudah omer ha'omer Yerushalayim lo amar klum* — Rabbi Yehudah holds that one who simply says "Yerushalayim" has said nothing of legal consequence. The question raised immediately is whether Rabbi Yehudah is rejecting the formula *ke'Yerushalayim* as well, or whether his objection is specifically to the bare form "Yerushalayim" without the comparative prefix *ke*. The *Gemara* will clarify this distinction in the discussion that follows.

---

## Miklal Lav Analysis

### Miklal Lav Assumption

The *Gemara* opens its analysis with the word *savruha* — "they assumed" — signaling a preliminary interpretation that may subsequently be revised. The working assumption is that *lachullin* operates via the principle of *miklal lav ata shomea hen*: from a negative statement one infers its positive counterpart. On this reading, saying "what I eat of yours is non-*chulin*" invokes, by logical inference, the positive status of *korban*, thereby rendering the food forbidden.

### Rabbi Meir Principle

The *Gemara* immediately raises a problem: if this is the mechanism, then whose position does the *mishna* reflect? If it is Rabbi Meir's, there is a difficulty — for Rabbi Meir explicitly rejects the principle of *miklal lav ata shomea hen*. The *Gemara* cites the relevant *mishna*: *Rabbi Meir omer kol tnai she'eino k'tnai B'nei Gad u'B'nei Reuven eino tnai* — any conditional stipulation not formulated like the condition of the tribes of Gad and Reuven is not a valid *tnai*.

### Bnei Gad Example

What was unique about the formulation in that episode? The Torah stated both sides of the condition explicitly: if they cross over with you, they will receive their inheritance on the eastern bank; and if they do not cross over, they will not receive it there. Rabbi Meir's position is that you cannot rely on one side of a conditional to imply the other. One might ask: is the Torah not simply being explicit about something logically obvious? Rabbi Meir's answer is precisely the opposite — the Torah states both sides *because* one side does not logically entail the other. The explicit statement of both halves demonstrates that without such explicit formulation, we may not infer the reverse.

### Rabbi Meir Logic

There are two distinct ways to understand Rabbi Meir's position. The first is that this is fundamentally a requirement of *speech acts*: regardless of what is logically deducible, the rules governing *tnai* or *neder* require that both sides be explicitly articulated. Perhaps in ordinary matters of intent (*da'as*) an implicit understanding would suffice, but a *tnai* is not merely a question of subjective intent. A *tnai* is an artificial legal mechanism — distinct from a case where someone simply never would have entered an agreement under certain circumstances — and such a mechanism demands precise verbal formulation. Similarly with *nedarim*: it is not what is in one's mind that counts, but what one actually said. The second way to understand Rabbi Meir goes further: he may be making a claim about logic itself.

### Propositional Logic

Anyone familiar with basic propositional logic will recognize that "if P then Q" does not entail "if not P then not Q." If it rains I will give you ten dollars — but even if it doesn't rain, perhaps I will still give you ten dollars. The only valid inference from "if P then Q" is "if not Q then not P." Thus, saying that if the tribes cross over they will receive their inheritance in *Ever HaYarden* does not logically imply that if they do not cross over they will forfeit it. There may be other grounds on which they would receive or not receive. On this reading, Rabbi Meir's objection is not merely procedural but substantive: the reverse proposition is simply not derivable from the original statement, and therefore one who says only "if P then Q" has not legally committed to "if not P then not Q." Applied to *nedarim*: saying "the food I would eat of yours is *chulin*" does not logically entail that the food is *korban*, since "not *chulin*" does not necessarily mean *korban* by logical necessity alone.

---

## Yad vs. Kinnuy

### Mishnah Attribution

Given that the *Gemara* has established that if *lachullin* works through *miklal lav*, the *mishna* cannot reflect Rabbi Meir's position, the *Gemara* initially suggests the *mishna* must follow Rabbi Yehudah — who does accept *miklal lav ata shomea hen*. But this creates a new problem: the *mishna* concludes with Rabbi Yehudah's own distinct ruling (*Rabbi Yehudah omer ha'omer Yerushalayim lo amar klum*), which implies that the rest of the *mishna* is not Rabbi Yehudah. Citing the end of the *mishna* as Rabbi Yehudah necessarily implies the beginning is not — a standard Talmudic inference (*mideseifa Rabbi Yehudah, reisha lav Rabbi Yehudah*).

### Tosafot Rid Position

This is precisely where the *Tosafot Rid* enters with a far-reaching observation. The initial assumption of the *Gemara* — the *savruha* — that *lachullin* works via *miklal lav* is, according to the *Tosafot Rid*, fundamentally mistaken, and this is the very assumption the *Gemara* ultimately rejects (though the exact point of rejection is debated). The *Tosafot Rid* argues that saying "this object is *lachullin*" is not a conditional inference at all. It is a direct description: the word *lachullin* is simply a synonym, or *kinnuy*, for *hekdesh*. If I say "you are impure," I am not inferring anything — I am saying you are *tamei*. The word "impure" means *tamei*; it does not mean "not pure" in the sense of a logical negation from which the positive must be inferred. Similarly, *lachullin* — non-*chulin* — simply means *korban*, and this has nothing to do with Rabbi Meir's principle.

### Yad Kinnuy Distinction

This analysis illuminates a deeper distinction: the difference between *yad* and *kinnuy*.
