A *yad* arises when a sentence is grammatically incomplete and something must be supplied to fill a blank; it is a kind of literary ellipsis. A *kinnuy* arises when the sentence is formally complete but a particular word requires interpretation — we must determine what that word stands for. When the *mishna* lists *tamei*, *notar*, *pigul*, *ke'imra*, *ke'mizbeach*, and *ke'Yerushalayim*, it is plainly operating in the register of *kinnuy*: each of these is a stand-in word for *korban*. Similarly, *lachullin* is a stand-in for *korban*. The person uttered a full sentence; the task is to decode what the word means.

This is why it is, in truth, strange that the *Gemara* introduced *miklal lav ata shomea hen* at all in this context — it is a principle about conditional propositions, not about vocabulary. If I call something "like the pen of sheep" (*kedirim*), I am not making a conditional statement; I am naming the object with a certain term. We do not say this involves *miklal lav*. The same logic applies to *lachullin*. The *savruha* imported a logical framework that does not naturally fit the category of *kinnuyim*, and the *Tosafot Rid* argues this is precisely what must be abandoned as the *sugya* proceeds.

### Ran's Categories

The *Ran* offers a complementary analysis that explains another structural feature of the *mishna*: why some *kinnuyim* require the prefix *ke* (like) and others do not. His answer concerns what each expression is actually doing linguistically. Terms like *tamei*, *notar*, and *pigul* foreground the *issur* status of the object itself — they describe it as having the identity of a forbidden *korban* substance. These terms highlight the halachic character of the thing being vowed, making the sentence meaningful without any comparative prefix.

### Ki Necessity

By contrast, when one says "this is *mizbeach*" or "this is Yerushalayim," those expressions do not themselves identify the object as a *davar assur*. If I say "this loaf of bread is the *mizbeiach*," the sentence is meaningless — bread is obviously not the altar. But if I say "this bread is *ke'mizbeiach*" — like the altar — I am drawing an associative comparison: I am relating this bread to the concept of things brought on the *mizbeiach*, and within that conceptual framework the bread acquires the status of a *davar hanadur*. The *ke* prefix creates the necessary semantic bridge. Without it, when the reference object is something like Yerushalayim or a sheep-pen, the statement is simply incoherent as a vow. This is exactly what Rabbi Yehudah is saying when he rules that *Yerushalayim* alone — without the *ke* — is ineffective: the bare word creates no meaningful associative link.

---

## Ki Yerushalayim

### Mishnah Attribution

With this framework in place, the *Gemara* resolves the authorship question by asserting *kulah Rabbi Yehudah hi* — the entire *mishna* is Rabbi Yehudah's position. Rabbi Yehudah is not arguing with the body of the *mishna*; he is adding a specification to it.

### Yerushalayim Distinction

Specifically, Rabbi Yehudah draws a line between *ke'Yerushalayim* and bare *Yerushalayim*. The earlier portion of the *mishna*, which lists *ke'Yerushalayim* among the valid *kinnuyim*, is Rabbi Yehudah's own ruling — *ke'Yerushalayim* works. What Rabbi Yehudah then adds, in the clause attributed to him, is that *Yerushalayim* without the *ke* does not work.

### Yerushalayim Scope

The reason is not arbitrary. *Ke'Yerushalayim* works because it directs the listener toward Yerushalayim's identity as the site of *korbanot* — the comparative form channels the association toward the *Beis HaMikdash* and the sacrificial service. But the bare word *Yerushalayim* encompasses an enormous range of things: the Knesset, museums, the Biblical Zoo, countless institutions and objects that have no connection to *korbanot* whatsoever. Without the *ke* to focus the comparison, saying "Yerushalayim" does not reliably invoke *korban* identity, and the vow is therefore without legal effect.

---

## Ki Yerushalayim (II)

### Braita Strictness

The *Gemara* then introduces a *braita* which presents an even stricter position: *Rabbi Yehudah omer ha'omer ki'Yerushalayim lo amar klum* — even *ke'Yerushalayim* is ineffective — *ad sheyidor bidvar hakorev biYerushalayim*, unless one explicitly vows by something actually offered in Yerushalayim. Even the comparative prefix does not suffice when the reference point is Yerushalayim itself, which remains too diffuse. The *Gemara* resolves the tension between this *braita* and the *mishna* by invoking *trei tanna'ei aliba d'Rabbi Yehudah* — there are two distinct traditions within Rabbi Yehudah's school, one of which holds that *ke'Yerushalayim* suffices and one that does not.

---

## Conditional Phrasing

### Permissible Formulas

The *Gemara* now turns to a *braita* that analyzes several formulations involving the word *chulin* itself. The *braita* rules that *chulin*, *hachulin*, and *kachulin* — whether one says "secular," "the secular," or "like the secular" — are all non-binding formulations. And this applies whether the person says *she'ochal lach* (that which I eat of yours is *chulin*) or *shelo ochal lach* (that which I do not eat of yours is *chulin*). These formulas are *mutar*.

### Forbidden Formula

By contrast, the *braita* rules that *lachullin she'ochal lach* — the food I eat of yours is *lachullin* — is *assur*. Here the prefix *la* transforms the word: *lachullin* means non-*chulin*, i.e., *korban*, and declaring one's food to be *lachullin* is therefore equivalent to declaring it *hekdesh*.

### Tosafot Rid Reversal

It is here that the *Tosafot Rid* locates the reversal of the *Gemara*'s opening assumption. The *braita* clearly demonstrates that *lachullin* is simply a word meaning *hekdesh* — a definitional synonym, not a logical inference. Even Rabbi Meir, who rejects *miklal lav ata shomea hen*, can accept that *lachullin* renders the food forbidden, because no conditional reasoning is involved. The word *lachullin* directly names the object as *korban*, just as the word "impure" directly names something as *tamei* without requiring any inferential step. The *Tosafot Rid* concludes that the *mishna* can therefore reflect Rabbi Meir's position after all, and the *savruha* at the top of 11a should be entirely abandoned. For completeness: other *rishonim* who do not accept the *Tosafot Rid*'s approach resort to more strained readings — one excises the problematic phrase from the text entirely, and the *Ra'avad* eliminates the *vav* and reads the formula as *le-challin*, i.e., *challot todah* (loaves of the thanksgiving offering), an interpretation the lecturer candidly characterizes as extremely forced.

### Conditional vs. Direct

The *Gemara*'s structure at this point becomes clearer when we attend to the precise mechanism at work in each formula. The cases of *chulin lo ochal lach* and *shelo ochal lach* that are ruled *mutar* both involve a kind of conditional or inferential structure: "your non-food is *chulin*" might seem to imply, via *miklal lav*, that your food is *korban* — but Rabbi Meir's principle blocks that inference, and therefore those formulas are *mutar*. By contrast, *lachullin she'ochal lach* is not a conditional statement at all. It directly describes the food as non-*chulin*, and non-*chulin* simply is *korban*. No inference is required or invoked.

### Permitted Formula

The third formula in the *braita* — *lachullin lo ochal lach*, "that which I will not eat of yours is *lachullin*" — is ruled *mutar*. Why? Because even granting that *lachullin* means *korban*, the person has not declared any specific food to be forbidden. They have said that the things they do not eat are *lachullin* — but this does not render the food in front of them *assur*. The statement does not focus on the *davar hanadur* in any meaningful sense; at most it refers abstractly to non-food objects or to the act of non-eating, neither of which constitutes a binding *neder*. The *Gemara* eventually clarifies, via the analysis of *she-ani* versus *she-eini*, that a valid *lashon neder* must attach to the object itself, not to the speaker's action.

---

## Le-Korban Strategy

### Le-Korban Mishna

The *Gemara* now introduces a later *mishna* presenting a parallel case: *le-korban lo ochal lach* — "that which I will not eat of yours is *le-korban*" — and records that Rabbi Meir rules this *assur*. This is initially puzzling. If Rabbi Meir rejects *miklal lav ata shomea hen*, why should declaring one's non-food to be *le-korban* render anything forbidden? The apparent reasoning would be: "my non-food is *korban*," therefore "my food is not *korban*" — but that is precisely the inference Rabbi Meir claims cannot be drawn.

### Rav Abba Reinterpretation

The *Gemara* resolves this through Rav Abba's reading: *na'aseh k'omer le-korban yehei, lefikhach lo ochal lach* — we interpret the person as having said "let it be a *korban*; therefore I will not eat it." On this reading, *le-korban* is parsed as *lekorban* — it should become a *korban* — and *lo ochal lach* is a natural consequence: since it is now a *korban*, I will not eat it. This is standard *konam* language: the speaker declares the object a *korban* and states the practical upshot. There is no *miklal lav* involved; the person simply said *konam* by another route, and even Rabbi Meir accepts this.

### Parallel Question

The *Gemara* then asks the obvious parallel question: if *lachullin* means *korban*, then *lachullin lo ochal lach* should be identical to *le-korban lo ochal lach*. Why, then, does the *braita* rule *lachullin lo ochal lach* as *mutar*? We should be able to apply the same parsing strategy — "it is *lachullin* (i.e., a *korban*), therefore I will not eat it" — and rule it *assur*.

### Braita Author Position

The *Gemara* answers with a principle of partial agreement: *hai tanna savar lah ke-Rabbi Meir b'chada u'palig leh b'chada* — the author of this *braita* agrees with Rabbi Meir in one respect but disagrees in another. The *braita* follows Rabbi Meir in rejecting *miklal lav ata shomea hen* — that is the basis for ruling the *chulin lo ochal lach* formulas *mutar*. But the *braita* does not follow the reading of the later *mishna* in which we parse the sentence as "it is a *korban*, therefore I will not eat it." Without that interpretive move, *le-korban lo ochal lach* would simply mean "my non-food is a *korban*," which says nothing about the food in front of the person and therefore carries no binding force.

### Abstract Concept

With this established, the *Gemara* can explain why *lachullin lo ochal lach* is *mutar* for this *tanna*. The sentence, read straightforwardly and without the "therefore" parsing, declares that the things one does not eat are *lachullin* — i.e., *korban*. But this refers to no concrete food object. The statement is, in effect, abstract — it either refers to non-food items or to the concept of non-eating, neither of which constitutes a *davar hanadur* with any practical force. Since a valid *neder* must attach to a real object that one would otherwise eat, this formula leaves all food *mutar*.

---

## She-Ani Debate

### Scope Examples

A practical illustration helps clarify the underlying principle. One cannot make one's computer or one's car forbidden through the language of *nedarim*, because these are not foods — there is no relationship of eating to be governed. The language of a *neder* must address an object that is in the domain of eating, not arbitrary items in the world.

### She-Ani Formula

This is why the classic formulation is *konam she-ani ochal lach* — "that which I would eat of yours is *konam*." The focus is on the food object: those things I would ordinarily eat are hereby declared *korban*. The second half of the statement ("therefore I will not eat") is not the *neder* itself but a natural description of its consequence. The *neder* is in the first clause, where the object is identified and its status declared.

### Object Focus

The principle that emerges is that *lashon neder* must focus on the object, not on the speaker's action. A *neder* is not a *shevuah*. A *shevuah* binds the person — "I swear I will not eat." A *neder* binds the object — "this food is *hekdesh* to me." If the language points to the speaker's action rather than to the object's status, it may constitute *lashon shevuah* at most, but it does not qualify as a *neder* in the technical sense.

### She-Eini Question

This principle generates a significant dispute among the *rishonim* concerning two variants of the same formula. *Konam she-ani ochal lach* — "that which I eat of yours is *konam*" — clearly refers to the food object, and is unambiguously a valid *neder*. But what of *konam she-eini ochal lach* — "that which I do not eat of yours is *konam*"? There is a *machloket rishonim* on this question. On one reading, this can still be parsed as "it is *konam*, therefore I will not eat it" — the *she-eini* being the consequence rather than the subject. On another reading, *she-eini ochal lach* is fundamentally a statement about what the speaker will do, not about what the object is, and therefore it does not constitute proper *lashon neder*. This maps directly onto the tension in the *Gemara* between the formula ruled *assur* in the later *mishna* (which requires the sentence-splitting interpretation) and the formula ruled *mutar* in the *braita* (which refuses to split the sentence and therefore reads everything as referring abstractly to the act of non-eating rather than to the food itself).

---

## Korban Statuses

### Status List

The *Gemara* now opens a new section of the *mishna*: *tahor v'tamai notar u'pigul assur* — one who declares food to be like that which is *tahor*, *tamei*, *notar*, or *pigul* has made a binding vow. The question is what, precisely, is being invoked by each of these terms.

### Shelamim Analogy

Rami bar Chama poses a pointed question: what is the status of one who says *harei alai ke-vasar zivchei shelamim le-achar zerikat damim* — "this [bread] should be upon me like the meat of *shelamim* offerings after the blood has been thrown"? The complication is that at the moment of the statement, the meat in question is in its permitted state — it is the very meat one is currently eating. Does this formulation function as a valid *kinnuy* for *korban*?

### Permitted State

The *Gemara* first clarifies the question. If the person explicitly stated the full formula — "like *shelamim* meat after blood-throwing" — they have clearly referenced the meat in its *mutar* state. Grabbing onto something in its permitted condition (*be-heteira kamatpis*) seems problematic as a basis for a *neder*: you have named a *davar hanadur* that is currently *mutar*, and a *davar hanadur* should be an object in a state of *issur*.

### Live Example

The *Gemara* therefore refines the scenario: imagine that someone is actively eating *shelamim* meat — the blood has been thrown, the meat is permitted, and the person is mid-meal — and another individual comes and places a piece of bread nearby, saying *ze ke-ze*: "this bread should be like this meat." What is the halachic status of the bread?

### Status Identity

This generates the *Gemara*'s central question: *be-ikaro kamatpis o be-heiter kamatpis* — is the person "grabbing onto" the original identity of the meat (as a *korban shelamim* prior to *zerikat damim*, when it was *assur*), or are they grabbing onto its current permitted status? The concept of *matpis* — latching the *neder* onto a pre-existing identified object to define the status of a new one — is crucial here. If the speaker intends to invoke the original *korban* identity of the meat, then this is a valid *kinnuy*: the bread is being declared like a *korban*, and the *neder* is binding. If the speaker is relating to the meat as it currently stands — a *mutar* food — then there is no *davar hanadur* with *issur* status onto which the *neder* can be anchored, and the *neder* would be ineffective. This question — whether *be-ikaro kamatpis* or *be-heiter kamatpis* — is left unresolved as the daf concludes, a fitting cliffhanger for a section whose every sentence proves inexhaustible.

---

---

# Nedarim 12

## B'Ikaro vs. B'Hashta

### Shelamim After Blood

The *daf* opens by picking up from the bottom of 11b, where Rami bar Chama poses a question about a case in which someone says: "This should be forbidden to me like the meat of a *shelamim* after *zrikat hadam*." The Gemara immediately objects: after *zrikat hadam*, a *shelamim* is permissible to be eaten — so the speaker has explicitly invoked something that is not in a forbidden state, making the question moot. The Gemara therefore reformulates the case. The man has before him a piece of *shelamim* meat after the blood has been sprinkled — he is in fact eating from it — and he gestures at a loaf of bread and says *zeh kazeh*, "this is like this." The question is: when he says "this," to what status of the *shelamim* is he referring?

Two possibilities present themselves. Either he refers to the object's current state (*b'hashta kamatpis*), in which case the *shelamim* meat is presently permitted and therefore not a *davar hanadur* in a forbidden sense, and the *neder* would have no effect. Or, he refers to the object's original state (*b'ikaro kamatpis*) — meaning the moment he originally sanctified the animal as a *shelamim*, when it was indeed a *davar hanadur* in a fully forbidden state — in which case the *neder* would take effect.

### Notar & Pigul

Rava responds: come and hear. Our *Mishnah* lists *notar* and *pigul* as valid objects of *matpis b'davar hanadur*. The *Mishnah* states that one may declare "behold this is like *notar*" or "behold this is like *pigul*," and this constitutes an effective *neder*. Crucially, both *notar* and *pigul* arise only *after zrikat hadam*. *Notar* is meat from a *korban* that was permitted for eating during the designated time, but which the owner left past the deadline; it is now forbidden by the Torah as *notar*, a prohibition entirely distinct from the original *neder*. The *pigul* prohibition — arising from an improper thought (*machshava*) during the *shechita* or *zrika* — conceptually precedes the *zrika* even if it is identified *l'achar zrikat hadam*, since the disqualifying *machshava* prevents the *zrika* from ever rendering the meat permitted. The *rishonim* therefore either excise *pigul* from the proof or treat it as *lav davka*, taking the operative case to be *notar*.

The significance of *notar* is this: during the period when the meat was permitted, the *neder* was not operative upon it — it was *mutar*. The *issur notar* that now applies to it is not a product of the original *neder*; rather, it is a distinct Torah prohibition comparable to *basar b'chalav*. As such, in its current state, the *shelamim* meat that became *notar* is a *davar ha'assur*, not a *davar hanadur*. Yet the *Mishnah* treats "behold this is like *notar*" as an effective *neder*. This implies that when one says "*zeh kazeh*," he is understood as referring back to the object's original state as *shelamim* — *b'ikaro kamatpis* — when it was indeed a fully operative *davar hanadur*. The word "*notar*" identifies the object; what the speaker intends is the status it held before it became permitted.

One might ask: why does the nature of *pigul* matter here? *Pigul* is indeed a function of *machshava* — the wrong intention at the time of the sacrificial act distorts the status of the offering, rendering it perpetually forbidden. The *rishonim* note that since *pigul* never passed through a state of being *mutar*, it is in a different category from *notar*, and the *Mishnah*'s mention of it alongside *notar* is not essential to the question of *b'ikaro* versus *b'hashta*.

### Notar Shel Olah

Rav Huna bei d'Rav Nasan objects to the proof from *notar*: perhaps the *Mishnah* is specifically discussing *notar shel olah*. An *olah* is never eaten by anyone — even after *zrikat hadam* it remains entirely forbidden to lay persons, and that prohibition is a direct consequence of the *neder* by which it was sanctified. Thus *notar shel olah* never passes through a stage of being permitted; it remains a *davar hanadur* in its forbidden state at all times. If so, one could invoke *notar shel olah* in its current state and still be *matpis b'davar hanadur* without needing to go back to an earlier status at all. This would mean the *Mishnah* offers no proof for *b'ikaro kamatpis* — it might be entirely consistent with *b'hashta kamatpis*, so long as there exists some scenario in which the word "*notar*" describes an object currently forbidden as a *davar hanadur*.

Furthermore, the principle of *stam nedarim l'hachmir* — that an ambiguous *neder* is interpreted stringently — would lead us to read a bare utterance of "behold this is like *notar*" as referring to *notar shel olah*, the stricter category, rather than to *notar shel shelamim*, the lenient one. If, however, the speaker specified "behold this is like *notar shel shelamim*," we would interpret his words according to the current state of the object, which is no longer forbidden as a *davar hanadur*, and the *neder* would not take effect.

### Why Call It Notar?

The Gemara raises a pointed question against this reading: if the concern is the *olah* category, why say "*notar shel olah*" at all? Why not simply say "*basar olah*" — the meat of an *olah*? There is no question that "behold this is like an *olah*" constitutes *matpis b'davar hanadur*; the animal is sanctified through your speech act and is entirely forbidden. What is added by labeling it as *notar*?

### Resolution on Olah

The Gemara answers: *lo mibaya ka'amar* — it goes without saying that "behold this is like an *olah*" is forbidden, since you are explicitly being *matpis b'korban*, invoking a straightforwardly forbidden *davar hanadur*. The *chiddush* is precisely the case of "*notar* of an *olah*." One might have thought that by saying "*notar*," the speaker emphasizes the *issur notar* dimension of the object rather than its *korban* dimension — and the *issur notar* is not a *davar hanadur* but a *davar ha'assur* — and therefore the *neder* should not take effect. The Gemara teaches us that this is not so: since the object is still an *olah*, since it never passed through a stage of being permitted, the invocation of its *notar* status merely emphasizes a layer of its *issur*, but the speaker is understood as being *matpis* in its *davar hanadur* dimension.

The analogy is instructive. If one were to say "behold this is like *basar b'chalav* of an *olah*," one would clearly be invoking the *basar b'chalav* prohibition — a *davar ha'assur* — and the *neder* would not take effect even though the underlying object is an *olah*. By contrast, "*notar shel olah*" is so deeply intertwined with the *korban* identity of the *olah* that we read it as invoking the *davar hanadur* status. Whether this analysis applies only when the speaker explicitly says "*notar shel olah*," or whether a bare statement of "*notar*" triggers *stam nedarim l'hachmir* to read it as *notar shel olah*, remains a point worth considering, though the Gemara does not resolve this definitively.

The broader interpretive question underlying all of this concerns how we determine what a speaker meant by his words. The answer, as this tractate makes clear throughout, is that it does not primarily matter what the speaker privately intended — it matters what the words objectively mean. A *neder* requires not merely intent but the correct verbal formulation, and even the speaker himself is bound by the meaning of his words as assessed by *halacha*, not by whatever he may have privately meant. If a statement has multiple possible meanings, the task is to determine which *halachic* meaning the words carry — and *stam nedarim l'hachmir* is the operative principle for resolving ambiguity. This is why, in many of these cases, we do not simply ask the speaker; even if we did, the answer could not override the *halachic* reading of what was said.

## Taanit & Yahrtzeit

### Meat & Wine Neder

The Gemara now introduces a *Mishnah* that brings a different kind of case to bear on the question of *b'ikaro* versus *b'hashta*. The *Mishnah* describes a person who says: "Behold I am [forbidden from eating] meat and drinking wine like the day on which my father died" (*k'yom shemeis bo aviv*), or like the day his *rebbe* died, or like the day Gedaliah ben Achikam was killed, or like the day he visited Yerushalayim and saw it in its destruction. The practice of accepting a *ta'anis* or forms of self-denial on a *yahrtzeit* is thus attested as a phenomenon going back to the earliest layers of the tradition.

This case introduces a conceptual abstraction. Whereas in the *shelamim* case the *davar hanadur* was a piece of meat, here the object of the *neder* appears to be a *day*. The model seems to parallel the case of *tzedakah*: just as money set aside for *tzedakah* acquires the status of a *davar hanadur*, and just as bread can become a *davar hanadur* through a declaration of *konam*, so too a day can be given a status of *ta'anis* through the spoken acceptance. The day itself becomes, in a sense, the *davar hanadur*. Five years ago, the man declared that a particular day — his father's *yahrtzeit*, or *Tzom Gedaliah* — was *assur alav* for eating meat and wine. That day thereby became a *davar hanadur*. Now, five years later, he says: "This [day] is like that day." He is being *matpis* in the *davar hanadur* of the earlier day.

### Shmuel's Explanation

Shmuel clarifies the *Mishnah*: *v'hu shenadar u'va m'oso hayom v'eilach* — the case is specifically one where he has been making this *neder* continuously from that original day forward. It is not that there was a single *neder* five years ago with four intervening years of non-*neder* status; rather, every year since his father's death he has accepted the same *neder* upon himself. Thus when he says on the current *yahrtzeit* "this is like my father's *yahrtzeit*," every instantiation of that day — including the most recent ones — carries the status of *davar hanadur*, and there is no ambiguity about which day he is invoking.

### Proof from Years

One might attempt to read the *Mishnah* as a proof for *b'ikaro kamatpis*: even if there were four intervening years in which the day passed without a *neder*, the speaker is still understood as invoking the *neder* status of the original day five years ago, going back past four years of *mutar* instantiations. The Gemara rejects this reading in light of Shmuel's clarification. Since Shmuel requires that the *neder* be ongoing — *shenadar u'va m'oso hayom v'eilach* — every year has been a *davar hanadur*, and there is no scenario in the *Mishnah* where the speaker is reaching back past years of *heter*. The *Mishnah* therefore offers no proof for *b'ikaro kamatpis*; it is perfectly consistent with *b'hashta kamatpis*, since in its current and ongoing state the day is a *davar hanadur*.

The conceptual elegance here is striking. The day of a *yahrtzeit* or *Tzom Gedaliah* cycles back each year as the same day with a potentially new or renewed status. When one says "this day is like that day," the question is which instantiation of the day one is invoking — the original *neder*-bearing instance, an intermediate *mutar* instance, or the most recent one. Shmuel's ruling forecloses the ambiguity by requiring that all instantiations share the same *davar hanadur* status.

### Neder on Prohibited

The Ran discusses what the *chiddush* of the *Mishnah* actually is, if the *Mishnah* presents no proof for or against *b'ikaro kamatpis*. The Gemara in *Shevuos* addresses this same passage and identifies the *chiddush* as follows: one might have thought that since *Tzom Gedaliah* is already *assur m'drabanan*, a *neder* accepted upon that day would not take effect — *ki nadar nami lo chayil neder*. Perhaps a *neder* cannot take hold on something already forbidden. The *Mishnah* teaches us that this is not so: even when a day is already forbidden by rabbinic enactment, a *neder* accepted upon that day does take effect. The person then bears both the rabbinic prohibition and the *neder* prohibition.

### Kraft Cheese Example

The Ran illustrates this with a practical example. If someone says "*neder konam* all [non-Jewish cheese] upon me" — even though such cheese is already *assur m'drabanan* — the *neder* takes effect and adds an additional layer of prohibition. One who thereafter eats such cheese violates not only the rabbinic prohibition but also his own *neder*. Consequently, if this same person were then to take a piece of permitted cheese and say "*harei zo* like [that non-Jewish cheese]," he would be *matpis b'davar hanadur* — piggybacking on the *neder* he had placed upon the first cheese — and the permitted cheese would also become forbidden. The Ran states explicitly: *v'hitpiso bahen d'matpis b'neder havei v'assur* — the *matpis* act upon something already *assur d'rabbanan* is effective, and a subsequent *zeh kazeh* on the *neder*-bearing object also takes effect.

## Teruma & Todah

### Teruma Permissible

The Gemara cites a further case from the *Mishnah*: *k'chalas Aharon u'k'trumaso mutar* — if one says "behold this is forbidden to me like the *challah* given to the *kohanim*" or like *teruma* given to the *kohanim*, it is *mutar*. Even though *teruma* is a *davar hanadur* — it acquires its status through the verbal act of separation — it is not fully *assur* to all people; *kohanim* may eat it freely. Since *teruma* does not carry an absolute prohibition flowing from the *neder*, it cannot serve as an effective anchor for *matpis b'davar hanadur*. For *matpis b'davar hanadur* to work, the *davar hanadur* must also be something that is fully *assur*. The Ran notes the distinction: a *davar ha'assur* does not take effect as an anchor for *matpis* because its prohibition is not *neder*-derived; a *davar hanadur* that is only partially forbidden likewise fails to serve as an anchor. Both aspects — *nadur* and *assur* — must be fully present.

### Lachmei Todah

The *Mishnah* then continues: *ha k'trumas lachmei todah assur* — if, however, one says "behold this is like the *terumah* of *lachmei todah*," it is *assur*. The *terumas lachmei todah* is the loaf separated from the forty loaves brought as a *todah* offering. Someone who brings a *todah* brings forty loaves: thirty *matzah* of three different types, and ten *chametz*. From each group of ten, one loaf is given to the *kohen* — this separated portion is called *terumas lachmei todah* and carries a status analogous to *teruma*, restricted to *kohanim*.

The *todah* offering presents a case directly analogous to the *shelamim* after *zrikat hadam*: by the time the *terumas lachmei todah* is separated and given to the *kohen*, the blood has already been sprinkled and the bread is now permitted to *kohanim*. It is no longer in a forbidden state. Yet the *Mishnah* rules that invoking *terumas lachmei todah* renders the *neder* effective — apparently because we look back to its earlier status, before *zrikat hadam*, when it bore the *kedushah* of a *korban* and would have involved *me'ilah* to eat. This seems to be a proof for *b'ikaro kamatpis*: we attribute the object's earlier forbidden status to the invocation, even though its current status is permitted.

### Separation Details

The Gemara raises a complication: is *terumas lachmei todah* truly always only found after *zrikat hadam*? In fact, it is possible to separate the *terumah* from the loaves before the blood is sprinkled. Moreover, the Gemara introduces an even more exotic scenario through a teaching of Rabbi Tuvi bar Kisna in the name of Shmuel. If someone baked his forty loaves as four enormous loaves — one of each of the four types, each the size of ten — he has fulfilled his obligation (*yatza*), though this is only a *lechatchila* deficiency, since the Torah specifies forty. However, the practical problem now arises: how does one separate the *terumas lachmei todah*? One cannot take one of the four gigantic loaves as the *terumah* for all the others, since *one must take one from each type separately* and may not substitute one type for another. Nor can one break off a partial loaf (*prusa*), since the requirement is for a whole unit.

The only solution is *d'aphrashinhu b'lisha* — one separates the dough designated as *terumah* while still kneading it. One takes a portion of the *chametz* dough and sets it aside, and similarly for each of the three *matzah* types — the *chalot*, the *rekikin*, and the *revucha*. The remaining dough of each type is then combined into a single large loaf. This demonstrates that it is possible — if unusual — for *terumas lachmei todah* to be separated before *zrikat hadam*, even at the stage of raw dough.

### B'Hashta Interpretation

The Gemara therefore reinterprets the *Mishnah*'s ruling on *terumas lachmei todah*. Rather than a proof for *b'ikaro kamatpis*, the case can be explained as *b'hashta kamatpis* applied with maximal stringency. When one says "behold this is like *terumas lachmei todah*," we interpret the words as invoking *terumas lachmei todah* in its current status as a *davar hanadur* — meaning the unusual but extant scenario of *terumas lachmei todah lif'nei zrikat hadam*, dough-stage *terumah* separated before the blood has been sprinkled. Just as the bare invocation of "*notar*" is read stringently as *notar shel olah* — because that is a scenario in which *notar* is currently a *davar hanadur* — so too *terumas lachmei todah* is read as the case in which the *terumah* is currently forbidden, namely the pre-*zrikat hadam* scenario. We are prepared, under *stam nedarim l'hachmir*, to find a reading of the speaker's words that places the object in a *currently* forbidden state as a *davar hanadur*, even if that scenario is unusual. What we may not be prepared to do is attribute to the speaker a reference to an *earlier* status that no longer obtains at all. The question of whether *b'ikaro kamatpis* is ever operative thus remains open, and the Gemara has not yet provided a conclusive proof for it.

## Bechor Debate

### Bechor Dispute

The Gemara now raises a *tannaitic* dispute that may directly bear on the question. Rabbi Yaakov holds that saying "behold this is forbidden to me like a *bechor*" is *assur*, while Rabbi Yehuda holds it is *mutar*. The central question is whether a *bechor* qualifies as a *davar hanadur*.

### Bechor After Blood

The Gemara asks: what exactly is the case? If the reference is to a *bechor* before *zrikat hadam* — while the animal is still alive and walking — why would Rabbi Yehuda permit? At that stage the *bechor* is a *korban* before *zrikat hadam* and seems fully forbidden. And if the reference is to after *zrikat hadam*, when the *bechor* has been slaughtered and its blood sprinkled and its meat is now permitted — why would Rabbi Yaakov forbid? The Gemara concludes that the case must be like the *shelamim* case: the meat of a *bechor* after *zrikat hadam* is lying in front of the person, along with some other permitted food, and he says "*zeh kazeh*" — this permitted food is like this *bechor* meat. The dispute thus maps precisely onto the question of *b'ikaro* versus *b'hashta*.

### Davar Ha'Assur View

Rabbi Yehuda's permitting opinion rests on a fundamental claim about the nature of *bechor*: a *bechor* is a *davar ha'assur*, not a *davar hanadur*. The Torah requires invoking a *davar hanadur* for *matpis* to be effective (*ki yiddor neder*, the principle being that one must be *matpis b'davar hanadur*), and a *bechor* does not qualify because it does not derive its *kedushah* from your verbal act. A *bechor* is *kadosh* from the moment of birth — *kadosh mei-imei imo* — without any declaration on your part. Its sanctity is inherent and automatic, not the product of a *neder*. Therefore invoking "behold this is like a *bechor*" is *matpis b'davar ha'assur*, which does not take effect.

### Sanctification View

Rabbi Yaakov's forbidding opinion does not deny that a *bechor* is *kadosh* from birth, but argues that a *bechor* is nonetheless a *davar hanadur* because there is a *mitzvah* to sanctify it. A *baraisa* teaches in the name of Rebbi: from where do we know that one born with a *bechor* in his house has a *mitzvah* to be *makdish* it? From the *pasuk* *hazachar takdish* — "you shall sanctify the male." Even though the animal is already *kadosh*, there is an obligation to add one's own verbal *hakdasha* to it. This means that a *bechor* also carries a *neder*-derived dimension of *kedushah*, and therefore it falls within the category of *davar hanadur*.

### Sanctity Discussion

Rabbi Yehuda's response to this argument is telling: *ki lo makdish leh mi lo mikdash* — even if one never sanctifies it, is it not already sanctified? The *mitzvah* of *takdish* is real, but its non-performance does not deprive the *bechor* of its *kedushah*. The fundamental identity of the *bechor* as a *korban* is not contingent on your words — it is inherent from birth. Whatever *kedushah* you add through your verbal sanctification is supplementary, not constitutive. The *bechor*'s basic identity is therefore that of a *davar ha'assur*, not a *davar hanadur*, and invoking it does not create an effective *neder*.

Rabbi Yaakov, for his part, could respond that even if the *bechor*'s inherent *kedushah* persists without your declaration, the fact that one's words *do* add a genuine dimension of *kedushah* is sufficient to classify it as a *davar hanadur* for purposes of *matpis*. The added human *kedushah* is not merely declaratory; it is real, and this reality places the *bechor* in the *neder* category. The rebuttal, however, is that this added dimension is not the central or essential identity of the *bechor* as a *korban* — and it is therefore insufficient to transform it from a fundamentally *ha'assur* object into a fundamentally *hanadur* one.

This distinction — between inherent sanctity and added sanctity, between *kedushah* that exists independently and *kedushah* that is constituted through human speech — carries profound implications well beyond *nedarim*. Rav Soloveitchik employed precisely this model in analyzing the *mitzvah* of *kiddush* on *Shabbos*. *Shabbos* possesses its own intrinsic *kedushah*, just as a *bechor* does. Yet there is a *mitzvah* of *kiddush* — to sanctify it with our words. The question is whether *kiddush* is merely a declaration acknowledging an existing reality, or whether it adds a genuinely human dimension of *kedushah* to what is already divinely given. Following the model of the *bechor*, one could argue that just as one has a *mitzvah lehakdisho* — to add one's own sanctification — even when the object already possesses independent *kedushah*, so too *kiddush* on *Shabbos* represents the human contribution of *kedushah* to the *kedushah* that *Shabbos* already bears in itself. This understanding of the *mitzvah* of *kiddush* — as the genuinely constitutive human act of sanctification rather than mere verbal acknowledgment — was, the lecturer notes, already anticipated by an earlier *rishon* who drew on this very comparison.

# Nedarim 14

## Davar Ha-Nadur Paradigm

### Davar Ha-Nadur Intro

The daf opens by revisiting the fundamental principle established in the preceding *mishnah*: that when a person wishes to invoke a model or paradigm for a *neder*, the object of comparison must be a *davar ha-nadur* — something whose forbidden status was itself created through a person's verbal act of dedication — and not a *davar ha-assur*, something forbidden by virtue of the Torah's own prohibition. No matter how severe the prohibition of *chazir*, *shekatzim u-remasim*, or *avodah zarah*, none of these qualify as a *davar ha-nadur*, because their forbidden status derives entirely from the Torah and not from any human speech act of consecration.

### Terumah/Challah Status

A question carries over from the previous discussion: why are *terumah* and *challah* not considered *davar ha-nadur*? After all, their status as *terumah* or *challah* is unquestionably created through a person's verbal designation. The *Ran* offers one answer — that since *terumah* is not forbidden in all respects, it reflects a Torah-imposed prohibition rather than a purely person-created status — though this reasoning is difficult to sustain, since the implications of the *terumah* status are in many ways analogous to those of an animal consecrated as a *korban*, which certainly qualifies as a *davar ha-nadur*.

Another approach suggested is that since the grain was already forbidden as *tevel* before the designation of *terumah*, the person is not truly creating a new forbidden status. One might even argue that the entire status of *tevel* is itself a function of the potential *terumah* latent within the grain, so that when one designates *terumah*, one is not so much creating a prohibition as completing or clarifying an existing one. An interesting test case for these questions would be *bikkurim*, which similarly is permitted to *kohanim* and forbidden to others, yet unlike *terumah*, failure to separate *bikkurim* does not render the produce *tevel*. Notably, no discussion in the *Gemara* or in the *Rambam* appears to treat *bikkurim* as a candidate paradigm for *nedarim*, which itself is striking.

### Rambam's Approach

The *Rambam* takes a substantially different approach to the requirement of *davar ha-nadur*, one that reconnects the entire institution of *nedarim* to the biblical concept from which it derives. Rather than defining *davar ha-nadur* solely as an object whose forbidden status was generated by a human speech act, the *Rambam* grounds it in the original biblical idea of a *neder* as a free-will offering to God. On his view, the *davar ha-nadur* must be the kind of thing that not only was created through one's speech but that emerged from a voluntary dedication to the Divine.

The obvious challenge to this position is: how then can one say "this should be like a *chattat*" or "like an *asham*," since those offerings arise from obligation rather than free will? The *Rambam* responds by noting the *Gemara* discussed previously: if one accepts upon oneself *nezirut*, one will under certain circumstances be obligated to bring a *chattat* and an *asham*, and so these offerings can in principle flow from an antecedent voluntary act. This also explains, according to the *Rambam*, why *terumah* and *challah* fail to serve as valid paradigms: they are not initiated by free will but by halakhic obligation, and therefore cannot be considered *davar ha-nadur* in the biblically grounded sense he requires.

What is particularly illuminating about the *Rambam*'s approach is how it restores the original biblical texture of the *neder*. The *Gemara*'s analysis elsewhere tends to shift attention away from the biblical model — in which the *neder* begins with a person voluntarily obligating himself to dedicate something to God, as when Yaakov took a *neder* to give *ma'aser* — toward a more abstract analysis of object-status. The concept of *nidrei mitzvah*, in which one takes a *neder* to perform a *mitzvah*, itself reflects this personal-obligation dimension: it begins with a personal commitment and ends with an object. The *Rambam* returns the analysis to precisely that framework.

### Ran's Question

The *Ran* raises a penetrating question at the very outset of the *masechet* that bears directly on all of this: what is, in fact, the classic formulation of a *neder*? The *pasuk* says *ki yidor neder*, and the requirement is *ad sheyidor bedavar hanadur* — until one vows with reference to a *davar ha-nadur*. But what does that mean for the structure of the vow itself?

One way to read it is that the paradigmatic statement of a *neder* involves the language of *korban* — saying *konam davar zeh alai* or *korban davar zeh alai*, with *konam* serving as the operative *kinuy*. On this reading, if one simply says *pat zeh asurah alai* without invoking *konam* or *korban*, that formulation works only as a *yad* — an implied reference to the full statement — because the concept of *korban* is implicit even if unstated.

But the *Ran* actually raises the possibility that the reverse is true: perhaps the paradigmatic statement of a *neder* is simply *davar zeh assur alai*, directly invoking one's own power to render something forbidden, which is itself the content of the biblical phrase *le'esor issar al nafsho*. On this reading, when one says *korban* or *konam*, it is that language which functions as a *yad* to the underlying direct statement of prohibition. The *Ran* observes that the rule of *davar ha-nadur* applies only when one chooses to use a comparative model — saying "this should be like that" — in which case the comparator must be a *davar ha-nadur* rather than a *davar ha-assur*. But the foundational speech act of *nedarim* does not require invoking any external paradigm at all.

### Speech Act Power

This question cuts to the heart of how we understand the power of *nedarim*. One instinct is to see the power of making something forbidden as borrowed or derived from the institution of *korban* — so that when one says *konam*, one is invoking the sanctifying power that attaches objects to the altar, and the *neder* draws its force from that. On this view, *konam* or *korban* is the paradigmatic statement, and saying *assur* without it is merely a shorthand or *yad*.

But the *Ran* suggests something more fundamental: that the Torah grants a person an intrinsic power to make something forbidden through speech alone. One does not need to borrow the conceptual force of *korban* or any other institution. Simply declaring *davar zeh assur alai* suffices to create a binding *neder*, because that is an independent power the Torah vests in human speech. The use of *korban* or *konam* language is an optional mode of expression, and if one chooses to employ a comparative model, that model must be a *davar ha-nadur*. But the *neder* itself is constituted by the direct declaration of prohibition, not by derivation from the *korban* paradigm.

This is a genuinely striking position, because it locates the force of *nedarim* not in the person's ability to replicate the consecrating act of *hekdesh*, but in an autonomous halakhic power of speech that stands on its own.

---

## Wife Like Mother

### Harei At Alai

The *mishnah* turns to the case of a man who says to his wife *harei at alai ke-ima* — you are forbidden to me as my mother. The *mishnah* illustrates an important principle: a man may render sexual relations with his wife forbidden to himself, notwithstanding the fact that marital relations constitute an obligation and a *mitzvah*. This works because the *neder* does not directly prohibit the *mitzvah* itself; rather, it renders the object — here, in effect, his wife insofar as he would derive a specific benefit — forbidden, and the inability to fulfill the *mitzvah* is a consequence of that status. The technical formulation would be *konam hanas tashmishcha alai* — the pleasure of intimacy with you is *konam* to me.

In the present case, however, the man has not used *konam* or *korban* language. He has said "like my mother," invoking an incest prohibition — that is, *matpis bedavar ha-assur*, not *bedavar ha-nadur*. The *mishnah* nevertheless requires him to undergo *hataras nedarim*, the process of annulment before a sage. The *Ran* explains this requirement on practical grounds: forbidding one's wife to oneself is not an uncommon occurrence in moments of anger, and if we were to say outright that no process is required because the language is technically invalid, people would draw the wrong lesson and become cavalier about *nedarim* that are halakhically valid.

### Abaye Resolution

The *Gemara* raises a challenge: a *baraita* states that if a man says *harei at alai kevasar ima* — you are to me like the flesh of my mother — or like his sister, or like *orlah* or *kilei hakerem* (both of which are forbidden in *hana'ah*), *lo amar klum* — he has said nothing. This seems to contradict the *mishnah*, which requires *hataras nedarim*. Abaye resolves the tension by drawing a distinction between levels of prohibition: *lo amar klum* means that the *neder* has no biblical force, but rabbinically one must still undergo the process of *hataras nedarim*.

### Talmid Chacham

Rava offers a different resolution: the *baraita* and the *mishnah* refer to different types of people. The *mishnah*'s requirement of *hataras nedarim* applies to an *am ha-aretz*, while the *baraita*'s ruling that nothing more is needed applies to a *talmid chacham*. The logic, as the *Ran* understands it, is not primarily about knowledge but about consequence: the concern driving the rabbinical requirement is that a person who knows his technically invalid *neder* requires no process will become lax and extend that casualness to genuine *nedarim*. A *talmid chacham* who understands the distinction between valid and invalid formulations will not draw the wrong conclusion from being told he need not go through *hataras nedarim* in this case. One might ask why a *talmid chacham* would utter such a formulation in the first place — perhaps, as noted, it was a way of venting anger with the knowledge that the words carry no legal force.

### Torah Vow Baraita

The *Gemara* introduces a *baraita* that maps precisely onto the three-part structure just discussed: *hanoder baTorah lo amar klum* — one who takes a *neder* "with the Torah" has said nothing, since the Torah's sanctity is not a *davar ha-nadur* — any more than it is a *davar ha-assur* in the conventional sense. Rabbi Yochanan adds that nevertheless one must undergo *she'eilah lechacham*, the process of seeking annulment from a sage. And Rav Nachman adds that a *talmid chacham* need not do so. This *baraita* thus provides a precise parallel to the three positions in the previous discussion: the base ruling (*lo amar klum*), the rabbinic requirement (*tzerich she'eilah*), and the exemption for the *talmid chacham*. It is worth noting that the statements of Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Nachman function as *amora'im* clarifying the *baraita*, in the same way that *amora'im* routinely clarify a *mishnah*.

The concern underlying the rabbinic requirement, as the *Ran* frames it, is not that one should be discouraged from taking such vows in the first place, but that one might extrapolate from the lenient treatment of an invalid *neder* to laxity about genuine ones. The *Ran* suggests that *amei ha-aretz* were in general considered conscientious in their observance of *nedarim*, which is precisely what makes the risk of mislearning significant: someone who takes *nedarim* seriously may incorrectly generalize from the ruling here and become lax about a binding *neder* on the assumption that it similarly requires no follow-through.

---

## Hanoder BaTorah

### Textual Analysis

The *Gemara* now returns to develop the case of *hanoder baTorah* in greater depth, examining what exactly is meant by the phrase *uvmah shekasuv bah* in the *baraita*: "one who vows with the Torah has said nothing; but one who vows with what is written in it — his words stand." A *tanya* on 14b teaches this formulation and then adds that if one says *bah uvmah shekasuv bah* — with it and with what is written in it — those words also stand.

The immediate question is: what is the difference between saying *bah* (in it) and *bemah shekasuv bah* (with what is written in it)? And why is it obvious, as the *Gemara* seems to imply, that adding *bah* alongside *bemah shekasuv bah* should suffice?

The *Gemara* offers an answer through Rav Nachman: *ha d'mancha oraissa a'ara* — if the Torah is lying on the ground — *ha d'nakit lah bidei* — and if one is holding it in one's hands. If the Torah is on the ground and one says *bemah shekasuv bah*, one may be referring to the parchment itself — the physical material on which things are written — rather than to the content. In that case, one is treating the Torah merely as a physical object, *geitei agvilei*, parchment, and the *neder* carries no force. But when one holds the Torah in hand and says *bemah shekasuv bah*, the mind is directed — *da'atei al hazkarot shebah* — toward the divine names written within it, and it is to those that the person is referring.

This analysis raises an underlying conceptual question: what exactly makes *bemah shekasuv bah* work as a *neder*? If one is referring to the *shem Hashem* — God's name written in the Torah — how does that serve as a *davar ha-nadur*? God's name is not a *davar ha-nadur* in any ordinary sense; its sanctity does not arise from a human speech act of dedication.

### Shvuah Explanation

The first explanation offered by the *Ran* is, in a sense, the most radical departure from the context: perhaps *hanoder baTorah* here does not mean a *neder* at all, but a *shvuah*. The *Ran* notes that the word *hanoder* sometimes denotes one who takes an oath rather than a vow in the technical sense. The scenario being described is one in which a person grasps a *sefer Torah* and declares "by this Torah" — much as one might place a hand on a Bible and swear in God's name. In that case, when one says merely *baTorah*, one is swearing by the physical Torah, without invoking God's name — and the *shvuah* is therefore ineffective. But when one says *bemah shekasuv bah*, one is invoking what is written within it — God's name — and is thereby taking a genuine *shvuah beshem Hashem*. On this reading, no question of *davar ha-nadur* arises at all, since we are dealing with a *shvuah*, not a *neder*.

### Raavad Explanation

The *Raavad* proposes a second, more structurally interesting explanation, one that preserves the reading of *hanoder* as a genuine *neder*. His claim is that the *azkarot* — the divine names written in a *sefer Torah* — are themselves a form of *davar ha-nadur*, because their sanctity is instilled through the intentional act of the *sofer* who writes them. The *sofer* must write God's name with specific *kavana* — conscious intent to write it as a divine name — and it is through that act of intentional inscription that the holiness of the name is created.

This raises a subtle but important question: do we understand the *sofer*'s act of writing as one in which he is the agent who instills the *kedushah* in the name? Or do we say that if he writes it correctly with the proper *kavana*, the Torah's own framework recognizes the result as *kadosh* — but it is not the *sofer* who is the source of that holiness? The *Raavad* leans toward the former view: the *sofer* instills the *kedushah* through his act of writing with intent, and therefore the *azkarot* can be said to be *davar ha-nadur* — their status originates in a human act of creation.

An analogy suggested to illuminate this is the requirement that a *get* be written *lishmah* — for the sake of the specific woman being divorced. There is a discussion among *rishonim* and *acharonim* about whether the husband's *lishmah* should be understood as him actively instilling in the *get* its directedness toward his wife, and whether it is precisely this instillment that explains the concept of *bitul get* — the nullification of a *get* before delivery — through which the husband can retroactively void it by declaring it null. If he instilled the *get*'s directedness, he can theoretically reverse that instillment.

The *Raavad*'s position here has an additional dimension: the sanctifying act of the *sofer* is not a pure speech act but a physical act of writing, accompanied by intent. One might wonder whether this suffices to create the quality of *davar ha-nadur*, which we have been analyzing as arising from a speech act. A possible response, however, is that the act of writing is itself a concretization of thought — the *sofer*'s *kavana* given physical form — so that it may be viewed as something closer to a speech act than, say, the physical separation of *terumah*. The *Ran* cites the *Raavad*'s position thus: *azkarot she-bah nodrin hein o nedurin hein*, the divine names in the Torah are either the act or the result of an act of dedication, *she-al yedei ha-ketivah ve-hachanah le-sheim kedushah hein kedushot* — because through the writing and preparation with intent toward holiness, they are made holy.

It is also worth noting that the divine names are not *assur behana'ah* in the ordinary sense. The Torah is used for reading and study; we do not typically categorize a *sefer Torah* as forbidden in benefit, subject to the rule of *mitzvot lav lehanot nitnu*. It has *kedushah* that demands a certain mode of treatment, but that is not the same as the standard *issur hana'ah* that attaches to *korbanot*. This makes the *Raavad*'s identification of the *azkarot* as *davar ha-nadur* all the more striking.

### Yerushalmi Explanation

The third explanation comes from the *Yerushalmi*, and it takes a different approach altogether. Rather than focusing on the *shem Hashem* written in the Torah, the *Yerushalmi* understands *bemah shekasuv bah* — "with what is written in it" — as a reference to the *korbanot* mentioned in the Torah. The *Yerushalmi*'s text reads: *ba-Torah lo amar klum, bemah shekasuv bah assur ke-kayamin ba-Torah bi-kdushat ha-Torah* — if you said "with the sanctity of the Torah," that is nothing; but if you said "with what is written in it," meaning the *korbanot* recorded therein, those *korbanot* are themselves *davar ha-nadur*, and one has made a valid *neder*.

This is analogous to the case of *bi-Yerushalayim*: Jerusalem itself is not a *davar ha-nadur*, but by saying "like Jerusalem" one may be taken to mean the *korbanot* brought there, and on that reading the vow is valid. Similarly, *bemah shekasuv bah* evokes the *korbanot* of the Torah, which are the paradigmatic *davar ha-nadur*, and therefore the *neder* takes effect.

A related point: if someone says *harei zeh alai ke-korban u-ke-vasar chazir*, one might ask whether the inclusion of an invalid comparator (*davar ha-assur*) undermines the valid one (*davar ha-nadur*). The intuition is that it should not — as long as the valid formulation is present, the additional invalid comparator does not cancel it. The *neder* remains in force on the strength of the *davar ha-nadur* element. This logic also supports the *Yerushalmi*'s position: *bemah shekasuv bah* encompasses many things, including *korbanot*; the fact that it also encompasses other material does not prevent the *korbanot* from doing the work of validating the *neder*.

### Why Bemah Works

The *Gemara* then addresses why it states explicitly that *bah uvmah shekasuv bah* — with it *and* with what is written in it — also works, given that *bemah shekasuv bah* alone already suffices. Rav Nachman's first answer, as noted above, distinguishes between whether the Torah is on the ground or held in hand: if it is on the ground and one says *bemah shekasuv bah*, one may be understood to mean the parchment (*geitei agvilei*), and the *neder* fails; but if one holds it, one is presumed to have one's mind on the *azkarot*, and *bemah shekasuv bah* alone works.

The *Gemara* then offers a second formulation: *ve-i ba'is eima*, perhaps in both clauses the Torah is on the ground, and the point is to teach that even when it is on the ground, saying *bemah shekasuv bah* suffices — and it goes without saying (*ein tzarich lomar*) that *bah uvmah shekasuv bah* also works, so the latter formulation is mentioned only in a *zu ve-eino tzarich lomar zu* construction.

A third formulation reads the entire matter as applying when one is holding the Torah: when holding it, even saying *bo* alone suffices, because holding it demonstrates that one's mind is on the content. On this reading, *bah uvmah shekasuv bah* teaches that when holding the Torah, one need not say *bemah shekasuv bah* — saying *bo* alone, which otherwise might be taken as a reference to the parchment, is treated as equivalent to *bemah shekasuv bah* because the physical act of holding it clarifies one's intent. In this third reading, the *vav* in *bah uvmah shekasuv bah* functions as "or" rather than "and."

To summarize: the *Gemara* has offered three distinct explanations for why *bemah shekasuv bah* works — as a *shvuah beshem Hashem* rather than a *neder*; as a *neder* in which the *azkarot* are themselves *davar ha-nadur* by virtue of the *sofer*'s instillment of *kedushah*; and as a *neder* in which the reference is to the *korbanot* written in the Torah, which are the paradigmatic *davar ha-nadur*. All three are genuinely illuminating, and each carries significant conceptual implications for the nature of *nedarim* and the mechanism through which a *neder* takes effect.

---

## Konam on Actions

### Mishnah Text

The *mishnah* now introduces a different class of *nedarim*: those in which a person appears to make an *action* rather than an *object* forbidden. The cases given are *konam she-ani yashen* — sleep is *konam* to me; *konam she-ani medaber* — speech is *konam* to me; and *konam she-ani mehalech* — walking is *konam* to me. The *mishnah* states *harei zeh belo yachel dvaro* — the prohibition of *lo yachel dvaro* applies. This formulation is itself notable: rather than simply stating that the person is *assur*, the *mishnah* frames the result in terms of the verse prohibiting the violation of one's word.

This *mishnah* stands in contrast to the final *mishnah* of the previous chapter, which addressed making a body part forbidden — there, the *mishnah* simply ruled *assur*. Here, where no body part and no physical object is mentioned, the *mishnah* uses the language of *belo yachel dvaro*, which sounds, if anything, even more emphatic.

### Rav vs. Nachman

The *Gemara* records a dispute: *konam einai besheina hayom im ishan lemachar* — my eyes are *konam* in sleep today, if I sleep tomorrow. The scenario is that today is the *tnai* (condition) and tomorrow is when the *neder* would take effect. If the person sleeps today, that triggers the condition; whether he then sleeps tomorrow will determine retroactively whether his action today constituted a violation of his *neder*.

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *al yishan hayom shema yishan lemachar* — one should not sleep today, lest one come to sleep tomorrow. The concern is that if the person sleeps today, activating the *tnai*, he will not be careful enough tomorrow to avoid sleep, and will retroactively have violated his *neder* by sleeping today. Rav Nachman disagrees: *yishan hayom velo chaishinan shema yishan lemachar* — one may sleep today; we trust the person to be sufficiently careful about his *neder* tomorrow.

The dispute turns on whether we trust a person who has already triggered the *tnai* — and thus placed himself in a situation where sleeping tomorrow would mean a retroactive violation of today's *neder* — to be sufficiently vigilant about tomorrow's *neder* obligation. Rav is concerned that the retroactive nature of the violation makes it psychologically remote enough that the person will not take it seriously. Rav Nachman holds that people can be trusted to fulfill their *nedarim*.

Rav Yehuda concedes, however, that all agree in the reverse case: *be-omer konam einai besheina lemachar im ishan hayom* — if my eyes are *konam* in sleep *tomorrow* if I sleep *today*, then one may sleep today. *Ki lo mizdahar bitnai'ah aval be-issura mizdahar* — because people may be lax about a *tnai*, but when the *issur* itself is tomorrow's obligation, we trust them to be careful about keeping it. The debate only arises when sleeping today merely triggers a condition, and tomorrow's sleep is both the content of the *neder* and the variable on which retroactive violation depends.

### Grammatical Problem

A more fundamental problem with the *mishnah* is now surfaced. We know from the *mishnah* in the previous chapter (*chomer bishvuot*) that *shvuah* differs from *neder* in one significant respect: a *shvuah* can apply to *davar she-ein bo mamash* — something non-physical — while *nedarim* apply only to *davar she-yesh bo mamash*, something with physical substance. Sleep, speech, and walking are all non-physical — they have no *mamash*. How, then, can a *neder* in the form of *konam she-ani yashen* take effect at all? The *mishnah* appears to assume that it does, but on what basis?

### Eyes Resolution

The *Gemara* resolves the problem by rereading the *mishnah*. The cases of *konam she-ani yashen*, *konam she-ani medaber*, and *konam she-ani mehalech* must be understood as shorthand for a formulation that does invoke a physical object. The *mishnah* must mean *konam einai besheina* — my eyes are *konam* in sleep — which inserts the eyes as the physical object to which the *neder* attaches. This mirrors the formulation of the final *mishnah* of the previous chapter, where body parts were explicitly mentioned. The *mishnah* here is read as doing the same thing implicitly, and the *Gemara*'s reinterpretation confirms that a *neder* cannot attach to a pure action without any physical referent.

---

## Impossibility & Nede (II)

### Shvuah Sleep

Even after inserting the eyes as the physical object, a further problem emerges. If the *mishnah* means *konam einai besheina* without a *tnai* — that is, my eyes are always forbidden in sleep, full stop — then we face a different difficulty. Rabbi Yochanan teaches: *shvuah she-lo yishan shelosha yamim, malkin oto ve-yashen le-alter* — one who swears that he will not sleep for three days receives lashes immediately and may go to sleep at once. The reason is that such a *shvuah* cannot possibly be fulfilled; it is physically impossible for a human being to go without sleep for three days. Because it is impossible, the *shvuah* is treated as a *shvuat shav* or *shvuat sheker* from the moment it is uttered, it never takes effect, and the person is free to sleep immediately.

The question posed by the *Gemara* is whether the same reasoning applies to a *neder*. If a person says *konam einai besheina* without qualification, he is in the same position: he cannot possibly fulfill this *neder*, since it is humanly impossible never to sleep. Does this mean the *neder* never takes effect?

---

## Konam on Actions (II)

### Itmar Debate

The *Gemara* presents the *itmar* — a recorded amoraic dispute — on the conditional vow *konam einai besheina hayom im ishan lemachar*. This is the precise case in which today is the *tnai* and tomorrow is the *neder*. The debate among the *amora'im* concerns whether the person may sleep today (trusting he will observe the *tnai* tomorrow) or must refrain today (lest he fail to fulfill the *tnai* and thereby retroactively violate the *neder*). This is the dispute between Rav and Rav Nachman discussed above. Rav holds that since a violation of the *tnai* would retroactively constitute a transgression — a form of retroactive violation — we cannot trust the person to be vigilant enough about the *tnai* and must therefore prevent him from sleeping today. Rav Nachman holds that we trust people to honor their *nedarim*, even when fulfillment depends on a future condition.

---

## Impossibility & Nede (II)

### Concept Difference

The conceptual comparison between *shvuah* and *neder* in cases of impossibility is illuminating and worth developing carefully. A *shvuah* is an obligation that the person takes on himself directly: "I will do such-and-such." When a *shvuah* contradicts what is halakhically permitted or what is physically possible — for instance, swearing to do something the Torah forbids, or swearing not to sleep for three days — there is a direct head-on collision between what the person is declaring and what he is able or permitted to do. In such cases, the *shvuah* is void from the outset.

A *neder*, by contrast, does not directly mandate or prohibit the person's conduct. It assigns a status to an object: my eyes are *konam* in sleep. The indirect consequence is that if the person sleeps, he will have derived benefit from those eyes in a way that violates their *konam* status — but the *neder* itself does not say "I will not sleep." It says "my eyes are forbidden." The impossibility argument therefore operates differently: when a *shvuah* to not sleep for three days is impossible, the *shvuah*'s content directly contradicts physical reality. When a *neder* renders the eyes forbidden in sleep, the *neder*'s content (a status assigned to an object) does not directly contradict physical reality in the same way — even if the practical consequence is that the *neder* cannot be honored.

This parallels the distinction between saying *tefillin* is forbidden to me, which creates a situation where I cannot fulfill my obligation of *tefillin*, versus saying I will not put on *tefillin*, which directly violates my obligation. The *neder* addresses the object; the consequences for my obligations or physical capacities are downstream. Thus the *Gemara*'s invocation of the *shvuah* comparison is noteworthy: it raises the question of whether impossibility of fulfillment is as fatal to a *neder* as to a *shvuah*, even though the mechanism of each is conceptually different.

### Tosafot View

*Tosafot* address this question directly. From the *Gemara*'s discussion — *mikan perushu de-neder she-iy efshar lekayem eino chal* — *Tosafot* derive that a *neder* which cannot be fulfilled does not take effect. The *Gemara* here appears to compare a *neder* that is impossible to fulfill to a *shvuah* that is *shav* — vain or impossible — and on that basis conclude that such a *neder* never takes hold.

*Tosafot* then raise a potential counterexample: what about a person who takes a *neder* on all the fruit in the world? Can one really go through life eating no fruit whatsoever? *Tosafot* clarify that such a *neder* is *not* the kind of impossibility that invalidates, since it is in principle possible to live without eating fruit. The point is not that we cannot imagine someone fulfilling it in practice, but that there is no categorical physical necessity that prevents fulfillment. The impossibility relevant to *nedarim* is one where fulfillment is inherently physically impossible — not merely difficult or practically unlikely.

### Physical Necessity

This brings us to the specific case of the eyes. The *neder konam einai besheina* — my eyes are forbidden in sleep — is not analogous to a *neder* on all fruit. It is not merely difficult for a person never to sleep; it is physically impossible, because the eyes will necessarily close. A person does not choose to sleep in the same way one chooses not to eat fruit; the closing of the eyes in sleep is a physical inevitability, not a volitional act that can simply be avoided indefinitely.

The comparison to food is thus instructive. If I declare all food forbidden to me, it is not possible for me to live without eating — but the food itself has no inherent tendency to be consumed by me. The physical necessity of eating is about my biological needs, not about the nature of the food. The *neder* makes the food a forbidden object; the food does not have to become available to me. By contrast, when I declare my eyes *konam* in sleep, the very nature of the eyes — as a physical organ that will necessarily close — means that the *neder* is aimed directly at an inevitability of the physical object's own nature, not merely at a human need that may or may not interact with the object.

Whether this distinction is fully persuasive or not, the *Gemara*'s analysis proceeds on the assumption that the impossibility of never sleeping is sufficiently analogous to the impossibility of a three-day sleepless oath to be relevant in the context of *nedarim* as well.

---

## Belo Yachel Resolution

### Reframed Case

The *Gemara* now undertakes a careful reanalysis of the *mishnah* to understand what case it is actually addressing and what exactly *harei zeh belo yachel dvaro* means. After the foregoing discussion, the simple reading — that the *mishnah* is telling us that *konam einai besheina* (my eyes are *konam* in sleep) binds the person such that sleeping is a violation of *belo yachel dvaro* — turns out to be either too trivial or too problematic to be what the *mishnah* intends.

If the *mishnah* merely meant to say that *konam einai besheina hayom* is a valid *neder* for today, that would be nothing new — it simply parallels the *mishnah* from the end of the previous chapter. If it meant that *konam einai besheina* applies indefinitely without any *tnai*, then as the *Gemara* has demonstrated, such a *neder* cannot take effect because it is impossible to fulfill.

So the *Gemara* argues that the *mishnah* must be addressing the *tnai* scenario. The case must be *konam einai besheina hayom im ishan lemachar* — my eyes are *konam* in sleep today, if I sleep tomorrow. Today is the *neder*; tomorrow is the *tnai*. One might have thought that *harei zeh belo yachel dvaro* means we forbid the person from sleeping today out of concern that he will sleep tomorrow and retroactively transgress. But the *Gemara* challenges this: if he is careful not to sleep tomorrow, there is no *belo yachel* at all — so the *mishnah*'s formulation of *harei zeh belo yachel dvaro* would only make sense if the *mishnah* is actually telling us that the person may sleep today, and the *belo yachel* is what he must avoid tomorrow.

### Semantic Puzzle

This creates a genuine semantic puzzle. *Harei zeh belo yachel dvaro* — in its natural sense — sounds like a statement of prohibition: this is the prohibition of *lo yachel*, meaning one must not violate one's word. But the *Gemara* is now being pushed to read it as a statement of permission: one may sleep today (*harei zeh*), and the *belo yachel* (*lo yachel dvaro*) is simply the rule that would apply tomorrow if one slept tomorrow. On this reading, *harei zeh belo yachel dvaro* does not mean "this constitutes a violation of *lo yachel*" but rather "this [situation — sleeping today] will subject one to the rule of *belo yachel* [tomorrow]."

The *Ran* takes note of the difficulty in reading the phrase this way and works through the problem carefully. The *Gemara* had initially wanted to read *harei zeh belo yachel dvaro* as prohibiting sleep today out of concern for tomorrow's *tnai*, but the argument was then made that *alman ka-issura mizdahar* — when it comes to tomorrow's actual *issur* (the *neder* itself), people are careful — and therefore sleeping today and trusting the person tomorrow is the correct approach. The *mishnah*'s *harei zeh belo yachel dvaro* would then be a warning about what awaits tomorrow if the *tnai* is not kept, rather than a prohibition of today's sleep.

### Final Resolution

The *Gemara*'s final resolution reads the *mishnah* as follows: the case is that the person *already slept* today — the *tnai* has been triggered. Given that, *harei zeh belo yachel dvaro* means that he must now be careful to keep his *tnai* tomorrow, i.e., not to sleep tomorrow, because if he does, he will retroactively have violated his *neder* through today's sleep. The *mishnah* is thus not deliberating about whether to permit or prohibit sleeping today; it is instructing the person who has already slept today that he is now under obligation to observe the *tnai* tomorrow, and the rule of *belo yachel dvaro* applies to that obligation.

This resolution accords with the position of Rav Nachman, who held that we trust a person to observe the conditions of his *neder*. The debate between Rav and Rav Nachman was about a prospective situation — whether to allow someone to sleep today knowing that doing so triggers the *tnai*. But the *mishnah* is addressed to a retrospective situation — the person has already slept today, and the *mishnah* tells him what he must do tomorrow. In that context, all agree: if you fell asleep today, you must keep your *tnai* tomorrow, for otherwise you will have transgressed *belo yachel dvaro*. The nuance is that the *mishnah* is not granting or withholding permission for today's sleep but rather delineating the consequent obligation that follows from it.

---

---

# Nedarim 15

## Rav Yehuda vs. Rav Nachm…

### Mishna on Konam

Today's *daf* is 15. We pick up where the *gemara* says *Ravina amar*, beginning with the word *le'olam*, approximately fifteen lines from the bottom of the page. By way of orientation, it is worth recalling what has been under discussion.

The *mishna* at the end of the previous *perek* dealt with a case in which someone said *konam pi medaber imach* — a *neder* directed at one's mouth as a physical body part, which constituted a *davar sheyesh bo mamash*, a prohibition bearing on something concrete. The *mishna* before us now, by contrast, speaks of a *konam* formulated as follows: my sleeping is *konam*, my speech is *konam* — which would seem to be a *davar she'ein bo mamash*, a prohibition directed at an entirely abstract entity.

### Condition-Dependent Neder

The *gemara*, however, opened not with this question about abstract objects but with a distinct debate that will occupy us through the better part of this *daf*: the disagreement between *Rav Yehuda amar Rav* and *Rav Nachman*. The case is one in which a person declares a *neder* — making something forbidden to himself today — conditional upon some action he will or will not take tomorrow. The question is whether we permit the person to act upon the *neder* today, trusting that he will be careful tomorrow not to trigger the *tnai* (the condition), or whether we are concerned that once the matter turns on the *tnai*, he will not treat it with the same weight he would give to a direct violation of the *neder* itself.

To clarify the mechanics: if the person does trigger the condition, then the *neder* takes retroactive effect, meaning that in hindsight he has violated the *neder*. But because the violation is established only retroactively and was uncertain at the time of the act, perhaps he will not take the *tnai* seriously enough. *Rav Yehuda amar Rav* holds that we do not permit the person to act today, precisely because he will not treat the *tnai* with the gravity he would apply to the *neder* itself. *Rav Nachman*, by contrast, holds that a person will indeed treat the *tnai* with the same seriousness and may therefore be trusted to observe it.

### Connecting Mishna to Deb…

The *gemara* attempted, somewhat forcibly, to read our *mishna* as a special case of this debate — as addressing the situation in which what one does today depends on what one will do tomorrow. The *gemara* itself acknowledges that this is a strained reading. One reason cited for why the *mishna* could not simply be taken at face value was a *mimanashach* argument: if the *mishna* is discussing making sleep forbidden as an abstract idea, a *neder* to that effect would not work; and if it means making one's eyes forbidden to sleep, that was already taught in a prior *mishna*. Since it cannot straightforwardly be either, the *gemara* proposed that it must be addressing the *tnai* case. That is where the previous *daf* concluded.

---

## Abstract Neder Derabbanan

### Ravina's Solution
