The *gemara* now offers a different and important answer. *Ravina amar*, beginning with *le'olam kedekatani*: the *mishna* means exactly what it says — that the *neder* was formulated as *konam* on the sleeping itself, as an abstract act. The natural question is how *bal yachel* can apply to a *davar she'ein bo mamash*. The *gemara*'s answer is *umai bal yachel mi-derabbanan* — the *bal yachel* that applies here is *mi-derabbanan*.

### Derabbanan Scope

This is a critically important point that was touched upon earlier but now receives explicit formulation: even though a *neder* takes effect at the biblical level only on something concrete, the rabbis extended the category of *neder* to encompass abstract matters as well. Accordingly, *konam* on my sleeping, *konam* on my walking — these take effect *mi-derabbanan*. From a conceptual standpoint, a significant gap remains between saying *shvua* I will not walk (which bears on the person himself) and saying *konam* on my walking (which is directed at the abstract act). But many of the practical distinctions collapse once we accept that both function *mi-derabbanan*. According to *Ravina*, then, the *chiddush* of our *mishna* is precisely this: even a *neder* formulated against an abstract action takes effect *mi-derabbanan*, and it is that rabbinic *bal yachel* which the *mishna* invokes.

### Bal Yachel Derabbanan

This leads the *gemara* to pose a sharp question: *umi ika bal yachel mi-derabbanan*? Would we ever apply the language of *bal yachel* — which is a *pasuk* in the *Torah* — to something that is only *derabbanan*? The *gemara* is not suggesting there are no rabbinic *nedarim*; there is ample evidence otherwise. The question is specifically about invoking the *pasuk* of *bal yachel* in this context. To illustrate the strangeness of the proposition: one would not say that eating chicken cooked in milk violates *lo tivashal gedi be-halev imo* — one would say it is *asur mi-derabbanan*. Would we similarly apply a *pasuk* of *bal yachel* to what is only a *derabbanan*? That is the *gemara*'s challenge.

---

## Minhag as Neder

### Baraita Minhag Issur

The *gemara* answers *in* — yes — and cites a *baraita* in support: *devarim ha-muttarim va-aherim nahagu bahen issur* — things that are permitted, which others have treated as forbidden through practice — *i attah rashai le-hattiran bifnehem*, you may not go ahead and tell them that their practice is baseless and that what they are doing is really entirely permissible, *she-ne'emar lo yachel devaro*, because it says, "his word shall not be violated." The *baraita* thus establishes that a pattern of religious practice creates a binding commitment, and that the verse of *lo yachel devaro* applies to it — even though no one imagines that this is a formal *neder* in the technical sense. There is therefore a category of *bal yachel mi-derabbanan*.

### Types of Minhagim

This passage opens onto an extraordinarily important domain of thinking about *nedarim* that is, interestingly, almost entirely absent from the explicit discussions of our *masechet*, which consistently focuses on the power of *neder* as it operates on objects. Yet it surfaces here and there, and the implications are far-reaching.

The *neder* that most of us think of in everyday life — when we say *bli neder*, for instance — tends to invoke the idea of personal religious commitment, of obligating oneself to do something. This is closer to the concept of *nidrei mitzvah*, such as *ashne ha-shana perek ze* — the commitment to study a particular chapter — and even there some *rishonim* held it was really a *shvua* rather than a *neder*. The biblical concept of *neder*, as in *vayiddor Yaakov neder lemor*, carries both the personal obligation and the dedication of an object. But for most people in practice, the concept of *neder* centers on that sense of personal religious obligation one takes upon oneself.

One classic formulation is what is said during *hattarat nedarim*: *kol davar tov she-nahagti shalosh pe'amim ve-lo amarti she-ye-he davar ze bli neder* — that performing some positive religious act three times in a row, without having explicitly exempted it from the status of a *neder*, constitutes a kind of *kabbalat neder* to continue the practice going forward. This is not about formal *mitzvah* obligations, which would not generate a *neder*-related consequence, but about voluntary religious practices.

### Hatam Sofer Minhag

The *Hatam Sofer*, who devoted considerable energy to combating religious reform and opposing the introduction of changes into traditional practice, drew heavily on precisely this idea. Even when a proposed change could be defended on technical halachic grounds, one powerful tool for resistance was the argument of *minhag* — that this is simply not the practice, and our practice is not the practice. The obvious weakness of this argument, standing alone, is that *minhagim* do change, and it is not in itself an overwhelming response if something is *halachically* permissible.

What the *Hatam Sofer* did to strengthen the force of *minhag* was to identify it with *neder*: every *minhag* is essentially a *neder* to act in that way, making every *minhag de-oraita* in force. In one *tshuva*, discussing what may have been a case of *bishul akum* or something similar, he reasons: even if the practice in question falls only in the *derabbanan* category, or does not fall in the *derabbanan* category at all and is therefore purely a matter of *minhag*, the *minhag* itself elevates it to *de-oraita* status through the force of *neder*. This is a strikingly powerful application of the *gemara*'s principle here.

It is worth pausing to appreciate how significant a *chiddush* this represents, and how far it takes us from what one might expect to find discussed in *Masechet Nedarim*. One opens this *masechet* expecting a discussion of vows about objects — and indeed that is what fills most of the tractate. And yet, through passages like this one, the concept of *neder* quietly encompasses the entire domain of adopted personal religious practices and communal *minhagim*, with consequences reaching into major halachic controversies of the modern period.

One might note in this context that *Tosafot* actually resists reading the *baraita* as an argument by mere analogy to our case of *neder* on abstract acts. *Tosafot* argues — see the line beginning *vachen nahagu bo issur teima mah inyan zeh le-nahagu bo issur*, followed by *yesh lomar de-hai namei she-nadar ve-nitkaven le-esor atzmo gam be-davar she-ein bo mamash, ein lecha minhag gadol mi-zeh* — that making a *neder* to forbid oneself from something abstract is itself the greatest possible form of *nahagu bo issur*; they are thus not two separate things but the same phenomenon. The simpler reading, however, is that the *gemara* is reasoning by analogy: just as a religious *minhag* generates a *derabbanan bal yachel*, so too does a rabbinic extension of *neder* to abstract matters.

### Minhag Issur vs. Heter

It is also important to note that the specific language of the *baraita* — *devarim ha-muttarim va-aherim nahagu bahen issur* — is carefully limited. It speaks of treating something as a *davar asur*, and this brings the discussion much closer to the world of *nedarim*. Consider, for example, someone who refrains from eating certain foods that mimic the taste or feel of *chametz* on *Pesach* even though they are technically permitted, or who does not travel on Fridays out of concern for arriving home before *Shabbos* in time, as the *gemara* in *Pesachim* discusses. In both cases one is treating something as *asur* — and whether the subject is an object (the pseudo-*chametz* food) or an abstract action (traveling on Friday), the prohibition is structured analogously to the world of *nedarim*, including the concept of *davar she'ein bo mamash*.

This stands in contrast to the other major category of *minhag*, which involves positive religious acts — taking on a practice of performing a *mitzvah*-adjacent act on a regular basis. That category is more analogous to the discussions of *ashne ha-shana perek ze* type commitments, which shade toward the *shvua* end of the spectrum. The *gemara* here, with its invocation of *bal yachel*, is addressing specifically the *minhag issur* form. The *gemara*'s conclusion, in any case, is that a *bal yachel mi-derabbanan* does exist, and this suffices to answer the challenge to *Ravina*'s position.

---

## Wife's Hana'ah Case

### Pesach Timeline Mishna

With the question of *bal yachel mi-derabbanan* resolved, the *gemara* returns to the unfinished debate between *Rav Yehuda* and *Rav Nachman*. The *gemara* introduces a *mishna* — one we will be studying in approximately a month — and attempts to derive from it a ruling in the debate.

The *mishna* presents the following case: a husband declares to his wife, *she'at nehenis li ad haPesach im telchi le-veit avicha ad heChag* — you may not derive benefit from me through *Pesach* if you go to visit your father's house at any point through *Succos*. The chronological structure is clear: *Pesach* falls first in the calendar year, followed by *Succos*. So the *issur hana'ah* runs from now until *Pesach*, and the *tnai* — the condition that would trigger it — is whether she visits her father at any point from now through *Succos*.

To lay this out concretely: if she visits her father's house during the period before *Pesach*, she has triggered the *tnai* and the prohibition on *hana'ah* takes effect, meaning she cannot derive benefit from her husband through *Pesach*. But the more interesting question is what happens during the period before she has triggered the *tnai*: may she be deriving *hana'ah* from her husband in the meantime? That is precisely the question of *Rav Yehuda* and *Rav Nachman*. *Rav Yehuda* would say no — we cannot trust her to refrain from visiting her father, so we do not let her derive *hana'ah* now. *Rav Nachman* would say yes — she can be trusted, and she may derive *hana'ah* with the expectation that she will not trigger the *tnai* later.

### Inference Hana'ah Permit…

The *gemara* proceeds to examine the language of the *mishna*. It says: *halcha lifnei haPesach asurah behana'aso ad haPesach* — if she went to her father before *Pesach*, she is forbidden from deriving benefit through *Pesach*. The *gemara* infers: *halcha lifnei haPesach asurah* — only if she has gone do we say she is forbidden; *lo halcha lo* — if she has not yet gone, it is permitted for her to derive *hana'ah*, and we simply trust her not to trigger the *tnai* later. This inference would appear to support *Rav Nachman*.

*Rabbi Abba*, however, rejects this reading. *Halcha lifnei haPesach asurah ve-loka* — the *mishna* means: if she has already gone to her father's house before *Pesach*, then the *tnai* is triggered, the prohibition is clearly in force, and if she were then to derive *hana'ah*, she would receive lashes. *Lo halcha* — if she has not yet gone, then *asurah be'alma* — she is simply forbidden, but without lashes, because we do not yet know whether the *tnai* will ultimately be triggered. The *mishna*'s statement *halcha asurah* is thus not saying it is only when she has gone that we prohibit; it is specifying the more severe consequence. Even when she has not yet gone, *Rav Yehuda* would hold that we do not trust her to maintain the *tnai* and would therefore not permit her to derive *hana'ah* — though the prohibition would not carry lashes at that stage, since it would have the character of *hatra'at safek*.

### Lashes Question

At this point a critical question arises: who, in fact, receives lashes? He made the vow; she derived the *hana'ah* — why should she bear the burden of his *nedarim* and be the one who faces lashes?

The *Ran* addresses this question directly. He says: *lokah hi* — it is she who receives lashes. *Aval ihu eino loke she-harei lo asah shum issur* — he has not done anything wrong, since *she-hedirah*, he merely made the vow; it was she who violated it. *Ude-tana nami hashmi'enu me-agav orchei* — perhaps part of the point of the *mishna* is to tell us that *de-alah rechiv issura* — the prohibition rests on her, *aval lo alav klal* — not on him at all.

### Ran vs. Rambam

The *Rambam* disagrees. *Loke hu she-hedirah* — he is the one who gets lashes, but only if *im he-henah otah* — if he actively caused her to derive *hana'ah*, say, by giving her a massage or directly providing the benefit himself. In that case, he has violated his own *neder*. *Aval hi eina loka* — she does not receive lashes, because *de-kivan de-lo nadrah klal* — she never took a *neder*. *Lo shayach bah lo yachel devaro* — the verse says do not violate *your* word; this is not her word, so even if she acts against it, she has not violated the biblical prohibition of *bal yachel*.

The *Ran*, however, argues that the *Rambam*'s position is untenable, citing a *sugya* in the later chapter *Ein Bein ha-Mudar* regarding *yesh milah be-konamos*. He arrives at the following principle: *ein ha-oser over klal* — the one who creates the *issur* does not transgress by virtue of the other person's violation — *ve-ha-mudar nami vadai avar* — and the one against whom the *neder* was directed is indeed the one who transgresses. The reasoning turns on the key phrase *lo yachel devaro*: *lo yachel a-dibur ka-amar* — what cannot be violated is the *word*, the *dibur*, as an abstract entity. It does not matter ultimately whose word it is; what matters is that a prohibition-status was created through speech, and anyone who violates that status violates that *dibur*.

This framing is entirely consistent with the central emphasis of our *masechet* on *neder* as creating an objective status in an object. I can make my coffee *asur* on you; the coffee acquires that status. If you then drink it, you have violated that status — you have violated the word that created it, *lo yachel devaro* — even though it was not your word. Just as one can sanctify an animal as a *korban*, and if another person misuses it they transgress, so too here: the person who crosses the line that should not be crossed is the one who transgresses, even though they did not draw that line.

The *Rambam*, by contrast, does not fully shift the focus away from the person who took the vow. Consistent with his view (discussed in the previous *daf*) that a *davar ha-nadur* must be the kind of thing one can bring as a free-will offering to God — connecting *neder* to the classical biblical act of obligating oneself to give something to the Divine — the *Rambam* understands *lo yachel devaro* as addressed first and foremost to the one who made the vow. For the *Rambam*, getting lashes requires that both conditions be met: the objective status of the object be violated, and the violation be committed by the very person who took the vow. Without both elements, there may still be a biblical prohibition, but the formal penalty of lashes does not apply.

The practical consequence is striking. If I declare *konam* on this coffee regarding you, and you drink it: according to the *Ran*, you receive lashes, because you violated the *dibur*-created status. According to the *Rambam*, you do not receive lashes because it was not your *dibur*, and I do not receive lashes because I did not perform the violating act — unless I actively caused you to drink it. In that case, the *Rambam* would say I get lashes as the one whose vow has now been violated by my own hand. If neither actively violated — if you simply drank what I passively left for you — then according to the *Rambam*, no one receives lashes, even though there may well be a biblical *issur* in play.

---

## Later Condition Violation

### Shaatnez Alternative

The *gemara* returns to the debate and presents what amounts to a mirror-image *mishna*. The case here is: *shaatnez li al hachag im telchi le-veit avicha ad haPesach* — she cannot derive benefit through *Succos* if she goes to her father's house before *Pesach*. Here the *issur hana'ah* extends all the way to *Succos*, and the *tnai* is limited to the period before *Pesach*. The structure is the reverse of the earlier case: the *tnai* window comes first, and the *issur* period extends far beyond it.

The *mishna* states: *halcha lifnei haPesach asurah behana'ah ad haChag* — if she went to her father's house before *Pesach*, she is forbidden from deriving benefit all the way through *Succos*. *U-muteres leilech achar haPesach* — and she is permitted to go to her father's house after *Pesach*. The *rishonim* discuss what the *chiddush* of this latter clause is; one reading is that we are not concerned that permitting her to go after *Pesach* will somehow lead retroactively or by extension to a prohibited going before *Pesach*. Then the *mishna* says: *halcha asurah, lo halcha lo* — if she went, she is forbidden; if she did not go, she is not.

### Rava's Clarification

The *gemara* again presses: *lo halcha lo* — does this mean that as long as she has not triggered the *tnai*, she is permitted to derive *hana'ah*? That would support *Rav Nachman*.

*Rava* answers: *hu hadin afilu lo halcha asurah* — the same logic applies here: even if she has not yet gone to her father's house, she is not permitted to derive *hana'ah*. *Halcha asurah ve-loka* — if she has already gone and it is before *Pesach*, then the *tnai* is triggered, the *issur* is in full force, and if she derives *hana'ah* she will receive lashes — whether she or he, depending on one's reading of the *Ran* and *Rambam*. *Lo halcha asurah be'alma* — if she has not yet gone, she is still forbidden from deriving *hana'ah*, but it is a lesser prohibition without lashes, because the *tnai* has not yet been triggered and we do not yet know its ultimate status. The *mishna*'s *lo halcha lo* is therefore not saying she is permitted to derive *hana'ah* in the interim; it is saying she will not face lashes in that period. Whether she may derive *hana'ah* in the interim remains the open question between *Rav Yehuda* and *Rav Nachman*, and the *pshat* of the *mishna* remains difficult for *Rav Yehuda*'s position.

---

## Meisivei Bread Case

### Bread Condition Case

The *gemara* raises a *meisivei* — a challenge from a *mishnaic* source. The case is: *kikar zo alai hayom im eilech le-makom ploni le-machar* — this loaf of bread is forbidden to me today if I go to Philadelphia tomorrow. The *mishna* then states: *achal, harei zeh be-val eilech* — if he ate the bread, he is now under a prohibition against going to Philadelphia tomorrow, as though there were a new biblical prohibition created by the *neder*.

### Permit or Forbid Eating

The *gemara* notes with some amusement the formulation *harei zeh be-val eilech* — as if there were now a new *lo ta'aseh*, "do not go to Philadelphia," which he has generated through his *neder*. But the *gemara*'s question is pointed: *mi katani ochel?* — does the *mishna* say he is *permitted* to eat the bread? It says *achal katani* — it says "if he ate," not "he may eat." The *mishna* is simply describing the consequences of having already eaten the bread; it never addresses whether eating the bread was permitted in the first place. This distinction is crucial for the debate between *Rav Yehuda* and *Rav Nachman*.

### Rav Yehuda Response

*Rav Yehuda* explains accordingly: the *mishna* sets up the case by assuming the bread was already eaten — not because it was permitted to eat, but because, from *Rav Yehuda*'s perspective, he was not supposed to eat the bread to begin with. Since the *mishna* could not say "you are permitted to eat" — because *Rav Yehuda* would say you are not — it framed the case as *achal*, taking the act as a fait accompli. Once the bread has been eaten, regardless of whether it should have been, the *mishna* then addresses the consequence: you are now under *bal eilech*, do not go to Philadelphia. *Ela ayadi de-tana reisha achal, de-lo mistani leh ochel* — since the first clause had to be framed around the fact of having eaten rather than the permission to eat, the *seifa* continues in kind, addressing what follows from that fact. Nothing can be inferred from this *mishna* about whether one was originally permitted to eat the bread before the *tnai* could be determined.

The *gemara*'s *maskana* is thus that the debate between *Rav Yehuda* and *Rav Nachman* remains unresolved by the *mishnaic* sources. Many *rishonim* observe that the *gemara* works so hard to deflect challenges to *Rav Yehuda*'s position — consistently providing him with answers — that one might infer the *gemara* is inclined to rule with him. The *Ran* leans toward *Rav Yehuda*: where a *neder* has been taken with a condition whose fulfillment is uncertain, we tell the person not to transgress the *neder* out of concern that he will trigger the *tnai* later.

---

## Neder for Action Control

### Indirect Action Control

This *sugya* invites us to step back and appreciate a broader phenomenon at work throughout these cases. A *neder* is about an object — it creates a status in a physical or semi-physical entity, making it *asur*. A *shvua*, by contrast, is about the person who swears. And there is a strong reluctance to take *shvuot* precisely because of *lo yenakeh Hashem et asher yisa et shemo lashav* — the gravity of invoking God's name in a false or unfulfilled oath. How, then, does one obligate oneself to do or to avoid doing a particular action, when one wants to avoid the weightier instrument of *shvua*?

The answer is to use *neder* instrumentally, directing it at an object in such a way that the *neder* will create indirect pressure on one's actions. The *neder* does not forbid the action; it makes the object *asur*, and then the stakes of the *neder* bear upon whether the action is taken.

### Fruit Trip Example

A concrete example: suppose I am trying to ensure that I actually make a long-deferred trip to Philadelphia. Rather than swear that I will go — which would invoke *shem shamayim* — I can say: all fruit in the world shall be *asur* to me if I fail to make this trip. Now I am strongly motivated to make the trip, not because the act of not going is directly forbidden but because I do not want to suffer the consequence of losing access to all fruit. The *neder* has translated into behavioral compulsion through the object.

The case of the loaf of bread works the same way, though it introduces a twilight zone of uncertainty. I said: this loaf is *asur* to me today if I go to Philadelphia tomorrow. Now, during this period, I do not know whether the *neder* will ultimately kick in. This is what generates the entire debate of *Rav Yehuda* and *Rav Nachman*: may I eat the bread and trust myself not to go tomorrow? The phenomenon is perfectly natural — using *nedarim* on objects to push oneself toward or away from certain actions — but the *tnai* structure introduces complexities about how much we can trust the person to maintain the condition.

---

## Husband Forbids Sex

### Konam Sex Mishna

The *gemara* now turns to a *mishna* that asks whether a husband can use *konam* to forbid conjugal relations: *ha-omer le-isha konam she-ani mishamshech harei zeh be-val yachel dvarav* — if the man says to his wife *konam* that I will not have sex with you, this is subject to *bal yachel*. Here we are operating, as the *mishna* established, in the *derabbanan* realm — the husband is forbidding not his body per se but the *hana'ah* of the act, the abstract pleasure of the sexual encounter, which is a *davar she'ein bo mamash*.

### She'ar Kesut Obligation

The *gemara* immediately challenges: *ve-ha mishtabed lah mid'oraita* — but he is biblically indebted to her, as it says *she'erah kesutah ve'onatah lo yigra* — he cannot withhold her food, clothing, or conjugal relations. One might think that this biblical obligation simply overrides any *neder* he could take. But that cannot be the full answer — after all, a person can make a *neder* that *tefillin* be *konam* on him, thereby indirectly undermining his biblical obligation to wear *tefillin*, since the *neder* forbids the object rather than directly confronting the *mitzvah*. The same logic would seem to apply here: let him forbid the *hana'ah* on her, and then when it comes time for the *mitzvas onah*, he simply cannot fulfill it because the object — as it were — is *asur*.

### Wife's Property Rights

The reason the *gemara* rejects this approach, however, is not the existence of an obligation but the existence of a *shibud* — a property claim. The *Ran* formulates this with precision: *de-lo matzi avid de-mid'oraita meshubed lah ve-havei ke-oser nichsei chavero al chaveiro* — he cannot make this *neder* because biblically he is *meshubed* to her, and his attempt to make his sexual pleasure *asur* on her is like trying to forbid a friend's property to that same friend. She has a form of property rights, a lien, on his body with respect to conjugal relations. It is hers, in a meaningful sense. And one cannot make *asur* on another person what already belongs to that person.

The distinction is important. Obligation alone would not block the *neder*; the indirect structure of *neder*-on-object routinely allows a person to undermine his own obligations. What blocks the *neder* here is *ownership*: she effectively owns a claim to his conjugal attention, and he therefore cannot make it *asur* to her.

### Pleasure Forbidden on Se…

The *gemara* therefore specifies the loophole: *be-omer hana'as tashmishech alai* — if instead the husband says, "the pleasure I would derive from you is *konam* on *me*," that formulation works. He is not forbidding her property to her; he is forbidding her property to himself. Anyone may make anything *asur* to themselves, including another person's property. He can make her car *asur* to himself; he can similarly make her sexual pleasure *asur* to himself. The *neder* thus takes effect. Indirectly, this prevents him from fulfilling *mitzvas onah*, but as we have established, indirect undermining of a *mitzvah* through *neder*-on-object does not invalidate the *neder*. They could not sustain the marriage under these conditions and would be required to divorce, but the *neder* itself is valid.

---

## Wife Forbids Sex

### Wife Forbids Pleasure

The *gemara* then turns to the reverse case. *Rav Kahana* states: if a wife says *tashmishi alecha* — my sexual pleasure is *konam* on you — then *kofin oso u-meshamshaseto* — we compel her nonetheless to have conjugal relations with her husband. She cannot make this *neder* effective against him.

### Husband's Shibud

The reasoning is exactly parallel to the earlier case. *De-shibuda meshubada lei* — her body, with respect to conjugal relations, is *meshubed* to him. Just as she has a property claim on him for *onah*, he has a corresponding claim on her. Therefore, when she attempts to forbid her sexual pleasure on him, she is in the same position as the husband who tried to forbid his sexual pleasure on his wife: she is attempting to make *asur* on the other person something that already belongs to that person. It cannot be done.

However, if she were to say *hana'as tashmishecha alai* — the sexual pleasure I would derive from you is *konam* on *me* — that formulation would work, on the same logic as the husband's case. She is making something *asur* to herself, and *she'ein machilin lo le-adam davar ha-asur lo* — one does not cause a person to receive what is forbidden to them. At that point, she is forbidden to have conjugal relations, and they would be required to divorce.

### Equal Marital Rights

This *gemara* is, in the context of the broader *masechet*, extraordinarily significant — and not only for the halachic mechanics of *nedarim*. What is striking is that the *gemara* begins with the husband's case, and there it posits not merely that he has a *mitzvah* to have sex with his wife, but that she holds an actual *shibud* on him — a property claim on his conjugal attentions. That framing is then replicated precisely and symmetrically in the wife's case: his *shibud* on her mirrors hers on him.

The conventional framing of marital sexuality in halachic literature centers on the verse *she'erah kesutah ve'onatah lo yigra* — his *mitzvah* to provide for her conjugal needs — and the wife's right to demand sex at regular intervals. What receives far less explicit attention is his corresponding right to have sex with her, and whether that right is personal obligation or property-claim. This *gemara* answers that question by using the exact same language in both directions: *meshubed lah* and *meshubeda lei*. The *shibud* is equal and parallel. One spouse cannot make forbidden to the other what that other person has a property claim upon, and this principle applies identically regardless of which direction the *neder* is attempted.

In a broader cultural context where woman as sexual property of the man has been the dominant framework for millennia, this *sugya* — encountered here in *Masechet Nedarim* of all places — quietly posits the man as equally the sexual property of the woman within the marriage, using precisely the same legal language in both cases. It is a remarkable conceptual statement about the nature of marital rights, and it emerges through the very particular lens of how *nedarim* interact with the property structure of conjugal obligations.

---

---

# Nedarim 16

## Neder vs. Shevuah

### Previous Daf Review

The present *daf* picks up from the *mishnah* at the bottom of 15b, which addressed a range of fundamental conceptual issues. Among them: the husband's and wife's respective rights over one another's person, and how that mutual quasi-ownership bears on the enforceability of a *neder*. The sugya also treated the concept of *bal yachel* — specifically, a rabbinic *bal yachel* applying even to abstract matters such as sleeping or walking, where no physical object is directly involved. Finally, it examined whether a *minhag* of treating certain things as forbidden can rise to the level of a *neder*, particularly in the context of *mitzvah*-related acts, which have their own relationship to the more biblical dimensions of the prohibition on vow violation.

### Ran vs. Rambam

One critical point from the previous discussion deserves brief review: the dispute between the Ran and the Rambam regarding who receives lashes for violating a *neder*. The Ran holds that lashes follow the violation of the object's status — once the object has been rendered forbidden, anyone who violates that status receives lashes. The Rambam disagrees. He maintains that *lo yachel devaro* — the biblical prohibition — is violated only by the person who both made the vow and then broke it. It is not that the Rambam permits a third party to violate the *neder*; rather, in his view, the biblical lashes are reserved for the person whose own word is being desecrated. The Ran focuses exclusively on the object's status; the Rambam focuses on the act of personal betrayal of one's own oath.

### Shevuah Actions

The *mishnah* now states: *shevuah she'aini yashen, she'aini medaber, she'aini mehalech — assur*. If someone takes a *shevuah* that he will not sleep, not speak, or not walk, it is forbidden. This is relatively straightforward, since a *shevuah* concerning actions — committing oneself not to perform a particular act — is the classic form of a *shevuah*. The notable *chiddush* was actually in the prior *mishnah*, which established that even a *konam* formulation applied to abstract actions like sleeping or speaking is binding, albeit only rabbinically.

### Neder Language

There is also an important linguistic distinction between the two instruments. A *shevuah* is articulated in the negative: *she'aini mehalech* — "I will not walk." A *neder*, by contrast, is articulated in the positive: *she'ani mehalech* — "my walking is forbidden," rendering the act itself a kind of *korban*-like prohibition. Furthermore, as the earlier analysis established, when the *neder* concerns an abstract action rather than a concrete physical object, its force is only rabbinic, whereas the *shevuah* in the same case operates at the biblical level.

---

## Korban Formulations

### Korban Lo Ochal

The *mishnah* now turns to a series of *neder* formulations involving the word *korban*, contrasting those that are binding with those that are not. Three formulations are presented as non-binding: *korban lo ochel lecha* ("a *korban* is my not-eating of yours"), *ha-korban she-ochel lecha*, and *lo korban lo ochel lecha*.

The first case is relatively clear. When someone says *korban lo ochel lecha*, they are framing the *neder* around the non-eating — essentially saying "a *korban* is my not eating your food." But a *neder* operates by rendering the object forbidden; the classic formulation is *korban she-ochel lecha* — "that which I would eat of yours is a *korban*." Framing the *neder* around the negative does not accomplish this. At most it could be read as an attempt to swear in the name of a *korban* that one will not eat — which is *lashon shevuah*, not *lashon neder* — and in any case one cannot take a *shevuah* in the name of a *korban*. So this formulation fails entirely.

### Ha-Korban Pause

The middle case is the most interesting. *Korban she-ochel lecha* — without the *heh* — would indeed be a binding *neder*: "that which I eat of yours is a *korban*." But if one says *ha-korban she-ochel lecha*, the addition of the *heh* followed by a pause transforms the meaning. Rather than using *korban* as the predicate describing the object's status, the speaker is now using *ha* as an interjection — "Behold! By a *korban*, I will eat of yours!" — which shifts the formulation into the realm of *lashon shevuah*: an oath taken in the name of a *korban*. And since one cannot take a *shevuah* in the name of a *korban*, this formulation also fails to bind.

### Klal Lav Atah

The third formulation — *lo korban lo ochel lecha* — might seem promising. If it is not a *korban* that I will not eat, one might reason by *miklal lav atah shomea hen* that what I will eat is indeed a *korban*. However, the *mishnah* does not accept this inference. Our *mishnah* follows the view of Rabbi Meir, who does not apply the principle of *miklal lav atah shomea hen* in this context. The double negative does not suffice to constitute a positive *neder*, and therefore the formulation is *mutar*.

### Gemara Mani

The *gemara* asks: *mani matnisin?* — whose view does our *mishnah* represent? The answer is Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda would not distinguish between *korban* and *ha-korban* at all, because in his view the very word *korban* without a prefix such as *ke-* does not constitute a valid *neder* formulation. Rabbi Yehuda requires *ke-korban lo ochel lecha* — without the *kaf*, neither formulation works. The *mishnah*, however, implies that *korban she-ochel lecha* would be sufficient, which reflects Rabbi Meir's position that prefixes are not required.

The *gemara* then turns to the end of the *mishnah* and notes an apparent tension. Elsewhere we have learned *li-korban lo ochel lecha* — Rabbi Meir says it is forbidden. This is explained by Rabbi Abba: *li-korban* is read as a sentence with a pause — "Let it be a *korban*" — full stop — "and therefore I will not eat of yours." But if that is so, why does the *mishnah* here rule that *lo korban lo ochel lecha* is permitted? The *gemara* answers: there is no difficulty. When one says *li-korban*, the prefix *lamed* signals an affirmative commitment — it should be a *korban*, therefore I will not eat. But when one says *lo korban*, one is saying it is not a *korban* — and to then infer that what I will eat is a *korban* would require applying *miklal lav atah shomea hen*, which Rabbi Meir rejects. The two rulings are thus fully consistent.

---

## Shevuah Works

### Shevuah Classic

Having established which *neder* formulations fail, the *mishnah* now contrasts these with the parallel *shevuah* formulations — all of which are binding. *Shevuah lo ochel lecha* — a *shevuah* that I will not eat of yours — is the straightforward case, a classic prohibitory oath.

### Ha-Shevuah

The more complex cases are *ha-shevuah she-ochel lecha* and *lo shevuah lo ochel lecha*, both of which the *mishnah* rules are *assur*. This is striking because the exact same linguistic structures that rendered the *neder* formulations invalid are now said to produce binding obligations. The puzzle is particularly sharp regarding *she-ochel lecha* — "that I will eat." Why should saying one will eat be interpreted as a prohibition against eating? And regarding *lo shevuah lo ochel lecha*, even if one reverses the double negative, one arrives at *shevuah she-ochel lecha* — and the same question recurs.

The *gemara* immediately seizes on this: *miklal d'ha shevuah she-ochel lecha — de-lo achilna mashma?* Are we really saying that a *shevuah* formulated as "I will eat" means one may not eat? The *gemara* cites the well-known *mishnah* in *Shevuot* — *shevuot shtayim she-hein arba* — where the four categories of *shevuah* include both *she-ochel* ("I will eat") and *she-lo ochel* ("I will not eat") as distinct and opposite types. Clearly, saying *she-ochel* in that context means one is obligating oneself to eat — not forbidding it. So how can our *mishnah* treat *shevuah she-ochel lecha* as a prohibition?

### Abaye Context

Abaye resolves this by appealing to context. The words *she-ochel* carry two potential meanings depending on the situation in which they are uttered. If people were pressing someone to eat — insisting again and again — and he finally relented and said *shevuah she-ochel* ("I swear I will eat"), then indeed *de-achilna mashma* — it means he is committing to eat. But if the person had been refusing — *lo achilna, lo achilna* — "I'm not eating, I'm not eating" — and then declared *shevuah she-ochel lecha*, the phrase functions differently. In that context, *she-ochel* is understood as a conditional: "Should I eat of yours, let me have violated a *shevuah*" — meaning, were I to eat, I would be transgressing. This is a refusal reinforced by oath, not a commitment to eat. The *she-ochel*, in context, means *de-lo achilna*.

The default meaning, as established by the *mishnah* in *Shevuot*, is that *she-ochel* means one will eat. Context of refusal can reverse this, but the reversal is entirely context-dependent.

### Rav Ashi Text

Rav Ashi takes a different approach entirely. Rather than appealing to contextual interpretation, he proposes an emended reading of the *mishnah*: the *mishnah* does not actually say *she-ochel* but rather *she-ei ochel* — with a prolonged *alef*, signifying "that I do not eat." This would make the *mishnah*'s ruling entirely straightforward — *shevuah she-ei ochel* is transparently prohibitory — without requiring any appeal to context.

The *gemara* then asks: if that is what the *mishnah* means, what is the *chiddush*? The answer is that one might have thought: perhaps someone who says *she-ei ochel* has simply mispronounced *she-ochel* — slipping up — and should be understood as intending to eat. The *gemara* therefore teaches that we do not reinterpret the words on that basis; the unusual phrasing *she-ei ochel* is taken at face value and treated as binding.

### Abaye Rejects

However, Abaye does not accept Rav Ashi's approach. The *gemara* notes, in strikingly unusual language — *Abaye lo amar ta'am k'Rav Ashi* — that Abaye distanced himself from Rav Ashi's reading. The reason is that Rav Ashi is changing the *girsa* of the *mishnah*: the *mishnah* as transmitted says *she-ochel*, and Rav Ashi emends it to *she-ei ochel*. Abaye refuses to alter the text.

Rav Ashi, in turn, does not say like Abaye — *nadi min ta'am d'Abaye* — because he rejects the entire framework of context-dependent meaning. His objection is principled: if *she-ochel* can mean "I will not eat" depending on context, then equally *she-lo ochel* could mean "I will eat" in the right circumstances. One could imagine a scenario where someone is rhetorically asked, "Should you not eat?" and responds *shevuah she-lo ochel* — meaning, were I not to eat I would have violated a *shevuah*, thus implying he must eat. If every formulation is context-dependent, nothing means anything with certainty, and the *mishnah* cannot be teaching reliable rules. The *mishnah* must therefore be taken to establish fixed, context-independent meanings: *she-ochel* means "I will eat" and *she-lo ochel* means "I will not eat." Abaye's contextual approach, however sensible in theory, cannot serve as the basis for a *mishnah* whose purpose is to teach definitive rules, since a teacher cannot transmit context along with a ruling.

### Tosafot Gezeira

One further difficulty with the *mishnah*'s ruling remains: why is *lo shevuah lo ochel lecha* binding? Even granting that one reverses the double negative to derive *shevuah she-ochel lecha*, we are back at the question of why that formulation is prohibited. Tosafot addresses this with a distinct argument: the binding force of *lo shevuah lo ochel lecha* rests not on logical inference but on a rabbinic *gezeira*. The concern is that a person might accidentally drop the first *lo*, transforming *lo shevuah lo ochel lecha* into *shevuah she-lo ochel* — a classically binding prohibitory oath. To prevent this slippage, the rabbis treated even the full *lo shevuah lo ochel lecha* as binding. This stands in contrast to the *neder* parallel — *lo korban lo ochel lecha* — where even if one drops the first *lo* and arrives at *korban lo ochel lecha*, that formulation is also non-binding. Hence there was no reason to decree stringency in the *neder* case, but there was such a reason in the *shevuah* case.

---

## Shevuah Stricter

### Zeh Chomer

The *mishnah* summarizes: *zeh chomer b'shevuot mib'nedarim* — this is the stringency of *shevuah* over *neder*. The cases just discussed — where the same linguistic formulations are binding when expressed as a *shevuah* but not when expressed as a *neder* — illustrate one dimension of this stringency. But there is also an earlier and more fundamental contrast. When the *mishnah* earlier taught that *shevuah she'aini yashen, she'aini medaber, she'aini mehalech — assur*, this too reflects a stringency of *shevuah* over *neder* — not because a *neder* on such matters fails entirely (for *konam she'ani mehalech* is indeed binding), but because the *shevuah* is biblically binding, whereas the *neder* on abstract actions — on walking, speaking, sleeping, things that are not physical objects — is only rabbinically binding. Biblical versus rabbinic: that is the weight of the contrast in the earlier formulations.

---

## Neder Stricter

### Mitzva Objects

Having shown how a *shevuah* is stricter than a *neder* in certain respects, the *mishnah* now turns to the reverse: *v'chomer b'nedarim mib'shevuot*. The example given: *amar konam sukkah she'ani oseh, lulav she'ani notel, tfillin she'ani maniach* — one declares the *sukkah*, *lulav*, or *tfillin* as *konam* upon him, whether for building, taking, or wearing.

### Neder Works

By a *neder*, such a formulation is binding. The person has not directly contradicted his biblical obligation to sit in a *sukkah* or take a *lulav*. He has instead spoken about the status of the object — rendering it forbidden to himself. When *Sukkot* arrives and he cannot use the object, his failure to fulfill the *mitzvah* is a downstream consequence, not a direct countermanding of God's command.

### Shevuah Fails

By a *shevuah*, however, this does not work — *she'ein nishba'in la'avor al ha-mitzvot*. One cannot take a *shevuah* to transgress a *mitzvah*. A *shevuah* operates in the domain of direct personal obligation: one commits to do or refrain from doing something. To take a *shevuah* not to sit in a *sukkah* is to directly pit one's oath against God's command — operating in *cheftzei Shamayim*, in God's domain rather than one's own. Such a *shevuah* does not take effect and remains non-binding. The person may sit in the *sukkah* without any violation of the oath. However, the act of having taken such a *shevuah* is itself a transgression: it constitutes a *shevuat shav* — an oath taken in vain — for which one receives lashes. The *shevuah* was stillborn from the moment of its utterance, but the utterance itself was a biblical violation.

---

## Shevuah Stricter (II)

### Biblical vs. Rabbinic

The *gemara* notes a possible ambiguity in the *mishnah*'s phrasing *zeh chomer b'shevuot mib'nedarim*. Does this refer to the cases just discussed regarding *korban* formulations, or to the earlier cases about sleeping and walking? The *gemara* concludes that it refers to the earlier section — *aseifa d'eidach baba katani* — the language about *shevuah she'aini yashen, she'aini medaber, she'aini mehalech*. In those cases, both a *shevuah* and a *neder* are binding, but the *shevuah* is weightier: it is a biblical prohibition, whereas the *neder* on abstract actions that are not physical objects is only rabbinic. That is the stringency: identical subject matter, but different levels of normative force.

---

## Cheftzei Shamayim

### Rav Gidel Source

The *gemara* now takes up the basis for the rule that one cannot take a *shevuah* to countermand a *mitzvah* obligation. Rav Kahana teaches in the name of Rav Gidel in the name of Rav; and Rav Tavyomi teaches the same in the name of Rav Gidel in the name of Shmuel. The question is: *minayin she'ein nishba'in la'avor al ha-mitzvot?* From where do we know this?

### Lo Yachel Devaro

The answer is *lo yachel devaro*. This verse applies both to *neder* and to *shevuah*, as the full *pasuk* reads: *ki yidor neder l'Hashem o hishava shevuah le'esor issar al nafsho lo yachel devaro* — whether he vows a *neder* to God or swears a *shevuah* to bind himself, he shall not desecrate his word. The prohibition of *lo yachel devaro* thus governs both instruments.

### Personal vs. Divine

The *gemara* derives from this verse: *devaro lo yachel aval meichalu hu l'cheftzei Shamayim* — regarding his own matters, he shall not violate his word; but regarding *cheftzei Shamayim* — God's matters — it may be violated, because it never took effect. The verse's application of *lo yachel* is to *devaro* — his word, in his domain. When a person attempts to make a binding commitment in God's domain, the commitment does not attach, and what was never binding can be set aside without transgression.

This distinction — *cheftzei* as a division between personal and divine domains — appears elsewhere in halachic literature as well. Regarding *Shabbat*, the verse *mimtzo cheftzecha v'daber davar* gives rise to the rule: *cheftzecha asurim ve-cheftzei Shamayim mutarim* — one's personal affairs are restricted on *Shabbat*, while matters of *cheftzei Shamayim* are permitted, which is why a *shul* may make announcements about communal Torah activities. Similarly, the principle of *osek b'mitzvah patur min ha-mitzvah* flows from *beshivtecha b'veitecha uvelachtecha vaderech* — *beshivtecha didach uvelachtecha didach* — when you are in your own sphere of action, the obligations of *mitzvot* apply; but when already engaged in God's domain, the calculus shifts.

### Gemara Question

A sharp question then arises. Both *neder* and *shevuah* appear in the same *pasuk* under the same rubric of *lo yachel devaro*, and both are said *l'Hashem*: *ki yidor neder l'Hashem* and *o hishava shevuah l'Hashem*. If the *l'Hashem* of the *shevuah* signals that one cannot operate in God's domain and thereby removes the binding force of such a *shevuah*, why does the *l'Hashem* of the *neder* not produce the same result? Why is a *neder* on *mitzvah* objects binding while a *shevuah* on *mitzvah* acts is not?

---

## Abaye Distinction

### Benefit vs. Use

Abaye answers that the difference lies not in the wording of the verse but in the inherent structure of the two acts. The critical formulations are: *hanat sukkah alai* — the benefit of the *sukkah* is forbidden to me — versus *shevuah she-lo ehena min ha-sukkah* — a *shevuah* that I will not derive benefit from the *sukkah*. In the *neder* formulation, one is not directly forbidding the act God commanded; one is rendering the object's benefit forbidden to oneself. When *Sukkot* comes, one cannot execute the *mitzvah* because the object is unavailable in the relevant sense — but one has not directly said "I will not sit in a *sukkah*." The *shevuah*, by contrast, directly targets the act itself and places a personal oath against the fulfillment of a divine command. That is why it fails.

### Rava Objection

Rava accepts the logical structure of Abaye's distinction but objects to the specific articulation. *V'chi mitzvot lehanot nitnu?* — Are *mitzvot* given in order to derive benefit from them? Performing a *mitzvah* is not classified as *hana'ah* in halachic terms. Therefore, saying *hanat sukkah alai* — the benefit of the *sukkah* is forbidden to me — would not prevent one from sitting in the *sukkah*, since sitting in a *sukkah* to fulfill the *mitzvah* does not constitute *hana'ah*. The *neder* on *hana'ah* would be ineffective in preventing the *mitzvah* in those terms.

---

## Hana'ah Definition

### Mitzvot Framework

The principle at stake here is *mitzvot lav lehanot nitnu* — *mitzvot* are not given for the purpose of deriving pleasure. This is not a sweeping theological statement about our attitude toward the commandments; it is a halachic classification of what counts as *hana'ah*. Halachic *hana'ah* is defined in this-worldly, physical terms. Fulfilling a religious obligation — accumulating, as it were, merit or spiritual satisfaction — does not qualify as physical benefit for the purposes of *neder* law.

### Knowledge Examples

A parallel illustration: may a non-*kohen* study a cadaver for the purpose of medical and anatomical education? The *poskim* generally permit it, despite the general prohibition against deriving *hana'ah* from a corpse. The reason is that intellectual expansion — gaining knowledge — is not classified as *hana'ah* in the operative halachic sense, even though from a broader perspective it may represent the highest form of human fulfillment. Similarly, *mitzvah* performance is not *hana'ah* in halachic terms, however central it is to Jewish life. This has a further wrinkle in contexts like *Tisha B'Av*, where Torah study is prohibited — but there the reason is *simcha*, joy, not *hana'ah*, pleasure, and the distinction between the two is meaningful.

---

## Abaye Distinction (II)

### Rava Solution

Given that *mitzvot lav lehanot nitnu*, Rava reformulates the operative *neder* language. Instead of *hanat sukkah alai* — which would be ineffective because *mitzvah* performance is not *hana'ah* — one must say *yeshivat sukkah alai* — the sitting in this *sukkah* is forbidden to me. This targets not the benefit derived from the object but a specific use of it. A *neder* can render an object forbidden with respect to particular actions or uses, not only with respect to conventional *hana'ah*. This is an important expansion of the concept of *neder*: it can prohibit certain modes of engagement with an object even where no conventional physical benefit is involved.

---

## Object Mention

### Non-Benefit Actions

The Ran draws out an important implication of this principle. Since a *neder* can operate on actions rather than only on *hana'ah*, one can in principle make a *neder* on a completely non-benefit action — his example is *konam zerikat tzor le-yam alav* — declaring this rock as *konam* upon him with respect to throwing it into the ocean. Even though there is no *hana'ah* in throwing a pebble into the sea, the *neder* is binding: *af al pi she'ein lo bi-zerikah zo hana'ah, assur le-zorko*.

### Explicit Requirement

However, the Ran adds a critical qualification: this works only if one is explicit. *Davka bi-meforesh* — one must specify the forbidden action. If one says *konam sukkah alai le-yeshivatah*, or *konam zerikat tzor* with the explicit action named, it is binding on that specific use.

### Default Hana'ah

But if one simply says *konam sukkah alai* or *konam tzor alai* — a generic declaration without specifying the forbidden mode of engagement — the default operative meaning of *konam* is *assur b'hana'ah*. The person would be forbidden to derive conventional benefit from the object but would be permitted to throw the rock into the ocean or to sit in the *sukkah* for *mitzvah* purposes (to the extent that is itself problematic). The word *konam*, standing alone, defaults to forbidding *hana'ah*. If the intention is to forbid something other than *hana'ah*, it must be made explicit.

### Tosafot Object

Tosafot offers a different position on a related question. The Ran holds that saying *yeshivat sukkah alai* — "the sitting in a *sukkah* is upon me as forbidden" — without mentioning the *sukkah* as a concrete object might be only a rabbinic *neder*, since the thing being forbidden is a *davar she'ein bo mamash* — an action without physical substance. Tosafot disagrees. In their view, the *neder* becomes fully binding, and is not classified as a *davar she'ein bo mamash*, as long as one mentions the name of some object in the formulation. Since *yeshivat sukkah alai* includes the word *sukkah*, even though the explicit subject is the act of sitting rather than the object itself, the mention of the object is sufficient to give the *neder* the status of one bearing on a physical thing, and it is therefore binding at the biblical level.

---

---

# Nedarim 17

## Neder vs. Shevua

### Opening & Prior Issues

The daf opens a new *mishna*, continuing the trend of the preceding pages in moving from technical language distinctions toward more fundamental conceptual issues. By way of review: earlier *mishnayot* had drawn a distinction between *shevua* and *neder* in terms of language, and then moved to discuss the ways in which *nedarim* are more stringent, or at least broader in their effect, than *shevuot*. The key point established there was that a *neder* can indirectly prevent the performance of a *mitzvah* by rendering an object forbidden — since the *neder* operates on the object itself — whereas a *shevua* directed against one's own obligation would not take effect, given that *mitzvot* are not considered a halakhic form of *hana'ah*. This also generated an important discussion about the scope of what a *neder* can prohibit: whether it is limited to the domain of eating and benefit, or whether it can extend to other types of interactions with an object.

### Language & Effect Scope

Central to those earlier discussions was the structural distinction between *neder* and *shevua*: a *neder* operates on an object, changing its status relative to the person; a *shevua* operates on the person, generating a personal obligation. The *neder*'s capacity to act on objects gives it a wider potential reach — it can, at least in principle, touch areas beyond benefit and eating — whereas the *shevua*'s direct confrontation with a pre-existing personal obligation creates its own set of limitations.

### New Mishna Overview

The *mishna* on daf 17 now introduces a further dimension of this *neder*-*shevua* distinction, one connected, though perhaps less directly, to the object-versus-person dichotomy: *yesh neder betoch neder ve'ein shevua betoch shevua* — one may make a *neder* within, or on top of, another *neder*, but one may not make a *shevua* on top of another *shevua*. The discussion that follows unpacks precisely what this asymmetry means and why it exists.

---

## Nazir Status Principle

### Nazir as Status

The *mishna*'s immediate example of a *neder* is striking: it chooses *nezirut*. This is not incidental. The Torah itself uses the word *neder* in connection with *nazir* — *ish ki yafli lindor neder nazir* — using the term twice, signaling that *nezirut* is a species of *neder*. More importantly, *nezirut* illustrates something essential about the nature of a *neder*: it is a speech act that changes a *status*. Rather than rendering an external object forbidden, the declaration of *nezirut* imparts upon the person himself the status of being a *nazir*. This, like other *nedarim*, is about using speech to effect a halakhic transformation — here applied to the person rather than to an object, but still operating through the logic of status-imposition. As will become clear, *nezirut* turns out to be the only form of *neder* that fits the *mishna*'s case, and the reason for this will emerge from the analysis below.

### Conditional Nazir

The *mishna* presents the case as follows: a person says *harei ani nazir im ochal* — "I will be a *nazir* if I eat" — and then immediately repeats the same declaration: *harei ani nazir im ochal*. He then eats. The *mishna* rules *chayav al kol achat ve'achat* — he is obligated for each one.

### Hovering Nezirut

A simple reading might suggest he becomes a double *nazir* — requiring two sets of *korbanot* at the end of thirty days, or receiving two sets of lashes for willful violation. But the *Gemara* does not read it that way. Rather, the *Gemara* understands the ruling to mean that after the first *nezirut* concludes, the second *nezirut* then takes effect. The result is a total of sixty days, structured as two successive periods of thirty: he completes the first, brings its *korbanot*, finishes that *nezirut*, and then begins and completes the second. The second *nezirut* was, during the first, in a kind of suspended state — hovering, waiting to take effect once the first status was removed.

### No Overlay Principle

This hovering phenomenon emerges from a fundamental principle that applies equally to *neder* and *shevua*: a second prohibition, status, or obligation cannot take effect on top of an existing one. The principle is *ein issur chal al issur* — one prohibition cannot take effect on top of another. Applied to *neder*, it becomes *ein neder chal al neder*; applied to *shevua*, *ein shevua chala al shevua*. What distinguishes *nezirut* is that the underlying status is intrinsically time-bound and terminal: it will end. Because it ends, the second *nezirut* does not simply disappear — it remains in suspension and takes effect the moment the first status is removed.

---

## Shevua Overlay

### Parallel Shevua Case

The parallel *shevua* case in the *mishna* is this: a person declares *shevua shelo ochal* — a *shevua* that he will not eat — and then immediately declares the same *shevua* again. He eats. The *mishna* rules he is *eino chayav ela achat* — liable only once. The second *shevua* simply did not take effect.

### Mushba Ve'omed

The reason invoked is the principle of *mushba ve'omed*: the person is already bound — either from *har Sinai* in the case of standing obligations, or from his first *shevua* in this case. A *shevua* cannot create an obligation on top of a pre-existing one. Since the person is already obligated not to eat this bread, the second *shevua* adding the same obligation is without effect.

### Shevua Concepts

This principle deserves careful examination, because it is less self-evident than it might appear. One must distinguish it from the case of a *shevua* that countermands an existing obligation — for example, a *shevua* that one will not sit in a *sukkah*. That would be a *shevuat shav*, a vain oath, and it would be a transgression at the moment of utterance, but it would not itself become a binding obligation. But a *shevua* to perform something one is already obligated in is a different matter. Why should it not take effect? Much depends on how one conceptualizes the nature of a *shevua*.

There are two ways to think about a *shevua* directed at the future. One view is that by swearing in God's name that one will do something, one has not so much created an abstract obligation as committed to a true or false statement about the future: if one does not do the thing, one will have sworn falsely, having invoked God's name for a declaration that turned out untrue. Under that framing, the question of whether the person was already obligated is somewhat beside the point — the issue is whether the oath was ultimately honored or not. If a person swears to put on *tefillin* and fails to do so, he has sworn falsely regardless of whether he was already biblically obligated.

But the rule of *ein shevua chala al shevua* implies a different conceptualization: the *shevua* is understood primarily as generating an obligation. The oath creates a halakhic duty. Under that model, one cannot generate an obligation on top of an already-existing obligation, because there is nothing new to obligate. I am already obligated — what does it mean to obligate myself a second time? This is the framework in which the rule makes internal sense, and it is a meaningful *chiddush*, because it moves the analysis away from the question of true-and-false swearing and toward the language of obligation and its creation.

### Shevua on Mitzvot

This tension surfaced earlier in the *Gemara* — on daf 8 — in the famous passage asking *minayin shenishba'in lekayem es hamitzvah*: how do we know one may swear to fulfill a *mitzvah*? The verse cited is *nishbati va'akayema lishmor mishpetei tzidkecha*. The *Gemara* there raised the objection: *vehalo mushba ve'omed mehar Sinai hu* — is he not already bound from *Sinai*? The resolution was *desharei lei le'inish lezarzuzei nafshei* — it is permitted for a person to do this in order to encourage and motivate himself. This implies that such an oath is not technically binding in a full halakhic sense, but is permitted as an act of self-encouragement, perhaps operative *miderabbanan* or in some looser form. The underlying analysis is precisely the point made above: if a *shevua* generates an obligation, you cannot generate what already exists; what is left is only a gesture of personal reinforcement.

---

## Status vs. Obligation

### Parallel Structures

The structural parallelism between the two principles can now be stated clearly: *ein neder chal al neder* and *ein shevua chala al shevua* are formally parallel, but they derive from different conceptual foundations. The *neder* operates by imposing a status of prohibition on an object; the *shevua* operates by generating a personal obligation. In both cases, the rule is that you cannot impose on what already exists.

### Logic Constraints

There is, however, a significant tension in the *neder* case that demands attention. The general principle *ein issur chal al issur* already applies to objects independently of any speech act: if something is already forbidden as, say, *neveilah*, does it then also become forbidden as *basar bechalav*? Perhaps not — because the object already carries a forbidden status, and one cannot layer a second forbidden status on top of the first. This is, admittedly, conceptually puzzling on its face, since one might ask why an object cannot carry multiple prohibitions simultaneously. But this principle exists and is operative in halakha. Given that, one might expect a *neder* — which also operates on an object — to face the same bar. And indeed it does. The crucial clarification is this: a standard *konam* declaration — *konam kikar zeh alai*, repeated twice — would be entirely ineffective the second time. The second *neder* on a normal forbidden object means nothing; *ein issur chal al issur*. It is only *nezirut* that behaves differently, for the reasons now to be examined.

The parallel question arises for *shevua*: if we understand a *shevua* as generating an obligation, then *ein shevua chala al shevua* follows directly. But if we instead emphasize the dimension of true-and-false swearing, the logic is less obvious, and the rule becomes a genuine *chiddush*. The fact that the rule exists at all thus tells us something important about how the *Gemara* conceptualizes the *shevua*: primarily as obligation-generating rather than primarily as a truth-commitment.

The resulting picture is this: by *shevua*, we focus on creating an obligation, and we say one obligation cannot take effect on top of another. By *neder*, we focus on creating a status, and we say one status cannot take effect on top of another. What we are left with as the genuinely distinctive case is *nezirut*.

### Nezirut Termination

*Nezirut* is intrinsically a bounded, terminal unit. Unlike a vague or indefinite prohibition, *nezirut* is structured: it is a defined period — thirty days by default — with a clear endpoint marked by the bringing of *korbanot*. When a person attempts to accept two *neziruyot*, the first is seen as a time-bound, temporary status; the second remains in suspension, hovering, ready to take effect the moment the first concludes. This hovering is the genuine *chiddush* of *nezirut*.

A natural question arises: why is hovering not available for a *shevua* or a standard *neder*? Consider a *shevua* not to eat a loaf of bread today: could a second identical *shevua* not simply hover and take effect the next day when the first one has run its course? The problem is that if the *shevua* is temporally defined — "not today" — then when today ends, there is no longer anything to hover over. And if the second *shevua* is open-ended — "not to eat this bread" — then one might wonder whether hovering could apply. But ultimately, the conceptual difference is that *nezirut* is a self-contained temporal unit, intrinsically designed to end and restart, which is precisely what makes the hovering model natural. For *shevua*, focused on personal obligation, there is no comparable termination-and-restart structure. The hovering model, then, is a *chiddush* peculiar to *nezirut* — and the interesting observation is that even a standard *neder* on an object does not share it.

---

## Rav Huna's View

### Distinction Required

*Rav Huna* addresses the question of precisely when the second *nezirut* can take effect. His answer: *lo shanu ela de'amar hareni nazir hayom hareni nazir lemakhar* — the rule of *yesh neder betoch neder* applies only when the person said "I am a *nazir* today" and then "I will be a *nazir* starting tomorrow." What is required is that the two *neziruyot* not be completely coextensive — that there be some temporal distinction between them.

### Extra Day Principle

The reason: *demigo deka mitosef yoma yetira* — since the second declaration adds an extra day beyond the first, the two *neziruyot* are not identical. The second will end one day later than the first. Because of this non-overlap, it takes effect.

### Two Interpretations

There are two ways to understand what *Rav Huna* requires. The first and perhaps more straightforward reading is that what matters is simply that the two *neziruyot* be conceptually distinct from one another. If you say the same thing twice, you have not introduced a second, hoverable *nezirut* — you have merely repeated yourself. But if you say something different, even slightly, you have designated a distinct second *nezirut*, and that distinctness is sufficient for it to be recognized as hovering. Under this reading, *Rav Huna*'s requirement is about the clarity of the speaker's intent to create something new.

The *Ran* offers a different understanding. He argues that the issue is not merely conceptual distinctness but actual effect: because the second *nezirut* begins one day later than the first, there is one day — day thirty-one — on which the second *nezirut* exists entirely by itself, with no first *nezirut* obstructing it. On that day, the second *nezirut* actually takes effect. And since the principle of *ein neziros pachot mishloshim yom* — *nezirut* cannot be for fewer than thirty days — once it takes effect for that one day, it retroactively obligates thirty days from that point. The extra day is therefore not just a signal of distinctness; it is the mechanism by which the second *nezirut* actually gets purchase.

This distinction between the two readings has practical consequences. Consider a person who accepts, say, a sixty-day *nezirut* and then, a week later, accepts an additional thirty-day *nezirut*. The two are clearly conceptually distinct — different durations, accepted at different moments. Yet according to the *Ran*'s reading, the second may never actually take hold, because there is no day on which it exists by itself, free of the first. On the simple reading, by contrast, their conceptual distinctness should be sufficient for the second to hover and await the conclusion of the first.

---

## Shmuel's View

### Complete Identity

*Shmuel* takes a broader position: *afilu amar hareni nazir hayom hareni nazir hayom* — even if the person said "I am a *nazir* today" and then immediately said "I am a *nazir* today" again, using an identical declaration with no temporal shift, *chala neziros aleha* — the second *nezirut* takes effect and hovers, waiting until the first concludes.

### Mishna Challenge

The *Gemara* presses *Rav Huna* from the *mishna* itself: if *Rav Huna* holds that only a shifted second *nezirut* takes effect, the *mishna* should have made this qualification explicit. It should have distinguished between *hareni nazir hayom hareni nazir lemakhar*, which would constitute *yesh neder betoch neder*, and *hareni nazir hayom hareni nazir hayom*, which would not. The *mishna*'s blanket statement — *yesh neder betoch neder* — without any such qualification suggests that even a completely identical repetition is sufficient, as *Shmuel* holds. The *Gemara* acknowledges this as a difficulty for *Rav Huna*: *kasha le'Rav Huna*.

---

## Shvuot: Figs Case

### Figs-Grapes Query

The *Gemara* now turns to the parallel *shevua* case and asks a sharper question. According to *Rav Huna*, the key feature that allows *nezirut* to be doubled up is that the two *neziruyot* are not completely coextensive — the second adds an extra day. The analogous case for *shevua* would then be: a person says a *shevua* that he will not eat figs, and then says a *shevua* that he will not eat figs and grapes. Here, too, there is a portion of the second *shevua* — the prohibition on grapes — that does not overlap with the first. Why, then, should the second *shevua* not take effect, at least with respect to the grapes?

At first glance, this might seem like an apples-and-oranges comparison. The *nezirut* case involves two *neziruyot* that are largely coextensive but for one additional day; the *shevua* case involves a prohibition on figs and an additional prohibition on an entirely different item. But the *Ran* argues that the *Gemara* is drawing a more precise analogy. The question is whether having a non-overlapping component is sufficient to allow the second item to take effect. On the *Ran*'s reading, the *Gemara*'s logic is: just as in *Rav Huna*'s view of *nezirut*, the extra day — the non-overlapping portion — is what grants the second *nezirut* its purchase, so too, the grapes — the non-overlapping portion of the second *shevua* — should grant the second *shevua* its purchase. And since we say it does not take effect, there must be a reason it fails even when there is non-overlap.

The second *shevua*, it should be understood precisely: the *Ran* reads it not as a *shevua* not to eat figs, combined with an independent *shevua* not to eat grapes, but as a single *shevua* not to eat figs and grapes together — i.e., in the same act or combination. Under that reading, the question becomes: can one be foresworn against eating figs-and-grapes-together when one is already foresworn against eating figs? One might say yes, since eating figs-and-grapes is conceptually a distinct act — and someone who violates the first *shevua* by eating figs would, upon then eating grapes, have also transgressed the second. Alternatively, one might say no: since one is already prohibited from eating figs, a prohibition against eating figs-and-grapes is without practical meaning, because one can never reach the state of eating figs-and-grapes while keeping *shevua* number one. The second *shevua* is effectively rendered redundant by the first.

### Rava's Example

*Rava* weighs in with a striking example that reveals his position. He posits: if a person took a *shevua* not to eat figs, then separately took a *shevua* not to eat figs and grapes, and then ate figs — thereby violating *shevua* number one — and then separated a *korban* for *shevua* number one, and thereafter ate grapes, what is the status of that grape-eating relative to *shevua* number two? *Rava* rules: *havei lei anavim chatzi shiur* — the grapes alone constitute only half a transgression of *shevua* number two. And since *ein mevi'in korban al chatzi shiur* — one does not bring a *korban* for half a transgression — no *korban* is owed at that point.

### Implication

The implication of *Rava*'s ruling is critical. By characterizing the grapes as *chatzi shiur* relative to *shevua* number two, *Rava* is implicitly affirming that *shevua* number two is operative — it took effect. Were it not in force, there would be no *shevua* number two to measure the grapes against. What the *korban*-separation does is segregate the fig-eating as a distinct, concluded act; now, viewing the grape-eating in isolation, it is only half of what *shevua* number two prohibits. But had the person eaten the figs and then, without separating a *korban*, immediately eaten the grapes, *Rava*'s logic implies he would have transgressed *shevua* number two as well — eating figs-and-grapes, the full prohibited combination.

This creates a direct challenge to the view that the second *shevua* in the figs-and-grapes case simply does not take effect. If *Rava* is correct, it does take effect. And if that is so, why does the *Gemara* present this as a case where the second *shevua* fails, in contrast to *nezirut*?

---

## Rav Huna vs. Rava

### Disagreement

The *Gemara* resolves the tension directly: *Rav Huna lo sevira lei ke'Rava* — *Rav Huna* does not hold like *Rava*. The two *amora'im* disagree on the underlying question of whether the figs-and-grapes *shevua* takes effect at all.

### Redundancy

*Rav Huna*'s position is that the second *shevua* is entirely without effect. The reasoning: since the person is already prohibited from eating figs by virtue of *shevua* number one, a prohibition against eating figs-and-grapes is meaningless. If one keeps *shevua* number one, one will never eat figs, and therefore will never be in a position to eat figs-and-grapes. The second *shevua* adds nothing to one's real-world behavior. It is not merely overlapping in some portion; it is substantively redundant, because the very act it prohibits — the combination — is already foreclosed by the first prohibition. This is the conceptual difference between *shevua* and *nezirut*: *nezirut* imposes a status, and a second status waiting to replace the first as it terminates has a clear identity as something distinct. But a *shevua* concerns what one will and will not do, and if you already cannot do something because of a prior *shevua*, it makes no halakhic sense to pile on an obligation that can never be independently triggered.

### Distinctness Model

*Rava*, by contrast, holds that as long as the second *shevua* is not the exact same thing as the first — as long as it has some distinct content — it takes effect. The grapes are something beyond what the first *shevua* covered, and that distinctness is sufficient. Under *Rava*'s view, the model works similarly to how *Rav Huna* himself applied it to *nezirut*: a non-overlapping element gives the second item a foothold, and once it takes hold in that area, it is effective across its full scope. *Rava* does not apply a separate conceptual framework for *shevua* versus *nezirut* — the distinctness principle operates the same way for both.

---

## Two at Once

### Single Statement

The *Gemara* raises a further case: *mi shenazar shtei nezirus* — someone who accepts two *neziruyot* in a single statement, declaring both at once rather than sequentially. This case will bear directly on the question of what *Rav Huna* truly requires and where his position finds its limit.

---

## Hataras Nedarim

### Case Setup

The scenario is as follows. Someone accepts two *neziruyot*. He counts through the first thirty days, and then, having completed the period and separated a *korban*, he goes to a *chacham* and performs *hataras nedarim* — the process by which a *chacham* retroactively dissolves a *neder* upon finding grounds for regret (*charata*). The possibility of regret even after the fact, even after one has lived through a *nezirut* and separated a *korban*, is presumably available — the *chacham* can inquire whether, had the person known how difficult it would be, he ever would have accepted it. Whatever the specific mechanism, the *chacham* dissolves the first *nezirut* retroactively.

### Retroactive Effect

The ruling: *alsa lo shniya barishona* — the second *nezirut* is deemed to have been fulfilled during those last thirty days. Retroactively, the person was not observing *nezirut* number one during that period — the *hatara* has eliminated it entirely, looking backward. But *nezirut* number two had been hovering throughout. When we now look back at those thirty days, we realize that *nezirut* one did not exist; consequently, *nezirut* two took effect during that time. The person has, retroactively, fulfilled *nezirut* number two. The *korban* he separated can be applied accordingly.

### Rav Huna Defense

This ruling poses a challenge to *Rav Huna*: the case as described says the person took two *neziruyot* — it does not specify that he said *hayom* and *lemakhar*, that is, that the two were temporally offset. If it was simply a double acceptance of identical *neziruyot*, *Rav Huna* would say the second one never took effect, and there should be nothing to retroactively credit. The *Gemara* therefore defends *Rav Huna* by reading the case as one where he had indeed said *hareni nazir hayom hareni nazir lemakhar* — with the required temporal offset. That would mean the second *nezirut* did hover and wait; but when the *hatara* retroactively eliminates the first, the second now accounts for only twenty-nine of the thirty days, one day remaining. Or, alternatively, the *Gemara* will propose a different reading of the case entirely.

---

## Two at Once (II)

### Rav Huna's Concession

The *Gemara* then introduces the case of *kibel shtei nezirus be'vas achas* — the person accepted two *neziruyot* simultaneously, in a single statement, explicitly designating two distinct *neziruyot* together. The *Gemara* indicates that even *Rav Huna* would agree in this case: the second *nezirut* hovers and, upon completion of the first, kicks in, even though the two are entirely coextensive in time.

This is a crucial clarification of *Rav Huna*'s position. His requirement of temporal offset — *hayom* versus *lemakhar* — is not a reflection of some conceptual difficulty with two coinciding *neziruyot* as such. *Rav Huna* has no objection to the model of complete overlap, where the second *nezirut* coincides entirely with the first and simply waits. What he objects to is creating that model through sequential, identical declarations. When someone says *hareni nazir hayom* and then, with the first *nezirut* already in place, repeats *hareni nazir hayom*, the second statement is simply a repetition — it is not doing anything.
