It does not introduce a second *nezirut*; it merely restates the first.

### Sequential vs. Simultane…

The distinction *Rav Huna* draws is therefore not about conceptual structure but about the mechanics of halakhic speech acts. A simultaneous declaration — "I accept two *neziruyot* beginning today" — is unambiguous: both are accepted at once, one takes effect, the other hovers. But a sequential declaration — *hareni nazir hayom*, and then later *hareni nazir hayom* — is a problem not because of any impossibility of overlapping *neziruyot* but because the second utterance, made after the first has already taken hold, is indistinguishable from mere repetition. If someone wanted to create a hovering second *nezirut* through sequential speech, he would need to say something meaningfully different — such as *hareni nazir lemakhar* — to signal that he is designating a distinct, second *nezirut* and not simply echoing the first.

---

## Hataras Nedarim (II)

### Ran's Solution

The *Ran* offers an alternative resolution to the challenge posed by the *hataras nedarim* case that does not require reading the case as one where *hayom* and *lemakhar* were explicitly specified. His argument is this: even if the two *neziruyot* were stated in identical terms — *hareni nazir hayom hareni nazir hayom* — and even according to *Rav Huna*, the retroactive voiding of the first *nezirut* through *hatara* is sufficient to make the second statement meaningful in hindsight. At the time of the second declaration, it appeared to be a meaningless repetition — the first *nezirut* was already in place, and the second seemed to add nothing. *Rav Huna* would indeed have said at that moment that it took no effect. But when the *chacham* subsequently performs *hatara* and retroactively eliminates the first *nezirut*, we now look back and see that the first statement was, in hindsight, void. With the first statement retroactively void, the second statement — which at the time seemed redundant — is now seen to have been meaningful after all: there was no first *nezirut* to block it, and so it took effect.

This is the force of the *Ran*'s approach: retroactive voiding (*lemafrei'a*) can transform the second statement from apparent superfluity to actual efficacy, because it changes the retrospective reality against which that statement is evaluated. *Rav Huna* need not concede that sequential identical *nezirut*-declarations work in the ordinary case; he can maintain his position while still accounting for the *hataras nedarim* ruling. One might raise the objection that if the second statement was not meaningful at the time it was uttered, it cannot retroactively become meaningful. This is a genuine difficulty, and it is the question with which the discussion concludes — a fascinating debate whose full resolution remains open.

---

---

# Nedarim 18

## Neder Betoch Neder

### Rav Huna vs. Shmuel

The daf begins at 18a, approximately four lines down, with *mative rav hamnuna* — a challenge posed by Rav Hamnuna. We are in the midst of the debate between Rav Huna and Shmuel concerning what the *mishnah* means when it says *yesh neder betoch neder* — that there is a neder within a neder.

The classic illustration involves the acceptance of *nezirut*. If someone says *hareini nazir hayom* and then says *hareini nazir lemachar*, Rav Huna requires that the two *neziruyot* not be identical — that there be some non-overlapping period. The Ran explains that when one day does not overlap between the two acceptances, that day — day thirty-one — causes an entirely new thirty-day *nezirut* to take effect. That is Rav Huna's position. Shmuel, reading the *mishnah* in its simpler sense, holds that even if the second acceptance is word-for-word identical to the first — *hareini nazir hareini nazir* — it nonetheless takes effect: not immediately, but held in abeyance until the first *nezirut* concludes, at which point the second kicks in automatically.

What emerged in the prior session is that even Rav Huna would concede that if someone accepted both *neziruyot* simultaneously — saying, for example, *harei alai shtei nezirut* — the phenomenon of one taking effect while the other hovers in abeyance is valid. His objection applies specifically to the sequential case, where one *nezirut* is already in force: attempting to accept the identical state upon oneself after it is already operative, he maintains, is a meaningless act.

### Ran's Approaches

It is worth noting that the Ran actually presents two distinct ways of reading the entire *sugya*, and we have been following only one of them. The approach we have been working with understands *neder betoch neder* as the second *nezirut* being suspended and held in abeyance, to take effect when the first concludes. This explains naturally why the phenomenon is unique to *nezirut*: only *nezirut* has a finite, time-bound character, which creates conceptual space for the second to hover.

However, the Ran also acknowledges a quite different reading: that *yesh neder betoch neder* means both *neziruyot* take effect simultaneously, making one a double *nazir*. Under this reading, if someone were to drink wine, he would incur two sets of lashes. The Ran does not favor this reading, but he recognizes it as a legitimate interpretation of the *Gemara*. More significantly, under this reading Rav Huna's insistence that the two acceptances differ makes excellent sense, because if they are absolutely identical, the principle of *ein issur chal al issur* — one prohibition cannot take effect upon another — would prevent the second from having any force. If, however, they differ slightly, the second qualifies as an *issur mosif* or *issur kolel*, and that distinction permits one to take effect upon the other within the *Gemara*'s framework for *ein issur chal al issur*. Crucially, this second reading would not confine the phenomenon to *nezirut* at all. The *mishnah*'s use of *nezirut* would be merely illustrative, and in principle one could say *konam kikar zeh alai konam kikar zeh alai* and create two stacked prohibitions on that loaf of bread, with the person incurring two sets of lashes for eating it.

These are genuinely two very different frameworks for understanding the *sugya*.

### Why Verse Needed

The *mishnah* says *yesh neder betoch neder* but goes directly to the case of *nezirut* without explaining what makes *nezirut* distinctive. Once we operate within the hovering framework — that the second *nezirut* waits and takes effect when the first ends — we understand the uniqueness of *nezirut*. But the question arises: why does a *pasuk* need to teach us this? The *Gemara* asks *heichi dami* — precisely which case requires the scriptural derivation?

### Qal VaChomer

To appreciate the need for a *pasuk*, the *Gemara* first reconstructs the *qal vachomer* one might have made in the opposite direction. The *Gemara* states: *ma shvua chamura, she'ein shvua chala al shvua* — a *shvua* is weightier, yet a *shvua* cannot take effect upon a *shvua*. If you take an oath not to eat a loaf of bread and then take a second oath to the same effect, the second one does not take effect, because you are already *mushba v'omed* — already obligated — and you cannot obligate yourself anew in the same matter. Therefore, reasons the *qal vachomer*, *nezirut kala lo kol sheken* — how much more so should the lighter category of *nezirut* be unable to double up?

The *Gemara* then states *talmud lomar nazir l'hazir* — the doubled language in the verse teaches that *nezirut chala al nezirut*, that *nezirut* does indeed stack. So the *pasuk* overrides what the *qal vachomer* would have predicted.

Now, *heichi dami* — what exactly is the case requiring that override? If it is Rav Huna's case — *hareini nazir hayom hareini nazir lemachar* — why would you even need a *pasuk*? Since there is a day of non-overlap, it is perfectly obvious that the second should take effect; no *pasuk* is needed. The *Gemara* therefore concludes: *ela lav d'amar hareini nazir hayom hareini nazir hayom* — it must be the case where someone said the identical thing twice, where the second acceptance completely coincides with the first. And the *Gemara* notes that since the *mishnah* teaches *nezirut chala al nezirut* — that even this works — it implies we are dealing with the non-obvious case. This seems to be a strong proof against Rav Huna.

The *Gemara* deflects: *hacha b'mai askinan k'gon shekibel alav shtei neziruyot b'vat achat* — here we are dealing with a case where the person accepted two *neziruyot* at once. That too is not obvious: since both are accepted for the same period beginning today, the second has no time in which it alone is operative. It is not obvious that the second one should be meaningful. Yet the *pasuk* teaches that it is — that the second hovers and will take effect when the first concludes. Crucially, Rav Huna agrees to this case. His objection is specifically to the sequential case where one is already in force when the attempt is made to add the second. When they are created together as a package, even he accepts the hovering phenomenon. And it is precisely that non-obvious case — *bat achat* — that requires a *pasuk*.

### Weight of Shvua

The *Gemara* then asks: *umai chumra d'shvua* — in what sense is a *shvua* said to be weightier, such that the *qal vachomer* runs from *nezirut* (the *kal*) to *shvua* (the *chamur*)? The *Gemara* first raises a possible answer and immediately complicates it: perhaps *shvua* is weightier because it takes effect even on matters that are non-physical — it obligates you to perform an action rather than conferring status on an object. But then *neder nami chamir* — a *neder* has its own weightiness: *sheken chal al mitzva k'reshut* — it can take effect on *mitzvah* objects and prevent you from performing a *mitzvah*. For instance, one can forbid all *sukkot* or all *tefillin* upon oneself, which a *shvua* cannot do, because a *shvua* that directly contradicts a Torah obligation is invalid, whereas a *neder* accomplishes the same end-result through a different mechanism.

Since each has an advantage over the other, the *Gemara* cannot identify a clean technical superiority. Instead, it concludes: *ela mishum d'chtiv ba bishvua lo yenakeh* — the reason *shvua* is considered weightier is that the Torah writes regarding it *ki lo yenakeh Hashem et asher yisa shemo lashav* — God will not cleanse one who takes His name in vain. This is not a technical distinction about the formal scope of each instrument; it is a statement about weight and gravity. A *shvua* invokes the divine name, and its violation carries a dimension of offense against God that a *neder* does not.

### Tosafot on Lo Yenakeh

There is a point worth flagging here, which Tosafot addresses. The *pasuk* of *lo yenakeh* is written in the context of *shvuat sheker* — a false oath about the past, where one invokes God's name to testify to the truth of a statement that is in fact false. That is the paradigmatic desecration of God's name: calling on God to bear witness to a lie. The *mishnah*'s case, however, involves *shvuat bituy* — an oath about future behavior, which creates an obligation. These are conceptually distinct: *shvuat bituy* is not primarily about calling God to witness a falsehood; it creates a positive obligation on the person. When you fail to fulfill it, retroactively you have backed your word with God's name and then not delivered on it — which resembles *shvuat sheker*, but the conceptual emphasis is on the obligation created rather than the invocation of the divine name.

Tosafot acknowledges that the *pasuk* of *lo yenakeh* is technically written in the context of *shvuat sheker*, and the *mishnah* deals with *shvuat bituy*, but concludes: *mikol makom chumra chashivuta shava hi* — nevertheless, as a category, *shvua* as a whole is weightier than *neder*, and the *Gemara* simply uses the most accessible expression of that weightiness. There are other respects in which *shvua* is more serious, which the *Gemara* in Shvuot elaborates; here the *Gemara* takes the straightforward one.

### Logic of Qal VaChomer

This is a good moment to clarify the logical structure at play. A *qal vachomer* runs from the *kal* to the *chamur*: if something is true for the lighter category, it certainly holds for the weightier one. Here, you might have wanted to argue: since *neder betoch neder* works by *nezirut*, which is *kal*, it should certainly work by *shvua*, which is *chamur*. But we know it does not work by *shvua*. The *Gemara*'s move is the logical contrapositive: if it does not hold for the *chamur*, it certainly should not hold for the *kal*. If *shvua* — which is *chamur* — does not permit *ein shvua chala al shvua* to be overridden, then *nezirut* — which is *kal* — certainly should not permit it. This is the structure of *if P then Q; therefore if not-Q then not-P*. You would have expected that just as *shvua* cannot double up, neither should *nezirut* be able to — and the *pasuk* comes to teach otherwise.

---

## Issur Cheftza vs. Ga (II)

### Order of Neder/Shvua

Before moving further in the *Gemara*, there is an important and conceptually rich discussion that the Ran develops on the basis of the *Yerushalmi*, concerning the interaction between *neder* and *shvua* across different categories — specifically, what happens when someone makes a *neder* following a *shvua*, or a *shvua* following a *neder*, on the same object.

The question: *shvua shelo ochal kikar ze* — I take an oath I will not eat this loaf — followed by *kikar ze konam alai* — I now make this loaf a *konam*, forbidden. Or conversely: first *konam*, then *shvua*. Does the second instrument take effect on top of the first?

### Cheftza Implies Gavra

The Ran's answer hinges on a fundamental conceptual distinction: *neder* operates as an *issur cheftza* — a prohibition that attaches to the object itself — while *shvua* operates as an *issur gavra* — a prohibition that attaches to the person. The Ran's core principle is that *issur cheftza* implies *issur gavra*, but not the reverse.

### Sukkah Example

The Ran illustrates with a paradigmatic case. If I have a *mitzvah* to sit in a *sukkah* — which is an *issur gavra*-style obligation upon me as a person — I can nonetheless subsequently make the *sukkah* forbidden to myself by declaring it a *konam*. The personal obligation and the object's status operate on different planes and do not directly contradict one another. Practically, the result is that I will be unable to honor both simultaneously, but the act of conferring a status on the object is not in direct conflict with the personal obligation. They are not in conversation with one another.

### Asymmetry of Order

From this emerges an asymmetry that is, at first glance, counterintuitive. If someone first says *shvua shelo ochal kikar ze* — I take an oath I will not eat this loaf — and then says *konam kikar ze alai*, the *neder* takes effect. Why? Because the *shvua* says nothing about the status of the loaf. The loaf is entirely neutral; the *shvua* is purely a statement about what I will do. Since the loaf retains neutral status, I can subsequently confer a prohibited status upon it through a *neder*. Similarly, if the *shvua* is in the reinforcing direction — I swear I will eat the loaf, and then I make it a *konam* — the *neder* still takes effect, even though it now creates a direct conflict between the *neder* and the *shvua*. The point is structural: the *shvua* made no claim about the object's nature, so the *neder* finds the object in a neutral state and can act upon it.

Reverse the order, however, and the result changes entirely. If someone first declares *konam kikar ze* — making the loaf forbidden — and then attempts to take a *shvua* on that loaf, whether to eat it or not to eat it, the *shvua* does not take effect. This is the surprising direction.

### Status Speaks to Person

Why? Because when the loaf is declared forbidden through a *neder*, that status is not merely a claim about the object in isolation. The Ran argues: what does it mean for an object to be forbidden if there are no people in the world to be affected by it? The forbidden status of the object is inherently a statement *to* the person — it says, you may not eat this. Once the *neder* has conferred a forbidden status on the loaf, that status has already implicated and addressed the person. It has already generated, as a direct consequence, an *issur gavra* — a personal prohibition upon the individual. Therefore, when the person subsequently attempts to make a *shvua* — a personal statement about what he will or will not do — the *shvua* finds that the personal dimension has already been spoken to. It is *lo chal*: the *shvua* cannot take effect, because there is no open space for it. The *issur gavra* generated by the *neder* preempts it.

This is the Ran's formulation: *issur cheftza* of *nedarim* generates *issur gavra* as well — *issur gavra nami ika bei* — because once the loaf is forbidden, the prohibition of *lo yachel devaro* applies, which is a personal obligation not to violate the *neder*. So the *neder* both establishes a status on the object and, as a consequence, speaks to the person. Whereas a *shvua* speaks only to the person and leaves the object's status entirely untouched. Hence the asymmetry: *neder* before *shvua* forecloses the *shvua*; *shvua* before *neder* does not foreclose the *neder*.

### Torah Lav Laws

This leads to a broader and genuinely important question about *issurim* in the Torah. When one first encounters the categories of *issur gavra* and *issur cheftza*, the natural case to consider is something like *chazir*. Our intuitive religious sense is that there is something intrinsically problematic about pork — that it is not merely neutral matter with a personal directive not to eat it, but that the thing itself has a problematic status. Yet the Torah's language often says *lo tochal* — you shall not eat — which is directed at the person and sounds like an *issur gavra*.

There are indeed those who argue that every prohibition in the Torah is technically an *issur gavra*, since the Torah always speaks to what you are not permitted to do, not about some inherent ontological status of the object. But the Ran's position, and the more nuanced view, is that these two categories are not mutually exclusive. A prohibition can start with an *issur cheftza* — the object has a problematic status — and then translate into an *issur gavra*: *and therefore* you may not eat it. Any *issur cheftza* carries with it an *issur gavra*. The converse, however, is not true: an *issur gavra* does not necessarily imply any *issur cheftza*.

The practical implication the Ran draws: since every *issur cheftza* entails an *issur gavra*, once you have started with a *neder* — which is an *issur cheftza* — you have, by the same act, already generated an *issur gavra*. There is therefore no room for a *shvua* to add anything on the personal level. But if you start with a *shvua* — which is purely *issur gavra* — the object remains wholly untouched, and a *neder* can still act upon it.

Furthermore, the Ran explains, every *lav* in the Torah is an *issur gavra* — that is, it is addressed to the person and tells them what not to do — but this does not mean it is *only* an *issur gavra*. Some *lavim* begin with the recognition that the object itself has a problematic character, and the prohibition on the person follows from that. The Ran's statement that a *lav* functions *kechol lo sa'aseh sheba-torah* — like any negative commandment in the Torah — does not collapse the distinction; it means the Torah's prohibitions always land, at minimum, on the person, but they may simultaneously reflect a status of the object.

### Ran's Text Analysis

Let us read the relevant passage in the Ran carefully. The Ran frames the question this way: one might have thought that just as an *issur cheftza* of *nedarim* can take effect upon an *issur gavra* of *shvuot* — since they are operating on different planes — so too should an *issur gavra* of *shvuot* be able to take effect upon an *issur cheftza* of *nedarim*. After all, if the *sukkah* argument works in one direction, why not in the other?

The Ran's answer: *mishum de-vinedarim ke-heichi de-ishei issur cheftza, issur gavra nami ika bei* — because in *nedarim*, once the *issur cheftza* exists, the *issur gavra* is already embedded in it. The moment the loaf is forbidden, the halacha of *lo yachel devaro* — you shall not violate your word — kicks in and is already speaking to the person. *Ve-hai lav issur gavra hu kechol lo sa'aseh sheba-torah* — this is a personal prohibition just like any negative commandment in the Torah. Thus the *neder*, as an *issur cheftza*, carries its *issur gavra* along with it. *Hilkach ein makom lishevuah shetachol al nedarim* — therefore there is no room for a *shvua* to take effect once a *neder* is already in place.

The Ran then cites the *Yerushalmi* in the first chapter of our tractate, which states: *bekikar echad mikeivan shehizkir alav shevuah keneveilah hu* — once someone declares a *neder* on a loaf, it is like a *neveilah*. From that point forward, if one attempts to make a *shvua* on it, it is as if one is trying to make a *shvua* take effect on top of an existing *issur* — and *ein shvuah chala al issurin*. Then *Rav Yudan* in the *Yerushalmi* states: this is specifically when the person first mentioned the *neder* and then the *shvua* — the *shvua* does not take effect. But if the *shvua* came first and the *neder* second, the *neder* does take effect, since the *shvua* left the object's status entirely open.

### Hekdesh Example

A question arises: what about *hekdesh*? When one is *makdish* something — consecrates it — it is simultaneously an *issur cheftza* and generates an *issur gavra* for any individual who might benefit from it. Is this not the same principle?

Precisely — the Ran's point applies equally to *hekdesh*. Every *issur cheftza* translates into an *issur gavra*. What is distinctive about *hekdesh*, one might note, is that the *issur cheftza* is capable of generating an *issur gavra* not just for the one who sanctified it but for any person who might interact with it. But this is not categorically different from the Ran's point; it simply illustrates the broader reach of an *issur cheftza*. A *neder* can similarly forbid a loaf to the entire world if the person who makes the *neder* owns that loaf. The principle that *issur cheftza* implies *issur gavra* holds across these cases. Indeed, the very concept of *kedushah* carries this inherently: the object's sanctified status is not merely an internal metaphysical fact about the object but speaks directly to what any person may or may not do with it.

### Meat and Milk

The conceptual framework of *issur gavra* versus *issur cheftza* opens onto a rich set of questions about Torah prohibitions generally. Take the prohibition of *basar b'chalav* — meat and milk. One approach holds that the primary prohibition of the Torah is simply not to eat them together; everything else — the prohibition on cooking them, on deriving benefit — is secondary and constructed to protect the eating prohibition. Under this view, the orientation is fundamentally personal and action-centered: there is nothing problematic about the combination per se, only about what you do with it. This is closer to a pure *issur gavra* orientation.

The opposing approach holds that the very phenomenon of meat and milk cooked together is intrinsically problematic — something akin to *kilayim* or *shatnez*, a fundamental disruption of natural categories. Under this view, the prohibition is not merely about protecting me from eating; it reflects a status of the *combined entity* itself, which then generates a series of downstream prohibitions: against cooking, against benefiting, against eating. This is the *issur cheftza* orientation.

The difference has concrete implications. The scope of the prohibition on *hana'ah* — benefit — is more naturally explained if there is something fundamentally objectionable about the object's status, which demands complete hands-off treatment, rather than merely a personal directive not to perform a specific action. The *issur achilah* alone suggests a narrower focus: it is about what you may or may not do, not about the thing being categorically tainted. These distinct orientations can be mapped onto the *issur gavra* / *issur cheftza* distinction and carry consequences for how we analyze the *halachot* of *basar b'chalav* throughout the tractate of Chullin.

For the purposes of *Nedarim*, the operative question is not whether a Torah prohibition is *issur gavra* or *issur cheftza* in the abstract, but whether the object in question is a *davar hanadur* — something whose forbidden status derives from speech-act dedication — or not. That is the criterion for whether a *neder* can use it as a reference point.

---

## Retroactive Effect

### Rava's Retroactivity

The *Gemara* now transitions to a related question. The *mishnah* establishes that when someone makes a *shvua* and then makes a second *shvua* on the same matter — *shvua shelo ochal v'achal eino chayav ela achat* — he violates only once. The second *shvua* does not take effect because one is already *mushba* and *omed*. Rava, however, asserts: *nish'al al rishona, shniya chala alav* — if the person petitions a *chacham* and has the first *shvua* dissolved through *heter*, the second *shvua* takes retroactive effect. Even though the second *shvua* was meaningless at the moment of utterance — since the first was already operative — once the first is removed, the second comes into force.

This is a striking principle. One might have argued that a statement which is entirely without force at the moment it is uttered is simply null — a *davar she'ein bo mamash*, a nothing. How can it hover and then retroactively take effect?

### Revach Concept

The *Gemara*'s language is illuminating. It does not say the second *shvua* is null; it says *revacha hu de-leit lei* — it has no *revach*, no space, no room in which to operate. This language is remarkable because it treats the *shvua* as something concrete — an obligation-object that requires physical space in which to exist. The first *shvua* occupies that space entirely, leaving no room for the second. But the second is nonetheless present, hovering, awaiting an opening. When the first is dissolved, the space opens, and the second takes effect. The obligations and statuses created by speech are being conceptualized with something close to physicality — they occupy space, they compete for room, they hover.

### Two Neziruyot

The *Gemara* attempts to derive Rava's principle from the case of two *neziruyot*. If someone accepted two *neziruyot* — *mi she-nadar shtei nezirot u-manat et ha-rishona ve-hifrish korban* — counted the first *nezirut*, separated a *korban*, and then obtained a *heter* on the first *nezirut*, *ala lo shniya bi-rishona* — the second *nezirut* is considered to have been operative from the start, and the days already counted apply retroactively to the second. The second *nezirut* hovered and, upon dissolution of the first, retroactively took its place. This seems to be strong support for Rava's principle.

### Bat Achat Status

The *Gemara* deflects the proof: *hacha b'mai askinan k'gon shekibel alav shtei neziruyot b'vat achat* — perhaps the case of two *neziruyot* refers specifically to the scenario where both were accepted simultaneously in a single utterance. In that case, we have already accepted that the simultaneous acceptance creates the hovering phenomenon: one takes effect, the other hovers, and if the first is dissolved, the second retroactively fills its place. This is structurally different from the sequential case, where one *shvua* was already in force before the second was uttered. In the *bat achat* scenario, because they were created together as a single package, the hovering status is constitutive and built-in. The *Gemara* is suggesting that perhaps Rava's extension to the sequential *shvua* case is not proven from the *nezirut* example.

### Sequential vs. Simultane…

And yet Rava's assertion stands: even in the sequential case, where the second *shvua* was uttered after the first was already operative, the second one nonetheless hovers — *revacha hu de-leit lei* — and will take effect if the first is dissolved. The *lishna achrina* of the *Gemara* reinforces this: *chiyuva hu de-leka, ha-shvuah ika* — the obligation to bring a *korban* or the liability for violation may not exist, but the *shvua* itself is still present. The practical implication — *le-mai hilchata* — is precisely *de-Rava*: if you dissolve the first *shvua*, *chala lo shniya tachteiha*, the second takes its place. Even by *shvua*, where we say *ein shvua chala al shvua*, the focus remains on the obligation-creating dimension of the *shvua*, and even there the second one hovers with just no room to operate, until the first is removed.

---

## Issur Cheftza vs. Ga (II)

### Power of Words

It is worth pausing over what *Masechet Nedarim* reveals about the nature of speech. The *Gemara*'s language — that the second *shvua* has no *revach*, no space — treats obligations and statuses created by words as if they were concrete, quasi-physical entities that occupy space, hover, and compete. This is not incidental to the *sugya*; it is, in a sense, its deepest teaching. When one says *konam* or takes a *shvua*, one is not merely expressing an intention. One is creating a status — of an object, of oneself — that now has an independent existence in the world of *halacha*. It competes with other statuses, it occupies conceptual space, it can hover waiting for room to take effect. The tractate of *Nedarim* is, among other things, a meditation on the creative power of speech: how words construct religious realities, generate obligations, transform the status of objects, and build what might be called a personal religious world alongside the pre-existing structure of Torah obligations. Much as a *bamah* was a personal, do-it-yourself site of worship — the *Gemara* elsewhere compares *nedarim* to this — so one who makes *nedarim* is in a sense constructing his own overlay of sanctity and prohibition on a neutral world. The statuses thus created are real, weighty, and interact with one another in all the ways we have been tracing.

---

## Stam Nedarim Lehachmir

### Opening Principle

The *mishnah* now presents a principle that addresses a question that has been hovering throughout the tractate: *stam nedarim lehachmir u-peirusham lehakel* — unspecified *nedarim* are given the stricter interpretation, while an articulated clarification is given the more lenient one. This principle speaks directly to the recurring question of why we do not simply ask the person what he meant. The answer embedded in the *mishnah* is that we do ask — and when he tells us, we follow the lenient interpretation. But when he does not tell us, or cannot tell us, we default to strict.

### Sacrificial Examples

*Keitzad* — what are the examples? The *mishnah* says: *harei alai k'basar maliach k'yayin nesech* — let this be forbidden to me like salted meat or like wine of libation. Two possible meanings present themselves. Salted meat is associated with sacrificial meat, since *kol korban chovatcha takriv melach* — all your obligatory offerings require salt. *Yayin nesech* — wine of libation — can refer either to *nesachim*, the wine poured on the altar as part of the Temple service, or to wine poured as a libation to *avodah zarah*. These are radically different referents with opposite halachic consequences.

*Im b'shel shelamim nadar* — if he meant like a sacrifice to God, *assur*: it is forbidden, because this is a *davar hanadur*, an object made forbidden through human speech-dedication. *Im b'shel avodat kochavim nadar* — if he meant like idolatrous libation or sacrifice, *mutar*: it is permissible. Why? Although food offered to *avodah zarah* is prohibited, it is not a *davar hanadur*. Its forbidden status does not derive from a speech-act of dedication; it derives from another mechanism entirely. Therefore it cannot serve as a reference point for a *neder*. *V'im stam* — and if he did not specify — *assur*: we give it the stricter interpretation and treat it as if he meant the sacrificial-to-God meaning.

The *mishnah* thus teaches both components of the principle simultaneously. The strict default (*stam lehachmir*) operates when nothing else is known. The lenient interpretation (*peirusham lehakel*) operates when the person clarifies that he meant the lenient referent — and his clarification is accepted and binding.

One might ask: what if the person says he had no particular meaning in mind, that he simply heard the phrase and used it without thinking of either the *shelamim* or the *avodah zarah* referent? The Ran and Tosafot address this. If someone says he intended to create the *issur* but had no idea what exactly the words meant, we would still apply the strict default. The requirement of intent (*piv velibbo shavin*) pertains primarily to the intention to create the status — the intention to obligate — not necessarily to detailed knowledge of precisely which referent is meant by the words chosen.

### Cherem Example

*Harei alai kecherem* — let this be upon me like *cherem*. *Cherem* admits of two referents: *cherem shel shamayim* — consecrated to the *Beit HaMikdash* — and *cherem shel kohanim* — dedicated to the *kohanim* for their use. The former is forbidden to all; the latter is permissible to those who receive it. *Im kecherem shel shamayim, assur* — that is a *davar hanadur* and forbidden. *V'im kecherem shel kohanim, mutar* — that is not forbidden to people, so it cannot serve as a *neder* reference point. *V'im stam, assur* — unspecified, we give it the strict meaning.

### Ma'aser Example

*Harei alai kema'aser* — let this be upon me like *ma'aser*. Again, two referents: *ma'aser behemah* — the animal tithe — and *ma'aser goren* — the grain tithe. *Im kema'aser behemah nadar, assur*: the animal tithe is a *korban* and is forbidden to be eaten by ordinary people; it is both a *davar hanadur* and a *davar ha'assur*. *V'im shel goren, mutar*: the grain tithe (*ma'aser rishon* or *ma'aser sheni*), while it is a *davar hanadur* in the sense that it is set aside through designation, it is not a *davar ha'assur* — it is permissible for consumption. Therefore it cannot serve as a reference point for creating a prohibition. *V'im stam, assur* — without clarification, the strict meaning governs.

### Terumah Example

*Harei alai kiterumah* — let this be upon me like *terumah*. Two referents: *terumat halishkah* — the annual donation to the *Beit HaMikdash* treasury (the *machatzit hashekel*) — and *terumah goren* — the priestly tithe separated from grain. *Im kiterumat halishkah nadar, assur*: this is forbidden to all and dedicated to the *Beit HaMikdash*, a clear *davar hanadur*. *V'im shel goren, mutar*: *terumah* of the grain is not a *davar hanadur* for the purposes of *neder* — either because it is not forbidden to all (being permitted to *kohanim*) or, as the Rambam suggests, because it is not a freely undertaken vow but a Torah-imposed obligation, and thus does not qualify as a *davar hanadur*. *V'im stam, assur* — the last statement is attributed specifically to Rabbi Meir, and it is this attribution that opens the door for Rabbi Yehudah's qualification.

---

## Rabbi Yehudah

### Terumah Regional

Rabbi Yehudah says: the strict default for unspecified *terumah* applies only in *Yehudah*, not in the *Galil*. *Stam terumah bi'Yehudah asurah, ba'Galil muteret* — in the *Galil* it is permitted even without clarification. The reason: *she'ein anshei Galil makirim et terumat halishkah* — the people of the *Galil* are not familiar with *terumat halishkah*. The *Beit HaMikdash* is not in their environment; the concept of *terumat halishkah* as a donation to the Temple treasury is not part of their daily consciousness.

### Default Modifier

This raises the deeper principle of what counts as a *stam* — a default meaning — and what requires a modifier. A word's default meaning is determined by its sociological and linguistic reality in a given context. In the *Galil*, when someone says *terumah*, they mean *terumah goren* — that is what the word means to them. If they want to say *terumat halishkah*, they will use the full phrase; the modifier is necessary. *Terumat halishkah* is not a *stam* meaning in the *Galil* because it is not part of the ordinary linguistic repertoire.

The phenomenon of what becomes the default and what requires modification is always a function of usage and familiarity. The default is what the unmodified word naturally evokes in its context. When digital watches were introduced, *digital watch* required the modifier — *watch* was *stam* the analog kind. Eventually, if enough shifts occur, the defaults can reverse, and the formerly default meaning needs a modifier. *Stam nedarim lehachmir* applies when the stricter meaning is a genuine, equally likely candidate for what the word means — when it could plausibly be what someone saying that word intends. Where one meaning has so dominated the word's use that the other meaning requires a modifier to convey, *stam* simply means the default meaning, and if the default is lenient, the result is *lehakel*.

### Cherem Regional

Rabbi Yehudah then applies the same logic in the opposite direction for *cherem*: *stam charamim bi'Yehudah mutarin, baGalil asurin*. In *Yehudah*, unspecified *cherem* is permissible; in the *Galil*, it is forbidden. Why? *She'ein anshei Galil makirin et charmei kohanim* — the people of the *Galil* are not familiar with the concept of *cherem* given to *kohanim*. In the *Galil*, the word *cherem* evokes only *cherem* consecrated to the *Beit HaMikdash*, which is the strict, forbidden category. *Cherem* given to *kohanim* would need a modifier there. Therefore *stam cherem* in the *Galil* is the strict meaning and the result is *assur*.

In *Yehudah*, by contrast, proximity to the *Beit HaMikdash* and familiarity with the *kohanim* means the word *cherem* commonly evokes *charmei kohanim* — the lenient category. Therefore *stam cherem* in *Yehudah* is treated as *mutar*.

### Logical Tension

The *Gemara* will press what seems to be a logical inconsistency in Rabbi Yehudah's ruling on *cherem* in *Yehudah*. Even granting that *cherem* in *Yehudah* commonly evokes *charmei kohanim*, the word can also mean *cherem haMikdash* in *Yehudah* — the Temple *cherem* is not unknown there. If both meanings are available in *Yehudah*, why does *stam lehachmir* not apply, as it does when there are two possible interpretations, one strict and one lenient? The principle of *stam nedarim lehachmir* would seem to demand that we take the strict meaning whenever both meanings are live options. Why does the existence of the lenient meaning (*charmei kohanim*) tip the entire default in *Yehudah* toward *mutar*, rather than triggering *lehachmir* precisely because both are possible?

The answer the *Gemara* will develop is that *stam lehachmir* presupposes that both meanings are roughly equally available and plausible. Where one meaning so dominates the sociological and linguistic reality that the other, while technically possible, is not the word's natural default meaning, we follow the actual default — whether strict or lenient. In *Yehudah*, *cherem* is simply what people mean when they say *charmei kohanim*; the *mikdash* meaning requires the fuller phrase. That dominance controls the *stam*, and no *lehachmir* override applies where the default itself is the lenient reading. This is not merely a logical rule but a sociological and linguistic reality that the *halacha* incorporates: what a word means — in its actual usage, in its actual community — determines what *stam* means.

---

---

# Nedarim 19

## Stam Nedarim Discrepancy

### Opening Discrepancy

The present daf continues a discussion of the principle of *stam nedarim le-hachmir, peirushan le-hakel* — that an ambiguous formulation of a *neder*, even when both possible interpretations would constitute a binding vow, is given the stricter construction. The *mishnah* dealt with cases where the language could be understood in two ways, one rendering the object a *davar hanadur* and the other not, and ruled that when the meaning is ambiguous we adopt the stricter interpretation. At the same time, the *mishnah* indicates that *peirusham le-hakel* — if the person were to clarify that he intended the lenient meaning, we would believe him. This raises the question of why we do not simply ask the person every time. Two explanations were offered: either the person is no longer available to ask, or the person genuinely had no specific intention, using language he heard others use without committing to one reading over another, in which case we supply the stricter meaning as a matter of legal principle.

The preceding *mishnah* also recorded a debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda concerning regional variation — specifically, how the standard meaning of the words *cherem* and *teruma* differs between *Galil* and *Yehuda*, such that the same term may produce a strict result in one region and a lenient result in the other.

### Three Explanations

The *gemara* opens by pressing a contradiction. We say *stam nedarim le-hachmir*, yet a different *mishnah* rules that *safek nezirut le-hakel* — a doubtful *nezirut* is resolved leniently. Since *nezirut* is itself a species of *neder*, why should the two be treated differently? The *gemara* identifies three possible directions for resolving this tension. The first would distinguish between cases where the doubt arises from the ambiguity of external circumstances versus cases where the doubt arises from the meaning of the vow's language. The second would draw a distinction intrinsic to *nezirut* itself, given its particular characteristics. The third — which the *gemara* actually pursues — is to declare the discrepancy a *machlokes tannaim*.

### Rabbi Zeira Resolution

Rabbi Zeira offers the resolution: *lo kashya, ha Rabbi Eliezer, ha Rabbanan* — there is no true contradiction, because the two rulings reflect the positions of Rabbi Eliezer and the *Rabbanan* respectively. The source is a *baraita*: if one consecrates all his *chaya* (wild animals) or all his *behema* (domesticated animals) to *hekdesh*, the question arises whether a *koi* — a hybrid creature of disputed zoological classification — is included. Rabbi Eliezer says it is not consecrated; the *Chachamim* say it is.

## Koi Consecration Cas (II)

### Koi Baraita

The *koi* is an animal whose status is genuinely uncertain, some holding it to be a *min bifnei atzmo* — a distinct species — rather than simply a doubtful case between *chaya* and *behema*. According to the *Ran* or *Tosafos*, Rabbi Eliezer holds that the *koi* is indeed a *min bifnei atzmo*, meaning it belongs to neither category, and therefore even if one says he is consecrating all his *chayos* and all his *behemos*, the *koi* would not be consecrated — it falls into neither. The *Chachamim*, by contrast, hold that the *koi* definitely falls into one of the two categories; we simply do not know which one, and therefore if one consecrates both categories it is certainly *kadosh*.

The *gemara* reads this dispute as reflecting a broader disagreement about what to do with a *safek* in the context of *hekdesh* — and since *nedarim* draws on the model of *hekdesh*, the same dispute should govern *nedarim* and *nezirut* alike. The *Chachamim*, who are *machmir* about consecrating property under conditions of doubt, would similarly be *machmir* when one makes himself a *nazir* under doubtful conditions. Rabbi Eliezer, who is *meikel* about consecrated property under doubt, would likewise be *meikel* about *nezirut*.

At this point the *gemara* makes a significant observation. One might have thought that there is a natural distinction between *nedarim*, which govern the status of objects, and *nezirut*, which governs a person's own status — and that people are more reluctant to impose obligations upon themselves than upon their property. Indeed, this distinction would have neatly resolved the original contradiction: for objects, we rule *stam nedarim le-hachmir*; for one's own person, *safek nezirut le-hakel*. The *gemara* explicitly signals awareness of this possible answer but sets it aside, preferring instead to treat both cases under a single framework and declare it a *machlokes tannaim*.

Woven into this discussion is the concept of *ma'eil inish nafshei le-sfeika* — whether a person would willingly subject himself to a doubtful status — and *ma'eil mamonei le-sfeika* — whether a person would willingly subject his property to such doubt. Until this point, one might have assumed that *stam nedarim le-hachmir* is purely a legal interpretive principle — a rule for how courts construe ambiguous language — with no reference to the vower's subjective intent. But the *gemara*'s introduction of the *ma'eil* framework suggests that the question of what a person would have wanted is itself part of the legal analysis. This can be understood as follows: rather than asking about this particular individual's intent, we adopt a general interpretive presumption — that people making these types of declarations typically intend either the broader or the narrower meaning — and apply that presumption uniformly as a matter of law. The *Ran* supports the more formalist reading: even if the person says he had no specific meaning in mind, the legal principle determines the meaning of his words regardless.

## Safek Bechoros Digre (II)

### Safek Bechoros

Abaye challenges the identification of *safek nezirut le-hakel* with Rabbi Eliezer. If that leniency is Rabbi Eliezer's position, then the same *mishnah* that rules *safek nezirut le-hakel* should reflect his position throughout. Yet the *mishnah* also rules on *safek bechoros* — cases of doubtful firstborn status — and the *gemara* cites a *baraita* stating that a *safek bechor* is forbidden for shearing and labor. If a cow gave birth to twins and it is unknown whether the firstborn was male or female, the male calf's *bechor* status is uncertain. In terms of monetary law (*Choshen Mishpat*), the principle of *hamotzi me-chaveiro alav ha-rayah* applies — the *kohen* cannot collect without proof. But in terms of *issur ve-heter*, since *bechorah* is a biblical obligation, *safek d'oraita le-chumra* applies and the animal is forbidden for shearing or work. This is a straightforward *safek d'oraita*, with nothing to do with Rabbi Eliezer's position — and yet it rules strictly, in contrast to the leniency by *nezirut*. The question stands: why are some doubtful cases treated leniently and others strictly?

## Koi Consecration Cas (II)

### Kedusha Types

The *gemara* answers by drawing a fundamental distinction: *ami ka-medamit kedusha ba'ah mei-eilya li-kedusha ba'ah bi-yedei adam* — why are you comparing a *kedusha* that arrives on its own to a *kedusha* that is conferred by a human act? The *bechor* animal either is or is not a *bechor* — its sanctity, if it exists, arrived independently of any human declaration. The question is purely one of fact: was the male calf born first? There is one factual reality, unknown to us, and based on that reality the animal is either definitively *assur* or definitively *muttar*. This is a classic *safek d'oraita*, and the rule *safek d'oraita le-chumra* applies.

### Facts vs. Interpretation

By contrast, when a person makes a *neder* or declares himself a *nazir* using ambiguous language, there is no unresolved factual question — the facts are fully known. The person spoke certain words. The question is entirely one of legal interpretation: how do we construe those words? What scope do we assign to that language? This is not a question about what happened in the world; it is a question about the legal meaning of a speech act. And if we adopt the legal principle that we interpret such language narrowly — *stam nezirut le-hakel* — then the *kedusha* was simply never conferred. The rule of *safek d'oraita le-chumra* does not apply because we are not uncertain about a fact; we have chosen, as a matter of interpretive law, to give the declaration its narrower construction.

This distinction — facts versus interpretation — is analytically powerful and the *gemara* presents it as resolving the question about *safek bechoros*. The case of *bechoros* cannot be compared to *nedarim* or *nezirut* because in *bechoros* we are uncertain about a fact, while in *nedarim* we are choosing how to interpret language.

## Safek Bechoros Digre (II)

### Liquids Tumah

Having resolved the *bechoros* question, the *gemara* turns to a more difficult challenge from the same *mishnah*. The *mishnah* rules: *safek mashkin le-tamei tamei, le-tamei acheirim tahor* — if there is doubt whether liquid was rendered *tamei*, we rule it *tamei* regarding itself but *tahor* regarding its capacity to transmit *tumah* to other objects. This is the ruling of Rabbi Meir, and the *mishnah* adds that Rabbi Eliezer agreed with this ruling. But the *gemara* challenges: does Rabbi Eliezer really hold that liquids become *tamei* under conditions of doubt? For there is a *baraita* stating that Rabbi Eliezer holds *ein tumah le-mashkin kol ikar* — there is no biblical basis for *tumah* of liquids whatsoever. The proof is the famous testimony of Rabbi Yose ben Yoezer of Tzereda, who testified about the *ayyal kimtza* locust that it is *dakhan* (the Aramaic equivalent of *tahor*, meaning kosher for consumption), and that *mashkin beit mitbachaya* — the liquids in the Temple slaughterhouse — are likewise *dakhan*, meaning they do not transmit *tumah*. The underlying principle is that *tumat mashkin* is only rabbinic, and in the *Beis HaMikdash* we revert to the biblical rule, eliminating the concern entirely.

If *tumat mashkin* is only rabbinic, then in a case of doubt whether liquid was touched, the rule of *safek d'rabanan le-kula* should apply, and we should be lenient. Yet Rabbi Eliezer, if he agrees with the *mishnah*'s ruling, appears to be strict even in this rabbinic doubt. How can that be reconciled with his leniency by the *koi*?

### Shmuel Resolution

The *gemara* offers a resolution attributed to Shmuel: the testimony of Rabbi Yose ben Yoezer should be understood as stating that the Temple liquids are pure only in the sense that they do not make other things *tamei* — *le-tamei acheirim* — but they themselves do become *tamei* at the biblical level. According to Shmuel, *tumat mashkin* at the level of the liquid becoming *tamei* itself is biblical; only its capacity to transmit *tumah* to other objects is rabbinic. This maps perfectly onto the *mishnah*'s split ruling: for the liquid becoming *tamei* itself, it is a *safek d'oraita* and we rule strictly; for the liquid making other things *tamei*, it is a *safek d'rabanan* and we rule leniently. *Safek d'oraita le-chumra, safek d'rabanan le-kula* — this is a clean and precise application of the principle.

However, according to Rav, who holds that *mashkin* are completely *tahor* at the biblical level (*dakhan mamash*), the entire *tumah* of liquids is rabbinic — yet Rabbi Eliezer is still strict when there is doubt. The *gemara* finds this difficult: if it is all rabbinic, why would Rabbi Eliezer be strict by *safek mashkin* yet lenient in the case of the *koi*? The *Ran* acknowledges that the comparison is not rigorous — the *bechoros* distinction (facts versus interpretation) does not map cleanly onto this new question, and the *gemara* seems to be reasoning more loosely, along the lines of: if Rabbi Eliezer is strict even about a rabbinic *safek* of liquids, it would be strange for him to be lenient about *safek nezirut*. This is admittedly not a tight argument. The *gemara* itself appears to treat it as something less than fully compelling.

In any event, the *gemara* concludes by abandoning the approach of Rabbi Zeira entirely. The whole framework identifying *safek nezirut le-hakel* with Rabbi Eliezer's position may have been based more on his particular view of the *koi* as a *min bifnei atzmo* than on a general principle about doubtful *kedusha*, and it does not survive scrutiny. The *gemara* therefore returns to the original problem fresh.

## Yehuda-Shimon Debate

### Grain Condition Case

The *gemara* proposes a new resolution: *ha Rabbi Yehuda, ha Rabbi Shimon* — the discrepancy between *stam nedarim le-hachmir* and *safek nezirut le-hakel* reflects a debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon specifically about *nezirut*. The source is a *baraita* from *Masechet Nazir*:

> *Haraini nazir im yeish be-keri zeh me'ah kor* — "I am a *nazir* if there are a hundred *kor* in this grain pile."

The person then goes to measure the grain and finds it was stolen or lost. There is now no way ever to determine whether the condition was met.

### Yehuda Matir Shimon Oser

Rabbi Yehuda says *matir* — the person is not a *nazir*. Rabbi Shimon says *oser* — the person is a *nazir*. This is a direct dispute about *safek nezirut*: Rabbi Yehuda rules leniently, Rabbi Shimon rules strictly. The *gemara* identifies Rabbi Yehuda's lenient position with *safek nezirut le-hakel* and Rabbi Shimon's strict position with the principle of *stam nedarim le-hachmir*, treating *neder* and *nezirut* as parallel throughout.

It is worth pausing to note an important conceptual difficulty that the *gemara* does not fully address. There is a significant difference between the question of how to interpret ambiguous language — which is the subject of *stam nedarim le-hachmir* — and the question of what to do when a clearly-intended vow is conditioned on a fact that remains unknowable. In the *stam nedarim* discussion, the person's language is ambiguous; we must choose a legal construction for words of uncertain meaning. In the grain case, the person clearly intended to become a *nazir* if a condition was met; the question is simply whether that condition was ever satisfied. These are logically distinct questions — one turns on interpretive principle, the other on factual uncertainty — and one could easily hold differently in the two cases. The *gemara*, however, treats them as equivalent and lumps them together as a single debate about whether *safek* produces stringency or leniency in the realm of *nedarim* and *nezirut*.

## Rava Explanation

### Safek Chamer

The *gemara* then raises a contradiction against Rabbi Yehuda himself: *mi amar Rabbi Yehuda lo ma'eil inish nafshei le-sfeika* — does Rabbi Yehuda really say that a person would not willingly subject himself to doubtful status? This is offered as the logical underpinning of his leniency in the grain case: since being a *safek nazir* is worse than being a *vadai nazir*, a person would never have intended for an ambiguous condition to bind him. Yet the same Rabbi Yehuda elsewhere states *stam terumah bi-Yehudah assurah* — that an ambiguous declaration of *teruma* in *Yehuda* is forbidden — and the *mishnah* records his position that *stam nedarim le-hachmir* applies whenever the language is genuinely ambiguous. This shows that Rabbi Yehuda endorses *stam nedarim le-hachmir* as a general principle.

Rava resolves the contradiction: *gabi keri kasavar kol safek chamur mi-vadai, lo ma'eil nafshei le-sfeika* — specifically regarding the grain pile case, the reason for leniency is that being a *safek nazir* is in fact worse than being a *vadai nazir*, and therefore a person would never have intended for his conditional vow to create that status. A *vadai nazir* completes his *nezirut* after thirty days, shaves his head, and brings his *korbanot*. A *safek nazir*, by contrast, cannot bring his *korbanot* — this would be *safek chulin ba-azarah* — and therefore can never formally conclude his *nezirut*. He is permanently suspended in an unresolvable doubtful status. Since this situation is demonstrably worse than being a definite *nazir*, the interpretive presumption is that no person would have wished to enter it. Therefore, any ambiguity in the condition is resolved in favor of the vow never having taken effect.

For a *neder*, by contrast, there is no analogous problem. If one's *neder* is treated as binding *mi-safek*, the consequence is that the object is prohibited — but this is a manageable restriction, not an impossible situation. One can live with a *safek neder* in a way that one cannot live with *safek nezirut*. Therefore by *nedarim* we say *stam le-hachmir*, while by *nezirut* we say *le-hakel*.

This resolution is elegant and analytically compelling. It means that the answer to the *gemara*'s original question — why *stam nedarim le-hachmir* but *safek nezirut le-hakel* — does not require positing a *machlokes tannaim* at all. The difference is intrinsic to the subject matter: a doubtful *neder* is tolerable, while a doubtful *nezirut* is a trap. Therefore we always interpret *nezirut* conditions in the more lenient direction, not as a matter of general dispute, but because of the specific nature of *nezirut* and its consequences.

### Nazir Olam

Rav Huna bar Yehuda pressed Rava: what if the conditional vow was phrased as *Haraini nazir olam* — a *nazir* forever? In that case, why would *safek* be worse than *vadai*? A *nazir olam* by definition never concludes his *nezirut*; the inability to bring concluding *korbanot* is no additional burden. There should therefore be no reason to resolve the doubt leniently. Rava answered that even by *nazir olam* the *safek* is worse than the *vadai*. A definite *nazir olam* has a special leniency: *hikhvid se'aro meikel be-ta'ar* — if his hair becomes too burdensome, he may trim it by bringing three *korbanot*, even though this does not terminate the *nezirut*. This is an unusual *halacha* that recognizes the extraordinary burden of lifelong *nezirut* and permits periodic relief through the *korban* process. A *safek nazir olam*, however, cannot avail himself of this leniency — bringing the *korbanot* would again raise the problem of *safek chulin ba-azarah*. Thus even *nazir olam* as a *safek* is worse than *nazir olam* as a *vadai*.

### Nazir Shimshon

Rav Huna bar Yehuda pressed further: what about a case where the person declared *Haraini nazir Shimshon* conditionally? *Nazir Shimshon* is a special category derived from the life of Shimshon, who was a *nazir* yet became *tamei la-meitim* and could never cut his hair. From Shimshon we learn that there is a form of *nezirut* in which one may become *tamei* to the dead — unlike a standard *nazir* — but can never cut his hair under any circumstances, even with the leniency that applies to *nazir olam*. By *nazir Shimshon*, neither a definite nor a doubtful status carries the leniency of hair-trimming, so there would again seem to be no difference between *vadai* and *safek*. Why then should the condition not be binding?

The *gemara* responded: *nazir Shimshon lo tanya* — the *mishnah* does not deal with the case of *nazir Shimshon*; it was not contemplated in the standard ruling. Abaye bar Avin replied that there is in fact a *baraita* that does address this scenario — a conditional vow of *nazir Shimshon* — and Rabbi Yehuda still rules leniently even there. Rava conceded: *im tanya, tanya* — if there is such a *baraita*, it stands, though he remained unpersuaded by its logic.

## Ki Yafla Principle

### Tarfon Position

Rav Ashi offers yet another approach. The leniency of *safek nezirut le-hakel* is not Rabbi Yehuda's own position at all — it is a ruling transmitted by Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Tarfon. The *baraita* reads: *Rabbi Yehuda mishum Rabbi Tarfon omer, ein echad me-hem nazir* — neither person is a *nazir*. The case described involves two people walking and seeing a figure in the distance: one says "I will be a *nazir* if that is so-and-so" and the other says "I will be a *nazir* if that is not so-and-so." Since one of the two propositions must be true, it seems that one of them must be a *nazir*. Nevertheless, Rabbi Tarfon rules that neither becomes a *nazir*.

### Ki Yafla Source

The reason: *she-lo nitna nezirut ela le-hafla'ah* — *nezirut* was given only for *hafla'ah*, a term derived from the biblical verse *ish o isha ki yafli lindor neder nazir le-hazzir la-Hashem* (Bamidbar 6:2). The word *yafli* is understood to mean an articulate, precise, and unambiguous declaration. *Hafla'ah* is the concept underlying all speech-act *kedusha* — *neder*, *shevua*, *nezirut*, and *hekdesh* are all effectuated through *hafla'ah*. Here, however, *ki yafli* is read as a requirement for clarity: if there is any ambiguity at the moment of declaration, the *nezirut* does not take effect. This is a pure legal principle, entirely independent of what the person wanted or what is in his mind. Even if the person believed with certainty that it was or was not the person in the distance — and was objectively correct — *nezirut* does not bind when the declaration was made in a context of uncertainty apparent to observers. *Nezirut* requires that it be unambiguously established from the outset.

This principle, rooted in the *pasuk*, provides the cleanest and most legally grounded answer to the question. It is not about what a person would or would not want; it is not about the consequences of doubtful *nezirut*; it is a textual requirement that *nezirut* take effect only through unambiguous declaration.

### Grain Lost Detail

The *gemara* notes a textual precision in the grain case: the *baraita* specifically says the grain was stolen or lost. If the principle of *ki yafli* means that *nezirut* cannot take effect whenever there is any ambiguity at the time of vowing, then even if the grain were present and measurable, since it was not clear at the time whether the condition would be met, the *nezirut* should not be binding — and the detail of theft or loss would be unnecessary. The *gemara* answers: you are correct that according to Rabbi Yehuda, citing Rabbi Tarfon, even if the grain were present and measurable, the person would not be a *nazir*, since the declaration was made in a state of uncertainty. The *baraita* specifies the case of theft or loss as a *chiddush* for Rabbi Shimon's strict position: Rabbi Shimon holds that a person is willing to enter into doubtful status (*ma'eil inish nafshei le-sfeika*), and therefore even though the condition can never be verified, the *nezirut* takes effect. The more striking *chiddush* is actually Rabbi Tarfon's leniency, but the *baraita* is framed around the case that provides the greatest *chiddush* for the strict position.

## Stam Teruma Regions

### Teruma Strict Lenient

The *gemara* now returns to the *mishnah* regarding regional linguistic variation. Rabbi Yehuda says: *stam terumah bi-Yehudah assurah, uva-Galil muteret* — an ambiguous declaration of *teruma* in *Yehuda* is forbidden, but in *Galil* it is permitted. The reason: in *Yehuda*, the word *teruma* can mean either *terumat hagoren* (the ordinary agricultural *teruma*) or *terumat halishka* (the Temple chamber contribution), and since *terumat halishka* is a *davar hanadur* while *terumat hagoren* is not, the ambiguity generates a genuine doubt, and *stam nedarim le-hachmir* applies. In *Galil*, however, the people are not familiar with *terumat halishka* — the term *teruma* in that region refers exclusively to *terumat hagoren*, which is not a binding *neder*. Since the word has only the lenient meaning in that locale, the declaration is not binding.

The *gemara* infers from this: if in *Galil* the people *were* familiar with *terumat halishka*, making the word ambiguous in their region as well, the declaration would be forbidden — *ha makirim, assurin*. This confirms that Rabbi Yehuda endorses the principle of *stam nedarim le-hachmir* in any case of genuine ambiguity.

## Stam Charamim Region (II)

### Charamim Permitted Forbi…

Immediately following is the parallel ruling about *charamim*: *stam charamim bi-Yehudah mutarin, uva-Galil assurin* — an ambiguous declaration of *cherem* in *Yehuda* is permitted, while in *Galil* it is forbidden. The reasoning: in *Galil*, the people are unfamiliar with *charmei kohanim* — the type of dedication that goes to the *kohanim* rather than to *hekdesh* — so the word *cherem* can only mean *cherem* dedicated to the *Beis HaMikdash*, which is a binding *neder*. In *Yehuda*, the word *cherem* could mean either *cherem* to *hekdesh* or *charmei kohanim*, and since the latter is not a *neder*, the ambiguity renders it permissible.

But this is the problem. If in *Yehuda* the word *cherem* can mean either the strict form (*cherem* to *hekdesh*) or the lenient form (*charmei kohanim*), why are we lenient? By the logic of *stam nedarim le-hachmir*, whenever there is genuine ambiguity we should be strict.

## Stam Teruma Regions (II)

### Yehuda Consistency

The proof that Rabbi Yehuda holds *stam nedarim le-hachmir* despite the leniency in *Galil* for *teruma* was already established — in *Galil* the word is not ambiguous, so there is nothing to be *machmir* about. The rule *stam nedarim le-hachmir* applies precisely when there is genuine ambiguity. Rabbi Yehuda's position is therefore entirely consistent: where there is real ambiguity he is strict; where the word has only one meaning in that locale he is lenient. This is not a *kula* in *stam nedarim*; it is a determination that the word is not, in that context, a *stam* case at all.

## Stam Charamim Region (II)

### Elazar b'Tzadok

The anomaly of the *cherem* ruling — where Rabbi Yehuda appears to be lenient despite genuine ambiguity in *Yehuda* — is resolved by Abaye: *seifa Rabbi Elazar be-Rebbi Tzadok hee* — the final ruling about *charamim* in *Yehuda* is not Rabbi Yehuda's position at all. It is the position of Rabbi Elazar be-Rebbi Tzadok. Rabbi Elazar be-Rebbi Tzadok holds that in *Yehuda* the word *cherem* is permissible precisely because there is ambiguity — and implicit in his ruling is the position that *stam nedarim le-hakel*.

This is a striking conclusion. The entire lengthy *sugya* grappled with the question of who holds *safek nezirut le-hakel*, passing through the positions of Rabbi Eliezer, the distinction between *kedusha ba'ah mei-eilya* and *kedusha al yedei adam*, the debate of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, Rava's explanation based on *safek chamer mi-vadai*, and Rabbi Tarfon's principle of *ki yafli* — and now, at the very end of the *daf*, the *gemara* points to Rabbi Elazar be-Rebbi Tzadok as someone who apparently says *stam nedarim le-hakel* directly. As the *Ran* notes, one could have explained the entire discussion by attributing *safek nezirut le-hakel* and the corresponding lenient positions to this view.

One could, alternatively, read Rabbi Elazar be-Rebbi Tzadok more narrowly: perhaps he agrees in principle with *stam nedarim le-hachmir* but holds that in *Yehuda* the word *cherem* is not genuinely ambiguous — that the usage of *charmei kohanim* is so prevalent there that the word *cherem* alone refers exclusively to that category, and anyone who wishes to say *cherem* to *hekdesh* would say *charmei mikdash* explicitly. On this reading, Rabbi Elazar be-Rebbi Tzadok is making a linguistic determination, not announcing a general leniency in *stam nedarim*. The *gemara*, however, does not adopt this reading and appears to understand his ruling as reflecting a general position that *stam nedarim le-hakel* — a position that, after all the preceding analysis, turns out to have a clear talmudic advocate. The connection between *nedarim* and *nezirut* underlying this entire discussion runs through the shared hermeneutical principle of *hafla'ah*, derived through a *gezeira shava* linking the language of *neder* and *nezer* — which is why the rules governing one apply to the other.

# Nedarim 21

## Marital Relations

### Completing Daf 20

We begin today by completing Daf 20, picking up at the bottom of 20b with the verse *velo tasuru acharei levavchem*. The preceding *sugyah* on Daf 20 constituted one of the most remarkable discussions in all of *Shas*, dealing at length with the question of which physical acts are permissible between husband and wife during marital relations. We encountered two poles: the position associated with *Imma Shalom* and Yochanan ben Dahavai — closely aligned with the stringent posture of Rabbi Eliezer, who would rush through the marital act lest he entertain an improper thought — and the opposing voice of Rabbi Yochanan, who rules definitively: *ein halakhah k'Yochanan ben Dahavai, ella kol mah she-adam rotzeh la'asot b'ishto oseh*. Whatever a man wishes to do with his wife, he may do. The language, it should be noted, reflects the male perspective of the *Gemara*, though it is typically paraphrased today as the couple being permitted to do whatever they wish together — and the underlying position is that this is entirely unproblematic, not merely technically permissible.

One striking feature of the *Gemara*'s rhetorical strategy here is worth noting. The discussion began with anxieties about how improper conduct would affect the children — a claim that, had it remained in the *halakhic* domain, would have had to contend with Rabbi Yochanan on *halakhic* terms. But Rabbi Yochanan's framing as *ein halakhah* essentially relocates Yochanan ben Dahavai's concerns outside the *halakhic* conversation altogether. Whatever metaphysical ideas one might hold about proper and improper conduct, the *Gemara* is insisting that those anxieties belong to a non-*halakhic* register. *Halakhically*, there is nothing problematic here.

### Intent vs. Use

Now, however, the *Gemara* makes an important shift. It introduces the verse *velo tasuru acharei levavchem* — you shall not stray after your hearts — and cites Rebbe: *al yishteh adam b'kos zeh v'yiten einav b'kos acher*. A person should not drink from one cup while setting his eyes on another — a metaphor for having marital relations with one's wife while thinking of another woman. Ravina sharpens this: *lo nitzrecha ella d'afilu b'shnei nashav* — this applies even between a man's two wives; he should not be intimate with one while his thoughts are directed toward the other.

This passage, notably, focuses not on *acharei eineichem* but on *acharei levavchem* — it is not about what the eyes perceive but about what the heart strays toward. The man sees the woman before him but is mentally elsewhere, straying after his own inner fantasy. The problem the *Gemara* is now identifying is not the nature of the physical act at all, but whether the act of intimacy is an act of genuine *relating* to the person in front of you, or merely *using* that person as a stand-in for someone else you would rather be with. That is the distinction — not the particular activity, but whether the person before you is truly present to you.

There is an important question lurking here about the role of fantasy in marital life generally, and some *poskim* do address it. However, the *Gemara* appears to be speaking specifically about a case where one imagines oneself with another person entirely and treats one's actual spouse as merely playing that role — a functional displacement rather than ordinary arousal. That is what is prohibited.

### Nine Traits

The *Gemara* continues with the verse *uvaroti mikem hamordim vehaposheim bi* — I will sift out from you those who rebel and sin against Me. Rabbi Levi reads this as a reference to *bnei tisha middot* — children conceived through nine types of deficient conduct. Where yesterday the *Gemara* was asking whether particular physical acts would produce physically flawed children — a claim resoundingly rejected — now it asks whether a different kind of deficiency, one of character and relational disposition, will produce children of poor character. The problem has shifted from the physical to the moral, from what kind of act was performed to what kind of relating was occurring between the spouses. The acronym *Asnat Mashgaach* encodes the nine types.

### Fear & Hatred

The first is *bnei eima* — children conceived when the wife is acting out of fear of her husband. The *Ran* explains: *lashon yira shehetil eima al ishto lehizakek lo shelo kirtzonah* — the husband has instilled fear in her such that she submits against her genuine will. Then *bnei anusa* — children of a woman who is literally coerced. Then *bnei senuah* — when he hates her; he feels no love, no care, but treats her as an available means of physical gratification. The *Ra'avad*, in his discussion of this passage, pointedly symmetrizes the case: it is the same whether he hates her or she hates him. Either way, one party is using the other purely for self-gratification rather than relating to them out of love or care.

*Bnei nidui* — children conceived while the husband is under a ban — is the one case in this list that stands apart, as it is simply a *halakhic* violation unrelated to the relational theme. *Bnei tmurah* — exchange — refers to a case of confusion, where one believes he is with one wife but is in fact with another. *Bnei meriva* — children of strife — means they are in the middle of a fight, not as makeup sex after reconciliation, but mid-conflict, where one thinks: we may be fighting, but we might as well have relations. *Bnei shichrut* — intoxication — means one or both are drunk, according to the *Ra'avad*, and not mentally fully present. *Bnei grushat halev* — divorced in the heart — means the husband has already decided, internally and unilaterally, to divorce his wife but has not yet told her; he proceeds with intimacy as if the marriage is still intact in spirit, which it is not.

*Bnei irvuvya* — children of confusion — is somewhat unclear: the *Ran* understands it as referring to relations with multiple partners, which would make it a case of adultery; Rashi suggests a case where a man cannot distinguish which of his wives he is with, similar to *tmurah*. Finally, *bnei chatzufa* — the audacious woman — we will return to shortly.

With the exception of *tmurah* and *chatzufa*, all of these cases share a single common feature: the spouse is being used as an object of self-gratification rather than genuinely encountered and related to as a person. This is what the *Gemara* identifies as the source of harm — not some physical impropriety, but the failure of genuine relational presence. Yesterday's discussion was about which physical acts are permitted; today's conclusion is that the real *halakhic* demand is not about the type of act but about whether intimacy is an act of connection or an act of use.

### Female Initiation

The *Gemara* now turns to *bnei chatzufa* — the audacious child — which the *Gemara* understands to mean that the wife demanded relations with her husband. One might have thought this was entirely praiseworthy. Indeed, the *Gemara* itself immediately raises the objection: *ayni?* Is that really true? Does it not say — *de'amar Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani amar Rabbi Yochanan* — that any man whose wife is *tova'ato*, who actively solicits him, will have children of extraordinary quality, surpassing even those of the generation of Moshe Rabbeinu? The proof: when Moshe called for men who are *chachamim u'nevonim*, he could not find people of *tevunah*. But the tribe of Yissachar, who are *yodei binah l'ittim*, did possess that quality — and Yissachar was conceived when Leah was *tova'at* Yaakov. The plain implication is that a wife actively soliciting her husband produces exceptional children.

The *Gemara* resolves the contradiction: *hahi d'martza artzuyei* — that was a case of seduction and persuasion, not outright demand. Leah seduced; she did not command. The permissibility, even the virtue, lies in *martza artzuyei* — hinting, enticing, drawing close — not in *tova'at b'peh*, an explicit verbal demand.

This distinction, however, naturally raises the question of where exactly the line lies between the two. The *teshuvah* of the *Yehuda Ya'aleh* reasons that since the *Gemara* validates what Leah did — and Leah said *elai tavo*, "come to me," which is already quite explicit — any expression short of an absolute demand ("you have no choice in the matter") would fall within the permitted category of *martza artzuyei*. What the wife cannot do is strip the husband of any say in the matter.

### Connection & Care

Even so, the very fact that the *Gemara* takes Leah's *tova'at* as a model that produces children greater than those of Moshe's generation is a striking recalibration of what might have been assumed to be a patriarchal assumption — that the husband always initiates, that the wife has no voice. The *Gemara*, far from affirming that assumption, holds it up and says: not only is female initiative acceptable, it is the paradigm of the ideal.

And with that, we complete the *perek* with *hadran alach ve'elu mutarin*. The conclusion of this entire extended discussion about marital intimacy is that *halakhah* is not primarily concerned with which physical acts are performed. What *halakhah* demands is that intimacy be an act of genuine connection — that each partner be present to and for the other, not using the other as a means to some private end. That is the core of what the *Gemara* is teaching about marital relations.

---

## Four Vows

### Four Categories

We now turn to a new area of the laws of *nedarim*. So far the *masechta* has been dealing largely with questions of interpretation: what words constitute a *neder*, how we read ambiguous formulations, to what extent a person's own interpretation of their language is credited, and so forth. One question that has not yet been addressed directly is that of *piv v'libo shavin* — the alignment of one's words and one's heart. What happens when someone utters the unambiguous language of a *neder* but was not truly intending to bind themselves? Not a case of misused words, where one meant *cherem* in the sense of a fishing net — but a case where the language was clearly *neder*-language, yet the speaker's frame of mind was simply not in sync with a genuine intention to be bound. That is what the *Mishnah* now addresses.

*Arba'ah nedarim hitiru chachamim* — the sages permitted four categories of vows, meaning these vows are not halakhically binding. The four are: *nidrei zeruzin* — spurring vows; *nidrei havai* — vows of nothingness or hyperbole; *nidrei shegagot* — vows made in error; and *nidrei onsin* — vows made under compulsion. In each case, the speaker used what sounds like *neder*-language and was aware that those were *neder*-words — yet because of their particular frame of mind at the time, the vow does not take effect.

### Spurring Vows

The example of *nidrei zeruzin*: a seller says *konam she-ani pocheis lach min ha-sela* — this object should be forbidden to you if I sell it for less than a *sela* (four *zuz*). The buyer counters: *konam she-ani mosif lach al ha-shekel* — it should be forbidden to me if I pay more than a *shekel* (two *zuz*). *Shneihem rotzim b'shloshah dinarim* — both of them are in fact aiming for three *dinarim*. Neither side actually intends to forbid anything; the vow-language is deployed as a haggling tool, a way of pressing the other side.
