Since neither party is genuinely serious about binding themselves, the vows do not take hold.

### Conditional Vows

The *Gemara* raises a question about the *tanna* behind this *mishnah*. Rav Abba bar Mamal reports in the name of Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah (the grandson of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) that the author is Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai, who said in the name of Rabbi Tarfon: *l'olam eino nazir lefi shelo nitnah nezirut ela l'hafla'ah* — a conditional vow of *nezirut* never takes effect because *nezirut* requires *hafla'ah*, precision and absoluteness at the moment of utterance. The relevance: the *zeruzin* case involves a conditional structure ("if I go lower than..."), and Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai may therefore be reading the permissibility as stemming from the conditionality itself, not from lack of seriousness. Even a completely serious conditional *neder* might not be binding.

Rava objects: *afilu teima rabanan* — one can explain this even according to the *rabbanan* who disagree with Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai on conditional *nezirut*. The *mishnah* does not say *shneihem ratzu*, "both wanted the same middle outcome and the conditions were therefore never really triggered." It says *shneihem rotzim*, they *want* the same thing — meaning from the outset, they never intended the vow to be binding at all. That is the reason it is not a *neder*: not some technical feature of conditionality, but the straightforward absence of genuine intent.

### Precision

Ravina then poses a sharper case to Rav Ashi: what if the seller said he will not go lower than *more than a sela* — say, four *zuz* and a fraction — and the buyer said he will not go higher than *less than a shekel*, say one *zuz* and a fraction? The parties are now being quite precise; they are not using round numbers. Precision in a financial negotiation might suggest genuine seriousness — the more exact your formulation, the more it looks like a real commitment rather than theatrical haggling. Perhaps in that case the vow *would* be binding?

### Exaggeration

Rava responds by pointing to a *baraita*: if someone was being persistently pressed by his friend to come eat at his house and finally said *konam beitecha she-ani nichnas*, "your house should be forbidden to me — I won't enter it," or even *tipat tzonen she-ani to'eim*, "I won't drink even a drop of cold water by you" — in such a case the person *is* permitted to enter the house and drink cold water. *Shelo nitkavein zeh ela l'shum achilah u-shtiyah* — the speaker's genuine intention went no further than refusing to participate in the meal.

The *Ran* explains: *af al gav d'nachis l'diyuka* — even though the person went down to minute precision, specifying "a drop of cold water," and thereby distanced himself far from what his friend wanted, nevertheless he did not literally mean it. The language of a single drop is recognizable as hyperbole, not as a real commitment to avoiding the house altogether.

This case raises a significant point: do we say that the exaggerated extensions simply fall away while the core intention remains binding, or that since the entire formulation was hyperbolic nothing is binding at all? The *baraita* implies the former: the person is permitted to enter the house and to drink water, but is presumably still bound by the core refusal to sit down for a meal. The exaggerated shell dissolves, but what the speaker genuinely intended — declining the invitation to eat — remains. That is a notable *chiddush*: *neder*-annulment is not always all-or-nothing; the exaggerated perimeter can be stripped away to reveal and enforce the actual intent at the core.

Returning to the question of precision: the *Gemara* distinguishes. *Tzaddikim omrim me'at v'osim harbeh* — righteous people promise little and deliver much. A person who says "I will give you just a drop of water" and then produces a feast is not being imprecise; he is using the conventional idiom of understatement. Inversely, someone who says he won't even accept a drop is using the conventional idiom of overstatement. In both cases the speaker's actual intention diverges from the literal words, and this is recognized social usage. The precise number in the haggling scenario, however, may be different — there it might genuinely signal that the speaker means exactly what he said. The *Gemara* concludes: *teiku*. The question of whether extreme numerical precision in a *zeruzin*-type context creates a real *neder* remains unresolved.

### Halakhic Authority

Rav Yehuda then reports in the name of Rav Assi: *arba'ah nedarim hallalu tzerichin she'eilah lehacham* — these four categories of vows still require formal release by a *hacham*. Even though the *chachamim* declared them permissible, one should still go through the process of *hatarat nedarim* to avoid treating vow-language lightly. When Rav Assi reported this ruling before Shmuel, Shmuel challenged it: the *tanna* explicitly teaches that the *chachamim permitted* these vows — which implies they are automatically non-binding and require no formal release. How can you say they require a *hacham*?

In light of this challenge, Rav Yosef teaches the tradition in a different formulation that does not carry the same vulnerability: *ein chacham rashai lehattir ella ke'ein arba'ah nedarim hallalu* — a *hacham* is not permitted to release a *neder* unless it approximates one of these four categories. This version of the statement shifts the function of the four categories: rather than being cases that themselves require release, they become the paradigm by which all *hatarat nedarim* is measured. A *hacham* releasing any *neder* must be able to bring the case into alignment with one of these four models.

---

## Vow Annulment

### Model of Annulment

With that formulation — *ein chacham rashai lehattir ella ke'ein arba'ah nedarim hallalu* — we arrive at the heart of the *halachah* of *hatarat nedarim*. The *Gemara* now uses these four categories as the template for understanding what *hatarat nedarim* is doing and how it works.

Consider the case: a person comes to a *hacham* to be released from a *neder* they clearly meant at the time. The question is, on what basis can the *hacham* permit it? The underlying logic of the four categories is that the person, in each case, was never truly and fully intending for the vow to be binding. In the haggling case this is obvious to everyone — no one seriously meant to forbid anything. But that same underlying structure — "at the time, I did not fully mean it to be binding" — is what the *hacham* must be able to reconstruct in any case where he releases a *neder*. The case before him will of course have appeared, from the outside, to be a genuine *neder*. That is why it needs a *hacham*. But the *hacham*'s work is to find the point at which the person's actual frame of mind at the time was not fully in sync with the binding force of what he said.

### Petach & Charata

This brings us to the central distinction in *hatarat nedarim* between two modes of release: *petach* and *charata*. A *petach* — an "opening" — is the identification of some consideration that the person had not thought through at the time of the vow; had they considered it, they would not have made the vow. A *charata* — "regret" — is the person's retrospective wish that they had never made the vow at all, independent of any specific unconsidered circumstance.

The relationship between *petach* and the *arba'ah nedarim* model is clear: the *petach* says, "you never fully meant it, because had you thought it through, you wouldn't have done it." That is structurally analogous to the haggling case — in both situations, the person's genuine will, properly understood, was not behind the vow. *Charata*, by contrast, concedes that at the time the person fully intended and meant the vow — but now, in hindsight, wishes they had not. That is a different kind of claim.

### Starting w/ Petach

Hence the principle — which follows directly from *ein chacham rashai lehattir ella ke'ein arba'ah nedarim hallalu* — of *ein potchin b'charata*: one does not open a *hatarat nedarim* process by asking the person whether they regret making the vow. You start with *petach*. You try to find some circumstance the person had not fully considered, such that you can say: had you thought this through, you would not have made the vow.

### Types of Charata

The *Ran* draws an important further distinction within *charata* itself. There is *charata me'ikara* — regret from the root — which means the person wishes they had never made the vow at all. And there is *charata dehashtah* — regret of now — which simply means that the person no longer wants to be bound going forward. The *Ran* notes that the second is not *charata* in any meaningful sense at all: every person who shows up seeking release from a *neder* no longer wants to be bound. That is why they came. True *charata* requires that the person genuinely wish that the vow had never been made in the first place — a retroactive reframing of the original moment.

### Rav Huna Case

The *Gemara* now presents a series of cases. Someone came before Rav Huna, who asked him: *libecha alecha?* — is your heart upon you? The person said: no. And Rav Huna released him.

The *Ran* explains this question as probing the person's frame of mind. The *Ran* paraphrases: *haya libecha meyushav alecha b'sha'ah shenadarta* — were you of settled mind when you made the vow? *V'gam achshav eincha toheh b'nidrekha ad hayom* — and have you also had no regret about it until now? *Ela shemehayom ulehalan ata rotzeh lachzor bach* — or is it only from today onward that you want to withdraw? That would be *charata dehashtah*, not *charata me'ikara*, and would not suffice. But if the person's answer of "no" means: no, I am *not* only changing my mind now — I actually regret ever having made it — then that is *charata me'ikara*, and Rav Huna releases him. This is therefore a case where *charata* is used as the basis for release, not *petach*.

One might ask whether this stands in tension with the principle of *ein potchin b'charata*. The answer appears to be that *ein potchin b'charata* means you do not *start* with *charata* — you prefer to find a *petach* — but *charata* remains a valid basis for release when it is genuine *charata me'ikara*.

### Middle Ground

Rabba bar bar Chana took a somewhat different approach in his case. He asked the person: *ilu hayu asara bnei adam sheyefaysucha b'ota sha'a, mi nadarta?* — if ten people had been there to calm you down and persuade you at the time, would you still have made the vow? The person said no, and Rabba bar bar Chana released him.

The *Ran* identifies this as occupying a middle ground between *petach* and *charata*. It is more than pure *charata* — rather than simply asking whether you regret it, it asks whether you could have been persuaded otherwise at the very moment of the vow. That slightly retrojects the counterfactual into the original moment, getting closer to the idea that the vow was not fully intended. But it falls short of a standard *petach*, which identifies a concrete circumstance the person had failed to consider — an internal lapse of reasoning rather than an external persuasion that might have intervened.

### Rabbi Yehuda

A *baraita* records Rabbi Yehuda's formulation: *omrim lo l'adam, lev zeh alecha* — you say to a person: is this same heart upon you? If he says no, you permit him. The *Ran* explains this similarly to Rav Huna: you are asking whether the person is simply changing their mind now, or whether they genuinely feel, in retrospect, that the vow should never have been made. "No, this is not the same heart I have now" — meaning: I am not the same person in the same state of mind who made that vow; I deeply wish it had never happened — is *charata me'ikara*, and suffices.

This leads to a practical point. The principle *ein potchin b'charata* means that a *hacham* should not begin with the *charata* question — not because *charata* never works, but because we take the language of vows seriously, and the preferred approach is to locate a *petach* that shows the person's genuine will was never fully behind the vow. *Charata* is harder — it concedes the full intentionality of the original moment and asks for release on the basis of subsequent regret. It works, but it is not where one begins.

### Rav Assi

Rav Assi asked a person who came before him: *kiduta shita* — are you astounded at what you originally did? The person said no — meaning, effectively, of course, how could I not be regretful of it? — and Rav Assi released him. The *Ran* notes the somewhat puzzling idiom: the person answers in the negative to what seems to be a question whose affirmative answer would grant release. The *Ran* suggests it was a rhetorical formulation — "am I *not* astounded?" — but in any event the substance is clear: this is another formulation aimed at eliciting *charata me'ikara*.

### Rabbi Eliezer Case

Someone came before Rabbi Eliezer, who asked: *be'ita nadur?* — do you want your vow to remain? The person replied: *ilu lo margizin li, lo be'inan klum* — had they not angered me at that time, I would never have wanted any of this. Rabbi Eliezer said: *tehei k'va'is* — let it be as you wished. The vow is released, because you only made it in anger and genuinely wish those circumstances had never arisen.

### Woman & Daughter

A final case: a woman had made her daughter forbidden to benefit from her — a severe vow of estrangement. She came before Rabbi Yochanan to be released. Rabbi Yochanan asked her: *ilu avita yadat d'amrin megirataikh, alu d'bartakh, ilu lo chama bat imma milin d'aziva, bechdi lo adarta* — had you known that your neighbors would say, "Look at her daughter — if her own mother made such a vow against her, the daughter must have done terrible things worthy of abandonment," would you have made the vow for no reason? The woman said no, and Rabbi Yochanan released her.

This is a clear case of *petach*. Had the woman stopped to think through the social implications of her vow — what it would signal to the neighbors about her daughter's character — she would never have made it. She was acting on anger without fully thinking through all the consequences. The *petach* here is not an internal circumstance she failed to consider but an external social reality: the vow itself, once made, would broadcast a devastating statement about her daughter to the world. That unconsidered implication is the *petach* through which Rabbi Yochanan opens the release. And it is a perfect illustration of the paradigm: you did not fully mean it, because had you fully thought it through, you would not have done it.

---

---

# Nedarim 22

## Charata vs. Pesach

### Charata and Pesach

The daf opens in the midst of a discussion about the practical process of *hataras nedarim* — releasing individuals from vows. Two foundational concepts govern this process. The first is *charata*: simple retrospective regret, the sense that "I wish I had never done this." The second is *pesach*: a retroactive disavowal grounded in an element of error, the sense that "had I been thinking clearly at the time, I never would have made this vow in the first place." This latter concept resembles the *arba nedarim* of our *Mishna*, where it is clear from the outset that the vow-taker did not fully mean what he said. The *pesach*, by contrast, involves demonstrating in hindsight that had the person been fully deliberate, he would not have intended the vow — making it a subtler but related form of the same underlying principle.

### Opening with Charata

Since *pesach* is the more substantive and concrete basis for release — it demonstrates with greater precision why the vow was never truly binding — one might assume it is always required. The question the *Gemara* is working through, then, is whether *potchin b'charata*: whether one may open the process of *hataras nedarim* with simple regret, or whether a specific *pesach* is always necessary.

## Rabbi Yannai Case

### Heaven Opens Ledger

The *Gemara* presents a series of cases in which different *Amoraim* released vows, some on the basis of *charata* and others on the basis of *pesach*. We now pick up three lines from the top of 22a. The grandson of Rabbi Yannai came before his grandfather seeking release from a vow. Rabbi Yannai opened with the following: "Had you known that when one takes a vow, the heavenly ledger is opened and your deeds are scrutinized — that the act of vowing triggers a divine audit of your entire conduct — would you have made the vow?" The grandson replied that he would not, and Rabbi Yannai thereupon released him.

### Verse Proof

Rabbi Abba identifies the scriptural basis for this principle: *ve-acharei nedarim levaker* — "after vows you will be inspected." The logic is that the vow-taker implicitly considers himself righteous enough to go beyond what the *Torah* has forbidden. The *Torah*, accordingly, responds by scrutinizing whether the person truly merits that self-assessment.

### Too Generic

This case is interesting on several levels simultaneously. At one level it concerns the formal *halakha* of how *hataras nedarim* operates. At another level it reflects the idea that the process depends on *pifo v'libo shavin* — the mouth and heart must be in agreement — so that a *chacham* can inquire into whether the vow-taker truly and fully intended the vow. And at yet another level, the case serves as an occasion to explore the religious status of vowing in general.

Yet whatever its virtues, Rabbi Yannai's opening is entirely generic. There is nothing case-specific about it: any vow-taker, in any situation, could be told that taking a vow triggers heavenly scrutiny. A proper *pesach* is meant to be concrete and particular — "had you been thinking about *this* specific consideration, you would not have made *this* vow." Rabbi Yannai's formulation, whatever its rhetorical power, does not achieve that.

## Rejecting Scare Tactics

### No Heavenly Ledger

The *Gemara* rules explicitly: even though Rabbi Yannai opened with the heavenly ledger, we do not open this way. The objection is twofold. First, as noted, it is too generic to function as a genuine *pesach*. Second, and crucially, the Ran explains that such an opening is a scare tactic: by confronting the petitioner with the specter of divine punishment, you may frighten him into saying he regrets the vow even if he does not genuinely feel that way. The danger is that you will elicit an answer that reflects fear rather than authentic reconsideration.

### Bamah Statement Rejected

The *Gemara* extends this ruling to another formulation. We also do not open with what was taught in a *braisa* in the name of Rabbi Natan: *ha-noder ke'ilu bana bamah, ve-ha-mekaymo ke'ilu makriv alav korban* — one who makes a vow is as if he built an unauthorized altar (*bamah*), and one who goes through with fulfilling it is as if he offered a sacrifice upon it.

### Bamah Philosophy

This is a striking and philosophically rich statement about the nature of vowing. The *bamah* metaphor deserves careful attention. The person who makes a vow is attempting to do more than what the *Torah* demands — to adopt additional prohibitions beyond those the *Torah* has already established. The implicit assumption is that self-denial is the paradigmatic religious act, so that doing more of it constitutes a higher level of piety. But this reasoning reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of what religious practice is.

The *bamah* comparison makes precisely this point. During a period when all sacrifice must be offered at the central *Beit HaMikdash*, building a private altar is not an act of greater piety — it is a transgression. Religion, in this view, is not a private, self-initiated enterprise but a communal, God-defined one. One does not earn credit by going off on one's own and constructing a personal religious supplement. And of course, the sin compounds itself: building the *bamah* is one violation, but actually offering upon it is a further and graver one. By analogy, making the vow is already problematic, but fulfilling it only deepens the problem — which is precisely why seeking *hataras nedarim* is so important.

It bears noting that there were historical periods when *bamot* were permissible — when there was no central *Beit HaMikdash*, private altars served a legitimate religious function. One can understand why a person might feel that the institutionalized framework of religion does not fully answer his spiritual needs, and that some personal religious initiative is called for. The *Gemara* is not denying that impulse entirely. But the specific context here — making things forbidden upon oneself beyond what the *Torah* requires — is the target of the critique.

### Ran's Analysis

The Ran addresses this directly. He writes that the reason we compare the vow-taker to one who builds a *bamah* is precisely because the vow-taker believes he is performing a *mitzvah*. His reasoning runs as follows: the *Torah* prohibits many things, and since the prohibition of things is itself a religious value, he can make himself even more religious by prohibiting yet more things upon himself. The *Gemara* — and the Ran in expounding it — declares this a fundamental error.

The Ran draws on a passage in the Yerushalmi in the perek *potchin lo*: "Is it not enough what the *Torah* has forbidden, that you must go and make more things forbidden upon yourself?" This is a trenchant formulation. The Rambam echoes this sentiment extensively in his discussions of the golden mean and the dangers of excessive self-denial: more restriction is not always a religious good, and may in fact be a religious failure.

The Ran adds a further dimension specific to the *neder* as a legal form: a *neder* draws its force from the *korban* model, since the prohibiting formula *konam* renders an object like a *korban*. If that quasi-*korban* is not desired by God — because the vow was not a legitimate religious act — then it is as though one has offered a sacrifice outside the *Beit HaMikdash*. Moreover, the Ran notes, the end of the *braisa* — "one who fulfills the vow is as if he offered a sacrifice upon the *bamah*" — can function as a *pesach* in the positive sense: to get out of the vow is to stop the process of bringing this unwanted quasi-sacrifice. Not seeking *hataras nedarim* means continuing to "offer" on an unauthorized altar.

### Abaye-Rava Debate

Despite all this, a debate arises as to whether we may at least open with the *beginning* of the statement — that making the vow was like building a *bamah* — even if we do not use the *end* of the statement about offering a sacrifice upon it. Building a *bamah* does not involve the same severity as actually bringing a sacrifice upon it; perhaps we can use the milder comparison without the scare-tactic concern.

Abaye says we open with the beginning of the statement; Rava says we do not. There is also a version of this dispute attributed differently to Rav Tavyumi, in which everybody agrees we do not open with the end — that it would be like bringing a *korban* outside the *Beit HaMikdash* — but Abaye and Rava dispute the beginning.

The final *halakha* is: *lo patchinin lo bereisha velo besayfa* — we open with neither the beginning nor the end. We do not say it is like building a *bamah*, and certainly do not say it is like bringing a *korban* upon it. The upshot is that we do not open with any of these scare-tactic formulations, however instructive they may be as theological statements about the nature of vowing.

## Anti-Scare Tactics

### Shmuel: Vow-Keepers Wick…

The *Gemara* continues: we also do not open with the statement of Shmuel. Shmuel taught that even one who fulfills a vow is called a *rasha* — a wicked person. This too would function as an extreme scare tactic: even going through with your obligation is sinful.

### Verse on Ceasing Vows

Rabbi Abbahu identifies the verse: *ve-chi techdal lindor lo yihyeh becha cheit* — "if you cease to make vows, there will be no sin in you." He then applies a *gezeira shava*, linking the word *chadala* (ceasing) in this verse to the same word appearing elsewhere: *sham reshaim chadlu rogez* — "there the wicked have ceased their anger and discord." The linguistic connection associates the cessation of vowing with the domain of the *resha'im*, confirming that one who makes vows and fulfills them is in some sense counted among the wicked.

### Sages' Teaching

Rav Yosef notes that the same idea appears in material we ourselves have studied: *kenidrei kesherim lo amar klum* — if someone says "this should be binding upon me like the vows of upright people," he has said nothing, because upright people do not make vows. But *kenidrei resha'im* — like the vows of wicked people — that is a binding formula, invoking *nazir*, *korban*, or *shvua*. Thus even the *Mishnayos* themselves encode the assumption that vow-taking is the province of the wicked, while those who are truly righteous do not vow at all.

The broader conclusion of this entire section is that the *Gemara* in *Nedarim* consistently presents vowing in a negative light — not as the only view in *Chazal*, but certainly as the dominant thrust of this *masechet*. The statements cited as potential *pesakim* are rejected not because they are wrong, but because they would function as scare tactics, potentially inducing people to claim regret they do not genuinely feel.

## Anger Digression

### Gehinnom & Anger

The *Gemara* now pivots into what it frames as a digression — though the connections to the surrounding material are not entirely incidental. Since the previous discussion mentioned *resha'im* and their anger, the *Gemara* transitions into a series of statements about the consequences of anger. Rabbi Yonatan — or Rabbi Yochanan — teaches: *kol ha-ko'es kol minei gehenom sholtim bo* — anyone who gets angry, all forms of *gehenom* take hold of him.

### Verse on Anger

The scriptural basis comes from *Kohelet*: *haseir kaas milibecha veha'aveir ra'ah mibsarecha* — "remove anger from your heart and remove evil from your flesh." The *Gemara* identifies *ra'ah* with *gehenom*, citing: *vegam rasha leyom ra'ah* — "and also the wicked person is destined for a day of evil" — where the "day of evil" denotes a concrete punishment awaiting him.

It is worth pausing over what the *Gemara* means here. The text of *Kohelet* is saying something relatively straightforward: anger eats away at you internally, affects how you think and act, and corrodes your life from within. The *Gemara*'s more graphic formulation — that all forms of *gehenom* control the angry person — may well be understood not as a description of otherworldly punishment but as a vivid depiction of the natural consequences of rage. Anger makes a person irrational; it leads him to transgress things he would never otherwise violate; it burns him from within and destroys his relationships and his better judgment. That is the *peshat* of the *pasuk* in *Kohelet*, rendered in the *Gemara*'s characteristic style.

### Physical Effects

The *Gemara* adds a further consequence: *ha-tachtoniyot sholtot bo* — hemorrhoids take hold of him as well. The *pasuk* is brought from *Devarim*: *venatan Hashem lecha sham lev ragaz* — God will give you there an angry heart — along with *vechilyon einayim* (dimming of the eyes) and *vedaavon nefesh* (languishing of the soul). The *Gemara* asks: what is the ailment that simultaneously afflicts the eyes and pains the soul? The answer: hemorrhoids. The connection to *kaas* and internal burning is the underlying physiological intuition — that extreme emotional agitation produces physical inflammation and internal distress. Indeed, the entire phenomenon here reflects a sophisticated understanding that emotional states have concrete bodily consequences.

### Chuza Murder Story

The *Gemara* presents a striking narrative illustrating where unchecked anger leads. When Ulla traveled up to *Eretz Yisrael*, two men from Chuza accompanied him on the journey. During the trip, one of them fell into a violent rage and killed the other.

### Ulla's Fear Response

The murderer then turned to Ulla and asked: *ya'u avdi?* — "Did I do well? Was it all right what I did?" Ulla, fearing for his own life, replied yes, and — depending on the textual variant — either himself exposed the neck of the murder victim or told the murderer to do so. When Ulla later came before Rabbi Yochanan, he expressed concern: *dilma chas veshalom achzeiki* — "perhaps, God forbid, I strengthened the hands of a sinner by affirming what he did?" Rabbi Yochanan reassured him: *nafshecha hatzalta* — you saved yourself. Under normal circumstances such a response would be impermissible, but the imperative of self-preservation overrides it here.

One might also raise a related question about the instruction to expose the murder victim's neck — whether hastening the death of someone already dying might touch on the *halachic* question of *chayei sha'ah*, and whether the imperative of *chiyuv hatzala* applies differently to someone whose life is terminal. These are complex questions that belong to the *poskim*, but the narrative at least provides a concrete case around which to think through the issues.

### Exile Requirement

What astonished Rabbi Yochanan was not Ulla's conduct but the fact that such murderous anger could have erupted at all. The verse says *venatan Hashem lecha sham lev ragaz* — God will give you *there*, in exile, an angry heart. The context is *Bavel*, the place of exile. How, then, could such anger manifest before crossing the Jordan into *Eretz Yisrael*? Ulla replied: *hahu sha'ata lo avrinan Yardena* — at that moment we had not yet crossed the Jordan; we were still in *chutz la'aretz*, and so the condition of exile-driven anger still applied. This is somewhat ironic given what is known historically of the intense sectarian passions that characterized life in *Eretz Yisrael*, but the *Gemara* reads the verse as limiting this particular form of rage to the exilic condition.

### Anger Consequences

The *Gemara* continues with several additional statements about the consequences of anger. Rabbah bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan teaches: *afilu Shechina eina chashuva k'negdo* — when a person is angry, he does not even care about God's presence. The *pasuk* cited: *rasha k'govah apo bal yidrosh ein Elokim kol mizmosav* — the wicked person, in the height of his anger, does not seek God; God is absent from all his thoughts. This rings psychologically true: rage is totalizing. Nothing matters to the person in its grip — not prior commitments, not relationships, not religious obligations.

Rav Yirmiyah of Difti adds: anger causes a person to forget his Torah learning and to become increasingly foolish. The verse: *ki cha'as b'cheik k'silim yanu'ach* — anger rests in the bosom of fools. And Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds a diagnostic dimension: if a person gets angry, it is a known indicator that his sins outweigh his merits. The verse: *u-va'al cheima rav pasha* — the person given to anger has abundant transgression.

### Sin and Scripture

Rav Ada, son of Rav Chanina, offers a remarkable observation. Had Israel not sinned in the *cheit ha-miraglim* — the sin of the spies — they would have received nothing more than the five books of the *Torah* and the book of *Yehoshua* alone. Why *Yehoshua*? Because *Yehoshua* addresses the value and the division of *Eretz Yisrael*, providing narrative closure to the *Torah*'s foundational story of the people entering the land. But the rest of *Tanach* — the *Nevi'im Acharonim* in particular — exists primarily to deliver *mussar* to *Bnei Yisrael* for their repeated failures. Had they not sinned, all the religious wisdom they needed would have been contained in the five books of Moshe.

The verse cited: *ki berov chochma rov kaas* — for in the abundance of wisdom there is an abundance of anger. The accumulation of wisdom through the prophetic books was itself a product of the accumulation of sin, which required a divine response. There is something simultaneously humbling and moving in this formulation: the magnificent corpus of *Nevi'im* that contains some of the most eloquent articulations of Torah values exists precisely because the people needed to be called back from their failures. The wisdom was real, but its occasion was loss.

## Elohei Yisrael Vows

### Rav Assi's Rule

The *Gemara* returns now to the main discussion. Rav Assi teaches: *ein nizkakim l'Elohei Yisrael* — we do not attend to vows made in the name of the God of Israel, with one exception: *shalom bayis*.

### Wife's Vow Case

The illustrative case: *konam ishti nehenet li* — "may my wife derive no benefit from me" — taken because she stole his wallet or struck his son. If it then becomes clear that she did neither of those things, the question of how to release the vow arises. One might note that if he explicitly stated these false premises as the basis of the vow, it could well be a case of *nidrei shegagot* — vows taken on false premises — which are inherently non-binding and would not require formal *hataras nedarim* at all. The Ran discusses this point and some commentators accordingly bracket that portion of the case.

### Neder or Shvua

There is a significant interpretive dispute as to what precisely is meant when someone vows "in the name of *Elokei Yisrael*." The Ran, along with *Tosfot* and the Rambam, understands this as referring to a *shvua* — an oath. Taking an oath in God's name is a distinct and weightier act than an ordinary *neder*, which derives its force from the *korban* framework rather than from invoking God directly. On this reading, the passage is discussing a situation that arose in the context of *hataras nedarim* but actually involves the question of whether a *chacham* can release a *shvua* taken in God's name.

This connects to the broader dispute between *Beit Shamai* and *Beit Hillel*: *Beit Shamai* holds that one never performs *hatara* for a *shvua*, since a *shvua* engages God's name and is about one's personal integrity and honesty in a way that a *neder* is not; *Beit Hillel* holds that *hatara* is available for a *shvua* as well. According to Rav Assi, even *Beit Hillel* would agree that a *shvua* taken specifically in the name of *Elokei Yisrael* is too weighty to release — unless it stands in the way of *shalom bayis*. The Ran draws a beautiful parallel: just as the *midrash* teaches that God allows His name written in holiness to be erased in water in order to make peace between husband and wife (in the *sotah* procedure), so too a *shvua* taken in His name can be undone for the sake of marital peace.

Rashi, however, reads the case differently: the formula *konam ishti nehenet li* is explicitly *lashon neder*, the language of a vow, and so we are speaking of an actual *neder* — but one made with God's name invoked alongside it, creating a hybrid between the *neder* and *shvua* forms. Even without the full weight of a *shvua*, using God's name in the context of a *neder* adds sufficient gravity that we are reluctant to release it absent a compelling reason like *shalom bayis*.

### Rav Assi to Woman

When the woman comes before Rav Assi to seek release, he says to her: *i nadart b'mohi, mizdakkekna lach* — had you used the term *mohi*, which functions as a *kinuy* (euphemism) for an oath, I would have attended to you and found a way to release you. *Hashta d'lo nadart b'mohi ela b'Elokei Yisrael, lo mizdakkekna lach* — but since you used not a *kinuy* but the name *Elokei Yisrael* itself, I cannot help you. The terminological distinction carries decisive *halachic* weight: a *kinuy* or euphemism for a *shvua* is releasable; a vow or oath taken explicitly in the divine name is not — except for *shalom bayis*.

The confusion in terminology throughout this passage — the word *nadart* used to describe what appears to be a *shvua* — is itself revealing. The *Gemara* is not always precise in distinguishing between *nedarim* and *shvuot*, a point the Ran explicitly acknowledges.

### Kahana-Yosef Story

The *Gemara* presents a telling anecdote. Rav Kahana came to the home of Rav Yosef, who offered him something to eat. Rav Kahana declined: *mari kula — lo ta'imna* — in the name of the Master of all, I will not eat anything. Rav Yosef replied in kind: *lo mari kula lo ta'imna lei* — in the name of the Master of all, I will not feed you anything. The *Gemara* notes that this makes sense from Rav Kahana's side — he took a *shvua* not to eat. But why did Rav Yosef need to invoke God's name at all? The *Gemara* concludes that Rav Yosef was not taking a new *shvua* of his own, but was rather communicating: since you have invoked God's name in your *shvua* not to eat, I am constrained — I cannot help you out of it. I am therefore unable to give you anything to eat. The story is instructive in demonstrating how casually and consequentially God's name was being invoked in everyday situations — something the *Gemara* clearly views as problematic.

## Halakha & Geonic Views

### Rav Nachman Ruling

The *Gemara* now delivers the bottom-line *halakha* through Rav Nachman: *hilchata potchin b'charata venizkakim l'Elohei Yisrael* — the law is that we open with *charata* (simple regret), and we do attend to vows taken in the name of *Elohei Yisrael*. Both rulings cut in the direction of accessibility and leniency: we do not require a specific *pesach*, and we do not treat the invocation of God's name as an absolute bar to release.

### Ran's Clarification

The Ran clarifies the scope of Rav Nachman's ruling: *potchin b'charata bein b'neder bein b'shvua* — we open with *charata* for both a *neder* and a *shvua*; and *nizkakim nami l'chatchila l'Elohei Yisrael* — we attend *l'chatchila* even to vows taken in God's name. The Ran further adds that this applies even if the person was holding a *Sefer Torah* while taking the oath. Being in physical contact with a *Sefer Torah* during an oath is a psychological intensifier — analogous to placing one's hand on a Bible — but it does not alter the fundamental *halachic* analysis. The *Sefer Torah* is relevant in the context of *shvuat ha-dayanim*, a court-administered oath, where such tangible contact is used to heighten solemnity; it does not render the *shvua* irrevocable for purposes of *hatara*.

### Gaon Disagreement

The Ran records that an unnamed *Gaon* ruled that one who swears in the name of the *Sefer Torah* or the *Aseret Ha-Dibrot* has no release ever — *ein lo hafara olamit*. The Ran dismisses this position unequivocally: *leita le-milta klal* — it has no standing whatsoever. The *din* is the *din* of the *Gemara*, which releases even *shvuot* through *charata*, and *kol she-ken* for *nedarim*.

### Rav Hai Gaon

Rabbeinu Hai Gaon takes a more measured but still significantly stricter position. Against the plain ruling of the *Gemara*, Rav Hai holds that for *nedarim* one must open with a *pesach* — not *charata*. His reasoning is that we should practice as Rav Ashi described, releasing vows only in a manner analogous to the *arba nedarim*: there must be a genuine ground for retroactive disavowal. *Charata* alone is too vague. Furthermore, Rav Hai holds that for *shvuot*, even a *pesach* is insufficient — we never release a *shvua* except in a case of *davar mitzvah* or *shalom bayis*.

### Mar Yehudai Gaon

Mar Yehudai Gaon goes further still. In his view, *nedarim* are to be treated like *shvuot*: we do not release either except in cases of *mitzvah* or *shalom bayis*, and even then only through a genuine *pesach*, not *charata*. He adds that the *pesach* in question must be one established by a *chacham* — *petach d'chacham* — not the husband's unilateral *petach* (*petach d'ba'al*), which is a different mechanism belonging to the realm of *hafara* rather than *hatara*.

### Final Ruling

Both the Rambam and the *Shulchan Aruch* rule in accordance with the *Gemara*, not the *Geonim*. Their position is that we are always available to release someone from either a *neder* or a *shvua*, whether taken in God's name or not, whether through *pesach* or through *charata*, and that no additional barriers beyond what the *Gemara* itself establishes should be placed in the path of one seeking release. The *Geonim* may have had policy reasons for their stringency — making vows feel weightier so that people would not take them lightly, knowing release would always be available — but as a matter of *ikar hadin*, their positions were not accepted.

There is a real tension embedded in this entire question. The easier it is to obtain release from a vow, the more it may encourage people to make vows casually. Yet the harder it is to obtain release, the more trapped people become in obligations that may be causing them real harm. The *Gemara* resolved this tension decisively in favor of accessibility — and the *Rambam* and *Shulchan Aruch* affirmed that resolution.

---

---

# Nedarim 24

## Kol Nidrei & Stipulation

### Kol Nidrei Recap

Today's daf is 24. Yesterday's shiur, delivered by a substitute, covered the central issues surrounding *kol nidrei* and the mechanism of making a *tnai* — a stipulation — to prevent one's vows from taking effect. By way of review: the *mishnah* presented the position of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who introduced the category of *nidrei zeruzin*, vows that are not genuinely intended to be binding.

### Nidrei Zeruzin

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov identified two related phenomena. The first and more transparent example involved two people haggling over the price of something, each making a *neder* in the course of the back-and-forth — a process that was obviously a kind of game, with no real intent that the vows should take effect. The second, somewhat less obvious case involved using a vow as leverage or pressure to get someone to do something — for instance, vowing that a friend's food will be forbidden unless he agrees to come for dinner. This calls to mind the story of Abaye and his wife, where a vow was deployed as an ultimatum; the inherent problem with ultimatums is that one must ultimately make good on them. The question is whether one can truly claim retroactively that the vow was never intended to be binding. That is precisely Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position: in such cases, where the person was using the vow purely as a form of pressure or encouragement and never genuinely wanted it to take effect, the vow is categorized as *nidrei zeruzin* and is not binding.

### Stipulation Mechanism

Alongside the *nidrei zeruzin* discussion, the *gemara* identifies a separate and independent mechanism: making an explicit stipulation at the outset — at the beginning of the year, for instance — declaring that any future vow one may take should not be considered binding if one does not remember having made it. The *gemara* raises an internal tension here: if you remember the stipulation and you go ahead and make a vow anyway, you presumably want the vow to be binding. Conversely, if your intent was always that it not be binding, you shouldn't be making the vow in the first place. The stipulation therefore helps only in cases where one genuinely forgets about it. This mechanism is analogous to, though not identical with, the institution of *moda'ah* in *dinei mamonot*: if someone is pressured into selling a plot of land, he may tell witnesses in advance that even though he will sign the document, he does not truly consent to the sale. Similarly here, one can declare in advance that any future vow should not be considered sincere. Rava offered a nuanced answer addressing certain intermediate cases where the person half-remembers the stipulation, but he did not, in principle, dispute Abaye's basic framework.

### Hatarat Nedarim

The practical upshot is that one may make such a declaration at the beginning of the year — at *Rosh Hashanah* — stipulating that any vows taken during the coming year, if forgotten, should not be binding. This is precisely the formula recited at the conclusion of the *hatarat nedarim* ceremony on *erev Rosh Hashanah*: *hareini mosar moda'ah lifneichem* — "I hereby make a proclamation before you" — followed by the declaration that any vow made from this day forward without being remembered shall be annulled from now. Of course, one observes that if this declaration truly worked comprehensively, one would not need to repeat *hatarat nedarim* every year; a single *moda'ah* would suffice indefinitely. But that, in any case, is the *gemara*'s mechanism.

The Ran then takes up the question of how all this bears on *kol nidrei*. The *hatarat nedarim* ceremony performed on *erev Rosh Hashanah* combines both dimensions explicitly: it annuls past vows through a generic expression of *charatah* — regret — and takes a stipulation for the future. The question of whether *charatah* alone, without specifying a *petach*, suffices for a generic annulment is one we have addressed previously; a generalized declaration of regret on behalf of the entire *tzibur* is somewhat unusual, since ordinarily the person seeking release must present himself and indicate *mischarait* — that he regrets the vow.

### Kol Nidrei Meaning

*Kol nidrei* presents its own complications. Unlike the formal *hatarat nedarim* ceremony, one is not presenting oneself individually, the formula combines past and future in an ambiguous way, and the halachic mechanism through which it operates is not entirely clear. The simple reading of the text suggests it is past-oriented, though Rabbeinu Tam, apparently for reasons related to this sensibility, proposed reorienting it toward the future — requiring certain grammatical adjustments to the text. Some *machzorim* preserve both the past-oriented and future-oriented *nuscha'os*, presenting them as alternate versions. An article on the grammar of *kol nidrei* by Dr. Richard Steiner offers a thorough analysis of this question for those interested in pursuing it.

It is worth noting that this question had significant real-world stakes. For much of Jewish history, the integrity of a business transaction with non-Jews was backed by a sworn vow. The perception that Jews would publicly release themselves from their vows on *Yom Kippur* night — effectively nullifying all commitments made over the preceding year — created serious problems and was used as grounds to question Jewish trustworthiness in commerce. This was part of the reason Rav Hirsch removed *kol nidrei* from the *Yom Kippur* liturgy in his community. The Ran's position that *kol nidrei* cannot coherently be understood as future-oriented — given the *gemara*'s concern, discussed below, about not publicizing the stipulation mechanism too broadly — also bears on how one understands the practical halachic meaning of the text.

---

## Rav Huna & Rava Dispute

### Rav Huna's View

The *gemara* now raises a question: should this mechanism of stipulation have been publicly announced? Rav Huna bar Chinana's position was that it ought to have been publicized broadly — at a *pirka*, a public gathering — so that everyone would know they could make a stipulation at the beginning of the year and thereby protect themselves from inadvertently transgressing their vows.

### Rava's Objection

Rava disagreed sharply. He pointed out that the *tana* had deliberately concealed this information — *mistam lei satumei* — by weaving the stipulation mechanism subtly into the *mishnah*'s case about *nidrei zeruzin*, rather than stating it as a separate and explicit principle. The reason: *kedei shelo yinhagu kalos rosh benedarim* — so that people should not treat their vows lightly. If everyone knew that a simple advance stipulation could nullify any future vow, there would be a strong temptation to take vows casually, confident that no real obligation was being incurred. Rava therefore challenges Rav Huna bar Chinana: the *tana* took care to obscure this information — and you propose to announce it in a public forum?

This passage is striking for two reasons. First, it offers a window into how the *gemara* sometimes understands its own hermeneutic activity. When the *gemara* reads a *mishnah* and extracts two distinct legal principles from what appears on its surface to be a single unified case, one might wonder whether the *gemara* truly believes this to be the *pshat* of the text or whether it is simply offering a legal reformulation that need not be taken as a reading of the *mishnah* itself. Here, remarkably, the *gemara* seems to be affirming that this is genuinely *pshat*: the very fact that the information was buried in the *mishnah*'s formulation, rather than stated explicitly, is itself legally significant — it was hidden intentionally.

### Sin vs Sloppiness

The second noteworthy dimension of this passage is the broader tension it reflects. This tension has run throughout *masechet Nedarim*: on one hand, you want to prevent people from actually transgressing their vows; on the other hand, if you make it too easy to avoid transgression — by providing ready-made mechanisms for annulment or by assuring people that certain vows are not really binding — you risk encouraging sloppiness in how people take vows in the first place. We have seen this tension elsewhere in the tractate: sometimes a *neder* is not technically binding, yet we require the person to go through the process of *hatarat nedarim* precisely so that the gravity of vow-taking is not undermined. Similarly, the *gemara* elsewhere formulates the principle of *halacha v'ein morin kein* — a ruling exists but is not publicized — and some halachic handbooks reflect this by presenting the public-facing ruling in the main text while reserving more nuanced leniencies for footnotes in Hebrew accessible only to *talmidei chachamim*.

Rav Huna bar Chinana's position, it should be noted, was presumably motivated by genuine concern: people were stumbling over vows they did not fully intend, and a publicly known mechanism could spare them that sin. Rava's response is not that the mechanism is invalid, but that broadcasting it too widely creates different harms. The *mishnah*'s deliberate obliqueness was thus not a failure of transparency but a considered halachic policy.

---

## Rabbis vs R. Eliezer

### Opening Question

The *gemara* now poses a new question: did the *rabbanan* disagree with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's categorization of *nidrei zeruzin*, or did they accept it? The stipulation mechanism, the *gemara* notes, would presumably be agreed upon by everyone — the debate about the *tnai* at the beginning of the year seems unrelated to the question of *nidrei zeruzin* per se. The real point of contention is whether the *rabbanan* accepted Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's broader category: when someone makes a vow not in the context of transparent haggling but as a form of one-sided pressure to get a result — "if you don't come to dinner, my food will be forbidden to you" — is that truly *nidrei zeruzin* and therefore not binding? One can imagine someone who genuinely would be offended at being refused, and who would sincerely intend the vow. Perhaps the *rabbanan* maintain that when the situation is not transparently a game, the vow stands. And a secondary question: if the *rabbanan* do disagree, how do we rule — like them or like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov?

### Gift Acceptance Case

The *gemara* adduces evidence from a *mishnah*. The case: someone says to his friend, *konam she'ani neheneh lecha im i attah notel livnecha kor shel chitin ushtei chaviyot shel yayin* — "my benefit from you shall be *konam* if you do not accept for your son this measure of wheat and these two barrels of wine." The speaker is trying to give a gift — perhaps a wedding present — and the intended recipient keeps refusing. In the middle of this friendly exchange, the giver declares that if the gift is not accepted, all benefit from the recipient will be forbidden to him. The *mishnah* rules: *harei ze yachol lehatir nidro shelo pi chacham* — he can get out of the vow without consulting a *chacham*, meaning the vow is not binding.

### Honor Satisfaction

The reasoning is as follows: *sheyachol lomar lo klum amarta ela bishvil kvodi zehu kvodi* — the recipient could say, "You only made that vow for the sake of my honor. Well, this is my honor — that you made me such an offer and I had the standing to decline it." In other words, the underlying purpose of the vow — to confer honor — has been achieved even without the gift being accepted. The person who refused the gift can claim he was honored by the very offer and by his ability to graciously decline. Therefore, it is as though the condition of the vow was satisfied, and the vow does not take effect.

One might observe that there is something not entirely gracious about this response. By insisting that the honor lies in declining, the recipient in some sense dishonors the giver by denying him the satisfaction of giving. The *Yerushalmi* addresses this directly: it says that if the giver responds, "I did not make the vow for your honor — I made it for mine, because it meant something to me to give this to you," then the vow is binding. The *Yerushalmi* thus contemplates the possibility that *lechvodi*, not *lechvodecha*, was the animating motivation, in which case the honorific logic fails. When the motivation is ambiguous, the question of whose honor drove the vow becomes determinative.

There is also a broader cultural dimension here. In the Roman world of patronage, the acceptance of a gift from a social inferior was itself a powerful statement of status. A *mishnah* in *Kiddushin* reflects something similar: one of the modes of *kiddushin* is the woman giving a gift to the man, with his agreement to accept it serving as the act of acquisition. In a world structured around patronage dynamics, the willingness of a more prominent figure to accept a gift carried real social weight, and the entire exchange could not be reduced to simple friendship.

### Case Classification

Having laid out the *mishnah*'s ruling, the *gemara* draws an inference. The *mishnah* says the vow is not binding because *zehu kevodi* — it is as though the honor was received. But this implies: were it not for that reasoning, the vow *would* be binding. So this is a genuine *neder*, not *nidrei zeruzin*. One might therefore conclude that the *rabbanan* argue with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov — that a one-sided vow used to pressure someone into accepting a gift is a real vow, not mere *zeruzin*.

The *gemara* rebuffs this inference: *le'olam Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov hu* — this *mishnah* can still be according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. But here, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov would concede that the vow is serious: *modeh Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov be'hai denidra havai*. Why? Because the giver says to the recipient: *lo kalba ana d'mit'hanina minech v'lo mit'hanita minai* — "I am not a dog, that I would be deriving benefit from you while you get nothing from me." Here the dynamic is reciprocal: the giver is saying, "I give things to you all the time; if you will not accept even this, then it is simply not a relationship where I can continue to take from you either." The vow runs in the opposite direction — if you do not accept from me, I will not take from you — and that introduces an element of genuine sincerity that distinguishes it from the simpler case.

---

## Reciprocal Vows

### Giver's Vow

The *gemara* now introduces the inverse case. *Ha'omer l'chavero konam she'ata nehenit li im ee ata noten livni kor shel chitin ushtei chavyot shel yayin* — "Your benefit from me shall be *konam* if you do not give my son this measure of wheat and these two barrels of wine." Here, instead of the giver making a vow about his own benefit from the recipient, he makes a vow about the recipient's benefit from him. Rabbi Meir says: *ad sheyiten* — until the recipient actually gives the gift, he cannot derive benefit from the giver. The *chachamim* say: *af zeh yachol lehatir et nidro b'lo pi chacham* — even here the vow is not binding without consulting a *chacham*. Why? *Sheyachol lomar hareni k'ilu hitkabalti* — because the giver can say, "It is as though I received the gift." This is similar in structure to the previous case: though the condition was not met, the giver declares it as effectively satisfied.

### Reciprocity Argument

Before returning to the question of *nidrei zeruzin*, the Ran raises an important question about the meaning of *ke'ilu hitkabalti*. One intelligible understanding is as follows: the giver wanted to receive an object; he could imagine a scenario in which Michael had given him the barrels of wine and he had then given them back. In that case, saying *ke'ilu hitkabalti* — "it is as though I received them" — has a plausible legal logic, because there is a concrete transaction one can imagine having occurred and been reversed. But what if the condition was not about a physical object? Suppose instead the condition was: "This is forbidden to you unless you go to the gym twice a week." In that case, *ke'ilu hitkabalti* is much harder to parse — what exactly is being treated as though it happened? The Ran raises this difficulty. He suggests that perhaps in all cases, the underlying logic is simply that the giver set a condition, the purpose of the condition was to satisfy a desire, and the giver can always declare that desire satisfied — which amounts to waiving the condition. Whether this is a conceptually clean legal mechanism or more of a pragmatic escape valve is a question the Ran leaves somewhat open.

In any case, the thrust of the *mishnah* — before the *gemara* addresses the question of *nidrei zeruzin* — is that this is a genuine *neder*, but one from which the giver can extract himself by invoking *ke'ilu hitkabalti*. The logical consequence: were that not available, the *neder* would be binding. So this seems to point toward the *rabbanan* holding that these pressure-vows are real vows.

### Ran's Analysis

The *gemara* again deflects: *le'olam Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov hu* — and the Ran's explanation makes this intelligible in terms of the *gemara*'s language. When the direction of the vow runs one way — "if you don't come to dinner, my food will be forbidden to *you*" — one might argue this is just an empty threat, a form of *zeruzin*. The person may be using the vow to encourage or pressure, but perhaps it is so hollow that even Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's category cannot make it binding. By contrast, when the vow runs in the reciprocal direction — "if you don't accept this from me, I won't get any benefit from *you*" — that reflects a genuine concern about the nature of the relationship. One is saying: what kind of relationship would it be if I give to you and you give me nothing in return? If this dynamic is allowed to continue, I simply do not want that relationship. Someone could sincerely feel this way, and therefore even Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov would concede that such a vow is binding.

The Rashba reads the distinction differently: he argues that what makes the case more serious is the weight of the gift involved — a larger, more significant gift warrants a more sincere vow, whereas an invitation to dinner is trivially easy to dismiss. However, this reading is difficult to reconcile with the actual language of the *gemara*, which never focuses on the size of the gift. The *gemara*'s language — *rav malka ana de-mahnina lach v'at la mahnit li* — points squarely to the reciprocity concern, not to the monetary value of the gift. When someone says, in effect, "Do you think I'm some kind of king who gives and expects nothing back?", the issue is relational symmetry, not the magnitude of any particular item. As anyone who has experienced that hollow feeling when the same person keeps arriving at *Shabbat* meals without ever hosting in return will recognize — that relational dynamic is a real source of grievance, and a vow expressing it could well be sincere.

### Initiated Vows & Ones

Mar Kashisha son of Rav Chisda raises yet another attempted proof from the *mishnah* dealing with *nidrei onsin* — vows that became impossible to fulfill due to circumstances beyond one's control. The case: I pressure someone to come eat at my house, and if he does not come, my food is forbidden to him. He was on his way but fell ill, or his son fell ill, or a river flooded and he could not cross. The *mishnah* holds that the vow is not binding, because I surely never intended the vow to apply in a case of genuine *ones*. What I wanted was for him to make his best effort to come; had he done so and been thwarted, I would never have wanted the prohibition to take hold.

This case sounds like *nidrei zeruzin*, since it is a one-directional vow used to encourage attendance at dinner. Yet the *mishnah* appears to treat it as a real vow that happens to be suspended due to *ones*. If it were truly *nidrei zeruzin*, the question of *ones* would be irrelevant — the vow would simply not be binding at all. This seems to imply that the *rabbanan* hold such a vow is genuinely binding when the condition is willfully not met.

The *gemara* once again deflects by reframing who initiated the vow. The case is not one where the inviter made the vow against the invitee; rather, *dizamina adrei l'mizamna* — the invitee initiated the vow. Michael had been wanting to come to dinner and felt that his host was not sincere about the invitation. So Michael pressed: "Come on, do you really want me to come? Make a vow to show me." The host, thus challenged, made the vow. In this scenario, the vow was not a *zeruzin* — it was not deployed to push Michael into doing something he was reluctant to do; Michael was already eager to come. The host made the vow to demonstrate sincerity in response to Michael's prompt. Therefore, the vow is a genuine *neder*, and when Michael cannot come due to *ones*, the *gemara* holds the vow does not take effect — precisely because it was not a vow of pressure but a vow of sincere commitment that circumstances rendered impossible to fulfill. This, the *gemara* argues, is still consistent with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov; it does not prove the existence of a *rabbanan* who dispute him.

After all this, the *gemara* has provided an answer to each attempted proof, but the weight of the evidence continues to suggest that there is indeed a stricter position in the background — one that treats these one-directional pressure-vows as genuine *nedarim*. The *gemara* has managed each time to distinguish the specific case, either through reciprocity, initiation, or *ones*, but the category of *nidrei zeruzin* as applied to simple one-sided encouragement-vows remains contested.

### R. Eliezer Extended

At this point, the *gemara* introduces a further statement: *yeter al ken amar Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov* — Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov went further. He said: *ha'omer l'chavero konam she'ani neheneh lecha im i attah mit'areach etzli v'tokhal immi pat chamah v'tishteh immi kos chamim* — "My benefit from you shall be *konam* if you do not come and stay with me as a guest, eat hot bread with me, and drink a cup of tea with me." And if the other party then responds in kind — saying similarly that he will derive no benefit from the host if the host does not reciprocate — *af elu nidrei zeruzin* — even these are *nidrei zeruzin*, says Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. The *chachamim* did not agree.

This statement is significant. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov is here extending his leniency to include even the reciprocal case — the very case the *gemara* had been treating as more sincere throughout the preceding discussion. Not only do the *rabbanan* refuse to follow him in this extension, but the *gemara* now asks what exactly the *rabbanan*'s disagreement covers: *lav afillu b'kammaita* — do the *rabbanan* not agree even with the original, non-reciprocal case? *U-shema mina pligi rabbanan alei* — from the phrasing here, it seems the *rabbanan* reject Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position across the board.

The *gemara* acknowledges, however, that there is an alternate *girsa* of the text according to which the *rabbanan*'s disagreement is limited to the reciprocal case alone; on the non-reciprocal case they might agree. What is clear in all *girsaos* is that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov himself holds that both cases are *nidrei zeruzin*.

---

## Ruling & Nidrei Havai

### Halakha Decision

The *gemara* concludes: *mai havya alah* — what is the practical ruling? *D'amar Rav Huna halakha k'Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov, v'khen amar Rav Adda bar Ahava halakha k'Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov* — Rav Huna ruled like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, and Rav Adda bar Ahava said the same. We rule like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

The Ran observes that this ruling effectively renders the first question — whether the *rabbanan* actually disputed Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov — moot. The entire investigation was driven by a *halachic* interest: does Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov stand alone or does he have opponents, and if opponents, who do we follow? Once we have the ruling, the prior question loses its urgency. The Ran notes that this is analogous to the Rambam's approach of presenting the final ruling without the surrounding dialectic — if the only interest is knowing what the *halacha* is, all the preceding discussion becomes academic. Of course, one might respond that learning the *gemara* has value beyond the bottom-line ruling, and the reasoning behind a position matters for understanding edge cases and borderlines. This also connects to the broader question of the principle of *yachid v'rabim halacha k'rabim* — ordinarily we follow the majority — and why in this case we deviate from it to follow Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. The considerations that go into such a ruling — the logic of the positions, the accepted practice in the field, the authority of the *Shulchan Aruch*, the clarity of the *gemara*'s own *pshat* — are the same considerations any *posek* must weigh, and there is no fixed hierarchy among them.

The practical scope of *nidrei zeruzin* as now defined is quite broad: not just the transparent mutual haggling case, but even one-sided pressure-vows and even reciprocal vows of the form "if you don't take from me, I won't take from you." All of these Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov — and now the *halakha* — considers *nidrei zeruzin*. The difficulty that remains is knowing precisely where the line falls. Abaye's own case, after all — where he made a vow as an ultimatum and still required a *hatarat neder* — seems to fall in the *zeruzin* category on its face. Yet it was treated as a genuine vow that needed formal release. Knowing which pressure-vows are mere *zeruzin* and which are sincere commitments that a person genuinely entertained — even if reluctantly — and which are the middle category of Abaye where the person was sincere but assumed the other party would comply, is a question that the *gemara* leaves without a fully explicit answer.

### Nidrei Havai Intro

The *mishnah* introduces the second category: *nidrei havai* — vain or empty vows. *Amar konam im lo ra'iti baderech hazeh k'olei Mitzrayim* — "This loaf is *konam* to me if I did not see on this road as many people as the Jews who came out of Egypt." Or: *im lo ra'iti k'nachash k'korat beit ha-bad* — "if I did not see a snake as thick as the beam of an olive press."

### Exaggeration vs Falsehood

The Ran distinguishes two different phenomena at play in the *mishnah*'s examples. The first case — seeing as many people as *olei Mitzrayim* — the Ran actually treats as a form of *guzma*, rhetorical exaggeration. When someone says "there were as many people as the Jews who came out of Egypt," everyone understands this as hyperbole meaning there were enormous crowds. On this reading, the person is actually telling the truth — he really did see massive throngs of people, and his vow condition was genuinely satisfied, expressed in the conventional idiom of exaggeration. The vow is therefore not binding, but for a different reason than one might expect: the *tnai* was actually fulfilled. The Ran's point here is really a principle about how to interpret exaggerated language in vows: *guzma* is read in its figurative meaning, not its literal one, so a vow conditioned on a patently hyperbolic statement is assessed according to what the speaker clearly meant, not the literal words.

The second case — a snake the size of an olive-press beam — is more interesting and more clearly within the *nidrei havai* category. This is not rhetorical exaggeration but an outright fantastical claim. The person is making a vow conditional on something everyone knows to be false. If you genuinely wanted to make the bread forbidden, you would simply say "this bread is forbidden to me." Why attach it to a condition you know to be false? The only sensible answer is that you are not actually trying to make the bread forbidden at all. What you are doing is using the vow to add rhetorical weight and colorfulness to your fish story — you want people to appreciate how enormous the snake was, and the vow formula serves as a rhetorical intensifier.

### Purpose Principle

This leads to the governing principle of *nidrei havai*: a *neder* is an instrument designed to make an object forbidden. When a vow is conditioned on something patently false — something everyone present knows to be untrue — the speaker clearly has no interest in making the object forbidden. He is using the vow for an entirely different purpose: to add drama and emphasis to a boastful or exaggerated statement. Since the vow is not being deployed for its intended function, it is not a *neder* at all, and nothing is forbidden.

---

## Nidrei vs Shevuot

### Shevuot Shav

The *gemara* introduces a *braita* that contrasts *nidrei havai* with *shevuot havai*. The version of the text before us reads: *nidrei havai mutarim shvuos havai asurim* — vows of the *havai* type are permitted, but oaths of the *havai* type are forbidden. An alternate *girsa* cited in the margin reads that both are permitted. To understand which is correct, the *gemara* points to the *mishnah* in *Shevuos* 29, which enumerates examples of *shvuat shav* — a false or vain oath. *Nishba l'shanot et hayadua la'adam* — swearing to contradict something universally known. For example: swearing that a stone pillar is made of gold, that a man is a woman, or that one did not see a snake like the beam of an olive press, or a flying camel. This is called *shvuat shav*. The *mishnah* in *Shevuos* thus categorizes these precisely as the type of oath the *gemara* is calling *shvuat havai*.

### Neder vs Shevua

The conceptual distinction between a *neder* and a *shevua* is essential here. The purpose of a *neder* is to make an object forbidden. The purpose of a *shevua* — particularly an oath about the past or present — is to back up one's word, to assert the truth of a statement with the weight of a divine invocation. These are fundamentally different instruments.

### Permitted vs Forbidden

When a person makes a *neder havai* — attaching a vow condition to a patently false or absurd statement — he has no interest in making any object forbidden. He is not using the *neder* for its proper purpose at all; he is co-opting the vow formula to add rhetorical color to a story. Therefore the vow is null, and nothing is forbidden. The *neder* simply does not function as one here.

When a person makes a *shevuat havai*, however — invoking an oath to back up a patently false claim — he is using the *shevua* for *exactly its intended purpose*: to lend credibility and weight to a statement. The fact that the statement is false does not mean the *shevua* is being misused; quite the contrary. Taking a *shevua* in order to back up one's word, even a false word, is precisely what a *shevua* does. And when it is invoked to back up a patently false claim, that is *shvuat shav* — forbidden by the Torah. So the asymmetry is principled: *nidrei havai* are permitted because the *neder* is not functioning as a *neder*; *shevuot havai* are forbidden because the *shevua* is functioning exactly as a *shevua*, and a *shevua* used to assert a falsehood — even an obvious one — is *shvuat shav*.

### Shevuat Havai Refined

The *gemara* then asks: what exactly would constitute a *shevuat havai*? If one says *shvua im lo ra'iti* — "an oath if I did not see such-and-such" — *midi ka'amar*? What kind of oath is that? An oath *if* you saw something is incoherent; the oath needs to be that you saw something. Abaye offers the straightforward formulation: *d'amar shvua she'ra'iti* — "a *shevua* that I saw a snake of such a size." That is indeed *shvuat havai* — you are invoking an oath to back up a patently false claim.

Rava objects, however, that this formulation is too obvious: it is simply the well-known category of *shvuat shav*, not a new principle. And furthermore, *dumiya d'neder katani* — the *shvuat havai* should be structurally parallel to the *nidrei havai* case. The case of *nidrei havai* involved a conditional structure: "this bread is forbidden to me if I did not see..." Rather than a direct assertion of the oath, Rava therefore reformulates: *b'omer ye'asru peros ha'olam alay b'shvua im lo ra'iti baderech hazeh k'olei Mitzrayim* — one says "by oath, all the fruit of the world is forbidden to me if I did not see on this road as many people as came out of Egypt." This is the genuinely novel case of *shvuat havai*: it is not a direct false assertion backed by an oath, but a conditional oath attached to a fantastical or exaggerated claim. That formulation is less obviously a simple *shvuat shav*, and it is here that Rava locates the real content of the category. Here too, one might observe intuitively, the oath is being used to give *oomph* to one's statement — the speaker is trying to convey the magnitude of what he witnessed, and the oath-formula is the intensifier he reaches for. We will resume this analysis in the next day's learning.

---

---

# Nedarim 25

## Nidrei Zeruzin & Havai

### Ein Piv Velibo Shavin

We pick up at the bottom of 24b, where the *mishnah* has already introduced us to the four categories of *nedarim* that are not binding. The unifying principle underlying all four is *ein piv velibo shavin* — the words spoken did not reflect the speaker's genuine intent. Even when the correct formulation was used, the vow lacks the essential congruence between speech and will that is required for it to take effect.

### Nidrei Zeruzin

The first category is *nidrei zeruzin* — vows made for the purpose of incentivizing or encouraging someone else. Whether the other party understood the speaker was not serious (as in the classic case of haggling) or genuinely believed the vow to be sincere, the bottom line is that the speaker never truly intended it to be binding. The vow was deployed as a social or rhetorical tool, not as a genuine act of prohibition.

### Nidrei Havai

The second category is *nidrei havai*. Here too the speaker never actually wants the object to become forbidden. Instead, the *neder* is used to lend weight to a statement — typically a patently false one. The *neder* functions as a kind of rhetorical emphasis, not as a genuine act of prohibition.

### Fish Stories & Guzma

The *mishnah* presents two examples of *nidrei havai*. The first — swearing that one saw as many people as those who left Egypt — is treated by the *Ran* as a case of *guzma*, a hyperbolic exaggeration. On his reading, the statement may not even be technically false; it is simply not to be taken literally, and therefore it does not properly belong to the category of *nidrei havai* at all. Setting aside the *Ran*'s somewhat distracting analysis, the essential case is the second one: claiming one saw a snake as large as the beam of an olive press. This is a transparently false statement — a "fish story," as it were. Just as people telling tall tales tend to embellish and pile on, so here the speaker adds a *neder* to back up the claim and give it emphasis. Since everyone understands the statement is false and the speaker never genuinely wanted anything forbidden, the *neder* does not take effect. In *nidrei zeruzin*, nobody takes the vow seriously, or at least the speaker does not. In *nidrei havai*, everybody knows the underlying claim is false, and the *neder* is merely its rhetorical backing.

---

## Shvuot Havai Analysis

### Tana: Nidrei/Shvuot

The *Gemara* on 25b opens with a *tanna* teaching: *nidrei havai mutarim* — vows of exaggeration are not binding — while *shvuot havai assurim* — oaths of exaggeration are forbidden. A second *girsa* reads instead *keshem shenidrei havai mutarim kach shvuot havai mutarim* — just as such vows are not binding, so too such oaths are not binding. The distinction between these two versions matters considerably, because the question of whether something is *assur* or *mutar* depends entirely on what one is looking at: is the question whether taking the *shvua* was forbidden, or whether the object the *shvua* was meant to prohibit actually becomes forbidden?

### Abaye's Translation

The *Gemara* asks: what exactly is a *shvuat havai*? If one says "a *shvua* that I did not see as many Jews as the *yotzei mitzrayim*," the *Gemara* objects — *midi ka'amar*? That formulation is grammatically incoherent; an oath attached to an "if" clause that goes nowhere says nothing. Abaye therefore reformulates: the oath is stated positively — *shvua she'ra'isi* — I swear that I did see so many Jews. This is the direct translation of the *neder* form into the oath form. Where the *neder* says "this will be forbidden if I did not see," the *shvua* says "I swear that I did see." In such a case — swearing to back up a patently false statement — the *shvua* would constitute a *shvuat shav*, an oath taken in vain, since everyone understands the statement to be false.

### Rava's Objection

Rava objects to Abaye's framing. If the case is simply that someone swore to back up an obviously false statement, we already know that is a *shvuat shav* — what is the novelty? Moreover, the *mishnah* in *Shvuos* frames the case in a way that must be analogous to the *neder*: not just backing up a statement, but actually making an object forbidden.

### Shvuat Shav vs. Forbiddi…

Rava therefore presents the properly analogous case: *be'omer ye'asru peiros ha'olam alai bishvua im lo ra'isi baderech hazeh ke'olei mitzrayim* — one says that all fruit of the world shall be forbidden to him by *shvua* if he did not see as many people as the *olei mitzrayim* on this road. This mirrors the *neder* precisely: in the *neder* case, one uses *konam* to prohibit food as backing for a false claim; here, one uses a *shvua* to achieve the same effect. Now the analysis splits into two distinct questions. First, was it permitted to take such a *shvua*? The *Ran* says no — it constitutes a *shvuat shav*, and one would receive lashes for it, because one is invoking God's name to back up what is obviously a false statement with no genuine intent to prohibit anything. Second, does the food actually become forbidden? Here the answer is no — the food remains permitted, because just as in the *neder* case the speaker never genuinely wanted the object to be prohibited, so here too the *shvua* was never about making food forbidden but only about lending rhetorical weight to a false claim.
