This explains the two *girsaot*: *shvuot havai assurim* refers to the act of taking such a *shvua*, which is forbidden as a *shvuat shav*. *Shvuot havai mutarim* refers to the food, which remains permitted. The parallel with cases like one who swears he will not sleep for three days or will not sit in the *sukkah* is instructive: those *shvuot* are not binding, which is precisely why they constitute *shvuat shav* — because they are purposeless, they were forbidden to take in the first place. So here too: because the *shvua* cannot genuinely prohibit the food, the act of swearing was itself a *shvuat shav*.

---

## Interpretation in Oaths

### Ravina: Anthill Case

Ravina poses a challenge to Rav Ashi. The *Gemara* had been discussing the case where one swears that one saw as many people as *olei mitzrayim* on a road. Ravina asks: perhaps this man had an anthill at home that he called "*olei mitzrayim*" — and perhaps he saw forty ants, which is exactly how many people he saw in the road? In that case, the *shvua* would actually be true, and the food might genuinely be forbidden. One might note that this is in a sense the inverse of *perushan le-hakel*: there, a lenient private interpretation is invoked to escape a *neder*; here, a stricter private interpretation is invoked to render the food forbidden — a kind of *perushan le-hachmir*. And there is a practical dimension as well: if the *Gemara* was about to impose *malkus* on someone for taking an oath in vain, that person might well claim he genuinely meant his anthill and therefore took no *shvuat shav* at all.

### Rav Ashi: Standard Meani…

Rav Ashi responds: *ki mishtava ada'ata didan mishtava* — when a person takes an oath, it is based on what we understand, not on whatever private meaning was going through his head. This is another expression of the principle of *devarim shebalev einam devarim*: one cannot retroactively assign a private meaning to words that everyone understands in a standard way.

This ruling appears to be in tension with the earlier discussion of *perushan le-hakel* by *nedarim*. The distinction is significant. A *neder* is fundamentally about establishing the status of an object — it operates between the person and the Almighty. A *shvua*, by contrast, is oriented toward other people: it is a way of backing up statements, making commitments, communicating promises. Because *shvua* is inherently communicative and interpersonal, it must go by what the words are understood to mean by others. You cannot unilaterally determine what your oath means when oaths exist precisely for the purpose of conveying meaning to others. The phrase *ada'ata didan* — based on what we think — captures this orientation exactly.

### Braita: Beit Din Oaths

The *Gemara* raises a challenge from a *braita*: when *beit din* administers an oath, they explicitly say to the oath-taker: *hevei yodea she-lo al tnai she-be-libcha anu mashbi'in otcha* — know that we are not administering this oath on the basis of whatever mental stipulation you have in your heart — *ela al dateinu ve-al da'at beit din*, but rather based on our understanding and on the understanding of *beit din*. If the general rule were already that oaths are interpreted according to communal standard meaning and never according to private intent, why would *beit din* need to state this explicitly? The need to declare it implies that in the ordinary case — outside *beit din* — one could in fact rely on one's own private interpretation.

### Chips of Wood Case

The *Gemara* asks: what case is *beit din*'s declaration coming to exclude? It is not coming to exclude the anthill interpretation — that would never be valid in any context, since calling one's anthill "*olei mitzrayim*" is a crazy interpretation that no one would accept. Rather, the declaration is coming to exclude a case like this: a borrower repaid his debt not in actual money but in chips of wood, to which he privately assigned the name "dollars." He then swears in *beit din* that he paid back the money. He is technically telling the truth — he gave "dollars" — but the word means something that no one else would recognize as payment. This type of technically-accurate-but-privately-defined usage is what *beit din* explicitly forecloses by declaring *al dateinu*. Outside *beit din*, one might have been entitled to rely on such a technically accurate — if misleading — private meaning.

### Rava's Staff Story

A famous story illustrates this principle. There was a man who owed money to a creditor. Rava instructed him to go and pay. The debtor claimed he had already paid. Rava said, then go swear to him. The debtor took his staff, had it hollowed out, placed the coins inside, and gave it to the creditor to hold while he picked up a *sefer Torah* to swear on. He then declared — according to the *Ran*'s *girsa* — *yahavti*, I gave you the money, which was technically accurate, since the coins were at that moment in the creditor's hands inside the staff. The creditor grew furious, smashed the staff, and the coins spilled out. The debtor declared: you see, I was telling the truth all along.

The *Ran* adjusts the *girsa* from *parei* (I repaid) to *yahavti* (I gave), because if he had said *parei*, even handing over money would not constitute repayment of a loan in the technical sense. But the broader point stands: the permissible range of interpretation extends to statements that are technically accurate, even if not what the other party would have assumed. What is never permissible is a genuinely crazy interpretation — calling chips of wood "dollars," or calling one's anthill "*olei mitzrayim*."

### Crazy vs. Technical

The *Gemara* thus draws a clear line. There are two distinct categories. The first is a genuinely absurd private meaning: I called my anthill "*olei mitzrayim*"; I call these chips of wood "dollars." Such interpretations are never valid, in *beit din* or outside it. The second category is a technically accurate meaning: the words, understood according to their normal semantic range, could validly describe what the speaker meant, even if that meaning was not what the listener assumed. Outside *beit din*, the speaker may rely on this technically accurate meaning. Inside *beit din* — or wherever a party explicitly declares *al dateinu* — even technical accuracy is insufficient; the words must carry their fully shared, standard meaning.

### Moshe & Arvot Moav

The *Gemara* brings a further proof from a *braita*: *ve-chein matzinu be-Moshe Rabbeinu* — we find the same principle by Moshe. When Moshe caused *Bnei Yisrael* to take an oath in *Arvot Moav*, he declared: *hevei yode'im she-lo al da'atchem ani mashbi'a eschem* — know that I am not administering this oath based on your understanding — *ella al da'ati ve-al da'as haMakom*. The verse supports this: *ve-lo itchem levadchem*, which the *Ran* interprets as "not what is within you alone" — not the private thoughts in your hearts. It was necessary for Moshe to make this explicit declaration in order to prevent *Bnei Yisrael* from later claiming that when they swore to worship God alone, they had privately meant their own gods by the word *Eloha*.

### God vs. Idols Name

The *Gemara* asks: does this prove that outside such an explicit declaration, one *can* rely on one's private interpretation? The *Gemara* answers no. The case of calling an idol "*Eloha*" is not a crazy interpretation at all — the Torah itself uses the word *Eloha* to refer to foreign gods, as in the verse *u-le-elohei Mitzrayim* (Shemos 12:12). So calling an idol "*Eloha*" is not a private eccentricity but a technically accurate usage. Moshe's declaration was therefore coming to exclude precisely the technically-accurate-but-non-standard case, not the crazy case. The crazy case — calling one's anthill "*olei mitzrayim*" — would never be valid regardless.

### Tech Accurate Rule

The *Gemara* thus arrives at its conclusion. The general rule, outside *beit din* or an explicit *al dateinu* declaration, is that one may rely on a technically accurate interpretation of one's words. What one may never do is give a genuinely absurd interpretation that no one would recognize as a valid meaning of the words. Inside *beit din*, even technical accuracy is foreclosed — the oath is administered on the basis of *da'at beit din*, the standard shared understanding. This is precisely why both Moshe and the institution of *beit din* needed to make their declarations explicit: they were extending beyond the ordinary rule to close off even the technically-accurate loophole.

---

## Unambiguous Language

### Specific Language Alt

The *Gemara* now entertains a digression. If the concern was that *Bnei Yisrael* might claim they understood "God" to mean their idols, why not simply formulate the oath in language that admits no other possible interpretation? The *Gemara* works through a series of alternatives. Why not have them swear to fulfill *mitzvos*? Because *mitzvos* can mean the commands of any king. Why not *kol mitzvos*? Because that might be interpreted as referring only to *mitzvas tzitzis*, which the *amora* says is equivalent to all the *mitzvos* together. Why not *Torah*? Because *Torah achas* might mean just one instance. Why not *Toros*? Because that would refer to *Toras haMincha*, *Toras haChatas*, *Toras haAsham* — the specific legal sections — but not to the whole. Why not *Toros u-mitzvos* together? Because they might be understood as two specific commandments rather than as a comprehensive phrase. Why not *Torah kula*? Because rejecting *avodah zarah* is itself equivalent to affirming the entire Torah, as the *braita* states: *chamura avodas kochavim she-kol ha-kofer bah ke-ilu modeh ba-Torah kula* — one who denies *avodah zarah* is as if he affirms the entire Torah. Even formulating it as *she-lo ya'avdu avodas kochavim ve-Torah kula* does not fully close the gap. Why not *taryag mitzvos*? Perhaps one might say, I call my dog *taryag mitzvos* — though the *Gemara* concedes that this might well have been unassailable.

### Moshe Practical

The *Gemara* concludes: *ela Moshe milta de-la tricha nakas* — Moshe simply did not want to go through the exercise of constructing a perfectly airtight formulation. He took the straightforward approach and declared: it means what I say it means, end of discussion. There was no point in going through the entire exercise when a simple *al da'ati* declaration accomplished the same thing.

---

## Snake Beam Example

### Snake Exists?

The *Gemara* now returns to the *nidrei havai* case involving the snake as large as a beam of an olive press. It raises the question: is such a statement truly impossible? Perhaps the claim is not as patently false as assumed.

### Shavor Malka Snake

The *Gemara* provides historical evidence: *de-hahu chivya de-hava be-shnei Shvor Malka* — there was a snake in the time of Shvor Malka to which they threw thirteen stableloads of grain. Snakes of extraordinary size, it seems, were not entirely unknown. So the statement may not be transparently false after all.

### Shmuel: Notched

Shmuel therefore clarifies: *be-taraf* — the case of *nidrei havai* concerns a snake that is *taruf*, notched or spotted along its back. *Kulo nachash mitraf tarfi* — all snakes have notching of some kind. No, the *Gemara* objects — *agavo taruf kamina* — the reference is to a snake notched specifically on its back, and snakes with that particular characteristic do not grow to the size of an olive-press beam. That is the kind of snake one would typically encounter, and swearing one saw such a snake that large is therefore a patently impossible claim.

### Beam Business Law

The *Gemara* then asks: why phrase it in terms of the snake being like a beam of an olive press, rather than simply saying the snake was *taruf*? The answer is: *milta agav urcha kama-shma lan* — the comparison incidentally teaches us a practical rule about the beam itself. *De-koras beit ha-bad gabo taruf* — a beam of an olive press has a notch on its back as part of its standard construction, used to attach the mechanism for pressing. *Le-mai nafka mina? Le-mekach u-mimkar* — this matters for business law. If one sells a beam designated for an olive press and the beam lacks the notch, the buyer may insist on a properly finished beam, since the term *korat beit ha-bad* by definition implies one equipped with that notch. The comparison between snake and beam thus simultaneously defines what kind of snake is meant and conveys a legal teaching about the commercial specifications of the beam.

---

## Nidrei Shegagot

### False Condition

We now arrive at the third category: *nidrei shegagot* — vows made in error. The first type involves a false factual premise. One says: this bread is forbidden to me if I had breakfast this morning — and at the moment of the *neder*, one genuinely believed one had not eaten. It subsequently emerges that one had in fact eaten. The *halacha* is that the *neder* is not binding. The speaker imposed a condition that he was certain would not be met; the condition was in fact met, but through no genuine intention on his part. Since when he took the *neder* he never wanted it to be binding, it does not take effect.

### Forgot Vow Later

The second type of *nidrei shegagot* involves a future-oriented condition. One says: *konam* this bread to me if I eat anything later today — genuinely intending to commit oneself to a diet. Then, later that day, one absent-mindedly reaches for a snack and eats it, having entirely forgotten the *neder*.

### Forget at Exec

This case is genuinely striking. Unlike the first type, when the *neder* was taken here the speaker was completely serious and fully intended it to be binding. Yet when the triggering act occurred — the snacking — the speaker had no memory of the *neder* at all. And the ruling is: the *neder* does not take effect.

### Piv/Libo at Trigger

The conceptual basis is an extension of *ein piv velibo shavin*. One might object: the act of snacking is not an act of taking a *neder* — it does not require the intention or presence of mind associated with establishing the *neder* in the first place. Why should the speaker's state of mind at the moment of triggering matter? And yet the *Gemara* treats it as decisive. The underlying reasoning appears to be that *nidrei shegagot* are invalidated not only at the moment of taking but also at the moment of triggering, provided that at that moment there was a genuine disconnect — in this case, complete forgetfulness — between what the *neder* required and what the speaker understood himself to be doing. The *neder*, as a creation of human language operating one step removed from direct divine prohibition, requires a minimal continuity of awareness. When that is wholly absent at the moment the condition is triggered, the *neder* fails to become *chal*. The contrast with ordinary violation is important: if one simply forgot the *neder* and ate the forbidden food, that is an *issur be-shogeg* — a violation committed inadvertently. But here, crucially, the *neder* is treated as never having taken effect at all.

### Mistaken Assumption

The second type of *nidrei shegagot* involves a mistake about the people involved. The *mishnah* gives the case of one who saw figures eating figs from his tree and declared: *harei aleichem korban* — let all these figs be *korban* to you. He was furious at what he took to be strangers helping themselves to his property. It then emerged that the group included his own father and brother. The *mishnah* adds another case: one who declared *konam ishti nehenet li* — my wife is forbidden to derive benefit from me — on the grounds that she had stolen his wallet or struck his child, and it later emerged that neither happened. In this case, the speaker did not use the word *im* — "if" — yet the *neder* was clearly premised on a factual assumption. Since the assumption was false, and the *neder* was transparently based on that assumption, it does not take effect. This is distinct from a *petach*: a *petach* is when one failed to consider some consequence of the *neder* that, had one thought about it, would have prevented one from taking it. Here, the *neder* was based on a mistaken belief about a core factual matter — who was present, or what had occurred — and that error goes to the very substance of the *neder* itself.

### Mixed Group Debate

What if the group included both the father and brother and other people as well? *Beit Shammai* say: the father and brother are permitted, but the others remain forbidden. *Beit Hillel* say: once any part of the *neder* is invalidated, the entire *neder* is invalidated — *neder she-hutar miktzato hutar kulo*. The case must be understood carefully: obviously, if one had said "Group A is forbidden and Group B is forbidden" and Group B was one's father and brother, Group A would plainly remain forbidden. The force of *beit Hillel*'s ruling is that when a single undivided statement is made — *harei aleichem* — and part of that statement was based on an error, the *neder* as a whole may fall away.

---

## Shvuot Shegagot

### Shvuot Rule

The *Gemara* teaches: *kesheim shenidrei shegagot mutarin kach shevuot shegagot mutarot* — just as *nidrei shegagot* are not binding, so too *shvuot shegagot* are not binding. The parallel cases from the *mishnah* would apply straightforwardly: one swore that a loaf would be forbidden if one had eaten breakfast, while mistakenly believing one had not; or one swore and then forgot the *shvua* at the moment of triggering. But the *Gemara* presents a far more interesting case.

### Rav Kahana Story

*Kegon Rav Kahana ve-Rav Assi* — it is like Rav Kahana and Rav Assi, who would sometimes dispute what their teacher Rav had actually said. One would declare: *shevuasa de-hachi amar Rav* — I swear that Rav said this! The other would respond: *shevuasa de-hachi amar Rav* — I swear he said no such thing; he said this other thing! *Ve-chol chad ve-chad ada'ata de-nafshei shapir kamishtava* — each one believed entirely that he was telling the truth.

### Sheker Beshogeig

This is the *chiddush*: if one of them was mistaken, that person took what amounts to a *shvuat sheker be-shogeig* — a false oath taken inadvertently. The *Gemara* teaches that such an oath is not binding and carries no culpability, because the person genuinely believed he was telling the truth. This is *shvuot shegagot*.

### Oaths Extension

This ruling is genuinely surprising. One might have thought: the entire purpose of a *shvua* is to back up one's words with the force of God's name. If those words turn out to be false, it might not matter that the speaker was in *shogeg* — the speaker was, after all, swearing to back up a claim, and that claim was false. The intuition would be that at least with regard to *shvuat sheker*, one ought to have been more careful before invoking God's name, and if one was wrong the *shvua* should still be problematic even in *shogeg*. The *chiddush* of this *Gemara* is that even here, where the *shvua* is functioning precisely as a vehicle for backing up a statement, if the speaker genuinely believed the statement to be true and was in error, the *shvua* is not binding.

The *Ran* focuses the analysis on whether fruit would become forbidden in such a case — i.e., if one said *shvua* that if Rav did not say X then fruit would be forbidden, and one was wrong about what Rav said. Even granting that this involves a mistake about the condition rather than a direct false backing of a statement, the *Ran* treats the question of the food's status as the analogue to the *neder* case. Whether the person committed any *issur* in taking the *shvua* the *Ran* leaves somewhat open. But the simpler reading of the *Gemara* — the case of Rav Kahana and Rav Assi swearing directly about what Rav said — suggests that even the direct function of a *shvua* as a verbal commitment to truth is subject to the *shegagot* principle.

---

## Petach & Void

### Consequence vs. Fact

A conceptual distinction must be drawn between two different ways in which part of a *neder* can be invalidated. In *nidrei shegagot*, the invalidation flows from a factual error — the speaker did not know that his father was among the group, or did not know that his wife had not actually struck the child. The error concerns what actually happened or who was actually present; it goes to the substance of the *neder* itself. A *petach*, by contrast, involves not a factual error but a failure of foresight: the speaker knew the relevant facts but did not think through the consequences of the *neder*. The classic *petach* is the *shabbat* and *yom tov* case: one who vowed never to drink wine clearly knows that *shabbat* exists and that a year includes *shabbat*; one simply did not stop to consider that the vow would apply there. That failure of attention requires a *petach* to undo; it does not automatically render the *neder* invalid.

### Days Permitted

The earlier teaching — prior to Rabbi Akiva's ruling — held: *otam hayamim mutarim ve-she'ar kol hayamim assurim* — those particular days (like *shabbat* and *yom tov*) are permitted, and all other days remain forbidden. The *petach* got the person out of the *neder* only with respect to the days he had not contemplated; the rest of the *neder* remained in force.

### Hutar Miktzato

Rabbi Akiva then taught: *neder she-hutar miktzato hutar kulo* — a *neder* that has been released in part has been released in its entirety. Once any portion of the *neder* is annulled, the whole *neder* falls away.

### Rava: Qualifier

Rava clarifies the parameters of the debate between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel*. Everyone agrees, he says, in the following case: if the person would have said, had he known his father was there, *kulchem assurim chutz me'abba* — you are all forbidden except for my father — then all agree that only the father is excluded and the rest remain forbidden. Why? Because the speaker himself says he would have maintained the statement *kulchem assurim*; he would simply have added a qualifier. Since the core statement was not in error, and the whole group would still have been included with just that one exception noted, the rest of the *neder* stands. The *machloket* between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* arises only when the person says: had I known my father was there, I would have said *Ploni va-Ploni assurim ve-abba mutar* — I would have named the others and excluded my father — meaning he would have formulated an entirely different statement. In that case, according to *Beit Hillel*, since the speaker would never have uttered the words *kulchem assurim* at all, the entire *neder* is void. *Beit Shammai* apparently maintains that even here the rest of the *neder* stands.

### Different Language

On Rava's first framing, then: where the speaker would have added a qualifier to the same basic language, everyone agrees the rest holds. Where the speaker would have used completely different language — never starting with *kulchem assurim* at all — that is where *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* disagree, with *Beit Hillel* voiding the entire *neder* by *hutar miktzato hutar kulo*.

### Rava Second

Rava then presents an alternative framing of where the *machloket* lies. On this second approach, the case of completely different language — where the speaker says he would have used an entirely different formulation — is so strong that even *Beit Shammai* would agree the entire *neder* is void. The *machloket* is then relocated to the qualifier case: where the speaker says he would have maintained *kulchem assurim* but added *chutz me'abba*, *Beit Hillel* still voids the entire *neder* by *hutar miktzato hutar kulo*, but *Beit Shammai* holds that the rest remains binding.

### Beit Shammai

We close at the question of *Beit Shammai*'s position in the qualifier case. What precisely is *Beit Shammai*'s reasoning when the speaker says he would have kept the core language and merely added an exception? This analysis will be taken up in the next session.

---

---

# Nedarim 26

## Nidrei Shgagot Review

### Mistaken Assumptions

We return briefly to a topic from yesterday's daf: *nidrei shgagot*, the category of vows made on the basis of a false assumption. The paradigmatic case is one who forbids something upon himself contingent on some state of affairs, believing that state of affairs does not obtain — when in fact it does. Because the vow was never intended to be binding under the actual circumstances, it is not binding. The *gemara* extends the same logic to *shvuat shgaga*, the mistaken oath.

There are two distinct scenarios of *shvuat shgaga*. The first, which the *Ran* treats as the more primary case, involves a person who simply swears that something happened or did not happen, genuinely believing his statement to be true — yet being mistaken. The second, to which the *gemara* gravitates, involves a conditional oath: "I swear I will not eat this if such-and-such occurred," where the person's false assumption about the facts renders the oath inapplicable.

### Rambam Shvuat Shgaga

What makes this analysis striking is the implication for the more obvious case: the person who takes an oath to back up a factual claim he sincerely believes to be true, only to discover he was wrong. One might have thought that since the entire point of taking a *shvua* is to stand behind a statement as true, someone who swears and turns out to be mistaken has committed *shvuat sheker*. Should he not have been more careful to verify the facts before invoking the divine name?

Nevertheless, the plain reading of the *gemara* is that such a person has not violated any prohibition — and this is precisely how the *Rambam* rules. In *Hilchot Shvuot*, Perek 3, the *Rambam* analyzes the category of *shvuat shgaga* and works through the implications with characteristic rigor. He notes that if a person swore he had not eaten and then recalled that he had — or swore he would not eat and then forgot and ate — these are classic instances of acting *beshogeg*, yet the *Rambam* classifies all such cases as *shvuat shgaga* for which the person is *patur*, entirely exempt.

### Subjective Truth Standard

This generates a paradox that the *Rambam* himself surfaces: if one is exempt whenever one swears falsely while believing oneself to be telling the truth, and exempt whenever one violates a future-oriented oath through forgetfulness, then the only remaining scenario of culpable *shvuat shgaga* — the one that incurs a *korban oleh v'yored* — is exceedingly narrow. The *Rambam* answers directly: the case of liability is where a person swore falsely knowing he was lying, and knew that swearing falsely was forbidden, yet did not know that such a violation incurs a *korban*. That ignorance of the *korban* obligation is the *shgaga* for which one is liable. In other words, the subjective intention of the oath-taker is the governing standard — if in your own mind you were telling the truth, you have not committed *shvuat sheker*, full stop. The *gemara* uses the term *mutarot*, indicating that such cases are not merely *patur aval assur* but reflect a fundamental non-violation.

---

## Father Exclusion Case

### Wine & Shabbat Case

With that review in place, we return to the central principle under discussion: *neder she'hutar miktzato hutar kulo* — when part of a vow is released, the entire vow is annulled. The *gemara* picks up from the previous daf, beginning from the passage on 25b. The foundational case involves a person who vowed never to drink wine. He is brought before a court and asked: had you considered that this vow would prevent you from drinking wine on *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov*? He says no, he had not thought that through. The early position was that only those days — *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov* — are released from the vow while all other days remain forbidden.

### Rabbi Akiva Principle

Then came *Rabbi Akiva*, who taught the principle of *neder she'hutar miktzato hutar kulo*: once any portion of a vow is released, the entire vow is annulled. The question now engaging the *gemara* is: what exactly are the parameters of this principle, and how do *Rabbi Akiva* and the *chachamim* disagree?

### Rabba's Analysis

*Rabba* draws a distinction that structures the entire discussion. Everybody agrees, he says, that if the vow-maker would say: "Had I known my father was among you, I would have said: all of you are forbidden *except for* my father" — that is, he would have made the same vow with a qualifier added — then the *neder* is not fundamentally undermined. The father alone is excluded, and the rest remain forbidden. In the *Ran*'s terminology, adding such a qualifier is called *mekayem devarav*: the speaker is essentially maintaining his original statement and merely appending a limitation to it.

The debate between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* in our *mishna*, says *Rabba*, concerns a different case: where the vow-maker says, "Had I known my father was there, I would never have said 'all of you' — I would have said specifically: so-and-so and so-and-so are forbidden, but my father is permitted." Here he claims he would have made a fundamentally different statement altogether — what the *Ran* calls *meshane devarav*. *Beit Hillel* says the entire original vow is void; *Beit Shammai* says only the father is released.

### Mekayem vs. Meshane

The conceptual hinge is thus the distinction between *mekayem devarav* and *meshane devarav*. When the speaker would merely have qualified his statement — adding an exception while leaving the underlying *neder* intact — *Rabba* holds that the *neder* stands and only the excepted person is released. When the speaker would have replaced his statement entirely with a different formulation, the question arises whether the original words retain any force at all.

### Beit Shammai vs. Hillel

*Rabba*'s reading of *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* places their dispute squarely in the *meshane devarav* case. Both schools agree that a pure *mekayem* — a qualifier added to an otherwise unchanged *neder* — leaves the *neder* intact for everyone except the excluded individual. Their dispute is over the case where the speaker insists he would have formulated an entirely different statement: *Beit Hillel* says the whole original *neder* is void, and *Beit Shammai* says the *neder* survives and only the father is released.

### Rava's Position

*Rava* adopts a more lenient reading of the same positions. He says that in the case of *meshane devarav* — a fundamentally different statement — everyone agrees the entire *neder* is void, even *Beit Shammai*. The dispute of *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel*, says *Rava*, is precisely over the *mekayem devarav* case: where the speaker would only have added a qualifier. *Beit Hillel* says even that degree of deviation from what he actually said is sufficient to void the entire *neder*. *Beit Shammai* says it is not.

In practical terms, *Rava*'s position is more lenient than *Rabba*'s. For *Rava*, holding like *Beit Hillel*, even a qualifier — *mekayem devarav* — is enough to collapse the entire vow. For *Rabba*, the entire vow collapses only when the speaker would have been *meshane devarav*, producing a categorically different statement.

### Rabbi Meir & Yose

The *gemara* maps this dispute onto the well-known debate between *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Yose* regarding the integrity of a statement. The case there involves someone who says of an animal: "*harei zo tmurat olah tmurat shelamim*" — a dedication that begins as an *olah* and ends as a *shelamim*. Since an animal cannot be both, the question is which declaration governs. *Rabbi Meir* holds *tfos lashon rishon*: the first expression is binding, and what is said later is irrelevant. *Rabbi Yose* holds *begmar devarav adam nitfas*: you cannot truncate a person's statement; you hear the whole thing and the complete statement determines the outcome.

The *gemara* applies this as follows. *Beit Shammai* holds like *Rabbi Meir* — the original *neder* stands because the first statement is what was actually said, and a qualifier at the end does not undo it. *Beit Hillel* holds like *Rabbi Yose* — you cannot freeze the statement midway; you look at the complete statement the speaker would have made, and since it differs from what he said, the original is void.

### Class Questions

Several questions arise naturally from this analysis. First, there is a technical point about whether the people subject to the *neder* must actually hear it pronounced — a question touching on *nidrei onsim*, which the *gemara* will address separately. More conceptually pressing is the question of why the *gemara* at all cares about what the speaker would *hypothetically* have said. The *neder* was made; it is in the world. Should we not simply assess the effect of removing one member of the group on the *neder* as it actually stands?

This is indeed a striking feature of the *gemara*'s analysis. The *gemara* is assessing not the structural quality of the *neder* itself — whether the group of people was named as a single unit, a collection of individuals, or a chain — but rather what the speaker would have articulated in an alternate reality. The reason the hypothetical matters seems tied to the principle of *piv velibbo shavin*: the binding force of a *neder* requires alignment between speech and intention. When a false assumption disrupts that alignment for part of the *neder*, the *gemara* asks how deep that disruption runs — and it answers by reconstructing the speaker's hypothetical alternative. This is admittedly unusual, since once language has been uttered, one would expect the analysis to focus on what was said rather than on a counterfactual. The discussion continues.

It is also important to note that the case of the father being unknowingly included falls under *nidrei shgagot* and requires no formal *hatarat nedarim*: once it is clarified that the father was present, the *neder* simply never applied to him. By contrast, the wine case — where the speaker knew all the facts but failed to think through their implications — does require a formal *hataras neder*, because there was no false assumption about the facts, only a failure to think them through. Both cases share the structural question of what happens to the remainder of the *neder* once part of it is removed, but they arrive at that question by different routes.

---

## Rabbi Akiva Mishna

### Language & Intent

The preceding discussion raises a deeper question about language and its binding power. What the *gemara* is effectively doing, one might observe, is reaching back into the speaker's mind after the fact — not to assess what he meant by the words he used, but to imagine what words he would have chosen under different circumstances. This is, as noted, a somewhat unusual mode of analysis. Ordinarily the question would be: given the *neder* as formulated, what is the structural impact of releasing one part of it? The *gemara* chooses instead to ask what the speaker would have said, and uses that hypothetical to determine how tightly bound the remaining elements of the *neder* are to the released portion. The intrinsic relationship between thought, language, and the facts on the ground is the governing concern — but the direction of analysis is from the hypothetical back to the actual, which is counterintuitive.

### Single Unit Case

The *gemara* now introduces a *mishna* that, at least in its initial formulation, seems to take the more intuitive approach. *Rav Pappa* raises a challenge to *Rava* from a *mishna* that elaborates on *Rabbi Akiva*'s principle. The *mishna* asks: how did *Rabbi Akiva* articulate *neder she'hutar miktzato hutar kulo*? If someone says *konam she'eini neheneh lekulchem* — my benefit is forbidden to all of you as a group — and for one member of the group the *neder* turns out not to apply (through *nidrei shgagot*, *hatarat nedarim*, or any other means), then it is void for all of them. The reasoning is that all of you together constitute a single unified *neder*, and removing one element dissolves the whole.

### Chain Structure

The *mishna* then presents a contrasting formulation: *she'eini neheneh lo laze velo laze velo laze* — not to this one, and not to this one, and not to this one, enumerating each person individually. Here the rule operates differently. If the *first* person named is released, all are released. If the *last* person named is released, only he is released and the rest remain forbidden.

### First Middle Last

The logic of the *mishna* is best understood as a chain structure. When someone says "not to you, and not to you, and not to you," each successive element is conceptually linked to what came before — like cells in a spreadsheet where each depends on the reference above it. Remove the first link and the entire chain collapses. Remove the last link and only that final element is affected, since nothing downstream depends on it. The *mishna* later adds that if a middle person is released, everyone from that point downward is released and those above remain forbidden.

This structure is categorically different from the group-unit case. In the group-unit case (*lekulchem*), the entire *neder* is a single whole; in the chain case (*lo laze velo laze*), the *neder* is a sequence of linked but distinct prohibitions, and the effect of releasing one depends entirely on its position in the sequence. Crucially, this analysis is about the nature of the *neder* as actually formulated — not about what the speaker would hypothetically have said. The question is whether the word structure creates a unified unit, a collection of independent units, or a daisy-chain of linked units.

---

## Reisha/Seifa Analysis

### Rabba's Reisha/Seifa

*Rava* now challenges *Rabba*: how does *Rabba*'s framework, which turns on what the speaker would hypothetically have said, accommodate this *mishna*? The *gemara* attempts to read the *mishna* through the lens of the *Rabba*–*Rava* dispute — specifically, to read the two cases of the *mishna* (the *lekulchem* case and the *lo laze velo laze* case) as corresponding to *meshane devarav* and *mekayem devarav* respectively.

According to *Rabba*'s reading, the *gemara* proposes: the *reisha* — the case where releasing one releases all — corresponds to a situation where the speaker would have said something fundamentally different (*lo laze velo laze* instead of *lekulchem*). The *seifa* — where releasing the first releases all — corresponds to a situation where the speaker would have said *lekulchem* (a completely different formulation) in place of the *lo laze velo laze* he originally used.

This is admittedly a forced reading. The *gemara* is attempting to map the structural analysis of the *mishna* — which asks about the intrinsic architecture of the *neder* — onto the hypothetical-speech analysis of *Rabba* and *Rava*, which asks what the speaker would have said in an alternate scenario. The two frameworks are not naturally aligned, and the *gemara*'s attempt to reconcile them requires assigning hypothetical alternative statements to the cases of the *mishna* in ways that are not immediately obvious.

### Rava's Objection

*Rava* presses his own objection against this reading. He argues that if the governing question is simply whether the speaker would have said a *qualifier* (which is sufficient to release all, according to *Rava*), then how does the *mishna*'s distinction between *rishon* (first) and *acharon* (last) make any sense? Whether one releases the first person or the last person has no bearing on what the speaker would hypothetically have said as an alternative formulation. The hypothetical-speech framework cannot explain why position in the sequence matters. The very distinction that the *mishna* draws — releasing the first releases all, releasing the last releases only him — is unintelligible if what we truly care about is the speaker's counterfactual intention.

This is a sharp observation. *Rava* is effectively pointing out that the *mishna* is operating on a different axis entirely. The *mishna* cares about the structure of the *neder* as uttered — specifically, whether the sequential formulation creates a dependency relationship among the named individuals. The *gemara*'s attempt to retrofit this into a framework of hypothetical speech does not hold.

### Daisy-Chain Logic

The *gemara* ultimately concedes the point and provides the correct reading. The *reisha* of the *mishna* — the *lekulchem* case — involves a single unified *neder* in which all named individuals form one coherent whole. The *seifa* — the *lo laze velo laze* case — involves individuals linked in a chain: *tla'an zeh bazeh*, each one is made dependent on the next. This is not about hypothetical speech; it is about the actual structure of what was said.

The *gemara* cites a *baraita* that corroborates this reading: *hutar ha'emtza'i* — if a middle person is released — then everyone from him downward (*heimenu ulemata*) is released, and those above him remain forbidden. This confirms the chain-dependency logic: a release propagates downstream through the chain but not upstream.

The *gemara* thus arrives at a position that, at least for the *mishna* of *Rabbi Akiva*, does not ultimately rest on the hypothetical-speech analysis of *Rabba* and *Rava*. The relevant variable is the structural quality of the *neder* itself — whether the language creates a unified unit, a collection, or a chain — and the effect of releasing one element is determined by that structure, not by what the speaker would have said otherwise. The *gemara* does not, however, abandon the hypothetical-speech framework entirely; it continues to apply it in subsequent cases.

---

## Kufri Onions Case

### Onion Vow

*Rav Adda bar Ahava* challenges *Rava* with a new case. A person declares: *konam batzal she'ani to'eim* — all onions are forbidden to me as a *korban* — *shehabatzal ra lalev*, because he has heard that onions are bad for the heart. This is the rationale behind the vow.

### Kufri Exception

He is then told: but the *Kufri* onion — a particular variety from a certain locale — is actually good for the heart. Therefore, it is clear he never intended to include the *Kufri* onion in his vow; regarding that variety, there was a *shgaga*. He is thus released from the *Kufri* onion: *hutar beKufri*.

The *baraita* then states: and not only from the *Kufri* is he released, but from all onions — *velo beKufri bilvad hutar ela bechol habetzalim*. This is an application of *hutar miktzato hutar kulo*.

### Question on Rava

The challenge to *Rava* is as follows. The *gemara* assumes that the speaker in this case would have said something like: "All onions are forbidden except for the *Kufri*" — that is, he would have maintained his basic statement with a qualifier (*mekayem devarav*). If *Rava* holds that even a qualifier is sufficient to release the entire vow, then this case would follow naturally from his position — no challenge to him here. But this also generates a question on *Rabba*, since *Rabba* holds that only *meshane devarav* releases the whole, yet the case seems to come out as though it does release the whole. The *rishonim* note that the question applies to *Rabba* as well, for reasons connected to *Rabba*'s association of his position with the stricter view of *Rabbi Meir*.

### Mishne Devarim Reply

The *gemara*'s answer is simple and decisive: who told you what this person would have hypothetically said? Perhaps he would have said not a qualifier but a fundamentally different statement — *meshane devarav*. He would have specified: these onions and those onions are forbidden, but the *Kufri* is permitted — enumerating types rather than adding a blanket qualifier. Under that reading, the case is one of *meshane devarav*, which releases the entire *neder* according to everyone: it satisfies *Rabba*'s requirement for complete nullification, and it resolves the difficulty with *Rabbi Meir* as well, since even *Rabbi Meir* would concede when the statement would have been entirely different, in accordance with *Rabbi Akiva*'s principle.

The deeper point, which the *gemara* is implicitly acknowledging throughout, is that there is no independent evidence in these cases for what the speaker would have hypothetically said. The *gemara* can always assign the hypothetical that fits the outcome. If the outcome demands *meshane devarav*, the *gemara* says that is what he would have said; if the outcome demands *mekayem devarav*, the *gemara* says that instead. This makes the hypothetical-speech framework somewhat less determinate than it might first appear.

---

## Figs in Basket

### Basket Vow

*Ravina* poses a further question to *Rava*. The case is: *nadar min hakalkala* — someone vowed that a basket (*kalkala*) is forbidden to him, intending to forbid everything in the basket. The basket turns out to contain *benot shuach*, a prized variety of fig. He then says: *ilu hayiti yode'a shebenot shuach betocha, lo hayiti noder* — had I known there were *benot shuach* in it, I never would have vowed. He loves *benot shuach* and would never have wanted to forbid them.

### Two Outcomes

From this declaration, two possible outcomes present themselves. Either the entire vow is released — because *hutar miktzato hutar kulo* — or only the *benot shuach* are released and the rest of the basket's contents remain forbidden.

### Mishne Devarim Assumed

The *gemara* initially assumes that this case reflects *meshane devarav*: the speaker would have made a fundamentally different statement had he known. Rather than saying "the basket is forbidden," he would have enumerated: these figs and those contents are forbidden, but the *benot shuach* are permitted. Under this reading, *Rava* — and indeed everyone — would say the entire vow is released, since *meshane devarav* produces universal nullification.

### Qualifier Option

But the *gemara* then considers the counter-assumption: perhaps the speaker's alternative formulation would have been a qualifier rather than a fundamentally different statement. He would have said: the basket is forbidden except for the *benot shuach* — *kol hakalkala asura uvenot shuach mutarot*. Under this reading, it is a case of *mekayem devarav*, and only the *benot shuach* would be released. *Tosfot* notes the apparent asymmetry: in the *Kufri* onion case, the *gemara* assumed a qualifier (*mekayem devarav*), while here it assumes a fundamentally different statement (*meshane devarav*). In both cases, however, the *gemara* essentially assigns the hypothetical that yields the desired result, and *Ravina*'s question remains formally unresolved — both alternatives are live possibilities, and the *gemara* does not definitively close the question.

---

## Baraita Resolution

### Five-Person Vow

The *gemara* concludes by identifying the *tanna* behind a *baraita* that synthesizes the entire discussion. The *baraita* states: *nadar michamishah benei adam ke'echad* — someone made a vow against five people as a single group. Two rules follow: (1) *hutar le'echad mehen hutru kullan* — if he was released from one of them, they are all released; (2) *chutz me'echad mehen, hu mutar vehen asurin* — except for one of them, that one is permitted and the others remain forbidden.

### Contradiction

These two statements appear to contradict each other. The first says releasing one releases all. The second says excluding one leaves the rest forbidden. The *gemara* understands this as two distinct positions, reflecting two different opinions — one in line with *hutar miktzato hutar kulo* and one that does not apply that principle.

### Rabba's Attribution

*Rabba* reads the *baraita* as internally coherent under *Rabbi Akiva*'s view. The *reisha* — *hutar le'echad hutru kullan* — reflects the case where the speaker would have been *meshane devarav*: he would have said an entirely different statement, and therefore the entire *neder* collapses. This is *Rabbi Akiva*'s position. The *seifa* — *chutz me'echad vehen asurin* — reflects the case where the speaker would have been *mekayem devarav*: he would have said the same statement with only a qualifier. In this case, *Rabba* says, even *Rabbi Akiva* agrees that the *neder* survives and only the excluded individual is released. Thus according to *Rabba*, the entire *baraita* is authored by *Rabbi Akiva* — the two clauses describe two scenarios within his framework, and the *seifa* captures the boundary of his own principle.

### Rava's Attribution

*Rava* reads the *baraita* differently. The *seifa* — *chutz me'echad vehen asurin* — represents the position of the *rabanan* who disagree with *Rabbi Akiva*. These *rabanan* hold that when the speaker would have been *mekayem devarav*, the *neder* stands and only the qualifier-exception is released. But the *rabanan* concede the *reisha*: when the speaker would have been *meshane devarav*, the entire *neder* is void — *divrei hakol*. Thus according to *Rava*, the *baraita* is authored by the *rabanan*, not by *Rabbi Akiva*, and its two clauses represent the *rabanan*'s own graduated position: *meshane devarav* → all released; *mekayem devarav* → only the one excluded. *Rabbi Akiva* himself goes further, holding that even *mekayem devarav* releases the entire *neder* — a position that does not appear in this *baraita* at all.

### Reconciliation

The *baraita* thus serves as the conceptual anchor for the entire sugya. The debate between *Rabba* and *Rava* over the scope of *neder she'hutar miktzato hutar kulo* — whether *meshane devarav* alone triggers universal release, or whether even *mekayem devarav* suffices — finds its textual basis precisely in this *baraita*'s juxtaposition of *hutar le'echad hutru kullan* against *chutz me'echad vehen asurin*. According to *Rabba*, the *baraita* is *Rabbi Akiva* articulating the limits of his own principle. According to *Rava*, the *baraita* is the *rabanan* articulating a position that partially concedes to *Rabbi Akiva*. Either way, the underlying machinery of the sugya — the hypothetical-speech analysis, the *mekayem*/*meshane* distinction, and the question of when partial release voids a *neder* entirely — is illuminated by this final *baraita*, which the redactor of the *Bavli* has placed at the conclusion of the discussion to crystallize what was at stake throughout.

---

---

# Nedarim 28

## Vows Under Duress

### Mishna Review

We open on daf 28 by returning to the *mishnah* that was introduced at the close of 27b, since it forms the primary focus of today's discussion. The *mishnah* belongs to a series of categories of *nidarim* that are not binding, and this particular category is *nidrei onasin* — vows made under duress.

### Nidrei Onasin

The broader context of the chapter has already explored the first category, which concerned *onus* in the sense of circumstances beyond one's control that prevent a stipulation from being fulfilled — a general question applicable to conditional formulations in any setting. The present *mishnah*, however, treats a more specific case: a *neder* made under a degree of compulsion, not absolute coercion, but pressure exerted to protect oneself from robbery or violence.

The *mishnah* states: *nodrim le-hargin u-le-charamin u-le-mochsin* — one may make a *neder* to those who would kill for money, to *charamin* (a similar category of extortionists), and to *mochsin*, tax collectors. The inclusion of tax collectors raises an immediate question: why are they treated as illegitimately taking one's money, given that taxes are ostensibly a legal obligation? The *Gemara* will address this directly.

The *mishnah* continues: *she-hi terumah* — one may vow that the produce is *terumah*, thereby deterring Jewish bandits who would not dare touch sanctified priestly portions. As the *Tosafos* observes with some wryness, there is a certain consistency to the moral hierarchy at play: people who had no compunction about robbery drew the line at consuming *terumah*. To make the claim credible, one takes a *neder* to back it up — *af al pi she-eino shel terumah*, even though it is not actually *terumah*. Similarly, one may claim the goods belong to the royal house, *she-hen shel beit ha-melech*, and swear accordingly, *af al pi she-einam shel beit ha-melech*, even though they do not.

### Shammai/Hillel Debate

The *mishnah* then records the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. Beit Shammai rules: *be-chol nodrim chutz mi-bishvua* — one may use any form of *neder* except a *shvua*. Beit Hillel rules: *af bishvua* — even a *shvua* is permitted. A further layer of the dispute concerns whether one may initiate the vow or must wait to be prompted. Beit Shammai holds *lo yiftach lo beneder* — do not open with a *neder* on your own initiative; wait for the extortioner to demand it. Beit Hillel rules *af yiftach lo* — one may even take the initiative. And regarding scope: if the extortioner says "vow that your wife will receive no benefit from you," may one expand it to include one's children as well? Beit Shammai rules that the wife is then permitted and the sons remain forbidden, while Beit Hillel holds *elu va-elu mutarin* — both are permitted.

### Shammai Stringency

Beit Shammai's general stringency regarding *shvua* reflects their more exacting treatment of oath-taking. At one level, this is a technical matter: a *shvua* invokes, explicitly or implicitly, the divine name, and carries with it the weight of *lo yenakeh Hashem* — God does not hold blameless one who takes His name in vain. But there is also a broader conceptual dimension. Beit Shammai's characteristic position — evident in the famous debate about how one praises a bride, where Beit Shammai insists one describe her only as she actually is, *kallah ka-mot she-hi* — reflects a thoroughgoing commitment to the alignment of word and truth. A *shvua*, whose very purpose is to affirm the veracity of one's statement, is for Beit Shammai not merely a formal halachic act but a claim to truthfulness. To deploy it in a context of deliberate misrepresentation, even under duress, compromises that integrity in a way that a *neder* — which functions more indirectly — does not.

This framework also illuminates the dispute about initiation and expansion. One reading of Beit Shammai's position is purely quantitative: whatever you do not say under direct compulsion is not compelled. If the extortioner did not demand a *neder* and you offered one, or if he demanded a *neder* about X and you added Y, those additional words are freely chosen and therefore binding, even if the overall circumstances were coercive. Beit Hillel, by contrast, holds that the entire situation compels you — without initiating or elaborating, you may not be believed, and so all of it falls within the scope of *onus*.

But Beit Shammai may also be making a deeper conceptual point. If the extortioner is essentially feeding you a script — demanding that you say precisely X — then in a sense those are not your words at all; you are merely voicing what he dictated. The compulsion is total and the speech-act is his, not yours, and therefore it carries no binding force. Any degree of initiative or elaboration on your part, however, reintroduces your own agency, and once those are your words, the duress of the surrounding circumstances is insufficient to sever you from your *neder*.

### Student Q&A

A question naturally arises about the structure of the *machlokes*: is the debate about the *neder* formulation a question of whether the *neder* is binding, or a question of whether one is permitted to make it in the first place? The answer differs depending on whether one is dealing with a *neder* or a *shvua*. With a *neder* — the formulation of *konam* making something forbidden — no one disputes that one is *permitted* to say it. There is no category of *neder sheker* or *neder shav*. The entire dispute concerns whether it is *binding*: the *neder* was never sincerely meant, and the question is whether the duress is sufficient to disassociate the speaker from those words. The *shvua*, by contrast, raises a prior question: are you *permitted* to make it at all? When you swear that this produce is *terumah*, you are asserting the truth of a false claim. That is where the concern of *shvuat sheker* or *shvuat shav* enters, and that is precisely what Beit Shammai forbids.

### Gemara Begins

With this framework in place, the *Gemara* opens its analysis by pressing on the classification of tax collectors. If *dina d'malchusa dina* — the halachic principle articulated by Shmuel that the law of the government is the law — governs our relationship to state authority, why does the *mishnah* treat the tax collector as an illegitimate extortioner rather than a lawful agent? That question launches the *Gemara's* extended discussion.

---

## Dina D'Malchusa

### Shmuel/Tax Collector

The *Gemara* raises the challenge directly: Shmuel's principle of *dina d'malchusa dina* holds that we are halachically bound by the laws of the governing authority. If so, why is the tax collector treated as someone from whom one may legitimately protect oneself through misrepresentation? The *mishnah* seems to assume that such taxation is unjust — but how can that be?

### Illegitimate Tax

The *Gemara* answers with two distinct explanations. The first, transmitted in the name of Shmuel himself through a chain of *amoraim*: *b'mochs she'ein lo kitzva* — we are speaking of a tax collector who operates without a fixed rate. The amount demanded is entirely arbitrary, governed by nothing more than his whim at the moment of collection. The second explanation, from the school of Rabbi Yannai: *b'mochs ha'omeid me'eilav* — a tax collector who is self-appointed, meaning one who simply positions himself and claims the right to collect by virtue of his own presence, not any governmental authorization. In this case, it is not a legitimate government whose laws are being enforced; it is, in effect, a private individual with a weapon.

### Ran Definition

The *Ran* clarifies the conceptual distinction between the two cases precisely. In the first case, the problem lies in the *din* component: *lav dina hu ela chamsanusa* — it is not law but robbery. An arbitrary, uncapped demand is not a *din*, a genuine legal norm with some objective standard; it is mere extortion dressed in official garb. In the second case, the problem lies in the *malchusa* component: there is no legitimate governmental authority standing behind the collector. Thus, *dina d'malchusa dina* requires both elements — a genuine *din* that meets some objective standard of lawfulness, and a genuine *malchusa* that constitutes a legitimate governing power. Where either element is absent, the principle does not apply.

### Roman/Babylon

Understanding why the *mishnah* does not articulate these qualifications explicitly requires attention to historical context. Throughout the *mishnayos*, tax collectors are treated as presumptively illegitimate — a stance that reflects the reality of Roman rule in the Land of Israel. Roman taxation in that period was often implemented through the practice of *tax farming*: the government sold the right to collect taxes in a given province to a private purchaser, who would then extract as much as he could, keeping the proceeds above whatever he had paid for the franchise. This arrangement is precisely the model of *mochs she'ein lo kitzva* — and explains why the figure of the tax collector appears alongside prostitutes and bandits in the literature of the period as emblematic of social degradation.

The statement of *dina d'malchusa dina*, by contrast, originates not from the *mishnah* but from Shmuel, who operated in Babylonia under the Sassanid Persian government — a regime that treated the Jewish community fairly and extended it considerable autonomy. Shmuel himself had a close personal relationship with the Persian king Shapur. It is therefore entirely coherent that a positive, binding relationship to civil authority would be articulated in that context, and that this principle would then be applied *retroactively* to explain the limiting conditions of the *mishnah*: when the *mishnah* treats tax collectors as illegitimate, it must be because they fall into one of the two categories — uncapped assessment or self-appointment — that fall outside the scope of genuine *dina d'malchusa*.

### Dina Scope

This discussion opens onto a broader set of questions about what precisely *dina d'malchusa dina* obligates. It clearly does not extend to ritual matters: a civil government cannot redefine the parameters of Jewish marriage, divorce, or any domain of religious law. That much goes without saying. A somewhat more contested question concerns the laws of inheritance. Civil inheritance law differs significantly from *halachic* inheritance law, and the overwhelming consensus among *poskim* has been that secular inheritance law does not override *din Torah* in this domain — hence the halachic importance of properly structured *halachic* wills. But even in the monetary domain where *dina d'malchusa* is most clearly applicable, an important distinction must be drawn.

### Debt vs. Payment

The critical distinction is between the *creation of obligations* and the *obligation to discharge them*. The principle of *dina d'malchusa dina* operates, based on the *sugya* in Bava Kamma, primarily in the domain of *dinei mamonos* — it determines questions of ownership and establishes who owes what to whom. What it does not do is override the separate halachic rules governing whether one is obligated to *pay* a debt one owes.

To illustrate: when a government levies a tax, *dina d'malchusa* determines that one genuinely *owes* that sum. The money the government collects in taxes is not considered stolen, and public infrastructure built with tax revenue may be used without concern. Similarly, when the government grants someone — say, through the mechanism of tax farming — the right to collect those taxes, one owes that individual the money, and failing to pay constitutes theft. But if the government itself is the direct creditor, *dina d'malchusa* establishes the debt without necessarily imposing the full halachic obligation to discharge it. The *Ran* makes this explicit in the passage found in the portion of his commentary preserved in the *Chisronos HaShas*: the appointed collector — one who collects on behalf of the government rather than having purchased the franchise — cannot *compel* a fellow Jew to pay, *im lo miyiras hamalchus*, unless the fear of governmental consequences comes into play. Because *dina d'malchusa dina*, in the end, creates no more than a debt, and halachic tradition recognizes that *hafka'as halva'ah* — extinguishing a debt without payment — is in principle permitted.

The practical and moral stakes of this position are considerable. There is a reported view — circulated privately and always disavowed publicly by its author — that on this basis one need not pay one's taxes. The halachic foundation invoked was this very principle: *dina d'malchusa* creates the obligation to owe but not necessarily to pay, and *hafka'as halva'ah* is permissible. The profound problem with this position, leaving aside its halachic merits, is the *chilul Hashem* it creates — a concern that the *Gemara* itself treats as dispositive even in discussions where some technical halachic latitude might otherwise exist.

### Tax Evasion Ethics

The *Gemara* in Bava Kamma that deals with related questions about obligations toward non-Jews introduced the issue of tax evasion in precisely these terms. The discussion there was sufficiently uncomfortable that the text was modified: references to *gezel goy* — taking from a non-Jew — were altered in many printed editions to *gezel Kena'ani*, so that the church, should it read the text, could be told that the discussion pertained only to the ancient Canaanites. Whatever one makes of the underlying halachic categories, the *Gemara* consistently inserts the *chilul Hashem* consideration as an override. When one's conduct — even if arguably within a technical halachic framework — creates the public impression that Jews cheat on their taxes or dishonor their financial obligations, that alone is sufficient grounds for prohibition. The recurring news stories of prominent figures prosecuted for financial crimes make this concern anything but theoretical. More fundamentally, it is ethically problematic to reduce the entire question to *chilul Hashem* as if the sole concern is the risk of being caught; the *rishonim* and *acharonim* increasingly recognize that the differential legal treatment of obligations toward non-Jews in earlier sources was predicated on specific historical conditions of oppressive and hostile regimes, conditions that do not characterize the contemporary context.

### Israel State

The *Ran*'s discussion of *dina d'malchusa dina* carries significant implications for the question of the halachic legitimacy of the modern State of Israel — a matter of ongoing controversy. The *Ran* quotes *Tosafos* to the effect that *dina d'malchusa dina* applies only to non-Jewish kings, and explains the underlying rationale: the basis for the king's authority to legislate is that he owns the land, and those who live on it are subject to his rules as a condition of residence — a feudal theory of sovereignty. By this logic, the principle does not apply in the Land of Israel, because *Eretz Yisrael kol Yisrael shutafim bah* — the entire Jewish people holds a share in the Land of Israel, and no individual sovereign can invoke the landowner's prerogative.

This *Ran* has been invoked by those who wish to deny the halachic legitimacy of the secular State of Israel: since *dina d'malchusa dina* does not apply in Israel, and the state does not operate through a recognized framework of *din melech* or *din Torah*, its legislative authority lacks halachic grounding. Others ground the state's legitimacy differently — either by arguing that the *Knesset* exercises something analogous to the authority of a *melech* in its contemporary democratic form, or by arguing that a democratically elected government represents a form of collective consent that generates its own binding norms. Each of these positions engages differently with the *Ran*. It should be noted that the *Ran* himself, in his *Drashos HaRan*, articulates the concept of *din hamelech* — the king's independent legislative authority to govern society beyond the parameters of *Torah* law — which suggests that even within the Land of Israel, some form of governing authority with real legislative power is recognized, even if it does not operate under the rubric of *dina d'malchusa dina*.

### Ran Tax Types

The *Ran* draws a further distinction between two types of tax collection that bears directly on the original *mishnah*. If an individual — including a Jew — *purchased* the right to collect taxes (the tax farming model), then one is fully obligated to pay him, because *dina d'malchusa* has legitimately created that right and the purchaser holds it. Attempting to misrepresent one's goods as *terumah* in order to avoid payment to such a collector would not be permitted. If, on the other hand, the collector has been *appointed* by the government to collect on its behalf — collecting for the king rather than for his own account — then one may not swear falsely, *deleika unsa*, because the situation is not one in which you are being forced to surrender what you do not legitimately owe. The debt is real.

### Ran Payment Force

But — and this is the *Ran*'s striking final point, preserved in the *Chisronos HaShas* passage — even in the case of a legitimately appointed government collector, the collector cannot *compel* payment. *Mihu ein memuneh zeh rashai lehachriach Yisrael chaveiro lifro'a lo et hameches* — this appointee does not have the right to force a Jew to pay him the tax. The reason: *dina d'malchusa dina lo yehei ela halva'ah* — *dina d'malchusa* creates no more than a debt, and *hafka'as halva'ah muteres* — extinguishing a debt without payment is halachically permissible. Therefore, one cannot swear falsely (since the debt is real), but one is not obligated to pay it either (since the duty to pay debts to non-Jews follows its own halachic logic). The *Ran*'s position thus creates an unusual asymmetry: *dina d'malchusa* generates genuine obligations of *ownership* and *debt-creation*, but leaves the question of actual payment discharge to separate halachic principles.

---

## Words vs. Intent

### Hidden Reservation

The *Gemara* now turns to the question of precisely how the vow described in the *mishnah* functions — that is, what formulation one actually uses when taking a *neder* to deflect bandits or tax collectors, and whether a purely mental reservation suffices to prevent it from being binding.

### Piv Ve-Libo

The *Gemara* cites Rav Amram in the name of Rav: the formulation is *ya'asru peirot olam alai im einam shel beit ha-melech* — let all the fruit of the world be forbidden to me if these do not belong to the king. The implication is that in one's heart, one does not mean it. This would appear to be a case of *ein piv ve-libo shavin* — one's mouth and heart are not in agreement. But the *Gemara* rejects this immediately: *keivan de-amar ya'asru, yetasru lei kol peirei alma* — once you have said "let them be forbidden," they are in fact forbidden. The Gemara will not allow a simple disclaimer of intent to dissolve the *neder*.

### Vow Modifiers

The *Gemara* therefore resolves the matter differently: *be-omer be-libo hayom* — one mentally qualifies the vow as applying only *today*, while the words spoken aloud are unqualified. Although in general *devarim she-be-lev einam devarim* — thoughts in one's heart do not constitute speech-acts with legal force — *legabei onsin shani*, in cases of compulsion the rule is different. The mental qualification is sufficient to limit the scope of the *neder* to the present day. Crucially, however, the *neder* is still operative for that day; one cannot eat the fruit today. The mental reservation narrows the *neder*; it does not nullify it.

### Zeruzin/Havai

This resolution raises a deeper question. At first glance, the *mishnah* appears to permit something stronger: a *neder* declared without any genuine intent, with the understanding that the duress alone prevents it from being binding. The *Gemara*'s limitation — that one may only *qualify* the vow, not entirely disclaim it — calls for explanation, particularly in light of the earlier categories of *nidarim* that are not binding. Consider *nidrei zeruzin*: if a seller says "I will not take less than ten *zuz* for this," the *neder* is not binding because the words patently do not reflect actual intent. Or *nidrei havai*: exaggerated speech like "I saw a snake as large as a house" is simply not treated as a sincere speech-act, regardless of what the words literally say. In both of those cases, the person's words do not match their intent — and we accept that the intent controls.

### Qualification Allowed

Why does the *Gemara* not permit the same in the case of a vow to bandits? The distinguishing factor appears to lie in the *context* in which the *neder* is made. In *nidrei zeruzin* and *nidrei havai*, the surrounding social context makes it immediately apparent — to everyone present, including the other party — that the words are not to be taken as a sincere vow. The vow is, as it were, transparent to all. But in the bandit scenario, the entire purpose of the *neder* is precisely to *project* sincerity — to convince the extortioner that the speaker genuinely means what he says. The *neder* is made within a context in which its literal import is the entire point; the other party is demanding it as a truth-verification mechanism. In that setting, one cannot invoke a purely private intention to dissolve what has been publicly performed as a sincere vow. The *beit din* cannot look past the context of the *neder* and treat it as though the speaker might simply not have meant it.

What one *can* do is reinterpret the vow's scope — the principle of *perushen lehakel*, that one may offer a limiting interpretation of what one's words meant. This is a legitimate move even in normal circumstances, though in some contexts it is limited to a *talmid chacham* capable of articulating such distinctions. In the *onus* context, it may be that even an ordinary person may invoke this interpretive approach. But the category of complete non-intent — *lo kavanti* in the fullest sense — is not available when the *neder* was made in a context where sincerity of intent was, by design, the entire point.

---

## Vows vs. Oaths

### Mishna/Braisa

The *Gemara* now addresses an apparent tension between the *mishnah* and a *braisa* on the question of what one may offer under duress. Our *mishnah* frames the debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel in terms of a *neder*: Beit Shammai rules *lo yiftach lo be-neder* — do not initiate a *neder*; Beit Hillel rules *af yiftach lo* — one may initiate. Rav Huna then cites a *braisa* that frames the debate differently: Beit Shammai rules *lo yiftach lo bishvua* — do not open with a *shvua*; Beit Hillel rules *af yiftach lo bishvua* — one may even offer a *shvua*. At first reading, these two formulations seem contradictory. The *braisa* implies that Beit Shammai permits initiating a *neder*, since only the *shvua* is restricted; the *mishnah*, however, implies that Beit Shammai restricts even the *neder*. And the *mishnah* implies that even according to Beit Shammai one may not respond with a *shvua* when the extortioner demands it, whereas the *braisa* seems to limit the prohibition only to *initiating* one.

The *Gemara* resolves this by recognizing that the *mishnah* and the *braisa* are each designed to teach a different *chiddush*. The *mishnah* addresses the *neder* case in order to convey the full stringency of Beit Shammai: Beit Shammai does not even permit *initiating* a *neder*. But when it comes to a *shvua*, Beit Shammai goes even further — one may not even *respond* with a *shvua* when it is demanded. The *braisa*, in turn, addresses the *shvua* case in order to convey the full permissiveness of Beit Hillel: Beit Hillel permits not merely responding with a *shvua* but initiating one. Thus: *tana mateisein be-neder lehodiah kocha de-Beit Shammai* — the *mishnah* teaches through the *neder* to show how far Beit Shammai restricts (no initiation even of a *neder*); *tana braisa bishvua lehodiah kocha de-Beit Hillel* — the *braisa* teaches through the *shvua* to show how far Beit Hillel permits (even initiating a *shvua*).

### False Oaths

The discussion raises a serious ethical question that the *Gemara* does not entirely sidestep. If Beit Hillel permits offering a *shvua* to deflect a bandit — and one swears, say, that these goods are *terumah* — is one not swearing a *shvuat sheker*? The *Gemara*'s answer, developed through the mechanism of *be-omer be-libo hayom*, suggests that the *shvua* too must be structured in a way that involves a qualifying mental reservation, not a wholesale false assertion. Whether swearing with *shem Hashem* that something is *terumah* — even with a mental qualifier in the form of a time-limitation — constitutes a truly permissible *shvua*, or whether some formulation short of directly swearing to the falsehood is required, remains an underlying tension in the analysis.

### Shammai Oaths

Rav Ashi offers a further reading of the *braisa* that reframes the issue entirely. The phrase *lo yiftach lo bishvua* in the *braisa* may not be referring to the bandit scenario at all. *Yiftach lo* — "opening" for someone — is the technical language of *she'elah*, the process by which a *beit din* releases someone from a *neder* or *shvua* through the mechanism of finding a *petach* or *charata*. Beit Shammai's position, on this reading, is *ein she'elah bi-shvua* — there is no process of halachic release from a *shvua*. One may obtain *hataras nedarim*, but Beit Shammai does not recognize an analogous *hataras shevuos*. This is entirely consistent with Beit Shammai's characteristically weighty treatment of the *shvua* as an irreversible commitment. One who takes a *shvua* and later regrets it has no recourse to a *beit din* for release. The gravity of a *shvua* is not something that can be undone by retroactive *charata*.

The parallel to the episode of *Yiftach Ha-Gil'adi* is striking and noted: Yiftach did not have his vow released precisely because no one opened (*yiftach*) the mechanism of *she'elah* for him. Beit Shammai's position may represent a principled insistence that such a mechanism ought not to exist for a *shvua*.

### Hillel Oaths

Beit Hillel, by contrast, rules *yesh she'elah bishvua* — the same process of halachic release available for a *neder* applies equally to a *shvua*. The full apparatus of *petach* and *charata* is available to someone who has taken a *shvua* and now seeks release from it. This is of a piece with Beit Hillel's broader approach throughout this chapter: the comprehensive circumstances of duress or regret are sufficient to engage the mechanisms of release, whether the original speech-act was a *neder* or a *shvua*.

---

## Kodashim Status

### Kadosh Status

With the analysis of *nidrei onasin* substantially complete, the *Gemara* transitions to a new *mishnah* that appears at first to be entirely unrelated. The four categories of non-binding *nidarim* — *havai*, *shegagos*, *onsin*, and the opening category of conditional *nedarim* — have all been addressed. Now the *mishnah* introduces a different conceptual dimension: the question of whether a *neder* can acquire a status analogous to *hekdesh*, sanctified property dedicated to the *Mikdash*.

### Rabbi Meir

This question arises from the very linguistic foundation of the *neder*. When one says *konam*, one is invoking a term drawn from the world of *korbanos* — *konam* is a cognate of *korban* — to render something forbidden. Rabbi Meir holds that this is not merely a formal parallel: when one says *konam* and renders something forbidden to all benefit, one has effectively instilled upon the object a status that draws genuinely from the world of *hekdesh*. Consequently, two concepts from *hilchos kodashim* apply: *me'ilah* and *pidyon*. *Me'ilah* is the transgression of deriving benefit from sanctified property, and according to Rabbi Meir, one who benefits from an object declared *konam* transgresses *me'ilah*, not merely the prohibition of *lo yachel devaro*. And *pidyon* — redemption — is the mechanism by which the sanctified status of an object may be transferred to a monetary substitute, after which the original object becomes permitted.

This is a conceptually remarkable position. *Me'ilah* in its classical sense involves misappropriating property that belongs to the *Mikdash*; but an object declared *konam* does not belong to the *Mikdash*. The operative concept in Rabbi Meir's view must be that *me'ilah* is not primarily about ownership but about violation of sanctified status — and that status can exist in the domain of *nedarim* just as it does in the domain of *hekdesh*.
