The verse acknowledges that Israel may be spiritually deficient in some respects, but they are not called uncircumcised in the default, physical sense. The term *arel* unqualified (*stam*) refers to non-Jews.

The *mishnah* adds: *ve'haya haplishtiti ha'arel hazeh* — and this Philistine, this uncircumcised one (I Samuel 17:26). The use of the term there is obviously derogatory — it would not have been remarkable simply to note that a Philistine was uncircumcised — and so it clearly functions as a marker of otherness and contempt. A further *pasuk*: *pen tismachna bnos plishtim pen ta'aloznah bnos ha'areilim* — lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised triumph (II Samuel 1:20). Here too, *areilim* is used as a general designation for the enemy, not a physiological description.

### Derogatory Usage

Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya adds: *me'usa hi ha'arla* — the foreskin is repugnant — in that it was employed as a way of deprecating the wicked, *shenitganu ba reshaim*, as the verse says *ki kol hagoyim areilim*. This is not merely a neutral label. The *mishnah* is quite candid: the term carries a strongly negative connotation, rooted in a categorical identification of non-Jews as *reshaim*. This reflects a pronounced *anachnu v'hem* — us-and-them — orientation, in which the foreskin becomes not merely a physical distinction but an identity and moral marker. And correspondingly, *milah* — circumcision — becomes not just a ritual act but the defining marker of Jewish identity, to the point where the label attaches even when the physical act was not performed.

---

## Brit Milah Aggada

### Brit Milah Greatness

The *mishnah* then opens into an extended *aggadic* collection on the greatness of *brit milah*, a passage notable for its placement within a *mishnah* on *nedarim*. The *Albeck* edition notes that this material appears to have been carried over from the *Tosefta*, where it reads as an expansion. Yet even the Kaufmann manuscript — generally considered the best manuscript of the *Mishnah* — already contains it within the body of the *mishnah*. That itself is striking.

The opinions are stacked one upon another. Rabbi Yishmael: *gedola mila shenichretu aleha shelosh esrei britos* — the greatness of *milah* is that thirteen covenants were cut over it, as the word *brit* appears thirteen times in the passage in which God commands Abraham regarding circumcision. Rabbi Yosi: *gedola mila shedocha es hashabbos hachamura* — great is *milah* in that it overrides *shabbat*, severe as *shabbat* is; the *brit milah* of the eighth day is performed on *shabbat* when it falls on that day. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: great is *milah* in that not even the righteous Moses — and it is notable that the *mishnah* uses *Moshe HaTzadik*, "Moses the Righteous," a designation one rarely encounters; the usual formulation is *Moshe Rabbeinu* — was given a moment's latitude when he was lax about performing the *milah* for his son at the *malon*. Rabbi Nechemyah: great is *milah* in that it overrides the laws of *nega'im* — a spot of *tzara'at* on the foreskin would be excised. *Rebbi*: with all the *mitzvot* that Abraham performed, he was not called *tamim* — whole, complete — until he circumcised himself: *His'halech lefanai ve'heye tamim*, walk before me and be perfect, followed immediately by the commandment of *milah*.

### Ultimate Importance

The final opinion reaches the highest level of claim: *gedola mila she'ilmale hi lo bara HaKadosh Baruch Hu es ha'olam* — were it not for *brit milah*, God would not have created the world. The source: *koh amar Hashem im lo brisi yomam va'laila chukos shamayim va'aretz lo samti* — so says God: if not for My covenant day and night, I would not have established the laws of heaven and earth. The word *brit* in this verse, usually taken to refer to *Torah*, is here read as referring to *milah*.

### Milah Wordplay

One might ask — and this question has no clean answer — why this collection appears here, in *Masechet Nedarim*, in the middle of a *mishnah* concerned with group-definition rules in *nedarim*. One might also ask why the discussion of *brit milah* does not appear in the *sugya* of Rabbi Eliezer in *Shabbat*, where the *halachic* details of performing a *brit milah* are analyzed at length, and where such *aggadic* material might seem more at home.

One thought — admittedly somewhat speculative — is the wordplay on *milah* itself. *Milah* means both circumcision and word. The entire third *perek* has revolved around the power of speech: what words create a *neder*, whether mouth and heart are aligned, what linguistic categories people use when they invoke a group's identity. At the conclusion of that *perek*, a reflection on *milah* in its dual sense may be intentional. And yet, there is a deep tension here: a *neder* takes a neutral world and gives it *halachic* status through words alone, with no physical change; whereas the entire weight of the *brit milah* discussion — especially *Rebbi's* opinion that Abraham was not *tamim* until he underwent *milah* — emphasizes the centrality of the physical act. Indeed, one might note the irony that a Jewish male who was never circumcised is nevertheless called a *nimul* in the language of the *mishnah*, suggesting that the *identity label* can function independently of the *physical reality*. There is something deeply interesting at the intersection of those ideas, even if the *mishnah* does not develop it explicitly.

On a different note: one might also observe that the *brit milah* discussion of Hatafat dam brit — as noted in connection with a convert who is already circumcised — demonstrates that the act is more than purely physical. The drop of covenantal blood required even of one already circumcised reflects a ritual and covenantal dimension irreducible to surgery.

### Moshe's Dilemma

The bottom of the page brings a *baraita* keyed to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's ruling that Moses was not given any grace period when he was lax about his son's *milah*. The *baraita* asks: but was Moses truly lax? Surely he had a reason. Indeed he did. He reasoned: if I perform the *brit milah* and then immediately set out on the journey God commanded — *lech shuv Mitzrayim*, return to Egypt — the danger to a newborn in the first three days after *brit milah* is well documented, as the verse says *vayihi bayom hashlishi biheyotam ko'avim*. Traveling with an infant three days post-circumcision is a genuine *sakana*. On the other hand, if I wait the three days, God has explicitly commanded me to go immediately. Moses was thus caught between two obligations, each of which made the other impossible to fulfill immediately.

### Moshe's Punishment

Why then was Moses punished at all? The *baraita* answers: *mipnei shenitasek b'malon techilah* — because upon arriving in the town, Moses first attended to his lodging arrangements before performing the *brit milah*. Had circumcision been his absolute first priority upon reaching the *malon*, the threat would not have materialized. But by addressing accommodations first — even understandably, even reasonably — he demonstrated that *brit milah* was not at the very top of his hierarchy in that moment. And for that, the verse says *vayifgeshehu Hashem vayivakesh hamito* — God encountered him and sought to kill him. The lesson, conveyed through the *aggadic* reading, is that even a man of Moses's stature and righteousness — and even when the delay is logically explicable — the *brit milah* admits of no postponement once the moment for it has arrived.

---

---

# Nedarim 32

## Opening & Brit Milah

### Daf Opening

We open today on daf 32a, completing the third *perek* before transitioning into the fourth. As we will see, this is not merely the next chapter but represents a genuine category shift from the issues we have been dealing with. We pick up two lines from the top of the page with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

### Brit Milah Identity

The *Gemara* here is focusing entirely on the *aggadata* appended to the *Mishna* concerning the importance of *brit milah*. The *Mishna* entered this territory because it discussed whether the terms *mulim* and *arelim* refer to the physical reality of who has or has not undergone *brit milah*, or whether they refer to Jews and non-Jews respectively. The *Mishna* determined the latter — these are identity categories, not anatomical descriptions. Accordingly, the *Gemara* proceeds with a series of *aggadot* about the supreme importance of *brit milah*. It is also worth noting that the *Gemara* in *Avodah Zarah* discusses this *Mishna* in the context of whether a woman can serve as a *mohelet*, again underscoring that *nimolim* is not purely about physical reality but about who is considered within the *brit* — an issue of identity. And of course, *ve-havai Arami hu* — one who is not within the *brit* is, by definition, outside.

### Physical vs. Conceptual

This placement at the close of the third *perek* of *Nedarim* is fascinatingly apt. *Nedarim* is a tractate about words creating reality, and *milah* itself also means word — so there is already something poetic here. The *aggadata* emphasizes how *brit milah* is about changing the physical reality of one's body, which stands in striking contrast to the phenomenon of *nedarim*, which changes the identity of things through words rather than through any alteration of the physical world.

### Milah vs. Neder

Yet the dialectic is not so simple, because returning to the beginning of the *Mishna*, who is considered *nimol* and who is considered *arel* is not determined purely by physical reality but also by the categories and words we use. There is thus an interesting tension throughout these first three *perakim* between the physical world of *issur ve-heter* — of things that create identity through bodily change — and the conceptual world shaped by thoughts and words, which is the world of *nedarim*. There may be no clean resolution, but the tension itself is illuminating.

## Tzipporah's Circumcision

### Moshe's Delay

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel teaches: it was not Moshe Rabbeinu whose life was at risk. The verse says that Moshe tarried and should have seized the first opportunity to perform the *brit milah* rather than first settling into the inn. The risk, however, fell not on Moshe but, as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel teaches, *ella le-oto tinnok* — upon the infant.

### Chatan Damim

The proof text is *ki chatan damim atah li* — "for you are a bridegroom of blood to me." The argument runs: go and see who is called a *chatan* here — it must be the infant. Admittedly, this is difficult, since if Tzipporah is the speaker, one would more naturally expect her *chatan* to be Moshe rather than her son.

### Rosh & Ran

The *Rosh*, in the left-hand column, addresses why the infant is called a *chatan*: *she-mitchatnin oto be-mitzvah rishonah* — one marries him off, as it were, through his first *mitzvah*, initiating him into the world of *mitzvot*. The *Ran* similarly explains *she-na'asah chatan al yedei brit* — he becomes a *chatan* by means of the *brit*. Both explanations have a somewhat circular quality — the infant is called *chatan* because through the *brit* one makes him a *chatan* — but there they stand. What is genuinely fascinating, however, is the underlying theological question: if it is the infant who was at risk, this is less a punishment of Moshe than a statement about the vulnerability of someone who deserves a *brit milah* and does not yet have one — someone who is, in a sense, not yet fully part of the Jewish nation, not yet within the *brit*.

### Blood Symbolism

In the way we actually perform a *brit milah*, the idea of *dam* — blood — is central to the ritual. There is the concept of *hatafat dam brit* for a conversion candidate who lacks a foreskin. The focus on *metzitzah b'peh* likewise reflects an intense ritual concern with blood. There is even a tradition that when a *brit milah* falls on *Rosh Hashanah*, the *ba'al tokei'a* who is also the *mohel* should not wipe the blood from his lips before sounding the *shofar*, so that the blood of the *brit milah* and the *korban* of Yitzchak are joined together.

This begins to tie the blood of *brit milah* to the blood of sacrifices. The entire episode of Tzipporah is, in fact, a *parasha* that foregrounds blood — blood as protection, blood as saving someone vulnerable from death. This clearly foreshadows what will happen in Egypt: the blood of the *Korban Pesach* saves those in the house from the *mashchit*. Here, too, something comes to destroy, and blood is what saves — presumably the infant. The blood of *brit milah* functions as a salvific, protective force, but this is unique to this *parasha*. Everywhere else in the *Torah*, *brit milah* is described in terms of removing the foreskin or making the covenant — *bayom ha-shmini yimol b'sar orlato*, *yimol lachem kol basar* — without any mention of blood. Only here does blood appear so prominently, tapping into the world of *korbanot*, which can itself be understood as a sublimation of child sacrifice: instead of sacrificing the child, you cut off the foreskin, shed some blood, and the child lives.

## Af & Cheima Angels

### Destructive Angels

Rabbi Yehuda bar Bizna expounds: at the moment that Moshe Rabbeinu was tardy regarding the *brit milah*, two destructive angels called *Af* and *Cheima* — wrath and rage — came and swallowed him up. The phrase *vayevakesh hamito* is here being translated into these personified destructive forces. *Ve-lo shayru mimenu ela raglav* — the only part of his body they did not swallow was his legs, though the *Ran* notes this is a euphemism for his penis.

### Tzipporah Acts

*Miyad vatikkach Tzipporah tzor* — immediately Tzipporah grasped what was happening and picked up a flint. *Vatikrot et orlat b'nah* — she circumcised her son, and *vayeiref mimenu* — the angels released Moshe at once. One might wonder how Tzipporah intuited the connection. Perhaps she tried many things and this was the one that worked.

### Divine Wrath

*Be-ota sha'ah bikesh Moshe Rabbeinu lehorgan* — at that moment Moshe wished to destroy those two angels, as the verse is read: *heref me-af va-azov cheimah* — release *Af* and abandon *Cheima* — understood as Moshe wishing to seize and eliminate them. God, however, indicated that the idea of divine anger is a necessary part of the world. The old question of why evil forces exist in a good world underlies this passage: to some degree these forces are necessary, even if the question remains whether they need to be quite as destructive as they are.

### Cheima Destroyed?

*Ve-yesh omrim le-Cheima harag* — some say Moshe actually did succeed in destroying *Cheima*, as implied by the phrase *Cheima ein li* — I no longer have *Cheima*. But then a later verse quotes Moshe himself saying *ki agorti mipnei ha-af ve-ha-cheima* — I was fearful of *Af* and *Cheima* — suggesting *Cheima* still existed at the end of his career. The *Gemara* resolves this: *trei Cheima havu* — there were two types of *Cheima*. Moshe destroyed one but not the other. Alternatively, *Gundat de-Cheima* — the verse refers not to *Cheima* itself but to the forces and retinue of *Cheima*, which Moshe could not eliminate even after destroying *Cheima* proper.

### Yetzer Hara

This episode calls to mind the *midrashim* that relate how, in the time of the Second Temple, the *Anshei Knesset Ha-Gedolah* convened and succeeded in destroying the *yetzer hara* of *avodah zarah*. The same theological question animates both traditions: if God gave us a good world, why do destructive forces persist? The answer seems to be that to some degree they are necessary — but the question of whether they must be as powerful and pervasive as they are remains open.

## Brit Milah Greatness

### Avraham's Mitzvot

A *baraita* is introduced: *Rebbi omer: gedola milah she-ein lecha mi she-nit'asek be-mitzvot ke-Avraham Avinu* — great is *brit milah*, for there was no one who was as devoted to *mitzvot* as Avraham Avinu — and yet he was not called *tamim*, whole and complete, except on account of *brit milah*. *She-ne'emar: hithalech lefanai ve-heyeh tamim* — walk before Me and be complete — followed immediately by *ve-etna briti beini u-veinecha* — and I will establish My covenant between Me and you. The verse from *brit milah* follows directly.

This raises a reflection worth pausing over. Avraham symbolizes, in one sense, Jewish identity as an ethnic or familial category — he predates the full system of *taryag mitzvot*, and all who descend from him are part of the Jewish family. This is the language of *Bnei Yaakov* to Shechem: *ki lo nuchal latet et achotenu le-ish asher lo orlah ki cherpah hi lanu* — it is shameful to give our sister to one who is uncircumcised. Here *brit milah* is pure ethnic-familial identity. By contrast, in the episode of Moshe, *brit milah* is connected to *Moshe Rabbeinu* and the world of *mitzvot* proper. These are two distinct models of what *brit milah* symbolizes, and they have implications for how one understands *geirus* as well.

Yet the *baraita* here, even while invoking Avraham, frames the greatness of *brit milah* squarely in the language of *mitzvot*: no one was as devoted in performing *mitzvot* as Avraham Avinu — not in the technical, commanded sense, but in the sense of alacrity and zeal in doing everything God asked — and still he was not *tamim* without *brit milah*. No matter how many *mitzvot* a person performs, this is the one that makes him, at least speaking of men, complete.

### Avraham Complete

*Davar acher*: great is *brit milah*, for without it Avraham was not *tamim* before God. The *pasuk* makes this explicit: the command to walk before God and be whole precedes and connects directly to the commandment of *brit milah*.

### Equal to All

*Davar acher*: *gedola milah she-shkula keneged kol ha-mitzvot she-ba-Torah* — great is *brit milah*, for it is of equal weight to all the other *mitzvot* in the *Torah*. The proof text is *ki al pi ha-devarim ha-eleh karati itcha brit ve-et Yisrael* — because of these matters I have established a covenant with you and with Israel. Since all *mitzvot* are part of a *brit*, and *brit milah* is itself a *brit*, it is therefore equal to all of them combined. One hears in such formulations an echo of the pressures of the Hellenistic period, when Greeks viewed *brit milah* as a disfiguring of the body and many Jews reversed their circumcision in order to compete in athletic contests in the nude. In that climate, declaring *brit milah* equal in weight to all other *mitzvot* was a powerful statement about whether one stands within or outside the Jewish people.

### Sustains World

*Davar acher*: *gedola milah she-ilmalei milah lo nitkaymu shamayim va-aretz* — great is *brit milah*, for were it not for *brit milah*, heaven and earth would not be sustained. The proof text: *im lo briti yomam va-layla chukot shamayim va-aretz lo samti* — if not for My covenant, day and night, I would not have established the laws of heaven and earth.

### vs. Torah

*U-fliga de-Rabbi Eliezer* — this position argues with Rabbi Eliezer, who taught: *gedola Torah she-ilmalei Torah lo nitkaymu shamayim va-aretz* — great is *Torah*, for were it not for *Torah*, heaven and earth would not be sustained — citing the very same verse. Both readings draw on the same *pasuk* but identify its referent differently: one says *brit milah*, the other says *Torah*.

### Elitism Debate

This disagreement is itself quite fascinating from a sociological perspective. The claim that *Torah* keeps the world going feeds into a certain kind of elitism: historically, only a very small percentage of people could truly say they devoted themselves to *talmud Torah* in the deep sense. If it is *Torah* that sustains the world, then it is the *talmidei chachamim* who sustain the world. If it is *brit milah*, it excludes fifty percent of the population, but fully and equally includes the other fifty percent. There is a meaningful difference between a populist and an elitist framing embedded in this dispute. An additional dimension worth noting: *brit milah* is something done *to* a person — the infant has no consciousness of it, no intention. *Nedarim*, by contrast, is all intention. The most important things are sometimes entirely outside one's control.

## Avraham Confused

### Avraham Trembles

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: at the moment that the Holy One Blessed be He said to Avraham Avinu *hithalech lefanai ve-heyeh tamim* — walk before Me and be complete — *ahazato ra'adah* — he was seized with trembling.

### Self-Doubt

Avraham said to himself: *shema yesh bi davar meguneh* — perhaps there is something unseemly, something disgraceful within me, that God must tell me to now become whole and complete? Is there some character deficiency I need to correct?

### God Clarifies

Then God said to him *ve-etna briti beini u-veinecha* — and I will establish My covenant between Me and you — and *nitkarrera da'ato* — Avraham's mind was cooled, calmed. He understood: it is not that his character is incomplete. It is something about his physical body, a *mitzvah* God has not yet commanded him. The incompleteness was not moral but physical — and the *brit milah* was the remedy.

## Mazal Discussion

### Avraham's Mazal

*Vayotze oto ha-chutza* — God took him outside. This passage is actually two *perakim* earlier in the *Torah* than the *brit milah* narrative. Avraham said before God: *Ribono Shel Olam*, I have looked into my *mazal* — my astrological sign — and one *girsa* reads *ein li ela ben echad* — I have only one son — though this does not fit, since this episode precedes the birth of Yishmael. The preferable *girsa* is *ve-eini ra'ui l'holid ben* — I am not suited to have children — which makes sense given Avraham's advanced age and lack of offspring until that point.

### No Mazal Israel

God responded: *tze me-istagninus shelcha* — leave your astrology — *ein mazal le-Yisrael* — there is no *mazal* for Israel. The Jewish people are *lemala min ha-mazal*, above and beyond the forces of the astrological constellations.

### Name Change

Rashi cites this teaching on the *Torah* and concludes: *Avram eino molid, Avraham molid* — Avram does not have children, that is what you see in your *mazal*, but Avraham — when your name changes — will have children. This is not merely a legal loophole. In the same *parasha* where God commands *brit milah*, God adds the letter *heh* to Avraham's name.

### Transcendence

This, I would suggest, is the deeper point connecting this passage to the *brit milah* discussion. The Greeks criticized *brit milah* as disfiguring what God gave you — the body is perfect, why mutilate it? But the message of *brit milah* is the opposite: we are not subservient to the forces of nature. We can change the course of things, rise above what the natural order would dictate. *Ein mazal le-Yisrael* — the commandment of *brit milah* is itself an act of transcendence over the natural order. You transform yourself, you change the course of nature, and with your new name you become capable of things that seemed naturally impossible.

## Tamim Character

### Reciprocal Wholehearted

Rabbi Yitzchak said: *kol ha-matmim atzmo ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu matmim imo* — whoever conducts himself with wholeheartedness, God deals with him wholeheartedly. The proof text: *im chasid titchasad, im gibbor tamim titamam* — with the righteous You act righteously, with the strong in his wholeheartedness You deal wholeheartedly.

### Success Follows

Rabbi Oshaya said: *kol ha-matmim atzmo sha'ah omedet lo* — whoever makes himself *tamim* will have great success. The proof text: *hithalech lefanai ve-heyeh tamim* — followed by *ve-hayita le-av hamon goyim* — and you will become the father of a multitude of nations.

### Physical to Internal

A subtle but important shift has occurred here. We have been speaking about the supreme greatness of *brit milah*, and how Avraham was not complete until he made this physical change in his body. Now we are saying that *tamim* — complete, whole, wholehearted — is a character trait, not a reference to *brit milah* per se. It is about how you conduct yourself in your inner life. The message of the *pasuk* has been extended from the physical act to the internal disposition. One might say the physical act is the external expression and the character is the internal: the external-internal relationship. But this is nonetheless a *chiddush* — it is not obvious, and the *Gemara* makes a point of it.

### Divination Rejected

The opposite of *tamim* is illustrated next. *Kol ha-menachesh lo nachash* — whoever practices divination will have the snake come back at him. *Tamim* means having pure, simple faith in God — not trying to beat the system, not trying to use magical devices to divine the future. Divination (*nachash*) reflects an anxiety-driven attempt to secure oneself against the unknown rather than trusting in God. The proof text cited is *ki lo nachash be-Yaakov* — there is no divination in Yaakov — though the *Gemara* notes the word is spelled *lo* with a *lamed-alef*, meaning "there is none," not *lo* with a *vav*, meaning "to him." The teaching is therefore grounded not in a textual reading but in the principle of *mida ke-neged mida*: if you try to circumvent God's way and figure things out through divination, it will come back to harm you. Simple faith is the best protection against anxiety about the future.

### Pure Faith Reward

Ahava bar Rabbi Zeira taught: *kol adam she-eino menachesh machnisin oto be-mechitza she-afilu malachei ha-sharet ein yecholim likanes betochah* — whoever does not practice divination is brought into an inner chamber so close to God that even the ministering angels cannot enter there. The proof text: *ki lo nachash be-Yaakov ve-lo kesem be-Yisrael* — there is no divination in Yaakov and no witchcraft in Israel — and the end of the verse: *ka-et ye'amer le-Yaakov u-le-Yisrael mah pa'al El* — now it will be told to Yaakov and to Israel what God has done. If you have pure faith in how God acts in the world and what God will do, you will know better than the angels what God is going to do. Actively trying to divine God's plans causes you to forfeit that closeness; simply trusting God elevates you beyond the angels.

## Avraham Punished

### Egypt Slavery

Rabbi Abbahu said in the name of Rabbi Elazar: why was Avraham Avinu punished and his descendants enslaved in Egypt for 210 years?

### Drafting Issue

The first explanation: *mipnei she-asah angarya be-talmidei chachamim* — because he conscripted *talmidei chachamim* into his army. The verse: *vayarek et chanichav yelidei beito* — he armed his *chanichav*, those trained in his household. The word *chanich* is understood, based on the *Ran*, as *le-chanech ba-Torah* — those initiated into *Torah* study — the *Torah* of Shem and Ever, where Yaakov later studied, the Torah inherited from Noach. This *Gemara* has been cited extensively in *Charedi* circles in Israel as a basis for exempting *yeshiva* students from military service: Avraham drafted *talmidei chachamim*, and for that his descendants were enslaved in Egypt. It is one of the more consequential applications of *aggadata* in contemporary policy debates.

### Exceeded Attributes

Shmuel offers a second, more textually direct explanation: *she-hifriz al middotav shel ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu* — he went too far regarding God's attributes, exceeded what was appropriate in challenging God. The verse: *bama eida ki irashenah* — by what shall I know that I will inherit the land of Israel? Rather than simply trusting in God's explicit promise, Avraham pushed further and demanded proof.

### Faith vs. Demand

This connects directly to the earlier *tamim* discussion. The theme of *tamim* is: have faith, trust that things will work out, and certainly when God explicitly promises you something, do not say *bama eida* — how will I know? That is the antithesis of the pure trust we described. Avraham, the one time he failed to embody *tamim* and demanded proof rather than accepting God's word, was punished accordingly. The drafting of *talmidei chachamim* is something of a digression from the central thematic thread; it is Shmuel's explanation that ties most naturally into the surrounding discussion.

## Lost Souls

### Separated People

Rabbi Yochanan said: the problem was that Avraham separated people from coming under the wings of the *Shechina*. He had an opportunity to bring people into the covenant, under God's protection, and he let it slip away.

### Melech Sedom

The verse: *ten li ha-nefesh ve-ha-rechush kach lach* — the King of Sodom said to Avram: give me the souls, the people you recaptured, and you may keep the spoils. Avram declined the booty — but he should have done the reverse: keep the people, let Sodom have the money. He had an opportunity to bring these people into his community, to serve God, and he lost them. He refused everything — the money and the people — when he should have insisted on keeping the people and surrendered only the spoils.

### Geirus Today

This teaching lends itself to applications as pointed as those from the *talmidei chachamim* passage, but in a very different direction. One could observe that when there are large populations — such as halachically non-Jewish *olim* — who could be brought under the wings of the *Shechina* through a proactive approach to *geirus*, and instead impossibly high standards and communal inaction mean they are left outside, the parallel to Avraham's lost opportunity is uncomfortable. The *aggadata* of the Talmud contains a multiplicity of voices, and one must be honest about the fact that different communities selectively cite those that support their agenda. Both the *talmidei chachamim* passage and this one are genuine voices in the tradition.

## Gematria Teachings

### Eliezer = 318

The *Gemara* continues with the episode of Avraham arming his household to pursue Lot's captors: *shmona asar u-shlosh me'ot* — 318. Rabbi Ammi bar Abba says: *Eliezer kineged kulam* — Eliezer was equivalent to all 318 in his capacity to wage war. Some say further: the 318 did not literally mean 318 people at all — it was just Eliezer alone. The proof: the *gematria* of *Eliezer* is 318. The *reish* is 300, the *lamed* and *ayin* together are 100, and the *yud-zayin-alef* are 18, totaling 318.

### Age Three

Rabbi Ammi bar Abba further taught: *ben gimel shanim hikir Avraham et boro* — Avraham recognized his Creator at the age of three. The proof: *ekev asher shama Avraham be-koli* — because Avraham listened to My voice. The *gematria* of *ekev* is 172. Avraham lived to 175. Therefore Avraham listened to God's voice for 172 of his years — meaning he recognized God at age three.

This is the occasion for a notable dispute between the *Rambam* and the *Ra'avad*. In the opening of *Mishneh Torah*, the *Rambam* describes Avraham coming to know God through philosophical inquiry and suggests Avraham became aware of God at the age of 40. The *Ra'avad* quotes this very *Gemara* in objection: the age was three, not 40. The disagreement reflects a deeper divide: the *Rambam* understood knowing God as an intellectual achievement requiring mature philosophical reasoning, and therefore could not accept the notion that a three-year-old *knew* God in any meaningful sense — he therefore preferred a different tradition, apparently from a *Midrash*, which gave the age as 40. The *Ra'avad*, more mystical in orientation, had no difficulty accepting that a three-year-old could intuit or experience God in a manner that counts as *recognition*. The *Rambam* effectively discounts the *aggadic* tradition of age three by privileging the philosophical model.

### Satan = 364

Rami bar Abba said: the *gematria* of *ha-Satan* — *shin-tet-nun*, along with the definite article *heh* — is 364. There are 365 days in the solar year. This means Satan has no power over Israel for one day of the year — which is Yom Kippur. The *gematria* works by the solar calendar even though our calendar is lunar; the point is the numerical symbolism, not calendrical precision.

### 248 Limbs

Rabbi Ammi bar Abba said: one verse says *Avram* and another says *Avraham* — what is the significance of the name change? Initially, God gave Avraham dominion over 243 of his limbs. A person has 248 limbs, and the *gematria* of *Avram* is 243. Ultimately, God gave him dominion over all 248 — *u-le-vasof himlicho al matayim ve-arba'im u-shmonah* — the addition of the *heh* in the name *Avraham* accounting for the five additional limbs.

### Five Control Limbs

Which were the five limbs over which he did not originally have dominion? *Shte einayim* — his two eyes, *u-shte oznayim* — his two ears, and *ve-rosh ha-geviyah* — the tip of his penis. The connection to *brit milah* is obvious. These are the organs of perception and desire: what we see and hear can lead us astray — *lo tasuru acharei levavechem ve-acharei eineichem* — and the sexual drive is what compels one to pursue what the eyes and ears have stirred. Avraham, through *brit milah*, gained mastery over those organs. One can try to stop up one's ears or close one's eyes, but the drives of perception and desire are not always within voluntary control. The *brit milah* represents symbolic — and perhaps more than symbolic — mastery over them.

### Control Drives

The *Rambam* in fact follows precisely this reading of *brit milah*: its purpose is to curb the sexual appetite. The *Rambam* states explicitly that *brit milah* decreases sexual pleasure, and that this is its intended function — we are meant to control and master our sexual drive rather than be controlled by it. This view has obvious contemporary resonance in debates about whether circumcision increases or decreases sexual pleasure, but regardless of the empirical question, the *Gemara* here establishes that *symbolically*, what *brit milah* is about is gaining control and mastery over one's drives rather than letting them dominate. And the insight of one of the students is well-taken: *brit milah* is done *to* the infant — he is passive — and perhaps the result is mastery over precisely those things in life over which one is passive. You cannot always control what enters your eyes and ears; what you can control is how you respond. The organs of reception become subject to your will.

## City Parable

### Siege Parable

Rami bar Abba expounds on a verse in *Kohelet*: *ir ketana* — a small city, *va-anashim bo me'at* — with few people — and a great king comes and lays siege to it, surrounding it. *Ir ketana zeh ha-guf* — the small city is the body. *Va-anashim ba me'at elu evarim* — the few inhabitants are the limbs.

### Interpretation

*Uva eleha melech gadol* — and a great king comes to besiege it: *zeh yetzer hara* — this is the *yetzer hara*. The small, weak body is besieged by the powerful forces of lust and drive seeking to take control.

### Sins Traps

*U-vanah aleha metzudim ve-charamim* — and he builds against it catapults and traps: *elu avonot* — these are the sins. The *yetzer hara* lays sins as pitfalls and snares for you to fall into. The siege is not only the initial assault but the accumulated network of temptations that progressively encircle the person.

### Yetzer Hatov

*U-matza vah ish misken ve-chacham* — and there was found in the city a poor but wise man: *zeh yetzer tov* — this is the *yetzer hatov*, that small quiet voice of conscience. *U-milat et ha-ir be-chochmato* — and he saved the city with his wisdom. And what is that wisdom? *Zu teshuvah u-ma'asim tovim* — repentance and good deeds.

### Teshuvah Future

The word *teshuvah* is striking here because it normally refers to repairing past sins — you have already transgressed, and now you repent. But in this *mashal*, the *teshuvah* is described as *saving* the city, that is, protecting it from future conquest. The resolution: when the *Gemara* says the sins are traps, it means not merely that you might sin, but that once you have committed some sins, those past sins become traps for the future. The *yetzer hara* whispers: you have already sinned, you are not a *tzaddik*, why try to live up to a higher standard? Past sins become an argument for future capitulation. And what saves you? The *yetzer hatov* saying: you can do *teshuvah*, you can actually live differently. So *teshuvah* functions here not only as a remedy for the past but as a protection against being snared by the past into further sin in the future.

### Forgotten Helper

*Ve-adam lo zachar et ha-ish ha-misken ha-hu* — but no one remembered that poor man. The city was saved, but not through a visible act of heroism — through quiet wisdom — and so the man was forgotten. *De-visha'at yetzer hara leit de-midkar leh le-yetzer ha-tov* — when your lusts and drives are seizing control of you, it becomes very difficult to remember the voice of conscience, to recall how it saved you before. The power of desire crowds out the memory of the quieter voice that once protected you.

### Wisdom Strength

*Ha-chochmah ta'oz la-chacham me-asarah shalitim* — wisdom gives strength to the wise man more than ten shields. *Zo teshuvah u-ma'asim tovim* — again, repentance and good deeds. And the ten shields that wisdom surpasses are identified as: *shte einayim* — two eyes, *u-shte oznayim* — two ears, *u-shte yadayim* — two hands (the sense of touch, which also leads astray), *u-shte raglayim* — two legs, which physically bring a person to places of sin, *ve-rosh ha-geviyah* — the tip of the penis, and *ve-ha-peh* — the mouth, through which one talks, arouses appetite through speech, and violates *lashon hara*. These are the ten things that will lead a person astray — and the *yetzer hatov*, the wisdom of repentance and good deeds, is stronger than all ten.

### Ten Temptations

The thematic arc here is important. We have moved from *brit milah* as the source of mastery over the five organs — the eyes, ears, and tip of the penis — to the *yetzer hatov* as the inner force that gives strength over all ten instruments of temptation. Just as we observed the shift from physical *tamim* to *tamim* as a character trait, here too the *Gemara* moves from the physical *brit milah* giving control over drives to the developed inner conscience of the *yetzer hatov* providing protection. *Brit milah* is the foundational physical reality; *yetzer hatov* is the internalized extension of that same principle.

## Kohenim Origin

### Shem Kohen

Rabbi Zechariah said in the name of Rabbi Yishmael: God originally intended to bring the *kehunah* — the priesthood — from Shem. Not from within Bnei Yisrael, not from among any particular Jewish tribe, but from the descendants of Shem son of Noach. They would be the *kohanim* of the world for all future generations.

### Malki-Tzedek

The proof: *ve-hu kohen le-El elyon* — and he was a *kohen* to the Most High God — referring to Malki-Tzedek, king of Shalem, whom *Chazal* identify as Shem son of Noach. This establishes that Shem already served as priest, and his descendants were slated to continue in that role.

### Universalism

One should pause to appreciate the striking universalist dimension of this idea. Our conventional framework is that the Jewish people are chosen, and within the Jewish people the *kohanim* occupy the highest rung of sacred service. But this *Gemara* envisions an alternative reality: the category of *kohanim* would have been *non-Jews* — descendants of Shem, but not Jews — serving in a role of highest holiness, perhaps even in the Temple. It is a genuinely remarkable universalist vision, at least in potential.

### Blessing Order

But *keivan she-hikdim birkat Avraham le-birkat ha-Makom* — since Malki-Tzedek placed the blessing of Avraham before the blessing of God — *hotzi'ah me-Avraham* — God transferred the *kehunah* to Avraham's line. The verse: *va-yevarechehu va-yomar baruch Avraham le-El elyon koneh shamayim va-aretz, u-varuch El elyon* — blessed is Avraham to the Most High God, owner of heaven and earth, and blessed is the Most High God.

### Avraham Correct

Avraham immediately objected: *ve-chi makdimin birkat eved le-birkat kono?* — does one give the blessing of the slave before the blessing of his master? You blessed me before you blessed God. *Miyad nitnah le-Avraham* — immediately the *kehunah* was given to Avraham. The proof text: *ne'um Hashem la-adoni* — God said to my master — where *adoni* refers to Avraham — *shev li-ymini* — sit at My right — *ad ashit oyvecha hadom le-raglecha* — until I make your enemies your footstool. And then the verse continues: *nishba Hashem ve-lo yinachem, atah kohen le-olam al dibrati Malki-Tzedek* — God has sworn and will not relent: you are a priest forever, because of (*al dibrati*) Malki-Tzedek.

### Words Matter

What does *al dibrati Malki-Tzedek* mean? The *Gemara* reads it as *al diburo shel Malki-Tzedek* — because of what Malki-Tzedek *said*, because of how he misspoke. *Ve-hu kohen, hu kohen, ve-ein zaro kohen* — he was a *kohen*, but his descendants are not *kohanim*. His improper speech cost his line the *kehunah* for all time.

### Words Final

And this is a remarkable note on which to conclude the extended *aggadata* of these three *perakim*. Throughout this entire *sugya*, a profound tension has run: the physical reality of *brit milah* versus the world of character and inner traits. Are you *tamim* because of the physical *brit*, or because of the integrity of your inner life? Does *brit milah* give you mastery over your drives, or does your *yetzer hatov*? And through all of this we are in *Masechet Nedarim* — the tractate of words. So what ultimately determines who is the *kohen*? Words. How *Malki-Tzedek* used words — whether properly or improperly — determined the entire future of the sacred service. In the end, the physical realities in which we live and the words that shape our realities are both indispensable. One might frame this entire *sugya* in contemporary terms as a tension between a behaviorist and a psychodynamic orientation: does a person change through behavior and physical action, or through the inner transformation of the self? The Talmud holds both in tension without resolving them — and perhaps that is the point.

## Fourth Chapter

### Scope Focus

We now turn to the fourth *perek*, which, as noted at the outset, is not merely the next chapter but a genuine category shift. The first three *perakim* addressed how *nedarim* are created: what words and intentions are required, what population is included when one uses particular formulations, and so forth. The fourth *perek* assumes the *neder* is already in force — it is valid and binding — and asks: what is the scope of the restriction? What exactly is forbidden and what is permitted?

### Pleasure vs. Food

The *Mishna* states: *ein bein ha-mudar hana'ah me-chavero le-mudar heimenu ma'achal* — there is no difference between one who is forbidden to derive any benefit (*hana'ah*) from his fellow and one who is forbidden only to derive food benefit (*hana'at ma'achal*). This seems counterintuitive: surely there is a vast difference between being forbidden all benefit and being forbidden only food-related benefit — there are countless types of benefit that have nothing to do with food.

### Exceptions

The *Mishna* goes on to enumerate the only differences: *ella drisat ha-regel* — the right to walk through someone's yard. If one is forbidden all benefit, one cannot cross through the person's property. But if the prohibition is limited to food benefit, one may traverse the yard. Similarly: *ve-ha-keilim she-ein osim bahem ochel nefesh* — vessels not used for food purposes. These too fall outside the scope of a food benefit prohibition.

### Money & Food

The *Gemara* will explain why these are virtually the only differences. When someone says *hana'at ma'achal* is forbidden, the correct interpretation is: you are forbidden from any benefit that can translate into money, because anything worth any money at all could potentially become food — if it is worth even a small amount, one could go and purchase something to eat. Therefore, the scope of a food benefit prohibition is nearly as broad as a general benefit prohibition.

### No Charge Items

The only benefits that escape this broad reading are those that have no monetary value associated with them — things for which no one would normally pay. Cutting through someone's yard is an example of such a benefit: one *could* charge for it, but ordinarily no one does, so it carries no dollar value and therefore cannot translate into food.

### Vessels vs. Clothing

What about *keilim* — vessels? Here a further distinction applies. If one would normally rent out a particular item — say, a rake — then borrowing it constitutes a monetizable benefit, and the person under a food benefit prohibition cannot borrow it. But if one normally lends such items freely as an act of neighborliness, without charge, then borrowing it is not a benefit that could translate into money, and it is permitted. However — and this is the key exception — even if one normally lends out food vessels without charge, those vessels remain forbidden to the person under a food benefit prohibition, because they relate directly to food preparation. By contrast, non-food items such as clothing — a shirt, a ring, a cloak, earrings — may be borrowed freely, since they bear no connection to food even when their monetary value might otherwise render them relevant. This distinction between food-related vessels and non-food items like clothing will be developed further in the discussion that follows.

---

---

# Nedarim 33

## Intro & Transition

### Welcome & Overview

Today's daf is 33, and we begin once again from the bottom of 32b — from the opening of the new chapter, the new *perek* — and its fresh *mishnah*. As noted in the previous session, we are now shifting from a discussion of *when* a vow is binding to a discussion of *what* is included in a vow once it has been established as binding. Specifically, the subject is what constitutes *hana'ah* — benefit — since the classic *neder* forbids the subject from deriving benefit from a particular person or object.

### Previous Perek Review

The previous *perek* addressed the conditions under which a *neder* is binding: examining the reasons behind it, the context in which it was made, and the motivations of the one who made it, in order to determine whether the person truly intended the vow and under what circumstances it takes effect. That entire discussion assumed the question of whether the *neder* is valid at all. The current *perek* makes a decisive shift: we assume the vow is valid and binding. The question now is what falls within its scope.

### Scope of Vows

The concept of *hana'ah* — benefit — is the organizing category. A generic *neder* forbids deriving benefit from a person or object in all its forms. But what counts as benefit? This is the central question that will occupy the daf. Closely related is the narrower formulation — forbidding only food-related benefit — and understanding the precise difference between these two types of vows is what the *mishnah* and subsequent *gemara* set out to clarify.

---

## Generic vs Food Hana'ah

### Ein Bein Formula

*Ein bein hamudar hana'ah mechavero lemudar heimenu ma'achal* — there is no difference between one who is forbidden all benefit from his friend and one who is forbidden only food from him. This formulation comes from the list of *ein bein* distinctions, familiar from Tractate Megilla. At first glance, one would expect an enormous gap between a comprehensive prohibition on benefit and a prohibition limited to food. The literal translation of *mudar heimenu ma'achal* is simply "forbidden from his food," which would seem to leave the vast majority of human interactions untouched. The *gemara* will have to explain why, in practice, the gap is so narrow.

The *mishnah* states that the only difference between the two is *drisas ha-regel* — the ability to cut across his yard — and *keilim she-ein osim bahem ochel nefesh* — the borrowing of vessels not used in food preparation. Under a generic prohibition on all benefit, one may not cut across his neighbor's yard and may not borrow anything at all: a rake, a car, anything whatsoever. But if the vow is limited to food benefit, one may cut through the yard and may borrow those categories of vessels.

### Mishnah Permitted Acts

The *mishnah* continues: *hamudar ma'achal mechaveiro* — if one is forbidden from deriving food benefit from his friend — *lo yash'ilennu* — his friend should not lend him *nafah ve-kivar ve-reichayim* — a sieve, another type of sieve, and a millstone or mill — *ve-tanur* — and an oven. All of these are prohibited because, even if one has vowed only against food benefit, it clearly encompasses things that lead to food or assist in obtaining it: objects that help one make food. A plate would fall into the same category.

On the other hand, *aval mash'ilo chaluk ve-tallit ve-tabba'at ve-nezamim* — one's friend may lend him a shirt, a cloak, a ring, and various other adornments. Between the forbidden category of food-preparation vessels and the permitted category of clothing, however, there remains a vast middle ground — most things in the world — whose status is not yet addressed by the *mishnah*.

### Gap in Understanding

A question naturally arises regarding the structure of the *mishnah*: the *seifa* — the second clause enumerating specific permitted items — appears redundant to the general phrase *ve-keilim she-ein osim bahem ochel nefesh*. It likely functions as a clarification of that terse *ein bein* formulation, which in its original context in Megilla was highly compressed. The *seifa* here may represent a later gloss or expansion, unpacking that concise statement with concrete examples.

---

## Vittur & Rabbi Eliezer

### Rabbi Eliezer Attribution

The *gemara* asks: *man tanna* — who is the author of this *mishnah*? *Amar Rav Adda bar Ahava: Rabbi Eliezer hi* — it is Rabbi Eliezer. This is demonstrated from a *braita*.

### Vittur Concept

*De-tanya: Rabbi Eliezer omer, afilu vittur assur be-mudar hana'ah* — even something that is a *vittur* — something not normally charged for, a giveaway, a freebie, something that people simply waive — is forbidden in a case of *mudar hana'ah*. Even something that no one would ever assign a monetary price to, that no one normally minds about, constitutes benefit if it passes from one person to another.

### Vittur Examples

The example given is the baker's dozen: if I sell twelve loaves and throw in a thirteenth at no charge, that thirteenth item is a *vittur*. More directly relevant is the case of *drisas ha-regel* — cutting through someone's yard. A person generally does not mind if his neighbor occasionally takes a shortcut across his lawn; he would never charge for it and would never think twice about it. Nevertheless, under a general prohibition on benefit, even this is forbidden. And so, if Michael has taken a vow that he cannot receive benefit from me, he may not cut across my yard — even though this is precisely the sort of thing people routinely overlook and do not care about.

The concept extends to other everyday informalities: borrowing someone's books, picking up a volume and leafing through it for a few minutes. People generally do not object. Perhaps the best translation of *vittur* is simply "things people don't mind about." Nonetheless, there is something received from the other person, and that is sufficient to constitute *hana'ah*.

### Abstract Benefits

It is worth noting that examples involving transactions — like the baker's extra item — are a somewhat lesser *chiddush*, because in those cases something concrete is being transferred as part of an existing commercial exchange. The more striking point is that Rabbi Eliezer's ruling extends to entirely abstract benefits: things that normally carry no monetary value and that people would never think to withhold. Even those, under *mudar hana'ah*, are forbidden. The ruling thus establishes that *hana'ah* is not defined by economic value or normal social practice, but by the bare fact of receiving something from another person.

---

## Hana'ah Leads to Food

### Sieve Problem

We turn now to the *gemara*'s central analytical challenge: *veha mi ma'achal nadar* — you only forbade food. So why is it forbidden to borrow the sieve? A sieve is not food. If the vow was limited to food benefit, on what basis do we prohibit borrowing vessels used in food preparation?

### Rav Shimon Interpretation

*Amar Rav Shimon ben Levi: be'omer hana'as ma'achalcha alai* — the formulation is not simply "your food is forbidden to me" but rather "the benefit of your food is forbidden to me." This subtly shifts the scope: not just eating the food, but deriving benefit from it. What would benefit from food look like? One could not use a cucumber to scratch one's back; one could not take wheat, chew it without swallowing, and apply it as a poultice to a wound. These are forms of benefit from the food itself that go beyond eating.

Tosafos notes that *hana'as ma'achalcha* might even encompass causing food to serve as the vehicle for benefit — not just using food directly but participating in a process by which food is made useful in some way. However, even with this expansion, the formulation does not obviously reach the sieve: borrowing a sieve is not benefit *from* food in any sense; it is benefit that helps one *process* food. The problem therefore remains.

### Rava Definition

The *gemara* therefore advances a broader interpretation. *Amar Rava: be'omer hana'ah hamevia lidei ma'achalcha alai* — I have forbidden myself any benefit that brings about — that leads to — food-related benefit. Accordingly, borrowing vessels that assist in the preparation of food is prohibited, because in doing so one is receiving something from the other person that ultimately translates into food benefit. The sieve helps one sift flour; the millstone grinds grain; the oven bakes bread. Each is a link in the chain from *hana'ah* to *ma'achal*. On this reading, any benefit received that constitutes a practical step toward food benefit falls within the scope of the vow.

### Monetary Savings

This principle — *hana'ah hamevia lidei ma'achal* — also explains why the gap between generic *hana'ah* and food *hana'ah* is so narrow in practice. A subsequent *mishnah* sheds light on this: *vechol davar she'ein osim bahem ochel nefesh, makom shemashkirin kiyotze bahem, assur* — any item not used for food preparation, if such items are normally rented out, is also forbidden. The logic is as follows: if Michael's neighbor normally rents out his donkey and Michael says to him, "Sure, go ahead, use it, no charge," then by not charging Michael, he has saved Michael money. And money saved is money that can be used to purchase food. Thus, monetary benefit — any concrete financial saving — is subsumed under food benefit, because money is the most direct path to food.

The picture that emerges is this: food benefit encompasses two categories. First, things that practically or directly contribute to the preparation or obtaining of food. Second, things that are normally rented — that is, things whose free provision saves money, which in turn can be used to acquire food. Anything that is neither used in food preparation nor normally rented — a category like cutting through one's yard or borrowing a book no one would ever charge for — remains outside the prohibition when the vow is limited to food.

This broader discussion also reflects a principle noted elsewhere in the *gemara*: the reason that the word *lo yochel* — do not eat — is understood, as Rashi explains, to encompass all forms of *issur hana'ah* is that virtually any benefit one receives can ultimately be converted into food. Food is the most fundamental category of human need, and therefore a prohibition on food benefit is inherently expansive.

---

## Rav Pappa Expansion

### Transportation Objects

*Amar Rav Pappa*: the category of food-related benefit includes not only objects used in the preparation of food but also objects used for the transportation of food. A sack to carry fruit — *sak lavei peirot* — or a donkey to transport produce — *chamor lehavi alav peirot* — are both included. A shopping cart would be the modern equivalent. Even *tzana be'alma* — a simple basket — falls under this category if used for the transport of food, because transporting food is part of the chain of benefit that leads to *ma'achal*.

### Rav Pappa Queries

However, Rav Pappa raises a series of further questions. *Sus lirkov alav* — a horse to ride on — *ve-tabba'at lera'ot bah* — a signet ring to display — *ve-mifsaya umizal be'armaya* — and cutting through someone's yard: what is the ruling in each of these cases?

### Getting to Food

The key distinction Rav Pappa is probing is the difference between objects that bring food to me or help me prepare food, and objects or situations that bring *me* to food. These cases are not about the food itself or its preparation; they are about facilitating my journey toward food. The yard example is perhaps the clearest: if I cut through your yard in order to get to a neighbor's barbecue, that does seem to be a *hana'ah hamevia lidei ma'achal* — but it is less directly connected to the food itself and more about my movement toward it. The horse is similar: borrowing a car to get to a dinner.

### Clothing & Appearance

The signet ring is more unusual. The *rishonim* explain that if one borrows impressive clothing or a signet ring and arrives at a meal looking important and distinguished, the hosts may seat him in a better section and serve him better food. So the ring or garment, by affecting one's appearance, can indirectly determine the quality of the food one receives. Is that *hana'ah hamevia lidei ma'achal*?

### Inconclusive Proof

The *gemara* attempts to resolve the question from the *mishnah*'s *seifa*, which permits lending clothing, rings, and the like. But the *gemara* responds: *eilima shelo lera'ot bahen* — perhaps the *mishnah* is discussing the ordinary case where the clothing is not being used to appear important, in which case *tzricha lemeimar* — of course it is permitted, since there is no food-related dimension at all. The *mishnah* need not be addressing the specific case of borrowing clothes to look distinguished at a meal. The *gemara* concludes *lo — leolam shelo lera'ot* — the *mishnah* is indeed speaking of the ordinary case, and the *seifa* only follows naturally from the *reisha*, without intending to resolve the harder question. The question of benefits that help one *get to* food or present oneself advantageously at a meal remains unresolved.

---

## Items Normally Rented

### Monetary Substitution

The second *mishnah* explains why the practical gap between generic *hana'ah* and food *hana'ah* is so narrow: any item that is normally rented out effectively constitutes monetary benefit when lent for free, and monetary benefit translates into food benefit. This is the mechanism by which the scope of food *hana'ah* expands far beyond what one might initially expect.

### Mashkirin Concept

*Mekom shemashkirin kiyotze bahen* — in a place where such items are rented out. The *gemara* raises a question about exactly what this criterion means. Does *mashkirin kiyotze bahen* require that people regularly rent this specific item on a personal, neighborly basis? Or does it mean that when one cannot borrow the item from a friend, one would have to rent it elsewhere — so the category is defined by the availability of a commercial alternative?

### Car Rental Example

The modern equivalent clarifies the principle well. Suppose Michael cannot get food benefit from his neighbor, and the neighbor says, "Of course, borrow my car, no problem." Even if neighbors routinely lend each other cars without any thought of charging, the fact remains: had the neighbor been unable to lend it, Michael would have had to go to a rental agency and pay. By lending the car, the neighbor has saved Michael money — money that could be used to buy food. That savings constitutes *hana'ah*, even if no one would ever have dreamed of charging in this particular social context. The point is not whether this neighbor *would* have charged, but whether the object is the sort of thing that can be and is rented commercially. If so, the free loan constitutes a monetary benefit, which in turn falls under food benefit.

### Attribution to Rabbi Eli…

The *gemara* asks *michlal de-reisha af al pi she'ein maskirin* — from the earlier clause, which deals with things like sieves and millstones, it appears that even items not normally rented are forbidden when they contribute to food preparation. This is true even though no one charges for the use of such items. *Man tanna hu?* — who holds this position? *Amar Rabba bar bar Chana: Rabbi Eliezer* — as established earlier, it is Rabbi Eliezer, consistent with his ruling that even *vittur* — things normally overlooked and not charged for — constitutes *hana'ah*. Even if no one in the world would charge to lend a sieve to a neighbor, if it contributes to food preparation it is forbidden. Perhaps the deeper principle here is: the question of whether people normally care is irrelevant. Whatever one receives from another person, even something routinely given for free, constitutes *hana'ah* in a legal sense if it falls within the prohibited domain.

---

## Mudar Hana'ah Paradoxes

### Three Permitted Acts

The *mishnah* now shifts to *hamudar hana'ah mechaveiro* — one who is entirely forbidden from deriving benefit from his friend — and enumerates three things that are nonetheless permitted. Each of these is, on its surface, a substantial benefit, and understanding why each is permitted requires careful analysis.

### Temple Tax

*Shokel et shiklo* — one may pay the other's *shekel* obligation to the *Beit HaMikdash*. On the surface, this appears to be a very real benefit: someone else is fulfilling my financial obligation to the Temple on my behalf. Why is this not *hana'ah*?

### Paying Off Debts

*Poreia et chovo* — one may pay off the other's debts. This is even more striking. If Michael owes a million dollars to a creditor and his neighbor pays it off, Michael's net worth has just increased by a million dollars. His liabilities column has been entirely erased. One would think this is among the most direct and significant forms of benefit imaginable. Yet the *mishnah* permits it.

### Lost Objects

*Umachzir lo et aveidato* — one may return his lost object to him. This third case is the most intuitively understandable: the finder is simply giving the owner back something that was already his. The finder performs a *mitzvah* of *hashavat aveidah*, and the owner receives his own property. Whatever service was rendered, in terms of what the owner actually receives, he receives only his own thing. One might wonder whether the gratitude or relief experienced constitutes *hana'ah*, but in terms of the actual transfer of property, no new benefit has been conferred.

### Payment for Return

A further nuance arises in cases where one would normally pay the finder for his time and effort — *makom she-notnu aleha sechar* — because the finder has taken time away from his regular work. In such cases, *tipol hana'ah le-hekdesh* — that *hana'ah* goes to *hekdesh*. Why must it go to *hekdesh*? The scenario is as follows: Reuven cannot get benefit from Shimon. Shimon finds Reuven's wallet and returns it — so far, so good: Reuven is only getting back his own property. Reuven wants to give Shimon twenty dollars for his trouble. Shimon says, "Forget it, keep your money." Now Reuven is in a bind: if Shimon waives the payment, and Reuven keeps the twenty dollars that he was prepared to give, he is now receiving something from Shimon — namely, Shimon's waiver of the fee. That becomes *hana'ah*. So the money must go to *tzedakah*, and Reuven cannot simply pocket it.

---

## Scaring Away Lion

### Creditors as Lions

The *gemara* provides a striking conceptualization of why paying off someone's debt is not considered conferring *hana'ah* upon him. *Avruchei ari be'alma hu ve-shari* — it is merely the scaring away of a lion, and therefore it is permissible. The image is of creditors as a lion bearing down on the debtor; paying them off does not give the debtor anything — it merely prevents an external force from taking something away from him. One is not providing a positive benefit; one is removing a threat. The lion metaphor is, admittedly, somewhat strained: a lion represents an undeserved, unjust attack, whereas a creditor has a legitimate claim. But the structural logic holds: one is not giving the debtor anything directly; one is pushing away an external claim. A model of *grama* — indirect causation — might have served equally well: you are not directly giving the debtor something good, but removing something bad.

### Chanan Case

*Amar Rabbi Oshaya: zu divrei Chanan* — this ruling reflects the opinion of Chanan. The *gemara* identifies the position with Chanan, a figure whose ruling appears in a *mishnah* in Ketubot. The case: a man went on a business trip without making any financial provision for his wife. A neighbor — Chanan — stepped in and provided money so the wife could purchase food, then sought reimbursement from the husband upon his return. The husband refused. Chanan ruled: *ibbad et me'otav* — the neighbor lost his money. Because no explicit stipulation was made with the husband, the neighbor was simply paying off the husband's creditor — his wife, who was owed maintenance. Since there was no agreement for repayment, and since paying off a creditor does not constitute concretely giving anything to the debtor, the neighbor cannot collect. The *benei kohanim gedolim* disagreed: *yishava kamma hotzi ve-yitol* — the neighbor may take an oath as to what he spent and collect accordingly. This is the debate about *mavriach ari* — whether removing a creditor's claim is or is not considered a genuine benefit to the debtor.

### Rava's Caveat

*Rava amar: afilu teima divrei hakol* — Rava argues that even the Rabbis who disagree with Chanan and hold that the neighbor can collect in that case would nonetheless agree that the *mishnah* here is permissible. He explains: *de-yahiv al menat shelo lifro'a* — the case in the *mishnah* involves a debt structured such that repayment could never be legally enforced. It is a loan in the sense that there is a personal moral obligation, but the creditor explicitly stipulated that he would never demand repayment in *beit din*. In such a case, even if paying off a real, enforceable debt would constitute *hana'ah*, paying off a non-enforceable debt would not — because it never appeared in the debtor's liabilities column in any legally meaningful sense. Shimon's payment freed Reuven from a moral weight, perhaps from social embarrassment, but never from any real financial liability. Accordingly, even the Rabbis would agree it is not *hana'ah*. This reading, however, is an *okimta* — a forced narrowing of the *mishnah* to a special case — and does not represent the straightforward *pshat* of the text.

### Deer's Horn Metaphor

The *gemara* then quotes the full *mishnah* from Ketubot. *Amar Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas ke-divrehem* — Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas sided with the *benei kohanim gedolim* that the neighbor can collect. *Amar Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai: yafeh amar Chanan* — Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai sided with Chanan. *Henniach me'otav al keren ha-tzvi* — the neighbor placed his money on the horn of a deer; he flushed it away. Since no stipulation was made with the husband, and since the act of paying a creditor is not seen as directly giving anything to the debtor, the neighbor cannot claim reimbursement. And by the same logic, it would not be prohibited by *issur hana'ah*.

### Rav Hoshaya Response

*Rava lo amar ke-Rav Hoshaya* — Rava did not follow Rav Hoshaya's approach. Rava preferred to read the *mishnah* as acceptable to all opinions — both Chanan and the Rabbis — by limiting it to the special case of a non-enforceable debt. Rav Hoshaya, on the other hand, would not accept this *okimta*, for two reasons. First, it requires an uncomfortable narrowing of the *mishnah*. Second, and more importantly: *gezerah shelo lifro'a mishum lifro'a* — even if we were to say that paying off a non-enforceable debt is not *hana'ah*, if we permit Shimon to pay off Reuven's non-enforceable debts, people will come to permit him to pay off Reuven's real, enforceable debts as well. As a protective *gezerah*, one would prohibit even the marginal case to prevent violation of the clearer case. Rav Hoshaya therefore maintains that the *mishnah* follows Chanan: paying off any creditor, real or nominal, is simply *mavriach ari*, and that is why it is permitted.

The *pshat* of the *mishnah* clearly aligns with Rav Hoshaya: Chanan's position is that *mavriach ari* is not *hana'ah*, and the *mishnah* can be read straightforwardly on that basis without requiring any special limiting case.

---

## Returning Lost Objects

### Rav Ami & Rav Assi

The *gemara* now addresses the third case in the *mishnah* — *machzir et aveidato*, returning a lost object — and reports a debate between Rav Ami and Rav Assi.

### Own Property Doctrine

*Chad amar: lo shanu ela be-she-nichsei machazir asurin al ba'al aveidah* — one opinion holds that the *mishnah*'s permission for the finder to return the lost object applies only when the finder's property is what is forbidden to the owner. That is, the owner cannot get benefit from the finder. In that case, *d'chi mahadar lei midam d'nafshei ka-mahadar lei* — when the finder returns the object, he is simply returning to the owner something that was already his own property. No new benefit passes from finder to owner; the owner merely receives back what was already his.

### Irony of Prohibition

*Aval nichsei ba'al aveidah asurin al machazir, lo ka-mahadar lei* — but here is the irony. What if the prohibition runs in the other direction: Shimon cannot get benefit from Reuven, and it is Shimon who has found Reuven's object? One would intuitively think this is entirely unproblematic — Shimon is giving *to* Reuven; Shimon is not getting anything. Why would that be a problem? The answer is surprising.

### Pruta of Rav Yosef

*De-ka-mahanei lei pruta de-Rav Yosef* — because Shimon is in fact getting benefit from Reuven, in the form of the *prutah* of Rav Yosef. The background: in Bava Metzia, there is a question about what level of *shomer* — guardian — the finder of a lost object is considered. Ordinarily one might say *shomer chinam* — an unpaid watchman — since no one is paying him to hold it. Rav Yosef, however, ruled that the finder is a *shomer sachar* — a paid watchman with a higher level of liability. The reason is that *osek be-mitzvah patur min ha-mitzvah* — one who is engaged in performing a *mitzvah* is exempt from other *mitzvos* that present themselves in the meantime. Therefore, if a *schnorrer* — a collector for charity — were to approach Shimon while Shimon is in the process of returning the lost object, Shimon would be exempt from giving *tzedakah* in that moment. That exemption — that saved dollar — is the *prutah* of Rav Yosef. It is a concrete benefit Shimon receives in the course of fulfilling the *mitzvah* of *hashavat aveidah*. And since it is Reuven's object that creates the occasion for this benefit, Shimon is, in effect, deriving benefit from Reuven.

The striking result: paying off a million-dollar debt is considered *mavriach ari* and not *hana'ah*, because the benefit is indirect. But the theoretical possibility of saving a single dollar in charity is considered *hana'ah* — because it is a concrete, direct benefit that accrues to the finder in the course of handling the owner's object. The contrast is remarkable, and it speaks to the precision with which the *gemara* defines *hana'ah*: not by magnitude, but by directness.

### Rarity of Benefit

The second opinion in the debate — *ve-chad amar afilu nichsei ba'al aveidah asurin al ha-machzir, mahadar lei* — holds that even when Shimon cannot get benefit from Reuven, Shimon may still return the lost object. *U-mishum pruta de-Rav Yosef lo shechiach* — the scenario of the *prutah* of Rav Yosef is simply too rare to take into account. The likelihood that a *tzedakah* collector will actually appear while Shimon is in the process of returning the object is low enough that we do not treat the act of returning the *aveidah* as inherently one that generates benefit. If it happens that a collector does appear and Shimon saves a dollar, that is a contingent outcome of a rare event — not a defining characteristic of the act itself. And therefore, in principle, returning the *aveidah* is not considered an act by which Shimon derives *hana'ah* from Reuven, and it remains permissible.
