# Nedarim 40

## Bikur Cholim

### No Limit to Bikur

The Gemara on 39b opens with a *baraisa*: *bikur cholim ein lah shiur* — there is no limit to the obligation of *bikur cholim*. The immediate question is: what precisely does this mean?

Rav Yosef proposed that *ein lah shiur* refers to the reward — that the reward for *bikur cholim* is limitless. Abaye pushes back sharply: is *bikur cholim* unique in this respect? Is there any *mitzvah* whose reward is capped? The Mishnah itself teaches *hevei zahir bemitzvah kalah kebachamurah she'ein atah yodeia matan secharan shel mitzvot* — be as scrupulous about a light *mitzvah* as about a weighty one, because we do not know the reward for the various *mitzvot*. That very formulation implies that all *mitzvot* may have unlimited or at least unknowable reward. To single out *bikur cholim* would imply the others do not share this quality, which is untenable.

### Gadol Etzel Katan

Abaye therefore offers a different interpretation: *afilu gadol etzel katan* — the statement that there is no limit to *bikur cholim* means that there is no threshold of social status that exempts one from performing it. A person of great standing cannot say that it would be beneath his dignity to visit someone of a lower station in life. The obligation admits of no such calculus. One sees this instinct at work during *shiva* calls as well — an important person does not decline to make a condolence call simply because the mourner is less prominent. The same holds for *bikur cholim*.

### Multiple Visits & Healing

Rava offers yet another reading of *ein lah shiur*: *afilu me'ah pe'amim bayom* — even one hundred times in a day. Having visited once, a person cannot simply check the obligation off his list. If the sick person needs human contact and no one else is providing it, the obligation to return remains. This parallels the formulation used elsewhere — *hakeim takem imo afilu me'ah pe'amim* — where the same act must be repeated as many times as circumstances demand.

The Gemara then cites Rav Acha bar Chanina: *kol mevaker choleh notel echad meshishim betza'aro* — whoever visits a sick person removes one-sixtieth of his suffering. (Some versions read *michol'yo*, of his illness, rather than *betza'aro*, of his anguish — a meaningful distinction, as the latter implies the visitor absorbs the suffering rather than eliminating it.) The Gemara immediately raises the obvious objection: if this is so, why not simply bring sixty visitors and cure the patient entirely? The answer is that this formula operates like the rule of *issur nechasim* from the house of Rebbi — in which each daughter's portion is calculated as a tenth of the remainder after the previous portions have been taken, rather than a flat tenth of the original estate. Similarly, each visitor removes a sixtieth of what remains of the suffering, not a sixtieth of the original whole, so that sixty visitors in sequence would not bring the patient to zero. Even if all sixty come simultaneously, the result is calculated as though they came sequentially and divided equally among them. Moreover, the effect applies only when the visitor is a *ben gilo* — someone of a cognate *mazal* — who possesses some sympathetic or harmonizing influence over the sick person.

### Rav Chelbo & R. Akiva

Rav Chelbo fell ill. Rav Kahana went and made a public announcement — *Rav Chelbo bish*, Rav Chelbo is sick — but no one came to visit. Rav Kahana then rebuked the people: did they not know the story of one of Rabbi Akiva's students who fell ill and the Sages did not come to visit him? Rabbi Akiva himself came, and because he honored the student — sweeping the floor and settling the dust of the room — *chaya*, the student recovered. The student said to him: *Rebbi, hechiyasani* — you have brought me back to life. Rabbi Akiva then went out and taught publicly: *kol mi she'eino mevaker* — anyone who does not visit the sick is as though he is spilling blood, since the act of visiting sustains the sick person's life.

It is worth noting what Rav Kahana's rebuke conspicuously does not record: that the people, having heard the *mussar*, then went and prayed for Rav Chelbo or visited him. The moral instruction stands on its own, whether or not it was successful in motivating action.

### Prayer & End-of-Life

When Rav Dimi came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he reported: *kol hamevaker chole gorem lo sheyichye* — whoever visits the sick causes him to live; *vechol mi she'eino mevaker es hachole yesh gorem lo sheyamus* — whoever does not visit causes him to die. The *Gemara* immediately scrutinizes the word *gorem*. Does it mean that the non-visitor actively prays for the patient's death? *Sheyamus salka deitach?* — can one seriously entertain that thought? Rather, the *Gemara* explains: one who does not visit simply does not pray — not for the patient's recovery, and not for his death. The passivity is the culpable act. By not being present, one never reaches the point of praying for the person, and therefore one bears some moral responsibility if the patient deteriorates.

This is a striking pivot in the Gemara's framing. The earlier passages — Rabbi Akiva sweeping the floor, Rav Acha bar Chanina's one-sixtieth principle — point to very concrete, practical dimensions of *bikur cholim*: attending to physical needs, providing human contact, emotional presence. Now the *stama deGemara* reframes the entire institution around prayer. One might ask why the Gemara makes this shift. The answer is left implicit, but the effect is the same: whether through practical care or *tefilah*, presence sustains the sick person, and absence — even if not malicious — is a form of abandonment.

At this point there is a remarkable *Ran* that carries great significance for discussions of medical ethics. The *Ran* begins: *nireh be'einai dehachi ka'amar* — it seems to me that this is what the Gemara is driving at. He writes that *pe'amim shetzarich levakesh rachamim al hachole sheyamus* — there are times when one ought to pray for a sick person to die. Specifically, when someone is *mitzta'er* greatly — in severe suffering — and *ve'i efshar lo sheyichye* — there is no possibility of recovery — then the most one can wish for this person is a swift and painless death, not a prolonged dying.

The *Ran* grounds this in the famous passage from *Perek Hanose* about Rabbi's maidservant. She observed that Rebbi was in great distress — having to go to the bathroom repeatedly and replace his *tefillin* each time — while his students continued to pray fervently for his recovery. She prayed: *yehi ratzon sheyachofu elyonim es hatachtonim* — may it be the will that the upper spheres overcome the lower spheres. The students' prayers were the lower spheres; clearly in heaven, it was Rebbi's time to die. She effectively prayed that his death not be prolonged by the students' well-intentioned but ultimately misdirected *tefilot*.

The *Ran* then applies this to the *Gemara*'s language: one who visits the sick person helps even through prayer — *afilu lehachyos*, even toward recovery if that is possible — *mipnei shehi tefilla yoser mo'eles*, because prayer offered in the presence of the patient is more effective. But one who does not visit fails on both counts: not only does he fail to pray for recovery when recovery is possible, but *afilu heicha de-ika lahna be-mituta* — even where the more modest prayer is called for, praying that the person should be able to die without prolonged suffering — *afilu ha nami lo mahanya*, even that prayer will not be effective, because it was never offered.

The *Ran* thus identifies a category of prayer for death that is not only permitted but at times obligatory — not a prayer that the person should die in a malicious sense, but a prayer that death, when it is the right outcome, should come gently and without delay. This has become foundational in discussions of end-of-life *halacha*. The central orienting principle is the distinction between prolonging life and prolonging death — one does not wish to stand in the way of a natural process of dying, but equally one does not interrupt interventions that are genuinely sustaining life. The *Ran* articulates this with precision: when recovery is not possible, the most one can do is pray that the passing be swift and merciful. The further question of whether a patient has personal autonomy in these decisions is a distinct and layered discussion. Rav Moshe Feinstein found a kind of indirect approach, arguing that when a patient's wishes are overridden, the resulting anguish can itself worsen the medical condition — so that respecting the patient's will is often the medically as well as halakhically indicated course. This argument does not translate easily to cases where the patient is unconscious, which is precisely where the hardest questions arise. The status of a *goses* — one already in the active process of dying — is a related but distinct category, involving a traditional prohibition against interfering with the natural process at that stage.

### Rava's Strategy

Rava's own practice regarding illness is instructive. On the first day he fell ill, he told those around him: *lo tiglu le-inshei* — do not tell people, *de-lo litra mazali* — so that his *mazal* should not be weakened. There is a sense that publicizing an illness makes it more of a concrete reality, and Rava wished to leave open the possibility that it would pass quickly and quietly. But once it became clear the illness was not passing, he reversed course entirely: *puku v'akhrizu b'shuka* — go and announce it in the marketplace. Two reasons converge here. First, *de'chol de'sani li richdu li* — those who hate him will rejoice at the news of his illness. Far from being a problem, Rava welcomes this, because the verse says *binfol oyvecha al tismach... pen yireh Hashem v'ra b'einav v'heshiv me'alav apo* — do not rejoice when your enemy falls, lest God see your rejoicing and remove His anger from your enemy. If Rava's enemies rejoice at his illness, God's attention will shift toward them and away from Rava, working to his benefit. Second, *u'derachim li libai rachamei* — those who love him will pray for him. Either way Rava gains. This passage carries a layer of biographical texture: Rava was known to have many detractors in *Mahuza*, a cosmopolitan city where he was an outspoken rabbinic authority whose rebuke was not always welcomed. His equanimity in invoking his enemies' anticipated pleasure is itself remarkable.

### Rewards for Visiting

The Gemara then enumerates the rewards for *bikur cholim*. Rav teaches: *kol hamivakeir et hacholeh nitzol midina shel Gehennam* — whoever visits the sick is saved from the punishment of *Gehennam*. The proof-text is *ashrei maskil el dal* — praised is the one who attends to the *dal*, the downtrodden or the poor, who here is understood to refer to the sick person, *ein dal ela choleh*, as supported by the verse *midala yivtza'eni*. *Biyom ra'ah yimalteihu Hashem* — on the day of evil, God will save him — and *ein ra'ah ela Gehennam*, "evil" here denotes *Gehennam*.

The Gemara then asks: is being saved from *Gehennam* not reward enough? What about reward in this world? The verse continues: *Hashem yishmereihu v'ichayeihu v'ushar ba'aretz ve'al titneihu b'nefesh oyvav* — God will preserve him and give him life and bless him in the land and not deliver him into the hand of his enemies. Each phrase corresponds to an aspect of the *bikur cholim* experience. *Hashem yishmereihu* — God will protect him from the *yeitzer hara*. *V'ichayeihu* — God will preserve him from suffering. *V'ushar ba'aretz* — that all will honor him, which the *Maharsha* connects back to the earlier principle of *gadol etzel katan*: just as even the great visit the lowly, so too will the one who visits be honored in turn by all strata of society.

The phrase *ve'al titneihu b'nefesh oyvav* — and not deliver him into the hand of his enemies — is phrased in terms of *nefesh* rather than simply "enemies," to convey something about the quality of one's friendships. The Gemara says *sheyihiyu lo rei'im keNa'aman sheripu es tzaraso* — may he have friends like those of Na'aman who helped cure him of his affliction. This is precisely what *bikur cholim* embodies: being a friend who shows up when someone has a problem. Conversely, *ve'al yizdamnu lo rei'im keRechavam shechilku es hamalchus* — may he not have friends like those of Rechavam, whose advice led to the splitting of the kingdom. The *nefesh* language alludes to the deep connection between a person and his advisors, whose counsel can either sustain or destroy.

A *baraisa* expands on this: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar teaches that if young people tell you to build and elders tell you to tear down, listen to the elders — because *binyan yeladim stirah*, the building of the young is ultimately a destruction, and *stiras zkeinim binyan*, the tearing down of the elders is ultimately a construction. The paradigm is Rechavam ben Shlomo, who listened to the young advisors who urged him to increase the people's burdens, with catastrophic consequences for the kingdom — while the elders' advice, which might have seemed like a weakening of royal authority, would in fact have preserved it.

### Timing & Divine Presence

Rav Sheshes the son of Rav Idi teaches: a person should not visit a sick person in the first three hours of the day, nor in the last three hours of the day. The reason: *ki heichi delo lisach da'ateih min rachamei* — so that he not lose the impulse to pray. In the morning (*tlas sha'ei kadmayasa*), the sick person often feels a temporary surge of energy and appears relatively well, so the visitor might conclude there is no urgent need for prayer. In the evening (*basrayasa*), when *takif chulsheih* — the illness is at its most acute — the visitor might feel that the situation is already hopeless and prayer futile. The middle of the day is therefore the appropriate time: the visitor sees the person in a state that properly motivates prayer.

It is worth observing what this implies. If *bikur cholim* were primarily about practical assistance and emotional support, the final hours of the day — when the patient is most distressed — would be precisely when the visit is most needed. The fact that the Gemara discourages visits at that time shows that prayer is being treated as the central function of the visit, and the timing is calibrated to maximize its effectiveness.

Ravin cites Rav for two further teachings. First: *minayin she'Hakadosh Baruch Hu zan es hacholeh* — how do we know that God sustains the sick person? From the verse *Hashem yisadeinu al eres devai* — God supports him on the bed of suffering — linking *sod* to the concept of *seuda*, sustenance. When a sick person cannot eat, it is God who sustains him. Second: *minayin she'hashechina shruya lemala mi'mitaso shel choleh* — how do we know that the divine presence hovers above the sick person? From the same verse: God supports him, which implies a physical presence above the bed.

A *baraisa* makes this practically operative: when visiting the sick, one should not sit on a couch, stool, or chair — *ella mita'atef ve'yoshev al gabei karka* — but should wrap oneself and sit on the ground, because the *shechina* is present above the sick person's bed and one must not position oneself at the level of the divine presence.

---

## Rivers & Mikvah

### Euphrates Testimony

The connection to what follows is that the preceding passage concluded with statements made in the name of Ravin citing Rav, and the Gemara now appends further statements attributed to the same chain of transmission. Ravin cites Rav: *mitra be'ma'arava sahada rabba Perat* — when there is rain in *Eretz Yisrael*, the great testimony to this is the Euphrates. When the Euphrates rises dramatically and its current runs fast and strong, this is evidence that there was heavy rainfall in Israel. The *mefarshim* explain that *Eretz Yisrael* sits at a higher elevation than the surrounding lands, so its rainfall runs off and eventually feeds into the Euphrates, causing it to swell. The observation has *halachic* significance, as we shall see.

### Underground Springs

This statement of Ravin stands in tension with a view of Shmuel. Shmuel holds *nahara mikafih mitbarech* — a river draws its blessing from its bedrock, meaning that rivers are primarily fed by underground springs rather than by rainfall. Shmuel even states elsewhere that every drop of rain from above is met by two drops drawn up from below — so that even heavy rainfall does not fundamentally alter the character of river water, which remains predominantly spring-fed.

The *halachic* stakes of this dispute are significant. A *mikvah* constructed from collected rainwater is valid only *be'ashboren* — when the water is settled and still, not flowing. A natural body of water fed by a spring, however — being a form of *mayim chayim*, living water — is valid even when moving (*zochalin*). If a river is primarily spring-fed, it retains the status of *mayim chayim* and may be used even when its waters are in motion. But if a river's water is predominantly rainwater or melted snow, then the moving water cannot be used for *tahara*, since it would have the status of a *mikvah* with the disqualifying property of *zochalin*.

### Moving Water & Tishrei

Shmuel's second statement, which contradicts his first, resolves the apparent consistency: *ein hamayim metaharim b'zochalin ela Perat miyomei Tishrei bilvad* — moving water is not valid for purification except for the Euphrates specifically during the month of Tishrei. The reasoning is that at other times of year there is cause for concern that the majority of the river's water derives from snowmelt (in spring) or from rainfall (in fall and winter), which would render the moving water invalid. Only during Tishrei — the fall, before the heavy rains arrive and after the snowmelt has subsided — can one be confident that the Euphrates's water is not predominantly rainwater, and only then is its moving water acceptable.

This second statement of Shmuel effectively concedes the point made by Ravin citing Rav: rivers cannot be assumed to be primarily spring-fed, and one must account for the possibility that their majority is rainwater or snowmelt. The two statements of Shmuel therefore conflict with each other, and it is this second, more stringent position — along with Ravin's observation about the Euphrates — that defines the operative *halacha*.

### Practical Mikvahs

Shmuel's father gave practical expression to this concern. *Avuha d'Shmuel avid lehu mikvatah l'banatei b'yomei Nisan* — he constructed *mikvahs* for his daughters during the spring (*Nisan*), when snowmelt would swell the rivers and render their moving water suspect as predominantly rainwater-derived. *Umartzipi b'yomei Tishrei* — and during Tishrei, he provided them with mats. The mats served a practical purpose: using a riverbed directly is uncomfortable and potentially dangerous (sharp rocks, slippery surfaces), and walking on the riverbed could raise concerns of *chatzitzah*. By providing mats, he enabled his daughters to use the Euphrates in Tishrei — when it was permissible — without those complications.

The *Ran* elaborates considerably on the *halachic* application of these principles. He notes that even at normal water levels, if a river frequently runs dry, there may be reason to suspect that even its ordinary flow is primarily rainwater-fed, since a river sustained by underground springs would not typically dry up. He thus extends the concern beyond high-water periods. On the question of how to *pasken*, Rabbeinu Tam attempts to rule leniently in accordance with Shmuel's first position — that rivers are always primarily spring-fed — but the *Ran* and virtually all other *Rishonim* reject this, holding that wherever there is genuine concern about rainwater or snowmelt, the river may not be used as moving water. The *Ran* also discusses a second possible leniency: that within the river, one might distinguish between sections that would have been valid *mikvah*-water even without the additional rainwater (since their baseline flow was spring-fed) and sections that exist only because of the rainfall. According to this approach, the former sections might remain usable even when the overall water is a majority rainwater, since the rainwater did not create or define those sections. This is a nuanced position and the *Ran* treats it at length.

The practical consequence of all this is significant. Oceans and natural lakes, being stationary, generally do not raise these concerns — though one must verify that a given lake is not man-made. Rivers, however, present a real and ongoing issue, since they are moving and their water composition varies substantially by season, geography, and precipitation patterns.

---

## Exile & Poverty

### Vessels of Exile

The Gemara now introduces a series of statements attributed to Ravin citing Rav, or in some textual traditions to Rabbi Ami citing Rav. The shift in topic is notable — these have nothing to do with *bikur cholim* or *Nedarim* — but the *Gemara* strings them together because they share the same chain of transmission. The verse in *Yechezkel* reads *ve'ata ben adam asei lecha k'lei gola* — and you, son of man, make for yourself vessels of exile. The *Gemara* identifies these minimal vessels as *ner*, a candle; *kearah*, a plate; and *shatiach*, a mat. These are the bare essentials for someone being driven from his home into exile, or in modern terms, the equivalent of the absolute minimum one needs to survive while displaced.

### Lacking Everything

This leads into an interpretation of the phrase *b'choser kol* — lacking everything — from *Devarim*. What does it mean to truly lack everything? Rabbi Ami citing Rav: *belo ner* — without even a candle — *belo shulchan*, without a table. Rav Hisda: *belo isha*, without a wife. Rav Sheshes: *belo shamash*, without an attendant — some household support. Rav Nachman: *belo de'ah*, without intellect. The *baraisa* adds: *belo melach*, without salt — the basic preservative and condiment — and *u'belo revav*, without something to dip one's bread in, some basic oil or fat. Each Amora identifies a different essential that, if missing, constitutes a state of total deprivation.

### Intellect & Sufficiency

Abaye draws a striking conclusion from Rav Nachman's position: *naktinan ein ani ela b'de'ah* — we hold that the only true poverty is poverty of intellect. This resonates with the Mishnah's formulation *eizehu ashir hasameach b'chelko* — who is wealthy? One who is satisfied with his portion. Abaye's teaching inverts this: true poverty is not a matter of material lack but of the absence of the wisdom and understanding that allow a person to navigate life and find meaning and sufficiency within whatever circumstances he faces. If one has *de'ah*, one can manage everything else; without it, no material possession is truly adequate.

The Aramaic saying from the west (*be'ma'arava*) captures the same thought in aphoristic form: *da de-bi kula bi* — if you have this (*de'ah*, understanding), you have everything; *de-la da bi mah bi* — if you lack this, what do you truly have? *De-kane da kane mah chasar* — if you acquire this, what are you missing? *De-la kane mah kane* — and if you have not acquired this, what have you acquired? The rhetorical structure reinforces the point: the possession of intellect and understanding is the one truly constitutive good, in the absence of which everything else is hollow.

# Nedarim 42

## Mishnah: Nedarim & Shemi…

### Opening Remarks

Today's daf is 42. We continue the discussion of what is or is not forbidden to someone who is *assur* — who cannot derive *hana'ah* from another person.

### Mishnah: Before Shemitah

The Mishnah opens: *hamudar hana'ah mechavero lifnei shevi'it* — one who is forbidden from deriving benefit from his fellow before *shevi'it*. This Mishnah turns out to be as much about *shevi'it* as it is about *issur hana'ah*. The ruling is: *eino yored letoch sadehu ve'eino ochel min haneti'ot* — he may neither enter the field nor eat from branches overhanging outside the field boundary.

As we have discussed previously, *hana'ah* is not limited to eating the fruit. Walking through someone's yard — the right of access to another's property — is itself a form of *hana'ah*. Trespassing on property one is forbidden to use constitutes a violation. Accordingly, someone forbidden from *hana'ah* may neither enter the field nor pluck fruit from overhanging branches outside it.

### Mishnah: During Shemitah

The Mishnah then states: *uveshevi'it* — and during *shevi'it*. This clause admits two readings, and the Gemara will explore them at length. On one reading, the *neder* was taken before *shemitah* and the question is what happens once *shemitah* arrives. On another reading, the *neder* itself was taken *on shevi'it* — meaning Reuven made the vow during the sabbatical year itself.

On *shevi'it*, the ruling is: *eino yored letoch sadehu* — he still cannot enter the field — *aval ochel hu min haneti'ot hanotos* — but he may eat from the overhanging fruit. Why? Because on *shevi'it*, the fruit is no longer Reuven's to forbid. The fruit belongs, in a meaningful sense, to everyone; it is not within the owner's power to make it forbidden. The land itself, however, remains Reuven's property — ownership of the land is not lost on *shemitah* — and so access to the field can still be rendered *assur* through a *neder*.

This raises an immediate question: on *shevi'it*, do the poor not have an inherent right of access to one's property for the purpose of gathering fruit? If so, how can Reuven make entry to his yard forbidden through a *neder*? After all, if that device were effective, every landowner could simply forbid access to his yard on *shemitah* and thereby prevent anyone from entering. The Gemara will address this at length; the short answer, for now, is that the fruit is not Reuven's to forbid, but the property and access to it remain his, and that access can still be made *assur*.

### Two Readings Explained

A second, clarifying section of the Mishnah addresses the case where only food — not general *hana'ah* — was forbidden: *nadar mimenu ma'achal lifnei shevi'it* — if the vow was only about food benefit, taken before *shevi'it*. Then *yored letoch sadehu ve'eino ochel min haperot* — he may enter the field (since entering the yard is not food), but he may not eat the fruit. And *uvashevi'it yored ve'ochel* — during *shevi'it*, he may both enter the field and eat the fruit, because on *shevi'it* the owner cannot make the fruit forbidden; it is no longer his.

The Mishnah is thus fairly straightforward in its basic contours. The central analytical question — which will dominate the Gemara's discussion — is whether the first part of the Mishnah, dealing with full *issur hana'ah*, means that *once shevi'it arrives* the previously forbidden fruit becomes permitted, or whether it means that *if the neder was taken on shevi'it* the fruit is not subject to prohibition. This question will turn into a deeper debate about the very nature of a person's power to forbid.

---

## Rav/Shmuel vs. R. Yochan…

### Rav & Shmuel Position

Rav and Shmuel both say: if someone declared *nechasim elu alecha* — "these properties are forbidden to you" — before *shevi'it*, then *eino yored letoch sadehu ve'eino ochel min haneti'ot* — he cannot enter the field and cannot eat from the overhanging fruit. And crucially: *af al pi shehigi'a shevi'it* — even once *shevi'it* arrives, this status does not change. Once the *neder* is in effect, it does not cease merely because the fruit becomes ownerless.

The reasoning is as follows. If I say "this book is forbidden to you" while I own it, and then I sell it to someone else, the forbidden status remains — because when I made the *neder* it was mine to make. The fruit that was in existence at the time of the *neder* and was rendered *assur* retains that status even as *shemitah* arrives, even though ownership of the fruit is effectively lost. New fruit that grows during *shemitah* would be a different matter entirely — the owner never had proprietary rights over that, and could not have forbidden it. But fruit that was already subject to the *neder* remains forbidden.

Accordingly, Rav and Shmuel read the Mishnah's statement *uveshevi'it* as referring to a *neder* taken *on shevi'it* — only then is the fruit permissible. But if the *neder* was taken before *shevi'it*, the prohibition persists even after *shemitah* arrives.

### R. Yochanan Position

Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish both say: if someone declared *nechasai alecha* — "my property is forbidden to you" — before *shemitah*, then *eino yored letoch sadehu ve'eino ochel min hanotos* — naturally, he cannot enter the yard or eat the overhanging fruit. But *hegia shvi'is* — once *shevi'it* arrives — *eino yored letoch sadehu aval ochel hu et hanotos* — he still cannot enter the yard, but he may now eat the overhanging fruit. The vow made before *shemitah* ceases to apply to the fruit once *shemitah* arrives, because the owner no longer owns that fruit.

### Property Access & Gezeir…

This position gives rise to a pointed observation from within the sugya. If forbidding access to one's field through a *neder* is effective on *shevi'it*, that would seem to be a highly convenient tool: one could effectively shut the poor out of one's land merely by declaring the property forbidden. But the Gemara does not regard this as an insuperable problem, because the person cannot forbid the new fruit that grows during *shemitah* — that was never his. And the stuff that already existed before *shemitah* could equally have been harvested and stored away before the sabbatical year began.

One might press further: what about fruit that exists on the tree but has not yet fully grown — fruit that will continue to develop once *shemitah* begins? Presumably the owner cannot forbid the additional growth, but practically speaking, how would anyone separate the permissible portion from the *assur* portion? This is a genuinely difficult question, and it points toward the broader tension in this Mishnah between formal legal categories and the practical realities of *shemitah* observance.

### Ownership & Power

The most conceptually compelling way to read the position of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish is as follows. Their ruling is not merely a function of what the person said or intended; it is a function of the limits of his actual power. A person's capacity to render something forbidden to another derives from his ownership and control over that thing. That power does not extend beyond the scope of his ownership. Therefore, once the fruit passes out of his domain — as happens with *shemitah* — the forbidden status he instilled in it cannot persist, because it was sustained only by his continued ownership.

This is a striking conceptual claim: it is not about intent, not about language, not about the terms of the *neder*. It is about the ontological limits of a person's power to prohibit. The Gemara, as we will see, will ultimately not accept this framing as the fundamental principle at stake — but it is worth pausing to appreciate its force.

---

## This vs. My Property

### Initial Proposal

The Gemara proposes that this is indeed the crux of the dispute. Rav and Shmuel hold: *adam oser davar she'birshuso afilu l'khesheyeitzei mershuso* — a person can render something in his possession forbidden, and that prohibition persists even after the object leaves his possession. Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish hold: *ein adam oser davar she'birshuso l'khesheyeitzei mershuso* — a person's power to forbid is coextensive with his ownership; it does not extend beyond it. This would be a profound and fundamental disagreement about the nature of *nedarim*.

The Gemara immediately challenges this framing: *v'sisbara* — but does this really hold together? If the debate were truly so fundamental, they should have stated their positions with respect to *nechasim elu*, "this property," as well — for if even generic language without any possessive is insufficient to sustain a prohibition past the loss of ownership, one would expect Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish to say so. Yet their formulation specifically uses *nechasai* — "my property." This already hints that the debate is not about the fundamental limits of one's power to forbid, but about the linguistic interpretation of the possessive.

Furthermore, the Gemara raises a proof from a Mishnah that clearly establishes the ability to render something forbidden even beyond one's lifetime and ownership: *omer livno konam she'atah neheneh li* — a father says to his son, "Korban — all my property is forbidden to you as benefit from me." If the father dies and the son inherits him: *yirshenu* — he inherits and may benefit. Why? Because inheritance does not constitute receiving something *from* the father. At the moment of death, the property passes automatically to the son's domain; the son is not receiving it *from* the deceased. Hence, if the father said only "from me," the prohibition does not apply to the inherited property.

But if the father said *bechayav uvemoto* — both in his lifetime and after his death — then *met lo yirshenu*: the son may not benefit from the property. The Ran here points out that this does not mean the son literally fails to inherit; the laws of inheritance operate automatically through *choshen mishpat* and cannot be stopped by a *neder*. What it means is that the son owns the property but may not derive benefit from it — he cannot sell it, use it, or profit from it in any way. This raises its own fascinating questions: can mere ownership, without benefit, itself constitute *hana'ah*? And what would the son ultimately be able to do with property he owns but cannot benefit from?

### Mishnah Evidence

The Mishnah just cited proves that one can render property forbidden *even after one's death* — even after one has entirely ceased to be the owner. This demonstrates conclusively that *adam oser davar she'birshuso l'khesheyeitzei mershuso* is not a contested position; it is universally accepted. But the Gemara notes: perhaps this requires explicit language — the father had to say *bechayav uvemoto*, explicitly extending the prohibition beyond his lifetime. Without such explicit language, one might still maintain that the default interpretation limits the prohibition to the period of actual ownership.

The Gemara then cites a further Mishnah that is decisive. The Mishnah teaches: if someone says *konam letoch beitecha she'ani nichnas* — "your house is forbidden to me, that I shall not enter it" — or *sadecha she'ani loke'ach* — "your field, that I shall not purchase it" — and then the owner dies or sells to another, the vow lapses: *mutar*, it is permitted. The prohibiting party said "your" house, "your" field — and once it is no longer *your* house, the prohibition dissolves. But if he said *le'bayit zeh she'ani nichnas*, *sadeh zo she'ani loke'ach* — "this house I shall not enter," "this field I shall not purchase" — and the owner dies or sells to another, the prohibition persists: *assur*.

This Mishnah is extremely clear. The use of the possessive — "your house," "your field" — limits the prohibition to the duration of that person's ownership. The use of the demonstrative "this house," "this field" — generic reference to the object itself — creates a prohibition that follows the object regardless of ownership. And note: in that Mishnah, the person forbidding is *not the owner at all* — he is the one seeking to enter or purchase. Yet even his prohibition is interpreted according to this possessive/demonstrative distinction. If the possessive limits *his* prohibition when the property is someone else's entirely, then certainly when I use the possessive about *my own* property, the limitation applies.

### Linguistic Resolution

Given this evidence, the Gemara concludes that there is no fundamental dispute between the Amoraim at all. The debate between Rav and Shmuel on the one hand and Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on the other is not about whether a person's power to forbid is ontologically bounded by ownership. Everyone agrees on the following: if one uses the demonstrative — *nechasim elu*, "these properties" — the prohibition persists even after one loses ownership. If one uses the possessive — *nechasai*, "my property" — the prohibition lapses once ownership ends.

When Rav and Shmuel said the *neder* remains in force even when *shemitah* arrives, they were speaking of a case where the declarant said *nechasim elu* — "these properties." When Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish said the fruit becomes permitted once *shemitah* arrives, they were speaking of a case where the declarant said *nechasai* — "my property." *Velo pligi* — they do not actually disagree. They are describing two distinct scenarios, and the Mishnah's ambiguity allowed each pair of Amoraim to read it in accordance with their respective case.

What remains is a striking *hava amina*: one might have thought that the power to forbid is inherently and always bounded by ownership, such that no *neder* could ever outlast one's control over the object — but at the end of the day we reject this and hold that the determinative factor is not metaphysical power but linguistic formulation. Generic, demonstrative language creates a prohibition that is object-bound; possessive language creates one that is relationship-bound and lapses with the relationship.

### Possessive & Demonstrati…

The Ran at the close of this section cites a fascinating *Yerushalmi* addressing a case where someone uses *both* a possessive and a demonstrative: *beitecha zeh* — "your house, this one." Which term governs the interpretation? Does "your house" limit the prohibition to the duration of the other person's ownership, or does "this" extend it to the object itself regardless of ownership? The *Yerushalmi* concludes: *mishum zeh* — you follow the final term. If he ended with the demonstrative "this," that is the operative word, and the prohibition follows the object. The principle is *holchin achar lashon acharon* — we follow the last formulation.

---

## Shemitah Rights & Access

### Rights vs. Vow

Returning now to the Mishnah's ruling that even on *shevi'it* the *neder* prevents the other party from entering the field: why should this be? On *shevi'it*, the poor have an inherent right of access to private fields in order to gather the ownerless fruit. If the Torah grants them this right of access, how can a *neder* override it? Indeed, one might ask more pointedly: if someone could simply declare *nechasim elu* over his field and thereby bar the poor from entering, this would effectively allow any landowner to protect his produce from the poor on *shemitah* simply by making a *neder* — which would seem to undermine the entire intent of the sabbatical year.

### Ulla's Limitation

Ulla answers: *be'omdim ilanot al ha-gvulin* — the Mishnah is speaking of a case where the trees are situated right at the boundary of the property. In such a configuration, the poor do not actually need to enter the field in order to gather the fruit. They can position themselves outside the border, place a ladder against the boundary, and reach the fruit without setting foot on the owner's land. The Torah's grant of access to the poor is a right of *entry for the purpose of gathering*, not an unlimited right of access. Where gathering is possible without entry, the right of entry does not exist. Therefore, the *neder* can effectively prevent entry — because the poor have no independent right to enter in the first place.

This is a genuinely striking limitation on the *shemitah* access rights we might have assumed the poor possess. The right is functional and proportionate: they may enter to the extent necessary to gather the fruit, and no more. If the fruit is accessible from outside, entry is not required and cannot be demanded.

### R. Shimon Gezeirah

Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim offers a related but distinct answer. The poor do have a right to enter the field to gather fruit, but they do not have a right to *linger* there after gathering is complete. The owner retains the right to insist they leave once they have collected what is owed to them. Now, through his *neder*, the owner has made any extended presence in his yard *assur* — the poor person who stays longer than necessary to collect the fruit would transgress the *neder*. Since the *neder* creates a real prohibition against lingering, the rabbis enacted a *gezeirah*: the poor may not enter the field at all, lest they come to tarry after gathering and thereby transgress.

This is a remarkable rabbinic safeguard, and it invites reflection. The *gezeirah* has the practical effect of barring all access to the field — which, as noted, might seem to provide an effective loophole against the obligations of *shemitah*. The question of why the rabbis would institute such a *gezeirah*, knowing its potential consequences for the poor's access to *shemitah* produce, is a genuine difficulty. Presumably, the individual owner's ability to benefit from this arrangement is circumscribed by other aspects of *shemitah* law — including the prohibition on commercial harvesting — but exactly how these constraints interact is worth further study.

---

## Lending & Selling Rules

### Mishnah Prohibitions

The next Mishnah addresses a person who is *mudar hana'ah me'chaveiro* — forbidden from benefiting from his fellow. The Mishnah states: *lo yash'ileinu* — he may not lend him objects; *ve'lo yish'al mimenu* — and may not borrow objects from him; *lo yelvennu* — may not lend him money; *ve'lo yilveh mimenu* — and may not borrow money from him; *lo yimkor lo* — may not sell to him; *ve'lo yikach mimenu* — and may not purchase from him.

### Gemara Question

The Gemara raises an immediate difficulty. *Bishlama lo yelvennu* — we understand why he may not lend him money: lending is a benefit conferred on the borrower. But *lo yilveh himenu* — why may he not borrow *from* him? What benefit is the borrower giving to the lender? The same question applies across the categories: we understand why the person forbidden from *hana'ah* may not receive objects, money, or goods — but why may he not give objects, lend money, or sell?

The Ran's *girsa* makes the structure of the Gemara's question cleaner: we understand *lo yilveh mimenu* — he may not borrow money — *ve'lo yikach mimenu* — may not purchase — *ve'lo yish'al mimenu* — may not borrow objects, because in all these cases he is receiving benefit. But why *lo yash'ileinu* — may he not lend objects — *ve'lo yelvennu* — and lend money — *ve'lo yimkor lo* — and sell to him? What benefit is flowing in those directions?

### R. Yose View

Rabbi Yose bar Chanina answers: the Mishnah is speaking of a case where both parties took mutual vows — *shenadaru hana'ah ze mize* — neither may benefit from the other. Under this reading, the Mishnah is not surprising: it is simply listing all the transactions that are prohibited when the *issur* runs in both directions. Each prohibition can be explained straightforwardly as preventing benefit to one or the other party. The difficulty with this reading is that it renders the Mishnah somewhat less interesting — it is merely applying the same principle twice, once in each direction.

### Abaye Gezeirah

Abaye offers a different answer: *gezera lish'ol mishum lehash'il vechein bekulhu* — it is a rabbinic *gezeirah*: even though in principle only one direction of each transaction is actually prohibited, the rabbis forbade the reverse direction as well, lest one come to do the forbidden direction. Don't borrow, lest you come to lend. Don't lend, lest you come to borrow. And so forth for all the categories. This reading is likely closer to the plain sense of the Mishnah.

### Sale Benefit & Avoda Zara

The discussion of sales raises a related point from earlier in the tractate: in a standard commercial transaction, who is the beneficiary? The Gemara's reasoning here seems to assume that primarily it is the buyer who benefits — which is why we understand why the *mudar hana'ah* cannot purchase, but need an explanation for why he cannot sell. The possibility that both buyer and seller mutually benefit from a transaction — an idea that surfaces elsewhere in the Gemara — would explain why the sale prohibition naturally runs in both directions without needing either Rabbi Yose's mutual-vow reading or Abaye's *gezeirah*.

This sugya has a striking parallel in the opening Mishnah of Avoda Zara, which lists a similar set of restrictions — no selling, no buying, no lending of money, no borrowing, no lending of objects, no borrowing — that apply to transactions with non-Jews in the three days before their holidays. The Gemara there similarly asks: we understand why one might not give benefit to a non-Jew before his holiday, but why may one not *receive* benefit from him? And Abaye there offers the same answer: it is a *gezeirah*, one direction is forbidden because of the other.

The parallel is illuminating. The collection of prohibited transactions here — lending, borrowing, buying, selling — does not operate purely as a technical consequence of *issur hana'ah*. As we saw throughout the previous chapter, many interactions remain entirely permissible even when *hana'ah* is forbidden: one may pay off another's debts, support his wife, visit him when ill. Yet this specific set of commercial and financial transactions is *assur* in both directions. It creates, in effect, a wall of separation. In the context of *nedarim*, this barrier is a legal consequence of the vow; in *Avoda Zara*, it expresses the social and religious distance between the Jewish community and idolatrous practice. That both contexts generate the same formal structure, and that Abaye's *gezeirah* appears in both, is worth noting as a reflection of how the Talmud thinks about the social meaning of prohibited transactions.

---

---

# Nedarim 44

## Hefker & Nedarim Intro

### Madir & Hefker Mechanism

We begin on daf 44a, though in order to organize the relevant background, we must first briefly revisit the mishnah that precedes it. The mishnah addresses a case of a *madir* — someone who has rendered another person (*mudar*) forbidden from deriving *hana'ah* from him. If the *madir* has made all of his possessions *assur* to the *mudar* and the two are traveling together, with only enough food for one, the question arises how the *mudar* might be permitted to eat. One solution suggested is that the *madir* declare his food *hefker* — he places it on a rock and announces that it is ownerless, available to whoever wishes to take it — thereby permitting the *mudar* to partake.

### Rabbi Yose's Objection

Rabbi Yose, however, rejects this solution. The *gemara* explains, through Rabbi Yochanan's analysis, why Rabbi Yose considers this approach ineffective.

### Rabbi Yochanan's Matana…

Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabbi Yose holds *hefker* to be analogous to a *matana*: a gift does not take legal effect until the recipient takes possession of it. Accordingly, until a third party actually comes and claims the *hefker* item, that item is still considered to be within the *reshut* of the original owner. Since it remains in the *reshut* of the *madir*, the *mudar* is still forbidden to benefit from it. Only after an intermediate party has claimed it and removed it from the *madir*'s *reshut* could it then pass to the *mudar*.

### Baalut & Ownership

This position carries an interesting implication: it suggests that there is no such thing in the world of *metaltelin* — movable property — that belongs to absolutely no one. Everything, at any given moment, resides in the *reshut* of some person and carries some degree of *baalut*. Parallels can be found in the laws of *nezikin*, where one who declares his *kad* ownerless in the *reshut harabbim* may still bear responsibility if someone trips over it — indicating that even an act of *hefker* does not necessarily sever all legal connection between an owner and his property. The word *hefker* itself means "consciously abandoned" — it requires verbalization, either to oneself or to others — and is distinct from *yeush*, the mere mental resignation to loss, which is itself a *machloket rishonim* as to whether it operates *mishum hefker*.

Although an earlier portion of the *sugya* appears to have raised a challenge to Rabbi Yochanan's explanation, the *gemara* continues to operate on the assumption that his position remains viable. That baseline — *hefker* is like a *matana* and requires *zechiyas* by another person before it exits the original owner's *reshut* — underlies everything that follows.

---

## Field Hefker & 3-Day Rule

### Why Make Fields Hefker

We now turn to the mishnah at the bottom of 43b, which serves as our primary text for the rest of the *sugya*. The mishnah states: one who declares his field *hefker* may retract within three days; thereafter he may not retract. If he declared it *hefker* for a limited period — one day, one week, one month, one year, or one *shavua* (a seven-year cycle; note that in the Talmud *shavua* means a *shemita* cycle, while *shabbat* denotes a seven-day period) — then as long as no one has taken possession, whether he himself or another, he may retract; once someone has taken possession, he may not.

Why would a person declare his field *hefker* in the first place? The reason is that *chiyuv* in *trumot u'maasrot* depends on ownership. A field that has been declared *hefker* and then repossessed from *hefker* is *patur* from *trumot u'maasrot*. So the scheme is: declare the field *hefker*, gamble that no one will immediately pounce on it, and then recollect it — now ostensibly exempt from *trumot u'maasrot* for that season. This is, to put it plainly, a sleazy practice, and the Talmud will have much to say about it.

### 3-Day Retraction Period

The mishnah's first clause tells us that for the first three days one may retract the *hefker* declaration. The Ran explains that even if someone has come along and claimed the field during those three days, the original owner may still retract. The logic here is that both parties are, in a sense, engaged in a kind of gamble: the owner hopes no one will take it, while an opportunistic third party — himself not entirely above suspicion — waits to claim it the moment it is declared *hefker*. During those first three days, the owner may say, "I withdraw; it was never really *hefker* after all."

Importantly, during those three days the field is also not *patur* from *trumot u'maasrot*. The owner does not get the benefit of *hefker* during the window when he retains the right to retract. After three days, however, he can no longer retract at all. If he wishes to recollect the field, he must do so as a fresh act of *zechiya* — claiming it from *hefker* just as anyone else would — not by retroactively voiding the *hefker* declaration.

The question naturally arises: why three days specifically? The answer offered is, essentially, that three days is the pragmatic middle ground — two days is too short, and four days is too long. The Rabbinic literature frequently uses three as a meaningful number, and common sense aligns with it as a period long enough to be meaningful but short enough to be definitive.

### Limited-Time Hefker

The second clause of the mishnah introduces a distinction. When a person declares his field *hefker* only for a limited period — a day, a week, a month, a year, or a seven-year cycle — the three-day retraction mechanism does not apply in the same way. Instead, the rule is: as long as no one has taken possession, whether the owner himself or another, he may retract; once someone has taken possession, he may not.

### Possession & No Retracti…

To clarify the practical distinction between retracting a *hefker* declaration and actively claiming the field from *hefker*: retracting means saying, "I withdraw the declaration; the field was never *hefker*." Claiming means going out and physically taking possession — building a fence, walking the boundaries — which is the standard method of acquiring a field. One who claims it thereby obtains it as *hefker* property, and if the *hefker* was valid, that acquisition carries a *petur* from *trumot u'maasrot*. Retracting, by contrast, is asserting that the field never left one's possession at all.

The question of whether the owner may then claim the field for himself as an act of *zechiya* — distinct from retraction — is meaningful. Taking possession as *zocheh* from *hefker* is an act consistent with *hefker* being real; retraction treats it as though *hefker* never occurred. If the owner takes possession as *zocheh*, the field is *patur* from *trumot u'maasrot*. If he retracts, it was never *hefker* and remains *chayav*. This distinction will become central in the analysis that follows.

---

## Reisha vs. Seifa Attribu…

### Rabbinic Three-Day Solut…

Having laid out the two clauses of the mishnah, the *gemara* now asks whether the *reisha* (the first clause, with the three-day rule) reflects the position of the *rabbanan*, while the *seifa* (the second clause, which ties retractability to possession rather than time) reflects the position of Rabbi Yose. The reasoning is as follows: the *seifa*, which allows retraction so long as no one has taken possession, fits naturally with Rabbi Yose's underlying view that *hefker* never truly exits the owner's *reshut* until someone claims it. The *reisha*, by contrast, which cuts off retraction after three days regardless of whether anyone has claimed it, seems to reflect the *rabbanan*'s view that *hefker* is a real act of dispossession.

### The Rammaim Problem

What motivates the *rabbanan*'s position in the *reisha*? They are troubled by the practice of *rammaim* — those who declare fields *hefker* with the full intention of reclaiming them in order to avoid *trumot u'maasrot*. The Rabbis were unwilling to allow this scheme to proceed unchecked.

### Rav's Patience Theory

Rav explains the logic: the *rabbanan* imposed a *de'rabbanan* *chiyuv* in *trumot u'maasrot* during the first three days — the period during which the *madir* retains the right to retract. Even though *de'oraita* the *hefker* may be valid and the field should be *patur*, the Rabbis said: as long as you can still retract, you remain *chayav de'rabbanan*. And, critically, Rav observes that the *rammaim* do not have the patience to wait longer than three days. They want their field back quickly. By making the three-day period a window of continued *chiyuv* — with freedom only arriving after three days — the Rabbis effectively neutralized the scheme: those who couldn't wait three days would be *chayav*, and those who did wait would find their *hefker* to be real and irrevocable.

One might ask: how can the Rabbis empower the original owner to retract even after a third party has taken possession *de'oraita*? The answer invoked is *hefker beit din hefker*: the *beit din* possesses the authority to dispossess and transfer property. The Rabbis, acting through this principle, can give the owner the right to retract his *hefker* even in circumstances where *de'oraita* he could not.

### Ulla: Both Rabbanan

Ulla takes a different approach to the *reisha*-*seifa* division. He maintains that both clauses of the mishnah reflect the position of the *rabbanan*, not a split between *rabbanan* and Rabbi Yose. The *gemara* challenges Ulla: if the *seifa* is also *rabbanan*, why does it condition retractability on whether someone has taken possession, rather than simply applying the three-day rule? Ulla's answer is: *shani shanah v'shavua de'la shechicha* — the cases of a limited-time *hefker* (for a day, a week, a month, etc.) are unusual enough that the *rabbanan* did not bother applying the three-day mechanism to them. The anti-*rammaim* legislation targets the standard *hefker* scenario, which is declaring the field fully ownerless without a time limit. The limited-time *hefker* is not the typical exploit the Rabbis were concerned about, and so they left it subject only to the basic rule: once someone has claimed it, there is no retraction.

One might press: if the scheme is to declare *hefker* for just one day, complete the harvest, and reclaim the field, isn't that even more efficient than waiting three days? The answer seems to be that the critical moment of *chiyuv* in *trumot u'maasrot* is connected to the land itself, not the harvested crop. Once produce has been brought into a *kri* — the storage pile — it becomes *chayav*, but the mechanism of *hefker* to avoid *trumot u'maasrot* operates at the level of the field's ownership at the time of harvest. Making the field *hefker* for a single day is simply too unusual a practice for the Rabbis to have specifically legislated against, and thus the limited-time *hefker* falls outside the three-day framework entirely.

---

## Reish Lakish: Both Yose

### Reish Lakish's Attributi…

Reish Lakish offers an entirely different reading of the mishnah. Rather than splitting the clauses between *rabbanan* and Rabbi Yose, or attributing both to *rabbanan*, Reish Lakish holds that both the *reisha* and the *seifa* reflect the position of Rabbi Yose. The *seifa* is identifiable as Rabbi Yose for the reasons already discussed — it conditions retractability on possession rather than time, consistent with Rabbi Yose's view that *hefker* remains in the owner's *reshut* until claimed. And since the *seifa* is Rabbi Yose, says Reish Lakish, the *reisha* must be as well.

But then why does the *reisha* impose a three-day limit at all? If Rabbi Yose's fundamental position is that you may retract at any time until someone takes possession, why did he institute a cutoff at three days? This requires explanation.

### Ran's Confusion Theory

The Ran offers what he considers the most coherent account of Reish Lakish's reading. Rabbi Yose, says the Ran, is concerned about a particular confusion that would arise if *hefker* were always revocable up to the moment of possession. If people knew that the owner could retract at literally any moment before someone claims the field — that the field is, in Rabbi Yose's view, still in the owner's *reshut* the entire time — they might begin to think that *hefker* is not really *hefker* at all, but simply a kind of deferred *matana*.

### Hefker vs. Matana Confus…

The Ran develops this concern. If the owner can retract up until the very moment someone takes possession, then from the perspective of the person who ultimately claims the field, what he received was not truly ownerless property — it was property that the original owner could have reclaimed at any instant. This makes the transaction look far more like a *matana* than a claim from *hefker*. And that confusion has practical consequences.

The person who claimed the field might reason as follows: since the owner retained *reshut* over this property until the very moment I claimed it, perhaps this field is still *chayav* in *trumot u'maasrot*, just as property received as a gift is *chayav*. If he thinks that, he will then try to separate *trumot u'maasrot* from this field for other fields, or from other fields for this one — generating a problem of *min ha-chayav al ha-patur* or *min ha-patur al ha-chayav*. That is a serious *de'oraita* concern: separating tithes from produce that is actually *patur* on behalf of produce that is *chayav*, or vice versa, invalidates the separation entirely.

To make this vivid: the field was declared *hefker*, but the owner could have retracted at any moment. The person who ultimately claimed it is in a state of genuine uncertainty. Was this a real *hefker*? Or was this more like receiving a gift from someone who retained ownership throughout? That uncertainty is precisely what Rabbi Yose sought to prevent.

### Terumot U'Maasrot Confus…

The Ran elaborates further on why this confusion is specifically dangerous in the context of *trumot u'maasrot*. He writes (at the top of 44b) that if we allow the owner to retract at any point before someone has claimed it, people will say: since the owner could have retracted even after a long period, that means the property must have been in his *reshut* the whole time, which in turn means that anyone who claims it is really receiving a *matana* — and therefore the field remains *chayav* in *trumot u'maasrot*.

The Ran's language is precise: *atu le-meimar de-chi lo chazar bo nami lizchei bah acher lo me-hefker ka-zachei* — someone who claims the field will not believe they are claiming it from genuine *hefker*, but rather from the owner's continuing possession. And: *venimtza she-ein ze zocheh min ha-hefker ella mekabel matanah* — it turns out that this person is not taking from *hefker* at all, but receiving a *matana*. And therefore: *ve-chasvri de-michayav be-maaser* — they will think the field is *chayav* in *maaser*, and they will then proceed to treat it as such, mixing *chayav* and *patur* produce in their *tithe* separations.

To make this concrete with an analogy: if someone announces a field is *hefker* but it is common knowledge that the owner can retract at any moment, then anyone rushing to claim it understands they are racing against the clock of the owner's own will. The field is "available" only because the owner permits it to be, and could close that window at any instant. This feels structurally identical to receiving a gift, not to claiming genuinely ownerless property.

It is therefore to prevent this confusion — the collapsing of *hefker* into *matana* in the public's legal understanding — that Rabbi Yose institutes the three-day rule. For three days, the owner may retract. That is consistent with Rabbi Yose's *de'oraita* position, since the property is still in his *reshut*. But after three days, Rabbi Yose institutes a *de'rabbanan* rule: you may no longer retract. This ensures that people understand there is a real *torat hefker* at work — a genuine legal category of ownerless property — and not merely an elaborate mechanism for making gifts.

---

## Gemara Challenge & Rava

### Three-Day Puzzle

The *gemara* now raises a sharp question against Reish Lakish's reading. If the point of the three-day limit is to ensure that people understand *hefker* is real — i.e., that *torat hefker* should not be forgotten — then why impose a three-day limit at all? If the concern is that people will confuse *hefker* with *matana*, the solution should be to declare *hefker* fully effective from day one, not to give the owner three days of retraction and only then declare it irrevocable. Why not simply make it *hefker* immediately, so that there is never any confusion?

### Rava: Rammaim Balance

Rava provides the answer: there are two competing considerations. On one side is the concern that *torat hefker* will be forgotten — that people will not understand *hefker* as a genuine legal category distinct from *matana*. On the other side is the concern about the *rammaim*: those who exploit *hefker* declarations to escape *trumot u'maasrot*. These two values must be balanced.

### After 3 Days Fully Hefker

The three-day period represents this balance. During the first three days, the owner retains the right to retract — consistent with Rabbi Yose's *de'oraita* position — and during this period the field remains *chayav de'rabbanan* in *trumot u'maasrot*, frustrating the *rammaim*. After three days, the *de'rabbanan* rule kicks in: the *hefker* becomes fully irrevocable, and the field is now genuinely *hefker de'rabbanan*, so that people understand it to be truly ownerless.

### Long-Term Reclaim Confus…

Without this three-day limit, a further problem would emerge. Suppose the owner declares *hefker* and simply waits — for weeks or months — until he is ready to reclaim the field. He then walks in and takes possession. According to Rabbi Yose's *de'oraita* position, that is entirely permissible: the field was in his *reshut* the whole time, and no one else has claimed it. But if the public observes this pattern — someone declares *hefker*, and then months later simply takes the field back — they will be deeply confused about the *chiyuv* in *trumot u'maasrot*. Did the person who eventually harvests this field acquire it from genuine *hefker*? Or is it still the original owner's property? That long-term ambiguity is even more dangerous than the short-term confusion the three-day rule is designed to address. By cutting off retractability at three days *de'rabbanan*, the system ensures that any claim made after three days is understood to be a fresh *zechiya* from *hefker*, carrying a *petur* from *trumot u'maasrot*.

---

## Baraita: Hefker Exemption

### Vineyard Hefker Baraita

A *baraita* is now introduced that challenges the positions developed above. The *baraita* states: one who declares his vineyard *hefker* and then, in the morning, rises and harvests it himself is *chayav* in *peret*, *olelot*, *shichecha*, and *pe'ah* — all the agricultural obligations associated with those categories — but is *patur* from *maaser*. The reason for the *petur* from *maaser* is derived from a *midrash* on the relevant *pasuk*: the double language of *azov ta'azov* that appears in connection with certain agricultural gifts does not appear with *maaser*, and therefore *hefker* exempts from *maaser* but not from those other obligations.

### Ulla Reconciliation

Ulla can accommodate this *baraita* within his framework without difficulty. According to Ulla, both the *baraita* and the mishnah follow the *rabbanan*. The *baraita* is describing the situation *de'oraita*: when the owner harvests his field on the morning after declaring it *hefker*, this falls within the three-day window during which, *de'rabbanan*, the *hefker* has not yet taken full effect. But *de'oraita* the *hefker* is real, and therefore the field is *patur* from *maaser de'oraita*. *De'rabbanan* there may be additional obligations, but the *baraita* is speaking of the *de'oraita* exemption.

### Reish Lakish Questions

Reish Lakish, however, has a problem. If the *baraita* follows the *rabbanan*, then during the three-day period the field should be treated as though it is still the owner's — *chayav* in *trumot u'maasrot* — as that is precisely the Rabbinic mechanism designed to foil the *rammaim*. Why then is the *baraita* telling us that he is *patur* from *maaser*? If the three-day rule is meant to maintain *chiyuv de'rabbanan* during that period, the *baraita* should be saying he is *chayav*, not *patur*. The *baraita* seems to undercut the very logic of the three-day Rabbinic legislation.

### Ran: Implicit Retraction

The Ran offers a resolution. The key is in what the owner did on the morning after declaring *hefker*. He simply went down to the vineyard and started harvesting — he never made any explicit declaration that he was reclaiming the field as his own through *zechiya* from *hefker*. Since he did not explicitly state that he was being *zocheh* from the *hefker*, the Ran says: *kivan de-lo parish she-hu zocheh bo... neima de-mehadar* — we interpret his action not as a fresh act of *zechiya* from *hefker*, but as an implicit retraction of the *hefker* itself. He changed his mind and reverted to treating the field as his own.

If this is a retraction, then according to Rabbi Yose — whose *de'oraita* position allows retraction at any point before someone has taken possession — the retraction is valid *de'oraita*, and the field was never *hefker*. If the field was never *hefker*, then it is *chayav* in *trumot u'maasrot* and not *patur*. But the *baraita* says *patur from maaser* — a result which, under this reading, fits precisely because the retraction is understood as a reversal within Rabbi Yose's framework, and the *baraita* is speaking to the resulting status.

### Reish Lakish: Attribute…

Reish Lakish sidesteps the difficulty entirely with a clean solution: he attributes the entire *baraita* to *rabbanan*, not to Rabbi Yose. In other words, Reish Lakish says: when I associated the mishnah with Rabbi Yose, that did not require me to associate this *baraita* with Rabbi Yose as well. The *baraita* can simply be understood as following the *rabbanan*, and the various technical details work themselves out under that attribution without generating the contradictions that plague the alternative reading.

---

## Two vs. Three Witnesses

### Two vs. Three Distinction

An alternative explanation (*i ba'it eima*) is offered to resolve the tension between the *baraita* and the mishnah without attributing them to different *tanna'im*. The distinction is not between Rabbi Yose and *rabbanan* at all, but between two different circumstances of *hefker*: whether the declaration was made in the presence of two people (*bifnei terei*) or three people (*bifnei tlata*).

When *hefker* is declared before only two people, the complexities discussed throughout — the right to retract, the three-day period, the ambiguity about *chiyuv* in *trumot u'maasrot* — all apply. The declaration is not maximally effective, and the various Rabbinic and *de'oraita* rules come into play. The mishnah, with its three-day retraction rule and all its attendant complications, speaks to this case.

### Three Witnesses Effective

But Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak, and Elazar ben Anas both hold that if *hefker* is declared before three people, it is fully and immediately effective. The declaration before three confers a qualitatively different legal status on the *hefker*: it is irrevocable from the outset, and its effect as genuine ownerless property — *patur* from *trumot u'maasrot* — is immediate. The *baraita*, which speaks of a *petur* from *maaser*, is therefore the case of *hefker* before three: the *hefker* took full effect immediately, and the owner who harvests the next morning is indeed *patur*.

### Three Witnesses Purpose

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds a further nuance. He holds that *devar Torah* — as a matter of pure Torah law — even declaring *hefker* before a single person is sufficient to render the property ownerless. The Rabbinic requirement of three is not because three are needed for the *hefker* itself to be effective, but for a purely practical purpose: one person to take possession of the *hefker* property, and two to serve as witnesses to that act of possession. The three-person rule is thus a procedural safeguard for proof, not a substantive requirement for the *de'oraita* validity of the *hefker* declaration itself.

---

---

# Nedarim 45

## Hefker & Ownership

### Hefker as Speech Act

The previous *perek* closed with a *machlokes* between Rabbi Yosi and the *Rabbanan* concerning how *hefker* operates, along with a dispute among the *Amora'im* about how to apply Rabbi Yosi's position, drawing on various *beraisos* and *mishnayos*. Before turning to the new *perek*, it is worth stepping back to examine the nature of *hefker* more broadly.

The case at the end of the prior *mishna* involved a person who was *mudar hana'ah* from another and placed food on a rock, declaring it *hefker*, so that the other person could freely take and benefit from it. The operative question is: what precisely does *hefker* accomplish? If *hefker* merely grants others permission to use an object without actually extinguishing the original owner's title — so that during the limbo period between the declaration and another person's acquisition the original ownership persists — then the *neder* would remain in effect wherever that *neder* depends on ownership. This would create a real difficulty for understanding how Rabbi Yosi's position functions in the *mishna*.

### Two Hefker Models

There are essentially two ways to understand *hefker*. The first model holds that *hefker* is a grant of permission to others to use or acquire the object, but does not transfer ownership until a second party actually acquires it. Under this view, the original owner's title lingers in that interim period. The second model holds that *hefker* is a complete and immediate severance of ownership — the moment one declares an object *hefker*, it passes out of one's *reshut* entirely.

Which model the *mishna* presupposes is precisely the question. The tension between these two models runs through many of the discussions that follow.

### Hefker & Nedarim

The Rambam observes that *hefker* is, in a certain sense, a kind of *neder*. This is not to say they are identical, but that in both cases one's words change the status of an object. With a *neder*, the words render the object *assur* or *mutar*; with *hefker*, the words alter to whom the object belongs. The Rambam's comparison is illuminated by the *Gemara* on daf 7, which asks whether *yad* functions for *hefker* — that is, whether the rules of partial verbal formulations that govern *nedarim* apply equally to *hefker*. That the *Gemara* even entertains the question demonstrates that these two categories share significant structural overlap as *speech acts* that change the *halachic* status of an object.

One can observe a similar dynamic with the separation of *terumah* and *maaser*: there too one employs words to change the legal standing of produce. In each of these cases — *hefker*, *nedarim*, tithing — it is a verbal act directed at an object, a *cheftza*, that produces a *halachic* transformation. The *masechta* has touched on this underlying pattern repeatedly.

### Hefker After Death

The comparison to *nedarim* carries one further striking implication: what happens if a person declares something *hefker* and then dies before anyone has acquired it? If *hefker* is a genuine *kinyan* — a real transfer of title to no one, with the property suspended in ownerless limbo — then the declaration should remain effective even after the owner's death; anyone who comes along afterward may acquire it. But if *hefker* is more akin to a *neder*, then it is a personal obligation of the declarer, and just as one's heirs are not obligated to fulfill the *nedarim* of their ancestor, they would not be bound to treat the property as ownerless. The property would simply fall back into the estate, having never truly left the owner's *reshut* — it was merely an attempted verbal transformation that lapsed upon death.

This is thus another domain in which the structural similarity between *hefker* and *nedarim* has concrete *halachic* consequences.

### Hefker Beit Din

The principle of *hefker beit din hefker* — that a rabbinic court possesses the authority to render property ownerless — also arose at the end of *amud alef*. Rabbi Shimon ben Hotzadak holds: *kol hamaphkir bifnei shlosha havi hefker* — declaring something *hefker* before three people constitutes valid *hefker*; before fewer than three it does not. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disagrees and says that *devar Torah*, even one person suffices, and the rabbis required three for a pragmatic reason: *kedai sheyihiyeh echad zocheh ushnayim me'idim* — so that one person may acquire the property and two may serve as witnesses.

These two positions suggest rather different theories of what the three-person requirement accomplishes. On Rabbi Shimon ben Hotzadak's view, one might read the requirement as analogous to a *beit din*, though it is equally possible he is not invoking formal judicial procedure at all. Rather, his concern may be with *publicity*: once three people know something, the matter becomes public — *avsha milta* — and acquires a standing in the communal sphere. Indeed, there is a known principle with *lashon hara* that once three people know of something it changes its status, because a certain *kol*, a communal voice, begins to form around that information. Under this reading, Rabbi Shimon ben Hotzadak's three-person requirement is about making the *hefker* publicly known, not about convening a *beit din*.

The principle of *hefker beit din hefker* itself comes up in several critical contexts. One striking application, to be encountered in *Kiddushin*, is the *sugya* of *afkinu rabanan lekiddushei minei* — the notion that under very circumscribed circumstances the rabbis possess the power to annul a marriage retroactively. At least according to some *Rishonim*, the mechanism is that the *beit din* declares that the money used for *kiddushin* was never truly the groom's — it was *hefker* — and thus the *kiddushin* never took effect. This illustrates the extraordinary reach of *hefker beit din hefker*.

### Goral & Authority

The *Gemara* in *Gittin* identifies two potential sources for *hefker beit din hefker*, and the two sources carry sharply divergent implications. The first source is the division of the land of Israel by *goral* — by lottery — when the Jewish people entered the land. At first glance this raises an obvious question: how did each person actually acquire his portion? The entire land was in some sense the collective inheritance of the Jewish people; no individual owned any of it; and yet through the *goral* each family received a defined tract. The mechanism by which this worked — by which the *beit din* could take something from the collective and vest it in an individual — is *hefker beit din hefker*. The *beit din* rendered the communal property ownerless with respect to all others and simultaneously designated it as belonging to a specific person.

This first source implies something quite far-reaching: *hefker beit din hefker* is not merely the power to make property ownerless, but the power to transfer ownership directly. The *beit din* can take from the collective and give to an individual. This reflects a model of communal or governmental ownership: the land ultimately belongs to God — *l'Hashem ha-aretz umlo'ah* — and the *beit din* functions as its administrator, capable of directing ownership where it chooses.

The second source is from Ezra, who exercised the power to confiscate — to declare *cherem* — the property of those who refused to ascend to the land of Israel. This source tells a different story. Here the *beit din*'s power is punitive and coercive: it is a policing authority, the capacity to fine or confiscate property from those who have violated communal norms. This is not a model of governmental ownership of everything, but a model of governmental enforcement power.

These two models — communal ownership with the *beit din* as administrator versus *beit din* as wielder of police power — represent genuinely different conceptions of what the Torah's governmental structure prescribes and what the principle of *hefker beit din hefker* means at its root.

A related but distinct question is whether the government may seize private land for public use. There are indeed such rules, traceable to Yehoshua's conquest of the land. The *Rambam* and the *Gemara* in *Bava Batra* enumerate approximately eight basic public-property-law rules that Yehoshua established: public easements through fields, specifications for road widths, rights of pasturage, and similar matters. These public-land-use questions constitute their own complex domain.

### Bitul Chametz

One other significant application of the concept of *hefker* is *bitul chametz*. According to Tosafot on Pesachim daf 2, *bitul chametz* — the nullification of one's *chametz* before Passover — operates through a mechanism related to *hefker*.
