It may not be that the act of *bitul* is identical to *hefker*, but rather that *bitul* causes one's *chametz* to become *hefker*. Under this view, a person who nullifies all his *chametz*, declares it ownerless, and simply closes the door on whatever remains — the Cheerios on the shelf, the residue on the frying pan — has in principle fulfilled his biblical obligation. The rabbinic requirements of *bedikat chametz* (searching), active destruction, and other measures were layered on top because *bitul* alone seems too easy.

### Ramban's Critique

The Ramban offers a sharp critique of Tosafot's position. He argues that *bitul chametz* cannot function through *hefker*, and that it operates through an entirely different mechanism — one closer to *bitul avodah zarah*. Just as a non-Jew who once worshipped an idol and then rejects it — smashing it, discarding it, or declaring it worthless — has performed a *bitul* that removes the idol's prohibited status, so too the person performing *bitul chametz* is not declaring the *chametz* ownerless but rather fundamentally reorienting his relationship to it: *eino ani rotzeh b'kiyumo* — I do not want this to exist for me any longer.

Under the Ramban's model, the decisive factor is a psychological-legal relinquishment of attachment to the *chametz*, not a formal act of ownership transfer. A person who simply does not want his *chametz* — who has inwardly and verbally severed his connection to it — has accomplished something *mide'oraita*, and the rabbis then required additional acts because this inner relinquishment alone seems insufficiently concrete.

One might press: with *avodah zarah*, the act of physical destruction demonstrates that the object is no longer worshipped — the idol's status is defined entirely by its being an object of veneration, and the owner's rejection makes that plain. But with *chametz*, what does a verbal declaration actually accomplish? Why should words alone have the power to change the *halachic* status of the *chametz*?

### Ran on Chametz

The Ran in *Psachim* — on daf 1 amud alef in the pages of the Rif — offers a distinctive answer. *Chametz* is categorically different from other property, the Ran explains, because the Torah itself declared *bal yera'eh u'val yimatzei* — two distinct prohibitions against owning or possessing *chametz* on Passover. These prohibitions have the effect of removing the *chametz* from one's *reshut* in a meaningful sense: the only dimension of "ownership" one retains over *chametz* on Passover is precisely the dimension that makes one liable for violating those two *mitzvot*. The *Gemara* itself uses language suggesting that the Torah places the *chametz* into one's ownership for the purpose of creating the violation. What remains of ordinary ownership is therefore only a residual sliver of connection, and to dissolve even that sliver requires only a much weaker mechanism than would be needed to declare ordinary property *hefker*.

This is the counterintuitive point: because the Torah has rendered the *chametz* so nearly outside one's *reshut* already, the bar for completing the severance is lower than for real property. It is not that *bitul chametz* is a full *hefker*; rather, the ownership that needs to be dissolved is itself attenuated, and so an attenuated act suffices.

The question of how all this fits with Rabbi Yosi's position — who holds that *hefker* does not fully remove ownership until another person acquires the property — is itself a subject the *Rishonim* address primarily from the perspective of the *Rabbanan*. Tosafot might resolve the difficulty by noting that *bitul chametz* is a different and weaker kind of *hefker* than ordinary *hefker*, one appropriate to the already-diminished ownership the Torah leaves one with respect to *chametz*. This would align, in spirit if not in precise mechanism, with the Ran's approach.

### Hefker Witnesses

Returning to the question of how many people are required for *hefker* to take effect: Rabbi Shimon ben Hotzadak holds that three people are required even *mide'oraita*, while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds that one suffices *mide'oraita* and three are required only *miderabbanan* (so that one may acquire while two serve as witnesses). The *Mishna* in the previous *perek* apparently involved a case with only two people — the *mudar hana'ah* and the one being *mafkir* — and the *Ritva* resolves this by invoking *sha'at hadachak*: because the person had nothing to eat, it was a pressing situation, and even if one follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and requires three rabbinically, the rabbis relaxed their requirement in a case of genuine need.

Alternatively, the *Machaneh Ephraim* draws a distinction between land (*karka*) and movable property (*metaltelin*). Ownership of movable objects is, in a sense, constituted more immediately by physical possession — you hold it, you own it; you put it down, and someone else picks it up, and it is *hefker*. Land, by contrast, involves a much more formal and layered structure of ownership, requiring public establishment of rights — analogous to filing a deed with a municipal office in modern law. On this view, even according to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, the rabbinic requirement of three applies only to land; for movable property, even *miderabbanan* one person suffices.

### Solo Hefker

A further question is whether *hefker* declared entirely by oneself — *hefker beino levein atzmo*, with no one present at all — takes any effect. The *Rosh* holds that it does work, at least at some level, and the *Kesef Mishnah* notes this position. The Rambam, by contrast, appears to hold that *mide'oraita* at least one person must be present, and *miderabbanan* three are required. The logic behind the Rambam's position is pointed: if you declare something *hefker* with no one around, what have you accomplished? Everyone else will continue to regard the object as yours, and in practical terms it functions as if you still own it.

This observation loops back directly to the question of *bitul chametz*: if the entire act of *bitul* is performed privately, with no one present and no external manifestation, does it accomplish anything? The debate between Tosafot and the Rambam about the nature of *hefker* bears directly on this.

### Shulchan Aruch Ruling

Interestingly, the *Shulchan Aruch* does not rule uniformly. In *Orach Chayim*, the *Shulchan Aruch* rules in accordance with the *Rosh* and accepts *hefker beino levein atzmo* in the context of *shevitat behemto* — the prohibition against allowing one's animal to work on *Shabbat*. If a person has lent his animal to a non-Jew who intends to plow with it on *Shabbat*, the owner may declare the animal *hefker* privately on *Shabbat* morning and thereby remove it from his ownership, dissolving the prohibition. In *Choshen Mishpat*, however, where the *Shulchan Aruch* addresses property law more directly, it rules like the Rambam — requiring at least one person present even *mide'oraita*, and three *miderabbanan*. The *Shulchan Aruch* thus applies different standards depending on the context: a leniency for *shevitat behemto* that it does not extend to ordinary property transactions.

---

## Perek Hashutfim

### Breira Concept

We now turn to *amud bet* and the opening of *Perek Hashutfim*. The *perek* introduces one of the most far-reaching and technically demanding topics in all of *Shas*: *breira*. The concept of *breira* — *huvar hadavar lemafrea* — asks whether something that happens later can retroactively clarify the status of something that was ambiguous or unresolved at an earlier moment. Can a subsequent event cast its light backward in time and determine what was true at the outset?

This question recurs across six or seven *sugyos* throughout *Shas*, with additional *gemaras* that echo those discussions — touching on *Gittin*, *Eruvin*, and the present *masechta*, among others.

### Terumah Example

The first classic case involves separating *terumah* and *maaser* from a barrel of wine on *Shabbat*, when such separation is rabbinically prohibited. The person wishes to drink from the barrel but cannot perform the separation formally. So he declares: whatever remains in the bottom of the barrel at the end will be the *terumah* and *maaser*, designated accordingly, and the rest is *chullin* and permitted. He makes sure to leave behind the correct proportion.

The difficulty is apparent: throughout the drinking, the wine in the barrel is all mixed together. No wine has actually been separated; one has merely designated *wine that has not yet been identified* as the future *terumah*. When the dregs finally remain at the bottom, the claim is that it has now been *huvar hadavar lemafrea* — retroactively clarified — that those dregs were always the *terumah*. This is *breira*.

### Yesh/Ein Breira

The fundamental *machlokes* is between *yesh breira* — there is *breira*, we can employ this mechanism — and *ein breira* — we cannot. The *halacha* as established based on a principle derived from *Beitzah* is that *yesh breira* applies to rabbinic prohibitions and *ein breira* applies to biblical prohibitions. The *Gemara* in the barrel-of-wine case is therefore not straightforwardly problematic, since separating *terumah* and *maaser* on *Shabbat* is a rabbinic prohibition, and for rabbinic matters we say *yesh breira*. The difficulty comes when trying to reconcile individual *sugyos* with this settled rule, since not every application fits neatly.

### Eruvin Example

The second classic case comes from *eruvei techumin*. On *Shabbat* one may not walk beyond the *techum*, the boundary outside a city. A person who wishes to walk to a *shiur* on *Shabbat* afternoon does not know which *shul* the *rebbe* will be speaking in. He therefore sets up two *eruvin* — one in each direction — so that he can walk in either direction and still reach his house afterward. Then, when the announcement is made on Friday night specifying where the *rebbe* will appear, he retroactively designates which of the two *eruvin* should have taken effect.

In some ways this resembles a *tnai*, a conditional statement: I make this *eruv* on condition that my *rebbe* comes to this *shul*. But the *Gemara* notes that *tnai* and *shaliach* apply only within the same category of act, and that *tnai* may not fit naturally here. The reliance is therefore not on *tnai* but on *breira*: the later event — the announcement of the *rebbe*'s venue — retroactively clarifies which *eruv* was always the intended and operative one.

---

## Partners Mutual Neder

### Mutual Neder Case

The *mishna* states: *ha-shutafin she-nadru hana'ah zeh mi-zeh, asurin likanes le-chatzer* — two partners who have each taken a *neder* against receiving any *hana'ah* from the other are forbidden from entering their shared *chatzer*. The scenario is two people, call them Reuven and Shimon, who own adjacent apartments and share a courtyard — something like the hallway of a modern apartment building. Each has declared a *neder* of *hana'ah* against the other, meaning each has sworn not to receive any benefit from the other. They intensely dislike one another.

### Tanna Kamma Position

The *Tanna Kamma* holds that since the *chatzer* is jointly owned, neither party may enter it at all. The reasoning: every square inch of the courtyard is co-owned by both partners. If Reuven walks across the courtyard, he is deriving benefit from that portion of the property which belongs to Shimon — and vice versa. Since each has taken a *neder* against benefiting from the other, and since there is no identifiable spot in the courtyard that belongs exclusively to one of them rather than jointly to both, neither may enter.

### Rabbi Elazar View

Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov disagrees: *zeh nichnas le-toch shelo ve-zeh nichnas le-toch shelo* — each one may enter into his own portion of the *chatzer*. The *Gemara* understands this disagreement as reflecting the *machlokes* on *breira*. The *Tanna Kamma* holds *ein breira*: one cannot retroactively determine which portion of the jointly owned courtyard was "yours," and therefore the entire space remains problematic. Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov holds *yesh breira*: once you are walking on a particular patch, it becomes retroactively clarified that that patch is the portion you own, and you are therefore walking only on your own property.

### Partnership Models

This forces a deeper question: what does joint ownership of a property actually look like? There are several possible models. One model: the ownership is like alternating stripes — Reuven fully owns patch 1, Shimon fully owns patch 2, Reuven fully owns patch 3, and so on, in a kind of checkerboard or striped pattern, with full independent ownership of each distinct strip. A second model: ownership is a grey blur — every single molecule of the property is owned fractionally by both parties, with each holding a percentage interest in every infinitesimal piece. A third model: the property is divisible into two halves, each partner owning one half outright as a separate and distinct parcel.

The practical stakes of this question are significant. Even according to *ein breira*, if the partnership arrangement can be understood as the third model — each person owns one clearly defined half — then perhaps each could technically tiptoe through his own half without ever setting foot on the other's. But if the ownership is the grey-blur model, there is no square inch that is unambiguously one partner's alone, and the *Tanna Kamma*'s blanket prohibition follows naturally.

### Ran Explanations

The Ran's discussion of this *mishna* is extensive. He offers multiple explanations for Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov's position, and these explanations are important because, as one looks more carefully at the *mishna*, the invocation of *breira* seems puzzling. Normal *breira* involves a one-time retroactive clarification — at the end of the barrel, the dregs are designated as *terumah*. But in the case of the *chatzer*, the partners are not passing through once; they live there and use the courtyard continuously. If walking in one direction is retroactively clarified as being on Reuven's portion, but tomorrow Reuven walks the same path, and yesterday Shimon walked it, the "clarification" seems to shift back and forth. It is not obvious that *breira* in the ordinary sense can bear the weight of this case.

Rabbeinu Tam, whose view is cited within the Ran, makes an observation along these lines: this case may not really be about *breira* in the standard sense at all. The Ramban suggests it is a *weaker* form of *breira* than usual because the situation is so anomalous. The Ran, interestingly, takes the opposite position: he argues this is actually a *stronger* form of *breira* than the ordinary case. In a barrel of mixed wine, there is no prior agreement that could have specified which wine would be the *terumah*. Here, by contrast, there was an original partnership agreement between two real people with real claims to defined portions of a real property. The terms of the agreement, however imprecisely articulated, always contained the seeds of a division. Retroactively clarifying who owned which portion, then, is not conjuring a clarification from nothing — it is drawing out what was implicit in the original agreement. That is a stronger and more legally grounded use of *breira* than the wine barrel case.

### Not Real Hana'ah

The first explanation the Ran entertains for why Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov permits entry is that walking across a courtyard may not constitute real *hana'ah* at all. The *neder* forbade *hana'ah* from the other person's property. But is the act of putting one's feet on shared property truly a benefit within the meaning of the *neder*? Traversing a space to get from point A to point B, with no enjoyment of the amenities of the space as such, may simply fall below the threshold of *hana'ah* that the *neder* was intended to prohibit.

If that is the case, then the mechanism that allows entry is not *breira* at all, and the case does not really turn on *yesh breira* versus *ein breira*. Walking is categorically outside the *neder*'s scope. This does not mean *breira* is irrelevant to the case — the *Gemara* still invokes *breira* as a factor in Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov's position — but it would mean that *breira* provides an additional layer of reasoning rather than the primary one. There is tension here that the *Gemara* will need to work through in the coming days.

### Millstones/Ovens

The second clause of the *mishna* states: *u-shneihem assurim le-ha'amid reichayim ve-tannur u-legadel tarnagolim* — both partners are forbidden from placing a millstone (*reichayim*) or an oven (*tannur*) in the *chatzer*, or from raising chickens there.

The *reichayim* referred to is not the great circular millstone but the hand-operated flat stone grinder — a large base stone with a smaller stone moved back and forth across it to grind flour. The Torah itself singles out the upper millstone as something that cannot be taken as collateral (*mashkon*) for a loan, precisely because a household grinds fresh flour regularly and confiscating the millstone would deprive the family of bread.

The *tannur*, the oven, presents a parallel issue. In the world of the *mishna*, ovens were clay tandoor-style structures kept not inside the home but in the *chatzer*, functioning as a communal resource for all tenants of the courtyard. If one of the partners now constructs a *tannur* in the *chatzer*, this becomes a permanent fixture of the shared space — and a fixture that the other partner would ordinarily have the right to use as co-owner of the *chatzer*.

Two distinct rationales could explain the prohibition. First, permanent installation: by placing a *reichayim* or *tannur* in the *chatzer*, the partner is occupying shared space permanently — and that occupancy itself constitutes a use of the *chatzer* in a way that touches on the co-ownership and implicates the *neder*. Second, communal-use introduction: by introducing a communal-use object into the *chatzer*, the partner creates something that the other partner, as co-owner, would naturally be entitled to use — but now cannot, because of the *neder*. This creates a structural conflict between the *neder* and the terms of the ownership agreement.

The third prohibited act, *legadel tarnagolim* — raising chickens — raises questions addressed in both the *Yerushalmi* and the *Bavli* here. One issue is the principle of *zeh neheneh ve-zeh lo chaseir*: if the chickens roam the courtyard but their presence does not actually diminish anyone else's use of the space, perhaps there is no real *hana'ah* problem. Chickens are property of one partner, but they occupy shared space the way any movable object might. The *Yerushalmi*'s treatment of this question will need to be revisited in more detail. A further issue is that the chickens, unlike the millstone or oven, are not stationary — they range across the entire *chatzer*, and one cannot invoke *breira* to argue they were always only on the owner's portion of the space.

### Unidirectional Neder

The *mishna* then shifts to a case where the *neder* is unidirectional: *haya echad mehem mudar hana'ah michaveiro, lo yikanes lachatzer* — if one of the partners has been forbidden from receiving *hana'ah* from the other, he cannot enter the *chatzer*.

This case is, on reflection, more difficult than the mutual-*neder* case. Here the person forbidden from the *chatzer* is a co-owner of that property. He owns fifty percent of it. How can the other partner's *neder* strip him of access to his own property? The principle *ein adam oser davar she'eino shelo* — a person cannot forbid something that does not belong to him — would seem to protect the co-owner's right of access, since the *chatzer* is also his.

Yet the *Tanna Kamma* permits this situation to arise. The *Tanna Kamma*'s position in the first clause — that joint ownership means every fleck of the *chatzer* is co-owned — creates this paradox: because every inch is partially his, every inch is also partially the other partner's, and so the forbidden party can find no spot in the *chatzer* that is uncontaminated by the other's ownership.

### Ran Explanations

Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov responds with two points. First: *yachol lomar l'toch sheli ani nichnas, v'eini nichnas l'toch shelcha* — the forbidden party can say, "I am entering into my portion, not yours." Through the mechanism of *breira*, he can treat his movement through the *chatzer* as movement exclusively through his own portion of the property. Second — and this is the *mishna*'s resolution of the impasse in the *Tanna Kamma*'s model:

### Forcing Sale

*V'kofin et hanoder limkor chelko* — we compel the partner who made the *neder* to sell his portion. The *neder* he made has created an impossible situation for the other co-owner: the other co-owner cannot access his own property because the *neder* has rendered every portion of the shared space potentially problematic. Since the situation is untenable, *beit din* forces the *noder* to sell his share to a third party. Once he has done so, the ownership structure changes, the *neder* no longer attaches to that person's property, and the formerly forbidden party may now freely enter the *chatzer*.

One might ask: must the sale be to the person forbidden under the *neder*? No — that would itself constitute *hana'ah*, since the person would be acquiring property from one he is forbidden to benefit from. The sale is to a third party or to some other arrangement that simply removes the *noder*'s ownership from the picture.

A close structural parallel exists in *halacha*: if two partners jointly own a slave and one frees his half, the slave is left in a state of *chatzyo eved chatzyo ben chorin* — half slave, half free — unable to marry a slave woman (as a free person) and unable to marry a free woman (as a slave). The *halacha* there, as here, resolves the impasse by compelling the other master to free him as well, because leaving a person permanently in this legal limbo would *levatel lo mi'periyah v'reviyah* — deny him the ability to fulfill the commandment of procreation. The coercive resolution in our *mishna* follows the same logic: an unworkable *halachic* conflict demands a structural remedy.

### Outsider Neder

The next clause of the *mishna* takes the case outward: *ha'echad min hashuk mudar be'echad mehen hana'ah, lo yikanes lachatzer*. An outsider — someone who neither lives in nor owns any part of the *chatzer* — has taken a *neder* forbidding himself from receiving *hana'ah* from one of the two partners. He, too, cannot enter the *chatzer*.

The reasoning is consistent with the *Tanna Kamma*'s model: since the *chatzer* is jointly owned, and since one of the two owners is the person from whom the outsider is forbidden to benefit, every portion of the *chatzer* contains an ownership stake belonging to that person. There is no spot the outsider can stand on without implicating the *neder*.

Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov again offers a way out: *yachol lomar letoch shel chavercha ani nichnas ve'eini nichnas letoch shelcha* — the outsider can say he is entering into the other partner's portion, not the forbidden partner's. Whether a visitor or outsider may rely on this mechanism — essentially claiming to use only the "half" of the *chatzer* belonging to the person from whom he is *not* forbidden — raises its own questions about trespass and permissible use of jointly owned space.

### Rented Property

The *mishna* then introduces a case involving rental: *hamudar hana'ah mechaveiro, veyesh lo merchatz uveit habad mushcharim ba'ir* — a person who is *mudar hana'ah* from another, where that other person owns a bathhouse and an olive press which are rented out to the public in the city. *Im yesh lo bahen tefisat yad, assur* — if the owner retains a *tefisat yad* in those properties, it is forbidden for the *mudar* to use them.

### Tefisat Yad

The concept of *tefisat yad* — literally "a hand's grasp" or residual grip — is the central analytical tool for this clause and will be the primary topic of the following day's discussion. The question is: once a property has been rented out, does the owner retain any meaningful rights over it? Clearly the owner retains legal title — ownership and rental are distinct — but during the rental period the renter holds exclusive use rights. Does the owner's residual connection to the property during the rental period constitute enough of a *reshut* that the *neder* extends to prohibit use of that property?

The *mishna* offers two positions: if the owner has *tefisat yad* — some form of residual use-right or access during the rental period — then the *mudar* is forbidden from using the property (*assur*). If *ein lo bahen tefisat yad* — the owner has fully transferred operational control and retains no use-rights during the rental — then the *mudar* is permitted (*mutar*), because the property is effectively no longer within the owner's *reshut* in the relevant sense.

The exact nature of *tefisat yad* — what kinds of residual rights during a rental qualify — is left for the *Gemara* to elaborate and will be the subject of the next day's learning.

### House/Field Neder

The *mishna* then introduces a *konam*-formulation: *ha'omer lachaveiro konam leveitcha she'ani nichnas, uvesadecha she'ani loke'ach* — one who says to his fellow: "Your house is forbidden to me as a *konam* that I shall not enter it," or "Your field is forbidden to me as a *konam* that I shall not take from its produce."

### Death/Sale

*Met o shemacharo le'acher, assur* — if the owner dies, or if he sells the property to someone else, the prohibition remains in effect. This clause was already employed as a proof-text approximately two weeks earlier in the discussion of what can dissolve a *neder*: specifically, whether making a *neder* against a person's property lapses when that property is transferred.

The language here is deliberate. The clause that follows the present one uses the formulation *konam bayit ze she'ani nichnas* — "this house is forbidden to me" — rather than "your house." The distinction is precise: saying "your house" implies that the prohibition is tied to your ownership, and if you sell it, the prohibition should lapse. Saying "this house" declares the object itself — the *cheftza* — forbidden, independent of who owns it. Therefore, even after death or sale, the prohibition adheres to the object and the person remains forbidden from entering or taking from it. This *mishna* was a critical proof-text in that earlier *machlokes*.

---

## Modern Applications

### Corporate Ownership

The foregoing discussion of partnership, *hefker*, *breira*, and ownership raises a question with profound practical ramifications: how does *halacha* treat corporate ownership in the modern sense? Most publicly traded companies conduct business on *Shabbat*. Shareholders own fractional interests in those companies. Does *halachic* ownership attach to those fractional shares in a way that creates *Shabbat* liability or *chametz* problems on Passover?

The *Minchat Yitzchak* addresses questions along these lines. David Zvi Hoffman in his *Melamed LeHo'il* has a *teshuvah* dealing specifically with the question of corporate ownership of *chametz* on Passover, arising from the case of a beer brewery. The underlying analytical question is whether a corporation constitutes a distinct legal entity — in which case shareholders own interests in the corporation, not in its assets directly — or whether shareholders are simply partners in a human partnership arrangement and directly co-own all corporate assets. If corporations can have genuine *halachic* personhood distinct from their shareholders, many of the problems dissolve; if shareholders are merely partners in the classical *shutafim* model, the same questions about joint ownership, *hefker*, and *breira* that animate the *mishna* of *Perek Hashutfim* apply with full force to every publicly traded company.

These are genuinely open and important questions, and one that the classical sources, composed before the advent of corporate law, could not directly anticipate. The *poskim* of the last century and a half have had to work carefully with the conceptual tools the *Gemara* provides to address a commercial world the *Tannaim* and *Amoraim* could not have foreseen.

# Nedarim 46

## Shutfin Mishnah Review

### Intro & Overview

Today's shiur covers *Nedarim* 46, the beginning of *Perek HaShutfin*. We begin by reviewing the *mishnah* that was introduced at the end of the previous *daf* before proceeding into the *gemara's* analysis. The *perek* concerns partners — *shutfin* — who hold joint ownership of a *chatzer*, perhaps a shared courtyard between two adjoining buildings or a communal hallway in a larger structure, and who have taken *nedarim* affecting their ability to derive *hana'ah* from one another or from the jointly owned space.

### Both Partners Forbidden

The *mishnah* opens: *hashutfin shenadu hana'ah zeh mizeh, asurim lehikanes lachatzer* — if two business partners have each taken a *neder* against deriving benefit from the other, both are prohibited from entering the jointly owned *chatzer*. Since each of them has partial ownership of that space, and since neither can receive *hana'ah* from the other's portion, the entire *chatzer* becomes inaccessible to both.

*Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov* disagrees: *zeh nichnas letoch shelo vezeh nichnas letoch shelo* — each one may enter into his own part. This ruling rests on the principle of *yesh breira*, the concept of retroactive clarification of the terms of an agreement. Even though the *chatzer* was held in undifferentiated joint ownership, *Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov* holds that it can become clear after the fact which portion belongs to which partner. Wherever a person walks at any given moment, he may claim retroactively that this was the portion designated for his use — so long as the *neder* against the other's property is not violated. On this view, each partner can navigate the entire *chatzer* by invoking *breira* to designate his current location as his own.

In addition to the prohibition on entering the *chatzer*, the *mishnah* states that *ushneihem asurim leha'amid reichaim vetannur ulegadel tarnigolim* — both are forbidden to place a millstone or an oven in the *chatzer* or to raise chickens there. Objects like a *reichaim* or a *tannur* are heavy, stationary, and permanently occupy a fixed portion of the space. Chickens, by contrast, range freely and effectively commandeer the entire *chatzer*. Both types of use therefore implicate the other partner's property in a way that triggers the prohibition.

One might ask: what meaningful *hana'ah* is at stake from merely walking through a communal *chatzer*? The *Ran* addresses this point based on the *gemara* in *Bava Batra*. Partners in a jointly owned *chatzer* each hold a right to protest certain encroachments — most notably the permanent installation of structures like the *tannur* and *reichaim*. The *Ran* suggests that the right not to exercise that veto — that is, refraining from lodging a protest — itself constitutes a form of *hana'ah*. It is the forbearance of the other partner, his tacit consent to one's use of the common space, that carries halachic weight.

### One Partner Forbidden

The *mishnah* then addresses a case where only one of the two partners has a *neder*: *haya echad mehem mudar hana'ah mechaveiro, lo yikanes lachatzer* — if one of them is *mudar hana'ah* from the other, he may not enter the *chatzer*. There is an important ambiguity here about how to read this case. One reading is that *Reuven* forbade *Shimon* from deriving benefit from his (*Reuven's*) property — that is, *Reuven* imposed the *neder* on *Shimon*. A second reading is that *Reuven* himself took a *neder* not to derive benefit from *Shimon*. This distinction matters greatly in light of the principle *ein adam oser davar she'eino shelo* — a person cannot render forbidden something that does not belong to him. If *Reuven* attempts to forbid *Shimon* from the *chatzer* despite the fact that *Shimon* holds partial ownership in it, the application of that principle becomes complicated. Some *Rishonim* therefore prefer the reading that it is *Reuven* who has taken the *neder* upon himself. Others hold that even the first reading is valid, because partial joint ownership creates sufficient intermingling of interests to allow one partner to restrict the other's access.

*Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov* again permits: *yachol hu lomar lo letoch sheli ani nichnas ve'eini nichnas letoch shelcha* — he can always say, "I am entering my portion, not yours." The *mishnah* adds: *vekofin et hanoder limkor et chelko* — the *beit din* compels the *noder* to sell his share. This detail provides important support for reading the *mishnah* as the first case — where *Reuven* imposed the *neder* on *Shimon*. If the situation were merely that *Reuven* forbade himself from *Shimon's* property, it would be difficult to understand why *beit din* would force *Reuven* to divest his own holding. The compulsion to sell suggests that *Reuven* is the one who has created an unbearable situation for *Shimon*, and it is *Reuven's* portion that must be removed from the equation. Both a textual and a conceptual argument thus exist on either side of this interpretive dispute.

### Third Party Forbidden

The *mishnah* moves to a third scenario: *haya echad min hashuk mudar be'echad mehen hana'ah, harei zeh lo yikanes lachatzer* — a third party from outside the *chatzer*, from the *shuk*, has taken a *neder* not to derive *hana'ah* from one of the partners. He may not enter the *chatzer* because every corner of it is jointly owned by both partners, and he cannot enter any portion without encountering the one from whom he is *mudar*.

*Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov* permits: *letoch shel chaverecha ani nichnas ve'eini nichnas letoch shelcha* — whenever this third party enters, he can invoke the principle that he is entering the other partner's portion, not the forbidden one's. Here again, *Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov* applies the same logic of retroactive designation.

This case raises the question of how a third party from outside acquires any right of access to the *chatzer* to begin with — given *ein adam oser davar she'eino shelo*, one cannot forbid what isn't his, and conversely, one does not ordinarily have rights in another's property. The *Ran* cites the *Rashba* and the *Ra'ah* on this point. The *Rashba* argues that the case applies *davka* when the outsider is entering *letzorekh hashutafut* — specifically in connection with business he is transacting with one of the partners. It is only because of an existing relationship with one of the residents that the *chatzer* is relevant to him at all; without such a relationship, his entry would be mere trespass and the *neder* would have no operative subject matter. The *Ra'avad* disagrees and permits more broadly, though the *Ran* finds the *Ra'avad's* reasoning unconvincing.

### Bathhouse/Press Case

The fourth case in the *mishnah*: *hamudar hana'ah mechaveiro veyesh lo merchatz uveit habad muskarin ba'ir* — a person is *mudar hana'ah* from another, and that other person owns a bathhouse or an olive press that are leased out in the city. *Im yesh lo bahen tefisat yad, assur* — if the owner retains *tefisat yad* in them, it is forbidden. *Ein lo bahen tefisat yad, mutar* — if he does not, it is permitted.

Understanding who is *mudar* from whom requires careful reading. The *mishnah* states *hamudar hana'ah mechaveiro veyesh lo merchatz* — the one who owns the *merchatz* appears to be the person from whom the *mudar* is forbidden. To draw the picture: the owner of the *merchatz* — call him *Reuven* — has leased it to *Shimon*. A third party, *Levi*, is *mudar hana'ah* from *Reuven*. The question is whether *Levi* using the bathhouse constitutes receiving *hana'ah* from *Reuven*. This depends on the nature of *Reuven's* lease arrangement with *Shimon*. If *Reuven* leases on a percentage basis — receiving a share of the proceeds — then every additional customer, including *Levi*, directly increases *Reuven's* income. In that case *Levi* is forbidden from using the *merchatz* because his patronage benefits *Reuven*. If, however, *Shimon* pays *Reuven* a flat fee regardless of how many customers use the bathhouse, then *Levi's* use generates no *hana'ah* for *Reuven*, and *Levi* is permitted.

The concept of *tefisat yad* thus points to a residual ownership interest expressed through ongoing financial stake — a percentage of the proceeds that keeps *Reuven* invested in the day-to-day success of the enterprise. The *gemara* at 46b will develop this point further, so a fuller treatment is reserved for the discussion of *tefisat yad* below.

### House/Field Ownership

The *mishnah* concludes with two related formulations. *Ha'omer lachaveiro konam leveitecha she'ani nichnas* — if a person says "your house is *konam* that I should not enter it" — or *vesadcha she'ani loke'ach* — "your field that I will not buy" — then *met o shemecharah le'acher, mutar*: if the original owner dies or sells it to another, the *neder* is dissolved. This is because the formulation was *beitecha* or *sadcha* — **your** house, **your** field — making the prohibition contingent on the object's ownership by that particular person. Once ownership changes, the operative condition no longer obtains.

By contrast: *konam bayit zeh she'ani nichnas* — "this house that I should not enter" — or *sadeh zo she'ani loke'ach* — "this field that I will not acquire" — *met o shemecharo le'acher, assur*: even after the owner dies or sells, the prohibition remains. Here the *neder* was directed at the object itself, not at the ownership relationship. The *mudar* would need to appear before a *beit din* to have the *neder* dissolved; there is no other mechanism by which he could ever enter that field.

This distinction invites the further question of what happens if the house is demolished and rebuilt. If the formulation was *beitecha*, it is plausible that rebuilding on the same property would preserve the force of the *neder*, since it is still "your house" on that site — though a completely new structure might challenge even that reading. If the formulation was *bayit zeh*, the rebuilt structure is arguably not *zeh*, that same physical building, and the *neder* would not apply to it. This parallels the well-known philosophical puzzle about the Ship of Theseus — at what point does incremental replacement of components change the identity of an object?

The *Rambam* in *Hilchot Nedarim*, *Perek* 8, *Halacha* 2, addresses an analogous case: a person who vows not to marry a certain woman because her father is wicked, or not to enter a house because there is a dangerous dog inside. If the father repents or the dog dies — *metu o she'asu teshuva, harei zeh mutar* — the *neder* lapses, because the original prohibition was implicitly conditional on the continued existence of the harmful circumstance. It is as if the person stipulated at the outset: this *neder* applies only so long as the problem remains.

The *Mishneh Lamelech* notes a further question raised by *Rabbi Eliyahu ben Chaim* (the *Ranach*): if the father did *teshuva* and then returned to his former ways, does the *neder* re-activate? The *Ranach* holds that it does — likening it to the house being rebuilt. The *Mishneh Lamelech* disagrees, arguing that the lapse of the *neder* upon the first *teshuva* was complete, and the subsequent relapse is a new development that cannot retroactively restore the old prohibition. The underlying question — whether a person who sins again after *teshuva* has retroactively invalidated that *teshuva*, or whether each episode is treated as a fresh transgression by a genuinely renewed individual — is itself a profound topic that runs through the literature on *teshuva* and is discussed in other contexts across *Shas*.

---

## Bidirectional vs Unidire…

### Bidirectional Question

The *gemara* opens with a formal *ibaya*: *benadru pligi?* — is the dispute in the *mishnah* about a case where each partner took a *neder* upon himself not to derive benefit from the other (*nadru*, they vowed), or is it about a case of *hediru ze et ze* — where each one imposed a *neder* on the other, forbidding the other from his property?

These are importantly different situations. In the *nadru* case, *Reuven* says "I will not derive benefit from *Shimon*" and *Shimon* says "I will not derive benefit from *Reuven*." In the *hediru* case, *Reuven* says "*Shimon*, you are forbidden from deriving benefit from my portion," and *Shimon* says "*Reuven*, you are forbidden from deriving benefit from my portion." The question the *gemara* poses: *mi amrinan binadru hu depligi aval behediru ze et ze modu lei Rabbanan leRabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* — do we say that the dispute exists only in the *nadru* case, but in the *hediru ze et ze* case the *Rabbanan* concede to *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov*?

Why would the *Rabbanan* concede in the *hediru* case? *Deki anusim damu* — because in that case each partner is *anus*, acting under duress. *Reuven* did not choose to make himself forbidden from the *chatzer*; *Shimon* unilaterally imposed that restriction on him. You cannot tell a person he is barred from his own home because his neighbor — who shares ownership of the entryway — chose to forbid him. The *ones* situation is foundational: the entire arrangement of joint ownership is now being weaponized against someone who had no say in it. This gives the *Rabbanan* grounds, perhaps, to agree with *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* that the partners must at minimum retain access to their own portions.

Alternatively, *o dilma afilu behediru ze et ze pligi Rabbanan* — perhaps the *Rabbanan* dispute *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* even in the *hediru ze et ze* case, and the fact of *ones* provides no relief. This is the *gemara's* open question.

### Forced Sale as Proof

The *gemara* attempts to resolve this question from the *mishnah's* second case — the unidirectional *neder*. The language of the *mishnah* is *haya echad mehem mudar hana'ah mechaveiro* — one of them was *mudar hana'ah* from his partner. The *gemara* suggests: *tani nadur* — read it not as *mudar* (imposed upon him) but as *nadur* (he vowed himself). That is, perhaps the *mishnah's* second case involves a person who voluntarily took upon himself a *neder* not to benefit from his partner.

However, the *gemara* immediately notes: *hachi nami mistabra detani seifa vekofin et hanoder limkor chelko* — the stronger reading is supported by the end of that clause, which says *beit din* compels the *noder* to sell his portion. If it were a case where *Reuven* voluntarily forbade himself from *Shimon's* property, why would we compel *Reuven* to sell his own share? He made a personal choice about his own conduct; there is no obvious reason to force a divestiture. The compulsion to sell makes sense only if *Reuven* is the one who imposed the restriction on *Shimon* — because then *Reuven* has created an impossible situation for *Shimon*, and the *beit din* acts to remedy it by removing *Reuven's* share from the equation.

This reading then implies that the *mishnah's* second case is precisely the *hediru* scenario — and the *Rabbanan* there still disagree with *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* despite the *ones* dimension. That would suggest the *ones* argument does not persuade the *Rabbanan*.

### Ones Paradox

But this produces a difficulty. If the *mishnah's* second case is one of *ones* — if *Shimon* was involuntarily subjected to *Reuven's* restriction — then why does the *gemara* need to force *Reuven* to sell? The *gemara* asks: *amai kofin oto, ha menanas anis* — if he is *anus*, why are we compelling him to divest his property? The very premise of *ones* is that the situation is against his will and not of his choosing — so it seems unjust to then impose the additional burden of forced sale on him.

The answer implied by the *gemara* is that the *ones* argument cuts the other way: precisely because the situation is one of *ones*, precisely because the partnership agreement has been rendered unworkable against *Shimon's* will, the *beit din* must intervene. The only equitable resolution is to compel *Reuven* — who created this situation by imposing the *neder* — to sell his portion and thus restore *Shimon's* ability to function. It is not a punishment of the *mudar* but rather the logical remedy when the structure of the joint ownership has been undermined. With this the *gemara* transitions to the debate between *Rabba* and *Rav Yosef* about whether the physical size of the *chatzer* affects the analysis.

---

## Courtyard Size Debate

### Rabba: Small = Permitted

*Amar Zeiri: machloket sheyesh bah kedei chalukah* — Rabba's position (cited here in the name of *Zeiri*) is that the dispute between the *Rabbanan* and *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* applies specifically to a *chatzer* that is large enough to be subdivided — *yesh bah kedei chalukah*. In such a case, the *Rabbanan* hold that even though each partner theoretically has his own portion, the undivided joint ownership renders entry by either forbidden partner problematic. *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* disagrees and permits entry on the basis of *zeh nichnas letoch shelo vezeh nichnas letoch shelo*.

But in a *chatzer* that is too small to be meaningfully subdivided — *ein bah kedei chalukah* — *divrei hakol mutar*: everyone agrees, including the *Rabbanan*, that entry must be permitted. The reason is that in such a small space the "private" portions of the two partners would necessarily overlap; there is no way to allocate each of them a distinct private zone. Given this physical reality, the logic of *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* becomes irresistible: each partner's use of any part of the *chatzer* simply is use of his own portion, because the space cannot be divided otherwise. The *Rabbanan* therefore concede to *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* when the *chatzer* is too small to divide.

### Yosef: BK Analogy

*Rav Yosef* challenges *Rabba's* position with a pointed analogy: *harei beit haknesset dechimi she'ein bo kedei chalukah dami* — consider the case of a *beit knesset*. A *beit knesset* functions like a *chatzer* that cannot be divided: its communal purpose makes it inherently indivisible regardless of its physical size. No one can claim a personal section of the synagogue the way a householder might claim a corner of his courtyard.

The *gemara* in *Megillah* explores the corporate character of *beit knesset* ownership. For a large city, the *beit knesset* was built with the broader public — including travelers and visitors — in mind, and therefore its ownership is so diffuse that the local residents cannot even sell it. For a small town, the *beit knesset* belongs more exclusively to its residents, who function as its shareholders. In either case, the space cannot be portioned out to individuals.

Yet the *mishnah* later rules that when two residents of the same city take *nedarim* against one another, *shneihem asurim bidvar shel otah ha'ir* — both are forbidden from communal assets of that city, including the *beit knesset*. The *beit knesset* thus parallels the small *chatzer* (which *Rabba* says should be *mutar*), yet the *mishnah* treats it as *assur*. If *Rabba* were correct that a space which cannot be divided defaults to *mutar*, the *beit knesset* case should also be *mutar*. The fact that it is *assur* defeats *Rabba's* position.

### Yosef: Size Distinction

*Rav Yosef* therefore proposes the inverse of *Rabba's* framework: *machloket she'ein bah kedei chalukah, aval yesh bah kedei chalukah divrei hakol assur* — the dispute between *Rabbanan* and *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* applies to the *small* courtyard that cannot be divided. There, *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* maintains that each partner can navigate by invoking *zeh nichnas letoch shelo*, while the *Rabbanan* hold that even this small space is entirely *assur*. In the *large* courtyard that is capable of division, however, everyone agrees it is *assur* — even *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* concedes that when the space is large enough to be genuinely subdivided, one cannot plausibly claim that wherever one happens to walk is automatically one's own designated portion. The discreteness of potential private zones undermines the blanket *breira* argument.

This is a striking reversal. *Rabba* had argued that the small *chatzer* is the easy case where all agree it is *mutar*; *Rav Yosef* argues it is the hard case where the dispute lies. The large *chatzer*, rather than being the contested scenario, is actually the one where both authorities agree the entire space is *assur*. The *beit knesset* analogy supports *Rav Yosef*: the synagogue, as an inherently indivisible communal space, is precisely the paradigm case where the dispute plays out — and the *mishnah* rules it *assur*, consistent with the *Rabbanan's* position in the small-*chatzer* dispute.

### Halacha Ruling

*Amar Rav Huna: halacha keRabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* — Rav Huna rules that the *halacha* follows *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov*. *Vechein amar Rabbi Elazar: halacha keRabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* — Rabbi Elazar likewise rules accordingly. The operative principle of *zeh nichnas letoch shelo vezeh nichnas letoch shelo* is therefore accepted as *halacha*, and *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's* invocation of *yesh breira* in this context becomes one of the recognized sources for applying *breira* in practice.

---

## Breira & Ones Concepts

### How Breira Works

With the *halacha* established, it is worth clarifying precisely how *breira* functions in this context. The principle of *yesh breira* holds that an ambiguous designation can be retroactively clarified by subsequent events. Here, the joint ownership agreement for the *chatzer* never specified which spatial portions belonged to which partner. When *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* rules *zeh nichnas letoch shelo*, he means that wherever a partner is standing at any given moment, that location is retroactively designated as the portion that was his — it was always going to be his portion; the current act of use simply brings that latent designation into focus. The *breira* is not a new legal act but a clarification of something that was, in a sense, always implicit in the original partnership.

This variety of *breira* is arguably more tractable than other applications of the concept precisely because there was a pre-existing purchase agreement undergirding the entire arrangement. Unlike cases of *breira* involving *terumah* or *tithes*, where the status of a particular quantity was indeterminate from the outset, here the two partners genuinely own the *chatzer* together. The task is not creating a new status but identifying what the existing ownership already implied.

### Why Ones Justifies Breira

The *ones* dimension reinforces the availability of *breira* in this context. The entire structure of the joint partnership was premised on mutual benefit and shared use. When one partner imposes a *neder* that forbids the other from accessing any part of the *chatzer*, that act fundamentally undermines the operating premise of the arrangement — not by agreement but by unilateral imposition. The partner who finds himself suddenly barred is *anus*; the situation is not of his choosing. This involuntary character of the restriction is precisely what makes it necessary to invoke *breira*: the original partnership agreement is being coercively subverted, and the retroactive designation of each partner's portion is the mechanism by which the equity of that original arrangement can be at least partially preserved.

### Partnership Assumptions

The concept of fifty-percent joint ownership is less straightforward than it initially appears. When two partners own a *chatzer* together, what exactly does each hold? Does each own fifty percent of every square *amah* simultaneously — a kind of gray undifferentiated co-ownership throughout the space? Or does the arrangement carry an implicit understanding that certain zones are more naturally associated with one partner, particularly the area directly in front of each partner's dwelling? Does "fifty percent" mean fifty percent of the space at all times, or does it contemplate alternating exclusive use — each partner enjoying full access on designated days?

These questions recur throughout *Shas* in contexts involving jointly owned animals, jointly owned tools, and jointly owned slaves. The fundamental ambiguity of what shared ownership operationally means is precisely the gap that *breira* is invoked to fill. In the context of the *chatzer*, the practical implication is that whatever portion a partner is actually using at a given moment may be understood as the portion that was always notionally his — at least when the alternative would leave him with no viable access to property he co-owns.

---

## Tefisat Yad Analysis

### Rav Nachman: 25% Thresho…

The *gemara* now returns to the *tefisat yad* case from the *mishnah* and asks: *vekamah tefisat yad* — how large must the owner's percentage stake be in order to constitute *tefisat yad* and thereby render use of the bathhouse or press *assur* to the *mudar*?

*Amar Rav Nachman: lemechtza, leshlish, uleravia* — Rav Nachman rules that *tefisat yad* applies when the lessor retains a profit share of one-half, one-third, or one-quarter of the proceeds. *Aval babatzir lo* — but if the percentage falls below a quarter, it does not constitute *tefisat yad*. On this view, only profit-sharing arrangements at or above the twenty-five percent threshold preserve sufficient residual ownership interest to make the *mudar's* use of the facility a prohibited *hana'ah* for the lessor.

### Abaye: All Percentages C…

*Abaye* disagrees: *afilu babatzir assur* — even a percentage below one-quarter creates *tefisat yad* and renders use *assur*. Abaye's logic is straightforward: if the arrangement is percentage-based at all, then each additional customer who uses the bathhouse or press directly increases the lessor's income. Even at ten percent, one more person using the *merchatz* means the original owner earns ten percent more from that visit. The lessor thus has a real and direct financial stake in every individual use of the facility, and the *mudar's* patronage therefore constitutes *hana'ah* flowing to the *mudar-mimenu*. Abaye's position appears to be the logically stronger one — if Rav Nachman accepts that a quarter-share creates *tefisat yad*, it is difficult to see why a tenth-share would not, since the mechanism is identical.

### Percentage vs Fixed Rate

The *gemara* resolves the apparent tension by identifying the case in which *tefisat yad* definitively does not apply: *heichi dami dishru, hamikabel betaska* — the permitted case is where the lessee pays a fixed fee, a *taska*. A *taska* is a flat annual payment to the lessor, independent of how many customers use the facility or how much revenue the business generates. When the arrangement is structured as a *taska*, the number of people who use the *merchatz* has no effect whatsoever on the lessor's income; he has already received his fixed payment. The *mudar's* patronage therefore generates no *hana'ah* for him, and use is permitted.

*Tefisat yad* is thus defined precisely as a percentage-of-proceeds arrangement — any arrangement in which the lessor's income is tied to the ongoing use and revenue of the facility. A *taska* (fixed rate) excludes *tefisat yad* entirely. Both Rav Nachman and Abaye agree on this structural point; their dispute concerns only the minimum percentage threshold at which a profit-sharing arrangement triggers *tefisat yad*.

### Market Practice Standard

The *gemara* invokes the phrase *machtela shilash verivea* — a standard formulation well-known from elsewhere in *Shas* (it appears, for instance, in the context of *geneiva* in *Bava Kamma*) — to indicate that the relevant percentages are not technically precise cutoffs but rather reflect common market practice for this type of transaction in this locality. The fractions of half, third, and quarter are not arbitrary; they represent the standard terms at which these leasing arrangements were conventionally structured in the marketplace. *Tefisat yad* is therefore defined not by an abstract numerical floor but by reference to market norms: whatever share of proceeds is typical for this kind of arrangement in this time and place defines the threshold. Below those conventional market rates, the arrangement is so attenuated that it no longer reflects genuine ongoing ownership interest; at or above those rates, the lessor's stake in the enterprise remains real and operative.

---

---

# Nedarim 47

## Houses & Ownership

### Mishnah intro

The daf opens with a *mishnah* presenting two distinct formulations of a *neder* concerning a house. In the first case, a person says to his friend, *konam le-veitecha she-ani nichnas* — your house is forbidden to me by *konam*, that I will not enter it. Similarly, *sadecha she-ani lokei'ach* — your field is forbidden for me to acquire. The *mishnah* rules: *meis o she-macharo le-acher mutar* — if the owner dies or sells the house to a third party, the prohibition is lifted. The *lashon* of the *neder* was precisely *le-veitecha*, your house; since it is no longer his house once he dies or sells it, the *neder* no longer applies.

However, if the person instead says *konam bayit zeh she-ani nichnas* — this house is forbidden to me — then *meis o she-macharo le-acher asur*: even if the owner dies or sells it to someone else, it remains forbidden. This *mishnah* had already been quoted in the *gemara* last week; we now arrive at the *gemara*'s analysis of it.

### Ran's distinctions

The *Ran* on 47a notes a striking feature of these two formulations: each carries its own *chumrot* in different contexts. Our *mishnah* establishes that *bayit zeh* is stricter regarding change of ownership — since it is the object itself that was rendered *asur*, rather than the object in relation to its owner, a transfer of ownership does not dissolve the prohibition. However, the *Ran* observes that *beitecha chamur le-inyan nefilah* — the formulation "your house" is actually stricter when it comes to the case of the house collapsing and being rebuilt. Since the *neder* was framed in terms of the owner's house, a new house built in the same place and owned by the same person would still fall under the *neder*. By contrast, with *bayit zeh* — this specific house — *keivan de-nafal azla*: once it falls, it is gone. The prohibition attached to that particular structure, and once that structure no longer exists, the *neder* dissipates.

### Shivrei keilim

This question of how much the rebuilding or reconstitution of an object preserves continuity with the original connects to a parallel in the laws of *tumah*. When vessels that are *tamei* break, *shivrei keilim* — broken vessels — ordinarily become *tahor*. However, the Rabbis instituted for certain types of vessels, particularly metal ones, that if you reconstitute the broken vessel — by soldering or forging the pieces back together — the *tumah yeshanah*, the old *tumah*, is reinstated in the newly remade vessel. The concern was that people would deliberately break a *tamei* metal vessel, render it *tahor*, and then immediately smelt it back together, avoiding the proper processes of purification — either immersion in a *mikveh* or, in cases of *tumat meis*, sprinkling with the ashes of the *Parah Adumah*. The institution of *tumah yeshanah* thus reflects a question parallel to the one in our *mishnah*: when you remake something, to what degree is it a continuation of the original object?

### Sukkah parallel

A further parallel emerges from a *gemara* in Sukkah 27a, in connection with the position of *Rabbi Eliezer*. *Rabbi Eliezer* holds that the *sukkah* one uses on *Sukkot* must be *re'uyah lekol shivah* — fit for use throughout all seven days. This creates a difficulty: what happens if the *sukkah* collapses during *Sukkot* due to circumstances beyond one's control — an *onus* — and is then rebuilt? The *gemara* raises the objection *hai achriti hi ve-einah le-shivah*: the rebuilt *sukkah* is an entirely new *sukkah* and was not fit for all seven days from the outset. The *gemara* resolves that even according to *Rabbi Eliezer* it would still be valid, and *Tosfos* there suggests that the dispensation may require rebuilding with the same materials. Using the same wood might render the rebuilt structure sufficiently continuous with the original *sukkah* — analogous to the question here of whether rebuilding a house on the same plot with the same materials constitutes the same house for purposes of the *neder*.

---

## Neder & possession

### Avimi's question

The *gemara* now poses a question attributed to *Avimi*. The case under discussion is *konam labayit zeh she-atah nichnas* — this house is forbidden for you to enter. The *gemara* notes that this must be referring to a house currently belonging to the person making the *neder*, because *ein adam oser davar she-eino shelo* — a person cannot render someone else's property forbidden to a third party. One can affect one's own status regarding one's own property, one's own status regarding another's property, or another person's status regarding one's own property, but one cannot alter another person's relationship to that person's own property. Therefore *konam labayit zeh* must mean: my house, which I am forbidding you to enter.

### Core question

The *gemara* then asks: *meis o she-mecharo le-acher mahu* — what is the law if that person, the owner who made the *neder*, subsequently dies or sells the property to someone else? The underlying question is formulated as: *adam oser davar she-birshuto lichshe-yeitzei me-reshuto o lo* — can a person forbid something that is currently in his possession even after it leaves his possession? The owner had legal control over the property at the moment of the *neder* and could thereby create the prohibition. But once the property changes hands — through death or sale — does the prohibition continue? Did the *neder* alter the intrinsic character of the house, or was the prohibition contingent on the ongoing ownership relationship, such that it dissipates once the connection is severed?

### Rava's proof

*Rava* offers a proof from a *sugya* in *Bava Kamma*. The case is: *ha-omer livno konam she-atah neheneh li* — a father says to his son that the son is forbidden from deriving benefit from him. If the father subsequently dies, *yirashenu* — the son may inherit from him. The rationale is that at the moment of death the father is no longer a living person in the same sense, and so the inheritance, which passes at that moment, is no longer really "the father's property" in the operative sense. However, if the father added in his *lashon* the phrase *be-chayai u-ve-moti* — during my lifetime and after my death — then *bemet lo yirashenu*: the son cannot inherit, because the explicit language extended the prohibition beyond the father's lifetime. *Rava* draws the conclusion: *shema mina adam oser davar she-birshuto lichshe-yeitzei me-reshuto* — a person does indeed have the legal power to create a prohibition over property in his possession that will persist even after it leaves his possession.

### Implicit vs explicit

This proof raises a related point about the role of explicit versus implicit language in the *neder* formula. The proof from *Bava Kamma* works specifically because the father made explicit mention of *be-chayai u-ve-moti*, extending the prohibition beyond death. Without that explicit language, the son could inherit. This suggests that the legal power to forbid an object after it leaves one's possession exists in principle, but whether it is activated in any given case may depend on whether the *neder*'s *lashon* makes that intention sufficiently clear — or whether, as in *Avimi*'s original case, the formula used (*bayit zeh*) is itself enough to implicitly carry that force.

### Ran's problems

The *Ran*, however, raises difficulties with *Rava*'s proof. The first concerns the principle of *zechia b'issurei hana'ah* — whether one can acquire ownership of something that is *assur be-hana'ah*, forbidden to derive benefit from. The *Ran* and the *Rashba* disagree on this point. The *Ran* maintains that yes, one may own property even if it is *assur be-hana'ah* — one simply cannot derive benefit from it. Ownership and permissibility of benefit are distinct categories. The *Rashba* questions this. This becomes relevant in the *Bava Kamma* case because the question of whether the son can have any legal relationship with the inheritance turns on whether one can hold ownership of something forbidden to benefit from.

### Inheritance paradox

The second difficulty the *Ran* raises is even sharper. In the *sugya* in *Bava Kamma*, it emerges that although the son cannot inherit the property — *lo yirashenu* — he can apparently pass it on to his own children, to the grandchildren of the original owner. But if the son truly cannot inherit, how can he pass anything on? One cannot transfer what one does not own. The *Ran*'s position — that the son does own the property but simply cannot derive benefit from it — allows for this: he holds title, he simply cannot extract personal benefit. On that reading, he could convey the property to his children without himself benefiting from the transaction. The alternative reading, that he has no ownership at all, makes the mechanism difficult to explain. One might characterize the son's ability to direct the property elsewhere as a form of *tovat hana'ah* — a vestigial interest — but even that framing requires some analysis, since *tovat hana'ah* itself can constitute a form of benefit.

### Hekdesh vs nedarim

*Rav Chaim* clarifies an important conceptual distinction that underlies this entire discussion: the difference between *hekdesh* and *nedarim*. *Hekdesh*, according to *Rav Chaim*, creates an absolute status within the object itself. It is entirely *cheftza*-based — the sanctified status inheres in the object regardless of who owns it, where it is, or what anyone's relationship to it may be. *Nedarim*, by contrast — even though we generally describe *nedarim* as operating on the *cheftza* — are in fact always sensitive to the relationship between the object and the person who declared the *neder*. This is part of what *ein adam oser davar she-eino shelo* reflects: the *neder* depends on the *noder*'s connection to the object. The *sugyot* here are therefore exploring precisely what happens when that connection is conditioned on continued ownership. The distinction also explains why one cannot be *makdish* something that is not one's own — not because *hekdesh* is relational in the same way, but because one lacks the legal power to act on an object one does not control. Once one does have that power, *hekdesh* creates a permanent, unconditional status, while a *neder* may be contingent on an ongoing relationship.

---

## Fruits & proceeds

### Mishna case

A new *mishnah* is introduced from later in the tractate. The *mishnah* states: *konam peirot ha-eilu alai* — if a person declares these fruits forbidden to himself — whether phrased *al pi* or *le-fi* — then he is *assur be-chilufeihem u-ve-giduleihem*: forbidden not only from the fruits themselves but also from *chilufeihem*, the proceeds obtained by selling those fruits, and from *giduleihem*, the produce that grows from the seeds of those fruits if they are planted. This bears a structural resemblance to the world of *korbanos* and *hekdesh* — specifically *temura* — and also to *terumah*, where there is a concept of *gidulei terumah*: produce that grows from *terumah* fruit takes on *terumah* status as well, whether *mid'oraita* or *miderabanan*.

### Rami's question

*Rami Bar Chama* poses a question on this *mishnah*. The *mishnah* describes a case where the person forbids the fruits to himself. But what if a person says *konam peirot ha-eilu al ploni* — these fruits are forbidden to another person? Does the *halacha* of *chilufeihem* — the prohibition extending to the proceeds — still apply in that case? Can this additional *chumra* operate when the *neder* is directed at someone else?

### Rami's analogy

*Rami Bar Chama* builds his question on an analogy. He notes two parallel limitations on the power of the *noder*. First: just as a person can make someone else's property (*peirot chaveiro*) forbidden to himself, but *cannot* make someone else's property forbidden to that other person — *ein adam oser peirot chaveiro al chaveiro* — so too there may be an asymmetry regarding *chilufeihem*. Second: *chilufeihem* has a character of *davar shelo ba l'olam* — something that does not yet exist. At the moment the *neder* is declared, the proceeds have not yet been generated; the money has not yet been spent for that purpose and has no connection to the *issur*. The purchase and the consequent designation of that money as *chilufei issur* will only occur later. Just as a person can make a *davar shelo ba l'olam* forbidden to himself — which the *mishnah* explicitly permits — but may not have the same power to make it forbidden to someone else, so too with *chilufeihem*. The analogy thus runs: one's power over another person's property and one's power over a *davar shelo ba l'olam* are parallel limitations — both represent things outside the *noder*'s full control. For oneself, the *halacha* is lenient in both directions; for another person, both limitations may apply.

When it comes to making something *assur* to oneself, the *noder* has broad latitude — the principle is almost *ha-peh she-asar ha-peh she-hitir*, that one can create *issurim* for oneself. One can make someone else's property forbidden to oneself, and one can make a *davar shelo ba l'olam* forbidden to oneself. When making something *assur* to another person, however, one lacks the power to make that person's own property forbidden to him, and — by the same reasoning — one may equally lack the power to extend the prohibition to *chilufeihem*, which have no current connection to the *issur* and are in that sense analogous to a *davar shelo ba l'olam* under third-party ownership.

### Two possibilities

The *gemara* thus presents two possibilities. The first: *chilufeihem* should be treated like *peirot chaveiro* — as something subject to the asymmetry between *al atzmo* and *al chaveiro* — in which case the prohibition on *chilufeihem* would operate only when the person is making the fruits forbidden to himself, but not when he is making them forbidden to someone else. The second possibility: *o dilma mishum de-chilufin ke-gidulin dami* — perhaps *chilufin* are structurally comparable to *gidulin*. Just as the produce that grows from the forbidden fruit is forbidden universally — regardless of whether the original *neder* was *al atzmo* or *al chaveiro* — because *gidulin* and *chilufin* are both listed together in the same *mishnah* and both partake of the character of *davar shelo ba l'olam*, perhaps *la shena hu ve-la shena chaveiro*: no distinction should be drawn between the case of the person himself and the case of his friend.

---

## Wife & creditors

### Wife case

*Rav Acha Bar Minyumi* offers a proof toward resolving *Rami Bar Chama*'s question. The case is: *ha-omer le-ishto konam she-ani neheneh lach* — a husband says to his wife that he cannot derive benefit from her. The *mishnah* then states that *lovin u-va'alei chovot ba'im ve-nifra'im* — creditors can come and collect the debt from the husband. The *gemara* asks: how does this work?

### Ran's caveat

Before proceeding, the *Ran* notes that this *neder* must have been made before *nisu'in*, before the formal completion of the marriage. The reason is that after *nisu'in*, the husband already has obligations to his wife by virtue of the *ketubbah*, and a *neder* to the contrary would directly contradict those contractual obligations. If the *neder* was made before *nisu'in*, however, the husband could have created this prohibition.

### Creditor question

The *gemara* then asks: *mai ta'ama ba'alei chovot nifra'im* — on what basis can the creditors extract the debt from the husband, given that he took a *neder* not to benefit the wife? When the husband pays off his wife's debts, is that not benefiting her? And if so, would those funds not constitute *chilufei issur* — an exchange deriving from the forbidden *hana'ah*? The *gemara* asks: *lav mishum de-chilufin lav ke-gidulin dami* — doesn't this suggest that *chilufin* are not like *gidulin*? The argument is that if *chilufin* functioned like *gidulin* — extending the prohibition universally — then the husband's paying the wife's creditors would be *assur* to her just as the original *hana'ah* would be. The fact that it is permitted would then suggest that *chilufin* are not analogous to *gidulin* and do not extend the prohibition to the second party.

### First answer

*Rava* rejects this as a conclusive proof. He says: *dilma lechatchila hu de-lo ve-im avad avad* — perhaps the distinction is only *lechatchila* and *bedi'avad*. That is, *lechatchila* the husband should not pay the wife's creditors in such a way that she benefits, but *bedi'avad*, if he did so, it stands. The reason is that when the husband pays off the creditor, the *hana'ah* to the wife is already two steps removed — the wife borrowed money, the creditor comes, and the husband pays the creditor. It is not a direct transfer of benefit from husband to wife, but something more triangular. Because of that remove, it is not fully captured by the *neder* in the same way — it is only *lechatchila* to be avoided, but not *assur bedi'avad*. Thus, the fact that the creditors can collect does not prove that *chilufin* are categorically different from *gidulin*; it may simply reflect the *bedi'avad* leniency of a two-step removal.

### Rava's orlah proof

Since *Rav Acha Bar Minyumi*'s case does not constitute a decisive proof, *Rava* brings a different one: *ha-mekadesh be-orlah eina mekudeshet* — if a man attempts to betroth a woman using fruits of *orlah* as *kiddushin*, the betrothal does not take effect. *Orlah* — the fruit of a tree during its first three years — is *assur be-hana'ah*, and so although fruit generally has the value of *shaveh perutah* required for *kiddushin*, the woman cannot receive *hana'ah* from it. The analogy between *issurei hana'ah* of *orlah* and the *issurei hana'ah* created by *nedarim* makes this case instructive.

### Orlah explained

Getting married constitutes *hana'ah*, as the tractate *Kiddushin* discusses extensively — cases range from a woman declaring that her *hana'ah* from watching a man dance shall serve as *kiddushin* money, to the extreme case of *adam chashuv*, where the woman's *hana'ah* from the distinguished man's willingness to accept a gift from her is itself the basis of the betrothal. Given that accepting *kiddushin* is *hana'ah*, and *orlah* is *assur be-hana'ah*, even if the woman accepts the *orlah* fruit she receives no valid *shaveh perutah* and the *kiddushin* fails. However, *micharan ve-kidesh bi-dmeihem harei zo mekudeshet* — if he first sold the *orlah* — even though doing so was itself an illegal act — and then used the money received from that sale as *kiddushin*, the betrothal is valid.

### Two-step removal

This case functions as *Rava*'s actual proof. The sale of the *orlah* and the use of the proceeds as *kiddushin* represents the same two-step removal seen in the wife-and-creditors case: it is not a direct transfer of the *assur* item but an indirect one. And yet *Rava*'s proof also demonstrates that *lechatchila hu de-lo ve-im avad avad* — the same logic applies. Just as in the wife case, where the creditor payment is only *lechatchila* problematic but stands *bedi'avad*, so too here: selling the *orlah* was *lechatchila* forbidden, but the proceeds are valid for *kiddushin bedi'avad* because they are sufficiently removed from the *issur* itself. Both cases thus reflect the principle that a two-step removal from the original *issur* places the resulting benefit outside the full reach of the prohibition.

### Legality discussion

One might ask whether there is a meaningful distinction between an illegal act — such as selling *orlah*, which is *assur be-hana'ah* — and the legal status of the proceeds. The answer seems to be that regardless of the illegality of the sale, the money received is simply money: it has attained a new status as currency and is not itself subject to the *issur* of *orlah*. The object has changed its form so thoroughly that the proceeds are no longer characterized as *orlah*, even if the transaction that generated them was impermissible.

### Orlah burning

A further point emerges regarding *orlah*. Since *orlah* must be burned — the fruits are subject to destruction by fire — one might ask: what if a person gives a large quantity of *orlah* and the woman then burns all of it? Would the ashes, being worth a *perutah*, count for *kiddushin*? The answer is no, because items that are *nisrafim* — required to be burned — attain a new status through burning. The principle of *panim chadashos ba'u l'kan* — a new entity has arrived — applies: the ashes are no longer *orlah* and are indeed a new object. Therefore, giving *orlah* to a woman with the expectation that she will burn it and use the ashes as *kiddushin* would not work. The act of burning transforms the object into something new that is no longer connected to what the husband originally gave her, meaning it would not function as the consideration for *kiddushin*.

---

## Rambam & inheritance

### Rambam ruling

Returning to the question raised earlier concerning the son forbidden from deriving benefit from his father's estate, the *Rambam* in *Hilchos Nedarim*, Perek 5, *halacha* 7 states: *asar bno be-hana'ah* — a person renders his son forbidden from deriving benefit from him — and the *Rambam* introduces a case where it is stated that if the son is a *talmid chacham* a specified mechanism may operate to permit him access. Moving to *halacha* 8, the *Rambam* rules: *zeh ha-ben ha-asur be-yerushat aviv im natan yerushat aviv le-achav o le-vanav harei zeh mutar* — the son who is forbidden from inheriting from his father may give the inheritance to his brothers or to his own children, and this is permitted.

### Ra'avad objects

The *Ra'avad* raises a sharp objection. He asks: *u-mah tzarich litna'o* — why does the *Rambam* in *halacha* 7 need to introduce the condition regarding the *talmid chacham* at all? If *halacha* 8 already says the son can simply give the inheritance to his brothers or children, why is any special condition necessary? The next *halacha* seems to render the condition in the previous one superfluous.

### Ownership question

The underlying tension in the *Ra'avad*'s objection points to a deeper unresolved question: does the son actually own the property — and merely cannot derive benefit from it — or does he have no ownership at all? The *Ran*'s position, as noted above, is that the son can hold ownership even over something that is *assur be-hana'ah* to him.
