On that view, the son owns the inheritance and can convey it to his brothers or children, even though he cannot himself benefit from it. The *Ra'avad*'s objection implies that this is difficult to sustain: how can one give away something one does not own? And if one can give it away — as the *Rambam*'s *halacha* 8 says — then why the need for any special condition in *halacha* 7? The question of whether the son possesses genuine ownership that is merely encumbered by a prohibition on benefit, or whether the prohibition on benefit entails a more fundamental absence of ownership, remains unresolved in this discussion.

---

## Cherem & communal

### Cherem cases

The *mishnah* now introduces cases involving the formula of *cherem*. *Hareini alecha cherem* — I am to you *cherem*, meaning my property is entirely forbidden to you — *ha-mudar asur*: the one upon whom the prohibition falls is forbidden. *Harei at alai cherem* — you are to me *cherem* — *ha-noder asur*: now the one who declared the *neder* is restricted. *Hareini alecha ve-at alai* — I am to you and you are to me — *shneihem asurim*, both are forbidden in their mutual restrictions, *ve-shneihem mutarim be-davar shel Olei Bavel* — yet both are permitted regarding things of *Olei Bavel* — *she-hefkirum Olei Bavel le-chol Yisrael*: because the returnees from Babylonia designated that property as belonging to all of Israel, it is essentially *hefker* for the entire Jewish people, and since neither party has individual ownership rights over it, neither has the power to forbid it to the other.

### Olei bavel defined

What constitutes property of *Olei Bavel*? The *mishnah* lists: *Har HaBayit, ha-azarot, ve-ha-bor she-be-emtza ha-derech* — the Temple Mount, the outer courtyards, and the wells along the road. *Har HaBayit* is owned by the entire Jewish people; no individual has the power to forbid it to another, since neither possesses individual proprietary rights. *Ha-azarot* — the extensions of *Har HaBayit* — represent a slightly distinct category, a point worth examining further. The *bor she-be-emtza ha-derech* refers to watering stations along the pilgrim routes — rest stops, *olei ha-regel* would pass through them and need to water their animals, and these too were established as communal property for all of Israel.

One might ask: what *hana'ah* would one even derive from *Har HaBayit* that the *mishnah* is concerned about? Whether simply walking there constitutes *hana'ah*, or whether it refers to bringing a sacrifice or observing the Temple service, requires further investigation.

### City property

The *mishnah* continues: *ve-asurim be-davar shel otah ha'ir* — but both are forbidden regarding things belonging to the city. What counts as communal city property? The *mishnah* lists: *ha-rachavah* — the town square, *ha-merchatz* — the public bathhouse (specifically a publicly owned one, not a privately held bathhouse, a distinction that appears frequently in the literature), *beit ha-keneset* — the synagogue, *ha-teivah ve-ha-sfarim* — the ark and the books, meaning *Sifrei Torah* and also *Sifrei Nevi'im u-Ketuvim* (since *sfarim* in *mishnaic* language refers broadly to the sacred books). These items belong collectively to the residents of the city, who are in a sense shareholders in communal ownership of these facilities.

### Radical implication

The radical implication of the *mishnah*'s ruling is striking. If two people declare mutual *cherem* on each other, and communal city property — including the streets — belongs to both of them as joint owners, then each has effectively forbidden the other from using the shared city infrastructure. This would include the streets themselves. A person who is subject to the other's *cherem* could not leave his house without using the streets, which now fall under the prohibition. The *mishnah* is therefore describing a situation in which mutual *cherem* renders both parties effectively housebound with respect to all shared municipal facilities. This is admittedly an extreme outcome, but it follows directly from taking seriously the logic of communal ownership: precisely because both parties are genuine shareholders in the city's public property, each has the power to impose a *neder*-based restriction on the other's use of their common share.

### Rabbi Elazar consistency

This raises a question about consistency with an earlier position in the *masechta*. *Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov*, whose *breira*-based position was discussed in the opening *mishnah* of the *perek*, would argue that since each party also owns part of the shared property himself, he retains enough rights to pass through, and one person cannot fully forbid another's own portion to him. If that reasoning is correct, why does *Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov* not register disagreement with the *mishnah* here, where the same logic of shared ownership is at work? That is an open question on the *mishnah* that warrants further examination.

---

## Writing to Nasi

### Ktiva solution

The *mishnah* presents a practical solution to the problem of mutual *cherem* locking both parties out of communal city property: *ha-kotev chelko la-nasi* — a person writes over his share in municipal property to the *Nasi*, the governor. By executing a *ktiva*, a document ceding his share in these public facilities to a designated third party, the person removes himself from the category of joint owner. Once he no longer holds a share, his *cherem* declaration cannot reach the other party's use of property in which he himself has no stake. The *Nasi* is identified as an ideal recipient for this transfer precisely because he functions as a natural representative figure.

### Rabbi Yehuda view

*Rabbi Yehuda* rules: *echad ha-kotev la-nasi ve-echad ha-kotev la-hedyot* — whether writing to the *Nasi* or to a commoner, the mechanism works. However, *Rabbi Yehuda* draws a procedural distinction: *she-ha-kotev la-nasi ein tzarich lizkot* — when writing over one's share to the *Nasi*, no formal act of *zechiya*, of acquisition by the recipient, is required. But *la-hedyot tzarich lizkot* — when writing to an ordinary person, a *hedyot*, the transfer requires an actual act of acquisition on the recipient's part.

### Rabbis' response

The *Chachamim* disagree: *echad zeh ve-echad zeh tzrichim lizkot* — both the *Nasi* and the *hedyot* require an actual act of *zechiya* for the transfer to be valid. The *Chachamim* add: *lo dibru ba-nasi ela ba-hoveh* — the *mishnah* mentions the *Nasi* not because of any special legal status he holds but simply because it is the realistic and customary way of doing it. There is no substantive *halachic* distinction between writing to the *Nasi* and writing to any other person.

### Galil exemption

*Rabbi Yehuda* further rules that *ein anshei Galil tzrichim lichtov* — the residents of the *Galil* do not need to execute this writing at all. The reason: *she-kevar katvu avoteihem al yadeihem* — their ancestors already signed over the relevant property in a similar manner generations ago. Since the land arrangements in the *Galil* were already transferred through prior generations' agreements, the matter is already settled for the inhabitants of that region, and no further document is needed.

---

---

# Nedarim 49

## Lashon & Cooking Terms

### Perek Overview

The sixth *perek* of *Nedarim*, *Hanoder Min Hamvushal*, is organized around a central preoccupation: the role of *lashon* — word choice — in determining the scope of a *neder*. The *perek* demonstrates repeatedly that the precise term a person selects when taking a vow is not merely stylistic but legally determinative. Sometimes the difference lies between a noun and a verb, sometimes between a more general and a more specific term, and in each case the halakhic outcome differs accordingly.

### Mvushal Prohibition

The *mishna* opens: *Hanoder min hamvushal* — if a person takes a *neder* not to eat cooked food — *mutar bitzali uvshaluk*, he is permitted to eat roasted or stewed food. The prohibition is specific: *mvushal* sounds precisely like boiled, and therefore no other method of preparation is included. Those familiar with the *mishna* in *Pesachim* at the tenth *perek* will recognize these cooking terms. The *mishna* there notes that on all other nights one may eat *basar tzali, shaluk, umvushal* — roasted, stewed, or boiled meat — whereas on the night of the *Korban Pesach* only roasted meat is permitted. That context will return shortly in the *sugya*.

### Tavshil Term

The *mishna* then introduces a second case: *amar konam tavshil she-eini to'em* — if a person says a *konam* that he will not taste a *tavshil*, a dish. The word *tavshil*, while derived from the same root as *mvushal*, refers to a broader category — a prepared dish, a side dish — rather than specifically boiled food. The *mishna* rules that such a person is *asur b'maaseh kederah rach*, forbidden to eat a soft, liquidy pot dish. However, he is *mutar b'aveh*, permitted to eat a very thick preparation of the same kind, since that would not qualify as a *tavshil*. The *gemara* will explain that the word *tavshil* denotes specifically something eaten together with bread; a thick *maaseh kederah* is eaten on its own and therefore falls outside the *neder*'s scope. We also see that a person who says *konam tavshil she-eini to'em* is permitted *b'veitzat turmusa* — a type of prepared egg — and *b'idlat hamrimutza*, a variety of stewed squash or pumpkin.

### Maaseh Kederah

The *mishna* continues: *Hanoder mimaaseh kederah* — if a person takes a *neder* specifically against *maaseh kederah* — *ein oser ela b'maaseh ritachta*, he is forbidden only from something actually boiled in a pot. *Tavshil* is a broader category that includes *maaseh kederah* as a subcategory; *maaseh kederah* is the narrower term. The practical hierarchy becomes clear: the more general term encompasses the more specific, and the person's chosen *lashon* determines which tier of the hierarchy is activated.

### Method vs. Type

A further case: *amar konam hayored lekederah she-eini to'em*, if a person says he will not eat anything that "goes into a pot." Here the focus shifts from the type of dish to the method of preparation — *asur bechol hamitbashlim b'kederah*, he is forbidden from anything cooked in a pot. The distinction is between saying, for instance, that one will not eat stew (a category of food) versus saying one will not eat anything prepared in a pot (a method). These overlap substantially in vocabulary, which is precisely what the *mishna* is working through.

### Stam Nedarim Rule

The broader principle underlying this *perek* is *stam nedarim le'hachmir*: when a person takes a *neder* without specifying what it covers, we interpret it inclusively and stringently. Once a person does specify, however, we take their words seriously on their own terms. Importantly, the specification need not come immediately — even if someone later comes to ask whether the *neder* covers a particular food, the person's explanation at that point is credited. Both the rule of stringency in ambiguous vows and the weight given to the person's own stated intent reflect the fundamental principle that *nedarim* track what a person actually means by the words they say.

---

## Oshaya Dispute

### Oshaya Forbids

The *gemara* now brings a *baraita*: *Tanya Rabi Oshaya oser* — Rabbi Oshaya forbids what the *tana kamma* of the *mishna* permitted. Recall that the opening line of the *mishna* permitted roasted and stewed food to someone who took a *neder* against *mvushal*. Rabbi Oshaya disagrees and holds that roasted and stewed meat are included in the prohibition as well. He acknowledges, however, that *af al pi she-ein raya l'davar*, he does not have a definitive proof — only *zecher l'davar*, a mnemonic support or allusion, drawn from the thirty-fifth chapter of *Divrei HaYamim* (2 Chronicles).

### Pesach Korban

The verse cited is *vayivashlu et ha-Pesach ba-esh kamishpat* — they "cooked" the *Pesach* offering in fire according to its law. This cannot mean they boiled it, since the *mitzvah* of the *Korban Pesach* requires roasting. The negative commandment is explicit: *lo tochlu mimenu na u-vashel mevushal ba-mayim* — do not eat it raw or boiled in water — and from this we derive *ki im tzali esh*, it must be roasted on fire. Yet the verse in *Divrei HaYamim* uses the word *vayivashlu*. The inference Rabbi Oshaya draws is that the root *b-sh-l* can function as a general term for cooking, encompassing roasting as well as boiling. Therefore, a *neder* against *mvushal* might include roasted food as well, since the word *mevushal* in its broader register means simply "cooked."

### Rabi Akiva Eiger

A sharp question appears in the *Gilyon HaShas* of Rabbi Akiva Eiger. He notes that there is a verse from *Parshat Re'eh* in *Devarim* that uses similar language in connection with the *Korban Pesach* — *u-vishalta ve-achalta* — you shall "cook" and eat it. This verse is in the *Torah* itself and makes the same point as the verse from *Divrei HaYamim*. Rabbi Akiva Eiger asks: why did Rabbi Oshaya quote from *Divrei HaYamim* rather than from the *Torah* directly? This question has also attracted attention from those who approach *Tanach* with a source-critical eye, since the usage of *levashel* in *Devarim* in connection with the *Korban Pesach* — which elsewhere clearly requires roasting — has been flagged as an apparent contradiction. The resolution offered by later commentators is that *Devarim* there is addressing not only the *Korban Pesach* (which must be from *tzon*, sheep) but also the *Korban Chagigah* that accompanies it, which may include *bakar* (cattle) and is a *Korban Shelamim* that would be boiled. Alternatively, the word *levashel* in all these contexts simply functions as the general term for cooking, precisely the point Rabbi Oshaya is making.

### Torah vs. Colloquial

The *gemara* initially frames the dispute in terms of a fundamental question about *nedarim*: *leima b'ha kamiflagi* — perhaps their disagreement turns on whether *nedarim* follow *lashon Torah* or *lashon bnei adam*. On this reading, Rabbi Oshaya holds *halach achar lashon Torah* — the *halachic* meaning of a word is determined by how it is used in the *Torah* — and since the *Torah* uses *levashel* to encompass roasting, a *neder* against *mevushal* would include roasted food. The *tana kamma*, by contrast, holds *b'nedarim halach achar lashon bnei adam* — in *nedarim* we follow colloquial usage, and in ordinary speech *mevushal* means specifically boiled. This connects to an earlier debate in the *masechta* regarding *kinuyei nedarim* — whether words like *konam, konas*, and similar terms are artificial constructions invented by the rabbis so that people would not pronounce the sacred terms *neder* or *korban* lightly, or whether they are simply foreign loan words absorbed into ordinary speech. The deeper question is whether *nedarim* as a *halachic* category is created by the *Torah* and then applied to human behavior, or whether the *Torah* is recognizing and giving structure to something people already do naturally. If the latter, then what matters is what words mean to the person saying them.

### Everyone Agrees

The *gemara* then reverses course: *la, dekulei alma b'nedarim halach achar lashon bnei adam* — in fact, everyone agrees that *nedarim* follow colloquial usage. Even Rabbi Oshaya does not hold *lashon Torah*. The true explanation is *mar ki atra umar ki atra* — each authority was following the way the word *mevushal* was actually used in his own locale. In Rabbi Oshaya's region, *mevushal* functioned as a general term for cooking — much as the word is used in modern Hebrew today — and therefore a *neder* against *mevushal* would include roasted food. In the locale of the *tana kamma*, the word *mevushal* meant specifically boiled, and so only boiling was prohibited. Both are right; they simply live in different places with different linguistic conventions.

### Regional Variation

The *gemara* spells this out: *be'atra de-Tana dilan, letzali karu lei tzali umevushal karu lei mevushal* — in the place of the *tana* of our *mishna*, roasted was called roasted and cooked was called cooked, each term having a distinct referent. *Be'atra de-Rabbi Oshaya, afilu tzali karu mevushal* — in Rabbi Oshaya's locale, even roasted food was called *mevushal*, cooked. The citation from *Divrei HaYamim* is therefore *asmachta be'alma* — nothing more than an *asmachta*. And indeed, Rabbi Oshaya himself signaled as much when he said *af al pi she-ein raya l'davar, zecher l'davar* — he explicitly disclaimed having a genuine proof.

### Asmachta Purpose

This raises a broader question: what is the function of *asmachta* in rabbinic literature? We know that some *mitzvot* are *d'oraita* and learned from *pesukim*, and others are *d'rabbanan*, introduced by the rabbis themselves. Why, then, do the rabbis sometimes attach their own *halachot* to biblical verses by way of *asmachta*, as though providing a scriptural anchor for what is ultimately a rabbinic idea? A significant answer is offered by the *Ritva* in his commentary to *Masechet Rosh Hashanah*, where the question of *asmachta* comes up in connection with whether *zichronot, malchuyot, ve-shofarot* on *Rosh Hashanah* might be *d'oraita*. The *Ritva* explains that *asmachta* is not wordplay or a rhetorical game. Rather, it reflects the essential relationship between *Torah she-bi-khtav* and *Torah she-be-al peh*: God embedded in the words of the written *Torah* the capacity to give rise to the oral *Torah*. When the rabbis find a hook for a rabbinic concept in a biblical text, that *asmachta* demonstrates the *Torah she-bi-khtav*'s *pluripotency* — its inherent capacity to generate and support the *Torah she-be-al peh* as well.

---

## Tavshil Definition

### Bread Definition

The *mishna*'s second case — *konam tavshil she-eini to'em* — now receives direct attention from the *gemara*. The *gemara* asks: *ha mitavshil nadar*, didn't he take a *neder* against *tavshil* — why then does the ruling not simply prohibit all cooked foods? *Amar Abbaye: hai tanna kol midei de-mitachal b'rifta tavshil karu lei* — this *tanna* holds that the word *tavshil* denotes anything eaten together with bread. It does not mean any cooked food whatsoever; it means specifically a side dish consumed alongside bread.

### Hamotzi Implications

This definition has direct *halakhic* implications. The accepted rule is that the *brachah* on *pat* — on bread — is *poteret ha-tavshil*, it exempts the recitation of a separate *brachah* on the side dishes. If *tavshil* means specifically something eaten together with and alongside the bread — not merely anything served at a meal where bread is also present — then the scope of the *hamotzi* exemption may be narrower than commonly assumed. The word *kol midei de-mitachal b'rifta* suggests something you actually eat the bread with or on — something you dip your bread into, spread on your bread, or eat bite by bite along with the bread. Questions follow naturally: does the *hamotzi* exemption extend to fruit served as a salad course, to dessert, to different kinds of drinks? These are questions the *poskim* address at length. It is worth noting that Rav Aharon Lichtenstein *zecher tzadik livrachah* was reportedly careful enough about this issue that on one occasion, when a melon was served as a salad course, he placed a piece of it on a roll specifically to bring it within the category of something eaten together with bread.

### Tosefta View

The *gemara* now raises a contradiction from the *Tosefta*: *vehanoder min hatavshil asur bechol minei tavshil* — a person who takes a *neder* against *tavshil* is forbidden from every kind of *tavshil* — *veasur betzali uveshaluk umevushal*, he is forbidden from roasted, stewed, and boiled meat — *veasur behitriyot rakot*, and he is forbidden from soft gourds or squashes, *shehacholim ochlin bahen pitam*, which sick people eat with their bread. This *Tosefta* appears broadly inclusive, treating *tavshil* as a wide category that encompasses roasted meat and soft gourds alike — which sets up the discussion that follows.

---

## Gourds & Health

### Rabbi Yirmiyah Story

The *Tosefta*'s final line — that sick people eat soft gourds with their bread — raises an immediate question: is this actually medically sound advice? *Eini, veha Rabbi Yirmiyah chalash* — is it not so that when Rabbi Yirmiyah fell ill, *al legabeih hahu asya leasuyei*, a certain doctor came to treat him? *Chaza kara demanach beveiteih, shakil venafak* — the doctor saw a gourd lying in the house, was alarmed, and left. The doctor's reaction seems to contradict the *Tosefta*'s implication that gourds are appropriate food for the sick. One commentator — the *Rashash* — notes that this is a peculiar way to practice medicine: if a patient is eating something harmful, you ought to advise him rather than simply walk out. However that may be, the doctor's statement upon departing was: *amar malach hamavet it lei ledein beveiteih, veana eiul leasuyei yateih* — the angel of death is in this man's house, and I am supposed to heal him? The presence of the gourd in the house was so alarming to the physician that he regarded the healing effort as futile.

### Soft vs. Hard

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *la kashya, ha berachichei, ha beashunei* — there is no difficulty. One case refers to the soft, tender flesh of the gourd, and the other to the hard outer shell or rind. Certain gourds have a very hard exterior that would be difficult and probably harmful for a sick person to eat, while the soft interior flesh is easily digestible and appropriate. *Rava bar Ulla* offers a variant formulation: *ha bekara gufa, ha beigabei* — one refers to the gourd's own flesh and the other to its shell. A further nuance emerges as well: younger gourds tend to be softer throughout, while older ones become tougher and thicker. Either way, the conclusion is that squash or gourd can be healthy for sick people to eat in certain forms but not in others.

### Vegetable Pairings

*Deamar Rav Yehuda: lulavei dekara besilka, lulavei dechitna bechucha* — it is good to eat the outer parts of the gourd with beets, and the stalks or seeds of flax with *kutakh*. *Kutakh* is the Babylonian condiment that the sages of *Eretz Yisrael* regarded with some revulsion — made from bread crusts, possibly moldy, and sour milk. It received attention in *Pesachim* in connection with the question of whether the *chametz* used in its production is halakhically significant or edible enough to matter.

### Am Ha'aretz Warning

*Ve-davar ze asur le-omro bifnei am ha-aretz* — and this matter should not be said in front of an *am ha-aretz*. The warning is clear, but its rationale is debated.

### Warning Reasons

Three distinct explanations are offered. The *Ran* suggests that if an *am ha-aretz* hears that flax stalks or seeds are healthy to eat, he will pull up all the flax plants to consume them — damaging the flax crop. *Tosafot* offers a different explanation: an *am ha-aretz* will mock the *gemara* for including seemingly obscure and irrelevant medical advice about which varieties of squash are healthy, and this mockery is precisely the kind of objection heard even today from those who ask why the *gemara* contains such material. The *mefaresh* here advances a third interpretation. On his reading, *am ha-aretz* refers not to an uneducated person in the general sense but to the technically defined halakhic category enumerated in *Berachot* — people who deliberately avoid certain *mitzvot* such as *tefillin*, *tzitzit*, and regular *Torah* study. On this reading, the concern is that one should not share this kind of detailed practical guidance with someone who has chosen to be malicious in their religious conduct. Each of these three explanations reflects a different understanding of both the category of *am ha-aretz* and the nature of the concern.

---

## Cholim Identity

### Rava's Statement

*Rava amar: man kholin? Rabbanan* — Rava says: who are these "sick people" mentioned in the *Tosefta*? They are the rabbis, not physically ill people in the ordinary sense.

### Shemoneh Esrei Source

*Rava le-ta'ameih de-amar Rava: ke-man matzlinan ak-tzirei ve-amriei?* — This follows Rava's own stated position about for whom we pray when we pray for *ktzirei* and *mriei*, both of which denote types of sick people. Looking at the *mefaresh*, *matzlinan ak-tzirei* refers to the prayer for the physically ill — *rofeh kholei ammo Yisrael*, the *brachah* in *Shemoneh Esrei* that God should heal the sick. But *mriei*, also a term for the unwell, is associated in the *brachah* with *pleitat sofreichem* — the flourishing of their scholars. Since we have a *brachah* covering both the physically sick and Torah scholars, and since both groups are described using the language of illness, it follows that the rabbis themselves are called *cholim*. *Ke-man? Ke-Rabbi Yosi* — this follows the position of Rabbi Yosi. *Mi-de-amar ktzirei u-mriei, shema mina: ktzirei ktzirei mamash, mriei rabbanan* — from the fact that the prayer uses both *ktzirei* and *mriei*, we infer that *ktzirei* refers to the genuinely physically ill, while *mriei* refers to the rabbis.

### Torah Study Weakness

Why should rabbis be considered sick to begin with? There is a well-known *midrash*, found also in the *gemara* in *Shabbat*, connected to *Parshat Chukat*: *zot torat adam ki yamut be-ohel* — this is the *Torah* of a person who dies in a tent. The *gemara* reads this as teaching that *Torah* is acquired only by one who, metaphorically speaking, kills himself over it — pushing himself to the point of physical exhaustion, studying intensively for long hours, not eating adequately, not exercising, and spending his days and nights in the *beit midrash*. Such a person would naturally become weakened. One commentator connects this to the famous story of *Resh Lakish* and Rabbi Yochanan: *Resh Lakish* had been a physically powerful man, but once Rabbi Yochanan persuaded him to commit himself to *Torah* study, his physical strength left him — as though dedicating oneself entirely to the life of the *neshamah* necessarily diminishes the body. This dynamic has even been noted sociologically: in the *Yeshivish* world, the image of manliness and greatness is not the physically robust outdoor type but rather the pale, bespectacled scholar hunched over his seforim — someone who, by the world's standards, might appear weak, but who embodies the highest communal ideal.

---

## Thick Kederah

### Thick Exemption

The *mishna* had ruled that one who takes a *neder* against *tavshil* is *asur b'maaseh kederah rach* — forbidden from a thin, soft pot dish — but *mutar b'aveh*, permitted to eat a thick one. The reasoning, as we have established, is that *tavshil* means something eaten together with bread, and a thick *maaseh kederah* would ordinarily be eaten on its own rather than as an accompaniment to bread.

### Bread with Bread

The *gemara* then notes: *matni de-lo ke-Bavlai* — the *mishna* does not reflect Babylonian practice. *De-amar Rabbi Zeira: Bavlai tipshai, de-achli lachma be-lachma* — Rabbi Zeira said: the foolish Babylonians eat bread with bread. What they would do is take a thick porridge — a hot cereal made from wheat or barley meal — and spread it on bread, creating a preparation of carbs on carbs. The comparison to a potato knish is apt: a starchy filling inside a starchy dough. Rabbi Zeira, who was himself a Babylonian who had made *aliyah*, was in a position to observe and critique this practice with some authority. This is one of several moments in the *gemara* where the food cultures of *Eretz Yisrael* and *Bavel* are contrasted, sometimes with pointed humor — we have already seen the *Eretz Yisrael* rabbis' disdain for *kutakh*, and the Babylonian rabbis reciprocated in kind regarding certain Israeli dishes.

### Kederah on Bread

The consequence for *halakhah* is direct: if Babylonians eat even a thick *maaseh kederah* by spreading it on bread — using it as a side dish or condiment to bread — then in Babylonia, even the thick preparation qualifies as *tavshil* and would fall under the *neder*. The *mishna*'s ruling that the thick version is permitted does not apply in the Babylonian context, because the premise of the ruling — that thick *maaseh kederah* is not eaten with bread — is false in Babylonia.

---

## Babylonian Foods

### Grain Pairings

*Amar Rav Chisda* — Rav Chisda raised the question of *da'itsa*: *heichei ma'alei, demichla dechittei belachma dechittei, udesia'arei belachma desia'arei* — given that porridge is eaten on bread in Babylonia, which pairing is preferable? Should you eat wheat porridge on wheat bread and barley porridge on barley bread, *o dilma dechittei bedesia'arei udesia'arei bedechittei* — or should you cross them, eating wheat porridge on barley bread and barley porridge on wheat bread? It is worth noting that *Tosafot* there cites *Rabbeinu Chananel* to the effect that *sea'arei* in this context may refer not to barley but to lentils — which would give the porridge a protein component and make the "carbs on carbs" critique somewhat less damning.

### Rava's Method

*Rava achlei bechasissei* — Rava ate his porridge with *chasissei*, meaning he ate it with roasted or toasted grain rather than in the way others prepared it, dipping his bread into the porridge. The *gemara* in *Pesachim* explains this practice further.

### Fingers & Taste

*Rabba bar Rav Huna ashkeichei leRav Huna deka'achil da'itsa be'etzba'ateih* — Rabba bar Rav Huna found Rav Huna eating porridge with his fingers. Rabba bar Rav Huna expressed surprise: *amai ka'achil mar beyadeih?* Why is my master eating with his hands? Rav Huna replied: *hachi amar Rav: da'itsa be'etzba'ateih bassim* — Rav taught that porridge eaten with the fingers tastes better, because you feel the texture and engage more fully with the eating experience. *Vechol doken bitartein* — and even more so with two fingers — *vechol doken bitlat* — and even more so with three. These were the Amoraim of Babylonia, who did not have forks and for whom the choice was essentially between eating with the hands and eating with a stick, as we shall see momentarily.

### Travel Advice

*Amar lei Rav leChiaya breih, vehachen amar lei Rav Huna leRabba breih* — Rav told his son Chiaya, and Rav Huna similarly told his son Rabba: *mezamnin lach lemachal da'itsa, ad parsa* — if people invite you to eat porridge, you should travel as much as a whole *parsa* to join them. *Lemachal bisra detora, ad tlata parsa'ei* — if people invite you for steak, you should go even three *parsa'ot*. Sound advice for any season.

### Spitting Rule

A further teaching: *kol midam lo tiflot kammai rabbach* — do not spit out your food in front of your teacher — *levar mikara veda'itsa* — except for gourds and porridge. These two foods are compared to *ptila shel avar* — the lead wire used in executions by *sreifah*, where molten lead was poured down the throat. The image is of something extraordinarily heavy and oppressive sitting in one's gut, potentially very painful. Therefore, *va'afilu kamei Shavur Malka pelot* — even in front of a king, one is permitted to spit them out.

### Fingers vs. Stick

*Rabbi Yose v'Rabbi Shimon* — two of the great *tannaim* — are brought anonymously here, presumably because the dispute involves something somewhat uncivilized and the *gemara* preferred not to attribute the positions explicitly. *Chad achal daisa b'etzbaotei* — one ate porridge with his fingers — *v'chad achal b'hutza* — and one ate with a stick. The one eating with a stick challenged the one eating with his fingers: *ad matay ata ma'achileni tzo'atecha* — how long will you keep feeding me your filth? Without washing one's hands, eating with the fingers would contaminate the shared pot. The finger-eater replied: *ad matay ata ma'achileni roka'acha* — and how long will you keep feeding me your saliva? The stick, having been in one's mouth, goes back into the communal dish on each bite. Each man's method of eating was, from the other's perspective, a source of contamination.

---

## Rabbi Yehuda Tales

### Figs Story

*Rabbi Yehuda v'Rabbi Shimon ayitu l'kameihu belusfin* — Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon were brought *belusfin*, which the *mefaresh* identifies as a kind of very overcooked or stewed figs. *Rabbi Yehuda achal, Rabbi Shimon lo achal* — Rabbi Yehuda ate them; Rabbi Shimon did not. Rabbi Yehuda asked why. Rabbi Shimon explained: *elu ein yotzim mibnei me'ayim kol ikkar* — these will never fully pass through the digestive system; they are too dense and will leave one feeling blocked up. Rabbi Yehuda responded: *kol shekein shenishmoch aleihen l'machar* — all the more reason to eat them now, so that I can rely on them to keep me full until tomorrow. Rabbi Yehuda's intention was not mere gluttony but economy: eating a satiating food now to carry him through the following morning.

### Rutabagas Story

*Rabbi Yehuda hava yativ kamei d'Rabbi Tarfon* — Rabbi Yehuda was once sitting before Rabbi Tarfon when Rabbi Tarfon remarked: *hayom panecha tzehubim* — today your face is shining, or perhaps very yellow or ruddy. Rabbi Yehuda explained: *emesh yatz'u avadecha lasadeh v'hevi'u lanu tardin v'achalnum b'lo melach* — last evening we went out to the field and they brought us *tardin* — large beets or rutabagas — and we ate them without salt. *V'im achalnum b'melach, kol shekein shehayu paneinu tzehubim* — had we eaten them with salt, our faces would have been glowing even more. The commentators observe that this was a deliberate act of modesty on Rabbi Yehuda's part: his face shone because of his Torah greatness, as we will see momentarily, but he did not wish to embarrass Rabbi Tarfon by suggesting his student outshone him. He attributed the radiance to the rutabagas instead.

### Wine Limits

*Amra hi matronita le-Rabbi Yehuda* — a Roman matron said to Rabbi Yehuda, addressing him with what amounts to a pun — *mora v'ravi*, which plays on *mori v'rabbi*, "my teacher." She accused him: are you teaching Torah while drunk? His face was so bright and flushed that she suspected him of inebriation. *Amar lah: heimanuta b'yada d'hahi itata* — he invoked a kind of oath and replied: have I ever tasted wine except for *kiddush* and *havdalah* and *arba kasse de-Pischa* — the four cups on *Pesach*? Rabbi Yehuda's self-description as a near-teetotaler was not just personal modesty. He added that from *Pesach* to *Shavuot* his head aches — *min ha-Pesach ve-ad ha-Atzeret* — from having drunk the four cups. This passage is frequently cited in discussions of whether the wine used for *kiddush* and *havdalah* must be genuinely alcoholic. The position attributed to Rav Moshe Feinstein in the *Igrot Moshe* is that wine with some measure of alcohol is required, based in part on this very story: Rabbi Yehuda, who avoided wine at great personal cost, did not substitute grape juice even when he might easily have done so. This implies that grape juice does not suffice for these *mitzvot*.

### Tzeduki Insult

*Amar lei hahu Tzeduki le-Rabbi Yehuda* — a *Tzeduki* said to Rabbi Yehuda: *panecha domim o ke-malvei ribit o ke-megadlei chazirim* — your face looks like either those who lend money at interest or those who raise pigs. The *mefaresh* suggests the *malvei ribit* comparison is because such people grow wealthy and therefore appear perpetually happy and flush. The image of Moses descending from Sinai with his face radiant is a relevant parallel, as is the verse from *Kohelet* that will appear momentarily. The *Tzeduki* seemed to be insinuating that Rabbi Yehuda's bright face reflected the contentment of someone engaged in prohibited activity.

### Latrine Visits

Rabbi Yehuda replied: *bi-yehudai tarveihu asiran* — for Jews, both of those activities are forbidden. He then offered the true explanation for his shining face: *ella esrin ve-arba'ah batei ha-kisse it li min beita le-bei midrasha* — there are twenty-four latrines on the way from my house to the *Beit Midrash*, *de-khol sha'ah ve-sha'ah ani nikhnas le-khol echad ve-echad* — and every opportunity I have, as I walk to the *Beit Midrash* each day, I make use of every one of them. That is the source of his radiant wellbeing. The *Tzeduki*'s challenge had also implicitly accused him of imitating the shining face that comes from ill-gotten ease; Rabbi Yehuda's answer — that *chokhmat adam ta'ir panav*, a person's wisdom brightens his face (*Kohelet*) — was the reply to the matron's accusation of drunkenness earlier. To the *Tzeduki* he gave a more earthly and pointed answer: proper bodily function, maintained rigorously on the walk to Torah study each day.

---

## Kiddush Wine

### Kiddush Status

The discussion of Rabbi Yehuda's wine consumption naturally raises the question of the *halachic* status of wine for *kiddush*. The *gemara* in *Pesachim* cites the *baraita*: *zakhor et yom ha-Shabbat le-kaddesho — zakhrehu al ha-yayin* — remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it; remember it over wine. This sounds like a *d'oraita* obligation derived directly from the verse of *zakhor*. Nevertheless, the consensus among the *Rishonim*, drawing on other *gemarot* as well, is that the requirement for wine at *kiddush* is only *d'rabbanan*. *Tosafot* in *Pesachim* suggests a middle position: holding a cup of wine during *kiddush* may be *d'oraita*, but actually drinking it is only *d'rabbanan*. The *mefaresh* in *Masechet Nazir* — who is not actually *Rashi* but a later author writing in that tradition — takes the more expansive view that having wine for *kiddush* is a *mitzvah d'oraita* in the full sense. The *daf* concludes here, at the bottom of 49b, and we will resume from that point at the next session.

---

---

# Nedarim 50

## Rabbi Yehuda's Radiance

### Three audiences respond

The daf opens by returning briefly to the series of three vignettes concerning Rabbi Yehuda's luminous complexion — described by the Aramaic word *tzahov*, which might suggest a yellowish tinge but almost certainly connotes a radiant, glowing countenance. Three different interlocutors posed the same question to him: his fellow *rabbanan*, a wealthy woman, and a *Tzeduki* (Sadducee). Each received a response calibrated to the questioner — more expansive and measured for some, brisk and dismissive for the heretic.

### Labor brings honor

From this point the Gemara moves forward. We are told that Rabbi Yehuda, when he would go to the *beit midrash*, would carry a barrel or large jug on his shoulders — *shakil gufa al katfeih* — and he would declare, *gedola melacha she-mechabedet et be'aleha*: labor is a great thing because it brings honor to those who perform it. At first glance this seems puzzling. He is, after all, simply transporting something to sit on, a kind of personal shtender. It is not immediately obvious why this constitutes a significant act of *melacha* of the sort that confers great *kavod*. Nevertheless, this was Rabbi Yehuda's lived demonstration of the principle that honorable labor dignifies the worker, however modest the task.

### Shared cloak blessing

The narrative continues with Rabbi Yehuda's wife, who went and acquired wool, *avda glima*, and fashioned a cloak. The arrangement was that when she would go out to the marketplace she wore it, and when Rabbi Yehuda would go to pray he wore it — *michasya umatzli*. On its surface, this passage conveys the remarkable austerity in which Rabbi Yehuda and his wife lived: a single cloak shared between husband and wife. When Rabbi Yehuda would wrap himself in it, he would recite a *bracha*: *Baruch she'atani me'il* — Blessed is God who has wrapped me in this cloak. Two points deserve attention here. First, this is a different *nusach ha-bracha* from the standard blessing recited upon wearing new garments. Second, the Rosh in Berachot cites this passage as proof that the threshold for reciting *Shehecheyanu* upon a new garment — or *Malbish Arumim* — is fundamentally subjective, determined by what brings genuine enjoyment and significance to the individual. For Rabbi Yehuda, who lived in poverty, this simple homespun cloak brought him real joy, and that was sufficient grounds for the blessing, regardless of how others might appraise its value.

### Unisex garment law

The shared cloak also raises a pointed *halachic* question concerning *beged ish u-veged isha* — the prohibition against men wearing women's garments and vice versa. How could Rabbi Yehuda and his wife both wear the same cloak? The implication appears to be that a garment made without specific intention for either a man or a woman — a genuinely unisex article — is permitted for both to wear, and this episode serves as evidence for that position.

## Yehuda's treasure

### Fast day refusal

The Gemara then introduces another story. *Zimna chada gazar Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel ta'anita* — one time Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who served as *nasi* of the *Sanhedrin*, decreed a fast day, presumably on account of drought, as was standard practice familiar from Masechet Ta'anit. Rabbi Yehuda did not appear at the gathering. We know from Ta'anit that the public fast involved bringing the *Sefer Torah* into the town square and conducting communal prayer there, partly to accommodate greater numbers and partly to lend the occasion the character of public supplication. Rabbi Yehuda's absence was noted.

### Refuses garment gift

The explanation offered was *leit lei kisuya* — he has no garment, no *ksut*, with which to appear. It is worth pausing on the terminology: *ksut* here refers to the outer wrap or cloak, as opposed to *beged*, which denotes more of an inner tunic. The distinction has relevance beyond this narrative — there are those who argue that the obligation of *tzitzit* as formulated in the *pasuk* in Devarim (*al arba kanfot ksutecha asher tichaseh bah*) attaches specifically to the outer wrap rather than to a smaller undergarment, which bears on the question of whether a *tallit katan* fulfills the *mitzvah* of *tzitzit* in the same sense as a *tallit gadol*, though this remains a matter of debate.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, himself of the wealthy *nasi* family — a family whose considerable resources, and whose occasional insensitivity to the poverty of *talmidei chachamim*, are documented elsewhere in *Shas*, most notably in the well-known episodes in Berachot where Rabban Gamliel embarrassed Rabbi Yehoshua until the extent of that sage's poverty became apparent — sent Rabbi Yehuda a new shirt. Rabbi Yehuda refused it. *Shadar lei glima velo kibel.* The refusal appears to reflect a kind of pride, or perhaps a principled self-sufficiency: his wife's cloak, however modest, was enough for him. He had said a *bracha* over it.

### Gold discovery

The story reaches its surprising conclusion at the top of daf 50a. Rabbi Yehuda lifted the mat he was sitting on and said to the messenger: *chazi mai ika* — look and see what is here. The *mefaresh* explains: beneath the mat, a miracle had occurred, and the entire space was filled with gold. *Na'asah li nes ve-nitmale kol oto makom zehuvim.* He was not, in other words, impoverished in any material sense. He simply chose not to avail himself of wealth. As the Gemara puts it: *lo nicha lei l'ithenuyei be-hadein alma* — it was not agreeable to him to derive *hana'ah* from this world. The refusal of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's shirt thus was not born of helplessness but of deliberate spiritual detachment from material comfort.

## Rabbi Akiva marriage

### Father's vow

The Gemara now transitions to the famous story of Rabbi Akiva's marriage — a story that appears as well in Ketubot 62b, and it would be worth comparing the two versions for their differences. *Rabbi Akiva ikadsha lei barteh de-Kalba Savua* — Rabbi Akiva married the daughter of Kalba Savua. The name *Kalba Savua* means "the satisfied dog," which is an unusual epithet. Some *mefarshim* suggest that people would come to him as hungry as a dog and leave fully satisfied — *savua* — because he was extraordinarily generous and wealthy. Whether this is the actual etymology or a folk explanation, it situates Kalba Savua as a man of great means.

When Kalba Savua learned of the marriage, he was furious. Rabbi Akiva at this point was poor, illiterate, and a simple shepherd — hardly what he envisioned for his daughter. He therefore made a *neder hana'ah* from all his property: Rabbi Akiva and perhaps his daughter as well would derive no *hana'ah* from his estate. The story thus arrives in Masechet Nedarim organically, though it is in substance an *agadata* about the *tanna'im*. The theme of *hana'ah* also resonates with the preceding episode: Rabbi Yehuda chose not to take *hana'ah* from this world; here, Kalba Savua weaponizes the *neder* to cut off *hana'ah* as a punitive measure.

### Straw house poverty

The young couple went to live together in a *bei tivna* — a straw house — sleeping on straw, *hava ganu be-itivna*. There, Rabbi Akiva would remove straw from her hair. There is a dispute among the *rishonim* here: the *mefaresh* understands that she would remove straw from his hair, but the Ran reads it as Rabbi Akiva removing the straw from his wife's hair — a small act of tenderness and care even within extreme deprivation, the two of them still tending to one another. Rabbi Akiva said to her: *ei hava lei ramina lach Yerushalayim de-dahava* — if I had the means, I would give you a *Yerushalayim shel zahav*, the golden Jerusalem circlet mentioned in the Mishnah in Shabbat — a tiara of gold, possibly engraved with the forms of Jerusalem's buildings or the Temple, a cherished piece of women's jewelry of that era. That this is the aspiration Rabbi Akiva articulates, even from within a straw house, speaks to his devotion to his wife.

### Elijah straw story

Then Elijah appears — as he must in any properly told *aggadic* tale — disguised as an ordinary person, knocking at the door and asking for a small amount of straw, because his wife had just given birth and they had nothing. Rabbi Akiva turns to his wife and says: *chazi gavra de-afilu tivna la it lei* — look, here is a person who does not even have straw. We, who have so little, still have something that another person lacks entirely. This moment of generosity and perspective from within utter poverty seems to be the catalyst. His wife immediately says to him: *zil havi be-rav* — go, study Torah.

What connects the Elijah episode to her instruction to go learn? Perhaps she recognized in that instinctive act of generosity — in his immediate concern for someone even poorer than himself — a greatness of character that demanded cultivation through Torah. It is also worth noting that in other sources, most prominently in *Avot de-Rabbi Natan*, the account of Rabbi Akiva's awakening to Torah study includes the celebrated image of water wearing away a stone: Rabbi Akiva, at the age of forty and still illiterate, observed water dripping onto rock, and reasoned that if soft water could penetrate hard stone, Torah could surely penetrate his heart. Here in our Gemara, it is his wife's instruction that sends him on his way.

### Twelve years learning

*Azal tartesrei shenei kamei de-Rabbi Eliezer ve-Rabbi Yehoshua* — he went for twelve years to study before Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua. Rabbi Eliezer here is Rabbi Eliezer ben Hurcanus, and Rabbi Yehoshua is Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananiah — two of the greatest *tanna'im* of their generation, known for different intellectual strengths, and themselves frequently in dispute with one another. It is notable that Rabbi Akiva studied under both simultaneously.

### Wife permits departure

After twelve years, Rabbi Akiva returned home. As he approached, he overheard a conversation from behind the house: a *rasha* — a wicked man — was saying to his wife that her father had been right, that she had married someone unsuitable, that her husband had been gone for twelve years and left her as *armalut chayot* — a living widow. Her response was striking: she said she wished that he would go and study for another twelve years.

Rabbi Akiva overheard this. *Ho'il ve-yahavat li reshu ahadar le-achorei* — since she has given me permission, I will turn back now and return to study. And he did. He did not stop to greet her. This troubles everyone who encounters the story. How could he not at least pause, spend even a short time at home, see how she was faring? The story is, in some sense, a parable — not necessarily a literal biographical record — but the message it may be conveying concerns the value of *siyum* without interruption, the irreplaceable quality of unbroken continuity in learning. Twenty-four consecutive years are not simply the arithmetic sum of two twelve-year periods with a break between them. What Rabbi Akiva represents, taken to an extreme, is the model of complete and undivided focus. The *rasha*'s observation that she was a *armalut chayita* is not, the Gemara acknowledges implicitly, without some force; but the story insists that this was her choice, that she understood and permitted it. How she sustained herself materially during this period, the text does not address, and these are genuinely difficult questions to sit with.

## Akiva returns

### Twenty-four thousand

*Hadar azal hava tartesrei shenei achranita* — he went back for another twelve years. *Ata be-esrin ve-arba alfin zugei talmidei* — he returned with twenty-four thousand pairs of students. The number is not incidental: one thousand students for each of the twenty-four years he spent in study. Everyone came out to greet him, *nafku kulei alma le-apei*, and she too rose to go out to meet him.

### Wicked man challenge

The same *rasha* from before appeared and said to her: *ve-at le-heicha* — and where are you going, as if to say, you really think you are actually his wife? She responded: *yodea tzaddik nefesh behemto* — a righteous person knows the soul of his animal. The saying is cryptic. One reading: just as a *tzaddik* can understand even the inner life of his animal, how much more certainly does he know me, his wife. Another reading, more self-deprecating: I have been living like a *behema*, with almost nothing, but even so the *tzaddik* is aware of that. There is something unsettling about the comparison, and the text does not resolve it cleanly.

### Wife deserves credit

When the crowd gathered around Rabbi Akiva and his wife was being pushed aside by the *rabbanan* pressing close, Rabbi Akiva said: *hanichu lah* — leave her be. *Sheli ve-shelachem shelah hu* — what is mine, and what is all of yours, belongs to her. Everything his students owed to him, he owed to her. The acknowledgment, rendered in a single sentence before the assembled thousands, is one of the more remarkable moments of public recognition in the Talmudic corpus. It comes at genuine cost to her — the sacrifice of a normal marriage, of family life, of presence — and Rabbi Akiva does not minimize that cost. The story of course raises larger questions about the tension between total commitment to *talmud Torah* and the obligations of married life, questions that have not become easier in subsequent generations.

## Six riches sources

### Vow annulment

*Shama Kalba Savua* — Kalba Savua heard of Rabbi Akiva's prominence. Twenty-four years earlier he had made a *neder* to ensure his son-in-law derived nothing from his property. Now that son-in-law had become the Rabbi Akiva known throughout *Shas* and the *Mishnayot*. *Ata ve-isha'il al nidrei ve-ishtarei* — he came and asked to have his vow annulled, and it was annulled.

This raises an important *halachic* difficulty. A *mishna* later in the tractate, at daf 64, rules *ein potchin be-nolad* — one cannot use a newly arisen circumstance as the *petach*, the opening, to undo a *neder*. If the rationale for annulling Kalba Savua's vow is that Rabbi Akiva turned out to be a great Torah scholar, that would seem to be precisely a *nolad* — a new fact that had not existed at the time of the vow. The resolution, apparently, is that the potential was always there. The greatness was *not* new; it was latent from the beginning. Kalba Savua could have known, and in some sense should have known, even at the time he made the vow, that this man had within him what was needed to become who he became. This is itself a striking claim: that Rabbi Akiva's genius and spiritual capacity were present even when he was an illiterate shepherd — that his wife saw what his father-in-law could not. The doubled expression *ishtarei ishtarei* may suggest something about the annulment's completeness or the emphasis with which it was granted; there is a suggestion from the Hagahos Ya'avetz that one instance of the word should perhaps be deleted, and the Ran and ArtScroll translations may reflect a reading where the annulment required more than a single process.

### From Kalba Savua

*Min shita milei i'atar Rabbi Akiva* — from six sources Rabbi Akiva became wealthy. The first is *min Kalba Savua*: once the *neder* was dissolved, his now proud father-in-law supported him generously. There is something almost ironic in this: Kalba Savua had always, it seems, wanted a great rabbinic son-in-law; he simply failed to see the potential standing before him. His daughter saw what he could not.

### Shipwreck treasure

The second source: *min ila de-sfinta* — from the mast of a ship. The Gemara explains that every ship contains a hidden cavity in the mast where valuables are concealed. One time, Rabbi Akiva was walking along the beach — *inshuya al kef yama* — and he had previously paid four *zuz* to some sailors to bring him back whatever they might find. They found nothing except a *gavza*, a chest or coffer, washed up on the shore, which they brought to him without opening. It was found to be full of gold coins. The sailors are presented as notably honorable — they brought back exactly what they found, without helping themselves to the contents.

One might ask whether there is any obligation to return such found property. The question is in fact live. The doctrine of *ye'ush* — renunciation of ownership through despair of recovery — would arguably apply once a ship sinks to the sea floor; the original owner, having given up hope of recovery, loses legal title, and the finder acquires the object. What the modern law of salvage looks like, and how far back the practical insistence on retained ownership of sunken vessels extends, is a separate question: the history of maritime insurance, going back to the origins of Lloyd's of London, reflects a consistent expectation that ownership of lost cargo does not simply evaporate. Whether the full conditions for *ye'ush* are met in a given case, and what a *posek* would say about underwater salvage today, are questions that merit their own careful *teshuvot*.

### Arabian traders

The third source involves a ship belonging to traders identified as *Sarukita* people — understood here as Arabian merchants — whose ship was tossed about at sea, *tavat sfintayeh*. The entire commercial cargo was placed into a chest, and that same chest was later found and brought to Rabbi Akiva. The narratives about shipwrecks and sea-chests cluster together and likely reflect both independent traditions about Rabbi Akiva's wealth and the special association of maritime fortune with the blessing of Zevulun — *sefunei tmunei chol*, things hidden in the sand and sea that become a source of riches.

### Matronita's gift

The fourth source is *min Matronita* — from a wealthy Roman noblewoman. The Ran quotes the full story: Rabbi Akiva and his students found themselves in need of funds and went to borrow from this *matronita*. She agreed, but stipulated an unusual condition: God and the sea would serve as *arevim*, as guarantors. If Rabbi Akiva could not repay her, she would look to them. A time for repayment was fixed. When the date arrived, Rabbi Akiva was ill — the Rosh notes explicitly that he fell sick at precisely the time payment was due — and could not pay. The *matronita* went down to the beach and prayed: You know that Rabbi Akiva is sick and cannot repay. You are the guarantor; I am holding You to it. Immediately, the daughter of Caesar was struck with a sudden fit — *nishtatit bito shel Keisar* — and she seized a chest full of precious stones and gold coins and threw it into the sea. The waves carried it to the exact spot where the *matronita* was sitting. She took it and went home.

Later, when Rabbi Akiva recovered, he came to repay the loan in full. She told him: *hazarti etzel ha-arev* — I went to the guarantor, and he paid it all, and more. She returned to Rabbi Akiva the surplus beyond what was owed him, and from this he became wealthy. The narrative is remarkable not only as a story of miraculous divine payment but as a demonstration of Torah's claim that *tzaddikim* operate within a framework where God's involvement in human affairs is direct and responsive.

### Turnusrufus wife

The fifth source is *min ishto shel Turnusrufus* — from the wife of Turnusrufus, the notorious Roman general, one of the great *resha'im* of the Talmudic period, and — as is noted — the very man responsible for Rabbi Akiva's eventual martyrdom. The Ran quotes this story as well: Turnusrufus came home troubled, and his wife asked what was wrong. He said that Rabbi Akiva was constantly taunting him publicly. She said: the God of these people hates licentiousness — give me permission and I will cause him to stumble. She went to seduce Rabbi Akiva. When Rabbi Akiva first saw her, he did three things: he spat, he wept, and he laughed. She asked him to explain. He said he would explain two but not the third. He spat because she came from a *tipa sruha* — a putrid drop, as the *mishna* says of every human being. He wept because such beauty would in the end be consigned to the earth and come to nothing. The laugh he did not explain at the time — but the Ran notes that he had seen through *Ruach Ha-Kodesh* that she would eventually convert and become his wife. Rabbi Akiva resisted the seduction, and through some further sequence of events, derived wealth from the encounter. The end of this story — including her conversion, their marriage, and what that says about Rabbi Akiva's later life — would require tracing across multiple *sugyot* and raises genuinely difficult questions about how the various biographical traditions about Rabbi Akiva fit together.

## Monkey pearls

### Pearl-finding monkey

The sixth source involves *Rav Gamda*, who similarly paid four *zuz* to sailors to bring him whatever they could find. They found nothing except a monkey, *kofa*, which they brought to him. The monkey ran off and began digging — *chafru batrei* — and was found to have been sitting atop a cache of pearls, *riva al marganita*. The honorable sailors brought all of the pearls back to him. Thus: a monkey led to discovery of precious gems, and this constitutes the sixth and final source of Rabbi Akiva's wealth.

### Torah vessel debate

Now the Gemara introduces a new episode. The daughter of Caesar says to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananiah: *Torah mefo'arah bi-chli mecho'ar* — such glorious Torah dwelling in such an ugly vessel. Rabbi Yehoshua was famously unbeautiful in appearance, and the Caesar's daughter poses the challenge with an almost philosophical directness: why should something so luminous be housed in such undistinguished physical form? That the daughter of a Roman emperor would regard the Torah as *mefo'arah* — magnificent — is itself noteworthy and the Gemara does not explain it further.

### Wine vessel analogy

Rabbi Yehoshua responded with a question: in your father's house, what do you store your wine in? She said: in earthenware jars, *manei de-pachra*. He said: everyone stores wine in earthenware — and even the imperial household does the same? Surely you should be storing it in vessels of silver and gold. She went and transferred the wine into silver and gold vessels — *ramat chamra be-manei de-chaspa ve-dahava* — and it went bad, *ve-sari*. Rabbi Yehoshua said: *af Oraita kein* — the Torah is just like this. Throughout *Shas*, Torah is compared to wine — something that begins well and deepens and improves with age. The *mishna* at the end of Kiddushin makes the parallel point that unlike physical crafts, which deteriorate as a person ages and loses strength and fine motor capacity, *talmud Torah* is a discipline in which one grows sharper and wiser with years of sustained effort.

She pressed further: but there are people who are both handsome and learned — *ve-ha'ika shapiran ve-gmiri*? He replied: if they were as ugly as I am, *havu gmiri tfei* — they would be even greater scholars.

## Shmuel criticism

### Judgment questioned

A woman came before Rav Yehuda in Nehardea for a legal judgment, *de-atai le-kamei de-Rav Yehuda min Nehardea le-dina*, and was found liable — *ve-it-haivat min dina*. She then challenged Rav Yehuda by asking whether his teacher Shmuel would have ruled the same way. Shmuel was the *rosh yeshiva* of Nehardea, so a litigant in Nehardea invoking Shmuel's name carried a local resonance. Rav Yehuda had studied under both Rav and Shmuel.

### Physical criticism

When Rav Yehuda asked whether she had known Shmuel, she answered in the affirmative — and then described not his *Torah* or his method of judgment, but his physical appearance: short, obese, dark-complexioned, with prominent teeth.

### Excommunication death

Rav Yehuda said to her: *u-ve-vizui ka atit* — did you come here to disgrace him? The parallel elsewhere in *Shas* is instructive: when an Amora traveling from Bavel to Eretz Yisrael was asked about the great teacher of his yeshiva and referred to Rav by the name *Abba Aricha* rather than his honorific, he was rebuked for failing to appreciate and properly name his master. This woman had presumably seen Shmuel in the streets of Nehardea but had no perception of who he truly was — his depth of *Torah*, his authority as a judge and legal decisor. Her challenge to Rav Yehuda's ruling rested not on a substantive legal objection but on a dismissive, superficial impression of the teacher from whom that ruling ultimately derived. Rav Yehuda placed the woman in *nidui* — excommunication — and the Gemara reports starkly: *paka u-mita* — she exploded and died.

## Medicinal eggs

### Turmaita definition

The Gemara returns to material from the Mishnah concerning the *beita turmaita*. The Mishnah had stated that even one who takes a vow not to eat *tavshil* — a cooked dish — may still eat *beita turmaita*. The Gemara now asks: *mai beita turmaita*? Shmuel explains that it is an egg prepared through an extraordinarily laborious process: it is placed alternately a thousand times in hot water and a thousand times in cold water — *alfa zimnei be-maya chamimei ve-alfa zimnei be-maya kerirei* — until it shrinks to very small size, *ad de-mizutra*, small enough to swallow whole. The reason it does not qualify as a *tavshil* may be that it is not something eaten with bread in the ordinary sense, or more precisely because it functions as a medicine rather than food. Its medicinal purpose is explicit: if one has intestinal trouble, the egg will absorb it on the way down and carry it out on the way up — or rather, on the way through. Because of the extraordinary difficulty of preparation, a skilled slave capable of making it was worth a thousand *dinarei*.

### Shmuel's medical use

The Gemara notes that Shmuel himself would use the *kulcha* vegetable — a different plant — for the same diagnostic and therapeutic purposes, testing himself with it to assess his own medical condition. He pressed this practice to such lengths that the members of his household were tearing their hair out with worry over how much pain he was enduring in the process.

## Fig jam dispute

### Jam comparison

The Gemara then discusses a case from the Mishnah in Ma'asrot concerning *kluvsin* — a variety of figs from which a kind of *laftei*, a thick jam or spread, is made. One who vows not to eat *bana'ot sheva* (another variety) may not eat *kluvsin*, and vice versa, because these are distinct species.

### Rabbi's disinterest

A legal dispute is brought before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. A man had given his slave to another person on the representation that the slave could prepare a thousand kinds of fig jam. The slave produced only eight hundred kinds. The aggrieved party brought the matter to Rabbi for adjudication. Rabbi's reaction is memorable: *avoteinu amru nashinu tova, anu afilu be-eineinu lo ra'inu* — our ancestors said they had forgotten good things, and even by our own eyes we haven't seen them. The point being that Rabbi, a man of considerable wealth and standing, had absolutely no frame of reference for these eight hundred, let alone a thousand, varieties of fig jam. The entire dispute seemed to him bewildering in its premises. Why was anyone litigating over two hundred missing varieties of fig jam?

### Wedding feast

*Rabbi avid lei hilula le-Rabbi Shimon be-Rabbi* — Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi made a wedding feast for his son Rabbi Shimon. The scale was prodigious: the *beit ganana*, the garden house or wedding canopy, alone cost 24,000 *ribvan dinarei* — an enormous figure. The celebration was lavish. And yet — *ve-lo azmanei le-Bar Kappara* — he did not invite Bar Kappara.

### Bar Kappara's rebuke

Bar Kappara's response was pointed. He said: *im le-overei r'tzono kach, le-osei r'tzono al achat kama ve-kama* — if this is the kind of feast put on for those who merely transgress God's will, how much more so will it be for those who fulfill it. Then, after Rabbi invited him in response to this, Bar Kappara sharpened the point: *le-osei r'tzono ba-olam ha-zeh kach, le-olam ha-ba al achat kama ve-kama* — if those who do God's will in this world receive such celebration, how much more extraordinary will be the reward of *olam ha-ba*. The Gemara breaks off here, and we resume from this point in the next session.

# Nedarim 51

## Rabbi's Wedding & Bar Ka…

### Wedding Feast Setup

The Gemara on 50b concludes a narrative concerning a wedding feast that Rabbi — *Rabbeinu Ha-Kadosh*, Yehudah Ha-Nasi — made for his son, Rabbi Shimon Be-Rabbi. As the *meforesh* had already noted, Rabbi conspicuously did not invite Bar Kappara, one of the great *Tannaim* of the generation — a remarkable omission that the story itself helps explain.

The text records that twenty-four million *dinarin* were spent on the wedding hall: *ktav a-beit ginana esrin ve-arba alfin ribo'in dinarin nafkan a-beit ginana dein* — an enormous sum, whether this was an inscription by Rabbi proclaiming his expenditure or graffiti of protest by Bar Kappara himself. Upon learning of the celebration from which he had been excluded, Bar Kappara remarked: *im le-ovrei retzono kach* — if even those who displease him merit such wealth and grandeur, then those who genuinely fulfill God's will should be rewarded all the more. The phrase *ovrei retzono*, those who transgress His will, is notable: Bar Kappara applies it almost ironically to himself, inverting the usual theological register in which it describes those who transgress God's commands, not merely those who have fallen out of favor with Rabbi.

Eventually the two reconciled, and Bar Kappara was invited. At that point he shifted his language entirely: *osei retzono ba-olam ha-zeh kach, le-olam ha-ba al achat kama ve-khama* — those who truly do God's will in this world merit such blessing, and how much more so in the World to Come. The shift from *ovrei retzono* to *osei retzono* marks the resolution of the personal quarrel, though the underlying tension between the two figures becomes clearer as the story continues.

### Suffering & Joking

The Gemara explains the deeper reason Rabbi had been reluctant to include Bar Kappara: *yoma de-michayach bei Rabbi ati pur'anuta le-alma* — any day that Rabbi would smile or take pleasure, suffering would enter the world. This startling statement is explained by the *Rishonim*, particularly with reference to a tradition cited in the *Ein Yaakov* (from *sof perek Yakin Yaakov*), that Rabbi had accepted upon himself personal physical suffering in order to shield others — apparently in the context of a prolonged drought — so that the broader world would be spared. On any day that Rabbi permitted himself to enjoy life, his self-imposed suffering was interrupted, and its protective effect correspondingly lapsed.

This concept is not without theological precedent in *Chazal*: the idea that great *tzadikim* absorb suffering on behalf of their generation appears in various places throughout *Shas*. It differs from the Christian theological framework of vicarious atonement in important structural ways — not least that in the rabbinic model it applies to specific *tzadikim* of the generation rather than to a single universal atoner — though the apparent resemblance is worth acknowledging as a point of theological interest.

Bar Kappara, being something of a *badchan*, a comic and wit, was precisely the sort of person whose company Rabbi had reason to avoid. Knowing this, Rabbi made Bar Kappara an unusual offer: *la tivadchan vehavna lach arba'in grivey chittey* — if you do not make me laugh, I will pay you forty measures of wheat.

### Wheat Joke Attempt

Bar Kappara accepted this arrangement and then proceeded to collect. He took a very large basket, coated it with pitch, carried it upside down on his head, and came before Rabbi demanding the forty measures of wheat: *leiti li Mar arba'in grivey chittey dedarshina bach* — give me, Mar, the forty measures of wheat that I am owed on account of my dealings with you. Rabbi responded: *lav azhartach dela tivadchan* — did I not warn you not to make me laugh? Bar Kappara replied: *chittey dedarshina ka nasivna* — I am only here to take the wheat that was promised to me.

The exact nature of the humor here is somewhat opaque to modern sensibilities. The combination of the oversized basket, the pitch coating, and the upside-down carrying seems to have constituted a kind of visual practical joke — perhaps the point being that he had no intention of actually collecting the wheat and was doing the whole thing in a manner calculated to be absurd, while simultaneously protesting that he was acting in complete seriousness. The joke, like many pieces of ancient humor, may require having been there. In any event, Rabbi apparently found it amusing enough to react, which meant Bar Kappara had technically violated the terms of their agreement — a paradox Bar Kappara was exploiting with evident relish.

### Arayot Derashot

At some point proximate to the wedding — apparently while Ben Elasa, Rabbi's wealthy son-in-law, was also present — Bar Kappara turned to Rabbi's daughter and said: *lemachar shatina chamra berikuda deavuch uvekirkunei deimmach* — tomorrow I will drink wine while your father dances and your mother sings or cackles. This passage has been cited in discussions of *kol isha*, the prohibition on listening to a woman's voice in song: the *Ya'avetz* lists it among passages in *Shas* where *Tannaim* and *Amoraim* appear to conduct themselves in ways that stand in tension with norms accepted as normative by later authorities. The *Meforesh* attempts to read the passage as referring to pouring wine rather than singing, but the *Ran* understands it as singing — and the plain meaning of the language appears to support the *Ran*.

Bar Kappara then proceeded to put his plan into effect. He approached Rabbi with a series of *drashot* on the terminology of *arayot* drawn from Vayikra chapters 18 and 20. The appropriateness of such a topic at a wedding has been questioned, though one possible context is the reading of the *parasha* of *arayot* on *Yom Kippur* afternoon — an occasion described in the last *Mishna* of Masechet Taanit as one of the two happiest days of the year, when young people would go out and engage in flirtatious behavior. Just as *Yom Kippur*, paradoxically a day of great joy, required awareness of *arayot* precisely because of the festive atmosphere, so too at a wedding the topic may have been deemed relevant as a kind of cautionary counterpoint to the celebratory mood.

Bar Kappara asked Rabbi: *mai To'evah* — what does the word *to'evah* mean, as it appears in the context of *arayot*? Every explanation Rabbi offered, Bar Kappara shot down: *kol de-amar lei Rebbe de-hachin hu to'evah parcha Bar Kappara* — every interpretation Rabbi proposed, Bar Kappara rejected. Finally, Rabbi asked Bar Kappara to explain it himself. Bar Kappara then requested that Rabbi's wife bring him a cup of wine, and told Rabbi himself: *kum rakod li* — get up and dance for me. This was the fulfillment of the scenario he had pre-announced to Rabbi's daughter: the father dancing, the mother serving. Having established the stage, he delivered his *derasha*: *de-hachin amar Rachmana to'evah — to'eh ata bah* — the word *to'evah* means "you are making an error with this," a *derashah* on the letters of the word.

After a second cup of wine, Bar Kappara asked: *mai tevel* — what is the word *tevel*, used in the context of bestiality? He again deflected every answer Rabbi offered and insisted Rabbi do as he had done before — dance, and have the wine poured. His explanation: *tevel hu — tavlin yesh bah* — the word *tevel* asks rhetorically whether there are spices in this, whether this act is in some way more enjoyable than any other. The *derasha* frames the Torah's prohibition as a kind of ironic question directed at the would-be transgressor.

A third cup followed, and Bar Kappara asked: *u-mai zimah* — what is the word *zimah*, associated in the *pesukim* of Vayikra with promiscuity and harlotry, the verse *ve-lo tizneh ha-aretz u-malah ha-aretz zimah*. Again the same sequence played out, and Bar Kappara's answer was: *zo mah hi* — this one, who is she? The implication is that *zimah* evokes the consequence of widespread promiscuity — children of unknown parentage — a concern that forms the subject matter of the fourth *perek* of Kiddushin.

### Ben Elasa Leaves

Notably, the Gemara does not say that Rabbi himself grew frustrated or offended. Some observe that Rabbi possessed such a deep love of Torah that he was genuinely engaged by the *derashot*, however oddly timed. It was his son-in-law Ben Elasa who could not tolerate the spectacle: *lo yachil ben alasa lemisbal* — Ben Elasa could not bear it, and so *kam ve-nafak hu ve-ittateih metaman* — he arose and left together with his wife, Rabbi's daughter.

## Ben Elasa's Haircut

### Ben Elasa Identity

The Gemara pauses to ask: who was this Ben Elasa, and what was he known for? The answer comes from a *baraita*: *lo le-chinam pizer ben alasa et ma'otav* — it was not for nothing that Ben Elasa spent his money lavishly. Rather: *ela lehar'ot bahen tisporet shel kohen gadol* — he spent his wealth in order to demonstrate to people what the haircut of the *kohen gadol* looked like.

Some background: there are three categories of figures obligated to maintain distinctive hairstyles. The king must have his hair cut every day, befitting his need to appear dignified and presentable — a rule connected to the verse *yofyecha techzenah einecha* and to the ruling in Yoma that a king may even wash his face on *Yom Kippur*. The *kohen gadol* must have his hair cut once a week, in a specific prescribed style. Regular *kohanim* must have their hair cut once a month.

Ben Elasa, as the son-in-law of Rabbi — who flourished around the year 180 CE, well after the destruction of the *beit hamikdash* — was living in a world where the *kohen gadol's* haircut had not been seen in living memory. His motivation appears to have been a form of preservation and anticipation: by replicating that haircut at great personal expense, he was showing people what it had looked like, and implicitly affirming his expectation that the Temple service would one day be restored. Whether it is halachically proper to replicate the *keilim* or practices of the *beit hamikdash* under current conditions is itself a disputed question — some hold it constitutes an *aveira* — but Ben Elasa's gesture is at minimum a striking expression of *messianic* longing.

The *baraita* cites the verse: *kasom yichsemu et rosheihem* — they shall surely trim their heads — which describes the *kohanim's* distinctive manner of cutting their hair.

### Lulianit Haircut

The *baraita* teaches: *ke-ein lulinit* — it resembles the *lulinit* style. But what exactly is the *lulinit* haircut? *Mai lulinit?* Rav Yehuda — one of the *Amoraim* — did not understand it and asked for a description. Rava explains: *rosho shel zeh betzad ikaro shel zeh* — the tip of one hair lies alongside the root of the next. This appears to describe an extremely close, even cut — somewhat like a very precise buzz cut — in which each hair's tip meets the base of the one beside it, reminiscent of the way the *lulav* or *hadas* is ideally described as growing. Achieving such precision without modern instruments would have been extraordinarily difficult and consequently very expensive — which explains why Ben Elasa needed to spend so much money simply to replicate it.

The *Rif* offers a different interpretation: something more akin to cornrows, where the hair lies in close parallel rows. The name *lulinit* may derive from the Latin word for wool, suggesting a texture or layered appearance — though this remains speculative. Whatever its precise appearance, it was clearly a haircut of elaborate and costly workmanship, and Ben Elasa's willingness to fund it for himself speaks to the depth of his commitment to honoring the memory of the Temple service.

## Tavshil & Dilat

### Tavshil Exception

The *Mishna* had previously stated that among the things exempt from a *neder* against *tavshil* — a cooked dish — are the *beitza* (the very hard-boiled egg whose medicinal character was discussed on the previous daf) and the *dilat haramuza*, a type of gourd or squash. As a point of context, the *Geonim* issued a *cherem* prohibiting the application of medical remedies mentioned in the Gemara, on the grounds that what worked in that era may not work in ours — so the medicinal dimension of the *beitza* is of historical rather than practical interest. The question now before the Gemara is what exactly the *dilat haramuza* is.

### Shmuel vs. Rav Ashi

*Mai dilat haramuza?* — what is this *ramuza* gourd? Shmuel says: *kara karkuzai* — it is the *karkuzai* type of squash, i.e., it is a particular species of gourd identified by that name. Rav Ashi disagrees: *dilat hatmuna beremetz* — it is a gourd buried and pit-roasted in hot coals, and the word *ramuza* refers not to a species but to a method of preparation. On Rav Ashi's reading, the *dilat haramuza* is distinguished from ordinary *tavshil* by its unusual preparation method — it is cooked in embers rather than in a pot — and that is why it is treated as an exception.

### Ravina Refutes Ashi

Ravina challenges Rav Ashi's position: *itvei Ravina le-Rav Ashi*. He cites a passage from Masechet Kilayim in which Rabbi Nechemia rules that the Aramean pumpkin (*dilat arammit*), which is identical to the Egyptian pumpkin (*dilat hamitzrit*), constitutes *kilayim* if cross-bred with the Greek pumpkin (*ha-yevanit*) — and similarly constitutes *kilayim* with the *ramuza* pumpkin.
