The logic of *kilayim* requires that the two varieties be sufficiently similar to count as the same species for cross-breeding purposes, yet distinct enough that mixing them is prohibited. The first *perek* of Masechet Kilayim catalogs precisely these relationships. The critical point is that *kilayim* terminology only makes sense if *ramuza* is a species name — you cannot have *kilayim* between a method of preparation and a type of squash. This proves that *dilat haramuza* refers to a distinct variety of gourd, not to a preparation method, and Rav Ashi's position is therefore refuted: *tiyuvta*.

By implication, Shmuel's position — that *dilat haramuza* is simply the *karkuzai* squash, another species — is confirmed. In the late *Amoraic* period, disputes between Ravina and Rav Ashi are common; here, unusually, it is Rav Ashi who loses, because Ravina brought a text from Kilayim that Rav Ashi had apparently not accounted for.

## Methods of Preparation

### Tavshil Scope

The *Mishna* being quoted here was actually stated earlier — it is not a fresh *Mishna* introduced at this point, which is itself somewhat unusual, as the Gemara normally would mark such a repetition with *gufa* or a similar indicator. The clause under discussion is: *ha-noder mimaseh kedeirah* — one who takes a *neder* against *maseh kedeirah*, a dish prepared in a pot. The ruling is: *ein assur ela mimaseh retachto* — he is only forbidden to eat something that is the characteristic boiled-up, pot-liquidy result of cooking in a pot.

However, if a person says *amar konam ha-yored likdeirah* — using the formulation "whatever descends into a pot" — then *assur be-khol ha-na'aseh ba-kedeirah*, everything prepared in a pot is forbidden. This distinction is fundamental to the entire *perek*: *maseh kedeirah* is the name of a dish, while *ha-yored la-kedeirah* describes a method of preparation. A *neder* against a dish type applies only to that dish in its characteristic form; a *neder* against a method of preparation applies to anything processed by that method.

### Pot vs. Frying Pan

The *Tosefta* elaborates: if a person took a *neder* against *ha-yored la-kedeirah* — whatever goes into the pot — he is also forbidden to eat *yored la-ilpas*, whatever goes into a frying pan. Why? *Shekevar yarad la-kedeirah kodem sheyarad la-ilpas* — because the pot precedes the frying pan: the food is first parboiled in the pot, and only then finished in the *ilpas* to crisp the exterior. Since the food has already entered the pot in the course of its preparation, a *neder* against the pot catches it at an earlier stage of the process.

The reverse does not hold: if a person takes a *neder* against *ha-yored la-ilpas* — whatever goes into the frying pan — he is permitted to eat whatever was only boiled in a pot, because that preparation never passed through the frying pan. Similarly, *min ha-na'aseh ba-kedeirah* — a *neder* against whatever is *prepared* in a pot — permits eating *na'aseh ba-ilpas*, whatever is prepared in a frying pan, since the frying pan represents a later, distinct stage. And *min ha-na'aseh ba-ilpas* permits *na'aseh ba-kedeirah* for the same reason — the two methods, once separated, do not implicate each other.

The governing principle throughout this entire discussion is *lashon bnei adam* — we follow ordinary colloquial usage. This *perek* is built on the premise that *nedarim* are interpreted according to how people actually speak, not according to technical or textual precision.

### Oven & Bread

The *Tosefta* continues: *ha-noder min ha-yored la-tanur* — one who takes a *neder* against whatever goes into an oven — *ein assur ela be-pat*, is forbidden only regarding bread. The *tanur* of Talmudic times was a conical or cylindrical clay oven, similar to a tandoor, into which flatbread was stuck against the inner walls to bake. While meat could also be roasted in such an oven — as we know from discussions in Pesachim and from the laws of *Shabbat* — the essential purpose and primary use of the oven was bread-baking. Roasting meat in the same oven was, in effect, a secondary use of the heat already generated for bread.

Accordingly, when someone says *yored la-tanur*, what goes into the oven, the natural referent in *lashon bnei adam* is bread, and only bread is forbidden. But if a person says *kol maseh tanur alai* — everything prepared in an oven is forbidden to me — then *assur be-khol ha-na'asim ba-tanur*, he is forbidden everything prepared there, including anything else one might bake or roast in that oven.

## Pickled & Prepared Foods

### Kavush & Shaluk

The *Mishna* on 51b opens with a series of cases about particular preparation methods. First: *min ha-kavush* — if a person takes a *neder* against *ha-kavush*, the pickled thing, using the definite article — *ein assur ela min ha-kavush shel yerak* — he is forbidden only from pickled vegetables. The *Ran* notes the significance of the *hei ha-yedi'ah*: because he said "the pickled," he is referring to the thing that people characteristically pickle, which is vegetables. Had he said simply *kavush* without the article, the *neder* would be broader in scope. This points toward the principle of *stam nedarim le-hachmir, peirushan le-hakel*: where the language is ambiguous, we would need to ask what the person actually meant.

One might observe that what counts as "the" pickled thing varies considerably by community — cucumbers in one setting, radishes, kimchi, or salted turnips in another. Corned beef, for instance, is itself a form of pickled meat. In communities where a wide range of foods are customarily pickled, the referent of *ha-kavush* would need to be determined by local usage. But if a person explicitly says *kavush she-eini to'em* — I will not taste any pickled thing — *assur be-khol ha-kevushim*, every form of pickle is forbidden.

The second case: *min ha-shaluk* — from *shaluk*, a preparation method for meat, perhaps best described as braising or prolonged stewing. Using the definite article again, the *neder* is *eino assur ela min ha-shaluk shel basar* — it applies only to red meat prepared in this manner. But if the person says *shaluk she-eini to'em* — braised I will not taste — then it applies to all braised foods, whether meat, poultry, fish, or vegetables.

### Rav Akha's Challenge

Rav Akha son of Rav Avya raised a challenge to Rav Ashi: *amar dikhvish mai, deshalik mai, detzali mai, demaliakh mai* — what if someone used not the form *ha-kavush* or *kavush*, nor the possessive *neder* formulation, but rather the participial form *dikhvish* (that which has been pickled), *deshalik* (that which has been braised), *detzali* (that which has been roasted), or *demaliakh* (that which has been salted)? When someone uses this formulation — "the thing that was prepared in this manner" — does that mean specifically the item characteristically prepared that way, or does it mean anything prepared in that manner at all?

The Gemara responds: *tiba'ei* — the question stands unresolved. In the language of *nedarim*, this is effectively a *teiku* — a question left without a definitive ruling.

### Tzali & Roasted

The *Mishna* next addresses *tzali*: *min ha-tzali, eino assur ela min ha-tzali shel basar* — from the roasted, a person is forbidden only from roasted red meat. This ruling is attributed specifically to Rabbi Yehuda — *divrei Rabbi Yehuda* — which is somewhat puzzling, since the parallel clauses about *kavush* and *shaluk* are stated anonymously. The attribution to Rabbi Yehuda suggests there may be a *machloket* about this somewhere else in the *sugyot*, though no explicit dispute is evident in this immediate context. As before, if the person says *tzali she-eini to'em* — roasted I will not taste — then *assur be-khol ha-tzluyim*, it applies to anything roasted.

## Fish Nidrei

### Maliakh Fish

The *Mishna* continues: *min ha-maliakh* — from the salted thing. As is well known from other contexts throughout *Shas*, whenever *maliakh* is used without further qualification, it refers specifically to salted fish — the dried, salt-cured variety, something resembling salt cod or another hard-dried salted fish rather than a brined pickle. The distinction between *maliakh* and *kavush* is that *kavush* involves immersion in a brine solution, while *maliakh* involves dry-salting, producing a much harder and more concentrated product that requires soaking in changed water before eating. This is also why consuming very salty fish at certain times of year was considered a health concern. Accordingly: *eino assur ela min ha-maliakh shel dag* — the *neder* applies only to salt-cured fish.

But if a person says *maliakh she-eini to'em* — salted I will not taste — then *assur be-khol ha-melukhim*, it applies to anything salted.

The *Mishna* then addresses a *neder* against fish more broadly: if a person says *dag she-eini to'em* or *dagim she-eini to'em* — fish, I will not taste — *assur bahen bein gedolim bein katanim bein melukhim bein tfelim bein chayim bein mevushalim* — it is forbidden in every form: large or small, salted or fresh, raw or cooked. The inclusion of raw fish is of some halakhic interest: the question of whether *bishul akum* — the rabbinic prohibition on food cooked by non-Jews — applies to sushi has been debated by contemporary *poskim*, since the *gezeirah* was not applied to foods normally eaten raw, and raw fish has in recent years become a normative food category. Some authorities, including material published by the Star-K, have addressed this question, though a range of opinions exists. Rice, which commonly accompanies sushi, has its own complicated status under *bishul akum*, further complicating the analysis.

By contrast: *umutar bit-rayta trufa u-vetzir* — one is permitted to eat the minced or chopped fish dish along with its brine. The precise character of this dish is not entirely clear, but it appears to resemble something like chopped herring — a minced preparation with accompanying liquid — distinct enough from ordinary *dag* to fall outside the *neder's* scope.

### Dag vs. Dagah

A *baraita* introduces the position of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, which complicates the *Mishna's* apparent equivalence between *dag* and *dagim*. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar rules: if a person says *dag she-eini to'em* — using the masculine singular — *assur ba-gedolim umuttar ba-katanim*, he is forbidden to eat large fish but permitted to eat small fish. Conversely, *daga she-eini to'em* — using the feminine or diminutive form — *assur ba-katanim umuttar ba-gedolim*, it is the small fish that are forbidden and the large fish that are permitted. And *dag daga she-eini to'em* — using both forms together — *assur bein ba-gedolim bein ba-katanim*, since the *neder* encompasses both forms, it applies to all fish regardless of size.

This *baraita* thus creates a grammatical distinction between *dag* and *dagah* based on the size of the fish in question: *dag* refers to large fish, *dagah* to small.

### Jonah Fish Story

Rav Pappa poses a challenge to Abaye: *mima'i de-dag she-eini to'em gadol hu* — what is the basis for saying that *dag* in the masculine form refers specifically to large fish? He points to the verse in Sefer Yonah: *vayeman Hashem dag gadol livloa et Yonah* — God prepared a large fish to swallow Yonah, which establishes *dag* as large. But then: *vayitpallel Yonah el Hashem Elohav mimi'ei ha-dagah* — Yonah prayed from within the innards of the fish, and there the word *dagah* is used. How can *dag* mean large and *dagah* mean small if the same fish is described by both words?

The Gemara answers that this apparent contradiction reflects a change in the fish itself: Yonah was initially swallowed by a large fish and remained there for three days without praying. When the fish then became more constricted — whether because God transferred him to a smaller fish or because the fish was otherwise diminished — Yonah found himself in a situation of *eit tzara*, genuine distress, and only then prayed. The *Maharsha* explains the transition differently: God transferred Yonah from a male fish (*dag*) to a female fish (*dagah*) that was filled with eggs, making it more crowded and prompting the prayer. Either reading explains why Yonah's prayer was elicited not by the initial swallowing but by a subsequent change in his situation — a point considered thematically relevant when the book of Yonah is read on *Yom Kippur* at *mincha*, evoking the image of approaching God from a place of constriction and need.

### Dagah Inclusive

Rav Pappa presses further: *dilma paltei dag gadol uvalei dag katan* — perhaps there is no size change at all; rather the large fish simply expelled Yonah underwater, and immediately a smaller fish swallowed him. In this reading there are two distinct fish in the narrative, and the change in terminology reflects a change in the fish rather than a change in its size. This would undermine the proof that *dag* means large and *dagah* means small, since both words in the Yonah narrative would simply describe whichever fish happened to be present.

The Gemara then introduces a different challenge to the *dag/dagah* distinction: *ella ve-ha-dagah asher ba-ye'or meta* — the verse describing the plague of blood says that the fish in the Nile died, using the word *dagah*. If *dagah* means only small fish, were only the small fish of the Nile killed while the large fish survived? Clearly that is not what the *pasuk* intends. The conclusion therefore is: *dagah mashma gedolim u-mashma katanim* — *dagah* is inclusive of all fish, both large and small.

This does not necessarily mean that *dag* cannot refer specifically to large fish — the masculine singular could still carry that meaning. But for practical purposes, the discussion is ultimately resolved on a different basis: *u-venedarim halach achar lashon bnei adam* — in matters of *nedarim*, we follow colloquial usage, and this holds *le-kulei alma*, by all opinions. Whatever the precise biblical semantics of *dag* versus *dagah*, what governs is how ordinary people use these words in their everyday speech. The *pesukim* from Tanach thus serve as evidence only insofar as they shed light on colloquial usage, and when they fail to do so consistently, we simply set them aside in favor of *lashon bnei adam*.

## Tzichna & Conclusions

### Tzichna Question

The *Mishna* states: *ha-noder min ha-tzachana* — one who takes a *neder* against *tzachana* (a form of prepared or pickled fish) — *assur be-tirya trufa*, is also forbidden the chopped minced fish preparation, *umuttar be-tzir u-ve-muryas*, but is permitted the fish brine and the *muryas* (a word of Latin origin meaning fish brine) which is the separately prepared pickling liquid.

On this, Ravina raises a question to Rav Ashi: *amar harei alai tzichin mai* — if a person declared forbidden upon himself *tzichin*, what is the law? Is *tzichin* simply the singular form of *tzachana*, such that one who is forbidden *tzachana* would obviously also be forbidden *tzichin*? Or are they distinct enough that a separate *neder* formulation would yield a different result? The Gemara offers no resolution: *tiba'ei* — the question is left open, a *teiku* on which we close the *daf*.

---

---

# Nedarim 52

## Dairy Products

### Milk & Whey Dispute

The *mishna* at the bottom of 51b opens with the case of one who takes a *neder* against *chalav* — milk. The ruling is *muttar b'kum*: the *kum*, the whey produced during the cheese- or yogurt-making process, is not included in the *neder* and remains permitted. Whey is the liquid that separates out when milk curdles, distinct from the protein solids that become cheese. *Rabbi Yose oser* — Rabbi Yose forbids the whey as well.

The way the Bavli understands this *machloket* is not as a technical dispute over how to classify whey in relation to milk, but rather as a question of *lashon bnei adam* — the vernacular usage of ordinary people — which is the animating principle throughout *Nedarim*. What do people mean when they say "milk"? The Yerushalmi, by contrast, appears to treat this as a genuine *machloket* between the *Tanna Kamma* and Rabbi Yose over the ontological nature of whey — whether it truly qualifies as milk. Worth noting as well: when a person says he is refraining from milk, he does not mean he is refraining from *milchik* broadly. The *neder* tracks the word, not the category.

### Lashon Bnei Adam

The entire framework of *nedarim* follows *lashon bnei adam* — what the speaker's words mean in ordinary usage. Points that might otherwise appear to be technical classification disputes turn out, at least in the Bavli's reading, to be more superficial questions about how people actually use certain words in their locale. The *mishna* thus encodes a sensitivity to lived linguistic practice rather than formal taxonomic reasoning.

There is an interesting tension worth pausing on. The *gemara* in *Shabbos* makes clear that the cheese-making process involves *mechabetz* — the curdling that separates solids from liquid — which is a *toladah* of *borer*, a derivative of the *melacha* of separating a mixture. That framing suggests that *halacha* conceives of milk as already a mixture of cheese solids and whey together. Yet our *mishna* treats whey as a new substance, distinct from the milk out of which it came. Reconciling these two positions is a genuine question that deserves further attention.

### Reciprocal Cases

The *mishna* continues with the reciprocal cases. If a person takes a *neder* against *kum* — whey — he is *muttar b'chalav*: even Rabbi Yose would agree that a *neder* against whey does not include milk. This is also noteworthy because it implies that the curdling process produces two genuinely new substances. Otherwise one might argue that since milk is simply a mixture of curds and whey, drinking milk always involves consuming whey, and a *neder* against whey would thus apply to milk as well. The *mishna*'s permissive ruling reflects the view that whey, once separated, is a new and distinct entity.

### Abba Shaul & Cheese

Abba Shaul adds: *ha-noder min ha-gevina asur bah bein melucha u'tefeila* — one who takes a *neder* against cheese is forbidden from eating it whether it is salted or unsalted. The novelty of the ruling is that one might have thought the term *gevina* in ordinary usage referred specifically to salted cheese, the more common form, and that unsalted cheese might not be included. Abba Shaul teaches that even unsalted cheese is called *gevina* — there is no other adequate word for it — and therefore both fall within the scope of the *neder*. This parallels other cases throughout the *mishna* where different preparation methods raise questions about which items are included in a given *neder* term.

---

## Meat & Flavor

### Meat/Gravy Rule

The *mishna* continues: *ha-noder min ha-basar muttar b'rotev* — one who takes a *neder* against meat is permitted to eat the gravy — *u'v'kippa*, and also the cracklings or drippings. The *rotev* is a gravy or sauce that carries the flavor of the meat and may contain small fragments of it, but is not itself a piece of meat. The *kippah*, according to the *mefaresh*, refers to a thick residue — drippings or compressed matter that accumulates during meat preparation, something like what falls to the bottom of the pan. Since the person's *neder* was against meat — a steak, a chicken leg, a discrete piece — the gravy and drippings are not included.

This point opens onto a major discussion in the *Ran* — which we will return to shortly — concerning *davar she-yesh lo matirin*, *bittul*, *min b'mino*, and *min b'she'eino mino*.

### Rabbi Yose Opinion

*Rabbi Yose oser* — Rabbi Yose forbids the gravy and cracklings as well. His reasoning is that the gravy contains pieces of meat and carries the *ta'am* — the flavor — of the meat, and therefore it falls within the scope of the *neder*.

### Rabbi Tarfon Case

Rabbi Yehuda adds a proof narrative: *ma'aseh v'asar aleinu Rabbi Tarfon b'veitzim she-nitbashlu imo* — there was an incident in which Rabbi Tarfon forbade eggs that had been cooked together with the meat to those who had taken a *neder* against meat. The scenario resembles a Sephardi-style stew where eggs are cooked directly in the meat pot and absorb its flavor. Rabbi Tarfon was *machmir* that even an egg cooked in a meat stew is considered meat for the purpose of *nedarim*. This serves as a *kal v'chomer* proof for Rabbi Yehuda's position that the gravy and *kippah* should similarly be forbidden.

The questioners responded: *amru lo kein hadavar — aval eimatai? Bizman she-yomar basar zeh alay* — granted, but under what circumstances does this apply? Only when the person specified *this* meat — *basar zeh*. The principle is: *she-ha-noder min ha-davar v'nitarev b'acher im yesh bo b'noten ta'am asur* — if one took a *neder* against something and it then became mixed with something else, it is forbidden only if there is enough of it to impart a *ta'am*, a flavor. The principle of *ta'am k'ikar* — that flavor carries the legal status of the substance itself — is a foundational concept in *kashrut* and *issur v'heter* broadly, and this passage is among its significant sources.

### Noten Ta'am Scope

The later *tannaim* thus clarify Rabbi Tarfon's position: *noten ta'am* applies only when the *neder* was articulated with *zeh* — "this" — as in *basar zeh*, this specific piece of meat. If the person simply said *basar* — meat in general — then even if a dish carries the full flavor of meat, it is not included. The logic is that the *neder* against a specific item causes that item's status to travel into whatever it subsequently flavors. A *neder* against meat in general, by contrast, is about the substance "meat" as a category and does not extend to *noten ta'am*.

This same framework applies to the question of whether funds from items made *asur* by a *neder* are themselves *asur*. If a person declared his entire purse *asur* to someone, would every subsequent coin spent in the marketplace carry that *issur*? The *gemara* implies that for consumable foods, *bittul* may apply — the prohibited item can be nullified in a mixture — a point that will be developed through the *machloket* between Rashi and the *Ran*.

---

## Wine & Flavor

### Wine Dishes

*Ha-noder min ha-yayin* — if one takes a *neder* against wine, *muttar b'tavshil she-yesh bo ta'am yayin* — he is permitted to eat a cooked dish prepared with wine, even one where the wine is a significant ingredient and its flavor is clearly detectable. Wine in a beef stew or a wine-braised dish is not "drinking wine" — it is eating a stew. The person who vowed against wine meant the wine itself, not every dish in which wine played a role. This stands in instructive contrast to the meat case: meat's *noten ta'am* is invoked only when the person said *basar zeh*, whereas with wine, ordinary *lashon* is already sufficient to exclude wine-flavored dishes.

It is worth noting as well the distinction between a *neder* against wine and a *neder neziroot*. A *nazir* acquires a comprehensive personal status — the prohibitions of *tameh meis*, grape products, and haircut are all bound together as dimensions of a single identity. Saying "I will be a *nazir* from wine" would actually create a full *nezirut*. But a *neder* against wine is simply a *neder* against wine, with no further extensions.

### This Wine

*Amar konam yayin zeh she'eini to'em* — if one said, "this wine I will not taste," and it subsequently fell into a dish, then *im yesh bo ta'am yayin harei zeh assur* — if it imparts a flavor to the dish, the dish is forbidden. The same *noten ta'am* principle that operates with *basar zeh* now operates with *yayin zeh*. Specifying *zeh* — this particular wine — causes that wine's prohibition to travel wherever its flavor travels.

A question arises regarding the precise role of the phrase *she'eini to'em* — "I will not taste" — as distinct from *zeh*. Why does the *mishna* formulate the wine case as *yayin zeh she'eini to'em* while the meat case uses *basar zeh alai*? One might distinguish between *issurei hana'ah* and *issurei achilah*, but this thread will be resolved more precisely through the *sugya* of Rami bar Chama, to be addressed below.

### Stam Yeinam

*Stam yeinam* refers to wine produced or handled by non-Jews, which is not necessarily wine used for *avodah zarah* but which carries a rabbinic prohibition extending from the concern over *yayin nesech* — libation wine. This prohibition may also be related to broader concerns about social mingling and the avoidance of close relationships that could lead to intermarriage, placing *stam yeinam* in the same family of rabbinic enactments as *bishul akum* and *pas akum*.

For purposes of *bittul*, *stam yeinam* follows a lower threshold than standard prohibited substances: it is *batel b'shisha* — nullified one-to-six — rather than the standard *batel b'shishim*. At one-in-six, the wine would certainly still be *noten ta'am*, so the ratio itself is set at a level that includes the *ta'am* threshold.

### Nine Days Custom

A related practical question concerns the *minhag* of *Ashkenazim* not to eat meat during the nine days before *Tisha B'Av*. What exactly does that *minhag* encompass? The *gemara* speaks of reducing *simcha* during *shavua she-chal bo* — the week in which *Tisha B'Av* falls — but the *Ashkenazi* community has extended and formalized the practice. This raises several questions: Does the *minhag* apply to chicken as well as beef? The *Magen Avraham* in *Shulchan Aruch* takes a stringent position that extends the restriction broadly. What about a dish that is technically *fleishig* — prepared with chicken broth — but contains no pieces of meat and has no detectable *ta'am* of meat? And what about grape juice, which carries the full *halachic* status of wine? These questions flow naturally from the *sugya*'s distinctions between the substance of a prohibited item and the flavor or derivative status it can impart.

---

## Meat & Flavor (II)

### Ran's Framework

Before turning to the *Ran*'s full conceptual analysis, it is worth establishing the question he is responding to. The *mishna* appears to assume that items made *asur* through a *neder* can in principle become *batel* in a mixture — that the usual rules of *bittul* apply. This assumption is what the *Ran* examines, because it intersects with the principle of *davar she-yesh lo matirin* and with the distinct phenomenon of *min b'mino*, each of which represents a case where *bittul* ordinarily does not operate.

---

## Davar She-Yesh Matirin

### Definition

*Davar she-yesh lo matirin* refers to something that can or will become permitted later. The general rule in *hilchot bittul* is that such an item cannot be nullified in a mixture. Even if the prohibited item is outnumbered sixty-to-one by the permitted substance it has fallen into, the fact that it will eventually become permitted on its own means we do not allow the mechanism of *bittul* to render it permitted now.

### Rambam Examples

The Rambam cites *chadash* — new grain — as a paradigmatic example. *Chadash* is prohibited *d'oraisa* until after the *omer* sacrifice is brought on the second day of *Pesach* (or, in the absence of the Temple, until that date passes). Since *chadash* will become permissible automatically after that date, it is *davar she-yesh lo matirin*, and a piece of *chadash* bread that falls into a basket of *yashan* — old-grain — flour cannot be nullified by the majority. The same logic could theoretically extend to *chametz* on *Pesach*: since *chametz* becomes fully permitted once *Pesach* ends, it too would appear to qualify as *davar she-yesh lo matirin*.

### Rashi Position

Rashi in *Beitzah* 3a explains the underlying rationale directly: since the prohibited item will eventually become permitted on its own, there is no need to rely on *bittul* — one should simply wait. *Bittul* is a mechanism for dealing with prohibitions that are inherently and permanently *asur*. Where the *issur* is time-bound, waiting is the appropriate response, and the Torah did not grant the mechanism of *bittul* for such cases.

### Mordechai View

The Mordechai takes issue with applying *davar she-yesh lo matirin* to *chametz* after *Pesach*. His argument is that *chametz* never truly becomes unconditionally *mutar*: every year it becomes *asur* again on *Pesach*. Its status is not simply "prohibited now, permitted later" but rather an ongoing cycle of alternating permissibility. Because of this vacillating nature, *chametz* does not fit the clean conceptual definition of *davar she-yesh lo matirin*, and so it should not be governed by that principle. The rabbinic prohibition on *chametz she-avar alav ha-Pesach* — *chametz* owned by a Jew over *Pesach*, which remains forbidden even after *Pesach* as a *knas* — is a further complication. That prohibition is *miderabbanan*, imposed as a penalty for failing to eliminate *chametz* before *Pesach*; it does not reflect the intrinsic nature of the substance.

### Ran Position

The *Ran* here mounts a fundamental challenge to Rashi's rationale. If the entire logic of *davar she-yesh lo matirin* is simply that one should wait for it to become permitted, then *nedarim* should also qualify as *davar she-yesh lo matirin* — one can always do *sheilah*, asking a *chacham* to be *matir* the *neder*. Yet our *mishna* clearly implies that items made *asur* through a *neder* can become *batel* in a mixture. This contradicts Rashi's explanation.

The *Ran* therefore offers a different conceptual framework, anchoring the principle of *davar she-yesh lo matirin* in the distinct phenomenon of *min b'mino*. The *gemara* in *Menachos* establishes that *min b'mino* — a substance mixed with something of the same kind — is not subject to *bittul*, deriving this from the *Yom Kippur* Temple service: even though the blood of the *par* (bull) vastly outnumbers the blood of the *se'ir* (goat), the *Torah* continues to reference each separately after they are mixed. The reason *min b'mino* is not *batel* is conceptual: *bittul* works through conflict — an *asur* item and a *mutar* item are sufficiently different that one can override the other. But when two items are of the same type, there is no conflict; they are too similar to contradict each other, and therefore neither nullifies the other.

The *Ran* extends this logic to *davar she-yesh lo matirin*: an item that will become *mutar* is not genuinely "in conflict" with the *mutar* substance surrounding it. A truly *asur* item — one that is permanently prohibited — exists in genuine tension with its *mutar* surroundings, which is precisely what allows *bittul* to operate. But *davar she-yesh lo matirin*, which is not a *davar ha-asur* in any absolute sense since it will become permitted, cannot be said to "conflict" with the permitted mixture in the way required for *bittul* to apply. The item's pending permissibility removes it from the category of genuine *issurim* that *bittul* is designed to address.

---

## Lentils Contradiction

### Lentil Problem

The *gemara* raises a *riminhu* — a contradiction — against what we have just seen in the *mishna*. A *braita* states: *min ha-adashim* — if one took a *neder* against lentils — *asur ba-ashishim* — he is also forbidden from *ashishim*. The *mefaresh* understands *ashishim* as some form of preparation made from lentil flour mixed with other flour and baked into bread, or perhaps lentils prepared with honey — a preparation that has undergone a meaningful transformation from plain lentils. The intuition that the transformation should matter — just as whey is permitted to one who took a *neder* against milk — would suggest *ashishim* should be permitted. Yet the *braita* forbids them.

The contradiction runs in both directions. The *Tanna Kamma* of our *mishna* permits whey to one who vows against milk, yet the *Tanna Kamma* of this *braita* forbids *ashishim* to one who vows against lentils. And Rabbi Yose, who forbids whey, here permits *ashishim*. Neither position is internally consistent on its face.

### Mar Ke-Atreih

The *gemara* resolves this with a principle already encountered earlier in the tractate: *mar ke-atreih mar ke-atreih* — each follows the vernacular of his place. The resolution is deliberately anti-theoretical. Do not attempt to construct a comprehensive conceptual account of why Rabbi Yose holds as he does in one case and differently in another, or why the *Tanna Kamma* takes the positions it does. The disagreements are not about ontology or classification at all — they are entirely about local usage. In one locale, the word for a thing extends to cover its derivatives; in another locale, it does not. The *halakha* of *nedarim* follows what words mean to the people who speak them.

### Milk Whey Terminology

The *gemara* makes this concrete: *be-atra de-rabbanan* — in the place of the Rabbis, meaning the *Tanna Kamma* — people call milk *chalba* and whey *kuma*. They are simply different words for different things. *Be-atra de-Rabbi Yose* — in Rabbi Yose's locale — whey is not called *kuma* but *kuma de-chalba*, "milk-whey." The word for milk is embedded in the very name of the whey. Consequently, when someone in Rabbi Yose's place takes a *neder* against *chalav*, the word *chalav* is heard in the name of the whey as well, and so it is included in the *neder*.

This is *lashon bnei adam* operating at a hyperlocal level. Not only do we follow how people generally speak — we follow how people speak *in a particular place*. The entire *machloket* dissolves into a question of regional terminology. The *braita* about lentils and *ashishim* follows the same logic: in the locale of the *Tanna Kamma* of that *braita*, *ashishim* is still called by a name close enough to lentils that it falls within the *neder*; in Rabbi Yose's locale, it does not.

---

## Grapes & Olives

### Grapes/Olives Rule

The *mishna* now turns to fruit: *ha-noder min ha-anavim muttar b'yayin* — one who takes a *neder* against grapes is permitted to drink wine. *Min ha-zeitim muttar b'shamen* — one who takes a *neder* against olives is permitted to use olive oil. The transformation from grape to wine, and from olive to olive oil, is sufficiently complete that wine is not thought of as grapes and oil is not thought of as olives. The process of producing wine does not merely extract something that was already inside the grape; it creates a new substance.

### Seven Mashkim

*Halacha* singles out wine and olive oil as two of the seven *mashkim* — the seven liquids that carry *halachic* significance, particularly in the laws of *tumah v'taharah*. The seven are wine, oil, blood, water, milk, dew, and *dvash* (bee honey). Only these seven liquids can render food susceptible to *tumah* or become *tameh* in the relevant ways. Other fruit juices — orange juice, for instance — do not carry this status. They are not considered *mashkim* in the *halachic* sense; from the *Torah*'s perspective they remain, as it were, extensions of the fruit itself rather than independent liquids.

This special status of wine and oil is also reflected in the distinct *brachot* recited over them. Wine receives *borei pri ha-gafen* and oil, in certain contexts, receives its own designation — in recognition of the transformation from raw fruit to processed liquid. Other juices, by contrast, take the same *bracha* as the fruit from which they came.

### These Grapes/Olives

*Amar konam zeitim va-anavim eilu she'eini to'em asur ba-hem u-va-yotzei ba-hem* — if one said "these olives, these grapes, I will not taste them," then not only the fruits themselves but also *kol ha-yotzei mei-hem* — whatever is produced from them — is forbidden. Just as *basar zeh* causes the meat's status to travel into whatever it flavors, and *yayin zeh* causes the wine's status to travel into whatever dish it enters, so too *eilu* — these specific fruits — causes the prohibition to extend to whatever emerges from them, including the wine pressed from them or the oil extracted from them.

But this applies only when one specifies *zeh* or *eilu* — "this" or "these." If one simply said *anavim* — grapes — without specification, the wine remains permitted.

### Rami Bar Chama Q

This generates a pointed question from Rami bar Chama: *eilu davka o she'eini to'em davka?* — Is it the word *eilu* — "these" — that is the operative element, or is it the phrase *she'eini to'em* — "I will not taste them"? The two elements appear together in the *mishna*'s formulation, and it is unclear which one is doing the legal work.

If it is *eilu davka*, then *she'eini to'em* should be superfluous — one could simply say "these grapes are *asur* to me" without adding "I will not taste them." Conversely, if it is *she'eini to'em* that is operative, then the word *eilu* is what requires explanation. Rami bar Chama's question sets up the *sugya* that follows, which will work through several attempted proofs before arriving at Rava's resolution.

---

## Fish Brine Case

### Rabbi Yehuda Baraita

The *gemara* revisits the *baraita* of Rabbi Yehuda with an eye toward Rami bar Chama's question. As established earlier, Rabbi Yehuda's proof from Rabbi Tarfon's case was qualified by the response that *noten ta'am* applies only when one says *basar zeh alai* — "this meat is forbidden to me" — after which everything that meat flavors is also forbidden. The *sugya* now attempts to leverage this *baraita* to determine whether the key variable is *zeh* specifically or *she'eini to'em* specifically.

### Fish Mishna

The *gemara* cites the *mishna* concerning *dagim* — fish. One who says *she'eini to'em dagim* — "I will not taste fish" — is forbidden from fish of all sizes and preparation methods, whether large or small, raw or cooked. The *mishna* also states *u'mutar b'tzir* — he is permitted the *tzir*, the brine or liquid that comes out of the fish. This appears to be a case involving *yotzei mehen* — the liquid produced by the prohibited item — and it is invoked here to try to answer Rami bar Chama's question. Notably, the *mishna* uses *she'eini to'em* without specifying *dag zeh* — "this fish" — which seems to suggest that *she'eini to'em* alone is sufficient.

### Rava Resolution

Rava intervenes to block this inference. The *tzir* that is *mutar*, he says, is only *kvar yatza mehen* — brine that had already come out of the fish before the *neder* was made. That pre-existing brine was never part of the fish at the moment of the *neder* and so was never included in its scope. But *tzir* produced from the fish *after* the *neder* — that is genuinely *yotzei mehen*, liquid emerging from a *davar ha-asur*, and would be prohibited. Rava's reading prevents the fish case from serving as direct proof one way or the other about the primacy of *she'eini to'em*.

### She'eini To'em

Despite Rava's qualification, the *gemara* ultimately resolves that *she'eini to'em* — "I will not taste" — is what generates the *issur* on *yotzei mehen*, not the specification of *zeh*. The fish *mishna* uses *she'eini to'em* without *dag zeh*, yet the post-*neder tzir* is still included. This demonstrates that when a person frames the *neder* in terms of tasting — "I will not taste X" — the prohibition extends to whatever emerges from X afterward, because whatever comes out of it also carries the taste he has foresworn. The word *zeh*, by contrast, serves a different function: it ties the prohibition to a specific object and its subsequent *noten ta'am* in other foods, rather than extending to *yotzei mehen*. The two formulations thus generate distinct *halachic* consequences, and Rami bar Chama's question is answered accordingly.

---

## Dates & Winter Grapes

### Dates/Date Honey

The *mishna* at the top of 53a turns to dates. *Ha-noder min ha-temarim muttar b'dvash temarim* — one who takes a *neder* against dates is permitted to eat date honey. The inverse is also stated: *min ha-dvash* — one who takes a *neder* against date honey — is permitted to eat dates. This contrasts with the grapes and wine case in an instructive way. Wine and olive oil are among the seven *mashkim*, halakhically independent liquids; date honey is not. It does not constitute a *mashkeh* in the technical sense — it is more properly understood as the syrup or extracted juice of the date rather than a transformed independent substance. The *neder* against dates, then, does not include date honey because date honey is simply a separate food, not an extension of the date in the way wine is an extension of the grape.

The question of whether *dvash* in the *Torah* refers to bee honey or date honey — with significant *nafka minas* for the prohibition on bringing honey as an offering and for the description of *Eretz Yisrael* as *zavat chalav u'dvash* — is a distinct and important topic. For the laws of the seven *mashkim*, the *dvash* that counts is *dvash devorim* — bee honey — not date honey, as established in *Masechet Machshirin*.

### Winter Grapes

*Istavnit* — winter grapes, or more precisely *istevimit* — are grapes that remain on the vine through autumn, either because they are too hard to ripen properly or because they are deliberately left late to develop a high acidity. The product made from them is something resembling vinegar — a very sour pressed liquid with a high content of malic and citric acids, similar to a *verjuice*. Alternatively, the reference may be to grapes left so long they become overly sweet, after which wine and then vinegar is made from them. One who takes a *neder* against winter grapes is *muttar b'chometz stavnit* — permitted to consume the vinegar made from them.

### Edible Principle

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar formulates a general principle: *kol she-darko le-ekhol ve-derekh ha-yotzeh mimenu le-ekhol* — anything that is itself customarily eaten and whose extracted liquid is also customarily eaten — such as dates and date honey — if one takes a *neder* against it, one is also forbidden from what comes out of it. And if one takes a *neder* against what comes out of it, one is forbidden from the item itself. The bidirectional inclusion follows from the fact that both the fruit and its liquid are regarded as edible foods in their own right, and neither is so distinct from the other as to escape the *neder*.

### Inedible Principle

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's principle has a second half: *kol she-ein darko le-ekhol ve-derekh ha-yotzeh mimenu le-ekhol* — anything not customarily eaten on its own, whose extracted liquid *is* customarily consumed — *nadar bo ein assur ela be-yotzeh mimenu*: if one takes a *neder* against such a thing, only what comes out of it is forbidden, because *she-lo nitkaven zeh ela le-yotzeh mimenu* — one's intention was only for the edible product it yields, not the inedible item itself.

Winter grapes appear to be precisely such a case, according to the Steinsaltz reading of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's position. Since the grapes themselves are not normally eaten, one who takes a *neder* against them had in mind only the vinegar or sour liquid they produce. Accordingly, the liquid is forbidden, but the grapes themselves remain *mutar*, even though the *lashon* of the *neder* named the grapes — because the person had no genuine intent toward the inedible fruit, only toward its edible derivative. This may place Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in tension with the earlier *mishna* that stated *ha-noder min ha-anavim muttar b'yayin*, or it may be that he simply excludes grapes and olives from his principle, treating their wine and oil as categorically different by virtue of their status among the seven *mashkim*. The *sugya* will continue into 53a.

---

---

# Nedarim 53

## Opening & Intro

### Intro & Schedule

We are presently in the middle of Nedarim 53a, having moved somewhat ahead in anticipation of the learning around Tisha B'Av. With that scheduling note aside, we turn directly to the substance of the *daf*.

### Wine, Oil, Honey

The *mishnah* midway down 53a opens with a sequence of specific exclusions from *nedarim*. *Hanoder min ha-yayin mutar b'yein tapuchim* — one who vows against wine is still permitted to drink apple wine, something akin to hard cider. The *mishnah* then continues: *min ha-shemen* — one who vows against oil — *mutar b'shemen shumshumin*, is permitted to use sesame oil, since oil, in the primary sense, means olive oil. And *min ha-dvash* — one who vows against honey — *mutar b'dvash tmarim*, is permitted to use date syrup, since *dvash* in the language of the *mishnah* already refers to bee honey, *dvash dvorim*.

### Tapuach & Charoset

The word *tapuach* merits a brief note. In Tanakh, *tapuach* may not refer to what we think of as an apple at all; it may denote some variety of citrus fruit, possibly an *etrog* or something related. This has practical implications, for instance regarding the preparation of *charoset*, since the *gemara* requires that *charoset* include *tapuchim*. Extensive research has been done on the range of ingredients — spices, wine, fruit — that appear in *charoset* traditions across Jewish communities, and the botanical identity of *tapuach* bears directly on that question.

---

## Lashon Bnei Adam

### Usage vs. Definition

The overarching principle animating these *mishnayot* is *lashon bnei adam* — common, everyday speech. One might suppose that these exclusions rest on technical botanical or culinary definitions: apple wine is not truly wine, sesame oil is not truly oil. But the *bavli*'s understanding, at least, is different. The debate is not about technical taxonomy but about what a person actually means when he utters a particular word. The power of human speech to create the *neder* is bounded by what the speaker intends, which in turn is determined by ordinary usage.

The *mishnah*'s cases make this clear. When a person says *dvash* today, no one — even in the most health-conscious of communities — intends agave nectar or maple syrup. Everyone understands *dvash* to mean bee honey. The meaning of *dvash* in Tanakh is a separate question; there it likely referred in many contexts to fruit syrup rather than a bee product. But by *lashon chachamim*, by the time of the *mishnah*, *dvash* had come to mean bee honey, and that is the *lashon bnei adam* that governs the *neder*.

### Vinegar & Sour Foods

The *mishnah* continues: *min ha-chometz mutar b'chometz stavniyot* — one who vows against vinegar is still permitted to use the vinegar produced from the winter grapes discussed in the previous *mishnah*. These are grapes left on the vine until winter, either unripened or overripened, which yield a sour condiment used in cooking. Since this is not the standard vinegar a person has in mind when he uses the word *chometz*, it falls outside the scope of the *neder*.

### Leeks & Plants

*Min ha-krishim mutar ba-kappalotot* — one who vows against *krishim* (leeks) is permitted to eat *kappalotot* (a different variety of leek). Many of the plants that appear throughout *mishnayot* — the *luf* plant in *Masechet Shevi'it* being a notable example — require specialized study to identify. There are dedicated works on the flora and fauna of the Talmud, and they are indispensable for understanding such passages with precision.

### Field vs. Garden

The *mishnah* then addresses an important distinction: *hanoder min ha-yerek mutar b'yarkot ha-sadeh* — one who vows against *yerek* (vegetables) is permitted to eat field vegetables, *yarkot ha-sadeh*, because the *neder* is understood to apply only to garden vegetables, *yarkot ginah*, the ones cultivated and sold in markets. The reason given is *she-hu shem levai* — field vegetables carry a distinctive, qualifying name. The concept of *shem levai* appears in other areas of *halacha* as well; for instance, the *mishnah* in *Parah* rules that the *ezov* used for the *parah adumah* must be the plain variety, not one that carries a qualifying name such as *ezov yavan* or *ezov kochli*.

One may ask whether the distinction between garden and field vegetables turns on species — whether certain species are inherently wild and uncultivated — or on the actual condition of the plant, whether a particular specimen happened to grow wild even if its species has been domesticated. This remains an interesting open question.

---

## Oil & Rov

### Oil in EY & Bavel

The *gemara* now introduces a *baraita* (introduced with *tanya*) from the *Tosefta* that elaborates on the *mishnah*'s ruling about oil. *Ha-noder min ha-shemen b'eretz Yisrael* — one who vows against oil in the Land of Israel — *mutar b'shemen shumshumin ve'asur b'shemen zayit*: he is permitted to use sesame oil but prohibited from olive oil, because in Eretz Yisrael, where olive trees are plentiful, olive oil is the default oil. *U'v'Bavel asur b'shemen shumshumin u'mutar b'shemen zayit* — in Bavel, where sesame is the primary oil crop, the *neder* against oil prohibits sesame oil and permits olive oil.

### Mixed Locales

The *baraita* then addresses a place where both oils are in use: *asur ba-zeh u'va-zeh* — both are forbidden. This seems obvious — *pshita*! The *gemara* responds: *la tzricha* — no, we need this ruling. *D'rov mi-chad mistapkin mahu* — what is the law in a locale where the majority of oil use comes from one type? One might have thought we should follow the *rov* and only prohibit the majority oil. The *baraita* therefore teaches us that even in such a case, both are forbidden, because *safek issura l'chumra* — in a case of doubt regarding a prohibition, we rule stringently.

This raises a deeper question about the nature of this *rov*. The *Beis Yosef* (in *Siman* 208 on the *Tur*) notes a crucial distinction. The standard application of *rov* is a case where the majority of the population uses one oil exclusively and a minority uses the other exclusively. But what if everyone uses both oils, simply in different proportions? In that scenario, no one truly thinks of one oil as *the* oil to the exclusion of the other. As the *Beis Yosef* points out, when everyone in a locale uses both, the *rov* argument loses its force, because *b'lashon bnei adam* everyone there understands that "oil" refers to both. The *baraita*'s statement that *asur ba-zeh u'va-zeh* may therefore be directed at a case where some people use only one and others use only the other — with a majority using one — and the ruling comes to teach that even the minority oil is included, because *safek issura l'chumra*.

### Safek Deoraita

This application of *safek issura l'chumra* to *nedarim* raises a broader question: would we not simply apply *safek deoraita l'chumra* here? This gets into a significant dispute among *rishonim*. The *Rambam*, most prominently in *Hilchos Tumas Meis* but also elsewhere, maintains that the principle of *safek deoraita l'chumra* is itself rabbinic in origin. According to the *Rambam*, on a *deoraita* level every *safek* is technically permitted, since one cannot establish the prohibition conclusively. The one exception the *Rambam* acknowledges is the *asham talui*, which one brings for doubts about certain *aveiros* — and even there the *Rambam* reasons carefully. The *Rashba*, by contrast, holds that *safek deoraita l'chumra* is itself a *din deoraita*, built into the structure of Torah law itself.

Against the backdrop of this dispute, the specific invocation of *safek issura l'chumra* for *nedarim* raises a further point. Even according to the *Rashba*, who makes *safek deoraita l'chumra* a biblical principle, one might have asked: why should a self-imposed *neder* — an *issur* that the individual created through his own speech — receive the same treatment? That requires its own *halacha*. And according to the *Rambam*, who holds the general principle is only rabbinic, perhaps *nedarim* could be treated with special stringency even at a *deoraita* level, given that a person has personally undertaken the obligation through his own words.

### Speech & Authority

This points to a broader dimension of *nedarim*: the authority of human speech to create prohibition must, in some measure, connect the speaker to the *Hakadosh Baruch Hu*. When a person vows, he is in some way placed in a position analogous to divine legislation — his words carry binding force. That parallel may be precisely why the *safek* in *nedarim* is treated with comparable gravity to a *safek* in Torah-ordained law. A proof for *safek deoraita l'chumra* as an explicit Torah principle may also be derivable from *Parshas Ki Seitzei*, where the verse concerning cutting down trees during a siege seems to indicate that a tree of doubtful status — neither clearly a fruit tree nor clearly otherwise — may not be cut down, which would constitute a direct textual grounding for treating *safek* in *deoraita* matters stringently.

---

## Shemita & Vegetables

### Shemita Distinction

The *mishnah* continues: *hanoder min ha-yerek* — one who vows against vegetables — *b'she'ar shnei shavua asur b'yarkot ha-ginah u'mutar b'yarkot ha-sadeh* — during the six ordinary years of the seven-year cycle, the *neder* applies to garden vegetables and not to wild field vegetables, since the latter carry a *shem levai* and were presumably not in the person's mind. *U'va-shvi'it asur b'yarkot ha-sadeh u'mutar b'yarkot ha-ginah* — but during a *shemita* year, the ruling reverses: the *neder* applies to wild field vegetables, not to garden vegetables. Why? Because during *shemita*, one cannot ordinarily be cultivating annual garden vegetables; it would be impermissible to maintain such a garden in most configurations. So the vegetables one actually means when saying *yerek* during *shemita* are the wild, field varieties.

An interesting question arises: if one vowed against *yerek* in the third year, does the meaning of that vow shift when the *shemita* year arrives, reflecting the changed *lashon bnei adam* of that time? Or does the *mishnah* apply only to a *neder* taken during the *shemita* year itself? The answer is not clear.

### Imports & Abbahu

Rabbi Abbahu, quoting Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel, qualifies the ruling: *lo shanu ela bimkom she'ein mevi'in yerek mi-chutz la'aretz* — this applies only to a place where vegetables are not imported from outside Eretz Yisrael. If there is no active import trade, then whatever vegetables are available during *shemita* must be the permissible field vegetables, and the *neder* is understood accordingly. But *aval bimkom she-mevi'in yerek mi-chutz la'aretz asur* — in a place where vegetables are imported from outside Eretz Yisrael, garden vegetables remain available even during *shemita*, and therefore the *neder* would apply to those as well.

The *gemara* notes that this is *ka-tanai* — analogous to a Tannaic dispute — and records the debate: one *tanna* holds that one may not import vegetables into Eretz Yisrael from outside at all (not only during *shemita* but at any time), while Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel permits the importation.

### Kedushat Shvi'it

Before moving on, it is worth noting that eating fruits and vegetables with *kedushat shvi'it* is not itself prohibited. On the contrary, the *Rambam* holds that there is a *mitzvah* to eat *peirot shvi'it*, derived from the phrase *lachem l'ochlah*. The various *heterim* employed by the *rabbanut* or other agencies to allow *shvi'it* produce into the marketplace are a separate and complex topic, but the underlying point is that one should not be anxious about eating such produce — that is precisely what it is there for. The *Rav Kook* reportedly suggested that one should wash one's hands before eating *kedushat shvi'it* fruits, not necessarily with a *bracha*, but as an expression of deference to the *kedusha* of those fruits, which carry the holiness of the Land of Israel.

### Tumat Met & Soil

What is the reason for the prohibition on importing vegetables into Eretz Yisrael according to the first opinion? *Amar Rabbi Yirmiya mishum gush* — Rabbi Yirmiya explains it on account of a clod of soil. Vegetables brought from outside Eretz Yisrael may carry soil from *chutz la'aretz*, and the soil of foreign lands carries a rabbinic *tumah* known as *eretz ha'amim* — *tumat meit m'drabbanan* — because of the concern that the soil of those lands may be mixed with fragments of bone from bodies buried throughout the terrain. Since one cannot know, the Rabbis applied a blanket *tumah* to the soil of lands outside Eretz Yisrael. This concern would be relevant primarily for those who maintain *chaverim* standards of purity.

---

## Vegetable Categories

### Cabbage & Asparagus

The *mishnah* continues with additional cases. *Min ha-keruv assur ba-isparagus* — one who vows against cabbage (*keruv*) is also prohibited from eating *isparagus*, which appears to be a subcategory of cabbage. The Steinsaltz edition describes *isparagus* as an energy drink prepared from a leafy green vegetable, possibly kale — a characterization that reflects the culinary discourse of our own era. Other *sugyot* in *shas* suggest it may be a prepared drink of some kind, though the precise preparation is unclear. In any case, *isparagus* is a sub-category of *keruv*, and therefore a *neder* against the more inclusive term encompasses it. *Min ha-isparagus mutar ba-keruv* — but if one vowed only against *isparagus*, the *neder* does not extend to cabbage generally, since *isparagus* is the more specific subcategory.

### Etymology & Modern

The word *keruv* also means the *keruvim*, the angelic figures on the *aron*. Our ancestors did not place two golden cabbages on the *aron*, so one wonders what the two words share. One possibility is that the way a cabbage's leaves fold tightly over each other resembles the way the *keruvim*'s wings enclosed their bodies — the same quality of folding inward and covering. In modern Hebrew, *keruvit* means cauliflower, while Brussels sprouts, being simply small cabbages, are called *keruv katan*. Whether the etymological connection between *keruv* the vegetable and *keruvim* the angels is biblical or post-biblical is itself an interesting question, as *keruv* in the sense of cabbage may not appear in Tanakh.

### Grits & Mikpeh

*Min ha-grisin assur ba-mikpeh* — one who vows against *grisin* (some kind of coarsely ground grain or bean, prepared into a thick porridge — roughly analogous to grits) is also prohibited from eating *mikpeh*, a specific prepared dish, perhaps a bean soup or grain porridge. *Mikpeh* appears elsewhere in *shas* in *Masechet Sukkah*, where the question of *yardu geshamim* (rain falling into the *sukkah*) is resolved when *mi-she-tisrach ha-mikpeh* — when the *mikpeh* is ruined by the rain. *Mikpeh* is more inclusive than plain *grisin*; it is a dish made with *grisin* as a principal ingredient.

### Garlic & Mikpeh

*Min ha-mikpeh assur ba-shum* — one who vows against *mikpeh* is even prohibited from eating garlic, because garlic was evidently a principal ingredient in *mikpeh*. When a person says *mikpeh*, the garlic is so central to that dish that even plain garlic falls within his intent. *Ve-Rabbi Yose matir* — Rabbi Yose disagrees and permits it, since he does not consider garlic to be encompassed by the word *mikpeh*.

This entire sequence of cases turns on the principle of *lashon bnei adam*. We are not living in the era of the *mishnah* and cannot know with certainty what each term evoked for its speakers. That is precisely why contemporary *poskim* who receive *shailot* about *nedarim* — and people do take *nedarim* inadvertently or with less than full appreciation of their severity — must carefully investigate what the person actually meant and whether grounds exist for *hatarah*, *petach*, or *charata*.

*Min ha-shum mutar ba-mikpeh* — but if one vowed only against garlic, he is permitted to eat *mikpeh*, because *mikpeh* is a complete dish in its own right, not reducible to garlic alone.

### Lentils & Bread

*Min ha-adashim assur ba-ashishim* — one who vows against lentils is prohibited from eating *ashishim*, a kind of lentil cake or bread made from lentil flour, because lentil bread is included in the person's intent when he says *adashim*. *Rabbi Yose matir* — Rabbi Yose permits it, holding that *ashishim* carries its own distinct name and is therefore a separate food. *Min ha-ashishim mutar ba-adashim* — but one who vows against *ashishim* specifically is permitted to eat plain lentils, since *ashishim* is the more specific term.

### Wheat Singular/Plural

The *mishnah* then discusses *chita chitin she-eini to'eim* — one who says "wheat I will not taste" — *asur bahen bein kemach bein ha-pat*: it is prohibited whether as flour or as baked bread. The word *chitin* in *mishnaic* Hebrew refers both to the grain and to wheat bread, since bread colloquially took its name from its primary ingredient. An interesting question arises about raw flour: since no one eats raw flour, one might argue a person never had raw flour in mind when saying *chitin*. Yesterday's *daf* touched on a related *machloket* about foods that are inedible in their natural state.

A *baraita* introduced with *tanya* records Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel's view: *chita she-eini to'eim* — if one says "wheat" in the singular — *asur le'afot* — it is prohibited to bake it into bread — *u'mutar lachos* — but permitted to chew raw kernels. Because *chita* in the singular refers to *pat shel chita*, a loaf of bread from wheat flour. But *chitin she-eini to'eim* — if one uses the plural form *chitin* — *assur lachos u'mutar la'afot* — it is prohibited to chew on raw kernels but permitted to bake, because *chitin* refers to the wheat grains themselves.

Rabbi Yehuda had earlier made a similar distinction between the singular *gris* and the plural *grisin*. The same logic applies: *gris she-eini to'eim assur levashel u'mutar lachos* — a vow against a single *gris* prohibits preparing it as porridge but permits chewing the raw grain; *grisin she-eini to'eim assur lachos u'mutar levashel* — a vow against the plural *grisin* prohibits chewing and permits boiling.

### Mishna Methods

This raises an important methodological question about how to read *mishnah*. When a later *tanna* states a position that overlaps with an earlier one, is he disagreeing, or is he clarifying what the earlier *tanna* already meant? The tendency to minimize *machloket* as much as possible — reading later opinions as specifications or elaborations rather than as genuine disagreements — is a recognizable approach, and one that the Artscroll edition tends to favor. Alternatively, one can read the editorial history of the *mishnah* as genuinely incorporating later opinions that diverge from earlier ones, which is not a defect but simply how law develops. Neither approach is obviously wrong; they reflect different methodological commitments about how *mishnah* was composed and what its editors intended.

---

## Perek 7: Yerek

### Gourds & Yerek

*Hadran alach ha-noder min ha-mevushal* — we have completed the sixth *perek* of *Nedarim* and begin the seventh. The seventh *perek* opens: *ha-noder min ha-yerek mutar b'diluim* — one who vows against *yerek* (vegetables) is permitted to eat *delu'im* (gourds, squash, pumpkins). One possible explanation: *yerek* may literally mean *greens*, referring specifically to leafy or green-colored produce, and *delu'im*, which come in shades of orange, yellow, and other colors, do not fit that description. Just as we speak of "getting some greens" and do not mean tomatoes or orange bell peppers, *yerek* may exclude gourds on coloristic or categorial grounds.

### Shaliach Test

*Ve-Rabbi Akiva oser* — Rabbi Akiva, however, prohibits *delu'im* as well. The *chakhamim* respond: *va-halo amar adam l'shlucho kach li yerek ve-hu omer lo matzasi ella diluim* — is it not the case that if a person sends a messenger (*shaliach*) to buy vegetables, and the *shaliach* returns saying "I'm sorry, they didn't have any *yerek*, they only had *delu'im*," the *meshale'ach* would be dissatisfied? The *shaliach* came back empty-handed because he concluded that gourds are not *yerek*. Does this not prove that *delu'im* are not included in *yerek*?

### Legumes & Merchants

Rabbi Akiva responds: *kein ha-davar* — is that really what would happen? *O shema omer hu lo matzati ella kitnit* — would the *shaliach* not rather say, "They didn't have anything except beans"? That is, the *shaliach* would return empty-handed when there were only *kitniyot* available — because *kitniyot* are clearly not *yerek* — but if *delu'im* were available, the *shaliach* would simply buy them and bring them back. *Ela she-ha-diluim bichlal yerek ve-kitniyot eino bichlal yerek* — gourds are included in the category of *yerek*, while beans are not. According to Rabbi Akiva, then, the *chakhamim*'s scenario is not realistic; a sensible *shaliach* would bring back the gourds. It is only beans that would provoke the response "they didn't have vegetables."

### Kitniyot Category

This brings us to the question of what *kitniyot* means as a category. We are familiar with the prevalent *Ashkenazi minhag* — and also the custom of some North African communities — to avoid certain foods on *Pesach*, including rice, various legumes, mustard, and possibly sesame. The word *kitniyot* reflects a broad taxonomic category already present in *mishnaic* law. The *Rambam* in *Hilchos Kilayim* recognizes a tripartite division of cultivated plants: *tevuah* (grain), *yerakot* (vegetables), and *kitniyot* — a broad intermediate category with its own *halachot* for *kilayim* and other areas. The *Ashkenazi Pesach minhag* of *kitniyot* does not necessarily encompass every plant in this rabbinic category, though the question of how broadly to apply it has generated ongoing debate. The rhetorical moves made by those who question the *minhag* — pointing to coffee beans or cocoa beans — reflect genuine engagement with where the category's boundaries lie.

### Ful Hamitzri

The *mishnah* concludes the *perek* with: *ve-assur b'ful ha-mitzri lach u'mutar b'yavesh* — one who vows against *yerek* is prohibited from eating fresh Egyptian beans (*ful ha-mitzri*) but permitted to eat them dried. The *ful* in Arabic-speaking cuisine of North Africa is a familiar staple, and this is almost certainly the same food. When fresh, *ful ha-mitzri* is a vegetable; when dried and hard, it becomes a *kitnit*. Green beans provide a useful analogy: fresh off the plant, with the pod still bright green and tender, they are a vegetable. Fully dried, the beans inside the pod become a legume.

This distinction has practical *halachic* ramifications: many families are willing to eat fresh green beans on *Pesach* even while observing the *minhag* of *kitniyot*, since the fresh bean in its pod is a vegetable, not a dried legume. The same transition point applies to peas — fresh pea pods are a vegetable; split peas are a legume. Fresh corn on the cob occupies a similar conceptual space: fresh, it reads as a vegetable; dried and ground, it approaches the status of a grain. The moment of transition from fresh vegetable to dried grain or legume is itself a meaningful taxonomic and *halachic* threshold.

---

## Gemara: Shaliach Role

### Yarkei Kedeira

The *gemara* now enters into the dispute between the *rabbanan* and Rabbi Akiva more analytically. A *meitivei* presses: if one who vows *mimini yerek* — from types of vegetables — is permitted, what is the exact content of the *neder* and what does it tell us about the dispute? *Amar Ulla be'omer yarkei kedeira alai* — Ulla explains: we are dealing with a case where the person said not simply *yerek* but *yarkei kedeira* — pot vegetables — are forbidden to me. This introduces a specific subcategory. In this framing, the *neder* targets pot vegetables specifically, leaving open the possibility of sending the *shaliach* to purchase a different kind of *yerek* that does not go in a pot. The dispute between the *rabbanan* and Rabbi Akiva would then concern whether *delu'im* qualify as *yarkei kedeira* or not.

### Cooked in Pot

The *gemara* challenges Ulla's reading: *ve-dilma yerek ha-ne'echal ba-kedeira ka'amar* — perhaps the person said a vegetable *eaten* from a pot, or as the alternate formulation has it, *yerek ha-mitbashel ba-kedeira*, a vegetable *cooked* in a pot? In that case, it is not a named subcategory but a universal description — any vegetable cooked in a pot — and that would encompass essentially all vegetables. Under this reading, Ulla cannot use the *yarkei kedeira* framing to explain why a *shaliach* might be sent to purchase a different kind of *yerek*: if all cooked vegetables are included, there is no remainder for the *shaliach* to retrieve.

### Messenger Test

With Ulla's resolution set aside, the *gemara* proceeds directly to the underlying dispute: *u'v'mai kamiflagi?* — what exactly do the *rabbanan* and Rabbi Akiva disagree about? *Rabbanan savri: kol milta de-tzarikh shaliach le-imlukhei aleih, lav mineihu* — the *rabbanan* hold that if the *meshale'ach* would consider dismissing the *shaliach* for having made the purchase, that demonstrates it was not what the *meshale'ach* meant. When we say a person would send back the *shaliach* for bringing *delu'im* when asked for *yerek*, that proves *delu'im* are not *yerek*. The standard of interpretation is the *meshale'ach*'s intent and expectation.

*Ve-Rabbi Akiva savar: kol milta de-mamlikh shaliach aleih, mineihu* — Rabbi Akiva holds that whatever falls within the *shaliach*'s range of reasonable judgment is included in the category. If the *shaliach* could plausibly have concluded that *delu'im* fulfill the request for *yerek*, then *delu'im* are indeed *yerek*. The *meshale'ach*'s subjective displeasure is not the determining factor; what matters is whether the *shaliach* had a reasonable basis for his decision.

### Shaliach Extension

This disagreement reflects a deeper question about the nature of *shelichut*. Is a *shaliach* an extension of the *meshale'ach* — *shaliach mi-din yad* — in which case the *shaliach* has no independent standing and every decision he makes is evaluated purely by reference to what the *meshale'ach* would have wanted? Under this model, the *rabbanan*'s position is entirely natural: the *shaliach* is only an arm of the *meshale'ach*, and the *meshale'ach*'s intent is the sole criterion. Alternatively, is the *shaliach* a newly empowered halakhic agent — someone to whom the *meshale'ach* has granted genuine authority to act? Under that model, the *shaliach* retains a measure of autonomous judgment, and the question shifts to what a reasonable agent in that role would determine.

### Shlucho Kemoso

This second model, in its most radical form, implies that what the *shaliach* decides *is* the *meshale'ach*'s will — legally, by definition. When the *meshale'ach* empowers a *shaliach* with full *shelichut*, he transfers his *ratzon* to the *shaliach*: whatever the *shaliach* does, the *meshale'ach* is bound by it, not because the *shaliach* guessed correctly, but because the *meshale'ach* empowered the *shaliach* to stand in his place. *Shlucho shel adam ke-moso* — a person's agent is as the person himself. This principle generates many further questions across *shas*, including whether *shaliach na'aseh eid* and whether *shaliach oseh shaliach*, and it remains a central topic in the *lomdishe sfarim* on *shelichut* broadly. We will continue from approximately the midpoint of 54a tomorrow morning, which will be *Rosh Chodesh Av*.

---

---

# Nedarim 54

## Pumpkins & Vegetables

### Intro: Pumpkin Exception

The *mishnah* states: *hanoder min hayerek mutar badiluim* — one who takes a *neder* not to derive benefit from vegetables is permitted to eat pumpkin. The immediate question is why pumpkin should not be included in the category of *yerek* in the first place.

### Ran's Explanations

The *Ran* at the opening of his commentary offers two distinct explanations. The first is: *dela havei yerek ela pri* — pumpkin is not a vegetable at all; it is a fruit. It grows on a vine and falls into the *pri* category rather than the *yerek* category. The second explanation offered by others is: *desatam yerek ne'echal kemoto shehu chai* — the ordinary meaning of *yerek* refers to something that is edible while raw. *Diluim* do not meet that criterion, and therefore fall outside the scope of the *neder*.

### Edible Raw Category

The question of whether something is *ne'echal kemoto shehu chai* — edible in its raw state — carries significant halachic weight across a range of areas. One prominent application is *bishul* on *Shabbat*. The *rishonim* discuss whether cooking a food that is already edible raw constitutes the *melacha* of *bishul*, and the *halacha* is that it does. *Tosafot* and the *Mordechai* raise the case of baked apples and similar foods where the item remains edible throughout but undergoes a qualitative transformation — becoming soft, mushy, and differently flavored — and even so, the conclusion is that such cooking is still *chayav*.

A clarifying example: boiling water. Water is edible cold and edible hot; functionally nothing has changed. Yet it remains subject to the prohibition.

The related question of partially cooked food generates a significant *machloket*. The *Rashba* holds that once a food has been cooked to the point of edibility, it is considered halachically cooked, and one is not *chayav mide'oraita* for cooking it further — for instance, returning a rare steak to the fire. The *Rambam* disagrees, holding that any improvement through further cooking, up to the point of full completion, continues to constitute the *melacha* of *bishul*. The *Shiltei Gibborim* goes even further, ruling that even fully cooked food, if further cooking would improve it — *mitztamek veyafeh lo* — remains subject to the *melacha de'oraita*, until the point at which it begins to deteriorate.

A second major application is *bishul akum*. A food that is edible in its raw state is exempt from the prohibition of *bishul akum*, since the non-Jew's involvement in its preparation is irrelevant — the food could have been eaten without any cooking at all. Carrots, for instance, are edible raw, and therefore cooked carrots present no *bishul akum* concern. The same logic has been applied to sushi, as eating raw fish has come to be regarded as normative.

### Rabbi Akiva's View

The *mishnah* continues: *v'Rabbi Akiva oser* — Rabbi Akiva prohibits eating pumpkin under such a *neder*. The *chachamim* challenge him: *vehalo omer adam lishlucho kach li yerek veomer lo matzati ela diluin* — is it not true that a person who sends a *shaliach* to buy vegetables, and the *shaliach* returns saying they had no vegetables but did have pumpkins, would report back in exactly those terms? The implication of the *chachamim* is that this return-and-report demonstrates pumpkin is *not* a vegetable — the *shaliach* came back empty-handed, distinguishing pumpkins from what was requested.

Rabbi Akiva, however, responds differently. He draws a contrast: if a *shaliach* came back and said they had no vegetables but did have *kitnit* — beans — no one would say that, because beans are too far removed from the vegetable category. The very fact that the *shaliach* specifically returns to report that pumpkins were available, and to ask whether pumpkins would be acceptable, is what interests Rabbi Akiva.

### Chachamim's Response

The *mishnah* also addresses the case of *ful hamitzri* — the Egyptian bean. *Vaasur beful hamitzri lach umutar beyavesh* — one is prohibited from eating it when fresh but permitted when dry. Fresh green beans are clearly a vegetable; dried beans are a different matter. This line supports Rabbi Akiva's position, demonstrating that even within the *kitnit* category, context determines whether a food falls within the scope of *yerek*.

### Machloket Framework

The *gemara* now articulates the underlying dispute. *Rabbanan savri kol milta d'tzarich shlicha l'amlokei alei lav minei hu* — the *rabbanan* hold that anything the *shaliach* feels the need to return and clarify is thereby shown to be *outside* the requested category. If he comes back and says "they had no vegetables but they did have pumpkins," he is implicitly distinguishing pumpkin from vegetable.

*V'Rabbi Akiva savar kol milta d'mimloch shlicha alei minei hu* — Rabbi Akiva holds the opposite: anything the *shaliach* returns to specify is shown to be *within* the category. The *shaliach* is saying: the only vegetable they had was pumpkin — do you want it? The act of asking the question itself indicates that pumpkin is understood to belong to the same general category as what was requested. The *machloket* thus turns on whether the need to specify is an act of inclusion or exclusion.

---

## Ulla's Precision

### Ulla's Requirement

The *gemara* questions the *mishnah*'s formulation from a different angle: *tanan hamudar min hayerek vehu min hayerek nadar* — but the *mishnah* simply says he took a *neder* from *yerek*, and *yerek* sounds inclusive enough that even Rabbi Akiva should concede that *diluim* would be included. The language seems too broad to generate the *machloket* described. *Amar Ulla beomer yarkei kedeirah alai* — Ulla therefore explains that the *mishnah* must be dealing with a case where the person used more precise language: "vegetables for the pot are forbidden to me."

### Gemara's Challenge

The *gemara* pushes back on Ulla's reading, suggesting alternative formulations: *vedilma yerek hane'echal bekedeirah ka'amar* — perhaps he said "vegetables that are eaten in a pot," or *beomer yerek hamitbashel bekedeirah alai* — "vegetables that are cooked in a pot." Any of these phrasings, while sounding more specific, would still be relatively inclusive, and Ulla's precision requirement would not meaningfully distinguish the case.

### Rashba's Extension

The *Rashba* extends the question raised here — whether *diluim* falls within the category of *yerek* — beyond the laws of *nedarim* entirely. Drawing on the *Yerushalmi*, the *Rashba* notes that the same categorical question applies in commerce and in the *halachot* of *hefker*. If a person declares all of his vegetables *hefker*, did he intend to include his pumpkins? The *Rashba*'s point is that this is a broadly applicable question about the scope of categorical language, not one confined to the specific domain of vows.

---

## Specification Principle

### Tanna Kamma Position

The *gemara* returns to articulate the positions more precisely. *Rabbanan savri kol milta d'tzarich shlicha l'amlokei alei lav minei hu* — the *tanna kamma* holds that anything requiring the *shaliach* to return and seek clarification is thereby shown to lie *outside* the category. The specification signals a distinction, not an inclusion.

### Rabbi Akiva Position

*V'Rabbi Akiva savar kol milta d'mimloch shlicha alei minei hu* — Rabbi Akiva maintains that the act of returning to specify is precisely what places something *within* the category. The *shaliach*'s clarification is a statement that the item is the only representative of the requested category available; it is not a concession that the item falls outside it.

### Abaye: Malkot vs. Issur

*Amar Abaye modeh Rabbi Akiva l'inyan malkot she'eino lokeh* — Abaye introduces an important distinction: even Rabbi Akiva concedes that one does not receive *malkot* for eating pumpkin in violation of a *neder* against *yerek*.
