In *min she-eino mino* mixtures, the rules differ. But the essential conceptual point stands: the *neder*'s status as reversible is what disqualifies it from the ordinary operation of *bittul*.

### Terumah Objection

The *gemara* immediately raises an objection. *Ve-harei terumah* — consider *terumah*. Just as a *neder* can in principle be reversed by approaching a *chacham* who may find grounds to annul it retroactively, so too can *terumah* be reversed: if a *chacham* determines that the original designation was made in error or without proper intent, the speech act can be undone and the grain retroactively becomes *tevel*. Yet we know that *terumah* is subject to *bittul* — there is a well-established rule that *terumah* that falls into a mixture of *chullin* is nullified if the ratio is one part in a hundred. Why does *terumah* not qualify as a *davar she-yesh lo matirin* and thereby escape *bittul*?

---

## Speech Acts & Status

### Power of Speech

To understand both the question and its answer, one must appreciate the deeper *halachic* structure shared by *nedarim* and *terumah*. Both prohibitions are created by a speech act. The prototype of a *neder* is rooted in the world of *korbanot*: one says of one's animal "this is a *korban*," and the speech act transforms the animal's *halachic* status. The *konam* formulation mirrors this: one says "this fruit is forbidden to me like a *korban*," and the speech act renders it so. *Terumah* operates the same way — one does not need to physically separate a portion of grain; one simply declares "this grain is *terumah*," and the designation is effected through speech alone.

Because both *nedarim* and *terumah* are rooted in speech, both are in principle reversible by undoing the speech act. A *chacham* can examine the intent and circumstances of the original declaration and, finding grounds, annul it — in effect, determining that the speech act never validly took effect. This is why both seem to qualify as *yesh lo matirin*.

### Theology & Derash

There is something profound in this structure. The speech act is a non-physical act of remarkable power: it can create an entire *halachic* world, rendering objects sacred, forbidden, or obligated. Yet precisely because it is rooted in speech — which is in turn rooted in will and thought — it carries within it the possibility of being undone. A *chacham* who releases a vow is not, so to speak, overpowering the original declaration; rather, he is determining that the person's deepest will was never truly aligned with the words they spoke. This is the inner logic of *hataras nedarim*: the vow is not broken but revealed to have been imperfect from the outset.

One might observe a certain theological resonance here. The power of divine speech to create the world, and the rabbinic enterprise of *Torah she-ba'al peh* as the interpretive unpacking of what divine speech truly means, parallel in some ways the structure of human vows and their release. Just as the *beis din* of scholars interprets what God's word actually requires, so the *chacham* interprets what the person's word actually meant. The analogy is not precise, but the structural similarity is striking.

### Terumah Batel Case

If *terumah* can also be reversed through a speech-act annulment, why is *terumah* not treated as a *davar she-yesh lo matirin*? The *gemara*'s first attempt at resolution is to restrict the scope of the question: perhaps *bittul* only applies to *terumah* that has already been given to a *kohen*. Once *terumah* has been transferred into the physical possession of a *kohen*, the speech act has had a concrete real-world effect: another person now owns the object and has relied on it. At that point, one cannot reverse the designation by approaching a *chacham* — the *kohen* would be deprived of property he has legitimately received. Since reversal is no longer possible, *terumah* in the hands of a *kohen* is no longer a *davar she-yesh lo matirin*, and *bittul* can apply.

---

## Terumah Transfer

### Terumah Pre-Transfer

The *gemara* tests this proposed limitation by examining the continuation of the *mishnah* it cited. The *mishnah* discusses *se'ah terumah tme'iah* — a unit of impure *terumah* — that fell into a mixture of fewer than a hundred units of *chullin*, which is insufficient for *bittul* since *terumah* requires a ratio of one in a hundred. The *mishnah* says: *tirakev* — let it rot. By implication, the *gemara* infers, if it had fallen into a hundred units, *ta'aleh* — it would be nullified and the mixture would be permitted. This establishes that *bittul* does apply to *terumah*.

But the *mishnah*'s continuation — *im hayeta tehorah*, the case where pure *terumah* became mixed — instructs that such a mixture should be sold to a *kohen*. This language, the *gemara* notes, indicates clearly that the *terumah* has not yet been given to a *kohen*; it is still in the possession of the Israelite who separated it. His only recourse is to find a *kohen* willing to purchase the entire mixture. Yet the *gemara* had proposed that *bittul* only applies after transfer to a *kohen*. Here we have *bittul* applying to *terumah* that has never been given to a *kohen*. The proposed limitation collapses.

### No Charge Rule

The *gemara* sharpens this point by examining a fine detail in the *mishnah*: *chutz midmei otah se'ah* — when selling the mixture to a *kohen*, the Israelite may charge for the ninety-nine units of *chullin* but may not charge for the one unit of *terumah* that is mixed in. He has an obligation to give the *kohen* the *terumah* portion; he is not entitled to sell it, only to give it. This rule confirms that the *terumah* was never previously given to a *kohen*, since if it had been received as a gift from a *kohen* grandfather — the scenario the *gemara* had been exploring — the Israelite owner would have full rights to resell it. The fact that he cannot charge for it proves we are dealing with *terumah* that originated with the Israelite himself and has never changed hands.

The conclusion is that *bittul* demonstrably applies to *terumah* that is still in the Israelite's possession and is entirely reversible. The simple restriction — that *bittul* only applies after transfer — fails. A different explanation is needed for why *terumah* is not a *davar she-yesh lo matirin* despite the theoretical possibility of its reversal.

---

## Rabbi Natan Critique

### R. Natan Source

The *gemara* now arrives at the definitive answer. *Bishlama konamot* — for *nedarim*, it makes sense that they are classified as *yesh lo matirin* and therefore not subject to *bittul*. The reason is stated explicitly: *mitzvah le'itshulei aleihu* — there is a positive obligation to seek release from a vow. And the source for this obligation is Rabbi Natan.

### Bamah Metaphor

Rabbi Natan states: *kol ha-noder ke'ilu bana bamah* — anyone who makes a vow is as though he built a *bamah*, a private altar. The *bamah* is a resonant image. In an era when the *Beit HaMikdash* stands, constructing a private altar — even with sincere devotion to God — is a transgression. The worshipper may believe he is enhancing his religious experience; he is not. He is setting himself up as a private religious authority, creating his own sacred space outside the framework of communal, institutionalized worship.

A *neder* functions similarly. The person who makes a vow imagines he is adding to the religious world, expanding the domain of the sacred, mimicking God's capacity to render things forbidden — *chazir*, *basar be-chalav* — by adding his own categories of prohibition. This impulse, however sincere, represents a form of private religion, a *bamah* of the soul. The communal religious experience is not meant to be supplemented by each individual's personalized system of prohibitions and obligations.

### Neder Fulfillment

Rabbi Natan continues with a further escalation: *veha-mekayemo* — one who not only makes a vow but then actually fulfills it, rather than seeking release — *ke'ilu hikriv alav umaktir aleha*: it is as though he has offered a sacrifice on that private altar and burnt incense upon it. Building the *bamah* is problematic; actually worshipping at it is worse. The person had an opportunity — indeed, an obligation — to dismantle the *bamah* by going to a *chacham* and being released from the vow. Having failed to do so and having instead lived out the *neder*, he has taken the private religious act to its full troubling conclusion.

### Critique Context

This is a remarkably sharp critique, and it is striking that the *gemara* returns to it repeatedly throughout *Masechet Nedarim*. The *masechet* does not offer much by way of a counterweight — a robust positive account of why *nedarim* might be a worthy religious practice — and the dominant tone, particularly as expressed through Rabbi Natan, is one of deep skepticism toward the entire enterprise of vow-making.

### Historical Context

This makes best sense against the historical background in which *nedarim* were an extraordinarily common practice in the Greco-Roman world of late antiquity. Saul Lieberman documented extensively how vow-making had become trivialized and widespread, not only within the Jewish community but throughout the broader culture. People made vows loosely and casually, without appreciating their weight. What the rabbis appear to be doing in this tractate — through both the intricate legal details they develop and through the explicit critique voiced by Rabbi Natan — is to reassert control over this phenomenon: to make vow-making a serious, weighty act that people would think carefully before undertaking, and ideally to discourage the practice altogether.

---

## Mitzvah to Reverse

### Mitzvah Reversal

Returning now to the legal question: since there is a *mitzvah* to seek release from a *neder*, the status of *neder*-based prohibition is categorically different from other *issurim*. The existence of a *mitzvah* to undo the *neder* means that the prohibition is, in a sense, already pointing toward its own dissolution. This is why it qualifies as a genuine *davar she-yesh lo matirin*: not merely that reversal is theoretically possible, but that reversal is what one is *supposed* to do. Rather than relying on *bittul* to navigate the practical consequences of the *neder*, one should simply go to a *chacham*, have the vow released, and the problem resolves itself entirely. That is the *halachically* preferred path, and because it exists, the tool of *bittul* is withheld.

### Terumah Obligation

By contrast, *terumah* carries no corresponding obligation to reverse it. Quite the opposite: separating *terumah* and giving it to a *kohen* is itself a *mitzvah*. The fact that reversal is theoretically possible does not make *terumah* a *davar she-yesh lo matirin*, because the entire thrust of the *mitzvah* points toward preserving and fulfilling the *terumah* status, not undoing it. Accordingly, *terumah* is subject to ordinary *bittul*, while *nedarim* are not. The distinction is not about the mechanics of reversibility but about the normative direction the *halacha* points: toward reversal in the case of *nedarim*, toward fulfillment in the case of *terumah*.

---

## R. Yochanan Case

### Replanted Tithes

The *gemara* now turns to a statement of Rabbi Yochanan that was cited earlier in the sugya and examines it directly. Rabbi Yochanan states: *litra betzalim she-tikna ve-zara* — if one had a *litra* of onions from which *terumot u-ma'asrot* had already been taken, and one then planted those onions, the subsequent produce is subject to *ma'aser* based on the total quantity — *mit'aseret lefi kulah*. One does not subtract the original unit from the calculation on the grounds that it had already been tithed; the entire yield, including the original unit, is treated as new *tevel* produce subject to a fresh round of *terumot u-ma'asrot*.

This is a striking ruling, and it raises the fundamental question about *bittul* in a new register. Evidently, when one actively plants already-tithed grain and it grows into a larger yield, the original unit's previously-fixed status is overridden: it becomes subsumed into the new *tevel* identity of the entire crop, and one must tithe from the whole.

### Chisda Objection

Rav Chisda's reaction to this teaching is memorable in its directness: *man tsayeis lach u-le-Rabbi Yochanan rabach?* — who would listen to you or your teacher Rabbi Yochanan in saying such a thing? His objection is: *heter she-bahen le-heichan halach?* — where did the *heter* portion go? That original unit was already tithed; it had *heter* status. Where did that status disappear to?

On the surface, this might seem like an ordinary *bittul* question — after all, *bittul* is precisely the mechanism by which items lose their distinct *halachic* status within a mixture. But Rav Chisda's question is more probing than that. *Bittul* works by erasing a problematic *halachic* status — a piece of *chazir* falls into a pot and its *issur* status is nullified by the majority. But here the dynamic runs in reverse: the original unit had *heter* status, and apparently, through the process of growth within the new crop, that *heter* status has been transformed into *issur* — the unit is now being treated as *tevel*, requiring a new round of tithing. Can *bittul* work not merely to erase *issur* but to impart a new *issur* status onto something that was *heter*? That is the genuinely counterintuitive question.

---

## Bittul Mechanics

### Ran Analysis

The *Ran* engages this conceptual difficulty directly. He explains that the ordinary mechanism of *bittul* works as follows: when forbidden material is present in a mixture in a quantity too small to be tasted, the *issur* status of that forbidden material becomes inoperative, since *halachic* prohibition is tied to the presence of identifiable taste or substance. The physical material may still be there — the piece of *chazir* has not literally vanished — but because it is undetectable, it ceases to exert its *issur* status. The result is that its status is erased.

In the standard growth case, the Ran frames the argument similarly: when the new growth of an onion dramatically exceeds the original quantity, the original forbidden portion is no longer detectable in the way that would warrant a distinct prohibition. The taste of the original *issur* is overwhelmed. Hence the new, larger onion may be permitted.

### Transform Question

But this analysis, the Ran continues, creates a difficulty for Rabbi Yochanan's ruling. When Rabbi Yochanan says that the whole expanded crop is subject to *ma'aser* including the original tithed unit, he is not erasing an *issur* — he is taking a unit that was *heter* and treating it as *tevel*. The *heter* status is being negated and replaced with a new obligatory status. This is not how *bittul* standardly operates. As the *gemara* frames it more simply: since when does *bittul* make *heter* into *issur*? *Bittul* removes *issur* — it does not create it.

### Mezuzah Case

One of the *acharonim* poses a related question that illuminates this conceptual point. If nine *mezuzot* written with proper intent are mixed with one *mezuzah* written without proper intent, does the one defective *mezuzah* become *kasher* through *bittul*? The intuitive answer is no — *bittul* does not work to impart a positive *halachic* status onto an object. It is a mechanism for eliminating *issur*, not for conferring *heter* or *kashrut*. This is the same structural question raised by Rav Chisda: can *bittul* go in the direction of imposing a status, rather than merely removing one?

---

## Onion Growth Split

### Six-to-Seven Year

The *gemara* now turns to the *mishnah* about the onion that grew from the sixth year into the seventh year of the *shmitta* cycle — what has been called throughout the *sugyya* the paradigmatic case. The *mishnah* addresses onions that began growing in the sixth year, continued through the transition into the seventh year, and were still in the ground during *shmitta*. The question is: what *halachic* status does the resulting onion bear?

### Black Leaves Test

The *mishnah* provides an observable criterion: *im hayu alin shelahen shchorin* — if the leaves of the onion are black, *assurin* — the onion is forbidden. *Horiku* — if the leaves have turned green, *mutarin* — it is permitted. The blackness or greenness of the leaves serves as an evidentiary indicator of when the decisive growth occurred. Black leaves suggest that the onion's significant growth happened during the *shmitta* year, while green leaves suggest it remained essentially a sixth-year product.

The *gemara* now asks: if the leaves are black and the onion is therefore *assur*, why is the *whole* onion forbidden? Surely some part of the onion grew in the sixth year, when there was no *issur*. One would expect only the portion that grew during the seventh year to be forbidden. Why does the *mishnah* speak of the onion as simply *assur*, apparently as a whole?

This language raises the very question about *bittul* in reverse: if the larger seventh-year portion renders the entire onion forbidden, it would appear that the seventh-year *issur* has been imposed not merely on the new growth but on the original sixth-year portion as well, transforming *heter* into *issur*. If so, the *gemara* would have evidence that *bittul* can indeed work bidirectionally — not only to erase *issur* but to impart it.

### New Growth Only

The *gemara* resolves the question by reinterpreting the *mishnah*'s language. *Mi savrat a-ikar katani* — do you think the *mishnah* is saying that even the original part of the onion is forbidden? *A-tosefet katani* — it is speaking only about the new growth. The *mishnah*'s ruling that the onion is *assur* refers specifically to the portion that grew during the seventh year. The original sixth-year core retains its *heter* status.

To be sure, since the two portions are thoroughly commingled within the same onion and cannot be physically separated, one must treat the entire onion with the stringency of *shmitta* produce as a practical matter — *agav orchiah*, as the *gemara* puts it. But as a matter of principle, only 80% (or whatever the actual proportion of seventh-year growth) is truly *assur*; the 20% that was sixth-year growth remains *heter*. The *mishnah* is not asserting that the original *heter* portion became *assur*. *Bittul* has not imposed a new status; the two portions simply coexist within the same physical onion.

---

## R. Gamliel Split

### Gamliel Position

With this reading established, the *gemara* examines the *baraita* that features Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel commenting on the same case. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states: *ha-gadel be-chiyuv chayav, ha-gadel be-fator patur* — that which grew during the period of obligation (*shmitta*) has the status of obligation; that which grew during the period of exemption (the sixth year) is exempt from *shmitta* restrictions.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is explicitly articulating the principle that different portions of the onion bear different statuses. He refuses to assign a single uniform status to the onion as a whole. The sixth-year growth remains sixth-year produce; the seventh-year growth is *shmitta* produce. They happen to share a physical onion, but their *halachic* identities remain distinct.

### Tanna Kamma Debate

The *gemara* infers that this position of Rabban Gamliel is being offered as a clarification or qualification of what the *tanna kamma* seemed to say. The *tanna kamma*'s language — that the onion is *assur* — appeared to attribute the *assur* status to the entire onion, potentially suggesting that the seventh-year growth transforms the sixth-year portion as well. Rabban Gamliel contests this reading and insists that the portions must be tracked independently.

The *gemara* proposes that our *mishnah* itself reflects the position of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel — and that the *tanna kamma* of the *baraita* may also be read consistently with this approach. On this reading, there is no actual dispute: everyone agrees that only the new seventh-year growth is *assur*, and the *tanna kamma*'s language is simply speaking about the new portion in shorthand. The *mishnah* and the *baraita*'s first opinion are thus harmonized under Rabban Gamliel's framework.

---

## Effort & Identity

### No Effort Case

Having established that in the onion case, where growth simply continued naturally from year six into year seven without any human intervention, the old and new portions retain distinct statuses — the *gemara* now asks whether this analysis is universal. Is it always true that *bittul* cannot transform *heter* into *issur*, or are there circumstances in which the original portion's identity genuinely changes?

The answer the *gemara* develops is that the key variable is *tarach* — effort or exertion. Where no effort is exerted, where the object simply continues to grow as part of an uninterrupted natural process, the original portion retains its independent *halachic* status. Old and new remain distinct. *Bittul* does not impose the new status on the old portion.

### Effort Exerted

But where effort is exerted — where the person actively intervenes and does something new to the object — the analysis may shift. The paradigmatic case of *tarach* in this context is planting: one takes the produce, makes a conscious decision to plant it in the ground, and the resulting growth is qualitatively different from mere continuation. The *gemara* suggests that this active intervention may be sufficient to redefine the object's identity entirely, such that even the original portion's status is transformed.

This is why Rav Chisda's question arises specifically in Rabbi Yochanan's case: the Israelite *actively planted* the already-tithed onions. That act of planting is the *tarach*, the deliberate exertion, that opens the possibility of identity transformation. When transformation occurs, the entire crop — including what derived from the original unit — takes on the new *tevel* status, and *ma'aser* must be taken on the whole.

### Vegetable to Seed

The *Ran* articulates this principle explicitly: *hani mili heicha de-lo tarach le-vatulei* — the rule that the original portion retains its status and only the new growth takes on the new status applies only where no transformative effort was made, as in the onion growing naturally from year six to year seven. But *aval heicha de-tarach* — where effort was invested, as when one took a unit of onions and planted them in the ground, *asu gidulim um-vatlin ikar le-gamrei* — the new growth comes up and completely transforms the original, to the point where even the original *heter* turns into *issur*.

The conceptual underpinning is this: when one takes produce and plants it, one has transformed the object from *vegetable* to *seed*. It is no longer the onion one had; it is a seed from which something new grows. The act of planting confers a new identity upon the original material. And once identity is transformed, the question of what the "original" status was becomes moot — there is no "original" in the relevant sense anymore. Everything that grows belongs to the new crop with its new status.

---

## Untithed Seed

### Ma'aser Contrast

The *gemara* immediately challenges this framework with a countercase. *Ve-harei litra ma'aser tevel de-ka-tarach* — consider the case of a unit of *ma'aser* that was *tevel* (meaning the *terumat ma'aser* had not yet been taken from it), and one went ahead and planted it. Effort was clearly exerted — planting is the paradigmatic *tarach*. Yet the *mishnah* or *baraita* in question rules that one does not simply treat the entire yield as new *tevel* and tithe from the whole. Instead, one still separately addresses the original unit's *ma'aser tevel* status. The original *tevel* status of that planted unit is not erased and replaced by the new crop's status; it persists.

This appears to be the same scenario — active planting of a unit that then grows — yet the outcome is the opposite of Rabbi Yochanan's case. In Rabbi Yochanan's case, actively planting already-tithed grain into a larger crop causes the original's *heter* to be absorbed into the new crop's *tevel* identity. Here, actively planting *tevel* grain apparently does not cause the original *tevel* unit's status to be absorbed into the new crop in the same way.

### Verse Limitation

The *gemara* resolves this tension by appeal to a *pasuk*: *aser ta'aser et kol tevuat zar'echa* — you shall tithe all the produce of your seed. The critical word, the *gemara* notes, is *zar'echa* — your seed. This verse is addressed to the person planting in the normal, standard manner: *de-hetra zari inshi* — normal people plant *heter* grain, grain from which they have already taken *terumot u-ma'asrot*. The verse presupposes this normal scenario and instructs that everything that grows from such planting is assessed together as new produce for purposes of *ma'aser*.

### Natural Planting

The key insight is that the Torah's mechanism of identity transformation — whereby planting causes the original to lose its prior status and become part of the new crop — only operates when one is doing the natural, expected thing. *Issura lo zari inshi* — people do not normally plant *tevel* grain, grain that has not been fully tithed. This is an aberrant act, outside the normative framework the verse addresses.

When one plants *tevel* grain, one is doing something unnatural in a *halachic* sense. And because the Torah's rule of identity transformation is designed for the normal case of planting *heter* grain, it does not apply here. The transformation principle is, so to speak, a privilege: one earns the ability to redefine the planted material's identity by doing what people normally do. If one is doing something unusual — planting grain that ought not to be planted in that state — the transformative mechanism does not engage, and the original material retains its prior identity.

### Dual Tevel Status

This produces a nuanced and somewhat complex result in the *ma'aser tevel* case. The new produce that grows from the planted *tevel* grain is indeed new *tevel* — it is produce that has not yet had its *terumot u-ma'asrot* separated, just like any other new crop. But the original unit of *ma'aser tevel* also continues to exist as such, with its own distinct *halachic* status that was never dissolved. There are thus, in a sense, two concurrent *tevel* statuses present in the field: the *tevel* of the new produce, and the unresolved *tevel* of the original planted unit, which must be separately addressed.

This is the resolution the *gemara* offers. The apparent symmetry between Rabbi Yochanan's case and the *ma'aser tevel* case is broken by the distinction between natural planting (*hetera*) and aberrant planting (*issura*). When one plants *heter* grain, identity transforms and the whole yield is new; when one plants *issur* grain, identity does not transform, the old status persists alongside the new, and both must be addressed independently.

# Nedarim 60

## Onion Bitul Resolution

### Rabbi Chanina's Onion

We open on daf 60 by returning to a statement introduced at the bottom of 59b. The Gemara cites *guffa* — returning to the matter itself — and quotes: *tzirtam Rav Yanai betzalim shel terumah sheneta'u verabu gidulav al ikaro mutar*. Rabbi Chanina reports in the name of Rav Yanai: if one plants an onion of *terumah* and the subsequent growth exceeds the original amount, it is *mutar* — permissible — because the original *terumah* onion is rendered *batel* by the new growth. This statement has been our primary focus throughout the preceding discussion: the question of whether *bitul* applies to this kind of growth at all, and whether *bitul* can even operate in a direction that converts *heter* into *issur* — the fascinating question raised in the prior session. Here, the Gemara accepts as its working premise that the growth does indeed effect *bitul*.

### Knockout Question

The Gemara now asks what it calls *le-meimra* — "does this suggest" — that *gidulei heter ma'alin et ha-issur*, that growth from permissible material nullifies the original forbidden quantity? And then comes the challenge: *ve-hatnan* — but we have already learned in a Mishna — *gidulei terumah, terumah*: growth from *terumah* is itself *terumah*. If whatever grows from a *terumah* onion is itself considered *terumah*, then the entire discussion of *bitul* seems beside the point. Before asking whether the new growth can nullify the original, one must ask whether the new growth is itself forbidden *terumah* by virtue of having grown from *terumah* in the first place. This is, as the Gemara essentially admits, a knockout question — and it is striking that it is posed only now, at the very end of the *sugya*, rather than at the outset where it would have reframed the entire discussion.

### Gidulei Gidulin

The Gemara's response is *begidulei gidulin amrinan* — Rabbi Chanina's statement was not referring to the second-generation growth, but to the third generation: growth from growth. When the Mishna says *gidulei terumah, terumah*, it means that the second-generation product retains *terumah* status. Rabbi Chanina's ruling about *bitul* concerns only the third generation.

This raises an immediate conceptual difficulty. With a crop like wheat, the notion of generational sequence is clear: one plants a seed, the seed disintegrates, new grain grows — that is the second generation. One then plants kernels of that harvested grain and a third generation of wheat emerges. But with an onion, which is a *davar she-ein zaro kalah* — something whose original seed does not disintegrate — how does one define a third generation? The onion simply continues to expand and produce shoots. One possibility is that a shoot is separated and replanted, akin to the horticultural technique of layering (*havrachah*) known from the laws of *Pe'ah*. The precise agricultural mechanics are not entirely clear from the text, but the conceptual point stands: the Gemara posits that a third generation of onion growth is analyzable.

The Gemara then anticipates an objection: we already know that *gidulei gidulin chullin* — that the third generation is *chulin* and no longer *terumah*. So what is the *chiddush* of Rabbi Chanina's statement? The Gemara answers: *afilu bedavar she-ein zaro kalah* — even in the case of an item whose seed does not disintegrate, such as an onion. By wheat, the ruling that the second generation is *terumah* and the third is not is comprehensible: each new generation involves the complete disappearance of the prior seed and a genuinely new plant. By the onion, one might have thought that since the original material is still physically present — *ein zaro kalah* — all subsequent growth, however remote, retains *terumah* status. The *chiddush* is that we do not reason this way: even for the onion, the third generation is *chulin*, and furthermore, it can effect *bitul* of the original.

### Terumah vs Tevel

The Gemara then introduces a further complication from a Mishna concerning *tevel* — grain from which *terumot u-ma'asrot* have not yet been separated. The Mishna states: *ha-tevel gidulav mutarin* — growth from *tevel* is permissible. So while *terumah* passes its status to the second generation, *tevel* does not. The Mishna qualifies this: *gidulav mutarin bedavar she-zaro kalah* — the second generation of *tevel* is permissible only if it is a crop whose seed disintegrates, such as wheat. *Aval bedavar she-ein zaro kalah, gidulei gidulav asurin* — but if the original seed does not disintegrate, even *tevel*, which is more lenient than *terumah* in not transmitting its status to the second generation, transmits its status through to the third generation.

This creates a seemingly insurmountable difficulty for the entire preceding discussion. If we are dealing with an onion — a *davar she-ein zaro kalah* — then: by *terumah*, the second generation is *terumah*, and by *tevel*, which is more lenient, even the third generation is still *tevel*-status. Under what circumstances could *bitul* ever apply? The new growth should always carry the forbidden status. This truly is, as one might ask, a question that should have appeared at the very beginning of the *sugya* rather than at its conclusion. The Gemara's having deferred it to this point is at once rhetorically effective and analytically puzzling.

### Sugya Conclusion

The Gemara's response reads: *ribuya de-rabu gidulin al ikaro mutar kamashma lan* — the novelty concerns the case where the new growth exceeds the original. This phrase is difficult to parse on its own terms, and it is precisely because of this difficulty that the *Rishonim* propose alternative readings.

### Ran's Resolution

The *Ran* offers a different *girsa* — textual reading — which he signals with *hachi garsinan*, and which provides the clearest resolution. The *Ran* reads the Gemara as follows: *hatam delo rabu gidula al ikaro* — when we say that the third generation of an onion remains forbidden even in a case of *tevel*, that ruling applies only when the new growth has not become a majority over the original. In that scenario, the onion is forbidden not because the new growth itself has acquired *terumah* or *tevel* status, but because the original forbidden piece is still physically present and has not been nullified. The new growth has not outnumbered it.

*Aval hacha gabi bitul shel terumah mishum she-rabu gidulei gidulim al ha-gidulim* — but in our case concerning *bitul* of *terumah*, the third-generation growth has become the majority over what preceded it. Under these circumstances, two conclusions follow: first, the new third-generation growth does not itself carry *terumah* status; second, it constitutes a majority sufficient to effect *bitul* of the original *terumah* onion.

The earlier Mishna's ruling that the onion remains forbidden through the third generation in the *tevel* case is thus reinterpreted: it was never saying that the growth itself acquires *tevel* status. It was simply saying that as long as the original *tevel* onion persists without having been nullified by a majority, the combined mass remains forbidden. Once the growth does constitute a majority — which is precisely the case Rabbi Chanina describes — *bitul* can and does apply. In this way, the *Ran* preserves the entirety of the *sugya*'s analysis by arguing that what grew from an onion is not itself *terumah*, that *bitul* is operative once the growth forms a majority, and that the Mishna's apparently restrictive ruling about the onion concerned only cases where no such majority existed. The conclusion: everything discussed over the preceding two days stands, circumscribed to the context of third-generation growth rather than second-generation growth.

---

## Temporal Language

### Today & Nightfall

Having concluded the lengthy discussion of the onion with *Hadran Alach Hanodea Min Hayarak*, the Gemara now opens a new *perek* focused on a different dimension of vows: not the object of the prohibition, but its temporal scope. If the preceding *perek* asked what is included in the noun specifying what is forbidden, this *perek* asks what is included in the time specification accompanying the vow.

The Mishna opens with a case: *konam yayin she'ani to'em hayom* — "Wine that I taste is *konam* for me today." The ruling is *eino asur ela ad shetechshach* — it is forbidden only until nightfall. The vow follows the halachic day, which ends at nightfall. Critically, this applies regardless of when during the day the vow was made: whether the person made the vow at noon or a minute before sunset, the prohibition ends when night falls. As a practical matter, this means the duration could be as brief as minutes or as long as nearly an entire calendar day.

### Weeks & Months

The Mishna proceeds to expand these principles across larger time units. *Shabbat zu* — "this Shabbat," meaning this week — renders wine forbidden *bechol ha-Shabbat*, the entire week. And the Shabbat day itself, the Mishna notes, counts *le-she'avar* — it belongs to the prior week rather than inaugurating the next. If one makes such a vow on Sunday, the coming Shabbat is included within "this week." This is treated as relatively obvious by the Gemara, with the *chiddush* being only that one not suppose the term *Shabbat* refers exclusively to the weekdays, excluding the Shabbat day itself.

Similarly, *chodesh zeh* — "this month" — forbids wine for the entire month, with *Rosh Chodesh* belonging to the next month and not included in the prohibition. The Gemara notes that this requires clarification specifically in the case of a full thirty-day month, where the thirtieth day is simultaneously the last day of the current month and the first day of *Rosh Chodesh* of the next. Since people call that day *Rosh Chodesh* — *kari inish kari lei Rosh Yarcha* — it is conceptually associated with the coming month, and the vow does not extend to cover it, even though technically it is the thirtieth day of the month in which the vow was made.

### Years & Rosh Hashana

*Shanah zo* — "this year" — forbids wine for the entire year, with *Rosh Hashana* belonging to the coming year. The Gemara observes that the Mishna uses different phrasing for *Rosh Chodesh* and *Rosh Hashana*: *Rosh Chodesh* is described as *lehaba* — what is coming — while *Rosh Hashana* is described as *le'atid lavo* — the future that is yet to come — suggesting perhaps a sense of greater temporal distance.

The seven-year *shemitah* cycle follows the same logic: *shavua zeh* forbids wine for the entire cycle, with the *shemitah* year itself belonging to the end of the prior cycle rather than beginning a new one.

### Duration Specificity

The Mishna then introduces a crucial distinction. If instead of saying "this day," "this week," "this month," or "this year," one specifies an absolute duration — *yom echad*, one day; *shabbat achat*, one week; *chodesh echad*, one month; *shanah achat*, one year — then the vow operates differently: *asur miyom leyom*, it goes from the moment of the vow forward for a full measured unit of time. If one makes a vow at 1:00 PM on Monday saying *yom echad*, the prohibition extends until 1:00 PM on Tuesday — a full twenty-four hours — rather than ending at nightfall that same day.

One might ask whether such duration-based vows calculate to the precise minute or only to the day. The Mishna does not resolve this fully for longer units such as a week or a month, though the logic of the rule implies a degree of precision: if one is on the third of *Adar* and takes a one-month vow, the vow presumably extends until the third of *Nissan*.

### Until Pesach Debate

The Mishna addresses the phrase *ad haPesach* — "until Pesach." If one uses the formulation *ad sheyagia* — until it arrives — the vow lasts until Pesach begins, and the phrase is read as exclusive: *ad velo ad bichlal*, until but not including. If one says *ad sheyehei* — until it has been — the vow lasts until Pesach concludes.

The Mishna then records a debate concerning the phrase *ad pnei haPesach* — "until the face of Pesach." Rabbi Meir holds *asur ad sheyagia*: the face of Pesach means its beginning, so the vow expires when Pesach arrives. Rabbi Yossi holds *ad sheyetze*: *pnei* refers to the receding face, i.e., the end of Pesach, so the vow continues through the entire festival. The correct *girsa* here, as noted in the margin and as established by *Rashi*, the *Ran*, and the *Rosh*, includes the word *pnei* in the Mishna text.

One might note the practical implication: a vow not to drink wine *ad pnei haPesach* could, depending on which position one follows, create an obligation to seek alternative means of fulfilling the *arba kosos* at the Seder — since *nedarim*, operating on objects rather than actions, can indirectly conflict with the performance of *mitzvot*.

### Gezeirah Logic

The Gemara turns to explore the ruling of Rabbi Yirmiyah that even though a vow said *hayom* — "today" — expires at nightfall, one nonetheless requires *she'eila lechacham*, a formal release from a sage, once night falls. The vow has lapsed; why is *heter chacham* necessary?

Rav Yosef explains: *gezeira hayom mishum yom echad* — it is a rabbinic decree, lest one who has experienced a *hayom* vow expiring at nightfall come to treat a *yom echad* vow as though it too expires at nightfall, when in fact it runs for a full twenty-four hours. If we allow a *hayom* vow to conclude without any formal act, one might reason by analogy that a *yom echad* vow likewise expires at the end of the calendar day.

Abaye challenges this: if so, should we not make the reverse decree as well — that a *yom echad* vow, even after twenty-four hours, requires *hatarat chacham* lest one mistakenly think that *hayom* means twenty-four hours too? Rav responds: *hayom beyom echad michlaf* — "today" could be confused with "one day," but *yom echad behayom lo michlaf* — "one day" cannot be confused with "today." Tosafot makes the underlying logic explicit. If one practices a *hayom* vow that expires at nightfall and then applies that experience to a *yom echad* vow, one would stop drinking too early. But if one practices a *yom echad* vow that runs twenty-four hours and tries to apply that experience backward to a *hayom* situation, the result is simply that one would abstain for longer — which causes no violation. The confusion is asymmetric: leniency in the *hayom* case could lead to improperly terminating a *yom echad* vow early, but leniency in the *yom echad* direction creates no practical error.

The Gemara then introduces a different framework through Ravina citing Ameimar in the name of Rav Yosef: this ruling of Rabbi Yirmiyah accords with the view of Rabbi Natan, who holds that anyone who makes a vow is as one who built a *bamah*, and one who fulfills it is as one who offered a sacrifice upon it. According to the *Ran*, the *gezeira* about *hatarat chacham* even after the vow has lapsed is not purely about preventing logical confusion between *hayom* and *yom echad*. Rather, the rabbinic antipathy toward vows as a category provides the underlying impetus: since vows are discouraged in principle, the rabbis imposed the requirement of *heter chacham* even for the most trivial of vows — the person who says "this item is forbidden to me until tonight" — precisely because such short, minor vows are perhaps the most prone to casual proliferation and need to be subjected to some procedural friction.

### Vows vs Fasts

The *Ran* addresses a practical corollary that flows naturally from this analysis. The custom of *ta'anit yachidim* — a private fast accepted at *mincha* time, observed from dawn until nightfall — follows the same temporal structure as a *hayom* vow: it expires at nightfall. Yet the *Ran* rules that at nightfall one does not require *hatarat chacham* to eat. *Velo gazru mishum yom echad* — no decree was made here lest one confuse it with a *yom echad* vow.

The reason: *hadavar yadua shedin shel ta'anis kach hi* — everyone knows that the law of a *ta'anis* is precisely this: it ends at nightfall. The practice of the *ta'anis* is a recognized institution with well-understood parameters, and no one observing a *ta'anis* will confuse it with a *neder* forbidding food for a full twenty-four-hour period. Moreover, *ein issuro kish'ar nedarim shekhvar kav'u lo chachamim zman* — its prohibition is not structured like ordinary *nedarim*; the sages already established its duration as a fixed matter. Even though a *ta'anis* is technically accepted through verbal declaration, the declaration does not create a *neder* in the sense of rendering all food forbidden as an object; it is an acceptance of a recognized institution that concludes at nightfall by established law. No one will confuse being in a *ta'anis* with having taken a vow that lasts a full day.

---

## Ambiguous Specifications

### Rosh Chodesh Dating

The Gemara raises a series of *ibayei lehu* — unresolved questions — that extend the Mishna's framework into more difficult territory. Before reaching these, however, the Gemara pauses to draw out the practical *halacha le-ma'aseh* implications of the ruling that *Rosh Chodesh* belongs to the coming month even when it falls on the thirtieth day of the preceding month — specifically, the question of how to date documents.

Tosafot addresses this directly. When writing a *ketubah*, a *shtar*, or a *get* on the first day of a two-day *Rosh Chodesh*, what date does one record? The first day of a two-day *Rosh Chodesh* is technically the thirtieth day of the prior month — so today, for instance, might be the thirtieth of *Shevat* — yet it is universally called *Rosh Chodesh Adar*. Tosafot rules: *kosvin yom ploni shehu Rosh Chodesh* — one writes the day of the week together with *Rosh Chodesh* of the new month. One does not record it as the thirtieth of the prior month, since in common usage — *lashon benei adam* — the day is called *Rosh Chodesh Adar*, not the thirtieth of *Shevat*. Since the Gemara elsewhere demonstrates that the laws of documents follow vernacular language in the same manner as *nedarim*, the same principle applies: one writes Monday, *Rosh Chodesh Adar*.

However, Tosafot adds that by a *get*, where precision is critical and error could determine whether a woman is bound or free, it is preferable to write both: *Rosh Chodesh Adar shehu yom shloshim le-chodesh Shevat* — identifying the day by both its popular name and its technical calendar position. Tosafot then cites Rabbeinu Tam as having followed this practice in the *ketubah* of his own daughter, and notes that this dual identification has become the accepted practice in *ketubot* as well. The distinction Tosafot draws — that the dual formulation is strictly required only for a *get* but recommended for a *ketubah* — is worth noting, since in practice both documents receive the fuller formulation.

### Unresolved 'Day'

The first *ibayei lehu* concerns a person who says *konam yayin she'ani to'em yom* — not *hayom* ("today") and not *yom echad* ("one day"), but simply *yom*, "day," without a demonstrative or numeral. The Mishna specifies outcomes for *hayom* (until nightfall) and for *yom echad* (twenty-four hours), but does not address the bare word *yom*. Which model does it follow?

The Gemara attempts to resolve this from the Mishna itself. One might reason: since the Mishna says *hayom* goes until nightfall, surely *yom* without the demonstrative *ha-* would be treated more like *yom echad* — a full day. The Gemara responds by pointing to the *seifa* of the Mishna, which rules that *yom echad* means twenty-four hours. Does not that imply by contrast that anything short of the explicit *yom echad* formulation — including bare *yom* — is treated like *hayom*? The Gemara rejects this reasoning: *ela meha lika le-mishma minah* — one cannot derive the answer from the Mishna, because the Mishna addresses only the two explicit cases and says nothing about what falls between them.

Rav Ashi then attempts to bring a proof from a *Beraita*: *konam yayin she'ani to'em hashana nitabra hashana asur bah u've'iburah* — if one says "this year" and the year is subsequently declared a leap year with an added second *Adar*, the vow extends through the added month as well. Rav Ashi suggests that the *chiddush* of this *Beraita* is not the leap-year extension — since if the year ends at the conclusion of *Elul*, the inclusion of *Adar Sheni* is entirely obvious — but rather that the *Beraita* was formulated using the word *shana* alone, without *ha-*, and yet it treats that as equivalent to *hashana*, "this year." By analogy, *yom* would be equivalent to *hayom*, ending at nightfall.

The Gemara rejects this argument: *le'olam de'amar hashana* — the *Beraita* was in fact saying *hashana*, "this year," all along, and its *chiddush* is precisely the leap-year point. The *hava amina* would have been: since most years are not leap years, one could follow the majority of years and hold that the vow ended with the ordinary *Adar* even in a leap year. The *Beraita* teaches that the vow follows the actual year in which it was taken, not the statistical norm. The word *shana* does not enter the analysis.

Since the question remains unresolved — *teiku* — practical *halacha* defaults to the more stringent position: *yom* is treated as *yom echad*, a full twenty-four hours.

### Yovel Cycle Debate

The Gemara next poses an *ibayei lehu* regarding the *Yovel* — the Jubilee year that concludes a fifty-year cycle. If one says wine is forbidden to him for "this *Yovel*," does the prohibition extend through the fiftieth year itself, or does the fiftieth year belong to the next cycle?

The parallel to the weekly and monthly cases is suggestive. Just as *Shabbat* was said to belong to the prior week rather than inaugurate the next, one might reason that the *Yovel* year, as the culmination of seven *shemitah* cycles, belongs to the period just concluded, and the vow therefore extends through it. But equally, one might argue as follows.

### Rabbi Meir vs Yehuda

The Gemara brings a *Beraita* recording a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis derived from the verse *vekidashtem et shnat ha-hamishim shana* — "you shall sanctify the fiftieth year." The *derashah* yields: *shnat hamishim ata moneh ve-ee ata moneh shnat hamishim ve-ahat* — you count year fifty as fifty, and you do not count it simultaneously as fifty and as one of the next cycle. The Rabbis derive from here that year fifty is the conclusion of the prior cycle; the following year begins a fresh cycle as year one. The fifty-year unit is a complete and closed unit.

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *yovel eino oleh le-minyan shavua* — the *Yovel* year does not count toward the seven-year cycle that follows it. Rather, *yovel oleh le-minyan shavua* — the *Yovel* year counts as year one of the next cycle. According to Rabbi Yehuda, the effective unit is forty-nine years, and what one calls the "fiftieth year" is simultaneously the first year of the subsequent cycle. This produces a practically significant consequence: the first cycle after a *Yovel* would have only five years of permitted planting, since the *Yovel* year itself is forbidden for agricultural work, and the immediately following year is *shemitah*, leaving only five intervening years.

The Rabbis challenge Rabbi Yehuda: the Torah says *shesh shanim tizra sadecha* — you shall plant your field for six years — yet according to his system, in the cycle immediately following a *Yovel*, there are only five plantable years. Rabbi Yehuda replies symmetrically: and according to you, the Torah says *ve-tziviti et birchati li-shlosh ha-shanim* — I will command My blessing for the three years — referring to the produce of year six sustaining the people through year seven (the *shemitah*), year eight (until the new harvest), and part of year six itself. But according to his interlocutors' system, at the boundary of a *Yovel* cycle, the produce of year six would need to sustain the people through year seven (*shemitah*), year eight (*Yovel*), and into year nine — four years, not three. The Gemara responds for both sides: in each case, the verse is speaking of the ordinary situation, not the boundary case involving *Yovel*. Each disputant's anomalous case is simply not the referent of that verse.

### Yovel & Vows

The Gemara closes by applying this dispute directly to the vow question: if someone says "this *Yovel* is forbidden to me," the question of whether the *Yovel* year itself is included depends precisely on whether year fifty belongs to the prior cycle (the Rabbis' view, in which case the vow runs through the *Yovel* year) or inaugurates the next (Rabbi Yehuda's view, in which case by the time the *Yovel* arrives, the "this *Yovel*" period has already concluded and wine becomes permissible).

---

## Hermeneutic Debate

### Ambiguity Principle

Turning to daf 60b, the Gemara addresses the broader interpretive principle underlying the debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yossi about *ad pnei haPesach*. The Gemara frames the dispute not merely as a question about the meaning of the word *pnei* but as a fundamental disagreement about how to interpret inherently ambiguous language in vows.

The Gemara formulates it thus: *Rabbi Meir savar lo ma'ayil inish nafshieh li-sfeika* — Rabbi Meir holds that a person does not wish to place himself in doubtful territory. Since the phrase *pnei haPesach* is ambiguous — it could mean the beginning of Pesach, the middle, or the end — Rabbi Meir assumes the speaker intended only the unambiguous, clear meaning: until Pesach begins, but not into the period of the festival itself, whose inclusion would be uncertain. *Rabbi Yossi savar ma'ayil inish nafshieh li-sfeika* — Rabbi Yossi holds that a person is willing to have his language carry ambiguous implications. The speaker using the word *pnei* may well have intended one of the possible meanings that extends into or through Pesach. Rabbi Yossi therefore rules that the prohibition extends until Pesach concludes.

### Marriage Ambiguity

The Gemara immediately raises a difficulty: the positions appear reversed in a different *sugya*. In a case where a man has two wives and from each wife has two daughters — an older daughter and a younger daughter — and he says *kidashti et biti ha-gedolah*, "I betrothed my older daughter," the Gemara in Kiddushin records a dispute about which daughter is meant. The terms *gedolah she-ba-gedolot* (the older daughter of the older wife), *gedolah she-ba-ketanot* (the older daughter of the younger wife), and *ketanah she-ba-gedolot* (the younger daughter of the older wife, who is "older" only in the sense of coming from the first wife) are all plausible referents of the term *gedolah*. The only daughter clearly excluded is *ketanah she-ba-ketanot* — the younger daughter of the younger wife, who cannot by any reading be called "older."

Rabbi Meir there rules *kulan asurot chutz min ha-ketanah she-ba-ketanot* — all daughters except the youngest of the younger wife are in a state of doubtful betrothal. Rabbi Yossi rules *kulan mutarot chutz min ha-gedolah she-ba-gedolot* — only the older daughter of the older wife is presumptively betrothed, since that is the narrowest and most definite meaning of *gedolah*. In Kiddushin, then, it is Rabbi Meir who extends the ambiguous possibilities and Rabbi Yossi who restricts interpretation to the unambiguous core — precisely the reverse of what the Gemara stated above regarding *pnei haPesach*.

### Reversed Positions

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by citing Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa in the name of Rav: *muchlefa ha-shita* — the positions are transposed. In our Mishna — concerning *pnei haPesach* — Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yossi should be understood in reverse of how they were first presented. The version of the debate in Kiddushin, where Rabbi Meir expands to all ambiguous possibilities and Rabbi Yossi restricts to the most definite meaning, reflects their true and consistent positions.

### General Principle

A *Beraita* then resolves the matter by formulating a general principle: *zeh ha-kelal, kol she-zmano kavu'a, ve-amar ad pnei* — whenever something has a fixed, defined time, and one uses the phrase *ad pnei*, Rabbi Meir rules *ad sheyetze* — until it concludes — and Rabbi Yossi rules *ad sheyagia* — until it begins. This *Beraita* is consistent with the Kiddushin ruling and confirms that the *muchlefa* applies to our Mishna: in the final understanding, Rabbi Meir includes the ambiguous duration and Rabbi Yossi restricts interpretation to the clear and definite beginning point. The underlying principle, on which both cases rest, is precisely whether one assumes a speaker intends his ambiguous language to carry its full possible range of meaning or only its most restricted and uncontested sense.

# Nedarim 61

## Harvest Vows

### Intro: Harvest Terms

The mishna at the center of today's daf concerns vows that employ agricultural time-markers. If someone says *ad hakatzir* — until the time of the grain harvest — or *ad habatzir* — until the grape harvest — or *ad hamasik* — until the time of the olive pressing — the rule is *aino assur ela ad sheyagia*: the person is forbidden only until that time arrives, meaning until it begins. This in itself is not a novel ruling; it follows directly from what was established earlier regarding *ad hapesach*. The *chidush* of this mishna lies in what comes next.

The mishna introduces its *klal* before its *prat*, which is somewhat unusual. The general principle is stated as follows: *kol shezmano kavua* — anything that has a fixed time — if one says *ad sheyagia*, one is forbidden until that time arrives. But if one says *ad sheyehei*, until it "becomes," the term is interpreted to mean until it is over — *assur ad sheyeitzei*. This is the rule established for Pesach in the previous mishna. The expression *ad sheyehei* points to when the event becomes a *haya*, a thing of the past; only then is the prohibition lifted.

The contrast — and the *chidush* — is the second half: *vechol she'ein zmano kavua*, anything that does not have a fixed time. In such cases, whether one says *ad sheyehei* or *ad sheyagia*, the result is the same: *aino assur ela ad sheyagia*, one is forbidden only until the season begins. The practical illustration given is *kayitz* — the gathering in of summer fruit. Whether one says *ad hakayitz* or *ad sheyehei hakayitz*, the vow expires when people begin bringing the fruit in their baskets, *ad sheyatchilu ha'am lehachnis bekalkalot*. If, however, one explicitly says *ad sheya'avor hakayitz* — until the *kayitz* passes — then the end point is *ad sheyekaplu hamiktzo'ot*, until the harvesting knives are folded and put away.

### Fixed vs. Unfixed

The conceptual core of this mishna is the distinction between *zmano kavua* and *ein zmano kavua*. The instinctive reading of *ein zmano kavua* is that one does not know when the season begins — every year the harvest starts at a different time, and so the phrase *ad sheyehei* cannot be pointing to a known endpoint. On this reading, when one says "until it happens" about something whose beginning is uncertain, the phrase naturally denotes the onset: it hasn't happened yet, and when it happens — meaning when it starts — that is when the vow expires. By contrast, when one says *ad sheyehei hapesach*, since everyone knows precisely when Pesach begins, "until it happens" cannot mean until it starts — that is already known. It must therefore point forward to when Pesach will have already occurred, will have become a thing of the past. This reading gives the principle considerable internal logic.

### Ein Zmano Kavua

The Ran, however, offers a different explanation of *ein zmano kavua*. He understands it to mean not that the beginning is uncertain, but that the *duration* is uncertain — one does not know when it ends. On this basis, he argues that we are disinclined to interpret *ad sheyehei* as meaning "until it is over," because when the endpoint is itself indeterminate, such a reading would leave the vow without any concrete terminus. We therefore fall back on the concrete beginning point rather than an open-ended conclusion.

One might find this somewhat puzzling: after all, the beginning of the harvest is also variable from year to year, so the asymmetry is not immediately obvious. But part of the Ran's point may be that the beginning of the harvest is in fact a milestone — a recognizable moment when people go out to the fields with their baskets — while the end tapers off gradually and is never marked by a clear, collective act of cessation. The onset has a definite social character; the conclusion does not. So while both are uncertain in the abstract, the beginning is in practice more determinate than the end, and *ad sheyehei* therefore tracks the beginning rather than the indeterminate close.

### Kayitz & Fruit

The Gemara elaborates on exactly what type of fruit defines the beginning of the *kayitz* season. A *tana* teaches: *kol kalkalah sheamru kol kalkalah shel teenim* — when the mishna speaks of people bringing in the baskets, it refers specifically to baskets of figs, not grapes. The reason, as a *braita* explains, is that *kayitz* as a word connotes hand-picking, and figs are picked by hand while grapes are cut with a knife. A *braita* further states: if someone takes a vow *miperot hakayitz* — from the fruits of the *kayitz* — he is forbidden only from figs.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees: *anavim bekhlal teenim* — grapes are included in the same category as figs. His reasoning is that when grapes become very ripe and the vine's supporting tendrils dry out, they too can be picked by hand — *ki mirdedu miktetzim beyado* — and therefore they are not categorically excluded from the definition of *kayitz*.

It should be noted that in the agricultural context of the Land of Israel, figs, dates, olives, and grapes were the primary produce. That the term *kayitz* attaches specifically to hand-picked fruits in this setting reflects the cultural and linguistic context in which these vows were made.

### End of Kayitz

The mishna states that the end of the *kayitz* season is marked by the folding away of the harvesting knives: *ad sheyachpilu hamiktzaot*. A *tana* specifies that the operative threshold is *rov hamiktzaot* — most of the knives, not all. This raises an immediate difficulty. If most of the knives in a given area have been put away, but a particular field-owner has not yet finished his harvest and his workers are still active, on what basis may anyone enter that field and take fruit?

The Tosefta states: *hukplu rov hamiktzaot mutarot mishum gezel* — once most of the knives have been folded away, anything remaining in the field is no longer prohibited as theft. The reasoning is that the owner has effectively abandoned the remaining produce — he has been *mafkir* it — and it is therefore also exempt from *ma'aser*. But this logic applies cleanly only when one can say with confidence that this particular owner has relinquished his claim. The use of *rov* introduces genuine ambiguity: how does one know that this specific field falls within the majority whose owners have finished harvesting? The apparent answer embedded in the rule is that the communal practice — the fact that most workers in the region have put their tools away — effectively forces a social reality in which even those who have not formally concluded simply cannot any longer harvest. The rule seems to impose a collective endpoint even on individual holdouts, perhaps on the theory that once the season is effectively over for the region, the remaining fruit is treated as abandoned. This tension will be explored through the stories that follow.

## Rov Hamaktzaot

### Huflu Rov Rule

The halacha of *huflu rov hamaktzaot* has clear social-welfare dimensions. Its promulgation appears to have been driven in part by the rabbis themselves, who actively demonstrated its application. The field-owners, it emerges from the stories below, were not always sympathetic to the rule — some may not have fully accepted it, or may have accepted it in principle while resenting its application in practice.

### Rabbi's Story

The first story: Rabbi and Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Yehuda came to a certain place — *iklu l'hahu atra* — at the time when most of the knives had been folded away. Rabbi began eating from the fruit of the trees they passed. Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Yehuda did not eat. The owner of the field arrived and said to them: why are the rabbis not eating? The knives have been put away — *hukplu rov hamaktzaot* — go right ahead. And even so, Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Yehuda did not eat. The Gemara explains: *kasavar mishum sanyus milta hu deka'amar hai gavra* — he suspected that the field-owner was not sincere, that he was saying this out of spite or resentment rather than genuine permission. This is entirely plausible given what we saw above: if the field-owner genuinely felt that *rov hamaktzaot* obligated him to yield his fruit, he would not have said it with evident bitterness. Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Yehuda read the social cue correctly.

### Rav Chama Story

The second story: Rav Chama bar Rav Chanina came to a certain place at the same time — *bizman shehukplu rov hamaktzaot* — and he was eating. He gave some to his attendant, but the attendant would not eat. Rav Chama told him: eat. This is what Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yossi transmitted in the name of his father Rabbi Yossi — that once most of the knives have been put away, it is permitted. The attendant apparently felt uncertain about the halacha or its application; Rav Chama had to actively instruct him and cite the ruling with rabbinic authority. The point seems to be that the rabbis were not merely themselves aware of this rule but felt it important enough to actively promote, even to their own household staff. There is something almost like a public-welfare function being performed: the rule exists, and the rabbis are demonstrating it by personal example and explicit teaching.

### Rabbi Tarfon Story

The third story is the most famous and most ethically complex. A certain man found Rabbi Tarfon in his field at the time when most of the knives had been put away, eating from the produce. The man put Rabbi Tarfon into a sack, hoisted him up, and was dragging him toward the river to throw him in — evidently under the impression that he had finally caught the thief who had been stealing from his vineyard all year. Rabbi Tarfon, from inside the sack, called out: *oi lo l'Tarfon sheze horgo* — woe to Tarfon, for this man is going to kill him. Upon hearing the name, the man dropped the sack and fled.

The rest of Rabbi Tarfon's life was shadowed by anguish over this incident. As Rabbi Abahu reports in the name of Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel: *kol yamav shel oto tzaddik haya mitzta'er al davar ze* — that righteous man was distressed about this matter for the rest of his days. His stated reason was: *oi li shenishtamashti b'kitra shel Torah* — woe to me that I used the crown of Torah. He felt he had no right to invoke his identity as Rabbi Tarfon to extricate himself, that some other means should have been found.

### Kitra Shel Torah

The Gemara buttresses this with a principle stated by Rabbah bar Bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *kol hamishtamesh b'kitra shel Torah ne'ekar min ha'olam* — anyone who uses the crown of Torah for his own purposes is uprooted from the world. The proof is a *kal vachomer* from Belshatzar. Belshatzar used the sacred vessels of the Beit Hamikdash — yet those vessels, the Gemara notes, had already been de-sanctified, as derived from the verse *u'va'u vah pritzim v'chililuha*: once the Beit Hamikdash was breached, its vessels became *klei chol*. The principle *kivan she'partzu na'asu chol* — once they have been broken into, they become ordinary — is a significant halachic principle with implications in many areas, including the status of synagogues that have been seized. Nevertheless, even though the vessels Belshatzar used had already been de-sanctified, he was killed for it that very night — *babeliyo kteil Belshatzar*. The *kal vachomer*: if the Torah itself — which can *never* be de-sanctified, which is *shechai v'kayam l'olam* — is misused, *al achat kama v'kama*, how much more severe the consequence.

The Gemara then raises a difficulty: given that Rabbi Tarfon was eating *during* the permissible period of *huflu rov hamaktzaot*, why was the man attacking him in the first place? The Gemara answers: *mishum dehu havei ganvi lei anveizi kol shatah* — that man had been having his grapes stolen throughout the year by someone, and when he stumbled upon Rabbi Tarfon, he was convinced he had finally caught his thief. The legality of *huflu rov hamaktzaot* was therefore irrelevant from the man's perspective — he thought he was dealing with a year-round criminal.

This sharpens the question of Rabbi Tarfon's anguish. If the man believed Rabbi Tarfon was a common thief and would not have been persuaded by a simple offer of payment or an invocation of the halachic rule, what alternative did Rabbi Tarfon have? The Gemara answers: *mishum de'Rabbi Tarfon ashir gadol havei, havei lei le-fayaso bi-damei* — Rabbi Tarfon was a very wealthy man. He could have offered substantial compensation, enough to satisfy the man for whatever had been stolen throughout the year. He was not compelled to identify himself as a great Torah sage. That, the Gemara concludes, is what he should have tried first, and his failure to explore that avenue — reaching instead for the announcement of his identity — is what caused him lasting remorse.

## Status & Identity

### Learning Motivation

A *braita* is now cited that addresses the proper motivation for Torah study, grounding the broader discussion in the *pasuk*: *le-ahavah et Hashem Elokecha lishmoa be-kolo u-le-davkah bo* — to love God, to hear His voice, to cleave to Him. A person should not say: I will study Torah so that people will call me a *chacham*. Nor: I will study Mishnah so that they will call me *rebbi*. Nor: I will study so that I will become an elder who sits in the *yeshivah* — though this motivation is somewhat different, since it may be more about the pleasure of learning than the honor it brings. Rather, one should *lemod me-ahavah* — learn out of love. And: *ve-sof ha-kavod lavo* — in the end, the honor will come. As the *pesukim* say: *koshrem al etzbe'otecha kotvem al luach libecha* — bind them to your fingers, inscribe them on the tablet of your heart — and *deracheiha darchei no'am*, its ways are ways of pleasantness, and *etz chayim hi lamachazikim bah*, it is a tree of life for those who hold fast to it.

The teaching does not deny the well-known principle that one should always learn even *shelo lishmah*, since *mitoch shelo lishmah ba lishmah* — from learning for ulterior motives, one arrives at learning for its own sake. But the ideal, clearly, is *lishmah* — learning for love of God and devotion to the Torah itself, not for the status it confers.

### Elazar's Teaching

Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok adds: *aseh devarim leshem pa'alam* — do things for the sake of their Maker — *ve-daber bahem lishmam* — and speak of them for their own sake. *Al ta'asem atarah lehitgadel bahem* — do not make them a crown for self-aggrandizement — *ve-al ta'asem kardom lihyot oder bahem* — and do not make them an agricultural tool, a spade to dig with. The same *kal vachomer* from Belshatzar follows: Belshatzar used vessels that had already been de-sanctified and was destroyed. One who uses the crown of Torah — which is never de-sanctified — *al achat kama v'kama*.

### Rava's Position

Against this background, Rava introduces a seemingly divergent position: *shari leih le-inish le-odoei nafshieh be-atra de-la yad'ei leih* — it is permitted for a person, and specifically for a *tzurba meirabanan*, to make himself known in a place where people do not know who he is. The proof-text is the verse in which *Ovadyah* identified himself to *Eliyahu*, saying *ve-avdecha yere et Hashem mi-ne'urav* — your servant has feared God since his youth. Ovadyah was in a situation where his identity and history were directly relevant, and he made them known. So too, Rava holds, a Torah scholar who arrives in an unknown town may identify himself rather than remaining anonymous. The line between appropriate self-identification and misuse of the Torah's crown is real but not always obvious. If a scholar comes to an inn and no one knows who he is, he may let it be known. This seems qualitatively different from exploiting one's status to override a just claim against oneself — but exactly where the line falls is not immediately clear from Rava's formulation.

### Known vs. Unknown

The Gemara itself then raises the tension with the Rabbi Tarfon story: but Rabbi Tarfon also identified himself in a place where the man did not know him — and he was anguished about it for the rest of his life. The Gemara's response returns to the argument already established: *inash gadol hayah va-hava leih le-payusei bi-dmei* — he was a great and wealthy man and could have offered compensation. But this still leaves Rava's position somewhat open-ended. Is it only permissible to identify oneself when there is no alternative available? That seems like an overly narrow reading of Rava's ruling, which appears to permit self-identification more broadly.

Rava himself then addresses an apparent internal contradiction in his position. The verse says *yehalelucha zar velo picha* — let others praise you, not your own mouth. How does that square with permitting self-identification? The Gemara resolves this cleanly: *ha b'atra d'yad'i lei ha b'atra d'lo yad'i lei* — in a place where people know who you are, you need not say anything; others will establish your identity, and the information will spread on its own. But in a place where no one knows you, you may speak on your own behalf. Rava does not appear to feel fully constrained by the Gemara's treatment of the Rabbi Tarfon narrative; his position seems more permissive — that a Torah scholar is genuinely entitled to acknowledgment and to the honor that properly accrues to his station, and that making this known is not the same as *mishtamesh b'kitra shel Torah*.

### Ran's View

The Ran resolves the tension with a principled distinction. He explains: the problem with what Rabbi Tarfon did was not that he identified himself per se. In the Ran's reading, the man, upon hearing the name Rabbi Tarfon, did not let him go out of a conviction that he was innocent — he let him go because he was unwilling to harm so prominent a Torah figure, even though he still believed Rabbi Tarfon had been stealing from him all year. That is *mishtamesh b'kitra shel Torah*: using Torah status to escape the *consequences* of something one is actually being held responsible for, regardless of whether that responsibility is just or unjust.

The Ran then draws the critical line: *liftor atzmo b'chvod Torah bamah she'eino chayav bo* — to use the honor of Torah to exempt oneself from something one is genuinely not obligated to do — that is permitted. And the examples that follow in the Gemara are all cases of legitimate entitlement. A *talmid chacham* may say he will not pay the poll tax — *lo yehavna karga* — because Torah scholars are genuinely exempt from that tax. He may say his case should be heard first at the court — *sharo li tigrai bereisha* — because that is an established right of Torah scholars, derived from *u-vnei David kohanim hayu*: just as a *kohen* receives priority — *kohen notel b'rosh* — derived from *v'kidashto* and developed by the school of Rabbi Yishmael to mean priority in reading Torah, in leading *Birkat Hamazon*, and in receiving the first and finest portion — so too does a *talmid chacham* receive priority. These are not instances of misusing the crown; they are the crown's proper exercise.

The Ran thus formulates the principle as follows: a *talmid chacham* may use his status for the benefits it genuinely entitles him to, just as *kohanim* and *leviyim* are entitled to *terumah* and *ma'aser*. What he may not do is use that status to get out of something that is legitimately being claimed against him — to escape accountability under cover of Torah honor. That is the authentic misuse. This reading has an elegant coherence, though it inevitably leaves open the further question of precisely what the entitlements of a *talmid chacham* are — a question the Gemara does not fully resolve but whose general contours are suggested by the examples cited.

## Tax Exemptions

### Poll Tax Exempt

Having articulated the principle through the Ran's framework, the Gemara now turns explicitly to the material benefits to which *talmidei chachamim* are entitled. Rava states: *shari lei l'tzurba meirabanan l'meimar lo yehavna karga* — a Torah scholar may declare that he will not pay the poll tax. The scriptural basis is the verse from Ezra: *minda blo vahalach lo shalit lemirmei aleihon* — it is not permitted to impose upon them. Rav Yehuda identifies each term: *minda zu manat hamelech* — a tribute to the king; *blo zu kesef gulgaltah* — the poll tax, literally a head tax; *vehalach zu arnona* — a third category, variously interpreted. The Ran understands *arnona* as some form of obligation to provision the king and his armies when they pass through. Tosafot, drawing on Latin etymology, understands it as corvée — forced labor. The JPS translation renders the three terms as tribute, head tax, and land tax.

This exemption has ancient and widespread precedent. Religious authorities and institutions were routinely exempted from taxation by ruling powers throughout history — from the account in the Yosef narrative, through the Persian edict in Ezra, through medieval European practice in which the Church enjoyed tax-exempt status. The practical dynamic often involved negotiation: the Jewish community would establish before the governing authority that these individuals served a religious function, and the exemption would follow from the recognized status of the religious class.

### Servant of Flame

Rava adds a further ruling: *shari lei l'tzurba meirabanan l'meimra avda d'nura ana* — it is permitted for a Torah scholar to say "I am a servant of the flame," in the context of the Zoroastrian Babylonian environment where a sacred, maintained flame was central to religious worship. By saying this, one would be understood by the tax authorities as belonging to or serving the Zoroastrian priestly class, whose members were also exempt from the poll tax. The result: *lo yavina acharga* — I will not pay the poll tax. The Gemara explains: *mai ta'ama l'salukei aria d'minei ka'amar* — he is only saying this to escape the lion pressing him for money, to avoid a payment he is in principle not obligated to make.

This is a striking ruling. The declaration creates the impression in the minds of the tax collectors that the speaker is affiliated with *avodat zarah*. This is not a small or casual misrepresentation. Relevant to the broader halachic literature is the question of whether such ambiguous speech is permissible in more extreme circumstances — such as to conceal one's Jewish identity during persecution — and this Gemara has been cited in that context.

### Ran's Justification

The Ran addresses the obvious difficulty. He offers two lines of reasoning. First, *de-mucha milsa de-amar hachi le-ashtomei mikarga* — it is transparent that the speaker is only saying this to evade the tax; the statement is not a sincere confession of religious identity, and its instrumental character is evident. But evident to whom? If it is evident to the non-Jewish tax collectors, why would the stratagem work? And if it is only evident to Jewish observers, the first justification is weaker than it appears.

The Ran therefore adds: a scholar does not become suspect of *avodat kochavim* simply because tax collectors take his ambiguous statement at face value. The scholar knows he is referring to God, who is described as *eish ochlah* — a consuming fire. The phrase *avda d'nura* is technically true of every servant of God.
