People would wonder: *mah ra'ah ima shel elu le-hisgareish* — what did the mother of these girls do to cause the divorce? They might suspect improper conduct on her part, or simply that she was not a suitable wife. And the daughters, having grown up in her household, would be viewed with wariness. The *mishna* is not creating this social reality; it is reflecting it, and using it as a lever to make the husband consider whether he would have made his *neder* had he appreciated all its consequences.

If the husband says *ilu hayiti yode'a she-kein lo hayiti noder* — had I known this I would not have made the *neder* — then *harei zeh mutar*, he is released.

---

## Woman's Appearance

### Ugly Neder

The *mishna* now turns to another case, already introduced in the prior *daf*: *konam she'ani nosei plonis ke'urah* — "Konam that I will not marry so-and-so, because she is ugly." The *neder* was made on the basis of an assumed characteristic of the woman.

### True Beauty Found

If it then emerges that she is actually beautiful — *ve-harei hi na'ah* — or that he mistakenly thought she was dark-skinned and she is actually fair, or that she was short but is actually tall, the *neder* is permitted. The *mishna* clarifies the reason: this is not a case of *nolad* — a circumstance that arose after the fact — because the woman did not *become* beautiful; she *was* beautiful and he simply did not realize it. This is therefore not a change in circumstances but a fundamental error of fact.

### Neder Ta'us

The *mishna* makes explicit: *lo mipnei she-ke'urah ve-na'aseis na'ah* — it is not because she was ugly and became beautiful, which would be a *nolad* situation. Rather, *she-ha-neder ta'us* — the *neder* was fundamentally erroneous. Because the *neder* was based on a false assumption of fact, it arguably does not even require a formal *heter*; the *ta'ut* is sufficient to undo it at its root.

### R. Yishmael Story

The *mishna* then recounts a *ma'aseh*: *uma'aseh be-echad she-nadar mi-bat achoto hana'ah* — a certain man took a *neder* against deriving benefit from his niece. It was customary in that era for men to be encouraged to marry their nieces, and this *neder* was evidently a mechanism to escape that social pressure. They brought the woman to the house of Rabbi Yishmael, and he and his household beautified her — *ve-ipe'uha*. Rabbi Yishmael then said to the man: *beni, mi-zu nadarta?* — "My son, was it about this woman that you made your *neder*?" The man replied: *lav* — no, he would never have made a *neder* about a woman like this. Rabbi Yishmael permitted her.

At that moment, Rabbi Yishmael wept and said: *bnos Yisrael na'os hein, ella she-ha-aniyus menaveltan* — the daughters of Israel are beautiful, but it is poverty that makes them appear unattractive. They are underfed, unable to bathe properly, without fine clothing. And when Rabbi Yishmael died, *hayu bnos Yisrael mekonenos kinah* — all the women of Israel would recite a lamentation, a formal *kinah* of poetic wailing. They declared: *bnos Yisrael al Rabbi Yishmael bechainah* — daughters of Israel, weep for Rabbi Yishmael. This is compared to the lament over King Shaul recorded in Scripture: *bnos Yisrael al Shaul bechainah*.

---

## Nolad Analysis

### Contradiction

The *gemara* now presses on the story: *maiseh listor* — is the *ma'aseh* a contradiction? The *mishna* began by saying that the permissibility of the *neder* is not because the woman became beautiful — that would be *nolad*. Yet the *ma'aseh* describes the man being shown a woman who has been made beautiful through cosmetic intervention. It sounds precisely like a case of *nolad* — she changed after the *neder* was made.

### Missing Text

The *gemara* resolves this through *chisorei mechsara* — there are missing words in the text, and the *mishna* must be read with an implicit addition.

### R. Yishmael Nolad

The reconstruction is: Rabbi Yishmael holds that *afilu ke'urah ve-na'aseis na'ah* — even if she was ugly at the time of the *neder* and subsequently became beautiful, one may still open with this as a *petach*. Rabbi Yishmael disagrees with those who would restrict this form of release only to cases where the woman was always beautiful and the man was simply mistaken. For Rabbi Yishmael, *poschin be-nolad* — one may use a circumstance that arose later as a basis for release — even in a case like this where perhaps the change was not entirely foreseeable. This aligns him with the position associated with Rabbi Eliezer earlier in the *masechta*, who permitted *petach* through *nolad*.

### Gold Tooth

The *gemara* then specifies what the beautification actually consisted of: *shen shel cheves hayta lah* — she had a replacement tooth of some kind, presumably an unattractive prosthetic material available at the time. *Aseh lah Rabbi Yishmael shen shel zahav* — Rabbi Yishmael had it replaced with a gold tooth, and that single change transformed her appearance sufficiently that the man no longer recognized her as the woman about whom he had made his *neder*. This clarifies why the *gemara* reads the story as a *nolad* case: the woman genuinely changed after the *neder* was made, rather than always having been beautiful.

### Rabbi Yishmael's Eulogy

When Rabbi Yishmael died, the *gemara* records that a male eulogizer opened with the following *hesped*: *bnos Yisrael al Rabbi Yishmael bechainah* — daughters of Israel, weep for Rabbi Yishmael — *ha-malbishechem ve-chulei* — he who clothed you, and so forth. Interestingly, the *gemara* does not record the remainder of the verse; it trails off with *ve-chulei*. The eulogy echoes the words found in the book of Shmuel regarding the lament over Shaul — *bnos Yisrael al Shaul bechainah* — and the parallel is intentional: as Shaul provided material abundance for the women of Israel, so Rabbi Yishmael took a personal interest in the welfare and dignity of Jewish women.

---

## Bar Bavel Story

### Dialect Difference

The *gemara* concludes the *masechta* with a famous and charming *ma'aseh* that, while seemingly a departure from the halakhic discussion, connects naturally to the overarching theme of *nedarim* — the interpretation of language, the gap between what one says and what one means, and the relationship between husband and wife. A man from Babylonia — *hahu bar Bavel* — went up to *Eretz Yisrael*, where they spoke Palestinian Aramaic rather than Babylonian Aramaic. The two dialects shared vocabulary but assigned different meanings to many terms. As one might say, the two communities were separated by a common language.

### Two Hooves/Lentils

He married a local woman. He said to her: *basheli li trei talsi* — "cook me two." In Babylonian Aramaic, this meant two legs or hooves of an animal — a substantial meat dish. In Palestinian Aramaic, the word could also mean lentil beans. She cooked him two lentils. Some explain that his "two" was simply a colloquial way of saying "some," and she took him quite literally.

### Escalation

He became angry — *ratah alah*. The next day, *basheli li garriva* — "cook me a large measure of it." She understood and cooked him an enormous quantity — taking his words literally once more. His frustration mounted.

### Melon vs. Candle

He then said: *zili ayiti li trei butzini* — "go get me two." In one Aramaic dialect, *butzina* means a melon; in the other, it means a lamp or candle. She brought him two candles — *ayita lei trei shargi*.

### Breaking on Head

At his wit's end, he told her: *zili tavrinhu al reisha d'Baba* — "go break them on the head of Baba." He meant: go break them at the gate, the *bava*, take them there. At that moment, Baba ben Buta happened to be sitting by the gate — *havai yativ Baba ben Buta ad d'baba* — adjudicating a court case. She went and broke the candles on his head.

The comic structure of the passage is unmistakable: *Baba* was sitting at the *baba*, and so the husband's instruction was fulfilled in the most literal and disastrous way possible.

### Pastoral Judgment

Baba ben Buta asked her: *mah deita avat* — what did you do? She replied: *kach tzivani ba'ali* — "that is what my husband commanded me." Baba ben Buta did not react with indignation.

### Husband's Will

Instead, he said to her: *asit retzon ba'alech* — you did your husband's will. This is the great irony of the episode: she demonstrably did *not* do what her husband intended, yet she did precisely what she understood him to say. Baba ben Buta chose to reframe the entire situation as one of good intent on all sides. He then blessed her: *ha-Makom yotzi mimcha shenei vanim k'Baba ben Buta* — may God bring forth from you two sons like Baba ben Buta.

The *gemara* closes the *masechta* here with *Hadran alach ha-Ma'adir* — the concluding formula of the tractate. The placement of this story at the very end is deeply apt. The entire *masechta* of *Nedarim* has been occupied with the question of how language is interpreted — what a person means when he speaks, how we assess the scope and intent of his words, and how *beit din* navigates the gap between utterance and intention. This final *ma'aseh* distills that theme into a scene of domestic miscommunication, where no one is acting in bad faith, yet the gap between what is said and what is understood produces chaos. Baba ben Buta's response — affirming the wife's good intent, reframing the situation as one of genuine effort rather than failure, and blessing the household — models a pastoral wisdom that transcends strict textual interpretation. Everyone was trying to do the right thing; the work now is to communicate more carefully.

---

---

# Nedarim 67

## Hafarah Overview

### Transition to Hafarah

The present daf opens at the very last line of 66b, marking a shift in the tractate's focus. While the preceding *perek* was devoted largely to *hatarah* — the mechanism by which a *beis din* retroactively releases a vow — *hatarah* itself was never the subject of a direct, foundational exposition. The *gemara* never paused to ask: from where do we derive that *hataras nedarim* is possible at all? That question remains, in a sense, suspended. What the Torah does address explicitly is a related but distinct institution: *hafarah*, the annulment or voiding of vows. It is this phenomenon that forms the subject of the new *perek*.

### Basic Halachot

The Torah establishes that a woman is always, conceptually, under the authority of some man. If she is in her father's house, her father has the power to annul her vows. If she is in her husband's house, her husband has that power. The Torah assumes no independent space for a woman between these two domains. Even if she never marries and remains in her father's home well into adulthood, she is conceptually under his authority. The passage from one domain to the other is precisely *nisuin* — the physical transfer from the father's house to the husband's house.

The exception the Torah carves out is explicit: *v'neder almanah u'grushah kol asher asra al nafsha yakum aleha* — the vow of a widow or divorcee stands, because she has left both domains and no man holds authority over her.

Several additional *halachos* govern this institution. First, annulment must occur *b'yom sham'o* — on the day the relevant party hears of the vow; the precise parameters of "that day" will be discussed as the *gemara* develops. Second, alongside the act of voiding, the Torah also recognizes *hakamah* — an affirmative declaration that the vow stands. If the husband or father actively establishes the vow, the opportunity for *hafarah* is lost even within that same day.

It bears noting that Chazal, in their reading of the Torah, do introduce a concept the Torah itself does not explicitly formulate: that once a girl reaches twelve and a half (*bogeres*), she is conceptually independent of her father. The Torah knows no such temporal boundary — in the Torah's framework, a woman moves from father to husband with no intervening independent stage. That independent stage is a rabbinic conceptual development.

### Hafarah vs. Hatarah

A third foundational point concerns the structural difference between *hafarah* and *hatarah*. *Hatarah* is retroactive. It is modeled on the concept of *ta'os* — the premise that had the person genuinely understood the implications of the vow, they would never have taken it. Undoing that misunderstanding retroactively dissolves the vow from its inception, as though it had never bound. *Hafarah*, by contrast, operates *me'kan u'laba* — from this point forward. It does not reach back. The mechanism is not intellectual dissolution but the assertion of authority: the husband or father exercises dominion over the woman's commitments and declares them void. The vow was binding until that moment; it is no longer binding from that moment onward. Accordingly, if a woman violated her vow prior to her husband's *hafarah*, she has genuinely transgressed — *hafarah* cannot reach back to undo that.

### Orphan Question

One might ask: according to the Torah's framework, what of a girl whose father has died and who has not yet married? In principle, she would be independent, since she has no father to place her under authority. Chazal, however, open up an entirely different conceptual landscape. Once the category of *bogeres* is introduced — independent adult status beginning at twelve and a half — the question of the orphaned girl largely loses its urgency. A girl who has passed twelve and a half is already independent regardless of whether her father is living. The large gap that opens up between *bas mitzvah* and *nisuin*, especially as *kiddushei ketanah* became uncommon, creates an expansive zone of female independence that the Torah itself does not map.

---

## Na'arah Me'orasah

### Mishnah Statement

The *mishnah* opens: *na'ara ham'urasa aviha u'va'alah mefirin nedareha* — the adolescent betrothed girl: her father and her husband annul her vows. This is a case of a woman occupying a genuinely intermediate status. She is a *na'ara* — between twelve and twelve and a half — and thus not yet a *bogeres* who has left her father's authority. At the same time, she is *m'urasa*, betrothed through *kiddushin*, though *nisuin* has not yet occurred. Critically, *nisuin* is the act of transition, the physical movement from the father's house to the husband's house. Until that transition occurs, she remains, in the most concrete sense, in her father's domain.

The *mishnah*'s language — "her father and her husband" — is itself the subject of the entire legal and textual discussion that follows.

### Ran's Analysis

The Ran opens his commentary with a foundational observation: *afilu nedarim she-nadra b'odah penuyah* — even vows she took before the *kiddushin* can be annulled in this framework. The *arus* (groom) can participate in annulling vows that predated his entry into her life entirely — but only *b'shutfuta d'av*, in partnership with the father. Furthermore, the *mishnah*'s use of the term *na'ara* is noted as excluding the *bogeres*: once she is twelve and a half, *d'ein aviha rishus bah* — her father no longer holds authority over her, and accordingly the *arus* too cannot annul, *b'lo shutfuta d'av lo matzi meifer* — without the partnership of the father he has no capacity to act.

This is a striking conceptual point. One might have expected that the *arus*, now that the father is out of the picture, would simply step into that role. But no: the *arus*'s capacity to annul is not an independent power. It is derivative of the father's authority. Where the father has no standing, neither does the *arus*.

### Groom Annuls Pre-Betroth…

This leads directly to an important conceptual clarification. Normally, a husband who enters *nisuin* cannot annul vows his wife took before the marriage. The logic is clear: his domain begins at the moment of *nisuin*, and what preceded it was outside his purview. Why, then, can the *arus* annul vows from before the *erusin*?

The answer follows directly from the principle just established: because it is fundamentally the father who annuls. The father's authority over his daughter is not bounded by the moment of *erusin*. He was always in authority. Since the *arus* acts in partnership with the father, and since it is really the father's power that drives the *hafarah*, the temporal boundary that would limit a husband acting alone does not apply here. The *arus* is, as the Ran puts it, tagging onto the father's participation. The father is primary; the groom is secondary.

The implication is sharp: when the father is absent — whether because the girl is a *bogeres* or because the father has died — the *arus* has no role at all. His power exists only in the shadow of the father's.

### Vows Age 11+1

The category is not limited to a *na'ara* in the strict sense. The Ran notes that the same *halacha* applies to a *ketanah* who is in her twelfth year — after eleven years and one day — because there is a separate principle in *hilchos nedarim* according to which vows taken in the year preceding *bar* or *bas mitzvah* are binding. For a girl who takes a vow in that year, she is still a *ketanah*, but her vow has force, and in that case, too, both the father and the *arus* together would annul it. This demonstrates, again, that the fundamental dynamic is not the girl's maturity but the structure of whose authority she is under.

### Joint Requirement

The *mishnah* continues: *heifer ha'av v'lo heifer ha'baal, heifer ha'baal v'lo heifer ha'av, eino mufar* — if the father annulled without the husband, or the husband without the father, it is not annulled. Neither party acting alone is sufficient. The *mishnah* adds: *v'ein tzarich lomar she'kiyam echad mehem* — and it goes without saying that if one of them performed *hakamah*, actively affirmed the vow, the annulment fails.

### Gemara Parsing

The *gemara* parses this *mishnah* carefully. The statement that if the father annulled alone or the groom annulled alone it does not work is necessary, because one might have thought that either party acting alone suffices. The *gemara* therefore notes: *mahu d'teima o aviha o va'alah* — lest one read the *mishnah* disjunctively, thinking either the father or the husband may act. The *mishnah* teaches that both must act together.

But then the *gemara* questions why the *mishnah* needs to state that *hakamah* by one of them ruins the process. If neither can annul alone, how much more so when one of them actively affirms! *Hashet'a yesh lomar heifer zeh belo zeh belo klum* — if one annuls without the other it accomplishes nothing, then *kiyam echad mehem lamah li* — why state the *hakamah* case at all? The *gemara* acknowledges this and says *tzaricha* — it is necessary to teach — and proceeds to explain in what unusual case the *hakamah* provision adds something new.

---

## Affirm vs. Void

### One Voids, One Affirms

The case the *gemara* constructs is this: party A performed *hafarah*, party B performed *hakamah*. Now, ordinarily, that is the end of the story — the *hakamah* has affirmed the vow and the prior *hafarah* of A is rendered ineffective, since the two must act together and B has instead gone the opposite direction. But the *gemara* introduces a twist.

### Hatarah on Hakamah

A *hakamah* is a verbal act — a declaration that the vow stands. As such, it is subject to *hatarah*: just as a vow itself can be retroactively released through a *chacham* who demonstrates it was made in error, so too a *hakamah* made in error (*hakamah b'ta'us*) can be retroactively released. The mechanism of *hatarah* applies to the *hakamah* just as it applies to any other consequential verbal commitment.

### Hakamah Reversal Problem

So the case is: A performed *hafarah*, B performed *hakamah*, and then B went to a *chacham* and had the *hakamah* released retroactively. The obvious intuition is: fine, the *hakamah* is undone as though it never happened, so A's *hafarah* still stands — now let B add his *hafarah* and it is complete. But the *gemara* rejects this.

### Gemara Conclusion

*V'chazar hamekayem v'nish'al al hakamaso* — and the one who affirmed went and sought release from his affirmation. *Mahu d'teima mai d'meifer me'ikara hashta v'eima* — one might think that what he voided initially, he has now reversed, so we are back to square one and can proceed. *Ka mashmalan d'ba'inan sh'neihem b'vas achas* — no, the *gemara* teaches that we need both parties to perform *hafarah* together, meaning A must now perform a new *hafarah*. The *hafarah* A performed before the *hakamah* cannot combine retroactively with B's new *hafarah* now that the *hakamah* has been undone.

The logic, though terse in the *gemara*, is roughly as follows. At the moment B performed *hakamah*, A's *hafarah* became effectively inert — not merely incomplete, but drained of any halachic potential. Even if that *hakamah* is later retroactively dissolved, the *hafarah* A performed had already passed through a period in real time during which it was entirely powerless. That passage is irreversible.

The Rambam takes this even further: not only can A's prior *hafarah* not combine with B's subsequent one, but A cannot even now perform a new *hafarah*. Once A's initial *hafarah* lost its effectiveness — even if for a reason later retroactively undone — A has exhausted his single opportunity. The rationale is that you cannot perform *hafarah* a second time after the first was already done, and since the first is now spent, A is out.

### Ran's Logical Question

The Ran raises a sharp objection to the *gemara*'s ruling. The entire power of *hatarah* is retroactivity. When we say the *hakamah* has been released retroactively, we are saying that in retrospect there was never a *hakamah*. It is as though it never happened. If so, why does A's *hafarah* suffer? Looking back, there was no *hakamah* intervening. The comparison the Ran invokes: if a man betroths a woman on condition that she has no outstanding vows, and she has vows at the time, and then she subsequently obtains a retroactive *hatarah* — the *kiddushin* takes effect retroactively, because retroactively she had no vows at the moment of betrothal. Why cannot the same retroactive logic restore A's *hafarah* to full effectiveness?

### Ran's Answer

The Ran offers two lines of response. The first is conceptual: even when *hatarah* dissolves a verbal act retroactively, it does not undo the fact that the act occurred. What it undoes is the binding force of the words. The act of *hakamah* — the physical speaking of words of affirmation — remains a historical fact, even if its legal consequences are erased. That act, having occurred, may be sufficient to create an obstacle, even after its effects are dissolved.

The second line of response reflects a structural asymmetry. *Hafarah* is a peculiarly fragile kind of act. Unlike *kiddushin*, which is a concrete act with immediate independent legal force, *hafarah* is purely verbal and, when only one party has acted, is inherently incomplete — it has no standing effect until the other party joins. It is waiting, in a state of suspended potential, for its partner. An act of such tenuous and inchoate character, which passed through a period in real time where it was not merely incomplete but actively foreclosed by the *hakamah*, loses that potential permanently. The Ran acknowledges he does not fully resolve the theoretical mechanism, but the *halacha* stands: even retroactively undoing the *hakamah* does not restore A's *hafarah*.

### Why Mention Hakamah

This returns us to the *gemara*'s question: why does the *mishnah* mention *hakamah* at all, given that it "goes without saying"? The Ran answers: the simple case — where one party does *hakamah* and that is the end of the story — indeed goes without saying. But the *mishnah* introduces *hakamah* specifically to teach that *hakamah* can create an obstacle even in more complex scenarios: specifically, the case where a *hakamah* is made and then retroactively dissolved, yet still manages to block the earlier *hafarah* from combining with a later one. That *chiddush* is not obvious, and it required the *mishnah* to mention *hakamah* in order to convey it.

---

## Scriptural Sources

### Reading the Pesukim

The *gemara* now turns to the scriptural grounding of *hafarah*, and we read through the relevant *pesukim* of Parashat Matot. The section opens: *vayedaber Moshe el rashei hamatot livnei yisrael lemor zeh hadavar asher tziva Hashem* — God spoke to Moses to tell the heads of the tribes. The phrase *rashei hamatot* is noted by Chazal as a small textual peg: normally the address would be *bnei yisrael*, so the mention of tribal heads, figures of authority, provides a hint in the direction of *hatarah* — though the text itself is entirely about *hafarah*. The textual basis for *hataras nedarim* itself is a separate discussion.

The first *pasuk* addresses the general case of vowing: *ish ki yidor neder la-Hashem o hishava shevua le-esor issar al nafsho lo yachel devaro ke-chol ha-yotze mipiv ya'aseh* — a man who takes a vow or an oath to prohibit something upon himself may not violate his word; he must do as he said. This *pasuk* establishes both the positive obligation and the prohibition of *bal yachel* for vows in general. It is worth noting that both *neder* and *shevua* are mentioned here, though in the framing of making something forbidden — which has been the consistent assumption throughout the tractate, where *nedarim* are understood primarily as prohibitions placed on objects.

### Father's Role

The text then shifts: *v'isha ki tidor neder la-Hashem v'asra issar b'veit aviha b'neureiha* — a woman who takes a vow while in her father's house in her youth. The father hears the vow and the prohibition she has placed upon herself. Notably, from this point the *shevua* drops from the text entirely — a fact consistent with the tractate's sustained analysis that *nedarim* are fundamentally about making objects forbidden, which is the core function of a *neder* rather than a *shevua*.

*V'hecherish lah aviha* — if the father is silent — *v'kamu kol nedareha v'chol issar asher asra al nafsha yakum* — all her vows and prohibitions stand. His silence functions as passive *hakamah*. *V'im hini aviha osa b'yom sham'o* — but if her father *hini* (annulled) it on the day he hears — *kol nedareha v'essareha asher asra al nafsha lo yakum* — they are not established. The word *hini* is an unusual term for annulment, but the content is clear: the father has the power to void his daughter's vows, and he must exercise it on the day he hears.

*V'Hashem yislach lah* — and God will forgive her — *ki hini aviha osa*. The phrase "God will forgive her" is unexpected: she has not necessarily violated anything, since the father annulled the vow. Chazal explain: the father annulled it without her knowledge, and she subsequently violated it, believing the vow to still be in force. On the level of objective action she committed no transgression — the vow was already void. But subjectively, in her own mind and intention, she experienced herself as transgressing. It is for that psychological act, that *kavanah* of transgression, that she requires divine forgiveness even in the absence of an objective *ma'aseh aveira*.

### Husband's Role

The second paragraph begins: *v'im hayo tihye l'ish* — if she comes to be to a man. The plain sense of *tihye* in many contexts in the Torah is *nisuin*, full marriage. *V'nedareha aleha* — and her vows are upon her from before. The husband hears, is silent, and the vows stand. If he annuls on the day he hears, they are dissolved, and *V'Hashem yislach lah*.

### Widow/Divorcee

At this point the Torah inserts the case of the widow and divorcee: *v'neder almanah u'grushah kol asher asra al nafsha yakum aleha*. Having left her father's house and her husband's house, she stands under no man's authority, and her vows stand unconditionally. No one can annul on her behalf.

### Vows During Marriage

The Torah then adds a third paragraph: *v'im beis isha nadra* — if she took the vow while already in her husband's house. This is a fresh vow, taken during the marriage itself. *O asra issar al nafsha b'shavua* — or she prohibited something upon herself by oath. The husband hears, is silent, and the vow stands. *V'im haifer yaifer osam isha b'yom sham'o* — if the husband annuls them on the day he hears — *kol motza sefaseha l'nedareha v'l'issar nafsha lo yakum* — all that issued from her lips will not stand. *Isha haiferam v'Hashem yislach lah*.

---

## Redundancy Problem

### Two Nisuin Cases?

The *gemara* now confronts a fundamental problem. We have two separate paragraphs about a husband annulling his wife's vows. The second paragraph explicitly concerns vows taken *b'veit isha*, during the marriage. The first paragraph, which says *v'nedareha aleha* — her vows were already upon her — seems to describe vows predating the marriage. If both paragraphs concern a *nesuah*, a fully married woman, and if the first establishes that the husband can annul even prior vows, then the second paragraph is entirely superfluous: the case it covers is less novel and less demanding than the first.

The redundancy is what forces Chazal to read the *pesukim* otherwise. If reading them both as *nisuin* creates an impossible redundancy, then one of them must be about something different.

The Ramban, in his commentary on the *parashah*, takes note of this problem explicitly. His position is that the *peshat* of the text reads both paragraphs as referring to a *nesuah* — a fully married woman. The repetition, on a *peshat* level, is a genuine difficulty, but it is the plain sense of the words. Nevertheless, he acknowledges, Chazal have read it otherwise, and he concludes *v'hakabalah tachria* — the received tradition adjudicates. That closing phrase is telling: the Ramban is not fully satisfied, but accepts the rabbinic reading as authoritative.

### Both Nisuin Theory

The *gemara* entertains the possibility that both paragraphs address *nisuin*. If so, why would the Torah need two paragraphs? Perhaps, the *gemara* suggests, the second paragraph — *v'im beis isha nadra* — comes to teach a *chiddush* about the first: specifically, *she'ein ha'baal meifer b'kodmin* — the husband cannot annul vows that predate the marriage. The first paragraph contains the phrase *v'nedareha aleha* — her vows were upon her — and one might have thought this means the husband can reach back to prior vows. The second paragraph, by emphasizing *beis isha*, "in her husband's house," would then be a corrective: his power of annulment extends only to vows made within the marriage, not before it.

This reading attempts to make both paragraphs work together around *nisuin* without redundancy. But the *gemara* refuses to accept it. Even if the second paragraph adds the *chiddush* that prior vows cannot be annulled, one is still left asking why the first paragraph is necessary at all. If the second paragraph already tells us everything — the husband can annul vows made during marriage, and cannot annul prior ones — what does the first paragraph add? *Sof sof lamah li* — ultimately, why do I need it? The redundancy is not dissolved; it is only shifted.

### Havayah = Erusin

The *gemara* then proposes a different approach: *havayah k'kiddushin mashma* — the word *tihye* (becoming) in the phrase *v'im hayo tihye l'ish* connotes *kiddushin*, betrothal, not *nisuin*. The *gemara* in tractate *Kiddushin* draws interpretive connections between the language of *havayah* and the language of betrothal, and on that basis Chazal read the first paragraph as describing an *arusah*, a betrothed woman, not a *nesuah*.

The Ran notes that this reading is not entirely straightforward. *Havayah* can mean *nisuin* as well — it can mean both. But since it can also be read as *erusin*, and since reading it as *erusin* resolves the redundancy, Chazal adopt that reading. With the first paragraph now understood as the case of an *arusah*, and the second as the case of a *nesuah*, the two paragraphs address different situations and each is independently necessary.

### Father-Only Theory

But even granting that the first paragraph addresses an *arusah*, a question remains: the paragraph mentions only the husband (or groom). How does Chazal's conclusion — that both father *and* groom must act — emerge from a text that seems to discuss only one party?

The *gemara* entertains a position consistent with the principle that the groom has no real authority before *nisuin*: *eima av lechudei meifer* — perhaps the father alone annuls. The mention of the groom in the *pasuk* would then serve a different purpose: not to give him a positive role, but to signal that if he performs *hakamah* he can block the process. The groom's only function is as a potential obstacle, not as a necessary co-participant.

This reading has a certain logical appeal. If we know that the father is the primary authority before *nisuin* and the groom has no genuine independent standing, why should we read the *pasuk* as requiring the groom's participation? Perhaps his mention is only cautionary — beware, if he affirms the vow, the father's annulment will fail.

### Father-Only Fails

The *gemara* rejects this reading, however, by noting that it makes the first paragraph of the *parashah* — the section about a girl in her father's house before she has any *arus* — completely unnecessary. If the father can annul alone even when there is an *arus*, how much more obviously can he annul when there is no *arus* at all. *Hashta yesh lomar bimkom arus meifer av lechudei* — if in the presence of a groom the father acts alone — *shelo bimkom arus mibaya* — is it necessary to tell me about the case without a groom? Of course the father's authority is established in the simpler case; you would never need to state it first.

The Ran explains what the *gemara* is driving at: the Torah clearly intends the opening section about the father to be a necessary teaching, not a redundant prelude. If the father-alone theory were correct, that opening section would be logically dependent on — and derivable from — the more complex *arus* case, which is backwards. You establish simple cases before complex ones; you do not require a complex case to be stated first in order to understand a simple one.

---

## Partnership Model

### Groom-Only Reading

The *gemara* now reverses course entirely and tests the opposite extreme: *eima arus lechudei meifer* — perhaps the groom alone annuls, with no need for the father. This is actually far closer to the *peshat* of the *pesukim*. The text speaks of the husband's role; if we are reading the first paragraph as *erusin*, then the plain sense is that the groom holds the authority. Perhaps the mention of the father in the structure of the *parasha* is merely contextual, and the groom, now that she is *m'urasa*, is the sole relevant authority.

### Husband Case Objection

But this reading too generates a redundancy problem. If the groom can annul entirely without the father, then the case of the *nesuah* — the fully married woman, *beis isha* — follows *kal vachomer*: if the groom can do it even when she is still conceptually in her father's house, then certainly the husband can do it after *nisuin* when she is fully under his authority. There would be no need for the Torah to state the husband's case separately.

*U'mah bimkom av arus meifer lechudei* — if in the presence of a father the groom annuls alone — *shelo bimkom av mibaya* — when the father is entirely out of the picture after *nisuin*, is it even a question? The *nesuah* paragraph would be entirely derivable by *kal vachomer* and would serve no independent purpose.

### Husband Limitation

The *gemara* attempts to rescue the groom-only reading by suggesting that the *nesuah* paragraph adds a genuine *chiddush* even in this framework: *she'eino meifer b'kodmin* — the husband cannot annul prior vows, only those made during the marriage. This would distinguish the *nesuah* case from the *arus* case, since the *arus* — acting in the context of a woman still fundamentally in her father's house — can reach prior vows.

But this response, the *gemara* observes, actually creates a new difficulty. If the *nesuah* paragraph's function is to teach that the husband cannot annul prior vows, then implicitly the *arus* paragraph teaches the opposite — that the *arus* can. But that implication of the first paragraph would then itself be informative in a way that makes the reader wonder: why can the *arus* do something the husband cannot? The answer, as we know, is *shutfuta d'av* — it is really the father doing it. But if that is the answer, the groom-only reading cannot be correct, because the father's involvement is the very explanation for the *arus*'s extended capacity. *Ela lav mishum shutfuta d'av* — is this not precisely because of the father's partnership?

### Shutfuta Resolution

The only reading that resolves all the tensions simultaneously is the *shutfuta* model: neither the father alone nor the groom alone, but both together. Each paragraph then serves an independent purpose: the first establishes the unique joint requirement for the *na'ara me'urasa*, and the second establishes the husband's independent but limited authority after *nisuin*. Neither is redundant, and neither is derivable from the other.

### Father's Fundamentality

Even within the *shutfuta* framework, it is essential to understand that the partnership is not between equals. The father remains the primary authority. The evidence is structural: when the father is absent — when the girl is a *bogeres* or the father has died — the *arus* can accomplish nothing at all. The *hafarah* is fundamentally the father's act; the groom participates but does not initiate. The reason the *arus* can annul vows predating the *erusin* is precisely this: since it is really the father's authority being exercised, temporal boundaries linked to the groom's entry into her life are irrelevant.

The final word of *b'yom sham'o* governs the entire structure. Anything heard more than a day before — whether heard by the father before the *kiddushin* or by both parties at different times — has already achieved its finalized status: either it was passively established by the father's silence or actively annulled. The groom's role pertains only to matters still within the window of *yom sham'o* at the time both parties are in a position to act. These complexities of timing — whose clock governs, what happens when the father hears on one day and the groom hears a week later — will be developed as the *perek* continues.

What this *perek* establishes at its outset is a new halachic reality, one the *pesukim* do not state plainly and that required Chazal to work carefully through the verses' apparent redundancy to uncover. The *arus* is given any role at all only because of his connection to the father's authority — and that is why the *parasha* cannot be reduced either to the father alone or to the groom alone. It is the *shutfuta*, the partnership, that the Torah encodes — with the father as the fundamental and primary partner, and the groom as the necessary but secondary one.

---

---

# Nedarim 68

## Review: Father-Husband

### Na'arah Status

Today's daf is 68. As with yesterday, there is relatively little *gemara* text here — much of the page is occupied by *Ran* — and the substantive *halachic* discussion follows closely in the spirit of what we saw on the preceding daf.

By way of review: the *mishnah* introduces the case of a girl who has not yet reached *bogeret* status, meaning she is still a *na'arah* — or in some circumstances even a *ketanah* whose *neder* is halakhically binding. Such a girl is considered, both physically and, more importantly, *halachically*, to be in her father's house. This remains true even after *kiddushin*, and continues until *nissu'in* — until the formal transfer at *chuppah* when she fully enters her husband's domain.

### Darsha Method

Nevertheless, *Chazal* read one of the *parashiyos* in the *Torah* that discusses the husband or father annulling a *neder* in a striking way. That *parasha* is understood to describe a case where the father and husband are *partners* in the act of *hafara* — specifically when the girl is a *na'arah murasah*, a betrothed minor. One might have expected that in this period, since she is still legally in her father's house, the father alone would hold the power of *hafara*. Yet *Chazal* read the *Torah* to teach that the husband participates as well, and that the two together annul the vow.

### Two Principles

Counterintuitively, however, even though the *parasha* the *gemara* draws upon speaks primarily of the husband, the father remains the primary and more central figure. Two important consequences flow from this. First, the *hafara* applies even to vows that predate the *kiddushin*, because it is fundamentally the father's authority that is operative. Second, if the girl has no father — if she is a *yesomah* with *kiddushin* — the husband alone cannot annul the *neder*. The father is indispensable.

---

## Two Categories

### Braita Reading

At the top of 68a, the *gemara* cites a *braita*: *tanya devei Rabbi Ishmael* — from the school of Rabbi Ishmael the following was taught. The *pasuk* reads: *bein ish l'ishto bein av l'vito b'neureha beis aviha* — "between a man and his wife, between a father and his daughter, in her youth in her father's house." The question is posed: the *Torah* has already stated *av l'vito* — why add *b'neureha beis aviha*? The plain reading of the *pasuk* would be that the section about the father applies when she is in his house, and the section about the husband applies after she marries. What, then, is the additional phrase teaching?

The *braita* answers: *mikan l'na'arah murasah she'aviha u'va'alah mefirin nedareha* — from here we derive the case of the *na'arah murasah*, whose father and husband together annul her vows. The *pasuk* is read not as describing two mutually exclusive scenarios but as identifying a single case that is simultaneously *bein ish l'ishto* and *bein av l'vito* — when she is a *na'arah* in her father's house who also has a husband. That is the *na'arah murasah*.

The *gemara* then asks: according to this *tanna* of the school of Rabbi Ishmael, what does he do with the other *pasuk* — *v'hayah tihyeh l'ish v'nedareha aleiha*? The answer is that he uses it for the other teaching of Rabbah, which we will encounter in approximately two *dafim*. That *drasha* addresses the case where one *arus* dies and she subsequently becomes betrothed to another: the double language of *v'hayah tihyeh* signals that the father's full authority over her — which he exercised before the first betrothal — is restored in the interval before the second.

### Inuy Nefesh

The *gemara* proceeds to ask: and what does Rabbah himself do with the *pasuk* of *bein ish l'ishto bein av l'vito*? The answer is that he uses it to derive a crucial *halacha* about the scope of the husband's power of *hafara*: what categories of vows can a husband annul?

The *Torah* repeatedly employs the phrase *le'esor issar al nafshah* — to make something forbidden upon herself — and the related *issar le'annot nefesh*, which refers to a type of self-denial or self-affliction. This is the same root used on *Yom Kippur* — *te'anu et nafshoteichem*. This explicit language establishes *inuy nefesh* — affliction-type vows — as one category the husband may annul.

### Devarim Shebeino

The second category is not stated explicitly but is derived. There are vows that do not rise to the threshold of *inuy nefesh* but that directly affect the dynamics of the husband-wife relationship. For example, she takes a vow that forbids her certain garments or modes of personal appearance. That may not constitute *inuy nefesh* in the strict sense, yet it plainly affects the marital relationship. For this second category — *devarim she'beino l'veinah*, matters between them — the *Torah*'s phrase *bein ish l'ishto* serves as the source. Thus the two categories the husband may annul are: *inuy nefesh* and *devarim she'beino l'veinah*.

### Ran vs. Rambam

An interesting question now arises: do these same two categories — and hence the same *limitations* — apply to the father as well? Or is the father's authority over his daughter absolute, unlimited by category?

The *Ran* cites the *Yerushalmi* explicitly. The *Yerushalmi* asks: we know that *inuy nefesh* vows fall under the husband's power, and that *devarim she'beino l'veinah* are derived from *bein ish l'ishto* — but what is the source for the father? The *Yerushalmi*'s answer is precise: just as the husband may only annul vows of *inuy nefesh* and *devarim she'beino l'veinah*, so too the father may only annul vows in those same two categories. The *Ran* states this explicitly.

The *Rambam*, however, takes a different position. In his view, the father's authority over his daughter is categorical and unlimited — he may annul any *neder* she takes, without restriction to these two categories. This is not made explicit in the *Bavli*, and the *Rambam* understands the father's control to be absolute. As the *Ran* notes, this is a direct *machloket Rishonim*, and it presumably reflects a deeper question about the extent of parental and spousal authority as understood by *Chazal*.

---

## Hafara Mechanics

### Question Setup

The *gemara* now raises a conceptual question about the mechanics of *hafara* in this partnership: *ba'al megez gayiz o miklesh kalesh?* When the husband — or, by extension, either partner — performs *hafara*, does he *cut off* half of the *neder*, or does he merely *weaken* it?

The *megez gayiz* position holds that each partner's act of *hafara* has an independent and concrete effect: each one cuts off his half. Under this view, if one partner does *hafara* and the other does not, something real has been accomplished — half the *neder* has been annulled, even if the other half remains. The *miklesh kalesh* position holds instead that the act of *hafara* by one party weakens the *neder* as a whole but does not sever a portion of it. The entire *neder* remains, just in a diminished state.

### Two Olives Case

The *gemara* illustrates the practical stakes with a concrete case. Suppose she took a vow not to eat two specific olives. The *arus* heard and performed *hafara*. She then ate both olives. If *megez gayiz* is correct — if he cut off half — then his *hafara* effectively released her from the prohibition on one of the two olives. She thus remained forbidden in one olive, ate it, and would be liable to *malkos*. But if *miklesh kalesh* is correct — if he only weakened the *neder* — then the entire prohibition remained in some attenuated form, and eating both olives would constitute a violation, but not one of sufficient weight to generate *malkos*.

### Student Challenge

One might raise a more fundamental objection: why assume that either partner's *hafara* has any independent effect at all? The structure of the partnership might suggest that nothing occurs until *both* parties act — like a system that requires two keys to be turned simultaneously before anything happens. If one key is turned without the other, nothing changes. This challenge is a serious one, and the *gemara* does not address it conceptually. Instead, it brings a *braita* as a proof-text and resolves the question from there.

---

## Father as Anchor

### Principle Statement

The *braita* opens by articulating the foundational principle: *met ha-ba'al nidrokna reshut la'av; met ha'av v'lo nidrokna reshut la'ba'al* — when the husband dies, his authority empties out to the father; when the father dies, his authority does not transfer to the husband. This is simply another formulation of the theme we have been developing: the father is the *anchor* of the *hafara* partnership. If the husband dies, full control reverts to the father — who was always the primary party anyway. But if the father dies, the husband is left without the essential partner, and his own rights cannot stand alone.

### Husband Dies Case

The *braita* now unpacks when it is that the husband's death empties his authority to the father. The answer: *bizman she-lo shama ha-ba'al kodem she-yamut* — when the husband had not heard the *neder* before he died, or when he heard and was silent, or when he heard and actively performed *hafara*.

### Three Scenarios

Three scenarios are thus identified where the husband did nothing problematic prior to dying. First, he never heard the *neder* at all. Second, he heard but died within that same day — meaning his silence never extended to a full period that would constitute *kiyum*. Third, he heard and actively performed *hafara*. In all three cases, he either did nothing or did nothing harmful, and the father may now take full control and annul the *neder*.

### Kiyum Problem

There are, however, two bad scenarios. The first is that the husband heard and performed an explicit *kiyum* — he actively confirmed the *neder*. The second is that he heard, remained silent for a full day's period, and then died — making his silence effectively a *kiyum* by inaction, a kind of pocket *kiyum*. In either of these cases, *ein yachol le-hafer* — even though he has now died and the father is the anchor, the husband has already put a stop to the possibility of *hafara*. That cannot be undone.

---

## Father Dies Case

### Father Hafara

The *braita* now turns to the reverse scenario: the father dies and the husband cannot annul, even when the father had already performed active *hafara*. The case: the father heard the *neder* and performed *hafara*, but the husband did not hear about it before the father died. One might reason that this case is particularly strong for the *neder* being annulled — the husband was not yet in the picture at all, the father alone acted, and the father did everything he was supposed to do. Perhaps the husband can now simply finalize what was all but completed?

The *Ran* notes that the *chidush* here is precisely to reject this reasoning. Despite the father having performed his *hafara*, despite the husband being entirely absent and peripheral, *met ha'av lo nidrokna* — the rights do not pass to the husband. The father is the anchor, and the *hafara* requires the father's presence all the way through. If the father dies, there is no completion. The husband cannot finish what the father began.

### New Vow

If she takes an entirely new *neder* after the father has died, the husband similarly cannot annul it — not until *nissu'in*. This is a point that underscores how thoroughly the husband's *hafara* authority is contingent on the father. Even if the two of them were the only parties involved, and she makes the *neder* after *kiddushin* but before *nissu'in*, he has no independent standing to annul. And even once they do marry and *nissu'in* occurs, he cannot annul retroactively a *neder* from before *nissu'in*, because retroactive *hafara* of prior vows is not within his power at that point.

### Partnership Required

The *braita* continues with a case that uses the explicit language of *shutafut*: *she'ein ha-ba'al meifer ela b'shutafut* — the husband can only annul as part of a *partnership* with the father. Here the father heard the *neder* and performed *hafara*, but the husband had not heard, and then the father died. Since the vow was taken while both the father and the husband were in the picture — even if the husband had not yet engaged with it — there remains a portion of the *hafara* that conceptually belongs to the husband. The father cannot supply that on his own after the husband's death, and certainly the husband cannot supply the father's portion. Without the *shutafut*, the *hafara* is incomplete.

---

## Father Takeover

### Scenario Setup

The *braita* now reaches its final and most complex case. The father heard the *neder* and performed *hafara*. The husband, however, died without ever having heard the *neder* at all — not just without having responded to it, but without even knowing it existed. This is an extreme case of the husband's non-involvement. One might argue that since he was never in the picture at all, the father's *hafara* should simply operate as though there were no husband — as the dominant and essentially exclusive party.

### Shammai v. Hillel

This case is disputed by *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel*.

### Shammai View

*Beis Shammai* holds: *chozer ha-av u-meifer chelko shel ba'al* — the father goes back and annuls the husband's portion. Notably, even *Beis Shammai* does not say the *neder* is simply annulled automatically now that the husband is gone. Rather, there is still a distinct act required: the father must perform an additional *hafara* specifically for the portion that would have been the husband's. Since the *neder* was taken while there was a *arus*, there is a portion of it that had been under his purview. Even though he never acted on it, that portion was not dissolved by the father's initial *hafara*. Upon the husband's death, the father now assumes that right and can annul it with a further act.

### Rabbi Natan

Rabbi Natan clarifies: this is the position of *Beis Shammai*, not *Beis Hillel*.

### Hillel View

*Beis Hillel* says: *ein yachol lehafer* — the father cannot annul the husband's portion. According to *Beis Hillel*, when the groom was in the picture and died, the right that was his does not simply pass to the father. Nobody now steps into the groom's role, and consequently the *neder* cannot be fully annulled. The girl remains bound by it — which, as one might note, may in some cases actually be her preference.

---

## Shma Mina

### Conclusion

The *gemara* now returns to its original question about *hafara* mechanics and draws the answer directly from this *machloket*. *Shma mina leBeis Shammai megez gayiz, leBeis Hillel miklesh kalesh* — we may conclude from this debate: *Beis Shammai* holds *megez gayiz*, that each party's *hafara* cuts off his half; *Beis Hillel* holds *miklesh kalesh*, that each party's *hafara* merely weakens the *neder* as a whole. *Shma mina* — this is the resolution.

### Ran Explanation

The *Ran* explains what precisely is at stake in each position, and why the *macholoket* about *hafara* mechanics maps onto the *macholoket* about whether the father can take over the husband's portion. The key concept the *Ran* introduces is *yerusha* — inheritance or transfer of rights. The question of whether the father can step into the husband's role is modeled on whether a *right* can be transferred, which in turn depends on whether that right is sufficiently concrete and substantial to function like a transferable object.

### Shammai Logic

According to *Beis Shammai*, the father's initial *hafara* annulled precisely his half — *chelko bilvad*. The husband's half was entirely unaffected — *lo nigrah klal* — it remained completely intact. That means there is something whole and substantial that was the husband's: the full right to annul the *neder* with respect to his portion, equivalent to one of the two olives in the earlier example. Because that right is intact and concrete — *chashuv hu* — it can be transferred and inherited by the father when the husband dies.

### Hillel Logic

According to *Beis Hillel*, when the father performed *hafara*, he did not sever a clean half. Rather, he weakened the *neder* as a whole — *miklesh kalesh* — affecting both portions together. What the husband is left with is therefore not a full, intact right to annul his half, but merely the right to act on a vow that has already been weakened. That is not substantial enough to constitute a transferable object — *eino chashuv lehorisho la'av*. Furthermore, since the father is still alive when this weakening occurs, his own portion of the *hafara* has not yet fully taken effect either; the *neder* sits in a weakened state. A weakened right is all the more incapable of being transferred, and thus the father cannot inherit it.

The *Ran* articulates the underlying model clearly: we are using the framework of *yerusha* — of transmissible rights — and for that framework to apply, the thing being transferred must be sufficiently object-like. A half-annulment that is whole and concrete can be conceptualized as a thing and passed on. An attenuation of the whole, with no clean half belonging to anyone, cannot.

---

---

# Nedarim 70

## Father & Groom Partnersh…

### Father's Death

The present *mishna* returns to the fundamental dynamic of the partnership between a father and an *arus* in annulling vows, after the preceding discussion of *hafarah* and *hakamah* performed in sequence. The *mishna* states: *meit av, lo nisroknah reshut l'baal* — if the father dies, his authority does not transfer to the husband. The underlying principle is that the father is the anchor of the entire annulment process. Even if the father has already performed his portion of the *hafarah*, the *arus* cannot complete it on his own, because the *hafarah* is fundamentally grounded in the father's presence and participation. Without the father, the process cannot be concluded.

### Groom's Death

The converse, however, obtains in the opposite direction: *meis habaal, nisroknah reshut l'av* — if the *arus* dies, his authority transfers back to the father. Whether the *arus* had already annulled his portion or had not yet done so, the father may now either complete the annulment or perform it in its entirety. The one exception is if the *arus* had performed *hakamah* before dying — in that case, the vow is confirmed and nothing further can be done. The asymmetry is telling: the father can absorb the *arus*'s role, but the *arus* cannot absorb the father's, because at bottom it is the father who is the principal actor.

### Power Comparison

The *mishna* then draws the comparison explicitly: *b'zeh yafeh koach ha'av mikoach habaal* — in this respect, the power of the father exceeds that of the *arus*. But then the *mishna* turns in a surprising direction: *b'davar acher yafeh koach habaal mikoach ha'av* — in another matter, the power of the *arus* exceeds that of the father. In what respect? *Shehabaal meifer b'bogeres, v'av eino meifer b'bogeres* — the *arus* can annul the vow of a *bogeres* (a young woman who has passed twelve and a half years of age), whereas the father cannot. The father's inability is readily understandable: once she becomes a *bogeres*, she is no longer *bi'neureiha beis aviha*, no longer subject to her father's household authority. But why does the *arus* have this power? We have been emphasizing throughout that the *arus* has no independent authority of his own — his power derives entirely from piggybacking on the father. If there is no father in the picture, either because she is a *bogeres* or because she is a *yesomah*, the *arus* should have no standing to annul. This question will be addressed momentarily.

### Verse Derivation

The *gemara* begins by asking the source for the rule that when the father dies, the *arus* cannot complete the annulment. The answer is the verse *bi'neureiha beis aviha* — in her youth, in her father's house. This phrase establishes that she is fundamentally located in her father's domain; the *arus* is an adjunct to that arrangement, not its foundation. Consequently, even if the father performed his part and then died, his absence renders the entire process incomplete.

On the other side, the *gemara* asks: from where do we know that when the *arus* dies, the father may take over even the *arus*'s share — not merely complete his own portion, but absorb the *arus*'s role entirely? Rabba answers from the verse *ve'im hayo tihyeh l'ish u'nedareiha aleiha* — "and if she shall come to be married to a man, and her vows are upon her." The doubling of *hayo tihyeh* — "having been" and "shall be" — is read as encompassing the case of successive marriages: she was betrothed to a first man, he died, and now she is to be betrothed to a second. The *gemara* derives from this that the father's rights before the second betrothal (*kodem havayah sheniyah*) are equivalent to his rights before the first betrothal (*kodem havayah rishonah*). Before groom number one appeared, the father had complete and sole authority to annul. So too, in the interval between groom number one's death and groom number two's arrival, the father's authority is once again complete.

### Rights Transfer

The *gemara* immediately presses this derivation with an objection. The analogy holds cleanly for vows that were never under the *arus*'s auspices — vows made after groom number one died, or vows he simply never heard of. Before groom number one entered the picture, the father's authority was unlimited and unencumbered. If the parallel is to vows equally free of prior entanglement, then of course the father's authority is complete in that parallel period. But what of vows that groom number one actually heard? In that situation, some residual dimension of the *arus*'s authority had attached to those vows. How do we know that, upon his death, it is specifically the father who inherits that dimension of authority?

The *gemara* resolves this elegantly. If the *pasuk* were needed only to tell us that vows the *arus* never heard revert to the father, it would be unnecessary — that ruling already follows from *bi'neureiha beis aviha* alone. A betrothed girl whose *arus* dies without having heard the vow remains *beis aviha* in every relevant sense, and the father's authority is self-evident. The very fact that the *pasuk* is needed to teach something implies it is teaching something non-obvious: namely, that even vows the *arus* had heard and over which he had authority revert to the father upon his death. The father is empowered to annul them in full.

## Groom Heard Vow

### Analogy Challenge

With the principle now established that the father's authority is restored upon the *arus*'s death even regarding vows the *arus* had heard, the *gemara* examines the analogy underpinning this ruling more carefully. The *hayo tihyeh* derivation equates the father's position before the second betrothal with his position before the first. But this analogy is most naturally read as applying to vows that were never under the first *arus*'s authority — since before the first betrothal, no *arus* had ever been in the picture at all. Does the analogy genuinely extend to vows that passed through the first *arus*'s *reshut*?

### Case Distinction

The *gemara* therefore entertains the possibility that the analogy should be read narrowly: *eima hanei milei bi-nedarim she-lo nir'u la-arus* — perhaps the father's restored authority applies only to vows that the first *arus* never heard. In those cases, there is a clean structural parallel: before groom number one, the father had full authority over vows made without any *arus* involvement; before groom number two, he has full authority over vows equally unrelated to groom number one. The cases are genuinely analogous.

But what of vows that the first *arus* did hear, over which he had some degree of control? One might argue that those vows carry a residual character different from vows that were always purely within the father's domain, and that the death of the first *arus* does not straightforwardly restore the father's authority over that peculiar category.

### Groom's Residual Rights

The *gemara* dismisses this concern, and its reasoning is important. If the *pasuk* were only needed to cover vows that the *arus* never heard, it would be superfluous — that ruling is already derivable from *bi'neureiha beis aviha* without any additional verse. A girl whose *arus* dies and whose vows he never heard about is simply back to being fully in her father's house; no new derivation is required. The *pasuk* must therefore be addressing a case not already covered — namely, vows the *arus* had heard and over which he had exercised some authority. The ruling is that even for those vows, the father's authority is restored in full upon the *arus*'s death.

This reinforces the conceptual framework that has been building throughout: the *arus*'s participation in the annulment process is not a free-standing right but a conditional one, wholly dependent on the father's continued presence and authority. When the *arus* dies, there is no independent *reshut* of his that persists or passes to another party independently — it simply dissolves back into the father's comprehensive authority.

## Bogeres Anomaly

### Groom > Father

We turn now to the second half of the *mishna*'s comparison: the case in which the *arus* has greater power than the father. The *mishna* states that the *arus* can annul the vow of a *bogeres* while the father cannot. This is genuinely puzzling. We have established that the *arus* has no independent *reshut* — his power is entirely derivative of the father's. How, then, can he have any authority in a case where the father has none?

### No Father Present

The *gemara* first considers the possibility that the case involves a woman who was betrothed while already a *bogeres* — that is, the father was never in the picture to begin with. If there was no father present at the time of the *erusin*, perhaps the *arus*'s authority does not need to piggyback on anything and stands on its own.

### Groom's Lack of Power

The *gemara* rejects this attempted resolution, and it should, because the logic does not hold. The absence of the father from the picture does not generate any new authority in the *arus*. We have established that even in cases where the father is gone — whether because he died or because she was always a *yesomah* — the *arus* as such has no power to annul vows. His authority arises only in conjunction with the father's. Simply removing the father does not fill the vacuum with *arus* authority; it leaves a vacuum. So the question remains: what is the source of the *arus*'s power over a *bogeres*?

## Later Mishna Reference

### 73b Mishna

To resolve the *bogeres* anomaly, the *gemara* points to a later *mishna* on 73b. The principle embedded in the current *mishna* is, in effect, borrowed from that later context, and understanding the later *mishna* is necessary to make sense of what appears here.

### R. Eliezer's View

The *mishna* on 73b addresses the case of a *bogeres* who waited twelve months after betrothal, or a widow who waited thirty days. Rabbi Eliezer rules: *hoil u'baal chayav bi'mezonoseha, yafeir* — since the husband is already obligated to provide for her sustenance, he may annul her vows. Rabbi Eliezer's position is that the arrival of the time designated for *nisuin* — the point at which the husband becomes financially responsible for her even though the marriage has not yet technically been consummated — is sufficient to grant him the annulment authority of a husband.

### Financial Obligation

The reasoning underlying Rabbi Eliezer's position, as the *gemara* explains it, is that once the husband has begun bearing the financial obligations of marriage, and the expected time of *nisuin* has arrived, the woman's vows are implicitly made with an understanding that her husband's acceptance is a condition of their binding force. He is now in a relationship of financial responsibility toward her, she knows she is about to enter *nisuin*, and in that context her vows carry an implicit *tnai* of spousal consent. Rabbi Eliezer is therefore prepared to treat her as effectively *nesuah* for purposes of *hafarah* from the moment those conditions obtain.

### Chakhamim Disagree

The *chakhamim* reject this position: *ein habaal meifer ad shetikanes lireshuto* — the husband does not have annulment power until she has actually entered into his domain through *nisuin*. Financial obligation alone, however significant, does not substitute for the formal entry into the marital relationship. On this view, the *arus* has no authority as *arus* regardless of how long the betrothal has persisted, and the arrival of the expected time of *nisuin* changes nothing legally.

## Mishna's Purpose

### Teaching Location

This raises the question: why does our *mishna* on 70a mention the *bogeres* case at all, given that the fuller treatment — including the time periods, the case of the *almana*, and the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and the *chakhamim* — belongs to the *mishna* on 73b? The *gemara* notes the apparent redundancy: *hasnina chada zimna* — we have taught this once already (or will teach it in its proper place), so why mention it here?

Before answering, the *gemara* first refines what the *bogeres* case in the later *mishna* actually means. The later *mishna* mentions a *bogeres* who waited twelve months. But the *gemara* objects: twelve months is the waiting period applicable to a *katana* or *na'arah* — a girl under twelve and a half. By a *bogeres*, the time of *nisuin* is expected to arrive much sooner, within thirty days. Why, then, does the later *mishna* attach the twelve-month figure to the *bogeres*? The *gemara* resolves this by reading the two conditions disjunctively: either she is a *bogeres* — in which case thirty days suffice — or she is a *katana* or *na'arah* who has waited the twelve months. The *mishna* on 73b is listing two parallel paths to the same legal threshold, not applying twelve months to the *bogeres* specifically.

### Parallel Structure

The *gemara* then offers two possible answers to the question of why the *bogeres* is mentioned in our *mishna* here rather than only in its natural location. The first answer is *ee ba'is eima hacha davka*: here in our *mishna* the mention of the *bogeres* is in fact the primary teaching, offered in a compressed form, and the later *mishna* on 73b then elaborates with the full details — the time periods, the *almana*, the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the *chakhamim* — that clarify precisely when this rule applies and according to whom. The second answer inverts this: *ve-ee ba'is eima*, the real and proper location for teaching the *bogeres* law is the later *mishna* on 73b, where the full discussion naturally belongs. Our *mishna* mentions it only incidentally — *ve-aydi de-nasiv reisha bazeh nasiv nami seifa bazeh* — because our *mishna* was structured around the phrase *bazeh yafeh koach ha'av mikoach habaal*, and the redactor wanted a parallel clause in the form *bazeh yafeh koach habaal mikoach ha'av*. To supply that parallel, our *mishna* borrowed the *bogeres* case from the later *mishna*, which is its true home.

### Conceptual Summary

The conceptual upshot must not be lost in these structural observations. The *arus* by himself has no independent power whatsoever. Even if the father is dead, even if she is a *bogeres*, even if he is the only man in her life — as *arus*, he has no *reshut* to annul her vows. His authority exists only as a piggyback on the father's authority. The single exception — and it is Rabbi Eliezer's position, disputed by the *chakhamim* — is when the time of *nisuin* has arrived. At that point, Rabbi Eliezer is prepared to treat her as effectively *nesuah* and to grant the husband full annulment power. A question that will require attention when the *mishna* on 73b is reached directly: if a *katana* reaches the time of *nisuin* according to Rabbi Eliezer, does the father still participate? When it is a *bogeres* with no father in the picture, the husband's full power at the time of *nisuin* is clean and unencumbered. But where the father is still legally present — because she has not reached *bagrus* — does Rabbi Eliezer's grant of husband-like power to the *arus* operate alongside or in place of the father's role? That question remains open.

## Successive Betrothals

### Multiple Divorces

The *gemara* now introduces a new scenario that pushes the logic of the father's authority further. A woman makes a *neder*, is betrothed (*arusa*), then divorced and re-betrothed — and this happens multiple times, even up to a hundred times in a single day (*bo bayom*). The stipulation that everything occurs on the same day is not incidental. Someone — either the father or the first *arus* — has heard the vow, the twenty-four-hour window has begun, and all the subsequent betrothals and divorces occur within that same window before the clock expires on whoever has not yet performed the annulment.

### Last Groom Powers

The *halakha* stated in the *mishna* is: *afilu l'meiah, aviha u'va'alah ha'acharon mefirin nedareha* — even if there were a hundred such betrothals and divorces, it is the father and the last *arus* together who annul her vows. The last *arus* in the chain is the one who participates in the annulment process, not any of the intermediate ones. And crucially, the last *arus* participates in annulling vows over which he was never directly a party — vows that groom number one may well have heard, over which groom number one had some authority, and which passed through potentially dozens of subsequent betrothals before reaching him.

### Father-Focused Logic

This result is, on reflection, powerful evidence that the entire framework is father-centered. What does groom number ten have to do with vows she made under groom number one? Nothing, in any direct sense. But viewed through the lens we have been developing, the answer becomes clear. Those vows were never really under groom number one's authority in any primary sense — they were always fundamentally under the father's authority. The *arus* at any stage is simply the individual who happens to be betrothed to her at the time of the annulment and who therefore joins the father in the process. Whether it is groom number one or groom number ten is irrelevant to the structure, because neither groom is the foundation; the father is the foundation. Groom number ten joins the father in the annulment the same way groom number one would have — not because he has any special connection to those vows, but because he is the current *arus* piggybacking on the father's authority.

### Continuous Control

The *mishna* then articulates the governing principle: *zeh haklal, kol she-lo yatz'ah li-reshut atzmah sha'ah achat* — the rule is that as long as she has never attained independent status for even a moment, the father retains continuous control. What would constitute independence for such a moment? Entry into *nisuin* followed by divorce or the husband's death; the death of the father himself; or the attainment of *bagrus*. If none of these has occurred — if she has passed through an unbroken chain of betrothal, divorce, and re-betrothal without ever exiting the father's domain — then *aviha u'va'al acharon mefirin nedareha*: the father and the current *arus* together annul her vows, regardless of how many intermediate *arusim* there have been.

## Verse Derivation

### Derivation Question

Having established the *halakha*, the *gemara* asks the obvious question: what is the textual source for the rule that the last *arus* can annul vows that the first *arus* heard? There is a significant distinction to draw here. We know from the earlier discussion that after groom number one dies and the father's authority is restored, the father can annul even vows groom number one had heard — that was derived from *bi'neureiha beis aviha* and the *pasuk*'s implicit teaching about the non-obvious case. But how do we know that a subsequent *arus* — not the father, but a new *arus* — gains the power to participate in annulling vows specifically heard by the first *arus*? The word *nir'u* ("were seen," i.e., came under the authority of) is used deliberately: once vows were presented to and heard by the first *arus*, they carry a distinct character. How does the second *arus* acquire authority over them?

### Shmuel's Derivation

Shmuel answers from the verse: *ve'im hayo tihyeh l'ish u'nedareiha aleiha* — "and if she shall have been married to a man, and her vows are upon her." The phrase *nedareiha aleiha* — "her vows upon her" — refers to vows she already carries with her. The *hayo tihyeh* construction, as established earlier, encompasses the case of successive marriages. Shmuel reads *nedareiha aleiha* in conjunction with *tihyeh*: the vows that were upon her from the first marriage (*hayo*) follow her into the second (*tihyeh*), and the second husband acquires authority over them.

### Word 'Aleha'

The *gemara* raises the objection that perhaps this derivation applies only to vows that were never under the first *arus*'s auspices — that is, the *hayo tihyeh* teaching addresses the transfer of vows the father controlled, not vows that had passed through the first *arus*'s *reshut*. The *gemara* responds: *aleha kra yeseira* — the word *aleha* is superfluous and carries additional legal weight. *Nedareiha aleiha* means "her vows, whatever was upon her" — in whatever state they existed, regardless of whether the first *arus* had heard them or not. She carries those vows into the new marriage, and the new *arus* acquires full authority over them as part of the joint annulment process with the father.

## Timing Questions

### Father's Clock Start

The *gemara* now identifies several unresolved timing questions that the foregoing analysis leaves open. The first concerns the father's twenty-four-hour window. When groom number one hears the vow, his twenty-four-hour clock begins. If he then dies and the father's authority is restored — including over the vows groom number one heard — does the father's own clock begin from the moment groom number one first heard the vow, or does it begin only from the moment the father himself becomes aware of the vow, which may be some hours after the *arus*'s death?

### Later Groom's Clock

A parallel question arises for the later *arus*. When groom number two or groom number ten enters the picture, from what point does his twenty-four-hour window run? Does it begin from when groom number one originally heard the vow — since the *hayo tihyeh* derivation in effect equates the second *arus*'s position with the first's — or does it begin only from when the later *arus* himself first hears about the vow?

### 24-Hour Definition

There is also the prior definitional question of what exactly the *mishna* means by the annulment window. The verse speaks of *miyom el yom* — "from day to day" — which implies a twenty-four-hour period. But the precise parameters of this window, and whether "day" means a calendrical day ending at nightfall or a full twenty-four-hour unit measured from the time of hearing, remains to be defined as the *gemara* continues. These questions are left open for subsequent discussion.

---

---

# Nedarim 71

## Erusin & Divorce Framewo…

### Opening

Today's daf is 71a. We pick up in the middle of the page at *tanya kevatei deShmuel*, but since there is time available, it is worth starting from the very beginning of the daf to set the frame.

### Mishnah: Multiple Divorc…

The daf opens with a *mishnah* presenting a striking scenario involving a *na'arah me'urasah* — a betrothed maiden — whose vow was made during *erusin*. The *mishnah* states: *nadra vehi arusa* — she made a *neder* while betrothed — *nisgaresh bo bayom* — and she was divorced that same day.
