We will return later to precisely why the same-day requirement matters; for now, the point is that at least the person who heard the vow has a twenty-four-hour window within which to act. *venisarsa bo bayom* — she then became betrothed again to a second man — *afilu leme'ah* — even if this sequence repeated a hundred times over on the same day — *aviha uba'al ha'acharon meferin nedareha* — the father and the last groom may nonetheless annul her vows.

This is initially surprising. For grooms two through one hundred, the *neder* was one she had made while betrothed to a different man — or, in the case of the first groom, a *neder* she may have made before the *erusin* altogether. And yet the *halacha* is that an *arus* is *mefer bekodmin*: he can annul even vows that predate him. This is because the mechanism of annulment is fundamentally the father's prerogative, and the *arus* merely participates. Since the father is always the anchor, and the *neder* has never left the father's jurisdiction, the current *arus* — whoever he may be — can always join the father's annulment.

### Father as Anchor

The governing principle is stated explicitly: *kol shelo yatza lireshut atzmah sha'ah achat* — as long as she has not gained independence for even a single moment. Independence is acquired through becoming a *bogeres*, through her father's death, or through *nisuin* — full marriage — any of which would remove her from the joint *erusin* framework. But as long as none of these have occurred, and she has always remained under her father's authority with grooms merely passing through, the rule is *aviha uba'al ha'acharon meferin nedareha* — it is the father and the last groom who perform the annulment together. The last groom piggybacks on what is fundamentally the father's right, and this is true regardless of how many prior grooms there may have been.

---

## Last Groom & Prior Heari…

### Niru L'Arus Rishon Q

The *Gemara* now probes a question that the *mishnah* leaves unanswered. The *mishnah* tells us that the last groom can annul together with the father — but it does not tell us whether the first groom had already *heard* the *neder*. This distinction matters. One might reason that if the first groom had already heard the vow, he was already an active participant in the process; his right had been engaged. Perhaps in that case the later groom cannot simply step in and take over what had already come under the first groom's purview. The later groom might be able to substitute only when working from a blank slate — that is, when the first groom had no involvement at all.

The *Gemara* formulates the question precisely: *minalan de'arus acharon mafer nedarim sheniru le'arus rishon* — from where do we know that the last groom can annul vows that had already been *nir'u le'arus rishon*, heard by the first groom? It is worth noting, as the term suggests, that *niru* here carries the meaning of *nishme'u* — they were heard, they came to the first groom's attention and fell within his capacity to act upon.

### Shmuel's Verse Proof

*Amar Shmuel de'amar kra* — Shmuel's answer is grounded in a verse. The Torah states *ve'im hayo tihyeh le'ish* — the double language *hayo tihyeh* implies a woman who has been married once (*hayo*) and then is married again (*tihyeh*) — *unedareha aleha* — and her vows remain upon her. The implication is that she carries her vows into the second marriage from the first: *nedarim she'hayu aleha kevar*, vows already upon her from the time of the first *hayo*, accompany her into the second *tihyeh*. Despite this carry-over, the final groom still participates in the annulment.

The *Gemara* immediately presses: *dilma hani mili shelo niru le'arus rishon* — perhaps the verse only applies when the first groom had not yet heard the vow, had not yet entered the process. If so, *aval nedarim sheniru le'arus rishon lo matzi mafer arus acharon* — but for vows that the first groom had already heard, perhaps the last groom cannot annul them. The word *aleha* in the verse is cited as a possible extra term pointing to this additional ruling, though its precise exegetical force is not entirely transparent from the text.

### Shmuel's Position

The *Gemara's* resolution is that the *halacha* of the *mishnah* extends even to the case where the first *arus* had full capacity to act — that is, even when it was *nir'u le'arus rishon*. The Ran notes something that is not self-evident from the way the passage is phrased: what we might have read as the *Gemara's* own assertion was, according to the Ran, Shmuel's intended point all along. Shmuel was not merely providing a verse-source for the *mishnah*. Rather, by citing the *pasuk*, Shmuel was asserting a reading of the *mishnah* that extended it to cover the case of *nir'u le'arus rishon* — the case where the first groom had already heard the vow. The Ran understands the *Gemara* as attributing to Shmuel not just the scriptural derivation but the substantive interpretive claim: the *mishnah's pshat* includes this harder case. This is, admittedly, not how the passage reads on its surface, but that is the Ran's understanding of what the *Gemara* knows about Shmuel's intent.

---

## Braita on Groom Death

### Braita Opening

With Shmuel's position established — that even vows heard by the first groom can be annulled by the last — the *Gemara* proceeds to cite a *braita* that it claims supports this view: *tani kavasei deShmuel*, we have a tradition that accords with Shmuel. The *braita* is complex, and as the Ran acknowledges in a lengthy analysis, the *Gemara* itself provides little explicit commentary. The basic scenario: *na'arah hame'urasah aviha veba'alah meferin nedareha* — a betrothed maiden, whose father and groom together annul her vows.

### Father Annuls, Groom Dies

The first scenario in the *braita*: *shama aviha veheifer lah* — the father heard the vow and annulled it — *velo hispik haba'al lishmo'a ad shemeis* — and the groom did not manage to hear before he died. *Venisarsa bo bayom* — she became betrothed to another man that day — *ve'afilu me'ah pe'amim* — even a hundred times over — *aviha veba'ala ha'acharon meferin nedareha* — the father and the last groom annul her vows. As stated, at this point we have not yet advanced beyond the *mishnah's* basic case, and the scenario explicitly describes the first groom as having died *before* hearing the vow — that is, it is a case of *lo nir'u le'arus rishon*. This is not yet a proof for Shmuel's more far-reaching claim.

### Groom Annuls, Father Fin…

The second scenario is more interesting: *shama ba'alah veheifer lah* — the groom heard and annulled his portion — *velo hispik ha'av lishmo'a ad shemeis haba'al* — and the father had not yet heard when the groom died. The father is the anchor of the entire process; we would therefore expect that since the father remains, he can complete the annulment. And indeed: *chozer ha'av u'meifer chelko shel ba'al* — the father goes back and annuls the groom's portion.

This formulation is striking. One might have supposed the father need only annul his own portion, since the groom had already done his. But the *braita* says the father must annul *chelko shel ba'al* — the groom's portion — as well as his own. The explanation appears to be that when the groom died, the effect of his *hafara* was lost — the annulment does not survive him. Yet the fact that he had staked a role in the process means someone must still play that role. The father therefore steps in and performs a double *hafara*: one in his own capacity as father, and one in the capacity of the deceased groom. This is consistent with the principle encountered earlier in the tractate — the father is the anchor, and the groom's rights, when they lapse, revert in some fashion to the father.

### Beit Shammai vs Hillel

*Amar Rav Natan*: *hein hein divrei Beit Shammai* — this represents the position of Beit Shammai, not an uncontested ruling. *Aval Beit Hillel omrim ein yachol lehafer* — Beit Hillel says the father cannot annul at all in this situation.

At first glance this seems to echo an earlier discussion about whether the groom's right, upon his death, is *migaz gayiz* — fully cut off and therefore transferable — or *miklash kalosh* — weakened but not cleanly severed, making it harder to transfer. But the present case, taken alone, seems to concern only one father and one groom; what does it have to do with our *mishnah's* question about whether a later groom can step in when it was *nir'u le'arus rishon*?

The answer, worked out by the Ran at considerable length, is that the *Gemara* reads the *braita* as addressing a scenario with *two* grooms. The first groom heard the vow, performed *hafara*, and then died. A second groom has now stepped in. When Beit Hillel says *ein yachol lehafer* — he cannot annul — the referent is the father together with the second groom. Even with a new groom on the scene, the father cannot complete the annulment. This is the case of *nir'u le'arus rishon* — but with the additional complication that the first groom not only heard the vow but actually performed *hafara* before dying.

---

## Debate Interpretation

### Beit Shammai Position

According to Beit Shammai: *nedarim she'niru le'arus nisrokna reshuto la'av umageiz gayiz* — vows that had come under the first groom's authority revert to the father when the groom dies, and the transfer (*migaz gayiz*) is effective. Even though the first groom staked his role in the process by performing *hafara*, Beit Shammai holds that his portion can nonetheless be transferred — first back to the father and, by extension, to a subsequent groom. The annulment process can therefore be completed.

### Beit Hillel Position

Beit Hillel disagrees: *aviha uba'al ha'achron meifirin nedareha, v'lo migaz gayiz* — the father and the last groom could in principle annul, but *lo migaz gayiz* — the transfer does not work. Once the first groom has exercised his right and performed *hafara*, he has positioned himself as a genuine stakeholder in the *neder*. His act created a role that is now his and his alone. When he dies, the effect of his *hafara* is lost — but the role he staked is not forgotten. According to Beit Hillel, once a groom has asserted and exercised that role, nobody else can step into it. The father cannot reclaim it, and neither can a later groom substitute for him. The *neder* therefore cannot be annulled, and the woman is left bound by it.

There is an irony worth noting: the outcome is actually worse when the first groom acted than when he did nothing. Had he merely heard the vow and then died without acting, his role would not have been staked, and the question of substitution would not arise. The father and later groom could simply proceed. But because he performed *hafara* — because he inserted himself as a participant in the annulment process — that act, though its effect dissipates with his death, leaves a residue that blocks anyone else from filling the void. He put his key in the lock, so to speak, and that act of engagement makes the role irreversibly his. This is *miklash kalosh* as opposed to *migaz gayiz*: the engagement weakened and transformed the *neder* in a way that entangles his portion with his identity as the one who acted, rather than cleanly cutting off a separable share.

### Hafara as Key Factor

The *Gemara* draws the crucial distinction: this entire debate — Beit Shammai against Beit Hillel — arises specifically because the first groom performed *hafara*. If he had merely heard the vow and done nothing — if he had *not* exercised his right — then even Beit Hillel would agree that his potential right creates no obstacle. It would simply revert to the father, or pass to a later groom, without complication. Both schools would concur that the final groom and father may proceed. The debate is *davka* because the groom acted.

The *braita* therefore does serve as a proof for Shmuel's broader claim, though not a direct one. The presumption underlying the debate of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel is that if the first groom merely heard the vow without performing *hafara* — the case of *niru* without action — then a later groom unquestionably can step in. This assumption is shared by both schools, and it is precisely Shmuel's point about the *mishnah*.

---

## Gerushin & Hakama

### Gerushin Status Q

The *Gemara* now raises a new and important question: *gerushin k'shtika damya o k'hakama damya?* — does the act of divorce function halachically as *shtika* (silence, i.e., doing nothing), or does it function as *hakama* (affirmation of the vow)?

The question has several layers. On one reading, divorce could be seen as *hakama* because it is causally related to the *neder*: when a husband divorces his wife rather than annulling the vow, his choice implies that he assumes the *neder* will remain in force. He had another option — *hafara* — and instead he divorced. This suggests that he accepts, or even endorses, the *neder's* continued existence. On another reading, the act of divorce itself — entirely apart from any inferred intention — constitutes an implicit *hakama* by virtue of the fact that the husband is formally relinquishing his right to perform *hafara*. The act of exiting the relationship, and with it the legal capacity to annul, might be categorized as an affirmation by conduct, regardless of what was going through his mind.

Alternatively, perhaps divorce is simply neutral — like *shtika* — a circumstantial exit from the marriage that says nothing about the *neder* one way or the other.

### Father's Right After Div…

The most direct *nafka mina* — practical consequence — is whether the father retains the ability to be *meifer* after the *arus* has divorced the woman. If *gerushin* functions as *shtika*, then the *arus* has simply exited the picture without having done anything to the *neder*, and the father can proceed and annul his own portion (and, arguably, the groom's as well). But if *gerushin* functions as *hakama*, then the *arus* has effectively affirmed the *neder* by divorcing her, and the father's ability to annul is compromised just as it would be had the *arus* explicitly confirmed the vow verbally.

This also raises an underlying question that the *Gemara* has not yet fully confronted: does *hakama* require a verbal act? *Nedarim* in general operate through formal verbal declarations — that is virtually the first principle of the tractate. Does *hakama*, which the *Gemara* in earlier contexts compared to a new *neder*, require the same formality? Or can it be constituted by a demonstration of will — an act, a choice, a conduct — without any words at all? The case of *gerushin* pushes precisely on this question, since divorce is accomplished through a written document (*get*), not through speech, and even setting that aside, the question is whether the *act* of divorce, irrespective of formality, can operate as an affirmation.

One example of *hakama* by conduct already encountered in the tractate: a woman says *hareini nezira* and her husband responds *va'ani* — "and so am I." This is treated as *hakama*. But there, the husband's words directly engage the *neder* and affirm it. The case of *gerushin* is both stronger and weaker: stronger in that the divorce formally alters the husband's legal position with respect to the marriage; weaker in that the act does not directly or verbally address the *neder* at all, but only demonstrates an assumption about it.

### Divorce & Remarriage Case

The specific scenario the *Gemara* constructs for this question: *k'gon she-nadra v'shama ba'alah v'gershah v'hachzirah b'yomei* — she made a *neder*, her husband heard it, divorced her, and took her back that same day. *I amar mar k'shtika damya* — if *gerushin* is like *shtika* — *matzi meifer leh* — he can still annul. *V'i amar mar k'hakama damya* — but if *gerushin* is like *hakama* — *lo matzi meifer* — he cannot.

The Ran notes an important qualification about this scenario: it cannot be a case of *nesuah* — a fully married woman — because if a married woman is divorced and then remarried, the vow would now have the status of *kodmin* with respect to the second marriage, and a husband cannot be *meifer bekodmin*. The case therefore must involve an *arusa*. With an *arus*, there is no *kodmin* problem, since the *arus* is always *meifer bekodmin* by virtue of the father's role. So the question is posed in the context of *erusin*: the *arus* heard the vow, divorced her, and then became betrothed to her again on the same day — can he now annul?

---

## First Proof Attempt

### Logical Challenge

The *Gemara* now attempts to prove from the *mishnah* itself that *gerushin* does not constitute *hakama*. Recall that the *mishnah* presents a case of *nisgaresh bo bayom venisarsa bo bayom* — she was divorced and remarried, cycling through multiple *arusim*, yet the father and the last *arus* can annul. *Shema mina gerushin k'shtika dami* — learn from this that *gerushin* is like *shtika* — *de'ei k'hakama dami, mi matzi arus acharon* — because if *gerushin* were *hakama*, how could the last *arus* possibly annul *nidrei de'ika arus rishon* — a *neder* that the first *arus* had already affirmed through his act of divorce? If each divorce constitutes *hakama*, then by the time she reaches the last *arus*, the *neder* has been affirmed repeatedly, and no one can annul it. Yet the *mishnah* says the last *arus* and father may annul — seemingly demonstrating that *gerushin* carries no weight as *hakama*.

This is a compelling argument.

### Mishnah Qualification

The *Gemara* deflects it: *hacha bemai askinan — b'shelo shama arus rishon* — the *mishnah* is dealing with a case where the first *arus* never heard the vow at all. If none of the prior *arusim* ever heard the *neder*, then their divorces are meaningless with respect to *hakama*; you cannot affirm what you do not know. Accordingly, the *mishnah* proves nothing about whether *gerushin* functions as *hakama* when the *arus* actually heard the vow — which is the operative question.

But this response creates a further difficulty: *mai irya bo bayom* — why does the *mishnah* specify that the divorces and re-betrothals all occurred *on the same day*? If the prior *arusim* never heard the vow, there is no ticking clock as far as they are concerned. *Afilu achar me'ah yamim nami* — even if she remarried after a hundred days, the *arus* who never heard would pose no *hakama* problem.

The answer is that the clock that is running belongs to the *father*, not to the prior *arusim*. It is the father who heard the *neder*, and the father who has a twenty-four-hour window. The *mishnah's* same-day requirement reflects the fact that the entire process — father and last *arus* annulling together — must be completed within the father's window. The scenario is constructed so that the father can act jointly with the last *arus* within the day on which the father heard. This also means, by implication, that presumably the father could in principle have annulled his own portion at any point within his window. But since the *arus* must also participate, and the *arus* can only act together with the father, it is structured as a joint same-day annulment timed to the father's hearing.

---

## Gerushin Braita Test

### Vow Divorce Remarry Brai…

The *Gemara* tries once more: *ta shema* — *nadara bo bayom, girsha vehachzira bo bayom, ein yachol lehafer* — she made a vow that day, he divorced her and took her back that day, and he cannot annul.

### Gerushin as Hakama

At first glance this is exactly the proof sought: the *arus* heard the vow, divorced her, and took her back — and he cannot annul. *Shema mina gerushin k'hakama dami* — this implies that the divorce functioned as an affirmation, thereby blocking the subsequent annulment.

### Nesuah Objection

But the *Gemara* immediately counters: *ami hacha benisua askinan* — this *braita* is discussing a *nesuah*, a fully married woman, not a betrothed maiden. *Vehai ta'ama de'ein yachol lehafer mishum de'ein haba'al meifer bekodmin* — and the reason he cannot annul is not because *gerushin* is *hakama*, but simply because a husband who has married a woman cannot be *meifer bekodmin* — he cannot annul vows that predate their marriage. After the divorce and remarriage, the vow now stands as *kodmin* relative to the new marriage, and that is what bars him from annulling.

### Ran's Nesuah Analysis

The Ran presses this further. One might try to salvage the proof by noting that two marriages are present — could one of them save the situation? The Ran explains why neither can. If the first marriage was *nisuin* and the husband then divorced and remarried as an *arus*, the new betrothal is an *erusin* without a father in the picture — because the *nisuin* removed her from her father's jurisdiction. An *arus* without a father has no capacity to annul at all. Conversely, if the second marriage is *nisuin*, there is no *kodmin* problem from the husband's side, but now the vow falls under the *nisuin* framework entirely, with no father. Either way, the *nesuah* scenario fails to isolate the question about *gerushin* and *hakama*, and no proof can be extracted.

---

## Hakama Nature & Form

### Gerushin Status Unresolv…

The upshot is that the question — *gerushin k'shtika damya o k'hakama damya* — remains unresolved. No available source definitively settles whether the act of divorce, when a groom has heard the *neder* and then divorces the woman, constitutes an affirmation of the vow or merely a neutral exit.

### Hakama & Verbal Acts

What the discussion does illuminate, however, is a broader and important question that underlies the entire inquiry: what does *hakama* require? Is *hakama* an act that must be performed verbally, in the same way that a *neder* requires a verbal declaration, or can it be constituted through conduct — through a demonstration of will or a change in legal status that implies an assumption about the *neder's* continuity?

We have seen from earlier in the tractate that *hakama* was in certain respects compared to a *neder*, such that it can itself be subject to a *hatara* — a release. That framing suggests a degree of formality. Yet the case of *gerushin* entertains the possibility that an act entirely unrelated to the *neder* in its formal verbal content — namely, the delivery of a *get* — might nonetheless count as *hakama* by virtue of what it implies about the husband's stance. The *Gemara* leaves this question open, and with it the larger question of whether *hakama* by conduct, without explicit speech directed at the *neder*, is halachically cognizable at all.

---

---

# Nedarim 72

## Pre-Marital Vow Annulment

### Daf Overview & Structure

We pick up on 72b, *amud bet*, with a new *mishna*. The *mishna* continues in the theme of the father and groom who together annul vows in partnership, but in doing so it raises — somewhat in passing — a central question that the *gemara* will open up and explore in depth.

It is worth noting that our *perek* in Nedarim follows a pattern common to many *masechtos* and *perakim*: it begins with the more obscure and in some ways more fascinating *halacha* — the intricate details of the partnership between father and groom, who is the *ikar*, how the combination functions, and so on — rather than starting from first principles. A more straightforward pedagogical approach would have first explained how *hafara* works, what the twenty-four-hour period entails, what *hakama* is, and so forth. Instead, all of that gets addressed along the way, as the *gemara* works through the more complex and nuanced cases. This is simply further confirmation that the *gemara* and the *mishnayos* were organized for those already in the conversation — not as Nedarim for beginners.

### Father & Groom Partnersh…

The *mishna* at the top of 72b opens with a striking phrase: *derech talmidei chachamim* — it is the way of Torah sages. It is worth pausing on this, as it is unusual for a *mishna* to invoke the category of *talmidei chachamim* so directly. The *mishna* then describes the following practice: before a man's daughter is about to leave his home — and *yotzes* here means *nissu'in*, marriage proper, since *kiddushin* and *erusin* leave her still legally in her father's house — a conscientious father would ensure that any outstanding vows were addressed. Once she becomes *nesu'ah*, the father exits the picture entirely: he can no longer annul, and her husband cannot annul vows that predate the *nissu'in* because they are *kodmim* — they preceded his jurisdiction. The only window for annulling such prior vows is before the *chuppah*.

So the *mishna* tells us: *derech talmidei chachamim*, before his daughter departs his home, a father would say to her, *kol nedarim she-nadart betoch beisi harei hein mefurim* — any vows you have taken in my house are hereby annulled. This is a blanket annulment, reminiscent in structure of *hataras nedarim* on *erev Rosh Hashana*. Clearly, he does not know the specific content of the vows; if he did, the situation would have played out differently, and the urgency of doing it now, before the window closes, would not have the same character. The *mishna* then adds: *vechain haba'al*, and so too the groom, before she enters his domain — since once she is *mekudeshes* his participation is already required — would similarly say: *kol nedarim she-nadart ad shelo tikanesi lirshusi harei hein mufarim* — any vows you may have taken before the *chuppah* are annulled. Because once the *chuppah* occurs and she is *nesu'ah*, he can no longer address vows that preceded his jurisdiction.

### Blanket Annulment Practi…

The implication of the *mishna* is immediately apparent: both the father and the groom are issuing blanket annulments of vows they have not heard. The framing could not be clearer — they say "any vows you may have taken," which indicates they are unaware of any specific vow. And crucially, there is no sense of a clock running out that would require them to speak now rather than later. The only urgency is the impending *nissu'in* after which the window closes entirely.

This raises an obvious question rooted in the *pesukim* in *Matos*: the Torah says *min hayom shema'o* — from the day he heard. It sounds as though hearing is a prerequisite for annulment. And one might add: if a husband can issue a standing blanket annulment without hearing, then presumably he could do so every night as a matter of course, and his wife's vows would always be pre-annulled. These are precisely the questions the *gemara* will now explore.

---

## Hearing Requirement Deba…

### Rami Bar Chama's Query

*Ba'i Rami Bar Chama* — Rami Bar Chama poses the question: *ba'al mahu sheyafer belo shmiya?* Can a husband — and the same question applies equally to a father, there is no distinction here — annul a vow without having heard it? *V'shama isha gabeyhu* — does the requirement that the husband hear function as the trigger that empowers him to annul? *O lav davka hu* — or is that phrase not to be read literally as a strict requirement?

It is almost striking to take a *pasuk* from the Torah and say *lav davka* — as if to say, the phrase doesn't really mean what it seems to say. But that is precisely what is at stake.

### Lav Davka Interpretation

What *lav davka* must mean here requires some unpacking. It would not be a wholesale dismissal of the phrase as meaningless. Rather, the more precise reading would be: the husband has twenty-four hours from the time he heard. He need not hear in order to perform the act of annulment, but once he has heard, he has only twenty-four hours remaining. Failure to annul within twenty-four hours of hearing is treated as *hakama* — tacit confirmation of the vow — since his silence upon learning of it for an entire day is construed as acquiescence. So *lav davka* would not mean hearing is irrelevant; it would mean that hearing is not a precondition for annulling, but it is the event that starts the twenty-four-hour clock. The *gemara* does not state this explicitly, but it appears to be the necessary *pshat*.

We should not simply say *lav davka* without accounting for the word's role at all. Rather, *b'yom shama'o* informs us of the consequences of hearing — the twenty-four-hour window — without making hearing itself a precondition for the act of annulment.

### Opening Conversation

*Amar Rava ta shma* — Rava says, come and hear from our *mishna* itself. The *mishna* says *derech talmidei chachamim* — and it is interesting to note that the *mishna* identifies this practice specifically with *talmidei chachamim*, perhaps because knowing that a blanket annulment of unknown vows is valid, and that hearing is not strictly required to perform it, itself requires significant *halachic* awareness. The *mishna* describes the father giving a comprehensive annulment of any vows the daughter may have taken — *ve-ha lo shama?* But he didn't hear them. So how does this work?

The *gemara* responds: *v'chi shama hu demifer* — no, what the *mishna* means is that he is not actually annulling now. Rather, he is opening the conversation with her. By saying "any vows you may have taken are hereby annulled," he is prompting her to disclose whatever vows she may have made, so that he can then perform the actual annulment upon hearing. So the *mishna*'s case involves a father who initiates the discussion precisely in order to get his daughter to articulate her vows — and only then does the formal annulment occur.

This is admittedly a significant reading into the *mishna*, which on its face sounds like a genuine blanket annulment of unspecified vows. The *gemara* then turns to the second half of the *mishna*: *vechain haba'al*, the groom likewise says this before the *nissu'in*. And here too the *gemara* applies the same logic — *hacha nami de-amar lah lechishe'eshma'enah* — he is saying that when he hears, the annulment will take effect. This is how the *gemara* reads the case: the act of annulment can be performed before hearing, but its effect is contingent on hearing.

Now this is a genuinely interesting middle position. One might have thought: if hearing is required for the effect, surely the very act of annulment cannot be initiated before that threshold is met — much like the case of *davar shelo ba le'olam*, where one cannot perform a legal act regarding something that does not yet exist. And yet the *gemara* here seems to carve out an intermediate stance: the act can be initiated prior to hearing, but the effect can only take hold once hearing has occurred.

### Father vs. Husband Timing

The Ran raises a pointed question: why is this resolution stated specifically regarding the husband, and not the father? The distinction is significant. For the father, if he performs the act of annulment now and hearing only occurs later, that "later" might well be after the *chuppah* — after which the daughter is entirely outside his domain. Since neither the moment of the act nor the moment of the effect corresponds to a time when he is genuinely empowered to annul, it is difficult to see how the two could combine into a valid *hafara*.

For the husband the situation is different. He performs the act now as an *arus* — he already holds the power to annul in partnership with the father. And when he later hears, he will hear as a *ba'al*, a fully married husband, at which point he has comprehensive authority over her vows. So the act performed at one valid stage and the effect triggered at another valid stage can indeed combine. The father, by contrast, must work within the *gemara*'s first reading: he initiates conversation, she discloses, and he annuls before the *chuppah* while he still can.

---

## Annulment Before Hearing

### Annulment of Future Vows

*Ta shma* — come and hear. The *gemara* now introduces a new *mishna* — which we find at 75a — that takes the question even further. The case: a man says to his wife before departing on a journey, *kol nedarim she-tidori mi-kan ad she-avo mi-makom ploni* — any vows that you make from now until I return from such-and-such a place.

### Non-Existent Vows Debate

These are not vows that exist and have merely not been heard — these are vows that do not yet exist at all. The *mishna* addresses two scenarios. If the husband says *harei hen kayamin* — I am confirming them, I am being *mekayem* — *lo amar klum*, his declaration is null. One cannot strengthen something that does not yet exist; *kiyum* requires the vow to already have some footing before it can be anchored. On this everyone agrees.

However, if he says *harei hen mufarin* — I am annulling them — then Rabbi Eliezer says it works, while the *Chachamim* say it does not.

### Prevention Logic

*Amar Rabbi Eliezer*: why should pre-emptive annulment be less effective than after-the-fact annulment? *Im hefer nedarim she-bau li-khlal issur, lo yafer nedarim she-lo bau li-khlal issur?* If he can annul a vow once it has already entered the realm of prohibition, surely he can act to prevent one from entering that realm altogether. Prevention is easier than cure; an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. This is also why the cases are not symmetrical: *kiyum* means strengthening, and you cannot strengthen what is not yet there. But *hafara* means preventing or removing — and surely preventing is even more achievable than curing.

### Establishment Requirement

The *Chachamim* respond from the *pasuk* itself: *ishah yekimenu ve-ishah yefirenu* — her husband shall establish it and her husband shall annul it. *Kol she-ba li-khlal hakam ba li-khlal hafer* — only something that can be subject to *hakama* can be subject to *hafara*. If a vow cannot be established — because it does not yet exist — it cannot be annulled either. This may reflect the mechanics of the annulment process, or it may simply be a *gezeirat ha-katuv*. Rabbi Eliezer's logic is conceptually appealing, but the *Chachamim* hold that the Torah's mechanism of annulment operates only on something already in existence.

One might note the irony: Rabbi Eliezer concedes that *kiyum* of a non-existent vow is impossible — but this is precisely the assumption that undermines his own *kal va-chomer*, since if *kiyum* cannot apply, and *kiyum* and *hafara* are treated as parallel categories by the *Chachamim*, then the same limitation applies to both.

In any case, this debate concerns only whether the act of annulment can precede the vow's existence. Nobody in the *mishna* raises the objection that the husband failed to hear the vow — neither Rabbi Eliezer nor the *Chachamim* flag hearing as a problem. This silence is itself informative.

### Effect Upon Hearing

*Ve-ha lo shama* — but he didn't hear these vows. This too doesn't seem to trouble either opinion in the *mishna*. The *gemara* once again resolves this: *hacha nami de-amar le-chi-ishmana* — here too, we read it as if he said the annulment would take effect when he hears about the vows. So again: the act is performed now, but the effect is held in abeyance until hearing occurs.

The *gemara* then asks: if that is the case, why does he need to make the declaration before he leaves? *Lechi yishma yeifer lah* — when he gets back and hears about any vow she made, let him annul it then. The answer: *kasvar dilma matreeda ha-hee sha'ata* — he is worried that upon returning from his trip, in the bustle of arriving home, he might be distracted and forget to annul in time. The twenty-four-hour window could expire. So he sets things in motion beforehand to ensure the annulment will take effect automatically once he hears, without relying on his future composure.

The *pshat* of the *mishna* clearly reads as genuine pre-emptive annulment. But the *gemara*, in order to preserve the requirement of hearing, consistently reads all such cases as: the act is permitted before hearing, the effect requires hearing. This is the framework the *gemara* applies throughout this *sugya*.

---

## Shaliach (Agent) Authori…

### Appointed Manager Role

*Ta shma* — the *gemara* brings a further case. A man about to leave on a trip says to his *apotropus* — his household manager or appointed agent — *kol nedarim she-tidor ishti mi-kan ad she-avo mi-makom ploni*, hafer lah: any vows my wife makes from now until I return, go ahead and annul them. The manager does so — *yachol yihiyu mufarim?* Could such an annulment be valid?

### Non-Delegable Power

*Talmud lomar isha yekimenu ve-ishah yefirenu* — the verse specifies the husband. The power of *hafara*, says Rabbi Yoshiah, cannot be transferred to an agent. It belongs exclusively to the husband himself.

### Shaliach Principle

Rabbi Yonatan objects: *matzinu be-chol ha-Torah kulo shlucho shel adam k'moto* — throughout the entire Torah, an agent stands in the place of the one who appointed him. Why should *hafara* be any different? Why can the husband not empower a *shaliach* to annul on his behalf?

### Hearing vs. Legal Act

The *gemara* then notes a deeper puzzle: even if the principle of *shaliach* could in theory apply, there is a conceptual difficulty. The *shaliach* would be the one who hears the vow — but the husband would not have heard it. If hearing is what empowers the husband to annul, then how could his *shaliach*'s hearing translate into the husband's ability to act?

The *gemara*'s answer — and this is spelled out more fully in the Ran and in Tosafot — is that hearing is not a legal act that can be delegated. One can transfer a legal power to a *shaliach*; one cannot make someone else do one's hearing. Hearing is circumstances, not agency. The circumstances of hearing create the empowerment; but those circumstances must attach to the person himself. As Tosafot states concisely: *inyan shmiah eino na'aseh shaliach* — the matter of hearing cannot be made into an act of agency.

### Shaliach Hears & Acts

Given all of this, the *gemara* concludes: even Rabbi Yoshiah, who holds that the power of *hafara* cannot be transferred, acknowledges that the reason is specifically *gezeirat ha-katuv* — the verse *isha yekimenu ve-ishah yefirenu* specifies the husband. Were it not for that verse, everyone would agree the power could in principle be transferred. *Aval d'chulei alma shlucho shel adam k'moto* — the baseline principle of *shaliach* would apply.

The *gemara* then works out how this case would function if the *shaliach* mechanism were valid: *de-amar lah le-chi shamana meifer lah* — the husband says to the *shaliach*, when you hear, annul it, and it will take effect when I hear. *Savar dilma matridna* — the husband anticipates being distracted upon his return, so he sets the *shaliach* in motion ahead of time. The *shaliach* performs the act upon hearing; the effect activates once the husband himself hears. In this way the *gemara* accommodates the case within its consistent framework: the act of annulment can precede hearing, but the effect requires the husband personally to have heard.

This entire discussion reinforces once more that the *pshat* of the *mishna* and *braita* is that hearing is not required to perform *hafara*. The *gemara*'s repeated accommodation — reading every case as a deferred effect contingent on future hearing — is the only mechanism by which it preserves any residual role for *b'yom shama'o* at all.

---

## Deaf Person Annulment

### Cheresh Query

*Ba'ei Rami Bar Chama* — Rami Bar Chama now poses a second question: *cheresh mahu sheyafer le'ishto?* Can a deaf person annul the vows of his wife? The question presupposes the conclusion of the previous discussion: if we have established — or are at least working with the assumption — that one need not actually hear a vow in order to annul it, then a deaf person's disability does not categorically prevent him from performing *hafara*. So the question must be sharper than that.

### Category of Hearer

*Im timtzei lomar ba'al meifer belo shemia* — if we say a hearing husband can annul without actually having heard a particular vow, perhaps the reason is *mishum debar shemia hu* — because he at least belongs to the category of one capable of hearing. *Aval cheresh de-lav bar shemia hu* — a deaf person, however, is not in that category at all. Perhaps that categorical exclusion disqualifies him from *hafara* altogether.

### Rabbi Zeira's Principle

This question connects to a broader principle articulated by Rabbi Zeira: *kol ha-ra'ui le-vila ein bila me'akevet bo, ve-chol she-eino ra'ui le-vila bila me'akevet bo* — whatever is fit to be mixed, the mixing is not actually indispensable; but if it is not fit to be mixed, then the mixing is determinative. The reference is to a *mincha* offering: the Torah requires the flour and oil to be mixed (*bila*), yet if one failed to mix them in a case where mixing was possible, the offering remains valid. But if the offering is of such a size that mixing is physically impossible — once the quantity exceeds what can be practically mixed — then its lack of fitness for *bila* disqualifies it entirely.

Tosafot flags the broader question this principle raises: how does one know when the *halacha* requires merely the potential for an act, and when it requires the act itself? The answer is not always clear. But the *gemara* here applies Rabbi Zeira's principle to suggest: perhaps *b'yom shama'o* is not eliminated entirely by our conclusion that hearing need not actually occur — perhaps it is reduced to the requirement of being in the *category* of a hearer. A hearing person who happens not to have heard a specific vow retains that potential; a deaf person has no such potential at all. *O dilma ve-shama isha lav me'akev* — or perhaps *ve-shama isha* plays no role whatsoever, not even as a categorical requirement.

### Braita Exclusion

*Amar Rava ta shma* — Rava resolves the question by citing a *braita*. The *braita* expounds *ve-shama isha* — her husband shall hear — and adds: *prat le'eshet cheresh*, to exclude the wife of a deaf person. The exclusion is explicit. A deaf man cannot annul his wife's vows.

From here, many *rishonim* draw the further implication: since the *braita* finds it necessary to explicitly exclude the case of the *cheresh*, it implies that merely not having heard a particular vow is insufficient to constitute a problem. The only disqualifying circumstance is being fully outside the category of hearing. This reinforces the position — consistent with everything seen in this *sugya* — that a hearing person need not actually have heard the vow in order to perform *hafara*. As this is a striking conclusion given the Torah's explicit language of *b'yom shama'o*, it bears emphasis: according to most *rishonim* and *poskim*, the *pshat* of the *sugya* is that actual hearing of the specific vow is not required for annulment to be valid.

---

## Multiple Wives Vows

### Simultaneous Annulment

*Iba'ya lehu* — a further question is raised: *ba'al mahu sheyafer li-sh'tei nashim be-vat achat?* Can a husband annul the vows of two of his wives simultaneously? He has vows from two wives on the same day and declares *mufar lachem* — it is annulled for both of you. Is that valid?

The question parallels the earlier inquiry into *ve-shama isha*: just as we asked whether *isha* — singular — is *davka*, implying the husband must address one wife at a time, so too we might ask about *yafer otah* — the annulment is of *her* vow. One might note that in the *pesukim* in *Matos*, the verb of *hafara* appears in the context of *kol nedareha ve-chol issar asher asra al nafsha* — her vows in their entirety — and the *hafara* there is on the *neder*, not on the person. The word *otah* in the sense of disallowing her personally (*yani otah*) is distinct from the *hafara* of the vow. So the textual basis for requiring individual treatment is not straightforwardly clear.

### Sotah Parallel

*Amar Rav Aina ta shma* — come and hear from the laws of *sotah*. *Ein mashkin sh'tei sotos ke'achat* — one does not administer the *sotah* waters to two suspected wives at the same time. Even if a man suspects both his wives of infidelity, the *sotah* process must be conducted separately for each. The reason given by the *tanna kama* is *mipnei she-liba gas ba-chaverta* — because one woman's heart becomes emboldened by her companion. Seeing her fellow undergo the drinking process without immediate consequence, she may not take the matter seriously, failing to appreciate that her companion may be innocent while she is guilty.

### Individual Requirement

Rabbi Judah disagrees with this rationale and offers instead a textual basis: *ela mishum she-ne'emar ve-hishka otah levadah* — because the verse says "and he shall make her drink *alone*," *levadah*, implying individual treatment is mandated by the *pasuk* itself. There is some discussion among the *rishonim* as to whether the *tanna kama* disputes Rabbi Judah's *derashah* entirely, or whether he agrees with the *pasuk* but is merely supplying the underlying reason behind it — in the manner of Rabbi Shimon who *doresh ta'ama di-kra*. The *gemara*'s conclusion on the question of simultaneous annulment for two wives appears to be that it must be done individually, though the precise resolution remains somewhat open.

---

## Bogeret & Widow Cases

### Ready-for-Marriage Cases

The *mishna* now addresses a distinct set of cases: a *bogeret* — a woman who has reached full maturity — who was betrothed (*mekudeshes*) and is now in the period that would naturally precede *nissu'in*, and similarly a widow who is betrothed for a second marriage. These are women who are fully ready to be married but have not yet entered the *chuppah*.

### Rabbi Eliezer Position

*Rabbi Eliezer omer*: since the *Sages* have ruled that the husband is now obligated in her *mezonos* — her financial support — he may annul her vows unilaterally, without the father's partnership, as though she were already *nesu'ah*.

This is a striking ruling. *De'oraisa* she is not yet *nesu'ah*, and the annulment would be *le-kula* — a leniency. How can the husband be granted unilateral authority that normally requires full *nissu'in*?

### Chachamim Position

*Chachamim omrim*: the husband cannot perform full *hafara* until she has actually entered his domain — until there is a real *chuppah* and genuine *nissu'in*.

### Rava's Comparison

*Amar Rava*: Rabbi Eliezer and the *mishna rishona* — the earlier teaching cited in Ketubot — express the same position. As the *mishna* in Ketubot teaches: *notnin li-vtula yod bet chodesh le-farnes atzma* — a virgin bride is given twelve months to prepare her trousseau and arrange for the wedding. *Higia yod bet chodesh* and the husband has not yet married her — his financial obligations kick in. *Ocheles mi-shelo* — he bears her food expenses.

### Truma Parallel

And further: *ocheles bi-truma* — if the husband is a *kohen*, she may even eat *truma*, despite the fact that ordinarily a woman must be genuinely *nesu'ah* to a *kohen* to be permitted *truma*. So there is a ritual-legal parallel: just as once twelve months have elapsed she is treated as *nesu'ah* for the purpose of eating *truma*, Rabbi Eliezer holds that she is treated as *nesu'ah* for the purpose of *hafara* as well.

By contrast, the *mishna* in Ketubot distinguishes the case of *yibum* — the *yavam*, the brother-in-law awaiting *yibum*. Even if six months passed under the deceased husband and six more under the *yavam* — or all twelve months in either configuration — they do not combine, and she may not eat *truma* by virtue of the *yavam*'s obligation. The later *beit din*, the *mishna rishona*'s successor ruling, went further and said: *ein ha-isha ocheles bi-truma ad she-tikanes la-chuppah* — she does not eat *truma* until she actually enters the *chuppah*. So even the *truma* leniency was subsequently restricted, reflecting the debate about how far we are prepared to treat her as *nesu'ah* for *issur* purposes before she formally is.

---

## Truma vs. Nedarim

### Rabbanic vs. Torah

*Amar lei Abaye* — Abaye challenges Rava's equation. Perhaps, says Abaye, the parallel between Rabbi Eliezer and the *mishna rishona* is not so simple. *Ad kan lo ashmian mishna rishona ela meichal bi-truma d'rabbanan* — the *mishna rishona* permitted her to eat *truma*, but *truma* in this context is a *rabbinic* matter. *Aval nedarim d'oraisa eima lo* — but *nedarim* is Torah law, and one might say Rabbi Eliezer would never have extended his position to allow a Torah-level *hafara* before actual *nissu'in*.

### Truma Sources

What does Abaye mean when he says *truma* here is *de-rabbanan*? This requires some background. *Mideoraita*, why may the wife of a *kohen* eat *truma* at all? Two potential *pesukim* are relevant. One is *anshei beiso heim yochlu be-lachmo* — the people of his household eat from his bread — pointing toward a *nesu'ah*, a woman established in his home. The other is *kinyan kaspo hu yochal be-lachmo* — that which he has acquired with his money, referring to *kiddushin* — pointing toward an *arusa*, a betrothed woman. The Yerushalmi understands the basis as *beiso*, requiring full *nissu'in* even *de'oraita*. The Bavli understands it as *kinyan kaspo*, so that *de'oraita* even an *arusa* may eat *truma*.

### Nesu'ah Requirement

If so, why did the *Sages* require *nissu'in* before she may eat *truma*? The reason is practical: she is still living in her father's house, among family members who are not *kohanim*, and would likely share the *truma* with them — which is forbidden. The *rabbinic* restriction is therefore a protective measure. Since her inability to eat *truma* before *nissu'in* is only *de-rabbanan*, it is not so significant to say: once twelve months have elapsed and it is truly time for the *nissu'in*, we will treat her as *nesu'ah* and allow her to eat. *Mah she-ein kein nedarim* — but for *nedarim*, which are *de'oraita*, how could the husband annul vows if she is not formally his *nesu'ah*? That is a much more serious claim, and Abaye holds that the parallel to *truma* therefore does not carry.

---

## Vows with Spousal Consent

### Spousal Presumption

The *gemara* introduces the position of Rav Pinchas in the name of Rava: *kol ha-noderet al da'as ba'alah hi noderet* — any woman who takes a vow does so with the presumption that her husband will agree. This is the conceptual key to Rabbi Eliezer's position. The woman's vow is not a unilateral declaration issued in disregard of her husband; it is made against the backdrop of her relationship with him, implicitly conditional on his acceptance. Since that implicit conditionality is built into the vow itself, the husband's annulment does not need to await formal *nissu'in* in the same way as a standard *hafara* would — because the vow's very force depends on his concurrence.

### Rabbi Eliezer's Logic

This explains why Rabbi Eliezer holds that once twelve months have elapsed and the husband is already obligated in her maintenance, the relationship has already reached a stage where her psychological orientation is effectively that of a *nesu'ah*. She is already thinking about him as her husband, and her vows are already being made *al da'at* him. The formal *nissu'in* has not yet occurred, but the relevant dynamic — the one the Torah was addressing when it invested the husband with the power of *hafara* — is already present. This is not merely a financial or technical marker; it reflects the actual state of the relationship.

### Implicit Condition

The Ran is careful to note, however, that one should not conclude from this that all formal requirements of *hafara* are suspended in such cases. The principle that a woman vows *al da'as ba'alah* does not mean that the husband's silent non-objection constitutes *hafara*, or that any expression of reluctance will do. The Ran writes explicitly: even granting that she vows on the presumption of his agreement, the husband must still perform a formal act of *hafara* using the language designated by the Torah. This is *gezeirat ha-katuv* — the Torah prescribed a formal mechanism with specific rules: a twenty-four-hour window, particular language, and so on. *Al da'as* explains the *reason* the Torah invested the husband with this power; it does not dissolve the formal requirements of how that power must be exercised.

One might think, for example, that if someone vows explicitly *al da'as* a specific individual — say, "I am taking this vow subject to So-and-so's approval" — that person could annul the vow without formal *hafara* language, simply by withholding consent. The Ran firmly rejects this: *vazu hi shegagas hora'ah* — this would be a genuine error in *psak*. The mechanism of *hafara* is formal and its rules are fixed; *al da'as* informs the underlying rationale but does not replace the formal act.

### Husband Category Expansi…

The Ran develops the point further in a direction that is conceptually illuminating. If *al da'as ba'alah* is the *reason* the Torah gave the husband power over his wife's vows, then we are essentially engaged in *darshinan ta'ama di-kra* — deriving the law from the reasoning behind the *pasuk*. And if so, when the Torah says *ba'al* — husband — we need to ask: what does the Torah mean by husband in this context? The Torah means the person standing in that relationship of presumptive agreement with her vows.

Once we frame it this way, Rabbi Eliezer's extension becomes intelligible. An *arus* who has been in a committed relationship with his betrothed for twelve months, who is already providing her with financial support, and in whose eyes she is already conducting herself as though married — such a person fits the Torah's category of *ba'al* for purposes of *hafara*, even though the formal *chuppah* has not yet occurred. The Torah's category of "husband" is not strictly limited to post-*chuppah* status; it encompasses whoever stands in the relevant relationship. At the twelve-month mark, with the *arus* already obligated in *mezonos*, the relationship has effectively reached that threshold.

This is not an unlimited expansion. The Ran is explicit: it would not extend to a stranger, a neighbor, or even a close friend, regardless of how much the woman trusted him or made her vows with him in mind. It extends only to someone who already fits within some recognizable form of the *ba'al* category — an *arus* at an advanced stage of betrothal. For such a person, the Torah's language of *ba'al* already includes him, given the reasoning that underlies the entire institution of *hafarat nedarim*.

---

---

# Nedarim 72b

## Perek Structure & Setup

### Intro: Perek Organization

The daf opens at 72b with a new *mishnah*, still within the broader theme of the father and the groom who together annul a daughter's vows. Yet as we will see, this *mishnah* raises — almost in passing — a central and far-reaching question that the *Gemara* proceeds to explore at length.

It is worth pausing at the outset to note something characteristic about the organization of this *perek*, as indeed of many *masechtos* and *perakim* throughout the Talmud. Rather than beginning with the most straightforward *halachos* — explaining what the twenty-four-hour window for *hafarah* consists of, what *hakama* means, how the process works in its basic form — the *perek* opens instead with the more obscure and in many ways more fascinating cases: the precise nature of the partnership between father and groom, who is the *ikar*, how the combination functions. All of the more foundational material gets addressed along the way, as it becomes relevant. This is simply another demonstration that the *Gemara* and the *Mishnayos* were organized for those already in the conversation, not as a beginner's introduction to the laws of *nedarim*.

### Mishnah: Blanket Annulme…

The *mishnah* at the top of 72b opens with a striking phrase: *derech talmidei chachamim* — it is the way of Torah scholars. It is notable that the *mishnah* directly identifies this practice with the category of *talmidei chachamim*; the term is common in the *Gemara* but relatively rare as a *mishnah*'s own formulation. Perhaps it means that one must actually be a *talmid chacham* to know that this practice is both possible and unproblematic — that he may annul vows he has not yet heard about.

The *mishnah* describes the following: before a man's daughter goes to *nisu'in* — and *yotzet me'etzlo*, leaving the father's house, conceptually means *nisu'in*, since during *eirusin* she remains in the father's domain — the father would say to her: *kol nedarim shenadart betoch beiti harei hem mufarim*, any vows you have taken in my house are hereby annulled. He gives her a blanket annulment, similar in spirit to the *hatarat nedarim* of *erev Rosh Hashanah*. The framing is deliberately open-ended: if she had already told him the specific vows, there would be no need for the general formula, and the clock would already be running. The phrasing makes clear that the father has not heard the specific vows; he is annulling whatever may exist.

### Father & Groom Roles

To understand why both father and groom must participate, it is necessary to recall the underlying structure. During *kiddushin*, the daughter remains conceptually in the father's house; *nisu'in* is when she leaves. The father alone can annul vows made before *kiddushin*, and in partnership with the *arus* he can annul vows made after *kiddushin* but before *nisu'in*. Once *nisu'in* occurs, the father is entirely out of the picture. If vows predate *nisu'in*, the husband cannot annul them unilaterally after *nisu'in* because they are *kodmin* — they precede his period of sole authority. The only window for addressing such vows is before *nisu'in*, which is precisely why the *mishnah* describes the father and groom each making their blanket declarations beforehand.

The *mishnah* continues: *vechen haba'al* — so too the groom, before she enters his domain, would say: *kol nedarim shenadart ad shelo tikanesi lirshuti harei hem mufarim*, any vows you may have taken before the *chuppah* are hereby annulled. Once *nisu'in* occurs, *eino yachol lehafer*, he can no longer address those earlier vows, for they are *kodmin*.

The clear implication of the *mishnah* is that neither the father nor the groom has actually heard the specific vows they are annulling. The blanket language and the absence of any running clock make this evident. And it is precisely this implication that the *Gemara* will take as its opening question.

---

## Shmiea Requirements

### Q1: Annul Without Hearing

*Ba'ei Rami Bar Chama* — Rami Bar Chama poses the question: *ba'al mahu sheyapir belo shemiah?* Can the husband — and the same question applies equally to the father — annul a vow without having heard it? Is *veshamah ishah* — and her husband heard — an absolute requirement, or is it *lav davka*, not strictly necessary?

It is almost comical, in a certain sense, to take a *pasuk* from the *Torah* and simply declare it *lav davka*. The question, however, is more nuanced than simple dismissal of the phrase. What *lav davka* likely means in this context is not that *beyom shmo'o* carries no significance whatsoever, but rather that it is not a prerequisite for the act of annulment. Its operative role would be different: from the moment the husband hears, the clock begins running and he has twenty-four hours to act. Failing to annul within twenty-four hours of hearing is treated as *hakama* — acquiescence by silence. On this reading, hearing is not what enables the annulment; rather, it is what starts the countdown. The husband could, in principle, annul even before he has heard, and *beyom shmo'o* would simply mean that having heard, he must now act within the day.

The *Gemara* does not spell this out explicitly, but it seems the most coherent *pshat* if one is going to say *lav davka* at all — it is not a wholesale dismissal of the phrase, but a reframing of its function.

### Opening Conversation

The *Gemara* seeks a proof from our *mishnah*: *ta shema*, come and hear — *derech talmidei chachamim ad shelo yatza bito me'etzlo amar lah kol nedarim shenadart betoch beiti harei hen mufarim — vehu lo shama*, and he did not hear. How does this work?

The *Gemara* offers an initial interpretation: *nehi d'chi shama hu d'mepar* — really, he only annuls when he hears. The declaration he makes now, before he has heard anything, is not itself an act of annulment. Rather, it is an opening to conversation — *orcha d'tzurba merabanan*, the way of a Torah scholar is *lehadurei*, to go back over it, to initiate a dialogue so that his daughter will articulate any vows she may have taken, and then he can properly annul them having heard. The blanket statement draws her into sharing, whereupon the real act of annulment can occur.

This reading is, admittedly, very difficult to square with the plain meaning of the *mishnah*. It imposes a great deal onto a text that reads simply as a completed act.

### Act vs. Effect Split

The *Gemara* then turns to the *seifa*: *vechen haba'al ad shelo tikanes l'rishuto amar lah* — the groom too says it before the *chuppah*. Here too, did he not act without hearing? The *Gemara* responds: *hacha nami d'amar lah l'chi shamana* — here too, he says to her: I will annul it when I hear. Some manuscript readings elaborate this in the same language as before; others give only the compressed formulation, *l'chi shamana*, meaning the annulment takes effect upon hearing.

This reading opens up a conceptually interesting middle position: perhaps hearing is required not for the *act* of annulment, but for the *effect* of annulment. The husband performs the act of *hafarah* now, but it takes hold only once he has actually heard. This is structurally somewhat reminiscent of debates around *davar shelo ba l'olam*: the puzzle of whether and when legal acts can be initiated regarding things that are not yet fully present. One might compare it to the case of a man who says *harei at mekudeshet li* before he has converted — not only is there an external impediment, but the very act seems to have no legal substrate. Yet the *Gemara* here is searching for a middle path: the act can be initiated now, and the effect will crystallize upon hearing.

### Ran: Father vs. Husband

The Ran raises a pointed question on this middle position: if this explanation works for the husband — he does the act now and it takes effect when he hears — why doesn't the *Gemara* give the same answer for the father? Why is the father's case handled differently, with the device of opening a conversation to get her to articulate the vow?

The Ran's answer turns on the difference in timing. For the father, the problem is that by the time he hears, it may already be after the *chuppah* — at which point his authority over her vows is entirely gone. At the moment of hearing, she is completely outside his domain. For that combination to work — the act done while she was still in his house, the effect crystallizing after *nisu'in* when he has no authority — neither moment is one in which he is actually in a position to annul. The two halves cannot meaningfully combine.

For the husband, the situation is different. He performs the act now as an *arus*, at which point he has at least partial authority. He will hear after *nisu'in*, when he is fully in the role of *ba'al* and unambiguously empowered to annul new vows. The act of annulment and the moment of hearing therefore both occur within legitimate windows of some authority, and it is coherent for them to combine. The effect taking hold upon hearing, at a time when he is fully in control, is a workable legal structure.

---

## Future Vows Debate

### Future Vows Mishnah

The *Gemara* brings another *mishnah* — located two pages later at 75a — as a further proof. The case: a man says to his wife, *kol hanedarim shetidderi mikan ad she'avo mimakom ploni* — any vows you make from now until I return from such-and-such place. He is about to leave on a trip and wishes to address whatever vows his wife may take in his absence.

### No Kiyum Before Existence

If he declares *harei hen kayamim* — I am establishing them — *lo amar klum*, he has accomplished nothing. There is a universal consensus on this: one cannot perform *kiyum*, the act of establishing or affirming a vow, on something that does not yet exist. *Kiyum* is about anchoring and strengthening an existing vow; there is nothing to anchor if the vow has not yet been taken.

### R. Eliezer: Hafarah Befo…

However, if he says *harei hen mufarim* — I am annulling them — *Rabbi Eliezer omer mufar*: Rabbi Eliezer holds this works. His reasoning: *im hefer nedarim sheba'u l'chlal issur, ra'uy yafer nedarim shelo ba'u l'chlal issur* — if one can annul a vow once it has already taken effect as a prohibition, how much more so should one be able to prevent it from ever taking effect in the first place. *Hafarah* is fundamentally about eliminating a prohibition; a preventive measure, he argues, is at least as valid as a curative one. The vow that does not yet exist is in an even more accessible state for annulment — there is less there to dissolve. This also explains why Rabbi Eliezer distinguishes *hafarah* from *kiyum*: *kiyum* requires something present to strengthen, whereas *hafarah* is about removal or prevention, and prevention is easier than cure.

### Chachamim: Parallel Requ…

The *Chachamim* respond from the verse: *ishah yekimenu ve'ishah yeferenu* — the husband shall establish it and the husband shall annul it. *Et sheba l'chlal hakeim ba l'chlal hafer, lo ba l'chlal hakeim lo ba l'chlal hafer* — only something that falls within the category of being establishable can be annulled; something that cannot be established cannot be annulled. This may be a *gezeirat hakatuv*, a formal Scriptural decree — the mechanism of annulment simply operates on existing vows — or it may reflect the logical symmetry that *ishah yekimenu ve'ishah yeferenu* presents *hakama* and *hafarah* as parallel operations on the same object. Either way, the *Chachamim* insist that the vow must exist before either operation can apply. Rabbi Eliezer concedes that *kiyum* requires existence, and the *Chachamim* argue that *hafarah* must be constrained in the same way.

### Act & Effect Upon Hearing

Now the *Gemara* returns to the *shmiea* question. In this *mishnah*, nobody — neither Rabbi Eliezer nor the *Chachamim* — raises any objection about the fact that the husband has not heard the vows. The entire debate is whether *hafarah* can apply to vows not yet in existence; the absence of hearing goes unremarked. The *Gemara* notes: *v'ha lo shama* — he has not heard — and yet this concerns no one?

The *Gemara* answers: *hacha nami d'amar lich'she'eshamana* — here too, he says, I am annulling it, and it will take effect when I hear. Once again: the act is performed now; the effect waits upon hearing. The *Chachamim*'s objection to Rabbi Eliezer is that the vow does not yet exist, not that hearing is missing. Both sides operate within the assumption that hearing is what the effect waits upon, but neither treats its absence as independently disqualifying the act.

### Why State It Now

This raises an obvious question: if the annulment only takes effect when he hears, why must he make the declaration before departing? Why not simply annul each vow as he hears about it upon his return?

The *Gemara* answers: *kasavar dilma matridna hi sha'ata* — he worries that he will be distracted at that later moment. Coming home from a trip, there are many demands on his attention. His wife might tell him about a vow she took, and by the time he has settled and remembered to formally address it, twenty-four hours will have passed and his silence will have been treated as *hakama*. He therefore initiates the process now, before he is distracted, setting things in motion so that the effect can crystallize upon hearing without risk of the window closing.

---

## Epitropos & Shaliach

### Epitropos Case

A further *mishnah* — also upcoming in the *masechta* — introduces the case of the *epitropos*: a man is about to leave on a trip and says to the steward running his household, *kol nedarim shenoderet ishti mikan ve'ad she'avo mimakom ploni* — any vows my wife takes from now until I return, *hafer*, annul them. The steward hears her take a vow and annuls it. Has the annulment taken effect?

### R. Yoshiya vs. R. Yonatan

Rabbi Yoshiya says no: *ishah yekimenu ve'ishah yeferenu* — only the husband can annul; this is not a power that can be transferred. Rabbi Yonatan responds: *matzinu bechol hatorah kullaha shelucho shel adam kemoso* — throughout the entire Torah, an agent stands in the place of the one who appointed him. Why should this power be different?

### Transferability of Powers

The *Gemara* notes that the debate between Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan concerns whether this particular power can be delegated. Not all legal capacities are transferable. There is a category of acts that are not merely about being invested with a power but about personally and physically performing something. *Chalitza* is the classic example — one cannot appoint a *shaliach* to perform *chalitza* on one's behalf, because the act is constituted by the personal participation of the principals. Similarly, one cannot appoint a *shaliach* to perform a *mitzvah* in the purely personal sense. The conceptual framework, developed in the Brisker tradition, distinguishes between a power invested in the person that can be transferred, and a personal act that cannot. The debate here is precisely which category *hafarah* falls into.

The *Gemara* adds a clarifying point: even Rabbi Yoshiya, who says the *epitropos* cannot annul, concedes that this is only *mishum gezeirat hakatuv* — because of the Scriptural decree of *ishah yekimenu ve'ishah yeferenu*. In principle, the act of annulment is of a type that *could* be transferred; it is the verse that restricts it to the husband. *Avald'chulei alma shelucho shel adam kemoso* — everyone agrees that absent that verse, transfer would be conceptually valid.

### Shaliach Hearing Problem

This concession generates a striking problem. If the *shaliach* could in principle annul on the husband's behalf, how would that work given that the *shaliach* heard the vow but the husband did not? If hearing is what empowers the annulment, and the husband has not heard, then the husband is not in a position to annul — and an agent cannot possess authority that the principal himself lacks.

### Ran: Hearing as Circumst…

The Ran resolves this by drawing a precise conceptual distinction. Hearing, he explains, is not itself a legal power — it is the *circumstances* under which the power to annul arises. One cannot transfer circumstances to a *shaliach*. What one can transfer is a legal power, once it has been activated by the relevant circumstances. The hearing itself — a passive, experiential state — is not the kind of act that can be delegated. The *shaliach* hearing is not equivalent to the husband hearing in any legally operative sense.

Once this distinction is drawn, the *Gemara*'s assumption becomes intelligible: if we could transfer the *power* of annulment (absent Rabbi Yoshiya's verse), the *shaliach*'s hearing would serve as the circumstances activating that power, and the husband's prior delegation would constitute the transfer of the now-activated power. But there is no way to delegate the *hearing itself* so as to produce the same result as if the husband personally heard. Hearing is circumstance, not power.

### Tosafot: No Shaliach for…

Tosafot's answer, found in manuscript traditions added to this *perek*, states the point more directly: *de'inyan shemi'ah eino na'aseh shaliach* — in the matter of hearing, one cannot make a *shaliach*. The reasoning implicit in this formulation is the same: hearing is not a legal act, and therefore not the kind of thing for which agency can be constituted. You can transfer a legal power; you cannot make another person hear for you in any legally operative sense.

The *Gemara*'s resolution in this case — *hacha nami de'amar lah lechish'shameina mefer lach* — is structurally the same as the previous cases. The husband tells the *shaliach*: annul when you hear, and it will take effect when I hear. The *shaliach* performs the act; the effect waits upon the husband's own hearing. Why use a *shaliach* at all if he can do it himself upon hearing? *Savar dilma mitradna* — he worries about distraction. The *shaliach* heard and acted; as soon as the husband hears, the effect crystallizes. The pattern is now entirely consistent across all the cases the *Gemara* has examined.

---

## Cheresh Question

### Can Cheresh Annul

Rami Bar Chama now poses his second question: *cheresh mahu she-yafer l'ishto?* Can a deaf man — a *cheresh* in the Talmudic sense of one who speaks but cannot hear — annul vows for his wife? This question is built on the assumption that the husband does not need to actually hear in order to annul. If hearing were literally required, the question would be moot. The question therefore presupposes at least some degree of *lav davka* in the *shmiea* requirement, and asks whether even the residual requirement — membership in the *category* of those capable of hearing — matters.

### Bar Shmiya Requirement

The formulation: *im timtzei lomar ba'al mefer belo shemia* — if you say the husband can annul without hearing — *mishum de-bar nishma hu*, it is because he belongs to the category of hearing. *Aval cheresh de-lav bar nishma hu* — but a deaf person who is not in that category — can he annul at all? This would apply the principle of Rabbi Zeira.

### R. Zeira's Principle

Rabbi Zeira's principle: *kol ha-rauy l'villah ein billah me-akevet bo, vechol she-ein rauy l'villah billah me-akevet bo* — anything fit to be mixed, the mixing does not actually prevent validity even if not performed; but if it is not fit to be mixed, then mixing — had it been possible — would have been required, and its impossibility renders it invalid. The context is the *mincha* offering: the Torah requires the flour and oil to be mixed, but if the *mincha* is of such a large quantity that mixing is physically impossible, it is invalid — whereas if mixing is possible but simply not done, it remains valid. Potential, not actual performance, is what matters; but the potential must be real.

Applied here: a normal husband is *bar shemia* — capable of hearing — and therefore the fact that he did not actually hear does not prevent annulment. But a *cheresh* lacks even the potential. The question is whether this disqualifies him.

Tosafot and others note a broader theoretical question lurking here: how does one determine, across different *mitzvos* and legal acts, when the principle of *rauy* — fitness or potential — is sufficient in place of actual performance? The *Gemara* does not resolve this general question but applies the specific query to the *cheresh*.

### Beraita: Prat L'Eishet C…

Rava brings a *beraita* in response: *veshamah ishah — prat l'eishet cheresh* — "and her husband heard" — this comes to exclude the wife of a deaf man. The exclusion is explicit and unambiguous.

### Category Membership Matt…

From this *beraita*, many *Rishonim* draw an important inference. The *beraita* specifically singles out the *cheresh* as excluded. If the mere failure to hear were itself a disqualification, there would be no need to identify the *cheresh* as a special case — anyone who did not hear would already be excluded. The fact that the *beraita* reserves its exclusion for the *cheresh* specifically implies that in ordinary cases, the husband's not having heard is not itself an obstacle. What disqualifies the *cheresh* is not that he failed to hear this particular vow, but that he is constitutively outside the category of hearing — he is *lav bar shemia*. A hearing husband who simply did not hear a particular vow remains *bar shemia*, and can therefore annul.

This is a striking conclusion. The *Torah* says *veshamah ishah*, and the *halacha* — as understood by most *Rishonim* — is that the husband need not actually hear. The *pshat* understanding of *beyom shmo'o* is perhaps best read as defining the window of *hakama*: from the moment of hearing, the husband has twenty-four hours before his silence becomes acquiescence. But the act of annulment itself is not contingent on prior hearing.

---

## Two Wives Question

### Two Wives Simultaneously

Rami Bar Chama poses a third question: *ba'al mahu she-yafer l'shtei nashav b'vat achat?* Can a husband with two wives annul vows for both of them simultaneously? He has two wives who have both made vows, and he says *mufar lachem* — it is annulled for you — addressing both at once. Is that effective?

### Singular 'Otah' in Verse

The question turns on the language of the *pesukim*. The relevant phrase is *yafer otah* — he annuls *her*, singular. The text consistently uses the singular form: *ve'im henia osah*, and her husband disallowed *her*; *ve'im bayom shmo'o isha yania osah*; *ve'hefer es nidrah*. The *hafarah* is grammatically directed at one woman at a time. Is this *davka* — meaning annulment must be performed individually for each wife — or *lav davka*, meaning the plural could be encompassed?

It is worth noting that in these *pesukim* the verb of *hafarah* applies to the *neder*, while the verb *yania* — disallowing — applies to *her*, the woman. The singular forms run through both verbs, suggesting the entire process is conceived as an individual act directed at one wife and her vow.

### Sota Parallel

Ravina brings a proof from *sota*: *ein mashkin shtei sotos ke'achas* — one may not administer the *sota* waters to two *sotos* simultaneously. The ritual involving a wife suspected of adultery must be performed individually, not for two women at once.

### Reason for Separation

The *mishnah* in *sota* records a dispute about the reason. The *Tanna Kamma* says: *mipnei she-libbah gas ba-chavertah* — because one woman's heart becomes emboldened by her companion. Seeing the other woman undergo the ritual without visible consequence, she may lose her fear and not confess even if guilty. Rabbi Yehuda says the reason is simply from the verse: *ve'hishkah osah levaddah* — and he shall make *her* drink, *levaddah* — alone, individually.

### Reason for Separation

The *Rishonim* debate whether the *Tanna Kamma* and Rabbi Yehuda are in substantive disagreement or whether the *Tanna Kamma* is simply explaining the rationale behind the verse, in the manner of Rabbi Shimon who is *doresh ta'ama dikra*. If the *Tanna Kamma* also relies on the verse fundamentally, then all opinions would require the procedure to be individual. This debate affects the parallel case of *hafarah*.

### Individual Annulment Req…

The *Gemara*'s apparent conclusion is that annulment must be performed for each wife individually. The consistent use of the singular throughout the *pesukim*, reinforced by the *sota* parallel, points in that direction. Precisely how the *Tanna Kamma*'s position in the *sota* case affects the *hafarah* parallel remains somewhat open, but the overall thrust of the *Gemara* is toward requiring individual annulment.

---

## Bogeret & Almanah

### Mishnah: Bogeret & Alman…

The daf concludes with a *mishnah* concerning several cases in which a woman is technically still in the stage of *eirusin* but the time for *nisu'in* has effectively arrived.
