A *bogeret* — a fully adult woman — who has waited twelve months after *kiddushin*; or an *almanah* — a widow — for whom *chazal* set only a thirty-day waiting period between *kiddushin* and *nisu'in* when that period has elapsed. These are scenarios in which *nisu'in* has not yet occurred but is expected imminently.

### R. Eliezer: Payment = An…

Rabbi Eliezer rules: *ho'il uba'alah chayav bimezonoseha* — since the husband is now obligated to provide for her food, this is sufficient to confer upon him the ability to annul her vows even without actual *nisu'in*. His financial obligation establishes his effective relationship to her as that of a husband, and therefore he can annul unilaterally — without the father's participation — even though *de'oraisa* she is technically still in the *eirusin* stage. This is puzzling: if she is not *halachically* a full wife, how can he have the annulment authority of a husband? The question presses especially given that this is a *leniency* — we are granting him a power he would not normally have.

### Chachamim: Actual Nisu'in

The *Chachamim* disagree: *ein haba'al mefer ad shetikanes lirshuto* — the husband cannot annul until she genuinely enters his domain through actual *nisu'in*. The formal legal status must be achieved; the financial obligation does not substitute for the real thing.

---

## Terumah & Status

### Rava: Reconciliation

Rava observes that Rabbi Eliezer's position here aligns with the *Mishnah Rishonah* — an earlier ruling — on a parallel question. *Rabbi Eliezer u-Mishnah Rishonah amru davar echad* — they said the same thing.

### Terumah After 12 Months

The *Mishnah Rishonah* in *Kesubot* ruled: *nosnin l'vsulah yod bet chodesh l'farnes atzmah* — a virgin is given twelve months to prepare her trousseau. If twelve months pass and the husband has not yet brought her to *nisu'in*, his financial responsibilities kick in — *ochelet mishelo*, she eats at his expense — and more strikingly: *ve'ochelet b'terumah* — if he is a *kohen*, she may even eat *terumah*, despite not yet being married. Normally a woman must be genuinely *nesuah* to a *kohen* to eat *terumah*. The *Mishnah Rishonah* extended this right to her based on the elapsed time, treating her effective status as already spousal even before *nisu'in*.

### Later Disallowance

A later *beit din* subsequently retracted this position: *eina isha ochelet b'terumah ad shetikanes l'chuppah* — a woman may not eat *terumah* until she has actually entered the *chuppah*. The later ruling tightened the requirement, refusing to extend spousal status for *issur* purposes before *nisu'in* had actually occurred. Thus the *Mishnah Rishonah* was willing to treat the twelve-month threshold as conferring near-marital status for *terumah* consumption; the later ruling was not. Rabbi Eliezer's position in our *mishnah* — that the husband's food obligation translates into annulment authority — maps onto the *Mishnah Rishonah*'s analogous expansion of spousal status.

---

## Abaye's Objection

### Terumah vs. Nedarim

Abaye objects to Rava's alignment: *dilma lo hi* — perhaps the two positions are not actually the same. The *Mishnah Rishonah* may have permitted *terumah* consumption only because *terumah bizman hazeh* is a *d'rabbanan* concern; the rabbis had the flexibility to relax it when circumstances warranted. But *nedarim* are *d'oraita* — the Torah itself controls who may annul. Even if the *Mishnah Rishonah* was willing to stretch the concept of spousal status for a rabbinic prohibition like *terumah*, it would never have granted the husband power to annul vows, which is a Torah-level matter. *Aval nedarim d'oraita eima lo* — for vows, we would not have extended that power.

### Rabbinic vs. Torah Issue

What does it mean to say *terumah* is *d'rabbanan* in this context? The Talmud elsewhere discusses which *pasuk* establishes the wife's right to eat *terumah*: is it *anshei beito hem yochlu b'lachmo* — people of his household — which would require *nisu'in*; or is it *kinyan kaspo hu yochal b'lachmo* — that which he acquired with his money — which would apply from *kiddushin*? The *Yerushalmi* reads *beito* and holds that even *d'oraita* she requires *nisu'in*. The *Bavli* reads *kinyan kaspo* and holds that *d'oraita* even an *arusa* may eat *terumah*. On the Bavli's reading, the restriction of *terumah* to *nesuot* is entirely rabbinic, making the *Mishnah Rishonah*'s leniency a relaxation of a rabbinic stringency — which is a very different matter from relaxing a Torah-level restriction on who may perform *hafarah*.

### Why Terumah Restricted

Why did the rabbis restrict *terumah* to *nesuot* in the first place if *d'oraita* an *arusa* is permitted? The most straightforward reason is practical: while still in her father's house during *eirusin*, she is likely to share the *terumah* with members of her family who are not *kohanim*, which would constitute a Torah violation. There is also a secondary concern — the possibility that the *kiddushin* will be undone by a *mekach ta'os*, retroactively rendering her never married, in which case her eating *terumah* would have been improper. Once the twelve months have passed and she is effectively standing at the threshold of *nisu'in*, the rabbis were willing — in the *Mishnah Rishonah* — to permit her to eat, since the sharing concern is less acute and the marriage is imminent. But this entire flexibility, Abaye argues, operates within the rabbinic sphere, and tells us nothing about the Torah-level rules of *hafarah*.

---

## Al Da'as Ba'al

### Implicit Husband Consent

The *Gemara* introduces the teaching of Rav Pinchas in the name of Rava: *kol hanoderet al da'as ba'alah hi noderet* — any woman who takes a vow, she vows with her husband's assent in mind. When a woman who is already in a marital relationship — or a relationship effectively equivalent to marriage — takes a vow, it is presumed that she intends the vow to be conditional upon her husband's acceptance. This is not an explicit *tnai* that she articulates, but a psychological reality about how she understands her own act.

### Psychological Intent

This reasoning applies specifically to a woman who has been betrothed for twelve months, the stage at which Rabbi Eliezer permits the husband to annul. At that point, her sense of herself as bound to this man — as living within the framework of their upcoming marriage — is sufficiently developed that when she takes a vow, her implicit orientation is toward a life with him. She vows, as it were, on the understanding that he would agree. This psychological fact, Rav Pinchas argues, is what grounds the husband's ability to annul at that stage.

### Vows vs. Terumah

This reasoning, however, applies to *nedarim* specifically. When a woman takes a vow, her subjective intent shapes the vow's structure. The concept of *al da'as ba'alah* captures something internal to the vow itself — it was taken with an implicit understanding. *Terumah* consumption, by contrast, is entirely an external legal status: she either has the right to eat *terumah* or she does not, and that depends on her formal legal standing, not on any psychological orientation she holds. The *Mishnah Rishonah* granted her *terumah* rights based on an analogous assessment of her practical status; the later *beit din* withdrew it. But for *nedarim*, the psychological dimension is different — the vow's own structure already incorporates the husband's hypothetical consent, and therefore *hafarah* is possible even before technical *nisu'in*.

---

## Ran: Redefining Husband

### Al Da'as Non-Husband

The Ran raises a sharp question against the *al da'as ba'alah* framework. If the mechanism is that she vowed with somebody else's assent in mind, can that person — whoever it is — now annul the vow? For instance, if someone says *al da'as* of a third party, not a husband at all, does that person acquire annulment power? And conversely, if *al da'as ba'alah hi noderet* is the operative principle, does the husband lose the twenty-four-hour window — can he annul at any time, since the vow was always implicitly conditional on his assent? The formal mechanics of *hafarah* — the specific language required, the twenty-four-hour limit — seem to sit in tension with a model that reduces *hafarah* to an implicit *tnai*.

### Formal Hafarah Mechanism

The Ran resolves this by insisting on the formal character of *hafarah*. *Hafarah* is not a *tnai* — it is not simply that the vow dissolves because a condition was not met. *Hafarah* is a formal Torah mechanism: it requires specific language, it operates within a twenty-four-hour window, it is a *gezeirat hakatuv* that the Torah invested in the husband. *U-gzeirat hakatuv hu, u-mishum hachi ein kol leshonot shavim bo* — proper language is required; not every formulation will do. Any view that reduces *hafarah* to the operation of an implicit *tnai* cannot account for why the husband must use the formal *lashon shel hafarah* or why a twenty-four-hour window applies at all.

### Torah's Rationale

So what role does *al da'as ba'alah* play? The Ran articulates it as follows: *hafarah* is indeed a formal Torah mechanism, complete with its own rules. But the Torah had a reason for investing this mechanism in the husband specifically. That reason is the presumption that the wife, when she takes a vow, does so with her husband in mind — *mishum d'al da'as ba'al hi noderet*. The Torah's decision to empower the husband is grounded in this psychological reality about the wife's mental state when she vows. This is a reading of the *ta'ama d'kra* — the reason behind the verse — and it is a strikingly woman-centric framing. The power is not given to the husband because he is the dominant party in whose house she lives and whose authority overrides hers. Rather, the Torah empowers him because the vow itself was implicitly made with him in mind, and it is therefore appropriate that he should be the one who can address it.

### Expanding Husband Catego…

From this understanding of the Torah's rationale, the Ran draws a conclusion about the scope of the category "husband" as the Torah uses it. If the reason the Torah empowers the *ba'al* is that the wife takes vows with him in mind, then the category of *ba'al* for purposes of *hafarah* should include any person who genuinely occupies that role in her psychological universe. After twelve months of *kiddushin*, when the relationship has matured to the point that she is practically living for the moment of *nisu'in*, when he is providing for her food, when she thinks of herself as functionally his wife — at that stage, an *arus* fits within the Torah's conception of *ba'al* for purposes of *hafarah*. The Torah says *ishah*, husband, and Rabbi Eliezer argues that the Torah would recognize the *arus* in this stage as falling within that category, precisely because the reason for the category is fully operative.

### Role-Based Limitation

The Ran is careful to confine this reasoning. It is not an invitation to say that any person whom a woman holds in high regard, or with whose approval she takes vows in mind, can thereby annul those vows. The power of *hafarah* flows through the formal Torah mechanism. What the *al da'as* reasoning does is define who fits within the Torah's category of *ba'al* for purposes of that mechanism. That category can be extended to an *arus* who stands in the husband's role — who is, in every relevant sense, the person she is married to, albeit not yet under *chuppah*. It cannot be extended to an arbitrary third party who is not in that role at all. The formal structure of *hafarah* remains intact; what expands, carefully and on principled grounds, is the definition of who qualifies as the *ba'al* whom the Torah empowered to perform it. This, the Ran concludes, is the most coherent account of Rabbi Eliezer's position — and it explains how *hafarah* before *nisu'in* is not a departure from the Torah's framework but a faithful application of its underlying logic.

---

---

# Nedarim 74

## Shomeret Yavam Intro

### Opening Remarks

The fifth *mishnah* of this *perek* continues the discussion of unusual cases — those that do not arise in the standard situation contemplated by the *Torah* — which the *perek* has chosen to focus upon: the case of the father and the *arus* acting in partnership in the annulment of vows, and now the case of the *shomeret yavam*, the woman who awaits *yibum*, levirate marriage.

### Yavam's Role

The *yavam*'s relationship with his *yevamah* is, on one hand, a carryover of the marriage of the deceased brother, which may itself have been at the level of *nesu'in*. The *yibum* relationship requires less deliberate intent to actualize into a full *nesu'in* — even an act of *bi'ah* performed without specific *kavanah* to create a marriage accomplishes it, because of the *zika*, the bond and remnant of the *kiddushin* that transfers from the dead husband to his brother. On the other hand, the relationship in its present, unrealized state is not equivalent to a full marriage: if the *yevamah* were to be with another man, it would not constitute *eshet ish*; and the release from the obligation can be achieved through *chalitzah* rather than a *get*.

### Yavam & Hafara

Given this ambiguous status, the question arises whether the *yavam* is needed and able to participate in *hafarat nedarim* together with the father. If the original marriage to the deceased husband had been at the level of *erusin*, the father remains in the picture entirely. The question then becomes whether the *yavam*'s relationship resembles *erusin* — in which case his participation in *hafara* is necessary but must be jointly with the father — or whether it rises to the level of *nesu'in*, in which case he would act alone. The *mishnah* uses the word *yafer* (he may annul), and it is not immediately clear which of these two possibilities that word entails.

## Mishnah Dispute

### Mishnah Setup

The *mishnah* presents the following case: a *shomeret yavam* — a woman awaiting *yibum* — whether she has one *yavam* or two. With two *yevamin*, the question is immediately more complex, since one cannot designate any particular one as being in a concrete relationship with her.

### R. Eliezer View

*Rabbi Eliezer omer yafer* — Rabbi Eliezer says the *yavam* may be *mefir*, whether there is one or two brothers-in-law. Whether this means he does so alone (as a *ba'al*) or together with the father (as an *arus*) remains to be clarified by the *Gemara*.

### R. Yehoshua View

*Rabbi Yehoshua omer l'echad aval lo lishnayim* — Rabbi Yehoshua says this authority applies only when there is one *yavam*, not when there are two. The reason is not merely epistemic uncertainty about which brother is "really" the one in the relationship, but something more fundamental: the relationship is indeterminate at its base, and therefore neither brother genuinely occupies the role of husband. It follows that if there are two *yevamin* and neither has the status of husband, the father annuls the vow by himself — not that the parties are paralyzed, but that the indeterminacy removes the *yavam* from the equation and leaves the father as the sole authority.

### R. Akiva View

*Rabbi Akiva omer lo l'echad velo lishnayim* — Rabbi Akiva rules that even a single *yavam* has no such status. In his view, even with only one brother-in-law, the relationship does not carry sufficient halachic weight to confer authority over her vows, and everything reverts to the father.

### Kal Vachomer

Rabbi Eliezer challenges Rabbi Akiva with a *kal v'chomer*. When a man marries a woman on his own initiative — *isha shekana hu l'atzmo* — he acquires the right to annul her vows. How much more so, then, in the case where heaven itself has designated the relationship — *isha shehiknu lo min hashamayim* — should he be in a position to be *mefir*? The very existence of a *mitzvah* of *yibum*, the concept of *yakum shem achiv hamet*, suggests this divinely ordained bond is stronger, not weaker, than one created by purely human initiative.

### R. Akiva Response

Rabbi Akiva rejects the comparison. *Im amarta b'isha shekana hu l'atzmo, she'ein l'acherim bah reshus* — when a man marries a woman entirely on his own, no one else has any share or claim to her. *Tomar b'isha shehiknu lo min hashamayim, sheyesh l'acherim bah reshus* — in the case of *yibum*, another brother also has a connection to her, and even after one brother acts, the other is not categorically excluded. The relationship is thus not exclusive, and for that reason the *yavam* does not stand in the same position as a husband. Rabbi Yehoshua presses back — *Akiva, peratzta b'shnei yevamim, mah atah meshiv al yavam echad?* — conceding that the argument works for two brothers but asking what Rabbi Akiva would say about a single *yavam*, where Rabbi Eliezer's *kal v'chomer* seems to apply in full force. Rabbi Akiva responds: *ein hayevamah gemurah layavam k'shem she'arusah gemurah l'isha* — the *yevamah* is not fully given over to the *yavam* the way an *arusah* is given over to her husband. The nature of the relationship is not as weighty; it is not marriage in the full sense, and therefore even a single *yavam* cannot be *mefir*.

## Zika & Relationship

### R. Akiva: No Zika

The *Gemara* now provides a conceptual framework for the three-way dispute. Rabbi Akiva's position is explained as *ein zika* — he does not recognize any concrete bond. *Zika*, as familiar from *Masechet Yevamot*, refers to whether the potential relationship awaiting actualization is itself given real halachic weight, such that we speak of an actual existing bond rather than a mere future possibility. One might have thought that even Rabbi Akiva could acknowledge *zika* while nonetheless maintaining that it is not strong enough to reach the level of *eshet ish* or to function like the bond of a husband for purposes of *hafara*. However, the *Gemara* prefers to frame Rabbi Akiva's position as a denial of *zika* as a concrete relationship altogether. There is a *mitzvah*, there is an *issur* of *lo tihiyeh eishet hamet hachutza*, but none of that has yet defined a real, concrete relational status — it remains a potential and an obligation, not an actualized bond.

### Yehoshua/Eliezer: Yes Zi…

Both Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer affirm *zika* as a real, concrete bond. The distinction between them is then straightforward: Rabbi Yehoshua holds that when there are two *yevamin*, the *zika* is fundamentally indeterminate — one cannot locate where it attaches — and so neither brother can invoke it. Rabbi Eliezer holds *ein b'reirah* is not a concern here, and even with two brothers some basis remains to recognize a *yavam*'s authority. The *Gemara* presses: even granted *zika*, how can Rabbi Eliezer hold that any particular one of two brothers is in a position to annul?

### Rav Ami Ukeimta

*Amar Rabbi Ami: k'gon she'asa ma'amar* — Rabbi Ami resolves the difficulty with an *ukeimta*, a recontextualization of the *mishnah*. He holds that the *mishnah* is not describing the baseline case of two brothers where neither has done anything. Rather, it speaks of a case where one of the brothers has performed *ma'amar* — the rabbinic act of *kiddushin* performed by a *yavam* with his *yevamah*. As is well known from *Masechet Yevamot*, *ma'amar* has no *d'Oraita* effect; the only halachically effective routes to completion are *bi'ah* for *yibum* or *chalitzah* for release. A *get* accomplishes nothing *d'Oraita*, and *kiddushin* on its own does nothing *d'Oraita*. Nevertheless, the Rabbis instituted *ma'amar* as a preparatory act — demonstrating intent, providing structure to the relationship, and in the case of multiple brothers, serving to designate which one is proceeding with the *yibum*. The Rabbis actually encouraged *ma'amar* even when there is only one brother, as a way of bringing formality and intention to the process before the act of *bi'ah* that constitutes the *yibum* itself. Once one of two brothers performs *ma'amar*, he is thereby designated as the one proceeding, and on that basis Rabbi Eliezer holds he is in a position to be *mefir*. This is the *ukeimta*: the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua concerns a case where *ma'amar* has been performed — Rabbi Eliezer holding it is sufficient to designate one brother for *hafara*, and Rabbi Yehoshua holding it is not.

### Ma'amar & Kinyan

The *Gemara* immediately notes a difficulty: *ma'amar* is rabbinic; why should a rabbinic act create a concrete enough relationship to confer the authority to do *hafara*? The answer is that *Rabbi Eliezer savar lah k'Beis Shammai*, for Rabbi Eliezer holds in accordance with Beis Shammai, *de'amri ma'amar koneh kinyan gamur* — that *ma'amar* effects a complete acquisition, a *kinyan gamur*, with real *d'Oraita* consequences. The Ran elaborates: according to Beis Shammai, *ma'amar* achieves the status of *k'nusah* — as if she has been fully brought into the marriage — such that if the *yavam* subsequently changes his mind, he need not perform *chalitzah*; he can dissolve the relationship with a *get* instead. This is a significant halachic consequence that demonstrates the *ma'amar* has genuinely redefined the relationship, moving it from the track of *yibum* onto the track of regular marriage with its attendant modes of dissolution.

## Beis Shammai Debate

### R. Elazar Narrow

At this point the *Gemara* introduces a complication. A certain *Rabbi Elazar* — distinct from Rabbi Eliezer of the *mishnah* — holds a narrower reading of Beis Shammai's position: *ma'amar l'Beis Shammai ein koneh ela lidchos b'tzara* — all *ma'amar* accomplishes according to Beis Shammai is to push aside the concern about the co-wife; it does not constitute a genuine *kinyan* in the broader sense. This narrow reading undercuts the premise that allowed Rabbi Eliezer's position in the *mishnah* to make sense, since without a true *kinyan gamur* from *ma'amar*, one cannot explain how one brother among two is designated as holding a concrete relationship with the *yevamah*.

### Three-Brother Example

To understand what "pushing aside the co-wife" means, consider a case with three brothers — call them Reuven, Shimon, and Levi — where two of them are married to sisters. If Shimon dies, Reuven has a *mitzvah* of *yibum* with Shimon's wife. But if he does so and then Levi dies, he is already married to the wife's sister and cannot perform *yibum* with Levi's widow. Conversely, if he does not perform *yibum* and Levi also dies, he faces the problem of *achot zekukato* — each woman is the quasi-wife's sister of the other because the *zika* to each renders the other an *achot zekukato* — and he cannot perform *yibum* with either.

### Beis Shammai Position

Now suppose Reuven performs *ma'amar* with Shimon's widow before Levi dies. When Levi subsequently dies, can Reuven say: "I have already acted upon my *zika* to Shimon's widow; Levi's widow can go free, since she is not in a genuine *zika* relationship with me in the same way"? Beis Shammai says yes — the *ma'amar* is sufficient to establish that Levi's widow need not concern him; she is the *tzarah* who is *nidchit*, pushed aside. Rabbi Elazar understands this narrowly: Beis Shammai is not saying *ma'amar* effects a full *kinyan*; it merely operates in this local context to remove the obligation with respect to the sister. Read this way, we are left without the broader *kinyan gamur* that would explain Rabbi Eliezer's position in the *mishnah*. The *Gemara* therefore turns to an alternative explanation.

## Mezonot Requirement

### Beit Din Obligation

The *Gemara* resolves the difficulty: *hacha b'mai askinan — k'gon she'amad b'din v'nitchayev lah mezonot*. The case is not simply one of *ma'amar* alone; it is a case where one of the brothers was brought before a *beit din* — presumably the older brother, to whom the obligation of *yibum* is first directed — and the *beit din* obligated him to pay *mezonot* to the *yevamah*. The logic is that this woman has been left without a husband, and if one particular brother is expected to fulfill the obligation and has been deferring, once a full year has passed she should not be left without support. The *beit din* therefore makes him financially responsible for her maintenance for as long as she continues to wait.

### Ran's Principle

This connects to a principle the Ran articulated in the previous *sugya*, cited here in the name of Rabbi Pinchas in the name of Rava: *kol hanoderet al da'at ba'alah hi noderet* — a woman who makes a vow does so with her husband's understanding in mind. The Ran was careful to explain that this principle is not a blanket rule that any person paying someone's bills can annul her vows. The mechanism requires someone who is already in a quasi-husband relationship, and to that pre-existing relationship one adds the further reality that he is paying her food bills and she sees herself as living in a relationship with him and about to be fully married to him. Under those conditions, her vows are presumed to be made *al da'ato*, in accordance with his understanding.

### Mezonot = Nisuin

The Ran draws out the practical consequence: paying *mezonot* combined with the existing *zika* relationship places this *yavam* into the *Torah*'s category of *ba'al*. More specifically, the Ran holds that this reflects a *nesu'in*-type relationship — and therefore, according to those who say the *yavam* can annul in such a case, he does so alone, without the father, as a *ba'al* and not merely as an *arus*. This resolves the earlier question about what *yafer* in the *mishnah* means: in the case where *mezonot* have been imposed, the *yavam* functions as a *ba'al* and acts independently.

## Textual Evidence

### Kal Vachomer Context

The *Gemara* now re-examines the text of Rabbi Eliezer's *kal v'chomer* in the *mishnah* in light of this reading. Rabbi Eliezer said: a woman he acquired for himself — *isha shekana hu l'atzmo* — he can annul her vows; how much more so a woman whom heaven designated for him. If, as Rabbi Ami holds, the *mishnah* is describing a case where *ma'amar* was performed, then this woman is not merely *min hashamayim* — she is *also* one whom he acquired himself through *ma'amar*, making her *kanah le'atzmo al yedei shamayim*. The *Gemara* notes this apparent over-description but dismisses it: it only strengthens the argument. He is saying, "This case is designated by heaven — and parenthetically he also acted himself on top of that — so surely this should be stronger than one who acted entirely alone."

### Rava's Question

The *Gemara* then observes that if we accept Rabbi Ami's reading of the *mishnah* as a *ma'amar* case, we can potentially resolve a question posed by Rava: *ma'amar l'Beis Shammai erusin oseh o nisuin oseh?* — does *ma'amar* according to Beis Shammai produce a state of *erusin* or a state of *nisuin*? This question arises because even if Beis Shammai holds *ma'amar* is a *kinyan gamur*, it is formally an act of *kiddushin*. Yet the nature of the *yibum* relationship — where *bi'ah* without any deliberate intent still consummates the marriage — suggests the entire structure might be closer to *nisuin* from the outset, such that *ma'amar* elevates it all the way to *nisuin* rather than stopping at *erusin*. The practical implications include whether *mezonot* is owed after *ma'amar* and the full range of questions attending to *nesu'in* status.

### No Father Mentioned

The *Gemara* proposes a resolution: since the *mishnah* states simply *yafer* — he annuls — without mentioning the father, it implies the *yavam* acts alone, as a *ba'al*, which would indicate *nisuin* status. The working assumption is that those who grant the *yavam* any authority do so because his relationship resembles *nisuin*, and therefore the *mishnah*'s omission of the father is significant.

### Rav Yitzchak View

Rav Yitzchak, citing Rav Ami, rejects this inference: *yafer beshutfut* — *yafer* means together with the father. The *yavam*'s status in that case is like an *arus*, not a *ba'al*, and his authority is not independent. The *mishnah*'s *yafer* does not resolve whether it is *erusin* or *nisuin*, and the question remains open.

## Braiyta Evidence

### Tosefta Citation

The *Gemara* now introduces a *braita* — a passage from the *Tosefta* — that parallels the *mishnah* debate. *Shomeret yavam bein yavam echad bein shnei yevamin*, Rabbi Eliezer says *yafer*, Rabbi Yehoshua says only for one and not for two, and Rabbi Akiva says neither one nor two.

### R. Eliezer Argument

Rabbi Eliezer's argument in the *braita* is formulated more precisely than in the *mishnah*. He says: *u'mah im isha she'ein lo chelek bah ad shelo tavo lereshuto* — a completely unrelated woman, toward whom he had absolutely no prior connection, once she enters his domain through an act of *kiddushin*, she is fully his and he can annul her vows. *Isha sheyesh lo chelek bah ad shelo tavo lereshuto* — but the *yevamah* is a woman to whom he already has a connection — the *zika*, the *mitzvah* of *yibum* — even before he has taken any additional step. How much more so, *mishebat'a lereshuto*, once she has come further into his domain, should he have that power? The Ran notes that the phrase *mishebat'a lereshuto* is chosen rather than *nichnesah lereshuto*, and suggests this reflects the language of *kiddushin* rather than *nesu'in* — the *Gemara* reads *ba'ah lereshuto* as referring to an act of *ma'amar* rather than completed *yibum*, since completed *yibum* would make her fully his wife and no one would debate it. This confirms Rabbi Ami's *ukeimta*: the case is one where *ma'amar* has been performed.

### R. Akiva Distinction

Rabbi Akiva's response in the *braita* is explicit. He distinguishes: *bekiddushin shekanah hu l'atzmo* — when a man performs *kiddushin* himself, *shekeshem she'ein lo chelek bah* before the marriage, *she'ein l'acherim chelek bah* either — nobody has any connection to her, and after *kiddushin* he closes out everyone else entirely. *Tomar b'isha shehiknu lo min hashamayim* — in the case of the *yevamah*, *shekeshem sheyesh lo imah chelek, ken yesh l'acher imah chelek* — just as he has a connection to her, so too another brother has a connection to her. Even after *ma'amar*, the other brother can theoretically perform *bi'ah* and complete the *yibum*; the exclusivity that characterizes an ordinary *kiddushin* is simply absent. This is the structural flaw in Rabbi Eliezer's *kal v'chomer*: ordinary *kiddushin* excludes all others; the *yavam*'s connection does not.

### R. Yehoshua Challenge

Rabbi Yehoshua again presses Rabbi Akiva: *Akiva, zu hi bishnei yevamin* — this reasoning about the lack of exclusivity holds when there are two brothers, but what do you say about a single *yavam*? When there is only one brother, there is no other claimant. Rabbi Eliezer's argument seems fully applicable.

### R. Akiva Final

Rabbi Akiva's answer is deliberately terse: *u'kesha'ar devarim ken nedarim* — just as in all other laws, so too with vows. Ben Azzai famously lamented — *chavalo l'cha Ben Azzai shelo shimasht et Rabbi Akiva* — that he had not attended upon Rabbi Akiva, implying the answer was so compressed that one needed deep familiarity with Rabbi Akiva's thinking to grasp it fully.

## Key Principle

### Ma'amar Presupposed

The *Gemara* now draws the conclusion that the *braita* confirms Rabbi Ami's *ukeimta*. The evidence: Rabbi Akiva himself says *bein asah ma'amar bein lo asah ma'amar* — whether or not he performed *ma'amar*, it makes no difference. This statement only makes sense if *ma'amar* was already on the table as a live option in the debate, which confirms that the scenario under discussion was one where *ma'amar* was part of the picture.

### Ba'at Lereshuto

Further confirmation comes from the *braita*'s formulation. The phrase *isha sheyesh lo chelek bah... mishebat'a lereshuto* — referring to the *yevamah* who has come further into his domain — can only refer to a state after *ma'amar*. If *ba'at lereshuto* meant the consummation of *yibum* through *bi'ah*, she would already be his wife and the debate would be meaningless. The phrase therefore presupposes that something beyond mere *zika* has occurred but that full *yibum* has not yet been completed — which is precisely the state after *ma'amar*. This confirms *ka pashit mineih d'keshe'asah bah ma'amar* — one can derive from this passage that the entire debate is framed around the *ma'amar* scenario.

### No Stoning = No Eshet Ish

Rabbi Akiva's clinching argument is now spelled out by Rava: *ee atah modeh she'ein chayavin sekilah k'na'arah hame'urasah* — you would have to admit that if the *yevamah* were to sleep with another man after *ma'amar*, she would not be liable to stoning as would a *na'arah hame'urasah*, the betrothed maiden. She is not *eshet ish* in the fullest sense. *U'kesha'ar devarim ken nedarim* — therefore, just as she lacks the full status of *eshet ish* in all other areas of law, so too with respect to *nedarim* she is not fully under his authority. No matter how robust the *zika*, no matter that *ma'amar* was performed, no matter that only one brother is in the picture — unless the relationship rises to the level of genuine *eshet ish*, the *yavam* cannot be *mefir*.

### Final Mishnah Phrase

The *Gemara* concludes by returning to the closing words of the *mishnah* itself, as cited by Rav Ashi: *ein yevamah gemurah l'ish keshem she'arusah gemurah l'ish* — the *yevamah* is not fully this man's wife in the way that a betrothed woman is fully her husband's *arusah*. This formulation encapsulates Rabbi Akiva's position: whatever the weight of *zika*, whatever the effect of *ma'amar*, the *yevamah* remains in a categorically incomplete relationship — not a fully constituted *eshet ish* — and therefore the *yavam* cannot perform *hafara*.

---

---

# Nedarim 75

## Pre-Annulment of Vows

### Opening Remarks

With this *daf* we move away from the extended discussion of the *aras* (groom) and the *yavam*, returning to what might be called more basic territory concerning the act of *hafarah* — though the cases examined remain anything but simple.

### Mishnah Text

The *mishnah* presents the following case. A husband about to depart on a business trip says to his wife: *kol hanedarim she-tadori mi-kan v'ad she-avo mi-makom ploni, ha-rei hen kayamim* — "All the vows you make from the time I leave until I return, I hereby affirm." The Ran notes that the husband says *mi-kan*, from here, i.e., from the moment of his departure, rather than *me-achshav*, from right now.

The *mishnah* rules: *lo amar klum* — he has said nothing. If, however, he declares *ha-rei hen mufarim* — that they are hereby annulled — then Rabbi Eliezer rules *mufar*, they are validly annulled in advance. The *chachamim* rule *eino mufar*: pre-annulment of a vow that does not yet exist is ineffective.

### Mekayem vs. Meifer

The distinction between these two rulings rests on the conceptual difference between *mekayem* (affirming a vow) and *meifer* (annulling it). To be *mekayem* a vow is to strengthen its reality as a binding *issur*, and one cannot strengthen what does not yet exist. But negating a vow — the *chachamim* and Rabbi Eliezer dispute whether annulment requires the prior existence of a vow in the same way.

### Rabbi Eliezer Kal Vachom…

Rabbi Eliezer presses his case with a *kal va-chomer*: *im heifer nedarim she-ba'u li-khlal issur, lo yafer nedarim she-lo ba'u li-khlal issur?* — If the husband can annul vows that have already taken effect and manifested as real-world prohibitions, how much more so should he be able to annul vows that have not yet come into existence? As the *gemara* will soon explore, the precise import of this argument — whether Rabbi Eliezer means the pre-annulment *prevents* the vow from ever taking effect, or whether it *annuls* the vow at the instant of its formation — is itself an open question.

### Chachamim Respond

The *chachamim* respond by invoking a scriptural link: *ishah yekimennu ve-ishah yeferennu* — "the husband shall affirm it and the husband shall annul it." From this verse they derive a parallel structure: *et she-ba li-khlal hakim, ba li-khlal hafer; lo ba li-khlal hakim, lo ba li-khlal hafer* — only something that is subject to affirmation can be subject to annulment. Since a vow that does not yet exist cannot be affirmed, it likewise cannot be annulled. The *kal va-chomer* may be logically appealing in principle, but the verse forecloses it.

### Act vs. Effect

The *mishnah* takes for granted that a husband may annul his wife's vows without having heard them — that question was addressed at length in the preceding discussion. The only issue here is whether annulment can precede the vow's very existence. One might ask whether the same conceptual move that was used earlier — splitting the act of *hafarah* from its effect, so that the act is performed now but takes hold only later — could be applied here to the *kiyum* side of the equation. The answer, however, is that such a maneuver cannot help the husband who wishes to be *mekayem*: since *kiyum* by definition requires a vow to strengthen, any attempted *kiyum* would necessarily await the vow's formation and would still be ineffective. The device of separating act from effect addressed only the *shemi'ah* problem; it has no traction here.

---

## Prevent vs. Annul

### Two Positions

The *gemara* opens with a formal question — *iba'ya lehu* — concerning the nature of Rabbi Eliezer's ruling. Granted that the husband's pre-issued *hafarah* is effective, what precisely does it accomplish?

### Annul After Effect

The first possibility: the vow does take effect, but simultaneously with its taking effect it is annulled. There is no moment in real time during which the wife stands bound — the annulment is instantaneous — yet conceptually the vow exists and is then negated.

### Prevent Effect

The second possibility: the husband's prior *hafarah* is preventative. The pre-annulment acts as an ounce of prevention, blocking the vow from ever acquiring any force or reality whatsoever. It never takes effect at all — *lo chail klal*.

### Ve-ani Case

The practical difference (*nafka mina*) between these two positions concerns the case of *hatfasah*. Suppose the wife declares *hareini nezirah*, and a bystander immediately says *ve-ani* — transferring the *nezirut* status to herself. The husband had, a week earlier, issued a blanket pre-annulment covering his wife's vows. If the vow took effect and was then annulled — the first interpretation — the bystander's *ve-ani* attaches to a real status that existed, if only for a conceptual instant, and her *nezirut* stands. If the vow never took effect at all — the second interpretation — there is no status to transfer, and the *ve-ani* is meaningless.

---

## Hafarah vs. Hatarah

### Example Setup

The *gemara's* example: the wife takes a vow, a companion says *ve-ani*, and the husband then annuls the wife's vow. The question is what consequences follow for the companion.

### Hatarah Question

This raises a further question. What if, instead of the husband's *hafarah*, the original person who made the vow went to a *chacham* for *hatarah* — formal dissolution? Would the companion who said *ve-ani* also be released?

### Ran's Distinction

Here the Ran articulates a distinction that is central to this entire *perek* yet, somewhat surprisingly, has not been foregrounded until now. *Hatarah* — dissolution by a *chacham* — is *oker ha-neder me-ikaro*: it retroactively uproots the vow from its very source. The mechanism of *hatarah* is to reframe the original vow as a *neder ta'ut*, a vow made in error, which means the vow is deemed never to have taken effect. *Hafarah*, by contrast, operates *mikan u-le-ha'ba*: it cuts off the vow going forward but does not retroactively undo the past. The husband does not uproot the vow; he severs it.

### Consequence

This distinction has direct practical consequences for the *ve-ani* case. When the first person obtains *hatarah* from a *chacham*, the retroactive effect means the original vow never existed, so all subsequent *hatfasah* — the status-transfers effected by those who said *ve-ani* — collapses as well. When the husband performs *hafarah*, however, the vow genuinely did exist (even if only for a conceptual instant), and that real, if momentary, existence is what the companion's *ve-ani* latches onto. The *hafarah* stops the wife's *nezirut* going forward, but the companion who said *ve-ani* transferred the status at the moment it existed and therefore remains bound.

### Nazir Parallel

This is not merely a *sevarah*-level inference; there is an explicit *gemara* in Nazir, 79b, that poses precisely this question: *ba'al me'akar akar, o migaz gayiz* — does the husband uproot the vow entirely, or does he merely cut it off from continuing? The *nafka mina* given there is identical: a woman vows *nezirut*, her companion says *ve-ani*, and the husband annuls the wife's vow. If the husband is *me'akar* — uprooting retroactively — then the companion too is released. If he is *migaz gayiz* — cutting it off going forward — the wife is released but the companion remains bound. The *gemara* in Nazir concludes: *ba'al migaz gayiz*; a *chacham* is *oker me-ikara*. This is an important and fundamental distinction that is, ironically, spelled out more explicitly in Nazir than in Nedarim itself.

### Ve-ani Timing

The Ran raises a second question worth addressing. By the time the companion says *ve-ani*, the wife's vow has already been annulled — so the wife is no longer a *nezirah* at that moment. Why should *ve-ani* not mean "and I am like you are right now," in which case the companion is equally free?

### Shelamim Analogy

The Ran resolves this by reference to a *gemara* concerning meat of *zivchei shelamim*. Before the blood is dashed on the *mizbeach*, the meat is forbidden; once it has been dashed, it is permitted. If someone then declares *ve-zeh ka-zeh* — "and this like that" — using the *shelamim* meat as the referent, the *gemara* asks: *be-ikaro kamatfis* — does he mean to compare to the object's current status (now permitted) or to its earlier status (when it was forbidden)? The *gemara* concludes *de-hashta kamatfis* — he refers to its present status — and therefore no *hatfasah* results. The Ran acknowledges this parallel, but distinguishes the *ve-ani* case on two grounds. First, the verbal form *ve-ani*, without the explicit comparative *kamoah* ("like her"), does not naturally carry the nuance "like her as she is right now." Second, and more substantially: what stands before the companion is the wife's act of declaration — *hareini nezirah* — and the *hafarah* itself is not present or visible. Given that backdrop, *ve-ani* most naturally refers to the *nezirut* status that that declaration created. Even if that status evaporated an instant later, it did exist, and it is to that status that *ve-ani* attaches.

To summarize the *nafka mina*: if the pre-issued *hafarah* means the vow took effect and was then immediately annulled, the companion's *ve-ani* latches onto the status that existed in that conceptual instant and the companion remains bound. If the pre-issued *hafarah* prevented the vow from ever taking effect, then there was never any status to transfer and the companion is free.

---

## Mishnah Language

### Eliezer's Logic

The *gemara* returns to the precise language of Rabbi Eliezer's *kal va-chomer*: if the husband can annul vows *she-ba'u li-khlal issur* — that have already come into the category of prohibition — should he not *a fortiori* be able to annul vows *she-lo ba'u li-khlal issur* — that have not yet entered that category? The natural reading of this argument is that Rabbi Eliezer claims the pre-annulment should prevent the vow from ever taking effect. That reading would resolve the earlier *ibaya* in favor of *lo chaylin*.

### Shelo Ba'u

The *gemara*, however, resists this reading. The phrase *shelo ba'u* does not mean vows that will never come into existence — *she-einan ba'in*. It means vows that have not yet come into existence — *adayin lo ba'u*. Rabbi Eliezer is not claiming that the pre-annulment defeats vows that would otherwise never take effect; he is speaking about vows that exist in the future but have not yet arrived.

### Challenged Status

The Ran offers a refined reading of the *kal va-chomer* in light of this correction. The argument is not that pre-annulment *prevents* the vow from taking effect. Rather: if the husband can annul a vow after it has taken hold in an unchallenged state, how much more so should he be able to annul a vow that comes into existence already challenged — *mumo imo*, bearing its defect from the very moment of its birth. The vow never existed in a pristine, unchallenged state; from the instant it came into being, the *hafarah* was already present. According to the Ran, this is Rabbi Eliezer's actual position: the vow does take effect, but it arrives already carrying the seeds of its own annulment.

### Own vs. Wife Vows

The *gemara* raises a further analogy. When a person makes a conditional pre-declaration — on the order of what is done on *Erev Rosh Hashanah* — that any future vows should be considered void, those vows do not take effect when subsequently made. Should we infer by *kal va-chomer* that a husband's pre-issued *hafarah* similarly prevents his wife's vows from taking effect?

### Two Mechanisms

The *gemara* deflects this inference: *ha ke-d'ita ve-ha ke-d'ita* — each case operates by its own mechanism. When a person pre-empts his own vows, the mechanism is *ta'ut*: the conditional declaration frames any future vow as an error, as something he never truly intended. The vow does not take effect because the *ta'ut* mechanism retroactively undermines the act of vowing. *Hafarah* of a wife's vow operates through an entirely different mechanism — annulment, not error — and the two cannot simply be mapped onto each other.

### After to Before

The Ran, however, finds this answer unsatisfying if taken at face value as the *kal va-chomer's* foundation, and offers a brilliant reinterpretation. The *kal va-chomer* does not claim that what works for one's own vows must work identically for a wife's vows. Rather, the analogy is structural: for one's own vows, where the operative mechanism is *ta'ut*, the pre-emptive declaration works *before* (via a *tenai*) even though one cannot undo one's own vow *after* by oneself. The structural lesson is: what works *after* should certainly work *before*. Now transpose to the wife's vows. There, the operative mechanism is *hafarah*, which concededly works *after*. By the same structural logic — if it works after, it should work before — the *hafarah* should work before the vow comes into existence as well. The mechanisms are different, but the logical form of the *kal va-chomer* is the same in both cases, and that is the argument's real force.

---

## Mikveh Analogy

### Mikveh Cleans

The *chachamim* respond to Rabbi Eliezer's *kal va-chomer* with a counter-example from the laws of *tumah*: *u-mah mikveh she-ma'aleh et ha-teme'im mi-tum'atan* — just as a *mikveh* restores a *tamei* person to *taharah* after the fact...

### Remove vs. Prevent

...nonetheless, *ein matzil et ha-tahor min ha-tumah* — being immersed in a *mikveh* does not prevent *tumah* from attaching. If a person is standing in a *mikveh* and simultaneously comes into contact with something *tamei*, or a bodily condition arises that would render him *tamei* — *tovel ve-sheretz be-yado* — he is *tamei*. The *mikveh* removes *tumah* after the fact but does not block *tumah* from taking hold in the first place. The *kal va-chomer* that "if it works after it works before" therefore does not hold as a general principle.

### Person's Role

The text continues with an additional line, noting: a person — *adam* — who cannot make a *tamei* object *tahor* (*she-ein ma'aleh et ha-tamei mi-tum'ato*), is it not logical that he should be unable to prevent *tahor* things from becoming *tamei*? Yet consider the case of *tumah blu'ah*: an object swallowed inside a person's body is shielded from *tumah* — it cannot become *tamei* — even though the person himself cannot make *tamei* things *tahor*. In other words, the mechanisms run in exactly opposite directions: a *mikveh* removes *tumah* but does not prevent it; a person prevents *tumah* (when absorbed internally) but does not remove it.

### Context-Dependent

The Ran explains the double thrust of the *chachamim's* argument. Point one: the *mikveh* itself demonstrates that something can remove without preventing — *kal va-chomer* logic from "after" to "before" does not operate in a vacuum. Point two: the comparison between the *mikveh* and the *adam* case demonstrates that across *halakhah*, the direction in which a mechanism operates is context-determined and cannot be extrapolated by *kal va-chomer* alone. The *chachamim* are not necessarily claiming that Rabbi Eliezer's *kal va-chomer* is logically incoherent, but that this class of inference is not ironclad — its force depends on what the surrounding *halakhic* framework supports.

---

## Pre-dunking & Seeds (III)

### Pre-dunking

The *chachamim* offer a second counter-example: *im matbilin kli tamei le-taharo* — if you can immerse a *tamei* vessel to render it *tahor*, can you pre-immerse a *tahor* vessel so that when it later becomes *tamei* the problem will have been solved in advance? The answer is obviously not. This is analogous to the person who says *echta ve-ashuv* — I will sin and preemptively repent. The *mikveh* does not work prospectively in that fashion.

### Suggests Haylan

Interestingly, the way the *chachamim* frame this counter-example — *yatbilu kli le-cheshe-yitma le-taharo*, "let them pre-immerse a vessel so that when it becomes *tamei* it will become *tahor*" — seems to presuppose that Rabbi Eliezer's mechanism is one in which the vow *does* take effect and is then reversed. The phrase *le-cheshe-yitma* implies: once it becomes *tamei*, the pre-immersion will kick in and render it *tahor*. This is the *haylan* interpretation — the vow takes effect, and the pre-annulment then resolves it.

### Conflicting Signals

At this point the *gemara* has two analogies pointing in opposite directions. The *mikveh*-in-use analogy — standing in a *mikveh* does not prevent *tumah* — suggests the *chachamim* are arguing against the *lo haylan* position: Rabbi Eliezer thinks pre-annulment prevents the vow from taking effect, and they counter that prevention does not work that way. The pre-dunking analogy, by contrast, suggests the *chachamim* are arguing against the *haylan* position: Rabbi Eliezer thinks the vow takes effect and is then reversed, and they counter that pre-applying a remedy for a future condition does not work. Two analogies; two different signals about what position they are attacking.

---

## Conclusion & Scriptu (II)

### Either Way

The *gemara* resolves this tension in a striking way. *Rabbanan lo kaymei lehu be-ta'ameih de-Rabbi Eliezer* — the *chachamim* themselves did not know precisely what Rabbi Eliezer's position was. Accordingly, *ve-hachi kamre lei* — their response was structured to cover both possibilities. They said to him: what is your view? If you hold *de-chayil u-mivtal* — that the vow takes effect and is then annulled — then the pre-dunking of the vessel is your refutation; we do not say that pre-applying the remedy solves the problem after the *tumah* attaches. And if you hold *de-lo chayil* — that the pre-annulment prevents the vow from taking effect entirely — then the *mikveh* is your refutation; being immersed in a *mikveh* does not prevent *tumah* from attaching.

---

## Pre-dunking & Seeds (III)

### Seeds Response

Rabbi Eliezer then responds with his own analogy. *U-mah zera'im teme'im, keivan she-zera'an be-karka taherun* — impure seeds, when planted in the ground, lose their *tumah* and become *tahor*. And we further know: *zeru'in ve-omdin lo kol she-ken* — things already planted cannot become *tamei* at all. Here is a case in which both mechanisms operate in tandem: planting removes existing *tumah* and simultaneously prevents future *tumah* from taking hold.

---

## Pre-dunking & Seeds (III)…

### Suggests Lo Haylan

If that is Rabbi Eliezer's chosen analogy, it points strongly toward the *lo haylan* interpretation. The seeds, once planted, are entirely immune to *tumah*; they do not become *tamei* and then become *tahor* — they simply cannot become *tamei* at all. Rabbi Eliezer appears to be saying that the pre-issued *hafarah* operates like the planting of the seed: it shields the vow from ever taking hold.

---

## Conclusion & Scriptu (II)

### Seeds Support

The *gemara* therefore concludes: *shema mina lo chaylin* — the seeds analogy supports the *lo haylan* interpretation, that according to Rabbi Eliezer the vow never takes effect at all. This resolves the *ibaya* in favor of the straightforward reading of the *kal va-chomer*: if *hafarah* can annul a vow that has taken effect, it should certainly be able to prevent a vow from taking effect in the first place.

### Uncertainty

Nevertheless, the *gemara* has already observed: *rabbanan lo kaymei lehu be-ta'ameih de-Rabbi Eliezer* — the *chachamim* themselves were uncertain which of these two positions Rabbi Eliezer held, and hence they armed themselves with counter-arguments sufficient to rebut either possibility.

### Scripture Over Logic

As for the *chachamim's* own ruling, the *gemara* notes that in the end their position does not rest solely on refuting the *kal va-chomer* but on a *gezerat ha-katuv*. The verse *ishah yekimennu ve-ishah yeferennu* establishes a parallel: only what can be established (*hakim*) can be annulled (*hafer*). A vow that does not yet exist cannot be established; therefore, it cannot be annulled. This is a scriptural limitation that operates independently of any logical inference.

### Ran's Synthesis

The Ran raises what seems like an obvious difficulty: if the *chachamim* have a *gezerat ha-katuv*, why did they spend so much effort deploying *kal va-chomer* counter-arguments and analogies from *tumah*? Why not simply cite the verse and be done with it? And conversely, if the *chachamim* reject this type of *kal va-chomer* as a matter of principle, why do we find elsewhere — as in the case of selling a daughter into slavery, where the *gemara* uses precisely this form of reasoning (*u-mekhurah kevar yotze'ah... eino din she-lo timakher*) — that the *chachamim* do accept "if it works to reverse, it works to prevent" as a valid *kal va-chomer*?

### Integrated Reading

The Ran's answer weaves the two together. The *chachamim* do accept this class of *kal va-chomer* as a legitimate form of inference — it is not categorically invalid. What they are saying in the earlier analogies is not "your logic is incoherent" but rather "your logic is not ironclad." Look at the breadth of *halakhah*: the *mikveh* works to remove but not to prevent; the *adam* prevents but does not remove; *tumah* and *taharah* operate according to their own principles and do not always follow intuitive inference. The *kal va-chomer* is a starting point, but *pesukim* frequently override it. That is the lesson the *chachamim* were teaching through all the earlier analogies: this type of inference is defeasible. And here, a *pasuk* does indeed override it — *ishah yekimennu ve-ishah yeferennu* establishes that the capacity for *kiyum* and the capacity for *hafarah* are coextensive, and no *kal va-chomer* can undo that. The earlier argumentation, understood in this light, was not a frontal assault on the *kal va-chomer's* logical form, but a preparation for the conclusion: even granting the *sevara*, a *pasuk* takes precedence, and here we have precisely such a *pasuk*.

---

---

# Nedarim 76

## Annulling Throughout Day

### Whole Day Principle

The *mishnah* on 76b opens with a foundational principle: *hafarat nedarim kol hayom* — the annulment of vows may be performed throughout the entire day. At first glance, one might read this as meaning twenty-four hours, a reading seemingly supported by the verse *miyom el yom*, "from day to day," which naturally suggests from this moment today until the same moment tomorrow. As the discussion will make clear, however, the *mishnah* and the final *psak halacha* actually mean something more restricted: until the end of the halakhic day, not a full twenty-four-hour window. That this point requires clarification is itself noteworthy; the *pshat* of *miyom el yom* had drawn many toward the twenty-four-hour reading.

The *mishnah* adds that this rule carries within it both a *kulah* and a *chumrah* — or, as the *Ran* explains, it is lenient in some cases and strict in others. The leniency is that a husband or father may have many hours in which to perform *hafara*. The stringency is that in certain cases, the window may be extraordinarily brief.

### Friday Night Case

The *mishnah* illustrates with a case involving *Shabbat*: if a woman made a *neder* on Friday night after *Shabbat* had begun, the husband may perform *hafara* that same Friday night and throughout *Shabbat* day — until it gets dark at *Shabbat*'s end (*ad shetecheshach*). The word *techeshach* ordinarily implies *tzet hakochavim*, nightfall proper, though the precise question of *bein hashmashos* remains.

The reverse case is equally instructive: if she made the *neder* just before *Shabbat* ended — one minute before dark — then the husband has only that one minute to perform *hafara*. If darkness fell and he did not act, the opportunity is gone permanently. The *mishnah* underscores this with urgency: *she'im chashecha velo hefer, eino yachol lehafer* — once night falls and he has not annulled, he can no longer do so.

The choice of *Shabbat* as the *mishnah*'s example is itself significant. *Shabbat* serves to illustrate that even when a *neder* is made on *Shabbat*, there is a pressing imperative to perform *hafara* on *Shabbat* itself — because that may be the husband's only opportunity. As the *Gemara* will clarify, this is what permits *hafarat nedarim* on *Shabbat* even when the *neder* has no bearing whatsoever on *Shabbat* observance — for instance, if she vowed that apples would be forbidden to her on Sundays. Even in such a case, if the *neder* was made on *Shabbat*, the husband may perform *hafara* on *Shabbat*.

### Tannaim Debate

A *baraita* records that this very principle is disputed among *Tannaim*. The *Tanna Kamma* holds *hafarat nedarim kol hayom* — annulment may be performed throughout the entire halakhic day. *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Eliezer b'Rabbi Shimon* dissent, ruling *me'eis le'eis* — a full twenty-four hours. A note on the side cites a *Tosefta* that attributes the *kol hayom* position explicitly to *Rabbi* (Rebbi); either way, the structure is a *Tanna Kamma* in favor of the halakhic day and two dissenting voices favoring twenty-four hours.

### Verse Reconciliation

The *Gemara* then asks after the reasoning on each side. The *Tanna Kamma* derives from the verse *b'yom shom'o* — "on the day that he hears" — that *hafara* must be performed on that same day. *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Eliezer b'Rabbi Shimon* derive from the verse *miyom el yom*, "from day to day," which sounds precisely like from now until the same time tomorrow — a full twenty-four hours.

The *Gemara* then reconciles each position with the verse it appears to discard. For the *Tanna Kamma*, who rules by the end of the halakhic day: why does the Torah also write *miyom el yom*? Because without that verse, one might have read *b'yom shom'o* as meaning only the daytime — excluding the nighttime hours. The verse *miyom el yom* comes to teach that the night is included within "the day," so that if she took the vow on Friday night, he may perform *hafara* that same Friday night. Yet the outer limit remains the end of that halakhic day.

For the position of twenty-four hours: why does the Torah also write *b'yom shom'o*? Because without it, one might have read *miyom el yom* as meaning from this Sunday until next Sunday — from one occurrence of a day to the same day of the following week. The verse *b'yom shom'o* constrains the window to one day's time. However, "one day's time" for these *Tannaim* means twenty-four hours, not the end of the calendar day.

Both readings are thus internally coherent and genuine engagements with the verses.

### Final Ruling

*Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi* said in the name of *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi*: *ein halacha k'oso hazug* — we do not rule like that pair. The *halacha* follows the *Tanna Kamma* and the *mishnah*: annulment must be performed by the end of the halakhic day. *Levi* had been inclined to follow the twenty-four-hour position, but *Rav* said in the name of his uncle *Rabbi Chiya*: we do not rule like that pair. That is the *halacha*.

---

## Shabbat Annulling

### Shabbat Overview

The discussion now turns to a *mishnah* cited from elsewhere: *mefirin nedarim b'Shabbat*, one may perform *hafarat nedarim* on *Shabbat*. As for *hataras nedarim* — the process of releasing a vow before a *chacham* — one may seek that release on *Shabbat* only when it is *letzorech haShabbat*, necessary for *Shabbat* itself. These two forms of vow dissolution are treated quite differently, and the *Gemara* proceeds to explain why.

### Beis Din Nature

*Hataras nedarim* is a *ma'aseh beis din* — an act of a court. It involves sitting judges who probe, inquire, and deliberate. Such an act is categorically problematic on *Shabbat*. The sole exception is when the *hatara* serves a *Shabbat* purpose: if one vowed not to eat meat and wishes to dissolve the vow in order to enjoy *cholent* on *Shabbat*, that qualifies as *letzorech Shabbat* and is permitted.

### Hafara Permitted

*Hafarat nedarim*, by contrast, is a fundamentally different act. It involves no inquiry, no deliberation, and no beis din process. The husband or father simply declares *mufar lach* — "it is annulled for you" — and the *neder* is dissolved. This is not a *ma'aseh beis din*.

Yet even *hafara* is not entirely without halachic complexity on *Shabbat*. Beyond the *beis din* concern, there is a separate issue: performing *hafara* effects a meaningful change in the world. One who takes *terumot u'ma'asrot* on *Shabbat* is prohibited because he is fixing the grain; one who immerses a vessel (*tovel a kli*) is prohibited because he is fixing the vessel. Similarly, dissolving a *neder* — even without the formality of a *beis din* — is some kind of significant, transformative act. That alone might be grounds for concern on *Shabbat*.

What overrides this concern is the urgency of the situation: *Shabbat* may be the husband's only opportunity to perform *hafara*. Because the *mishnah* rules that *hafara* must be performed within the halakhic day and cannot carry over to the next, the urgency of that last window is precisely what permits the act on *Shabbat* — even when it serves no *Shabbat* purpose whatsoever.

### One-Minute Case

The *Gemara* initially entertained the possibility that just as *hatara* is limited to cases of *letzorech Shabbat*, perhaps *hafara* too is only permitted on *Shabbat* when it serves a *Shabbat* purpose. A *baraita* attributed to the school of *Rav Pappi* indeed stated: *ein meferin nedarim ela letzorech haShabbat* — one may perform *hafara* only for a *Shabbat* need.

*Rav Ashi* refutes this from our *mishnah*. The *mishnah* teaches that if she made her vow one minute before *Shabbat* ended, the husband must perform *hafara* before dark. Now: can any *Shabbat* purpose conceivably be served in that one final minute? Manifestly not — it is the last moment of *Shabbat*, and whatever the *neder* touches cannot be remedied for *Shabbat* at that point. Yet the *mishnah* does not say he is forbidden to perform *hafara* in that minute; on the contrary, it instructs him to do so. If *hafara* were limited to *Shabbat* purposes, it would be forbidden at that very moment — and indeed at any moment on *Shabbat* when the *neder* poses no *Shabbat* constraint. The *mishnah* would have had nothing to say about that final minute.

### Tannaim Dependency

The *Gemara* resolves the tension by referring back to the *Tannaim* debate. The permissibility of *hafara* on *Shabbat* without a specific *Shabbat* purpose depends entirely on whether one rules like the *Tanna Kamma* (the end of the halakhic day) or like *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Eliezer b'Rabbi Shimon* (twenty-four hours).

According to the view that one has only until the end of the halakhic day — *kol hayom* — *hafara* is permitted on *Shabbat* even when it serves no *Shabbat* purpose, because *Shabbat* is the husband's only and final opportunity. Of course we allow it.

According to the twenty-four-hour view, there is no such urgency. After *Shabbat* ends, time still remains — the full twenty-four hours has not elapsed. Therefore, under that view, *hafara* on *Shabbat* is permitted only when there is a specific *Shabbat* need; otherwise, one should simply wait until *Shabbat* is over. Since we rule like the *Tanna Kamma* — the end of the halakhic day — we also rule that *hafara* on *Shabbat* is permitted across the board, even without *letzorech Shabbat*.

### Negligence Question

The *Gemara* now raises a question about *hataras nedarim* specifically: when we permit *hatara* on *Shabbat* because it is *letzorech Shabbat*, does this apply even when the person had ample opportunity to perform *hatara* before *Shabbat* and simply failed to do so? Or do we deny the *Shabbat* leniency when the person was negligent?

The case is vivid: a person vowed on Friday morning that he would not eat meat. He had all of Friday to find a *chacham* and dissolve the vow; he did not bother. Now it is *Shabbat* and he cannot eat his *cholent*. He wishes to seek *hataras nedarim* now. On one hand, this is genuinely *letzorech Shabbat*. On the other hand, he should have handled it beforehand. The question is whether his prior negligence forfeits his right to the *Shabbat* leniency. This parallels discussions among later *poskim* regarding *shvus d'shvus b'makom mitzvah*: some hold that if one was negligent and could have arranged things properly before *Shabbat*, no allowance is given on *Shabbat* itself; others hold that whatever the cause, the present need must be addressed.

### Negligence Permitted

The *Gemara* resolves the question from a real-life precedent: *izdakkaku lei rabanan livrei d'Rav Zutra brei d'Rav Zeira* — the rabbis responded to the needs of the son of *Rav Zutra*, son of *Rav Zeira*, and performed *hatara* even for *nedarim* that he could have dissolved before *Shabbat* but did not. They did not withhold the leniency on account of his prior negligence. The *Gemara* notes that this is in fact the dominant ruling among *poskim* in analogous cases — whatever the reason one finds oneself in the situation, the present halachic need must be addressed.

---

## Hataras Requirements

### One Expert Rule

The *Gemara* now addresses the question of who may perform *hataras nedarim* and under what conditions. *Rav Yosef* proposes that when *hataras nedarim* is permitted on *Shabbat* — in a case of *letzorech Shabbat* — it may only be performed before a *yachid mumcheh*, a single qualified expert. It may not be performed before three *hedyotos*, three lay people who together constitute the alternative form of a valid *beis din* for *hatara* purposes.

This requires some background. The basic structure of *hataras nedarim* is that it may be performed before either a *yachid mumcheh* — a single recognized expert — or before three lay people. (The precise meaning of *mumcheh* — what qualifications it requires — is a question for another discussion.) Most of the cases in *aggadata* and *halacha* involve a single rabbi, because a qualified rabbi is a *mumcheh* and suffices alone. But the option of three lay people also exists. *Rav Yosef*'s position is that on *Shabbat*, even where *hatara* is permitted, one may only use the *yachid mumcheh* option — not the three-*hedyotos* option.

### Appearance Concern

The reason *Rav Yosef* gives is *mishum d'michzei k'dina* — because three people sitting together to perform *hatara* looks like a full *beis din*. Even if the underlying act is permitted, it creates the appearance of conducting formal legal proceedings on *Shabbat*, which is itself problematic. Therefore, when we extend the *Shabbat* leniency, we extend it only in its least court-like form: a single expert. Three people — even lay people — is too suggestive of a *beis din* sitting in judgment.

### Abaye Refutes

*Abaye* rejects *Rav Yosef*'s position. He argues that given what we know about the leniencies that apply to *hataras nedarim*, it simply cannot be said to look like a *beis din* at all — whether it involves one person or three. Since the very nature of *hataras nedarim* is manifestly not that of a formal court proceeding, the concern of *michzei k'dina* does not apply, and the three-*hedyotos* option remains available even on *Shabbat*.

### Non-Formal Features

*Abaye*'s proof rests on the accumulated leniencies that apply to *hataras nedarim*: it may be performed *me'umad* — while standing; it may be performed *balayla* — at night; and it may be performed *b'krovim* — by relatives. None of these features are consistent with a *beis din*. A *beis din* must sit; it must convene in the daytime; its members may not be relatives of the parties or of one another. The fact that *hataras nedarim* permits all of these departures from *beis din* norms means that no reasonable observer could mistake it for one. The appearance-of-*beis-din* concern therefore simply does not apply.

### Conceptual Status

This leads directly to a deeper conceptual question: is *hataras nedarim* fundamentally an act of a *beis din* — albeit with many procedural exceptions — or is it something categorically different from a *beis din* act altogether?

One could argue that it remains a *beis din* act in essence, with certain relaxed procedures. After all, even in *Sanhedrin*, a *yachid mumcheh* is treated as equivalent to a full *beis din* in certain respects. Under this view, the departures from standard *beis din* procedure (standing, night, relatives) are explicable as exceptions, and one would need to account for each one. The act itself, however, remains a form of judicial proceeding.

Alternatively — and this is the more radical position — the cumulative weight of these exceptions may prove that *hataras nedarim* is not a *beis din* act at all. This is particularly compelling with respect to relatives: it is impossible to constitute a *beis din* of relatives. Standing and nighttime are merely procedural variations; one could argue those remain within the range of *beis din* flexibility. But relatives? A *beis din* composed of relatives is no *beis din*. Their inclusion in *hataras nedarim* suggests that the process belongs to an entirely different category.

Even if one concludes that it is not a *beis din* act, this does not mean it is entirely unrestricted on *Shabbat*. Even *hafarat nedarim* — which is certainly not a *beis din* act — is problematic on *Shabbat* for the separate reason that it effects a real change in status. *Hataras nedarim* similarly effects a change, and therefore remains something that requires specific *Shabbat* justification. The key insight is that once we recognize it is not a *beis din* act, the three-*hedyotos* option is no more problematic on *Shabbat* than the *yachid mumcheh* option, and *Abaye*'s refutation of *Rav Yosef* stands.

---

## Night/Standing/Relatives

### Rav's Silence

The *Gemara* now records a tradition in the name of *Rav Abba*, who said in the name of *Rav Huna* in the name of *Rav*: the *halacha* is that *hataras nedarim* may be performed at night. The *Gemara* immediately challenges: is that not already explicit in the *mishnah*? After all, the *mishnah* permits *hafara* on Friday night — surely it is obvious that vow dissolution can occur at night. The *Gemara* therefore corrects the tradition: what *Rav* meant was not *hafarat nedarim* at night — that requires no demonstration — but *hataras nedarim* at night. That is the genuine *chiddush*: the process before a *chacham*, which resembles a *beis din* proceeding, may be performed at night.

Once this correction is made, *Rav Abba* turns to *Rav Huna* and asks: did *Rav* actually say this? *Rav Huna* fell silent — *ishtik*. The *Gemara* then probes the nature of that silence: was it *ishtik* in the sense of "be quiet, I reject this," meaning *Rav* did not agree? Or was it *shasik* — a silence of approval? The text leaves the question somewhat ambiguous. Different *girsaot* handle this differently, but the overall sense is that *Rav*'s agreement with the ruling of nighttime *hatara* remains uncertain from this exchange alone.

### Standing Example

A second tradition resolves the question in practice. *Rav Ika bar Avin* reported that *Rav* himself had performed *hataras nedarim* for *Rabba* — in a small chamber of the *beis midrash* (*kituna d'vei Rav*), while standing, alone, and at night. Three features in a single act: standing, without the formal quorum of three, and at night. The "alone" element, it should be noted, is not necessarily problematic if *Rav* qualifies as a *yachid mumcheh*; the significant departures from *beis din* norms are the standing and the nighttime. This incident establishes that at least *Rav*'s practice embodied these leniencies, even if his explicit ruling had been ambiguous.

### Nachman Ruling

*Rabba* then said in the name of *Rav Nachman*, consolidating the *halacha* explicitly: *nishalin nedarim omeid, yachidi, u'valayla, u'v'Shabbos, u'v'krovim* — *hataras nedarim* may be performed while standing, alone, at night, on *Shabbat*, and by relatives. The ruling on *Shabbat* still operates within the earlier framework — it appears to refer to cases of *letzorech Shabbat*, and the addition that this applies *va'afilu haya lahem pnai mib'od yom* — even if they had time before *Shabbat* — confirms that prior negligence does not forfeit the *Shabbat* leniency.

### Rambam View

The *Rambam*'s formulation is particularly clear and worth noting. He writes: *hakrovim matirin lahatir nedarim, u'matirin balayla u'me'umad, she'ein hatara zu din* — relatives may perform *hataras nedarim*, and it may be performed at night and while standing, *because this release is not din*. The *Rambam* does not frame these as exceptions to an otherwise *beis din*-like process; he states flatly that *hatara* is categorically not *din*. This makes the leniencies not anomalies requiring justification but natural consequences of the fundamental nature of *hataras nedarim*. The one remaining question — why then are three people involved at all, if it is not *din*? — is perhaps the easiest thing to ask and the hardest to answer simply, but the *Rambam*'s framing makes clear that the *requirement* of three does not transform the act into a *beis din* proceeding.

---

## Sitting vs Standing

### Gamliel Example

The *Gemara* now raises a challenge from a famous story involving *Rabban Gamliel*. The *baraita* records that when *Rabban Gamliel* performed *hataras nedarim*, he dismounted from his donkey, wrapped himself in his *tallit*, and sat down — only then proceeding to release the *neder*. This appears to contradict the position that standing is permitted, since *Rabban Gamliel* took explicit care to sit.

### Opening Method

The *Gemara* resolves this by invoking the dispute over *potchin b'charata*. The question is: what must the *chacham* do to release a *neder*? One view — *potchin b'charata* — holds that it suffices to open with a question of regret: "Do you regret having made this vow?" If the person says yes, the *chacham* declares *mutar lach* and the *neder* is dissolved. No elaborate probing of circumstances is required. Another reading — *ein potchin b'charata* — holds that simple regret is insufficient. The *chacham* must investigate the concrete circumstances surrounding the *neder*: what the person was thinking, what he failed to consider, whether had he taken those circumstances into account he would not have made the *neder*. This is a deliberate, probing process that uproots the *neder* (*me'aker nidra*) through careful analysis (*ba'i iyunei*).

Under the latter view, real deliberation is required — not as a formal technical requirement for the *hatara* to take effect, but because the nature of the act demands that it be given proper weight and focus. *Rabban Gamliel*, who held this view, accordingly sat, wrapped himself in his *tallit*, and gave the matter his full and serious attention. Not because sitting is a formal *din*, but because proper deliberation practically requires it.

### Simple Regret

*Rav Nachman*, who ruled that standing is permitted, held the position that simple regret suffices. If all that is needed is for the person to express regret — *are you sorry you made this vow? yes, fine, mutar lach* — then there is no need for deep deliberation, and therefore no need to sit. One can stand, or even occupy oneself with other things, because the act is so simple and direct that it does not require focused concentration. This is what the *Rosh* suggests is the proper context for the earlier account of *Chiyya bar Rav*, who performed *hataras nedarim* while shooting arrows, and *Rabba bar Rav Huna*, who moved around the room without full concentration: those stories belong precisely here, illustrating what it looks like when the *potek b'charata* approach is taken to its logical conclusion.

One might be troubled by such a picture. Does not trivializing the process of *hatara* also trivialize the gravity of making *nedarim*? This tension is real, and the subsequent discussion in the *Gemara* about the sinfulness of making vows — even fulfilled ones — may itself be understood as a corrective: even if the *hatara* process is straightforward, the act of having made the *neder* at all is not without moral consequence.

### Rashba Distinction

The *Rashba* offers a nuanced position. He acknowledges that *potchin b'charata* is the operative ruling: the *chacham* may begin by simply asking whether the person regrets the *neder*. If the answer is yes, *mutar lach* suffices and no further deliberation is needed. Suppose, however, the person says no — he does not regret it. The *chacham* must then probe for a *petach*, a grounds for release based on something the person had not considered at the time. This requires genuine deliberation. Even so, the *Rashba* holds that standing remains permitted even in this second phase, because the *opening* of the process — *ikar dina* — was begun while standing; therefore the *conclusion* of the process may also be concluded while standing.

### Ran Critique

The *Ran* is unpersuaded. He writes explicitly: *v'lo yaradeti l'ta'amo* — I do not follow his reasoning, and since I do not understand it, I cannot rule accordingly. The *Ran*'s position is that once actual deliberation becomes necessary — once one must truly probe and investigate — the practical requirement of sitting and focusing applies.
