Whatever was done standing before does not carry forward to justify standing through a phase of the process that genuinely requires concentration. The mode of the proceeding must match the demands of what is being done at each moment.

---

## Vow as Sin

### Prayer Needed

The *Gemara* closes with a striking moral teaching occasioned by a real case. *Rava* reported to *Rav Nachman*: a rabbi who had come from *Eretz Yisrael* said that the rabbis had performed *hataras nedarim* for the son of *Rav Huna bar Avin*, dissolving his *neder*, and then said to him: *zil u'vei rachmei a'nafshecha de'chatat* — go and pray for your soul, for you have sinned. This is remarkable. The *hatara* was successful; the *neder* was dissolved and, retroactively speaking, never truly bound him. Yet the rabbis told him to pray for his soul for having sinned.

### Sinner Status

The *Gemara* grounds this in a *baraita* of *Rabbi Dimmi*, brother of *Rav Safra*: *kol ha'noder, af al pi she'mekayemo, nikra chotei* — anyone who makes a *neder*, even if he fulfills it, is called a sinner. One might note that the *Gemara* could have cited the more vivid formulation — *kol ha'noder ke'ilu banah bamah*, he who makes a vow is as one who built an *illicit altar* — where the *Ran* explains that fulfilling the vow is even worse, analogous to actually sacrificing upon it. But the formulation chosen here makes a distinct point: even the act of making the *neder*, independent of fulfillment or violation, is itself sinful. In the case at hand, the *neder* was dissolved — and yet the moral stain of having made it remained. The rabbis were right to tell the young man to pray.

### Cease Making Vows

*Rav Zvid* then adds a verse in support: *ve'ki techdal lindor lo yihyeh vecha cheit* — if you cease from making vows, there will be no sin in you. The logical inference is clear: if you do not cease, there is sin — *even if you fulfill* the vow. And with even greater force: if the *neder* is dissolved through *hatara* and technically never existed in a halachic sense, the underlying act of having made it is still a moral failing that requires *tefillah* and seeking forgiveness.

### Qiyyum vs Hafara

The *Gemara* closes with a *baraita* that draws an important distinction between *qiyyum* — ratification — and *hafara* — annulment. If a husband says to his wife: "Any vows that you make, I do not want you to make them" — or "they are not vows" — *lo amar klum*: he has said nothing. This is not a valid *hafara*. Expressing displeasure is not annulment; declaring that the *neder* is not a *neder* does not change the fact that it is one. *Hafara* requires a formal, active act of annulment with precise language.

### Implicit Qiyyum

The opposite case yields the opposite conclusion. If the husband says: "Well done, there is no one like you — had you not made those vows, I would have made them for you," then *devarav kayamim* — his words constitute a valid *qiyyum*, a ratification of the vow. For *qiyyum*, even implicit expressions of approval suffice. Indeed, as the *Ran* notes, we will see later in the *Gemara* that *qiyyum* does not even require verbal expression at all — if in his heart the husband desired the vows, that alone constitutes *qiyyum*.

### Formal Language

The contrast between *qiyyum* and *hafara* thus reflects a deep structural asymmetry. *Qiyyum* requires no formal language; it follows from will and desire. *Hafara* requires specific, formal verbalization — not merely an expression of sentiment or wish, but the actual performative act of annulment. To say "I don't want these vows" or "these are not real vows" conveys a state of mind, but it does not perform the act. The language of *hafara* must be language *of* annulling, not language *about* annulling. This distinction — between performing an act through speech and describing one's attitude through speech — is what separates effective *hafara* from words that, whatever they may express, accomplish nothing.

---

---

# Nedarim 78

## Hafara & Hatara Basics

### Non-Judicial Status

The sugya opens by revisiting the foundational distinction between *hafara* — annulment of a vow by a husband — and *hatara* — annulment by a sage. Earlier discussion established that the panel performing *hatara* shares certain formal features with a *beit din*: it requires either three individuals or a single *mumche*, an expert of sufficient standing. Yet the *Gemara* makes clear that this body does not function as a proper *beit din* in the adjudicating sense. It may convene at night, its members may stand rather than sit, and relatives (*krovim*) are not disqualified — all departures from ordinary judicial procedure. This non-judicial character is not a peripheral detail; it is central to understanding several practical *halachos* that follow.

### Shabbat Permissibility

One immediate implication of the non-judicial status of *hafara* and *hatara* concerns performance on *Shabbos*. *Hafara* by a husband may always be performed on *Shabbos*, because the husband has only until the end of the day to annul — there is therefore always an immediate need (*tzorech*), and when there is a need it does not matter by what formal arrangement it is performed. *Hatara* may similarly be performed on *Shabbos* when it is needed for the sake of *Shabbos* itself (*letzorech Shabbos*). Moreover, precisely because the act of *hatara* is not a *maaseh beit din* in the formal judicial sense, there is no prohibition on performing it with three individuals rather than one, since even when three people act together they are not constituting a formal *beit din*. The non-judicial character thus dispenses with the concern that would otherwise make such an act on *Shabbos* problematic.

### Standard Language

The *Gemara* turns to the appropriate language for annulment, particularly on *Shabbos*. A man should not say to his wife on *Shabbos* the standard weekday formula — *mufar lichi*, *batul lichi*, "it is annulled to you, it is void to you" — as one would ordinarily say during the week. Rather, he should say to her: *tli ve-ochli*, *tli ve-shtei* — "take and eat, take and drink" — and the *neder* is automatically void (*veneder batel meilav*). This is instructive on two levels. First, it establishes what the standard, direct language of annulment is. Second, it demonstrates that even in cases where a more direct formulation would be appropriate, indirect language can suffice when circumstances call for it — in this case, the concern about performing an overtly legal verbal act on *Shabbos*.

### Intent Requirement

Rabbi Yochanan adds a critical qualification: *vetzarich sheyivatel belibo* — it is not sufficient to utter the indirect words alone; the husband must simultaneously hold in his heart an intention to annul (*bitul belibo*). The words spoken need not themselves be words of *bitul*, but the inner intention must be genuinely present. This formulation is reminiscent of the *bitul* of *chametz* before Pesach, where one who cannot perform *biur chametz* may instead annul it in the heart (*mevatel belibo vedaio*), rendering it ownerless. The parallel invites reflection, though the cases are distinct. Critically, as the *Ran* emphasizes and as the *Gemara* will clarify more explicitly, purely internal *bitul* without any accompanying verbal act would be insufficient. What is required is a combination: words that, while not explicit declarations of annulment, implicitly convey it — together with genuine inner intention. Neither element alone is adequate.

---

## Shammai vs. Hillel

### Shammai Position

A *baraisa* presents an explicit dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on this question. Beit Shammai holds that on *Shabbos*, a husband should annul *belibo* — with inner intention accompanied by indirect language, as described above — but that on a weekday he must be more explicit, articulating the direct formula *mufar lichi*, *batul lichi*. The *Ran* clarifies that even Beit Shammai does not mean the husband annuls by thought alone on *Shabbos*; rather, the indirect verbal act combined with inner intention, as described in the previous passage, is what Beit Shammai permits when circumstances prevent direct articulation.

### Hillel Position

Beit Hillel holds that the same indirect approach suffices both on *Shabbos* and during the weekday: *echad ze ve-echad ze mevatel belibo ve-ein tzarich lehotzi bisfasav* — in both cases he annuls in his heart without needing to articulate the formula explicitly. On its face this sounds as though Beit Hillel requires no verbal act whatsoever, only internal intention. Yet as the *Ran* insists, and as a later passage in the *Gemara* makes clear, pure internal *bitul* without any verbal component would not be effective. Beit Hillel's position is therefore that the indirect verbal act is always sufficient — it is not a special dispensation limited to *Shabbos* — while Beit Shammai would prefer direct articulation when possible and treats the indirect form as an accommodation to *Shabbos* rather than an equally valid alternative.

### Heart Intent Synthesis

This raises the question of whether Beit Shammai would validate indirect annulment on a weekday after the fact (*bedi'avad*). It is reasonable to conclude that Beit Shammai would — their position is that direct language is preferred when there is no obstacle, not that indirect language is categorically invalid. Beit Hillel, by contrast, simply does not distinguish between the two modes: if it works, it works, regardless of when and under what circumstances it is employed. What is clear from both positions is that there is an irreducible combination at work: implicit verbal expression and genuine inner intention operating together. And of course, if one does say *mufar lichi* explicitly, that simultaneously fulfills whatever inner intention is required — the explicit formula carries the inner meaning by definition.

### Meifer vs. Mevatel

Checking the *Rambam* on this point reveals a striking distinction that requires closer examination. In *Hilchos Nedarim* 13:7 (*yud gimel*, *zayin*), the *Rambam* rules as follows: a husband who performs *hafara* of his wife's or daughter's vow must articulate it verbally — if he performs *hafara* only in his heart, it is not effective. But one who performs *bitul* — the annulment from a different angle — does not need to articulate it verbally; *bitul belibo* alone suffices, and the *neder* is thereby void. The *Rambam* in the passage there appears to treat *meifer* and *mevatel* as two distinct processes with differing requirements. The standard formula often cited — *mufar lichi*, *batul lichi* — may in fact be the *Rambam*'s way of referring to two separate acts, one of *hafara* and one of *bitul*, with different formal requirements for each. This distinction deserves further analysis, but at minimum the *Rambam* agrees with the *Ran* that some combination of verbal act and inner intention is operative, even if he parses the components differently.

---

## Language Specificity

### Explicit vs. Implicit

The *Ran* raises a pointed question. Earlier in the *Gemara*, a case was discussed in which a husband says to his wife: *konam, nedarim shetiduri, i efshi shetiduri* — "I do not wish you to make such vows" — or *ein ze neder* — "this is not a vow." The *Gemara* ruled that such language is ineffective: *lo amar klum*, he has said nothing of consequence. But if the *Ran* just established that indirect language is sufficient provided the husband has *bitul belibo*, why did that earlier formulation fail? After all, it too is a form of indirect expression.

### Vow Negation Problem

The resolution lies not in the directness of the language per se but in whether the language is *implicitly* an act of annulment at all. Consider the phrase "go ahead and eat it." If a wife has made a vow forbidding herself from eating something and her husband tells her "go ahead and eat it," there is only one coherent way to understand that instruction: the husband must have annulled the vow, because otherwise his instruction would be meaningless. The implication of annulment is thus inherent in and inseparable from the statement. By contrast, if the husband says "this is not a vow," he is making a factual claim — and a false one at that, since it plainly is a vow. He is not saying "I am making it not a vow" or "I am annulling it"; he is asserting a state of affairs that does not exist. Similarly, "I do not wish you to make vows" is a statement about his preferences, not an act of annulment. It leaves entirely open whether he intends to annul or merely to express displeasure. A statement that communicates annulment implicitly must actually communicate annulment — not every indirect locution accomplishes that. The crucial requirement, therefore, is not merely that the language be indirect but that the indirect language unambiguously implies the act of annulment. A statement of factual negation or personal preference does not clear that bar.

---

## Wrong Language Rule

### Language Swapping Invalid

Rabbi Yochanan teaches: *chacham she-amar bi-leshon ba'al u-va'al she-amar bi-leshon chacham lo amar klum* — if a sage employs the language appropriate to a husband, or a husband employs the language appropriate to a sage, neither has accomplished anything. The case contemplated is not one of confusion about which process to perform; rather, it is a case where the actor knows what process he intends but uses the wrong terminology. A sage conducting a *hatara* who says *mufar lach* instead of the appropriate language of the sage has not effected *hatara*. A husband performing *hafara* who says *mutar lach* has not effected *hafara*. This ruling emphasizes that verbal articulation is not merely instrumental — it is constitutive of the act. Wanting to do the right thing while saying the wrong thing is insufficient.

One might wonder whether the principle of *yad la-neder* — where language that partially and ambiguously gestures toward a neder is nonetheless treated as binding — could apply here in reverse, validating an act whose language approximates but does not match the required formula. The answer appears to be no, precisely because the husband and the sage are performing fundamentally different processes. The *ba'al*'s act of *hafara* operates going forward — it dissolves an existing vow from the moment of annulment onward. The *chacham*'s act of *hatara* operates retroactively — it treats the vow as though it never existed. These are not merely formally different; they are conceptually opposed. Using the other's language does not create an approximate version of one's own process; it describes the other process entirely. There is no room for a *yad* construction when the language accurately describes something real, just the wrong thing.

### Torah Derivation

A *baraisa* grounds this in the *pasuk* from *Mattos*: *zeh hadavar asher tzivah Hashem — ish ki yidor neder* — "this is the matter that God commanded — a man who takes a vow." The phrase *zeh hadavar* — "this is the matter" — is read restrictively: *chacham matir ve-ein ba'al matir*, only the *chacham* performs *hatara*, not the husband. Now, one might have argued the contrary by a *kal va-chomer*: if a *chacham*, who lacks the power of *hafara*, can nevertheless perform *hatara*, then surely a *ba'al*, who possesses the greater power of *hafara*, should a fortiori be able to perform *hatara* as well. It is something of an irony — the husband's unique power is invoked as the basis for expanding his authority into the sage's domain. Nevertheless, *talmud lomar zeh hadavar*: no, only the *chacham* performs *hatara*, and not the husband.

### Hafara Authority

A second *baraisa* derives the mirror proposition. *Zeh hadavar* — again read restrictively — establishes that *ba'al meifer ve-ein chacham meifer*: only the husband can perform *hafara*, and the *chacham* cannot. Here too a *kal va-chomer* suggests itself in the other direction: if the husband, who lacks the power of *hatara*, can nevertheless perform *hafara*, then surely the *chacham*, who possesses the power of *hatara*, should a fortiori be able to perform *hafara*. Again, *talmud lomar zeh hadavar*: no. Each authority is confined to its own domain. The *Gemara* notes that these derivations do not prove quite as much as Rabbi Yochanan's rule might require — they establish that the actual *processes* are exclusive, not necessarily that using the other's language while performing one's own process would fail. But the broader point stands: since the two processes are conceptually distinct and the *devar* that defines each is specific to its actor, using the language that describes the other's process cannot constitute one's own.

### Ran Language Analysis

This raises a practical question: what exactly is the language of the *chacham*? The language of the *ba'al* is explicit in the *Torah* — *va-im hafer yafer osah me-ishah*, the language of *hafara* belongs to the husband. But where does the *Torah* specify that a *chacham* says *mutar lach*?

The *Ran* addresses this at the end of 77b. His first answer draws from the verse *lo yachel devaro* — "he shall not profane his word." From here we learn the role of the *chacham*: others can render his word *chullin*, ordinary and non-binding. Since *chullin* is the category of the non-sanctified and unrestricted, the term *mutar* — permissible — is the apt language for what the *chacham* does. This answer, as the *Ran* himself concedes, is not entirely persuasive.

At the very top of 78b, however, the *Ran* cites the *Yerushalmi* for a more compelling resolution. The *Yerushalmi* records: *ha-ba'al omer mufar lach, ve-ha-zaken omer ein kan neder ein kan shvu'a* — the husband declares "it is annulled to you," while the elder declares "there is no vow here, there is no oath here." This formulation clarifies the conceptual logic. *Mufar* — from *meifer* — means dissolved going forward: the vow existed and is now annulled from this point onward. *Mutar* — and equivalently *ein kan neder* — means it was always permissible; there never was a binding vow. This is the nature of the *chacham*'s act: *hatara* renders the vow as though it never came into existence. And this is precisely why the husband cannot use that language — to say *ein kan neder* or *mutar lach* is to claim that the vow never existed, but the husband's role presupposes that a vow did exist and is now being dissolved prospectively. He cannot retroactively undo its existence; he can only cut off its future effect.

This analysis casts light on the *nusach* of *hataras nedarim* recited on *erev Rosh Hashanah*. The formula includes *hakol mutar lach, hakol sharui lach* — *mutar* and its Aramaic equivalent *sharui*, both indicating that the thing was always permissible. It also includes *hakol mechulin lach*, which carries a somewhat different connotation — *mechila* suggests erasure of something that existed, somewhat closer in spirit to *hafara*. Whether *mechulin* was always part of the original *nusach* may be worth investigating. And crucially, the formula also includes *ein kan lo neder ve-lo shvu'a ve-lo nezirus ve-lo cherem ve-lo issur ve-lo konam* — there is no vow here, no oath, no *nezirus*, no *cherem*, no prohibition, no *konam*. All of these are the language of the *chacham*: retroactive annulment treating the original commitment as though it never took legal hold.

---

## Three Laypeople Source

### Zeh HaDavar Link

The *baraisa* continues with a *gezeira shava* — a textual analogy based on a shared phrase. The phrase *zeh hadavar* appears in *parshas Mattos* in the context of *nedarim*, and it appears again elsewhere in the *Torah* in the context of *shchutei chutz* — the prohibition against slaughtering a consecrated animal outside the *Beis HaMikdash*. The *baraisa* proposes linking them: just as by *shchutei chutz* the *Torah* states *daber el Aharon ve-el banav ve-el kol b'nei Yisrael* — applying the law to Aharon, his sons, and all of Israel — so too, *parshas nedarim* applies to all of Israel, not only to *rashei ha-matos*. And conversely, just as *parshas nedarim* emphasizes *rashei ha-matos* — heads of the tribes — so too *shchutei chutz* must be understood to involve *rashei ha-matos*.

### Three Hedyotos Valid

What does it mean for *parshas nedarim* to extend to *kol Yisrael* beyond *rashei ha-matos*? Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains: *lehachshir shlosha hedyotos* — to validate three laypeople as a qualified panel for *hataras nedarim*. The *parsha* focuses on *rashei ha-matos*, which establishes that a *yachid mumche* — a single qualified individual of sufficient stature — may annul vows. The inclusion of *kol Yisrael* then signals a second, broader category: ordinary people, provided there are three of them. The logic of choosing three, as the *Ran* explains, is that once we know one individual is not enough in this second category, the next coherent institutional form is that of a *beit din*, which requires three.

But this conception of a *beit din* deserves careful definition. The body that performs *hataras nedarim* is not a *beit din* in the adjudicating sense — it may convene at night, it may include relatives, its members need not be seated. How then is it meaningful to call it a *beit din*? Rav Soloveitchik observed in a number of contexts that *beit din* does not always function as an adjudicating body. The *Sanhedrin* that goes out in the case of *eglah arufah* and declares *yadeinu lo shafchu es hadam hazeh* is not adjudicating anything — it is representing the Jewish people. Similarly, when *beit din* sanctifies the new month or proclaims a leap year, it acts not as a court but as a representative leadership body. *Rashei ha-matos* is itself a leadership role, not a juridical one. The institution of *beit din*, understood as a representative leadership body rather than a judicial one, is the natural parallel. This may also explain why it is three specifically: not because three *dayanim* are needed, but because three is the constitutive number for a recognized communal body, and the *beit din* in its representative — as distinct from its adjudicating — capacity provides that form. The *Torah* elsewhere refers to the *beit din* using different terms at different points — *zekenim*, *shoftim*, *Elohim* — and it is the *zekenim* formulation, connoting communal leadership rather than strict adjudication, that applies here.

### Shchutei Chutz Link

Returning to the *gezeira shava*: what role do *rashei ha-matos* play in the context of *shchutei chutz*? Rav Sheshet explains: *lomar she-yesh she'eila b'hekdesh* — to teach that *rashei ha-matos* can perform *she'eila* regarding *hekdesh*, that is, a *chacham* can annul a consecration (*hekdesh*) just as he can annul a *neder*. This creates a significant practical opening: if someone slaughtered a consecrated animal outside the *Beis HaMikdash* and is thereby liable to *kareis*, he may go to a *chacham* and argue that had he been aware of certain circumstances he would never have consecrated the animal. The *chacham* performs *hatara* on the original act of *hekdesh*, which retroactively undoes the consecration, rendering the animal ordinary (*chullin*). The slaughter then turns out to have been of an unconsecrated animal, and no *aveira* was committed at all.

This, however, is the position of Beit Hillel, which holds that *she'eila* — the process of retroactive annulment on grounds of error — applies to *hekdesh*. Beit Shammai disagrees: *ein she'eila b'hekdesh*. Even if one consecrated an animal in error, the *hekdesh* is binding. Since the entire mechanism of *hatara* works by reclassifying the original act as having been made in error (*b'to'us*), and Beit Shammai holds that even *hekdesh b'to'us* is fully valid, Beit Shammai denies that *rashei ha-matos* play any role by *shchutei chutz*. Consequently, for Beit Shammai the *gezeira shava* linking *parshas nedarim* and *shchutei chutz* does not hold — they do not derive the law of three *hedyotos* from this source.

### Moshe Derivation

For Beit Shammai, then, where do three *hedyotos* come from? The *Gemara* answers: *nafka lehu mi-deRav Assi bar Nasn* — from the teaching of Rav Assi bar Nasn. The *pasuk* states: *vayedabeir Moshe es moadei Hashem el b'nei Yisrael* — "and Moshe spoke the appointed times of God to the children of Israel." A *baraisa* records a dispute. Rabbi Yosi HaGlili says: the *pasuk* speaks of the *moadim* and does not mention *Shabbos Bereishis* alongside them — which is puzzling, since in *parshas Emor* where the *moadim* are listed, *Shabbos* appears first, *sheshes yamim* and so on. Rebbi (*Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi*) says: the *pasuk* speaks of the *moadim* and does not mention *parshas nedarim* alongside them — which is equally puzzling, given that *parshas nedarim* in *Mattos* follows immediately after the *moadim* of *Pinchas*.

Rav Assi bar Nasn was troubled by this *baraisa* and went to find Rav Sheshet to ask him about it. He traveled first to Naharda'ah and, not finding Rav Sheshet there, followed him to Mechuza.

### Moadim Requirement

Rav Sheshet resolved the difficulty. The *baraisa* is not making a claim about what appears adjacent in the text; it is drawing a *halachic* distinction. *Moadei Hashem tzrichim kiddush beit din* — the appointed times require sanctification by *beit din*. The *moadim* are proclaimed through *kiddush hachodesh*, the *beit din*'s sanctification of the new moon. *Shabbos Bereishis ein tzricha kiddush beit din* — *Shabbos* requires no such sanctification; it has its sanctity independently, without any action by *beit din*. The verse *asher tikre'u osam bemo'adam* — "that you shall proclaim in their appointed time" — applies only to those occasions whose timing is declared by *beit din*, not to *Shabbos*.

Similarly — and this is the key point for our topic — *moadei Hashem tzrichim mumche*: the *moadim* require an expert panel, specifically a *beit din* of *mumchim*, for the sanctification of the new moon. *Ve-ein parshas nedarim tzricha mumche*: but *parshas nedarim* — the process of *hataras nedarim* — does not require a *mumche*-level panel. The word *eileh* — "these" — in *eileh moadei Hashem asher tikre'u osam* is restrictive: only *these* require a *beit din* of *mumchim* for their proclamation. *Shabbos* does not, and *parshas nedarim* does not. From here Beit Shammai derives that *hataras nedarim* is valid even when performed by *hedyotos*, laypeople without expert credentials.

The *Gemara* then raises the obvious difficulty: but *parshas nedarim* says *rashei ha-matos*, which implies people of stature and expertise — so how can laypeople suffice? The answer, attributed to Rav Chisda and alternatively to Rabbi Yochanan: *b'yachid mumche* — ​*rashei ha-matos* refers to the case of a *yachid mumche*, a single individual of sufficient standing. When it is a *yachid*, he must be a *mumche*. But the separate teaching about *kol Yisrael* — and for Beit Shammai, the teaching from *eileh* — establishes the alternative: three *hedyotos* without individual expert status.

---

## Mumche Definition

### Mumche Relativity

This raises the critical question of who qualifies as a *mumche* for the purpose of a *yachid* performing *hataras nedarim*. One might suppose that the *mumche* required here is parallel to the *mumche* required for *kiddush hachodesh* — a member of a *beit din* whose authority derives from an unbroken chain of *semicha* going back to Moshe Rabbeinu. On that reading, no *yachid mumche* could perform *hataras nedarim* today, since the chain of *semicha* has been severed and such a *beit din* no longer exists.

The *Rambam*, however, rejects this interpretation. In *perek* 12 of *Hilchos Shevuos*, the *Rambam* rules that any *rav muvhak* — a distinguished authority — may perform *hataras nedarim* as a *yachid*. The *mumche* required here is not the same *mumche* as the one required for *kiddush hachodesh*. The power to sanctify the new month derives from a specific authority transmitted from Moshe Rabbeinu through an unbroken chain; the power to annul vows as a *yachid* derives from something different — expertise, knowledge, standing in the realm of *halacha* — and that kind of *mumche* exists in every generation. There is no requirement of *semicha* in the technical genealogical sense.

### Knowledge Minimum

But what exactly is the knowledge threshold, and does it apply differently to a panel of three than to a *yachid*? Here one must distinguish between the requirements for a *yachid mumche* and the minimum competence required even for a *beit din* of three. The *Ran* asks pointedly: if laypeople suffice, why can one not convene three people who are entirely ignorant of the laws of *nedarim*? The answer, which the *Ran* derives from other passages in the *Gemara* — discussed earlier in the tractate — is that some minimum knowledge is required even from a panel of three. This is not a formal credential requirement but a functional one: if the members of the panel do not know what they are doing, they are not performing *hataras nedarim* at all. The act of *hatara* requires analysis — identifying a *petach* or a *charata*, understanding why the vow would not have been made had certain circumstances been known, and declaring the vow dissolved on that basis. A panel that mechanically recites words without any comprehension of the process is not conducting *hatara*; it is performing a meaningless verbal exercise.

The practical minimum for a panel of three is therefore that at least one member must genuinely understand the process and be capable of explaining it to the others. The other two must at minimum be able to understand the explanation when it is given — they need not be *gamir*, knowing the law independently, but they must be *savir*, capable of following reasoning and understanding the substance of what they are affirming. One must know and explain; the others must be able to understand. Below that threshold, the panel's declaration is without legal effect.

### Gadol HaDor Requirement

The *Ran* takes a stronger position regarding the *yachid mumche*. Citing *Rabbeinu Shmuel* in *perek Yayin Nesech*, the *Ran* notes that a *yachid mumche* must be *baki b'Gemara*, a thorough expert, *klomar rav muvhak* — that is, a distinguished rabbinic authority. But the *Ran* presses further. If being a *mumche* means simply possessing expert knowledge of the relevant laws, why does a *Gemara* elsewhere entertain the possibility that Rav Huna might not have the standing to annul a *neder* as a *yachid*? Rav Huna was certainly a great scholar; if expertise alone sufficed, he would plainly qualify. The *Ran* concludes from this that *mumche* for the purpose of *yachid* annulment requires more than expert knowledge. The *Torah* says *rashei ha-matos* — the heads of the tribes — and this implies that the annulment of vows was entrusted to those who are *yoshvim u-frukkim she-ba-dor*: the preeminent figures of their generation. It is not enough to be well-versed in the laws; one must be counted among the *gedolim* of the generation.

This produces a three-tiered analysis. The first possibility — that one must have *semicha* traceable to Moshe Rabbeinu, like the *beit din* of *kiddush hachodesh* — is rejected; that standard would make the role practically impossible and is not what the *Torah* intends here. The second possibility — that any expert scholar suffices — is also rejected by the *Ran*, since that would not explain the *Gemara*'s doubt about Rav Huna. The correct standard, according to the *Ran*, is a relative one: the *yachid mumche* must be the preeminent rabbinic authority of his generation, the *gadol ha-dor* in a real sense. This is a demanding but not impossible standard. Every generation has its *gedolim*, and among them, those at the very top are the ones who possess the standing to annul vows as a *yachid*. It is not an absolute metric but a generational one.

---

## Modern Application

### Rosh Hashanah Question

This analysis gives rise to a serious practical question about the widespread custom of *hataras nedarim* performed on *erev Rosh Hashanah*. The ceremony is conducted publicly, with groups of people serving as the panel before whom the petitioner declares nullification of vows made over the past year. Often the participants — both those serving as the *beit din* and those seeking *hatara* — have limited familiarity with the relevant laws and proceedings. Given the standards just established — that even a panel of three requires at minimum one member who genuinely understands the process, with the others capable of following the explanation — it is legitimate to ask whether the Rosh Hashanah ceremony typically meets halachic requirements.

### Petach vs. Charata

The ceremony as commonly practiced does not proceed through the formal *petach* model of *hatara*, in which the *chacham* identifies a specific new consideration that, had the person known it at the time of making the vow, would have caused him not to take it on at all — thereby establishing that the vow was made in error. Instead, the Rosh Hashanah ceremony operates primarily on the model of *charata* — remorse — where the petitioner expresses regret over vows made, and the panel affirms the nullification on that basis. There is a question among *poskim* as to whether the Rosh Hashanah practice constitutes a genuine *hataras nedarim* according to the stricter understanding, or whether it functions primarily as a *mesirat moda'ah* — a declaration of intent for the future — signaling that vows one may inadvertently take in the coming year should not be considered binding.

If *charata* alone suffices without going through the *petach* process, and if the *charata* model requires a less intensive analytical engagement, one might argue that the bar of *gamir ve-savir* is lower in that context, and that the ceremony thus has greater validity than the stricter analysis might suggest. Nevertheless, the concern remains that participants who do not understand the words being recited — or who recite them in a language they do not comprehend — are not meaningfully engaged in any process at all. The correct practice is for the words to be said in whatever language the participant understands. The broader question of whether the Rosh Hashanah ceremony reliably accomplishes genuine *hataras nedarim* is, by honest assessment, an open and serious one.

---

---

# Nedarim 79

## Mumcheh & Beit Din

### Hatarat Nedarim Overview

We begin today's *daf* at the bottom of 78b, in the middle of a discussion concerning *hatarat nedarim*. The Gemara has established that *hatarat nedarim* — the annulment of vows — may be performed either by a *yachid mumcheh*, a single expert authority, or by a court of three laypeople.

### Defining Mumcheh

The precise definition of *mumcheh* is itself a matter of dispute. One view holds that it requires *semicha* from Moshe Rabbeinu — a chain of ordination reaching back to Sinai — a standard that effectively renders the category inapplicable in post-Talmudic times. A second view requires an extraordinarily high level of knowledge and brilliance, a threshold so demanding that even some *Amoraim* may not have attained it. The third approach, which appears to be the inclination of the Ran, is that *mumcheh* simply means *rashei hamatot* — someone who stands among the distinguished Torah authorities of his generation. On this view, every generation has its *mumchehim*; it is not an exclusive club of five, but neither is it open to all.

### Shulchan Aruch Mumcheh

The *Shulchan Aruch*'s position appears to set an even more accessible standard. It initially frames *mumcheh* in terms of *gimur vesavir* — full mastery and comprehension of the relevant *halachot* of *nedarim* — suggesting that genuine expertise in this area suffices. Interestingly, however, the *Shulchan Aruch* adds that in the present day, no one qualifies as a *mumcheh*. The apparent tension between these two statements — a relatively modest theoretical threshold paired with the practical conclusion that no one meets it — is not easily resolved.

### Beit Din Members

When *hatarat nedarim* is performed by a court of three, the question arises as to the required qualifications of each member. All authorities agree that the members cannot be entirely ignorant of what is transpiring; each must be sufficiently engaged to meaningfully participate in the process. The intuitive position, therefore, is that at least one member must possess *gimur vesavir* — genuine mastery — while the other two need only *savir*, the capacity to understand what is explained to them. On this model, one person truly knows the material, explains it to the others, and they comprehend it well enough to function as legitimate members of the *beit din*.

### Savir Standard

Here too, however, the *Shulchan Aruch* introduces a surprising ruling: it appears to hold that all three members need only meet the *savir* standard. This raises an obvious difficulty — if all three are merely *savir*, who is doing the explaining? Presumably some fourth party, not a formal member of the *beit din*, would need to provide the necessary background. The *Shulchan Aruch* does not resolve this, but the ruling reflects a notably permissive approach to the qualifications required for *hatarat nedarim*.

---

## R. Chanina Silence

### Silence Indicates Intent

Picking up approximately five lines down on 78b, the Gemara records a striking interpretation attributed to Rabbi Chanina. The Torah states that if a husband remains silent for a day upon hearing his wife's vow, the vow is established — *yekimenu*, it becomes *hakamah*, and he loses the power to annul. Rabbi Chanina proposes a radical reinterpretation of this rule. The reason silence constitutes *hakamah*, he argues, is not the silence itself but rather what the silence indicates. If a husband is quiet for an entire day without annulling the vow, we infer that he was genuinely accepting of it — he was effectively ratifying the *neder* through his inaction. The *pasuk*, on this reading, is not establishing a categorical rule about silence but rather a presumption about what silence reveals.

### Spite Silence

This interpretive move opens the door to significant qualification. If the husband is silent not because he accepts the vow but for some other reason — say, to cause his wife anxiety, to manipulate her emotionally, to let her remain uncertain about whether the *neder* will stand — then his silence does not indicate acceptance at all. He has his own agenda, entirely unrelated to *hakamah*. In such a case, argues Rabbi Chanina, the silence should not be treated as *hakamah*, and the husband's ability to perform *hafarah* should remain intact.

### Heifer After 10 Days

Rabbi Chanina follows this reasoning to its conclusion: even after ten days have passed, if the silence was clearly motivated by spite or manipulation rather than genuine acceptance, the husband retains the right to perform *hafarah*. The operative concept is *yom shamo* — the day is defined by what the silence indicates. Where silence plainly does not indicate acceptance, the clock does not run on the husband's ability to annul.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava challenges this position from a Baraita that enumerates the circumstances under which a father regains control over his daughter's vows after the husband's involvement. The Baraita states: *eimatai amru met habaal nishkena reshut la'av* — when does the father regain authority? When the husband neither heard the vow, or heard it and remained silent (*shama veshatak*), or heard it and annulled it and then died on that very day. By contrast, if the husband was *mekayem* — actively affirming the vow — or was silent and then died after 24 hours, the father cannot annul. Rava notes that this Baraita appears to make no distinction based on the reason for the silence. Any silence sustained past the end of the *halachic* day appears to constitute *hakamah* regardless of intent.

### 24 Hour Silence

Rava's logic is pointed: the Baraita simply states that silence beyond the day is *hakamah*, without qualifying whether the silence was motivated by acceptance or by spite. If Rabbi Chanina were correct that spite-motivated silence never constitutes *hakamah*, one would expect the Baraita to distinguish between the two cases. Its failure to do so seems to imply that all silence, whatever its motivation, yields *hakamah* by the end of the day.

### Shatak Purpose

The Gemara responds with a distinction. When the Baraita speaks of *shatak* — of silence — it is specifically referring to silence undertaken with the intent of *kiyum*, of ratifying the vow. That is the ordinary case: a husband who is making up his mind, uncertain whether to annul, and lets the day pass without acting. That silence constitutes *hakamah* by the end of the day. The Baraita was never addressing the exceptional case of silence motivated by spite. Rava's challenge therefore does not compel Rabbi Chanina's defeat.

The Gemara then presses further. If *shatak al menat lekayem* — silence specifically intended as *kiyum* — is the case under discussion, that is effectively identical to an explicit verbal *kiyum*. Why distinguish it from the Baraita's earlier phrase *shama vekiyem*, where the husband actively ratified the vow? The Gemara's answer, as explained by the Ran, is that there are two meaningfully distinct scenarios.

### Ran's Two Scenarios

The Ran explains that *hakamah* does not require verbalization. A husband who, at a given moment, genuinely and actively desires to be *mekayem* the vow right now — even without saying a word — has performed a valid *kiyum* immediately. His silence in that instant, if it is apparent that this is his intent, is sufficient. By contrast, if the husband is in a state of deliberation — thinking about doing *kiyum* at some later point, not yet resolved — then we cannot credit him with an immediate *kiyum*, because his intent is not yet evident. In that case, it is only the passage of the full *halachic* day without *hafarah* that resolves the ambiguity and renders the silence meaningful as *hakamah*.

Thus *shama vekiyem*, where the husband actively ratifies, and *shatak al menat lekayem stam* — neutral deliberative silence — are not identical: the first works immediately, the second requires the full day. The classic ruling that silence until the end of the day constitutes *hakamah* addresses only the intermediate *stam* case, where the husband is neither actively ratifying nor actively spiting, but simply undecided.

---

## Hakeimah vs Heifer

### Chomer in Each

The Gemara now introduces a Baraita cited by Rav Chisda asserting that there are respects in which *hakamah* is stronger than *hafarah*, and respects in which *hafarah* is stronger than *hakamah*.

### Hakeimah Non-Verbal

The first area where *hakamah* is stronger: silence itself can produce *kiyum*. As established above, the passage of the full day without *hafarah* constitutes *hakamah* even without the husband ever uttering a word.

### Heifer Verbal Only

By contrast, silence never produces *hafarah*. *Hafarah* requires verbalization — some form of explicit speech — and no amount of silence, however prolonged, can serve as an annulment of the vow.

### Kiyum In Heart

These two points are, in fact, deeply connected. The Baraita states: *kiyem belibo kiyem; heifer belibo eino mufar* — if one ratified the vow in his heart, it is ratified; if one annulled the vow in his heart, it is not annulled. *Kiyum* does not require verbalization; it can be achieved through internal intention alone. *Hafarah* must be spoken aloud. The reason silence over the course of the day yields *hakamah* is precisely because we infer from that silence that the husband's internal disposition is one of acceptance — and since *kiyum* operates through internal disposition, the inference suffices. *Hafarah*, which operates exclusively through speech, cannot be accomplished in this indirect manner.

One can see immediately how these two points reinforce each other: the effectiveness of silent *kiyum* explains why the passage of time without speech yields *hakamah*, and the requirement of speech for *hafarah* explains why no analogous inference can work in the opposite direction.

### Mutual Exclusion

The Baraita then notes one area of symmetry: *kiyem ein yakhol lehafer; heifer ein yakhol lekayem* — once one has performed *kiyum*, *hafarah* is no longer available; once one has performed *hafarah*, *kiyum* is no longer available. This mutual exclusivity applies in both directions equally.

The Baraita promised an area where *hafarah* is stronger than *hakamah*, yet so far only areas of *hakamah*'s strength have been identified.

### Undoing Hakeimah

The Gemara supplies the answer in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *nish'alin al ha-hekem ve-ein nish'alin al ha-hefer* — one may seek release from *hakamah* through a *chakham*, but not from *hafarah*. Since *hakamah* operates by reinforcing the *neder* — by treating it as fully affirmed — it partakes of the character of a *neder* itself, and just as a *neder* may be undone through *hasharat nedarim* before a *chakham*, so too a *hakamah* may be unwound in that way. *Hafarah*, once performed, cannot be undone. In this respect, *hafarah* is definitively stronger.

---

## Three Tyufot

### Tyufa 1: Spite

The Gemara now marshals three successive Tannaitic challenges against Rabbi Chanina's position. The first is brought by Rav Kahana. The Baraita addresses a case of *shoteik al menat lemekat* — a husband who is silent specifically to cause his wife distress — and rules that by the end of the *halachic* day, this silence nonetheless constitutes *hakamah*. This appears to be a direct and explicit rejection of Rabbi Chanina, who held that spite-motivated silence should not yield *hakamah* regardless of how much time has passed.

### Three Silences

The Gemara responds by questioning whether the Baraita is indeed addressing spite-motivated silence, suggesting it might be referring to the more ordinary case of silence aimed at eventual *kiyum*. The Gemara then resolves the matter by noting that the word *hecherish* — "he was silent" — appears three times in the relevant *pasuk*. Each mention extends the ruling to an additional type of silence: one occurrence addresses silence where the husband intends immediate *kiyum*; a second addresses deliberative silence; and the third — the surplus mention — extends the law to even spite-motivated silence. The Torah's threefold use of the word of silence is thus read as a deliberate textual signal that all forms of silence, irrespective of motivation, yield *hakamah* by the end of the day. This constitutes a clear refutation of Rabbi Chanina.

### Tyufa 2: Shabbat

The second challenge is raised by Rava. The Gemara elsewhere permits a husband to perform *hafarah* on *Shabbat* — an act that would otherwise seem to raise concerns — specifically because if the vow was taken as *Shabbat* was ending, he must have the opportunity to annul before the day closes. The reasoning is: if he cannot perform *hafarah* on *Shabbat*, then the day ends and the vow becomes established. The very fact that we permit *hafarah* on *Shabbat* to prevent this outcome is Rava's basis for a powerful argument.

### Shabbat Inference

Consider the logic carefully. If a husband cannot perform *hafarah* on *Shabbat* — whether due to a rabbinic prohibition — then his silence on that day is not a free choice. He is silent because *halacha* prevents him from acting, not because he wishes to ratify the vow. According to Rabbi Chanina, such silence — silence whose reason is clearly not acceptance — should not become *hakamah*. If that were so, he would not lose the right to perform *hafarah* at the end of *Shabbat*, and we would have no reason to permit *hafarah* on *Shabbat* in the first place. The very existence of the dispensation to perform *hafarah* on *Shabbat* demonstrates that the reason for one's silence is legally irrelevant — any silence sustained through the end of the day becomes *hakamah*, period. This is another *tyufta* against Rabbi Chanina.

### Tyufa 3: Ignorance

The third challenge comes from Rav Ashi. The Gemara addresses a case where a husband says: I knew that my wife took a vow, but I did not know that I had the power to perform *hafarah*. He was never taught the relevant laws. Three days have now passed. The ruling: *yaper* — he may still perform *hafarah*. The reasoning is that *beyom shamo* — "on the day that he heard" — is defined not from the moment he first heard the words of the *neder*, but from the moment he became aware that he was in a position to act on it. Hearing without the contextual knowledge that one has the ability to respond is not halachically meaningful hearing.

### Hearing Debate

This ruling sets up a related debate about a parallel case. What if the husband says: I knew I had the power to perform *hafarah*, but I did not realize that what my wife said constituted a *neder*? Rabbi Meir rules that this still counts as hearing; the husband heard the words, knew he had the relevant legal power, and his failure to recognize the statement as a *neder* does not reset the clock. The *chakhamim* disagree and hold that this is analogous to the previous case — without realizing it is a *neder*, one has not truly "heard" it in the halachically operative sense, and the day begins only when full awareness is achieved.

What is notable for our purposes is what both Rabbi Meir and the *chakhamim* appear to agree upon: once the clock does begin — once hearing is established — the reason for the husband's subsequent silence does not matter. If a man is silent because he is clueless about *halacha*, that too becomes *hakamah* by the end of the day. The debate is only about when the clock starts, not about whether the motivation behind silence modulates the *hakamah* rule. This is the third and final *tyufta* against Rabbi Chanina's intent-based limitation.

---

## Ran & R. Akiva Eiger

### Ran On Silence

Returning to the Ran's discussion, the Gemara's principle that *kiyum* may be accomplished non-verbally — indeed, through the very mechanism of silence — requires explanation. The Ran addresses this directly: we learn from the law of silence on the day of hearing that *hakamah* does not require verbalization. The fact that sustained silence through the end of the day yields *hakamah* demonstrates that *kiyum* operates through internal disposition, not through speech.

### Intent Evidence

Why, then, does the silence need to last until the end of the day? The Ran explains: until sunset, it is simply not yet clear what the silence means. Perhaps the husband is planning to perform *hafarah* shortly. The ambiguity cannot be resolved before the day ends. Only once the full day has passed without any act of *hafarah* does the silence become unambiguous evidence that the husband's disposition is one of acceptance. As the Ran puts it: since we are going exclusively by what the husband intends, and we do not have direct access to his inner state, we require the accumulated weight of an entire day's silence to establish that his intent is indeed *kiyum*.

### Active Desire

From this the Ran draws a further inference: if the husband at some earlier moment during the day genuinely and actively desires — not merely contemplates — *kiyum*, that intent is effective immediately, without needing to wait until sunset. The Ran describes this as analogous to crossing a finish line: if you have actually crossed it, you do not need to wait for the race to be over. In such a case it is as though the full day has already been discharged, because the husband's will is unambiguously directed toward *kiyum* at this very moment.

### Akiva Eiger Problem

Rabbi Akiva Eiger raises a sharp challenge against this position. The Ran has argued, on the one hand, that since *kiyum* operates through internal intent, and since we cannot access a person's internal thoughts directly, we require the silence of a full day as evidence of that intent. But on the other hand, the Ran also holds that if the husband actively desires *kiyum* right now, his intent is immediately effective — without waiting for the day to end. The difficulty is this: if, as the Ran acknowledges, we normally cannot access what a person is thinking, and if we therefore require observable evidence (the passage of the full day) to establish *kiyum* — then how can an immediate unspoken desire for *kiyum* ever work? In the case of immediate intent, there is no equivalent evidence. The husband has said nothing and done nothing; we simply have no basis on which to credit his inner desire with halachic effect.

### Evidence Requirement

The *Gilyon HaShas* addresses this challenge. The underlying principle, he explains, is that internal thoughts — *devarim shebelev* — do not generally carry halachic significance. However, where those thoughts are *muchach uvalui lechol* — evident and manifest to observers — they do acquire halachic weight. This is the logic of the silent *hakamah* that accrues over the course of the day: the sustained silence renders the husband's inner acceptance evident to those around him. By the end of the day, *galui lanu kavanato* — his intent is disclosed to us — and that is why it is legally effective.

### Observable Evidence

Applying this framework to Rabbi Akiva Eiger's challenge, the *Gilyon HaShas* resolves that even in the case of immediate *kiyum*, there would need to be some form of observable evidence — something visible to others — for the immediate intent to take legal effect. Merely thinking, with nothing to disclose the thought to any observer, would fall under the general rule that unmanifest internal states carry no halachic weight. Silence accumulated over the day provides precisely such evidence; a bare internal desire, unaccompanied by any observable act or signal, does not. The question of immediate *kiyum* is thus left with some difficulty, though the *Gilyon HaShas*'s framework at least clarifies what form of evidence would theoretically be required.

---

## Heifer Categories

### Nedarim To Meifer

With the beginning of the final chapter of the tractate, the Gemara turns from the question of *who* may perform *hafarah* and *when* to the question of *which* vows are subject to *hafarah* at all. The opening of the *perek* establishes: *ve-elu nedarim shehu mefer* — these are the vows that a husband annuls. Before proceeding, it is worth noting the Ran's observation that the same categories applicable to the husband — *inuy nefesh* and the relational category of *bein ish leishah* — apply equally to the father with respect to his daughter, at least according to the Ran's position. The Rambam disagrees and holds that the father's authority over his minor daughter's vows is unlimited; the more restricted categorization applies only to the husband, who is dealing with an emancipated adult.

### Inuy Nefesh

The Torah frames the husband's authority over his wife's vows around the phrase *leanot nefesh* — to afflict the soul, or more precisely, to afflict the body. The first category of vows subject to *hafarah* is accordingly those involving *inuy nefesh*, vows whose effect constitutes a form of bodily affliction.

### Inuy Examples

The *Mishnah* offers two initial examples of *inuy nefesh*: a vow to refrain from bathing and a vow to refrain from wearing makeup. These are presented as paradigmatic cases of self-denial that rise to the level of *inuy nefesh*.

### Bein Ish Leishah

The second category is derived from the Torah's phrase *bein ish leishah* — between a man and his wife — and encompasses vows that, while perhaps not constituting bodily affliction, directly affect the marital relationship and the dynamics between husband and wife. This category opens a separate channel of authority for the husband beyond the *inuy nefesh* framework.

### R. Yosi Position

Rabbi Yosi disputes the *Mishnah*'s classification. He holds that refraining from bathing and refraining from makeup do not rise to the level of *inuy nefesh*. This is a striking position, particularly given the Roman-era context in which the Talmud was composed, where public bathing was a regular and socially normative practice. Yet Rabbi Yosi maintains that *inuy nefesh* requires a higher threshold — something closer to a complete and significant deprivation — and that these examples fall short. Instead, Rabbi Yosi proposes his own paradigm cases of *inuy nefesh*. What Rabbi Yosi does with bathing and makeup, then, is presumably to place them in the *bein ish leishah* category rather than *inuy nefesh* — an important distinction, as the Gemara will go on to explain.

### Non-Inuy Examples

Rabbi Yosi's conception of *inuy nefesh* is notably demanding. He illustrates with two cases where *hafarah* is *not* available: if a wife vows to abstain from the fruit of a particular country, that is not *inuy nefesh*, because fruit from other countries remains available — *yavi mimedina acheret*, go fetch it from another region. Similarly, if she vows to abstain from produce purchased at a particular storekeeper's shop, that too is not *inuy nefesh*, since she can simply shop elsewhere. These cases lack the quality of genuine, inescapable deprivation that *inuy nefesh* requires.

### Sole Supplier

There is, however, an exception to the storekeeper case. If the husband's only practical supplier of food was that particular storekeeper — for example, because the storekeeper was the only one who would extend him credit, while no other vendor would deal with him on those terms — then forbidding the produce of that storekeeper's shop does constitute *inuy nefesh*. Whatever the theoretical availability of alternatives, the practical reality is that this family's food supply depends entirely on that one source, and to eliminate it is genuine deprivation. The Ran further applies this principle to the country case: when the *Mishnah* says that forbidding fruit from a particular country is not *inuy nefesh* because one can obtain it from elsewhere, this presupposes that the alternative country is genuinely comparable — both are secondary sources. If the forbidden country is in fact the primary source of the household's food, the analysis would follow the storekeeper model and the vow would indeed constitute *inuy nefesh*.

---

## Permanence Analysis

### Only Inuy Mufar

The Gemara initially reads the *Mishnah* as holding that only *inuy nefesh* vows are subject to *hafarah* by the husband. Vows lacking *inuy nefesh* cannot be annulled.

### Baraita Citation

A Baraita immediately challenges this reading by citing the Torah's phrase *bein ish leishah bein av levito* — explicitly establishing that vows *bein ish leishah*, in the relational category, are also subject to *hafarah*. The Baraita confirms that both categories — *inuy nefesh* and *bein ish leishah* — lie within the husband's authority.

### Why Distinguish

This raises a pointed question. If the husband can annul vows in both categories, why does Rabbi Yosi insist that bathing and makeup are *not inuy nefesh*? If they fall into the *bein ish leishah* category, the husband can annul them anyway. What halachic work is the categorical distinction doing?

### Suggested Theory

The Gemara proposes a theory: although the husband can perform *hafarah* on both categories, the categories differ in their duration of effect. *Inuy nefesh* vows, when annulled, are annulled permanently — *meifer le-olam*. But *bein ish leishah* vows, when annulled, are effective only during the marriage; upon divorce, the *neder* reasserts itself. On this theory, the mechanism of *hafarah* differs between the two categories: in the case of *inuy nefesh*, the husband possesses genuine annulment authority; in the case of *bein ish leishah*, his power is more like a right to suspend the vow's operation for as long as the marital relationship continues. This would explain why Rabbi Yosi needs to distinguish the categories — whether a vow falls into *inuy nefesh* or merely *bein ish leishah* has real consequences for the permanence of the *hafarah*.

### R. Yochanan Nuri

This theory is supported, at least prima facie, by the ruling of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri in the *Mishnah*. If a wife takes a vow forbidding the product of her labor to her husband — *maaseh yadeha* — the husband is not technically required to annul it, since that labor belongs to him anyway. But Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri advises that he should annul it regardless. The reason: if they later divorce, he would no longer own her labor, and the vow — never having been formally annulled — would spring back into effect and forbid her labor to him. This would prevent them from remarrying, since no marriage can function if the wife's labor is forbidden to her husband. The advice to annul proactively demonstrates that *hafarah* of a *bein ish leishah* vow can have lasting effect — it will protect against the vow's reinstatement even after divorce. This seems to support the theory that *hafarah* of such vows does indeed carry some lasting force.

### Theory Rejected

The Gemara ultimately rejects the theory that *bein ish leishah hafarah* lapses upon divorce. Even after the couple divorces, a *hafarah* that was performed during the marriage remains effective. The case of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri confirms this: the whole point of his advice is that the husband should perform *hafarah now* so that it will remain in effect even if they divorce — which would make no sense if *bein ish leishah hafarah* automatically lapsed upon divorce.

### Refined Distinction

The Gemara therefore refines the distinction. Both *inuy nefesh* and *bein ish leishah* vows, when annulled, remain annulled even after divorce. The difference lies in what happens if the woman subsequently marries another man. For *inuy nefesh* vows, the original husband's *hafarah* is effective *bein le'atzmo bein le'acheirim* — both for himself and for others, meaning the vow remains annulled even with respect to a new husband. For *bein ish leishah* vows, the *hafarah* is effective *le'atzmo* — for himself — but not *le'acheirim* — not for a new husband. Once she marries another man, the vow reasserts itself in her new relationship.

The underlying logic is that *bein ish leishah hafarah* is not a free-standing annulment of the *neder* but rather a suspension rooted in the particular marital relationship. After divorce, the couple might still remarry, and in that potential relationship the *hafarah* retains its relevance — it remains *bein ish leishah* even in the divorce state, since the bond has not been fully severed beyond all prospect of reunion. But once she marries another man, the original marital context that grounded the *hafarah* is definitively gone, the old husband's sphere of authority over this *neder* is extinguished, and the *neder* reasserts itself in her new marriage. With *inuy nefesh*, by contrast, the husband's authority is absolute: he possesses genuine annulment power, and what he annuls stays annulled regardless of subsequent relationships.

---

---

# Nedarim 81

## Wellspring Dispute

### Two Towns Setup

The daf picks up at the bottom of 80b, continuing the larger discussion of what constitutes a *neder inuy nefesh* — a vow of self-affliction that a husband is entitled to annul — alongside the category of *beino l'veina*, matters that pertain specifically to the dynamic between husband and wife. The Gemara introduces a *baraita* (found in the Tosefta to Bava Metzia) with the formula *v'rammi d'Rabbi Yosi ad d'Rabbi Yosi* — a contradiction is raised between two rulings of Rabbi Yosi.

The *baraita* presents the case of a *ma'ayan shebnei ha'ir*: a natural wellspring that originates in one town and flows toward another. The question is how to adjudicate competing water needs between the two towns across a hierarchy of uses.

### Life & Animals

The hierarchy proceeds as follows. First: *chayeihem v'chayei acheirim* — the lives of the townspeople who possess the wellspring take precedence over the lives of the people in the other town. This is entirely unsurprising; it reflects the foundational halachic principle of *v'chai achicha imach* — *chayecha kodmin l'chayei achicha*, your own life takes priority over that of another. Second: *behemtam u'vehemat acheirim* — their animals take precedence over the other town's animals. Third: *kvisatan u'kvisat acheirim* — their laundry takes precedence over the other town's laundry. All three of these rulings follow naturally from the principle of self-priority.

### Laundry Priority

The surprising ruling comes next. The *baraita* poses the case of *chayei acheirim u'kvisatan*: what if the other town's people need the water for basic sustenance — their lives — while the town with the wellspring needs it only for laundry? The anonymous first voice of the *baraita* rules *chayei acheirim kodmin l'kvisatan*: the other town's lives take precedence over laundry, which seems obvious. But then: *Rabbi Yosi omer, kvisatan kodemes l'chayei acheirim* — Rabbi Yosi rules that their laundry precedes the other town's lives.

This is, on its face, a startling ruling. Someone in the next town needs water to survive, and Rabbi Yosi permits the first town to keep the water for laundry?

### Tosafot Reading

Tosafot offers an important qualification. He reads *kodemet* not as a categorical denial of water to the other town, but as a question of temporal priority. The wellspring flows naturally from town A to town B. Town A is permitted to first pause or dam the water in order to complete their laundry, after which the water continues downstream to town B. On this reading, nobody in the second town ultimately goes without — they simply have to wait. The *chiddush* is only about the order of access, not about a permanent withholding, and Tosafot presumably frames it this way because the assumption is that no one will actually die from the delay.

### Ethics & Charity

The Ran, by contrast, appears to favor a more literal reading, which creates genuine moral tension. One might try to defend the position with reference to the principle that even a limb of one's own body takes precedence over another person's life — the *psak halacha* being that one is not obligated to risk a limb to definitively save another's life, even though objectively a life outweighs a limb. If even one's own limb takes precedence, perhaps something central to one's bodily dignity and well-being — clothing one wears, the state of one's physical environment — might similarly precede a more distant person's claim on one's resources. This is admittedly harsh, and the lecturer does not endorse a literal reading. But it invites comparison to Peter Singer's well-known critique: every day people spend significant sums on dinners, consumer goods, and personal luxuries while lives elsewhere could be saved with those same funds. The distance and abstraction of the need makes it feel different — but morally, is it? Here, the context is less abstract: these are fellow Jews in a neighboring town. The tradition of *pidyon shvuyim* illustrates that when Jews are in acute need nearby, significant personal sacrifice is expected. A mitigating interpretation of *chayei acheirim* is also possible — perhaps it refers not to imminent death but to a lower level of well-being, a harder life rather than a life-threatening emergency.

### Tzedakah Priority

This ruling opens onto a broader question about the competing metrics within *tzedakah* obligations. Halacha articulates two distinct hierarchies: one based on proximity (*aniucha ve'aniyei ircha, aniucha kodmin* — your own poor take precedence over those of another city) and one based on degree of need (*ani ve'ashir, ani kodem* — the poor take precedence over the wealthy even in loan contexts). What happens when proximity and need pull in opposite directions? The poor of one's own city need education, while the poor of a neighboring city need food — to whom does one's primary obligation run?

The Chasam Sofer holds that need always governs first: one must ensure that basic needs everywhere are met before ascending to higher-level needs, beginning with those closest. The Aruch Hashulchan, by contrast, emphasizes that primary obligation always tracks proximity. Something of this tension plays out in the *baraita*: even granting that we should not imagine people literally dying, one can still ask whether one town's laundry precedes another town's general welfare. These are genuinely unsettled questions in the application of *tzedakah* priorities, and the Gemara surfaces them here without fully resolving them.

---

## Medical Dangers

### Shmuel's Health

Having established that Rabbi Yosi elevates laundry to a remarkable degree of importance, the Gemara now presents a medical teaching from Shmuel that contextualizes this. *Arvuvita dereisha* — the tangling and filth of the hair from not washing — *mayti lidei avira*, leads to blindness. *Arvuvita demani* — the filth of one's garments from not doing laundry — *mayti lidei sha'amimuta*, leads to a kind of mental disturbance or psychological deterioration. *Arvuvita degufa* — bodily filth from not bathing — *mayti lidei shichney vekivi*, leads to sores and blisters.

### Contradiction Resolved

This teaching sharpens the original contradiction. If not bathing causes sores and blisters, how can Rabbi Yosi say bathing is not *inuy nefesh*? And if not laundering causes psychological deterioration — seemingly worse — why does Rabbi Yosi use laundry to such great rhetorical effect while dismissing bathing? The Gemara's resolution is that Rabbi Yosi does not doubt Shmuel's medical claims. Rather, his position is that not laundering is genuinely weighty — enough that one may prioritize laundry over other competing claims — yet that still does not automatically make the *deprivation* of laundering the kind of *inuy nefesh* that rises to the level activating a husband's annulment power. The distinction is between what is medically serious and what crosses the formal halachic threshold of *nidrei inuy nefesh*.

---

## Three Warnings

### Hygiene Warning

The Gemara records that *shalchu mitam* — they sent from Eretz Yisrael — three warnings. The first: *hizahru b'arvuvsa* — be careful regarding filth, the neglect of bathing and laundering. Given Shmuel's medical teachings, the community has a responsibility to ensure that even those without means have access to the basic hygiene that protects health.

### Chavruta Warning

The second warning: *hizahru b'chavura* — be attentive to community, which the *rishonim* explain as a reference to learning in *chavruta*, in partnership. Torah study is not meant to be a solitary enterprise; the maintenance of a learning community is presented as a communal priority on a par with the first warning.

### Poor Children

The third and most extensively discussed warning: *hizahru bivnei aniyim* — take special care of the children of the poor, for *shemehem taitzei Torah* — from them Torah will ultimately go out. The verse cited is *yizal mayim midalyav* — water will flow from his lowly ones — where *dal* (lowly) is read as the source of *mayim* (water), and water is Torah.

### Torah Transmission

This leads the Gemara to pose a question: *umipnei mah einam metzuyin talmidei chachamim l'taitzei talmidei chachamim mibeineihen?* Why do we not consistently see the children of *talmidei chachamim* themselves becoming great *talmidei chachamim*? Logic would seem to favor it — Torah is spoken in the home, learning is prioritized, the culture is saturated with it. And indeed, one can point to dynasties like that of Rashi — Rashbam, Rabbeinu Tam, the Ri — where Torah did pass with remarkable depth across generations. Yet the Gemara treats the absence of such dynasties as the norm requiring explanation.

### Three Explanations

Three *amoraim* offer explanations. Rav Yosef says: *shelo yomru Torah yerusha hi lahem* — so that no family should come to feel that Torah is their *yerusha*, their inheritance. A *yerusha* is something received without effort; it arrives by default. The children of *talmidei chachamim*, if Torah passed automatically from father to son, would have no incentive to labor for it. The *bnei aniyim*, by contrast, receive nothing for free and must work for every opportunity. Their Torah therefore comes from genuine effort and urgent appreciation.

Rav Sheshet bar Rav Idi adds: *k'dei shelo yitgadru al hatzibur* — so that they should not become haughty over the community. If one family maintained a sustained monopoly on Torah learning across generations, the inevitable result would be a kind of aristocratic elevation — the family of Torah, set above and apart, a protected hierarchy. God arranges matters so this does not solidify.

Mar Zutra frames the same point as consequence rather than prevention: *mishum shehen mitgabrim al hatzibur* — it is because such families, when Torah does concentrate in them, do become overbearing toward the community. The loss of the dynasty is recompense for that pattern.

Rav Ashi offers a final reason: *mishum d'karu l'inshei chamrei* — because they call other people donkeys. When a family comes to regard itself as the sole bearers of Torah, they come to view laypeople as inherently inferior — *am ha'aretz hadomeh k'veheimah* — and that contempt, when rooted in a sense of innate superiority rather than earned distinction, generates its own punishment.

### Torah Universality

There is a deeper point underlying all three explanations. The *Beit HaMikdash* was hierarchical by design: physical proximity to it mattered, access was stratified, and *kehunah* was exclusively hereditary — a genuine *yerusha* for the *bnei Aharon*. Torah, by contrast, is the one of the *shlosha k'tarim* of which the Gemara says *kol harotzeh yavo v'yitol* — whoever wishes may come and take it. Chazal created the institution of universal education. The warning to care for *bnei aniyim* is in part a reminder that the universality of Torah is not self-maintaining; it requires active communal protection. Even something that should be as radically open and non-hierarchical as Torah can drift toward becoming a protected, centralized institution if the community is not vigilant.

---

## Blessing Over Torah

### Verse & Blessing

The Gemara now cites the verse: *mi ha'ish ha'chacham v'yaven et zot — al mah avdah ha'aretz* — who is the wise person who will understand this: why was the land destroyed? The Gemara records that the sages could not answer, the prophets could not answer, until God himself answered: *al azvam et Torati asher nasati lifneihem velo sham'u bekoli velo halchu bah* — because they abandoned My Torah and did not listen to My voice and did not walk in it.

### Voice & Blessing

The apparent redundancy of *velo sham'u bekoli* and *velo halchu bah* — not listening to God's voice and not walking in the Torah seem to describe the same failure — occasions the teaching of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: *she'ein mevarchin baTorah techila* — they did not make the *bracha* over Torah first. "Not listening to My voice" refers to the failure to make the blessing before learning.

### Torah Business

What is the connection between not making a *bracha* and the problem of Torah becoming a family inheritance? A *bracha* is not merely a formality. *Asher kideshanu bemitzvotav vetzivanu* — it is an act of recognizing that one learns because God commanded it, that Torah is a gift received from outside oneself, a *mitzvah* being performed in response to divine demand. The danger for a family in which Torah has become the family business across generations is that this sense evaporates. Learning becomes what one's father did, what one's grandfather did, the professional substrate of one's life. When Torah is simply the family trade, one does not make a *bracha* over it — not because one is impious, but because it no longer registers as a treasure being encountered. One is not *listening to God's voice*; one is simply doing what one does. This loss of orientation — the failure to experience Torah as a commanded gift rather than a familial possession — is, according to Ravina, the deeper cause behind both the abandonment of Torah and the failure of dynasties to sustain genuine Torah scholarship.

---

## Vardimus Question

### Vardimus Confused

Isi bar Yehuda stopped attending Rabbi Yosi's *beit midrash* for three days. When Vardimus bar Rabbi Yosi — Rabbi Yosi's son, bearing a name apparently of Greek derivation — encountered him and asked why he had not come, Isi bar Yehuda replied: *ki ta'ameh de'avuch lo yad'ana heichi asina* — if I cannot understand the reasoning of your father, how can I keep attending? Vardimus asked him to state what he did not understand, saying perhaps he could explain it. Isi bar Yehuda cited the ruling: *Rabbi Yosi omer kvisatan kodemet lechayei acheirim* — that one's laundry precedes the other town's lives. This, he said, makes no sense, and he could not continue attending a *beit midrash* where he heard such things without comprehension.

### Levite Suburbs

Vardimus then offers a textual derivation. The verse states: *umigrasheihem yihyu livhemtam ulechol chayasam* — the surrounding fields of the Levitical cities shall be for their animals and for all of their *chayasam*. The question is: what does *chayasam* mean? If it means wild animals — deer and the like — that is already included in *behemtam*. The verse would be redundant.

### Chayasam Meaning

Therefore, *chayasam* must refer to something that sustains life — *chayusa mamash*. But if it means literal life-sustaining activities, that too seems obvious and need not be stated. The derivation therefore pushes further: it must refer to something that comes next in the hierarchy of needs after *behema* — and consulting the order of the *baraita* (lives, then animals, then laundry), that next category is laundry. Laundry is thus included in the term *chayasam* — things that sustain life — because *de'ika tzaar degivshusa*, the neglect of laundry brings real physical harm (the filth, the associated ailments discussed by Shmuel). This is how Vardimus grounds his father's ruling: laundry is classified as life-sustaining activity and therefore may, under the framework of *chayecha kodmin*, be prioritized even against the competing needs of others.

---

## Bathing & Makeup

### Not Inuy Nefesh

The Gemara returns to the central case. *Amar Rabbi Yosi: ein elu nidrei inui nefesh* — Rabbi Yosi rules that vows involving the prohibition of bathing or the application of makeup do not fall within the category of *nidrei inuy nefesh*. The husband, therefore, cannot exercise his annulment power on that basis.

### Beino L'Veina Question

A question is then raised: even if these vows are not *inuy nefesh*, does Rabbi Yosi hold that they qualify as *devarim shebeino l'veina* — matters pertaining to the direct relationship between husband and wife — for which the husband also has annulment authority? The Gemara attempts to answer from Rabbi Yosi's own phrasing: *ein elu nidrei inui nefesh* sounds as though he is making a categorical ruling about the classification, not simply saying he cannot annul them. This might imply that they are not even in the *beino l'veina* category.
