But the Gemara deflects: perhaps Rabbi Yosi is only addressing the Rabbis who placed these in the *inuy nefesh* category, and his statement is *l'didchu* — addressed to those who take that position. He is saying: at minimum concede they are not *inuy nefesh*. His own view may go further and remove them from *beino l'veina* as well. Whether they belong there is therefore left open by this exchange.

### Rav Adda vs. Huna

Two *amoraim* dispute the matter. Rav Adda bar Ahava holds that the husband can annul — these vows do fall within *devarim shebeino l'veina*. Rav Huna holds he cannot annul.

### Fox Metaphor

Rav Huna's reasoning is captured by the saying: *shelo matzinu shual shemet b'afar pir* — we have never found a fox that died from the dust of its own burrow. A creature is not harmed by the familiar environment it has grown accustomed to. Applied here: if a husband's wife does not bathe or apply makeup, that is part of the physical reality of their shared life together. People adapt to and tolerate what becomes their normal environment. On this view, the husband has no genuine complaint, and therefore the vow does not rise to the level of *beino l'veina* in a way that would justify annulment.

---

## Annulment Categories

### Inuy Nefesh Rule

The *baraita* then sets out the governing categories systematically. Vows that carry *inuy nefesh* — genuine self-affliction — the husband may annul *bein beino l'veina bein beino l'veina ve'acheirim*: whether the vow directly concerns their relationship or involves her deprivation by a third party. The operative question for *inuy nefesh* is entirely about the nature and degree of harm to her, not about who is the subject of the vow. If her being deprived of something constitutes real *inuy nefesh*, it does not matter whether that thing comes from her husband, from another person, or from the world at large.

### Examples List

This is illustrated concretely. If she says *konam peirot eilu alai* — all fruit is forbidden to me — he can annul it. It does not matter whose fruit. If she says she is forbidden from benefiting from a particular person — her father, her brother, his brother, his father — or says she will not give straw before his animals or water to his cattle, he *cannot* annul. The reason: even though such vows may cause him annoyance or inconvenience, and even though they affect his household and family relationships, they are not directly about the intimate dynamic between the two of them. Since they do not rise to *inuy nefesh* either, neither basis for annulment applies. The *chiddush* here is that vows which create indirect irritation or hardship for the husband — even regarding his animals, his family members — fall outside both categories.

### Beino L'Veina Examples

By contrast, if she vows not to apply *kechol* or *afros* (the various forms of eye and face makeup), or not to have sexual relations — *shelo eshamesh mitatecha* — he can annul, *mishum devarim shebeino l'veina*, because these directly concern their relationship. The vow implicates something between the two of them in a direct and personal way.

### Obligatory Acts

But certain acts she cannot effectively vow away at all, because they fall within her existing obligations to him: *shelo atzia lecha mitatecha* (making his bed), *shelo emzog lecha et hakos* (mixing his wine), *shelo erchatz lecha panecha yadecha veraglecha* (washing his face, hands, and feet). As established in Ketubot, even a wife who brings a hundred maidservants into the household is still obligated to perform these acts of intimate service for her husband personally. Since she lacks the halachic standing to vow away something she is already obligated to provide, such a vow is simply ineffective — *ein tzarich lehafer*, the husband does not even need to formally annul.

---

## Rabban Gamliel

### Lo Yachel Devaro

That said, Rabban Gamliel holds that even with respect to vows that are technically ineffective — those covering acts she is already obligated to perform — the husband should nonetheless go through the process of annulment. The basis is *lo yachel devaro*: he should not let his word become violated. The Ran observes that the verse does not say *lo yachel nidro* or *shvuaso* — it says *devaro*, his *word*. The implication is that even speech that is not technically binding as a *neder* carries weight. Dismissing it entirely, treating it as though it never happened, is itself a form of disregard. The process of annulment, even where not strictly required, honors the gravity of speech and restores clarity.

### Son's Oath

This resonates practically. A son returned from camp having made some kind of conditional declaration — not technically a *neder* under strict halachic analysis — but he was distressed by it and wanted resolution. The technically correct answer that "it means nothing" was insufficient; he needed the formal process. The father said *mutar lach, mutar lach*, and only then did the son feel genuinely released. The words had weight, and the weight needed to be formally addressed. That is the thrust of Rabban Gamliel's ruling.

### Self-Annulment

A digression is prompted by the verse *lo yachel devaro*: *mikan lechacham she'ein matir nidro atzmo* — a Torah scholar cannot annul his own vow. The verse implies that one can *violate* one's words — meaning the words retain binding force on the person who spoke them. Someone else can annul, but the person himself cannot. As the aphorism goes: a prisoner cannot release himself from jail.

---

## Bathing & Makeup (II)

### Baraita Attribution

Returning to the *baraita*: who is the *tana* who placed the prohibition of applying *kechol* and *afros* in the category of *devarim shebeino l'veina*? The question matters because the *tanna kamma* of the *mishnah* places bathing and makeup in the *inuy nefesh* category. The *baraita* placing these in *beino l'veina* — a lesser category — can only reflect the view of Rabbi Yosi, who holds they are not *inuy nefesh*. This is therefore strong evidence that Rabbi Yosi, despite saying these do not qualify as *inuy nefesh*, does hold they belong in *beino l'veina* — resolving the earlier question in favor of Rav Adda bar Ahava.

---

## Sexual Relations

### Forbidden Pleasure

The Gemara now turns to the case of sexual relations. The *baraita* said that if she vows *shelo eshamesh mitatecha* — she will not have sexual relations with him — he can annul, *mishum devarim shebeino l'veina*. But the Gemara presses: what exactly is the case? If she says *hana'at tashmishi alecha* — the pleasure of my sexual service is forbidden to you — why would annulment even be necessary? *Hameshubdedet leih* — she is obligated to him in this regard; it is not hers to forbid.

### Rav Kahana

The case must therefore be, the Gemara concludes, *k'Rav Kahana*. Rav Kahana rules: if a woman says *hana'at tashmishi alecha* — my sexual service is forbidden to you — *kofin u'meshamshto*: she is compelled to fulfill her obligation regardless. The vow does not take effect, because it targets something that is not hers to withhold. But if she says *hana'at tashmishcha alai* — the pleasure of your sexual service is forbidden to me — then *yafer*: he must annul. This version of the vow does take effect.

### Wife Obligation

The reason the second formulation takes effect while the first does not relates to the principle *she'ein ma'achilin et adam davar ha'asur lo* — one may not force a person to consume something forbidden to them. She did not say she would not fulfill her duty; she said she would not benefit from him. Nevertheless, when the time comes to fulfill her obligation, she cannot be placed in the position of performing a transgression. Her obligation is therefore effectively neutralized by the vow, even though it was structured indirectly. And since this creates a genuine disruption in the dynamic between them, it falls within *beino l'veina* and he has the power to annul.

The Gemara takes for granted that a wife is *meshubdedet* — obligated — to have sexual relations with her husband. A wife who refuses is classified in halacha as a *moredet*, a rebel. The Rashba grounds this obligation not in a specific biblical verse but in the implicit structure of the marital bond: when a couple stands under the *chuppah*, the commitment they undertake includes mutual sexual fidelity and availability. It is not merely a contractual arrangement but a fundamental dimension of what marriage is.

### Rambam Problem

The Rambam offers a different account, one rooted in the *kinyan* model of *kiddushin*. On the Rambam's view — as elaborated by the Netziv and implicit in the Rambam's own formulation — the act of *kiddushin* involves an acquisition of the woman for marital purposes; her body, in the context of sexual relations, is in a sense her husband's domain. Therefore, she cannot make forbidden to herself what does not, on this account, fully belong to her to make forbidden. This reasoning is halachically potent but ideologically fraught, and can be read as providing halachic cover for marital coercion. The meaning of *kofin* in this context — whether it means legal compulsion or physical force — is itself disputed, and there is a documented history of women bringing complaints to rabbinic authorities and receiving inadequate redress on exactly these grounds.

### Custom Practice

The Gemara closes with a teaching about the weight of established practice: *devarim hamutarim ve'acheirim nahagu bahem issur, ee ata rashai linhog bahem heiter kedei levatlam* — if something is genuinely permitted but a community has adopted a practice of treating it as forbidden, one may not simply act in defiance of that practice to demonstrate its technical permissibility. The basis is once again *lo yachel devaro* — even informal speech and practice carry a kind of moral weight that demands respect. This is in the same register as Rabban Gamliel's ruling: even when there is no binding *neder*, the words and practices that people have taken seriously are not to be dismissed.

---

## Husband Annulling

### Matir vs. Meifer

Finally, the Ran raises a distinct and important question: can a husband serve as the one who is *matir* — who permits — his wife's vows, rather than simply being *meifer*, the one who annuls? The two roles are conceptually different. *Hafarah* is the husband's specific statutory power to annul within the marriage framework. *Hatarat nedarim* is the rabbinically prescribed process of releasing a vow through a sage or panel. The question is whether a husband can function in the latter capacity for his wife.

### Vested Interest

The Ran's analysis turns on the principle of *nogea badavar* — an interested party. If the husband has a personal stake in the vow being dissolved — because it is a *beino l'veina* matter, or because it implicates him in some way — he cannot serve as *matir*, since an interested party is disqualified from serving in that role. But if the vow does not affect him, the question becomes whether his status as her husband — governed by the principle of *ishto k'gufo*, that a wife is as one's own body — disqualifies him from serving as *matir* even when he has no direct interest. This is an open dispute between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Yehuda in a *mishnah*, and the question of how we *pasken* on it remains unresolved.

---

---

# Nedarim 82

## Inuy Nefesh vs. Beino L'…

### Bathing & Makeup

The present daf picks up from the bottom of 81b, where the Gemara had been wrestling with the distinction between *inuy nefesh* — vows of genuine self-denial over which a husband holds broad annulment power — and *devarim shebeino l'veina*, matters bearing on the intimate spousal relationship alone. The discussion established that according to the *Rabbanan*, a woman's vow not to bathe and not to wear makeup constitutes *inuy nefesh*. According to Rabbi Yosi, however, those same restrictions do not rise to the level of *inuy nefesh* but rather fall into the category of *devarim shebeino l'veina*.

### Rabanan vs. R. Yosi

The Gemara had further examined whether even Rabbi Yosi's category of *devarim shebeino l'veina* would encompass such vows, and concluded that it would. This distinction matters because the two categories carry different halachic weight: *inuy nefesh* allows for full annulment, while *devarim shebeino l'veina* grants the husband only a more circumscribed power.

### Husband's Limited Power

The Gemara underscored an important limitation: even where a vow qualifies as *devarim shebeino l'veina*, the husband can annul only that portion of the vow that directly affects the marital relationship between the two of them. He cannot, by virtue of that annulment, remove the vow's effect on her interactions with all other people. This sets the stage for the Gemara's next inquiry.

---

## Tashmish HaMita Question

### The Question Posed

Resuming two lines from the bottom of 81b, the Gemara records that Rava posed a question to Rav Nachman: *tashmish hamita l'Rabbanan* — the denial of marital relations according to the *Rabbanan* — does it constitute *inuy nefesh*, or does it fall instead under *devarim shebeino l'veina*?

The framing of this question is significant. For Rabbi Yosi, we had asked whether the denial of bathing was even sufficient to qualify as *beino l'veina*. The *Rabbanan*, by contrast, operate with a considerably lower threshold for *inuy nefesh* — they are more ready to classify deprivations as genuine self-affliction. The question is therefore whether the *Rabbanan* would regard the denial of sexual relations as crossing into *inuy nefesh*, or whether by its very nature it remains a matter fundamentally about the husband-wife bond and therefore categorized as *beino l'veina*.

### Rav Nachman's Answer

Rav Nachman responded that the answer may be derived from a *mishnah*. The *mishnah* teaches the case of a woman who declares *netulah ani min hayehudim* — that she is "removed from Jews" — meaning she has forbidden herself from receiving sexual benefit from any Jew. In such a case, the husband *yafar chelko*, he annuls his portion of the vow, with the result that *u'meshameshta*, she may have marital relations with him. However, should the couple ever divorce, she remains forbidden to all other Jewish men — an outcome that would make remarriage exceedingly difficult. What the *mishnah* thus demonstrates is that the husband's power extends only to that dimension of the vow that affects him personally. He cannot remove the vow's restriction vis-à-vis the rest of the world. The implication of Rav Nachman's proof is that denial of sexual relations is treated as *beino l'veina* rather than as *inuy nefesh*, since if it were *inuy nefesh* the husband would possess full annulment power.

### Rava's Objection

Rava pushes back: *l'Rabbanan ki ba'ei lach* — that was the question I asked according to the *Rabbanan*. But the *mishnah* Rav Nachman cited is *Rabbi Yosi katani lah* — it reflects the view of Rabbi Yosi. And Rabbi Yosi, as established, holds a far more restrictive definition of *inuy nefesh*. For Rabbi Yosi, bathing and makeup do not constitute *inuy nefesh*, so it follows naturally that sexual relations, too, would fall outside *inuy nefesh* and be classified as *beino l'veina* at most. The question was what the *Rabbanan* hold, and citing a *mishnah* that reflects Rabbi Yosi's position provides no answer.

### Attribution to Rabbi Yosi

This prompts a striking observation: *de'amar Rav Huna kulei pirkan Rabbi Yosi hi* — Rav Huna states that the entire remainder of this *perek* is authored by Rabbi Yosi. The basis for this claim is a textual cue in the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* concludes with the phrase *divrei Rabbi Yosi*, explicitly attributing a statement to Rabbi Yosi. The Gemara reads this as not merely closing out one ruling but as introducing Rabbi Yosi's voice as the governing voice for all subsequent *mishnayos* in the *perek* — *mikan v'eilach Rabbi Yosi hi*. This is a remarkable hermeneutic move: the repetition of *divrei Rabbi Yosi* at the end of a *mishnah* is taken as signaling that Rabbi Yosi is the *stam* author of what follows.

The practical consequence is that Rava's objection stands: the *mishnah* Rav Nachman cited, which shows that *tashmish* qualifies only as *beino l'veina* and not *inuy nefesh*, reflects Rabbi Yosi's narrower standard. It offers no guidance regarding the *Rabbanan*'s position.

### Nature of Marriage

The Gemara therefore leaves the question unresolved. The Ran, in the narrow columns, notes that since the question was not definitively answered — *baya v'lo ipashta* — we adopt the stringent position: *nekitinan l'chumra v'eino meifer ela devarim she'beino l'veina*. The husband cannot perform a blanket annulment of such a vow; his power extends only to its *beino l'veina* dimension.

The Ran, however, adds that some authorities infer from a later statement of Shmuel — which we will encounter shortly — that even without explicit Talmudic resolution, *tashmish* falls within the *inuy nefesh* category according to the *Rabbanan*.

This ambiguity is genuinely striking. The *rishonim* note — in connection with other halachic discussions, such as the question of whether a woman in a dangerous medical situation may use certain forms of birth control — that the *halacha* cannot simply counsel a couple not to have marital relations. Sexual relations are regarded as constitutive of marriage itself. Given that, the notion that a permanent denial of sexual relations might not rise to the level of *inuy nefesh* — while not bathing does — presents an intuitive challenge that the Gemara's inconclusiveness does not fully resolve.

The classification of *inuy nefesh* also raises a related question of method. The Gemara appears to operate with formal, categorical judgments: once a category of deprivation — food, bathing, makeup — is deemed *inuy nefesh*, it applies as a class regardless of individual variation. The *mishnah* does not ask whether a particular woman cares greatly about makeup; it classifies makeup categorically. This formal approach raises questions about scope and duration that the Gemara gestures toward but does not resolve here.

---

## Shmuel's Principle

### Shmuel's Ruling

The Gemara now introduces a statement of Shmuel transmitted in the name of Levi: *kol nedarim ba'al meifer l'ishto* — a husband may annul all of his wife's vows, with one exception. If she declares that a specific individual may not receive benefit from her, the husband cannot annul it, because *she'eino meifer* — such a declaration imposes no deprivation on her; another person's inability to benefit from her is not *inuy nefesh* for her.

### One Source Suffices

Here is Shmuel's *chiddush*: *hana'as Ploni alai meifer* — if she says "I may not receive benefit from Reuven," the husband *can* annul it. This is categorized as *inuy nefesh*. The innovation is that *inuy nefesh* is not assessed by asking: if this vow stands, will she actually be living in an afflicted state? The answer to that question might well be no — there are many other people who can provide her with fruit, assistance, or whatever benefit she has forsworn. Instead, Shmuel holds that the determination depends on whether the *type* of thing being denied is intrinsically a form of *inuy nefesh*. If fruit in general constitutes *inuy nefesh*, then denial of fruit from even a single source is sufficient to invoke the *inuy nefesh* category, and the husband may annul the vow.

This is a significant *chiddush* — and, as the Gemara immediately observes, one that appears to collide directly with our *mishnah*.

### Mishnah's Objection

The *mishnah* states: *peirot medinah zo alai* — if a woman declares that the fruit of a particular country is forbidden to her, *yavi lah mimedinah acheret* — her husband should bring her fruit from a different country, and since she retains access to the same type of item through another source, the vow does not constitute *inuy nefesh*, and the husband cannot annul it. This is a direct challenge to Shmuel's position: the *mishnah* explicitly rules that if another source is available, there is no *inuy nefesh*.

### Difficult Reading Propos…

To salvage Shmuel's position, Rav Yosef — and the Gemara working through this — proposes a forced reading of the *mishnah*. The case, on this reading, is not that she simply forbade herself from a country's fruit; rather, she said: "I may not have the fruit of this country *that you, my husband, bring.*" On this interpretation, she has not really denied herself access to that fruit at all — she can still obtain it through anyone else. Because the deprivation is purely contingent on the husband's role as provider, and she retains full access through any other channel, it falls outside *inuy nefesh* and the husband cannot annul it.

The difficulty with this reading is not merely that it strains the plain meaning of the *mishnah*. It also requires reconciling it with a subsequent case in the same *mishnah*: *peirot Chonvoni ze alai* — if she says that the fruit of a specific storekeeper is forbidden to her, the *mishnah* rules that the husband likewise cannot annul it. The Gemara suggests the same forced reading: she is only denying herself the storekeeper's fruit as conveyed by her husband; anyone else may still bring it to her. This reading is admittedly far from *peshat*.

### Sole Provider Case

The forced reading collapses under the *mishnah*'s own internal evidence. The *mishnah* continues: *lo hayta parnasato ela mimenu* — if the husband's sole source of food provision is this very storekeeper, then *harei ze yafer*, the husband may annul the vow. The reason is that in such a circumstance, she is genuinely denied access to that fruit regardless of any alternative channel.

But if the entire *mishnah* is about vows she made only contingent on the husband being the one who conveys the fruit — then even in the case of the sole-provider storekeeper, her access is not actually blocked: someone other than the husband could simply go to that same storekeeper and bring the fruit to her. Why, then, does the *mishnah* permit annulment in the sole-provider case? The forced reading cannot account for this.

### Mishnah's Plain Reading

The Gemara concludes: *ela mide'seifa delo maisi ba'al* — since the end of the *mishnah* clearly envisions a case where the husband's conveyance is not the operative variable, it follows that the *reisha* likewise is not conditioned on who brings the fruit. She has forbidden the fruit to herself categorically, regardless of the source. *Harei reisha ein yachol lehafer* — the husband cannot annul in the opening case simply because she can always obtain the same fruit elsewhere.

The plain reading of the *mishnah* thus stands as a straightforward rejection of Shmuel's position. The *mishnah* holds that so long as another source exists, the vow does not constitute *inuy nefesh*, and the husband has no power to annul it.

However, Shmuel has a response: *u'matnitin Rabbi Yosi hi* — as Rav Huna established, the entire *mishnah* in this *perek* reflects Rabbi Yosi's view. For Rabbi Yosi, who operates with a narrow definition of *inuy nefesh*, it makes sense that deprivation must be total — from all sources everywhere — before *inuy nefesh* applies. The *Rabbanan*, who operate with a broader category, would hold that even denial from a single source suffices. Shmuel therefore aligns himself with the *Rabbanan* and is undisturbed by the *mishnah*'s apparent contradiction, since that *mishnah* represents Rabbi Yosi's stricter position.

The corollary noted parenthetically by the Gemara — *meifer nedarim she'beino l'veina* — is that even where Shmuel cannot establish full *inuy nefesh*, the *beino l'veina* avenue may yet be available, though the Ran notes this is not a logical continuum: something may simply not bear on the marital relationship at all and therefore not qualify on either ground.

---

## Two Loaves Case

### Two Loaves Setup

The Gemara now presents a new case, transmitted by Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel. A woman takes a vow forbidding herself from two loaves of bread. One is fine white bread — *b'achat nit'aneh*, a genuine deprivation not to be permitted to eat it. The other is bran bread or a stale inferior loaf — *b'achat ein nit'aneh*, something whose loss imposes no meaningful affliction. Half of her single, unified vow falls within *inuy nefesh*; half does not.

It is worth pausing to note the underlying assumption: that even a vow about a single loaf of bread — a narrow scope — is treated categorically as *inuy nefesh* once food of that quality is in the *inuy nefesh* class. The Gemara does not evaluate the magnitude of the deprivation in context; it reasons formally from the category.

### Shmuel's Position

Shmuel rules: *mitoch shehu meifer l'mit'aneh, meifer l'she'eino mit'aneh* — because the husband can annul the portion of the vow that involves genuine *inuy nefesh*, he can annul both portions of the vow. The vow was made as a single, unified utterance; and since the husband holds annulment power over part of it, Shmuel extends that power to the whole.

### Ran's Explanation

The Ran explains the logic carefully. The Gemara will establish later that the husband cannot perform a *hafara* on only *part* of a vow: *hafara* is all-or-nothing. He cannot say "I annul this vow for three days but not the rest," or "I annul it for these fruits but not those." The *pasuk* indicates that his act of *hafara* must operate on the vow as a whole.

Given this constraint, the husband confronts two options: either he has no power at all — because he cannot do a complete *hafara* of a vow over which he only has partial authority — or we must extend his authority to cover the whole vow, precisely because only a complete *hafara* is a valid act of *hafara*. Shmuel adopts the latter position: since the husband is entitled to annul the *inuy nefesh* portion, and since *hafara* can only be executed on the vow in its entirety, we conclude that he is therefore empowered to annul the whole. The Ran articulates this not merely as a consequence of *hutar miktzato hutar kulo* — the principle that once part of a prohibition is dissolved the rest dissolves with it — but as a direct requirement of how *hafara* functions: the act itself must engage the entire vow, and so the husband must be regarded as authorized to perform it completely.

### Beino L'Veina Exception

One might wonder how this all-or-nothing logic squares with the earlier case of *netulah ani min hayehudim*, where the husband annuls only *chelko* — his portion — leaving the prohibition with respect to all other men intact. The Ran explains that *beino l'veina* is categorically different in kind from *inuy nefesh* annulment. When a husband annuls a vow on grounds of *beino l'veina*, he is not undoing the *neder* wholesale; he is exercising an override rooted in the fact that the vow impinges upon *their* relationship. The annulment is inherently relational and partial in nature — it removes the vow's force to the degree that it affects him, while leaving the rest untouched. This is why, for instance, if the couple divorces, the prohibition reasserts itself: the *hafara* never dissolved the underlying *neder*, it only suspended it within the bounds of the marriage. *Beino l'veina* annulment is by its very nature targeted and relational, not a complete removal of the *neder*. A *hafara* grounded in *inuy nefesh*, by contrast, is a substantive abrogation of the *neder* itself — and therefore must be complete.

---

## R. Yochanan's View

### Partial Annulment Only

Rabbi Yochanan — or in one version, Rav Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan — disagrees with Shmuel's position on the two-loaves case. His ruling is *meifer l'mit'aneh v'eino meifer l'she'eino mit'aneh*: the husband annuls only that portion of the vow that constitutes *inuy nefesh*, and the part that is not *inuy nefesh* remains in force. Rabbi Yochanan does not accept the all-or-nothing logic that Shmuel invokes. In his view, the husband's authority is precisely calibrated to his domain: he has complete power over *inuy nefesh* and no power beyond it, so the non-*inuy nefesh* component of the vow stands unaffected.

### Nazirite Case

The Gemara raises an objection against Rabbi Yochanan's position from a *mishnah* concerning *nezirus*. The *mishnah* teaches: if a woman took a vow of *nezirus* and was going around drinking wine and contracting corpse-impurity — thereby violating her *nezirus* — she receives lashes. If, however, her husband annulled the *nezirus* without her knowledge, and she continued drinking wine and contracting impurity thinking she was violating it, she does not receive lashes — because objectively, the *nezirus* had already been dissolved.

The Gemara's challenge focuses on this case. The objection asks: if Rabbi Yochanan is correct that a husband can only annul the *inuy nefesh* portion of a vow, perhaps when the husband annulled the *nezirus* he only annulled the wine prohibition — which is the aspect that causes genuine deprivation, *inuy nefesh* — while leaving intact the prohibition against grape skins and grape pits, and possibly the *tumas meis* prohibition. If so, might she still be liable for violating those remaining prohibitions, even after his annulment?

### Nazirite is Package Deal

Rav Yosef resolves the objection: *ein nezirus l'chatzoim* — there is no such thing as a partial *nezirus*. A *nezirus* is a unified, indivisible package. One cannot be a *nazir* only with respect to wine, or only with respect to *tumas meis*. The obligations of *nezirus* — the prohibition of wine and all grape products, the prohibition of corpse-impurity, and the prohibition of cutting one's hair — constitute an all-or-nothing commitment. Therefore, when the husband annulled his wife's *nezirus* by virtue of his power over the *inuy nefesh* aspect — the wine prohibition — the entire *nezirus* necessarily dissolved, because there is no intermediate state of a partial *nezirus* that could remain.

This is what distinguishes the *nezirus* case from the two-loaves case. In the two-loaves case, it is entirely possible for the vow to stand as to one loaf and be annulled as to the other — there is a coherent residual state. In *nezirus*, no such residual state exists. And because *ein nezirus l'chatzoim*, the husband's annulment of the wine aspect brings the entire edifice down. There is therefore no contradiction with Rabbi Yochanan: his *hafara* works precisely as he describes — it annuls the *inuy nefesh* component — and as a consequence, because of the indivisible nature of *nezirus*, the whole vow dissolves.

### Abaye's Clarification

Abaye accepts Rav Yosef's resolution but sharpens the formulation. Rav Yosef said *ein nezirus l'chatzoim* — there is no half-*nezirus* — which speaks to the qualitative indivisibility of *nezirus*: one cannot be a *nazir* for only some of the prohibited categories. Abaye adds the parallel point about duration: *ein nezirus l'chatzoim bein korban l'chatzi nezirus* — there is no half-*nezirus* in duration either, meaning that if a woman began a *nezirus* of, say, thirty days and her husband annulled it after fifteen days, she cannot bring the *korban* associated with completing a *nezirus*, because a *korban* requires the full term to have been fulfilled. Abaye wished to make explicit that the indivisibility of *nezirus* applies both to its qualitative scope and to its temporal duration.

The broader debate between Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan regarding the two loaves thus remains intact. Shmuel holds that once the husband possesses authority over the *inuy nefesh* component of a unified vow, he must be understood as empowered to annul the whole — because *hafara* is by nature an act on the complete *neder*, and empowering him to act on part necessarily requires empowering him to act on the whole. Rabbi Yochanan holds that the husband's authority is precisely and exclusively coextensive with *inuy nefesh*: he annuls everything within that domain and leaves everything outside it entirely untouched.

---

---

# Nedarim 83

## Annulling Partial Vows

### Rav Yehuda/Shmuel

To situate today's discussion, we begin by recalling the debate introduced earlier on this daf. The gemara had presented the position of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: when a woman takes a vow encompassing two objects — one of which constitutes *inuy nefesh* (self-affliction) and one of which does not — and the husband annuls the vow with respect to the part that is *inuy nefesh*, the entire vow is dissolved. The question was how to understand the mechanism. One approach would invoke the principle of *neder shehufar miktsato hufar kulo* — a vow annulled in part is annulled in its entirety. The Ran, however, frames it somewhat differently: the Torah empowers the husband to annul the whole precisely because, in order to annul the part to which he is entitled, the annulment must necessarily encompass the whole.

### Rabbi Yochanan Debate

Rabbi Yochanan disputes this. In his view, the husband annuls the part that is *inuy nefesh* and that part alone; the remainder of the vow stays intact. The gemara had noted that *devarim shebeino leveinah* — matters pertaining specifically to the dynamics between husband and wife — may operate under a different principle, where the husband annuls his portion while the rest remains. The present debate, however, concerns vows that fall into the category of *inuy nefesh*, and it is there that Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel diverge.

### Nezirus Package

The gemara then challenged Rabbi Yochanan from the case of *nezirus*. When a husband annuls his wife's Nazirite vow, the entire *nezirus* falls away, even though strictly speaking the only element of *nezirus* that qualifies as *inuy nefesh* is the prohibition on wine. The gemara resolved this by invoking the principle of *ein nezirus b'chatzayin* — there is no such thing as a half-Nazirite. *Nezirus* is an indivisible package: one cannot be a *nazir* with respect to some of its components while exempt from others. Therefore, even Rabbi Yochanan would agree that when the wine prohibition is annulled, the entire *nezirus* collapses — not because of the general rule about partial annulment, but because *nezirus* by its nature admits of no partial status.

### Abaye's Korban Clarif.

Abaye sharpens this point further. It is not merely that there is no partial Nazirite status — there is also *ein korban nezirus lachatziyin*: no Nazirite offering can be brought for an incomplete *nezirus*. The practical implication is this: even if a woman observed her *nezirus* faithfully for, say, fifteen days before her husband annulled it, she was fully a *nezirah* throughout that period and would even incur lashes had she willfully violated the *nezirus* with proper warning. Nevertheless, since the thirty-day period was never completed — or whatever term she accepted upon herself — no *korban nezirus* is ever brought. The *korban* attaches only to the completion of the Nazirite term, and without completion there is nothing to which the offering can attach.

A question naturally arises: if a woman accepted *nezirus* for sixty days and her husband annulled it after thirty days — a complete standard term — does she bring the *korban nezirus* then? This is left open; the answer is not clear.

---

## Tamei in Nezirus

### Woman Tamei Baraita

The gemara now introduces a *baraita* to challenge the principle that no *korban* is brought for an incomplete *nezirus*. The case: a woman vowed *nezirus*, became *tamei* in the course of her *nezirus*, separated out a *behemah* for the *asham* that a *nazir* who becomes *tamei* is required to bring, and thereafter her husband annulled her vow. What happens?

It is worth noting the structure of the *korbanos* brought when a *nazir* becomes *tamei*. Three offerings are required: an *olas ha-of*, a *chatas ha-of*, and an animal for the *asham*. The baraita tells us the woman separated out the animal for the *asham* and then the husband annulled. It then states: she brings the *chatas ha-of* but not the *olas ha-of*.

Tosafot flag a striking textual difficulty here: the baraita mentions that she separated out the *behemah* for the *asham* and then says nothing further about it. It does not tell us whether she brings it or what becomes of it. Tosafot leave this as an unresolved question, and there is no obvious answer beyond what they themselves acknowledge. In any event, the focal point for the gemara is the *chatas ha-of*.

### Chatas Ha-Of Question

The gemara presses: if the principle of *ein korban nezirus lachatziyin* is correct and no *korban* is brought for an incomplete *nezirus*, why is this woman bringing a *chatas ha-of* at all? Surely the fact that she is bringing even one of the Nazirite *korbanos* demonstrates that some obligation persists even when the *nezirus* is cut short.

One might think, before getting to the answer, that the *korbanos* associated with *tum'ah* are a categorically distinct matter. A *nazir* who becomes *tamei* brings those offerings in the middle of the Nazirite term, not at its conclusion — their purpose is to restart the *nezirus*, not to mark its completion. Still, one could reason that even if she is no longer a *nezirah* by virtue of the husband's annulment, she had become *tamei* and was obligated in those *korbanos* at the time of her *tum'ah*, and perhaps that obligation persists. So the gemara's challenge has force.

### Not General Rule

The gemara deflects by turning the challenge back on itself: if bringing a *korban* for an incomplete *nezirus* were in fact the rule, the baraita should have simply said that. It should have told us straightforwardly that a woman whose *nezirus* is annulled mid-term brings her standard three *korbanos* — *chatas*, *olah*, and *shelamim*. The fact that the baraita instead presents a narrow, specific case — *tum'ah* in the middle of *nezirus*, with only one of the three *korbanos* brought — is itself the proof. Clearly, the general rule is that a woman whose *nezirus* is terminated before completion brings no standard *korbanos*. This case is exceptional on multiple fronts: it arises specifically because of *tum'ah*, and it involves only the *chatas ha-of* rather than the full complement of offerings.

### Chatas Ha-Of Safek

The gemara then provides the positive account of why the *chatas ha-of* is uniquely suited to this situation. It draws on a principle from an entirely different context. The gemara elsewhere discusses the case of a *yoledes* — a woman who gave birth or suffered a miscarriage — where there is doubt as to whether her circumstances genuinely created *tumas leida*. Was the miscarriage after forty days of conception or before? Such a woman finds herself in a bind: if she is indeed *tamei*, she cannot eat *korbanos* or enter the *Beis Hamikdash* until she brings her *korban leida*, which is a *chatas ha-of*. But if she is not *tamei*, she cannot bring a *chatas* to which she has no genuine obligation. The Torah resolves this through a *mesorah* — a tradition derived from *pesukim* — that she may bring a *chatas ha-of al hasafek*, a *chatas ha-of* in a state of doubt. The blood is sprinkled, the bird is not eaten, and she becomes *tehorah*. This establishes that the *chatas ha-of* is a category of *korban* capable of functioning in inherently ambiguous and indeterminate situations, unlike most *korbanos* which demand a definite, concrete obligation.

The *chatas ha-of* is thus not merely a *korban* for a known *chet*; it is a *korban* designed to address a gray zone — a situation that is *nisht ahin, nisht aher*, neither fully resolved one way nor the other.

### Resolution

With that foundation in place, the resolution becomes clear. This woman — who became *tamei* during her *nezirus* and then had the *nezirus* annulled by her husband — finds herself in precisely such a gray zone. She genuinely did become *tamei* and incurred an obligation in *korbanos* at that time. Yet she is no longer a *nezirah*, so the purpose of those *korbanos* — to restart the *nezirus* — no longer applies. She is thus in an inherently indeterminate state. Conveniently, the *korban* she needs is a *chatas ha-of*, which is the very type of offering the Torah designates for such ambiguous situations. She therefore brings the *chatas ha-of*, not because it represents a general rule that *korbanos* are brought for incomplete *nezirus*, but because the *chatas ha-of* is precisely the instrument for addressing this kind of gray-area obligation.

The Rishonim add a further dimension from another sugya dealing with this same baraita: there is an opinion of Rabbi Shimon that a *nazir* is considered a *chotei* — one who has sinned — because he deprived himself of wine, *shetzi'er atzmo min hayayin*. For this reason as well, there is value in the *chatas ha-of* even once the *nezirus* is no longer in force, as an element of atonement for the very essence of the Nazirite deprivation. The bottom line: the *chatas ha-of* in this case proves nothing about a general obligation to bring *korbanos* for an incomplete *nezirus*. The rule of *ein korban nezirus lachatziyin* stands.

---

## Wine vs. Tumah

### Restate Baraita

The gemara now returns to the central debate — whether a husband can selectively annul only the *inuy nefesh* portion of a vow — and brings the same baraita again: a woman vowed *nezirus*, became *tamei*, and the husband then annulled. She brings the *chatas ha-of* and not the *olas ha-of*.

### Hypothetical Split

The gemara now poses a pointed question. Recall that Rabbi Yochanan's position is that the husband annuls only the *inuy nefesh* portion of a vow and not the rest. Applied to *nezirus*: the *inuy nefesh* of *nezirus* is the wine prohibition. The prohibition against becoming *tamei l'meis* — the prohibition on contracting corpse-impurity — is not obviously *inuy nefesh*. So suppose the husband's *hafarah* annulled only the wine element of the *nezirus*. What happens to the *tum'ah* element?

If the annulment left intact the prohibition against becoming *tamei*, then she is still a *nezirah* with respect to *tum'ah*. And if that is so, then the *korban* she must bring upon becoming *tamei* is not merely the limited *chatas ha-of* of a gray zone — it is the full complement of *korbanos* appropriate to a *nazir* who became *tamei* and must restart the *nezirus*, because she still has an active *nezirus* to restart (at least regarding *tum'ah*). The fact that the baraita says she brings only the *chatas ha-of* and not the *olas ha-of* would then be difficult to explain: why not the full set of *korbanos* for a *nazir* who became *tamei*?

The Ran explains the *hava amina* underlying this challenge. It is known that there exists a form of *nezirus* called *Nazir Shimshon* — modeled on Samson, who avoided cutting his hair and abstaining from wine but regularly contracted *tumas meis* in the course of killing Philistines. The gemara derives from this that the prohibition on *tumas meis* is in principle separable from the other elements of *nezirus*. If so, one might entertain the idea — at least as a *hava amina* — that the husband's annulment of the wine prohibition left in place a *nezirus* limited to the *tumas meis* prohibition, and that she therefore has an ongoing *nezirus* to complete and a full *korban tamei nazir* to bring.

The Ran notes that this is a difficult position; we have never before heard of a regular *nezirus* that covers only *tumas meis* without wine and hair. The only exception is *Nazir Shimshon*, which is explicitly labeled as such. Nevertheless, the gemara entertains it for the sake of the answer.

### Tumah = Inuy Nefesh

The gemara responds: *tumas meis* is also *inuy nefesh*. Not being permitted to become *tamei l'meis* — not being able to attend funerals, visit a *beis kvoros*, go to a *beis avel* — is itself a form of self-denial. The proof is from the verse *v'hachai yiten el libo* — the living shall take it to heart. The baraita expounds in the name of Rabbi Meir: one who eulogizes others will be eulogized when he dies; one who weeps for others will be wept over; one who buries others will be buried. The message is that participating in communal mourning and burial is a fundamental social responsibility and act of belonging. Being barred from that — being unable to go to a funeral, to enter a *beis kvoros*, to fulfill one's obligations as a member of the community — is a genuine *inuy nefesh*.

This carries a significant practical implication beyond the Nazirite context. If a woman were to vow that she will not become *tamei* or visit a cemetery or attend a funeral, the husband would be able to annul that vow, since it qualifies as *inuy nefesh*.

### Package Deal Affirmed

With *tumas meis* established as *inuy nefesh*, both the wine prohibition and the *tum'ah* prohibition fall within the domain of *inuy nefesh*. When the husband's *hafarah* operates on the *nezirus*, it annuls the entire *nezirus* at once — wine and *tum'ah* together. Since the *nezirus* is entirely terminated, there is no ongoing Nazirite status of any kind, and therefore no obligation to bring the standard *korbanos* of a *nazir* who became *tamei*. The only *korban* that persists is the *chatas ha-of*, for the reasons articulated above. The principle that *nezirus* is an indivisible package is thus reaffirmed: the husband cannot annul only the wine element and leave the *tum'ah* element standing. The entire *nezirus* falls away at once.

The Ran notes that even if the gemara could have relied solely on the package-deal principle — *ein nezirus b'chatzayin* — to explain why the husband cannot annul only one element, by adding the point that *tumas meis* is itself *inuy nefesh* the gemara achieves a *nafka mina*: it establishes that a standalone vow against contracting *tumas meis* or attending funerals is annullable on its own merits, not merely as a consequence of the indivisibility of *nezirus*.

The debate between Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan — whether the husband who annuls the *inuy nefesh* portion of a mixed vow thereby annuls the whole — thus remains unresolved by the Nazirite case, precisely because in *nezirus* every element qualifies as *inuy nefesh* and the entire structure collapses together.

---

## Benefit from All

### Mishnah Stated

The gemara moves to the next mishnah. A woman declares *konam she-ani nehenis l'vriyos* — "let it be *konam* that I receive benefit from people," meaning she forbids herself all benefit from other human beings. The mishnah rules: the husband cannot annul this vow. This is striking. If any vow is *inuy nefesh*, one would think it is this one — forbidding oneself benefit from all of humanity. Why can he not annul it?

The answer, which the gemara will develop, is that when a woman says "all people," she implicitly excludes her husband. The husband can still provide for her, sustain her, and serve as her conduit to the world. Since she is not wholly cut off — her husband remains available as a source of support — it is not considered *inuy nefesh* at the level that would trigger the husband's right of annulment. This is admittedly a counterintuitive result, and the gemara will need to work through several layers of analysis to make it coherent.

It should also be borne in mind that the entire chapter follows the position of Rabbi Yossi, who maintains a particularly narrow definition of *inuy nefesh*. That narrowness will inform the answers that follow.

### Ran's Logic

The Ran anticipates an obvious difficulty. Earlier in the tractate there is a case involving a *chanvani* — a storekeeper. If a woman vows not to benefit from a particular storekeeper, and that storekeeper is the only one who will sell to her household, the husband can annul the vow, because sealing off that single source of supply constitutes *inuy nefesh*. But then: in the present case the woman has sealed off the entire world of people. Why is that not *inuy nefesh*, if blocking one storekeeper is?

The Ran resolves this with a precise distinction. In the storekeeper case, the woman vowed not to benefit from *the fruit of that storekeeper*. This is a prohibition on the object — those specific goods. Even if her husband goes and purchases the fruit from that storekeeper and brings it home to her, she is still receiving the fruit of that storekeeper; the husband's role as intermediary does not change the identity of the forbidden object. If that store is the only available source of food, the vow completely seals off all food, regardless of who physically retrieves it.

### Intermediary Role

In the present case, however, the woman did not say "the objects of all people are forbidden to me." She said she will not receive *hana'ah* — benefit — from people. *Hana'ah* here means direct benefit. The prohibition attaches to the act of direct receipt, not to the objects themselves. This creates a crucial aperture: the husband can go to any person in the world, receive benefit from them on his own account, and then convey it to her. When she receives it from his hand, she is receiving benefit from her husband, not from those other people. Since the objects themselves are not the forbidden item — only the direct interaction is — and since the husband can serve as an intermediary, she retains access to the entire world's resources through him. Therefore, this does not rise to the level of *inuy nefesh* under Rabbi Yossi's stringent standard.

### Gemara Question

The mishnah adds that she may still benefit from *leket*, *shichachah*, and *pe'ah* — the agricultural gifts left for the poor — since these have been rendered *hefker* (ownerless) by their original owners. Collecting them is not receiving benefit from a person; it is taking from what has become ownerless. This further moderates her situation.

The mishnah then addresses a related case: if a woman vows that *Kohanim u'Levi'im* shall not benefit from her, they may take *trumah u'ma'aser* against her will, because the obligation to give those gifts is not in her control — it is an entitlement of the *Kohanim* and *Levi'im* independent of her will. If she specifies *these particular Kohanim and Levi'im*, she may direct her *trumah u'ma'aser* to others.

The gemara then presses the logic of the mishnah. If the husband cannot annul because she is still being sustained by him — *efshar d'mitazna midilei* — this implies *michlal d'ba'al lav b'chlal briyot hu*: the husband is not included in the category of *briyot* when she makes this vow. The gemara then reads the end of the mishnah — *v'yachola l'ehanot b'leket shikchah u'pe'ah* — and observes that if she is still being sustained by the husband, she is not poor, and would not be entitled to collect *leket shikchah u'pe'ah* under ordinary agricultural law. The mention of *leket shikchah u'pe'ah* thus implies she is not being supported by the husband, which seems to contradict the premise that the husband is excluded from her vow.

---

## Benefit from All (II)

### Three Positions

The gemara presents three distinct positions in response to this difficulty. Each takes a different stance on whether the husband is included within the term *briyot* when a woman declares *konam she-ani nehenis l'vriyos*, and each reads the mishnah accordingly.

---

## Ulla: Husband Excluded

### Ulla Position

Ulla answers: the husband is fundamentally not included in the category of *briyot* when she says "all people." When a woman uses this formulation, she means all other people — not her husband, who stands in an entirely different relationship to her. It is therefore not *inuy nefesh*, because her husband can still provide for her directly.

### Leket Support

The mention of *leket shikchah u'pe'ah* in the mishnah, according to Ulla, is a supplementary point: even setting aside the husband's support, she has an additional avenue — the ownerless agricultural gifts. The mishnah is telling us both reasons she is not sealed off from the world, and the primary reason the husband cannot annul is the husband's own continued availability.

---

## Rava: Hefker Solves It

### Rava Position

Rava disagrees. In his view, the husband is included within *briyot* — she has genuinely forbidden herself benefit from everyone, including him. The reason the husband cannot annul is not that she can still receive from him, but solely that she can still be provided for from *leket shikchah u'pe'ah*, which is *hefker* and therefore not benefit from any person. Under Rabbi Yossi's exceedingly narrow conception of *inuy nefesh*, the mere availability of ownerless food is sufficient to prevent this from rising to the level of *inuy nefesh* that would empower the husband to annul.

### Ran Challenges

The Ran finds this position deeply difficult. The very reason the *chanvani* case constitutes *inuy nefesh* — even according to Rabbi Yossi — is that sealing off a primary food source is real deprivation. But in the *chanvani* case, the woman could in principle collect *leket shikchah u'pe'ah*. Why didn't Rabbi Yossi say there too that it is not *inuy nefesh* because she can still get food from *hefker*?

### Seasonal Leket

The Ran proposes a resolution that is itself startling: perhaps the *chanvani* case is set in winter, when *leket shikchah u'pe'ah* is not available because there is no harvest. In summer, when gleaning is possible, even the *chanvani* case might not constitute *inuy nefesh* under Rava's reading of Rabbi Yossi. This is an extraordinarily narrow reading of *inuy nefesh*, but it follows from Rava's position.

---

## Rav Nachman: Conditional

### Rav Nachman Position

Rav Nachman returns to the position that the husband is not included in *briyot* — when she says "all people" she implicitly means everyone other than him. The reason: the husband occupies a categorically different position relative to her while they are married, and it is natural to assume that the vow, in its ordinary meaning, did not encompass him.

### Divorce Scenario

Where Rav Nachman diverges from Ulla becomes clear in how he reads the mishnah's mention of *leket shikchah u'pe'ah*. Rav Nachman reads the mishnah as saying: *if she is divorced* — *nitgarshah* — then she is left with *leket shikchah u'pe'ah*. Once she is no longer married, the husband reverts to the *briyot* category, and she can no longer benefit even from him. At that point, her only recourse is the ownerless agricultural gifts. This reading makes the *leket shikchah u'pe'ah* clause make sense: it describes her situation post-divorce, when the "exception" for the husband no longer operates.

The difference between Ulla and Rav Nachman is thus: according to Ulla, the husband is categorically and permanently outside the scope of the vow — even after divorce, presumably, the vow never encompassed him. According to Rav Nachman, the husband was always in principle included in *briyot*, but the marital relationship created a temporary inapplicability. Once that relationship ends, he falls back into the category to which he naturally belongs, and the vow operates against him as well.

### Status Change Question

This leads the Ran into an extended discussion of a broader question: what happens when the circumstances relevant to a vow change during its duration? The gemara elsewhere discussed a case where a woman vowed not to benefit from *yordei hayam* — sailors — and someone's status as a sailor changed after the vow was taken. Does the vow's scope reassess itself as circumstances change?

According to Rav Nachman's reading, it seems we do reassess: the husband begins as effectively excluded from the vow and then, upon divorce, becomes included. The Ran notes, however, that this may be a special case. The husband was never fundamentally outside the vow — he was always within the category of *briyot* in principle; the marriage simply created an override. When the marriage ends, he does not switch categories; he returns to the category he was always in. This is different from the *yordei hayam* case, where the question is about a person genuinely moving from one category to another. Here the husband's fundamental category never changed — only the practical applicability of the vow shifted with the marital status.

---

## Nituah Challenge

### Nituah Mishnah

Rava now challenges Rav Nachman with a proof from another mishnah. That mishnah concerns a woman who declares that she is *netuah* — removed, meaning she forbids herself sexual pleasure from all people. This is a vow of sexual estrangement that encompasses the entire world.

### Rava's Proof

Rava argues: if the husband were truly not included in the category of *briyot* when a woman says "all people," then this vow would not touch him at all, and it would already be *inuy nefesh* by virtue of excluding everyone else. There would be no need for any further action on the husband's part. Yet the mishnah states explicitly that the husband annuls his portion — *yafer chelko* — and then has conjugal relations with her. The necessity of the husband's annulment demonstrates that he was included in the vow to begin with.

### Husband Annuls Share

The ruling is that the husband annuls the part of the vow that pertains to him, and she remains forbidden to all other men. This confirms that he was included in the original vow — otherwise, there would be nothing for him to annul.

### Context Determines

The gemara resolves the apparent contradiction between this case and the *konam she-ani nehenis l'vriyos* case as follows: *shani hacha demuchach miltha* — here the matter speaks for itself. In the *nituah* case, the woman says she is forbidden sexual pleasure from *Yehudim* — from all Jews. But she already has no permitted sexual relationship with anyone other than her husband. If the vow means "everybody except my husband," it is entirely meaningless: she already cannot have relations with anyone else. A vow that says nothing is not a vow. Therefore, in this context, the husband must be included — otherwise the declaration has no content at all.

### Meaningfulness Test

The governing principle that emerges is this: whether the husband is included in a formulation of "all people" depends on whether the vow has meaningful content without him. In the *nituah* case, including only the rest of the world would render the vow pointless — the husband must be included for it to say anything at all. In the *konam she-ani nehenis l'vriyos* case, by contrast, a vow not to benefit from all other people is entirely meaningful on its own, even without the husband. In such a case, we read the vow according to its natural implication: "all people other than you," and the husband is not within its scope.

---

---

# Nedarim 85

## Mishnah & Annulment

### Benefit Forbidden

The *mishnah* with which we open Daf 85 is one we have encountered before, still situated within the broader discussion of which *nedarim* a husband may annul on behalf of his wife — specifically, what qualifies as *d'varim shebeino l'veina* (matters between them) or *d'varim shel inui nefesh* (matters of self-denial). The case the *mishnah* presents is the following: a woman declares "*konam she'ani osa al pi abba, v'al pi avicha, v'al pi achi, v'al pi achicha*" — that anything she produces shall be forbidden in benefit to her father, her husband's father, her brother, or her husband's brother.

### Tanna Kamma

The *Tanna Kamma* rules that the husband cannot annul this *neder*, and on two distinct grounds. First, it does not qualify as *inui nefesh*, since she is not forbidding any pleasure to herself. Second, it does not qualify as *d'varim shebeino l'veina*: although the practical consequences may certainly annoy the husband — the couple cannot host her father or his brother for a meal — the *neder* itself does not directly forbid anything as between the two of them. The further ruling of the *mishnah* is that if she were instead to say "*she'ani osa al picha*" — what I produce is forbidden to you, the husband — he does not need to annul even that, because the husband already holds a lien on his wife's *ma'aseh yadayim* (the products of her labor). Since it is not fully hers to forbid, the *neder* cannot effectively take hold on something that is already his.

### Rabbi Akiva

*Rabbi Akiva* disagrees: "*yafer, shema ta'adif alav yoter min hara'uy lo*" — he should annul the *neder*, lest she produce more than she is strictly obligated to provide. Recall the *mishnah* in *Ketubot* that enumerates the minimum labor a wife is required to perform. If she exceeds that minimum, the surplus — the *hadafah* — is something the husband has no strict legal entitlement to, even if in practice he would benefit from it. The *neder* would therefore take effect on that excess. *Rabbi Akiva* thus provides two reasons for annulment: first, it qualifies as *d'varim shebeino l'veina*; and second, he risks transgressing inadvertently if he benefits from her extra production.

### Rabbi Yochanan

*Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri* takes a different position: "*yafer, shema yigarshena v'tei'asur alav*" — he should annul it lest he divorce her and she become forbidden to him. His concern is not the *hadafah* at all; he may well accept that the husband is entitled to her extra production. His worry is forward-looking: right now the *neder* does not take effect because the husband holds a lien on her *ma'aseh yadayim*. But if they were to divorce, that lien dissolves, the labor returns to her ownership, and the *neder* — held in a kind of abeyance — would then kick in and take effect. The consequence would be that they could not remarry, since it would be untenable to live together with him unable to benefit from her work. Better, therefore, to annul it now and remove it entirely, rather than leave it suspended.

This position of *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri* implicitly establishes something important: an annulment grounded in *d'varim shebeino l'veina* remains effective even after divorce, at least for the period in which she is not yet remarried. If the annulment would evaporate upon divorce, the entire concern of *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri* would be pointless — for the annulment would need to be operative precisely in that post-divorce moment.

What the *Gemara* is now going to focus on, however, is a more fundamental question: before we even get to the husband's annulment, how does this *neder* manage to remain in abeyance at all? If her *ma'aseh yadayim* are not hers at the time she makes the vow, should the *neder* not be null and void on the spot? Why is it not simply extinguished the moment it is uttered?

## Shmuel & Ownership

### Shmuel's Ruling

"*Amar Shmuel, halacha k'Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri*" — Shmuel rules in accordance with *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri*, affirming both that the annulment is effective in the post-divorce period and that we must be concerned about what happens if they divorce, even though the *neder* has not taken effect at the time of its utterance.

The *Gemara* immediately draws a comparison to *hekdesh*: "*l'meimra d'kasavar Shmuel adam makdish davar shelo ba l'olam?*" — is Shmuel thereby implying that a person can sanctify something that does not yet exist? The parallel is direct: when she declares her *ma'aseh yadayim konam*, those products are not yet hers — they belong to the husband by right. Yet *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri* holds that the *neder* will take effect once she reclaims them upon divorce, just as if someone were to declare an animal he does not yet own as *hekdesh*, expecting it to take effect once he acquires it.

### Hekdesh Challenge

But this creates a contradiction, for the *Gemara* cites a *baraita*: "*hamakdish ma'asei yedei ishto, harei zu osa v'ocheles*" — if a husband himself sanctifies his wife's labor as *hekdesh*, she may continue working and consuming the proceeds without concern. The reason: at minimum in one reading of the case, the husband is not providing her food, and therefore he holds no entitlement to her *ma'aseh yadayim*. Since his rights to her labor depend on his maintenance of her, absent that maintenance his *hekdesh* cannot take hold on something he does not own. She also has the recourse of declaring "*eini nizonis v'eini osa*" — I will not be supported by you and I will not work for you — thereby freeing herself from the arrangement and leaving him with no claim to her labor.

The *baraita* continues with the *mosar* — the surplus beyond her basic obligation. Here, curiously, the text seems to assume the husband *is* entitled to it, with *Rabbi Meir* declaring it *hekdesh* and *Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar* declaring it *chullin*, non-sanctified. The underlying dispute, as the *Gemara* in *Ketubot* works out through a rather forced *ukimta*, appears to concern whether the husband's *hekdesh* can take effect on something not yet produced — a *davar shelo ba le'olam*. *Rabbi Meir* holds it can; *Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar* holds it cannot.

"*V'amar Shmuel halacha k'Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar*" — and Shmuel rules like *Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar*: one cannot sanctify a *davar shelo ba le'olam*. This is striking. In one place Shmuel rules like *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri*, apparently validating a *neder* on something not yet in the woman's possession, even potentially years in the future. In another, he rules like *Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar*, explicitly rejecting the capacity to make *hekdesh* on something not yet existing. How are these two rulings consistent?

One might attempt to resolve this by reading Shmuel's ruling in favor of *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri* narrowly — perhaps he was only endorsing *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri*'s dismissal of *Rabbi Akiva*'s concern about the *hadafah*, affirming that the husband is entitled to the surplus as well and that there is therefore no danger of inadvertent transgression. But the *Gemara* rejects this reading: if that were all Shmuel intended, he should have simply ruled like the *Tanna Kamma* — who says the same thing — or stated explicitly that the law does not follow *Rabbi Akiva* regarding the *hadafah*. Saying "the law follows *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri*" plainly implies endorsement of that opinion's central and distinctive claim: that the husband must annul lest the *neder* take effect upon divorce. And that claim presupposes that such a *neder* can remain in abeyance and later take effect — which looks very much like sanctifying a *davar shelo ba le'olam*.

### Konamos Different

*Rav Yosef* offers a resolution that will be familiar from an earlier *sugya*: "*shani konamos*" — vows expressed through the *konam* formula are different. The principle he invokes is that a person can make another's fruit forbidden to himself, even without owning it. Since *nedarim* can operate on objects one does not own — making them forbidden *to oneself* — they can also apply to things that do not yet exist. This is in contrast to *hekdesh*, where the act of sanctification is fundamentally one of ownership transfer, which requires that one actually possess the object being transferred.

## Hands as Entity

### Abaye Challenge

*Abaye* presses back on *Rav Yosef*'s solution with precision: "*bishlama adam oser peiros chaveiro alav* — granted, I can make your fruit forbidden to me, *sheharei adam oser peirosav al chaveiro* — because you can also make your own fruit forbidden to someone else." The logic requires that at least one of two relationships hold: either the person making the *neder* controls the object (forbidding his own fruit to others), or he controls himself (forbidding himself from another's fruit). But there must be a genuine hook somewhere.

What the woman is attempting, however, is something different: she is trying to make her *ma'aseh yadayim* — which (a) does not yet exist, and (b) she will not be entitled to until some indefinite future point if and when she is divorced — forbidden *to her husband*. That is doubly problematic. She neither controls the object (it is not yet produced and belongs to the husband by lien) nor is she making it forbidden to herself. The rule that *nedarim* work on things one doesn't own applies only when the one making the *neder* is making it forbidden to himself. But forbidding something to another person — "*eino oser peiros chaveiro al chaveiro*" — that she cannot do. So we are back to the fundamental question: how does *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri*'s position work at all?

### Physical Hands

The *Gemara* answers: "*ela amar Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua b'omeres yikdeshu yadai l'oseihem*" — the resolution lies in the formulation of the vow itself. When the woman declares her hands forbidden, she is not making a vow about an abstract future object that does not exist. She is making a vow about her hands — the physical, present, tangible hands — declaring them forbidden for what they produce, *l'ma'aseihem*. The hands are here, in the world, right now. Whatever the precise phrasing — and the *Gemara* notes that this phrase may have originated in the context of actual *hekdesh* sanctification, where *l'oseihem* could refer to the Creator, but is here being repurposed or applied by analogy — the operative point is "*yadai isneihu b'olam*": the hands exist in the world.

This answer addresses one dimension of the *davar shelo ba le'olam* problem — that the product has not yet been produced. By re-framing the object of the *neder* as the hands themselves rather than their future output, the *Gemara* resolves the question of non-existence. But the second dimension of the problem immediately reasserts itself: "*meshubada yadehah l'ba'al*" — her hands are subject to the husband's lien. If the *neder* is to take effect only *lich'she-tisgaresh*, upon divorce, we are once again dealing with a future contingency that she does not presently control. How, given Shmuel's position that one cannot sanctify a *davar shelo ba le'olam*, does this work?

## Analogies

### Field Analogy

*Rabbi Ila* attempts to demonstrate through analogy that the concept should be intuitively workable. He envisions someone saying to a friend: "*sadeh zu she-ani mocher lach, lech-she-ekachena mimmeka takdish*" — "this field I am about to sell you, when I buy it back from you I will sanctify it." *Rabbi Ila* assumes that this pre-sanctification would indeed take effect at the moment of repurchase. The intuitive basis is that at the time of the declaration, the field is fully in the owner's control; he could sanctify it right now if he wished. He is therefore performing a genuine act of sanctification in the present, with the effect deferred to the moment the field returns to his control after the intervening sale.

### Yirmiyah Challenge

*Rabbi Yirmiyah* challenges this analogy sharply: "*mi dami?*" — how can you compare the two cases? In the field case, at the moment the declaration is made, the field is entirely in the owner's control — "*hashta be-yadeih*" — and he could sanctify it immediately if he chose. But is a married woman similarly positioned with respect to her *ma'aseh yadayim*? She is not. The moment she is married, she no longer has the capacity to freely sanctify her labor. The more apt analogy, *Rabbi Yirmiyah* argues, would be: "*sadeh zu she-macharti lach, lech-she-ekachena mimmeka takdish*" — "this field I have already sold you, when I buy it back it will be sanctified." But this formulation exposes the problem rather than solving it: if you have already sold the field, you cannot now sanctify it. The past ownership is irrelevant; what matters is the present, and right now you have no rights to it. The same is true for the woman.

### Collateral Analogy

*Rav Pappa* takes a different approach, arguing that *Rabbi Yirmiyah*'s counter-analogy is too extreme in the other direction. When one sells a field outright, "*pesika miltayhu*" — the matter is entirely settled, the field is completely out of the seller's hands. But the woman's situation is not like that. The husband has a lien on her *ma'aseh yadayim*, but it is not the case that her hands have been fully alienated from her. She retains title; it is just that the husband's lien encumbers all benefits flowing from that title. A better analogy, *Rav Pappa* proposes, is: "*sadeh zu she-mashkanti lach, lech-she-efdenah mimmeka takdish*" — "this field that I have given you as collateral, when I redeem it from you it will be sanctified." In this case the field has not been sold; the owner retains title, but the holder of the collateral is entitled to all its produce. This maps neatly onto the wife's situation: she retains title to her hands, but the husband, by virtue of the marital arrangement, is entitled to all their productive output. *Rav Pappa* assumes intuitively that since title remains with the owner, one has sufficient grounds to make a declaration today that will take effect upon redemption.

### Control Objection

*Rav Sheshet bar Rav Idi* objects: "*mi dami? sadeh beyado l'fdotah*" — the field analogy still fails because in the collateral case, it is in the owner's power to redeem the field. If he gathers enough money, he can pay off the lender and reclaim the field. The decision to redeem is his. But "*ishah beyadah l'garesh?*" — is it in the woman's power to bring about a divorce? It is not. The husband decides whether to divorce her. She cannot compel the situation. Since she is not in a position to reclaim her *ma'aseh yadayim* through her own action, how can her present declaration have any operative force?

*Rav Sheshet* then attempts a refined analogy: a field given as collateral for a period of ten years, during which redemption is contractually prohibited. If the owner declares "*lichi afdena mimcha titkadesh*" — "when I do redeem it after the ten years it will be sanctified" — that should work, since after the ten-year period has elapsed the right to redemption automatically comes into effect. At least there is a fixed endpoint. But this only sharpens the problem with the woman's case.

### No End-Point

*Rav Ashi* presses further: "*hatam kayitz*" — in the field case, there is a defined terminus. After ten years, the period of encumbrance ends by its own terms. But "*ishah mi it lah kaitza?*" — by the woman, there is no fixed end-point at all. The marriage could last indefinitely. There is no moment that is structurally guaranteed to arrive at which she will regain her *ma'aseh yadayim*. If the woman lacks the capacity to redeem her labor and there is no fixed point at which the situation must resolve in her favor, what possible basis does she have for making a declaration today that will take effect in that indeterminate future?

## Kedushat Haguf

### Identity Transform

Having exhausted the analogies, *Rav Ashi* now provides the genuine resolution: "*shani konamos, d'hachi kedushat haguf dami*" — *konamos* are different, because they operate like *kedushat haguf*.

To understand this, one must distinguish between two modes of sanctification. *Kedushat damim* — sanctification of monetary value — is what occurs when one donates a field or animal to *bedek habayit*, Temple maintenance. The object is not fundamentally transformed; it simply changes ownership, in effect entering *hekdesh*'s account, to be sold and converted into funds. Because this is a transaction in the domain of ownership, all the standard rules governing ownership apply: one can only sanctify what one owns, liens can block the transfer, and so forth.

*Kedushat haguf* — sanctification of the body or substance of the object — is categorically different. When one consecrates an animal as a *korban*, its very identity is transformed. It is no longer merely a cow that belongs to *hekdesh*; it has become an *olah*, a sacrifice. The *kedushah* has redefined what it is, not merely who holds title to it. Because the sanctification is operating on the plane of identity rather than ownership, the ordinary rules of ownership and lien do not apply in the same way.

The *Gemara* invokes the principle stated by Rava: "*hekdesh chametz veshichrur mafki'a midei shi'abud*" — sanctification, *chametz*, and the freeing of a slave override existing liens. A *konam*, *Rav Ashi* argues, functions like *kedushat haguf* — it transforms the identity of the object rather than simply transferring its ownership. And because the woman retains title to her hands even though the husband holds a lien on their output, she has just enough of a foothold to invoke this identity-transforming power. The husband's monetary lien cannot block a process that is not operating in the monetary domain of ownership.

### Slave Example

The case of the slave provides the most vivid illustration. Suppose a creditor holds a lien on a slave owned by his debtor. If the debtor were to attempt to sell that slave to a third party, the creditor could intervene: the lien encumbers the slave, the debtor lacks the freedom to transfer ownership against the creditor's interest. But if the debtor frees the slave, the result is different. Freeing a slave is not a transfer of ownership from one party to another — it is a transformation of the slave's fundamental status. He is no longer a slave; he is now a free man. The creditor cannot assert that his monetary lien gives him rights over a free person. The process of changing the slave's status operates on a different plane from the monetary arrangements, and because the owner still retains title despite the lien, the transformation takes effect. The creditor may still be owed money, and in principle he retains a claim, but he may well lose the practical ability to enforce it through that particular asset.

### Hekdesh Chametz

The same logic applies when an encumbered animal is consecrated as a *korban*. The creditor cannot interpose his monetary lien to prevent the animal from achieving its new identity as a sacrifice. And similarly with *chametz*: if someone failed to destroy his *chametz* before *Pesach* and the *chametz* is now *assur behana'ah*, a non-Jewish creditor operating within the halachic framework cannot claim his lien on the *chametz* remains actionable, because the *chametz*'s identity has fundamentally changed. Its transformation into something forbidden overrides prior monetary claims.

In each of these cases, the key feature is that the one effecting the transformation retains some form of title even if a lien encumbers the object's use. That residual title is sufficient to activate the identity-transforming power, and once activated, monetary liens fall away as irrelevant.

Applied to the *mishnah*: the woman's declaration of *konam* on her hands is, by the mechanism *Rav Ashi* describes, not merely a declaration of ownership-based prohibition but an invocation of *kedushat haguf*-like power through the *konam* formula. Since she retains title to her hands even during the marriage — it is only the *benefit* of her labor that the husband has a lien on — that title is sufficient for the *konam* to take hold and transform their status. The husband's lien, being a monetary arrangement, cannot block a process of identity transformation.

## When Does It Work?

### Divorce Question

This resolution, however, immediately generates a new difficulty. The *Gemara* asks: "*ee hachi, lama lee shema yigarshena?*" — if *konamos* carry this identity-transforming power that can override liens, why does *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri* frame his entire concern around the scenario of divorce?
