If the *konam* works by *kedushat haguf* and thereby mafki'a the husband's lien, it should take effect right now, not only upon divorce.

The *Gemara* responds by emending the reading of *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri*: "*tani ve'od shema yigarshena*" — read the text as saying "and furthermore, lest he divorce her," meaning that the *konam* does take effect immediately, and the concern about divorce is an additional consideration layered on top, not the sole or primary mechanism. The *Ran* grapples with this interpretation, acknowledging that it sits somewhat uneasily in context. For if one accepts that the *konam* takes effect right now — which *Rav Ashi*'s principle would support — then the *Tanna Kamma* and *Rabbi Akiva* simply do not accept that the *konam* has this power. The *Tanna Kamma*, in particular, likely holds that while *kedushat haguf* does *mafki'a midei shi'abud* in cases of actual *korban*, *hekdesh*, or *shichrur*, a mere *neder* — even one formulated as a *konam* — does not carry that same transformative capacity, and therefore the husband's lien blocks it entirely.

*Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri*'s response, as rendered after the *Gemara*'s emendation, is that the *konam* does work now by virtue of this principle, and *uve'od* — and even if one does not accept the full philosophical argument that it takes effect immediately — one should at the very least be concerned that it will become operative upon divorce. The circularity of that position is not lost on the *Gemara*: if one rejects the underlying principle, one would presumably reject the post-divorce concern as well, since both rest on the same foundation. How the *Ran* resolves this is its own discussion, but it is a notably striking way for the *sugya* to conclude — with the logical tension between the two positions left in some degree of productive suspension.

---

---

# Nedarim 86

## Specificity in Annulment

### Mistaken Identity Cases

The *mishnah* on 86b continues the discussion of a husband's power of *hafarah*, shifting focus from the content of vows — what constitutes *inuy nefesh* or *devarim shebeino l'veina* — to the mechanics of the act of annulment itself. The *mishnah* presents a series of cases in which a husband attempted to annul or affirm a vow under some form of mistaken identity or misclassification. *Nedar ishto vesavar shenadar bito* — his wife took a vow but he thought it was his daughter, or *nedar bito vesavar shenadar ishto* — his daughter took a vow but he thought it was his wife. *Nadra benazir vesavar shenadra bekorban* — she vowed to be a *nazir* but he thought she used *korban* language, or the reverse. *Nadra mite'einim vesavar shenadra min ha'anavim* — she vowed not to eat figs but he thought the vow was about grapes, or vice versa.

In each case, the husband was mistaken either about the identity of the woman whose vow he was acting upon, the subject matter of the vow, or the type of the vow. The *mishnah* rules: *harei zeh yachzor veyafer* — he must go back and annul properly if he wants the annulment to take effect.

### Three Requirements

The principle emerging from the *mishnah* is that for an act of *hafarah* — and as the *gemara* will clarify, *kiyum* as well — to be valid, the husband must know for whom he is acting, what object the vow concerns, and what type of vow it is. The *mishnah* is not primarily concerned with the subjective reasons a husband might have for preferring to annul one vow over another, though one could argue that the reason he might annul a *nazir* vow differs from his reason for annulling a *korban* vow, and similarly that what he wishes to annul for his wife may differ from what he wishes to annul for his daughter. The *mishnah* treats these as formal requirements of knowledge rather than merely motivational ones.

### Timing from Hearing

One might ask whether a mistaken annulment resets the clock of *beyom shamo* — the requirement that the husband act on the day he hears the vow. The answer appears to be no. Since in all these cases the husband did know he had the power to annul and did know he was dealing with a *neder* he could address, the original time period is not reset. The clock runs from the day he actually heard the vow. The *mishnah* does not treat this category of error as analogous to cases — discussed in upcoming *mishnayot* — where the husband did not realize he had the power to annul or did not recognize the vow as one he could address.

### Mode of Hearing

One question that arises is how a husband could mistake his wife for his daughter or vice versa. The simplest reading is that he heard from behind a door and confused their voices. The *Ran*, however, writes that *she'amru lo shebito nadra umitoch kach hefer o kiyem* — it was reported to him incorrectly, and on the basis of that report he annulled or affirmed. This is somewhat puzzling, since an earlier discussion established that the husband must hear the vow personally, which was the basis for ruling that he cannot appoint a *shaliach* to hear on his behalf. How the *Ran*'s formulation fits that requirement is a question that deserves further attention.

### Otah Analysis

The *gemara* takes up the *mishnah* with the observation: *l'memra d'otah davka* — the word *otah* ("her") in the relevant verse is specific. He must know precisely who the woman is whose vow he is annulling.

### Knowing the Vow

The *Rosh* here explains: *dichtiv v'ini otah d'mashma she-makkir ha-ishah ha-noderes* — the word *otah* implies recognition of the woman who made the vow, *umashma nami hadichtiv v'heifer et nidrah* — and the phrase "her vow" implies that he must also recognize the specific vow. *Tosafot*, by contrast, understands the word *otah* in *v'ini otah* to refer not to the woman but to the vow itself. We noted earlier that the plain meaning of the verse is that *v'ini otah* means "prevent her" — the woman — while *nidrah* refers to the vow. Thus the *Rosh* draws on both to derive both requirements, while *Tosafot* reads *otah* as referring to the vow directly. Either way, the conclusion is the same: the husband must know both the woman and the vow.

---

## Explicit vs. Interna (II)

### Keriah Wrong Person

Having established that the husband must have specific knowledge, the *gemara* raises a challenge from *keriah* — the rending of garments in mourning. The verse speaks of David rending his garments *al Shaul v'al Yehonatan beno*, explicitly naming those for whom the rending was performed. One would therefore expect that rending garments for the wrong person ought not to count, just as annulling the wrong person's vow does not count.

### Baraita Contradiction

A *beraisa* is cited: *amru lo met aviv ve-kara* — someone was told his father had died and he rent his garments, *ve-achar kach nimtza beno* — and it turned out it was actually his son who had died. The *beraisa* rules *yatza yedei keriah* — he has fulfilled his obligation of *keriah*, even though the act was performed under a mistaken identity. This seems directly analogous to our case, and yet the ruling goes the other way. The verse contains *al* — just as specific as *v'ini otah* — and still we do not require that the *keriah* be performed for the correct person.

A second *beraisa* appears to contradict the first: *amru lo met aviv ve-kara, ve-achar kach nimtza beno, lo yatza yedei keriah* — he did not fulfill the obligation. The *gemara* resolves this apparent contradiction: *lo kashya, ha bistam ve-ha bemeforesh* — it is not difficult; the two *baraitot* address different cases. The distinction turns on whether the act was explicitly labeled as being for a particular person or whether the mistaken identity was only internal.

### Explicit Mislabel

The *Ran* explains the resolution more precisely. The first *beraisa*, which rules that *keriah* counts even though it was done for the wrong person, is not describing a case where they explicitly told him his father had died. Rather, *be-she'amru lo met* — they told him only that someone had died, *ve-savar aviv ve-nimtza beno* — and he assumed it was his father, when in fact it was his son. Since the act was not explicitly labeled as a rending for the father, *keriah* performed in the context of a family member's death is valid even though his internal assumption was wrong. The second *beraisa*, which rules that *keriah* does not count, describes the case where they told him explicitly that his father died — that is, the act was explicitly labeled as being for the father — and then it emerged that it was the son. An explicitly mislabeled act cannot be reassigned.

This principle — that what matters is not internal intention but external, explicit labeling — is striking. One might have thought that *keriah* could tolerate internal error because it is an outward, physical demonstration in a real-world context of loss, whereas an act of *hafarah* or *hakamah* requires much more specific engagement with the substance of the vow, and *kiyum* in particular requires no verbal act at all. That the same principle of external labeling would govern all of these is somewhat counterintuitive, though the *gemara*'s development of the *keriah* analogy pushes in precisely that direction.

### Apply to Annul

Translating this principle back to *hafarah* and *hakamah*: as long as the husband has not explicitly labeled his act as an annulment of a specific person's specific vow — as long as he simply heard a vow and declared *meifer ani* — the act is not mislabeled. Even if internally he was thinking about the wrong woman or the wrong vow, the act stands: there was a vow, he had the power to annul, and he performed the act of *hafarah*. It is only where he explicitly designated the act — "I am annulling my daughter's vow" — and it turned out to be his wife's vow, that the *hafarah* fails.

This is admittedly a surprising extension of the *keriah* analogy. The sense in which an act of mourning has objective meaning in the context of a real death — regardless of what was in the mourner's mind — is not identical to the sense in which a husband's act of annulment has meaning regardless of whom he was thinking of. But the *gemara*'s logic treats the two as parallel.

---

## Toch Kedei Dibur

### Rav Ashi Correction

*Rav Ashi* goes further: *kan betoch kedei dibbur kan le'achar kedei dibbur* — the difference between the two *baraitot* on *keriah* is not a question of explicit versus internal labeling, but of timing. Even if the act was explicitly mislabeled — even if they told him his father had died and he rent his garments — if the discovery that it was actually his son occurred *betoch kedei dibbur*, within the time window of *toch kedei dibbur*, the act can be redefined and the *keriah* counts.

### Simultaneity Concept

The concept of *toch kedei dibbur* — roughly, "within the time of speech," understood as approximately the time it takes to greet a teacher (*shalom alecha rabbi*) — normally applies to verbal acts, where a speaker can reconsider and amend a declaration within an immediate window. It is less intuitive when applied to a physical act like *keriah*, where there is no speech to extend or amend. What *Rav Ashi* seems to be saying is that the discovery itself, occurring *toch kedei dibbur*, allows the earlier act to be retrospectively redefined — not by redoing anything, but simply by virtue of the temporal proximity of the new awareness.

### Keriah Discovery

The *gemara* supports this with a *beraisa*: *mi sheyesh lo choleh b'toch beito* — someone has a gravely ill person at home, *ve-chedumeh shemet* — and the person appeared to have died (stopped breathing), *ve-kara* — and he rent his garments, *ve-achar met* — and then the person actually died shortly afterward. *Lo yatza yedei keriah* — he did not fulfill the obligation. Then comes a gloss attributed to *Rav Shimon ben Pazi* in the name of *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* in the name of *Bar Kappara*: *lo shanu ela shemet achar k'dei dibbur* — this ruling applies only if the person died after *k'dei dibbur* had elapsed; *aval b'toch k'dei dibbur k'dibbur dami* — but if the person died within *toch kedei dibbur*, it counts, because within that window, the moment of the act and the moment of the death are treated as contemporaneous.

The combined teaching of this section is therefore: first, *keriah* need not be intentionally directed at the correct person — it must only not be explicitly mislabeled; second, even explicit mislabeling can be corrected if the correction or discovery occurs *toch kedei dibbur*; third, the same principles apply by analogy to *hafarah* and *hakamah*.

---

## Explicit vs. Interna (II)

### Keriah Before Death

The most extreme and philosophically difficult implication of *Rav Ashi*'s ruling is the *beraisa* just cited: the man rent his garments before the person had actually died, and yet it counts as valid *keriah* provided the death followed *toch kedei dibbur*. This is a genuinely difficult case. It is one thing to say that an act performed in the correct context — someone has died, a family member rends garments — is valid even if the mourner's internal assumptions were wrong. But here the precondition for *keriah* — actual death — had not yet obtained at the moment the act was performed. How can an act be valid for an event that had not yet occurred?

---

## Toch Kedei Dibur (II)

### Pre-Condition Problem

This question is genuinely difficult. For *toch kedei dibbur* to apply to a matter of intent or a verbal act, one can say that the speaker's mind or declaration remains open and continuous within that window, allowing a later moment within it to redefine an earlier one. But here the difficulty is ontological: you are trying to pull a future event — the actual death — backward to give meaning to a prior act. It is not merely a question of redefining one's frame of mind; the very condition that would make the act halachically meaningful did not exist yet.

### Time Granularity

One possible resolution is that *halachah* measures time in *toch kedei dibbur* increments, not in seconds. The clock of *halachah*, so to speak, does not tick in units finer than *toch kedei dibbur*. Just as the principle of *i efshar letzamtzem* addresses the impossibility of perfect precision, one could suggest that *halachah* treats the entire span of *toch kedei dibbur* as a single temporal unit — anything occurring within it is halachically simultaneous with anything else in that window. Under this reading, the *keriah* and the death occur in the same halachic moment, even if, measured by an ordinary clock, the death came fractionally later.

This interpretation does have limits. The *gemara* rules elsewhere that certain acts cannot be remedied even within *toch kedei dibbur*. For example, if a husband betroths a woman who at that same moment receives a *get* from a previous husband, the *kiddushin* does not take effect. So the principle of halachic simultaneity does not resolve every case. The temporal-granularity approach may explain the *keriah* case — where one is merely relabeling an act in the context of a real death — but the full philosophical implications of *toch kedei dibbur* as applied to preconditions that do not yet exist remain genuinely challenging.

---

## Exceptions to Toch

### Four Exceptions

The *gemara* concludes with the operative *halachah*: *v'hilchasa, toch kedei dibbur k'dibbur dami* — the rule of *toch kedei dibbur* applies as a matter of law, *chutz mimigadef v'oved avodas kochavim u'mekadesh u'mgaresh* — except for blasphemy (*megadef*), idolatry (*oved avodah zarah*), betrothal (*kiddushin*), and divorce (*gerushin*). In these four cases, a retraction or correction within *toch kedei dibbur* has no legal effect.

All the *rishonim* note that this entire framework — the general principle and its exceptions — appears to be *d'oraisa* in its application. The *mishnah* we are analyzing concerns *hafarah* and *hakamah*, which are themselves *d'oraisa* matters. This creates a significant difficulty for the view of *Rabbeinu Tam*, who held that *toch kedei dibbur* is a rabbinic *takkanah* designed to ease commercial transactions by giving parties a brief window to reconsider. The *gemara* here applies *toch kedei dibbur* across a range of *d'oraisa* contexts without any indication that it is a rabbinic overlay.

### Weighty Acts

No explicit verse is cited as the source for excluding the four cases. The *rishonim* explain it on the basis of *sevara* — logic. The *Ran* writes: *bishar mili d'lav chamiri kulei hai, k'she-adam oseh otam lo b'gemar da'ato hu oseh* — in ordinary matters of life, a person acts without having fully made up his mind, always holding a small reservation, *da'ato she-yuchal lachazor bo toch k'dei dibbur* — expecting that he can still reconsider within that brief window. The act is undertaken with a kind of built-in tentativeness, which is what *toch kedei dibbur* accommodates.

### Intent Finality

But *hani kivan d'chamiri kulei hai, ein adam oseh otam ela b'haskamah gemurah* — since these four acts are so weighty, a person never undertakes them without complete and unreserved intention. There is no residual tentativeness to be accommodated. Therefore, *mishum hachi chazarah afilu toch k'dei dibbur lo mahani* — any attempt to retract is legally null, because the *da'as* at the moment of the act is considered to have been full and final.

One could alternatively formulate the principle as follows: rather than asking about the actor's internal state, one could say that an act of such weight is itself final by virtue of what it is. The act speaks for itself and cannot be relabeled or retracted, regardless of whether the actor's frame of mind was technically tentative or not. Whether the focus is on the finality of *da'as* or the finality of the act itself, the functional conclusion is the same: for *megadef*, *oved avodah zarah*, *kiddushin*, and *gerushin*, *toch kedei dibbur* provides no relief.

---

## Partial Acts Debate

### Figs Grapes Vow

The *mishnah* introduces a new scenario. A woman declared: *konam te'einim v'anavim eilu she-ani to'emet* — these figs and grapes are forbidden to me regarding my tasting of them. The husband then acted on only one part of the vow.

### Partial Effects

The *mishnah* rules: *kiyam le'te'einim, kulo kiyam* — if he affirmed the vow regarding figs, the entire vow is affirmed. *Heifer le'te'einim, eino mufar ad she-yafer af la-anavim* — but if he annulled regarding figs, it is not annulled at all until he annuls the grapes as well. The principle: a partial *hakamah* works for the whole *neder*, but a partial *hafarah* works for nothing. The *neder* already exists as a reality; to affirm what is already there, even a partial affirmation is sufficient to root the entire *neder* in place. To annul, however, requires rejecting the whole, and a partial annulment accomplishes nothing.

The *Ran* suggests a different reading of the *mishnah* — namely, that *hafarah* on part does work for that part, and the phrase *eino mufar* until he annuls the grapes means only that the grapes remain bound until he addresses them separately. But this is not the *pshat* of the *mishnah*, and the *Ran* himself appears to acknowledge as much. The plain reading is all-or-nothing.

### Separate Language

A second case in the *mishnah*: *amar konam te'einah she-ani to'emet ve-anavah she-ani to'emet* — she used the phrase *she-ani to'emet* separately for each item, applying it to the fig and to the grape individually. *Harei hu shenei nedarim* — this constitutes two separate vows. The consequence is that a *kiyum* on one does not establish the other, and a *hafarah* on one is effective for that one. The repetition of the verbal formula *she-ani to'emet* suffices to break the single vow into two independent vows, even without repeating the word *konam* for each item.

### Yishmael All/Nothing

The *gemara* identifies the *mishnah* with *Rabbi Yishmael*. A *beraisa* is cited to spell out his position: *isha yekimenu ve-isha yeferenu* — the husband shall establish it and the husband shall annul it. If she said *konam te'einim v'anavim eilu she-ani to'emet* — figs and grapes that I shall not taste — *kiyem le'te'einim, kulo kiyem* — if he affirmed for figs, it is all affirmed; *heifer le'te'einim, eino mufar ad she-yafer af la-anavim* — if he annulled for figs only, it is nothing until he annuls the grapes as well. These are the words of *Rabbi Yishmael*. The *mishnah* is thus fully aligned with his position.

### Akiva Linked

*Rabbi Akiva* disagrees. He reads the juxtaposition in the verse — *isha yekimenu ve-isha yeferenu* — as linking *hakamah* and *hafarah* so that they operate with equal efficacy. The *gemara* then asks: where does the concept of partial *hakamah* producing full effect come from? The *drasha* is from the word *yekimenu*: the *mem* suffix is read as *mimmenu* — "from it" or "of it" — yielding *yakim mimmenu*, meaning that affirming even a part of the vow constitutes a full *hakamah*. From this, *Rabbi Akiva* derives by *hekesh* — analogy — that *af yesirenu mimmenu*: just as a partial *hakamah* is a full one, a partial *hafarah* is also effective. Both work partially and completely in parallel.

*Rabbi Yishmael* would counter: *mi ketiv yafer mimmenu?* — the word *mimmenu* appears only by *yekimenu*, not by *yeferenu*. You cannot derive the partial *hafarah* from the partial *hakamah* without a specific textual basis. *Rabbi Akiva* responds that the verse *hekesh*'s the two — they are explicitly linked — so *ma hakamah mimmenu af hafarah mimmenu*. The debate is thus clear: both agree that partial *hakamah* operates fully; they disagree on whether the same follows for *hafarah*.

### Sages Position

*Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan* introduces a third opinion, that of the *Chachamim*. According to the standard *girsa*: *ma hafarah ma sheheifer heifer af hakamah ma shekiyam kiyam* — just as *hafarah* works for what was annulled (and only for that), so too *hakamah* works only for what was affirmed (and only for that). This reading rejects the all-or-nothing framework entirely: partial *hafarah* is effective for the part addressed, and partial *hakamah* is effective only for the part affirmed.

The *Ran*, however, presents an alternative *girsa* found in *k'tzat sefarim*: *aval chachamim omrim mah hafarah mah shehefir lo hefir af hakama mah shekiyam lo kiyam* — just as a partial *hafarah* does nothing, so too a partial *hakamah* does nothing. The *Ran* further notes that this is the *girsa* of *Rabbeinu Moshe bar Nachman* in his *halachot*. Under this reading, the *Chachamim* represent the third logical possibility in an all-or-nothing framework: Rabbi Yishmael holds that partial *hakamah* is everything and partial *hafarah* is nothing; Rabbi Akiva holds that both are everything; and the *Chachamim* hold that both are nothing. Three logically coherent positions given an all-or-nothing premise.

### Rambam Ruling

The *Rambam*, in chapter 13 of *Hilchot Nedarim*, halachah 10, rules as follows: *asah te'einim va'anavim bein bishvuah bein she'asar atzmo bechol hamin vekiyam lite'einim vehefir la'anavim o shekiyam la'anavim vehefir lite'einim mah shekiyam kiyam mah shehufar mufar* — if the figs and grapes were treated as separate matters, and he affirmed the figs and annulled the grapes, or vice versa, what he affirmed is affirmed and what he annulled is annulled. The *Rambam* thus follows the standard *girsa* of the *Chachamim*, ruling that partial *hafarah* and partial *hakamah* each take effect for their respective objects.

---

## Oaths Parallel

### Rava Shimon

*Rava* observes: *masnitin Rabbi Shimon hi* — the *mishnah* reflects the position of *Rabbi Shimon*. The reference is to the debate regarding multiple oaths: *de'amar ad sheyomar shevuah lechol echad ve'echad* — Rabbi Shimon holds that separate liability for each oath requires that each be designated separately. In the case of one who borrowed from five people and denied each debt, a single blanket denial-oath produces only one *korban*, whereas separate declarations of *shevuah* for each person produce separate obligations.

### Separation Needed

The parallel to our *mishnah* is that combining the figs and grapes in a single vow creates a single *neder*, just as combining the oaths in a single declaration creates a single oath. The repetition of *she-ani to'emet* for each item functions analogously to repeating the word *shevuah* for each creditor — it creates the necessary separation. *Rava*'s point is that our *mishnah*'s requirement of explicit separate language to divide a compound vow into independent *nedarim* mirrors *Rabbi Shimon*'s requirement in the realm of oaths.

---

## Next Mishnah Intro

### Know Vows Case

The *gemara* closes with the opening of the next *mishnah*: *yodeia ani sheyesh nedarim* — "I know that there are vows." This sets up the question of when the husband's time window for annulment begins in a case where he knew vows existed but lacked full knowledge of their specifics — the timing question that the upcoming discussion will develop further.

---

---

# Nedarim 86b

## Specificity in Hafara

### Wife vs. Daughter

The *mishna* on 86b continues the discussion of *hafara* by a husband, shifting focus from the categories of *inui nefesh* and *devarim shebeino l'veinah* to the act of *hafara* itself. The *mishna* presents several cases of confusion: a man's wife took a vow but he thought it was his daughter, or his daughter took a vow but he thought it was his wife; a woman made a vow using *nazir* terminology but he thought she used *korban* language, or vice versa; she made a vow not to eat figs and he thought she made a vow not to eat grapes, or the reverse.

These cases span three distinct categories of confusion: the identity of the person whose vow is being acted upon, the object of the vow, and the type of vow made. The distinction between a *neder* made using *nazir* language and one using *korban* language is not merely terminological — these represent genuinely different types of *nedarim*, and the basis on which a husband might wish to annul one could differ substantially from his basis for annulling the other. Of course, one could argue the same for wife versus daughter: what he wishes to annul for his wife may not be what he wishes to annul for his daughter. But it seems the *mishna* is not primarily concerned with the substantive motivation in each case. The operative point is structural: you must know whom you are annulling for and what exactly you are annulling.

### Types of Vows

In all these cases of confusion, the *mishna* rules: *harei ze yachzor veyafer* — he must go back and be *mefer* if he wishes the annulment to take effect. One natural reading is that he attempted *hafara* while mistaken, and so he must try again. But the *Ran* suggests — and both readings may in fact be true simultaneously — that the *mishna* also contemplates the case where he was *mekayem* the vow under a mistaken impression. Since a *kiyum* made in error is not a binding *kiyum*, he retains the ability to go back and be *mefer*. Whether the act was *kiyum* or *hafara*, the *gemara* will make clear that one must know for whom the vow was made, on what object, and of what type.

### Reattempt Needed

This raises a timing question: does the confusion reset the clock, giving him until the end of a new day from when he realized his error? The answer appears to be no. The *mishna* seems to assume that the husband knew he was empowered to annul, knew he was dealing with a type of *neder* he could annul, and knew all the general circumstances — he simply had the details wrong. Because he did have that fundamental awareness when he first heard the vow, the operative day remains *beyom sham'o*, the day he heard it. The discovery of his error does not restart the twenty-four-hour window.

### How Husband Hears

A separate question arises: how did the husband confuse his wife for his daughter, or vice versa? One natural answer is that he heard through a door, the voices were similar, and he simply mistook one for the other. However, the *Ran* offers a surprising reading — that the case involves someone reporting the vow to him incorrectly: *sha'amru lo shebito nadra umitoch kach hefer o kiyem*, "they told him his daughter had vowed, and on that basis he annulled or affirmed." This is striking, because earlier in the tractate there was an extensive discussion establishing that the husband must personally hear the vow — he cannot appoint an agent to hear it on his behalf. The *Ran*'s formulation seems to imply that being told about a vow suffices for *hafara* to take effect, which sits in tension with that earlier position. This point is worth noting even if a full resolution is not readily at hand.

---

## Explicit Mislabeling

### Otah Davka

The *gemara* opens its analysis with the phrase *lema'imra di'otah davka*: the word *otah* — "her" — in the verse *yani otah* is precise and exclusive. He must know exactly which woman's vow he is annulling. Not only is there specificity required regarding the person, but the *gemara* draws the same inference from the phrase *v'heifer et nidrah* — "he shall annul her vow" — meaning he must know the specific *neder* he is annulling: *she-yakir ha-neder*. The *Rosh* here draws both requirements from the two components of the verse: the *otah* specifying the woman, and *nidrah* specifying the vow. Interestingly, *Tosafot* takes a different approach and understands the word *otah* by *yani otah* as referring not to the woman but to the vow itself. Either way, both *Rosh* and *Tosafot* arrive at the same practical conclusion: the husband must know both the person and the vow he is annulling.

### Keriah Analogy

The *gemara* then raises what appears to be a strong counterexample from the laws of *aveilus*. The verses regarding *keriah* use the formulation *al Shaul v'al Yehonatan beno* — explicitly naming for whom the rending is performed — suggesting that *keriah* must be done with a specific person in mind. Yet a *brayta* teaches: *amru lo meit aviv v'kara* — they told him his father died and he rent his garments — *v'achar kach nimtza b'no*, and it turned out it was actually his son who had died. Despite this, *yatza yedei kriya* — he fulfilled his obligation. On its face, this seems to contradict the principle that the act must be specifically directed, since the *al al* formulation in the *pesukim* appears at least as demanding as *otah davka*.

### Mind vs. Labeling

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *ha b'stam v'ha b'meforesh* — the cases differ based on whether the misdirection was merely internal or was made explicit. What renders an act as being "for X" is not what is silently passing through one's mind, but rather explicit labeling. If a person performs *hafara* or *kiyum* — or *keriah* — while thinking of the wrong person, but without that mistake being verbally or explicitly declared, it does not disqualify the act. Only if the act is explicitly labeled as being for the wrong person does it fail.

Applied to the *brayta* about *keriah*: the case where *yatza* is ruled, the *Ran* explains, is not actually where they explicitly told him his *father* had died — for then it would be labeled as a *keriah* for the father. Rather, the case is where they said to him only that someone died (*amru lo meit*), he assumed it was his father (*v'savar aviv*), and then it emerged it was actually his son. Since his assumption was entirely internal and was never made explicit, the *keriah* succeeds.

### Keriah Efficacy

The *gemara* then brings a second *brayta* that distinguishes the two scenarios precisely. Where someone was explicitly told his father had died and rent his garments, and it later emerged it was his son — *lo yatza yedei kriya*, he did not fulfill the obligation. But where they told him only that someone had died (*amru lo meit lo meit*), he assumed it was his father, rent his garments, and it turned out it was his son — *yatza yedei keriah*, he fulfilled it.

This resolution is notable and somewhat counterintuitive. For *hafara* and *kiyum*, one might expect internal awareness of the correct person to be especially critical — after all, *kiyum* need not even be verbal; the *rishonim* earlier in the tractate established that *kiyum be-lev* suffices. An act of annulment or affirmation is, by its nature, an expression of approval or disapproval, and it seems to require knowing the actual circumstances, not merely performing the external act in the right general context. *Keriah*, by contrast, is a physical act that derives some of its meaning from the objective reality of rupture and mourning, regardless of what is precisely in one's head. Yet the *gemara* draws the analogy, and apparently *hafara* and *kiyum* similarly do not require specific internal intention toward the correct person — they require only that the act not be explicitly mislabeled for the wrong person.

---

## Toch Kedei Dibbur

### Rav Ashi's Rule

*Rav Ashi* goes further: *kan be-toch kedei dibbur, kan le-achar kedei dibbur* — the distinction between the two *braitot* is not about explicit versus implicit mislabeling at all. Rather, even explicit mislabeling can be corrected, provided the correction occurs within *toch kedei dibbur*. This is a significant extension. Normally, *toch kedei dibbur* is associated with acts of speech — the idea that within the immediately subsequent moment one can still define or redefine what one has said. It is more difficult to apply it to a physical act like *keriah* where no further speech follows, and where there is no continuing act being performed that one's subsequent thoughts might redirect.

### Death Later Case

According to *Rav Ashi*, then, the first *brayta* — where *yatza* is ruled — applies to a case where the discovery was made *toch kedei dibbur*, even if the act was explicitly labeled for the wrong person. The second *brayta* — where *lo yatza* is ruled — applies to a case where the discovery came only *le'achar kedei dibbur*, after the window had closed. A further *brayta* is adduced in support: someone had an ill person in his house who appeared to have died, and in that belief rent his garments, but it then emerged the person had actually died only a short time afterward. *Lo yatza yedei kriya* — he did not fulfill the obligation. To this, *Rav Shimon ben Pazi* in the name of *Rav Yehoshua ben Levi* in the name of *Bar Kappara* adds the qualification: *lo shanu ela shemet le'achar kedei dibbur* — this ruling applies only where the actual death followed the *keriah* by more than *kedei dibbur*. But *aval betoch kedei dibbur k'dibbur dami* — if the death occurred within *kedei dibbur* of the *keriah*, it is treated as simultaneous and the *keriah* counts.

### Discovery Timing

This last case is perhaps the most difficult in the entire discussion of *toch kedei dibbur*. It is one thing to say that an explicit mislabeling can be corrected within *toch kedei dibbur* — one could argue that within that window the act remains in a process of definition, and a corrective realization somehow relabels it. But in the case of the *brayta*, the problem is not mislabeling at all. The problem is that at the moment of *keriah*, the person had not yet died. The *keriah* was performed before the triggering circumstance even existed. For *toch kedei dibbur* to salvage this is not a question of relabeling — it seems to require treating *keriah* performed before a death as valid for a death that occurs afterward.

### Pre-Circumstance Acts

This raises a fundamental conceptual puzzle. *Toch kedei dibbur* is normally understood as an opportunity to correct or redefine an act while still in its immediate orbit. But one cannot straightforwardly correct an act done before the circumstances that would validate it even came into being. This seems categorically different from, say, correcting a mistaken *beracha* by immediately saying the right one. The person did *keriah* for someone not yet dead, then the person died within *kedei dibbur* — and the *gemara* says the *keriah* counts. How can one perform an act of mourning before there is anything to mourn?

### Simultaneity Concept

The most coherent way to understand this is that *toch kedei dibbur* is here being deployed as a concept of legal simultaneity rather than as an opportunity for relabeling or correction. *Halacha* does not measure time in seconds. It measures in *toch kedei dibbur* increments. Anything occurring within the same *toch kedei dibbur* window is treated as occupying the same legal moment — the same "tick" of the halakhic clock. On this understanding, the *keriah* and the death are legally simultaneous because they fall within the same *kedei dibbur* unit, and therefore the *keriah* validly marks the death. This is a striking and demanding application of the concept, and it does not obviously generalize. One would not say, for instance, that betrothing a woman takes effect retroactively because she received her *get* from a prior husband within *kedei dibbur* — yet the logic of simultaneity would seem to suggest that. Accordingly, it seems more precise to say that the function of *toch kedei dibbur* here is specifically about whether the act and the triggering event can be treated as occurring within the same legally indivisible unit of time, in a way that *halacha* demands but does not extend indiscriminately to all acts.

To summarize the structure of the *sugya*: first, specificity of intent is required — the act must not be explicitly labeled for the wrong person. Second, even if it is explicitly mislabeled, correction within *toch kedei dibbur* remedies this. And the same principles apply, by parallel, to *hafara* and *hakama*, where — despite the fact that *kiyum* is internal and one would expect much more is demanded by way of specific awareness — the same permissive framework operates.

---

## Exclusions to TKD

### Five Exclusions

The *gemara* concludes with a *hilchasa*, a ruling on the practical *halacha*: *toch kedei dibbur k'dibbur dami* — within *kedei dibbur* is treated as the statement itself. However, there are five categories excluded from this rule: *chutz mi-megadef v'oved avodas kochavim u-mekadesh u-megaresh* — blasphemy, idolatry, *kiddushin*, and *geirushin*. If someone uttered a blasphemy and immediately retracted, saying he did not intend God, or someone bowed in worship and then claimed he intended the *davening* posture, or someone betrothed a woman and *toch kedei dibbur* said he takes it back, or delivered a *get* and immediately claimed he did not mean it — in none of these cases does *toch kedei dibbur* provide any remedy.

Before examining the reasoning, an important structural point must be noted. All the *rishonim* observe that the framework of *toch kedei dibbur* being applied here — including to *hafara* and *hakama*, which are *d'oraisa* — is evidently a *d'oraisa* concept. This creates a serious difficulty for the position of *Rabeinu Tam*, who held that *toch kedei dibbur* is a rabbinic *takkanah* instituted to ease commerce, allowing parties to back out of a transaction within the first few moments. The application of *toch kedei dibbur* throughout this passage to biblical-level obligations makes *Rabeinu Tam*'s characterization very difficult to sustain, and all the *rishonim* raise this objection.

### Complete Intent

The *Ran* addresses the rationale for excluding the five cases. He writes: *u'l'chol milei d'lav chamiri kulei hai* — for ordinary matters that are not especially weighty, *k'she'adam oseh osam lo b'gmar da'ato hu oseh* — when a person does them, he never acts with fully resolved intention. There always remains a degree of tentativeness, an implicit reservation, a sense that within *kedei dibbur* he can still reconsider. Therefore *toch kedei dibbur* allows for retraction. But *hani keivan d'chamiri kulei hai ein adam oseh osam ella b'haskama gmura* — these five matters, being of such gravity, are never undertaken unless one's intention is completely unreserved and final. There is simply no subjective reservation being held. Therefore *chazara afilu toch kedei dibbur lo mahani* — even a retraction within *kedei dibbur* cannot undo them, because the *da'as* at the time of the act was already complete.

### Acts Speak

An alternative explanation does not focus on the internal state of the actor but on the objective weight of the act itself. Acts of such significance — idolatry, blasphemy, *kiddushin*, *geirushin* — are so weighty that *halacha* treats them as speaking for themselves and as inherently final. Even if one were to argue that subjectively the person maintained some reservation, the act itself is of a category that cannot be redefined by subsequent second thoughts. The act's weight forecloses the possibility of relabeling it through any later awareness or retraction, however immediate.

---

## Partial vs. Whole

### Mishna Position

The next *mishna* introduces a new scenario: *amrah konam te'einim va'anavim elu she'ani to'emes* — a woman vowed that these figs and grapes are forbidden to her in terms of her eating them. *Kayam l'te'enim kulo kayam* — if the husband affirmed the vow with respect to the figs, the entire *neder* is affirmed. *Heifer l'te'enim* — if however he annulled only the figs — *eino mufar ad sheyafer af l'anavim* — it is not annulled until he also annuls the grapes.

The straightforward reading of this *mishna* is that *hakama* and *hafara* operate on an all-or-nothing basis, but asymmetrically. Since the *neder* already exists and is a real, established thing, even a partial affirmation is enough to root and confirm it in its entirety. Annulment, however, must contend with the full *neder*: a partial *hafara* accomplishes nothing. To erase the vow, the husband must reject it in its entirety. An ounce of *kiyum* goes a long way; a partial *hafara* does nothing at all.

The *Ran* proposes an alternative reading of the *mishna* — that *eino mufar ad sheyafer af l'anavim* means the grapes are not annulled until he annuls them, but the figs *are* annulled by the partial *hafara*. On this reading, partial *hafara* works for the part it covers. This reading is, however, not the *pshat* of the *mishna*, and the *Ran* himself acknowledges as much. The plain sense remains: partial *kiyum* affirms everything; partial *hafara* accomplishes nothing.

### Separate Language

The *mishna* then introduces a limiting case: *amar konam te'enah she'ani to'emes v'anavah she'ani to'emes* — if she used the word *she'ani to'emes* separately for each item, *harei elu shenei nedarim* — these constitute two separate *nedarim*. Once the two items are treated as separate *nedarim*, the all-or-nothing framework applies independently to each one. Performing *kiyum* or *hafara* on one does not affect the other.

The natural question is what makes language sufficiently separating. If she had separately said *konam* before each item, they would clearly be two vows. Here she did not repeat the word *konam*, but she did repeat the verbal phrase *she'ani to'emes* for each item individually. Is that sufficient? The *mishna* says it is, though the *gemara* will examine how this connects to a broader debate about what constitutes the separation of *nedarim*.

### Rabbi Yishmael

The *gemara* asks: *mani matnitin* — whose view does our *mishna* represent? *Rabbi Yishmael*. This is established from a *brayta* that reproduces the *mishna*'s ruling almost verbatim: *ishah yekimenu v'ishah yeferenu* — her husband shall affirm it and her husband shall annul it. If he affirmed the figs, *kulo kayam* — the whole thing is affirmed. If he annulled the figs, it remains fully in force *ad sheyafer af l'anavim* — until he also annuls the grapes. *Divrei Rabbi Yishmael* — these are the words of *Rabbi Yishmael*. The *mishna* as we have it straightforwardly reflects *Rabbi Yishmael*'s position.

### Rabbi Akiva

*Rabbi Akiva* disagrees. He begins from the same verse: *ishah yekimenu v'ishah yeferenu*. The linkage of *hakama* and *hafara* in a single verse implies they must operate with comparable efficacy. But what is the *drasha* that produces the rule that even a partial *hakama* works? *Rabbi Akiva* reads *yekimenu* as *yakim mimenu* — the *mem* in the word becomes the preposition *min*, yielding: he affirms even *from* it, meaning from a portion of it. A partial *hakama* of even one component affirms the entire vow. And since *hafara* is *hekesh*-ed to *hakama* by the same verse — *mah hakama mimenu af hafara mimenu* — partial *hafara* likewise works as a full *hafara*. On *Rabbi Akiva*'s view, both *hakama* and *hafara* operate symmetrically: partial works as complete for both.

*Rabbi Yishmael* would respond that the *drasha* of *mimenu* applies only to *yekimenu* — there is no such formulation by *yesirenu*. *Rabbi Akiva* would counter that the *hekesh* between them in the verse bridges that gap. The debate thus has a clear formal structure: *Rabbi Yishmael* reads partial *hakama* as complete by *drasha*, with no such extension to *hafara* — partial *hafara* is nothing. *Rabbi Akiva* uses the same *drasha* but extends it via *hekesh* — partial works as complete for both.

### Chachamim

*Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba* said in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: those are the positions of *Rabbi Yishmael* and *Rabbi Akiva*. But the *chachamim* say: *makish hakama le-hafara* — they compare *hakama* to *hafara* in the opposite direction. *Mah hafara ma she-heifer heifer, af hakama ma she-kiyam kiyam* — just as *hafara* works on what is annulled, so *hakama* works on what is affirmed. The apparent meaning is that partial works for both — what is affirmed is affirmed, what is annulled is annulled — and neither sweeps the whole *neder* in its wake.

If we map out the logical possibilities, assuming an all-or-nothing framework, there are three: partial *hakama* is everything and partial *hafara* is nothing (*Rabbi Yishmael*); partial is everything for both (*Rabbi Akiva*); and partial is nothing for both. The *chachamim* as rendered here seem to represent a departure from all-or-nothing entirely, saying that partial works for the part it covers — a genuinely distinct fourth possibility.

### Ran's Girsa

The *Ran* reports a different *girsa* found in several manuscripts and attributed to *Rabbeinu Moshe bar Nachman* in his *hilchos*: *aval chachamim omrim mah hafara ma she-heifer lo hufar af hakama ma she-kiyam lo kiyam* — what he annulled is not annulled, and what he affirmed is not affirmed. On this *girsa*, the *chachamim* hold that partial *hafara* is nothing *and* partial *hakama* is nothing. This preserves a clean all-or-nothing structure across all three opinions: *Rabbi Yishmael* (partial *hakama* is everything, partial *hafara* is nothing), *Rabbi Akiva* (partial is everything for both), and *chachamim* (partial is nothing for both). On this reading, all three positions remain within the all-or-nothing framework, distributed across the logical possibilities.

### Rambam

The *Rambam* in *Hilchos Nedarim* 13 rules in accordance with our *girsa* of the *chachamim*, holding that partial works for both: if he affirmed the figs and annulled the grapes, *mah she-kiyam kiyam u'mah she-hufar mufar* — what he affirmed is affirmed and what he annulled is annulled. Each part is governed independently by whatever act was performed upon it.

---

## Oath Analogy

### Rava/Rabbi Shimon

On the question of what language is needed to separate a single compound vow into two distinct *nedarim*, *Rava* invokes *Rabbi Shimon*'s position from the laws of oaths. The case there involves someone who denies debts owed to multiple creditors with a single oath. If he says "I swear I owe none of you anything," that is one oath and incurs one *korban* if he lied. If he says "I swear I don't owe you, and I swear I don't owe you," addressing each creditor separately with the word *shvuah*, those are five separate oaths and incur five *korbanos*. The debate is what happens when he uses a form like "I swear I don't owe you or you or you" — one use of the oath-word covering multiple people. *Rabbi Shimon* holds that the oath-word must be repeated for each person individually — *ad sheyomar shvuah l'chol echad v'echad* — to produce separate oaths.

*Rava* says our *mishna* reflects this same position applied to *nedarim*. When the woman says *she'ani to'emes* separately for each item — figs and grapes — this is analogous to, though not perfectly identical with, reusing the oath-word. It is not as complete a separation as repeating *konam* before each item would be, but it is sufficient to constitute two *nedarim* according to the view that requires more explicit separation to break a compound declaration into its components.

### Next Mishna

The next *mishna* opens the topic of *yodeia ani sheyesh nedarim* — the husband's knowledge regarding which types of *nedarim* he has the ability to annul and how that affects the timing of the *hafara*. This is a topic we had touched on earlier in the context of when the *yom sham'o* clock begins to run, and it will be explored there in detail.

---

---

# Nedarim 88

## Unawareness of Hafara

### Existence of Hafara

The *daf* for today is 88, and we pick up at the bottom of 87b with a new *mishna*. We remain in the domain of *hafara* — the husband's power to annul his wife's vows — and the *mishna* we now encounter introduces a nuanced question about what it means to truly "hear" a vow.

The *mishna* presents the following case: a husband says, *yodea ani sheyesh nedarim* — I know that there is such a thing as a halachic *neder* — but *eini yodea sheyesh mefirim* — I did not know that there exists such a thing as *hafara*, or that anyone is empowered to act as a *meifer*, an annulling authority. Perhaps he assumed that *hafara* was an ancient biblical institution no longer in practice. Perhaps he simply never considered that such a mechanism was available to him at all. In such a case, the *mishna* rules *yafeh* — he may still annul the vow. The reason is that the day on which the vow was made is not considered *yom shamo*, the halachically operative "day of hearing." Since he was entirely unaware that *hafara* was relevant to his situation, he was not truly "hearing" the *neder* in any meaningful sense. It is only the day he realizes that he possesses this power that becomes his *yom shamo*, and that is the day he may perform *hafara*.

### Yom Shamo Defined

This raises an important conceptual question: one might argue that *yom shamo* should be defined purely in terms of the physical act of hearing — one either heard or did not. If we begin to sever the physical act of hearing from its practical significance and meaning, perhaps neither day qualifies as *yom shamo* and the husband finds himself unable to annul at all. The *mishna* rejects this approach, at least in the case where a person was entirely outside the *parsha* — entirely unaware that *hafara* existed or applied to him. In such a case, the day genuine awareness arrives is the operative *yom shamo*, and *hafara* is valid on that day.

### Relevance Anecdote

The underlying principle is that if something is not perceived as relevant to you, it does not register — even if it is technically within your sensory range. If a person does not know that commercial vehicles are prohibited on certain roadways, a sign reading "no commercial vehicles" simply does not register as one passes it. And if one does not know that a mechanism of *hafara* exists or applies to him, the words of the *neder* he overhears do not truly constitute hearing in the sense the Torah has in mind. *Shmi'ah* — the kind of hearing that activates the husband's right and obligation to respond — means a meaningful, cognizant apprehension of what one has heard and its implications.

---

## Partial Hearing Debate

### Specific Neder Unknown

The more complex and analytically rich case appears at the end of the *mishna*: *yodea ani sheyesh mefirim aval eini yodea shezeh neder* — I know that I possess the power of *hafara*, and I know that the world of *nedarim* is in principle my concern, but I did not realize that this particular utterance of my wife's constituted a *neder*. Perhaps he thought a certain key word was required and it was absent; perhaps he believed this topic fell outside the category of *devarim shebeino leveinah*. In any case, he was not entirely outside the *parsha* — he knew he was someone who could be a *meifer* — but he misjudged the specific details that would make this vow operative.

Is this sufficient to constitute *yom shamo*? The *mishna* records a dispute: *Rabbi Meir omer lo yafer* — Rabbi Meir says he cannot annul — while *Chachamim omrim yafer* — the Sages say he may.

### Ran's Explanations

The *Ran* offers two distinct explanations of this dispute, and they represent genuinely different readings of the underlying halachic positions.

### Realization as Hearing

The simpler explanation — which the *Ran* presents second but which flows most naturally from the *reisha* of the *mishna* — begins with the position of the *Chachamim*. The *Chachamim* hold that the husband may perform *hafara*, meaning: on the day he realizes that this utterance was in fact a halachic *neder*, that day becomes his *yom shamo*, and he may annul just as in the first case of the *mishna*. When the pieces come together and full awareness is achieved, that constitutes *yom shamo*.

Rabbi Meir, on this reading, disagrees. He holds that since the husband already knew he was within the *parsha* — he knew *hafara* was relevant to him as a general matter — that initial day of hearing already constituted *yom shamo*. One could therefore not retroactively designate the later day of fuller comprehension as *yom shamo*. The question then becomes whether Rabbi Meir would permit *hafara* on the original day of hearing itself. In principle, yes — if, for example, his wife urged him to perform *hafara* even though he himself was uncertain whether it was relevant, and he complied, that would presumably be valid according to Rabbi Meir. The operative point is that the day one knew one was in the *parsha* is *yom shamo*, and no later day can serve as a substitute.

### Two Half-Hearings

The first and more striking explanation the *Ran* offers presents Rabbi Meir as holding a far more restrictive position: the husband cannot annul either that day or the next. The reasoning is as follows. On the day of hearing, he knew he was within the *parsha*, but he lacked the specific knowledge that this was a *neder*. On the later day when he realizes it was a *neder*, too much time has passed — the clock of *yom shamo* already began ticking when he first heard and recognized his general capacity. Neither half constitutes a complete *shmi'ah*: the first half is sufficient to preclude the later day from serving as *yom shamo*, but it is not itself sufficient to permit *hafara*, because the hearing was incomplete. The second half completes the knowledge but falls outside the operative window. Rabbi Meir thus splits the hearing into two partial *shmi'ahs*, neither of which individually suffices.

According to this reading, the *Chachamim* disagree and hold that on the day the husband first heard — even with incomplete knowledge of the specifics — that constitutes adequate *yom shamo*, and he may perform *hafara* on that day if he chooses. The partial initial hearing, according to the *Chachamim*, is sufficient. In summary, under the second *Ran* explanation: Rabbi Meir holds that partial hearing is never sufficient — two halves do not make a whole — while the *Chachamim* hold that the initial partial hearing is adequate for *hafara* on that day itself.

---

## Blind Person Paralle (II)

### B'lo Ra'ot

Having laid out the *mishna*'s debate, the *Gemara* now poses a challenge from an entirely different area of halacha: the laws of accidental manslaughter and *galus*, exile to a city of refuge. The verse describes a case where one person kills another *b'lo ra'ot* — without seeing. The scenario is the standard one: a person is chopping wood in a forest, the blade flies off the handle, and someone is killed. The verse's phrase *b'lo ra'ot* generates a dispute about the status of a *suma*, a blind person, who by definition always acts without seeing.

The *Gemara* cites the following: *b'lo ra'ot prat l'suma*, divrei Rabbi Yehuda — Rabbi Yehuda holds that *b'lo ra'ot* excludes a blind person. The logic is that *b'lo ra'ot* means one who could have seen but did not; a blind person, who can never see, is in a categorically different situation and is exempt from *galus* entirely. Rabbi Meir, by contrast, holds *l'rabot et hasuma* — that *b'lo ra'ot* includes the blind person. Now, the *Gemara* perceives a structural parallel to our *mishna*: the debate about the blind person concerns whether partial awareness — a kind of awareness-without-seeing — suffices to place someone within the legal category at hand. This maps, the *Gemara* suggests, onto the debate about partial hearing in the context of *hafara*. Yet something striking emerges: the positions appear to be reversed.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Derivation

The *Gemara* explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning as follows. The verse in the context of *galus* also contains the phrase *v'asher yavo et re'ehu baya'ar* — and one who comes upon his friend in the forest — regarding which the *Gemara* observes: *kol d'var me'ilei laya'ar hu* — any person who enters a forest is included. A blind person is perfectly capable of entering a forest, so the verse begins by assuming a blind person is included in the law of *galus*. When we then encounter *b'lo ra'ot*, there is no need to use it to include the blind person — that has already been accomplished. The only remaining function of *b'lo ra'ot* is therefore to exclude the blind person. This is the principle of *ein ribui achar ribui ela lema'et*: a second inclusion, when the item is already included, must function as an exclusion.

### Rabbi Meir's Derivation

Rabbi Meir proceeds from the opposite starting point. A different verse in the passage uses the phrase *b'li da'at* — without awareness — and Rabbi Meir reads this as referring to someone who is *bar meda*, capable of full awareness. A blind person, he argues, is not fully capable of such awareness — *suma lav bar meda hu* — and so the passage, read from the outset, implies that a blind person is excluded. When the verse then says *b'lo ra'ot*, there is nothing left for it to do by way of exclusion — the blind person is already excluded. Therefore, this phrase must function to include the blind person. This is the principle of *ein miyut achar miyut ela lerabos*: a second exclusion, when the item is already excluded, must function as an inclusion.

### Partial Awareness Drive

The *Gemara* therefore concludes with *Rava*'s statement: *hacha me'inyana de'kra v'hacha me'inyana de'kra* — in each case, the outcome is driven by the specific language of the verse, and therefore the positions in the *galus* dispute need not be consistent with one's general view on partial awareness. What appears to be a reversal of positions is in fact the result of each *tanna* being driven by different textual starting points.

The *Ran*, however, goes further and offers a deeper reading of how positions on partial awareness actually *drive* the textual interpretations rather than being independent of them. The *Ran* aligns the *galus* dispute with the second explanation he gave of our *mishna*. According to that reading, Rabbi Meir holds that partial awareness — a half-hearing — is never sufficient. This is his general orienting principle. When Rabbi Meir approaches the *parsha* of *galus*, he therefore begins by assuming that a blind person, who has only partial awareness, is excluded, since his default approach is that the partial does not count. The extra verse then has no exclusionary work to do and must therefore include the blind person. Rabbi Yehuda, who is presumably the position of the *Chachamim* in our *mishna*, begins from the opposite principle: partial awareness is meaningful and sufficient. Accordingly, he reads the *parsha* of *galus* as initially including the blind person, since his default is that partial suffices. The extra verse then has no inclusionary work left and must therefore exclude.

On this reading, the positions are not merely reversed by textual accident. Rather, the deeper halachic intuition about whether partial awareness suffices shapes how each *tanna* reads the verse, and the resulting textual conclusion comes out in the opposite direction from where each would land in the context of *hafara*. The *Ran* is careful to observe that this is specifically true under the second reading of the *mishna*'s dispute — the reading in which Rabbi Meir holds that two half-hearings, each insufficient alone, leave the husband unable to perform *hafara* at all.

---

## Neder/Son-in-Law Pr (III)operty

### Vow Setup

We now turn to the next *mishna*. The case involves *hamadir hana'ah mechasno* — a father-in-law who takes a vow prohibiting his son-in-law from deriving any benefit from him. Having done so, he nonetheless wishes to give money to his daughter. The question the *mishna* grapples with is how the father-in-law can give property to his daughter in a way that does not benefit his son-in-law.

### Automatic Transfer

The difficulty is rooted in the principle of *kol shekansah isha kanah ba'alah* — whatever a wife acquires, her husband acquires. If the father simply gives money to his daughter, the husband immediately acquires it, and the father-in-law has thereby indirectly caused his son-in-law to benefit from his property, in violation of his vow. The father therefore faces a challenge: how does one give a gift to a married daughter without the benefit flowing through to the son-in-law?

---

## Blind Person Paralle (II)

### Different Verses

The *Gemara*'s resolution through *Rava* — that in each domain the verse operates according to its own logic — applies specifically to the question of how the blind person debate in the laws of manslaughter maps onto the partial hearing debate in the laws of *hafara*, and the analysis belongs with the *galus* discussion above rather than being reintroduced here. What the context of the son-in-law *mishna* requires is a separate analysis of how the wife's acquisition operates and whether the father's stipulation can interrupt the automatic transfer to the husband.

---

## Neder/Son-in-Law Pr (III)ope…

### Noseies V'Notenes

The *mishna* provides a solution: the father must give the money with the stipulation *mah she'at noseies v'notenet l'ficha* — "whatever you take and give over into your mouth." This phrasing goes beyond a simple declaration that the husband has no rights; it defines the moment of the daughter's acquisition in a specific and constrained way.

### Stipulation Fails

The *Ran* explains why a simple stipulation — saying merely that the husband shall have no rights over the gift — is insufficient according to the *mishna*. The reason lies in the principle of *yad isha k'yad ba'alah*, which the *mishna* is understood to follow in accordance with the position of Rabbi Meir. If the wife's hand is halachically equivalent to her husband's hand — that is, if she is not a legally independent acquisitional entity but rather an extension of him — then a stipulation excluding the husband's rights is logically incoherent. One cannot give something to a person's hand while simultaneously excluding that person from ownership. If her hand *is* his hand, the transfer goes to him directly and there is no mechanism to interrupt it.

The *mishna*'s solution, as the *Ran* explains it, is that the father is not truly transferring ownership to his daughter at all. The money remains, in effect, the father's. What he is granting is something far more limited: the right to consume. As she is in the act of placing the food or its equivalent into her mouth — and only at that moment — he permits her to benefit from it. At that instant of consumption, the benefit accrues to her directly, and there is no opportunity for it to pass through her hand into her husband's. Whether this applies only to consumables or extends to non-consumable goods such as clothing is a question the *Ran* considers separately: one might argue that a non-consumable is possessed at the moment she takes hold of it and could then pass to the husband; alternatively, one could argue that even then the item remains the father's, which she is merely permitted to use, and it never enters the chain of acquisition that leads to the husband.

---

## Rav vs Shmuel

### Yad Isha Identity

At this point the *Gemara* sets out the conceptual distinction underlying the dispute between Rav and Shmuel, who debate whether the *mishna*'s stringent formulation is in fact required as a matter of *halacha*.

The conceptual foundation of the entire discussion turns on the precise meaning of *kol shekansah isha kanah ba'alah* versus the stronger formulation of *yad isha k'yad ba'alah*. These two principles are not equivalent. The first formulation describes an automatic transfer: the wife possesses property, but it immediately flows to the husband. One can visualize this as automatic email forwarding — the item enters her account and is instantly redirected to his. Under this model, she does have her own *yad*, her own acquisitional capacity; it is simply that her account is configured to forward everything to her husband's. If this is correct, perhaps one could interrupt the forwarding — perhaps the father can stipulate that what he deposits in her account shall not be forwarded.

The second and stronger formulation — *yad isha k'yad ba'alah* — holds something more radical. Her hand is not merely connected to his; it *is* his. She has no independent acquisitional standing at all. There is no separate account that then forwards; there is only his account. Under this model, no stipulation can change the outcome, because there is no interstitial stage of her ownership in which to intervene. The only approach that can work is the one the *mishna* describes: eliminating the transfer entirely by ensuring she never "acquires" in the standard sense, but only benefits at the precise moment of consumption.

Rav holds in accordance with this stronger model — and the *Gemara* will note that this aligns with Rabbi Meir's position — and therefore requires the full formulation of *noseies v'notenet l'ficha*. Shmuel holds the more moderate position and therefore maintains that a simple stipulation against the husband's rights suffices.

---

## Neder/Son-in-Law Pr (III)ope…

### Money vs Food

One further question requires attention: why does the *mishna* specify that the father gives his daughter *money* rather than food directly? The *Ran* explains that food is a categorically different case. The husband is obligated to feed his wife. If a third party directly provides food to the wife, that provision satisfies the husband's existing obligation to feed her. The property, in other words, is discharging what is already his debt. Since what he owes her is her food, that food belongs to her by virtue of his obligation and does not carry with it any residual right for him to claim benefit. The father's gift of food would therefore be free of the problem entirely — the husband never acquires rights over what satisfies his own obligation to her.

The indirect benefit to the husband from not having to spend money on food himself is, the *Ran* notes, an instance of *mavriach ari* — warding off a lion, preventing a loss — which is not halachically treated as conferring direct benefit on the person in question. Therefore the father wishing to give food would face no difficulty at all. It is specifically money — and, by extension, non-food property — that presents the problem addressed by the *mishna*, because money given to the wife flows through her hand into the husband's in a way that food designated for her sustenance does not.

---

## Rav vs Shmuel (II)

### Rav: Both Phrases

The *Gemara* now presents Rav's position directly. *Lo shanu ela de-amar lah mah she-at noset ve-notenet be-ficha* — Rav taught that the *mishna*'s permission applies only if the father explicitly uses the formulation of "what you place into your mouth." *Aval amar mah she-tirtsi asi* — but if he says "do with it as you wish," even though this is functionally equivalent to saying "your husband has no rights over it," in that case *kana bahen baal* — the husband acquires it nonetheless. According to Rav, a simple declaration that the husband has no rights is legally ineffective. The only mechanism that prevents the husband from acquiring is the construction in the *mishna* whereby the wife does not fully acquire until the moment of consumption.

### Shmuel: Stipulation Only

Shmuel disagrees. *Afilu amar mah she-tirtsi asi* — even if the father merely says "do with it as you wish," conveying that it is entirely hers and the husband has no rights, *lo kana bahen baal* — the husband does not acquire it. Shmuel holds the more moderate view of *kol shekansah isha kanah ba'alah* — the automatic transfer model — and maintains that since the wife does possess her own acquisitional capacity, it is possible to interrupt the forwarding mechanism through explicit stipulation. Under Shmuel's position, the *mishna*'s formulation of *noseies v'notenet l'ficha* is not legally required; a straightforward condition that the husband shall have no rights is sufficient.

The *Ran* is careful to note that Shmuel is not disputing the internal logic of the *mishna* itself. Rather, Shmuel holds that the *mishna* reflects the position of Rabbi Meir — who applies *yad isha k'yad ba'alah* in its stronger sense — but that as a matter of practical *halacha*, we do not rule like Rabbi Meir on this point. Rav, by contrast, holds that the *mishna*'s stringent position is the operative *halacha*.

---

## Shitur Mevo'ot Example

### Shitur Concept

The *Gemara* now raises a challenge to Rav's position from a different context entirely: the laws of *shituf mevo'ot*. To understand the challenge, a brief description of the institution is necessary. In a shared alleyway — a *mavoi* — all the courtyards whose residents use that alleyway must establish a form of joint ownership in a single food item in order for the alleyway to be treated as a unified domain and carrying within it to be permitted on Shabbat. This is the *shituf mevo'ot*. Each courtyard is independently populated by residents of separate households, and each household is legally distinct. In order to unify all of these distinct entities into a single corporate-like domain, they all become joint owners of a single communal food item — typically a barrel of wine.

The practical question is how to effect this joint ownership efficiently. Rather than going door to door collecting a contribution from each household, a simpler method is available: one person takes the barrel and declares *harei zeh lechol bnei hamavoi* — this is hereby transferred to all the residents of the *mavoi*. This person confers ownership on everyone. But this act of conferring ownership requires a third party — someone who is not the owner — to take possession of the barrel and hold it on behalf of all the other residents. The owner cannot transfer something to himself; the acquisition must pass through an independent hand.

### Wife as Third Party

The *mishna* governing this process — a *stam mishna*, presumed to reflect the position of Rabbi Meir — lists the parties who may serve in this role. *Umezakeh lahen al yedei avdo veshifchato ha'ivrim* — one may effect the transfer through one's Hebrew male or female slaves. *Ve'al yedei beno uvito hagedolim* — through one's adult sons or daughters. *Ve'al yedei ishto* — and through one's wife.

The rationale for including adult children and Hebrew slaves is that even though they exist in a close relationship with the owner, they are halachically recognized as distinct legal persons capable of independent acquisition. The mention of the wife in this list is what creates the difficulty.

The community's *eruv* is handled in practice in a manner consistent with this principle: a rabbi takes a box of matzahs — which remain usable over an extended period — gives them to a designated individual, and says that this person is taking possession on behalf of all members of the community who reside in the relevant domain. The wife is listed as one who can perform this function for the *shituf mevo'ot*.

### Rabbi Meir Problem

Here lies the tension. If Rabbi Meir holds *yad isha k'yad ba'alah* — that the wife's acquisitional capacity is simply an extension of the husband's — then giving the barrel to one's wife is no different from giving it from one's right hand to one's left. There is no independent legal entity receiving it; it simply remains in the husband's domain. *Ve'i amart kneyah shon ba'alah* — and if you say that the husband invariably acquires whatever comes into his wife's hand, with no possibility of stipulating otherwise — then *eruv lo nafik mereshuteih deba'al*: the *eruv* barrel never leaves the husband's domain, and he cannot use her to effect the transfer to the rest of the *mavoi*. How then can the *stam mishna* — which follows Rabbi Meir — include the wife as a valid agent for this *kinyan*?

### Rava's Caveat

Rava resolves the apparent contradiction: *af al gav de'amar Rabbi Meir yad isha k'yad ba'alah, modeh Rabbi Meir le'inyan shituf, dekeivan d'lezakot l'acherim hu, miyad ba'alah zachyah* — even though Rabbi Meir holds that the wife's hand is like her husband's hand, he concedes in the case of *shituf* that she can serve as the acquisitional agent, because here the transfer is from the husband's hand and is intended to confer ownership upon others. In this circumstance, the wife successfully represents an entity distinct from the husband.

The *Ran* and *Tosafos* both emphasize that the critical element here is *miyad ba'alah* — that it is the husband himself who is initiating the transfer. The reasoning is as follows. The principle of *yad isha k'yad ba'alah* is not a metaphysical description of what a wife is; it is an imposed legal structure. Unlike the case of a non-Hebrew slave — whose status as the master's property is fundamental and cannot be severed by act of will — a wife retains full legal personhood within *halacha*. She can be a litigant, own property under certain conditions, and is in no way a chattel. The characterization of her *yad* as equivalent to her husband's is therefore a legal construct that was instituted and that, importantly, can be removed. The only party empowered to sever that connection is the husband himself. He can, by an act of explicit intention, declare that he is releasing his claim and that she is to function as a genuinely independent entity for purposes of this transaction.

A third party could not accomplish this. If someone other than the husband places an item in the wife's hands and says "this is for other people," the *yad isha k'yad ba'alah* structure is not disrupted — it takes what is going into her hand and redirects it to the husband. Only the husband, as the one whose relationship with her generates that legal structure, can choose to step outside it.

This is to be distinguished from reading the *Gemara*'s language as emphasizing *lezakot l'acherim* — the fact that the transfer is destined for others. On an alternative reading, one might argue that when a wife takes possession for the sake of parties other than herself, we view her as standing in for those third parties rather than as an extension of her husband, and therefore the *yad isha k'yad ba'alah* structure simply does not apply. Under this reading, the critical variable would be the destination of the property rather than the identity of the giver. However, the *Ran* and *Tosafos* both reject this reading and emphasize that it is specifically *miyad ba'alah* — the husband's active, explicit participation as the giver — that breaks the structural equivalence.

---

## Wife Standing Limit

### Wife Contradiction

The *Gemara* now identifies a further complication. *Aesivay Ravina l'Rav Ashi* — Ravina posed to Rav Ashi a challenge from another Tannaic source: a *baraita* that explicitly enumerates the parties who can and cannot serve as the acquisitional agent for the *shituf mevo'ot*. On the permissible side, it lists adult children and Hebrew slaves — precisely as in the *stam mishna*. On the impermissible side — *elu she-ein zachin lahen* — it lists minor children, Canaanite slaves, and *v'ishto* — the wife. This creates a direct contradiction: one Tannaic source explicitly permits the wife to serve in this role and another explicitly prohibits it.

### Property Interest Requir…

Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction. The *stam mishna* that permits use of the wife does not apply across the board. *Matnitin besheyesh lah chatzer be'oto mavoi askinan* — the *mishna* refers specifically to a case where the wife herself owns a house in that very *mavoi*. *Demigo dezachyah l'nafshah zachyah l'achrinei* — since she has independent standing to acquire for herself in this context, she can also acquire on behalf of others.

### House Ownership

The logic of Rav Ashi's answer is as follows. Even when the husband is willing to sever the *yad isha k'yad ba'alah* structure, and even when he is the one giving explicitly — as Rava established — Rabbi Meir still requires that the wife have some form of genuine independent legal standing in the relevant context in order for her acquisition to be recognized as belonging to a distinct entity. If she is simply his wife with no independent connection to the *mavoi*, she remains, even in the best of circumstances, primarily an extension of him and cannot serve as a genuinely independent *kinyan* vessel. But if she independently owns a house in that *mavoi*, she is already recognized as her own legal presence within the shared domain. That pre-existing standing — *miggo dezachyah l'nafshah*, since she is capable of acquiring for herself in this setting — enables her to acquire on behalf of others as well.

It bears noting that for the wife to independently own a house in the *mavoi* in a manner that is not subject to the husband's rights, it would likely have to have been brought into the marriage under conditions that explicitly excluded the husband's claims — perhaps as a prenuptial arrangement. Once inside the marriage, any newly acquired property would, according to Rabbi Meir's strong position, pass immediately to the husband's domain.

A further observation emerges from this entire discussion: the transfers being analyzed here appear to concern not merely the husband's right of *ochel peiros* — his entitlement to the usufruct of his wife's property while she retains title — but full transfer of ownership itself. The *shituf mevo'ot* question is about who holds title to the barrel of wine, not about who profits from it. This suggests that the halachic principle under discussion operates at the level of full ownership, a point that would require further elaboration beyond what this *Gemara* explores directly.

---

## Final Halacha

### Shmuel Ruling
