The *Gemara* concludes with the question of practical *halacha*: do we rule like Rav or like Shmuel? The general principle is *halacha k'Shmuel b'dinei mamonot* — we follow Shmuel in monetary law. Although the dispute arises here in the context of *issur* — the prohibitions of *nedarim* — the *Ran* makes clear that the underlying debate is fundamentally one of *dinei mamonot*, concerning the nature of the wife's acquisitional relationship with her husband. Accordingly, the *Ran* cites the ruling of the *Nagid* Rabbeinu Shmuel HaLevi in the name of Rav Amram Gaon that the *halacha* follows Shmuel: *halacha k'Shmuel*. Furthermore, the *Ran* observes that Rav aligns with Rabbi Meir and Shmuel with the *Rabbanan* — the *Chachamim* — and that the general tendency of the *sugya* runs in Shmuel's direction. The practical consequence is that a father who gives his daughter a gift with an explicit condition that her husband shall have no rights over it — *al menat she'ein l'ba'alech reshut bahen* — that stipulation alone is halachically sufficient, and the elaborate formulation of *noseies v'notenet l'ficha* is not required.

### Alternative Positions

The *Ran* notes, however, that not all *poskim* accept this conclusion. There are authorities who rule like Rav and require the stricter formulation of the *mishna*. The precise scope of the debate — including how to read exactly what "do with it as you wish" implies and whether there are intermediate positions — is subject to further discussion among the *rishonim*. The *Ran* acknowledges these alternative views without fully resolving every dimension of the question.

---

---

# Nedarim 89

## Widow/Divorcée Vows

### Introduction

The final *perek* of *Nedarim* arrives at the end of a sustained treatment of vow annulment that began with the father's authority over his daughter, moved through the complex case of the *na'arah me'orasah* who stands under the joint control of father and *arus*, and then devoted considerable attention to the husband's power of *hafara* over his wife. Now, three *dapim* from the end of the tractate, the *mishnah* turns to the case that the Torah addresses in what appears to be the most straightforward fashion: the woman who is entirely her own person, subject to no man's authority.

### Torah Source

The *pasuk* in question is *v'neder almanah u'grushah kol asher asra al nafshah yakum aleha* — the vow of a widow or divorcée, whatever she has forbidden upon herself, shall stand. At first glance, this seems to require no derivation at all: if there is no father and no husband, there is obviously no one to annul her vow. The *mishnah* therefore signals, by opening with this verse, that the *pasuk* is coming to teach something less obvious. The *chiddush* is not the bare case but a more nuanced one — and it is in unpacking that nuance that the *perek* begins.

### Delayed Vow Case

The case the *mishnah* presents is the following. A woman who is independent — a *bogeret*, an *almanah*, a *gerushah*, any woman not under a man's control — declares: *hareini nezirah achar shloshim yom*, I will become a *nezirah* after thirty days. Before those thirty days elapse, she gets married. The vow then takes effect when she is already married to a husband who, in principle, has the power to annul her vows. Can he annul it?

The *mishnah* answers: *af al pi shenisset b'toch shloshim yom eino yachol l'hafer* — even though she married within the thirty days, he cannot annul it. The *chiddush* of the *pasuk* is precisely this: the husband's authority to annul is not determined by when the vow takes effect but by when the vow was made. Since she was an *almanah* or *gerushah* at the moment of utterance, the vow is established as hers alone, and no subsequent marriage can strip it of that character.

### Reverse Case

The reverse case follows naturally. A married woman — *nadrah v'hi b'reshut habaal* — declares while under her husband's authority: *hareini nezirah achar shloshim yom*. He has the power to annul her vow. The *mishnah* rules that he may in fact annul it, *af al pi shenit'almanah o nitgarshah b'toch shloshim yom* — even if she is widowed or divorced within those thirty days, before the vow ever takes effect. He need only perform the annulment during the period of their marriage; the fact that when the thirty days finally expire she is no longer his wife is irrelevant. He cannot, of course, annul her vows after she is widowed or divorced, but he can annul before it takes effect during the marriage, and that annulment holds. Again, the controlling moment is the time of utterance, not the time of effect.

### Same-Day Rule

The *mishnah* then presents a compressed and striking scenario: *nadrah bo bayom v'nitgarshah bo bayom v'hechezirah bo bayom* — she took a vow, was divorced, and was then remarried to the same man, all on the same day. Can he annul it, given that it was made while she was his wife and she is his wife again at the moment he seeks to annul? The *halachah* is *eino yachol l'hafer* — he cannot. The reasoning draws on two related principles. First, a husband cannot be *meifer* for vows that predate him — *ein ba'al meifer b'kodmin* — and the second marriage, even to the same man, is a new marriage. From the perspective of that second marriage, the vow was made prior to it and is therefore beyond his reach. Second, the divorce, even for a moment, granted her independence, and that moment is legally transformative.

### Governing Principle

The *mishnah* closes with the formulation *zeh haklal: kol sheyatzah l'reshut atzmah sha'ah achat eino yachol l'hafer* — the governing rule is that once she enters her own domain, even for a single moment, he loses the power to annul. This serves as the practical articulation of the *pasuk*'s teaching. The independence of the *almanah* and *gerushah* is not merely a biographical state but a legal threshold: once crossed, it cannot be erased by subsequent remarriage. The possibility raised in discussion — that his act of divorcing her might itself function as a kind of *kiyum*, a ratification of the vow through the very act that created her independence — is worth considering, even if the *halachah* does not depend on it.

---

## Yishmael vs. Akiva

### Baraita Case 1

A *baraita* now presents the underlying *machloket tanna'im* in explicit form. The first case: an *almanah* or *gerushah* — a woman fully independent — declares *hareini nezirah l'cheshe'inasei*, I will become a *nezirah* when I get married. She then does get married.

### Yishmael: Effect

*Rabbi Yishmael omer yafer* — Rabbi Yishmael holds that the husband can annul. His reasoning: the determinative moment is when the vow takes effect, i.e., when it becomes operative. The vow takes effect upon marriage, which means it takes effect precisely when she is under his authority. The fact that it was formulated before the marriage is irrelevant; what matters is the moment at which the prohibition becomes real. Rabbi Yishmael thus focuses on the *sha'at chal* — the time of effect.

### Akiva: Utterance

*Rabbi Akiva omer lo yafer* — Rabbi Akiva holds that the husband cannot annul it, because the controlling moment is *sha'at amira* — the time of utterance. She uttered the vow when she was independent, and that character attaches to the vow permanently. The *seiman* introduced here — *yelali* — encodes the alternating pattern of *yafer / lo yafer* in Case 1 and *lo yafer / yafer* in Case 2, since the positions reverse in the second case.

### Baraita Case 2

The second case is the mirror image: a married woman declares *hareini nezirah l'cheshe'etgaresh*, I will become a *nezirah* when I get divorced. The husband, cooperatively or otherwise, then divorces her, and the vow takes effect at the moment of divorce.

### Positions Reversed

The positions now reverse. *Rabbi Yishmael omer lo yafer*: since the vow takes effect when she is divorced and no longer under his authority, his annulment is meaningless — he had no power over it at the moment it became operative. *Rabbi Akiva omer yafer*: since the vow was made during the marriage, the husband had the power to annul it on the day she made it, and it does not matter that the effect only came later. The reversal is not surprising once the underlying logic is clear: each *tanna* is applying a single consistent principle across both cases, and the two cases simply instantiate the tension between the two principles in opposite directions.

### Torah Exegesis

The Talmud then presents the scriptural foundations for each position. Rabbi Yishmael derives his view from the phrase *veneder almanah u'grushah* — the word *veneder*, he argues, refers not to the act of vowing but to the actual standing reality of the vow itself. The focus of *veneder almanah u'grushah* is on when the vow *exists* as an operative prohibition: is it in existence when she is an *almanah u'grushah*, i.e., independent, or when she is married? That is the question. *Ad she-hi neder besha'at almanut v'gerushin* — we look to the state she is in when the vow is in effect.

Rabbi Akiva derives his view from the phrase *kol asher asra al nafshah* — the word *asra*, she forbade, focuses attention not on the standing reality of the prohibition but on the act of prohibiting. *Ad she-isur neder besha'at almanut v'gerushin* — was she independent at the moment she performed the act of forbidding? That is the question, and it is answered by looking at the *sha'at amira*, the moment of utterance.

### Mishna Attribution

Rav Chisda states the obvious conclusion: *matnitin Rabbi Akiva hi* — our *mishnah*, which consistently governs by the time of utterance, reflects Rabbi Akiva's position.

---

## Abaye's Resolution

### Thirty-Day Vow

Abaye, however, challenges this. He argues: *afilu teima Rabbi Yishmael* — one might say the *mishnah* is consistent even with Rabbi Yishmael's position. The key distinction lies in how the vow is formulated. In the *mishnah*, the vow is time-indexed: the woman says it will take effect after thirty days. The date of effect is fixed independently of her marital status. It is possible that over the course of those thirty days, nothing changes: she remains in exactly the same legal position she was in when she uttered the vow. The change in her status — the marriage or divorce — happens to occur incidentally within that window, but it is not built into the structure of the vow itself.

### Event-Based Vow

In the *baraita*, by contrast, the vow is status-indexed: *l'cheshe'inasei*, when I get married; *l'cheshe'etgaresh*, when I get divorced. The event of taking effect is definitionally tied to a change in legal status. By the very structure of the vow, the act of utterance and the moment of effect are categorically different moments — the vow was designed to span a transition from one legal domain to another. It is this intrinsic opposition between the two moments — utterance in one status, effect in another status — that Rabbi Yishmael focuses on and that triggers his rule of *sha'at chal*.

### Incidental Change

But in the *mishnah*'s thirty-day case, Abaye argues, even Rabbi Yishmael might agree that the *sha'at amira* governs. The vow was expressed as taking effect after a certain number of days — *shalmu yomei velo nitgarsha, shalmu yomei velo mitnasba* — and it was entirely possible that those thirty days would run out without any change in her status at all. The change that happened to occur was adventitious, not intrinsic to the vow. Since Rabbi Yishmael's principle focuses on cases where the two moments are by design in opposition, when the status change is merely incidental he may concede that the original status, the one in which the vow was made, is the one that counts. This is the *ra'n*'s formulation: *keivan shebitchilato haya raui haneder lachul beoto reshut shehaya beshaat amira* — since at the outset the vow could have taken effect within the same legal domain as the utterance, the original domain defines it even in Rabbi Yishmael's view. The *halachah* in any case follows Rabbi Akiva, both because *halacha ke-Rabbi Akiva mechavero* and because the *mishnah* is a *stam mishna* — though whether it is in fact a *stam mishna* depends on whether one accepts Abaye's resolution.

---

## Leaving Father

### Ketubot Precedent

The *gemara* now turns to the closing line of the *mishnah* — *zeh haklal kol sheyatzah l'reshut atzmah sha'ah achat eino yachol l'hafer* — and reads it alongside a parallel *zeh haklal* from tractate *Ketubot*, which dealt with the *na'arah me'orasah*. That *klal* in *Ketubot* establishes the following: as long as the daughter has not fully left her father's authority, the father retains his right to participate in the annulment of her vows jointly with the *arus*. The formulation *zeh haklal kol shelo yatzah mereshut ha'av aviah u'vaalah mefirin nedareha* is broad: even if her departure from the father's domain is partial or ambiguous — for example, if the father or his messengers accompany the husband's messengers on the way — she is still considered within the father's authority, and the father may still annul.

The *leatuyei* — the case the *klal* in *Ketubot* comes to include — is the scenario where the father accompanies, or sends his representatives to accompany, the husband's emissaries. Even in that borderline situation, since she has not fully exited her father's control, he remains in the picture. The *klal* reaches broadly in favor of maintaining the father's presence so long as any connection remains.

### Our Perek Klal

The *zeh haklal* of our *perek* — *Elu Naarot* — operates in the opposite direction and addresses the threshold from the other side. Once she has been handed over to the husband's messengers without the father or his representatives present — *masar ha'av lishluchei habaal o shemasru shluchei av lishluchei habaal* — she has left her father's control, and any prior vows can no longer be annulled by the husband under the rule of *ein ba'al meifer b'kodmin*. Interestingly, at this precise moment she has not yet entered *reshut habaal* in the full sense — she has not seen her husband, there has been no *chuppah*, she is simply in transit with his messengers. Yet since the father has stepped back, the opportunity for the husband to annul vows from the betrothal period is now gone.

The *mishnah*'s language of *yatzah l'reshut atzmah* is therefore somewhat forced in this reading, since she has not become independent in any straightforward sense — she is on her way to *reshut habaal*. The better reading seems to be *yotzet mereshut ha'av*: she is leaving the father's domain, not entering her own. But the practical consequence is the same: once the father is no longer present, the window for annulling prior vows closes.

### Betrothal Status

The question this raises is worth pressing: vows she made during *erusin* — the betrothal period — were subject to annulment by the father and the *arus* jointly. Once she transitions to full *nisuin*, those vows from the betrothal period become prior to the husband's status as full husband and cannot be annulled. The moment she is handed over to his messengers without the father functions, in this analysis, as a kind of threshold event equivalent to *chuppah* for purposes of the annulment window. The husband had the opportunity to annul betrothal-period vows while she was still betrothed and still partially in her father's domain; once that threshold is crossed, the father's authority is gone, and from the husband's vantage point, those vows preceded his authority and are beyond his reach.

---

## Nine Cases

### Three by Three

The *mishnah* now presents what appears to be an elaborate multiplication of cases, though the underlying structure is simple: there are three ways a woman becomes *yatzah l'reshut atzmah* — independent — and the *mishnah* takes each of those three and shows that various other circumstances that might seem to add complexity are in fact irrelevant. The *Yerushalmi* is cited to note that Rabbi Yehuda taught this *mishnah* *l'chahed bo et hatalmidim* — to sharpen the students — and indeed the exercise has the quality of a deliberate puzzle rather than a necessary elaboration of the law.

The three fundamental categories are: a woman who has been married and divorced (*yetomah b'chayei ha'av*, an emancipated minor despite her father's being alive); a true orphan (*yetomah*, whose father has died); and a *bogeret*, a woman who has reached adulthood. Within each of these categories, the *mishnah* varies circumstances that make no legal difference — whether she is a *bogeret* or a *na'arah*, whether the father is alive or dead — to arrive at nine cases. The key point is that once the essential condition is met, the additional factors are legally superfluous.

An important clarification: for a girl to achieve independence through marriage and divorce, the marriage must have been *nisuin*, full marriage, not merely *erusin*. If she became widowed or divorced during *erusin*, she never left her father's authority in the first place. Only genuine *nisuin* — *masi bito* — fully removes her from the father's domain, such that a subsequent divorce or widowhood renders her truly independent.

### Divorced Category

The first group focuses on the *yetomah b'chayei ha'av* — the woman who has been married and divorced while her father is still alive. Within this group, three variations are presented: she is a *bogeret* and also happens to be a *yetomah b'chayei ha'av* (emancipated through divorce); or she was a *na'arah*, became a *bogeret*, and is a *yetomah b'chayei ha'av*; or she is a *na'arah* who has not yet become a *bogeret* but is a *yetomah b'chayei ha'av*. In all three cases, the controlling factor is simply that she has been married and divorced. The other circumstances are irrelevant.

### Orphan Category

The second group focuses on the woman whose father has actually died — the true *yetomah*. Again, three variations: she is a *bogeret* and her father has died; she was a *na'arah*, became a *bogeret*, and her father died; or she is a *na'arah* who has not become a *bogeret* and whose father has died. In each case, what renders her vows binding is simply that there is no father.

### Adult Category

The third group focuses on the *bogeret* — the woman who has attained adulthood. Here the variation is somewhat different, since by definition this group is about the *bogeret* status itself. The cases are: she is a *bogeret* and her father is alive; she was a *na'arah* who became a *bogeret* and her father is alive. One might note that one could have generated a third variation — adding whether she was married and divorced — to produce a full twenty-seven case matrix, but the *mishnah* (and *Rabbi Yehuda*) stops at nine.

### Rabbi Yehuda

After presenting the nine cases, the *mishnah* adds a ruling attributed to Rabbi Yehuda: *af hamasi bito haktana v'nitalmana v'nitgarsha v'chazra etzlo* — even a man who marries off his minor daughter, and she becomes widowed or divorced and returns to him, *adayin hi na'arah* — even if she is still a *na'arah* and not a *bogeret*, since she has had *nisuin* and is now divorced, she is independent. Her vows are binding. This is not adding a new principle but rather illustrating what *yetomah b'chayei ha'av* means — the father is alive, she is still a minor, but the experience of full *nisuin* followed by divorce has emancipated her in the eyes of the law.

### Chachamim Simplify

Rav Yehuda cites Rav: *zo divrei Rabbi Yehuda, aval Chachamim omrim shalosh naarot nidreihen kayamim* — this elaborate enumeration is Rabbi Yehuda's teaching, but the Sages state the matter simply: three categories of women have binding vows — a *bogeret*, a *yetomah* (in the literal sense), and a *yetomah b'chayei ha'av* (divorced after *nisuin*). The *ra'n* quotes the *Yerushalmi* explicitly: *she'af Rabbi Yehuda lo amar ella l'chahed et hatalmidim* — Rabbi Yehuda's nine cases were pedagogical, not substantive. The Sages' three categories contain all nine within them.

---

## Konam Cases

### Konam 1

The following *mishnah* presents two *konam* formulations that test the edges of the husband's annulment authority. The first: *konam she'eini nehenet l'abba u'l'avicha im ose ani al picha* — a vow that the wife will receive no benefit from her own father or from her father-in-law, conditional on her husband benefiting from her. The two parts of the package work in opposite directions: if the husband eats what she produces, the *tnai* is triggered and she cannot benefit from either father — which constitutes *inui nefesh*; but if he does not eat, the *tnai* is not triggered, yet the vow sits over him as a reason not to eat from what she makes, which affects *devarim shebeino l'veina*.

### Package Analysis

One way or the other, this vow touches on something within the husband's domain: either it will produce *inui nefesh* for his wife, or it will constrain the marital dynamic between them. The first *mishnah* rules that he can annul it.

The second part of the *mishnah*'s first case raises a harder question. The wife says: *she'eini nehenet l'abba u'l'avicha im ose ani al pi abba u'al pi avicha* — I will receive no benefit from you (my husband) if my father or your father benefit from anything I do. Now, if the *tnai* is triggered, the result is clearly *devarim shebeino l'veina* and *inui nefesh* — she cannot benefit from her husband. But one might ask: can she simply go through life ensuring that neither father benefits from her, thereby never triggering the vow? If so, there is no *inui nefesh* and no *devarim shebeino l'veina* in the untriggered state — the husband cannot derive marital benefit from whatever she gives to her father or father-in-law, and they do not benefit from her. Why should he be able to annul?

The *Ra'n* explains that since it is so highly likely that the fathers will at some point benefit from her activity, the vow is treated as effectively anticipating a result that is *devarim shebeino l'veina* and *inui nefesh*, and therefore he may annul it. One might add — building on what we already saw in the previous *mishnah* — that the *mishnah* there already established that a husband can annul a vow before it takes effect. If we know that once the *tnai* is triggered the vow would be squarely within the categories he may annul, then the question of whether it is certain to be triggered may not be the threshold question at all; it is enough that if it takes effect it would be his to annul, and he may act on that potential.

Other *Rishonim* — the *Rosh* among them — prefer a different reading: the package as a whole, even in its untriggered state, is *devarim shebeino l'veina*. The *tnai* itself is structurally tied to the marital relationship — the triggering event is him benefiting from her, and the consequence is her being forbidden to benefit from him — and this interconnection places the entire construct within the scope of *beino l'veina*, not merely as an indirect annoyance but as something that directly configures the relationship between the two of them. On this reading, the *mishnah* is not relying on probabilistic anticipation but on a structural analysis of the vow itself.

A previous *mishnah* established that if she makes a vow about her father or his father's not benefiting from her, that is not *beino l'veina* — he may be indirectly upset, but it does not directly touch the marital relationship. Here, the difference is that her inability to give her father benefit is linked by *tnai* to a vow that is explicitly about the two of them. That linkage transforms the package into something *beino l'veina*, at least according to these *Rishonim*.

### Konam 2

The second *konam* is the *mishnah*'s bolder case: *menu'ah ani min haYehudim im meshameshetcha* — the benefit of marital relations with any Jewish man is forbidden to me if I have marital relations with you. This is clearly *beino l'veina* and *inui nefesh*. The *mishnah* rules he may annul it. The mechanism is worth noting: the vow does not directly say she will not have marital relations with her husband; it says the *hana'at tashmish* of all men — which, since it excludes no one, includes him — is forbidden to her. This formulation is permitted, whereas directly forbidding marital relations with him would be *batel* outright. As a vow of *hana'at tashmish*, the husband is included among those she may not be with if the *tnai* is triggered. So one way or another, the vow affects *tashmish* with her husband.

### Baraita Dispute

A *baraita* records a debate. The case is the first *konam* — the wife will not benefit from her father or father-in-law if the husband benefits from her. *Rabbi Natan omer lo yafer* — Rabbi Natan says the husband cannot annul it. *Chachamim omrim yafer* — the Sages say he can.

The *Ra'n* explains Rabbi Natan's position strikingly: Rabbi Natan holds that *hafara* — the annulment of a vow — can only be performed after the vow has actually taken effect. *Eina ba'al meifer ela im kein chal haneder* — the husband cannot be *meifer* unless and until the *neder* has *chal*. Therefore, in the first *konam* case, where the *tnai* has not yet been triggered and the vow has not yet taken effect, Rabbi Natan says he cannot annul it. The *chachamim* disagree and hold that the husband may be *meifer* even before the *neder* takes effect.

This position of Rabbi Natan is striking in context, because it seems to echo the view of Rabbi Yishmael that annulment timing should track the time of effect. Yet Rabbi Natan was not drawn into that earlier discussion. The two principles are related but not identical: Rabbi Yishmael was speaking about which party has the *power* to annul (father vs. husband) based on the woman's status at the time of effect; Rabbi Natan is speaking about whether annulment can occur at all before the vow takes effect. They are parallel intuitions operating in different analytical registers.

---

## Worldly Deprivation Story

### The Vow

The *gemara* now introduces a story that illuminates the debate between Rabbi Natan and the *chachamim* and then leads into a broader question about *hatarat nedarim*. A certain man forbade himself all benefit from the world — *asar hana'at d'alma alei* — conditional on his getting married before he had had the opportunity to learn *halachah*. His intent was to motivate himself: he wanted to spend a period of genuine study in *yeshiva* before marrying, and he took this vow as a spur to his own commitment. He was not merely saying he would try; he set a substantive goal of *taninan hilcheta* — mastering the essential corpus of legal learning.

### Temptation

He tried with every possible effort — *rehat b'agpei v'tuvlei*, running with his staff and flask, or a ladder and pulley, depending on the reading; all idioms for maximum exertion — but he was unable to accomplish the learning he had set out to do. He could not find the right teacher, or could not succeed in understanding, or the circumstances simply did not permit it. He remained unmarried, bound by the social and personal pressures of not having fulfilled his vow's condition. Then Rav Acha bar Rav Huna came and, as *piteihu* — he misled him — told him that since he had tried as hard as he could, he had satisfied his vow and could proceed to marry. The man did so.

Subsequently — and this is where the tar or mud comes in — Rav Acha bar Rav Huna apparently caused the man to realize, through some kind of practical intervention, that he might in fact be bound by his vow after all. The exact nature of the intervention is debated among the *Rishonim*: one reading has him throwing dirt on the man's garments, making him unable to get them cleaned without deriving benefit from the world; another reading has him applying tar to make the man unrecognizable. One plausible reading is that having gotten the man to marry, Rav Acha bar Rav Huna then made him feel that his vow had actually taken effect — i.e., that the marriage had triggered it — so that the man would now be in a position to seek a formal *hatarat nedarim*. The man's embarrassment in coming to Rav Chisda may explain why he concealed his identity.

### Appeal

The man came before Rav Chisda and laid out the situation: he had tried as hard as he could, he had taken a wife, and he was now uncertain whether his vow had taken effect. He asked to be released from it.

### Strategy

Rava then reflects on what Rav Acha bar Rav Huna had done and praises it: *man hakim le-mevad ki hai milta i lav Rav Aha bar Rav Huna* — who but Rav Acha bar Rav Huna would have been clever enough to set this up? The genius of the strategy, Rava explains, was that Rav Acha bar Rav Huna understood that the same *machloket* between Rabbi Natan and the *chachamim* that applies to *hafara* — whether the vow must take effect before annulment — *hacha nami paligi b'she'eila*, might also apply to *she'eilat chacham*, the process of a sage releasing someone from a vow. Rabbi Natan might hold that just as a husband cannot be *meifer* until the *neder* takes effect, so too a *chacham* cannot release a vow until it has taken effect. Rather than leave the man in the position of seeking release from a vow that had not yet definitively triggered, Rav Acha bar Rav Huna arranged for the vow to take effect — by having the man get married and thereby trigger the condition — so that the release could proceed cleanly even according to Rabbi Natan's view.

### Hatarat Debate

This raises the explicit question: is the debate between Rabbi Natan and the *chachamim* limited to *hafara* by the husband, or does it extend to *hatarat nedarim* by a *chacham*?

### Textual Proofs

Rav Papa answers: *mahloket b'hafara* — the debate between Rabbi Natan and the *chachamim* is only about *hafara*. Rabbi Natan holds *eina ba'al meifer ela im kein chal haneder*, and derives this from the verse *ve-hafrah ha-levanah* — playing on the similarity between *ve-hafrah* and *hafara*, and reading *ha-levanah* as *chal* the *bamah* (since *kol ha-noder ke-ilu boneh bamah*, one who vows is as if he builds a *bamah*): *hafara* operates when *chal* the vow, i.e., when the vow has taken effect. The *rabanan*, for their part, derive that *hafara* may occur even before the vow takes effect from the verse *mefer mahshevot arumim* — God annuls the schemes of the devious — meaning one can annul even a thought, even something not yet actualized.

### Universal Rule

However, when it comes to *she'eilah* — releasing through a *chacham* — *divrei ha-kol ein chacham matir klum ela im kein chal haneder*: everyone agrees, both Rabbi Natan and the *chachamim*, that a sage cannot release a vow until it has taken effect. The source is the verse *lo yahel devaro* — he may not violate his word — from which we derive that *others* may release his word for him; but the word *yahel* contains within it the word *chal*, teaching that the release operates only once there is *chal devaro*, once the vow has taken effect.

The logic of this is admittedly difficult. The mechanism of *hatarat nedarim* is that the *chacham* retrospectively identifies the vow as having been made *b'ta'ut* — in error — as though the person would not have wanted to take it had he foreseen the circumstances. Retroactive recharacterization of this kind should not, intuitively, require the vow to have taken effect. Yet the formal requirement stands: the process of *hatarat nedarim* has an independent formal structure, and that structure, according to all opinions, requires *chal* as a prerequisite. This is why Rav Acha bar Rav Huna's strategy was not merely playing it safe with respect to Rabbi Natan's position on *hafara* but was in fact necessary from the perspective of *hatarat nedarim* according to everyone.

---

---

# Nedarim 90

## Hatarat Nedarim

### Conditional Vows

We pick up in the middle of daf 90, approximately eleven lines down, at the words *leima mesayei lei*. The preceding discussion had introduced a complicated case from our *mishnah* involving the prohibition of *hana'ah* — benefit — and a *braita* that recorded the position of Rabbi Dosa concerning a woman who said, in effect, "I am forbidden to have sex with you if I have sex with you." The question raised was: why cannot the husband be *meifer* such a vow? After all, it seems clearly to fall within the categories of *inuy nefesh* or *devarim shebeino leveinah*.

### Rabbi Dosa's View

The *Gemara* established that Rabbi Dosa's position is that a husband cannot be *meifer* a *neder* until it has actually taken effect — *ad sheyachol haneder*. The *chachamim* disagree with this requirement.

One might initially find this surprising. Intuitively, *hafara* — the husband's annulment — seems to be precisely the kind of power that operates on an existing vow: the husband confronts a *neder* already in force and overrides it. It is *hatara* — annulment by a *chacham* — that seems to operate retroactively, going back to the original speech act and declaring it to have been made in error. One might therefore have expected the requirement of prior effectuation to apply more naturally to *hafara*, while *hatara* could plausibly function even before the vow has taken hold.

### Rav Acha's Story

This tension is illustrated by a story about Rav Acha bar Rav Huna, who tricked someone into triggering the *tenai* — the condition — of his vow so that it would become *chal*, and only then sought *hatara* from a *chacham*. The *Gemara* explained that Rav Acha bar Rav Huna believed the same debate that governs *hafara* applies to *hatara* as well, and he therefore wanted to satisfy the position of Rabbi Dosa by ensuring the *neder* had taken effect before seeking its dissolution.

### Rav Pappi Position

The *Gemara* then advances an even more far-reaching position, attributed to Rav Pappi: the debate between Rabbi Dosa and the *chachamim* applies only to *hafara*, but when it comes to *hatara*, there is no debate at all — even the *chachamim* agree that a *chacham* cannot be *matir* a *neder* until it has taken effect. This is striking precisely because it runs counter to the intuition outlined above. One would expect *hatara*, with its retroactive character, to be the procedure more capable of operating before effectuation, yet Rav Pappi places the stricter requirement there.

### Lo Yachel Devaro

Rav Pappi derives this from the verse *lo yachel devaro* — "he shall not profane his word" — the very source from which we learn that a *chacham* has the power to annul a *neder*. The word *yachel* shares its root with *chal*, to take effect. The implication, on this reading, is that the vow can only be voided after it has first been *chal*: it can only be un-*chal* once it has been *chal*.

---

## Konam She'eini

### Woman's Dual Vow

The *Gemara* now attempts to bring a supporting proof for Rav Pappi's position. The *braita* reads: a person says *konam she'eini ne'eneh li-Ploni* — a *konam* prohibiting benefit between himself and Ploni — and adds that whoever serves as the *chacham* to grant *hatara* on this *neder* will also be forbidden to him. The Ran reads the case as Ploni being prohibited from benefiting from the person making the vow, though the grammar of the vernacular formulation remains ambiguous even at this late stage of *Maseches Nedarim*.

What results is a kind of Möbius *neder*: two people are rendered *assur* — Reuven and the as-yet-unidentified *chacham* who will grant the *heter*. The *braita* then rules that one must first obtain *hatara* for the first prohibition — the one involving Reuven — and only afterward obtain *hatara* for the prohibition that thereby fell upon the *chacham* who granted it.

The mechanism is this: the first *chacham*, say Rabbi Cohen, is *matir* the *neder* as it pertains to Reuven. At the moment he does so, the condition is met and the prohibition against him personally takes effect. A second *chacham* must then be *matir* that prohibition. The two must be sequential, not simultaneous, because a *chacham* who is himself a party to the *neder* — a *nogea ba-davar* — cannot serve as its *matir*.

The *Gemara* argues from this *braita* in favor of Rav Pappi: the *braita* instructs that one must first resolve the prohibition against Reuven, allowing the prohibition against the *chacham* to take effect, and only then seek *hatara* for that second prohibition. This ordering proves that *hatara* requires the *neder* to have taken effect first. If *hatara* could work before a *neder* takes effect, one could simply approach a second *chacham* and preemptively undo the prohibition against the first *chacham* before that first *chacham* even renders his ruling.

### Rishon Reinterpreted

The *Gemara* deflects the proof by arguing that *rishon* in the *braita* need not mean "the first one you took" — it may simply mean "do one and then do the other." The *braita* need not be teaching that the first *neder* chronologically must be dissolved before the second; it may merely be instructing that the two dissolutions must be sequential rather than simultaneous, without specifying which comes first. This is, however, an unsatisfying reading of the *braita*, both because such a banal instruction scarcely requires a *braita* to communicate it, and because the word *rishon* in context naturally implies chronological priority.

### Yesh Breira Problem

There is a further objection that the *Gemara* does not raise, though it seems compelling in its own right. Even setting aside whether the *neder* against the *chacham* has yet taken effect, there is a *yesh breira* type of difficulty: at the time one seeks to preemptively undo the prohibition against the *chacham*, we do not yet know who that *chacham* will be. One might intend to go to Rabbi Cohen, but then change one's mind and go to a different *chacham*. How can one be *matir* a *neder* whose subject has not yet been determined? The parameters of the *neder* are themselves unknown. Why the *Gemara* does not invoke this argument — which seems to be the more obvious objection — and instead resorts to the weaker reinterpretation of *rishon*, is unclear. Nevertheless, the *Gemara* proceeds as it does.

---

## Nazir Triggered

### Neder Plus Nazir

The *Gemara* attempts a cleaner proof from a second *braita*: one declares *konam she'eini ne'eneh le-Ploni* — a *konam* prohibiting benefit from Reuven — and adds that if this *neder* is ever dissolved, he will become a *nazir*. The *braita* rules that one must first be *nish'al* — seek *hatara* — on the *neder*, and only afterward seek *hatara* on the *nezirut*. This case is far less ambiguous than the previous one. The two objects are clearly distinct: the *neder* and the *nezirut*. There is no question of which is *rishon* and which is *sheini*.

### Order Proof

Why must they be resolved in that order? Because the *nezirut* does not yet exist when the *neder* is first made — it is triggered only when the *neder* is dissolved. The *braita*'s instruction to first obtain *hatara* on the *neder* before obtaining *hatara* on the *nezirut* presupposes that the *nezirut* must actually have come into existence before it can be dissolved. This appears to be a straightforward proof that *hatara* requires the *neder* to be in effect.

### Reverse Order

The *Gemara* asks: according to the view that *hatara* can work before a *neder* takes effect, why not dissolve the *nezirut* first? One could approach a *chacham* and say: I undertook *nezirut* contingent upon a certain condition being met, I regret having done so, and I wish it not to take effect when that condition is triggered. The fact that the *braita* insists on the opposite order seems to prove that the condition must be triggered — the *nezirut* must become *chal* — before *hatara* is possible.

### Rabbi Natan

The *Gemara* responds: this *braita* may represent only the position of Rabbi Natan, not a consensus ruling. The *braita* is admittedly taught anonymously, which ordinarily suggests broader agreement. Nevertheless the *Gemara* maintains that the proof is limited — the *braita* establishes clearly that this one position requires effectuation before *hatara*, but it does not demonstrate that the view is universally held, as Rav Pappi claimed.

---

## Rav Pappi Alt

### Mareimar Report

The *Gemara* now introduces an entirely different version of Rav Pappi's position. Ravina reports in the name of Mareimar, who transmitted it in the name of Rav Pappi: the debate between Rabbi Dosa and the *chachamim* applies only to *hafara*, but when it comes to *hatara*, everyone agrees that a *chacham* can be *matir* the *neder* even before it takes effect. This is the exact inverse of the previous version of Rav Pappi. Both versions agree that the dispute is limited to *hafara*; they disagree only on which direction the consensus regarding *hatara* runs.

This second version actually accords more naturally with the intuition developed at the outset. Since *hatara* operates by retroactively identifying an error in the original speech act, there is no obvious reason it cannot be applied to a speech act that has not yet produced a binding effect. If anything, the retroactive character of *hatara* makes it more suited to early intervention, not less.

### Emphasis on Divro

This version of Rav Pappi also draws from *lo yachel devaro*, but with a different emphasis. Where the first version stressed the word *yachel* — implying that the *neder* must first be *chal* before it can be undone — this version stresses *devaro*, "his word." The moment a person utters the vow, the speech act itself exists and is available for a *chacham* to address. The effectuation of the *neder* is not what renders it subject to *hatara*; the act of speaking is sufficient.

### Counterargument

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this version by reinstating the same *braitot* considered earlier. First, the *braita* about the dual *konam* affecting Reuven and the dissolving *chacham*: if *hatara* is available before effectuation, why must the dissolutions occur in sequence at all? The *Gemara* repeats its answer — *rishon* simply means one before the other, not necessarily the first chronologically — which is equally unsatisfying here.

The second *braita* about the *neder* and the conditional *nezirut* poses the real difficulty. The *Gemara* asks: according to this version of Rav Pappi, why cannot one dissolve the *nezirut* first, before the *neder* is even dissolved and the *nezirut* triggered? The *Gemara* pronounces *tiyuvta* — a refutation. This version of Rav Pappi appears to be defeated by the *braita*, which requires that the *neder* be dissolved and the *nezirut* triggered before the *nezirut* itself can be dissolved.

### Conditional vs Postponed

Here a conceptually important distinction emerges. The *braita* about the *nazir* case involves a genuinely conditional *neder* — one whose effectuation is contingent upon the occurrence of a specific event that may or may not come to pass. This is categorically different from a *neder* whose effect has been postponed — for example, a vow stated to take effect in thirty days. In the postponed case, effectuation is certain; the *neder* will definitely become *chal*, it simply has not done so yet. In the conditional case, there remains a genuine question whether the condition will ever be triggered and whether the *neder* will ever take effect at all.

The argument of Rabbi Natan and the supporting *braitot* may be specifically addressing the conditional case. If a *neder* is conditional and might never take effect, it is unclear what a *chacham* is dissolving — there may be nothing there to dissolve. By contrast, a postponed *neder* that will certainly take effect at a future date represents a genuine vow from the moment of its utterance, and the question of whether *hatara* can be performed before the appointed date may remain genuinely open.

---

## Halakhic Ruling

### Ran's Ruling

The *Ran* at the top of 90b states the *halakha* explicitly: *le-inyan she'eila kaima lan k'Rav Pappa d'lo machlokes b'hafara aval b'she'ela divrei hakol ein chacham matir ad sheyachol haneder* — when it comes to *hatara*, we rule like the first version of Rav Pappi that everyone agrees a *chacham* cannot dissolve a *neder* until it has taken effect. The *Ran* notes that the great authorities ruled this way *l'chumra*, as the strict position, though he acknowledges that another position exists maintaining the debate applies equally to *hatara*.

With respect to *hafara*, the case is clearer. The earlier *sugya* — involving a woman who took a vow while married but whose vow took effect thirty days later after her divorce, with Rabbi Akiva ruling that the husband could annul the vow at the time it was taken — already implicitly established that we rule like the *chachamim* that *hafara* can occur before the *neder* takes effect. The story of the man tricked into triggering his *tenai* might seem to complicate this — the *chacham* there was concerned to satisfy the position of Rabbi Natan — but the *Ran* notes that the overwhelming consensus of the *Gemara* is that we do not rule like Rabbi Natan even by *hafara*.

### Postponed Vows

The *Ran* also addresses the question of postponed, as opposed to conditional, vows for purposes of *hatara*. He records two views. One position holds that a *chacham* may dissolve a postponed *neder* even before its appointed time arrives, reasoning that since the *neder* will certainly take effect, there is effectively already a *neder* in existence — it has merely been deferred. The other position holds that even in such a case, since the person has not yet become *assur*, a *chacham* cannot yet be *matir*. The *Ran* states his preference for the first view: *sevara kama tritza tefei* — there is a meaningful conceptual difference between a conditional *neder*, which might never materialize, and a postponed *neder*, which will certainly take effect.

The practical distinction turns on how we understand Rav Pappi's ruling. If the prohibition on *hatara* before effectuation is grounded in the uncertainty of the conditional case — we cannot treat something as a *neder* when we do not know whether it will ever function as one — then once the outcome is certain, even a pre-effectuation *hatara* may be permissible. If, however, the ruling is understood more literally — a *chacham* simply cannot act until the *assur* actually exists — then the certainty of future effectuation is irrelevant, and *hatara* must wait in all cases. The general ruling follows Rav Pappi: *hatara* requires effectuation, with the question of postponed vows remaining subject to the views just described.

### Transition

With that, we arrive at the final *mishnah* of the tractate — a *mishnah* whose *halakhic* implications extend far beyond the narrow domain of *nedarim* and whose reach into questions of marriage, divorce, belief, and human dignity makes it among the most consequential texts in the entire *masekhet*.

---

## Women's Divorce

### First Stage

The *mishnah* opens: *barishona hayu omrim, shalosh nashim yotz'ot ve-notlot ketubbah* — they used to say that three categories of women are granted divorce and collect their *ketubbah*. This opening formula signals what will follow: a two-stage ruling in which an initial policy is reversed. The three women are those who bring claims that, under the initial ruling, were believed without requiring independent corroboration. Not only are they forced to divorce, but the divorce is treated as no fault of their own — hence they receive their *ketubbah* as well.

### Tamei Claim

The first category is *ha-omeret teme'a ani lach* — a woman who tells her husband "I am *tame'ah* to you." This means either that she was violated — which would be directly relevant if her husband is a *kohen*, since even a raped woman becomes forbidden to her *kohen* husband — or that she committed adultery. But if the woman committed adultery, why would she receive her *ketubbah*? This prompts the *Gemara* to conclude that the receipt of the *ketubbah* applies specifically to the case of an *eshet kohen* who was raped: she was the victim, bears no culpability, and is therefore entitled to her *ketubbah*. The initial policy of believing her, however, presumably extends to both cases — *ketubbah* or not.

Underlying this policy is the principle of *shavya nafshah chatikhah de-issura*: by making this declaration, the woman effectively defines herself as forbidden. One might also argue that the initial policy was simply grounded in the assumption that a person would not make such a claim without it being true. The husband may insist he does not believe her, but if in practice he does believe her, that becomes a separate problem we will return to. At this first stage, the *mishnah* says: we believe her, we compel divorce, and — in the *kohen* case — we require the *ketubbah* to be paid.

### Shamayim Beini

The second category is *shamayim beini u-veinecha* — "heaven is between us." This phrase signals a claim that only God can attest to, meaning it pertains to some aspect of their intimate life that no external witness could observe. The *Gemara* understands this as a claim that the husband is incapable of *yoreh ke-chetz* — of normal ejaculation — and consequently cannot give the wife children. She is therefore demanding a divorce on the grounds that she cannot have children with him.

One might object: since a woman is not commanded in *pru u-rvu*, why should her inability to have children constitute grounds for a forced divorce? The *Gemara* in *Ketubot* addresses this and concludes that a woman has a legitimate human interest in having children — framed in part as a concern for who will care for her in old age — and that this constitutes a sufficient claim. It is worth noting that the claim here is not about the *mitzvah* of *onah*, of marital intimacy itself. Even if the husband cannot produce children, the couple can presumably have marital relations; it is specifically the inability to give her children that drives the claim. That the failure to fulfill *onah* is not itself raised as grounds for divorce is an interesting implication.

Under the initial policy, the wife is believed on this claim as well, the divorce is compelled, and the *ketubbah* is paid — again on the assumption that she has been wronged and is not at fault.

### Estrangement

The *Ran* raises the possibility that *shamayim beini u-veinecha* carries a broader meaning than the *Gemara*'s technical reading. He cites the *Yerushalmi*, which reads the phrase as a claim about marital distance: *k'ma d'Shamayim rechuka min ar'a, kach hi iteta rechika m'ba'alah* — just as the heaven is distant from the earth, so is this wife distant from her husband. On this reading, the claim need not be specifically about the husband's physiological incapacity; a general assertion of profound marital estrangement would itself constitute a cognizable basis for divorce, and the wife would be believed on that claim alone.

The *Ran* acknowledges that the Babylonian *Gemara* understands the phrase as referring specifically to *yoreh ke-chetz*, and supports this with a paraphrase: *Elokim eid beini u-veinecha d'kushta kamina she-davar zeh eino yadua bo ela la-Shem* — God alone is witness to this, for this matter is known to none but God. On the *Gemara*'s reading, the claim must be about something that only God can testify to, and something specific — namely, the inability to have children. Nevertheless, the *Ran* notes that according to the *Yerushalmi*, the language *efshar d'lashon Hashamayim beini l'veinecha kolel hakol* — perhaps the phrase encompasses both ideas: the physiological claim and the claim of estrangement.

The *Rambam* bridges these positions in a different way. He frames the woman's claim in terms of marital intimacy itself: she declares that she finds her husband so intolerable that she cannot bear to have sex with him. This formulation makes the claim not about whether children are possible but about whether marital life is sustainable. The *Rambam* holds that no person can be compelled to remain in a marriage in which intimate relations have become impossible to tolerate, and that principle grounds the entitlement to divorce.

### Nezurah

The third category is *netulah ani min ha-Yehudim* — she has taken a vow prohibiting herself from having relations with any Jew. This is why the case appears in *Maseches Nedarim*. But the logic requires unpacking. If she has forbidden herself relations with all Jews, she will be unable to have relations even after the divorce — so why does the marriage need to end?

The answer is that if a woman has reached the point of taking a vow of this extremity, we assume she cannot tolerate marital relations. Whether the cause is physiological, psychological, or otherwise, the assumption is that something has driven her to this drastic declaration, and it would be unconscionable to compel her to remain in the marriage under such circumstances. Why, one might ask, cannot the husband simply annul the vow through *hafara* — since it is a *devarim shebeino leveinah* — and continue the marriage? And in fact, as we will see, under the revised ruling, that is precisely what happens with respect to his portion. But under the initial ruling, we believe her claim as to the circumstances that led to the vow and accordingly compel the divorce.

---

## Reversal & Consequences

### Chazru Lomar

The *mishnah* continues: *chazru lomar* — they reconsidered and revised the ruling. This formula signals a deliberate reversal of the initial policy. The same three categories of women who had been believed and given both divorce and *ketubbah* are now treated differently across the board.

### Natna Eineha

The stated reason for the reversal is *shelo tehei ishah notenet einehah be-acher u-mekaklelet al ba'alah* — that a woman should not set her eye on another man and thereby ruin her marriage. The concern is that the original policy, however well-intentioned, created a mechanism for abuse: a woman who wished to leave her husband for another relationship could simply manufacture one of the three qualifying claims, obtain a divorce together with her *ketubbah*, and face no adverse consequences for doing so.

### New Requirements

Under the revised ruling, *ha-omeret teme'a ani lach tavi ra'ayah li-devareha* — a woman who claims she is forbidden to her husband must now bring proof. If no proof is forthcoming, the couple remains married. For the claim of *shamayim beini u-veinecha*, the ruling is *ya'aseh derekh bakashah* — the husband is asked to make efforts to placate her or address her grievance. The *Yerushalmi* suggests something as concrete as making her a fine meal; the *Gemara* understands this as an attempt at reconciliation, whether through marital counseling or similar means.

### No Divorce/Ketubah

For the case of *ha-nezurah min ha-Yehudim*, the ruling under revision is that the husband annuls his portion of the *neder* — *yafer le-chelko* — since it pertains to *devarim shebeino leveinah*, and they continue marital relations. If she is eventually divorced for other reasons, she remains bound by the vow as it applies to all other Jews, since the husband's annulment covers only his own portion. The practical result is that we are in effect saying we do not believe her — or at least that we will not act as if we believe her. If we are not going to force a divorce based on her claim, then we will require her to continue in the marriage as though the underlying concern did not exist.

What is notable is how binary this treatment is. One might have expected a middle position: believe her enough to compel a divorce, but not enough to grant a *ketubbah*. That would impose a financial cost on making the claim while still providing relief to a woman in a genuinely intolerable situation. This is indeed the position of the *Rambam* when a woman says she finds her husband physically intolerable: he rules that she receives a divorce but forfeits her *ketubbah*, the financial disincentive serving as a filter against bad-faith claims while preserving a genuine avenue of relief. That middle position is not adopted here. Under the revised ruling it is all or nothing: either we believe her fully, or we do not believe her at all, and there is no divorce.

### Agunah Problem

The real-world consequences of this reversal are far-reaching. A woman who genuinely cannot tolerate her marriage — whether because of estrangement, because her husband has treated her terribly, or because the marriage has broken down in every meaningful sense — finds herself without recourse. This is the dynamic that produces the *agunah* situation in its various forms. Courts invoking *shalom bayit* as a response to such claims are in fact carrying forward the logic of *chazru lomar* — the reversal itself.

It is crucial to be precise here: what the *mishnah* is actually saying, in its initial ruling, is that these conditions are genuinely intolerable and warrant divorce. The only thing that shifted in the revision is the question of proof and the fear of abuse. But the downstream consequence is that the framework of "try to work it out" and "we are not going to believe you" becomes the default response to women's claims of marital breakdown — even in cases where evidence eventually becomes available, or where the claims are clearly substantiated.

The asymmetry is also worth noting. A man who wishes to leave his marriage may simply do so, within the limits of *beit din* authority; even *beit Shammai* requires cause, but the threshold for the husband is structurally lower. A woman who wishes to leave must overcome the presumption created by *chazru lomar*, no matter how compelling her situation. That asymmetry, rooted in a polygamous social structure in which a man can have multiple wives and a woman can have only one husband, is the foundation upon which all of this rests.

---

## Shavya Nafsha

### Non-Belief Framework

This brings us to what is perhaps the deepest and most philosophically challenging problem raised by the *mishnah*. The revised ruling says we do not believe the woman. But what does it mean for *halakha* to officially refuse to believe something that may be true — or that the husband himself believes to be true?

The principle of *shavya nafshah chatikhah de-issura* holds that a person's own declaration can create a binding prohibition for themselves, regardless of whether witnesses can corroborate the claim. One hundred witnesses may testify that a piece of meat is *kosher*; if I declare it to be *chazir*, I am bound by my own declaration and may not eat it. My self-assessment creates a binding legal reality for me, independent of the broader legal determination. So here: if a woman declares herself forbidden to her husband — whether through a claim of adultery, rape, or a vow — why does *chazru lomar* dissolve the force of *shavya nafsha*? And if the husband himself believes his wife and says so, does not his belief create a *shavya* for him as well?

### Hafkat Kiddushin

One answer proposed by the *rishonim* is *afkinu rabbanan le-kiddushin mineih* — the rabbis retroactively annul the *kiddushin*. On this approach, in those cases where the woman's claim is in fact true, the rabbis exercise their authority to undo the marriage from the outset, which means the *kiddushin* never had legal force, and accordingly neither the prohibition that would normally result from adultery — nor the concern about *shavya nafsha* — ever attaches. The husband and wife continue living together because they are, retroactively, as though never halakhically married.

This is a radical position. And the *rishonim* themselves note its limits: it does not resolve the case of an *eshet kohen* who slept with a non-Jew while married, since the prohibition on her is not derived from the marriage itself but from a separate status that *hafkat kiddushin* cannot undo.

A second, somewhat less radical answer focuses on the specific textual source of the *kohen* prohibition. The verse forbidding a *kohen* from living with a woman who has been defiled speaks to the *kohen* — it is his prohibition. The woman herself has no separate Torah prohibition against living with her *kohen* husband as a result of her status. So even if she knows she has become forbidden to him according to his *issur*, she is not herself in violation by continuing to live with him. His prohibition and hers are asymmetric. This answer, however, applies only to the *kohen* case and does nothing to resolve the adultery scenario involving a *yisrael*.

What appears ultimately to be the underlying position — even if the *rishonim* do not state it so starkly — is that *halakha* defines reality. If the legal system has determined as a matter of policy that this class of claims is not to be believed, then the legal effect of those claims is suspended. The *shavya nafsha* principle may itself be overridden when the relevant declaration falls into a category that *halakha* has ruled non-cognizable. The declaration simply has no legal traction within the system that has decided not to credit it.

### Tosafot Solution

*Tosafot* addresses the problem of the husband directly and practically. At the end of the *Tosafot*, in the widest lines, *Tosafot* states: *d'af le-mishnah achronah im omeret ishah teme'ah ani lakh v'amar ha-ba'al she-ma'amina* — even under the revised ruling, if the wife says "I am *tame'ah* to you" and the husband says that he believes her, she becomes forbidden to him through his *shavya*. And if subsequently the wife reverses her claim and says it was in fact under duress — *b'ones* — so that perhaps his *shavya* should dissolve along with the underlying claim, *Tosafot* rules that once he is bound by *shavya*, he cannot undo it through her retraction.

*Tosafot* then records a further position: *v'yesh omrim d'mshamtinan lei al she-garam she-tei'aser ishto alav* — some authorities say we place the husband in *cherem* if he chooses to believe his wife, because by doing so he effectively forces a divorce upon her against her will, in violation of *cherem de-Rabbeinu Gershom*. The wife, under the revised ruling, has a legal right to remain married; she is believed when she says she wants to continue the marriage, even if she made a contrary claim previously. If the husband invokes *shavya nafsha* based on her prior claim, he is unilaterally imposing a divorce on a woman who does not wish to be divorced, which is precisely what *Rabbeinu Gershom* forbade.

The practical implication is that the husband is counseled: do not say you believe her. Not because the law prohibits him from having private beliefs, but because if he articulates that belief, he will find himself in *cherem*. The threat of *cherem* operates as a kind of legal prophylactic against the problem of *shavya*.

### Official vs Real

What *Tosafot*'s ruling reveals is an attempt at communal policy-making that navigates a genuinely impossible tension. The law officially does not believe the woman. The husband, who lives with her, who knows her, may believe her completely. But the legal system says: as long as you do not officially say you believe her, *shavya* does not engage and the marriage can legally continue. And the community reinforces this by threatening *cherem* against anyone who invokes *shavya nafsha* in this context.

This is the point at which *halakha* and lived reality come into sharpest conflict. A husband who privately believes his wife was raped, or that she committed adultery, or that their marriage is genuinely broken, is told: for the legal system to function as it has been designed to function, you may not say this publicly, and if you do, you bear the consequences. The pastoral and psychological dimensions of this — how a couple is supposed to rebuild or continue a marriage under such conditions, how a woman is supposed to process her own experience within a framework that officially denies its legal relevance — are largely left unaddressed by the formal *halakhic* discussion. That silence is itself significant.

---

---

# Nedarim 91

## Belief & Disbelief

### Mishnah Overview

The daf before us is 91, the last daf of Nedarim, and we pick up at 91b at the *gemara* following the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* presents a powerful set of cases: a woman who claims she has been raped, or who claims that she committed adultery, or who claims that she is otherwise unable to remain with her husband — and the question is whether she is believed. The *mishnah* wrestles with the consequences of that belief, particularly regarding the *ketubah*.

### First Position

The opening position of the *mishnah* — the *mishnah rishona* — holds that the woman is believed, and that her belief extends even to the *ketubah*. There is no concern that she might be fabricating her claim in order to force a divorce; she is credited fully, even though believing her provides her with no financial disincentive to lie.

### Second Position

The later position — the *mishnah acharona* — reverses course. There, the *rabbanan* express concern that the woman is inventing the entire account in order to extract a *get*, and therefore she is not believed in any of these cases.

### Rambam Middle Path

Between these two poles lies the Rambam's middle position, highly significant in its practical implications: if a woman declares that she finds her husband so intolerable that she cannot bear to live with him and cannot maintain intimate relations, the Rambam holds that she is believed — but she does not collect her *ketubah*. Critically, the Rambam rules that the husband is compelled to grant her a *get*. This position, which has largely been abandoned in the *Ashkenazi* world, bears directly on contemporary *agunah* discussions as a path that has been foregone.

---

## Terumah & Doubt

### Terumah Question

The *gemara* opens with a *she'elah*: in the case of a wife of a *kohen* who claims she was raped — which is the paradigm case for the *mishnah*, since rape renders such a woman forbidden to her *kohen* husband while it would not render the wife of a *Yisrael* forbidden — and who is not believed according to the *mishnah acharona*, what is her status with respect to *terumah*? Can she continue eating *terumah*? How thoroughly do we disbelieve her?

### Rav Sheshet

*Rav Sheshet* rules that she continues to eat *terumah*. To act otherwise — to tell her to refrain from *terumah* — would be to communicate to the world that she has a doubtful status, that there is a *safek* regarding her. We cannot adopt a position that formally says we do not believe her and simultaneously signal to the outside world that we half-believe her.

### Shelo Totzi La'az

The operative concern is *shelo totzi la'az al baneha* — that casting doubt on her status will raise questions about her children's legitimacy as *kohanim*. If she is actually forbidden to her husband and subsequently bears children, those children would be *chalalim*. Any public signal of ambiguity regarding her status would therefore taint the status of children born during the marriage. So *Rav Sheshet* insists: we must project a complete, unambiguous position that she is fully permitted to her husband.

### Rava Position

*Rava* disagrees. He rules that she should not eat *terumah*. His reasoning is that abstaining from *terumah* does not necessarily communicate a problematic status to the outside world — *efshar d'achla chullin*, she might simply be eating the *chulin* food in the house rather than the *terumah*. The practical oddity of this logic is readily apparent: it is hardly inconspicuous when someone consistently avoids a particular category of food, and those who visit would certainly notice. Nevertheless, that is *Rava*'s position.

### Rava's Qualification

*Rava* adds, however, that even *Rav Sheshet* would agree that if she becomes widowed or divorced, she should stop eating *terumah*. Why? Because while her husband was alive and she was eating *terumah*, any children born during that period will be assumed by observers to have been born under a period of her uncontested status. If, after her husband's death, people notice she has stopped eating *terumah*, they will naturally assume something occurred *after* the husband died — a subsequent rape or other incident — and that will not retroactively cast doubt on the children born during the marriage. Thus, *Rav Sheshet*'s policy of protecting her status for the sake of the children can, in *Rava*'s view, be suspended once the marriage has ended, since the temporal gap protects the children's status regardless.

Yet this is a deeply strange position. *Rava* is saying that we should instruct this woman to begin adopting a practice that will broadcast to the community that she has a problematic status. The underlying tension is significant: *Rava* is unable to fully set aside his discomfort with entirely disbelieving her. He cannot fully let go of the possibility that her claim might be true, and that unease resurfaces once she leaves the marriage.

What is most striking is that both *Rav Sheshet* and *Rava*, despite their disagreement on practical policy, are each reflecting a residual uncertainty. Neither has fully made peace with the position that she simply is not believed. *Rav Sheshet* sets aside his discomfort for reasons of public policy; *Rava* cannot. But both are signaling that the doubts have not been fully extinguished.

---

## Standards of Belief

### Cheskas Tahara

Setting aside the question — which arose in the previous discussion — of *shavya nafshah chaticha de'issura*, of what she herself knows in her own mind, it is worth stepping back to recall that it is not so straightforward that a woman's self-report should be automatically credited to change her status. Consider the analogy: if a pile of grain had an established *chezkas tahara* and a single witness reported that a *tamei* person touched it, there would be a genuine question about *eid echad ne'eman be'issurin* versus the force of an existing *chazaka*. The question of whether testimony is effective when the subject is *beyado* — within the person's own control or knowledge — versus when it is not, adds further complexity. Personal status raises these questions with even greater intensity. It is simply not self-evident that a woman's own testimony about herself is sufficient, for all purposes, to change her status vis-à-vis the rest of the world.

### Proof Threshold

This raises the deeper threshold question: what standard of proof is actually required to establish that a woman is forbidden to her husband, or to compel a husband to divorce his wife? If one were asked *ab initio*, the answer would not be "whatever she says is sufficient." So when the *mishnah rishona* declares that she is believed and the *mishnah acharona* declares she is not, the shift may be less dramatic than it appears. The bigger structural problem, as noted previously, is that according to her own words she is claiming to be engaged in an *aveira* by continuing to live with her husband — which makes it difficult to understand how we can compel her to remain in the marriage regardless. That tension does not disappear simply because we formally decline to believe her.

### Takana Logic

One way to understand the shift from the *mishnah rishona* to the *mishnah acharona* is as a *takana* — a rabbinic enactment that simply overrides the default rule and refuses to credit her testimony regardless of what the *halacha* would otherwise require. The alternative understanding is that once the possibility of ulterior motive has been raised — once the concern of *shema einah natna be'acher* has been introduced — this is enough to reassess her believability altogether, not as an override, but as a genuine recalculation that brings us back to the status quo of her being permitted to her husband. Under this reading, there is no *takana* at all; it is simply a recognition that once motive and veracity are called into question, she no longer meets the threshold of credibility needed to change her status.

Both *Rav Sheshet* and *Rava*, as noted, suggest that whatever the mechanism, the doubts have not fully dissipated — and that lingering uncertainty is what animates their respective positions on *terumah*.

---

## Ones & Ketubah

### Rav Pappa Quiz

*Rav Pappa* reports that *Rava* posed a question to them as a kind of test: if the wife of a *kohen* was raped and is therefore forbidden to continue living with her *kohen* husband and must be divorced — does she collect her *ketubah* or not? The intuitive answer would seem to be yes, since it is not her fault. But the *hava amina* runs as follows: since *ones* — rape — in the case of the wife of a *kohen* is equivalent in its legal consequences to willful adultery in the case of the wife of a *Yisrael*, in the sense that both require a divorce, perhaps she should receive no *ketubah*, just as the willfully adulterous wife of a *Yisrael* receives none.

### Woman's Counter

The *gemara* frames the counter-argument in a striking way. Rather than resting simply on the absence of fault, it has the woman say, in effect: *ana hazina* — I am actually fit. My personal status has not been compromised. Even after being raped, I remain fully eligible to marry a *Yisrael*. *Degavra hu denistachfa sadeh* — it is you, the husband, whose field has been flooded. The disability that requires the divorce is a function of your status as a *kohen*, not of any fault of mine. The *gemara* is not suggesting the woman bears any moral blame — the *Torah* itself declares *velanaarah lo ta'aseh davar*. Rather, the question being probed is: when divorce is required and neither party is at fault, does the *ketubah* attach? And the answer the *gemara* works toward is that since the cause of the divorce is rooted in the husband's status as a *kohen*, it is, to some degree, attributable to him.

### Resolution

The resolution comes from the *mishnah* itself. The *mishnah* discusses a woman who says *tme'ah ani lach* — "I am forbidden to you" — and rules that she has a *ketubah*. The *gemara* works through the possible cases: if she is the wife of a *Yisrael* claiming willful adultery, she would not receive a *ketubah*; if she is the wife of a *Yisrael* claiming rape, she is not forbidden to her husband at all, so there is no question. The only case that makes sense of the *mishnah* is the wife of a *kohen* claiming rape. And the *mishnah* rules she receives her *ketubah*. *Rav Pappa* and the other students informed *Rava* that they could prove the answer from the *mishnah* itself — and they passed the test.

---

## Gerashtani Question

### Case Intro

The *gemara* now turns to a new question: *amra leh lebaal gerashtani* — a woman says directly to her husband's face, "You divorced me," without producing a *get*. She claims the *get* was lost, but insists the divorce occurred. What is her status?

### Rav Hamnuna

*Rav Hamnuna* reasons from the *mishnah*. Even according to the *mishnah acharona*, which rules that a woman is not believed when she claims rape or adultery, the reason for the disbelief is that *hatam hu demeshakra* — there we suspect her of lying. What enables her to lie in those cases? *Deyad'a debaa'la lo yada bah* — she knows that her husband has no way of independently verifying her claim. She knows he cannot contradict her. This, combined with the possibility that she harbors ulterior motives — *shema einah natna be'acher* — is what makes her statement insufficiently credible. But in the case of *gerashtani*, even if she has motivations to be free of the marriage, *hayad'a bah* — the husband would know whether or not he gave her a *get*. A man does not forget whether he divorced his wife. And therefore, *chazaka ein isha me'iza paneha bifnei ba'alah* — there is a presumption that a woman will not brazenly lie to her husband's face about something he knows to be false. In such a case, *Rav Hamnuna* rules, she is believed.

### Husband Knows

The deeper implication of *Rav Hamnuna*'s position is significant: the *mishnah acharona*'s refusal to believe the woman is not an absolute, overriding *takana* that silences her in every conceivable circumstance. Rather, the *mishnah acharona* has raised doubts and questions about her credibility in specific types of cases. Those doubts can be overcome where there are stronger countervailing reasons to believe her. The *chazaka* of *ein isha me'iza paneha bifnei ba'alah* supplies such a reason.

---

## Rava Counter

### Shame Logic

*Rava* challenges this analysis. He argues that even the *mishnah rishona*'s decision to believe the woman did not reflect a general disposition to credit whatever she says. Rather, it rested on specific circumstances that made her claim particularly credible — namely, that nobody would make a claim of rape or adultery if it were false, because even for the victim, even in a case where she bears no moral blame, such a disclosure carries an element of shame and vulnerability. The *mishnah rishona* believed her *davka* because of that logic — and even then, the *mishnah acharona* ultimately chose not to believe her.

### Motivation Override

For the case of *gerashtani*, *Rava* disagrees with *Rav Hamnuna*. He acknowledges the force of *chazaka ein isha me'iza paneha*, but argues that when a woman is sufficiently motivated to exit the marriage — *dezimnin detakif lah min gavra* — she can summon the resolve to confront her husband directly and lie to his face. The desire to leave the marriage, when powerful enough, overrides the *chazaka* that she would be too ashamed to lie in his presence.

### Absolute Position

This raises the further question of whether *Rava*'s position amounts to saying that the woman can never be believed once we have reached the *mishnah acharona*. It is possible that *Rava*'s view has a categorical dimension: given that even in the *mishnah rishona*, where the case for believing her was at its strongest — where there was genuine *davka* reason to credit her — the *mishnah acharona* nevertheless refused to do so, *Rava* may be unwilling to permit any exceptions. Having established a regime of non-belief, he may hold that it admits no case-by-case reappraisal.

---

## Testing Positions

### Hashamayim Case

*Rav Mesharshya* raises a challenge to *Rava* from the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* includes the case of a woman who says *hashamayim beini u'veinecha* — "heaven is between you and me." As the *Bavli* reads this phrase, it is a claim about the husband's inability to father children — specifically, a claim that he cannot ejaculate with sufficient force. The *mishnah rishona* believes her in this case. But if *Rava* is correct that the *mishnah rishona* only believed the woman in cases where her claim was intrinsically credible due to the shame involved in making it, how does the *hashamayim* case fit? Here she is saying something embarrassing about *him*, not about herself. There is no shame to her in making this claim, and yet the *mishnah rishona* credits her. This seems to undercut *Rava*'s reading of the *mishnah rishona*'s rationale.

### Fertility Claim

*Rava* responds that the case is more specific than it appears.
