For the woman to invoke *hashamayim beini u'veinecha* in the relevant sense, she cannot simply speak in vague terms — she must articulate explicitly the nature of the deficiency, specifically that he *ein yorek ke-ḥetz*, that he cannot ejaculate with the force of an arrow. And *Rava* argues that this explicit formulation — describing intimate physiological detail about her husband in front of a *beit din* — is itself something that she would not say if it were not true. Even though the embarrassment attaches to him rather than to her, the sheer intimacy and specificity of the statement, made in a public judicial forum, is such that she would not articulate it unless it were accurate.

### Rava Reasserts

Thus *Rava* reasserts his position: the *mishnah rishona* believed her across all its cases *davka* because each case presented a specific and identifiable reason to credit the claim. In no case did the *mishnah rishona* operate from a general presumption of female credibility. And in each case, notwithstanding those reasons, the *mishnah acharona* declined to believe her.

### Acharona Test

The *gemara* then runs the test in the other direction: if *Rav Hamnuna* is correct that the *mishnah acharona*'s regime of disbelief admits exceptions when the husband would know the truth of the matter, should the *hashamayim* case also constitute an exception under the *mishnah acharona*? After all, the husband knows whether or not *ein yorek ke-ḥetz* applies to him — he is the one to whom it is happening. If she is willing to say that to his face, and he would know whether she was lying, should she not be believed even under the *mishnah acharona*?

### Self-Conviction

*Rav Hamnuna*'s position here is that she would not be believed even in this case under the *mishnah acharona*, because *michezi debe'iah yada* — while the husband may be aware of what occurs during the act of intercourse itself, *beyoreh ke-ḥetz lo yada* — he does not have independent clarity about the precise nature of how he ejaculates in the technical sense relevant to the claim. More to the point: it is not what the husband actually knows that determines whether the woman will lie, but what she can convince *herself* that he does not know. If she can persuade herself that he might have doubts, or that he won't be able to definitively refute her, that is enough for her to be willing to make the claim. *Umishum hachi meshakra* — and for that reason she will lie. The decisive variable is her own psychology of rationalization, not the objective state of the husband's knowledge.

---

## Halakhic Ruling

### Follow Hamnuna

The *halakhic* ruling is that we follow *Rav Hamnuna* against *Rava*. The principle of *chazaka ein isha me'iza paneha bifnei ba'alah* is accepted broadly throughout the *gemara*, and the ruling here is in line with that general acceptance. The implication is significant: it is not only that we believe a woman when she says *gerashtani* — it is that the *mishnah acharona*'s regime is not absolute, and there are circumstances in which a woman will be believed even within it.

### Ran on Relations

The *Ran* draws out a further consequence. Once we accept *Rav Hamnuna*'s principle — that where the husband would know the truth of the matter, she will be believed even under the *mishnah acharona* — it follows that a woman who says her husband refuses to have intimate relations with her altogether would also be believed. *She'omeret eino nizkak imi klal* — she claims he will not be with her at all. Since the husband knows whether this is true, and since she would not lie to his face about something he knows, she is believed — *keivan deba'ala yada bah afilu lemishna acharona meheimna* — and he is compelled to give her a *get* and pay her *ketubah*.

### Ketubah Categories

The *Ran* notes the broader *halakhic* implication: a man who refuses to have relations with his wife is failing to fulfill the *mitzvah* of *onah*, and the woman's testimony about that refusal is sufficient to compel divorce and payment of *ketubah*. Similarly, the *Ran* cites the principle that if a man refuses to have relations unless they remain clothed — if he will not fulfill *onah* in the manner *halakhically* required — he must also *yotzi ve-yitein ketubah*, divorce her and pay her *ketubah*. In all these cases, the woman's claim is credited precisely because the husband would know its truth, and the *chazaka* of *ein isha me'iza paneha* therefore applies.

### Ran's Caveat

The *Ran* adds an important qualification, attributed to the *Ri*: the woman is believed and receives her *get* and *ketubah* only when her expressed demand is for the *get* itself — for the divorce. If she draws attention to the *ketubah*, if she emphasizes the financial dimension of her claim, this introduces a new motive and weakens her credibility. The focus on money raises fresh concerns of the same kind as *shema einah natna be'acher*. But if she says simply that she wants to be free of the marriage and demands a *get*, without foregrounding the monetary claim, she will receive both the *get* and the *ketubah*. In practice this points to the need for careful framing — which, as *Tosafot* noted somewhat wryly, is precisely why one needs competent legal counsel.

---

## Story One

### Daily Ritual

The *gemara* now presents a series of narrative cases that conclude the *perek*. The first involves a woman who, as a regular intimate gesture following relations with her husband, would wash his hands. The *Ran* suggests she may have done this for reasons connected to *tumah* — perhaps her husband was a *kohen* — though what precisely this would address is not entirely clear, since more significant *tumah* concerns require immersion in a *mikveh*. In any case, it functioned as a gesture of intimacy.

### Husband Surprised

One day, the husband noticed she had brought water to wash his hands, even though, as he told her, they had not had relations that day. Why was she performing this ritual?

### Wife's Explanation

Her response was striking: if it wasn't you, then it must have been one of those non-Jewish fragrance merchants — *ahaloyei*, aloe merchants — who had been present in the area. It must have been dark, she must have heard someone she took to be her husband, and she went to him. It was essentially the same logic as the classic case of mistaken identity in the dark, familiar from other contexts in the *gemara*.

The reason the *gemara* specifies that the other man was a non-Jew is relevant to the question of her status: for the wife of a *kohen*, even a mistaken or coerced act renders her forbidden, so the identification of the man as a non-Jewish stranger is the legally operative detail that would create her prohibition. For the wife of a *Yisrael*, even if her account were believed, she would not be forbidden to her husband since she acted under the belief that it was her husband — a case of *shogeg* that would not render her forbidden.

### Rav Nachman

*Rav Nachman* ruled: *ein anu mashgichin bah* — pay no attention to her. *V'leit bei mashasha b'mila* — there is no substance to her words. She is seeking a divorce and has constructed an ingenious account — one designed to appear as if the disclosure was involuntary, drawn out by the husband's question rather than volunteered — precisely in order to make it look credible. Despite how convincing the circumstantial presentation might seem, *Rav Nachman* rules categorically that we do not believe her.

This is noteworthy: the ruling is categorical, not case-by-case. *Rav Nachman* does not undertake a granular assessment of the plausibility of her story. This connects to the earlier discussion about whether the *mishnah acharona*'s disbelief is absolute or contextual. Here, the ruling appears to favor the categorical approach — and, as we noted, this actually serves the interests of a woman who does not want to be divorced, since by not believing her we allow the marriage to continue.

---

## Story Two

### Painful Relations

The second case involves a woman who was visibly not in a good mood with her husband. He asked her why. She replied that she had never experienced such pain during relations as she had that day.

### No Relations

Her husband told her: we did not have relations today.

### Merchants Again

She responded: if that is so, then it must have been those non-Jewish fragrance merchants who had been present in the house that day — *dilma chad minhon*, perhaps one of them.

### Another Man

*Rav Nachman* again ruled: do not pay attention to her — *natna einayha be'acher hi hi*, she has set her eyes on another man. Once more, despite the apparent circumstantial weight of the evidence, the ruling is categorical. The couple's ability to remain married is preserved precisely through that categorical disbelief.

---

## Story Three

### Caught & Run

The third case is different in kind. A man was hiding behind closed doors with a married woman — not his wife — when the husband came home. The man broke through the wicker gate and fled.

### Hiding Logic

*Rava* ruled: *itteta sharya* — the woman is permitted. His reasoning: *im itta de-avar issura*, had he actually committed adultery with her, *mikhse hava mirchas* — he would have hidden more carefully. He would have taken greater care to ensure that he was not seen fleeing. The very brazenness of his visible escape suggests that there was nothing he needed to conceal.

### Ran Clarifies

The *Ran* addresses a question that lurks beneath the surface of this ruling: does this mean that without *Rava*'s reasoning, the circumstantial evidence of a man found hiding with a married woman would be sufficient to render her forbidden to her husband? The *Ran* is explicit that it does not. *She-ein itteta niaseret al ba'alah* except through *kinnuy ve-stira* — the formal *sotah* procedure involving a witnessed warning followed by witnessed seclusion — *o be-eidei davar barur*, or through witnesses who observe the act itself with substantial clarity. Circumstantial evidence alone, however suggestive, is insufficient to render a woman forbidden to her husband.

### Reassurance

If that is so, what is *Rava* accomplishing with his reasoning? The *Ran* explains: *hayu romi b'chei hai gavna v'chol bar nafesh d'chush al atzmo k'dei la'asot yedei shamayim* — the husband, even without a *halachic* obligation to divorce his wife, might nevertheless feel that morally or personally he cannot remain in the marriage given what he witnessed. He suspects that something occurred even if he cannot prove it. *Rava*'s reasoning is directed at *him* — at calming his fears and providing him with a rational basis for concluding that his suspicions are unfounded. The rabbinic authority here operates not only on the level of formal *halacha* but as a form of pastoral reassurance, requiring considerable confidence and leadership on the rabbi's part.

---

## Story Four

### Cress & Snake

The final case is the most vivid. An adulterer — described as such, though the irony of that label will become apparent — had entered a woman's home and was hiding behind the door or in the closet when the husband arrived. On the table was cress that a snake had bitten from. The concern about uncovered food bitten by a snake — *gilu'i*, the category of leaving food exposed — is that snake venom may be left behind.

### Life-Saving Warning

The husband, unaware of the danger, was about to eat from the poisoned cress. *B'lo da'ata de-itteta* — and the wife, who may have known about the snake but had not noticed her husband was about to eat, was also unaware of what was happening in that moment. The man hiding in the closet, seeing the husband about to eat the poisoned food, called out: *lo teichul mihanech d'tam'inhu chivya* — do not eat from that; the snake has bitten from it. He exposed himself in order to save the husband's life.

### Rava's Logic

*Rava* ruled: *itteta sharya* — the woman is permitted. *Ei ita de-avad issura* — had he actually committed adultery with her, *nicha lei de-leichul ve-leimut* — he would have wanted the husband to eat the poisoned cress and die. The *gemara* supports this from a verse: *ki nafu ve-dam biyadeihem* — they committed adultery and blood was on their hands. An adulterer, the logic runs, would not recoil from the husband's death; indeed he would welcome it.

### Secret Affair

The *gemara* anticipates the counter-argument: perhaps he *did* commit adultery, and yet *davka* wanted the husband to live — *ke-dei de-tehavi itteta leh*, so that the woman would remain available to him as a secret lover. For as the verse says, *mayim genuvim yimtaku ve-lechem setarim yinam* — stolen waters are sweet and hidden bread is tasty. He prefers the clandestine intrigue of adultery over marriage; he has no interest in the husband's death and every interest in his continued existence. The *gemara* rejects this counter-argument and maintains *Rava*'s ruling: the presumption is that an adulterer would want the husband out of the way, and the man's life-saving warning is therefore proof that he did not commit adultery. The woman is permitted to her husband.

---

## Shalom Bayis Synthesis

### Perek Context

It is worth pausing to observe where these stories appear. They close an entire *perek* whose central subject is a husband's power to annul his wife's vows. Whatever dimension of power that dynamic reflects, it also represents a *halakhic* mechanism aimed at reducing sources of marital tension — an instrument for preventing or dissolving vows that generate discord between husband and wife.

### Dual Method

The concluding stories operate with a dual method. On the formal *halakhic* level, the *gemara* consistently refuses to believe the woman's claim that she committed adultery or was violated — a categorical disbelief that, paradoxically, protects the integrity of marriages in which neither party actually wants a divorce. On the informal level, the *gedolei Yisrael* appearing in these stories — *Rav Nachman*, *Rava* — employ circumstantial reasoning and pastoral reassurance to address the husband's fears and suspicions, providing him with a rational and emotional basis for remaining in the marriage.

### Goal

The dual method — formal disbelief combined with circumstantial reassurance — achieves the goal of reducing marital discord while maintaining *halakhic* integrity. The *chazal* are not simply dismissing the woman's words; they are navigating an intricate balance between the demands of *din*, the welfare of the marriage, and the dignity of both parties. The final image of the *gemara* — the man hiding in the closet calling out to warn the husband not to eat the poisoned food — is almost cinematically resonant: the would-be adulterer becomes, in the end, the husband's unlikely rescuer, and *itteta sharya*.

---

---

# Nazir 2

## Intro to Nazir

### Opening & Dedication

We begin today *Maseches Nazir*. Today's daf is Nazir 2a. Today is also the *yahrtzeit* of my mother, *Chana bas Mordechai Eliezer*, Anat Linzer, and this learning is dedicated to her memory. A few brief words in her honor appear at the end of this shiur.

*Maseches Nazir* logically continues *Maseches Nedarim*. The first word to say before jumping in is that *nazir* is a type of *neder* — a status created through an act of speech, just as we learned regarding *neder* in general. A *neder*, as distinct from a *shavuah*, is not an oath to do or refrain from doing something; it is a speech act that effects the status of an object, renders an object or a person forbidden to another. A *nazir*, similarly, is constituted through a speech act that does not focus on what is being prohibited, but rather creates a status and defines the person as a *nazir*. As the Torah states, *ish o ishah ki yafli lindor neder nazir* — a man or a woman can undertake *nezirut*. We encountered several cases of a woman taking a vow of *nezirut* and her husband annulling it in the preceding *masechet*.

The consequences of *nazir* status are threefold: the person may not drink wine or consume any grape products, may not become *tamei* to the dead, and must allow his or her hair to grow wild. This is not an oath; it is not a focus on forbidding a particular act. It is a status — analogous to designating an animal as a *korban*, which generates a host of *halachos* governing what may or may not be done with that animal. So too here, the speech act instills a status, and from that status flow the attendant obligations and prohibitions.

### Nazir vs. Neder

The first *mishnah* of *Nazir* very closely parallels the first *mishnah* of *Nedarim*, in that both address the types of speech acts that are legally sufficient to effect the relevant status. The question in both cases is: what precisely must one say, and how formal or precise does that language need to be?

### Textual Sources

Before turning to the text, a word about the structure of the page and the available commentaries. Unlike *Nedarim*, where the *Tosfos* running along the side was not the standard genre — more a running commentary than the dialectical, critical engagement we associate with *Tosfos* proper — here in *Nazir* the *Tosfos* is a fully standard *Tosfos*, asking pointed questions from other sugyos and working toward resolutions. There is no *Ran*, as the need for that kind of running commentary is less acute here. However, the pseudo-*Rashi* — which is not the authentic *Rashi*, though the identity of its true author remains a matter of scholarly discussion — will likely be consulted more frequently precisely because *Tosfos* is now functioning in its standard role rather than as a running commentary. The *Rosh* also provides something of a running commentary here. We will refer to all of these as occasion demands.

One should also note that while the page looks more standard than *Nedarim*, the external *rishonim* on *Nazir* are sparser. On *Nedarim* one finds the *Ramban*'s *Hilchos Nedarim* paralleling the *Rif*, as well as a *Ritva*, *Nemukei Yosef*, and *Rashba*. For *Nazir*, the broader corpus of *rishonim* simply does not exist to the same degree — a curious fact, perhaps partly explained by the limited practical relevance of the laws of *nezirut* in the absence of the *Beis Hamikdash* (since *nezirut* cannot be concluded without the requisite *korbanot*), though since when has practical relevance determined whether *rishonim* write on a *masechet*? It is also worth noting that both *Nedarim* and *Nazir* appear to reflect a somewhat different editorial tradition than most of the Bavli — current scholarly consensus suggests a different *yeshiva* center in *Bavel* rather than the main academies, which accounts for certain differences in terminology and idiom, though nothing radical.

### Seder Nashim Context

The *gemara* will address momentarily why *Nazir* belongs in *Seder Nashim*. The simplest answer — discussed by *Tosfos* and the *Rosh* — is that it follows *Nedarim*, and *Nedarim* belongs in *Seder Nashim* because the primary locus of *nedarim* in the Torah concerns the husband's and father's right to annul the vows of a wife or daughter. That familial, marital context is what anchors *Nedarim* in *Nashim*, and *Nazir* follows naturally in its wake. The *gemara*, however, will offer a more substantive reason, to which we now turn.

---

## Kinuyim & Yadot

### Kinuyim Principle

The *mishnah* opens: *kol kinuyei nezirut ke-nezirut* — all substitute expressions for *nezirut* carry the same legal force as *nezirut* itself. Even non-standard terminology, if it functions as a stand-in for the formal term, suffices to make one a *nazir*.

### Elliptical Speech

The *mishnah* then states: *ha-omer ahei, harei zeh nazir* — one who says "I will be," without completing the sentence, is a *nazir*. This is striking: the sentence is entirely open-ended. One could fill in that blank with any number of things. The *gemara* will explain that this case applies specifically where a *nazir* is passing in front of the speaker, such that the context fills in the ellipsis.

The *mishnah* continues: *o ahei na'eh* — "or I will be beautiful." Here too, the meaning is not self-evident. The word *na'eh* means beautiful, not *nazir*. Yet either because a *nazir* was passing before the speaker and the phrase means "I will be beautiful like that *nazir*," or because the speaker is understood to be gesturing toward his own hair, the phrase carries legal force. *Tosfos* and the *Rosh* place *ahei na'eh* in the category of *yad* — an elliptical or incomplete expression — though it occupies an interesting intermediate space between a pure *yad* (an unfinished sentence) and a *kinuy* (a substitute term that carries meaning through convention). A pure *kinuy* involves a substitute word standing in for the term *nazir* itself. *Ahei na'eh* is a complete sentence, but its meaning is carried by context rather than by the word's own semantic content.

### Substitute Words

The *mishnah* then addresses: *nazik, naziach, paziach* — words that are clearly variations of the word *nazir*, with slight phonetic distortions. *Harei zeh nazir* — such a person is a *nazir*. These are the classic *kinuyim*: substitute terms that stand in for the formal word. One can see how *nazik* and *paziach* are distortions of *nazir* — take the *nun* and deform it slightly into a *pei*, draw a line through the *reish* to arrive at *paziach*.

There is a debate in the *gemara* in *Nedarim* as to whether these words constitute *lashon shebadu chachamim* — a language invented by the rabbis — or *lashon umos*, the vernacular of other nations. The latter option seems difficult to sustain: it would be rather remarkable if foreign languages had their own terminology for *nezirut* that happened to closely mirror the Hebrew, and these words sound more like inventions than genuine foreign vocabulary. Yet the question has real *halachic* bite: if the rabbis simply invented these terms, does that make them a less-than-formal language? Does using them create a full-fledged *nezirut d'Oraita*?

The *Ran* in *Nedarim* argued that the entire concept of language is conventional — there is no objective standard for what constitutes a "real" language. Once a convention is established and people understand what the terms mean, it becomes a valid language for the purposes of *nezirut*, regardless of whether the rabbis originated it. The analogous case in *Nedarim* concerns *konam* and related terms. The *gemara* there explains that the substitute terminology was instituted so that a person would not begin by saying *korban* and complete the utterance with *l'Hashem*, thereby invoking God's name in a potentially frivolous context. That logic applies more naturally to *nedarim* involving the word *korban* than to *nezirut*, where the concern is less obvious — though the general desire to signal the weightiness of the act through substitute language may still apply.

---

## Allusions & Context

### Allusive Phrases

The *mishnah* continues with further examples: *harei ka-ze* — "I am like this one," presumably said while looking at a *nazir*; *harei alai mesalsel* — "I will twirl my hair"; *harei alai mechalkel* — similarly referring to attending to one's hair; and *harei alai l'shaleach pera* — "I will let my hair grow wild." In all these cases, *harei zeh nazir* — the person is a *nazir*. These are what one might call allusions with legal force: the words do not literally mean *nazir*, but the phrase, taken in context, communicates an unambiguous intent to accept *nezirut*.

### Bird Offerings

A more ambiguous case follows: *harei alai tziporin* — "I hereby undertake [an obligation of] birds." Bird offerings are indeed part of the *nazir*'s *korbanot* at the conclusion of *nezirut*, but they are also the offering of a *metzora*. The statement thus does not unambiguously point to *nezirut* specifically.

### Rabbi Meir Dispute

*Rabbi Meir omer Nazir* — Rabbi Meir holds that such a person is a *nazir*. *Chachamim omrim eino Nazir* — the Sages disagree. The *gemara* will elaborate on this dispute, but the underlying question is whether the allusion to bird offerings alone is sufficient to constitute an act of accepting *nezirut*, or whether the ambiguity of the reference defeats the speech act.

---

## Kinuyim & Yadot (II)

### Tosfos Analysis

*Tosfos* raises a pointed question about the *chiddush* of *kinuyim*. If these are simply words in another language — or even in a made-up language that has become conventionally understood — what is the novelty? You can obviously become a *nazir* by saying so in any language. So the *mishnah*'s listing of *nazik, naziach, paziach* would be trivially obvious.

*Tosfos* answers: *ein hachi nami d'gam b'sha'ar lishonot im hikkir v'hevin v'nitkaven lekabel alav nezirut havei nazir* — it is certainly true that in any other language, if one understood and intended to accept *nezirut*, one becomes a *nazir*. The *chiddush* of these particular terms, says *Tosfos*, is that *mishum d'dami tefai v'lashon haTorah* — because they closely resemble the formal Torah language of the word *nazir*, they bind a person even without specific intent, in a way that ordinary foreign-language equivalents do not.

### Intent & Convention

This is a striking position, because the entire foundation of *nedarim* and *nezirut* is *piv v'libo shavin* — one's words and one's heart must be aligned. One might object: if you say *harei ani nazir* without intending it, the words alone do not make you a *nazir*. So how can *Tosfos* say that saying *nazik* or *paziach* binds you even without intent?

The most reasonable reading is that *Tosfos* does not mean "zero intent." Rather, there must be some general intent to undertake something significant — but the speaker may not have focused specifically on *nezirut* as opposed to some other form of *hafla'ah*, some other verbal act of self-imposition. The argument would then be: when the words used are so close to the formal Torah language of *nazir*, that proximity carries its own interpretive weight and locks in the meaning of *nezirut* even if the speaker had not consciously specified it. Whether spoken in French or English or any other language, only precise, specific intent would suffice. But when the words are near-formal Torah language, that specificity is supplied by the formal register of the words themselves.

*Tosfos* further elaborates on the position of *Reish Lakish*, who holds that these are *lashon shebadu chachamim* — invented words. *Tosfos* asks: according to *Reish Lakish*, how can one bring a *korban* on the basis of invented language? Would this not be *chullin ba-azarah* — bringing non-consecrated animals into the Temple precincts? *Tosfos* answers: *keivan de-mitkavein lindor be-nazir ve-yodeia she-lashon zeh badu chachamim lindor bahem be-nazir, kabbalah gemurah hu ke'ilu amar bi-lashon ha-katuv ba-Torah* — since the person intends to accept *nezirut* and knows that this is the language the rabbis instituted for that purpose, it constitutes a complete acceptance, as though one had spoken in the formal language of the Torah itself.

What is interesting here is the phrase *ke'ilu amar bi-lashon ha-katuv ba-Torah*. There is, strictly speaking, no single prescribed verbal formula in the Torah for accepting *nezirut*. Yet *Tosfos* writes as though such a formal text exists. Both parts of the *Tosfos* — the first part, which suggests near-formal language binds even without full intent, and this second part, which describes the invented language as equivalent to the Torah's formal language — seem to presuppose a kind of formal register of sacred speech that occupies a different normative space than ordinary language, even intentional ordinary language. One might not resolve this tension entirely, but it reflects a coherent underlying intuition: the closer one's words are to the formal idiom of Torah obligation, the more fully they function as legal speech acts.

### Lashes vs. Korbanot

*Tosfos* cites one final possibility, attributed to *Ravya bar Chiya*, who explains *Reish Lakish*'s position as applying specifically to *malkut* — lashes — rather than to *korbanot*. That is: one who violates *nezirut* accepted through these invented terms receives lashes, but does not bring a *korban*. This is a curious intermediate category, positing a *nezirut* that is weighty enough to generate corporal liability upon transgression, yet not substantial enough to obligate the full complement of Temple offerings. The question of how such a middle tier is conceptually coherent is left open, but the possibility itself reflects the deeper uncertainty about whether invented convention, even when widely accepted and intentionally employed, creates a fully *d'Oraita* legal status.

---

## Why Seder Nashim

### Gemara Opening

The *gemara* opens by asking: *tana be-seder nashim ka-ei* — we are in *Seder Nashim*. *Mai ta'ama tani Nazir?* — what is the reason *Nazir* is taught here? As noted above, the simplest answer is that it follows *Nedarim*, and *Nedarim* belongs in *Nashim* because the Torah's primary treatment of *nedarim* concerns the husband's and father's power to annul. *Nazir* follows naturally in that wake.

### Sotah & Wine

The *gemara*, however, offers a substantive reason of its own: *tana kra ka-ei* — the *tanna* is anchored in a biblical context. The verse discusses a husband divorcing his wife because of *ervat davar* — presumed adultery. *Mi garam lah la-aveirah?* — what caused her to sin? *Yayin* — wine. And therefore: *kol ha-ro'eh sotah be-kilkulah* — anyone who sees a *sotah* in her disgrace, as her hair is disheveled and she undergoes the ordeal, should recognize that her downfall was caused by wine and the pursuit of sensual pleasure. The appropriate response is *yazir atzmo min ha-yayin* — to disavow wine, that is, to become a *nazir*. It is worth noting the irony that this reasoning is addressed entirely to a male audience — it is the man who sees the *sotah* and resolves to become a *nazir*. One might have expected the reasoning to apply symmetrically, but the *gemara*'s framing reflects how completely the lens here is male.

### Nazir-Sotah Link

Because *nazir* is thus connected to *sotah*, and *sotah* is placed in *Seder Nashim*, *nazir* belongs there as well — and indeed, *Maseches Sotah* follows *Maseches Nazir* directly in the ordering of the *seder*. Moreover, in the Torah itself, *nazir* and *sotah* are juxtaposed in the very same section of *Bamidbar*. The placement in *Seder Nashim* is therefore not merely a structural afterthought; it reflects a deliberate thematic and scriptural linkage.

---

## A-B-B-A Structure

### Missing Yadot

Having established why *Nazir* belongs in *Seder Nashim*, the *gemara* turns to an internal structural question about the *mishnah* itself. The *mishnah* opened by stating *kol kinuyei nezirut ke-nezirut* — the principle of *kinuyim* — but its first concrete example was *ahei*, which is not a *kinuy* at all, but a *yad*, an elliptical sentence. So the *mishnah* seems to announce one principle and immediately illustrate a different one.

*Rava* (and some say it was stated anonymously) resolves this by the principle of *hisurei mihasra ve-hachi katani* — the *mishnah* is missing text and must be read as follows: *kol kinuyei nezirut ke-nezirut, ve-yadot nezirut ke-nezirut* — both *kinuyim* and *yadot* are effective. The *mishnah* implicitly includes *yadot* alongside *kinuyim*. The examples of *ahei* and *ahei na'eh* are then the illustrations of *yadot*, while *nazik, naziach, paziach* are the illustrations of *kinuyim*.

But this raises a further question: if we are inserting both categories, and the *mishnah* announced *kinuyim* first, why does it illustrate *yadot* first? The *gemara* notes that the *mishnah* appears to follow an A-B-B-A structure — announcing two categories and then discussing them in reverse order. Why would it do so?

### Precedent Examples

The *gemara* adduces parallel examples from other *mishnayot*. *Bameh madlikin u-vameh ein madlikin* — the *mishnah* in *Shabbos* discusses what one may and may not use as a wick, and it discusses what one may *not* use first. *Bameh tomnin u-vameh ein tomnin* — the *mishnah* about insulating food discusses the prohibited cases first. *Bameh ishah yotza u-vameh eino yotza* — the *mishnah* about what a woman may carry on *Shabbos* similarly starts with the prohibited. In all these cases, the *mishnah* names both options (A and B) and then discusses B before A — a classic A-B-B-A structure.

### Exception Rules

However, the *gemara* notes that this is not a universal rule. *Bameh behemah yotza u-vameh eino yotza* — the *mishnah* about what an animal may wear on *Shabbos* starts with the permitted cases, not the prohibited. And *yesh nochalin u-manhilin* — the *mishnah* about inheritance begins with the primary case (those who both inherit and bequeath), not the last category mentioned.

So neither A-B-B-A nor A-B-A-B is a fixed rule. The *gemara* therefore articulates the underlying logic case by case. When the subject concerns personal prohibitions — what *you* may or may not do — the *mishnah* leads with the prohibited, because that is what demands attention and care. When the subject concerns the animal rather than the person directly (*behemah*), there is less urgency to foreground the prohibition, and the *mishnah* begins with the permitted. When the topic is inheritance (*nochalin*), the *mishnah* starts with the primary, normative case before moving to exceptions.

### Yadot Derasha

What then is the logic here in *Nazir*? Why illustrate *yadot* before *kinuyim*? The *gemara* answers: *yadot hava de-atu leh midrashah chavivi leh* — the concept of *yad* is derived from a *pasuk* through *derasha*. Things derived through rabbinic *derasha* from scriptural texts occupy a beloved place; the rabbis cherish what they have derived from close reading of *pesukim* and wish to discuss it first as the concrete illustrative case. Hence, even though *kinuyim* was announced first, the *yadot* are illustrated first because they carry the prestige of scriptural derivation.

### Final Order

Yet if *yadot* are so beloved, one might ask: why not open the *mishnah* itself with *yadot* rather than *kinuyim*? The *gemara* answers: *ki matchil, matchil be-ikar korban* — when beginning, one begins with the more primary act. The use of substitute terms (*kinuyim*), even though these may in some cases be conventional or invented language, is a more basic, self-evident concept: you use a different word that means the same thing, and of course it counts. The concept of *yad* — that an *incomplete* sentence, never even articulating what you are accepting, can nonetheless constitute a binding speech act — is a far greater *chiddush*. Indeed, the very fact that a *derasha* was necessary to establish *yadot* proves that *kinuyim* is the more fundamental concept; *kinuyim* needs no scriptural derivation because it is simply the obvious principle that language works by meaning, not by arbitrary form.

So the structure is: the *mishnah* opens by announcing *kinuyim* as primary, then (via the implicit insertion of *yadot*) introduces the concept of *yadot* as well. When it comes to concrete illustration, it illustrates *yadot* first — because they are derived from *derasha* and cherished — and then returns to illustrate *kinuyim*. This produces the A-B-B-A pattern: announce *kinuyim*, introduce *yadot*, illustrate *yadot*, illustrate *kinuyim*.

---

## Ahei Case

### Shmuel Context

The *gemara* now homes in on the specific case of *ahei* — "I will be." The difficulty is obvious: how does an incomplete sentence become legally binding? The person has not said what he will be. *Dilma ahei be-ta'anis kamar* — perhaps he means "I will undertake a fast," or any of a thousand other possibilities. Shmuel's answer is: *kegon she-hayah Nazir over lefanav* — the case is where a *nazir* was walking in front of him. That context fills the ellipsis and makes the meaning clear.

### Yad Categories

This leads the *gemara* to examine Shmuel's position through a three-tier conceptual framework. There is a *yad mokhiach* — a contextually obvious ellipsis. There is a *yad she-eino mokhiach* — an ellipsis that probably points to a certain meaning but is not entirely unambiguous. And there is something that is not a *yad* at all — so open-ended that it cannot even be treated as a truncated speech act.

### Ketubah Example

The clearest example of a *yad mokhiach* comes from a parallel discussion in *Kiddushin*: a man standing under the *chuppah* says *harei at mekudeshes* without adding *li* — "to me." Strictly speaking, he might be acting as an agent for someone else. But given that he is present at his own wedding ceremony, surrounded by family, the omission of *li* is transparently a *yad mokhiach* — so obvious from context that there is no real ambiguity. He did not complete the sentence, but no reasonable person would doubt what he meant.

### Nazir Before Him

Since Shmuel specifies that the *mishnah*'s case requires a *nazir* to be passing before the speaker, the *gemara* infers that Shmuel may hold that only a *yad mokhiach* suffices — a fully transparent contextual ellipsis. A *yad she-eino mokhiach* would then not be adequate. The *gemara* raises this as a question about Shmuel's position, noting that the same issue arises in the *Kiddushin* context where Shmuel also opines.

The *gemara* then qualifies: even with a *nazir* walking past, the case is not so simple. When there is a *nazir over lefanav*, *leika le-safukei be-milsa achrina* — there is no room to suspect that the speaker meant anything other than accepting *nezirut* upon himself. Without a *nazir* present, however, *amrina dilma ahei be-ta'anis kamar* — we would simply say he might have meant a fast, and the statement would not be a *yad* at all. The point is that bare *ahei* with no context is not even on the spectrum of *yad* — it is too indeterminate. Shmuel's example of *nazir over lefanav* establishes the minimum context required, but does not resolve what Shmuel holds regarding intermediate cases.

### Korban Alternative

A further complication: even with a *nazir* walking in front, the *gemara* raises the possibility that *ahei* does not mean "I will be a *nazir*" at all, but rather "let it be upon me" — meaning the speaker intends to assume responsibility for that *nazir*'s *korbanot* at the conclusion of his *nezirut*. Strange as it sounds, one person can indeed undertake to finance another's *korbanot*, relieving the *nazir* of that obligation. So even the most natural contextual reading — a *nazir* before you, you say "I will be" — admits of an alternative interpretation: not *nezirut* itself, but commitment to the other's offerings.

### Clarification Suffices

The *gemara* resolves this by noting that the case is one where the person subsequently clarified his intention — *de-kamar be-libo*, he said (or it became clear) that he meant *nezirut*. The *gemara* then asks: if he clarified it afterward, is that not obvious? Why does the *mishnah* need to tell us anything? The answer is: *mahu de-teima be-inan piv u-libo shavin kamashma lan* — one might have thought that we require a complete alignment between words and intent at the moment of the speech act itself, such that the words must be fully self-explanatory. The *mishnah* teaches that this is not required: subsequent clarification of intent can work together with the original words to constitute a valid acceptance.

### Yad Works

This brings the discussion to its conclusion. What has been illustrated here is precisely a *yad she-eino mokhiach*. The words *ahei*, even with a *nazir* passing by, are not entirely transparent — there is the alternative reading of assuming the *korban* obligation. The words in context "probably" point to *nezirut*, but not with full certainty. The *chiddush* is that this is sufficient: a *yad she-eino mokhiach*, joined with subsequent clarification of intent, constitutes a valid speech act. Since the person intended *nezirut* and subsequently clarified that intention, we can say that that is indeed what the words expressed. The principle of *piv u-libo shavin* does not require that the words be maximally explicit at the time of utterance; it requires that the words and the intent be aligned — and that alignment can be established in conjunction with subsequent clarification.

---

## Nazir Ethics

### Nazir Sinner?

Tomorrow's discussion — which we had hoped to reach today — concerns the question of whether the *nazir* is a *chotei*, a sinner. The Talmud's treatment of this question is nuanced and important, and we will address it in full then.

### Two Models

By way of preview, one might note that the standard understanding in the *gemara* of why the *nazir* might be considered a *chotei* is that he deprives himself of the pleasures of this world. But this opens onto a deeper question about what constitutes the primary form of religious engagement. One model of *kedushah* holds that a person reaches spiritual heights through separation — growing one's hair wild as a mark of social estrangement, avoiding contact with the dead, refraining from any engagement with the physical in order to transcend it. That is one vision of holiness. But there is a very different conception of *kedushah*, expressed in *Rabbi Yisrael Salanter*'s famous principle: *yenems gashmiyus iz dayn ruchnius* — the other person's physical needs are your spiritual obligation. On this understanding, genuine holiness is not found in withdrawal from the world but in full engagement with it, in understanding and attending to the real human needs of those around us.

### Mother's Model

This daf is dedicated to the memory of my mother, *Chana bas Mordechai Eliezer*, *aleha ha-shalom*. If I were to identify the image that most captures who she was, it would be this: answering calls in the middle of the night — midnight, later — to arrange a *taharah*, and going immediately to perform it. The *nazir* achieves holiness by distancing himself from contact with the dead. My mother achieved *kedushah* by running toward it, by being *metamei le-meitim* in the deepest and most selfless sense, extending herself at the moments when no one else was there.

There is also the other dimension — what people shared at the *shiva*: that when families moved into the community, she was the one who welcomed them, who made them feel invited and at home, who remembered, years later, what a friend's favorite dish was and made sure it appeared on the *Shabbos* table when that friend returned after a long absence. What it does to a person — to know that they are remembered, that they matter, that someone has held them in mind across years — is not a small thing. That kind of *kedushah*, the *kedushah* of attentiveness to other human beings and their real needs, is the alternative model to the *nazir*'s separation. It is the model my mother lived. May her memory be a blessing.

---

---

# Nazir 3

## I will be beautiful

### Ehei Na'eh classification

The daf opens with the phrase *ehei na'eh nazir* — "I will be beautiful, [I will be] a *nazir*." If someone declares "I will be beautiful," that person is considered to have accepted *nezirut*. The question is how to classify this statement. A *yad* is typically a truncated, elliptical sentence — "I will be" — where one must fill in the blank. Here, by contrast, a complete sentence has been uttered: "I will be beautiful." The issue is not incompleteness but rather what the word "beautiful" signifies in this context. One could therefore suggest that this functions more as a *kinuy* than as a *yad*, though it does not fit the standard definition of *kinuy* either. A *kinuy* normally involves a technical substitute word — *nazik*, *paziyach*, *naziyach* — standing in for the word *nazir*. The word *na'eh* does not mean *nazir*; it means beautiful. It is only by contextual interpretation that it is understood to refer to *nezirut*. The categorization therefore remains somewhat ambiguous, somewhere between *yad* and *kinuy*.

### Challenge to meaning

The Gemara immediately presses: how do we know that *na'eh* refers to being a *nazir*? Perhaps *ehei na'eh lefanav bamitzvot* — "I will make myself beautiful before God in *mitzvot*" — as the *Braisa* in the *Mekhilta* expounds the verse *zeh Eli ve'anveihu*: "This is my God and I will glorify Him." The *Braisa* explains *anveihu* as *ehei na'eh lefanav bamitzvot* — I will glorify myself before God through the performance of *mitzvot* — and gives examples: *sukkah na'eh*, *lulav na'eh*, *tzitzis na'eh*, *sefer Torah na'eh*. This is the concept of *noi mitzvah*, beautifying the objects of the commandment. Even within a religious register, then, the phrase *ehei na'eh* need not refer to *nezirut*. The challenge stands: even setting aside entirely secular interpretations, the phrase could carry a meaningful religious sense without triggering any vow of *nezirut*.

### Samuel: hair context

Shmuel resolves the difficulty by appeal to context: *she-tefus be-sa'aro ve'amar ena'eh* — the speaker is grabbing hold of his hair while saying "I will be beautiful." With that physical gesture providing the frame, what else could he mean? The long hair of a *nazir* is being contemplated as something beautiful, and the gesture of seizing one's hair gives the necessary context to interpret the declaration as an acceptance of *nezirut*.

### Nazir as sinner

This resolution, however, raises its own difficulty. The Gemara objects: *nezira milsa de'aveira* — being a *nazir* is a matter associated with sin. If *nezirut* is sinful, how can it be described as "beautiful," and how can we halakhically anchor that description? The Gemara acknowledges the point but deflects it: *de'afilu le-Rabbi Elazar HaKappar de'amar nazir chote, hani mili gabbei nazir tamei* — even according to Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, who holds that the *nazir* is a sinner, that characterization applies specifically to a *nazir tamei*, a *nazir* who has become ritually impure. That is the context of the Torah's language *asher chata al hanefesh* — "who sinned against the soul" — which appears in the portion dealing with a *nazir* who became *tamei*. Why is the *nazir tamei* a sinner in a way that goes beyond the mere fact of impurity? Because *de'aydi deba'ei mistar* — since he must now reverse his entire count and begin again, as the Torah says *vehayamim harishonim yipplu* — the first days fall away — there is a concern that *dilma ati leme'evar al nezirutei* — he will come to transgress his *nezirut* altogether. As the *Rishonim* note, drawing on a *gemara* encountered in *Nedarim*, a *nazir tamei* whose *nezirut* drags on indefinitely may come to regret having undertaken it at all, thereby undermining the *leshem shamayim* dimension of the vow. That compromised sincerity is what earns the designation *chote*.

### Tahor nazir not sinner

The Gemara then states: *aval nazir tahor lav chote kari bei* — a *nazir tahor*, one who has successfully maintained purity throughout, is not called a sinner. Consequently, according to everyone, including the more skeptical voices regarding *nezirut*, a *nazir tahor* can genuinely be described as *na'eh*. The statement "I will be beautiful," uttered while seizing one's hair, is therefore an entirely coherent acceptance of *nezirut*.

### Tosafot on mixed nature

Tosafot, however, raises a pointed difficulty. In every other context where Rabbi Elazar HaKappar is cited, his position is precisely the opposite: his *chiddush* is that the term *chote* — which the Torah applies textually to the *nazir tamei* — extends equally to a *nazir tahor*. That is the whole force of his ruling. It is therefore surprising that this Gemara restricts him to the *nazir tamei* case. Tosafot resolves this tension through a nuanced reading: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar holds that *nezirut* is always a mixed phenomenon. The *perishat atzmo min hayayin* — the self-denial of wine — or more broadly the aspiration to attain holiness through separating from society rather than engaging it, is genuinely problematic. Yet there is also something worthy in the gesture: a form of sincere religious striving, a personal acceptance of discipline. If the *nazir* managed to remain *tahor*, the positive element dominated, and we can say the overall experience was good — *hein na'eh*. But the *cheit* element was always present; the negative was not eliminated, merely outweighed. If the *nazir* became *tamei*, the negative dominates entirely and the designation *chote* is unambiguous. This reading allows Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's position to be consistently one of complexity: the *chote* element always applies even to the *nazir tahor*, but when purity is maintained, the balance tips toward the positive.

This picture of *nezirut* as an inherently ambivalent institution — neither straightforwardly praiseworthy nor simply condemned — is worth holding in mind as the tractate unfolds. In *Nedarim*, the dominant voice was decidedly negative toward vow-making: one who makes a *neder* is likened to one who builds a *bamah*, and the presumption was that *resha'im* make *nedarim*. Whether *Nazir* will sustain that register or modulate toward something more ambivalent remains to be seen.

---

## Incomplete expressions

### Harei kazeh context

The Gemara turns to the phrase *hareini kazeh* — "I am like this." Does this constitute a declaration of *nezirut*? The Gemara immediately asks the same question it posed before: how do we know what "like this" refers to? The answer given is *she-tefus be-sa'aro* — the speaker was holding his hair, the same contextualizing gesture used earlier. Without some such framing, the phrase is too open-ended to anchor.

### Complete vs incomplete

Tosafot draws an important structural distinction arising from these cases. When a sentence is left incomplete — "I will be" — we look to the external surroundings to fill it out. If a *nazir* is passing by, that context supplies the missing content: "I will be like that." However, when a complete sentence has been uttered, the interpretive logic changes. "I will be beautiful" is a full declaration about oneself; one does not naturally look outward to nearby figures to supply its meaning. The necessary context must therefore be intrinsic — the speaker holding his own hair — rather than external. Similarly, if one said "I will be" while holding his hair, Tosafot suggests that would not necessarily produce an acceptance of *nezirut*: an incomplete sentence looks to the passing *nazir* for completion, not to a gesture the speaker is making to himself. Conversely, "I will be beautiful" with a *nazir* walking past — but without the speaker touching his own hair — would likewise be insufficient, since the completed sentence points inward and should be interpreted in relation to the speaker's own words and actions. The asymmetry follows from the structural difference between an incomplete sentence reaching outward for completion and a complete sentence that is self-contained.

### Silsul discussion

The Gemara next considers *hareini mesalsel* — "I will *salsel*." What does *silsul* mean, and why should it refer to *nezirut*? The Gemara cites the maidservant of Rabbi, who appears in several contexts in *Megillah* and *Rosh Hashanah* as a repository of authentic biblical Hebrew — a language increasingly distant from the spoken vernacular of the period, which had shifted toward Aramaic. She said to a certain man, *ad matai ata mesalsel be-se'arekha* — "How long will you keep twirling your hair?" — thereby establishing that *silsul* can refer to playing with or twirling one's hair. However, the Gemara counters: perhaps *mesalsel* means one intends to devote himself to Torah study, as the verse says *salseleha u-teromemeka* — "delve into it and it will raise you up" — where *silsul* connotes deep engagement and immersion. Shmuel's answer is consistent with what he has said throughout: *hacha nami she-tefas be-sa'aro* — here too, the speaker must be holding his hair. With that gesture, *silsul* clearly refers to the hair and not to Torah study.

One might ask whether *silsul* — twirling or playing with one's hair — creates any tension with the *nazir*'s obligation *gadel pera se'ar rosho* — to let his hair grow wild and unruly. The underlying verse describes hair that grows loose and untamed, whereas *silsul* implies active handling. The Gemara does not raise this as a formal objection, and the discussion of *psik reisha* and intent would apply, but the juxtaposition is worth noting.

It is also worth pausing over the contextual framings the Gemara has consistently provided. Of the two standard contexts that render these ambiguous declarations meaningful, one involves seeing another person and wishing to emulate them — a motivation that is, at best, externally driven — and the other emphasizes the beauty or length of the hair. Neither framing represents the most elevated motivation for undertaking *nezirut*. The Gemara may not have had any other practical choice, but both the mimetic impulse and the focus on personal appearance are less than ideal as foundations for a sacred vow.

The Gemara then considers *hareini mechalkel* — a declaration apparently referring to some manner of tending the hair. The Gemara cites a *mishnah* about the minimum quantity of plaster carried into the public domain, where Rabbi Yehudah specifies *kedei la-sud kalkal* — enough to plaster down the temple hair. Rav Papa explains *bastidan* (which Rashi glosses *templa be-la'az* — "temple" in the vernacular) as the hair by the temples that one folds or flattens down in order to secure a covering over it. However, the Gemara counters that *kilkul* can also mean sustaining or feeding the poor, as in the verse *va-yechalkel Yosef es aviv ve-es echav* — "and Yosef sustained his father and brothers." Once again, Shmuel provides the same answer: *she-tefas be-sa'aro* — he was holding his hair. The consistency of Shmuel's approach throughout this passage underscores what is at stake in his position. Recall that the Gemara earlier asked what Shmuel holds regarding a *yad she-einah mochiachat* — an unclear *yad*. The systematic provision of a contextualizing condition for every case in the *mishnah*, conditions that the *mishnah* itself does not mention, reflects Shmuel's insistence on a higher threshold of clarity. The *mishnah* appears to accept these phrases as self-sufficient; Shmuel requires either the holding of hair or a *nazir* passing by to make them evidently meaningful.

### Shalach pera

The Gemara arrives at what seems the most obvious case: *hareini meshalleach pera* — "I will send forth my wild hair." This should be unambiguous. Nevertheless, the Gemara asks: *mimai de-hadin shiluach ribuya hi* — how do we know *shiluach* means to let grow? Perhaps it means to remove, as in *ve-shilach mayim al pnei chutzos* — "to cast the water outward" — meaning one intends to cut off and discard one's hair. The Gemara resolves this by invoking the *gezeira shava* of *pera-pera*: the *nazir*'s verse reads *kadosh yihyeh gadel pera se'ar rosho* — "holy shall be the growing of the wildness of his hair" — and the verse in *Yechezkel* regarding ordinary *kohanim* reads *u-pera lo yishalechu* — "they shall not send forth wild hair" — i.e., *kohanim* must cut their hair every thirty days. The *Tosafot Rosh* notes that the primary function of this *gezeira shava* is in fact to define the *kohen*'s restriction: just as a *nazir*'s *pera* is defined by the standard term of *nezirut*, which is thirty days, so too a *kohen* who allows his hair to grow for thirty days has transgressed. But the link also establishes that *shilu'ach pera* by the *kohanim* — letting the hair grow wild — is the same *pera* as the *nazir*'s. Therefore *shiluach pera* means the growing of wild hair, not its removal. The Gemara adds an alternative: *v'iba'is eima, ha'i meshale'ach mayim nami ribuya hu* — even the verse about casting water can be read as referring to growth, since *d'chimaski lehu maya l'peirei* — when one waters fruits, they grow. For *hareini meshalleach pera*, no additional contextual gesture is required; the phrase is sufficiently clear on its own.

---

## Birds dispute

### Rabbi Meir birds

The *mishnah* now introduces a significant dispute: *harei alai tzipporim* — "I accept upon myself birds." Rabbi Meir holds this constitutes *nezirut*; the Sages disagree. What is Rabbi Meir's reasoning? Reish Lakish explains: *tzipporim semuchim le-se'ar kibel alav* — birds appear in a verse juxtaposed to hair. The verse in Daniel reads: *ad di se'areh k'neshrin raba v'tiprohi k'tziporin* — "until his hair grew like an eagle's and his nails like birds'." The word *tzipporin* appears in the context of *se'ar*, hair, and therefore Rabbi Meir holds that birds carries the meaning of its adjacent term, referring to the *nazir*'s characteristic hair. It is a considerable interpretive leap — the more directly juxtaposed word in the verse is *neshrin*, eagle, not *tzipporin* — but one can also observe a linguistic connection: the Aramaic *tiprohi* shares resonance with *tzipornav*, fingernails, which in turn is connected to *tzipor*, bird. In any case, Rabbi Meir's principle is explicit: *matpisin b'davar ha-samuch lo* — one can perform a *hatpasa*, borrowing the meaning of a nearby word.

The term *hatpasa* carries technical weight from *Masechet Nedarim*, where it describes the transfer of status: if item A has been rendered *assur* by a *neder konam*, and one then says *zeh kazeh*, one is *matpis* the second item with the status of the first. Here the usage is somewhat different — one is not transferring a status but borrowing a semantic meaning from an adjacent word in a verse — yet the technical vocabulary is deliberately introduced.

### Sages reject borrowing

The Sages hold *lo matpis inish bemidi d'samich leh* — one does not borrow meaning from a nearby word. Their more straightforward understanding of the declaration *harei alai tzipporim* would be that the speaker intends to bring bird sacrifices in the context of *nezirut*: since a *nazir tamei* brings bird offerings as part of his *korban*, saying "I accept birds upon myself" might mean "I accept the type of *nezirut* that involves bringing birds." That is the more direct semantic connection, and notably it reflects somewhat negatively on the speaker's framing — accepting *nezirut* with anticipated impurity built into the conception is a troubling starting point, given everything the earlier discussion established about the *nazir tamei*. But that is the Sages' reading of what Rabbi Meir himself must mean. The Sages say that even this more direct connection is insufficient: you cannot anchor a declaration of *nezirut* in a term that is itself neutral simply because a related term appears nearby.

### Rabbi Yochanan view

Rabbi Yochanan offers a different account entirely. He holds *dekuli alma lo matpis* — everyone agrees that one cannot borrow meaning from a nearby word. The disagreement between Rabbi Meir and the Sages is not about the *hatpasa* principle at all. Rabbi Meir's reasoning, according to Rabbi Yochanan, is *de-chayshinan shema tzipporei nazir tamei kibel alav* — we are concerned that perhaps the speaker meant to accept upon himself the bird-sacrifices of a *nazir tamei*. That is the practical connection: a *nazir tamei* brings bird sacrifices, and saying "I accept birds" in that context may be understood as a declaration of *nezirut* with the attendant *korbanot* in mind.

The Gemara presses: if we are operating on "perhaps that is what he means," why not say *dilma tzipporei nedavah kibel alav* — perhaps he simply meant to bring a voluntary bird offering as an *olah*? The Gemara responds: if that were his intent, he would have said *harei alai kan* — the standard idiom for a pair of bird offerings. Since he said *tzipporim* without the standard term *kan*, the voluntary-offering reading is less natural. The Gemara continues: perhaps he meant to donate birds for a *metzora*'s purification ritual, where the verse uses the word *tzippor* repeatedly — *ve-shachat et ha-tzippor ha-chayah*, *ve-et ha-tzippor*, *be-dam ha-tzippor ha-shechutah*. Tosafot explains this as meaning: perhaps he intended that if any *metzora* in the world requires birds for his *tahara* process, he accepts upon himself to donate them.

### Reish Lakish differs

These challenges reveal that even Rabbi Yochanan's explanation requires an additional condition to eliminate alternative readings. The Gemara therefore concludes: *kegon shehaya nazir tahor over lefanav* — the case is one in which a *nazir tahor* was walking in front of the speaker. With that context, the declaration "I accept birds upon myself" is understood as relating to *nezirut*, and not to any of the alternative possibilities. This answer applies equally to Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning and to Reish Lakish's.

### Nazir context required

If both Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish ultimately require a *nazir* walking in front of the speaker, the question arises: *mai beinaiahu* — what is the practical difference between their positions?

### Tosafot reconciles

The Gemara resolves this: *ika beinaiahu kegon d'amar tzipporim ha-semuchim le-se'ar alai* — the difference emerges in a case where there was no *nazir* passing by, but the speaker explicitly said "I accept upon myself birds that are written next to hair." According to Rabbi Yochanan, even this explicit formulation is insufficient without a *nazir* present; the contextual anchor is required regardless. According to Reish Lakish, this explicit invocation of the verse's juxtaposition is itself sufficient: by referencing birds in the specific context of that *pasuk* in Daniel, the speaker has made clear that "birds" carries the meaning of the adjacent "hair," and therefore of *nezirut* — without any need for a *nazir* to be passing by.

This allows Reish Lakish's account to explain the underlying debate between Rabbi Meir and the Sages in the *mishnah* as stated, where no special external context is mentioned at all. Rabbi Meir holds that the invocation of a word whose neighboring term in a verse has the desired meaning is sufficient; the Sages hold it is not. On that reading, the *mishnah*'s formulation makes sense: Rabbi Meir requires no passing *nazir*; he relies on the semantic borrowing from the text. The Sages reject that borrowing.

The Gemara then raises a challenge to the Sages' position from a *Braisa*: *ha-omer yamin harei zo shevu'ah* — one who says "by my right hand" has made a valid oath. How can the mere utterance of "right hand" constitute a *shevu'ah*? Is that not precisely borrowing the meaning of a neighboring term — since the verse says *va-yarem yemino u-smolo el ha-shamayim va-yishava b'chai ha-olam*, where *yamin* appears alongside *shevu'ah*? The Gemara rejects this comparison: *mishum d'yamin gufei ikrei shevu'ah* — because the word *yamin* itself has acquired the independent meaning of oath, as the verse *nishba Hashem bi-yemino* demonstrates: God swore "by His right hand," meaning God took an oath in the form of "By my right hand I will do X." The meaning of *yamin* as oath is therefore intrinsic to the word through usage, not merely borrowed from an adjacent term. This distinction vindicates the Sages' position: they reject the borrowing of neighboring meaning, but acknowledge that words can organically develop new meanings through the contexts in which they consistently appear.

---

## Partial nezirut

### All-or-nothing rule

The *mishnah* introduces a new and conceptually important case: *harei ani nazir min ha-chartzanim* — "I am a *nazir* from the grape-skins," or *min ha-zagim* — from the seeds, or *min ha-tiglachat* — from shaving, or *min ha-tumah* — from impurity. The person has declared *nezirut* but attempted to limit it to only one of its constituent restrictions. The *mishnah* rules: *harei zeh nazir ve-chol dikdukei nezirut alav* — that person is nonetheless a *nazir*, and all the detailed laws of *nezirut* apply. It is an all-or-nothing institution: one cannot accept the status of *nazir* piecemeal.

### Not Rabbi Shimon

The Gemara immediately notes: *masnisin d'lo k'Rabbi Shimon* — the *mishnah* does not reflect the position of Rabbi Shimon.

### Rabbi Shimon view

A *Braisa* is cited: Rabbi Shimon holds *eino chayav ad she-yidom mikulam* — one is not bound by *nezirut* unless one vows regarding all of its restrictions. If someone attempts only a partial acceptance, he has done nothing at all.

### Sages' reasoning

The Sages hold the opposite: *afilu nazar ela be-echad min ha-nehon havei nazir* — even if one accepts only one restriction, one becomes a *nazir* subject to all of them. The logic is that *nezirut* is a unified package; a partial acceptance drags the whole structure along with it.

### Biblical sources

What are the biblical sources for these positions? Rabbi Shimon derives his view from *mikkol asher ye'aseh mi-gefen ha-yayyin me-chartzannim ve-ad zag* — "from everything that is made from the grapevine, from the skin to the pit." The word *mikkol* — from everything — implies that one must accept the full scope; a partial acceptance falls short of the whole and is therefore nothing. The Sages derive theirs from *mi-yayin ve-shachar yazir* — "from wine and intoxicating drink he shall become a *nazir*." The verse names only wine, yet we know full well that a *nazir* is bound by far more than wine alone. Evidently, naming only wine — only part of the obligation — is sufficient to constitute *nezirut* for everything. Even a partial declaration triggers the full status.

---

## Nazir and wine mitzvot

### Wine mizvot issue

The Gemara now asks: since the extra language *mi-yayin ve-shachar yazir* is not needed to tell us about the all-or-nothing rule (the Sages deriving their position from elsewhere), what does this verse come to teach? The answer: *la-shavyei mitzvah ke-reshut* — to equate even a *mitzvah* involving wine with an ordinary permitted act. That is, the *nazir*'s prohibition on wine applies even when drinking wine would fulfill a *mitzvah*. The verse's inclusive language covers wine consumed in the performance of commandments.

### Kiddush problem

What *mitzvah* would be implicated? *Kiddushta ve-avdalta* — the wine of *kiddush* and *havdala*. Even for those, the *nazir* is forbidden. This seems unremarkable. But the Gemara then produces what is, by any measure, a striking statement: *harei mushba ve-omed hu me-Har Sinai* — but is he not already sworn and obligated from Sinai? The implication appears to be that since one has a *Sinai*-level obligation to make *kiddush*, that obligation pre-empts the *nazir*'s prohibition: *mushba ve-omed* — a pre-existing oath or obligation cannot be overridden by a subsequent vow. The *Rishonim* are confounded. Wine for *kiddush* is not *d'Oraita* in the first place — there is no verse in the Torah requiring *kiddush* on wine specifically; one may make *kiddush* on bread. And even if there were a Torah-level obligation to make *kiddush* on wine, the principle of *mushba ve-omed* would not straightforwardly apply, because accepting *nezirut* does not constitute a direct declaration against the *kiddush* obligation. One could compare it to declaring a *sukkah* forbidden to oneself: such a declaration does not directly negate the obligation to dwell in a *sukkah*, but focuses on the object; and yet it effectively prevents fulfillment of the *mitzvah* when the time comes. The same logic applies to *nezirut*: by accepting the status of *nazir* one does not say "I will not make *kiddush*" — one merely takes on a status that renders wine *assur*, which then gets in the way.

### Kiddush not d'Oraita

The *Rishonim* therefore struggle to make sense of this *gemara* as a straightforward statement. The basic analytic objections are twofold: first, wine for *kiddush* is *de-Rabbanan*, not *d'Oraita*; second, even for a *d'Oraita* obligation, the *mushba ve-omed* principle does not apply when the newer vow operates obliquely rather than directly against the standing obligation.

### Rabbeinu Tam rhetorical

Rabbeinu Tam cuts through the difficulty with characteristic boldness: the Gemara's statement is not a declarative assertion but a rhetorical question expressed with astonishment — *bitmiha*. The Gemara is not saying that *mushba ve-omed* prevents *nezirut* from taking effect regarding *kiddush* wine. It is asking incredulously: do you really think there is a Sinai-level obligation to drink wine for *kiddush*? Of course there is not. The whole premise of the question collapses, and the verse's teaching that *nezirut* applies even to wine connected with *mitzvot* stands uncontested.

### Rava case

The Gemara then presents Rava's formulation of a related case: *shavu'ah she-eshteh* — if one takes an oath that he will drink, *ve-chazar ve-amar hareini nazir* — and then declares himself a *nazir*, *chalah nezirut al shavu'ah* — the *nezirut* takes effect notwithstanding the oath.

### Nezirut vs shevua

This case is the clean illustration of the principle at stake. A person has sworn an oath to drink wine and subsequently accepted *nezirut*. His *nezirut* is fully operative, and he is now forbidden to drink. But this does not mean the *nazir* simply overrides his *shevua*: it means the *nezirut* takes effect as a status, and when the time arrives to fulfill the oath, the *nazir* status stands in the way — just as making all *sukkot* forbidden to oneself does not directly violate the obligation to sit in a *sukkah* but renders fulfillment impossible when *Sukkot* arrives. The *nezirut* does not go head-to-head against the *shevua*; it operates laterally, focusing on the person's status rather than directly contradicting his prior commitment. That is why *nezirut* takes effect — it is not *mushba ve-omed* in the direct sense.

The overwhelming consensus of the *Rishonim*, including the extended discussion in the *Tosafot Rid* in *Arvei Pesachim*, is to follow Rabbeinu Tam's reading: the *gemara*'s *mushba ve-omed* statement is rhetorical, wine for *kiddush* is *de-Rabbanan*, and *nezirut* can take effect even in the face of a *shevua* because the two operate on different planes. A small number of *Rishonim* do attempt to read the *gemara* literally — concluding, for instance, that a *nazir* would be permitted to drink *kiddush* wine, or entertaining related anomalies — but these readings are widely regarded as untenable. The *sugya* resolves cleanly on Rabbeinu Tam's account, and with that the daf reaches its conclusion.
