# Nazir 4

## Shimon vs. Rabbanan

### Nezirut Indivisible

The *mishna* establishes that *nezirut* is an all-or-nothing commitment: one cannot accept upon oneself only a partial form of *nezirut* — only from grapes, only from hair-cutting, or only from *tumah*. It is a complete package. The *gemara* then engages Rabbi Shimon's position, which likewise treats *nezirut* as indivisible, but with an additional and sharper implication: if one attempted to accept *nezirut* from only one aspect of its obligations, one has done nothing at all. There is a conceivable third position — that partial *nezirut* is in fact valid — but this is a position the *gemara* rejects. The one exception, which will emerge in the coming *mishna*, is *nazir Shimshon*, since Shimshon himself became *tamei* regularly. Beyond that, there is no phenomenon of partial *nezirut*.

### Shimon: All or Nothing

The *gemara*, as it often does, seeks to identify the *pasuk* from which each side derives its position, and then to ask what the opposing side does with that same verse. In this context, the central *pasuk* under analysis is *miyayin veshechar yazir* — that a *nazir* will abstain from wine and intoxicating liquid. As discussed previously, the Sages understand that in the context of *nezirut*, *shechar* does not carry its ordinary meaning of non-wine intoxicants such as beer or mead, but refers only to wine-based mixtures — a reading that is admittedly not the straightforward *pshat* of the verse.

The *gemara* had explained that the *rabbanan* use this verse to teach that even an attempt to accept *nezirut* from only one element draws in the entire package. If so, what does Rabbi Shimon do with that verse? He holds that the verse comes to tell us that even a type of wine one might have thought should be excluded remains forbidden to the *nazir*.

### Miyayin Veshechar

The *gemara* initially suggests that the excluded wine might be the wine of *kiddush* and *havdalah*, but this is rejected. The *gemara*'s language — *mushba ve'omed me'har sinai* — is read by most *rishonim*, following Rabbeinu Tam, as ironic or rhetorical: obviously a *nazir* cannot drink the wine of *kiddush* and *havdalah*. No verse is needed to establish that.

The *gemara* therefore identifies a more meaningful case, introduced by Rava: suppose someone takes a *shevuah* that he will drink wine, and immediately afterward declares himself a *nazir*. One might have thought that the prior oath to drink wine cannot be overridden by the subsequent *nezirut*, and that he must therefore drink the wine. The verse *miyayin veshechar yazir* comes to teach that the *nezirut* does indeed take hold, and he is forbidden from that wine as well.

### Yayin Mitzvah Issue

The underlying principle here is that one cannot take a *shevuah* that directly countermands an existing obligation — *mushba ve'omed*. I cannot swear not to sit in a *sukkah* on *Sukkot*, for instance, since I am already obligated. Nor can I swear to drink wine and then swear not to drink wine; the second oath would directly contradict the first obligation. However, a *neder* operates differently. A *neder* works indirectly: if I declare all *sukkahs* forbidden to me, I am not directly countermanding my personal obligation. I am making the physical object of the *sukkah* forbidden, and then when the *mitzvah* arrives, I simply cannot fulfill it — the object is forbidden.

Similarly, when one declares oneself a *nazir*, one is not saying "I will not drink wine." One is changing one's status, one's identity. The natural consequence of having assumed the status of *nazir* is that wine becomes forbidden, but this is not a direct countermand of the prior *shevuah* to drink. One relates to the object — or in the case of *nezirut*, one becomes the object — and everything flows from that new status. This is why *nezirut* can override even an existing oath, because it is a change of personal status rather than a direct acceptance of individual obligations.

### Nezirut as Status

This distinction is crucial: when a person says *harei ani nazir*, he is not directly obligating himself not to drink wine, not to cut his hair, not to become *tamei*. He is imparting upon himself the status of *nazir*, and from that status all the individual *issurim* flow by Torah law. He himself becomes, in a sense, the object — the bearer of the status — and the prohibitions attach to him through that status, not through direct vow.

Returning to the *gemara*'s give-and-take: the *rabbanan* counter that they too need the verse *miyayin veshechar yazir* to teach the case of the wine that was the subject of a prior *shevuah*. If so, they cannot use that verse for the all-or-nothing teaching. But the *gemara* responds: if the only purpose of the verse were to teach that this particular wine remains forbidden, it would have sufficed to say "from wine." The fact that it adds *veshechar* — the extra element — must come to teach something additional: namely, that even if one attempted *nezirut* only from *shechar*, one becomes a *nazir* with respect to everything. Rabbi Shimon's purpose for the word *shechar* is then asked: he holds that *shechar* in this verse comes to establish a *hekesh*, a comparison, between the law of the *nazir* and the law of the *Beit HaMikdash*.

## Shechar Definition

### Tziruf Concept

The verse in the context of the *Kohanim* — *yayin veshechar al teisht ata u-vanecha itach* — prohibits a *kohein* from entering the *Beit HaMikdash* in a state of intoxication. That verse likewise uses the phrase *yayin veshechar*. Since by *nazir* we establish that *shechar* cannot mean non-wine intoxicants but must refer to wine-based mixtures, the *hekesh* between *nazir* and *Mikdash* teaches that the same is true for a *kohein*: only wine, not other intoxicating liquids, would trigger the prohibition of entering the *Mikdash*. In both contexts, the prohibition extends specifically to wine-based drinks.

### Kohen Application

The technical distinction matters: for a *kohein* and wine, there is a formal measure — a *revi'is*, approximately three and a half ounces, which is less than the size of most *kiddush* cups. For *shechar* in the ordinary sense, the prohibition requires actual intoxication. The *gemara* reasons that since *shechar* cannot carry its plain meaning in the context of *nazir*, and the verse in *Mikdash* uses the identical phrase, it too must be restricted to wine-based drinks.

### Rabbi Yehuda: Broad Shec…

This leads to a rejection of Rabbi Yehuda's position. A *baraita* records that Rabbi Yehuda holds: if a person ate pressed figs from Ke'ilis, or drank honey and milk, and then entered the *Beit HaMikdash*, he is liable — because all of these substances, even some that are solid foods rather than drinks, can cause a state of intoxication and are therefore encompassed within *shechar*. For Rabbi Yehuda, *shechar* extends to anything that produces this state of being intoxicated or somewhat elevated, regardless of whether it is a beverage at all.

### Shechar Wine-Based

The *rabbanan* reject this broad reading. Only wine-based substances are encompassed by *shechar*; other intoxicating substances — *sha'ar devarim hamishkarin* — are not included. There is a significant gap between these positions. Rabbi Yehuda takes the word *shechar*, which refers to a specific type of intoxicating beverage, and extends it to anything that produces this physiological state. A reasonable position might have rejected Rabbi Yehuda's extension to solids while still reading *shechar* literally as beer or mead. Yet the *gemara* here implies that even for entering the *Beit HaMikdash*, only wine-based substances are included. It should be noted that this is not the way we rule in practice: the *halacha* does in fact hold that *shechar* is included, and we tend to rule like Rabbi Yehuda that even other intoxicating substances are prohibited.

### Hora'ah Digression

This discussion naturally gives rise to a related practical question: if a person consumed a substance that caused intoxication — whether a food like fermented figs or a medication taken for serious pain that produced an altered state — would that disqualify him from rendering a *halachic* ruling or sitting on a *beit din*? The prohibition against *hora'ah* while intoxicated is not limited to wine; if we rule like Rabbi Yehuda that other intoxicating substances are included, then medication that produces a high might equally disqualify a *dayan*. One practical distinction found in the *Shulchan Aruch* is that if a person is merely relating what is already written explicitly in the books — not rendering a novel ruling — that is not considered *paskening* and would be permitted even in an intoxicated state. As was wryly observed: if one can remember the *siman* in *Shulchan Aruch*, perhaps one is not genuinely incapacitated.

## Isur Chal Al Isur

### No Double Prohibition

The *gemara* continues. The *rabbanan* need the verse *miyayin veshechar yazir* for the case of the *shevuah* to drink wine; they use it to teach that even that wine remains forbidden after one accepts *nezirut*. But there is an alternative explanation for what Rabbi Shimon does with this verse. The *gemara* suggests: Rabbi Shimon does not hold the principle of *isur chal al isur* — that one forbidden status cannot take hold atop another. Because he rejects this principle generally, he needs a verse to establish that *nezirut* does indeed create a prohibition even where a prior *isur* already exists.

### Neveila/YK Case

The *gemara* brings a *baraita* to illustrate Rabbi Shimon's position: Rabbi Shimon says that one who eats a *neveila* on *Yom Kippur* is exempt from violating *Yom Kippur*, because there is no *isur chal al isur*. This is a striking *gemara*. One can understand the principle when it applies to the status of an object: if a piece of meat is already a *neveila* and one then cooks it in milk, one might argue that the object cannot acquire the additional status of *basar b'chalav* — it already bears a forbidden status, and the second prohibition does not attach. That logic is coherent.

But the *Yom Kippur* case is far more puzzling. The prohibition of *Yom Kippur* does not rest on the status of the object; it rests on me — on the person's obligation of *inuy*, self-affliction. What does the forbidden status of the *neveila* have to do with whether I have violated my personal obligation of *Yom Kippur*? I have still engaged in an act of eating on *Yom Kippur*. Why should I be exempt? This is the primary case from which Rabbi Shimon derives his principle, and yet it is the most difficult to understand.

### Oath vs. Nezirut

The *gemara* applies this to *nezirut*: suppose one took a *shevuah* not to drink wine — the mirror image of the earlier case — and then declared himself a *nazir*, and then drank wine. According to Rabbi Shimon, the verse *miyayin veshechar yazir* establishes that even in this case he is forbidden on the wine through *nezirut* as well — not only through his prior *shevuah*. This is a case where *isur chal al isur* does apply even according to Rabbi Shimon, because the verse teaches it explicitly. The principle applies whether the prior *shevuah* was to drink the wine or not to drink it; in either case, the *nezirut* remains operative.

This again connects to the insight that *nezirut* functions as a change of status rather than a direct assumption of obligations. When one declares *harei ani nazir*, one is not directly confronting the prior oath at all; one is transforming one's identity, and the prohibitions follow from that.

## Shimon: No Shiur

### Combining Products

The *gemara* turns to the verse the *rabbanan* use for their all-or-nothing teaching. Rabbi Shimon had used *mikkol asher ye'aseh migefen ha-yayin* to mean that one must accept *nezirut* from everything, and that accepting only part produces nothing. What do the *rabbanan* do with this verse? They read it as teaching the law of *tziruf* — that the various grape-derived products forbidden to a *nazir* combine with one another. If one ate a small amount of grape skin and a small amount of seeds and some raisins, and together these combine to constitute a *kezayit*, one has violated the prohibition. The word *mikkol* — from all — indicates that all the different categories of forbidden grape products join together to form the minimum measure.

### Kol Shehu L'Malkos

What then does Rabbi Shimon do without this teaching of *tziruf*? The *gemara* cites a *baraita*: Rabbi Shimon holds *kol shehu l'malkot* — even the smallest amount is sufficient for lashes. This is a general principle Rabbi Shimon advances throughout *Shas*, argued most fully in *Masechet Makkot*: wherever the Sages require a minimum measure, Rabbi Shimon holds that one violates the prohibition even with the smallest amount and is liable even to lashes.

### Shiur for Korban Only

Rabbi Shimon does allow for a minimum measure — but only in one specific context: *lo amru kezayit ela l'inyan korban* — the *kezayit* measure was stated only with respect to the *korban*. If one acted unintentionally and the question is whether one must bring an atonement offering, a minimum threshold applies. But for purposes of punishment — including lashes — even the smallest amount constitutes a full violation. This is a fascinating idea: willful transgression, even of a minute quantity, is a complete violation. Unintentional transgression triggers a *korban* only once it reaches a certain degree.

By *nezirut*, Rabbi Shimon therefore has no need for *tziruf*. For lashes, he does not need a *kezayit* of any single type, let alone a combination — even the tiniest amount suffices. For a *korban*, one would need a minimum measure, but by *nezirut* one does not bring a *korban* for violating the prohibition on grapes and wine. The *korban* is brought either upon the completion of *nezirut* or when one becomes *tamei*. There is therefore no context in which *tziruf* would be necessary according to Rabbi Shimon.

A *kezayit* measure does remain relevant according to most authorities, with Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that *chatzi shiur* — less than the minimum amount — constitutes an *issur de'oraita* (unlike Resh Lakish's position), though not at the full degree of violation. Rabbi Shimon's position goes further: he holds there is no minimum at all, even for purposes of punishment.

## Nazir Shimshon

### Identifying Shimshon

The *mishna* introduces the institution of *nazir Shimshon*. If someone says *harei ani k'Shimshon* — behold I am like Shimshon — or *k'ven Manoach*, like the son of Manoach, or *k'ba'al Delilah*, like the husband of Delilah, or *k'mi she'akar daltot Azza*, like the one who tore down the doors of Gaza, or *k'mi shenakru Pelishtim et einav*, like the one whose eyes the Philistines gouged out — in any of these cases one becomes a *nazir Shimshon*. The larger *chiddush* here is not merely which phrases work, but that there exists this distinct institution of *nazir Shimshon*, in which one does not violate — or does not violate to the same degree — through becoming *tamei*, since Shimshon himself became *tamei l'met* routinely.

### Clarification Debate

The *gemara* asks: why does the *mishna* need to list all of these formulations? The answer is that each one is necessary. If one said only *harei ani k'Shimshon*, one might be referring to another Shimshon entirely — there are many people by that name. The *mishna* therefore adds *k'ven Manoach*. But if one said only *k'ven Manoach*, there might be other people called ben Manoach; the *mishna* therefore includes *k'ba'al Delilah*. And so on, each phrase clarifying and building upon the previous ones.

This raises an interesting question about how to read the *mishna*. On the surface, the *mishna* appears to offer these phrases as alternatives — any one of them suffices. But the *gemara*'s reasoning seems to suggest that they are cumulative: one must say *k'Shimshon*, then *k'ven Manoach*, then *k'ba'al Delilah*, each phrase required to remove ambiguity introduced by the prior one.

### Tosafot Reading

*Tosafot* addresses this tension. They hold that the first set of phrases — *k'Shimshon k'ven Manoach k'ba'al Delilah* — do indeed require one another, meaning all must be said together before *nazir Shimshon* status is established. However, *Tosafot* maintains that the final phrases — *k'mi she'akar daltot Azza* and *k'mi shenakru Pelishtim et einav* — are sufficiently explicit on their own. Even so, this reading does not align naturally with the straightforward *pshat* of the *mishna*, which seems to present each phrase as independently sufficient, nor does the *gemara* state this distinction explicitly.

This reading is in fact consistent with a theme we have encountered in the previous two days: the *mishna* appears to permit relatively vague formulations to be effective, while the *gemara* requires far greater specificity — as we saw with Shmuel's ruling that one must have a *nazir* standing in front of him and be holding one's hair. The *gemara* here similarly tightens the requirements of the *mishna*, which is fully consistent with what we have seen throughout the opening of this tractate.

## Olam vs. Shimshon

### Nazir Olam Details

The next *mishna* asks: *mah bein nazir olam l'nazir Shimshon* — what is the difference between a *nazir olam* and a *nazir Shimshon*? Both are permanent forms of *nezirut*, but they are mirror images of one another. A *nazir olam* is one who accepts *nezirut* upon himself forever, with no intention to terminate it. The reader will be aware that Rav Kook had a student known as "the Nazir" who accepted *nezirut* and remained a *nazir* for his entire life, since there is no *Beit HaMikdash* in which to bring the *korban* that would terminate *nezirut*. It is worth noting, however, that *nazir olam* is a specific institution: one who declares himself a *nazir* but never brings the concluding *korban* is not thereby a *nazir olam* — he is simply a *nazir* who has chosen not to end his *nezirut*. A *nazir olam* is one who by the very nature of his declaration intends it to be permanent.

The *gemara* notes that the *mishna* has introduced the comparison without having first established what *nazir olam* is. It therefore fills in: *michsarei michsara vehachi katani* — the *mishna* is incomplete and should be read as having stated: one who says *harei ani nazir olam*, behold I am a *nazir* forever, is a *nazir olam*. Now, what is the difference between a *nazir olam* and a *nazir Shimshon*?

The *mishna* states: *nazir olam hichbid se'aro meikel beta'ar umevi shalosh behemot* — a *nazir olam*, when his hair becomes too heavy, is permitted to trim it with a razor, and when he does so he must bring three animals as offerings. This is remarkable: by all appearances, cutting one's hair violates a biblical prohibition for a *nazir*, yet the Sages derive from the case of Avshalom that this allowance exists for a *nazir olam*. We are learning from actual cases in *Nach* — Shimshon and Avshalom — that variant forms of *nezirut* exist which carry leniencies not found in the *Torah*'s presentation of *nezirut*. A *nazir Shimshon* may become *tamei lemet*; a *nazir olam* may trim his hair when it becomes excessively burdensome. Both seemingly violate biblical prohibitions, yet both are learned out from these later figures.

### Avshalom Source

*Tosafot* in the last *tosafot* of the *daf* explains: the requirement to bring three animals when cutting one's hair is a *halacha* transmitted to Moshe at Sinai, with support derived from the verse concerning Avshalom, who declared *ashaleim nidri* — I will fulfill my vow. The vow is understood as the same three-animal sacrifice — *chatat*, *olah*, and *shelamim* — that a *nazir tahor* brings upon completing his *nezirut*. In a certain sense, bringing these offerings constitutes a virtual completion of the *nezirut*, opening a window that permits the hair to be cut, even though the *nezirut* itself continues forever.

### Three Korbanot

When the *nazir olam* brings these three offerings and cuts his hair, he has not ended his *nezirut*. He must continue observing all the laws of *nezirut* going forward. The *korbanot* serve as a kind of partial punctuation — a moment of release from the burden of accumulated hair — while the fundamental status of *nazir* remains intact. The laws of *tumah* for a *nazir olam*, by contrast, are standard: *ve'im nitma meivi korban tumah* — if he becomes *tamei*, he must bring the *korban tumah* just as any other *nazir* would. There is no leniency by *tumah*.

### Shimshon Leniencies

*Nazir Shimshon* is precisely the reverse. *Hichbid se'aro eino meikel* — even if his hair grows impossibly heavy, he is not permitted to trim it. There is no allowance regarding hair. This, of course, reflects what we know of Shimshon himself: the relationship between scissors and his hair was not a favorable one. But *ve'im nitma eino meivi korban tumah* — if he becomes *tamei*, he is not obligated to bring a *korban tumah*. There is an allowance by *tumah*. The two institutions are thus mirror images, each reflecting the actual reality of the figure from whom they take their name.

It should be noted that *Tosafot* adds another difference between the two institutions that the *mishna* does not mention: a *nazir olam* can have his *nezirut* revoked by a *chacham* through *she'eila*, whereas a *nazir Shimshon* cannot. Since the *mishna* wished to enumerate differences in the practical observance of *nezirut* rather than in the manner of its dissolution, this distinction was not included.

## Nezirut on Shimshon

### Korban Paradox

The *gemara* now raises a sharp question about the *mishna*'s formulation. The *mishna* says that a *nazir Shimshon* does not bring a *korban tumah* — implying that becoming *tamei* is still prohibited but does not trigger a *korban*. But this creates an apparent paradox: if *nezirut* applies fully to a *nazir Shimshon* in all other respects, why would he not be obligated to bring a *korban tumah* upon becoming *tamei*?

*Mani matnitin?* the *gemara* asks — who is our *mishna* following? The answer is: neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Shimon, as their positions will be shown to be more extreme than the *mishna* implies.

### Rabbi Yehuda Permits

A *baraita* records that Rabbi Yehuda holds: *nazir Shimshon mutar letamei lametim* — a *nazir Shimshon* is permitted *lechatchila* to become *tamei* to corpses, since that is precisely what we find that Shimshon himself did. His becoming *tamei* was not a violation at all.

### Shimon Rejects

Rabbi Shimon, on the other hand, holds: *ha'omer harei ani nazir Shimshon lo amar klum* — one who says "behold I am a *nazir Shimshon*" has said nothing whatsoever. The reason: *shelo matzinu b'Shimshon sheyatza nezirut mipiyu* — we do not find that Shimshon ever verbally accepted *nezirut* upon himself. The angel declared it; the status was conferred from birth. Shimshon's father did not accept it for him, and Shimshon himself never articulated an acceptance. There was no *halachic* act of vowing.

The *gemara* then resolves who the *mishna* follows: it must go like Rabbi Yehuda. The reason the *mishna* used the conditional formulation *im nitma* — "if he became *tamei*" — is only because the parallel structure required it: since by *nazir olam* the *mishna* stated *im nitma meivi korban tumah*, it mirrored that formulation for *nazir Shimshon*. But the true content of Rabbi Yehuda's position, as the *gemara* clarifies, is that a *nazir Shimshon* is *lechatchila* permitted to become *tamei*.

## Vow vs. Automatic

### Becoming Nazir Shimshon

The *gemara* now explores how exactly one becomes a *nazir Shimshon* according to Rabbi Shimon's understanding. All the phrases listed in the *mishna* — *k'Shimshon*, *k'ven Manoach*, *k'ba'al Delilah*, and so on — are formulations in which one says "I wish to be like Shimshon." This is not, on reflection, the acceptance of an independent institution called *nazir Shimshon*. What one is actually saying is: I want to take Shimshon's *nezirut* status and transfer it to myself. This mechanism of transferring a status from one object or person to another is called *hatfasah*.

### Hatfasah Concept

*Hatfasah* — the act of "grabbing," of connecting one thing to another that already bears a status in order to transfer that status — is a recognized mechanism within the world of *nedarim*. If a sanctified animal is standing before me, and I point to a loaf of bread and say *zeh ka-zeh* — this is like that — I have transferred the *kedushah* of the first object to the second. This works because both the original object and the new one are operating within the same world of *nedarim*, the world in which status is imparted through speech acts.

But what if the first object's status was never imparted through words? What if it became *kadosh* automatically, without a human vow? Can one then use *hatfasah* to transfer that status to another object? This is the crux of the debate.

### Davar Hanidur

Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon dispute a principle called *davar hanidur* — whether *hatfasah* is effective only when the original status came into being through a *neder*, a verbal act of consecration. Rabbi Shimon holds that *hatfasah* requires a *davar hanidur*: the original status must have been created through words. A status that came about automatically — like the status of *nazir* conferred upon Shimshon from the moment of his birth through the angel's declaration, without any human speech act — cannot be transferred through *hatfasah*. Since every formulation by which one becomes a *nazir Shimshon* is an act of *hatfasah* — I want what Shimshon had — and since Shimshon's status was not a *davar hanidur*, the declaration is meaningless.

## Bekhor Debate

### Bekhor Transferability

The *gemara* tests this principle through the parallel case of *bekhor*. A *baraita* records a dispute: if one says *harei alai k'bechor* — this loaf of bread shall be like this firstborn animal — does the *hatfasah* work? A *bekhor* is indeed *kadosh* and forbidden in benefit, but it became *kadosh* automatically, through birth, without any human *neder*. Rabbi Yaakov holds that the *hatfasah* works — the loaf is forbidden. Rabbi Yossi holds that it does not work.

The *gemara* initially suggests that Rabbi Yehuda follows Rabbi Yaakov — holding that *hatfasah* is effective even when the original status was not imparted through words — and that Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Yossi. But the *gemara* then retracts: in fact, everyone agrees that *hatfasah* fundamentally requires a *davar hanidur*. The entire dispute between Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Yossi concerns only whether *bekhor* can be considered a *davar hanidur* despite the automatic nature of its sanctity.

How so? The verse says *ki tidor neder laHashem* — when you vow a vow to God. The extra phrase *laHashem* is taken to extend the law to include certain cases one might not have expected. Rabbi Yaakov reads *laHashem* as including the *bekhor*: even sanctity that began automatically as belonging to God can be part of the *hatfasah* system. Rabbi Yossi disagrees: *laHashem* is needed to include *chatat* and *asham*, which one might have thought are excluded from *hatfasah* because they are not voluntary offerings but obligatory ones. Their sanctity was imparted through speech — one does sanctify the animal — but they are not classic *nedarim* in the motivational sense; one was compelled to bring them. The *laHashem* establishes that even obligatory offerings are part of the *hatfasah* world. Having used the verse for that purpose, one cannot further stretch it to include *bekhor*, whose sanctity was never imparted through any speech act at all.

### Yossi: No Words

Rabbi Yossi's position is thus: the *bekhor* is categorically different from *chatat* and *asham*. A *chatat* and *asham*, even though they are obligatory, have their sanctity imparted through the owner's speech — one goes and sanctifies the animal. The status came through words. Therefore there is reason to include them in the *hatfasah* world: *matfisan bineder*, their status was grabbed through a *neder*-type act. But a *bekhor*: *ein matfiso bineder* — its status does not come through words at all. It is automatically sacred from birth. There is therefore no basis to include it in the *hatfasah* world even through the extension of *laHashem*.

### Yaakov: Sanctification

Rabbi Yaakov's response is that a *bekhor* does in fact have a dimension of status imparted through words. A *baraita* from the school of Rebbe teaches: from where do we know that one who has a *bekhor* born in his flock has a *mitzvah* to actively sanctify it — even though it is already automatically *kadosh*? From the verse *hazachar takdish* — the male you shall sanctify. Even though the *bekhor* is already sacred, there is a positive commandment to perform an act of sanctification upon it.

Rabbi Yaakov argues that this obligatory act of sanctification means that the *bekhor*'s status does have a dimension that comes through words, through a speech act of *hakdashah*. Therefore it can participate in the *hatfasah* world. Rabbi Yossi's counter is that this *mitzvah* of sanctification is ultimately superfluous — *i-lo makdish lei mi lo kadosh*? — even if one does not perform this act, the *bekhor* is already sacred. If one's words do not actually affect the *bekhor*'s status — since it would have been sacred regardless — then one has not imparted status through a *neder*, and it cannot serve as the basis for *hatfasah*.

The Rav offers a beautiful application of this dispute. When we recite *kiddush* on *Shabbat* — *zachor et yom hashabbat l'kadesho* — one might ask: does our *kiddush* actually add anything to *Shabbat*'s sanctity, which exists independently of us? Following Rabbi Yossi's logic, one might say that *kiddush* is merely an act of acknowledgment — we are recognizing a holiness that exists without us, and our words change nothing. But following Rabbi Yaakov's logic, one might say that our act of *kiddush* does add a human dimension of *kedushah* to a *Shabbat* that already possesses its own *kedushah*. The parallel is striking.

## Bekhor Debate (II)

### Shimshon Mystery

Having established that everyone agrees *hatfasah* requires a *davar hanidur*, the *gemara* leaves unresolved an important question: if this is indeed the rule, how does Rabbi Yehuda permit a person to become a *nazir Shimshon*? If Shimshon never verbally accepted *nezirut*, his status was not a *davar hanidur*, and one cannot transfer it to oneself through *hatfasah*. The *gemara* does not provide a direct answer.

### Rosh Solutions

The *Rosh* offers three possible resolutions. First: perhaps the verse by *nazir* uses the phrase *l'hazir laHashem*, and this *laHashem* extends to include *nazir Shimshon* — the same way some hold that *laHashem* by *neder* includes *bekhor*, so too it might include the *nezirut* of Shimshon. Second: Rabbi Yehuda may hold that Shimshon in fact did verbally accept *nezirut* upon himself when he came of age and became *bar mitzvah* — this is what the angel's instruction pointed toward, and naturally Shimshon fulfilled this obligation through an act of acceptance. Third: Shimshon's father may have made him a *nazir* when he was a child, as a father has the authority to do — *ish madir et beno b'nazir* — making the *nezirut* rest on a human verbal act after all.

According to these resolutions, everyone agrees that *nazir Shimshon* works by the mechanism of *hatfasah* — by transferring Shimshon's status — not by accepting an independent institution. The question is only how to establish that Shimshon's original status was itself a *davar hanidur*. The debate about Shimshon's *bar mitzvah* acceptance is, as one participant put it, an imaginative but halachically serious reconstruction.

## Shimon HaTzadik

### Refusing Asham

The *gemara* uses the phrase *l'hazir laHashem* in the verse for a different teaching entirely. A *baraita* reports: Shimon HaTzadik — from the era of the *Beit HaMikdash* — said: *miyamai lo achalti asham nazir tamei* — in all my days I never ate the *asham* brought by a *nazir* who had become *tamei*. He would eat other *ashamos*, which also arise from sin — unintentional sin — and therefore could theoretically raise similar concerns. But a *tamei nazir* was different in his eyes. Becoming *tamei* during *nezirut* means one must start the entire process again from the beginning. The concern the *gemara* had expressed was that such a person might retrospectively regret having ever accepted *nezirut*, rendering the entire *nezirut* retroactively invalid — something like a *neder* made in error — making the animal effectively *chullin ba'azarah*. Therefore, Shimon HaTzadik refused to eat the *asham* of such a person.

### Shepherd Story

He makes one exception. A man came to him from the south, *yafeh einayim v'tov roi* — beautiful eyes, a fine appearance — and his hair was extraordinary, flowing in layered locks. Shimon HaTzadik asked him: my son, what moved you to become a *nazir*? For at the end of his *nezirut*, this man would have to shave off this magnificent hair. This is an interesting irony: we have encountered earlier the suggestion that a *nazir*'s growing hair might itself be a source of attraction and pride, yet here the conclusion of *nezirut* demands that it all be cut off.

### Repentance Motivation

The man replied: I was a shepherd for my father in my village. I went to draw water from the well, and I saw my reflection. My *yetzer hara* was stirred up within me and sought to draw me down from this world into a life of self-indulgence and hedonism. I said to it: *reika* — empty one — why do you take such pride in a world that is not yours, a passing temporal world whose end is worms and maggots? *Ha'avodah* — I swear — I will shave this hair for heaven's sake. And so he became a *nazir* in order to redirect his life toward holiness and away from the pull of vanity.

### Right Motivation

Shimon HaTzadik stood and kissed him on his head, and said: *kamosecha yirbu nezirim b'Yisrael* — may there be many *nezirim* in Israel like you. And about you, the verse says: *ish ki yafla lindor neder nazir lehazir laHashem* — a man who makes his vow as a *nazir* to be separated for God's sake. The *laHashem* of the verse, the *gemara* thus teaches, is not a *halachic* point about the mechanism of *hatfasah*. It is a moral and religious point: *nezirut* must be truly and genuinely for God. A *nezirut* arising from the right motivations — redirecting one's life from the pull of the self toward dedication to the divine — is the *nezirut* that the verse envisions.

This reflects the *gemara*'s ongoing ambivalence about *nezirut*. Throughout *Masechet Nedarim*, the *gemara* was deeply skeptical of *nedarim* — one who vows is called a *chotei*, a sinner. *Nazir* is more nuanced. On one hand, a *nazir* is someone striving for holiness; on the other hand, the *gemara* worries about wrong motivations, about separation from society, about the *nazir tamei* who probably regrets everything. The ending of this *daf* captures that ambivalence beautifully: yes, *yirbu nezirim b'Yisrael* — there should be many *nezirim* — but only, and precisely only, when the motivation is truly *laHashem*.

---

# Nazir 5

## Nazir Shimshon

### Shimshon Status

The *gemara* on daf 4b picks up in the middle of a discussion about *Nazir Shimshon* and *Nazir Olam*. The background question concerns whether Shimshon accepted his *nezirut* himself, through a *neder*, or whether the *nezirut* was externally imposed. This is halachically significant because the mechanism for one person to declare himself a *Nazir Shimshon* — to transfer Shimshon's status onto oneself — depends on whether Shimshon's own *nezirut* originated through a vow. This was the subject of a *tannaitic* dispute reviewed previously.

### Angel's Declaration

The *gemara* now asks: *v'Shimshon lav nazir havae* — and was Shimshon not a *nazir*? The question seems strange at first glance, since nobody denied that he was a *nazir*. The debate was specifically about whether his *nezirut* came about through a *neder*. The *gemara* presses: *v'ha-ksiv* — does the verse not say *ki nezir elohim yihye hana'ar min habaten*, that the child would be a *nazir* to God from the womb? To this, the *gemara* responds: *hasam malach d'ka-amar* — there it was only the angel saying so, not Shimshon himself.

Fitting this into the preceding discussion, the objection would be: didn't he accept his *nezirut* through a *neder*? The angelic declaration would not demonstrate that Shimshon undertook his *nezirut* in the normal way. The answer is that it was only the angel's directive, not a formal vow. More broadly, though, one may read this passage as addressing a simpler version of Rabbi Shimon's position. Rabbi Shimon said *lo amar klum shelo matzinu b'Shimshon sheyatza nezirut mipiv* — he never uttered a declaration of *nezirut*. This can be read in two ways: either he was a *nazir* but not through a vow, and therefore the status cannot be transferred; or, more radically, that according to Rabbi Shimon, Shimshon never formally held the halachic status of *nazir* at all. The *gemara*'s question and answer may be hinting at this second reading — the angelic announcement did not itself confer a halachic *nezirut*.

### Contact with Dead

The *gemara* continues: *u'minah d'itmei l'meisim* — how do we know that a *Nazir Shimshon* carries an allowance to become *tamei meis*? Shimshon certainly killed many people, but how do we know he directly touched them? The *gemara* first suggests a proof from the verse *lechi hachamor hikeisi elef ish* — with the jawbone of an ass I slew a thousand men. Since he was wielding that instrument at such close range, presumably he came into contact with the bodies. The *gemara* pushes back: *dilma giruy garu beih* — perhaps he threw it at them, never touching them directly. Questions of *tuma b'chiburin* — *tumah* transmitted through an intermediate object — are at play, but if he threw the jawbone as a projectile, no direct contact need be assumed.

The *gemara* then proposes a different verse: *vayach mehem shloshim ish vayikach es chalitzosam* — he smote thirty men and took their garments. If he removed their clothing after killing them, he must have touched them. The *gemara* responds: perhaps he stripped them first and then killed them. To this, the *gemara* answers *vayach vayikach ksiv* — the verse says "he smote and he took," in that order: he struck them first and took their garments afterward. Yet the *gemara* still resists: *v'dilma gosesin shavinahu* — perhaps he only rendered them mortally wounded but not yet dead when he took the garments, so that he still did not touch full corpses.

### Tradition on Contact

With all textual proofs exhausted, the *gemara* concludes: *ela fayn, gemara gemira lah* — this is simply a received tradition that Shimshon did in fact come into contact with some of those he killed. That closes the discussion of *Nazir Shimshon*.

---

## Nazir Olam

### Absalom Example

The *gemara* turns to the concept of *Nazir Olam* and asks: *v'nazir olam heicha ktiv* — where in Scripture is the idea of a *Nazir Olam* sourced? This refers not simply to someone who chooses indefinitely to remain a *nazir*, but to a formal status in which the *nezirut* is permanently constitutive — and which paradoxically permits periodic hair-cutting. A *braita* answers: *Rabbi omer: Avshalom Nazir Olam hayah* — just as *Nazir Shimshon* is derived from a narrative in *Tanach*, so too *Nazir Olam* is derived from the story of Avshalom.

### Absalom Narrative

The relevant verse is *vayehi miketz arba'im shanah* — and it came to pass at the end of forty years — at the point when Avshalom was plotting his rebellion against David. He says to the king: *elchah na va'ashalem et nedarai asher nadarti l'Hashem b'Chevron* — let me go and I will fulfill my vows that I made to God in Chevron. We also know that he would cut his hair *echad l'shneim asar chodesh* — once every twelve months, as Rabbi derives from the phrase *vayehi miketz yamim l'yamim* — and it was at the end of days upon days.

What is being read into these *pesukim* is that Avshalom's declaration "let me fulfill my vows" means he needed to bring the three *korbanot* that normally conclude a *nezirut*. For a *Nazir Olam*, these offerings do not terminate the *nezirut* — they open a halachic aperture allowing the *nazir* to cut his hair. Thus Avshalom would periodically bring these *korbanot* and trim his hair, yet his *nezirut* persisted permanently. The phrase *yamim l'yamim* is understood to indicate that he did this on a yearly basis.

It is worth noting an irony here that connects to the previous *sugya*. The discussion concluded with the case of a man who became a *nazir* for the purpose of eventually cutting his hair, and there was a contrast with the *mishnah* as Shmuel reads it — a person who grabs his hair and says "I will be beautiful, therefore I will be a *nazir*." The question of whether the *nazir*'s long hair represents beauty or social displacement is genuinely complex. The *pshat* of *pera* suggests the hair grows wild and unkempt, marking the *nazir* as outside normal society. Yet Avshalom's hair is described in *Tanach* precisely as something strikingly beautiful — which makes the *Nazir Olam* example an interesting counterpoint.

### Walled City Link

Rabbi derives that Avshalom's yearly hair-cutting cycle comes through a *gezeirah shavah* between the word *yamim* as it appears in the Avshalom narrative and the word *yamim* as it appears in the laws of houses in a walled city. The relevant *pasuk* there reads *yamim tihyeh ge'ulato* — his right of redemption shall be for *yamim* — and then subsequently, *ad melot lo shanah temimah* — until a full year has been completed. The *gemara* derives: *yamim* there means twelve months, a full year. Therefore *yamim l'yamim* by Avshalom also means a full year.

*V'yalif yamim yamim mibatei arei chomah, ma hasham yud-bet chodesh, af kan yud-bet chodesh* — just as *yamim* there means twelve months, so too here. This is how Rabbi concludes that a *Nazir Olam* cuts his hair once a year.

The *gemara* immediately raises a challenge. Rabbi himself holds elsewhere that *yamim* in that very *pasuk* about the walled city means literally two days — *ein yamim pachus mishnayim* — so that the seller must wait at least two days before exercising his right of redemption. How then can Rabbi use *yamim* in that *pasuk* to mean a full year?

The *gemara* answers: *hai gezeirah shavah mishum koved gamir, uvishenei yamim leika koved* — the *gezeirah shavah* is established on account of the weight of the hair becoming burdensome, and the hair certainly does not become burdensome after two days. Since the *gezeirah shavah* for the *Nazir Olam* case is premised on the notion of hair growing heavy, the *yamim* of the *gezeirah shavah* must refer to a period long enough for hair to become burdensome — which brings us to the fuller reading of that *pasuk*, identifying *yamim* with a complete year.

### Qualified Yamim

Having established that Rabbi links *yamim* to a full year via *batei arei chomah*, the *gemara* considers whether Avshalom's *yamim* could be linked to some other verse that carries *yamim* with a different duration.

First: *ve'eima beis shana* — perhaps it means two years? There is a verse that reads *vayehi mikeitz shenasayim yamim* — and it came to pass at the end of two years of days — where *yamim* appears in the context of two years. The answer: *danin yamim she'ein imahem shanim miyamim she'ein imahem shanim* — we derive *yamim* (unqualified) from *yamim* (unqualified). The verse by Avshalom says *yamim l'yamim* with no attached qualifier, and the verse by *batei arei chomah* says *yamim tihyeh ge'ulato* also without a qualifier. But *shenasayim yamim* has the word *yamim* immediately juxtaposed with *shenasayim*, making it a qualified usage. One may not learn from a qualified *yamim* to an unqualified one. *Al yochiach zeh sheyeish imo shanim*.

Second: *ve'eima sheloshim yom* — perhaps thirty days? There is a verse that reads *ad chodesh yamim* — until a month of days — where *yamim* appears alongside the word for month. The same answer applies: *danin yamim she'ein imahem chodashim miyamim she'ein imahem chodashim* — *yamim* without a month-qualifier is learned from *yamim* without a month-qualifier. *Ve'al yochiach zeh sheyeish imo chodashim*.

Third: *ve'eima meihacha miyamim yamimah* — perhaps we should learn from the verse about the daughters of Israel who would go to commemorate the daughter of Yiftach, described as coming *miyamim yamimah*, four times a year. If they came four times a year, perhaps the unit of *yamim* represents a three-month interval? The *gemara* responds: *danin yamim miyamim ve'ein danin yamim miyamimah* — we derive *yamim* from *yamim*, not from *yamimah*, which is a slightly different morphological form of the word. A *gezeirah shavah* requires the closest available verbal match.

The *gemara* then asks: *umai nafka mina* — why should the morphological form matter in a *gezeirah shavah*? Does a *gezeirah shavah* require identical words? The *gemara* invokes the well-known *braita* of the school of Rabbi Yishmael regarding *tzara'at* in a house, where the *kohen* "returns" (*veshav*) and "comes" (*uva*) — two different words used to describe the same act — and the *gemara* uses them interchangeably: *zo hi shivah zo hi biah*. This seems to suggest that *gezeirah shavah* tolerates links of meaning even without identical words. The *gemara* answers: *hani mili heicha deleika dedami leih* — that principle applies only when there is no closer match available. *Aval heicha de'ika dedami leih, midedami leih yalpinan* — but where there is an exact verbal match, the *gezeirah shavah* must follow the more precise link. Since *yamim* unqualified is available as a match, we do not resort to *yamimah*.

A further reason not to learn from the Yiftach narrative: *mena yade'ah dechol tlata yarchi chad zimna* — who says the four annual visits were evenly spaced at three-month intervals? *Dilma arba zimnei beshata*, four times a year, but irregularly distributed — perhaps *arba yarchi chad zimna*, then *trei yarchi bechad zimna*, and so on. Since the visits need not have followed a fixed interval, one cannot extract any standard unit of time from *miyamim yamimah*.

A student raised the structural observation that the *braita* of Rabbi Yishmael — who is associated with the school of *dibra Torah k'lashon b'nei adam* and generally tends toward meaning over precise morphology — is being read here as if it were making a point about *gezeirah shavah* as a formal technique, when in fact that *braita* may not be using *gezeirah shavah* at all. Rabbi Yishmael's comparison of *shivah* and *biah* may simply be a recognition that two words are synonymous in context, not a *gezeirah shavah* in the technical sense. This touches on the broader question of what *gezeirah shavah* originally meant. There is an early *mishnah* in which Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel invoke a *gezeirah shavah* in the context of two rabbinic laws — possibly the *eiruv techumin* case — suggesting that in its earliest form, *gezeirah shavah* may have meant something more like a logical analogy between comparable concepts, rather than the formal technique of word-linking that automatically transfers an entire body of law from one domain to another.

The upshot of all of this is that Rabbi's derivation stands: Avshalom is understood to have been a *nazir*, periodically bringing his *korbanot* and trimming his hair on a yearly basis (*miyamim l'yamim* = once a year), and this is how Rabbi establishes that a *Nazir Olam* may trim his hair annually.

### Nehorai: 30 Days

Rabbi Nehorai disagrees and says *megale'ach achas lishloshim yom* — a *Nazir Olam* may cut his hair once every thirty days. This is a substantial allowance: patterned after the standard unit of *nezirut*, after one has completed an equivalent period, one may get a trim. The basis is *gabei kohanim* — derived from the laws of *kohanim*, who may not allow their hair to become *gadel pera*, wild growth. *Mishum d'ika koved* — after thirty days, hair is considered to have become heavy and burdensome. *Hacha nami ika koved* — the same applies here: once the hair reaches the thirty-day threshold, it is considered burdensome and the allowance to trim kicks in.

Tosafot notes the circularity in this reasoning: the only reason we know that the *kohen* prohibition of *gadel pera* means more than thirty days is that we learn it from the standard *nezirut*, where thirty days' hair growth is defined as wild. So the chain of reasoning goes: a standard *nazir* has thirty-day *nezirut*, during which the hair must be *gadel pera*; this means thirty days defines wild hair; a *kohen* may not have *gadel pera* hair, so thirty days is the threshold; and now we use that threshold to tell us when a *Nazir Olam* may trim. Tosafot suggests the reasoning may prefer *kohanim* as the intermediate reference rather than deriving *Nazir Olam* directly from ordinary *nezirut*, since it may be preferable not to derive a *Nazir Olam*'s law directly from the temporary *nazir* (*Nazir Sha'ah*).

One genuinely puzzling question that this raises: when a *Nazir Olam* receives his trim, must his hair still maintain the *pera* state? If he trims every thirty-one days — cutting off only the hair that grew after the previous trim — his hair would cycle in and out of the *pera* threshold. On day twenty-nine it would not yet qualify as *pera*; on day thirty or thirty-one it would; then he trims and returns below the threshold. Is the *Nazir Olam* then living most of his life with hair that does not qualify as *pera*? This seems strange, since one would expect the condition of *pera* to be a permanent characteristic of the *nazir*'s state, not merely a momentary threshold he crosses before trimming back down. The *gemara* does not resolve this explicitly.

### Yosi: Weekly

Rabbi Yosi is more radical still: *megale'ach me'erev Shabbos le'erev Shabbos* — a *Nazir Olam* may cut his hair every *erev Shabbos*. The reasoning is *shekein matzinu bivnei melachim shemegalchin me'erev Shabbos le'erev Shabbos* — this is the grooming standard of princes, who cut their hair weekly, and since Avshalom was a prince, he presumably maintained this standard.

This position is striking on multiple levels. First, if Avshalom trimmed his hair weekly, how did his hair become so famously long that it caught in the tree? One answer offered is that his weekly trim was minimal — perhaps only split ends — and the hair overall remained long. Second, and more fundamentally, if a *Nazir Olam* gets a weekly haircut, his hair may never truly reach the state of *pera* at all after the first month. He would look entirely presentable at all times — essentially indistinguishable from anyone else. This seems to suggest that the *Nazir Olam*'s outward appearance is qualitatively different from that of a standard *nazir*, which is itself quite strange.

The *gemara* asks *mai ika beinei v'sha'ar echav* — how would Avshalom look different from his non-*nazir* brothers, the other princes, who also cut their hair weekly? What is the practical *nafka mina* between Avshalom's regimen and theirs? Two answers are given. First, *yom tov shechal lihayos b'emtza Shabbas* — if a *yom tov* fell mid-week, the other princes could get haircuts for *kavod yom tov*, but Avshalom, being a *nazir*, could not cut mid-week. Second, *ur l'giluychi mitzafra d'ma'alei Shabata* — his brothers could cut their hair Friday morning, whereas Avshalom, who had to wait out the full permitted interval, could not cut until *panya*, just before sunset on Friday. Tosafot adds that this may also reflect the requirement that Avshalom could not cut without first bringing his *korbanot* — so the distinction between him and his brothers was visible in the timing, even if not in the length of his hair.

### Forty Years

The *gemara* raises a chronological difficulty: *hanei arbayim shana mai avidteihu* — what are these forty years counting from? David's entire reign lasted only thirty-seven years, so "forty years after" the beginning of David's kingship is impossible. Rav Nehorai says in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua: *l'ketz mem shana she'sha'alu lahem melech* — the forty years count from when the Jewish people first asked for a king from Shmuel. The rebellion of Avshalom against his father mirrors the original rebellion of *Bnei Yisrael* against divine sovereignty when they demanded a human king — an act that Shmuel regarded as a rejection of God's kingship. Forty years later, Avshalom rebels against his father's earthly kingship. A *tanna* adds: *osa shana she'sha'alu lahem melech hi shenas eser l'Shmuel HaRamasi* — the year of that request was the tenth year of Shmuel's career, a chronological anchor that explains how all the dates in the narrative align.

---

## Standard 30 Days

### Mishnah Text

The *mishnah* states simply: *stam nezirut sheloshim yom* — standard, unexplicated *nezirut* lasts thirty days. If a person says "I am a *nazir*" without specifying a duration, the assumed period is thirty days, after which he brings his *korbanot*. We return here to ordinary *nezirut*, setting aside the special cases of *Nazir Shimshon* and *Nazir Olam*.

### Gematria Method

The *gemara* asks: *mani milei* — what is the source for thirty days? Rav Matna derives it from the verse *kadosh yihiyeh, gadel pera se'ar rosho* — holy shall it be, the growing wild of his hair. The word *yihiyeh* in *gematria*: *yud* (10) + *heh* (5) + *yud* (10) + *heh* (5) = 30. *Yihiyeh be-gematria tlasin havu* — *yihiyeh* in *gematria* equals thirty.

It is worth noting that this is a case where the *gemara* deploys *gematria* in service of an actual *halacha*. It seems fairly clear, however — given that Bar Pada immediately offers an entirely different derivation — that both authorities likely began with a received tradition that *stam nezirut* is thirty days, and each then sought to connect that tradition back to the *pesukim*. When everyone assumes a law and the debate is only about which verse supports it, that pattern typically indicates a tradition in hand rather than a derivation in process. This dynamic recurs frequently in the *sugyot* of *Chazal*: sometimes they derive the law from the verse, and sometimes they start with the tradition and find the verse afterward.

### Pada Counts

Bar Pada offers a different derivation: *k'neged nazir neziru ha'amurim ba'torah lamed chasar achas* — count the occurrences of the words *nazir* and *neziru* in the Torah and you will find twenty-nine. Interesting: if one actually counts all occurrences of *nazir* and related forms in the Torah, the total comes to thirty. Bar Pada's position is that one occurrence must be excluded — either because it is needed to introduce the concept and cannot count, or because, as the *rishonim* suggest, the phrase *ki nezer elohav al rosho* uses *nezer* to mean a crown rather than *nezirut*, and therefore does not count toward the tally. This leaves twenty-nine — and that, as we shall see, leads Bar Pada to conclude that *stam nezirut* is in principle twenty-nine days, not thirty.

### Word Usage Debate

The *gemara* challenges: why does Rav Matna not use Bar Pada's counting method? Rav Matna replies: *hahu ledrasha* — each extra occurrence of the word *nazir* in the Torah is there to teach a specific law. As we have seen, for example, *miyayin veshechar yazir* with its doubled form teaches *le'esor yayin mitzvah keyayin reshut* — that even wine consumed in fulfillment of a *mitzvah* is prohibited to the *nazir*; and the doubled expression *ki yafuli lindor neder Nazir lehazir l'Hashem* teaches *melamed she'nezirut chala al nezirut* — that one *nezirut* can take effect while another is still running, hovering in abeyance until the first concludes. Since every occurrence is pressed into service for an independent law, Rav Matna cannot simply count them up as a calendar.

### Pada Defense

Bar Pada responds: *leit chad min'hon d'lav ledrasha* — there is not a single occurrence that does not teach something. His point is that even those occurrences used for counting are not simply superfluous; rather, their very presence is meaningful. Since it is impossible that all twenty-nine (or thirty) instances teach independent *drashot* — there are not that many independent laws of *nezirut* to be derived — at least some of them must be there for counting purposes. *Ela mide'hahu leminyana, kulhu nami leminyana* — since one is established as being for counting, all may be treated as counting toward the total. The ones that do teach specific laws serve a dual function: they teach the law and they count. The key principle is that once any of the occurrences cannot be assigned an independent *drasha*, it establishes that the function of enumeration is operative across all of them.

---

## Matna vs. Pada (III)

### Matna: 30 True

Having established the two methods of derivation, the *gemara* now draws out their substantive legal disagreement. For Rav Matna, the true duration of *stam nezirut* is thirty days. The *korbanot* ending the *nezirut* are brought on day thirty-one, after the thirty days are complete.

### Pada: 29 True

For Bar Pada, the true duration is twenty-nine days in principle. However, since the *korbanot* cannot be brought at night, and one reaches the end of day twenty-nine at nightfall, one must wait until day thirty to bring the *korbanot* in practice. So the *nezirut* ends functionally on day thirty — but this is merely a practical constraint, not the halachically defined duration.

The *gemara* now tests these positions against the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* states *stam nezirut sheloshim yom* — thirty days. For Rav Matna this is straightforward. For Bar Pada it is a difficulty: he says twenty-nine. Bar Pada responds: *idi ve'idi yom sheloshim d'megaleach umeiti korbanotav nami* — in all cases, it is on day thirty that one shaves and brings *korbanot*, because one can never end it before day thirty even on the twenty-nine-day theory. Hence the *mishnah* says "thirty days" as the practical day of completion, even though the underlying duration is twenty-nine.

The *gemara* next examines the *mishnah*: *mi she'amar hareini Nazir megaleach yom sheloshim ve'echad* — one who simply says "I am a *nazir*" cuts his hair on day thirty-one. For Rav Matna this is straightforward: thirty-day duration, *korbanot* on day thirty-one. For Bar Pada it is a difficulty: he should be able to bring his *korbanot* on day thirty. Bar Pada responds: *eima seifa* — look at the end of that *mishnah*: *im gilach beyom sheloshim yatza* — if he cut on day thirty, he has fulfilled his obligation *bedi'avad*. Bar Pada can explain this: the *nezirut* was twenty-nine days, and day thirty is the proper day of completion. The *seifa* is actually in his favor. The *reisha*, which says to wait until day thirty-one *lechatchila*, Bar Pada explains as a precautionary measure: *na'aseh ke'omer shleimim* — we are concerned that one may have said "I am a *nazir* for a full month," in which case full thirty days are required. Since the difference between twenty-nine days and a month is not substantial in people's minds, we require everyone to wait until day thirty-one *lechatchila* to avoid confusion. In principle, for *stam nezirut*, day thirty is the correct and sufficient day.

### Matna Resolution

For Rav Matna, the *reisha* is straightforward — thirty days, bring *korbanot* on day thirty-one — but the *seifa* is the difficulty. How does day thirty work *bedi'avad* if the duration is thirty days? *Kasavar miktzas hayom kekulo* — Rav Matna holds the principle that part of a day counts as the whole day. One need not complete all of day thirty; having entered day thirty, the thirty-day requirement is satisfied, and the *korbanot* may be brought. The reason we nonetheless say *lechatchila* to wait until day thirty-one is that we prefer not to rely on *miktzat hayom kekulo* as a first resort. But *bedi'avad*, bringing the *korbanot* on day thirty itself is valid.

---

## Partial Day Princip (III)le

### Principle Overview

The principle of *miktzat hayom kekulo* — that part of a day counts as the whole — is familiar from other areas of *halacha*. In *aveilus*, the seven days of mourning: one rises at the beginning of the seventh day, with that partial day counting as the full seventh. Similarly, a *zavah* who counts seven clean days may immerse at the beginning of the seventh. Importantly, this principle does not always operate as a *lechatchila* standard; in some contexts, such as *niddah*, one must wait until the full end of the seventh day. Whether and when one may rely on *miktzat hayom kekulo* is itself context-dependent, which is part of why Rav Matna treats it as a *bedi'avad* resource rather than a first-choice option.

---

## Matna vs. Pada (III)

### Consecutive Cases

The *gemara* now examines back-to-back *neziriyot*. The *mishnah* states: *mi shenazar shtei neziriyot megaleach et harishona yom shloshim ve'echad vehashniya leyom shishim ve'echad* — one who takes on two consecutive *neziriyot* cuts for the first on day thirty-one and for the second on day sixty-one. The same questions arise. For Rav Matna: straightforward, thirty-day duration each, so day thirty-one ends the first and day sixty-one ends the second. For Bar Pada: why wait until day thirty-one for each? On his view the *nezirut* is twenty-nine days.

---

## Partial Day Princip (III)le…

### Full Days Exception

The *gemara* then examines the *mishnah*'s statement: *hareini nazir shloshim yom* — if one explicitly says "I am a *nazir* for thirty days" and then cuts on day thirty, *lo yatza* — one has not fulfilled the obligation. This holds for both opinions. For Bar Pada, who does not invoke *miktzat hayom kekulo*, this is simple: once one has specified full days, the full count must be satisfied. For Rav Matna, the question is sharper: why doesn't *miktzat hayom kekulo* apply here? The *gemara* answers: *be'omer shleimim* — because one said "full days." When one explicitly articulates a full thirty-day *nezirut*, the *miktzat hayom* principle is preempted; the statement of intent requires complete days, not a partial final day.

### Day 30 Hinge

In the case of back-to-back *neziriyot*, day thirty-one ends the first and begins the second. But if one went ahead and ended the first *nezirut* on day thirty — either through *miktzat hayom* (Rav Matna) or because it was a twenty-nine-day *nezirut* (Bar Pada) — then day thirty itself serves as the pivot: it ends the first and begins the second. Accordingly, the second *nezirut* started on day thirty, and adding thirty days (with the same *lechatchila* logic) brings one to day sixty for the second shaving. This is exactly what the *mishnah* says: *ve'im gilach et harishona leyom shloshim, megaleach et hashniya leyom shishim* — if one shaved for the first on day thirty, one shaves for the second on day sixty.

---

## Matna vs. Pada (III)…

### Pada Resolution

Returning to Bar Pada's resolution of the back-to-back case: the *seifa* of the *mishnah* — that shaving the first on day thirty means shaving the second on day sixty — works for Bar Pada because on his view the first *nezirut* was twenty-nine days, properly concluded on day thirty, and the second likewise. The *reisha*, which says to wait until day thirty-one and day sixty-one *lechatchila*, Bar Pada again explains as *be'omer shleimim* — or as a precautionary measure to account for cases in which one has articulated a full month, so that everyone is asked *lechatchila* to wait the extra day in order to avoid confusion between *stam nezirut* and an explicitly month-long *nezirut*.

---

## Partial Day Princip (III)le……

### Double-Dip Issue

For Rav Matna, the *seifa* of the back-to-back *mishnah* requires that *miktzat hayom kekulo* operate in two directions simultaneously on day thirty. On Rav Matna's view, the first *nezirut* was thirty days; ending it on day thirty requires invoking *miktzat hayom kekulo* — a portion of day thirty counts as the full thirtieth day of the first *nezirut*. But then day thirty also counts as day one of the second *nezirut*, which in turn requires invoking *miktzat hayom kekulo* in the other direction — that entering day thirty is treated as a full first day of the new *nezirut*. The *gemara* presses: can we truly double-dip in this way?

The *gemara* explains: *mahu detaima, hani mili le'inyan chada nezirut, aval lishtei nezirut lo* — one might have thought that *miktzat hayom kekulo* can be invoked for one *nezirut* but not to simultaneously serve two *neziriyot*. If the logic of the principle is that we treat the portion of day thirty as if it were the full final day of the first *nezirut*, then that day is, conceptually, fully consumed by the first. How can that same partial day also be treated as a fresh opening day of the second? The *gemara*'s resolution is that the *mishnah*'s explicit ruling — *yom shloshim oleh lekan ulekan*, day thirty counts in both directions — establishes this as a genuine *chiddush*: the same partial day can simultaneously close one *nezirut* and open another, applying *miktzat hayom kekulo* in both directions at once.

---

---

# Nazir 6

## Rav Masna vs Bar Pada

### 30 vs 29 Days

The daf opens in the middle of 6a, picking up a dispute introduced in prior sessions. *Rav Masna* and *Bar Pada* disagree about the fundamental structure of *stam nezirus* — standard, unspecified *nezirut*.

*Rav Masna* holds that *nezirut* is, in principle, thirty days. Since a series of *mishnayot* makes clear that a *nazir* may bring his *korban* on day thirty — thereby completing his *nezirut* on that day — *Rav Masna* must account for this by invoking the principle of *miktzas hayom kekulo*: a partial day counts as the whole. Just as a mourner rises from *aveilus* on the morning of the seventh day without completing a full seventh day, so too the *nazir* who enters day thirty has, in principle, satisfied his thirty-day obligation. This also explains why the *mishna* specifies that *lechatchila* — as the preferred initial practice — one should wait until day thirty-one to bring the *korban*. If *miktzas hayom kekulo* applies, there is still some practical reason to wait, which will become clearer as the discussion unfolds.

*Bar Pada*, by contrast, rejects *miktzas hayom kekulo* entirely. In his view, *stam nezirus* means twenty-nine days — not thirty — but twenty-nine *complete* days, with no partial-day principle at play. The *nazir* brings his *korban* on day thirty as a matter of course, because by that point twenty-nine full days have already elapsed. Why *lechatchila* one should still wait until day thirty-one on his account is less clear — perhaps to accommodate cases where the *nazir* explicitly stipulated thirty days — but his fundamental position is twenty-nine full days, no *miktzas hayom*.

### Miktzas Hayom Kekulo

One might ask: what precisely is the conceptual basis for *miktzas hayom kekulo*, and when does it apply? There is a related but distinct principle, *rubo kekulo* — the majority counts as the whole — but these are not equivalent. The principle of *rubo kekulo* operates when the goal is to achieve a particular state: for instance, in *shechita*, one need not sever the trachea and esophagus entirely; cutting the majority of each is sufficient, because the required state — severance — is considered achieved. Similarly, in *eiruv*, a wall need not be continuous along the entire perimeter; as long as the majority is enclosed, the area is considered walled off. In each case, what matters is achieving a recognized condition, not completing a precise physical act.

*Miktzas hayom kekulo* is better understood as a principle specific to durations — periods of time framed as units rather than as counts. When one asks whether a person "completed a week" or "completed a month," the focus is on the conceptual unit, not on the literal number of hours. Once a person has entered the final day of that unit, one can say that the unit has, in a meaningful sense, been achieved — because the unit, not its constituent days, is what matters. This is why the principle is most naturally applied to things like mourning periods, *nezirut*, or any framework structured around temporal units rather than discrete counts.

### Rubo Kekulo

This distinction has real *halachic* consequences. *Rubo kekulo* and *miktzas hayom kekulo* each have their domain. When a goal is to achieve a state, the majority suffices. When a goal is to complete a duration understood as a unit, entering the final day may suffice. But where one is literally counting discrete actions — say, eating a *kezayis* or completing all eighteen blessings of *shemoneh esrei* — neither principle straightforwardly applies. The appropriate application of each principle depends on how one analyzes the underlying obligation.

---

## Consecutive Nezirut

### Day 30 Double Count

The *gemara* now cites a *mishna* with a striking implication. The case involves a person who has accepted two consecutive *neziruyot*, one immediately following the other. The rule is that *lechatchila* one should bring the *korban* for the first *nezirut* on day thirty-one. If, however, one did so *bedieved* — after the fact — on day thirty, that too is valid. Day thirty then becomes day one of the second *nezirut*, so the second *korban* should *lechatchila* be brought on day sixty — which is day thirty-one counting from that new starting point. And if *bedieved* one brought the second *korban* on day fifty-nine, that is also valid, for the same reason: day fifty-nine of the combined count is day thirty of the second *nezirut*.

The critical principle the *mishna* articulates is *oleh lakan ulakan* — that day thirty counts toward both the ending period and the beginning period. The arithmetic makes the point starkly: two units of thirty days should require sixty days, yet the *mishna* validates completion in fifty-nine. The only way to reconcile this is if the middle day — the day of the *korban* — is counted in both directions simultaneously. This is the *chidush* implicit in *oleh lakan ulakan*.

### Bar Pada's Challenge

The *gemara* asks: *bishlama* according to *Rav Masna*, this makes sense. His position is that *nezirut* is fundamentally thirty days, and *miktzas hayom kekulo* allows day thirty to function as the completion of the first unit and — simultaneously — the beginning of the next. One can say the partial day counted as a full thirtieth day for the first *nezirut*, and also as day one for the second. But according to *Bar Pada*, what is the *chidush*? If *nezirut* is twenty-nine full days, then by the end of day twenty-nine the obligation is already complete. Of course day thirty will work — there is nothing surprising about it counting toward the next *nezirut*, because it was never required for the first.

### Oleh Lakan Ulakan

*Bar Pada* responds: the *mishna*'s language of *oleh lakan ulakan* is actually where he derives his position. The reason day thirty can count toward the beginning of the next period is precisely because it was not needed for the previous one. This is, admittedly, a somewhat counterintuitive reading of the phrase — *oleh lakan ulakan* sounds like double-counting in both directions, yet *Bar Pada* reads it as conveying the opposite: that the day is available for the next period because it was never part of the prior one.

From *Rav Masna*'s perspective, the *chidush* of *miktzas hayom kekulo* is that bringing the *korban* midway through day thirty counts as completing the first *nezirut* and simultaneously initiates the second — a double application of the principle in a single day. *Bar Pada* finds this conceptually untenable. How can one day be counted twice? His answer is that the *mishna* is teaching something different: the principle is that *nezirut* is truly only twenty-nine days, and therefore there is no double-counting. Day thirty was never in play for the first unit, and it simply initiates the next.

It is worth noting that *Tosafot* here — whose commentary on this *daf* is unusually extensive and reads more like sustained running exposition than the familiar dialectical give-and-take — takes up much of the analytical burden that the *Ran* typically bears in *Nedarim*, precisely because the standard *Rashi* on *Nedarim* is not authentic *Rashi*.

The *gemara* at this point does not resolve the dispute by ruling definitively. The *gemara*'s primary goal is to explore and articulate each position rather than always to reach a *halachic* conclusion, and both positions remain alive.

---

## Tumah on Day 30

### Tamei Soter Hakol

The *gemara* now cites another *mishna*: if someone said *hareini nazir* and became *tamei* on day thirty, *soter et hakol* — the entire *nezirut* is undermined and must be restarted.

According to *Rav Masna* this is immediately intelligible. The *nazir* may bring his *korban* on day thirty by virtue of *miktzas hayom kekulo*, but that same principle carries a vulnerability: if something happens later in day thirty that is fundamentally incompatible with *nezirut*, we cannot retroactively affirm that the partial day counted as a complete and valid thirtieth day. Drinking wine or getting a haircut after the *korban* is brought does not undo anything — those are acts made permissible by the *korban* itself. But *tumah* is categorically different: it does not merely violate the *nazir*'s restrictions; it retroactively impugns the integrity of the entire period, requiring him to start over. Since we relied on *miktzas hayom kekulo* to say the beginning of day thirty counted as a complete thirtieth day, we can only maintain that position if the remainder of the day is consistent with it. If *tumah* occurred later that day, we must step back and say: we cannot call that a *yom tahara* — a day of purity — and therefore cannot count it as the thirtieth day at all.

### Retroactive Negation

This is a striking idea: the *halachic* status of the beginning of the day is, in a sense, conditional on what unfolds in the remainder. When we say *miktzas hayom kekulo*, we are making a legal determination that the partial day counts as the whole — but that determination is open to reassessment if subsequent events within that day fundamentally contradict the status we assigned it. The *korban* does not lock in the result irrevocably; what happens for the rest of day thirty can redefine what the beginning of that day meant.

A useful analogy: in *shechita*, if one cuts the majority of the trachea and esophagus and then, in attempting to complete the cut, performs the remaining portion in a disqualifying manner, there is a serious opinion that the entire *shechita* is invalidated. One could have stopped while ahead — the majority was sufficient — but once the problematic cut was made in the remaining portion, it retroactively undermined the whole. The same logic applies here: once the day has run its full course and *tumah* occurred within it, we cannot sustain the fiction that the earlier portion of the day was equivalent to a complete, untainted thirtieth day.

### Zava Analogy

An illuminating parallel comes from the laws of *zava*. A woman who experiences three consecutive days of non-menstrual bleeding must count seven consecutive clean days. On the seventh day, she need not wait until nightfall — she may immerse in the *mikvah* during the day itself, invoking a form of *miktzas hayom kekulo*. However, if she immerses during day seven, then has relations with her husband, and then bleeds again before nightfall, the entire count is retroactively undermined — she was always in the status of *zava*, the immersion was void, and she must begin a new seven-day count. This is precisely why *halacha* prescribes that even after immersing on day seven, she should wait until nightfall before resuming marital relations — or better yet, wait to immerse at all until nightfall — so as not to create the conditions for this retroactive collapse.

### Lechatchila Day 31

This is exactly the reason why *lechatchila* one should wait until day thirty-one to bring the *korban*. If the *korban* is brought on day thirty and the *nazir* then becomes *tamei* before nightfall, the entire *nezirut* is invalidated — every day of it — because day thirty cannot be counted as a valid conclusion. By waiting until day thirty-one, the *nazir* ensures that even if *tumah* occurs on that day, it falls entirely outside the completed thirty-day unit, which by then is unambiguously in the past. The *lechatchila* is thus a safeguard: it protects against a scenario in which *tumah* on the final day would force a complete restart.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer's 30 Days

### 7 vs 30 Contradiction

The *gemara* continues by examining the end of the *mishna*, where *Rabbi Eliezer* disagrees with the ruling that *tumah* on day thirty undermines everything: *Rabbi Eliezer* says it undermines only seven days. This makes sense if *Rabbi Eliezer* holds that day thirty is already beyond the completed *nezirut* — whatever happens there cannot retroactively erase what preceded. But now the *gemara* presents a second case in the same *mishna*: a person explicitly vowed a hundred days of *nezirut* and became *tamei* on day 100. Here *Rabbi Eliezer* says the *tumah* undermines thirty days, not seven and not a hundred.

This is deeply puzzling. According to *Rav Masna*'s framework, *Rabbi Eliezer* holds *miktzas hayom kekulo* in its most absolute form — an iron wall descends at the moment the partial day begins, making everything that follows completely irrelevant. On that account, *tumah* on day 100 should undermine only seven days, not thirty. And according to *Bar Pada*'s framework, *Rabbi Eliezer* holds there is no *miktzas hayom kekulo* at all — which would mean that on day 100 of an explicitly stated hundred-day *nezirut*, the *nazir* has not yet completed his obligation, so *tumah* would require him to do the entire hundred days over again.

Neither framework produces thirty days. *Rabbi Eliezer* seems to contradict himself.

### Bar Pada Sides Eliezer

*Bar Pada* now clarifies his position. He states that regarding the earlier *mishna* — the standard thirty-day case where *Rabbi Eliezer* said only seven days need be redone — he concedes the *chachamim*'s theoretical framework. The *chachamim* hold that thirty days are required and debate with *Rabbi Eliezer* only over how to conceptualize *miktzas hayom kekulo*: whether the partial day leaves the remainder of the day still consequential (the *chachamim*'s view) or closes everything off completely (what *Rav Masna* attributes to *Rabbi Eliezer*). *Bar Pada* concedes that the *chachamim*'s position on thirty days is internally coherent, but aligns himself with *Rabbi Eliezer* — whom he understands as holding twenty-nine full days and no *miktzas hayom kekulo*. On that account, when someone becomes *tamei* on day thirty of a standard *nezirut*, it is already past the completion point, so *tumah* there cannot impinge on the main unit — hence only seven days.
