But this still leaves *Rabbi Eliezer*'s ruling of thirty days in the hundred-day case unexplained, on any account.

### Last Day Exception

*Reish Lakish* provides the answer: there is a special *halacha* — not derived from logical extension of either *miktzas hayom* or the twenty-nine-day principle, but from a specific *drashah* on a *pasuk* — that applies uniquely when one becomes *tamei* on the very last day of a *nezirut*.

### Torah Verse Proof

*Reish Lakish* cites the verse: *zot tihiyeh torat ha-Nazir b'yom melot yemei nizro* — "this shall be the law of the *nazir* on the day that the days of his *nezirut* are completed." The *Torah* is teaching: if one becomes *tamei* specifically on the *yom melot* — the final day of the *nezirut* — then *ten lo torat nazir*, give him the law of the *nazir*, meaning a standard *nezirut* of thirty days. This is not derived from any general principle about *miktzas hayom*; it is a discrete *halacha* extracted from the verse. If you become *tamei* on your final day, whatever the duration of your *nezirut*, you do not redo the entire *nezirut* — you do a standard one.

This explains *Rabbi Eliezer*'s ruling of thirty days in the hundred-day case. A hundred days were explicitly stipulated; *miktzas hayom* is irrelevant for *Bar Pada* who rejects it. The *nazir* became *tamei* on day 100 — the final day. The verse's special *halacha* kicks in: he does a standard *nezirut* of thirty days, not a hundred. And in the earlier case — *tumah* on day thirty of a standard *nezirut* — according to *Bar Pada*, day thirty is already past the twenty-nine-day completion point, so day thirty is not the "last day" in the relevant sense; day twenty-nine was. Therefore the special *halacha* of *tumah* on the last day does not apply, and *tumah* on day thirty is simply *tumah* that occurs after the *nezirut* concluded, requiring only the standard seven-day purification process. *Reish Lakish* concedes there is no logical derivation for the thirty-day ruling; it is a *halacha* extracted from the *Torah*'s formulation.

---

## Melot Hayamim Debate

### Yoshiya vs Yonatan

The *gemara* now asks whether the dispute of *Rav Masna* and *Bar Pada* mirrors a prior *tannaitic* debate, cited in a *braita*. The relevant verse reads: *ad melot hayamim asher yazir l'Adonai... kadosh yihye gadel pera sear rosho* — "until the fullness of the days that he consecrated to God... he shall be holy; he shall let the hair of his head grow wild."

*Rabbi Yoshiya* derives from this that there is no *gidul pera* — the required hair growth that is the hallmark of *nezirut* — in fewer than thirty days: *ein gidul pera sear pachos mishloshim*. His proof-text is the phrase *kadosh yihye gadel pera* — specifically the word *yihye*, whose *gematria* is thirty.

*Rabbi Yonatan* says the thirty-day requirement needs no derivation from *yihye*; it follows from the phrase *ad melot hayamim* itself. The concept of "days that need to be filled" implies a unit that can be either full or less than full — and the only temporal unit that admits of such variability is a month. A week is always seven days; it admits no partial version. A year is counted by months, not by days (as the *Rabbanan of Kisari* will clarify below), so a year does not yield a number of days in the relevant sense. A month, however, can be twenty-nine or thirty days — it can be full or deficient — and the notion of "filling" days points precisely to that structure.

### Gematria Yihye

The *gematria* of *yihye* — *yud* (10), *heh* (5), *yud* (10), *heh* (5) — equals thirty. *Rabbi Yoshiya* uses this *gematria* to establish the thirty-day minimum for *nezirut* from the word *yihye* in the verse. This is the hermeneutic *Rav Masna* is associated with in the *gemara*'s analysis.

### Rav Masna's Unity

*Rav Masna* argues that the two *tannaitic* positions — *Rabbi Yoshiya* and *Rabbi Yonatan* — are not actually in dispute about the number of days. Both agree that thirty days are required. Their disagreement concerns the interpretive question of *ad v'ad bichlal*: does the word *ad* (until) mean "up to and including" or "up to but not including"? *Rabbi Yoshiya* reads *ad* as exclusive — "until but not including" — and therefore cannot derive thirty days from *ad melot hayamim* alone; he supplements with the *gematria* of *yihye* to reach thirty. *Rabbi Yonatan* reads *ad* as inclusive — "until and including" — and therefore *ad melot hayamim* by itself implies thirty full days, the full month inclusive.

On this reading, *Rav Masna* can claim that both *tannaim* support his view: everyone agrees that thirty days are required. The interpretive dispute about *ad* is purely internal to the verse and does not affect the substantive ruling. This is the stronger posture for an *amora*: demonstrating that one's position is consistent with all *tannaitic* opinions.

### Ad Inclusivity

*Bar Pada*'s position, by contrast, requires conceding that *Rabbi Yoshiya*'s view does not support him. *Bar Pada* can align himself only with *Rabbi Yonatan*, and specifically with a particular reading of *Rabbi Yonatan*: that *ad melot hayamim* means "until the fullness of the days," with *ad* understood as exclusive — up to but *not* including the thirtieth day. On that reading, the verse points to twenty-nine days. This is, admittedly, a somewhat strained reading of *Rabbi Yonatan*, since *Rabbi Yonatan*'s own stated logic seems to lead to thirty days, but *Bar Pada* exploits the ambiguity in the word *ad* to extract a twenty-nine-day reading from it.

### Rabbanan Kisari

The *gemara* asks: why not interpret *melot hayamim* as referring to a year rather than a month? A year also admits of variability — Hebrew years can be shorter or longer depending on whether months are full or deficient and whether an extra month is intercalated. The *gemara* answers by citing the *Rabbanan of Kisari*, who teach: *minayin she'ein monin yamin leshanim?* — how do we know that years are not counted by days? From the verse *lechodeshei hashana* — "for the months of the year." Years are reckoned by months, not by days. Since *melot hayamim* invokes the counting of *yamim* — days — it cannot refer to a unit measured by months. Only a month, whose duration is itself measured in days and which can genuinely be full (thirty days) or deficient (twenty-nine), fits the category of a unit whose "days need to be filled."

---

## Indefinite Expressions

### Big/Small Nezirut

A *mishna* now establishes the practical scope of *stam nezirut*. If someone says *hareini nazir achat gedola* — "behold I am a *nazir*, a single big *nezirut*" — or *hareini nazir achat ketana* — "a single small *nezirut*" — he is a *nazir* for thirty days. The qualifiers "big" and "small" are meaningless without a specified duration. A person who says "big" or "small" has still said only that he is a *nazir*; and *stam nezirut* is thirty days. Since no number was given, no number can be derived. "Big" might mean it will feel big, or require great effort — but it does not communicate a time.

### Distance Limits

More striking is the *mishna*'s ruling: even if someone says *hareini nazir mikan ad sof ha'olam* — "behold I am a *nazir* from here to the end of the world" — he is nonetheless a *nazir* for thirty days. The expression *ad sof ha'olam* here is locative, not temporal — it describes a physical distance ("from here to China," as it were), not a duration of time. Since *nezirut* is measured in days, not in distance, distance language does not translate into an extended *nezirut*. The *gemara* explains: when someone says this, the intent is hyperbolic — this *nezirut* is going to feel as long as the journey from here to the end of the world. But since no time duration was specified, only the default *stam nezirut* of thirty days applies.

---

## Mishna-Braita Reconcilia…

### Braita Distance-Time

A *braita*, however, seems to rule differently. If someone says *hareini nazir mikan ve'ad makom ploni* — "behold I am a *nazir* from here until such-and-such place" — we calculate how many days it takes to travel from here to that place. If the travel time is less than thirty days, he is a *nazir* for thirty days (since *nezirut* cannot be less than thirty). If the travel time is more than thirty days, he is a *nazir* for the actual number of travel days. Here, distance is explicitly being translated into time duration, in apparent contradiction to the *mishna*.

### Rava on Journey

*Rava* resolves the contradiction: the *braita* is discussing a case where the person *hechzik baderech* — has already set out on the journey. Once he is already traveling, saying "from here until that place" naturally expresses duration rather than mere spatial distance. When you are on the road and say "until we get there," you are measuring in time — thinking about how long until we arrive, not how many miles remain. In that context, translating distance into travel time is perfectly natural. But if a person is sitting at home and says he will be a *nazir* from here to the end of the world, there is no journey underway, no natural conversion of distance to duration, and the expression is best understood as rhetorical emphasis, not as a specification of time.

*Tosafot* adds a further nuance: when one is on a journey, the vow may carry an element of seeking divine protection for the duration of the travel, which further explains why distance would be understood as defining the time frame of the *nezirut*.

### Miles Question

One might ask: even in the *mishna*'s case, where the person is not on a journey, could the distance at least yield a number — and could that number then indicate *how many* sequential *neziruyot* the person has accepted? After all, if the world is a certain number of *parsa'ot* across, then "from here to the end of the world" might mean that many sequential units of thirty-day *nezirut*. The same question applies to *Rava*'s case: why not say that each *parsa* of the journey represents one separate *nezirut*?

### Rav Pappa No Units

*Rav Pappa* answers: *be-atra de-lo manu parsei* — in a locale where distances are not measured in *parsa'ot*. Without a fixed, conventional unit of measurement, no determinate number emerges from the distance expression. "From here to that place" does not yield a number if there is no standard way of measuring the intervening distance. And since no number can be extracted, no count of sequential *neziruyot* can be established. The same logic disposes of the question of counting by overnight lodgings along the route: even if one tried to count nightly stops, that still runs into the underlying problem that the vow was framed in spatial terms and there is no fixed unit that converts cleanly into a number of *neziruyot*.

---

## Countable vs Uncountable

### Nazir Olam Forms

A final *mishna* presents cases that at first appear similar but yield dramatically different results. If someone says *hareini nazir ke-afar ha-aretz* — "like the dust of the earth" — or *ke-sear roshi* — "like the hairs of my head" — or *ke-chol ha-yam* — "like the sand of the sea" — he is a *nazir olam*, a *nazir* forever, and cuts his hair every thirty days. The mechanism here is conceptually distinct from a single extended *nezirut*: the person has accepted upon himself an effectively infinite sequence of sequential thirty-day *neziruyot*, each terminating with a *korban* and immediately followed by the next. In practice he will be a *nazir* for his entire life, bringing a *korban* at the end of each thirty-day unit and immediately beginning the next.

This raises the question: why does "like the dust of the earth" — clearly a spatial or quantity reference — translate into an infinite number of sequential *neziruyot*, while "from here to the end of the world" — also a spatial reference — translates into only one thirty-day *nezirut*?

### Ketzisusa Principle

The *gemara* articulates the principle: *kol milta d'is bei ketzisusa lo k'tani* — anything that has a fixed, determinate number is not what was taught. That is: expressions like "the hairs of my head" or "the sand of the sea" are understood as conveying an uncountable, practically infinite quantity. No one seriously believes they can enumerate every grain of sand on the sea or every hair on a head. The expression is understood as meaning an unlimited, indeterminate number — and therefore it is taken as expressing an intention to accept an unlimited series of *neziruyot*.

By contrast, "from here to the end of the world" — despite sounding equally hyperbolic — could in principle yield a concrete number depending on what unit of measurement is applied. The circumference of the world, as the *gemara* elsewhere records, is a specific figure (five hundred *parsa'ot*). Because a determinate number *could* be extracted, even if we do not know which unit the speaker has in mind, the expression does not clearly convey an infinite sequence. Since no definite time duration is specified and no definite number of sequential *neziruyot* is clearly implied, the vow defaults to a single standard *nezirut* of thirty days.

The principle, in short: where a spatial or quantity expression is so vast that no number can concretely emerge from it — sand of the sea, hairs of the head — the vow is taken as infinite sequential *neziruyot*. Where the expression, however expansive it sounds, could theoretically be resolved into a concrete number, it is treated as mere emphasis and yields only the default single *nezirut*. The remainder of this complex sugya will be taken up in the following session.

---

---

# Nazir 8

## Default & Scope

### Stam Nezirut Intro

The eighth daf of Nazir continues the discussion of *stam nezirut* — the default, unqualified acceptance of *nezirut* — which carries a duration of thirty days. The previous daf dealt with complicating cases: what happens when someone says something like "from here, a large one" or "from here until the end of the world"? In those cases, the rule is that since no particular quantity, time, or unit was specified, the vow is interpreted as a single, standard *nezirut* of thirty days. The contrast is with a case where the person does specify time — as in the earlier *mishnah* where someone says "I am a *nazir* for thirty days and one hour." Since there is no such thing as an hour-long *nezirut*, that statement is interpreted to mean thirty-one days. The organizing principle, then, is threefold: if someone speaks abstractly (big, far, great), that does not translate into additional time or units; if someone specifies time, that redefines duration; and if someone specifies units, that generates multiple *neziruyot*.

### Singular vs. Plural

One subtle point worth noting is that the *mishnah* employs the feminine form in the phrase *hareini nazir achat gedolah*, which is grammatically curious. The *nazir* is masculine, yet *achat gedolah* is feminine, suggesting the underlying referent is *nezirut achat* — one unit of *nezirut* — rather than a masculine *nazir gadol*. This linguistic observation anticipates a theme the *gemara* will develop at length: the difference between using the word *nazir* in the singular versus using the word *nezirut* or *neziruyot*, and whether that grammatical distinction carries legal weight.

---

## Fill of Box

### Hair/Dust/Sand

The *mishnah* opens with a series of cases: *hareini nazir kisa'ar roshi* — "I am a *nazir* like the hairs of my head"; *ukhe'afar ha'aretz* — "or like the dust of the earth"; *ukhechol hayam* — "or like the sand of the sea." The ruling is *harei zeh nazir olam* — this person is a *nazir* forever. This does not mean a *nazir olam* in the technical sense of an uninterrupted, permanent *nezirut*, but rather that the person has accepted upon himself an effectively infinite number of discrete *neziruyot* in sequence. Because hairs, dust, and grains of sand are all discrete countable units, the vow is interpreted as: "I accept upon myself as many separate *neziruyot* as the number of hairs on my head" — or grains of sand, or specks of dust. Since that number is functionally infinite, the person will forever be cycling through thirty-day *neziruyot*, each ending with the full complement of *korbanot* and shaving, followed immediately by the next.

This must be distinguished from a true *nazir olam*, who accepts a single uninterrupted *nezirut* with no end date, and who is permitted to trim his hair periodically — some hold once a week, some once a month, some once a year — precisely because otherwise the hair would become unmanageable. The person who says "like the hairs of my head" is a *nazir le'olam* in a colloquial sense: he will be a *nazir* forever as a practical matter, cycling through one thirty-day term after another, but he completes each one with a full shaving and *korbanot*. He is not in the legal category of *nazir olam*.

### Rabbi's Position

*Rebbi* disagrees with the *tanna kamma*. He says: *ein zeh megale'ach achat lishloshim yom* — this person does not shave every thirty days. *Rebbi*'s position is that since the speaker used the word *nazir* in the singular — not *neziruyot* in the plural — he did not accept multiple units upon himself. The reference to hairs on his head does not translate into a specific number of *neziruyot*, because units only become significant if the speaker has framed the vow in terms of multiple units. If he used the singular *nazir*, then no matter how vast the comparison, he is simply one *nazir* for thirty days. The number of hairs on his head tells us only that he felt the vow was enormously significant — it does not redefine the scope.

*Rebbi* then clarifies what *would* mean multiple *neziruyot* with shaving every thirty days: *ha'omer harei alai neziruyot kisa'ar roshi* — "upon me are *neziruyot* like the hairs of my head." Only the use of the plural *neziruyot* transforms the comparison into a multiplicity of units. Without that plural, the singular *nazir* limits the vow to one thirty-day term.

### House/Basket Case

The *mishnah* then presents the case of *hareini nazir melo habayis o melo hakupa* — "I am a *nazir* like the fill of the house" or "like the fill of this basket." Here, the rule is *bodkin oso* — we examine him, we ask him what he meant. If he says *achas gedolah nazarti* — "I accepted one large *nezirut*" — meaning the comparison to the fill of the house was meant only to convey magnitude, not to specify a number of units, then he is simply a *nazir* for thirty days. He did not give us time, he did not give us units, he just expressed that it felt like a very large thing. Fine — one *nezirut*.

But if he says *stam nazarti* — "I declared *nezirut* without any particular intention" — then the words themselves must be interpreted. The *mishnah* rules: *ro'in es hakupa ke'ilu hi mele'ah chardal* — we view the basket as if it were filled with mustard seeds, and the person is a *nazir* for all the days of his life, since the number of mustard seeds that fill a basket is functionally uncountable. This is striking. The very premise requires examination: why does saying "like the fill of the box" translate into a number of discrete units at all? The person used the word *nazir* in the singular. And even granting that the phrase somehow implies units, why interpret it as the most numerous possible units — mustard seeds — rather than the fewest, such as watermelons or gourds?

### Distance Cases

The *mishnah* also addresses *hareini nazir mikan ad makom ploni* — "I am a *nazir* from here to such-and-such a place." The rule is *omdin kama yamim mikan ad makom ploni* — we estimate how many days of travel it takes to get from here to there. If the distance is less than thirty days' travel, the person is a *nazir* for thirty days, since *nezirut* cannot be less than thirty days. If the distance is more than thirty days' travel, then *keminyan hayamim* — the number of travel days defines the duration of the *nezirut*.

This was discussed earlier in the context of the *mishnah*'s statement that saying "from here to the end of the world" does not lengthen the *nezirut*. The question there was: if "from here to Chicago" translates into a duration, why does "from here to the end of the world" not do the same? Tosafot raises the possibility that people do have a fixed assumption about the distance to the end of the world, which would make it no different from any other measurable journey. Rabbah's resolution was that this case applies when the person is already on the trip — when someone is traveling and declares *nezirut* for the duration of the journey, the distance naturally converts into time. Tosafot adds another dimension: the person may be accepting *nezirut* as a *neder* seeking divine protection for the journey, in which case "until I get there" is the natural scope.

### Solar Year

A parallel case: *hareini nazir keminyan yemot hachama* — "I am a *nazir* like the number of days of the solar year." The *mishnah* rules *moneh neziros keminyan yemot hachama* — the person must fulfill 365 *neziruyot*, one after another. Critically, the formula is "the *number* of days of the solar year," not "for the *duration* of a solar year." The word *keminyan* — "like the number of" — signals that we are counting discrete units, not measuring a span of time. Accordingly, we count 365 separate thirty-day *neziruyot*, each requiring its own completion and *korbanot*. At thirty days per *nezirut*, that amounts to approximately thirty years.

*Rabbi Yehudah* reports that there was an actual such case, and by the time the man finished all 365 *neziruyot*, he had died. This anecdote is cited not merely as a curiosity but as proof of the legal ruling: we do not interpret "the number of days of the year" as one year-long *nezirut*, but as 365 discrete *neziruyot*. The man spent the better part of his life fulfilling them.

### Mustard vs. Watermelon

The *gemara* addresses the obvious question raised by the fill-of-the-basket ruling. It asks: *b'mai* — why mustard seeds? *Delachzei ke'ilu mele'ah kishuin vedilu'in* — why not view the basket as filled with cucumbers and gourds? Tosafot sharpens the question: why not view it as filled with dough? A single mass of dough, no matter how large the container, could constitute one piece filling the entire basket, which would yield a single *nezirut* of thirty days. The *gemara* is pressing the question of whether ambiguous language should be resolved strictly or leniently.

Tosafot notes that there is a *mishnah* in *Taharos* that states *safek nezirus lehakeil* — in cases of doubt regarding *nezirut*, we rule leniently. That principle would point toward interpreting the basket as filled with the fewest, largest units possible. The *gemara* then reveals that this is in fact a dispute between *Rebbi Shimon* and *Rabbi Yehudah*, and that the stringent interpretation of mustard seeds reflects the position of *Rebbi Shimon*.

---

## Shimon vs. Yehudah

### Safek Principle

The *gemara* introduces the broader principle: what do we do when there is doubt about *nezirut*? *Rebbi Shimon* holds *safek nezirus lehachmir* — in cases of doubt, we rule strictly. *Rabbi Yehudah* holds *safek nezirus lehakeil* — in cases of doubt, we rule leniently. This dispute is directly cited by the *gemara* as the backdrop for the fill-of-the-basket case. *Rebbi Shimon* is strict and therefore interprets the basket as filled with mustard seeds, yielding an uncountable number of *neziruyot*. *Rabbi Yehudah* is lenient and would presumably interpret it more narrowly.

It should be noted that the two cases under this debate are not entirely parallel. One is a question of language: how do we interpret ambiguous words? The other is a question of whether a condition was actually met. These are conceptually distinct — one concerns the meaning of the vow, the other concerns whether the vow took effect at all. The *gemara* treats them together, but the difference matters, as we will see in *Rabbi Yochanan*'s subsequent clarification.

### Conditional Case

A *baraita* is introduced: *hareini nazir al m'nas sheyehei becheri zeh me'ah kor* — "I am a *nazir* on the condition that there will be in this pile of grain one hundred *kor*." The person then went to measure the pile and found it gone — either stolen or lost. The question is whether the *nezirut* took effect. *Rebbi Shimon* rules that the person is forbidden — *safek nezirus lehachmir*, we treat the uncertainty strictly and assume the *nezirut* applies. *Rabbi Yehudah* rules that the person is permitted — *safek nezirus lehakeil*, and since we do not know whether the condition was met, the *nezirut* does not take effect.

One way to frame *Rabbi Yehudah*'s position: when the person said "on condition that there are one hundred *kor* in the pile," what he really meant is "on condition that we *find* one hundred *kor* in the pile." Since one went and the pile was gone, one never found one hundred *kor* — regardless of whether the hundred *kor* were there before being stolen. On that reading, the condition was demonstrably not met. But the *gemara*'s broader framing is that the dispute is simply about whether uncertainty triggers leniency or stringency.

### Safek Worse Problem

The *gemara* then introduces a striking and counterintuitive claim: *adam machnis es atzmo ledavar shesefeko chamur mivado* — a person can put himself into a situation where the *safek* (doubt) is actually more stringent than the *vadai* (certainty). How is being a *safek nazir* worse than being a definite *nazir*?

The answer: if one is a definite *nazir*, one completes thirty days, brings the *korbanot* — *olah*, *shelamim*, *chatat*, and *asham* — and is released. But if one is a *safek nazir*, one must observe the prohibitions of *nezirut* since one might be a *nazir*. Yet at the end of thirty days, one cannot bring the *korbanot* that complete and terminate the *nezirut*, because those *korbanot* — particularly the *chatat* and *asham* — may only be brought by a definite *nazir*. They cannot be brought as voluntary offerings by someone who may not be a *nazir* at all. The result is that the *safek nazir* is trapped: obligated to maintain the restrictions indefinitely because the *nezirut* has not been formally closed, yet unable to close it because doing so requires *korbanot* one cannot bring under uncertainty.

### Solution Strategy

There is, however, a way out of this trap. The *safek nazir* can make the following declaration: "If I am already a *nazir* from my earlier statement, I am doing nothing now. But if I am not yet a *nazir*, then I hereby accept *nezirut* upon myself right now." This conditional statement converts the ambiguous situation into a *vadai* either way. If the first acceptance worked, nothing changes. If it did not, the new declaration is unconditional and definitive. Either way the person is now a certain *nazir*, can complete thirty days, bring the *korbanot*, and be released.

### Tamei Scenario

Tosafot notes, however, that even this solution does not always work, and that is precisely why *safek* remains worse than *vadai* in principle. Consider the following scenario: the person is a *safek nazir* and is about to recite the conditional formula to resolve his status — but before he can do so, he becomes *tamei* (ritually impure). Now the problem compounds. If he was already a *nazir* before becoming *tamei*, he brings the *korbanot* of a *nazir tamei*, which include a *chatat* ha-of and other specific offerings, and he restarts his *nezirut* from the beginning. But if he was not yet a *nazir* when he became *tamei*, and he now accepts *nezirut* upon himself, he does *not* bring the *korbanot* of a *nazir tamei* — because those are only for someone who was already a *nazir* when the impurity occurred. The conditional formula therefore does not resolve the problem in this scenario; one remains stuck in genuine uncertainty with no clean exit. This demonstrates that being a *safek nazir* can be structurally worse than being a *vadai nazir*, even accounting for the partial solution.

The *gemara*'s conclusion is clear: *Rebbi Shimon* is fully aware that his stringency places the person in a worse position than the stringency of a definite obligation — and he is willing to accept that consequence, because his view is that whenever there is doubt in *nezirut*, we go strict. *Rabbi Yehudah* disagrees and refuses to impose *nezirut* under uncertainty.

---

## Yehudah Position

### Status Quo Logic

*Rabbi Yochanan* intervenes with a crucial distinction: *afilu teima Rabbi Yehudah* — one can say even *Rabbi Yehudah* would agree with the strict ruling in the fill-of-the-basket case. The key is *hasam lo nachis lei l'nezirus, hacha nachis lei l'nezirus* — there, in the conditional case of the pile of grain, the person never definitively entered into *nezirut* in the first place. Since we do not know whether the condition was met, we do not know whether *nezirut* ever began. *Rabbi Yehudah*'s leniency operates precisely in this space: the person's current status is non-*nazir*, and without certainty that the condition was fulfilled, we preserve that status quo. We do not impose *nezirut* on the basis of doubt.

But in the fill-of-the-basket case, the person has certainly entered *nezirut* — at minimum, even the most lenient interpretation (one watermelon) means he became a *nazir*. Once *nezirut* has definitely begun, *Rabbi Yehudah* might agree that we do not allow doubt to terminate or limit it. The question is no longer whether *nezirut* begins; it has already begun. The question is whether it continues and extends. And on that question, perhaps even *Rabbi Yehudah* would say: *b'mai islukey minei?* — what force would remove him from his *nezirut*? Since he is already a *nazir*, doubt does not extricate him.

### First Ends Status

Tosafot complicates *Rabbi Yochanan*'s proposed distinction. One might think that after the first thirty-day *nezirut* is completed, the person has fully exited *nazir* status — and therefore when the question arises whether a second *nezirut* begins, we are back to the same situation as the conditional case: the person is currently not a *nazir*, and doubt should not create one. In other words, Tosafot is pointing out that *Rabbi Yochanan*'s logic — that the person already entered *nezirut* — applies only during the first term. Once that term ends, the person's status reverts to non-*nazir*, and the rationale for stringency dissolves.

### Second Term Start

This leads to the *gemara*'s sharper formulation of the difficulty. After the first thirty days conclude, the person's first *nezirut* is definitively complete. The question becomes: does a second *nezirut* begin? At this moment, the person is not a *nazir*. If *Rabbi Yehudah* holds that we do not impose *nezirut* under doubt when the person's status quo is non-*nazir*, then at the end of each thirty-day cycle, he should be permitted to stop — because the question of whether the next term begins is itself uncertain, and the status quo is not-*nazir*. The *gemara* raises this as a genuine challenge to *Rabbi Yochanan*'s proposed reconciliation.

The *gemara*'s response is that perhaps the entire fill-of-the-basket case is treated as one *nezirut* whose length is uncertain — rather than multiple *neziruyot* of uncertain number. If *Rabbi Yehudah* holds like *Rebbi* (as the *gemara* will now develop), then saying *nazir* in the singular with a vague quantifier might mean one very long *nezirut* of indefinite duration, not thousands of discrete separate *neziruyot*. In that framing, the question is never "does the next *nezirut* begin?" but rather "when does this one end?" — and since it has already begun, the uncertainty about its endpoint keeps it running, consistent with *Rabbi Yehudah*'s logic.

---

## Yehudah = Rabbi?

### Singular Test

To establish whether *Rabbi Yehudah* could hold like *Rebbi*, the *gemara* must first determine whether *Rabbi Yehudah* actually agrees with *Rebbi*'s core principle. *Rebbi*'s ruling, as stated in the *mishnah*, is that using the word *nazir* in the singular — even combined with "like the hairs of my head" — means only one *nezirut* of thirty days, because the plural *neziruyot* is required to generate multiple units. The *gemara* proposes that perhaps *Rabbi Yehudah* holds this same view, which would explain how our *mishnah* (the fill-of-the-basket case with its stringent ruling) could be attributed to *Rabbi Yehudah*: he agrees it is one *nezirut*, but since it definitely began and we don't know when it ends, it continues indefinitely.

### 365 Days Proof

The *gemara* immediately challenges this hypothesis. It cites the very case discussed in the *mishnah*: *hareini nazir keminyan yemot hachama* — "I am a *nazir* like the number of days of the solar year." The *mishnah* rules that the person must fulfill 365 *neziruyot*. And *Rabbi Yehudah* himself endorses this ruling by citing the story of the man who died before completing all 365. The verb *hishlim* — "completed" or "finished them all" — implies a plurality of obligations the man had to discharge one by one. Clearly, *Rabbi Yehudah* holds that when you say *nazir* in the singular combined with "like the number of days of the year," you mean 365 *discrete* *neziruyot*, not one long one.

This directly contradicts the hypothesis that *Rabbi Yehudah* holds like *Rebbi*, since *Rebbi* would say: you used the word *nazir* in the singular, therefore you mean one *nezirut*. *Rabbi Yehudah*, by contrast, treats the reference to number as generating multiple units even when the word *nazir* is in the singular. So on the surface, *Rabbi Yehudah* does not hold like *Rebbi*.

### Number Difference

The *gemara* responds: *minyan shani* — the use of the word *minyan* (number, quantity) is different. When someone explicitly says *keminyan* — "like the *number* of" — everyone may agree that this generates discrete units, regardless of whether the word *nazir* or *neziruyot* was used. The word *keminyan* is inherently about counting, about discrete enumeration, and its presence in the formula is sufficient to signal that the person intends multiple units. This is not the same as saying *nazir* in the singular combined with a vague comparison like "like the hairs of my head" — which contains no explicit number language.

To verify whether *Rebbi* himself holds this distinction, the *gemara* introduces a *baraita*. The *baraita* presents the case of *hareini nazir keminyan yemot hachama* — just as in the *mishnah* — and the *tanna kamma* rules 365 *neziruyot*, and a parallel case of *keminyan yemot halevana* (like the number of days of the lunar month), yielding 29 or 30 *neziruyot*. *Rebbi* then says: *ad sheyomar neziruyot alai keminyan yemot hachama* — the person must use the plural *neziruyot* combined with the number language before we count multiple units. According to *Rebbi*, even the phrase "like the *number* of days of the year" is insufficient if the word used is the singular *nazir*. Only the plural *neziruyot* creates multiple units, regardless of what else is said.

This proves that *Rebbi* does not distinguish between cases with and without *minyan* language. For *Rebbi*, the singular *nazir* always means one — full stop. Therefore, the *gemara*'s attempt to reconcile *Rabbi Yehudah* and *Rebbi* by appealing to the *minyan* distinction runs into trouble: that distinction may be *Rabbi Yehudah*'s but is not *Rebbi*'s.

### Figs/Paths Proof

A further *baraita* is brought to confirm *Rabbi Yehudah*'s independent position. *Rabbi Yehudah* himself says in a *baraita*: *hareini nazir minyan helktei kayitz* — "I am a *nazir* according to the number of mounds of drying figs," or *minyan shvilei shemitah* — "the number of paths cut through the field during *shemitah*." In both cases, *Rabbi Yehudah* rules *moneh neziros keminyan helktei kayitz, keminyan shvilei shemitah* — the person must fulfill that many *neziruyot*. This confirms that *Rabbi Yehudah* holds that when *minyan* language is used, even with the singular *nazir*, the result is multiple discrete *neziruyot*. He clearly does not hold like *Rebbi*, who would require the plural *neziruyot* in any event.

---

## Yehudah = Rabbi? (II)

### Partial Agreement

The *gemara* resolves the tension with a nuanced formulation: *Rabbi Yehudah savar lah kavatei bichada upaliga alei bichada* — *Rabbi Yehudah* agrees with *Rebbi* in one respect and disagrees in another. The *gemara* has now established that *Rabbi Yehudah*'s position is a middle ground between *Rebbi* and the *chachamim*, and the specifics of that middle ground are worked out in the following section.

---

## Middle Position

### Alone = One

*Rabbi Yehudah* agrees with *Rebbi* on the following: if someone says the word *nazir* in the singular — without any *minyan* language, without any explicit quantifier — then even if he adds a comparison that involves vast quantities (like the hairs of my head, like the sand of the sea), that comparison does not transform the vow into multiple *neziruyot*. The singular *nazir* without a number word attached to it means one *nezirut*. On this point, *Rabbi Yehudah* concurs with *Rebbi*: the word *nazir* alone, in the singular, limits the vow to one term. The vast comparison expresses only the subjective weight of the acceptance, not the number of units.

### Plus Minyan = Many

Where *Rabbi Yehudah* disagrees with *Rebbi* is when *minyan* language — explicit number-counting — is introduced. When someone says *hareini nazir keminyan yemot hachama*, or *keminyan helktei kayitz*, the word *keminyan* is an explicit quantifier that converts the vow into discrete units. For *Rabbi Yehudah*, that number language overrides the singular form of *nazir* and generates multiple *neziruyot* equal to the stated count. For *Rebbi*, by contrast, even this does not suffice — only the plural form *neziruyot* creates multiple terms, and nothing else.

This middle position elegantly accounts for the *baraita*ic rulings cited in *Rabbi Yehudah*'s name. In every case where he rules multiple *neziruyot*, explicit *minyan* language was present. In cases without *minyan* language — the vague fill-of-the-basket case, the hairs-on-the-head case without the number word — *Rabbi Yehudah* would agree with *Rebbi* that the singular *nazir* means one term.

This resolution also clarifies *Rabbi Yochanan*'s original argument. The fill-of-the-basket case, where the *mishnah* rules that *stam* (no declared intent) means an uncountable number of *neziruyot*, uses the construction *hareini nazir melo hakupa* — the word *nazir* in the singular, with no explicit *keminyan*. If *Rabbi Yehudah* agrees with *Rebbi* in such cases that the singular *nazir* means one, then the fill-of-the-basket case could indeed go like *Rabbi Yehudah* — interpreted as one indefinitely long *nezirut* rather than multiple discrete ones. The stringency is not about multiplying *neziruyot* but about the ambiguous endpoint of a single, already-begun *nezirut*.

One further observation complicates the picture, raised toward the end of the discussion. The grammatical point is well taken that *nezirut* in the singular is itself an abstract noun — it is not simply the singular of *neziruyot*. If *nezirut* denotes an abstract, endless state, then *Rebbi*'s use of *neziruyot* to denote multiple units is linguistically precise: *neziruyot* as a true plural of a count noun implies discrete enumerable instances, while *nezirut* as an abstract noun implies a single undifferentiated state. This grammatical substructure runs beneath the entire *sugya* and lends precision to what might otherwise seem like a merely formal distinction.

The *baraita* toward the end of the chapter summarizes by presenting the full range of cases — *hareini nazir* plus one (*v'achat*), plus more (*v'od*), plus again (*v'shuv*) — yielding two, three, and four *neziruyot* respectively. The *gemara* briefly entertains whether *v'shuv* could be interpreted as retroactively doubling everything that came before, potentially reaching six. It concludes that *v'shuv* simply means one additional unit, so the total is four.

---

## Closing Greek Terms

### Hen/Digon/etc.

The *perek* concludes with a *baraita* attributed to Sumchos, a *tanna* whose name reflects Hellenistic cultural influence. Sumchos enumerates Greek numerical terms as they apply to *nezirut*: *hen* (one) means one *nezirut*; *digon* (two) means two; *trigon* (three) means three; *tetragon* (four) means four; and *pentagon* (five) means five. If someone declares *nezirut* using these Greek number-words, the *halacha* recognizes them as valid specifications of quantity, and the person must fulfill the corresponding number of *neziruyot*.

The terms *trigon*, *tetragon*, and *pentagon* are cognates of the Greek words for three-sided, four-sided, and five-sided figures — the same roots as "triangle," "tetragon," and "pentagon" in English. The word *digon* is less immediately obvious but refers to a two-sided figure. These terms appear in the Talmud as evidence that Greek numerical and geometric vocabulary had penetrated the everyday speech of Jews in the Talmudic period, sufficiently so that *halacha* had to address vows made using that vocabulary.

### House Shapes

A second *baraita* follows, also employing these geometric terms, this time in the context of *nega'im* — the laws of *tzara'at* affecting houses. The *baraita* states: *bayis agul* — a circular house — or a house shaped as a *digon*, *trigon*, or *pentagon* does not become *tamei* with *nega'im*. Only a *tetragon* — a four-sided, rectangular house — can become *tamei*. The reason derives from the verse's repeated use of the word *kir* (wall): the Torah mentions walls multiple times in describing a house afflicted with *nega'im*, and the *gemara* derives from these repetitions that four walls are required. A house without four distinct walls — whether round, triangular, or pentagonal — falls outside the category of house subject to *tum'at nega'im* altogether.

With this, the *perek* concludes: *hadran alach kol kinuyei*.

---

---

# Nazir 9

## Nazir Grogrot

### Perek Sheini Intro

With the opening of the second perek, *Hareini Nazir*, we enter terrain that overlaps with themes from the first perek, though with a distinctly new focus. Much of *perek* 1, as in the parallel tractate Nedarim, addressed the different formulations of language a person might use to declare *nezirut* — not only whether a particular declaration makes one a *nazir*, but also how many units of *nezirut* are created, whether we interpret the vow as binding for the standard duration or a longer period, and the special categories of *Nazir Olam* and *Nazir Shimshon*. The second perek now takes up a different kind of question: what happens when the language of the declaration is internally incoherent?

### Mishna Statement

The opening *mishna* presents the following case: *Hareini nazir min hagrogros umin hadvela* — "I am a *nazir* from dried figs and pressed dates." Neither *grogros* (dried figs) nor *dvela* (pressed dates) are grapes or wine. They have no connection to the world of *nezirut*, whose prohibitions, as the Torah specifies, all derive from *kol asher ye'aseh migefen hayayin* — everything produced from the grapevine.

### Beis Shammai/Hillel

*Beis Shammai* rules that such a person is indeed a *nazir*. *Beis Hillel* rules that he is not. The immediate difficulty, of course, bears on *Beis Shammai*: how can declaring oneself a *nazir* from something entirely outside the domain of *nezirut* — figs and dates — create *nezirut* at all?

---

## Rav Yehuda Reframe

### Rav Yehuda's Statement

*Rav Yehuda* attempts to reframe *Beis Shammai*'s position: *ad kan she'omru Beis Shammai, lo amru ela be'omer harei hen alai korban* — "Even when *Beis Shammai* said it, they only said it in the case where one says 'these are upon me like a *korban*.'" That is, *Rav Yehuda* reads *Beis Shammai* as holding that the declaration *Hareini nazir min hagrogros* is not interpreted as *nezirut* at all, but rather as a *neder* — a vow rendering those figs forbidden. On this reading, *Beis Shammai* never actually says the person becomes a *nazir* in the conventional sense; rather, the statement is recast as a prohibition on the figs themselves, as though one said *harei hen alai ke'korban*. Alternatively, the word *nazir*, as Tosafot notes, can itself carry the meaning of *lehazir* — to separate — and thus the phrase *Hareini nazir min hagrogros* is read simply as "I hereby separate myself from these figs," a declaration of personal prohibition rather than a *kabbalat nezirut*.

### Nazir = Removal

Whether the reframing proceeds through the language of *lehazir* or through the analogy to *korban*, *Rav Yehuda*'s point is the same: *Beis Shammai* does not hold that uttering the word *nazir* in conjunction with figs actually triggers *nezirut*. The statement is translated into its most plausible halakhic meaning — a self-imposed prohibition on those items.

### Neder/Shvua Parallel

This interpretive move is familiar from the opening discussions in Nedarim. The *gemara* there explored at length the question of *neder belashon shvua, shvua belashon neder* — using the technical term for one type of vow when one clearly intended the other. Since a *neder* applies to objects and a *shvua* to actions, a person who says "a *neder* that I will not enter this house" is understood by many *rishonim* to have actually made a *shvua*, because that is the only form that fits the content. The wrong term is treated as a *yad* — a handle or indicator — pointing toward the actual intent. So too here: the word *nazir*, under *Rav Yehuda*'s reading of *Beis Shammai*, functions as a *yad* for a *neder* forbidding the figs.

### Beis Shammai Problem

The problem, however, is that the *Tanna Kamma* of the *mishna* does not read *Beis Shammai* as *Rav Yehuda* does. On the straightforward reading of the *mishna*, *Beis Shammai* holds that the person is genuinely a *nazir* — not merely forbidden from eating figs, but a full *nazir* in all its dimensions. How can a declaration that mentions only dates and figs — items wholly foreign to *nezirut* — create actual *nezirut*? This is the question the *gemara* now addresses directly.

---

## Rabbi Meir Principle

### Ein Adam Motzi

The *gemara* explains: *Beis Shammai savrei ke'Rabbi Meir, de'amar ein adam motzi devarav levatala* — *Beis Shammai* holds like Rabbi Meir, who says that a person does not utter his words for naught. A meaningful halakhic principle operates here: when someone makes a formal declaration in a halakhic context, we do not simply dismiss the statement as nonsense. We seek a legally coherent interpretation.

### Erech/Damim Example

The *gemara* grounds this in Rabbi Meir's classic case. The Torah provides a system of *arachin* — fixed valuations based on a person's age and sex — distinct from *dmei*, the market value of something. If someone says *erech kli alai* — "the *erech* of this vessel is upon me" — this is a problematic formulation, since *erech* as defined by the Torah applies only to human beings, not to objects. Rabbi Yehuda would say the person is not liable for anything, because the statement is simply incoherent. Rabbi Meir, invoking *ein adam motzi devarav levatala*, says we reinterpret the word *erech* as *dmei* — the person meant to say "the *value* of this vessel is upon me" — and they are obligated accordingly. The declaration, though technically misphrased, is given a coherent halakhic reading rather than being discarded.

### Why Different?

Applying this to our case, however, reveals a significant tension. When someone says *erech kli alai*, the fix is clean: substitute *dmei* for *erech*, and the entire statement makes sense. But *Hareini nazir min hagrogros* cannot be saved by a simple terminological substitution. Even if we accept *ein adam motzi devarav levatala* and refuse to dismiss the statement outright, we are still left with a nonsensical clause: *min hagrogros*. Under the *nazir* framework, figs are irrelevant. So *Beis Shammai*, in applying Rabbi Meir's principle here, is doing something more aggressive than Rabbi Meir's original example: not just reinterpreting a term, but actually discarding the second half of the statement entirely, retaining only the first word — *nazir* — as binding.

### Student Question

This raises an obvious question: why not do both? If the first part of the statement (*Hareini nazir*) is binding and the second part (*min hagrogros*) represents some additional intent, why not say the person is both a *nazir* and also forbidden from figs — treating the two halves as independent halakhic acts? The *mishna* offers no such intermediate position. *Beis Shammai*, on the *Tanna Kamma*'s reading, says the person is a *nazir* — full stop. Nobody says the person is both. The *gemara* will develop why, but the question is well-taken: logically, a "both" position is conceivable.

---

## Begmar Devarav

### Rabbi Yosi Position

*Beis Hillel*, the *gemara* explains, holds *ke'Rabbi Yosi, de'amar begmar devarav adam nitpas* — a person is "caught" — meaning bound — by the conclusion of his words. We do not freeze the analysis at the first clause of a statement; we read the statement as a whole, and the final portion of what was said carries interpretive weight for what preceded it.

### Neder Pitcho Imo

The operative concept here is *neder upitcho imo* — a vow that carries its own "opening" for dissolution within itself. Normally, dissolving a vow requires presenting a *chacham* with a *petach*, an opening — some basis for regret. Here, the very terms of the declaration themselves constitute that opening: by saying *min hagrogros*, the person has revealed that his entire concept of *nezirut* was built around abstaining from figs, which is not *nezirut* at all. The statement as a whole is self-undermining. *Beis Hillel* does not stop at *Hareini nazir* and declare it binding; they allow the speaker to finish, and what emerges is a statement that never coherently constitutes *kabbalat nezirut*. Notably, the *gemara* could have explained *Beis Hillel* more simply — as merely rejecting *ein adam motzi devarav levatala* — but instead it grounds *Beis Hillel* within Rabbi Yosi's framework, affirming that even if we accept the principle that one's words must mean something, the complete statement here, taken as a whole, produces a self-canceling result.

### Tosafot Explanation

Tosafot elaborates on how this works. The key passage, several lines into Tosafot's discussion, explains: since *begmar devarav adam nitpas*, we are "caught" by the conclusion — which is the mention of *grogros* — and since there is no *nezirut* with respect to *grogros*, the person is not a *nazir*. Even though at the outset he said *Hareini nazir*, by adding *min hagrogros* he effectively reversed himself *toch k'dei dibbur* — within the halakhic window of speech that is treated as continuous. It is as though he found a *petach* for his vow, a ground for dissolution, immediately upon completing the utterance. Since *nidro upitcho imo* — his vow and its opening came together — nothing takes effect at all.

### Tosafot Question

Tosafot then raises the precise question that arose above: the *gemara* in the context of *tmura* records that Rabbi Yosi holds that when someone says *harei zeh tmurath olah tmurath shelamim* — this animal is an exchange for both an *olah* and a *shelamim* — Rabbi Yosi does not declare the whole statement void. Rather, he says the animal has both *kedushas* and it cannot be brought as a single *korban*, but can be redeemed, with half the proceeds going to each. There, even though the two parts of the statement are logically contradictory, Rabbi Yosi says both are operative. Why, then, in our case, don't we say both parts of the statement are operative — the person is a *nazir* and also a *nadur* from figs?

---

## Why Not Both?

### Safa Explains Reisha

Tosafot's resolution is precise. In the *tmura* case, *tmurath olah* and *tmurath shelamim* are two independent, equal-weight clauses. Neither explains or qualifies the other; they simply sit side by side as separate declarations. When two parts of a statement are genuinely independent and non-overlapping, we say both are meant and both take effect. But in our case, the situation is different: *min hagrogros* is not an independent second clause. It is the speaker's own explanation of what he means by *nazir* — his conception of *nezirut* is that it consists of abstaining from *grogros*. The *safa*, the end of the statement, comes *lifaresh* the *reisha* — to explain the opening. The speaker is not making two separate declarations; he is elaborating on the one declaration, and that elaboration reveals it to be incoherent.

### End Contradicts Start

This creates a structural problem. Once we read the second half as explaining the first, the whole sentence effectively says: "I am a *nazir*, and by *nazir* I mean someone who abstains from figs." But that is not *nezirut*. The *safa* has thus not merely added a second layer; it has retroactively undermined the entire content of the first.

### One or Two Parts?

The underlying hermeneutic question is whether we are dealing with one statement or two. If they are two independent parts — as in *tmurath olah tmurath shelamim* — we say both. If the second part is an interpretation or elaboration of the first — as in *nazir min hagrogros*, where the *grogros* clause explains what the speaker thought *nazir* meant — then the *safa* is the key to the whole utterance, and since the *safa* reveals a fundamental misunderstanding, the statement as a whole produces nothing. That is what *begmar devarav adam nitpas* means in this context: we wait until the speaker is finished, and only then assess the whole.

---

## Multiple Versions

### Version 1

Having established the main conceptual framework, the *gemara* notes that the *mishna* does not align with a certain *tanna*: *matnitin delo ke'hai tanna*. A *braita* records Rabbi Natan citing a different version of the dispute. According to Rabbi Natan, *Beis Shammai* says the person is *nadur ve'nazir* — both forbidden from the figs (a *neder*) and a *nazir*. *Beis Hillel* says *nadur ve'ein nazir* — he is forbidden from the figs but is not a *nazir*. This version is notably different from the *mishna*. Here, everyone salvages the entire statement in some way. *Beis Shammai*, by saying both parts are independently binding, preserves the full declaration — the word *nazir* creates *nezirut*, and *min hagrogros* creates a *neder* on the figs. *Beis Hillel*, rather than voiding the whole statement, gives it a coherent unified meaning: *nazir min hagrogros* is read as *nadur min hagrogros* — the word *nazir* is interpreted as *neder* language, and the person is simply forbidden from figs.

### Positions Explained

The *gemara* explains the theoretical underpinnings of this version as well. *Beis Shammai savrei ke'Rabbi Meir uke'Rabbi Yehuda*. *Beis Shammai* here applies *ein adam motzi devarav levatala* (the principle of Rabbi Meir) to both halves of the statement: *nazir* means *nazir* and *min hagrogros* means *nadur min hagrogros* (as *Rav Yehuda* had originally read *Beis Shammai*). Nothing in the sentence is wasted; both parts carry independent halakhic force. *Beis Hillel savrei ke'Rabbi Yosi* — applying *begmar devarav adam nitpas* to read the statement as one coherent whole, they give the entire declaration the meaning of *nadur min hagrogros*, the only reading that renders the complete sentence meaningful.

### Version 2

A second textual tradition (*lishna achrina*) within Rabbi Natan's account presents yet another variation: *Beis Shammai omrim nadur ve'eino nazir* — the person is forbidden from the figs but is not a *nazir*. This is precisely the reading *Rav Yehuda* attributed to *Beis Shammai* at the outset of the discussion. *Beis Hillel* says *lo nadur velo nazir* — neither; he is nothing at all. This version maps neatly onto *Beis Shammai* following *Rav Yehuda*'s interpretation and *Beis Hillel* following Rabbi Shimon's approach of *lo hitnadev k'derech hamitnadvim* (to which we return shortly).

### Three Options

Surveying all the material, there are three distinct positions one could occupy when applying *ein adam motzi devarav levatala* to this case. First: the person is a *nazir* and we discard the *min hagrogros* clause — the first part of the statement was binding, the second part is treated as either irrelevant or as a failed attempt at reversal. Second: the person is *nadur min hagrogros* but not a *nazir* — the whole sentence is given a single coherent meaning by translating *nazir* as *nadur*. Third: the person is both a *nazir* and *nadur min hagrogros* — both halves of the statement take independent effect. All three positions stem from the shared refusal to read the statement as meaningless, but they differ in how they distribute that meaning across the two clauses. *Beis Hillel*, for its part, is willing to look at the complete statement and conclude that it never coherently achieved anything halakhically binding.

---

## Mincha Parallel

### Mincha Variations

The *gemara* now introduces a parallel set of cases from a *mishna* elsewhere: *Ha'omer harei alai mincha lehavi min hase'orim* — someone who says "I accept upon myself to bring a *mincha* from barley." Since there is no voluntary *mincha* brought from barley (barley *minchot* are restricted to specific obligatory cases such as *minchat sotah*), the declaration is internally inconsistent. Nevertheless, the *tanna* rules: *yavi min hachittim* — he brings it from wheat. Similarly: one who said he would bring a *mincha* from *kemach* (bran or coarse flour) must bring it from fine flour (*solet*), since there is no *mincha* from *kemach*; one who said he would bring it without oil and *levona* (frankincense) must include them; one who said *chatzi issaron* (a half-measure, which has no standing as a *mincha*) must bring a full *issaron*; and one who said one and a half *issaronot* must bring two, rounding up to the nearest valid unit. In all these cases, the *tanna kamma* holds: we strip away the invalid qualifier, identify the core intent as a *mincha*, and obligate accordingly.

### Rabbi Shimon

*Rabbi Shimon* exempts in all these cases: *shelo hitnadev k'derech hamitnadvim* — this person did not make a vow in the manner of those who normally vow. If the only halakhically coherent interpretation of the whole statement requires discarding a significant portion of what was actually said, *Rabbi Shimon* would rather declare the entire declaration non-binding than artificially reconstruct it. This is a direct and close parallel to the *Hareini nazir min hagrogros* case: just as there is no *nezirut* from *grogros*, there is no *mincha* from barley as a freewill offering, and *Rabbi Shimon* would treat both declarations identically — as generating no obligation at all.

### Tanna Kamma ID

*Chizkiyah* is the first to address the question of who the *tanna kamma* is in the *mincha* case. He identifies the *tanna kamma*'s position as equivalent to that of *Beis Shammai*: just as *Beis Shammai* says *Hareini nazir min hagrogros* creates *nezirut* by ignoring the invalid *min hagrogros* clause, so too the *tanna kamma* says *mincha min hase'orim* creates an obligation to bring a *mincha* by ignoring the invalid *min hase'orim* clause. The structure of the reasoning is identical in both cases.

---

## Rabbi Yochanan

### Understandable Mistake

*Rabbi Yochanan* disagrees with *Chizkiyah*'s identification. The *tanna kamma* in the *mincha* case can be understood even according to *Beis Hillel* — it need not reflect the position of *Beis Shammai* at all. Why? *Be'omer ilu hayiti yode'a she'ein nodrim kach, lo nadarti kach ella kach* — because the case is one where the person can be presumed to say: "Had I known that one cannot vow this way, I would not have said *min hase'orim*, I would have said *min hachittim*." The declaration is treated as binding not because we mechanically ignore its invalid clause, but because the mistake was an understandable one. Most people do not carefully distinguish between barley and wheat when thinking about bringing a *mincha*; the commitment to bring a *mincha* is genuine and the specification of *se'orim* was simply an error that, if caught at the time, the person would immediately have corrected. In such a case, we say the fundamental intent was to bring a *mincha*, the qualifier was mistaken but not misconceived, and therefore the obligation stands.

### Barley vs Lentils

This principle, *Rabbi Yochanan* implies, has a sharp limit. An "understandable mistake" is one within the normal range of confusion — where the gap between what was said and what could have been said is relatively small. *Min hase'orim* vs. *min hachittim* is a modest error; barley and wheat are both grains, both familiar, and easily confused in the mind of someone unfamiliar with the precise laws of *minchot*. But if someone says *mincha min ha'adashim* — a *mincha* from lentil beans — that is a categorically different kind of error. No one making a sincere vow about a *mincha* confuses lentil beans with wheat. Such a statement reflects not a small mistake but a fundamental misunderstanding of what a *mincha* is, analogous to someone who thinks *nezirut* means not eating figs. In that case, the speaker is not simply misspecifying a detail; the whole concept they are operating with is wrong, and we cannot say their "fundamental" intent was to bring a valid *mincha*.

### Chizkiyah Initial

*Chizkiyah* initially argues that the *mincha* dispute is parallel to the *Beis Shammai/Beis Hillel* dispute, implying that even a radical departure from the norm — like lentil beans — should be treated consistently: we drop the invalid qualifier and obligate the *mincha*. On his view, there is no halakhically meaningful distinction between small and large mistakes in this context. The principle of ignoring the nonsensical second clause operates uniformly, regardless of how far outside the realm of *minchot* the stated qualifier falls.

### Gemara Challenge

The *gemara* challenges *Chizkiyah*'s position by pressing the parallel he himself established. *Chizkiyah* had identified the *tanna kamma* by the *mincha* case as following *Beis Shammai*. But *Beis Shammai* holds — even in the case of *Hareini nazir min hagrogros* — that the person becomes a *nazir*, despite the radical absurdity of the qualifier. *Ve'adashim legabei mincha kegrogros legabei nazir damu* — lentil beans in the context of a *mincha* are like *grogros* in the context of *nezirut*: both are wildly off-base. But *Beis Shammai* rules the person is a *nazir* even in the *grogros* case. By his own analogy, *Chizkiyah* should conclude that even lentil beans would obligate a *mincha*. Yet *Chizkiyah* himself had said that the *adashim* case produces nothing. This is internally inconsistent.

### Chizkiyah Reverses

*Hadar bei Chizkiyah* — *Chizkiyah* reversed himself. Faced with this challenge, he conceded that the distinction between small and large mistakes is indeed operative, and came around to the position of *Rabbi Yochanan*: the *mincha* obligation in the case of *se'orim* rests on the fact that it was an understandable mistake, not on a blanket rule of ignoring all invalid qualifiers. Large, radical mistakes — like *adashim* — do not generate a *mincha* obligation.

---

## Why Only Barley?

### Rava's Explanation

*Rava* explains why *Chizkiyah* ultimately capitulated: *matnisin kashya lei* — he was troubled by the *mishna* itself. *Mai irya d'tani min hase'orim* — why did the *mishna* give specifically the example of *barley*? If the rule were that we always strip away the invalid qualifier and require a valid *mincha* regardless of how outlandish the qualifier was, the *mishna* could have — and should have — made the point more powerfully by giving an extreme case: *lisni min ha'adashim*, "even if you said lentil beans, you still bring a *mincha*." The fact that the *mishna* chose *barley* as its example demonstrates that the case is specifically calibrated to the range of understandable mistakes. *Se'orim* is at the boundary — close enough to a real *mincha* that we can say the person genuinely intended a *mincha* and simply got the grain wrong.

### Small Mistake Logic

When someone says *mincha min hase'orim*, the underlying intent is clear: this person wants to bring a *mincha*. The specification of barley was a detail they got wrong, but it does not transform their core commitment. We therefore ignore the mistaken qualifier and obligate them in a normal *mincha*.

### Big Mistake Logic

When someone says *mincha min ha'adashim*, the situation is qualitatively different. Lentil beans have nothing to do with the *mincha* as an institution. Someone who thinks they can bring a *mincha* of lentils is not merely confused about a detail; they are operating with a fundamentally different conception of what they are doing. We cannot say they "fundamentally wanted to bring a *mincha*" and the lentils were an incidental error. They were trying to do something outside the framework of *minchot* entirely, and that attempt generates no halakhic obligation.

---

## Rabbi Yochanan Refined

### Rabbi Yochanan Final

After *Chizkiyah* reverses himself and accepts *Rabbi Yochanan*'s position, the *gemara* presents *Rabbi Yochanan*'s own response to the challenge about lentil beans. Remarkably, *Rabbi Yochanan* now asserts: *afilu min ha'adashim* — even if someone says *mincha min ha'adashim*, they are still obligated to bring a *mincha*. This appears to contradict his earlier stated position. The *gemara* clarifies: *Rabbi Yochanan* is not abandoning his reasoning but rather arguing *lidvarav de'Chizkiyah* — speaking according to *Chizkiyah*'s own framework. *Rabbi Yochanan* is pressing *Chizkiyah*: you, *Chizkiyah*, should have stayed with your original position that we always drop the nonsensical qualifier. Your reason for reversing was that the *mishna* only mentioned *se'orim*; but that proves nothing, because there are other explanations for why the *mishna* chose that example.

### Reversal Theory

One such explanation: *dilma lo mibaya ka'amar* — perhaps the *mishna* is making its point *a fortiori* in the opposite direction. If someone says *min ha'adashim*, that is such an obviously impossible qualifier that it must be read as a *chazara* — a reversal. The person is effectively saying, "I'm not really committing to a *mincha*." But *tefos lashon rishon* — we hold them to the first statement. Since the second clause is so clearly absurd, we treat it as an attempted (and ineffective) retraction rather than as a genuine explanation, which means the first statement stands and the *mincha* obligation is even more obviously binding. On this reading, *adashim* is *kal vachomer* — if anything, it makes the case for obligation more compelling, not less.

### Genuine Intent Theory

A second alternative explanation for why the *mishna* used *se'orim*: when someone says *mincha min hase'orim*, it is genuinely ambiguous whether they are making a mistake or expressing a genuine and specific preference. Perhaps they specifically want to bring something like a *minchat omer* or a *minchat sotah*, which are indeed barley-based. If such a thing exists, I want to bring it; if not, I don't want to bring anything at all. If that is the case, the person has not "fundamentally wanted to bring a *mincha*" with barley as a mistaken qualifier — rather, they specifically wanted *that* type of *mincha* and nothing else. The *mishna* therefore has to affirmatively teach us that even in this ambiguous case we say they are obligated to bring a regular *mincha* from wheat, because we interpret the qualifier as a mistake rather than a precise condition.

### Intent Question

The *gemara* thus surfaces a deeper conceptual question running beneath the entire discussion: what is the nature of the mistake being made? If the error is small and within the normal range of confusion, we can confidently say the person's fundamental intent was to perform the *mitzvah* in question, and the qualifier reflects a genuine misunderstanding of the details. But if the error is large — if the qualifier reflects a radically different conception of the act itself — the question becomes whether this represents an attempted reversal, a completely different undertaking, or simply a bigger version of the same kind of mistake. These three framings lead to different conclusions, and the *amoraim* are divided on which framing correctly captures the logic of the *tanna kamma*.

---

## Final Synthesis

### Beis Shammai Lock

At the core of the entire sugya is a fundamental disagreement about how to evaluate a declaration that contains an incoherent element. *Beis Shammai*'s approach, as it emerges across all the versions of the debate, is essentially one of *tefisah* — locking in the first meaningful word that was uttered. Once someone says *nazir*, that word carries halakhic force, and it is exceedingly difficult to walk it back or requalify it. The subsequent clause — *min hagrogros* — does not redefine what was said; it arrives too late to undo what the first word already accomplished. Whether one explains this as an application of *ein adam motzi devarav levatala* (giving the statement force by focusing on its first viable clause), or as *ein she'eila b'hekdesh* (the principle that *nezirut*, like *hekdesh*, cannot be dissolved), or as a refusal to permit *chazara* once the declaration has taken effect, the result is the same: *Beis Shammai* is highly resistant to allowing a speaker to escape a statement they have already made.

### Beis Hillel Whole

*Beis Hillel*, by contrast, insists on reading the declaration as a whole before assigning it any binding force. *Begmar devarav adam nitpas* — a person is assessed by the entirety of what they said. When we look at the complete statement *Hareini nazir min hagrogros*, we see that the speaker's own conception of *nezirut* is built on something that has nothing to do with *nezirut*. The statement is not two parts in tension; it is one coherent (if confused) statement that, taken whole, fails to constitute any recognized halakhic act. In the *mincha* parallel, this translates to: when the qualifier is radically off, it shows that the speaker was not, at bottom, trying to bring a valid *mincha* — they were trying to do something else, something that does not exist within the halakhic framework, and therefore nothing is binding.

### Limits of Principle

The principle of *ein adam motzi devarav levatala* is thus powerful but bounded. It operates most cleanly where the statement is almost right — where a small terminological error can be corrected by reinterpretation, as in *erech kli alai* being read as *dmei kli alai*. It becomes strained when the invalid portion of the statement is not a minor terminological error but a fundamental reconception of what the *mitzvah* is — *grogros* instead of *yayin*, lentil beans instead of *solet*. In those cases, *Beis Hillel* (and ultimately *Chizkiyah* as well) concludes that the speaker simply was not doing what they thought they were doing, and no binding obligation results. *Beis Shammai*, unwilling to leave any utterance without halakhic consequence, finds a way to impose one regardless — but at the cost of effectively ignoring everything the speaker said except the very first word.

---

---

# Nazir 10

## Talking Cow Mishna

### Cow's Declaration

Daf 10 opens with what will likely be one of the most memorable *mishnayot* encountered in the course of learning *Nazir*. The *Mishnah* presents the following scenario: a man reports that a cow declared, *hareini nezira im omedet ani* — "I will be a *nazira* if I stand up." Or alternatively, that a door declared, *hareini nezira im niftach ani* — "I will be a *nezira* if I am opened." The man comes before us reporting, in apparent seriousness, that he witnessed these declarations by a cow and a door.

### Beis Shammai/Hillel

*Beis Shammai* rules that the man is a *nazir* — not the cow or the door, but the man himself is a *nazir*, presumably contingent on whether the stated condition was fulfilled. *Beis Hillel* rules that he is not a *nazir*. The *Gemara* will clarify the precise nature of this dispute.

### R. Yehuda Position

*Rabbi Yehuda* adds a qualification: even when *Beis Shammai* said the man is a *nazir*, they did not mean he becomes a full *nazir*. Rather, their intent was only that whoever says *harei para zo alai korban im omedet hi* — "this cow is upon me as a *korban* if it stands" — the cow becomes forbidden to him. This is analogous to the earlier *Mishnah* where a man says he is a *nazir* from dates (*develah*): *Rabbi Yehuda* held there that the dates become forbidden to him rather than that he actually assumes full *nezirut*. So too here, the cow becomes forbidden, not that a full *nezirut* takes effect. How this reasoning extends to a talking door is left somewhat open, but presumably the door would become forbidden to him in some analogous sense.

The natural reaction to all of this is: of all the things one might ask about this *Mishnah*, the debate over whether this constitutes *nezirut* or a *korban*-like prohibition seems almost beside the point. What on earth is going on with a cow that declares itself a *nezira*?

---

## Gemara Response

### Rami bar Chama

The *Gemara* asks the obvious question: *para mi ka mishtaya* — since when does a cow talk? *Rami bar Chama* proposes the following reading: *kegon shehayesa para revutza lefanav* — we are dealing with a case in which a cow was crouched down before the man. He observes it and says, *kisvura para zo eina omedet* — this cow must be thinking that it is not going to be able to stand up. It appears so thoroughly crouched that one would say it has given up on rising.

### Meat Nazirut

With that as the backdrop, *Rami bar Chama* explains the man's actual statement as *hareini nazir mibesara im amda me'aleha* — I will be a *nazir* from its flesh if it stands up on its own. And then the cow did in fact stand up on its own. The condition was thus met. This immediately reduces the *Mishnah* to a parallel of the preceding one, since the question now becomes: what does it mean to declare oneself a *nazir* from the meat of a cow?

### Debate Repetition

The *Gemara* notes that *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel* simply follow their respective positions — *ve'azlu Beis Shammai leshitasan veBeis Hillel leshitasan* — the same positions they took in the earlier *Mishnah* regarding dates and *develah*. *Beis Shammai* holds that if someone says he is a *nazir* from dates or from meat, he is indeed a *nazir*, because we look past the odd object named and recognize the underlying intent to accept *nezirut*. *Beis Hillel* holds that such a declaration is meaningless, since one cannot be a *nazir* "from" meat any more than one can be a *nazir* "from" dates, and so he is not a *nazir* at all. The immediate question the *Gemara* raises is: why must this debate be repeated? *Beis Shammai* already stated this position once in the earlier *Mishnah*.

---

## Two/Three Times

### Multiple Cases

*Rava* answers: *trei telas* — two or three times we are shown variations of the same principle. And so teaches *Rabbi Chiya*, and so says *Rabbi Yoshiya* as well: there are multiple illustrations of the same debate, and that is intentional.

### Dates/Grapes

But the *Gemara* goes further and insists that each case is necessary — *u'tzricha*. Had the *Mishnah* only taught the case of *grogros u'develah*, dates and dried figs, one might have thought that *Beis Shammai*'s ruling applies only there. Why? *Mishum demichalfin ba'anavim* — because dates and grapes are genuinely similar. They are both smallish, darkish fruits. It is not entirely unreasonable for someone to confuse the two, to think that what the *Torah* prohibits to a *nazir* under the category of grapes somehow extends to or includes dates. And so *Beis Shammai* could be saying: you clearly wanted to be a *nazir* and simply got confused about which fruit was meant, and therefore your declaration takes effect.

### Meat Distinction

But meat and grapes — *lo michalef* — nobody confuses those. So if the *Mishnah* only taught the case of meat, one might assume the opposite: that the case of dates would not work for *Beis Shammai*, since the confusion between dates and grapes is more plausible and *Beis Shammai* might be relying on that confusion to impose *nezirut*. The case of meat would then need its own logic.

### Wine/Meat Link

That logic runs as follows: *bevishra vechamra* — wine and meat go together. A good meal, a life of sensual indulgence, is classically represented by meat and wine. The institution of *nezirut* is understood by many to represent a form of asceticism, a withdrawal from physical pleasure. It is therefore not at all unreasonable to suppose that when a person says "I am a *nazir* from meat," they are thinking: a *nazir* abstains from the pleasures of meat and wine together. As the *Gemara* notes, *de'amar mar*, there is a teaching that an *onen* — a mourner in the acute stage of mourning — is forbidden from wine and meat. These two are linked as the classic expression of physical indulgence. Indeed, it is worth pausing over this association, because the prohibition of wine for a *nazir* is not solely about hedonism. The *pasuk* in *Yirmiyahu* — *vatashku es hanezirim yayin ve'al hanevi'im tzivisem leimor lo tinavu* — speaks of giving the *nezirim* wine to drink and commanding the prophets not to prophesy, suggesting that wine is problematic not merely because of physical pleasure but because it clouds the mind and distracts from devotion to God. Nonetheless, the popular association of *nezirut* with abstaining from both wine and meat is understandable, and *Beis Shammai* might be saying: when you declared yourself a *nazir* from meat, you were really expressing a desire to be a *nazir* in the full sense. Had the *Mishnah* only told us the meat case, however, I might have thought the dates case is too far-fetched for *Beis Shammai* to accept — dates have no association with *nezirut*.

### Door Example

And then there is the door. Had the *Mishnah* only given us the cases of dates and meat, one might have concluded that *Beis Hillel* concedes in those cases — that even *Beis Hillel* agrees that when there is some basis for the confusion or association, the declaration works. The door case eliminates that possibility. By including a case of complete absurdity — *aval deles*, but a door — the *Mishnah* shows that *Beis Shammai* maintains its position even when the appended object is total nonsense, and *Beis Hillel* maintains its position even in cases where the association might seem coherent. All three cases together establish the full scope of the dispute.

---

## Tosafot Solutions

### Mapik Hey

Having understood the *Gemara*'s reduction of the *Mishnah* to a straightforward debate about declaring oneself a *nazir* from meat or from a door, *Tosafot* now attempts the harder task: making sense of the actual language of the *Mishnah* on its own terms.
