The *Mishnah* says *amra para zu* — this cow said — and then quotes the cow as saying *hareini nezira im omedet ani*. How does one read those words in a way that produces the *Gemara*'s conclusion?

*Tosafot*'s first approach invokes anthropomorphism. The idea is that we project human intention onto an animal. The cow is crouched and straining — it *looks* as though it is telling us something. Just as the verse in *Yonah* says *veha'oniyah chishvah lehishaver* — the ship *thought* it would break — the ship of course was not literally thinking; the language is anthropomorphic, conveying that the ship was on the verge of breaking. So too here, when the *Mishnah* says the cow *said* it would be a *nezira*, it means the cow's posture and behavior are *telling* us that it cannot stand.

### Grammar Fix

That handles the first part of the *Mishnah*. But the second part presents a grammatical challenge. The word *nezira* is feminine. How does a man declare himself a feminine *nezira*? *Tosafot* offers a brilliant grammatical observation: the *hei* at the end of *nezira* is a *mapik hei* — a suffix meaning "from it." So *hareini nezira* does not mean "I will be a *nezira*" in the feminine sense; rather, it means *hareini nazir heimena* — I will be a *nazir* from it, from the cow. This transforms the declaration into exactly what the *Gemara* requires: a statement that the man will be a *nazir* from the cow's meat if it stands. The only remaining difficulty is the word *ani* at the end — *im omedet ani*, "if I stand" — which does not fit naturally, since it is the cow that would be standing, not the man. *Tosafot* acknowledges this difficulty but regards the rest of the reading as compelling despite that loose end.

### Literal Approach

*Tosafot*'s second approach takes the *Mishnah* more at face value. According to this reading, the man is genuinely reporting a story — he came and told us: I saw this cow, and it appeared to say that it would be a *nezira* if it stood up. The *Mishnah* records this as a straightforward narrative of what the man reported.

### Story/Meaning

Since what the man reports is complete nonsense — a cow cannot be a *nezira* — we interpret the telling of this absurd story as a *de facto* declaration of *nezirut* on the man's part. As *Tosafot* puts it: *heichah kesheadam mesaper lefaneinu kach bedaito lekayem alav sheyehe nazir mivesara* — when a person comes and tells us this strange story about a cow, what he is really communicating is that he intends to accept upon himself *nezirut* from the cow's meat. The story about the cow is the vehicle; the real content is his declaration of *nezirut*.

One might note that according to this second approach, the primary *chiddush* of the *Mishnah* shifts. It is no longer simply another illustration of the *Beis Shammai*/*Beis Hillel* debate about declaring *nezirut* from non-grape objects. Rather, the novel ruling would be that we interpret an absurd story about a cow as a declaration of *nezirut* altogether — that we translate bizarre narrative into legally operative speech. The *Gemara*'s focus on the *Beis Shammai*/*Beis Hillel* debate then becomes a secondary point following from that primary *chiddush*.

---

## Rava's Version

### Rava Objection

*Rava* now raises an objection to the entire framework of *Rami bar Chama*. *Mi ktani im amda me'aleha* — does the *Mishnah* actually say "if it stood up on its own"? It does not. And if that is the *Gemara*'s complaint, one might ask: of all the liberties one could take with a *Mishnah* about a talking cow, why is the insertion of the words "on its own" the sticking point? *Tosafot* essentially reads *Rava*'s objection as a more general dissatisfaction with the entire reading — a way of saying that the explanation of *Rami bar Chama* simply does not reflect what is actually happening in the *Mishnah*, and the missing words "on its own" are the marker of that problem.

### Inverted Condition

*Rava* then offers his own reframing. The cow is still crouched down in front of the man, but *Rava* changes the nature of the condition. Rather than the man saying *im amda* — if it stands — *Rava* reads the condition as *im lo amda* — if it does not stand. The man declares *hareini nazir miyayin* — I will be a standard *nazir* from wine — *im lo amda* — if it does not stand. And then the cow stood up on its own — *ve'amda me'aleha*.

One might immediately note that *Rava* himself is inserting a word — *lo* — that does not appear in the *Mishnah*, having just criticized *Rami bar Chama* for inserting the phrase "on its own." *Tosafot* acknowledges this asymmetry but suggests that a missing *lo* is a more tolerable emendation than a missing qualifying phrase, though the reasoning is admittedly strained.

### Ability to Raise

The dispute between *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel* now takes on an entirely different character. The man said he would be a *nazir* if the cow does not stand. The cow did stand. So why should he be a *nazir* at all? *Beis Shammai savri tursa de-hai gavra mishum okmei biyadei hu* — *Beis Shammai* holds that the man's focus, his *tursa*, was on whether he himself would be able to get the cow to stand. His statement "if it does not stand" was not a neutral observation about the cow's posture; it was a wager or a declaration of intent: "If I cannot get it to stand, I will be a *nazir*." The cow ultimately stood up on its own, but the man was not the one who caused it to stand. The condition — *im lo ukma biyadei*, if I cannot raise it — was therefore met, and he is a *nazir*.

*Tosafot* asks: where does the *Gemara* derive this reading of the man's psychology? The answer, *Tosafot* explains, is that the *Gemara* is trying to understand why a person would ever make such a condition. It makes sense if the man was trying to demonstrate his own ability to get the cow up — essentially making a deal: "I bet I can get it to stand; if I can't, I'll be a *nazir*." That is an intelligible psychological motivation. The cow's crouching is what prompts this, and the man's declaration is really about his own agency in resolving the situation.

### Standing Fact

*Beis Hillel* disagrees about the *tursa*. *U-Beis Hillel savri turpei d'hai gavra mishum terviahu* — *Beis Hillel* holds that the man's focus was simply on the crouching. He was upset that the cow was crouched down, and his declaration was: "If this cow doesn't get up, I'll be a *nazir*." It does not matter who or what caused it to stand — the relevant fact is simply whether the cow ended up on its feet. *Ha kama* — it stood. The condition was met in the most straightforward sense, and he is not a *nazir*.

---

## Resolution

### Rabbi Yehuda Limit

*Rava*'s reframing now runs into difficulty with *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position. If, as *Rava* explains, the man explicitly declared *hareini nazir miyayin* — I will be a *nazir* from wine — then why does *Rabbi Yehuda* limit even *Beis Shammai*'s ruling to saying that merely the cow becomes forbidden to him? If the man said outright that he would be a *nazir* from wine, there is no basis for *Rabbi Yehuda* to reduce the outcome to a mere prohibition on the cow.

### Must Be Meat

The *Gemara* resolves this by reverting to the formulation of *Rami bar Chama*: the case must be one in which the man said *hareini nazir mibesara* — I will be a *nazir* from its meat — not from wine. We return, in other words, to the same debate we have seen before: the man declared *nezirut* from a non-standard object — meat — and the three-way dispute of *Beis Shammai*, *Beis Hillel*, and *Rabbi Yehuda* plays out exactly as it did in the case of dates. *Beis Shammai* holds that he is a *nazir*, *Beis Hillel* holds that he is not, and *Rabbi Yehuda* holds that the meat becomes forbidden to him. The *tna'i* — the condition about the cow standing — is now layered on top of this debate.

### Concession

The *Gemara* then stages an exchange between the two schools. *Beis Shammai* addresses *Beis Hillel*: even according to your own logic, concede to us — *odu lan mei'ha* — that in this case the man's *tursa* was on the crouching, and the cow stood, so the condition was not met, and he should not be a *nazir* even according to you. *Beis Shammai* is saying: whatever you think about *nezirut* from meat in general, at least agree that in this specific case the condition was fulfilled — the cow stood — and therefore *Beis Hillel* should not impose *nezirut* here.

### Hillel Counter

*Beis Hillel* responds: *lav turpei d'hai gavra mishum okmei biyadei* — no, we read the man's focus as being on *his ability* to get the cow to stand, not merely on whether it stood. He was not the one who got it to stand, so the condition — from *Beis Hillel*'s perspective — was in fact not met, and the man is not a *nazir*. *Beis Shammai* in turn insists: *turpei d'hai gavra mishum okmei biyadei v'halo ukme* — his focus was indeed on whether he could get it to stand, and he did not, so the condition was met and he is a *nazir*.

---

## Simple Reading

### Core Claim

Stepping back, the simplest way to characterize what the *Gemara* has done is this: the talking cow is, in the end, a distraction. Whatever elaborate story the *Mishnah* constructs about a cow declaring *nezirut* from its crouched position, the operative legal content reduces to a man saying *hareini nazir mibesara* — I will be a *nazir* from its meat — with some kind of condition attached about whether the cow stands.

### Why Illustrations

The multiple illustrations — dates, meat, door, and now the cow — serve the purpose identified earlier: to demonstrate that the dispute between *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel* applies across the full range of cases, from the marginally understandable to the completely absurd.

### Parallel Structure

The *Mishnah* of the talking cow thus runs in exact parallel to the earlier *Mishnah* about dates. *Beis Shammai* says the man is a *nazir*, *Beis Hillel* says he is not, and *Rabbi Yehuda* says the cow — or the dates, or the door — is forbidden to him. *Rava*'s version adds one further layer: a debate about whether the condition embedded in the declaration was actually met, turning on whether the man's intent was simply that the cow would stand, or specifically that he himself would succeed in raising it. What the talking cow and the talking door have to do with this precise dispute about the nature of a conditional vow remains, to say the least, an interesting question — but there it is, laid out in the *Gemara* of *Nazir* daf 10.

# Nazir 11

## Partial Nezirus Intent

### Beis Hillel/Shammai

Daf 11 opens by returning to the terrain of ordinary *nezirus* after the extended discussion of unusual formulations — including the debate of *Beis Hillel*, *Beis Shammai*, and *Rebbi Yehuda*'s interpretation of *Beis Shammai* — regarding what it means to declare oneself a *nazir* from something that is not itself one of the prohibited categories of *nezirus*. The question there was whether such a declaration constitutes full *nezirus*, no *nezirus* at all, or merely a prohibition on the specific item named. With that backdrop in place, the *Mishnah* now turns to more standard cases.

### Cup of Wine Case

The first *Mishnah* on this daf presents a person who is offered a cup of wine — *mazgu lo es hakos* — and declares, *hareini nazir mimenu*, "I am a *nazir* from it." The word *mimenu* is somewhat ambiguous: it could mean "from wine" generically, or it could mean "from this particular cup." One might therefore have thought that the person was merely declining this specific serving rather than genuinely accepting *nezirus*. Nevertheless, the ruling is that such a person is a *nazir*.

### Partial = Full

This ruling reflects a principle established in an earlier *Mishnah*: accepting *nezirus* with respect to any one component of *nezirus* — wine, haircuts, or *tumas meis* — constitutes full *nezirus*. The position of the *Chachamim* is that *nezirus* is a package deal; if you accept any piece of it, you have accepted all of it. Since this declaration concerns wine, which is a genuine element of *nezirus*, even *Beis Hillel* agrees that the person becomes a *nazir* in full.

It is worth noting that had the person said *hareini nazir min hakos hazeh* — "I am a *nazir* from this cup" — the result might well have been different, since that formulation makes explicit that the reference is to a particular vessel rather than to wine as such. The formulation *mimenu* is general enough to be read as referring to wine, which is why the ruling applies.

## Drunk Woman Story

### Woman's Declaration

The *Mishnah* then presents a contrasting case: *maaseh be-isha achas she-haysah shikorah* — there was a woman who was drunk, and people were offering her another cup of wine. She declared, *hareini nezirah mimenu*, "I am a *nezirah* from it" — the very same formulation used in the previous case.

### Limited Intent

Despite the identical language, the *Chachamim* rule that she did not become a *nezirah*. Their reasoning is that *lo nis-kavnah zo ela lomar harei hu alai k'korban* — she merely intended to forbid this specific cup to herself as a *neder*, as a *konam*. She was not accepting *nezirus* from wine generally; she meant only to refuse this particular cup.

### Contradiction Question

This immediately raises a sharp question: why is the context of the second case any different from the first? In both instances, the identical phrase *mimenu* was used. The *Gemara* presses this directly: *maaseh listor*? Is the story being brought in order to contradict the ruling just stated? You declared at the outset that *harei zeh nazir*, and then you tell us of a case where the same words yield the opposite result?

Before examining the *Gemara*'s resolution, it is worth pausing on a broader question raised by this passage. One might invoke the principle of *perushan le-hakel*, familiar from *Nedarim*, according to which ambiguous *nedarim* are read leniently. If *nezirus* is a species of *neder*, should the same principle not apply here — permitting the person to explain what he or she actually meant? The *Gemara* throughout this tractate has largely not pursued that avenue; rather than asking the declarant what was intended, the discussion proceeds to determine meaning objectively from context and language. The principle of *piv v'libo shavin* — that words and intent should align — is one the *Gemara* is aware of, but its actual deployment in these *sugyos* is more limited than one might expect. The question of when subjective intent can override the plain import of words, and when we say *ein piv v'libo shavin* renders a declaration non-binding, will resurface explicitly later in this *daf*. For now, the *Gemara* proceeds by asking not what she meant to say, but what, objectively, her situation tells us about what she was saying.

### Chasorei Mechasra

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction with the technique of *chasorei mechasra vehachi katani* — the *Mishnah* is missing a clause and must be read as though it contained an explanatory transition. The missing clause establishes that when an ordinary person, in an ordinary social setting, is offered a cup of wine and says *hareini nazir mimenu*, that person is a *nazir*; but if the person was drunk at the time and made the same declaration, the result is different.

## Drunk Woman Logic

### Strong Language Tactic

The *Gemara* then explains why the drunk person's declaration is treated differently: *keman de'amar harei alai korban hu* — it is as if the person said this cup is forbidden to me like a *korban*. But one might ask: if that is what the person meant, why not simply say those words? The *Gemara* answers: *savar meitina achrina umitza'aru li* — the drunk person is thinking that if he or she says merely "this cup is forbidden to me," those around will simply continue offering wine. The person wants to communicate something categorical and absolute, something that will make clear that no further pressure should be applied. By invoking the language of a *nazir*, the person is deploying a rhetorical tactic: *eima lehu hamiltha*, saying something that signals total abstention, *depaska lehu*, cutting off the attempt entirely.

### Social Pressure

*Tosafos* elaborates on this reasoning helpfully. The passage describes a social reality: *derech b'nei adam l'haftzir b'shikor she'yishteh* — it is common practice to pressure a drunk person to keep drinking. People find it amusing to encourage further intoxication, and the drunk person, who genuinely does not wish to drink more, cannot make that refusal stick by merely declining a particular cup. The only language powerful enough to end the pressure is the language of *nezirus*, which conveys an absolute and apparently binding commitment. *Tosafos* concludes: *aval k'she'eino shikor ein derech l'haftziro* — but when a person is not drunk, there is no social pressure of this kind. If a sober person declines a cup of wine and no one is pressing the matter, there is no need to invoke the language of *nezirus* merely to get people to back off.

### Sober Contrast

This contrast explains the ruling in the first part of the *Mishnah*. When a sober person, who is under no special pressure to drink, uses the language of *nezirus* in response to being offered a cup of wine, that person is genuinely invoking the concept. There is no ulterior communicative purpose being served. The heavy word carries its actual weight, and since the person is declaring *nezirus* from wine — a genuine component of *nezirus* — the full status applies. *Tosafos* states this explicitly: *v'l'kach omer d'nazir mikulehu* — when you use the strong word *nazir* without any social pressure compelling you toward theatrical language, you really mean to be a *nazir* from wine, and being a *nazir* from wine pulls along the rest.

## Conditions on Torah

### Conditional Declaration

The next *Mishnah* presents a new category of case. A person declares: *hareini nazir al mnas she'ehei shoteh yayin umitamei lameitim* — "I will be a *nazir* on the condition that I may still drink wine" or "on the condition that I may still become *tamei* through contact with the dead."

### Conditions Void

The ruling is unambiguous: *harei zeh nazir v'assur bekulan* — this person is a *nazir* and is forbidden in all the relevant respects. None of the conditions are honored.

There are two ways to understand why. The first approach, and the one the *Gemara* will confirm in the name of Ravina, is that the person has accepted full *nezirus* and then attempted to attach conditions to a Torah-mandated status. This triggers the principle of *matneh al mah shekatuv ba-Torah*: any stipulation that contradicts what the Torah requires is void. The person has genuinely accepted the *nezirus*; we simply discard the conditions. The second approach reads *al mnas* not as "with a condition upon" the whole of *nezirus* but as equivalent to *chutz* — "except for." Under this reading, the person was attempting to accept partial *nezirus*, which brings us back to the earlier debate about whether partial acceptance constitutes full *nezirus*. The *Gemara* will return to both of these frameworks.

## Mistaken Understanding

### Unaware of Wine Ban

The *Mishnah* then introduces two further cases involving mistaken understanding. In the first, the person declares *nezirus* but states: *yodea ani sheyesh nezirot aval eini yodea shehanazir assur beyayin* — "I know that the institution of *nezirus* exists, but I did not know that a *nazir* is forbidden wine." Perhaps, he imagined, *nezirus* is simply about growing one's hair long and nothing more.

### Chachamim vs. Shimon

The ruling of the *Chachamim* is *harei zeh assur* — this person is bound as a *nazir*. Ignorance of one of the *halachos* does not void the acceptance. *Rabbi Shimon*, however, rules that the person is not a *nazir* at all.

### Expected Dispensation

The third case involves a different kind of mistake. Here the person knew full well that a *nazir* is forbidden wine, but declares: *savur hayiti she-Chachamim matirin li* — "I assumed that the rabbis would grant me a dispensation," either because he is someone who cannot function without wine, or because his livelihood as a gravedigger requires him to become *tamei* regularly.

### Positions Reversed

Remarkably, the positions of the *Chachamim* and *Rabbi Shimon* are now reversed. In this third case, the *Chachamim* rule *muttar* — this person is not bound as a *nazir* — while *Rabbi Shimon* rules *assur*. And lest there be any confusion: *muttar* here means the person does not become a *nazir* at all. A partial *nezirus* is not an option except in the case of *Shimshon*.

This reversal is genuinely striking, and the *Gemara* devotes considerable attention to explaining it.

## Partial Acceptance L (II)

### Partial Nezirus

Before addressing the reversal directly, the *Gemara* first asks why there is apparently no debate regarding the first case — the person who says *hareini nazir al mnas she'ehei shoteh yayin*. If *Rabbi Shimon* holds that when a person did not realize wine was included, the *nezirus* is not binding — because the person was in effect only accepting a partial *nezirus* — why does *Rabbi Shimon* not say the same when the person explicitly stipulates that wine should be excluded?

The answer given by *Rebbi Yehoshua ben Levi* is that *Rabbi Shimon* in fact does dispute that first case as well; it simply was not recorded separately in the *Mishnah*.

## Conditions on Torah (II)

### Matneh al Torah

Ravina, however, takes a different position: *Rabbi Shimon* genuinely concedes in the first case. The reason is *matneh al mah shekatuv ba-Torah*: the person has accepted the full *nezirus* and then attempted to impose conditions on a Torah-defined status. The conditions are simply voided, and the full *nezirus* stands. This is distinct from the second case, where the person never understood or accepted the full package in the first place. As *Tosafos* puts it: *d'k'sh'amar hareini nazir chal alav nezirus l'chol mili* — when you say *hareini nazir*, full *nezirus* takes effect immediately on all its components; *v'ki amar al mnas matil tnai al mah shekatuv ba-Torah u'vatel ha-tnai* — and when you then say "on condition," you are attempting to make a stipulation against what the Torah prescribes, and that stipulation is void.

By contrast, in the second case, what the person was internally accepting was a *nezirus* that did not include the wine prohibition — because that is all they knew *nezirus* to be. That is not a case of full acceptance plus a void condition; it is a case of genuinely partial acceptance. And the question of what partial acceptance amounts to is the subject of the ongoing debate.

## Partial Acceptance L (II)

### Partial Debate

With that foundation in place, the *Gemara* turns to explaining why *Rabbi Shimon* and the *Chachamim* reverse their positions between the second and third cases. The key is to appreciate that the second case — where the person did not know wine was prohibited — is a case of partial *nezirus*. In the person's own conception, *nezirus* meant only the hair-related practices; in accepting *nezirus*, that is all they were accepting.

This brings us back to the debate that was introduced in an earlier *Mishnah*. If a person says *hareini nazir min ha-yayin*, or any formulation indicating acceptance of only one component of *nezirus*, the *Chachamim* hold that accepting any piece of *nezirus* constitutes accepting the whole thing — it is a package deal. *Rabbi Shimon*, by contrast, holds *ad sheyidor mikulan* — unless you explicitly accept all components, you have accepted nothing; a partial package counts as nothing.

So in the second case, the person was in their mind accepting partial *nezirus*. The *Chachamim* say partial acceptance equals full *nezirus*, and therefore the person is bound. *Rabbi Shimon* says partial acceptance equals nothing, and therefore the person goes free.

### Hitur Request

Now the third case. Here the person knew exactly what *nezirus* entailed. What they believed was that they would receive a *heter* — a dispensation — because of their particular circumstances. The *Gemara*'s most elegant explanation is that this case involves not the process of *kabbalah* — acceptance — but the process of *hatara* — dissolution. The person in fact accepted full *nezirus*, and now, in effect, is coming before the *Chachamim* and seeking to be released from one component of it: the prohibition on *tumas meis*, because they are a gravedigger.

The question then becomes: if someone seeks *hatara* — dissolution of a *neder* — on the basis of *charata* regarding only one element of the *neder*, does that partial *charata* dissolve the entire *neder*, or must *charata* attach to the whole?

### Parallel Processes

This is where the elegance of the mirror-image explanation becomes clear. The process of *kabbalah* and the process of *hatara* are structurally parallel. The *Chachamim* hold that just as accepting *nezirus* for one component sweeps in the whole, so too being *mitcharet* — expressing regret — for one component dissolves the whole. *Neder she-hutar miktzato hutar kulo*: a *neder* that is dissolved in part is dissolved entirely. Therefore, when this person comes with *charata* over the gravedigger element, the *Chachamim* say that dissolves everything, and the person is *muttar*.

*Rabbi Shimon*, maintaining his consistent position, holds that both processes require totality. Just as you must accept the full package to become a *nazir*, you must be *mitcharet* over the full package to be released. Partial *charata*, focusing only on the *tumas meis* component, does not constitute a valid *hatara*, and therefore the person remains bound — *assur*.

This explanation makes sense at the level of process rather than end-state. One might wonder: if the *Chachamim* say that accepting the wine component alone makes one a *nazir* for everything, why should expressing *charata* over the *tumas meis* component dissolve the wine component as well? Shouldn't the wine component remain in force, and a *nazir* who is still obligated on wine is still a *nazir* in full? The answer is that we are looking not at what formal obligations happen to remain, but at the act itself: the act of *kabbalah* can be partial and still be valid, and the act of *hatara* can likewise be partial and still be valid, because the two processes are structurally analogous.

## Alt Explanations

### Nidrei Onesim

The *Gemara* offers an alternative framework for explaining the third case: the dispute concerns *nidrei onsin* — coerced or circumstantially compelled vows. The *Mishnah* in *Nedarim* records four categories of *nedarim* that the *Chachamim* released: *nidrei ziruzin* (vows of encouragement or haggling), *nidrei havai* (exaggerated or nonsensical vows), *nidrei shegagot* (vows made under mistaken beliefs about conditions), and *nidrei onsin*. A *neder ones* is illustrated by a case where one says "my possessions shall be forbidden to you if you do not come to my celebration," and the other person does not come — but only because of circumstances beyond their control, such as an unavoidable delay. The vow-maker never intended the prohibition to take effect under those conditions.

The *Gemara* applies this framework to the third case: the person who accepted *nezirus* thinking they would receive a dispensation is, in some sense, in a position analogous to *nidrei onsin* — they would never have accepted *nezirus* had they known it would interfere with their livelihood as a gravedigger, and that interference is a kind of *ones*.

### Hatara Requirement

The debate between the *Chachamim* and *Rabbi Shimon* in this framework tracks the dispute between *Shmuel* and *Rav Assi*. *Rav Yehuda* cites *Rav Assi* to the effect that even these four categories of *nedarim*, though fundamentally non-binding, still require a formal process of *hatarat nedarim* — the *Chachamim* should formally pronounce *muttar lach* — and this is *derabbanan*. When this position was reported before *Shmuel*, he responded: the *Mishnah* says *hatiru Chachamim* — the *Chachamim* released them — meaning they are simply not binding; no formal process is required. The *Chachamim* in the *Mishnah* on this *daf* follow *Shmuel*: the *neder* is simply not binding, hence *muttar*. *Rabbi Shimon* follows *Rav Assi*: the *neder* is not binding in a fundamental sense, but one must still go through a process of dissolution — meaning it is *assur* in the sense that it is presently binding until formally undone.

### Ein Piv V'libo

*Tosafos* offers a further alternative. Looking at a line in *Tosafos* that begins with the word *nami*, *Tosafos* argues that the third case is not really a matter of *nidrei onsin* at all. Rather, it is a case of *ein piv v'libo shavin* — the person's words do not match their inner intent. The person said *hareini nazir*, but their mental state at the time of declaration was that *nezirus* would not require them to give up their gravedigging work. What they said and what they intended diverged fundamentally.

The debate then maps onto the same *Amoraic* dispute about *ein piv v'libo shavin*: does this situation require no formal process at all, because the declaration was never truly binding, or does it require going through *hatarat nedarim* even though the *neder* was fundamentally defective? One position says the *neder* is simply not binding and no process is needed; the other says it is presently binding until a formal *hatara* is performed, if only to avoid trivializing the whole institution of *nedarim*. When we say *assur* in this context, we mean not that it is permanently binding, but that it requires formal dissolution — as in the story of a son who returned from camp troubled by a vow he had made, where the *halachic* response of *muttar lach, muttar lach, muttar lach* provided the needed closure, whether for his psychological ease or to preserve the gravity of the institution.

## Korbanot Responsibility

### Dual Obligation

The final *Mishnah* of the *daf* introduces a new scenario. A person declares: *hareini nazir v'alai l'galeach nazir* — "I am a *nazir*, and I accept upon myself the responsibility to shave another *nazir*," which means taking on the financial obligation to bring the *korbanot* for another *nazir* at the conclusion of that person's *nezirus*.

### Mutual Help

The *Mishnah* then describes the optimal practical arrangement. If both parties are clever — *im hayu pikchin* — they will each bring the other's *korbanot*. This way, each person fulfills only one set of *korbanot* rather than two, and neither needs to search for a stranger whose *korbanot* they have obligated themselves to bring. If they cannot arrange this mutual arrangement, each must go and find another *nazir* whose *korbanot* they can bring. The *Mishnah* notes that the second person declared *v'ani v'alai l'galeach nazir* — "and me, and I also take responsibility to shave a *nazir*."

### V'ani Coverage

This formulation raises a question for the *Gemara*: if the second person had said only *v'ani* — "and me" — without the additional clause *v'alai l'galeach nazir*, would that abbreviated statement have covered both obligations, the *nezirus* itself and the responsibility to bring another's *korbanot*? Or does *v'ani* alone cover only part of what the first person said?

## Partial Statement Analys…

### Full vs. Partial

The question the *Gemara* formulates is precise: does *v'ani* go on *kulei dibura* — covering the full statement made by the first person — or only *palga d'dibura* — covering part of it? And if only part, which part: the *reisha*, the first element of the declaration (the *nezirus* itself), or the *seifa*, the concluding element (the responsibility to bring another's *korbanot*)?

### Text Analysis

The *Gemara* brings an initial proof from the *Mishnah* text itself. Since the *Mishnah* had the second person say both *v'ani* and *v'alai l'galeach nazir*, it appears that both clauses were necessary. If *v'ani* alone had covered everything, why would the *Mishnah* have required the additional clause? The inference follows: *shma mina v'ani al techilat dibura mashma* — *v'ani* alone picks up only the first element of the statement, the *nezirus*, while the *v'alai l'galeach* clause is necessary to cover the second obligation. This reading seems natural: one would expect "and me" to echo the most immediate referent — the *nezirus* — leaving the additional responsibility to be stated explicitly.

### V'ani Omnibus

*Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua* challenges this proof before Rava. He argues that *v'ani* could in fact cover everything — both the *nezirus* and the obligation to bring another's *korbanot*. If so, why does the *Mishnah* have the second person also say *v'alai l'galeach*? The answer is that this added phrase is not adding halachic content; it is simply explanatory — *alai be-ha milta*, "upon me, this thing," meaning the speaker is spelling out what *v'ani* already implied. The *Mishnah* gives us a full sentence not because the sentence was required to create the halachic effect, but for the sake of clarity.

In support of this reading, *Rav Huna* points to the *Mishnah* that follows in the text: *harei alai l'galeach chatzi nazir*, where a person accepts responsibility to bring the *korbanot* for half of another *nazir*'s obligations. There too, the second person says a full sentence — *v'ani alai l'galeach chatzi nazir* — even though in that case only one thing is at stake, namely the responsibility for another's *korbanot*, with no personal *nezirus* involved. If *v'ani* were truly insufficient and required supplementation, why does the *Mishnah* not simply record that the second person said *v'ani* in a case where there is only one thing to echo? The fact that the *Mishnah* still has that person say a full sentence suggests that the full sentence is the *Mishnah*'s way of giving an example of what was said, not a halachic requirement. And if so, in our case as well, *v'ani* alone would have sufficed.

### Rava's Logic

Rava rejects this argument. His reasoning is that the two *Mishnayos* can be read together in a way that avoids making both of their full-sentence formulations superfluous. If in the first *Mishnah* — our case — *v'ani* was insufficient and the additional clause was genuinely necessary, then we can account for the second *Mishnah*'s full sentence by saying: *tani seifa d'lo tzricha mishum reisha d'tzricha* — the *seifa* includes a clause that was not technically required, but it does so in order to parallel the *reisha* where the clause was required. This is an acceptable halachic literary technique: one case is formulated in full because it needed to be, and the parallel case adopts the same formulation for consistency.

### Supplementation Needed

But Rava argues that the reverse reading creates an insupportable result. If *v'ani* already covers everything, then in both *Mishnayos* the additional phrases are purely superfluous. Having two independent cases each containing a legally unnecessary clause — purely for stylistic reasons — is not how a *halacha* text operates. One can accept superfluity in the *seifa* where it mirrors necessary language in the *reisha*, but one cannot accept gratuitous superfluity in both. Therefore Rava concludes: *v'ani* alone, without supplementation, is insufficient to create the full halachic effect of both obligations. The first *Mishnah* required both clauses because both clauses do real work: *v'ani* picks up the *nezirus*, and *v'alai l'galeach* adds the obligation to bring the other's *korbanot*. Here the *daf* concludes.

# Nazir 12

## Agent & Unknown Woman

### Mishnah Setup

The daf begins at the bottom of 11b, introducing a *sugya* that, at first glance, appears to have little connection to the topic at hand. To recall the context: the *mishnah* dealt with two men, each of whom declared, "I am a *nazir* and I accept upon myself to shave a *nazir*" — meaning, to bring another *nazir*'s *korbanot*. The *mishnah* observes that if they are clever, they will simply take care of each other's *korbanot*, a kind of mutual arrangement not unlike the practice of two poor people exchanging *Mishloach Manot* so that each fulfills his obligation for *Seudas Purim*.

### Unspecified Marriage

With that *mishnah* in mind, the *gemara* cites a ruling of Rav Yosef bar Yosef in the name of Rabbi Yochanan. If a man says to his *shaliach*, "*Tze ve-kadesh li isha stam*" — go out and marry any woman for me, whoever says yes first — and the *shaliach* departs but never returns with any report, then the man who sent him is forbidden to marry any woman in the entire world.

The reasoning proceeds in two steps. First, there is a presumption — *chazaka shaliach oseh shelichuto* — that an agent carries out his mission. We therefore assume the *shaliach* did in fact betroth someone. Second, since the man gave no specification as to which woman the *shaliach* should approach, he has no idea who his *shaliach* married on his behalf. Any woman he might now wish to marry could be a sister, mother, or daughter of the woman who is already, unknowingly, his wife. He is therefore forbidden to everyone.

This ruling calls to mind, in a somewhat whimsical vein, the *vort* that *Lavan* sought to destroy everything (*bi-kesh Lavan avinu la-akor et hakol*) — for if *Avraham*'s servant had married a woman without specification and never returned, *Yitzchak* would have been unable to marry anyone, since every woman in the world might be a relative of that unknown wife. The joke collapses, of course, since *Avraham* did in fact give *Eliezer* specificity — "*lo sikach isha livni mibnos Kena'ani*" — but the *gemara* here serves as its basis.

### Tosafot Fine

Tosafot immediately raises an obvious difficulty: if this man is forbidden to every woman because any one of them might be his wife's sister or mother, then by the same logic, how can any man in the entire world marry any woman? Perhaps the woman he wishes to marry is the very woman the *shaliach* betrothed?

Tosafot resolves this by invoking the position of Rabbeinu Tam that women are believed when they testify that they were not the ones who accepted *kiddushin*. So any adult woman can simply testify on her own behalf. But this does not help with *ketanot* — minor girls who would not know whether their father accepted *kiddushin* on their behalf. How, then, can anyone marry a minor?

Tosafot answers that on a *d'Oraita* level, the man can actually marry any woman. We follow the majority — *azlinan batar ruba* — since most women are not relatives of the woman the *shaliach* married. The prohibition on the man himself is not a genuine *issur* but rather a *knas b'alma* — a fine — imposed upon him for having sent a *shaliach* with no specification at all, handing him a blank check without identifying even a general pool of eligible women. Other people in the world are not subject to this fine; it is targeted solely at the one who acted irresponsibly.

### Kavua Principle

Tosafot presses further: even granting the majority principle, why should this not constitute a *kavua* situation and therefore trigger a fifty-fifty *safek* rather than a lenient *rov*? The principle *kol kavua k'mechtza al mechtza dami* holds that when a forbidden thing occupies a fixed place, we cannot simply dissolve it into percentage probabilities; we must treat it as an even doubt.

The classic illustration: if one finds a piece of meat on the ground and does not know which butcher shop it came from, and the majority of shops in the neighborhood sell kosher meat, one may follow the majority and assume it is kosher — *kol d'parish meruba parish*, what has separated itself has separated from the majority. But if one walked into a store, purchased meat, and later cannot remember which store one entered, the analysis changes. One is not simply asking about the identity of the meat in the abstract; one is asking which specific store — each standing in its fixed place — one walked into. Since each store is concrete and recognizable, not dissolved into an abstract mixture, we treat the question as fifty-fifty.

The logic is difficult to articulate precisely, and the *gemara* cites a *pasuk* as its basis. One way to approach it: when the forbidden option has a fixed, concrete identity that stands before you, you cannot simply think away from it by invoking percentages. It is not lost in a mixture. The forbidden store is right there; you cannot pretend it is only abstractly possible.

Tosafot raises the question of whether the women in this case should constitute *kavua* — the *shaliach* went to wherever the woman was, she was in her home, that is a fixed place, analogous to the store he entered. Why should we not apply *kavua* and treat every woman as a fifty-fifty doubt?

Tosafot's answer is that *kavua* applies only when the forbidden thing is distinctly recognizable as itself — *nikkar l'atzmo* — and the permitted thing is equally recognizable as itself. You know which store sells *treif*, you know which sells *kosher*; you simply do not know which one you entered. That is the scenario where you cannot ignore the concrete possibility. But in the case of the woman, it is not that you have a woman standing before you whom you know to be your wife's sister but are unsure whether you entered "that house." It is simply a question of identity in the abstract: you do not know who the *shaliach* married, and you do not know whether this woman has any relationship to that unknown person. That is closer in structure to finding meat on the floor — a question of abstract identity — not to walking into a fixed store. *Kavua*, therefore, does not apply.

## Reish Lakish Challenge

### Bird Pairs Lost

Reish Lakish poses a challenge to Rabbi Yochanan from a related domain. There is a category of *korban* — brought by a woman who has given birth, a *zavah*, or a *zav* — that consists of a pair of birds, one to serve as a *chatas* and one as an *olah*. One may purchase these as a unit, a *kan*, and both birds are immediately sanctified, but their respective identities — which is the *chatas* and which the *olah* — remain unspecified until a later point. This is called a *kan stuma*, an unexplicated pair.

If one bird from a *kan stuma* flies away, or flies into a group of birds that must be put down and is lost among them, or dies, the remaining bird can simply be paired with a new replacement, since no identity has yet been fixed. This is the advantage of the *stuma* arrangement. Had the pair been explicit — *kan meforeshas* — the loss of one bird would have been far more problematic, since one would not know whether the *chatas* or the *olah* had been lost.

The challenge Reish Lakish raises concerns all the *kinim* in the world. One of these birds has flown somewhere out there, carrying a sanctity — an unresolved *kedushat korban* — as it wanders. How can anyone ever bring a bird as a *korban* again? Any bird one now brings might be that escaped bird, already designated for someone else's *korban*. The parallel to Rabbi Yochanan's ruling is exact: just as any woman might be the *shaliach*'s unknown wife, any bird might be the escaped *korban* bird.

Tosafot notes that this challenge is not simply about other people. Even the person who lost the bird faces the question: when he goes to bring a new *korban* using birds, how does he know that none of these birds is his own escaped one?

### Fixed Places

Rabbi Yochanan's response draws precisely the distinction Tosafot had articulated. *Kamina ana isha d'lo nayda* — I am speaking of a woman, who does not simply fly off. People have fixed places; they live somewhere, they can be found. Even if a woman goes to the marketplace, *hadar lenichusa* — she returns home. Women are therefore more analogous to the stores standing in their fixed places than to things dissolved into an anonymous mixture.

Birds, by contrast, are fundamentally mobile. A bird that has flown out into the world is genuinely lost in the mass of birds everywhere. That is a question of abstract identity — like the piece of meat found on the floor — and for such cases one simply follows the majority. There is no *kavua* concern because there is no fixed place.

### Recognizable Forbidden

Following on from Rabbi Yochanan's response, the *gemara* cites Rava, who clarifies the limits of the position. Rabbi Yochanan concedes that if the woman one wishes to marry has no living relatives whatsoever — no daughter, granddaughter, mother, grandmother, or sister — one may marry her even under the shadow of the unknown *shaliach* marriage, since there is no relative whose identity could create a problem.

The more striking ruling is this: even if the woman did have a sister — and that sister was married to another man at the time the *shaliach* was appointed — one may marry this woman. The reasoning is *d'ba'ei sha'ata d'kamar lei havah nasuy l'gavrei*: at the moment the *shaliach* was appointed, the sister was already married to someone else. She was, at that moment, unavailable. And the principle is *ki mashvi shaliach bemilta d'kaima kamei* — one only empowers a *shaliach* in matters that stand before one as currently available options. *Bemilta d'lo kaima kamei lo mashvi shaliach* — for things not currently available, one simply does not grant the *shaliach* power.

This is a striking and counterintuitive *halacha*. The implication is that even if the sister subsequently became divorced — after the *shaliach* was appointed but before he carried out the marriage — and even if the *shaliach* then married her, it would not be binding, because he was never empowered to take that action. His authority was fixed at the moment of appointment, limited to what was then accessible. The *gemara* will develop the implications of this principle.

## Agent Empowerment

### Sister Divorced Later

The rule that a *shaliach* is empowered only in currently available matters now connects directly to the *mishnah*. But before reaching that connection, the *gemara* pauses to clarify what the underlying principle actually is.

The case in question: I sent a *shaliach* to marry a woman for me. This woman has a sister who, at the time I appointed him, was married. Subsequently — sometime during the year I have not heard from the *shaliach* — the sister gets divorced. Can I now marry this sister?

The answer is yes, and the reason is that the *shaliach* was never empowered to marry the sister in the first place, because she was unavailable at the time of appointment. Since she could not have been the woman he married on my behalf, she poses no danger of being my wife or my wife's sister. I may therefore marry her freely.

The scenario that creates the genuine difficulty is the following: the *shaliach* departs, the sister subsequently gets divorced, and the *shaliach* — now encountering the sister in her state of availability — goes ahead and betroths her. Why should this not be binding? He is marrying a perfectly available woman, on behalf of a man who has authorized him to marry anyone.

### Thought vs. Power

One might understand the limitation as a matter of *da'at* — the man's intention at the time of appointment. When he sent the *shaliach*, he was only thinking about women who were then available; the sister simply was not in his mind. This reading suggests the limitation is cognitive: if he had explicitly said "and for any woman who becomes available later," it would work.

But the *gemara* moves toward a different and more fundamental understanding: this is not merely a question of what was in the man's mind. It is a structural limitation on the power of *shelichut* itself.

### Current Availability

The *gemara* articulates the principle explicitly: *lo mashvei inish shaliach ela bemidi demati avid hashta* — a person can only empower a *shaliach* in something that he himself is currently capable of doing. *Bemidi delo mati avid lei hashta, lo mashvei* — for something outside his current capability, he simply cannot grant the power of agency.

This is a remarkable limitation. It seems to say that the scope of *shelichut* is not merely what one intends or instructs, but is bounded by what one could actually have executed at the moment of appointment. If I cannot do a given act right now — even though I will be able to do it later, and even though by the time the *shaliach* acts the situation will have changed — I never succeeded in granting the *shaliach* that power in the first place.

### Future Nazirite

The connection to the *mishnah* now becomes clear. The *gemara* asks: *bishlama batra* — it is understandable that the second man's vow to care for a *nazir*'s *korbanot* can include the first man, who was already a *nazir* when the second man made his declaration. *Ela kamai* — but what about the first man? When he declared that he would take care of a *nazir*'s *korbanot*, the second man had not yet become a *nazir*. How can his vow cover someone who did not yet exist as a *nazir*?

The *gemara* resolves this by reading the vow's intent: *im eshkachna dehavi nazir* — what the man meant was, whoever I find to be a *nazir* when the time comes for me to fulfill my vow. He is not committing to care for a specific, currently existing *nazir*; he is committing to care for whoever will be a *nazir* at the relevant time. This reading suggests that one's commitments naturally extend to future contingencies.

By the same logic, one might argue that when I send a *shaliach* to marry a woman, I implicitly mean: whoever is available when you get around to it, including women who become available after I send you. *Im eshkachna demigaresha* — if you find a woman who has since been divorced, go ahead and marry her for me.

But the *gemara* rejects this: *lo mashvei inish shaliach ela bemidi demati avid hashta*. Even if this is within my *da'at* — even if this is what I intended — the structural rule of *shelichut* prevents it. I cannot grant power for something I could not have done at the moment of appointment. The *mishnah* case works for a different reason: the man is not appointing a *shaliach* at all. He is making a personal vow about his own future action, and personal vows can certainly be directed at future contingencies. The limit applies to *shelichut*, not to personal undertakings.

## Vow Annulment

### Guardian Annuls

The discussion of *shelichut* and current availability raises a further question, tested against a case from the laws of vow annulment. If a man, about to depart on a journey, tells his *epitropos* — his estate manager, the one who holds his power of attorney — to annul any vow his wife makes during his absence, and the *epitropos* does indeed annul such vows upon hearing them, can those annulments stand?

### Yoshiya vs. Yonatan

Rabbi Yoshiya says no. He derives this from the verse *isha yekimenu v'isha yiferenu* — the husband himself must confirm or annul; there is a specific textual requirement that the husband perform this act personally. An agent cannot substitute for the husband here.

Rabbi Yonatan disagrees: *matzinu bechol makom she-shlucho shel adam kemoto* — we find everywhere that one's agent is as oneself. The one place in the *mishnah* where this principle is stated explicitly is in the context of a *shaliach tzibur* for *Shemoneh Esrei*, as cited in Berachot 34b. Why should the principle not apply here as well?

### Verse Obstacle

The *gemara* now uses this debate to test the principle of *shelichut* and current availability. The husband who appoints the *epitropos* cannot himself annul his wife's future vows at the moment of appointment, because those vows do not yet exist. The question is whether this constitutes an argument against appointing the *epitropos* at all.

The *gemara* reasons: if we assume that the husband himself is incapable of pre-annulling vows — that is, if we follow the *chachamim* who say in a related context that *lo matzi mefer* — then the very act of appointing an *epitropos* is a case of empowering a *shaliach* for something one cannot currently do. And yet Rabbi Yonatan says it works. This seems to directly contradict the principle that one can only empower a *shaliach* in currently available matters.

The *gemara* resolves this by suggesting that perhaps both Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan are operating according to the view of Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that a husband *can* pre-annul his wife's future vows. Under Rabbi Eliezer's view, there is no contradiction: the husband already has the current capability to annul future vows himself, and he therefore has the full power to delegate that capability to an *epitropos*. The reason he is appointing an *epitropos* rather than simply pre-annulling the vows himself is not inability but practicality — he might forget when he returns, or he might be angry, or distracted, and the annulment window will close.

### Pre-annul Question

But this only pushes the question back: if Rabbi Eliezer's position allows the husband to pre-annul his wife's vows right now, why bother with the *epitropos* at all? Just do it yourself before you leave.

Tosafot addresses this. Looking at the *tosafot* discussion of *dilma mishtalyana*, he explains that a husband who pre-annuls his wife's vows explicitly — saying to her directly, "any vow you make while I am away, I hereby void" — creates a confrontation. *Tipul ketata beineihem*: it leads to a fight. It is disempowering to a wife to be told before any vow is even made that her vows mean nothing. But if the *epitropos* handles it quietly in the husband's absence, reacting to each vow as it arises, the wife's dignity is preserved and a direct confrontation is avoided. The husband prefers not to raise the issue at home before he leaves — and certainly not face-to-face — which is precisely why he makes the arrangement quietly with the *epitropos*.

The *gemara*'s own answer to this question is somewhat unsatisfying, and Tosafot's response fills the gap. In any case, the *gemara*'s conclusion is that the limitation on *shelichut* — that one can only empower an agent in currently available matters — remains intact. The *epitropos* case does not contradict it, because under Rabbi Eliezer, the husband does have current capability.

## Half Nazirite

### Two Men Half

The *gemara* now returns to the *mishnah* at hand. The next *mishnah* presents the following case: one man says *harei alai legaleiach chatzi nazir* — I accept upon myself to shave half a *nazir*, meaning to bring the *korbanot* for half a *nazir*. Another man hears and says the same thing.

### Meir vs. Sages

Rabbi Meir says: each of them is obligated to bring a full set of *korbanot* for a *nazir shaleim*. The *chachamim* say: each is only obligated to bring half.

Tosafot notes that the second man is structurally superfluous to the core debate; the real question is simply what the phrase *alai legaleiach chatzi nazir* means for a single individual. The *mishnah* introduces two men only to parallel the structure of the previous *mishnah*.

### Grammar of Half

Rava clarifies the terms of the dispute. Everyone would agree on the following: if one explicitly says *chatzi korbanot nazir alai* — half of the *korbanot* of a *nazir* I accept upon myself — one brings half the *korbanot*. The word *chatzi* is clearly modifying *korbanot*, and half an offering is what one owes.

Conversely, if one says *korbanot chatzi nazir alai* — the *korbanot* of a half-*nazir* I accept upon myself — one brings a full set of *korbanot*. Why? Because *d'ha lo askan nezirut le-palga* — there is no such thing as a half-*nazir*. A person who is half a *nazir* is simply a *nazir*. "Half a *nazir*" is simply a *nazir*, and whoever is such a person has a full complement of *korbanot*. When one says *chatzi nazir*, the word *chatzi* attaches to the person, and that person's *korbanot* are full.

The dispute in the *mishnah* concerns the language *alai legaleiach chatzi nazir*, which reads as though *chatzi* is modifying *nazir* — in which case, following the above logic, one would owe a full *korban*. This is, on its face, Rabbi Meir's position. What requires explanation is why the *chachamim* read this differently.

Rabbi Meir's reasoning: *keivan de'amar harei alai*, once one has said *harei alai*, one has obligated oneself in the full *korbanot* of *nezirut*. When one then says *chatzi nazir*, that addition is simply vacuous — *lav kol kemeineih* — it cannot undo what *harei alai* already established.

The *chachamim*'s reasoning: *neder u-fetach imo hu* — there is a vow and its opening together. The latter part of the phrase explains and limits the earlier part. The entire declaration must be read as a unit, with the end clarifying the scope of the beginning.

### Tosafot Grammar

What remains puzzling is why, if the phrase *alai legaleiach chatzi nazir* looks structurally parallel to *korbanot chatzi nazir*, it should produce a different result for the *chachamim*. In both cases, *chatzi* seems to be modifying the word *nazir*, which should yield a full *korban*.

Tosafot grapples with this. The conclusion Tosafot reaches is that the presence of the word *alai* up front, before *legaleiach*, makes a structural difference. When one says *harei alai legaleiach chatzi nazir*, the *alai* — the acceptance of obligation — comes first, and then *chatzi* follows. According to the *chachamim*, *chatzi* is thus understood as modifying the *alai*, the scope of what one is accepting: I am accepting upon myself half of the obligations involved. This is equivalent in import to saying *chatzi korbanot nazir alai*, with *chatzi* clearly modifying the quantum of obligation rather than the identity of the *nazir*.

It must be admitted that this distinction is subtle, and the grammatical argument does not yield itself to clean exposition. The fundamental point, however, is that the debate turns on whether the word *chatzi* in this construction limits the person — a half-*nazir*, who is a full *nazir* — or limits the obligation — half the *korbanot* of a *nazir*.

## Conditional Birth

### Vow Upon Birth

The final *mishnah* of the daf introduces a new type of conditional *nazir* vow. A man declares: *hareini nazir liksheyihyeh li ben* — I will be a *nazir* when I have a son. If a son is subsequently born to him, he becomes a *nazir*.

### Tumtum Question

What if the child born is a daughter, or a *tumtum* — a child whose genitalia are covered, making the sex indeterminate — or an *androgynos*, a child with both male and female genitalia? In all these cases, *eino nazir* — he is not a *nazir*. The vow specified a *ben*, a definite male child. Even a *tumtum*, who represents a *safek* as to sex, does not satisfy the condition, because when one says *ben* one means a certain, unambiguous male.

If, however, the man had said *kesheyihyeh li valad* — when I have a child — then even a daughter, a *tumtum*, or an *androgynos* triggers the *nezirus*, since the word *valad* encompasses all offspring.

If his wife miscarried, *eino nazir* — he is not a *nazir*, because the vow specified *nolad*, the child being born. A miscarriage does not satisfy *nolad*.

### Doubtful Status

Rabbi Shimon, however, takes a different position. He holds that if the fetus miscarried but might have been viable — *ben kayama* — and might have been male, then the man is in a state of *safek nezirus*. Rabbi Shimon's reasoning is twofold: first, he considers a miscarriage of a potentially viable fetus to qualify as *leidah* for the purposes of this vow; second, he treats even a *safek* outcome as sufficient to create a *safek* vow obligation.

Being a *safek nazir* is a deeply problematic position. One must observe *nezirus* because one might be a *nazir*, but one cannot bring the concluding *korbanot* because one might not be a *nazir* at all. The situation is entirely unresolvable.

Rabbi Shimon therefore prescribes a declaration to escape the bind. The man should say: if the first child was a viable male — *im haya ben kayama* — then *harei ani nazir hova*, I am now completing the obligatory *nezirus* already triggered. And if it was not — *ve-im lav* — then *harei ani nazir nedava*, I am now taking on *nezirus* as a voluntary act. By this formula, the man commits himself either way to observing *nezirus* and may bring his *korbanot*, since regardless of which scenario obtains, he is now definitively a *nazir* under one heading or the other.

### Second Child

If the wife then gives birth a second time — a viable child — the *chachamim*'s analysis is straightforward: the second birth is what triggers the *nezirus*, and *harei zeh nazir* — he is a *nazir*.

For Rabbi Shimon, however, the situation is more layered. Since the first child already placed the man in a state of *safek nezirus*, the second child now creates a new *safek*: perhaps the first child was the triggering event, in which case the *nezirus* has already been completed (or is in process), and the second child is irrelevant. Or perhaps the first was not triggering, and the second is the true trigger — creating yet another *safek nezirus*.

Rabbi Shimon again prescribes a two-part declaration. The man should say: if the first child was viable, *harishon hova* — the first period of *nezirus* I am now completing was the obligatory one, and *vezu nedava* — the *nezirus* I now take on for the second child is voluntary. If the first was not viable, *harishon nedava* — the first period was voluntary, and *vezu hova* — this one, for the second child, is the obligatory fulfillment of my vow.

---

---

# Nazir 13

## Conditional Nezirut

### Opening Review

Today's daf is 13. We begin by revisiting the *mishnah* at the bottom of 12b, which was briefly introduced at the close of the previous session but requires a full reading before proceeding to the *gemara*.

### Son/Daughter Status

The *mishnah* opens: *hareini nazir l'khsheyihyeh li ven* — "I will be a *nazir* if I have a son." If a son is indeed born, *harey zeh nazir* — he becomes a *nazir*. But what if the child born is a daughter, a *tumtum*, or an *androgynous*? A *tumtum* is a person whose genitalia is concealed, so one cannot determine whether the child is male or female. An *androgynous* child possesses both sets of genitalia, raising its own *halachic* classification questions. In all such cases, the *mishnah* rules *eino nazir* — he does not become a *nazir*.

The implied *chiddush* here is that when a man vows *nezirut* contingent on having a *ben*, a *tumtum* does not suffice to trigger the vow even as a *safek*, because *ben* is understood to mean a definite son. If, however, he had said *l'khsheyihyeh li vlad* — "when I have a child" — then even if the child born is a daughter, a *tumtum*, or an *androgynous*, he becomes a *nazir*, since he used the more inclusive term.

### Miscarriage Case

The *mishnah* continues: *hipilah ishto eino nazir* — if his wife miscarried, he is not a *nazir*. The underlying assumption of the *mishnah* appears to be that if the miscarried child had been considered viable — *kalu lo chadashav*, having reached full term — it would in principle fall within the category of *vlad* and potentially trigger the vow. Nonetheless, the *tanna kamma* rules that the person is not a *nazir*, and the *gemara* will explain why.

There is an important distinction worth noting here between a *nefel* — a miscarriage of a non-viable fetus — and what might be termed *nolad met*, a stillbirth of a child that had been viable until the moment of death. The *mishnah* uses the term *hipilah* precisely because the status of the child is uncertain, and that uncertainty is what drives the *halachic* discussion that follows.

### Tanna Kamma vs R. Shimon

The position of the *tanna kamma* is identified by the *gemara* as that of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds *lo nachis inish nafshai l'safeka* — a person who makes a conditional vow does not intend to be bound when the condition is in doubt. The reasoning is that being a *safek nazir* is worse than being a *vadai nazir*: you must observe all the restrictions of *nezirut* but have no means of ending it, since you cannot bring the *korbanot* of a *nazir* without certainty that you are one. Rabbi Yehuda therefore concludes that the person intends his vow to take effect only if the condition is definitely fulfilled. Since there is doubt whether the miscarried child was viable, the vow does not take effect at all.

Rabbi Shimon disagrees and holds that the person is indeed a *safek nazir* and must grapple with that status.

### Safek to Vadai

Rabbi Shimon provides a practical resolution. The *mishnah* states: *yomar* — the person should declare — *im hayah ben kayama, hareini nazir chovah* — "if that child was viable, I am a *nazir* by virtue of my original vow." *V'im lav, hareini nazir nedavah* — "and if it was not viable, I now accept *nezirut* as a freewill gift." By conditioning the current *nezirut* on both possibilities, the person transforms himself from a *safek nazir* into a *vadai nazir* in either case. He can then complete his *nezirut*, bring his *korbanot*, and be done.

### Second Child Born

The *mishnah* then addresses the scenario where *chazrah v'yaldah* — his wife subsequently gives birth to a living child. According to the *tanna kamma*, the first miscarriage did not satisfy the condition, so this birth does. The person is unambiguously a *nazir*.

According to Rabbi Shimon, however, the situation is once again uncertain. It is possible that the first child was viable and the first *nezirut* was obligatory, making the current birth trigger only a new freewill consideration. Or the first child was not viable, in which case the first *nezirut* was freewill, and now the obligatory *nezirut* has been triggered. Rabbi Shimon applies the same resolution: *yomar, im harishon ben kayama, harishon chovah v'zo nedavah* — "if the first was viable, my first *nezirut* was obligatory and this new one I accept as freewill." *V'im lav, harishon nedavah v'zo chovah* — "if the first was not viable, my first was freewill and this one is my obligatory *nezirut*." For each ambiguous birth, the person resolves *safek nezirut* into *vadai nezirut* through conditional declaration.

---

## Gemara Analysis

### Initial Question

The *gemara* opens with *hai mai l'memra* — what is the point? The opening clause of the *mishnah* — that one who vows *nezirut* contingent on having a son, and has a son, becomes a *nazir* — seems self-evident. The *gemara* answers that the *chiddush* lies in the subsequent clause.

### Ben vs Child

The *gemara* first addresses why it was necessary to state the case of *ben*. Perhaps, the *gemara* suggests, one might have thought that *ben* is not strictly "son" but rather derives from the root *l'hibanot*, meaning "to be built" — and thus *ben* functions as a generic term for child. The *mishnah* therefore teaches *kamashma lan d'lo* — we do not interpret it that way. *Ben* means son.

The answer is admittedly not fully satisfying. There are many other words in biblical Hebrew that function as generic terms for offspring. The more interesting *chiddush*, one might argue, concerns the *tumtum*: a *tumtum* is a *safek* — either a son or daughter — so why does the presence of a *tumtum* not trigger even a *safek* obligation? Moreover, what happens if some time later the membrane covering the *tumtum*'s genitalia is removed and the child is discovered to be male — does one retroactively become a *nazir*? The *gemara* does not pursue this line of inquiry, but it is a striking question.

### Tumtum Problem

The *gemara* similarly questions the *chiddush* of the *vlad* case. If he said "when I have a child," it seems obvious that even a daughter, *tumtum*, or *androgynous* would qualify. The *gemara* responds that one might have thought *vlad d'michshav beinei inshi ba'inan* — that "child" means a child considered significant in the eyes of people, which is to say, a son. Society's historical preference for male children is the subtext of the *gemara*'s observation. The *mishnah* therefore teaches that we take his words literally: he said *vlad*, and any child qualifies.

The *gemara* then turns to the *chiddush* of the miscarriage case, which is identified as the real crux of the *mishnah*. The question of who holds this position leads the *gemara* to identify the *tanna kamma* as Rabbi Yehuda, based on an earlier ruling involving a conditional vow about a threshing floor. The principle is the same: *lo nachis inish nafshai l'safeka* — one who makes a conditional vow intends certainty, not doubt.

### Retroactive Viability

With this framework established, the *gemara* considers whether and how the birth of a subsequent child might retroactively resolve the doubtful status of a previously miscarried child.

### Animal Sanctification

*Ba'i minei Rav Abba mi'Rav Huna* — Rav Abba posed a question to Rav Huna. The case: a man says *hareini nazir l'khsheyihyeh li ven* — "I will be a *nazir* if I have a son" — and his wife miscarried. Operating under Rabbi Yehuda's principle, he is definitively not a *nazir*. Nonetheless, he separated out an animal as a *korban*. His wife then gives birth to a living child. The question is: was he a *nazir* from the time of the first child, and is the animal already sanctified?

The *nafka mina* is practical: if one were to use the animal for shearing or labor — *legizato ul'avoda bo* — would one be in violation of *me'ilah*? If the animal was sanctified when he set it aside, it is *asur*; if not, it is permitted.

The *gemara* immediately clarifies: according to Rabbi Shimon, there is no question. From the moment of the miscarriage, the man was already a *safek nazir* under Rabbi Shimon's ruling. The interesting question arises specifically according to Rabbi Yehuda, who would normally have said the person is not a *nazir* at all. Does the subsequent birth of a living child retroactively establish that the miscarried child was in fact *ben kayama* — viable — and that the man was therefore a *nazir* from the earlier point?

The *gemara* is probing a nuanced middle position: perhaps the evidence supplied by the second living child is sufficient to move Rabbi Yehuda from his default position of non-obligation. It might not render the man a *vadai nazir* from that earlier moment — which could make him *chayav me'ila* — but perhaps enough to impose some form of obligation. The *gemara* asks: *kadosh o lo kadosh* — is the animal sanctified or not? The *gemara* concludes *teiku* — the question is left unresolved.

### Twin Viability

The question of whether the birth of the second child can retroactively establish the viability of the first is complicated by a further consideration. *Tosafot* observes that the *gemara*'s implicit assumption — that the second child's viability would prove the first's — may not be warranted. The key variable is whether these are identical or fraternal twins.

If the twins are identical, they derive from the same fertilized egg split in two, and they are biologically the same age. In that case, the viability of the second child would indeed establish that the first was also viable. If, however, they are fraternal twins, two separate eggs may have been fertilized at different times — perhaps one egg fertilized on the first day after intercourse and another on the third. This could mean that the twins differ by as much as two days in gestational age, which in turn could place one at the threshold of viability and the other just below it.

*Tosafot* makes this explicit, citing the language *deshema miktzat hatipah nikletah miyad umiktzat hatipah hashniyah lo nikletah ad achar shney yamim* — that perhaps part of the semen was absorbed immediately and part only two days later. If that is the case, then the twin born alive may actually have been conceived slightly earlier, and the one who was miscarried, though appearing to be the same age, was in fact two days younger and had not yet crossed the threshold of *ben kayama*. This explains why the *gemara* leaves the question unresolved as *teiku*, rather than simply concluding that the second birth settles the matter.

---

## Two Nezirut Declarations

### And Me Question

*Ba'i minei Ben Rechumi me'Abaye* — Ben Rechumi posed a question to Abaye. The case: a man declares *hareini nazir l'khsheyihyeh li ven* — "I will be a *nazir* when I have a son" — and a companion overhears him and says *ve'alai* — "and upon me." What does this mean? Is the companion saying he will be a *nazir* when he himself has a son, or when the original speaker has a son?

### Alai vs Ani

The *gemara* proceeds to a parallel case. What if rather than saying *ve'alai*, the companion says *va'ani* — "and I"? At first glance, both seem to convey the same meaning. Yet the *gemara* probes whether *va'ani* might carry a different intent. One possibility is *anfshah ka'amar* — he is speaking about himself, meaning "and when I have a son, I too will be a *nazir*." The other possibility is *ve'rachimna lach kvatich* — "and I care for you as I care for it," expressing not a personal vow inspired by the other's example, but rather an expression of solidarity with the speaker. In this reading, *va'ani* means: "Because of my bond with you, if you have a son, I too will be a *nazir*."

The distinction between *alai* and *ani* is subtle. *Alai* — "upon me" — places the obligation directly on oneself, stepping away, so to speak, from the original speaker. *Ani* — "and I" — may instead be oriented toward the relationship: "I am with you in this," suggesting that the *nezirut* is conditioned on the original speaker's son rather than one's own.

An alternative version of the text, noted in the margin (*samech alef*, denoting *sfarim acherim*), has the original vow formulated as *l'khsheyihyeh lecha ven* — "when you have a son" — making the question even more pointed. If Michael says "I will be a *nazir* when you have a son" and Dov says "and me," does "and me" follow Michael's formulation (conditioned on Michael's son) or does the principle of *adam karov eitzel atzmo* — one is closest to oneself — pull the declaration toward Dov's own son?

### Ksifa Interpretation

The *gemara* then introduces the concept of *ksifa lei milta* — embarrassment in another's presence — as a factor shaping intent. *Tosafot*'s reading is as follows: when the companion says *va'ani* in the presence of the original speaker, there is a social pressure not to appear indifferent to the other's situation. Accordingly, *va'ani* in the presence of the speaker would naturally be understood as "and I am here for you — if you have a son, I too will be a *nazir*," because to say "and I, when I have a son" in that moment would be to ignore the person standing before you. The embarrassment of appearing self-focused in front of someone who has just expressed so much significance to having a son pulls the declaration toward the other person's condition.

### Third Party Case

The *gemara* then raises the case of a third party: *amar hareini nazir l'khsheyihyeh l'ploni ven* — Michael says "I will be a *nazir* if Charlie has a son." Charlie is not present. If Dov then says *va'ani*, there is no direct social pressure to express loyalty to Charlie, since Charlie is not in the room.

### Loyalty Motivation

The question is whether the dynamic of loyalty still operates indirectly. Even though Charlie is absent, Dov has witnessed Michael's deep commitment to Charlie's welfare — so much so that Michael is prepared to accept *nezirut* on Charlie's behalf. Dov may therefore feel a pull not of loyalty to Charlie, but of loyalty to Michael. The reasoning would be: Michael, I see how much you care for Charlie. Because I care for you, I will also be a *nazir* if Charlie has a son.

This analysis reveals two distinct psychological models at work in these declarations. In the first model, someone observes a *nazir* or hears a vow and says "me too" — inspired by the idea and adopting it for themselves. In the second model, the "me too" is not about inspiration but about solidarity — not "you gave me a good idea" but "I am with you in this." The two models yield different *halachic* conclusions about whether the companion's vow is conditioned on his own child or on the original speaker's. The *gemara* leaves this as *tiku* — unresolved.

---

## Immediate/Delayed Start

### Two Nezirut Setup

The next *mishnah* presents the following case: *hareini nazir v'nazir k'sheyihyeh li ven* — "I will be a *nazir* [starting now] and a *nazir* when I have a son." The *mishnah* is working through the interaction between a *nezirut* that begins immediately and one conditioned on a future event.

### Order Problem

The subtlety lies in the order of the declarations. When the man says "and a *nazir*" without specifying a future time, even though it was his second statement, it is understood to take effect immediately. What he has in effect said is: my second *nezirut* begins now, and my first *nezirut* — the one conditioned on having a son — will begin when the condition is met.

This creates an unusual inversion: the person is currently practicing his *second* *nezirut* while his *first* *nezirut* has not yet taken effect. When his son is born and the first *nezirut* comes due, it preempts the second: *maniach et shelo u'moneh shel beno* — he sets aside his own ongoing *nezirut* and counts the thirty days of the son-*nezirut*. Then, *achar kach mashlim et shelo* — he completes the remaining days of his own *nezirut*.

### No Shaving

The *mishnah*'s use of the word *mashlim* — completing or making up — carries an important implication. *Tosafot* makes explicit what the *mishnah* leaves implicit: it is impossible that the man would have shaved at the conclusion of the son-*nezirut* before completing his own, because the remaining days of his own *nezirut* would then be fewer than thirty. The requirement of *giddel pera* — the growth of hair for the requisite period — means that one cannot validly conclude a *nezirut* without at least thirty days of uninterrupted hair growth since the last shaving. Accordingly, there is no shaving between the two periods; the man does a straight continuous run and brings his *korbanot* only at the end.

This yields a significant practical consequence: because of the unusual order in which these *neziruyot* took effect, the man avoids bringing two separate sets of *korbanot*. Normally, two accepted *neziruyot* require the first to conclude — with shaving and *korbanot* — before the second begins. Here, because the second was already underway before the first came due, the first is entitled to preempt the second without requiring the second to formally conclude first. And since the second was never formally concluded, it does not need to restart from scratch — only the remaining days need to be completed.

### Hundred Days

To appreciate the full scope of the issue, it is helpful to look ahead to the *mishnah* on 15a, which presents a variant: *hareini nazir l'khsheyihyeh li ven v'nazir mei'hayom* — "I will be a *nazir* when I have a son and a *nazir* starting now for a hundred days." Here the immediately-effective *nezirut* is one of a hundred days rather than the standard thirty.
