Tosafot raises the question of why the subject does not simply admit the vow by his silence when the first pair testifies, given the principle of *shtika kehoda'ah* — silence as admission. Tosafot resolves this with two possible scenarios: either the subject actively denies everything, or both pairs came before the *beit din* simultaneously, in which case the internal contradiction between them means the subject has no reason to respond.

There is also a question about intention: since so much of the law of *nedarim* and *nezirut* concerns the alignment of *piv velibo* — one's words and one's heart — one might wonder whether a *beit din* may compel *nezirut* based on testimony if the subject claims he did not mean the words. The *Gemara* does not address this directly, but the implicit logic of the *Mishnah* seems to be that once witnesses have testified to the words and there is no overriding context that would redefine them, the external court proceeds on the basis of the statement as made.

### Rabbi Yishmael

The *Gemara* notes that the *Mishnah*'s framing of the dispute — as between two competing pairs of witnesses — is not universally accepted. A *baraita* in the name of Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka states that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not actually disagree in the case of two separate pairs of witnesses. In that case, everyone would agree with the principle of *yesh bichlal chamesh shtayim* — the overlap is clear enough, and the *nazir* must observe two periods. The genuine dispute, Rabbi Yishmael argues, concerned a single pair of witnesses whose members contradict each other internally — one witness says two years and the other witness says five years.

In that scenario, Beit Shammai says *nechleka ha'edut* — the testimony is divided, and a pair whose members cannot agree on what they witnessed cannot stand as valid *edut*. Beit Hillel says even here *yesh bichlal chamesh shtayim* applies: the witness who says five implicitly includes the claim of two, so the two witnesses share common ground on the two-year period and combine to form valid testimony for that duration.

This reframing is illuminating. In the case of two separate pairs, the intuitive force of the overlap argument is relatively strong: it is hard to say that a pair testifying to five years *contradicts* a pair testifying to two, since five is simply a larger claim. The disagreement is about whether two pairs saying different things can generate a combined testimony — a higher standard, but not an inherently unreasonable one. In the case of a single internally divided pair, however, the question is sharper: to what extent can two witnesses who disagree with each other be said to be testifying to the same thing and thus join to create unified *edut*? That is where the real debate lies, and Rabbi Yishmael's *baraita* locates the dispute there.

### Discrete Units

Rav introduces an important qualification: *hakol modim b'moneh* — everyone agrees in the case where the witnesses are counting discrete units. If the first pair testified that the subject said "I will be a *nazir* one time and two times," and the second pair testified that he said "three times, four times, and five times," there is no genuine contradiction between them, and everyone would agree that the testimonies combine. The distinction turns on how the *nezirut* is described. When the subject is reported to have declared a single block — "two years" or "five years" — the two testimonies describe conceptually different units, and the question of overlap is genuinely contested. When the subject is reported to have declared individual discrete units one by one, the testimonies address individual instances and can be seen to agree on the specific units each covers.

Tosafot explicates the case of *moneh* as follows: the first pair said he declared one time and two times; the second pair said he declared three times, four times, and five times. Alternatively, one could construct the case so that the overlap is even more literal — the first pair reports one and two, the second reports one through five — but either way, when the claims are atomized into individual units, the logic of combination is considerably more intuitive than when they are expressed as aggregates.

The *Gemara*'s exchange between Rav Chama and Rav Chisda clarifies the precise scope of the *moneh* principle. If one witness says five and explicitly not two — that is, he positively excludes the lower number — then the testimonies actively contradict each other and cannot combine. The *moneh* principle applies only where the witnesses enumerate units sequentially and no such exclusion is implied.

---

## Va'ani Declarations

### Cascading Status

The next chapter opens with a *Mishnah* presenting the case of cascading *nezirut* declarations. One person says *hareini nazir* — I am a *nazir* — and his companion hears and says *va'ani* — and I as well. A third person hears the second and says *va'ani*. The *Mishnah* rules that *kulam nezirim* — all of them are *nezirim* — because each piggybacks on the one before.

The *Mishnah* then addresses what happens when the chain is disrupted. If the first person obtains a *heter* — retroactive annulment — they are all released, *hutru kulam*. The logic is that each subsequent person's *va'ani* is not merely an independent declaration of *nezirut* made in a context created by the first. Rather, it functions as *hatfasa* — a transfer of status. The later declarant is saying, in effect: whatever status applies to you applies to me. This is structurally analogous to *ze k'ze* in the laws of *nedarim*, where the *kedusha* of one object is transferred to another. If the first person's *nezirut* never truly took effect — retroactively voided by the *heter* — there was no status to transfer, and the subsequent declarations are vacuous.

Conversely, if the last person in the chain obtains a *heter*, only he is released. The first person's status is independent and self-standing; the last person's annulment has no upstream effect.

### Wife First

A related *Mishnah* addresses the husband-wife scenario. A husband declares *hareini nazir*, and his wife, upon hearing, says *va'ani*. In this case, the husband may annul his wife's *nezirut* — which is his prerogative as a husband — and his own *nezirut* remains standing. Her *nezirut* derived from his and is therefore subject to his *hafera*; his does not depend on hers and is unaffected.

Now consider the inverse: the wife declares *hareini nezira*, and the husband, upon hearing, says *va'ani*. The *Mishnah* rules *eino yachol lehafer* — he cannot annul it. There are two ways to understand this ruling. One reading is that annulling his wife's *nezirut* would, as a practical matter, undo his own, since his *va'ani* piggybacked on her status. Since *lo yachel devaro* — a person cannot annul his own vow — this indirect route of annulment is also closed. A second reading, which the *Gemara* favors, is that the moment the husband said *va'ani* in response to his wife's declaration, he performed an act of *kiyum* — ratification. Having ratified the wife's *nezirut*, he can no longer perform *hafera* upon it, since *kiyum* and *hafera* are mutually exclusive. On this reading, the reason he cannot annul is not that it would affect him, but that he has already forfeited the right to annul through the *kiyum* itself.

### Husband First

The *Mishnah* continues with further variations. If a husband says *hareini nazir v'at* — I am a *nazir*, and how about you — and the wife responds *amen*, he may annul her vow while his own remains standing, since her *nezirut* derived from his. If the wife says *hareini nezira v'ata* — I am a *nezira* and you as well — and he responds *amen*, he again cannot annul, for the same reason as above: his *amen* constitutes *kiyum* of her vow. Whether the mechanism is *lo yachel devaro* or *kiyum*, the practical result is the same — *hafera* is unavailable to him.

The question is raised whether, in the case where the husband performed *kiyum* through his *va'ani* or *amen*, he could subsequently seek *hatara* from a *chakham* for his own *va'ani*, thereby undoing his own *kiyum* and then annulling his wife's *nezirut* from beneath. The *Gemara* leaves this as a live question. It is worth noting that the earlier discussion in the tractate of whether a *chakham* can be *matir* a *kiyum* is directly relevant here, though no final resolution is offered at this stage.

### Reish Lakish

Reish Lakish, sitting before Rabbi Yehuda Nesia — the grandson of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi — articulates a crucial limiting principle: *vehu she-hitpisu kulam betoch kedei dibbur* — the entire sequence of *va'ani* declarations is valid only if all of them occurred within *tokh kedei dibbur* of the first person's statement.

The assumption underlying Reish Lakish's formulation at this stage is that all subsequent declarants are piggybacking directly on person number one — not on the person immediately before them, but on the original *nazir*. This assumption will be revisited, but it drives the *tokh kedei dibbur* requirement: since each later declarant is extending and participating in the first person's speech act, the temporal connection must be to that original act.

This is a significant point. In the classic case of *yad* — where a *nazir* passes before someone who then says *va'ani* — the *va'ani* works because the passing *nazir* creates a context that gives meaning to the word. That is a different mechanism: the context frames the later utterance. Here, however, what is happening is not merely context-creation but actual *hatfasa* — the later declarant is attaching to and extending the earlier one's speech act itself. That is why *tokh kedei dibbur* is required: one can only be said to participate in another's speech act if one does so within the window during which that speech act is still, legally speaking, live.

### Tokh Kedei Dibbur

The *Gemara* asks: how long is *tokh kedei dibbur*? The answer given is *kedei she'eilat shalom* — the time it takes to extend a greeting, as in *shalom alecha*. But then a further question arises: is it the greeting from a student to a teacher — *shalom alecha rebbi* — or from a teacher to a student? The difference is not merely ceremonial. A student greeting a teacher would say something like *shalom alecha rebbi u'mori*, which is a somewhat longer phrase than a teacher's brief *shalom alecha*. Whether *tokh kedei dibbur* spans two words or three words has practical significance for how many people can realistically fit their *va'ani* declarations within that window.

A response is offered to Reish Lakish: *lo shavkat ravcha le-talmidah* — you have not left room for the student. The implication, as Tosafot understands it, is that Reish Lakish's strict application of *tokh kedei dibbur* — measured from the original speaker's statement — creates problems in cases where a natural interruption intervenes, such as a student pausing to greet his arriving *rebbi* before saying *va'ani*. The push-back suggests that the window may be slightly more generous than Reish Lakish implies.

There is in fact a conceptual distinction worth drawing here. The rule of *tokh kedei dibbur* is classically invoked when a *speaker* wishes to retract or amend something they themselves said. In that context, the window is measured from the end of one's own speech. Here, however, a different party is joining in. One might therefore argue that the window for the subsequent declarant need not be identical to the classical *tokh kedei dibbur* of self-correction. Perhaps the second person's *va'ani* merely needs to occur in close proximity to the first person's statement — not necessarily within the exact same three-word window, but immediately in its wake. This would mean that even after the first person's *tokh kedei dibbur* has closed — after their own window for self-correction has elapsed — a second party could still validly say *va'ani* in the brief moment immediately following. The analogy to other cases of context-driven legal acts supports this reading: in *kiddushin*, for instance, if a couple has been discussing marriage at length, the handing of a ring without explicit words can suffice because *asukin b'oto inyan* — they are still engaged in that matter — and this extends well beyond any *tokh kedei dibbur* of the last spoken word. Here, by contrast, we are not merely saying the context gives meaning to the second person's words; we are saying the second person is actively participating in the first person's speech act. That participation must therefore be temporally proximate to the speech act itself, even if the precise measure of that proximity may differ from the self-correction model.

A *baraita* is cited: *mi she'amar hareini nazir v'shama chaveiro v'shaha kedei dibbur v'amar va'ani, hu assur v'chaveiro mutar* — if the companion waited a *kedei dibbur* before saying *va'ani*, only the first person is a *nazir*, not the second. This supports Reish Lakish's position that *tokh kedei dibbur* is the operative standard, not something more generous.

### Piggyback Chain

With the *tokh kedei dibbur* framework established, the *Gemara* turns to the question of whose statement each subsequent declarant is piggybacking on. Reish Lakish assumed they all connect back to person number one. But the *Mishnah* describes a scenario with persons two and three saying *va'ani* sequentially, and the *Gemara* asks: *chad batar chad matpis* — does each person grab onto the one immediately before him — *o dilma bekamma matpis* — or do they all grab onto person number one?

The *nafka mina* is considerable. If each person piggybacks on the one immediately before, the chain can theoretically extend indefinitely: person two connects to person one, person three connects to person two, person four connects to person three, and so on, each within *tokh kedei dibbur* of the prior speaker. If they all connect to person number one, the chain is limited to however many people can fit their *va'ani* declarations within *tokh kedei dibbur* of that first statement — only a handful at most.

A further *nafka mina* follows from this regarding the effect of a middle person's *heter*. If each person connects to the one before, then annulling person two releases persons three and four and everyone below, while leaving person one unaffected. If everyone connects to person one, then annulling anyone other than person one affects no one else.

The *Gemara* attempts to resolve the question from the *Mishnah* itself. The *Mishnah* says: *hutar ha-rishon hutru kullan* — if the first is released, all are released. The inference (*ha emtzai lo*) would be that only the first person's annulment has this cascading effect; a middle person's annulment would affect no one. This would support the view that everyone connects to person one. But the *Gemara* deflects: perhaps the *Mishnah* focused on the first person not because he is the only one whose annulment matters, but because using the first person allows one to say *hutru kullan* — all are released — which is the most dramatic formulation. A middle person's annulment would release only those below, making it a less useful teaching vehicle.

Similarly, the *Mishnah* says: *hutar ha-achron, ha-achron mutar ve-kullan asurin* — if the last person is released, he is permitted and all before him remain forbidden. The inference would be that an intermediate person would affect only those who follow. But the *Gemara* resists: the *Mishnah* may be using *achron* loosely to mean anyone other than the first person.

### Baraita: Sequential

The resolution comes from an explicit *baraita*: if the first person is released, all are released; if the last is released, only he is released; if a middle person is released, *heimenu u-lemata mutar, heimenu u-lemala assur* — from him downward is permissible, from him upward is forbidden. This explicitly distinguishes the middle person's annulment from the last person's and from the first person's. *Shema mina chad batar chad matpis* — this demonstrates conclusively that each person piggybacks on the one immediately before him, not all on person one.

This conclusion has a natural quality to it. When person three says *va'ani*, the most immediate referent for those words is person two, who just spoke. The chain is sequential. The practical implication — that the chain can extend indefinitely, each link connecting within *tokh kedei dibbur* of the prior link — follows directly.

The *Gemara*'s conclusion also returns us to a question that runs beneath the entire discussion: to what extent is this the default legal interpretation of *va'ani*, and to what extent does it depend on the specific circumstances? One can readily imagine cases where person three was facing person one and clearly intending to connect to that original declaration, not to person two. Whether halacha would honor that stated intent, or whether the sequential *hatfasa* model operates objectively regardless of subjective direction, is a question the *Gemara* does not definitively resolve. As a default in the absence of clarifying context, the rule is *chad batar chad matpis* — each connects to the one immediately before.

---

---

# Nazir 25

## Reish Lakish vs. R. Yoch…

### Nazir Death/Annulment

The daf opens with a debate concerning a foundational halacha of *nazir*: when a *nazir* dies or a husband annuls his wife's vow of *nezirut*, and money has been sanctified and set aside for the *korbanot* without specification as to which *korban* each sum was designated for, the entire pile is assigned to an *olah*. The Gemara understands this case to involve a pile that would have contributed to all of the *nazir*'s *korbanot*, including a *chatat* — making the ruling a genuine *chiddush*. It is not as if the entire pile could have gone to an *olah* in the ordinary course of events; some portion of it was destined for a *chatat*. And yet, the halacha is that once the funds can no longer be used for their *nazir* purpose, the entire pile is directed toward an *olah*.

### Halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai

Rabbi Yochanan holds that this ruling is a *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* — a tradition received from Sinai with no textual derivation. On his view, the halacha distinguishes between *stumim* (undesignated funds) and *meforashim* (designated funds): if the pile was non-designated, this special dispensation applies; if individual sums were explicitly designated — this pile for the *chatat*, this for the *olah*, this for the *shelamim* — then the halacha was not said, and each sum follows its own designation. Since it is a *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*, no logical questions can be pressed against it. It operates as an arbitrary rule confined to its precise parameters, and one cannot ask why similar scenarios are treated differently.

### Reish Lakish's Pasuk

Reish Lakish, by contrast, derives this halacha from a *pasuk*: *le-chol nidreihem u-le-chol nidvosem* — "for all their vows and for all their free-will offerings." He understands *nezirut* as something that begins as a *neder* (a vow), and leftover or unusable funds therefrom can be directed toward a *nedava*, which paradigmatically refers to an *olah* — the quintessential free-will offering that is entirely given over. The Gemara, however, presses Reish Lakish: if the derivation is from this *pasuk*, why should the halacha be limited to undesignated funds? Even if the money was explicitly designated, it originated from a *neder* and now becomes a *nedava* — so let it go to an *olah* regardless.

### Rava's Objection

Rava responds: designated funds cannot be repurposed. This principle is already established from the *braita* of the school of Rabbi Yishmael. Once funds carry a concrete designation, they remain within that category — just as a *tmura* or *vlad* (derivative sanctities) retain the identity of their parent *kedusha*. Accordingly, since we already know that anything with a designated *kedusha* cannot be redirected, the *pasuk* learned by Reish Lakish can only be speaking to a pile of undesignated funds. That is precisely where the *chiddush* lies: even though it was clear that *chatat* money was present in that pile, since it had not been formally designated, the *pasuk* permits the entire pile to be used as an *olah*.

---

## Vlad & Tmura

### Rak Kodashecha Pasuk

The Gemara now turns to unpack the *braita* of Rabbi Yishmael, which grounds the broader principle about derivative sanctities. The *pasuk* reads: *rak kodashecha asher yihyu lecha u-nedarecha tisa u-vata el hamakom asher yivchar Hashem* — "Only your holy things that you possess, and your vows, shall you lift up and come to the place that God shall choose." The *pasuk* concludes: *ve-asita olotecha habasar vehadam al mizbe'ach Hashem Elokecha vedam zevachecha yishapech al yesod mizbe'ach Hashem v'habasar tochel* — bring your *olot*, and the blood and flesh of your *shelamim* upon the altar, and eat the meat. Since there are ample other *pesukim* instructing one to bring *korbanot* to the *Beit Hamikdash*, this *pasuk* must be communicating something additional. The *midrash halacha* identifies that additional teaching: *bevladei kodashim u-vitmurasam hakatuv medaber* — the *pasuk* is speaking of the offspring of consecrated animals (*vlad*) and substituted animals (*tmura*), both of which represent derivative *kedusha*.

### Bringing Derivatives

One might have supposed that such derivative sanctities — since they are not the original consecration — should be left to graze until they develop a blemish and are redeemed. The *pasuk* of *tisa u-vata* instructs that they be brought to the *Beit Hamikdash*. But perhaps the intent is merely to bring them there and withhold food and water until they die — *yimna mehem mayim u-mazon bi-shvil she-yamusu*. Therefore the *pasuk* continues: *ve-asita olotecha habasar vehadam* — you shall actually bring them as sacrifices. The principle derived is: *ke-derech she-ata noheg ba-olah noheg bi-tmurata* — treat the *tmura* of an *olah* as an *olah* is treated; and *ke-derech she-ata noheg bi-shlamim noheg bi-vladeihem* — treat the offspring of a *shelamim* as a *shelamim* is treated.

A subtle point underlies the pairing of examples. An *olah* must be male — *im olah korbano min ha-zachar* — and therefore cannot produce a *vlad*. Accordingly, the example of a derivative *olah* is a *tmura*, not a *vlad*. A *shelamim*, by contrast, may be female, so it can produce offspring; hence the example of a derivative *shelamim* is a *vlad*. The *pasuk* thus instructs that each type of derivative is brought in the manner appropriate to its original *kedusha*.

One might further ask: *yachol af vlad chatat u-tmurat asham kein* — perhaps the same applies to the offspring of a *chatat* or the *tmura* of an *asham*, and those too should be brought as their respective *korbanot*? To this, the *pasuk* responds with the word *rak* — "only" — which excludes the *chatat* and *asham*. This is the position of Rabbi Yishmael. The rationale is well-established: a *chatat* that cannot be brought for its original purpose — whether it is the offspring of a *chatat*, the *chatat* whose owner died, the *chatat* whose owner was already atoned for by another offering, the *chatat* that passed its year, or a *tmurat chatat* — must be let to die. This rule encompasses five cases, recalled by the mnemonic *vitmanah* (ו-ת-מ-נ-ע): *vlad chatat*, *tmurat chatat*, *metu ba'aleha*, *nitkapru be-acher*, and *avrah shnatah*. For all five, the animal is starved until death, and this is a *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*.

### Rabbi Akiva Position

Rabbi Akiva holds that one need not derive the exclusion of the *chatat* and *asham* from the word *rak*. Rather, a separate *pasuk* states *asham hu* — "it is a guilt-offering" — from which the Gemara derives *ba-havayato yehei*: the *asham* retains its identity and cannot be redirected to serve any other function. Implicitly, the same applies to the *chatat*.

The distinction between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva is not immediately transparent, since both are learning from ancillary textual indicators. Rabbi Akiva's preference for *asham hu* over *rak* may stem from the fact that *rak* is a generic exclusion whose precise scope is uncertain, whereas *asham hu* speaks specifically to the *asham* and communicates directly that its identity is fixed and cannot be overridden.

### Why Learn from Pasuk?

This leads to a pressing question that the Gemara raises at multiple junctures: *lama li kra, hilchata g'miri lah* — why do we need a *pasuk* at all? We already have the *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* that the five *chatot* die and that whatever would require a *chatat* to die by an *asham* instead requires it to graze (*kol she-be-chatat metah be-asham ro'eh*). Why, then, does the *braita* appear to be deriving these very rulings from *pesukim*?

The Gemara's resolution differs for Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva. For Rabbi Yishmael, the *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* establishes that the animal cannot be validly brought (*lo kasher*), but the *pasuk* of *rak kodashecha* adds a further dimension: if one were to bring such a *chatat* in these circumstances, one would violate a *lav ha-ba mi-klal aseh* — a prohibition implicit in a positive command. The positive command *ve-asita olotecha* covers only *olot* and *shelamim* in their derivative forms, implicitly excluding the *chatat*. Bringing the *chatat* in this state thus constitutes a transgression of an *aseh*. The *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* tells us the act is invalid; the *pasuk* tells us it is additionally a transgression.

For Rabbi Akiva, who does not connect the matter to the *pasuk* of *rak kodashecha*, this resolution is unavailable. The Gemara therefore says the *pasuk* of *asham hu* comes to teach the ruling articulated by Rav Huna in the name of Rav — a ruling about the *asham*'s capacity for transformation, discussed in the following section.

The Gemara notes, moreover, the broader methodological point that this entire *midrash halacha* presupposes the *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*. Tosafot observes that the plain sense of the *braita* suggests Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva are both deriving the basic rule about the *chatat* dying — but the Gemara refuses to read it that way. Since it is committed to the view that this halacha is already known from *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*, it assigns each *tanna* a distinct teaching derived from the *pasuk*, even at the cost of departing from the surface reading of the *braita*. Tosafot candidly acknowledges this tension.

---

## Hava Amina: Olah/Shelamim

### Hava Amina Explained

Before reaching the question of why the *pasuk* is needed, the Gemara addresses the *hava amina* — the initial assumption — that the *pasuk* must overcome in the first place. The initial assumption is not that one would starve derivative *olot* and *shelamim* everywhere; rather, it is something more peculiar: *yachol ya'aleh le-veit habechira ve-yimna mehem mayim u-mazon bi-shvil she-yamusu* — one might have brought them up to the *Beit Hamikdash* and let them die there.

This *hava amina* arises from the structure of the *pasuk* itself. The first part, *tisa u-vata*, instructs bringing these animals to the *Beit Hamikdash*. One might read this as: bring them there, and then — since they are not eligible to be brought as original consecrations — leave them there to die. The *pasuk* then adds *ve-asita olotecha habasar vehadam*, teaching that they must actually be offered as sacrifices. The *hava amina* is therefore a perfectly logical reading of the sequence of the *pasuk*, and the conclusion (*ka mashma lan d'lo*) dispels it.

### Bring as Sacrifices

The *pasuk* thus teaches: bring derivative *olot* and *shelamim* — whether *tmura* or *vlad* — and offer them as the *korban* that their original *kedusha* represents. The derivative *olah* is brought as an *olah*; the derivative *shelamim* is brought as a *shelamim*. The word *rak* then comes to limit this dispensation.

### Chatat Must Die

The word *rak* excludes the *vlad chatat* and *tmurat asham* from this permission. The *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* of the five *chatot* that die is well established, and the Gemara is resolute that it not be displaced by a *pasuk*-derived rule. This is why, for Rabbi Yishmael, the *pasuk*'s purpose is re-understood: rather than establishing that these animals cannot be brought (which is known from *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*), the *pasuk* establishes the additional *issur aseh* one incurs by bringing them improperly. For Rabbi Akiva, the *pasuk* of *asham hu* teaches the more nuanced halacha of Rav Huna — that the *asham*'s identity can transform, but only once it has been formally handed over to pasture.

---

## Asham's Identity Transfo…

### Asham Given to Pasture

The Gemara resolves the question of why Rabbi Akiva needs the *pasuk* of *asham hu* by invoking the teaching of Rav Huna in the name of Rav: *asham she-nitak le-re'iya u-shechato le-shem ola kasher* — an *asham* that has been handed over to graze, if one then *shechts* it with the intent that it be an *olah*, it is valid as an *olah*. Once the *asham* has been set into the process of grazing — the process by which it will eventually develop a blemish, be redeemed, and have its funds applied to an *olah* — its *kedusha* has already functionally transformed. Even though the animal itself has not yet been redeemed, the act of handing it over to the shepherd initiates a shift in its identity such that a *shechita* performed *le-shem olah* at that point is effective.

This halacha applies specifically to an *asham* that cannot be used for its original purpose — a *tmurat asham*, an *asham* whose owner has died, or whose owner has already been atoned for by another offering. For such an *asham*, the *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* prescribes that it graze until it develops a blemish, at which point the animal is redeemed for its monetary value and that money is brought as an *olah*. The transformation is not of the money to another *asham* or *chatat* — since the original purpose can no longer be served — but specifically to an *olah*. The *pasuk* of *asham hu* comes to teach, according to Rabbi Akiva, that this process of identity transformation is real and operative — and that it is only once the *asham* is handed over to the shepherd that its *kedusha* begins to shift.

### Transformation Conditions

The condition is precise: *taima d'nitak* — the reason for the transformation is that the *asham* was actually handed over for pasture. *Ha lo nitak lo* — if it was not yet handed over, even if the owner knows full well that this *asham* can no longer serve its original purpose, the animal's identity has not yet shifted. *D'amar kra hu, asham hu, ba-havayato yehei* — the *pasuk* affirms that it retains its status as an *asham* unless and until something actually initiates the transformative process.

There is a significant Tosafot on this sugya, since Rabbeinu Tam takes the position that the requirement of handing over to pasture is only *derabbanan*, not *de'oraisa*. On his reading, what truly shifts the animal's identity at the *de'oraisa* level is the *kavana* at the time of *shechita*: if one *shechts* it *le-shem olah*, it is valid as an *olah*, even without having first handed it to a shepherd; if one *shechts* it *le-shem asham*, it does not work. The plain sense of the Gemara, however, appears to establish the handing-over-to-pasture as the operative *de'oraisa* criterion, and Rabbeinu Tam's reinterpretation departs significantly from that reading in order to reconcile it with another *sugya* that seems to undercut the *de'oraisa* status of the pasturing requirement.

---

## Beyond Nazir

### Single Obligation, Multi…

The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's formulation, which described the rule as a *halacha* specifically in *nazir*. The Gemara asks: is this truly unique to *nazir*? Surely the same halacha applies in other analogous cases. The Gemara answers: *tana nazir ve-chayvei kinim d'damu lei* — the *tanna* taught *nazir* because it is the paradigm, but the halacha extends to all cases that resemble *nazir* — namely, any situation in which a single obligation generates multiple *korbanot*.

### Yoledes Case

A *braita* establishes the parallel case: those obligated to bring *kinim* (pairs of bird-offerings) — of whom the *yoledes* is a classic example — who set aside money for their birds, and subsequently come into greater wealth such that they are now obligated to bring animal sacrifices rather than birds. Since their pile was set aside for an open-ended *chovah* (obligation), without specifying how much goes to the *chatat*-bird and how much to the *olah*-bird, the same principles apply: *rotzeh le-havi bahen chatat behemah yavi, olat behemah yavi* — one may direct the whole pile toward the animal *chatat* or toward the animal *olah*.

Tosafot engages carefully with the language used in setting aside such a pile. If one says "this is for my *korbanot*," Tosafot understands this to mean that both *korbanot* must come from this pile, even though it remains unspecified which sum is for which. If one says merely "this is for my obligation," the language is open-ended enough that the whole pile could go toward a single *korban*. This distinction matters because the *chiddush* of the halacha — that after the person's death the pile can go entirely to an *olah* — is greatest when the pile was understood to contain both *chatat* and *olah* money, yet the halacha redirects the whole to an *olah*. If the pile was open-ended enough that even while the person lived it could be assigned entirely to one *korban*, there is less novelty in the post-death ruling.

In the *yoledes* case: if she dies and the pile is *stumim* (unspecified), *yiplu le-nedavah* — it falls to an *olah*. This is precisely the same ruling as in *nazir*, confirming that the halacha is not limited to *nazir* but extends to any single obligation that generates multiple *korbanot*.

### Two Independent Obligati…

The contrast case is introduced to delineate the scope of this principle precisely. The *braita* describes a person who is obligated in a *chatat* (arising from one cause) and who separately accepts upon himself an obligation of an *olah* (a completely unrelated *neder*). He sets aside money and says *harei eilu le-chovotai* — this is for my obligations. Since he has two entirely independent obligations, the pile contains both *chatat* money and *olah* money: *rotzeh le-havi bahen chatat behemah lo yavi, olat behemah lo yavi* — he may not use the entire pile for either the animal *chatat* or the animal *olah* alone. Each obligation's funds must be distinguished and directed appropriately.

When such a person dies with this unspecified pile, *yelchu le-yam ha-melach* — the money must be thrown into the Dead Sea. The reason is that this is not a case of one obligation generating multiple *korbanot*; it is two separate, independent obligations that happen to share a single pool of funds. Since *chatat* money is present and cannot be repurposed, and since the *chatat* money cannot be separated out with precision, the entire pile is lost. One cannot extract the *olah* money from the mixture because no individual coin can be identified as specifically belonging to one obligation or the other. The sanctification of a coin is concrete — it is not merely a symbolic representation of general monetary value that can be reassigned — and thus the intermingling of *chatat* funds with *olah* funds, where the former cannot be redirected, disqualifies the entire pile from any further use.

This stands in contrast to the *nazir* or *yoledes* case, where the single origin of the obligation means that even a pile containing identifiable *chatat* and *olah* funds can, upon the person's death, be directed entirely toward an *olah* through the special halacha derived either from *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* or from the *pasuk* of *le-chol nidreihem u-le-chol nidvosem*.

---

## Unspecified vs. Designat…

### Rav Ashi's Requirement

Rav Ashi clarifies the precise meaning of *meforashim* — explicitly designated — which serves as the cutoff beyond which the special halacha of redirecting funds to an *olah* no longer applies. His teaching refines what "unspecified" must mean in order for the halacha to operate.

### Naming Korbanos

One might assume that "designated" refers only to the clearest case: where the *nazir* said explicitly *elu le-chatasi ve-elu le-olasi ve-elu le-shalmi* — "these coins are for my *chatat*, these for my *olah*, these for my *shelamim*." Rav Ashi teaches that this is not the only case. Even if the person said *elu le-chatasi u-le-olasi u-le-shalmi* — "this pile is for my *chatat*, my *olah*, and my *shelamim*" — without further specifying which sum is for which, this is already considered *meforashim*. The explicit naming of the *chatat* as one of the intended recipients of this pile sufficiently concretizes the *chatat*'s identity within that pile, and therefore the pile can no longer be redirected to an *olah* after the *nazirut* is annulled or the *nazir* dies.

### Obligation vs. Korbanos

A second formulation attributed to Rav Ashi extends the principle further: *lo teima ad d'amar elu le-chatasi u-le-olasi u-le-shalmi* — do not say that only when one names the specific *korbanot* is it considered designated. Rather, *afilu amar elu le-chovati harei hein ke-meforashim* — even if one says merely "this pile is for my obligation," that too is treated as designated, and the *chatat* money it contains cannot be redirected.

This leads to a subtle question: if even saying "for my obligation" is considered sufficiently explicit to constitute *meforashim*, what formulation remains genuinely *stumim* and qualifies for the special halacha? Tosafot wrestles with this directly. He argues that saying *le-korbanot neziruti* — "for my *nazir*-offerings" — is marginally less concrete than *le-chovati*, because while both imply that all the *korbanot* are to come from the pile, the formulation *le-korbanot neziruti* does not explicitly invoke a *chatat* by name or category. Nevertheless, Tosafot acknowledges that even this formulation refers to all the *korbanot*, and therefore he is not entirely satisfied that this represents a true functional difference. The Gemara's *chiddush* — that a *stumim* pile containing *chatat* funds can go entirely to an *olah* — thus operates in an increasingly narrow band of cases, and the exact dividing line between *stumim* and *meforashim* remains genuinely difficult to pin down.

---

## Separating Chatat Money

### Pile Becomes Concrete

Rava teaches a further principle that extends the concretization logic in a striking direction: *im hifrish d'mei chatat mibeineihem harei hen ke-meforashim* — if one separates out the *chatat* funds from an otherwise unspecified pile, then even the remaining funds — which consist only of *olah* and *shelamim* money, with no *chatat* money remaining — are treated as though the entire pile has become designated.

The intuition one might bring to this case would be exactly the opposite: now that the *chatat* money has been cleanly removed, there is no longer any admixture of *chatat* funds. Surely the remaining pile should now qualify for the special halacha and go entirely to an *olah*? Rava rules otherwise. The act of separating out the *chatat* funds draws the entire pile out of the indeterminate, amorphous state in which the special halacha operates. Once something about the pile has been made concrete and real — even if it is only the *chatat* portion being segregated — the pile as a whole crosses from that indeterminate state into a more determinate one. Its identity has begun to solidify, and the special mechanism by which an unspecified pile is redirected to an *olah* is no longer available.

### Must Divide Remaining Mo…

The practical consequence is that after the separation, the remaining *olah* and *shelamim* funds must be divided between an *olah* and a *shelamim* in the appropriate proportions; the entire remainder cannot simply be assigned to an *olah*. The pile has, in Rava's framing, entered the real world of determinate identity. Just as the Gemara's broader analysis draws on the image of sanctified funds as concretely attached to specific purposes — each coin, once designated, is not merely symbolic monetary value but carries a fixed *kedusha* — so too the act of beginning to apportion that pile triggers a kind of irreversible concretization. From that point forward, the remaining funds must be treated according to their actual proportional designations, and the special halacha of *stumim* no longer applies.

---

---

# Nazir 26

## Maot Stumot Rule

### Intro: Money to Olah

The sugya on 26b opens with a ruling transmitted in the name of Rav Huna citing Rav: *lo shanu ela maot* — this principle applies only to money. The principle in question is the rule of *maot stumot*: if a *nazir* set aside an unspecified pile of money intended for his *chatat*, *olah*, and *shelamim*, and then died or had his *nezirut* annulled, that money is used entirely toward an *olah*. This is what we have been discussing. But Rav's ruling now introduces a critical limitation: *aval beavehemah, harei hi kimefureshet* — if instead of money it was animals, those animals are treated as if they were already explicitly designated.

### Animals vs Money

The question is: what exactly is the case of animals? If the animals in question were the precise three offerings a *nazir* is required to bring — a male lamb, a female lamb, and a ram — then the ruling would be self-evident. Each animal is inherently self-identifying, and of course each would be brought for its appropriate sacrifice. The case must therefore involve something less obvious.

*Tosafot* works out that the *gemara* is discussing a situation in which someone set aside three cows — animals that are within the category of valid sacrifices but are not themselves the required offerings for this particular *korban nazir*, which must come from sheep. The owner declares that these animals are sanctified for the purpose of his sacrifices, intending that they will be sold, the proceeds redeemed, and the money then used to purchase the required animals. The question is why this situation is treated differently from an unspecified pile of money.

### Tosafot: Cow Kedushah

*Tosafot*'s analysis turns on a careful distinction regarding *kedushah* and the ability to transfer it. To appreciate the problem, consider three scenarios. First: if one sanctifies a cow for *bedek habayit* — for the upkeep and operating expenses of the *Beit Hamikdash* — it may be sold immediately, just as one might donate a car or any object of value. Second: if one sanctifies a cow to be brought itself as an *olah*, then that *kedushah* cannot be transferred and the cow cannot be sold until it develops a *mum* — a blemish — since only the onset of a blemish can release it from the sanctity that had designated it as the animal itself to be offered.

The interesting middle case — the one *Tosafot* grapples with — is where one sanctifies a cow with the *kedushah* of an *olah*, but not because the cow itself will be brought as that *olah*. Rather, since the *nazir*'s *olah* must be a sheep, the cow is being sanctified solely as a funding mechanism: sell the cow, take the proceeds, buy the sheep. One might have thought that because the cow itself was never going to be brought, the *kedushah* could simply be transferred through a sale without waiting for a *mum*. But *Tosafot* concludes, drawing on the logic of this very *sugya*, that the answer is otherwise. Since the cow belongs to the world of valid *korbanot* — since in theory a cow could be brought as an *olah*, even though that is not the *kedushah* designated here — the *kedushah* clings to it with full force, and cannot be removed without a *mum*. By contrast, if one were to sanctify a chicken — which is not a valid candidate for an *olah* of an animal — that could simply be sold outright without waiting for any blemish, because the chicken does not inhabit the world of animal *korbanot* and therefore the *kedushah* does not attach to it in the same way.

This conclusion has direct implications for our *halakha*. The question of whether animals are treated as *mefureshet* or as *maot stumot* depends heavily on whether they can be freely liquidated, which in turn depends on whether a *mum* is required before sale.

### Rav Nachman: Tmimah

The *gemara* now provides the ruling of Rav Nachman, which clarifies the scope of Rav's statement: *ha de-amrinan be-behemah harei hi ke-mefureshet — lo shanu ela bitmimah*. When we say that animals are treated as explicitly designated, that applies only to an unblemished animal, a *tmimah*. Such animals, because of the *kedushah* problem just described, cannot be sold until they develop a *mum*, and this waiting period gives them a different legal character. *Aval ba'alat mum* — but if the animal already has a blemish — *harei hi kistumah* — it is treated like unspecified funds, like *maot stumot*.

This raises the obvious question: why should the presence or absence of a *mum* matter to our *halakha* about whether the funds ultimately go toward an *olah*? Even animals without a *mum* will eventually develop one, or be sold, and the proceeds will be divided among the required *korbanot*. Why should the ease or difficulty of liquidation determine whether the pile counts as specified or unspecified?

### Mezuman Definition

To answer this, the *gemara* offers two approaches. The first is formal: the *halakha* of *maot stumot* is a *halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*, and it was transmitted specifically regarding money — *maot* — not regarding other things. If one has non-cash items with *kedushah* mixed in — including potential *chatat* funds — and the case does not fall within the ambit of this *halakha*, then the proper resolution is to cast the money into the *Yam HaMelach*, because the *chatat* component cannot be used and the entire pile must be destroyed. On this formal approach, the *halakha* simply was not said about anything other than cash, and that is the end of the matter.

But then what is the line between cash and not cash? Here the concept of *mezuman* becomes operative. The Hebrew word for cash in modern parlance is *mezuman* — literally, "something ready." The underlying idea is that something readily and immediately convertible to money, with minimal delay or friction, shares the legal character of money. An animal with a *mum* has no *kedushah* impediment to its sale — one simply brings it to market and sells it. That is cash. An unblemished animal cannot be sold until it develops a blemish; it must sit, grazing, for an indeterminate period. That is not cash. Similarly, a *niska* — a bar of precious metal — was regarded by some as sufficiently difficult to sell at the right price that it too falls outside the *mezuman* category, while others, as Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rules, disagree and consider even metal bars to be cash-equivalent. A *shura d'korei* — a pile of lumber or beams — is clearly not cash, since finding a buyer willing to inspect and purchase raw timber requires locating someone building a house and negotiating terms.

The second approach offers a logic beyond the formal rule. When one has three unblemished cows that must wait for a *mum* before they can be sold, one may, over time, mentally begin to pre-designate: "Bessie will go toward the *olah*, that other cow toward the *chatat*." Even if this mental designation was never verbalized, the extended waiting period creates the conditions for this kind of private assignment, and the pile accordingly begins to take on the character of *mefureshet* — as if it were already explicitly divided. This is, admittedly, a somewhat rabbinic-sounding concern, and *Tosafot* grapples with whether an unspoken mental designation can actually alter the legal status of the pile. But as a framework for understanding the distinction, it at least provides some logic, even if the cleaner approach remains the formal rule: the *halakha* was said only about *mezuman*, about things that are readily liquidated, and an animal without a *mum* simply does not qualify.

---

## Halakha Scope Debate

### Shimi: Metal & Wood

Rav Shimi bar Ashi poses a direct question to Rav Papa: *mai tama d'Rabbanan d'amri d'maot v'lo behema v'lo naska* — what is the reason that the Rabbis said this *halakha* applies to money and not to animals, not to metal bars, *v'lo shura* — and not to a pile of beams? He has just been told that the rule is formally limited to *maot* — cash or cash-like items — and he is challenging the basis of that limitation.

### Birds Case

But Rav Shimi presses further with what turns out to be the most interesting extension of this question: *maot v'lo ofot* — money, and not birds? To understand what he means, one must recall a distinct *halakha* involving *kinei yoledes* — the two birds that a woman who has given birth must bring, one as an *olah* and one as a *chatat*. There, the *halakha* is that she need not specify at the time of purchase which bird is which; the specification can be made either by the owner at the time of purchase or by the *kohen* at the time of bringing. What would happen, then, if such a woman purchased two birds without specifying, and then died before either stage of specification occurred?

One would naturally assume that since one bird is an *olah* and one is a *chatat*, the *kohen* should simply bring whichever one he designates as the *olah* and let the *chatat* die — since a *chatat* cannot be brought on behalf of someone who has died. But the question arises: should we treat those two unspecified birds the way we treat *maot stumot*? The birds have the same problem — there is a *chatat* and an *olah* mixed together in an unspecified pile, the owner has died, and perhaps we should simply bring both as an *olah*, just as we do with unspecified money. On the other hand, given that the *gemara* has been consistently narrowing the scope of the *maot stumot* rule — excluding animals, excluding metal bars, excluding lumber — perhaps birds too fall outside its ambit, and in that case both birds could not be brought as an *olah*.

This is the tension Rav Shimi is articulating. The initial assumption of the *gemara* is that these birds, having not yet been specified — neither by the owner at purchase nor by the *kohen* at the time of the offering — retain the status of *stumim*, unspecified. And if they are *stumim*, and the *halakha* of *maot stumot* applies broadly, then both should go toward an *olah*. But given how sharply the *gemara* has been limiting the rule, maybe not.

*Tosafot* here raises three possible readings of this passage, and the one that emerges as most coherent is the following: the *gemara* is not merely asking a hypothetical about whether the rule should apply to birds, but rather grounding its reasoning in the language Rav Chisda used — *mitparshot* — which will now become the pivot of the discussion.

### Rav Chisda: Birds

The *gemara* invokes the teaching of Rav Chisda: *ein hakinim mitparshot ela o belakichat bealim o ba'asiyat hakohen* — birds are not explicated, are not rendered *mefureshet*, except either at the moment the owner purchases them or at the moment the *kohen* performs the offering. The word Rav Chisda chose is significant. He did not say that the birds' identity is not *established* or not *fixed* — he said they are not *mitparshot*, not rendered explicit. And *mitparshot* is the precise opposite of *satum*. By using this language, Rav Chisda implicitly assigned the birds the status of *stumim* whenever neither the owner nor the *kohen* has yet acted. If the woman dies before either stage, the birds remain *satum*.

And if their status is *satum*, what follows? The *gemara* reads Rav Chisda's language as implying that such unspecified birds follow the *halakha* of *maot stumot* — if the owner dies, they are both brought as an *olah*, as a *nedava*. But then Rav Shimi's question bites: you have just been told the rule only applies to money, not to animals, not to metal, not to lumber. So why should birds be different? Why would the *halakha* of *maot stumot* apply here?

The *gemara* responds: *v'litameich* — according to your counter-reasoning, that we should not limit the rule to money at all and should apply it across the board to anything unspecified. If that is so, there is an immediate problem from the *Mishnah* cited by Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: *heivi shalosh behemot velo peireish* — if one brought three animals without specifying which is which, and those three animals happen to be the precise animals required — a male lamb, a female lamb, and a ram — then *harauya lechatas tikarev chatas, le-olah tikarev olah, ulishlamim tikarev shelamim* — each is brought for its appropriate sacrifice. The *kedushah* is apportioned correctly.

### Objection Logic

But if one wishes to apply the *maot stumot* rule to everything that is unspecified, one should be troubled by this ruling. The *gemara* says these animals were not specified — *behemah lav kimeforeshet dami* — animals are not like *mefureshet*. If animals truly share the status of *stumim*, then even these three animals — the exact right animals for the sacrifice — should follow the rule of *stumim* and we should bring them all as an *olah*. Why instead does each animal go to its appropriate sacrifice? This seems to directly contradict the position that *stumim* applies broadly to all unspecified items regardless of their form.

### Response: Gender

The response is sharp — almost dismissive. *Hacha nekeiva, hacha zachar* — here, the *chatat* is female and the *olah* is male. These animals are not unspecified in any meaningful sense. A male sheep and a female sheep are self-identifying. Of course they cannot have the status of *stumim* — it is perfectly clear which is which. The question was, frankly, absurd. *Stumim* describes a situation where it genuinely cannot be determined which item belongs to which category. If you have the exact right animals and their sex alone tells you which goes where, there is nothing unspecified about the situation. It is as though one had three piles of money with signs reading *olah*, *chatat*, and *shelamim* — that is not *stumim* at all.

So the broader debate remains: is the *maot stumot* rule formally limited to money and cash-equivalent items, or does it apply broadly to any genuinely unspecified constellation of *kodesh* items? The case of birds sharpens this question because birds present a genuine case of *stumim* — identical in appearance, capable of being brought as either *olah* or *chatat*, and unspecified until the act of the owner or *kohen*. If the rule is broad, both birds go toward an *olah* when the owner dies. If the rule is narrow and limited to money, the birds must be handled differently.

---

## Braita: Son & Father

### Setup: Father Dies

The *gemara* now introduces a *braita* found in full on 30b, which the text here cites in abbreviated form. The *braita* poses the question: *keitzad amru ish megaleiach al nezirus aviv* — when does a person get to shave — meaning, when does a son get to use his deceased father's money to bring the *korbanot* for his own *nezirut*? The *braita* sets up the scenario: a father was a *nazir*, set aside unspecified money for his *nezirut*, and then died. Without the son's involvement, that money would simply go toward an *olah*, as we have established. The question is whether the son can step in and use that money for his own *korbanot* instead.

### Case 1: After Death

The first case: *v'amar hareini nazir al m'nas she'agaleach al ma'os abba* — the son declares himself a *nazir* on condition that he gets to use his father's money to bring his *korbanot*. This declaration was made after his father died. In this case, the son succeeds. The money was standing there, its original purpose no longer achievable since the father had died, and its ultimate destination had not yet been determined. The son stepped in at precisely the right moment, accepted *nezirut* explicitly tied to the use of that money, and is therefore entitled to use it. *Zehu she-megaleiach al ma'os aviv* — this is the case where the son actually does bring his *korbanot* with his father's money.

### Case 2: Simultaneous

The second case: *aval mi shehaya hu v'aviv nezirim* — he and his father were both *nezirim* at the same time, meaning the son had already accepted *nezirut* while his father was still alive. The father subsequently set aside money for his *nezirut* and then died. The son now says he wants to use that money for his own *korbanot*. *Harei elu yiplu l'nedavah* — in this case, he cannot do so. The money falls to *nedava*, following the standard rule of *maot stumot*. The son cannot claim it because he was already a *nazir* before his father died; there was no moment where the money was available and his *nezirut* was formed with the intent to use it.

### Specified Animals

The *braita* then addresses the parallel case involving animals. *Haysa lo behemah mefureshet* — if the father had specifically designated particular animals — *chatat tamus* — the *chatat* animal dies since it cannot be brought, *olah tikarev olah* — the *olah* is brought as an *olah*, *shelamim yikrevu shelamim* — the *shelamim* is brought as *shelamim*. Each specified animal follows its designated *kedushah*, and there is nothing unusual about this outcome.

---

## Mum Status

### Inference: Unspecified M…

The *gemara* now draws an inference from the *braita*. When the *braita* contrasts unspecified money — which goes toward an *olah* as *nedava* — with specified animals — where each goes to its designated sacrifice — the *gemara* asks: *mai lav afilu ba'alat mum* — does this not apply even to animals with a blemish? That is, the *braita* seems to be drawing a contrast between money and all forms of animals. If so, even animals with a *mum*, which we have suggested are cash-equivalent, would still fall on the "animal" side of the ledger and would be treated as *mefureshet* rather than as *maot stumot*. This would undermine what Rav Nachman had ruled earlier.

### Braita Scope

The *gemara* rejects this inference. *Lo, tmimah* — no, the *braita* is speaking of unblemished animals, or more precisely, it is speaking of clearly specified animals, where each animal's identity as *chatat*, *olah*, or *shelamim* was already made explicit by the owner. The *braita*'s contrast is not between money and all animals, but between unspecified money and explicitly designated animals. *Aval ba'alat mum k'stumah dami* — but an animal with a blemish retains the status of *stumim* and is treated like money.

This generates a further question from the *gemara*: if animals with a *mum* are truly cash-equivalent, then why does the *braita* not make this clear? Why contrast unspecified money with specified animals, when there is an intermediate category — unspecified blemished animals — that behaves just like money? Why not illustrate the *halakha* using that intermediate case?

### Mum as Money

The *gemara* responds: *hachi nami* — in fact, animals with a *mum* are simply included in the category of money. *Ba'alat mum l'mai kadeshah? Lidmei* — when an animal with a blemish is sanctified, what is its sanctity directed toward? To its monetary proceeds. It will be sold, and the *kedushah* will transfer to the money received. *D'mei haynu maot* — proceeds are money. When the *braita* says "money," it means anything whose *kedushah* operates through its monetary value, including blemished animals. The *braita* was not being incomplete; it was using "money" in a sense broad enough to encompass everything that is sold for its value and whose *kedushah* transfers to the proceeds.

### Final Principle

The *gemara* thus arrives at its final principle. The *halakha* of *maot stumot* — that an unspecified pile of funds intended for a *nazir*'s *korbanot* goes toward an *olah* when the owner dies — applies to anything whose *kedushah* operates through its monetary value: actual coins, blemished animals, and according to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, even metal bars. It does not apply to unblemished animals that cannot be sold until they develop a *mum*, and it does not apply to things like lumber that require significant effort to liquidate. The line is *mezuman* — readiness, liquidity, the practical ability to convert immediately into cash. Anything on the *mezuman* side of that line follows the *halakha* of *maot stumot*; anything that requires waiting or exceptional circumstances to convert falls outside it and is treated as *mefureshet*, as already designated, because the extended holding period creates the conditions for mental pre-designation or simply because the formal *halakha* was never transmitted for such cases in the first place.

---

---

# Nazir 26b

## Maot Setumot

### Unspecified Money Intro

The Gemara on 26b opens with a statement of Rav Huna in the name of Rav: *lo shanu ela ma'ot* — the rule we have been discussing, whereby unspecified funds set aside for the *korbanot* of a *nazir* (the *chatat*, *olah*, and *shelamim*) are directed toward an *olah* when the *nazirut* is annulled or the *nazir* dies, applies only when those funds are literally money. *Aval behemah harei hi k'mefureshet* — but if instead of money, animals were set aside, those animals are treated as already specified, as though each animal's identity has been designated.

### Animals vs. Money

What exactly is the case under discussion? The Gemara is terse here, and Tosafot works through the possibilities at some length in order to establish the basic *pshat*. One might have thought the case involved the precise animals a *nazir* is obligated to bring — a female lamb for the *chatat*, a male lamb for the *olah*, and a ram for the *shelamim*. But if those are the animals in question, it is self-evident that each is already identified: they are three distinct species, and there is no ambiguity whatsoever. The *olah* animal, the *chatat* animal, and the *shelamim* animal identify themselves. In that case it would be trivially obvious that the animals are *mefurashim* — specified — and there would be nothing to teach.

Tosafot therefore concludes that what the Gemara has in mind is a different scenario: the person sanctified three cows — animals that are within the world of *korbanot* in some sense but are not themselves the animals required for the *korban nazir*, which demands a sheep for the *olah*. The intent would be to sell the cows, take the proceeds, and use the money to purchase the required animals. Now the question becomes: when three cows are sanctified with the *kedusha* of *korbanot*, and they will eventually be sold and their proceeds divided among the various sacrifices, why should they not be treated like an unspecified pile of money? Which cow's proceeds are going to which sacrifice? Surely this should be *stumah* — unspecified — in exactly the same way as an indistinct pile of coins.

### Three Cows Case

To understand why animals are not treated like unspecified money, it is necessary to work through an important distinction that Tosafot develops and that will prove central to the Gemara's entire discussion. The question is what happens when one sanctifies an object with the *kedusha* of a *korban* but the object itself is not of the type that could be brought as that *korban*. For example, if one were to sanctify a digital recorder with the *kedusha* of an *olah*, the recorder cannot itself be placed on the *mizbei'ach*; what happens is that the *kedusha* transfers to the proceeds of its sale, and those proceeds are then used to purchase the required animal. This is a normal and unproblematic transfer.

Now consider a different case: one sanctifies a cow with the *kedusha* of an *olah* for a *nazir*, which must be a sheep. The cow is within the world of *korbanot* — it is the kind of animal that could, in the right circumstances, be brought as a *korban*. Does that make a difference? According to Tosafot, it does, and it makes a critical one.

### Kedusha Transfer

The principle at work is this: if an object is sanctified for *bedek ha-bayis* — for the maintenance fund of the *Beis HaMikdash* — it has no identity as a sacrificial animal and can simply be sold at any time. If an animal is sanctified to be brought itself as a *korban olah*, its *kedusha* cannot be removed and the animal cannot be sold until it develops a *mum* — a disqualifying blemish — because only a blemish releases it from the realm of *korbanot* and permits its sale. The intermediate case is when an animal is sanctified with the *kedusha* of an *olah* but is not itself going to be brought as one — as with our cow, whose proceeds will fund a sheep *olah*. Does this middle case follow the rule of *bedek ha-bayis*, permitting immediate sale, or does it follow the rule of a *korban* animal, requiring a *mum* before sale?

Tosafot concludes from the present *sugya* that because the cow is intrinsically relevant to the world of *korbanot* — it is, after all, the kind of animal that could in principle serve as a *korban* — its *kedusha* cannot simply be transferred through a sale. The *kedusha* remains stuck to the cow until the cow develops a *mum* and thereby exits the world of *korbanot*. By contrast, if one were to sanctify a chicken with the *kedusha* of an *olah*, since a chicken is wholly outside the world of animal *korbanot*, the *kedusha* presents no obstacle to an immediate sale. It is this distinction — whether the object is *relevant* to the world of *korbanot* or not — that gives meaning to the distinction between animals with a *mum* and animals without one.

## Temimah vs. Mum

### Rav Nachman Tmimah

Against this background, Rav Nachman adds a crucial qualification to Rav's statement: *lo shanu ela temimah* — the rule that animals are treated like *mefureshet* (specified) applies only to an unblemished animal. The reason is now clear: an unblemished cow that has been sanctified with the *kedusha* of a *korban* cannot be sold until it develops a *mum*. It will sit in the owner's field for an extended and indeterminate period. During that time, as will be developed shortly, there is reason to think its identity may become fixed in the owner's mind in a way that distinguishes it from an undifferentiated pile of money.

### Ba'alat Mum

*Aval ba'alat mum harei k'stumah* — but if the animal already has a blemish, it is treated like unspecified funds. An animal with a *mum* is not subject to the *kedusha* restriction that prevents sale; it can be readily sold and converted to cash. That ready convertibility places it, for halachic purposes, in the same category as cash — and therefore it follows the *halacha* of *ma'ot setumot*.

## Maot Setumot (II)

### Cows Unspecified?

This still leaves a question unanswered. Even granting that an unblemished cow presents complications around *kedusha* and sale, why should those cows ultimately be treated as *mefureshet* — specified? When the question was posed at the outset — three cows, no specification of which one's proceeds go to which sacrifice — surely this should be treated as *stumah*, unspecified, just like a pile of money. Why does the Gemara say otherwise?

## Limits of Maot

### Two Approaches

There are two ways to understand the limits of *maot setumot*. The first approach is that the entire *halacha* is a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* — a received tradition from Sinai — and that tradition was stated specifically with respect to *ma'ot*, cash, and not with respect to other forms of property. Under this view, even if one's three cows are genuinely unspecified — there is no clarity about which animal's proceeds will fund which sacrifice — it simply does not matter, because the *halacha* was never said for anything other than money. The cows remain non-*stumah* not because they are in fact specified, but because the special *halacha* of *setumim* never applied to them in the first place. The practical consequence is that the money cannot be directed toward an *olah*; since *chatat* funds are mixed in with everything else, the entire amount would have to be cast into the *Yam HaMelach*.

But if this is purely a formal rule limited to money, one might wonder: what about animals with a *mum*, which Rav Nachman just said are treated like *setumah*? Animals with a *mum* are also not cash. So the question becomes: where exactly is the dividing line?

### Mezuman Definition

The word that illuminates this is *mezuman* — the modern Hebrew word for cash. The root meaning is something like "ready" or "at hand," and the concept it captures is immediate transferability. The *halacha* of *setumim* was stated for things that are readily liquidable — readily converted into money for the purpose of purchasing the required *korbanot*. Something that can be sold quickly and easily in the normal course of commerce is functionally equivalent to cash and falls within the scope of the *halacha*. Something that requires time, negotiation, or waiting for the right buyer does not. On this reading, animals with a *mum* — which, since they bear no *kedusha* restriction, can be taken to market and sold without delay — are considered *mezuman*, cash-equivalent, and therefore fall within the *halacha* of *setumim*. Animals without a *mum*, which cannot be sold until a blemish appears, are not *mezuman*, not cash-equivalent, and therefore fall outside the *halacha*.

### Pre-Designation Logic

The second approach attempts to supply an internal logic for why unblemished animals are treated as *mefureshet* — specified — rather than simply excluded by a formal rule. The reasoning is as follows: when an unblemished animal has been sanctified and cannot be sold until it develops a *mum*, it may sit in the owner's possession for a long time. Over the course of that extended waiting period, the owner is likely to begin mentally allocating the animals — thinking to himself that the proceeds from this cow will fund the *olah*, and the proceeds from that cow will fund the *chatat*. If such mental pre-designation occurs, the animals are no longer genuinely unspecified; they have been informally assigned in the owner's mind, even if no formal declaration has been made.

This reasoning has an obvious difficulty, which Tosafot acknowledges: a mental assignment that has not been verbalized ordinarily has no halachic standing. Thoughts in the mind, without an act or declaration, do not usually alter the status of *kodshim*. For this reason, the cleaner and more defensible approach is simply the formal one: the *halacha* of *setumim* is limited to things that are readily liquidable — to *mezuman*, cash or cash-equivalents. Anything that requires extended time to convert to money falls outside the *halacha*, and the question of whether its identity has been mentally pre-designated is beside the point.

## Rav Shimi Challenge

### Metal vs. Wood

The foregoing discussion raises a further question about exactly where to draw the line between what counts as *mezuman* and what does not. One position implies that a *nascha* — a bar of precious metal, silver or gold — does not qualify as cash-equivalent, because selling a bar of precious metal requires waiting for the right price and is not as immediate as selling a blemished cow in an agricultural market. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak disagrees: *afilu nascha* — even a bar of metal is *mezuman* for this purpose, and the *halacha* of *setumim* applies to it. What is excluded, on his view, is *sovi d'karei* — beams of lumber. Wood requires finding a buyer who is in the market to build a house and who must inspect the material; it is simply not liquid. The precise line between metal and lumber as measures of liquidity may be somewhat surprising — one might have thought precious metal, which sells by weight, would be at least as liquid as livestock — but such is the Gemara's assumption about the relative ease of these markets.

### Money Not Birds

Rav Shimi bar Ashi poses a sharp question to Rav Pappa: the *rabbanan* say the *halacha* was stated for *damim* — money — and not for *behemah*, not for *nascha*, not for *sovi*. Very well. Then it should equally be: *damim v'lo ofot* — money and not birds. What does he mean by birds?

## Two Birds Case

### Unspecified Birds

The case Rav Shimi has in mind is not simply birds that someone happened to sanctify for a vague purpose. The classic *halacha* is that a *yoledes* — a woman who has given birth — is obligated to bring two birds, one as an *olah* and one as a *chatat*. She need not specify at the time she acquires the birds which is which; specification can happen either when the owner herself declares it at the time of purchase, or when the *kohen* designates the birds at the time he performs the service. This is a well-established *halacha* governing *kinnim* — pairs of birds brought for such obligations.

Now consider what happens if the woman acquires the two birds without specifying their identities and then dies before bringing them. She has two birds, one of which is a *chatat* and one an *olah*, but no one has yet declared which is which. One natural approach would be to bring the matter to the *kohen* and let the *kohen* make the designation — declaring one an *olah* and bringing it, and disposing of the other, since the *chatat* cannot be brought after the owner's death. But there is another possibility: could we treat those two unspecified birds like a pile of *ma'ot setumim*? In an unspecified pile of money containing both *chatat* funds and *olah* funds, the *halacha* is that the entire pile goes toward an *olah*. Why not apply the same *halacha* here and bring both birds as an *olah*?

Rav Shimi's challenge is essentially this: the question of whether the *halacha* of *setumim* extends to birds is not academic. Either the *halacha* is limited to money — in which case it should not apply to birds, and bringing both birds as an *olah* would be incorrect — or the *halacha* is not so limited, in which case why was it ever restricted to money in the first place?

### Counter Position

The counter-position is that the *halacha* of *setumim* should not be artificially restricted. Whether one has an unspecified pile of money, unspecified animals, unspecified bars of metal, or unspecified birds — if the *kedusha* is genuinely undifferentiated and the owner has died, the property follows the *halacha* of *setumim* and is directed toward a *nedava*, an *olah*.

### Rav Chisda Birds

Rav Chisda taught: *ein ha-kinnim mitparshot ella im be-likichat ba'alim o be-asiyat ha-kohen* — pairs of birds do not become specified except either at the time the owner purchases and designates them or at the time the *kohen* performs the service. The significance of Rav Chisda's formulation, as Tosafot explains, lies in his choice of the word *mitparshot*. He did not simply say that the birds' identity is not *nikva'im* — not established. He said they are not *mitparshot* — not explicated. *Mitparshot* is the precise opposite of *satum*. By framing it this way, Rav Chisda implicitly communicates that until one of those two events occurs — owner's designation at purchase or *kohen*'s designation at service — the birds' halachic status is *satum*, unspecified.

### Mitparshot Inference

If the birds have the status of *setumim* prior to designation, then when the owner dies before designation occurs, the normal *halacha* of *setumim* should apply: both birds go toward an *olah*, offered as a *nedava*. The inference from Rav Chisda's use of *mitparshot* is thus that birds do fall within the *halacha* of *setumim* — which challenges the position that the *halacha* is limited strictly to money.

## Birds Distinction

### Specified Animals

The Gemara responds to Rav Shimi's challenge with a counter-question. If one wishes to say the *halacha* of *setumim* applies equally to everything — money, animals, metal, birds, without distinction — then one must contend with what Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel teaches in the Mishnah: *heivi shalosh behemot v'lo peresh* — if someone brought three animals for his *korban nazir* without specifying which is which, and it happens that he brought precisely the three required animals (a female lamb, a male lamb, and a ram), then *harau'ya le-chatat tikarev chatat, le-olah tikarev olah, ve-li-shelamim tikarev shelamim* — each animal is assigned to its appropriate identity. The female goes as the *chatat*, the male lamb as the *olah*, the ram as the *shelamim*.

The counter-position maintains that animals too should follow the *halacha* of *setumim* and are not treated as specified. If so, how does the *kedusha* of this unspecified pile of three animals divide itself so neatly? The answer is that this is not at all a difficult case: these three animals, being the exact required animals, are self-identifying. They are not genuinely unspecified in any meaningful sense. Asking why they are not treated as *stumim* is like asking why a pile of money with a large sign reading "*chatat*" on one portion and "*olah*" on another should be treated as unspecified — the question answers itself.

### Torah Process

What actually distinguishes the bird case and explains why birds can be *setumim* is that the Torah itself specifies the process by which birds receive their identity: *ve-lakach ve-asah* — the owner takes and the *kohen* does. The birds' identity is assigned at one of precisely two moments — acquisition or service — and until one of those moments arrives, the Torah itself leaves them undesignated. There is no analogous Torah-mandated process in the case of animals; an animal's identity as *chatat*, *olah*, or *shelamim* is determined at the moment of designation, and when the owner brings three distinct and self-identifying animals, the designation is obvious.

### Three Animals

The point is further underscored by the observation that the *chatat* of a *nazir* is a female animal and the *olah* is a male animal — *hacha nekeva hacha zachar*. When you have a female sheep and a male sheep in front of you, it is simply not possible to speak of genuine non-specification. The *chatat* is the female; the *olah* is the male. There is nothing *satum* about it. By contrast, two birds of the same species brought for a *yoledes*, neither yet designated, are genuinely indistinguishable. That is why the Torah's process — designation at purchase or by the *kohen* — is both necessary and meaningful in the bird case, and not applicable in the case of clearly self-differentiating animals.

## Mum Equivalence

### Hamnuna Challenge

Rav Hamnuna raises a challenge against the position that an animal with a *mum* is treated like *setumah* — like unspecified funds. The argument in favor of that position was that a blemished animal, which bears no *kedusha* restriction and can be sold immediately, is *mezuman*, cash-equivalent, and therefore falls within the *halacha* of *setumim*. But one might question whether this is correct. After all, an animal with a *mum* is still an animal; it is not money. Even on the view that certain things are treated as money-equivalents, does a blemished animal really belong in that category? Rav Hamnuna brings a *braita* to probe this question.

## Father's Funds
