### Father Dies

The *braita* — which is quoted here in abbreviated form, with the full version appearing at 30b — addresses the *halacha* of a son who shaves (i.e., brings the concluding *korbanot*) for his father's *nezirut*. The case is: the father was a *nazir*, set aside money for his *korbanot* (*hefrish maot le-neziruto*), and then died. Normally, when a *nazir* dies, unspecified money goes toward an *olah*. But if the son then declares: *hareini nazir al menat she-agalei'ach al maot Abba* — I will take upon myself *nezirut* on condition that I may use my father's money for my *korbanot* — and he makes this declaration after his father's death, then the money was set aside for the father's *nezirut*, the father has died, the money is available and not yet redirected, and the son becomes a *nazir* specifically to use those funds. In this case the son does get to use the father's money.

### Both Nezirim

The second case in the *braita* is where the son does not wait for his father to die. Both the father and the son are *nezirim* simultaneously. The father sets aside money for his own *nezirut* and then dies. The son then says he will use his father's money. Here he cannot, because when the father died with money set aside for his own *nezirut*, and the son was already a *nazir* at that time, the son is not entitled to redirect those funds. The money falls to *nedava* — it follows the normal *halacha* of unspecified funds and goes toward an *olah*.

### Specified Unspecified

The *braita* continues: *haitah lo behemah meforeshet* — if the father had animals that were already specified, *chatat tamut* — the *chatat* animal is left to die — *olah tikarev olah* — the *olah* animal is brought as an *olah* — *shelamim yiplu li-shelamim* — the *shelamim* animals are brought as *shelamim*. Unspecified money follows one rule; specified animals follow their own designations individually.

## Mum Equivalence (II)

### Animals Not Money

The Gemara now draws an inference from this *braita* relevant to Rav Hamnuna's challenge. The *braita* contrasts unspecified money, which goes to *nedava*, with specified animals, which go to their respective purposes. The Gemara asks: *mai lav afilu ba'alat mum* — is the contrast not saying that even animals with a *mum* do not have the *halacha* of *setumah*? That is, even blemished animals are treated as specified (and thus go to their own designated purposes), not like unspecified money? This would undermine the position that a blemished animal is equivalent to *ma'ot setumot*.

But the Gemara immediately notes that this inference is strained: the *braita* is explicitly speaking of *behemah meforeshet* — clearly specified animals. It is not making any statement at all about unspecified animals with blemishes. The contrast is between unspecified money and clearly specified animals, not between unspecified money and every possible type of animal. One might respond that the *braita* should have made its point more directly — if blemished animals are truly cash-equivalent, why not contrast unspecified money against unspecified blemished animals, which would be a more illuminating comparison?

### Dmei Hayinu Maot

The Gemara's resolution is clean and decisive: *ba'alat mum le-mai kedishah? Li-dmei* — a blemished animal's *kedusha* is oriented toward what? Toward its monetary value. It is going to be sold; its *kedusha* lives in its sale price. *Demei hayinu ma'ot* — and proceeds are themselves money. When the *braita* speaks of *ma'ot setumot*, unspecified money, this already encompasses blemished animals, because a blemished animal's *kedusha* is money-in-waiting. There was never a category distinction to begin with; the *braita*'s reference to money naturally includes anything whose *kedusha* is expressed through monetary proceeds.

This resolution clarifies the overall shape of the *sugya*. The *halacha* of *setumim* — the rule that unspecified funds go toward an *olah* — applies to money and to anything functionally equivalent to money: things that are readily liquidable and whose *kedusha* is carried by their monetary value. A blemished animal fits squarely within that category. An unblemished animal that cannot be sold pending the appearance of a *mum* does not. And the specific *halacha* of birds is governed not by the money-equivalence analysis but by the Torah's own process of designation through *likichat ba'alim* or *asiyat ha-kohen*, which leaves the birds genuinely *setumim* until one of those moments arrives.

---

# Nazir 28

## Unspecified Funds

### Intro: Pile of Funds

We pick up in the middle of 27b, at the point where *masiv Rava* — Rava raises a challenge. We are finally wrapping up the *sugya* concerning the pile of unspecified funds that goes toward an *olah* in the case of a *nazir*. Recall the background: the three *korbanot* of the *nazir* — the *shelamim*, the *chatas*, and the *olah* — could in principle come from a single pile of unspecified funds, and the *halacha* directs such funds toward the *olah*. We had been working through a long discussion about whether that *halacha* is limited to money or whether it applies to other objects as well — things like beams of wood, bars of precious metal, or animals with a blemish. Even within the position that it applies only to money, we did not take "money" entirely literally. The argument was that anything capable of being quickly and easily liquidated should be treated as equivalent to money — including, perhaps, blemished animals, which on account of their *kedusha* would presumably find a ready market and would not require an extended valuation process.

### Money vs. Objects

That is the backdrop for the current discussion. The question is whether blemished animals properly belong in the "money" category — that is, whether the *halacha* that unspecified funds go toward the *olah* would apply to them as well. If a person sanctified three blemished animals as non-specified funds for his *nezirut* and the *nezirut* was subsequently nullified, would those animals fall under this rule?

### Blemished Animals

Consider further: if one sanctified three cows — animals that cannot themselves be used as *korbanot* of a *nazir* — and then the person died or the *nezirut* was annulled, does the *halacha* that the unspecified *kedusha* devolves upon an *olah* apply? The answer would depend on whether those cows, blemished or otherwise inappropriate for sacrifice, are treated as equivalent to money or to specified sacrificial animals. This is the question one more attempt will try to resolve, before we proceed to the *mishna* on the following *daf*.

---

## Rava's Challenge

### Korban - Personal Sin

Rava raises a challenge from a *braita* that bears directly on this entire discussion. The *braita* draws on the *pasuk* describing the *chatas*: *nefesh ki techeta* — if a soul sins — *v'heivi korbano seirat izim al chatato asher chata* — he shall bring his *korban*, a she-goat, for the sin that he has sinned. The language of the verse is highly specific: it is his *korban*, for his sin. The *braita* proceeds to unpack that specificity at length.

*Bekorbano hu yotzei v'eino yotzei b'korban aviv* — a person fulfills his obligation with his own *korban*, not with his father's. This is the governing principle: a *chatas* is bound absolutely to the person who committed the transgression and to the specific sin for which it was designated. This principle, as we have been consistently noting, is why an animal sanctified as a *chatas* that cannot be used must be left to die — it cannot be redirected elsewhere.

There is, of course, a striking counterpoint in the law of *nezirut*: if a father sets aside an unspecified pile of money for his *nezirut* and then dies, a son who subsequently accepts *nezirut* with the express intention of using that money may in fact do so. The money may thus be redirected from father to son. But that is a special application of the rule of unspecified funds — and, crucially, it is only possible when the funds are *stumim*, unspecified, not when they have been designated for a particular *korban*. That distinction is central to everything that follows.

### Father's Chatas

The *braita* begins by positing the most apparently extreme case and then walking toward what might seem more lenient. Perhaps one cannot use his father's *korban* when the animal was set aside for a lighter category of sin and he wishes to apply it to a weightier category — *min hakal al hachamur* — or from a weightier to a lighter — *min hachamur al hakal*. In those cases the identity of the *korban* has been substantially altered, and clearly it cannot serve. But perhaps, the *braita* suggests, if one keeps it within the same category of sin — light for light, weighty for weighty — maybe using the father's *korban* for the son's equivalent obligation would be permissible?

*Talmud lomar: korbano* — the *pasuk* says "his," explicitly and deliberately. It is his *korban*, not his father's — even if the category of sin is identical.

### Chatas Specificity

The *braita* then introduces the next layer: *yachol lo yetze b'korban aviv uvehemah she-hifrish afilu min hakal al hakal min hachamur al hachamur* — perhaps it is clear that one cannot use his father's sacrifice even if it is within the same category, when the father actually sanctified a specific animal. That we understand. But what about a case where the father only set aside money, not a designated animal?

The justification for this concern is drawn from the *halacha* of *nezirut* itself. *She-harei adam megalayach al maot aviv b'nezirot bizman she-hen stumim v'lo bizman she-hen meforashim* — a person may use his father's money for his own *nezirut*, but only when those funds are *stumim*, unspecified. Once the father has designated a particular pile for a particular *korban* — this pile for the *chatas*, this pile for the *olah* — the son may not reassign it. The capacity to reassign exists only when the funds remain amorphous and undirected.

Nevertheless, the *braita* presses the question: since we do observe at least some flexibility with money in the context of *nezirut* — a son can use a father's unspecified funds — perhaps that flexibility extends to *chatas* money as well. If the father set aside money specifically designated for his *chatas* and died, perhaps the son can use it for the son's own *chatas*, on the theory that money is inherently more reassignable than a designated animal.

*Talmud lomar: korbano* — again the verse says "his." Even money that the father sanctified for a *chatas* cannot be used by the son. The *halacha* of unspecified funds permitting a son to use his father's money for *nezirut* does not extend to *chatas*. A *chatas* must be specifically his — from the outset, not inherited or redirected from someone else — whether the sanctified object is an animal or a pile of money.

### Own Money Limits

The *braita* now advances to a further question: what about reassigning one's own *chatas* funds? We have established that a person cannot use his father's *chatas* *korban* — not an animal, not money. But what about using his own money, sanctified for one *chatas*, for a different *chatas*?

*Yachol lo yetze b'behemah she-hifrish l'atzmo min hakal al hakal u-min hachamur al hachamur* — perhaps even for oneself, one cannot reassign an animal from one sin to another, even keeping it within the same category. And indeed the *braita* offers a demonstration of why not: if one set aside an animal for *chelev* and then slaughtered it with the intention of bringing it for *dam*, or vice versa — *sheharei lo ma'al v'lo kiper* — he has neither committed *me'ila* nor achieved atonement. He has not achieved atonement, because the animal cannot be reassigned from one sin to another; and because he has not succeeded in reassigning it, he has not technically misused *hekdesh* in the full sense. The attempted reassignment simply failed.

One might note that this argument is somewhat circular — it more assumes than proves the conclusion — but the *braita* takes it as established that an animal designated as a *chatas* for a specific sin cannot be reassigned even to a different sin of one's own.

This raises an interesting question: if I sanctified an animal for *chelev* and slaughtered it intending to bring it for *dam*, am I still *yotzei* for *chelev*? I have certainly not fulfilled my obligation for *dam*. But the animal was a *chatas* — just brought *shelo lishma*, for the wrong sin. The question of whether it might still satisfy the original designation is genuinely interesting, though we set it aside here.

The *braita* continues: *aval yotzei b'maot* — perhaps money, though, is more freely reassignable. If the father set aside money for *chelev* and the son wishes to use it for *dam*, or if a person set aside his own money for one *chatas* and wishes to redirect it to another — perhaps that works. The logic would be: *sheken im hifrish l'atzmo ma'ot min hachelev v'heivi al hadam... sheharei ma'al v'kiper* — because with money, if one were to redirect his *chatas* funds from one sin to another, he would actually have committed *me'ila* and achieved atonement. Unlike the animal case, where the reassignment simply fails, with money something seems to happen: an act of *me'ila* has occurred, and its effect may be to discharge the *kedusha* and allow the funds to be reapplied. The *talmud lomar: al chatato* — the verse says "for his sin," meaning *ad she-yehei korbano l'shum chatato* — his *korban* must be for the specific sin. Even money designated for one *chatas* cannot be redirected to another. The verse leaves no opening.

### Money & Me'ila

At this point, *Tosafot* provides an illuminating explanation of the logic underlying the *braita*'s argument about money and *me'ila*. *Tosafot* notes the correct textual reading: *she'ein mo'al v'kiper she'hame'ot ein bahem kedushat haguf* — the money does not possess *kedushat haguf*, intrinsic sanctity. This distinction is essential.

There are two levels of *kedusha* for objects dedicated to the *Beit HaMikdash*. *Kedushat haguf* refers to an object that is itself intrinsically sanctified — an animal designated as an *olah*, for instance, whose very body is consecrated for use. *Kedushat damim* refers to an object whose sanctity consists only in its monetary value — it is destined to be sold, with the proceeds used to acquire whatever is actually needed. Money set aside for a *korban* is *kedushat damim*: the money itself is not going to be burned on the altar; it will be used to purchase an animal.

This distinction bears directly on the laws of *me'ila*. When one misuses *hekdesh* in error — *be'shogeg* — the effect of that *me'ila* is to transfer the object out of *hekdesh*. But this desanctification operates differently for *kedushat haguf* versus *kedushat damim*. An object with *kedushat haguf*, even if misused, retains its intrinsic sanctity — one violation does not strip an *olah* of its identity as an *olah*. But an object with only *kedushat damim* is more loosely bound to the domain of *hekdesh*; it is essentially property of the *Beit HaMikdash* waiting to be liquidated. If such an object is misused *be'shogeg*, the act of *me'ila* effectively removes it from *hekdesh*, much as an act of theft removes something from its owner's domain.

Two conditions, then, govern whether *me'ila* results in desanctification: the misuse must be *be'shogeg* — not intentional — and the object must have *kedushat damim*, not *kedushat haguf*. Money designated for a *chatas* satisfies both: it has only *kedushat damim*, and if misused accidentally it would constitute *me'ila* that strips the *kedusha*. *Tosafot* articulates the inference: *dehazi lemifak l'chulin al yedei me'ila* — the money is susceptible to losing its *kedusha* through *me'ila*, which demonstrates that its *kedusha* is less permanently affixed to its identity. One might therefore argue that the *kedusha* is more fungible, and that a conscious reassignment to a different *chatas* should similarly be effective — since *be'shogeg* the act of reassignment would have worked, perhaps *be'mezid* it can work as well: *ho'il v'shayeich bo shinui b'shogeg*. This is the *braita*'s argument for why money *should* be reassignable to a different *chatas*.

The *talmud lomar: al chatato* closes the door even on this reasoning. Whatever the theoretical flexibility of money's *kedusha*, the verse insists that the *korban* must be designated for this specific sin. There is no room to reassign — not from father to son, not from one sin to another, whether the sanctified object is an animal or money.

It is worth noting the parallel this discussion bears to the concept of *shinui* in the laws of *geneiva*. When a thief effects a qualitative change — *shinui ma'aseh* or *shinui haguf* — in a stolen object, this can vest ownership in the thief under certain conditions. Here, the very act of *me'ila be'shogeg* functions as a kind of *shinui reshut*, a change of domain, that removes the object from *hekdesh*. There are *gemarot* that draw precisely this parallel between *ye'ush* and *shinui reshut* in the laws of theft and certain cases of *me'ila*.

One should also note that this *braita* is stylistically unmistakably *midrash halacha* — it moves verse by verse through the *pasuk*, deriving each successive rule from a subtle textual reading. While the *Gemara* does not signal whether a given *braita* derives from a *tosefta* or a *midrash halacha*, the sustained focus on the *pesukim* makes the origin here transparent.

### Braita Relevance

One might wonder what the relevance of this lengthy *braita* is to our original question about blemished animals and unspecified funds. The connection lies in one of the *braita*'s early moves: when considering whether money might be reassignable, the *braita* notes that a person can use his father's money for his own *nezirut* — but only when those funds are *stumim*, unspecified, *v'lo bizman she-hen meforashim*. The *braita* drew a contrast between money and animals: even in *nezirut*, a son cannot use his father's sanctified animal. It is only an unspecified pile of money that carries this reassignability.

That contrast — between money and animals in the context of what a son may use for his own *nezirut* — is what our *sugya* wants to analyze. The question is: when the *braita* says a son cannot use his father's animal, does *behemah* mean only the specifically designated unblemished sacrificial animals? Or does it also include blemished animals that cannot themselves be offered? The answer to that question determines whether blemished animals fall in the "money" category or the "animal" category for purposes of the *halacha* of unspecified funds.

---

## Objects = Money

### Blemished Animals?

The *Gemara* now draws on that line in the *braita* directly. *Katani miha* — at least the *braita* teaches: a son cannot reuse his father's animal for *nezirut*, but he can reuse his father's money. When the *braita* says "animal," does it mean *afilu ba'alet mum* — even a blemished animal? If so, then even blemished animals are not in the money category and cannot be reassigned — which would mean they do not fall under the *halacha* of unspecified funds going toward the *olah*.

The *Gemara* rejects this reading: *lo temimah* — no. When the *braita* said "animal" in the context of things a son cannot reassign for his own *nezirut*, it was referring to unblemished animals, the properly designated sacrificial animals. Those are the ones whose identity is so concretely fixed that they cannot be reassigned even in *nezirut*.

### All = Money

The *Gemara* then presses further: *aval ba'alet mum mai?* — but what do you want to say about blemished animals? Would you say *kistuma damya* — that they are treated like an unspecified pile of money and may be reassigned? If so, then why does the *braita* mention only money — *maot she-hifrish aviv* — as the category of things a son may use? Why not also mention blemished animals, or beams of wood, or any other non-sacrificial object?

The answer is straightforward: *hacha nami* — those other objects are equally included. *D'lamai khazya? Lidmai* — for what are they fit? For their monetary value, their proceeds. Anything that is not itself going to be used as the sacrifice — whether it is cash, a blemished animal, a beam of wood, or any other object — is fit only to be sold, with the proceeds going toward the ultimate purpose. In that sense, everything in this category is equivalent to money. *Demei hani maos* — it is all in the same category as the pile of money.

The *Gemara*'s method here is instructive. The difficulty throughout this long *sugya* arose because the *mishnayot* and *braitot* dealt with two poles — an amorphous pile of money on one side, and a concretely specified sanctified animal on the other — leaving ambiguous everything that falls between. The *Gemara* now resolves that ambiguity definitively: the critical distinction is not between money and animals in the abstract, but between objects that will themselves be used as *korbanot* and everything else. Everything else — regardless of its form — is treated as money, because its *kedusha* is *kedushat damim*, value-based rather than identity-based. The mention of money in the *braita* was representative, not exhaustive.

With that, the *Gemara* brings this extended *sugya* to a close, and we turn to a new *mishna*.

---

## Annulment at Sacrifice

### Blood Sprinkled

The final *mishna* of this section addresses the annulment of a woman's *nezirut* by her husband at an extremely inopportune moment — not merely after she has set aside funds or animals, but while the *korbanot* are actually being brought. The husband has been away; he returns, finds his wife concluding her *nezirut* at the *Beit HaMikdash*, and seeks to annul her vow on the spot. The day of his return is the *yom shmoa* — the day he first learned of the vow — and so according to the laws of annulment, this is in principle the day he may act.

*Nizrak aleha echad min hadamim eino yachol lehafer* — if the blood of one of the sacrifices has already been sprinkled on her behalf, the husband can no longer annul. The reason is not procedural inconvenience. After even one *korban* has been completed, the restrictions of *nezirut* fall away from her. She may immediately drink wine. Since the husband's power to annul is grounded in the *nazir* vow's character as *inuy nefesh* — an affliction of the soul, a category encompassing vows that restrict the woman's conduct or impact their relationship — once the restrictions are lifted, that footing is gone. He no longer has any basis on which to annul.

### R. Akiva: Slaughter

*Rabbi Akiva omer afilu nishchata aleha achas mikol habehemah eino yachol lehafer* — Rabbi Akiva holds that he cannot annul even earlier, immediately after one of the animals has been slaughtered but before the blood has been sprinkled. At this moment, the woman is technically still bound by the restrictions of *nezirut* — the *korban* is not yet complete — and therefore the *Tanna Kamma* would permit the husband to annul. Rabbi Akiva disagrees.

The reason is *hefsed kodashim*. If the husband annuls after the animal has been slaughtered but before the blood is sprinkled, the *korban* — specifically, as the *Gemara* will clarify, the *chatas* — cannot be completed, since the woman is no longer a *nezirah*. The blood cannot be sprinkled for a *chatas* that no longer belongs to an obligated *nazir*, and the entire animal must be destroyed. This represents a devastating waste of a sacred object. Rabbi Akiva holds that the trivial benefit of escaping one final minute of the wine restriction does not justify this destruction. What would she even do — drink wine in the *Beit HaMikdash*? The disproportion between gain and loss is so stark that Rabbi Akiva forbids the annulment at this stage.

*Tosafot* raises a fascinating question: if the husband ignores this ruling and annuls anyway, does the annulment take effect? The question is whether *yesh koach beyad chachamim la'akor davar min haTorah* — whether the Sages can void what would otherwise be a biblically valid annulment on policy grounds. *Tosafot* leaves this unresolved.

### When Annul Ends

The positions of the *Tanna Kamma* and Rabbi Akiva thus represent different thresholds. The *Tanna Kamma* holds that once the blood of even one *korban* has been sprinkled, the husband can no longer annul — since the restrictions have lapsed. Rabbi Akiva extends the prohibition one step earlier: even after slaughter, before sprinkling, if annulling would destroy the *chatas*, he cannot annul. Both positions turn on the interplay between the husband's residual standing to annul and the cost — in wasted *kodashim* — of exercising that standing at this late stage.

---

## Tamei & Shaving

### Tamei Case

The *mishna* draws a distinction between *tiglachat tahara* — the normal shaving that concludes *nezirut* after a complete, uninterrupted term — and *tiglachat tumah*, the shaving that follows after the *nezirah* has become ritually impure. In the *tumah* case, the woman must begin her *nezirut* anew — an additional full month stretches ahead of her. In such a case, *yafeh* — even if the *chatas* from the *tumah* process has already been slaughtered and the blood has not yet been sprinkled, or even after the blood has been sprinkled, the *Tanna Kamma* holds that the husband can still annul. Why? *Shehu yachol lomar: ee efshi b'isha menuvelat* — because he can say, I do not want a wife whose appearance is disorderly. But more substantively, since there is a full month of *nezirut* still ahead of her, the *nezirut* is far from over. The reason annulment was barred in the *tahara* case was that after one *korban* the restrictions were effectively finished. Here, with a full month remaining, there is ample basis for the husband to annul, regardless of what stage the *korbanot* have reached.

### R. Meir: Final Stage

*Rabbi Meir omer: af betiglachat tahara yafer mipnei she-yachol lomar ee efshi b'isha megulachat* — Rabbi Meir holds that even in a normal *tahara* process, even after all three animals have been brought and only the final shaving remains, the husband may annul. His justification: he can declare that he does not want his wife to shave her head. Even at the final moment, that declared preference constitutes sufficient grounds for annulment, and the *halacha* entitles him to prevent that last stage.

---

## Chatas & Shelo Lishma

### Olah/Shelamim OK

Rabbi Zeira challenges the ruling of Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Akiva had held that after the animal is slaughtered but before the blood is sprinkled, the husband cannot annul because the *chatas* would be destroyed. But Rabbi Zeira asks: *v'amai? V'lizrok daman shelo lishman v'yishtarei b'chamra* — why is there any problem at all? Even after the annulment, simply sprinkle the blood — it will be brought *shelo lishma*, for an unintended purpose, since the woman is no longer a *nezirah*, but an *olah* or *shelamim* brought *shelo lishma* is still *kasher*. The meat will be permissible; the *korban* is not wasted.

### Shelo Lishma Valid

The *Gemara* supports this from a *braita* concerning *kivsei atzeret* — the lambs brought on *Shavuot* in conjunction with the *shtei halechem*. If those lambs were slaughtered *shelo lishman*, or before or after *Shavuot*, the ruling is: *hadam yizarek v'basar ye'achel* — sprinkle the blood and eat the meat. Even brought at the wrong time or for the wrong purpose, they remain valid. If it fell on *Shabbat*, the sprinkling should not be done *ab initio* — since the wrong purpose removes the basis for overriding *Shabbat* — but if done, it is valid, and the *imurin* are burned that evening.

The *braita*'s relevance is that it demonstrates the general principle: *korbanot* other than a *chatas*, brought *shelo lishma*, remain valid. The case of *kivsei atzeret* is particularly instructive because it also encompasses situations where the intent may be correct but the context is wrong — bringing at the wrong time, for instance, is itself a form of *shelo lishma*. The annulment case is analogous: the person slaughtering may intend correctly, but by virtue of the woman's no longer being a *nezirah*, the *korban* is by definition not being brought for its intended purpose. Nevertheless, it remains valid.

Thus, if we are dealing with an *olah* or *shelamim*, Rabbi Akiva would have no objection to annulling — simply complete the *korban* as a voluntary offering.

### Chatas Unique

*Aval hacha b'mai askinan? K'gon she-shachat chatas b'reisha* — the case Rabbi Akiva is addressing is specifically where the *chatas* was slaughtered first. The *halacha* is *gilach al achat mishaloshan yatza* — shaving over any one of the three *korbanot* concludes the *nezirut*, so the *chatas* need not be first in order — but Rabbi Akiva's ruling applies to the scenario where the *chatas* is the first animal slaughtered. A *chatas* brought *shelo lishma* is invalid — unlike an *olah* or *shelamim*, a *chatas* for the wrong person or wrong purpose does not merely fail to satisfy its obligation; it is an entirely invalid *korban* and must be destroyed. Therefore, once the *chatas* has been slaughtered, annulling the *nezirut* before the blood is sprinkled would leave an unusable carcass. There is no option of simply completing it as a valid offering. This is why Rabbi Akiva says: we will not allow the annulment, even though technically the woman is still bound by the restrictions for one more moment — because the cost, the total destruction of the *chatas*, is wildly disproportionate to the benefit.

If the first animal slaughtered had been the *olah* or the *shelamim*, Rabbi Akiva would agree with the *Tanna Kamma*: the husband may annul, since those animals can still be validly offered even after the annulment, *shelo lishma*.

---

## Tamei & Shaving (II)

### Wig Debate

We return to complete the *mishna*. The *Tanna Kamma* holds that in a normal *tahara* conclusion, once the blood of one *korban* has been sprinkled, the husband can no longer annul. Rabbi Meir holds that he may annul even at the final stage — even after all three *korbanot* have been brought — to prevent her from shaving, declaring *ee efshi b'isha megulachat*: I do not want a bald wife.

The *Tanna Kamma* responds: *efshar b'pe'ah nachris* — she can wear a wig. The husband's complaint that he does not want a shaved-headed wife is not a compelling objection if the condition is remediable through a wig. Since she can cover the shaved head, the claimed hardship is not real, and the husband has no standing to annul merely to prevent the shaving.

Rabbi Meir, however, is not persuaded: *depei nachris idi d'zuama lo nicha lei* — a wig, being foreign hair, has an unfamiliar smell. It does not smell like her own hair. The husband may legitimately object to that difference, and therefore his stated preference not to have her undergo the shaving remains a genuine and valid basis for annulment, even at this final stage.

---

---

# Nazir 29

## Father Making Son Nazir

### Age Limits Debate

The Gemara opens with the suggestion that the Amoraic debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish — concerning whether a father's power to impose *nezirut* on his son derives from a special *halacha* or from the rabbinic concept of *chinuch* — may be rooted in an earlier Tannaitic dispute. The Gemara introduces a *baraita* with the question: *ad matai madzir beno benazir* — until what age can a father make his son a *nazir*?

### Rabbi's Halacha View

Rabbi answers: *ad sheyavi shtei se'arot* — until the son brings two pubic hairs, i.e., until the son reaches full halachic adulthood at thirteen. In Rabbi's view, the father retains the power to impose *nezirut* on his son as long as the son remains a minor in the complete sense. Even if the son may have already acquired a certain degree of independence in the realm of vows, the son is still fundamentally under the father's jurisdiction as long as he has not reached full maturity.

### R. Yose Chinuch View

Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda takes a different position: *ad sheyagia le'onat nedarim* — until the son arrives at the age of vow-making. This refers to the year preceding *bar mitzvah*, during which a child who sufficiently understands the meaning and gravity of a vow may make one that is halachically binding. This status is known as *mufla samuch l'ish* — literally, one who can enunciate vows and is close to adulthood. The capacity to make independent vows, according to Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda, removes the son from his father's sphere of authority in this domain. The underlying rationale is that *chinuch* — the father's obligation to train his son in *mitzvot* — is the conceptual basis for the father's power here. Once the son can himself function as an agent in the area of *nedarim*, the justification for *chinuch* falls away.

### Gemara Reconciliation

The Gemara pauses before concluding that this Tannaitic debate straightforwardly maps onto the Amoraic one. The positions could align, but it is not self-evident that they must. The debate between thirteen and twelve does not automatically imply a debate about *halacha* versus *chinuch*, because each of those two conceptual positions could potentially lead to either age cutoff. The Gemara therefore explores two distinct approaches to reading the Tannaitic dispute.

### Halacha Approach

The first approach posits that *dechulei alma halacha hi benader* — both Rabbi and Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda agree that the father's power to impose *nezirut* on his son is a *halacha*, not a rabbinic device of *chinuch*. The point of contention is a different one: *vehacha bemufla samuch le'ish kamiflagi* — they disagree about the legal status of *mufla samuch l'ish*.

Rabbi holds that *mufla samuch l'ish d'rabanan* — the son's independent vow-making capacity in the year before *bar mitzvah* is only a rabbinic institution. Since the father's power derives from a *halacha* — and this Gemara clearly assumes that *halacha* here means *d'oraita* — *ve'ata de'oraita dachi d'rabanan*: a biblical rule overrides a rabbinic one. Therefore, the father retains the power to impose *nezirut* on his son even during the year of *onat nedarim*.

Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, holds that *mufla samuch l'ish de'oraita* — the son's independent capacity for vows during that year is a biblical status. And since *nezirut* is itself a form of vow, even a *halacha*-based power in the father cannot override the son's biblically recognized independence in that very domain.

### Halacha L'Moshe Status

This raises an important question about the nature of *halacha* itself. The Gemara never actually uses the phrase *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* — it says only *halacha*. The assumption that *halacha* means *d'oraita* is operative in this sugya, but deserves scrutiny. There are cases where *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* is used rhetorically or metaphorically rather than literally — a notable example appears in a *mishnah* in Eduyot, which uses the phrase *halacha* to describe what is clearly a rabbinic obligation regarding *terumos u'maasros* in lands outside of Israel. Scholars have traced how the concept evolved across the Tannaitic and Amoraic periods, and the phrase does not invariably signal *d'oraita* status.

A second consideration: there is a view, associated with the Netziv, that the word *halacha* in certain contexts — particularly as Rashi uses it — may mean simply an ancient tradition, without carrying the full force of *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*. These caveats notwithstanding, the Gemara's own logic in this passage clearly treats *halacha* as *d'oraita*. The critical point is that the *halacha* here is not an entirely independent law but rather a detail within the existing *d'oraita* framework of *nezirut*. When a *halacha* supplies a parameter internal to a *d'oraita* category, it is naturally folded into that category's biblical standing. That is presumably why *halacha* here is treated as carrying *d'oraita* weight: it tells us something about how the *d'oraita* laws of *nezirut* operate, not about some independent, externally-derived rule.

### Chinuch Approach

The second approach argues in precisely the opposite direction: *dechulei alma k'dei l'chancho b'mitzvot* — everyone agrees the father's power is based on *chinuch*, and the entire institution is rabbinic. Here too, *mufla samuch l'ish* is *d'rabanan*. The question becomes which of two competing rabbinic institutions prevails.

According to Rabbi: *asi chinuch d'rabanan v'dachi mufla samuch l'ish d'rabanan* — the father's rabbinic obligation of *chinuch* overrides the son's rabbinic independence in vow-making. The father's role as trainer retains priority; the son's ability to make his own vows does not terminate the father's *chinuch* jurisdiction in this area. This is striking given that this framework already requires overriding numerous other halachic principles — *chullin b'azarah*, considerations of *shechitah*, and so forth. Adding one more override is consistent with the broader latitude the rabbis extended to the father's *chinuch* role.

According to Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda, once the rabbis established that a son of twelve has recognized independence in the realm of *nedarim*, that recognition itself removes him from the category of one requiring *chinuch* in this domain. The rabbis' acknowledgment of the son's capacity is not merely an incidental permission to make vows; it is a statement that the son is no longer a subject of the father's *chinuch* in this particular area. Therefore, *lo asi chinuch d'rabanan v'dachi mufla samuch l'ish* — the father's *chinuch* authority cannot override that recognized independence.

## Rabbi Chanina Story

### Chanina Story Setup

Having established the theoretical Tannaitic background, the Gemara now transitions to a concrete narrative. A *baraita* records: *ma'aseh b'Rebbi Chanina she'hadiro aviv b'nazir* — there was an incident involving Rabbi Chanina whose father had made him a *nazir*. When the *nezirut* was completed, he was brought before Rabban Gamliel. *V'haya Rabban Gamliel bodek bo leida im hevi shtei se'arot im lav hevi* — Rabban Gamliel examined him to determine whether he had brought two pubic hairs. The question was whether the father had validly imposed *nezirut* on the son, or whether the son had already been an adult at the time — in which case the father's act would have had no effect. Rabbi Yose, for his part, holds that what Rabban Gamliel was checking was not *shtei se'arot* but whether the boy *higia l'onat nedarim* — had reached the age of vow-making — meaning that the decisive question was whether the child was twelve and sufficiently understood the nature of vows.

### Chanina's Response

Before Rabban Gamliel could complete his inquiry, Chanina himself spoke up: *Rabbi, al tista'er livdok kani* — do not trouble yourself to examine me. *Im katan ani, eyei bishvil abba* — if I was a minor when my father imposed *nezirut* on me, then I am a *nazir* by virtue of my father's act. *Im gadol ani, eyei bishvil atzmi* — and if I was an adult, I hereby accept *nezirut* upon myself. Either way, I am a *nazir*. There is no need for the examination because the outcome is the same regardless.

### Gamliel's Praise

Rabban Gamliel was moved by this response. *Amar Rabban Gamliel venashko al rosho* — Rabban Gamliel kissed him on the head and declared: *muvtach ani be-zeh she-moreh halacha be-Yisrael* — I am certain this young man will grow up to render halachic decisions in Israel. The *baraita* records that it was not long before this prediction was fulfilled.

### Middle Adulthood Problem

The Gemara now presses harder. For Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda — who holds that the cutoff is *onat nedarim* — the case is relatively straightforward. If the boy had reached the age of vow-making, the father could not have imposed *nezirut*; if he had not, the father's imposition stands. Either way, Chanina's statement works: if he was still within the father's authority, the father's *nezirut* holds; if he was independent enough to make vows himself, he can accept *nezirut* on himself at that point. The analysis proceeds fluently.

The Gemara's challenge is directed primarily at Rabbi, who holds the threshold is *shtei se'arot* — full adulthood. There are three possible scenarios for when Chanina became an adult: before the father imposed *nezirut*, after the completion of the thirty-day period, or somewhere in the middle. The first two cases are manageable. If he was already an adult when the father acted, his silent acquiescence — or perhaps his verbal acceptance — makes him a *nazir* on his own terms. If he only became an adult after the thirty days were complete, the father's *nezirut* runs its course uninterrupted.

The problem is the third scenario. It emerges — explicitly in the *Tosefta*, and implicitly from the Gemara's reasoning — that if a son becomes a full adult *in the middle* of the thirty-day period his father imposed, that transition of legal status terminates the father's *nezirut* even without any active protest. The son's transition to independent legal standing simply dissolves the earlier imposition. If so, Chanina's statement — "either way I am a *nazir*" — is not accurate for every scenario. If Chanina became an adult on, say, day ten, the period that preceded his adulthood would be invalidated, and he could not simply count backward from the start and claim he completed a full *nezirut*.

### Adult Status Interrupts

The Gemara probes the asymmetry between *onat nedarim* and full adulthood more carefully. If it is the age of vow-making that matters, the fact that a boy arrives at *onat nedarim* mid-*nezirut* does not terminate the father's imposition. The father was entitled to impose the *nezirut* at the outset; the son's newly acquired capacity to make his own vows does not retroactively disrupt an already-operative process. The son's basic legal status has not fundamentally changed. He is still a minor in the general sense; he has merely acquired a limited, specific independence in the realm of vows.

Full adulthood, however — marked by *shtei se'arot* — is categorically different. Becoming a *bar mitzvah* represents a total transformation of legal status. It is not a narrow expansion of one competency; it is the complete emergence of the person as an independent legal subject. Therefore, according to Rabbi, who holds that the threshold is *shtei se'arot*, adulthood reached in the middle of the thirty-day period would genuinely rupture the father's *nezirut*. This is what makes Chanina's statement potentially problematic under Rabbi's view.

### Dual Acceptance

The Gemara's resolution involves a careful rereading of what Chanina actually said. Chanina's statement was not simply binary. It can be understood as an acceptance of *nezirut* from that very moment forward, regardless of when he became an adult. The question becomes whether this simultaneous declaration can cover all scenarios. For the scenario where Chanina became an adult precisely at the end of thirty days, the father's *nezirut* is intact and complete. For the scenario where he became an adult at the very beginning, his own verbal acceptance covered the *nezirut* from the start. The difficult case — adulthood in the middle — requires that Chanina's declaration on that day be treated as an independent acceptance of *nezirut* effective from that moment, with a full thirty days running from that point. By accepting *nezirut* upon himself regardless of circumstances, Chanina ensured that *mimah nafshach* — in any event — he would emerge as a valid *nazir* who completed a full thirty-day period: either his father's from the outset, or his own from whatever point adulthood arrived.

This observation about the difference between what terminates paternal *nezirut* and what merely precluded the father from imposing it in the first place is worth underscoring. Even Rabbi, who holds that the father retains authority until *shtei se'arot*, concedes that once *shtei se'arot* arrive, the father's *nezirut* ends — even mid-process and even without any active objection from the son. It is a structural termination, not a volitional one. The son's ability to object, mentioned in an earlier *mishnah*, operates on a different axis: even as a minor, a son can terminate the father's imposition through protest. That is a separate mechanism. The present case addresses the automatic legal effect of reaching adulthood itself.

## Using Father's Funds

### Mishnah Rule

The next *mishnah* introduces a distinct but related topic: the ability of a son to make use of funds his father had set aside for his own *nazir* sacrifices. The rule stated is that a son may use such funds, but a daughter may not: *ha'ish megalei'ach al nezirut aviv ve'ein ha'ishah megalei'achat al nezirut aviha*.

### After Death Case

The *mishnah* presents one configuration for this law: *mi shehaya aviv nazir vehifrish ma'ot stumim al neziruto umet* — a father who was a *nazir* and set aside undesignated funds for his *nezirut* and then died. Under normal circumstances, unspecified funds dedicated for *nezirut* go to an *olah*. But if the son thereafter declares: *hareini nazir al menat she'agalei'ach al me'ot abba* — I become a *nazir* on the condition that I may use my father's set-aside funds — the *mishnah* addresses whether this stipulation is effective. The *chiddush* is that funds which would otherwise be channeled to a communal *olah* can instead be redirected to the son's own *korbanot*, provided the son explicitly stipulates this at the time he accepts *nezirut*.

### Simultaneous Nazirs

A second configuration involves a case where father and son are *nezirim* simultaneously. The father sets aside funds for his own *nezirut* and then dies mid-process. May the son use those funds for his own *korbanot*?

The text of the *mishnah* and an accompanying *baraita* present the opinions of Rabbi Yosi and others, and there is a notable textual difficulty: *Tosafot* cites a *girsa* of the *mishnah* that is the exact reverse of what appears in the standard printed text. In the *girsa* consistent with the *baraita* that the Gemara quotes, Rabbi Yosi holds that the son may use the funds only if he accepted *nezirut* after the father's death, stipulating at that moment that he would use the father's funds. If the son and father were *nezirim* simultaneously, Rabbi Yosi holds *harei elu yiplu li-nedavah* — those funds go to a communal contribution and may not be used by the son. Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Yehuda appear to hold the opposite on the simultaneous case — that when son and father are *nezirim* at the same time, the son may use the father's funds.

The intuition behind the simultaneous case is suggestive: when father and son undertake *nezirut* together, it has the character of a shared family enterprise. The funds the father set aside are not entirely his alone in some moral sense; they belong to a joint endeavor. Accordingly, when the father dies, the funds pass naturally to the son who is continuing the same communal *nezirut*. In the after-death case, by contrast, the son's *nezirut* is an entirely independent undertaking — he has no special claim to the father's funds without an explicit stipulation.

### Halacha Reason

One might ask what halachic basis underlies any of this. The Gemara poses precisely this question — *mai ta'ama* — and Rabbi Yochanan responds simply: *halacha b'nazir hi*. There is no derivable source, no *pasuk*, no extension of *chinuch*. It is, as Rabbi Yochanan characteristically states in this tractate, simply a received tradition pertaining to *nezirut*. Reish Lakish, who elsewhere offers alternative reasoning, is silent here — presumably because there is no alternative to offer.

### Son-Only Rule

The Gemara then asks: is it not obvious that only a son and not a daughter is entitled to use the funds, given that a son inherits from his father and a daughter does not? The Gemara answers that this is not at all obvious. Consider a case where the deceased father left only a daughter — *de-leit lei ella barta* — and she stands to inherit all his other property. One might argue that since we learn the son's entitlement from the concept of *yerusha*, and she inherits just as he does, she should also be entitled to use the funds. The Gemara therefore must address this: *mahu de-teima yorshin gamrinan lah* — lest one say we derive her entitlement from the laws of inheritance. To this, Rabbi Yochanan's answer stands — *halacha b'nazir hi*, and the *halacha* specifies sons, not daughters. Even a daughter who would inherit all the father's ordinary property cannot use the dedicated *nazir* funds for her own *korbanot*. The *halacha* carries its own internal definition of who qualifies, independent of the general laws of *yerusha*.

This point illuminates a broader feature of *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* in this context. Not only does the *halacha* establish the basic rule that a son may use the father's funds — it also defines the precise contours of that rule: only sons, not daughters, even in a case where the daughter would be the sole heir. Without that component of the *halacha*, one would be tempted to extend the rule through reasoning from *yerusha*. The *halacha* forecloses that extension.

### Baraita Positions

The Gemara then asks whether the *rabanan* who disagree with Rabbi Yosi dispute his ruling at the first point — the case where the son accepts *nezirut* after the father died — or at the second point, the simultaneous case, or both. The *baraita* quoted in response makes Rabbi Yosi's position explicit: the son may use the funds when he stipulates this after the father's death, but not when they were *nezirim* simultaneously. Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Yehuda are cited in the *baraita* as holding that the simultaneous case also works — but the *baraita* does not make entirely clear whether they dispute the first case as well or only add the second. What does emerge is a spectrum of positions: Rabbi Yosi endorses only the after-death stipulation; others extend the permission to the simultaneous case; and whether any authority holds that the simultaneous case works while the after-death case does not remains to be resolved.

## Multiple Sons Funds

### Rava's Splitting

Rava raises a question that pushes at the limits of the *halacha*: what if a father had two sons, both of whom are *nezirim* and both of whom wish to use the father's dedicated funds? *Mahu* — what is the rule? Is this *halacha* a purely independent tradition within *nezirut* — one that operates without reference to *yerusha* — such that we say *kol dekadim galach galach*, whoever gets there first and uses the funds gets them, first come first served? Or does the *halacha*, despite its independent status, nonetheless draw upon the framework of *yerusha* in certain respects, such that the funds are divided equally between the two sons?

### Yerusha Connection

The question is whether the *halacha* is fully self-contained or whether it rides atop a *yerusha* infrastructure. If it is *yerusha*-governed in its details, then just as two sons would split the father's ordinary estate equally, each would receive an equal share of the *nezirut* funds to apply toward his *korbanot*. If it is purely independent, there is no particular reason why the funds should not simply go to whichever son acts first. The tension is meaningful: we have already seen that this *halacha* does not follow *yerusha* in every respect — daughters are excluded even when they are the only heir. But exclusion of daughters does not tell us how the funds are divided among multiple qualifying sons.

### Bechor Double Share

Rava's second question sharpens this further: what if one of the sons is a *bechor* — a firstborn son — and the other is a *pashut*, an ordinary son? In the normal laws of inheritance, the *bechor* receives a double portion. Does that double portion apply here as well? *Hilkheta gamrinan lah* — do we say this is purely a matter of *halacha* and therefore the *bechor* does not receive a double portion? Or do we say *yerusha hi* — the *yerusha* framework applies, and just as the *bechor* takes two portions of the father's ordinary estate, *hacha nami megale'ach* — so too he receives double the funds toward his *korbanot*?

### Chulin vs Hekdesh

The Gemara introduces a further distinction within the question about the *bechor*. Even if we say the *yerusha* framework applies, perhaps it applies only to *chulin* — ordinary property — and not to *hekdesh* — consecrated property. To understand this, the Rosh offers a more precise reading of the Gemara's language. He points out that the *gemara's* question about *chulin* and *hekdesh* is not a freestanding inquiry; it is a refinement of the *bechor* question specifically. According to the Rosh, the Gemara's formulation should be read as follows: even if we conclude that the *yerusha* framework governs how the funds are divided among the sons — so that each son receives a proportionate share — it might still be true that the *bechor*'s double portion does not apply, because the *bechor*'s entitlement to a double share may be categorically limited to *chulin*.

### Bechor Inapplicable

The basis for this distinction lies in the scriptural language used for *bechor* — *bechol asher yimatze lo* — the firstborn gets a double portion of all that is *found*, meaning all that is available. The term implies accessible, ordinary wealth. *Hekdesh* funds, however, are pre-designated and consecrated; they are not simply *found* in the estate as available resources. Therefore, even if the general *yerusha* framework extends to dividing *nezirut* funds between sons, the specific entitlement of the *bechor* to a double portion may not apply, because *hekdesh* property does not satisfy the criterion of *bechol asher yimatze lo*. The Rosh emphasizes that the *chulin*-*hekdesh* distinction is not a separate question the Gemara entertains alongside the *bechor* question — it is part of the *bechor* question itself, clarifying why the *bechor*'s double portion might not apply even under a *yerusha*-governed model.

### Different Nazir Types

Rava then asks: what if the father and son were different types of *nezirim*? For example, the father was a *nazir olam* — a perpetual *nazir* — while the son is a *nazir stam*, a standard thirty-day *nazir*. (A *nazir olam* does periodically bring *korbanot* — the *nezirut* of a *nazir olam* permits a haircut once every thirty days or annually, accompanied by the appropriate *korbanot* — so the dedicated funds are not without purpose.) The question is whether the *halacha* that permits the son to use the father's funds operates only when both are the same type of *nazir*, or whether it functions even across different categories of *nezirut*.

*Tosafot* notes that one could further ask whether the *halacha* applies even when both are *nazir olam* — perhaps the rule was only ever formulated for standard *nezirut*, not for *nezirut* of the *olam* variety. And even if both *nazir olam* types can access the funds, perhaps that only holds when father and son share the same type, not when one is *olam* and the other *stam*. In any event, if the different types of *nezirut* are both *nezirut tahara* — both involving purity-related sacrifices — there is an argument that the funds can be redirected, since they are fundamentally the same category of *korban*.

### Tamei-Tahor Funds

The final question is posed by Rav Ashi and concerns a more fundamental divergence. What if the father's funds were dedicated not for *nezirut tahara* but for *nezirut* in a state of *tumah* — the father had become *tamei* and set aside funds for the *korbanot* a *tamei* *nazir* must bring, which involve birds rather than the standard animals? Can the son, who is a *nazir tahor*, use those *korbanot tumah* funds for his own *korbanot tahara*? Conversely: *aviu nazir tahor vehu nazir tamei mai* — what if the father was *tahor* and the son is *tamei*?

These are not merely different *types* of *nezirut* — they represent categorically different *korbanot*, with different animals and different ritual contexts. The question is whether the *halacha* that transfers the father's dedicated funds to the son operates even across this kind of disparity. The Gemara leaves both versions of the question unresolved — *teiku*.

With that, the daf concludes: *hadran alach Mi She'amar*.

---

---

# Nazir 29b

## Father Making Son Nazir

### Yochanan vs. Reish Lakish

The *sugya* opens by asking whether the debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish — regarding whether a father's power to impose *nezirut* on his son is a special *halacha* particular to *nezirut*, or whether it derives from the rabbinic concept of *chinuch* — maps onto a parallel dispute among *Tannaim*. The *Gemara* introduces a *braita*: *ad masai madzir beno benazir* — until what age may a father make his son a *nazir*? Rabbi holds: until the son brings two pubic hairs, i.e., until he becomes a full adult at the age of thirteen. Rabbi Yose b'Rebbi Yehuda holds: until he reaches *onat nedarim* — the stage at which a minor may make binding vows.

This concept of *onat nedarim* requires some elaboration. A child — whether boy or girl — reaches *onat nedarim* one year before the age of majority: a year before a girl's *bat mitzvah* and a year before a boy's *bar mitzvah*. At this point, provided the child understands that he or she is making a vow to God and has basic comprehension of the act, the vow is considered binding. This status is known as *mufla samuch l'ish* — the ability to enunciate a vow while not yet a full adult. Whether this category is *d'oraisa* or *derabbanan* is itself a subject of considerable debate, as we will see.

### Tannaim: 13 vs. 12

The *Gemara* asks whether this *Tannaitic* dispute mirrors the *Amoraic* one. The initial reading suggests that Rabbi's position — that the father retains power until the son becomes a full adult with two pubic hairs — is consistent with viewing the father's authority as a *halacha*, an intrinsic legal power over his minor son. Even if the son has already reached *onat nedarim* and can make his own vows to some degree, the father's power is conceived broadly: the son is still a minor in the overall legal sense, and the father retains dominion over him until the son becomes a full adult. Rabbi Yose b'Rebbi Yehuda's position, by contrast — that the father's power ends already at *onat nedarim* — seems consistent with the *chinuch* framework: once the son has some independent standing in the domain of vows, the father's role as educator in that area becomes inapplicable.

### Halacha Debate: Mufla

The *Gemara* rejects this initial alignment, however. It offers a first alternative resolution: *d'chulei alma halacha hi b'nazir* — perhaps all agree that the father's power is a *halacha*, not merely *chinuch*. The debate concerns a different question entirely: what is the legal status of *mufla samuch l'ish*?

According to Rabbi, *mufla samuch l'ish* is *derabbanan*. The son's independent standing in vows at age twelve is only a rabbinic enactment. Since the father's authority to impose *nezirut* is a *halacha* — operating at the *d'oraisa* level — it overrides the son's merely rabbinic independence. Hence the father retains his power even past *onat nedarim*, all the way until the son is a full adult.

According to Rabbi Yose b'Rebbi Yehuda, *mufla samuch l'ish* is *d'oraisa*. If the son possesses biblically recognized independence in the domain of vows, then even a *halacha* granting the father power over his son should not extend into an area where the son is biblically autonomous. Since *nezirut* is itself a form of *neder*, and the son is independently recognized by the *Torah* as a party to vows, the father cannot impose *nezirut* on him once he reaches *onat nedarim*. The dividing line is therefore not *chinuch* versus *halacha*, but rather *d'oraisa* versus *derabbanan* status of the son's independence.

A natural question arises: does the *Gemara* actually use the phrase *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*, or merely *halacha*? In fact, the *Gemara* uses only the word *halacha*. The assumption that *halacha* implies *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* and therefore *d'oraisa* status is standard, but two qualifications deserve mention. First, there are well-known instances where *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* is used rhetorically rather than literally — the *Mishnah* in *Eduyos* speaks of *halacha* that Ammon and Moav tithe *ma'aser ani* in the seventh year, a ruling that is clearly *derabbanan*, yet the phrase is used. Second, some authorities, including the *Netziv*, suggest that *halacha* in certain contexts may simply denote an ancient tradition without carrying the full technical weight of *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*. Nevertheless, the *Gemara* here clearly operates on the assumption that *halacha* functions at the *d'oraisa* level, since the entire dynamic depends on the father's authority being able to override the son's *derabbanan* independence — not his *d'oraisa* independence. What may further support treating it as *d'oraisa* here is that we are not dealing with a wholly new independent ruling, but rather with a parameter internal to the *d'oraisa* laws of *nezirut* themselves — a detail about the scope of the *Torah*'s framework already in place.

### Chinuch Framework

The *Gemara* then presents a second approach: *d'chulei alma k'dei l'chancho b'mitzvot* — perhaps all agree the father's authority is based on *chinuch*, and the entire institution is *derabbanan*. Moreover, *mufla samuch l'ish* is also *derabbanan* on all views. We therefore have two rabbinic forces in tension: the father's *chinuch* obligation on one side, and the son's rabbinic independence in vows on the other.

Rabbi holds that in this collision, we tip in favor of *chinuch*: *ati chinuch d'rabbanan v'dachi mufla samuch l'ish d'rabbanan*. The father's *chinuch* role prevails, and the son's limited rabbinic independence in vows does not terminate the father's power. This approach also helps explain why *chinuch* in the context of *nezirut* can override other principles — such as *chullin ba'azarah* and *shechitah l'of* — that are similarly *derabbanan*: we are already in a domain of rabbinic accommodation.

Rabbi Yose b'Rebbi Yehuda holds the reverse: once the rabbis recognized the son's independent standing in the area of *nedarim*, that recognition itself removes him from the *chinuch* framework in this domain. *Chinuch* is predicated on the child being a non-agent in the relevant area. Once the child can act independently — even rabbinically — the father's *chinuch* role falls away.

The *Gemara* concludes that the *Tannaitic* dispute cannot be cleanly mapped onto a single underlying question. Either it is about the *d'oraisa* versus *derabbanan* status of *mufla samuch l'ish* within an overall *halacha* framework, or it is about which rabbinic principle prevails when two *derabbanan* institutions conflict. The lines do not divide neatly.

---

## Rabbi Chanina Case

### Chanina's Story

The *Gemara* introduces a *braita* containing a real-life illustration of this debate: *maaseh b'Rabbi Chanina* — there was a case involving Rabbi Chanina whose father had made him a *nazir*. He was brought before Rabban Gamliel, who wished to investigate the matter. Rabban Gamliel sought to determine whether the boy had already reached adult status when his father imposed the *nezirut* — because if the son had already been a full adult at that point, the father's act would have been ineffective. The question, as framed by the two opinions, was either whether the boy had two pubic hairs (Rabbi's position — the test for full adulthood), or whether he had already reached *onat nedarim* (Rabbi Yose b'Rebbi Yehuda's position — the earlier threshold).

The young Chanina, demonstrating remarkable presence of mind, said to Rabban Gamliel: do not trouble yourself with the examination. If I was a minor when my father imposed *nezirut* on me, then I am a *nazir* on account of my father — *eheye bishvil aba*. And if I was already an adult, then I accept *nezirut* upon myself now regardless — *eheye bishvil atzmi*. Either way, I am a *nazir*.

Rabban Gamliel rose and kissed him on his head, and declared: *muvtach ani beze sheyoreh halacha beyisrael* — I am confident that this young man will one day teach *halacha* in Israel. And indeed, we are told, it was not long before that prediction came true.

### Mid-Period Majority

The *Gemara* initially poses what the *Rosh* characterizes as a somewhat throwaway question — noting that it is easy to understand Chanina's reasoning according to Rabbi Yose b'Rebbi Yehuda, since reaching *onat nedarim* is that opinion's threshold, and Chanina's statement that he would accept *nezirut* himself if he had reached *onat nedarim* fits naturally. The harder question, according to Rabbi, is this: if the test is two pubic hairs and full adulthood, then when Chanina said "if I am an adult, I accept it for myself," he was presumably speaking of that same standard. But then the *Gemara* quickly moves to what is the real question.

The *Gemara* identifies three scenarios: the son was already an adult when his father made him a *nazir*; he became an adult after the thirty days of *nezirut* concluded; or he became an adult in the middle of the thirty-day period. The first two cases are straightforward. If he was already an adult at the outset, his acquiescence — whether silent or verbal — renders it his own *nezirut*, and it concludes after thirty days. If he became an adult only after the thirty days ended, the *nezirut* was entirely that of the father and it concludes naturally.

But the middle case is genuinely difficult. The *Tosefta* makes explicit what the *Gemara* assumes: if a son becomes a full adult in the middle of the *nezirut* his father imposed, becoming an adult in itself terminates whatever his father had begun — just as the *Mishnah* earlier discussed how the son's protest or the relatives' shaving terminates the *nezirut*. Reaching full legal adulthood functions as an automatic termination, even without any explicit act of protest. This creates a significant problem for Chanina's declaration.

### Termination Criteria

The *Gemara* now asks why the analysis differs depending on whether the dividing line is *shtei se'arot* (two pubic hairs, full adulthood) or *onat nedarim* (the ability to make vows). The answer turns on a fundamental distinction between these two thresholds.

Reaching *onat nedarim* grants the son a limited form of independence in the specific domain of vows. But it does not change his overall legal status. He is still a minor in every other sense. Consequently, while *onat nedarim* would be strong enough to prevent the father from imposing *nezirut* at the outset — since in the area of *nedarim* the son is now an independent actor — it is not strong enough to terminate a *nezirut* already underway. The father was fully empowered to impose *nezirut* before *onat nedarim* arrived. The fact that the son now has some limited independence in the realm of vows does not retroactively undo what was validly imposed. His fundamental legal status remains that of a minor.

By contrast, *shtei se'arot* — full adulthood — represents a complete transformation of legal status. The son is now a new legal person in every domain, not merely in one limited area. That complete transformation is powerful enough to terminate whatever the father had begun, even mid-period, without any explicit protest.

### Counting Periods

This asymmetry resolves the *Gemara*'s problem according to Rabbi Yose b'Rebbi Yehuda. Under that opinion, reaching *onat nedarim* mid-period does not interrupt the *nezirut* at all. The thirty days run continuously from when the father imposed it. So Chanina's declaration — "either way I am a *nazir*" — works perfectly: whether the father's *nezirut* was valid from the start or not, thirty days from the outset suffices.

Under Rabbi's opinion, however, things are more complicated. If Chanina became an adult in the middle of the thirty days, the *nezirut* imposed by his father ended at that point. He would need to begin a fresh thirty-day count from the moment of adulthood, and bring his *korbanot* at the end of that period. So he cannot simply say "either way thirty days from the outset." He would need to account for the possibility that he became an adult partway through.

The *Gemara* resolves this: according to Rabbi, one would have to be more precise. If it became clear that Chanina became an adult mid-period, the appropriate approach would be to complete the father's thirty days, and then — if adulthood had not been reached at the very outset — accept a new *nezirut* from that moment forward, bringing *korbanot* only at the conclusion of an additional thirty days. In practical terms, since the precise moment of adulthood cannot always be established, one might need to accept *nezirut* and bring *korbanot* in a way that covers both possibilities. The *Gemara* leaves the precise resolution open but establishes that unlike Rabbi Yose b'Rebbi Yehuda's clean answer, Rabbi's position requires two separate counting periods depending on when adulthood was reached.

One might raise a comparison to *giur katan* — a minor who converts and upon reaching majority has the option to repudiate the conversion. There are genuine structural similarities: in both cases, a status was imposed on someone who was a minor, and full adulthood triggers a reassessment. Similarly, the *Minchas Chinuch* raises the celebrated question of a child who becomes a *bar mitzvah* in the middle of *sefiras ha'omer* — does the counting before adulthood count toward the *d'oraisa* obligation of counting fifty days, or was it entirely without legal meaning? The same logic applies here.

What emerges from this *sugya* is a subtle distinction: the threshold that prevents imposition going forward (*onat nedarim*) is not necessarily the same threshold that terminates an ongoing *nezirut* (*shtei se'arot*). Nor is a minor's right to protest — which can end the *nezirut* even without adulthood — identical to the automatic termination triggered by becoming an adult. Each operates by its own logic.

---

## Son Using Father's Funds

### Mishna Scenarios

The *Gemara* now turns to the next *Mishnah*, which addresses a distinct but related father-son question: may a son use funds that his father had designated for his own *nezirut* sacrifices? The *Mishnah* opens with the ruling that a son may do so — but a daughter may not. The details of how and when this applies are then spelled out.

The *Mishnah* distinguishes two scenarios. In the first, which Rabbi Yosi presents as the case where the mechanism does *not* apply, a son becomes a *nazir* after his father has already died, and declares: *hareini nazir al menas she'agale'ach al ma'os abba* — I accept *nezirut* on condition that I use my father's funds. In the second scenario, which Rabbi Yosi identifies as the case where it does apply: the son and the father were both *nezirim* simultaneously, the father set aside unspecified funds — *ma'os setumim* — for his own *nezirut*, and then the father died.

It should be noted that this is the *girsa* supported by the *braita* quoted shortly thereafter in the *Gemara*, which is the reverse of what appears in some printed versions of the *Mishnah*. Relying on that *braita*, where Rabbi Yosi's position is stated explicitly, we read the *Mishnah* as well with Rabbi Yosi holding that only the simultaneous case works — not the post-death acceptance.

What underlies the difference between these two scenarios? When father and son are *nezirim* at the same time, there is something that might be described as a family religious undertaking — a shared *nezirut* enterprise. In that context, when the father dies, the funds he designated flow to the son as a natural extension of what had already been a shared process. When the son only accepts *nezirut* after the father's death, he is an entirely independent actor, and the father's designated funds — which are *hekdesh*, consecrated property — cannot simply be redirected for someone else's *korbanot*.

There is also a first version of this mechanism, which in the *Mishnah* as initially read seems to be the case that works: the son stipulates from the outset that he will use the father's money. In that version, the logic is different. Unspecified funds — *ma'os setumim* — have a certain indeterminacy about their destination; they normally go to an *olah*. If the son at the moment of accepting his own *nezirut* declares that his *nezirut* is predicated on using those funds, he creates a link between his *nezirut* and those funds from the beginning.

### Halacha: Son Not Daughter

The *Gemara* asks for the rationale underlying the son's ability to use his father's funds. Rabbi Yochanan answers simply: *halacha hi b'Nazir* — it is a *halacha* specific to *nezirut*. There is no *pasuk*, no *chinuch* argument, no logical derivation. This is a traditional ruling. Notably, unlike other places where Rabbi Yochanan offers *halacha* as one possible explanation alongside others, here it appears to be the only available answer, and Reish Lakish offers no alternative.

The *Gemara* then asks: is it not obvious that only a son and not a daughter may use the father's funds? A son inherits his father; a daughter does not, except in the absence of sons. Since these are *hekdesh* funds, the ability to use them follows an inheritance-like logic, and of course a daughter inherits differently. The *Gemara* responds: *lo tzricha d'leis lei ela barta* — the *chiddush* is needed for the case where the father had only a daughter, who would in that case inherit all his other property. One might think that since the *halacha* is framed in terms of inheritance and she is the heir, she should be entitled. The *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* — or the *halacha* itself — tells us this is not so. The right belongs specifically to a son, not to a daughter, even when she is the sole heir.

This is a striking ruling. The *halacha* is acknowledged to be somewhat arbitrary in its parameters — there is no broader principle that straightforwardly generates these details. That is precisely what makes it a *halacha*: it is an ancient tradition whose contours are simply received rather than derived.

### Braita Positions

The *Gemara* then raises the question: do the *rabbanan* actually disagree with Rabbi Yosi, and if so, on which point? As noted, Rabbi Yosi (working with the *girsa* supported by the *braita*) holds that the mechanism works when the son accepts *nezirut* after the father's death with explicit stipulation. The rabbis might agree with this and add that it also works when they were *nezirim* simultaneously — a broader position. Or the rabbis might hold the exact mirror image of Rabbi Yosi, saying it works only when they were *nezirim* simultaneously and not after death. Or there may be an even broader position that both scenarios work.

The *braita* is then cited: it presents Rabbi Yosi's position explicitly — the post-death stipulation works; simultaneous *nezirut* does not. It then records that Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Yehuda all hold that the simultaneous case also works — *zehu shemegalei'ach al maos aviv*. What remains unclear is whether these latter authorities also include the post-death case or limit themselves to the simultaneous scenario. The *Gemara* notes this ambiguity and does not fully resolve which cases the *rabbanan* include or exclude. What is visible is the range: Rabbi Yosi anchors one position; Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Yehuda take a broader view regarding simultaneous *nezirut*; and the exact scope of their disagreement with Rabbi Yosi remains partially open.

---

## Multiple Sons & Yerusha

### Two Sons Division

With the basic framework established, the *Gemara* turns to a series of questions probing how far the analogy to *yerusha* — inheritance law — governs the operation of this *halacha*. These questions are raised as *ba'yot* by *Rabbah* and *Rava*.

The first: what if the father left two sons, both of whom are *nezirim* and both of whom wish to use their father's designated funds? Do we say that this entire institution has nothing to do with *yerusha* — in which case it is simply first come, first served: *kol de-kadim gille'ach gille'ach*, whoever brings his *korbanot* first gets to use the funds? Or do we say that *yerushah gemiri lah* — this *halacha* is nonetheless shaped by the principles of inheritance — in which case each son receives half?

One might further ask: at what point must both sons be *nezirim* in order for both to assert a claim? If one son becomes a *nazir* twenty days into the other's *nezirut*, or after the first son's thirty days are already complete but before the first son has brought his *korbanot*, does the second son have standing to claim half? The *Gemara* does not explore these complications here, focusing on the simpler case where both sons are *nezirim* simultaneously. The question of principle remains: is this a pure *halacha* with no *yerusha* logic embedded in it, or does it import *yerusha* principles?

### Bechor Double Portion

*Rava* sharpens the question: what if one son is a *bekhor* — a firstborn — and the other is a *pashut*, an ordinary son? By the laws of *yerusha*, the *bekhor* receives a double portion: *pi shenayim*. Does that double portion apply here as well?

If we say *halakhah gemiri lah* — this is a pure *halacha* with no *yerusha* logic — then perhaps the sons divide equally, and the *bekhor* has no special claim. If we say *yerushah hi* — it follows *yerusha* principles — then the *bekhor* should receive twice what his brother receives of the father's *hekdesh* funds, just as he would receive a double portion of ordinary estate property.

But the *Gemara* then adds a further refinement, reflecting the analysis of the *Rosh*. Even if we generally apply *yerusha* principles, perhaps the *bekhor*'s double portion is a special case that does not extend to *hekdesh*. The *bekhor*'s entitlement to *pi shenayim* is derived from the verse *b'chol asher yimatzei lo* — from whatever is found, whatever is available to him. The word implies accessible, available assets. *Hekdesh* funds, however, are not "available" in the ordinary sense — they are pre-consecrated property. One might argue that the *bekhor*'s special double portion, grounded in this language of availability, simply does not apply to *hekdesh* funds, even if the general *yerusha* principle of division between sons does.

The *Rosh* argues that the phrase *u-ve-chullin hu de-it leh pi shenayim aval be-hekdesh lo* — that the *bekhor* gets a double portion from *chullin* but not from *hekdesh* — is not raising an entirely new question but rather clarifying the question about the *bekhor*. It is not, as *Tosafos* suggests, a matter of how the father verbally designated the funds (whether he said *nezirusi* versus *korbanos nezirusi*). The *Rosh* dismisses that reading as *pirush zar* — a strained explanation — since there is no meaningful legal difference between those formulations.
