Rather, the question is structural: even granting that *yerusha* principles govern the division of funds between sons, does the *bekhor*'s specific entitlement to *pi shenayim*, which is textually anchored in the concept of available assets, extend into the realm of *hekdesh*? That is the unresolved question.

### Nazir Types

The *Gemara* then asks a further question: what if father and son are different *types* of *nezirim*? The case: the father is a *nazir olam* — a lifelong *nazir* — and the son is a *nazir stam*, a standard thirty-day *nazir*. Or the reverse. Can funds designated for one type of *nezirut* be used by someone observing a different type?

A brief clarification: a *nazir olam* does not bring *korbanot* at the conclusion of a fixed term, since there is no fixed term. Rather, a *nazir olam* takes a haircut periodically — once every thirty days by some views, once a year by others — and brings *korbanot* at that time. So the question of designated funds is still relevant.

The question is whether the *halacha* allowing the son to use the father's funds was formulated specifically for standard *nezirut* — *stam nezirut* — or whether it extends to any combination of *nezirut* types. *Tosafos* further notes that one might even question whether this *halacha* applies when both are *nazir olam* — perhaps it was specifically calibrated for standard *nezirut* alone.

### Tamei/Tahor Transfer

Finally, *Rav Ashi* poses the most acute version of the question: what if the father's funds were not merely designated for a different *type* of *nezirut*, but were designated for a qualitatively different sacrificial purpose? Specifically, if the father had become *tamei* — ritually impure — and set aside funds for *korbanot* of *nezirut tumah* (which involve different animals, including birds), and the son's *nezirut* is *nezirut tahara* — pure *nezirut* — may the son use those funds? The *korbanot* of *nezirut tumah* and *nezirut tahara* are not merely different in magnitude or proportion; they are categorically distinct offerings. And the reverse: if the father's funds were for *nezirut tahara* and the son's *nezirut* is *tamei* — what then?

The *Gemara* leaves this unresolved: *teiku*. The questions about two sons, the *bekhor*, the different types of *nezirut*, and the *tamei/tahor* transfer remain open, marking the close of the tractate's final discussion.

*Vehadran alach Mi She'amar.*

---

---

# Nazir 31

## Hekdesh Ta'us Intro

### Shammai/Hillel Dispute

Perek Hamishi opens with a dispute that, at first glance, seems to belong more naturally to the laws of *hekdesh* than to *nezirut*. The *mishnah* states: *Beis Shammai omrim hekdesh ta'us hekdesh* — Beis Shammai holds that a mistaken consecration is nonetheless a valid consecration. Beis Hillel disagrees: *ein hekdesh* — the consecration does not take effect. Taking the *mishnah* at face value, the question is whether an act of *hekdesh* grounded in a mistaken premise has any legal force.

### Link to Perek Sheini

This dispute does not arise in isolation. All the way back in Perek Sheini (daf 9), the *mishnah* records a parallel controversy: if someone declares *hareini nazir min ha-gerogerot u'min ha-devilah* — "I am a *nazir* from figs and pressed dates" — Beis Shammai says he is a *nazir* while Beis Hillel says he is not. The Gemara there explained: *Beis Shammai leta'myahu d'amri ein she'elah b'hekdesh, u'cheivan d'ein she'elah b'hekdesh ein she'elah b'nezirut* — Beis Shammai reasons that just as one cannot obtain release from *hekdesh*, so too one cannot obtain release from *nezirut*, since the Torah applies the word *kodesh* to the *nazir*, as in the *pasuk*: *kadosh yihyeh gadal peras se'ar rosho*. The stickiness of *hekdesh* thus anchors Beis Shammai's broader position on the irrevocability of *nezirut*.

### Shammai's Logic

Beis Shammai's reasoning, then, is that *hekdesh* is an unusually durable legal category — once something is consecrated, it cannot simply be undone. That same quality of durability is what Beis Shammai invokes here: if *hekdesh* cannot be released, it follows that even a mistaken *hekdesh* should take hold, since the underlying legal mechanism admits no exceptions.

### Three Cases

The *mishnah* provides three concrete illustrations. First: one declares that the first black ox to emerge from his house shall be *hekdesh*, but a white ox emerges instead — Beis Shammai says it is *hekdesh*, Beis Hillel says it is not. Second: one declares that the first gold coin to come up from his pocket shall be *hekdesh*, but a silver coin comes up — again Beis Shammai says *hekdesh*, Beis Hillel disagrees. Third: one declares that the first barrel of wine that comes to hand shall be *hekdesh*, but it turns out to be oil — same dispute. Three cases, seemingly making the same point. The reason the *mishnah* requires all three will become clear as the Gemara proceeds.

---

## Temurah Explanation

### Beginning/End Parallel

The Gemara opens its analysis by asking: what is Beis Shammai's rationale? The first answer offered is *yalfinan techilat hekdesh mi-sof hekdesh* — we derive the rule governing the inception of *hekdesh* from the rule governing a later stage of *hekdesh*.

### Temurah Logic

The specific comparison is to *temurah* — the act of attempting to substitute one animal for a consecrated one. Once an animal is *hekdesh*, it cannot be redeemed simply by designating a replacement; instead, both animals become consecrated. Crucially, *temurah* operates even when the substitution is mistaken: if one said "this black ox in exchange for my *korban*" and it turned out to be white, the *temurah* is still valid. The argument is therefore: *ma temurah afilu b'ta'ut af hekdesh afilu b'ta'ut* — just as *temurah* works even with a mistaken identification, so too the initial act of *hekdesh* should work even when mistaken.

### Hillel's Objection

Beis Hillel rejects this comparison on two grounds, both noted by Rashi. First, *temurah* is a *gezerat hakatuv* — a specific biblical decree — and one cannot extrapolate from a unique legal rule to a general principle. Second, and more substantively, there is a conceptual difference between making a mistake *within the realm of hekdesh* — as in *temurah*, where *kedushah* is already present — and mistakenly *bringing something into* the realm of *hekdesh* in the first place. Beis Hillel's formulation is: *hani milei temurah, u'le-kho de-hekdesh b'ta'ut lo machtinan* — that rule applies to *temurah*, but I will not allow an item to enter *hekdesh* through a mistake at the outset.

### Timing Challenge

The Gemara presses Beis Shammai further. Consider a case where someone says, "Let this animal be a *temurah* as of noon today" — the *temurah* would not take effect at the moment of speech, but only when noon arrives. The condition must be fulfilled before the legal change occurs. By the same logic, in our *mishnah*, the person said the *black* ox — so why should anything happen before a black ox actually emerges? The white ox that came out is not what was specified, and the *temurah* analogy would seem to support waiting until the specified condition is met rather than allowing the wrong item to be consecrated.

---

## Rav Pappa Reinterpret

### First Black Ox

At this point, Rav Pappa offers a different approach entirely. Rather than defending the *temurah* comparison, he reframes the *mishnah*'s case: *lekach ne'emar rishon le-khesheyetze rishon, ve-hashor shachor ka'amar* — what the person actually meant was "the first black ox to come out." The *mishnah* is not describing a scenario with only two oxen — one black, one white — where the wrong one emerged. Rather, the person owned multiple oxen, including several black ones, and designated "the first of the black oxen to come out of my house." When the white ox walked out, that was simply irrelevant to his declaration. The first black ox to subsequently emerge is then consecrated.

### Not Actually Mistake

This reinterpretation fundamentally changes the character of the case: it is no longer, strictly speaking, a *ta'us* at all. The speaker was deliberate and specific; there was no error in the premise of his declaration. So why does the *mishnah* frame this as a case of *hekdesh ta'us*?

### Ta'us Redefined

The Gemara explains that *ta'us* here does not mean an outright mistake but rather an ambiguous or non-definitive statement — as distinct from a clear, unambiguous act of *hekdesh*. The declaration "the first one to come out of my house shall be *hekdesh*" has an element of imprecision that invites reinterpretation, and it is this quality that the *mishnah* calls *ta'us*.

### Gemara Objects

The Gemara challenges Rav Pappa: the *mishnah* says "the first to come out of my house," not "the first black one." If the person truly meant "the first of the black ones," the phrasing of the *mishnah* seems to point in a different direction. One could answer that "from my house" is simply specifying the location as opposed to another outbuilding, and that the primary criterion was the color — but the textual difficulty remains.

### Pappa Responds

Rav Pappa of Barnish responds to Rav Ashi: *mishum de-ati le-diburei kama* — because the declaration as stated comes across as somewhat misleading or ambiguous relative to what was actually intended. The face value of the words suggests one thing, while the speaker's real intent was another. It is precisely this gap between surface meaning and actual intent that requires reinterpretation and that justifies applying the label of *ta'us* to what is, in reality, a deliberate but loosely worded declaration.

---

## Shammai True Ta'us

### Question Setup

Having established Rav Pappa's model — in which the *mishnah*'s case is not a genuine mistake but a deliberately ambiguous formulation — a natural question emerges: does Beis Shammai actually hold that a true *hekdesh ta'us*, a real mistake in the underlying premise, would be valid? The reinterpretation implies that a genuine *ta'us* might in fact not work even according to Beis Shammai, since the whole effort was to show that the *mishnah*'s case is not a *ta'us* at all.

### Neder/Chacham Case

The Gemara raises a *mishnah* that bears directly on this question: *mi she-nadar be-nazir ve-nishal le-chakham ve-hittiro, ve-hayetah lo behemah meforeshet, tetzei ve-tir'eh ba-eder* — if someone vowed to be a *nazir*, consulted a *chakham* who released him, and had already set aside a specific animal for his *korban*, that animal goes out to graze freely among the flock. The reason is that the *chakham* is *oker ha-neder me-ikaro* — he uproots the vow retroactively, as if it never existed. Since the *nezirut* never legally occurred, the animal designated for its *chatat* was never truly consecrated.

### Hillel Challenges

Beis Hillel invokes this case against Beis Shammai: *i attem modim be-she-hekdesh b'ta'ut ve-tetzei ve-tir'eh ba-eder?* — do you not concede that in this case, which involves a *hekdesh ta'us*, the animal is not consecrated and simply grazes freely? If Beis Shammai truly holds that *hekdesh ta'us* is valid *hekdesh*, the animal should remain consecrated even after the *chakham* releases the vow.

### Status Change Analysis

The answer — which both Rav Pappa's framework and, as Tosafot notes, straightforward analysis would supply — is that this is not a *hekdesh ta'us* case at all. The person fully intended to be a *nazir* and deliberately designated the animal; there was no mistake in the premise. What subsequently changed was not the discovery of an error but a conscious legal act: the *chakham*'s retroactive release of the vow. There is a fundamental difference between a *ta'us* — where the very premise of the consecration was mistaken from the outset — and a deliberate act that is later undone through a recognized legal mechanism. Beis Shammai can therefore concede this case entirely without any concession regarding genuine *hekdesh ta'us*. According to Rav Pappa, moreover, our *mishnah*'s case is itself not a genuine *ta'us*, so the entire exchange is operating on a separate track from the *mishnah*'s core ruling.

---

## Abaye Past Tense

### Vocalization Difference

Abaye offers a third explanation of the *mishnah*, one that depends on a subtle difference in vocalization. The letters *shin-yud-tzadi-alef* can be read either as *she-yeitzei* — "that will come out," future tense — or as *she-yatza* — "that came out," past tense. The *mishnah*, as typically read, seems to use the future: one declares in advance that whatever black ox will emerge from his house shall be *hekdesh*. But the letters themselves are equally consistent with a past-tense reading, and Abaye proposes that this is precisely how the *mishnah* should be understood.

### Past Tense Reading

On Abaye's reading, the *mishnah* describes not a prospective declaration but a retrospective one: the speaker is standing in the afternoon or evening, after an animal has already come out of his house. He declares, "The black ox that came out of my house — let it be *hekdesh*."

### First Animal Intent

The case then proceeds as follows: it becomes known — or is pointed out — that the animal which actually emerged was white, not black. The speaker responds: had I known it was a white ox that came out, I would have said "the white ox." My intention was simply to consecrate the first animal, whatever it was. The color was incidental to the declaration; what mattered was that it was the first to come out. Beis Shammai holds this consecration valid.

### Extension Problem

What makes Abaye's explanation elegant for the first case creates a difficulty for the other two. The *mishnah*'s second case uses *she-ya'aleh* — "that will come up" — in connection with the gold coin, and the third uses *she-ta'aleh* in connection with the barrel of wine. These forms are clearly future tense and do not naturally admit the same vocalic shift that worked for *she-yatza*.

### Vocalization Solutions

The Gemara resolves this by adjusting the vocalizations of the other two cases as well. For the coin, read *she-ala* instead of *she-ya'aleh*; for the barrel, read *she-altah* instead of *she-ta'aleh* — both past-tense forms. On this reading, all three cases follow the same model: the speaker designated something after the fact, mistakenly identifying it by a secondary attribute (color, material, contents), when his actual intent was simply to consecrate whatever had come to hand first.

---

## Eye Framework Analysis

### Rav Chisda Principle

With the three explanations of the *mishnah* laid out, the Gemara shifts to a related analysis introduced by Rav Chisda. He states: *ukma b'chivrei lakya, chivrei b'ukmei lakya* — a black ox among white ones is inferior, and a white ox among black ones is also inferior. In a white herd, a black ox stands out unfavorably; in a black herd, a white ox is at a disadvantage. This principle of relative quality among livestock now becomes the lens through which the three *mishnah* cases are examined.

### First Case Quality

The first case — the black ox — thus involves an item of lesser quality, given that the herd is presumed to be white. If Beis Shammai holds that this consecration is valid, one might infer that a person can consecrate *b'ayin ra'ah* — in a "bad eye," with a less generous disposition, giving *hekdesh* an inferior item while keeping the better one. The difficulty is determining whether Beis Shammai's ruling reflects that standard or a more generous one.

### Second Case Quality

The second case complicates the picture. The person said *zahav* — gold — but a silver coin emerged. Gold is more valuable than silver, so the person had intended to give the better item and ended up giving the lesser one. This would suggest he was consecrating *b'ayin yafah* — with a "good eye," intending generosity toward *hekdesh* — yet Beis Shammai says even the lesser silver coin is consecrated.

### Third Case Quality

The third case adds further complexity. Wine was declared, oil emerged. Whether wine or oil is the superior commodity depends on region: in Galilee, wine is more valuable, making this a case of giving the lesser item; in other places, oil is more valuable, reversing the quality calculus entirely. The three cases thus seem to move back and forth between *ayin yafah* and *ayin ra'ah* without a consistent pattern.

### Resolution by Use

Rav Chisda resolves the difficulty by introducing a use-based framework: *ukma le-mashcha, sumka le-visra, chivra le-radya* — a black ox is best for leather (the hide), a red ox is best for eating, and a white ox is best for plowing. The quality of an animal is not absolute but relative to its intended purpose. With this principle, each of the three cases can be assigned a consistent value — whether the consecrated item represents a more or a less desirable choice depends on what the item is being used for. As for the first case, Rav Chisda adds: when I said that a black ox in a white herd is inferior, I was speaking of a particular type of ox — *turei d'Karmonaye*, oxen of that specific province — not of oxen in general. In ordinary circumstances, the black ox can in fact be the more valuable one, depending on its intended use. This allows all three cases to be read consistently.

---

## Maaser Proof

### Miscount Scenario

Beis Shammai now presses its case for the validity of *hekdesh ta'us* by mounting a counter-proof from the laws of *maaser behemah*. The argument runs as follows. When counting one's animals to designate the tithe, the tenth animal to pass under the rod becomes *maaser*. But what happens if the count goes wrong? The *mishnah* addresses a case where someone miscounted and called the ninth animal the tenth, the tenth animal the ninth, and the eleventh animal the tenth — thereby producing three animals, each called "tenth" at some point in the counting.

### All Three Sanctified

Despite the error, all three animals acquire the sanctity of *maaser*. The biblical verse states: *kol asher ya'avor tachat ha-shevet ha-asiri yihyeh kodesh l-Hashem* — whatever passes under the rod as the tenth shall be holy. The law sanctifies the tenth animal through the act of the rod passing over it, and the miscounting does not undo the consecration that attached to each animal at the moment it was designated.

### Shammai's Proof

This, says Beis Shammai, is a clear demonstration that *hekdesh ta'us* is valid: the person made an obvious mistake — one cannot have three different animals each genuinely be the tenth — and yet all three become *maaser*. If the Torah permits *hekdesh* through *ta'us* in the case of *maaser*, the same should apply to *hekdesh* generally.

### Hillel Rejects Proof

Beis Hillel rejects the proof: *lo ha-shevet kidsho* — it is not the person's speech that consecrates the animal; it is the rod. The *kedushah* of *maaser behemah* is a *gezerat hakatuv*, a specific biblical decree, and the mechanism of consecration is the physical act of the rod touching the animal, not the verbal designation. Since the source of the *kedushah* is the rod rather than the spoken word, one cannot draw conclusions about the validity of verbal *hekdesh b'ta'us* from this case.

### Hillel Logic

Beis Hillel reinforces the point with a reductio: *u-mah ilu ta'ah be-hanahat ha-shevet al shemini ve-al shenim asar shema asah klum* — if someone mistakenly placed the rod on the eighth animal or the twelfth, nothing would happen; no *kedushah* would result. This proves that it is not the person's declaration or intent that drives the consecration in the *maaser* case. Rather, as Beis Hillel concludes: *ela ha-katuv she-kiddesh asiri* — it is the scriptural verse itself that consecrates the tenth, making this an entirely sui generis mechanism. The *maaser* case therefore provides no basis for the broader principle Beis Shammai seeks to establish.

---

## Nazir/Status Distinction

### Animal Status Question

Having worked through Beis Shammai's proof from *maaser* and Beis Hillel's rebuttal, the Gemara returns to the case introduced earlier: why is the animal designated for the *chatat* of a *nazir* not consecrated once the *chakham* releases the vow? If Beis Shammai holds that *hekdesh ta'us* is valid, and the designation of the animal was made under the assumption of a *nezirut* that turned out never to have legally existed, should that not be a *hekdesh ta'us* that Beis Shammai would validate?

### Conscious Act Distinction

The answer is that this is simply not a case of *hekdesh ta'us*. The person who designated the animal did so consciously, deliberately, and with full intent. There was no mistake in the premise at the moment of the act. What happened subsequently — the *chakham*'s retroactive release of the vow — is an entirely different legal phenomenon. An intentional act that is later reversed by a recognized legal mechanism is categorically distinct from an act that was mistaken in its very premise from the outset.

### Summary Distinction

The distinction that emerges from the entire sugya is therefore this: *hekdesh ta'us*, as the term is used in the *mishnah* and debated by Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel, refers to a situation where the premise underlying the consecration was erroneous at the moment of the declaration. It does not encompass a case where a person consciously and correctly performed an act of *hekdesh* and subsequently undid it through legitimate means. Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel agree on the latter — the animal goes out to graze — and their dispute is confined to the former.

---

---

# Nazir 32

## Nezirut B'Taaut Setup

### Opening Context

The *mishna* at the bottom of 31b continues the theme of *ta'ut* — error — that has occupied the preceding discussion. The previous *mishna* established that *hekdesh b'ta'ut* is *hekdesh* according to *Beit Shammai*, and the current *mishna* builds on that foundation by turning to the intertwined questions of *nezirut b'ta'ut* and *hekdesh b'ta'ut* together.

### Refused Heter Case

The *mishna* opens: *mi shenadar b'nazir venishal l'chacham ve'asaro* — someone took a vow of *nezirut* and went to a *chacham* to obtain a *heter*, but the *chacham* was unable to release him. One might ask how such a case is to be understood according to *Beit Shammai*, who does not generally accept the framework of *nezirut b'ta'ut* as grounds for release. *Tosafot* addresses this directly: for the *mishna* to function according to *Beit Shammai*, what the person asked the *chacham* must not have been a standard *heter* based on *ta'ut* or *petach* — which *Beit Shammai* would not recognize — but rather a claim that the formula of the vow was insufficiently precise. The *masechet* itself opened with the various formulations that constitute valid or invalid acceptance of *nezirut*, and there are cases where one might legitimately ask whether the precise formula was ever uttered. That type of challenge is one even *Beit Shammai* would entertain. According to *Beit Hillel*, of course, a broader claim of *ta'ut* — had I thought it through I would not have accepted — is itself sufficient grounds for a *chacham* to release the vow. In this *mishna*, whatever the basis of the request, the *chacham* ruled that he could not help, and the person remains bound.

### Beit Shammai View

The *mishna* teaches that in such a case the person counts his *nezirut* from the time he originally accepted the vow — *monei mishaa shenadar*. On its face this seems obvious: of course he counts from the onset. The *gemara* will therefore assume that the *chiddush* of the *mishna* is that this is true even if, in the interim, the *nazir* violated his *nezirut*. Perhaps the very reason he was going to the *chacham* in the first place is that he had forgotten himself and drunk wine, or violated the *nezirut* in some other way, and was now seeking retroactive release. Very appropriately, the *chacham* refused. The teaching of the *mishna*, then, is that he does not lose his accumulated days. Being made *tamei* triggers a *korban* and a fresh start, but other violations — drinking wine, shaving — do not restart the count; they incur punishment, but the duration of the *nezirut* remains anchored to the day it was originally accepted.

### Counting from Onset

The *gemara* will now explore exactly what this counting entails and whether any days need to be made up for violations — but before proceeding to that analysis, the *mishna* introduces the second case, which concerns the animal that was sanctified in anticipation of the *korban nezirut*.

---

## Hekdesh Ta'us Debate

### Animal Goes Free

The *mishna* continues: *nishal l'chacham vehitiro* — now suppose the *chacham* did grant a *heter*. *Hayta lo behema mufreshet* — the person had already sanctified an animal as a *korban* of his *nezirut*. *Tetzei v'tir'eh ba'eder* — it goes free and grazes with the flock. Since retroactively he was never a *nazir*, there was never a valid context for sanctifying an animal as a *korban nezirut*. As *Tosafot* explains, this is analogous to a person who sanctifies an animal as a *chatat* without ever having the sin that obligates a *chatat*: the act of sanctification is void, not merely erroneous.

### Beit Hillel Argument

*Amru Beit Hillel l'Beit Shammai* — *Beit Hillel* said to *Beit Shammai*: do you not concede this very point? There is something striking about the structure of this exchange. *Beit Hillel* is appealing to an earlier *mishna*, universally accepted, and using it to make an argument against *Beit Shammai*. This phenomenon — where *Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai* refer to a *mishna rishona*, an earlier ruling that predates their dispute — offers a window into the historical development of the *mishna* itself. The argument is: *ee atem modim b'ze she'hu hekdesh ta'ut sheteitzei v'tir'eh ba'eder* — do you not concede that this is a case of *hekdesh b'ta'ut* and that the animal goes free? If so, this earlier *mishna* demonstrates that *hekdesh b'ta'ut* is not *hekdesh*, and how can *Beit Shammai* maintain otherwise?

### Ma'aser Behema Counter

*Beit Shammai* responds with a counter-example from *ma'aser behema*. The process is well known: animals born that year are counted one by one as they emerge from the pen, and every tenth one is struck with a marked staff and consecrated as *ma'aser behema*. If one miscounts and calls the ninth animal *ten*, or calls the eleventh *ten*, the *halacha* is that all three — nine, ten, and eleven — are consecrated. *Beit Shammai* presses: *ee atem modim b'mi she'ta'ah v'kara l'tshi'i asiri* — do you not concede that when you mistakenly call nine *ten*, or ten *nine*, or eleven *ten*, all three acquire *kedushah*? This, says *Beit Shammai*, is proof that *hekdesh b'ta'ut* is *hekdesh*.

### Different Mechanism

*Beit Hillel* responds: *lo hashevet kidshah* — it is not the staff that consecrates, not the act of designation driven by intent. The proof is that if one were to accidentally call the eighth animal *ten*, or the twelfth, it would not be consecrated at all. The rule of nine and eleven is not a general principle about the power of erroneous sanctification. Rather, *ela katuv shekidesh asiri hu kidesh tshi'i v'et achad asar* — the Torah itself defines the tenth in a way that encompasses a margin of error: nine and eleven called *ten* through an honest mistake fall within the category of what the Torah designates as *ma'aser*. But this is a specific *halacha* in *ma'aser behema* about how the Torah defines *ten* — it is not a general principle of *hekdesh b'ta'ut*. The proof is that even within *ma'aser behema*, calling the eighth *ten* produces nothing, demonstrating that the mechanism is the Torah's definition of the tenth, not the general power of erroneous consecration.

### Basic Criteria Principle

One might then ask: why does *Beit Shammai* not respond to *Beit Hillel's* original argument — that the animal of the person who retroactively was never a *nazir* goes free? *Tosafot* explains that *Beit Shammai* did not need to respond because that case is not *hekdesh b'ta'ut* at all in the operative sense. That case involves missing the fundamental criteria that would enable the sanctification in the first place. If one is not a *nazir*, one cannot consecrate an animal as a *korban nezirut*. If one has not eaten *chelev* and thus bears no obligation of a *chatat*, one cannot consecrate an animal as a *chatat*. The absence of the basic legal context is not a case of *ta'ut* in the relevant sense — it is a case where the very precondition for the *hekdesh* never existed.

*Tosafot* phrases it precisely: *vechan hanezirus leisa hekdesh nami leisa vegarua zeh mehekdesh ta'ut* — here, since the *nezirut* itself does not exist, the *hekdesh* likewise does not exist, and this is something even weaker than *hekdesh b'ta'ut*. And therefore: *afilu Beit Shammai modu detivtal le'alter keivan dene'ekar haneder legamrei* — even *Beit Shammai* concedes that it is retroactively void, since the entire *neder* is uprooted completely. It is as if one who has no obligation declares an animal to be *lechatas* — *lo amar klum*, it is as though nothing was said, even according to *Beit Shammai*.

The *gemara* then draws this principle out symmetrically, noting that the same logic applies on *Beit Hillel's* side with respect to *temurah*. *Rabbi Yirmiyah* observes: *mi-deBeit Shammai nishma leBeit Hillel* — from *Beit Shammai* we can derive the position of *Beit Hillel* as well. *Beit Shammai* holds that *hekdesh b'ta'ut* is *hekdesh*, and yet they would concede that if the *nazir* obtains a *heter* and retroactively was never a *nazir*, the animal is not consecrated — *keivan de-iglei milta d'lav shapir nazar*, once it emerges that he was never properly a *nazir*, the fundamental basis for the *hekdesh* is gone. By the same token, *Beit Hillel*, who hold that *temurah b'ta'ut* is *temurah* — *hani milei heicha d'ika ikar hekdesh*, that applies when the original animal is indeed consecrated. But if the original *hekdesh* itself is undermined — *itakar ikar hekdesh, itakar nami temurah* — the *temurah* falls away as well. For *Beit Hillel*, the original animal must be *hekdesh* before *ta'ut* can operate; for *Beit Shammai*, one must actually be a *nazir* before an animal can be sanctified as a *korban nezirut*. In both cases, *ta'ut* is a principle that can apply within a valid framework — but it cannot substitute for the framework itself.

---

## Making Up Days Debate

### Violation Assumption

The *gemara* turns to the first clause of the *mishna* — *moneh mishaa shenadar*, that one counts from the day one accepted the *nezirut* — and asks: *mani masnisin?* Whose view does this *mishna* represent? And the *gemara* answers, surprisingly: *lo Rabbi Yosei velo Rabbanan* — it fits neither *Rabbi Yosei* nor the *Rabbanan* as they appear in a *braita*. The *gemara* is assuming throughout that the *mishna* is addressing a case where the *nazir* violated his *nezirut* — by drinking wine, for example — and that the *chiddush* is that despite the violation, one does not lose the days already counted.

### Days Makeup Dispute

The *braita* teaches: *mi shenadar ve'avar al neziruso, ein nizkakin lo ela im kein moneh bahen issur keyamim shenahag bahen hetter* — one who vowed and violated his *nezirut* is not received, meaning we do not accept his *korbanos*, unless he first makes up, through days of prohibited conduct, as many days as he conducted himself permissibly. So if he accepted a *nezirut* of a hundred days and drank wine for forty-five, he must complete a full hundred days of abstention before the *korbanos* can be brought. *Rabbi Yosei* disagrees: *dayo shloshim yom* — thirty days is sufficient, a complete standard unit of *nezirut*, even if many more were violated.

Either way, according to both *Rabbi Yosei* and the *Rabbanan*, some makeup is required. Yet the *mishna* appears to say simply that one counts from the onset, with no mention of additional days. The *gemara* notes that if this is the *Rabbanan*, the *mishna* is difficult in a case of *nezirut mu'etes* — a short *nezirut* — because the full amount of violated days must be made up. And if it is *Rabbi Yosei*, it is difficult in a case of *nezirut meruba* — a long *nezirut* — because even thirty additional days must be made up, and the *mishna* implies none are required.

### Both Views Possible

The *gemara* resolves this by offering a dual reading: *ee ba'is eima Rabbi Yosei, ee ba'is eima Rabbanan* — one can read the *mishna* as consistent with either position, provided one specifies the length of the *nezirut* involved.

Reading the *mishna* according to *Rabbi Yosei* is possible in one of two ways. One bold reading is that *dayo shloshim yom* does not mean *make up thirty days* but rather *thirty days is enough* — meaning *Rabbi Yosei* fundamentally rejects the requirement to make up violated days. The *braita* addresses a *nezirut mu'etes*, and *Rabbi Yosei's* statement means: he has served his thirty days, I do not require anything further. Under this reading, *Rabbi Yosei* and the *mishna* align perfectly — neither requires makeup days — and the *mishna* can be speaking of a long *nezirut*. A second reading takes *dayo shloshim yom* to mean that thirty additional days must indeed be made up when many were violated, but that for a short *nezirut* with few violations, *Rabbi Yosei* may not require makeup at all. The *mishna* would then address a *nezirut mu'etes* with few violations.

Reading the *mishna* according to the *Rabbanan* requires a more radical re-reading of the word *mishaa* itself. Rather than *moneh mishaa shenadar* — he counts from the moment he accepted — the *gemara* suggests reading it as *moneh ke-mishaa shenadar*, meaning he must recount all the days that have elapsed since he accepted the *nezirut*, because those are precisely the days he spent in violation. By inserting a *chaf* of comparison, the *mishna* is no longer saying he counts forward from the start but that he must reckon and make up every day since the start. Though no violation is explicitly mentioned in the *mishna*, the *gemara* takes for granted that this is the operative assumption — otherwise the *mishna* would be stating something entirely obvious.

---

## Stolen Animal Case

### Animal Stolen Setup

The following *mishna* addresses a different form of *nezirut b'ta'ut*, this one based on a mistaken factual premise at the time the vow was accepted. *Mi shenadar b'nazir ve-halach le-havi et behemto, matza she-nigneva* — someone accepted *nezirut* and went to retrieve his animal in anticipation of bringing his *korbanos*, only to discover it had been stolen. This person is coming to a *chacham* and claiming: I am a poor man; I only ever intended to become a *nazir* on the assumption that this animal was available to me. Had I known it was stolen, I never would have accepted *nezirut*. So what is the *halacha*?

The case of the stolen animal unfolds across what follows, but the essential analytical framework is introduced here. It involves the principle known as *ein potchin b'nolad* — one cannot use as the basis for a *heter* something that did not yet exist or was not yet known at the time the vow was made. The *nazir's* claim depends on the animal's status at the time of his vow, and the *mishna* will draw a precise line depending on exactly when the theft occurred relative to when the vow was taken.

### Before/After Knowledge

*Im ad she-lo nigneva behemto nadar, harei zeh nazir* — if the theft occurred only after he had already accepted the *nezirut*, then he is a *nazir*. At the time he took the vow, his assumption was correct: the animal was his. The subsequent theft could not have been anticipated and cannot retroactively define his state of mind as having been mistaken. *Ve'im mishe-nigneva behemto nadar, eino nazir* — but if the animal had already been stolen at the moment he accepted the *nezirut*, even though he was unaware of this, then he is not a *nazir*. In this case, the factual premise underlying his acceptance was false at the very moment of the vow. A *chacham* can question him: had you known at the time you accepted *nezirut* that your animal had already been stolen, would you have done so? He says no. That constitutes a classic *ta'ut* — the vow was accepted under a mistaken factual assumption, and under *Beit Hillel's* framework (since *Beit Shammai* does not really accept *nezirut b'ta'ut*), the *chacham* can release him.

The release in such a case works through the process of *hatara* as it operates in *hilchot nedarim* generally. When a vow is taken on the basis of an unexplicated assumption that turns out to be false, a *chacham* can serve as the mechanism for release. This is not explicit in the *mishna* itself — we are reading in what we know from *Masechet Nedarim* — but that is the operative framework.

---

## Future Destruction E (II)

### Ein Potchin B'Nolad

The principle at stake in the next case is *ein potchin b'nolad*: one may not open the door for a *heter* by invoking something that had not yet come into being at the time the vow was taken. Had the theft not yet occurred, it was not a fact in the world and not something the person could have anticipated. We are not fortune tellers. One cannot retroactively say: had I known what the future held, I would not have taken the vow — because there was no way to know the future. However, if the thing in question was something reasonably foreseeable — a *nolad hashachiach*, something likely to occur — then it may be used as a *petach* even if it had not yet occurred at the time of the vow. The precise line between what could and could not have been anticipated will be central to the discussions that follow.

---

## Stolen Animal Case (II)

### Nachum HaMedai Case

The *mishna* introduces the following arresting case: *keshe'alu nezirim min ha-golah* — when *nezirim* came up from the exile to bring their *korbanos* in Jerusalem — *u'matzu Beit HaMikdash charev* — and found that the *Beit HaMikdash* had been destroyed. This is a remarkable historical vignette: people who had accepted *nezirut* in the diaspora, who had not yet heard of the destruction, arriving in Jerusalem with their animals ready to bring *korbanos*, only to encounter the ruins. *Nachum HaMedai* addressed them and asked: *ilu heyissem yodim sheBeit HaMikdash charev, hayissem nozrim?* — had you known that the *Beit HaMikdash* would be destroyed when you accepted your *nezirut*, would you have become *nezirim*? They said no. And *Nachum HaMedai* released them.

---

## Future Destruction E (II)

### Nachum's Reasoning

*Nachum HaMedai's* reasoning follows the logic of *nezirut b'ta'ut*: since the purpose of *nezirut* is ultimately to bring a *korban* in the *Beit HaMikdash*, and had they known the *Beit HaMikdash* would be destroyed they would not have accepted *nezirut*, their original vow was made under a false premise. This is precisely the structure of a *ta'ut* that a *chacham* can address. The difficulty, however, is that what *Nachum HaMedai* used as the basis for the *heter* was the future destruction of the *Beit HaMikdash* — something that had not yet occurred at the time they accepted *nezirut* and indeed something they could not have anticipated. This is a textbook application of *ein potchin b'nolad*, which is exactly why the *chachamim* overturned his ruling.

### Chachamim Response

*U-cheshe'va davar etzel chachamim amru* — when the matter came before the sages, they ruled: *kol she'nazar ad she-lo charav Beit HaMikdash, nazir* — anyone who accepted *nezirut* before the destruction of the *Beit HaMikdash* remains a *nazir*. The fact that the *Beit HaMikdash* was subsequently destroyed cannot retroactively release a vow accepted when it was still standing. *U-meshecharav Beit HaMikdash, eino nazir* — but if someone accepted *nezirut* after the destruction, having not yet heard of it, then he is not a *nazir*. In that case, the destruction was already a fact in the world at the moment of the vow; he simply was unaware of it. That is genuine *ta'ut* — the vow was predicated on a state of affairs that had already ceased to exist. But using a future event — the anticipated destruction — as the basis for releasing someone who accepted *nezirut* while the *Beit HaMikdash* still stood: that is *ein potchin b'nolad*, and *Nachum HaMedai* erred.

---

## Potchin B'Nolad Debate

### Rabbi Eliezer Silenced

*Amar Rabba: shetaflu Rabbanan l'Rabbi Eliezer v'okmu b'shitasaihu* — the Rabbis overwhelmed *Rabbi Eliezer* and brought him into line with their position. *Rabbi Eliezer* in fact holds *potchin b'nolad* — as the *mishna* elsewhere records, *d'tannan: potchin b'nolad, divrei Rabbi Eliezer, va-chachamim ossrin* — *Rabbi Eliezer* holds that one may open a door for a *heter* based on something that came into being after the vow, while the *chachamim* forbid it. *Rabbi Eliezer* was active at the time of the *churban ha-Bayit* and might have been expected to defend *Nachum HaMedai's* ruling. Yet his voice does not appear in the *mishna* challenging the *chachamim*. *Rabba's* explanation is that the *Rabbanan* simply overwhelmed him — pressed him into silence, whether by persuasion or by sheer weight of consensus. This is a striking *gemara*: it does not record *Rabbi Eliezer* being convinced, only that he was silenced.

### Conditional Future

*Va'amar Rava* — and *Rava* introduces a subtle distinction: *af al pi d'amri Rabbanan ein potchin b'nolad, aval potchin b'tnai nolad* — even though the *Rabbanan* say one may not open with a *nolad*, one may open with a *conditional nolad*. The *gemara* explains: *ami lehon, ilu ata inish ve'ami l'chon de'charav Beit HaMikdash, mi haveisa nadrisah?* — you could say to the *nezirim*: not *had you known the Beit HaMikdash would be destroyed* — that would be *ein potchin b'nolad* — but rather: *had people come to you and told you that the Beit HaMikdash might be destroyed any day now, would you still have accepted your nezirut?*

The initial reading of this distinction is that it resembles *nolad hashachiach* — invoking a likely future event rather than an unknowable one. Perhaps the *nezirim*, had they stopped to take honest stock of the political realities and the military situation, might have recognized that destruction was a serious possibility. Had someone they trusted confronted them with this reality, would they have proceeded? And had they answered no — well, that is not asking them about something unknowable; it is asking whether, had they thought clearly and been properly informed, they would have acted differently.

### Rosh Advice Theory

*Tosafot* reads this differently, emphasizing the phrase *ilu ata inish ve'ami l'chon* — had *people* come and *told* you. The point is not merely about the objective probability of destruction but about what the *nezirim* would have done had they actually been pressured by advisers. The *Rosh* elaborates on this reading at length: *ilu hayu baim anashim v'hayu nosnim lachem eitzah she'lo tidru ulai yecharav Beit HaMikdash terem klos neziroschem, klum hayitem nozrim? Ve'omru ken hayinu nimlachim v'shomim l'atzasam* — had people come and counseled you not to take the vow, because the *Beit HaMikdash* might be destroyed before your *nezirut* concluded, would you have accepted? And they would say: yes, had they advised us, we would have listened to their advice. The *Rosh* states that this constitutes a valid *petach*: *pesach havei af al pi she'haeitzah tluyah b'nolad* — it is a valid opening even though the advice itself concerned a future *nolad*, because the *charat* is rooted in what people would have told them and what they would have listened to, not in the objective occurrence of the *nolad* itself. *Kivan she'machmas atzasam hayah chozer* — since their turning back would have been on account of the advice of others, this does not fall under the prohibition of *potchin b'nolad*.

The difficulty with this reading is genuine: the people never actually received such advice. Why should it matter that they would have listened to advisers who never came? Perhaps what this is really capturing is something like: had you been thinking clearly, had you had access to good judgment, would you have done this? The *petach* is not about the social pressure of friends but about what a reasonable, well-informed person in their position would have done.

### Prophetic Warning

*Amar Rav Yosef: ei havai hatam, hava amina lehon: ha-ketiv, Heichal Hashem Heichal Hashem Heichal Hashem heima* — *Rav Yosef* says: had I been there, I would have released them by citing the *pasuk* from *Yirmiyahu*, where the people foolishly declare *Heichal Hashem* — the Temple of God will protect itself — and *Yirmiyahu* is warning them of their false confidence. The implication, as *Tosafot* notes, is that the *pasuk* speaks implicitly of both a first and a second *Beit HaMikdash*: people trusted that God would protect the *mikdash*, and *Yirmiyahu* prophesied otherwise. *Rav Yosef's* argument would be that the *nezirim* should have known — from *Yirmiyahu's* warning and from the historical precedent of the first *churban* — that destruction was a real possibility. This would function as a *nolad hashachiach*: something one could and should have anticipated. Had you genuinely internalized what *Yirmiyahu* was telling you, would you have taken *nezirut*?

### Timing Objection

*Amar Abaye: nehi de-yadeitun lehu de-yicharav, mi yadeitun le-eimas?* — *Abaye* objects: granted, perhaps they should have known in some broad sense that the *Beit HaMikdash* was vulnerable to destruction; but did they know *when*? Even if they had absorbed *Yirmiyahu's* warning and the lessons of history, there was no reason to believe it would happen within the span of their *nezirut*. *Va-achti mi yadeina be-hai yoma?* — and even the additional *pasuk* from *Daniel* about seventy *shavuim* does not help, because even if one were to derive that destruction was four hundred and ninety years away, the precise timing was not knowable. To say that they should have foreseen not just that destruction would eventually come but that it would come *now*, within their *nezirut*, is to demand too much. The *gemara* accepts *Abaye's* objection and leaves *Rav Yosef's* approach unresolved.

This discussion also prompted a broader exchange about the human capacity for self-deception in precisely such circumstances. Even after the *churban* of the first *Beit HaMikdash*, people clung to the faith that God would not allow it to happen again — that the precedent was irrelevant, that this time was different. The historical parallels noted in the *Rosh's* comment are sharp: *she'hayu misyaashim min ha-puranus* — they despaired of punishment; *im yeicharev Heichal Hashem od yibaneh lanu bayit sheni, im yeicharev gam oso od yibaneh lanu shelishi* — if it falls, God will build another; if that falls too, another will come for the days of *Mashiach*. The capacity to rationalize confidence in the continuation of what one loves is not a failure unique to any generation. The very fact that *Yirmiyahu* was right once does not, as one might observe, persuade the next generation that he is still right.

---

## Six People Case

### Conditional Vows

The final *mishna* on the *daf* presents an intricate series of conditional vows. Six people are walking on a road when an unidentified man approaches. Each of the six makes a conditional *neder* of *nezirut* tied to the identity of the approaching person.

Person one says *hareini nazir shezeh ploni* — I will be a *nazir* if that is Reuven. Person two says *hareini nazir she-ein zeh ploni* — I will be a *nazir* if that is *not* Reuven. Person three says *hareini nazir she-echad mikem nazir* — I will be a *nazir* if one of you is a *nazir*. Since one of the first two must necessarily be correct — either it is Reuven or it is not — person three seems by all appearances destined to be a *nazir*. Person four says *hareini nazir she-ein echad mikem nazir* — I will be a *nazir* if none of you is a *nazir*. And also one of them may not be — since one of the first two must be wrong — so person four's condition is also not obviously unmet. Person five says *hareini nazir sheshneichem nezirim* — I will be a *nazir* if both of you are *nezirim*. Person six says *hareini nazir she-kulchem nezirim* — I will be a *nazir* if all of you are *nezirim*.

### Beit Shammai: All Nezirim

*Beit Shammai omrim kulam nezirim* — all six are *nezirim*. This is the position of *Beit Shammai*, who holds that *nezirut b'ta'ut* is *nezirut*. Everyone in this group wanted to become a *nazir*, and everyone thought their condition was being met, even if some were factually mistaken. The desire to accept *nezirut* was present; the error concerned the factual condition, not the intention. Under *Beit Shammai's* framework, that error does not undo the *nezirut*.

### Beit Hillel: Condition M…

*Beit Hillel omrim: eino nazir ela mi shelo nitkaymu devarav* — only those whose conditions were met become *nezirim*. The *gemara* notes that this formulation is puzzling on its face, since it seems to say only those who were *wrong* become *nezirim*. The *gemara* immediately corrects this to mean the opposite: only those who were *right*, whose conditions were fulfilled by the objective facts, are *nezirim*. Under *Beit Hillel's* understanding, if your condition was not met, you are simply not a *nazir* — there is no vow to be retroactively affirmed by the fact that you thought you were right.

### Rabbi Tarfon: None Nezir…

*Rabbi Tarfon omer: ein echad mehem nazir* — not one of them is a *nazir*. *Rabbi Tarfon* takes the opposite extreme from *Beit Shammai*: *lo nitna nezirut ela lehafla'ah* — *nezirut* was given only for *hafla'ah*, clear articulation, drawn from the verse *ki yafli lindor neder nazir*. Since at the time each person accepted *nezirut* there was genuine uncertainty about whether the condition would be met, the vow lacked the clarity required. Even persons three and four, who might seem to have had their conditions certainly met, are not *nezirim* according to *Rabbi Tarfon*: since persons one and two lacked the requisite clarity and are thus not *nezirim*, person three's condition — *one of you is a nazir* — was not met, and person four's condition — *one of you is not a nazir* — must be read narrowly, as *Tosafot* explains, to mean one is not and one is, which also fails if neither one nor two is a *nazir*. Persons five and six, who conditioned their *nezirut* on the *nezirut* of others, are therefore likewise released.

### Person Turns Away

*Hechezir panav le'achorav* — now suppose the approaching person turned away and his identity was never established. Within the framework of *Beit Hillel*, who holds that *nezirut* depends on whether the condition is met, what happens when the condition can never be evaluated? The *mishna* rules: *eino nazir* — he is not a *nazir*. If there is unresolvable doubt about whether your condition was met, you do not become a *nazir* under *Beit Hillel's* approach. This stands in contrast to *Beit Shammai*, under whose view everyone is a *nazir* regardless, and to the question *Rabbi Shimon* will now address.

### Rabbi Shimon: Safek Nazir

*Rabbi Shimon omer* — *Rabbi Shimon* says the logical position in the case of the person who turned away is that one is a *safek nazir*. The status is genuinely doubtful, and a *safek nazir* faces a particular practical problem: how does the *nezirut* ever conclude? One cannot bring a *korban* if one is in doubt about whether one is a *nazir* at all. *Rabbi Shimon's* solution is that the *safek nazir* must say: *im haya kidevarai, hareini nazir chovah* — if my condition was met, then I am a *nazir* by virtue of what I originally accepted; *ve'im lav, hareini nazir nedavah* — and if not, then I hereby accept *nezirut* as a free-will *neder* in any case. By accepting an optional *nezirut* in this conditional form, the person ensures that whatever his original status, he is now definitively a *nazir*, and can bring his *korbanos* and conclude.

What emerges from this final *mishna* is a clean spectrum of positions. *Beit Shammai* holds that *nezirut b'ta'ut* is *nezirut* — intending to be a *nazir* is enough, regardless of whether the condition was met. *Rabbi Tarfon* requires *hafla'ah*, absolute clarity at the moment of acceptance, and rejects *nezirut* whenever doubt was present at that moment. *Beit Hillel* stakes out the middle ground: *nezirut* depends on whether the condition is objectively satisfied. And *Rabbi Shimon*, working within the *Beit Hillel* framework, provides the practical resolution for the case of permanent uncertainty — the *safek nazir* accepts an additional, unconditional *nezirut nedavah* to bring the matter to a definitive close.

---

---

# Nazir 33

## Six Vows Re: Reuven

### Mishna Text & Translation

The *mishna* at the bottom of 32b opens with a vivid scene: six people are traveling together when a stranger approaches from the opposite direction. One of the six declares, *hareini nazir she-zeh Ploni* — "I will be a *nazir* if that is Reuven." A second, disagreeing, says *hareini nazir she-ein zeh Ploni* — "I will be a *nazir* if that man is not Reuven." So far these two are clearly in direct opposition to one another.

### Each Condition Analyzed

Person three says *hareini nazir she-echad mikem nazir* — "I will be a *nazir* if one of you is a *nazir*." This condition seems logically guaranteed: either the stranger is or is not Reuven, so one of the first two must have their condition met. Person four says *hareini nazir she-ein echad mikem nazir* — "I will be a *nazir* if one of you is not a *nazir*." The *gemara* understands this not as "none of you is a *nazir*" but rather as asserting that one of them is not, which mirrors what person three said in reverse. Person five says *hareini nazir she-shneichem nezirim* — "I will be a *nazir* if both of you are *nezirim*," understood as referring to the first two. Person six says *hareini nazir she-kulchem nezirim* — "I will be a *nazir* if all of you are *nezirim*," which seems plainly impossible, since at most only some of the conditions can be met. Prima facie, only a subset of the group should become *nezirim*.

### Beit Shammai: All Nezirim

*Beit Shammai* says *kulam nezirim* — they are all *nezirim*. This is a striking ruling, and the principle behind it is that *hekdesh b'ta'ut* — a dedication made in error — is nonetheless valid *hekdesh*, and similarly a *nazir b'ta'ut* is nonetheless a *nazir*. The parallel is to the case discussed earlier of one who says "the first black cow that comes out of my house," where the underlying intent is simply to consecrate the first cow. The stipulation reflects an assumption about reality, not a genuine open condition. So too here: each person is not merely rolling the dice. Each is assuming they know the truth and expressing that assumption. Since they fundamentally want to be a *nazir* and are simply mistaken about the facts, *Beit Shammai* holds that the *nezirut* takes effect regardless.

### Hekdesh B'Taout Principle

One might ask why the concept of *hekdesh b'ta'ut* applies to *nezirut* at all, given that it does not apply to *nedarim*. Two considerations emerge. First, *nezirut* involves *korbanot*, so there is a dimension of *hekdesh* inherent in it, and the principle of *hekdesh b'ta'ut* operates within that framework. Second, and independently, the *nazir* is described as *kadosh yihiyeh gadel perah sear rosho* — there is a status of sanctity attached to the *nazir* himself that *nedarim* lack. This holiness-status is precisely what distinguishes *nezirut* from *nedarim* in *Beit Shammai*'s analysis.

There is also the question of whether *Beit Shammai*'s logic would extend even to a genuine *tnai* about the future — where you truly do not know what will happen — as opposed to a *ta'ut*, where you mistakenly assumed you knew the present reality. This may depend on how one reads the earlier *mishna* about the black and white cow.

### Beit Hillel: Conditional…

*Beit Hillel* rules *eino nazir ela mi she-lo nitkaymu devarav* — the only one who is a *nazir* is the one whose condition was not met. The *gemara* will address the obvious anomaly in this formulation; the intended meaning is that only those whose conditions were met become *nezirim*. In short, *Beit Hillel* applies the ordinary logic of conditional vows: you become a *nazir* when and only when your stated condition is fulfilled.

### Rabbi Tarfon: No Nezirim

*Rabbi Tarfon* takes the opposite extreme from *Beit Shammai*: *ein echad mehem nazir* — none of them is a *nazir*.

### Lo Nitna Nezirut Princip…

The *gemara* explains that *Rabbi Tarfon* holds the principle of *lo nitna nezirut ela l'hafla'ah*, derived from the verse *ish o isha ki yafli lindor neder nazir* — *nezirut* must be enunciated in a clear, unambiguous, black-and-white manner. Any element of stipulation or doubt at the moment of declaration undermines the foundational requirement. This would seem to imply that even a *tnai* about the future would be insufficient for *nezirut* according to *Rabbi Tarfon*, since the declaration must be fully resolved at the time it is made.

It is worth noting that the language of *hafla'ah* appears in the verse about *nezirut* but not in the parallel verse about *nedarim*, where the formulation is simply *ish ki yidor neder* without *hafla'ah*. This linguistic distinction is what grounds the *lo nitna nezirut ela l'hafla'ah* principle specifically in *nezirut* rather than in *nedarim* generally.

One can understand *Rabbi Tarfon*'s position as reflecting the gravity of *nezirut*: because it is such a weighty commitment — and because unlike a physical act, it exists entirely as a speech act and therefore must be fully real on its own terms — it cannot be contingent or stipulated. *Nezirut* demands absolute clarity, a quality that a conditional vow by definition lacks.

---

## Stranger Turns Back

### Stranger's Departure

The *mishna* then introduces a complication: *hirtiah leachorav* — the stranger turned back and went away before anyone could determine his identity.

### Beit Hillel: Condition U…

For *Beit Shammai* and *Rabbi Tarfon*, this development changes nothing — their positions are not contingent on whether the condition was ultimately verifiable. The discussion that follows concerns *Beit Hillel*'s position. According to *Beit Hillel*, since there is no way to determine whether the condition was met, the *tanna kamma* holds that no one becomes a *nazir*.

### Safek Nazir Debate

This conclusion might seem surprising: surely each person should be a *safek nazir*, a doubtful *nazir*. Indeed, that is precisely what *Rabbi Shimon* says.

### Rabbi Shimon's Dual Acce…

*Rabbi Shimon* rules that everyone becomes a *safek nazir*, and he prescribes a specific formulation to resolve the legal difficulty. Each person must declare: *im haya kidvarai harei ni nazir chova* — if my condition was indeed met, then I am obligated in *nezirut* by virtue of my original declaration; *veim lav, harei ni nazir nedava* — and if my condition was not met and I am therefore not a *nazir* by that vow, I now accept *nezirut* upon myself as a voluntary gift. This two-pronged acceptance ensures that one way or another, the person is a genuine *nazir* and is not trapped in the impossible status of *safek nazir*, which would require observing all the stringencies of *nezirut* with no mechanism to conclude it through a *korban*.

---

## Gemara on Conditions Met

### Beit Hillel's Anomaly

The *gemara* homes in on *Beit Hillel*'s formulation: *eino nazir ela mi she-lo nitkaymu devarav* — the one whose condition was *not* met is the *nazir*? Why would that person be a *nazir*?

### Rav Yehuda's Textual Fix

*Rav Yehuda* proposes the simplest solution: simply remove the word *lo* from the *mishna*. The correct reading should be *mi she-nitkaymu devarav* — the one whose condition *was* met is the *nazir*. This is what *Beit Hillel* intends, and the word *lo* is a scribal or transmission error.

### Abaye: Self-Reversal

*Abaye*, at the top of 33b, offers an alternative reading that preserves the *mishna*'s text. The case, he says, concerns a person who reversed himself *toch kedei dibbur* — within the unit of speech. For example, a person said "I will be a *nazir* if this man is Reuven — actually, if he is *not* Reuven." He rescinded and reversed his initial condition within the same utterance.

### Earlier vs. Later Statem…

On this reading, *lo nitkaymu devarav* — "his conditions were not fulfilled" — refers specifically to his *earlier* statement, *devarav harishonim*, even though his *later* statement, *devarav ha'acharonim*, was fulfilled. The *mishna* is saying: the person whose first condition was not met but whose second condition was, that person is a *nazir*. This is admittedly a strange way to transmit the ruling — requiring the reader to understand that *lo nitkaymu devarav* means only the first part of a self-contradicting utterance — but it is what the *mishna* requires on this interpretation.

### Identifying the Tanna

Having established that the final section of the *mishna* (where the stranger turns back) must reflect *Beit Hillel*'s framework — since for *Beit Shammai* and *Rabbi Tarfon* the stranger's departure is irrelevant — the *gemara* asks whose position within the *Beit Hillel* camp is being represented. Specifically, the *mishna* indicates that *if* the condition could have been verified as met, the person would be a *nazir*, but if it cannot be verified, he is not even a *safek nazir* (according to the *tanna kamma*). Whose opinion is that?

### Rabbi Tarfon Excluded

*Rabbi Tarfon* can be ruled out immediately. If it were *Rabbi Tarfon*, then even when the condition is verifiably met, the person would not be a *nazir*, since at the moment of declaration he did not know whether the condition was met — *keivan d'bishata d'kanazar lo yada i Ploni hu v'ilo* — and so the *nezirut* never took effect. But the *mishna* clearly implies that the status of the condition matters, meaning that if verified, the person would indeed be a *nazir*. This is incompatible with *Rabbi Tarfon*'s position. Through this analysis of the end of the *mishna*, the *gemara* is simultaneously clarifying the logic that underlies *Rabbi Tarfon*'s ruling.

---

## Braita: Rabbi Yehuda

### Grain Pile Case

Having ruled out *Rabbi Tarfon*, the *gemara* identifies the relevant authority through a *braita*: *hareini nazir al menas she-yehei b'kri zeh meah kor* — "I will be a *nazir* on condition that this grain pile contains one hundred *kor*." The person then goes to measure the pile and finds it has been stolen or lost, making it impossible to verify whether the condition was met.

### Rabbi Shimon: Safek Nazir

*Rabbi Shimon* says this person is *oser* — he is in a state of prohibition, meaning he is a *safek nazir*. This is the same *Rabbi Shimon* who appears in our *mishna*, and the parallel is precise.

### Rabbi Yehuda: No Nezirut

*Rabbi Yehuda* says *matir* — the person is entirely permitted, meaning he is not a *nazir* at all. When the condition cannot be verified, there is no *nezirut*. The *gemara* identifies this as the opinion matching the *tanna kamma* of the *mishna*: if the stranger turns back without being identified, no one becomes a *nazir*. Since the *mishna* does hold that the person would be a *nazir* if the condition were verified as met, this is not *Rabbi Tarfon*'s position but rather *Rabbi Yehuda*'s.

### Rabbi Shimon's Logic

*Rabbi Shimon*'s reasoning: *keivan d'ilu lo nignav dilma hava bei meah kor v'hava nazir* — since had it not been stolen, the pile might well have contained a hundred *kor*, and the person would have been a *nazir*, therefore even now, in doubt, he is a *nazir* — *misafek*. The same logic applies to the case of the stranger: since had he come before us and been identified as Reuven, the person who vowed on that condition would have been a *nazir*, therefore even when identity is uncertain, he is a *safek nazir*.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Logic

*Rabbi Yehuda*'s reasoning is articulated by *Tosafot* on the phrase *ela Rabbi Yehuda dikree hu*: *d'lo machis inish nafshei l'safeika* — a person does not intend to include cases of doubt within his condition. When one says "if this pile contains a hundred *kor*," the implicit meaning is: if it is definitively proven that the condition is met. A case of doubt is not something the person consciously included in his vow. Therefore, *Rabbi Yehuda* holds that the *tnai* applies only when its fulfillment is unambiguous and proven; in cases of doubt, the person has not activated his vow and is not a *nazir*. This concludes the *gemara*'s analysis of the first *mishna*, having clarified along the way both *Rabbi Tarfon*'s principle of *lo nitna nezirut ela l'hafla'ah* and *Rabbi Yehuda*'s principle that a *tnai* does not extend to *safek* cases.

---

## Seven Vows Re: Koy

### What Is Koy?

The next *mishna* introduces a new case, structured similarly to the first but involving a very different subject: the *koy*. The *koy* is an animal of uncertain zoological classification — some type of hybrid, perhaps between a deer and another species — whose halachic status the rabbis were unable to determine. The essential question is whether the *koy* is a *chayah* (a wild animal) or a *behemah* (a domesticated animal), or perhaps belongs to some third category altogether.

### Koy's Halachic Status

The distinction between *chayah* and *behemah* carries significant halachic consequences in two directions. First, regarding blood covering: the verse *ish ki yatzud tzeid chayah o of asher yeiachel veshafachta et damo vechiso be'afar* — one who slaughters a *chayah* or a bird must cover the blood. A *behemah* is not subject to this requirement. Second, regarding *chelev* (forbidden fat): the *chelev* of a *behemah* is forbidden because the *behemah* is a species brought on the *mizbeiach*, whereas the *chelev* of a *chayah* is permitted since the *chayah* is not a sacrificial species. Because the *koy*'s category is unknown, the rabbis imposed both stringencies: its blood must be covered and its *chelev* may not be eaten.

The *koy* also invites a broader reflection. The question of whether reality must be binary — whether every animal must be either *chayah* or *behemah* — parallels discussions about the *androgynous*, who has both male and female features. Did the rabbis consider the possibility that such an individual constitutes a third category rather than being forced into either existing one? These questions carry obvious resonance with contemporary discussions, but they arise organically from the rabbinic texts themselves.

### Mishna's Seven Vows

The *mishna* then describes a group that sees a *koy* and makes conditional *nezirut* vows. Person one says *hareini nazir she-zeh chayah* — "I will be a *nazir* if this is a *chayah*." Person two says *hareini nazir she-zeh eino chayah*. Person three says *hareini nazir she-zeh behemah*. Person four says *hareini nazir she-ein zeh behemah*.

### Both/Neither Conditions

Person five says *hareini nazir she-zeh chayah uvehemah* — "I will be a *nazir* only if this animal falls into both categories simultaneously." Person six says *hareini nazir she-ein zeh lo chayah velo behemah* — "I will be a *nazir* only if it falls into neither category."

### Collective Vows

Person seven says *hareini nazir she-echad mikem nazir* — "if one of you is a *nazir*." Person eight says *hareini nazir she-ein echad mikem nazir* — "if one of you is not a *nazir*." Person nine says *hareini nazir she-kulchem nezirim* — "if all of you are *nezirim*."

### All Nine: Nezirim

The *mishna* rules: *harei kulam nezirim* — they are all *nezirim*. This is striking. If one takes the *koy* as either a *chayah* or a *behemah*, then only some of the conditions could be met and some could not. How can all nine become *nezirim*?

*Tosafot* explains that this need not be *Beit Shammai*'s position. It can be read according to *Rabbi Shimon*, who holds that in cases of doubt they are all *safek nezirim*. What *harei kulam nezirim* means, on this reading, is that they are all in the status of *safek nazir*. There remains some ambiguity about whether persons seven through nine might be *vadai nezirim* rather than *safek nezirim* — for example, if *she-ein echad mikem nazir* means "one of you is definitely not a *nazir* (and I will be one if that's true)," then that condition may be definitively met, making person eight a *vadai nazir*. Alternatively, *she-kulchem nezirim* might mean "all of you are *safek nezirim*," in which case the condition is met and person nine is a *vadai nazir*. *Tosafot* leaves these questions open but finds it possible to read the entire *mishna* as consistent with *Rabbi Shimon* and *Beit Hillel*, with all nine being *safek nezirim*.

---

## Nine Nezirim or Nezirut?

### Braita: Nine People

The *gemara* notes a discrepancy between two *braitot*. The first *braita* describes the *mishna*'s case as involving *tisha nezirim* — nine *nezirim*, meaning nine separate individuals who each made one conditional vow.

### Braita: One Person

The second *braita* describes it as *tisha nezirot* — nine *nezirut* statuses, implying that one person made all nine conditional declarations and consequently bears nine distinct obligations of *nezirut*.

### Cancellation Problem

The second reading raises an immediate difficulty. If one person said both "I will be a *nazir* if this is a *chayah*" and "I will be a *nazir* if this is not a *chayah*," only one of those two conditions can logically be met. One might think the two should cancel each other out or that together they produce at most one *nezirut*, not two. Similarly with all the paired conditions. So how does one person accumulate nine separate *nezirut* statuses?

### Rav Sheshet's Answer

The *gemara* also presses on the final three conditions, which reference "you" — the other people — and cannot easily be said by a single individual about himself. *Rav Sheshet* resolves this by positing a two-stage process: nine people each made the declarations corresponding to the first portion of the *mishna*, giving rise to nine *nezirim*. Then one of them additionally declared *hareini nazir unezirot hakol alai* — "I accept upon myself all the *nezirut* statuses that you have all undertaken." This one person thereby accumulates all nine *nezirut* obligations.

### No Cancellation Principle

The deeper *chidush* of the *tisha nezirot* reading — whichever mechanism produces it — is that contradictory conditions do not cancel each other out. When a person declares *nezirut* conditionally on the *koy* being a *chayah*, that *nezirut* takes effect *misafek*. When the same person declares *nezirut* conditionally on the *koy* not being a *chayah*, that *nezirut* also takes effect *misafek*. We do not step back and say: since logically only one can be true, only one counts. Each declaration stands independently.

### Legal Indeterminacy

This conclusion connects to a deeper point. The reason the contradictory conditions do not cancel is not simply a procedural rule about how vows are processed. It reflects the underlying nature of the *koy*'s status. Whether an animal is a *chayah* or a *behemah* is not a brute empirical fact that we happen not to know; it is a *legal* determination, and in the *koy*'s case, that legal determination is genuinely indeterminate. There is no objective fact of the matter that resolves it. This is analogous to what *Rav Soloveitchik* said about *bein hashmashot*: one view holds that *bein hashmashot* is simply a period within which we cannot identify the precise moment night begins; but the alternative view holds that *bein hashmashot* is by definition a liminal period, neither day nor night, not merely an unknown but an ontological gray zone. On the second view, it makes no sense to say *mi-manafshach* (one way or the other). The period simply is what it is. So too with the *koy*: since its classification is legally indeterminate — it may be both, neither, or a third category — all the conditional possibilities remain perpetually open, none cancels the others, and all the *nezirut* statuses coexist.

---

## Three Prohibitions

### Three Prohibitions Listed

The *gemara* now turns to a new *mishna* that opens the following chapter. *Shloshah minim asurim b'nazir* — there are three categories of prohibition for a *nazir*: *hatumah*, contracting ritual impurity through contact with the dead; *hadiglachas*, shaving or cutting the hair; and *hayotze min hagefen*, consuming products of the vine. The subsequent discussion focuses primarily on the third category.

### Grape Products Combine

The *mishna* states that *hayotze min hagefen mitztarefin zeh im zeh* — all products of the vine combine with one another toward the minimum required amount. So if a *nazir* consumes a small quantity of wine, a small quantity of grapes, and a small quantity of grape skins, these amounts aggregate.

### Kezayit Standard

The minimum measure for violation is a *kezayit* — the volume of an olive — of grape matter.

### Mishna Rishona: Revi'it

The *mishna* notes explicitly that there was an earlier *mishna* — a *mishna rishona* — which stated the measure as a *revi'it* of wine (*ad she-yishte revi'it yayin*), roughly three to three-and-a-quarter ounces. The relationship between these two measures requires clarification: the *mishna rishona* may have applied specifically to wine as a liquid, measured in the standard liquid unit of a *revi'it*, while the current ruling of *kezayit* applies to solid grape matter. Or it may be that originally even solid matter was conceptually measured against the liquid standard of wine — since the prohibition of grape products is conceptually derivative of the prohibition of wine — and the current position departed from that approach. The *gemara* will elaborate on this distinction.

---

## Individual Grape Parts

### Rabbi Akiva: Soaked Bread

*Rabbi Akiva* extends the prohibition to *mishrat anavim*: even if a person did not consume a *kezayit* of actual grape matter, if he ate a piece of bread that was soaked in wine, and the total volume of that bread is a *kezayit*, he is liable. The wine need not constitute a *kezayit* itself; it is the soaked bread that reaches the measure. *Rabbi Akiva* derives this from the verse *v'chol mishrat anavim lo yochal* — anything soaked in wine shall not be eaten. This verse creates an independent prohibition based on the totality of the soaked item, not solely on the quantity of wine absorbed.

This principle will lead into a broader discussion applicable to *kashrus* generally — specifically the question of how forbidden and permitted substances combine when mixed, whether liability is measured by the *issur* alone or by the composite. This *sugya* is studied in the context of *Yoreh De'ah* and the laws of *kashrus*.

### Each Part Separately

The *tanna kamma* holds that each of the four vine-derived categories — wine, grapes, *chartzanim* (which, as we will see, are the seeds), and *zagim* (the outer skin) — individually triggers liability if consumed in a *kezayit* quantity. The basis is the verse *meichartzanim v'ad zag lo yochal* — "from the seeds to the skin he shall not eat" — which enumerates each component separately.

### Rabbi Eleazar: Two & One

*Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah* introduces a stringency specific to the *chartzanim* and *zag*. He derives from the verse's plural and singular forms that liability for these components requires consuming two *chartzanim* and one *zag*. It is not enough to have a *kezayit* of seeds alone; one needs at least two seeds and one skin (or the reverse, depending on which term refers to which). Presumably the *kezayit* requirement remains in force alongside this, raising the question of how these two criteria interact when the quantities partially overlap.

### Chartzanim & Zag

Which term refers to the seeds and which to the skin? The *gemara* quotes the *tanna kamma*'s identification: *hachartzanim eilu hachitzonim* — the *chartzanim* are the outer part, meaning the skin; *hazagim eilu hapnimiyim* — the *zagim* are the inner part, meaning the seeds. That is the view of *Rabbi Yehuda*.

### Rabbi Yosi Corrects

*Rabbi Yosi* disagrees and offers a mnemonic to prevent confusion: *kezug she-beveheimah* — like the bell worn by an animal. A bell (*zug*) is the outer casing, while the internal clapper that strikes it is called the *inval*. Therefore, *zag* — related to *zug* — denotes the outer skin, and *chartzanim* — being plural — denotes the seeds, since each grape contains multiple seeds but only one skin. This makes intuitive sense. *Rabbi Yosi*'s identification is the accepted ruling: *chartzanim* are the seeds (as confirmed by modern Hebrew usage, where *beli chartzanim* means "seedless") and *zag* is the outer skin.

---

## Yotzei Min HaGefen Scope

### Gefen Itself Excluded

The *gemara* now interrogates the scope of *hayotze min hagefen*. The phrase *hayotze min hagefen* — that which issues from the vine — but not the *gefen* itself. The actual wood of the vine is excluded.

### Rabbi Eliezer: Leaves

*Rabbi Eliezer* holds a much broader position: *afilu alim velulavim bemashma* — even the leaves and the vine tendrils are included in the prohibition. The *mishna*, which does not enumerate these, is therefore inconsistent with *Rabbi Eliezer*'s view. The *lulavim* here are not the palm branches of *Sukkot* but rather the vine tendrils, the climbing appendages of the vine that wrap around supports.

### Hermeneutic Methods

The dispute between *Rabbi Eliezer* and the *rabbanan* flows from a fundamental difference in hermeneutic methodology. *Rabbi Eliezer* employs the method of *ribui u'miyut*, associated with the school of *Rabbi Akiva*, while the *rabbanan* employ *klal u'prat*, associated with the school of *Rabbi Yishmael*. This is the same distinction articulated in the thirteen hermeneutic principles recited at the conclusion of the morning blessings.

### Ribui U'Miyut Explained

The *ribui u'miyut* method operates as follows. If the Torah states a broad inclusive expression and then narrows it with a specific limiting expression, the ריבוי *ribui* has already broadened the scope to everything, and the *miyut* then narrows it by excluding only the category most unlike the items specified. If there is a further *ribui*, we are already at the stage of maximum inclusion and only the most dissimilar item is excluded.

### Klal U'Prat Explained

The *klal u'prat* method works differently. A general statement (*klal*) followed by a specific statement (*prat*) limits the scope entirely to the items specified — *ein baklal ela mah shebaprat*. If there is a subsequent *klal*, giving a structure of *klal prat u'klal*, then the scope expands again to anything similar to the items in the *prat*, but only things similar to them.

The verse concerning the *nazir* reads: *miyayin v'shechar yazir* — a specification (wine and strong drink); *mikol asher ye'aseh mi-gefen hayayin* — a general inclusion (anything made from the vine); *meichartzanim v'ad zag lo yochal* — a return to specifics (from seeds to skin). This is the structure of *prat klal u'prat*, which is the reverse of the more common *klal prat u'klal*.
