## Where Shaving Occurs

### Baraita Text

The *Gemara* cites a *braisa*: *v'gilach hanazir pesach ohel moed* — the *nazir* shaves at *petach ohel moed*. The *braisa* connects this with the *shelamim*: since the *shelamim* is described as being brought *pesach ohel moed* — *u'shchato pesach ohel moed* — and the *nazir*'s shaving is described with the same language, the shaving is being conceptually linked to the ritual of the *shelamim*. Indeed, beyond the *nazir* context, there is a *halacha* that if the doors of the *ohel moed* are not yet open when the *shelamim* is slaughtered, it is *pasul* — the phrase *pesach ohel moed* carries substantive weight in the *shelamim* ritual specifically. Applying that same phrase to the *nazir*'s shaving therefore connects the two.

### Literal vs. Metaphoric

One might ask: perhaps *pesach ohel moed* is not a metaphoric association but a literal geographic description — that the *nazir* performs his shaving literally inside *Makom HaMikdash*, in *Ezras Yisrael*. For a *nazir tahor* completing his thirty days, this is not a *taharah* problem — he is fully *tahor* and permitted in *Makom HaMikdash*. So conceivably the *Torah* is directing that the shaving literally take place at *pesach ohel moed*. The *Gemara* addresses and rejects this possibility.

### Rabbi Yoshaya

Rabbi Yoshaya argues that the literal reading cannot be correct, on grounds of *bizayon* — disrespect to the sanctity of *Makom HaMikdash*. He derives this from a *kal v'chomer*: the *Torah* says *lo ta'aleh b'ma'alos al mizbachi* — do not ascend the altar by stairs — because even the legitimate *avodah* of a *kohen* walking up steps might involve some slight exposure that is considered disrespectful. If even the *avodah* itself must be performed with such care regarding dignity, then surely the act of shaving — which is not an act of *avodah* — must not be performed within *Makom HaMikdash* itself, where it would constitute a *bizayon*. Therefore the phrase *pesach ohel moed* cannot mean literally there; it must be describing the connection to the *shelamim*. A parallel version of this *drashah* is cited from a *Midrash* in *Parshas Naso*, with slightly different wording but the same conclusion.

### Rabbi Yitzchak

Rabbi Yitzchak offers a different textual argument for the same conclusion. The *Torah* says *v'lakach et se'ar rosh nizro v'natan al ha'esh* — he takes the hair of his head and places it on the fire. The implication is *mi she'eino mechusar ela lekicha u'netina* — that all that intervenes between taking and placing is the act of taking and placing themselves. If the shaving took place in *Makom HaMikdash*, the *nazir* would then have to carry his hair out to where his *shelamim* is cooking — creating additional steps of *hava'ah* between the taking and the placing. The *Torah*'s language implies they occur in the same location. Therefore the shaving must take place where the *shelamim* is being cooked — which is outside *Makom HaMikdash*, in *Ezras Nashim* or even elsewhere in *Yerushalayim*. (Indeed, *lehalacha* there was an actual *lishkas nezirim* — a chamber in the *Ezras Nashim* — where the *nazir* would shave and cook his *shelamim* together.) A parallel formulation of this argument is cited in an alternative version: *makom shehu mevashel sham hayah megaleach* — where he cooks, there he shaves.

### Abba Chanan

Abba Chanan, in the name of Rabbi Eliezer, offers a position somewhat closer to the literal reading: *v'gilach hanazir pesach ohel moed kol zman she'ein pesach ohel moed pasuach eino megaleach* — the *nazir* shaves at *pesach ohel moed*, and if the doors of the *ohel moed* are not open, he may not shave. This takes the phrase *pesach ohel moed* not as a pure metaphor but as imposing a real condition: the shaving is only valid when the doors are open, wherever the shaving physically occurs. This is analogous to the rule about *shelamim* — a *shelamim* slaughtered when the doors are not yet open is *pasul*.

### Shimon Shizuri

Rabbi Shimon Shizuri offers a distinct *drashah* that moves in a different direction entirely. He reads: *v'gilach hanazir pesach ohel moed v'lo nezira* — a male *nazir* shaves at *pesach ohel moed*, but a female *nazirah* does not. According to *Tosafos*, what this means practically is that the *nazir* shaves in the vicinity of the grounds — in *Ezras Nashim* or wherever the *shelamim* is being cooked — an area that is frequented by *kohanim*, while the *nazirah* shaves in a private, modest location (*makom tzanua*) elsewhere in *Yerushalayim*. The reason: *shema yisgaru ba pirchei kehuna* — lest the young *kohanim* be aroused by her, since her hair is uncovered during the shaving.

### Sotah Objection

The *Gemara* raises an objection: the *sotah* also stands before the *kohanim* with her hair uncovered — *v'he'emidah lifnei Hashem* — and we do not invoke any concern of *shema yisgaru ba pirchei kehuna*. Why should the *nazirah* be treated differently?

### Sotah Response

Rabbi Shimon Shizuri responds: *zu kocheles u'pokeses* — the *nazirah* wears cosmetics and presents herself attractively, and it is in that state that she is shaving and her hair is uncovered. *Zu eina kocheles u'pokeses* — the *sotah*, by contrast, is being subjected to a public, degrading process; she is disheveled, not adorned. A woman in an attractive state with uncovered hair raises a concern of arousal that does not apply to a woman undergoing the humiliating *sotah* ordeal. It is for this reason that the *nazirah*, unlike the *nazir*, must shave in a modest, private location.

---

---

# Nazir 47

## Opening Mishnah & Tumah

### Opening & Daf Overview

We open today with daf 47, amud alef, picking up with the *mishnah* at the very top of the page. We are concluding one *perek* and beginning the next.

### Beard Shaving Q&A

Before turning to the text, one clarification worth noting: a *nazir* is only prohibited from cutting the hair of the head. Shaving the beard presents no problem whatsoever, since the prohibition of *nezirut* concerns only the long hair of the head.

### Mishnah: Blood & Tumah

The *mishnah* reads: *mi shenizrak alav echad min hadamim venitma* — one upon whom one of the blood-sprinklings has been performed and then became *tamei*. To set the context: we have just concluded the extended discussion in which the *chachamim* hold that even a single *korban* completes one's *nezirut*. The *mishnah* now addresses the case where, after one *korban* has already been brought, the *nazir* becomes *tamei*. What is the consequence?

### Eliezer vs. Chachamim

*Rabbi Eliezer omer soter et hakol* — Rabbi Eliezer says it undoes everything. This is a natural extension of Rabbi Eliezer's position from earlier, that *achar ma'aseh kulam* — one requires all the *korbanot* to complete *nezirut*. Since the *nezirut* was not yet concluded, the subsequent *tumah* destroys whatever had been accomplished.

*Vachachamim omrim yavi shear korbanotav veyit'har* — the *chachamim* say that the *nezirut* is indeed finished. The *tumah* does not undermine anything; the *korban* already brought remains valid. All that remains is the obligation to bring the remaining *korbanot*, which she completes after becoming *tahor*.

---

## Tosafot: Tahara Before K…

### Tosafot: Veyit'har Order

The language of the *mishnah* — *yavi shear korbanotav veyit'har* — might seem to suggest that one brings the *korbanot* first and only afterwards becomes *tahor*. Tosafot addresses this directly, explaining that *veyit'har* in this context means: *lichsheyit'har* — only once one has become *tahor* may the remaining *korbanot* be brought. The order in the *mishnah* should not be read literally as "bring and then purify," but rather "bring [once purified]."

### Sources: Yerushalmi & Pe…

Tosafot cites the *Yerushalmi*, which reads the *mishnah* straightforwardly as requiring *taharah* first and only then bringing the *korbanot*: *kach mefaresh biyerushalmi stam matnita d'tahara v'achar kach yavi korbanotav*.

The basis for this reading lies in the *pesukim* themselves. The *Torah*, when addressing a *nazir* who became *tamei meit*, describes a process in which he first achieves full *taharah* and only on the eighth day brings his *korban*. This reflects an implicit *Torah* demand: a *nazir* may not have his *korbanot* of *nezirut* brought while in a state of *tumah*. There is a broader *halachic* discussion about *tamei meshalayach korbanotav* — whether a *tamei* person may have *korbanot* brought on his behalf — and the ruling is that only certain light levels of *tumah* permit this. One who is *tamei meit*, or one who is a *metzora* or *zav*, certainly cannot be *meshalayach korbanotav*. But Tosafot's point is more specific: even if one might debate the general rule, in the particular context of a *nazir* who is *tamei meit*, the *pesukim* make clear that the *Torah* insists on full *taharah* before any *korbanot* of *nezirut* are brought.

### Why Tumah Can't Destroy…

Once we understand this, Tosafot explains why the *tumah* cannot destroy what has already been accomplished. The *korban* that was brought while the *nazir* was still *tahor* was valid — *harei hu kodem shenitma ra'uy litiglachas*, before he became *tamei* he was fit for the *tiglachat*, and the *korban* was brought in a state of *hechsher*. There is therefore no basis to disqualify it retroactively. However, any *korban* brought after the *tumah* but before achieving *taharah* would indeed be invalid: *aval hazevachim shehikriv mishenitma yistor* — whatever he brought after becoming *tamei* and before becoming *tahor* does not count.

The principle Tosafot articulates is: *dekapid kra sheyavi korbanot neziroot betaharah* — the *Torah* insists that the *korbanot* of *nezirut* be brought in a state of *taharah*. After the *nazir* undergoes *taharah*, including the *hazayah* of days three and seven, he may then bring the remaining *korbanot*.

---

## Eliezer: Soter Korba (II)

### Tosafot Clarification

This leads naturally to a clarification of what Rabbi Eliezer actually means when he says *soter et hakol*. The phrase sounds sweeping — it destroys everything — but we already know from an earlier *mishnah* that Rabbi Eliezer ruled that *tumah* after the full thirty days of *nezirut* requires only seven additional days, not the full thirty. So *soteret hakol* cannot literally mean all the days.

Tosafot makes this explicit in his very first comment here: *v'nitma Rabbi Eliezer omer soter hakol v'lo kol hayamim k'mforesh ba-Gemara d'Rabbi Eliezer hu d'amar l'eil nitma l'achar milo soter zayin ela soter korbanot kama* — Rabbi Eliezer says it destroys everything, but not all the days, as the *Gemara* clarifies; Rabbi Eliezer is the same one who said earlier that becoming *tamei* after the full thirty days requires only seven additional days. What is destroyed is not the count of days but the *korbanot* — the prior *korbanot* are nullified, and any subsequent *korbanot* are also invalid until the *nazir* properly completes his *nezirut*.

The context of the *mishnayot* throughout this section has been precisely this: whether the *korbanot* already brought remain valid or are destroyed. This is the *machloket* between Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim*, and the relationship to the number of days is secondary — a natural consequence of whether the *nezirut* itself was complete, but not the primary focus.

---

## Miriam from Tarmod Story

### Miriam's Daughter Dies

The *chachamim* bolster their position with a practical precedent: *ma'aseh b'Miriam haTarmodit* — there was a story involving Miriam from Tarmod. She had taken upon herself a *neder* of *nezirut* and one of the blood-sprinklings had already been performed on her behalf — *shenizrak aleha echad min hadamim*. At that moment, she was informed that her daughter was in mortal danger. She ran to her daughter and found that she had died — *vehalcha umatza shemeta*. She thus became *tamei meit* after one *korban* had already been brought.

### Chachamim's Ruling

The *chachamim* ruled: *tavi shear korbanoteha v'tit-har* — let her bring the remaining *korbanot* once she becomes *tahor*. Her *nezirut* was complete after that first *korban*; the subsequent *tumah* did nothing to undermine it. The *korban* that had been brought stood, and her obligation was only to complete the remaining *korbanot* after achieving *taharah*.

This ruling stands as a direct practical refutation of Rabbi Eliezer's position. Rabbi Eliezer holds that the *tumah* destroys the *korbanot* and effectively nullifies what was accomplished; the *chachamim* demonstrated through the case of Miriam that this is not so.

---

## Eliezer: Soter Korba (II)

### Gemara: Soter Definition

The *Gemara* now steps back and presses the question: the *mishnah* states that Rabbi Eliezer says *soter et hakol*, and elsewhere Rabbi Eliezer ruled that *tumah* after the full thirty days requires only seven additional days — so what does *soter* mean here? *Amar Rav mai soter d'ka'amar Rabbi Eliezer soter korbanotav* — Rav states: the *soter* Rabbi Eliezer refers to is that it destroys the *korbanot*. Any *korban* previously brought is nullified, and any *korban* brought in an improper state is likewise invalid. The *chachamim*, by contrast, hold that the first *korban* remains fully valid — *hacha nami savarta d'chachamim im tavi shear korbanoteha v'tit-har, shma mina* — as the case of Miriam from Tarmod confirms: let her bring the remaining *korbanot* once she becomes *tahor*, and this resolves the question.

The focus, then, in both the *mishnah* and the story of Miriam, is on the *korbanot* — not on the number of days. Days are implicated insofar as destroying *nezirut* means more days are required, but what is immediately at stake is whether the *korbanot* already brought retain their validity.

---

## Transition to Kohanic Tu…

### Perek Summary & Tumah Fo…

With the declaration of *hadran alach sheloshah minim*, we conclude the *perek* of *sheloshah minim*. That *perek* was structured around the three core prohibitions of a *nazir*: wine, shaving, and *tumah*. These three areas opened broader *halachic* discussions with general relevance. The wine prohibition led into the discussion of *ta'am ke'ikar* — the principle that taste functions like substance in matters of forbidden mixtures. The prohibition on shaving led to an examination of what constitutes shaving with respect to the beard and the *pe'ot*. And the prohibition on *tumah* opened the discussion of *tumat kohanim* — whether a *kohen* or *nazir* who is already *tamei meit* transgresses again by becoming *tamei* again, and the laws of *meit mitzvah*.

### Preview: Nazir-Kohen Pri…

Now, as we enter the new *perek*, we continue and deepen the discussion of *tumah*, because there is much more to learn from the relationship between *nazir* and *kohen* with respect to the restrictions on *tumah*. The central organizing principle of the coming *perek* is the rule known as *kol tumah she'ein haNazir megale'ach aleha ein Kohen muzhar aleha* — any *tumah* for which a *nazir* does not shave, a *kohen* is not prohibited against.

This principle might seem to refer only to *tumat sheretz*, *tumat neveilah*, *zivah*, *tzara'at*, and the like — types of *tumah* that are simply outside the scope of what *nezirut* addresses. But in fact it reaches further: even within the domain of *tumat meit* itself, there are categories that, by received tradition, do not trigger the obligation for a *nazir* to shave or to restart his *nezirut*, and therefore a *kohen* is likewise not prohibited against them. This creates an important area of inquiry — things that are technically *tumat meit* and yet fall outside the prohibitions both of *nezirut* and of the *kohen*'s restrictions against *tumah*. This has direct practical relevance for contemporary questions involving *kohanim*.

---

## Kohen Gadol, Nazir & Mei…

### Priority: Kohen Gadol vs…

The *mishnah* states: *Kohen Gadol veNazir ein mitamim likroveihem* — a *kohen gadol* and a *nazir* do not become *tamei* even to their immediate relatives. This is a striking parallel. A normal *kohen* may become *tamei* to his seven close relatives; a *kohen gadol* cannot. Conceptually, the *kohen gadol* is always in a state of readiness to serve — *min hamikdash lo yeitzei* — he is never permitted to remove himself from that role, even for the death of an immediate family member. The *nazir*, interestingly, shares this same restriction according to the *pesukim*: he too cannot become *tamei* even to an immediate relative.

Both, however, do become *tamei* for a *meit mitzvah*: *aval mitamim lemeit mitzvah*. This is not stated explicitly in the *Torah* but is understood by the *rabbis* from the *pesukim*, as the *Gemara* will explain. The *mishnah* then addresses the question of priority: *hayu mehalchim baderech u-matzu meit mitzvah* — if a *kohen gadol* and a *nazir* are traveling together and encounter a *meit mitzvah*, who should become *tamei* first?

The underlying issue here touches on the concept of *hutra* versus *dichuya* — whether in situations like *meit mitzvah* or *pikuach nefesh*, the prohibition is entirely suspended (*hutra*), or merely overridden by a competing value (*dichuya*). The *dichuya* perspective leads naturally to the effort to minimize the degree of override: if only one person needs to become *tamei* to fulfill the obligation, we try to determine which person's *tumah* is least consequential.

### Eliezer: Kohen Gadol Pri…

Rabbi Eliezer says: *yitma Kohen she'eino meivi korban al tumato v'al yitma Nazir shemeivi korban al tumato* — let the *kohen* become *tamei*, because a *kohen*'s *tumah* (under normal circumstances) does not require him to bring a *korban* as part of the consequences. The *nazir*, on the other hand, whose becoming *tamei* destroys his *nezirut* and requires him to bring a *korban*, suffers far more grievous consequences. Even though under normal circumstances both would be violating a *lav*, the practical fallout for the *nazir* is far weightier. Therefore, protect the *nazir* and let the *kohen gadol* become *tamei*.

One might ask about a *nazir Shimshon* — such a *nazir* does not bring a *korban* for *tumah* to begin with, since a *nazir Shimshon mitamei lemeitim* in any case. But that would be a moot point, as the *nazir Shimshon*'s status is sui generis.

### Chachamim: Nazir Priority

The *chachamim* respond with a fundamentally different framework: *yitma Nazir she'ein kedushato kedushat olam v'al yitma Kohen shekedushato kedushat olam* — let the *nazir* become *tamei*, because the *nazir*'s *kedushah* is only a *kedushah* of time, a temporary status, while the *kohen*'s *kedushah* is permanent.

The argument is not about the practical consequences of becoming *tamei*, but about the quality of the violation. When a *kohen*'s *kedushah* is breached, something essential to his very identity is transgressed. A *nazir*'s *kedushah*, while real and meaningful, is a status he accepted upon himself, not an intrinsic identity. It may even be a temporary status — though Tosafot notes that even a *nazir olam* does not change this calculus, because the fundamental character of *nezirut* as a *kedushah sha'ah* remains. The *chachamim* go further: they maintain this principle even as against a *kohen hedyot*, not just a *kohen gadol*. For Rabbi Eliezer, even a *kohen gadol* becomes *tamei* before a *nazir*; for the *chachamim*, even a *nazir* becomes *tamei* before a *kohen hedyot*. This explains why the *girsa* shifts in the text when recording the *chachamim*'s position — they ground the priority in *kedushat olam*, which belongs to any *kohen*, not only the *kohen gadol*.

The tension between the two positions is illuminating: Rabbi Eliezer measures by *halachic* consequence, the *chachamim* by the ontological weight of the violation.

---

## Two Kohen Gadolim Cases

### Anointed vs. Garmented

The *Gemara* now proceeds through a series of thought experiments involving cases where two figures of comparable but not identical status encounter a *meit mitzvah* together. The first case: *Mashuach beshemen hamishcha u'merubeh bivgadim* — one *kohen gadol* who was anointed with the anointing oil, and another who attained the office of *kohen gadol* by having worn the eight priestly garments (*merubeh begadim*). The anointing oil was secreted away in the time of King Yoshiyahu, so the question concerns what would have been the rule had such a scenario existed.

The *Gemara* rules: *mashuach beshemen hamishcha adif* — the one anointed with the anointing oil has the higher status and is therefore protected from *tumah*. The reason: *de'illu mashuach beshemen hamishcha meivi par al kol hamitzvot* — there is a special *halacha* in Masechet Horayot that if a *kohen gadol* who was *nimshach beshemen hamishcha* issued an incorrect ruling and then followed his own ruling, he brings a special *par* as an *atonement korban*. This privilege and the elevated status it reflects belongs only to the *mashuach beshemen hamishcha*, not to the *merubeh begadim*. Therefore, the anointed one has an objectively higher status and is accordingly protected.

The question of how such a scenario could realistically arise — with both simultaneously alive and both either equally active or equally retired — is something Tosafot addresses, though the precise reconstruction is complex.

### Off-Duty vs. Active

The second case: *mashuach she'avar u'merubeh begadim* — a *mashuach beshemen hamishcha* who is no longer in active service, alongside one who is *merubeh begadim* and currently serving. The ruling here reverses the first: *merubeh begadim adif*, *de'merubeh begadim avid avodah* — the one currently in active service takes priority and is protected. The reason is straightforward: what overrides the inherent prestige of having been anointed with the oil is the immediate practical reality that this person is actively performing *avodah*, and *tumah* would interfere with that. *Ve'ilu mashuach she'avar lav bar avodah hu* — the one who has been permanently removed from service cannot perform *avodah* regardless; there is no comparable disruption if he becomes *tamei*.

### One-Day vs. Permanent Is…

The third case: *avar machmas kiryo ve'avar machmas muma* — two *kohanim gedolim* who are both currently off duty. One was temporarily removed because he was a *ba'al keri* (a seminal emission), and the other because of a bodily blemish. The ruling: *avar machmas kiryo adif* — the one temporarily off duty due to *keri* is protected, *de'hu chazi le'avodah lemachar* — because he will be able to return to *avodah* the following day after immersing in the *mikveh*. The one removed due to a blemish, *ve'ilu avar machmas muma lo chazi le'avodah* — cannot currently serve, and Tosafot adds that even if the blemish is potentially temporary, one does not know when it will heal, whereas the *ba'al keri*'s disqualification is precisely one day. All three of these cases follow a clear logical structure: the one whose active relationship with the *avodah* is more immediate and more restorable is always the one whose *taharah* is more protected.

---

## Mashuach Milchamah vs. S…

### Question Posed

Now the *Gemara* raises a question that is less immediately obvious: *iba'ya lehu mashuach milchama ve'sgan hai minaihu adif* — which has higher priority, the *mashuach milchama* or the *sgan*?

The *mashuach milchama* is the *kohen* anointed to lead the people into battle — the one who addresses the people before war with the words *mi ha'ish hayarei ve'rach halevav yelech ve'yashuv leveiso*. He holds a specially anointed role of considerable stature. The *sgan* is the vice *kohen gadol*, whose role is to stand ready to substitute for the *kohen gadol* should he become *tamei*, particularly on *yom kippur* when a *kohen gadol* is absolutely indispensable.

Both are a rank below the *kohen gadol*, functioning as executive vice-presidents of sorts. The question: if they both encounter a *meit mitzvah*, which one is protected and which one must become *tamei*? The *mashuach milchama* has an active, weighty role — he is not merely waiting in the wings, he is on stage. The *sgan*, one might think, is essentially defined by his readiness to step in, which only rarely becomes relevant. So perhaps the *mashuach milchama*'s status warrants protection?

### Baraita Answer

The *Gemara* cites a *baraita* in response: *tashma detanya, ein bein mashuach milchama lesgan ela she'im hayu mehalchim baderech u'matzu meit mitzvah, yitamei mashuach milchama ve'al yitamei sgan* — the only difference between the *mashuach milchama* and the *sgan* is this: if they are going on the way and find a *meit mitzvah*, the *mashuach milchama* becomes *tamei* and not the *sgan*. So the *sgan* is the one who is protected.

### Rationale: Sgan's Role

The rationale is precisely what makes this a striking ruling. The *sgan*'s entire job description is to remain *tahor* and ready. *Rebbi Chanina ben Antigonus omer: lama tiknu sgan lekohen gadol? she'im ye'arei bo psul harei nichnas umeshamesh tachtav* — why did they institute a *sgan* for the *kohen gadol*? So that if the *kohen gadol* becomes disqualified, the *sgan* enters and serves in his place. His primary responsibility is not some active task he is currently performing — it is the maintenance of his *taharah* and readiness. Becoming *tamei* would be a fundamental violation of the *sgan*'s core function in a way that the *mashuach milchama*'s becoming *tamei* is not. The *mashuach milchama*'s role does not require him to preserve his *taharah* as its central purpose; the *sgan*'s role does, almost by definition.

---

## Two Different Priorities

### Contradiction Noted

But this ruling seems to contradict another *baraita*: *mashuach milchama kodem lesgan* — the *mashuach milchama* comes before the *sgan*, apparently suggesting that the *mashuach milchama* has higher priority. Does this not contradict the rule that the *sgan* is protected from *tumah*?

### Two Contexts, Two Rules

The *Gemara* resolves: *le'inyan hachayoso mashuach milchama adif* — when it comes to saving a life, the *mashuach milchama* takes priority. *Mai ta'ama? detali beih rabim* — because the welfare of many depends on him. If one must choose whose life to save, the *mashuach milchama*'s role in protecting the entire people gives him priority, much as one would prioritize saving the Secretary of Defense over a deputy official whose role is primarily one of readiness.

*Ule'inyan tumah sgan adif* — but when it comes to *tumah*, the *sgan* is given priority and is protected. *Detanya Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus omer: lama tiknu sgan lekohen gadol* — because the entire rationale for the *sgan*'s existence is to remain *tahor* and ready to serve if needed. These are two different questions yielding two different answers, and there is no contradiction.

### Tosafot: Hierarchy Clari…

Tosafot raises an important point here. The *baraita* states *ein bein mashuach milchama lesgan* — there is no difference between them except for this matter of *tumah*. But this seems plainly incorrect: there are in fact many significant differences between the two. The *mashuach milchama* wears the garments of the *kohen gadol*, while the *sgan* wears the garments of a *kohen hedyot* — even when performing his role, and even in the context of *yom kippur*, when the *kohen gadol* himself wears *bigdei lavan*. Moreover, the five restrictions enumerated in the *parasha* for the *kohen gadol* — not disheveling his hair, not rending his garments, not becoming *tamei* to the dead, not marrying a widow, and being required to marry only a *betulah* — all of these apply to the *mashuach milchama* but not to the *sgan*.

This means the *mashuach milchama* is effectively a quasi-*kohen gadol* in a different sphere: not in the *Beit HaMikdash* but in the domain of the battlefield and the camp. So what does the *baraita* mean by *ein bein*?

Tosafot explains: the *ein bein* means that there is no area in which we give greater weight to the *sgan* over the *mashuach milchama*, except for this one matter — that the *sgan* does not become *tamei* when they encounter a *meit mitzvah* together. In every other domain, the *mashuach milchama* has equal or greater status. But in this one instance, because the *sgan*'s entire identity is bound up with maintaining *taharah*, that is the single exception where the *sgan* is protected and the *mashuach milchama* is not.

---

## Individual Override for…

### Individual Permission

Having completed the analysis of who takes priority when a *kohen gadol* and *nazir* travel together, the *Gemara* steps back to address the foundational premise. *Ad kan lo peligi ela be-Kohen Gadol ve-Nazir ki ka azli bahadi hadadi* — all the debate has been about who takes priority when they are traveling together. *Aval chad chad le-chudei bartzit meiyei inun* — but if each of them is alone, it is taken for granted that each one individually is permitted to become *tamei* to a *meit mitzvah*.

### Source Question

This prompts a fundamental question: *minani milei* — where does this come from? The *Torah* never states explicitly that a *meit mitzvah* overrides the prohibitions on *tumah* for a *kohen gadol* or a *nazir*. What is the textual source?

---

## Pesukkim: Al Kol Nafshot…

### Pesuk: Le'aviv U'le'imo

The *Gemara* cites the relevant *pesukim*. Regarding the *kohen gadol* it is written: *al kol nafshot met lo yavo* — he shall not approach any dead person, and separately: *le'aviv u'le'imo lo yitama* — not even to his father and mother shall he become *tamei*.

### Kal Va'chomer Logic

The *Gemara* asks: who is the subject of *al kol nafshot met lo yavo*? If it is addressing non-relatives, this would be redundant — *kal va-chomer hu*. A normal *kohen* who may become *tamei* to his relatives may not become *tamei* to non-relatives; how much more so a *kohen gadol* who cannot even become *tamei* to relatives — surely he cannot become *tamei* to non-relatives. There would be no need for the *Torah* to state this explicitly. Tosafot frames the same point more directly, without the circularity of a formal *kal va-chomer*: a *kohen gadol* is already a *kohen*, and as such is already prohibited against *tumah* to non-relatives in his basic capacity as a *kohen*. Therefore *al kol nafshot met* cannot be teaching us about non-relatives.

### Both Phrases Extra?

It follows that *al kol nafshot met lo yavo* must be referring to relatives — the *Torah* is telling us that a *kohen gadol* may not become *tamei* even to his own family. If that is so, then the subsequent phrase *le'aviv u'le'imo lo yitama* — not to his father and mother — appears to be entirely redundant. We have already been told he cannot become *tamei* to any relative. Why repeat it for father and mother specifically?

### Extra Words Teach New Ru…

Because both phrases are extra, each can be expounded to teach something new. *Le'aviv* — "to his father" — is cited as an example: *ha mitamei hu le-met mitzvah* — but he does become *tamei* to a *meit mitzvah*. The specific mention of *le'aviv* signals that there is someone to whom he may become *tamei* — and this is the *meit mitzvah*. The logic follows the principle of *miyut achar miyut ela lerabbot*: two restrictions in sequence imply that within those restrictions there is a permitted category. The *Torah* has already said he cannot become *tamei* to relatives; adding "not to the father" implies — but there is one case where he can, namely a *meit mitzvah*.

---

## Gezeira Shava: Le'imo Co…

### Nazir's Le'imo Scope

The *Gemara* now turns to *le'imo* — "to his mother" — and brings a *braisa* in the name of *Rebbi* that opens with the *nazir*. A *nazir* is told *lo yitama lahem bemotam* — he shall not become *tamei* to them in their deaths. The word *bemotam* — "in their deaths" — is significant: it specifies *tumat meit* as the prohibited *tumah*, thereby implying that other types of *tumah* — such as *tzara'at* or *zivah* — do not fall under the *nazir*'s prohibition. *Gabi nazir bemotam eino mitamei aval mitamei hu lenigam ulezivatam* — for a *nazir*, the prohibition is specifically against becoming *tamei* through death-related *tumah*; contact with a *metzora* or a *zav* is not prohibited.

This might seem obvious, since the *nazir*'s prohibition is textually framed around corpse-*tumah*. But it sets up the crucial *gezeira shava*.

### Applied to Kohen Gadol

With respect to the *kohen gadol*, the question is different. The *pesukim* say *le'aviv u'le'imo lo yitama* — not to his father and mother shall he become *tamei*. These words do not specify *bemotam*; they simply say he shall not become *tamei*. One might therefore think the prohibition encompasses any *tumah* his father or mother might have — whether *tumat meit*, *tzara'at*, or *zivah*. *Bekohen gadol minalan* — how do we know that for a *kohen gadol* as well, the restriction is limited to *tumat meit*?

The answer is a *gezeira shava*: *ne'emar imo benazir vene'emar imo bekohen gadol* — the word *imo* ("his mother") appears both by the *nazir* and by the *kohen gadol*. This verbal parallel licenses a *halachic* connection: *mah imo ha'amur benazir bemotam eino mitamei aval mitamei hu lenigam ulezivatam* — just as by the *nazir*, the prohibition is limited to *tumat meit* (as established by *bemotam*), *af imo ha'amur bekohen gadol bemotam eino mitamei aval mitamei hu lenigam ulezivatam* — so too by the *kohen gadol*, the restriction is only against *tumat meit*, and contact with a *metzora* or *zav* is not prohibited.

### Redundancy Analysis

The overall structure of the exposition is now complete. Since *al kol nafshot met lo yavo* must refer to relatives (as argued above), both *le'aviv* and *le'imo* are redundant within the *pesuk*. Each extra phrase comes to teach a distinct *halacha*: *le'aviv* teaches that there is a case — *meit mitzvah* — where even a *kohen gadol* becomes *tamei*; and *le'imo*, through the *gezeira shava* with the *nazir*, teaches that the *kohen gadol*'s prohibition is restricted to *tumat meit* and does not extend to other forms of *tumah*. These are not references to the *kohen gadol*'s specific father or mother — once *al kol nafshot met* encompasses all relatives, *le'aviv* and *le'imo* become free to carry new independent *halachic* content, as extra words in the *Torah* are never without purpose.

---

---

# Nazir 48

## Kohen Gadol & Nazir

### Meis Mitzvah Override

The daf opens in the middle of 48a, approximately fifteen lines down, at the margin notation *Bamidbar* 6. The sugya is concerned with establishing the source for a striking principle: the prohibitions against *tumah* incumbent upon a *kohen gadol* and a *nazir* are each exceptionally severe and categorical — neither may become *tamei* even to his closest relatives — and yet both prohibitions are overridden when a *meis mitzvah* is at stake. The question the *gemara* sets out to answer is: what is the textual and logical basis for this override?

### Kohen Gadol Source

By the *kohen gadol*, the Torah states: *al kol nafshos meis lo yavo, l'aviv u'l'imo lo yitama* — he shall not enter upon any dead soul, and shall not become *tamei* for his father or mother. The *gemara*, as framed by *Tosafos*, reasons as follows: since a *kohen gadol* is already a standard *kohen*, he is already forbidden to become *tamei* to non-relatives by virtue of the general *kohen* prohibition. The phrase *al kol nafshos meis lo yavo* need not therefore be read as restricting him from non-relatives — that is already known. Rather, it must be addressing relatives. And if relatives are already implicit in the opening clause, what purpose does the separate phrase *l'aviv u'l'imo lo yitama* serve? Since a prohibition followed by a further limiting phrase — a *miyut achar miyut* — implies an implicit permission, we derive that while for his father he is prohibited, a *meis mitzvah* overrides even this. The word *aviv* teaches no to relatives but yes to *meis mitzvah*. And the word *imo* is used to link — through a *gezeirah shavah* — to the corresponding passage in the laws of *nazir*, establishing that the prohibition applies only to *tumat meis* and not to other forms of *tumah* such as *tzara'as* or *zivah*.

### Kal Vachomer Attempt

With the *kohen gadol*'s exception established, the *gemara* turns to the *nazir*: how do we know that a *nazir*'s prohibition is similarly overridden for a *meis mitzvah*? One might have proposed a *kal v'chomer*: if a *kohen gadol*, whose sanctity is permanent and eternal, may become *tamei* for a *meis mitzvah*, then a *nazir*, whose sanctity is limited in time and assumed voluntarily, should certainly be overridden for a *meis mitzvah*. However, the *gemara* rejects this inference. The *kal v'chomer* can be reversed: a *kohen gadol* who becomes *tamei* intentionally violates a prohibition and receives lashes, but there is no *korban* associated with his violation. A *nazir* who becomes *tamei*, by contrast, must bring a *korban* and restart his *nezirut*. The *tumah* carries far heavier practical consequences for the *nazir*, and so one might argue that his *kedushah* is more precarious rather than less severe, and that a *meis mitzvah* therefore would not override it. The *kal v'chomer* fails, and a *pasuk* is needed.

---

## Nazir Braita Drasha

### Nefesh Meis Analysis

The *gemara* transitions to the laws of *nazir* and introduces a *braita*. The relevant verse states: *al nefesh meis lo yavo* — the *nazir* shall not enter upon a dead soul — followed by *l'aviv u'l'imo l'achiv u'l'achoso lo yitama lahem b'mosam*. The *braita* begins by asking whether the phrase *nefesh meis* might include even an animal carcass, since an animal is also called a *nefesh*, as in the verse *makeh nefesh behemah*. The *braita* resolves this by noting that a dead animal is called a *neveilah*, not a *nefesh meis* — *nefesh meis* denotes a human corpse specifically.

### Tanna Kamma vs Yishmael

The *tanna kamma* derives this restriction from the word *meis* itself: the verse speaks of *nefesh adam*, a human being. Rabbi Yishmael disagrees and says there is no need to derive it from the word *meis*. The verse says *lo yavo* — he shall not enter the same space — not merely *lo yiga*, he shall not touch. The only form of *tumah* that operates through *biah*, through being under the same roof without direct contact, is *tumat meis* of a human corpse. All other forms of *tumah* operate only through touch or carrying. Since the verse prohibits *lo yavo*, it is implicitly addressing only human corpses: *benefashot hamitamot b'viah hakatuv medaber* — the verse speaks of those corpses that convey *tumah* through entry into the same space. One who enters the same room as the corpse, even without touching, becomes *tamei* — and this is true only of human corpses. Whether this extends to non-Jewish corpses with respect to *tumat ohel* is itself a matter of *machloket* among the *tannaim*, but for Jewish corpses there is no question.

### Aviv v'Imo Signal

With this established, the *braita* proceeds: *l'aviv u'l'imo eino mitamei aval mitamei hu l'meis mitzvah* — for his father and mother he does not become *tamei*, but for a *meis mitzvah* he does. The words *aviv* and *imo* are understood as carrying a surplus meaning. Before explaining the precise function of each word, the *braita* notes that one might have thought the exception for *meis mitzvah* could be derived by logic alone: *ad shelo yomar yesh li badin* — even before the verse says so, I could have reasoned it out.

### Why Not Kal Vachomer

The logic would be a *kal v'chomer*: a *kohen gadol* whose sanctity is permanent — *kedushato kedushat olam* — may nonetheless become *tamei* for a *meis mitzvah*. A *nazir* whose sanctity is inherently time-limited — *she'ein kedushato kedushat olam* — should certainly be overridden for a *meis mitzvah*. But as already noted, the *kal v'chomer* can be deflected: a *kohen gadol* does not bring a *korban* for his *tumah*, whereas a *nazir* brings a *korban* and must restart entirely. This counter-argument — *lo im amarta b'kohen gadol she'kein eino meivi korban al tumato* — is sufficient to defeat the *kal v'chomer*.

The *braita* next considers another possible interpretation of *l'aviv u'l'imo*. Perhaps these words are not teaching that relatives are forbidden while *meis mitzvah* is permitted. Perhaps the reverse is intended: for his father and mother he is forbidden, but for other corpses — non-relatives — he is permitted? This *hava amina* has a certain logic: with relatives, the emotional pull is so strong that any boundary might dissolve. With strangers, there is less risk of overreach, so perhaps only relatives are restricted. However, the *gemara* dismisses this reading via a *kal v'chomer* from the ordinary *kohen*: even a standard *kohen hedyot*, whose level of *kedushah* is far lower, is *tamei* to relatives but not to non-relatives — relatives are the easier case for a *kohen*, not the harder one. If a lower-grade *kohen* may become *tamei* for relatives but not for non-relatives, then certainly a *nazir*, who may not become *tamei* even for relatives, cannot be *tamei* for non-relatives. So *l'aviv u'l'imo* is not telling us non-relatives are permitted.

What then is the function of these words? *L'aviv u'l'imo she'eino mitamei aval mitamei hu l'meis mitzvah* — they are extra, and their surplus signals the permission of *meis mitzvah*.

A difficulty remains, however: for the *kohen gadol*, the opening clause was already understood as referring to relatives because he is already a standard *kohen* and is obviously forbidden to non-relatives. The extra words therefore pointed to *meis mitzvah*. But for a *nazir*, there is no such prior prohibition against non-relatives. A *nazir* does not begin from a baseline of being forbidden to any corpse. Therefore, the opening clause *al nefesh meis lo yavo* might itself be needed to establish the prohibition against non-relatives, leaving no surplus at all. If the opening clause addresses non-relatives, then *aviv* is needed to teach relatives, and there is nothing left over for *meis mitzvah*.

### Gezeirah Shavah Setup

The *gemara* works through this carefully. Ultimately it concludes: *aviv* teaches that relatives are forbidden — that is its function for the *nazir*, in contrast to the *kohen gadol* where the same role was played by the opening clause. And *imo* is reserved for the *gezeirah shavah* connecting the *nazir*'s verse to the *kohen gadol*'s verse on the matter of *b'mosam* — teaching that the prohibition applies only to *tumat meis* and not to other *tumot*. That leaves *achiv* — "his brother" — as the word that teaches *meis mitzvah* is permitted. And *achoso* remains to teach something further, which we will reach shortly. The *gemara* thus maps the words as follows for the *tanna kamma* (Chachamim) approach: the opening *al nefesh meis* establishes non-relatives; *aviv* establishes relatives; *imo* functions in the *gezeirah shavah* establishing that only *tumat meis* is covered; *achiv* teaches yes to *meis mitzvah*; and *achoso* teaches something additional.

It is worth noting that the entire structure of this *sugya* is built around an interplay between the authority of the text and the authority of human reasoning. The very phrase *ad shelo yomar yesh li badin* — I could have reasoned it out even without the verse — reflects a principle found elsewhere in the *gemara*: *lama li kra, sevara hu* — why do I need a verse, this is logical. The verse is needed only where the logic is genuinely ambiguous. Where the conclusion follows clearly from reason, a verse would be superfluous.

---

## Meis Mitzvah Application

### Pesach & Milah Case

The *braita* now takes up the function of *achoso* — "his sister" — and what that word comes to teach. *U'l'achoso mah talmud lomar?* A case is presented: someone is on his way to slaughter his *korban Pesach* or to perform a *bris milah* for his son — both of which are *mitzvos aseh* whose violation carries *kares* — and he hears that a relative has died. Must he interrupt what he is doing and become *tamei* to attend to the burial? The instinct might be that yes, the obligation to bury relatives is powerful, perhaps powerful enough to override these other *mitzvos*.

### Tosafot Weighing

*Tosafos* in the discussion of *u'l'achoso mah talmud lomar* clarifies the scope of this rule: it applies even to a regular person — not a *kohen gadol* and not a *nazir* — who is in the process of performing *Pesach* or *milah*. *Tosafos* explains: *lo ati aseh d'tumah she'ein bah kares, d'dachi aseh d'Pesach u'milah she'yesh bahem kares* — a positive commandment to become *tamei* for a relative, which is a *mitzvah* without *kares*, does not override a weightier positive commandment associated with *kares*. One might have thought that the obligation to attend to a deceased relative, given how seriously the *gemara* treats *meis mitzvah*, would override even these powerful *mitzvos*. The *chidush* here is that it does not — at least in a situation where others are available to attend to the deceased, so that the relative does not become a *meis mitzvah*. If the person himself abandons *Pesach* or *milah* to attend to the burial, he violates the principle. This is a significant ruling given the general weight we assign to caring for the deceased.

### Achoso Drasha

But the verse then continues: *yachol lo yitamei l'meis mitzvah* — perhaps even in the case of a *meis mitzvah* he should not become *tamei*, even while performing other *mitzvos*? The answer: *talmud lomar achoso* — the word *achoso* teaches that by a *meis mitzvah*, he does become *tamei*, and moreover, *meis mitzvah* overrides even his being actively engaged (*osek*) in the *mitzvos* of *korban Pesach* and *milah*. *Achoso* therefore teaches the outer limit of *meis mitzvah*'s power: not only does it override the *kedushah* of a *nazir* and a *kohen gadol*, it overrides one's active engagement in these other critical *mitzvos*.

---

## Tanna Kamma & Akiva

### Tanna Kamma Method

To summarize the *tanna kamma*'s (Chachamim's) *drasha*: *aviv* establishes that relatives are forbidden; *imo* serves the *gezeirah shavah* to establish that only *tumat meis* is at issue (not other *tumot*); *achiv* teaches that *meis mitzvah* overrides; *achoso* teaches that *meis mitzvah* overrides even when one is *osek* in *Pesach* and *milah*.

### Akiva's Opening

Rabbi Akiva offers an alternative *drasha*. He says: *nefesh ilu ha'rechokim, meis ilu ha'kerovim* — within the opening clause *al nefesh meis lo yavo*, the word *nefesh* already addresses non-relatives, and the word *meis* addresses relatives. Two separate words, two separate categories. This means that by the time we reach the subsequent listing of *aviv, imo, achiv, achoso*, we have already excluded both non-relatives and relatives from any permission, and the words that follow are entirely free to teach other things. Consequently, Rabbi Akiva does not need *aviv* to prohibit relatives — he has already accomplished that from the opening clause.

### Akiva Aviv, Imo, Achiv

For Rabbi Akiva, *l'aviv u'l'imo eino mitamei aval mitamei hu l'meis mitzvah* — both *aviv* and *imo* together teach that *meis mitzvah* is permitted. This immediately raises a question: why are both words needed to convey a single ruling? The *gemara* will address this. Rabbi Akiva's use of both *aviv* and *imo* for *meis mitzvah* also creates a problem for the *gezeirah shavah* — if *imo* is occupied here, how can it simultaneously serve as the connecting word for the *gezeirah shavah* establishing that the prohibition applies only to *tumat meis*? That too will be addressed. *Achiv* and *achoso*, now freed from their earlier roles, are available for further teachings.

---

## Akiva Achiv & Achoso

### Akiva Achiv

For Rabbi Akiva, *achiv* teaches the following: *she'yehei kohen gadol v'hu nazir, l'achiv eino mitamei aval mitamei hu l'meis mitzvah* — this refers to a person who is both a *kohen gadol* and a *nazir* simultaneously. We already know from Rabbi Akiva's system that *meis mitzvah* overrides a *kohen gadol* alone, and that it overrides a *nazir* alone. But what of a person carrying both statuses at once, a double accumulation of prohibitions?

### Achiv Necessity

One might have thought that although a *meis mitzvah* overrides a single *lav*, it would not override two simultaneous *lavin*. Perhaps the quantitative increase in the number of prohibitions tips the scales. *Achiv* therefore comes to teach that *meis mitzvah* overrides even this double status: *mah li chad lav, mah li trei lavin* — whether there is one *lav* or two *lavin*, the *Torah*'s dispensation for *meis mitzvah* applies equally.

---

## Gezeirah Shavah Logic

### Problem Setup

This creates an apparent difficulty for Rabbi Akiva. If both *aviv* and *imo* are together needed to teach that *meis mitzvah* is permitted for a *nazir*, then neither word is free at either end of the analogy, since they are both actively employed in the verse about the *nazir*. Equally, up at the verse of the *kohen gadol*, both words would presumably also be needed to teach *meis mitzvah* there. If so, *imo* is not free at either end, and the *gezeirah shavah* between the two passages — which requires at least one word to be free — cannot be constructed.

### Solution: Already Known

The *gemara* answers concisely, and *Tosafos* elaborates: *kivan d'amar mar im hayah kohen gadol v'nazir l'achiv eino mitamei aval mitamei hu l'meis mitzvah, mah li kohen gadol lachudei, mah li nazir v'kohen gadol* — since Rabbi Akiva's own *drasha* on *achiv* already teaches that *meis mitzvah* overrides a person who is simultaneously a *kohen gadol* and a *nazir*, we have thereby already established that *meis mitzvah* overrides the *kohen gadol* as well. Once *meis mitzvah*'s override of the *kohen gadol* is already known from *achiv*, the word *imo* in the *kohen gadol*'s verse no longer needs to convey that ruling — it is freed. And once it is free at that end, the *gezeirah shavah* can be constructed even without the word being free at both ends. *Imo* is therefore available to serve the *gezeirah shavah* linking the *nazir* and the *kohen gadol* on the restriction of *tumat meis* exclusively.

---

## Akiva Achiv & Achoso (II)

### Akiva Achoso

Having established the function of *achiv* in Rabbi Akiva's system, the remaining word is *achoso*. For Rabbi Akiva, where *achoso* is no longer needed to teach the double-status case (already derived from *achiv*), *achoso* retains the role it plays in the *tanna kamma*'s system: teaching that *meis mitzvah* overrides even when one is actively engaged in other *mitzvos*, namely *korban Pesach* and *milah*. As the *braita* had stated: even if one is already on the way to perform these time-sensitive *mitzvos aseh she'yesh bahem kares*, if a *meis mitzvah* arises, he must stop and attend to it. And by way of parallel — for the *tanna kamma* (*Chachamim*), this same ruling was derived from *achoso* as well, but they needed *achiv* first for the basic *meis mitzvah* exception, having no other available word. Rabbi Akiva, having derived *meis mitzvah* from *aviv* and *imo* and double-status from *achiv*, uses *achoso* for this final teaching about overriding active engagement in other *mitzvos*.

---

## Aviv & Imo Necessity

### Aviv Alone Problem

We must now address the question of why Rabbi Akiva needs both *aviv* and *imo* to teach *meis mitzvah* — why would one of them alone not suffice? The *gemara* explains with two distinct *hava aminas*. Had the verse stated only *aviv* — the father — one might have thought: the reason the *nazir* is restricted from becoming *tamei* to his father is specifically because paternity is established by *chazakah* alone. You never know with absolute certainty who one's father is. Perhaps that very uncertainty is what generates the stringency — there is a measure of doubt about the relationship. But if so, the *tumah* restriction to the father might reflect that doubt rather than the general principle of *kedushah*. By implication, the mother — *deyadi'an deyaldasei*, whose identity as the birth mother is certain — might be permissible. So *aviv* alone could have been misread as indicating that only relationships characterized by paternal uncertainty are restricted, not maternal relationships.

### Imo Alone Problem

Conversely, had the verse stated only *imo* — the mother — one might have thought the opposite. The reason the *nazir* is restricted from becoming *tamei* to his mother might be because she is not part of the patriarchal family identity. The Torah everywhere speaks of family in terms of the father's line: *l'mishpechotam l'beit avotam*. The mother's side is not the primary identifier of lineage or family in the Torah's structure. So if the verse said only *imo*, one might have understood: yes, the mother's side is restricted precisely because it falls outside the primary family definition, but the father's side — which *is* the family — should certainly be permissible. *Imo* alone could have been misread as limiting the prohibition to the non-patriarchal line.

### Both Combined Solution

Therefore, the verse states both *aviv* and *imo*. When read together, they convey nothing that the opening clause had not already established — all relatives are prohibited. The combination adds nothing new in terms of scope, and this is precisely the point. Because the combination does not limit the prohibition to one parental line over the other, it does not subtract from what the opening clause established. The words are therefore truly surplus, and a *miyut achar miyut* — a repeated restriction after an already-complete restriction — serves to *permit* rather than to further restrict. The surplus of both words *combined* is what signals the permission for *meis mitzvah*. Had only one been present, it might have been read as a limiting clarification rather than a permissive signal. With both present, neither misinterpretation is possible, and the *drasha* emerges cleanly: they are extra, and their surplus message is that *meis mitzvah* is permitted.

This is what the lengthy *Tosafos* on this passage ultimately establishes. It navigates carefully through the apparent circularity — the words were used to teach *meis mitzvah*, yet the *gemara* seems to focus on why you need both to maintain the prohibition on relatives — and concludes that the necessity of both words is precisely what ensures the *drasha* for *meis mitzvah* is not susceptible to misinterpretation. You must say both to prevent the reader from thinking the verse is narrowing the prohibition rather than opening an exception.

---

## Kol & Nefesh Usage

### Kol Nafshos Role

The *gemara* returns to the opening clause of the *kohen gadol*'s verse — *al kol nafshos meis lo yavo* — and asks, given everything Rabbi Akiva has now derived from subsequent words, what does *kol nafshos* teach? The answer is that it establishes the general prohibition against *tumah* from non-relatives: *l'afukei rechokim* — to exclude the thought that any leniency might apply even to distant persons.

### Nafshot Plural

The plural form *nafshos* serves a distinct function: *l'afukei revi'is dam sheyatza mishnei meitim* — to exclude a quarter-*log* (*revi'is*) of blood drawn from two separate corpses from the principle that a *revi'is* of blood from a single corpse conveys *tumah* through *ohel*. Normally, a *revi'is* of blood from one body represents a sufficient quantity to convey *tumat ohel*, and a *kohen gadol* or *nazir* would be prohibited. One might have thought that if the same volume is drawn from two separate corpses, it does not represent a complete single *meis* and therefore ought not convey *tumat ohel*. The plural *nafshos* — *kol nafshos* — teaches that even blood from two separate corpses combining to form a *revi'is* does convey *tumat ohel*, and is therefore prohibited for a *kohen gadol* and a *nazir*.

With this, the *sugya* of 48a reaches its conclusion. The bottom line of the entire discussion, shared by both the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Akiva despite their different methods of *drasha*, is consistent: both a *kohen gadol* and a *nazir* are prohibited from *tumat meis* for all relatives, but both are obligated to attend to a *meis mitzvah*, and that obligation supersedes even their heightened *kedushah* — and in fact supersedes active engagement in other weighty *mitzvos* as well.

---

---

# Nazir 49

## Intro & Overview

### Opening Remarks

Today's shiur picks up on 49b and will cover, God willing, through daf 50 as well.

### Perek Focus & Exceptions

This *perek* has been focused on the prohibition against a *nazir* becoming *tamei*. We have spent considerable time understanding how *meis mitzvah* overrides the restrictions of both a *nazir* and a *kohen gadol*, and the question of priorities when those statuses are combined. Now the *mishnah* turns to the actual parameters of the *nazir*'s *tumah* restrictions — specifically, the minimum sizes and types of materials derived from a corpse that render a *nazir tamei*.

To some degree this brings us into territory that touches on broad sections of *Meseches Taharos*, but we will not be entering all of that. What makes this *perek* particularly interesting is a handful of cases where something causes *tumas meis* and yet the *nazir* does not shave as a result. There are a few such exceptions, learned from tradition — *halacha l'Moshe m'Sinai* — where even though *tumas meis* technically obtains, the *nazir* is somehow excluded from the full consequence. This matters beyond the narrow context of *nezirus*, because the parameters of *tumas kohanim* are learned from the restrictions of the *nazir*. So these exceptions, though they may initially seem obscure, carry genuine practical weight.

### Practical Relevance

One might ask: how relevant is any of this today? The answer is that *tumah* for a *kohen* remains practically relevant. Beyond that, these *halachos* apply only to someone who actually takes a *nazir* vow — which, while uncommon, is halachically available.

---

## First Impurity List

### First List Items

The *mishnah* opens: *al eilu tumos hanazir megale'ach* — for the following *tumot* does a *nazir* shave his head, destroying his current count of *nezirus*, obligating him to bring a *korban* and begin again.

The first item is *al hameis* — an entire corpse. Then *al kezayis min hameis* — even just an olive-sized piece of flesh from the corpse. The *kezayis* measure is notable here: it is normally associated with food, but it functions as a kind of default minimum in many contexts. The tradition is that even an olive-sized portion of the flesh of a corpse causes *tumas meis*.

It should be noted that all the items in this first list — until we reach the final item — cause *tumas meis* even through *ohel*, that is, even if one is merely under the same roof. There are three modes of *tumah* conduction from a *meis*: *maga* (touching), *massa* (carrying), and *ohel* (tenting — being under the same roof, or being over the *meis*, or having the *meis* over you). The *Torah* emphasizes *ohel* particularly in the context of a full human corpse — *adam ki yamut b'ohel* — and one can conceptually understand that what *tumat ohel* is doing is identifying something sufficiently representative of the whole. This is why the *shiurim* for *ohel* are somewhat different: some very small items cause *tumah* through touch but not through *ohel*.

The third item in the list is *al kezayis netzel* — a *kezayis* of *netzel*, a substance we will examine closely in the *Gemara*. In brief, it refers to flesh that has dissolved and then recongealed, or to juices that ran off the flesh and then congealed through boiling. It retains the status of flesh for purposes of *tumah*.

Next is *melo torvad rekev* — a ladle-full of *rekev*, the decomposed matter of a body that has turned to dust. This is not flesh that liquefied and resolidified; it is the natural dusty decomposition of the body. Several of these *shiurim*, as we will see, are *halacha l'Moshe m'Sinai*.

The *mishnah* then lists *al shidra v'al gulgoles* — the spinal cord and the skull, whether that means either one alone or the combination will be clarified. Then *al ever min hameis* — a complete limb of the dead body — and *al ever min hachai* — a limb that fell off from a living person. This last item is striking. Until now one might have thought the list is about things that representatively stand in for the whole corpse. But here the person is not dead. A limb severed from a living person is itself treated as a kind of *meis*, independent of whether the person survives. The *ever* must have upon it *basar karuy* — enough flesh that, were it still attached to the body, the limb could heal over and scar. It cannot be bone alone.

### Half-Kav Bones

The *mishnah* continues: *v'al chatzi kav atzamos* — a half of a *kav* of bones. A *kav* is a volume measure; a half-*kav* is roughly one and a half to two and a half quarts in the range of contemporary estimates. Tosafot notes that this is not referring to just any random collection of bones. The bones must come from *rov minyano o rov binyano* — either a majority of the number of bones in the body, or a majority of the body's structural bones. That quantity itself, *rov minyan v'rov binyan*, causes *tumat ohel*.

Tosafot continues: *rov binyan* refers to the two hips, or one thigh, or the equivalent — the major structural bones of the body. And then Tosafot introduces the key point: even though *tumat ohel* is caused by a *rova* (a quarter of a *kav*) of bones that come from *rov minyan* or *rov binyan*, the *nazir* does not shave unless there is a full half-*kav*. This is stated explicitly in the first chapter of *Ohalos*. So here we encounter the first of the exceptions: a quarter-*kav* of bones from *rov minyan* or *rov binyan* causes *tumas meis d'Oraisa*, yet the *nazir* does not shave on account of it.

### Quarter-Kav Exception

The *halacha* that a *nazir* shaves only on a half-*kav* and not a quarter-*kav* is itself a *halacha l'Moshe m'Sinai*. This may seem like a minor technical distinction, but the principle is important: there exist cases of *tumas meis* that do not trigger *nazir megaleach*. These exceptions also bear on *tumas kohanim*, since the *nazir*'s laws govern those parameters. A *kohen* who would otherwise be prohibited from contracting *tumah* is likewise not bound by this prohibition (*ein kohen muzhar alav*) in cases where the *nazir* does not shave — such as *tumat ohel* from a quarter-*kav* of bones.

### Three Modes of Tumah

The first list concludes: *v'al magaan v'al masaan v'al ahilan* — touching them, carrying them, or being in their *ohel*. Everything on this list causes *tumah* through all three modes.

---

## Second Impurity List

### Barley-Grain Bone

The *mishnah* then introduces a second, shorter list: *v'al etzem k'se'ora* — even a tiny chip of bone the size of a barley grain. This causes *tumah*, but only through *al maga'o v'al masa'o* — touching and carrying — not through *ohel*. The key distinction between the two lists is therefore this: most things that cause *tumas meis* through contact also cause it through *ohel*. But bones are different. For *tumat ohel*, you need either the skull or the spinal cord, or *rov minyan* or *rov binyan* expressed in the minimum volume. For *tumah* through contact, even a tiny sliver of bone the size of a barley grain suffices.

### Consequences of Impurity

When a *nazir* contracts *tumah* from any of these sources, the consequences are: *u'mazeh bashlishi u'va'shvi'i* — sprinkling of the purification-water on days three and seven; *soter es ha'kodmin* — all prior days of the *nezirus* count are destroyed; and he does not begin counting again until he becomes *tahor*, brings his *korbanot*, and only then begins the new count. The chip of bone the size of a barley grain, though it causes *tumah* only through touch and not through *ohel*, still triggers this full set of consequences for the *nazir*.

---

## Sumchos Incident

### Yehuda's Warning

The *Gemara* opens this section with a *baraisa*: after the passing of Rabbi Meir — *achar petiraso shel Rabbi Meir*, literally "after his departure" — Rabbi Yehuda said to his students: do not allow Rabbi Meir's students into our *beis medrash*, because they are *kantranim* — troublemakers. They do not come with a sincere desire to learn *Torah*; they come *lekapacheini bahalachos* — to harass through *halachic* argumentation, treating *halacha* as an intellectual exercise and mind game rather than as a genuine search for truth.

### Sumchos Forces Entry

Despite this, *dachak Sumchos v'nichnas* — Sumchos forced his way in. Sumchos was one of Rabbi Meir's most distinguished students. He came and reported: *kach shana li Rabbi Meir* — this is how Rabbi Meir taught me this *mishnah* — listing both *al hameis* and *al kezayis min hameis* explicitly.

### Yehuda's Objection

Rabbi Yehuda grew angry and said to his students: did I not warn you? Don't let Rabbi Meir's students in here — they are troublemakers. His objection was: *al kezayis min hameis megaleach, al hameis lo kol shekein?* If you shave for a *kezayis* of flesh from the corpse, is it not obviously true all the more so for the entire corpse? Why state *al hameis* at all? It is entirely implicit. The irritation is understandable: it is not merely that Rabbi Meir's version includes an extra phrase. It is that Sumchos is insisting on it, presenting it as halachically significant. "What are you doing?" is the implied complaint. "You're just making trouble — it's obvious."

### Yosi's Defense

Rabbi Yosi's response is itself worth pausing over. He says: *yomru Meir shachav, Yehuda ka'as, Yosi shatak — Torah mah tehei aleha?* They will say: Meir passed away (*shachav* — he went to lie down), Yehuda grew angry, and Yosi was silent — what will be of the *Torah*? Rabbi Yosi is saying: I must defend Rabbi Meir's honor, and more importantly, his *Torah*, even though I am Rabbi Yehuda's colleague. The personalities are getting in the way. The *Torah* has to be defended regardless.

So Rabbi Yosi offers a justification: *lo nitzrecha ela l'meis she'ein alav kezayis basar* — you need the explicit statement of *al hameis* for the case of a corpse that has no *kezayis* of flesh remaining. Imagine a body that has decomposed so that only bones remain — there is no *kezayis* of flesh. Yet it is a complete corpse.

### Nefel Discussion

The *Gemara* objects: but that is also covered by the other items in the list — limbs, or *rov binyan*, and so on. If you shave even for a single limb, surely you shave for the whole body?

The *Gemara* then brings Rabbi Yochanan's formulation: *lo nitzrecha ela l'nefel shelo nitkashru evarav begidin* — it is needed for the case of a *nefel*, a stillborn or miscarried fetus, whose sinews have not yet developed. Because there are no *gidin*, the halachic concept of an *ever* does not apply. Such a *nefel* could be very underdeveloped — possibly as early as day forty — and might have neither a *kezayis* of flesh nor a developed skeletal structure sufficient to trigger the other items on the list. In that case, only *al hameis* covers it. Why the absence of *gidin* also excludes the *shidra* and *gulgoles* categories is not fully explored, but there seems to be an assumption that if the fetus is so small and undeveloped, those thresholds are also not met.

### Rava's Answer

Rava offers yet another resolution: *lo nitzrecha ela l'rov binyano o l'rov minyano she'ein bahen rov atzamos* — it is needed for a case where you have *rov minyan* and *rov binyan*, but not the minimum volume. If the corpse is very small — such as a very tiny skeletal structure — you could theoretically have a majority of the number of bones and a majority of the body's structure, and yet not reach the minimum volume threshold.

This is an important clarification: *rov minyan* and *rov binyan* are not independent of volume. As Tosafot demonstrated, the requirement is *rov minyan* or *rov binyan* expressed in at least a *rova* (for ordinary *tumas ohel*) or a half-*kav* (for *nazir megaleach*). Even a full *rov minyan* and *rov binyan*, whole and uncrushed, without that minimum volume, does not cause *tumat ohel*. So a very small corpse could have *rov minyan* and *rov binyan* — every structural bone present — and yet fall below the minimum volume. In that case, the explicit *al hameis* is what covers it.

### Torah vs. Personalities

One student made a beautiful observation worth noting. The *Gemara*'s language — *Meir shachav, Yehuda ka'as, Yosi shatak* — is not merely narrative background. It captures something deeper. When all the focus falls on personalities — Meir passed away, Yehuda grew angry, Yosi stayed silent — the *Torah* is forgotten. That is precisely what Rabbi Yosi was responding to. His statement, *Torah mah tehei aleha*, is a reorientation: stop thinking about the people, start thinking about the *Torah* being taught. It is also worth noting that the *Gemara*'s terminology of death is notably dignified — *petira* (he took his leave), *shachav* (he went to lie down) — language that preserves a sense of the soul continuing and of departing to another realm, rather than reducing death to mere bodily dissolution.

This same *sugya* appears, in a more developed literary form, in Kiddushin 52b. There, the *mishnah* in question concerns whether a *kohen* can effect *kiddushin* with *basar kodshei kodashim* — meat of the innermost sanctified offerings, which has monetary value even if the woman cannot eat it herself. The absurdity Rabbi Yehuda objects to is: what is a woman doing in the *Azara* conducting a *kiddushin* ceremony? That makes the nature of his complaint clearer — Rabbi Meir's students are not pursuing practical *halacha* but are constructing fanciful, practically impossible scenarios as intellectual exercises. And the *Gemara* there provides a charming series of answers about how a woman could legitimately be in the *Azara* — her father is there as the recipient, or she sent a *shaliach* — and the final answer plays directly off *dachak Sumchos v'nichnas*: *dachka venichnesa* — perhaps she simply forced her way in. So the literary structure of that *sugya* illuminates our own and explains why the troublemaker framing resonates so strongly.

---

## Netzel Discussion

### Netzel Definition

The *mishnah* lists *kezayis netzel* among the things for which a *nazir* shaves. The *Gemara* now asks: *ve'eizu netzel* — what exactly is *netzel*? Two answers are given: (1) *basar hameis shekarash* — flesh of the dead that had liquefied and then recongealed; and (2) *mochal she'hirtiach* — juices that ran off the flesh and then were boiled and congealed.

### Identifying Netzel

The *Gemara* then asks: what is the case? If we simply do not know whether this congealed substance came from the flesh or from some other liquid of the body — like saliva or mucus — then the act of congealing tells us nothing about its identity. Those other bodily fluids are not *metamei* as *tumas meis* in their own right; they may carry indirect *tumah* from contact with the dead, but they are not themselves the *meis*.

So the *Gemara* clarifies: *ella diyaadina dedidahu* — we know that it came from the flesh. And then the question becomes: even so, does congealing matter? Even in dissolved or liquid form, since we know it came from the flesh, it should cause the same *tumah*. What does congealing add?

Rabbi Yirmiyah answers: *bistam* — in an ambiguous case, where we do not know whether this liquid came from the flesh or from *keicho v'ni'o* (phlegm and mucus), congealing is the identifying factor. *I karash* — if it congeals — *mochal hu* — then we know it is from the juices of the flesh, since those other bodily fluids would not congeal in the same way. *Lo karash* — if it does not congeal — then it may well be mucus or saliva, and we cannot be certain.

So the *chiddush* of the *Gemara* is that the *tumah* status of the dissolved flesh does not actually depend on it being solid — even in liquid form, flesh-derived *netzel* is *metamei*. The congealing or the boiling is not a condition for *tumah* but rather a diagnostic tool to establish identity.

Tosafot extends this reasoning to the *hirtiach* case: we know the substance came from the body, but we do not know whether it is *mochal* from the flesh or from *keicho v'ni'o*. If it boils and bubbles in a characteristic way (*de'avar ritchus*), then it is identifiably from the flesh. If not, it may be mucus. The precise logic of why boiling identifies it as such — rather than simply being another test of viscosity — is not entirely clear, but Tosafot is fitting it into the same structural framework as the congealing case.

### Netzel for Animals

Abaye poses a question to Rava: *yesh netzel livheimah o ein netzel livheimah* — does the principle of *netzel* apply to animals and *tumas neveilah*, or is it unique to *tumas meis*? The question is whether this is a *halacha* about the definition of flesh as such — in which case it should apply broadly — or whether it is a tradition specific to human corpse *tumah*.

Two possible positions frame the question: perhaps the tradition of *netzel* is specifically *d'ati mi-adam* — derived from human remains, as part of *tumas meis* — and does not extend to *tumas neveilah*. Or perhaps there is no distinction, and liquefied animal flesh counts as flesh for *tumas neveilah* as well.

### Tumat Chamurah Doctrine

Whether this question is even practically relevant, however, depends on another dispute. The *Gemara* introduces the principle: *tumah chamurah ad lager, v'tumah kalah ad lekelev*. The heavier *tumah* — specifically *tumas neveilah*, the carcass of an animal that is itself a primary source of *tumah* — is measured by fitness for human consumption. This is derived from the verse *lager asher bish'arecha titnenah ve'achalcha*: the carcass may be given to the *ger* to eat; from here we learn *ha-raui lager karui neveilah she-eino raui lager eino karui neveilah* — only what is fit for human consumption bears the status of *neveilah* and its accompanying *tumah*.

This principle is itself somewhat counterintuitive, since most *avot hatumah* have nothing to do with edibility — a *zav*, a *niddah*, a *metzora* — none of those derive their *tumah* status from being food. Nevertheless, for *tumas neveilah*, which inherently concerns the flesh of what would normally be edible, the tradition is that the *tumah* dissipates once the flesh is no longer fit for human consumption.

*Tumah kalah ad lekelev* is parenthetical to our discussion: it refers to foods that conduct *tumah* from elsewhere — the threshold for something to be considered "food" in that context may be as low as being fit for consumption by a dog. This is a familiar distinction from *hilchos Pesach* and elsewhere, where different areas of *halacha* operate with different definitions of food.

### Question Moot

Now, if *tumah chamurah ad lager* is correct — that *tumas neveilah* requires fitness for human consumption — then the question of whether *netzel* from an animal is considered *neveilah* is moot. The juices of decomposing flesh are not fit for human consumption, and therefore they are simply *tahor* regardless of whether they conceptually count as "flesh." The question only has force if *tumah chamurah ad lekelev* — if even *tumas neveilah* requires only fitness for dog consumption, and one holds that decomposing animal juices remain fit for a dog.

The *Gemara* then brings a *tosefta*: if you melt *neveilah* fat over fire, it remains *tamei*; if you leave it to decompose in the sun and it liquefies, it is *tahor*. One might think this proves the *lekelev* opinion wrong — even liquefied flesh is *tahor* — but the *Gemara* deflects this. When left out in the sun, the flesh first putrefies (*asrach*) before it liquefies; at that point it has become like dust, no longer fit even for a dog. So the *tosefta* is *tahor* not because liquefied flesh cannot qualify as *neveilah*, but because the particular process of sun-rotting renders it unfit even for *lekelev*.

The conclusion, therefore, is that if one holds *tumah chamurah ad lekelev*, and one imagines a scenario where the liquefied animal flesh remains fit for a dog, the question of whether *netzel* applies to *neveilah* is genuinely unresolved. The *Gemara* leaves it as a *teiku*.

---

## Nitzok Mishnah

### Pouring Not Connected

The *Gemara* now transitions to a *mishnah* from *Machshirin*: *kol hanitzok tahor* — all instances of pouring are *tahor*. The scenario is this: I have a *tamei* carcass, and I am pouring water from a vessel onto it. The water that actually contacts the carcass becomes *tamei* — it is a *rishon*. But what of the water still in the vessel above? Is the stream of water connecting them treated as one unit, rendering the water in the vessel *tamei* as well? The answer is no: the poured liquid does not constitute a single connected unit with the source. Only what actually makes contact becomes *tamei*.

### Honey Exception

The *mishnah* provides exceptions: *chutz midevash hazifim* — except for a very thick type of honey — *v'hatzapichit* — and the waxy cakes of honey that come directly from the beehive. These substances are so thick that they are considered more like a solid, and the normal rule of *nitzok* does not apply to them. They are treated as sufficiently solid — or sufficiently connected — to constitute a single unit.

### Beit Shammai View

Beit Shammai add: *af hamikpah shel gerisin v'shel pol* — even a thick porridge of oat-groats or lentils can constitute a connected unit, *mipnei shehi soledet leachoreha* — because it "pulls back." What this means is: if you invert the vessel mid-pour, a watery liquid will simply fall away entirely, while something sufficiently viscous will partially retract back into the vessel. That pulling back demonstrates connectedness and coherence. Notably, the term *soledet*, meaning to recoil or pull back, echoes the *shiur* of *yad soledes bo* — the threshold of heat in the laws of cooking on Shabbos, where one's hand recoils from contact. Both uses of the root share the idea of a reactive withdrawal.

---

## Nitzok for Foods

### Nitzok Question

Building on this *mishnah*, the *Gemara* now asks: *yesh nitzok le'ochlin o ein nitzok le'ochlin* — does the principle of *nitzok* apply to foods? Specifically: if something that began as solid food is liquefied — say, ground down or cooked into a thick flowing mass — and then poured onto a source of *tumah*, is the remaining portion in the vessel considered connected to what flows out, or not?

### Two Criteria

The question turns on which of two principles underlies the *mishnah*'s ruling. The first possibility: *mishum d'is behu riri* — the reason thick honey and similar substances are considered connected is that they possess *riri*, sticky strands that cling and cohere. If that is the criterion, then even a very thick liquefied food that lacks these clinging strands would not be considered connected.
