The second possibility: *mishum d'smichi* — the reason is simply thickness itself, not the quality of stickiness. If that is the criterion, then any sufficiently thick liquefied food would be connected regardless of whether it forms such strands.

For Beit Shammai, the criterion is clearly *riri*: they explicitly speak of the substance *soldin leachoreha* — pulling back — which is precisely the behavior of something sticky and cohesive. But the question is what the *Tanna Kamma* holds. When the *Tanna Kamma* mentions only the very thick honey, is it because honey has *riri*, or because honey is thick? It would seem intuitive that honey also has *riri*, and so both could be true of honey. Beit Shammai's contribution would then be extending the principle to things that have *riri* but are less thick than honey. But the *Gemara* does not resolve this definitively.

### Fat of Corpse Proof

Rava brings a proof from a *mishnah*: *cheilev hameis she'hu shaleim, v'hisicho — tamei*. If the fat of a corpse is whole — meaning present in the minimum quantity sufficient for *tumah* — and then liquefied, it remains *tamei*. However, *hayah mefurad v'hisicho — tahor*: if the fat was already separated into pieces individually below the minimum, and then melted together, it is *tahor*. The logic of that second ruling concerns a broader question: can something that lost its *tumah* status by falling below the minimum regain it once the volume is reconstituted? The *mishnah* assumes it cannot, at least for *tumah* through contact.

### Liquefied Fat Paradox

What concerns us is the first clause: once the fat is liquefied, it remains *tamei*. But here a paradox emerges. The *Gemara* is exploring the possibility that *ein nitzok le'ochlin* — that liquefied food is *not* considered one connected unit. If that is so, then even the fat sitting at the bottom of the vessel is not connected to the fat at the top. The fat, once liquefied, is simply a large collection of microscopic droplets, no more united than any poured liquid. So how can one say the entire quantity is *tamei*? One is not touching all of it simultaneously.

This challenge is more striking than it may first appear, because the question of *nitzok* is not limited to the act of pouring. Even if the liquid is stable within a vessel, it may not constitute a single halachic unit. The *Gemara* is suggesting that liquid is not "connected" in the halachic sense even when it is sitting undisturbed in a container — and this makes the case of the liquefied fat puzzling.

### Rav Zeira Answer

Rav Zeira, together with Mar the son of Rav Avina, offers an answer: *kegon debehadei demartach lei, salik amuda denura lefuma demana, vekarash* — we are speaking of a case where, in the very process of liquefying the fat over a fire, a column of flame reached the opening of the vessel and caused the fat to recongeal at the surface. In other words, the fat never became fully and stably liquid; in the same moment that the fire melted it, the heat at the opening caused it to solidify again. The whole quantity is therefore treated as congealed and unified. This is admittedly a forced reading of the *mishnah*'s plain language, which speaks straightforwardly of the fat being liquefied, but Rav Zeira is constraining the case to preserve coherence.

### Ravina-Ashi Answer

Ravina said to Rav Ashi: come and hear a proof from Beit Shammai — *Beit Shammai omrim af hamikpah shel gerisin v'shel pol mi-she-hen soladin leachoreha* — you can see that for Beit Shammai, the criterion is *riri*, stickiness, not mere thickness. The fact that the porridge pulls back is what makes it connected.

The *Gemara* deflects: *midi irya?* Is that relevant? *Hasam mishum desmichin, hacha mishum riri* — there, perhaps the *Tanna Kamma*'s honey is about thickness; here, Beit Shammai are about *riri*. In other words: Beit Shammai's criterion is clearly *riri*, but we do not know whether the *Tanna Kamma* agrees with that criterion or operates on thickness alone. The case of honey is compatible with both — honey is both thick and sticky — so it cannot disambiguate. The *Gemara* therefore leaves the original question unresolved: whether for the *Tanna Kamma*, a very thick but non-sticky liquefied food constitutes a connected unit for *tumah* purposes remains a *teiku*.

---

---

# Nazir 49b

## Overview & Context

### Opening Remarks

Today's daf continues our forward pace through the masechta, picking up on 49b, with the expectation of covering through daf 50 as well.

### Perek Focus

This *perek* has been centrally concerned with the prohibition against a *nazir* becoming *tamei*. The earlier material established that a *nazir* may become *tamei* for a *meit mitzvah*, and we devoted considerable time to understanding how that exception is derived from the relevant verses — including how *meit mitzvah* overrides the restrictions of both a *nazir* and a *kohen gadol*, even when those sanctities are compounded. The question of priority — whose *kedushah* one must protect first when there is some element of choice — also occupied us. The present *mishnah* turns to the actual parameters of a *nazir*'s *tumah* restrictions: specifically, what types and quantities of a dead body trigger the *nazir*'s obligation to shave.

### Tumah Parameters

To some degree, this *mishnah* covers territory one might expect to find in *masechta Taharot*, cataloguing the minimum sizes of a dead body and its parts that cause *tumat meit*. We will not be immersing ourselves in every corner of those laws, but the *mishnah* does give us the basic framework: what objects, in what quantities, cause *tumat meit*, and in particular which of those require the *nazir* to shave his head, nullifying his prior count, requiring a *korban*, and necessitating a fresh start.

### Halacha L'Moshe Exceptio…

An important nuance emerges: in a few cases, something causes *tumat meit* as a matter of *d'oraita* law, and yet the *nazir* is nonetheless not obligated to shave. These exceptions are derived from *halacha l'moshe misinai* — received tradition without explicit scriptural derivation. This distinction is not merely theoretical. Since the parameters of *tumat kohanim* are learned from the restrictions of the *nazir*, these exceptions carry practical relevance for *kohanim* as well, and one should keep that in mind as the discussion unfolds.

---

## Mishnah: Tumah Items

### Mishnah Introduction

The *mishnah* opens: *al elu tumos hanazir megalei'ach* — on the following *tumot* does a *nazir* shave his head, destroying his prior count of *nezirut*, requiring the relevant *korbanot*, and beginning the count again only after becoming *tahor*.

### Corpse & Flesh

The first item is *al hameit* — an entire corpse — and *al kezayit min hameit* — even a *kezayit*-sized piece of the flesh of the corpse. The choice of *kezayit* is notable. In most contexts, *kezayit* is a standard measure for foods; here it functions as a kind of default minimum size, the received tradition being that even an olive-sized piece of a corpse's flesh causes *tumat meit*. It is worth emphasizing from the outset that the items on this first list all cause *tumat meit ba'ohel*: that is, not only through direct contact or carrying, but through being under the same roof — through *ahel*.

### Definition of Ahel

*Ahel* — tenting — encompasses several configurations: you may be beneath the same roof as the *meit*, the *meit* may be above you, or you may be above it. The Torah's language of *adam ki yamut ba'ohel* provides the scriptural anchor for this concept. Conceptually, what *tumat ohel* is capturing is the idea of something representative of the whole — a part of the dead body significant enough to stand in for the complete person. That is why the *shi'urim* for *tumat ohel* tend to be somewhat larger or more specific than those for *maga* alone.

One might wonder about more complex spatial configurations — for instance, whether a *meit* on an upper floor causes *tumah* to someone in a basement with a floor separating them. The short answer is that this is precisely what *masechta Oholot* is about, with the key principle being that a roof with a *tefach* of airspace beneath it can, under most circumstances, interrupt the *tumah* and prevent it from passing through. The reason that flying over a cemetery remains a problem is that there is no *tefach* cavity — the coffin itself is treated as an extension of the *meit* rather than a barrier.

### Netzeil Definition

The *mishnah* continues: *v'al kezayit netzeil* — on a *kezayit* of *netzeil*. The *gemara* will define this precisely, but the basic concept is flesh that has liquefied and subsequently recongealed, which carries the same *halachic* status as the flesh itself.

### Rekev Amount

*V'al melo tarvad rekav* — on a ladle-full of *rekav*, the decomposed matter of the body. This is not flesh that liquefied and resolidified; this is the body reduced to dust, the biological endpoint of decay. The *gemara* will have more to say about these distinctions. Some of these categories are rooted in *halacha l'moshe misinai* without explicit derivation.

### Spine & Skull

The *mishnah* adds: *al hashidra v'al hagulgollet* — the spinal column and the skull, whether they operate jointly or severally will become clearer from context.

### Limb Sources

*V'al eiver min hameit* — a complete limb from a dead body — and, perhaps more surprisingly, *v'al eiver min hachai* — a limb severed from a living person. This second case is striking. Until this point, one might have understood the principle as synecdoche: the part represents the whole person who has died. But here the person is alive. The limb itself, when severed, takes on an independent status akin to a *meit*. It is not representing a corpse; it is itself treated as a kind of *meit* in its own right. This has practical implications — a limb lost to amputation, for example, would require burial. For a limb from a corpse or from a living person to carry this status, there must be adequate flesh on it: *sheyesh alav basar karaui*, sufficient flesh that, were the limb still attached to the body, it would be capable of healing over.

### Bones Requirement

*V'al chatzi kav atzamot* — on a half-*kav* of bones. Roughly speaking, this is a volume of a few ounces to perhaps a liter or more, a not entirely trivial quantity.

### Tosafot: Bone Amounts

*Tosafot* here makes an important observation that deserves careful attention. The *mishnah* specifies a half-*kav*, but *Tosafot* notes that it is not simply any random collection of bones. The bones must derive from either *rov minyan* — a majority of the count of the bones in the body — or *rov binyan* — a majority of the structural mass of the body. Once one has bones satisfying that criterion, and they are crushed, and one scoops out a half-*kav* from that pile, that quantity triggers the *nazir*'s obligation to shave.

*Tosafot* further clarifies *rov binyan*: it is exemplified by the two hip-bones and one thigh-bone, or the reverse — the largest structural bones of the body.

The key distinction *Tosafot* draws, however, concerns the relationship between *tumat ohel* and the *nazir*'s shaving obligation. The *halacha* for *tumat ohel* in general is a quarter-*kav* — *rova hakav* — as stated explicitly in *perek* 2 of *masechta Oholot*. Yet the *halacha l'moshe misinai* for the *nazir* requires twice that amount: a half-*kav*. This is one of the cases where an amount that genuinely causes *tumat meit d'oraita* does not obligate the *nazir* to shave. A quarter-*kav* of bones from *rov minyan* or *rov binyan* causes *tumat ohel*, but the *nazir* does not shave until the quantity reaches a half-*kav*.

A *kohen* in such a case would technically not be in violation of the *lav* — just as we say *ein kohen muzhar alav* in such a context — and could theoretically become *tamei* through *tumat ohel* from this quarter-*kav* without violating the prohibition. These fine distinctions, though they may seem remote, matter for practical *hilchot kohanim*.

### Blood Amount

*V'al chatzi log dam* — on a half-*log* of blood. Here again, the same principle applies. A *revi'it* of blood from a corpse causes *tumat ohel* — this was established at the end of the previous daf's discussion. Yet once more, for the *nazir* to be obligated to shave, the quantity must be double: a half-*log*. So both for bones and for blood, the threshold for *tumat ohel* in general is half the quantity required to trigger the *nazir*'s shaving obligation — another instance of *halacha l'moshe misinai* creating a distinction between causing *tumah* and obligating the *nazir*.

### Three Types Tumah

Everything on this first list causes *tumah* through all three modes: *maga* — touching, *masa* — carrying, and *ahel* — tenting. The *mishnah* states this explicitly: *v'al maga'an v'al masa'an v'al ohilan*.

### Second List: Bones

The *mishnah* then pivots to a second, shorter list: *v'al etzem k'se'ora* — even a chip of bone as small as a barleycorn. This tiny fragment causes *tumat meit*, but only through *al maga'o v'al masa'o* — touching and carrying — not through *ahel*. This is the principal asymmetry in the laws of *tumat atzamot*: bone fragments of a certain mass cause *tumat ohel* — either *rov minyan* or *rov binyan* with the requisite volume, or the skull or spine — but for *tumat maga*, even the most minuscule fragment suffices. A barleycorn-sized chip of bone, therefore, causes *tumat meit* through contact, obligating the *nazir* to shave, even though it would never cause *tumat ohel*.

### Tumah Consequences

When any of these *tumot* apply, the *nazir* shaves his head, has the *mei chatat* — the waters mixed with the ashes of the *parah adumah* — sprinkled upon him on the third and seventh days, and all prior days of *nezirut* are nullified: *soter es hakodmin*. He does not begin counting anew until he becomes *tahor* and brings his *korbanot*; only the following day does his fresh count commence.

---

## Sumchus Story

### Entry Prohibition

The *gemara* introduces a *baraita* that establishes the context for the ensuing discussion. After Rabbi Meir passed away — the *gemara* uses the term *petirah*, "he took his leave," which already signals a certain dignity of expression — Rabbi Yehuda addressed his students: *al yikansu talmidei Rabbi Meir l'chan* — do not permit Rabbi Meir's students to enter this *beit midrash*. His reasoning: *mipnei she'kantarin hem* — they are provocateurs — *v'lo lilmod Torah hen ba'in* — they do not come with a sincere desire to learn Torah — *ella l'kapechani bahalachot hen ba'in* — they come only to best me in *halachic* debate, using the learning as an intellectual exercise rather than as a pursuit of *pesak* and truth. We have all encountered students whose motivation seems to be winning rather than learning; Rabbi Yehuda evidently felt Rabbi Meir's disciples embodied this tendency.

### Sumchus Enters

Nonetheless, *dachak Sumchus v'nichnas* — Sumchus forced his way in. Sumchus was among Rabbi Meir's most distinguished students. Once inside, he reported that Rabbi Meir had taught the *mishnah* in the following form: *al elu tumat hanazir megalei'ach al hameit v'al kezayit min hameit* — explicitly listing both the entire corpse and a *kezayit* of the corpse, rather than mentioning only the *kezayit*.

### Yehuda's Challenge

Rabbi Yehuda was incensed. He turned to his students: did I not tell you not to let Rabbi Meir's students enter? Then he pressed the substantive objection: *al kezayit min hameit megalei'ach al hameit lo kol sheken?* — if one shaves for a *kezayit*, is it not self-evidently true that one shaves for an entire corpse? Why does Rabbi Meir's version of the *mishnah* need to state the entire corpse separately? The redundancy seemed pointless, and the insistence on the fuller formulation struck Rabbi Yehuda as precisely the kind of mind-game he had warned against — not pure Torah learning but intellectual provocation dressed up as precision.

### Yosi Defends Meir

Rabbi Yosi would not remain silent. He framed his intervention memorably: *yomru Meir shachav* — they will say Meir has gone to his rest — *Yehuda ka'as* — Yehuda grew angry — *Yosi shatak* — and Yosi was silent? *Torah mah tehei aleha?* — what then will become of the Torah? Here we see Rabbi Yosi standing not merely as a defender of Rabbi Meir's reputation but as a defender of Torah itself. Rabbi Meir's teaching cannot be dismissed as mere provocation; it must be understood and vindicated.

### Yosi's Answer

Rabbi Yosi offers the first explanation: *lo nitzrecha ella meit she'ein alav kezayit basar* — the separate mention of the entire corpse is necessary for the case of a dead body that has no remaining flesh. A skeleton stripped entirely of flesh does not have a *kezayit* of *basar*; yet the entire body, the full corpse, still causes *tumah*. Were the *mishnah* to list only the *kezayit* of flesh, this case would be left without explicit coverage.

The *gemara* pushes back: but the *mishnah* also mentions a limb from the corpse, and we know that *eiver* causes *tumah* — so *kal vachomer*, if even for a single limb one shaves, surely for an entire body? Rabbi Yosi's answer does not fully resolve the redundancy on its own.

### Yochanan: Stillbirth

Rabbi Yochanan provides a more precisely targeted answer: *lo nitzrecha ella nefel shelo nitkashu evarav begidin* — the separate listing of the entire corpse is needed for a *nefel*, a stillborn or miscarried fetus, whose sinews have not yet developed. Without *gidin*, the *halacha* of *eiver* — limb — does not apply, since a *halachic* limb requires the connective structure of sinews. And such a *nefel* may be so small and undeveloped that it also lacks a *kezayit* of flesh. It may furthermore lack the skeletal volume needed for *rov minyan* or *rov binyan*. Yet it is a complete *meit*, and as such the separate mention of the entire corpse is necessary to include it. It remains somewhat unclear why the *shidra* and *gulgollet* — the spine and skull — also fail to apply in this case, though perhaps the assumption is that at such early stages of development these structures have not yet formed adequately.

### Rava: Skeleton Volume

Rava offers yet another explanation: *lo nitzrecha ela lerov binyano ulerov minyano she'ein bahen rova atzamot* — the listing is needed for a case where one has *rov minyan* and *rov binyan* — a majority of the skeletal structure in both number and form — but the total volume does not reach the minimum of *rova kav* (or, more precisely for the *nazir*, *chatzi kav*) required to impose the shaving obligation. Even with a complete skeletal majority, if the body is so small — perhaps a very young fetus — that its bones lack the minimum volume, the *nazir* would not otherwise be obligated from any of the other categories. The separate mention of the entire corpse thus covers this gap. Rava's mention of *rova atzamot* here is likely not a precise reference to the *nazir*'s threshold of *chatzi kav* but rather the general minimum for *tumat meit*, since his point is about *tumat meit* in general. The underlying principle, however, confirmed by *Tosafot*'s earlier analysis, is that *rov minyan* and *rov binyan* are not independent of volume requirements — even a complete majority of bones, uncrushed and whole, fails to cause *tumat ohel* if it lacks the minimum quantity. This intersection of structural majority and volumetric threshold is fundamental.

### Death Terminology

It is worth pausing over an aspect of the language in this *gemara* that is easy to overlook. The discussion began with the word *petirah* — "he took his leave" — and Rabbi Yosi's protest employed *shachav* — "he has gone to lie down." Both are deliberate euphemisms, dignified circumlocutions that resist the objectifying language that necessarily dominates the surrounding *halachic* discussion of body parts and minimum quantities. There is something instructive in the contrast: the *halacha* demands precision about flesh and bone and volume, but the *gemara* simultaneously insists on a more humane register when speaking of the person who died.

One participant made a perceptive observation about Rabbi Yosi's formulation — *Meir shachav, Yehuda ka'as, Yosi shatak* — pointing out that by framing everything in terms of what people will say about the named personalities, Rabbi Yosi is actually critiquing the very dynamic he is interrupting: everyone has become focused on the individuals and their reputations rather than on the Torah being taught. His exclamation *Torah mah tehei aleha* is a deliberate reorientation, pulling the discussion back from personalities to the substance of what matters.

This same *gemara* also appears in *Kiddushin* 52b, where its original literary context may be clearer. There the *mishnah* discusses what objects a man may use to effect *kiddushin*, including *basar kodshei kodashim* — meat of the most sacred offerings, which has monetary value even if the woman cannot personally consume it. Rabbi Meir's version of that *mishnah* prompted Rabbi Yehuda's complaint in strikingly similar terms; the scenario of performing *kiddushin* with meat while standing in the *Azarah* struck Rabbi Yehuda as an absurd theoretical exercise rather than practical *halacha*. The *gemara* there then offers a series of answers for how a woman might legitimately be in the *Azarah* — through a *shliach*, through her father accepting on her behalf, and finally in a flourish that mirrors the opening narrative, *dachakah v'nichnesah mai* — perhaps she simply forced her way in, just as Sumchus had forced his way into the *beit midrash*. The literary symmetry is unmistakable, and that context illuminates what it means to be a *kantran*: not a troublemaker in the crude sense, but one who treats *halacha* as a vehicle for intellectual jousting rather than for arriving at the truth.

---

## Netzeil Discussion

### Netzeil Definition

The *gemara* now returns to the *mishnah*'s mention of *netzeil* to define it precisely. *Netzeil* is flesh of a corpse that has liquefied and subsequently congealed: *basar hameit shekarash*.

### Two Versions

The *mishnah* offers two variations. The first is flesh that liquefied naturally and recongealed on its own. The second is *mohel she'hirtiach* — some type of liquid that ran off from the flesh and then was boiled and congealed. These may represent two distinct physical processes: in the first, it is the flesh itself that dissolved; in the second, it is more the juices or fluids that separated from the flesh and then, through heat, solidified.

### Identity Question

The *gemara* poses a fundamental question about the first case. *Ilima d'lo yadiana d'didei hu* — if we simply find some congealed mass and do not know its origin, does the fact of its congealing tell us anything? At first glance, one might ask: if we do not know whether this material came from the flesh or from some other bodily liquid, then congealing alone proves nothing. But the *gemara* probes further: suppose we do know it came from the body — *ela dyadinan d'dideihu* — why then should it matter whether it congealed or not? Once we know the material is dissolved flesh, it should cause the same *tumah* as the flesh itself regardless of its physical state. Dissolved flesh, one might think, is still flesh.

### Congealing Indicator

Rabbi Yirmiyah resolves the matter: *bistam* — in a case of uncertainty about the liquid's identity. The *halacha* regarding *netzeil* applies where we do not know whether the liquid before us derived from the flesh or from other bodily secretions such as saliva or mucus, *keicho v'nie'o*, which are not themselves sources of *tumat meit*. In such a case, congealing serves as an indicator of identity: *ei karash, mohel hu* — if it congeals, it derives from the flesh and carries the *tumah* of a *kezayit* of the corpse; *lo karash, dilma keicho v'nie'o hu* — if it does not congeal, it may be spit or mucus and does not carry that *tumah*. The congealing, then, is not a condition of the *tumah* itself but a diagnostic tool for determining the substance's origin.

### Tosafot Tests

*Tosafot* extends this analysis to the second variant — *mohel she'hirtiach*, the liquid that boiled. There too, *Tosafot* explains, we are dealing with a case of uncertain identity: *dyadinan d'ba mizeh hameit aval lo yadinan mohel zeh mibasaro o mikeicho v'nie'o* — we know the liquid came from the body but not whether it originated from the flesh or from other secretions. If upon heating the liquid it boils vigorously — *hirtiach v'hadar rasach* — that indicates it derives from the flesh and is therefore *tamei*. If it does not exhibit this behavior, it is presumably saliva or mucus and is *tahor*. The underlying logic of the two versions is thus parallel: whether congealing or boiling, these are diagnostic tests to establish identity, not conditions of the *tumah* itself. One might note that the *gemara* does not itself address the *hirtiach* case directly; it is *Tosafot* who fills in the parallel reasoning.

---

## Animal Neveilah

### Netzeil for Animals

Abaye poses a question to Rava: *yeish netzeil l'beheimah o ein netzeil l'beheimah* — does the principle of *netzeil* extend to animal carcasses for the purposes of *tumat neveilah*? In the preceding discussion, *netzeil* functioned within the framework of *tumat meit* — the unique *tumah* associated with human corpses, relevant to the *nazir* and to *kohanim*. But *netzeil* might alternatively be understood as a general definitional statement about flesh: dissolved flesh retains the *halachic* identity of flesh. If so, that principle could apply equally to *tumat neveilah*, the *tumah* conveyed by the carcass of an animal.

### Human vs. General

Two approaches present themselves. One holds that the *netzeil* principle was received as a *halacha* specifically for *tumat meit* — *gemiri netzeil d'asi me'adam* — and does not extend beyond that domain. The other holds that it reflects a general definition of flesh that applies wherever flesh is the operative *halachic* category, including *tumat neveilah* — *lo shena*, it makes no difference.

### Consumption Fitness

The *gemara* notes that whether this question has practical significance depends on a prior dispute. *Hanicha leman d'amar tumah chamura ad lager v'tumah kala ad lekelev shapir* — the question is only live according to the view that distinguishes between a *tumah chamura*, whose continued force depends on the substance remaining fit for human consumption, and *tumah kala*, whose continued force requires only that the substance remain fit for a dog.

The underlying principle for *tumat neveilah* is derived from the verse *lager asher bish'arecha titnenah v'achalah* — you may not eat this *neveilah*, give it to the stranger in your gates and let him eat it. From here the tradition derives that *haraui lager karui neveilah v'she'eino raui lager eino karui neveilah* — what is fit for human consumption is called *neveilah*; what is not fit for human consumption is not called *neveilah* and loses its *tumah* status. This is *tumah chamura ad lager*: the weighty *tumah* of the *neveilah* as an *av hatumah* endures only so long as the carcass is fit for a human being to eat. The mention of *tumah kala ad lekelev* — that a lesser *tumah*, such as the capacity of a food substance to conduct *tumah* from another source, may persist even when the substance is only fit for dogs — is parenthetical to the main question.

If *tumah chamura* requires fitness for human consumption, then the liquefied juices running off a decomposing animal carcass are presumably not fit for human consumption, and the question of whether they retain the *halachic* identity of flesh is moot — they have already lost their status as *neveilah* regardless. But if one holds that *tumah chamura* requires only fitness for a dog — *tumah chamura ad lekelev* — then the juices, which might well be consumable by a dog, could retain their status. In that case, Abaye's question becomes pressing: do they retain the identity of flesh for *neveilah* purposes?

### Liquefied vs. Decomposed

A *baraita* is introduced as potential evidence: *himchehu ba'or tamei bachama tahor* — if a *neveilah* was liquefied by placing it over fire, it remains *tamei*; if it decomposed by being left in the sun, it becomes *tahor*.

### Decomposition Results

The *gemara* asks: if *tumah chamura* extends to whatever is fit for a dog, then even the sun-decomposed matter should remain *tamei*, since surely it is still fit for a dog? The *gemara* responds: *eimat matchilei, basar de'astrich* — when does the *neveilah* liquefy in the sun? Only after it has putrefied. And once it has putrefied, *bechama kivan de'astrich havei lei afar* — it becomes like dust, no longer fit even for a dog. The sun-decomposition case therefore does not resolve the question about juices that remain fit for a dog, because the *baraita*'s case involves matter that has crossed the threshold into unfitness for any consumption whatsoever.

The conclusion, then, is that whether the liquefied juices of an animal carcass carry the *tumah* of *neveilah* remains unresolved. If one holds that *tumah chamura* requires human consumption fitness, the question is moot — the juices fail that test. If one holds that fitness for a dog suffices, the question turns on whether the liquids carry the definitional identity of flesh, and on that the *gemara* leaves us without a definitive answer.

---

## Niztok Mishnah

### Pouring Rule

The *gemara* introduces a *mishnah* from *masechta Machshirin*: *kol hanitzok tahor* — all instances of pouring liquids remain *tahor*. The operative question is whether a liquid being poured constitutes a single halachic unit connecting the source vessel to the point of contact. If, for example, one pours water from a vessel onto a *neveilah*, the water that physically contacts the carcass becomes *tamei*. Does the act of pouring render the water still in the vessel a single object with the water that touched the *neveilah*, thereby making the contents of the vessel *tamei* as well? The answer of the *mishnah* is no — *kol hanitzok tahor* — the flow of liquid does not create a halachic connection. Only what actually contacts the *tamei* object becomes *tamei*.

The exceptions involve extremely thick substances: *midvash haziphim* — the very thick honey of the *ziphim* — and *hatzapichit* — what may be the dense cakes of honey from the honeycomb — substances so viscous they function more like solids than liquids, and which are therefore treated as connected.

### Beit Shammai View

*Beit Shammai* extends the category further: *af hamikpa shel gerisin v'shel pol* — even a very thick porridge of crushed legumes is considered connected, *mipnei shehi soledet leachoreha* — because it pulls back. The criterion articulated by *Beit Shammai* is *soledet*: when you tilt or interrupt the flow of such a viscous substance, it does not simply fall away completely — some of it adheres and pulls back toward the source. This quality of adhesion or retraction is the basis for treating it as a single unit. The term *soledet* appears also in the context of *yad soledet bo* — the threshold temperature for *halachic* cooking — where the sense of recoiling from heat is similarly the governing intuition.

### Niztok & Foods

The *gemara* uses this *mishnah* as a springboard to ask: *yeish nitzok le'ochlin o ein nitzok le'ochlin* — does the concept of *nitzok* apply to foods as well as to liquids? That is, if one takes a food substance that has been liquefied — pulverized or processed into a thick, flowing mass — and pours it onto a *tamei* source, is the material in the vessel considered connected to what has touched the *tamei* object?

### Thick Foods Criteria

The question turns on why the thick honey qualifies as connected according to the *chachamim* and why *Beit Shammai* extends the principle to thick porridge. Two distinct rationales are possible. The first — *mishum de'it behu riri* — is that the relevant property is the presence of *ririn*, sticky stringy components that adhere and pull back, creating the physical connection that underlies the *halachic* unity. The second — *mishum desmichin* — is that sheer thickness alone is sufficient, even without the adhesive quality of *ririn*. For *Beit Shammai* the answer is clear: the criterion is *soledet*, the pulling-back quality, which is precisely the *riri* factor. But the *tanna kamma*'s inclusion of honey could reflect either view — honey is both thick and sticky, so it is consistent with either rationale.

---

## Fat Liquefaction

### Fat Status

A *baraita* is now introduced: *chelev hameit shehu shalem, vehiticho, tamei* — the fat of a corpse, when whole — meaning present in the minimum quantity required for *tumah* — and then liquefied over fire, remains *tamei*. *Haya meforad vehiticho, tahor* — if the fat was fragmented below the minimum and was then liquefied and reassembled, it is *tahor*. The second ruling reflects the general question of whether *tumah* can be reacquired once a substance has fallen below the minimum threshold through physical separation; the *baraita* assumes it cannot, at least for purposes of *tumat maga*.

### Liquids Not Combined

The first ruling, however, raises a pointed question. We have just established that *kol hanitzok tahor* — liquid is not considered a unified connected object. If so, when one liquefies the fat of a corpse, the result is a liquid that, by this principle, is not a single unit. The person who touches part of the liquefied fat is not touching the full minimum quantity. Why, then, does it remain *tamei*?

### Container Question

This is a genuinely surprising implication. The *nitzok* principle is typically discussed in the context of liquid being actively poured, and one's intuition might be that liquid sitting stably in a container constitutes a single unit. But the *gemara*'s analysis here suggests that the principle of liquid not being combined applies even to liquid at rest in a vessel — the liquid at the bottom of the container and the liquid at the top are not, in *halachic* terms, a single object. That being so, how does liquefied fat retain its *tumah* status?

### Recongealing Answer

Rabbi Zeira, together with the son of Ravina, offers a resolution: *anah u'mar brai d'Ravina targumina* — we explained this together. *Kegon d'bahadi d'martach lei, salik amuda d'nura l'puma d'mana, v'karash* — the *baraita* is speaking of a case where, in the very process of liquefying the fat over fire, the flame reached the opening of the vessel and caused the contents to recongeal partially. Thus the fat was never fully in a liquid, uncombined state — at the moment of its liquefaction, heat simultaneously caused recongealing. This allows the fat to remain *tamei* because it retained something of its solid, unified character even during the cooking process. This answer departs from the *p'shat* of the *baraita*, which simply describes the fat as having been liquefied, but it is the explanation offered.

### Stickiness Debate

Ravina raises the question to Rav Ashi, returning to the unresolved matter of *Beit Shammai*'s criterion. *Beit Shammai* says: *af hamikpa shel grisin v'shel pul, mimeshehen sollin leachoreih* — the porridge is connected *because* it pulls back. This clearly makes the *soledet* quality — the *riri* factor — the operative criterion. But the question about the *tanna kamma* remains: when the *tanna kamma* includes honey, is that because honey has *ririn*, or simply because it is thick? The *gemara* responds: *midi irya — hasam mishum desmichin, hacha mishum riri* — these are two different considerations; *Beit Shammai*'s criterion is *riri*, but the *tanna kamma*'s criterion may be *smichut*, thickness alone.

### Unresolved Question

The *gemara* thus concludes without resolving the question. For *Beit Shammai*, the stickiness factor — *riri*, the adhesive pulling-back quality — is clearly the determinative criterion. But for the *tanna kamma*, whose exemplar is honey (which is both thick and sticky), it cannot be determined whether thickness alone suffices without the *riri* factor. The case of a substance that is very thick but not sticky — lacking *ririn* — therefore remains a *teiku* in the *gemara*: an unresolved question as to whether such a substance is considered combined through *nitzok* or not.

---

---

# Nazir 52

## Incomplete Animals & Bir…

### Missing Ant Limb

The *daf* for today is 52. We pick up at the bottom of 51b, where the *Gemara* has been engaged with the topic of *rekev* — the dust produced by a decomposed corpse — and the narrow circumstances under which it generates *tumah*: primarily, a naked body in a marble casket, along with any additional criteria the *Gemara* may impose. Three lines from the bottom of 51b, the *Gemara* introduces a question posed by Rava.

*Bei Rava* — Rava asked: if you have an ant (*nemalah*) that is missing a limb, yet remains viable, what is the *halacha*? This question arises from the concept of *biryah* — the principle that consuming an entire creature, even one smaller than a *kezayit*, carries the same legal weight as consuming a *kezayit* of a forbidden substance, because the integrity of a complete entity constitutes a qualitative substitute for the quantitative *shiur*. The question is whether this qualitative status holds when the ant is missing a leg but can still survive, or whether the *biryah* status requires, in the end, translation into a quantitative measure, such that any deficiency renders it incomplete.

More precisely, Rava's question is: *shiura gmarina lei* — do we ultimately translate the *biryah* into a fixed quantity (the volume of the whole ant), so that anything less than that full volume is insufficient? Or do we say *biryah gmarina lei* — that as long as the creature remains a viable, living entity, it retains its qualitative *biryah* status regardless of a missing limb?

### Biryah & Quantity

It should be noted that the law of *biryah* applies to prohibitions of eating, not to the *shiurim* for *tumah*. Nevertheless, the underlying conceptual question — whether *biryah* is an irreducibly qualitative standard or whether it ultimately resolves into a quantitative measure — is what Rava is probing.

The *Gemara* proceeds to seek a resolution. *Amar Rav Yehuda miDiskharta* — Rav Yehuda of Diskharta says: *ta shema*, come and hear.

### Sheretz & Lentil

The *Gemara* returns to the domain of *tumah*, specifically to the *sheretz* — a creeping creature whose carcass conveys impurity. Two *pesukim* are at play: one says *kol asher yiga bahem* ("whatever touches them"), suggesting contact with the entire creature; the other says *kol asher yipol mehem* ("whatever falls from them"), suggesting that even a part suffices. The *Gemara* resolves this tension: *bahem* implies the whole, *mehem* implies a part — but the resolution is that one must touch *miktzatan shehu kekulan*, a portion that is representative of the whole.

How is a part deemed representative of the whole? *Veshi'eru hachamim ke'adasha* — the sages established the measure as the size of a lentil bean. The reasoning: *shekein hachomet techilat briato ke'adasha* — the *chomet* (identified variously as a snail or a type of limbless lizard) is the size of a lentil bean at the very beginning of its formation. This smallest of the *shratzim*, at the moment of its initial creation, is the size of a lentil. Therefore, the minimum quantity that can represent an entire *sheretz* is the size of a lentil bean — a piece of a dead mouse of that size renders one *tamei*.

The *Gemara* then draws a conclusion: *shema mina shiura gemiri lah* — we see that it is a matter of *shiurim*, not of *biryah*. Even where one begins with the concept of something that represents the whole, one ultimately arrives at a fixed quantitative number. The conceptual point is significant: even though the *sheretz* analysis does not work precisely the same way as the *biryah* analysis for eating (which is case-by-case, ant by ant, rather than a universal lentil-bean standard), the *Gemara*'s direction is clear — we seek to quantify. The *biryah* status, rather than remaining an open-ended qualitative assessment, gets translated into a number: the volume of the complete creature.

### Tosafot on Full Creature

*Tosafot* reads the proof somewhat differently. Two lines into the narrow commentary at the top of the *daf*, *Tosafot* writes: *bishlama shiura gemiri midba'inan ke'adasha* — since we require the size of a lentil bean, we see it is about *shiur*. Why? Because when we derived the lentil-bean measure, we derived it from the *chomet* in its full form, with its legs and horns intact. Even though one could theoretically cut a small piece of the *chomet* that would leave it lacking a leg and still capable of surviving, we do not say the *shiur* is the minimum size at which a *chomet* could live. Rather, *ba'inan ke'adasha mamash keviyata* — we require the full size of a complete *chomet*. This shows that the operative standard is the full creature, not a reduced creature that might still be viable.

In contrast to *Tosafot*'s emphasis, one might stress the more conceptual point: the *Gemara* shows that we consistently seek to translate the *biryah* concept into a fixed quantity, and that once we do so, any deficiency from that quantity is disqualifying.

### Soul & Shiur

The *Gemara* is not yet finished. *Amar Rav Shemaya*: *ki ba'inan shiura* — when do we need a *shiur* in the case of the *chomet* and the lentil-bean measure? *Devalo hachi ke'adasha lo metamei dela nafla beh neshama* — because without the lentil-bean size, the *chomet* would not yet convey *tumah*, since a soul has not yet entered into it.

This is somewhat cryptic, but *Tosafot* explains as follows: even though it is true that an animal can be missing a limb and still survive, this is only the case after it has been fully born. If the baby *chomet* were to be born without a leg, it would be born smaller than the size of a lentil — too small to be viable at all. Therefore, the reason we do not consider a sub-lentil-size *chomet* — one that might theoretically be missing a leg — is that no such viable creature exists before the soul has entered into it. However, if a *chomet* or ant was already born, already living, and then lost a limb, it remains viable. Whether such a living creature with a missing limb retains its *biryah* status for the purposes of the prohibition of eating — that question, Rav Shemaya implies, remains open.

The deeper conceptual point is worth appreciating: normally we think of a quantitative *shiur* as what lends qualitative significance to an act. But here the *Gemara* is working from the opposite direction — *biryah* is a qualitative substitute for the quantitative significance of a *kezayit*, and the *Gemara* asks whether that qualitative status is always anchored to a fixed quantity, or whether it can float contextually depending on the individual creature in front of us.

---

## Backbone & Skull

### Intro Backbone

We turn now to a related but distinct domain: the backbone (*hashidra*) and the skull (*hagulgoles*) as sources of *tumah*. These are bone-based sources, and bone operates differently from flesh in the laws of *tumah*. A small piece of bone — the size of a barley grain — conveys *tumah* through touch, but to convey *tumat ohel* (impurity under a shared roof), one needs enough bone to represent the body in a more substantial way. Two primary *shiurim* govern *tumat ohel*: either *rov binyano* (majority of the body's structure) or *rov minyano* (majority of the body's bone count), and even without meeting those thresholds, a *rova* or *chatzi kav* of bones from such a significant collection will cause *tumat ohel*. The backbone and skull constitute a separate category — the question before us is whether you need both together or whether either one alone suffices.

### Backbone No Ribs

*Iba'ya lehu* — the *Gemara* raises the question: when the *mishna* says *shidra ve-gulgoles*, does it mean the backbone and the skull together, or the backbone or the skull, either one independently? This is not merely a linguistic question about the *vav* in Hebrew; it is a substantive *halachic* question.

*Amar Rava ta shema* — come and hear. *Shidra shegirer rov ila'in sheba, tehora* — a backbone from which most of the ribs have been broken off is *tahor*; it does not convey *tumat ohel*. *Uvakever, afilu meshuberes o meforekes temea mipnei hakever* — but if it is in a grave, even if it is broken or dismembered, it remains *tamei* because of the *kever* itself. This is a *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* — the grave is treated as combining the fragments into a single unified object, even when they are broken, and rendering the contents *tamei*. The *chiddush* is twofold: first, that a backbone without most of its ribs is no longer deemed a backbone for purposes of *tumah*; second, that the grave overrides this and causes *tumah* nonetheless.

### Both or Either?

Now the *Gemara* asks what this teaches about our question. *Ta'ama mishum degirei* — the reason the backbone without ribs is *tahor* is because the ribs are broken off. *Ha lo girei tamei* — if not, it would be *tamei*. This implies that the backbone alone — with its ribs intact — suffices to cause *tumat ohel*, even without the skull.

But the *Gemara* deflects: *halo katani* — did we actually say that? Perhaps the passage is only telling us what happens when the ribs are broken. *Dechi girei tahara itztreicha lach* — what the passage needed to tell us is that when the ribs are broken, it is *tahor*. Whether this means the backbone alone (with ribs) is enough, or whether the skull is also needed, is not determined by this ruling. Perhaps even if you need both the backbone and the skull, once the backbone loses most of its ribs it is no longer halachically a backbone, and so the *tumah* fails — but that does not tell us whether an intact backbone alone suffices.

The discussion then turns to the story of Dustai the doctor (*Todos HaRofei*).

### Dustai Story

*Rabi Yehuda omer: shisha devarim Rabbi Akiva metamei ve-Chachamim mitaherin* — there were six matters in which Rabbi Akiva held something to be *tamei* and the *chachamim* held it *tahor* with respect to *tumat meis*, and Rabbi Akiva eventually reversed himself on most of them. The occasion for identifying these six was a famous episode:

Boxes filled with bones were brought to the *beit knesset* of the metalworkers — the craftsmen did not want to bring them inside, lest the *kohanim* present become *tamei*, so they placed the boxes in the open air of the courtyard. This episode itself illustrates an important feature of the *beit knesset* in the *Tannaic* period: it served as a communal gathering space (*beit am*), not merely as a place of prayer — which is why the doctors and rabbis convened there. *Venichnas Todos HaRofei vekhol harofim imo* — Todos the doctor came with all the other physicians, and they declared: *ein kan shidra mimeit echad* — there is not here a backbone coming from a single corpse.

The point of the doctors' testimony was that even if the bones collectively constituted a quantity sufficient for *tumah*, they came from multiple bodies. This is directly relevant to the debate between Rabbi Akiva and the *chachamim* about whether bones from multiple corpses can be combined.

### Single Bone Suffices

The *Gemara* initially reads this episode as resolving our question about backbone and skull: *ta'ama deleka shidra michada* — the reason it was *tahor* is that there was no backbone from a single body. *Ha ika o shidra o gulgoles michada* — if there had been a single backbone or a single skull from one body, *denazir megale'ach alei* — it would have been sufficient for a *nazir* to shave, and would have caused *tumat ohel*.

This would seem to confirm: *shema mina o shidra o gulgoles* — it is either one or the other that suffices, not both together.

But the *Gemara* again deflects with the formula of *lo miba'ya ka'amar*: not only was there no backbone-and-skull together from one corpse, there was not even a backbone alone from one corpse, nor a skull alone. The case was simply one of total absence. We cannot infer from the doctors' statement what would have been ruled had there been an intact backbone — whether that alone would have sufficed, or whether the skull would also have been required.

The simple reading of all these *braitot* supports the "either one" reading, but the *Gemara* consistently rebuts each proof, maintaining that the question remains open.

---

## Multiple Bodies

### Six Cases Setup

The *Gemara* now quotes the passage that lists the six matters in dispute. *U-ma hen shisha devarim she-Rabbi Akiva metamei ve-Chachamim metaherin* — what are the six things that Rabbi Akiva declared *tamei* and the *chachamim* declared *tahor*?

### Limbs & Blood

The first: *al ever min ha-mes she-ba mi-shnei mesim* — a limb assembled from parts of two separate corpses (e.g., the top of a finger from one body and the bottom from another). This is the most striking case — a limb would seem to derive its significance from its integrity as an entity, and combining parts from two bodies would seem to undercut that integrity entirely. Yet Rabbi Akiva held it *tamei*.

The second: *al ever min ha-chai she-ba mi-shnei bnei adam* — a limb from a living person composed from two separate living individuals.

The third: *al chatzi kav atzamot she-ba mi-shnei mesim* — a half-*kav* of bones from two separate corpses. Rabbi Akiva held that such bones, even from two different bodies, combine to cause *tumah*; the *chachamim* disagreed.

The fourth: *al reviet dam ha-ba'ah mi-shnayim* — a *reviet* (approximately three to four ounces, the same measure used for *kiddush*) of blood from two corpses. Here *Tosafot* notes a subtle distinction: the standard for a *nazir*'s obligation to shave is *chatzi kav* of bones and *chatzi log* of blood, while the standard for *tumat meis* more generally is *reviet kav* of bones and *reviet log* of blood. The *braita* mentions *chatzi kav* of bones (the *nazir* standard) but then mentions *reviet* of blood (the *tumat meis* standard) — a slight asymmetry worth noting.

### Split Barley Bone

The fifth: *al etzem k'se'orah she-nechelak li-shnayim* — a bone the size of a barley grain that has been split into two pieces. This case is notably different from the others: it does not involve bones from two separate bodies, but rather a single bone divided into two. It also differs in type — this is a case of *tumat maga* (impurity through contact) rather than *tumat ohel*. One might understand the ruling: a barley-grain-sized bone is already the minimum for contact-based *tumah*, and dividing it into two might cause each piece to fall below any meaningful threshold, even if they are placed back together.

### Count Clarification

This raises the question of enumeration: listing both backbone-and-skull and the above cases would produce seven, not six. The *Gemara* offers several answers.

First: *kol heicha de-palgi alei rabbim* — when we count six, we mean six cases in which *rabbim*, many sages, argue against Rabbi Akiva. *L'afukei etzem ka'siora* — excluding the split barley bone, because there it is only Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri who disagrees with Rabbi Akiva, not the *chachamim* collectively. The core dispute of Rabbi Akiva with the *chachamim* is about combining from two separate bodies — and the barley-bone case, involving division of a single bone, does not fit that pattern.

Second alternative: *ki tani eiver min hamet eiver min hachai lo katani* — when we count six cases related to corpses, *ever min ha-chai* (a limb from a living person) was not being counted, since it is not a matter of *tumat meis* per se.

Third alternative: perhaps *ever min ha-mes* and *ever min ha-chai* are treated as a single combined case, since they are closely related.

Fourth alternative: *ki tani kol heicha denazir migale'ach al achila* — we are counting cases that involve *tumat ohel* and *nazir megale'ach*, which excludes *etzem ka'siora* since that is only *tumat maga*.

Fifth: *ki tani kol heicha de-hadar beih* — the six refer to those cases on which Rabbi Akiva ultimately reversed himself. Though seven are listed, he reversed himself on only six — not on the *reviet* of blood. That brings us to the next discussion.

### Akiva's Reversal

*Ve-hadar bo Rabbi Akiva* — Rabbi Akiva reversed himself on most of these positions. But on the *reviet* of blood from two bodies, he did not reverse himself. One can appreciate why: blood from different bodies is naturally indistinguishable. Todos the doctor could look at bones and determine that they came from different individuals, but blood — before blood typing was possible — would have appeared as a single homogeneous mass. Rabbi Akiva therefore held firm.

*De'amar lei Rebbi le-Bar Kappara: lo tish'na reviet dam be-chazara* — Rebbi told Bar Kappara not to include *reviet dam* in the list of reversals. *She-hi limuda she-Rabbi Akiva beyado* — Rabbi Akiva kept his teaching firmly in hand. *Ve-od hamikra mesaye'o* — and furthermore, a *pasuk* supports him: *ve-al kol nafshot met lo yavo* — the word *nafshot* is in the plural, and given that *ki hadam hu hanafesh* — blood is the life — the plural implies that blood from multiple persons of the dead (in the plural) still generates *tumah*. This *drasha* grounds Rabbi Akiva's position in a *pasuk*, which is also why the *braita* mentions *reviet dam* (the *tumat ohel* measure) rather than *chatzi log* (the *nazir* measure): Rabbi Akiva's *limud* begins with *reviet* as the primary quantity.

### Shimon Testimony

*Rabi Shimon omer: ad yamav haya metame* — Rabbi Shimon testified that his entire life, Rabbi Akiva held his position on the blood. *Im mishemet hazar bo ani lo yodea* — if after Rabbi Akiva died he reversed himself, Rabbi Shimon says he does not know.

The *Gemara* then cites a *braita*: *hushcharu shinav mipnei taniyotav* — Rabbi Shimon's teeth turned black from the many fasts he undertook in repentance for having made this irreverent remark (implying that Rabbi Akiva might reverse himself post mortem). The humor of the remark was not lost on the *Gemara* itself, which also repeated it — and apparently both the *Gemara* and the audience understood the joke. Nonetheless, Rabbi Shimon recognized it as disrespectful toward his *rebbi* and took it seriously enough to fast in penance.

---

## Majority Bones

### Majority Debate

The *Gemara* now introduces a dispute between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* regarding the *rov atzamot* requirement for *tumat ohel*. *Beit Shammai omrim: rov atzamot min ha'atzamim o mishnayim u'mishlosha* — Beit Shammai holds that the requisite *chatzi kav* (or *rova*) of bones may come from as few as two or three bones; they need not come from a broad representation of the body's full skeletal structure. *Beit Hillel omrim: rova min hageviya, mi-rov binyano o mi-rov minyano* — Beit Hillel requires that the bones represent the majority of the body's structure (*rov binyan*) or the majority of its bone count (*rov minyan*).

### Yehoshua's Proof

*Amar Rabbi Yehoshua: yachol ani la'asot divrei Beit Shammai ve-divrei Beit Hillel ke-echad* — Rabbi Yehoshua claimed he could reconcile the two positions. The apparent contradiction between "two or three bones" and "*rov binyan* or *rov minyan*" is not a genuine dispute, he argued.

### Anatomy Proof

Rabbi Yehoshua explains: when Beit Shammai said "two or three bones," they specifically meant *mishtei shokaim ve-yerech echad o mishtei yerechayim ve-shok echad* — either two calves and one thigh, or two thighs and one calf. This combination of three bones — taken from the lower limbs — constitutes *rov govho shel adam*, the majority of a person's height. And this, Rabbi Yehoshua argues, is precisely what Beit Hillel means by *rov binyan*: the structural majority of the body.

The anatomical reasoning is that the thighs and calves together account for more than half of a person's standing height. (The pelvis sits slightly higher than the midpoint of the body, so where the thigh attaches is approximately at the midpoint; the combined leg bones below that represent the majority of the height.) Furthermore, not only do the thigh-and-calf bones represent the majority of the body's height, but taking a majority of those four bones (two thighs and two calves) — i.e., any three of the four — represents the majority of the body's primary structural bones. This is what Beit Shammai meant: not that any random two or three bones suffice, but that these specific two or three from the legs are the bones that constitute *rov binyan*.

*Tosfot* notes here that the *Gemara* in Ohalot assumes *rmach evarim* — 248 limbs — in a person, citing the principle that *kuf kaf hey hem rov minyan*, meaning 125 bones constitute a majority. This figure of 248 *evarim* (which likely here means bones rather than full limbs, since 248 discrete limbs would be anatomically impossible) underlies the *rov minyan* calculation.

As for *rov minyan*, Beit Hillel's position is that the majority of the bone count may actually be found concentrated in the small bones of the hands and feet — the *mifarkei yadayim ve-raglayim*. Thus one could have *rov minyan* without having *rov binyan*, if all the tiny bones of the extremities were present. Rabbi Yehoshua's reconciliation is that Beit Shammai was articulating *rov binyan* in anatomical terms, while Beit Hillel was stating the principle more broadly (encompassing both *rov binyan* and *rov minyan*) — but both agree that some form of body-representation is required.

### Single Bone Sammai

The *Gemara* now quotes the line that is directly relevant to the backbone-and-skull question: *Shammai omer afilu etzem min ha-shidra o min ha-gulgoles* — Shammai himself (not Beit Shammai collectively, but Shammai) held that even a single bone from the backbone or the skull suffices to cause *tumat ohel*.

This is the leniency of Shammai in the context of bone *tumah*: whereas Beit Shammai required two or three specific bones (*rov binyan*), Shammai went further and said even one bone from the skull or backbone is enough. What then is the opposing position? Presumably, Beit Hillel or the *chachamim* would require the whole backbone or skull. But Shammai says even one bone from either of those structures is enough — an extremely stringent position as to what qualifies, even if the single bone is minimal in size.

### Resolution Ambiguity

The *Gemara* attempts to infer what the opposing *Rabbinic* position must be: *u-lishmeih d'ta'ama d'Beit Shammai d'machmir, hanei Rabbanan ad d'ika shidra ve-gulgoles* — if the *rabbinic* position were simply requiring both together (the whole backbone and the whole skull), we could read the debate that way. But the *Gemara* pushes back: one cannot determine from Shammai's extreme stringency (accepting even one bone from either structure) what exactly the opposing position demands. The *Rabbanan* only disagree about the single bone; where Shammai says one bone is enough, they say you need the whole thing. But do they mean the whole skull *or* the whole backbone (either one), or the whole skull *and* the whole backbone (both together)? This ambiguity remains unresolved. The evidence consistently leans toward "either one" — all the cases discussed, including the Todos the doctor episode, speak only of finding a single backbone, with no mention of needing a skull as well. But the *Gemara* repeatedly declines to accept these as conclusive proofs.

### Rambam Rules

At this point, one may consult the *Rambam* in *Hilchos Tumat Meis*, Perek 8. The *Rambam* rules: *hashidra ve-hagulgoles, rov binyano ve-rov minyano* — these are the bones that convey *tumah* for a corpse. *Shidra sheshleimah harei hi ke-meis shalem* — a complete backbone is treated like a whole corpse. *Gulgoles sheshleimah harei hi ke-meis shalem* — a complete skull is likewise treated as a whole corpse. The *Rambam* thus rules that either one alone suffices — which is clearly where all the evidence in the *Gemara* was pointing, even if the *Gemara* itself declined to resolve the question with formal proof.

---

## Partial Backbone Question

### Quarter Kav Question

The *Gemara* now raises a new question posed by Rami bar Chama. *Ba'ei Rami bar Chama: rov atzamot min ha-shidra ve-ha-gulgoles mai?* — what is the law if one does not have a whole backbone or skull, but has a quantity of bones derived from the backbone or skull?

To understand this question properly, one must recall the framework. For *tumat ohel*, bones convey *tumah* either when they constitute *rov binyan* or *rov minyan* of the body (or a *chatzi kav* / *rova kav* coming from such a significant collection), or when one has an entire backbone or skull. Now Rami bar Chama asks: what if one has only a partial backbone — not the whole thing — but enough of it to constitute the relevant *shiur* of bones? Since the backbone and skull are themselves *significant* bone structures (indeed, they are treated as equivalent to a whole corpse when complete), perhaps a *shiur* derived from them should carry special weight.

More specifically, Rami bar Chama frames the question in terms of *nazir megale'ach*: when is a *chatzi kav* of bones required? *Heicha de-ika mish'ar evarav* — normally when the bones come from the general skeletal remains of the body — its ordinary bones. But since the backbone and skull are of heightened significance (*de-chamiri*), such that even a single one causes *tumat ohel*, perhaps *afilu rova atzamot* — even a *rova kav* (quarter-*kav*) of bones derived from the backbone or skull — should be sufficient for a *nazir* to shave, equivalent in weight to the *chatzi kav* required from ordinary bones.

In other words, Rami bar Chama assumes as his premise that a *shiur* of bones from the backbone or skull does convey *tumah* even if the backbone or skull is not whole. His question is only whether the *shiur* in such a case is reduced to a *rova* (due to the enhanced significance of these bones) rather than the standard *chatzi kav*.

### Rava's Proof

*Amar Rava ta shema* — come and hear. The *mishna* that governs the *nazir* discusses *chatzi kav atzamot* and separately lists *shidra ve-gulgoles*. If a *rova atzamot* from the backbone or skull were also a distinct operative measure for *nazir megale'ach*, it should have been mentioned in the *mishna* alongside these other categories. Its absence suggests that no such reduced *shiur* exists: the only quantity-based measure is the *chatzi kav*, and the only backbone/skull-based measure is the complete structure. A partial backbone or skull generating *tumah* at a reduced *shiur* finds no place in the *mishna*.

### Alternative Explanation

The *Gemara* then raises a complication. Rava himself is reported to have stated in another context: *lo nitzrecha ela le-shidra ve-gulgoles she-ein bahem rova atzamot* — that a ruling was necessary specifically for a case of backbone or skull that does not contain a *rova atzamot*. The implication is that even without the requisite *rova* quantity, the intact backbone or skull alone causes *tumah*. Conversely, if the backbone or skull were large enough to contain a *rova*, then the *rova* itself would be the operative measure — not the completeness of the structure.

(This statement is formulated in the *Gemara* as referring to *rova atzamot*, not *chatzi kav atzamot* — which is intriguing, since it seems to align with Rami bar Chama's suggestion that by backbone and skull, the *shiur* is a *rova* rather than a *chatzi kav*.)

This creates an internal tension: Rava used the *mishna* to refute the idea of a reduced *shiur*, yet his own statement in another context seems to presuppose exactly that reduced *shiur*. The resolution proposed is that Rava's earlier statement was made before he had fully considered Rami bar Chama's question; after hearing the challenge, he reconsidered and took the position that the *mishna's* silence on the *rova* measure from backbone/skull is dispositive.

### Unresolved Status

Ultimately, the question is left unresolved. The *Gemara* cannot confirm whether a partial backbone or skull generates *tumah* as a quantity measure, and if so, what that quantity is. Rava's proof from the *mishna* — that the absence of a *rova*-from-backbone category implies no such category exists — stands as the strongest argument. But Rava's own earlier statement, which the *Gemara* here attributes to a pre-reconsideration position, muddles the picture. The sugya thus concludes in an unresolved state, to be continued.

---

---

# Nazir 53

## Skull & Backbone

### Individual Bones

We are in the middle of a discussion concerning the portion of the *mishnah* that focuses on the skull and the backbone — *shidra v'gulgollet*. The first question to establish was whether it is only the two of them combined that are *metamei b'ohel*, or whether each one alone suffices. All the evidence pointed to each alone, and that is the way the Rambam rules.

### Quantity Requirements

The next question concerns cases where one does not have the whole skull or backbone, but has a sufficient quantity of them. We have already learned that a quarter of a *kav* — *revi'it kav* — of the majority of bones by number (*rov minyan*) or by structure (*rov binyan*) causes *tuma b'ohel*, and that double that amount, a half-*kav*, is the threshold for *nazir megaleach*: the *nazir* must shave his head and reverse the entire process. These two cases thus present a different threshold for the *nazir* to shave versus what causes *tuma b'ohel* in the ordinary sense.

The assumption, then, is that the same structure applies to *shidra v'gulgollet*: a *revi'it kav* drawn from the skull or backbone — even if one does not have their entirety — causes *tumas ohel*, and a half-*kav* would be the threshold for *nazir megaleach*.

### Rami bar Chama's Q

Against this assumption, Rami bar Chama raised the following question: since *shidra v'gulgollet* are far weightier than ordinary bones — there are only two of them and each one alone represents the entire body — perhaps even a smaller quantity of them should trigger *nazir megaleach*. That is, perhaps for *nazir megaleach* one does not need the standard half-*kav*; perhaps a *revi'it kav* — the same amount that normally causes *tuma* from ordinary bones — would suffice. This question remains before us as we enter the top of 53a.

---

## Shammai's Position

### Shammai: One Bone

The *Gemara* brings a potential proof: *ta shema* — come and hear. Shammai says: *etzem echad min hashidra u'min hagulgollet* — even one bone from the backbone or from the skull causes *tuma* and triggers the *nazir*'s obligation to shave. The question is whether we can extrapolate from Shammai's ruling what the opposing opinion holds.

### Cannot Infer Opposition

The *Gemara* dismisses this attempt: *shani Shammai d'machmir tfei* — Shammai is simply exceptionally stringent. From his stringency in one direction, one cannot infer the precise contours of the opposing view. The opposing position might hold, first, that you need the whole skull and backbone, and second, that if you have a certain quantity, you need a standard half-*kav* — not conceding any reduced threshold for *shidra v'gulgollet*. Just because Shammai is so strict does not mean the other school agrees to his degree of stringency; they might simply apply the ordinary rule of a half-*kav*.

The *Gemara* then attempts to reason in the other direction: perhaps Shammai's strictness implies that the opposing opinion is as lenient as possible — requiring the full half-*kav*. But the *Gemara* rejects this too: *dilma ad kan lo pligi rabanan alei d'Shammai ela b'etzem echad aval b'rov atzamot revi'it kav afilu rabanan modei* — perhaps the Rabbis disagree with Shammai only regarding a single bone being sufficient, but would agree that a *revi'it kav* of the majority of bones suffices. We simply cannot know.

The same point was made previously in a different discussion: from Shammai's position alone, one cannot infer how wide the *machloket* is. Shammai is very strict — even one bone from the skull or backbone. The opposing view might require both skull and backbone together, or might require skull or backbone individually but demand a full half-*kav* of their substance, or might concede that a *revi'it kav* suffices. All remain open. The question of whether, for the *tuma* relevant to the *nazir*, a half-*kav* or a *revi'it kav* from *shidra v'gulgollet* is required therefore remains unresolved. The broader lesson is that from one position in a *machloket* one cannot infer how wide that *machloket* extends.

---

## Historical Shiurim

### First Elders

Having established this unresolved question, the *Gemara* introduces a statement by Rabbi Eliezer that provides historical and conceptual background to the entire doubling of the *shiur* for *nazir megaleach*. The doubling is admittedly quite strange: why should the threshold for the *nazir* shaving be specifically double the amount that causes ordinary *tumas ohel*? If this were a universal rule it would be one thing — but why is it only with bones and blood that the *shiur* for *nazir megaleach* is double the ordinary *shiur* for *tumas ohel*?

Rabbi Eliezer explains: *zekeinim ha-rishonim* — the original early elders — were themselves divided. One group among them held *chatzi kav atzamot ve-chatzi log dam le-kol*: a half-*kav* of bones and a half-*log* of blood was the universal *shiur* for all purposes — *tuma*, *teruma*, *nezirut*, *Pesach*, *kodashim*. This was their single undifferentiated *shiur* for *tumas ohel*. The quarter-*kav* and quarter-*log* played no role in their system.

### Second Elders

A second group among the early elders took the opposite position: *af rova atzamot ve-revi'it dam le-kol* — the quarter-*kav* of bones and the quarter-*log* of blood suffice for everything. They likewise drew no distinction between *nazir*, *oseh Pesach*, *teruma*, and *kodashim*. The debate between these two groups was simply: half-*kav* or quarter-*kav*, half-*log* or quarter-*log* — with no internal differentiation by category. One notes that the existence of this debate already complicates any simple claim that all *shiurim* are *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*, a point the *Gemara* itself will address.

### Final Beit Din

The *beit din* that came after them — *beit din shel achareihem* — established the following ruling: *chatzi kav atzamot ve-chatzi log dam le-kol* — a half-*kav* of bones and a half-*log* of blood is the *shiur* for all purposes. This is because if one has double the standard *shiur*, obviously everyone is rendered *tamei* under any category. But — and this is the essential point that must be read alongside the first part — *rova atzamot ve-revi'it dam le-teruma ve-kodashim aval lo le-Nazir ve-oseh Pesach*: the quarter-*kav* of bones and the quarter-*log* of blood constitute *tuma* only with respect to *teruma* and *kodashim*, not for the purposes of the *nazir* (triggering the obligation to shave and bring *korbanot*) and not for the *oseh Pesach* (affecting one's ability to bring the Passover offering).

### Nazirite vs Terumah

The practical upshot is this: if one has only the quarter-*kav* or quarter-*log*, one is considered *tamei met* for the purposes of *teruma* and *kodashim* — one would need to become *tahor* — but this would not destroy one's *nezirut* and force the full shaving and *korban* process. Similarly, it would not prevent one from bringing a *korban Pesach* — though the *Gemara* does not spell out explicitly whether such a person would then be permitted to eat the *korban Pesach*.

The most natural analytical framework for this distinction would be to say that the half-*kav* is the *de-oraita* threshold, while the quarter-*kav* is a *mi-de-rabbanan* stringency — one we apply for *teruma* and *kodashim* but do not apply when the consequences are particularly weighty: we would not on account of a merely *de-rabbanan* status of *tamei* prevent someone from bringing a *korban Pesach*, nor would we force a *nazir* to bring a *korban* he is not truly *de-oraita* obligated to bring. This exact structure was applied earlier on 42b in the context of *tumat chiburin*, where Rav Yannai said: *lo amru tuma be-chiburin ela le-teruma ve-kodashim, aval le-Nazir u-le-oseh Pesach lo*. The *Gemara* there also drew the same line between *teruma* and *kodashim* on one side, and *nazir* and *oseh Pesach* on the other — suggesting a *de-oraita*/*de-rabbanan* framework. However, that is not where our *Gemara* ultimately lands.

---

## Third Opinion Status

### Not a Compromise

The *Gemara* raises a pointed challenge: *michdi ein hachra'ah shelishit machra'at* — a third opinion does not qualify as a compromise position that decides the *halacha*. What does this mean?

When a third opinion occupies the middle ground between two extremes, we might be inclined to rule according to it — we treat it as a *hakhra'ah*, a deciding compromise. But that inclination applies only when the third opinion is genuinely a midpoint within the same conceptual universe as the other two. If the third opinion is not really a compromise but rather introduces an entirely new concept that neither of the first two positions acknowledges as a legitimate axis of distinction, then it is simply a third independent view — not a *hakhra'ah*. In that case, the three opinions are simply three equal positions, and the fact that one appears numerically "in the middle" does not give it any special decisional weight.

Here: the first group of elders said the *shiur* is a half-*kav*, full stop, for everything. The second group said the *shiur* is a quarter-*kav*, full stop, for everything. Neither group drew any distinction between *nazir* and *oseh Pesach* on the one hand and *teruma* and *kodashim* on the other. The third position — the *beit din shel achareihem* — says: for *nazir* and *oseh Pesach* the *shiur* is half-*kav*, for *teruma* and *kodashim* the *shiur* is quarter-*kav*. This is not a compromise; it is an entirely new conceptual category that the first two groups never acknowledged. To use an analogy: if one party insists on living in New York and the other insists on Los Angeles, declaring that they will live in Ohio is not a *hakhra'ah* — it is a completely independent position of its own. Kansas City, by contrast, would be a genuine *hakhra'ah*.

Since both earlier groups spoke in absolute, undifferentiated terms — half-*kav* for everything, or quarter-*kav* for everything — the final *beit din*'s categorical distinction between types of *tuma* purposes is not a compromise between them. It is a third opinion that neither side prepared the conceptual ground for. And precisely because it is not a *hakhra'ah*, the question becomes: on what authority do we adopt it? Why does this third position carry the day?

### Prophetic Tradition

The *Gemara* answers through a statement of Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi: *mipi shemu'ah amru* — this ruling was transmitted as a received tradition. Specifically, it was a tradition going back to *mipi Chagai Zechariah u-Malachi* — Chaggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, the last of the prophets, at the beginning of the Second Temple period. The ruling is not the independent reasoning of the later *beit din*; they had an ancient tradition supporting this very distinction.

The *Gemara* notes — and the Rambam states explicitly — that this is *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*. Yet it is also worth noting that *mipi shemu'ah* and *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* may not be identical. As the Netziv explains, when the *Gemara* uses the term *halacha*, Rashi often glosses it as *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*, but the Netziv argues that it may simply mean an exceedingly ancient tradition whose original rationale has been forgotten — a tradition of great antiquity, but not necessarily one with the formal claim of Sinaitic origin.

One might ask why the tradition is attributed specifically to Chaggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. The *Gemara* does not explain this attribution. Nor does it fully clarify whether they transmitted this distinction by virtue of their status as *nevi'im* — which would raise complex questions about the role of prophecy in the *halachic* process — or whether they transmitted it simply as the last links in the chain of tradition as members of the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah*, in which case the authority is that of transmission rather than of prophetic revelation. These questions are not resolved here. What is clear is that the distinction between *nazir* and *oseh Pesach* on one side and *teruma* and *kodashim* on the other is, in the *Gemara*'s final conclusion, a genuine *ikar halacha* — not merely a rabbinic stringency applied selectively, but a substantive distinction grounded in received tradition.

---

## Mishnah List Analysis

### Complete List

The *mishnah* teaches: *al elu nazir megaleach* — over these does the *nazir* shave. The list comprises the backbone, the skull, a limb from a corpse or from a living person bearing sufficient flesh (*basar ka-rauy*), a half-*kav* of bones, a half-*log* of blood, and finally — in a separate category — a bone the size of a barley grain (*etzem ke-se'orah*), which causes *tuma* through touching and carrying (*maga* and *masa*) but not through *ohel*.

### Al Elu Function

The *Gemara* explains that the phrase *al elu* — "over these" — serves an exclusionary function. It comes to exclude the *etzem ke-se'orah* from the *ohel* category: *de'al maga ve'al masa in, ve'al ohel lo* — for touching and carrying, yes; for being under the same *ohel*, no. The *mishnah* is thus organized into two sub-lists: one pertaining to *tumas ohel*, and one pertaining to *tumas maga u-masa*.

What is striking is that the *Gemara* here takes something of a *Rabbi Yishmael*-like approach — *dibra Torah kileshon bnei adam* — to the *mishnah* itself, treating each additional word as carrying halachic weight rather than as ordinary linguistic usage. The *mishnah*'s first *al elu* divides the two internal lists (those causing *tumas ohel* from those causing only *tumas maga*), while the *ve'elu* at the *mishnah*'s close divides it from the *mishnah* that follows on 54a, which lists cases where the *nazir* does *not* shave — including, as we will see, cases such as an overhanging stone (*even ha-sochech*).

---

## Half-Kav Bones

### Gemara's Question

The *Gemara* now doubles back to the *mishnah*'s ruling on *chatzi kav atzamot* — a half-*kav* of bones causes *tumas ohel* and *nazir megaleach* — as opposed to *rov atzamot*, the majority of bones, which is not stated here. The *Gemara* asks: *heichi dami* — what is the actual scenario? If the bones are all individually the size of a barley grain, then even without a half-*kav*, a single bone suffices — *teipok lei mishum etzem ke-se'orah*, it comes out from the rule of *etzem ke-se'orah*. There is no need for a half-*kav* in that case.

### Dust Resolution

The *Gemara* therefore resolves: *ela de-ikmach chamuchei* — the bones must have been ground into dust, pulverized to such a degree that there is not even a single *etzem ke-se'orah* among them.
