In that case, no individual bone meets the *shiur* for *tumas maga*, yet the aggregate quantity of a half-*kav* still causes *tumas ohel*.

### Tosafot Analysis

Tosafot notes the difficulty here: *tzarich iyun, mai ka parich* — why is the *Gemara* asking this question at all? We are discussing *tumas ohel*, and an *etzem ke-se'orah* does not cause *tumas ohel* regardless. What prompted the *Gemara*'s challenge? Tosafot offers a complicated answer: the *Gemara* understood that the *mishnah*'s ruling on *chatzi kav atzamot* implicitly excludes scenarios involving *less* than a half-*kav* — not merely from causing *tumas ohel*, but from causing *tuma* at all. What scenario would that be? One where the bones have been entirely pulverized to dust. In that condition, less than a half-*kav* of dust would not be *metamei* at all, not even through touching. The half-*kav* threshold, when reduced to dust, is what preserves the *tuma* even without any individual bone meeting the *shiur*.

---

## Limb w/o Flesh

### Flesh Requirement

The *mishnah* then turns to *ever min ha-met ve'ever min ha-chai she-yesh alav basar ka-rauy* — a limb from a corpse or from a living person that has sufficient flesh upon it. *Basar ka-rauy* means flesh of an amount sufficient to heal if the limb were reattached to a living person.

The *Gemara* proceeds with what reads as a somewhat unusual reverse order through the *mishnah*, having already addressed the bones, the *rov minyan* and *rov binyan*, and the skull and backbone. Now it turns to the *ever*. Before examining the *ever* with sufficient flesh, the *Gemara* raises a prior question:

### R. Yochanan: No Shaving

*Eiver she-ein alav basar ka-rauy mai* — what is the law when a limb does not have sufficient flesh upon it? The answer is obviously that it does not cause *tumas ohel*. The real question is: does it still cause *tuma* through *maga* — through touching? Could one argue that a limb retains halachic significance as an *ever*, even when lacking sufficient flesh, such that touching it renders the *nazir* obligated to shave?

Rabbi Yochanan rules: *ein ha-nazir megaleach aleihem* — the *nazir* does not shave over them. His reasoning: *de-katani b'reisha* — the first *mishnah* explicitly requires *she-yesh alav ke-zayit basar*, and the implicit reading is that without that amount of flesh, it does not cause *tuma*. Furthermore, if a limb lacking sufficient flesh could cause *tumas maga*, it should have appeared on the *maga* list in the *mishnah*. It is on neither list, and therefore the *nazir* is not *megaleach*.

### Reish Lakish: Tumah via…

Reish Lakish disagrees: *megaleach*. He derives this from the fact that the second *mishnah* — the one listing cases where the *nazir* does *not* shave — does not include *ever she-ein alav basar ka-rauy* in its list. Since it is absent from that negative list, Reish Lakish infers that the *nazir does* shave upon touching it — it is a case of *tumas maga*, not *tumas ohel*.

To understand the force of this debate, it is essential to appreciate the structure of the two *mishnayot*. The first *mishnah* (on 49b) lists cases of *nazir megaleach*; its list includes *ever min ha-met ve-ever min ha-chai she-yesh alav basar ka-rauy*, along with the *etzem ke-se'orah* for *maga*. The second *mishnah* (on 54a) lists cases of *ein hanazir megaleach*: places like a field of graves (*beit ha-pras*) and *eretz ha-amim*, and physical categories such as the tombstone (*golel* and *dofek*), *revi'it dam*, and *rov ha-atzamot* — this last corresponding to the *revi'it ha-kav*. Critically, *ever she-ein alav basar ka-rauy* does not appear in the second *mishnah*.

### Implicit vs Explicit

The *Gemara* presses Rabbi Yochanan: if the logic is that anything not appearing in the first list is excluded, why does the second *mishnah* go to the trouble of listing *reva'it atzamot* — the quarter-*kav* of bones — which is already implicitly excluded by the first *mishnah*'s requirement of a half-*kav*? The second *mishnah* apparently does mention things that are already implicit exclusions from the first.

### Implicit Exclusion

Rabbi Yochanan answers: *kol heicha d'mashma miklala lo tana b'seifa* — wherever the exclusion is genuinely implicit in the *klal* of the first *mishnah*, the second *mishnah* does not need to repeat it. The second *mishnah* only mentions something when, without the explicit statement, one might have drawn an erroneous inference.

In the case of *reva'it atzamot*, had the second *mishnah* not stated it explicitly, one might have thought that less than a half-*kav* is not *metamei* even through *maga* or *masa*. The explicit statement therefore comes to clarify: the quarter-*kav* is excluded only from *ohel*, not from *maga*. Even less than a half-*kav* of bones still causes *tuma* through touching. That clarification was necessary and thus warranted explicit mention.

As for the *revi'it dam* appearing in the second *mishnah*, Rabbi Yochanan explains: *l'afukei midivrei Rabbi Akiva* — it is stated there to exclude Rabbi Akiva's persistent position that *revi'it dam* drawn from two corpses causes *tumas ohel*. The *mishnah* wishes to explicitly reject that view and therefore states it. In principle, the second *mishnah* does not need to restate things already implicit in the first.

Returning to *ever she-ein alav basar ka-rauy*: since the first *mishnah* explicitly conditions the *ever* on *she-yesh alav basar ka-rauy*, the implication that a limb without sufficient flesh is excluded is fully embedded in the first *mishnah*. There is no need to repeat it in the second *mishnah*. Thus, the *nazir* does not shave for it.

Reish Lakish, by contrast, reads the two lists differently: the first *mishnah* organizes by modality — *ohel* cases and *maga* cases — and the second *mishnah* enumerates everything that does not trigger *nazir megaleach*. If a scenario is absent from the second *mishnah*, it is *megaleach*. The *she-yesh alav basar ka-rauy* of the first *mishnah* implicitly suggests the case of *she-ein alav basar ka-rauy*, and since that case is not listed in the second *mishnah* among the non-*megaleach* categories, Reish Lakish concludes that it is *megaleach* through *maga*. Rabbi Yochanan's position seems the stronger reading of the *mishnah* as a whole, but as we will see, Reish Lakish draws support from *midrashei halacha*.

---

## Midrashic Derivations

### Braita Sources

The *Gemara* cites a *braita* that provides scriptural grounding for the categories of *tumas ohel* and *tumas maga*. The *pasuk* read for *ohel* is: *ve-chol asher yiga al pnei ha-sadeh u-ve-chalal cherev o ve-meit o ve-etzem adam o ve-kaver* (Bamidbar 19:16). The *Gemara* reads *al pnei ha-sadeh* as referring to *ha-me'ahil* — one who is an *ohel* over these sources of *tuma*. The phrase *al pnei* — literally "upon the face of" — is understood as superfluous given the word *yiga* ("touch"), and from this superfluity the *drashah* derives that the *pasuk* speaks of *tumas ohel*.

### Chalal Cherev

From the word *be-chalal* the *braita* derives *eiver min ha-chai* — specifically, a limb from a living person that *yesh lo le-haalot arucha*, has enough flesh that it could heal if reattached. The word *chalal* suggests something that has been struck or wounded but is not yet fully dead — the limb, so to speak, is "the dead thing" while the person remains alive.

### Cherev & Vessels

*Cherev* gives rise to the famous principle *cherev harei hu ke-chalal* — a metal vessel is halachically equivalent to a *chalal*. This means that metal *keilim* that come into contact with a *meit*, or are present in the same *ohel* as a *meit*, acquire the *tuma* of the *meit* itself and become *avi avot ha-tuma* rather than merely *av ha-tuma*. They are not merely secondary sources of *tuma* but are elevated to the primary level of the corpse itself. This principle will be discussed further in the next *daf*.

*O ve-meit* — from *meit* the *braita* derives *eiver ha-nechlal min ha-meit*, a limb that is part of a corpse — that is, *ever min ha-meit*, where the whole body is the *meit* and the limb is extracted from it, as opposed to the *chalal* case where only the limb itself is the "dead thing."

*O ve-etzem adam* — from *etzem adam* the *braita* derives *rov atzamot*, the majority of bones. Though *etzem* sounds like a single bone, the *drashah* understands it as referring to the bone that represents the entire person — *rov atzamot*. The list from this *pasuk* thus covers *eiver min ha-chai*, *eiver min ha-meit*, and *rov atzamot* — most of the *mishnah*'s *ohel* categories — though notably not the blood or *ke-zayit basar* categories as yet.

### Ohel vs Touching

The *braita* on *tumas ohel* is then set alongside the parallel *braita* on *tumas maga*, derived from a different *pasuk*: *ve-al ha-nogei'a be-etzem o be-chalal o be-meit o be-kaver* (Bamidbar 19:18). Rav Yehuda introduces this *braita* as a *tena* — a tannaitic source — dealing with touching. The two *beraitot* share much of the same language but serve different halachic functions: the first defines sources of *tumas ohel*; the second defines sources of *tumas maga*.

From *be-etzem* in the touching *pasuk*, the *braita* derives *etzem ke-se'orah* — a bone the size of a barley grain causes *tuma* through touching. This is the distinctive *shiur* for *maga* that does not apply to *ohel*.

*O ve-kaver* in the *ohel* list gives rise to *kever satum* — a sealed grave. The *halacha* of *kever satum* is that if a body is enclosed in a sealed coffin or burial chamber, the entire enclosure is treated as the *meit* itself: the *tuma* spreads across the full dimensions of the casket and bursts upward (*tumah boka'at ve-olah boka'at ve-yoredet*), passing through the covering and continuing upward, because the sealed grave is treated as an extension of the corpse. This is why overflight of cemeteries is a concern. If the burial chamber were not sealed — lacking full sides — the *tuma* would stop within a *tefach* of the body at the covering above and would not proceed further upward, since the covering would function as an *ohel* to block it.

### RL: Flesh-Deficient Limbs

The key contribution from the *maga* braita for the Reish Lakish dispute is the following. Where the *ohel* braita derived from *be-chalal* the case of *eiver min ha-chai she-yesh lo le-haalot arucha* — a limb with sufficient flesh — Reish Lakish reads the same word *chalal* in the *maga* braita to yield a different derivation: *zeh eiver ha-nichleh min ha-chai ve-ein bo le-haalot arucha* — a limb from a living person that does *not* have enough flesh to heal. Similarly, *o be-meit* in the *maga* braita yields *eiver ha-nichleh min ha-meit* without sufficient flesh. The two *beraitot* thus present a parallel structure: the *ohel pasuk* gives us *eiver min ha-chai* and *eiver min ha-meit* with sufficient flesh; the *maga pasuk* gives us the same two categories without sufficient flesh — and these latter cause *tuma* only through touching, not through *ohel*. This is the explicit scriptural support for Reish Lakish's position: a limb from a corpse or a living person lacking sufficient flesh is *metamei* through *maga*, even if it does not cause *tumas ohel*.

The parallel structure between the two *beraitot* is also visible in the bone categories: *etzem adam* in the *ohel pasuk* refers to *rov atzamot*, while *be-etzem* in the *maga pasuk* refers to the smaller *etzem ke-se'orah*. So too with *chalal* and *meit* — each appears in both *pesukim* but yields a different level of *tuma* depending on context.

The final word in the *maga pasuk* — *o ve-kaver* — receives a striking interpretation from Reish Lakish: *zeh kever she-lifnei ha-dibbur* — the grave before the giving of the Torah at Sinai. What this mysterious phrase means, and its full halachic significance, will be taken up in the next session.

---

---

# Nazir 54

## Tumat Met Framework

### Ohel vs. Touch

The daf opens by returning to a foundational question in the laws of *tumat met*: which objects generate *tumah* through *ohel* — that is, by being under the same roof as a *met* — and which generate *tumah* only through direct contact? The two *pesukim* that govern *tumat met* both appear, at the level of *peshat*, to be discussing touch: *vechol asher yigah al p'nei hasadeh* — "and anyone who touches on the face of the field" — refers specifically to the open field, meaning not under a roof, so it is not *tumat ohel*. The second *pasuk*, *ve'al hanogea*, similarly seems to address touch. Yet the *midreshei halakha* read *al p'nei hasadeh* as describing a situation where a person is *over* the face of the *met* — leaning above it without making direct contact — and thereby interpret this *pasuk* as speaking about *ohel*. From this reading, the first *pasuk* yields the items that convey *tumah* through *ohel*, and the second yields the items that convey *tumah* through touch.

### Pesukic Sources

From the first *pasuk*, the *midreshei halakha* derive that *chalal*, *cherev*, *met*, *etzem adam*, and *kever* all cause *tumah* through *ohel*. These five categories are not identical in their natures, and unpacking what each term signifies is essential to understanding how the system operates.

### Cherev Doctrine

*Chalal* in this context is understood to mean something that was once an *eiver min hachai* — a limb severed from a living person — that is now dead in isolation, even without a complete corpse. *Cherev* introduces what is perhaps the most striking principle: *cherev harei hu kechalal* — the sword is like the corpse itself. The significance of this principle is considerable. A *met* is an *avi avot hatumah*, meaning that whoever touches it is rendered an *av hatumah* and is *tamei* for seven days. The rule of *cherev harei hu kechalal* extends this status to the sword — or more broadly, as we will see, to certain metal vessels — such that whoever touches it also becomes an *av*, not merely a *rishon*, and is *tamei* for seven days. The sword does not go down a level of *tumah* by virtue of having been in contact with the *met*; it retains the full status of the *met* itself.

### Mishkav Analogy

This is conceptually parallel to another domain of *halakha*: the *mishkav u'moshav* of a *zav*. A *zav* is an *av hatumah*. When a *zav* sits or lies upon something, that object — the *mishkav* or *moshav* — does not become a *rishon* as an ordinary vessel would through contact. It becomes an *av hatumah* by virtue of its identity as the seat of the *zav*. Famously, this applies even if the *zav* is separated from his seat by many cushions — the image invoked is of a princess and the pea — because what defines the *mishkav* is not physical contact but a status relationship. In a similar conceptual register, *cherev* acquires the full status of the *met* not by simple contact but by something more like identity-level association. Although we will arrive later in today's daf at a broader definition of what counts as *cherev* — potentially extending to all metal vessels that shared an *ohel* with a *met* or touched it — the basic principle is that these objects are conceived as *avi avot hatumah*, just as the *met* itself.

### Tumat Ohel Items

The five items that cause *tumat ohel* are thus: *chalal*, *cherev*, *met*, *etzem adam*, and *kever satum*. The last of these, *kever satum* — a sealed coffin — requires explanation. One might have thought that a coffin would function as an *ohel* and thereby *contain* the *tumah*, preventing it from spreading upward. But the *halakha* of *kever satum* holds that if the coffin is sealed on all sides — walls and top — then the entire coffin is treated as the *met* itself, and the *tumah* is *metamei* not only in line with the *met* but in line with the entire coffin. The coffin does not serve as an *ohel*; it is, in legal terms, a *met*. This is a critical principle underlying the *halakha* of graveyards: one cannot simply argue that the coffin contains the *tumah*.

### Bone Amount Distinctions

The category of *etzem adam* introduces the most significant difference between *tumat ohel* and *tumat maga*. For *tumat ohel*, the bone must be of sufficient quantity to represent the person — *rov minyan*, *rov binyan*, a *shidrah*, a *gulgolet*, or a corresponding quantity of bones. This is *etzem adam*. For *tumat maga*, however, even a bone the size of a barley grain — *etzem kese'orah* — causes *tumah* through touch. This distinction between *etzem adam* and *etzem* is the principal point of divergence between the two *pesukim*, and it will become the pivot of the Talmudic debate immediately to follow.

---

## Braita Analysis

### Reish Lakish Position

The discussion of the second *pasuk*, which the *midreshei halakha* read as governing *tumat maga*, provides the occasion for a major dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan. Reish Lakish contends that there exists a category of *eiver min hachai* and *eiver min hameis* — severed limbs — that lacks sufficient flesh to survive if reattached, yet still causes *tumah* through touch. His proof comes from a *braita*.

### Braita Text

Rav Yehuda introduces the relevant *braita* with the word *tanya*. The *braita* expounds the *pasuk* *ve'al hanogea be'etzem o vechalal*: "touching a bone" refers to *etzem kese'orah*; "or a *chalal*" refers to an *eiver* that was severed from a living person and does not have sufficient flesh to heal — *ein bo lehaalos arucha*; "or a *meis*" refers to *eiver min hameis*; "or a *kever*" — and here Reish Lakish interjects that this *kever* is *kever shelifnei hadibbur*, the grave before the divine speech, a phrase we will return to shortly.

### Eiver Definitions

Within the *braita*, the distinction between the two types of severed limbs is as follows. An *eiver min hachai* or *eiver min hameis* that has sufficient flesh — enough that the limb could survive if reattached — is the standard case that causes *tumah* through *ohel*. An *eiver min hachai* or *eiver min hameis* that does not have sufficient flesh is the more unusual case, and it is this case that Reish Lakish says the *braita* addresses in the context of *tumat maga*.

### Limb Analysis

The *gemara* then presses: what exactly is the case of *eiver min hameis* in this *braita*? If the limb contains an *etzem kese'orah*, then it already causes *tumah* as a bone — *hainu hanogea be'etzem*. So the *braita* must be speaking of a case where the bone within the limb is insufficient to qualify independently. There is, then, a limb with insufficient bone to cause *tumah* as a bone, insufficient flesh to heal, and yet it causes *tumah* through contact. This, says Reish Lakish, demonstrates that a limb without sufficient flesh retains independent *tumah*-causing status by virtue of being a limb, and the *Torah* includes it explicitly — *rachmana rabyei*. The relevance to our *masechta* is that Reish Lakish infers that a *nazir* should also be *megaleach* upon touching such a limb, even though the *mishnah* listing the causes of *nazir megaleach* mentioned only limbs with sufficient flesh. The *mishnah* may have omitted it, but the *midrash halacha* makes clear that the *tumah* exists.

### Rav Yochanan Rebuttal

Rabbi Yochanan responds: *le'olam de'is beih* — the limb in the *braita* does in fact contain an *etzem kese'orah*. The apparent redundancy of the *braita* mentioning this limb separately from "bone" is not because it is teaching a new category; it is teaching a different mode of *tumah*-transmission. *V'ei eino inyan lemaga, tanehu inyan lemassa* — if the text is not needed to teach about *touching*, apply it to teach about *carrying*. This is the standard *talmudic* principle of *im eino inyan l'zeh, tnehu inyan l'zeh*.

### Masa Derivation

The structure of the two *pesukim* establishes two modes of *tumah*: *ohel* and *maga*. But there is a third mode — *massa*, carrying — and it needs a Scriptural source. Rabbi Yochanan's position is that there is no independent category of *eiver* without sufficient flesh causing *tumah* through touch; there is simply a second application of *etzem kese'orah*, and the redundancy derives *tumat massa*. The *halakhic* rule that carrying is equivalent to touching — as stated in the *mishnah* — still needs a textual basis, and that is what the apparent duplication in the *braita* provides. This is the substance of the Reish Lakish–Rabbi Yochanan dispute as it stands on this *amud*.

---

## Kever Lifnei HaDibbur

### Tosafot Interpretations

We now return to the striking phrase that Reish Lakish appended to his reading of the *braita*: the *kever* mentioned in the *pasuk* governing *tumat maga* is *kever shelifnei hadibbur* — the grave before the divine speech. *Tosafot* identifies two possible interpretations of this phrase.

### Non-Jew Status

The first interpretation understands *lifnei hadibbur* as referring to the period before *Matan Torah*. The underlying question is: what was the status of graves and the *tumah* they generate before the Torah was given? *Tosafot* links this to the broader question of when the people of Israel shifted from the status of *bnei Noach* to the status of *Yisrael*. Was it from the moment Avraham received *brit milah*? From *ma'amad Har Sinai*? There is an entire work — attributed to the *Mishneh Lamelech*, entitled *Parshat Drachim* — that works through the *midrashim* through this lens. One famous illustration: the debate between Yosef and his brothers, in which he accused them of eating *eiver min hachai*, turned precisely on this question. Yosef believed they already had the status of *bnei Yisrael* and were subject to more stringent obligations; they believed they retained the status of *bnei Noach*.

*Tosafot* notes, however, a difficulty with this first interpretation. If one accepts the view of *Rabbanan* and Rabbi Shimon that non-Jews are *metamei* through *ohel* — that is, if the rule *atem atem keruyim adam* limiting *tumat ohel* to Jews is not accepted — then there would be no need for a special *pasuk* to teach that a grave from before *Matan Torah* conveys *tumah* through *maga*. Everyone already concedes that non-Jews convey *tumah* through touch; that is uncontested even by Rabbi Shimon. So what novel teaching is *kever shelifnei hadibbur* adding? If the point were about the status of the person — Jewish versus non-Jewish — and if touching a non-Jew's grave already conveys *tumah*, why do we need a *drasha* about the period before the Torah was given?

### Pre-Legislation Theory

This leads *Tosafot* to offer a second interpretation, which is, one might argue, the more natural reading. The *dibbur* in question is not the moment of *Matan Torah* as a whole, but the specific moment when the particular *parasha* of *tumat met* was legislated. The *parasha* of *adam ki yamut b'ohel* appears in *Chukat*, far into the forty years in the wilderness — not at Sinai. It is entirely possible that between *Matan Torah* and the giving of that specific *parasha*, people came into contact with the dead and entered a state of *tumah* before those laws existed. What is the status of such a person once the *parasha* is given?

### Ritva Solution

The *Ritzba* — cited within *Tosafot* — addresses this question by distinguishing between the metaphysical reality of *tumah* and the legal legislation that addresses it. The *Ritzba* holds that Jews possess *tumah* status even before the law is given; what *kever shelifnei hadibbur* teaches is that the laws, once legislated, apply retroactively to those who entered that status beforehand. This is not a punitive or retroactive legislation in the ordinary legal sense; rather, it reflects a presumption that *tumah* is a metaphysical condition that exists independently of whether *halakha* has yet defined its consequences. Once the *halakha* is given, it addresses the person's actual state, whatever the origin of that state.

### Parallel Cases

*Tosafot* draws a parallel to other areas of *tumah*. A *pasuk* in *Perek Haba al Ha'arayot* similarly derives the status of a *zav shelifnei hadibbur* — a man who experienced a *zov* before *Parshat Zavim* was given. The same question applies to a woman who had her period before *Parshat Niddah* was legislated: is she a *niddah* from the moment that *parasha* takes effect? The *drasha* answers that yes, even if the condition arose before the legislation, these laws apply. What this implies is that these *tumot* are not created by the law; the condition exists, and the law governs it once it is given.

### Metaphysics & Law

This raises a genuinely profound question: to what degree is *tumah v'tahara* a metaphysical reality, and to what degree is it purely a legal construct? If *tumah* is only a legal category, then it cannot exist before the law is enacted, and any attempt to apply it retroactively would be incoherent. But if *tumah* has an independent metaphysical reality — if it is a condition that attaches to a person regardless of legislation — then the law, when given, simply addresses a pre-existing state. One practical formulation: it is not that the person is held liable for having entered the *Mikdash* or otherwise violated a prohibition before the law was given — they violated nothing, since no prohibition existed. But from the moment the *parasha* is given, the person's current state is what it is: they are *tamei*, they must wait seven days, they must undergo the sprinkling of *parah adumah*, and all the attendant *halakhot* now apply to their actual condition. The law did not create the condition; it chose to address it.

---

## Nazir Non-Megaleach List

### Sprinkling Rules

The *mishnah* concludes with the phrase *umaza bashlishi uvisvi'i vesoteis* — he sprinkles on day three and day seven, and it destroys the earlier days. A *nazir* who contracts one of the qualifying forms of *tumat met* must undergo the full *tahara* process, including *hazayah* on days three and seven, and the days of *nezirut* already completed are invalidated. The *nazir* may not begin counting anew until he becomes *tahor*, and he brings his *korbanos* as required.

### Counting Dispute

The *gemara* raises a question about the precise reading of the *mishnah's* phrase *ad she-yit-har* — until he becomes *tahor*. Does this mean he begins his new count on day seven, once *tahara* is technically achieved, or only on day eight, after the *korbanos* are brought? *Tosafot* notes that the version of the *mishnah* available to the *gemara* did not include the phrase *umeivi es korbanosav* — "and he brings his *korbanos*" — so the question is genuinely open from the text alone.

### R. Eliezer vs. Rabbanan

The *gemara* frames the dispute as follows. If *ad she-yit-har* means until the end of day seven — at which point *ha'erev shemesh* has passed and *tahara* is complete — then the *mishnah* follows Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that the *nazir* begins counting his *nezirut taharah* on day seven, since he is fully *tahor* by nightfall. If *ad she-yit-har* means until after the *korbanos* are brought, which occurs on day eight, then the *mishnah* follows the Rabbanan, who hold that *nezirut taharah* does not take effect until day eight.

### Braita Comparison

The *gemara* resolves the question by cross-referencing the *mishnah* immediately to follow — the list of things for which a *nazir* is *not* *megaleach*. That *mishnah* states: *umaza bashlishi uvisvi'i umatchil umoneh miyad* — he sprinkles on day three and seven and begins counting immediately. In this case, since the *nazir* is not *megaleach*, he does not bring *korbanos*, and *miyad* naturally refers to the moment he becomes *tahor* on day seven after the sprinkling. If "immediately" in the non-*megaleach* case means right after day seven, then "until he becomes *tahor*" in the *megaleach* case must refer to something later — namely, day eight after the *korbanos*. The contrast between the two formulations reveals that *miyad* is the earlier start point and *ad she-yit-har* is the later one.

### Day Eight Start

The *gemara* concludes: *manu Rabbanan hi d'amri nezirut tahara ad shemini lo chayila* — this accords with the Rabbanan, who hold that *nezirut tahara* does not take effect until day eight. The *nazir* who must bring *korbanos* cannot begin counting toward his new *nezirut* until after those *korbanos* are offered. The comparison with the non-*megaleach* case, where counting resumes immediately after day seven, establishes that the requirement to bring *korbanos* is what delays the start in the standard *megaleach* case, and that delay continues until day eight.

---

## Tumat But Not Megaleach

### Beit HaPras

The *mishnah* now presents a list of things for which a *nazir* is *not megaleach*. The first items are *beit hapras* and *eretz amim*. A *beit hapras* is a field over which a grave was plowed. The rabbis decreed that one who passes through such a field is *tamei*, out of concern that tiny fragments of bone may have been scattered across a wide area. Biblically, however, this decree does not apply: the area is too large, the fragments too small, and the concern too attenuated to rise to the level of *de'oraita tumah*. Since a *nazir* is only *megaleach* for qualified *tumat met de'oraita*, *beit hapras* does not trigger *megaleach*.

### Eretz Amim

*Eretz amim* — the land outside *Eretz Yisrael* — was declared *tamei* by rabbinic decree. The reasons given are multiple. One is a concern that Jewish bodies are buried throughout the diaspora, though the practical force of this reasoning is complicated. A more compelling explanation, which *Tosafot* states explicitly and which we will revisit, is that this decree was enacted as a social and national measure to encourage Jews to remain in *Eretz Yisrael*. There may also be a theological dimension — *Eretz Yisrael* as the uniquely sanctified land, and the outside as *eretz hatzmei'ah*. In any case, the *tumah* of *eretz amim* is rabbinic, and a *nazir* is not *megaleach* for it.

### Golel ve'Dofek

*Golel ve'dofek* is a category subject to a dispute between Rashi and *Tosafot* regarding its physical referent. Rashi, in *Perek Kama* of *Ketubot*, explains that the *golel* is the cover of the coffin and the *dofek* refers to the side panels. *Tosafot* disagrees, citing the *gemara* in *Perek Bameh Madlikin* which derives *golel ve'dofek* from the phrase *al p'nei hasadeh*, which implies objects that are exposed above ground, not buried. Rabbeinu Tam therefore explains that *golel* is the tombstone — the *matzeiva* — and *dofek* refers to the stones upon which the tombstone leans for support. A third possibility, raised in discussion, is that these terms refer to the stone sealing a catacomb, which accords with archaeological evidence that both above-ground and below-ground burial practices coexisted.

### Golel Status

What is significant about *golel ve'dofek* is that it is *de'oraita tumah* — specifically *tumat meis de'oraita* — and yet a *nazir* is not *megaleach* for it. The *Torah* derives from *al p'nei hasadeh* that the tombstone and its supporting stones carry biblical *tumah*, yet they are not included in the list of *nazir megaleach*. This is a striking principle: *de'oraita* status does not automatically entail *nazir megaleach*. The previous *mishnah* establishing when a *nazir* is *megaleach* never mentioned touching a *kever satum* on a part not directly opposite the *met*; the present *mishnah* clarifies that *golel ve'dofek*, though biblically *tamei*, is excluded from the *megaleach* requirement.

The practical corollary emerges from *Masechet Smachot*, which states: *kol meis she'ein hanazir megaleach alav, ein kohen muzhar alav* — any *tumah* for which a *nazir* is not *megaleach* is also one for which a *kohen* is not prohibited. This principle extends the significance of the *megaleach* list well beyond *nezirut* into *kohen* law.

### Revi'is Dam

*Revi'is dam* — a quarter-*log* of blood from a corpse — causes *tumah de'oraita*, whether through touch or *ohel*. Yet the *nazir* is not *megaleach* for it, because the qualifying quantity for *nazir megaleach* by blood is *chatzi log*, not *revi'is*.

### Ohel Rova Atzmos

Similarly, *ohel rova atzmos* — being under the same roof as a quarter-*kav* of bones — constitutes *tumat meis de'oraita* through *ohel*, yet it does not trigger *megaleach*. The threshold for *nazir megaleach* by bones in an *ohel* context is *chatzi kav*, not *rova kav*. These cases represent the other face of the distinctions that dominated the previous days of the *daf*: smaller quantities of blood and bone are *de'oraita tamei*, but they fall below the threshold at which *nazir megaleach* applies.

### Vessels Touching Corpse

The next category is *keilim hanogaim b'meis* — vessels that touched the corpse. The more interesting reading of this case, and the one with the most *halakhic* consequence, is that these are vessels falling into the category of *cherev harei hu kechalal*. Such vessels do not merely become an *av* through contact; they acquire the status of *avi avot hatumah*, like the *met* itself. A *nazir* who touches such a vessel would become an *av* and be *tamei* for seven days — a full *tumat meis* by all accounts. Yet the *mishnah* teaches that a *nazir* is not *megaleach* for this. These vessels are *de'oraita tumat meis* at the level of *avi avot*, and still not *megaleach*.

### Rav Goren Innovation

This ruling has a remarkable practical application in the *halakhot* of *kohanim*. We noted earlier the principle from *Masechet Smachot*: *kol meis she'ein hanazir megaleach alav, ein kohen muzhar alav*. If a vessel that has acquired the status of *cherev harei hu kechalal* is one for which a *nazir* is not *megaleach*, it follows that a *kohen* is not prohibited from touching such a vessel.

Rav Goren — not Rav Herzog, as initially misstated — proposed an innovative *halakhic* solution to the question of whether a *kohen* may study medicine and thereby come into repeated contact with corpses. The background is as follows: even granting the position that a *kohen* who is already *tamei meis* cannot become *re-tamei* simply by touching the *met* again, there remains the concern that active contact with the *met* raises the level of the *kohen's tumah*. Rav Goren's solution: bring metal rings into the room where the *met* is located. These rings thereby acquire the status of *cherev harei hu kechalal* — they become *avi avot hatumah*, as *tamei* as the *met* itself. Since a *kohen* is permitted to touch these rings (a *nazir* would not be *megaleach* for them, and accordingly a *kohen* is not *muzhar* on them), the *kohen* can then wear these rings while handling the *met*. By wearing an object that is already at the *avi avot* level, the *kohen* is not raising his level of *tumah* through direct contact with the *met* — he is already in contact with something of equivalent status. The logical and *halakhic* elegance of this approach generated significant controversy; Rav Moshe Feinstein reportedly had a strong reaction against it.

### Metzora Case

The *mishnah* then turns to entirely different categories of *tumah* — those that are not *tumat meis* at all. A *metzora* in the stage of *yimei gmaro* — the second week of quarantine, when the spot has already spread and the *kohen* has sealed a full determination — or in *yimei seforo* — the subsequent seven-day counting period during which the *metzora* undergoes *tahara* before bringing *korbanos* on day eight — is a full *metzora* in the *halachic* sense. Tzaraas *tumah* is its own *de'oraita* category. Yet since it is not *tumat meis*, there is no *megaleach*. For these cases, the *mishnah* states: he is not *megaleach*, he sprinkles on days three and seven because there is *tumat meis* as well (since whatever *tumat meis* he may have contracted still requires *hazayah*), earlier days are not destroyed, and he begins counting *miyad* — immediately — once he becomes *tahor*.

The *mishnah* also clarifies that he does not bring the *korban* associated with *nazir megaleach*, since no *megaleach* has occurred.

### Light Tumot Counting

*Umbe'emes amru* — in truth they said — the *mishnah* adds a further distinction. *Yimei hazav v'hazavah* — the days in which a man is a *zav* or a woman is a *zavah* — and *yimei hesgeiro shel metzora* — the days of the first week of a *metzora's* quarantine, before a definitive diagnosis — not only do not trigger *megaleach*, they can actually count positively toward the *nazir's* total count of days. Since none of these constitute *tumat meis*, they do not prevent *nezirut* days from accumulating.

One might think this is obvious — what *tumah* other than *tumat meis* would interrupt *nezirut*? The real *chiddush* is what this implies by contrast with the first case. The *mishnah* contrasting these lighter cases with the case of the *metzora* in *yimei gmaro* or *yimei seforo* reveals something important: even for the heavier *metzora*, it is not *tumat meis* that prevents counting — it is the *tzaraas* state itself. The *nazir* in that state cannot count those days toward his *nezirut*, and must wait until he exits the *metzora* status entirely before resuming. The reason is not yet fully explained by the *gemara* and will require further examination.

### Sakkot & Peraot

The *gemara* now defines the terms *sakkot* and *peraot* from the *mishnah*. *Sakkot* are trees that overhang the ground — *ilan hamaysach al ha'aretz*. *Peravot* are stones protruding from a wall — *avanim hayotzos min hageder* — adjacent to a cemetery. Walking under either constitutes only a rabbinic *tumah*, and therefore a *nazir* is not *megaleach* for either.

### Sakkot Non-Ohel

*Tosafot* explains, citing *Perek Kama d'Niddah*, that a tree is not a valid *ohel* from a *de'oraita* perspective because the branches are spread apart and do not constitute a solid *tefach* of coverage. The leaves and branches vary in density, and there is no reliable *tefach-by-tefach* roof. Even if there is certainly a *kezayit min hamet* buried beneath one of these trees, one who walks under it is *tahor mi-de'oraita*. Even walking under all of them would not create *de'oraita* liability, because one was never under a proper *ohel*. The rabbinic decree imposes *tumah* on one who passes beneath such trees, but since it is rabbinic, *nazir* is not *megaleach*.

### Peraot Rabbinic

The case of *peraot* is different in its rationale. A stone overhang can in principle constitute a proper *ohel* — that is not the issue. The issue is uncertainty about whether there is a *meis* beneath any given stone. *Tosafot* explains: this is a wall adjacent to a cemetery, and there may be a *nefel* — an infant who did not survive — buried beneath one of the protruding stones. The scenario of a protruding stone above a cemetery wall raises the question of how the *tumah* passes around or through the wall to the other side, which is why the case is framed in terms of a burial near or beneath the stone itself rather than across from a grave. In any case, one does not know with certainty whether there is a *meis* beneath the specific stone under which one walks. This is *sefeik tumah b'reshut harabbim* — a doubtful *tumah* in a public domain — which the rule of the *Torah* renders *tahor*. It is only by rabbinic decree that one is considered *tamei* for passing beneath such a stone. Since the *tumah* is rabbinic, *nazir* is not *megaleach*.

The distinction between the two cases is thus: by *sakkot*, the *ohel* itself is not a valid *de'oraita ohel* — the branches are insufficiently solid. By *peraot*, the *ohel* is potentially valid, but there is *sefeik* regarding the existence of a *meis* beneath it. In both cases the result is the same — only rabbinic *tumah*, and therefore no *nazir megaleach*.

---

---

# Nazir 54b

## Mishna Review

### Opening

We begin on 54b, five lines down in the *Gemara*. The *Mishnah* presented a list of categories of *tumah* for which a *Nazir* is not *megale'ach* — does not shave his head, does not lose the earlier days of his *nezirus*, and does not bring a *korban*. Some of these exclusions apply because the *tumah* in question is only *d'rabbanan*; others apply even to *tumah* that is nominally *d'oraisa*, such as *tumas meis*, but that nevertheless fall outside the category that triggers *nazir megale'ach*. An important parallel principle, found not in our *Gemara* but in *Masechet Smachot*, states that whatever does not cause a *Nazir* to shave also does not fall within the prohibitions incumbent upon a *Kohen* — a point of great significance to which we will return.

### Categories Overview

The *Mishnah*'s list of exclusions from *nazir megale'ach* divides into two broad categories. The first consists of cases where there is no doubt that *tumah* is present, but the mechanism by which it is transmitted is only *d'rabbanan*. The second consists of cases where the *tumah* itself may be *d'oraisa* in origin but is nonetheless excluded from the operative category. The upcoming discussion focuses primarily on the first type: cases where a genuine dead body may well be present, but the manner of transmission does not rise to the biblical standard.

### Trees & Walls

Two examples of rabbinically-based *tumah* appear in the *Mishnah*: overhanging trees and outcropping walls. In the case of the trees — most plausibly trees growing over a cemetery — *Tosafot* explains that while there is indeed a corpse buried underneath, the branches and leaves in any given span do not constitute a *tefach* by *tefach* surface and therefore cannot form a *d'oraisa ohel*. In the case of the outcropping stone walls, the scenario involves something buried on the outside of the cemetery wall — sometimes fetuses, buried there due to uncertainty about their status. Because the burial is uncertain, the *tumah* is a *safek tumah b'reshut harabbim*, and the person remains biblically *tahor*. Both cases thus represent categories where the *Nazir* does not shave, and where — by the parallel principle of *Masechet Smachot* — the *Kohen* is not formally prohibited.

---

## Beis Hapras

### Intro

We now take up a new category in the *Mishnah*'s list: *beis hapras* and *eretz ha'amim*. *Beis hapras* refers to a field through which a grave was accidentally plowed, scattering fragments of bone throughout. Biblically, there would ordinarily be no sufficient basis for *tumah* without actual contact with the bone itself, but rabbinically one may not walk through such a field. The *Gemara* gives this only brief treatment here; it is *eretz ha'amim* — the lands outside of *Eretz Yisrael*, which are deemed *tamei* — that will occupy the bulk of our discussion.

### Air vs. Ground

The *Gemara* poses a pointed question about the nature of *tumas eretz ha'amim*: *eretz ha'amim ibaya lehu* — they raise the question: *mishum avira gazru aleha* — was the decree directed at the airspace itself? Or *mishum gusha gazru aleha* — was it directed at the ground?

To understand the stakes: if the concern is the ground (*gusha*), then the *tumah* operates within the standard framework of *tumas meis* and *ohel*. Just as one who stands over a corpse is *tamei* by virtue of being in the same *ohel*, so too one who walks or stands over the ground of *eretz ha'amim* would be *tamei* if we assume the ground harbors the dead. Critically, however, if one were inside a structure or on an elevated platform that effectively forms an *ohel* between oneself and the ground, one would be protected — the floor below serving as an *ohel* separating the person from whatever lies beneath.

### Avira & Gusha

*Avira*, by contrast, means that even this protection is unavailing. Even if one is entirely shielded from what is beneath — sealed above an *ohel*, standing on the second floor of a building — one remains *tamei* by virtue of being within the airspace of *eretz ha'amim*. There are, after all, no dead bodies floating in the air; there is no physical rationale for *tumas avira*. This observation itself points toward something important about the nature of this decree: it cannot be explained as a straightforward extension of ordinary *tumas meis* and *ohel*. It must be motivated by something else.

---

## Tosafot Airspace

### Transport Cases

*Tosafot* introduces precisely the cases the *Gemara* will shortly bring: *k'gon mahalach b'shidah tevah u'migdal* — one who is transported through *eretz ha'amim* inside a large box, wagon, or tower. The box must be larger than forty *se'ah* — the size of a *mikveh* — because below that volume it qualifies as a *kli*, a vessel, and as a vessel it could not serve as an *ohel* and would itself be susceptible to *tumah*. Assume instead a massive box, like the crate a large appliance comes in, with an open top. If you are standing inside it, elevated on a platform within it, then the floor of the box constitutes an *ohel* between you and the ground of *eretz ha'amim*. You should, by normal *ohel* logic, be protected. Similarly, if you travel through *eretz ha'amim* by wagon or boat, the structure of the vessel stands between you and the ground.

### Stricter Rules

Yet *Tosafot* states: *she'hechmiru vo yoter mib'ohel hameis* — the Sages were more strict regarding the airspace of *eretz ha'amim* than the ordinary rules of *ohel* and corpse-*tumah* would require. Even though one is above an *ohel* that would normally be fully protective, the mere fact of being within the airspace renders one *tamei*. This is a stringency that has no parallel in standard *halachot* of *tumah*.

### Policy Rationale

The key phrase in *Tosafot* is: *shelo yeitzei me'eretz l'chutz la'aretz* — so that people should not leave *Eretz Yisrael* for *chutz la'aretz*. This is a remarkable statement. The *tumah* of *eretz ha'amim* is not grounded in a practical concern about contact with the dead. It is a policy instrument — an application of *halacha* as a form of social legislation designed to discourage emigration from *Eretz Yisrael*. The immediate practical effect falls most heavily on *Kohanim*, for whom *tumah* carries formal prohibitions, but the designation of the outside world as *eretz tmei'ah* presumably carries a broader cultural weight as well, reinforcing the attitude that *chutz la'aretz* is categorically inferior — a place one should not wish to inhabit.

There is already a separate prohibition, *assur latzeit me'eretz Yisrael l'chutz la'aretz*, applicable to all Jews. One might ask: is that not sufficient? Perhaps. But *Kohanim*, it seems, were especially responsive to the framework of *tumah v'taharah*, and the designation of *eretz ha'amim* as *tamei* would have had particular force for them. Beyond the formal prohibition, the very label of *eretz tmei'ah* shapes how one relates to the outside world. This stands in interesting tension with the recognition — which we noted based on a student's observation — that *Eretz Yisrael* itself has, through the millennia of invasion and massacre, become saturated with the dead. Every building project today in Israel uncovers old graves. That irony only reinforces the conclusion that the fundamental motivation of *tumas eretz ha'amim* must be this *kedei shelo yeitzu* rationale, whatever form it ultimately takes in *halachic* application.

---

## Gusha Alternative

### Dead Bodies

*Tosafot* also considers the *gusha* position: that the decree operates only through the ground and the normal laws of *ohel*, without the additional stringency of *avira*. On this reading, one would be *tamei* by walking over or being within a normal *ohel* relationship with the ground of *eretz ha'amim*, but protected if one stands above an *ohel* that intervenes. The question is what bodies would ground this *gusha*-based *tumah*. *Tosafot* offers two answers: *mipnei metei mabul* — because of the dead of the Flood, who, according to certain *gemarot*, were swept into *Bavel* (identified with *Shin'ar*) and are buried beneath its ground; and *mipnei rov Yisrael shenehergu b'chutz la'aretz* — because the majority of Jews who were killed throughout history died outside of *Eretz Yisrael*.

### Practical Issues

Both answers face serious difficulties. The *mabul* dead were not Jewish, and the standard ruling is that only Jewish corpses convey *tumas ohel*. One might argue that the first answer assumes we rule that non-Jews also convey *tumas ohel* — but that is far from settled. Moreover, *Bavel* is not all of *chutz la'aretz*. As for the second answer: even granting the tragic historical claim that many Jews perished outside of *Eretz Yisrael*, the major mass deaths of the *Beis HaMikdash* period occurred predominantly within *Eretz Yisrael* itself. There is no clear empirical basis for assuming that Jewish dead are uniformly distributed throughout *chutz la'aretz* in quantities sufficient to ground a *gusha*-based *tumah* with the force of *tumas ohel*. Rightly understood, even the *gusha* account does not rest on solid physical reasoning — it cannot be a straightforward application of ordinary *tumah* law.

### Policy Underlying

This is why *Tosafot*'s policy rationale — *kedei shelo yeitzu* — is likely the underlying motivating force regardless of which account one adopts. The question between *avira* and *gusha* is then not whether the decree is policy-driven, but rather how far the Sages extended it: did they apply ordinary *tumas ohel* logic with the ground as the source (*gusha*), or did they go further and declare the very airspace *tamei* even when one is otherwise protected by an *ohel* (*avira*)? Both represent departures from purely physical *tumah* reasoning; *avira* simply departs further.

---

## Nazir-Kohen Link

### Principle

At this point the broader principle connecting *nazir megale'ach* and *kohen muzhar* comes into focus. The principle, as formulated in *Masechet Makkos* and echoed here, is: *kol tumah she'ein ha'nazir megale'ach aleha, ein ha'kohen muzhar aleha* — any *tumah* that does not cause a *Nazir* to shave does not trigger the formal biblical prohibition for a *Kohen*. This linkage is structurally important: it means that the entire question of what constitutes operationally significant *tumah* — the *tumah* that the Torah treats as the most serious kind — is defined by the *Nazir*'s shaving requirement.

### Application

The application to *eretz ha'amim* and *beis hapras* follows directly. Because these are *d'rabbanan* forms of *tumah* that do not cause a *Nazir* to shave, a *Kohen* entering *eretz ha'amim* or *beis hapras* does not incur *malkus d'oraisa* and is not in violation of a biblical prohibition. There remain *issurei d'rabbanan* — the rabbinic prohibitions are real — but the *Kohen* is not *muzhar* in the full biblical sense, does not receive lashes, and is not subject to a *d'oraisa issur*. This distinction between the biblical and rabbinic levels of prohibition will prove critical in the discussions that follow.

---

## Gemara Resolution

### Sprinkling Proof

The *Gemara* now attempts to resolve the *avira*-versus-*gusha* question from a ruling found in the *Mishnah* itself: *u'mazei bashlishi uvashvi'i* — one who entered *eretz ha'amim* must be sprinkled with the purification waters of the *parah adumah* on days three and seven of the purification process. The *Gemara* reasons: *v'ei amart mishum avira* — if the *tumah* is based purely on the airspace, then this is a novel, free-standing form of *tumah* with no basis in the framework of *tumas meis*. If it is not grounded in *tumas meis*, there is no logical basis for applying the *haza'ah* on *shlishi v'shvii* — the sprinkling cycle is inherently part of the *tumas meis* purification process. On the *avira* account, the Sages invented a new *tumah*; they cannot then borrow the ritual mechanics of an entirely different *tumah* to define its purification.

### Conclusion

The *Gemara* initially appears to conclude that the sprinkling requirement points to *gusha* — the *tumah* operates within the *tumas meis* framework, and therefore the standard purification ritual applies. But the *Gemara* immediately rejects this inference: *le'olam eima lach mishum avira* — one can still say it is *avira*-based. The sprinkling mentioned in the *Mishnah* does not apply to every item on the list. The *Mishnah* mentions *shlishi v'shvii* with respect to some categories, such as *sechachos*, *pera'os*, and *beis hapras*, which are extensions of *tumas meis* and therefore appropriately purified through *haza'ah*. But other items on the list — *metzora* being the clearest example, since the *parah adumah* sprinkling is obviously irrelevant to *tzara'as* — are not subject to *shlishi v'shvii*. On the *avira* reading, *eretz ha'amim* falls into the second category: it is a distinct *tumah* to which *shlishi v'shvii* does not apply.

The *Gemara* then adds that this conclusion is supported by another consideration: *mideka tanni v'keilim hanog'im b'meis* — the *Mishnah* also includes vessels that touched a dead body among the categories for which a *Nazir* does not shave. *Hani keilim benei haza'ah nin?* — Are such vessels subject to sprinkling on days three and seven? Clearly not, in the *Gemara*'s assumption. This demonstrates that the *Mishnah*'s mention of *shlishi v'shvii* cannot be read as applying to every item enumerated. Therefore, *eretz ha'amim*'s exemption from *shlishi v'shvii* is consistent with the *avira* interpretation and does not refute it.

---

## Cherev Ke'Chalal

### Vessels Assumption

This raises a significant question. The *Gemara* assumes without explanation that *keilim* that touched a dead body would not require *shlishi v'shvii* sprinkling. Let us examine why. Under ordinary *halachot* of *tumah*, a vessel that touches a *meis* becomes an *av hatumah*. A person who then touches that vessel becomes a *rishon l'tumah* — a first-level derivative — and is *tamei* for only one day. The one-day *tumah* has no connection to the seven-day purification process and *shlishi v'shvii*; those apply only to *tumas shivah*, the full seven-day *tumah* associated with direct contact with a corpse or its equivalent. So if we are talking about ordinary vessels, the logic is clear: no *shlishi v'shvii*. But then a different question arises: if it is such a routine form of *tumah*, why does the *Mishnah* bother mentioning it at all?

### Tosafot Question

This is precisely *Tosafot*'s question. *Tosafot* asks: *v'im tomar* — why not read the *Mishnah* as referring to metal vessels under the principle of *cherev harei hu k'chalal* — a sword is like a corpse? Under *cherev k'chalal*, a metal vessel that was in contact with a corpse is treated as if it were the corpse itself — an *av hatumah* in the fullest sense. Anyone who touches it becomes *tamei* with a seven-day *tumah* and requires *shlishi v'shvii* sprinkling. If that is the *Mishnah*'s intent, then two things follow: first, it is a genuine *chiddush* worthy of mention, and second, the person *would* require *shlishi v'shvii*, so the *Mishnah*'s reference to sprinkling would apply here too, undercutting the *Gemara*'s proof.

Why, then, does the *Gemara* assume the *Mishnah* is not talking about metal vessels under *cherev k'chalal*?

### Rabbeinu Tam

*Rabbeinu Tam*'s answer is direct: *de'al karchach lo miktamah masnisin b'klei matechos* — the *Mishnah* cannot be speaking of metal vessels under *cherev k'chalal*, because *de'im kein hanazir megale'ach, d'cherev harei hu k'chalal* — if it were, the *Nazir* would be *megale'ach*. If the vessel is treated like the corpse itself and the *Nazir* who touches it is thereby *tamei tumas shivah*, there is no known *Gemara* that exempts such a *Nazir* from shaving. *Rabbeinu Tam*'s position is that *cherev k'chalal* would indeed trigger *nazir megale'ach*, and therefore the *Mishnah*, which teaches that the *Nazir* does *not* shave for *keilim hanog'im b'meis*, cannot be discussing *cherev k'chalal* at all. The *Mishnah* must be speaking of ordinary vessels under ordinary *tumah* rules.

---

## Rabbeinu Chaim

### House Metaphor

*Tosafot* then records the famous exchange between *Rabbeinu Tam* and *Rabbeinu Chaim HaKohen*. *Rabbeinu Chaim* sent *Rabbeinu Tam* a letter, opening with the verse *aizeh bayis asher tivnu li, v'aizeh makom menuchati* — "What house can you build for Me, and what place shall be My resting place?" — invoking the divine rhetorical question to pose one of his own: he is a *Kohen*, and *Rabbeinu Tam* is telling him that any metal vessel that was ever in a house with a *meis* is now itself like the *meis* — and the *Kohen* is biblically prohibited from being in the same space as it. *Aizeh bayis asher tivnu li* — what house can you build for me in which I could ever live?

### Metal Problem

The argument is a *reductio ad absurdum*. *Rabbeinu Chaim* invokes the principle *kol tumah she'hanazir megale'ach aleha kohen muzhar aleha* — everything that requires *nazir megale'ach* also triggers the *Kohen*'s prohibition. He observes: *v'ein lecha bayis she'ein bo shum klei machos she'hayah b'ohel hameis o shum masmer* — there is no house that does not contain some metal vessel or nail that was at some point under the same *ohel* as a dead body. In the Middle Ages nails were not manufactured fresh from a factory; they were reused from house to house, passed through markets, carried across generations. Any such nail, if *cherev k'chalal* applied in full force, would render the *Kohen* biblically prohibited from entering any ordinary home. The implication is patently impossible as a practical matter.

### Conclusion

*Rabbeinu Chaim HaKohen* therefore concludes that even metal vessels — even when *cherev k'chalal* applies and the person who touches them is *tamei tumas shivah* — do not cause a *Nazir* to shave and do not trigger the formal biblical prohibition for a *Kohen*. This is what the *Mishnah* is teaching when it lists *keilim hanog'im b'meis* among the cases where a *Nazir* does not shave: the *chiddush* is specifically about metal vessels under *cherev k'chalal*, and the ruling is that even there, the *Nazir* is not *megale'ach* and the *Kohen* is not *muzhar*. This position represents the accepted *halacha*.

---

## Rambam Position

### All Vessels

The *Rambam* takes the discussion in a striking direction. Not only does he affirm *cherev k'chalal*, but he extends its scope beyond metal vessels. In *Hilchos Tumas Meis* 5:3, he writes: *keilim she'nitme'u b'meis bein b'maga bein b'ohel, harei hanogei'a bahen k'nogei'a b'meis atzmo* — vessels that became *tamei* through a corpse, whether through direct contact or through *ohel*, render one who touches them as if one had touched the corpse itself. Just as a corpse conveys seven-day *tumah* whether to a person or to vessels, so too do vessels that became *tamei* through the corpse — whoever or whatever subsequently touches them is *tamei tumas shivah*.

### Derivation

And the *Rambam* derives this not only from tradition (*mi'pi hashmu'ah*) but from a novel reading of the verse. He asks: *v'chi ya'aleh al da'atcha* — would it enter your mind that someone who killed another person would be *tamei* for seven days even if he had no physical contact with the body? Surely the verse *kol horeg nefesh* cannot mean one who shot an arrow from a distance. It must refer to killing with a sword — *horeg nefesh b'cherev* — in which case the verse teaches that the sword itself becomes like the corpse, and its bearer is *tamei tumas shivah* through the contact with the sword. From there the *Rambam* derives that all vessels that touched a *meis* — *bein klei matechos, bein klei shetef uvgadim*, whether metal, cloth, or other materials — share this status.

### Three Positions

The discussion thus yields three distinct positions. The first restricts *cherev k'chalal* to metal vessels (*klei matechos*) and holds that touching them creates *tumas shivah*; the question then is what follows for a *Nazir* and a *Kohen*. The second position — *Rabbeinu Tam*'s, which is rejected *l'halacha* — holds that if *cherev k'chalal* applies to metal vessels, the *Nazir* is *megale'ach* and the *Kohen* is *muzhar*; therefore the *Mishnah* cannot be speaking of metal at all. The third position — *Rabbeinu Chaim HaKohen*'s, representing the accepted ruling — holds that *cherev k'chalal* does apply to metal vessels and does create *tumas shivah*, but the *Nazir* does not shave and the *Kohen* is not *muzhar* even for metal. And the *Rambam* goes furthest of all: *cherev k'chalal* applies to all vessels regardless of material, but here too the *Nazir* does not shave. The *Rambam*'s additional ruling — that even the obligation of *shlishi v'shvii* sprinkling does not apply to a *Nazir* in this case, despite the seven-day *tumah* — is, frankly, a striking *halacha* that demands further attention of its own.

The common thread across all positions that have halachic standing is the impossibility of the alternative. If touching any vessel or any metal vessel ever in contact with a *meis* were to impose biblical prohibitions on *Kohanim* with the full force of *tumas meis*, no *Kohen* could function in ordinary life. The *reductio ad absurdum* of *Rabbeinu Chaim HaKohen* — what house can you build for me? — captures the underlying principle: *halacha* cannot be read in a way that makes normative life for a *Kohen* simply impossible.

---

## Tannaitic Debate

### Box Case

The *Gemara* now proposes to resolve the underlying *avira*-versus-*gusha* question by reference to a *tannaitic* dispute: *lema katannai* — let us say this is a debate among *Tanna'im*. The case is: *haniknas l'eretz ha'amim b'shidah tevah u'migdal* — one who enters *eretz ha'amim* while enclosed in a large box, crate, or tower. *Rabbi* (Judah HaNasi) says he is *tamei*; *Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda* says he is *tahor*. On its face, this looks like an exact parallel to the *avira*-versus-*gusha* question. The box, as we have noted, would constitute an *ohel* between the person and the ground. If one holds *gusha*, the person should be protected and *tahor*. If one holds *avira*, the open-topped box leaves the person exposed to the airspace and *tamei*. *Rabbi*'s position that he is *tamei* would thus reflect *avira*, and *Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda*'s position that he is *tahor* would reflect *gusha*.

### Initial Interpretation

This is the straightforward reading — *mai lav*, the *Gemara* asks, is *Rabbi* not holding *mishum avira*, and *Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda* holding *mishum gusha*? If so, we have our resolution: the *tannaitic* debate maps directly onto the *avira*-versus-*gusha* question, and the debate remains unresolved at the *tannaitic* level. But the *Gemara* does not rest with this.

### Ohel Zaruk

*De'chulei alma mishum gusha* — the *Gemara* proposes that in fact both *Tanna'im* agree the issue is the ground, not the airspace. The disagreement is instead about whether the box, which is being transported, constitutes a valid *ohel*. A moving *ohel* — one that is being carried rather than standing stationary — is called an *ohel zaruk*, a "thrown" or "projected" *ohel*. The question is: *mar savar ohel zaruk shemei ohel u'mar savar lo shemei ohel* — one *Tanna* holds that a moving structure constitutes a valid *ohel* and therefore protects the person inside; the other holds it does not. On this reading, the dispute is not about the source of *tumas eretz ha'amim* at all, but about a general principle in *hilchos ohel* — one that has implications far beyond *eretz ha'amim*, including, as was noted, the question of aircraft today.

A *baraita* is then cited in which *Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda* himself teaches that if a box filled with *keilim* is thrown in front of a *meis* so that it flies over it as an *ohel*, the *keilim* inside are *tamei* — because the flying box does not constitute an *ohel*. If the same box were stationary, suspended on poles above the *meis*, the *keilim* inside would be *tahor*, because then it is a genuine *ohel*. This *baraita* appears to demonstrate that *Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda* himself holds *ohel zaruk lo shemei ohel* — and that would seemingly contradict his position that the person in the transported box in *eretz ha'amim* is *tahor*.

*Tosafot* resolves this by distinguishing between degrees of *zaruk*. A box that is literally thrown through the air — or a *talis* flapping in the wind with no support from the ground — is a classic *ohel zaruk* and is *lo shemei ohel* by everyone's agreement. A box being carried by bearers who stand on the ground is a more ambiguous case: it is moving, and thus not fully stationary, but it is anchored to the ground through the bodies of those carrying it. The debate between *Rabbi* and *Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda* may then concern precisely this intermediate case of a transported, but ground-anchored, box — not the extreme case of a box in free flight.

---

## Transport Baraita

### Status Problem

The *Gemara* then advances to a third possible framework for the debate, and before presenting the *baraita* that supports it, it is worth flagging a conceptual difficulty in the second framework (the *lo shechiach* account). The principle *davar lo shchiach lo gazru beih rabbanan* — that the Sages did not apply a rabbinic decree to unusual, rare cases — is a rule about prohibiting *actions*. When the Sages prohibit a category of conduct, they intend their prohibition for the normal range of cases; if a situation is so unusual that it was simply not contemplated, the prohibition may not apply. But applying this principle to the *status* of *tumas avira* is conceptually jarring. If the Sages declared the airspace of *eretz ha'amim* to be *tamei*, that is a categorical assignment of *tumah* to a space — it is not a prohibition of a particular action. To then say that one can be within that airspace through an unusual method and thereby escape the *tumah* is a strange application of the *lo shechiach* principle: it is not prohibiting a rare action, it is selectively withdrawing a status based on the rarity of the method of contact.

### Transport Types

The *baraita* reads: *haniknas l'eretz ha'amim b'shidah tevah u'migdal, tahor* — one who enters *eretz ha'amim* in a box or tower is *tahor*. *U'vakaron u'visfinah u'veis'karya, tamei* — but one who enters by wagon, boat, or *eis'karya* (apparently the mast or rigging of a ship) is *tamei*. The distinction the *baraita* draws between these two groups is the central question.

### Normalcy Test

One might initially think the difference relates to *ohel* status — perhaps a wagon or boat does not constitute an *ohel* while the box does. But this analysis does not hold. Both a box and a wagon can provide the same physical separation from the ground. Both can, in principle, be analyzed under the *ohel zaruk* framework. The only consistent difference between the two groups is the normalcy of the mode of transport. How does one normally enter *eretz ha'amim*? By wagon, by boat, by ship. These are the standard means of travel. Being carried through *eretz ha'amim* enclosed in a large box is by contrast an entirely unusual scenario. The *baraita*'s distinction, then, supports the interpretation that the *tumah* is *avira*-based, but was decreed only for normal modes of entry into the airspace — not for the unusual case of the box.

---

## Leaning Theory

### Presumption

The *Gemara* offers yet a third possibility: *ve'iba'it eima, hacha shema yotzi rosho verubo lesham pligi* — if you wish, say that the debate concerns a different issue altogether. On this reading, everyone agrees that *eretz ha'amim*'s *tumah* is *gusha*-based, and everyone agrees that the box constitutes an *ohel* that would normally protect its occupant. Nevertheless, one might say the person in the box is *tamei* because of a presumption that he will lean out — that he will extend his head or the majority of his body outside the box, at which point even the *gusha*-based *tumah* would reach him through normal *ohel* logic. The *Hachamim* who rule him *tamei* immediately may be acting on this presumption: we are sufficiently confident he will lean out that we treat him as *tamei* from the outset.

### Yosei Position

*Tosafot* brings a *baraita* in which *Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda* explicitly addresses this: *hanichnas l'eretz ha'amim b'shidah tevah u'migdal tahor, ad sheyotzi lesham rosho o rubo* — one who enters in a box is *tahor* until he actually extends his head or the majority of his body outside, at which point he becomes *tamei*. This formulation strongly suggests that the operative concern is indeed the act of leaning out, and that *Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda* refuses to presume it in advance — he requires it to actually occur. The *Hachamim* who rule *tamei* immediately presumably accept the presumption and act on it preemptively.

One might ask: if this is really about *gusha* and *ohel* logic, why does it require specifically *rosho verubo* — the head or majority of the body — to trigger *tumah*? Even a small part of the body extending beyond the *ohel* might seem sufficient. The *Gemara* does not fully resolve this tension, and it remains a difficulty with the *gusha*-leaning interpretation.

### Summary

We thus have a range of interpretive possibilities for the *tannaitic* debate and for the underlying question of *tumas eretz ha'amim*. The first possibility: the debate is directly about *avira* versus *gusha* — *Rabbi* holds *avira* and therefore rules the person in the box *tamei* despite the *ohel*, while *Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda* holds *gusha* and rules him *tahor* because the *ohel* protects him. The second possibility: both agree the issue is *gusha*, but disagree whether the transported box constitutes an *ohel zaruk* that fails to protect. The third, supported by the *baraita* about wagon, boat, and mast: both agree the issue is *avira*, but the decree applies only to normal modes of entry — the box is too unusual a method to have been included. The fourth: both agree the issue is *gusha* and the box is a valid *ohel*, but one *Tanna* presumes the occupant will lean out and rules him *tamei* preemptively, while the other requires the leaning to actually occur. Each of these frameworks carries different implications for how broadly or narrowly *tumas eretz ha'amim* applies — and each illuminates a different dimension of what the Sages were trying to accomplish with this remarkable decree.

---

---

# Nazir 55

## Metzora Stages

### Mishnah Overview

The *daf* opens at the bottom of 55a, five lines from the bottom, with the words *umatchil umoneh*. The *mishnah* presents two halachic situations involving a *nazir* whose days do not count toward his *nezirut*. The first concerns someone who is *tamei tumas meis* only *derabbanan* — or subject to one of those forms of *tumas meis* that does not require the *nazir* to shave, such as *golel*, *dofek*, or *kelim* — and the second concerns a *metzora* who is in the process of becoming *tahor*. In both cases, the earlier days of *nezirut* are not destroyed, but the days during the period of *tumah* do not count toward the *nezirut*. This makes sense for *tumas meis*, since *tumah* of that kind is fundamentally antithetical to *nezirut*. The *mishnah*'s inclusion of the *metzora* requires elaboration.

### Three Metzora Stages

There are three stages a *metzora* passes through, and it is important to understand each one clearly.

A person develops a suspicious mark and must present himself to a *kohen*. The *kohen* examines the mark and, if uncertain, declares a waiting period of one week. During this week the person is called a *musgar* — quarantined, under observation — and is considered *tamei* with a full level of *tumah*. At the end of the week, the *kohen* returns. If the mark has cleared, the person simply immerses in a *mikveh* and is *tahor*; he does not become *tamei* retroactively. If the mark has not cleared, the *kohen* declares him a *muchlat* — a definite, fully confirmed *metzora*. The word *muchlat* conveys absoluteness, in contrast to the tentative status of *musgar*. Once declared *muchlat*, the person remains in this state indefinitely, until the mark clears.

### Tahara Ritual

Once the mark clears, the *kohen* comes and examines the *metzora* and confirms the healing: *vehineh nirpah nega hatzara'as min hatzarua*. At that point an elaborate *tahara* process begins. Two birds are taken, one is slaughtered over a clay vessel containing spring water, and the living bird together with cedar wood, crimson thread, and hyssop is dipped in the blood and water and used to sprinkle the *metzora* seven times. The *metzora* then launders his garments, shaves all his hair — *kol se'aro*, not only the hair of the head but all bodily hair — immerses in water, and returns to the camp. At this point, however, the process is not yet complete.

### Gamro vs. Sipro

The period during which the *metzora* is *muchlat* — that is, the indefinite quarantine from the time he is declared a confirmed *metzora* until the mark clears — is called *yemei gamro*. The stage that follows the initial *tahara* ritual is called *yemei sipro*, the seven-day counting period. During *yemei sipro*, the *metzora* dwells outside his tent but inside the camp. After those seven days, he shaves all his hair a second time, launders his garments, and immerses. Only then is he ready for the final stage.

### Final Purification

On the eighth day following *yemei sipro*, the *metzora* brings a *korban*. The Torah specifies: *uv'yom hashemini yikach shtei torim o shenei venei yona* — two doves or two pigeons — along with additional offerings, completing the *tahara* process.

To summarize the full arc: first, the *musgar* stage, an uncertain quarantine; if confirmed, the *muchlat* period (*yemei gamro*), indefinite until the mark clears; then the *tahara* ritual of birds, sprinkling, first shaving, and return to the camp; then *yemei sipro*, seven days of counting; then a second shaving, immersion, and finally the *korban*. Our *mishnah* stated that during *yemei gamro* and *yemei sipro*, the days do not count toward the *nazir*'s *nezirut*, though they do not destroy the earlier days either.

---

## Rav Chisda's View

### Short vs. Long

The *Gemara* opens with a statement of Rav Chisda: *lo shanu ela bi'nezirut mu'etet* — the *mishnah*'s ruling that the days of *yemei gamro* and *yemei sipro* do not count toward the *nezirut* applies only to a short *nezirut*. But *aval bi'nezirut merubah masak nami salikan* — in the case of a long *nezirut*, those days do indeed count.

### Hair Growth Logic

What lies behind this distinction? Rav Chisda's actual position is that fundamentally those days *do* count. After all, a *metzora* is not *tamei meis* — why should his status affect the counting of *nezirut*? The reason the *mishnah* says they don't count is not a matter of principle but of practical necessity: the *nazir* will always require thirty days of *gidul se'ar* — hair growth — before his *nezirut* can conclude, and the *metzora* process requires shaving twice, leaving him with no hair. So if a *nazir* had completed five days of a thirty-day *nezirut* and then became a *metzora*, there is no point in saying those middle days count, because no matter how many days he had banked, he will need a full thirty days of hair growth after the shaving. In practice, therefore, saying the days count would never help him — it is effectively as though they do not count.

However, in a *nezirut merubah* — a long *nezirut*, say of one hundred days or, as the *Gemara* will illustrate, fifty days — the situation differs. Suppose the *nazir* had completed twenty days before becoming a *metzora*, and the entire *metzora* process takes another fifteen days or so. He will then have thirty days remaining anyway, providing the required *gidul se'ar*. In such a case, those middle days can in principle count, since there is no practical obstacle. This is what Rav Chisda means: the real *halacha* is that the days count; the *mishnah*'s ruling that they do not applies only where, practically speaking, it makes no difference.

### Rav Sharvaya's Challenge

Rav Sharvaya challenges this. He points to the language of the *mishnah* itself: *nitdakah lo manin miyad* — as soon as he becomes *tahor* he begins counting immediately. This phrasing implies that he does not lose his earlier days. But if Rav Chisda's reasoning is merely about the practical need for thirty days of hair growth, then in the case of a short *nezirut*, the *metzora* would not merely fail to count his middle days — he would actually lose his earlier days as well, because he is going to need a full thirty days regardless. The *mishnah*, however, says the earlier days are not lost.

Consequently, the *mishnah* must be speaking of a case where those earlier days are genuinely preserved — which means it cannot be speaking of a simple thirty-day *nezirut*. It must be speaking of a long *nezirut*. And even so — even in that long *nezirut* — the *mishnah* says the middle days do not count. This directly contradicts Rav Chisda, who said they do count in a long *nezirut*.

---

## Fifty-Day Case

### Hypothetical Scenario

Rav Chisda attempts to resolve this. He responds: *hu mative lah ve-hu mefarek lah* — he raises the objection and he answers it himself. The *mishnah*, he suggests, is describing a fifty-day *nezirut*. The *nazir* completed twenty days before becoming a *metzora*, then went through the shaving process, and afterward would do another thirty days — *de-nazir de-it lei gidul se'ar*. In this configuration, Rav Chisda can maintain his position: the earlier twenty days are not lost (which is why the *mishnah* says he starts counting immediately), and yet the middle days do not count — not as a matter of principle, but because they would not help him anyway, since he still needs thirty days at the end. The *mishnah* thus describes a case where the days are neither *soter* (destroying earlier days) nor *oleh* (counting toward the total), but only because of the *gidul se'ar* requirement.

### Real Halacha Problem

The problem with this approach is that it requires an oddly narrow reading of the *mishnah*, tailored specifically to a fifty-day *nezirut*. More importantly, Rav Chisda's assertion is that fundamentally the days *are* counted toward the *nezirut* — it is only the practical constraint of *gidul se'ar* that prevents them from helping. But the *Gemara* is about to demonstrate from a *baraita* and from a complex case involving double uncertainty that fundamentally *ein olim lo* — those days simply do not count, irrespective of whether the *nazir* will or will not have enough days of hair growth at the end.

---

## Safek Double Status

### Case Setup

The *Gemara* introduces a striking case: *nazir shehayah tamei besafek umuchlat besafek* — a *nazir* who may have contracted *tumas meis* (in the manner that would require shaving and nullify earlier days), and who may also be a *muchlat metzora*. These two conditions of uncertainty overlap, creating a complex halachic problem.

### Safek Resolution

The *rishonim* note a conceptual difficulty: can one be a *muchlat* in a state of *safek*? *Tzara'at* is unique in that a person only acquires the status of *metzora* through the ruling of a *kohen*. The *kohen* examines the mark and either declares the person *tamei* or *tahor*.
