There are prescribed rules governing how the *kohen* rules in cases of doubt, but once those rules are applied, the person's status is definite. So there is no true *safek muchlat* in the ordinary sense. The *rishonim* understand the case as involving, for example, uncertainty about whether the *kohen* who ruled was a valid *kohen* — some suggest the *kohen* may have been a *safek challal* — or some other meta-level doubt about the validity of the ruling itself.

### Timeline: 60 & 120 Days

The *halacha* in this double-*safek* case is: *ochel be-kodashim le-achar shishim yom* — he may eat *kodashim* after sixty days; *ve-shoseh yayin u-mitamei le-meitim le-achar me'ah ve-esrim yom* — he may drink wine and contract *tumas meis* (that is, he may complete and conclude his *nezirut*) after one hundred and twenty days. These numbers require explanation.

First, note that the sixty-day threshold is about removing any doubt of *metzora* status, since a *metzora* cannot eat *kodashim*. Being *tahor* of *tumas meis* is a separate matter — the sprinkling on days three and seven of the *parah adumah* ashes resolves that. A *nazir tamei* who has completed the sprinkling is *tahor* for the purpose of eating *kodashim*, even if he has not yet brought his *korban* or done the *giluach* of *nezirut tumah* and restarted his *nezirut tahara*. The sixty days are therefore needed to resolve the *metzora* doubt, not the *tumas meis* doubt. The remaining sixty days — from day sixty to day one hundred and twenty — are then needed to fully conclude the *nezirut* under conditions of uncertainty.

### Triple Shaving Structure

To understand how these numbers are derived, one must trace the three required *giluachim* through the double-*safek* case. The *nazir* might be a *nazir tahor* who cannot shave until the end of his *nezirut*. At the same time, if he is a *metzora*, the *mitzvah* of *giluach* for *metzora* overrides the prohibition against shaving during *nezirut* — but only if he is definitely a *metzora*. Since he is only a *safek metzora*, there is no overriding justification. Therefore, he must wait thirty days before the first *giluach*, so that if he is a *nazir tahor*, those thirty days will suffice for his *nezirut* to conclude and he may shave. He brings an *olah* with a *tenai* — if he is a *nazir tahor*, this is his *korban olah*; if not, it is a mere *nedavah* — and shaves.

After thirty days and the first *giluach*, if he is a *nazir tamei*, he still needs thirty more days before the second *giluach* (which would serve for *metzora*'s *yemei sipro* or for the *nazir tamei* shaving). He cannot assume those thirty days counted, since he might have been a *nazir tahor* and those days were *yemei gamro* or *yemei sipro* — *ein olim lo*. Thus, another thirty days pass and a second *giluach* is performed. At sixty days, he is free of any *metzora* status doubt and may eat *kodashim*.

### Shaving Non-Doubling

But he cannot declare his *nezirut* concluded at sixty days, because the shaving done for *metzora* does not simultaneously count as the shaving for *nezirut*. This is the critical *halacha*: if a person was genuinely both a *metzora* and a *nazir*, the *giluach* performed as a *metzora* cannot be credited as the *giluach* for the *nazir*. They are two separate requirements and the same act cannot discharge both. Consequently, even if the first two shavings resolved his *metzora* status, if he was truly a *metzora* then those shavings were for *metzora* and did not serve the *nazir*. And since he might have been a *metzora*, we cannot credit those shavings toward his *nezirut*. He must therefore wait yet another thirty days and perform a third *giluach* — bringing the total to one hundred and twenty days — before concluding his *nezirut*.

The *Gemara* confirms: if it were a year-long *nezirut* and the same double *safek* applied, the numbers scale accordingly. *Ochel be-kodashim le-achar shtei shanim* — it would take two years to resolve the *metzora* doubt; *ve-shohai et ha-metama le-meitim le-achar arba shanim* — and four years to conclude the *nezirut*. This last figure is telling. If *yemei gamro* and *yemei sipro* fundamentally counted toward the *nezirut*, then once the *metzora* doubt is resolved after two years, the *nazir* would need only thirty additional days to conclude his *nazir tahor* status, and another year for *nazir tamei*, yielding three years and thirty days — not four. The fact that four full years are required demonstrates that none of the days during *yemei gamro* and *yemei sipro* count toward the *nezirut* at all. This directly refutes Rav Chisda's position that the days fundamentally count and the *mishnah*'s ruling is merely a practical consequence of *gidul se'ar*.

---

## Baraita Proof

### Rav Ashi's Question

Rav Ashi raises the question: *ein li ela yemei tumah she-ein olim lo min ha-minyan* — I know only that the days of *tumas meis* (in the case that is *soter*, i.e., that destroys earlier days) do not count. *Yemei chaluto minayin?* — from where do I know that *yemei chaluto*, the days when the *nazir* is a *muchlat metzora*, do not count? What is the biblical source for this rule?

### Graveyard Nazir Logic

The *Gemara* attempts a *kal va-chomer*. At the end of the *tumas meis* period, the *nazir* shaves and brings a *korban*; similarly, at the end of the *metzora* period, there is shaving and a *korban*. By analogy, just as *yemei tumah* do not count, *yemei chaluto* should not count either.

But the analogy is challenged: *tumas meis* is weightier — it destroys earlier days — and that is why it does not count toward new days. *Tzara'at*, by contrast, does not destroy earlier days and is therefore less weighty. Perhaps then *yemei chaluto* do count?

The *Gemara* responds with a *kal va-chomer* in the other direction: consider the *nazir be-kever* — a person who accepts *nezirut* while standing in a graveyard. Since he was already *tamei meis* when he began his *nezirut*, he never had a period as a *nazir tahor* who subsequently became *tamei*, and therefore he is not required to undergo the shaving and *korban* of *nezirut tumah*. His hair, the very hair on his head when he accepted the *nezirut*, is preserved — *se'aro ra'ui le-tiglachat nezirut* — it will be the hair shaved at the conclusion of his *nezirut tahara*. And yet, *ein olim lo min ha-minyan* — while he remains *tamei meis*, those days do not count. This is despite the fact that his hair is fully intact and will serve the final *nezirut* shaving.

Now compare: a *nazir* who is a *muchlat metzora* — his hair will definitely be shaved off before his *nezirut* concludes. The hair does not survive to the final *giluach* of *nezirut*. If even the *nazir be-kever*, whose hair is preserved, has days that do not count — how much more so (*lo kol she-ken*) should *yemei chaluto* not count, where the hair itself is going to be shaved away, representing a fundamental challenge to the *nazir*'s hair-preserving *nezirut* status.

### Shaving & Korban

The *baraita* identifies the distinguishing features that render *yemei gamro* and *yemei sipro* as *ein olim lo*: the requirement for *tiglachat* (shaving) and for bringing a *korban*. These parallel the defining characteristics of a *nazir tamei* whose days do not count — shaving and a *korban*. It is this dual requirement that marks the *metzora*'s *muchlat* and *sipro* periods as analogous to *tumas meis* for purposes of *nezirut* counting.

### Musgar Stage Counts

The *baraita* then asks: *yachol af yemei hasgiro?* — perhaps the same rule applies to the first stage, when the *nazir* is a *musgar*? The answer is no. *Im amarta bi'yemei chaluto shekein chaluto ta'un tiglachat u-meivi korban* — in the *muchlat* stage there is shaving and a *korban*, and that is why those days do not count. *Tomar bi'yemei hasgiro she-ein ta'un tiglachat ve-eino meivi korban* — in the *musgar* stage there is no shaving and no *korban*. The *musgar* who is cleared will simply go to the *mikveh* and be done. Therefore, *l'fichach ya'alu le-minyan* — those days do count toward the *nezirut*.

### Fundamental Non-Counting

The *baraita* concludes: *yemei sipro ve-yemei gomro ein olim lo min ha-minyan* — these two stages do not count, because of the shaving and *korban*. But *yemei hazav ve-hazavah* and *hesgeiro shel metzora* — *harei eilu olim lo* — these do count, because they lack the shaving requirement (or both shaving and *korban*) that characterizes the non-counting periods.

Now the *Gemara* deploys this *baraita* against Rav Chisda with full force. When the *baraita* deliberated whether *yemei chaluto* might be *oleh min ha-minyan*, it was plainly contemplating a case in which the *nazir* would have his thirty days of *gidul se'ar* at the end regardless — that is, a *nezirut merubah*. There would be no reason to consider the possibility of *oleh* if we were dealing with a short *nezirut*, because in that case the *gidul se'ar* problem alone would answer the question. The *baraita*'s discussion thus assumes a long *nezirut* — and yet it concludes *ein olim lo min ha-minyan*. *Alma lo silik lei* — clearly, in principle they do not count. The *baraita* is not concerned with *gidul se'ar* as the operative reason; it assumes the *nazir* will get his *gidul se'ar*, and still rules that the days do not count. *Shema mina* — this is a definitive proof against Rav Chisda.

---

# Nazir 55b

## Metzora & Nazir

### Metzora Stages

The *mishna* on this *daf* discusses the status of a *nazir* who finds himself simultaneously subject to another form of ritual impurity or process that prevents him from completing his *nezirut*. Before engaging with the *Gemara's* analysis, it is worth clarifying the three distinct stages of a *metzora's* progression, since the *mishna's* ruling depends critically on understanding them.

When a person develops a suspicious skin condition, a *kohen* must examine it. If the *kohen* cannot render an immediate determination, he declares the individual a *musgar* — quarantined for observation — and returns after a week to reassess. During this first stage, the individual is *tamei* at a full level of *tumah*, yet the situation remains tentative: the *kohen* has not rendered a definitive verdict. If upon the second inspection the condition has not resolved, the *kohen* declares him a *muchlat* — a confirmed, definitive *metzora*. The term *muchlat* conveys the absolute, locked-in nature of the status: there is no longer any ambiguity about his condition. This period of confirmed *metzora* status, which continues until the condition clears, is referred to in the *mishna* as *yemei gamro*. During *yemei gamro* the *metzora* is sent outside the camp entirely.

Once the condition clears, the *kohen* examines the individual and initiates the *tahara* process. On the day the condition is found to have healed, the *kohen* performs the bird ritual — taking two living, *tahor* birds, cedar wood, crimson thread, and hyssop; slaughtering one bird over an earthenware vessel containing spring water; and sprinkling the blood seven times upon the person being purified. The individual then shaves all his hair, immerses in a *mikveh*, and is permitted to re-enter the camp, but must remain outside his tent for seven days. This seven-day counting period that follows the initial ritual is called *yemei sifro*. On the seventh day of *yemei sifro*, he shaves all his hair a second time, immerses again, and on the eighth day brings his *korbanot*. Only then is he fully *tahor*.

The structure, then, is as follows: *musgar* — the first tentative quarantine stage; *muchlat* and *yemei gamro* — the confirmed indefinite period of *metzora* status until the condition clears; and *yemei sifro* — the seven-day counting period following the initial *tahara* ritual, culminating in a second shaving and the offering of *korbanot*.

### Mishna Rule

Our *mishna* establishes that during *yemei gamro* and *yemei sifro*, the days do not count toward a *nazir's* tally of *nezirut*, though they do not destroy (*soter*) the days already counted beforehand. This parallels the rule for a *nazir* who is *tamei meis* in a way that does not trigger *giluch* and *korban* — such as one who contracted a rabbinic-level *tumas meis*, or who touched a *golel*, *dofek*, or *kelim* that had been in contact with a corpse. In those cases, the days of *tumah* do not count, but neither do they nullify the earlier days.

By contrast, if the *metzora's* condition was caught at the *musgar* stage and cleared without advancing to *muchlat*, the episode is treated like a *zav* or *zava* — it has no effect whatsoever on the *nazirut*. Similarly, a *nazir* who becomes a *zav* or *zava* experiences no interruption to his *nezirut*. The *mishna's* ruling of *ein olim lo* — the days do not count — applies specifically to *yemei gamro* and *yemei sifro*, the stages characterized by *giluach* and *korban*.

## Rav Chisda

### Rav Chisda's Theory

The *Gemara* records the opinion of Rav Chisda, who distinguishes between a short and a long *nezirut*: *lo shanu ela binezirut mu'etet, aval binezirut merubah misak nami salikan lei* — the rule that those days do not count was stated only regarding a short *nezirut*, but in the case of a long *nezirut*, those days do in fact count. This is a striking position, because it essentially challenges the plain reading of the *mishna*.

Rav Chisda's reasoning is rooted in the requirement of *gidul se'ar* — thirty days of hair growth — that must precede the final *giluach* of a *nazir tahor*. A *nazir* who goes through the *metzora* process will have his hair shaved not once but twice before emerging from that process. By the time he is *tahor*, his head is bare. He will therefore require a full thirty days of hair growth regardless of how many days he counted beforehand. In a standard thirty-day *nezirut*, then, this practical reality means that the days spent as a *metzora* cannot contribute anything meaningful — even if they "count" in principle, you will still need a full thirty days at the end. Hence the *mishna's* language of *ein olim lo* is, in Rav Chisda's view, not a statement of fundamental law but a practical consequence of the *gidul se'ar* requirement.

For a long *nezirut*, however — say, one of fifty or one hundred days — if a *nazir* had already completed twenty days before becoming a *metzora*, and the *metzora* process occupied an additional stretch of time, he may still have enough days remaining that, even accounting for thirty days of *gidul se'ar* at the end, those middle days can effectively be credited. In such a case, Rav Chisda holds that they fundamentally do count, and the *mishna* simply does not address this scenario.

### Rav Mesharsheya

Rav Mesharsheya raises a challenge to Rav Chisda's position. He observes that the *mishna* states *ve'eino mevatel bahen et hakodmin* — these days do not destroy the earlier ones. He argues: if the *mishna* were speaking of a short *nezirut*, then it should have said the opposite — that the earlier days *are* destroyed — because in practice, a *nazir* with a thirty-day *nezirut* who undergoes this entire process and has his hair shaved twice will need the full thirty days thereafter regardless of what he accumulated beforehand. Saying merely that the middle days *do not count* without nullifying the earlier ones presupposes a scenario where one already has days that are worth preserving. That is only meaningful, Rav Mesharsheya argues, in the context of a long *nezirut* — *nezirut merubah* — yet even there, the *mishna* rules *ein olim lo*. This directly contradicts Rav Chisda, who held that in a *nezirut merubah* the days should count.

### Fifty-Day Case

Rav Chisda responds by proposing a specific scenario that fits the *mishna's* language of neither *soter* nor *oleh*: a fifty-day *nezirut* in which the *nazir* had completed twenty days before becoming a *metzora*, then undergoes the *metzora* process — involving two shavings — and afterward must count another thirty days of *gidul se'ar* before the final *giluach*. In this case, the twenty days beforehand are preserved and not destroyed, but the middle days of the *metzora* process cannot be used either, because the *nazir* will need those thirty days at the end regardless. This accounts for the *mishna's* formulation.

Rav Chisda concedes that in a truly long *nezirut* — one where enough days remain that the middle days could be credited and still leave thirty days for *gidul se'ar* at the end — those middle days would in principle count. He maintains that the *mishna's ein olim lo* is not a fundamental halakhic statement but rather a practical limitation born of the *gidul se'ar* requirement. The rest of the *Gemara* will proceed to demonstrate that this position is untenable, and that the days fundamentally do not count.

## Double Safek

### Double Safek Setup

The *Gemara* now raises a complex case: a *nazir* who may have become *tamei meis* in a way that would require *giluach* and *korban* — that is, a *tumah* of the *soter* variety — and who is also a *muchlat b'safek*, a doubtful confirmed *metzora*. The intersection of these two *safekot* creates a situation where multiple *giluchim* may be required under different conditions, but performing any one of them without justification could violate the *nezirut* itself.

One might ask how a person can be a *muchlat b'safek*, since the *halacha* of *tzaraas* is that the status of *metzora* is determined entirely by the *kohen's* declaration — once the *kohen* renders a ruling according to the established procedures, the status is definitive. The *rishonim* acknowledge this difficulty and note that a precise scenario is hard to identify; one possible construction is that there was doubt about the *kohen's* own qualifications. Regardless of the exact framing, the *Gemara* treats the double *safek* as a valid case and proceeds to work through its consequences.

### Sixty to 120 Days

The *Gemara* rules that such a *nazir* may eat *kodshim* only after sixty days, and may drink wine and contract *tumas meis* — that is, fully complete his *nezirut* — only after one hundred and twenty days.

The logic is as follows. In order to eat *kodshim*, the *nazir* need not yet fully resolve his *nazir tamei* status — from a standpoint of *tumah v'taharah*, once he has undergone the sprinkling of *parah adumah* on days three and seven, he is fully *tahor* and may eat *kodashim* even without yet bringing his *korbanot* of *nezirut*. What must be resolved first is his possible *metzora* status, since a *metzora* cannot eat *kodshim*. It takes sixty days to exit the *metzora* status in light of the *safek*, for reasons the *Gemara* will explain. Completing the *nezirut* entirely, however — which requires resolving the *nazir tamei* and *nazir tahor* obligations — takes a full one hundred and twenty days.

### Conditional Korbanos

The *Gemara* and *Tosafot* work through the mechanics in considerable detail. The procedure unfolds across multiple thirty-day intervals, with each *giluach* separated by thirty days because of the need for *gidul se'ar*.

Initially, the individual cannot shave immediately upon the clearing of the condition, because he may be a *nazir tahor* — and a *nazir tahor* may not have his hair cut before the completion of his *nezirut*. Therefore one must wait thirty days before performing the first *giluach*, ensuring that even if he were a *nazir tahor*, the minimal period required has elapsed. At that point, a conditional *korban olah* is brought: if he is a *nazir tahor*, this serves as his *korban* for *nezirut*; if not, it is a voluntary *nedava*. The *halacha* that *gilach al echad min hadamim yatza* — even a single *korban* can serve *bedi'eved* to complete the *giluach* of a *nazir tahor* — allows this to work. After thirty days, the first *giluach* is performed, covering both the possible *metzora giluach* and the possible *nazir tahor* or *nazir tamei giluach* as applicable.

However, the matter is not resolved. One cannot proceed to the second *metzora giluach* — which would normally take place seven days after the first — because the *nazir* may actually have been a *nazir tamei* rather than a *nazir tahor*. If so, the first *giluach* served only the *nazir tamei* role, and thirty more days are needed before the second *giluach* can take place for the *nazir tahor*. Thus a second *giluach* with its own conditional *korban* occurs at day sixty.

After sixty days and two *giluchim*, the *metzora* process — if it was ever real — is fully complete, and the individual can eat *kodshim*. But the *nezirut* is not yet done. If the individual was actually both a *metzora* and a *nazir tamei*, then the *halacha* is that the *giluach* of a *metzora* does not count toward the *giluach* of a *nazir*; they cannot serve double duty. This means the first sixty days of *giluachim* may not have counted for the *nazir* at all in such a scenario. The individual must therefore wait another thirty days and perform a third *giluach*, and then yet another thirty days with a fourth *giluach*, to cover all possible configurations. In each interval, conditional *korbanot* are brought with the appropriate *tnai*.

The key principle underlying this entire structure, and the one the *Gemara* intends to prove through it, is *ein olim lo* — the days of *yemei gamro* and *yemei sifro* do not count toward the *nezirut*. The fact that the concluding period requires not a mere thirty days but a full doubling of the *nezirut* period demonstrates that those middle days contribute nothing. This point is pressed against Rav Chisda's position in the next section.

## Braita Proof

### Rav Ashi's Query

The *Gemara* introduces a further proof — and, more fundamentally, the textual source for the entire principle — when Rav Ashi poses the question: *ein li ela yemei tumah she'ein olim lo min haminyan* — I know only that the days of *tumah* do not count; *yemei chaluto minayin* — what is the source that the days of *yemei gamro* do not count?

It is important to clarify what is meant here. The baseline case that does not count is a full *tumas meis* with *giluch* — and that case is actually *soter*, not merely *ein olim lo*. The question Rav Ashi is asking is grounded in a *Midrash Halacha* from the *Sifrei*: given that we have a source for the *nazir tamei* not counting days, what is the derivation that the *metzora's* days in *yemei gamro* also do not count?

### Kal Vachomer

A *kal vachomer* is proposed. A *nazir* who accepts *nezirut* upon himself while standing in a graveyard — a full *tamei meis* condition — does not need to perform the *giluach* and *korban* of a *nazir tamei*, because he never transitioned from *tahor* to *tamei* during the *nezirut*. Crucially, his hair at that point is preserved: it will not need to be shaved as a result of his *tumah*, and it remains available for the final *giluach* of his *nezirut taharah*. Yet even this person, whose hair is intact and whose case appears less disruptive than a *metzora's*, has his days of *tumah* not count. How much more so, then, should the days of a *nazir muchlat* not count — for the *metzora's* hair will inevitably be shaved off before the *nezirut* is complete, representing a direct contradiction to the integrity of the *nezirut*.

The argument runs: *kal vachomer* — just as the *nazir bakever* whose hair is *raui letiglachat nezirut* (fit for the final shaving of *nezirut*) nonetheless has his days not count, the *muchlat* whose hair is *she'ein saro raui letiglachat nezirut* (not fit, because it will be shaved off prematurely) should *a fortiori* have his days not count.

This *kal vachomer* is then challenged: *tumas meis* is weightier because it destroys the earlier days — that is why it doesn't count. But *yemei gamro* does not destroy the earlier days, suggesting it is less disruptive and perhaps its days should count. The *braita* responds: *lo, kal vachomer* — and reframes the *kal vachomer* to rest on the comparison of *giluach* and *korban*.

### Braita Categories

A *braita* then organizes the categories systematically. *Yemei gamro* and *yemei sifro* — the periods characterized by *giluach* and *korban* obligation — do not count toward the *nezirut*. The analogy to *nazir tamei* holds: both involve shaving and *korban*, and in both cases those days are *ein olim lo min haminyan*.

By contrast, the days of a *zav*, a *zava*, and the *musgar* stage of a *metzora* all count toward the *nezirut*. The distinguishing criterion is the absence of *giluach* and *korban*. A *zav* and *zava* do bring a *korban* at the conclusion of their status, but they do not shave. The *musgar* has neither *giluach* nor *korban* — if the condition clears at that stage, he simply immerses in a *mikveh* and is *tahor*. Therefore, *harei elu olim lo* — those days count.

The *braita* addresses the question of whether *yemei hasgiro* — the *musgar* stage — should also not count, given that it too involves the same level of *tumah* as *yemei gamro*. The answer is decisive: it is the *giluach* and *korban* that render *yemei gamro* and *yemei sifro* analogous to *nazir tamei* and generate the rule of *ein olim lo*. Without them, there is no basis to exclude those days.

The *braita* thus provides the *midrash halacha* foundation for the *mishna's* rule: *yemei sifro viyemei gamro ein olim lo min haminyan* — because they bear the halakhic signature of *giluach* and *korban* that marks days of significant ritual disruption to the *nezirut*.

### Fundamental Non-Counting

With the *braita* in hand, the *Gemara* now delivers its decisive refutation of Rav Chisda. The *braita* had considered the possibility that *yemei gamro* might be *oleh min haminyan*. At what point would such a position be coherent? Clearly not in the case of a *nezirut mu'etet* — a standard thirty-day *nezirut* — because there one would need thirty days of *gidul se'ar* regardless, and the days could never practically count. The only scenario in which one could meaningfully *consider* those days as counting is in the case of a *nezirut merubah*, where there would be more than thirty days remaining and the *gidul se'ar* requirement could still be satisfied at the end.

Yet the *braita* entertains precisely this scenario and then concludes: *ein olim lo min haminyan* — they do not count. *Alma lo salik leh* — the *braita's* conclusion is that fundamentally, as a matter of principle, those days do not count. This has nothing to do with *gidul se'ar*. The *braita* is operating in a *nezirut merubah* context — the very scenario Rav Chisda claimed would allow the days to be credited — and rules that they do not count regardless. *Shema mina*: this is a conclusive proof that the *halacha* of *ein olim lo* is not a practical consequence of the *gidul se'ar* requirement, as Rav Chisda maintained, but a fundamental halakhic principle in its own right.

---

---

# Nazir 56

## Nezir & Mikdash Entry

### Intro: Exceptions

The final section of this *perek* opens with a *mishnah* that draws a striking parallel between two distinct bodies of law: the rules governing when a *nazir* must shave his head as a result of *tumas hameis*, and the rules governing liability for entering the *Beit Hamikdash* in a state of *tumah*. Throughout the preceding *perek*, we encountered a series of cases in which a *nazir* who contracted a form of *tumas hameis* was nonetheless exempt from the obligation of *nezir megaleach* — cases such as the *metzora* and certain other categories where, despite the *tumah* being biblical in nature, the *mesorah* indicates that it does not trigger the shaving requirement or nullify the *nezirut*. The *mishnah* now establishes a general principle: these two domains — *nezir megaleach* and *biat mikdash* — track each other precisely.

The rule, stated by Rabbi Eliezer in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua, runs as follows: *kol tumah min hameis shehanazir megaleach aleha chayavim aleha al biat mikdash* — any *tumah* from the dead that causes a *nazir* to shave also renders one liable for entering the *Beit Hamikdash* while bearing that *tumah*. Conversely, *kol tumah min hameis she'ein hanazir megaleach aleha ein chayavim aleha al biat mikdash* — any *tumah* from the dead that does not obligate a *nazir* to shave similarly carries no liability for *biat mikdash*.

It is worth noting the practical scope of this rule. *Tumas meis* ordinarily permits entry into the *Machaneh Leviyah* and even into the *Ezrat Nashim*, right up to the *Azarah* itself. What is at stake here is therefore entry into the temple precinct proper. The *mishnah* thus tells us that those categories of *tumas meis* that are exceptional with respect to *nezir megaleach* are equally exceptional with respect to *biat mikdash* — they carry no liability even at the biblical level.

### Meir's Objection

Rabbi Meir registers a sharp objection: *lo tehei zu kallah min hasheretz* — surely this *tumah* should not be treated more leniently than touching a dead rodent. His point is intuitive. Even if a particular variety of *tumas meis* does not activate the *nazir*'s obligation to shave — perhaps because it is categorized as a lesser or anomalous form — it is still *tumas meis*. And any *tumah* whatsoever, even touching a *sheretz*, renders a person liable for entering the *Beit Hamikdash* in that state. The cases under discussion are not rabbinic enactments like *sechochot u'praot* or *Beit Hapras*, where no one would argue the point. These are assumed to be *d'oraita tumot*. How, then, can one say that a person bearing such *tumah* is exempt from liability for *biat mikdash*?

### Gemara Source

The *gemara* is not primarily interested in the substance of this dispute, but in the transmission of the tradition itself. It notes that the principle attributed in the *mishnah* to Rabbi Eliezer in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua — the *stam* Rabbi Yehoshua being Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya — was in fact received through an intermediate link: Rabbi Yehoshua bar Mama. A *beraita* fills in the background.

Rabbi Eliezer relates that he once traveled to Ardaskaya, where he encountered Rabbi Yehoshua ben Peter Rosh seated and presenting his analysis before Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Peter Rosh articulated the same rule: *tumah* from the dead that causes a *nazir* to shave also entails liability for *biat mikdash*, and *tumah* that does not obligate shaving likewise entails no such liability. Rabbi Meir pushed back with precisely the argument recorded in the *mishnah* — that this *tumah* should at minimum be no lighter than *tumas sheretz*.

At that point, Rabbi Eliezer intervened, asking Rabbi Meir whether he was acquainted with the authority of Rabbi Yehoshua bar Mama. Rabbi Meir confirmed that he was. Rabbi Eliezer then reported: *kach amar li Rabbi Yehoshua bar Mama mishum Rabbi Yehoshua* — this is what Rabbi Yehoshua bar Mama told me in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua, that he had received the tradition *shamati* — I heard — that any *tumah* from the dead that obligates a *nazir* to shave also carries liability for *biat mikdash*, and any that does not obligate shaving carries no such liability. Rabbi Eliezer thereby backed the position of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Peter Rosh, establishing that it was a received tradition from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya himself.

### Chain of Tradition

This background raises an obvious question: if Rabbi Eliezer's immediate source was Rabbi Yehoshua bar Mama, who in turn received it from Rabbi Yehoshua, why does our *mishnah* cite Rabbi Eliezer in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua directly, skipping the intermediate link?

The *gemara* derives from this a general principle about the reporting of traditions: *kol shma'teta d'mitamra b'bei tlata* — any tradition that was transmitted through three stages, *kadmaya uvatraya amrinan* — we cite the first and the last, *metzaya la amrinan* — but the middle link need not always be mentioned. It is not required to enumerate every step in the chain of transmission.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak illustrates this with a further example. Nachum HaLavlur declares his tradition going back *miRabbi Mayasha shekibel me'abba shekibel min hazugot shekiblu min hanevi'im* — from Rabbi Mayasha who received from his father who received from the *zugot* who received from the prophets — a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* concerning one who plants dill and mustard seed in two or three different locations in a field, that *pe'ah* is given from each separate location. What is instructive here is not the content of this *halacha* but the structure of its citation: it proceeds from Nachum HaLavlur all the way back to the prophets, yet it omits Yehoshua and the *zekenim* who, according to *Pirkei Avot*, stood between Moshe and the prophets in the chain of tradition. The *gemara* concludes *shema mina*: it is indeed not necessary to cite every intermediate link.

One might reasonably ask — and the *gemara* invites this observation — that Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua were in fact contemporaries, both teachers of Rabbi Akiva. How peculiar, then, that Rabbi Eliezer would receive this tradition three removes away rather than directly from his colleague. Perhaps this reflects circumstances surrounding Rabbi Eliezer's *cherem*, or some other reason they did not communicate directly on this matter. The question is a natural one, and it was noted.

---

The same *halacha* has a parallel formulation in *Masechet Smachot* that is considerably more relevant in practical terms: *kol tumah she'ein hanazir megaleach aleha ein kohein muzhar alav* — any *tumah* that does not obligate a *nazir* to shave likewise does not constitute a biblical violation for a *kohein*. This raises the broader question — touched upon throughout the *perek* — of whether certain anomalous categories of *tumas meis*, those associated with *cherev k'chalal* or *keilim hanoge'im b'meit*, also create exceptions in the laws of *tumas kohanim*.

## Logic vs. Tradition

### Akiva's Argument

The next *mishnah* introduces a fascinating exchange between Rabbi Akiva and his teacher Rabbi Eliezer, followed by a contrasting encounter with Rabbi Yehoshua. The discussion touches on a theme that runs through much of the *perek*: many of the laws of *nezirut* resist logical explanation and appear almost arbitrary. Rabbi Yochanan, as we have seen elsewhere, would often say simply *halacha hi b'Nazir* — it is a law that applies to the *nazir*, with no further derivation offered.

Rabbi Akiva opens by presenting an argument before Rabbi Eliezer. He begins with two established facts. First, a bone the size of a barley grain — *etzem k'se'orah* — does not cause *tumah* through *ohel*, i.e., being in the same enclosed space as a corpse. It lacks the minimum mass to produce *tumas ohel*. And yet, a *nazir* who touches or carries such a bone must shave and loses his accumulated *nezirut*. Second, a *revi'it* of blood — *revi'it dam* — does cause *tumas ohel* at the biblical level. A person who is in the same space as a *revi'it* of blood from a corpse becomes *tamei*.

From these two facts, Rabbi Akiva constructs a *kal vachomer*. If a tiny chip of bone that cannot even produce *tumas ohel* is nonetheless sufficient to obligate a *nazir* to shave when he touches or carries it, then certainly a *revi'it* of blood — which does produce *tumas ohel* — should at minimum obligate a *nazir* to shave when he touches or carries it. It is important to note that Rabbi Akiva carefully limits his argument to *maga* and *masa* — touch and carrying — not *ohel*, because the bone only causes liability through those two modes, and a *kal vachomer* cannot extend beyond its premise.

The practical implication is significant. The established rule requires a *chatzi log* of blood — half a *log* — before a *nazir* is obligated to shave due to blood. Rabbi Akiva argues this is too high a threshold, at least for touch and carrying. A *revi'it* of blood should suffice for those modes, given that a *revi'it* produces *tumas ohel* while the tiny bone does not produce *tumas ohel* at all.

### Eliezer Dismisses

Rabbi Eliezer's response is blunt: *ma zeh Akiva, ein danim kan mi-kal vachomer* — what are you doing, Akiva? There is no place for a *kal vachomer* here. This amounts to a flat dismissal: these laws are arbitrary, they do not respond to logic, and Rabbi Akiva's reasoning, however clever, is simply beside the point.

### Yehoshua Validates

Unsatisfied with this response, Rabbi Akiva brought his argument to his other teacher, Rabbi Yehoshua. Rabbi Yehoshua's reaction was strikingly different: *yafeh amarta* — you argued well. The argument is valid. And yet, he continued, *ela kach amru halacha* — nonetheless, this is the received tradition, and the tradition stands.

The difference in approach between the two teachers is pedagogically significant. Rabbi Eliezer simply rejected the argument without engaging it. Rabbi Yehoshua validated the argument intellectually while explaining why it ultimately cannot prevail: the domain in question is governed not by logical inference but by *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* — a tradition transmitted from Sinai. A good argument does not override a received tradition; it simply illuminates why logic alone is insufficient here.

### Eliezer vs. Akiva

This exchange is not merely a disagreement about a specific *shiur* of blood. It reflects a deeper tension about the nature of *Torah she-ba'al peh*. Rabbi Eliezer, by his own example and by the famous characterization of him in rabbinic literature, never transmitted anything that he had not received from his teacher. His entire orientation is toward received tradition. Rabbi Akiva, by contrast, represents the power of human intellect and logical derivation — the idea that law can and should be reasoned out from principles, not merely inherited.

This tension has an older precedent. When the question arose whether a *korban Pesach* overrides *Shabbat* when *Erev Pesach* falls on *Shabbat*, Hillel HaBavli spent the entire day presenting *kal vachomers* and analogies to the assembled authorities, and they would not accept his conclusion. It was only when he said *kach mikublani miShemaya v'Avtalyon* — I have received this as a tradition from Shemaya and Avtalyon — that they accepted the ruling. The implication is that tradition remains the ultimate authority, even when logic independently arrives at the same conclusion.

It is in this spirit that Rabbi Eliezer was more dismissive of Rabbi Akiva's *kal vachomer*. For Rabbi Eliezer, the very act of deploying a logical argument in a domain governed by tradition was a category error. Rabbi Yehoshua, perhaps more generous in temperament, acknowledged the logical force of the argument before setting it aside. And Rabbi Akiva — who elsewhere is identified as the one who first established that a *revi'it* of blood constitutes the minimum *shiur* for a *nazir* with respect to touch and carrying — evidently continued to press this position based on his *kal vachomer*, a position grounded in his distinctive approach to legal derivation.

## Halacha Exception

### Which is Exception

The *gemara* now raises a precise question: *ibaya lehu* — the following problem was raised. When Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua said that the *kal vachomer* is inapplicable because this domain is governed by *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*, which rule exactly is the *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*? Is it the rule governing the bone — that even a tiny *etzem k'se'orah* is sufficient to obligate a *nazir* to shave through touch and carrying — or is it the rule governing the blood — that even a *revi'it* of blood causes *tumas ohel*?

This question is not as simple as it first appears. One might have assumed that anything constituting *tumas meis* would obviously obligate a *nazir* to shave, and that the exceptions are what require *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*. But as *Tosafot* notes, the *pesukim* concerning the *nazir* emphasize *tumas ohel*: *al kol nafshos meis lo yavo* — he shall not come near any dead person. The straightforward reading might suggest that a *nazir* is only obligated when exposed to something that produces *tumas ohel*, or at minimum to something powerful enough to produce that category of *tumah*. If so, the rule that even a tiny chip of bone — which lacks the mass for *tumas ohel* — suffices to obligate a *nazir* to shave is itself a *chiddush*, a departure from the plain meaning of the *pesukim*. That departure could be the *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*.

Alternatively, the *chiddush* could be on the side of the blood. The *pesukim* concerning the *kohein* use the phrase *al kol nafshos meis* as well, and *Tosafot* suggests that reading *nafshos* in the plural implies the minimum blood of two people, which would amount to a *chatzi log*. On that reading, the *pesukim* would support requiring a *chatzi log* of blood to produce *tumas ohel*, making the rule that a *revi'it* is sufficient the *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* — a transmitted tradition that goes beyond what the *pesukim* alone would support. If so, it is the *revi'it* of blood that is the anomalous exception, and Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua were telling Rabbi Akiva: do not build a *kal vachomer* beginning from the *revi'it*, because the *revi'it* itself is the exception.

### Beraita Answer

The *gemara* resolves this through a *beraita* that states the matter explicitly: *etzem k'se'orah halacha v'revi'it dam kal vachomer* — the rule governing the tiny bone is the *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*, while the rule that a *revi'it* of blood causes *tumas ohel* is derived through *kal vachomer*. In other words, the anomaly is on the side of the bone; the *revi'it* of blood is the logically derived rule, and the bone is the exceptional tradition.

### No KV from Exception

This immediately clarifies why Rabbi Akiva's *kal vachomer* cannot stand. He sought to argue from the bone — which obligates a *nazir* to shave through touch and carrying despite producing no *tumas ohel* — to the *revi'it* of blood, which does produce *tumas ohel*. But the bone is itself an exception, a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* that departs from what logic would dictate. *Ein danim kal vachomer me-halacha* — one cannot build a *kal vachomer* from a premise that is itself a received anomaly. A *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* is *sui generis*; it stands on its own and is not meant to serve as a logical premise from which further laws are inferred. The bone's rule is true, but it tells us nothing about what the law should be elsewhere, precisely because it exists outside the domain of rational derivation.

This raises a broader conceptual point. One might have thought that a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*, being the most authoritative form of tradition, would constitute the strongest possible foundation for a *kal vachomer*. In fact, the opposite is the case. The force of logical inference depends on its premises being part of a coherent, rationally accessible system. A *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* that represents an exception to what logic would otherwise dictate is precisely not such a premise; it is a standalone received tradition, valid within its own scope, but incapable of generating further inferences.

## Two Nzirim Safek

### Mishnah Setup

We now turn to an entirely different topic, though one that touches on realities of *tumas meis* in a very concrete way. The *mishnah* presents the following scenario: *shnei nezirim* — two *nezirim* — to whom one person says: *ra'isi echad mikem she-nitma* — I saw one of you become *tamei*, perhaps by entering an area with a grave, *v'eini yodeia eizeh mikem* — but I do not know which of you it was. Each *nazir* is now a *safek nazir tamei*. Neither knows with certainty whether he is the one who contracted *tumas meis*.

This creates a complex halachic predicament. A *nazir tamei* must go through the process of bringing a *korban tumah* and then counting new days of *nezirut*, culminating in the *korban tahara*. But one cannot simply bring a *korban* if one is not certain one is obligated. Nor can one simply shave without being certain of one's status. The solution for a single individual in this situation would involve waiting out the minimum period of *nezirut* — thirty days — then shaving and bringing minimal *korbanot* with appropriate stipulations. The *olah*, for instance, could be brought with the condition that if one is obligated as a *nazir tamei* it counts as the obligatory *olah*, and if not it is a voluntary *olat nedavah*. The *chatat ha'of* — a bird offering — may be brought even in a state of doubt, this being a special *halacha*. The *asham*, however, cannot be brought conditionally or on the basis of doubt. So one never fully satisfies that component of the *korban tumah* in a state of *safek*.

## Two Nzirim Safek (II)

### Safek Tumah Rules

Before addressing the practical solution for the two *nezirim*, the *gemara* raises a fundamental question: why are they *safek tamei* at all?

The principle governing doubtful *tumah* is derived from the laws of *sotah*. The Torah describes the *sotah* as having gone into seclusion — *venistara* — in a private space. From this, the *gemara* derives the general principle: *safek tumah birshut hayachid sefeko tamei* — doubtful *tumah* that occurred in a private domain is treated as *tamei*, while *safek tumah birshut harabim sefeko tahor* — doubtful *tumah* in a public domain is treated as *tahor*. This applies even at the biblical level, *d'oraita*.

### Domain Question

The *gemara* notes, however, that the analogy to *sotah* requires that only two people be present in the private space — the woman and the man with whom she secluded herself. The rule of *safek tumah birshut hayachid* applies when there were only two people in the relevant space, paralleling the *sotah* scenario. Here, however, there are three people: the two *nezirim* and the witness who observed them. With three people present, this should constitute a *reshut harabim*, and *safek tumah birshut harabim sefeko tahor*. If so, both *nezirim* should simply be presumed *tahor* — yet the *mishnah* treats them as *safek tamei* and requires them to act accordingly.

### Reshut Hayachid

The *gemara* resolves this through Rabbah bar bar Chana, who explains that the case involves a witness who saw the two *nezirim* from a distance — *be'omer ra'isi tumah shenizreka beineichem* — who observed from afar and could not make out which of them was involved. The witness was not physically present in the same space as the two *nezirim*; he observed from outside. The space the two *nezirim* occupied was therefore a *reshut hayachid*, and the witness's presence at a distance does not convert it into a *reshut harabim*.

Rav Ashi adds that this reading is supported by the language of the *mishnah* itself: *v'eini yodeia eizeh mikem* — I do not know which of you — implies not that the witness forgot, but that he never knew, which fits precisely the scenario of someone watching at a distance who could not identify which individual was which.

Importantly, throughout this entire analysis the *gemara* assumes that the *safek* retains its status as a genuine doubt, treating it as *safek tamei* rather than *vadai tamei*. *Tosafot* raises the point that when we say *safek tumah birshut hayachid* is *tamei*, the normal rule is that we treat the person as *vadai tamei*, not merely as *safek tamei* — mirroring the *sotah*, where the presumption becomes essentially a certainty for legal purposes. However, since it is impossible for both *nezirim* to be *vadai tamei* — only one of them actually became *tamei* — the *gemara* here retains the language and substance of *safek*, operating within a framework where both individuals carry genuine uncertainty.

### Paired Offerings

The *mishnah*'s solution for the two *nezirim* is elegant. Between the two of them, there must be one *korban tumah* and one *korban tahara*. Each *nazir* shaves and they bring together both a complete *korban tumah* and a complete *korban tahara*. The stipulation each makes is: *im ani hu hatamei korban tumah sheli v'korban tahara shelcha* — if I am the one who was *tamei*, the *korban tumah* is mine and the *korban tahara* is yours; *v'im ani hu hatahor korban tahara sheli v'korban tumah shelcha* — and if I am the one who was *tahor*, the *korban tahara* is mine and the *korban tumah* is yours.

After the first thirty days, the *nezirim* count an additional thirty days. At the end of those sixty days, one of them has definitively completed a full *nezirut taharah* following an episode of *tumah*, and the other has completed a standard *nezirut taharah*. Each brings a complete set of *korbanot*, again with appropriate stipulation: the *korban* of the second thirty days belongs to whichever of them was indeed the one who was *tamei* and has now completed his *taharah*. The attribution flows to the person for whom it is obligatory.

### Two-Person Advantage

The advantage of having two *nezirim* in this situation rather than one is substantial. When a single *nazir* faces this uncertainty alone, he is limited to bringing minimal *korbanot* — primarily an *olah* on a conditional basis — because he cannot bring the full *korban tumah* when he does not know himself to be obligated. He can never bring the *asham* at all. With two *nezirim*, however, the situation is different: since one of them is definitively obligated in the *korban tumah* and the other is definitively obligated in the *korban tahara*, both complete sets may be brought without any conditional framing. The only stipulation required is to direct each set toward the person for whom it applies. *Tosafot* notes that in this configuration the stipulation is almost formulaic — it is simply an attribution, not a genuine conditional offering. No *olat nedavah* is necessary, no incomplete *korban* is brought; each person brings a full set and declares to whom it belongs.

## Double Shaving

### Hakafah Problem

Having described the practical solution for the two *nezirim*, the *gemara* identifies a difficulty that had been lurking beneath the surface. The *mishnah* envisions each *nazir* shaving twice: once at the end of the first thirty-day period and once at the end of the second. But if one of them was in fact *tahor* all along, then his second shaving — undertaken so that he can fulfill the *mitzvah* of *nazir megaleach* in the event that he was *tamei* — is a shaving that he does not need and that he may not need halachically to perform. And the act of shaving all the hair of one's head implicates the prohibition of *hakafat rosh* — the prohibition of *lo takifu*, shaving the sideburns in a manner that makes a circuit of the head.

The *gemara* is thus asking: even granting that the shaving itself is not *me'akev* — that *nezirut* is formally complete without it — we still have to account for the fact that we are permitting a *nazir* to shave in circumstances where the shaving may constitute a violation of *hakafat rosh*. Why do we permit that?

### Shmuel: Woman/Minor

Shmuel answers that the *mishnah* is speaking of a woman or a minor. A woman is excluded from the prohibition of *lo takifu* because the prohibition against shaving the beard — *lo yashchitu pe'at zekanam* — does not apply to women, who ordinarily have no beard. And since there is an assumption that whoever falls outside the prohibition of shaving the beard also falls outside the prohibition of shaving the sideburns, a woman is entirely exempt from *hakafat rosh*. A minor likewise falls outside these prohibitions in a way that eliminates the concern. Therefore the *mishnah* is addressing a case where the two *nezirim* are women, or one of them is a minor, such that the double shaving creates no violation.

### Inference: Hakafah

The *gemara* immediately draws an inference from Shmuel's answer. One might have suggested a far simpler resolution to the problem: leave the *nezirim* as adult males and simply hold that *hakafat kol harosh lo shemah hakafah* — that shaving all the hair of the head does not constitute the prohibited form of *hakafah*. The prohibition of *lo takifu*, on this reading, refers specifically to making a defined perimeter cut around the head, leaving a circle of hair — like shaving around a circuit so that the remaining hair describes a line. When one shaves the entire head smooth, there is no circling, no defined sideburn — there is simply baldness. Perhaps that does not implicate the prohibition at all.

Had Shmuel accepted this position, he could have resolved the *gemara*'s difficulty without invoking the special status of women and minors. He did not. *Midela mokim lah hachi* — since he does not explain it this way — *shema mina kasavar Shmuel hakafat kol harosh shemah hakafah* — we infer that Shmuel holds that shaving all the hair of the head does constitute the prohibited *hakafah*. This is a clear inference. For Shmuel, an adult male who shaves his entire head violates the prohibition of *lo takifu* just as surely as one who makes a circular perimeter cut. The only way to permit the double shaving of the *mishnah* is therefore to situate the case among those who are outside the prohibition entirely — women and minors.

## Shaver/Shavee

### Huna: Shaver Independent

The *gemara* then cites a further teaching: *amar Rav Huna hamakif et hakatan harei hu chayav* — Rav Huna rules that one who shaves a minor is liable. This challenges the apparent implication of Shmuel's answer, which seemed to suggest that when the *shavee* — the person whose hair is being cut — is a minor, the act is entirely permitted. Rav Huna disagrees, or at least introduces a critical distinction.

The underlying conceptual question is how to read the *Torah*'s formulation of the prohibition: *lo takifu pe'at roshchem*. To whom does the *Torah* speak? *Pe'at roshchem* — the sideburns of your head — seems addressed to the person whose sideburns are being cut, i.e., the *shavee*. But *lo takifu* — do not make a circuit — seems addressed to the one who performs the cutting, i.e., the *shaver*. Are these two aspects of a single integrated prohibition, or are they independent obligations that can be separated?

Rav Huna holds that the *shaver* bears an independent obligation. If the *shaver* is an adult male, he is liable regardless of who the *shavee* is. Even if the *shavee* is a minor — who is himself outside the prohibition — the adult male performing the shaving violates the prohibition from the *shaver*'s side.

### Adda Challenges

Rav Adda bar Ahava challenged Rav Huna directly: *vedidach man megaleach lehu* — your own children, who do you have shaving them? Presumably Rav Huna's children had their sideburns cut, yet Rav Huna had just ruled that an adult male shaver is liable regardless of the shavee's status. If an adult male shaved Rav Huna's children, that adult male would be violating the prohibition. Who, then, was doing the cutting?

### Huna Response

Rav Huna answered simply: *Chovah* — his wife. Since a woman is exempt from the prohibition — as Shmuel established, and as the logic of the *Torah*'s formulation confirms — a woman acting as the *shaver* violates nothing. The shavee is a minor, and the shaver is a woman. Neither occupies the position of an adult male in the chain of the act.

This generates a coherent model. The prohibition operates along two independent axes: the *shaver* axis and the *shavee* axis. An adult male cannot occupy either position without violating the prohibition — he cannot be the one who cuts and he cannot be the one whose sideburns are cut. But women and minors are outside the prohibition on both axes. A woman can serve as the *shaver*, and a minor can serve as the *shavee*, without creating any violation. The only constraint is that an adult male must not appear in either role.

### The Curse

The exchange, however, did not end peacefully. Rav Adda bar Ahava responded to the name *Chovah* — Rav Huna's wife — by invoking it ominously: *tekavrinehu Chovah livneih* — may Chovah bury her children. Whether this was intended as a genuine curse or as an exclamation of disbelief — the *Rosh* understands it as rhetorical, something like "does she want to bury her children? How can you allow this?" — the words carried consequence. The *gemara* records that for all the years of Rav Adda bar Ahava's life, Rav Huna had no further children. The *gemara* does not say that Chovah had no further children — pointedly, it focuses the consequence on Rav Huna himself. The power of such utterances, even when not intended as a curse, appears repeatedly in the *gemara*, and this episode is a striking illustration.

### Huna's Model

To summarize Rav Huna's position as it emerges from this discussion: the prohibition of *lo takifu* operates independently on the *shaver* and the *shavee*. An adult male cannot serve as the *shaver* — even if the *shavee* is a minor or a woman — and an adult male cannot serve as the *shavee* — even if the *shaver* is a woman or a minor. Women and minors, however, may occupy either role freely. Thus a woman shaving a minor creates no violation on either side, and Rav Huna's own practice — having his wife Chovah cut his children's sideburns — was entirely consistent with his ruling.

---

---

# Nazir 56b

## Tumah & Mikdash Entry

### Rabbi Eliezer's Ruling

The *perek* concludes with two *mishnayot* that are considerably less intense than the intricate debates we have been navigating throughout this chapter regarding the various forms of *tumas meis* and their consequences for the *nazir*. The first of these opens with a sweeping principle attributed to Rabbi Eliezer in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua: any *tumah min hameis* for which a *nazir* shaves his head — thereby nullifying his earlier *nezirut* — is also the category of *tumah* for which one incurs liability upon entering the *Beit Hamikdash* while in that state of *tumah*. Conversely, any *tumah min hameis* for which the *nazir* does not shave carries with it no liability for *bias mikdash*. The two categories mirror each other precisely.

It is worth recalling the context: *tumas meis* is unusual in that it is tolerated even within *Machaneh Leviyah* — one may proceed as far as *Ezras Nashim* — and the liability we are discussing applies only upon actual entry into the *Azarah* itself. With that in mind, the principle the *mishnah* is establishing becomes clear: whatever constitutes a *nazir*-invalidating *tumah* is also the threshold for *Mikdash* liability.

### Rabbi Meir's Challenge

Rabbi Meir pushes back sharply. His argument is straightforward: even granting that there exist forms of *tumas meis* that do not require the *nazir* to shave — and we spent much of this *perek* cataloguing those cases — these are still forms of *tumah* derived from contact with the dead. How can they possibly be less severe than touching a *sheretz*, a dead rodent? Any *tumah* whatsoever generates liability upon entering the *Beit Hamikdash*. The *mishnah* is not discussing the rabbinically derived categories such as *skachos*, *praos*, or *Beis Hapras*, but rather cases that are assumed to be biblically rooted — cases that, despite their biblical status, are nonetheless exceptions to the rule of *nazir megalayach*. Rabbi Meir insists that the *nazir* exception cannot translate into an exception for *bias mikdash*; the person is still *tamei meis*, and that is enough to be liable.

### Beraitah Discussion

The *Gemara* is less interested in the substance of this debate than in a secondary observation: how did Rabbi Eliezer come to state this principle in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua? A *braisa* is introduced in which Rabbi Eliezer recounts that when he traveled to Ardaskaya, he found Rabbi Yehoshua ben Peser Rosh sitting and presenting his analysis before Rabbi Meir — and the content of that teaching was precisely the principle articulated in our *mishnah*: the categories of *tumah* that trigger *nazir megalayach* are the same that trigger liability for *bias mikdash*, and those that do not trigger the former do not trigger the latter. When Rabbi Meir responded with his challenge — again invoking the comparison to *sheretz* — it was Rabbi Eliezer who intervened.

### Rabbi Eliezer's Source

Rabbi Eliezer turned to Rabbi Meir and asked: are you familiar with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Mamo, and do you know how weighty an authority he is? Rabbi Meir replied that he was. Rabbi Eliezer then stated: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Mamo transmitted this ruling to me in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua — the *stam* Rabbi Yehoshua, that is, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya — and the content of that tradition is precisely this principle. With that citation, Rabbi Eliezer gave backing to the position of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Peser Rosh and confirmed the ruling in our *mishnah*.

This raises an obvious question: if Rabbi Eliezer received the tradition through Rabbi Yehoshua ben Mamo, why does our *mishnah* present it simply as Rabbi Eliezer saying it in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua, skipping the intermediate link entirely?

---

## Tradition Transmission

### Kadmaya and Batraye

The *Gemara* draws from this episode a principle about how chains of tradition are reported. From the fact that Rabbi Eliezer states a tradition as going directly from himself to Rabbi Yehoshua — omitting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Mamo, the authority from whom he actually received it — we learn that when a tradition passes through multiple links, it is sufficient and indeed standard practice to cite only the *kadmaya* and the *batraye*, the originator and the final transmitter. The intermediate authorities — the *metziaye* — need not always be enumerated.

### Nachman Example

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds a parallel illustration. Nachman haLavlur is quoted as saying: this is what I received from Rabbi Measha, who received it from his father, who received it from the *zugot* — the early paired authorities of the Second Temple era, such as Hillel and Shammai and those before them — who received it from the *neviim*, and this constitutes a *halakha leMoshe miSinai* going back to Moshe Rabbeinu. The specific content concerns planting dill and mustard seed in two or three separate locations in one's field, and the requirement to leave *peah* — a corner portion — independently for each section rather than one combined corner for the whole.

The precise details belong to the laws of *peah*, but the point the *Gemara* draws on is the structure of the transmission: Nachman haLavlur gives a chain that proceeds from himself through several generations back to the *neviim*.

### Omitted Authorities

The *Gemara* immediately asks: but where in this chain are Yehoshua and Chalev? We know from *Pirkei Avot* that Moshe transmitted the Torah to Yehoshua, Yehoshua to the *zekenim*, and the *zekenim* to the *neviim* — yet Nachman haLavlur's chain jumps directly from the *neviim* to earlier links without specifying Yehoshua and the *zekenim*. This confirms, *shema mina*, that one need not enumerate every intermediate step in a chain of tradition. Some steps may be skipped while still faithfully representing the lineage.

---

## Rabbi Akiva's Logic

### Kal Vachomer Argument

The next *mishnah* shifts to a debate between Rabbi Akiva and his teacher Rabbi Eliezer, and it is notable that the discussion is introduced with the same formula used earlier: *danti lifnei*, I laid out my argument before him. Rabbi Akiva formulates the following *kal vachomer*: a bone the size of a barley grain does not cause *tumah* through *ohel* — it lacks the power to render someone *tamei* by being in the same covered space — and yet a *nazir* must shave if he touches or carries such a bone. Now, a *revi'is* of blood — a quarter-*log* — does cause *tumah be'ohel*. Should it not follow, by an inference *a fortiori*, that a *nazir* who touches or carries a *revi'is* of blood should certainly be obligated to shave?

The elegance of the argument is worth pausing over. Rabbi Akiva is careful not to argue that the *revi'is* should cause *tumah be'ohel* for the *nazir* — that would require a different *kal vachomer*. He argues only about *maga* and *masa*, touch and carrying. If the little bone — which cannot even cause *ohel tumah* — is sufficient to obligate a *nazir* to shave when touched, then a *revi'is* of blood, which can cause *ohel tumah*, should certainly be sufficient to obligate shaving when touched. The existing rule held that shaving was triggered only from a half-*log* of blood, and Rabbi Akiva was pressing: why demand a half-*log* even for *maga*?

### Rabbi Eliezer Rejects

Rabbi Eliezer's response was terse: *mah zeh Akiva, ein danim mi-kal vachomer* — what are you doing, Akiva? Logical inference has no place here. These are arbitrary rules, and this is not the arena for your *kal vachomers*. He neither validated the argument nor explained why it was inapplicable; he simply dismissed it. This reaction reflects something fundamental about Rabbi Eliezer's orientation toward Torah: he famously never stated anything he had not received from his teacher, and the application of human logic to these received rules struck him as fundamentally misplaced.

### Rabbi Yehoshua Validates

Rabbi Akiva was unsatisfied with this response and brought the argument to Rabbi Yehoshua. Rabbi Yehoshua's reply was strikingly different in tone. He said: *yafeh amarta* — you have argued well. The argument is sound. But: *ella kach amru halacha* — nevertheless, this is the received tradition, and it stands as it is.

The distinction in approach is instructive. Both Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua arrive at the same bottom line — the *kal vachomer* does not change the *halacha*. But Rabbi Yehoshua validated the argument's internal logic while explaining why it nonetheless cannot override the tradition. Rabbi Eliezer simply rejected the enterprise of reasoning altogether. This dynamic reflects a broader tension running through the tradition between those who see *Torah she-be'al peh* primarily as the custodianship and transmission of received law, and those who see it as an ongoing intellectual engagement with text and logic. Rabbi Eliezer was paradigmatically the former; Rabbi Akiva — who brought unprecedented creativity and derivation to *halacha* — represented the latter. It is no coincidence that Rabbi Eliezer was more dismissive.

---

## Halakha L'Moshe Question

### Which Exception?

The *Gemara* now raises a pointed question: when Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua say that the *kal vachomer* is inappropriate because this is a *halacha*, what exactly is the *halacha leMoshe miSinai* being referenced? The *Gemara* presents two possibilities. One: the *halakha leMoshe miSinai* is the rule that even a bone the size of a barley grain — which lacks the power of *tumas ohel* — is sufficient to obligate a *nazir* to shave. Under this reading, the bone is the anomaly, and you cannot build a *kal vachomer* on an anomaly. Two: the *halacha leMoshe miSinai* is the rule that a *revi'is* of blood causes *tumas ohel* at all. Under this reading, the *revi'is* of blood is the anomaly, and it cannot be invoked as the stronger horn of a *kal vachomer*.

The reasoning behind the second possibility draws on the verse: *al kol nafshot meis lo yavo*. As *Tosafot* explains, a plain reading of the *psukim* might imply that the minimum for *tumas meis* is a half-*log* of blood — because *nafshot* in the plural suggests an amount sufficient for two lives, which would be two *revi'is*, totaling a half-*log*. On this reading, the *revi'is* of blood causing *tumas ohel* is itself a *chiddush*, a departure from what the verses suggest, and therefore cannot serve as the stronger premise of a *kal vachomer*.

### Bone as Exception

The *Gemara* resolves the question by citing a *braisa* explicitly: the rule that a bone the size of a barley grain obligates a *nazir* to shave is the *halacha leMoshe miSinai*. The *revi'is* of blood is not a *halacha leMoshe miSinai* in this context; Rabbi Akiva was attempting to derive it by *kal vachomer* from the bone. But since the bone is itself a designated exception — a *halacha leMoshe miSinai* — it cannot serve as the basis of derivation.

### Kal Vachomer Principle

This brings us to a broader principle established here: *ein danin kal vachomer me-halacha* — one cannot construct a *kal vachomer* using a case that is itself labeled as a *halacha leMoshe miSinai*. The reason is conceptual. A *halacha leMoshe miSinai* is, by its nature, a sui generis received tradition — it is not intended to convey a larger principle from which further law may be derived. The entire enterprise of *kal vachomer* depends on the premise that the stronger case is stronger because of some underlying logic. When a rule is categorized as a *halacha leMoshe miSinai*, it stands outside that logical framework. It is simply tradition, not a proposition whose implications can be extended by human reasoning.

One might ask why this should be so — surely a tradition received at Sinai carries the highest possible authority, and if anything one might expect it to be the most reliable premise from which to derive. The answer seems to lie in the nature of the two modes of *halacha*. When we engage *pesukim* through the thirteen hermeneutical principles, we are working within a system of intellectual derivation where each ruling participates in a larger logical discourse. *Halacha leMoshe miSinai*, by contrast, is pure received tradition, standing apart from that discourse. To borrow its specific ruling as a logical stepping stone would be to misappropriate it — treating as a logical proposition something that is, by definition, a tradition unto itself.

---

## Two Nazirims Safek

### Safek Setup

The next *mishnah* presents a new scenario. There are two *nezirim*, and a third person informs them: I saw one of you become *tamei* — perhaps he walked unknowingly into a burial ground — but I do not know which one of you it was. Each of the two *nezirim* is now a *safek nazir tamei*, a *nazir* of doubtful *tumah* status.

### Solution with Stipulation

The *mishnah* provides a practical resolution for this predicament. Since one of the two is definitely obligated in a *korban tumah* and the other is definitely obligated in a *korban tahara*, they do not each need to bring both sets independently with stipulations. Rather, they bring their respective sets together and stipulate: if I am the one who was *tamei*, then my *korban* is the *korban tumah* and yours is the *korban tahara*; and if I am the one who was *tahor*, then mine is the *korban tahara* and yours is the *korban tumah*. Because one of each is definitively owed, the full set of obligatory *korbanot* — including the *chatat ha-of* for *tumah* — can be brought without resorting to a *nedava* framework.

This approach is considerably more efficient than what a single *safek tamei nazir* would face. A single individual in that state cannot bring a full *korban tumah* set, since he may not be obligated, and faces additional complications around the *asham*, which cannot be brought either *misafek* or *bitnai*. Having a partner in the same predicament allows the full sets to be brought and directed appropriately.

---

## Two Nazirims Safek (II)

### Two Periods

Following the initial *korban* sequence, the two *nezirim* count an additional thirty days. One of them has just concluded — if he was the *nazir tahor*, he is now finished. But the other — if he was the *nazir tamei* — must now complete his reconstituted *nezirut*. At the conclusion of the second thirty-day period, again one of them is definitively obligated in a full *korban tahara*, and again a stipulation is issued: whoever is the *tamei* one, the earlier set thirty days ago was his *korban tumah*; whoever is the *tahor* one, the earlier set was his *korban tahara*. And now, the *korban tahara* brought at day sixty belongs to whichever of them still needs it. In this way, the full halakhic obligations of both possible scenarios are discharged without either person needing to know his own status.

---

## Safek Tumah Domains

### Sotah Principle

The *Gemara* raises an unexpected question on the entire framework of the *mishnah*: why are the two *nezirim* treated as *safek tamei* at all? The principle governing *safek tumah* — learned from the case of the *Sotah* — is: *safek tumah birshut hayachid, safeiko tamei; safek tumah birshut harabbim, safeiko tahor*. Doubtful *tumah* in a private domain is treated as *tamei*; doubtful *tumah* in a public domain is treated as *tahor*. This principle, derived conceptually from the *Sotah* case — where *v'nistra*, she went into seclusion, implies that only two parties were present — applies whenever a doubt arises in a setting of two people.

### Three Make Public

If there were two *nezirim* plus the witness who observed the incident, that is three people. Three people constitute a *reshut harabbim* for the purposes of this rule. And if it is a *reshut harabbim*, then *safeiko tahor* — both *nezirim* should be ruled *tahor*, and the entire elaborate procedure of the *mishnah* would be unnecessary. This is a striking problem.

*Tosafot* raises a further complication from the other direction. Even if we were to apply the *reshut hayachid* principle, the *halacha* in that case does not merely treat the person as *safek tamei* — it treats him as *vadai tamei*, definitively *tamei*, until cleared. Yet the entire *mishnah* operates within a framework of *safek*, not *vadai*. *Tosafot* resolves this by noting that since it is impossible for both of them to be *vadai tamei* — only one actually is — we cannot apply the *vadai* consequence to both simultaneously. The situation therefore remains in the realm of *safek*, even in a *reshut hayachid*, because the absolute ruling cannot be consistently applied.

### Distance Witness

The *Gemara* resolves the domain question through Rabba bar bar Huna: the case concerns a witness who was standing at a distance from the two *nezirim*. He observed them from afar — perhaps he saw a piece of a corpse thrown in their direction, or simply could not make out who was who — and did not share the same space. The two *nezirim* were therefore in a *reshut hayachid* unto themselves, since the witness was not with them in that enclosed space. This reading is reinforced by Rav Ashi, who notes that the precise language of the *mishnah* — *eini yodeia eizeh mikem*, I do not know which one of you — implies not that the witness forgot what he saw, but that he never knew in the first place, which fits naturally with the scenario of observing at a distance and being unable to identify which individual was involved.

---

## Shaving Problem

### Hakafa Concern

The *Gemara* now raises a difficulty with the mechanics of the *mishnah*'s solution. Both *nezirim* shave at the end of each thirty-day period. But if one of them is *tahor*, he has no obligation to shave the second time. He shaves anyway — to discharge the possible obligation of the one who is *tamei*. Yet in doing so, he shaves all the hair of his head. This raises the concern of *hakafa*: the prohibition of *lo takifu pe'at rosheichem*, not to cut the sidelocks in a circular manner. Even setting aside the question of whether this person's *nezirut* is over, does shaving all the hair of one's head violate this prohibition?

The *Gemara* notes that the *giluach* itself is not *me'akeiv* the completion of *nezirut* — one's *nezirut* ends regardless of whether one shaves. So one might argue: why not simply have both *nezirim* shave only once at day thirty, and forgo the second shaving, thereby avoiding any possible transgression? The *mishnah* nevertheless prescribes shaving twice. The question is how that is permitted.

### Shmuel's Answer

Shmuel resolves the difficulty: the *mishnah* is dealing with a case of a woman or a minor. A woman is excluded from the prohibition of *hakafa* because that prohibition is linked to the prohibition against shaving the beard — and since women do not typically have beards, they are outside the category entirely. Anyone excluded from the prohibition of shaving the beard is correspondingly excluded from the prohibition of *hakafa* of the sideburns. Thus, if the two *nezirim* are women, there is no *hakafa* concern, and both may shave freely at both junctures.

### Full Head Alternative

The *Gemara* challenges this: why did Shmuel resort to the case of a woman or minor at all? Another solution was available: perhaps shaving the entire head does not constitute a violation of *hakafa* in the first place. *Lo takifu* means to make a circular cut — to create a hairline that encircles the head. If one shaves everything and is left entirely bald, there is no hairline at all, and therefore no *hakafa* in any meaningful sense.

### Shmuel's Position

Since Shmuel does not offer this answer and instead specifies the case of a woman or minor, we may infer — *shema mina* — that Shmuel holds *hakafat kol harosh shemah hakafa*: shaving the entire head does constitute the prohibited *hakafa*. Under ordinary circumstances, an adult male who shaves all the hair of his head without halakhic justification violates this prohibition. The only way to permit the second shaving, therefore, is to situate the case where the individuals are not subject to the prohibition at all — hence women or minors.

---

## Four Shavings Case

### Mishnah Setup

Mar Zutra reports that Shmuel's discussion is presented not in connection with our *mishnah* but with a subsequent one, which we encountered in a recent *daf*: a *nazir* who is *safek tamei* and *safek metzora*. Such a person must spread out his obligations over sixty days and performs four separate shavings across that period. As a *metzora*, he shaves at the onset of his *tahara* process and again a week later at its conclusion; as a *nazir tamei*, he shaves at the end of his *tumah* period and again at the completion of his reconstituted *nezirut*. If he is *safek* in both categories, the four shavings are spaced across sixty days to accommodate all possibilities. Yet in each case, the possibility that a given shaving is unnecessary raises the same *hakafa* concern.

### Same Question Applied

The question and resolution follow the same logic. The *Gemara* asks why we permit an individual who may not be obligated to shave repeatedly, given the prohibition of *hakafa*, and Shmuel's answer is the same: *be-ishah ve-katan*, a woman or a minor. Since Shmuel requires this qualification rather than relying on the argument that shaving the full head is not *hakafa*, the inference stands: Shmuel maintains that shaving the entire head does constitute *hakafa* and is prohibited for an adult male under ordinary circumstances.

---

## Shaver Independence

### Adult Shaver Liable

At this point Rav Huna introduces a position that cuts against the implicit assumption in Shmuel's answer. Shmuel resolved the *hakafa* concern by making the *nazir* a woman or minor — implying that if the *shavee* is exempt from the prohibition, the shaving is permissible. Rav Huna challenges this framing: *ha-makif et ha-katan harei hu chayav* — one who shaves a minor is nonetheless liable. The prohibition of *lo takifu* operates independently for the *shaver*: if the shaver is an adult male, he transgresses regardless of who the *shavee* is, even if the *shavee* is a minor or a woman entirely outside the prohibition.

### Wife Shaving Issue
