Throughout the tractate, the *mishnayot* and *beraitot* have repeatedly assumed that women can be *nezirot*, as the *pasuk* itself states *ish o isha ki yafli lindor neder nazir* — "a man or a woman who takes a *nazir* vow." Women are not in the category typically excluded; they are explicitly included in the *parashah*. It is non-Jews who are singled out here as excluded.

### Women/Slaves Status

Having established that both women and slaves have *nezirut*, the *mishna* notes a stringency that applies to women but not to slaves: *she'hu kofeis avdo* — a master can force his slave in the matter of his *nezirut*, meaning he can effectively override his slave's *nezirut* and prevent him from maintaining it. *V'eino kofeis ishto* — a husband, however, cannot force his wife. This is notable because one might expect a husband to have the right to annul his wife's *nedarim*, particularly those touching on their relationship. Whether the *nezirut* restrictions — abstention from wine, prohibition from becoming *tamei* to the dead — constitute *devarim she'beino l'veina* such that the husband could annul them is an open question; the prohibition on cutting hair might theoretically fall within that category since it affects appearance, yet the *mishna* says he cannot override it.

The pseudo-Rashi on this passage clarifies: if a slave took a *nazir* vow, his master may force him to drink wine — i.e., to violate the *nezirut*. But if a wife took a *nazir* vow and the husband did not annul it in time, he can no longer nullify it, and he certainly cannot force her to violate it. The slave's *nezirut* remains revocable at the master's discretion; the wife's, once the window for annulment passes, becomes fully binding.

---

## Bnei Yisrael Source

### Bnei Yisrael Exegesis

The *gemara* asks: *minan hani mili* — from where do we know that non-Jews have no *nezirut*? The *baraita* answers: *Daber el Bnei Yisrael* — the Torah says "speak to the *Bnei Yisrael*," excluding non-Jews. Before returning to the exclusion of non-Jews, the *gemara* asks why the *baraita* also needs a verse to *include* slaves, since ordinarily slaves are obligated in all *mitzvot* that women are obligated in. Rava answers: one might have thought that the phrase *le-esor issar al nafsho* — "to bind a restriction upon oneself" — applies only to *b'mi she-nafsho kenuyah lo*, one who fully owns himself and can direct his own conduct. A slave, whose person is legally the property of his master, might not be in a position to impose binding restrictions upon himself. Therefore the *baraita* needs *ve'amarta aleihem* to include slaves — expanding beyond the *Bnei Yisrael* framework to encompass them. Curiously, this framing suggests that while a slave may not be capable of making an ordinary *neder* binding, his *nezirut* can nonetheless take effect — though his master may override it — which is itself a remarkable position.

Returning to the exclusion of non-Jews, the *gemara* notes that the phrase is *Daber el Bnei Yisrael*, excluding non-Jews. But *Daber el Bnei Yisrael ve'amarta aleihem ish o isha ki yafli lindor neder nazir* — the same passage also says *ish*, "a person," which is a broader inclusive term. By *erchin*, the *gemara* observes a parallel dynamic: *Daber el Bnei Yisrael* excludes non-Jews from being *ma'arich* — the one who declares another's value — yet *talmud lomar ish* comes back to include non-Jews in the category of *ne'erach*, the one whose value is declared. There is thus a "middle position" in *erchin*: non-Jews can be *ne'erach* but not *ma'arich*. One might ask whether the same logic applies to *nezirut*: *Bnei Yisrael* partially excludes non-Jews, but *ish o isha* partially includes them, yielding some middle status.

### Erchin Half-Status

The question is therefore sharpened: by *erchin*, we have a verse that generates a genuine half-status — non-Jews are inside the *parashah* as objects of valuation (*ne'erach*) even though they are outside it as active participants (*ma'arich*). Why can't we say the same about *nezirut*? *Bnei Yisrael* restricts their full participation; *ish o isha* might still grant them some partial entry into the *parashah*. What that middle position would look like is not immediately obvious — perhaps they observe *nezirut* without bringing a *korban*, or perhaps they have some attenuated form of the status — but the structural question is whether any partial inclusion is possible.

The *gemara* responds: *shani hacha d'amar kra* — this case is different, because the verse says *l'aviv ul'imo lo yitama* — the *nazir* may not become *tamei* to his father and mother. This locates the *nazir*'s laws within a framework of someone who has *tumah* — someone who *can* become *tamei*. From here the *gemara* begins its analysis of whether non-Jews fall within that framework at all.

---

## Tumah/Tahara Link

### Father Concept

The first attempt at reading *l'aviv ul'imo lo yitama* as an exclusion of non-Jews focuses on the word *aviv* — "his father." Perhaps non-Jews have no legally recognized father, such that the verse simply cannot apply to them. This is rejected immediately: *Rabbi Chiya bar Avin said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan* that a non-Jew does inherit from his father by Torah law, as the verse states *ki yerusha l'Esav natati et Har Se'ir* — "for I gave Mount *Se'ir* as an inheritance to *Esav*." The Torah itself recognizes the paternal line among non-Jews as legally meaningful for purposes of inheritance. The claim that non-Jews have no legal father is therefore untenable.

The *gemara* then asks whether the exclusion might derive from the *mitzvah* of *kibbud av* — perhaps the verse means to speak only about someone who has an obligation of honoring a father. Non-Jews are not obligated in *kibbud av*. The *gemara* rejects this as well: *mi ketiv kibbud avicha, kaveid avicha* by *nazir*? The *nazir* verses say nothing about *kibbud av*; they simply say father and mother. Moreover, the logic of being *mitamei* to relatives is not limited to parents — a regular *kohen* becomes *tamei* to siblings and children as well, where there is no *kibbud* relationship involved. Whatever the conceptual foundation of this category, it is not *kibbud av* per se.

It is worth noting that the idea of being *mitamei* to relatives is conceptually linked to *avelut* — it is from the *kohen*'s obligation to become *tamei* to the seven *krovim* that the obligation of *avelut* itself is derived, at least according to those who hold *avelut* is *d'Oraita*. So while *kibbud av* may be the most concrete expression of a child's responsibility toward a parent, the *gemara*'s category here is the broader one of relational obligation to *krovim*, and that does not map neatly onto *kibbud* alone.

### No Tumah = No Nezirut

The *gemara* then arrives at its key insight: *l'aviv ul'imo lo yitama* speaks only *b'mi she-yesh lo tumah* — about someone who has the capacity to become *tamei*. *Yatza akum she-ein lo tumah* — a non-Jew is excluded because a non-Jew does not become *tamei*. Since *tumah* is the organizing concept of the *nazir*'s prohibition to his parents — you cannot be prohibited from contracting *tumah* if *tumah* does not apply to you — non-Jews are categorically outside this *parashah*.

This is a striking *gemara*. It is not that the *halacha* lacks practical implications regarding non-Jews and *tumah*; quite the contrary. If a non-Jew touches a dead body and a Jew then touches him, determining the *Jew's* status requires knowing whether the non-Jew contracted *tumah* in the first place. These statuses matter even when they are not part of the non-Jew's own legal obligations.

### Parah Adumah Source

The *gemara* asks: *minayan dileis lehu tumah* — from where do we know that non-Jews have no *tumah*? The answer is a verse concerning the *parah adumah*: *veha'ish asher yitma velo yitchata venichreta hanefesh ha'hi mitoch hakahal* — a person who becomes *tamei* and does not undergo the *chitat* (sprinkling of the *parah adumah* ashes) and then enters the *Mikdash* or eats *kodshim* will be cut off *mitoch hakahal*, from the community. The word *kahal* refers specifically to *Klal Yisrael*. *Yatza zeh she'ein lo kahal* — one who has no share in *kahal*, i.e., a non-Jew, is excluded.

### Tahara-Tumah Link

The *gemara* anticipates an objection: perhaps all this verse teaches is that a non-Jew is not subject to *karet* for entering the *Mikdash* while *tamei* — *dilma kares hu d'lo mechayev* — but perhaps a non-Jew nonetheless *does* contract *tumah*. The *gemara* responds by citing a second verse: *vehizah hatahor al hatamei* — the *tahor* person sprinkles upon the *tamei* person. From here: *kol she'yesh lo taharah yesh lo tumah, vekol she'ein lo taharah ein lo tumah* — whoever has *taharah* has *tumah*, and whoever lacks *taharah* lacks *tumah*. Since a non-Jew lacks *taharah* — specifically the *taharah* of *parah adumah*, which the verse in *Parshat Chukat* restricts with *vehaysa la'adat Bnei Yisrael lemishmeret* — he therefore lacks *tumah* as well.

*Tosafot* notes a further question here: perhaps the linkage between *taharah* and *tumah* via *vehizah hatahor al hatamei* is drawn for a different *drasha* entirely, or perhaps the exclusion from *parah adumah* covers only that particular form of *taharah*, not all *taharah* generally — perhaps a non-Jew has *taharah* via *mikvah*, for instance. The *gemara* answers by citing *veha'ish asher yitma velo yitchata*, which explicitly connects *tumah* to the *chittui* of *parah adumah* through the phrase *velo yitchata*. That extra phrase, which would be unnecessary if the verse simply said *veha'ish asher yitma*, underscores that *tumah* and the *taharah* of *parah adumah* are inextricably linked. Since non-Jews are excluded from that *taharah* by *Bnei Yisrael* language in *Parshat Chukat*, and since *tumah* follows *taharah*, non-Jews have no *tumah* of any kind.

The upshot of this chain: non-Jews are excluded from *nezirut* because *l'aviv ul'imo lo yitama* requires the capacity for *tumah*; non-Jews lack *tumah* because they lack *taharah*; they lack *taharah* because the *parah adumah* is restricted to *Bnei Yisrael*; and the link between *taharah* and *tumah* is derived from *vehizah hatahor al hatamei* and *veha'ish asher yitma velo yitchata*.

### Nachala Alternative

Rav Acha bar Yaakov offers an alternative derivation. Rather than proceeding through *tumah* and *taharah*, he returns to the phrase *l'aviv ul'imo lo yitama* and argues that the word *aviv* is not fully applicable to non-Jews for a different reason. The verse in the context of slaves reads *vehenchaltem otam livneichem achareichem* — "you shall bequeath them to your children after you." From this: *kol she'yesh lo nachala yesh lo tumah* — whoever participates in this category of *nachala* (specifically, the bequeathing of slaves from one generation to the next) is within the *parashah* of *nazir*. *Kol she'ein lo nachala ein lo tumah* — whoever lacks this *nachala* is excluded.

Non-Jews, while they do inherit property from their fathers — as established earlier from *ki yerusha l'Esav* — do not legally bequeath slaves to their children in the manner recognized by *halacha*. The *halacha* recognizes that Jews own *avadim kena'anim* as legal property passed down through generations; it does not recognize the equivalent institution among non-Jews. Therefore, the *avir* of the non-Jew is not the full *aviv* the *pasuk* contemplates, and this excludes them from the *parashah*.

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: *i hachi avadim nami lo* — if the criterion is *nachala* of slaves, then slaves themselves would also be excluded from *nezirut*, since slaves obviously do not own and bequeath other slaves. Since we know slaves *do* have *nezirut*, this derivation fails. Accordingly, the *gemara* abandons Rav Acha bar Yaakov's approach and returns to Rava's formulation, which we take up next.

---

## Korban Exclusion

### Rava's Logic

Having set aside Rav Acha bar Yaakov's alternative, Rava presents a broader logical argument for why non-Jews are *categorically* excluded from *nezirut* — not merely partially excluded — and why the analogy to *erchin* (where a half-status exists) does not apply here.

The question, recall, is why *Bnei Yisrael* and *ish o isha* cannot generate the same middle position for *nezirut* that *Bnei Yisrael* and *ish* generate for *erchin*. Rava argues: *im mishum korban lo mehacha nafka leh* — if you were to say the partial exclusion would concern the *korban* — that non-Jews are excluded from *Bnei Yisrael* when it comes to bringing a *korban nezirut* but included via *ish o isha* in the status of *nezirut* itself — we don't need the *Bnei Yisrael* verse to tell us that. We already know from elsewhere that non-Jews cannot bring a *korban nezirut*.

The source is a verse in *Vayikra* 22:18: *daber el Aharon ve-el banav ve-amarta aleihem ish ish mi-beit Yisrael u-min hager be-Yisrael asher yakriv korbano le-chol nidreihem u-le-chol nidvotam asher yakrivu l-Adonai le-ola* — despite the phrase *mi-beit Yisrael*, the repeated *ish ish* expands the scope to include non-Jews, who may vow and bring *korbanot*. However, the verse concludes *le-ola* — only an *olah*. We accept an *olah* from a non-Jew; we do not accept other types of *korbanot*. Rabbi Yossi HaGlili derives explicitly: *le-ola perat le-nezirot* — the word *le-ola* excludes a *korban nezirut*, which comprises an *olah*, a *chatat*, and a *shelamim*. Since a non-Jew may only bring a *nedavah* *olah* and not the distinctive *korbanot* of *nezirut*, they cannot bring a *korban nezirut*.

Therefore, when we arrive at the *parashah* of *nezirut* and read *Bnei Yisrael*, the partial exclusion — the *korban* — is already accomplished. The only work left for *Bnei Yisrael* to do is *complete* exclusion. There is no room for a middle status, because the middle was already occupied by the earlier derivation.

### Half-Status Hypotheticals

The *gemara* examines whether other potential half-statuses might nonetheless have been entertained, such that we would need *Bnei Yisrael* to exclude them specifically and *ish o isha* to include them in some residual way.

The first suggestion: perhaps *Bnei Yisrael* excludes non-Jews from *nezirut olam* — permanent *nezirut* — but *ish* still includes them in ordinary, time-limited *nezirut*. Rabbi Yochanan dismisses this: *mi ketiv nazir olam*? Nowhere in the *pesukim* is *nezirut olam* even mentioned. If the *pesukim* do not address *nezirut olam* as a category, one cannot construct a partial exclusion based on it.

The second suggestion: perhaps *Bnei Yisrael* excludes non-Jews from the ability to impose *nezirut* on their children, while *ish* still includes them in their own personal *nezirut*. Again, Rabbi Yochanan answers: *halacha hi be-nazir* — the ability to make one's child a *nazir* is not derived from the *pesukim* at all. It is a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*, a tradition entirely outside the textual framework of the *pesukim*. Since it is not in the *pesukim*, the *pesukim* cannot be read as splitting on it.

### Child Nezirut

A third suggestion parallels the second: perhaps *Bnei Yisrael* excludes non-Jews from the *halacha* of *megalchim al nezirut avihem* — the practice whereby a son may shave, or bring a *korban*, in connection with his father's *nezirut* (a case discussed elsewhere in the tractate where a father and son accepted *nezirut* simultaneously, or where the son carries out the *nezirut* on behalf of the father in some capacity). Again, Rabbi Yochanan responds: *halacha hi be-nazir* — this too is *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*, not derived from the *pesukim*, and therefore the *pesukim* cannot be generating a partial inclusion or exclusion based on it.

The structure of Rava's argument thus emerges clearly: any partial exclusion of non-Jews from *nezirut* that might have been entertained is either already accomplished through other *pesukim* (the *korban* via *le-ola*), not actually contained in the *pesukim* of *nezirut* (the derivative *halachot* of child *nezirut* being *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*), or simply not referenced in the *pesukim* at all (*nezirut olam*). Since no coherent half-status remains possible, *Bnei Yisrael* in the *parashah* of *nezirut* can only serve as a complete exclusion — and the earlier derivation from *l'aviv ul'imo lo yitama* through *tumah* and *taharah* establishes the categorical ground for that exclusion.

---

---

# Nazir 62

## Non-Jews Excluded

### Prior Discussion Review

The *daf* opens in the middle of a sustained discussion about who is included in and excluded from *nezirut*. The *mishnah* includes women and slaves, and excludes non-Jews. The *gemara* had established that non-Jews are excluded from *nezirut* based on the *pasuk* of *daber el bnei Yisrael* — the commandment is addressed specifically to the Children of Israel. The *gemara* had then explored whether non-Jews might be partially included, following the model of *erchin*, where the phrase *ish ki yafli neder be-erkecha* creates a balance between *bnei Yisrael* and *ish*, yielding a middle position: non-Jews cannot make an *erech* vow, but they can be the subject of one — that is, a Jew who vows to pay the *erech* valuation of a non-Jew fulfills his vow according to the *Torah*'s fixed tables of valuation.

The *gemara* had considered whether a parallel middle position might exist for *nezirut*, and had rejected it on two grounds. First, the *pasuk* of *l'aviv u'l'imo lo yitama* — the *nazir*'s prohibition against contracting *tumah* for a parent — is inapplicable to non-Jews, who are not governed by the *Torah*'s *tumah* laws. Second, and more fundamentally, there is no logical middle position available for *nezirut*. The proposed middle position — that non-Jews would not bring a *korban nazir* but would remain bound by the other restrictions of *nezirut* — collapses, because their exclusion from the *korban nazir* is already established from a separate *pasuk* indicating that non-Jews may bring *korbanot* only as a *nedavah*, a free-will *olah* offering, not as a *korban nezirut*. With no middle position available, the *psukim* excluding non-Jews from *nezirut* must be understood as a total exclusion. The *gemara* had further considered other partial categories — *nazir Shimshon*, *nazir olam*, *madir et beno b'nazir* — and dismissed each, since those categories derive from *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* or from principles not dependent on the relevant *psukim*. The conclusion reached was that non-Jews are entirely excluded from *nezirut*.

### Erchin vs Nezirut

With that discussion resolved, the *gemara* pivots back to examine the *erchin* discussion more carefully. On 62a, the *gemara* asks: *ei hachi, ish ki yafli neder be-erkecha be-erchin lama li?* — given what was just established, why does the *Torah* need the word *ish* to include non-Jews partially in *erchin*? The *gemara* notes that *erchin* is explicitly linked to *nedarim*: the very *pasuk* that establishes *erchin* — *ish ki yafli neder be-erkecha* — frames an *erech* vow as a type of *neder*. And regarding *nedarim* generally, a separate principle already establishes the inclusion of non-Jews.

### Non-Jews as Subject/Obje…

The *baraita* cited is from Vayikra 22, where the *pasuk* reads: *ish ish mibeit Yisrael u'min hager b'Yisrael asher yakriv korbano l'chol nidreihem u'l'chol nidvotam asher yakrivu l'Hashem l'olah*. The double expression *ish ish* is interpreted as *lerabbot et ha-ovdei kochavim she-nodrim nedarim u-nedavot ke-Yisrael* — to include non-Jews who take vows and make free-will offerings like Israel, with the scope of that inclusion being *l'olah*, that is, *korbanot* of the free-will type. This encompasses not only animal offerings but vows of monetary gifts to the *beit hamikdash* and, by extension, *erchin* vows. Since non-Jews are already included in the *parsha* of *nedarim*, and *erchin* is a type of *neder*, they are already implicitly included in *erchin* — making the word *ish* in the *erchin pasuk* apparently redundant.

There is also a subtle double question embedded here. The prior discussion had concluded that non-Jews can be the *object* of an *erech* vow but not the *subject* — they can be *ne'erach* but cannot be the *maarich*. Yet the present discussion, which derives their inclusion from the fact that they can make *nedarim*, seems to imply that they can be the one making the *erech* vow. The tension between being the subject and being the object of *erchin* will be addressed shortly.

## Ish Ki Yafli Analysis

### Why Ish in Erchin

The *gemara* resolves the redundancy of *ish* in the *erchin pasuk* as follows: *ela hai ish miba'ei leih le-atuyei mufla samuch le-ish* — the word *ish* by *erchin* is needed not to include non-Jews in the *parsha* of *erchin* (which we already know), but rather to establish the principle of *mufla samuch le-ish*.

### Erchin Linked to Nedarim

Before developing this principle, it is worth pausing to appreciate the structure of the *gemara*'s reasoning. Since *erchin* is linked to *nedarim* — and the inclusion of non-Jews in *nedarim* is independently established — the word *ish* in the *erchin pasuk* must be doing something else. The *gemara* identifies that something else as the principle of *mufla samuch le-ish*, and once we understand that principle, we understand that *ish ki yafli* in the *erchin pasuk* (and, by extension, by *nedarim* and *nezirut*) teaches us something specifically about the maturity threshold for vow-making.

### Mufla Samuch L'Ish

The principle of *mufla samuch le-ish* is discussed in a *mishnah* in *Niddah* and related contexts. The idea is that a boy or girl within the year before reaching *bar* or *bat mitzvah* respectively — within the year before their age of majority — may have their vows tested. The question posed is: *nidrehem nivdakim* — do they understand what they are vowing? Specifically, do they appreciate the weight and significance of making a vow to God? If they demonstrate that understanding — *leshem mi nadaru* — then their vow is binding even during that year before majority. This principle applies not only to *nedarim* but to all categories that fall under *hafla'ah*, speech acts that create a change of status: *nezirut*, *hekdesh*, *korbanot*, and all the related categories discussed throughout *masechet Nedarim*.

There is an interesting question about whether this principle is *de'oraita* or *derabbanan*, and that question is now introduced. If it is *de'oraita*, then the *pasuk* of *ish ki yafli* is its source. If it is only *derabbanan*, then the *pasuk* must be doing something else — and the *gemara* proposes that in that case, *ish ki yafli* comes to teach the parallel principle as applied to non-Jews.

## Mufla Samuch L'Ish Theory

### Tosafot's Question

The *gemara* now articulates the apparent anomaly: *ha nicha le-man de-amar mufla samuch le-ish de-oraita* — that works well if this is a biblical principle derivable from the *pasuk* of *ish ki yafli*. *Ela le-man de-amar derabbanan*, but if it is only rabbinic for Jews, then the *pasuk* is freed up and *ish ki yafli* in the *erchin* context comes to teach *mufla samuch le-ish* for non-Jews: *le-atuyei mufla samuch le-ish de-ovdei kochavim*. This is a striking and counterintuitive result: the principle of *mufla samuch le-ish* would be only *derabbanan* for Jews but *de'oraita* — having a biblical source — for non-Jews.

*Tosafot* on 61b raises this very question and offers an answer. The relevant *Tosafot* explains: *d'vadai Yisrael d'lo havei bichlal bal yachel ad d'havei gadol* — a Jew is not yet subject to the prohibition of *bal yachel devaro* (do not violate your word) until reaching adulthood. And once he does become an adult, he is immediately included in *bal yachel*. The principle derived from the *gemara* in the *perek* of *yotzei dofen* is: *kol deleis b'bal yachel leis b'hafla'ah* — anyone who is not yet in the category of *bal yachel* is not yet capable of binding *hafla'ah*. Since the *mitzvot* governing vows do not apply to a minor, the speech act of vowing has no legal reality for him yet — he is not yet fully in the *parsha*, and therefore the vow cannot bind. This is why *mufla samuch le-ish* requires *derabbanan* reinforcement for Jews: without it, the minor before his year of *mufla samuch le-ish* would simply not be in the category at all.

### Bal Yachel & Formalism

A non-Jew, however, is never subject to *bal yachel* — that *mitzvah* is not part of *sheva mitzvot b'nei Noach*. Since the formal halachic category of *bal yachel* never applies to a non-Jew at any age, the logic of *kol deleis b'bal yachel leis b'hafla'ah* cannot be used to exclude a young non-Jew from making a binding vow. There is no formal line saying: until this age, you are not yet in the category. Hence the principle of *mufla samuch le-ish* can apply to non-Jews directly from the *pasuk*, without the same logical obstacle that necessitates rabbinic reinforcement for Jews.

This can be elaborated further. For Jews, what fundamentally matters is the formal halachic category: you are either in the category of *bar mitzvah* or you are not. The formal rule is absolute and does not yield to contextual assessment. By contrast, *sheva mitzvot b'nei Noach* does not operate with the same level of rigid formalism.

### Sheva Mitzvos Flexibility

This difference between Jewish law and *sheva mitzvot b'nei Noach* in terms of formalism and defined thresholds appears to be a broader structural feature. Consider *gezeila*: for Jews, there is no violation for stealing less than a *shaveh prutah*, because the *Torah* establishes that minimum threshold as the legal definition of meaningful money. For non-Jews, the prohibition of theft applies even to *pachos mishaveh prutah*. Similarly, consider abortion: for Jews, a fetus in utero is not legally classified as a *nefesh*, and the act is not subject to the full category of *lo tirtzach*. For non-Jews, the prohibition of *lo tirtzach* extends to include a fetus, as derived from the *pasuk* of *shofech dam ha'adam ba'adam damo yishafech* — *eizehu adam ba'adam*, what is a person within a person, that is a fetus. Notably, this is not a distinction based on the identity of the fetus but on the applicable law: a Jew aborting a non-Jew's fetus is not subject to *lo tirtzach*, and a non-Jew aborting a Jew's fetus is. The governing variable is the law applicable to the actor, not the status of the fetus.

What seems to emerge is that *sheva mitzvot b'nei Noach* does not draw formal lines — minimum monetary amounts, specific developmental thresholds, precise ages — in the same way that Jewish law does. Jewish law creates clear, observable, quantifiable criteria: this side of the line yes, the other side no. For non-Jews, the law operates in a less formalized mode, more sensitive to the concrete reality of each situation.

This structural difference illuminates the *mufla samuch le-ish* question in a new way. For Jews, the entire system of vow-making operates through formal categories: are you *bar mitzvah*? If yes, binding; if no, not binding; and perhaps there is a year before that has its own status — but even that is a formal rule, debated as to whether it is *de'oraita* or *derabbanan*. There is no room for a case-by-case assessment of individual cognitive maturity once you are past the threshold. For non-Jews, who is to say there is a formal age of majority at all? And even if there is, does it operate with the same categorical rigidity? The *gemara*'s approach — that non-Jews are assessed based on whether they understand what they are doing — reflects precisely this less-formalized framework. The question of whether a non-Jew has an age of majority, and what that age would be, remains genuinely open; but what is clear is that the assessment proceeds differently, without the hard formal lines of Jewish law.

## Yodea L'haflot Standard

### Ki Yafli Inclusion

The *gemara* now reconsiders the relationship between the debate about who is the subject and who is the object of *erchin* by non-Jews, and how *ish ki yafli* functions within each position. The *gemara* presents both sides of the debate. According to the view that *bnei Yisrael ne'erchin ve-ein ovdei kochavim ne'erchin* — Jews can be the object of an *erech* vow but non-Jews cannot be the object — the word *ish* comes to teach that non-Jews can be the subject, the *maarich*, which is already established through the *nedarim* connection, and *ki yafli* teaches the principle of *mufla samuch le-ish* for either Jews or non-Jews. That approach fits naturally with everything discussed so far.

According to the other view — *bnei Yisrael maarichin ve-ein ovdei kochavim maarichin* — Jews are the subject of the *erech* vow but non-Jews cannot make the vow, though they can be the object — the word *ish* comes to include non-Jews as valid objects of *erchin*, which the *gemara* notes applies even to an infant: *afilu tinok ben chodesh barucheihu*, even a month-old child can be the *ne'erach* since the tables of valuation in the *Torah* already account for that age. This is admittedly an odd exclusion: a non-Jew who can make all other types of *nedarim* and *korban* vows, who can be *makdish* property to the *beit hamikdash*, is nonetheless excluded specifically from making the *erech* vow. The *pasuk* excludes him from this particular formalized category, even while leaving him in every adjacent category.

If that is the case, then *ki yafli* is no longer needed to establish *mufla samuch le-ish* in the direction of including under-age individuals who understand what they are doing. Instead, *ki yafli* now functions in the other direction.

### Non-Jews Case-by-Case

*Amar Rav Adda bar Ahava*: *le-atuyei oved kochavim gadol d'af al gav d'gadol hu im eino yodea lehaflot* — *ki yafli* comes to teach that even an adult non-Jew, if he does not know what he is doing, if he does not understand the act of *hafla'ah*, his vow is not binding. This is exclusively applicable to non-Jews. For a Jew who is an adult, there is no case-by-case investigation into whether he understood the nature of his vow; he is an adult, and the vow is binding. Unless there is a clearly established and severe cognitive disability, the formal category of adulthood overrides any claim of ignorance. But for a non-Jew, even adulthood does not suffice — the question is whether he was *yodea lehaflot*.

This creates a perfectly symmetrical picture. For Jews: formal age of majority determines binding status; *mufla samuch le-ish* may be applied in the year before majority, but this is at most *derabbanan*, and the framework is categorical. For non-Jews: there is no formal line; a minor who understands what he is doing can be bound, and an adult who does not understand is not bound. The assessment is contextual and individual, not categorical and formal — precisely consistent with the broader structural distinction between Jewish law and *sheva mitzvot b'nei Noach* described above.

*Tosafot* notes that according to the opinion that non-Jews cannot be the *maarich* in *erchin*, the principle of *yodea lehaflot* derived from *ish ki yafli* is applied not to *erchin* itself but to all the other *nedarim* that non-Jews can make — *korbanot*, *hekdesh*, and similar categories. Even though they are excluded from the specific *parsha* of *erchin*, the *pasuk* speaks in the context of *erchin* but teaches a principle applicable to all their *hafla'ah* acts.

## Ki Yafli & Yad

### Ki Yafli by Nezirut

Having established what *ish ki yafli* teaches by *erchin*, the *gemara* now asks the parallel question about *nezirut*: *ela ki yafli d'chtav rachmana gabei nezirut lama li?* — why does the *Torah* also write *ki yafli* by *nezirut*? The relevant *pasuk* there is *ki yafli lindor neder nazir*. Since *nezirut* is explicitly linked to *nedarim* — *itkash nezirut l'nedarim* — anything derived from *ki yafli* by *nedarim* regarding *mufla samuch le-ish*, whether for Jews or non-Jews, automatically applies to *nezirut* as well. So what additional teaching does *ki yafli* provide in the *nezirut* context?

The *gemara* answers: *le-atuyei yadayim she'einan mochiachot* — to include the case of *yadayim* (handles, shorthand formulations of vows) that are not self-evident. A *yad* is an incomplete or elliptical expression that implies the rest of a vow — for example, a person walking in front of a *nazir* says *ehei*, "I will be," without completing the sentence. If the meaning is implied, it is a *yad mokhiach*, an evident handle, and it is binding. If it is not clear what was implied — a *yad she'einah mokhiach*, a non-evident handle — the question is whether such an expression is nonetheless binding.

### Abaye vs Rava Debate

*D'itmar yadayim she'einan mochiachot: Abaye amar havyan yadayim*, Abaye holds that even a non-evident handle is binding; *Rava amar lo havyan yadayim*, Rava holds it is not binding. According to Abaye, *ki yafli* by *nezirut* includes even the case of a *yad she'einah mokhiach* — even an ambiguous handle can constitute a valid *hafla'ah*. But for Rava, who holds that a non-evident handle is not binding, what is *ki yafli* teaching?

It should be noted that there is a well-known textual difficulty here: in other *gemarot* Abaye and Rava appear to hold the reverse positions from those attributed to them here, and *Tosafot* discusses various versions of the text and attempts to harmonize them with the positions found elsewhere. The ambiguity turns on how one understands the word *yafli* itself. If *yafli* connotes clear, articulate expression, then *ki yafli* could be read as demanding a high standard of explicitness — which would *exclude* a non-evident handle rather than include it.

### Rabbi Tarfon Position

For Rava, *ki yafli* by *nezirut* comes to support the position of Rabbi Tarfon: *ve-khid-Rabbi Tarfon, d'tanya Rabbi Yehuda omer mishum Rabbi Tarfon: ein echad me-hem nazir le-fi she-lo nitnah nezirot ela le-hafla'ah* — *nezirut* is valid only when it is made with complete and clear articulation. Rabbi Tarfon's position arises from the *mishnah* involving a chain of conditional *nezirut* vows, where various people vow to be a *nazir* depending on whether another person is or is not a *nazir*, with circular or indeterminate conditions. Rabbi Tarfon declares that none of them is a *nazir*, because the vow was never explicitly and unambiguously articulated at the moment it was made. According to this reading, *ki yafli* demands a degree of clarity and articulation that a *yad she'einah mokhiach* fails to provide. One could add that even a *yad mokhiach* involves incomplete articulation, though it is completed by inference — and *ki yafli* may come to include that case as well, while excluding the purely non-evident handle.

For the *rabbanan* who do not accept Rabbi Tarfon's stringent position, *ki yafli* by *nezirut* must be teaching something else entirely. And here the *gemara* arrives at a striking conclusion.

## Hattarat Nedarim

### Chagigah Mishna

The *gemara* cites: *hattarat nedarim porkhin ba-avir ve-ein la-hem al mah she-yismokhu* — the institution of *hattarat nedarim*, the annulment of vows, is as if floating in the air, with no biblical text to support it. This is in fact a *mishnah* in *Chagigah*, and it is striking that we have gone through the entirety of *masechet Nedarim* and all of *Nazir* without this *mishnah* having been placed more centrally in the discussion. There is a distinction worth drawing: the *mishnah* in *Chagigah* elsewhere describes certain areas of law as *harim ha-teluyin be-sa'arah* — mountains hanging by a hair, meaning there is at least *some* textual peg, however slender. *Hattarat nedarim*, by contrast, is described as floating entirely without support.

### Rabbi Eliezer Position

*Rabbi Eliezer omer yesh la-hem al mah she-yismokhu, she-ne'emar ish ki yafli, ki yafli shtei fe'amim* — Rabbi Eliezer disagrees and holds that *hattarat nedarim* does have a biblical basis: the fact that *ki yafli* appears twice, once by *nezirut* and once by *nedarim*. One mention of *ki yafli* establishes the *hafla'ah* of creating a vow; the other establishes the *hafla'ah* of annulling a vow: *echad hafla'ah le-issur ve-echad hafla'ah le-hetter* — one speech act of *hafla'ah* binds, and another speech act of *hafla'ah* releases.

### Hafla'ah Creates & Annuls

This is a conceptually significant framing. Until now, the understanding of *hattarat nedarim* has generally been rooted in the concept of *ta'ut* — the *chacham* identifies some element of error or mistaken assumption that was present when the vow was made, and on that basis declares it void retroactively. Even when *poskim* were lenient and did not require the person to identify a specific error he had at the time of the vow, the conceptual framework remained oriented around the idea of retrospective invalidity.

Rabbi Eliezer's derivation from *ki yafli shtei pe'amim* frames *hattarat nedarim* differently: it is itself an act of *hafla'ah*, a formal speech act by the *beit din* that produces a change of status. Just as the individual's *hafla'ah* creates the obligation, the *beit din*'s *hafla'ah* annuls it. This is not necessarily rooted in identifying a *ta'ut*; it is the exercise of a formal power. This is analogous to the husband's *hafarah* of his wife's vow, which works *mikan u-le-haba* — going forward, not retroactively — and is also understood as an annulment rather than a declaration that the vow was never made. *Heter neder* works retroactively, but under this conceptualization it may be understood as an exercise of a formal *hafla'ah* power rather than as a discovery of antecedent error.

One might observe that this framework has implications for the broader question of the power of *beit din* to act in the domain of *kiddushin* — the question of *hafka'at kiddushin* — where similarly the debate is whether *beit din*'s power rests on *ta'ut* (the marriage was always implicitly conditional on *beit din*'s approval) or on an independent formal power of annulment. The present *gemara* offers a suggestive parallel.

## Wife vs Slave Vows

### Annulment Distinction

The *gemara* moves to the next *mishnah* (62b): *chomer be-avadim mibanashim she-hu meifer nidrei ishto ve-eino meifer nidrei avdo* — there is a respect in which vows are more binding for slaves than for women, in that a husband can annul his wife's vow but cannot annul his slave's vow.

The asymmetry runs in both directions. A husband who annuls his wife's vow on the day he hears it annuls it permanently — *heifer olamit*. Even if he subsequently divorces her, or dies, the vow has been removed entirely. Whatever happens afterward, the *nezirut* is gone. This is a true *hafarah*, an annulment.

### Override Distinction

Conversely, a master has a power over his slave's vow that he does not have over his wife's vow: he can *kofe* — compel — his slave to violate his *nezirut*, requiring him to perform tasks that are incompatible with *nezirut* even if that means incurring *tumah* or drinking wine. He cannot do this to his wife. This is not an annulment but an override — the master's authority over his slave's labor and body allows him to demand behavior that conflicts with the slave's self-imposed restrictions, but it does not dissolve the *nezirut* itself.

This distinction is important: what the master exercises is a power of override grounded in his authority, not a power of annulment grounded in a spousal relationship. The slave, who is bound by *mitzvot* as a partial Jew, would — if compelled to incur *tumah* — need to undergo the relevant purification process and restart his *nezirut* count, even if the master's demand was halachically legitimate as an exercise of his authority.

### Slave Freed

If the slave is subsequently freed, the full *nezirut* becomes binding upon him: *yatza le-cherut mashlim neziruto*. The *mishnah* states this, and the *gemara* will develop it further.

## Override Nezirut, Not Ne…

### Comparative Power

The *gemara* now raises a question that was implicit in the *mishnah*: *lama ravo kofe le-nezirut aval lo le-nedarim u-le-erchin* — why does the master have the power to override his slave's *nezirut* specifically, but not to override other binding vows (*nedarim*) or *erchin* commitments? (Some versions of the text substitute *shevua* for *erchin*.) This seems puzzling, because the *pasuk* that would logically support the master's override — *le-esor isar al nafsho*, restricting oneself — appears in the context of *nedarim*, not *nezirut*. The *pasuk* continues: *b'mi she-nafsho knuya lo*, in the case of one who owns himself; *yatza eved she-ein nafsho knuya lo* — this excludes a slave, whose self is not his own. If this exclusion is read as rendering the slave's vow fundamentally non-binding, it would seem to apply to *nedarim* just as much as to *nezirut*. So why is the master's power limited to *nezirut*?

### Rav Sheshet Answer

*Amar Rav Sheshes*: The answer is circumstantial. The case under discussion by *nedarim* is one where a slave said *konam* on a specific cluster of grapes in front of him — *kegon she-hayah eshkol shel anavim munach lefanav*. By *nedarim*, forbidding that particular cluster does not significantly impede his service to his master: *deki nami mitzar be-hai lo mitzar be-achrinim* — even though he is restricted regarding this item, he is not restricted regarding other grapes. The master can simply direct him to eat other food. *Lo matzi kapi lei* — the master cannot compel him to eat that cluster, since there are alternatives.

But if the slave undertakes *nezirut*, the situation is categorically different: *deki mitzar be-hai mitzar be-khulhu* — the restriction on grapes applies to all grapes without exception. If the master requires him to eat grapes, or requires him to work in a vineyard and consume the produce, there is no alternative. *Matzi kapi lei* — the master can therefore override the *nezirut* and compel him to drink.

The *gemara* immediately challenges this answer as overly circumstantial. The same situation could arise by *nedarim*: if the slave made a *neder* on the only available food and would grow weak without eating it, *d'ilo achil lei chalish*, the same logic would seem to apply. Moreover, one might argue that *nedarim* are actually more likely than *nezirut* to interfere with a slave's service, since *nezirut* restricts only grape products, *tumah*, and haircuts — none of which arise in most ordinary work situations — while a *neder* could be made on any food, any activity, anything at all. If the criterion is whether the vow gets in the way of serving the master, *nedarim* would seem to pose at least as great a risk as *nezirut*. Rav Sheshet's answer, while constructing a case where *nezirut* does interfere, does not establish a categorical difference.

### Haroa O Haitiv

*Ela amar Rava*: Rava reformulates the case: imagine there were grape seeds — *chartzan* — in front of the slave. His *neder* applies only to these seeds; *be-hai hu de-mitzar lo matzi kapi lei* — the master cannot force him to eat them, since grape seeds are not essential nourishment and the slave can manage without them. But if he is a *nazir*, *d-mitzar nami be-achrinimi*, his restriction extends to all grape products. If the master needs him to eat grape seeds — however implausible — he can compel him. The *gemara* raises the same objection: *u'gabei nedarim mi lo askinan d'leika ela hai chartzan d'ilo achil lei chalish?* — what if the grape seeds are literally all that is available and the slave would grow weak without them? Again the distinction is purely circumstantial.

*Ela amar Abaye*: Abaye offers a fundamentally different answer. The question is not whether the vow happens to interfere with the slave's labor in a given situation, but rather what the law says about the binding nature of such vows in the first place. The *pasuk* of *leharei o lehaitiv* — said by the context of *shevua* — establishes that an oath is binding only when it restricts you from something you are permitted to do: *ma hatava reshus af hara'a reshus* — just as doing good is volitional, so too the bad one swears to must be volitional. This excludes an oath to harm others — *yatza leharei le-acherim she-ein reshus be-yado* — since one does not have the right to harm another person, an oath to do so is not binding.

Abaye extends this principle: when a slave takes a *neder* or *shevua* that restricts his service to his master, he is in effect doing harm to his master — *leharei le-acherim*. Since he has no right to harm his master in this way, the *neder* or *shevua* is simply not binding in the first place. This is why the master does not need to override it: there is nothing to override. This is a striking reversal of expectations. One might have thought the *neder* is binding but the master has power to override it; Abaye concludes that the *neder* is not binding at all.

For *nezirut*, the situation is different. The *pasuk* of *le-esor isar al nafsho b'mi she-nafsho knuya lo* applies, and the *gemara* had previously derived from this that the slave's *nezirut* is binding — but subject to the master's override. The exclusion there is categorical-sounding: *yatza eved she-ein nafsho knuya lo*. Yet the *halacha* treats it not as a total invalidation but as a situation where the *nezirut* is binding and the master has the power to override when necessary. The result is that for *nedarim* and *shevuot*, the slave's restricting vow is not binding at all, while for *nezirut* it is binding but overridable — which is, as the *gemara* notes, somewhat ironic, since the *pasuk* excluding the slave reads as a more categorical exclusion by *nezirut* than the *leharei o lehaitiv* reasoning does by *nedarim*.

## Slave Ran Away

### Rabbi Meir vs Yose

The *gemara* then presents the case of a slave who ran away from his master. Rabbi Meir says *lo yishteh* — the slave may not drink wine; his *nezirut* is binding even when he is not in his master's presence. Rabbi Yose says *yishteh* — he may drink; the *nezirut* is overridden even when the slave has run away.

### Mafkir Question

The *gemara* first asks whether this dispute reflects the ruling of Shmuel. Shmuel holds: *ha-mafkir avdo yatza le-cherut ve-ein tzarich get shichrur* — if a master renounces monetary ownership of his slave, the slave automatically acquires free personal status without needing a formal *get shichrur*, a writ of manumission. The reasoning is that a slave's monetary status and his personal status are linked: loss of the former automatically produces the latter. If the slave ran away and the master has effectively abandoned his claim, perhaps this constitutes *mafkir*, and the slave is now free — in which case, according to Rabbi Meir who holds like Shmuel, the slave would be fully free and therefore fully bound by his *nezirut*; while Rabbi Yose, who does not hold like Shmuel, would say the slave is still a slave and his *nezirut* remains overridable.

The *gemara* rejects this framing: *d'kulei alma isleih d'Shmuel* — everyone could hold like Shmuel. The case here is not one where the master has truly renounced ownership; he expects the slave to return or to be recaptured. The master's monetary claim is still in effect. The question is therefore not about personal status at all but about the master's interest.

### Master's Interest

The entire rationale for the master's power to override the slave's *nezirut* is that the master needs the slave to serve him effectively, and the *nezirut* gets in the way of that service. The override is justified by — and limited to — the master's practical interest. The question when the slave has run away is therefore: what does the master's interest dictate?

According to the position that says *yishteh* — Rabbi Yose — the master still wants the slave to drink wine and remain strong: *savar sof sof mehadar hadar ve-ati gabei* — the master expects ultimately to recapture the slave or have him return. Therefore, *lishki chamra ke-heichi d'lo likhush* — the master wants him to drink now so he stays strong for when he is recaptured. The same interest that justifies the override when the slave is present — keeping him strong and capable of service — applies even when he is away.

According to the position that says *lo yishteh* — Rabbi Meir — the master's interest when the slave has run away is precisely the opposite: *savar lihavy leh tzara ke-heichi d'lahadar gabei* — the master wants the *nezirut* to remain binding and the slave to be restricted, so that the slave will be motivated to return in order to escape the discomfort of his restrictions. On this view, the override does not apply when the slave is away, because the master's interest is now served by *allowing* the *nezirut* to bind, not by overriding it.

Both opinions agree that the master has not renounced ownership and the question turns entirely on how we assess the master's interest in the slave's absence — a purely circumstantial determination with no categorical resolution, dependent on the specific relationship between the master's authority and the slave's situation in each case.
