# Nazir 63

## Nazir Discovers Tumah

### Opening Topic

The mishnah at the top of daf 63 introduces a substantially new topic. The preceding discussion concerned which categories of persons are subject to the laws of *nezirut* — concluding, for instance, that a Canaanite slave (*eved*) is included while non-Jews are not. Now the mishnah turns to an entirely different question: the case of a *nazir she-gilach ve-noda lo she-hu tamei* — a *nazir* who completed his thirty-day term, brought his *korbanot*, shaved, and only then discovered that at some point during his *nezirut* he had been *tamei*. Perhaps someone has just informed him that the house he entered a week earlier contained a corpse. He now confronts the realization that his *nezirut* was retroactively compromised, that he brought his *korbanot* in a state of *tumah*, and that seemingly his entire *nezirut* was invalidated.

### Tumah Yeduah vs. Tehom

The mishnah distinguishes between two categories of *tumah*. If it was *tumah yeduah* — a known *tumah*, meaning one that was known to others even if not to the *nazir* himself — then *soter*, his entire *nezirut* is retroactively demolished. He must begin the thirty days again, bring new *korbanot*, and shave again, just as if he had discovered the *tumah* at the moment it occurred. However — and here lies the *chiddush* of the mishnah — if it is *tumat ha-tehom*, *tumah* of the depths, a particular category of hidden *tumah*, then *eino soter*: his *nezirut* is not invalidated, and he has fulfilled his obligation through his *korbanot* and his shaving.

### Tumat Tehom Exception

The concept of *tumat ha-tehom* is at first striking, because in both cases the *nazir* was, in fact, *tamei* in hindsight. In neither scenario did he know about it at the time, and yet only one category — *tumah yeduah* — destroys his *nezirut* while the other does not. The *chiddush* of the mishnah, then, is this exception: a certain class of hidden *tumah*, if discovered only after the *nezirut* is complete, does not retroactively undermine it.

### Before/After Shaving

The mishnah adds a critical qualification: *im ad she-lo gilach, bein kach u-vein kach soter* — if he discovered the *tumah* before he shaved, then regardless of whether it was *tumat ha-tehom* or *tumah yeduah*, his *nezirut* is destroyed and he must begin again. The *chiddush* of *tumat ha-tehom* applies only when he discovers the *tumah* after he has finished — that is, after he has shaved. The mishnah's emphasis on shaving (*gilach*) as the operative endpoint raises a question about the structure of the rule.

### When Does Nezirut End

The mishnah's emphasis on *gilach* as the critical boundary invites a question: does this formulation assume that *nezirut* is not complete until the *nazir* has shaved? This would align with the position of Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that *tiglachat me'akevet* — the shaving is indispensable and the *nezirut* is not concluded until all the *korbanot* and the shaving have been performed. By contrast, the Rabbis hold that *keivan she-nizrak alecha echad min ha-damim yatza* — once one blood-offering has been sprinkled on the *nazir*'s behalf, his *nezirut* is concluded. One might therefore wonder whether the mishnah's reference to shaving is specifically tied to Rabbi Eliezer's position, or whether the rule of *tumat ha-tehom* independently creates a requirement to wait until shaving. The *gemara* will resolve this: the operative principle is whether the *nezirut* is over, whatever that point is determined to be. If we adopt Rabbi Eliezer's view, then "before he shaved" is simply the way of saying "before his *nezirut* concluded." If we adopt the Rabbis' view, then safety comes once he has brought his first *korban* — the shaving is simply the marker of completion under Rabbi Eliezer's framework, not an independent requirement of *tumat ha-tehom*.

---

## Cave Example

### Immersion Scenario

The mishnah proceeds to illustrate the concept of *tumat ha-tehom* with a concrete case. *Yarad litbol be-mearah* — he descended to immerse himself in a cave, and afterward it was discovered that there was a *met*, a corpse, *tzaf al pi ha-mearah*, at the mouth or opening of the cave. The precise topography here requires some interpretation. Based on Tosafot, it appears that the body was located at or near the entrance of the cave, in the same body of water in which the *nazir* immersed, so that if the body was there at the time of his immersion, he would have been beneath the same roof (*ohel*) as the corpse. The question is whether the body was there when he immersed — he did not see it, but it has now been discovered.

### Floating Meaning

The word *tzaf*, ordinarily translated as "floating," generates some puzzlement in context. What does it mean for a corpse to be floating at the mouth of a cave? The most coherent reading, aided by Tosafot, is that the body was floating in the water at the entrance — that is, the body of water in the cave extended to the mouth, and the corpse was found floating in that same water. If the corpse was there when the *nazir* immersed, he would have been in *ohel* relationship with it — beneath the same enclosed roof of the cave. The question of whether he was *tamei* turns on whether the corpse was actually present during the immersion.

### Floating vs. Buried

The mishnah then draws a distinction that is the heart of the *tumat ha-tehom* rule. *Nimtza tzaf* — if the corpse was found floating, exposed to the open air, then *tamei*: this is not *tumat ha-tehom*, and the *nazir*'s *nezirut* is destroyed. *Nimtza meshuka be-karka ha-mearah* — if the corpse was found buried in the floor of the cave, and the *nazir* went down *le-hakir*, to cool himself, then *tahor*: this is *tumat ha-tehom*, and his *nezirut* stands. The core distinction is between *exposed* and *buried*. Something that was out in the open — even if neither the *nazir* nor anyone else happened to see it — is categorically not *tumat ha-tehom*. Something buried beneath the ground is. Neither scenario involved the *nazir* knowing about the *tumah* at the time, yet only the buried case qualifies.

### Tosafot Explanation

One might ask why the mishnah switches its language mid-case — using *tovel* (immersing) in the floating scenario and *le-hakir* (cooling oneself) in the buried scenario — since the reason one entered the cave would seem irrelevant to the *halakha*. Tosafot explains that the switch is deliberate and reflects a double *chiddush*. When a person enters water for the purpose of *tevila*, he is being scrupulous about his *tahara* and presumably attentive to any potential source of *tumah*; yet even such a careful person is considered to have encountered *tumat ha-tehom* if the body was buried — while still being considered *tamei* if the body was exposed, even though he missed it. In the reverse direction, a person who entered simply to cool off is presumably less vigilant; yet even for such a person, if the body was buried, it is *tumat ha-tehom*. Both directions of the switch carry a *chiddush*.

### Burial + Unknowable

The mishnah focuses on the distinction between buried and exposed, but it leaves implicit a second requirement that the *gemara* will make explicit: the *tumah* must not only be buried but must also have been entirely unknown — *ein echad makirah be-sof ha-olam*, not known to anyone anywhere in the world. If a body is buried but the local community is aware of the grave — even if the *nazir* himself did not know — that is not *tumat ha-tehom*. A *beit ha-pras*, for example, would not qualify, since people are generally aware of it. The mishnah does not spell this out, but the *gemara* will.

---

## Purification Case

### Tumah During Purification

The mishnah introduces a further limitation on *tumat ha-tehom*. *Yarad litaher mi-tumat met* — if he descended to immerse not simply as a general act of purification but specifically to complete his purification from a prior *tumat met*: he had already been in contact with a corpse, undergone the sprinkling of the ashes of the *parah adumah*, and was now going to the *mikveh* to finalize his *tahara*. During this immersion, it is subsequently discovered that there was a buried, unknown corpse — the very type of buried, unknowable *tumah* that in the earlier case would have qualified as *tumat ha-tehom*. Nevertheless, the mishnah rules: *tamei*, his *nezirut* is *soter*. The principle of *tumat ha-tehom* does not apply here.

### Chazakah Principle

The mishnah explains the ruling with the principle: *shechazkat tamei tamei, shechazkat tahor tahor, she-raglayim la-davar* — the presumptive status (*chazaka*) of a *tamei* person is *tamei*, and the presumptive status of a *tahor* person is *tahor*, and there is a *raglayim la-davar*. The operative logic is *chazaka*: this person entered the *mikveh* with the legal status of *tamei*. His status was already *tamei*, and the discovery of a buried corpse would have, if anything, extended or compounded that *tumah*. Since his *chazaka* was *tamei*, we do not apply the benefit of *tumat ha-tehom* to spare him — his starting status was already compromised. The *tumat ha-tehom* exception was designed for a person who began from a *chazaka* of *tahor* and encountered a wholly hidden *tumah*; it does not extend to one whose legal status was already *tamei*.

### Chazakah vs. Evidence

It is worth distinguishing between *chazaka* and what the mishnah calls *raglayim la-davar*, which the mishnah uses in conjunction with the *chazaka* principle. *Chazaka* is not a probabilistic claim. It does not assert that a person is *more likely* to have retained a certain status; it is a legal operating principle by which, for *halachic* purposes, we treat a person's status as unchanged until we have affirmative information otherwise. Whether I touched a *tamei* object or not is a factual matter about which *chazaka* says nothing in terms of likelihood; it simply instructs the *halacha* to presume status quo. *Raglayim la-davar*, by contrast, normally denotes circumstantial evidence — factual grounds that give some support to a conclusion. Used here alongside *chazaka*, the phrase perhaps means that the *chazaka* itself gives the status "legs," a kind of permanence and solidity, rather than referring to independent circumstantial evidence. Alternatively, *raglayim la-davar* might be used loosely. The distinction between these two modes of legal reasoning — presumptive status versus circumstantial support — is worth bearing in mind throughout the discussion.

One might also observe that the mishnah's phrase *tamei* vs. *tahor* in describing the outcomes of these cases is itself somewhat imprecise. As the Rambam's language makes clear, the real question in all of these cases is *soter* vs. *lo soter* — whether the *nezirut* is retroactively invalidated. Even when the mishnah says *tahor* in the *tumat ha-tehom* case, the *nazir* is not literally *tahor*: he still must go through the process of becoming *tahor* (sprinkling of *parah adumah* ashes, *mikveh*, etc.). What the *halakha* means is that his *nezirut* and his *korbanot* were not destroyed. The Rambam consistently frames these cases in terms of *soter* and *eino soter*, and that is the more precise formulation.

Regarding the ultimate source of *tumat ha-tehom*, one might anticipate that such a counterintuitive principle — that a person retroactively known to have been *tamei* is nonetheless treated as having fulfilled his *nezirut* — must derive from a specific *pasuk*, and the *gemara* will indeed explore textual sources. But it is worth noting now that the mishnah itself offers no derivation, and the *gemara* will ultimately conclude that *tumat ha-tehom* is a *halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*, or at minimum a very ancient tradition (*gemara gemiri lah*) whose source cannot be traced through standard *drashah*.

---

## Sources Drashah

### Pesuk Nazir

The *gemara* asks *mina hanei mili* — from where do we derive this extraordinary rule? Rabbi Elazar cites a *pasuk* from the laws of *nazir*: *ve-chi yamut met alav be-feta pitom* — "and if a dead body dies upon him suddenly" (Numbers 6:9). The phrase *alav* — "upon him," meaning in his clear awareness — is read to indicate *be-mechuveret lo*, that which is manifest to him. When the death is sudden and plain (*pitom*), the *nazir* is *tamei*. The implication is that when the *tumah* was *not* manifest to him — not sudden, not in his direct awareness — a different rule applies, creating the category we are calling *tumat ha-tehom*.

### Pesuk Pesach

Resh Lakish derives the principle from a different *pasuk*, one concerning the *korban Pesach*: *ki yihyeh tamei la-nefesh o be-derech rechoka* — "if a man is *tamei* for a dead body or on a far road" (Numbers 9:10), which describes when a person brings *Pesach Sheni*. The key word Resh Lakish focuses on is *derech*, a road or path. *Mah derech be-galuy* — just as a road is exposed and open to public view, *af kol be-galuy* — so too any *tumah* that qualifies under this verse must be "out in the open." By implication, the criterion of *tumat ha-tehom* for *Pesach* is that the *tumah* was *not* in the open — it was covered and buried. Thus from this *pasuk* we derive the "exposed vs. buried" element of the rule.

### Combining Sources

Together, these two *pesukim* could in principle yield both criteria of *tumat ha-tehom*: from *alav* ("upon him") we derive the requirement of unknownness — the *tumah* must not have been in the awareness of the person or, as we will see, of anyone; and from *derech* ("road") we derive the requirement of being covered and buried, not exposed. One might thus synthesize the two and construct the full definition of *tumat ha-tehom* from these verses. However, the *gemara* raises a difficulty. The *baraita* on *tumat ha-tehom* requires not merely that the *nazir* was unaware, but that *ein echad makirah be-sof ha-olam* — not a single person in the world knew of the *tumah*, even someone at the farthest end of the earth. If one uses the *pasuk* of *alav* as the source, one might conclude only that *the nazir himself* was unaware, and that if anyone at the far end of the world happened to know, it would still be *tumat ha-tehom*, since it was still not "upon him." The *gemara* observes that the *pasuk* of *derech* might support the notion that the *tumah* must be unknown to all — since a path implies public awareness — but the derivation is strained. Ultimately, the *gemara* concludes that these *pesukim* cannot satisfactorily yield both criteria.

### Baraita Dead Body

The *gemara* quotes a *baraita* that articulates the critical case: *ha-motze met mushkav le-rochbah shel derech* — if one finds that a corpse was laid out spanning the full width of a road. Here there is no *safek* about whether the traveler passed over the *met*: since the corpse covered the entire width of the path, anyone who walked that road definitively passed over it and was under *ohel* with it. For ordinary *tumah* purposes, *be-tumat ha-met* — the person is *tamei*. But *benazir ve-oseh Pesach tahor* — for the *nazir* and the one performing the *Pesach* offering, the *baraita* declares them *tahor*, meaning their obligations were not invalidated.

This is a striking case because it is not a *safek* — it is a certainty, in hindsight, that the person was *tamei*. Yet *tumat ha-tehom* saves him for purposes of *nezirut* and *Pesach*. This will be important later when the *gemara* considers whether *tumat ha-tehom* requires an element of doubt (*safek*) or operates even in cases of retrospective certainty.

Given the difficulties in deriving *tumat ha-tehom* from *pesukim*, the *gemara* concludes: *tumat ha-tehom gemara gemiri lah* — it is a received tradition. The Rambam characterizes it as *davar zeh halakha mi-pi ha-kabalah*. Whether *gemara gemiri lah* is precisely synonymous with *halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* is a matter of some discussion. Rashi in several places treats them as identical. The Netziv, drawing on the Rambam and other *rishonim*, suggests that *halakhata gemiri lah* may refer to an ancient, enshrined tradition of very early *batei din* whose source is no longer known — not necessarily a tradition transmitted orally from Sinai in the technical sense, though it carries full *de-oraita* authority. The phrase *halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* is itself sometimes used loosely in *tannaitic* literature, as the gemara's preference for the Aramaic formulation here may simply reflect linguistic register rather than a substantive distinction.

As for the practical scope of *tumat ha-tehom*: the *halakha* applies specifically to *nazir* and *oseh Pesach*, not to *terumah* or other categories of *tahara*. If someone ate *terumah* and subsequently discovered he had been subject to a *tumat ha-tehom*, he does not benefit from any exemption — he violated the prohibition, albeit *be-shogeg*. The *halakha* of *tumat ha-tehom* is a specific leniency carved out for *nezirut* and *Pesach*.

---

## Rami's Question

### Timing Question

Having established that *tumat ha-tehom* was defined as a *halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*, and that the mishnah's emphasis on shaving reflects the position of Rabbi Eliezer, the *gemara* turns to a question posed by Rami bar Chama. This is distinct from the *tumat ha-tehom* context — Rami bar Chama is asking about an ordinary *tumah yeduah*. His question: *nitma be-toch melot ve-noda lo le-achar melot mahu* — if the *nazir* became *tamei* during his thirty days, but the discovery occurred only after the thirty days were complete, what is the *halakha*? Does the timing of discovery matter? Specifically: *batar yedi'ah azlinan* — do we follow the moment of discovery? And since the discovery was after the thirty days, is it treated more leniently, analogously to a case where *tumah* occurred after the thirty days?

To frame the question precisely: Rabbi Eliezer holds that *tumah* occurring *after* the thirty-day term does not destroy the entire *nezirut* — the *nazir* need not restart thirty days, but merely waits seven days to become *tahor* before bringing his *korbanot* (*soter shiva*). The question Rami bar Chama raises is whether *tumah* that occurred *during* the thirty days but was only *discovered* afterward might be treated similarly, on the grounds that the discovery came late — or whether the factual reality that *tumah* occurred during the *nezirut* is determinative, regardless of when it was discovered.

### Rava First Answer

Rava responds by directing attention to the mishnah: *ta shema, ad she-lo gilach, bein kach u-vein kach soter* — even in a case of *tumat ha-tehom*, if he discovered the *tumah* before he shaved, the *nezirut* is destroyed either way. The force of this proof: the phrase *bein kach u-vein kach* ("either way") implies that the mishnah is addressing a case where the discovery came after the thirty days but before the shaving — since if he discovered it *during* the thirty days, the ruling would be obvious and not worth stating. Therefore, the mishnah teaches: even when discovery occurs after thirty days have elapsed, if it was before shaving (and thus, per Rabbi Eliezer, before *nezirut* was concluded), the *nezirut* is *soter*. This would appear to resolve Rami bar Chama's question: we do not follow the moment of discovery; we follow the moment of *tumah*.

### All vs. Seven Days

The *gemara* does not rest here, however. Even granting that it is *soter*, a further question emerges: *kulo soter o shiv'ah soter mahu* — does the *tumah* destroy the entire thirty days, requiring the *nazir* to recommence from the beginning, or does it only obligate a seven-day waiting period (*soter shiva*)? This question becomes interesting specifically in the context of Rabbi Eliezer. The Rabbis hold that *tumah* requiring a restart is always thirty days; under their view, whether the *tumah* occurred during or after the term, the outcome is thirty days. But Rabbi Eliezer's position is more nuanced: he holds that *tumah* occurring after thirty days is *soter shiva* only. The mishnah under discussion is, as established, the position of Rabbi Eliezer. So now: under Rabbi Eliezer, if the *nazir* became *tamei* during the thirty days but discovered it only afterward — is that treated like *tumah* after thirty days (*soter shiva*), or like a standard mid-*nezirut* *tumah* (*soter hakol*)?

The *gemara* raises the possibility that *soter shiva* might apply here, reasoning that since the *yedi'ah* came after *melot*, perhaps Rabbi Eliezer would treat it similarly to *tumah* occurring after the term. Conversely, since the *tumah* itself occurred during the thirty days, perhaps it destroys the full *nezirut* even for Rabbi Eliezer.

### Mishnah Conclusion

The *gemara* concludes by observing that the mishnah employs the language *bein kach u-vein kach soter* — "either way it is *soter*" — without distinguishing between the case of becoming *tamei* during the term and discovering it during the term, on the one hand, and becoming *tamei* during the term and discovering it afterward, on the other. Tosafot, the Rosh, and the pseudo-Rosh on this *daf* all read the *gemara*'s conclusion as follows: since Rabbi Eliezer rules that *tumah* after thirty days is *soter shiva*, and since the mishnah draws no distinction between that case and the case of *tumah* during thirty days discovered afterward, the *gemara* equates them — and the conclusion is that even *tumah* occurring *during* the thirty days, if discovered only afterward, is *soter shiva* under Rabbi Eliezer's view. This reading is, as must be acknowledged, not immediately transparent from the *gemara*'s language. The argument is that since the mishnah does not differentiate, we infer that the case of late discovery is treated identically to the post-term *tumah* scenario — which Rabbi Eliezer rules is *soter shiva* rather than *soter shloshim*. This is a striking conclusion, and the reading requires some care.

---

## Full Baraita

### Road Span Case

The *gemara* now quotes the full *baraita* on *tumat ha-tehom*. The first case: *ha-motzi met mutal le-rochbah shel derech* — a corpse discovered lying the full width of a road, buried and unknown (*tumat ha-tehom*). The ruling: *le-trumah tamei* — for *terumah* purposes the person is *tamei*; *u-venazir u-ve-oseh Pesach tahor* — but for *nazir* and *oseh Pesach*, the principle of *tumat ha-tehom* applies and his obligations were fulfilled. The use of *tahor* here is somewhat loose, as noted above: he is not literally *tahor* and must still undergo the purification process; the meaning is that his *nezirut* and *Pesach* obligation are not invalidated.

### Escape Route

The *baraita* immediately qualifies this ruling: *bameh devarim amurim she-ein lo makom la-avor* — when is this true? When there was no space to pass around the body — the corpse genuinely spanned the entire width, leaving no room for the traveler to have avoided it. *Aval yesh lo makom la-avor* — but if there was a small strip of the path, even a foot's width at the edge, that the corpse did not reach, such that a person walking that extreme edge would have avoided the *met*, then even for *terumah* the person is *tahor*.

### Public Domain

The reason is the principle of *safek tumah be-reshut ha-rabim*: a public road is a *reshut ha-rabim*, and a *safek* about *tumah* in a *reshut ha-rabim* is ruled *tahor*. Even if the probability of having walked in that narrow strip is very small — 5% of the road's width was clear, 95% covered — the existence of any possibility that one avoided the corpse is sufficient in a *reshut ha-rabim* to declare the person *tahor* for all purposes, including *terumah*.

### Body Condition

The *baraita* adds a further qualification: *bameh devarim amurim she-matza'o shalem* — when is the ruling about a clear path being sufficient to be *tahor* applicable? Only when the body was whole. *Aval meshubar o mefurak* — if the body was broken apart or dismembered, even if there was a clear path, *chayshinan bein perakim avar* — we are concerned that the traveler may have woven through the gaps between the limbs, which means he could have passed through the space occupied by the body without walking over any single part. The logic is that a dismembered body presents multiple gaps, and it is possible that the traveler threaded his way through them rather than walking over any portion. In such a case, even the possibility of having avoided the corpse does not save him, because we are concerned that he may in fact have passed between the limbs and thus been in *ohel* with the body through the gaps.

### In Coffin

However: *u-ve-kever* — if all the limbs, even if dismembered, were enclosed in a coffin that spanned the full width of the path, then *afilu nishbar u-meforak tamei*, even if dismembered, the person is *tamei*. The reason is *mipnei she-ha-kever mitztarfo* — the coffin unites all the contents as a single legal unit. One may recall that a coffin (*kever*) itself has the status of the *met* it contains; everything within the coffin is treated as a single entity. Therefore there are no "gaps" through which the traveler could have passed — the entire coffin is the *met*, and one cannot weave between its contents.

### Walking vs. Carrying

*Bameh devarim amurim* — all the above leniencies concerning the possibility of having avoided the body apply *be-mahalech be-raglav*, when the traveler was walking on foot. *Aval ta'un o rachuv* — if he was carrying a burden or riding on an animal, then *tamei* even where there might have been a narrow escape route. The reason: *lefi she-ha-mahalech be-raglav efshar lo she-lo yiga ve-shelo yasit ve-shelo yahil* — a person walking on his feet can be precise enough in his movements to potentially avoid touching, shifting, or creating an *ohel* over the corpse. But *ee efshar she-lo yiga ve-shelo yasit ve-shelo yahil* — a person burdened with a load or mounted on an animal cannot control his movements to the same degree; he will inevitably have leaned, swayed, or extended over the space in a way that creates *tumah*. The *halakha* here is calibrated to circumstantial reality: not every claimed scenario is evaluated individually, but a general assessment is made that a mounted or burdened traveler cannot achieve the precision of avoidance that a careful walker might.

### Definition Criteria

After all these cases, the *baraita* provides the formal definition: *ve-eizehu tumat ha-tehom, kol she-ein makkirin otah be-sof ha-olam* — *tumat ha-tehom* is any *tumah* that is unknown to anyone, even at the far end of the world. *Makkira echad be-sof ha-olam, ein zo tumat ha-tehom* — if even one person anywhere knew of it, it does not qualify. This is the unknowability criterion.

### Straw vs. Crevices

The burial criterion is also specified precisely. *Hayah tamun be-teven o bi-tzrorot* — if the body was buried under straw or under pebbles, *harei zu tumat ha-tehom* — this is *tumat ha-tehom*. The *chiddush* is that even covering as light as straw is sufficient to qualify as "buried" for this purpose. On the other hand, *be-yamim u-va-afelah u-venekikei ha-sla'im* — if it was in water, in darkness, or in a crevice of a rock, *ein zo tumat ha-tehom* — these do not qualify as "buried." The apparent paradox is that a body in a rock crevice — which might be very difficult to see — is considered exposed, while a body under straw is considered buried. The best understanding is that "buried" in this context means covered *in a manner that the ground conceals it*, whereas a crevice, even a deep one, is part of the open landscape and thus "exposed" in the relevant legal sense. The precise limits of this distinction are not fully spelled out by the *baraita*.

### Met Only

Finally, the *baraita* closes: *ve-lo amru tumat ha-tehom ella met bilvad* — the entire principle of *tumat ha-tehom* applies only to *tumat met*, the *tumah* of a corpse. This makes sense: *tumat ha-tehom* is the specific exception carved out for *nazir* and *oseh Pesach*, and the relevant *tumah* for both of those contexts is *tumat met*. Other forms of *tumah* (such as *tumah* from a *sheretz*, etc.) are not subject to this exception.

---

## Floating Objects

### Sheretz Floating

The *gemara* uses the case in the mishnah — which involved a *met* that was described as *tzaf*, floating — as an occasion to examine an entirely separate *halakha* regarding floating and *safek tumah*. The principle to be established: a floating *tumah* — not related to *tumat ha-tehom*, but a floating *sheretz* (one of the eight creeping creatures whose carcass conveys *tumah*) — creates a *safek* that is treated more leniently than a standard *safek tumah be-reshut ha-yachid*. The *baraita* states: *safek tumah safa, bein bi-kelim bein bi-karka, tehorah* — a doubt about *tumah* involving a floating object, whether floating in a vessel or floating in the ground, is ruled *tahor* according to the *tanna kamma*, even in a *reshut ha-yachid*, where ordinarily a *safek tumah* would be ruled *tamei*.

### On Earth Drashah

The basis for this ruling: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi derives it from a *pasuk*. The verse states *be-khol ha-sheretz ha-shoretz* — "all creeping things that creep," which would imply that contact with any *sheretz* anywhere renders one *tamei*. But the verse also says *al ha-aretz* — "on the ground." Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi reconciles these by distinguishing between *vadai maga'o* and *safek maga'o*. If one *certainly* touched the *sheretz*, one is *tamei* wherever the *sheretz* is — on the ground, in water, floating anywhere. But if there is a *safek* whether one touched it, then *al ha-aretz* — one is only *tamei* when the *sheretz* was on the ground. If it was floating, and there is a *safek* about the contact, one is *tahor*.

### Floating Tahor

The logic, on reflection, is that floating objects are in some sense less "present" in a space than objects resting on the ground. The principle of *safek tumah be-reshut ha-yachid tamei* operates on the premise that the *tumah* source is fixed and present in a private domain; the *safek* is purely about whether contact occurred. But a floating object is not anchored — it is less definitively "there" — and the verse *al ha-aretz* limits the *safek tumah* rule to cases where the *tumah* source is resting on solid ground. In a *reshut ha-rabim*, this distinction is academic since *safek tumah be-reshut ha-rabim* is always *tahor*; the ruling matters only in a *reshut ha-yachid*, where the floating exemption overrides what would otherwise be a presumption of *tumah*.

### Shimon Vessels

Rabbi Shimon disagrees with the *tanna kamma* in one respect: *bi-kelim tamei, bi-karka tahor* — if the *sheretz* was floating in a vessel, a *safek* about contact renders one *tamei*; if floating in the ground (i.e., in a body of water naturally in the ground), one is *tahor*. Ulla explains Rabbi Shimon's source: the verse *akh mayan u-vor mikveh mayim yihyeh tahor* — "but a spring, a pit, or a collection of water shall be *tahor*" — establishes that water naturally contained in the ground has a special status of *tahara*. But the verse also states *yitma* — implying that in other contexts *tumah* does apply. Rabbi Shimon reads this as distinguishing between floating in a natural body of water in the ground (*tahor* for a *safek*) versus floating in a vessel (*tamei* for a *safek*). Tosafot raises the question of whether the same principle would apply to an object flying through the air rather than floating in water — if a *sheretz* was thrown and one is uncertain whether it struck him, does the "not on the ground" exemption similarly apply? The question is raised but not resolved.

# Nazir 65

## Single Unknown Burial

### Body in Normal Position

The *mishnah* at the bottom of 64b opens with a case that has little direct connection to *nazir* per se, but picks up on thematic associations with the opening *mishnah* of the tractate — particularly the principle of *tumat hatehom* and the phrase *raglayim ladavar*. The *mishnah* begins: *hamotzei meit techila* — if someone discovers a dead body that was previously unknown, *mushkav kedarko*, lying in the normal burial position. As the *gemara* will clarify, this specification is not incidental; it comes to exclude certain other cases, as we will see.

The scenario presupposes a body that has been discovered, perhaps in the middle of a road or a field — somewhere it does not belong in the public sphere. In ancient times, if someone died while traveling, the practical exigencies of the moment might have compelled companions to bury the body wherever they happened to be, with the intention perhaps of returning later to relocate it properly. The paradigmatic case from *Tanach* is that of *Rachel*, about whom it is written *vatikaver sham bederech Ephrat* — she was buried right there on the road. Such a burial was understood not to confer a permanent right on that location.

### Removal & Reburial

Given that such a burial was understood as temporary and not conferring a permanent claim to the site, the *mishnah* rules: *notlo v'et tfusato* — one removes the body together with its *tfusa*. The word *tfusa* derives from *l'tpos*, to grab or seize, and refers to the surrounding earth that is taken up along with the body. The body is then to be reburied in a proper cemetery. The rationale for the relocation is to ensure that *kohanim*, *nezirim*, and others obligated to avoid *tumat meit* are not prevented from using the road or area.

### Purpose of Dirt

Why is the surrounding dirt taken as well? At first glance this might seem puzzling. After all, bodily fluids in themselves, once the person has died, do not necessarily constitute a primary source of *tumah* — the classic categories of *tumat meit* are flesh, bone, and blood in specific quantities. One might ask, then, what is the concern that drives the requirement to remove the surrounding earth?

The answer seems to be that the concern is not purely about *tumah* in the technical sense but about *kevura* — the dignity and integrity of the burial. One wants all the remains of the *meis* to be reinterred together. There is also a possibility, as the *gemara* will elaborate, that some material in the surrounding earth genuinely could contribute to the halakhic quantities of *rekev* — the decomposed matter of a corpse — that do cause *tumah*. The *mishnah* continues: if two bodies are found, *shnayim notlan v'et tfusatan* — you take both and the surrounding dirt of each and rebury them. But the critical ruling comes next.

## Shechunat Kvarot

### Two Bodies

The discovery of a single body, or even two bodies, does not by itself trigger any assumption of a graveyard. Each is treated individually: you remove it with its surrounding earth and rebury it elsewhere. No special investigation of the surrounding area is required. It is only when three bodies are found that the analysis shifts fundamentally.

### Three Bodies Threshold

*Matza shlosha* — if three bodies are discovered — *im yeish bein zeh l'zeh arba amot ad shmoneh*, if there is between them a spacing within a range of four to eight *amot*, then *harei zeh shechunat kvarot* — this constitutes a *shechunat kvarot*, a neighborhood of graves, that is to say, a graveyard. The logic of the four-to-eight *amot* range is that this corresponds to the spacing one would expect in a crypt or cemetery. If the bodies were too close together, one might suspect a mass burial under some tragic circumstance rather than a planned cemetery. If they were too spread out, they would simply appear to be isolated individual graves with no relation to one another. Within this particular range, the arrangement reflects what one would expect of a deliberately organized burial site.

What precisely the four-to-eight *amot* range means in terms of the layout of the three bodies is itself a matter of detailed discussion. *Tosafos* engages at length with this question in light of a *gemara* in *Bava Basra* concerning how bodies were placed in *kuchim* — burial niches or crypts. *Tosafos* offers the possibility that two of the bodies are within four *amot* of each other, while the full range extends to eight *amot* for all three, though the precise geometric arrangement remains somewhat unclear.

### Twenty-Cubit Radius

Once three bodies are found within this range and the location is declared a *shechunat kvarot*, the *mishnah* mandates a further investigation: *bodeik mehemenu u'lehalan esrim ama* — one must check outward from this point twenty *amot*. The presumption is that if this is indeed a graveyard, there may be further burials beyond those three initially discovered, and one must determine the full extent of the graveyard.

If within that twenty-*ama* radius another grave is found, then *bodeik mehemenu u'lehalan esrim ama* — you must check again, another twenty *amot* from that new discovery. The graveyard is assumed to be continuing, and the investigation must keep pace with each new find. The phrase the *mishnah* invokes for this cascading investigation is *raglayim ladavar* — there is good circumstantial evidence warranting continued suspicion that the graveyard extends further.

This is one of the two reasons this *mishnah* appears here rather than simply in a tractate dealing with purity law. First, the subject matter involves buried *tumah* of unknown provenance — *tumat hatehom* — which connects to the opening *mishnah* of the tractate. Second, the phrase *raglayim ladavar* appears here and connects textually to the *mishnah* that preceded it, though in that earlier context the phrase carried a somewhat different nuance: there it referred to a pre-existing basis — the person had already been *tamei*, and that prior status formed the foundation upon which a new *tumah* was assessed. Here, *raglayim ladavar* carries its more common meaning of circumstantial evidence justifying ongoing investigation.

### Context Matters

The *mishnah* concludes with an important interpretive point: *she'ilu techila matza'o notel et tfusato* — had you found that one body alone, in isolation, you would simply have removed it with its surrounding dirt and reburied it elsewhere. You would not have been required to conduct any twenty-*amot* investigation, and even had you proactively done so and found another grave twenty *amot* away, you would not have declared the area a graveyard. You would have treated each grave as a separate isolated burial.

But now, because you began with a cluster of three graves, and this additional grave falls within the twenty *amot* radius of that cluster, the interpretive context is entirely different. The same grave that in isolation would have been treated as a lone burial is now read as part of the graveyard. This is a striking illustration of how the identical physical fact — one grave — can carry entirely different legal significance depending on what has already been established about the surrounding context.

Implicit in the *mishnah*, though not stated explicitly, is a principle the *gemara* spells out: once a location is determined to be a *shechunat kvarot*, the bodies there are not to be disinterred. They have a right to remain where they are. The original permission to disinter a lone grave rests on the assumption that the burial there was incidental — no one plants a permanent cemetery in the middle of a road. But if there is a graveyard, the graveyard predates the road, the road was built over the graveyard, and the bodies have every right to their place. In that case, you do not disinter the graves; you reroute the road.

## Exceptions & Exclusions

### Discovered vs. Known

The *gemara* proceeds to interpret each qualifying term in the *mishnah* as excluding a category of case. The method is one of *prat lezeh* — each word of the *mishnah* functions to exclude something, though the *gemara* notes somewhat wryly that this sounds like the style of *derashah* applied to a biblical verse, whereas here it is being applied to a *mishnah*. Nevertheless, the *mishnah* clearly articulates criteria, and those criteria function to exclude cases that do not meet them.

*Matza* — discovered — *prat lematzuy*: this applies specifically to a body whose existence was previously unknown. If a grave was always known to exist in a particular place, that changes the analysis entirely. A known grave is not subject to disinterment; its location was established and has always been recognized. The permission to move a grave depends on the assumption that it was an incidental or emergency burial; a known grave carries with it the presumption that it was intentionally placed there.

### Murdered Bodies

*Meit* — if it is a dead body — *prat le'harug*, as opposed to someone who was murdered. The *gemara* is about to cite the principle that these rules apply only when the body is whole, and a murdered or dismembered body would by definition not be whole. This explains the exclusion, at least in part, though *Tosafos* acknowledges that the rationale for excluding a murdered body is not made fully explicit.

### Position Criteria

*Mushkav kedarko* — lying in the normal way — *prat leyoshev*, as opposed to sitting upright, and *prat leroshon munach bein yarchosav*, as opposed to a fetal position with the head placed between the knees. These exclusions address cases where the burial posture suggests the body may be that of a non-Jew. The normal Jewish burial practice was to lay the body horizontally; sitting or fetal positions were associated with non-Jewish burial customs. Notably, Bronze Age burials in the land were often in a sitting position, so this is not merely a theoretical concern. If the body is non-Jewish, then *tumat ohel* does not apply according to the ruling that a non-Jew does not convey *tumat ohel*, and therefore the entire apparatus of investigation becomes irrelevant.

### Incomplete Bodies

*Tani Ulla bar Chanina*: a *braita* teaches that if the body is incomplete — *meit she'chasar ein lo tfisah* — there is no requirement to take the surrounding dirt, *velo shechunat kvarot* — and if three such incomplete bodies are found, one does not establish a *shechunat kvarot* from them.

This ruling raises a genuine question. The consequence in all these exclusion cases is not that one is prohibited from disinterring — it is, if anything, more lenient: one *can* disinter without the additional stringencies. One need not take the surrounding earth, and one need not worry that three such bodies establish a graveyard. The only case where disinterment is clearly prohibited is the case of a *known* grave — *prat lematzuy* — where the presumption is that the grave has a right to remain in place.

But *Tosafos* raises the question: what is the logic for saying that an incomplete body does not establish *shechunat kvarot*? The answer given is *halacha leMoshe miSinai* — which *Tosafos* acknowledges is, formally speaking, something of a last resort in terms of explanations, though it acknowledges that the tractate has had occasion to invoke *halacha leMoshe miSinai* repeatedly.

As for the cases where the exclusion is based on the possibility that the bodies are non-Jewish — there are two possible consequences: either you are still allowed to disinter but without the stringencies of *tfusa* and *shechunat kvarot*, or, if we assume the bodies are non-Jewish, you may simply move on entirely, since a non-Jewish body does not convey *tumat ohel* and there is no *tumah* concern driving the investigation in the first place.

### Head-to-Foot Burial

*Matza shnayim, rosho shel zeh b'tzad marglotav shel zeh, v'rosho shel zeh b'tzad marglotav shel zeh* — if two bodies are found buried in a head-to-foot, head-to-foot arrangement, lying parallel to each other in alternating orientation — *ein lahem tfusa v'lo shechunat kvarot*. Here too one does not take the surrounding dirt, and three such burials do not establish a *shechunat kvarot*. This type of arrangement is not consistent with normal Jewish burial practice, suggesting once again that these may be non-Jewish graves, or at least that something atypical is occurring that should not trigger the full apparatus of the graveyard rules.

### Mixed Known/Unknown

*Matza shlosha, echad yadua u'shnayim techila* — if three bodies are found, one of which was always known and two of which are newly discovered — or, switching to a group of four, two known and two newly discovered — *ein lahem tfusa v'ein lahem shechunat kvarot*. Even though three or four bodies are present, if the group is a mixture of known and newly discovered graves, neither *tfusa* nor *shechunat kvarot* applies in the same way.

*Tosafos* explains the logic for the *shechunat kvarot* exclusion, which at least makes a certain amount of sense. The category of *shechunat kvarot* applies either to three bodies that were all previously known — in which case they constitute a recognized graveyard — or to three bodies all newly discovered — in which case we infer that this must be a forgotten graveyard. But a mixture of the two does not fit either category. If it were a recognized graveyard, one would have known about all three. If it were a forgotten graveyard, one would have found all three newly. The mixed case falls between the categories; one can simply assume that the known graves were always there and the newly discovered ones are coincidental additions. There is no basis to declare the entire area a graveyard.

As for why *tfusa* also does not apply in the mixed case, *Tosafos* quotes the *Rashbam* who invokes *halacha leMoshe miSinai*.

## Yeshevav & Akiva

### Yeshevav's Attempt

The *gemara* records a historical incident: *maaseh b'Rabbi Yeshevav she'badak u'matza shnayim yeduyim v'echad techila* — there was a case involving Rabbi Yeshevav who investigated and found two graves that were previously known and one that was newly discovered. He sought to declare this combination a *shechunat kvarot* and to cordon off the surrounding twenty *amot* for investigation.

### Akiva's Rebuke

Rabbi Akiva said to him: *kol she'yagata l'rik yagata* — all the effort you have put in is for nothing. The phrase is striking and evokes something of the sensibility of *Kohelet* — all our efforts amount to naught. But the legal point is sharp: *lo amru shechunat kvarot ela l'gimel yedua'im o l'shlosha techila* — the category of *shechunat kvarot* was said only when all three are previously known or all three are newly discovered.

### Pure Graveyard Status

The requirement is, in other words, categorical uniformity. Either three known graves — a recognized graveyard — or three newly discovered graves — a forgotten graveyard. Any mixture of the two, and one does not have grounds to declare the area a *shechunat kvarot*. Rabbi Akiva's rebuke also carries a practical dimension: declaring large areas to be graveyards has significant consequences for the public, foreclosing movement through those areas for *kohanim* and others who must avoid *tumat meit*. There is therefore good reason to be precise about when the threshold is met.

## Tfusa & Soil

### Tfusa Definition

The *mishnah* says *notlan v'et tfusatan* — one takes the bodies and their *tfusa*. The *gemara* asks: *heichi dami t'vusa* — what exactly constitutes the *tfusa*?

### Egypt Derivation

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar kra* — Rav Yehuda derives it from a biblical verse: *amitatni miMitzrayim* — "take me up from Egypt," the words of Jacob to Joseph regarding his burial. The *drasha* reads into the phrase the idea that Jacob was asking that some of Egypt — some of the earth — come with him. Rashi explains this as connected to the notion that Jacob did not want to remain in *adama tme'ia*, impure soil, and wished to be brought back to the land of Israel along with some of the surrounding earth.

### Three Fingers Earth

Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok specifies: *notel afar tichuach* — one takes the loosened, dug earth, *v'chofer b'vetula* — and one also digs into the virgin, undisturbed earth beneath the body, *gimmel etzba'ot* — three finger-widths deep. The rationale is that bodily fluids are assumed to have seeped even into the undisturbed earth beneath the corpse.

### Coffin & Shards

The *gemara* then raises a *braita* that appears to give a different account of the *tfusa*: *v'kama hi tfusa — peirash Rabi Elazar b'Rabi Tzadok: notel et hakismin v'et hatzrorot*. Here the *tfusa* is described in terms of taking *kismin* — splinters, presumably from the coffin — and *tzrorot*. *Tosafos* explains *kismin* as material rubbed off from a marble coffin, and as for *tzrorot*, Rashi explains them as clumps of earth that have absorbed blood and brain matter from the body — *tzrorot adama shenit'havu min hadam u'min hamuach* — so that they may contain substance that contributes to the halakhic quantities of the *meis*.

### Sifting Remains

What is significant about this *braita* is that it does not simply say one takes all the surrounding earth indiscriminately. Rather, there is a process of sifting and discrimination: *v'zorek et havada'in* — you discard that which is certainly not part of the *meis*; *u'maniach et hasfeikot* — you set aside in a secluded place that which may possibly contain part of the *meis*, so that people engaged in matters of *tahara* should not come into contact with it; *v'hashar mitztaref l'rov binyano shel meis u'l'rov minyano u'l'mlo tirvad rekav* — and what is clearly identified as part of the body itself combines toward the threshold quantities: the majority of the body's structure (*rov binyano*), the majority of the body's count of bones (*rov minyano*), or the *melo tirvad rekav* — a full ladle's worth of the decomposed matter of the corpse — all of which are the halakhic thresholds for *tumat meis*.

This is notable because it addresses the question raised earlier about *why* the surrounding dirt is removed. It is not a blanket concern about any fluid; it is because specific identifiable material — material that genuinely constitutes part of the *meis* or its decomposition — may have mingled with the earth, and that material contributes to the *shiurim* that convey *tumah*. One does not remove everything; one tries to identify what genuinely matters.

The *gemara* notes that the earlier formulation — simply taking three finger-widths of dug and virgin earth — reflects the view of a different *tanna*, and that *Rav Yehuda amar Rav* follows that position. The *braita* of sifting and selecting follows a different approach.

### Rekev Problem

*Tosafos* raises a difficulty connected to this passage. For material to count as *rekev* — decomposed matter of a corpse — and to contribute to the *shiur* of *melo tirvad rekav*, it must be pure, uncontaminated by foreign matter. But if the body was buried with fragrances, spices, or other materials placed in the *aron*, as was apparently common practice, then any decomposed matter would be contaminated by these foreign substances and would not qualify as *rekev*.

*Tosafos* addresses this by suggesting that the *kismin* in the *braita* refer to ground-off fragments of a *marble* coffin — *aron shel shayish shenichtat* — rather than a wooden coffin. The reason is that a wooden coffin would itself decompose along with the body and potentially disqualify the *rekev*. If the coffin is marble, this problem is avoided. But this solution in turn raises its own difficulty: if the coffin is marble, how would bodily fluids seep out far enough into the surrounding earth to be a concern? The discussion illustrates how intricate these questions become once one tries to reconcile the *braita*'s details with the underlying halakhic requirements for *rekev*.

## Sequential Discovery

### Third Body Found

*Amar Rava*: suppose one checks and disinters, then checks again and disinters, and then on a third occasion finds another body — *badak ufina, badak ufina, badak ve'ashkach, mahu* — what is the law? The question is this: if a person had already removed the first two bodies and then discovered a third, the three together would constitute a *shechunat kvarot*. But the two have already been disinterred. What now?

### Retroactive Graveyard

The tension is between two considerations. On one hand, retroactively one can say this was a *shechunat kvarot* all along, and therefore the bodies had a right to remain where they were and should not have been disinterred. On the other hand, the disinterment of the first two had already been completed before the third was found; at that point in time there was no reason to suspect a *shechunat kvarot*.

### Rava's Compromise

Rava rules: *lo hai mafni leh legabi hanach terei, velo hani terei legabi hai chad* — you do not move the third to join the two that were disinterred, since you now know it was part of a graveyard; but you do not need to reinter the two alongside the third either. Each situation is left as it currently stands. The two that were already moved remain where they were reinterred, and the third remains in its original location.

### Continue Disinterring

*Ika d'amri* — there is an alternative formulation of Rava's ruling: *keivan she'nasna reshut lefanot, mefaneh lehawn* — once permission to disinter was granted, one may continue and disinter the third as well. Since the process was already legitimately begun — two were already moved — and since practically speaking there is a communal interest in having all bodies in proper cemeteries rather than scattered about fields and roads, once one has started one may continue.

### Ilu Matzu Principle

The *gemara* asks: *velishavinhu shechunat kvarot* — why not simply declare this a *shechunat kvarot* and leave all three in place? Reish Lakish answers: *ilu matzu v'tiharu Eretz Yisrael* — they found an excuse and thereby purified *Eretz Yisrael*. The idea is that there is a broader interest in keeping *Eretz Yisrael* accessible and navigable for *kohanim*, for those engaged in *taharos*, and for the public generally. When any excuse presents itself to treat a site as not a *shechunat kvarot* — thus permitting the bodies to be removed to a proper cemetery — one avails oneself of it. In the sequential discovery case, the excuse is that when each body was disinterred, there was no known graveyard; the third body was found only afterward. Therefore one is permitted to use this as the *eila* — the legal basis — to avoid declaring the site a *shechunat kvarot*.

This principle, it should be noted, has a somewhat ironic dimension. The formal halakhic posture is that *Eretz Yisrael* is *tahora* and *Eretz Ha'amim* is *tamei*. Yet here the *gemara* reveals that this presumption of purity for *Eretz Yisrael* was maintained precisely *because* the rabbis used any available excuse to clear areas from *tumah* suspicion. The presumption of purity is not simply a given; it is actively constructed through halakhic creativity.

### Rosh's Reading

The *Rosh* reads the *ilu matzu* principle more broadly. He comments that Reish Lakish's statement reflects a general operating principle: *ba'alila muetes uvisvara katana tiharu Eretz Yisrael mishum kohanim v'osei taharos* — with a small excuse and a modest argument, they purified *Eretz Yisrael* for the sake of *kohanim* and those engaged in *taharos*. This is not merely a rule for the specific sequential-discovery case; it is a general stance that a low threshold of reasoning suffices to establish purity of a place, because practical life in *Eretz Yisrael* requires it.

The *Rosh* adds: *v'lo dami l'kever yadua d'asur lifnos d'ein kan yedia vada'is* — and this is not comparable to a definitively known grave, which cannot be disinterred, because in the case of sequential discovery there is no truly certain knowledge that this was a graveyard. The discovery was piecemeal, and when each disinterment occurred, the graveyard status had not yet been established.

## No Find in Radius

### Twenty-Cubit Question

The *gemara* poses a further question: *badak kaf ama v'lo matza mahu* — if one checked twenty *amot* and found nothing, what is the status? The question is somewhat ambiguous. *Tosafos* understands it as asking about checking in one direction and finding nothing — but as *Tosafos* notes, one does not understand why finding nothing in one direction should mean anything, since the graveyard might extend in the other direction. Nevertheless, that is how *Tosafos* reads the question.

### Still a Graveyard

*Amar Rav Nachman bar Yirmya amar Rav: shechunat kvaros* — it remains a *shechunat kvarot*. Now, one would expect *shechunat kvarot* to be the stringent ruling — the one that prevents disinterment. But *Tosafos* understands this as a *kula*, a leniency: the answer is that having found nothing, you may assume that you have reached the end of the graveyard and need not continue checking further in that direction. This reading, as *Tosafos* acknowledges, does not sit perfectly with the words of the *gemara*, but that is how *Tosafos* resolves it.

### Intentional Burial

The *Rosh* offers a fundamentally different reading of the question and answer. According to the *Rosh*, the question is: after finding three bodies and checking all twenty *amot* around in all directions — finding nothing — may you now disinter those original three? Perhaps the failure to find anything else in the radius suggests it is not really a *shechunat kvarot* after all, just three coincidental graves; and if not a *shechunat kvarot*, then they can be disinterred.

The answer, says the *Rosh*, is no: *harei zeh shechunat kvarot* — it remains a *shechunat kvarot*. *U'pshita lei keivan d'gimmel hem muchzak lei shechunat kvarot af al pi shelo matza* — once three bodies are found, the presumption of *shechunat kvarot* is established even if the twenty-*amot* investigation yields nothing further. Three bodies in the appropriate configuration is sufficient to establish that this was an intentional burial site. Perhaps it was a small graveyard with only three graves; that is still a graveyard, and those bodies may not be removed. According to this reading, the *ilu matzu* line that appears in some manuscripts is a copyist's error transferred from the preceding discussion, and the *Rosh* removes it from his text.

## Tzaraat Doubts

### Initial Purity

The next *mishnah* has no connection to *nazirut* at all, except that it employs structural principles parallel to those seen in the earlier *mishnayot* — particularly the principle of *raglayim ladavar* and the concept of *chazaka*. The *mishnah* states: *kol safek negaim bit'chilatah tahor* — all doubts regarding *negaim* before the person has been declared *tamei* are resolved in favor of *tahara*. *Ad shelo nizkak l'tumah* — as long as the person has not yet been formally established as *tamei*, any doubt as to whether a skin lesion qualifies as *nega tzara'at* is resolved leniently.

The underlying principle is *chazaka* — status quo. The person was *tahor* before; absent a definitive determination that the *nega* meets all requirements for *tumah*, the prior status is maintained.

### Established Impurity

*Mishenizkak l'tumah* — once the person has been formally established as *tamei*, *sfeko tamei* — any subsequent doubt is resolved in favor of *tumah*. If there is a question whether the *nega* has cleared sufficiently to render the person *tahor*, the status quo of *tumah* is maintained. This mirrors the principle from the opening *mishnah* of the tractate: a person already *tamei* is not saved by a subsequent *tumat hatehom* being retroactively unknown, because *raglayim ladavar* — there was already a pre-existing basis of *tumah*.

The *mishnah* invokes the phrase *mipnei she'chezkatam tamei* — because the presumptive status is *tamei*. The mechanism is pure *chazaka*: whatever the prior status was, it is maintained in the face of doubt.

### Two People Case

The *Rosh* provides a vivid illustration of how this *mishnah* operates in practice, drawing on cases from tractate *Negaim*. Two people come before the *kohen* at the same time. One has a lesion of a certain smaller size; the other has a lesion the size of a *sela* — a coin, larger than a *gris*. Neither is yet declared *tamei*; both are examined and locked up for a week of assessment. When they return after the week, both lesions are now the size of a *sela*. One of them has clearly spread — having started smaller, it grew — and is therefore *tamei*. The other, which started at *sela* size and remained at *sela* size, did not spread and was never even the minimum size, so it is *tahor*. But the *kohen* has forgotten which person had which initial lesion size, and neither person remembers either. The ruling: both are *tahor*. Even though one of them is objectively *tamei*, since neither can be identified as the *tamei* one, both retain their initial *chezkat tahara*.

### Lesion Progression

The *Rosh* then presents the reverse scenario. Two people come, one with a lesion smaller than a *gris*, one with a lesion the size of a *sela*. Both are examined and locked up. They return and both have lesions the size of *sela va'od* — larger than a *sela*. Both have spread; both are declared *tamei*. They are locked up again. They return once more, and now both lesions have diminished, returning toward a *sela* in size. The question is: when does each of them become *tahor*?

### Baseline Return

The answer is: each person must return to the size they had *initially*, before any spread. For the person who began with a *sela*-sized lesion, returning to a *sela* suffices to establish *tahara* — that is the original baseline. For the person who began with a smaller lesion, a return to *sela* size is not enough; the lesion must return all the way to its original smaller size. Now if both return to *sela* size simultaneously and the *kohen* cannot recall who started with which size, both remain *tamei*. The one who started smaller has not yet returned to baseline; the one who started at *sela* has. But since one cannot determine which is which, both retain their *chezkat tumah* until the matter can be clarified.

## Nega Appearance Order

### Verse on Purity

The *gemara* asks: *mena hani milei* — what is the source for the principle of initial *tahara* in cases of doubt? *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav amar kra: letaharo o letame'o* — the verse says "to purify or to make *tamei*." The fact that the verse mentions *tahara* first — *ho'il ufatah bo hakatuv betahara techila* — since the Torah opened with *tahara*, this indicates a disposition toward *tahara* as the starting point.

### Purity Objection

The *gemara* immediately objects: *ei hachi, afilu mishenizkak l'tumah nami sfeko tahor* — if the verse teaches a general inclination toward *tahara*, then even once a person has been declared *tamei*, any subsequent doubt should also be resolved in favor of *tahara*. That would contradict the second half of the *mishnah*. So the verse cannot be the source of the principle stated in the *mishnah*.

### Hair Whitening

The *gemara* resolves this by relocating the verse's teaching: *ela ki itmar deRav Yehuda amar Rav aha itmar* — this verse was cited by Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav for a different *halacha* entirely. The verse is not the source for the status quo principle; that principle rests on the general rule of *chazaka*, which operates independently. The verse instead addresses a specific case: *im beheret kadma lese'ar lavan tamei, ve'im se'ar lavan kodem labeheret tahor* — if the *baheret* lesion appeared first and then the hair within it turned white, the person is *tamei*; but if the hair was always white before the lesion appeared, the person is *tahor*, since the *baheret* did not cause the hair to whiten. *Safek* — if one does not know which occurred first — the person is *tamei*.

This case is structurally different from the ordinary doubt: it is not a question of two separate individuals whose identities are confused. It is a question about the order in which two events occurred in the same person. The general principle of *chazaka* does not straightforwardly resolve this, since one knows the person previously had naturally white hair but also knows the lesion is present. It is in this specific case that the verse supplies a rule.

### Unknown Order

Rabbi Yehoshua comments *kehe* — which Rav Yehuda explains as meaning *tahor*. The *Rosh* understands Rabbi Yehoshua as providing the rationale for why the order-of-events doubt resolves to *tahara*: the verse opens with *letaharo*, establishing that when the order is unknown, one presumes *tahara* based on the textual priority given to purity. This is the unique contribution of the verse in this specific context, as distinct from the *chazaka*-based principle governing the general cases in the *mishnah*.

## Zav Checks

### Seven Factors

The penultimate *mishnah* — again unrelated to *nazirut* but brought here for the phrase *raglayim ladavar* — deals with the law of *zav*. *Beshiv'ah derachim bodkim et hazav* — in seven ways one examines the *zav*, the man with an abnormal penile discharge. The context requires some clarification. A man can have two types of emission: seminal emission (*keri*), which conveys a lighter degree of *tumah*, or *zivah*, an abnormal non-seminal discharge, which conveys a heavier degree. The law of *zav* applies to the latter. A man becomes a *zav* after two such discharges; a third requires him to bring a *korban* upon purification. The seven-way check applies *ad shelo nizkak le'zivah* — before he has yet been established as a *zav* — meaning before he has seen two such discharges.

The seven factors are potential external causes that, if present, would explain the discharge as something other than *zivah*, thus exempting the emission from counting toward *zav* status.

### External Causes

The seven factors are: *bemachal uv'mishteh* — something he ate or drank that may have caused the discharge; *bemassa* — carrying a heavy load, physical exertion; *uv'kfitzah* — jumping, again exertion; *uv'choli* — illness. If any of these factors were present, and the man has not yet seen two discharges to establish *zav* status, the emission is attributed to the external cause and does not count.

### Sight & Thoughts

The remaining factors are: *uv'mareh uv'hirhur* — something he saw and thoughts that arose from it, referencing visual stimulation and sexual thoughts that might have prompted the discharge through a pathway analogous to arousal. Though counted separately, these two are understood as connected — something seen leading to *hirhur*, mental dwelling, which in turn might cause the emission through something akin to seminal stimulation even if the discharge itself is not semen.

### Pre-Zav Leniency

Before *zav* status is established — *ad shelo nizkak le'zivah* — if any of these seven factors is present, the emission is attributed to the external cause rather than to *zivah*, and the man does not advance toward *zav* status. The logic is that until the pattern is established, any available explanation for the emission is taken seriously and used leniently.

## Zav Status

### No Exemption

*Mishenizkak le'ziva* — once the man has been established as a *zav* by having two qualifying emissions, the calculus changes entirely. *Ein bodkin oto* — one does not investigate these seven factors anymore. Even if exertion, illness, or other factors are present, a subsequent discharge is treated as *zivah* regardless. The established condition is presumed to be the cause.

### Ones & Semen

*Onso vesfeko veshichvat zaro tme'im* — once he is a *zav*, discharges that would otherwise be attributed to *ones* — external compulsion — are *tamei*; discharges that are in doubt as to their nature are *tamei*; even an emission of semen from a *zav* is treated as *tamei*, on the possibility that it contains *zivah* mixed within it. All categories of discharge, once *zav* status is established, are presumed to be manifestations of the underlying condition.

### Attributed to Condition

The reason given is *sheraglayim ladavar* — because there is now a pre-existing basis, a *raglayim ladavar*, that all emissions are attributable to his condition. Once the condition is established, there is no need to search for alternative explanations; everything is attributed to the *zivah*. This is the third application of *raglayim ladavar* in these *mishnayot*, and here it carries its clearest meaning: a pre-established factual basis that governs the interpretation of all subsequent ambiguous events.

## Fatal Wound

### Mortal Wound

The final *mishnah* brought in this cluster — again for *raglayim ladavar* — addresses a capital case: *hamakeh chavero* — one who strikes another, *ve'amduhu lemitah* — and the victim is assessed as likely to die from the wound. The striker faces potential execution for murder if the victim dies.

### Recovery & Relapse

*Vehekel mimah shehaya* — but then the victim improves. The wound appeared mortal, the prognosis seemed clear, but the person begins to recover. Does this improvement change the legal analysis? Then: *v'le'achar mikan hichbid umet* — after the initial improvement, the victim deteriorates and ultimately dies. Does the death still trace back to the original wound?

### Death Attributed

The first opinion: *chayav* — the striker is liable. The fact that the victim temporarily improved does not break the causal chain. The injury was declared mortal at the outset, and the victim ultimately died. The improvement is simply part of the natural and unpredictable course of a fatal wound, and the death is attributed to the original act.

### Different Cause

*Rebbi Nechemiah omer patur* — Rabbi Nechemiah says he is exempt. The improvement, in Rabbi Nechemiah's view, is itself legally significant evidence. It is *raglayim ladavar* — circumstantial evidence — that the original wound was not in fact fatal; something else intervened to cause the ultimate death, and one cannot attribute the death to the original striker.

### Circumstantial Evidence

This use of *raglayim ladavar* is distinct from the earlier applications. In the graveyard case, *raglayim ladavar* referred to positive evidence justifying ongoing suspicion. In the *zav* case, it referred to an established condition that governed interpretation of subsequent ambiguous events. Here, Rabbi Nechemiah uses *raglayim ladavar* to mean that the circumstantial evidence — the fact of improvement — points away from the original wound as the cause of death. The improvement gives *raglayim* — legs, grounds — to the inference that the original wound was survivable, and therefore the striker is exempt. The *tanna kamma*, by contrast, reads the circumstances as confirming the original assessment: the victim was fatally wounded and ultimately died, with the improvement being an interlude that does not change the fundamental trajectory.

---

---

# Nazir 66

## Raglayim L'Davar

### External Causes Dismissed

The *Gemara* on daf 66 opens at the bottom of 65b, picking up from a *Mishnah* that, while having little direct connection to *Nazir*, introduced the phrase *raglayim l'davar* — the same phrase that appeared at the beginning of the *perek*. The *Mishnah* concerned a *zav*, a man who has experienced the abnormal genital discharge designated as *zivah* by the Torah. Before a man becomes a full *zav*, we check whether each sighting of the discharge might be attributable to some external cause — *ones* — such as exertion, illness, or certain foods. If so, that sighting is discounted. Once he has had two flows, however — making him a *zav* in the preliminary sense — any subsequent flows are relevant either because a third flow obligates him to bring a *korban* or because any flow during the seven clean days he must count will reset that count entirely. The principle of *raglayim l'davar* teaches that for these subsequent flows, we no longer concern ourselves with the possibility of external causes: since the man is already a *zav*, we assume the continued flow stems from his condition, not from something incidental.

### V'Hazav Et Zovo

The *Gemara* then asks: *minah hanei milei* — what is the scriptural source for this distinction? Rabbi Natan answers by citing the verse *v'hazav et zovo* — "and the one who flows, his flow" (Leviticus 15:3) — and notes that the verse concludes *l'zachar ul'nekeivah*, "whether male or female," drawing an analogy between the male *zav* and the female *zavah*. The difference between the two is instructive. For a woman, the operative distinction in the Torah is between *niddah* — menstrual bleeding occurring during the expected cycle — and *zavah* — bleeding outside the menstrual period. The question for her is entirely about *when* the blood flows, not *what* is flowing. For a man, by contrast, the distinction is between *shichvat zera*, a seminal emission, which is natural and its own category of *tumah*, and *zivah*, which is an abnormal discharge distinguishable from semen by its consistency, as described in the *Mishnah*. For a woman, external causes are entirely irrelevant — the *tumah* applies regardless. The verse *v'hazav et zovo l'zachar ul'nekeivah* is therefore read as establishing when the male *zav* is treated like the female: after the double language of *zovo* — implying two prior flows — external causes cease to matter for him as well. From the third sighting onward, he is analogized to the woman for whom *ones* is never a consideration.

### Rabbi Eliezer vs. Rabban…

A *baraita* is then cited that appears to complicate this picture. Rabbi Eliezer holds that even for the third flow — the one that would obligate a *korban* — we still check for external causes. According to him, it is only the fourth flow and beyond (those that could interrupt the seven clean days) for which we no longer check. The *tanna kamma*, by contrast, holds that from the third sighting onward, *ones* is already irrelevant.

### Et Particle Dispute

The *Gemara* traces this disagreement to a hermeneutical dispute over the word *et* in *v'hazav et zovo*. The *rabbanan* do not treat the particle *et* as expanding the scope of the verse, and so they read *v'hazav zovo* — two flows — as the threshold after which external causes are dismissed; the third flow is therefore already governed by the rule of *raglayim l'davar*. Rabbi Eliezer, by contrast, applies the standard exegetical principle associated with Rav Nachum Ish Gamzu and does *darish et* — reads the particle as adding to the count — yielding three flows as the threshold, so that only the fourth flow is beyond scrutiny. All authorities agree, in any event, that from a certain point onward, *ones* is simply not a consideration.

---

## Safek Regarding Emission

### Identity of Emission

The *Mishnah* then lists additional categories treated as *tamei*: *ones*, *safek*, and *shichvat zera*. Having addressed *ones*, the *Gemara* now turns to *safek*. Rava clarifies that the *safek* in the *Mishnah* does not refer to a case where one is uncertain whether anything came out at all. Such a doubt would not be governed by *raglayim l'davar* — the mere fact that a man is already a *zav* does not allow us to assume that a new flow occurred when there is no evidence of one. Rather, Rava explains: *vadai chaza safek machmat shichvat zera safek machmat re'iyah* — something definitely emerged, but its identity is unknown. The doubt is whether what came out was the result of a seminal emission or whether it was *zivah* flowing on its own.

### Zivah with Semen Rules

Why does this distinction matter? *Tosafot* clarifies by reference to a rule taught elsewhere: *zivah* that is mixed together with semen — *depeticha bei shichvat zera* — destroys only one day of the man's clean count, whereas *zivah* that flows on its own — *delo peticha bei shichvat zera* — destroys all seven days and requires him to start again from the beginning. The practical stakes are therefore significant. If a man is, say, on day three of his seven clean days, and something occurs: if it was a seminal emission, there is no interruption at all. If it was a mixed emission — *zivah* together with semen — he cannot count that one day but may continue counting the rest. If it was *zivah* alone, he must begin the entire count anew. The *safek* of the *Mishnah* addresses the case where one finds evidence of both substances — stains of each — and cannot determine whether they emerged together or separately.

### Strict Assumption

Rava concludes: *keivan shenizkak l'tumah, sfeko tamei* — since the man has already established himself as a *zav*, we invoke *raglayim l'davar* and adopt the stricter reading. We assume that the *zivah* came out on its own, not mixed with the semen, and the man must restart all seven days.

---

## Zav's Semen Status

### Semen Tumah by Masa

The *Mishnah* includes *shichvat zera* — semen — as *tamei*. The *Gemara* asks: *l'mai hilchata* — for what practical *halachah*? If the point is merely that touching the *zav*'s semen renders one *tamei*, that would hardly be remarkable: even the semen of any ordinary man who is *tahor* is itself an *av hatumah* and conveys *tumah* by contact. The *Gemara* therefore concludes that the *Mishnah* must be establishing something more: *zaro shel zav metamei b'masa* — the semen of a *zav* conveys *tumah* even through carrying (*masa*), not merely through contact. This would place it in the same category as the *zivah* flow itself, which is *metamei b'masa*.

### Rabbi Eliezer vs. Yehosh…

The *Gemara* then identifies which *tanna* holds this position, by citing a *baraita*: Rabbi Eliezer says that the semen of a *zav* is *not metamei b'masa*; Rabbi Yehoshua says it *is metamei b'masa*. Rabbi Yehoshua's reasoning is not that semen inherently achieves this status — rather, he reasons that since the man is a *zav*, it is impossible that any penile emission would not contain within it at least some droplets of *zivah* — *tzikhtzukhei zivah*. It is those droplets, not the semen itself, that account for the stringent *tumah*.

### Droplets Explanation

This seems a perfectly serviceable reading of the *Mishnah*: our case involves a known *zav*, and *raglayim l'davar* allows us to assume that any emission will be contaminated with *zivah* — this is precisely why we treat even his semen strictly. The *Gemara*, however, pushes back: *afilu Rabbi Yehoshua lo amar ella mishum tzikhtzukhei zivah, aval b'inei lo amar* — even Rabbi Yehoshua does not say that pure semen alone, entirely free of any *zivah*, would be *metamei b'masa*. This is an abstract distinction — in practice there is indeed no way to separate the emissions — but the *Gemara* treats it as meaningful in principle, and so will not read the *Mishnah* as making a statement solely about the droplets.

### Rav Ada Bar Ahava

Instead, the *Gemara* cites Rav Ada bar Ahava: *lomar she'ein tolin bah* — the *Mishnah*'s reference to *shichvat zera* is teaching that once a man is a *zav*, we do not attribute a subsequent *zivah* flow to the seminal emission that preceded it. This interpretation connects back to the laws of *ones*: among the external causes that would ordinarily discount a *zivah* is a prior seminal emission. The reasoning is that the body may be weakened or affected by the ejaculation, and a flow following it closely may therefore be attributed to that cause rather than to the *zivah* condition itself.
