The *gemara* offers three possible resolutions. *Ibba'it eima nasiv u-ferash*: perhaps Ben Azzai did marry but subsequently separated from his wife — he left the marriage to devote himself to Torah study, and this tradition records that episode. *Ibba'it eima me-rabeih shemia leih*: alternatively, he heard this measure from his *rabbi* and reported it as authoritative tradition, without it being derived from personal experience. *Ve-ibba'it eima*: and if you prefer — *Torah hi ve-lilmod ani tzarich* — this is Torah and I must learn it; Ben Azzai was, in the well-known tradition, one of those who studied the most intimate dimensions of human life as pure Torah, possessing knowledge through sacred learning rather than personal encounter. Finally, *sod Hashem liyreiav* — the secret of God is with those who fear Him: perhaps Ben Azzai simply knew, in the manner of one whose fear of Heaven grants him a form of direct apprehension.

---

---

# Sotah 5

## Bread & Prostitution

### Bread without washing

The *daf* continues from where we left off on 4b, where the *Gemara* had surveyed a range of opinions regarding the *shiur bi'ah* — the minimum duration of the act of intercourse — and one of those opinions had invoked a metaphor involving reaching a hand into a basket of loaves of bread, citing a *pasuk* in the process. The *Gemara* now builds upon that *pasuk*, offering a series of *drashot*.

Rav Avira taught — sometimes transmitting the teaching in the name of Rav Ammi, and sometimes in the name of Rav Assi — that whoever eats bread without *netilat yadayim* is as if he had intercourse with a woman who is a prostitute (*zonah*), as it is stated (Mishlei 6:26): *ki be'ad ishah zonah ad kikar lachem* — "for on account of a woman who is a prostitute, a man is reduced to a loaf of bread." The homiletic connection is drawn between one's treatment of a loaf of bread and the domain of sexuality: just as eating can be invested with *kedushah* — through handwashing, blessings, and intentionality — or can be reduced to mere self-gratification, so too with sexuality. The eating of bread with *kedushah* parallels sexuality within marriage, while eating without proper preparation parallels the indulgence of appetite without sanctity.

### Rava's reread

Rava, characteristically attentive to the precise wording of a *pasuk*, raises a grammatical objection to Rav Avira's reading. The verse opens with the *zonah* and concludes with the loaf of bread; if the intent were to compare the improper eating of bread to illicit relations, the verse should have been phrased in the reverse order. Rather, Rava reads the *pasuk* according to what is likely its *pshat*: *kol haba al ishah zonah lesof mevakesh kikar lachem* — whoever habitually consorts with a prostitute will in the end become impoverished and go begging for a loaf of bread. That is the natural and primary meaning of the verse.

### Mayim rishonim/acharonim

Whatever the precise interpretation of the *pasuk*, the underlying concern with *netilat yadayim* generates further discussion. Rav Zreika in the name of Rabbi Elazar states that whoever treats *netilat yadayim* lightly — *hamizalzel binetilat yadayim* — will be uprooted from the world. This is a striking formulation.

Rav Chiya bar Ashi in the name of Rav specifies the proper technique: for *mayim rishonim*, the first washing before eating bread, one must hold one's fingers upward; for *mayim acharonim*, the final washing after the meal, one must hold the fingers downward. A *baraita* confirms this: *hanotel yadav tzarich sheyagbi'ah yadav lemalah* — one who washes hands must raise them upward — lest the water flow below the wrist and then run back over the fingers, thereby rendering them *tamei* once again.

The underlying logic requires some background. The practice of washing hands before eating bread derives from the *kohanim*, who would eat *terumah* — bread made from *terumah* flour — and for whom ritual purity was therefore essential. The rabbis established that unwashed hands carry the status of a *sheni letumah*, a second-degree derivative of impurity, sufficient to render *terumah* *tamei*. Rather than requiring full immersion in a *mikvah* to purify the hands, the rabbis instituted the washing of hands as a means of restoring *taharah*. Ordinary Jews adopted this practice in parallel, treating their eating as if they were *kohanim* consuming *terumah*, thereby elevating the sanctity of their meals.

The mechanics of the washing require two pourings. The first water — *mayim rishonim* — purifies the hands, but in doing so becomes *tamei* itself; indeed, liquids that come into contact with impurity acquire a special status and themselves become *tamei*. The second water then purifies the first water. The practical concern is this: if during the first pouring the water flows past the wrist onto the forearm, it becomes *tamei* there, but the second pouring reaches only up to the wrist. The water sitting on the forearm has thus not been rendered *tahor* by the second pouring. If one then lowers the fingers, that *tamei* water may run back down onto the hands, rendering them *tamei* once more. Hence the requirement to keep the fingers elevated during *mayim rishonim*.

It should be noted that there is a dispute among the *rishonim* as to precisely which joint serves as the boundary — whether the relevant threshold is the wrist or the knuckle where the fingers attach to the palm. The normative practice is to ensure the entire hand is washed; in pressing circumstances, *besha'as hadechak*, one may rely on the more lenient position that requires only the fingers. In any case, the essential rule is clear: fingers up for *mayim rishonim*.

The reason the fingers must be held *downward* for *mayim acharonim* is different in nature. *Mayim acharonim* serve to remove *melach Sedomit* — a particularly harsh salt associated with Sodom — and other unpleasant residues from the fingers. The purpose is to push the undesirable material away from oneself, hence the fingers point downward so that the water and residue drain away.

### Drying hands

Rabbi Abahu adds a further dimension: *kol ha'ochel pat belo niguv yadayim ke'ilu ochel lechem tamei* — whoever eats bread without drying one's hands afterward is as if eating *tamei* bread, as the verse states (Yechezkel 4:13): *kacha yochlu venei Yisrael et lachmam tamei* — "so shall the children of Israel eat their bread in a state of impurity." The hands at that point are technically *tahor*, but Rashi explains that the act is *ma'us* — disgusting — and therefore treated rhetorically as equivalent to ritual impurity. There is something instructive here about the dual register of religious motivation: for some, the sense of ritual significance (*tamei*) is more compelling; for others, it is the aesthetic and moral dimension (*ma'us*) that resonates.

---

## Gasut haruach

### Haughty soul & adultery

The *Gemara* now returns to the same *pasuk* in Mishlei (6:26) and focuses on its concluding phrase: *ve'eshet ish nefesh yekarah tatzud* — "and a married woman ensnares a precious soul." Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *kol adam sheyesh bo gasut haruach lesof nichshal be'eshet ish* — whoever possesses haughtiness of spirit will ultimately stumble in the sin of adultery with a married woman, because the very haughtiness that leads one to feel entitled to anything will lead one to transgress even in the domain of another man's wife. The *pasuk* is read as: a *nefesh yekarah*, a precious soul — understood here as a haughty soul, one that considers itself supremely important — will be "captured" by a married woman. This resonates with the narrative at the end of *Parashat Bereishit*, where the *benei Elokim* seized *benot ha'adam* as they pleased — taking married women directly from the *chuppah* — reflecting a complete breakdown of boundaries born of a sense of absolute entitlement.

Rava, however, again scrutinizes the *pasuk*. If the intent is to speak of a haughty soul, the verse should have said *nefesh gevoha*, a high soul, rather than *nefesh yekarah*, a precious soul. Furthermore, if the married woman is to be the active subject ensnaring someone, the verse should have read *hi tatzud* — "she will ensnare" — making the married woman the grammatical subject. Since the verse does not align with the desired reading, Rava offers an alternative: *kol haba al eshet ish* — whoever has intercourse with a married woman — *afilu lamad Torah* — even if he is a *nefesh yekarah*, a precious soul, who has learned *Torah*, which is described as more precious than jewels (*yekarim mipninim*) and whose bearer is even greater than a *Kohen Gadol* who enters the innermost chambers — *hi titzudennu ledina shel Gehennom* — the married woman's sin will ensnare him all the way to the judgment of *Gehennom*. Here it is the *sin*, not the woman, that ensnares; the sinner is not ensnaring her but is himself being drawn in to the gravest punishment.

### Haughtiness = idolatry

Because the topic of *gasut haruach* — haughtiness of spirit — has now been introduced, the *Gemara* embarks on an extended exposition of its gravity. It is worth pausing to note that the term is *gasut ruach*, a heaviness or thickness of spirit — and one cannot help but observe the resonance with the *pasuk* at the heart of *Sotah*: *ve'avar alav ruach kinah*, a spirit of jealousy came over him. This juxtaposition invites reflection on whether the spirit of jealousy driving the husband may itself be entangled with a spirit of haughtiness.

Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: *kol adam sheyesh bo gasut ruach ke'ilu oved avodat kochavim* — whoever has haughtiness of spirit is as if he worshipped *avodah zarah*. The one who is haughty recognizes no authority above themselves and is effectively a law unto themselves. The connection is drawn through the shared term *toavah*: the verse states *toavat Hashem kol geva lev* (Mishlei 16:5) — an abomination to God is all who are of haughty heart — and separately the verse states *ve'lo tavi toavah el beitecha* (Devarim 7:26) — do not bring an abomination into your home — referring to *avodah zarah*. The same term *toavah* links them.

### Haughtiness = denial

Rabbi Yochanan himself, speaking in his own name rather than in the name of his teacher, goes further: *ke'ilu kafar be'ikar* — it is as if one denied the very existence of God. The verse cited is *ve'ram levavecha ve'shachachta et Hashem Elokecha* (Devarim 8:14) — "your heart will be lifted up and you will forget the Lord your God." There is a subtle distinction in the progression here. Worshipping *avodah zarah* involves rejecting one authority in favor of another; outright *kefira* is the rejection of divine authority altogether, with oneself as the sole authority. Haughtiness, Rabbi Yochanan argues, belongs to this latter and more radical category.

### Consequences of pride

The *Gemara* continues with further characterizations of haughtiness. Rabbi Chama bar Chanina says it is as if one had relations with all the *arayot*, all the forbidden sexual relations: *ke'ilu ba al kol ha'arayot*. The shared word *toavah* links the haughty heart (*toavat Hashem kol geva lev*) with the entire category of *arayot*, which is collectively described as *kol ha'toavot eleh* (Vayikra 18:27). The logic is that the unrestrained ego will ultimately give free rein to all desires.

Ulla offers yet another formulation: *ke'ilu bana bamah* — it is as if he built a *bamah*, a private altar outside the *Beit HaMikdash*. The verse cited is *chadlu lachem min ha'adam asher neshamah be'apo ki bameh nechshav* (Yeshayahu 2:22) — "cease from the man whose breath is in his nostrils, for what is he worth?" The homiletic reading takes *bameh nechshav* — "what is he worth?" — and vocalizes it as *bamah*, reading it as: such a person *is* a *bamah*. Rashi notes that a *bamah* was characteristically built on elevated ground, on high mountains and prominent places — an image perfectly fitting of one who elevates himself.

This comparison to a *bamah* is instructive in the way it complements the two previous comparisons. *Avodah zarah* represents a total substitution of divine authority with another. *Kefira* is an outright rejection of God. But a person who is haughty may still be observant and God-fearing. Such a person is not worshipping another god and is not denying God; yet they are nonetheless a law unto themselves, bypassing communal norms and institutions. That is the *bamah*: still worshipping God, perhaps, but doing so on one's own terms, outside the sanctioned framework — as though saying, everyone else goes to the *Beit HaMikdash*, but I will do it my own way.

### Charity despite pride

The *Gemara* then takes up the phrase from the same *pasuk* that introduced the abomination of the haughty heart: *yad leyad lo yinakeh* — "hand to hand will not go unpunished" (Mishlei 11:21). The question is what "hand to hand" alludes to in relation to haughtiness.

Rav interprets it as referring to intercourse with a married woman — though the *Bach* notes that the correct reading, as attested by Rashi and others, is that the subject remains the haughty person. Even if such a person has recognized God's mastery over heaven and earth, as Avraham Avinu declared *harimosi yadi el Hashem El Elyon koneh shamayim va'aretz* — "I have lifted my hand to God, Master of heaven and earth" — *lo yinakeh midinah shel Gehennom*, he will not be cleansed from the punishment of *Gehennom*. The haughty person may sincerely affirm that God is the ultimate authority, and yet the practical effect of his haughtiness — his sense of entitlement and the way he treats others — remains a grave transgression.

*Devei Rabi Sheila* objects to this reading: if the verse intends to allude to Avraham's declaration, it should have said *yadi* rather than *yad leyad*, echoing *harimosi yadi*. They therefore offer an alternative: even if such a person received *Torah* at the level of Moshe Rabbeinu, of whom it is written *miyimino esh dat lamo* — the fiery law was given from God's right hand — *lo yinakeh midinah shel Gehennom*. Even the greatest *Torah* scholarship does not neutralize the haughtiness.

Rabbi Yochanan in turn objects to *devei Rabi Sheila*'s reading: if the verse meant to allude to God giving the *Torah* to Moshe's hand, it should have said *yad miyad* — from one hand to another — not *yad leyad*. Rather, Rabbi Yochanan interprets *yad leyad* as referring to the act of giving: hand extended to another's hand — that is, *tzedakah*. Even if such a person performs *tzedakah baseser* — gives charity anonymously, in a way that preserves the recipient's dignity, with no public recognition — and even though we know from the verse *matan baseser yichaper af* (Mishlei 21:14) that giving in secret appeases divine anger — nevertheless, because of the haughtiness, *lo yinakeh midinah shel Gehennom*. The sin of haughtiness is not neutralized even by this. The cumulative force of these three readings is striking: a haughty person may acknowledge God as Master of all, may have acquired enormous *Torah* knowledge, and may give *tzedakah* with complete anonymity and discretion — and yet none of this is sufficient to offset the fundamental wrong of haughtiness.

### Prohibition source

The *Gemara* now asks: *azhara legasut haruach minayin* — what is the source of a prohibition against haughtiness in the *Torah*? Rava, or some say Rabbi Zeira, cites the verse *shimu veha'azinu al tigbahu* (Yirmiyahu 13:15) — "hear and give ear, do not be haughty." Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites instead the verse in Devarim: *ve'ram levavecha ve'shachachta et Hashem Elokecha* — "your heart will become lifted and you will forget God" — in conjunction with *hishamer lecha pen tishkach et Hashem Elokecha* — "guard yourself lest you forget the Lord your God." Rabbi Avin, transmitting from Rabbi Ila, establishes the principle that wherever the *Torah* uses the language of *hishamer*, *pen*, or *al*, these constitute negative prohibitions — *lo ta'aseh*. Since the verse warns *hishamer lecha pen tishkach*, and since allowing one's heart to grow proud leads directly to forgetting God, the prohibition against forgetting God encompasses within it a prohibition against the pride that causes it.

---

## Consequences & rewards

### Diminishment & repentance

Rav Avira taught — again sometimes in the name of Rav Assi and sometimes in the name of Rav Ammi — that whoever possesses haughtiness will in the end be diminished: *kol adam sheyesh bo gasut haruach lisof mitma'et*. The verse cited is *romu me'at* — "lift up a little" — read homiletically as: if you lift yourself up, you will become *me'at*, diminished. And lest one think the consequence is merely a slight reduction in stature while one continues to exist and have an impact in the world, the verse continues *ve'einenu* — and he is no more — meaning his memory will be obliterated entirely, as if he had never existed.

However, if the person returns in *teshuva*, *ne'esaf bizmano ke'Avraham Avinu* — he will be gathered in his time, that is, he will live a full life, like Avraham Avinu. This suggests that the punishment for unrepented haughtiness is not merely diminishment but premature death, since the alternative to repentance is dying before one's time. The verse concludes *vehumchu kechol yikfatzun* — they will be brought low and gathered in like all — and if one does make oneself humble through *teshuva*, they will be gathered in like *bakol mikol kol*: like Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov, each of whom the *Torah* describes with that phrase, indicating a life of complete fullness.

### Head of husk debate

The verse under discussion concludes: *uchrosh shibolet yimalu* — "like the head of the husk they will wither." Rav Huna and Rav Chisda debate what this image means. One says it refers to the *kisa d'shivalta* — the hairs that crown the top of the husk of wheat, the thin tendrils that extend upward. The other says it refers to the *shibolet atzmah* — the husk itself, and its top specifically.

If it refers to the hairs at the crown, the verse is straightforward: just as those hairs are cut away, so too will the haughty be cut down. The objection arises for the one who says it refers to the husk itself: what then does *kerosh* — the head — add to the image? Rav Assi, and likewise the school of Rabbi Yishmael, offer a parable: a person entering his field will pick the tallest stalks first. The tallest ones are gathered first and removed. So too the one who raises himself highest draws attention and is cut down first. The first image — the hairs being snipped from the crown — is perhaps more vivid, but both convey the same essential point: it is precisely what is most elevated that is most vulnerable to being cut down.

### God with lowly

The *Gemara* moves to a *pasuk* in Yeshayahu (57:15) that speaks of God dwelling *et daka ushefal ruach* — with the downtrodden and the lowly of spirit. Again Rav Huna and Rav Chisda disagree. One interprets the verse as: *iti daka* — God says "bring the downtrodden to me; I will raise them up." The other interprets it as: *ani et daka* — "I will go down and be with the downtrodden where they are." The *Gemara* concludes that the second interpretation is the more compelling, *umistavra*, because we know that God passed over all the great mountains and rested the *Shechinah* on *Har Sinai* — the lowest of the mountains — and did not raise *Har Sinai* up to the level of the others but came down to where it was.

This is not merely a logical point but a deeply pastoral one. When a person is in a state of bleakness, depression, or despair, the message that God will *eventually* lift them up may feel irrelevant or unbelievable. What is needed — and what the *Gemara* is affirming — is the knowledge that God is present *there*, in the darkness, in the lowliness itself.

### Learning from God

Rav Yosef draws a practical lesson: *le'olam yilmad adam mida'as kono* — a person should always learn from the conduct of his Creator. Just as God passed over all the great mountains and chose to rest the *Shechinah* on the lowly *Har Sinai*, so too a person should cultivate humility. A variant of this teaching adds: just as God rested the *Shechinah* not in grand trees but in the humble thorn bush (*sneh*), so too human beings should model themselves on this divine preference for the lowly.

### Deserve cutting down

Rabbi Elazar states: *kol adam sheyesh bo gasut haruach ra'uy legado ke'asheirah* — whoever has haughtiness of spirit is deserving of being cut down like an *asheirah*, an idolatrous tree. The verse states *veramei hakoma gedu'im* (Yeshayahu 10:33) — "the tall ones will be cut down" — and the verse regarding *asherot* states *va'asheihem tigde'un* (Devarim 7:5) — "their *asherot* you shall chop down." The combination of the two verses, sharing the root *gimel-dalet-ayin*, associates the fate of the haughty with the command to destroy idolatrous trees. The language is stark. One might note that the verse about *asherot* carries the force of a commandment — *you shall cut them down* — which is somewhat unsettling when applied to haughty people, and the practical implications of such rhetoric require care in interpretation. But at minimum, the *Gemara* is saying that the haughty are in their spiritual character akin to something that is an abomination and fit to be eliminated.

Rabbi Elazar adds a second teaching: *kol adam sheyesh bo gasut haruach ein afro ninar* — whoever has haughtiness of spirit, his dust will not be stirred at the time of *techiyat hameitim*. The verse states (Yeshayahu 26:19): *hakitzu veranenu shochnei afar* — "awaken and rejoice, those who dwell among the dust." The verse does not say *shochvei be'afar* — those who have lain down in the dust, which would refer to all the dead — but *shochnei afar* — those who have made their dwelling among the dust, meaning those who were humble and low in their lifetimes. Only they will be roused; the haughty, who disdained such lowliness in life, will not merit *techiyat hameitim*.

### God cannot dwell

Rav Chisda, or some say Mar Ukva, states: *kol adam sheyesh bo gasut haruach amar Hakadosh Baruch Hu: ein ani vehu yecholim lador ba'olam* — God says of the haughty: "I and he cannot dwell in the same world." If the haughty person fills all the space and acknowledges no authority, there is no room for God. The verse states (Tehillim 101:5): *malshni baseser re'ehu oto atzmit; gevah einayim urechav levav oto lo uchal* — "one who slanders his friend in secret I will cut down; one of haughty eyes and broad heart, him I cannot endure." The *Gemara* reads the final phrase not as *oto lo uchal* — "him I cannot endure" — but as *ito lo uchal* — "with him I cannot be." God and the haughty cannot coexist.

The *Gemara* notes that some teach this statement in the context of those who speak *lashon hara*, since the first half of the verse concerns slander; on this reading, it may be the *lashon hara* born of haughtiness — rather than the haughtiness itself — that is the primary focus of the verse.

---

## Extended homilies

### Little wind disturbs

Rabbi Alexandri teaches: *kol adam sheyesh bo gasut haruach afilu ruach kima ocharto* — whoever has haughtiness, even a small wind will disturb him. The haughty person is hypersensitive to any perceived slight, constantly alert to whether others are sufficiently recognizing their status and authority. The verse states (Yeshayahu 57:20): *vehareshaim kayam nigrash* — "and the wicked are like the driven sea." The comparison: the sea contains vast quantities of water, and yet even a small wind disturbs its surface. *Adam she'ein bo ela revit* — a human being has only a *revi'it* of blood, which is the *Gemara*'s understanding of the minimal vital fluid — and yet the haughty person, driven by *gasut haruach*, is as easily agitated as the ocean. The *reshaim* here are those identified with haughtiness.

### Talmid chacham arrogance

Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi in the name of Rav states: *talmid chacham tzarich sheyehe bo echad mishmini shebishminit* — a *talmid chacham* requires within himself one sixty-fourth of haughtiness. A *talmid chacham* represents the *Torah* and carries its dignity. If someone slights him, they are slighting not merely a private individual but the *Torah* he embodies. Therefore a minimal measure of self-respect — a derivative of a derivative, an eighth of an eighth — is appropriate. The formulation is deliberately attenuated: not one-eighth, but one sixty-fourth, as though to say that even this is only barely tolerable and only at the greatest remove from real *gaivah*. Yet the *Gemara* has also already stated that even one who received *Torah* at the level of Moshe will not be cleansed from *Gehennom* if he has haughtiness. *Torah* scholarship can become a source of precisely this dangerous pride — the same thing it is meant to guard against.

### Crowns like husk hairs

Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua adds: *uma'atra lei ke-sasa l'shibulta* — and this minimal amount of pride crowns the *talmid chacham* like the hairs on top of the husk of wheat. This, of course, deliberately echoes the earlier image of those same hairs being cut off as a punishment for haughtiness. The image is inherently ambivalent: the very thing that adorns can, in excess, become the thing that is severed. A tiny amount is a crown; any more and it becomes a liability.

### Rava's resolution

Rava concludes that this is an impossibly fine line: *beshamta de'is bei uv'shamta de'leis bei* — a *talmid chacham* is deserving of *cherem* if he has [too much] pride, and is deserving of *cherem* if he does not have [any]. Too much, and the *Torah* has made him insufferable and contemptuous of others; too little, and he fails to uphold the dignity of the *Torah* he represents. The balance is real, delicate, and in practice extraordinarily difficult to maintain.

### Total rejection

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cuts through the complexity with a unilateral ruling: *lo minah velo miktzatah* — I want none of it, not a drop, not even the smallest fraction. His reasoning: is it a trivial matter when the verse states *toavat Hashem kol geva lev* — an abomination to God is all who are of a haughty heart? If the *Torah* calls it an abomination, one must keep far away from it entirely. The tension between Rav Nachman's total rejection and the recognized need for a *talmid chacham* to maintain some measure of dignity is left standing. The *Gemara* does not resolve it so much as present the full range of the challenge. A well-worn *yeshiva* joke captures it: the *Gemara* says a *talmid chacham* should have one sixty-fourth of arrogance, but some seem to be very *machmir* on the *shiur*.

---

## Value of humility

### Heart like flesh

Chizkiyah teaches: *ein tefilaso shel adam nishma'at ela im kein mesim libo k'vasar* — a person's prayer is heard only if he makes his heart like flesh (*basar*) — not like stone, not like a haughty elevated spirit, but soft, flexible, impressionable. The verse cited is (Yeshayahu 66:23): *vehayah midei chodesh bechodsho yavo kol basar lehishtachavot* — "all flesh shall come to bow down." It is *basar* — flesh — that comes to the *Beit HaMikdash* to prostrate. The one who approaches God must approach as *basar*.

### Flesh vs. adam

Rabbi Zeira observes a distinction within the laws of *tzara'at*. When *tzara'at* appears on *basar* — on flesh — the verse indicates *venerpa*, it will heal. When the verse speaks of *adam* — a person — who has *tzara'at*, this phrase of healing does not appear. The point is not that *tzara'at* on a person cannot clear up, but that one who thinks of himself primarily as *adam* — a person of stature, a human being in his full dignity — finds healing and change more difficult. The one who regards himself as *basar* — humble flesh — is more open to the possibility of healing and transformation.

### Adam & basar acronyms

Rabbi Yochanan expands this further, offering *gematric* and acronymic readings of both words as a reminder of human frailty. *Adam* may be read as an acronym for *eifer, dam, marah* — ashes, blood, and bile. *Basar* may be read as *bushah, sruchah, rimah* — shame, putrefaction, and worms. An alternative tradition reads the middle letter as *shin* rather than *sin*, yielding *Sheol* — the netherworld — in place of *srucha*. These readings are not intended to produce despair but to provide an antidote to haughtiness: whatever one's achievements, the body decomposes into these elements.

### Se'et & sapachat

Rav Ashi applies this to haughtiness directly: *kol adam sheyesh bo gasut haruach lisof nifchat* — whoever has haughtiness will in the end be brought low. The verse cited is *ulaseit velasfachat* (Vayikra 13:2), referring to types of *tzara'at*. The *derasha* reads *se'eit* as related to the language of elevation — *se'eit* means lifting up, as in *ve'al kol heharim haramim ve'al kol hageva'ot hanisa'ot* — and *sapachat* as something secondary and adhesive, something that clings to and is subordinate to another. The haughty person who is *se'eit* — elevated — will be brought down to the status of *sapachat* — a mere addendum.

### Greatness of lowly

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches: *bo ur'ei kama gdolim nemuchei haruach lifnei Hakadosh Baruch Hu* — come and see how great are those of lowly spirit before God. When the *Beit HaMikdash* stood, one who brought an *olah* received the merit of an *olah*; one who brought a *minchah* received the merit of a *minchah*. But one who possessed a lowly spirit, it is as if he brought all the sacrifices together. The lowly spirit surpasses any individual sacrifice that one could bring.

### Broken spirit greatest

The verse confirms this: *zivchei Elokim ruach nishbarah* (Tehillim 51:19) — "the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit." The plural *zivchei* — sacrifices — refers to all sacrifices collectively, and the broken spirit encompasses them all. And furthermore, *ein tefilato nima'eset* — his prayer will not be despised, as the verse concludes: *lev nishbar venidkeh Elokim lo tivzeh* — "a broken and crushed heart, God will not despise."

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds one final teaching: *kol hasham orchotav ba'olam hazeh zocheh vero'eh bishu'ato shel Hakadosh Baruch Hu* — whoever weighs and assesses his paths in this world will merit seeing God's salvation. The *Rambam* cites this teaching as foundational, grounding in it the principle that all one's actions should be directed and evaluated *leshem shamayim*. The word *vesham* in the verse (Tehillim 50:23) is read not as "there" but as a form of *shuma* — assessment and evaluation. Whoever consistently weighs his direction in this world will behold the salvation of God.

This extended passage on pride and humility is not a mere digression. The *ruach* — spirit — that animates *gasut haruach* stands in pointed juxtaposition to the *ruach kinah* — spirit of jealousy — with which *masechet Sotah* opens. The question of what kind of *ruach* is driving the jealous husband is one the *Gemara* seems deliberately to be placing before us.

---

## Kinui & forbidden acts

### Warning contradiction

The *Gemara* now returns to the *halacha* of *Sotah* and the mechanics of the *kinui* — the formal warning that a husband must give his wife. The process has been substantially legalized and limited by *Chazal*: witnesses, *beit din*, and a carefully defined sequence of acts are required. The *Gemara* addresses an apparent internal contradiction in the *Mishnah*.

The *Mishnah* states that the husband warns his wife in front of two witnesses not to speak with a particular man — *al tedabri im ish ploni zeh*. The implication would seem to be that *dibbur*, speech, constitutes the legally significant act, equivalent to *stirah*, seclusion. Yet the *Mishnah* immediately thereafter states that if she spoke with the man she remains *muteret le-veitah* — permitted to her husband — and *muteret le'echol bitrumah* — permitted to eat *terumah* if her husband is a *kohen*. The internal contradiction is stark: the first clause implies that speaking is the relevant act, while the second clause implies that it is not. *Ha gupa kashya* — this passage is self-contradictory.

### Abaye's resolution

Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining how the *Mishnah* must be read. The *Mishnah* is enumerating several scenarios in which the woman remains permitted: whether he warned her not to speak and she spoke; whether he warned her not to speak and she went into *seclusion* (*nistera*); whether he warned her not to go into seclusion and she spoke — in all these cases, *adayin muteret le-veitah muteret le'echol bitrumah*. She remains permitted in all of them, because in each case either the warning does not match the act, or the act alone is insufficient. The warning and the forbidden act must align: the warning must be against the act that generates the legal consequence.

### Final forbidden state

The one case in which she becomes forbidden is specified: *nichnesa imo leveit haseser veshahat kedei tumah* — she entered with him into a private place and remained there for sufficient time to have intercourse (*kedei tumah*) — after having been warned specifically against seclusion. In that case alone, *asura le-veitah va'asura le'echol bitrumah* — she is forbidden to her husband and forbidden to eat *terumah*. The warning must be against seclusion, the act must be seclusion, and there must be sufficient time. All three elements together constitute the forbidden state. Here the *daf* concludes, and the shiur will continue from *amud bet* at the next session.

---

---

# Sotah 6

## Sotah Status & Yibum

### Sotah Suspected Status

We begin on 6b, approximately ten lines from the bottom, with the words *umet choletzet*. The subject is an interesting application of *yibum* law — a topic familiar to those who have studied Maseches Yevamos — arising from the case of the *sotah*.

To review the basic framework: a woman who has been warned (*kinui*) and subsequently secluded herself with the man against whom she was warned now carries the status of a *sotah*. Halakhically, she is a *safek* — a doubt — but she is treated as a *vaday*, a certainty, because the language of the *Torah* declares *venistarah vehi nitma'ah*. Based on the evidence accumulated at this stage, the *Torah* treats her as though *tumah* has been established, even though the ultimate clarification awaits the ritual at the *Beit HaMikdash*.

The practical consequence of this *safek*-treated-as-*vaday* status is that she is forbidden from having marital relations with her husband, and her husband is forbidden from having relations with her. Furthermore, if she is married to a *kohen*, she may not eat *terumah*. There is something deeper here than a mere technical prohibition: the bond of marriage has been, in some sense, weakened or compromised, which is why the *Torah*'s declaration of *v'nitma'ah* reaches beyond the bedroom and touches even her right to eat *terumah*. This will be developed further when we encounter the word *v'nitma'ah* appearing multiple times in the relevant *pesukim*.

### No Yibum Rule

Against this background, the *Mishnah* teaches that if the husband dies before the *sotah*'s status has been clarified — before she has had the opportunity to drink the bitter waters — the brother, in a case where the couple has no children, may not perform *yibum*. The reasoning is almost self-evident: *yibum* is an act of sexual intimacy, it establishes a sexual relationship with this woman, and it does so precisely because the brother steps into the shoes of the deceased husband. But the husband himself was forbidden from having relations with her. How, then, could the *Torah* mandate the brother to do what the husband could not?

At the same time, because the matter remains a *safek* — she has not been definitively proven guilty — she is not simply released. The brother must still perform *chalitzah* to sever the *zika*, the levirate bond that has transferred to him.

One might wonder: what if the man against whom she was warned and with whom she secluded herself was, in fact, the brother? In that case, the calculus would shift — but that is a separate discussion. The *Mishnah*'s case is the standard one, and the *Gemara* now asks the obvious opening question: *amay*? Why?

### Peshat Derivation

The *Gemara* first asks: why indeed can the brother not perform *yibum*? And then: if he cannot perform *yibum*, why must *chalitzah* be done at all?

Rav Yosef provides a scriptural basis: *v'yatz'ah mibeito v'halchah v'haytah l'ish acher* — "she shall leave his house and go to be with another man" (Devarim 24:2). This verse describes a woman who is divorced in a context of *matza bah ervat davar*, the discovery of some act of nakedness. The *drasha* extends the verse: we read it as applying not only to divorce but to any scenario in which a *sotah* is no longer with her first husband — whether through divorce or death — and the phrase *l'ish acher*, "to another man," is expounded as *ish acher v'lo yavam*: she may go to a completely different man, but not to the *yavam*, the brother-in-law.

This is admittedly a narrow and unusual reading of the *pesukim*. Rashi notes that the *drasha* treats *v'yatz'ah mibeito* as encompassing any manner by which she leaves the marriage — not just divorce — and then focuses on the next phrase: *v'halchah v'haytah l'ish acher*, her subsequent relationship must be with someone entirely unrelated to her first husband, not with someone who is essentially a continuation of that husband's legal persona. As a student rightly noted, this is clearly not the *peshat* of the verse. The verse describes a divorced woman, not a widow, and *yibum* applies in cases of death, not divorce. This is, in every sense, a *drasha* — a hermeneutical reading that reads particular significance into precise language.

## Yibum Prohibition Logic

### Abaye's Refutation

The *Gemara* immediately presses the internal logic. Abaye raises a sharp objection: *ella me'ata chalitzah nami lo tiba'i* — if the *sotah* is excluded from *yibum* by this *pasuk*, she should be excluded from *chalitzah* as well. If the verse categorically removes her from the domain of levirate law, why should the brother have any obligation toward her at all?

Rav Yosef responds: *ilu itei leva'al mi lo ba'ei get* — if the husband were still alive, would he not need to sever the bond with a *get*? The relationship does not dissolve on its own, even in cases of adultery or suspicion. The husband would still need to formally sever the marital bond through a *get*. Similarly, the *zika* that transfers to the brother upon the husband's death does not dissolve automatically. Even if *yibum* is unavailable, the bond must be formally severed, and that severance takes the form of *chalitzah*.

Tosafot, however, points out a problem with this logic. There are many situations in which a brother cannot perform *yibum* and yet is equally exempt from *chalitzah*, even though a husband in those same cases would still need to give a *get*. For example, if the widow is an *ervah* to the brother — a forbidden relative — the brother has no obligation of *chalitzah*, even though had the husband been alive, a *get* would have been necessary to dissolve the marriage. The principle that "the husband needs a *get*" does not automatically entail that "the brother needs *chalitzah*." So the argument does not quite hold.

### Voluntary vs Mandated

Rav Yosef offers a second version of the derivation. The *Torah* says *v'yatz'ah mibeito v'halchah v'haytah l'ish acher* — she goes to another man, to someone who, the *Gemara* explains, is *acher* in a particular sense: *acharei desani lah*, because she has become problematic for the household. The first husband did the right thing — he rid himself of a woman whose conduct had undermined the marriage. The language of *ish acher* carries a negative valence: the man who subsequently marries such a woman occupies a lower moral standing than the first husband who had the clarity to end the relationship. He was prepared to marry a woman suspected of adultery, described as a *rishah* in the context of *matza bah ervat davar*, and he *hichnis rishah l'toch beito* — he brought this problematic woman into his house.

The *Gemara* then asks pointedly: *v'at amrat tityabem nami yibumei?* — and you are proposing that the *Torah* would now mandate the brother to marry this woman under compulsion? The whole point of the verse was that removing her from this household was the right and proper response. How could the *Torah* turn around and require another man to take her on involuntarily?

Abaye pushes back: *ella me'ata le'acher lo tinasei* — if the logic is that she is the kind of woman no one should be entering into a relationship with, then she should be forbidden to everyone, not just to the brother. Every subsequent marriage should be prohibited. The *Gemara* responds: *mi ka ramina lah aleih be'al korchei?* — no one is forcing anyone to marry her. A third party who chooses to marry such a woman does so of his own free will; caveat emptor. But the *Torah* cannot mandate — cannot compel — a man to enter a relationship with a woman about whom these serious questions have been raised.

### Tosafot Resolution

As noted above, Tosafot acknowledges that neither of these derivations is fully satisfying as a formal logical proof. The real logic, Tosafot concludes, is more fundamental: if sexual relations are forbidden between this woman and her husband, then how can the *Torah* mandate *yibum*, which is a direct continuation of the husband's marital relationship — in effect, mandating the very act that was forbidden? That is the core of the argument. Because the suspicion is not definitive — it remains a *safek* — she cannot be fully excluded, and *chalitzah* is still required. But the mandate of *yibum* cannot stand where sexual relations were themselves prohibited with the man whose place the *yavam* is taking.

### House-Wrecker Logic

Tosafot here cites a beautiful elaboration from Rabbeinu Chananel. Where does the phrase *listore l'beito*, "to wreck the household," come from? Rabbeinu Chananel — and Tosafot says *hit'im devarav*, he sweetened the words, he gave them flavor — notes that it is the precise inverse of *asher lo yivneh et beit achiv*, "that he shall build his brother's house," which is the defining obligation of *yibum*. This woman, suspected of adultery, is in the category of a home-wrecker — *listore l'beito*. How could she be brought into the *mitzvah* of building a house? The very language of *yibum* contradicts the nature of what is being proposed.

### Remarriage to Others

The *Gemara* then tests the second version of Rav Yosef's argument — the *ish acher* reading — from a different angle. Abaye raises the following case: she was suspected of adultery while married to her first husband. Her first husband dies, or divorces her, and she subsequently marries a second man — an *ish acher*, in the language of the *pasuk*. They have a happy marriage, undisturbed by any suspicion of adultery. The second husband then dies without children, leaving his brothers obligated in *yibum*. Should the brothers of the second husband now be prohibited from performing *yibum* with this woman, on the grounds that the *pasuk* calls her second husband an *ish acher* — implying that marrying her was a poor choice, and no one should be mandated to do so?

The *Gemara* responds: *gavi d'hai mi b'shem tov hu ka'i* — but in the context of the second husband, she carries a good reputation. The successful second marriage has changed the picture. Whether it indicates she did *teshuva*, or that the problem lay with the first relationship rather than with her as a person, the point is that we now assess her relationship status through the lens of the second marriage. It is that relationship — the second husband's household — whose continuity the *yibum* obligation is meant to serve. The *ish acher* label applied to the second husband was appropriate in hindsight — he took a risk by marrying a woman with a questionable past — but by the time we reach the question of *yibum*, the relevant relationship is the second marriage, in which she was unimpeachable.

### Rava's Kal Vachomer

Rava offers a different approach: a *kal vachomer*. The act that caused her to become a *sotah* made her forbidden to her husband — the man she was *muttar* to, the man she was married to. If this compromised status is strong enough to forbid her to the person who had the most legitimate relationship with her, how much more so should it create a barrier to the person who, while her husband was alive, was *arayos* to her — her husband's brother, who was doubly forbidden to her as both a married woman's relative and her husband's brother. If the suspicion is potent enough to sever the permitted relationship, it should certainly be potent enough to prevent the creation of what had previously been a forbidden one.

### Kohen Gadol Example

The *Gemara* tests this *kal vachomer* with a counterexample. Consider a *kohen hedyot* — an ordinary priest — who dies, leaving his widow to the *yibum* obligation of his brother. But the brother in this case is a *kohen gadol*, and a *kohen gadol* is forbidden to marry a widow (*almanah*). Does the *kal vachomer* apply here? Could we say: since she is forbidden to the *kohen gadol* who was muttar to her — wait, no — he was never *muttar* to her. The *Gemara* dismisses this case: *ha asirah ve-kaima* — she was always forbidden to him. The *kal vachomer* requires a situation in which some new development turned a previously permitted relationship into a forbidden one. The *kohen gadol*'s prohibition against marrying a widow predated everything; it is not the result of any new status affecting her.

### Rape Case Analysis

The *Gemara* tries a better counterexample. A woman married to a *kohen* was raped. The rape, tragically, renders her forbidden to her husband — a *kohen* may not remain married to a woman who has been violated, even involuntarily. The husband dies, and the brother — who is a *challal*, the son of a *kohen* who married a *gerushah*, making the offspring a *challal* — is obligated in *yibum*. According to the *kal vachomer*, one might reason: the act of rape made her forbidden to the husband she was *muttar* to; how much more so should it make her forbidden to the brother! But this would prohibit the *challal* from performing *yibum*, which seems incorrect.

The *Gemara* responds: *ones be-yisrael mishra sharei* — rape by a non-*kohen* does not create any prohibition. The *challal* occupies the status of a non-*kohen* with respect to marriage restrictions. And *gavi d'hai leika issura* — there is no prohibition applicable to the brother in this scenario. The *kal vachomer* fails here because the prohibition created by rape is *kedushah*-specific: it is a restriction that applies only within the domain of *kehunah* and does not carry over into relationships where *kehunah* is not a factor. The *sotah*'s case is fundamentally different: the suspicion of adultery creates a prohibition that is relevant in any intimate relationship, not one limited to a particular domain. Therefore, it does transfer, so to speak, and the *kal vachomer* does hold: if it forecloses the permitted relationship with the husband, it certainly forecloses the continuation of that relationship through *yibum* with the brother. *Chalitzah* alone is what remains.

## Forbidden to Terumah

### Enumeration Cases

The *Mishnah* now turns to enumerate the women who, while carrying their unresolved *sotah* status, remain forbidden to eat *terumah*. The underlying structure of this list is important: each case represents a scenario in which the *sotah* process will never reach its completion through the actual drinking of the waters. The only way to lift the prohibition on *terumah* eating is to resolve the question — either by the ritual working or by some other definitive clarification. When that resolution becomes impossible, the prohibition remains in place. It is therefore somewhat pointed that the *Mishnah* frames these cases as *asurot milachol biterumah* — forbidden to eat *terumah* — since that framing emphasizes not just what happened, but what can never now be undone.

### Guilt & Witnesses

The *Mishnah* lists first: *ha'omeret temei'a ani lach* — if she herself admits that she has committed adultery, the process stops immediately. Similarly, if witnesses arrive and testify that she committed adultery — *v'shavu eidim she-hi temei'ah* — the process is halted. In both cases, the *sotah* ritual is superfluous. The matter has been resolved by direct evidence. These cases may seem obvious — if she is unquestionably guilty, of course she cannot eat *terumah* — but the *Mishnah* is making clear that the *terumah* prohibition, having attached, does not lift simply because the ritual is no longer going to take place. She must receive a *get* and the prohibition persists.

### Refusal Cases

The *Mishnah* continues: *ve'omeret eini shotah* — if she refuses to drink, the process ends. And: *o she-ha-ba'al eino rotzeh le-hashkotah* — if the husband refuses to go through with giving her the waters, the process equally ends. In all of these cases, the ritual will never take place. The *Mishnah* is teaching us what the practical consequence is when the process is interrupted at this stage: she gets divorced — without a *ketubah*, if it was her own refusal; possibly with a *ketubah*, if it was the husband who chose not to proceed — and she remains in her state of prohibition, since the situation will never be resolved.

### Husband Violation

Finally, the *Mishnah* lists: *ve-shavah ba'alah baderech* — if the husband had marital relations with her while she was in the process of being brought to undergo the ritual. By doing so, he violated the restrictions that the *sotah* status imposed on both of them. Once this violation occurs, one does not go through with the waters. Again the process is terminated, and again the prohibition on *terumah* eating remains unresolved.

A brief but important structural observation: the *Torah* grounds the entire *sotah* process in the husband's jealousy — *ruach kin'ah* — which is fundamentally subjective. Chazal sought to objectify the process, placing it under *beit din* supervision, requiring objective evidence of warning and seclusion, and so forth. But this created a tension: once the process is formalized and removed from the husband's unilateral control, a husband can no longer simply retract his suspicion and end the matter. The machinery, once set in motion, follows its own juridical path.

## Witnesses Overseas

### Rav Sheshet's Point

Rav Amram reports in the name of Rav Sheshet: *sotah she-yesh lah eidim bimdinat hayam ein ha-mayim bodkin otah* — if there is a *sotah* whose guilt is known to witnesses somewhere overseas (*medinas hayam*), in a distant place, the waters will not work on her. The scenario is this: those witnesses are unknown to the *beit din*; the woman and her husband proceed through the entire *sotah* ritual; the waters appear to have no effect; everyone concludes she is innocent. Rav Sheshet says: no. The reason the waters had no effect is not that she was innocent — it is that there existed objective evidence of her guilt elsewhere in the world, and the ritual is designed for the domain of unresolvable doubt. When concrete evidence exists — even unknown, even far away — the ritual is neutralized.

The *Gemara* immediately notes the epistemic problem this creates: how do we ever know *why* she came out appearing clean? The *Gemara* will address this.

Rav Sheshet adds: *ve-anhir lah einan mimatnisin* — and he illuminated his teaching from the *Mishnah* itself. The *chiddush* was not new; it was embedded in the *Mishnah*.

### Scriptural Basis

What is the scriptural basis for Rav Sheshet's ruling? The *Gemara* cites: *venistarah vehi nitma'ah ve-eid ein bah* — "and she was secluded and became *nitma'ah* and there is no witness" (Bamidbar 5:13). The phrase *ve-eid ein bah*, there is no witness who knows, is read precisely: *deleka deyadah bah*, there is nobody who knows of her guilt. *Le'apukei ha de-ika deyadah bah* — this excludes the case where someone does know, even from afar. In that case, the waters cannot function as a clarifying mechanism, because the truth is not hidden — it is merely inaccessible.

A question arises: does *ve-eid ein bah* require specifically two witnesses — *eidim* — or does even a single witness (*ed echad*) neutralize the ritual? This is a genuine question, since we have a principle that a single witness is believed after *kinui* and *stirah*, and can prevent the drinking from proceeding. Would a single distant witness similarly neutralize the waters? Tosafot is not certain. The question extends further: does a single witness who appears *after* the ritual has been performed have the same effect retroactively?

### Witnesses Post-Ritual

The *Mishnah* states that witnesses who arrive to testify she is *temei'ah* result in her not eating *terumah*, and the *Gemara* asks the diagnostic question: *de-atu eidim eimat* — when exactly do these witnesses arrive? If they arrive before she drinks, the case is trivial — she is proven guilty and of course does not eat *terumah*. The *Mishnah*'s formulation would then be unremarkable. The *Mishnah* must therefore be referring to a case where the witnesses arrive *after* she drank. Having drunk, and having appeared to emerge unharmed, she would seem to have been vindicated by the waters.

Yet the *Mishnah* says we still believe the witnesses. This, says the *Gemara*, makes perfect sense *bishlama* if we accept Rav Sheshet's principle — that when witnesses exist, the waters do not function as a truth-revealing mechanism. The waters' apparent silence proves nothing in that case; we now understand why the ritual seemed inconclusive. We therefore believe the witnesses, and her *terumah* prohibition remains.

But if, on the contrary, we maintain that the waters function even when witnesses are present elsewhere, then the waters' silence would constitute strong proof of her innocence — and the subsequent arrival of witnesses should retroactively render them liars. *Tiggalei milta le-mafrea de-sahadei shikrei ninhu* — it would become retrospectively clear that these witnesses were lying. Here the *Gemara* makes a remarkable implicit move: the *sotah* ritual, embedded within a juridical framework of *beit din*, objective evidence, and formal procedure, is treated as a category of valid evidentiary proof — strong enough, in principle, to override witness testimony. The fact that the *Mishnah* clearly trusts the witnesses even after the ritual therefore proves Rav Sheshet's point.

## Merit & Efficacy

### Rabbi's Merit View

Rav Yosef challenges Rav Sheshet's proof. *Le-olam eima lach mayim bodkin otah* — the waters do function even when overseas witnesses exist. How then do we explain the *Mishnah*'s ruling that we believe the witnesses who arrive after the ritual? *Ve-ha eimur zekhut tolah lah* — because there is another possible explanation for why the ritual had no apparent effect: the woman possessed *zechut*, merit, which suspended the waters' action. The witnesses are believed not because witnesses neutralize the ritual, but because there are other reasons the ritual might not have worked.

The *Gemara* then identifies what the two positions are debating: *be-minvella de-Rabbi* — the question of deterioration, as articulated by Rabbi in a *baraita*. Rabbi says: *zekhut tolah ba-mayim ha-marim* — merit suspends the effect of the bitter waters. But it does not suspend it indefinitely without consequence. She does not give birth normally, and she does not improve in her health: *ela minvella ve-holechet* — rather, she progressively deteriorates, until ultimately she dies in the manner the *Torah* described. It is a delayed reaction: the merit purchases time, but the end is the same.

### Rabbis' Position

The Rabbis disagree with Rabbi. According to the Rabbis, *zechut* is fully *tolah* — it fully suspends the effect of the waters, and she does not die at all. The *zechut* is complete. The question then becomes: do the Rabbis agree that she at least visibly deteriorates, even if she does not die? Or do they hold that there is no observable effect whatsoever — the waters simply do not work?

### Sheshet Interpretation

Rav Sheshet reads the debate as follows: *bein le-Rabbi bein le-Rabbanan hi misnavna* — whether according to Rabbi or according to the Rabbis, she deteriorates. The Rabbis may disagree with Rabbi about whether she ultimately dies, but they agree that some visible deterioration occurs. If that is correct, then the apparent complete absence of effect — the ritual seemingly working perfectly with no ill consequence — cannot be attributed to *zechut*. If *zechut* always produces at least observable deterioration, then when there is no deterioration at all, the only explanation is either that she is genuinely innocent, or that the waters were neutralized by the existence of overseas witnesses. And since the *Mishnah* credits the witnesses who arrive afterward, Rav Sheshet concludes that his position stands proven: the witnesses neutralize the waters.

### Yosef Counter

Rav Yosef reads the debate differently: *le-Rabbi hi misnavna, le-Rabbanan lo havya misnavna* — according to Rabbi, she deteriorates; according to the Rabbis, she does not deteriorate. Nor, for that matter, does she die — the Rabbis hold that with sufficient *zechut*, the waters have no effect whatsoever, and she lives her life undisturbed. If that is a possible outcome, then the waters' complete silence — no deterioration, no ill effect — could simply reflect that she had *zechut*. There is therefore no need to invoke the principle that witnesses neutralize the waters. The witnesses who arrive after the ritual are believed because they establish actual adultery; the ritual's silence is explained by *zechut*. The two explanations coexist, and neither requires the other.

## Shimon's Objection

### Policy Concern

Rabbi Shimon bar Ashi raises a fundamental objection to the entire framework of *zechut* suspending the waters' effect. *Ein zechut tolah ba-mayim ha-marim* — Rabbi Shimon categorically rejects the idea. His argument is one of policy and systemic legitimacy. If *zechut* can suspend or neutralize the waters' effect, then the entire ritual is undermined. *Madche ata et ha-mayim bifnei kol ha-nashim ha-shotot* — you have effectively discredited the waters in the eyes of all women who undergo this ritual. Anyone can point to a case where a woman who seems guilty emerged apparently unscathed, and attribute it to *zechut* rather than innocence. *Ve-ata motzi shem ra al ha-tehorot she-shatu* — you have cast aspersions on all the women who legitimately emerged innocent, because people will suspect that they too were actually guilty and simply benefited from their merit. The guilty will think they can get away with it; the innocent will be suspected of guilt. The entire mechanism is corrupted.

Rabbi Shimon's argument is striking precisely because it grounds a halakhic conclusion not in textual derivation but in policy reasoning. The logic of what a well-functioning institution would look like determines what the *halacha* must be.

### Parallel Logic

The *Gemara* then extends Rabbi Shimon's critique directly to Rav Sheshet's principle. *Ve-im ita yesh eidim bimdinat hayam nami ata motzi shem ra al ha-tehorot she-shatu* — if we accept that overseas witnesses neutralize the waters, then exactly the same systemic problem arises. Every woman who emerges apparently clean will be suspected of having gotten away with it because there are witnesses far away who know the truth. The same logic that Rabbi Shimon deploys against *zechut* applies with equal force to the principle of overseas witnesses.

### Shimon Rejects Both

How does the *Gemara* respond? *Rabbi Shimon ka-amrat?* — you are asking about Rabbi Shimon? *Rabbi Shimon midei de-zechut lo tali eidim nami lo talu* — Rabbi Shimon rejects both. He does not accept that *zechut* interferes, and he equally does not accept that witnesses interfere. But the *Gemara* is operating within the position that does accept these interferences, and within that position, both *zechut* and overseas witnesses play parallel roles. The argument is: if you accept one form of interference, you must accept that the same systemic concern applies to both, and yet both remain valid.

## Minchah Status

### Minchah Sequence

The *Gemara* now turns to the *sotah*'s *minchah* offering and what becomes of it in various interrupted scenarios. The sequence of the *minchah* process is key to understanding the analysis. The *minchah* is brought; it is placed in a *kli sharet* — a consecrated vessel — at which point it acquires *kedushat ha-guf*: the body of the offering is sanctified, and it can no longer be redeemed. The *kometz* — the prescribed handful — is then separated and offered on the *mizbe'ach*; the remainder (*shirayim*) would normally be eaten by the *kohanim*. The question is what happens to the *minchah* at each stage if the *sotah* process is interrupted.

### Rav's Argument

The *Gemara* connects this to the debate about overseas witnesses. The *Mishnah* taught that among the cases where the *minchah* is burned is the case where witnesses arrive to testify she is guilty — *ushev'u lah eidim she-hi temei'ah*. The *Gemara* asks the diagnostic question: when do the witnesses arrive? If before the *minchah* was placed in the *kli sharet*, it could simply be redeemed — *tifrok ve-teichulin*. The case in the *Mishnah* must therefore be where the witnesses arrive after the *minchah* was already placed in the *kli sharet*.

Now, says the *Gemara*, if we accept Rav Sheshet's position — that the waters function when there are no witnesses, but are neutralized when witnesses exist — then at the time of sanctification, there were no witnesses (or they were unknown), the process was valid, the *minchah* was properly sanctified, and its *kedushah* stands. When the witnesses subsequently arrive, the process is terminated, but the *minchah* retains its sanctity and must be burned. This is coherent.

But if we say the waters function even with overseas witnesses — meaning the waters are not neutralized by their existence — then we are forced to say that even had the witnesses not come, the process would have been ineffectual from the outset. The sanctification was therefore in error from the very beginning: *de-kadosh me-ikara be-ta'ut kadosh*. If so, the *minchah* was never truly sanctified, and rather than burning it, one should be able to take it out as ordinary *chulin* — *tipok le-chulin*. The fact that the *Mishnah* says it must be burned, and not simply redeemed or eaten as *chulin*, thus appears to support Rav Sheshet.

### Yehuda Limitation

Rav Yehuda mi-Diskarta offers a solution that limits the scope of the problem. He says: *kegon she-zinta ba-azara* — the scenario in the *Mishnah* is one where the witnesses testify not that she committed adultery a year ago in some distant city, but that she committed adultery *right now*, in the *azarah* itself, after the *minchah* was already placed in the *kli sharet*. In that case, at the time of sanctification, there were genuinely no witnesses — none existed anywhere. The sanctification was valid. The witnesses then come and testify about a brand new act of adultery, which independently terminates the process. The *minchah* was properly sanctified, but the process is now terminated, so it must be burned.

The *Gemara* playfully notes the practical difficulties with this scenario — she has an escort of young priests (*pirchei kehunah*). The objection is answered in several ways: she could have committed adultery with one of the escorting priests themselves, or she may have needed to use the bathroom and took advantage of that moment of relative privacy.

This answer, though technically valid, applies only to a narrow subset of cases. It does not resolve the general principle for the more common case of witnesses who arrive with testimony about prior adultery.

### Papa's Solution

Rav Papa offers the definitive resolution, one that operates without restricting the case. *Le-olam ke-da-amrinan me-ikara* — maintain the original scenario: witnesses arrive with testimony about prior adultery, long before and far away. Technically, one could argue the sanctification was retroactively in error and the *minchah* is simply *chulin*. But this cannot be permitted in practice. *Mi-de-rabbanan gezeira shema yomru motzi'in mi-kli sharet le-chol* — by rabbinic decree, we do not permit what appears to everyone to be a *kli sharet*-sanctified offering to be simply treated as ordinary food. The appearance of sanctity, once established in the public eye, cannot be undone without communal confusion and the undermining of *kedushah* as a category. Therefore, even if technically the sanctification was in error, we burn the *minchah* — not as a genuine *korban*, not on the *mizbe'ach*, but in the *beit ha-deshen*.

## Minchah Scenarios

### Pre-Sanctity Contamination

Rami bar Rav Mari enumerates the various scenarios systematically. If the *minchah* became *tamei* before it was placed in the *kli sharet*, it has not yet acquired *kedushat ha-guf*: *harei hi ke-chol ha-menachot ve-tipade* — it is treated like any ordinary *minchah* in that state, and may be redeemed.

### Death After Sanctity

If the *minchah* was already placed in the *kli sharet* and then became *tamei*, it has *kedushat ha-guf* and cannot be redeemed. The process is terminated, and: *harei hi ke-chol ha-menachot ve-tisaref* — it must be burned.

### Kometz Offered

If the *kometz* was already separated and offered on the *mizbe'ach* but the *shirayim* had not yet been eaten — and in the meantime either the husband or the wife died, terminating the process — the *kometz* offering was brought legitimately, at a time when everything was in proper order. In that case: *harei ke-chol ha-menachot ve-tei'achel* — the *shirayim* are eaten normally. The offering was brought in proper context.

### Doubtful Minchah

The case of *shel safeik ba'ah mitchila* — a *minchah* that from the very outset was brought in circumstances of doubt — is resolved by the principle of *kippurah s'fika v'halcha la*. Rashi clarifies that *kippurah* here does not mean *atonement* in its technical sense, but rather that the offering accomplished its purpose: it was brought as it was meant to be brought, in a context of genuine doubt, and that context was legitimate. The fact that retrospectively the doubt was never going to be resolved — because, say, one of the parties was going to die — is irrelevant, since at the time of bringing, everything was appropriate.

### Witnesses Post-Ritual

When witnesses arrive after the ritual: *minchasah tisaref* — the *minchah* is burned. As explained by Rav Papa, this is by rabbinic decree to preserve the appearance of *kedushah*. It is burned in the *beit ha-deshen*, not as an offering on the *mizbe'ach*.

### Zomemin Witnesses

Finally, if the original witnesses — those whose testimony established the *kinui* and *stirah* — were subsequently proven to be *eidim zomemin*, false witnesses contradicted by other witnesses, the entire basis for the *sotah* process collapses. *Minchasah chulin* — the *minchah* reverts to *chulin* and may simply be eaten. There is no obligation to burn it and no need to redeem it; it was never sanctified.

One might object: did we not just say that even when sanctification is retroactively in error, we burn for appearance's sake? The *Gemara* answers: *eidim zomemin kala is lehu* — the exposure of false witnesses is a public event. When witnesses are contradicted and proven to be liars by additional witnesses, the entire community becomes aware that the original testimony was fabricated. It becomes broadly understood that the *sotah* process was initiated on false grounds, and therefore the *minchah* was never sanctified. There is no danger of anyone thinking that a legitimately sanctified offering is being desecrated; the public knowledge of the *eidim zomemin* provides full transparency.

## Shimon Reconciliation

### Text vs Policy

Having established, in Rav Papa's framework, that the *minchah* in the witnesses-after-the-ritual case is burned by rabbinic decree, the *Gemara* returns to Rabbi Shimon's policy objection. Rabbi Shimon had argued that accepting any interference with the waters — whether from *zechut* or from overseas witnesses — systematically undermines the legitimacy of the entire *sotah* process. One might therefore think that Rabbi Shimon's objection strikes at the very source from which Rav Sheshet derived his principle.

The *Gemara* clarifies that this is not so. Rabbi Shimon's policy argument is powerful, but it cannot override a textual derivation (*drasha*). The question is: is there a textual basis that survives Rabbi Shimon's critique?

### Vetohorah Source

The *Gemara* cites the derivation from the word *vetohorah* — "and she will be pure" (Bamidbar 5:28). The verse states that if she is innocent, the waters will prove her pure and she will conceive. The word *vetohorah* is read as implying a limiting condition: the waters function as a mechanism of *taharah* only under specific conditions. *V'lo she-yesh lah eidim bimdinat hayam* — not when there are witnesses overseas who know she is guilty. And similarly, *v'lo she-tola lah zechus* — not when *zechut* is operative.

### Gossiping Peshat

The verse also yields a third case: *v'lo she-yisu v'yitnu bah mozeros b'levana* — not when she is the subject of widespread gossip among women knitting in the moonlight. This is a striking *drasha*: if her alleged adultery has become so publicly known that it is the talk of the community, the waters will not function as a revelation of hidden truth, because the matter is no longer truly hidden. The textual basis is the same word *vetohorah* — the waters are effective only when her status is genuinely unresolved and concealed; not when it has entered the domain of public knowledge, however informal.

### Rarity Mitigation

Rabbi Shimon's position is then reconciled with these derivations as follows. Rabbi Shimon's policy concern — that exceptions undermine legitimacy — is not without force, but it does not reach every possible case. The case of *zechut* was his primary target, and he rejects it entirely as too corrosive. The case of overseas witnesses is different. *Lo shchicha* — it is not common. Cases where witnesses exist in distant lands, unknown to the *beit din*, who could testify to her adultery, are genuinely rare. The textual derivation from *vetohorah* compels us to acknowledge this as a valid limiting condition, but its rarity means that it will not, in practice, generate the systemic suspicion that Rabbi Shimon feared. The waters' legitimacy is not meaningfully undermined by an exception that almost never arises. Rabbi Shimon can therefore concede the textual point while maintaining his broader objection to *zechut*, whose pervasive applicability would indeed corrode the entire institution.

---

---

# Sotah 7

## Private to Judicial

### Previous Context

The previous *mishna* dealt with circumstances that would prevent the *sotah* procedure from going forward — cases where the woman remained forbidden to eat *terumah*, including situations involving *edim* in *medinat hayam* and cases of admission. That *mishna* serves as a necessary background, because the present *mishna* now addresses what happens once none of those impediments apply: the procedure is cleared to proceed, and we turn to a description of how it would actually unfold.

### Woman to Beis Din

The *mishna* opens with the question *keitzad oso lah* — what would you do with her once she has acquired the status of a *sotah*, having been warned and having gone into seclusion? The answer: *molicho l'veit din she'be'oto makom* — you bring her to the *beit din* of that locale.

This is already a striking departure from the *Torah*'s presentation of the *sotah* procedure. In the *Torah*, the husband brings his wife directly to the *Beis HaMikdash* for the ritual. Here, however, the first stop is the *beit din*. That choice is not incidental — it is a statement about what this process fundamentally is.

### Chazal's Authority

The *mishna*'s framing makes a clear declaration: this is a matter of *din*. What had begun as a husband's jealousy, his private suspicion of his wife, has been converted into a judicial proceeding. The witnesses, the circumstantial evidence, the formal warning — all of it transforms the dynamic from one of passion and individual initiative into one of institutional supervision and objective adjudication.

This move is characteristic of *Chazal* more broadly. The authority of *Chazal* and *beit din* is grounded in the *pasuk* of *al pi hatorah asher yorucha v'al hamishpat asher yomru lecha ta'aseh lo tasur yamin u'smol* — but that *pasuk* in the *Torah* is addressed *el hakohanim v'el hashofet asher yihiyeh bayamim hahem*, with the *kohanim* far more prominent than the singular *shofet*. At the time of the *Beis HaMikdash*, institutional authority resided far more with the *kohanim* than with the rabbis. Yet *Chazal*, in describing the reality of how these procedures were conducted, consistently assert their own authority. We find this, for example, in the way the *beit din* would determine whether a *kohen* was fit for *avodah* when questions arose about his *yichus*.

The *sotah* procedure illustrates both dimensions of this assertion simultaneously. First, *Chazal* are taking something rooted in the husband's passion and making it objective — grounded in testimony and evidence rather than in one man's unilateral discretion. Second, they are taking something that belonged to the *kohanim* and the *Beis HaMikdash* and placing it under the authority of *beit din*. Both moves are reflected in the single word *keitzad*: what do you do? You bring her to a *beit din*.

---

## Two Sages

### Shema Yavo Aleha

Once the local *beit din* has received the case, the *mishna* continues: *u'mosru lo shnei talmidei chachamim* — they hand over two Torah sages to the husband, who will serve as escorts, accompanying the couple on their journey to *Yerushalayim*. The stated reason is *shema yavo aleha baderech* — lest he have relations with her along the way.

This detail is layered with significance. Once a woman has acquired the status of a *sotah*, husband and wife are forbidden to have relations with each other until the matter is resolved. The concern is not merely one of general propriety but of practical efficacy: we learn that the *sotah* waters function only when the husband himself is free of sin. If he were to violate the prohibition en route, the entire proceeding would be undermined. The waters would no longer be effective.

The presence of the two escorts therefore serves a concrete halachic purpose. But notice what it also does to the character of the whole process. At no point from here on is this the husband dragging his wife to judgment. The *beit din* has dispatched its agents; they are the ones accompanying this woman to the next stage. The husband is no longer the driver of events — the *beit din* is. This interestingly mirrors the description in *Yoma* of the *beit din*'s oversight of the *Kohen Gadol* before *Yom Kippur*, where the *mishna* uses the very same language: *mosru lo shnei talmidei chachamim*, the *beit din* hands over two sages to accompany the *Kohen Gadol* as he prepares for the *avodat hayom*. In that context too, a *Beis HaMikdash* ritual of the highest order is being overseen and structured by the *beit din*.

### Rav's Position

The *Gemara* asks why two representatives were needed rather than one. The fact that there are two escorts plus the husband makes three men in total, and the *Gemara* suggests this might support a teaching of Rav. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *lo shanu ela be'ir* — the rule that two men and a woman do not constitute *yichud* applies only when they are in a city, but *aval be'derech*, on a journey, *ad de'ika tlasa*, you need three men to avoid concern of *yichud*. The reason: *shema yitztarech echad me'hem le'nekavav* — one of the men may need to attend to his bodily needs. In a city, stepping away for that purpose does not create meaningful seclusion; but on a journey in open terrain, the man who steps away from the group to find some privacy in the brush or forest will leave the remaining man and the woman alone in what would constitute *yichud*. Hence the need for a third person to ensure someone is always present.

On this reading, the requirement for two escorts rather than one follows directly from Rav's principle: because they are traveling, three people are required to prevent any situation of *yichud* arising along the route.

### Witnesses Role

The *Gemara* does not ultimately accept that as the explanation, however. *Lo*, it says — *hacha hainu ta'ama ki heichi de'lehavu alah sahadei*: here the reason is so that they should serve as witnesses. What would they be witnessing? As Rashi explains, if the husband were to go ahead and have relations with his wife during the journey, these two escorts would be positioned to testify to that fact, which would then disqualify the proceeding from going forward. A single witness would not suffice to establish that the husband and wife had relations on the journey — that requires the standard two-witness evidentiary threshold. Hence two escorts are needed to function as a proper *beit din*-style testimony mechanism.

### Talmidei Chachamim

This still leaves a question open: why must the escorts specifically be *talmidei chachamim*? If the purpose is simply to provide two witnesses, any two competent witnesses would do.

The *Gemara* initially considers whether this supports another teaching of Rav — *lo shanu ela ke'sherim aval prutzim afilu asara nami lo* — that the principle allowing two men to be alone with a woman without concern for *yichud* applies only to upstanding individuals, but if the men are *prutzim*, licentious in sexual matters, even ten such men with a woman cannot be trusted. The concern is not that those other men will exercise moral restraint; it is that a man known to be *parutz* will not be inhibited by their presence. The *Gemara* cites a case in which ten men actually smuggled a woman out of a city concealed in a bed for illicit purposes.

But the *Gemara* again sets this aside: *lo, hacha hainu ta'ama de'yad'i l'atruyei bei* — the reason we need *talmidei chachamim* is that they will know to give him *hatra'ah*, a formal halachic warning. Rashi explains: if the husband is on the verge of violating the prohibition of having relations with his *sotah*, they will recognize what is happening and be positioned to issue a valid *hatra'ah* before the act, which is necessary for him to incur *malkos*.

This is, admittedly, a somewhat surprising rationale.
