It is one thing to want the proceeding to go forward without being compromised — but why does it matter to us that this man specifically receives a warning so that he can then be liable for *malkos*? In isolation, the concern for ensuring a particular transgressor receives his due punishment is not typically something we go out of our way to engineer proactively.

But the logic becomes clear when you recognize what this does to the character of the procedure. To send *talmidei chachamim* who are capable of giving *hatra'ah*, who function in effect as a small traveling *beit din* throughout the journey, is to make the most emphatic possible statement that this entire proceeding is framed within the world of *din*. Witnesses, warning, liability for lashes — these are the very structural elements of rabbinic judicial process. By foregrounding all of them, *Chazal* are foregrounding *din* itself. The *talmidei chachamim* are not incidental chaperones; they are representatives of the *beit din* whose presence at every stage of the journey makes clear that this is, above all, a judicial matter.

### Arei Miklat Parallel

*Tosafos* notes that this same language and structure appear in a different context — the case of one who kills accidentally and is sent to an *ir miklat*. There too, the *Gemara* records that two *talmidei chachamim* accompany the exile, *shema ye'hargenu baderech* — lest the *go'el hadam* kill him on the way. The *Gemara* there similarly explains that the two are needed so that if the *go'el hadam* is about to kill this man, they can issue a proper warning and, if necessary, intervene to stop him.

*Tosafos* observes that in both cases — the *sotah* and the accidental murderer — the *Gemara* grounds the requirement for *talmidei chachamim* in the need for *hatra'ah*. The parallel is striking and deliberate. At the beginning of the study of *sotah*, it was observed that several scenarios in the *Torah* involve something that begins as vigilante justice, as taking the law into one's own hands, and the process by which *Chazal* and sometimes the *Torah* itself bring these situations under institutional control. The *go'el hadam* is precisely the paradigm case: the *Torah* already legislates *arei miklat* as a structured response to the otherwise unbounded right of the blood-avenger. *Chazal*'s treatment of the *sotah* follows the same trajectory — taking what was a private act of jealousy and passion, placing the *beit din* at the center of the proceedings, and asserting its supervisory presence at every stage, from departure to arrival. The presence of two *talmidei chachamim* accompanying the accused, just as two *talmidei chachamim* accompany the accidental murderer, makes the parallel explicit and structural.

---

## Rabbi Yehuda

### Ba'ala Ne'eman

Having established the position of the *Tanna Kamma* — that the *beit din* dispatches two *talmidei chachamim* to accompany the couple — the *mishna* records a dissenting view: *Rabbi Yehuda omer ba'alah ne'eman aleha*, Rabbi Yehuda holds that the husband is trusted, and no escorts are needed. If he is trusted not to have relations with her en route, there is no reason to send two *talmidei chachamim* along. And this difference is not merely logistical — it fundamentally changes the character of the journey. Is the experience one of the *beit din*'s agents bringing this woman toward judgment, or is it the jealous husband bringing his wife? Rabbi Yehuda's position restores something of the *Torah*'s original dynamic.

### Kal V'Chomer

A *beraita* records Rabbi Yehuda's argument in the form of a *kal v'chomer*: *u'mah niddah she'hi b'kares ba'ala ne'eman aleha* — in the case of a *niddah*, whose prohibition carries the penalty of *kares*, a very serious transgression, we trust a husband and wife to sleep in the same room without having relations. *Sotah she'hi b'lav* — a *sotah*, whose prohibition is merely a negative commandment, *lo kol sheken* — how much more so can we trust him not to transgress?

### Rabbis Counter

The Rabbis respond with the phrase *hi hanosenes* — that very argument is the reason we *don't* trust him. *Niddah d'kares chamira lei u'meheiman* — a *niddah* prohibition, being so weighty, will restrain him; we can rely on him. *Sotah b'lav lo chamira lei v'lo meheiman* — a *sotah* prohibition, being only a simple negative commandment, is not weighty enough to serve as a reliable deterrent, and we cannot trust him to observe it.

### Biblical Source

A second *beraita* records the same dispute, but with different attribution. There, Rabbi Yosei presents the *kal v'chomer* argument, and the Rabbis push back with two objections. The first: *im amarta b'niddah she'yesh lah heter* — with a *niddah*, there is an eventual release; after she immerses in the *mikveh*, she becomes permissible again, and the prohibition has a cyclical, expected quality. *Tomar b'sotah she'ein lah heter* — with a *sotah*, if she is found guilty, she will never be permissible to him again. This finality might make him feel that relations during the journey are his last opportunity, creating a far more powerful temptation. The second objection adds: *mayim genuvim yimtaku* — stolen waters are sweet. Now that she is forbidden to him, the very fact of her prohibition may itself heighten the temptation. *Tosafos* explains why this second argument was necessary: one might have argued that since he has been with her before, there is no special urgency — but the very novelty of her forbidden status can make her more tempting, not less.

In that second *beraita*, Rabbi Yehuda's position is stated not as a *kal v'chomer* but as a direct appeal to the *pasuk*: *v'heivi ha'ish es ishto el hakohen* — the man brings his wife. This is the *Torah*'s own description of who initiates and executes this procedure.

### Chazal's Role

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction between the two *beraisos* by explaining that Rabbi Yehuda first presented the *kal v'chomer* argument, which the Rabbis refuted. He then fell back on the *pasuk* itself: regardless of whether the *kal v'chomer* holds, the *Torah* says the man brings his wife, and that should be sufficient.

The *Gemara* then asks: *Rabbi Yehuda haynu Tanna Kamma* — isn't Rabbi Yehuda's position the same as the first *tanna*'s? Both concede that from the *Torah*'s perspective, it is the man who brings his wife. The *Gemara* answers: *ika beinaihu aval amru* — the difference is entirely in what *Chazal* added. Everyone agrees that on the *Torah*'s own terms, the husband brings his wife. The dispute is whether the Rabbis are authorized to change that procedure by adding their own supervisory layer. The *Tanna Kamma* holds that they did so and appropriately so. Rabbi Yehuda holds that we should not alter what the *Torah* prescribed. He is not necessarily denying that there is some basis for concern — but he does not want to transform the fundamental nature of the process to the degree that the *Tanna Kamma*'s position implies. He wants to keep it closer to its biblical form, where the husband is the driving force, rather than converting it into an exercise in institutional supervision.

---

## Beis Din Hagadol

### To Jerusalem

The next *mishna* describes the subsequent stages. *Hayu maalin osah le-Beis Din Hagadol she-bi-Yerushalayim* — they bring her to the Supreme Court in *Yerushalayim*. Again, notice the framing: not directly to the *Beis HaMikdash* for the ritual, but to the *Beis Din HaGadol*. It is true that the *Beis Din HaGadol* was situated within the *Beis HaMikdash* complex, in the *Lishkat HaGazit*, but that is not the point. The *mishna* is presenting the journey as proceeding from one *beit din* to the next — from the local *beit din* to the Supreme Court — and from there only then to the *kohanim* for the ritual itself. At no stage does the *mishna* describe this as simply a husband bringing his wife to the *Beis HaMikdash*.

### Intimidation

*U'me'ayemin aleha ke'derech she'me'ayemin al edei nefashot* — they frighten her in the manner in which witnesses in capital cases are frightened. In capital cases, the concern is that a witness might fill in gaps in his knowledge, might testify to something he is not fully certain of, and so the *beit din* would impress upon such witnesses the enormous weight of their testimony — that if an innocent man dies based on their words, his blood and the blood of his descendants would be on their hands. This cuts in both directions: if the witness truly knows, he must testify; but if there is any uncertainty, he must stand down. The purpose is to ensure that only reliable testimony enters the proceedings.

Here, the *beit din* applies analogous pressure to the *sotah* herself. The explicit parallel to capital cases is drawn — and the *mishna* makes no apology for it. The *sotah* proceeding is being framed within the same institutional framework as the gravest matters of *din*.

### Appeals to Admit

The *mishna* then describes what the *beit din* says to her: *biti, harbeh yayin osah* — my daughter, wine often causes people to act in ways they would not otherwise act. They invite her to confess by offering her mitigating circumstances: *harbeh se'chok osah*, excessive frivolity, *harbeh yaldus osah*, the passions and poor judgment of youth, *harbeh shechenim ra'im osim*, the corrupting influence of bad company and bad neighbors. They are, in effect, making it possible for her to admit by reducing the apparent weight of moral responsibility. They do not require her to present herself as a fully deliberate sinner — they offer her a range of explanations that would allow her to acknowledge what happened without bearing its full shame.

### Shelo Yimacheh

The culminating appeal is: *asi lishmo hagadol she'nichtav bi'kedushah shelo yimacheh al hamayim* — act for the sake of God's great Name, which is written in holiness, so that it should not be dissolved into the water. This is a striking inversion. The purpose of the *sotah* procedure is precisely to dissolve the Divine Name into the water so that it can be administered to the woman. But here, the *beit din* presents that prospect as something to be avoided. The purpose, they are saying, is *shelo yimacheh* — not to erase it.

This raises a genuine question: if we trust that the ritual works, why are we working so hard to prevent it from being used? One might argue it is better for the sinner to confess of her own accord; or one might invoke the various reasons explored in earlier discussion about why the ritual's efficacy might be unreliable in practice. But the *mishna*'s focus here is revealing: it does not frame the goal as arriving at the truth, or even as vindicating the innocent. The goal, as stated, is to avoid erasing God's Name. Everything is oriented toward obtaining an admission and thereby bypassing the ritual.

### Admission Consequence

If she responds *tme'ah ani* — I am impure, I am guilty — the consequences are clear: *shoveret ktuvatah*, she loses her *ketubah*, *v'yotzah*, and she is divorced. Admission ends the proceeding. She leaves without the financial protection of her *ketubah* and without her marriage.

### Maintains Innocence

If she says *tehorah ani* — I am pure, I am innocent — the proceedings advance. *Maalin otah leshaar hamizrach* — they bring her to the eastern gate, which is directly opposite the *shaar Nikanor*.

---

## Eastern Gate Ritual

### Eastern Gate

The eastern gate of the *Beis HaMikdash* is the entry point into the *ezrat nashim*. Proceeding westward through the *ezrat nashim*, one reaches the top of a series of steps leading into the *azarah* proper, where the *mizbe'ach* stands. At the top of those steps is the *shaar Nikanor*, the gate that transitions from the *ezrat nashim* into the *azarah*. The *mishna* tells us that the *sotah* is brought to the eastern gate, facing this *shaar Nikanor*, because that is where the *sotot* drink, where newly delivered mothers come for their purification, and where *metzora'im* undergo parts of their purification ritual.

### Gate Theology

The *shaar Nikanor* is a gate in a wall, and like ancient city gates it has physical thickness — a substantial passage of stone. That liminal space within the gate's thickness did not carry the *kedushah* of the *azarah*; it had only the *kedushah* of the *ezrat nashim*. This made it a legal threshold available to those who could not yet enter the *azarah* but whose ritual required some form of proximity to it.

A *yoledet*, a woman who had given birth, needed to bring a *korban* as part of her purification, but was not yet *tahor* in a way that allowed her into the *azarah*. By standing in the *shaar Nikanor*, she could be present for the bringing of her *korban* without entering the prohibited space. A *metzora* needed the blood of his *korban* applied to his thumbs and toes, but similarly could not yet enter the *azarah*. He would stand in the thickness of the gate and extend his thumb and toe into the *azarah*, allowing the *kohen* to apply the blood — though this raises the separate halachic question of *bi'ah b'miktzas shemah bi'ah*, whether partial entry into the *Beis HaMikdash* while *tamei* constitutes a prohibited entry.

The *sotah*, too, would stand in this liminal space. And what is striking is the company she is placed in. The *mishna* describes her alongside the *yoledet* and the *metzora* — people undergoing processes of *tum'ah* and *taharah*. This is no accident. The *Torah*'s own language for the outcome of the *sotah* procedure is *v'nitme'ah* and *hi lo nitme'ah* — she is *tamei* or she is not *tamei*. The procedure is being reframed not only as a matter of *din* but also as a process of *taharah*, of determining and rectifying a state of spiritual impurity. This is a different kind of framing than the trial-by-ordeal model, and perhaps a more accessible one — we know there are *taharah* processes that involve unusual rituals, birds, blood on fingers, strange mixtures. A *minchah* offering, words dissolved in water, a woman drinking — situated within that framework, the ritual becomes less anomalous.

### Garment Tearing

*Hakohen ochez bi'vgadeha* — the *kohen* takes hold of her garments. *Im nikre'u nikre'u v'im nifremu nifremu* — if they tear, they tear; if they split entirely, they split. The *kohen* holds her garments and does not release them regardless of how extensively they rend, continuing until *ad she'hu megaleh libah* — he has exposed her chest. He also undoes her hair, *v'soter et se'arah*, which echoes the *Torah*'s own language for this stage of the procedure.

### Modesty Limits

Rabbi Yehuda dissents in a specific case: *im haya libah na'eh lo haya megalehu* — if her chest was particularly attractive, he would not expose it, and *im haya se'arah na'eh lo haya sotro* — if her hair was beautiful, he would not undo it. The underlying tension is obvious: this degradation ritual involves uncovering parts of the body that are normally covered, and in doing so risks transforming what is meant to be a shameful and sobering spectacle into something erotically charged for the onlookers. Rabbi Yehuda attempts to set limits precisely at the point where the degradation threatens to tip into something else.

### Degradation

If she had been wearing white garments, she is dressed in black. If she wore golden jewelry — *k'lei zahav, ve'katliyot, ve'nezamim ve'tabba'ot* — various chokers, earrings, and rings — *ma'avirin mimena*, they are removed from her, *kedei lena'velah*, in order to dishevel her and render her repulsive. This is a systematic process of degradation, stripping away the markers of status and beauty and replacing them with their opposites. Then an Egyptian rope is taken and bound above her breasts to hold up the garment after it has been torn, so that it does not fall entirely. The sequence likely proceeds as follows: first the black garments are substituted and the jewelry removed; then the *kohen* tears the garments; then the rope is tied to hold them.

### Public Spectacle

*V'chol ha'rotze lir'ot ba v'ro'eh* — and whoever wishes to come and see may come and see. This is a public spectacle, and notably it is one that has no direct source in the *Torah*. The *Torah*'s *sotah* procedure is not a public event. *Chazal* have made it one.

This transformation is worth pausing over. The movement from a private matter between a jealous husband and his wife to a public spectacle before all of *Yerushalayim* mirrors a broader pattern in *Chazal*'s treatment of *Beis HaMikdash* rituals generally. The *Yom Kippur* service, for instance, is explicitly marked in the *Torah* as a moment of singular divine intimacy: *v'chol adam lo yihyeh b'ohel mo'ed b'vo'o l'chaper bakodesh*. Yet in the *mishna*'s description of *Yom Kippur*, the service becomes a public ritual — the people gather to see the lot selected, to watch the red string, to hear the reading of the *Torah*. *Chazal* consistently push these rituals into the public sphere.

And there is a further dimension here, drawn from the work of Yishai Rosen-Zvi, who wrote on *Masechet Sotah* in his book *Ha-tekes she-lo hayah* — the ritual that never was. Rosen-Zvi argues that the *mishna* proceeds throughout with an assumption of the woman's guilt. The entire procedure is oriented not toward clarifying her status but toward punishing her. One way to see this is in the scaring: when the *beit din* frightened the *sotah*, they appealed only in one direction — please confess, spare us the need to erase God's Name. When *beit din* frightens witnesses in capital cases, by contrast, they press in both directions: testify if you truly know, but do not testify if you are uncertain. Here, the *beit din* does not say: if you are truly innocent, go forward so that the waters can vindicate you and restore you to your husband. The assumption is that she did it, and the *beit din*'s appeals are structured accordingly.

This presumption of guilt also helps explain the public spectacle. A neutral judicial proceeding aimed at determining guilt or innocence does not need an audience. But if the outcome is already understood — if this is, in effect, a public punishment — then gathering the people makes perfect sense, both as a form of communal shaming and as a deterrent. The *Torah* itself provides the underlying principle: *v'chol ha'am yishme'u v'yira'u*.

### Who May Watch

*Chutz me'avadeha u'shifchoteha* — with one exception: her servants may not be present. The reason given is *mipnei she'libah gas bahen* — their presence would bolster her sense of confidence and importance. She might be less willing to confess with her servants watching; she might feel less the weight of the proceedings if surrounded by people over whom she has authority. The goal of obtaining a confession or at least ensuring the degradation achieves its full psychological effect requires that she be stripped of those familiar sources of comfort and status.

*V'chol ha'nashim mutarot lir'otah* — but all women are permitted and indeed encouraged to see her. The *mishna* quotes a *pasuk* from *Yechezkel*: *v'niv'ssru kol ha'nashim v'lo ta'asena k'zimatchena* — all the women shall take heed and not do as she did in her lewdness. The *sotah* proceeding, in its public form, serves the same function as *kol ha'am yishme'u v'yira'u* in capital cases: punishment as public instruction and deterrent, the logic of *din* made visible.

---

## Beis Din Authority

### Deriving Rule

The *Gemara* asks: *mena hani millei* — from where is this derived? How do we know that the *sotah* must be brought before the *Beis Din HaGadol* in *Yerushalayim*? Rabbi Chiyya bar Gamda said in the name of Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina: the derivation comes from a *gezeirah shavah* of *Torah-Torah*. It is written here, by the *sotah*: *v'asah lah ha'kohen et kol ha'Torah ha'zot* — the *kohen* shall do all of this *Torah*, this ritual. And it is written there, by the *zaken mamre*: *al pi ha'Torah asher yorucha* — in accordance with the *Torah* they teach you. *Mah le'halan b'shivim v'echad* — just as a *zaken mamre* who rebels against the ruling of the *Sanhedrin* requires a court of seventy-one, *af kan b'shivim v'echad* — so too here, the *sotah* procedure requires the oversight of a *beit din* of seventy-one.

### Zaken Mamre

The *kal v'chomer* from *zaken mamre* is an instructive choice of parallel. The *zaken mamre* is a Torah sage who rules contrary to the *Sanhedrin HaGadol*, the supreme authority, and whose defiance carries the penalty of death. The *Sanhedrin*'s authority in that case is total and essential — without their involvement the case cannot proceed. The *Gemara* is drawing on that model to establish the *Beis Din HaGadol*'s centrality to the *sotah* process as well.

### Chronology Problem

*Tosafos* raises a powerful difficulty with this derivation. The *halacha* of *zaken mamre* applies only when the *Sanhedrin* is sitting in its designated place within the *Beis HaMikdash*. Historically, we know that the *Sanhedrin* left the *Beis HaMikdash* — they moved out of the *Lishkat HaGazit* — before the *churban*, because they did not wish to bear responsibility for adjudicating capital cases. Yet the evidence indicates that *sotah* rituals continued even after the *Sanhedrin* had left the *Beis HaMikdash*. If the *sotah* procedure truly required a *Beis Din HaGadol* sitting in the *Beis HaMikdash*, on the model of *zaken mamre*, then *sotah* should have ceased the moment the *Sanhedrin* relocated. But that does not appear to be what happened.

### Warning Not Required

*Tosafos* resolves the difficulty as follows: *d'iyum lo haya ma'akev* — the intimidation, the warning administered by the *Beis Din HaGadol*, was not *me'akev*. It was not a blocking condition. *D'im lo hayu me'ayimin klal, af al pi chen haysa shosah* — even if the *beit din* had not issued the warning at all, she could still have gone through with the drinking of the waters. The *sotah* ritual would still function. *Hilchach haysa nohages afilu achar hagalus* — therefore the practice continued even after the *Sanhedrin*'s departure from the *Beis HaMikdash*.

### Chazal Paradox

This resolution is, on reflection, remarkable. *Tosafos* is telling us that for all the elaborate *beit din* scaffolding that has been constructed around the *sotah* procedure — the local *beit din* receiving the case, the two *talmidei chachamim* accompanying the couple, the *Beis Din HaGadol* in *Yerushalayim* issuing its solemn warning — none of it is ultimately *me'akev*. None of it is strictly necessary. At its core, the *sotah* procedure is a *Beis HaMikdash* ritual: the man brings his wife to the *kohen*, and the *kohen* administers the waters. The entire *beit din* superstructure could theoretically be dispensed with, and the procedure would still be valid.

This paradox runs in both directions. *Chazal* foreground *beit din* authority at every stage, insist on its presence, draw explicit parallels to *din*, and embed witnesses and *hatra'ah* into the very journey to *Yerushalayim* — and then the sources reveal that it was all optional. This also provides an answer to the earlier question that the first *Tosafos* implicitly raised: why, if *sotah* requires a *beit din* of seventy-one on the model of *zaken mamre*, is it not listed in *Perek Kamma* of *Sanhedrin* among the cases requiring a *beit din* of seventy-one? The answer is precisely because the *sotah* proceeding is not, at its base, something that requires a *beit din* of seventy-one. It is a *Beis HaMikdash* ritual. The *beit din*'s role, however elaborate and however prominently *Chazal* present it, is ultimately not constitutive of the ritual's validity.

What we are left with is a picture of extraordinary complexity: a ritual that the *Torah* conceived as a husband's private action in the *Beis HaMikdash*, which *Chazal* systematically transformed into a judicial proceeding saturated with the language and structure of *din* — while simultaneously acknowledging, when pressed, that the transformation was always optional and the underlying reality remained a pure *Beis HaMikdash* ritual.

---

---

# Sotah 7b

## Warnings & Severity

### God's Name Erased

The Gemara opens with a discussion of the foundational concern underlying the *sotah* ritual: the erasure of God's name. The *mishnah* had established that the *beit din* impresses upon the woman the severity of what she is about to undergo — just as witnesses in capital cases are solemnly warned — because of the prohibition against erasing God's name unnecessarily. The relevant phrase is *assur lishmo hagadol shenichtav bikdushah shelo yimcha al hamayim*: the great name, written in holiness, must not be erased over the water without cause.

This concern is central to understanding the *sotah* ritual's inner logic. Part of the ritual's profound beauty, as reflected in *aggadata*, is that God is willing to have His name erased in order to restore *shalom bayit* between a husband and wife. Nevertheless, the prohibition against erasing God's name remains in force, and so the *beit din* works to prevent that erasure wherever possible.

### Paradox of Warnings

The Gemara then raises what appears to be a sharp contradiction. A *baraita* from the *Tosefta* expands on the notion of warning the woman and states: *kederech shema'amin aleha shelo tishteh kach ma'amin aleha shetishteh* — just as we warn her not to drink, so too we warn her to drink. This seems paradoxical. If the entire purpose of warning her is so that she will not go through with the ritual and thereby cause God's name to be erased, what could it possibly mean to warn her to drink?

The *baraita* itself elaborates: we tell her, "If it is clear to you that you are innocent, stand firm and drink, because the bitter water is like a dry medicine placed on raw flesh — if there is a wound, it dissolves into it and takes effect; if there is no wound, it does nothing." In other words, if she is innocent, the water will have no effect and it is actually beneficial for her to proceed with the ritual. The destruction of God's name will then serve a purpose.

### Before/After Erasure

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya kan kodem shenimchakah hamegillah kan le'achar shenimchakah hamegillah* — there is no difficulty, because these are two distinct stages. Before the *Megillat Sotah* has been erased into the water, the *beit din* tries to encourage the woman to admit guilt, so that the erasure of God's name is avoided altogether. Once the *megillah* has already been erased, however, we do not want that erasure to have been in vain, and so we now encourage her to drink and affirm her innocence, telling her the water will benefit rather than harm her.

The *mishnah* had stated that they say before her *devarim she'einam kedai lishoman* — things that are not suitable to be heard, yet are said to her anyway. The Gemara clarifies that these are *devarim shel aggadah*, aggadic narratives, stories that will move her emotionally. Why are they described as *einam kedai lishoman*? That becomes clear as the Gemara provides its examples.

### Judah & Reuben

The Gemara's *baraita* specifies the content of these narratives. We tell her stories from the earlier writings, from the lives of the founding figures of Israel, citing a verse from Iyov: *asher chakhamim yagidu velo kichadu me'avotam* — the wise ones have spoken of these things and have not hidden them from their ancestors. Two paradigmatic examples are then given.

*Yehudah hodah velo bosh* — Yehuda admitted his sin and was not embarrassed. *Mah hayah sofo? Nachal chayei ha'olam haba* — his end was that he inherited the life of the World to Come. Similarly, *Reuven hodeh velo bosh mah hayah sofo nachal chayei ha'olam haba* — Reuven admitted his sin and was not embarrassed, and he too inherited the World to Come.

Here the rabbis are making use of the *pshat* reading of narratives that, from the perspective of *Torah she-be-al peh*, are generally understood more carefully. We are told in *Megillah* that the story of Reuven is not translated into *Targum* during public reading, precisely so that people should not be misled by the *pshat* understanding — which sounds as though Reuven literally slept with his stepmother, while *Chazal* maintain the incident was something less severe. Yet here, the Gemara is explicitly drawing on the *pshat* reading of these stories as emotionally powerful examples of repentance and admission of guilt. This reflects a broader tension in rabbinic thought about how to read *Tanach* and how much to engage with the personalities of its protagonists as real, flawed human beings capable of sin and *teshuvah*.

The reason these narratives are *einam kedai lishoman* — not suitable to be heard — is precisely because they reflect badly on great *tzaddikim* or on figures who appear prominently in the *Torah*. Yet they are told to the *sotah* anyway, because inspiring her to confess and repent overrides that concern. The *Rema* cites this principle in one of his *teshuvot*, noting that the concern of embarrassing a *talmid chakham* can be overridden in the context of a process aimed at eliciting confession and restoring *shalom bayit*.

### Judah's Punishment

The Gemara then asks: we said both Yehuda and Reuven inherited *Olam Haba* — what further reward is there to discuss? *Ela mah secharan ba'olam hazeh* — what was their reward even in this world?

For Reuven, the *pasuk lahem levadam nitnah ha'aretz* hints at his being among the tribes who received the first inheritance on the east side of the *Yarden*, a share in *Eretz Yisrael* that was his own. For Yehuda, we know he admitted his sin because the *pasuk* says explicitly: *vayakker Yehuda vayomer tzadkah mimmeni* — Yehuda recognized and said, "She is more righteous than I." But how do we know that Reuven admitted his sin? The Gemara cites Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: what does it mean when Moshe blesses Reuven at the end of *Sefer Devarim*, saying *yechi Reuven ve'al yamot*, "Reuven shall live and not die"? And immediately following is the blessing for Yehuda, introduced with the unusual word *vezot* — a connection that the Gemara draws upon to link the two.

The Gemara then presents a striking teaching: *kol otan shanim shehayu Yisrael bamidbar hayu atzmotav shel Yehuda mitgalgelin ba'aron* — throughout the forty years that the Jewish people were in the desert, the bones of Yehuda were rolling around in the ark, dislocated, until Moshe prayed on his behalf. The specific punishment was *eivarei deshapa* — his limbs were disjointed from their sockets — an image that Rashi connects to the *treifah* discussed in *Chullin* on daf 42b, *buka d'atma deshaph midukhtei*, the dislocated hip joint. Even in death, Yehuda was punished for his role in the episode with Tamar.

What prompted Moshe's prayer? *Amar lefanav Ribbono shel Olam mi garam leReuven shehodeh* — who was it that caused Reuven to do *teshuvah*? It was Yehuda. Yehuda's character, his willingness to admit wrongdoing publicly, inspired Reuven's own *teshuvah*. And so it was not even Yehuda's own *teshuvah* directly that earned him this redemption, but the fact that his example had inspired another person to repent. This is a striking teaching about the ripple effects of genuine admission of sin.

The Gemara then parses the blessing of Yehuda in *parashat v'zot habracha* as a series of remedies for the punishments Yehuda had suffered. *Shema Adonai kol Yehuda* — God heard Yehuda's cry, releasing him from his dislocated bones. *V'el amo tevi'enu* — bring him back to his people, meaning they finally allowed him into the *yeshivah* of heaven, the *metivta d'rakiya*, from which he had been excluded. *Yadav rav lo* — his hands were strengthened, corresponding to his now being permitted to participate in the *shakla v'tarya*, the back-and-forth of debate in the heavenly *beit midrash*, from which he had previously been barred even after gaining entry. And *v'ezer mizarav tihyeh* — let there be help against his enemies, meaning he could finally arrive at halakhic conclusions, *aliba d'hilkhata*, in his learning.

### Reuven's Public Apology

The Gemara then returns to Reuven and poses a question. *Bishlama biYehuda ashkechan de'odei* — we understand why Yehuda had to make a public admission of his sin: *ki heichi d'lo tisoraf Tamar*, so that Tamar would not be burned. Yehuda had no choice but to speak publicly to save her life. But why did Reuven need to make a public admission? *Lama lei de'odei* — there was seemingly no practical purpose; no one's life was at stake. Moreover, does not Rav Sheshet say that it is brazen to publicize one's own sins, *chatzip alai diprat chataei*?

The Gemara answers: *ki heichi d'lo lyechshadu achvohi* — Reuven was concerned that if he did not publicly acknowledge what he had done, his brothers would fall under suspicion. Something had become known, but without knowing who was responsible, people might have suspected any of his brothers. By making a public declaration, he ensured that no one else would be considered *chashud* for that sin.

This reflects the broader principle, noted especially in the *Rambam*, that for sins *bein adam lachavero*, there is an obligation to publicly acknowledge and apologize, because another person has been hurt and public rectification is part of the repair. For sins *bein adam lamakom*, by contrast, it is generally preferable to keep the matter private, between the person and God, without unnecessary public disclosure. Reuven's case was exceptional: the public nature of his admission was not self-serving, but was required specifically to protect his brothers from wrongful suspicion.

---

## Woman's Confession

### Ketubah Receipt

The Gemara then transitions to the case in which the woman admits to having committed adultery. *Im amra tmea ani* — if she says she is impure, *shovrim ktubatah* — we break her *ketubah*. The question is what exactly this means. *Shmaat mina kotvim shovar* — does it mean we write a receipt acknowledging that the *ketubah* has been settled, leaving the original document in place? Or does it mean something else?

Abaye proposes emending the reading: *tni mikrat*, we should read it as *koraat*, she tears up the *ketubah*. If you tear up the *shtar* itself, the instrument of debt is destroyed and cannot be claimed. Rava objects: *veha shoveret katani* — the *mishnah* uses the word *shoveret*, which implies breaking, not tearing. You cannot simply change the *mishnah*'s language.

### Ketubah Document

Rava therefore offers a different resolution: *bemakom she'ein kotvim ktubah askinan* — we are discussing a locale where it was not the practice to write a physical document for the *ketubah*. The *ketubah* obligation existed, but was conducted entirely orally. In such a case, there is no document to tear. The *mishnah*'s language of *shovrim* then means that we write a receipt — a *shovar* — to formally dissolve her claim.

This is a noteworthy window into the historical development of the *ketubah* as an institution. The *sugyot* across *Shas* present a complex picture: in some places the *ketubah* appears *d'Oraita*, in others *d'Rabbanan*. The *Rambam* at the beginning of *Hilchot Ishut* formulates it strikingly, stating that the *mitzvah* of *kiddushin* requires marriage *bekiddushin uvektubah* — the *ketubah* is part of the *mitzvah* of *kiddushin* itself.

Rashi at the bottom of the page notes two alternatives for how, in a place without a written *ketubah*, a woman would collect her entitlement. If divorced, *mishenitgarsha motzia gita vegova ba* — she brings the *get* itself as proof of her status and collects on the basis of that. If widowed, *u'chshenitalmena mevia edei mita vegova* — she must bring witnesses who testify to her husband's death before she can claim from his estate. This latter process is considerably more burdensome, requiring *edei mita* rather than simply producing a document. In a certain sense, one can trace in this the practical impetus for institutionalizing the written *ketubah*: the difficulty for a widow of having to produce testimony made it far simpler, ultimately, to give the woman a *shtar* she could hold in her hand.

---

## Eastern Gate Ritual

### Nikanor Gate

The *mishnah* continues: *de-in amarta tehorah ani ma'alin ota le-sha'ar hamizrach* — if she says she is innocent, they bring her up to the eastern gate, which is the *Sha'ar Nikanor*, the great gate at the boundary between the *Ezrat Nashim* and the main *Azarah* of the *Beit Hamikdash*. This gate had fifteen steps ascending to it and two smaller doors on either side. It was the central point for those who had no reason to enter the *Azarah* itself — *Yisraelim*, women, and others — who nevertheless came to the *Beit Hamikdash*.

The Gemara asks: *ma'alin ota* — what does it mean they bring her up? *Hatam ka'ima* — she was already there, since the earlier stages of the ritual had already taken place at the *Sha'ar Nikanor*. The Gemara clarifies: *ma'alin ota* refers to bringing her up from the *Beit Din Hagadol she-biYerushalayim*, the *Lishkat Hagazit*, which straddles the boundary between the *Azarah* and the *Ezrat Nashim* — half *kodesh* and half *chol* — but which is also adjacent to the *Sha'ar Nikanor*. The Gemara notes that it is precisely here, *lifnei Hashem*, that the woman must be made to drink, as the *pasuk* requires: *ve-he'emid ha-kohen et ha-ishah lifnei Hashem*.

The same location requirement applies to the *metzora*, whose purification process also requires the *kohen* to stand him at the entrance of the *Mishkan* or *Beit Hamikdash*: *ve-he'emid ha-kohen ha-mitaher*. The symbolic power of this is notable — the *metzora* is excluded even from walled cities, and then for his *taharah* he is brought back inside, to the very threshold of the sacred.

### Making Her Weary

The Gemara then states: *ma'akimim ota u-mekifim ota kedei le-yage'ah* — they make her walk all around the *Har Habayit* in order to tire her out. The purpose is to wear her down so that, if she is guilty, she will be more likely to admit it rather than proceed to drink the water. Conversely, if she is genuinely innocent, the fact that she is willing to drink even after this exhausting ordeal demonstrates the sincerity of her claim.

### Witnesses Comparison

A *tanna* draws an explicit comparison to the procedure in capital cases. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states: *Beit Din mesa'in et ha-edim mi-makom le-makom kedei she-titaref da'atan aleihem ve-yahzeru ba-hen* — the *beit din* makes witnesses in capital cases schlep from place to place in order to tire them out and induce them to reconsider whether they really wish to testify. The parallel is precise: in capital cases the witnesses may be putting an innocent person to death if they are lying, and we create disincentives for false testimony. At the same time, if they are telling the truth, they are absolutely obligated to testify — indeed, it is a great *mitzvah* to do so. The same dual dynamic applies to the *sotah*.

The Gemara also notes the broader question of who else must present themselves at the *Sha'ar Nikanor*. A *yoledet*, a woman who has given birth, must bring her *korban* there as well, by the rule that *ein korbano shel adam karev ela im ken omed al gabav* — a person's sacrifice cannot be offered unless that person is present. The Gemara raises *zavim* and *zavot* as additional examples of *mechusei kapparah*, and concludes that the *mishnah* simply listed one representative case — *tana chada mineihu nakat*.

### Two Sotahs Together

The *baraita* states: *ein mashkin shtei sotos ke'achas* — one may not administer the *sotah* water to two women simultaneously. The concern expressed by the first opinion is *kedei shelo yehei libah gas bechavertah* — one woman should not be emboldened by the presence of the other. If two women are undergoing the ritual together and both are stubborn, each one may be emboldened by the other's stubbornness into proceeding to drink the water even if guilty.

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees not with the ruling but with its basis: *lo min hashem hu zeh ela amar kra osah levadah* — this is not derived from *sevara*, from logical reasoning, but directly from the *pasuk*, which says *osah levadah*, "her alone." This is a *gezeirat hakatuv*. This constitutes a good example of a *machloket* in which both *tanna'im* agree on the *halakhah* but differ on whether its source is logical or scriptural. Notably, the Gemara treats a compelling *sevara* as carrying *d'Oraita* force — *tana kamma*, identified as Rabbi Shimon, holds that we *darshin ta'ama dekra*, we interpret the *pasuk* in light of its reasoning, so the *gezeirat hakatuv* is bounded by the logic behind it.

The *nafka mina* between the two opinions concerns a woman who is *rotetet* — particularly fearful and visibly trembling. According to Rabbi Shimon, such a woman could theoretically be made to drink alongside another *sotah*, since there is no concern that she would be emboldened by the other woman's presence. According to Rabbi Yehuda, the *gezeirat hakatuv* is absolute regardless of the circumstances. The *Tosafot HaRosh* adds that one would still need to account for the case where one woman is fearful but the other is not — the latter could still embolden the former, requiring the prohibition to cover both scenarios.

The Gemara then introduces a broader principle: *ein osin mitzvos chavilos chavilos* — one may not bundle *mitzvot* together. Rashi explains that this is because doing so gives the appearance of treating *mitzvot* as a heavy burden one is trying to rush through, as though eager to discharge one's obligations and move on — *nire'eh kemo shehayah alav lemassoi u-memaher leforok masa'o*. *Tosafot* in *Moed Katan* offers a different and more positive framing: just as we do not combine one celebration with another — *ein me'arvin simcha besimcha* — so too each *mitzvah* deserves its own separate focus and its own *simcha shel mitzvah*. One of the *acharonim*, Rav Yosef Engel, notes an additional technical dimension: the principle of *osek bemitzvah patur min hamitzvah* — one who is occupied with a *mitzvah* is exempt from another *mitzvah* — may itself create a structural barrier to performing two *mitzvot* simultaneously.

The *baraita* lists further applications of *ein osin mitzvos chavilos chavilos*: two *metzoraim* cannot undergo the purification ritual simultaneously; two *avadim Ivrim* cannot have their ears pierced at the same time; two *agalot arufot* cannot be performed together. Notably, all of these examples involve performing two instances of the *same mitzvah* rather than two different *mitzvot* in parallel — an important distinction, since no one would suggest that one cannot *daven minchah* while simultaneously shaking a *lulav* simply because they are two different *mitzvot*.

The *machloket* over whether the piercing of a slave's ear is a *mitzvah* at all — and therefore subject to *ein osin mitzvos chavilos chavilos* — is itself debated by later authorities. The *Chazon Ish* holds it is a *reshut*, entirely optional, and the master could refuse even if the slave requests to remain; the *Magen Avraham* holds that once the slave requests to be *nirtza*, it becomes obligatory for the master.

The Gemara ultimately resolves the apparent tension between the principle of *ein osin mitzvos chavilos chavilos* and the possibility of having two *sotahs* drink on the same day: *lo kashya kan bekohen echad kan beshnei kohanim* — there is no contradiction, since the prohibition applies to a single *kohen* who would be performing the ritual for two women. Two different *kohanim* could each administer the water to a different *sotah*, even at the same time, since neither *kohen* individually is bundling *mitzvot*.

---

## Exposure & Humiliation

### Uncovering Hair

The *baraita* cites the *pasuk* *u-farah et rosh ha-ishah* — the *kohen* unbraids or uncovers the woman's hair. The Gemara asks: from *roshah* alone, we know only about her head. From where do we derive that her body itself must also be exposed? The Gemara answers: the *pasuk* does not say merely *u-farah et roshah* but rather *u-farah et rosh ha-ishah* — the full word *ha-ishah*, "the woman," is included, extending the obligation to expose her body as well. And if so, what does the specific mention of *roshah* teach? *Melamed shehakohen soter et se'arah* — it teaches that the *kohen* undoes and loosens her hair specifically.

### Hirhurim Concern

Rabbi Yehuda raises a consideration: what if the woman is particularly attractive? This brings into focus a broader question: how concerned are we about *hirhurim*, inappropriate sexual thoughts, among those witnessing the *sotah* ritual? *L'meimra de'Rabbi Yehuda chaish l'hirhur* — it would appear that Rabbi Yehuda is concerned about *hirhurim* arising from the public exposure of the *sotah*. And *v'rabbanan lo chaishi* — the Rabbanan are less concerned.

### Execution Comparison

However, the Gemara notes that this apparent alignment seems to be precisely the reverse of what these same authorities hold elsewhere. In the context of execution by *skilah*, a *baraita* states that a man is stripped of all clothing except *perek echad milfanav* — one piece of cloth in front. A woman, by contrast, receives two pieces — *echad milfaneha v'echad milachareha* — because, as Rashi explains, *she'beit haboshet ne'erat mishnei tzadim*, a woman's private area is exposed from both sides and therefore requires coverage on both sides. But notably, even according to this *baraita*, a woman's entire torso would be uncovered during execution by *skilah* — indicating that the Rabbanan are not especially concerned about *hirhurim* in that context. Yet that is described as *divrei Rabbi Yehuda* — Rabbi Yehuda's position. Meanwhile, *v'chachamim omrim ha'ish niskal arom, v'ein ha'ishah niskalet aroma* — the Sages say a man is stoned completely naked, but a woman is not stoned naked at all; she must be clothed.

This presents a puzzling inversion: in the context of *sotah*, Rabbi Yehuda appears more protective of the woman from *hirhurim*, while in the context of *skilah* the Rabbanan are the ones who require that a woman not be exposed naked.

### Raba's Rationale

Rava resolves both the internal contradiction within Rabbi Yehuda's position and that within the Rabbanan's position simultaneously: *de-Rabbi Yehuda ad-Rabbi Yehuda lo kashya*, and *de-rabanan ad-rabanan nami lo kashya*. The concern in the *sotah* case is not *hirhurim* per se — it is *mishum venissaru kol hanashim*, because all women must witness the *sotah*'s fate and be warned by her example. The humiliation of the *sotah* serves a broader deterrent and educational purpose. In the case of execution, however, *ein lecha yisur gadol mizeh* — there is no humiliation greater than death itself, and there is no need to add further degradation.

Rava identifies a more specific concern driving the *sotah* case: *sh'ma totzi mibeit din zakai v'yitgaru bah pirchei kehunah* — perhaps she will leave the *sotah* ritual having been found innocent after drinking the water, and the young *kohanim* who are present in the *Azarah* (*metzuyin ba'azara*, as Rashi notes) will be stirred by inappropriate thoughts about her. If she has been exposed in public in the course of the ritual, these *kohanim* will have seen her, and that sight will provoke *hirhurim*.

But why not apply that concern to execution as well? *Hatam mistalka* — in the case of execution, she is gone; she has died. The *kohanim* will not see her again. *Gemiri d'ein yetzer hara sholet ela b'ma she'einav ro'ot* — it is a received principle that the *yetzer hara* only takes hold with respect to what a person's eyes have actually seen. Once she is dead, there is no ongoing exposure to provoke ongoing *hirhurim*. But in the *sotah* case, if she is found innocent, she returns to her husband and continues to live in the community, and the *kohanim* who saw her exposed will encounter her again.

### Bru Lo Mitah Yafah

The Gemara then raises the question of whether we should administer both punishments — expose her publicly *and* execute her — in the case of a guilty *sotah*. The answer draws on one of the most fundamental principles of rabbinic capital law: *ve'ahavta lere'acha kamocha beru lo mitah yafah* — from the verse "love your neighbor as yourself," the rabbis derive that one must provide an appropriate death, a *mitah yafah*, even to one who is executed. This *drashah* is invoked repeatedly throughout *Sanhedrin* in connection with all four *mitot beit din*, consistently functioning to pull back from what the *Torah* might appear to mandate explicitly, in order to preserve the physical integrity of the human body.

As Professor Lorberbaum has argued, the underlying principle is *tzelem Elokim* — the human being possesses a physical form that reflects the divine image, and capital punishment must therefore be carried out in a manner that does not deform or disfigure the body. *Beru lo mitah yafah* does not necessarily mean the most pleasant death, but the death that leaves the body most intact and unspoiled. By this standard, adding public humiliation on top of execution would violate the principle — we cannot require someone to be both publicly exposed and put to death.

### Pain vs. Humiliation

The Gemara then addresses a specific *machloket* regarding what *mitah yafah* means in practice, directly relevant to the question of execution: *mar savar bizyona adif lah tfei mitza'ara d'gufa* — one opinion holds that emotional humiliation is worse than physical pain, and therefore being executed naked (which accelerates death by removing cushioning from the stones but is more humiliating) is actually the *better* death — more pain, less humiliation. *U-mar savar tza'ara d'gufa adif lei tfei mibizyonei* — the other opinion holds that physical pain is worse, and therefore being clothed at execution (which cushions the impact but prolongs death) is preferable — more humiliation, but less physical suffering. Both opinions apply the principle of *mitah yafah*, but they disagree about which factor is the dominant consideration in determining the most appropriate death.

### Removing Jewelry

The *mishnah* states that if the woman was dressed beautifully — wearing white garments or fine jewelry — she is dressed in ugly or worn clothing for the ritual. The Gemara initially treats it as obvious (*pshita*) that her jewelry must be removed, since the entire purpose of the process is *nivvul*, to make her look degraded. But the Gemara raises a counterintuitive possibility: *behanei it lah bizyuna tfei* — perhaps leaving her jewelry on is actually *more* humiliating, because of the common proverb about a person who walks around naked but wearing shoes. That is, a figure who retains tokens of elegance and status while being otherwise degraded is in some respects more pitiable and embarrassing than one who is stripped completely. The Gemara concludes — *kamashma lan* — we do not apply this reasoning; the jewelry is removed.

### Egyptian Rope

After the tearing of the garment, the *kohen* brings a *chevel hamitzri*, an Egyptian rope, and ties it above her breasts to prevent her clothing from falling down entirely. The *Yerushalmi* offers two explanations for why specifically an Egyptian rope: either because her conduct recalled the licentiousness of Egypt, *k'ma'aseh eretz mitzrayim*, or alternatively the term is not *chevel mitzri* but *chevel matzui* — a common rope woven from palm fronds, rough and coarse, which was the standard material of the time.

The Gemara records a question posed by Rav Abba to Rav Huna: is the *chevel hamitzri* *me'akev* — is it an indispensable part of the *sotah* ritual, without which the process is invalid? Two possible explanations for its use are considered. If the reason is simply *shelo yishm'tu bgadeha me'aleha*, so that her clothes do not fall down, then even a small cord would suffice and the specific Egyptian rope would not be essential. But if the reason is rooted in *middah keneged middah*, corresponding to her having provocatively girded herself, then the specific rope carries substantive significance and might be *me'akev*.

The Gemara resolves the question by citing a more expanded version of the *mishnah*, a *baraita*, which makes explicit that the reason for the rope is purely functional — *k'dei shelo yishm'tu bgadeha me'aleha* — so that her garments do not fall. Since the reason is purely practical, the specific Egyptian rope is not *me'akev*.

*Tosafot* at the top of the following page raises an additional question prompted by the *Yerushalmi*: the rope is purchased from *mishirei halishkah*, public temple funds. This raises a parallel question about other instruments of capital punishment — the sword used for beheading, the cord used for *chenek* — whether those too are purchased with public funds, and how far the parallel between *sotah* and *mitat beit din* extends.

---

## Witnesses to Ritual

### Contradiction Resolved

The Gemara notes that the *mishnah* appears to contradict itself. On one hand it states *ve-chol ha-rotzeh lir'ot bah yera'eh* — whoever wishes to see may come and see, with no distinction between men and women. On the other hand, the *mishnah* also states *kol ha-nashim mutarot lir'otah* — all women are permitted to see her, implying that women yes, men no.

Abaye attempts to resolve the contradiction by suggesting *targemah anashim* — that even the first clause refers only to women. Rava objects: *ve-ha kol ha-rotzeh lir'ot bah yera'eh* — but the first clause clearly says "whoever wishes," which is inclusive language, not restricted to women.

### Women Obligated

Rava offers a different resolution: *kol ha-rotzeh lir'ot bah ro'eh lo shena gavrei ve-lo shena nashei* — whoever wishes to come and see, whether men or women, may come and see. Both are permitted. The second clause, however, conveys something more: *nashim chayavot lir'otah* — women are not merely permitted but *obligated* to attend.

### Women's Lesson

The obligation for women to witness the *sotah* ritual is derived from the *pasuk*: *ve-nissaru kol ha-nashim ve-lo ta'aseina ke-zimatchanah* — all women are to be chastened and warned so that they do not engage in the same *zimah*, the same prohibited sexual behavior, that the *sotah* may have committed. Women must be present specifically so that they will internalize the lesson and be deterred from similar conduct. Men are permitted to attend but are not obligated; women are not merely permitted but are required to come and witness.

---

## Middah Keneged Middah

### Measure for Measure

The final *mishnah* of the chapter introduces the principle of *middah keneged middah* — the manner in which a person conducts himself or herself is precisely the measure by which God responds. *Be-middah she-adam moded bah modedin lo.* The *sotah*'s punishment corresponds exactly to her sin. *Hi kishtah atzmah la-aveirah, ha-Makom nivvelah* — she adorned herself with jewelry for the sake of her sin; God therefore takes away her beauty. *Hi giltah et atzmah la-aveirah, ha-Makom gilah aleiha* — she revealed herself for her sin; God therefore reveals her.

### Order of Punishment

The *mishnah* specifies the sequence of the *sotah*'s physical punishment: *be-yarech hitchilah ba-aveirah* — she began her sin with her thigh, a euphemism for her genitalia. *Tcilah ve-achar kach ha-beten* — and then her womb, corresponding to the concern about pregnancy from the adulterous relationship. Therefore, *lokah ha-yarech tcilah ve-achar kach ha-beten* — the punishment begins with the thigh and only then affects the womb. *Ve-sha'ar kol ha-guf lo palat* — the rest of the body is entirely unaffected by the *sotah* water; only those specific parts of the body that were implicated in the sin are punished. The Gemara will elaborate on these *pesukim* and their implications in the discussion that continues on daf 8b.

---

---

# Sotah 8

## Warning & God's Name

### Warnings & Erasure

The *gemara* opens on 7b with the phrase *uma'amin aleha* — the *beit din* impresses upon the *sotah* the gravity of what she is about to undergo. The *mishnah* had already stated that they warn her just as they warn witnesses in capital cases, and the reason given is *asur lishmo hagadol shenikhtav bikdusha shelo yimacheh al hamayim* — it is forbidden to erase God's name, which has been written in holiness, upon the water for no reason. The *megillas sotah* is inscribed with God's name, and the ink is then scraped into the bitter water. This is, in one sense, one of the most striking features of the *sotah* ritual: God is willing to have His name erased in order to restore *shalom bayit* to a couple. Nevertheless, erasing God's name carries a genuine *issur*, and so the *beit din* works strenuously to avoid bringing about that erasure unnecessarily.

### Drinking Paradox

The *gemara* then raises what appears to be a contradiction. A *baraita* from the *Tosefta* states that just as we scare her out of drinking, so too we scare her into drinking — *kederech shema'amin aleha shelo tishteh kach ma'amin aleha shetishteh*. This seems paradoxical: if the entire purpose of the warnings is to prevent the erasure of God's name, how can it also be our goal to encourage her to drink?

### Water as Medicine

The *baraita* resolves this by explaining that if she is certain of her innocence, she is told: *omrim lah bitti im barur lach hadavar shetehorab at omdi al boryich ushti* — if it is entirely clear to you that you are pure, stand firm and drink. The water, the *baraita* explains, is like a dry medicine placed upon raw flesh: *lefi she'ein mayim hame'arerim domim ela lesam yavesh shemunach al basar chai*. If there is a wound, the medicine dissolves into it and takes effect; if there is no wound, it does nothing at all. The implication is clear: if she is innocent, the water will have no effect and the ritual will demonstrate her innocence. If she is guilty, the ritual will run its course as designed. The *gemara* thus resolves the contradiction: there are two distinct stages of the ritual.

### Before/After Megillah

Before the *megillas sotah* has been erased, the goal is to encourage the woman to confess so that God's name need not be effaced at all. After the *megillah* has already been erased, that concern is moot — God's name is already gone — and it would now be wasteful and purposeless for her to refuse to drink. At that point, she is instead encouraged to drink: the water will prove her innocent if she is indeed innocent, and the erasure of God's name will have served its purpose. These are different encouragements suited to different moments in the proceeding.

---

## Judah & Reuben

### Aggadic Stories

The *mishnah* had said that they tell her *devarim she'einam kedai lishmo'an* — things not fit to be heard — in order to move her emotionally. The *gemara* explains: *tanu rabbanan omer lefaneha devarim shel aggada uma'asim she'iru baksuvim harishonim* — they tell her *aggadot* and stories that occurred in earlier generations. The specific source cited is from *Iyov*: *asher chachamim yaggidu velo kichadu me'avosam* — that the wise of earlier times would tell of these things and not conceal them from their ancestors. As *Rashi* explains, these are things written in the *Torah* about events of ancient times — stories in which great and wise people were able to acknowledge their sins openly. The phrase *devarim she'einam kedai lishmo'an* refers to the fact that, under normal circumstances, one would not publicize these stories, as they could be embarrassing to figures of great stature whose full standing the tradition wishes to protect.

### Judah & Reuben

Two figures are given as examples. *Yehuda hoda velo bosh* — Judah admitted his sin and was not embarrassed. *Mah haya sofo? Nachal chayei olam haba* — and what came of it? He inherited a share in the *olam haba*. Similarly, *Reuven hoda velo bosh, mah haya sofo? Nachal chayei olam haba* — Reuben admitted his sin and was not embarrassed, and he too inherited the *olam haba*.

### Peshat & Derash

This passage is striking because the *gemara* here goes against what the tradition generally maintains in other contexts. As we know from Tractate *Megilla*, the rabbinic view — at least from the perspective of *Torah she-be'al peh* — tends to be that Judah and Reuben did not actually commit the transgressions that the *peshat* of the *Torah* seems to imply. When the *parshiyot* dealing with Reuben are read publicly, the *targum* is withheld, so that listeners will not be misled by the surface reading — for the *peshat* of the story of Reuben suggests that he literally violated his stepmother, while *Chazal* understand it as something considerably less severe. Yet here the *gemara* reads these stories according to their *peshat* in order to draw a moral lesson — that great people can admit wrongdoing. The reason these words are *she'einam kedai lishmo'an* is precisely because they are potentially embarrassing to figures who are elsewhere treated as towering *tzaddikim*.

This connects to the broader contemporary debate about approaching figures in *Tanach begova ha-einayim* — relating to biblical personalities as fully realized human beings — and how much that is permissible from the rabbinic perspective. The story of Judah and Tamar raises precisely this question: in the *peshat*, Judah says *tzadka mimeni*, acknowledging that Tamar was right and he was wrong. The *gemara* here appears to authorize reading the story as it reads, even if other contexts demand a more interpretive layer, in order to achieve the goal of inspiring the *sotah* to confess. The *Rema* in one of his *teshuvot* cites this passage as a proof that even embarrassing a *talmid chacham* can be part of what is legitimately permitted in the broader context of the *sotah* process — bringing people to confession and restoring *shalom bayit*.

### Reuben's Repentance

Having established that Judah admitted his sin, the *gemara* asks: *ela Reuven menalan de'hodi* — how do we know that Reuben admitted to having sinned? The proof comes from *Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani* citing *Rabbi Yochanan*, who reads the connection between *yechi Reuven ve'al yamot* in Moses's blessing to the tribes at the end of *Devarim* and *vezot liYehudah*, which follows immediately. *Rashi* notes that the blessing of Judah is the only one that opens with the unusual word *vezot*, suggesting a textual linkage between Reuben's life-and-death fate and Judah's admission. The *gemara* understands this connection to mean that Reuben's fate depended upon Judah's own repentance and what it inspired.

### Judah's Punishment

The *gemara* then describes what Judah suffered in the *midbar*. All forty years that *Bnei Yisrael* wandered in the desert, Judah's bones were rolling around in his coffin — *kol otan shanim she'hayu Yisrael bamidbar hayu atzmotav shel Yehuda mitgalglim ba'aron* — until Moses stood and prayed for him. Moses argued before God: *mi garam l'Reuven she'hoda* — who was it that inspired Reuben to do *teshuvah*? It was Judah. Thus Judah was rewarded not because of his own *teshuvah* alone, but because his character and his admission inspired Reuben to do *teshuvah* as well. That is why the next phrase in the blessing is *shema Adonai kol Yehudah* — God hears Judah's prayer and responds, releasing him from his posthumous suffering.

What was the precise nature of that suffering? *Rashi* here connects *evarai deshaffa* — his limbs were dislocated — to the *treifah* discussed in *Chullin* 52b, *buka de'atma deshaf biduchteh*, the hip socket displaced from the hip joint. The punishment of forty years of rolling bones was understood as a consequence of whatever connection existed between Judah and his conduct regarding Tamar — even as he had acknowledged his failing and been forgiven. *Tosafot* in the *gemara* raises the question of why Judah was still being punished for forty years, and *Rashi* connects it to a *niduy al tenai* — some form of conditional *cherem* — though this requires further investigation.

Beyond the rolling bones, Judah suffered additional penalties. *Velo hava ka'aylin lei lemtivta dirakia* — they would not admit him into the heavenly *yeshiva*. Even once he was admitted, *velo hava ka yada mishkal bishmayta bahadei rabanan* — he could not participate in the *shakla vetarya*, the back-and-forth of halakhic debate with the *rabbanim* in heaven. And then, *velo hava kasalik lei shemayta aliba dehilkhata* — he could not bring his *sugyot* to their proper halakhic conclusion. Moses's blessing *ve'ezer mitsarav tihyeh* — that the *Torah* should be a protection from his enemies — is read as the remedy for this final deficiency, enabling Judah to learn *sugyot aliba dehilkhata* at last.

### Reuben's Motivation

The *gemara* then distinguishes between Judah's case and Reuben's. *Bishlama Yehuda de'odi kehikhi delo tishraf Tamar* — Judah had an obvious reason to admit publicly: if he had not done so, Tamar would have been burned. But what motivated Reuben to confess? *Ve'amar Rav Sheshet*: *chatsifa alai demafrat chatatei kehikhi delo tishdu achohi* — he was concerned that if he did not publicly admit what he had done, his brothers would be suspected. Under normal circumstances, he might have gone to Jacob privately, but since others who knew something had happened would not know who was responsible, Reuben had to make a public declaration to clear his brothers' names.

### Public vs. Private

This leads to a broader principle. The *Rambam*, drawing on the *gemara*, distinguishes between *mitzvot bein adam lachaveiro* and *mitzvot bein adam laMakom* when it comes to the question of public versus private apology. For sins between a person and another person, one must publicize the apology, because another person was genuinely hurt and public acknowledgment is part of making it right. For sins between a person and God, it is preferable to keep the matter private — there is no reason to publicize a transgression of that kind, and doing so only adds another dimension of exposure without any remedial benefit. The case of Reuben illustrates that even when a public apology might magnify the problem in some ways, the concern of allowing others to remain under unjust suspicion can override that consideration.

---

## Breaking Ketubah

### Ketubah Dispute

The *gemara* turns to the practical consequences if the woman admits to adultery during the *sotah* proceeding. *Im amart tameia ani* — if she says she is impure, *shomein sheovrim ketubatah* — the *gemara* infers that we break her *ketubah*. But what does *shovrim* mean here?

### Abbaye vs. Rava

*Shma mina kotvim shovar* — one might think it means we write a receipt canceling the obligation of the *ketubah*. *Amar Abaye tani mikra* — Abaye says we should emend the *mishnah* to read *korei'a*, meaning we simply tear up the *ketubah* document itself. If a physical *shtar* is torn up, there is no way for the holder to claim the debt it represents, and the matter is closed. The question of which approach is better turns on where the burden lies: does the husband need a receipt proving the *ketubah* was discharged, or is it sufficient to simply destroy the document? *Amar lei Rava* — Rava objects that the *mishnah* says *shoveret*, not *koriat*, and one cannot simply amend a *mishnah*. Therefore the *mishnah* must be read as written.

*Ela amar Rava bimkom she'ein kotvim ketubah askinan* — Rava resolves the issue by saying the *mishnah* is discussing a case where no physical *ketubah* document was written at all. The *ketubah* obligation was undertaken orally. In such a case, there is no document to tear up, and so *shovrim* — breaking the *ketubah* — means writing some form of receipt or acknowledgment that the obligation has been discharged.

### No Document Cases

*Rashi* at the end of this passage offers two related scenarios in which a woman might claim her *ketubah* without a physical document. In a case of divorce, *mishenitagresha motzi'ah gittah ve'govah bah* — she produces the *get* itself as proof of the divorce and uses it to collect her *ketubah*. In a case of widowhood, *mevi'ah edei mitah ve'govah* — she brings witnesses who can testify to her husband's death, and on that basis she collects from the estate. The latter is a considerably more burdensome process, reflecting the general principle of *hamotzi mechaveiro alav hara'ayah* — that the one seeking to extract money from another bears the burden of proof.

One can trace in these cases the historical development of the *ketubah* document itself. At an earlier stage, the *ketubah* was apparently an oral obligation, and the woman had to marshal independent evidence — witnesses to the divorce or death — in order to collect. The rabbis subsequently instituted the practice of writing a physical *ketubah* document precisely to ease this burden, enabling the woman to collect simply by presenting the *shtar* she held in her hand.

---

## Ritual Locations

### Eastern Gate

The *mishnah* states: *de'imar amart tehorah ani ma'alin osah lisha'arei mizrach* — if she says she is pure, they bring her up to the eastern gate, which is the *Sha'ar Nicanor*, the great gate standing between the *Ezrat Nashim* and the main *Azarah* of the *Beit Hamikdash*. The *Sha'ar Nicanor* featured two smaller doors on either side and fifteen steps ascending to it, and it constituted the central meeting point for those who had reason to be in the *Beit Hamikdash* but not in the *Azarah* proper — including women and other *Yisraelim* who gathered in the *Ezrat Nashim*.

The *gemara* asks: what does *ma'alin osah* mean — she was already there? The answer is that she had first been brought to the *Beit Din Hagadol*, the *Lishkat Hagazit*, which straddles the border between the *Azarah* and the *Ezrat Nashim*. From there she is brought up to the *Sha'ar Nicanor* for the actual drinking of the water.

### Walking Around

*Umakkifin osah kedei l'yage'ah* — they make her walk all around the *Har Habayit* to tire her out. A weary woman, if guilty, will be more inclined to admit it; and a woman who drinks the water despite exhaustion demonstrates more convincingly that she genuinely believes herself innocent. The *gemara* draws a parallel to a *baraita*: *Rebbe Shimon ben Elazar omer beit din masin es ha'edim mimakom lemakom kedei shetitaref da'atan aleihem veyachzeru bahen* — the *beit din* also makes witnesses in capital cases travel from place to place in order to wear them down. The goal is to create a genuine disincentive to false testimony — if you are lying, make it hard enough that you will reconsider — while simultaneously affirming that if you are telling the truth, it is a great *mitzvah* to do so regardless of the difficulty.

### Where She Drinks

The *mishnah* establishes that the *sotah* drinks at the *Sha'ar Hamizrach*. The *gemara* asks: is this rule also applied to the *metzora* and the *yoledet*? For the *sotah*, the *pasuk* is explicit: *veha'emid hakohen es ha'ishah lifnei Adonai* — it must be done before God, meaning at the entrance of the *Beit Hamikdash*. For the *metzora*, the *pasuk* similarly says *veha'emid hakohen hamitaher* — the *kohen* must stand the *metzora* at the entrance of the *Mishkan*, and so the same location applies. The symbolism here is powerful: the *metzora* is excluded even from walled cities during the period of impurity and must dwell outside, and then the *taharah* process brings him back inside, to the very threshold of the sacred precincts.

### Yoledet & Korban

What about the *yoledet*? The *gemara* asks: if the reason a *yoledet* must appear at the *Sha'ar Nicanor* is simply *de'ika mikaima akorbaneihu* — that anyone bringing a *korban* must be present for its offering — then by the same logic, *zavin vezavot* should also be listed. The *gemara* answers: *hachi nami vetana chada mineihu nakat* — indeed the same rule applies to them as well; the *mishnah* simply listed one representative example, the *yoledet*, but intended all *mechusarei kaparah*. *Tosafot* in multiple places in *Shas* grapples with the general problem of *mishnayot* that appear to make sweeping inclusive or exclusive statements but in practice admit of many exceptions. The principle of *tana veshayer* — the *tanna* left out cases — is one of the standard resolutions.

---

## Two Sotahs Rule

### No Two Together

The *gemara* introduces a *baraita*: *ein mashkim shtei sotot k'achat* — one cannot give two *sotot* the water simultaneously. The stated reason is *kedei shelo yehei libah gas bachaverta* — so that she should not become emboldened by the presence of another *sotah* alongside her. If two women who are both guilty were made to drink together, each might draw a kind of stubborn courage from the other and refuse to confess, even to the point of drinking the water despite her guilt.

One might observe from this rule that the *sotah* ritual is not deferred until the *regalim*. If it were, one would likely accumulate multiple *sotot* and be tempted to process them together — which is precisely what this rule prohibits.

### Rabbi Judah's View

*Rabbi Yehudah omer lo min hashem hu zeh ela amar kra otah levadah* — Rabbi Judah disagrees with the reason. He says the rule is not grounded in the *sevara* of *libah gas bachaverta* at all. Rather, it is a *gezeirat hakatuv*: the *pasuk* simply says *otah levadah*, just her alone, and that suffices. This is a meaningful *machloket*: both *tanna'im* agree on the *halacha*, but they disagree about its source. The *tanna kama* treats the rule as a *sevara* — a logical inference — and Rabbi Judah treats it as a direct *pasuk*. As the *gemara* then clarifies, *vetana kama hinu Rabbi Shimon dedarish ta'ama d'kra* — the *tanna kama* is Rabbi Shimon, who agrees the *pasuk* says *otah levadah* but reads the *pasuk's* limitation as deriving from and coextensive with the underlying logic. This reflects a broader *machloket* between Rabbi Judah and Rabbi Shimon throughout *Shas* regarding *darshinan ta'ama d'kra* — whether understanding the reason behind a *pasuk* can expand or contract the parameters of the *halacha* derived from it.

### Fearful Woman

*Mai beinaihu? Ika beinaihu rotetet* — what is the practical difference between the two positions? The case of a woman who is particularly fearful and trembling about the *sotah* water. According to Rabbi Shimon, whose reason is *libah gas bachaverta*, a *rotetet* woman would not be emboldened by the presence of another *sotah* — her extreme fear would override any such effect — and so two *sotot* could theoretically be processed together in such a case. According to Rabbi Judah, the *pasuk* says *otah levadah* regardless, and the prohibition is absolute. *Tosafot HaRosh* raises the question of what happens when one of the pair is *rotetet* but the other is not: even then, one might worry that the more composed woman will embolden the other, and therefore we remain *choshesh* in that case as well.

### Bundling Mitzvot

The *gemara* asks: and can one really make a *rotetet* woman drink at all? And then it challenges even more fundamentally: *vaha ein osin mitzvot chavilot chavilot* — we have a principle that one may not bundle *mitzvot* together. Even without the specific concern of *libah gas bachaverta*, performing two *sotah* rituals simultaneously would violate this broader rule.

*Rashi* explains the reason for *ein osin mitzvot chavilot chavilot*: it appears as though the *mitzvot* are a heavy burden that one rushes to discharge. *Shenireh k'mo shehayah alav l'masoy umemaher l'farek masao* — it looks like someone hurrying to unload a heavy pack. Performing *mitzvot* hastily and in bulk conveys that they are merely obligations to be disposed of, rather than things of genuine value to be cherished. *Tosafot* in *Moed Katan* offers a different rationale: just as *ein me'arvin simcha b'simcha* — we do not hold a wedding on *Chol HaMoed* because we want each *simcha* to receive its own full attention — so too each *mitzvah* deserves its own dedicated focus and its own *simcha shel mitzvah*. One of the *Achronim*, *Rav Yosef Engel*, adds yet another conceptual lens: the principle of *osek b'mitzvah patur min hamitzvah* means that performing one *mitzvah* technically exempts one from another, and therefore bundling two *mitzvot* together may be not merely inadvisable but technically impossible.

### Bundling Examples

A *baraita* lists additional cases: *ein metaherin shtei metzoraim k'achas* — one cannot perform the purification ritual for two *metzoraim* simultaneously. *Ein rotzin shtei avadim k'achas* — one cannot pierce the ears of two *eved Ivri* together at the same ceremony. An *eved Ivri* who, after six years of service, declares *ahavti es adoni* and wishes to continue as a slave undergoes a formal ear-piercing, with the *pasuk* stating *va'avado l'olam*. A *machloket* exists between the *Chazon Ish* and the *Magen Avraham* about the nature of this: the *Chazon Ish* holds that even when the slave seeks to remain, the master may refuse, making it entirely a *reshut*; the *Magen Avraham* holds that once the slave actively wishes to be *nirtza*, it becomes obligatory for the master.

*Ein orfin shtei eglos k'achas* — one cannot perform two *egla arufa* rituals simultaneously. While it would be tragic indeed for a city to require two such rituals at once, if it did, each would have to be performed separately. The *baraita* concludes: *lefi she'ein osin mitzvot chavilot chavilot*. It is worth noting that all the examples in this *baraita* involve doing two instances of the *same* mitzvah at once — not two different *mitzvot* performed together. The concern is not that one cannot daven and shake a *lulav* simultaneously; it is the ceremonial repetition, the bundling of identical solemn procedures, each of which demands its own dedicated attention and process. The *eved Ivri* must be brought before the court, the *egla arufa* requires traveling out to a remote location — these are elaborate, ceremonial proceedings that cannot be rushed together.

### One vs. Two Kohanim

*Amar Abaye ve'isayma Rav Kahana: lo kashya kan b'kohen echad kan bishnei kohanim* — the resolution is that a single *kohen* cannot administer the water to two *sotot*, but two *sotot* could theoretically be processed on the same day — perhaps even simultaneously — by two different *kohanim*, since in that case each *kohen* is performing a single, undivided act and there is no violation of *mitzvot chavilot chavilot*.

---

## Sotah Clothing

### Tearing Clothes

The *gemara* states: *vekohen ochez b'vgadeha* — the *kohen* holds onto her clothing. The procedure described in the *mishnah* involves tearing open her garments and then securing them with an Egyptian rope above her breasts. The *gemara* asks about this in relation to concerns of *hirhurin* — inappropriate sexual thoughts — that the ritual might occasion.

### Stoning Clothes

*Lemimra d'Rabbi Yehuda chaish l'hirhur* — is Rabbi Judah concerned about *hirhur* while the *Rabbanan* are not? The *gemara* notes that this seems to be inverted from what we know elsewhere. A *baraita* states: when a man is executed by *skilah*, he is covered with *perek echad milfanav* — a single cloth in front.
