A third: just as in his youth David humbled himself before those greater than him for the purpose of learning Torah, so too in his greatness he maintained that same humility. The connection between David's *michtam* and Tamar's modesty is thus sustained: the quality that saved Tamar — her *tzniyut* in Yehudah's house — becomes an inheritance for the Davidic line, expressed as the humility and purity that characterize David himself.

---

## Yehudah admits

### Recognition items

*Haker na* — do you recognize these? Yehudah is presented with the signet, cord, and staff.

### Haker circularity

Rabbi Chama the son of Rabbi Chanina observes: *be-haker biser le-aviv* — with the word *haker* he informed his father. The brothers had earlier sent Yosef's coat dipped in blood to Yaakov, saying *haker na ha-ketonet bincha hi im lo* — recognize now, is this your son's coat? And immediately after that episode, the Torah records *va-yered Yehudah me-eit echav* — Yehudah went down from his brothers — and the story with Tamar begins. The same word *haker* now returns to measure out Yehudah's reckoning.

### Jacob echo

The literary and moral parallel is precise. By Yaakov, the sons kept their distance and presented the evidence indirectly — they let the father recognize the coat himself rather than confront him with what they had done. Here too, Tamar does not confront Yehudah directly but sends the evidence and lets him recognize it. In both cases, the person given the *haker* moment is allowed to arrive at the truth through their own recognition.

### Teshuva opening

This structure is what makes Yehudah's *teshuva* genuine. Had Tamar accused him directly, the dynamic would have been defensive — denial, deflection, dismissal. By presenting the evidence and giving him an opening, she allowed him to come forward and claim the truth himself, to own it. That is the moment of authentic *teshuva*.

### Recognition theme

The *mida k'neged mida* dimension here reaches further back still. The pattern of *vayaker* and *haker* runs from Yaakov and Esav — where Yaakov used the *gedei izim* and Yitzchak *lo hikiro* — through the brothers using *gedei izim* dipped in blood to make Yaakov recognize something false — through Yehudah's reckoning here — and further still to *vayaker Yosef et echav v'hem lo hikiruhu* by the Yosef story. The word *haker* is a thread stitched through the entire family narrative, and it is always about recognition, concealment, and the moment of moral accounting.

---

## Yehudah's confession

### Tzaddka statement

*Vayaker Yehudah vayomer tzadka mimeni* — Yehudah recognized and said: she is more righteous than I.

### Joseph vs Yehudah

Rabbi Chanin bar Bizna said in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida: Yosef, who sanctified God's name *ba-seter* — in private — by withstanding the advances of Potifar's wife, *zacha ve-hosifu lo ot achat mishmo shel HaKadosh Baruch Hu* — merited that one letter of God's name was added to his: *eydut bi-Yehosef shemo*, the extra *heh* making his name יהוסף. Yehudah, who sanctified God's name *be-farhesia* — in public — by openly acknowledging his sin, *zacha ve-nikra kulo al shemo shel HaKadosh Baruch Hu* — merited that his entire name contains the letters of God's name: יהודה contains a *yud*, a *heh*, a *vav*, and a *heh*.

### Bat kol promise

At the moment Yehudah said *tzadka mimeni*, a *bat kol* went forth: *ata hitzalta Tamar u-shnei baneha min ha-or* — you have saved Tamar and her two children from the fire.

### Three names

*Chayecha she-ani matzil bi-zchutcha gimel mi-banecha min ha-or* — in your merit I will save three of your descendants from the fire. *Man ninhu? Chananya, Mishael, ve-Azarya* — those thrown into Nevuchadnezzar's furnace and saved.

### Divine origin

The Gemara then reads *tzadka mimeni* not only as "she is more righteous than I" but as a divine utterance: *mimeni yatzu kevushim* — from Me went forth these hidden decrees. The entire chain of events, the *bat kol* declares, was God's design.

---

## Union resolution

### Separation read

*Ve-lo yasaf od le-da'atah* — he no longer knew her. The plain reading is that after this episode Yehudah and Tamar had no further sexual contact.

### Marriage alternative

Shmuel Saba, the father-in-law of Rav Shmuel bar Ami, citing Rav Shmuel bar Ami himself, offers a different interpretation: *keivan she-yad'ah* — once he knew her, reading *da'atah* not as sexual knowledge but as recognition of her righteousness and her *l'shem shamayim* motivation, *shuv lo pasak mimena* — he did not cease from her. They began to live together as husband and wife.

### Textual variant

The proof is a *gezeirah shavah*: *ve-lo yasaf od le-da'atah* is read in parallel with *kol gadol ve-lo yasaf* — the great voice that did not cease. Just as that voice continued without interruption, so too the relationship continued. The word *yasaf* in both contexts is read as cessation that did not occur.

### Happy ending

This alternative ending is remarkable in the context of a tractate about sexual sin and its consequences. Here the narrative that began with lust and moral failure — Yehudah mistaking his daughter-in-law for a prostitute — resolves into a proper marital union. Because he did the right thing, because he admitted, the story ends not in separation and shame but in legitimate relationship. The framework of *mida k'neged mida* is fulfilled in the positive direction: genuine *teshuva* and honest reckoning restore what was broken.

---

## Zonah vs kedesha

### Cult prostitute

When Yehudah wished to send payment, he dispatched his friend the Adullamite, who was told to ask for *ha-kedeshah hi be-Einayim al ha-derech* — the *kedeshah* who sat by the road at Enaim. *Kedeshah* technically refers not to an ordinary prostitute but to a cult prostitute — a woman who served in pagan temples as part of idolatrous practice, a phenomenon attested widely across the ancient Near East.

### Face-saving

Robert Alter notes the discrepancy: when Yehudah first encountered her, the Torah says he thought her a *zonah* — an ordinary prostitute. But when he sends his friend to make payment, he instructs him to ask for a *kedeshah*. Alter's insight is that Yehudah was attempting to save face among the local population. Asking a neighbor to help locate a *zonah* you had slept with is frankly embarrassing. Asking for a *kedeshah* carries a different connotation — something more exotic, perhaps quasi-religious — and sounds more dignified than having to admit you visited a common streetwalker. It is, in short, a face-saving euphemism.

### No cult here

The neighbors' response is pointed: *lo hayta bizeh kedeshah* — there has been no *kedeshah* here. *Zonahs* we may know about; *kedeshas* we do not. The very attempt at euphemism fails, and the word the neighbors use brings Yehudah right back to where he started.

---

---

# Sotah 11

## Absalom's Hair

### Intro: Absalom

Today's daf is 11. We pick up at the bottom of 10b, in the middle of a story about Absalom (*Avshalom*) within the larger context of *midah keneged midah* that began with the *sotah* and her punishments. Now we turn to Absalom: his hair was the most beautiful, almost divine thing about him, and ultimately it proved to be his downfall.

The *Gemara* opens with a *baraita*: *Tanu Rabbanan* — Absalom rebelled through his hair, as it says, "And like Absalom there was no man as beautiful... and when he shaved his head — for it was heavy upon him and he shaved it — he weighed the hair of his head at two hundred *shekalim* by the king's weight." *Rashi* reminds us, in case we have forgotten what we learned in *Masechet Nazir*, that the *Gemara*'s understanding is that Absalom was a *nazir olam* and was therefore permitted to shave his hair once every twelve months. The hair provided him a pretext — gathering people around him and leading an insurrection — and presumably filled him with the sense that he was deserving of the kingship, though the *Gemara* does not say that explicitly.

### Hair & Pride

The *Gemara* then offers a *derasha* on the phrase "the king's weight," identifying it as a standard measure used by the people of Tiberias and Tzipori. From this flows the moral consequence: *lefichach nitlah besearo* — therefore he was caught by his hair. He was, as it were, hoisted by his own petard. As it says, "And Absalom rode before the servants of David, and Absalom rode upon the mule, and the mule went under the thick branches of the great terebinth, and his head caught in the terebinth, and he was suspended between heaven and earth, and the mule that was under him passed on."

### Tree & Death

The *Gemara* then addresses a natural question: why did he not simply cut himself free? It says he took a sword and wanted to cut his hair — but at that very moment, *tanna d'vei Rabbi Yishmael* teaches, the depths of *Sheol* opened up beneath him. The insight offered in discussion resolves the difficulty elegantly: Absalom could not cut his hair because he now faced a second peril — if he cut himself free, he would fall into the abyss that had opened below him. That explains his paralysis.

Following Joab's killing of Absalom, the report of his death was brought to King David, who went up to the gate and wept, crying out: *bni Avshalom, bni bni Avshalom, mi yiten muti ani tachtecha Avshalom bni bni* — "My son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom, would that I had died in your place, Absalom my son, my son." And then again: *Avshalom bni bni*. It is difficult to overstate the pathos of these verses — arguably the saddest passage in all of *Tanakh*. No matter what Absalom had done, David's anguish is complete and unconditional. That is precisely what makes it so unbearably poignant.

### David's Lament

The *Gemara* asks: *hanei tmanya bni lama* — why are there eight utterances of "my son"? Seven of them, it explains, correspond to the seven chambers of *Gehinnom*: each one of David's cries raised Absalom up from one level of the depths, each one lifting him a little closer to the surface. The eighth utterance — according to one opinion — served to reconnect Absalom's severed head to his body (though this detail does not appear explicitly in the biblical text); according to another opinion, David's prayer actually brought Absalom to *Olam Haba*.

### Gehinnom & Prayer

This last point raises an important question taken up by *Tosafot*: the principle stated in *Chelek* is *bra mezakei aba* — a son's merits can benefit his deceased father — but not *aba mezakei bra*, a father cannot bring benefit to his son in this way. How, then, did David's prayer avail Absalom?

*Tosafot* offers two responses. First, Absalom had not worshipped idols, and therefore the case may be different from those situations in which a sinner is wholly beyond redemption. Second, and more directly: the principle that *aba lo mezakei bra* means only that out of respect for the father, we do not ordinarily count the son's deeds as accruing to the father's merit — but that is a matter of formal accounting. Prayer, however, is different: *aval tefila mo'eles* — prayer is effective. And David prayed for Absalom.

This raises a deeper conceptual issue. *Kaddish* operates on a somewhat different logic: the son's recitation of *kaddish* sanctifies God's name in the world, and since the deceased father brought into the world a child who now performs this act, the merit redounds indirectly to him — *bra mezakei aba* in the classic sense. But praying directly for the welfare of another's soul is a distinct concept from performing good deeds whose merit flows back through a causal chain. One is asking God to act; the other is creating a new meritorious act attributable to the deceased through the child.

It is interesting, in passing, to note the parallels with the legends that grew up around the death of Shabtai Tzvi — the myths about prayer campaigns to elevate him from *Gehinnom* and bring him to *Olam Haba*. He remained so powerful a figure in the popular imagination that people could not accept that his sin was the final word. Something similar seems to be at work in the *Gemara*'s wrestling with whether David's prayer could ultimately bring Absalom to *Olam Haba*. On the question of gradations: once a soul has been removed from punishment, it is one further step to *Olam Haba* — not to the highest level, but to some entry-level portion. The *Gemara* in *Rosh Hashanah* does speak of the *reshaim* dwelling in a kind of temporary state for twelve months before their final judgment, something not entirely unlike the concept of purgatory in other traditions.

### Monument

The *Gemara* continues: "And Absalom had taken and set up for himself a monument in his lifetime." The *Tanakh* reports that after his death it was recalled that Absalom had already erected this monument, calling it *Yad Avshalom*, because he said, "I have no son to keep my name in remembrance."

The *Gemara* asks: *mai lakach* — what does "he had taken" mean? *Reish Lakish* says: just as *Vayikach Korach* means that Korach made a bad transaction, so too here — *shelakach mekach ra le'atzmo* — he had made a bad investment for himself. Whether this refers to his foreseeing his own death by erecting a monument, or to the entire disastrous enterprise of the rebellion, is left somewhat open.

*Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa* adds: *be'etzah amukah shel malko shel olam* — this was all part of the deep counsel of the King of the universe. *Rashi* explains this with reference to the punishment decreed upon David after the sin of Bathsheba — God had told him that evil would arise from within his own house — *hineni mekim alecha ra'ah mi'beitecha*. Without diminishing Absalom's own *bechirat chofshit*, the episode unfolded in accordance with a divine plan. The *Gemara* draws a parallel to the story of Joseph: *Vayishla'chehu me'emek Chevron* — he was sent from the valley of Hebron. *Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa* reads *emek* here as "deep counsel," the deep strategy of that righteous one buried in Hebron, namely Abraham, and connects this to the divine decree of *yado'a teda ki ger yihyeh zar'acha* — "Know well that your descendants will be strangers." Joseph's being sent to his brothers was all part of the mechanism by which that divine promise would come to be fulfilled. The question of *hashgacha pratit* and *bechirah chofshit* operating simultaneously is, as the *Gemara* itself seems to acknowledge, a formidable one — and the text moves on.

### Children & Wheat

The *Gemara* now addresses the monument's stated rationale: *ki amar ein li ben* — Absalom said he had no son. But this is puzzling, since the *Tanakh* earlier reports that he had three sons and one daughter. *Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi* explains: he had no son *hagun lemalkhut* — no son fit to inherit a kingdom. This detail itself implies that even at the time he erected the monument, Absalom was already anticipating his bid for the throne — for why else would fitness for kingship matter?

*Rav Chisda* adds a *gemiri* — a received tradition: whoever burns another's grain (*tevuato shel chavero*) will leave no son to inherit him. This explains why Absalom's sons predeceased him, though *Rav Chisda* acknowledges the tradition is transmitted as a general principle. The underlying logic is a form of *midah keneged midah*: just as one destroys the fruit of another's labor — that which was planted and nurtured — so one's own progeny, the fruit of one's own life, will be cut down.

The episode being referenced is Absalom's burning of Joab's wheat field. After Absalom had been permitted to return to Jerusalem but the king still refused to receive him, Absalom needed to compel Joab to intercede on his behalf. Since Joab was not responding to his messages, Absalom instructed his servants: "Go and set fire to Joab's field." And so they burned the field. That act of destruction ultimately led to his restoration in the eyes of the king — and set in motion the chain of events that would culminate in the rebellion.

---

## Miriam & Measure

### Miriam Hovers

The *Gemara* now returns to the *Mishnah*, which teaches that just as there is *midah keneged midah* for punishment, so there is *midah keneged midah* for good — and the example is Miriam, who waited over Moses for one hour, and in the end the entire nation of Israel waited for her seven days when she was stricken. But *Abaye* raises an objection: can this really be called *midah keneged midah*? She waited one hour — *hatam chada sha'ata* — while Israel waited seven days. That is not measure for measure; it is vastly disproportionate. *Abaye* therefore proposes reading the *Mishnah* as saying that for *midah tovah* it is specifically not so — the reward is greater.

*Rava* objects: the *Mishnah* says *vechen linyan hatovah* — "and likewise for good." You cannot simply change the *girsa*. The concept is the same; what differs is only the quantity. The resolution is that *midah keneged midah* applies to both directions, but *mida tovah* is always *merubah* — greater — than *midat puranut*.

### Math: Hour & Days

*Tosafot* picks up the mathematical precision of this point. *Tosafot* notes that when the *Mishnah* says Miriam waited "one hour," it cannot be taken literally as a full hour. For the *Tosefta* teaches that *mida tovah merubbah mimiddat puranut al achat chamesh me'ot* — the measure of good exceeds the measure of punishment by five hundred times. Calculating: seven days contain 168 hours. If the ratio is 500:1, then Miriam must have waited only approximately one-third of an hour — roughly twenty minutes — not a full hour. *Tosafot* says "a third or a quarter," though the arithmetic points more precisely to a third.

*Tosafot* then notes a further difficulty: regarding the spies, the punishment was *yom lashanah* — a year for each day they spent scouting, which yields a ratio of 365:1. That is *midat puranut*, not *mida tovah*. But 365:1 is less than 500:1, yet the *Tosefta* claims that *mida tovah* exceeds *midat puranut* fivefold. Is then the *midat puranut* of the spies greater than the *mida tovah* of Miriam? The *Gemara* in the first chapter of *Chagigah* complicates things further: *Rabbi Yochanan* expounds the verse "they seek Me daily" to mean that whoever engages in Torah even one day is regarded as if he engaged all year — again a ratio of 365:1 — and the *Gemara* there explicitly equates this with the punishment of the spies. So are the two measures actually equal after all? The *Gemara* leaves the precise arithmetic to God.

### Divine Protection

Returning to the verse *vatitatzav achoto merachok* — "and his sister stood from afar" — *Rabbi Yitzchak* teaches: this entire verse was said in the name of the *Shechina*; it was the divine presence that was hovering there to protect Moses, not merely Miriam standing watch. He demonstrates this by showing that each word of the verse is elsewhere associated with God: *vatitatzav* — to stand — appears in *vayavo Hashem vayityatzav*; *achoto* — sister — in *emor lechochma achoti at*, where wisdom, which is close to God, is called "sister"; *merachok* — from afar — in *merachok Hashem nirah li*; *lada'at* — to know — in *ki el de'ot Hashem*; *mah ya'aseh* — what will be done — in *ki lo ya'aseh Hashem Elokim davar*; and *lo* — to him — in *vayikra lo Hashem shalom*. Every word in the verse, on its own, connects back to God.

---

## Pharaoh's Plan

### New Pharaoh

With this the *Gemara* opens into the broader narrative of Moses and the Israelites in Egypt — a backdrop that will occupy the remainder of the daf. *Rav* and *Shmuel* disagree about *vayakam melech chadash al Mitzrayim* — "and a new king arose over Egypt." One says he was literally a new king; the other says that in fact his decrees were renewed — his entire approach toward Israel changed. The support for the first view is simply the word *chadash* — it says "new." The support for the second view is that the text never says the old king died (*vayamot vayimloch*), implying continuity of the person with a radical change in policy. As for *asher lo yada et Yosef* — "who did not know Joseph" — the one who holds the policy-change view explains: he acted *keman dilo yadalei klal*, as if he had never known Joseph at all.

The *Gemara* notes: *hu hitchil be'eitzah techila* — Pharaoh was the one who initiated the plot against Israel first, and therefore *lefichach lakah techila* — he was struck first, as it says: "and upon you and upon your nation and upon all your servants the frogs shall come up" — he was the first one hit by the plagues. This is the *midah keneged midah* of the initiator.

### Water Plan

The verse *hava nitchachma lo* — "come, let us deal wisely with them" — uses the singular *lo* where the plural *lahem* would be expected. *Rabbi Chama b'Rabbi Chanina* understands this as deliberate: *bo'u venitchacham lemoshi'an shel Yisrael* — let us outwit the Savior of Israel. The *lo* refers not to the Israelites but to their divine protector. And the plan was calibrated precisely around the principle of *midah keneged midah*: Pharaoh knew that God avenges measure for measure, and so he sought a method of oppression that God could not repay in kind.

Should we destroy them by fire? But Scripture says "Behold, God comes with fire" — God will repay us with fire. By the sword? But "with His sword against all flesh" — repayment in kind. Therefore: *ela bo'u venidonam bamayim* — let us cast them into the water. For God had already sworn never to bring another flood upon the world, as it says, "for this is as the waters of Noah to me, for I have sworn that the waters of Noah shall not again pass over the earth."

### Pot Metaphor

Their miscalculation, the *Gemara* explains, was twofold. First, *she'al kol ha'olam kulo eino meivi* — God swore He would not bring a flood upon the entire world, but He said nothing about destroying one nation by water. Second — and more pointedly — *aval hem ba'im venoflim betocho* — when the Egyptians pursued Israel, they ran into the sea themselves. God did not drown them; they came and fell into it of their own accord, as it says *uMitzrayim nasim likrato* — "and the Egyptians were fleeing toward it." *Rabbi Elazar* crystallizes this: the verse says *ki vadavar asher zadu aleihem* — in the very matter in which they schemed against them. And the word *zadu*, the *Gemara* notes, is the language of cooking — as in *vayazed Yaakov nazid*, "and Jacob cooked a stew." *Bekdeira shebishlu bah nitbashlu* — in the very pot in which they cooked, they themselves were cooked.

One might ask whether this entire passage — attributing to Pharaoh an awareness of *midah keneged midah* and a calculated effort to circumvent it — is consistent with his statement elsewhere that he does not recognize God's authority at all. It is a genuine tension: a *Midrash* that quotes verses from Isaiah anachronistically and posits a Pharaoh who is theologically sophisticated enough to scheme against the God of Israel sits uneasily alongside the Pharaoh who says "I do not know the Lord." This is a place where *midrash* and *peshat* do not align — and where the *Midrash* transforms the entire dynamic of the narrative in a profound way, making Pharaoh from the very outset a figure who knows and fears God, rather than one who simply refuses to recognize His authority.

### Three Advisors

*Rabbi Simai* teaches: three were in that council who advised Pharaoh on how to deal with Israel — Balaam, Job, and Jethro. Balaam was the one who gave the advice; he is, after all, the figure who throughout the tradition counsels other nations on how to harm Israel — *ba v'iyaatzcha*, "come and I will advise you," and later it is Balaam's counsel that lies behind the incident of the daughters of Midian. For this, *neherag* — he was ultimately killed in the war against Midian.

Job was silent. He neither agreed nor protested — he lacked the courage to oppose Pharaoh. For this, *nidon b'yisurin* — he was afflicted with suffering. This is a striking passage, for it presents us with an answer to the question that the entire book of Job never explicitly resolves: why did Job suffer? Here the answer is that he was a silent enabler. There is a powerful parallel here to the famous *baraita* at the opening of *Masechet Avodah Zarah*, where the three sages before the Romans — one who praised Rome, one who was silent, and one who criticized — are treated not as morally equivalent but in terms of the degree to which their conduct constituted collaboration. Silence in the face of evil is itself a form of complicity.

Jethro fled. Whether he also protested before fleeing is implicit in his departure — his running away was itself a form of refusal, even if incomplete. For this, *zachu mibnei banav sheyeshvu b'lishkat hagazit* — his descendants merited to sit in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, the seat of the Sanhedrin. As the verse says, "the families of scribes who dwell in Yavetz" — *Tirathites, Shimeathites, Sucathites, these are the Kenites who came from Chamath, the father of the house of Rechab* — and the Kenites are identified as the descendants of Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses. They became the scribes and members of the Sanhedrin, serving in the *Beit Hamikdash*. The *midah keneged midah* here is of counsel: because Jethro's response was ultimately the right one, his descendants came to be the very advisors of the nation of Israel.

---

## Treasure Cities

### Brick Ruse

The *Gemara* now turns to *vayasimu alav sarei misim* — "and they placed upon him taskmasters." The use of the singular *alav* rather than the plural *aleihem* is noted, and a *baraita* from the school of *Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Shimon* explains: *she'hevi'u malben vetalu lo l'Paroh betzavaro* — they brought a form of a brick and hung it around Pharaoh's own neck. The ruse was to announce a great communal building project and have Pharaoh himself participate on the first day, so that no Israelite could claim to be too refined for the work. And indeed: if any Israelite said *istinis ani* — "I am too delicate for this" — they were told: "Are you more refined than Pharaoh himself?" In this way, everyone was pressed into labor on that opening day.

The *Gemara* continues with another grammatical tension: *lema'an anoto besivlotam* — the verse mixes singular and plural. The resolution offered is that *lema'an anoto* refers to Pharaoh — they oppressed that one for that single day — while *besivlotam* refers to Israel — all of this was for the sake of impressing the Israelites into their burdens. It was, in other words, a one-day ruse that served as the instrument of a far larger enslavement.

### Pithom/Raamses

The *Gemara* addresses the word *miskenot* in *arei miskenot* — "treasure cities." *Rav* and *Shmuel* disagree: one says *she'mesaknot et ba'aleihen* — these buildings endanger their builders (*Rashi* understands this as a general observation about construction projects, not limited to this specific case); the other says *she'memaskenot et ba'aleihen* — they impoverish their owners. As the tradition goes: *kol ha'osek bevinyan mitmasken* — anyone involved in building projects will come to poverty.

Regarding Pithom and Raamses themselves, again *Rav* and *Shmuel* disagree. One says: Pithom was the city's actual name, and it was called Raamses descriptively — *she'rishon rishon mitroses* — because as soon as they would build it, each new course of construction would crumble and shatter. The other says: Raamses was the actual name, and the name Pithom came from *pi tehom bola'o* — the mouth of the abyss swallowed everything they built, since the ground was swampy and each construction sank immediately.

### Purposeless Work

This detail inspired a beautiful observation about the nature of *avodas parech*: beyond the physical brutality of the labor, what was most demoralizing was its utter purposelessness. Everything they built collapsed or sank — like Sisyphus, condemned to roll the stone up the hill only to watch it roll back down. The practice of making men do women's work and women do men's work — which the *Gemara* will shortly address — partakes of the same logic. *Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani* citing *Rabbi Yonatan* explains *befarech* as *shehaya machlifim melachet anashim lenashim umelachet nashim la'anashim* — they would interchange the work of men and women and the work of women and men. *Rashi* notes: *vezu kashah shelo hayu regilim bekach* — this was especially harsh because they were completely unaccustomed to it. It was demoralizing on two levels: not only the backbreaking nature of the work but the stripping of dignity that comes with being forced to do that which is alien to your nature and training.

### Multiplying Promise

The verse *veka'asher ya'anu oto ken yirbeh veken yifrotz* — "as they afflict him, so shall he increase and so shall he spread" — uses the future tense where past tense (*rabu vefaretzu*, "they increased and they spread") would be expected. *Reish Lakish* explains: *ruach hakodesh mevasertan* — the divine spirit is announcing it. The oppressors say "afflict him," and God's voice comes back: "so shall he increase and so shall he spread." There is also a formulation that is even sharper: *atah amarta pen yirbeh, ani omer ken yirbeh* — you said "lest they multiply," I say "so they shall multiply." The echo of *pen yirbeh* and *ken yirbeh* makes the *midah keneged midah* almost structural: the exact same word, with the negative particle of fear replaced by the affirmative particle of divine promise. Conceptually, punishment operates like contraction, while blessing is expansive — which is precisely why the multiplier for *mida tovah* exceeds the multiplier for *midat puranut*.

---

## Righteous Women

### Women's Sustenance

*Rabbi Avira* expounds: *bisechar nashim tzidkaniyot shehayu beoto hador nigalu Yisrael miMitzrayim* — it was in the merit of the righteous women of that generation that Israel was ultimately redeemed from Egypt. The account is this: when the women would go to draw water, God would arrange that small fish would enter their pails alongside the water — *mesaknot lahem dagim ketanim bekadeihen* — so that their buckets came up half water and half fish. They would then set two pots on the fire, one to heat the water and one to cook the fish, and bring both out to their husbands in the field. There they would wash them, anoint them, feed them, and give them drink — and through this process restore their strength and their spirit until desire returned, and they would lie together *bein shefatayim* — between the folds.

One need not try to resolve every detail of this account with others. The broader theme here is important: it is the woman who is the agent of redemption, through acts of sustenance and intimacy — an echo of the *Yehudah* and *Tamar* story, where again it was the woman who was the initiator, again through an act of intimacy, and again it was ultimately connected to the chain that leads to *David Hamelech*. The drive that can lead to destruction when it crosses the boundaries of what is permitted — as with the *sotah* with whom this tractate began — can equally be the force that brings about the *geulah* when directed toward what is right.

The verse invoked is *im tishkevun bein shefatayim* — "if you lie down between the folds" — and through the merit of that lying down, *zachu Yisrael levizat Mitzrayim* — Israel merited the spoils of Egypt, as the verse continues: "the wings of a dove covered in silver and her feathers in a filigree of gold."

### Apple Trees

Once pregnant, the women would return home, and when the time of birth came, they would go out to give birth in the field — *tachat hatapuach*, under the apple tree — away from the eyes of the Egyptians. What exactly a *tapuach* is remains uncertain: apples are not indigenous to the Middle East, and various commentators have suggested the *etrog* or other fruits. Notably, the word "apple" in many languages originally carried the generic meaning of "fruit" — hence *tapuach adamah* for potato. The *Shir Hashirim* verse *tachat hatapuach orarticha* — "under the tapuach I aroused you" — is applied here to this context of birth.

God Himself, the *Gemara* continues, would send something from the heavenly realms to care for the newborns — cleansing them, preparing them, as a skilled midwife prepares a newborn infant, and providing them nourishment. The verse from *Yechezkel* is invoked: "on the day that you were born, your navel cord was not cut, and you were not washed with water" — the text of the *Haggadah*'s *derasha* connects here, where the entire metaphor of *Yechezkel* 16 about the founding of the nation is read literally as describing these miraculous births. God supplied them with *devash misela veshemen mechalmish tzur* — honey from the rock and oil from the flinty stone — as the verse in *Devarim* says: *vayenikehu devash misela* — He suckled them with honey from the rock.

### Ground & Grass

Once the Egyptians became aware that births were occurring, they came to kill the infants. At that moment, a miracle occurred: *venivla'in bakarka* — the babies were swallowed into the ground. The Egyptians then brought oxen and plowed over the places where the babies lay buried, but they were too deep and were protected. After the Egyptians left, *hayu mevatzbetzin veyotzin* — the babies would sprout out from the ground *ke'esev hasadeh*, like the grass of the field. The verse *revava ketzamach hasadeh nesatich* is cited — the very verse from the *Haggadah* that forms part of the *derasha* on that passage in *Yechezkel*: "I caused you to increase like the plant of the field." The *Gemara* is reading that verse with full literalness. The metaphor of the birthing of the nation and the literal birth of these children are collapsed into one.

When these children grew up, *ba'in adarim adarim levateihem* — they would come home in flocks, like flocks of animals from the field. The verse is read *al tikrei ba'adi adayim ela be'edrei adarim* — do not read "in jewels" but "in flocks." The image is striking: born in nature, swallowed by the earth, sprouting like grass, and returning home as flocks — they are almost animals of the field, untamed, raised by the earth itself.

### God Recognition

When God revealed Himself at the sea, *hem hikiruhu techila* — they were the first to recognize Him. And why? Because they had already encountered Him in the field when they were infants — it was through God's care that they had been bathed, nourished, and protected. And so at the sea they were able to cry out *zeh Keili ve'anveihu* — "this is my God and I will glorify Him." They recognized Him because they had known Him before.

---

## Midwives

### Shifra & Puah

*Rav* and *Shmuel* disagree about the identity of the two midwives. One says they were a mother and daughter (*isha uvita*), the other says a daughter-in-law and mother-in-law (*kala vechamotah*). The one who holds they were a mother and daughter identifies them as Yocheved and Miriam. The one who holds they were a daughter-in-law and mother-in-law identifies them as Yocheved and Elisheva, Aaron's wife.

A *baraita* sides with the mother-daughter view. *Shifra zu Yocheved* — Shifra was Yocheved. Why was she called Shifra? *Shemeshaperet et havelad* — she would beautify and care for the newborn; and additionally, *sheparu veravu Yisrael beyameha* — Israel was fruitful and multiplied in her days. *Puah zu Miriam* — Puah was Miriam. Why was she called Puah? *She'hayeta po'ah* — she would coo in order to help the child emerge, using soothing sounds to help the infant along. An alternate explanation: *she'hayeta po'ah beruach hakodesh* — she would speak with the divine spirit, saying: "My mother is destined to give birth to a son who will be the savior of Israel." And indeed, *moshi'an shel Yisrael* — the savior of Israel — is the very phrase we encountered earlier in Pharaoh's council, where the plan was to outwit *moshi'an shel Yisrael*. There, one might have taken it as referring to God; here, retrospectively, it becomes clear it refers to Moses.

*Tosafot* cites the explanation of *Rabbeinu Chananel* regarding *po'ah*: it refers to an incantation whispered to ease childbirth — *lo chashot lichisha* — and the practice of whispering such incantations to a woman in labor was common even in Tosafot's own time.

### Birth Signs

Pharaoh instructs the midwives: *beyaledchem et ha'ivriyot* — when you deliver the Hebrew women — and he specifies the *avnayim*, the birthing stones. *Rabbi Chanan* explains: Pharaoh gave them a sign by which to know that birth was imminent. When a woman crouches to give birth, *yarchoteiha mitztanenot ka'avanim* — her thighs become cold as stone — and that is when the midwives would need to be present to intercept the newborn.

An alternative explanation connects *avnayim* to the image of the potter's wheel: *va'ered beit hayotzer vehinei hu oseh melachah al ha'avnayim* — the potter works the stone, with one side here and one side there and the pedestal in the middle. Similarly, in childbirth: one thigh on this side, one thigh on the other, and the child coming out in the middle. The word *avnayim* thus becomes a metaphor for the birthing position.

### Refusal & Protection

*Rabbi Chanina* teaches that Pharaoh also gave the midwives a sign by which to distinguish boy from girl even before an examination: *ben panav lematah* — a boy comes out face down; *bat paneha lema'alah* — a girl face up. This connects to the *Gemara*'s broader understanding of conception: since the *Gemara* assumes the male is above and the female below during intercourse, the child is born in the position corresponding to its parent — a boy in the father's position, a girl in the mother's.

The verse says the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt had commanded them *aleihen*. The use of *aleihen* rather than the expected *lahen* prompts *Rabbi Yose bar Chanina* to suggest that Pharaoh had also tried to seduce them to sin sexually — *she'tav'an lidvar aveirah* — using *alav* in the sense of *lavo eleiha*, which the *Gemara* reads as a euphemism for sexual approach. They refused on that account as well.

### Women as Beasts

*Vatechayena et hayeladim* — "and they gave life to the children." A *baraita* teaches: not only did they not kill the children, they actively provided them with water and food to sustain them.

The midwives' excuse to Pharaoh — *ki lo ka'nashim hamitzriot ha'ivriyot ki chayot hena* — "for the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they are *chayot*" — is read carefully by the *Gemara*. Does *chayot* mean midwives? The *Gemara* objects: *atu chaya mi lo tzaricha chaya achrita* — surely a midwife when she herself gives birth needs another midwife! A barber needs a barber to cut his own hair. So *chayot mamash* cannot be the meaning here.

Rather, *ela amru lo: uma zu kechaya nimshala* — they told him: this nation is compared to an animal. They give birth without help, as animals of the field do. And this is supported by the very tribal blessings of Jacob: Judah is a lion cub, Dan is a serpent, Naphtali a swift deer, Issachar a burdened donkey, Joseph a firstborn ox, Benjamin a wolf. For those tribes where the comparison is explicit in the text, it is written; and for those where it is not, the verse *mah imcha laviya bein arayot* — "your mother was a lioness among lions" — covers the rest. All of Israel, in some sense, is likened to animals.

This is, in fact, a deeply layered *peshat*. The women who gave birth under the apple trees in the field, whose infants were swallowed into the earth and sprouted like grass, who came home in flocks — they are, in the most literal sense of the *Gemara*'s narrative, being born as creatures of the natural world, beyond the reach of Pharaoh's machinery. But there is another dimension as well. Part of the process of enslaving a people is dehumanizing them — reducing them in the eyes of the oppressor to something less than human. Pharaoh could believe the midwives' claim precisely because he had already begun that process of dehumanization. Yet the *Gemara* turns that very trope on its head: yes, they are like animals — and that is their glory, their resilience, their source of redemption.

---

---

# Sotah 12

## Midwives & Batim

### Intro & Framework

We pick up seven lines from the bottom of 11b, in the midst of the *aggadata* concerning the enslavement in Egypt — particularly fitting for *Chol HaMoed Pesach*. The broader context is the *mishnah*'s principle of *midah keneged midah*, measure for measure: just as God repays the *sotah* according to what she did, so too does the divine calculus operate throughout history.

### Rav vs. Shmuel

The *pasuk* states: *vayehi ki yar'u hameyaldot et haElohim vaya'as lahem batim* — when the midwives, identified with Yocheved and Miriam, feared God, He made for them *batim*, houses. A dispute between Rav and Shmuel turns on the meaning of these *batim*. One opinion holds *batei kehunah veleviyah*: houses of priesthood and Levitical service, referring to Aharon and Moshe who descended from Yocheved. The other holds *batei malchut*: houses of kingship. The first interpretation is relatively straightforward — Aharon stands at the head of the *kehunah* and Moshe is the preeminent of the Levites. The second requires more unpacking.

### Calev & Miriam

How does kingship emerge from Yocheved and Miriam? The Gemara answers: *David nami miMiriam ka'ati* — David himself descends from Miriam. The relevant *pesukim* are in Divrei HaYamim, where Calev marries a woman named Azuvah, and then takes Efrat, who bears him Chur. Separately, David is called *ben ish Efrati*. The Gemara links these together: Calev ben Yefuneh married Miriam, who is identified with both Azuvah and Efrat. David descended from Calev and therefore, ultimately, from Miriam herself.

---

## Miriam's Genealogy

### Calev Marries Miriam

The *pasuk* in Divrei HaYamim reads: *veCalev ben Chetzron holid et Azuvah isha ve'et Yeriyot* — Calev son of Chetzron "begot" Azuvah the wife and Yeriyot. Several difficulties immediately arise. First, the *pasuk* says *ben Chetzron*, but we know him as Calev *ben Yefuneh*. The Gemara resolves this: *ben Yefuneh* is a descriptive epithet — *she'pinah me'atzat hameraglim*, he turned himself away from the counsel of the spies — while Chetzron is his father's proper name.

A further complication: Calev is also called *haKenizi*, associated with Kenaz, since the *pasuk* in Shoftim describes Osniel ben Kenaz as *achi Calev*, the brother of Calev, implying they share a father. Rava resolves this: Calev was Kenaz's stepson, not his biological child. The designation *haKenizi* reflects that he was raised in Kenaz's household without being his natural son. *Shema mina* — this resolves all identifications, and the Calev in the *pasuk* is Calev ben Yefuneh.

Now, *zo Miriam* — Azuvah is Miriam. Why was she called Azuvah? *Shekol azvuha mitchilatah* — everyone had abandoned her, for she was sickly and no one wished to marry her. As for the word *holid* — "he begot" — the Gemara asks the obvious: surely he married her, he did not beget her? *Vehalo minsav hava nasiv lah* — of course he married her. This sets up the next teaching.

### Marriage L'Shem Shamayim

Rabbi Yochanan derives from here: *kol hanos'e isha l'shem shamayim ma'aleh alav hakatuv ke'ilu yeladah* — whoever marries a woman *l'shem shamayim*, for the sake of Heaven, Scripture accounts it as though he had fathered her. Here, Calev married Miriam not out of desire or attraction — she was sick and abandoned, with no one to care for her — but purely for her benefit and for the sake of Heaven. Therefore the Torah uses the language of *holid*, as if he had given birth to her. The image of a husband as father-figure is striking to modern sensibilities, but reflects the reality of a society where such a marriage was genuinely an act of protection and selfless provision.

The *pasuk* also mentions *Yeriyot* alongside Azuvah. Rather than reading this as a second wife, the Gemara interprets it as another name for Miriam: *she'hayu paneha domin liyeriyot* — her face resembled *yeriyot*, curtains, drawn and pale from illness. The following phrase, *ve'eileh baneha*, "these are her children," is read *al tikri baneha ella boneha* — not her children but that which built her, describing how Calev's marriage restored and strengthened her.

### Sons' Names Interpreted

The three sons listed — Yashar, Shovav, and Ardon — are interpreted not as literal children but as descriptions of Calev himself and what he accomplished. *Yashar*: *she'yishar et atzmo* — he made himself straight, whether by resisting the *meraglim* or by taking the upright path of marrying Miriam when others would not. *Shovav*: *she'shovev et yitzro* — he subjugated his *yetzer*, his inclination, again in resisting the *meraglim* or in choosing Miriam over someone more conventionally attractive. *Ardon*: *she'rada et yitzro* — he subdued his desire similarly. An alternative tradition reads *Ardon* as *she'panav domin levered* — his face was ruddy as a rose.

### Ashur & Tekoa

The *pasuk* continues: *veAshur avi Tekoa hayu shtei nashim Hel'ah veNa'arah* — Ashur the father of Tekoa had two wives, Hel'ah and Na'arah. The Gemara identifies Ashur with Calev once more. Why is he called Ashur? *She'hush'cheru panav beta'aniyot* — his face grew dark from the fasts he undertook, praying for the strength to withstand the pressure of the *meraglim*. This is a remarkable detail: the same Calev who stood before all of Bnei Yisrael with seemingly unshakeable courage could not rely on his own fortitude alone, but had to pour out his heart to God through fasting and prayer.

*Avi* — father: *she'nasa lah ke'av*, he became like a father to Miriam. *Tekoa*: *she'taka libo le'aviv she'bashamayim* — he drove his heart like a stake into his Father in Heaven, whether in the context of the *meraglim* or in his decision to marry *l'shem shamayim*.

As for the "two wives," Hel'ah and Na'arah: *na'asit Miriam k'shtei nashim* — Miriam became like two wives. *Lo Hel'ah veNa'arah hava* — these are not two distinct women. Rather, originally she was *Hel'ah*, sickly, and ultimately she became *Na'arah*, as strong and healthy as a young woman.

The children listed as *bnei Hel'ah* — Tzereth, Tzohar, and Etnan — are likewise interpreted in terms of this transformation. *Tzereth*: *she'na'asit tzarah lechaveroteha* — she became a rival to all the women around her, so stunning had she become. *Tzohar*: *she'hayu paneha domim ketzohorayim* — her face shone like midday. *Etnan* — which ordinarily refers to a harlot's payment — is interpreted here as: *shekol haro'eh otah molich etnan le'ishto*, that any man who saw her was so stirred that he would go and seek intimacy with his own wife, even offering her something akin to payment. The image is jarring, but conveys the idea of Miriam's remarkable transformation.

### Path to David

With all this established, the *batei malchut* interpretation is complete. Miriam married Calev ben Yefuneh of the tribe of Yehudah, and David descended from that union. Thus the houses God made for the midwives include the house of kingship that ultimately produced David HaMelech.

---

## Pharaoh's Decrees

### Drowning Edict

The Torah states: *vayetzav Paroh lechol amo* — Pharaoh commanded his entire nation that every son born should be thrown into the Nile. Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina notes that the phrase *lechol amo* indicates that the edict extended even to Pharaoh's own people — Egyptian children as well. Rashi, drawing on the Midrash Tanchuma, explains why: Pharaoh's astrologers had seen that the savior of Israel would be born on that day, but could not determine whether he was Egyptian or Hebrew. Since the identity was ambiguous — and indeed Moshe grew up in Pharaoh's palace and was even called *ish Mitzri* by the daughters of Yisro — Pharaoh cast the net wide and commanded that all male children born that day be drowned.

### Three Decrees

Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina also enumerates three distinct decrees that Pharaoh issued. First, the instruction to the midwives: if it is a boy, kill him. Second, the broader command to throw every Hebrew male newborn into the Nile. Third, the final sweeping edict to his own people to cast even their own sons born on that day into the river. The decrees thus escalated in scope and cruelty.

### Amram Divorces

The Torah then says: *vayelech ish mibeit Levi* — a man went from the house of Levi. This is Amram taking Yocheved. But the word *vayelech*, "he went," requires explanation. Rav Yehuda bar Zvina says: *she'halach be'atzat bito* — he followed the advice of his daughter. This is the famous *midrash* connecting back to Miriam.

*Amram gadol hador hayah* — Amram was the preeminent figure of his generation. Once Pharaoh's edict to throw every newborn son into the Nile was issued, Amram reasoned: *l'shav anu ameilim* — it is for nothing that we labor, meaning that the effort of having children was futile if the boys would immediately be murdered. The word *ameilim* is slightly unusual here — it is the women who bear the burdens of pregnancy and birth — but the sense is clear. He then rose and divorced his wife. The purpose of the public divorce, rather than simply ceasing marital relations, seems to have been to make a statement that would prompt others to follow: *amdu kulam vegeirshu et neshoseihem* — all the men rose and divorced their wives.

### Miriam's Argument

Miriam confronted her father: *abba, kasha gzeiratecha yoser mishel Paroh* — Father, your decree is harsher than Pharaoh's. The argument unfolds in three parts. First: Pharaoh decreed only against the males, but your act ensures that no female children will be born either. Second: Pharaoh decreed only for this world; by not bringing children into existence, you deny even those potential souls their share in *olam haba* — for even a child who is killed immediately has a soul that merits *olam haba*. Third — and this is the most striking element: *Paroh harasha, safek miskayemet gezeiraso safek einah miskayemet* — Pharaoh is a *rasha*, and it is uncertain whether his decrees will be fulfilled. But you, *tzaddik*, your decrees will certainly be fulfilled: *she'ne'emar vetigzar omer veyakom lach* — for it is said that when the righteous decree, it is established. Therefore, what you are doing is actually more harmful than what the *rasha* is doing.

### Remarriage Celebration

*Amad vehechezir et ishto* — Amram listened to Miriam and remarried Yocheved. *Amdu kulam vehecheziru et nesheihem* — and all the men followed suit. The *pasuk*'s language of *vayelech ish* and *vayikach et bat Levi* sounds as though this is a first marriage. This is precisely why the Gemara had to construct this backstory: Aharon and Miriam are clearly older than Moshe, as the *pasuk* later says *vatitatzev achoto merachok* — his sister stood at a distance — so there must have been earlier children. The divorce and remarriage account explains the *pasuk*'s language while preserving the chronology.

Rabbi Yehuda bar Bizna adds: *she'asah lah ma'aseh likuchin* — he made of this remarriage a grand first-wedding celebration. *Hoshivah b'apiryon* — he seated her on a throne; *ve'Aharon veMiryam merakedin lefaneha* — Aharon and Miriam danced before her; *malachei hashareit amru* — the ministering angels proclaimed: *eim habanim semeichah* — the mother of children is rejoicing. Whether this refers to Yocheved's existing children or anticipates the birth of Moshe, the setting is one of great celebration and joy — which provides the backdrop for the conception and birth of Moshe.

---

## Yocheved's Birth

### Age Question

The *pasuk* calls Yocheved *bat Levi*, daughter of Levi, which implies youthfulness. The Gemara raises the difficulty: *efshar bat me'ah ushloshim shanah hava'i vekari lah bat?* — is it possible to call her a *bat*, a daughter, when she was 130 years old at the time of Moshe's birth? The tradition establishing her age is as follows: if she was born when Yaakov's family descended to Egypt and she was then 130 years old when Moshe was born, that aligns with Moshe being 80 years old at the time of the Exodus, having been born 130 years into the Egyptian sojourn.

### Yocheved Born in Egypt

Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina addresses this through a textual reading: *zo Yocheved she'horatah baderech veleIdatah bein hachomot* — Yocheved's conception occurred while her mother was traveling down to Egypt, and she was born at the very moment of entry. The proof is the *pasuk*: *asher yaldah otah le-Levi beMitzrayim* — which is read as: her birth (*leidatah*) was in Egypt, but her conception (*horatah*) was not in Egypt. This could only be the case if she was born at the precise instant of entry into Egypt — between the walls, *bein hachomot*, at the city gates.

### 70 Souls Problem

This interpretation resolves a well-known difficulty in the *pesukim*. When the Torah enumerates the souls who descended to Egypt, the count comes to 69, yet the Torah states there were 70. The answer is Yocheved: she was only being gestated during the journey, so there were 69 persons traveling, but the moment they entered Egypt she was born, making 70. This is the interpretive motivation for Rabbi Chama's reading.

If Yocheved was born upon the entry to Egypt and the sojourn lasted 210 years, with Moshe being born 130 years in and living to 80 at the time of the Exodus, then Yocheved was indeed 130 years old at Moshe's birth. The question of how she can be called *bat* remains.

### Yocheved's Youth

Rabbi Yehuda answers: the signs of her youth returned to her, as they had to Sarah — she regained the physiological markers of youthfulness, including the ability to conceive. The *Ibn Ezra* raises a sharp objection: by Sarah, the Torah makes an enormous point of the miraculous nature of her conceiving at 90, yet here at 130 the Torah passes over it without comment. The *Ramban* responds at length, noting that there are many hidden miracles the Torah does not record explicitly. In any case, this is the Gemara's position.

### Three-Month Pregnancy

Rav Yehuda bar Zvina adds a further detail that will become important shortly: Yocheved was already three months pregnant at the time of Amram's remarriage. The great celebratory *vayikach* — all that fanfare of the wedding, the dancing, the angels singing — occurred when she had already been carrying Moshe for three months. We will see momentarily why the Gemara requires this detail.

---

## Moshe's Birth

### Painless Birth

The *pasuk* says *vatahar ha'isha vateled ben* — the woman became pregnant and gave birth to a son. If she was already pregnant at the time of the remarriage, why does the Torah speak of her pregnancy as beginning now? Rav Yehuda bar Zvina answers: *makish leidatah le-horatah* — the Torah juxtaposes her giving birth to her conceiving in order to teach something. *Mah horatah she'lo betza'ar af leidatah she'lo betza'ar* — just as her conception was without pain, so too her birth was without pain.

The connection between conception and birth here teaches the principle: *mikan l'nashim tzidkaniyot she'lo hayu befitko shel Chava* — righteous women are not subject to the curse of Chava, who was told she would give birth in pain. It is worth noting that when the epidural became available and voices in some religious communities raised objections on theological grounds — citing the curse of Chava — there was never any corresponding objection from the Jewish community. For us, a curse is not something to be preserved but to be escaped, and here the Gemara makes clear that righteous women stand outside it.

### House of Light

The Torah says *vatere oso ki tov hu* — she saw that he was good. The question is what this means. Every mother finds her child beautiful; what does this observation tell us that is exceptional? The sages offer multiple answers.

The view of the Sages is that when Moshe was born, *nitmalei habayis kulo or* — the entire house filled with light. This is the image most are familiar with, as Rashi quotes it on the *pasuk* in the Torah. The connection to *ki tov* is drawn from a *gezerah shavah*: the same phrase appears at the creation of light — *vayar Elokim et ha'or ki tov* — and just as God saw the light and called it good, Yocheved saw Moshe and perceived the divine light radiating from him.

### Name Interpretations

Rabbi Meir says: *tov shemo* — *ki tov hu* simply means his name was Tov. This gives Moshe a Hebrew name bestowed by his mother, which is meaningful since *Moshe* is in fact an Egyptian name — present, for example, in *Rameses*, which means *Ra-Moshe*, born of Ra. *Ki min hamayim meshisihu* — "for I drew him from the water" — uses a Hebrew root that in context carries an Egyptian connotation of birth from water. Rabbi Meir's reading restores a Hebrew name to him.

Rabbi Yehuda says his name was Tuvia — reading *ki tov hu* as *tov* plus *Yah*, the divine name: God is good. Rabbi Nechemia says: *hogun lenevu'ah* — she perceived that he possessed the potential for prophecy, though the text does not indicate how she perceived this. *Acheirim* say he was *nolad keshe'hu mahul* — born already circumcised, without a foreskin, which was itself a visible sign of his singular nature.

### Three-Month Hiding

*Vatispenehu shlosha yerachim* — she hid him for three months. The Gemara asks: why only three months? Why could she not simply continue hiding him? The answer requires understanding how the Egyptians were tracking the situation. When the Egyptians saw that the Hebrew men had remarried their wives, they began counting nine months forward from that date, anticipating when births would occur. They then sent informants to locate hidden babies through a disturbing method: *kol heichah de'hava shamei Mitzrayim demisyalid yanuka, mamtu yanuka hatam* — wherever Egyptians heard that a baby was expected, they would bring an infant of their own, slap it to make it cry, and the hidden baby would cry in response, revealing its location. Based on a *pasuk* in Shir HaShirim — *achazo lanu shualim shualim ketanim* — the small foxes, little babies used to ferret out other babies.

Here the three-month detail becomes crucial. *Delo manu Mitzrayim ela mish'as hadra* — the Egyptians counted nine months from the date of the remarriage. But Yocheved was already three months pregnant at that point. So they expected birth nine months from the remarriage, while Moshe was actually born six months after the remarriage — three months earlier than the Egyptians anticipated. This bought Yocheved three months of undetected concealment. Once that window closed and the Egyptians began actively searching, she could no longer hide him.

---

## The Basket

### Wicker Material

*Vatikach lo teivat gome* — she took a basket of wicker reeds. Why specifically wicker? Rabbi Elazar says: *mikan l'tzadikim shemamounam chaviv aleihem yoter migufam* — from here we learn that the righteous value their money more than their bodies, choosing inexpensive materials. And why are they so careful with money? *Lefi she'ein poshtin yedeihem begazel* — because they scrupulously avoid theft, they are equally careful with what they spend. This is a striking interpretation, and the Gemara immediately senses the difficulty: being economical is one thing, but applying that principle to a basket meant to save your child's life seems misplaced. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani therefore offers a more functional explanation: wicker was chosen because it is flexible — *davar rach she'yachol la'amod bifnei davar rach uvifnei davar kasheh* — it can absorb impact whether it encounters something soft or something hard. A rigid material would risk puncturing and sinking; a flexible one could bend without breaking.

### Plastering Method

*Vatachmira vachamer uvazafet* — she plastered it with slime and pitch. A *tanna* teaches: *chamer mibifnim vezafet mibachutz* — the slime was on the inside and the pitch was on the outside. The reason: *kedei shelo yariach oso tzaddik rei'ach ra* — so that the *tzaddik*, the infant Moshe, should not have to smell the foul odor of the pitch. The plaster layer on the interior served to insulate him from the smell of the tar on the outside.

### Placement in Reeds

*Vatasem basuf* — she placed it among the *suf*. Rabbi Elazar says this refers to *Yam Suf*; Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says *suf* simply means a swamp or reed bed, as the *pasuk* elsewhere uses *kaneh vasuf* to refer to reeds, making *suf* a species of aquatic plant.

### Pharaoh's Daughter

*Vaterd bat Paroh lirchotz al haYe'or* — Pharaoh's daughter went down to bathe at the Nile. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai explains: *melamed sheyardah lirchotz migilulei aviha* — she went to cleanse herself from the excrement, meaning the idolatry of her father. The washing was a conversion ritual. The proof: the *pasuk* in Yeshayahu uses the image of washing to describe the removal of spiritual filth — *im rachatz Hashem et tzoa'at bnot Tzion* — establishing that washing can represent purification from sin rather than physical bathing.

### Maidservants Killed

*Vena'aroteha holchot* — her maidservants were walking alongside her. Rabbi Yochanan reads *holchot* here as a euphemism for death, in the same way the *pasuk* says *hineh anochi holech lamut* — I am going to die. When the maidservants saw that Pharaoh's daughter intended to rescue Moshe, they protested: even when the whole world does not obey a king's decree, his own household should. How could she violate her father's *gezeirah*? *Ba Gavriel vechavatam bakarka* — the angel Gavriel came and struck them into the ground, killing them.

The parallel to the earlier narrative is worth noting. Amram issued a *gezeirah* and his daughter Miriam rose to undermine it through persuasion. Here, Pharaoh issued a *gezeirah* and his daughter bat Paroh rose to violate it through action. A *tzaddik*'s decree is certain to stand; a *rasha*'s is not. The same principle echoes through both episodes.

One maidservant was left alive. *Delav orcha de-bas malka lemeikam lechudeih* — it would not be proper for the king's daughter to stand entirely alone without an attendant. Gavriel spared one for the sake of decorum.

---

## Discovery & Rescue

### Extended Arm

*Vatishlach et amatah vatikacheha* — she sent her *amah* and took the basket. A dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemia: one says *amah* means her hand — from *amah*, the cubit measure, referring to her arm — and the other says it means her maidservant, the standard meaning of *amah*. The one who reads *shifchah*, maidservant, asks: if you mean hand, why not use the clearer word *yad*? The one who reads *amah* as arm asks: if you mean maidservant, it should have said *shifchah*; the word *amah* is ambiguous.

If *amah* means her arm, then what does the text convey by using this unusual word? *De'ishtarbovei ishtarbuba* — her arm miraculously extended, stretching out an *amah* beyond its natural reach to grasp the basket. This is compared to Achashveirosh extending the scepter to Esther, and to the *pasuk*: *shinei resha'im shibarta* — Resh Lakish reads not *shibarta*, "you broke their teeth," but *sherivavta* — "you caused them to elongate," another miraculous extension in a different context.

### Seeing Divine

*Vatiftach vatireihu et hayeled* — she opened the basket and saw the child. The Hebrew uses *vatireihu* — she saw *him* — when we might have expected simply *vatire*, she saw the child. Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina explains: *she'ra'atah Shechinah imo* — she saw the divine presence accompanying the child. *Vatireihu* — she saw God *et hayeled*, with the child. This connects directly to the earlier teaching that the house filled with light at Moshe's birth: here too, bat Paroh perceives something supernatural.

### Child Crying

*Vehinei naar bocheh* — there was a child crying. The text uses two different words: *yeled*, an infant, and *naar*, a young man. A *tanna* offers: *hu yeled vekolo ke'naar* — he was an infant in body but his voice was that of a young man, a powerful, adult cry. This is the view of Rabbi Yehuda.

### Voice & Blemish

Rabbi Nechemia objects: *im kein asita lo l'Moshe Rabbeinu b'mum* — you have made Moshe Rabbeinu into a person with a defect. For an infant to have so deep and powerful a voice would itself be a physical anomaly, a blemish. Rashi adds an additional dimension: since the Levites served as singers in the *Beit HaMikdash*, such an aberrant voice in childhood would, somewhat anachronistically, invalidate someone from that service.

Rabbi Nechemia therefore offers an alternative reading: *melamed she'asta lo imo chuppat ne'urim* — his mother had made him a small *chuppah*, a wedding canopy, inside the basket. *Bateivah amrah: shema lo ezkeh l'chuppato* — in placing him in the basket she thought, perhaps I will never live to see his wedding, so let me make him one now. The word *naar* thus refers not to his voice but to this miniature *chuppah*, recalling the wedding celebration that had marked his parents' remarriage.

### Circumcision Recognition

*Vatomer miyaldei ha'ivrim zeh* — she said, this is one of the Hebrew children. How did she know? Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina: *she'ra'atah oso mahul* — she saw that he was circumcised. This is presumably distinct from the earlier tradition that he was born without a foreskin — here the implication is that he had been circumcised in the ordinary manner.

### Unwitting Prophecy

The word *zeh* — "this one" — receives close attention. Rabbi Yochanan says: *melamed she'nisnaveit shelo mida'atah* — she prophesied without knowing what she was saying. *Zeh nofel, ve'ein acher nofel* — this one was cast into the Nile, and no other would be. The moment Moshe was placed in the Nile, the astrological sign that had prompted the edict was read as fulfilled, and the decree ceased. Bat Paroh's words were thus an unconscious prophecy: *this* child, and no other, was "the one cast into the Nile" in the sense the edict had in mind.

---

## Astrologers Confused

### Saw by Water

Rabbi Elazar now brings a *pasuk* from Yeshayahu that mocks those who practice necromancy and divination: *hamitzpitzpim vehamehaggim*, those who chirp and mutter. The Gemara reads this as a description of astrologers generally: *tzofim* — they see something — *mitzpitzpim* — they read signs — *ve'einam yodim mah tzofim* — but they do not fully understand what they are seeing; *mahagim* — they speak — *ve'einam yodim mah mahagim* — but they do not fully understand what they are saying.

What did Pharaoh's astrologers see? *Ra'u shemoshi'an shel Yisrael bamayim hu lokeh* — they saw that the savior of Israel would be punished by water. On this basis they issued the decree to cast all male children into the Nile.

### Edict Ceased

*Keivan deshadyuhu le-Moshe* — once Moshe was thrown into the Nile, *amru: tu lo chazina ki hai simana* — the astrologers said, we no longer see that sign in the heavens. *Batlu legezerataihu* — and they annulled the decree. Their reasoning: the savior has been cast into the water, punished, and is presumably dead. There is no longer cause for alarm. *Vehem einam yodim* — but they did not understand.

### Mei Merivah

*Ki al Mei Merivah hu lokeh* — the savior would not be punished by the Nile but by the waters of Merivah. The sign the astrologers saw was real; their interpretation was wrong. Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina derives this from the *pasuk*: *hemah Mei Merivah asher ravu* — these are the waters of Merivah, the very same waters that the astrologers of Pharaoh had seen *vetau*, and about which they were confused. They saw water, they thought the Nile; the true referent was Merivah, where Moshe would later strike the rock rather than speak to it, and for that he would be denied entry into the land.

### Moshe's Credit

Finally: *shesh me'ot elef ragli* — the word *ragli* is read by the Gemara not as "foot soldiers" but as *bishvili*, "because of me." Moshe says to Israel: *bishvili nitzaltem kulchem* — all 600,000 of you were saved because of me. When I was cast into the Nile, the astrological sign was read as fulfilled, the edict ceased, and you were spared.

Tosafot raises the obvious objection: the entire edict was made in the first place because of Moshe, since it was his birth that the astrologers feared. How can he take credit for ending a decree that he caused? Tosafot answers: once Moshe was cast into the Nile and the astrologers declared the sign fulfilled, not only did the decree targeting Moshe's generation end — even the older, pre-astrological impulse to persecute and destroy the Israelites, which had manifested even in the initial orders to the midwives, ceased entirely. In that broader sense, Moshe brought about the complete cessation of the murderous decrees, and it is for this that he takes credit.

---

---

# Sotah 13

## Moshe's Birth & Miriam

### 21st Nissan Dating

The daf opens in the midst of a series of *midrashim* surrounding *yetziat mitzrayim*, specifically the birth of Moshe Rabbeinu. We pick up with Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa, who derives from the word *zeh* in the *pasuk* a precise date for when Moshe was discovered by *Bat Pharaoh*. His position is that *oto yom esrim ve'echad b'Nissan haya* — that day was the 21st of Nissan. On that basis, the heavenly angels said before God: *Ribbono shel olam*, the one who in the future will sing the *shira al hayam* on this very day — should he be smitten on this very same day?

### 6th Sivan Alternative

Rabbi Akiva bar Rabbi Hanina disagrees. According to him, *oto yom shisha b'Sivan haya* — the day Moshe was discovered was not the 21st of Nissan but the 6th of Sivan, the very day the Torah would later be given at Har Sinai. The angels' protestation is framed accordingly: the one who in the future will receive Torah from Har Sinai on this day — should he be smitten on this day? Both opinions derive their respective dates from the emphatic use of *zeh* in the *pasuk* — *miyaldei ha'ivrim zeh* — understanding the word as pointing toward a day of particular cosmic significance.

### 7th Adar Birth/Death

The *Gemara* now examines which opinion is internally coherent with the tradition that Moshe was hidden for three months before his discovery. The underlying datum is the teaching: *beshiva b'Adar met uveshiva b'Adar nolad* — Moshe died on the 7th of Adar and was born on the 7th of Adar. His death date on the 7th of Adar is derived from the account in *Sefer Yehoshua*: Bnei Yisrael mourned Moshe for thirty days, after which God told Yehoshua to cross the Jordan, and that crossing, as the *pesukim* in Yehoshua make clear, occurred on the 10th of Nissan — counting back thirty days yields the 7th of Adar. The birth date on the same day is derived from the principle that *tzaddikim* live out complete years, dying on the anniversary of their birth, along with Moshe's own declaration *ben me'ah ve'esrim shana anochi hayom* — "today I am exactly 120 years old" — implying that the day of his death was precisely the day of his birth.

### Leap Year Timing

The *Gemara* asks: *bishlamah* for the opinion that Moshe was discovered on the 6th of Sivan, the arithmetic works out elegantly — three months from the 7th of Adar yields Adar, Nissan, Iyar, Sivan, arriving at the 6th or 7th of Sivan, aligning with *Matan Torah*. But for the opinion that he was discovered on the 21st of Nissan, how can three months from the 7th of Adar reach only the 21st of Nissan? The *Gemara* resolves this: *osa shana me'uberet hayita* — that year was a leap year. Moshe was born on the 7th of Adar Rishon; he had the remainder of Adar Rishon, the entirety of Adar Sheni, and 21 days of Nissan — most of the first month, all of the middle month, and most of the third month, satisfying the requirement of *rubo shel rishon*, *rubo shel acharon*, and *emtza'ei shalem*.

### Nursing Refusal

The *Gemara* then turns to the verse *ha'elech vekarati lach isha meneiket min ha'ivriyot* — shall I go and call a nursemaid from the Hebrew women? Why specifically Hebrew women? The *Gemara* teaches: *melamed she-hechziru l'Moshe al kol hamitzriyot* — they had already attempted to have Moshe nurse from Egyptian women, and he refused from every one of them. The reasoning given is: *peh she'atid ledaber im haShechina yanik davar tamei* — the mouth that would one day speak directly with the Divine Presence, should it suckle something impure? The impurity referred to is not the person of the Egyptian woman herself, but the non-kosher food she consumed, the effects of which pass into a nursing mother's milk. This *aggadic* passage carries real halakhic resonances among the *poskim* regarding whether the food of a nursing mother must meet kosher standards, given that the infant, who is below the age of *chinuch*, would still be receiving some spiritual or physical effect of *metamtem et halev* — the heart-dulling quality that the *Gemara* elsewhere attributes to non-kosher food.

### Knowledge Verses

The *Gemara* connects Moshe's refusal to nurse from Egyptian women to the verse: *l'mi yoreh de'ah v'et mi yavin shemu'ah gemulei mechalav atikei mishadayim* — "To whom shall one teach knowledge, and who shall understand the tradition? One who weans himself from milk and removes himself from the breast." This verse is now understood as a reference to Moshe, who as an infant refused the milk of Egyptian women, thereby preserving the sanctity of the mouth destined to speak before God.

The *Gemara* then addresses the verse *vattomer lah Bat Pharaoh lechi*, in which *Bat Pharaoh* tells Miriam to go. Rabbi Elazar derives from the subsequent *vattelech ha'almah* — "and the young woman went" — that she went *bizrizut k'almah*, with the alacrity of a young woman. The *Gemara* then notes *vattelech ha'almah vatikra et em hayeled*, and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani explains why she is called *ha'almah*: *she-he'elimah et dvareha* — she concealed her words, presenting Yocheved as merely a Hebrew nursing woman without revealing that she was Moshe's own mother.

The verse then continues: *vattomer lah Bat Pharaoh heichi et hayeled hazeh* — here, take this child. Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina observes: *misnave'ah ve'einah yoda'at mah misnave'ah* — she prophesied without knowing what she was prophesying. The word *heichi*, parsed as *hei* and *sheleichi*, carries the meaning "here is what is yours" — *Bat Pharaoh* unknowingly declared that this was Yocheved's own child. Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina adds a broader principle: *lo dayam latzaddikim she-machzirim lahem avedatan* — it is not sufficient for the righteous that their lost objects are returned to them; *ela she-notnim lahem scharam* — they are also paid for retrieving what was already theirs to begin with.

### Miriam's Prophecy

The *Gemara* transitions to the verse at *Shirat Hayam*: *vattikach Miriam hanevia achot Aharon*. The question is posed: why does it say *achot Aharon* — Aaron's sister — and not Moshe's sister? The answer, cited in the name of Rav Amram citing Rav, and some say Rav Nachman citing Rav: *melamed she-nitnave'ah k'she-hi achot Aharon* — this teaches that she had already attained the status of *nevia* while she was only Aaron's sister, before Moshe was born. This implies that her prophecy concerned Moshe's birth: *atida imi sheteleid ben* — my mother will give birth to a son. Her father kissed her on her head and said, *bitti, nitkayma nevuatecha* — my daughter, your prophecy has been fulfilled — and, as a result, he restored his wife, bringing Yocheved back.

### Miriam's Witness

Yet once Moshe was placed into the Nile, the father struck Miriam on her head and said: *bitti, heichan nevuatecha* — my daughter, where is your prophecy now? This explains the verse *vatitatzav achoto merachok lada'at mah yei'aseh lo*: Miriam stood at a distance not merely to watch over her brother, but *lada'at mah yihyeh b'sof nevuatah* — to see what would ultimately become of her prophecy, whether it would in fact be fulfilled. The contrast between Miriam's long-term prophetic perspective and Amram's immediate, reactive responses — first to Pharaoh's decree by divorcing Yocheved, then to Moshe's placement in the Nile by striking Miriam — runs as a recurring thread through this section of the *Gemara*.

---

## Yosef Buries Yaakov

### Entourage Precedence

The *Gemara* now moves to the burial of Yaakov, examining the *pasuk*: *vaya'al Yosef likbor et aviv vaya'alu ito kol avdei Pharaoh* — Yosef went up to bury his father, accompanied by all the servants of Pharaoh. The *Gemara* notes that on the way out, Pharaoh's entourage preceded Yosef's own family — *kol beit Yosef ve'echav u-veit aviv* — yet on the return journey, the order was reversed: *vayashov Yosef Mitzraima hu ve'echav v'hadar kol ha-olim ito likbor et aviv*, where Yosef and his family are mentioned first. Rabbi Yochanan explains: *batchila shelo ra'u bikhvodan shel Yisrael* — initially the Egyptians had not yet witnessed the honor afforded to Israel, so they did not show them honor; *ul'vasof she-ra'u bikhvodan, nahagu bahem kavod* — in the end, once they witnessed that honor firsthand, they treated them accordingly. The *Gemara* now turns to where this transformation of honor occurred.

### Atad & Crowns

The *Gemara* cites the verse *vayavo'u ad goren ha-Atad* — they came to the threshing floor of the Atad, meaning thornbushes or thistles. The *Gemara* asks: *v'chi goren yesh l'atad* — who makes a threshing floor for thorns? Rabbi Abbahu explains: *melamed she-hikifuhu ktarim l'arono shel Yaakov* — what the verse is describing is that they surrounded Yaakov's coffin with crowns, the various kings who came to pay their respects each placing a crown there. The word *atad*, with its connotation of sharp thorns, thus evokes the image of a *goren* — a threshing floor — surrounded by a fence of thorns, which Rashi understands as a barrier to keep animals out. But the deeper image is of Yaakov's coffin encircled by the pointed crowns of kings.

### Descendants' Arrival

A *Braitah* is cited: *kulam lemilchamah ba'u* — they had not come to pay honor but to make war. Bnei Esav, Bnei Yishmael, and Bnei Keturah — all the descendants of Avraham outside of the line of Yaakov — came with the intention of attacking the Israelite family as they returned with Yaakov's coffin into the land they had been occupying.

### Yosef's Crown

Yet when they saw Yosef's crown suspended over Yaakov's coffin — *kivan she-ra'u kitro shel Yosef taluy be'arono shel Yaakov* — Yosef being the viceroy of Egypt and the most powerful figure present — their intention shifted. *Natlu kulam kitreihem u-tla'um be'arono shel Yaakov* — they all took their own crowns and hung them on Yaakov's coffin as well. The irony is apparent: the Egyptians in Pharaoh's entourage came to show honor to Yosef as an Egyptian dignitary, not specifically to honor Bnei Yisrael — and yet the net effect was a massive public demonstration of honor to Yaakov.

### 36 Crowns

A *Braitah* teaches: *sheloshim ve-shishah ktarim nitlu be'arono shel Yaakov* — thirty-six crowns were ultimately hung on Yaakov's coffin. Rashi notes that one can roughly arrive at this number by tallying the princes listed in the genealogies of Esav and Yishmael, arriving close to thirty-six even if the count does not come out exactly.

### Esav's Claim

When they arrived at *Me'arat haMachpelah*, Esav came to obstruct the burial.
