The *Gemara* provides background via the teaching of Rav Yitzchak: *Kiryat Arba, arba zugot hayu* — the name Kiryat Arba, the city of the four, refers to the four pairs buried there: Adam and Chavah, Avraham and Sarah, Yitzchak and Rivkah, and Yaakov and Leah. Three and a half pairs were already interred. Esav argued: Yaakov buried Leah in his portion, and the remaining niche is mine. Even if I sold the privileges of the firstborn, *peshitosah mi zvini* — I did not sell my basic rights as a regular son, and therefore my share of the cave remains mine.

### Document Dispute

Bnei Yaakov responded that he had in fact sold all rights, citing Yaakov's own declaration *bekivri asher kariti li* — "my grave that I have acquired for myself." Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak explains: *ein kirah ela leshon mekhirah* — the word *kira* in this *pasuk* means not to dig but to purchase, as on the islands (*karkei hayam*) the word for purchase is *kira*. Thus Yaakov's insistence on *kariti li* — I acquired this for myself — strongly implies that his ownership of the specific niche was not merely ancestral but was actively established and transferred to him. Esav demanded proof: *havu li igarta* — show me the document. Bnei Yaakov replied that the document had been left behind in Egypt.

### Naftali's Mission

There was no difficulty in retrieving it quickly: *nizil Naftali* — let us send Naftali, *dekal ke'ayalta* — who is as swift as a hind, as the *pasuk* says *Naftali ayalah shelucha ha-noten imrei shefer* — Naftali is a swift deer who delivers beautiful words. Rabbi Abbahu applies *al tikri* here: *al tikri imrei shefer ela imrei sefer* — do not read "beautiful words" but "words of the document," for Naftali was being sent to fetch the written proof.

### Chushim Kills Esav

While everyone waited for Naftali to return from Egypt, Chushim son of Dan was present. He was *yakiran leh udneih* — hard of hearing, literally his ears were heavy. He asked what was happening, and was told that Esav was holding up the burial until Naftali returned from Egypt with the document. Chushim's reaction was immediate: *ve'ad de'ati Naftali me'ara demitzrayim yehei avi abba mutal be-vizayon?* — Until Naftali returns from Egypt, my father's father should lie there in disgrace? He took a rod, struck Esav on the head, and Esav's eyes fell out and landed on Yaakov's lap — the coffin being evidently open. *Patchinhu Yaakov le'einei* — Yaakov opened his eyes and smiled. The *Gemara* cites the verse *yismach tzaddik ki chaza nakam* — the righteous will rejoice when he sees retribution done, *pe'amav yirchatz bedam harasha* — and will wash his feet in the blood of the wicked.

One might note a difficulty: the *pesukim* seem to record a genuine reconciliation between Yaakov and Esav. Why is this narrative, with its violent resolution, the satisfying endpoint? The *Gemara*'s presentation here likely reflects the perspective of *Chazal* who, living under Roman — and later other — oppressive powers, understood Esav as a recurring historical antagonist to Bnei Yisrael. What read as personal reconciliation in the *pesukim* becomes, in the broader sweep of history, an unresolved tension that demands ultimate resolution. There is something genuinely comforting, from within that framework, in the image of the righteous smiling at the sight of justice.

### Yaakov Laughs

*Be'otah sha'ah nitkayma nevo'atah shel Rivkah* — at that moment the prophecy of Rivkah was fulfilled. She had said *lamah eshkal gam shneichem yom echad* — why should I be bereaved of both of you in one day? Although Yaakov and Esav did not die on precisely the same day, *kevuratam miha beyom echad hava* — their burials occurred on the same day, and in that sense her prophecy found its fulfillment.

---

## Yosef-Moshe Parallel

### Yosef's Leadership

The *Gemara* raises a question about the earlier *pasuk*: if Yosef's brothers were also involved in carrying Yaakov up to Canaan — as the verse *vayisu oto vanav artza Kena'an* indicates — why does the primary *pasuk* credit Yosef alone? The *Gemara* explains: *amru hanichu lo* — the brothers said, let Yosef take the lead, *kevodo bi-mlachim yoter mibedyotot* — it is greater honor for Yaakov to be buried by kings than by ordinary people. They did not remove themselves from the burial; they deferred to Yosef's royal prominence to maximize the honor afforded to their father.

---

## Yosef-Moshe Parallel (II)

### Moshe's Care

Just as Yosef was the most prominent figure of his generation and took the lead in burying Yaakov, so too Moshe — the greatest of his generation — took it upon himself to carry Yosef's bones out of Egypt. The *Gemara* draws this as an explicit and intentional parallel, underscoring a principle of reciprocal care for the dead across generations. The narrative of Yosef carrying Yaakov's bones from Egypt to Canaan is thus mirrored in Moshe carrying Yosef's bones from Egypt to Canaan. There is moreover a deep sense of closure in this: the long arc of Yosef's oath to the brothers, the period of enslavement during which the hope of redemption may have seemed forgotten, and the ultimate fulfillment of the return to the land — all are gathered together in the act of Moshe lifting Yosef's bones.

---

## Moshe Gets Yosef

### Moshe & Mitzvot

*Tanu Rabbanan*: come and see how precious the *mitzvot* were to Moshe — *shechol Yisrael kulan nit'asku beviza* — all of Israel was occupied with the spoils of Egypt, the gold and silver and borrowed vessels, *vehu nit'asek bemitzvot* — while he devoted himself to the *mitzvah* of carrying Yosef's bones. This is what is meant by *chacham lev yikach mitzvot* — the wise of heart will take on *mitzvot*.

### Serach bat Asher

How did Moshe know where Yosef was buried? *Amru: Serach bat Asher nishtayra me'oto hador* — Serach daughter of Asher was the sole survivor still living from the generation of Yosef. Moshe went to her and asked: *klum at yoda'at heichan Yosef kavur?* The *Gemara* frames this detail with quiet pathos: if Bnei Yisrael had maintained the hope of redemption alive during the years of enslavement, one would expect them to have preserved the tradition of Yosef's burial place. That only this one elderly woman knew suggests how completely *yisrael* had despaired. It is also notable, as has been observed throughout this *sugya*, that it is women — Miriam, Serach — who serve as the keepers of tradition and the carriers of hope.

### Metal Casket

Serach told Moshe: *Aron shel matechet asu lo Mitzrayim* — the Egyptians had made Yosef a metal casket, *ukeva'uhu baNilus* — and they had sunk it in the Nile, *kedei sheyitbarchu meimav* — so that the waters of the Nile would be blessed by Yosef's presence. Yosef's capacity for sustaining Egypt through the famine had left such an impression that even in death the Egyptians sought to harness his blessing for their river.

### Moshe Calls Yosef

*Halach Moshe ve'amad al sfat Nilus* — Moshe went and stood at the bank of the Nile and called out: *Yosef, Yosef, higa zman she-nishba HaKadosh Baruch Hu* — the time has come that God swore to redeem, *ve-higi'ah ha-shvu'ah she-hishbata Yisrael* — and the oath that you made Israel swear has also arrived. *Im ata mareh atzmacha mutav; ve'im lav, harei anu menukim mi-shvu'atecha* — if you show yourself, good; if not, we are absolved of your oath. We have done everything we can. Immediately, *miyad tzaf arono shel Yosef* — Yosef's coffin floated to the surface.

### Elisha Analogy

The *Gemara* anticipates the obvious question: how does iron float? It cites the episode from *Sefer Melachim* in which Elisha caused a borrowed iron axe-head that had fallen into the water to float by throwing a piece of wood into the spot where it had sunk. From this a *kal vachomer* is constructed: if the iron floated for Elisha, who was a student of Eliyahu who was a student of Moshe, *bifnei Moshe Rabbeinu al achat kamah vechamah* — how much more readily would iron float for Moshe himself.

### Crypt Alternative

Rabbi Natan offers an alternative tradition: Yosef was not buried in the Nile at all but *bikvarnit shel melachim* — in the royal crypt, the catacombs of the kings of Egypt. According to this view, Moshe went to the royal crypt, made the same declaration — *Yosef, higi'a et she-nishba HaKadosh Baruch Hu she'ani go'el etchem* — and at that moment *nizdaze'ah arono shel Yosef*, Yosef's coffin shook free from its niche, and Moshe removed it.

### Two Arks Travel

*Vechol otan shanim she-hayu Yisrael bamidbar hayu shnei aronot halalu mehalchim zeh im zeh* — all those years that Israel traveled in the wilderness, these two arks traveled together: *echad shel met* — one containing a dead body, Yosef, *ve'echad shel Shechinah* — and the other the *aron* of God's presence containing the *Luchot HaBrit*. They were not side by side in the strict sense — the *Gemara* elsewhere derives from Yosef that a corpse may enter the *machaneh Leviyah* but not the *machaneh Shechinah* — but they traveled in close proximity.

### Passersby Question

*Vehayu ovrim u-shavim omrim: mah tivan shel shnei aronot halalu* — passersby would ask: what are these two *aronot*? They would be told: one contains a dead body and the other contains the divine presence. *Vechi mah darko shel met le-halech im Shechinah* — what right does a dead body have to travel alongside the divine presence? The image is genuinely startling — and, as one might observe, carries a visual resonance that would have seemed deeply disturbing from the outside. The *Gemara* does not shy away from this tension.

### Yosef Fulfilled

The answer given: *kiyem zeh kol mah she-katuv bazeh* — this one, Yosef, fulfilled everything written in that one, the *luchot*. The *Gemara* connects this to the practice, known from other contexts, of placing a *sefer Torah* in the *aron* of a great *talmid chacham* during his *levayah*, and saying *ki ein zeh mah she-katuv bazeh* — for this one fulfilled what is written in that one. Yosef is thus presented as the original paradigm of one whose life so completely embodied the Torah that his *aron* properly accompanies the *aron* of the *Shechinah*.

### Israel's Role

The *Gemara* then poses the same structural question it raised earlier regarding Yosef and Yaakov: *ve-illu asik beh Moshe, Yisrael lo havu ma'aski beh?* If Moshe had not taken the initiative, would Israel not have done it themselves? Indeed, the *pasuk* says *et atzmot Yosef asher he'elu Bnei Yisrael mi-Mitzrayim kavru be-Shechem* — and Bnei Yisrael buried the bones that *they* brought up. A further question: and if all of Israel would not have done it, would not Yosef's own children have seen to it? For another *pasuk* links the land of Shechem specifically to *bnei Yosef* as an inheritance.

The answer follows the same logic as before: *amru hanichu lo*. Bnei Yosef said, let Bnei Yisrael do it, *kevodo bi-mrubeh yotze mi-mi'ut* — the honor is greater when the multitude carries it out than when only a few do. And Bnei Yisrael in turn said, let Moshe do it, *kevodo bigdolim yoter mibiketanim* — it is greater honor when a great one does it than when lesser ones do.

### Completion Gets Credit

But then there is a direct contradiction in the *pesukim* — one verse says *vayikach Moshe et atzmot Yosef imo*, Moshe took the bones, and another says *asher he'elu Bnei Yisrael* — which Bnei Yisrael brought up. Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina resolves this with a general principle: *kol oseh davar velo gmaro, u-va acher u-gmaro, ma'aleh alav ha-katuv al she-gmaro ke-illu asao* — whoever begins something and does not complete it, and another comes and completes it, the credit goes entirely to the one who finishes. A *mitzvah* is called by the name of the one who completes it — *ein ha-mitzvah nikret ela al shem gomrah*. Since it was Bnei Yisrael who ultimately buried Yosef in Shechem, the *pasuk* attributes the entire act to them.

Rabbi Elazar adds a sobering corollary: *af moridin oto migdulato* — one who begins and fails to complete is not merely passed over but is brought down from his greatness. The *pasuk* records *vayehi ba'eit vayered Yehuda* — Yehuda went down — because he set in motion the effort to save Yosef but did not see it through. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani extends this even further: such a person may even bury his wife and children, as indeed Yehuda did — *vatamat bat Shua eishet Yehuda*, and *vayehi vayamat Er ve-Onan*. The *Gemara* presents this as *mussar* — pointed moral instruction — rather than strict legal analysis.

### Bones Self-Reference

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav asks: why did Yosef refer to himself with the word *atzmotai* — my bones — during his own lifetime, saying *ve-ha'alitem et atzmotai mizeh itchem*? The answer: *mipnei she-lo micha bikhvod aviv* — because he failed to protest on behalf of his father's honor. When his brothers stood before him without yet knowing who he was, they referred to Yaakov as *avdecha avinu* — your servant our father — and Yosef said nothing to correct the disrespectful formulation. Because he did not defend his father's dignity, his own honor was diminished, and he spoke of himself as *bones* — a term of lowered status — even in life.

### Early Death

Rav Yehuda citing Rav — and some say Rav Chama bar Rabbi Chanina — asks further: *mipnei mah meit Yosef kodem le'echav* — why did Yosef die before his brothers? *Mipnei she-inhig atzmo be-rabbanus* — because he conducted himself with an air of authority. The word *hinhig atzmo* implies that he gave himself superior airs, throwing his considerable weight around, asserting his status and position. This — rather than simply holding authority, which was unavoidable given his position as viceroy — is the fault attributed to him.

### Brought Down Egypt

The *Gemara* returns to the verse *Yosef hu hurad Mitzraima* — Yosef was brought down to Egypt. Rabbi Elazar applies *al tikri*: *al tikri hurad ela horid* — do not read "was brought down" but "brought down," for Yosef ultimately brought down *itztigninei Pharaoh migdulatan* — the astrologers of Pharaoh from their greatness. He alone could interpret the dreams that confounded them all, and in doing so he effectively displaced them.

### Potiphar & Castration

The verse *vayiknehu Potifar saris Pharaoh* raises a question: what is a *saris* — a eunuch — doing with a wife? Rav explains: *sheknaho le'atzmo* — he bought Yosef for his own personal use, meaning his intentions toward Yosef were sexual in nature, and he was not yet a *saris* at the time of purchase. Thereupon *ba Gavriel ve-sirso* — the angel Gavriel came and castrated him. The *Gemara* also notes a variant reading *ufara'o*, which Rashi explains as referring to the *peri'ah* — a more complete form of mutilation, analogous to the second stage of *milah* in which the thin membrane beneath the foreskin is pulled back. The linguistic evidence is the shift in the text: the name first appears as *Potifar* and subsequently as *Potifera*, the added syllable reflecting the act of *peri'ah* performed upon him.

---

## Moshe's Final Days

### Enough for You

The *Gemara* now turns to God's response to Moshe's repeated entreaties to be permitted to enter the land: *rav lach* — it is enough for you, or more precisely, *rav lach* — it is too much for you. Rav Levi observes a kind of measure-for-measure quality in the language: *be-rav bisar, be-rav bisru* — Moshe informed others with the word *rav* — *rav lachem bnei Levi* — and he himself was informed with the word *rav*: *rav lach*.

### Rav Lach

The *Gemara* offers multiple interpretations of *rav lach*. One: *rav yesh lach* — Moshe, there is already a *rav* here, a leader in the wings, and that is Yehoshua. Rashi adds that this also carries the implication that it is no longer Moshe's turn — Yehoshua's time has come. Another interpretation: *she-lo yomru ha-rav kama kasheh ve-hatalmid kama sarvan* — if Moshe continues petitioning, people will say: how intransigent is the master, and how pressuring is the student. Neither God's reputation nor Moshe's is served by the continued back-and-forth.

### High Standards

Why was God so exacting with Moshe to begin with? *Tana devei Rabbi Yishmael: lefum gamla shichna* — based on the camel is the load. The load placed on a camel corresponds to its capacity to bear it. Because Moshe was on such an elevated level, he was held to account for things that would not be reckoned against a lesser person. The great are measured by a higher standard.

### 120 Years Old

Moshe declared to Israel: *ben me'ah ve'esrim shana anochi hayom* — I am 120 years old today. The *Gemara* asks: why does it say *hayom* — today — unnecessarily? *Hayom malu yamai u-shnotai* — to tell you that today, this very day, my years are complete. This is also the proof that *tzaddikim* die on the anniversary of their birth: *God* fulfills *mispar yamecha amalei* — the number of your days I will fill — precisely, from day to day and from month to month.

### Gates of Wisdom

Moshe then says *lo uchal od latzet velavo* — I can no longer go out and come in. One might assume this refers to physical movement, but the *Gemara* objects: *u-Moshe ben me'ah ve'esrim shana bemoto lo chahat eino velo nas lecho* — at his death his eyes had not dimmed and his strength had not left him. Indeed, a *Braitah* teaches that when God told Moshe to ascend Har Nevo, *shtem esrei ma'alot hayu sham, u-psa'an Moshe be-psi'ah achat* — there were twelve elevations from the plains of Moav to the mountain, and Moshe traversed them all in a single leap. He clearly retained his full physical vigor.

### Leap to Nebo

Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan therefore explains: *latzet velavo be-divrei Torah* — I can no longer go out and come in through words of Torah. *Melamed she-nistatmu mimenu sha'arei chochmah* — the gates of wisdom had been closed to him. He had lost his capacity for the kind of vigorous intellectual engagement with Torah — the going in and out, the argumentation and analysis — that had defined his entire life. There is something at once poignant and, perhaps, merciful in this: Moshe may have found it more possible to accept his death once he recognized that the faculty most precious to him was already departing.

---

## God Buries Moshe

### Shared Sabbath

The *Gemara* notes the verse *vayeilech Moshe ve-Yehoshua ve-yityatzevu be-Ohel Moed* — Moshe and Yehoshua went and stood in the *Ohel Moed*. A *Tanna* teaches: *otah Shabbat shel dyo-zugi hayta* — that *Shabbat*, that particular period, was one of shared pair-leadership. *Nitlah me-zeh ve-nitnah le-zeh* — authority was being taken from Moshe and transferred to Yehoshua. The use of the word *Shabbat* here deliberately echoes the rabbinic institution of *Shabbat shel mi hayta* — whose week was it? — referring to the practice of rotating authority between two leaders, a phenomenon the rabbis were familiar with in their own institutional life. The *Gemara* uses that resonance to say that here, uniquely, the two were briefly able to share the moment of transition.

### Death & Burial Sites

*Amar Rabbi Yehuda: ilmalei mikra katuv iy efshar le-omro* — if it had not been written in the verse, one could not say such a thing. The verse *vaya'al Moshe me-arvot Moav el Har Nevo* places Moshe's death at Mount Nevo, which lies in the portion of Reuven, as Bnei Reuven are recorded as having built *et Nevo*. Yet Moshe was buried in Gad's portion, as the verse *vayar reshit lo ki sham chelkat mechokek safun* — "for there is the hidden portion of the lawgiver" — is understood to refer to Moshe's burial place in Gad's territory. Between the site of his death in Reuven and his burial in Gad, the distance was four *mil* — approximately four kilometers. A considerable distance to traverse, and the question is: who transported him?

### Divine Transport

*Melamed she-hayah Moshe mutal be-chanfei Shechinah* — Moshe lay cradled in the wings of the divine presence, which carried him the four *mil* to his burial place. This image closes the circle opened by our *Mishnah*: Moshe carried Yosef's *aron*, and God carried Moshe's body. The parallel is exact and intentional.

### Angels' Eulogy

The heavenly angels accompanied Moshe and declared: *tzidkat Hashem asah u-mishpatav im Yisrael* — he performed the righteousness of God and God's laws with Israel. This verse from the end of *Devarim* serves as the angelic eulogy at Moshe's burial.

### God's Lament

God's own expression of mourning: *mi yakum li im mere'im, mi yityatzeiv li im po'alei aven* — who will rise with me against the wicked? Who will stand firm with me against those who do iniquity? The death of Moshe is experienced, as it were, as a loss of an irreplaceable ally in the ongoing work of justice in the world.

### Sages' Responses

The *Gemara* then records several Amoraic responses, each apparently citing a verse that captures what was lost. Shmuel cites *mi ke-he-chacham u-mi yodea pesher davar* — who is the wise one who knows the explanation of things? Rabbi Yochanan cites *ve-hachokhmah me-ayin timatzei* — and from where now shall wisdom be found? Rav Nachman simply states *vayamot sham Moshe* — and there Moshe died. A further voice, *Samayon*, declares: *vayamot sham Moshe safra rabba de-Yisrael* — the great scribe of Israel has died.

Whether these Amoraim are understood as voicing what the angels said, what God said, or as themselves participating virtually in the *levayah* of Moshe — the *vav* connecting them (*ve-Shmuel amar*, *ve-Rav Nachman amar*) gives the passage something of the quality of a gathering of mourners, each adding their eulogy in turn, until the last voice simply names the fact: the great scribe of Israel is gone.

---

---

# Sotah 14

## Moshe's Death & Burial

### Perek Transition

Daf 14 brings us to the close of the first *perek* and the opening of the second, situated within a sustained aggadic passage surrounding the death of Moshe. The thematic thread has been the chain of burial: Yosef buried his father Yaakov, Moshe buried Yosef, and God Himself buried Moshe. The preceding material contained a vivid description of Moshe's *levayah*, carried on divine wings and accompanied by the angels. We now pick up at the bottom of 13b.

### Lo Meis Moshe

Four lines from the bottom of 13b, the Gemara introduces a striking teaching: *V'yesh omrim lo meis Moshe* — and some say Moshe did not die. The famous parallel is of course *Yaakov Avinu lo meis*, but the case of Moshe is harder. By Yaakov, the verse omits any explicit statement of death — it says *vayei'asef el amav* but never says *vayamas*. By Moshe, however, the Torah states explicitly *vayamas sham*. How, then, can the Gemara maintain that he did not die?

The Gemara's resolution is a *gezeirah shavah*: *kesiv hacha vayamas sham* — it says he died there — *ukesiv hasam vayehi sham im Hashem* — and it says there he was with God. Just as when Moshe was *sham* with God at Sinai he was in attendance before God, so too here he is in attendance before God. The implicit reasoning is worth dwelling on: Moshe spent forty days and forty nights at Sinai without eating or drinking, existing in some manner beyond normal physicality. Perhaps during that time something fundamental shifted in the nature of his body, and perhaps what occurred at his death was similarly an apparent departure — his body lies there, but his spirit remains in attendance before God, connected as it was during those forty days. It is not that all souls are with God after death, but rather that Moshe had not completely departed; his connection to God mirrors what occurred at Sinai. In this reading, the death is real in some external sense but not in the ultimate spiritual sense.

This teaching arises naturally in the wake of Moshe's *levayah* and *hesped*. There is a profound difficulty in accepting the finality of Moshe's death — he is the lawgiver, the supreme *navi*, the figure through whom all Torah flows. The Torah's own language wraps his end in mystery: *velo yada ish et kevurato*. Once the Torah signals that mystery, once God is the sole witness to the burial, it becomes possible — even understandable — that a tradition would develop holding that he never truly died at all.

### Hidden Grave

The Torah provides three identifying markers for Moshe's burial place: in the valley, in the land of Moav, opposite Beis Peor. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Brachya observed that there is a *siman b'soch siman* — an identifier nested within an identifier. And yet, *va'afilu hachi velo yada ish et kevuraso*: even with all these markers, no one has ever been able to find it. The text proceeds to explain why this is not accidental.

The evil kingdom — Rome — sent to the leader of Beis Peor demanding: *hareinu heichan Moshe kavor* — show us where Moshe is buried. When the searchers stood at a high elevation, the site appeared to be below them. When they descended, it appeared to be above. They divided into two groups to cover both possibilities, but those above still saw it below, and those below still saw it above. A miracle prevented discovery regardless of approach.

The meaning of this is clear. If Moshe's burial place were known, it would become a site of pilgrimage and veneration, and Moshe would be at risk of being deified. The entire point of the transition into the Land of Canaan was to happen without Moshe — indeed, the Torah closes with the words *lo kam navi od beYisrael*, and specifically because he was the greatest, the people had to be capable of living their lives without him. Thus: *lekayem ma shene'emar velo yada ish et kevuraso*.

### Rabbi Chama

Rabbi Chama b'Rabbi Chanina adds a further dimension: even Moshe himself did not know where he was buried. The textual basis is a *gezeirah shavah* on the word *ish*: *velo yada ish et kevuraso* — no *ish* knew his burial — and *vezot haberachah asher berach Moshe ish ha'Elokim* — Moshe is called *ish*. Thus the verse itself tells us that even Moshe the *ish* did not know.

Rabbi Chama b'Rabbi Chanina then asks why Moshe was buried specifically near Beis Peor. The answer: *kedai lechaper al ma'aseh Peor* — to atone for the sin of Peor, the sin of Bnos Moav, which occurred in that very location.

---

## Imitatio Dei

### Walking After God

The same Rabbi Chama b'Rabbi Chanina continues with a teaching that, while not directly linked to what precedes it, is introduced at this point because it is his. He asks: what does it mean when the Torah says *acharei Hashem Elokeichem telechu* — you shall walk after Hashem your God? Is it literally possible for a person to walk after the *Shechinah*? The Torah itself declares *ki Hashem Elokecha esh ochlah hu* — God is a consuming fire. How can one aspire to closeness with or imitation of such a God?

### Six Acts Enumerated

The resolution: *leilech achar midotav* — to follow after God's *attributes*, the concrete ways in which God acts in the world. The Gemara enumerates these:

God clothed the naked, as it is written that He made for Adam and his wife garments of leather and dressed them — so too you should clothe the naked. God visited the sick, as it is written that God appeared to Avraham at the plains of Mamre after his *brit milah* — so too you should visit the sick. God consoled mourners, as it is written that after Avraham's death God blessed Yitzchak his son — and that blessing is understood as a visit of consolation — so too you should console mourners. God buried the dead, as it is written *vayikbor oto bagai* — and this ties directly back to the preceding material — so too you should bury the dead.

### Character vs. Actions

This *drasha* is worth holding up against another classical formulation of the same obligation: *mah hu rachum af ata rachum, mah hu chanun af ata chanun* — as God is merciful so you should be merciful, as God is gracious so you should be gracious. The two formulations represent fundamentally different approaches to ethics. One focuses on character traits — *rachum*, *chanun* — asking the person to cultivate an inner disposition that mirrors God's. The other, as in the Gemara before us, focuses entirely on concrete actions: it does not matter whether you are naturally inclined toward compassion; what matters is what you actually do in the world.

This maps onto a broader debate in ethical thought. One tradition, exemplified by the Rambam in his *Peirush Hamishnayos* on *Pirkei Avot*, holds that the perfection of character is the ultimate goal, and that actions serve primarily as a means to that end. This is the consistent thread of the *Shemonah Perakim*: every ethical deed is described as a means toward perfecting one's character rather than as an end good in itself. A famous illustration is the Rambam's reading of the dictum *hakol lefi rov hama'aseh velo lefi godel hama'aseh* — it is all according to the quantity of the deed, not the size. Rambam explains that it is better to give one dollar of *tzedakah* a hundred times than a hundred dollars at once, because the repeated act cultivates the character of generosity more effectively. The goal is the internal transformation.

By contrast, the formulation in our Gemara emphasizes what you actually do. In a Kantian register, one might even argue that doing a good deed against one's inclination, out of sheer sense of obligation, reflects a purer ethical commitment — what matters is the good accomplished, not the personality of the one accomplishing it. The two approaches are genuinely in tension: is *imitatio Dei* a program for self-cultivation, or a program for making the world better through concrete action?

One might note an additional dimension here: the concretization itself is significant. The general commandment of *ve'ahavta lere'acha kamocha* encompasses all of these obligations in principle, but left at that level of abstraction, no one would reliably fulfill them. Because *Chazal* speak with great concreteness about *nichum aveilim*, *bikkur cholim*, *hachnasat orchim*, and *halvayat hames*, these obligations become identifiable, actionable, and deeply embedded in communal practice. There is a real power in the concrete over the abstract, and in that sense the emphasis on actions rather than character traits also has a practical pedagogical valence.

The connection to the surrounding material is suggestive as well. The passage follows the account of Moshe's burial — an event at which the impulse to worship and deify Moshe had to be actively prevented. The response is not to explain Moshe philosophically but to say: figure out how to act like him. You cannot be God, you cannot be Moshe, but you can do what God and Moshe did.

### Torah Bookended

Rabbi Simlai continues the theme. His *drasha*: *Torah techilasah gemilus chasadim vesofah gemilus chasadim* — the Torah begins with acts of loving-kindness and ends with acts of loving-kindness. At the beginning: *vaya'as Hashem Elokim le'adam ule'ishto katnos or vayalbishem* — God clothed Adam and his wife. At the end: *vayikbor oto bagai* — God buried Moshe. Rabbi Simlai is not listing these as two examples among many; he is pointing to the structural architecture of the Torah itself. Whatever else the Torah contains — all its commandments, all its narratives — it opens and closes with *gemilus chasadim*. This should tell us something essential about what the Torah is fundamentally about.

---

## Moshe & Eretz Yisrael

### Mitzvot in Land

Rabbi Simlai continues, now turning to a different question: *mipnei mah nisaveh Moshe Rabbeinu lehikanes le'Eretz Yisrael* — why did Moshe so desperately desire to enter the Land of Israel? Was it to eat its fruit? To enjoy its goodness? The Gemara answers in Moshe's own words: *harbeh mitzvos nitzvu ve'ein mitkaymim ella be'Eretz Yisrael* — many *mitzvot* were commanded and can only be fulfilled in the Land of Israel. *Ekanes ani la'aretz kedei sheyitkaymu kulan alai* — let me enter so that all of them may be fulfilled through me.

### God's Response

God's response is striking: *kelum atah mevakesh ella lekabel sachar?* — is it nothing but reward that you seek? And then, immediately: *ma'aleh ani alecha ke'ilu asitam* — I will credit you as if you had done them. The Gemara then expounds a passage from Isaiah 53 to support this.

### Isaiah 53 Exegesis

The verse *lachen achalek lo varabbim ve'et atzumim yachalek shalal* — therefore I will divide his portion among the many and with the mighty he will divide the spoil — is parsed in detail. *Lachen achalek lo varabbim*: one might think this means Moshe's reward will be like that of later great figures, but not like the earliest great ones. *Talmud lomar ve'et atzumim yachalek shalal*: no, with the mighty — meaning Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov, who were mighty in Torah and *mitzvot*.

*Tachat asher he'erah lamavet nafsho*: because he exposed himself to death — *she'masar atzmo lemitah* — referencing his declaration *ve'im ayin mecheni na misifrecha*, his readiness to be destroyed along with Israel rather than see them destroyed.

*Ve'et poshim nimnah*: he was counted among sinners — *she'nimnah im metei midbar* — he was reckoned among those who died in the wilderness, like a captain who does not abandon his ship.

*Vehu chet rabbim nasa*: he carried the sin of the many — *she'kiper al ma'aseh ha'egel* — he atoned for the sin of the golden calf.

*Velafoshim yapgia*: for sinners he would entreat — *she'bikesh rachamim al poshei Yisrael she'yachzeru biteshuvah*, he prayed for God's mercy that sinners should repent. The word *pegiah* means entreaty, as in the verse *ve'al tifga bi* — do not entreat me — directed at Moshe when God wished him to stop praying.

### Reward & Mitzvot

The exchange raises an immediate question. The Mishnah in *Pirkei Avot* states *al tihyu ka'avadim hameshameshim et harav al menat lekabel peras* — do not be like servants who serve the master in order to receive a reward. How, then, does God's response — *kelum atah mevakesh ella lekabel sachar?* — make sense as a critique of Moshe? Who said Moshe was only in it for the *sachar*?

A famous story about the Vilna Gaon is relevant here. The Gaon once saw someone on *Sukkot* with an exceptionally beautiful *etrog* and asked to use it. The owner agreed on the condition that he receive all of the Gaon's *sachar* for the *mitzvah*. The Gaon agreed, took the *etrog*, and performed the *mitzvah* — and his students had never seen him so joyful. When they asked why, he said: every other time he could not be certain that some part of his motivation was the *sachar*; this time he knew with certainty he was doing it purely *leshem hamitzvah*, because there was no *sachar* to be had.

The deeper question is what this passage suggests about the value of *Eretz Yisrael*. The Gemara reduces Moshe's desire to enter the Land entirely to the issue of fulfilling *mitzvot hateluyot ba'aretz* — the commandments dependent on the land. But one might have expected something grander: the actualization of Israel as a national entity under God, defined by Torah, building a civilization with a *beit hamikdash*, realizing the whole vision of what it means to be the people of God in their land. Is the entire point really just to accumulate more *mitzvot*?

This connects to Rabbi Simlai's teaching at the end of Masechet Makkos — the same Rabbi Simlai who authored the teaching here. There it says *darash Rav Simlai: sheish me'os ushlosh esrei mitzvos ne'emru lo leMoshe mi'Sinai*, and the preceding *mishnah* states *ratza HaKadosh Baruch Hu lezakot et Yisrael lefichach hirbah lahem Torah umitzvot*. The abundance of *mitzvot* is itself the mechanism of *zekhut*; the more you do, the greater the *sachar*. This framework — the quantity of *mitzvot* as a measure of spiritual standing — pervades both contexts, and it is possible that Rabbi Simlai is deploying it consistently as part of a larger theological program emphasizing the *ribbu'i mitzvot* as the core of Jewish identity and divine favor.

Some scholars have suggested that the statement *hirbah lahem Torah umitzvot lezakot et Yisrael* is a polemical response to Christian theology, which characterized the law as reflecting bondage rather than liberation — *the covenant from Mount Sinai bears children who are slaves*. The counter-claim is precisely that the abundance of *mitzvot* is not bondage but the vehicle of merit and spiritual elevation.

One might also read God's response to Moshe — that he will receive credit as though he had performed the *mitzvot* without having entered the land — as a post-*churban* consolation of sorts. Jewish identity and the *kiyum mitzvot* do not depend on actually being in *Eretz Yisrael*. Moshe himself, who could not enter, receives the full credit. This reading understands the passage as addressing the exilic condition: one need not be in the Land to realize one's full spiritual potential through *mitzvot*.

---

## Sotah's Minchah

### Egyptian Basket

We now turn to the second *perek*. The *mishnah* states: *haya mevi et minchatah besoch kefifah mitzrit* — the husband would bring her *minchah* inside an Egyptian basket. Note that it is the husband who is the actor here; looking at the *pesukim*, it is the husband who brings the woman to the *beit hamikdash* and brings her *minchah*. *Venosan al yadeha* — and he places it on her hands — *kedei leyaga'ah* — in order to weary her.

The *mishnah* then notes the contrast with all other *menachot*: *kol menachot techilatan vesofan bichli sharet* — all *menachot* begin and end with a *kli sharet*, a sanctified vessel. But this *minchah* begins not in a *kli sharet* but in this lowly, mundane vessel — *vezo techilasah bekefifah mitzrit* — and only at the end, *vesofah bichli sharet*, when it must actually be offered, is it placed in a *kli sharet*.

Similarly, all *menachot* require oil and frankincense, while this *minchah* requires neither. (The Gemara will note that the *minchat chotei*, the sinner's meal-offering, also lacks oil and frankincense, and will address this.) All *menachot* come from wheat; this one comes from barley. There is one other *minchah* that uses barley — the *minchat ha'omer* — but even that barley is ground into *geresh*, a very fine and refined barley flour comparable in quality to the *soles* of wheat offerings. The *sotah's* offering, by contrast, comes as a coarse bran — *kemach* — not refined at all.

Rabban Gamliel supplies the interpretive key: *kesheim shema'aseha ma'aseh behemah kach korbanah ma'achal behemah* — just as her actions were the actions of an animal, so her sacrifice is the food of an animal. This is a striking formulation. The *mishnah* throughout has been conveying degradation through ritual means — the lowly vessel, the coarse grain, the absence of oil and frankincense — but it is Rabban Gamliel who connects the dots explicitly: the deliberate lowliness of her offering mirrors a moral judgment about her conduct.

This also reinforces the posture of presumed guilt that pervades the *sotah* procedure. The repeated emphasis on *kedei leyaga'ah* — wearying her — operates on the assumption that she sinned and should be induced to confess. And the *middah keneged middah* logic that ran through the earlier material in the *masechet* continues here: each degrading element of the procedure corresponds to her presumed transgression.

### Tosafot Reordering

Tosafot raises a pointed question on the *mishnah's* organization. *Ein seder hamishnah keseder haparshah mechuvonim* — the order in the *mishnah* is not aligned with the order of the *parshah* in the Torah. Tosafot then reconstructs the Torah's sequence:

First comes *kinuy* and *setirah*. Then the husband brings her and brings her *minchah*. Then the *kohen* prepares the water — the earthenware vessel, the half-*log* of water from the *kiyor*, the dust from the floor. Then the woman is brought to the Sha'ar Nikanor and her garments are disheveled. Then the *minchah* is placed on her hands while the *kohen* holds the bitter waters. Then the oath is administered. Then the *megillah* is written, the name erased into the water, and she drinks. Then the *minchah* is transferred from the Egyptian basket to a *kli sharet*, the *kometz* is taken, and it is offered on the *mizbe'ach*.

But in our *mishnah*, the disheveling of the woman's garments and the rending of her clothing — discussed in the previous *perek* — came before the *minchah* is introduced. So the *mishnah* has reordered the material. Tosafot raises this without fully resolving it: either there is some literary or pedagogical reason for the *tanna*'s reorganization, or we should assume that the *halakhic* sequence in practice follows the Torah's order, and the *mishnah* has organized things differently for its own expository purposes. What seems untenable is that the *tanna* would silently invert the Torah's sequence and expect us to understand that the Torah's own order should be disregarded — without explicitly signaling that, as the Gemara does in other contexts, such as the *Kohen Gadol's avodah*.

### Wearying Purpose

A *baraita* is cited: *tanya Abba Chanin omer mishum Rabbi Eliezer* — why does the procedure use the Egyptian basket and place the *minchah* on her hands? *Kedei leyaga'ah* — to weary her — *kedei she'tachzor bah* — so that she should repent and confess her sin. And from this Abba Chanin draws a *kal va'chomer*: if God shows such concern for those who transgress His will — wanting her to confess and be spared rather than suffer the punishment of the *mei hamarim* — how much more so does God care for those who do His will.

### Water & Minchah Order

The Gemara immediately challenges this interpretation. *Umimai mishum de'chasah hu?* — how do you know the reason for wearying her is concern for her welfare? *Dilma ki heichi de'lo timachak megillah?* — perhaps the intent is to prevent the unnecessary erasure of God's name? This is a very different concern. Other *mishnayot* make clear that there is a strong prohibition against erasing God's name unnecessarily; perhaps the entire effort to induce confession is motivated by that concern, not by concern for the woman herself.

The Gemara resolves this: the *tanna* who attributes the motivation to concern for the woman must hold the position that *mashke ve'achar kach makriv et minchatah* — she drinks the water first, and only afterward is the *minchah* offered. If that is so, then by the time we are still urging her to confess and spare herself, God's name has already been erased — the *megillah* has already been scraped into the water she has drunk. There is no longer any protective purpose regarding God's name. The only remaining reason to continue urging her to confess would be concern for her life and well-being.

Rashi explains the mechanics: she drinks, and then the *minchah* is brought — and critically, the physical effects of the water are suspended until the *minchah* is offered. The *minchah*, in this view, is the final trigger. She has drunk the water, but nothing will happen until the *kometz* is placed on the fire. So even after drinking, she can confess, the *minchah* will not be offered, and she will be spared.

This sounds counterintuitive — we naturally imagine the drinking as the climactic act — but as Tosafot's careful reconstruction of the *pesukim* confirms, this is precisely what the Torah's own sequence suggests: *ve'hishkah... venatan al yadeha* — she drinks, and then the *minchah* is waved and offered. The Gemara is drawing out an opinion that takes that sequence seriously, however strange it appears to us.

---

## Menachot Comparison

### Standard Procedure

The *mishnah* stated that all other *menachot* begin in a *kli sharet* while the *sotah's* begins in an Egyptian basket. The Gemara challenges this from a *mishnah* in Menachot describing the standard procedure for bringing a *minchah*: a person brings it from home *bekaltot shel kesef veshel zahav* — in vessels of gold and silver — and only upon arriving at the Temple does he transfer it into a *kli sharet*. This suggests that even ordinary *menachot* do not begin in a *kli sharet* but rather in mundane home vessels. So what is distinctive about the *sotah's* basket?

### Kli Sharet Debate

Rav Papa resolves the apparent contradiction: the *mishnah's* claim should be read as saying that all other *menachot* begin in vessels that are *fit* to serve as a *kli sharet* — meaning gold and silver vessels — even if they are not formally sanctified as such. The *kefifah mitzrit*, the Egyptian wicker basket, is not merely unsanctified but is categorically unfit to serve as a *kli sharet*.

This implies that a wicker vessel is disqualified from being a *kli sharet* altogether. The Gemara asks: like whom is this position? It aligns with Rebbi (Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi) against Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda, as a *baraita* teaches: if *klei sharet* were made of wood, Rebbi disqualifies them while Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda validates them. Since wicker is treated as a form of wood, the *mishnah's* assumption that the *kefifah mitzrit* is disqualified from *kli sharet* status follows Rebbi's position.

The Gemara then attempts to reconcile the *mishnah* even with the position of Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda: even he would only validate wooden *klei sharet* that are *chashuvim* — finely crafted and respectable. He would not validate lowly, crude wicker vessels. And why not? Because of the principle *hakrivehu na le'pechatecha* — would you offer this to a governor? — meaning that what is not suitable to bring before a human authority is certainly unfit as a vessel for divine service. This principle is not merely an ethical consideration; it has operative *halakhic* force, actually disqualifying an otherwise potentially valid vessel.

### Respect Principle

The principle *hakrivehu na le'pechatecha* operates as a genuine standard. What is fit to be presented to a person of authority is fit for the *mizbe'ach*; what would be embarrassing to offer a governor is certainly unfit for God's altar. This raises a question of application: who determines whether a given vessel meets this standard? If a gold vessel were mangled or degraded, would it be disqualified despite being made of precious metal? The principle seems to address both the material and the manner of craftsmanship together.

There is also a notable tension here with the principle of *ein aniyut bemakom ashirut* — there is no poverty in a place of wealth — which governs the *beit hamikdash* and precludes the use of cheap or inadequate materials in divine service. The *sotah's* basket is thus doubly notable: not only is it not a *kli sharet*, it is the kind of vessel that would be disqualified from ever becoming one.

### Sanctification Acts

The *mishnah* describing the standard *minchah* procedure states that once placed in a *kli sharet*, you sanctify it — *umekadsho bichli sharet*. The Gemara notes that this language implies an act of sanctification distinct from the mere placing into the vessel. Does the *kli sharet* automatically sanctify whatever is placed in it, or must there be a specific intention to sanctify?

The Gemara suggests that the language *notna bichli sharet lekadsho bichli sharet* — placing it in the *kli sharet* in order to sanctify it — could reflect intention, but equally could simply mean that the result of placing is sanctification. The question remains open as to whether intentional sanctification is a prerequisite. It is noted that the owner's earlier verbal declaration — *harei zu minchas* — constitutes *kedushat peh*, verbal sanctity, which does not yet confer the full *kedushat ha-guf*, intrinsic sanctity, that determines whether the object can be redeemed, whether removal from the Temple precincts is consequential, and so forth. That full *kedushat ha-guf* comes only through placement in the *kli sharet*.

---

## Altar Placement

### Two Verses

The standard *minchah* procedure includes the act of *hagashah*: *magishah bekeren dromit ma'aravit keneged chudah shel keren vedayo* — you touch it at the southwest corner of the altar, at the very tip of the corner, and that suffices.

To understand why the southwest corner, the Gemara draws on two verses. One verse says *lifnei Hashem* — before God — which directs us toward the west side of the *mizbe'ach*, the side facing the *Heichal*. The other verse says *el pnei hamizbeach* — at the face of the altar — which directs us toward the south, where the ramp ascends and the altar faces when you approach it. Neither verse alone is sufficient:

A *baraita* articulates the tension precisely: *lifnei Hashem yachol bema'arav* — perhaps in the west? *Talmud lomar el pnei hamizbeach* — the face of the altar, meaning the south. *I el pnei hamizbeach yachol badarom* — perhaps in the south? *Talmud lomar lifnei Hashem* — before God, meaning the west. *Ha keitzad?* — how then? *Magishah bekeren dromit ma'aravit* — you place it at the southwest corner, satisfying both directions simultaneously.

To visualize this: the *Heichal* stood on the west end of the *Azarah*, opening eastward. The *mizbe'ach* stood in the courtyard east of the *Heichal*. The *ramp* of the *mizbe'ach* ascended from the south, making the south face the *pnei hamizbeach*. The *Heichal* was to the west, making the west side of the *mizbe'ach* the side facing *lifnei Hashem*. The southwest corner is the precise geometric point that satisfies both demands simultaneously.

### Hermeneutic Rule

Rabbi Eliezer offers a different approach, though one that reaches the same conclusion through a broader hermeneutic principle. Rather than looking for a compromise position that satisfies both verses simultaneously, he articulates a general rule: *kol makom she'atah motzeh shenei mikra'ot* — wherever you find two verses — *echad mekayem atzmo umekayem divrei chaveiro ve'echad mekayem atzmo umevatel divrei chaveiro* — one of which can satisfy itself and also satisfy the other, while the other can only satisfy itself at the expense of the first — *menichim et zeh shemekayem atzmo umevatel et chaveiro vetofsim et shemekayem atzmo umekayem chaveiro* — you set aside the exclusive one and follow the inclusive one.

In this case: if you follow *lifnei Hashem* in the west literally, you are on the west side of the *mizbe'ach* and have no element at all of *pnei hamizbeach* in the south — the two are mutually exclusive. But if you follow *el pnei hamizbeach* — the south face — and specifically at the southern end, the question is whether that position can still be described as *lifnei Hashem*, before God. According to Rabbi Eliezer's view, it can, because even from the south face of the *mizbe'ach* one stands facing the *Heichal*. Thus the south position satisfies itself and also preserves something of *lifnei Hashem*, while the west position satisfies only itself and sacrifices the south entirely.

### Vedayo & Parallels

The word *vedayo* — and that is sufficient — requires explanation. One might think that beyond touching the vessel at the corner, the *minchah* itself must physically touch the *mizbe'ach*. *Vedayo* tells us: no, touching the vessel is sufficient; the *minchah* within the vessel need not itself contact the altar.

Rav Ashi draws a parallel: just as when the *kohen* sanctifies the blood of a *korban*, the sanctification comes through the vessel that catches the blood — the *kli sharet* of the *shechitah* being the knife itself — and not through the blood physically touching the altar, so too by the *minchah*, contact of the vessel with the altar suffices.

### Altar Position

Rav Ashi offers yet another resolution to the two verses, independent of the southwest-corner solution. He argues that the *tanna* who generated this *drasha* held that *kulo mizbe'ach batzafon kai* — the entire altar was situated in the northern portion of the *Azarah*. If the *mizbe'ach* was shifted entirely northward, then its southern face would align precisely with the midpoint of the *Azarah*, directly opposite the opening of the *Heichal*. In that configuration, standing at the south face of the *mizbe'ach* places you squarely *lifnei Hashem* — directly before the *Heichal* — while also satisfying *el pnei hamizbeach* by being at the face of the altar. Both verses are satisfied without recourse to the corner at all.

---

## Kometz Preparation

### Frankincense Removal

The *mishnah* on the standard *minchah* procedure states *umesalek et halevonah letzad echad* — the *kohen* moves the frankincense to one side before taking the *kometz*. The reason is straightforward: the *kometz* must consist solely of the flour mixed with oil. *Ki heichi dela tikmotz behadi mincha* — so that when he scoops the handful, he does not inadvertently include any frankincense. As the Gemara elsewhere teaches, if when the *kohen* took the *kometz* he found in his hand a pebble, a grain of salt, or a single granule of *levonah*, the *kometz* is *pasul* — because his handful must be entirely of the *minchah* itself, nothing else.

Similarly, *vekometz mimakom shenitrabah shamanah* — the *kometz* is taken from the portion of the *minchah* where the oil is most thoroughly mixed in. The Scriptural basis is *misaltah umishmanah* — from its flour and from its oil — which the Gemara reads as mandating that the *kometz* come from a portion rich in oil.

### Double Sanctification

Once the *kohen* has taken the *kometz*, *venotno letoch kli sharet umekadsho bichli sharet* — he places the *kometz* into a *kli sharet* and sanctifies it therein. The Gemara asks: the *minchah* was already sanctified in the *kli sharet* when it was first transferred from the home vessels — why does the *kometz* require yet another act of sanctification in a second *kli sharet*?

The Gemara answers by drawing a parallel to the blood of a *korban*: *dam af al gav dekadisheih sakin betzavar behemah* — the blood is already sanctified by the knife, which is a *kli sharet* and which sanctifies the blood at the moment of *shechitah* — *hadar mikadshei leih bichli sharet* — and yet the blood is caught again in a *kli sharet*, which constitutes a second act of sanctification. The first sanctification establishes the sacred status of the blood; the second elevates it to the level required for application to the *mizbe'ach*. So too by the *minchah*: the first placement in the *kli sharet* sanctifies the *minchah* as a whole; placing the *kometz* in a second *kli sharet* brings it to the level of sanctity required for offering on the altar. *Hacha nami lo shana* — here too, it is no different.

---

---

# Sotah 15

## Mincha Process

### Frankincense Transfer

The daf begins at the bottom of 14b, where the Gemara resumes its account of the process of bringing the *mincha* of the *sotah*. Before returning specifically to that ritual, the Gemara completes its citation of a *braita* that describes the standard procedure for bringing any *mincha* — useful background for the discussion that follows.

The *braita* states: *umalket et levonata venotnah al gabav* — the *kohen* gathers the *levona* (frankincense) from the original vessel in which the *mincha* was presented and transfers it to the separate *kli sharet* (sacred vessel) into which the *kometz* (handful) has already been placed. The verse cited is *ve-et kol ha-levona asher al ha-mincha* — "and all the frankincense that is upon the *mincha*" — which he then offers upon the *mizbeach*.

### Handful Offering

The top of 15a states: *umaale umaktir bichli sharet* — he brings it up and offers it in the *kli sharet*. This formulation raises a question: is he actually burning up the *kli sharet* itself? Rashi notes a different *girsa* of the text: *maktirah* cannot be read as "he has already burnt it," since the next line states that he first salts it. Rather, the reading should be *maale bichli sharet lehaktirou* — he brings it up in the *kli sharet* for the purpose of offering it, which both clarifies that the *kli sharet* is not itself being consumed and that the burning has not yet taken place. First, he salts it — *umolcha* — in fulfillment of the verse *vechol korban minchatcha bamelach timlach*, that all *korbanot* must be salted. Only then does he place it on the fire: *venotnah al gabei ha-ishim*. Afterward, *karev ha-kometz sheyarayim ne'echalin* — once the handful has been offered, the remainder (*sheyarayim*) becomes permissible to be eaten.

### Handful Timing

A *tannaitic* debate addresses the precise moment at which the *kometz* is considered to have been offered, thereby permitting the remainder. Rabbi Chanina holds that it is once the fire has taken hold: *mishe-tishlot bo ha-ur*. Rabbi Yochanan holds a stricter standard: *mishe-tatzit ha-ur berubo* — once the fire has caught the majority of it. This is a more advanced stage, requiring that the fire has not merely ignited the *kometz* but has actually taken hold of most of it.

### Mixing Ingredients

The *braita* continues: the *kohanim* may then mix into the remainder wine, oil, and honey — anything they wish — provided they do not allow it to become *hametz*. The reason: the verse says *lemoshcha* — the remainder is to be treated in a manner befitting dignity, *kederech shehamelachim ochlim*, in the way that kings eat. One might have thought that mixing in additional foodstuffs diminishes the sanctity of the *korban*; the *braita* teaches that on the contrary, eating in a dignified, refined manner is not only permitted but appropriate. The sole limitation is that one may not allow the remainder to become leavened.

### Leavening Prohibition

The source for this prohibition is the verse *lo teafeh hametz chelkam* — do not make even their portion into *hametz*. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish derives from the word *chelkam* that even the priests' portion — the remainder left after the *kometz* is offered — may not be allowed to become *hametz*. One might wonder how leavening is even possible once a *mincha* has already been cooked or placed on fire, a question that belongs more properly to Masechet Menachot, where an entire chapter is devoted to the *issur* of *hametz* in the context of *menachot*. Different *menachot* involve different modes of preparation — some are placed directly on coals, some are made on a flat pan (*machavat*) or deep pan (*meracheshet*), and there is even a *minchat ma'afeh tanur* baked in an oven — which is part of why Masechet Menachot is so extensive.

---

## Menachot Comparison

### Sinner's Mincha

Having completed the background *braita*, the Gemara now returns to the *minchat sotah* and opens with the statement from the Mishnah that all *menachot* require oil and frankincense, with the exception of the *mincha* of the *sotah*. The Gemara immediately challenges this: *vehaika minchat chotei* — what about the *minchat chotei*, the meal offering of a sinner? At the end of Parashat Vayikra, a category of *korbanot* called *oleh veyored* (variable offerings, scaled to one's means) provides that for certain specified sins, a person of limited means may bring a *mincha* in lieu of an animal *chatat*. That offering — the *minchat chotei* — is also explicitly stated in the Torah to require neither oil nor frankincense: *lo yasim aleha shemen velo yitein aleha levonah*, followed by *ki chatati* — because it is a sin offering. So the *sotah*'s *mincha* is not unique in lacking oil and frankincense.

### Three Qualities

The Gemara resolves this by reframing the Mishnah's claim. *Hachi ka'amar* — what the Mishnah is actually saying is not that all other *menachot* have both oil and frankincense, but rather that all other *menachot* possess at least one of three positive qualities: they contain *shemen* (oil), *levona* (frankincense), or they are made from refined wheat flour (*soles*) that comes from wheat (*chitin*). Every *mincha*, without exception, has at least one of these distinguishing positive characteristics — though some have only one, while others have all three.

### Sota Mincha Qualities

To illustrate: the *minchat chotei*, the sinner's meal offering, lacks oil and frankincense, yet it is made from refined wheat flour (*soles min ha-chitin*) — one redeeming quality remains. The *minchat ha-omer*, though it comes from barley rather than wheat, still requires oil and frankincense and is prepared from refined barley flour (*geres*) — it retains two of the three positive qualities. By contrast, *ve-zo* — the *sotah*'s *mincha* — has none: it has no oil, no frankincense, it is made from barley (*se'orim*) rather than wheat, and it is made from coarsely ground flour (*kemach*) rather than refined flour (*soles*) — that is, whole grain with the bran still present, the opposite of *soles*. It is thus uniquely deficient across all three dimensions, a point the Gemara emphasizes as expressive of its degraded symbolic character. And yet, as an aside, the *kohanim* are still obligated to eat it — they receive no prize for that particular assignment.

---

## Sota Mincha Reasoning

### Rabbi Shimon's View

A *braita* is cited presenting Rabbi Shimon's analysis of the underlying logic. He argues that by strict reasoning, the *minchat chotei* — the standard sinner's meal offering — *should* have required oil and frankincense: *she-lo yehei chotei niskar* — so that the sinner should not benefit by having a less costly or less elaborate offering. Why should he be let off easy? Yet the Torah does not impose this additional expense. Why? *She-lo yehei korbano mehurdar* — because it is more important that the offering not be beautiful or embellished, since its symbolic function — communicating the gravity of sin — outweighs the concern about the sinner's financial ease. The symbolic message takes precedence over the punitive economic logic.

### Sin Offering Parallel

Rabbi Shimon extends this reasoning. He argues that by the same logic, a *chatat* for a standard sin (conventionally referred to as a *chatat cheilev*, since the passage establishing the *chatat* in the Torah is juxtaposed to the prohibition of eating forbidden fat) *should* have required *nesachim* (libations — the accompanying wine, oil, and flour offerings that come with many animal sacrifices). Rashi notes that the juxtaposition is not incidental: the laws of *chatat* in the Torah are written directly adjacent to the passage about *cheilev* and *dam* being offered on the *mizbeach*, making *chatat cheilev* a natural reference point. The same logic applies: the sinner should not benefit from the absence of *nesachim*. But they are not required — *she-lo yehei korbano mehurdar* — so that the offering not be embellished.

Importantly, Rabbi Shimon is here giving a *ta'ama d'kra* — a reason-based interpretation of the Torah's ruling. The question raised is whether he is merely *describing* the known law by offering an explanation, or whether he is actually *deriving* the law from his interpretive principle and using it to determine halacha in cases we do not yet know. The first possibility is significant because Rabbi Shimon is generally one who *darshinan ta'ama d'kra* — who applies the reason of a verse to determine legal conclusions in other cases. The Gemara will test which of these readings is correct.

### Metzora Exception

Rabbi Shimon continues: the *chatat* and *asham* of a *metzora* (a person afflicted with *tzara'at*) *do* bring *nesachim* — and this is because they are not brought on account of sin. The *metzora*'s purification offerings are not *kaparah* for transgression but rather part of a *taharah* process. Rashi notes that this is not derived by Rabbi Shimon alone from logical inference — the Gemara elsewhere (Masechet Menachot, chapter *Shtei Middot*) actually has a specific *drasha* to include the *metzora*'s offerings in the requirement of *nesachim*. So according to Rashi, Rabbi Shimon's statement here is *descriptive*: he knows the law and is explaining *why* these offerings are the exception.

The Gemara then objects: is it really true that the *metzora*'s offerings have nothing to do with sin? Does not the Gemara elsewhere (Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan) state that *nega'im* come for seven sins? The Gemara answers: there, the *nega* itself serves as the atonement for the sin — *hu d'ichpar lei*. By the time the person brings the *korban*, it is not to atone for sin but simply to be reinstated in the world of *kodshim*: *l'ishtarei b'kodshim hu d'ka-mayti*. The *korban* is purely a part of the *taharah* process, not an act of *kaparah* for the original transgression.

### Nazirite Challenge

The Gemara presses further: according to Rabbi Shimon's logic, a *chatat* of a *nazir* should also require *nesachim*, since it too is not brought on account of sin. We know that in practice a *nazir*'s *chatat* does not have *nesachim* — so the challenge is: does this refute Rabbi Shimon's explanatory principle entirely, or does it merely reveal that we are working with established *halacha* and testing whether his explanation is consistent with the data?

This is a subtle and important question about the nature of the argument. If the Gemara is actually using Rabbi Shimon's principle to determine what the law *should* be, it would be proposing a real change in *halacha*. But that seems not to be the case — the Gemara appears to know the *halacha* and is asking whether Rabbi Shimon's explanation is coherent given the data. Either way, the challenge stands: the *chatat nazir* does not bring *nesachim*, yet according to Rabbi Shimon's framework it should, since it is not brought for sin.

Tosafot notes a more fundamental formulation available: the underlying rule is simply that only a *korban* that can be brought *beneder uvenidava* — as a freewill offering — brings *nesachim*. An *olah* and *shelamim* fall into that category and therefore always bring *nesachim*, even when obligatory (as in *musaf* offerings). A *chatat* and *asham*, which are by nature always obligatory and never voluntary, do not bring *nesachim* — with the single exception of the *metzora*'s *chatat* and *asham*, which the Torah explicitly associates with *nesachim*. This is the real rule. Rabbi Shimon is offering a *ta'ama d'kra* — an explanatory rationale — for why the rule works out the way it does, not a derivation of the rule itself.

### Nazirite Resolution

The Gemara resolves the challenge: *savar lah keRabbi Eliezer haKappar* — Rabbi Shimon holds in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer haKappar, who maintains that a *nazir* is also considered a sinner. Therefore, even the *chatat* of a *nazir* is brought in the context of sin, and the data remains consistent with Rabbi Shimon's explanation.

Tosafot raises a difficulty by noting that other passages in the Gemara discuss the extent of Rabbi Eliezer haKappar's position. Some *Gemarot* suggest that only a *nazir tamei* — one who became ritually impure and thereby failed to complete his *nezirut* — is considered a sinner by Rabbi Eliezer haKappar, because through impurity he undermined his commitment. Other *Gemarot* suggest that even a *nazir tahor* — one who completed his *nezirut* without any impurity — is considered a sinner simply because he denied himself the permitted pleasure of wine; even without regret, there is an element of improper self-denial. The present Gemara, Tosafot observes, seems to require that even the *nazir tahor* be considered a sinner according to Rabbi Eliezer haKappar — because it is specifically the *nazir tahor* whose *chatat* is an animal offering of the type that could theoretically require *nesachim*. The *nazir tamei* brings a different type of sacrifice. So the challenge and its resolution only cohere if Rabbi Eliezer haKappar's category of "sinner" encompasses the *nazir tahor*.

---

## Rabban Gamliel

### Animal-Like Actions

The Gemara now introduces a *braita* in which Rabban Gamliel offers an independent explanation for why the *sotah*'s *mincha* is made from barley. He addresses the sages — referred to here as *sofrim* — with a certain formality, saying *hanichu li ve'edreshenu kemin chomer* — "leave me and I will expound it beautifully." The phrase *kemin chomer* is interpreted by Rashi as something golden and beautiful, like a fine clasp; Tosafot suggests it may mean a pearl or jewel. Either way, Rabban Gamliel signals that he has a particularly elegant formulation to offer. The dynamic is intriguing: one wonders whether the designation *sofrim* here reflects a distinction between those whose specialty is *halacha* — Rabban Gamliel's primary domain — and those whose specialty is *drash* and symbolic interpretation, prompting his somewhat pointed request to be allowed to speak. A similar dynamic appears elsewhere in the literature, as when Rabbi Akiva is told that his area is the hardest legal tractates like *nega'im* and *ohalot*, not *aggadah*.

Rabban Gamliel's explanation: *kesheim shema'aseha ma'aseh beheimah kach korbanah ma'achal beheimah* — just as her actions were like those of an animal — following her desires without human moral restraint — so too her offering is the food of an animal. This is, of course, a deeply dehumanizing framing, and, as has been noted throughout these pages, it presumes her guilt.

### Wealth Objection

The preceding explanation, attributed to Rabbi Meir, was that since she fed her lover the delicacies of the world (*ma'adanei olam*), her offering is the food of animals (*ma'achal beheimah*). Rabban Gamliel's objection to Rabbi Meir is that this reasoning works only for a wealthy woman who could actually feed her lover delicacies. What about a poor woman? The explanation simply does not account for all cases.

### Universal Explanation

Rabban Gamliel's explanation, by contrast, applies universally. It does not depend on what she fed her lover or what her financial means were. Regardless of her economic situation, the characterization of her actions as animal-like — as driven by appetite rather than moral agency — is the same. Therefore, the offering that symbolizes those actions is uniformly the food of animals.

---

## Water Ritual

### Vessel and Water

The Gemara now presents the next Mishnah, which describes the preparation of the bitter waters. The *kohen* would bring a *pili shel cheres* — a pottery vial or vessel — and place into it *chatzi log mayim min ha-kiyor*, half a *log* of water from the *kiyor* (the laver in the Temple). A half-*log* is approximately double a *revi'it*, corresponding to something like six or seven ounces — roughly the size of a standard cup.

### Quarter-Log Measure

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees, holding that only a *revi'it* of water is required. His reasoning will be explained later: since Rabbi Yehuda holds that less text was written on the scroll that is erased into the water (*keshem shemi'at bichtav*), less water is needed to dissolve it.

### Heichal Procedure

The *kohen* would then enter the *Heichal* — the inner sanctum of the Temple, where the *Shulchan* and *Menorah* were located — and turn to his right. This rightward turn reflects the general principle in the Temple that all turns are made to the right, the direction associated with primacy and strength. (The same principle governs, for instance, the direction in which the *Sefer Torah* is carried around, which results in a counter-clockwise procession, since one always moves to one's right. Similarly, the *kallah* circles the *chatan* in this direction.)

### Marble Tile

At a specific location in the *Heichal*, there was a space of one cubit by one cubit (*ama al ama*) covered by a marble tile (*tavla shel shayish* — *tavla* being a Latin-derived term). Set into this tile was an iron ring, allowing the tile to be lifted.

### Retrieving Dirt

The *kohen* would lift the tile — presumably recessed into the floor so as not to be a hazard — and retrieve dirt from the natural ground beneath it.

### Dirt in Water

He would then place this dirt into the water, enough so that it was visible floating on the surface: *kedei sheyeira'eh al hamayim*. The verse cited is: *min ha'afar asher yihyeh bekarka hamishkan yikach hakohen venatan el ha-mayim* — "from the dust that shall be on the floor of the *Mishkan*, the *kohen* shall take and place into the water."

---

## New Vessel Debate

### New Vessel Required

The Gemara cites a *tanna* who states that the pottery vessel must be new — *pili shel cheres chadasha* — in the view of Rabbi Yishmael. His reasoning is a *gezerah shavah*: he derives *kli kli* — from the shared term "vessel" — connecting the *sotah* ritual to the *metzora* ritual, where the Torah also specifies *kli cheres*. Just as by the *metzora* the vessel must be new, so too here.

### Metzora Comparison

How do we know that the *metzora*'s vessel must be new? The verse states: *veshachat et hatzippor ha'achat el kli cheres al mayim chayim* — the bird is slaughtered over a pottery vessel containing living water. The Gemara derives: just as the *mayim chayim* (living water — water drawn directly from a natural spring, never processed or used) has never been worked with, so too the vessel must never have been used — *kli shelo na'asta bo melacha*.

This generates a further question: if we are connecting the *sotah* ritual to the *metzora* ritual through this *gezerah shavah*, should we also require *mayim chayim* for the *sotah*? The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yishmael himself holds this position — he rules that the water of the *kiyor* comes from an underground spring and therefore qualifies as *mayim chayim*. The *Chachamim*, however, hold that the water of the *kiyor* need not be *mayim chayim* and can be drawn from other collected sources.

The Gemara then challenges the derivation itself: *ika l'mifrach* — one can challenge the extension from *metzora* to *sotah*. The *metzora* ritual involves additional requirements — cedar wood, hyssop, and crimson thread (*etz erez, ezov, ushni tola'at*) — which impose multiple demands on the ritual. Perhaps those additional requirements justify the further demand that the vessel be new. By the *sotah*, where no such parallel demands exist, we might not extend that conclusion.

### Blackening Invalidation

Rava resolves the matter in a way that applies to the *Chachamim*'s position — that the vessel need not be entirely new. He states: *lo shanu* — the teaching that the vessel need not be new applies only when it has not become blackened. *Aval nitachmu panav, psulin* — if its surface has blackened from use, the vessel is invalid.

### Unchanged Vessel

The reason: *dumya d'mayim* — the vessel must parallel the water. Just as the water must be *shelo nishtanu* — unchanged from its natural state — so too the vessel must be *shelo nishtaneh* — unchanged from its original condition. A vessel that has blackened through use has undergone a fundamental transformation and therefore no longer meets this standard.

Tosafot raises a difficulty here, noting that another Gemara in Avoda Zara makes a similar comparison — *kemayim, shelo nishtaneh* — in the context of *bishul akum*, yet that application does not map cleanly onto all the parameters of that law. Tosafot therefore concludes that the derivation here is an *asmachta* — a rabbinic enactment with scriptural support — and that the requirement that the vessel be in its unchanged condition is *derabbanan*, not *d'oraita*. By implication, Tosafot is similarly suggesting that *bishul akum* is rabbinic in nature, though that is not his primary point here.

---

## Nidcha Question

### Refiring Question

Rava poses a question: if the vessel had become blackened — and is therefore invalid — and was then refired in a kiln until it became white again, what is the law? *Mi amrinan kivan de'idchu idchu* — do we say that once it was pushed away (*nidcheh*) from eligibility, it can never return, even after being restored? This is the principle of *dichui* — that once an object has been rejected for sacred use, it cannot be reaccepted even if the defect is remedied. Or do we say *kivan de'hadar hadar* — since it has returned to a fit state, it is once again valid? Alternatively, one might argue that since the blackening was a transitory condition that has now been reversed, it was perhaps never a true *dichui* in the first place — perhaps comparable to a *mum over* (a passing blemish) that does not permanently disqualify.

### Metzora Items Invalid

To shed light on this question, the Gemara cites Rabbi Eliezer: the cedar, hyssop, and crimson string used in the *metzora* ritual — if they were used to form a strap to carry a pack on one's back — are *psulin*, invalid for subsequent use in the ritual. Presumably the concern is that they were bent or otherwise altered.

### Permanent Damage

The Gemara attempts to derive from this that even if such items could theoretically be straightened out, they remain invalid. It responds: *hatam de'iklaf iklufei* — there, the bending may have caused actual peeling or permanent structural damage that cannot truly be undone. Therefore the *pesul* is permanent not because of *dichui* per se, but because the physical object cannot be fully restored. This response limits the case's applicability to the *nidcha* question about the vessel: since the vessel *can* be fully restored through refiring, perhaps it does return to valid status.

### Melacha Question

Tosafot raises a difficulty with the Gemara's framing. In a *Tosefta* to Nega'im (chapter *Ein Metzora*), Rabbi Eliezer himself states that the cedar, hyssop, and crimson thread used in the *metzora* ritual must not have had *melacha* performed with them. This suggests that the invalidation in that case is not primarily about the bending at all, but about the prohibition of *melacha* with these items — yet the Gemara focuses entirely on the bending. Tosafot does not resolve this difficulty, but it highlights a real tension: if *melacha* is the operative concern, the Gemara's analysis of whether the bending is correctable seems beside the point.

The question also connects to the broader discussion of *dichui* in contexts beyond *korbanot*. The classic principle of *nidcheh* applies most clearly to sanctified *korbanot*. It becomes less clear how it applies to objects used in rituals associated with the Temple but not themselves sanctified — like the items for the *metzora* or the vessel for the *sotah*. There is also a distinct question about *bigdei kehunah*: Tosafot notes that a Gemara in Zevachim holds that priestly garments which became soiled or torn invalidate the Temple service if worn in that state, yet if laundered they are restored to valid status. Priestly garments are sanctified objects, yet a correctable defect does not permanently disqualify them. One might contrast this with the blackened vessel, where the restoration requires refiring — perhaps a more drastic intervention — and ask whether that more fundamental transformation constitutes permanent *dichui*. These various permutations — *korban*, *mitzvah* object, Temple ritual object that is not a *korban*, and sanctified garments — each raise distinct questions about whether and how the concept of *dichui* applies.

---

## Dirt Sources

### Mishkan Ground

The Gemara turns to a *braita* analyzing the verse: *min ha'afar asher yihyeh bekarka haMishkan yikach hakohen venatan el ha-mayim*. One might have thought that the *kohen* could simply bring dirt from outside and carry it in. The *Talmud lomar* — the teaching that counters this — is *bekarka haMishkan*: the dirt must come from the floor of the *Mishkan* itself, not from an external source.
