On the other hand, one might have thought that *bekarka haMishkan* requires the *kohen* to actually dig up the floor with a shovel — and this too is rejected. *Asher yihyeh* — "that shall be" — indicates dirt that simply happens to be on the floor, not dirt that must be actively excavated. The practical upshot: *yesh sham havei, ein sham ten sham* — if there is already loose dirt there, use it; if not, pre-lay some dirt on the floor so that it will be available when the time comes.

### Alternative Source

A second *braita* takes an entirely different approach. Reading *asher yihyeh* as the operative phrase rather than *bekarka haMishkan*, this opinion holds that any dirt will do — dirt can even be brought from outside. The word *bekarka haMishkan* is then available to teach something else entirely.

### Multiple Locations

According to this reading, *bekarka haMishkan* serves to include other locations beyond the original *Mishkan* in the wilderness. Issi ben Yehuda teaches: the verse comes to include the *karka* of Shilo, Nov, Givon, and even *Beis Olamim* — the permanent Temple. Dirt from the floors of any of these sacred locations would be valid for the *sotah* ritual.

### Nov Givon Problem

Rashi is deeply troubled by the inclusion of Nov and Givon and therefore maintains a different *girsa* of the text, excluding them and limiting the *ribbuy* to *Beis Olamim*. His reasoning: Shilo requires no *ribbuy* at all, since it was the actual *Mishkan* relocated from the wilderness — obviously it is included in the plain meaning of the verse. Nov and Givon, by contrast, had a diminished status: they functioned as a *bamah*, a high place, without the *Aron* and without the full status of a central sanctuary, and crucially, the *sotah* ritual would not have been performed there — it was not a place where individual communal rituals of this kind were conducted. Therefore Rashi considers it a corruption of the text to include Nov and Givon, and restricts the expansion to *Beis Olamim* alone.

Tosafot disagrees with Rashi's emendation of the *girsa* and defends the inclusion of Nov and Givon on the grounds that Issi ben Yehuda may follow the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda (cited in chapter *Ba Siman*) that individual ritual offerings performed at the *Ohel Mo'ed* in the wilderness could also be performed at the *Ohel Mo'ed* at Gilgal — suggesting there is a position according to which individual rituals like *sotah* could indeed be performed at Nov and Givon. To emend the text entirely on the basis of a difficulty, Tosafot says, is going too far.

### Kal V'Chomer

Issi ben Menachem holds that no *ribbuy* is needed to include *Beis Olamim*. A *kal v'chomer* suffices: if, regarding the lesser *tumah* of ordinary ritual impurity, the Torah makes no distinction between the *Mishkan* and the permanent *Beit HaMikdash* — one may not enter either while *tamei* — then certainly the weightier moral *tumah* of *eshet ish* (suspected adultery, referred to in the Torah as *venitme'ah*) should equally apply to the *Beit HaMikdash*. Therefore *Beis Olamim* requires no special *ribbuy*. What, then, does *bekarka haMishkan* teach according to Issi ben Menachem? Simply that one cannot bring dirt from a basket — it must come from the floor, as explained earlier.

This *kal v'chomer* is, frankly, a striking and puzzling one. The comparison being drawn is between two very different senses of *tumah*. The *tumah* of ordinary ritual impurity is a specific halachic status governed by the laws of entering sacred precincts. The *tumah* of *eshet ish* is a moral and spiritual designation — the Torah says *venitme'ah*, meaning she has become defiled through her actions — but this never generates a *halacha* that a known adulteress is forbidden to enter the *Beit HaMikdash*. Furthermore, the *kal v'chomer* itself runs in a counterintuitive direction: if ordinary *tumah* is kept *out* of the Temple, then the weighty *tumah* of *eshet ish* should... be processed inside it? The inference does not flow in an obvious way. Nevertheless, the analogy between these two distinct domains of *tumah* — the halachic-ritual and the moral-spiritual — is a fascinating one, and the *kal v'chomer*, however structurally unusual, serves to ground the *sotah* ritual's connection to the permanent *Beit HaMikdash* in a principle rather than a mere *ribbuy* of the text.

---

---

# Sotah 16

## Dirt Source & Location

### Pre-laid vs. Fresh Dirt

The daf opens with a question about the source of the dirt used in the *sotah* ritual. The verse states *asher yihyeh be-karka ha-mishkan* — the dirt that will be on the ground of the *mishkan* — which raises the question of whether the *kohen* must actually dig the dirt from the ground of the *mishkan*, or whether it suffices to bring dirt in and pre-lay it there. As we saw at the close of the previous daf, the possibility of pre-laying dirt — placing it beneath the floor tiles rather than digging it afresh — is on the table.

### Two Tannaitic Positions

Two tannaitic positions emerge from the *braisa* at the top of the daf. Issi ben Menachem holds that *be-karka ha-mishkan* establishes a requirement that the dirt be placed on the ground — that is, the dirt must rest on the floor of the *mishkan* — but does not require it to be dug from there. Issi ben Yehudah takes a broader interpretive step: he understands *be-karka ha-mishkan* not as a procedural requirement about the dirt's placement, but as a geographic marker whose function is to exclude what might otherwise have been excluded, thereby teaching that the *sotah* ritual is valid not only in the *mishkan* itself.

### Geographic Scope

According to one version of Issi ben Yehudah's position, the verse extends the validity of the ritual to Shilo, Nov, and Givon — the intermediate sites of the *mishkan* before the permanent Temple was built. Rashi is uncomfortable with this extension and crosses it out, since the *sotah* procedure resembles the offering of an individual — a *korban yachid* — and there is a question whether such offerings could be brought at Nov and Givon, which had the status of a *bamah* and permitted individual altars. Tosafot, however, defends the inclusion, explaining that this reflects the view that a *korban yachid* could in fact be brought at Nov and Givon. In any case, the verse also extends the ritual to the *beit olamim* — the permanent *beit hamikdash*.

### Three Interpretive Models

Returning briefly to the discussion from the previous daf, it is worth noting that the *gemara*'s treatment of the *sotah* ritual reflects three distinct conceptual frameworks. The plain sense of the *pesukim* frames the ritual as a mechanism for determining guilt or innocence. The *mishnah*'s emphasis, by contrast, presumes guilt and frames the ritual as punishment. A third lens — and the one particularly relevant here — is that of purification: the *sotah* brings a *korban*, she stands in the section of the Temple where *teme'im* stood (at the Sha'ar Nicanor, the place where those afflicted with *tzara'at* and women after childbirth would stand), and she undergoes a rite at the *beit hamikdash*. This lens of *tumah* and purification runs through the discussion in ways that are not immediately obvious from the text, and the *gemara* itself draws on the *sotah*'s category of *tumah* as a precedent for laws of *safek tumah* in entirely unrelated contexts — such as the rules of *safek tumah be-reshus ha-rabim* and *safek tumah be-reshus ha-yachid*, which are derived from the *sotah*'s act of secluding herself in a *reshus ha-yachid*.

### Beit HaMikdash Inclusion

One might ask: why does the *torah* need a verse to include the *beit hamikdash*? Is the permanent Temple not always presumed to be included wherever the *torah* says *mishkan*? Tosafot addresses this directly and offers an illuminating answer: the difficulty is that the verse says *be-karka ha-mishkan* — the ground of the *mishkan* — and the *beit hamikdash*, unlike the *mishkan*, has a paved floor. One might therefore have thought that the *beit hamikdash* is specifically excluded, since the verse emphasizes *karka* — ground — and the Temple's interior is covered with stone flooring. The special inclusion is therefore necessary to override that potential exclusion.

---

## Ashes vs. Dirt Question

### No Dirt Scenario

The *gemara* now raises a new question: *ein sham afar, mahu sheyiten efer?* — what if there is no dirt available? May ashes be used in its place? This question arises within the context already established: we have concluded that the dirt need not be dug from the ground; at most, it must be placed upon the ground. Given that latitude, might ashes — which the *torah* itself sometimes calls *afar* — also qualify?

### Beit Shammai Position

*Aliba de-Beit Shammai lo tivaei lach* — according to Beit Shammai, there is no question at all. Beit Shammai holds *lo matzinu efer she-karui afar*: ashes are never called *afar*. The two words — *afar* (dirt) and *efer* (ashes) — are categorically distinct, and no verse establishes that *efer* falls under the rubric of *afar*. The question therefore simply does not arise for Beit Shammai.

### Beit Hillel Position

The question becomes pressing according to Beit Hillel, who holds *matzinu efer she-karui afar* — there is indeed a case where ashes are called *afar*. The source is the verse *ve-lakach me-afar sereifat ha-parah* — "he shall take from the *afar* of the burning of the *parah*" (Numbers 19:17). The *parah adumah* leaves ashes, yet the verse calls them *afar*. Beit Hillel reads this as evidence that the word *afar* can encompass *efer*. Beit Shammai responds that *afar sereifa* is a compound term meaning "the dust of burning," which is a way of referring to ashes — but the word *afar* standing alone does not mean ashes.

### Blood-Covering Halacha

The practical application of this dispute extends to *kisui ha-dam* — the commandment to cover blood after *shechita*, as the verse says *ve-kissehu be-afar* (Leviticus 17:13). May ashes be used? Beit Shammai says no, since ashes are not called *afar*. Beit Hillel says yes, since *afar sereifat ha-parah* demonstrates that *efer* can be called *afar*. According to Beit Hillel, one may fulfill *kisui ha-dam* with ashes.

### Dirt Type Requirement

The *gemara* now asks whether the reasoning that allows ashes for *kisui ha-dam* according to Beit Hillel would also permit them for the *sotah*. One might argue that it should, since in both cases the operative word is *afar*. But the *gemara* raises a counterargument: *af al gav de-ikarei afar, hacha be-karka ha-mishkan ktiv* — even granting that *efer* can be called *afar*, the *sotah* verse specifically says *be-karka ha-mishkan*, which implies a connection to the nature of *karka*. Perhaps the contextual emphasis on *karka* restricts the *afar* here to something that genuinely resembles ground, and ashes — however legitimately called *afar* in another context — do not qualify.

### Two Readings

Rashi explains *be-karka ha-mishkan* to mean that even if you may take dirt out of a basket without digging, it must still be the type of substance that *could* be the *karka ha-mishkan* — it must genuinely resemble ground. Alternatively, one may read *be-karka ha-mishkan* as conveying the territorial teaching of Issi ben Yehudah and Issi ben Menachem — not a qualitative requirement about the nature of the dirt itself — in which case the word *afar* might remain open enough to include *efer* according to Beit Hillel. Whether *be-karka ha-mishkan* is a qualitative restriction on the substance or merely a territorial and procedural teaching is thus the crux of the question left open at this point.

---

## Halacha Okevet HaMikra

### Rabbi Yishmael's Princip…

The *gemara* now pivots to a celebrated ruling: *ta shema, de-amar Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Yishmael* — come and hear, as Rabbi Yochanan says in the name of Rabbi Yishmael. *Be-shelosha mekomot halacha okevet mikra* — in three places the *halacha* undermines the plain sense of scripture. The word *okevet* — which may be translated as "undermines" or "overrides" — captures the idea that in these three cases, if one were to follow the simple reading of the verse, one would arrive at a *halacha* different from what the tradition mandates. Rashi explains that *halacha* here means *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* — an ancient received tradition — and it is this received tradition that stands in apparent tension with the plain sense of the text.

### Kissui HaDam

The first case is *kisui ha-dam*. The *torah* says *be-afar* — with dirt — yet the *halacha* is *be-chol davar* — with anything that can grow seeds. This is not a limitless expansion; one cannot, for example, cover blood with a book. But the tradition permits substances that resemble dirt in its seed-growing capacity, such as ground pottery shards, even though they are not literally *afar*.

### Nazir Hair Cutting

The second case as quoted in the *gemara* is the *nazir*. The verse states *ta'ar lo ya'avor al rosho* — a razor shall not pass over his head — yet the *halacha* extends the prohibition to any instrument that removes hair. The *nazir* is forbidden from cutting his hair with anything, not only a razor.

### Get Writing Surface

The third case is the *get*. The verse uses the word *sefer* — a document or book — yet the *halacha* permits writing a *get* on any surface that is detached from the ground: a leaf, an animal's horn, the arm of a slave. The received tradition does not confine the *get* to parchment or any particular material.

### Rashi's Girsa Correction

Rashi takes issue with the second case as presented — the *ta'ar* of the *nazir* — and argues that this is actually not a case of the *halacha* undermining scripture but of the *halacha* expanding and intensifying scripture. The *torah* says a razor is forbidden; the *halacha* adds that all instruments are forbidden. This is being more *machmir* than the verse, not contradicting it. Rashi acknowledges a somewhat forced explanation — that it "undermines" in the sense that lashes would be administered for violations involving other instruments even though the verse does not explicitly require them, thereby raising the specter of lashing an innocent person — but Rashi finds this unsatisfying.

Rashi therefore prefers a different *girsa* (textual reading), citing the *Yerushalmi* in Tractate Kiddushin, where the three cases are: *sefer* — the *get*; *afar* — *kisui ha-dam*; and *martzea* — the awl used to pierce the ear of the slave who refuses his freedom (Exodus 21:6). As quoted by Rashi: *be-masechet Kiddushin Yerushalmi matzati mishna zu* — the three cases are the *sefer*, the *afar*, and the *martzea*. The *halacha* by the slave's ear is that any piercing instrument works — *afilu sul ve-sira* — even a thorn or similar implement. Rashi adds: *vehu nireh be-einai me'od de-hach de-ta'ar tosefet hi* — it seems very clear to him that the *ta'ar* version is an addition that does not belong, since it adds to rather than contradicts the verse.

### Why These Three Cases

Rashi raises a deeper question: given that *midrash halacha* regularly reinterprets verses — sometimes expanding them, sometimes narrowing them — what makes these three cases distinctive enough to be labeled *halacha okevet mikra*? The answer Rashi provides is that in all the other cases where the *halacha* diverges from the plain sense, there is a *drasha* — a hermeneutical derivation embedded in the verse — that allows one to say the alternate reading is present within the *mikra* itself. One may disagree about whether a given *drasha* is compelling, but there is a method that links the *halacha* back to the text.

Rabbi Yishmael, however, holds that for these three cases, no such *drasha* exists. Other *tanna'im* do offer *drashot* for these laws — they find ways to derive *be-chol davar* for *kisui ha-dam* from the verse, ways to read the *sefer* of *get* as including any surface, and so on. But Rabbi Yishmael does not accept those *drashot*. As Rashi writes: *de-Rabbi Yishmael lo mashme' lei kra'i de-vechasav lah de-marbina minei le-rabot kol davar* — Rabbi Yishmael does not read the verse "and he shall write for her" as yielding an expansion to include all surfaces. *Ella halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai samchina* — the only basis is the received tradition. And any verse that appears to support it is merely an *asmachta*. *Hilkach, she'ar midrashim... lo chashiv lei Rabbi Yishmael ke-halacha okevet* — all other *drashot* throughout the *torah* do not constitute *halacha okevet* in Rabbi Yishmael's view, because in those cases there is a legitimate hermeneutical derivation that accounts for the *halacha*. But these three he cannot derive. The tradition stands and the simple sense of the verse is genuinely overridden. Rabbi Yishmael is prepared to live with that disparity.

---

## Midrash HaLacha Origins

### Tradition vs. Derivation

This discussion opens a broader question that is genuinely debated among *rishonim* and modern scholars alike: in *midrash halacha*, did *Chazal* begin with a received tradition about what the *halacha* is and then return to the *pesukim* to locate support for it, or did they begin with the text and derive the *halacha* through hermeneutics? The answer is almost certainly not uniform — sometimes one approach, sometimes the other — and the evidence internal to the *gemara* often points toward which method was operative in a given case.

### Forced Drasha Evidence

When a *drasha* appears highly forced — when one wonders whether any independent reader of the verse would have arrived at this interpretation — it is a strong signal that *Chazal* started with the practice and worked backward. The classic example is the *gemara*'s discussion of *pikuach nefesh docheh Shabbos*: it is manifest that the *halacha* was known and established, and the *gemara* is proposing various possible pesukim to serve as its textual anchor. When the *drasha* seems genuinely embedded in the verse, one may more plausibly conclude they started with the text and reasoned forward.

### Rabbi Yishmael's Stance

What is remarkable about Rabbi Yishmael's position is that it goes even further. Most situations where *Chazal* start with the tradition can still, in the end, produce a *drasha* — perhaps forced, perhaps creative, but one that anchors the *halacha* in the *pasuk* retroactively. Rabbi Yishmael is saying something more striking: even after the fact, even knowing the *halacha*, he cannot in good conscience say that the *pasuk* contains it. It is pure tradition, and the verses remain in apparent contradiction to it. This is why the term *okevet* — undermining — is apt for Rabbi Yishmael in a way it would not be for others: he is the one for whom the *halacha* genuinely overrides and does not resolve with the *mikra*. Other *tanna'im* have *drashot* that resolve the tension; for Rabbi Yishmael, the tension remains.

---

## Ashes Omission Explained

### Why Not Ashes?

The *gemara* now returns to the question of ashes in the *sotah* ritual and poses a pointed challenge. If ashes can in fact serve as *afar* for the *sotah* according to Beit Hillel — and if this represents a case where the *halacha* expands beyond the plain sense of *afar* — why is this not on Rabbi Yishmael's list of three places where *halacha okevet mikra*? This is, as Tosafot notes, a genuinely puzzling question for multiple reasons. First, Rabbi Yishmael presumably holds like Beit Shammai that *efer* is never called *afar*, and therefore there would be no expansion at all — no *okevet* to record. Second, if one follows Beit Hillel and *efer* is legitimately called *afar*, then the *halacha* is actually consistent with the *mikra*, not overriding it — and so again there is nothing to list. Tosafot struggles with the question, yet the *gemara* poses it and proceeds to answer it.

### Abbreviated List Theory

The *gemara*'s first answer is *tana ve-shayer* — the list is incomplete; items were left off. The list says "three" but is not exhaustive; there are additional cases that also exemplify *halacha okevet mikra* beyond the three recorded. Ashes for *sotah* may be one such omission.

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: *u-mai shayer de-hai shayer?* — if you claim the list is abbreviated, there must be more than one omitted item, because one would never compile a list and leave off only a single case. If you're going to say things were left off, show us another omission as well.

The *gemara* proposes: *shayer metzora* — the shaving of the *metzora* was also left off. The relevant verse, from the seventh day of the *metzora*'s purification process, reads: *ve-haya ba-yom ha-shvi'i yegalach et kol se'aro* — and on the seventh day he shall shave all his hair. The verse then specifies: *et rosho ve-et zakano ve-et givot einav* — his head, his beard, and his eyebrows. It then returns to a general formulation: *ve-et kol se'aro yigalach* — all his hair shall he shave. This is a classic structure of *klal u-frat u-klal* — general, specific, and general — from which we derive *ein atah dan ella ke-ein ha-frat*: we include anything similar to what was specified. The *frat* describes places where hair is gathered and visible (*mekom kinus se'ar ve-nireh*), so we include the pubic hair (*se'ar ha-raglayim*, as Rabbi explains), while excluding underarm hair (*beit ha-shachi*) — which, even when naked, is not visible unless one raises one's arms — as well as individual stray hairs elsewhere on the body.

The plain sense of the verse, following this *klal u-frat u-klal*, would limit the shaving on day seven to the gathered, visible areas. Yet the *halacha* — *megalcho ke-dala'at* — requires shaving the *metzora* completely bald, like a gourd. This appears to be another case of *halacha okevet mikra*.

### Addition vs. Contradicti…

But the *gemara* rejects this reasoning. *Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* objects: *ki ka chashiv halacha okevet mikra* — when Rabbi Yishmael lists cases of *halacha okevet*, he means cases where the *halacha* genuinely contradicts and displaces the plain sense of the verse. *Ha okevet midirabanan hi* — this case undermines not the plain sense of the *mikra* but the *drasha* of the *mikra*. The *mikra* itself says *kol se'aro* — all his hair — which on its face sounds comprehensive. It is only because of the *klal u-frat u-klal* derivation that we would narrow it to gathered areas. The *halacha* of shaving like a gourd contradicts the narrowed *drasha*, not the plain verse. This is therefore not the same category as the three cases Rabbi Yishmael listed.

Rav Pappa offers a second reason the *metzora* case does not belong on the list: *ki chashiv halacha okevet ve-okaret* — the three listed cases involve situations where following the *halacha* means you would *not* be fulfilling the *mikra*'s instruction. Writing a *get* on a leaf means you are not writing it on a *sefer*; covering blood with pottery shards means you have not covered it with *afar* in the simple sense. The *halacha* displaces what the verse required. But by the *metzora*, shaving the entire body *includes* the areas the verse specified — one is doing the bunches of hair *and more*. The *halacha* is *okevet u-mosefet* — it overrides but adds — and one who shaves the *metzora* completely has certainly also shaved his head, beard, and eyebrows. It does not undermine the *mikra*; it fulfills it and exceeds it.

### Metzora Derasha Methods

The *gemara* records the full *drasha* for both hermeneutical approaches. According to *klal u-frat u-klal* (Rabbi Yishmael's method): *klal* — *ve-et kol se'aro*; *frat* — *et rosho ve-et zakano ve-et givot einav*; *klal* — *ve-et kol se'aro yigalach*. *Ain atah dan ella ke-ein ha-frat*: we include *mekom kinus se'ar ve-nireh* — places where hair gathers and is visible. Rabbi rules that this includes *se'ar ha-raglayim* — the pubic hair — because it is visible when unclothed. It excludes *beit ha-shachi* (underarm hair) and individual strands across the body.

According to *ribbuy u-miut u-ribbuy* (Rabbi Akiva's method): *riba* — *ve-et kol se'aro* (expansion); *mi'et* — the listed body parts (limitation); *riba* — *ve-et kol se'aro yigalach* (expansion again). When you have *ribbuy, miut, ve-ribbuy*, you include virtually everything, excluding only the most categorically different thing. *Ma mi'et* — what is excluded? *Mi'et se'ar she-betoch ha-chotem* — the nose hair. Everything else is included, and one shaves him like a gourd.

### Rabbi Akiva vs. Rabbi Yi…

This analysis generates Rav Ashi's third and cleanest answer to why the *metzora* shaving does not belong on Rabbi Yishmael's list. *Ha matnita mani? Rabbi Yishmael hi* — the *braisa* listing the three cases of *halacha okevet* is the position of Rabbi Yishmael himself. *De-darash klal u-frat* — Rabbi Yishmael applies *klal u-frat u-klal*, which yields on day seven only the shaving of bunches of hair. According to Rabbi Yishmael, that is precisely what the *halacha* of day seven *is*: you do not shave the *metzora* like a gourd on day seven. The position that requires shaving like a gourd on day seven belongs to Rabbi Akiva, *de-darash ribbuy u-miut* — who reads *ribbuy, miut, ve-ribbuy* and therefore includes the whole body. This is not *halacha* against *drasha*; it is simply Rabbi Yishmael's *drasha* against Rabbi Akiva's *drasha*. There is no *okevet* at all from Rabbi Yishmael's perspective.

We thus have three separate reasons why the *metzora* shaving is not on Rabbi Yishmael's list: first, it contradicts only the *drasha* and not the plain verse; second, it adds to rather than displaces the *mikra*'s requirement; and third, it is not Rabbi Yishmael's *halacha* in the first place.

### Partial Resolution

With all three answers in place, we return to the original question: why are ashes not on the list? No fully satisfying resolution emerges. The *gemara* offers the partial answer of Rav Huna bar Ashi quoting Rav: *ein sham afar, mevi rakvuvit yerek* — if there is no dirt, one may bring decomposed vegetable matter and use it to sanctify the water. This is not ashes; it is something that grew from the ground and naturally decomposed, and it retains enough of the character of *karka* to be considered a form of *afar*.

But the *gemara* immediately qualifies: *ve-lo hi* — that is not a true equivalence. *Rikvuvit yerek hu de-havei afar* — decomposed vegetable can be considered *afar*. *Efer lo havei afar* — ashes cannot. So even the partial resolution expands *afar* only modestly — to naturally decomposed organic matter — and explicitly stops short of including ashes. The question of ashes remains without a clean resolution, and the question of why they do not appear on Rabbi Yishmael's list remains similarly open.

---

## Visibility Requirement

### Three Visible Items

The *gemara* now introduces a *braisa*: *shelosha tzerichim she-yeira'u* — three things must be visible. These are: the *afar* of the *sotah* when placed in the water; the *efer parah* — ashes of the *parah adumah* — when placed in the water; and the *rok yevamah* — the spit of the *yevamah* in the *chalitzah* ceremony. The verse by *chalitzah* states *ve-yarkah be-fanav* and *le-einei ha-zekenim*, requiring that the *zekenim* actually see the spit. In each of these cases, the relevant substance must be visible when combined with the water or present before the observers.

### Bird Blood Addition

*Mishum Rabbi Yishmael amru* — in the name of Rabbi Yishmael, they added a fourth: *af dam tzippor* — the blood of the bird used in the *metzora*'s purification. When the bird is slaughtered and its blood falls into the water, that blood must be visible.

### Bird Blood Source

The *gemara* provides the derivation. The verse states: *ve-taval otam be-dam ha-tzippor ha-shechutah u-va-mayim ha-chayim* — he shall dip them in the blood of the slaughtered bird and in the living water. A *braisa* is then cited: one might have thought you dip only in the blood, without water — therefore the verse says *ba-mayim* (in the water). One might have thought you dip only in the water, without blood — therefore the verse says *be-dam* (in the blood). *Ha keitzad?* — how is this resolved? *Mevi mayim she-dam tzippor nikar bahem* — you bring water in which the blood of the bird will remain recognizable. The blood and the water are combined, but the blood must remain *nikar* — recognizable, visible — within the mixture. Rabbi Yishmael accordingly includes this among the things that must be seen.

---

## Blood-Water Mixture

### Blood Prominence

Rabbi Yishmael's requirement that the blood be *nikar* in the water is not merely a technical formality. The verse says *be-dam ha-tzippor ha-shechutah* — in the blood of the slaughtered bird — rather than simply "in them," and Rabbi Yishmael reads this as establishing that the blood must retain its essential character. You are fundamentally dipping into *blood* — water is added to it, but blood is what the dipping is about.

### Revi'it Measure

The practical consequence of this position is a limit on the amount of water: *revi'it*. If more than a *revi'it* of water is added, the blood will be so diffused that it can no longer be said to be *nikar*. At a *revi'it* or less, the blood remains visibly and substantively present.

### Mamshut Principle

Tosafot deepens this analysis. The word *nikar* does not mean merely that one can detect that blood was once present, the way a forensic trace might indicate a prior substance. Tosafot explains that the blood must retain its *mamashus* — its essential, physical substantiality. The question is framed this way: are we looking at blood that has had some water added, or at water that has had some blood added? Rabbi Yishmael requires the former. There must be enough blood relative to the water that the mixture can still be characterized as *dam* — blood — into which one is dipping. The verse *ve-taval otam be-dam ha-tzippor* obligates one to dip into *blood*, and therefore the *mamashus* of the blood must remain. This is why the water is limited to a *revi'it*: at that volume, one can still say the blood is present as blood, not merely as a colorant dissolved into water. This point parallels broader questions of *bittul* — at what point has a substance ceased to be present in its essential form and become merely a trace?

### Simple Mixture View

The Rabbis who do not share Rabbi Yishmael's position — and who accordingly did not include the bird's blood in their list of items requiring visibility — understand the verse differently. *Ha-hu le-gufei* — the separate mention of blood and water is not to establish that the blood must predominate; rather, it teaches the simple fact that blood and water must be combined. The instruction *be-dam u-va-mayim* means: dip in a mixture of both. The blood need not retain its *mamashus*; what matters is that both components are present.

Rabbi Yishmael objects: if the verse only intended to say "combine them," it should have written *ve-taval bahem* — dip in them — rather than specifying *be-dam* and then *ba-mayim* separately. The separate specification of *be-dam* teaches that the blood must be prominent — *le-nikar*. The Rabbis counter: if the verse had only written *ve-taval bahem* — in them — one might have thought the dipping in blood and the dipping in water are done separately in sequence, first one and then the other. The explicit mention of both together teaches that they must be combined. Rabbi Yishmael responds that this teaching — the need to combine them — is already derived from a different verse: the verse *ve-shachatu et ha-tzippor ha-achat el keli cheres al mayim chayim* — the bird is slaughtered over a vessel of water, so the blood naturally falls into the water, producing an automatic combination. The Rabbis reply that one could technically comply with *shachatu al mayim chayim* while preventing the blood from mixing — for instance, by slaughtering near the vessel and diverting the blood into a separate container. Therefore a verse is still needed to teach the requirement of combination.

---

## Bird Size Problem

### Extreme Cases

Rav Yirmiya poses a challenge to Rabbi Zeira targeting the *revi'it* measure. *Gedola u-madachat et ha-mayim* — consider a very large bird: its blood will be so abundant that a *revi'it* of water will be entirely overwhelmed, with no meaningful presence of water remaining. *Ktana ve-nimchit mipnei ha-mayim* — consider a very small bird: its blood will be so scant that even a *revi'it* of water will overwhelm it, and no meaningful presence of blood will remain. How can a single fixed measure of a *revi'it* work across the full range of bird sizes?

### Sparrow Standard

Rabbi Zeira's response carries an implicit rebuke: *lav amina lach lo teippek nafshach levar me-hilchata* — haven't I told you not to try to outsmart the *halacha* in this way? The *revi'it* measure was calibrated specifically for the *tzippor dror* — the sparrow — which is the standard bird used for this ritual.

### Normal Range Solution

Within the range of sparrows, Rabbi Zeira explains, the measure holds: *ein lach gedola she-madachat et ha-mayim* — there is no sparrow large enough that its blood will overwhelm a *revi'it* of water — *ve-ein lach ktana she-nimchit mipnei ha-mayim* — and there is no sparrow small enough that its blood will be overwhelmed by a *revi'it* of water. The *shiur* of a *revi'it* was established with the normal range of sparrows in mind, and within that range it is an accurate and workable measure. Extreme hypotheticals about oversized or undersized birds are not the target audience of the *halacha*.

---

## Mixing Order Debate

### Dirt-First Rule

The *gemara* returns to the *sotah* ritual and the question of sequence. A *braisa* states: *hikdim afar le-mayim — pasul* — if the dirt was placed in the vessel before the water, the mixture is invalid. The verse *ve-natan el ha-mayim* — "and he shall put into the water" — implies that the water must already be present when the dirt is added.

### Rabbi Shimon's View

Rabbi Shimon disagrees: *Rabbi Shimon machshir* — Rabbi Shimon validates the mixture even if the dirt was placed first. His reasoning is derived from a comparison to the *parah adumah*, where, as we will see, both orderings have textual support, and he reads the two rituals as linked by a *gezeira shava*.

### Gezeira Shava

The connection between the two rituals rests on the shared word *afar*. The *sotah* verse speaks of *afar*, and the *parah adumah* verse speaks of *afar sereifat ha-parah* — also called *afar* by the verse, as Beit Hillel established. Rabbi Shimon draws a *gezeira shava* between the two uses of *afar* to allow each ritual to teach something about the other.

### Reverse Direction

What does the *sotah* teach about the *parah adumah*? That the substance must be visible on top of the water — *afar al gabei mayim*. The *sotah* ritual implies that the dirt or its equivalent rests visibly upon the water's surface. Rabbi Shimon applies this teaching to the *parah adumah* as well: when the ashes are placed in the water, they too must be *nikar* — visible — on the water.

### Order Flexibility

And in the reverse direction: what does the *parah adumah* teach the *sotah*? That the order of mixing can be reversed. Since the *parah adumah* has textual support for both orderings — as the *gemara* now explains — the *gezeira shava* extends that flexibility to the *sotah* as well. Even if the dirt is placed before the water in the *sotah* ritual, Rabbi Shimon holds it remains valid.

---

## Red Heifer Verses

### Alav - Ashes First

The *gemara* now examines the two verses in the *parah adumah* passage that seem to point in opposite directions regarding the order of mixing. The first verse is *ve-natan alav mayim chayim el keli* — "he shall put upon it living water into a vessel." The word *alav* — "upon it" — implies that the ashes are already present when the water is added, meaning the ashes go first.

### El Keli - Water First

The second reading emerges from the phrase *mayim chayim el keli* — "living water into a vessel." If one reads this phrase as indicating that the living water is placed into the vessel at the outset, the implication is that the water is in the vessel first, and the ashes are added afterward. Thus the same verse seems to support both sequences: *alav* implies ashes first; *el keli* implies water first.

### Flexible Order

Rabbi Shimon reconciles the two: *ratza zeh noten, ratza zeh noten* — one may do it either way. The two formulations in the verse are not contradictory but complementary, each validating a different order. By the *parah adumah* both sequences are valid, and through the *gezeira shava*, both sequences become valid for the *sotah* as well.

---

## Rabbis' Order Rule

### Machshir on Top

The Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Shimon in both cases. Their principle is: *mimah matzinu be-chol makom machshir le-mala* — we find universally that the *machshir* — the potent, active ingredient — goes on top. The water is the base solution, a passive medium. The special substance — whether dirt, ashes, or blood — is the *machshir*, the component that actually activates the ritual. And that component must be placed second, on top of the water already in the vessel.

### Reinterpretation

Given this principle, the Rabbis reinterpret *ve-natan alav* to mean something other than "the ashes are placed first." Once the water is already in the vessel, the ashes are added, and then *alav* — upon it — the water is stirred over and mixed through the ashes. The word *alav* describes not an initial placement of ashes but a subsequent folding of the water over the ashes after they have been added. The *machshir* (the ashes) still goes second — after the water — and then the mixing is described by *alav*.

### Three Examples

The Rabbis find support for water-first in three parallel cases. By *sotah*, the plain sense of the verse requires water first: *ve-natan el ha-mayim* means you put the dirt into the water already present. By the *parah adumah*, the Rabbis read *mayim chayim el keli* as mandating water first in the vessel. And by the blood of the *metzora*'s bird, *al mayim chayim* — upon living water — similarly implies the water is there first and the blood descends into it. In all three, the water precedes the special substance.

### Water as Base

The underlying logic is consistent: the non-water element — dirt, ashes, blood — is in each case the special, ritual-defining component, the *machshir*. The water is simply the medium. The ritual logic therefore demands that the medium be in place first, and the defining ingredient be introduced into it. This ordering is *me'akev* according to the Rabbis — it is not merely a preferred sequence but a requirement, and reversing it invalidates the mixture. Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, drawing on the *gezeira shava* and the flexibility encoded in both verses of the *parah adumah*, holds that either order is valid in both rituals.

---

---

# Sotah 17

## Writing the Megillah

### Opening & Mezuzah

Daf 17 opens with a new *mishnah* that continues the procedure for the *sotah*. The preceding *mishnayot* had addressed the collection of the dirt and its placement into the vessel — the questions of where the dirt should come from, whether it should be visible on the surface of the water, and so on. Now, having established that the woman has already brought her *minchah*, the *mishnah* turns to the next stage: writing the *megillah* and scraping its contents into the water. The *kohen* comes to write the *megillah* — *ba lo lichtov et ha-megillah* — and the question immediately arises: from which point in the relevant passage does he begin writing?

### Biblical Pesukim Order

Before examining the *mishnah*'s answer, it is worth pausing to review the order of the *pesukim* in *Parshat ha-Sotah*, since the *mishnah*'s presentation does not straightforwardly follow that order.

The passage begins with the husband bringing his wife to the *kohen* along with her offering of a tenth of an *eifah* of barley flour — *lo yitzok alav shemen v'lo yitein alav levonah* — no oil or frankincense, for it is a *minchah* of jealousy, a memorial offering that recalls iniquity. That is where our *perek* began. The *kohen* then presents her before God, takes holy water in an earthen vessel, and adds dust from the floor of the *Mishkan* to the water — *v'natan el ha-mayim* — which is what the previous *mishnah* covered.

Then comes: the *kohen* stands the woman before God, dishevels her hair, places the *minchah* in her hands — and in the *kohen*'s hands are the bitter, curse-inducing waters. This passage already mentions disheveling her hair, which in fact appeared much earlier in the *mishnayot*' treatment. Next: *v'hishbia otah ha-kohen* — the *kohen* makes her take an oath, saying: "If no man has lain with you, and if you have not gone astray in impurity under your husband, *hinaki mi'mei ha-marerim ha-eileh* — be cleansed of these bitter, curse-inducing waters." Then the conditional curse: "And you, if you have gone astray under your husband, and if you have become impure, and a man has given his seed in you apart from your husband — *yitein Hashem otach l'alah v'lishvuah b'toch amech* — may the Lord make you a curse and an oath among your people, may the Lord cause your thigh to fall and your belly to swell. *Uva'u ha-mayim ha-marerim ha-eileh b'me'ayich* — and let these bitter waters enter your innards to swell the belly and cause the thigh to fall." *V'amrah ha-ishah amen amen* — and the woman shall say: amen, amen.

Then: *v'katav et ha-alot ha-eileh ha-kohen ba-sefer u-machah el mei ha-marim* — the *kohen* writes these curses in a book and scrapes them into the bitter water — and then *v'hishkah et ha-ishah*, he makes her drink.

Importantly, the *mishnah* skips entirely over the *kohen*'s oral administration of the oath and proceeds directly to the writing. This omission will prove significant later.

### Mishnah: Writing Point

The *mishnah* asks: from where does the *kohen* begin writing? The answer is: from *v'im lo shachav ish otach* — "if no man has lain with you." That is the opening of the oath formula proper, beginning with the conditional declaration of innocence. 

The *mishnah* then adds that the *kohen* does not write the instructional text embedded in the *pesukim* — *eino kotev v'hishbia ha-kohen et ha-ishah*, the narration that "the *kohen* shall make her swear." The text to be written contains, as it were, quotation marks: the quoted speech of the oath, not the stage directions. And at the conclusion, the *mishnah* states *eino kotev v'amrah ha-ishah amen amen* — the woman's response of *amen amen* is likewise not written, for that is her reaction to the oath, not the oath itself. This, the *mishnah* implies, is the position of the *tanna kamma*.

### Tanna Kamma View

The *tanna kamma*'s approach, then, is to write the full quoted text of the oath — both the conditional declaration of innocence ("if no man has lain with you, be cleansed") and the curse that follows — while omitting the narrative instructions embedded in the middle of the *pesukim* and the woman's concluding response of *amen amen*.

One might ask whether it is problematic to omit the middle section of the *pesukim*. This is precisely the concern raised by the *tanna kamma*'s formulation: you are not cutting *within* any one *pasuk*, but rather excising what is, in context, parenthetical instruction. The quoted speech continues uninterrupted; only the interposed narrative direction is dropped. That is a natural reading — you write the words in quote marks, so to speak, and skip the words outside them.

### Rabbi Yehudah View

*Rabbi Yehuda* takes a far more restrictive position. *Kol atzmo eino kotev ela* — his entire point is to write nothing other than the curse formula itself: *v'yitein Hashem otach l'alah u'lishvuah b'toch amech, uva'u ha-mayim ha-marerim ha-eileh b'me'ayich* — may the Lord make you a curse and an oath, and let the waters enter your innards. *Rashi* explains *kol atzmo* as an idiom indicating that one must be scrupulously careful to write only the curse phrase and nothing beyond it.

*Rabbi Yehuda* agrees with the *tanna kamma* that *v'amrah ha-ishah amen amen* is not written. But he goes far further: he also omits the opening conditional — the clause about being cleansed if innocent — and writes nothing of the conditional framing of guilt. Only the curse itself goes into the *megillah*.

This position is striking in light of a theme that has run throughout the *mishnayot*: the *sotah* procedure is presented throughout with a presumption of guilt. The process has consistently been framed not as a clarification of her innocence but as the administration of punishment for her transgression. *Rabbi Yehuda*'s view reflects this most sharply — the *megillah* contains only the curse; there is no trace in the written text of the possibility that she is innocent.

One might argue, as was raised in discussion, that *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position is not necessarily about a presumption of guilt, but about a more precise understanding of the *mechanics* of the water's power. The water is the *me'arerim* — the cursing water. What makes it cursed is the written curse scraped into it. The curse-producing element is specifically the curse text. If she is innocent, the water will not harm her regardless — so perhaps the rationale is about the function of the *megillah* rather than any presumption about her guilt.

That said, the objection remains: if one thinks about the *power of the verses entering the water*, then the water itself is also conditional — because the full *pasuk* presents a conditional reality. If she is innocent, *v'niktah v'nizre'ah zara* — she will be cleansed and will bear seed. Not including those words means, in a sense, that only the curse element is being placed into the water. This tension is not fully resolved in the *mishnah* and awaits the *Gemara*'s analysis.

## Gemara Debate

### Rabbi Meir: Implicit

The *Gemara* asks: *b'mai kamifligi* — what is the source of the disagreement? *B'hai kra kamifligi* — they dispute the reading of the following *pasuk*: *v'katav et ha-alot ha-eileh ha-kohen ba-sefer* — he shall write these curses in the book.

*Rabbi Meir* — who is identified as the *tanna kamma* — holds that *alot*, the curses, means *alot mamash*, the actual curse text. The additional *hei* at the beginning — *ha-alot* — is a *ribui*, an expansion: *l'rabot klalot ha-ba'ot machamat brachot* — to include the curses that come by way of the blessing. What does this mean? The phrase *hinaki mi'mei ha-marerim* — be cleansed from the bitter waters — is ostensibly a blessing. But it implies a curse: if you are not innocent, you will not be cleansed. The *hei* of *ha-alot* therefore includes even this implicit curse — the conditional statement of innocence — within what must be written, because it is the flip side of the curse.

Then *eileh* — "these" — serves to limit: *l'ma'utei klalot she'be-Mishneh Torah* — to exclude the curses that appear in *Parshat Ki Tavo*, which uses the same language of *alah*. Those *klalot* are not to be included. And *ha-eileh*, with the additional *hei*, further limits — *l'ma'utei tzava'ot v'kabalot amen* — to exclude the instructional portions and the woman's *amen amen*.

### Rabbi Yose: No Cutting

*Rabbi Yose* accepts the overall framework of the *derashah* but extends it in a different direction. He holds that *et ha-alot ha-eileh* — the word *et* — comes to include the instructional text of the *pesukim* and the woman's response of *amen amen*. That is, *et l'rabot tzava'ot v'kabalot* — the *et* expands what is written to include the entire *pasuk* without interruption. His concern, in effect, is that one does not chop a *pasuk* in the middle. Starting from the beginning of the oath and including the conclusion — the woman's *amen amen* — he writes the entire passage without cutting any portion out.

*Rabbi Yose*'s position is thus actually broader than the *tanna kamma* on the question of the instructional text embedded in the middle. The *tanna kamma* cuts out the narrative directions; *Rabbi Yose* does not cut anything.

### Meir Responds

*Rabbi Meir*, by contrast, is *esin lo darish* — he does not accept *et* as a *ribui*. He is simply not impressed with the word *et* as a basis for including additional content. Therefore, unlike *Rabbi Yose*, he does omit the narrative instructions and the *amen amen* response.

### Yehudah: Minimal

*Rabbi Yehuda* takes the same words — *alot*, *ha-alot*, *eileh*, *ha-eileh* — but reads all of them as *mi'utim*, limitations, rather than expansions. *Alot mamash* — curses, yes, but only the actual curse text. *Ha-alot* — the *hei* is not a *ribui* but a *mi'ut*: *l'ma'utei klalot ha-ba'ot machamat brachot* — specifically to exclude the conditional innocence clause at the beginning, which is not itself a curse. *Eileh* — to exclude the curses of *Mishneh Torah*. *Ha-eileh* — to agree that the narrative instruction and the *amen amen* are excluded. Thus *Rabbi Yehuda* uses every extra letter to narrow, narrowing the written text to only the curse formula at the end.

The *Gemara* thus presents a spectrum: write everything (*Rabbi Yose*), write the full oath but omit the instructions and *amen amen* (*tanna kamma / Rabbi Meir*), or write only the curse (*Rabbi Yehuda*).

It is worth pausing to consider whether these *derashot* reflect genuine hermeneutic differences — about when a *hei* expands versus when it limits, or whether *et* carries *ribui* — or whether each *tanna* began with a different intuition about what makes sense, and then found the hermeneutic language to support it. One position finds it logically indispensable to include both sides of the conditional; another feels that only the curse need enter the water; a third insists that one does not interrupt a *pasuk*. It is an open question whether the hermeneutic generated the conclusion or the conclusion generated the hermeneutic.

### Hei Analysis

The *Gemara* itself asks a sharp question: both *ha-alot* and *ha-eileh* contain an extra *hei* — yet *Rabbi Meir* treats *ha-alot* as expansive and *ha-eileh* as restrictive. Why does the same letter do opposite work in each location?

The *Gemara* answers: it depends on context. *Hei de-gabei de-ribuiya hi* — when the *hei* attaches to a word that is inherently expansive, as *alot* is (since you are being told to write the *alot*, which implies writing what belongs to them), the *hei* expands further, including even the implicit curses at the beginning. *Hei de-gabei de-mi'uta* — when the *hei* attaches to a word that is inherently limiting, as *eileh* ("these" already restricts), the *hei* reinforces the limitation, excluding even the narrative instruction and the *amen amen*.

In the end, the dispute distills to four positions about what gets written: the *pasuk* in full without excision (*Rabbi Yose*); the full oath text minus embedded instruction and the woman's response (*tanna kamma*); the full oath text including the innocence clause, minus instruction and *amen amen* (*Rabbi Meir*, which on one reading is the same as *tanna kamma*); or only the bare curse formula (*Rabbi Yehuda*).

## Inverse Inference

### Meir & Inference

The *Gemara* now raises a pointed challenge to *Rabbi Meir*. *Rabbi Meir* holds that the opening conditional clause — "if no man has lain with you, be cleansed" — is an *implicit curse*, and that is why the *hei* of *ha-alot* includes it. But *Rabbi Meir* is famously of the opinion that *mi-klal lav attah shomea hen* — from a negative formulation you cannot infer a positive, and from a positive you cannot infer a negative. In other words, if the *pasuk* says "if you are innocent, be cleansed," one cannot automatically infer the inverse: "if you are guilty, you will not be cleansed." Yet that inference is precisely what makes the innocence clause an *implicit curse* according to *Rabbi Meir*'s analysis.

This principle is established in the context of *tena'im* — the formal conditions that must be stated when making stipulations. *Rabbi Meir* holds that a *tenai kaful* — a double condition — is required: you must spell out explicitly both sides of the stipulation. The model is Moshe's agreement with *Bnei Gad u-Bnei Reuven*: *im ya'avru chalutzim* — if they cross in arms before their brothers and the land is subdued, they receive their portion *me-ever la-Yarden*; *v'im lo ya'avru* — and if they do not cross, they will settle among you in Canaan. Both sides must be stated, because you cannot logically derive the inverse from a single conditional statement alone.

Indeed, as anyone who has studied formal logic knows, if P then Q does not entail if not-P then not-Q. The statement "if it rains, we will not play ball" does not mean "if it does not rain, we will play ball" — it only means that if we did play ball, it cannot have rained. So "if you are innocent, be cleansed" does not strictly imply "if you are guilty, you will be punished." You would need that to be stated explicitly.

The question is whether *Rabbi Meir*'s principle that one cannot infer the inverse applies broadly and universally, or whether it is limited to formal *tena'im* — where the concern is about the strict legal sufficiency of a stipulation's formulation. If it is a broad principle, then *Rabbi Meir* cannot treat "be cleansed if innocent" as implying an inverse curse for guilt, and the whole basis of his *derashah* unravels.

### Tanchum: Chinaki

*Rabbi Tanchum* resolves this difficulty with a linguistic observation: *chinaki ktiv* — the *pasuk* reads *hinaki*, which can be parsed as *chinaki*, meaning "be strangled." If you read the conditional clause with that double valence — if you are innocent, *hinaki*, be cleansed; but embedded in the very word is also *chinaki*, be strangled — then the clause is not merely a statement of potential innocence from which a curse must be inferred inversely. The curse is, in a sense, already there within the word itself, as a play on its letters. This makes the clause less *implicitly* cursed and more directly so, giving *Rabbi Meir* firmer ground to include it as part of the *alot* that must be written.

### Akiva: Fire

At this point the *Gemara* introduces a celebrated *derashah* of *Rabbi Akiva*. *Ish v'ishah* — man and woman. Take the letters of *ish*, aleph-yud-shin, and *ishah*, aleph-shin-hei. God's name, *yud-hei*, is distributed within the words of man and woman: the *yud* in *ish*, the *hei* in *ishah*. *Zachu* — if they merit — *shechina beineihem* — the divine presence is between them. If they do not merit — *lo zachu* — *esh ochaltan* — fire consumes them. Remove the *yud* and the *hei* and what remains in both words is *aleph-shin*, *esh*, fire.

*Rashi* explains *zachu* in concrete moral terms: *lalechet be-derech yesharah* — to walk on the straight path — *shelo yehei hu no'ef v'lo hi no'efet* — that he should not be an adulterer and she not an adulteress. This is a striking formulation, because it reintroduces the man as a potential offender on equal terms with the woman. It is worth noting that technically, under *halacha*, a man commits adultery only when he sleeps with a *married woman*; sleeping with an unmarried woman, while prohibited, is not the technical offense of *ni'uf* against his own wife. Yet *Rashi* here seems to read the moral register more broadly: cheating on one's spouse — regardless of the technical legal category — tears the marriage, and then *esh ochaltan*.

The *Gemara* continues: *amar Rava, v'de-ishah adifa mi-de-ish* — *Rava* observes that the woman's fire is greater than the man's. In the word *ish*, the *aleph* and *shin* of *esh* are separated by the *yud* — God's letter stands between the fire-letters and keeps them in check. In *ishah*, the *aleph* and *shin* are adjacent — *mitzarfis* — the fire letters are already joined. *Rashi* glosses: *esh shel ishah kashah u-mi-maharet le-echol* — the woman's fire is fierce and swift to consume. Whether this reflects something about the nature of temptation, the social dynamics of the household when infidelity occurs, or some other concern, the *Gemara* does not spell out fully, and the plain meaning remains somewhat open.

The connection of this *derashah* to the *sotah* procedure is worth appreciating. The entire process takes place in the *Beit ha-Mikdash*, where God's presence dwells. God's name is being written on the parchment and then scraped into the water. If the couple's relationship has deteriorated to the point that God's name is not sufficiently present in their marriage to avert this crisis — that the fire has not been kept in check — then the procedure is an attempt to bring God's name more directly into the situation and, through it, resolve the conflict. If she is innocent, the water — containing the divine name — douses the fire. If she is guilty, the fire consumes. It is a fitting thematic arc.

## Dust & Divine Name

### Rava: Merit

*Amar Rava* — why does the *Torah* prescribe bringing *afar*, dust, for the *sotah*? *Zachtah, yotzei mimenah ben k'Avraham Avinu* — if she merits, she will bring forth a son like *Avraham Avinu*, of whom it is written *afar va-efer* — dust and ashes. *Lo zachtah, tachzor la-afarah* — if she does not merit, she returns to her dust.

The connection to *v'niktah v'nizre'ah zara* — she will be cleansed and bear seed — is thus given a more specific content: the child she will bear is compared to *Avraham Avinu*. And if not, she reverts to dust — a fitting end.

### Abraham: Merit

The *Gemara* continues with a *derashah* of *Rava*: because *Avraham Avinu* said *v'anochi afar va-efer* — and I am but dust and ashes — his descendants merited two *mitzvot* connected to *afar* and *efer*: *efer parah* — the ashes of the *parah adumah* — and *afar sotah* — the dust of the *sotah*.

The *Gemara* immediately asks: but there is also *afar kisuy ha-dam* — dust used to cover blood after *shechita* — which is also a *mitzvah* involving dust. The answer: *hasam hachsher mitzvah ika, hana'ah leka* — there it is merely the performance of a *mitzvah*, but there is no concrete benefit. Here, both the *efer parah* and the *afar sotah* produce tangible benefit — the ashes of the *parah adumah* restore *taharah*, and the dust of the *sotah* resolves strife between husband and wife.

### Derasha: Efer

The *Gemara* then records a second *derashah* of *Rava*: because *Avraham* said *im mi-chut v'ad s'roch na'al* — from a thread to a sandal strap, I will take nothing of the spoils of *Sdom* — his descendants merited two *mitzvot*: *chut shel techelet* — the thread of *techelet* in *tzitzit* — and *retzuah shel tefillin* — the strap of *tefillin*, which, like a shoelace, is made of leather.

Again the *Gemara* requires that these be *mitzvot* with concrete this-worldly benefit. *Retzuah shel tefillin* — this is established by the *pasuk*: *v'ra'u kol amei ha-aretz ki shem Hashem nikra alecha v'yare'u mimeka* — all the peoples of the earth will see that God's name is called upon you, and they will be in awe of you. A *baraita* identifies this with the *tefillin she-ba-rosh* — and *Rabbi Eliezer ha-Gadol* confirms it. Wearing *tefillin* on one's head causes others to perceive one's connection to God and generates protective awe.

### Techelet: Throne

Then the *Gemara* asks: *ela chut shel techelet mai hi* — in what way does wearing *techelet* produce concrete benefit? *Detanya, Rabbi Meir omer*: *mah nishtanah techelet mi-kol minei tzivonin* — what distinguishes *techelet* from all other colors? Because *techelet* resembles the sea, the sea resembles the sky, and the sky resembles the *kise ha-kavod* — the divine throne. This is supported by two *pesukim*: *v'tachtat raglav k'ma'aseh livnat ha-sapir u'che'etzem ha-shamayim la-tohar* — and under His feet was like the work of a sapphire brick, like the very essence of the sky in its purity — and *k'mareh even sapir dmut kise* — like the appearance of a sapphire stone is the form of the throne. The *techelet* thus draws one's gaze upward — from sea to sky to throne — and creates a genuine connection to God, a benefit of a different order than financial gain but concrete and real nonetheless.

The pattern in all these *derashot* is consistent: *Avraham*'s merit produced *mitzvot* for his descendants that carry not merely the reward of performance but a palpable this-worldly effect — purification, domestic peace, divine awe, and connection to God.

## Writing Materials

### Surfaces

A new *mishnah* addresses the physical requirements for writing the *megillah*. The *kohen* may not write on a *luach* — *Rashi* explains this as a wooden tablet — nor on *neyar*, paper, which *Rashi* describes as made from a fibrous material, presumably a papyrus-like substance. Nor may he write on *diphera*, which is untreated or incompletely treated hide. Rather he must write on the *megillah*, that is, on properly prepared parchment — *klaf*.

It is interesting that the *mishnah* uses the word *megillah* here rather than *klaf*, since the *Torah* itself uses the word *sefer*. The *mishnah* contrasts *diphera* with *megillah* rather than with *klaf* — the constructed *megillah* as an object, not merely the raw parchment. The *pasuk* cited is *she-ne'emar ba-sefer* — for so the *Torah* says: in a *sefer*.

### Ink Requirements

The *mishnah* continues: one may not write using *komos* — *Rashi* identifies this as a tree sap — nor *kankantom*, which is copper sulphate, nor with any substance that leaves a permanent mark — *kol davar she-roshem*. The concern is indelibility: if the ink is absorbed into the parchment such that even scraping leaves a residue, the substance is invalid. The ink must sit on the surface of the parchment without being absorbed, so that it can be fully scraped off and dissolved into the water.

The valid substance is *deyo* — the standard ink used for *Sifrei Torah* and the like, which sits on the surface and can be scraped off cleanly. The *pasuk* cited is *she-ne'emar u-machah* — the *Torah* says "and he erased" — requiring *ketav she-yachol le-himachot*, writing that can be erased. This implies not merely that the ink can be removed, but that when scraped it leaves nothing behind — the words must be fully dissolved into the water.

## Validity Conditions

### Nighttime Invalid

*Rava* rules: *megillat sotah she-ketavah ba-laylah pesulah* — if the *megillah* was written at night, it is invalid. The source is a *gezerah shavah*: *v'asah lah ha-kohen et kol ha-Torah ha-zot* — the *kohen* shall perform for her all this instruction — is linked to *al pi ha-Torah asher yoru-cha v'al ha-mishpat* — according to the instruction they teach you and according to the judgment. Just as judgment must take place during the day — *mishpat ba-yom* — so too *megillat sotah* must be written during the day.

### Backward Invalid

If the *megillah* was written *le-mafrea* — in reverse order, writing from the end backwards even if the final product reads correctly — it is invalid. The source: *v'katav et ha-alot ha-eileh* — write these curses — meaning write them *ke-heichi de-chtivei*, in the order they are written. The *pasuk* implies forward sequential writing, not writing that arrives at the correct text by working backwards.

### Pre-Oath Invalid

If the *megillah* was written before the woman accepted the oath — *kodem she-tikabel aleha ha-shevuah* — it is invalid. The source: *v'hishbia* — he made her swear — *v'achar kach v'katav* — and afterwards he wrote. This is the explicit sequence of the *pesukim*, and it must be followed. Notably, the *mishnah* itself skipped over the oath-taking entirely and moved directly to the writing, yet the actual *halacha* requires that the oath precede the writing. This underscores what *Tosafot* will observe: the order of the *mishnah* does not determine the *halachic* order.

### No Scoring Invalid

*Ketavah iggeret pesulah* — if it was written as a letter, it is invalid. *Rashi* explains this as writing without *shirtut* — scoring. *Sifrei kodesh* are written with scored lines on the parchment; if the *megillah* was written without this scoring, it is considered a mere letter and not a *sefer*, and therefore invalid. The derivation: *ba-sefer amrah Rachmana* — the *Torah* said it must be in a *sefer*, meaning with the formal requirements of *sifrei kodesh*.

### Two Parchments

If the *megillah* was written on two separate pieces of parchment — say, the text did not fit on one piece — it is invalid: *sefer echad amrah Rachmana, v'lo shenayim u-sheloshah sefarim* — the *Torah* required one book, not two or three.

### Intermittent Invalid

Finally, if the *kohen* wrote one letter and scraped it off, wrote the next letter and scraped it off — so that the entire text was never present on the parchment at one time — this is invalid: *d'chtiv v'asah lah ha-kohen et kol ha-Torah ha-zot* — the entire text must be present at once before it is scraped into the water.

## Tosafot Analysis

### Sefer Distinction

*Tosafot* raises an extensive question about the ruling that writing on a *luach* or *neyar* is invalid. In other halachic contexts — for example, a *get* — the *Torah* uses the language of *v'katav lah sefer keritut*, and the rabbis derive from the word *sefer* there that one may write a *get* on virtually any surface, even a cow's horn. Why, then, is the *megillat sotah* restricted to parchment?

The distinction *Tosafot* draws is the preposition *bet*. By the *sotah*, the *Torah* says *ba-sefer* — in a book — which places the emphasis on the physical object itself. The *megillah* must be a *sefer* in the full, physically realized sense. By the *get*, the *Torah* says *sefer keritut* — a document of severance — and the word *sefer* there is taken by the rabbis as *sefirat devarim be'alma*, a mere recounting of separation, emphasizing the content rather than the physical form. Hence the broad permissiveness for writing surfaces by a *get* but strict limitation to *klaf* by the *megillat sotah*.

Separately, the *Yerushalmi* raises the question of whether parchment from a non-kosher animal may be used. One consideration there is: if the woman refuses to drink and the *megillah* is not erased, you would be leaving God's name written on parchment from a non-kosher animal, which is unseemly. The *Yerushalmi* also asks whether the *megillah*, before being erased, has *kedushah* — does it convey impurity to the hands the way sacred *sifrei kodesh* do? The tentative answer is that it may not, because it was written for the purpose of being erased, which may deprive it of the standing of a sacred *sefer*. These remain interesting questions about the status of an object whose nature is fundamentally transitional.

On the matter of the nighttime invalidation, *Tosafot* addresses what type of judgment *sotah* resembles. *Dinei mamonot* — monetary cases — must begin during the day but may conclude at night. *Dinei nefashot* — capital cases — must be conducted entirely during the day, beginning and end. *Tosafot* rules that *sotah* resembles *dinei nefashot*: *kol din sotah, bein gmar bein techilah, pasul ba-laylah* — every aspect of the *sotah* process, whether beginning or completion, is invalid if performed at night. This framing of *sotah* as analogous to *dinei nefashot* is significant: it reflects the understanding that what is being adjudicated is, in effect, a capital matter. If found guilty, the woman will die — and *Chazal* understand this even though the *pesukim* do not state death explicitly. Treating it as *dinei nefashot* is therefore consistent with that thematic reading of the entire procedure.

### Scoring Requirement

*Tosafot* then turns to the requirement of *shirtut*. Why does the *pasuk* need to tell us that writing without scoring invalidates the *megillah*? There is already a rule elsewhere — derived at the opening of *Gittin* — that one may not write even three words from a *pasuk* without scoring, even in the context of ordinary correspondence. Given that this is already a general prohibition, surely the *megillat sotah* must also be written with scoring. What novel information does the *pasuk* add?

*Tosafot*'s answer: the existing requirement establishes a prohibition on writing without scoring, but a prohibition does not automatically mean that an object produced in violation of that prohibition is halachically invalid. One might have violated the rule and yet produced a valid *megillah*. The *pasuk* comes to tell us that here, the absence of scoring is not merely a procedural violation — it renders the *megillah* itself *pesulah* as an object. The formality of *ba-sefer* is *me'akev*, not merely *l'chatchilah*.

### Tosafot Question

*Tosafot* then develops an extended analysis of when *shirtut* is required and when it is not, working through the case of *tefillin*, where the *pesukim* are written without the full scoring applied to a *Sefer Torah*. *Tosafot* proposes distinguishing between two types of scoring: a perimeter score around the entire section, which satisfies the general prohibition against writing three words of a *pasuk* without any scored border, and the line-by-line scoring required for full formal *sifrei kodesh*.

At the conclusion, *Tosafot* cites a tradition in the name of *Tosafot Rabbeinu* from *Masechet Gittin*, transmitted in the name of *Rabbi Eliyahu ha-Tzarfati*: when one quotes the language of a *pasuk* in correspondence not as a direct citation of a *pasuk* but as flowery Hebrew expression — *amira be'alma lifrosh b'shalom* — using the words as literary idiom rather than as scripture, there is no obligation of *shirtut*. But if one is writing a letter and explicitly cites a *pasuk* as such — "as the *pasuk* says..." followed by the quoted text — then *ki hai gavna assur le-michtav belo shirtut*, one may not write it without scoring.

*Tosafot* then adds its own question — and notably does not resolve it: *v'lo yadana minan li-michtav be-peirushin pesukim belo shirtut* — we do not know the source permitting the writing of *pesukim* in commentaries without *shirtut*, in cases where the *pasuk* is being brought as an explicit citation. Commentaries on *Torah* and *Gemara* routinely cite *pesukim* explicitly as *pesukim* without performing *shirtut*. How is this permitted? *Tosafot* leaves the question open.

A parallel question concerns quoting partial *pesukim* — whether citing only a portion of a *pasuk*, particularly when that portion includes *shem Hashem*, is permissible. *Rav Ovadia Yosef* addresses this in a *teshuvah* and concludes that the *Gemara* itself quotes partial *pesukim* containing *shem Hashem* without concern, demonstrating that the rule of *kol pasuk de-lo paskei Moshe* — not dividing a *pasuk* — applies specifically to a ritual recitation context, not to learning, discussion, or citation in analysis. The *megillat sotah* itself, as a ritual act, might be governed by that stricter standard, while ordinary Torah discourse is not. But the question of *shirtut* in correspondence and commentary remains, as *Tosafot* acknowledges, unresolved.

---

---

# Sotah 18

## Ketivah & Mechika Lishmah

### Two Scrolls, One Vessel

The daf opens with a question posed by Rava (*ba'ei Rava*) concerning the practical mechanics of the *sotah* ritual. Suppose a *kohen* is processing two *sotot* simultaneously and writes two *megillot* — one for each woman — and then scrapes them both into a single vessel. May both women drink from that one vessel?

### Individual Process Requi…

The underlying issue is the requirement of *ketivah lishmah* — that the scroll must be written specifically for her, as the verse states *vechatav lah hakohen*, "and the priest shall write for her." This requirement has already been established: the scroll cannot be pre-written, and it must be composed after she takes the oath. The *ketivah lishmah* requirement is clearly satisfied here, since each scroll was written individually for its respective woman. But the Gemara raises a further possibility: perhaps *mechika lishmah* is also required — that the act of scraping must itself be individualized for each woman.

The concern with simultaneous scraping is that even if one's knife moved across one woman's parchment for her sake and across the other woman's parchment for hers, the overall *process* of producing the bitter waters was not focused on one individual woman. Rather, it was a single process being conducted for two women at once. Whether *lishmah* requires that the action be understood as distinctly oriented toward a single individual — not merely labeled in one's mind — is the substance of the question.

### Mixed Waters Problem

The Gemara then extends the question through a series of progressive scenarios. Suppose one concedes that *mechika lishmah* is required, and proceeds correctly: each woman's scroll is scraped into its own separate vessel. Now, however, the contents of those two vessels are poured together into one. The *ketivah* and *mechika* were each performed properly and individually, but the resulting waters are now commingled. Is that a problem?

The Gemara formulates this concern sharply: *hai lav didah ka shatya v'hai lav didah ka shatya* — each woman is drinking water that is not exclusively hers. The question is whether drinking requires that the water be precisely the water prepared for that individual.

### Breira & Re-division

The Gemara carries the inquiry one step further: suppose after mixing the waters, one then re-divides them into two separate vessels. Is this valid? The Gemara invokes the concept of *breira* — the legal principle of retroactive determination. Do we say that upon re-division, each vessel is deemed to contain the water that was originally hers? Or do we say *ein breira*, and the re-division accomplishes nothing, since the waters cannot magically self-separate along their original lines?

The Gemara concludes all three sub-questions with *teiku* — the matter remains unresolved.

One might note how peculiar it would be to invoke *breira* in the conventional sense here. Normally, *breira* concerns situations where something was never distinctly identified at the outset and we ask retroactively which portion was always meant to belong to a particular party — such as brothers dividing an inherited estate, or grain designated as *terumah* only after the fact. In those cases, nothing was mixed; rather, something existed in an undifferentiated state and was eventually assigned. But here, two separately prepared, distinguishable waters were fully merged. Saying that upon re-division each woman receives precisely her original water seems to invoke not *breira* in the usual halakhic sense but something approaching outright magic.

### Tosafot on Breira

Tosafot addresses this difficulty directly and at length. Tosafot begins by noting that ordinary *breira* cannot mean that a fully diffused mixture retroactively resolves back into its original components. If that were possible, one could solve any case of *taarovet* — say, *terumah* wine mixed into *chullin* wine — simply by pouring into two vessels and declaring that the *terumah* went into one of them. Clearly that is untenable.

Tosafot therefore reframes the Gemara's question. The real concern with commingling the waters, Tosafot argues, is not that each woman happens to drink water that belongs to another woman. Drinking someone else's water is not itself the problem. Rather, when the two separately prepared waters are merged into a single vessel from which both women drink, the two distinct ritual processes are effectively collapsed into one. The individuality of each woman's *sotah* ordeal is dissolved when everything ends in a single common cup.

If that is the correct framing, then what the Gemara means when it asks about *yesh breira* after re-division is not whether the waters physically self-separate along their original lines — that is impossible and Tosafot explicitly rejects it — but rather whether re-dividing into separate vessels restores the appearance and legal reality of two distinct processes. Once each woman is drinking from her own cup — a cup dedicated exclusively to her, in which only she is drinking — the *mechika* performed for her and the *ketivah* written for her can again be understood as a complete, individualized ritual, even if some of the other woman's water happens to be admixed within. The re-division may be sufficient to reconstitute the distinctiveness of the process in each woman's case.

Tosafot acknowledges that this reading is difficult and the full formulation remains complex, but the thrust is: *yesh breira* in this context means not physical self-selection but rather that re-division re-establishes the ritual distinctiveness that the commingling had disrupted. The Gemara, notably, frames all of this in purely halakhic terms — whether the process was conducted *for her* — rather than in terms of any metaphysical power inhering in the waters themselves.

---

## Drinking Methods

### Straw/Sieve Drinking

Rava poses an additional question: *hashka besiv* — what is the law if the woman drank through a fiber, or through a straw (*bishfoferet*)? Is that a valid mode of drinking? The operative question is *miderech shtiah bekach o ein derech shtiah bekach* — is this a normal manner of drinking or not? The Gemara concludes *teiku*.

Tosafot notes a parallel case discussed elsewhere in the Talmud regarding eating *matzah* when it is wrapped in fiber (*karchah besiv*) — whether that constitutes valid *achilah*. However, Tosafot points out that the cases are distinguishable: when food is encased in something, the casing interposes between the food and the throat, raising a question of *chatzitzah*. By contrast, a straw or fiber tube does not actually surround the liquid as it passes down the throat; it merely conveys the liquid from cup to mouth. The question here is therefore more genuinely whether drinking via a conveyance is *derech shtiah* — the normal manner of drinking as envisioned by the Torah — rather than whether there is an interposition.

The *Aruch* is cited with an interpretation that sheds further light. According to the *Aruch*, the fiber (*siv*) was placed into the water, absorbed it like a sponge, and then the saturated fiber was brought to her mouth, from which she sucked the water out. This makes the question considerably more compelling, since it is far less obvious that sucking water from an absorbent material constitutes *derech shtiah* in the manner of the verse *vehishka et hamayim* — "and he shall make her drink the water."

### Spilled Water

Rav Ashi raises a final question: *nishpechu mehen venishtayru mehen* — what if some of the water spilled and she drank only what remained? The Gemara again concludes *teiku*.

---

## Two Oaths & Curse

### Repeated Oath in Torah

Rabbi Zeira, citing Rav, raises the question: *shtei shevuot ha'amurot beSotah lamah* — why does the Torah mention the making of an oath twice in the *sotah* passage? The structure of the relevant verses is as follows: the first instance of *vehishbia otah hakohen* introduces the conditional formulation — if you have not gone astray you will be cleared, and if you have gone astray... — without completing the consequence.
