The second instance of *vehishbia hakohen et ha'ishah bishvuat ha'alah* then introduces the explicit curse: God shall make you an *alah* and an oath among your people, the water shall enter your belly.

One might have thought that one oath precedes the scraping of the scroll and the other follows it. But Rava objects: both oaths as they appear in the text clearly precede the scraping. That interpretation is therefore untenable.

### Oath with/without Alah

Rava therefore offers an alternative: one instance refers to a *shvuah she'yesh imah alah* — an oath accompanied by a curse — and the other to a *shvuah she'ein imah alah* — an oath without a curse. The first, more conditional presentation is an oath without an explicit curse, while the second invokes the full force of the *alah*.

### Defining Shvuah Sheyesh…

The Gemara then struggles to define precisely what constitutes a *shvuah she'yesh imah alah*. Rav Abba citing Rav offers: *mashpiani alayich she-lo nitmeis she-im nitmeis yavo'u bach* — I am making you swear that you did not sin, because if you sinned the water will come upon you. The curse functions as the motivating consequence of the oath — swear truthfully and understand that if you are lying, this is the result.

Rava objects that this construction leaves the curse as a separate, parallel element: the *alah* stands on its own and the *shvuah* stands on its own, but the oath does not actually incorporate the curse. Rava therefore proposes: *mashpiani alayich she-im nitmeis yavo'u bach* — I am making you swear that if you have sinned the waters will come upon you. But Rav Ashi counters: that formulation contains a curse but where is the oath? She is merely being told what will happen; she is not attesting to anything.

Rav Ashi ultimately proposes: *mashpiani alayich she-lo nitmeis v'im nitmeis yavo'u bach* — I am making you swear that you did not sin, and if you sinned let the waters come upon you. The precise distinction between this and Rav Abba's original formulation is not entirely transparent, and the Gemara acknowledges the difficulty.

### Rashi on Two Oaths

Rashi offers a clarifying framework. In Rashi's reading, the *shvuah* of the woman is exclusively her attestation to the truth of her declaration: *mashpiani alayich she-yehai emes mah she-amart lefaneinu she-lo nitmeis* — I am making you swear that what you have said before us — that you did not sin — is true. That is the *shvuah* in the strict sense: the woman swears to the veracity of her own statement.

The second element — *v'im nitmeis yavo'u bach mayim* — is the *alah*, the curse, which the *kohen* calls upon to take effect upon the woman if she is lying. Rashi understands this as the *kohen* forswearing the curse to do its duty — invoking the *alah* as one might invoke witnesses or heavenly forces — in the manner of *ha'azinu hashamayim va'adabera*, calling upon heaven and earth as witnesses. The *kohen* is not administering the curse as an addendum; he is actively summoning it into its role. Thus there are genuinely two distinct acts: the woman's oath attesting to her truthfulness, and the *kohen*'s invocation of the curse to operate upon her if her oath is false. The *shvuah* and the *alah* are separate in nature but bound together in the ceremony.

---

## Amen Amen & Scope

### Double Amen

The Mishnah states that the woman responds *amen amen* — the double affirmation. The Gemara explains: *amen al ha-alah, amen al ha-shvuah* — one *amen* accepts the *alah* and one *amen* affirms the *shvuah*. That is, with one *amen* she declares: yes, I accept the consequence — let the water come upon me if I have lied. With the other she declares: yes, I am swearing that I am telling the truth. Rashi accordingly reads *amen shelo nitmesi* as *kabbalas shvuah* — acceptance of the oath — and *amen v'im nitmesi yavo'u vi* as *kabbalas alah* — acceptance of the curse.

The principle of *gilgul shvuah* is also operative here. Once a party has been validly brought before the court and compelled to take an oath on some matter, additional oaths may be attached. Consequently, since the husband is entitled to compel her oath regarding the specific man of suspicion, the court can also extend the oath to cover any man — she is swearing to her fidelity broadly, not only with respect to the particular individual named in the *kinui*.

### Different Men & Periods

The Mishnah further specifies: *amen me'ish zeh, amen me'ish acher* — one *amen* affirming she did not sin with this man, and one *amen* affirming she did not sin with any other man. The *sotah* ritual thus functions as an occasion to extend the scope of the oath well beyond the specific suspected incident.

### Arusah & Nesuah

The Mishnah states: *amen shelo satisi arusah unesua'ah* — she says *amen* that she did not commit adultery when she was an *arusah* and when she was a *nesuah*. The husband can ordinarily initiate the *sotah* process only during the period of *nisuin*, but since the oath is being administered, its scope may extend retroactively to her period of *eirusin* as well. Were she to have committed adultery during *eirusin*, she would have been forbidden to him; therefore the oath may encompass that period.

### Shomeret Yevam Status

The Mishnah adds: *veshomeret yevama mekunesah* — the oath may also extend to conduct during her period as a *shomeret yavam*, after her first husband died and before the *yavam* performed *yibbum*. This raises an immediate difficulty: it is not at all obvious that a *shomeret yavam* who sleeps with another man is thereby forbidden to the *yavam*. The prohibition of *lo tihiyeh eshes hameit hachutzah le'ish zar* is an *issur lav*, a negative prohibition, but that does not automatically mean that such conduct renders her *asurah* to the brother-in-law in the way that adultery renders a woman forbidden to her husband. The Mishnah's inclusion of this case implies that it does — and the Gemara will interrogate that implication.

The Mishnah concludes with the principle: *zeh klal, kol she-bi-ybeah lo haytah asurah lo, lo hayah matneh imah* — any circumstance in which intercourse with another man would not render her forbidden to him is outside the scope of the oath. The converse likewise holds: wherever such intercourse would render her forbidden, that period falls within the scope of the oath.

---

## Shomeret Yevam Forbidden?

### Rav Hamnuna Position

Rav Hamnuna draws a significant halakhic conclusion from the structure of the Mishnah: *shomeret yavam she-zintah asurah li-yvamah* — a woman awaiting *yibbum* who commits adultery is forbidden to the *yavam*. His argument is straightforward: the Mishnah allows the *yavam* to extend the oath to cover her conduct as a *shomeret yavam*. But the Mishnah also states explicitly that oath extension is only possible where intercourse would have rendered her forbidden. The only way both clauses can coexist is if sleeping with another man as a *shomeret yavam* does in fact render her forbidden to the *yavam*.

### EY Disagreement & Akiva

The Sages of Eretz Yisrael, however, rule otherwise: *leis hilkheta ke-Rav Hamnuna*. Despite acknowledging that Rav Hamnuna's reading of the Mishnah is compelling as *peshat*, they reject his conclusion. Their reasoning: the Mishnah's inclusion of the *shomeret yavam* case reflects a minority opinion. *Ha manni Rabbi Akiva hi* — this is the position of Rabbi Akiva.

### Why Not Rav Hamnuna

Rabbi Akiva holds a sweeping general principle: *ein kiddushin topsin be-chayavei lavin* — *kiddushin* is not binding when contracted with one who is prohibited by a negative commandment. Moreover, the offspring of such a union is a *mamzer*. Under Rabbi Akiva's framework, any prohibition at the level of *issur lav* is treated with extraordinary legal weight: not merely does one violate the prohibition, but the relationship itself is legally unrecognized, the *kiddushin* is void, and the child bears the status of *mamzer*.

Applied to *shomeret yavam*: the prohibition *lo tihiyeh eshes hameit hachutzah le'ish zar* is an *issur lav*, and under Rabbi Akiva's general approach any relationship entered into in violation of a *lav* is treated as if it were a prohibited union in the full sense — *kiddushin* does not bind, and the offspring is a *mamzer*. It is this general position of Rabbi Akiva that explains why, in his view, a *shomeret yavam* who sleeps with another man would be forbidden to the *yavam*: not because *yibbum* constitutes a quasi-marriage in some special sense, but because Rabbi Akiva weights every *issur lav* so heavily.

Rav Hamnuna's approach, by contrast, was not premised on Rabbi Akiva's general principle. He argued from the distinctive nature of *yibbum* itself: the *zikah* — the halakhic bond connecting the widow to the brother — is a form of quasi-marriage, and betrayal of that bond is akin to adultery. That is why, in his view, she is forbidden to him.

The Sages of Eretz Yisrael make a crucial distinction: the Mishnah's extension of the oath to the *shomeret yavam* case is not a universally held position. It reflects Rabbi Akiva's particular view. We do not rule like Rabbi Akiva here, and therefore a *shomeret yavam* who sleeps with another man is not, in the view of the majority, rendered forbidden to the *yavam*. The *kiddushin* of another man with her would be binding, she does not produce a *mamzer*, and she remains eligible for *yibbum*.

It is worth noting that there is no other case of an *issur lav* that creates the kind of relational context in which "sleeping with another man" could constitute something analogous to adultery. The only two legal frameworks in which a woman's sexual conduct with another man impinges upon an existing relational obligation are *nisuin* and *shomeret yavam*. Rabbi Akiva's position about *chayavei lavin* is thus distinctively operative precisely in the *shomeret yavam* case — not because *yibbum* is uniquely quasi-marital, but because Rabbi Akiva's principle is general, and *shomeret yavam* happens to be the only *issur lav* context in which the question of such betrayal can even arise.

---

## Oath Scope Extension

### Previous & Later Marriag…

Rabbi Yirmiah raises a further pair of questions regarding the extension of the *sotah* oath. First: *mahu she-yatne adam al nisuin harishonim* — can a man stipulate that the oath cover conduct during a previous marriage between them? That is, if a man divorced his wife and then remarried her, and now in the second marriage she is undergoing the *sotah* process, can he extend the oath to encompass any adultery she may have committed during the first marriage? Second: *al nisuei achiv* — can a *yavam* who performed *yibbum* extend the oath to cover conduct during the *arusah* period of the deceased brother's marriage, when that deceased brother was the husband?

These questions should be understood in light of the Mishnah's concluding principle: oath extension is permissible only where intercourse would have rendered her forbidden. Both scenarios above would satisfy that condition. Were she to have committed adultery during their first marriage, she would currently be forbidden to him in the second marriage. Were she to have committed adultery during the period when she was married to the deceased brother, she would have been ineligible for *yibbum*; the *yavam* could not have married her at all.

### Forbidden = Oath Allowed

The Gemara resolves Rabbi Yirmiah's questions by citing the Mishnah's general rule: *kol shetiba'el velo te'aser lo, lo hayah matneh imah* — wherever intercourse would not forbid her to him, he cannot stipulate; the logical contrapositive confirms that wherever it would forbid her, he may stipulate. Since in both of Rabbi Yirmiah's cases the conduct in question would render her forbidden in the relevant relational context, the oath extension is permitted. *Shema mina* — this may be derived from the rule.

One may also note a subtle point regarding the word *matneh*. Throughout this discussion, when the Gemara refers to the extension of the oath beyond its immediate default scope, it consistently uses the language of *matneh* — stipulation, active extension. This implies that such extensions are not automatic. The *yavam* or husband must explicitly extend the oath if he wishes it to apply to these additional circumstances; they do not take effect without such stipulation.

### Future Marriage Limits

Rav Ashi poses the converse case: *mahu she-yatne adam al nisuin ha'achronim* — can a man, in the context of Rabbi Meir's position that the oath can be future-oriented, stipulate that the oath cover conduct during a potential second marriage between them, if they were to divorce and remarry? The argument in favor: if she were to commit adultery after they remarried, she would be forbidden to him in that second marriage. The argument against: in the context of the current marriage, that future adultery does not render her presently forbidden. *Hashta meiha lo asira lei* — right now she is not forbidden to him.

The Gemara resolves this from the Mishnah's language as well. The Mishnah specifies that he cannot stipulate about the period of divorce, but does not say he cannot stipulate about a future remarriage. By implication, stipulating about conduct during a potential remarriage is permissible — just as he may stipulate about conduct during a prior marriage — since in both cases, were she to sin at those times, she would be forbidden to him in that marital context. The symmetry is exact: past first marriage and future second marriage are treated equivalently. *Shema mina*.

---

## Double Jeopardy

### Three Jeopardy Views

The *baraita* is introduced: *zot torat hakanot* — "this is the law of jealousy." The *tana kama* reads *zot torat* as an expansive formulation: *melamed she-isha shota ve-shona* — a woman may be made to drink the waters twice. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *zot* is a limiting word, implying *she'einah shota ve-shona* — she may not be made to drink a second time.

The *Chachamim* introduce a third position: *ein isha shota ve-shona bein be-ish echad bein bishnei anashim* — a woman never undergoes the ordeal a second time, whether the second instance involves the same husband or a different one.

Thus the full spectrum: the *tana kama* permits a second ordeal even with the same husband; Rabbi Yehuda permits it with a different husband but not the same; the *Chachamim* prohibit a second ordeal altogether, regardless of the husband.

### Nechunya Testimony

Rabbi Yehuda reports: *maaseh ve-heid lefaneinu Nechunya Chofer Shichin* — Nechunya the Digger of Wells testified before us that a woman may drink twice — but this was accepted only *bishnei anashim*, with two different husbands, not with the same husband. Tosafot cite a *Yerushalmi* in which a woman named Korkemit actually underwent the ordeal three times before Shemaya and Avtalyon — evidence that the ritual did occur historically, and that the debate about double jeopardy reflects a genuine and consequential disagreement. Whether Nechunya's testimony was to a received halakhic tradition or to something he personally witnessed is left open.

The Gemara's presentation of three positions — unlimited repetition, repetition with a different husband only, and no repetition at all — remains to be analyzed further in the discussion that follows.

---

---

# Sotah 19

## Multiple Sotah Tests

### Torah vs. Zot

The daf opens by revisiting a *braita* that was quoted at the close of 18b. The *braita* begins with the phrase *zot torat ha-kena'ot* — "this is the *torah* of jealousies" — and the interpretive tension is immediately apparent: the word *torah* is an expansive, inclusive term, while *zot* is a narrowing, limiting one. These two words pull in opposite directions, and it is precisely this tension that generates the three-way dispute among the *tanna'im*.

The *tanna kamma* fastens onto the word *torah* to allow for multiple occurrences of the *sotah* procedure. That is, a woman who has been suspected, warned before witnesses, and made to drink the bitter waters could, if later suspected again under fresh circumstances, be subjected to the entire process a second time. *Torah* signals multiplicity.

### Rabbi Yehuda Position

*Rabbi Yehuda* counters by emphasizing the exclusive force of *zot*: *she-en isha shota ve-shona* — a woman cannot be made to undergo the procedure twice. There is no double jeopardy. He does, however, qualify this position based on testimony. The *braita* records that *Nechunya Chofre Shichin* — Nechunya the ditch-digger — testified before the sages that a woman could in fact be made to drink a second time, and this testimony was accepted, but only in a limited context: *bi-shne anashim* — if it involves two different husbands. *Rabbi Yehuda*'s reasoning is that when the same husband suspects his wife a second time, the problem may lie more with the husband than with the woman. But if an entirely different husband brings the accusation, that represents a genuinely different set of circumstances, and the procedure may be repeated.

### Chakhamim Rejection

The *chakhamim* — identified in the *braita* as *Rabbanan Batrai*, the later sages — take a more sweeping position: *en isha shota ve-shona ben be-ish echad ben bi-shne anashim* — a woman can never be made to drink again, whether the suspicion comes from the same husband or from two different ones. This represents a rejection even of the testimony of *Nechunya*, and applies across the board.

### Gemara's Question

The *gemara* is not content to leave the dispute as a simple three-way disagreement, because the positions must account for both textual signals — the inclusive *torat* and the exclusive *zot*. The *gemara* therefore presses: does the *tanna kamma*, who emphasizes *torat*, have no use for *zot*? And conversely, does the *Rabbanan Batrai*, who effectively reads the law as prohibiting a second procedure in virtually every case, have no use for *torat*? These questions prompt *Rava* to offer a comprehensive analytical framework.

---

## Rava Framework

### Identical Circumstances

*Rava* maps out the full logical space of possibilities. At one extreme: *be-ish echad u-vo'el echad* — the same husband, and the same individual suspected as the adulterer. Here everything is perfectly identical. The husband was unsatisfied with the first result and wishes to repeat the process against the same person. This is pure double jeopardy in the strictest sense, and *de-khule alma lo pligi* — all opinions agree that this is prohibited. The word *zot* performs its exclusionary function precisely here: this case of absolute identity is excluded by all.

### All Different

At the other extreme: *bi-shne anashim u-shne bo'alim* — two different husbands, and a different suspected adulterer in each instance. Here every relevant circumstance has changed. The woman has never been tested with respect to this husband or this suspected paramour; nothing about the prior proceeding is being relitigated. Here too all opinions agree — but in the opposite direction: *de-isha shota ve-shona* — she may undergo the procedure again. The word *torat* achieves its inclusive purpose precisely in this case.

### Middle Cases

The dispute among the three *tanna'im* therefore concerns only the two intermediate cases: one husband who suspects his wife of having conducted herself inappropriately with two different men (*ish echad u-shne bo'alim*), and two different husbands who each suspect their wife of involvement with the same individual (*shne anashim u-vo'el echad*).

### Tanna Kamma Logic

The *tanna kamma* adopts the most permissive position. He reads *torat* as broadly inclusive — *lerabbuye kulhu* — encompassing virtually all cases. The word *zot* serves only to exclude the one scenario on which everyone agrees: identical husband, identical suspected adulterer. Everything else — both middle cases included — is permitted. The *tanna kamma* is the maximalist here.

### Rabbanan Batrai Logic

The *Rabbanan Batrai* adopt the inverse approach. *Zot limute kulhu* — the exclusive term excludes virtually everything — both middle cases are prohibited. The word *torat* serves only to include the one scenario on which all agree: different husband, different suspected adulterer. Everything short of total difference in circumstances is excluded. The *Rabbanan Batrai* are the minimalists.

### Rabbi Yehuda Balance

*Rabbi Yehuda* stakes out the middle position with elegant symmetry: *zot limutei tartei, torah lirboyei tartei* — *zot* excludes two cases, and *torat* includes two cases. The two excluded cases share a single variable: the same husband. Whether that husband is suspicious of the same man or a different man, if it is the same husband a second time, the procedure cannot be repeated. The two included cases share the opposite variable: different husbands. Whether those two husbands suspect her of involvement with the same man or different men, the fact of a different husband constitutes a genuinely different set of circumstances, and the procedure may be repeated. This makes intuitive sense as well: since the *sotah* procedure is fundamentally about the wife's relationship with her husband, it follows that cases involving the same husband form a natural category of exclusion, while cases involving a different husband form a natural category of inclusion — even if the suspected adulterer happens to be the same person.

---

## Menachah Process

### Who Takes It

The third *perek* opens with the *mishnah* describing the ritual steps of the *sotah*'s *mincha* offering. The *mishnah* states that "he" would take the *mincha* from a wicker basket (*kefifah mitzrit*) and place it into a *kli shareis* — a sanctified temple vessel — and then place it upon her hand. The identity of the "he" is disputed. *Rashi* understands this to refer to the husband, reasoning that until the offering is placed into a *kli shareis* it has not yet entered the domain of the *kohen*'s responsibility. *Tosafot*, by contrast, argues that this must refer to the *kohen* himself, since the *pasuk* speaks of the *kohen* taking it from her hand.

### Sanctification

Once the *mincha* is placed into the *kli shareis*, it becomes sanctified. It is then returned to the woman's hands, so that she holds the now-sanctified offering. At this point, the *kohen* places his hands underneath hers — *maniach yado tachat yadah* — preparing for the waving.

### Five Steps

The *mishnah* enumerates the steps of the *mincha* procedure. First, the *kohen* waves the offering (*tenufah*), with his hands underneath and her hands on top, as a single joint act. Second, he brings it close to the *mizbe'ach* (*hagashah*). Third, he takes the *kometz* — a handful of the offering. Fourth, he burns the *kometz* on the *mizbe'ach* (*haktarah*). Fifth, the remainder (*shirayim*) is eaten by the *kohanim* in the *Beis Hamikdash*. These five steps — *waving, touching the altar, taking the handful, burning, and the remainder being eaten* — constitute the full procedure for every *mincha*, and the *sotah*'s offering is no exception.

---

## Order Dispute

### Tanna Kamma Order

Having described the steps of the *mincha*, the *mishnah* now turns to the question of order: does the drinking precede the *mincha*, or does the *mincha* precede the drinking? The *tanna kamma* holds that first she drinks and only then is the *mincha* brought. The understanding implicit in this position is that once the *mincha* is subsequently brought, it triggers or activates the effect of the bitter waters that she has already consumed.

### Rabbi Shimon Order

*Rabbi Shimon* reverses the order: *makriv et minchatah ve-achar kach mashkeh* — first the *mincha*, then the drinking. And *Rabbi Shimon* does not rest on inference alone; he cites an explicit *pasuk*: *ve-achar yashkeh et ha-ishah et ha-mayim* — "and afterwards he shall cause the woman to drink the waters." The word *ve-achar*, "afterwards," appears after the verses describing the *mincha* procedure, making the sequence clear — or so it would seem. The *pasuk* appears to place the drinking explicitly after the *mincha* offering.

### Rabbi Shimon Concession

Despite his clear preference, *Rabbi Shimon* concedes that if the order was reversed — if she drank first and the *mincha* was brought afterward — the *mincha* is nonetheless *kesherah* (*be-di'avad*, after the fact). The procedure is valid retroactively. This concession, as we will see, becomes important when the *gemara* tries to understand what *Rabbi Shimon* does with the earlier *pasuk* that seems to place the drinking first.

---

## Waving Process

### Owner Waving

Before turning to the textual analysis of the order dispute, the *gemara* records a separate exchange. *Rabbi Elazar* said to *Rabbi Yoshiya* of his generation — notably a colleague rather than an elder, which is why the pointed manner of the remark was appropriate — that he should not sit down until he could explain: *minayin le-minchat sotah she-te'unah tenufah* — whence do we know that the *sotah*'s *mincha* requires *tenufah*, waving? At first glance this question is surprising, since the *pasuk* explicitly states that the *kohen* shall wave it. *Rabbi Elazar* clarifies: that the *kohen* waves it is explicit. The question is, whence do we know that the *owner* — the woman herself — must also participate in the waving?

### Gezeirah Shavah

The answer is derived through a *gezeirah shavah* — a verbal analogy between two passages. By the *sotah*'s *mincha*, the verse states *ve-lakach ha-kohen mi-yad ha-isha* — the *kohen* shall take from the hand of the woman. By the *shelamim*, the peace-offering, the verse states *yadav tevi'enah* — his hands shall bring it — and this verse speaks about the owner's hands in the context of waving the breast and leg of the *shelamim*. The shared term "hand" links the two passages and allows us to apply the rules of each to the other.

### Joint Action

The *gezeirah shavah* runs in both directions: just as by the *sotah* we have a *kohen* performing the waving, so too by the *shelamim*; and just as by the *shelamim* the owner participates in the waving, so too by the *sotah*. The practical upshot is that this is not accomplished in two separate acts. *Maniach yado tachat yad be'alim u-menif* — the *kohen* places his hands underneath the hands of the owner and they wave together as one. The owner is in direct contact with the offering because it flows from her and is connected to her; the *kohen*'s hands underneath represent the transition from personal ownership toward the *mizbe'ach*.

---

## Mishnah Structure

### Gemara Reading

When the *mishnah* lists the steps — *henif, higish, kamatz, hiktir* — and then says "he would have her drink and then bring the *mincha*," a difficulty arises: the *mishnah* has already said *hiktir*, that he burned the *kometz*. How can it then say he would first have her drink and only then bring the *mincha*, if the *kometz* has already been described as burned?

The *gemara* resolves this by distinguishing between two separate discussions embedded in the *mishnah*. The first part of the *mishnah* — *henif ve-higish kamatz ve-hiktir, ve-ha-sha'ar ne'echal la-kohanim* — is answering a structural question: *seder mincha keitzad?* What is the procedure of the *mincha*? What are its steps? The *mishnah* is describing the internal sequence of the *mincha* offering itself, not yet addressing when it occurs relative to the drinking. Only after completing this description does the *mishnah* turn to the separate question of the relationship between the drinking and the *mincha*.

### Sequence Debate

With that structural clarification established, the *gemara* proceeds to the substantive debate. *Rabbanan* hold: *mashkeh ve-achar kach makriv* — first she drinks, then the *mincha* is brought. *Rabbi Shimon* holds the opposite: *makriv et minchatah ve-achar kach mashkeh* — first the *mincha*, then she drinks — as the *pasuk* explicitly states with the word *ve-achar*. And *Rabbi Shimon* concedes *be-di'avad*: if she drank first and the *mincha* was brought afterward, it is *kesherah*. The challenge, then, is to explain how the *chakhamim* can argue against *Rabbi Shimon* given the apparent clarity of the *pasuk*. This requires a careful analysis of all three drinking references in the relevant verses.

---

## Three Pesukim Analysis

### First V'Hishkah

The *gemara* identifies three distinct references to drinking in the passage in *Bamidbar* 5. The first — *ve-hishkah* — appears immediately after the verse describing the scraping of the *megillah* into the water (*ve-chatav et ha-alot ha-eleh ha-kohen ba-sefer u-macha el mei ha-marim*), and states that he shall cause the woman to drink the bitter, cursing waters. This occurs before any mention of the *mincha* procedure in the *pesukim*.

### V'Achar Yashkeh

The second reference — *ve-achar yashkeh et ha-ishah et ha-mayim* — appears explicitly after the *pesukim* describing the *kohen* taking the *mincha* from her hand, waving it, performing *hagashah*, taking the *kometz*, and burning it on the *mizbe'ach*. It then says "and afterwards he shall cause the woman to drink the waters." *Rabbi Shimon* reads this as the operative instruction for timing: the word *ve-achar*, "afterwards," places the drinking definitively after the *mincha*.

### Third V'Hishkah

The third reference — *ve-hishkah et ha-mayim* — appears yet again following the second reference, in the context of what happens once she has drunk. This repetition creates the exegetical problem: if the second *ve-hishkah* already addressed the drinking after the *mincha*, what work does the third do? And if the first *ve-hishkah* already addressed the drinking before the *mincha*, how does *Rabbi Shimon*, who privileges the second reference, account for the first? These three *pesukim* become the terrain on which *Rabbanan* and *Rabbi Shimon* stake out their respective positions.

---

## Rabbi Shimon Counter

### Three Prerequisites

The *gemara* quotes a *braita* that draws on *Rabbi Shimon* and *Rabbi Akiva* jointly: *ve-achar yashkeh* — the word *ve-achar* teaches that the drinking comes *l'achar kol ha-ma'asim kulan ha-amurim le-ma'alah* — after everything enumerated above. And specifically, *maggid she-shloshah devarim me'akvin bah* — three things must precede the drinking for it to be valid: the *kometz* must have been offered, the *megillah* must have been fully erased, and the woman must have already accepted the *shvuah*.

---

## Prerequisites Analysis

### Kometz Requirement

The first prerequisite — *ad she-lo karav ha-kometz* — is precisely the point at issue between *Rabbi Shimon* and the *rabbanan* in the *mishnah*. The *braita* records *Rabbi Shimon le-ta'ameih*: he is consistent with his own position — first the *mincha*, then the drinking, exactly as the *pasuk* indicates.

### Full Erasure

The second prerequisite — *ve-ad she-lo nimchakah megillah* — seems puzzling at first. Of course she cannot drink if the ink has not yet been scraped into the water; there would be nothing to drink. The *gemara* therefore asks: *ela mai mashkeh lah?* — What exactly would she be drinking if it hasn't been erased?

### Rav Ashi Clarify

*Rav Ashi* resolves this: *lo nitzrecha ela le-shirumo nikkar* — the requirement is not simply that some erasure has occurred, but that the erasure must be total and complete. If words were scraped into the water but faint traces of the writing remained visible on the *megillah* — *rishumo nikkar* — the water cannot be drunk. The *pasuk*'s requirement of erasure demands that the writing be entirely undetectable; a partially erased *megillah* renders the water invalid.

### Oath First

The third prerequisite — *ve-ad she-lo tekabbel aleha ha-shvuah* — teaches that the woman must have already accepted the oath before she can drink. The *gemara* raises a subtle point here: this sounds as though the restriction is only that she cannot drink before the oath, but that the *megillah* itself could have been written beforehand. Yet *Rava* elsewhere states clearly that a *megillat sotah* written before the woman accepted the *shvuah* is entirely invalid — *lo asah ve-lo klum*. The order of the *pesukim* must be followed: first the oath, then the writing of the *megillah*, then the erasing, and then the drinking. The *gemara* acknowledges that the inclusion of the oath requirement as a distinct point here was perhaps to round out the list to three, since the underlying rule — that the oath must precede the writing — is already established elsewhere.

---

## Rabbanan Interpretation

### First Mention

Having established *Rabbi Shimon*'s reading of *ve-achar yashkeh* as the primary timing instruction, the *gemara* now explains how *Rabbanan* — who hold that the drinking precedes the *mincha* — account for all three *pesukim*. Their logic rests on the principle that the first mention establishes the operative timing. *Rabbanan savri ve-hishkah kama legufo de-mashkeh ve-achar kach makriv* — the *Rabbanan* treat the first *ve-hishkah*, which appears before the *mincha* steps, as the authoritative statement of sequence: she drinks first, and only then is the *mincha* brought.

### Rishumo Nikkar

If the first *ve-hishkah* establishes timing, then what does the second reference — *ve-achar yashkeh* — teach? *Rabbanan* say it is not about timing at all, but about a separate *halakhah*: *mi-ba'ei lei she-rishumo nikkar* — it teaches the *din* of *rishumo nikkar*. The word *ve-achar*, "afterwards," is read not as "after the *mincha*" but as "after everything that preceded the drinking has been properly completed" — including, most critically, the requirement that the *megillah* be fully erased with no faint writing remaining. The verse is a parenthetical reminder: before the actual drinking takes place, ensure that all prior steps — particularly the erasure — were properly performed.

### Forcing Compliance

The third *ve-hishkah* — *ve-hishkah batra* — teaches the position of *Rabbi Akiva*: *she-im nimchakah megillah ve-amrah eini shotah, me'arin otah u-mashkin otah be-al karchah* — if after the *megillah* was erased the woman declares that she will not drink, we press her and cause her to drink against her will. The final mention of drinking is thus not about timing, but about the obligation to ensure compliance: once the *megillah* has been scraped into the water, the process must be seen through, even coercively. In this way, *Rabbanan* derive three distinct teachings from the three *pesukim*, while maintaining that the first *ve-hishkah* governs the actual sequence: drinking first, *mincha* second.

---

## Rabbi Shimon Counter (II)

### Afterwards Explicit

*Rabbi Shimon* takes the opposite approach. *Ve-achar yashkeh legufo* — the explicit *ve-achar yashkeh* is the primary timing instruction, and it places the drinking definitively after the *mincha*. This is not a parenthetical point about proper procedure; it is the statement of the correct sequence: first the *mincha*, then the drinking.

How then does *Rabbi Shimon* handle the first *ve-hishkah*, which appears before the *mincha* steps? He reads it as establishing the *be-di'avad* ruling: *she-im hishkah ve-achar kach hikriv et minchatah, kesherah* — if the order was reversed and she drank before the *mincha* was brought, the procedure is nonetheless valid after the fact. The earlier *ve-hishkah* is not saying "now have her drink"; it is saying that even if you were to have her drink at this earlier point, you could still go forward with the *mincha* and the *sotah* procedure would remain intact. It establishes retroactive validity for an out-of-order sequence, while the true *lechatchila* sequence is governed by *ve-achar yashkeh*.

The third *ve-hishkah batra* — like *Rabbi Akiva*'s reading — teaches that if the *megillah* was erased and the woman refuses to drink, she is compelled.

*Rabbanan*, for their part, refuse to accept that the *pasuk* would open with a *be-di'avad* scenario. Since the *pasuk* describes drinking before the *mincha*, that must be the *lechatchila* order, not a concession to a substandard procedure. This is the crux of why *Rabbanan* resist *Rabbi Shimon*'s reading: the *pshat* of the *pesukim* — however much *Rabbi Shimon*'s overall reading may commend itself — militates against treating the earlier mention of drinking as a mere *be-di'avad* allowance.

---

## Rabbi Akiva Force

### Rabbi Yehuda Force

The *gemara* now raises a challenge against the attribution of forced drinking to *Rabbi Akiva*. A separate *braita* records a dispute about what happens when the *megillah* has been erased and the woman refuses to drink. *Rabbi Yehuda* states that an iron jaw-spreader — *kalbos shel barzel* — would be placed into her mouth to force it open, and she would be made to drink against her will in any such case.

### Akiva Purpose

*Rabbi Akiva* rejects this. The purpose of the entire procedure, he argues, is *le-vodkah* — to test her, to determine whether she committed adultery. The bitter waters are an instrument of investigation, not punishment in their own right. If the very prospect of drinking has caused her to admit guilt — *ve-halo bedukah ve-omedet*, she is already as good as proven — then the waters have achieved their purpose. The name of God has been erased and this has produced the desired result: a confession or its equivalent. There is no basis to compound this by forcing the water upon her as well.

### Akiva Distinction

Yet *Rabbi Akiva* is not categorically opposed to forced drinking. He draws a temporal line: *ad she-lo karav ha-kometz, yekholah la-chazor bah* — before the *kometz* has been offered, the woman can retract. *Mishe-karav ha-kometz, einah yekholah la-chazor bah* — once the *kometz* has been offered, she cannot retract, and she is made to drink.

### Akiva Contradiction

This distinction seems initially puzzling. If the entire basis for *Rabbi Akiva*'s leniency is that her refusal constitutes an implicit confession — rendering forced drinking unnecessary because the waters have already served their purpose — then why does it matter whether the *kometz* has been offered or not? An implicit confession is an implicit confession regardless of where in the procedure one stands. The *gemara* presses this internal tension within *Rabbi Akiva*'s position.

---

## Trembling Analysis

### Fear vs. Guilt

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction within *Rabbi Akiva*'s position by introducing a crucial distinction between two types of refusal. The fundamental question underlying *Rabbi Akiva*'s entire framework is: can we reliably read her refusal to drink as an implicit admission of adultery? The answer is: not always. There is a real concern that the ritual's terrifying nature — the solemn oath, the divine name being erased, the entire theatre of the *Beis Hamikdash* — may have so overwhelmed an innocent woman that she refuses out of sheer panic, not out of guilt. If that is the case, her refusal is not a confession at all; it is a symptom of fear.

### Calm Refusal

*Rabbi Akiva*'s categorical position against forced drinking applies specifically to *be-riyuta* — a calm, collected demeanor. If a woman is composed and deliberately says she will not drink, that is unmistakably an implicit admission. She understands precisely what is at stake; she is not overwhelmed by terror; and she is choosing not to proceed. *Rabbi Akiva* therefore holds: *kol machamat briyuta klal klal lo shatya* — whenever the refusal comes from a calm, composed state, we never force her under any circumstances. That refusal is treated as a confession, and the waters have served their purpose.

### Before Kometz

The more complex case is *retita* — a woman who is trembling and visibly terrified. Here *Rabbi Akiva* cannot confidently read her refusal as a confession; the trembling suggests that fear, not guilt, may be driving her behavior. In this case, *Rabbi Akiva* draws his distinction based on when in the procedure the refusal occurs.

Before the *kometz* is offered, *Rabbi Akiva* holds that she may retract — she cannot be forced to drink. *Rav Ashi* explains: either the *megillah* has not yet been erased, or — following *Rashi*'s interpretation of *Rabbi Akiva*'s position — the *megillah* was erased, but the *kohanim* did so prematurely, before the *kometz* was brought. Since the proper order, according to *Rabbi Akiva*, should be *mincha* first and then erasure, a *kohen* who erased the *megillah* before the *kometz* was offered acted improperly — *she-lo ke-din avud kohanim de-machki*. In that case, the woman had more time rightfully available to her before being confronted with the erased water, and the situation was precipitated by the *kohanim*'s jumping ahead. Given both the trembling and the procedural irregularity, *Rabbi Akiva* does not treat her refusal as a confession, and she may back out — *matzi hadra bah*.

### After Kometz

Once the *kometz* has been offered and the erasure was performed in the proper order — *ke-din avud kohanim de-machki* — the situation changes. Everything has been done correctly; all proper steps have been completed. Now, even though she is trembling and her refusal might stem from fear, *Rabbi Akiva* holds that we cannot grant her an exit. The trembling means we cannot confidently interpret her refusal as an admission of guilt, and therefore the logic that "the waters have already served their purpose" does not apply. Paradoxically, it is precisely because she may be innocent but simply terrified that *Rabbi Akiva* insists she must drink — *lo matzi hadra bah* — and if necessary, she is compelled.

This elegant resolution reconciles the apparently contradictory positions. *Rabbi Akiva* never forces a calm woman, because her composure makes her refusal a clear implicit admission. He never forces before the *kometz* when a trembling woman refuses, because procedural considerations allow her to withdraw. But he does force after the *kometz* when a trembling woman refuses, precisely because her trembling renders the refusal ambiguous rather than confessional, and since the procedure has been properly completed, it must be seen through. Two *tanna'im* debate exactly where *Rabbi Akiva* placed this line — the earlier *braita* suggests the critical factor is the erasure of the *megillah*, while this *braita* places it at the offering of the *kometz*. The *gemara* resolves this as *trei tanna'ei ve-aliba de-Rabbi Akiva* — two *tanna'im* each transmitting a version of *Rabbi Akiva*'s position.

---

## Retraction Question

### Case Setup

The *gemara* now poses a further question. The case of the calm woman whose refusal is read as an implicit admission has been established. But what happens when that woman subsequently changes her mind? She said *eini shotah* — calmly and clearly, without trembling — and *Rabbi Akiva* has read this as a tacit confession of adultery. But then she reverses course and says *shotah ani* — "I will drink." Does she get to retract?

### Cannot Retract

One view holds that she cannot retract. *Keivan de-amrah eini shotah, teme'ah ani ka-amrah* — since she said she would not drink, she implicitly declared herself to have committed adultery. And *keivan de-achzik nafshah be-tum'ah, lo matzi hadra bah* — once she established her status as one who committed adultery, she cannot undo it. The *gemara* notes the suggestive force of the word *de-achzik* — "established" — which invokes a quasi-judicial framework: she has fixed a *halakhic* status for herself, and one cannot simply reverse such an establishment.

### Fear-Based Refusal

The opposing view argues that we should not be so quick to finalize the admission. *Keivan de-amrah shotah ani, galya da'ata de-machamat biyututa hu de-amrah* — now that she is willing to drink, it becomes clear that even what appeared to be a calm, collected refusal may have been rooted in fear rather than guilt. The external appearance of composure may not perfectly track inner states. Since she never explicitly confessed — she only implicitly did so through refusal — and since she is now reversing that refusal, perhaps we should not press the implicit admission further and should allow her to drink.

### Teiku

The *gemara* leaves this question unresolved: *teiku*. The tension between treating an implicit admission as irrevocable and allowing the woman's demonstrated willingness to drink to recast the prior refusal as fear-based cannot be adjudicated here.

---

## Water Bitterness

### Bitter Additive

The daf concludes with a ruling of *Avuyei di-Shmuel* — the father of *Shmuel*. He holds that the *sota*h's water must contain an actual bitter additive: *tzarich she-yitein mar le-tokh ha-mayim* — something physically bitter must be placed into the water, independent of any effect produced by the erasing of the curses.

### Textual Proof

The source for this requirement is the redundant language of the verse itself: *mei ha-marim ha-marim* — the bitter, bitter waters. The word for bitterness appears twice, and *Avuyei di-Shmuel* reads this as indicating two independent sources of bitterness. The *meararim* — the cursing quality — is produced by the erasing of God's name and the curses into the water. But the *marim* — the physical bitterness — must be present independently. *Marim ke-var* — the waters must already be bitter before the spiritual dimension is added. The physical bitterness of the water is thus a freestanding requirement, not a byproduct of the spiritual process.

---

---

# Sotah 20

## Review & Opening

### Mincha & Megilla Review

Daf 20 continues the tractate's systematic walk through the *sotah* ceremony. The previous daf addressed the *mincha* — its composition and preparation — as well as the writing of the *megilla*: the ink, the parchment, and the requirement that it be written only after she took the *shvua*. Notably, the *mishna* itself omits any mention of the *shvua*, but the requirement emerges from other sources. The daf also treated the scraping of the *megilla* into the water.

### Drinking Order

A major debate occupied the previous daf as well: which comes first, the drinking of the water or the bringing of the *mincha*? The ambiguity arises directly from the *psukim*, which first describe the drinking and then the *mincha*, yet conclude with the phrase *v'achar yashke et ha'isha et hamayim* — "and afterward he shall make the woman drink the waters." Whatever the precise *halachic* order, it is clear that the *mishna* deliberately reserves the drinking for last, since it is the climax of the entire procedure. The dominant position, in any event, appears to be that the drinking follows the *mincha*, consistent with *v'achar yashke et ha'isha et hamayim*. With that backdrop established, the *mishna* of daf 20 now turns to the drinking itself.

## Refusal to Drink

### Before Erasure

The *mishna* opens with the case in which the woman refuses to drink before the *megilla* has been erased. If she says *eini shota* — "I will not drink" — she does not thereby admit guilt, but the proceedings cannot be completed through her refusal. In that case, *megillata nignenzet* — the *megilla* is placed in *gniza*. Since it bears God's name, it cannot simply be destroyed, yet it cannot be reused, as the *megilla* must be written specifically for that particular *sotah*. It is therefore stored away.

### Tzir & Wearing

Rashi explains that there was a small designated space near the walls of the *heichal* where it would be buried. Tosafot, however, cites a striking *Yerushalmi*: *megillata nignenzet tachat tziro shel heichal* — it would be placed beneath the *tzir* of the *heichal*, the hinge-socket or pivot of the door. The *Yerushalmi* adds that this was done *bishvil leshachaka* — in order to wear it down gradually. Small amounts of water would flow there and continue to dissolve the writing. This is a remarkable practice: rather than direct erasure, they arranged for the *megilla* to be worn away through *grama*, an indirect process. Why they would seek to cause it to be worn away rather than simply keep it buried is not entirely clear, but the *Yerushalmi*'s account is what it is.

### Mincha & Single Use

Similarly, the *mincha* — once it had entered a *kli sharet* — could not be redeemed or removed from the *azara*. The *mishna* states *u'minchata mitpazeret al hadeshen*: it would be scattered on the ashes, meaning burned in the *Beit hadeshen*, the section of the *azara* designated for *korbanot* that had become *pasul*. The *mishna* also states explicitly: *v'ein megillata kesheira lehashkot ba sotah acheret* — a *megilla* written for one woman cannot be used for another. This is precisely why it must be placed in *gniza* rather than reused. If she refuses to drink, she would be divorced without her *ksuva* — not because she admitted guilt, but because she is the cause of the proceedings' failure to complete.

## After Erasure

### Forced to Drink

The *mishna* then turns to the case in which the *megilla* has already been erased and she then says *eini shota*. If she were to admit guilt at this point, the procedure would still be halted; but without an admission, the situation is entirely different. Now that God's name has been erased into the water, the proceedings cannot simply be abandoned at her whim. The *mishna* rules: *m'ar'arin otah u'mashkin otah al karchah* — they confuse her, agitate her, and force her to drink against her will. Some form of physical compulsion, such as a device to keep her mouth open, is implied.

### How Much Erased?

Tosafot cites an important *Yerushalmi* on this point: *kama yimachak?* — how much of the *megilla* must have been erased before we reach the threshold of compulsion? *Tani Rabbi Chanina: Beit Shammai omrim ot achat, Beit Hillel omrim shtei otiyot* — Beit Shammai holds that even one letter of erasure triggers the obligation, while Beit Hillel requires two letters. Rabbi Ila explains Beit Hillel's reasoning: the threshold is *kedei lichtov Yud Hei* — enough to have written two letters of God's name. This implies that the concern is specifically reaching God's name itself. It is worth noting that one could technically transgress the *issur mechikat hashem* even by erasing a single letter of the divine name — perhaps that is Beit Shammai's position. In any case, the *Yerushalmi* makes clear that they had to reach the point of erasing *shem Hashem* for the compulsion to apply.

## Physical Effects

### Manifestation Signs

Once she drinks — whether willingly or by compulsion — the *mishna* describes the consequences in vivid terms: *eina maspeket lishtot ad shepaneiha morikot* — almost instantaneously, her face turns green or jaundiced; *v'eineiha boltot* — her eyes bulge out; *v'hi mitmaleit gidim* — and she is filled with protrusions. Rashi explains *hagidim shebilchayeiha* — the sinews or veins of her jaw — *noffin venirin kemalei gidin*: it looks as though her entire face is swollen with distended veins. *Vegam besarah naaseit shitah shitah shel nefichah* — her flesh becomes puffed up in rows. The *Sifri* describes it as though poles are thrust into her, so she has ridges protruding from her flesh.

### Removal & Impurity

The *mishna* concludes this passage with: *v'heim omrim hotziuha, shelo tetamei ha'azara* — the attendants say, take her out, so that she does not render the *azara* impure. Notably, the *mishna* does not state that she dies. Yet the urgency of removing her strongly implies she is about to die, and the *gemara* will qualify this point further.

### Presumption Guilt

One striking feature of this *mishna* is that it does not say *im hayeta temei'ah* — "if she was impure" — or *keshehayetah temei'ah*. It simply describes these physical effects as the natural, expected outcome. The *mishna* thus speaks from a presumption of guilt, without conditional language. This is a significant editorial choice.

## Zechus Toleh

### One-Three Years

The *mishna* continues: *im yesh lah zechut hayetah tolah lah* — if she had merit, it would hold the punishment in abeyance. The *mishna* specifies that merit can suspend the punishment for one year, two years, or three years, depending on the degree of merit. The *gemara* understands this as *bedavka* — precise — and will discuss it accordingly.

This concept of *zechut tolah* raises immediate difficulties. If women are seen going through the *sotah* procedure without apparent consequences, it undermines public confidence in the efficacy of the waters. This very concern, as we shall see, prompted one of the *tannaim* to object to the concept altogether. Nevertheless, this is the *mishna*'s position.

One might ask whether *teshuva* could forestall the punishment entirely. This depends on how one understands the nature of the procedure. If the *sotah* process is viewed as a purely divine punishment — a matter between the woman and God — then *teshuva* might logically be effective. There is a well-known responsum, likely from the *Noda Biyehudah*, addressing a parallel case: a person who is *chayav misa* and performs sincere *teshuva* before execution. The ruling is that the court carries out the sentence nonetheless. Divine forgiveness is between the person and God; the court operates by different parameters. The same principle may apply here. Yet this very distinction underscores a tension in the *sotah* procedure: to whatever degree it functions as a court-supervised process — the couple appeared before the court, the court sent her to the *Beit HaMikdash*, there are witnesses — it is not simply a private matter between the woman and God. As we will discuss at the end of the *daf*, this tension becomes increasingly significant as the *gemara* develops the concept of *zechut tolah*.

Relatedly, the concept of *zechut tolah* is very disruptive to the practical reality of the procedure. If the proceedings appear to work — husband and wife resume marital life — and then two or three years later it becomes apparent she was guilty, what does that do for the husband's understanding of what transpired? How can they resume normal life if the water has not definitively proven anything in the immediate aftermath? The *gemara* offers various explanations for when the water fails to take effect — if the husband is not *menukeh me'avon*, if she has *zechus*, and so on — but one wonders whether these explanations arose precisely in response to periods when the procedure did not appear to be functioning as intended.

### Teaching Women

The *mishna* draws an explicit conclusion from the concept of *zechut tolah*: *mikan omer Ben Azzai: chayav adam lelamed et bito Torah*. From here, Ben Azzai derived that a person is obligated to teach his daughter *Torah*. The reasoning is direct: if a woman drinks the water and experiences no immediate effect, she might conclude that the entire system is a fraud. However, if she has been taught *Torah* and specifically this *halacha* — that *zechut* sometimes suspends the punishment — she will understand that the absence of immediate effect does not invalidate the system. Knowledge of the system preserves faith in it.

### Ben Azzai & R. Eliezer

Rabbi Eliezer disputes this directly: *kol hamelamed et bito Torah ke'ilu melamdah tiflut* — whoever teaches his daughter *Torah* is as though he taught her *tiflus*, a term with clear sexual connotations, which Birnbaum translates as promiscuity. The context makes this meaning unmistakable. Rabbi Eliezer's concern is precisely the inverse of Ben Azzai's optimism: yes, knowing how the system works produces trust in it — but it also reveals how to work around it. If she knows that *zechut* can suspend punishment, she might reason that by accumulating *zechus* in other areas of life, she can commit adultery and defer consequences indefinitely. A little knowledge, on this view, is a dangerous thing.

This raises the broader question of why the debate is framed specifically around women. The same concern could theoretically apply to men: someone who has learned *Nezikin* thoroughly can find technically permissible ways to act improperly in business. There is even a tradition recorded in the *gemara* that one who learns *Torah shelo lishma* in the sense of manipulating the system would have been better off not being created. The reason the debate focuses on women is likely twofold. First, men are already obligated in *talmud Torah*, so whatever potential negatives exist, the *mitzva* is not up for debate. What is open for debate is whether women, who are not so obligated, should be actively educated — and there one can weigh costs and benefits. Second, there may be a dimension here of how Rabbi Eliezer views women specifically: the final line of the *mishna* will make this clearer.

It is also worth noting that Ben Azzai's formulation is about preserving the woman's confidence in the system, not about enabling *zechut* to shield her. Rabbi Eliezer's concern is not that *talmud Torah* itself will give her the *zechut* to evade punishment — *zechut* only suspends, it does not fully exempt — but rather that knowing the mechanics of the system will teach her how to acquire *zechus* strategically in other ways. The distinction matters. One might also note an argument entirely absent from the *mishna*'s debate: that teaching a woman *Torah* might elevate her character and make her less inclined toward wrongdoing in the first place. The *mishna* does not entertain this possibility.

A further point: the *Rambam*, when codifying this material, uses the language *aval amru chachamim: kol hamelamed et bito Torah ke'ilu melamdah tiflut* — he frames it as rabbinic guidance rather than an outright prohibition, with the formulation *amru chachamim* suggesting policy direction rather than strict *isur*. To what degree this entire debate is a *halachic* debate, as opposed to a matter of *da'at Torah*-style communal guidance, is worth considering.

### R. Yehoshua View

The *mishna* concludes this section with Rabbi Yehoshua's famous statement: *rotzah isha b'kav v'tiflut mitishah kabim u'prishut* — a woman would rather have one measure of sustenance and be able to have her sexual pleasure than nine measures with the requirement of abstinence. On this view, women are more prepared to sacrifice material wellbeing in order to maintain access to physical intimacy, and therefore cannot be trusted with knowledge that might give them theological cover for transgression.

The *mishna* then lists, in what appears to be Rabbi Yehoshua's name, figures who destroy the world: *chasid shoteh* — a foolish pietist; *rasha arum* — a crafty wicked person; *isha prushah* — a woman who is abstinent; and *makkot perushim* — the lashes of the ascetics. Rashi explains *makkot perushim* in the *gemara* as someone who strikes himself against walls to appear humble and modest — a performative false righteousness that has lost sight of genuine *frumkeit*.

The inclusion of *isha prushah* is striking. Rabbi Yehoshua has just argued that women inherently prefer physical pleasure over abstinence, and yet here he lists an abstinent woman as one who destroys the world. The implication appears to be that a woman who presents herself as *prushah* is dissembling — all women, on this view, are ultimately seeking physical intimacy, and the woman who performs abstinence is the most dangerous of all. This connects directly to the broader question that runs through the entire *masechet*: how one understands the cheating woman and where blame is located. Some threads in the *gemara* have refocused or at least included the husband in the picture; here, the lens is firmly on the woman as the locus of sexual transgression. The debate about teaching women *Torah* is not purely an educational policy discussion — it reflects fundamentally different views of what the *sotah* represents and who bears moral responsibility.

## Ink Debate

### Two Accounts

The *gemara* now records a tradition transmitted by Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, in the name of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Meir was a scribe (*lavlar*), and he reported that when he was learning *Torah* with Rabbi Akiva — *keshehaiti lomed Torah etzel Rabbi Akiva* — he would add *kankantom* to his ink, *v'lo amar li davar*: Rabbi Akiva said nothing to him. When he subsequently came to Rabbi Yishmael — *keshebati etzel Rabbi Yishmael* — Rabbi Yishmael asked him about his trade, and upon learning he was a scribe, told him: *hevei zahir shemelachtacha melachat shamayim hi* — be very careful, for your work is the work of heaven. If you add or omit even one letter — *shema tachsir ot achat o tatir ot achat* — you could destroy the entire world: *nimtzata ata machriv et ha'olam kulo*.

### Divine Work

Rashi illustrates why this is no hyperbole in terms of theological consequence: if one erases the *aleph* from *emet*, or the *heh* from *Elohim*, or adds a letter to *Bereishit* such that it reads as though something created God — one letter transforms the meaning entirely. The analogy to "let's eat grandma" versus "let's eat, grandma" captures the principle: punctuation, or in this case a single letter, saves worlds.

### Kankantom Purpose

Rabbi Meir responded to Rabbi Yishmael's warning by saying: I already know the precise spellings — *debaki ana b'chasirut veyitirut* — but there is an additional concern beyond correctness at the moment of writing. Even after writing, *dilma ati veyativ akarna de'dalet* — perhaps a fly will land on the protruding corner of a *dalet* and smudge it, *u'mashvei lei reish* — turning it into a *reish*. Therefore, *davar acher yesh li she'ani matil l'toch hadyo v'kankantom shemo* — I add *kankantom* to the ink to ensure indelibility, so that no smudging can corrupt the letters after the fact.

Rabbi Yishmael's response: *vechi matilim kankantom l'toch hadyo? Ha-Torah amrah u'macha* — the *Torah* requires that the *megillat sotah* be erasable, and therefore the writing must be of a kind that can be erased. Indelible ink violates this requirement, at least for the *megillat sotah*.

## Source Contradiction

### Order Contradiction

The *gemara* immediately challenges the account: *v'hatanya* — we have a *braisa* that tells a different version. In that *braisa*, Rabbi Meir says it was when he was learning with Rabbi Yishmael that he used *kankantom* and Rabbi Yishmael said nothing — and it was when he came to Rabbi Akiva that Rabbi Akiva forbade it. So we have two contradictions: first, the order of apprenticeship (which teacher came first?), and second, who actually objected to the *kankantom* (Rabbi Yishmael or Rabbi Akiva?).

### Learning Sequence

The *gemara* says: *bishlama shimush a-shimush lo kashya* — the apparent contradiction in order of apprenticeship can be resolved, because both sequences are true. *Me'ikara asa l'kamei d'Rabbi Akiva* — he first came to Rabbi Akiva. *Keivan d'lo matzi ka'ei alibeih* — but he could not follow what Rabbi Akiva was getting at. This is, incidentally, a remarkable statement about the future Rabbi Meir — the very sage whom no one else could fully understand — who in his youth could not keep up with Rabbi Akiva. He then went to Rabbi Yishmael and *gamar gemara* — he acquired the tradition, the foundational knowledge. Rabbi Yishmael's approach was more about transmitting tradition, while Rabbi Akiva's was more about analysis and creative reasoning. *Hadar asa l'kamei d'Rabbi Akiva savar svara* — he then returned to Rabbi Akiva and learned how to analyze and break down that foundation. So both sequences are accurate: it was Rabbi Akiva first and then Rabbi Yishmael, and also Rabbi Yishmael and then Rabbi Akiva.

### Who Forbade?

However, the contradiction about who forbade the *kankantom* cannot be resolved similarly. The *gemara* concludes: *ela asrah a-asrah kashya* — this remains a genuine difficulty, meaning the two *braisot* reflect a disagreement about what actually happened. The *gemara* leaves this as an unresolved contradiction between the sources.

## Torah Ink Rules

### Parshat Sotah

A *braisa* then records Rabbi Yehuda's account of Rabbi Meir's ultimate position: *l'chol matilin kankantom l'toch hadyo* — for all purposes one may add *kankantom* to the ink, *chutz mi-parshat sotah bilvad* — except for *parshat sotah* alone. Rabbi Meir was unwilling to abandon his practice of using *kankantom* for scribal work generally; he accepted the restriction only for the *sotah* passage.

### Sefer vs. Mikdash

Rabbi Yaakov then refines this further in Rabbi Meir's name: *chutz mi-parshat sotah she-ba-mikdash* — the restriction applies only to the *parshat sotah* that is actually written in the *Mikdash* for the procedure itself; the section as it appears in a *Sefer Torah* does not require erasable ink.

The *gemara* asks: *mai beinaihu* — what is the practical difference between these two formulations? Rabbi Yirmiyah answers: *limchok limdinata ika beinaihu* — the debate concerns whether one may use the *parshat sotah* as written in a *Sefer Torah* for the actual *sotah* procedure. The question is thus not merely academic: can the *kohen* open a *Sefer Torah* to the relevant passage and erase it into the water, or must a dedicated *megilla* be written separately for this purpose?

Tosafot explains the underlying logic: since the *Torah* states *u'macha* — "and he shall erase" — there is an understanding that any text functioning as the *parshat sotah* must be written in a form that is capable of being erased. If the passage in a *Sefer Torah* could in theory be used for the procedure, then the *Torah* itself would demand that this passage be written in erasable ink. Conversely, if one holds that the *Sefer Torah* passage can never serve as the *megillat sotah*, there is simply no requirement that it be written with erasable ink.

This debate connects to a broader parallel about ink and *Sifrei Torah* generally. The ability to correct a *Sefer Torah* depends on the ink being erasable — it rides on the surface of the *klaf* and can be scraped away. Were the ink to be absorbed into the *klaf*, correction would be impossible. This capacity for erasure is almost a practical necessity, given that scribes do make mistakes. Similarly, a *Sefer Torah* need not be written *ksidran* — in order — which means corrections can be made without invalidating the entire scroll. The *Rambam* rules that writing with erasable ink is *mitzva min hamuvchar*, the preferred manner, but that *bedieved*, if one wrote with *kankantom* or similar indelible materials — *she-hu omed v'eino nimchak* — the scroll remains *kasher*. The practical *halacha* thus aligns with Rabbi Akiva's general principle, at least *lechatchila*.

### Megilla Reuse

The *gemara* then introduces an independent debate: *ein megilla kesheira lehashkot ba sotah acheret* — a *megilla* written for one woman cannot be used to administer the waters to another woman. This is the standard position. But Rabbi Akha berabbi Yoshiya holds the contrary: *megilla kesheira lehashkot ba sotah acheret* — the same *megilla* can indeed be reused for another woman. This is a position we have not encountered until now. (One must also contend with the earlier ruling of Rava that the *megilla* cannot be written before the woman took the oath — Tosafot notes that this *gemara* appears to ignore that requirement, and raises the question of how to harmonize the two. One possibility is that both women in this scenario had already taken their oaths before the writing occurred.)

The *gemara* proposes that this debate about reuse is structurally parallel to the debate about whether the passage in a *Sefer Torah* can be used: if you cannot reuse a *megilla* written for one woman for another, perhaps the same logic prevents using the generic *Sefer Torah* text for any woman; and if you can reuse it, perhaps the generic text suffices.

However, Papa then demonstrates — *dilma la hi* — that these debates need not align. The *tanna kamma*'s reason for prohibiting reuse is not about *lishmah* per se but about *keivan de'itkazai leshum Rachel*: once the *megilla* has been assigned to Rachel, it cannot be reassigned to Leah. But a *Sefer Torah* is *stama kesiva* — written generically — and was never assigned to any particular woman, so perhaps it *can* be used. Conversely, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak argues the reverse: Rabbi Akha berabbi Yoshiya permits reuse *keivan de'ichtiv leshum alos v'alah* — because the *megilla* was written for the purpose of functioning as a curse, regardless of which woman it serves. But a *Sefer Torah* written *lilmod kesiva* — to be a *Sefer Torah* for learning — was never written for the purpose of being a curse at all, and *hacha nami delo machakinan* — one cannot use it for the *sotah* procedure.

The *gemara* thus elegantly demonstrates that there are independent considerations in each case pointing in opposite directions, and one cannot simply map one debate onto the other.

A challenge is then raised from the laws of *gittin*: if a man wrote a *get* for his wife and changed his mind, and a townsman found him and said *shmi keshimcha v'shem ishti k'shem ishtecha* — my name is the same as yours and my wife's name is the same as your wife's — may he use that *get*? The answer is clearly no: *ha-hu pasul legarsheto bo*. A *get* written for one woman is invalid for another. This would seem to support the view that a *megilla* likewise cannot be reused. The *gemara* responds that *gittin* and *sotah* are not governed by the same principles: by a *get*, the *Torah* states *v'chatav lah* — "and he shall write for her" — making *lishmah* the essential act of writing. But for *sotah*, the operative term is *v'asah lah* — and what does "doing" mean in this context? *Mechikah* — the erasing. It is the act of erasing into the water that must be done for her; the writing itself may not require the same standard of *lishmah*.

## Fear & Niddah

### Sudden Fear

The *gemara* now returns to the question raised by the *mishna*'s statement that they say *hotziuha* — take her out of the *azara*. The *gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama* — why must she be removed? Is it because she will die, and they want to prevent a corpse from rendering the *azara* impure?

The *gemara* challenges this reasoning: a corpse is in fact permitted in *machaneh Leviyah*, as derived from the verse that Moshe took the bones of Yosef *imo b'mchitzato* — with him in his camp, and Moshe was in *machaneh Leviyah*. Furthermore, the area where the *sotah* stands — *Sha'ar Nikanor*, at the boundary between *Ezrat Nashim* and *Ezrat Yisrael* — has only the sanctity of *Ezrat Nashim*, which is *machaneh Leviyah*, not *machaneh Shechinah*. Even if she were to die there, a corpse would technically be permitted.

Abaye therefore offers a different explanation: *shema tifros niddah* — the concern is not that she will die, but that the physical trauma and shock of the experience will cause her to emit blood and become a *niddah*. A *niddah* is forbidden in *machaneh Leviyah* because *tumah yotzei migufo* — impurity that issues from the body — renders one prohibited from entering that domain. This is also why, in contemporary times, those who ascend to Har HaBayit are advised regarding their status with respect to both *ba'al keri* and *niddah*.

### Fear Types

This leads the *gemara* to ask: *l'meimra d'be'isusa marafya* — does fear cause the body to loosen and bleed? Yes: *dechtiv vatischalchal hamalka* — Esther trembled greatly — and *amar Rav shepirsah niddah* — Rav says that she became a *niddah* from the trembling.

But a difficulty arises: we have a *mishna* that rules that a woman hiding in a cave, afraid of bandits, need not fear that she has begun her period, because fear suppresses bleeding. Which is it — does fear cause bleeding or prevent it?

The *gemara* resolves this with a distinction: *pachda tzamit* — chronic anxiety, the kind that has been present for some time, causes the body to constrict and suppresses bleeding; *be'isusa marafya* — sudden shock causes the body to loosen and triggers bleeding. Rashi explains *pachda* as prolonged worry, as distinguished from the sudden seizure of fear. It is this sudden shock — *be'isuta* — that the *gemara* identifies as the concern when the woman drinks the *sotah* waters, and therefore the attendants must remove her from the *azara* before she becomes a *niddah* there.

One might note a secondary implication: a woman who wished to delay or obstruct the *sotah* proceedings could theoretically do so by ensuring she became a *niddah*, since the procedure cannot be conducted while she is in that state. Whether this would be treated analogously to simply refusing to drink — resulting in divorce without *ksuva* — is an interesting question left open.

## Suspension Durations

### Three Months

The *gemara* asks: *man masnisin?* — which *tanna* authored our *mishna*, which states that *zechut* can suspend punishment for one, two, or three years? It turns out that at least three other *tannaim* hold positions inconsistent with this formulation. The *braisa* records: if she has merit, it suspends punishment for three months — *kedei hakcarat ha'ubar* — just long enough for a pregnancy to become visible. This is the view of Abba Yossi ben Chanan. His reading of the verse *v'niktah v'nizra'ah zera* is that *v'niktah* refers not only to the *tehorah* woman but also to the meritoriously guilty one, and the suspension lasts until *v'nizra'ah zera* — when a pregnancy would be recognizable, not when it is conceived.

### Nine Months

Rabbi Elazar ben Yitzchak ish Kfar Darom reads *v'nizra'ah zera* differently: *zera* refers to the time it takes for a child to be born. The suspension therefore lasts nine months. A secondary reading he offers draws from *zera ya'avdenu yesupar* — "the seed that serves him will be told" — i.e., *zera hara'uy lesaper*, seed mature enough to speak. This would extend the period further, but the primary position is nine months.

### Twelve Months

Rabbi Yishmael holds: *shneim asar chodesh* — twelve months. Even though there is no direct *rava* for this, there is a *zecher ladavar* — a hint — from the story of Daniel and Nebuchadnezzar. Daniel advised Nebuchadnezzar: *lahen malka malki yishpar alach, v'chatayach b'tzedaka ferok, va'avayach bemichan inayin* — redeem your sins through righteousness, your iniquities through generosity to the poor — and Nebuchadnezzar's well-being would be extended. The verse then records: *u'liktzas yarchin terei asar* — after twelve months, all these things came upon Nebuchadnezzar. He had followed Daniel's advice, performed righteous acts, and thereby postponed the divine punishment by a full year. So merit forestalls punishment for twelve months.

### Three Years

None of these positions, however, reaches three years. The *gemara* resolves this by saying that the *mishna* indeed follows Rabbi Yishmael's twelve-month view, but adds a multiplier from the verse: *ko amar Hashem: al shelosha pish'ei Edom v'al arba'ah lo ashivenu* — "for three transgressions of Edom and for four I will not reverse it." The verse implies that for three sins, God holds back punishment; the model of one year per instance is multiplied threefold, yielding three years. Even though this is only a *zecher ladavar* rather than a definitive proof, it accounts for the *mishna*'s formulation.

## Divine vs. Court

### Model Shift

The final movement of the *daf*'s discussion marks a significant conceptual shift. As the *gemara* elaborates on *zechus toleh*, it moves away from the specific dynamics of the *sotah* procedure — the *v'niktah v'nizra'ah zera* of the relevant *parshat sotah* — and toward a much more generic model: any person who deserves divine punishment may have that punishment forestalled by merit. The proof from Nebuchadnezzar's twelve-month reprieve is the clearest illustration: Nebuchadnezzar is not a *sotah*, not subject to any court proceeding, not even Jewish — yet the same principle of merit suspending divine punishment applies to him.

### God vs. Court

This shift has a positive dimension: it normalizes the *sotah* within a broader theology of divine justice and human merit. The guilty woman is not being treated as a unique category of sinner with her own special divine mechanism; she is simply a person whose deserved punishment can be forestalled, just like anyone else. This arguably *downplays* the hyperfocus on the adulterous woman as an exceptional figure.

At the same time, this shift pulls in a direction that complicates the court-supervised nature of the entire proceeding. If *zechut tolah* is understood as simply a matter of divine punishment operating between the woman and God — forestalled by merit, regardless of *teshuva* or any court action — then the entire procedure begins to look less like a legal determination and more like an occasion for divine intervention. As was pointed out in the earlier discussion of *teshuva*: the more one sees *zechus toleh* through this lens of purely divine punishment, the more it becomes a matter between her and God alone, with the court serving only as the context in which God acts — not as the body that determines her fate. The question of how this interacts with the husband's ability to resume marital relations, and whether the procedure has genuinely "proven" anything if the water does not take immediate effect, remains a deep tension within the entire *masechet* — one that the subsequent *dafim* will continue to address.

---

---

# Sotah 21

## Merit Forestall Puni (II)

### Merit Three Years

The *mishnah* established that *zechus* can forestall the punishment of the *sotah* for as long as three years. The *gemara* now asks: *zechus d'mai*? What type of merit possesses sufficient power to delay punishment for that length of time?

The *gemara* raises two possibilities. The first is *zechus d'Torah* — perhaps it is the merit of learning Torah. Yet this is immediately challenged: *ha einah metzuva v'osa* — a woman is not commanded to learn Torah, and therefore, as an *eina metzuva v'osa*, the merit she accumulates through Torah study does not carry the full weight that *talmud Torah* ordinarily confers. The second possibility is *zechus d'mitzvah* — the merit of other *mitzvos* she has performed. But this too is called into question. *Zechus d'mitzvah mi magna kulei hai?* Since when does a *mitzvah* wield that kind of protective power?

### Ner Mitzvah Torah Or

To press this challenge, the *gemara* cites a *braita* in the name of Rabbi Menachem bar Rabbi Yosi, a teaching entirely general in character, concerned with the relative protective power of *mitzvah* as against Torah. *Ki ner mitzvah v'Torah or* — for a *mitzvah* is a candle and the Torah is light. The verse, says the *braita*, deliberately compares the *mitzvah* to a *ner* and the Torah to *or*, and the lesson drawn from each comparison is distinct.

*Ma ner einah megina ela lefi sha'ah* — just as a candle provides light or protection only for a limited time, so too *af mitzvah einah megina ela lefi sha'ah*, a *mitzvah* only protects for a brief period. *Torah*, by contrast, is compared to *or* in the broader sense of light itself — *ma or magin l'olam*, light illuminates perpetually — and so *af Torah megina l'olam*, Torah protects forever.

The *gemara* then cites the verse from Mishlei: *b'hishalchecha tancha osach, b'shochbecha tishmor alecha, v'hakitzosa hi tisichecha*.
