The *braita* reads this verse as a sequence. *B'hishalchecha tancha osach* — when you walk, it will guide you — *zeh l'olam hazeh*, this refers to Torah's guidance in this world. *B'shochbecha tishmor alecha* — when you sleep, it will guard you — *zu misah*, Torah protects even in death. *V'hakitzosa hi tisichecha* — and when you awaken it will speak for you — *l'asid lavo*, in the future world, where the Torah one has learned will serve as an advocate.

The difficulty this creates for the *gemara*'s question is now clear. If a *mitzvah* protects only briefly, it would seem insufficient to forestall punishment for as long as three years. And if the relevant *zechus* is Torah, the power of that protection would seem unavailable to a woman at full strength, since she is an *eina metzuva v'osa*.

One might argue that the protective power of Torah does not derive from the *kiyum hamitzvah* of *talmud Torah*, but from the intrinsic quality of Torah as *dvar Hashem* — from connecting with the word of God — and that this power operates regardless of whether one is commanded. That argument is available, and it is not without force. Yet the *stam* of the *gemara*, at least at this stage of the discussion, appears to proceed on the assumption that the protective quality of Torah flows through the value of fulfilling the *mitzvah* of *talmud Torah*, not from some independent sacramental power of Torah itself. This raises a further question: even if a woman's Torah study is understood merely as *hechsher mitzvah* — a means of learning the *halachos* of what she must do — how could that instrumental learning confer greater protection than the *mitzvos* it enables her to perform? If a *mitzvah* protects only briefly, the learning that enables it cannot protect longer. The *gemara* thus leaves both possibilities in difficulty.

Before moving to the *gemara*'s resolution, it is worth noting an apparent tension in the tradition's broader framework. The *Shulchan Aruch* rules that women do not recite a *bracha* over *mitzvas asei shehazman grama* if they choose to perform them, yet women do recite *birchas haTorah* in the morning. The Soloveitchik analysis holds that *birchas haTorah* is not a *birchas hamitzvah* in the ordinary sense but rather a *bracha* on the *cheftza* of Torah itself — as evidenced by the blessing's own language: *asher kidshanu b'mitzvosav v'tzivanu la'asok b'divrei Torah* points toward the *mitzvah* dimension, but *v'ha'arev na*, *melamed Torah l'amo Yisrael*, and *bocher asher bachar banu* address Torah's intrinsic character as *Nosen HaTorah*. On this view, the protective power of Torah could indeed be understood as independent of *kiyum hamitzvah*. Yet, as noted, this is not the path the *gemara* chooses to take.

The *braita* then adds a second formulation: *aveira mechaba mitzvah, v'ein aveira mechaba Torah* — a sin extinguishes a *mitzvah*, but a sin cannot extinguish Torah. Rashi explains that "extinguish" here refers not to the protective power of the *mitzvah* but to its *s'char* — its reward. One who has performed *mitzvos* and also committed *aveiros* may find that *le'atid lavo* they cancel each other out. But *aveiros* will not cancel the reward of Torah. This is supported by the verse *mayim rabim lo yuchlu lechabot es ha'ahavah* — great waters cannot extinguish the love. The *Maharsha* observes that the imagery is striking: Torah is generally compared to water, yet here the *aveiros* are the water and Torah is the flame — the *ner*, the *or* — that cannot be quenched. So *mitzvos* afford brief, momentary protection that may ultimately be neutralized by *aveiros*, while Torah confers a lasting, encompassing protection that endures. Neither option, then, cleanly solves the *gemara*'s problem.

### Parable Traveler

To illustrate the difference between the protection of *mitzvah* and the protection of Torah, the *braita* of Rabbi Menachem bar Rabbi Yosi offers a *mashal*. A person is traveling in the darkness of night, *b'ishon layla va'afeila*, and he fears the thorns, the pits, the thistles, the wild animals, and the bandits. He also does not know which path to take.

He then chances upon a torch — *avuka shel or*. The torch immediately delivers him from the thorns, the pits, and the thistles — he can now see what lies immediately before him. Yet he is still afraid of the wild animals and the bandits, and he still does not know which path to take. When dawn breaks — *keivan she'ala amud hashachar* — the daylight saves him from the animals and the bandits, for these are dangers of the night that the light of day dispels. Yet even now he still does not know which way to go. When he reaches a crossroads — *parshas drachim* — he is saved from everything and knows the right path.

The *mashal* is clear in its first two stages. The torch is the *ner mitzvah*: it provides immediate protection from immediate dangers, but its reach is limited. The light of day is the *or Torah*: it is broader, more comprehensive, and protects from graver threats. But what is this *parshas drachim*, this crossroads where one finally knows the right direction? The *gemara* will address this — and the three opinions about its meaning constitute a striking discussion in their own right.

---

## Rav Yosef Answer

### Rav Yosef Position

Rav Yosef proposes a resolution that cuts through the apparent impasse. He distinguishes between two dimensions of protection — protection from punishment and protection from sin — and argues that *mitzvah* and Torah provide these in different combinations.

*Mitzvah b'idna d'asik bah megana u'matzla* — a *mitzvah* while you are in the course of performing it both protects you from punishment and, as Rashi explains based on the continuation of the *gemara*, saves you from sin. *B'idna d'lo asik bah* — once you have finished, *aguni magnei* — it still forestalls punishment, but *atzulei lo matzla* — it no longer protects you from sinning. Torah, by contrast, *bein b'idna d'asik bah u'vein b'idna d'lo asik bah*, whether you are actively learning or not, *megana u'matzla* — it both forestalls punishment and protects from sin. The educative power of Torah shapes character in a lasting way, setting a person on a more elevated path even when he is not sitting in the *beit midrash*. On this account, a *mitzvah* does forestall punishment even after it is completed, and that is sufficient to explain how this *sotah*'s merit delayed her punishment for up to three years. Torah's additional power is the ongoing protection from future sin.

### Rava Doeg Challenge

Rava challenges Rav Yosef's position. *Ela me'ata* — if Torah protects one from sinning even when not actively learning, how do we account for Doeg and Achitophel? These two figures, prominent in rabbinic literature as great *talmidei chachamim*, nonetheless sinned grievously, pursuing and attacking David. *Mi lo askei beTorah* — they certainly engaged in Torah study. *Amai lo higina aleihu* — why did their Torah learning not prevent them from sinning? The objection is fundamental: there are those who learn Torah and nonetheless go badly astray. Rav Yosef's formulation that Torah protects from sin while not learning cannot be sustained if it is falsified by such prominent counterexamples.

### Rava Revision

Rava therefore revises the framework. Torah, *b'idna de'asik bah*, while one is actively learning, *magna u'matzla* — protects from punishment and saves from sin. *B'idna delo asik bah*, when not learning, *aguni magna* — it still forestalls punishment, but *atzulei lo matzla* — it does not necessarily prevent sin. A person can learn Torah and then leave the *beit midrash* and sin. *Mitzvah*, meanwhile — *bein b'idna de'asik bah bein b'idna delo asik bah* — whether performing or not, *aguni magna* — protects from punishment, but *atzulei lo matzla* — cannot protect from sin, even during the act of performance. (It is at least theoretically possible, as the *Mishnah Berurah* hints regarding *lashon hara* in a *sukkah*, to be engaged in a *mitzvah* while simultaneously sinning in another way.)

This revised formulation serves the *gemara*'s purpose. The advantage of Torah over *mitzvah* is now narrowly defined: Torah, uniquely, prevents sin *while one is actively learning*. Both Torah and *mitzvah* forestall punishment after their performance is complete. This explains how a *sotah*'s merit of *mitzvah* could protect her for up to three years. It also accounts for Doeg and Achitophel — men who learned Torah but sinned when they left their learning. The difficulty with Rava's formulation is that it substantially attenuates the lovely imagery of the *braita*, which suggested Torah's protection was far more sweeping and enduring. But this is where the *gemara* arrives.

---

## Ravina Women Merit

### Ravina Merit Enable

Ravina offers a different resolution entirely, one that returns to the original question about the *sotah* rather than reconstructing the topology of *mitzvah* and Torah protection. *Le'olam zechus Torah* — it is in fact the merit of Torah that protects this woman. And as for the objection that she is an *eina metzuva v'osa* and therefore her Torah learning lacks full merit — *nihi depikudei lo mifkada* — it is true she is not commanded, *be'agra demakrin u'matnyan bnaihu* — but she shares in the reward that accrues from causing her sons to read *pesukim* and study *mishnah*, and *u'natrin lehu le'gavreihu ad de'atu mi-bei midrasha* — from waiting patiently for her husband to return from the study hall, maintaining the home, and enabling him to learn. *Mi lo palga bahadayhu?* — does she not receive a portion of that reward? By enabling the Torah learning of the men in her life — her sons and her husband — she participates in their *mitzva ve'oseh*, and it is that participation which confers upon her the *zechus Torah* that can forestall punishment.

### Women Enablers

This answer is candid about its assumptions: a woman's own Torah learning, as *eina metzuva v'osa*, does not carry the full protective weight of a man's Torah learning. The merit she acquires comes not from her own direct engagement with Torah as a commanded act, but from her role as enabler. She sends her children to *cheder*; she waits for her husband to return from the *beit midrash*.

This is not a *gemara* that necessarily sits easily with contemporary sensibilities, and it is worth noting that the *gemara* did not have to construct the question this way. The *mishnah* earlier cited Nevuchadnezzar's capacity for *zechus* to forestall punishment for three years — and his merit was simply giving charity to the poor. Nothing required the *gemara* to introduce the *braita* of *ner mitzvah v'Torah or*, to reject the possibility that an ordinary *mitzvah* could carry this power, or to resist the idea that a woman's Torah study as *eina metzuva v'osa* might nonetheless provide protection. The *gemara* chose this path. And the path it chose has a pointed contextual relationship with what follows: the later *mishnah* contains both Ben Azzai's view that one is obligated to teach one's daughter Torah and Rabbi Eliezer's opposition. Ravina's answer, appearing immediately before that discussion, effectively frames women's relationship to Torah learning in instrumental rather than intrinsic terms — their real merit lies in enabling men's Torah, not in their own engagement with it as an independent value.

The contrast with the *sotah* herself is also worth observing. The *sotah* was waiting — apparently — for her paramour. The righteous woman whom Ravina describes is waiting for her husband to return from learning Torah. The *gemara* appears to be drawing a deliberate contrast between two types of waiting.

---

## Merit Forestall Puni (II)

### Crossroads Interpretatio…

The *gemara* now returns to the unresolved element of the parable — the *parshas drachim*, the crossroads where the traveler is finally saved from everything and knows which path to take. *Mai parshas drachim?* Three *amoraim* offer interpretations, and taken together they form a suggestive continuum.

Rav Chisda says: *zu talmid chacham v'yom ha-misa* — this is a *talmid chacham* and the day of death. The Torah has guided one through life, protected from dangers both immediate and profound, and the *parshas drachim* is that final threshold — the moment of departing this world for the next. At that crossroads, one does not yet know whether the path leads to *olam ha-ba* or not — *al ta'amin b'atzmecha ad yom mosecha* — yet having arrived there through the guidance and protection of Torah, one now knows the Torah has led one through to the end, set one on the right path. The image is almost entirely sacramental: Torah, sustained throughout a lifetime of learning, carries a person through to the final reckoning.

Rav Yitzchak says: *zeh talmid chacham b'yirat chet* — this is a *talmid chacham* with fear of sin. For Rav Yitzchak, Torah illuminates the world and shows what is right, but Torah alone cannot guarantee that one will choose correctly. *Ra'eh nasati lefanecha hayom et ha-chayim v'et ha-tov v'et ha-mavet v'et ha-ra* — one now knows the two paths, but will one choose the right one? That depends on bringing to the *parshas drachim* a quality that Torah cannot by itself supply: *yirat chet*, the internalized fear of sin. Torah is necessary but not sufficient.

Mar Zutra says: *zeh talmid chacham d'sakla shma'ta aliba d'hilchasa* — this is a *talmid chacham* who successfully brings legal reasoning to its correct *halachic* conclusion. For Mar Zutra, even choosing to act rightly is not enough if one's Torah learning leads to incorrect *halachic* conclusions. Torah shows what is right in principle, but one must be able to translate that learning into sound *halacha l'maaseh*.

These three positions form a continuum from the mystical to the rational. For Rav Chisda, Torah has an almost intrinsic, sacramental protective power — sustain it till you die, and it will carry you through. For Rav Yitzchak, Torah is necessary but must be complemented by character, by *yirat chet*, the quality that ensures one actually chooses rightly when confronted with the fork in the road. For Mar Zutra, Torah must be disciplined into correct *halachic* reasoning — even character and good intent are insufficient if one's learning has led to wrong conclusions. Each of the latter two answers also implicitly pulls back from the claim that Torah does everything: one can be a *talmid chacham* without having the right character; one can learn Torah without arriving at the correct *halacha*.

---

## Aveira Sin Extinguish

### Aveira Mechabah

The *gemara* now returns to the formulation encountered earlier: *aveira mechaba mitzvah, v'ein aveira mechaba Torah* — a sin extinguishes a *mitzvah*, but a sin cannot extinguish Torah. The verse from Shir HaShirim is adduced: *mayim rabim lo yuchlu lechabot es ha'ahavah* — great waters cannot extinguish the love, where "love" signifies Torah. The *Maharsha* notes the poignancy of the imagery: elsewhere Torah is compared to water, but here the *aveiros* are the water and Torah is the flame — the *ner*, the *or* — that cannot be drowned.

### Doeg Achitophel

Rav Yosef introduces a *drasha* by Rabbi Menachem bar Rabbi Yosi on a verse that Doeg and Achitophel might have encountered — and which, had they properly understood it as Rabbi Menachem bar Rabbi Yosi did, *lo radfu batar Dovid*, they would not have pursued David.

Their reasoning, it appears, ran as follows. The verse *v'lo yeira'eh becha ervat davar v'shav me'acharecha* teaches that a sin of forbidden sexual relations causes God to withdraw. David had sinned in the matter of Bathsheba. Therefore, they concluded, God had abandoned David, and he was now susceptible to attack. *Leimor Elohim azavo* — God has forsaken him.

What they failed to understand — *v'hein einam yodim* — is precisely the principle of *aveira mechaba mitzvah, v'ein aveira mechaba Torah*. It is true that a *sin* can extinguish the protection of a *mitzvah*. But it cannot extinguish the protection of Torah. David was not merely a performer of *mitzvos*; he was a *talmid chacham*, a man of Torah. And because Torah's protection cannot be extinguished by an *aveira*, God did not forsake David. Doeg and Achitophel, brilliant scholars though they were in their own right, misread the verse and drew the wrong conclusion — they did not reckon with the distinct and indelible protective power of Torah.

The *gemara* then turns to the verse *im yitein ish es kol hon beiso b'ahavah boz yavozu lo* — if a man were to give all the wealth of his house for love, people would scorn him. The discussion of Hillel and his brother Shevna illuminates an ideal: Hillel devoted himself entirely to Torah without relying on material support from others, unwilling to trade any portion of his Torah's reward for financial ease. When Shevna proposed a *Yissachar-Zevulun* arrangement, a *bat kol* emerged and cited this very verse. Hillel would not commodify his Torah, would not give up so much as a fraction of his *talmud Torah* for worldly benefit. Ulla notes that this surpasses the model of those who learned Torah under the support of a brother or a *nasi* — worthy arrangements, but not the highest ideal.

---

## Teach Daughters Torah

### Ben Azzai Teach

With the new *amud* the *gemara* turns to the next *mishnah*, which contains a debate about teaching one's daughter Torah. Ben Azzai states: *chayav adam l'lamed es bito Torah* — a person is required to teach his daughter Torah. The reason is connected to the *sotah* procedure: the *mishnah* establishes that *zechus* can suspend the effects of the water, and a woman who has learned Torah will understand this — she will know why the water may have failed to act immediately and not suppose the *sotah* ritual has been definitively disproven. There is at least a practical argument for teaching women the relevant Torah.

Yet the discussion that follows is inflected by the *gemara* we have just completed. If teaching one's daughter Torah confers upon her the *zechus* of Torah — or at least, as Ravina suggested, enables her to become an instrument of Torah's merit — one might think there is every reason to teach her. But the opposing view raises a different concern entirely.

### Rabbi Eliezer Tiflus

Rabbi Eliezer states: *kol ha-melamed bito Torah k'ilu melamdah tiflus* — whoever teaches his daughter Torah is as though he has taught her *tiflus*. The term *tiflus*, which in context is clearly juxtaposed with *perishus* and tied to sexual transgression, most naturally denotes sexual licentiousness or conduct of a sexually improper character. Several sources confirm this reading: the *gemara* elsewhere connects *tiflus* to the disqualification of women and slaves from *zimmun* together, and the word appears in descriptions of the banquet of Achashverosh where the officers competed in boasting about women.

Why would teaching one's daughter Torah be equivalent to teaching her *tiflus*? Several possibilities present themselves. The most direct, and most relevant to the *sotah* context, is that Torah knowledge shows her the loopholes — she learns the *halachos* and learns how the system works, and that knowledge enables her to exploit it. A second possibility: Torah study develops nuance and analytical subtlety, and that capacity for fine distinctions can be turned to finding ways around prohibited conduct. A third, more structural concern is that Torah's *zechus* will protect her from punishment, thereby removing the deterrent effect of the *sotah* ritual.

### Torah Effect Tiflus

The *gemara* clarifies that Rabbi Eliezer's statement cannot be taken literally — Torah is obviously not itself *tiflus*. *Ela eima k'ilu limda tiflus* — it is as if he taught her *tiflus*, because the effect of her having learned Torah is equivalent in its practical consequences to having been taught licentiousness. It is not that Torah is shameful; it is that in this context, for this person, the knowledge functions as an opening toward transgression.

### Wisdom Craftiness

Rabbi Abbahu identifies the underlying principle of Rabbi Eliezer's position: *d'ksiv ani chochma shakanti arma* — I am wisdom, I have dwelt with craftiness. *Keivan she-nichnas chochma b'adam nichnesa imo armumis* — once wisdom enters a person, craftiness enters with it. Wisdom and cunning travel together; learning sharpens the mind, and a sharper mind finds more ways to achieve what it desires. The concern, then, is not that Torah is corrupting in any direct sense, but that it arms one with intellectual tools that can be turned in any direction.

The obvious question arises: what of men? Men learn Torah and thereby also acquire *arma* — craftiness. Rabbi Abbahu's principle seems to apply universally. The *gemara* does not resolve this question explicitly here. One might say that men are obligated to learn regardless and cannot be exempt on account of this danger, or that the tradition places greater trust in men's use of those tools — though neither answer is articulated in so many words.

### Rabbanan Three Positions

The Rabbanan who disagree with Rabbi Eliezer ask: *hai ani chochma mai avdi lei?* What do they do with the verse *ani chochma shakanti arma*? They apply it differently. Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina reads *arma* not as craftiness but as nakedness — *ein divrei Torah miskaymin ela b'mi she-ma'amid atzmo arom aleihen* — Torah endures only in one who makes himself naked for it, strips away all other pursuits and devotes himself entirely. Rashi, however, reads it as a variant of the craftiness interpretation: one who schemes and maneuvers to find every possible opportunity to learn Torah, seizing moments wherever they appear. Rabbi Yochanan adds: *ein divrei Torah miskaymin ela b'mi she-mesim atzmo k'mi she-eino* — Torah endures only in one who makes himself as nothing, practicing a radical self-negation and self-sacrifice for the sake of learning. *V'hachochma me'ayin timatzei* — wisdom comes from nothingness; make yourself nothing, and Torah will find its home in you.

These three readings of *arma* — the sacramental (nakedness, total devotion), the strategic (seizing every opportunity to learn), and the spiritual (self-negation) — stand in contrast to Rabbi Eliezer's use of the same word. Rabbi Eliezer sees *arma* as the danger that Torah's wisdom produces; the Rabbanan see *arma* as precisely the quality one must bring *to* Torah in order to truly acquire it.

### Yerushalmi Matron

Tosafot cites a crucial passage from the Yerushalmi that illuminates the full scope of Rabbi Eliezer's position. A *matrona* — a Roman noblewoman — posed a genuine question to Rabbi Eliezer: why did the sin of the golden calf, which was one sin, result in three different forms of death? Rabbi Eliezer refused to answer her. *Ein isha chachma ela bapalach* — a woman's wisdom is only in her weaving. The school in Israel called *Pelech* derives its name from this phrase, chosen deliberately and ironically.

When his son Horkenos reproached him — *bishvil shelo le'ashivah davar echad min haTorah*, you refused to answer a single question of Torah to this woman, and by insulting her you have cost me three hundred *kor* of *ma'aser* annually — Rabbi Eliezer replied: *yisrefu divrei Torah v'al yimsaru divrei Torah l'nashim* — better that the words of Torah be burnt than that they be transmitted to women.

This was not merely the concern about *melamdah tiflus*. Rabbi Eliezer held a principled, sweeping opposition to women receiving Torah. The image is striking in context: in the *sotah* ritual, Torah is dissolved into water to be tested against the woman; here, Rabbi Eliezer would rather Torah burn than be given over to women. In both cases, Torah must be protected from a certain kind of contact with women — though obviously for entirely different reasons and with very different valences.

The Yerushalmi also provides important context for Ben Azzai's position. Ben Azzai is said to follow the view of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, who expounded the verse of *hakhel*: *ha'anashim, v'hanashim, v'hatef* — the men came to learn, *nashim ba'os lishmoa*, the women came to hear. As Tosafot explains, this means women's participation in *hakhel* is not for the sake of *zechus Torah* per se, but *kedei sheyeidu lekayeim mitzvah* — so that they know how to fulfill *mitzvos*. This establishes a middle position between the poles of the debate: it is not an intrinsic *Torah lishma* for women, but neither is it *melamdah tiflus*. There are thus three positions in the tradition: Torah study for women has intrinsic value; Torah study for women is valuable as instrumental knowledge enabling *kiyum mitzvos*; and Torah study for women is actively dangerous.

---

## Rabbi Yehoshua Woman

### Kav Tiflus Nine

Rabbi Yehoshua's statement returns the discussion to the sexual dimension that runs throughout the tractate. *Rotze isha bekav ve'tiflut mitisha kabim u'frishus* — a woman prefers one measure of sustenance with *tiflus* over nine measures with *perishus*, with asceticism and separation.

### Income Presence

Two readings of this statement emerge from the *rishonim*. Rashi understands *tiflus* in the general sense of greater sexual freedom, and the contrast is between a modest life that affords greater sexual opportunity and an affluent one with more separation. Rabbeinu Chananel, cited by Tosafot, makes the *pshat* more specific and more domestic: a woman would rather her husband be a donkey driver who comes home regularly — once a week on *Shabbat*, providing *onah* — earning a modest income of one *kav*, than have him be a camel driver who travels on long routes, comes home only once every thirty days, and earns the much larger income of nine *kabim*. *Chavivah aleiha onah bechol Shabbat vekav echad mitisha kabim u'frishus sheloshim yom*.

One might observe that this preference — for the husband's presence over material wealth — seems entirely natural and even admirable. Yet in context Rabbi Yehoshua presents it as a concern, because the same drive, misdirected, becomes the source of the *sotah*'s downfall. And the teaching connects back to the question of Torah instruction: the danger of teaching a woman Torah, in Rabbi Eliezer's view, is that Torah arms her with the tools to pursue what she desires. Rabbi Yehoshua simply asserts that what she desires, at bottom, is this.

---

## Four Destroyers

### Chasid Shoteh

In the same context, the *mishnah* records a teaching attributed to Rabbi Yehoshua: there are those who destroy the world, and among them is the *chasid shoteh*, the foolish pious person. *Heichy dami chasid shoteh?* — what does a *chasid shoteh* look like? *Kegon deka taveia itta benahra, ve'amar lav orach ara listakulei bah, ve'atzulah* — a woman is drowning in the river, and he says it is improper to gaze at a woman, and he fails to save her.

Tosafot cites a parallel from the Yerushalmi: an infant is drowning, and the *chasid shoteh* says, let me first remove my *tefillin* and then I will save him — *ad shecholeitz tefillin yatzah nishmato*, and by the time he finishes removing his *tefillin*, the child has died. There is also the neat wordplay embedded in the Yerushalmi version: *echlotz* — I will remove — echoes the language of *tefillin* removal, *chalitzah*, while the word itself sounds like a cry of urgency. The point in both cases is the same: piety that is divorced from practical moral reasoning, that privileges the form of righteousness over its substance, destroys lives.

### Rasha Arum

The *rasha arum*, the crafty wicked person, is the counterpart of the *chasid shoteh*. Where the *chasid shoteh* is conspicuously righteous while causing harm through his failure to engage with reality, the *rasha arum* conceals his wickedness behind a facade of ordinariness or even apparent virtue. What ties this figure to the others in the list is the same element — he is not what he appears. His *rishus* is executed *b'armimus*, with craftiness, such that it is not apparent to observers that anything wrongful has occurred.

### Early Case Judge

Rabbi Yochanan identifies the *rasha arum* as *zeh hamati'im devarav le'dayan kodem sheba ba'al din chaveiro* — one who presents his version of the case to the judge before the opposing litigant arrives. Even if the judge intends to be impartial, once a case has been framed in a particular way it is very difficult to genuinely reorganize one's understanding around the opposing account. First impressions in litigation create a bias that is hard to dislodge. There is in fact a prohibition against hearing one *ba'al din* in the absence of the other, and Rabbi Yochanan's identification of this as *rasha arum* behavior underlines why: it is subtle, it does not appear to be a violation of anything, and yet it has a real and corrupting effect on the judicial process.

### Poor Disqualify

Rabbi Abbahu identifies the *rasha arum* as one who gives a poor person just enough money to push him over the threshold of eligibility — *zeh ha-nosein dinar le'ani le'hashlim lo masayim zuz*. The rule, as the *mishnah* establishes, is that one who possesses two hundred *zuz* may not take *leket*, *shichecha*, *peah*, or *maaser ani* — he is not considered an *ani*. One who has one *dinar* less than two hundred *zuz* is an *ani* and may receive these gifts in full. By giving the poor person precisely the *dinar* that brings him to two hundred *zuz*, the donor appears to be performing an act of generosity — he gives the man something! — while in fact cutting him off from all future entitlement to *matnos aniyim*. The one-time gift costs the donor a *dinar*; the loss to the poor person is potentially enormous.

### Estate Sale

Rav Assi, citing Rabbi Yochanan, identifies a further instance of the *rasha arum*: *zeh ha-masi eitza limkor b'nechasim mu'atim* — one who counsels the sale of a small estate in circumstances where this advice will harm the orphaned daughters.

The legal background, as Rabbi Yosi cites in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, is the rule that if male heirs from a small estate sell it prematurely, *mah she-machru machru* — what they have sold is sold. In a small estate, all the assets are in principle earmarked to support the daughters — *mezonos* for the unmarried sisters — until they marry. The sons technically have no share. Yet if the sons liquidate the estate, the daughters' claim, which lies against real property, cannot follow the proceeds; the sale stands and the daughters' support disappears.

The *rasha arum* here is not the son who sells — Tosafot notes that even the son's action may not be strictly forbidden. What is wrongful is the unsolicited outsider who, having no stake in the outcome, volunteers advice that serves one party at the direct expense of another and subverts the intent of the original estate arrangement.

Abaye adds a variant: *zeh ha-masi eitza limkor b'nechasim k'Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel*. The relevant dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel concerns a gift made with a subsequent gift-over: I give my property to Reuven, and after Reuven, to Shimon. If Reuven sells the property during his lifetime, Rabbi holds that Shimon can reclaim it from the purchasers; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that Shimon receives only what Reuven leaves over — if Reuven sold it, it is gone. The *rasha arum* advises Reuven to sell under the authority of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position, thereby defeating Shimon's expectation under the original gift. Again, it is not the advice itself that is necessarily wrong if solicited by one's client, but the uninvited intervention to harm one party for the benefit of another that constitutes *rasha arum* conduct.

---

---

# Sotah 22

## Women's Torah Study

### Opening & Tiflus Issue

Today's *daf* is 22 in *Sotah*. We pick up at the very bottom of 21b, having just worked through a series of fascinating and contested reflections on the question of teaching one's daughter *Torah*. The Gemara raised the concern of *tiflus* — the idea expressed in the famous formulation *kol hamelamed bito Torah ke'ilu limdah tiflus*, that teaching a daughter *Torah* is as if one taught her foolishness or licentiousness. This issue was itself preceded by a broader Gemara discussion about the value of *Talmud Torah* for women, arriving at the question indirectly by asking what kind of *zechus* is *toleh* for women — and exploring women's role as *eina metzuvah ve'osah*. The Gemara then moved into Rabbi Yehoshua's skepticism about women who present themselves as ascetic and uninterested in physical pleasure, and from there into the broader theme of people who do not present themselves as they truly are.

### Historical Context

Before returning to the Gemara, a brief word on the *tiflus* debate is in order. Historically, women were often not educated simply because women were not educated in general society — not necessarily from any religious conviction. But in the modern era, when women's education became both possible and expected, the question of women learning *Torah* and specifically *Torah Sheba'al Peh* became, for some communities, a serious ideological and *halachic* position grounded in the concept of *tiflus*, and for others — including the *Rav* and the Lubavitcher Rebbe — something considered absolutely essential. The real battleground has far more to do with broad sociological and religious attitudes than with the precise interpretation of this single line.

### R. Eliezer's Position

As we saw, *Tosfos* quotes the *Yerushalmi* where Rabbi Eliezer takes not merely a cautionary position about *tiflus* as a loophole in *sotah* proceedings, but an outright harsh stance on the value of women learning *Torah* altogether: *mutav yisrefu divrei Torah ve'al yimsru lenashim* — it is better that the words of *Torah* be burned than transmitted to women. Whatever one makes of the attitude toward women underlying that statement, it reflects a very strong position. And yet the *Gemara* does not come down definitively on one side of the Rabbi Eliezer versus Ben Azzai debate, leaving open the question of how to rule — or even whether this is a matter of *psak* at all, rather than competing positions in *aggadic* literature.

### Rambam's Approach

The *Rambam*'s treatment is instructive here. He rules that a woman *can* learn *Torah* and that she is like *eina metzuvah ve'osah* — she performs an act that is not obligatory upon her — but he affirms *yesh lah s'char*, she receives reward for it. Then, introduced with the formula *aval amru chachamim*, he cites *kol hamelamed bito Torah ke'ilu limdah tiflus*. The phrasing *aval amru chachamim* signals explicitly that the *Rambam* is not presenting this as *halachah*, but rather as a form of religious direction or advice. He is not *paskening* it as a binding ruling.

### Context & Realities

Several distinct considerations shape how one understands Rabbi Eliezer's position. First, there is the question of whether the Gemara establishes any definitive ruling at all. Second, even within Rabbi Eliezer's own statement, how much is it *halachah* and how much shaped by the particular social realities of women in his era? Third — and this is the crucial contemporary dimension — how much do present-day realities demand a fundamentally different response, such that following Rabbi Eliezer's approach today would be not only counterproductive but genuinely destructive? The reason different communities take different positions on women's *Torah* education is not primarily because they interpret this one line differently; it is because they hold different broader views about women's roles, intellectual capacities, and relationship to society. The interpretation of the line follows from those views — not the other way around.

---

## Deceptive People

### Theme Introduction

Returning now to the Gemara, we are in the midst of a discussion about people who do not present themselves as they truly are. The earlier material included Rabbi Yehoshua's comment about the *isha perushah* — the woman who presents herself as ascetically pious but whose motives are suspect — and the *chassid shoteh*, someone who has absorbed the externals of *chassidus* without grasping its essence, drawn entirely toward outward form rather than inner reality. There was also the *rasha arum*, the deceptive wicked person who appears righteous while scheming in the background.

### Rav Sheshet

The Gemara continues at the bottom of 21b. *Amar Rav Sheshet*: the *rasha arum* is one who *machtiya acherim b'orchotav* — who tips other people toward his path. *Rashi* explains: *reu v'asu kamoni, l'chu b'drachai* — "Look at me, follow my example, walk in my ways." The person presents himself as a model of righteousness, saying "imitate me," while in truth this performance is designed to deflect suspicion from his real conduct. The outward *chassidus* is a cover for inner corruption: *lo nitkaven zeh l'harot atzmo k'chassid b'einei habriyot v'ein tocho k'baro*. Admittedly, this does not fit the Gemara's language perfectly. *Tosfos* offers what feels like a more compelling reading: this person gives advice to others that ultimately serves his own interests rather than theirs. Like an advisor who steers a client toward an investment because it benefits himself — the guidance appears altruistic, but is entirely self-serving. This relates to the prohibition of *lifnei iver*, though the Gemara's concern here is not with cataloguing specific *issurim* but with identifying character types: the sort of person who always presents as deeply generous and other-directed, while every move serves himself.

### Lenient to Self

*Amar Rabbi Zreika amar Rav Huna*: the *rasha arum* is *zeh hameikal le'atzmo u'machmir le'acheirim* — one who is lenient for himself and stringent toward others. This person projects an image of great *frumkeit*; whenever asked a *sha'ila*, he responds with the strictest ruling. But privately, when no one is watching, he applies the most lenient standard to himself. The rigorous public persona is inversely related to his private behavior.

### Ulla's Category

*Ulla amar*: such a person is one who *kara ve'shana velo shimish talmidei chachamim* — who learned *Mikra* and *Mishna* but never genuinely attended upon Torah sages.

### Shimush Debate

What is the precise problem with *velo shimish*? *Rashi* explains: *lilmod sevarat haGemara b'ta'amei haMishna* — the person knows all the material but has never engaged in the kind of rabbinic discourse that reveals what it actually means. *She'ein Torato al boryah* — his *Torah* learning lacks depth — *ve'ein lilmod heimenno*, one cannot simply learn from *Mishna* alone, because *sheharei al yedei hata'amim yesh chilluk be'issur ve'heter, be'dinei mamonot leZakot uleChayev, uvetahara letamei uletaher* — only by understanding the reasoning behind rulings does one grasp the distinctions governing *issur ve'heter*, monetary law, and matters of *tahara*. The *Gemara* itself is always asking *mai ta'ama amar hachi* — what is the underlying reason — and tracing *ika beineihum* — the practical differences that flow from competing rationales. Without that conceptual scaffolding, a person cannot actually apply the *halachah* properly.

But why is this person an *arum*, a schemer? The Gemara explains: *vearum hu shemashmi'a kolo ve'shoneh mishnayotav*, *kasevar hu shevaki b'ta'ameihem*, *ve'nohegin bo kavod ke'talmidei chachamim* — he broadcasts his erudition, recites *mishnayos* with great confidence, and people assume he is a genuine *talmid chacham* and defer to him accordingly. We all know people of this type: very erudite, able to cite a thousand sources, impressive in their fluency — but with no real depth of understanding. The Gemara elsewhere captures this as *chamor nosei sefarim*, a donkey carrying books — all the information on its back, none of it genuinely internalized.

One might also suggest that *shimush talmidei chachamim* points to something beyond intellectual comprehension. The purpose of attending upon Torah sages is not only to acquire the conceptual tools for *halachic* reasoning, but to observe how *Torah* actually transforms character — how it shapes the small, daily ways in which one interacts with other people. A person who has only pursued the knowledge, without that investment in personal development, remains in some sense a *rasha arum*: his unrefined character traits persist beneath a surface that looks entirely like that of a *talmid chacham*.

### Xerox & Education

This discussion connects in an interesting way back to the earlier conversation about women's *Torah* education. The Gemara's concern about *tiflus* was in some quarters associated specifically with *Torah Sheba'al Peh* as distinct from *Torah Shebichtav*. In certain *chareidi* schools, the approach has been to teach girls *Mikra* but not *Rashi*, on the grounds that *Torah Sheba'al Peh* is the dangerous knowledge. There was even a period when the "progressive" approach to women studying *Gemara* was to allow it only from a photocopied sheet — as if physical distance from the *Gemara* itself mitigated something. The point is that learning *Mikra* and *Mishna* without *Gemara* and without genuine depth is not only intellectually incomplete; it is, in the Gemara's framework, precisely the profile of someone who appears knowledgeable but cannot actually navigate *halachah*. And part of what makes *Torah Sheba'al Peh* feel threatening to some may be exactly that it is empowering — it is the knowledge that actually governs how we live and act.

### Am Ha'aretz Status

Having described the person who learned but did not attend upon sages, the Gemara now assigns him a category. *Rabbi Eliezer omer: harei zeh am ha'aretz* — he is like a commoner. This is notable because the *am ha'aretz* designation, while often carrying negative connotations in rabbinic literature, is actually a step back from the *rasha arum*. An *am ha'aretz* is not necessarily malicious — he is simply someone whose *halachic* practice cannot be relied upon and who is outside the rabbinic world. Perhaps he is a fine person who loves learning but lacks intellectual depth, or who has no bad intentions but simply cannot represent himself as more knowledgeable than he is. The *am ha'aretz* is better than the *rasha arum*, though one also cannot trust his *halachic* precision.

### Bur Classification

*Rav Nachmani omer: harei zeh bur* — worse still, he is a complete ignoramus. This is surprising, and *Tosfos* himself flags it: *teima, keman sevira lei?* How can someone who has learned *Mikra* and *Mishna* be worse than an *am ha'aretz*? The intuition may be that knowledge without understanding is, in a certain sense, more problematic than simple ignorance. The *am ha'aretz* at least knows what he does not know. The person who has memorized masses of material without grasping it occupies a more confused and dangerous epistemic position — though calling him a *bur*, a word associated with the most complete kind of ignorance, remains a harsh verdict.

### Kuti Analogy

*Rabbi Yannai omer: harei zeh kuti* — a Samaritan. This is a striking escalation. *Rashi* explains that since this person has not attended upon sages, *eino makpid al divrei chachamim lada'atam* — he does not concern himself with rabbinic rulings because he does not even want to know what they are. *Velo shana ela leharot atzmo ketalmid chachamim* — and whatever he has learned was only to present himself as a *talmid chacham*.

But *Rashi*'s comparison to the *Kutim* is worth examining more closely. The *Kutim* were not simply lax observers. They had a fundamentally different authority structure: a different *Sefer Torah*, a different understanding of *Torah*, and a complete non-recognition of rabbinic authority — not a failure to comply with it, but a wholesale rejection of it. So *Rashi*'s point, reflected in the prohibition on eating their bread and wine, is not merely that they were punctilious in the wrong things, but that *keivan shelo shimish chachamim, eino makpid al divrei chachamim lada'atam* — because he has not attended upon sages, he does not recognize rabbinic authority as binding on him at all. Someone who says "I want to know the texts but I don't care what the rabbinic tradition has to say about them" — who effectively becomes an authority unto himself — is more threatening than someone who is simply ignorant. The ignorant person at least knows where the authority lies. This figure rejects the entire system, like a kind of intellectual priesthood-of-the-laity: "I'll learn these texts and I won't care what anyone else has determined." *Eino makpid al divrei chachamim lada'atam* — he doesn't even want to know.

### Magus Category

*Rav Acha bar Yaakov omer: harei zeh magus* — a mage. *Rashi* interprets this as *mechashef ve'ochez et ha'einayim ve'gonev et halevavot* — someone who casts illusions, bewitching people into believing he is brilliant when there is no substance behind it. This is in the spirit of the *rasha arum*: he casts his spell, and people fall under it. One might also note, as was raised in discussion, that in the world of the Gemara a *magus* referred to a Persian priest — a figure who represents an entirely different religious tradition and authority system, not merely a charlatan. On that reading, the *magus* represents yet a further step along the same axis as the *Kuti*: not just a rejection of rabbinic authority, but an allegiance to an altogether foreign system.

### Magus & Tana

The Gemara then clarifies the comparison. *Amar Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: mistavra keRav Acha bar Yaakov*, because people say: *rati magusa* — the magus chants — *velo yada mai amar* — and he has no idea what he is saying. He recites his incantations as pure gibberish, with no comprehension of their content. And similarly, *tani tana velo yada mai amar* — the *tana*, the memorizer of *Tannaitic* material, recites what he has memorized without understanding a word of it. As Saul Lieberman once remarked, what the rabbis wanted in their *tanna'im* — the small-*tav tanna'im*, not the *tanna'im* of the *mishnaic* period — were people with excellent memories and very little creativity. You wanted them to transmit the text accurately; you did not want them to think about it, because then they would introduce their own ideas. The comparison to the *magus*, then, is ultimately about the complete absence of comprehension beneath an imposing performance of erudition: it looks like knowledge, but it is ignorance all the way down.

---

## Am Ha'aretz

### Shema Criterion

The Gemara now asks directly: *tnu rabanan, eizehu am ha'aretz?* — Who is an *am ha'aretz*? The first answer: *kol she'eino korei kri'as shema shacharis ve'arvis* — whoever does not recite *Kri'as Shema* morning and evening.

### Shema Significance

This criterion is tied to a teaching elsewhere in the Gemara — in *Menachos*, if I recall correctly — that someone who recites *Kri'as Shema* morning and evening has fulfilled the verse *lo yamush sefer hatorah hazeh mipicha vehagisa bo yomam valaylah*: if you merely frame your day with *Torah* at its beginning and end, it is as if *Torah* has not departed from your mouth the entire day. The *am ha'aretz* who does not even recite *shema shacharis ve'arvis* is, in the Gemara's view, someone entirely outside the world of *Torah*. One thinks perhaps of the figure of Tevye in Fiddler on the Roof, who has almost certainly never learned a word of *Gemara* in his life, but who understands viscerally that sitting in the *beis knesses* and learning the holy books is what he should aspire to. That self-understanding — that connection, however tenuous — is what distinguishes him from someone who has entirely vacated the world of *Torah*.

### Berakhot Significance

The Gemara adds *u'birchasa* — even the *berachos* of *Shema* matter here, and notes that these are *miderabbanan*. This is significant: the *berachos* surrounding *Kri'as Shema* double as *birchos haTorah* — someone who forgets *birchos haTorah* can rely on the *berachos* of *Kri'as Shema*, because those blessings are fundamentally about God's having chosen us and given us *Torah*. They frame the recitation of *Shema* itself as an act of *Talmud Torah*. Being outside even that minimal rabbinic framing places a person outside the entire enterprise.

### R. Meir Opinion

*Divrei Rabbi Meir* — this is Rabbi Meir's position: the *am ha'aretz* is defined by failure to recite *Shema* morning and evening.

### Tefillin Criterion

*Vachachamim omrim: kol she'eino meni'ach tefillin* — the Sages define the *am ha'aretz* as one who does not put on *tefillin*. This criterion shifts the focus from *Torah* knowledge to a fundamental daily practice: even if you are not deeply learned, at minimum the wearing of *tefillin* marks your participation in the world of *mitzvos*.

### Tefillin History

This is actually quite striking historically. We tend to hold a romanticized view of how universally observant communities were in earlier centuries. Yet we have evidence from the period of the *Rishonim* — I believe it is the *Smag*, though I am not certain — that there were communities where *tefillin* wearing was seriously challenged, and this authority would travel from town to town urging people to begin putting on *tefillin* and affixing *mezuzos* to their doors. The assumption that these practices were universal even in ostensibly observant communities may not be warranted.

### Symbolic Meaning

There is also a symbolic dimension worth noting. The *Shema* itself contains *vehayu le'os al yadecha* — and they shall be a sign upon your arm — and *uletotafos bein einecha* — and frontlets between your eyes. *Tefillin* is, in a sense, the physical embodiment of the *Shema*'s own words: even if one is not engaged in daily *Torah* study, wearing *tefillin* represents a binding of *Torah* to oneself, an external sign of internal connection. Someone who does not even perform that minimal act of symbolic identification has removed himself from the chain entirely.

### Ben Azzai

*Ben Azzai omer: kol she'ein lo tzitzis bevigdo* — whoever does not have *tzitzis* on his garment. This too is part of the *parshiyos* read in *Kri'as Shema*, and similarly functions as an outward symbol of Jewish identity and connection to *Torah*, even apart from the level of one's actual learning.

### R. Yonatan

*Rabbi Yonasan ben Yosef omer: kol sheyesh lo banim ve'eino megadlam leTalmud Torah* — whoever has children and does not raise them toward *Talmud Torah*. We are back here to the *Torah* axis. Significantly, the phrasing is not simply *eino melamdam Torah* — he does not teach them *Torah* — but *eino megadlam leTalmud Torah*, he does not raise them *toward* it. The question is whether one sees *Torah* education as an aspiration worth striving for and investing in, even if one cannot provide it directly. Is it something you see your children as needing? Does it matter to you?

### Acheirim

*Acheirim omrim: afilu korei ve'shoneh velo shimish talmidei chachamim* — even one who has learned *Mikra* and *Mishna* but has not attended upon Torah sages — *zehu am ha'aretz*. This brings us back precisely to where we began in the prior discussion. Knowledge without genuine engagement — without the character development and deep understanding that come from *shimush* — does not lift a person out of the *am ha'aretz* category.

### Severity Scale

The Gemara then establishes an escalating scale of severity. *Kara velo shanah* — one who knows *Mikra* but not *Mishna* — *harei zeh bur*, is a complete ignoramus in all of rabbinic discourse. And *lo kara velo shanah* — one who has learned nothing at all — *alav hakasuv omer*: the verse says *vezarati es beis Yisrael ve'es beis Yehudah zera adam vezera beheimah* — I will plant the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man and the seed of animals. In context, that verse is a *beracha* about the repopulation of the land. Here, it is deployed with the implicit suggestion that someone entirely outside the world of *Torah* is, in a certain sense, like an animal.

---

## Women & Talmud

### Question

Where do women fit within all these criteria for *am ha'aretz*? This is an entirely fair and pointed question. The Gemara has just laid out a comprehensive taxonomy — reciting *Shema*, wearing *tefillin*, wearing *tzitzis*, raising children for *Talmud Torah*, pursuing *shimush talmidei chachamim* — and women are exempt from, or simply absent from, most of these categories.

### Connection

This brings us back directly to the opening discussion. Juxtapose *kol hamelamed bito Torah ke'ilu limdah tiflus* with the full weight of everything the Gemara has now said about what it means to be disconnected from *Torah* — the escalating scale from *am ha'aretz* to *bur* to *kuti* to *magus* — and the tension becomes very sharp indeed. Women are told, in one tradition, that too much *Torah* learning is a problem; and yet the framework the Gemara has built places the absence of *Torah* engagement among the most troubling characteristics a person can have.

---

## Am Ha'aretz (II)

### Tosfot Complexity

*Tosfos* raises a critical point that cannot be passed over: *teima lari de'amar perek Hanizakin* — there is a *baraita* in *Gittin* that defines *am ha'aretz* as whoever does not eat *chullin* in a state of *tahara*, *divrei Rabbi Meir* — and the criteria there are entirely different from what we have here. *Tosfos* resolves this by stating *upirush deharbei inyanei am ha'aretz hein* — *am ha'aretz* means different things in different contexts. Sometimes the term disqualifies a person from serving as a witness; sometimes it concerns trustworthiness regarding *tithes* and *purity*; sometimes it touches on *zun*, *shemitah*, or the acquisition of certain goods. The categories can be contradictory with one another precisely because they are not describing a single unified group.

This point has broader historiographic significance. There has been considerable scholarly work — including a paper by Yair Furstenberg on the status of *am ha'aretz* in *Chazal* — arguing that we should not assume the Rabbis were always referring to a single identifiable sociological group. The term may function more like a concept — a flexible category that plays different roles in different *halachic* and social contexts. There was certainly a time when it referred to a very concrete population. But once it enters the fabric of rabbinic literature as a concept, it begins to operate in more abstract ways, and the contradictions between different *gemarot* reflect that flexibility rather than simple inconsistency. The parallel in our own world might be the whole spectrum of what it means to call someone "not *frum*" — a label that encompasses an enormous range of people and behaviors, none of which are really equivalent.

The Gemara then cites: *yera Hashem beni umelech, ve'im shonim al titarev* — fear God and the king, and do not mix with those who are *shonim*. *Amar Rabbi Yitzchak: elu sheshonim halachos* — these are people who merely recite *halachos* by rote. One might think *halachos* sounds more advanced than *Mishna* — you are actually studying law. But *halachos* here refers to apodictic legal statements memorized without any underlying discussion or reasoning, which is functionally equivalent to the problem already described. And of course, there is the famous teaching *kol hashoneh halachos bechol yom muvtach lo shehu ben olam haba* — one who reviews *halachos* every day is assured a share in the world to come. The Gemara addresses this: the problem is not the memorization itself but thinking one can *pasken* from it. *Mahu deteima* — one might have thought *shonim becheta* meant repeated sinners, as per Rav Huna's teaching *keivan she'avar adam aveirah veshana bah hutra lo* — once a person transgresses and repeats it, it becomes, as it were, permitted to him; or as Rav Yisrael Salanter reportedly added, if you do it a third time it becomes a *mitzvah*. But no — *kamashma lan* — the *shonim* here are those who merely mouth *mishnayos* without comprehension.

---

## Tannaim & Memorization

### Baraita Claim

*Atanna'im meval'ei olam* — the *tanna'im*, the memorizers of *Mishna*, destroy the world. One can appreciate the irony: the *tanna* who had to memorize this *baraisa* was memorizing a statement about how memorizers destroy the world.

### Ravina Clarification

*Mavlei olam salka daitach?* — Do they really destroy the world? *Amar Ravina*: of course not. The problem is not memorization itself — we need those people to preserve the *Mishna* with accuracy. The problem is *she'morim halacha mitoch mishnasam* — that they believe they can *pasken halachah* directly from what they have memorized.

### R. Yehoshua

*Tanya nami hachi, amar Rabbi Yehoshua: vechi mavlei olam hein? Vahala miyashvei olam hein* — are they not in fact settlers of the world? — *shenemar halichos olam lo*. The entire Talmudic discussion is built upon the foundation of memorized *mishnayos*. *Kol hashoneh halachos bechol yom* is the indispensable substrate. Without accurate memorization, there is no tradition to discuss.

### Core Issue

*Ela she'morim halacha mitoch mishnasam* — the problem is not memorizing, it is thinking one can issue rulings on its basis. The *tanna* who memorizes is *miyashvei olam*; the one who thinks his memorization qualifies him to *pasken* is *mevallei olam*. The distinction matters enormously, and the Gemara's care in making it reflects a deep awareness of how dangerous a little learning can be when misapplied.

---

## Mavlei Olam

### Isha Perushah

*Isha perushah* — the woman who presents herself as separated from physical pleasures — is among the *mavlei olam*, the destroyers of the world. The skepticism, as established earlier, is that her presentation of austere piety conceals something else entirely.

### Three Types

The Gemara now adds additional categories: *tanu rabanan, besulah tzalya-nis* — a praying virgin — *ve'almanah shovevis* — a wandering widow — *ve'katan shelo kalu chodashav* — a minor whose months have not been completed — *harei elu mavlei olam*, these destroy the world. The *besulah tzalya-nis*, according to *Rashi*, is someone always engaged in prayer and devotion, projecting an image of extraordinary piety. The *almanah shovevis* is a widow constantly traveling through the community, visiting everyone. *Rashi* suggests she is a gossip — though as was noted, that does not perfectly fit the model of someone presenting themselves as other than they are; perhaps the better reading is that she visits presenting herself as motivated by care and concern when her real motivation is social engagement or information-gathering. The *katan shelo kalu chodashav* the Gemara will clarify momentarily.

### Pious Virgin

*Ve'amar Rabbi Yochanan: lamadnu yiras cheit mibesulah* — we can learn fear of sin from the young woman, *ve'kibul sachar mei'almanah* — and the meaning of receiving reward from the widow. What is the story of the *besulah*? *Rabbi Yochanan shama lah le'hahi besulah de'nafla apei* — Rabbi Yochanan heard this young woman fall on her face in prayer — *ve'amra: ribbono shel olam, baras Gan Eden u'varas Gehennom, baras tzaddikim baras reshaim* — You have created Paradise and *Gehennom*, righteous people and wicked people — *yehi ratzon milfanecha shelo yikashlu bi bnei adam* — may it be Your will that people not stumble through me, that men not sin on my account.

### Problematic Aspects

This is presented as a model of *yiras cheit* — and in one sense it is striking. True *yiras cheit* is not merely fear that *I* will sin, but fear that I might inadvertently cause *others* to sin. One is reminded of the prayer recited before entering the *beis hamidrash* — *shelo yikashlu*, that my colleagues not stumble through anything I say. To be so attuned to the possibility of causing harm, even unintentionally — that is a profound expression of moral seriousness.

At the same time, there is something deeply troubling here. *Yiras cheit* properly begins with concern for one's own conduct. The framing of this prayer — in which a woman's central religious preoccupation is with male desire and male sin, and in which she understands her own body as the primary locus of danger — reflects and reinscribes a way of thinking about women that is, to put it plainly, very deeply problematic. It connects to the entire fabric of *Maseches Sotah* and its preoccupations. These difficulties do not disappear simply because the text presents it as admirable.

### Righteous Widow

The story of the *almanah* who demonstrates *kibul sachar*: there was a certain widow in whose neighborhood there was a synagogue, yet every day she would come and pray in Rabbi Yochanan's *beis hamidrash* rather than in the closer *beis haknesseth*. Rabbi Yochanan said to her: *biti, lo beis haknesseth be'shivvuseich?* — is there not a synagogue in your community? She replied: *rabbi, lo sechar psios yesh li* — do I not receive the reward for the extra walking? The lesson in *kibul sachar*: she extended herself beyond what was required, internalizing a disposition of exerting extra effort for the sake of *mitzvos* even when the effort was not strictly necessary.

### Question Raised

Yet both examples are, on closer examination, somewhat awkward as ideals. The *yiras cheit* of the young woman is entangled with the male gaze and the internalization of responsibility for male desire. The *almanah*'s extra walking, while representing admirable devotion, raises its own questions — *is* it better to pray in a *beis hamidrash* than a *beis haknesseth*? And can it be that this widow is also, perhaps, seeking connection to the world of *Torah*, which may be why she extends herself specifically to come to Rabbi Yochanan's *beis hamidrash* rather than the local synagogue? Perhaps that dimension is part of the point. But regardless, both examples are in some sense extreme, and one must ask whether extremity in this direction is genuinely praiseworthy or instead reflects an excess that has its own distortions. How can the Gemara claim these figures are *mavlei olam* when the examples are so clearly righteous?

### Specification

The Gemara resolves the tension: *ki ka'amar* — the original teaching does not refer to all widows and virgins, but to specific types. *Kegon Yochni bat Retivi* — like this woman Yochni bat Retivi. *Rashi* explains — drawing on what appears to be a *mesorah* not found elsewhere in rabbinic literature — that this woman was a witch who made her *parnassa* as a midwife: she would use incantations to prevent a woman from giving birth, then be called in to help, reverse the incantations, and earn a great reputation. The details of *Rashi*'s source are unclear, and he sometimes provides *aggadic* backdrop that does not appear in other texts, but the point is clear: it is *that* kind of widow who is *mavlei olam*, not every widow who moves through her community.

### Young Scholar

Back to *katan shelo kalu chodashav*: *hacha targimu* — here in *Bavel* they explained it as *zeh talmid chacham hamiva'eit berabbotav* — a young Torah scholar who is dismissive and disrespectful of his teachers and of those with greater age and authority, overly impressed with his own attainments.

### Gap Year Problem

*Tosfos* quotes a *Yerushalmi*: *Rabbi Chilkiya beshem Rabbi Simon: zeh shehu gadol baTorah shelo befirko, umevazeh et hagedolim mimenu* — someone who is genuinely beyond his years in *Torah* knowledge and therefore feels entitled to denigrate those who are chronologically or institutionally his seniors. This is, regrettably, a recognizable phenomenon: students who return from a year of intensive study abroad suddenly finding themselves, in their own estimation, the world's greatest *talmidei chachamim*, while their community rabbi appears to them as inadequate. The brilliance is real; the judgment is not.

### R. Abba

*Rabbi Abba amar: zeh talmid shelo higia lehora'ah* — not the relationship to others but the effect on the community: a student who has not reached the level of *hora'ah* and yet issues rulings. This is what makes such a person *mavlei olam* in the deepest sense. And the failure here is not necessarily one of knowledge. A person might be genuinely brilliant and yet not ready to *pasken*, because *hora'ah* demands wisdom, understanding of people, judgment about circumstances — not merely *sefarim*.

---

## Piskening Readiness

### Verse Application

*D'amar Rabbi Abbahu amar Rav Huna amar Rav: mai d'chtiv, ki rabim chalalim hipila* — what is the meaning of the verse "many are those she has caused to fall"? (The verse, drawn from the context of a seductive woman, is now applied to an entirely different situation.) *Zeh talmid chacham shelo higia lehora'ah u'moreh* — this refers to a *talmid chacham* who has not yet reached the level of *hora'ah* and yet rules. *Rashi* notes a play on *hipila* and *nefel* — a premature birth — connecting back to *katan shelo kalu chodashav*: like an infant born before its time, this scholar's rulings are a kind of miscarriage of judgment. He is, in effect, murdering people through his premature *psak*.

### Opposite Case

*Ve'atzumim kol harugeha* — "and great are all those she has slaughtered." *Zeh talmid chacham shehigia lehora'ah ve'eino moreh* — this refers to a *talmid chacham* who has reached the level of *hora'ah* and does not rule. If you are qualified to *pasken* and you withhold that service, you are equally culpable — perhaps more so. You leave the field open to those who are not qualified, you fail the people who need your guidance, and you close your eyes to your own responsibility. *Rashi* reads *atzumim* as a play on *otzem einav* — closing one's eyes. The *Maharsha* reads it differently: *atzum* means great, powerful — you are great, you are fit, and yet you do not act.

### Rav Moshe

This tension is captured with great personal immediacy in Rav Moshe Feinstein's introduction to the *Igros Moshe*. He writes that he was deeply hesitant to *pasken* — who was he to rule, and what if he ruled incorrectly? The Gemara itself warns: *zeh talmid shelo higia lehora'ah u'moreh, rabim chalalim hipila*. Yet Rav Moshe could not simply decline to *pasken*, because the very next line says *ve'atzumim kol harugeha* — if you are *higia lehora'ah ve'eino moreh*, you are equally causing destruction. The obligation is real and cannot be evaded by excessive humility once one has genuinely reached the level of *hora'ah*.

### 40 Years

*Ve'ad kamah* — until what age must one wait? *Arbaim shanah* — forty years. *Aini?* — Is this really so? *Ve'ha Rabbah ori* — Rabbah ruled on *halachic* matters, and he lived only until forty! The Gemara answers: *b'shavi* — only if one is equivalent to the *poskim* of one's generation.

### Rashi vs. Tosfot

There is a notable dispute between *Rashi* and *Tosfos* about how to read this. *Rashi* holds that if you are equivalent to the *poskim* of your generation, you may rule even before forty — you are only prohibited from ruling before forty if you are below their level. *Tosfos* reads it differently: equivalence alone is insufficient — only if you are better than everyone around you may you rule before forty; equivalence requires waiting. The distinction is between adequacy and superiority as the threshold for early *hora'ah*.

### Modern Application

*Tosfos* also clarifies that forty years does not mean forty years of age but forty years of learning — which would imply an even later start for most people. Yet one can understand the number in terms of what it was trying to achieve: *psak* requires not just accumulated knowledge but life experience, judgment, and knowledge of people — not only of *sefarim*. And contemporary *poskim* note that much of the reason for that lengthy formation was the sheer volume of material that had to be internalized from memory. Now that all the material is available in written and printed form, some of those considerations change substantially.

---

## Seven Types of Prushim

### Machos Perushim

*U'makkos perushim* — the smitings of the ascetics — constitute the final category of those who destroy the world. The term *perushim* here carries a double valence: it means both Pharisees and people who separate themselves from ordinary life in the pursuit of piety. *Rashi*'s understanding is that these are people who engage in self-flagellation and the externals of extreme piety while fundamentally missing what righteousness actually requires — and worse, presenting that performance to the world, perhaps even to themselves, as genuine holiness.

### Seven Listed

*Tanu Rabbanan: shiva perushim hein* — there are seven types of false pietists. *Parush Shichmi, Parush Nikpi, Parush Kizai, Parush Meduchya, Parush Machovasi*, *Parush Mei'ahava*, and *Parush Mi'yira*.

### Shichmi Type

*Parush Shichmi: zeh oseh ma'aseh Shechem* — one who performs the deeds of Shechem. *Rashi* explains: the people of Shechem underwent *bris milah* not out of genuine religious conviction but to serve ulterior interests. The act was performed but for entirely the wrong reason. The *Maharsha* adds a sharper dimension: the sequence matters. Shechem first committed a terrible act and then undertook *bris milah* — so the religious performance functions as a cover-up for prior wrongdoing. It is not even simply misguided motivation; it is a kind of religious whitewashing of genuine transgression. The principle *mitoch shelo lishmah ba lishmah* — that improper motivation can eventually lead to proper motivation — does not apply when the religious act is being used to conceal something already done wrong.

### Nikpi Type

*Parush Nikpi: zeh hemenakeif et raglav* — who walks very daintily. *Rashi* says this person minces his steps to project an image of humility and piety. It is entirely performative — a presentation of holiness through gait, with nothing behind it.

### Kizai Type

*Parush Kizai* — *kizai* meaning bloodletting. *Amar Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: zeh hamakiz dam lektalin* — one who bangs into walls and causes himself to bleed. *Rashi*: this person is too scrupulously *frum* to look at a woman and therefore walks into walls. The absurdity is intentional — and it calls to mind the experience of excessive scrupulosity taken to a self-harmful extreme.

### Meduchya Type

*Parush Meduchya: demishapei k'meduchya* — bent over like a pestle. The pestle has a distinctive curved shape. This person walks hunched over to display humility. Again: purely external show, with no genuine substance behind it.

### Machovasi Type

*Parush Machovasi*: this person says *mah chovati tu va'esenu* — tell me what my obligation is and I will fulfill it. At first the Gemara protests: *ma'alyusa hi* — that is admirable! Tell me what I need to do and I will do it. But no — the *Gemara* clarifies: the problem is the full phrasing: "I have done everything required of me; *if* there is anything more, tell me and I will do it." The person presents themselves as having already discharged all responsibilities, seeking only to identify any remaining obligations. The posture of prior completion is the problem — the claim to have already done everything, combined with the performance of eagerness to do more.

### Ahava & Yira

*Parush Mei'ahava* and *Parush Mi'yira* — motivated by love of reward or fear of punishment. These sound problematic but are actually defended. *Amar lei Abaye ve'Rava letana: ha lo tisni* — do not include these in the problematic list. Even if the *ahava* is love of reward and the *yira* is fear of punishment — improper motivations — these are not categorically bad.

### Rav Support

*De'amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav: le'olam ya'asok adam beTorah u'vemitzvos af al pi shelo lishmah, shemitoch shelo lishmah ba lishmah* — a person should always engage in *Torah* and *mitzvos* even if not *lishmah*, because acting *shelo lishmah* will ultimately lead to *lishmah*. The problem with all the other false pietists was that they were presenting themselves as something other than what they were. Here the motivation is impure, but it is not a deception that harms others — and it carries within itself the seed of genuine transformation.

---

## Hidden vs. Revealed

### Hidden vs. Revealed

*Amar Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: demitamera mitamera, demigalya migalya* — what is hidden stays hidden, what is revealed stays revealed. We have just spent considerable time cataloguing people who present as something they are not. The practical reality is: we know what we know. We cannot peer behind the facade. What is hidden from us remains hidden.

### Divine Justice

*Beis dina rabba le'iparei mehani dechafu gundei* — but the ultimate High Court will ultimately bring justice to those who have wrapped themselves in a *tallis* and presented as pious when they were not. Human judgment is limited; divine judgment is not.

### King Yannai

*Amar lei Yannai Malka l'devasei* — King Yannai, who had caused the deaths of many of the Sages, says to his wife on his deathbed: *al tishari min haPerushim* — do not fear from the Pharisees. And *velo mi'mi she'einam Perushim* — nor from those who are not Pharisees. The genuinely righteous will not harm you even after what was done to them; the genuinely wicked are no threat to you either, as they have no moral standing to act.

### Tzvu'im Defined

*Ela min hatzvu'in* — fear only the *tzvu'im*, the chameleons — *she'domin laPerushim*, who appear to be ascetics and Pharisees, *shema'aseihem ma'aseh Zimri*, but whose deeds are the deeds of Zimri — who violate the most fundamental prohibitions — *umevakshim sachar k'Pinchas*, while demanding reward as if they were Pinchas.

### Final Image

This is the closing image of the *daf*, and it is a powerful one. The Gemara has traveled a long arc: from the question of women's *Torah* education and the concern about those who appear as what they are not, through the *rasha arum* and his many incarnations, through the *am ha'aretz* and *bur* and *kuti* and *magus*, through the *tanna'im* who cannot *pasken* and the scholars who can but will not, through the seven false pietists — and arrives here at the *tzvu'im*: people who act like Zimri and claim the reward of Pinchas. They are, in the Gemara's reckoning, the most dangerous figures of all — not the openly wicked, not the genuinely righteous, but those who commit transgressions while wrapping themselves in the garments of holiness. Against them, human vigilance has limits. Only divine judgment, in the end, can see through.

---

---

# Sotah 23

## Zimri & Pinchas

### Zimri & Pinchas

The daf opens by returning to the close of the *aggadata* passage that concluded the previous amud. The Gemara had been exploring the phenomenon of women who appear one way and are in reality another — the *isha perusha* who presents outward piety while concealing inner corruption. But as the discussion developed, the Gemara broadened its scope considerably, recognizing this as a wider human phenomenon that applies to men no less than to women. This broadening itself is worth noting: even within a tractate devoted to the *sotah*, the Gemara is attuned to the question of whether we are examining something specific to women's sin or something universal in human nature.

### Broader Phenomenon

The final line of the *aggadata* before the *mishna* is worth savoring for the precision with which it captures a particular personality type — one that has since become a stock figure in Rabbinic literature: *ma'aseihem kema'asei Zimri u'mevakshim sachar kePinchas* — they act like Zimri yet expect to be rewarded like Pinchas. The figure is not merely about duplicity before others, the hypocrite who performs righteousness publicly while sinning in private. At a deeper level, it describes people who have somehow convinced themselves of their own righteousness, who have internalized the self-image of Pinchas while their conduct mirrors Zimri.

### Zenut & Kina

The pairing of Zimri and Pinchas is especially resonant in this context. Zimri sins through public sexual transgression with a Midianite woman, while Pinchas is the *kanai*, the zealot, whose defining act is *kina* — zealotry. The concept of *kina* runs through the Torah on multiple levels. On one plane it describes the jealous husband; on another it describes God's own demand for exclusive fidelity: *El kana hu*, God is a jealous God. The metaphor of Israel's worship of other gods is framed throughout the Torah as *zenut* — *ve'zanah acharei elohei nechar ha'aretz* — a betrayal of the covenantal relationship with God, depicted as a kind of spiritual adultery. Pinchas acts *asher kina l'elohav*, as one who is jealous on God's behalf, because Zimri's act was simultaneously an act of physical *zenut* and a form of abandonment of God through entanglement with the deities of Midian. The intersection of the metaphorical *zenut* and the literal *zenut* is striking, and it also reinforces that this passage is not exclusively about women — it is about men, about the fundamental human capacity for self-deception in matters of fidelity and devotion.

---

## Zechut Toleh Debate

### R. Shimon: No Zechut

The *mishna* now opens with a striking position: *Rabbi Shimon omer ein zechut tola b'mayim hamarim* — Rabbi Shimon flatly denies that merit ever caused the bitter waters to suspend their judgment. It is worth pausing on the epistemological strangeness of this debate. Generations after the *Beit HaMikdash*, the Tannaim are debating what actually occurred when a woman drank the *mayim hamarim*. No doubt all parties could observe that sometimes a woman drank the water and nothing happened. The question is how to interpret that fact: does it mean she was genuinely innocent, or that her *zechut* suspended the judgment? The observable facts may have been shared; the dispute is about what those facts mean.

### Public Trust Problem

Rabbi Shimon's argument against *zechut tola* is primarily a policy argument. *Ve'im atah omer hazechut tola* — if you were to say that merit can suspend the effects of the waters, then *madhe ata et hamayim bifnei kol hanashim* — you undermine the waters' credibility in the eyes of all women. The *Sifrei* formulates this as *makhshikh gavno*, you cause it to become blurry, to lose its potency in the public's perception. The image is almost that of muddying the water itself. Two distinct harms follow. First, people will see a woman emerge unaffected and say: I know this woman committed adultery, and yet nothing happened — the water does not work. Second, the innocent women suffer: *motzi shem ra al hatehorot*. Women who were genuinely innocent and whose innocence was confirmed by the waters will now be suspected retroactively — people will say, *tme'iot hayu*, they were really guilty, *ela shetaltah lahen hazchut*, it is just that their merit suspended the punishment. For Rabbi Shimon, this double injury to the institution's integrity proves it cannot be so.

One might further note the practical problem raised in this connection: if *zechut tola* were operative, how would a husband ever know that he could resume marital relations with his wife? You might answer that he works with the *chazakah* — what has been observed provides a presumptive basis for conduct.
