But once you introduce the possibility of *zechut tola*, you have complicated that presumption considerably, and the question of when the husband and wife may resume their relationship becomes genuinely difficult.

### Rebbi: Zechut Works

Rebbi disagrees. *Hazechut tola bamayim hamererim* — merit does suspend the judgment of the bitter waters. But Rebbi's position is more nuanced than simply affirming *zechut tola* without qualification. He adds: *ve'einah yoledet ve'einah meshabbachat* — even when merit suspends the negative judgment, the positive effect of the waters is not realized either. The waters, had she been innocent, would have brought enhanced fertility — *ve'niketah ve'nizre'ah zara*. If she is guilty but her *zechut* intervenes, she escapes the physical destruction, but she does not receive the blessing. She does not bear children.

### Observable Signs

Rebbi's answer to Rabbi Shimon's concern is built on observability. If a woman drank the waters and afterward bore healthy children and her body flourished, people can see she was innocent. If a woman drank and received no blessing of children, people will say: the *pasuk* promises *ve'niketah ve'nizre'ah zara* — and she has not been *nizre'ah zara*. We can infer that her *zechut* must have been operative. Rebbi goes further still: *ela mitnavnevet ve'holekhet* — not only does she fail to bear children, but she actually deteriorates. And *sof hi meta be'otah mitah* — ultimately she dies from it, in the same recognizable way, only stretched over a longer period. So the public will see a clear spectrum: women who drank and flourished, whose innocence is confirmed, and women who drank and deteriorated, whose guilt is evident even if the timeline is extended. This, Rebbi argues, is a reasonable answer to Rabbi Shimon's concerns about the water's reputation. What is striking throughout this entire discussion is how the Tannaim construct the reality of what *must* have happened based on what the halacha and policy require — an argument from necessity rather than from direct observation.

---

## Mincha Tamei

### Before Sanctification

The *mishna* now transitions, somewhat abruptly, back to the *mincha* of the *sotah*. The assumed order of the *sotah* procedure is: the *mincha* is brought and offered, and then she drinks the water — *ve'achar yashkeh et hamayim*. The *mishna* doubles back, however, to address what happens if the *mincha* becomes *tamei* at different stages of the process. If the *mincha* became *tamei* before it was placed into the *kli sharet*, it is treated like any other *mincha* in that pre-sanctified state. At that stage it has only *kedushat peh* — a sanctity conferred through verbal designation — and such sanctity can be transferred: the *mincha* can be redeemed for money and a new *mincha* brought in its place.

### After Sanctification

Once the *mincha* has been sanctified by the *kli sharet*, however, it acquires *kedushat haguf* — an intrinsic, constitutive sanctity that defines its very identity rather than being merely instilled upon it. Once something attains *kedushat haguf*, it cannot be redeemed and cannot be removed from the *azarah*. If it subsequently becomes *tamei*, it must be burned within the *azarah*. This is not a law specific to the *minchat sotah*; it is the universal rule for all *menachot*. The *mishna* establishes this baseline in order to set up the more specific cases that follow.

---

## Mincha Burned

### Intro: Mincha Burned

Having established when an ordinary *mincha* must be burned on account of *tum'ah*, the *mishna* now introduces a related but distinct category: *ve'elu sheminchoteihem nisrafot* — the following women are those whose *mincha* is burned even though it has not become *tamei*. The *minchat sotah* has a set of unique circumstances under which the offering is rendered without purpose, and in those cases, since the *mincha* has already been sanctified in the vessel and cannot be redeemed, it must be burned. The fire is not on the *mizbe'ach* — it is on the ash pile within the *azarah*, where *pesulim* are burned.

### Confession

The first case: *ha'omeret tme'ah ani lach* — if the woman confesses her guilt. She is not subject to execution under these circumstances, since there were no witnesses and no formal warning, but her confession renders the entire *sotah* procedure moot. There is no longer any purpose for the *mincha*. Since it has been sanctified, it cannot be redeemed, so it is burned, and she is divorced without receiving her *kesubah*.

### Witnesses

The second case: witnesses come forward and testify to her guilt. Even without a formal confession, the existence of witness testimony eliminates the need for the ordeal. Again the *mincha* is burned, and she is divorced without her *kesubah*.

### Refuses to Drink

The third case: *ha'omeret eini shota* — she refuses to drink. This is a kind of *nolo contendere*: she neither admits guilt nor contests the charges, but she refuses to submit to the process. The result is that she is divorced without her *kesubah*, since she is the one obstructing the mechanism by which her innocence could be established. The husband remains in a state of prohibition relative to her, and since she is preventing resolution, she bears the consequence. The *mincha* is burned.

### Husband's Relations

The fourth case is distinctive in that the fault lies with the husband: *ve-she-ba'alah ba aleha baderech* — the husband had sexual relations with her after she became a *sotah* and before the ordeal was completed. The Torah conditions the efficacy of the waters on the husband being *nikah me'avon* — free from sin in this matter. If he is not, the waters will not work. Once it is known that this condition has been violated, there is no point in proceeding with the *mincha* or the ordeal, and the *mincha* is not brought. In this case, since it is the husband's conduct that has nullified the process, she would presumably receive her *kesubah* — though the *mishna* notes this as a matter to be examined further.

---

## Wife of Kohen

### Shared Ownership

The *mishna* now arrives at an entirely different category of *nisrafot*: *ve-chol hanesu'ot le-kohanim minchateihem nisrafot* — all women married to *kohanim* have their *mincha* burned. This burning is of a different character from the burning of the *pesul* cases above. The rule of *minchat kohen kalil tihyeh lo te'achel* — the *mincha* of a *kohen* must be entirely consumed, burned on the *mizbe'ach* — applies here. The question is why the wife of a *kohen* should have her *mincha* treated as a *minchat kohen*.

The answer is that the husband is considered a part-owner of the *mincha*. Rashi explains this in relation to the broader rule that a husband is obligated to pay for his wife's obligatory *korbanot* — a principle derived from the Gemara in Nazir. The husband foots the bill; she is the *mitkapeir*, the one for whom the atonement is being made and on whose behalf the offering is brought. Tosafot raises the question of whether this applies equally to a *minchat nedava*, a voluntary offering, since the financial obligation of the husband is specifically tied to obligatory *korbanot*. There, perhaps, he does not bear the cost even if, technically, *kinyan isha kana ba'alah* — the husband's acquisition of his wife entails some rights in her property. But for the *minchat sotah* specifically, the case is especially strong: *ve-hevi ha'ish et ishto* — the Torah frames the entire process as the husband bringing his wife. It says *ve-hevi et korbanah aleha* — he is the one who brings the *korban* on her behalf. More than any other case where the husband merely writes the check, here the Torah explicitly casts him as the active agent bringing the offering for her. Consequently, it is both her *mincha* and his *mincha*, and since it is his *mincha*, the rule of *minchat kohen* applies and the remainder may not be eaten.

### Rashi: Beis Hadeshen

Rashi, however, reads the *mishna*'s term *nisrafot* differently. In his commentary, Rashi states: *ve'afillu karav hakometz ke-hilchato ve-lo nitme'u nisrafim shirayim be-veit hadeshen* — even though the *kometz* was offered properly and nothing became *tamei*, the *shirayim* are burned in the *beis hadeshen*. On Rashi's reading, the burning of the remainder is not a burning on the *mizbe'ach* as a true *minchat kohen* would be, but rather a burning on the ash pile within the *azarah*, the same place where *pesulim* are burned. This anticipates the Gemara's discussion of two competing positions: is the remainder burned on the *mizbe'ach* as befits a genuine *minchat kohen*, or is it burned in the *beis hadeshen* because this *mincha* is a hybrid of two statuses? The *beis hadeshen*, it should be noted, is located within the *azarah* itself — it is not *chutz la-machaneh* — but it is distinct from the *mizbe'ach*.

---

## Gender Differences

### Kohenet Status

The *mishna* then pivots to a broader discussion, introduced by the contrast between the wife of a *kohen* and a *kohenet* — a woman who is herself a daughter of a *kohen* — who marries an Israelite. *Ve-hakohenet she-niset le-Yisrael minchatah ne'echelet* — her *mincha* is eaten in the normal fashion, because she carries no *kohen* status herself and her husband is not a *kohen*, so the *mincha* is treated as a standard *minchat Yisrael*. The *kometz* is burned on the *mizbe'ach* and the *shirayim* are eaten by the *kohanim*.

It is worth noting the terminology here. Throughout the Talmud, a woman who is a daughter of a *kohen* is almost always referred to as *bat kohen*. The usage of *kohenet* is relatively unusual. It is striking that a *mishna* which calls her *kohenet* proceeds to demonstrate that she has virtually no *kohen* status in practice. The identity of the tribe, particularly with respect to priestly lineage, flows through the male line. A woman's tribal identity is defined by the man she marries, not the family she was born into. This is reflected in law throughout: a *bat kohen* who marries an Israelite loses access to *terumah*; a woman who marries a *kohen* gains access to it. The discussion of the *mishna* is organized around a question: *mah bein kohen le-kohenet* — what is the difference between a *kohen* and a *kohenet*?

### Chalalah

The *mishna* states: *kohenet mitchalelet, ve-kohen eino mitchalel* — a *kohenet* can have her status compromised; a *kohen* cannot. The concept of *chalalah* refers to a woman whose priestly fitness has been violated, rendering her forbidden to a *kohen*. This status does not belong only to daughters of *kohanim* — any woman, whether *bat kohen* or *bat Yisrael*, who engages in certain categories of forbidden sexual acts becomes *pesulah le-kohen*. For example, an *almanah* who has relations with a *kohen gadol* becomes a *chalalah* and is forbidden even to a *kohen hedyot*. The act of sex is what determines her status; the precise scope of the husband's transgression — whether his violation requires *kiddushin* or obtains even without it — is a *machloket rishonim*, with the Rambam holding that the *kohen* only transgresses in the context of *kiddushin* while other *rishonim* disagree.

What is remarkable, and what the *mishna* draws attention to, is the asymmetry. A *kohen* who commits any sexual sin under the sun does not lose his *kehuna* status through his own action. His sanctity is not penetrable from without. He can be born a *chalal* — if he is the product of a forbidden union — but a born *kohen*'s status cannot be forfeited through his own conduct. There are *halachot* of social censure — a *kohen* currently married to a woman he is forbidden to marry is not permitted to *duchan*, for example — but these are social mechanisms of pressure, not a change in fundamental status. The disparity here mirrors a broader asymmetry: for a married woman, sexual infidelity constitutes adultery and violates her personal status; for a married man, sexual relations with an unmarried woman are not technically adultery in the same sense, and his personal status is not affected. The woman can be rendered *tamei* and forbidden; the man's status persists unchanged. This is reflected as well in the *kehuna* context: the woman's priestly fitness can be violated; the man's cannot.

### Tumah Differences

The *mishna* continues: *kohenet mitame'ah le-meitim, ve-ein kohen mitame'ah le-meitim* — a daughter of a *kohen* is permitted to become *tamei* through contact with the dead; a male *kohen* is not. The source for this distinction is *emor el ha-kohanim benei Aharon* — the prohibition of *tum'at meit* is addressed to *benei Aharon*, the sons of Aaron, *ve-lo benot Aharon* — not the daughters of Aaron. The *Tosefta* also notes the related case, conspicuous in its absence from the *mishna*, that a *kohen* serves on the *mizbe'ach* — *kohen omed u-makriv al gabei ha-mizbe'ach* — which plainly does not apply to a *kohenet*.

### Eating Offerings

The *mishna* concludes: *kohen ochel be-kodshei kodashim, ve-ein kohenet ochelet be-kodshei kodashim* — a *kohen* eats from the *kodshei kodashim* such as *chatat* and *asham* within the *azarah*, but a *kohenet* does not. The source is *kol zachar bi-vnei Aharon yochlenu* — all males among the sons of Aaron shall eat from it. The Torah is explicit.

### Summary: Kohenet

The irony of this entire *mishna* is profound. It designates the woman as *kohenet* — a term that implies an affirmative priestly identity — yet enumerates exclusively cases where she lacks any distinct status on account of her father being a *kohen*. Every item in the list demonstrates that she is, in terms of *halachic* identity, simply a woman, with no privileges and no restrictions that differ from those of an ordinary *Yisraelit*. Even the *chalalah* status, which might seem like a priestly restriction, applies to any Jewish woman. The *kohenet* of this *mishna* is, functionally, a *bat kohen* with no operative *kohen* status of her own.

---

## Hybrid Mincha

### The Problem

The Gemara now examines the central legal puzzle embedded in the *mishna*: what exactly happens to the *minchat sotah* of a woman married to a *kohen*? The Gemara frames it as follows. *Kol hanesu'ot li-khehunah minchatam nisrafet* — all women married to *kohanim* have their *mincha* burned, regardless of whether the woman is a *kohenet*, a *leviyah*, or an *Israelite*. The reason is *mipnei she-yesh lo chelek bah* — because the husband has a share in it. Insofar as it is his *mincha*, *lo te'achel* — it may not be eaten. But then: *ve-ein olah kalil, mipnei she-yesh lah chelek bah* — you cannot simply offer the whole thing on the *mizbe'ach* as a single unit, because she has a share in it. A true *minchat kohen* is offered whole, without the separation of *kmitzah*; but here, because the woman is not a *kohen*, you must take a *kmitzah*, as would be done for any *minchat Yisrael*. So the *mishna* resolves it: *ela ha-kometz karev be-atzmo ve-ha-shirayim kreivim be-atzmam* — the *kometz* is offered by itself, and the remainder is offered by itself. You perform the *kmitzah* in deference to its identity as a *minchat Yisrael*, and you burn the remainder in deference to its identity as a *minchat kohen*. The difficulty, however, is immediately apparent: once part of the offering has been placed on the *mizbe'ach* — namely the *kometz* — is it permitted to place the remainder on the *mizbe'ach* as well? The *pasuk* teaches: *ki kol se'or ve-chol devash lo taktiru mimenu isheh la-Hashem*, and the *drasha* from *mimenu* is that once part of a *korban* has been offered on the *mizbe'ach*, the remainder is forbidden to be placed there. This is a general principle: even the uneaten meat of a *korban* that is not an *olah* — the innards are offered on the *mizbe'ach*, but the remaining flesh that is designated for eating is forbidden to go up on the *mizbe'ach*.

### R. Eliezer: Eitzim

The Gemara answers in the name of Yehudah the son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi: *de-masik lehu le-shem eitzim* — you burn the remainder by designating it as firewood rather than as a *korban*. The *mizbe'ach* always requires fuel; you are not offering the remainder as a sacrifice but as combustible material to feed the fire. This is the position of Rabbi Eliezer, as found in a *baraita*: Rabbi Eliezer reads the phrase *lerei'ach nicho'ach* as a limiting qualifier. The prohibition is *lo ya'alu lerei'ach nicho'ach* — you may not offer it up as a pleasing fragrance, as a *korban*. But you may place it on the *mizbe'ach le-shem eitzim* — as firewood, which is not the same act as bringing a *korban*. The context for this *sevara* is a dispute about what to do when pieces of *korbanot* have become mixed together — say, limbs from an *olah* and limbs from a *chatat*, and it is no longer possible to determine which is which. According to Rabbi Eliezer, you may put all of them on the *mizbe'ach* and designate the *chatat* limbs as firewood; according to the Rabbis, you may not do this — you must allow them to become *pasul* and then burn them, passively, without putting them on the *mizbe'ach* at all.

### Tosafot's Question

Rashi, in his commentary on this passage, speaks of a *tenai* — a conditional designation — that one makes when burning the remainder: if the *kometz* was not truly a proper *kmitzah* and the whole thing should be treated as a *minchat kohen*, then this burning is valid as an offering; and if it is a *minchat Yisrael* and the *shirayim* are truly *shirayim*, then these are to be regarded as firewood. Tosafot objects to this framing. A *tenai* presupposes a *safek* — an uncertainty as to which of two possibilities obtains. By the legs of the mixed lambs, you genuinely do not know whether a given limb came from the *olah* or the *chatat*, and so a conditional designation makes sense. But here there is no uncertainty. This *mincha* is simultaneously a *minchat kohen* and a *minchat Yisrael* — both statuses coexist in it at the same time. It is not a question of which it is; it is both. The situation is analogous to an *androgynos* who is both male and female, or to a *chatzi eved ve-chatzi ben chorin* — the half-slave, half-free individual, familiar from discussions in *Minchat Chinuch*. You cannot make a *tenai* between two simultaneous realities. Tosafot's resolution is that you simply accept the best possible compromise: the remainder is burned, it is not eaten, and it is not offered as a proper *korban* — it occupies an intermediate status that satisfies neither identity fully. As the *shiur* puts it, a compromise is not when everyone is happy; a compromise is when everyone is equally unhappy.

One further question arises from this discussion: when burning *le-shem eitzim*, does the act require the same standards of *haktarah* that a proper offering does? Does it need to occur by day? Must there be proper *kavana*? Tosafot, citing the *Yerushalmi*, explores whether the requirement of intent for *haktarah* applies when the material is being burned as firewood rather than as a *korban*. The implicit answer seems to be that if you are genuinely burning it *le-shem eitzim*, the technical requirements of *haktarah* do not apply — it is not being brought as a *korban* in any formal sense.

### R. Elazar b.R. Shimon

But the Gemara has proceeded on the assumption of Rabbi Eliezer's position. The Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Eliezer — who hold that you cannot designate the mixed limbs as firewood — would be unable to use that solution here. The Gemara therefore pivots to the ruling of Rabbi Elazar beRebbi Shimon, found in a *baraita*: *ha-kometz karev le-atzmo ve-ha-shirayim mitpazrin al beit ha-deshen* — the *kometz* is offered on the *mizbe'ach* on its own, and the remainder is scattered on the *beis hadeshen*. This is precisely the reading Rashi adopted for the *mishna*.

The case Rabbi Elazar beRebbi Shimon was originally addressing is a third scenario: a *kohen* who brings a *minchat chotei* — the meal offering that serves as the poverty-tier substitute in an *oleh ve-yored* obligation. When the Torah describes this offering it says *ve-hayeta la-kohen ke-minchah* — it shall be for the *kohen* like a *mincha*. The question is: like which *mincha*? Rabbi Elazar beRebbi Shimon argues that the word *ke-minchah* — like a *mincha*, not like *his* *mincha* — means it is to be treated like a standard *minchat Yisrael* in one respect: a *kmitzah* is taken. The word is *ke-minchah*, not *ke-minchat kohen*. However, since it is still a *minchat kohen* in some sense, the *shirayim* cannot be eaten. So he reaches the same intermediate resolution: *kmitzah* is taken, the *kometz* is offered, and the remainder cannot be eaten and cannot be properly offered, so it is burned in the *beis hadeshen*. The Rabbis, by contrast, hold that *ke-minchah* means it is fully like a *minchat kohen* and the whole thing is burned on the *mizbe'ach*. Their disagreement with Rabbi Elazar beRebbi Shimon is specifically about this case, which they regard as a straightforward *minchat kohen*, not a hybrid.

### Rabbanan Agree

The Gemara then makes a crucial concession: *ve-afillu Rabbanan lo paligi alei de-Rabbi Elazar beRebbi Shimon ella be-Minchat Chotei shel Kohanim de-vat akrava hi* — even the Rabbis only disagree with Rabbi Elazar beRebbi Shimon in the case of the *minchat chotei* of a *kohen*, which they regard as a genuine *minchat kohen* that should be fully offered. But in the case of the wife of a *kohen*, where the *mincha* is genuinely a hybrid — simultaneously carrying the status of a *minchat kohen* and a *minchat Yisrael* — *afillu Rabbanan modu* — even the Rabbis concede that you cannot eat the *shirayim* and cannot properly offer them on the *mizbe'ach*. You take the *kmitzah*, you offer it, and the remainder is burned in the *beis hadeshen*. This is the position that Rashi had already adopted in the *mishna*, and which now receives its Talmudic grounding.

---

## Gender Differences (II)

### General M/F Diffs

The *mishna* transitions again, now moving from the specific *kohen*/*kohenet* dichotomy to a general enumeration of differences between men and women across a range of *halachic* contexts. The Gemara supplies the *pesukim* underlying each distinction.

### Metzora Hair

The *mishna* states: *ha'ish poreia u-forem* — a man who is a *metzora* must let his hair grow wild and rend his garments. A woman does not. The Gemara derives this from the *pasuk*. The *Torah* begins the laws of *tzara'at* with *ish ish ki yihyeh be-or besaro* — it opens with *ish*, man. One might have thought that women are entirely exempt from *tzara'at* laws. The *pasuk* then says *ve-ha-tzarua asher bo ha-nega* — using a general term for the *metzora* without specifying gender — to teach that a woman too can be a *metzora* and is subject to *tum'at tzara'at*. The *hava amina* from *ish* is not that women are exempt from *tum'ah*, but that some of the active behavioral obligations incumbent upon a *metzora* — letting the hair grow wild, rending the garments — apply specifically to men by virtue of that initial *ish*.

### Nazirite Vow

*Ha'ish madir et beno be-Nazir* — a man can make his son a *Nazir*, even without the son's consent or explicit agreement, *ve-ein ha-ishah maderet et benah be-Nazir* — but a woman cannot impose a *nazirite* vow on her son. The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan: *halacha hi be-Nazir* — this is a *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* with respect to the laws of *nezirut*. Reish Lakish had offered a different rationale, rooting the distinction in the laws of *chinuch* — the obligation to educate a child in *mitzvot* — and holding that *chinuch* falls specifically on fathers with respect to sons but not on mothers with respect to daughters. But that was Reish Lakish's reading; the Gemara here follows Rabbi Yochanan and grounds the law in *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*.

### Nazirite Inheritance

*Ha'ish megalei'ach al nezirut aviv* — a man who himself became a *Nazir* after his father was a *Nazir* may, under certain circumstances, make use of his father's remaining *korbanot* for his own *nezirut*, *ve-ein ha-ishah megale'ichat al nezirut aviha* — but this does not apply to a woman. Again Rabbi Yochanan: *halacha hi be-Nazir* — this too is *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*.

### Father Marries Daughter

*Ha'ish mekadesh et bito* — a father can arrange the *kiddushin* of his daughter, giving her in marriage, *ve-ein ha-ishah mekadeshet et bitah* — a mother cannot. The source is the *pasuk*: *et bitti natati la'ish ha-zeh* — "I gave my daughter to this man" — the father speaking. This right belongs to the father *de-oraita*; *de-rabbanan* a mechanism was created for the mother as well, but the Biblical institution is paternal.

### Sale to Slavery

*Ha'ish mocher et bito* — a father can sell his daughter as a slave in certain circumstances of poverty; *ve-ein ha-ishah mocheret et bitah* — a mother cannot. The source is *ki yimkor ish et bito* — the Torah specifies *ish*, the father.

### Stoning Execution

*Ha'ish niskal arom* — a man who is stoned is stoned while naked; *ve-ein ha-ishah niskelet arumah* — a woman is not. The Gemara derives this from *ve-ragmu oto kol ha-edah* — they shall stone him, and *oto* is taken to mean him in his own state, without his garments. The Gemara preempts the possible misreading: *oto* cannot mean to exclude women from capital punishment altogether, since the Torah elsewhere explicitly says *ve-hotzeita et ha-ish ha-hu o et ha-ishah ha-hi el she'arecha* — you shall bring out that man or that woman to your gates, and execute them. Rather, *oto* teaches *oso be-lo chesuto ve-lo osah be-lo chesusah* — him without his clothes, but not her without hers.

### Hanging

*Ha'ish nitlah* — after execution by stoning, a man's body is hung; *ve-ein ha-ishah nitlit* — not a woman. The source is *ve-talita oto al ha-eitz* — and you shall hang him, *oto ve-lo otah*. This raises the perennial question in the *Torah*'s legislative language: since the default gender of Hebrew is masculine, when does the masculine pronoun limit the law to men, and when is it inclusive? The *gemara* consistently addresses this on a case-by-case basis, and the masculine genitive is not always read as exclusionary. In these cases, it is.

### Sale for Theft

*Ha'ish nimkar bi-gnivato ve-ein ishah nimkeret bi-gneivatah* — a man who steals and cannot repay is sold into slavery by *beit din*, but a woman is not. The *pasuk* says *ve-nimkar bi-gnivato* — the word *bi-gnivato*, using the masculine possessive, is the basis: *bi-gnivato ve-lo bi-gneivatah* — for his theft, not for her theft. The *beit din* has no authority to sell a woman in satisfaction of her theft debt.

The *Tosefta* in chapter 2, *halacha* 8, supplements this list considerably: a *kohen* serves on the *mizbe'ach*, which a *kohenet* does not; the father retains rights to his minor daughter's found objects, her earnings, and the power to annul her vows; a man is obligated in *mitzvot asei she-ha-zman geramah* while a woman is not; a man transgresses *bal takif* and *bal tashchit* — shaving the sidelocks and beard — and the prohibition of *tum'at meitim* for a *kohen*; only a boy can be a *ben sorer u-moreh*; a man can be sold into slavery more than once, and a woman cannot be; a man undergoes *retziah* — ear-piercing to mark perpetual slavery — and a woman does not; and various other distinctions related to the laws of *eved ivri*. The *mishna*'s list, while substantial, is thus only a selection from a fuller catalogue of male-female *halachic* differences.

---

---

# Sotah 24

## Arusa & Shomeret Yavam

### New Perek Overview

With *daf* 24, we arrive at a new *perek*. Having completed the step-by-step description of the *sotah* procedure in the previous chapters, the *Mishnah* now returns to the more characteristically Talmudic mode of analysis: identifying categories, determining who qualifies and who does not, and working through the criteria that govern the *sotah* process. This is the kind of sustained halakhic analysis more familiar from tractates like *Kodashim*, where the procedure has already been described and the focus shifts to the underlying rules.

Before proceeding, it is worth noting a common misconception about the *sotah*: neither the *Torah*, the *Mishnah*, nor the *Gemara* actually states that she dies. The single dramatic line — "remove her lest she make the *Azarah tamei*" — is interpreted by the *Gemara* to mean that she may be about to become a *niddah*. The popular imagination has embellished this considerably beyond what the sources actually say.

### Arusa Definition

The *Mishnah* opens: *arusa v'shomeret yavam lo shotot v'lo notlot ktubatah* — a betrothed woman and a woman awaiting levirate marriage neither drink nor collect their *ktuba*. The *arusa* is a woman who has accepted *kiddushin* — the ring or its equivalent — from her husband, rendering her fully married in law. If she commits adultery, it is a genuine act of adultery: the children would be *mamzerim*, she would be forbidden to her husband, and all attendant legal consequences apply. The sole distinction between *eirusin* and *nisuin* is that the couple has not yet begun a shared life together. They are not living together, they are not intimate, and the reciprocal obligations of married life have not yet commenced. She remains, in that sense, a marriage on paper — complete in its legal weight, but not yet actualized in lived reality.

### Shomeret Yavam

The *shomeret yavam* is the woman whose husband has died childless, leaving her bound by the tie of *zika* — a quasi-marital connection — to her deceased husband's brother, the *yavam*. She awaits either *yibbum* or *chalitzah*. She is prohibited by an *issur lav* from marrying or sleeping with any other man. Although this bond is not a full marriage, it is understood as a continuation, in potential form, of the marriage with the deceased brother, now existing in a kind of anticipatory relationship with the living brother.

### Cannot Drink/Ktuba

In both cases, if *kinui* was issued and the woman subsequently entered seclusion, she cannot be compelled to drink, and she does not collect her *ktuba*. The logic runs as follows: she becomes forbidden to her husband as a *sotah* — the *Mishnah* treats this as implicit — but since the process cannot be completed, the only resolution is divorce without *ktuba*. The general principle is that when the inability to complete the procedure is attributable to the wife, she forfeits her *ktuba*; when it is attributable to the husband, she collects it. In these cases, even though no one is formally at fault — she simply is an *arusa* or *shomeret yavam* — she is nonetheless considered responsible, because she need not have entered seclusion with another man after her husband warned her. She made that choice, and the consequence follows.

A question was raised about the language of the *Mishnah*: why does it say *lo notlot ktubatam* rather than the more familiar formula *v'teitzei blo ktuba* — "she goes out without a *ktuba*"? The answer lies in structure. The *Mishnah* is about to present cases where women *do* collect their *ktuba* despite not drinking — *lo shotot v'notlot*. The parallel formulation *lo shotot v'lo notlot* sets up that contrast neatly, and the stylistic symmetry justifies the phrasing.

### Rashi-Tosafot Dispute

The question of the *shomeret yavam* is particularly rich. *Rashi* explains that even if she were not halakhically forbidden to the *yavam* by virtue of her suspected conduct, the brother would still be entitled to declare that he refuses to marry such a woman. That refusal alone is sufficient to dissolve the *zika* without her collecting a *ktuba*.

*Tosafot* objects. The rule established earlier in the tractate is that if the act itself — had it actually occurred — would not have rendered her forbidden, then the suspicion of having done it cannot render her forbidden either. It would be strange if the *sotah* process made her status worse than actual proven misconduct would. *Tosafot* therefore resolves the matter by working from the premise that a *shomeret yavam* who sleeps with another man would in fact be forbidden to the *yavam*. On that premise, the *sotah* process is coherent: since proven infidelity would forbid her, suspected infidelity similarly triggers the *sotah* status.

A further question was posed: if there are multiple brothers, who among them is entitled to issue *kinui*? And if one brother does so and she becomes forbidden on account of his *kinui*, does she remain permissible to the other brothers? This is a genuinely difficult question that does not appear to have been resolved in the discussion.

### Textual Derivation

The textual basis for excluding the *arusa* and *shomeret yavam* from drinking comes from the phrase *asher tisteh ishah tachat ishah* — "that a woman strays from her husband" — where *ishah* denotes a complete husband, not merely an *arus* or a *yavam*. This excludes cases where the marriage is not yet full. The *Gemara* will explain how the beginning of the *parasha* — the phrase *daber el Bnei Yisrael v'amarta* — is interpreted to include the *arusa* and *shomeret yavam* within the ambit of *kinui* even while they are excluded from the drinking. The two phrases thus operate on two different parts of the process.

---

## Forbidden Marriages

### Widow/Divorcee Cases

The *Mishnah* turns to a different category: women in marriages that, while legally binding, are in violation of a negative prohibition. If a prohibition carries the weight of *issur kareit* — incest, for example — the marriage is not binding at all. But if the prohibition is merely an *issur lav*, the marriage takes legal effect even though it transgresses the law. The question is whether such a husband may charge his wife as a *sotah* and bring her through the procedure, when one might argue that the entire marriage ought to be dissolved regardless.

The examples given are: a *kohen gadol* married to a widow (*almanah*); a divorced woman or a *chalutza* married to an ordinary *kohen* (*kohen hedyot*) — with the note that the *Bavli* tends to treat the prohibition of a *chalutza* marrying a *kohen* as rabbinic rather than biblical; a *mamzeret* or *netina* married to a regular *Yisrael*; and conversely, a regular Jewish woman married to a *mamzer* or *netin*.

### Mamzer/Netin Cases

These cases all share the characteristic that the marriage involves a violation of a negative prohibition touching on personal status. The specific prohibition varies — in some cases it concerns priestly restrictions (*issurei kehunah*), in others it concerns lineage (*mamzer*, *netin*). In all of them, however, the marriage is technically valid even as it transgresses the law.

### Cannot Drink Rule

The ruling in all such cases is *lo shotot v'lo notlot ktubatam*: they do not drink and they do not collect the *ktuba*. The reason they do not drink is that the marriage is not recognized as a legitimate *ishah* — not a marriage that should remain in place. Since the whole framework of the *sotah* process presupposes a valid marriage worth protecting, these marriages fall outside that framework. And since the women themselves are held responsible for having entered seclusion after being warned, they forfeit their *ktuba* as well.

---

## Process Failures

### Confession/Witnesses

The *Mishnah* now shifts to a different class of cases — not those where the nature of the marriage disqualifies the woman, but those where the *sotah* process breaks down for other reasons. The list opens: if a woman confesses her guilt, or if witnesses testify that she committed adultery, there is nothing left to establish through drinking. The process becomes superfluous. In such cases, she does not drink and does not collect her *ktuba* — the outcome is determined by evidence rather than by the ordeal.

### Woman Refuses

If the woman simply refuses to drink, she is likewise forbidden without a *ktuba*. She is the obstacle. Even though she has not confessed and there are no witnesses, her refusal creates a situation that cannot be resolved in her favor, and since the inability to complete the process is attributable to her, she bears the consequence.

### Husband Default

The cases shift when the fault lies with the husband. If the husband declares *eini mashkeh* — "I will not make her drink" — and withdraws from the process, or if the husband has relations with her after she has become a *sotah* and before the process was completed (which he is prohibited from doing, and which renders the *mei sotah* ineffective in any case), then the ruling changes: *notlot ktuba v'lo shosot*. She collects her *ktuba* even though she cannot drink. He is the responsible party. Notably, she remains forbidden to him in her status as *sotah*, since there is no mechanism to resolve the suspicion.

### Husband Dies

The most complex case in this section is where the husband dies before the process is completed — an act of God, without fault on either side. Here *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* disagree. *Beit Shammai* holds that she collects her *ktuba* and does not drink; *Beit Hillel* holds *o shotot o lo notlot ktubasan* — either drink or forfeit the *ktuba*, and since she cannot drink, she does not collect. The underlying question is how to allocate the consequences when no one is at fault. *Beit Shammai* appears willing to attribute the problem to the husband, since he is the one who died, even without moral fault; *Beit Hillel* takes the position that the inability to complete the process, absent a responsible party, falls on the wife.

---

## Forbidden Marriages (II)

### Nursing/Pregnant Women

A further category is introduced: *u'uveres chavairta u'meinekes chavairta* — a woman who is pregnant with another man's child, or nursing another man's child, and whose husband married her during that period. The prohibition here is not about personal status or a violation of Torah law; it is rabbinic in origin and rooted in a specific concern. If a man marries a woman who is nursing an infant from her deceased first husband, the concern is that the new husband — for whom the child is not his — will not weigh the infant's welfare appropriately. He may engage in marital relations, she may become pregnant, and the demands of a new pregnancy and new infant will compromise her ability to nurse and care for the existing child. The *Gemara* here reflects a recognition that having children in close succession can be harmful to an infant, particularly when the decision is made by a party without skin in the game.

This emerges into a law: a man should not marry a nursing or pregnant woman until the child has passed the two-year nursing period. The *Gemara*'s acknowledgment of this concern, while framed as a prohibition rather than a permission to use contraception, resonates with the practice documented in the name of *Rav Yosef Eliyahu Henkin*, who would regularly grant *heterim* for women to use contraception for two or more years after giving birth, in order to allow focused care for the existing child.

If such a man then issued *kinui* and seclusion followed, is this treated like the cases of prohibited marriages — where the couple should not remain married and therefore the full *sotah* process cannot proceed — or is it different?

### Meir vs Sages

*Rabbi Meir* applies the same principle as in the cases of *issurei kehunah*: since they should not be married right now, the *sotah* procedure cannot be pursued. She neither drinks nor collects her *ktuba*.

The *Chachamim* disagree. They distinguish this case from the earlier prohibited marriages on a crucial ground: in this case, the man is not required to divorce his wife. He could live separately from her during the two-year period and then resume the marriage. Since we would not demand a divorce, the marriage retains its legitimacy, and therefore the *sotah* procedure may be carried out. *Rabbi Meir* applies the principle broadly — any reason they should not be married currently disqualifies the *sotah* process. The *Chachamim* apply it narrowly — only where the marriage is so defective that divorce is required does the process become unavailable.

---

## Infertile Women

### Infertile Categories

*Aylonit v'zkeinah u'she'eina re'uya l'yeled* — an *aylonit*, an elderly woman, and a woman who cannot bear children — these are the next cases considered. The *aylonit* is a woman with markedly masculine characteristics who is considered not only infertile but physically distinct in ways the *Gemara* associates with that condition. The *zkeinah* is simply an older woman past childbearing age. *She'eina re'uya l'yeled* — *Rashi* understands this as a woman who drank a sterilizing potion; *Tosafot* offers a different explanation, and also asks why the *Mishnah* does not simply use the standard term *akara* (barren woman), which the Torah uses for classic infertility.

One might ask: why does infertility raise a question about the *sotah* process at all? The issue is not the verse *v'nikta v'nizra zara* — that she will be purified and bear seed — though that might be a passing thought. The concern parallels the earlier cases: the man has a *mitzvah* of *pru u'revu*, an obligation to have children. If his wife cannot bear children, perhaps the marriage is one that should not continue, and therefore falls outside the framework of a legitimate *ishah* that the *sotah* process presupposes. This question arises even in a marriage of fifty years — he could theoretically always take an additional wife and thus fulfill his obligation, but the concern is whether this marriage, as it stands, is one the *Torah* views as a *sotah*-eligible union.

### Cannot Drink/Ktuba

The *Mishnah*'s ruling: *lo notlet ktuba v'lo shotah* — she does not collect her *ktuba* and does not drink.

### Rabbi Eliezer View

*Rabbi Eliezer* dissents: *yachol hu v'yissa isha acheret v'yifros v'ya'amod im zu* — he can simply marry another woman and thereby fulfill his obligation of *pru u'revu*, while remaining married to his current wife. On this view, there is no reason to dissolve the marriage or to bar the *sotah* process, since the man has an available remedy that does not require divorcing his wife. Intuitively, *Rabbi Eliezer*'s position has considerable force: there is nothing inherently wrong with this marriage, particularly in a halakhic framework that permits polygamy. If his *mitzvah* of *pru u'revu* can be satisfied through a second marriage, the first marriage need not be undone, and the *sotah* process should apply normally.

---

## Mixed Cases

### Arayot Cases

*Al yedai kol ha'arayot mikanyin* — the *kinui* process applies even when the woman is suspected not merely of adultery but of another forbidden sexual relationship. One might have supposed that when the suspicion involves an entirely separate category of prohibition — sleeping with a close relative, for instance — the case should be analyzed through that other framework rather than through the *sotah* framework. The *chiddush* here is that the *sotah* process is not dislodged by the presence of a concurrent prohibition. The *kinui* and the *sotah* status remain operative, and if she undergoes the ordeal and is cleared, this clears up both the adultery question and the *arayot* question simultaneously.

### Minor/Non-Man

The exception: a woman cannot be made a *sotah* based on suspicion of having been with a minor (*katan*) or with someone who is not a man (*mi she'eino ish*). The phrase *mi she'eino ish* is deliberately opaque, and the *Gemara* will address it on a subsequent *daf*.

The question of the *katan* is not about physical capacity but about legal significance. The act, even if it occurred, would not carry sufficient legal weight to create *sotah* status. A question was raised about a non-Jew: would suspicion of sleeping with a non-Jew similarly disqualify the *sotah* process? The suggestion that *mi she'eino ish* might encompass a non-Jew was floated, though this was not resolved. Both the *katan* and the potential non-Jew share the characteristic of not being *tofes kiddushin* — not being able to effect a legally binding betrothal — and that may be the relevant common denominator, though this remains to be seen in the *Gemara*.

---

## Beit Din Authority

### Cases for Intervention

*V'elu she'beis din mikanyin lahen* — the following women, whose husbands are not in a position to issue *kinui*, will have *beit din* step in on the husband's behalf. The cases are: the husband became a *cheresh* (deaf-mute, who lacks full legal competence); the husband became a *shoteh* (mentally ill, not in the sense of being demented but of having a mental condition that disrupts his ability to function legally); or the husband is *chavush b'veit ha'asurim* — imprisoned and unable to monitor or respond to his wife's conduct.

This raises an important conceptual question. Earlier in the tractate, there was a debate about whether it is *assur l'kanos* — forbidden for a husband to issue *kinui* — or *mutar*, or even a *chiyuv*. If it is *assur l'kanos* when the husband acts out of his own jealousy and subjective passion, perhaps when a third party — *beit din*, an objective body with no personal stake — observes concerning behavior, they bear a responsibility to address it that the emotionally invested husband does not.

### First Opinion

The first opinion sharply limits what *beit din* can accomplish: *lo lehashkotah amru ela lefoslah miktuvatah* — the *Sages* did not say that *beit din* can represent the husband to the point of compelling her to drink. All they can do is disqualify her from collecting her *ktuba*. The immediate consequence of *beit din*'s intervention, therefore, is that the situation moves toward divorce without *ktuba* — since there is no mechanism to complete the *sotah* process when the husband is incapacitated, and the *sotah* status cannot be resolved, the only exit is dissolution of the marriage.

This raises a searching question about what has actually been achieved. If the woman knows that the only possible outcome is divorce without *ktuba*, has her behavior been deterred? It seems unlikely. Perhaps the purpose is not deterrence of her current conduct but protection of his interests — ensuring that when and if he returns to capacity, he will not be required to pay a *ktuba* to a wife who behaved this way in his absence. But even that framing is not fully satisfying, since his financial interests seem an insufficient reason for *beit din* to intervene as actively as it does.

Another possibility is that *beit din* is acting on halakhic grounds: they believe this marriage should end, not merely for his financial protection, but because they suspect adultery has occurred and they do not want the couple to remain married in such circumstances. On this reading, *beit din* is acting to achieve a halakhic result — dissolution of a marriage they believe should not continue — and the *ktuba* consequence is a tool toward that end.

A further wrinkle: in the cases of *cheresh* and *shoteh*, a *get* cannot be arranged even from a distance, since the husband lacks legal competence to issue one. Only in the case of the imprisoned husband could a *get* potentially be arranged from prison. So what *beit din* has accomplished in the *cheresh* and *shoteh* cases is, in effect, a kind of conditional verdict — setting the stage so that if the husband ever recovers capacity, divorce without *ktuba* is the pre-determined result.

### Rabbi Yosi

*Rabbi Yosi* goes further: *af lehashkotah* — *beit din* is empowered to authorize her actually drinking, *liksheyeitzei ba'alah mibeit ha'asurim yashkenah* — when the husband is released from prison, he can make her drink on the strength of *beit din*'s prior *kinui*. This is a significant expansion. On *Rabbi Yosi*'s view, the *kinui* issued by *beit din* has full legal force, and the process is merely suspended — not foreclosed — until the husband regains the ability to bring it to completion. In the interim, the woman is in a kind of *agunah* state, unable to move forward, but the path to resolution remains open. The husband, upon release, could choose either to complete the *sotah* process or, if the *sotah* process vindicates her, to resume the marriage — he need not necessarily divorce her.

### Philosophy/Analysis

The conceptual architecture here is striking. The *Mishnah* has already shown, across several categories, that *sotah* status can be created even in cases where the process can never be completed — where from the very outset there is no possible *sotah* outcome. The *Torah* permits this intermediate status, even without any path to resolution, apparently because the suspicion and the conduct that created it are themselves legally significant, independent of whether the ordeal can be performed. *Beit din*'s intervention extends this logic to cases of an absent or incapacitated husband, authorizing the creation of that status through a surrogate.

The question of whose interests are being protected is not straightforwardly answered. If it is about deterrence, it is unlikely to deter, because once the *sotah* status is established and no resolution is possible, the woman has nothing further to lose. If it is about his financial interests, the magnitude of *beit din*'s involvement seems disproportionate to a monetary concern. The most coherent account may be halakhic: *beit din* acts because it views the continuation of this marriage under these circumstances as a problem the law demands they address, and stripping the *ktuba* is the mechanism available to them in his absence. And as a secondary consideration, there is also the deterrent function for future cases — if women know that their conduct during a husband's incapacity will be met with a consequence, even a delayed or partial one, that knowledge may shape behavior.

---

## Kinui Derivation

### Gemara Question

The *Gemara* now takes up the question implicit in the *Mishnah*: since the *arusa* and *shomeret yavam* cannot drink, how can *kinui* apply to them at all? *Mishna hu d'lo shatya* — the *Mishnah* presupposes that *kinui* can be issued but drinking is unavailable. *Ha'kinui mikanei lah* — *kinui* does apply. *Mna hani mili* — from where do we derive this?

The *Gemara* cites a *baraita*: the phrase *daber el Bnei Yisrael v'amarta* at the opening of the *parshat sotah* — the doubled language of "speak" and "say" — is interpreted as an expansion. It includes the *arusa* and *shomeret yavam* within the *kinui* stage of the *parasha*, even though they are excluded from the drinking stage by the later phrase *tachat ishah*. The opening of the *parasha* draws them in; the closing phrase cuts them off before the final step.

### Yoshiya vs Yonatan

A *baraita* records a debate between *Rabbi Yoshiya* and *Rabbi Yonatan* that cuts against the *Mishnah*'s unanimous ruling. *Rabbi Yonatan* — whose position matches the *Mishnah* — excludes both *arusa* and *shomeret yavam* from drinking. He reads *tachat ishech* as excluding the *shomeret yavam* first (since that is the more obvious exclusion for him), and a second phrase, *asher tisteh isha tachat ishah*, as excluding the *arusa*.

*Rabbi Yoshiya* takes the opposing view: he uses the double language of *ish ish* to *include* the *shomeret yavam* in the full *sotah* process, up to and including drinking. For *Rabbi Yoshiya*, the *shomeret yavam* is sufficiently married — or nearly so — that she drinks just as a fully married woman would. It is only the *arusa* who is excluded.

### Conceptual Debate

The underlying conceptual disagreement is this: which of the two relationships — *eirusin* or *zika* — is more weighty, more fully an *ishut*?

*Rabbi Yoshiya* (and the position associated with him in the *Gemara*) holds that the *arusa* relationship is more of a marriage. The man actively chose it; he performed an act of *kiddushin*; she bears full capital liability for adultery. The relationship is enormously weighty, even if not yet a lived marriage. The *shomeret yavam*, by contrast, had this bond thrust upon her without choice, and her liability for sleeping with another man is more limited. So *eirusin* is closer to full *ishut* and harder to exclude; *zika* is more peripheral and more easily read out of the *parasha*.

*Rabbi Yonatan* takes the opposite view. The *shomeret yavam* is more obviously included — and thus more surprisingly excluded by the verse — because her path to full marriage requires no additional act. She does not need *kiddushin*, she does not need a formal wedding ceremony. Sexual relations alone, even unintentional ones, immediately actualize the *zika* into full marriage. The marriage is almost there; it could happen in an instant. The *arusa*, despite her weighty legal status, still requires the full process of *nisuin* to actualize. So the *shomeret yavam* is the one you would expect to be more included in *parshat sotah*, and therefore she is the first one the verse needs to exclude.

This conceptual debate is not merely academic — it maps onto a disagreement in the *Gemara* between *Rav* and *Shmuel* about the legal effect of sexual relations in the *yibbum* context, which the *Gemara* explores in the next section.

---

## Consummation Requirement

### Baraita Rule

*Rabbi Acha bar Chanina* came from the south and brought a *baraita* with him: *mishekadma shchivat ba'al l'vo'el* — the *sotah* process can only apply if the husband consummated the marriage before the suspected act of infidelity occurred. *V'lo shekadma shchivat bo'el l'ba'al* — if the suspected act came first and the marriage was never consummated, the husband cannot subject her to the *sotah* ordeal. This is derived from the phrase *miba'aladei ishech* — "other than your husband" — with emphasis on *u'nitein ish bach et shichvato*, implying that the husband's intimacy must precede the other man's.

This is a rule not stated explicitly in the *Mishnah* itself, but one the *Gemara* adopts as authoritative. It raises the question of what, precisely, consummation adds to the legal picture. One possibility is that it is simply another dimension of *ishut* — the marriage must be fully realized, not only in its formal structure but in its physical consummation, before the *sotah* framework applies.

### Zera Concern

A deeper dimension of this requirement may be found in the *Gemara*'s language. The *parasha* uses the phrase *shichvat zera* — "a lying of seed." Halakhically, intercourse without ejaculation would carry the same prohibition, so the phrase seems to have no strictly legal content. The *Ramban* explains this as pointing to the real engine of the husband's jealousy: the concern about *zera* — whose children these are. If another man has lain with his wife, the fundamental fear is that the children he is raising may not be his. The end of the *parasha* echoes this — *v'nikta v'nizra zara*, she will be cleansed and bear seed.

This same concern animates the position of the *Tzitz Eliezer* in the modern debate about artificial insemination with donor sperm. He cited precisely this *Ramban* to argue that another man's *zera*, even without a sexual act, constitutes a form of quasi-adultery. *Rav Moshe Feinstein*, by contrast, dismissed this entirely: halakha deals only with acts, and without a sexual act there is no adultery. He regarded the *Tzitz Eliezer*'s concern as imported from outside values rather than grounded in *Torah* — a remarkable response, given that it is *pshat* of the *psukim* and the *Ramban* says it explicitly.

Applied here: is it possible that the consummation requirement is connected to this concern about *zera*? If the husband has never been intimate with his wife, he has no reason to worry about the paternity of her children; any future children would obviously not be his. The concern about *zera* that drives the *sotah* process only becomes relevant once he has been intimate with her. One cannot say this with certainty — the *Gemara* does not state it this way — but the thematic resonance is present.

### Arusa Case

This creates a puzzle for the *Mishnah*'s discussion of the *arusa*. If consummation is required for the *sotah* process, why does the *Mishnah* need a separate verse to exclude the *arusa* from drinking? She has not yet consummated the marriage; she is automatically excluded under the consummation requirement.

The *Gemara* resolves this via *Rami bar Chama*: *mashkachat lah k'egon sheba al arusato b'veit aviha* — the exclusion is still needed for the case where the husband had relations with his *arusa* while she was still living in her father's house. She is still an *arusa* — they have not yet made a home together, she has not yet entered the *chuppah* — but the marriage has in fact been consummated. (The *Gemara* notes, citing what we will encounter in *Ketubot*, that in *Yehuda* it was the practice for a betrothed couple to spend private time together, and this sometimes led to sexual relations.) In that case, consummation alone does not transform her into a *nesua*. *Rashi* describes such relations as *b'znut* — not in the context of beginning a married life, and therefore not actuating *nisuin*. For that case, the verse *tachat ishah* is needed to exclude her from drinking.

---

## Yavam Marriage Status

### Challenge

The *Gemara* then turns the same question on the *shomeret yavam*: *kehavata gabei shomeres yavam* — how do you have a case of a *shomeret yavam* after sexual relations who is still a *shomeret yavam*? The challenge is sharp: the moment *yibbum* relations occur, she should automatically become his full wife — *ishto me'aleta hi*. Why would you ever need a verse to exclude a *shomeret yavam* if the moment she has relations with the *yavam* she is no longer a *shomeret yavam* at all?

### Rav's View

*Rav* holds *kanah l'chol davar* — that sexual relations between a *yavam* and his *yevama*, regardless of intent or context, create a complete and full marriage in every respect. On *Rav*'s view, there is never a case of a *shomeret yavam* after relations — she is immediately and fully his wife. The *Gemara* notes that this means *Rav* must say like *Rabbi Yoshiya*, who holds that the *shomeret yavam* does drink. But the *Gemara* will complicate this.

### Shmuel's View

*Shmuel* disagrees: *lo kanah ela l'devarim ha'amurim b'parsha* — relations in the context of *yibbum*, when not accompanied by the intent to begin a married life together, do not create full *nisuin*. She becomes legally his wife in certain respects specified in the *parasha* — adultery would be a capital crime, he inherits his brother's estate through her (*l'hakim shem achiv hamet*) — but she does not achieve the status of full *nisuin*. She remains, in some sense, more like an *arusa* than a *nesua*. On *Shmuel*'s view, there can be a *shomeret yavam* after relations, and that is precisely the case the verse needs to address.

### Resolution

The *Gemara* draws the natural inference: *Rav* must hold like *Rabbi Yoshiya* and *Shmuel* must hold like *Rabbi Yonatan*. But both *Rav* and *Shmuel* push back against this assignment.

### Final Reconciliation

*Rav* says: I could actually say like *Rabbi Yonatan* — that the *shomeret yavam* does not drink even after relations. Here is why: *mideitztrich kra lemoutei, miklal d'ishto me'aleta hi* — the very fact that a verse was needed to exclude the *shomeret yavam* demonstrates, according to *Rav*, that without the verse she would be considered completely his wife. She is fully married after relations, as *Rav* maintains — and yet the verse nonetheless excludes her from the *sotah* process. The reason, on this reading, is not that the marriage is incomplete, but that a marriage entered through *yibbum* — through the continuation of the dead brother's bond rather than through an independent act of will — is categorically different from a marriage the man chose. Even though she is fully his wife, it is not the kind of marriage the *Torah* placed within the *sotah* framework.

*Shmuel* responds in kind: I could actually say like *Rabbi Yoshiya* — that the *shomeret yavam* does drink. *Mideitztrich kra l'rabuyei, miklal d'lav ishto hi klal* — the verse needed to include the *shomeret yavam* in the *sotah* process, which shows that without it she would not be considered fully his wife at all. That matches *Shmuel*'s view that relations without intent to begin a married life do not create full *nisuin*. Nevertheless, the verse includes her sufficiently in the *parasha* to make her drink — even this incomplete marriage is enough to trigger the *sotah* ordeal.

The final picture is thus: *Rav* says relations create full marriage, and yet a verse excludes the *yevama* from *sotah* because of the particular nature of *yibbum* marriages. *Shmuel* says relations without marital intent do not create full *nisuin*, and yet a verse includes the *yevama* in the *sotah* process because even that partial bond is sufficient for the *parasha*. Both amoraim can therefore align with either *tanna*, because each is reading the textual derivation through his own understanding of what kind of relationship *yibbum* creates.

With this, the *daf* concludes.

---

---

# Sotah 25

## Overes Al Das & Warning

### Definition of Overes Al Das…

The daf opens with a fresh topic, framed as an *ibayahu* — a question raised by the rabbis. Before examining that question, however, it is worth establishing the meaning of the central term: *overes al das*, a woman who transgresses the norms of married life. This concept originates in a *mishnah* in *Kesubos* that distinguishes between *das Moshe* — biblical norms — and *das Yehudis* — the recognized practices of Jewish women. The category is not about a woman who sins against God; it is specifically about behaviors that affect the marriage itself. The Gemara's examples of *overes al das Moshe* include a woman who does not go to the *mikvah* or who feeds her husband non-kosher food. Notably, the Gemara does not include *chilul Shabbos* in this list, because a woman who violates Shabbos has sinned between herself and God — that transgression does not intrinsically damage the marital relationship. By contrast, *overes al das* describes conduct that compromises the intimacy of the marriage, or that, in the idiom of the Mishnah, attracts unwanted attention from other men.

The Mishnah enumerates behaviors such as going out with uncovered hair, nursing in public, or engaging in flirtatious interactions with men outside the household. Translated into contemporary terms, these are behaviors perceived as undermining the private sphere of the marriage — drawing the gaze, or worse, the involvement, of other men, whether practically or in the imagination. These behaviors resemble the *sotah* situation in spirit, though they fall short of it in substance: a woman who has not committed adultery, and has not even been subjected to *kinuy* and *stirah*, may nonetheless be acting in ways that garner her husband's jealousy and compromise the relationship. If the husband seeks to divorce her on account of such conduct, he may do so without paying her *kesuvah* — she is considered to be at fault, and it is a fault divorce. That is the legal framework of *overes al das*.

### Warning Requirement?

The Gemara now poses its question: does a woman who is *overes al das* require warning — *hasra'ah* — in order to forfeit her *kesuvah*? The framing of the question is important. The Gemara is not asking whether *hasra'ah* is required in the same sense as in criminal law, where warning is necessary to establish *meizid* and enable corporal punishment. Rather, the Gemara is asking whether the husband — or *beis din* — must first inform the woman that her behavior is unacceptable and that continued conduct will lead to divorce without a *kesuvah*, before that consequence can take effect.

The Gemara lays out two sides of the question. On one hand, *keivan d'overes al das hi lo ba'ei hasra'ah*: since she has already acted inappropriately in a way that damages the marriage, perhaps no warning is needed — she has forfeited the *kesuvah* through her own conduct. On the other hand, perhaps she does require warning, *d'hadra bah* — so that she has the opportunity to mend her ways. This second framing is revealing: the concern is not that her conduct was technically insufficient, but that a broader, more humane consideration applies. Breaking up a marriage is a serious matter, and perhaps the healthier approach — one that the rabbis who establish the rule would endorse — is to first attempt repair rather than rushing to the most severe consequence. Warning signals that the situation can still be corrected, and that divorce without a *kesuvah* should be a last resort rather than an automatic outcome.

It is worth noting that this same logic does not apply where adultery has actually occurred. In that case there is a *halachic* reality — the woman is forbidden to her husband — and no amount of willingness to repair the relationship can set that aside. But *overes al das* operates in a different register: there is no absolute *halachic* prohibition, the relationship is not destroyed in a formal sense, and so the possibility of repair is genuine. Additionally, even if a husband wishes to claim that his wife was *overes al das* and refuse to pay her *kesuvah*, he would need to bring objective evidence before a court — the *kesuvah* is an obligation, and he cannot simply declare himself exempt.

One might also ask whether *shogeg* — the woman not realizing she was forbidden from acting in a certain way — bears on the question. The Gemara does not frame the issue in those terms. It does not say that *hasra'ah* is needed because she was acting unknowingly and therefore should not be penalized as harshly. Instead, the focus is on the broader consideration of preserving the marriage. It is nonetheless worth observing that the degree to which conduct damages a marriage may be affected by whether it was done knowingly or in ignorance — a woman who defies a known standard has communicated something different about her relationship than one who simply did not understand what was expected of her.

### Arusah/Shomeret Yavam

The Gemara attempts to resolve the question from a source. *Ta shema*: an *arusah* and a *shomeret yavam* do not drink and do not collect a *kesuvah*. What is accomplished by the husband performing *kinuy* in such cases? The Gemara initially suggests: *lav l'afsidei kesuvaseh* — it must be to cause her to forfeit her *kesuvah*. If so, this would prove that *kinuy* is required for that purpose, meaning that the mere fact of her going into seclusion with another man is not sufficient — you need the additional step of *kinuy*, which functions as a form of *hasra'ah*. Why else would the husband need to go through the process of warning her if she were going to lose her *kesuvah* simply by having gone into seclusion?

Abaye pushes back: *lo, le'osrah alav* — perhaps the purpose of the *kinuy* is not to cause her to lose her *kesuvah* at all. Rather, the husband performs *kinuy* because he wants to impose upon her the status of *sotah*, making her forbidden to him. This is a distinct legal goal — it is not about the money, but about creating a formal forbidden status. The *kinuy* can be used, in other words, not as a financial measure but as an act of imposing a religious-legal status that goes beyond the civil consequence of losing the *kesuvah*.

Rav Papa offers another answer: *lehashkosah k'she'yinasu* — the husband performs *kinuy* now, while she is an *arusah*, intending that if she later goes into seclusion after *nisuin*, he will be able to make her drink on the basis of the earlier warning. There is a *baraisa* that makes this explicit: one cannot make an *arusah* drink while she is an *arusah*, but one can perform *kinuy* while she is an *arusah* so that if she goes into seclusion after *nisuin*, she becomes a *sotah* on the basis of that prior warning. This is a legitimate strategic use of *kinuy* — keeping one's options open — and therefore the *kinuy* in the case of an *arusah* is fully explained without needing to appeal to the *kesuvah* at all.

Rava then offers a much stronger proof. *Ta shema*: the *mishnah* enumerates cases of *issurei lavin* — women whose marriages, though formally binding, are biblically prohibited. These include, for example, a widow married to a *Kohen Gadol*, a divorcée or *chalutza* married to an ordinary *kohen*, a *mamzeres* or *nesinah* married to a Yisrael, or a daughter of Israel married to a *mamzer* or *nasin*. In all these cases, the *mishnah* rules that such women do not drink and do not collect their *kesuvah*. Yet the husband still goes through the process of *kinuy*. Why?

This is a brilliant point because it eliminates both of Abaye's and Rav Papa's answers simultaneously. The answer *le'osrah alav* — to make her forbidden to him — cannot apply here, because she is already forbidden by a biblical prohibition; *hai issura deka'i* — the prohibition already stands. And the answer *lehashkosah k'she'yinasu* — to make her drink after *nisuin* — also cannot apply, because they are already in a state of *nisuin*; there is no future *nisuin* to wait for. So why is *kinuy* necessary at all? *Ella lav l'afsidei kesuvaseh* — it must be solely to cause her to forfeit her *kesuvah*. And the implication is that the *stirah* alone — the mere fact of her going into seclusion — would not have been sufficient. Something more was needed, and that something more is the *kinuy*, which here functions as a warning.

Rav Yehuda of Diskarta then steps in to rescue the earlier approach: *le'osrah labo'el k'ba'al*. The purpose of *kinuy* in the cases of *issurei lavin* is to make her forbidden to the man she is suspected of having slept with, just as she is forbidden to her husband. A *sotah* — a woman suspected of adultery — becomes forbidden both to her husband and to the man she is suspected of. If the husband performs *kinuy*, establishes the *sotah* process, and then for whatever reason divorces her without her ever having a chance to drink — because he never brought her to the *Beis HaMikdash*, or the *Beis HaMikdash* was destroyed — she remains forbidden to that other man. This is a significant and independent legal consequence of *kinuy*, entirely separate from the *kesuvah*. Therefore, one still cannot prove that *hasra'ah* is required for the *kesuvah* from these cases.

### Beit Din Acts for Incapa…

The Gemara pivots to a cleaner proof. *Ta shema*: the *mishnah* teaches that *beis din* steps in and performs *kinuy* on behalf of a husband in certain cases — when the husband became a deaf-mute, became insane or mentally incapacitated, or is imprisoned. And the *mishnah* specifies the purpose explicitly: *lifoslah miksuvashah* — to cause the wife to lose her *kesuvah*. This is not framed as being about making her forbidden to her husband or forbidden to the suspected paramour. It is stated plainly that *beis din* acts for this specific purpose.

This seems decisive. If going into seclusion were sufficient on its own to cause her to forfeit the *kesuvah*, why would *beis din* need to perform *kinuy* at all? The witnesses to her *stirah* could simply testify, and she would lose the *kesuvah* without any further step. The fact that *beis din* found it necessary to go through the process of *kinuy* indicates that *stirah* alone is insufficient — some form of warning is required, and in the absence of a capable husband, *beis din* steps in to provide that warning through *kinuy*.

### Conclusion: Warning Need…

The Gemara, however, entertains the possibility of distinguishing this case. Perhaps the reason *hasra'ah* is required for the *beis din* cases, even though in ordinary circumstances it would not be needed, is that the husband is absent. When the husband is not present — when he is deaf, insane, or imprisoned — the wife's behavior will naturally be less constrained, and her conduct therefore does not carry the same weight of defiance as it would if she were knowingly acting against her present husband's wishes. In that context, one might say that she cannot be penalized without warning, since her behavior is not as blameworthy. But when the husband is present and she still acts this way, it is worse — and perhaps there no warning would be needed.

The Gemara rejects this distinction. The conclusion stands: *ba'ei hasra'ah* — warning is required for a woman to lose her *kesuvah* on account of *overes al das*. This is a resolution that, remarkably, does not appear explicitly in *Kesubos*, where the entire topic of *overes al das* is discussed at length. The foundational question of what kind of evidence or warning is needed to forfeit the *kesuvah* is answered here, in *Sotah* — making this *sugyah* an essential clarification of material studied in a different tractate entirely.

---

## Husband's Right to Waive

### If Husband Doesn't Mind?

The Gemara now raises a second *ibayahu*, which is in many ways the more fundamental question. The scenario: the wife has been *overes al das*, but the husband does not object — *lo kapid*. He is aware of her behavior and is not troubled by it, or at least does not wish to end the marriage on account of it. Can he simply continue the marriage as if nothing happened, or does the court step in and require that the marriage be dissolved?

*Kapida* — or *hakpada* — is perhaps best rendered as something one finds deeply objectionable, something that genuinely disturbs. The question is whether the husband's subjective disposition — his not finding the behavior objectionable — has legal force in this context. The Gemara frames this as: *mi amrinan b'kapida d'ba'al tala Rachmana* — do we say that the whole structure of *overes al das* is contingent on the husband's *kapida*? And if he is *lo kapid*, the whole framework simply does not apply?

Or do we say, on the other side, *keivan deka kapid kapid* — meaning, since this behavior is the sort of thing that *should* bother him, it matters even if he says it does not? Rashi explains this phrase as: since this is conduct that is objectively objectionable, his claimed indifference is beside the point. This can be understood in two ways. One is psychological: perhaps he says he does not mind, but we know that deep down he does, and the marriage is being damaged even if he is not willing to acknowledge it. The other is societal: even if he genuinely does not mind, there is a broader communal interest in not allowing such behavior to be implicitly sanctioned by the continuation of the marriage. The court's involvement in marking certain conduct as unacceptable is not merely for the benefit of this particular husband; it sends a message about the standards of marriage in the community.

This is admittedly a striking position — the idea that a rabbinical court would compel the dissolution of a marriage that both parties wish to continue. But the comparison is apt: *halacha* already determines whether marriages can continue at all, and *beis din* is already empowered to intervene in ways that override the personal preferences of the individuals involved. The question is only how far that authority extends into the domain of conduct that, while objectionable, does not create an absolute *halachic* prohibition.

### Personal vs. Objective

The Gemara seeks to resolve the question from the *mishnah* about *beis din* stepping in for a deaf-mute, insane, or imprisoned husband. If the law were entirely subjective — if the husband's *kapida* were the sole determining factor — then *beis din* would have no basis to act on his behalf, since the husband might recover or be released from prison and then express that he does not mind his wife's behavior. How can *beis din* presume to act against his potential interests?

The Gemara responds with *stama demilta*: generally speaking, *keivan d'avras adas*, since she has violated these norms, we assume that *nicha lei* — it is in his interest for *beis din* to act. The presumption is that a normal husband would want his wife's *kesuvah* forfeited under such circumstances, and *beis din* acts on that presumption. This answer does not resolve the underlying debate — it does not tell us definitively whether a fully capable husband who explicitly states he does not mind can preserve the marriage — but it demonstrates that the mere theoretical possibility of his indifference does not paralyze *beis din* from acting in his name. The question of *ratzah lekayem mekayem* remains formally open at this stage of the discussion, though the trajectory of the *sugyah* implicitly moves toward an answer.

---

## Revoking Kinuy

### Retract Kinuy?

The Gemara now turns to a third *ibayahu*, this one concerning the *kinuy* in the *sotah* context proper rather than the *overes al das* framework. The husband has issued a *kinuy* — he has formally warned his wife not to enter into private seclusion with a specific man — and then he changes his mind. He becomes *mochel*: he forgives, or withdraws, his warning. Can the *kinuy* be revoked?

The Gemara frames the question around the phrase *tala Rachmana*, which now applies literally, since we are dealing with the *sotah* case: *kinuy* is rooted in the husband's jealousy and *hakpada*. One side says: since it was all driven by his objection, and he has now stopped objecting, the *kinuy* dissolves — *kinuyo machul*. The other side says: once he has created this formal legal act, he cannot simply retract it — *lo matzi machil leh*. This second position may be grounded in the idea that the *kinuy* is not merely the expression of a subjective emotional state but the invocation of a formal legal process that, once set in motion, operates independently of whether he continues to feel aggrieved.

More substantively, one can frame this as a question about what the *kinuy* fundamentally is. At the beginning of the *masechet*, this tension was already present: is *sotah* all about the husband's jealousy and *hakpada*, an outgrowth of the subjective dynamics of the marriage, or has the Gemara transformed it into an objective legal proceeding driven by *raglayim ladavar* and the involvement of *beis din*? If the former, then when he stops being jealous, the whole structure collapses. If the latter, then the process, once initiated, belongs to an objective domain and is no longer his to withdraw.

### Revoke After Stira?

The Gemara then raises the more challenging case: can the husband revoke his *kinuy* even after the wife has gone into seclusion — after *stirah* has occurred? At that point she has already become a *sotah*. He now says: I retroactively retract my *kinuy*. Can he do this?

The stakes of this question are high. If revocation is possible even after *stirah*, then the entire *sotah* process is ultimately dependent on the husband's ongoing willingness to pursue it, and the objective legal reality established by *stirah* counts for little. If revocation is not possible after *stirah*, then the moment she enters seclusion, the case passes from the subjective realm of his jealousy into the objective domain of *beis din*, and his feelings at that point become legally irrelevant.

The Gemara attempts several proofs.
