And now Rabbi Yehoshua ben Horkenos — a student of your student, your halachic grandchild — has demonstrated that it was love all along. *V'halo Yehoshua talmid talmidecha limed she-me-ahavah asa* — look at what your student's student has taught. Even in disagreement with the master, the student vindicates the deepest aspiration: that Torah be clarified, and that its most profound truths come to light.

---

---

# Sotah 28

## Identity of Him

### Who is "Him"?

The *mishnah* with which we conclude the fifth *perek* opens with two parallel principles: just as the waters check her, they check him, and just as she is forbidden to the husband, she is forbidden to the adulterer. Before proceeding further, the *Gemara* pauses to ask a basic question: when the *mishnah* says the waters check *otoh* — him — who exactly is "him"? There are two candidates: the husband (*ba'al*) or the adulterer (*bo'el*).

### Waters Check Both

The *Gemara* raises the possibility that the waters check the husband. But what would the husband have done wrong? The *Gemara* considers that perhaps the husband himself sinned — for example, by sleeping with his wife after she had already acquired the status of a *sotah*, thereby rendering that act of intercourse forbidden. The *Gemara* immediately rejects this: if the husband is not free of sexual sin, the waters do not merely fail to check him — they fail to check *her* as well. The *baraita* is explicit: *venikah ish me'avon vehishah hahi tisa et avonah* — the man will be clean of sin and the woman will bear her sin. *Bizman she'ish menukah me'avon*, when he is clean of that specific sin, the waters are effective. If he is not, the waters are effective for neither of them. So the waters cannot be "checking him" in any sense that's useful — if he has sinned, nothing gets checked at all. The *otoh* must therefore refer to the *bo'el*, the man she is suspected of having had relations with.

### Parallel Language

This raises a stylistic difficulty. If the *mishnah* intends the *bo'el*, why not name him as such? Later in the very same *mishnah*, when it says she is forbidden to the husband just as she is forbidden to the adulterer — *keshem she'asurah laba'al kakh asurah labo'el* — the *mishnah* uses the explicit term *bo'el*. So why say *otoh* in the first clause instead of *bo'el*?

The *Gemara* resolves this elegantly: *reisha aidei detana otah tana otoh* — because the opening clause describes what happens to *her*, using the word *otah*, the natural parallel is *otoh*. The linguistic symmetry of *otah/otoh* dictates the phrasing. In the second clause, where the *mishnah* introduces the word *ba'al* for the husband, the natural parallel becomes *bo'el*. The parallel pairs are *otah/otoh* and *ba'al/bo'el* — and in both cases, the referent is the same man: the one she is suspected of having had relations with.

### Yerushalmi & Gematria

*Tosafot* on 27b quotes a *Yerushalmi* that develops this theme richly, and it is worth pausing over because the *Bavli* itself contains no parallel discussion. The *Yerushalmi* in the name of Rav Tanchuma observes that the *gematria* of *hamar'arim* — the cursed waters — equals 248 times two, corresponding to the 248 limbs in his body and the 248 limbs in her body: *minyan hamar'arim neged remach evarim sheyesh bo veneged remach evarim sheyesh bah*. The word *mar'arim* contains a *resh-mem-resh-mem* for 240, and the remaining letters bring the total to 480 — that is, 248 doubled. The waters thus symbolically destroy two complete bodies, his and hers.

The *Yerushalmi* then adds a further and striking observation: the waters check her for every act of forbidden intercourse she receives from her husband after she has slept with the *bo'el* — *keshem shemayim bodkin otah al kol biah shehi mekabeles miba'alah le'achar habo'el kakh heim bodkin otoh*. This is surprising on multiple levels. First, it implies that the waters' effect is not a single event but cumulative, potentially multiplying across repeated violations. Second, it implies that the *bo'el* is held responsible not only for his own act but for the cascade of forbidden acts that follow from it — her subsequent, now-prohibited intercourse with her husband. He is punished, as it were, for her sins that occur after his sin, because he is the root cause of all that follows.

This also challenges a common assumption — that the *sotah* waters simply kill the guilty woman. The *Yerushalmi* pictures something more complex: an ongoing, iterative consequence that unfolds over time.

The *Yerushalmi* then addresses the legal logic of why her status works through her: *lo eshet amisecha lo sitein shichavsecha lezara litam'ah bah* — you make yourself *tamei* through *her*. Her status is the operative one. *Im haysa mezidah asurah, shogeges muteres* — if she was fully intentional, she is forbidden; if she was unwitting, she may be permitted to her husband.

---

## Forbidden Status Effects

### Brother Restriction

The *Yerushalmi* adds another striking consequence: *ukhshem she'asurah le'achiv shel ba'al kakh asurah le'achiv shel bo'el* — just as she is forbidden to the *ba'al's* brother (in the case of *yibum*), so too she is forbidden to the *bo'el's* brother. The case of the husband's brother is understandable: the marriage has been compromised, and therefore the *mitzvah* of *yibum*, which depends on the legitimacy of that marriage, can no longer apply. But that she is forbidden to the *bo'el's* brother is far more difficult to understand. What is the mechanism? What logic connects her status to the family of the man she is suspected of having sinned with?

One might suggest — and this is an appealing idea — that the concern is a practical one: if she were permitted to marry the *bo'el's* brother and then that brother died, the result would be a *yibum* obligation with the *bo'el* himself, to whom she is forbidden. We thus preemptively prohibit the marriage to the brother in order to foreclose that possibility. That would at least offer a functional rationale, even if the prohibition seems unusual at first glance.

### Status Works Through Her

The underlying principle that emerges from the *Yerushalmi* is that her status is entirely operative through her, not through the man. A man who commits adultery with a married woman does not change his own personal status. So if the suspected man actually committed adultery not with her but with some other woman, the waters will not affect him when she drinks, because it all passes through her. The principle is: *bah hadavar talui* — it is all dependent on her.

---

## Asymmetrical Outcomes

### Him Affected Only

The *Gemara* now considers an unusual scenario: what if she drinks the waters and he is affected but she is not? The immediate explanation offered is *zechus toleh* — merit. She must have done it, since otherwise the *bo'el* would not have been affected. But her merit delayed or concealed the impact on her. This explains the phenomenon, but only according to the view that merit prevents the waters from showing any visible effect. If she is definitely guilty but her merit shields her temporarily, yet the *bo'el* had no such merit, then he is affected and she appears unaffected.

### Intentional/Unwitting

But this explanation fails according to the view that even when merit protects someone, the effect is nonetheless visible — the person begins to deteriorate, even if slowly. Under that view, if she showed no sign whatsoever, the *zechus* explanation is insufficient.

The *Gemara* then considers and rejects the possibility that he drank contaminated water (*mayim megulim*) independently — the effects of snake venom do not replicate the specific physiological signs of the *sotah* waters, namely the belly swelling and the thigh collapsing.

The *Gemara* ultimately resolves the case: *she'hayah hu mazid vehee shoggeget* — he was intentional, she was unwitting. He knew he was sleeping with a married woman; she, through some unusual circumstance, did not — perhaps she mistook him for her husband. According to *Rashi*, the paradigmatic case of *shogeg* for the *sotah* is exactly this: both parties thought they were sleeping with their own spouses. Because she was *shogegget*, the waters do not affect her. Because he was *mazid*, he is affected.

One must ask: what exactly constitutes *shogeg* in the context of adultery? The *Gemara* and *Rashi* define it narrowly — she must have genuinely believed the man was her husband. This is far more restrictive than simply believing the act was permitted. A famous responsum addresses a case where a woman was told by a man claiming to be Elijah the Prophet that sleeping with him would bring the *Mashiach*, and she believed him. The *posek* ruled she was not considered *shogegget*, because she knew she was transgressing against her husband — the only valid *shogeg* is genuinely mistaking the man for one's spouse.

### Her Affected Only

The *Gemara* then considers the reverse: she is affected by the waters but he is not. The immediate explanation is again *zechus* — his merit prevented the waters from affecting him. This works according to the view that merit shields someone entirely, but fails according to the view that merit still allows visible deterioration. Contaminated water is again raised as an alternative explanation and again rejected for the same reason.

The simplest explanation is that she committed adultery with a different man altogether — *ela ani omer im acher nistarah* — and the man we suspected is innocent. That accounts for why he was unaffected.

### Marriage Question

If he was truly unaffected because he was not the adulterer, might she now be permitted to him if she is divorced? The *Gemara* says no: *tifater she'hayah hu shogeg vehee mezidah* — we must entertain the possibility that he was the adulterer but was *shogeg* while she was *mezidah*. Since he was *shogeg*, the waters did not affect him. But since she was *mezidah*, she remains forbidden to him. We cannot read his non-reaction as proof of innocence.

### Four Cases Summary

The *Gemara* now systematically works through all four combinations of intentionality. If he was *mazid* and she was *shogegget*: the waters affect him, not her; she is permitted to continue living with her husband. If he was *shogeg* and she was *mezidah*: the waters affect her, not him; she is forbidden to her husband, and she cannot go and be with the *bo'el* — *efshar lomar yatza mitachas yado vehayeta le'ish acher*, could it be that she divorces from her husband on account of her adultery and then goes to live with the very man she committed adultery with? The answer is no. If he was *mazid* and she was *mezidah*: both are fully affected. If he was *shogeg* and she was *shogegget*: perhaps neither is affected, and theoretically those two might end up together — although this is a deeply unusual case.

The operative principle in all of this: she cannot become permitted to the *bo'el* as long as one of them was *mazid*. The only scenario in which they could perhaps eventually be together is if neither had any intentional culpability.

---

## Source from Verses

### Vav or Repetition

Returning to the *Bavli* proper, the *Gemara* at the top of 28a takes up the question of the *drashot* underlying the *mishnah's* opening clause. The waters are described in the *Torah* text using the word *ba'u* — they shall enter — and this word appears three times in the relevant *parsha*. Moreover, in two of those appearances, the word is prefaced by a *vav*, giving *uva'u*. The question: is the *drasha* that the waters affect the *bo'el* derived from the extra *vav* (i.e., *uva'u* rather than *ba'u*), or from the repetition of the entire word *ba'u* itself?

The *Gemara* attempts to resolve this from the second clause of the *mishnah* — *nitme'ah venitme'ah* — where similarly a word appears with and without a *vav*. But the *Gemara* notes that the same question applies there as well, so it cannot resolve our question from that source.

The resolution comes from the explicit statement of *Rebbi* later in the *mishnah*, who says *shenei pe'amim* — twice, i.e., the derivation is from the repetition of the word itself, not from the extra *vav*. From this we infer by contrast that *Rabbi Akiva* — the one from whose position *Rebbi* is departing — does indeed derive *drashot* from the extra *vav*. This is consistent with Rabbi Akiva's well-known method of deriving meaning from every additional letter in the text, a method he received from Nachum Ish Gamzu.

### Six Instances Explained

According to Rabbi Akiva, then, there are effectively six textual units requiring explanation: the three appearances of *ba'u* and the three accompanying *vav*s — *shita krai ketivei*. Each pair of units — one for her and one for him — teaches something distinct about the manner in which the waters operate.

### Tzava, Asiyah, Yedia

The three categories are *tzava*, *asiyah*, and *yedia*. The *tzava* is where the *pasuk* issues a divine declaration, as it were, dictating what the waters will do — *uvau hamayim hamarerim litzvot beten* — this is the moment of commanding or establishing the reality of what the waters accomplish. The *asiyah* is where the *pasuk* describes what actually happens in practice — the water enters and her belly swells. The *yedia* is where the *kohen* informs her explicitly what she should expect.

The *yedia* carries a specific legal significance. There is an apparent contradiction in the *psukim* about the order in which the waters take effect. In one place, the *Torah* speaks of the thigh collapsing first, then the belly swelling — which corresponds to the anatomical sequence of the act of relations, progressing downward. But when the waters actually take effect, the belly is affected first, because that is the order in which the water physically enters the body. The *kohen* must inform her of this discrepancy explicitly, so that she does not think the waters failed to work because they did not proceed in the order she expected. The pair of *vav*s attached to each of these three categories indicates that the same framework — command, action, and informing — applies equally to the *bo'el*.

### Three Instances

*Rebbi* disagrees. He does not derive *drashot* from extra *vav*s — *tlata krai ketivei*, there are simply three instances of the word *ba'u*, one for each of the three categories: *tzava*, *asiyah*, and *yedia*. Under this approach, since every appearance of the word *ba'u* is already needed for those three contexts, how does *Rebbi* know that the waters affect the *bo'el* at all?

The *Gemara* answers: from the phrase *litzvot beten velanpil yarech* — to cause a swelling of the belly and a collapsing of the thigh — where the *Torah* does not use the feminine possessive. Elsewhere the *Torah* says *vetzavtah betnah venaphlah yerechah* — her belly and her thigh, with the female possessive. Since that verse already covers her belly and her thigh, the earlier, unpossessed phrase is redundant if applied to her. Its purpose must therefore be to indicate that his belly and his thigh will also collapse — *betno veyerecho shebo'el*.

Rabbi Akiva can then respond: according to him, the unpossessed phrase serves a different purpose — it is the *yedia*, the *kohen*'s informing her of the order of effects (belly first, then thigh). *Rebbi* counters: if that were all, the *Torah* would have simply written *betnah verechah*, with the female possessive. The deliberately generic phrasing signals that two things are being taught simultaneously: first, the order of effects for her, and second — by virtue of the absence of the feminine possessive — that the same effects apply to him.

---

## Three Consequences

### Rabbi Akiva's View

The *Gemara* now cites a *baraita* addressing the word *nitme'ah*, which appears three times in the *parsha*. According to Rabbi Akiva, each appearance teaches a distinct consequence of her *tum'ah* status. The first: she is forbidden to her husband. The second: she is forbidden to the *bo'el*. The third: *echad litrumah* — she is disqualified from eating *terumah*. If she is the wife of a *kohen*, or even a *bat kohen*, her status has been so fundamentally compromised that she may no longer partake of *terumah*. *Divrei Rabbi Akiva.*

### Kal Vachomer

Rabbi Yishmael responds with a *kal vachomer* that derives a fourth consequence. There exist women who are forbidden to marry a *kohen* — such as a *grushah* — and yet who may still eat *terumah* as daughters of *kohanim*. These women have a compromised marital status relative to *kehunah* but retain their *terumah* rights through their lineage. Now: if this *sotah* woman cannot even eat *terumah* — as Rabbi Akiva derives — *eino din she'asurah likhehunah*? How much more so must she be forbidden to marry a *kohen* altogether? This is not a disagreement with Rabbi Akiva but an extension: Rabbi Yishmael adds a fourth *halacha* using the existing three as a springboard.

The practical significance of this point is noteworthy. *Rashi* clarifies: *afilu hi bat kohen uba'alah kohen, nifselah min haterumah* — even if she is herself the daughter of a *kohen* and her husband is also a *kohen*, she is disqualified from *terumah*. This is not merely a consequence of the marital relationship being compromised; it affects her personal status as a *bat kohen*. So even if her husband dies and the marital basis for eating *terumah* is gone, she remains disqualified on the basis of her own defiled status. That is precisely what gives Rabbi Yishmael's *kal vachomer* its force: since even her personal status as a *bat kohen* has been overridden by her *sotah* status, certainly she cannot now marry a *kohen*.

---

## Presumed Guilty Status

### Why Repetition?

The *Gemara* then poses a sharp question: given that the *Torah* itself repeatedly acknowledges uncertainty — describing both the case where she became *nitme'ah* and the case where she did not — why does it use the word *nitme'ah* repeatedly as though her guilt were established? *Im nitme'ah lamah shoseh? Ve'im lo nitme'ah lamah mashkeh?* If she is definitely guilty, why go through the process? And if she is innocent, on what basis does the husband have the right to subject her to it?

### Definitely Forbidden

The answer is that the *Torah* is telling us something precise: *magid lecha hakatuv shehasafek asurah* — she is forbidden by virtue of the doubt alone. The repeated use of *nitme'ah* is not a declaration of certain guilt; it is a declaration that the *safek* itself confers a definite forbidden status. She is *vadai asurah* not because we know she sinned, but because the formal process of *kinui* and *stirah* — warning and seclusion — has created an objective status of *issur* that persists until resolved.

This is a remarkable *chiddush*. The normal approach to a *safek* in *halacha* is either to be stringent as a precautionary measure or to permit on the basis of a *chazakah*. What is unusual about the *sotah* is that the *safek* itself — independent of any probability assessment — creates a *vadai* prohibition. She knows whether she sinned or not. She could be entirely innocent. And yet, the moment she formally becomes a *sotah* through the required legal process, she is objectively and certainly forbidden to sleep with her husband. This is not merely "we are being cautious because we don't know." It is a real, positive *issur*.

### Issur Asei Nature

*Tosafot* develops this point carefully. The question is raised: why does the Torah need to establish this special status at all? A *safek* of adultery would presumably be *assur* anyway on general principles. The obvious answer is that she herself knows the truth — but *Tosafot* presses further.

*Tosafot* notes that the *issur* here is an *issur asei* — a prohibition derived from a positive formulation. The *Torah* does not say "do not sleep with your husband"; it describes her as *tamei*. The operative prohibition flows from that status: *venitme'ah* — she is *tamei*, and therefore sleeping with her husband violates the status that has been declared. This is structurally similar to other cases of *issur asei*, such as the derivation that consuming human flesh is prohibited through the positive command *kol beheima tehorah tocheilu* — since human flesh is not a *beheima tehorah*, consuming it violates that positive imperative implicitly.

The consequence is significant: *afilu hi tehorah ne'eneshes b'veis din shel ma'alah im ba'alah k'chayvei asei* — even if she is entirely innocent of adultery, if she sleeps with her husband while she formally holds the status of a *sotah*, she has violated an *issur asei*, and she will be held accountable before the heavenly court together with her husband. The waters clearing her do not retroactively permit what was done while she held the *sotah* status. The prohibition is real and present from the moment the status attaches.

---

## Safek Tumah Principle

### Comparison to Sheretz

From the principle that the *sotah's* doubtful status creates a definite *issur*, the *Gemara* extrapolates to general laws of *tum'ah*. *Mikhan attah dan lesheretz* — from here you can derive the rules governing *safek tum'ah* for ordinary *tumah* cases such as contact with a *sheretz*.

The *kal vachomer* proceeds as follows. By a *sotah*, we do not treat *shogeg* as equivalent to *mazid*, and we do not treat *ones* as equivalent to *ratzon* — that is, involuntary exposure does not make her a *sotah*. Yet despite this, *asah bah safek kevadai* — the doubt is treated as certainty. By a *sheretz*, in contrast, the law makes no distinction at all between *shogeg* and *mazid* or between *ones* and *ratzon* — any contact creates *tum'ah* regardless of intent. Therefore, how much more so should a *safek* contact with a *sheretz* be treated as *vadai tum'ah*?

This is the source for the principle of *safek tum'ah bireshut hayachid safeko tamei* — a doubtful *tum'ah* in a private domain is treated as *tamei*.

### Private Domain

The *Gemara* then applies the parameters of the *sotah* case to define when this rule operates. *Umah sotah reshut hayachid af sheretz reshut hayachid* — just as the *sotah* situation involves a *reshut hayachid*, the *safek tum'ah* rule applies only in a *reshut hayachid*, not in a *reshut harabbim*. One might immediately note that *seclusion* and *reshut hayachid* are not identical concepts. The definition of *reshut hayachid* for purposes of *safek tum'ah* is not the same as the Shabbat definition. It has more to do with the degree of privacy and the question of who was present and capable of observing what occurred.

### Kinui & Sitrah

*Tosafot* raises a pointed question about the comparison. By a *sotah*, the reason we treat the doubt as a definite *issur* is that there are *raglayim ladavar* — circumstantial grounds for suspicion: there was a *kinui* (warning) and a *stirah* (seclusion in defiance of that warning). By a simple *safek tum'ah* case — did the *sheretz* touch the food or not? — there are no such grounds. How can the comparison hold?

*Tosafot* answers by reframing the role of *kinui* and *stirah* in the *sotah* case. The *kinui* and *stirah* do not establish that it is *likely* she committed adultery — they merely elevate the situation from irrelevant seclusion to a genuine *safek*. Without *kinui*, a woman going into seclusion with a man would not constitute a *safek* at all, because we operate with a *chezkas kashrus* — a presumption of propriety. We do not assume that every private encounter involves adultery. The *kinui* strips away that presumption and converts the situation into a genuine 50-50 *safek*. Once it is a genuine 50-50 *safek*, it is comparable to a simple *safek* of whether the *sheretz* touched the food. The *raglayim ladavar* do not tip the balance toward guilt; they merely create the *safek* in the first place.

### Knowledge Requirement

The second parameter derived from *sotah*: *umah sotah davar sheyesh bo da'at lisha'el* — the *sotah* situation is one in which someone could in principle be asked what happened, namely the woman herself. Therefore, *af sheretz davar sheyesh bo da'at lisha'el* — the rule of *safek tum'ah bireshut hayachid* applies only where there is someone present who could have knowledge of what occurred.

Why should this matter? One approach is that the function of treating the *safek* as a *vadai issur* is to force the matter toward resolution. If someone is present who knows what happened, declaring the situation *tamei* creates pressure for that knowledge to surface. If no one could possibly know, the declaration of *tum'ah* serves no such clarifying function. This is also why *reshut harabbim* tends toward *tahor* — not simply because many people were present, but paradoxically because in a very public setting, no one specific individual can be said to have observed what occurred. It is the intermediate case — a few people present, one of whom could know — that triggers the rule.

*Tosafot* notes an application of this principle to the case of a woman with a doubtful *niddah* status when others were present: even if people were nearby, they could not observe anything about her internal status. The "someone who could be asked" must be someone with actual epistemic access to the relevant facts.

### Final Rule

The *Gemara* concludes with the fully articulated rule: *davar sheyesh bo da'at lisha'el bireshut hayachid safeko tamei* — if someone could be asked and the event occurred in a private domain, the *safek* is treated as *tamei*. *Bireshut harabbim safeko tahor* — if it occurred in a public domain, the *safek* is treated as *tahor*. *Veshein bo da'at lisha'el, bein bireshut hayachid uvein bireshut harabbim, safeko tahor* — and if there is no one who could be asked, whether in a private or public domain, the *safek* is *tahor*.

---

---

# Sotah 29

## Sotah & Safek Tumah

### Intro: Sotah to Terumah

Today's daf is 29, and we pick up at the bottom of 28b. The sugya has now transitioned from *sotah* to *terumah* — which, somewhat surprisingly, will be the focus of this entire daf. The immediate reason for the shift is not primarily the connection between *sotah* and *terumah* as such, but rather that our *mishnah* of this *perek* recorded a series of *drashos* under the heading *bo bayom darash Rabbi Akiva*, several of which concern *tumah*, and it is those *drashos* that will occupy us.

The original connection was that from the case of *sotah* — a wife who secluded herself (*yichud*) with another man after her husband's formal warning — we derived the broader principle governing *safek tumah bereshut hayachid*. The *sotah's* status demonstrates that once the relevant circumstances are established, the presumption shifts: she is treated as definitively forbidden rather than merely doubtfully so.

### Sotah Status & Tosafos

The *halacha* is that a *sotah* is *vadai assur* — definitively forbidden — on the basis of the *safek*. This status holds until it is clarified through the formal procedure of drinking the bitter water. *Tosafos* draws out an important implication: even if it later becomes clear that she had not in fact committed adultery, or even if she herself knows she has not, the violation of her current status — such as sleeping with her husband before the matter is resolved — constitutes a genuine transgression. Her situation is one of definitive prohibition, not merely doubtful prohibition.

### Safek Tumah Principle

From this, the Gemara derives the general principle of *safek tumah bereshut hayachid*. The language of *tumah* in the *sotah* context carries its own specific meaning, but the transfer to the general laws of *tumah* throughout the Torah is significant. The conditions are formal and precise: the doubt must arise in a *reshut hayachid*, a private domain, and there must be *yesh bo da'at lisha'el* — someone present who is capable of being asked about the circumstances.

One way of understanding why the *safek* generates *vadai tumah* is that treating the matter as definitively impure, pending clarification, creates incentive for resolution: witnesses may come forward, participants may remember. This social function, however, only makes sense when there is actually someone present who might know something — hence the requirement of *yesh bo da'at lisha'el*. If no one is present who could be questioned, *ein bo da'at lisha'el*, then even in a private domain the doubt is resolved leniently as *tahor*.

### Kinuy & Stira Model

*Tosafos* raises a pointed question about the analogy between *sotah* and *safek tumah*. In the case of ordinary *tumah*, the doubt is a straightforward fifty-fifty uncertainty. By contrast, the *sotah* case seems to involve *raglayim ladavar* — circumstantial indicators suggesting guilt — and not a mere equipoise. Where, then, is the fifty-fifty doubt?

*Tosafos* introduces a crucial conceptual framework in response. The *kinuy* (the husband's formal warning) and *stira* (the subsequent seclusion) together produce a fifty-fifty doubt. Without them, the situation would not even qualify as a genuine *safek* in the first place. The *kinuy* and *stira* are thus not evidence of guilt; they are the precondition that elevates the situation to the status of a doubt worth taking seriously. This is an important lens through which to understand the *sotah* institution, and one that had not been fully foregrounded in earlier discussion.

It should also be noted that *reshut hayachid* in this context does not carry its Shabbos meaning. Here it refers more to a private location, and the determination is functional rather than spatial.

### Three Restrictions

To close the introductory survey, the Gemara recaps the three restrictions the *sotah* incurs from the word *venitma'ah*: she is forbidden to her *ba'al* (her husband), forbidden to the *bo'el* (the suspected adulterer), and forbidden to eat *terumah*. The last applies whether she is the wife of a *kohen* — in which case her marital status no longer entitles her to *terumah* — or a *bat kohen* herself, in which case this act is understood to invalidate her personal entitlement as well. It is worth noting, as was observed in discussion, that while her husband's financial obligations toward her presumably continue during the pendency of the process, the prohibition from *terumah* takes immediate effect.

---

## R. Akiva vs. R. Yishmael

### R. Yishmael's Kal VaChom…

Rabbi Yishmael, responding to Rabbi Akiva's derivation of *terumah* from *venitma'ah*, proposes a *kal vachomer*: if there exist women who are forbidden to marry a *kohen* yet are still permitted to eat *terumah* — such as a *gerushah* who is a *bat kohen* — then a woman who cannot eat *terumah* at all should certainly be forbidden from marrying a *kohen*. The scenario being contemplated is where this woman's husband subsequently dies; her status as a presumed adulteress or as a *sotah* should, by this logic, render her permanently forbidden to a *kohen* just as a *zonah* is.

Rabbi Akiva's position, as introduced in the *mishnah*, had been that she is forbidden to the *ba'al*, forbidden to the *bo'el*, and forbidden to eat *terumah* — three distinct restrictions, each derived from a separate word or letter. The Gemara now examines whether Rabbi Yishmael's *kal vachomer* was meant as an addition to Rabbi Akiva's teaching or as a disagreement with it.

### Gemara's Challenge

The Gemara raises a sharp challenge: according to Rabbi Akiva, where does the prohibition of *kehunah* come from? And if Rabbi Akiva would say he simply does not need a *pasuk* for *kehunah* — because a woman who commits adultery acquires the status of a *zonah*, and since we treat *safek* like *vadai* we would say *safek zonah ke-zonah*, rendering her forbidden to a *kohen* automatically — then the same argument should equally spare him the need for a *pasuk* regarding *terumah*. The prohibition of a *zonah* from *terumah* is already established by the verse *u'vat kohen ki tihyeh le-ish zar hi betrumas hakodashim lo tochel*, which Rabbi Akiva interprets to cover a woman who has relations with a man forbidden to her. So why would he need a separate *pasuk* to tell him she is forbidden to *terumah*?

This is a tight and well-constructed challenge: if the logic of *zonah* status can do the work for *kehunah*, it should equally do the work for *terumah*, leaving Rabbi Akiva's three *venitma'ah* derivations without adequate content.

### Akiva's Four Pesukim

The Gemara resolves the difficulty by noting that according to Rabbi Akiva there are in fact four textual indicators, not three. The word *venitma'ah* appears three times in the *sotah* section, but one of the instances is preceded by a *vav* that Rabbi Akiva treats as generating an additional derivation. So we have three *venitma'ahs* plus one *vav* — four sources in total. One teaches that she is forbidden to her *ba'al*, one that she is forbidden to the *bo'el*, one that she is forbidden to *terumah*, and one — derived from the extra *vav* — that she is forbidden in *kehunah*.

The need for the *kehunah* derivation from the *vav* is that we cannot simply assume her status as a *zonah* provides it. Evidently Rabbi Akiva holds that a woman in the uncertain status of *sotah* does not automatically become a *zonah* in a way that would independently establish all the attendant restrictions. Hence the *pasuk* must supply the *kehunah* prohibition explicitly.

### Yishmael's Three + Logic

Rabbi Yishmael, by contrast, does not derive from the extra *vav*. He therefore has only three *venitma'ahs*: one for *ba'al*, one for *bo'el*, and one for *terumah*. From *terumah* he then constructs a *kal vachomer* to *kehunah*: since she is forbidden from eating *terumah*, she should certainly be forbidden from marrying a *kohen*.

### Relevance Framework

The Gemara presses: how does Rabbi Yishmael know that the third *venitma'ah* teaches *terumah* rather than *kehunah*? One could argue the reverse — that the third *venitma'ah* establishes the prohibition of *kehunah*, and that *terumah* would then be permitted, since we know there are women forbidden to marry a *kohen* who nevertheless retain the right to eat *terumah* (a *gerushah bat kohen* being the paradigm case).

Rabbi Yishmael's response is elegant: the third *venitma'ah* should be read in parallel with the first two. What do the first two establish? Prohibitions that take effect *m'chayim* — while everyone is still alive: she is forbidden to her husband and to the suspected adulterer here and now. A prohibition of *terumah* similarly applies immediately: she is a *bat kohen*, say, and she loses her right to eat *terumah* at this moment. A prohibition of *kehunah*, by contrast, only becomes relevant if her husband dies — only then would the question of whether she may marry another *kohen* arise. Rabbi Yishmael therefore concludes that the third *venitma'ah* must be targeting the immediately applicable prohibition, which is *terumah*, and *kehunah* is then derived by *kal vachomer*.

### Akiva Rejects Dumiya

Rabbi Akiva does not accept this framework of *dumya de-ba'al u-vo'el* — the comparison that presumes the third *venitma'ah* must, like the first two, address something immediately applicable. In his view, the third *venitma'ah* might well teach the lesser *chiddush*, namely the prohibition of *kehunah*, which applies only post-mortem, while *terumah* would remain unknown without an additional source. That is why he requires the extra *vav* — to capture *kehunah* — while dedicating the third *venitma'ah* to *terumah*.

### Redundancy Principle

Alternatively, the Gemara suggests, Rabbi Akiva might agree that in principle a *kal vachomer* could yield the *kehunah* prohibition, but he nonetheless uses the *vav* to state it explicitly. The principle invoked is *milsa d'asi b'kal vachomer tarach v'kasav lah kra*: something that could have been derived logically, the Torah nevertheless troubled itself to write explicitly.

This principle stands in interesting tension with the Gemara's occasional declaration elsewhere of *lama li kra, sevara hi* — why do I need a *pasuk*, I could figure it out myself? That formulation reflects the remarkable weight accorded to human reason and *sevara* in the tradition of *Torah she-be'al peh*, to the point that a verse can be set aside or interpreted non-literally when it conflicts with what logic demands. The flip side, captured by *milsa d'asi b'kal vachomer tarach v'kasav lah kra*, is that this same rational force does not make a scriptural reaffirmation unwelcome or superfluous. It is not a problem for the Torah to state explicitly what one could have derived — the two sources are not in conflict, they simply converge on the same conclusion from different directions.

---

## Safek Tumah from Korban

### Safek Tumah Rules

Rav Gidal said in the name of Rav: the rule that *davar she-yesh bo da'at lisha'el* in a *reshut hayachid* yields *safek tamei*, while *ein bo da'at lisha'el* yields *safek tahor* regardless of domain — this rule is not derived primarily from *sotah*. It is derived from a different *pasuk* entirely.

### Korban Meat Source

The source is the verse *ve-habasar asher yiga b'chol tamei lo ye'achel* — meat of a *korban* that touches anything *tamei* may not be eaten. The Gemara reads this carefully: *vadai tamei hu de-lo ye'achel* — it is only if it is definitively known to be *tamei* that it may not be eaten; if there is doubt, *ha-safek tamei safek tahor*, it may be eaten.

### Safek Tahor Logic

This reading, however, creates an apparent contradiction. The end of the verse states *kol tahor yochal basar* — whoever is *tahor* may eat the meat — from which one might derive that it is only when one is definitively *tahor* that eating is permitted, and that *safek tamei* is therefore forbidden. The beginning of the verse seems to teach *safek tahor* while the end teaches *safek tamei*. The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between contexts: one clause addresses the case where no person is on the scene — only the object, *ein bo da'at lisha'el* — and the doubt about the meat itself is resolved leniently; the other clause addresses the case where a person is present, *yesh bo da'at lisha'el*, and in that case doubt is resolved strictly.

One might have proposed a different distinction — that the beginning of the verse speaks about doubt concerning the meat and the end about doubt concerning the person — but the Gemara does not adopt this reading. The determining factor is not which party is in doubt but whether anyone capable of being consulted is present in the situation at all.

### Domain Distinction

If one had only this *pasuk* from *korban* meat, one might have concluded that the *yesh bo da'at* / *ein bo da'at* distinction applies equally regardless of whether the incident occurred in a public or private domain. It is the *sotah* case that teaches the additional variable of *reshut hayachid* versus *reshut harabbim*.

### Two Sources Combined

Conversely, if one had only the *sotah* model, one might have concluded that *safek tumah* in a *reshut hayachid* requires *da'at* on the part of both parties — the one who touches and the one who is touched — since in *sotah* both the man and the woman are present and aware of the circumstances. By *sotah* alone, one might limit the strict ruling to cases where both the *tamei* and *tahor* parties have *da'at*, making the rule inapplicable when, for instance, a rodent touches an object with no human witness. It is the *korban* meat *pasuk* that teaches the rule requires only that some person be on the scene who is capable of being asked — not that both parties to the contact must have *da'at*.

Both sources are therefore necessary: *sotah* supplies the *reshut hayachid* dimension, and the *korban* meat verse supplies the *da'at* principle in its correct formulation.

---

## Shlishi LeTerumah

### R. Yehoshua's Challenge

The Gemara returns to the *mishnah*, where Rabbi Akiva's *bo bayom* teachings include a derivation from the *pasuk* of *kli cheres*: *kol asher betocho yitma* — anything inside an earthenware vessel contaminated by a *sheretz* becomes *tamei*. Rabbi Akiva's *drasha* of *yitma* — reading it as *yitamei*, meaning it has the capacity to further transmit *tumah* — establishes that food can become a *shlishi*, a third-degree derivative of *tumah*, with respect to *terumah*.

Rabbi Yehoshua's famous reaction was: *mi gala afar me'einecha, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai?* — "Who removed the dust from your eyes, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai?" The comment is pointed: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai had taught that the concept of *shlishi biterumah* rests only on a *kal vachomer*, not on an explicit *pasuk*. Rabbi Akiva's derivation demonstrated that it has a scriptural basis after all, sparing it from challenge. The remark comes in appreciation — the earlier master had said we must acknowledge the weakness of the derivation, and the later master has now shored it up.

### Pre-Akiva Status

This leads the Gemara to ask: if before Rabbi Akiva there was no *pasuk*, why did everyone nonetheless assume that food could become a *shlishi* with respect to *terumah*? Why was it treated as *tamei* without scriptural warrant?

### Rav Yehuda's Explanation

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: although there was no explicit *pasuk*, there is nevertheless a *din kal vachomer* — the concept of *shlishi* for *terumah* can be derived logically. The *halacha* was assumed based on this *kal vachomer* even before Rabbi Akiva supplied the *pasuk*.

### Tevul Yom Kal VaChomer

The *kal vachomer* proceeds as follows: a *tevul yom* — a person who has immersed in a *mikvah* but for whom sunset has not yet arrived — is *mutar b'chullin*, permitted with respect to non-sanctified food, meaning he is not considered *tamei* in a way that would compromise ordinary *chullin*. Yet *poseil bitrumah* — he invalidates *terumah* that he touches. Now, a *kikar sheini* — a loaf of bread that is a second-degree derivative of *tumah* — is itself *pasul b'chullin*, meaning it already creates a problem even at the level of non-sanctified food. Surely, then — *eino din sheyaaseh shlishi biterumah* — this loaf, which is already *tamei* with respect to *chullin*, should certainly be able to render *terumah* it touches *pasul* as a *shlishi*.

The structural logic of the *kal vachomer* calls for something that is *tahor* with respect to *chullin* yet invalidates *terumah*, from which we argue *a fortiori* that something *tamei* with respect to *chullin* should certainly invalidate *terumah*. The *tevul yom* approximates the first role — he does not disqualify *chullin* yet he cannot eat *terumah*. There is, however, an acknowledged imprecision in comparing a person to a loaf of bread, and one might equally observe that a *tevul yom* is not formally classified as a *sheini betu'mah*; his status is its own category of residual *tumah*. But that is the argument as it stands, and we proceed to examine where it can be challenged.

---

## Tzad HaShaVeh Analysis

### Avi HaTumah Objection

The *kal vachomer* is immediately open to challenge: *mah letevul yom she-kein avi hatumah*. The *tevul yom*'s residual *tumah* may seem weak, but it originated from something weightier. The person in question began as an *av hatumah* or at least a *rishon* — perhaps he was a *baal keri* who himself had the status of an *av hatumah*, or at minimum he had directly touched a *sheretz* and began as a *rishon*. The residual *tumah* of a person who started at a higher level may be more potent than the initial *tumah* of a *kikar sheini*, which never started above *sheini*. One cannot therefore conclude from the *tevul yom*'s power over *terumah* that a *sheini* of food equally has that power.

### Gemara's Middle Ground

The Gemara attempts to circumvent this objection by substituting a different *tevul yom*: *tevul yom de-sheretz*, a person who touched a *sheretz* and then immersed. Such a person was only a *rishon*, not an *av hatumah*, and his residual *tumah* after immersion started from a lower point. If even the residual *tumah* of someone who started only as a *rishon* is powerful enough to disqualify *terumah*, then the argument toward *sheini* of food should be stronger.

### Persons vs. Foods

But this middle ground still does not close the gap. *Mah letevul yom de-sheretz she-kein bemino avi hatumah* — even in the case of *tevul yom de-sheretz*, the *tumah* of persons belongs to a category that is intrinsically more potent, because a person is capable, at least in principle, of becoming an *av hatumah*. Food, by contrast, can never become an *av hatumah* no matter what it touches — even if food were to come into contact with a *meit*, it becomes a *rishon* at most, never an *av*. The *tumah* of persons may therefore be categorically weightier than the *tumah* of foods, and one cannot use residual personal *tumah* as a lever to prove anything about the initial *tumah* of a *sheini* in food. This distinction — that the category of personal *tumah* carries an intrinsic weight that food *tumah* does not, even before considering the actual degree — is striking and conceptually important.

### Combined Sources

Since the *kal vachomer* from *tevul yom* cannot stand alone, the Gemara introduces *kli cheres* as a second source and proposes learning from a *tzad hashaveh* — a common denominator between the two. The argument runs as follows: a *tevul yom* (a person with residual *tumah*) can invalidate *terumah*; a *kli cheres* that is a *rishon* (and which, like food, can never become an *av hatumah*) can invalidate *terumah*. Since we have two instances — one a person, one a vessel — we can extract what is common to both and argue that anything sharing that common feature should similarly invalidate *terumah*.

The *kli cheres* case is useful because it removes the objection about personal *tumah* being categorically weightier: *kli cheres* is not a person, it cannot become an *av hatumah*, and yet it invalidates *terumah*. Against this, one might note that *kli cheres* is a *rishon*, not a *sheini*, and its case involves *tumah me'aviro* — it transmits *tumah* even without direct contact through the airspace of the vessel — which is a distinctive stringency not found in the *tevul yom*. Hence neither source is free of distinctive characteristics.

### Weakness Eliminated

This is precisely the *chozar ha-din* dynamic: each of the two sources has characteristics that might explain its power over *terumah* that the other does not share, and neither characteristic is present in the *kikar sheini*. The argument oscillates between the two — one deflects the objection raised against the other — until we are left not with a true *kal vachomer* but with a *tzad hashaveh*.

### Common Denominator

The *tzad hashaveh*, as formulated by Rashi (who emends the text from *she-mutarin b'chullin* to *she-metammim*, since a *kli cheres* that is a *rishon* does in fact render *chullin* a *sheini*), is that both a *tevul yom* and a *kli cheres* are called *tamei* and both invalidate *terumah*. Anything that is called *tamei*, including a *kikar sheini*, should therefore invalidate *terumah*. This is the *tzad hashaveh*, and it is, as the Gemara notes, a weaker form of argument than the original *kal vachomer* — it is more analogical than deductive, resting on the extraction of a common property rather than on a strict hierarchy of stringency.

---

## Tzad Chamur Challenge

### Tzad Chamur Objection

The vulnerability of any *tzad hashaveh* is well known: it is always possible to object that the distinctive characteristics of the two source cases — rather than their common denominator — are what explain the *halacha* in each instance. If that is so, then the common denominator cannot carry the *halacha* to the new case. This is the *tzad chamur* challenge. In our case, the distinctive characteristics are: the *kli cheres* transmits *tumah* through airspace (*me'aviro*), which is a unique stringency; and the *tevul yom* either originated from a higher level of *tumah* or belongs to the categorically weightier domain of personal *tumah*. A *kikar sheini* has neither of these features, and one cannot therefore conclude from the *tzad hashaveh* that it invalidates *terumah*.

### Generational Challenge

This *tzad chamur* objection is what later generations raised against the derivation. The Gemara notes that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was apparently not troubled by this challenge — perhaps because raising a *tzad chamur* objection against every *tzad hashaveh* would effectively eliminate all such arguments from the tradition, which he was unwilling to do. But the later generation was not prepared to rest easy with a *tzad hashaveh* that could be challenged, and it was Rabbi Akiva's contribution that saved the *halacha* from ongoing uncertainty.

### Akiva's Pesach Source

Rabbi Akiva's derivation from the *kli cheres pasuk* gave *shlishi biterumah* an explicit scriptural foundation. Once there is a *pasuk*, the *tzad hashaveh* and its attendant vulnerability to *tzad chamur* objection become moot. The *halacha* rests on the *derasha*, not on the logical argument, and the challenge of the later generation is answered. This is a concrete illustration of the principle noted earlier: a *pasuk* is more secure than a *sevara*, because *sevara* can always be countered by a counter-*sevara*, while an explicit scriptural derivation — or one firmly grounded in *drasha* — cannot be similarly dislodged.

---

## Revi'i BeKodesh

### R. Yosei's Question

The Gemara continues: given that we now know *shlishi biterumah*, how do we derive the parallel rule for *kodesh* — namely, *revi'i bekodesh*, that a fourth-degree derivative of *tumah* invalidates sanctified food? A *braita* records Rabbi Yosei's question: *minayin lerevi'i bekodesh she-pasul?* The answer, he says, is a *kal vachomer*.

### Mechusar Kipurim Analogy

The *kal vachomer* parallels the one used to derive *shlishi biterumah* from *tevul yom*, but operates one level higher. *Mechusar kipurim* refers to a person who has completed the immersion and waited for sunset but whose *tahara* process is not yet complete because he still must bring a *korban* — such as a *zav*, *zavah*, or *yoledet*. After sunset, such a person may eat *terumah*, but remains forbidden from eating *kodashim* until the *korban* is brought the next morning. This is an even more residual *tumah* than that of a *tevul yom*: by *mechusar kipurim* it is barely a *tumah* at all, yet it is enough to bar the person from *kodashim*.

The *kal vachomer* runs: if a *mechusar kipurim*, who is *mutar biterumah* — permitted to eat *terumah* — is nonetheless *pasul bekodesh* — barred from *kodashim* — then *shlishi she-pasul biterumah* — something that is a *shlishi* and has thereby become invalid for *terumah* — surely should be *pasul bekodesh* as well. The parallel to the original *tevul yom* argument is tight: just as the residual *tumah* of *tevul yom* proves that *sheini* of food creates a problem for *terumah*, so the residual *tumah* of *mechusar kipurim* proves that *shlishi* of food creates a problem for *kodesh*, yielding the status of *revi'i bekodesh*.

### Shlishi LKodesh Source

Before arriving at *revi'i*, however, we must first establish *shlishi lekodesh* — that food which is a *shlishi* is invalid for *kodashim*. This is derived from the verse *ve-habasar asher yiga b'chol tamei lo ye'achel*, which concerns meat of a *korban*. The Torah called food that fell into a *kli cheres* contaminated by a *sheretz* — a *sheini* — by the term *tamei* (as established earlier in the *pasuk* of *kol asher betocho yitma*). Thus when this verse says that meat of a *korban* that touches anything *tamei* — including a *sheini* — may not be eaten, it establishes that if *korban* meat becomes a *shlishi* by touching a *sheini*, it is forbidden. *Shlishi lekodesh* is therefore scripturally grounded.

### Revi'i Derivation

From *shlishi lekodesh* being established by the *pasuk*, we then derive *revi'i* by the *kal vachomer* from *mechusar kipurim* as described: if someone whose *tumah* is so residual that he may eat *terumah* yet cannot eat *kodashim*, then *shlishi* food — which genuinely cannot be eaten as *terumah* — should certainly be able to invalidate *kodashim* it touches, producing a *revi'i bekodesh*.

### R. Yochanan's Problem

Rabbi Yochanan, however, objects sharply: *ta'am de-Rabbi Yosei ani yode'a, mahu? She-harei teshuvato betzido* — I understand what Rabbi Yosei is doing, but the refutation is built right into the argument. *Ochel ha-ba machmas tevul yom yochiach* — consider food that has been rendered *pasul* by contact with a *tevul yom*. Such food is *pasul biterumah* — it invalidates *terumah* — yet *eino oseh revi'i bekodesh* — it does not create a *revi'i* for *kodesh*.

This is a striking counter-example. The entire *kal vachomer* rested on analogizing the *shlishi* in food to the *mechusar kipurim* — if a person with only residual *tumah* can bar *kodashim*, then food at the *shlishi* level should certainly do so. But the case of food touched by a *tevul yom* reveals that the analogy between persons and foods in this chain does not hold cleanly: food touched by a *tevul yom* is *pasul biterumah* and yet does not produce a *revi'i bekodesh*. This breaks the very logical bridge on which the *kal vachomer* depends, and the full resolution of this challenge must await further analysis.

---

---

# Sotah 30

## Sheini/Shelishi/Revii

### Tvul Yom & Mechussar

The discussion on this *daf* picks up from the bottom of 29b, deep in the analysis of the degrees of *tumah* and how they propagate across different categories of food. The foundational structure of the argument is this: we learn that there is a concept of *shlishi bi-terumah* — that *terumah* can become *tamei* at a third degree of remove — from the case of a *tvul yom*, a person who has immersed in a *mikvah* but whose *taharah* is not yet complete until nightfall. Such a person, though carrying only residual *tumah*, is forbidden to eat *terumah* but is permitted to eat *chulin*. The analogy then runs: if a person with residual *tumah* is forbidden to eat *terumah*, then food which is itself *tamei* — a *sheini* — should certainly be capable of rendering *terumah tamei*, producing a *shlishi*.

The second step extends the logic further. A *mechussar kippurim* — one who has immersed and whose *taharah* is complete but who has not yet brought the required atonement offerings — is permitted to eat *terumah* but is forbidden to eat *kodashim*. By the same analogical structure, if a person with this residual status cannot partake of *kodashim*, then food which is itself *tamei* for *terumah* — a *shlishi* — should certainly be capable of rendering *kodashim tamei* at a fourth degree, producing a *revii*. These derivations proceed via *kal va-chomer* or *gezerah shavah*, not as *halachah le-Moshe mi-Sinai*.

### Yochanan's Challenge

Rabbi Yochanan objects to the entire structure of this *drashah* attributed to Rabbi Yose, declaring that he cannot understand it — *ta'am b'Rebbi eini yodea* — because the refutation lies right alongside the argument. He introduces a counterexample: *ochel ha-ba machmat tvul yom* — food that was touched by a *tvul yom*. Such food, namely *terumah* touched by a *tvul yom*, would effectively be a *shlishi*. According to the logic of the derivation, it should then be capable of rendering *kodashim* into a *revii*. Yet we know that this is not the case: such food is *pasul bi-terumah* — it invalidates the *terumah* — but *eino oseh revii ba-kodesh*, it does not go on to produce a *revii* in *kodashim*. The existence of this category — things that are *pasul* for *terumah* and yet do not transmit *tumah* further into *kodashim* — undermines the inference from *mechussar kippurim* to *shlishi bi-terumah* making *kodashim* into a *revii*. If the pattern were consistent, Rabbi Yochanan argues, why should we assume that a *shlishi* of *terumah* — which proceeds through food all the way down — passes the *tumah* into *kodashim* when the analogous case of food derived from a *tvul yom* does not?

### Tvul Yom Food Status

The question is how we know that food touched by a *tvul yom* does not make *kodashim* into a *revii*. The Gemara cites a *Braitah* in which a dispute among *Tannaim* is recorded. Abba Shaul holds a stringency *de-rabbanan*: a *tvul yom*, when it comes to matters of *kodashim*, is treated as a *rishon*, not merely as a *sheini*. The formulation is *metamei shnayim u-fosel echad* — he renders two levels *tamei* and invalidates one further level. In practical terms, for *kodshim* purposes, the *tvul yom* touching food makes the food a *sheini*, which touching further food makes it a *shlishi*, and that *shlishi* touching *kodesh* renders it *pasul* as a *revii*. So according to Abba Shaul, the *tumah* deriving from a *tvul yom* does in fact descend all the way to a *revii* in *kodashim*. Rabbi Meir holds that the *tvul yom* is treated as a *sheini* — *metamei echad u-fosel echad* — making *terumah* into a *shlishi*, which then renders *kodesh* into a *revii*. So according to both Abba Shaul and Rabbi Meir, the *tumah* of the *tvul yom* does proceed through to a *revii* in *kodashim*.

The position that creates a genuine counterexample is that of the *Chachamim*, who say: just as a *tvul yom* invalidates *terumah* food and liquid, so too he invalidates *kodashim* food and liquid — but it stops there. The food that he invalidated as a *shlishi* does not go on to render *kodashim* into a *revii*. If we rule like the *Chachamim*, then food touched by a *tvul yom* is indeed a counterexample to the proposed derivation from *mechussar kippurim*.

### Rav Pappa Defense

Rav Pappa challenges this framing: *be-mai* — upon what basis does Rabbi Yochanan's objection rest? It rests on the assumption that the ruling follows the *Rabbanan*, who say the *tvul yom*'s *tumah* stops at the *shlishi* and does not extend to a *revii* in *kodashim*. But perhaps the *drashah* of Rabbi Yose follows the position of Abba Shaul, who holds that the *tvul yom*'s *tumah* does reach a *revii* in *kodashim*. According to Abba Shaul, even though this represents a rabbinic stringency in its characterization of the *tvul yom* as a *rishon*, the underlying principle is that *tumah* deriving from a *tvul yom* can descend two full levels to render *kodashim* into a *revii*. Under that view, there is no counterexample at all.

### Countermove Analysis

The Gemara responds that if we accept Abba Shaul's position — that the *tvul yom*'s *tumah* does pass all the way through to render *kodashim* into a *revii* — then there is a different problem. If this is consistent rather than a counterexample, then there is no need to derive the rule about *revii* in *kodashim* from the case of *mechussar kippurim* at all. The Gemara proposes an alternative derivation: *u-mah ochel ha-ba machmat tvul yom* — if food that comes from a *tvul yom*, who himself is *mutar be-chulin*, whose *tumah* starts at a relatively weak point, nonetheless generates *tumah* that descends all the way to produce a *revii* in *kodashim*, then certainly *ochel shlishi ha-ba machmat sheni* — food that is a *shlishi* deriving from a *sheini* — where the *sheini* itself, unlike the *tvul yom*, is *assur be-chulin*, should certainly produce a *revii* in *kodashim* by *kal va-chomer*. The Gemara is asking: why did the *drashah* run to the case of *mechussar kippurim* when, if Abba Shaul is correct, there was a ready inference available from the case of food touched by a *tvul yom*?

### Tzad Hashaveh

The Gemara then considers whether one might deflect this proposed inference with a *pircha*: perhaps the *tvul yom* case cannot serve as the basis for the derivation because *mah la-tvul yom she-ken av tumah* — the *tvul yom* could be an *av tumah*, a primary source of *tumah*, which is a stringency that food can never possess. Food can never be an *av tumah*, and so one cannot argue from the *tvul yom*'s *tumah* extending to a *revii* in *kodashim* to the same being true for food that is itself *tamei*. The Gemara notes that this same *pircha* would apply equally to the case of the *mechussar kippurim* — he too is a person, who could potentially be an *av tumah*.

### Person-to-Object Challen…

The challenge of learning from a person to food is a recurring structural problem in this entire *sugya*. The *tvul yom* and the *mechussar kippurim* are both persons, and persons have a dimension of *tumah* — their potential to be an *av tumah* — that food simply does not share. This asymmetry means that any inference from the person's *tumah* behavior to what food does with *tumah* is potentially flawed by this *pircha*. It is worth noting that this objection could have been raised much earlier in the entire deliberation; indeed, it was, and the Gemara dealt with it by invoking a *tzad ha-shaveh* involving *keli cheres*, drawing on the *Sotah* context in which the very problematic of persons being *tamei* generating rules about objects being *tamei* is central to the tractate.

### Summary & Closure

To summarize the core of this difficult passage: the Gemara seeks to establish, through derivation, that a *sheini* can make *terumah* into a *shlishi*, and that a *shlishi* of *terumah* can make *kodashim* into a *revii*. The first is derived by analogy to the *tvul yom* who is forbidden from *terumah* yet permitted with *chulin* — so *chulin* that is itself *tamei* as a *sheini* should make *terumah* into a *shlishi*. The second is derived by analogy to the *mechussar kippurim* who may eat *terumah* yet is forbidden from *kodashim* — so *terumah* that is itself *tamei* as a *shlishi* should render *kodashim* into a *revii*. The Gemara's challenge comes from the case of food touched by a *tvul yom*, which is *pasul* for *terumah* yet — according to the *Chachamim* — does not pass its *tumah* on to *kodashim*. This is a counterexample if we follow the *Chachamim*; but if we follow Abba Shaul and say it is not a counterexample, then why was it not itself used as the basis for the derivation? The Gemara leaves the tension unresolved in a fully satisfying way, and ends by noting that the challenge of learning from a person to food — the *pircha* that persons can be *avos tumah* while food cannot — remains a relevant critique of both potential sources of derivation, even if it was not formally pressed to its ultimate conclusion.

---

## Shelishi Limits

### Rav Assi Statement

The Gemara now introduces a broad statement from Rav Assi in the name of Rav — with an alternative tradition attributing it to Rabba bar bar Assi in the name of Rav — establishing that the following *Tannaim* all share a single foundational position: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yose, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Elazar — all of them hold *de-ein sheni oseh shlishi be-chulin*, that a *sheini* does not make a *shlishi* in ordinary *chulin*. The category of *shlishi* is limited to *terumah*; ordinary *chulin* does not achieve third-degree *tumah* status. This point is worth pausing on, because the *limudim* of the preceding discussion — the *tvul yom* and *mechussar kippurim* derivations — were in each case explicitly about *terumah*. The *tvul yom* who may not eat *terumah*, the *mechussar kippurim* who may not eat *kodashim* — both derivations operated within the world of *terumah* and *kodashim*, never extending the rule of *shlishi* to *chulin*. Nevertheless, Rashi on the *Mishnah* had noted that Rabbi Akiva's derivation from the *pasuk* of *kol asher yipol me-hem el tocho yitma* — *yitma le-tamei acherim*, that the loaf in the *keli cheres* is *tamei* to make other things into a *shlishi* — contains nothing in its text specifically limiting it to *terumah*. It sounds as though Rabbi Akiva's *pasuk*-based derivation would extend *shlishi* even to *chulin*. The Gemara now reinforces that the consensus of *Tannaim* restricts *shlishi* to *terumah*, and proceeds to demonstrate this from each authority's rulings.

### Rabbi Meir Position

Rabbi Meir is sourced from a *Mishnah*: *kol ha-ta'un bi'at mayim mi-divrei soferim* — anything that requires immersion by rabbinic decree. The paradigmatic case of rabbinic *tumah* requiring immersion is human hands. Hands were assigned a default status of *sheini le-tumah* by rabbinic enactment, because their condition is uncertain — one does not know what they have touched. This is a *tumah* that exists only *de-rabbanan*; *de-oraita* it is impossible for a part of the body to be *tamei* while the rest is not, but rabbinically they assigned this status. The consequence is that one washes hands before eating *terumah* since hands in this *sheini* status cannot handle *terumah* — and this practice eventually extended to washing before eating bread even for non-*kohanim*.

The rule the *Mishnah* articulates is: *kol ha-tamei mi-divrei soferim metamei et ha-kodesh u-fosel et ha-terumah*. Anyone who is *tamei* by rabbinic decree — thus effectively a *sheini* — *metamei et ha-kodesh*, renders *kodesh tamei*, and *fosel et ha-terumah*, invalidates *terumah*. The distinction between *metamei* and *fosel* is crucial: *metamei* means the *tumah* can be transmitted one further level, whereas *fosel* means it invalidates but does not transmit further. So if such a person touches *kodesh*, they make it a *shlishi*, and that *shlishi* can render other *kodesh* into a *revii* — since *kodesh* goes up to *revii*. But if they touch *terumah*, it is merely *pasul* without passing on further. And the continuation: *u-mutar be-chulin u-ve-ma'aser* — this person is permitted to handle *chulin* and *ma'aser*; *chulin* is entirely unaffected. This is explicit: a *sheini* does not produce a *shlishi* in *chulin*. These are the words of Rabbi Meir. The *Chachamim* add *ma'aser* to the list of things that are affected — the debate about *ma'aser* concerns whether *ma'aser* is treated for these purposes like *kodesh* — but both Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* agree unambiguously that *sheini* does not make a *shlishi* in *chulin*.

### Rabbi Yose Position

Rabbi Yose's position is sourced from the very derivation discussed earlier in this *sugya* — *ha d'amaran*, the entire preceding analysis. The evidence that Rabbi Yose does not hold *sheini* makes *shlishi* in *chulin* comes not from what he said but from what he did not say. Had Rabbi Yose held that *chulin* could become a *shlishi*, his derivation would have needed to go further: *de-im ita, leisei le-revii bi-terumah va-chamishi be-kodesh*. If *chulin* itself could be a *shlishi*, then *terumah* should have been able to reach a *revii*, and *kodesh* should have been able to reach a *chamishi*, a fifth degree. The logic flows from the same *tvul yom* analogy: a *tvul yom* who is *mutar be-chulin* renders *terumah tamei*, so *chulin tamei* as a *sheini* should render *terumah* into a *shlishi*. But if *chulin* could be a *shlishi*, then by the same logic *chulin tamei* as a *shlishi* should render *terumah* into a *revii*, and then *terumah* as a *revii* should render *kodesh* into a *chamishi*. The fact that Rabbi Yose's derivation stopped at *revii* for *kodashim* demonstrates that he holds *chulin* reaches only to *sheini*, and it is *terumah* that reaches *shlishi* and *kodesh* that reaches *revii*. The hierarchy is clean: the greater the sanctity of the object, the more susceptible it is to progressively attenuated *tumah*. As one of the participants observed, this is structurally analogous to the principle that *tzaddikim ha-kadosh baruch hu medakdek aleihem ke-chut ha-sa'arah* — those who are holier attract even the most residual forces of *tumah*; or conversely, the forces of *tumah* can adhere even to the most attenuated *tumah* precisely when it encounters the most sacred objects.

### Rabbi Yehoshua Position

Rabbi Yehoshua's position emerges from a *Mishnah*: Rabbi Eliezer says that if one eats food that is *rishon* one becomes a *rishon*; if one eats food that is *sheini* one becomes a *sheini*; if one eats food that is *shlishi* one becomes a *shlishi*. The principle is, in effect, that you are what you eat — eating *tamei* food assigns you the same *tumah* status as that food. Tosafot notes that this operates on two levels of rabbinic enactment: the first level holds that if you eat something like a *sheini*, you cannot then eat *terumah*, since people would perceive the *terumah* as going into a stomach that contains *sheini* and being rendered *tamei* there. The second level goes further — after eating it, you are treated as being at that level even for purposes of what you touch.

Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees and says: one who eats *rishon* or *sheini* becomes a *sheini*; one who eats *shlishi* becomes a *sheini* only for *kodesh* — *sheni be-kodesh ve-ein sheni bi-terumah* — meaning it would affect *kodesh* but not *terumah*. What kind of food that was a *shlishi* could one have eaten? The *Mishnah* specifies: *be-chulin she-naasu al taharas ha-terumah* — *chulin* that was treated with the same care and stringency as *terumah*. This leads to the next subsection.

### Chulin Al Taharas

When a *kohen* has *terumah* in the house continuously and wishes to maintain a single uniform standard of purity, he may treat his *chulin* as if it were *terumah* — handling it with the same care and scrutiny. This practice is called *chulin she-naasu al taharas ha-terumah*. The halachic consequence is that the *chulin* that is handled with this *terumah*-level care acquires — by rabbinic enactment — the same *tumah* susceptibility as *terumah*. If a *sheini* touches standard *chulin*, nothing happens. But if a *sheini* touches *chulin* treated *al taharas ha-terumah*, that *chulin* becomes a *shlishi*. The Gemara draws out the implication: *al taharas ha-terumah in*, yes — only if it was treated with the care of *terumah* does it achieve *shlishi* status — *al taharas ha-kodesh lo*, not if it was merely treated with the care of *kodesh*. Rashi's text simply reads *chulin lo* — that standard *chulin* simply does not become a *shlishi*. The conclusion is the same either way: *alma kasavar ein sheni oseh shlishi be-chulin* — it is clear that Rabbi Yehoshua holds a *sheini* does not make a *shlishi* in standard *chulin*.

### Rabbi Elazar Formula

Rabbi Elazar's position comes from a *Braitah*: *shloshtan shavin* — the following three are equivalent in one respect. Whether one has a *rishon* in the world of *kodesh*, of *chulin*, or of *terumah*, it is *metamei shnayim u-fosel echad be-kodesh* — it transmits *tumah* two levels down and invalidates one more, meaning it reaches all the way to *revii* in *kodesh* and there stops. Then: *metamei echad u-fosel echad bi-terumah* — in the world of *terumah*, the *rishon* goes down two levels, making a *sheini* and then a *shlishi*, and stops. And *u-fosel echad ba-chulin* — in the world of *chulin*, the *rishon* goes down only one level to a *sheini* and stops. This is a beautifully clear formulation: *chulin* ends at *sheini*, *terumah* ends at *shlishi*, and *kodesh* ends at *revii*.

---

## Shelishi Limits (II)

### Challah Case

Rabbi Eliezer's position is derived from a *Mishnah* concerning *challah*: *Rabbi Eliezer omer, challah nitelet min ha-tehorah al ha-teme'ah* — *challah* may be taken from *tahor* dough on behalf of *tamei* dough. The background is as follows: if one's dough became *tamei*, the *challah* separated from it becomes *terumah teme'ah*, which the *kohen* cannot eat and can only burn. Rabbi Eliezer rules that if the dough was made *tamei* deliberately — *be-meizid* — one is required to separate *tahor challah* from *tahor* dough on behalf of the *tamei* dough as well, so that the *kohen* receives a *tahor challah*. The practical challenge is how to accomplish this while keeping the doughs connected for purposes of the separation.

---

## Challah Dispute

### Eliezer Leniency

Rabbi Eliezer's solution is to interpose a small piece of *tahor* dough between the *tahor* and *tamei* portions. The quantity of this interposing piece is critical: it must be *pachos mi-kebeitzah*, less than a *kebeitzah* in volume. This is because food that is less than a *kebeitzah* can become *tamei* itself but does not transmit *tumah* further. The piece in the middle will be rendered *tamei* by contact with the *tamei* dough, but since it is less than a *kebeitzah*, it will not pass the *tumah* on to the *tahor* dough on the other side. The three portions — *tamei* dough, small interposing piece, *tahor* dough — are thereby treated as one connected mass, and *challah* can be taken from the *tahor* portion *mi-n ha-mukaf*, as if taken from a connected whole. The *Chachamim* forbid this arrangement.

---

## Challah Dispute (II)

### Kebeitzah Mechanics

A second *Braitah* reports that Rabbi Eliezer permitted this even with a *kebeitzah*-sized interposing piece, not only with less than a *kebeitzah*. This version of the ruling is more striking, because a *kebeitzah* of food does transmit *tumah*. How then could Rabbi Eliezer permit using a *kebeitzah* of *tahor* dough in the middle without concern that it will become a *shlishi* and transmit *tumah* to the *tahor* dough on the far side? The configuration would be: *tamei* dough — a *rishon* — touching the interposing piece making it a *sheini*, which then contacts the far *tahor* dough making it potentially a *shlishi*.

### Gemara Analysis

The Gemara initially assumes that the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the *Chachamim* is precisely about whether *sheini* makes *shlishi* in *chulin*: *mai lav be-ha kamifligi* — is this not the crux of their disagreement? The *Tamei* dough is a *rishon*, the interposing dough becomes a *sheini*, and the question is whether the far *tahor* dough becomes a *shlishi*. Rabbi Eliezer holds *ein sheini oseh shlishi be-chulin* — no, it stops at *sheini* — so the scheme works. The *Chachamim* hold *sheini oseh shlishi be-chulin* — yes, the *tumah* would reach the far dough — so they forbid it.

An additional assumption underlying this reading is *chulin ha-tevulim le-challah lo ke-challah damu* — dough from which *challah* has not yet been separated is treated as ordinary *chulin*, not as *challah*/*terumah*, even though it contains actualized potential *challah* within it.

### Rav Mari Resolution

Rav Mari son of Rav Kahana resolves the apparent debate differently. Since we have already shown from so many *Tannaim* that all agree *ein sheini oseh shlishi be-chulin*, it cannot be that this is the point of contention between Rabbi Eliezer and the *Chachamim*. Instead, *ve-hacha be-chulin ha-tevulim le-challah kamifligi* — what they actually debate is whether *chulin* from which *challah* has not yet been separated is treated as *challah* (*terumah*) in its *tumah* susceptibility, or as plain *chulin*. The *Chachamim* hold *ke-challah damu* — it is like *challah*, and therefore the interposing dough can become a *shlishi*, making the scheme impermissible. Rabbi Eliezer holds *lo ke-challah damu* — it remains *chulin*, cannot become a *shlishi*, and the scheme is therefore permissible. Alternatively, the Gemara offers a second resolution: *de-chulei alma chulin ha-tevulim le-challah lo ke-challah damu ve-ein sheini oseh shlishi be-chulin* — everyone agrees on both of these points, and the dispute is actually about *ha-mutar ligrom tumah le-chulin she-be-chutz la-aretz* — whether one is permitted to cause *tumah* to spread to *chulin* outside of the Land of Israel. Rabbi Eliezer permits deliberately spreading *tumah* to the interposing *chulin* dough for the constructive purpose of enabling *challah tehorah* to be separated on behalf of everything combined. The *Chachamim* hold this is forbidden: *assur ligrom tumah le-chulin she-be-chutz la-aretz*. The upshot in any case is that virtually every *Tanna* agrees that *shlishi* is limited to *terumah*; the consensus is overwhelming, even if Rashi's observation about Rabbi Akiva's *pasuk*-based derivation raises a lingering question about whether the *Mishnah* itself implies a broader reach.

---

## Techumin Drasha

### Levitic Cities

The Gemara now transitions to a different *drashah* of Rabbi Akiva: *bo bayom darash Rabbi Akiva*. The *pesukim* about the *arei ha-Leviyim* — the Levitic cities — contain an apparent contradiction. One *pasuk* speaks of a thousand *amah* around the cities and another speaks of two thousand. Rabbi Akiva's resolution is that a thousand *amah* represents one measure — the immediate surrounds, fields or yards — while two thousand *amah* represents the city limit proper.

### Akiva Derivation

The halachic significance of establishing a two-thousand *amah* city limit is its relevance to *Shabbat* boundaries. If Rabbi Akiva is deriving a two-thousand *amah* measure from these *pesukim*, it is presumably because this establishes *techumin* — the *Shabbat* boundary — as a *de-oraita* concept, derived from these very verses.

### Debate Framework

The Gemara frames the underlying debate as follows: *mar savar techumin de-oraita u-mar savar de-rabbanan* — one authority holds that *techumin* is a biblical prohibition and the other holds it is rabbinic. If Rabbi Akiva's *drashah* establishes a two-thousand *amah* city limit for the *Leviyim*, the point of the derivation — what *nafka mina* does it serve — is presumably to establish that the prohibition of leaving the *Shabbat* boundary is *de-oraita*. The other *Tanna* who does not accept this reading of the *pesukim* would instead understand the two thousand *amah* as describing where the *Leviyim*'s fields and vineyards lay, not as establishing a halachic limit for *Shabbat*.

### Tosafot Nuance

Tosafot raises a nuance: the dichotomy need not be absolute. Perhaps even one who reads the *pasuk* as describing the *Leviyim*'s agricultural land could still derive *techumin de-oraita* from a different *pasuk*. Conversely, perhaps Rabbi Akiva could acknowledge that the two-thousand *amah* figure also describes the *Leviyim*'s land without that undermining the *Shabbat* application. However, at minimum, Rabbi Akiva's derivation is most coherent if he is drawing a *de-oraita* norm about *Shabbat* boundaries, since for him the verse's import cannot simply be the agricultural distribution to the *Leviyim*. One might also note that there is another potential application of knowing the city limit of the *arei ha-Leviyim* — namely, establishing when one is considered to be within the city for purposes of *arei miklat*, cities of refuge, which function as Levitic cities. Yet the Gemara specifically frames the debate around *techumin de-oraita* versus *de-rabbanan*, and this is the most naturally compelling reason why Rabbi Akiva would need to derive a precise two-thousand *amah* measure from these *pesukim*.

---

## Song at Sea

### Song Setup

The next *drashah* of Rabbi Akiva concerns the *Shirah* at the sea — *Az Yashir Moshe*. The *Braitah* introduces the scene: when Israel ascended from the sea, *natnu eineihem lomar shirah* — they set their eyes upon saying *shirah*. The question is: how did they say it? The word *lemor* in the verse — *vayomru lemor Ashira la-Shem* — suggests a responsive mode, but what exactly does this mean?

### Akiva Responsive
