Rabbi Akiva's position is that *lemor* refers to responsive singing analogous to the way an adult *makri* reads *Hallel* for a congregation when that congregation is largely unlettered. The adult would chant each section, and the congregation — not knowing the full text — would respond with the opening words of the first verse: *Ashira la-Shem*. So Moshe would say *Ashira la-Shem ki ga'oh ga'ah*, and they would respond *Ashira la-Shem*; Moshe would continue, and they would again respond *Ashira la-Shem* — a recurring *refrain* that constituted their participation. This is like the practice of *Hodu la-Shem ki tov, Hodu la-Shem ki tov* — a responsive verse that allows full participation without requiring knowledge of the entire text. The *lemor* thus means: Moshe said it, and they responded with the opening line.

### Eliezer Repetition

Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Yose HaGelili holds differently. He compares it to the case where a *katan*, a minor, reads *Hallel* for the congregation. Since a minor cannot discharge the obligation of adults, the congregation cannot simply respond *Amen* and be *yotzei*; they must repeat every word themselves. So here too, *lemor* means that for every word Moshe said, all of Israel repeated that word — complete word-for-word repetition, which also explains how they knew the text: they simply repeated after Moshe.

### Chachamim Unison

The *Chachamim* interpret the verse differently. *Vayomru* — they all said it — indicates that everyone recited the entire *Shirah* simultaneously, in unison. *Lemor* means that Moshe opened first — *d'patach Moshe be-reisha* — and then everyone said it together with him. This is analogous to the way *Shema* was recited in the *beit ha-knesset*, where the *sofer* or *sheliach tzibbur* would open and then everyone would join in unison, rather than responding responsively or repeating word by word. But this position raises the obvious question: how did all of Israel know the words if Moshe composed the song on the spot?

### Yose HaGelili Answer

Rabbi Yose HaGelili addresses this question directly in a *drashah*: *b'sha'ah she-alu Yisrael min ha-yam, natnu eineihem lomar shira* — when they came up from the sea, they wanted to say *shira*. How did they all know to say exactly what they said? His answer: *ol mutal al birkei imo* — a toddler sitting on his mother's lap — and *tinok yonek mi-shadei imo* — an infant nursing from its mother's breast. When the *Shechina* revealed itself at *Yam Suf*, the toddler lifted his neck and the infant released the breast from his mouth, and they said: *Zeh Eli ve-anvehu*. The miracle is that even infants were imbued with prophecy and song at that moment. The people did not need to learn the words from Moshe; they were supernaturally inspired to sing.

### Infants Midrash

The *pasuk* cited as the proof text is *mi-pi olelim ve-yonkim yisadta oz* — from the mouths of toddlers and infants You established strength — where *oz* echoes *Ozzi ve-zimrat Yah*, the opening of the *Shirah* itself, suggesting that the *oz*, the strength of song, came even from the youngest. The image is deliberately vivid and even graphic: the infant releases the nipple from his mouth to sing. The Gemara records that this text was once cited at a *brit*, which is perhaps not surprising.

### Meir Enhancement

Rabbi Meir goes further still: *minayin she-afilu ubarim she-be-me'ei imman amru shira* — how do we know that even the fetuses in their mothers' wombs said *shira*? The proof text is *be-makhelot barechu Elohim, Hashem, mi-mekor Yisrael* — in the assemblies bless God, from the *mekor* of Israel — where *mekor* is the rabbinic anatomical term for the womb, the source that nurtures the child. The objection is immediately raised: *va-halo lo chazu* — the fetuses could not see anything. Rabbi Tanchum resolves this: *keres na'asa lahem ke-aspaklarya ha-me'irah* — the womb became for them like a luminous transparent glass, and they could see through it and behold the divine presence. What the infants perceived through sight, the fetuses perceived through a miraculous transparency of the womb itself.

---

## Job Love vs Fear

### Lo Ambiguity

The *daf* concludes with a discussion of *Iyov* and the question of whether his service of God was *me-ahavah* or *mi-yirah* — from love or from fear. The *Mishnah* had cited the verse *hen yikteleni, lo ayachel* — even if He kills me, I will still hope in Him — as evidence that Iyov served from love. However, as the *Mishnah* noted, *adayin ha-davar shakul* — the matter is still uncertain — because the word *lo* could be written with a *lammed alef* meaning "not" — I will not have faith — or with a *lammed vav* meaning "for Him" — I will maintain my faith in Him. The Gemara asks the obvious question: let us simply look at how the word is written. It is in fact written with a *lammed alef*. Does that not settle it?

### Written Form Challenge

The Gemara challenges the reliability of reading the written form as definitive by bringing another *pasuk*: *be-chol tzaratam lo tzar* — in all their afflictions, He is not afflicted — where *lo* is also written with a *lammed alef*, yet the meaning, given the continuation of the verse (*u-malach panav hoshi'am*, and His angel saved them), must be *lo* with a *vav* — meaning God is afflicted by their suffering. So the written *lammed alef* cannot be read as determinative; it can carry either meaning. The Gemara notes that this is not a standard *keri u-chtiv* discrepancy; rather, a *lammed alef* itself can mean *lo* with a *vav*. This may reflect archaic orthographic ambiguity: just as the feminine pronoun *hi* was sometimes written with a *vav* rather than a *yod* in older Hebrew texts, the *alef* in *lo* may have functioned as a vowel placeholder rather than a semantic indicator of negation.

### Meir Approach

Rabbi Meir resolves the question differently, without relying on the written form of the word at all. He notes that *Iyov* is described as *yere Elokim*, fearing God — and so is *Avraham*, of whom the *pasuk* says *ki ata yadati ki yere Elokim atah* — now I know that you fear God — after the *Akeidah*. Since we know from another *pasuk* that Avraham is called *ohavi* — My beloved, the one who loves Me — the description of Avraham as *yere Elokim* did not preclude but rather included *ahavah*. By *gezeirah shavah* of the common phrase *yere Elokim*, the same is true of Iyov: *yirah* in Iyov's case also emerged from a foundation of *ahavah*.

### Reward Differential

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar articulates the practical difference in reward between those who serve *mi-yirah* and those who serve *me-ahavah*. One who serves from fear — *ze taluy le-elef dor* — the reward extends for a thousand generations. One who serves from love — *le-alpayim dor* — two thousand generations. The Gemara supports this from two *pesukim*. In one, *le-alafim le-ohavai u-le-shomrei mitzvotai* — thousands of generations for those who love Me and keep My commandments — *alafim* (thousands) is juxtaposed to *ohavai* (those who love Me). In the other, *le-ohavav u-le-shomrei mitzvotav le-elef dor* — for those who love Him and keep His commandments, a thousand generations — *elef* (one thousand) is juxtaposed to *shomrei mitzvotav* (those who keep His commandments). The distinction turns on what each word is adjacent to: love is paired with thousands, observance without the same quality of love is paired with one thousand.

### Two Students

The *sugya* concludes with an aggadic coda. Two students sat before Rava. The first said: I was told in my dream — *ma rav tuvcha asher tzafanta li-rei'echa* — how great is Your good that you have stored away for those who fear You. The second said: I was told in my dream — *ve-yismechu vecha kol chosei vach, le-olam yeranenu ve-ya'altzu vach ohavei shemecha* — and all who take shelter in You will rejoice; forever those who love Your name will sing.

### Rava Judgment

Rava said to both of them: *travaychu rabbanan tzadikei gemurei atun* — you are both complete *tzaddikim*. But: *mar me-ahavah u-mar mi-yirah* — one serves from love, and one serves from fear. The first student's dream cited a verse about *rei'echa*, those who fear; the second student's dream cited a verse about *ohavei shemecha*, those who love Your name. Each man's dream reflected his own spiritual mode of service — and Rava affirmed that both paths lead to the status of *tzaddik gamur*, a fully righteous person, even as they are not identical in their nature or their reward.

*Hadran alach ha-Shole'ach.*

# Sotah 31

## Opening Mishnah

### R. Eliezer: Bird Claim

The daf begins two-thirds of the way down the page, at the opening of a new *perek*. The *mishnah* returns to the very first *mishnah* of the *masechta*: the case of *mi she-kina le-ishto ve-nistara* — a man who warned his wife not to go into seclusion and she did so anyway. The question before us is: what quality of proof is required to establish that she went into seclusion, so as to permit or compel the continuation of the *sotah* process?

Rabbi Eliezer's position, already stated in the opening *mishnah*, is stated here in its most radical form: *afilu shama mi-of pore'ach* — even if one merely heard the claim of a passing bird. No matter how tenuous the assertion, any claim that she went into seclusion suffices as the basis for the *sotah* process. This is, by any measure, a strikingly unfair standard for the woman.

The consequence the *mishnah* states is *yotzi ve-yiten ketubah* — he divorces her and pays the *ketubah*. This phrasing is initially puzzling: one might have expected it to say that he must make her drink the *sotah* water, not that he must pay the *ketubah*. Rashi explains the logic: once the *sotah* process is triggered, she is forbidden to him. He has two options — either she undergoes the drinking, or, if neither party wishes to pursue that path, he divorces her and pays the *ketubah*. If she refuses to drink and the process is abandoned, she leaves without the *ketubah*. The *mishnah* states the case from the perspective of the husband who chooses not to proceed with the drinking.

### R. Yehoshua: Rumors

Rabbi Yehoshua requires something more substantial. His formulation is *ad she-ye-hayu nos'ot ve-notnot bah nashim ba-matyah ba-levanah* — until the women who sit and spin by moonlight begin to gossip about her. This somewhat colorful idiom conveys the requirement that there be actual social rumor circulating about her conduct.

Rabbi Yehoshua's standard, understood correctly, is that one needs two proper witnesses that she went into seclusion. The case of gossip here is not a *halacha* about rendering her forbidden to her husband as a *sotah*; there are no witnesses to seclusion at all. Rather, the issue is with the phrase *tehorah hi* — she is pure — which appears in connection with the *sotah* water. Once her reputation has been publicly tarnished, the waters will not be effective in any case. So the option of drinking is no longer on the table.

At the same time, since there are no formal witnesses to seclusion, she has not been rendered *teme'ah* as a *sotah*. The husband could theoretically remain married to her — there is merely this cloud of rumor. But if he chooses to divorce her because of this reputation, he must pay the *ketubah*. The result is an asymmetry in how *yotzi ve-yiten ketubah* functions in each case: for Rabbi Eliezer, it implies she *is* a *sotah* and may be compelled to drink; for Rabbi Yehoshua, she is not a *sotah*, but the husband who wishes to leave must nonetheless pay. This is, as Rashi reads the *mishnah*, a difficult but defensible reading.

## One Witness After

### Slave/Maidservant Testim…

Assuming the standard of Rabbi Yehoshua — two witnesses to seclusion — the *mishnah* now addresses the consequences of testimony regarding the act of adultery itself. The *halacha* is that once the predicate of warning and seclusion has been established, a single witness who comes and says *ani ra'iti she-nitme'ah* — "I saw that she became *teme'ah*," that is, that she committed adultery within that seclusion — is believed. The consequence is not execution, for which two *kosher* witnesses would be required, but rather that she may not drink the *sotah* water; she is considered a proven adulteress, and upon divorce she forfeits her *ketubah*.

The *mishnah* extends this further: *afilu eved afilu shifchah harei elu ne'emanim* — even a male or female slave would be believed for this purpose. The one witness who testifies to the act of adultery need not be a *kosher* witness in the formal sense. The consequence of such testimony is that she loses her *ketubah*.

### Jealous Relatives

The *mishnah* then lists five categories of women who are presumed to harbor enmity toward the wife: the mother-in-law (*chamot*), the mother-in-law's daughter, the co-wife (*tzarat*), the widowed sister-in-law who stands to be subject to *yibum* with the husband, and the husband's daughter from another wife. These women all have identifiable personal interest in the wife's downfall and their credibility is therefore diminished.

Nevertheless, the *mishnah* rules *harei elu ne'emanos* — they are believed — but with a qualification: *ve-lo le-fosla mi-ketubatah ella shelo tishteh*. Their testimony is sufficient to stop the *sotah* drinking process — we treat their claim as sufficiently credible that we will not proceed with the water — but it is *not* sufficient to strip the wife of her *ketubah*. The husband must divorce her and pay the *ketubah*. So she loses the option of drinking and clearing her name, but she retains her financial protection.

## Opening Mishnah (II)

### Kal vaComer Logic

The *mishnah* then raises the question of how we know that the *eid echad* is believed for the testimony of adultery at all. One might have constructed a *kal va-chomer* that would have led to the opposite conclusion. The reasoning would proceed: the first testimony — that she went into seclusion — is a less severe form of evidence, since even after seclusion is established she still has the option of the *sotah* water to clear her name. Yet even for this less consequential testimony, the Torah requires two witnesses. All the more so, then, for the second testimony — the one that actually seals her fate and makes her permanently forbidden — should we not require two witnesses?

This is a compelling argument. The *mishnah* answers by citing the verse *ve-eid ein bah* — there is no witness against her, implying that even one witness suffices. The *mishnah* reads this as: if there *is* even one witness against her, there is a problem; she may not drink.

The *mishnah* then runs the *kal va-chomer* in the opposite direction. Now that we have established from this verse that one witness suffices to seal her fate in the more consequential second testimony, we might reverse the logic: *kal va-chomer*, the first testimony about seclusion, which is less consequential because the *sotah* water remains available, should also be achievable with one witness. That would unravel the entire structure, eliminating the requirement for two witnesses to seclusion.

To block this reversal, the *mishnah* cites the verse *ki matza bah ervat davar* — when the husband finds "a matter of nakedness" regarding her, with the word *davar* (*matter*) linked by *gezeirah shavah* to the verse *al pi shenayim eidim yakum davar* — a matter is established by two witnesses. From this parallel, the *mishnah* derives that the seclusion testimony requires two witnesses: *mah lehavalahn al pi shenayim af kan al pi shenayim*.

This *gezeirah shavah* is somewhat surprising in context, since the verse *ki matza bah ervat davar* appears in the laws of *get* and not in the *sotah* passage itself. The *mishnah* reads it as referring to the husband's suspicion, which is precisely the situation of seclusion. The *Gemara*, however, will read both the *derashot* and this *pasuk* somewhat differently.

The *Gemara* interjects: why do we need this *gezeirah shavah* from the word *davar*? There is a simpler derivation. The verse *ve-eid ein bah* that grants believability to the single witness uses the word *bah* — "regarding her." This word *bah* is limiting: it is specifically in regard to the act of adultery itself that a single witness is believed. For *kinuy* and *stirah* — the warning and seclusion stages — the verse offers no such license, and those require two. The *Gemara* concludes *hachi nami ka'amar* — yes, that is indeed what the *mishnah* means to convey: *bah* — regarding the act itself one witness is believed, *ve-lo be-kinuy ve-lo be-stirah*.

A further question arises: once we know that in the *sotah* context one witness is believed for the act of adultery when building on the seclusion, might one extend this to suggest that one witness would always be believed to accuse a woman of adultery even without the prior structure of warning and seclusion? The answer comes from the same *gezeirah shavah*: *ne'emar kan davar ve-ne'emar lehavalahn davar* — the word *davar* appears here and in the verse about two witnesses, establishing that outside the specific *sotah* framework, testimony of adultery requires two. The *sotah* context is the exception; the general rule remains two *kosher* witnesses.

## Default Two Witnesses

### No Two Witnesses

The *Gemara* now turns to the section of the *mishnah* dealing with one witness against one witness, where the *mishnah* appears to say they neutralize one another and the drinking proceeds. Before engaging with that debate, the *Gemara* establishes the foundational principle: *minani mili* — from where do we know that one witness is believed for the act of adultery in the *sotah* case?

The *Gemara* cites a *baraita*: *ve-eid ein bah bi-shnayim ha-katuv medaber* — when the verse says "there is no witness against her," the Torah is speaking about two witnesses. That is, "no witness" means no *two* witnesses. The verse is understood as: there are no two witnesses against her, only one — and she was not raped — in which case she is forbidden and the drinking is halted.

This reading may seem counterintuitive. The plain reading of the *mishnah* seemed to say that "no witness" permits drinking, and "one witness" prohibits it. The *Gemara* instead understands the verse as: no two witnesses — only one — and that one witness suffices to stop the process.

### Eid = Two Default

How do we know that the unqualified word *eid* means two? The *Gemara* derives this from the verse *lo yakum eid echad be-ish le-chol avon* — one witness may not rise up against a person for any offense. The *Gemara* asks: since *eid* is already singular in form, why does the verse need to specify *echad* — one? It must be that the word *eid* by itself ordinarily denotes two witnesses, and the qualifier *echad* is needed to indicate that only one is meant.

This yields a general *klal*: *kol makom she-ne'emar eid harei kan shnayim ad she-yafrit lecha ha-katuv echad* — wherever the word *eid* appears, it means two witnesses, unless the text explicitly specifies *echad* to indicate a single one. This is a far-reaching principle that recurs throughout the *Gemara* in matters of testimony.

With this principle established, the *Gemara* can read *ve-eid ein bah* as referring to the absence of two witnesses: the Torah is saying there are no two witnesses against her, there is only one — and it is that one witness, acting in the context of established seclusion, who is believed to render her forbidden.

## Competing Testimonies

### Ulla: Cannot Neutralize

With the foundational principle established, the *Gemara* turns to the *mishnah*'s statement that one witness saying she became *teme'ah* against one witness saying she did not would neutralize one another, allowing the drinking to proceed. Rashi notes that the witness who says *lo nitme'ah* is not claiming to have observed the room and seen that nothing happened; rather, he is saying something more modest — "your observation is not reliable" or "I was with you and I know you could not have seen what you claim." It is a contradiction of credibility, not an affirmative counterclaim.

The *Gemara* immediately challenges the premise that such a contradiction could have any force at all. The first witness — the one who says she became *teme'ah* — is not an ordinary witness. He comes equipped with the prior testimony of warning and seclusion, which form a *raglayim la-davar*, a factual foundation for the suspicion. The Torah, given this foundation, has granted this witness extraordinary weight, treating his single testimony as authoritative. How, then, can a single witness offering a mere contradiction — without any comparable foundation — neutralize this specially-empowered testimony?

This is Ulla's principle: *kol makom she-min ha-Torah eid echad harei kan shnayim* — wherever the Torah accords special believability to a single witness, that witness effectively counts as two. And *ein dvaro shel echad bi-makom shnayim* — the word of an ordinary single witness has no weight against two. If the specially-empowered witness counts as two, the ordinary contradiction counts as one, and one cannot override two. It follows that the contradiction is simply ineffective, and we would consider her *teme'ah*.

Ulla therefore proposes a different *girsa* of the *mishnah*: where the *mishnah* reads *hayetah shotah* — she would drink — in the case of one against one, Ulla reads *lo hayetah shotah* — she would *not* drink. The one who says she became *teme'ah* wins, and the process is stopped. Rabbi Yitzchak adopts the same reading.

### R. Chiya: Simultaneous

Rabbi Chiya, however, retains the original text of the *mishnah*: in the case of one against one, *hayetah shotah* — she would drink. The two testimonies neutralize one another, and the process continues. The *Gemara* notes that Ulla's argument — based on the specially-granted weight of the first witness — poses a genuine difficulty for Rabbi Chiya. It is not merely that Rabbi Chiya disagrees with Ulla's opinion; Ulla's position has compelling logical force, grounded in the structure of the Torah's grant of special believability.

### Timing: Simultaneous vs…

The *Gemara* resolves this tension by distinguishing between the timing of the testimonies. *Kan be-vat achas, kan be-zeh achar zeh* — in one case the witnesses arrive simultaneously, in the other they arrive sequentially. Rashi specifies that "simultaneously" means within *toch kedei dibbur* — the brief interval of a normal utterance.

The logic of this distinction is as follows. If both witnesses arrive at the same time, the court has not yet accorded full weight to the first witness's claim. Two people step forward together; one says she became *teme'ah* and the other immediately disputes this. Since the challenge is present from the outset, the testimony of the first has never been fully established, and the situation remains unresolved — she drinks. This is the case Rabbi Chiya is addressing, and it does not contradict Ulla's principle, because Ulla's principle applies once the testimony has been accepted.

If, however, the first witness testified and the court recognized his testimony — if that testimony has been received and accorded its special weight — then a witness who arrives afterward cannot dislodge it. The first testimony, once accepted, is treated as two witnesses, and nothing that comes subsequently can override it.

## Two-Against-One Cases

### 1 vs 2: Neutralizes

The *Gemara* now turns to the *mishnah*'s next case: one says she became *teme'ah* and two say she did not — *hayetah shotah*, she would drink. The two neutralize the one, and the process continues. This makes immediate sense in light of everything established: if even a single opposing witness can neutralize the one who says *teme'ah* (when they arrive simultaneously), two opposing witnesses can certainly do so.

This is also why Rashi insists that *lo nitme'ah* does not mean the witnesses actively observed innocence; if two witnesses had positively testified that she did not commit adultery, the question would be entirely settled and she obviously would not drink. Their testimony is a contradiction of the first witness's claim, not an affirmative attestation of innocence.

### 2 vs 1: Two Win

The final case in the *mishnah*: two say she became *teme'ah* and one says she did not — *lo hayetah shotah*, she would not drink. Two prevail over one and the process stops. This seems almost self-evident. One might wonder: if two witnesses testified that she committed adultery, why is she not executed? The *Gemara* implies they may not be *kosher* witnesses.

The *Gemara* notes an interesting structural point. The *mishnah* had just stated that one against one neutralizes (at least simultaneously). If so, the case of two against one — where the two win — does not seem to add much; by the same logic, one against one stopping the process ought to follow even more readily. And conversely, if the point of two against one stopping the process is to suggest that one against one would *not* stop it — that one against one would neutralize — then this aligns with Rabbi Chiya's reading.

The *Gemara* then presses: doesn't the case of two beating one (*lo hayetah shotah*) prove that one against one *would* let her drink — a problem for Ulla, who rules that even one against one stops the process? Rabbi Chiya responds: *al tameich, eima seifa* — look at the final clause of the *mishnah*. Two say *teme'ah*, one says not — she would not drink. Would you then say that one and one she *would* drink? That would also follow from the same logic. The *mishnah*'s final clause cannot be read as implying that two and one is different from one and one in terms of which direction they cut. Something else must be the purpose of these final clauses, and the *Gemara* now explains what that is.

## R. Nechemya: Majority

### Majority When One Witness

The *Gemara* concludes that the closing section of the *mishnah* — the two-against-one cases in both directions — is not addressing the debate between Ulla and Rabbi Chiya at all. Rather, *kula be-pasulei edus ve-Rabbi Nechemya hi* — the entire passage concerns witnesses who are not *kosher* in the formal sense, and it follows the opinion of Rabbi Nechemya.

A *baraita* records Rabbi Nechemya's principle: *kol makom she-he'emina Torah eid echad halach achar rov de'os* — wherever the Torah has granted believability to a single witness, you follow the majority of opinions. The reasoning is fundamental. The Torah's ordinary framework of testimony requires two *kosher* witnesses. The *sotah* case has already broken that framework by accepting a single witness, and by accepting witnesses who are not formally *kosher*. Once the normal rules are set aside, the remaining organizing principle is simply numerical: whichever side has more voices prevails.

In the normal law of testimony, two witnesses are formally equivalent to one hundred — quantity above the threshold of two is irrelevant. But when we have already departed from the formal framework, we revert to a more intuitive standard: more voices on one side carry greater weight.

### Gender Parity

Rabbi Nechemya extends this logic explicitly: *afilu shtei nashim be-ish echad ki-shnei anashim be-ish echad* — even two women against one man are equivalent to two men against one man. One might have thought that a single *kosher* male witness carries inherently greater weight than women, who are ordinarily *pasul* for testimony. Rabbi Nechemya rules otherwise. Since the entire framework of formal testimony has been suspended, there is no basis for preferring a *kosher* witness's testimony over that of a *pasul* witness. Two is simply more than one, and two women beat one man.

This is a remarkable *chiddush*. The *mishnah* in its closing cases is teaching precisely this: two women can override one man, and the majority — in either direction — determines the outcome.

### Male Witness Lock-In

At this point the *Gemara* introduces a qualification. The full reach of Rabbi Nechemya's principle — that women can override a man even when they arrive later — may be too broad. A secondary opinion holds: *kol heicha de-ata eid echad kosher me-ikara afilu me'ah nashim nami ke-eid echad damyan* — if a single *kosher* male witness testified first, even one hundred women who came afterward count as only a single witness. His testimony locks in.

The question concerns sequential testimony, and here the *Gemara* takes the discussion in a direction that goes beyond the earlier Ulla–Rabbi Chiya debate. Ulla and Rabbi Chiya agreed: once a witness testifies and is accepted, later testimony cannot undo it. Rabbi Nechemya's *rov de'os* principle seemed to challenge this: perhaps if enough people testify afterward — even women against a man — the later majority prevails.

One position within the discussion of Rabbi Nechemya's view accepts this: even if the first witness was a man, the later majority can override. The second position, which the *Gemara* ultimately elaborates, resists this conclusion where a *kosher* witness testified first. In that case, his testimony acquires the status of formal *kosher edut*, equivalent to two proper witnesses, and that cannot be overridden by any subsequent accumulation of *pasul* witnesses. The *Gemara* therefore explains the *mishnah*'s case: *ve-hacha be-mai askinan ke-gon de-asi ishah me-ikara* — the case in the *mishnah* where later testimony does override must be one where the first witness was herself a woman. When the first to testify is a woman, her testimony does not attain the status of formal *edut*, and a later majority of women can override it.

### Strict vs Lenient

One further question: why does the *mishnah* need to give *both* two-against-one cases — two saying *teme'ah* against one saying not, *and* one saying *teme'ah* against two saying not? If the principle is simply that the majority prevails, both cases follow automatically.

The *Gemara* answers: *ma d'teima ki azlinan basar rov de'os le-chumra aval le-kula lo azlinan* — one might have thought that we follow the majority only when it produces the stringent outcome, but not the lenient one. That is, if the majority says *teme'ah*, we follow them because it is *le-chumra* to stop the process; but if the majority says she did not become *teme'ah*, perhaps we would not follow them *le-kula* to permit her to drink. The *mishnah* therefore needed both cases to teach that the majority principle operates symmetrically: we follow the greater number regardless of which direction the leniency or stringency cuts.

Rashi's view of what constitutes *chumra* and *kula* here is interesting. He reads it as lenient to believe the witness who says she committed adultery, since the consequence — that she does not drink and goes out without her *ketubah* — spares her from the risk of the waters. Others might read the *kula* as permitting her to drink and clear her name. Either way, the *mishnah*'s teaching is that the majority principle is not asymmetric: it applies in both directions.

To summarize the overall architecture of this *Gemara*: the one witness who testifies to adultery in the *sotah* context carries extraordinary weight, grounded in the prior testimony of warning and seclusion. Ulla holds that once accepted, this testimony is unassailable by a single contradicting voice — it is treated as two witnesses. Rabbi Chiya limits this to sequential testimony; simultaneous contradiction still neutralizes. Rabbi Nechemya introduces the further principle that when the Torah has suspended the formal rules of testimony by accepting a single witness, the remaining criterion is the majority of voices — and this majority operates across gender lines and, in some views, even overrides testimony already accepted, provided the first witness was not a *kosher* male witness whose testimony locks in as formal *edut*.

# Sotah 32

## Previous Perek Review

### Eliezer vs. Yehoshua

Before turning to the new *perek*, it is worth revisiting two points from the material just completed. The *Mishnah* presented a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding the circumstances under which a husband would divorce his wife and provide a *kesuvah*. Rabbi Eliezer held that even a rumor as tenuous as what one might overhear from a passing bird would suffice. Rabbi Yehoshua required something more substantial — people actually witnessed the two together in circumstances suggesting impropriety.

Rashi understood this dispute as relating to the earlier debate about what constitutes valid *stira* — the act of seclusion required to trigger the *sotah* process. That reading, however, sits awkwardly with the plain text of the *Mishnah*. Tosafos offers a considerably cleaner approach: the two Tannaim are actually debating something entirely different. In the cases they discuss, there is no *kinuy* and no *stira* at all — only rumors. The debate concerns what kind of rumors are sufficient to warrant advising the husband to divorce his wife. Since there is no proper halachic basis for the *sotah* procedure, the husband must in any event provide a *kesuvah*. Tosafos's reading is the more natural one.

### Witnesses & Timing

The second point concerns the case of two witnesses who contradict one another — one testifying that the woman became *temei'ah* and the other that she did not. The question is whether they are neutralized by one another only when they testify simultaneously, or also when one comes after the other.

Rashi explains "simultaneously" as meaning within *toch k'dei dibbur* — the brief interval considered legally contemporaneous with speech. Tosafos disagrees. According to Tosafos, once *beis din* has already heard and ruled on the first testimony, a subsequent contradicting witness carries no weight. But if both witnesses appear before *beis din* before any ruling is issued, they neutralize one another, regardless of whether one spoke a moment before the other.

### Elu Ne'emarim Intro

With those clarifications in place, we now open a new *perek* — *Elu Ne'emarim*. While it begins with a point about *sotah*, the *perek* is in fact broad and consequential, addressing the *halacha* of reciting texts: which texts must be recited specifically in *lashon hakodesh*, and which may be said in translation.

---

## Bechol Lashon

### Sotah & Ma'aser

The *Mishnah* opens: *elu ne'emarim bechol lashon* — the following may be recited in any language. The first two items are *Parshas Sotah* and *viduy ma'aser*.

*Parshas Sotah* refers to the verbal component of the *sotah* procedure — the priest's address to the woman, her response of *amen amen*, and so forth. This is striking: the text is written in Hebrew, and the document is scraped into the water in Hebrew, yet the recitation itself may be in any language.

*Viduy ma'aser* is the declaration made at the end of the third year, in which the person states that all accumulated *ma'aser* has been properly distributed and removed from his home. The *Torah* provides a specific text for this declaration. That both of these — cases where the *Torah* itself specifies a formal text — may nonetheless be recited in translation is a considerable *chiddush*.

### Shema & Tefillah

The *Mishnah* continues its list: *Krias Shema*, *tefillah* (meaning *Shemoneh Esrei*), and *Birkas HaMazon* may all be recited in any language. One might pause and ask: for *tefillah* and *Birkas HaMazon*, the *Torah* provides no fixed text — it simply requires that one thank and bless God. Why would I have assumed these must be in Hebrew at all? Perhaps the *Mishnah*'s point is that even where there is no prescribed text, one might have thought there exists an inherent sanctity to the Hebrew language that demands its use even in open-ended recitation. The *Mishnah* dispels this: in all these cases, any language is valid.

### Shvuas Ha'Eidus

The *Mishnah* also lists *shvuas ha'eidus* and *shvuas hapikadon* as permissible in any language. *Shvuas ha'eidus* arises when someone adjures witnesses to testify on his behalf, and they falsely deny having seen anything relevant — they are liable to bring a *korban* for this oath. *Shvuas hapikadon* arises when someone denies having received an object for safekeeping, swears falsely to that effect, and later admits the truth — similarly requiring a *korban*. Both may be administered and taken in any language.

### Tosafot: Shomeia

Tosafos makes an important observation about the phrase *elu ne'emarim bilshonam* — they are recited in *their* language. He explains: *u'peirush kol adam bilshono she'hu shomeia* — the meaning is that each person recites in a language he actually understands. The example he gives is telling: one cannot fulfill the obligation by reciting in a foreign language he does not comprehend. Interestingly, however, Tosafos concedes that Hebrew — even if not understood — would still be valid, which opens a broader question about *kavana* and the degree of comprehension required for each individual area of *halacha*.

Tosafos then raises a tension: the word *bechol lashon* in the *Mishnah* seems to imply any language whatsoever, without any requirement of understanding — *bein shomeia bein eino shomeia*. And yet, as the *Gemara* will show regarding *Shema*, understanding does seem to matter. Tosafos thus flags the question of whether one can recite a translated text in a language he does not understand and still fulfill his obligation.

### Tosafot: Other Items

Tosafos raises a further question: the *Mishnah* lists certain items that may be said in any language, but omits a great many others — *Hallel*, *Shir HaShirim*, *Kiddush* of Shabbos, *brachos* before food, *birkas hamitzvos*, and so forth. Why are these not listed?

One might suggest the *Mishnah* limits itself to *de-Oraisa* obligations, but Tosafos dismisses this: *tefillah* is most likely *de-Rabbanan*, *Krias Shema* is *de-Rabbanan* according to some views, while *Kiddush* is *de-Oraisa*. The categories do not align neatly enough to support such a distinction.

### Tosafot: No Shomeia

Tosafos resolves this by drawing a distinction between two types of items. The items the *Mishnah* lists — *Parshas Sotah*, *viduy ma'aser*, *Krias Shema* — may be said in any language, but only if the speaker understands what he is saying. The items Tosafos mentions as omitted — *brachos* before food, *birkas hamitzvos*, and the like — may be said in any language even without understanding. Because those items operate differently, they are not comparable to the *Mishnah*'s list and were therefore not included. This distinction is admittedly difficult to explain on principled grounds, but Tosafos acknowledges it clearly.

---

## Bilshon Hakodesh

### Hebrew Texts List

The *Mishnah* then turns to texts that must be recited specifically in *lashon hakodesh*: *Mikra Bikkurim* (the declaration of *aram oveid avi* when bringing first fruits), *chalitza* (including the woman's declaration of *kacha ye'aseh la'ish* and the accompanying shoe removal and spitting), *brachos* and *klalos* on *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eival*, *Birkas Kohanim*, the blessing of the *Kohen Gadol* on *Yom Kippur* when he reads from the *Sefer Torah*, *Parshas Hamelech* at *Hakhel*, and *Parshas Eglah Arufah* — the declaration of the elders: *yadeinu lo shafchu es hadam hazeh*.

One item that stands out as particularly surprising is the address of the *mashuach milchama* — the *kohen* anointed for war — when he speaks to the troops. He informs them: whoever has built a new house, planted a vineyard, or betrothed a wife may return home. This is not a ritual recitation in any conventional sense; it is a practical communication designed specifically to be understood. If there is any context in which we would expect translation to be permitted — indeed required — it would be this one. And yet this too must be in *lashon hakodesh*.

It should be noted: just because the recitation must be in Hebrew does not necessarily mean the *chalitza* itself is invalid if the text is not recited in Hebrew. That is a separate question treated elsewhere.

As for *brachos* and *klalos* on *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eival*: this is not an ongoing *halachic* obligation but a historical event. The reason it is mentioned in the *Mishnah* is that it serves as the exegetical basis — the *gehezera shava* anchor — for the other items requiring *lashon hakodesh*, as the *Gemara* will now explain.

### Mikra Bikkurim

How do we know that *Mikra Bikkurim* must be in *lashon hakodesh*? The *Gemara* points to the juxtaposition of two phrases. By *bikkurim* the *Torah* says *ve'anita ve'amarta lifnei Hashem elokecha* — you shall respond and say before God. By the *brachos* and *klalos* on the mountains, it says *ve'anu haLevi'im ve'amru* — the Levites shall respond and say. The combination of the verbs "respond" and "say" appears in both contexts. Just as the *brachos* and *klalos* on *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eival* were in *lashon hakodesh*, so too *Mikra Bikkurim* must be in *lashon hakodesh*.

### Chalitza

The same *gezera shava* applies to *chalitza*. By *chalitza*, the *Torah* writes *ve'aneta ve'amra* — she shall respond and say. By the Levites on the mountains, it says *ve'anu haLevi'im ve'amru*. The same dual-verb construction creates the link: just as the mountains required *lashon hakodesh*, so does *chalitza*.

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees. He holds that by *chalitza* there is no need to derive the Hebrew requirement from the mountains via this *gezera shava*. The *Torah* itself says *ve'amra kacha* — she shall say "thus," meaning she must say it in precisely this manner — *ad she'tomar balashon hazeh*, until she says it in this very language. The word *kacha* itself implies the exact wording, which is inherently the Hebrew text as given.

---

## Har Gerizim & Eival

### Geography

Having established that the *brachos* and *klalos* on *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eival* serve as the foundation for the other *lashon hakodesh* requirements, the *Mishnah* now describes that ceremony in detail. It begins with the geography.

Once the Jewish people crossed the Jordan, they came to *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eival*, which are in *Shomron*, alongside *Shechem*, near *elonei Moreh*. The *Torah* provides these geographic markers, and the *Gemara* explains how we know that *elonei Moreh* refers to *Shechem*: the *Torah* elsewhere says that Avram passed through the land *ad mekom Shechem ad elon Moreh*. Just as *elon Moreh* in that earlier verse refers to *Shechem*, so the *elon Moreh* mentioned in connection with *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eival* likewise refers to *Shechem*.

### Arrangement

Six tribes ascended *Har Gerizim* and six ascended *Har Eival* — those on *Har Gerizim* for the *bracha*, those on *Har Eival* for the *kelala*. It is worth noting that even today *Har Gerizim* is covered with vegetation while *Har Eival* is entirely barren — a striking natural correspondence to the roles each mountain was assigned.

The *kohanim*, *Levi'im*, and the *aron* stood below in the middle, between the two mountains. The *kohanim* encircled the *aron* as an inner protective ring; the *Levi'im* encircled the *kohanim*. All the remaining Israelites stood on both sides — six tribes on each mountain. This is supported by the verse in *Yehoshua*: *vechol Yisrael uzekanav veshotrav veshofetav omdim mizeh umizeh la'aron*.

### Brachos & Klalos

The *Mishnah* then describes the recitation. They turned toward *Har Gerizim* and opened with the *bracha*: *baruch haish asher lo yaaseh pesel umasecha* — blessed is the man who does not make a graven image. Both groups — those on *Har Gerizim* and those on *Har Eival* — responded *amen*. This is notable: despite the two mountains representing two opposing paths, the *amen* response came from all of Israel together. Then they turned toward *Har Eival* and recited the corresponding *klala*: *arur haish asher yaaseh pesel umasecha* — and again, both groups responded *amen*.

The sequence alternated — *bracha*, *klala*, *bracha*, *klala* — until all the *brachos* and *klalos* were completed. This interleaving is natural and deliberate: the two choices are set before the people together, blessing and curse side by side.

### 70 Languages

After completing the *brachos* and *klalos*, they brought the stones and built the *mizbeiach* — the *Mishnah* understands that the inscribed stones and the altar stones were one and the same — plastered them over with lime and wrote upon them *kol divrei haTorah beshivim lashon*, the entire *Torah* in 70 languages. The source for this is the *Torah*'s instruction to write these words *be'er heitev* — very clearly and well explicated.

What makes this deeply significant in context is the juxtaposition. The *brachos* and *klalos* — which must be in *lashon hakodesh* — serve as the basis for other things that must be in *lashon hakodesh*. And yet standing right alongside them, at this very same moment of national commitment, is the writing of the *Torah* in all 70 languages. This will become directly relevant when the *Gemara* later discusses the principle of *kol haTorah kulah bechol lashon ne'emra*.

After the ceremony, the stones were dismantled, and the people went and spent the night in their place — Rashi identifies this as *Gilgal*. There is some complexity here, as *Yehoshua* describes twelve stones taken from the feet of the *kohanim* at the crossing of the *Yarden*, which seem to be a distinct monument erected at *Gilgal* to commemorate the crossing. A degree of conflation between the two accounts exists, but the *Mishnah* does not address it directly.

---

## Gezera Shava

### Sotah Language

The *Gemara* now asks: how do we know that *Parshas Sotah* may be recited in any language? The source is the verse *ve'amar hakohen laisha* — the priest shall say to the woman. Rashi cites the parallel verse *ve'amar el haisha* — to the woman — which implies that the recitation is about reaching her, communicating to her in a way she takes to heart. The word *amar* is a generic verb of communication, as opposed to the double-verb construction (*ve'anu ve'amru*) that signals a specific formal text. The sense of *el ha'isha* is *devarim hanichnasim belibah* — words that enter her heart — meaning any language that she understands.

### Woman's Understanding

A *baraisa* makes this explicit: *mashmi'in osah bechol lashon shehi shoma'as* — she is informed in any language that she understands. This connects to Tosafos's earlier point about *shomeia*: in translation, the requirement of understanding the language is operative.

### Four Topics

The *baraisa* then specifies the four topics that must be communicated to her: *al ma hi shotah uvmah hi shotah, al mah nitmes uvmah hi nitmes* — why she is drinking and in what vessel, and for what she has become *tamei* and by what means.

These four topics are not uniform in character. *Al ma hi shotah* — why she is drinking — refers to the formal halachic criteria: there was *kinuy* and *stira*; this is why the procedure is taking place. *Uvmah hi shotah* — in what she is drinking — refers to the earthenware vessel used, a detail chosen for its demeaning quality, signaling the diminished state she has brought upon herself.

*Al mah nitmes* — for what she became *tamei* — is not halachic criteria but *mussar*: *al iskei schok veyaldus*, it comes from frivolity and immaturity, from conduct that opens the door to such situations. *Uvmah hi nitmes* — by what means — returns to halachic territory: *beshogeg o bemeizid, be'ones o beratzon* — was it inadvertent or deliberate, coerced or willing? This matters greatly because only the willful and uncoerced transgression is tested by the waters.

The reason all of this is spelled out to her — at least the last point — is *shelo lehotzi la'az al hamayim hamarim*: so she should not emerge and claim the waters have no power, having drunk them without effect. She must understand that certain circumstances — *shogeg*, *ones* — exempt from the trial, and her survival in those cases reflects nothing about the efficacy of the waters.

### Praise & Faults

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai teaches: a person should speak his own praises in a low voice, and his own faults loudly. How do we know praises should be in an undertone? From *viduy ma'aser*: the declaration is in essence a statement of everything one did correctly — *asisi kechol asher tzivisani, hashkifa mimon kodshecha* — yet the *Torah* does not say *ve'anu ve'amru*, the language of proclamation; it simply says *ve'amarta*, you shall say. Quietly, without fanfare.

And how do we know one's pain or difficult circumstances should be proclaimed? The *Gemara* says: from *Mikra Bikkurim*. There, *matchil bignus* — one begins with the difficult opening, *arami oveid avi*, evoking the suffering of our ancestors and the precarious origins of our people — and this is recited publicly and aloud.

### Viduy as Praise

The *Gemara* observes that the parallel drawn here is somewhat imprecise. *Viduy ma'aser* is straightforwardly self-praise, but *Mikra Bikkurim* is not exactly *gnus* in the sense of personal fault. It is more in the category of *tza'ara* — difficulty, pain, a less than triumphant chapter of one's story. The teaching therefore is refined: one should not merely hide sinful conduct; rather, one should feel free to share one's suffering openly, because doing so invites others to pray on one's behalf. This is the deeper point: *kol mi she'ira bo davar tzarich lehodi'a lerabbim, verabbim mevakshim alav rachamim* — whoever experiences hardship should make it known, so that others may seek mercy on his behalf.

This is illustrated by *vetamei tamei yikra*: the *metzora* sent outside the camp is required to announce his condition — *tzarich lehodi'a tza'aro lerabbim verabbim mevakshim alav rachamim*. The pastoral point is powerful: people who are suffering often conceal it, either out of pride or a reluctance to burden others. The *Torah* and *Chazal* take a different view — sharing one's pain opens the door for communal support and prayer.

### Tefillah Undertone

Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, teaches: why was *tefillah* established as a silent, undertone recitation? We know the model from *Chana* — *vekolah lo yishama* — but why did *Chazal* adopt that model? *Kedei shelo levayesh es ovrei aveirah* — in order not to embarrass those who have sinned. When a person stands before God in *tefillah*, he should feel free to speak honestly about his failures and transgressions. If *tefillah* were recited aloud, people would be inhibited. The intimate, private character of silent *tefillah* allows for genuine, unguarded honesty.

This observation also carries with it an implicit point: *tefillah* is not merely the recitation of a fixed text. One is expected to add personal words within *Shemoneh Esrei* — to speak to God about one's own life, needs, and failures. The structure exists to enable that conversation, not to replace it.

### Chatas & Olah

The same principle — protecting the sinner from public embarrassment — is illustrated from the laws of *korbanos*. A *chatas* and an *olah* are both slaughtered in the northern part of the *azarah*. Because they share the same location, a bystander watching someone bring an animal cannot tell from the place of *shechita* whether that person has sinned and is bringing a *chatas* or has done nothing wrong and is bringing an *olah*. The *halacha* itself is structured to protect a sinner's dignity.

### Blood Distinction

The *Gemara* immediately raises a challenge: is the distinction truly concealed? The application of the blood differs — *dam chatas lemala*, the blood of a *chatas* is applied to the horns at the top of the *mizbeiach*, while *dam olah lemata*, the blood of an *olah* is cast on the lower walls. A careful observer could discern the difference.

The *Gemara* responds: *hasam kohen hu deyada* — only the *kohen* knows. By the time the blood is being applied, it is the *kohen* performing the service, and the layperson watching from the *azarah* may not readily follow the technical details of blood application. Tosafos, however, raises the obvious question: are we really to assume that observers are so inattentive? The *Gemara* accepts the answer but the difficulty is real.

### Gender Concealment

The *Gemara* raises a further challenge: a *chatas* must be a female animal and an *olah* must be male. If observers can see which sex of animal a person hands to the *kohen*, the distinction is transparent.

The *Gemara* answers: *chasuy mechasya be-alyah* — the fat tail of a sheep covers and conceals the genitals, so passersby cannot readily determine the animal's sex. The *Gemara* thus assumes that for sheep specifically, the distinction is not obvious. Tosafos again notes the somewhat strained assumption that people are carefully observing these details.

### Avodah Zarah

The *Gemara* then presses the point: what about a *chatas* brought specifically for *avodah zarah*? That *korban* may only be a female goat, and a goat has no concealing fat tail. The sex of the animal is visible, and therefore the nature of the sin is apparent to anyone watching. How does the principle of concealment apply here?

The *Gemara* responds: *hasam nichsof ve-nechsi ki heichi de-niskapar lei* — in the case of *avodah zarah*, a measure of additional embarrassment is not only appropriate but perhaps necessary. The severity of the sin of *avodah zarah* demands a more complete process of atonement and shame, and the public visibility of one's *korban* contributes to that process. For ordinary sins, the *Torah* protects the sinner's dignity; for *avodah zarah*, it does not — and this is entirely fitting.

---

## Shema Language

### Shema Any Language

The *Gemara* turns to *Krias Shema*. How do we know it may be recited in any language? From the word *shema* — *be-chol lashon she-ata shomea* — "hear" means: in any manner and language in which you can understand. The *Gemara* is treating the first word of *Krias Shema* as itself a legal instruction, indicating that understanding is central and therefore any language that conveys understanding is valid.

It should be noted that this *Gemara* treats *Krias Shema* as *de-Oraisa*. As Tosafos discusses at length, other *Gemoras* seem to suggest it may be *de-Rabbanan*, and no fully settled position emerges from the *stam* of the *Gemara*. But the present sugya proceeds on the assumption that at least the first *pasuk* or first paragraph carries biblical force.

### Rabbi vs. Rabbanan

A *baraisa* records the dispute directly. Rabbi says: *Krias Shema ki-ksava* — it must be read exactly as it is written, meaning in Hebrew, and cannot be recited in translation. The Sages say: it may be recited in any language.

### Rabbi's Ve'hayu

Rabbi's reason: the verse says *ve'hayu hadevarim ha-eileh al levavecha* — "and these words shall be upon your heart." The word *ve'hayu* — they shall be — implies that the words must remain exactly as they are, in the form in which they were given. This is analogous to the principle of *kacha* in *chalitza*: the formulation demands the precise original text.

### Rabbanan Shema

The Sages, by contrast, emphasize *shema* — hear, understand. The central obligation is comprehension, and comprehension is achievable in any language. As for *ve'hayu* — the Sages use it to derive a different *halacha* entirely: *shelo yikra lamafreia* — one may not recite *Krias Shema* out of order. The words, the sentences, the paragraphs must follow their proper sequence. *Ve'hayu* thus governs order rather than language.

Where does Rabbi derive the prohibition against reciting *Krias Shema* out of order, given that he uses *ve'hayu* for the language requirement? The *Gemara* answers: from the doubling of the expression — *ve'hayu hadevarim*, rather than simply *ve'hayu devarim*. The additional *heh* signals an additional requirement. The Sages do not accept this kind of inference from the extra *heh* and therefore have no need to overload *ve'hayu* with both requirements.

### Hearing Requirement

What does Rabbi do with the word *shema*? *Lehashmia oznecha mah she-ata motzi mi-picha* — you must let your ears hear what comes out of your mouth. This is the *halacha* of audibility: one must recite *Shema* at a volume that at minimum is audible to oneself.

The Sages, on the other hand, hold in accordance with the view that *hakore es Shema v'lo hishmia l'ozno yatza* — one fulfills the obligation even if one does not hear oneself. For the Sages, *shema* means language comprehension, not audibility.

The result is that Rabbi is strict on both dimensions: Hebrew is required, and audibility is required. The Sages are lenient on both: any language is valid, and audibility is not required. One might have expected the correlations to run differently — those who require the formal Hebrew text might care less about audibility (since the focus is on the text, not comprehension), while those who permit translation might specifically demand audibility (since comprehension is the goal). Tosafos notes and explores these possibilities, but the *Gemara* as it stands presents Rabbi and the Sages each internally consistent on their respective positions.

---

## Torah Bechol Lashon

### Deduction

The *Gemara* now raises a broader question flowing from the dispute between Rabbi and the Sages. Can we infer from Rabbi's position — which requires *Krias Shema* in Hebrew and derives this from *ve'hayu* — that Rabbi holds *kol haTorah bechol lashon ne'emra*, that the general rule is that Torah texts may be recited in any language? For if Rabbi's default were that everything must be in Hebrew, why would he need *ve'hayu* to establish that *Krias Shema* must be in Hebrew? That would simply follow from the general rule.

The *Gemara* deflects: the verse was still necessary because of the word *shema*, which could have implied that even Rabbi permits any language here. *Ve'hayu* is therefore needed to counter that inference and confirm that even in this case, the general requirement of Hebrew applies.

Similarly, one might infer from the Sages' position that they hold the default is Hebrew — otherwise, why would they need the word *shema* to permit any language? The *Gemara* deflects again: *shema* was still necessary because *ve'hayu* could have been read as an exception demanding Hebrew even for those who in principle permit any language. Both proofs are thus deflected, and neither Rabbi nor the Sages can be definitively assigned to one side of the broader principle.

### Default Rule

The principle of *kol haTorah kulah bechol lashon ne'emra* — Torah was given in all languages — is best understood as a question about the default rule. When the *Torah* requires a text to be recited, is the baseline assumption that any language will serve, or is the baseline Hebrew? The position of *bechol lashon ne'emra* holds that all languages are inherently valid; items requiring specifically *lashon hakodesh* are exceptions to that default. The opposing view holds that *lashon hakodesh* is the default, and explicit permission is needed to allow translation.

As the Tosafot Shantz explains, the practical implication is this: when the *Torah* provides a text for recitation and says nothing explicit about language, does the text remain inherently open to translation, or does it presumptively require Hebrew?

### 70 Languages Link

This entire discussion connects powerfully to what the *Mishnah* described earlier. At the very moment the Jewish people crossed the *Yarden* and committed themselves anew to the *Torah*, the first thing they did was write the entire *Torah* in 70 languages — *beshivim lashon*, with the instruction *be'er heitev*, to write it clearly and accessibly. This is an astonishing counterpoint to the *brachos* and *klalos* that must be in *lashon hakodesh* and that serve as the basis for other requirements of Hebrew. Standing alongside those requirements is the vision of *Torah* written in all the languages of the world.

This suggests that *kol haTorah kulah bechol lashon ne'emra* is not merely a legal default rule but reflects something fundamental: the *Torah* is inherently accessible to all peoples in all languages. Where the *Torah* demands *lashon hakodesh* specifically — as it does in the cases derived in this *perek* — that is an exception, requiring its own source and justification. Where no such demand is made, the *Torah*'s native posture is openness to every language.

It is worth noting that Rashi and Tosafos raise the question of whether this principle relates to whether a *Sefer Torah* itself may be written in another language — a separate and well-known debate. But that does not appear to be what the *Gemara* here is discussing. The present discussion concerns something more fundamental: whether Torah recitation, as a category, was always understood to allow for translation — a position grounded in the very act with which Bnei Yisrael began their life in the land.

---

---

# Sotah 33

## All Languages: Sotah, Vi…

### Sotah, Viduy, Shema

The daf opens in the middle of a discussion about which ritual declarations may be recited in any language. Already mentioned are *sotah* — not the writing of the *parsha* but the reciting of it — along with *viduy maaser* and *shema*. All three derive from the *Torah*, and the Mishnah has established that each may be performed in any language.

### Tefillah & Rachamim

*Tefillah* is now addressed. The Gemara states: *rachamei hi* — it is supplication to God, direct communication with God — *vechol heicha deba'i matzlei*, and so one may pray however one needs to speak. Because *tefillah* is at its core a matter of personal address to the Almighty, it is most appropriate that it be expressed in whatever language allows a person to be most articulate.

### Avot vs. Korbanot

This is a significant point, because the word *rachamei* carries a precise conceptual weight in the Gemara. It stands in contrast to the classic debate in Berakhot over whether *tefillah* is *keneged avot* or *keneged korbanot* — whether it corresponds structurally to the *korbanot*, with all their prescribed forms and regulations, or whether it corresponds to the way Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov prayed, which involved no fixed text, no fixed time, and was very much of the heart. The Gemara's conclusion in Berakhot is that at its core *tefillah* is *keneged avot*, though the structure and timing of the *korbanot* have been layered upon it. When the Gemara wants to invoke that core dimension — that *tefillah* is fundamentally personal communication — it uses the phrase *rachamei ninhu*. And it is precisely because of that core that *tefillah* may, in principle, be offered in any language.

### Rav Yehuda & Aramaic

The Gemara immediately challenges this. *Vetefillah bechol lashon?* Is it truly the case that *Shemoneh Esrei* may be said in any language? Does not Rav Yehuda say *leolam al yishal adam tzarachav bilshon Aramit* — one should never make a personal request in Aramaic? And does not Rabbi Yochanan add that whoever makes their request in Aramaic, *ein malachei hasharet nizkakim lo* — the ministering angels will not attend to them?

### Angels & Aramaic

The reason given is *lefi she'ein malachei hasharet makirim bilshon Aramit* — they do not recognize Aramaic. This is a striking idea: that there is something a heavenly being would fail to recognize. Some *Rishonim* qualify this, suggesting it applies specifically to Aramaic rather than to all non-Hebrew languages, and that the issue is not literal non-recognition but a kind of disapproval — the angels regard Aramaic as a corruption of Hebrew, being itself a Semitic language. In any event, the principle is that one should not recite *tefillot* in Aramaic because the angels serve as the bearers of prayer, and they will not convey what is said in that language.

### Individual vs. Communal

The Gemara resolves the tension: *lo kashya — ha beyachid ha betzibur*. The question depends on whether one is praying privately or communally. When one prays as part of a community, God's presence is found directly among the congregation, and there is no need for angelic intermediaries. When one prays privately, the angels are needed to carry the prayer upward, and in that context the Aramaic restriction applies.

One can also understand this on a more conceptual level that extends beyond the specific issue of Aramaic. When one recites the fixed Hebrew text, even if it somewhat constrains one's ability to express oneself with full personal feeling, what is achieved is connection — to the tradition, to the weight and depth of the words themselves, and to a sense of community through a shared text. When one is already praying *betzibur*, that sense of communal connection and *mesorah* is present regardless, and it therefore becomes permissible to pray in another language. But when one is praying alone, the Hebrew text may itself serve as the vehicle that connects the individual to something larger than the private moment.

### Women & Vernacular

This distinction generated discussion among the *Rishonim* because in practice, women — and others not fluent in Hebrew — would recite *Shemoneh Esrei* even when praying privately. This led some *Rishonim* to refine the distinction: the relevant factor is not whether one is literally praying among others, but whether one is reciting a communal prayer as opposed to a wholly personal, self-composed text. If it is a communal prayer like *Shemoneh Esrei*, it may be recited in translation even by someone praying alone — perhaps because God hears the communal prayer wherever it is said, or because one praying *Shemoneh Esrei* at home is, in some sense, joining the larger community offering that same prayer. It may also be that when one composes a personal prayer in one's own words, using one's own language is the most natural approach. In any case, the *Rishonim* ultimately tend to limit Rav Yehuda's restriction specifically to Aramaic, so that once Aramaic ceased to be the vernacular, the practical import of the restriction largely disappeared.

### Angels & Languages

The Gemara now turns to the underlying premise and challenges it directly. *V'ei malachei hasharet makiri belashon Aramit* — is it truly the case that the angels do not know Aramaic? A *baraita* is cited: Yochanan the *Kohen Gadol* heard a *bas kol* from the *Kodesh Hakodashim* — Rashi explains this occurred while he was performing the *avodah* on Yom Kippur — and the voice proclaimed *nitzchu talyaya de'azlu le'agacha kerava le'Antyocha*, that the young men of the *Chashmonaim* who went to battle against the Seleucids were victorious. A second story follows: Shimon HaTzaddik heard a *bas kol* from the *Kodesh Hakodashim* declaring *batlis avidata de'amar sanay le'aysay al heichala* — the campaign that the enemy had planned against the *Beis Hamikdash* has been nullified — and that a certain Greek ruler had been killed and his decrees annulled. The time was recorded, and it was found to correspond exactly to the moment those events occurred. In both cases, *uvelashon Aramit hayah* — the *bas kol* was delivered in Aramaic. Since a *bas kol* presumably passes through an angel, this seems to demonstrate that the angels do know Aramaic.

The Gemara offers two responses. First: *bas kol shani* — a *bas kol* is different, *de'le'ishtamuei avida*, because its very purpose is to be heard and understood by people, so perhaps a special angel delivers such proclamations specifically in the people's language. Second: *ve'i bayit eima Gavriel hava* — perhaps it was Gavriel who was speaking, and Gavriel is the one angel who knows all languages, *de'amar mar ba Gavriel velimdo shivim lashon* — as the master taught, Gavriel came and taught Yosef all seventy languages. These two possibilities resolve the challenge, and the restriction on Aramaic prayer stands as stated.

---

## Birchat Hamazon

### Hamazon Source

The Mishnah next establishes that *birchat hamazon* may also be recited in any language. This requires discussion because *birchat hamazon* is clearly grounded in a *pasuk* in the *Torah*: *ve'achalta vesavata uverachta et Hashem Elokecha* — you shall eat and be satisfied and bless the Lord your God. The fact that it derives from a *Torah* verse might lead one to think that Hebrew is required.

### Rashi vs. Tosafot

Rashi reads the Gemara as simply noting the *pasuk* to indicate that there is no fixed text — since the verse just says "bless," without specifying any particular wording, there is no reason to require Hebrew. On Rashi's reading, the Gemara is not answering a question but simply observing that of course it can be in any language, since there is nothing to translate. Tosafot, however, records a different *girsa* of the Gemara — one that begins with the question *mena hanei milei*, from where do we know this — and argues that Rashi's text has been altered. On Tosafot's reading, the Gemara does need to derive that *birchat hamazon* may be said in any language, because the presence of the word *uverachta* might have led us to think — by comparison to other *brachot* such as *birchat kohanim* that must be said in Hebrew — that here too Hebrew is required. The *pasuk* must therefore be cited to show that it may be said in any language. This is a genuinely striking point: even when there is no fixed textual formula to translate, there is still reason to think that perhaps Hebrew specifically is required — and a *pasuk* is needed to dispel that assumption.

### Hamazon & God

What is the proof from the verse? Tosafot explains: *uverachta et Hashem* — since the *bracha* and the praise are directed *klapei haShechinah*, toward God directly, one may bless in any language one chooses. When the communication is purely between the person and God, with no ritual dimension addressed to others, the language barrier dissolves. This is, notably, quite parallel to the justification for *tefillah* as *rachamei* — direct address to God removes the requirement of a specific sacred tongue. Yet, as Tosafot makes clear, even in such a case the principle needed to be explicitly derived, since there remains an independent reason to require Hebrew even when no prescribed text exists.

---

## Holy Tongue Required

### Oaths in Any Language

The Mishnah also includes *shevuat ha'eidut* — the oath administered to a witness who denies knowing relevant testimony — and derives its permissibility in any language from the verse *v'nefesh ki techeta v'shama kol alah*, since it says *bechol lashon she'hi shoma'at*, in whatever language she hears. The need for a *pasuk* here, too, indicates that even for something not purely ritualistic, there is reason to suppose Hebrew might be required. *Shevuat hapikadon* — the oath regarding a withheld object — is derived from *shevuat ha'eidut* through a *gezeirah shavah* on the word *techeta* appearing in both contexts, and similarly may be administered in any language. The Mishnah's list of things permitted in all languages is thus complete; the *Rishonim* note that many other *brachot* and recitations are of course also said in other languages, but these are the specific items singled out by the Mishnah.

### Lashon Hakodesh List

The Mishnah then turns to the contrasting category: *v'eilu ne'emarim belashon hakodesh* — the following may only be said in *lashon hakodesh*: *mikra bikkurim*, *chalitzah*, *brachot v'klalot*, and others enumerated in the Mishnah.

### Mikra Bikkurim

The Gemara addresses each in turn. For *mikra bikkurim*, the Mishnah derives the requirement from the verse *v'anita v'amarta lifnei Hashem Elokecha* — you shall respond and say before the Lord your God. The double verb *v'anita v'amarta* — respond and say — also appears in the passage of the Levites at *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eival*, where it is written *v'anu halevi'im v'amru el kol ish Yisrael kol ram*. By means of *gezeirah shavah* on the term *aniyah*, we learn: just as there by the *brachot v'klalot* it is in *lashon hakodesh*, so too here by *mikra bikkurim* it must be in *lashon hakodesh*. This is a notable ruling, because one might have thought that *mikra bikkurim* — which is an expression of personal gratitude to God — should be in the language that most allows the individual to speak from the heart. Nevertheless, the *gezeirah shavah* establishes that it requires Hebrew. Perhaps because the declaration in the *Beis Hamikdash* is a public ritual, heard by all present, its formal and communal character calls for the sacred tongue.

### Brachot v'Klalot Source

The Gemara then asks: how do we know that the *brachot v'klalot* of the Levites were themselves in *lashon hakodesh*? The answer comes through another *gezeirah shavah*: the verse by the Levites uses the expression *kol ram* — a loud voice — and separately, in the passage of *matan Torah*, it says *Moshe yedaber vehaElokim ya'anenu b'kol* — Moshe would speak and God would answer him with a voice. Just as there, when God spoke, it was clearly in Hebrew, so too the *kol ram* of the Levites must be in *lashon hakodesh*.

### Chalitzah & Kacha

For *chalitzah*, the Mishnah presents two approaches. The *rabbanan* learn from the double verb *v'ansa v'amra* — she shall respond and say — the same pattern of *aniyah v'amirah* that signals *lashon hakodesh*. Rabbi Yehuda, however, does not require this derivation for *chalitzah* because he learns it from the word *kacha* in the verse *kacha ye'aseh* — so shall it be done. Rabbi Yehuda reads *kacha* rather than the simpler *ko* as indicating two things: the declaration must be in Hebrew, and furthermore, it is specifically the physical acts of *chalitzah* — not the verbal declaration — that are indispensable for the *chalitzah* to be valid. The *rabbanan*, who do not read the elongated *kacha* as teaching two separate points, use it only to establish that the acts are essential, and derive the requirement of Hebrew from *v'ansa v'amra* instead.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Method

The Gemara asks: if Rabbi Yehuda uses *kacha* for both points and does not use *v'ansa v'amra* by *chalitzah*, what does he do with that phrase? The answer is that he needs it to teach regarding the Levites that the *brachot v'klalot* are in *lashon hakodesh*. Rabbi Yehuda's entire chain of derivation thus runs differently from that of the *rabbanan*: he learns that *chalitzah* must be in Hebrew from *kacha*, then uses *chalitzah* to teach that *brachot v'klalot* are in Hebrew, and from there applies the *gezeirah shavah* to *mikra bikkurim*. The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda does not simply learn the Levites' *brachot v'klalot* from the *gezeirah shavah* on *kol* connecting to Moshe and God's voice, as the first approach had done. The answer is that the *gezeirah shavah* on *aniyah* is the tradition he received, while the *kol-kol* connection is not his tradition — at a certain point one cannot ask why one *gezeirah shavah* was chosen over another, as these are matters of received tradition.

### Baraita Rule

A *baraita* is then cited in support of Rabbi Yehuda's view: *kol makom she'ne'emar ko, kacha, aniyah, v'amirah, einu ela lashon hakodesh* — wherever the *Torah* uses the expressions *ko*, *kacha*, *aniyah*, or *amirah*, the requirement is that it be in *lashon hakodesh*. The Baraita applies this to three instances: *ko tevarachu et bnei Yisrael* — referring to *birchat kohanim*; *kacha d'chalitzah* — the *kacha* of *chalitzah*; and *aniyah v'amirah d'Levi'im* — the *aniyah v'amirah* of the Levites by *brachot v'klalot*. From that last anchor point, the derivation extends further to *mikra bikkurim*.

---

## Har Gerizim & Eival

### Location Description

The Mishnah speaks of the ceremony on *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eival*, and the Gemara now examines a *baraita* addressing the precise location of those mountains as described in the verses. The *baraita* cites the verse *halo hemah b'ever haYarden*, behold they are across the Jordan. The phrase is then parsed: *me'ever l'Yarden u'l'halan divrei Rabbi Yehuda* — on the other side of the Jordan, and further beyond, according to Rabbi Yehuda. On this reading, *ever haYarden* denotes the east bank, and the mountains are described as being at a substantial distance from it. *Acharei derech mevo hashemesh* — after the way of the coming of the sun — is read as *mekom she'chamah zorachat*, the place where the sun rises, i.e., from the east. This is admittedly not the simple *peshat* of the verse, but the intent is to emphasize that the mountains are located far from the eastern side of the Jordan.

Continuing: *b'eretz ha'Kna'ani hayoshev ba'aravah* — in the land of the Canaanites who dwell in the valley. This, according to the *baraita*, refers to *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eival*, where the *Kuti'im* (Samaritans) dwell in the current era. *Mul haGilgal* — opposite Gilgal, *samuch l'Gilgal* — near Gilgal, because these mountains are located well to the west of the Jordan, in the direction of Gilgal. *Etzel elonei Moreh* — near *elonei Moreh*, which is identified as *Shechem*. The *baraita* then cites the parallel verse from the story of Avraham — *v'ya'avor Avram ba'aretz ad mekom Shechem, Alon Moreh* — to establish by *gezeirah shavah* that *Alon Moreh* here too means *Shechem*.

A second *baraita* is cited, in which Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Yose recounts that with this very passage he demonstrated to the Samaritans that their *sifrei Torah* were falsified. The Samaritans, who rejected the oral tradition, claimed that *Elon Moreh* by *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eival* referred to *Shechem* — the location they held sacred. Rabbi Elazar responded: *zieftem Toratechem v'lo alissem b'yedchem klum* — you have falsified your Torah and gained nothing thereby — for we too agree that *Elon Moreh* is *Shechem*. But we know this through a *gezeirah shavah* from the verse about Avraham. You, who reject the oral tradition, have no such derivation — where did you learn it from? The precise logic of this exchange requires closer examination; the Gemara's point seems to turn on something beyond the simple identification of the name, though exactly what that additional element is remains somewhat opaque in the text.

### Rabbi Elazar

A different approach to the verse is now presented. Rabbi Elazar says: *halo hem b'ever haYarden — samoch l'Yarden*. The word *ever* does not mean a far distance but rather immediately near. The mountains are located just on the other side of the Jordan — immediately to the west, as soon as one crosses. This contrasts with Rabbi Yehuda's reading of the verse as pointing to a location far from the eastern bank. Rabbi Elazar supports his reading: one cannot interpret the verse as pointing far away from the Jordan, because another verse says *v'haya b'ovrechem et haYarden* — it will be when you cross the Jordan — implying that the erection of the stones and the ceremony of *brachot v'klalot* follow immediately. The phrase *b'yom asher tavru* — on the day that you cross — reinforces that this was to take place immediately upon crossing.

On Rabbi Elazar's reading, *acharei derech mevo hashemesh* means toward the setting of the sun — i.e., to the west — which coheres naturally with a location just across the Jordan on the western bank.

### Problems & Responses

His reading, however, presents difficulties.
