The verse describes the location as *b'eretz ha'Kna'ani*, yet the territory immediately west of the Jordan at the crossing point is the land of the *Chivi*, not the *Kena'ani*. Furthermore, the verse says *hayoshev ba'aravah* — who dwells in the valley — but the *Chivi'im* dwell among mountains and hills, not in a valley. And *mul haGilgal* — opposite Gilgal — is problematic because Gilgal was itself some distance from the actual crossing point, so one could not truly say that the crossing spot faces Gilgal.

### Second Direction

These difficulties lead to the interpretation of Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov: *lo ba hakatuv ela l'harot lahem derech bishniya k'derech sheher'a lahem berishona* — the verse from *mul haGilgal* onward is not describing the location of *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eival* at all. Rather, it is providing directional guidance for entering the land. When they left Egypt, the *Bnei Yisrael* were guided by the *ananei kavod*; now, entering the land a second time without those clouds, the Torah provides geographical markers to orient their movement. The mention of the valley, Gilgal, and the land of the *Kena'ani* are thus waypoints for the journey into the land — not descriptors of where the ceremony took place. Rashi adds that following this path through the valley, past Gilgal, and through the land of the *Kena'ani* ensures that they penetrate deep into the land rather than remaining near the Jordan crossing.

---

## Jordan Crossing

### Aron Crosses First

A *baraita* describes how the *Bnei Yisrael* actually crossed the Jordan. On a normal day of travel through the wilderness, the order was: two of the tribal camps would march first, then the *aron* would follow behind the first two *degalim*. But on the day of the crossing, *nasa techila* — the *aron* went first. This was necessary because the *aron* carried by the Levites entering the water is what caused the waters to stop flowing. The verse is cited: *hinei aron habrit adon kol ha'aretz over lifneichem baYarden* — the *aron habrit* of the master of the whole world passes before you into the Jordan.

### Three Times

Ordinarily it was the *Levi'im* who carried the *aron*, but on the day of the crossing, *nas'u hakohanim* — it was the *kohanim* who carried it. The verse confirms: *vehaya kenach kapot raglei hakohanim nosei aron Hashem* — when the feet of the *kohanim* bearing the *aron of Hashem* came to rest in the Jordan. A *baraita* adds: Rabbi Yosei says there were three occasions on which the *kohanim* specifically carried the *aron* — when they crossed the Jordan, when they circled Yericho, and when the *aron* was returned to its permanent place when Shlomo brought it into the *Kodesh Hakodashim*.

### Waters Back Up

As soon as the feet of the *kohanim* touched the water, *chazaru hamayim le'achoreihem* — the waters turned backward. Unlike the splitting of the *Yam Suf*, where a sea was divided, here the Jordan was a rushing river; the oncoming water met resistance and could no longer flow forward, while the water already below drained away, leaving dry ground. The verse is cited: *vaya'amdu hamayim hayordim milmala, kamu ned echad* — the waters descending from above stood, forming a single wall.

### 12 Mil Dimensions

How high did this wall of water rise? Rabbi Yehuda says: *shneim asar mil al shneim asar mil, keneged machaneh Yisrael* — 12 *mil* by 12 *mil*, corresponding to the size of the camp of Israel. The width of the Jordan itself was approximately 50 *amot* (which corresponds closely to the river's present width of about 60 feet). The dimensions of 12 *mil* by 12 *mil* therefore describe not the width of the wall across the river, but the extent to which the water backed up — 12 *mil* in depth along the river and 12 *mil* in height. A *mil* is 2,000 *amot*, approximately a kilometer, so 12 *mil* represents roughly 12 kilometers. The camp of Israel was understood to occupy a square of 12 *mil* by 12 *mil* when they traveled.

### Water Speed

Rabbi Eliezer ben Shimon challenges Rabbi Yehuda's calculation. *Adam kal o mayim kalim* — which moves faster, a person or flowing water? *Hevei omer mayim kalim* — clearly the water is faster. If the wall was only 12 *mil* high, and water moves faster than people, then by the time the *Bnei Yisrael* finished crossing — which took as long as it would take to traverse 12 *mil* — the rushing water from upstream would have risen far higher than 12 *mil* and would have simply crashed over that wall and drowned them. *Im ken bayim mayim veshotef otam* — if so, the waters would have come and swept them away.

### 300 Mil Height

The answer: *ela melamed shehayu mayim nikdashim ve'olim kippin al gabei kippin* — rather, the waters were sanctified and piled up in layers upon layers, *yoter mishlosh meot mil* — more than 300 *mil* in height. This reflects the assumption that water travels approximately 25 times faster than people walk, and so in the time it took the nation to cross, the backed-up water rose to more than 300 *mil* high.

### Kings' Response

The miraculous scale of the event was such that *ad she'ra'u otam kol malchei mizrach uma'arav* — until all the kings of the East and the West saw it. The verse in Sefer Yehoshua is cited: when all the kings of the Amorites on the western side of the Jordan heard how God had dried up the waters of the Jordan before the *Bnei Yisrael* until they had passed through, *vayimas levavam* — their hearts melted — and *velo hayah bahem od ruach mipnei bnei Yisrael* — they no longer had any spirit to stand against the *Bnei Yisrael*.

The Gemara adds that even before the crossing of the Jordan, Rachav had told Yehoshua's messengers about the earlier miracle of the *Yam Suf*: *ki shamanu et asher hovish Hashem et mei Yam Suf* — we heard how God dried up the waters of the *Yam Suf* — and *venishma vayimas levavenu velo kamah od* — and we heard and our hearts melted and no spirit remained. The parallel phrasing between Rachav's account of the *Yam Suf* and the verse describing the reaction of the kings to the Jordan crossing underscores that the miracles at both bodies of water formed a unified arc of Divine intervention that broke the resolve of *Bnei Yisrael*'s enemies. The discussion of the Jordan crossing will continue on the following daf.

---

---

# Sotah 34

## Jordan Crossing

### Daf 34 Overview

Daf 34 picks up twenty lines down, at the words *odam ba-Yarden* — "while they were still in the Jordan" — in the midst of a *baraita* drawn from the *Tosefta*. The broader context is the *Mishnah*'s discussion of what may be said in any language versus what must be recited specifically in *lashon ha-kodesh*. The *Mishnah* had ruled that the blessings and curses pronounced on Har Gerizim and Har Eival could only be said in Hebrew, and the *Gemara* has been unfolding a detailed account of everything that accompanied the crossing of the Jordan into Canaan: the erection of the stones, the building of the *mizbe'ach*, and the proclamation of the *brachos* and *klalos*. Daf 34 continues from within that narrative.

### Joshua's Condition

While the *kohanim* were still standing in the Jordan — and indeed all of *Bnei Yisrael* were still in the river — Yehoshua addressed them: *de'u al mah atem overim et ha-Yarden*, "understand for what purpose you are crossing the Jordan." He stated the condition explicitly: *al menat she-torishu et yoshvei ha-aretz mi-pneichem* — you are crossing on the condition that you commit yourselves to driving out the inhabitants of the land. The *baraita* cites the verse in Bamidbar, *ve-horashtem et kol yoshvei ha-aretz mi-pneichem*, and adds: if you fulfill this, well and good — but *im lav*, if you do not, *ba'u mayim u-shotefim etchem*, the waters will come and drown you. Whether this means that failure to agree at that moment would bring immediate catastrophe, or that failure to ultimately carry it out would lead to that consequence, the text leaves somewhat open; the latter reading seems more natural. The *Gemara* then notes the unusual phrasing *otichem* — "you" — and derives that Yehoshua was saying *oti ve-etchem*, the waters will come and destroy me together with you. He included himself in the threat.

### Twelve Stones

Again while standing in the Jordan, Yehoshua instructed them: *harimu lachem ish even achat al shichmo le-mispar shivtei Yisrael* — each man should take up one stone on his shoulder, corresponding to the twelve tribes, taken from the Jordan itself, and erect them after crossing over. The verse states: *le-ma'an tihyeh zot ot be-kirbechem* — this shall be a sign in your midst — so that when future generations ask, *mah ha-avanim ha-eleh lachem*, "what are these stones?", they will be told that the forefathers crossed the Jordan. This language resonates with the *pasuk* about the *Korban Pesach* and the exchange recalled in the *Seder*. The purpose of the stones, the *Gemara* says, is as a *siman la-vanim she-avru avot ha-Yarden* — a sign for children that the forefathers crossed the Jordan.

A further instruction followed: *se'u lachem mizeh mi-toch ha-Yarden mi-matzav raglei ha-kohanim* — take from where the *kohanim* are standing twelve stones, carry them with you, and place them *ba-malon asher talinu vo ha-laila*, in the place where you will sleep that night. One might have thought this meant they should carry the stones to every encampment — but the *Talmud* derives from the phrase *asher talinu vo ha-laila*, "where we will sleep this night," that only the first encampment is meant.

Rashi's comment at the verse *seu mizeh mi-toch ha-Yarden mi-matzav* is worth noting: he explains that the people lifted up stones, the *kohanim* stood on them, and the stones were then taken from beneath the feet of the *kohanim*. Rashi further states that these were the very stones later erected on Har Eival, upon which the *mizbe'ach* was built and the *Torah* inscribed *be'er heitev* — and that they were subsequently taken down and re-erected in Gilgal. The precise relationship among the three distinct elements — the altar, the writing of the *Torah* on the stones *be'er heitev*, and the twelve commemorative stones — is not straightforward, and working out their interconnection is no simple matter.

### Grape Cluster

The *baraita* records that Rabbi Yehuda — or according to another reading, Rabbi Yose — reported that Abba Chalafta, Rabbi Eliezer ben Matya, and Chananya ben Chakinai once stood on those very stones, and measured that each stone weighed the equivalent of forty *se'ah*, an enormous weight. A received tradition (*gemiri*) teaches that the load a person can lift and hoist onto his own shoulders is only one-third of what he can carry if another person loads him. Since Yehoshua instructed them to have the stones lifted onto their shoulders — implying they were loaded by others — this shows that each carrier could bear the equivalent of 120 *se'ah*. From this calculation, the *Gemara* derives: *mikan ata mitchashev la-eshkol* — from here you can reckon the size of the grape cluster.

The verse says the spies carried the grape cluster *bamot bishnayim*, with a pole between two. But if a pole already implies two carriers, why does the verse add the word *bishnayim*? The *Gemara* answers: *bishnei motot* — there were two poles. Rabbi Yitzchak adds the term *turtani ve-turtani de-turtani* — poles upon poles — indicating not merely two poles but four. Rashi explains the arrangement: two poles running in parallel and two crossing beneath them in an X formation, providing additional support. Eight people in total carried it.

This raises an obvious question about the sheer weight: if a single person, when loaded by another, can carry 120 *se'ah*, and eight people are carrying together with four poles, the cluster must have been of staggering proportions. The *Gemara* elaborates: one person carried a pomegranate, one carried a fig, eight carried the single cluster of grapes — and Yehoshua and Kalev carried nothing at all. Two explanations are offered: either *mishum de-chashivei*, because they were too distinguished to carry anything, or *she-lo hayu be-oto eitzah* — because they were not part of the scheme. The bringing back of the fruit was, in their view, part of the strategy to frighten the people and was not a genuine celebration of the land's bounty.

### Formation Debate

The *Gemara* records a dispute between Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzchak Napcha concerning how the Israelites crossed the Jordan. This connects to the earlier debate — recalled from the previous daf — about how high the waters piled up. Rabbi Yehuda had held that the waters rose twelve *mil*, because the camp was twelve *mil* across, and the time it took the camp to cross was the time during which the waters accumulated. Rabbi Eliezer b'Rabbi Shimon disagreed sharply, saying the waters rose 300 *mil* — twenty-five times the camp's width — because water moves far faster than people walk.

One opinion among Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzchak Napcha holds: according to Rabbi Yehuda, *ke-chaniyatan avru* — they crossed just as they were encamped, in a twelve-by-twelve square formation — and that is why it took the length of time it did to traverse the Jordan, producing a twelve-*mil* accumulation of water. According to Rabbi Eliezer b'Rabbi Shimon, *be-fispecha achat avru* — they crossed in a more elongated procession, something closer to a marching line rather than a square — and therefore it took far longer to pass through, causing the waters to pile much higher. This reading is somewhat surprising, since Rabbi Eliezer b'Rabbi Shimon's stated position was simply that water travels faster than people, not that they marched in a different formation — but the *Gemara* suggests this may also be part of his position.

The other opinion holds that *bein mar u-vein mar ke-chaniyatan avru* — both authorities agree that they crossed in the same square formation as they were encamped. The debate is purely about speed: *mar savar adam kal*, one holds that a person travels as fast as the water (an admittedly difficult image), while *mar savar mayim kalim*, the other holds that water moves far faster than people. This second reading appears to be the more straightforward account of what the earlier dispute actually was.

Tosafot engages in an extended analysis arising from the fact that the Jordan was only fifty *amot* wide. If Yehoshua addressed all of *Bnei Yisrael* while they were standing in the river, and if the camp measured twelve *mil* — which equals 2,400 *amot* — then there would need to be 480 units of people in a fifty-*amot*-wide riverbed to accommodate the entire camp, meaning the people would have had to move steadily downstream as more entered behind them. Tosafot attempts to calculate whether the Jordan itself was even long enough to contain them all simultaneously, and the mathematics are far from trivial.

---

## Spies Mission

### Shlach vs. Devarim

Since the discussion has been centered on Yehoshua, the crossing into the land, and the figures of Yehoshua and Kalev who brought back fruit from Canaan, the *Gemara* transitions naturally to the episode of the spies. The text now takes up the relationship between the two accounts of that mission: the version in *Shlach* and the retelling in Devarim.

In *Shlach* the Torah reads *shlach lecha anashim* — send men. Reish Lakish explains: *shlach lecha mada'atcha* — "go ahead, do it from your own mind," meaning God was granting permission, not issuing a command. This reconciles the two accounts: in Devarim, Moshe recalls that the people came to him requesting the mission; in *Shlach*, God responds by permitting it. The question is then implicit: would God have commanded something that ended so catastrophically? The answer is evidently no — *vachi adam zeh borer chelek ra le-atzmo*, would a person really choose a bad portion for himself? Clearly God would not have ordained this; it was only a concession to the people's request.

This is also the meaning, Reish Lakish continues, of the verse *va-yitav be-einai ha-davar* — "and the matter was good in my eyes." Reish Lakish reads it: *be-einai ve-lo be-einav shel makom* — it seemed good to me, but not in God's eyes. God gave allowance, but it was not God's own preference — as the catastrophic outcome made plain.

The *Gemara* then adds: *vayachperu lanu et ha-aretz* — "and let them search out the land for us." Rabbi Chiya bar Abba comments: the spies intended from the outset nothing less than the shaming of Eretz Yisrael. He draws a verbal parallel: *vayachperu* here echoes the verse *ve-chafra ha-levanah u-vosha ha-chamah* — the moon shall be shamed and the sun shall be embarrassed — showing that *vayachpor* carries the connotation of shame. Their mission was aimed at disgracing the land.

### Spies' Names

The *Gemara* then lists the names of the spies as the Torah records them, beginning with *le-mateh Reuven Shamua ben Zakur*. Rabbi Yitzchak states: we have a received tradition going back through the generations — *masoret be-yadeinu me-avoteinu* — that the spies were called by the names they bore in the Torah because those names reflected their deeds, *meraglim al shem ma'aseihem nikre'u*. Whether this means their parents providentially gave them names that came to describe their actions, or whether the Torah assigns them names that function as epithets, the *Gemara* does not resolve definitively. But the principle stands: the names encode what they did.

However, Rabbi Yitzchak acknowledges, we have only managed to work this out for one of them: *Satur ben Michael*. *Satur* — from the root meaning to undermine or destroy — *satar ma'asav shel ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu*: he undermined God's design, which was to bring the people into the land. *Michael* — the name contains *El*, God — *she-asah atzmo mach*: he made God appear weak, as though God lacked the power to bring them in.

Rabbi Yochanan then takes up the challenge and proposes an additional example: *Nachbi ben Vafsi*. *Nachbi* — *she-hechbi devarav shel ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu* — he concealed God's words, hiding the truth about what God could and would do. *Vafsi* — *she-pisa al midotav shel ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu* — he strode over, as it were, leaped past God's attributes, failing to acknowledge divine power.

### Caleb's Separation

The verse in the *parasha* reads *va-ya'alu ba-negev va-yavo ad Chevron* — they went up through the south and he came to Hebron. The singular *va-yavo* is striking; it should read *va-yavo'u*, in the plural. Rava derives from this: *melamed she-parash Kalev me-atzat ha-meraglim* — the singular teaches that Kalev broke away from the conspiracy of the spies. Not only did he refuse to participate in their scheme, but he physically separated himself from the group. *Va-halach ve-nishtate'ach al kivrei avot* — he went and prostrated himself on the graves of the forefathers — Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov — who are buried in Chevron, along with the *Imahos*. He prayed: *avosai bikshu alai rachamim* — my fathers, seek mercy for me, that I be saved from the conspiracy of the spies, for it was enormously difficult to stand up against that pressure.

The Torah's statement — *ve-avdi Kalev ekev hayta ruach acheret imo* — that Kalev possessed a different spirit — is thus explained by this act: he went to Chevron, he prayed, and that inner strength was what distinguished him. Of course there is a further point of connection: Kalev ultimately received Chevron as his portion when the land was divided. And Rashi notes on the verse *va-avi'osiv el ha-aretz asher ba shama* — "and I will bring him to the land he went to" — this language is purposefully specific. It is not a general promise of entry into Canaan; it is a promise of the very place, Chevron, that Kalev had visited to pray.

Tosafot raises a pointed question about this episode: the *Gemara* elsewhere teaches that the dead are unaware of what transpires in this world — *meisim lo yad'ei midi*. If so, what is the purpose of prostrating oneself and praying at the graves of the forefathers? Tosafot answers: when a person prays in this way, they inform the deceased in heaven that someone below is praying and seeking their intercession, and those holy souls can then themselves pray to God on that person's behalf. There is also support from the *baraita* that asks why people go out to cemeteries — the answer given is *k'dei she-yivakshu aleihem meisim rachamim*, so that the dead will pray for mercy on behalf of the living. The matter is theologically sensitive — rationalist authorities were wary of any formulation that might slide into the appearance of praying *to* the dead rather than asking them to pray — but the passage makes clear that there is a recognized tradition here, and both the metaphysical question (do the dead have awareness?) and the theological question (what is the proper role of an intermediary?) warrant careful handling.

### Joshua Protected

Yehoshua did not need to go pray at the graves of the forefathers because Moshe had already prayed on his behalf. The verse states: *va-yikra Moshe le-Hoshea bin Nun Yehoshua* — and Moshe called Hoshea the son of Nun "Yehoshua." The name *Yehoshua* encodes the prayer: *Yah yoshia'acha me-atzat ha-meraglim* — may God save you from the plot of the spies. Moshe's *tefilla* for Yehoshua thus preceded and preempted the need Kalev felt to go seek intercession for himself.

The *Gemara* then returns to the verse *ve-avdi Kalev ekev hayta ruach acheret imo* and notes that the subsequent promise — *va-avi'osiv el ha-aretz asher ba shama* — refers precisely to Chevron, the land to which he came to pray. As Rashi underscores, the Torah does not say he will enter Canaan in general, but specifically the land he went to, which is Chevron.

### Giants Names

The verse records: *ve-sham Achiman Sheshai ve-Talmai yelidei ha-anak* — there were Achiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of the giant. The *Gemara* interprets each name. *Achiman* — *meyuman she-ba-echav* — the most capable among his brothers, the strongest. *Sheshai* — *she-mesim et ha-aretz ke-shechitut* — he caused the earth to collapse beneath him as he walked, leaving deep craters, he was so massive. *Talmai* — *she-mesim et ha-aretz telamim telamim* — he plowed furrows in the earth with each step. A second interpretation, framed as *davar acher*, shifts from etymology to historical record: *Achiman bana Anat*, Achiman built the city of Anat; *Sheshai bana Alash*, Sheshai built Alash; *Talmai bana Talbush*, Talmai built Talbush. As for the phrase *yelidei ha-anak*, the *Gemara* notes that *anak* relates to the word for neck: Rashi explains that their necks appeared to pierce through the heavens — or through the sun itself — so towering was their stature.

---

## Hebron's Qualities

### Hebron vs. Zoan

The verse states: *ve-Chevron sheva shanim nivnesa lifnei Tzoan Mitzrayim* — Chevron was built seven years before Tzoan of Egypt. The *Gemara* immediately asks: *mai nivnesa* — what does "built" mean here? If taken literally, it would mean that Chevron as a city was constructed before Tzoan. But this is difficult: Canaan was the youngest son of Cham, while Mitzrayim — after whom Egypt is named — was an older son, as the verse enumerates: *bnei Cham Kush u-Mitzrayim u-Put ve-Chanaan*. Would a father really build a city for his youngest son before his older son? And Tzoan was Mitzrayim's city.

The *Gemara* therefore reinterprets: *she-hayta mevunah echad mi-shiva be-Tzoan* — Chevron was seven times more *mevunah* — more built up, more developed — than Tzoan. The point is comparative quality, not chronological construction.

This is where the statement becomes striking. The *Gemara* observes: *ein lecha tarshin be-chol Eretz Yisrael yoter mi-Chevron* — there is no place in all of Eretz Yisrael that is more rocky and barren than Chevron — *de-kivrei bei shichvei* — which is precisely why the dead are buried there, since the ground is not useful for agriculture. Yet *ein lecha me'ulah be-chol ha-aratzot yoter mi-Eretz Mitzrayim* — there is no land in the world more fertile than Egypt, compared to the Garden of God, as the verse says — and *ein lecha me'ulah be-chol Eretz Mitzrayim yoter mi-Tzoan* — and within all of Egypt, there is no more fertile and distinguished region than Tzoan, where the high dignitaries of Israel resided during their dealings with Egypt.

And yet: *afilu hachi*, even so, Chevron is seven times more *mevunah* than Tzoan. The nature of that superiority — rocky Chevron surpassing the most fertile place in the most fertile land — suggests that Rashi's reading, *meyushevet be-peiros*, "settled with fruits," may itself be pointing toward something more than agricultural output. It is perhaps more natural to understand this as a spiritual statement about the quality of the place rather than a claim about its physical productivity.

### Rocky Land Grazing

One might object: is it really true that Chevron is so rocky? The *Gemara* cites a verse — *va-yehi mi-ketz arba'im shanah va-yomer Avshalom el ha-melech elcha na* — and Avshalom, requesting leave to go to Chevron, said he wanted to bring a sacrifice. Rabbi Avyu, and some attribute this to Rabbah bar bar Chana, explains: *Chanan she-halach le-havi kevasim mi-Chevron* — he went to bring lambs from Chevron. And a *baraita* teaches: if you want fine rams, you get them from Moav; if you want the best lambs, you get them from Chevron. This appears to contradict the characterization of Chevron as barren and rocky: how can the best lambs come from such inhospitable terrain?

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction directly: *aidi de-klisha ar'a avda ra'aya, ve-shamin kinyana* — it is precisely because the land is thin and poor that it produces excellent grazing, and so you get fat, prized flocks. Rocky, sparse land is ideal grazing country; the animals forage over wide, lean terrain and produce superior quality. The paradox resolves itself: Chevron's very poverty as agricultural land is what makes it outstanding for flocks. And with that observation, the *Gemara* continues into the next daf.

---

---

# Sotah 35

## Meraglim & Lashon Hara

### Kalev at Chevron

The *aggadeta* on this daf opens in the midst of a long narrative touching on the crossing of the *Yarden* at the time of Yehoshua, with digressions into related topics — most immediately, the story of the *meraglim*. The *gemara* had already noted that the verse describing the spies' arrival at Chevron employs the singular form — *vayavo ad Chevron* — and derives from this that only Kalev went to Chevron, where he prostrated himself at the graves of the *avot* and prayed: *bikshu alai rachamim*, "pray for mercy on my behalf." Rashi observes that this detail provides a satisfying closure to a parallel found later in Yehoshua's narrative: it is Kalev who ultimately receives Chevron as his inheritance — *ha'aretz asher darach bah* — a fitting reward for the very place where he had gone to seek the protection of the ancestors.

### Tosafot: Dead & Prayer

There is a pointed question raised by Tosafot on this passage. The *gemara* in the chapter *Mi She-meto* concludes that the dead are not aware of what transpires in this world — *lo yad'in midi* — and this applies even to the *avot ha-olam*, to Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov themselves. If so, what is the point of praying that the *avot* should intercede on one's behalf, as Kalev did?

Tosafot resolves this by suggesting that the dead do not directly hear prayers addressed to them, but they are informed — *modi'in lahem* — that someone below has prayed that they should in turn pray on his behalf. They receive, as it were, a summary of what has been requested of them. Tosafot adds corroborating sources: the practice cited in the second chapter of Ta'anis of going out to the cemeteries so that the *meitim* should pray on behalf of the living, and the episode in the chapter of the *chasidim* involving Rabbi Mana who prostrated himself at his father's grave. These precedents reflect a clearly encoded *minhag*, observed particularly during the *aseres yemei teshuva*.

### Intermediaries & Worship

The deeper concern with this practice, however, is not primarily whether the dead have awareness — Tosafot's answer addresses that — but whether the practice remains properly directed. The ideal, as understood by Tosafot and by the *gemara*, is that one requests of the deceased that they pray to God on one's behalf; they function as an intermediary in petition, not as the object of worship. The problem is that this line becomes quite blurred in practice. When people go to a *beit ha-kevarot*, it is very likely that they direct their prayers to the *meitim* themselves, not merely asking them to carry prayers forward to God. At that point, it becomes a *tefillah* addressed to a being other than God — something that would deeply disturb the Rambam, and which touches on a fundamental question about the nature of worship.

This concern is distinct from the concept of a *shaliach tzibbur*, who represents the congregation but remains a this-worldly representative praying together with the community, not an intermediary in any theologically charged sense. Similarly, the liturgical passage of *Machnisei Rachamim*, in which we ask angels to bring our prayers before God, occupies its own category.

The contrast with certain Christian practices is instructive here. Many Christian communities pray directly to deceased saints — not "please bring my prayer to God," but "Saint so-and-so, please help me" — where the saint is effectively the one prayed to, not merely the conduit. This is understandable in a theological framework where God has taken human form and where deceased holy individuals are correspondingly relatable objects of petition. But it is precisely this blurring — from intermediary to the thing prayed to — that raises serious concerns in the Jewish framework.

One might raise the concept of *zechut avot* in this context, but that is fundamentally different. *Zechut avot* is not a matter of directing prayer to the ancestors; it is a theological accounting in which one stands before God and invokes the accumulated merit of prior generations. The two concepts are not merely adjacent on a continuum — one is a claim about how God reckons merit, the other is a question about the very object of worship.

### Spies' Report

After this digression, the *gemara* returns to the narrative of the spies, picking up from *daf* 34b. The verse reads: *vayashuvu mitur ha'aretz miketz arba'im yom* — and they returned from scouting the land. A subsequent verse says *vayelchu vayavo'u* — they went and they came. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai derives from the juxtaposition of the going and the coming — *makish halicha livi'ah* — that just as their return was characterized by *etza ra'ah*, an evil plan or collusion, so too their original departure was already undertaken with that same evil design. They left with bad intentions.

The spies' report itself begins with a remarkable blend of truth and slander. They affirm that the land is indeed flowing with milk and honey and offer its fruit as evidence — *vegam zavat chalav udevash hi* — but then immediately pivot: *efes ki az ha'am*, the people are too strong for us. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir derives a principle from this structure.

### Lashon Hara & Truth

The principle is striking: *kol lashon hara she'ein bo devar emet bit'chilato ein mitkayem besofo* — any *lashon hara* that does not contain some element of truth at the outset will not endure. A skilled purveyor of harmful speech knows that proximity to the truth lends credibility and staying power. By contrast, slander that contains no factual core fails to take hold. It is worth noting that the *Chafetz Chaim* draws a careful distinction between *lashon hara* — true but harmful speech — and *motzi shem ra* — false slander. The *gemara* here uses *lashon hara* in its more generic sense of harmful speech, without that technical distinction, but the practical observation is about slander: it is most destructive when anchored in verifiable truth.

### Kalev's Strategy

The verse then says *vayahas Kalev et ha'am el Moshe* — Caleb silenced the people before Moses. Rava interprets *vayahas* as *she'hisitam bidvarim* — he incited or seduced them with words, a way of drawing them in before pivoting. The question arises: why was it Kalev who spoke and not Yehoshua?

### Rosh Ketiah

The answer is that Yehoshua did try to speak, but the people dismissed him immediately: *dein rosh keti'ah yemallel* — should this "cut-off head" speak? Rashi explains that Yehoshua had no children, and therefore the people reasoned that he had no personal stake in the outcome — he would not inherit the land himself and thus had no basis to advocate for entering it. His words carried no weight in their eyes.

The *Aruch* offers an alternative interpretation: *rosh keti'ah* alludes to the letter *yud* at the beginning of Yehoshua's name. Moshe had renamed him *Yehoshua* — adding a *yud* to *Hoshea ben Nun* — and a *yud* is a tiny, seemingly "cut-off" letter. The remark was simply a dismissive insult: this shrimp should speak? Either way, Kalev saw that whatever Yehoshua said, the people would find some way to be dismissive of him.

### Kalev's Counterargument

So Kalev calculated differently. He reasoned: *im ishta'ina, amrei bi milta, vachasmi li* — if I try to speak directly against them, they'll find a way to silence me too. So he said to them: *vachi zo bilvad asa lanu Ben Amram* — is this the only thing the son of Amram did to us? Note that he uses the dismissive epithet *Ben Amram* — a degrading way of referring to Moshe — as a rhetorical device. The people thought he was about to say something against Moshe and fell silent to hear the complaint. He had them. And then he pivoted: *hotzianu miMitzrayim, uvaka lanu et hayam, vehe'echilanu et haman* — he took us out of Egypt, split the sea, fed us the manna. And even if he told us to make ladders and climb to heaven, would we not listen? The structure is a direct parallel — and almost the inverse — of what the *gemara* said about *lashon hara* that must begin with truth. Here, a false premise — the suggestion that Moshe had wronged them — was used to gain the audience's attention, and then the truth was deployed to make the real point. It is, as one student aptly noted, a case of coming to praise Caesar by first seeming to come to bury him.

### Land Consumes Inhabitants

Returning to the body of the spies' report: *eretz ochelet yoshveha hi* — it is a land that consumes its inhabitants. Rava expounds: God says, *ani chashavti letova* — I arranged this for their benefit. Whenever the spies passed through, a prominent person among the local inhabitants died — *meis chashiva didehu ki heichi denitardu* — so that the locals would be distracted by mourning and would not investigate who these strangers were. There is a second version: it was Iyov who died at that time, and all the world was occupied with his *hespeda*, which additionally removed the *zechut* that had protected the Canaanites — *sar tzilam me'aleihem* — since Iyov's merit had served as a kind of shield for them. But what the spies interpreted as ominous devastation was in fact divine protection in disguise. *Hem chashvu leraa*.

### Liars or Interpreters?

Finally, the *gemara* reaches the spies' claim: *vanehi be'eineinu kachagavim vechen hayinu be'eineihem* — we were in our own eyes like grasshoppers and so too in their eyes. Hamasharshiya declares bluntly: *meraglim shikrei havu* — the spies were liars. This is presented as something of a *chidush*, since until this point the spies had not said anything demonstrably false — *eretz ochelet yoshveha* is an interpretation of facts, not a fabrication. But now Hamasharshiya says outright they were lying. 

*Bishlama vanehi be'eineinu kachagavim lachayei* — granted, their self-assessment as grasshoppers is subjective and could be true. *Ela vechen hayinu be'eineihem mna yadei* — but how did they know how they appeared to the Canaanites?

The *gemara* pushes back — *velo hi* — and offers a resolution. Since there were constant deaths among the inhabitants, the spies would observe them providing *havra'ah* — the meal of condolence — to mourners under cedar trees. Bnei Yisrael, needing to conceal themselves, climbed up into those very cedar trees. From there they overheard the locals saying: *kachazinan inshei dedamu lekamzei be'ilanei* — we see people up there that look just like grasshoppers in the trees. The cedar trees appear in the story for a simple reason: they had to be elevated to hear what was being said at the level of giants, and concealment in the trees is what allowed them to overhear the remark at all. So the *gemara* concludes: they were not liars — they had actual evidence for their claim.

---

## Punishment & Plague

### Crying & Tisha B'Av

The verse states: *vatissa kol ha'eda vayitnu et kolam vayivku ha'am balayla hahu* — the entire congregation lifted their voice and the people wept on that night. Rabba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan identifies the timing: *oto halayla erev Tisha B'Av haya* — that night was the eve of the 9th of Av. God declared: *hem bachu bechiya shel chinam* — they wept for nothing. So God responded: *ani ekba lahem bechiya l'dorot* — I will establish for them a night of weeping for all generations. The report of the *meraglim* thus marks the very first of the catastrophes associated with Tisha B'Av.

### Stoning & Divine Presence

The verse continues: *vayomru kol ha'eda lirgom otam ba'avanim* — the congregation said to stone them with stones. Immediately the verse adds that *kevod Hashem* appeared in the *Ohel Mo'ed*. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba teaches: this teaches that they actually took stones and threw them upward — *klapei ma'ala* — toward God Himself. This reading connects to the earlier teaching about *mimenu* — greater than Him — in which the spies had implicitly disparaged even God's power. The throwing of stones at the divine presence is of a piece with that blasphemy.

### Spies' Plague

The verse then records: *vayamutu ha'anashim motzi'ei dibat ha'aretz ra'ah ba-mageifah* — the men who spread the evil report of the land died in the plague. The word *ra'ah* is read in conjunction with *mageifah* — it was a particularly terrible plague, a *mitah meshunah*, an unusual death.

### Worm Cycle Death

Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish teaches, citing the *drasha* of Rav Shila of Kefar Tamarta: their tongues stretched downward and fell to their navels — *nishtarbev lishonam v'nafal al tiburam* — and worms emerged from their tongues and entered their navels, and then cycled back from their navels to their tongues. The punishment was calibrated to the sin: they had misused their speech through *lashon hara*, and so the tongue became the locus of their grotesque death. The *tibur* — the navel — is significant as well, since the *gemara* in Yoma discusses the navel as a marker of the seat of life; the worms thus invaded the very center of their being and cycled between the organ of their sin and the core of their existence.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers an alternative: they died of *askara*, croup — again, a disease of the throat and tongue, fitting punishment for those who destroyed through speech.

---

## Jordan Crossing & Ar (II)

### Waters Return

The *gemara* returns now from the digression about the *meraglim* to the narrative of Yehoshua. *V'keivan she-alah ha-acharon she-b'Yisrael min ha-Yarden* — when the last Israelite left the Jordan, *chazru mayim limkomam* — the waters returned to their place. The verse quoted is *vayhi ba-alot ha-kohanim nosei aron brit Hashem mi-toch ha-Yarden*, when the *kohanim* emerged from the Jordan, at which point *nitku kapot raglei ha-kohanim el ha-charavah* — the soles of their feet stepped onto dry land — and *vayashuvu mei ha-Yarden limkomam*, the waters returned. They returned *al kol gedotav* — to their full banks — because, as the earlier *psukim* indicate, the Jordan was at peak strength following the snowmelt.

### Ark Lifts Carriers

A problem arises when one reads the *psukim* carefully. The Jordan split as soon as the *kohanim* stepped in — *as soon as their feet touched the water, the waters stopped*. That means the *kohanim* themselves never crossed the Jordan; they stepped in from the east bank, the waters held, all of Israel passed through, and then the *kohanim* stepped back out — onto the east bank, not the west. The *gemara* states this explicitly: *nimtza aron v'nos'av v'kohanim mi-tzad echad* — the *aron* and its carriers and the *kohanim* ended up on the east side of the Jordan, while all of Israel was on the west side.

The resolution: *nassa aron et nosav* — the *aron* lifted up those who were carrying it and miraculously transported them across. The *aron* was *nosei et nosav* — it carried those who bore it. The proof-text is the verse *vayhi ka'asher tam kol ha'am la'avor vaya'avor aron Hashem v'ha-kohanim lifnei ha'am* — when all the people had finished crossing, the *aron* passed and the *kohanim* were before the people. The logical reading of that verse is that the *kohanim* caused the *aron* to pass; but the *gemara* inverts this: it was the *aron* that passed and, in doing so, carried the *kohanim* over.

---

## Uzza's Punishment

### Uzza's Error

It was precisely a failure to appreciate this power of the *aron* that brought about the punishment of Uzza. The verse recounts how, during King David's attempt to transport the *aron* to Jerusalem, they arrived at *goren Kidon*. *Vayishlach Uza yado le'echoz et ha'aron* — Uzza extended his hand to grab the *aron*, thinking the oxen had slipped and it was about to fall — *ki shamtu ha-bakar*. He was struck down on the spot.

---

## Uzza's Punishment (II)

### God's Rebuke

The *gemara* frames God's rebuke of Uzza as follows: *nosav nasa, atzmo lo kol sheken* — the *aron* lifted those who were carrying it; surely it can take care of itself without your assistance. *Vayichar af Hashem b'Uzza vayakehu sham al ha-shal* — God's anger burned against Uzza and He smote him there on the *shal*, the error. The *gemara* emphasizes the word *shal* — it was not *meizid*, a deliberate sin. Uzza was trying to do something that appeared good. Yet the consequence was fatal — a pattern recognizable from the story of Nadav and Avihu, and from the broader principle that God holds the righteous to a more exacting standard, *medakdek im ha-tzadikim*.

The power-plant analogy is apt here: the presence of God is like a power plant that gives light and energy to the entire world, but proximity without proper protection — approaching incorrectly, doing the wrong thing — carries severe consequences. This is not a negation of the source's beneficence; it is a function of its intensity.

### Uzza's Merit

Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar debate the nature of *al ha-shal*. One says it refers to the error itself — the act, though well-intentioned, constituted a transgression of protocol. The other says *shal* means he relieved himself in its presence — a reading that attempts to account for why the consequences were so severe by suggesting a secondary disrespect. Rashi reads *shal* through the lens of *nashal zeitecha*, something that falls away.

Rabbi Yochanan, however, consistent with his framing of Uzza's act as an error rather than deliberate sin, rules that *Uza ba le'Olam Haba* — Uzza enters the world to come. The proof-text is the verse *vayamat sham im Aron Ha'elokim* — he died there *with* the *aron* of God. Just as the *aron* endures forever, so too Uzza will come into the world to come.

### David's Zmirot

The *gemara* then asks: why was David also deserving of punishment in the context of this episode? *Mipnei she-kara l'divrei Torah zmirot* — because he referred to the words of Torah as *zmirot*, as songs. The reference is to the verse in Tehillim: *zmirot hayu li chukecha b'veit megurai* — your statutes were to me like *zmirot* in the house of my dwelling.

This requires some unpacking. David's dancing before the *aron* is not the problem — that was an expression of joy and was regarded as proper honor. The concern is specifically that he characterized the *chukim* — the statutes of Torah — as *zmirot*. *Shira* is elevated poetic composition; *zemer* is a common tune. The distinction matters because one is expressing that Torah is a source of joy, which is legitimate, while the other is recasting the very genre of the words themselves — as if calling Torah a *zemer* places it in a different literary category, something lighter, something comparable to any pleasurable reading.

The *gemara* draws a contrast: if David had said Torah is a *sha'ashua*, a plaything, that remains clearly a metaphor for how one experiences it. But calling it *zmirot* is recasting the text itself as belonging to a different genre of writing, and that is what seems to trouble the *gemara*.

### Treating Torah Lightly

God's response to David is: *divrei Torah she-katuv bahem hata'if einecha bo v'eineno* — the words of Torah are such that if you but flutter your eye away, they disappear. You called them *zmirot*? *Hareini machshilcha b'davar she-afilu tinokot shel beit raban yod'in oto* — I will cause you to stumble in a matter that even schoolchildren know.

The connection between the *zmirot* rebuke and the *hata'if einecha* verse may initially seem opaque. But the logic runs as follows: if you treat Torah only as a source of pleasant entertainment — *zmirot* — and never as something requiring serious, careful attention, then you will not pay sufficient care to its words. That carelessness will cost you. And indeed: *u'vnei Kehos lo nasan ki avodat ha-kodesh aleihem b'katef yisa'u* — the Torah states explicitly that the *aron* was to be carried on the shoulder, not on a wagon. Every schoolchild knows this. Yet David had the *aron* transported on a wagon — *va'atun asinu ba'agalah* — an error that directly precipitated the tragedy of Uzza. The consequence of treating Torah lightly is that one commits errors that children know better than to make.

---

## Jordan Crossing & Ar (II)

### Ark's Autonomy

The broader principle the *gemara* has been developing is that the *aron* is not merely a sacred object that requires protection — it is itself a source of divine power that protects those who carry it, indeed that carries those who carry it. This is the inverse of what Uzza assumed when he reached out to steady it. The *aron* is *nosei et nosav*: it bears its bearers. Like a power plant, it is the source of energy and protection for those who relate to it correctly; but approached incorrectly, it is lethal. This principle connects the miraculous transport of the *kohanim* across the Jordan, the death of Uzza, the smiting of the men of Beit Shemesh who looked at the *aron* dismissively while continuing to harvest — and, in a different register, the punishment of David for treating the Torah with insufficient gravity.

The *gemara* relates the episode of Beit Shemesh as well: when the *aron* was returned by the Philistines, the people of Beit Shemesh were smitten. One opinion holds that the problem was they kept on harvesting in the field while the *aron* passed through — continuing their mundane work without pausing to acknowledge the moment. A second opinion holds that they went further and spoke dismissively of it: *man amricha de'mrayat, u'man asach de'puyasat* — who got you so angry? And who appeased you? — addressing the *aron* in a personified but contemptuous fashion. Either way — passive impassivity or active dismissal — the *aron* is not an object that tolerates being taken lightly.

---

## Three Stone Sets

### Moshe's Stones

Moving on, the *gemara* establishes that there were three distinct sets of stones erected in connection with the giving and writing of the Torah. The first was erected by Moshe in *Eretz Moav*, before the crossing of the Jordan. The connection is made through the parallel language of *be'er*: the opening of Devarim says *ho'il Moshe be'er et ha-Torah ha-zot* — Moshe began to explicate this Torah — and the commandment later uses *ba'er heiteiv*, explicate well. The *gemara* links the two instances of *be'er* to establish that Moshe himself performed a similar act of inscription.

### Yehoshua's Stones

The second set was erected by Yehoshua within the Jordan itself. The verse states: *ushteim esreh avanim hekim Yehoshua besoch ha-Yarden* — Yehoshua erected twelve stones in the midst of the Jordan.

### Gilgal Stones

The third set was the re-erection of those same twelve stones at Gilgal after the crossing. The verse states that they took the stones from the Jordan and erected them at Gilgal.

### Writing Method Debate

A *baraita* addresses the question of how exactly Israel wrote the Torah on the stones, given that the Torah also commands *vesadta osam ba-sid* — you shall plaster them with plaster. The intersection of carved inscription and plaster covering requires explanation.

### Yehuda's Method

Rabbi Yehuda says: *al gabei avanim kesavuha* — they wrote it directly on the stones, as the verse states, *vechasavta al ha-avanim et kol divrei ha-Torah ha-zot*. And afterward, *sadu osan ba-sid* — they covered the stones with plaster. Presumably the inscription was carved into the stone, so it would remain legible beneath the plaster, though the readability would certainly be compromised.

### Shimon's Challenge

Rabbi Shimon challenges Rabbi Yehuda directly: *lidvarecha, heich lamdu umot she-be'oto ha-zman Torah* — according to your view, how did the nations of that time learn Torah? This is a striking assumption embedded in the question: the purpose of writing the Torah *ba'er heiteiv* in *shivim lashon* was not merely internal — not merely so that Israel would know its own covenant — but so that the nations would have access to it. The Torah of Israel was to serve as a model for the world. If the inscription was then covered with plaster, how could the nations have read it?

### Plaster Printing Press

Rabbi Yehuda responds: *binah yeseirah nasan bahem ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu* — God granted the nations particular wisdom and understanding. They sent their scribes, *veshigru notirin shelahem*, and those scribes *vekilpu et ha-sid* — peeled off the plaster — and carried it away. 

This is, on reflection, a brilliant solution. When text is carved into stone and plaster is poured over it, the plaster hardens in relief, with the letters raised on its surface — which is precisely how printing type functions. The peeled plaster becomes a perfect printing surface, a mirror image that can be pressed onto other materials to produce copies. The nations sent their scribes, who removed the plaster and thereby obtained what amounts to a printing press for the Torah in seventy languages. The *ba'er heiteiv* — the clear, detailed exposition — was not destroyed when the plaster was applied; it was preserved in a form ideally suited for distribution.

### Writing on Plaster

Rabbi Shimon's own alternative view is: *al gabei sid ktavuha* — they wrote directly on top of the plaster, not on the stones beneath. And underneath — *vechatav lahem lemata* — was written the verse *leman asher lo yilamdu etchem la'asot kechol ha-to'evot* — so that they should not teach you to do all of their abominations — a verse about why the seven nations must be destroyed. On Rabbi Shimon's view as well, the plaster was pulled off and sent to the nations, but it was written on top of the plaster rather than transferred from the stone beneath. Either way, both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon are answering the same practical question: if the writing was meant for the *umot ha-olam*, how did they receive it when the stones stood in Eretz Yisrael? The answer is that the plaster itself — whether as printing press or as inscribed surface — was sent to them.

---

## Nations & Repentance

### Nations Could Repent

Rava bar Shila asks: what is the reasoning behind Rabbi Shimon's view? The verse beneath the inscription — *leman asher lo yilamdu etchem* — contains within it an implication: *ha lamadeta she'im hayu chozrim bi-teshuva, hayu mekabelin otan* — this teaches that had the nations repented, they would have been accepted. The very fact that God provided the Torah to the nations — that it was published for them in seventy languages — meant that repentance and acceptance were genuinely available to them. Rabbi Shimon understands that even the seven nations, had they changed their ways, could have been received rather than destroyed.

Rashi extends this: not only would they not have been destroyed, they could even have converted. The publication of Torah in seventy languages was a genuine invitation.

### Plaster Metaphor

The verse then cited is: *vehayu amim misrephot sid* — the nations will be like the burning of a plaster pit. Rava bar Shila reads this as *al iskei sid* — because of the plaster. The nations had the Torah given to them through the medium of the plaster in seventy languages, and they failed to learn from it. Therefore they will burn like plaster. The plaster that was meant to transmit Torah to them becomes the symbol of their judgment.

### Seven Nations Debate

Rabbi Yehuda reads the same imagery differently: *mah sid ein lo takana ela sreifa* — just as plaster has no remedy other than burning, *af otam ovdei kochavim ein lahem takana ela sreifa* — so too those nations have no remedy other than destruction. On this reading, the *gemara* is establishing a debate specifically about the *shiva amamin*, the seven Canaanite nations. Rabbi Shimon holds that even they, had they repented upon receiving the Torah through the plaster, would have been accepted. Rabbi Yehuda holds that *ein lahem takana* — they were destined for destruction regardless, with no possibility of reprieve.

This debate is focused specifically on the seven nations and not on the *umot ha-olam* generally. Regarding the general nations, neither opinion could hold *ein lahem takana* — otherwise the entire exercise of publishing Torah in seventy languages would have been pointless. The debate is thus a narrow one about whether the Canaanite nations, whom Israel was commanded to destroy upon entering the land, had any theoretical avenue of escape through repentance — and on this, Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda disagree.

---

---

# Sotah 36

## Stones & Torah Writing

### Pesukim Review

We begin at the bottom of 35b, in the midst of a debate concerning the details surrounding the erection of the stones and the writing of the Torah. Before proceeding, a correction is in order regarding what was said in the previous session. A more careful reading of the relevant *pesukim* clarifies considerably what the *gemara* is about to do.

### Three Stone Sets

The *gemara* identifies three distinct sets of stones. The first are those that Moshe erected on his side of the *Yarden* — a fact not stated explicitly in the *pesukim* but derived by the *gemara* through a *gezeira shava* on the word *be'er*, "well." The second are the stones that were set in the *Yarden* itself: *vayusham sham ad hayom hazeh* — they were erected there and remain there to this day, hidden beneath the water, their erection symbolic, their presence known but unseen. These are distinct from the third set, the twelve stones taken *out* of the *Yarden* and subsequently erected in *Gilgal*.

### Deuteronomy 27 Analysis

It is important to examine the *pesukim* in Devarim 27 carefully, because they generate a significant textual ambiguity. The Torah commands: *ve-hayah bayom asher tavru et ha-Yarden... ve-hakemota lecha avanim gedolot ve-sata otam ba-sid* — on the day you cross the *Yarden*, you shall erect large stones and plaster them with lime. It then commands: *ve-katavta aleihem et kol divrei ha-Torah ha-zot* — and you shall write upon them the entire Torah. So far, it appears the Torah is to be written on the erected stones. The text then continues: *ve-hayah be-ovrechem et ha-Yarden takimu et ha-avanim ha-eleh... be-Har Eival ve-sata otam ba-sid* — you shall erect these stones on Har Eival and plaster them. Then follows the command to build a *mizbeiach* of whole, unhewn stones, offer *olot* and *shelamim*, eat, and rejoice.

The ambiguity is this: the Torah speaks of writing on the stones and then speaks of building a *mizbeiach* from *avanim shelemot*, and then concludes with the instruction to write *et divrei ha-Torah ha-zot ba'er hetev* — the words of this Torah, explained well. Are we returning to the erected stones, or is this writing upon the *avnei ha-mizbeiach*? The *pesukim* are genuinely ambiguous.

### Tosafot: Malon vs. Mizbe…

*Tosafot* on 35b, *keitzad katvu Yisrael et ha-Torah*, addresses this directly. A *Tosefta* records that Rabbi Yehudah holds *al gabi ha-mizbeiach katvuha* — it was written on the *mizbeiach*. But the *Yerushalmi* preserves a different tradition: *al avnei ha-malon nichtevu* — it was written on the stones of the lodging place, i.e., the erected stones. The practical difference is significant. According to the view that it was written on the *avnei ha-malon*, the nations of the world could send their scribes day after day to transcribe the Torah, which was written in seventy languages, from this enduring public monument. According to the view that it was written on the *avnei ha-mizbeiach* — *lo le-sha'ah hayu ve-nignazu*, they were not permanent and were eventually hidden away. The *gemara* there resolves that even so, God placed understanding in the heart of every nation and they somehow acquired the Torah that was written in seventy languages.

*Tosafot* also raises the linguistic difficulty: for those who say it was written on the *avnei ha-mizbeiach*, what does *ve-sata otam ba-sid* — and you shall plaster them — refer to? The answer given is *bein kol even va-even* — the plaster between each stone, i.e., the mortar binding the *mizbeiach* together, not a surface coating for writing.

### Two Separate Events

There is a second layer of complexity that emerges from the narrative in *Yehoshua*, namely the apparent separation of the stone erection and the Har Gerizim/Har Eival ceremony into two distinct events. The Torah in Devarim seems to present everything — erecting the stones, writing the Torah, building the *mizbeiach*, and the *brachot* and *klalos* — as one unified event at Har Gerizim and Har Eival. But in *Yehoshua*, these come apart.

### Geographic Timeline

A look at the geography and the narrative sequence in *Yehoshua* reveals the full extent of this problem. *Gilgal*, where the Israelites camped after crossing the *Yarden*, was right at the eastern edge of *Yericho*: *vayachanu ba-Gilgal biktzeh mizrach Yericho*. Har Gerizim and Har Eival are far to the interior — the *gemara* later says more than sixty *mil* away, a journey of multiple days. And the narrative in *Yehoshua* does not conflate these events at all.

Perek 4 of *Yehoshua* records that *Yehoshua* erected the twelve stones taken from the *Yarden* in *Gilgal*, with no mention of writing Torah and no mention of building a *mizbeiach*: *ve-et shteim esrei ha-avanim ha-eleh asher lakechu min ha-Yarden hekim Yehoshua ba-Gilgal*. The purpose stated for the stones is purely commemorative — so that future generations would know that Israel crossed the *Yarden* on dry land, *lema'an da'at kol amei ha-aretz ki yad Hashem ki chazaka hi*. Then the narrative proceeds to the wars of *Yericho* and *Ha'Ai*, and the episode of *Achan*, spanning multiple *perakim* of wars and battles. Only at the end of Perek 8 does the text say: *az yivneh Yehoshua mizbe'ach l'Hashem Elokei Yisrael be-Har Eival* — and there, in Perek 8, it describes the building of the *mizbeiach*, the writing: *vayichtav sham al ha-avanim mishne Torat Moshe*, and the performance of the *brachot* and *klalos*.

This means that according to the plain reading of *Yehoshua*, the erection of the stones happened immediately after crossing the *Yarden*, and the *mizbeiach*, the writing of the Torah, and the *brachot* and *klalos* happened weeks or months later, well into the land, after several significant military campaigns. The Torah's account in Devarim, by contrast, presents it all as a single integrated sequence of events occurring upon entry. The *gemara* is faced with the task of reconciling these two very different presentations.

### Malbim's Theory

One approach to the ambiguity of the sequence of plastering and writing is that of the *Malbim*, who proposes that the writing of the Torah on the plaster occurred at multiple stages. His view is that first, while the plaster was just beginning to dry — a state when one can still inscribe into it — they wrote the Torah. This would correspond to what occurred at or near the *Yarden*. Subsequently, when they built the *mizbeiach* and the *olot* were offered, the stones were plastered again, the plaster dried somewhat, and they wrote the Torah yet again. This approach attempts to honor both the Devarim and the *Yehoshua* accounts by distributing the writing across different moments. However, this is a complex theory and we must set it aside for now to turn to what the *gemara* itself requires.

---

## Teshuvah & Seven Nations

### Rava on Rabbi Shimon

Returning now to the main *gemara*: the discussion concerns a debate between Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Shimon regarding the nations who witnessed the writing of the Torah on the stones. Six lines from the bottom of 35b, *Rava bar Shila* explains the reasoning behind Rabbi Shimon's position. The verse states: *ve-hayu amim misrofot sid* — the nations shall be as burning lime. Rabbi Shimon reads this *al iskei sid* — as referring to the matter of the lime, the plaster. Had the nations learned from what was written on the plaster, they would not have been destroyed. The implication of Rabbi Shimon's view is that the option of *teshuvah* and acceptance was genuinely open to them.

### Rabbi Yehudah's View

Rabbi Yehudah, by contrast, reads *kesid* — just as lime has no remedy other than burning, so too these nations have no remedy other than destruction. For Rabbi Yehudah, their fate is unconditional; *teshuvah* would not have altered it.

### Yefat Toar & Canaanites

A *baraita* is cited that connects to this debate: *ve-shavita shivyo* — the laws of *yefat toar* — is read as including *Kena'anim* who were outside the land of Israel, meaning that if they were to do *teshuvah* they would be accepted: *im chozrin be-teshuvah mekabelin otam*. The *gemara* concludes that this *baraita* follows the position of Rabbi Shimon, since it is Rabbi Shimon who holds that *teshuvah* would have been effective for the seven nations. Rabbi Yehudah, by contrast, maintains that the obligation to destroy the *shiva umot* applies regardless, even outside of Israel, even if they do *teshuvah*.

### Tosafot on Rachav

*Tosafot* raises a sharp question: *teima heich kibelu la l'Rachav* — how was *Rachav* accepted, given that she was from *Kena'an* within the land, as is established in the *Sifri*? This is a serious difficulty for any reading that would accept *Kena'anim* under certain conditions.

### Yefat Toar Override?

*Tosafot* addresses both this question and a related difficulty. Regarding *Rachav*, *Tosafot* explains: *im hayu chozrin az be-teshuvah be-sha'ah she-kasav et ha-Torah, afilu Kena'anim she-be-tocha hayu mekabelin* — had the *Kena'anim* done *teshuvah* at the time the Torah was written on the stones, even those within the land would have been accepted, and this holds even according to Rabbi Yehudah. The critical distinction is the timing. The debate about whether *teshuvah* is effective pertains to the period after the war had already begun. *Rachav*'s acceptance thus occurred within the pre-war window, before the conflict was joined in earnest. Once war commenced, that is where the dispute between Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Shimon becomes operative, and Rabbi Yehudah holds that subsequent *teshuvah* would not exempt them — whereas the *Kena'anim* outside the land remain under discussion.

The second difficulty *Tosafot* raises is whether *yefat toar* could itself constitute an exception to the obligation to destroy the *shiva umot*: *dilma be-yefat toar afilu Rabbi Yehudah modeh* — perhaps even Rabbi Yehudah would agree that the laws of *yefat toar* override the obligation to destroy them, given that the *gemara* holds *yefat toar* waives even the prohibitions of *kehunah*. *Tosafot* responds that the laws permitting sexual relations with a captive woman do not carry with them an exemption from the separate affirmative *mitzvah* to destroy the seven nations. The *mitzvah* to eliminate the *shiva umot* outside of Israel, according to Rabbi Yehudah, would not be overridden by the *heter* of *yefat toar*. These are, in sum, several intertwined questions: the degree to which there is an obligation to destroy the *shiva umot* outside of *Eretz Yisrael*, whether *teshuvah* would have constituted a remedy, how to handle the case of *Rachav*, and whether *yefat toar* could serve as a basis for exception.

---

## One Day Narrative

### Sixty Mil Journey

The *gemara* now returns to the central narrative and its harmonization of the *Yehoshua* account with the Devarim commands. *Bo re'eh* — come and see — *kama nisim na'asu be-oto ha-yom*: how many miracles were performed on that very day they crossed the *Yarden*. The *gemara* states that *Bnei Yisrael* crossed the *Yarden* and then came to Har Gerizim and Har Eival — *yoter mi-shishim mil*, more than sixty *mil* away, which is approximately sixty kilometers. This is a remarkable claim. The point is precisely that the *gemara* is taking the events of Perek 8 of *Yehoshua* — the *mizbeiach*, the writing of the Torah, the *brachot* and *klalos* — and asserting they occurred on the same day as the crossing of the *Yarden*.

### Bracketing Battles

This requires bracketing the battles described in Perakim 6 and 7 of *Yehoshua* — the conquest of *Yericho* and the campaign against *Ha'Ai* — and treating them as narratively displaced from their chronological position. This is essentially the principle of *ein mukdam u-me'uchar ba-Torah* applied to the book of *Yehoshua*: the battles of *Yericho* and *Ha'Ai* did not occur on that first day but are recorded out of sequence. *V'ein kol beryah yechola la'amod bifneihem* — no creature was able to stand against *Bnei Yisrael*; *ve-chol ha-omed bifneihem haya nisraz* — anyone who tried was immediately, let us say, undone.

### Fear Before Them

The *gemara* draws upon a verse: *ve-es emasi ashalach lefanecha ve-hamoti et kol ha-am* — I will send My fear before you and I will disturb all the people. *Rashi* explains *ve-hamoti* as *lashon mehumah ve-irvuv ha-guf mah she-betocho* — a language of confusion and disordering of the inner body, i.e., causing the enemy to lose control of his bowels. And the verse continues: *tipol aleihem eimatah va-fachad* — fear and trembling will fall upon them.

The *gemara* then applies a *derasha* to the verse *ad ya'avor amcha Hashem / ad ya'avor am zu kanita* — the two halves of the verse are read as referring to two distinct entries into the land. The first half, *ad ya'avor amcha Hashem*, refers to *bi'ah rishonah*, the first entry in the time of *Yehoshua*. The second half, *ad ya'avor am zu kanita*, this nation that You have acquired, refers to *bi'ah sheniyah*, the second entry in the time of *Ezra*. The *gemara* observes: *amru me'atah re'uyim hayu Yisrael la'asot lahem nes be-vi'ah sheniyah ke-vi'ah rishonah* — it would have been fitting for miracles to accompany the second entry as they had the first. *Ela she-garam ha-chet* — but sin caused otherwise. *Rashi* makes the important observation that it was not merely the absence of miracles that was at stake, but the fundamental nature of the entry itself: in the second entry, *Bnei Yisrael* entered as subjects of the Babylonian kingdom, *mishta'abdim le-malchut*, settling the land by permission rather than conquering it as a sovereign nation.

### Stones Round Trip

The *gemara* continues: *ve-achar kach hevi'u et ha-avanim u-vanu et ha-mizbe'ach ve-sadu va-sid ve-chatvu aleihem et kol divrei ha-Torah be-shivim lashon*. This is the *gemara*'s resolution of the ambiguity in the *pesukim*: the same stones that had been erected in *Gilgal* were transported to Har Gerizim and Har Eival, where they were used to build the *mizbeiach*, plastered, and the Torah was written upon them in seventy languages. The *olot* and *shelamim* were offered, they ate, drank, rejoiced, performed the *brachot* and the *klalos* — *ve-kiplu et ha-avanim* — and then folded up, so to speak, the stones. This phrase raises a question: if the stones were brought all the way to Har Gerizim and Har Eival, when did they get erected in *Gilgal*, as *Yehoshua* describes? The answer is that after all this was done, they brought the stones back. *Ve-ba'u va-lanu be-Gilgal* — and they came and lodged in *Gilgal*. As the verse says, *ve-ha'avartem otam imachem ve-hinachtem otam ba-malon* — you shall carry them with you and place them at the lodging place. One might ask: perhaps any lodging place would do? The *gemara* derives from the phrase *asher talinu bo ha-lailah* — where you sleep that night — that it refers to one specific place. And then the verse in *Yehoshua* records: *ve-et shteim esrei ha-avanim ha-eleh asher lakechu... hekim Yehoshua ba-Gilgal* — the twelve stones were erected in *Gilgal*. According to the *gemara*'s reading, this erection in *Gilgal* happened after the round trip to Har Gerizim and Har Eival, not before.

### Synthesis & Resolution

It is worth pausing to appreciate the full scope of what the *gemara* has accomplished here. There were two distinct problems in the *pesukim*. The first was the internal ambiguity in Devarim 27: was the Torah written on the erected stones or on the *avnei ha-mizbeiach*? The *gemara*'s answer is that these were the same stones — the stones erected in *Gilgal* became the stones of the *mizbeiach* at Har Gerizim and Har Eival, and the Torah was written on them in that dual capacity. The second problem was the apparent disjunction between Devarim, which presents the erection of the stones, the building of the *mizbeiach*, the writing of the Torah, and the *brachot* and *klalos* as one integrated event, and *Yehoshua*, which places the erection of the stones in *Gilgal* immediately after the crossing and the *mizbeiach* and *brachot u-klalos* many chapters and months later in Perek 8. The *gemara* resolves this by collapsing both accounts into a single miraculous day: the stones were taken from the *Yarden*, transported more than sixty *mil* to Har Gerizim and Har Eival, used for the *mizbeiach* and the writing of the Torah, and then brought back to *Gilgal* — all on the same day — while the battles of *Yericho* and *Ha'Ai* are treated as occurring at a later time, bracketed out of chronological sequence. This is a *gemara* that is solving problems in the *pesukim* that one would not have recognized without reading the narrative of *Yehoshua* alongside Devarim with great care.

### Tzira Debate

The *gemara* cites a *tanna*: *tzira lo avra imahen* — the *tzira*, the wasps, did not cross over with them into *Eretz Yisrael*. The verse had promised: *ve-shalachti et ha-tzira lefanecha* — I will send the wasps before you. So why does the *baraita* say they did not cross? Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish explains: *al sfat ha-Yarden amda* — they stood at the bank of the *Yarden*. They did not enter the land but remained hovering at its border, and from there they launched their attack. *Ve-zarka bahen mara* — they spat their venom across, blinding the enemy: *ve-simta eineihem mi-l'mala* — blinded their eyes above — *ve-sersatan mi-l'mata* — and castrated them below. This was, in effect, a long-range assault — a kind of guided weapon that operated from outside the border of *Eretz Yisrael*. The verse in Amos confirms both aspects: *va-ashmid piryo mi-ma'al* — I destroyed the fruit from above — *ve-sharashav mi-tachat* — and the roots below.

### Two Tzira

Rav Papa offers a different resolution: *shtei tzirot havai* — there were two distinct *tzirot*. One was associated with Moshe, and one with *Yehoshua*. The *tzira* of Moshe did not cross over into *Eretz Yisrael*, while the *tzira* of *Yehoshua* did cross and operated within the land, fulfilling the verse *ve-shalachti et ha-tzira lefanecha*. What problem is Rav Papa solving by positing two? It is difficult to say with certainty, and a closer examination of the *Maharsha* would be required. The *Maharsha* does observe that the verse referring to the *tzira* specifies only the *Kena'ani* and the *Chiti* and does not mention the other nations — which may be part of what the *gemara* is working through. The matter requires further study.

---

## Division of Tribes

### Six on Each

The *gemara* now turns to the actual events at Har Gerizim and Har Eival. Six tribes went up to the top of Har Gerizim and six to Har Eival. The verse in *Yehoshua* states: *chetzyo el mul Har Gerizim ve-ha-chetzyo el mul Har Eival* — half facing Har Gerizim and the [other] half facing Har Eival. What is the significance of the *ve-ha-chetzyo*, the particular phrasing of "the half"?

### Ephod Stones

Rav Kahana answers: *ke-derech she-chalukim kan, kach chalukim be-avnei efod* — just as they are divided here on the mountains, so are they divided on the stones of the *efod*. The *ve-ha-chetzyo* alludes to a division recognized elsewhere in the Torah, namely on the two precious stones worn on the shoulders of the *Kohen Gadol*. The *gemara* challenges this with a *baraita*.

### Ephod Letter Count

The *baraita* teaches: *shtei avanim tovot hayu lo le-Kohen Gadol al ketfav* — the *Kohen Gadol* had two precious stones on his shoulders, one on each side. On them were written the names of the twelve tribes: six names on one stone and six on the other. The verse states: *shishah mi-shemotam al ha-even ha-achat ve-et shemot ha-shishah ha-no'tarim al ha-even ha-sheniyah ke-toldotam*. The *baraita* notes that *ke-toldotam* — by their birth order — applies to the second stone but not the first. Why? Because on the first stone, *Yehudah* is listed first even though he is the fourth-born, since he is the leader — *mipnei she-Yehudah mukdam*. The *baraita* further states: *va-chamishim otiyot hayu* — there were fifty letters in total — *esrim va-chamishah al even zo ve-esrim va-chamishah al even zo* — twenty-five on each stone, a perfectly equal division.

### Rabbi Chanina View

Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel disagrees with the first opinion. He holds that the division on the *avnei efod* did not follow the order found in *Chumash ha-Pekudim*, i.e., *Bamidbar*, but rather the order found in *Chumash Sheni*, i.e., *Shemot*. The opening of *Shemot* lists: *Reuven, Shimon, Levi, Yehudah, Yissachar, Zevulun, u-Vinyamin* — and then: *Dan, Naftali, Gad, ve-Asher* — and the section concludes with *Yosef*. The *gemara* explains that in this listing, *benei Leah* appear in their birth order together, while *benei Rachel* appear one at the beginning (*Binyamin*) and one at the end (*Yosef*), with the children of the *shefachot* in the middle: *benei Rachel echad mi-kan ve-echad mi-kan, u-venei shefachot be-emtza*.

But this raises a difficulty: the verse says the names were inscribed *ke-toldotam* — and the second stone in this arrangement is not in birth order at all. The *gemara* resolves: *ki-shmos she-kara lahem avihen, ve-lo ki-shmos she-kara lahem Moshe* — it means by the names their father gave them at birth, not the tribal appellations used by Moshe later. Thus *Reuven* and not *Re'uveni*, *Shimon* and not *Shimoni*, *Dan* and not *ha-Dani*, *Gad* and not *ha-Gadi*. The intent is not a sequential birth order but rather personal names given at birth. This is a subtle and meaningful distinction: the *avnei efod* bore not the names of the tribes as national entities — as they appear in the census of *Bamidbar* — but the names of the twelve sons of *Yaakov* as individual human beings, as they appear in the opening of *Shemot*. There is something deeply personal about this understanding: the *Kohen Gadol* carried these twelve men on his shoulders, not twelve tribes in the abstract.

The *gemara* then challenges Rav Kahana: the *ve-ha-chetzyo* of Har Gerizim and Har Eival corresponds to neither of these two divisions on the *avnei efod*. The arrangement on the mountains — *Shimon, Levi, Yehudah, Yissachar, Yosef, u-Vinyamin* on Har Gerizim, and *Reuven, Gad, Asher, Zevulun, Dan, ve-Naftali* on Har Eival — does not match either the *Bamidbar* order or the *Shemot* order on the stones of the *efod*. *Tiyuvta de-Rav Kahana tiyuvta*: Rav Kahana's position is refuted.

### Ve'hachetzyo Problem

The *gemara* therefore returns to the question: if *ve-ha-chetzyo* does not refer to the division of the stones of the *efod*, what does it mean? The answer comes from a *tanna*: *hatziyah shel mul Har Gerizim merubah me-hatziyah shel Har Eival* — the half facing Har Gerizim was larger in number than the half on Har Eival. The *ve-ha-chetzyo* on Har Eival highlights that it was the lesser half.

### Levi Below Solution

The reason for this disparity: *mipnei she-Levi lemata* — because *Levi* was below, not on top of Har Gerizim. Since the *Levi'im* and *Kohanim* stood below in the valley rather than ascending the mountain, the side of Har Gerizim was diminished by their absence. One might object: *adaraba*, since *Levi* was below, that should make the Har Gerizim side smaller — yet the *gemara* says it was larger. The *gemara* clarifies: even though *Levi* was not fully counted in the Har Gerizim side, nevertheless the Har Gerizim side was still numerically greater.

### Yosef's Population

The reason is *bidei Yosef imahem* — because *benei Yosef* were on Har Gerizim, and *Yosef*'s population was enormous, more than enough to compensate for the absence of *Levi*. The proof is from *Yehoshua*: *vayidabru bnei Yosef et Yehoshua lemor, madua natata li nachalah goral echad ve-chevel echad va-ani am rav* — the children of *Yosef* complained to *Yehoshua* that he had given them only one portion even though they were so numerous. *Yehoshua* replied: *aleh lecha ha-ya'arah* — go up into the forest and take more land. The *gemara* interprets this exchange with a remarkable aside: *amar lahem lechu ve-hachvi'u atzmechem ba-ye'arim she-lo tishlot bachem ayin ha-ra* — *Yehoshua* was in effect telling them: you are so many, go hide yourselves in the forests so the *ayin ha-ra* will not afflict you. They responded: *zar'eih de-Yosef lo shaltah beih eina bisha* — the seed of *Yosef* is not subject to the evil eye. The verse itself confirms: *ben porat Yosef, ben porat alei ayin* — Rabbi Abbahu reads *alei ayin* not as "by the spring" but as *olei ayin*, rising above the evil eye. Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina derives the same from the *berachah* of *Yaakov*: *ve-yidgu la-rov be-kerev ha-aretz* — they shall multiply like fish within the land. Just as fish in the sea are covered by water and the eye has no power over them, so too the descendants of *Yosef* are not subject to the *ayin ha-ra*.

### Census Math
