*Tosafot* on 36a, *mahi ve-ha-chetzyo*, takes the discussion further by actually performing a tabulation from the census at the end of *Bamidbar* — the census taken at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, after the generation of the desert had died, as is established by *Seder Olam*. *Tosafot* computes the actual numbers tribe by tribe and concludes: *timtza be-minyan shvatim she-amdu al Har Gerizim odef al otam she-amdu al Har Eival tish'at alafim chasar kuf-lamed* — the tribes on Har Gerizim exceeded those on Har Eival by nine thousand minus 130. So the Har Gerizim side was indeed larger, consistent with the *gemara*. Crucially, *Levi* numbered approximately eight thousand. If one removes *Levi* from the Har Gerizim side, the difference narrows to only about one thousand, rendering the two sides nearly equal. This is entirely consistent with the *gemara*'s statement that it was *Levi*'s absence below that nearly equalized the sides, and that *Yosef*'s large numbers made the difference in keeping Har Gerizim the larger side.

### Fifty Letters

The *gemara* now raises an arithmetical problem. The *baraita* had stated that there were fifty letters across the two stones of the *efod*, twenty-five on each. But when one actually counts the letters in the twelve tribal names, the total is forty-nine, not fifty — and the division is twenty-five and twenty-four, not twenty-five and twenty-five. *Hamishim ve-ki chada havei* — fifty? It is forty-nine.

### Yehosef Solution

Rabbi Yitzchak offers the first solution: *Yosef hosifu lo ot achat* — an additional letter was added to *Yosef*'s name. The verse states: *edut be-Yehosef samo be-tzeto al eretz Mitzrayim* — there is a verse in *Tehillim* where *Yosef* appears with an extra *heh*, written *Yehosef*. It was this spelling that was inscribed on the *efod* stone, adding one letter to reach fifty total, with exactly twenty-five on each stone.

### Binyamin Shalem

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak challenges this: the *baraita* says *ke-toldotam* — the inscription must reflect the names as given at birth. *Yehosef* was not a name by which he was known during his lifetime in that form; it appears only in a late verse in *Tehillim*. Therefore, the name *Yehosef* does not satisfy the requirement of *ketoldotam*. Instead, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proposes a different solution: throughout the entire Torah, *Binyamin* is written without a *yud* — *Binyamin chaser* — but when he was born and his father named him, the verse reads *va-aviv kara lo Binyamin* — and this spelling is with the full *yud*, *Binyamin shalem*. It is precisely this birth spelling that satisfies *ke-toldotam* — the name as called at birth — and that provides the fiftieth letter, yielding twenty-five letters on each stone.

---

## Yosef's Temptation

### Yosef Sanctifies Name

Since we have been speaking of *Yosef* and the extra letter added to his name, the *gemara* now tells us why he merited this distinction. Rav Chana bar Bizna in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida teaches: *Yosef she-kidesh Shem Shamayim be-seter, hosifu lo ot achat mi-shmo shel Hakadosh Baruch Hu* — *Yosef*, who sanctified God's name in private, was rewarded with one letter from God's name: the *heh* of *Yehosef*.

### Yehudah Public Sanctific…

The contrast is drawn immediately: *Yehudah she-kidesh Shem Shamayim be-farhesia, nikra kulo al shemo shel Hakadosh Baruch Hu* — *Yehudah*, who sanctified God's name publicly, merited that his entire name reflects God's name. Indeed, *Yehudah* contains the letters *yud, heh, vav, heh* — the four letters of the divine name — with only an additional *dalet*. We will return tomorrow to the public sanctification of *Yehudah*, which the *gemara* will identify not with the *Yehudah* of this week's *parsha* but with the story of *Nachshon ben Aminadav* at the *Yam Suf*. For now, the focus is on *Yosef*.

### Temptation Scene

The *gemara* cites the verse: *va-yehi ke-hayom ha-zeh va-yavo ha-bayta la'asot melachto* — it was on such a day and he came to the house to do his work. Rabbi Yochanan says: *melamed she-shneihem li-dvar aveirah nitkavnu* — both of them, *Yosef* and the wife of *Potiphar*, intended that day to sin. What pushes Rabbi Yochanan to this unflattering reading about *Yosef*? *Tosafot* explains that it is the juxtaposition of *va-yavo ha-bayta* — "and he came to the house" — a word *va-yavo* associated with *bi'ah*, with *la'asot melachto*, doing his work. On this reading, the text hints that his coming was charged with intent. *Rav u-Shmuel* debate this directly: one says *la'asot melachto mamash* — to do his actual work — and the other says *la'asot tzorachav nichnas* — he entered to fulfill his desires.

*Ve-ein ish me-anshei ha-bayit sham ba-bayit* — none of the household staff was present. How could such a large household be completely empty? *Tana de-bei Rabbi Yishmael* explains: *oto ha-yom yom chagam haya* — it was a festival day of theirs, *ve-halchu kulam le-veit avodah zarah shelahem* — and all of them went to their house of idol worship. She told them she was ill and remained behind. *Amra*, she said to herself: *ein li yom she-nizkak li ke-hayom ha-zeh* — I will never have an opportunity like today.

### Yaakov's Image

At that critical moment, *va-titpesehu be-vigdo lemor*, she grabbed him by his garment. It was at this moment that *ba'ah demut dyukno shel aviv* — the image of his father appeared to him — *ve-nirah lo ba-chalon*, in the window. And the image spoke. *Yaakov*'s image said to him: *Yosef, atidim achecha she-yikkatvu al avnei efod* — your brothers are destined to be inscribed on the *avnei efod*, *ve-ata beneihem* — and you are among them. *Retzoncha she-yimacheh shimcha mi-beneihem* — do you want your name erased from among them? This warning carries a profound resonance, given the context in which the *gemara* has placed it. We have spent considerable time discussing the writing of names on the *avnei efod* and the erasure of names — and now the threat to *Yosef* is precisely the erasure of his name from among his brothers on those very stones. One might also detect here a deeper echo: the concept of *mechiyat ha-shem*, the erasure of the divine name, is particularly associated with grave sexual transgression. The warning is simultaneously about physical erasure from the *efod* and about the theological weight of such a sin.

*Ve-tikara ro'eh zonot* — and you will be called a shepherd of prostitutes. The verse in Mishlei says: *ro'eh zonot ye'abed hon* — one who shepherds prostitutes wastes great treasure. This was the warning. People dissipate immense reservoirs of dignity and honor by following their desires.

### Physical Resistance

*Miyad* — immediately — *va-teshev be-eitan kashto* — he placed his strength in his bow. The bow is transparently a phallic metaphor for the tension of sexual arousal. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir reads: *she-shav kashto le-eitano* — his bow returned to its strength, or alternatively, his *keri* returned to its source. *Va-yaphozu zero'ei yadav* — and the sinews of his arms were scattered. He pressed his fingers into the ground to prevent ejaculation. *Va-yetze shichvat zera mi-bein tzippornei yadav* — the seminal emission came out through his fingernails. This graphic account is conveying something important about the nature of what *Yosef* was resisting: he had come to a point where resistance was physiologically nearly impossible, where the body's drive was so powerful that even in holding back, the seed had to discharge somehow. He redirected it at enormous personal cost.

### Shepherd Role

*Midei avir Yaakov* — from the power of *Yaakov*. Who caused it that his name was ultimately inscribed on the *avnei efod*? *Avir Yaakov* — the strength of *Yaakov*, whose image appeared and pulled him back. *Misham ro'eh* — the *gemara* now returns to the image of the shepherd. Because he resisted and became worthy of having his name inscribed on the *efod*, *misham zachah ve-na'aseh ro'eh* — from there he merited and became a shepherd. *She-ne'emar: ro'eh Yisrael ha'azinah, noheig ke-tzon Yosef* — the verse says, Shepherd of Israel, hear, who leads like the flock of *Yosef*. *Yosef*, who might have become a *ro'eh zonot*, a shepherd of prostitutes, instead became the shepherd of *Bnei Yisrael*.

---

---

# Sotah 37

## Joseph's Restraint

### Joseph Intro

The daf opens against the backdrop of a broader discussion about the division of tribes at *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eival* and the figures of Yosef and Yehoshua. The Gemara had noted that two individuals are paradigmatic of *kiddush shem shamayim*: Yosef performed it *b'seter* — in secret — while Yehudah performed it *b'rabbim* — in public. The Gemara now turns to examine each case in depth, beginning with Yosef.

### Twelve Tribes from Joseph

A *tanna* teaches: *haya ra'ui Yosef latzeit mimenu yud-bet shvatim* — Yosef should rightfully have fathered all twelve tribes, just as Yaakov his father did. The textual basis is the juxtaposition in *Bereishit*: *Eleh toldot Yaakov Yosef* — "These are the generations of Yaakov: Yosef." The language suggests a direct parallel, as if Yosef were to be to his generation what Yaakov was to his. The *toldot* formula ordinarily introduces a genealogical listing, and the singular mention of Yosef implies he was meant to carry that generative role in full.

### Benjamin's Ten Sons

Yet this potential was forfeited at the decisive moment of temptation with the wife of Potifar: *ela sheyatza shichvat zaro mibein tzipornei yadav* — his seed went forth from between his fingernails. The act of restraint was heroic, yet it entailed a real loss. The Gemara notes, somewhat ruefully, that even though the occasion was a *kiddush shem shamayim*, the circumstances that led to it could perhaps have been avoided altogether. As the old distinction goes: a wise person never enters the situation a clever person needs to escape.

Nevertheless, *ve'af al pi chen yatze'u miBinyamin achiv* — the ten tribes Yosef was meant to father emerged instead from his brother Binyamin. *Vekulan nikre'u al shemo* — all ten of Binyamin's sons were named in memory of Yosef and the separation between them. The names are parsed one by one: *Bela*, because Yosef was *nivla bein ha'umot* — swallowed among the nations; *Vacher*, because Yosef was at least the firstborn of their shared mother; *Ashbel*, because God had taken him captive (*shevao Kel*); *Gera*, because he dwelt in exile like a lodger (*ger be'achsanyot*); *Naaman*, because he was exceedingly pleasant; *Achi v'Rosh*, my brother who was also my head, my elder; *Mupim v'Chupim* — I did not see his wedding (*chupah*) and he did not see mine. Rashi adds that *Mupim* also alludes to *piv k'fi Yaakov Avinu*, the teaching he received from Shem and Ever; and *Ard* — who descended among the nations, or according to another opinion, whose face resembled a rose (*vered*). What is striking is the intimacy of the naming: Binyamin, who was perhaps ten years old when Yosef was sold, named every one of his children as an expression of that unrelenting grief and longing.

---

## Joseph in Egypt

### Pharaoh's Test

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: when Pharaoh declared to Yosef, *uviladecha lo yarim ish et yado* — no man shall lift a hand without your authority — the astrologers of Pharaoh objected. *Eved shelekachato b'esrim kesef* — a slave purchased for twenty pieces of silver, you would set him over us? Pharaoh responded that he perceived in Yosef the *ginunei malchut* — the qualities of royalty — citing wisdom, strength, and beauty. The astrologers countered: if this is to be so, then let him demonstrate fitness for such office by knowing all seventy languages, as befits a man of truly royal upbringing.

### Gabriel & Languages

*V'ata Gavriel v'limdo shivim lashon* — the angel Gavriel came and taught Yosef the seventy languages. There is something deliberately inverted about this in relation to the story of Moshe, where Gavriel moved the infant's hand from gold to coals, resulting in Moshe's becoming *kvad lashon* — heavy of speech. Here the movement is in the opposite direction, opening Yosef's linguistic capacity rather than constraining it. Yet even with Gavriel's instruction, Yosef could not master the learning: *lo hava ka gamir*. At that point, *hosifu lo ot achat mishmo* — God added one letter of His own name to Yosef's name, transforming it into *Yehosef*, as the verse states: *eidut bi'Yehosef samo b'tzeito al eretz Mitzrayim*, with the completion of the verse *sfat lo yadati eshma* — a language I did not know I now hear. The letter unlocked what instruction alone could not.

This detail connects back to the theme of *kiddush shem shamayim b'seter*: the reward for Yosef's hidden sanctification of God's name is precisely this hidden gift — *ot achat mishmo shel Hakadosh Baruch Hu* — one letter from God's own name. And it is worth noting the contrast this creates with Pharaoh, who presented himself to the world as a divine figure: the one who truly carries that *element* of divinity is Yosef, through the letter of God's name embedded in his own.

### Hebrew Language Secret

The next day, whatever language Pharaoh tried, Yosef responded in kind — the test was passed. Then Yosef spoke to Pharaoh in *lashon hakodesh*, in Hebrew, and Pharaoh did not understand. Pharaoh asked Yosef to teach him this language. Yosef tried, but Pharaoh could not learn it — Gavriel was not there for him. Pharaoh then asked Yosef to swear that he would never reveal to anyone that there existed one language Pharaoh did not know, since a king who was worshipped as a god could not be known to lack mastery of any tongue. *V'ishtaba lei* — and Yosef swore.

The relevance of this oath surfaces later, at the end of Yaakov's life, when Yosef tells Pharaoh: *avi hishpiani leimor* — my father made me swear to bury him in *Kena'an*. Pharaoh replied: *zil tishol ashvuatcha* — go and seek release from your oath. Yosef responded: *v'eishul nami ashvuatach* — if I seek release from my oath regarding my father, I will also seek release from the oath I made to you, the oath to keep your linguistic secret. And though Pharaoh was displeased, he had no choice: *alei ukvor et avicha ka'asher hishbi'echa* — go, bury your father as he made you swear. The Midrash reads *ka'asher hishbi'echa* as indicating that Pharaoh's acquiescence was entirely conditioned on the weight of the oath, and the passage subtly explains why Pharaoh honored it at all.

### Oath Annulment

Tosafot raises a sharp halachic question on the phrase *v'eishul nami ashvuatach*. One who swears an oath to another person cannot seek *hatarat nedarim* — annulment of that vow — without that person's knowledge, or at least without some form of acquiescence, analogous to the episode of Tzidkiyahu and Nevuchadnetzar. Pharaoh never agreed to Yosef's annulling the oath made to him; he only agreed to release Yosef from his father's oath. So how could Yosef even threaten to do so?

Tosafot works through several possibilities before concluding: *veshema okminehu adigeizum* — perhaps Yosef was simply bluffing. He threatened something he in fact could not halachically have done, but Pharaoh did not know that. *Lo haya yachol lehishael alav velo nicha lei lePharaoh* — Yosef truly could not have obtained release from that oath, and Pharaoh was not happy about the situation, but Pharaoh did not know Yosef lacked the means to carry through. So Yosef's leverage was a bluff — and it worked.

---

## Judah's Leadership

### Benjamin Jumps First

The Gemara turns to the tribe of Yehudah and its *kiddush shem shamayim b'rabbim* at *Kriat Yam Suf*. A *tanna* teaches in Rabbi Meir's name: when the Jewish people stood at the sea, the tribes competed with one another — *zeh omer ani yored techilah layam, vezeh omer ani yored techilah layam* — each declaring that it would descend first. While they argued, *kafatz shivto shel Binyamin veyarad layam techilah* — the tribe of Binyamin leaped and went down into the sea first. The proof text is *sham Binyamin tzair verodem*, which is read: *al tikri verodem* — do not read "rules them" — *ela rad yam* — but "went down into the sea."

The response of Yehudah was not gracious: *vehayu sarei Yehudah rogmem otam* — the princes of Yehudah were stoning them, as the verse states *sarei Yehudah rigmatam*. The implication, though not spelled out explicitly in the Gemara, is that Yehudah felt this was their prerogative, stolen from them by Binyamin's initiative. *Lefichach* — therefore — *zacha Binyamin hatzaddik venaaseh ushpizin lagvura* — Binyamin merited to become the host of the Divine Presence, as the verse promises: *uvein ktefav shachan* — between his shoulders it dwelt. This connects to the well-known geographical-theological point that the *Kodesh Kodashim* fell within Binyamin's *chelek*, even as the broader *Har Habayit* fell within Yehudah's — two tribes of *Bnei Rachel* and *Bnei Leah* standing right at the threshold of the Divine dwelling.

Tosafot cites a *mashal* from the *Tosefta* or *Mechilta* that frames this somewhat differently. A king had two sons; he told the younger to wake him at sunrise, and the older at the third hour. The younger came to wake the king at sunrise, but the older prevented him, insisting the time was wrong. While they argued, the king rose on his own and said: *mah banai l'kape'ach s'charchem* — I will not deprive you of your reward. Binyamin's reward for going first was *Shechinah b'chelko* — the Divine Presence resting in his portion. Yehudah's reward for its role — for the leadership it embodied even in the dispute — was *malchut*, as the verse implies: *ein rad ela malchut*. This version is notably more generous to Yehudah: both tribes were doing something they understood to be right, and each received a corresponding reward.

Yet the Gemara's version is harder on Yehudah. The stoning of Binyamin's tribe hardly sounds like an act of leadership. One response to this tension is that the *Tosefta* version reframes the dispute as a principled disagreement about *timing* — Yehudah believed the moment had not yet come — whereas the Gemara's account suggests a competition over privilege. The *Kotzker Rebbe* is said to have reconciled the two opinions: during the theoretical argument, everyone was talking; when the actual moment of action arrived, Binyamin moved — and *lo palgi ahadedi*, the two accounts do not truly contradict.

### Nachshon's Faith

Rabbi Yehudah offers a different version entirely: *lo kach hayah ma'aseh* — that is not how it happened. In Rabbi Yehudah's account, *kafatz Nachshon ben Aminadav veyarad layam techilah* — Nachshon ben Aminadav leaped first into the sea. The verse *v'Yehudah od rad im El* is read as "Yehudah went down with God," or on account of his faith in God.

And the verse cited immediately afterwards — *hoshieini Elokim ki va'u mayim ad nafesh* — "save me, God, for the waters have reached my soul" — makes clear that the sea did not split immediately. Nachshon had gone in, and the waters were at his throat. *Tavati b'yevein metzulah v'ein ma'amad* — I have sunk into the deep mire and there is no footing. This is the Gemara's way of squaring the famous narrative question: who split the sea — Nachshon or Moshe? The answer given here is that both acts occurred, but sequentially, and with a frightening interval between them.

### Nachshon Drowning

While Nachshon was drowning, *hayah Moshe maarich bitfilah* — Moshe was prolonging his prayer. God responded: *yedidai tov'im bayam* — My beloved ones are drowning in the sea — interestingly in the plural, perhaps echoing the famous Midrash that God's own handiwork was drowning: *ma'aseh yadai tov'im bayam v'atem omrim shirah*. God says to Moshe: *v'atah maarich bitfilah l'fanai?* — and you are prolonging your prayer before Me? Moshe replied: *Ribbono Shel Olam, u'mah b'yadi la'asot?* — Master of the Universe, what else should I do? And God's answer: *daber el Bnei Yisrael veyisau* — speak to the children of Israel and let them go forward — and then lift your staff.

This is an extraordinarily powerful moment that is not always appreciated in its full depth. Moshe was doing the entirely natural, even obligatory, thing: he was praying, awaiting divine instruction. And God essentially says: stop. There is a time for prayer, a time to wait for instruction — and a time to simply *know what you have to do and do it*. Nachshon embodied that third mode. He did not wait for the sea to split. He did not wait for instruction. He understood, at some deep level, that if this is the situation, this is what God wants — and he leaped.

This also illuminates the famous verse after the crossing: *vaya'aminu b'Hashem uvMoshe avdo* — and they believed in God and in Moshe His servant. If they had seen all the plagues and wonders, what does it mean that only now did they believe? The answer is that *emunah* here is not abstract theological belief, not assent to God's existence. It is live, active, embodied faith — the kind of faith that acts before it sees, that jumps into the water before the water parts. Nachshon demonstrated that faith before anyone else.

### Judah's Kingdom

*Vezachu Yehudah la'asot memshalah b'Yisrael* — Yehudah merited to exercise dominion in Israel. The verse: *haysah Yehudah l'kodsho, Yisrael mamshelosav* — Yehudah was for God's holy one, Israel for His dominion. And the reason: *mishum dehayam ra'ah vayanos* — because the sea saw and fled, because of the actions of Yehudah. It was the act of *Nachshon* — and the tribe that followed — which, together with Moshe's subsequent lifting of his staff, brought about the splitting of the sea.

It is worth noting the contrast between Yosef and Yehudah that runs beneath the surface here. Yosef operates throughout in a mode of *histapkut* — trusting that God is working through events, saying to his brothers *al te'atzvu*, do not be distressed, it is all God's doing. This is admirable from a theological standpoint, but it is not the posture of a leader. Yehudah, by contrast, says *anochi e'ervenu* — I take personal responsibility. The reward for Binyamin's leap was *Shechinah* — God's Presence. The reward for Yehudah's leadership was *memshalah* — dominion, kingship. Faith and leadership are not identical, and both have their distinct expressions and rewards.

---

## Gerizim & Eival

### Levi's Position

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov opens a new problem: *iy efshar lomar Levi lemattah* — it is impossible to say that Levi was below, at the foot of the mountains, because the Torah's own division places Levi on *Har Gerizim*. But neither can one say they were above on the mountains, because the account in *Yehoshua* places the *Kohanim* and *Levi'im* in the center, with the *Aron*, below. How to reconcile?

The Gemara's answer: *ziknei kehunah v'leviya lemattah* — the elders of the *kohanim* and *Levi'im* were below with the *Aron*, while the remaining members of the tribe were above on the mountain, as the Torah prescribes.

Rabbi Yoshiya offers an alternative: everyone fit for *avodah* — those between the ages of 30 and 50, the active years of Levitical service — was below, while the rest were above.

### All Below Mountains

Rebbi disagrees with both: *elu v'elu lemattah* — both groups, all the tribes, were below. This resolves a different textual tension. The Torah says *eleh ya'amdu al Har Gerizim*, which sounds like they stood *on* the mountain. The account in *Yehoshua* says *mul Har Gerizim* — facing, or at the foot of, Har Gerizim. Rebbi reads *al* not as "upon" but as "near," *besamuch*, and marshals a parallel: the verse *venasata al hamareches levonah zakah* — you shall place the frankincense *on* the arrangement of the *lechem hapanim* — cannot mean literally atop the bread, as the incense sat in the space between the two stacks. So too *al* in this context means adjacent, not literally upon. Just as Rebbi in a separate *braita* rules *al besamuch* regarding the frankincense of the *lechem hapanim* — deriving this from the verse that the *parochet* shades *over* the *Aron* without literally resting on it — so too here: everyone stood *near* the mountains, not on them.

The image that results is of the entire people gathered in the valley between the two mountains, all below, all present, all participants.

### Facing Mountains

*Hafchu pneichem klapei Har Gerizim* — they all turned to face Har Gerizim — *upetchu b'bracha* — and they opened with the blessing. Then they turned toward *Har Eival* and opened with the *klala*. The choreography is total participation: no one stands apart while others recite; the entire people face the mountain of blessing and then face the mountain of curse. Every voice is included. The Torah's language confirms this: *v'anu kol ha-am v'amru amen* — all the people answered and said *amen*. One might feel that the original image — tribes positioned on visually distinct mountains, one lush and abundant, one barren — carries a certain dramatic power. But what this arrangement achieves is that every person owns every blessing and every curse, and no one is merely an observer.

---

## Covenant Framework

### Three Covenants

The Gemara now counts: *baruch bikhlal baruch biprat, arur bikhlal arur biprat* — there is a general blessing and a specific blessing, a general curse and a specific curse. Beyond that, each *mitzvah* has four dimensions: *lilmod u'lelamed lishmor v'la'asot* — to learn, to teach, to observe, and to do. For each of those four dimensions there is a corresponding *baruch*, and for each a corresponding *arur*. That is four plus four equals eight; eight blessings and eight curses equals sixteen dimensions per *mitzvah* — sixteen *britot*. And this was enacted three times: at *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eival*, at *Sinai*, and at *Arvot Moav*. Three times sixteen yields forty-eight *britot* — forty-eight covenantal dimensions — for every single *mitzvah* in the Torah.

Rabbi Shimon, however, disputes whether *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eival* constituted one of the three *brit*-moments at all. His alternative three loci are *Har Sinai*, *Ohel Moed*, and *Arvot Moav*. His reasoning reflects a conceptual reframing: we have shifted from counting *brachot* and *klalot* to speaking of *brit* — covenant. And when the question is where the covenant was established, *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eival* are a ceremony of *baruch* and *arur*, not the *ikar brit*. The covenant proper is sealed at *Sinai*, elaborated at *Ohel Moed*, and renewed at *Arvot Moav*.

### Generalities & Details

This dispute maps onto a deeper *tannaitic* disagreement. Rabbi Yishmael holds: *klalot ne'emru b'Sinai, pratot b'Ohel Moed* — the general principles were stated at Sinai, the specific details at the Tent of Meeting. Rashi illustrates: the verse *vezavachta alav et olotecha ve'et shelamecha* — you shall offer your burnt offerings and peace offerings upon it — was stated in the context of Sinai, but it gives no detail about *matan damim*, the application of the blood, or *haktarat emurin*, or *hafshat v'nituach*. All of those details appear only in *Sefer Vayikra*, which is the Torah of *Ohel Moed*. On this reading, everything in the Torah from *Vayikra* onward is the *prat* of what was sketched at *Sinai*. This also implies a natural reading of what *Sinai* encompasses: it need not be limited to the *Aseret HaDibrot* alone, but may extend through *parshat Mishpatim*, where Moshe descended, read the Torah to the people, and sealed the *Sefer HaBrit* — the covenant scroll — at the end of *Mishpatim*. That is the natural terminus of the *Sinai* revelation as a legal-covenantal unit, and including *Mishpatim* makes it considerably more plausible to view it as the repository of *klalot* from which all subsequent detail is drawn.

Rabbi Akiva disagrees: *klalot u'pratot ne'emru b'Sinai* — both generalities and specifics were stated at Sinai. *V'nishnu b'Ohel Moed* — and they were repeated at the Tent of Meeting. *V'nishtalshu b'Arvot Moav* — and repeated a third time at Arvot Moav. On this view there are three fully parallel transmissions of the entire Torah, each in its own setting and context.

This is a dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva that extends well beyond the immediate question of covenant-locations. Rabbi Yishmael's famous principle is *dibra Torah kilshon bnei adam* — the Torah speaks in human language, in accessible, contextually organic terms — and his approach to hermeneutics tends toward restraint, not pressing every detail to yield independent legal force. Rabbi Akiva, who *darshens* every letter, would naturally hold that even the details were already present at *Sinai* in their fullness — nothing was communicated in a lesser or more mediated mode. The question of how many times the Torah was transmitted, and whether details were already embedded in the original revelation or unfolded progressively, appears to track these broader commitments. This axis is, of course, a central concern of Heschel's *Torah Min Hashamayim*.

### 48 Covenants Math

The mathematical upshot: once we have 48 *britot* per *mitzvah* (16 × 3), and this applies to every individual *mitzvah* in the Torah, we have 48 *britot* per *mitzvah* multiplied across 613 *mitzvot*. But Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda of Kfar Akko, citing Rabbi Shimon, goes further: *ein lecha mitzvah u'mitzvah she'ktuvah baTorah shelo nichratu aleha arbaim u'shmonah britot shel shesh me'ot elef u'shloshet alafim v'chamesh me'ot v'chamishim* — for every single *mitzvah*, the 48 *britot* are covenanted not just once but 603,550 times — the number of adult men counted in the census. For every *mitzvah*, each individual Israelite carries 48 covenantal obligations, and there were 603,550 individuals. The Gemara then notes: for every individual Israelite, the total number of covenantal obligations equals 603,550.

### Mutual Guarantee

Rav Mesharshaya explains the distinction between the two positions: *arva d'arva ika beinaihu* — the second position adds the dimension of *arvut* upon *arvut* — guarantee upon guarantee. On the first reading, one might simply be multiplying the total *britot* across the total population, an arithmetic aggregation. But Rav Mesharshaya's point is different: each individual does not merely have 48 *britot* for each *mitzvah*. Each individual is also an *arev* — a guarantor — for every other individual's 48 *britot*. So for every *mitzvah*, each person carries 48 obligations on their own account, plus responsibility for 603,549 others, each carrying their own 48. The numbers become astronomical.

And one can extend the logic: I am not only responsible for your keeping your 48 *britot*, I am also responsible for your discharging your *arvut* obligations toward everyone else. That level of *arvut d'arvut* makes the total obligation truly exponential — and Rav Mesharshaya appears to intend exactly that, which is why he adds this observation rather than simply restating what came before. Tosafot works through some of the arithmetic, though by that point the numbers have grown well beyond the scope of a brief calculation.

---

## Curses & Adultery

### Adultery Theme

Rabbi Yehudah ben Nechemia, the *meturgamana* — the public announcer — of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, offered a striking interpretation: *kol haparsha kula lo ne'emra ela b'mna'ef u'mna'efet* — the entire section of *brachot* and *klalos* was stated only with reference to an adulterer and adulteress. This is a striking return to the *Sotah* theme, and it is notable that the formulation includes the male sinner, not only the woman. The *parasha* is not, on this reading, a general moral catalogue — it is a unified statement about the consequences of sexual betrayal within marriage.

### Curses Explained

The Gemara then proceeds to trace every *arur* back to the act of adultery, with varying degrees of directness. *Arur ha'ish asher ya'aseh pesel u'masecha* — the verse curses one who makes an idol. But, the Gemara explains, this means one who committed adultery, produced a *mamzer*, and that child — excluded from *Bnei Yisrael* — went among idol worshippers and worshipped *avoda zara*. The sin of adultery cascades into idolatry: *sheken garmu lo* — for they caused it.

Rashi extends the reading systematically: the adulterer fathers a *mamzer*; the child, shamed and excluded, turns to the nations and their worship. Similarly, *shochev im behemah* is read in the context of the *Sotah* ordeal: *eishes ish she'asa ma'aseh behemah she'mna'efet*. *Mikalel aviv v'imo* — one who curses his father and mother — is the child of an adulterous union, born into a household whose shame brought disgrace on the parents who raised such wrongdoing. *Mashgeh iver* — who misleads the blind — is the seducer of a married woman: *m'fateh eshet ish*, blinding her to the weight of the sin she is being drawn into, since *she'isuma badavar v'eino yodei'a onsho kamohu* — she is blinded in the matter and does not fully perceive the punishment as he does. *Masig gevul re'ehu* — who removes a neighbor's boundary — is one who takes another man's wife: *ba'al ishto, harei zeh hesig gevul*. *Makeh re'ehu baseter* — who strikes his neighbor in secret — is one who causes the bitter waters of the *Sotah* to work their effect through whispered manipulation. *Lokei'ach shochad l'hakot nefesh* — one who takes a bribe to cause death — is the one who accepts payment to aid the adulterer in seducing a married woman and thereby brings about her death through the *Sotah* ordeal.

The final verse — *mateh mishpat ger yatom* — the Gemara concedes: *eini yodei'a lidrosh* — I do not know how to interpret it in this framework. The intellectual honesty of that admission is, in its own way, as noteworthy as all the interpretations that preceded it.

---

## Blessings & Curses

### Alternating Pattern

The Mishna states: *Tanu Rabanan*: the verse *venasata et habracha al Har Gerizim ve'et haklala al Har Eival* — why does the Torah need to state this, given that the allocation of tribes to each mountain has already been specified? The answer is: *ela l'hakdim bracha laklala* — to establish that the blessing is pronounced before the curse. And lest one think this means all the *brachot* are recited together before all the *klalos*, the singular language — *bracha v'klala* — indicates: one blessing, then one curse, then the next blessing, then the next curse. They alternate, one by one, individually.

### Seven Parallels

The Mishna then enumerates seven structural parallels between the *brachot* and the *klalos*. Each of the following features that characterizes the *klalot* applies equally to the *brachot*: they were pronounced by the *Levi'im* (*ma klalos b'Levi'im af brachot b'Levi'im*); they were said in a loud voice (*ma klala b'kol ram af bracha b'kol ram*), as the phrasing *v'anita v'amarta* implies; they were in *lashon hakodesh* (*ma klala b'lashon hakodesh af bracha b'lashon hakodesh*) — which connects this passage directly to the discussion that opened the tractate; they had both a general and specific form (*ma klala b'klal u'vfrat af bracha b'klal u'vfrat*); and finally, for both, *elu v'elu onim v'omrim amen* — both these and those, all the people together, answered and said *amen*. Not half the people for the blessings and the other half for the curses — everyone said *amen* to both. The structural symmetry is total: in form, in voice, in language, in scope, and in communal response, blessing and curse are mirror images of one another.

---

---

# Sotah 38

## Intro: Birkat Kohanim

### Daf 38 Overview

Daf 38 marks a transition away from the *agadata* and returns to the *mishnayot*, specifically to the category of things that must be said in any language — *ne'emarin bechol lashon* — as well as those requiring *lashon hakodesh*. The daf now turns its attention to *birkat kohanim*.

### Why in Sotah

It is worth pausing to note how much of the *halachot* of *birkat kohanim* come to be discussed precisely here, in Masechta Sotah. The reason is structural: *birkat kohanim* appears in the *mishna* as one of the items requiring *lashon hakodesh*, and so Sotah becomes the occasion for a full treatment of the subject. The same dynamic explains why the laws of *egla arufa* — which might more naturally have found a home in Kodshim — end up receiving an entire *perek* here: because *egla arufa* is mentioned in the *mishna*'s discussion of *lashon hakodesh* versus *bechol lashon*, and one topic pulls the other in its wake.

### Mishna: Birkat Kohanim

The *mishna* asks: *birkat kohanim keitzad* — how is *birkat kohanim* performed? The *keitzad* here is not asking how to recite the blessing in *lashon hakodesh*; that requirement is taken for granted. Rather, the *mishna* uses this as an opportunity to address the broader laws of how *birkat kohanim* is conducted.

### Three Issues

Three issues are addressed. First, the number of blessings: *bamedina omer osa shalosh berachos* — outside the *mikdash*, the blessing is divided into three, meaning the congregation responds *amen* after each of the three verses (*Yevarechecha*, *Ya'er*, *Yisa*), treating each as a separate unit. *Ubamikdash bracha achat* — in the *Beis HaMikdash*, they do not interrupt with *amen* between the verses, and so the entire blessing constitutes one. In the *mikdash*, the response was *baruch shem* rather than *amen*, and since this does not interrupt the flow of the three verses, they are treated as a single unified blessing.

Second, the divine name: *bamikdash omer es Hashem kichsavov* — in the *mikdash*, God's name is pronounced as written, that is, the *shem hameforash*, the four-letter name that is not sounded outside the *mikdash*. *Ubamedina bekinuyov* — outside the *mikdash*, the name is pronounced in its customary substitute form. Rashi explains: *kichsavov be-Yud-Heh*, *bekinuyov be-Aleph-Dalet*.

Third, the position of the hands: *bamedina kohanim nosim es yedeihen kneged kitfeihen* — outside the *mikdash*, the *kohanim* lift their hands to shoulder height. *Ubamikdash al gabei rasheihen* — in the *mikdash*, the hands are raised above the head. The reason given is that the *shechina* rests in the *mikdash*, and the hands should therefore be raised high enough that the divine presence is, in a sense, above them. An exception is made for the *kohen gadol*, *chutz mikohen gadol she'eino magbiya yadav lema'la min hatzitz* — his hands should not rise above the *tzitz* on his forehead. *Rabbi Yehuda* disagrees, holding that even the *kohen gadol* raises his hands above the *tzitz*, citing the verse *vayisa Aharon es yadav el ha'am vayivarchaim* — and since Aharon was a *kohen gadol*, the word *vayisa* implies a particularly high elevation.

### Mishna Structure

The *mishna*'s organization is notable. The pattern alternates between *medina* and *mikdash*: the first ruling goes *medina-mikdash*, the second goes *mikdash-medina*, and the third returns to *medina-mikdash*. This may simply be a mnemonic device — each clause flows into the next through an ABBA-like alternation. There may also be a more deliberate reason: when it comes to the issue of pronouncing God's name as written, the *mishna* places the *mikdash* practice first, because pronouncing the *shem hameforash* is a matter of such gravity that it cannot be mentioned as an afterthought. The other issues are more historically remote and so their secondary mention is less problematic.

---

## Language Requirement

### Koh Tevarchu

The *gemara* opens with a *baraita*: *koh tevarchu* — the word *koh* indicates that the blessing must be given in *lashon hakodesh*. The *baraita* asks: perhaps it may be said in any language? Perhaps *koh* does not carry this implication?

### Gezerah Shava

The *gemara* resolves this through a *gezerah shava*. The word *koh* appears here in *koh tevarchu*, and the word *eileh* appears elsewhere: *eileh ya'amdu levarech et ha'am* — the blessing pronounced on Har Gerizim. Just as the blessing at Har Gerizim was given in *lashon hakodesh*, so too *birkat kohanim* must be in *lashon hakodesh*: *mah lehalan bi-lashon hakodesh af kan bi-lashon hakodesh*.

### Tosafot Question

Tosafot raises an incisive question: why derive the requirement from Har Gerizim? One could equally argue the opposite — learn from the verse *ve'achalta ve'savata u'verachta*, which governs *birkat hamazon*, and which we know may be said in any language. The *gezerah shava* could just as well have pointed toward *bechol lashon*.

### Text vs. Non-Text

Tosafot answers: it is more compelling to derive *birkat kohanim* from the blessings of Har Gerizim, because both are instances where the Torah provides an explicit text — *dil'shteihen meforash ba'Torah*. The text of the *kohanim*'s blessing is fully spelled out in the Torah; similarly, the blessings and curses at Har Gerizim are spelled out. By contrast, the text of *birkat hamazon* is not specified in the Torah — the verse *ve'achalta ve'savata u'verachta* simply requires expressing gratitude, and any adequate formulation suffices. Since there is no prescribed text, the question of original versus translation does not arise, and of course it may be said in any language.

This points to a deeper conceptual distinction. The requirement to speak in *lashon hakodesh* is, in many cases, really a requirement to recite the original text rather than a translation. When the Torah provides a specific text, the question becomes: must you say the original, or may you say it in translation? Things permitted in any language may simply be those for which no specific text is mandated — in which case the concept of "original versus translation" is inapplicable, and naturally any language will do.

### Categorization

Examining the lists in the *mishna* bears this out. Those items requiring *lashon hakodesh* — *mikra bikkurim*, *chalitzah*, *berachot ukelalot*, *birkat kohanim*, *parshat hamelech*, *parshat egla arufa*, and *mashuach milchamah* — nearly all have a specific Torah text. Those permitted *bechol lashon* that have no formal text — like *tefilla* and *birkat hamazon* — are of course open to any language. And some things with a formal text — like *parshat sotah*, *vidui ma'aser*, and *kriat shema* — are permitted in any language, meaning translation is acceptable. The one exception in the *lashon hakodesh* list is *birkat kohen gadol* on Yom Kippur, which has no fixed text, making it the outlier. On this reading, the emphasis of *lashon hakodesh* is less about the Hebrew language per se and more about the obligation to use the original text rather than a translation.

---

## Two Approaches

### Rabbi Yehuda

*Rabbi Yehuda* holds that no derivation from Har Gerizim is necessary. *Koh* itself — "exactly like this" — is sufficient to teach that the blessing must be recited in precisely this form, in this language. No external source is needed.

---

## Standing Requirement

### Koh Tevarchu

A further *baraita* derives from *koh tevarchu* that the blessing must be given while standing. Perhaps, the *baraita* asks, the *kohanim* may be seated? The verse provides the initial opening.

### Eileh Ya'amdu

A *gezerah shava* resolves the question. *Eileh ya'amdu levarech* — "these shall stand to bless" — at Har Gerizim makes clear that standing is required: *mah lehalan be'amida af kan be'amida*.

---

## Standing Requirement (II)

### Lesharto Ulevarech

*Rabbi Natan* holds that the standing requirement need not be derived from Har Gerizim. The verse *lesharto ulevarech bishmo* — the *kohanim* are chosen to serve God and to bless in His name — is itself sufficient. This verse powerfully links the priestly role of service with the role of blessing.

### Avodah Connection

The derivation proceeds as follows: just as priestly service (*sheirut*) must be performed while standing, so too the blessing must be given while standing — *mah mesharet be'amida af mevarech be'amida*. And how do we know that priestly service itself requires standing? From the verse *la'amod lesharet* — "to stand and to serve."

---

## Two Approaches (II)

### Rabbi Natan

As the discussion develops, a clear structural pattern emerges. One approach — that of *Rabbi Yehuda* and those who derive requirements from *koh tevarchu* combined with *eileh ya'amdu levarech* — situates *birkat kohanim* within the category of a *beracha*. The relevant constellation is the nature of blessing itself: *koh* points us to the blessing text, and Har Gerizim provides a parallel instance of blessing. The priestly identity is not the hermeneutic focus.

*Rabbi Natan* adopts an entirely different orientation. He consistently derives the requirements of *birkat kohanim* from *lesharto ulevarech bishmo* — framing *birkat kohanim* as a form of *avodah*, priestly service. The model is not "how does one give a blessing" but "what do *kohanim* do in their role as servants of God."

### Conceptual Dispute

This is not merely a technical dispute about which verse to use. The two approaches reflect a deeper disagreement about what *birkat kohanim* fundamentally is. Is it a *beracha* — an act of blessing that happens to be performed by *kohanim* — or is it an *avodah* — a form of priestly service that happens to take the form of a blessing? Both approaches reach the same practical conclusions so far, but the underlying framework diverges significantly.

### Different Conclusions

The stakes of this dispute become visible when one asks whether *birkat kohanim* is a *mitzvah de'oraita* outside the *Beis HaMikdash*. If one learns everything from how *berachot* work — and especially from Har Gerizim, which itself took place outside any *mikdash* — then there is no inherent reason to confine the *mitzvah* to the *mikdash*. The practice outside the *mikdash* is straightforwardly a *mitzvah de'oraita*. But if one learns everything from *sheirut* — from priestly service in the *mikdash* — then one might well conclude that *birkat kohanim* is fundamentally a *mikdash*-centered *avodah*, and whatever is practiced outside is something of a lesser status. This question will continue to resonate throughout the subsequent discussions.

---

## Hand Position

### Nesi'as Kapayim

A further *baraita* derives from *koh tevarchu* that the blessing requires *nesi'as kapayim* — the lifting of the hands. The verse itself might not make this obvious, so the *baraita* turns to a *gezerah shava*: *ne'emar kan koh tevarchu* and *ne'emar lehallan vayisa Aharon es yadav el ha'am vayivarchaim* — Aharon lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them. Just as there the blessing was given with raised hands, so too here.

### Rabbi Yonatan Challenge

*Rabbi Yonatan* challenges this derivation. If we are going to learn from Aharon's blessing, we are obligated to learn all the contextual circumstances of that blessing: Aharon was the *kohen gadol*, the occasion was *Rosh Chodesh*, and it followed a series of *korbanos tzibbur* at the time of the *miluim*. If we learn from there, perhaps *nesi'as kapayim* is only required when all these circumstances converge — when it is a *kohen gadol*, on *Rosh Chodesh*, after public offerings.

### Hu Uvanav Kol Hayamim

*Rabbi Natan* responds: the derivation from Aharon's blessing is unnecessary. The verse *lesharto ulevarech bishmo hu uvanav kol hayamim* — "to serve and to bless in His name, he and his sons, all the days" — provides the needed answer. From *hu uvanav*, we learn that just as Aharon performed *nesi'as kapayim*, so too his sons do the same — eliminating the restriction to *kohen gadol*. And from *kol hayamim* — "all the days" — we learn that the practice is not limited to special occasions like *Rosh Chodesh*.

### Eliminating Circumstances

This disposes of two of the three limiting circumstances: the *kohen gadol* restriction falls away through *hu uvanav*, and the *Rosh Chodesh* restriction falls away through *kol hayamim*. The question of the structural link is then addressed: the verse *hu uvanav kol hayamim* speaks of *la'amod lesharet* — priestly service — and we connect the *beracha* to the *sheirut* through the other verse, creating the *hekesh* between *beracha* and *sheirut* that makes the *avodah* comparison operative. The general principle is then stated: just as *avodah* is performed the same way by ordinary *kohanim* as by the *kohen gadol*, and under ordinary circumstances as under special ones, the same applies to *birkat kohanim*.

### Tosafot: Korban Type

Tosafot raises a further question. Even granting all of the above — even accepting that *nesi'as kapayim* is not limited to the *kohen gadol* and not limited to *Rosh Chodesh* — how do we know it applies in the absence of a *korban tzibbur*? In the case of Aharon, the setting was a *korban tzibbur*, and *kol hayamim* could itself be satisfied by the *korban tamid*, which is itself a *korban tzibbur* offered every single day. So perhaps *nesi'as kapayim* is required every day — but only because every day there is a *tamid*, a public offering. How do we know it would apply by a *korban yachid*?

### Tosafot Answer

Tosafot resolves this by accepting the implicit premise: in fact, *birkat kohanim* in the *mikdash* was only performed in the context of *korban tzibbur*, not *korban yachid*. This is documented explicitly in the fifth *perek* of Masechta Tamid, which describes the *kohanim* descending after placing the limbs on the ramp, gathering in the *lishkat hagazit*, reciting the *aseret hadibrot*, *shema*, and other prayers, and then blessing the people — and the same practice applied at *musaf* and at the afternoon *tamid*. *Rabbi Yonatan*'s challenge about *korban yachid* was therefore not truly a challenge at all: *nesi'as kapayim* was always tied to *korban tzibbur*.

But this answer carries a consequence that Tosafot makes explicit: if *birkat kohanim* in its full *halachic* form was tied to *korban tzibbur*, then the question of whether the *mitzvah de'oraita* applies outside the *Beis HaMikdash* becomes acute. The *avodah*-centered approach has now established that the practice is inherently bound to the context of communal sacrifice in the *mikdash*.

---

## God's Name

### Vesamu Et Shemi

The *gemara* turns to the question of the divine name. A *baraita* teaches: *koh tevarchu es benei Yisrael beshem hameforash* — since the verse says *koh*, and the word *koh* specifies the exact form, one reads the name as it is written, yielding the *shem hameforash*. But perhaps one may use only a *kinuy*, a substitute pronunciation?

The *baraita* resolves this from the verse *vesamu es shemi al bnei Yisrael* — "and they shall place My name upon the children of Israel." *Shemi hameyuchad li* — my distinctive, unique name. That name is the *shem hameforash*.

### Outside Mikdash Question

But one might ask: if that is the source, perhaps the *shem hameforash* is to be used even outside the *Beis HaMikdash*? After all, the verse *vesamu es shemi* does not itself specify a location.

The *baraita* answers through a verbal analogy: *ne'emar kan vesamu* and *ne'emar lehallan lasum et shemo sham* — "the place that God has chosen to place His name there." The word *vesamu* here echoes *lasum et shemo sham* there. Just as *lasum et shemo sham* refers to the *Beis Habechira*, the chosen place, so too *vesamu es shemi* applies only in the *Beis Habechira*. Outside the *mikdash*, only the *kinuy* is used.

### Bechol Hamakom

*Rabbi Yoshiya* holds that no such derivation is necessary. He cites the verse *bechol hamakom asher azkir es shemi avo eilecha uverachticha* — "in every place where I will cause My name to be mentioned, I will come to you and bless you." From this verse he derives that wherever God's name is mentioned — meaning wherever the *kohanim* invoke it — God will come and bless.

### Gemara Resistance

The *gemara* resists the straightforward reading of this verse. *Bechol makom salka deitach?* — does it truly mean everywhere? Rashi explains the difficulty on two levels. First, there is a circular problem: the verse *ze shemi leolam veze zichri* already teaches that God's written name is not pronounced as written — *lo keshe'ani nichtav ani nikra* — so the idea that the *shem hameforash* would be used everywhere already runs against an established principle. Second, and more substantively, Rashi notes: *vechi bechol makom shechina ba'ah vesharah* — does the *shechina* truly descend and rest in every place? The verse says *avo eilecha* — "I will come to you" — which implies divine presence descending. That is not a universal phenomenon.

### Reading Out of Order

The *gemara* therefore concludes: *ella mikra ze mesuras hu* — this verse must be read out of sequence. The correct reading is: *bechol hamakom asher avo eilecha uverachticha* — wherever I choose to come and bless you, wherever I cause My *shechina* to dwell — *sham azkir es shemi*, there I will cause My name to be mentioned. The location of *avo eilecha uverachticha* is the *Beis Habechira*, and it is there that *azkir es shemi* occurs. Rashi adds that *bechol hamakom* refers to the various sacred sites — such as *Shilo* — that served as the chosen location before the permanent *Beis HaMikdash* was established.

### Theological Balance

Placing the *gemara*'s rearrangement alongside the plain meaning of the verse reveals a profound theological tension. On one side stands *hamakom asher bachar Hashem Elokecha lasum es shemo sham* — one specific, chosen place where God places His name. On the other stands *bechol hamakom asher azkir es shemi* — which, on its face, sounds like God's presence can be invoked anywhere. These two verses pull in opposite directions: one speaks of radical particularity, the other of apparent universality. The *gemara* resolves this tension by rearranging the universal verse so that it, too, points back to the one chosen place. But the tension itself is theologically significant.

### Kohanim's Role

There is a reading of the *psukim* that preserves both dimensions rather than collapsing the universal into the particular. *Lasum es shemo sham* — God places His name in the *Beis HaMikdash*. But the *kohanim* are *vesamu es shemi al bnei Yisrael* — they place God's name upon the people. They do not live only in the *mikdash*; their role, as stated in *koh tevarchu es benei Yisrael*, extends to all of Israel. When they perform *birkat kohanim* and invoke the divine name, they are causing God's name to be mentioned — *azkir es shemi* — and God responds: *avo eilecha uverachticha*, *va'ani avarchem*. On this reading, the verse is not rearranged but understood as a description of the full dynamic of *birkat kohanim*: God concentrates His presence in one place (*lasum es shemo sham*), but commissions the *kohanim* to carry that name outward (*vesamu es shemi*), and promises that wherever they do so, He will bless the people (*bechol hamakom asher azkir es shemi avo eilecha uverachticha*). The universal and the local are both real — the *kohanim* are the bridge between them.

Returning to the structural debate: it is noteworthy that the second approach — the *avodah*-centered one — is precisely the one that resists the universal reading and rearranges the verse. The first approach, less invested in tying *birkat kohanim* to *mikdash*-based service, is more compatible with the universalist implication of *bechol hamakom*. The *avodah* approach needs to pull the verse back toward the *Beis Habechira*; the *beracha* approach is less compelled to do so.

Both approaches, it should be noted, seem to presuppose that *birkat kohanim* applies outside the *mikdash* as a *mitzvah de'oraita* — the *baraitot* in this section treat the distinction between *mikdash* and *medina* as a question of *how* the *mitzvah* is performed (with or without the *shem hameforash*), not *whether* it exists outside. Yet the internal logic of the *avodah* approach — with its emphasis on *sheirut*, *korban tzibbur*, and *mikdash* — creates real hermeneutical pressure toward the conclusion that the full *mitzvah de'oraita* belongs in the *mikdash* alone.

---

## Additional Requirements

### Who Receives

A further *baraita*: *koh tevarchu es benei Yisrael* — one might think this limits the blessing to native-born Israelites. The verse *emor lahem* — "say to them" — extends it to all, including *geirim* and freed slaves.

### Face to Face

Another *baraita*: *koh tevarchu* — the blessing is given *panim keneged panim*, face to face. Perhaps the *kohanim* could face away from the congregation? The verse *emor lahem* teaches otherwise: just as one speaks to a friend — *ke'adam she'omer lachaveiro* — so here, the *kohanim* must face those they bless.

### Audible Voice

Another *baraita*: *koh tevarchu bekol ram* — the blessing must be given in a loud, fully audible voice. Perhaps a whispered recitation suffices? Again, *emor lahem* teaches: one speaks to a friend in an ordinary, audible manner.

### Calling Kohanim

*Abaye* teaches: *naktinan* — we hold the position that when there are two *kohanim*, the *chazzan* calls out *kohanim* to prompt them to begin. When there is only one *kohen*, the *chazzan* does not call out *kohen*; the single *kohen* begins on his own. The source is *emor lahem* — here read in the liturgical sense, as the caller addressing those who will bless. *Lahem* implies a plural audience; one person alone does not require the call.

### Rav Chisda View

*Rav Chisda* adds a further position: *naktinan*, we hold that a *kohen* may call out *kohanim* to prompt his fellow *kohanim*, but a *Yisrael* leading the service does not call out *kohanim*. His source: *amira mishelachem* — the calling must come from among their own. It may be that having a *Yisrael* instruct *kohanim* to perform their sacred role is considered inappropriate.

### Ruling

The *halacha* follows *Abaye* and not *Rav Chisda*. The *chazzan* calls *kohanim* when there are two, not when there is one — but the caller need not himself be a *kohen*.

It is worth noting that these discussions about the *chazzan* calling *kohanim* are evidently conducted in a contemporary *tefilla* context entirely outside the *mikdash*, which retrospectively confirms that the earlier statements about *oleh laduchan* and the obligations of *birkat kohanim* are also addressed to the *shul* reality — not exclusively to the *mikdash* setting.

---

## Rabbi Yehoshua ben L (II)

### God's Desire

*Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* teaches: how do we know that God desires *birkat kohanim* to be performed? From the verse *vesamu es shemi al bnei Yisrael va'ani avarchem* — "they shall place My name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them." The phrasing suggests not merely that if the name is placed God will bless, but that God needs this to happen — that the *kohanim* placing His name enables God to bless Israel. God, so to speak, desires to bless His people and requires the *kohanim*' invocation as the vehicle for that blessing.

### Kohen Blessed

*Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* further teaches: any *kohen* who gives the blessing is himself blessed — *kol kohen hamivarech misbarech*. But a *kohen* who does not give the blessing is himself not blessed. The source: *va'avaracha mevarachecha* — "I will bless those who bless you." The *kohen* who blesses the people places himself within the covenant blessing promised to Avraham, receiving blessing in return.

### Three Mitzvot

*Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* adds: any *kohen* who does not go up to the *duchan* transgresses three positive commandments — *koh tevarchu*, *emor lahem*, and *vesamu es shemi*. This is striking: alongside the encouragement that the blessing kohen is himself blessed, there is a hard obligation — failure to go up is an active transgression of three *aseis*.

### Ben Gerusha

However, a *kohen* who does not go up on every occasion does not necessarily arouse suspicion on each absence. The *gemara* distinguishes: if a *kohen* goes up *leprakim* — occasionally — then people understand he simply did not go up on this particular occasion, and no one suspects he is a *ben gerusha* or *ben chalutza* (a *kohen* rendered unfit by illegitimate lineage). But if a *kohen* never goes up at all, he arouses suspicion that his lineage disqualifies him. These are two separate concerns — the halachic transgression attaches each time he fails to go up; the social suspicion attaches only to one who never goes up. Rashi explains *leprakim* as referring to *chagim umoadim*, which may reflect the *Ashkenazi* practice of performing *birkat kohanim* only on *yom tov* — though the plain meaning of the *gemara* is simply "sometimes," without specifying which occasions.

---

## Rabbi Yehoshua ben L (II)

### Timing Restriction

*Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* further teaches: a *kohen* who does not go up *ba'avoda* — while the *shliach tzibur* is in the midst of the *retzei* blessing — may no longer go up afterward. *Shuv eino oleh*. The source: *vayisa Aharon es yadav el ha'am vayivarchaim vayered me'asos hachatat veha'olah vehashlamim* — Aharon blessed the people while still in the context of the *korbanot*, before descending from the *mizbeach*. The blessing must take place while the *avodah* is still in active progress. Translated into the *shul* setting: the *kohen* must begin his ascent to the *duchan* while the *retzei* is still being recited — not after the *beracha* is complete.

---

## Timing in Tefilla

### Aaron's Context

This principle — that the blessing must occur within the context of the *avodah* — is itself a remarkable statement about the structure of *tefilla* as it corresponds to the *mikdash*. Even when *birkat kohanim* is performed entirely outside any *mikdash*, the *gemara* insists on situating it within the *avodah* context, represented in *tefilla* by the *retzei* blessing. The verse *vayered me'asos hachatat* makes clear that Aharon had not yet descended — he blessed the people while still above, in the very midst of the sacrificial service.

### Beginning Movement

The *gemara* then asks: *Rav Ami* and *Rav Assi* — who were themselves *kohanim* — apparently went up to perform *birkat kohanim* after the *beracha* of *retzei* was complete. Does this not contradict the ruling just stated? The *gemara* resolves this: *meikara havu akiri kora'aihu matu lo havu matu* — from the beginning they were lifting their legs, they had begun the physical movement, they simply had not yet arrived at the *duchan* by the time the *beracha* was completed. The process of going up was already underway during *retzei*.

### Leg Lifting

This is given a more general formulation by *Rabbi Oshaya*: *lo shanu ela shelo akar raglav* — the rule that one may not go up after the *beracha* ends applies only when the *kohen* has not yet lifted his leg at all during *retzei*. But once he has lifted his leg — even slightly — he may go up even after the *beracha* has concluded.

### Shliach Tzibur

This same principle resolves a related question: if the *shliach tzibur* is himself a *kohen*, may he interrupt his role to perform *birkat kohanim* and then return? The answer is: if he is certain he can do so without losing his place — *im havtachto she-nosei kapav ve-chozer litfilato* — he is permitted. But the difficulty is that as *shliach tzibur*, he was standing at the *amud* reciting *shemoneh esrei* during *retzei*, not moving toward the *duchan*. How can he be considered to have begun the movement?

### Movement Suffices

The *gemara* answers: *hacha nami de'akar porta* — here too, the slightest movement suffices. Even the faintest physical beginning — even a shift of weight, a barely perceptible forward motion — is enough to situate the *kohen* within the *avodah* context and permit the subsequent ascent. The principle is that the connection to *avodah* does not require completed movement; intention expressed in even the most minimal physical act is sufficient.

---

## Character & Generosity

### Tov Ayin

*Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* teaches: *ein nosnim kos shel bracha levarech ela letov ayin* — the cup of blessing for *birkat hamazon* is given only to one who is *tov ayin*, of a generous and benevolent disposition. The reasoning: a *beracha* is not only words. The spirit in which a blessing is given matters. A person with a generous heart blesses from abundance; such a blessing carries weight.

### Generous Disposition

The source verse: *tov ayin hu yevorach ki nasan milachmo ladal* — the one of good eye will be blessed, for he gave of his bread to the poor. The *gemara* reads this *midrashically*: do not read *yevorach* (he will be blessed) but *yevarech* (he will bless) — the same quality of generosity that leads one to give to the poor qualifies one to bestow blessings upon others.

### Birds Know

*Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* further teaches: even birds recognize the stingy person — *afilu ofos makirim betzarei ayin*. A person's character is communicated not only through words but through every dimension of his presence. Someone who is stingy broadcasts that quality non-verbally, and even creatures who do not understand speech can sense it. The source: *ki chinam mezorah hareshes be'einei chol ba'al kanaf* — "for in vain is the net spread in the sight of every winged creature." The birds see someone scattering seed and they know it is a stingy person who will take and not give; they do not come to him. The deeper point is about the *kohanim*: the *beracha* is not merely a verbal formula. A *kohen* of generous spirit communicates that generosity through the blessing itself, and the non-verbal dimension of the blessing is as real as the words.

### Stingy Transgression

*Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* concludes: *kol haneheneh mitzarei ayin over belav* — one who benefits from a stingy person transgresses a negative commandment.

### Ra Ayin

The source: *al tilcham es lechem ra ayin* — do not eat the bread of one who has a bad eye. *Ki kemo sha'ar benafsho hu* — his soul is pained by it. He may say *echol ushesah* — "eat and drink" — but he does not mean it. His outward hospitality is empty; inwardly, he resents the giving. To accept from him is to take what was never truly offered, which is a form of wrongful acquisition.

### Two Lavin

*Rav Nachman* adds: in fact, such a person transgresses not one but two negative commandments — *al tilcham* and *al sis'av*, the second derived from the continuation of the verse: "do not desire his delicacies." Both the act of eating and the cultivating of desire for what a stingy person offers constitute separate transgressions.

---

---

# Sotah 39

## Tov Ayin & Egla Arufa

### Intro: Tov Ayin

The daf opens in the middle of the *sugya* on *birkas kohanim*, picking up from the bottom of 38b. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi had offered a string of statements around *birkas kohanim*, including the principle that a *bracha* communicates not merely through words but through the inner disposition of the one who gives it. The ideal is *tov ayin* — a generous, well-wishing spirit. The *tzar ayin*, by contrast, communicates its stinginess even nonverbally, even to the birds, regardless of what is said aloud. This non-verbal dimension of blessing is the backdrop for what follows.

### Tzar Ayin & Egla Arufa

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi continues: *ein egla arufa ba ela bishvil tzaray ha'ayin* — the ritual of *egla arufa*, which addresses cases of unsolved murder, only becomes necessary on account of those who are stingy of eye. The scriptural basis is the declaration made by the elders: *yadeinu lo shafchu es hadam hazeh v'eineinu lo ra'u* — our hands did not spill this blood and our eyes did not see. The Gemara notes the obvious question: would anyone suspect the elders of the court of murder? The answer is that the declaration addresses a different kind of culpability. *Ela lo ba l'yadeinu ufataruhu belo mezonos* — he came to our hands and we dismissed him without food; *velo re'inuhu vehinachnuhu belo levayah* — and we did not see to it that he had accompaniment on his journey.

### Abandoned Traveler

The scenario implied is that a traveler passed through town without receiving food or escort, and as a consequence — Rashi suggests he may have attempted to rob someone for food and was killed in the encounter — something went wrong. The stinginess of the community, its failure to take responsibility for the vulnerable person passing through, lies at the root of the tragedy. It is therefore fitting that *egla arufa* is connected to *tzar ayin*: the communal failure flows from an absence of the generous, caring spirit that *birkas kohanim* is meant to embody. It is also worth noting that the very next chapter of the tractate deals with *egla arufa*, making this a natural thematic bridge.

---

## All Kohanim Congregation

### Kulo Kohanim Question

The Gemara now introduces a ruling of Rav Simlai: *beis hakeneses shekula kohanim, kulam olim laduchan* — in a synagogue where all the members are *kohanim*, they all ascend to the *duchan*. The Gemara immediately raises the obvious question: *lemi mevarchin* — to whom do they give the blessing? If everyone is on the *duchan*, who remains to receive it?

### Am Besadot & Absent

Rav Zeira answers: *l'acheihem shebasados* — to their brothers in the fields. The blessing goes out to those who are part of the community even if not physically present in the synagogue. The Gemara supports this with the verse *v'es asher einenu poh imanu hayom* — and those who are not here with us today — suggesting that people who belong to the community, even if absent, can receive the blessing.

### Ones vs. Reshus

But the Gemara raises a challenge from a *baraisa* of Abba the son of Rav Minyamin bar Chiyya: *am she'achorei kohanim einam bikhlal bracha* — those who stand behind the *kohanim* are not included in the blessing. The requirement is *panim k'neged panim*, face to face. If those who are merely behind the *kohanim* are excluded, certainly those outside the synagogue entirely should be excluded. The Gemara resolves this: *lo kashya, ha d'anisi, ha d'lo anisi* — it is not difficult. The distinction is between those whose absence is coerced (*ones*) and those whose absence is voluntary (*reshus*). Those who could have been present but chose not to be have effectively removed themselves from the community and do not receive the blessing. Those whose absence is beyond their control remain connected to the *tzibur* and receive the blessing. The people standing behind the *kohanim* are in a position they could have changed — they could have been in front — and so their being behind reflects a voluntary self-exclusion.

### Split Arrangement

A *baraisa* of Rabbi Simi from Bei Bersa addresses this practically: in a congregation of all *kohanim*, some go up to the *duchan* while others remain below to answer *amen*. The ideal arrangement, then, is to split the *kohanim* so that a receiving congregation remains below.

### Minyan Requirement

The Gemara clarifies the conditions: *ha d'ishtayer bei asara, ha d'lo ishtayer bei asara* — the question is whether ten remain below or not. If the congregation is exactly ten, there is no way to send some up while keeping a *kahal* below. But if there are more than ten, some may ascend while a *minyan* remains as the receiving *tzibur*.

### Kahal Requirement

This leads to a broader principle: *vecho sevarchu es benei Yisrael* — the *bracha* is addressed to *benei Yisrael* as a collective. One does not perform *birkas kohanim* without a *tzibur* present to receive it. The *bracha* is inherently communal in character.

This raises a series of practical questions that flow naturally from the discussion. If *birkas kohanim* requires a *minyan*, what happens if the *minyan* dissipates after *shemoneh esrei* has begun? For *Sefardim* who perform *birkas kohanim* daily, this could arise in principle; for *Ashkenazim* it is largely a *Yom Tov* question. The relationship between *birkas kohanim* as a component of *chazaras hashatz* and as an independent act requiring its own *minyan* is genuinely complex.

A further nuance emerges: one needs a *minyan* present in the synagogue in order to perform *birkas kohanim* at all, but one does not require a *minyan* physically below to receive the blessing — the *am shebesados* fills that role. Ideally, however, if it can be arranged so that a *minyan* remains below, it should be. Crucially, the *kohanim* who ascend to the *duchan* do not count toward the *minyan* of those receiving the blessing, but they do count toward the overall *minyan* required to hold the service. The scenario of nine *Yisraelim* and an indefinite number of *am shebesados* filling out the quorum by themselves is plainly untenable.

The question of what constitutes the relevant community for *am shebesados* also bears consideration. In the classical case of a town where many people are out in the fields during *davening*, the connection to the local community is clear. But what of a tiny congregation where there are simply no others nearby — would the blessing extend to *Klal Yisrael* broadly, or must there be some communal association? The *sugya* seems to assume the latter.

---

## Exclusion & Position

### Behind Kohanim Excluded

Having established who is included in *birkas kohanim* through the lens of *ones* and *reshus*, the Gemara now takes up the formal *baraisa* of Abba the son of Rav Minyamin bar Chiyya directly: *am she'achorei kohanim einam bikhlal bracha* — those standing behind the *kohanim* are excluded from the blessing.

### No Hefsek: Height/Teivah

The Gemara immediately asks: is it not obvious? It proceeds to clarify what does *not* constitute an interruption. *Aricha be'appei gutzi* — a tall person standing in front of a shorter person — *lo mafsik*, that does not interrupt. As Rashi notes, there would be no end to this if height were an issue; we cannot require stadium seating in the synagogue. Similarly, *teiva lo mafsik* — the *teiva*, the reading platform or *bimah*, does not constitute a *hefsek* even if it sits between the congregation and the *kohanim*. The Gemara then raises the harder case: *mechitzah mai* — what about someone standing behind a partition?

### Tosafos: Self-Exclusion

Tosafos reframes the question importantly. He argues that the case of the *mechitzah* must be referring to someone who is not *anus* — because if they were *anus*, it is obvious that a *mechitzah* is no worse than being out in the fields entirely, and such a person would clearly receive the blessing along with the *am shebesados*. But if they are not *anus*, Tosafos raises a pointed question: why should being behind a *mechitzah* but in front of the *kohanim* be better than being behind the *kohanim* without a *mechitzah*? The person without a *mechitzah* who stands behind the *kohanim* seems less physically blocked, and yet they are excluded. Tosafos resolves this by explaining that standing behind the *kohanim* — *achorei oref* — is a statement. *Mar'im d'atzman ke'ilu ein habracha chashuvah b'eineihem* — they demonstrate that the blessing is not important to them. The Torah uses the language of *panim k'neged panim*; to place yourself behind them is to opt out of the face-to-face relationship. By contrast, someone standing behind a *mechitzah* but facing the *kohanim* has not made that statement. They are oriented toward the blessing, even if physically obstructed.

### Iron Wall & Connection

The Gemara then cites the well-known teaching of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *afilu mechitzah shel barzel einah mafsekes bein Yisrael l'avihem shebashamayim* — even an iron wall does not divide between Israel and their Father in heaven. This provides the conceptual foundation: physical barriers do not sever the spiritual relationship.

### Mechitzah & Core Minyan

Tosafos addresses the apparent tension with other *sugyos* that seem to require people to be in the same physical space in order to be *mitztaref* for a *minyan*. The resolution that Tosafos offers, which has become broadly accepted, distinguishes between two questions. To constitute a *tzibur* in the first place — to be able to perform *chazaras hashatz*, *devarim shebikdusha*, and *birkas kohanim* — one needs a core *minyan* in the same location. Once that core *minyan* exists and is performing these acts, then others who are behind *mechitzos* or in adjoining rooms can connect to and be included in what that *tzibur* is doing. The mechanic has something of the quality of *hashakah* in a *mikvah*: the connected body must maintain its core integrity, and from there extension is possible.

### Tosafos Drush: God's View

Tosafos closes with a passage of striking beauty. Citing the *gemara* in *Perek Ein Omdin* (32b) where Rabbi Elazar states that since the destruction of the *Beis Hamikdash*, an iron wall has separated Israel from their Father in heaven, Tosafos notes that these two teachings are not in contradiction. The *gemara* in *Berachos* is referring to the diminished reception of prayer in the absence of the *Beis Hamikdash* — *ein tefilasam miskabeles kemo shebizman Beis Hamikdash kayam*. But with respect to whether the *tzibur* is blessed through *birkas kohanim* or discharged through the *shliach tzibur* — *d'klapi avinu shebashamayim lo tali b'hefsek mechitzah* — from God's perspective, the walls between us simply do not register. There may be walls that affect how our prayers ascend, but there is no wall that prevents God's blessing from reaching Israel. This, Tosafos notes, lends itself to a broader *drush*: from God's vantage point, the barriers we perceive between ourselves and Him are not acknowledged on His side.

### Standing to the Side

The Gemara raises a further question: *tzadadim mahu* — what about those who are not behind the *kohanim* and not directly in front, but standing alongside them?

### Parah Adumah Analogy

The answer comes from a *mishnah* about the sprinkling of *parah adumah* waters. The rule there is: if one intended to sprinkle in front and the water landed behind, or intended to sprinkle behind and it landed in front, the *hazayah* is invalid. But *lefanav vehizzah al tzadadim shebifanav* — if one intended to sprinkle in front and it landed on the sides, the *hazayah* is *kesherah*. Rashi clarifies that *tzadadim shebifanav* means things that are alongside, not directly in front and not behind — and yet they are treated as "in front." The principle follows: being alongside the *kohanim* is included within the category of being in front of them. It would not make sense otherwise — in a large hall, no one could literally stand directly facing the *kohanim* at all times, and those alongside them are naturally part of the facing congregation.

---

## Washing Hands

### Washing & Holiness

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches: *kol kohen she'lo natal yadav lo yisa kapav* — a *kohen* who has not washed his hands may not lift his hands to bless. The source is the verse *se'u yedeikhem kodesh u'varchu es Hashem* — lift up your hands in holiness and bless God. The word *kodesh* in the verse indicates that the hands must be sanctified — which is achieved through washing — before the blessing can be given.

### Rashi: Immediate Before

Rashi explains that this washing must take place *lifnei aloto laduchan* — immediately before ascending to the *duchan*. The requirement is not merely that the *kohen* washed at some point that day, but that the washing is proximate to the act.

### Tosafos: When Washing
