Tosafos engages critically with a version of Rashi's text that appears to say that morning washing suffices and that a *kohen* who washed his hands in the morning and was careful (*natar*) need not wash again before ascending. Tosafos questions whether this line is authentic to Rashi or was inserted by a student — *ke'imdumeh she'hu hageh mi'hagahos talmid* — because Rashi's own language in explaining the Gemara implies that the washing must be truly proximate, *mamash samuch*, to the ascent. The Gemara itself reinforces this by quoting the verse *se'u yedeikhem kodesh u'varchu* — suggesting that *netilat yadayim* and *birkas kohanim* are to follow immediately one upon the other. The practical implication is familiar: when the *shliach tzibur* is himself a *kohen*, he must wash before the service begins so that he can proceed without interruption.

An underlying question, discussed before the *daf* began, concerns how one conceptualizes this washing — as an element of *avodah*, aligned with the *kohanim*'s washing before Temple service, or as something unique to *birkas kohanim* reflected in this particular verse. The choice of verse is telling: the Gemara does not cite the general *pasuk* about washing before *avodah*, but this specific verse connecting holiness, hands, and blessing. One might argue this makes the *netilah* particular to *birkas kohanim*, though the word *kodesh* in Biblical Hebrew does not technically mean washing the way *kiddesh* does in Mishnaic usage — itself perhaps a deliberate play on the resonance between sanctification and cleansing.

### Bracha Formula

The Gemara proceeds to ask: what *bracha* does a *kohen* recite? Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua, in the context of explaining his longevity, mentions that he never performed *nesias kapayim* without first making a *bracha* — implying that this was not universal practice. The formula articulated by Rav Zeira citing Rav Chisda is: *asher kidshanu b'mitzvosav u'vikdushaso shel Aharon v'tzivanu levarech es amo Yisrael b'ahava*.

### Aharon's Sanctity

This *bracha* is structurally distinctive. The standard form of a *birkas hamitzvah* is *asher kidshanu b'mitzvosav v'tzivanu*, but here an additional phrase is inserted: *u'vikdushaso shel Aharon* — and through the sanctity of Aharon. This insertion serves a necessary clarifying function. The word *kidshanu* with its plural suffix raises a question: who is the "we"? *Birkas kohanim* is not a *mitzvah* incumbent upon all of Israel. So the *bracha* specifies: we — the *kohanim* — possess a *kedushah* rooted in Aharon, and it is by virtue of *kedushas Aharon* that we are commanded in this *mitzvah*. This is not a claim of superiority but a necessary statement of which *kedushah* grants the obligation. It would be worth examining whether a parallel *nusach* applies to other distinctly *kohen* obligations — for instance, the *bracha* before eating a *chatas* — whether there too the *sheiltas Aharon* language appears in the formula.

### B'ahava (With Love)

The final word of the *bracha* — *b'ahava* — brings the discussion full circle. The verse *vecho sevarchu* does not itself contain the word *ahava*. Its inclusion in the *bracha* formula directly echoes the opening theme of the *sugya*: that *birkas kohanim* is not merely a ritual act but must be animated by genuine love and generosity of spirit — the *tov ayin* that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi placed at the center of authentic blessing. The *nusach* of the *bracha* is thus a theological statement: this blessing works only when it flows from *ahava*.

---

## Birkas Kohanim Choreogra…

### Yehi Ratzon Prayer

The Gemara now details the choreography of *birkas kohanim* step by step. *Ki akar krei'ei mai amar* — as the *kohen* begins moving his legs toward the *duchan*, what does he say? He recites a *yehi ratzon*: that the blessing should contain no *michshol v'avon* — no stumbling and no sin.

The specific content of the *yehi ratzon* invites reflection on what *michshol v'avon* might mean in this context. One reading — and a compelling one — is that the *kohen* is praying that the very blessing he is about to convey should not itself become a source of stumbling for those who receive it. Wealth, success, and divine favor can become *michsholim* when they lead people to arrogance or sin. The *kohen* standing as a conduit of blessing is thus asking that what flows through him be genuinely good for those who receive it — a prayer for the blessing's positive effect, not merely its transmission. This reading resonates with a parallel seen in the *tefillah* recited upon leaving the *beis medrash*, where one prays that Torah study not become a source of harm.

### Ribbono Shel Olam

After the blessing is complete and the *kohanim* turn their faces back toward the *aron*, the Gemara asks what they say at that moment. Rav Chisda expounded before Rav Ukva: *Ribbono Shel Olam asinu mah she'gazarta aleinu* — Master of the Universe, we have done what You decreed upon us; *aseh immanu mah she'hivtachtanu* — now do for us what You have promised us. The prayer then quotes *Hashkifah mi'me'on kodshecha min hashamayim u'varech es amcha Yisrael* — look down from Your holy dwelling in the heavens and bless Your people Israel.

What is striking about this formulation is the shift in pronouns. The *kohanim* say "do for *us*" — not "do for *them*." Having performed their distinctive role as the conduit of blessing, they now re-enter the general community of Israel as recipients. The *hivtachtanu* alludes to *Va'ani Avarchem* — and I will bless them — God's own assurance in the *pasuk* that He will confer the blessing upon Israel when the *kohanim* pronounce His name. The *Ribbono Shel Olam* does not quote this verse explicitly, and perhaps wisely so — there is a certain *chutzpah* in saying "You promised, now deliver." Instead, the *kohanim* invoke the closing verse of *Hashkifah mi'me'on kodshecha* as a request, while the implicit allusion to *Va'ani Avarchem* provides the theological grounding.

### Fingers Straight Until

Rav Chisda rules that the *kohanim* may not fold their fingers back until they have turned their faces away from the congregation. Even after the blessing is complete and *amen* has been said, the hands remain extended as long as the *kohanim* are still facing the *tzibur*. The reason is not stated explicitly, but one attractive reading is that folding the fingers might feel like a withdrawal — like taking back what has been given — and as long as one faces the congregation the gesture of blessing remains open.

### Sequencing Rules

Rav Zeira citing Rav Chisda now lays out a precise series of sequencing rules, each one requiring a stage to be fully completed before the next begins. The *korei* — the one who calls out "kohanim" — may not do so until the congregation has fully finished its *amen* to *Retzei*. The *kohanim* may not begin their *bracha* until the *korei* has finished calling. The congregation may not answer *amen* until the *kohanim* have completed their *bracha* — all the way to the final word. And the *kohanim* may not begin the next *bracha* until the congregation's *amen* to the previous one is fully concluded. Each act must be given its full space.

### Remain Until Sim Shalom

The choreography extends further. The *kohanim* may not turn their faces away from the congregation — *l'hachzir p'neihem min hatzibur* — until the *shliach tzibur* has begun *Sim Shalom*. And they may not step down from the *duchan* — *la'akor ragleihem* — until the *shliach tzibur* has completed *Sim Shalom*. The sequencing is layered: turn away only when *Sim Shalom* begins; descend only when it concludes. The sense is one of sustained presence and dignified transition rather than a quick departure once the ritual words are done.

### Tosafos: Hearing Concern

Tosafos analyzes the reason behind these sequencing requirements by asking whether they are based on the principle of *trei kali lo mishtamei* — that two voices speaking simultaneously cannot both be heard. Tosafos notes a difficulty: the Gemara elsewhere implies that when something is *chaviv*, beloved and important, *trei kali* are indeed *mishtamei*. Moreover, the *kohanim* themselves constitute multiple voices, yet they speak simultaneously without concern. Tosafos resolves that the sequencing rules are not fundamentally about the general public failing to hear. They are about the individual worshiper who is still saying *amen*: if that person is in the middle of their own *amen* when the *kohanim* begin the next *bracha*, that specific person will not be able to hear the new *bracha* they are in the midst of responding to. The concern is thus for the experience of each individual — the *kohanim* must wait not because sound is technically inaudible but because, as a matter of consideration, one should not begin a new stage while any member of the *tzibur* is still meaningfully engaged in the previous one. The Gemara's framing, however, does not seem quite so focused on the hearing of specific individuals — it has more the quality of giving each act its proper, non-overlapping space.

---

## Torah & Haftarah Order

### Aliyah Before Haftarah

Rabbi Tanchum citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *hamaftir banavi tzarich sheyikra baTorah techila* — one who reads the *haftarah* must first receive an *aliyah* in the Torah. One cannot leap directly to the *haftarah* without first being called to the Torah reading. The proper sequence of sacred acts requires traversing them in order.

### Roll Torah First

Continuing in the same sequence of teachings, Rabbi Tanchum citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules: *ein hamaftir rashai lehaftir banavi ad sheyigolel Sefer Torah* — the *maftir* may not begin the *haftarah* from the prophets until he has rolled up the *Sefer Torah* and completed that prior act. One finishes with the Torah before turning to the *haftarah*.

### Kvod Hatzibur: Coverings

Rabbi Tanchum citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds: *ein shaliach tzibur rashai lehafshit es hateiva betzibur* — the *shliach tzibur* may not remove the decorative coverings from the *teiva* while the congregation is still present, *mipnei kvod hatzibur*. After *kriat haTorah*, the elaborate coverings and cloths adorning the reading platform would be put away. To do so while the congregation is still assembled is disrespectful — stripping the *teiva* bare in their presence demeans the setting in which they have gathered.

### Torah Removal Timing

Rabbi Tanchum citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules further: *ein hatzibur rasha'in latzeit ad sheyinnatel Sefer Torah veyaniach bimkomo* — the congregation may not leave until the *Sefer Torah* has been taken and restored to its place. In the time of the Gemara, the *Sefer Torah* would sometimes be carried to a more protected private home for safekeeping. Shmuel, however, says: *ad sheyeitzei* — until it goes out, the congregation must wait, even before it has been fully restored to its destination. The Gemara resolves the apparent disagreement: *lo pligi* — they do not actually argue. *Ha d'ika pitcha achrina* — if there is another door in the synagogue, the congregation may leave by the other door while the *Sefer Torah* exits by the first, since they are not walking ahead of it. *Ha d'leika pitcha achrina* — if there is only one door, the *Sefer Torah* must go first.

### Torah Goes First

The concluding verse that grounds this entire sequence of rulings: *Acharei Hashem Elokeichem teleichu* — after God shall you walk. The *Sefer Torah*, as the tangible representation of *dvar Hashem*, goes first. The people follow. This principle of sequencing — giving precedence to what is sacred, waiting until the sacred act is complete before moving on — runs through the entire *sugya* and finds its most elemental expression here: you follow after God, not before.

---

---

# Sotah 40

## Response to Kohanim

### Pesukim During Blessing

The *daf* begins at the bottom of 39b, in the midst of the discussion of *birchas kohanim* — one of the rituals that must be performed in Hebrew. The *gemara* poses the question: *bizman shehakohanim mevarchin et ha'am mah hem omrim* — when the *kohanim* bless the people, what do the people say?

Nowadays, *siddurim* print *pesukim* for the congregation to recite silently — a verse corresponding to each word of the blessing — though many people simply scan the text with their eyes. The assumption in the *gemara*, however, is more active: the congregation would say something during the blessing itself, something that relates not merely to each individual word but to the very fact of receiving a divine blessing through the *kohanim*. This is distinct from the *amen* said at the conclusion; what is described here occurs during the blessing itself.

### Shacharis Response

Rabbi Zeira said in the name of Rav Hisda: the congregation recites the closing verses of Psalm 103 — *barechu Hashem malachav gibborei ko'ach*, praise God, His angels of great strength; *barechu Hashem kol tzeva'av meshartav osei retzono*, all His hosts, those who serve God and do His will; *barechu Hashem kol ma'asav bechol mekomos memshalto barchi nafshi et Hashem*, all His creatures in all places of His dominion should praise Him — my soul shall bless God.

The inner logic here is striking: the *kohanim* declare that God will bless the people, and the people respond, as it were, in kind — praising and blessing God in return. God blesses you, and you, in gratitude, call upon all of creation to bless God back.

### Musaf Response

For *Shabbas Musaf* — an additional *Shemoneh Esrei* — Rabbi Assi states that the congregation recites: *Shir hama'alos hinei barechu et Hashem kol avdei Hashem* (Psalm 134:1), behold, bless God all you servants of God; *se'u yedekhem kodesh uvarechu et Hashem* (ibid. 2), lift up your hands in holiness and bless God; and *baruch Hashem mitziyon shokhen Yerushalayim halleluyah* (Psalm 135:21), blessed is God from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem, praise God.

The *gemara* notes, however, that the third *pasuk* is taken from a different *perek* in *Tehillim*. Why not use *yevarekhekha Hashem mitziyon*, which appears in the same *perek* as the first two verses? Yehudah the son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi explains: since the theme of the congregational response is blessing God — mirroring the blessing the *kohanim* channel toward the people — one must end with a verse that blesses God. *Baruch Hashem mitziyon* accomplishes this. *Yevarekhekha Hashem mitziyon*, by contrast, speaks of God blessing you — precisely what the *kohanim* are already saying. The response must be a reciprocal blessing directed toward God, not a repetition of what is being received.

One observes, as well, that just as there are three *pesukim* of *birchas kohanim*, so too there are three *pesukim* of response — one corresponding to each.

### Taanis & Yom Kippur

For *mincha* on a *taanis* — when *birchas kohanim* is performed because there is no concern that the *kohanim* have been drinking — Rav Acha bar Yaakov provides a markedly different set of verses: *im avonoseinu anu vanu Hashem aseh lema'an shemekha* (Jeremiah 14:7), though our sins testify against us, God act for the sake of Your name; *mikveh Yisrael moshio be'eis tzarah* (ibid. 8), O Hope of Israel, its savior in time of distress; *lamah tihyeh keger ba'aretz lamah tihyeh khe'ish nidham kegibor* (ibid. 9), why should You be like a stranger in the land, like a mighty man who cannot save?

This is notably different in character from the other responses. Rather than blessing God in return for the blessing received, the congregation uses the occasion as an opening to pray for the very purpose of the *taanis* — to importune God to answer and to act. Receiving a blessing and standing in connection with God, they seize the moment to beseech Him.

At *ne'ila* on *Yom Kippur*, Mar Zutra (and some say this appears in a *baraisa*) gives: *hinei ki chen yevorach gever yere Hashem* (Psalm 128:4), behold, so shall the man who fears God be blessed; *yevarekhekha Hashem miTziyon ure'eh betuv Yerushalayim kol yemei chayekha ure'eh vanim levanekha shalom al Yisrael* (ibid. 5–6), God should bless you from Zion and may you see Jerusalem's goodness all the days of your life, and see your children's children — peace upon Israel.

Here, at the close of *Yom Kippur*, the response is neither a return-blessing to God nor a petition for rain. Instead it expresses the aspiration of a *yerei Hashem*, a God-fearing person receiving blessing, looking forward to a year of life and continuity and peace. Of all the responses enumerated, only the standard *shacharis* version — where one blesses God in response to receiving blessing from God — follows the pure structure of reciprocal praise.

### Timing of Verses

The *gemara* raises the question of where exactly within *birchas kohanim* these *pesukim* would be recited. Rabbi Elazar says: between each *bracha* — that is, after each of the three *pesukim* of the blessing. Rav Sheshet says: at the mention of God's name — *b'hazkarat Hashem* — since hearing the divine name in the context of this blessing is itself what calls forth the response of praise.

Rav Mar and Rav Zevid dispute the structure of the response. One holds that it was *pasuka likaval pasuka* — one response-*pasuk* corresponding to each *pasuk* of the blessing. The other holds that upon each *pasuk* of the *kohanim*, the congregation recited all three *pesukim* of the response.

---

## Only in Mikdash

### Chiya bar Abba View

Having established that these *pesukim* were said, the *gemara* turns to whether they may be recited outside the *Beis Hamikdash*. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba rules: *kol ha'omram bigvulin eino ela to'eh* — whoever recites them outside the *Beis Hamikdash* is simply making a mistake. The rationale is that these verses were a response to the power of hearing the explicit divine name pronounced in the *Mikdash*. Whether one holds that the *pesukim* were said at *shem Hashem* or between the *brachot*, the sense of God's manifest presence bestowing blessing — which invokes this particular response — belongs specifically to the *Mikdash* context.

### Chanina bar Pappa

Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa goes further and disagrees more fundamentally. He says: *teda* — know — that not only are they inappropriate outside the *Mikdash*, they should not be said even in the *Mikdash*. His reasoning: *klum yesh lecha eved shemevarchin oto vehu machzir* — is there a slave who, when receiving a blessing, talks back? Even if his words are grateful and responsive, should one not simply listen attentively to the blessing being given? The argument implies that the *pesukim* are said during the blessing itself — during the words of the *kohanim* — which makes Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's objection coherent. One is supposed to receive the blessing, not be murmuring verses simultaneously.

This framing, however, sits in some tension with Rabbi Elazar's view that the *pesukim* are said between the *brachot*, not during them — and the *gemara* does not fully reconcile these positions.

### Yitzchak bar Chanina

Rav Yitzchak bar Chanina takes the opposite position: *teda* — know — that it is entirely appropriate to say them even outside the *Beis Hamikdash*. His counter-argument mirrors Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's imagery but inverts it: *klum yesh eved shemevarchin oso ve'ein mekabbel panim* — is there a slave who, when blessed, shows no acknowledgment at all? If one receives a blessing, one ought to demonstrate gratitude and respond in kind. This reasoning aligns naturally with the view that the *pesukim* are said between the *brachot* rather than during them — a moment of response, not of distraction.

### Abahu's Practice

Rabbi Abahu reports: *merish hava amina lehu* — I used to recite these *pesukim* outside the *Beis Hamikdash*. But once he observed Rabbi Abba of Akko not saying them, he too stopped. The specific weight Rabbi Abahu gave to this behavior will become clear momentarily, in light of his deep respect for Rabbi Abba as a man of exceptional humility.

### Humility Digression

Rabbi Abahu also relates: I used to think of myself as a humble person — *anvetana ana*. But once I observed Rabbi Abba of Akko's conduct, I realized that I was not.

What was Rabbi Abba's conduct? When Rabbi Abba would convey a teaching to his *amora* — together with the reasoning behind it — the *amora* would then stand up and announce to the assembled crowd his own reason instead of, or in addition to, Rabbi Abba's. This requires some explanation of the role of the *amora*. In the academies, the term *tana* referred not only to the sages of the *Mishnah* and *baraisa* era but to a specific functionary: a person who had memorized all the *mishnayos* and *baraisos* and would recite them upon request — a living repository. Similarly, the *amora* (from *amira*, speech) was a kind of loudspeaker: the rabbi would say his *shiur* quietly, and the *amora* would repeat it loudly so the entire crowd could hear.

What Rabbi Abba's *amora* would do was substitute — or supplement — Rabbi Abba's reasoning with his own. Perhaps he would say: "Rabbi Abba teaches this *halacha*, and here is my reason." Rabbi Abba *lo kapid* — he did not mind at all.

The most plausible reading, in order to reconcile this with the obligation to teach Torah accurately, is that the *amora* announced his own reasoning in his own name — explicitly — and Rabbi Abba allowed him to use the public platform to do so. The humility displayed was not just tolerance of being contradicted, but the willingness to let a subordinate elevate himself to a seemingly equal footing in public.

By contrast, Rabbi Abahu's own humility — which he now recognized as lesser — consisted of the following: the wife of Rabbi Abahu's *amora* told Rabbi Abahu's wife: "Ours doesn't need yours. My husband is capable enough to give his own *shiur* — he bends down to hear Rabbi Abahu and then stands up to announce it only as a gesture of respect, because Rabbi Abahu has connections to the government (*bei Keisar*). But he could manage entirely on his own." Rabbi Abahu's wife went and told him this. His response: *mai nafka lach minha* — what does it matter to you? *Minei uminah yitkales ila'ah* — between me and him, God's name is elevated. He was not *makpid*. Let the man think he gives just as good a *shiur* — who is harmed?

But Rabbi Abahu recognized that this was a private remark, made to a wife — not a public act of self-elevation like what Rabbi Abba's *amora* had done. The degree of humility demanded to truly not mind, as Rabbi Abba of Akko did not mind, was of a different order entirely.

A further story about Rabbi Abahu's regard for Rabbi Abba: when the rabbis considered appointing Rabbi Abahu as *Rosh Yeshiva* — a position that brought with it significant material support — Rabbi Abahu saw that Rabbi Abba of Akko was burdened with many creditors and owed considerable debts. He told the rabbis: there is a greater rabbi — appoint Rabbi Abba of Akko. This would allow Rabbi Abba to pay off his debts through the income that came with the position.

### Jewels & Knickknacks

The *gemara* now relates a famous episode directly involving Rabbi Abahu and Rabbi Chiya bar Abba. The two came together to a certain town. Rabbi Abahu delivered a *shiur* in *agadata* — a *midrash*, a sermon, a meaningful message. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba delivered a serious *halacha shiur* with rigorous sources and analysis. Everyone left Rabbi Chiya bar Abba's lecture and went to hear Rabbi Abahu. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba was despondent.

Rabbi Abahu consoled him with a *mashal*: to what may this be compared? To two merchants who come to a village — one selling precious gems and pearls, the other selling small knickknacks, needles, and trinkets. *Al mi koftzin* — to whom does everyone rush? To the one selling the knickknacks, of course, because everyone can buy something small and useful. Nobody can afford the jewels. Your *shiur* is clearly at a far higher level, Rabbi Abahu was saying — your Torah is the jewels. But it is simply beyond these people. They come to me not because my Torah is greater, but because it is more accessible to them.

Every day, Rabbi Chiya bar Abba would escort Rabbi Abahu to his lodging — *mishum yekara d'vei Keisar* — as a gesture of honor, since Rabbi Abahu's proximity to the imperial government gave him special status. On that day, in recognition of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba's true greatness in Torah, Rabbi Abahu reversed the gesture and escorted Rabbi Chiya bar Abba to his lodging instead. And even so, *lo itosev da'tei minei* — it did not fully settle Rabbi Chiya bar Abba's spirit. Being told that one possesses extraordinary Torah is gratifying, but it does not entirely substitute for feeling that people want to hear from you.

---

## Modim Response

### Modim Concept

The *gemara* now transitions naturally: having discussed what the congregation says when receiving *birchas kohanim*, it asks what the congregation says when the *shaliach tzibbur* recites *modim* during *chazaras hashatz*. This is one of the two signature moments of the *chazara* — alongside *kedusha* — where communal participation is most essential. During *kedusha*, the congregation sanctifies God's name together; during *modim*, the congregation echoes the *shaliach tzibbur*'s expression of communal gratitude, each person saying their own *modim* while he says his.

So *mah hem omrim* — what does the congregation say? Rav says: *Modim anachnu lach Hashem Elokeinu al she'anu modim lach* — we thank You, God our Lord, for the fact that we thank You. This is a remarkable formulation. Rashi explains: we thank You for having given us the capacity and the closeness to You that enables us to thank You — gratitude for the very ability to be grateful. In one's own silent *Shemoneh Esrei*, one has already thanked God for all one has prayed for; now, in the repetition, the congregation says: we are so thankful to be a people who stand before You in prayer and are able to offer You thanks.

### Modim Variations

Shmuel elaborates: *Elokei kol basar al she'anu modim lach* — God of all flesh, that we thank You. Rabbi Simai elaborates further: *Yotzreinu yotzer bereishis* — our Creator, Creator of the beginning — *al she'anu modim lach*.

The sages of Nehardea add, in the name of Rabbi Simai, something more concrete: *berachos vehoda'os lishmecha hagadol al shehecheyisanu vekiyamsanu* — blessings and thanks to Your great name for having given us life and sustained us — *al she'anu modim lach*. Now the thanks are no longer purely reflexive; something specific is named: life itself. Rav Acha bar Yaakov then appends a *bakasha* to Rabbi Simai's formulation: *ken techayeinu usechaneinu* — so too may You give us life and be gracious to us — *vetikabetzeinu ve'esof galuyoseinu lechatzros kodshecha* — gather us to Your holy courtyards — *velishmor chukecha vela'asos retzonecha belevav shalem* — to observe Your laws and do Your will wholeheartedly — *al she'anachnu modim lach*.

At this point the formulation has traveled quite far from its origin. The elegant core — *modim al she'anu modim*, thanksgiving for the capacity of thanksgiving — has been expanded into petition, and the *netziv* of *Modim Derabbanan* as commonly recited today includes this fuller material. Something of the purity of that original formulation is worth pausing over.

Rav Pappa concludes: since all of these formulations contain beautiful and fitting content, we say all of them together — which is precisely what became our practice.

### Community Respect

Rabbi Yitzchak states: a leader should always have *eimas tzibbur* upon him — a sense of reverence for, and obligation toward, the community. The *gemara* derives this from *birchas kohanim*: when the *kohanim* bless the people, their faces are toward the people and their backs are, as it were, toward the *Shechina* — toward where the *Aron* stands, the front of the sanctuary. Such is the degree of respect shown to the congregation.

Rav Nachman derives the same principle from a verse in Divrei Hayamim: *vayakom hamelech David al raglav vayomer shim'uni achai ve'ami* — King David rose to his feet and said, hear me, my brothers and my people. The *gemara* asks: if they are *achai*, my brothers — his equals — why call them *ami*, my people? And if they are *ami*, his subjects — why call them *achai*? Rabbi Elazar explains: David was saying, if you are prepared to listen to me willingly, then I will treat you as brothers, as equals. *Ve'im lav ami atem va'ani rodeh eschem bemakkel* — and if not, I will treat you as subjects and compel you. The honor and equality offered to the community is thus conditional on their responsiveness — but the baseline posture of a leader toward his community is one of respect.

The *rabbanan* then bring this discussion back to *birchas kohanim* with the teaching: *ein kohanim rashaim la'alos besandaleihem laduchan* — *kohanim* may not ascend the *duchan* wearing sandals. This is one of the nine *takanos* of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakai.

---

## Blessing Halacha

### Kohanim Sandals

The *gemara* asks: what is the reason for this *takana*? The obvious suggestion is *kevod tzibbur* — when the *kohanim* lift their arms and the hem of their garments rises, muddy sandals are exposed, and this is unseemly before the congregation.

Rav Ashi, however, disagrees. The real concern is different: *shema nifsika lei retzu'a besandalo* — perhaps the strap of a *kohen*'s sandal breaks on the way up to the *duchan*, and he bends down to retie it. Everyone else continues up to perform *birchas kohanim*, and he is left crouching on the ground. People will say: he is not going up because he is a *ben grusha o ben chalutza* — the son of a divorced woman or a woman who performed *chalitza* — and is therefore disqualified from performing *birchas kohanim*. To avoid this source of suspicion, the *takana* requires all *kohanim* to remove their sandals before ascending.

### One Blessing

The *mishna* states: *bamikdash bracha achas* — in the *Mikdash*, *birchas kohanim* was recited as a single uninterrupted blessing. The reason: *lefi she'ein onim amen bamikdash* — because *amen* is not said in the *Beis Hamikdash*. Since there is no *amen* following each of the three *pesukim*, they are not treated as three separate *brachot* but as a continuous unit.

This creates a notable tension with the earlier discussion in the *gemara*. The *gemara* above spoke of reciting *pesukim* in the *Mikdash* between or during the *brachot* — and that would seem to break them up. *Tosafos* resolves this by suggesting that *baruch shem kavod malchuto le'olam va'ed* — said at *shem Hashem*, in the middle of a *bracha* rather than at its conclusion — would not constitute a division between the three *pesukim*. This works well according to the opinion that the *pesukim* were recited at *shem Hashem*. According to the opinion that they were said between the *brachot*, the difficulty remains, and the *gemara* does not directly address it.

### No Amen Mikdash

The *gemara* asks: from where do we know that *amen* is not said in the *Beis Hamikdash*? The source is the verse in Ezra: *kumu barchu et Hashem Elokeichem min ha'olam ve'ad ha'olam* — rise and bless God from this world to the next world — which encapsulates the liturgical formula *baruch shem kavod malchuto le'olam va'ed* as the response in the *Mikdash*.

And from where do we know that this response is given after each individual *bracha*? From the verse: *veyivarchu shem kevodecha umeromam al kol bracha usehilla* — and they shall bless Your glorious name, which is exalted above every *bracha* and praise — teaching that for every single *bracha*, one gives praise. That praise takes the form of *baruch shem kavod*, not *amen*.

Why is *amen* not said in the *Mikdash*? The *Maharsha* offers an explanation involving *gematria*. A more compelling approach may be conceptual: *amen* is fundamentally the response of a follower — one who hears another initiate a blessing and affirms it. There is power in this role; the *gemara* elsewhere speaks at length of the extraordinary spiritual weight of *amen*. But in the *Beis Hamikdash*, where one stands in the direct presence of God, perhaps the expectation is different. If one is going to respond to a blessing of God at all, one must do so with one's own active blessing — *baruch shem kavod* — not merely with a secondary affirmation of someone else's.

---

---

# Sotah 41

## High Priest's Blessi (II)

### High Priest Intro

The *mishna* on 40b opens a new topic: having concluded the extended discussion of *birchas kohanim*, the *mishna* turns to other rituals that must be performed specifically in Hebrew. The first of these is *birchas kohen gadol* — and by introducing it this way, the *mishna* uses the occasion to explore how these ceremonies were actually conducted. Some of the rituals described in this section of *Sotah* are primarily historical in character, like the *brachos u'klallos*; others, like *birchas kohanim*, remain practically operative. *Birchas kohen gadol* falls somewhere in between — it was fully operative when the *beis hamikdash* stood, and the *mishna* treats it as an opportunity to reconstruct what it looked like.

The context is *yom hakippurim*. After all the *korbanos* have been brought and the *sa'ir* has been sent *l'azazel*, the *kohen gadol* and the assembly conduct a *keriat hatorah* in the *azarah*. This occurs at the conclusion of the *avodas hayom*, when the bulk of the unique service has been completed. It is worth noting that the *mishna* in *Yoma* records an interesting variant: the reading could be performed either in the white *bigdei kehuna* of *yom kippur* or in a special cloak prepared for this service — a detail that raises its own questions about how fully this reading was incorporated into the structure of the *avoda* proper.

### Torah Passing Ritual

The *mishna* describes the ceremony of transferring the *sefer torah* in detail. The *chazzan haknesset* — the attendant of the synagogue who handles all the practical affairs of the *knesset*, whom *Rashi* describes as the *shammash* who bears responsibility for all the workings of the synagogue, bringing things in and out, preparing everything — takes the *sefer torah* and gives it to the *rosh haknesset*. The *rosh haknesset* is the one who makes the decisions: who reads the *haftarah*, who leads the prayers. *Rashi* captures this distinction sharply: *al piv nechtachin divrei haknesset* — on his word all matters of the *knesset* are decided. The roles correspond, roughly, to what we today combine in the *gabbai*. The *rosh haknesset* then passes the *sefer torah* to the *segan*, the deputy *kohen gadol*, who in turn gives it to the *kohen gadol* himself.

One might pause here to ask: which *knesset* is this? Are we speaking of a synagogue on *har habayit*? Was there some formal communal institution in *yerushalayim* that the *chazzan haknesset* represented? This is genuinely unclear. What is evident is that the ritual is synagogue-like in character — a ceremonial reading of the *torah* — yet the precise identity of the *knesset* in question remains uncertain.

### Reading Sections

Once the *sefer torah* reaches him, the *kohen gadol* stands and receives it, and reads from *acharei mos* — the *avodas yom hakippurim* — and from *ach ba'asor*, the section in *Emor* in *Vayikra* describing the *musafin* of *yom kippur*, drawn from the cycle of *musvei yom tov*. After reading these sections, he rolls the *sefer torah* closed, holds it against his chest, and declares: *yoser mi-mah she-karasi lifneichem kasuv kan* — more than what I have read before you is written here. He is signaling that there is an additional section he will recite, but which he will not read from the scroll. That additional section — *u'va'asur sheb'chumash hapekudim* — is the corresponding passage in *Pinchas* in *Bamidbar*, which also describes the *musaf hayom* of *yom kippur*. He recites this second passage by heart, *al peh*, rather than reading it inside the scroll.

The reason he does not simply scroll to *Pinchas* will be addressed by the *gemara*, but the statement itself requires explanation. Why does he feel compelled to announce that more is written here than he read? Because he then proceeds to recite something without reading from the *sefer torah*, one might suspect that the text he is reciting is simply not found in it. To dispel any suspicion that there is some deficiency in the *sefer torah*, he preemptively declares that everything is indeed written — he is simply not reading it from inside. This logic, as we will see, connects directly to the broader *halachic* principle of *tircha d'tzibura*.

After completing both readings, the *kohen gadol* recites eight *brachos*. The *mishna* lists them: on the *torah*, on the *avoda*, on the *hoda'ah* (thanksgiving), on *mechilas avon* (forgiveness of sin), on the *mikdash*, on *yisrael*, on the *kohanim*, and on *yerushalayim* — with a final element described as *v'hashar tefillah*, a general supplication.

What is striking about these *brachos* is that they are not merely *birchos hatorah* in the ordinary sense. Rather, the completion of the *keriat hatorah* is being used as a framework for reciting *brachos* over the entirety of the *avoda* that has just culminated. The *al ha'avoda* is, according to *Rashi*, the *retzei* — the prayer asking God to accept the service — though *Rashi* notes in *Yoma* that the concluding formula cannot be the *hamachazir shechinaso l'tziyon* of our *shemoneh esrei*, since that does not fit the context of an *avoda* just completed. Instead, it may correspond to the *retzei* found in the context of *birchas kohanim*: *she'otcha levadcha b'yirah na'avod*, which carries precisely the sense that the *avoda* is being performed right now. *Rashi* adds the principle: *achar zevichah hoda'ah* — after the sacrifice one gives thanks — which is why the *al ha'avoda* leads naturally into the *al ha'hoda'ah*, corresponding to *modim* of the *shemoneh esrei*.

The structure thus mirrors the *shemoneh esrei* in a loose way: *retzei*, *modim*, and then the hope that the *avoda* will effect *mechilas avon* — corresponding to the *atah bechartanu* type of blessing in which God is described as *melech mochel v'solei'ach la'avonot*. This is followed by *birchos* on the *mikdash*, on *yisrael*, and so on. *Rashi*'s formulations for some of these are suggestive: *baruch asher bachar baMikdash*, *baruch habocher b'amo Yisrael*. The shape of the *davening* is recognizable, even though one is entering it, so to speak, from the middle. What is notable is that this is not fundamentally about the *keriat hatorah* at all — it is using the reading of the *torah* as the occasion to offer a comprehensive liturgical response to everything that has just happened on *yom kippur*.

---

## Honor Display

### Tosafot's Query

The *gemara* draws an inference from the chain of transmission: since the *sefer torah* passed from *chazzan* to *rosh haknesset* to *segan* before reaching the *kohen gadol*, one might conclude that we practice *cholkin kavod l'talmid bimkom harav* — we honor the lesser figure even in the presence of the greater one. But this reading, while initially plausible, does not survive scrutiny.

*Tosafot* sharpens the problem considerably. The obvious inference — that all these intermediate stages are simply meant to heighten the honor of the *kohen gadol* by approaching him through multiple steps — is exactly right. The question is more specific: granted that you want to demonstrate the *kohen gadol*'s elevated status by passing the *sefer torah* upward through the hierarchy, why was it necessary to include the *rosh haknesset* at all? Why not go from the *chazzan* directly to the *segan*? Skipping the *rosh haknesset* would still produce an ascending chain — *chazzan* to *segan* to *kohen gadol* — which would equally serve to highlight how high the *kohen gadol* stands. The *rosh haknesset* is, after all, considerably lower in the hierarchy than the *segan* or the *kohen gadol*. Who is slighted by bypassing him?

*Tosafot* answers its own question: even the *segan* would be slightly dishonored if the *sefer torah* arrived in his hands having come directly from someone two levels below him rather than from the person immediately beneath him in the hierarchy. But *Tosafot* then presses further — and this is where the genuine insight lies — why should we care? If the entire enterprise is about the honor of the *kohen gadol*, let the *segan* be slighted. What is wrong with going from *chazzan* to *segan*, bypassing the *rosh haknesset*, and then from *segan* to *kohen gadol*?

### Abaye's Answer

Abaye's answer is: *kulo mishum kevodo d'kohen gadol* — the entire protocol, including every intermediate stage, is entirely for the sake of the *kohen gadol*'s honor. This is not a concession to the lesser figures in the middle. Rather, having every step proceed in careful, orderly sequence — one rung at a time — itself amplifies the honor of the person at the top. To bypass any intermediate figure, even if it would only slightly reduce the honor of those bypassed, would diminish the cumulative effect of the ascent. Every stage of the ceremony increases the *kavod* of the *kohen gadol*, not merely the final transfer.

This reading represents a significant refinement over the simpler understanding. *Rashi* might have read the chain as a natural courtesy to the intermediate figures. *Tosafot*, and through them Abaye's principle, establishes something more precise: the staged ascent is not a balance between honoring multiple parties but a single coherent act of honoring one supreme authority. Even a subtle disruption to the continuity of that ascent — even bypassing the *rosh haknesset* — would undermine the message that the entire ceremony is designed to convey.

---

## Torah vs Haftarah

### Jump Rules

After establishing that the *kohen gadol* reads from *acharei mos* and then from *ach ba'asor*, the *gemara* raises a contradiction. There is a principle that one may jump (*medalgin*) in the *navi* — that is, when reading the *haftarah* one may skip from one passage to another — but one may not jump in the *torah*. Yet here the *kohen gadol* is apparently jumping from one section of the *torah* to another. How is this permitted?

### Translator Timing

Abaye offers a first resolution: *lo kashya* — there is no contradiction. The distinction depends on whether the skip can be completed before the *meturgeman* — the translator — finishes rendering the preceding passage. If the reader can reach the next *pasuk* before the translator concludes, there is no pause, no moment of waiting, and the jump is permissible. If not, there is a pause, and that is *tircha d'tzibura*.

But the *gemara* then cites a *braita* that complicates this resolution. The *braita* teaches: one may jump in *navi*, one may not jump in *torah* — and then specifies that even in *navi*, jumping is permitted only up to the point where the translator has not yet finished. This implies that even in *navi*, you cannot create a pause. But the *braita* is also saying that in *torah*, even if you can reach the next *pasuk* before the translator finishes, you still cannot jump. Timing alone, then, cannot be the full criterion. So Abaye offers a second, more refined resolution.

### Theme Continuity

*Lo kashya* — there is no difficulty. The real distinction is between jumping within a single theme (*inyan echad*) and jumping between different themes (*shnei inyanim*). In the *torah*: you may jump if you are staying within the same subject matter and can complete the jump before the translator finishes. In the *navi*: you may jump even between different themes, but still only if you can do so before the translator finishes. And within the *navi*, you may not jump from one *sefer* of *navi* to another — with the exception of *trei asar*, the twelve minor prophets, which form a single *sefer*. Even there, however, one may not go backwards within the *sefer*, as that would create confusion for the listeners.

### Listener Focus

*Rashi* provides a beautifully precise explanation for why you cannot jump between themes in the *torah* even with adequate timing. When a person's mind is engaged with one subject, it does not immediately disengage and redirect itself toward a new theme. The listener cannot easily switch attention. In the context of reading the *torah* — where the purpose is not merely ritual but genuine instruction in the *mitzvos* — this matters enormously. *Rashi* puts it sharply: *she'ein halev shehu nimshach achar inyan echad mmaher latzet mimenu lishmoa lehavin divrei inyan echad* — a heart drawn along one line of thought does not quickly exit it to absorb a different subject.

And the stakes are high. The *torah* is the source of the *mitzvos* that people are obligated to perform. Reading the *torah* publicly is an opportunity for people to hear and internalize what is required of them. If a listener is shifting between topics and cannot follow properly, a *pasuk* goes ununderstood, it passes over him — *over alav v'eino mekayma* — and he will not fulfill it. In this light, it is better not to read the passage at all than to read it in a way that guarantees the listener will not absorb it. Switching themes mid-reading ensures exactly that failure.

The *navi*, by contrast, does not carry the same weight of obligatory practice. Missing a nuance or losing the thread in the *haftarah* does not produce the same halakhic consequences. Hence the asymmetry: in *torah*, thematic continuity is a precondition; in *navi*, it is not required.

---

## High Priest's Blessi (II)

### No Scrolling Rule

Having established the framework for jumping in the *torah*, the *gemara* returns to the earlier question: why does the *kohen gadol* recite the passage from *pinchas* by heart rather than reading it inside? The *gemara* phrases the question with apparent surprise — *velirkacha lesifra vlikrei*, why not just scroll and read? This is puzzling because the issue seems already to have been addressed. *Rashi* in fact explains that what was happening is that while the *kohen gadol* was scrolling from *acharei mos* toward the next section, the *meturgeman* was translating the last *pasuk* — they were working simultaneously so there would be no perceived pause. It is *pasuk* by *pasuk*, not section by section, that the translation proceeds, and the scrolling and translating overlap.

But a further question is articulated explicitly: *v'ha'amar Rav Huna bar Yehuda amar Rav Sheshet* — because *ein golin sefer torah b'tzibur*, one does not scroll the *sefer torah* before the public. The act of visibly scrolling while the congregation sits and waits is itself a form of *tircha d'tzibura*, not merely the passage of time but the spectacle of delay. Even if time is being used productively — even if the translator is speaking — the visual fact of a pause in the reading, with the scroll being moved, is unseemly. It is not the absolute quantity of time that constitutes *tircha* but rather the felt sense of waiting and hesitation.

One might then ask: why not simply bring a second *sefer torah* opened to *pinchas*? *Rav Huna bar Yehuda* addresses this as well: *mishum pigmo shel rishon* — because it raises the appearance of a defect in the first *sefer torah*. If the *kohen gadol* sets aside one scroll and takes up another in the middle of his reading, the onlookers will wonder why. There must be something wrong with the first one. *Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish* adds an additional reason: bringing a second *sefer torah* within the same *aliyah* would necessitate an additional and superfluous *bracha* — *bracha she'eina tzricha*. The *bracha* attaches to the *cheftza*, the *sefer torah* itself, and to bring a second one in the midst of the same reading implies an additional *bracha* over it, which is unnecessary and therefore improper.

The *gemara* then asks whether this concern about *pigmo shel rishon* is really coherent, since we know from *Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha* that on a *shabbat* that coincides with *rosh chodesh* and *chanukah*, three *sifrei torah* are brought out simultaneously. How is that not *pigmo*? The answer: *tlat gavrei b'tlat sifei leika pgama* — when three different people read from three different scrolls, there is no implication that any one scroll is defective, since each person has his own scroll for his own *aliyah*. But *chad gavra b'trei sifei ika pgama* — when the same person, in the same *aliyah*, sets aside one scroll and picks up another, the contrast is inescapable. Why was the first one abandoned? That generates the suspicion of a defect. The solution, then, is to recite the passage from *pinchas* entirely from memory, with the statement *yoser mi-mah she-karasi kasuv kan* serving to assure the congregation that the omission of that passage from the reading was a matter of protocol, not of deficiency.

### Eight Blessings

The *mishna* lists eight *brachos* recited by the *kohen gadol* following the reading. A *braita* elaborates: the *bracha al hatorah* follows the form used in the synagogue — *asher natan lanu torat emet*. The *brachos al ha'avoda*, *al ha'hoda'ah*, and *al mechilas ha'avon* follow their established formulations familiar from the *shemoneh esrei*. Then come separate *brachos* for the *mikdash*, for *yisrael*, for the *kohanim*, and for *yerushalayim*, each as a discrete *bracha* unto itself. The *braita* concludes: *v'hashar tefillah* — a final petition, described as *techina*, *rina*, and *bakasha*, for whatever *yisrael* needs, concluding with the *chatimah* of *shomea tefillah*.

The count raises a question. If each of the seven named categories constitutes one *bracha*, and *v'hashar tefillah* is an eighth, the tally reaches eight. But the *braita*'s description of that final element as a *bracha* containing *techina*, *rina*, and *bakasha* does not clearly resolve whether it is to be counted separately or understood as subsumed within one of the seven. *Rashi*'s explanation here does not fully clarify the matter, and a parallel difficulty arises from noting that some textual traditions omit the *bracha* for *yerushalayim*, apparently following a *girsa* in *Yoma* and the *Yerushalmi* that does not list it, while *Rashi* does mention *yerushalayim* but omits the *kohanim* as a separate category.

What is clear in any case is that the *brachos* as a whole are not oriented toward the *torah* reading alone. They are a comprehensive liturgical response to the entire *yom kippur* experience: acknowledging the *avoda* that has just been performed, giving thanks for it, praying that it has effected atonement, and invoking God's connection to His *mikdash*, His people, His city. The *keriat hatorah* provides the occasion; the *brachos* are the substance of what the occasion demands. There is something deeply interesting about how this draws the whole congregation into participation in what was otherwise entirely the *kohen gadol*'s private service.

---

## King's Reading

### Hakhel Intro

The next *mishna* introduces *parshas hamelech* — the reading of *hakhel*. The *hakhel* ceremony, described in *devarim* as occurring at the conclusion of the *shmita* year, gathers all of *klal yisrael* for a public reading of the *torah*. The *torah* itself says *tikra es hatorah hazos* without specifying that it is the king who reads, yet the *mishna* takes for granted that the king performs the reading. The ceremony takes place *b'motzei yom tov harishon shel chag* — the *gemara* will shortly clarify that this means not the second day of *succos* but rather the eighth year, *bishminis*, following the *shmita*.

### King's Platform

A large wooden platform — *bima shel etz* — is constructed in the *azarah*. As with the *kohen gadol*'s reading, the *gemara* will confirm that *azarah* here means the *ezrat nashim*, which is the only space large enough to accommodate the full assembly of *klal yisrael*. The king sits upon this platform. The significance of this detail will become apparent shortly, since kings who are not of *malchei beit david* are not permitted to sit in the *azarah* proper; the *ezrat nashim* resolves this difficulty.

The chain of transmission of the *sefer torah* is identical to what was described for the *kohen gadol*: from *chazzan haknesset* to *rosh haknesset* to *segan* to *kohen gadol*, and then from the *kohen gadol* to the king. The king stands to receive the scroll and then sits to read it — *v'hamelech omed u'mekabel, v'korei yoshev* — which is the prerogative of *malchei beit david* in the *azarah*.

### Agrippas's Stand

Agrippas the king — the last king of *yisrael* before the *churban*, a descendant of Herod — stood both to receive the *sefer torah* and to read from it, declining to exercise his privilege of sitting while reading. The sages praised him for this. He chose to show honor to the *torah* by standing, setting aside his royal prerogative.

But when Agrippas reached the passage *lo suchal laseis alecha ish nochri* — you may not set a foreigner over you — his eyes filled with tears. He recognized that this *pasuk* disqualified him: he was descended from Herod, who was of servile and non-Jewish origin, and he therefore could not claim fully Jewish lineage on his father's side. The assembled people called out to him: *al tisra Agrippas, achinu atah, achinu atah* — do not fear, Agrippas, you are our brother. *Rashi* explains that they said this because his *mother* was Jewish — *imo mi'yisrael* — which they held sufficient to regard him as one of them.

### King's Text

The sections read at *hakhel* are drawn from *sefer devarim*. The king begins from the opening of *devarim* — understood as *mishneh hatorah hazos* — reading through to *shema*. He then reads the *shema* itself, which *Rashi* identifies as the declaration of *kabalat malchus shamayim*. He continues with *v'haya im shamoa*, *Rashi* noting that this constitutes *kabalat ol mitzvos* — again, our familiar structure from *keriat shema*. He then reads *aser t'aser* and *ki tichaleh l'aser*, passages concerning *ma'aser* and the gifts to the *aniyim*, because this is the time of *zman ha'asif* — the harvest season of *succos* — and these obligations are particularly timely. *Rashi* explains that the passage *parshat hamelech* intervenes between *aser t'aser* and *ki tichaleh*, but it was read together with the surrounding material so as not to break up the *ma'aser* reading, with *parshat hamelech* read immediately afterward. Finally, he reads the *brachos u'klallos* from *ki tavo* and continues through to the end of the entire *parsha*. *Rashi* identifies the *birchos u'klallos* as the acceptance of the *bris* of the *torah*, the covenant — *kabalat britot shel Torah*.

After the reading, the king recites the same eight *brachos* as the *kohen gadol*, with one modification: instead of *al mechilas ha'avon* — which is appropriate to *yom kippur* — he substitutes a *bracha* for the *regalim*, concluding with *mekadesh yisrael v'hazmanim*, which fits the *succos* setting.

The translator, *Rashi* notes, does not accompany the king's reading. There is no *meturgeman* when the king reads. This creates an apparent difficulty regarding the jumping between passages in the *torah* — if there is no translator, there is no framework within which to evaluate whether a skip is made before the translator finishes, since there is no translator at all. *Rashi* resolves this by saying that the absence of a translator means the constraint of *birkat she'ein tzricha* and *tircha* operate differently, though this explanation is acknowledged to be somewhat difficult to fully work out.

### Hakhel Day

The *gemara* then asks: if the *mishna* says *motzei yom tov harishon shel chag* — after the first day of *yom tov* of *succos* — does this mean *hakhel* is done on the second day of *succos*? *Bishmini salka dach'tacha*? The *gemara* resolves this: *ela eima bishminis* — no, it means in the eighth year, the year following *shmita*.

The *gemara* then asks why all the different temporal designations in the *pasuk* are necessary — *miketz sheva shanim*, *hashmita*, *b'moed*, *b'chag hasuccos*, *b'vo kol yisrael*. It answers that each one is required to exclude a different mistaken inference. *Miketz sheva shanim* alone might have been taken to mean seven years from the time *moshe* gave the *torah*, not the end of the *shmita* cycle. *Hashmita* alone might have meant the very end of the *shmita* year, rather than the beginning of the following year's *yom tov*. *B'moed* is necessary to tell you it is a *yom tov*, excluding *rosh hashanah*. *B'chag hasuccos* specifies which *yom tov*. And *b'vo kol yisrael* tells you it is at the beginning of the *chag* when they are arriving, not the last day.

---

## Honor Display (II)

### King's Progression

The *gemara* repeats its earlier observation in the context of the king's ceremony: the chain of transmission from *chazzan haknesset* to *rosh haknesset* to *segan* to *kohen gadol* to king again prompts the inference *shema mina cholkin kavod l'talmid b'makom harav* — and again Abaye supplies the same answer: *kula mishum kevod hamelech*. All the intermediate stages exist solely to magnify the honor of the king. The principle applies identically in both contexts: a staged, orderly ascent through every level of the hierarchy, without skipping, is itself the most powerful expression of honor for the person at the top.

---

## Kingly Honor

### King's Honor

Having established that Agrippas stood to read and was praised for it, the *gemara* raises a question: the sages praised him — *shivchuhu*, implying that it was well done — but how? A king is forbidden to waive his honor. The principle is stated explicitly: *melech she-machal al kevodo ein kevodo machul* — a king who relinquishes his honor has not succeeded in relinquishing it. The basis for this principle is the verse *som tasim alecha melech she-tehei imato alecha* — set a king over you, that his fear should be upon you. This is not merely an expectation or a convention; it is a legal requirement. The people need the institution of monarchy to carry its full weight of awe, and the king has no authority to unilaterally diminish that weight. By contrast, a *nasi* or any other officeholder who waives his honor — even the opinion that this is permitted applies to them, according to *amar Avatya*: *nasi she-machal al kevodo kevodo machul*. But the king is categorically different.

Then comes the answer: *mitzvah shani* — for the sake of a *mitzvah*, it is different. When a *mitzvah* is at stake, the king may set aside the protocol of his honor.

### Mitzvah Exception

*Tosafot* raises a powerful objection. The principle *mitzvah shani* — that a *mitzvah* overrides the prohibition of a king compromising his honor — cannot be unlimited. There are cases in the *gemara* where a king is said to be *makhal al kevodo* in the context of a *mitzvah*, such as honoring guests (*hachnosas orchim*) or honoring a bride and groom (*chosson v'kallah*), and yet the ruling there appears to be that even so, *ein kevodo machul*. If *mitzvah shani* applied universally, how could that be?

*Tosafot* distinguishes between types of *mitzvos*. When the king stands to read the *torah* out of honor for the *torah* itself — which is honor for the *shechina* — he is, in effect, saying: my honor means nothing in the presence of God's honor. The *kavod* he is yielding is entirely subordinated to and absorbed by a higher *kavod*: *kavod shamayim*. Similarly, in cases such as whether a king may perform *chalitzah* or *yibbum*, the king does what he does in order to fulfill *mitzvas hamelech* — God's command — which is, in a direct sense, subjugating himself to God's authority.

### Interpersonal Mitzvot

By contrast, when the *mitzvah* in question is *bein adam l'chaveiro* — honoring a *kallah* or rising before a *talmid chakham* — what is brought to the forefront is not God's honor but the other person's honor. Even though there is a *mitzvah* from God to perform these acts, the relational dynamic of the act itself is human-to-human. In that context, the king is effectively trading his honor for theirs. That is not *mitzvah shani* in the relevant sense; it more closely resembles the king simply being *makhal al kevodo* in favor of another human being.

*Tosafot* adds a further dimension: in such cases, the other party — the *kallah*, the *talmid chakham* — themselves bear an obligation to honor the king. There is therefore a countervailing *mitzvah* on the other side: the obligation *upon them* to give the king honor. The king cannot waive what is not solely his to waive; others are bound to honor him, and that obligation is not erased by the king's willingness to forgo it.

---

## Agrippas & Flattery

### The Restriction

When Agrippas reached the passage *lo suchal laseis alecha ish nochri*, he wept. A *tanna* taught in the name of *Rabbi Natan*: on that day, the enemies of *yisrael* — the *gemara*'s euphemism for *yisrael* itself — became deserving of destruction, because they flattered him: *she'hechnifu lo l'Agrippas*. They called out *achinu atah, achinu atah* — and by doing so, they assured him that he was fit, that there was no problem, when in fact there was.

### Genealogy Req.

The question immediately arises: what exactly was wrong? If his mother was Jewish — *imo mi'yisrael* — is he not halakhically Jewish? And if he is Jewish, what precisely is the deficiency that the *pasuk* is pointing to? *Rashi* says that regardless of his mother's status, his descent from non-Jewish ancestry made him *unseemly* for kingship, and the sages were wrong to reassure him.

*Tosafot* goes considerably further. Normally, we follow the rule that for various positions of authority that are restricted to those with proper Jewish lineage, *imo mi'yisrael* — a Jewish mother — is sufficient to satisfy the requirement. But *Tosafot* argues that the office of king is uniquely stringent. The verse itself uses the phrase *mi'kerev acheicha tasim alecha melech* — from *among your brothers* you shall set a king over you — and *Tosafot* reads this as requiring that the king be *mikerev*, fully from within, on *both* sides: *me'aviv u'me'imo mi'yisrael*. The *parsha* of the king thus sets a stricter standard than the general rule about *serarah* and Jewish lineage. Agrippas's father was not Jewish, and therefore, regardless of his mother, he did not meet the *torah*'s requirement for kingship.

### Flattery Defined

If *Tosafot*'s reading is correct, then Agrippas was not merely of questionable lineage — he was legally disqualified by the *torah* from holding the kingship. His kingship was *b'zroa she'lo k'din torah* — established by force and in violation of *din torah*. The people who called out *achinu atah* were not merely being tactful or kind; they were actively affirming that he was fulfilling a *mitzvah* when in fact he was violating a *toraitic* prohibition. *V'chizku b'kach* — they strengthened him in this course of action.

This is the real nature of *chanufah* as the *gemara* will go on to discuss. *Chanufah* is not simply flattery in the ordinary sense of the word — empty praise or unwarranted compliments. It is the act of telling someone who is doing something in violation of the *torah* that what they are doing is perfectly fine and legitimate, and thereby reinforcing them in their transgression. The sages did not just say something kind to Agrippas; they *machzik*-ed him, they gave him the stamp of approval for conduct that the *torah* forbade. That distinction — between flattery as pleasant speech and *chanufah* as endorsement of wrongdoing — will carry the discussion forward into the next *daf*.

---

---

# Sotah 42

## Meshauach Milchama

### Hebrew Requirement

The new *perek* opens with the institution of the *meshiach milchama* — the *kohen* specially anointed for war — and immediately establishes that his address to the people before battle must be delivered specifically in *lashon ha-kodesh*, Hebrew. This is somewhat counterintuitive: if the entire purpose of the address is to reach the hearts of the soldiers and steel their courage, one might expect that the most widely understood vernacular would be preferred. Yet the *mishnah* is clear — *b'lashon ha-kodesh hayah medaber*.

The derivation proceeds from the verse *v'hayah k'korovchem el hamilchama v'nigash ha-kohen v'diber el ha-am* — when you draw close to battle, the *kohen* shall draw near and speak to the people. The *Gemara* then links this *dibbur* to another instance of the same root elsewhere, in the context of the giving of the Torah: *Moshe yedaber veha-Elokim ya'anenu be-kol* — and just as that speech was in *lashon ha-kodesh*, so too this one. The *Gemara* acknowledges that there are many instances of *dibber* throughout the Torah, and *Tosafot* engages with this directly. The *Yerushalmi* formulation runs as follows: why does the word *v'dibber* alone establish Hebrew? After all, *keri'at shema* also uses the related form *ve-dibarta bam*, yet it may be recited in any language. The *Yerushalmi* answers that what is decisive is the combination of *dibber* and *amirah* together — *v'diber ha-kohen v'amar* — and then proceeds to distinguish the case of *viduy ma'aser*, which also contains a form of *amirah* yet may be recited in any language. Rabbi Chagai then offers the alternative derivation through a *gezeirah shavah* of *hagashah*: *v'nigshu ha-kohanim* corresponds to another instance of *hagashah* spoken in *lashon ha-kodesh*, and therefore here too the language must be Hebrew.

The underlying logic may be that there is a spiritual power to the use of the sacred tongue, particularly when one is invoking divine protection. In any case, the requirement stands.

### Brothers vs Enemies

The *meshiach milchama* begins his address with the words *Shema Yisrael — atem k'revim ha-yom el ha-milchama al oyveichem*: you are drawing close today against your enemies. The emphasis on *al oyveichem* — against your *enemies* — is deliberate. He continues: not against your brothers, not Yehudah against Shimon or Shimon against Binyamin. This is a distinction that carries real weight, because internecine conflict did occur during the pre-monarchic period and even afterward. The reasoning given is *she-im tiplu b'yadam yerachamu aleichem* — if you were to fall in the hands of your brothers, they would have compassion on you. By contrast, these are your enemies, and if you fall in their hands they will have no mercy. So the address begins by clarifying the stakes: this is not a civil war with its implicit safety net; this is war against those who will show no quarter.

### Pekach & Oded

The proof-text for the brotherly compassion argument comes from the incident of *Pekach ben Remalyahu*, as summarized by *Rashi* at the end of the *perek*. *Pekach*, king of the northern kingdom of *Yisrael*, waged war against *Achaz* of *Yehudah* and took many captives from *Bnei Yehudah*. A prophet named *Oded* went out before the returning army of *Yisrael* and declared: God was angry at *Bnei Yehudah* and therefore delivered them into your hands — but you have smitten them without restraint, and now you intend to enslave them? *Hashivu et ha-shivya* — return the captives.

The *pasuk* then relates: *va-yakumu ha-anashim asher nikre'u vi-shemot va-yachaziku ba-shivya* — those who were designated by name took hold of the captives, clothed the naked from the booty, shod them, fed them, gave them drink, anointed them, placed the ones who could not walk on donkeys, and brought them to *Yericho*, city of palm trees, to their brethren — and then returned to *Shomron*. This is what happens when you fall among brothers. The *meshiach milchama* invokes this episode to sharpen the contrast: your current enemy will not treat you this way.

### Courage Speech

Having made the soldiers aware of exactly what they face, the *meshiach milchama* turns to fortifying their resolve. *Al yerach levavchem v'al tira'u v'al tachpezu v'al ta'artzu* — do not let your heart grow faint, do not fear, do not tremble, do not be terrified. He then enumerates the specific psychological weapons the enemy will deploy: the braying of the horses, the clashing of swords, the clamoring of shields — *Rashi* explains that armies would deliberately bang their shields together to spread fear among the opposing side — the hordes of enemy soldiers, and the blasting of horns. Each of these is a form of psychological warfare, and the address names them explicitly so the soldiers know what to expect.

The cure for all of it is theological: *ki Hashem Elokeichem holech imachem* — God is going with you. The address continues: *hem ba'im be-nitzchono shel basar va-dam* — they come with the strength of flesh and blood, *ve-atem ba'im be-nitzchono shel Makom* — and you come with the strength of God. Two examples are then marshaled. The Philistines came with the valor of Goliath — *mah hayah sofo?* — what was his end? *U-lesof nafal be-cherev* — he fell by the sword, and his people fell with him. The Ammonites came with the valor of *Shovach* — what was his end? He too fell by the sword, and his nation with him. But you are not like them, for God goes with you to fight for you, you come with the *aron*, and you will be victorious.

What is striking about this formulation is that the address does not minimize the threat. The soldier is told precisely how terrible his enemy is, and precisely how little mercy he can expect. The courage comes not from illusion but from faith. The *meshiach milchama* strengthens hearts not by misrepresenting the danger, but by orienting the army toward the source of genuine power.

### Kohen Authority

The *Gemara* now asks: *yachol kol kohen she-yirtzeh* — might any *kohen* who wishes step forward and deliver this address? After all, the verse does not specify a particular appointment. The *Gemara* answers from a *kal va-chomer* or analogy to the *shotrim*, the officers who speak afterward (*mi ha-ish ha-yarei ve-rach ha-levav — yeilech ve-yashuv le-veito* and so on): just as the *shotrim* hold formally appointed positions — presumably appointed by the *shofetim*, the judges they serve — so too the *kohen* who speaks must be someone specifically appointed to that role. *Mah shotrim bi-memunah — af kohen bi-memunah*.

One might then suggest that it must be the *kohen gadol*. But this is rejected by analogy to the *shoter* as well: just as the *shoter* is appointed yet has someone above him in the hierarchy, so the *kohen* here must be someone appointed yet with a superior over him. The *kohen gadol* does have the king above him in certain respects — as we have seen, the king hands the *Sefer Torah* to the *kohen gadol* at *Hakhel* — but within the realm of *avodah*, of the Temple service itself, no one outranks the *kohen gadol*. The comparison to a *shoter* who has a *shofet* over him therefore does not fit the *kohen gadol* in that domain. The *meshiach milchama* must thus be someone appointed to this specific task yet subordinate to the *kohen gadol*.

### Sgan HaKohanim

The natural candidate would then seem to be the *sgan* — the deputy or vice *kohen gadol*. But the *Gemara* rejects this too: *sgan lav memunah hu* — the *sgan* does not hold the kind of appointment that qualifies here. The *Gemara* supports this from a *baraita*: Rabbi Chanina, who was himself the *sgan ha-kohanim*, states that the sole purpose of the *sgan*'s appointment is *she-im yei'ara bo psul be-kohen gadol — nichnas u-meshamesh tachtav* — if the *kohen gadol* becomes disqualified or dies, the *sgan* enters and serves in his place. He is the vice president. He has no independent mandate beyond standing ready to replace the *kohen gadol* when necessary.

*Tosafot* raises an interesting difficulty here. A *baraita* in *Sanhedrin* states that when the *kohen gadol* was receiving mourners, *ha-sgan u-meshiach milchama omed bi-ymino* — the *sgan* and the *meshiach milchama* would stand to his right. This implies that the *sgan* does play some active role alongside the *kohen gadol*, rather than simply waiting for him to die. *Tosafot* resolves this by distinguishing between rabbinic and biblical appointment. The *sgan* was certainly given certain tasks by his fellow *kohanim* — there is a *mishnah* that describes the *memuneh* giving instructions, and there are various roles assigned. But these were internal arrangements made by the *kohanim* among themselves, similar to how they might appoint a *markal* (overseer) or a *gizbar* (treasurer). What the *sgan* lacks is a *biblically recognized status* of appointment that would make him the *kohen* who speaks before battle. His only Torah-level appointment is to be ready to replace the *kohen gadol*; everything else is institutional arrangement, not a recognized *minui* from the Torah itself. The *meshiach milchama* must therefore be a distinct appointment — someone designated specifically for this function.

---

## David & Goliath

### Shema Yisrael

The *Gemara* pauses on the opening words of the *meshiach milchama*'s battlefield address — *Shema Yisrael* — and asks: *mai shna Shema Yisrael?* Why specifically this formulation, so resonant with the declaration of God's unity? Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai explains: God says to *Yisrael* — even if you have fulfilled nothing other than *keri'at shema* of the morning and evening, you will not be delivered into their hands. The *zechus* of reciting *Shema Yisrael* twice daily is sufficient protection. This is a notably accessible guarantee — not dependent on extraordinary merit, but on the most basic and universal Jewish practice.

---

## Two Addresses

### Timing & Content

The *Gemara* now establishes that the *kohen* spoke to the people not once but twice. *Pa'amayim medaber imahem* — he would address them on two separate occasions. The first was *ba-sfar* — at the border city, before the army had actually left the land of *Yisrael* proper. The second was *ba-milchama* — at the battlefield itself, immediately before engagement. At the border, the content was essentially administrative: *shimu divrei ma'archei milchama ve-chazru* — hear what the officers are telling you about who is eligible to return, and return accordingly. That is, the *shotrim* would there enumerate the categories of those who should go home — one who has built a house and not dedicated it, betrothed a woman and not yet married her, planted a vineyard and not redeemed it, and the one who is fearful and soft-hearted.

The address at the battlefield itself was the courage speech: *al yerach levavchem al tira'u v'al tachpezu v'al ta'artzu*. This sequence — first sending home those who should not be there, then inspiring those who remain — is logically the reverse of the order in which the verses appear in the Torah. The Torah presents the encouragement of the *kohen* before the *shotrim* announce the exemption categories. The *Gemara* does not comment directly on this discrepancy but it is evident that the practical sequence makes more sense: eliminate the fearful first, and deliver the courage speech to those who are actually going into battle.

### Four Tactics

The four expressions of fear — *al yerach*, *al tira'u*, *al tachpezu*, *al ta'artzu* — correspond to four specific things that enemy armies would do in order to break the morale of the opposing force. They would clang their shields (*magifim*); they would blast the horns (*meri'im*); they would let out war cries (*tzovchim*); and they would trample forward with their armies (*romsim*). Each phrase in the *kohen*'s address is a counter to one of these tactics, reassuring the soldiers against each specific form of psychological warfare.

---

## David & Goliath (II)

### Goliath Brazenness

Rabbi Yochanan offers a *drasha* on the name *Golyat* itself: *she-amad be-giluy panim* — he stood with brazenness before God. The source is his challenge: *baru lachem ish v'yered elai* — choose for yourselves a man and let him come down against me. The *Gemara* reads this as a direct affront to the divine, since *v'ein ish ela Ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu* — the word *ish* in certain contexts refers specifically to God, as in the verse *Hashem ish milchama*, God is a man of war. Goliath was therefore not merely challenging the army of Israel; he was effectively saying: send down your God and I will fight Him. God's response: *hareini mapilo al yedei ben ish* — I will bring him down through the hands of a *ben ish*, a son of a man, a mere youth — as in the verse *ve-David ben ish Ephrati*, David son of a man of Ephrat. The wordplay is pointed: Goliath invoked *ish* as a challenge to God, and it is through a *ben ish* that he is undone.

### Self-Trapping Words

Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir identifies three specific moments where Goliath's own words sealed his fate. First, *baru lachem ish v'yered elai* — the word *v'yered*, let him come down, implies a descent upon Goliath, a conquest. Second, *im yuchal le-hilachem iti ve-hikani* — if he will be able to fight me and smite me; even phrased conditionally, Goliath articulated his own defeat. Third, his taunt to David — *ha-kelev anochi ki ata ba elai be-maklot* — am I a dog that you come to me with sticks? — ultimately described how he would be beaten, like a dog.

One might ask: David also makes a forceful declaration — *ata ba elai be-cherev u-ve-chanit u-ve-kidon* — you come to me with sword and spear and javelin — does this not similarly describe David being attacked? The *Gemara* answers no, because David immediately continues: *ve-anochi ba eleicha be-shem Hashem Tzeva'ot elokei ma'archot Yisrael* — but I am coming against you in the name of God. David's statement is not a prediction of his own defeat; it is precisely the declaration the *meshiach milchama* would make — we come in the name of God. The contrast between their respective sources of power is the entire point.

The connection to the earlier theme is explicit: Goliath would come out *ha-shakem ve-ha'arev* — early in the morning and in the evening — precisely at the times of *keri'at shema shacharit ve-arvit*, in order to prevent Israel from reciting *Shema*. This echoes Rabbi Yochanan's earlier teaching: the *zechus* of *Shema* is what protects in battle, and Goliath knew exactly what to undermine.

### Beinayim

The *pasuk* describes Goliath as *ish ha-beinayim* — a man of the *beinayim*. The *Gemara* explores several interpretations of this term. Rav says *she-mevuneh mi-kol mum* — he was perfectly constructed, without any blemish or defect. Shmuel says *beinoni she-b'achav* — he was merely the middling one among his brothers; if you think Goliath was large, you should see his older brothers. The school of Rabbi Shila says *she-hu asuy ke-vinyan* — he was built like a building, massive and solid. And Rabbi Yochanan says *bar me'ah papi ve-chada nani* — he had a hundred fathers and one mother.

*Rashi* elaborates on this last reading: *ben ha-ta'arovet* — a son of mixture — because many men came upon his mother in a single night and she conceived from one of them. One is the biological father and all the others are adulterers. *Rashi* adds that *nani* is the word for father in Persian.
