The *drasha* on *beinayim* — from the root *bein*, between — thus suggests he emerged from *bein anashim harbei*, from among many men. *Rav Yosef* adds in the same vein: *she-ha-kol dashim et imo ke-gat* — everyone trampled his mother like a *gat*, a winepress. The word *me'aros* in the phrase *mime'aros Plishtim* is read *ma'archos*, and *she-ha-kol he'eru be-imo* — everyone performed the act of *giluy arayot* with his mother. The portrait being drawn is of a man of illegitimate and sordid origins, despite his fearsome appearance.

### Harpa/Arpa

A later *pasuk* in *Sefer Shmuel* refers to four sons born *le-Harpa be-Gat* — to *Harpa* in *Gat*. These four, who fell in battle against David and his servants, appear to be Goliath's brothers, and *Harpa* is their mother. Yet elsewhere her name appears as *Arpa*. This *Arpa* is, of course, known from the story of *Rut* — she is the sister-in-law of *Rut* who kissed her mother-in-law *Na'omi* and turned back, rather than accompanying her to the land of *Yisrael*. The *Gemara* now draws the connection between the two.

*Rav u-Shmuel* debate the two names. One holds that her name was *Harpa*, and she was called *Arpa* because *she-ha-kol orfin otah me-achoreiha* — everyone would approach her from behind, the word *oref* denoting the back of the neck. The other holds that her name was *Arpa*, and she was called *Harpa* because *she-ha-kol dashim otah ka-arifot* — everyone trampled her like *harifot*, the crushed or milled grain. Two *pesukim* are adduced in support of the *harifot* reading: the woman who spread a cloth over the pit and scattered *arifot* upon it as a trap (*va-tishpach aleha ha-arifot*), and the verse *im tichtosh et ha-evil ba-machtesh be-toch ha-arifot* — if the foolish one is ground up in the mortar among the grain. Both images carry the sense of something being violently broken down. The point in all of these interpretations is consistent: the mother of these giants was a woman of profound immorality, and her sons' enormous physical power is in inverse proportion to the legitimacy of their birth.

### Four Children

*Rav Chisda* identifies the four sons born to *Harpa* in *Gat*: *Saph u-Madon Golyat ve-Yishbi ve-Nov* — names that appear in the text of the *pesukim* themselves. Each fell *be-yad David u-ve-yad avadav* — at the hands of David and his servants in separate engagements. The connection to *Rut* is now drawn explicitly: *de-kasiv va-tishak Arpa la-chamotah ve-Rut davkah bah* — *Orpah* kissed her mother-in-law and *Rut* cleaved to her. Rabbi Yitzchak states in the name of God, as it were: *yavo benei ha-neshukah* — let the children of the one who gave the goodbye kiss come forth, *ve-yippelu be-yad benei ha-devukah* — and let them fall at the hands of the children of the one who cleaved. The symmetry is striking and purposeful: the choice *Orpah* made on the road to *Yisrael* — the kiss of farewell — determined the fate of her descendants.

### Orpah's Reward

*Rava* adds a dimension of nuance to *Orpah*'s story. *Be-schar arba d'maot she-horida Orpah al chamotah* — in the reward of the four tears that *Orpah* shed for her mother-in-law, *zachta ve-yatza mimenah arba'ah gibborim* — she merited that four mighty warriors emerged from her. The four tears are derived from the verse *va-tisenah kolam va-tivkena od* — *Rashi* understands this as weeping from both eyes, making two, doubled by the word *od* to four. *Orpah* was not simply a wicked person; she wept genuinely for *Na'omi* and accompanied her a significant distance before turning back. Her failing was not cruelty but a lesser degree of self-sacrifice than *Rut*. And so she received a reward — four sons of extraordinary physical power — even as those sons ultimately fell at the hands of David, the descendant of *Rut*, *Orpah*'s counterpart.

### Praising Wicked

The *Gemara* notes a textual detail about Goliath's description: *k'siv chetz chanito ve-karinan etz chanito* — the written form of the text says *chetz*, the arrow of his spear, while the read form (*keri*) says *etz*, the wood of his spear. Rabbi Elazar draws the following conclusion from the sparse description of Goliath's might: *adayin lo higanu le-chatzi shevacho shel oto rasha* — we have not even reached half of the praise due to that wicked one. The Torah's description, impressive as it is, captures less than half of his actual power and stature.

The *Gemara* immediately asks: if that is so, why describe him at all? *She-asur le-saper be-shivchen shel resha'im* — it is forbidden to enumerate the praises of the wicked. The answer: *lo dumi shavkei d'dami* — you cannot omit it entirely, because you must describe Goliath's greatness in order to convey the magnitude of David's achievement. The praise of Goliath is not for Goliath's sake; it is for David's. Without knowing what David overcame, one cannot fully appreciate the victory.

---

## Shovach Army

### Shovach Names

The *Gemara* returns to the motif introduced earlier in the *meshiach milchama*'s address — *Bnei Amon ba-u be-nitzchono shel Shovach* — the Ammonites came to battle relying on the valor of *Shovach*, their general, whose story is recounted in *Sefer Shmuel*. However, in *Divrei ha-Yamim* the same figure is called *Shofach*. The *Gemara* notes: *k'siv Shovach u-ch'siv Shofach* — both names appear in the text.

*Rav u-Shmuel* debate his true name. One holds that his name was *Shofach*, and he was called *Shovach* because *she-asui ke-shovach* — he was built like a pigeon coop, extraordinarily tall and imposing. The other holds his name was *Shovach*, and he was called *Shofach* because *she-kol ha-ro'eh oto nishpach le-fanav ke-kiton* — everyone who saw him would spill out before him like a pitcher, perhaps losing control of their bowels or simply dissolving in fear before him.

### Ashpato Meaning

The *Gemara* then turns to a *pasuk* about the armies of *Nevuchadnezzar*: *ashpato ke-kever patuach kulam gibborim* — his quiver is like an open grave; they are all mighty men. The word *ashpato* can mean a quiver for arrows, but it can also mean a garbage heap or *ashpah*. *Rav u-Shmuel* — or in another version, *Rav Ami ve-Rav Asi* — debate the meaning. One holds that *ashpato* refers to the quiver of arrows: *b'sha'ah she-zorkim chetz osim ashpah ashpah shel chalalim* — when they shoot their arrows they make mound upon mound of corpses, each mound like an *ashpah*, a garbage heap. One might then think that this merely reflects their skill at archery rather than their personal might — therefore *Talmud lomar kulam gibborim*, the verse concludes that they are all personally mighty men as well.

### Excrement View

The other opinion reads *ashpato* differently. *B'sha'ah she-osim tzorcheihem osim ashpah ashpah shel zevel* — when they relieve themselves, they make mound upon mound of excrement, suggesting by their sheer physical size the enormous quantities they discharge. This too is a form of praising their might, if an unusual one. Here again the verse's conclusion is necessary: *kulam gibborim* — they are indeed mighty, not merely large in an unhealthy way.

*Rav Mari* draws a practical medical inference from this discussion: *shema minah — hai man de-nafish zivlei cholei me'ayim hu* — one who produces excessive excrement is to be presumed to have intestinal illness. The *nafka mina* is *le-itpuchi be-nafshei* — the person should attend to his own welfare and seek medical attention. *Rashi* explains this as: *le-vakesh alav refu'ot* — to go seek healing.

---

## Worry & Health

### Managing Worry

The *Gemara* cites the verse *da'agah be-lev ish yashchenah* — if there is worry in a man's heart, he should do something with it (*yashchenah* or *yassichennah*, depending on how one reads the vowels). *Rav Asi* introduces the discussion and notes two competing readings of the operative word, both using a *sin* — *yassichennah*.

### Therapy Methods

The two readings yield two opposing therapeutic strategies. One says *yassichennah mi-da'ato* — push it out of his mind, distract himself from the worry, deal with problems by redirecting his attention elsewhere. The other says *yassichennah la-acherim* — speak about it to others, share the burden of the concern. The *Gemara* here reflects a genuine debate about how human beings should manage anxiety: suppression and distraction on one side, disclosure and conversation on the other. The *Gemara* presents both as legitimate readings of the verse without definitively resolving between them — though the pairing with the discussion of intestinal health in the preceding lines creates a suggestive context, implying that unexpressed worry has a way of manifesting physically.

---

---

# Sotah 43

## Meshuch Milchama Speech

### Priest & Ark

The daf opens at the very last line of 42b, continuing the discussion of the *meshuch milchama* — the anointed priest who addresses the troops before battle. The Torah declares: *Hashem elokeichem hu haholeich imachem* — "Hashem your God is the one who walks with you." The *gemara* asks: *vechol kach lama* — what is the purpose of all of this? The obvious answer is that it gives the soldiers courage. But the question, as Rashi frames it, is more precise.

### Rashi on Halicha

Rashi explains that the question is not why this statement is made at all, but what is the emphasis of the word *haholeich* — "walking" or "going" — rather than simply "is with you." The answer is: *mipnei sheHashem vechol kinuyav munachim ba'aron* — because God's name and all of the various divine appellations are actually present in the *aron*. It is therefore not merely an abstract declaration that God accompanies the army; it is a statement that the physical object representing God's presence — the *aron* — is literally going with them into battle. This raises the interesting question of whether the *aron* itself was taken out of the *Beit Hamikdash* or the *Mishkan* and brought to the battlefield, and there is a view that a separate *aron* was used for battle, distinct from the one that resided in the sanctuary.

### Midian War Example

The *gemara* then brings a proof from the war against Midian: *vayishlach otam Moshe elef lamateh latzava, otam ve'et Pinechas ben Elazar hakohein latzava uchelei hakodesh vechatzotzrot hateruah beyado*. The *gemara* identifies the components: *otam* refers to the Sanhedrin; *Pinechas ben Elazar* is the *meshuch milchama*; *uchelei hakodesh* — the holy vessels — refers to the *aron* and the *luchot*; and *vechatzotzrot hateruah* — the trumpets of the blast — is rendered as *shofrot*. This last identification is noteworthy: *chatzotzrot* are the metal trumpets, while *shofrot* are made from an animal's horn. The *gemara* elsewhere indicates that in the Amoraic period these two terms exchanged their meanings in vernacular usage, which may explain why the *gemara* here renders the *chatzotzrot* of the *pasuk* as *shofrot*.

### Pinchas Genealogy

The *gemara* then adds: *lo chinam holeich Pinechas lamilchama* — it was not for nothing that Pinchas went to war against Midian. He went specifically to avenge the honor of his mother's father, as Scripture records: *vehamidanim machru oto el Mitzrayim* — the Midianites sold Yosef into Egypt. This implies that Pinchas descended from Yosef on his maternal side.

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: is Pinchas really descended from Yosef? The *pasuk* states that Elazar ben Aharon took a wife from the daughters of *Putiel*, and she bore him Pinchas. So who is this *Putiel*? The *gemara* presents the classic explanation that *Putiel* alludes to Yitro — *shepitem agalim l'avoda zara* — who fattened calves for idol worship, giving rise to the name *Puti El* in the sense of fattening for the gods. This would make Pinchas a descendant of Yitro on his mother's side, not of Yosef.

The *gemara* then invokes the well-known *aggadic* tradition that after Pinchas slew Zimri, the tribes mocked him: *re'item ben Puti zeh* — "have you seen this descendant of Puti?" — *shepitem avi imo agalim l'avoda zara* — "whose grandfather fattened calves for idol worship?" — *veharag nesi miYisrael* — "and yet he had the audacity to slay a leader of Israel?" This *aggadic* understanding runs deep enough that one cannot simply discard the derivation from Yitro. The *gemara* therefore resolves the tension: Pinchas was descended from both lineages on his mother's side. Either his maternal grandfather descended from Yosef and his maternal grandmother descended from Yitro, or the reverse. The *gemara* notes that the word *Putiel* is pointed in a way that implies two roots — *dayka nami dektiv mibnot Putiel*, *trei mashma*, "the word implies two." He therefore avenged the honor of his ancestor Yosef by leading the war against the very people who sold him.

---

## Military Exemptions

### Three Categories

The *gemara* turns to the next *mishnah*, which addresses the speech of the *shotrim* — the officers — to the assembled troops. The Torah instructs them to announce three categories of exemption: one who built a new house and did not yet inaugurate it; one who planted a vineyard and did not yet perform *chilul*; and one who betrothed a woman and did not yet marry her. Those who qualify return from the front. Alongside this, there is a category of soldiers who do not go back to the front line but remain in service providing support — supplying food, water, and maintaining the roads.

### House Exemption

The *mishnah* broadens the house category significantly. It is not limited to a standard dwelling: *echad haboneh beit hateven beit habakar beit ha'etzim* — whether it is a barn for straw, a stable for cattle, a shed for wood, or any storage facility with a roof. What matters is that it is a structure of some substance. Nor does one need to have built it himself: whether one built it, purchased it, inherited it, or received it as a gift — all are included.

### Vineyard Exemption

The vineyard exemption is likewise broad. The word *chilulo* in the *pasuk* — "and did not perform *chilul*" — is understood by the *gemara* to refer to the fourth year of *neta revai*, when the owner performs *chilul* by redeeming the fruit's sanctity onto money and spending that money in Jerusalem. This provides a window of four full years from the time of planting during which one is eligible for the exemption. (Some medieval commentators suggest that *chilul* may allude to a dedication ceremony, similar to *chanacho* by the house, but the *gemara* reads it as referring specifically to the fourth-year *kerem revai* process.)

The *mishnah* then expands the category of *kerem*: it includes not only a full vineyard but also five fruit-bearing trees — since the minimum *kerem* for purposes of other *halakhot* consists of five vines — even from five different species. And, parallel to the house, it includes not only planting but also *mavrich* (layering a branch underground to take root elsewhere), *markiv* (grafting), purchasing, inheriting, or receiving as a gift.

### Betrothal Exemption

The third category — betrothal — is similarly expanded. Whether the woman is a *betulah* (never-married virgin), a widow (*almanah*), or even a *shomeret yavam* — a woman awaiting *yibum* — the exemption applies. Remarkably, the *mishnah* extends this even to a case where a soldier heard during battle that his brother died in the war, leaving behind a widow: he returns as well, because he now has the obligation of *yibum*.

### Support vs. Leave

Those in these categories do not simply go home. They return from the front line but remain in national service, as the *mishnah* specifies: *umsapkim mayim umazon umtaknim es hadrachim* — they provide water and food and repair the roads. They serve the army in a support capacity without engaging in combat.

### No Exemption Cases

The *mishnah* then identifies cases where one does not return even to support duty. If one built a *sha'ar*, *achsadra*, or *mirpeset* — a gatehouse, colonnade, or porch — that does not qualify, because these are not habitable structures. If one planted only four fruit trees, or planted five trees that are of a species that does not bear fruit, that does not qualify. If a man remarries his own divorced wife — *hamachazir gerushato* — that does not qualify, since she is not a new wife to him. And if the betrothal or marriage involves a forbidden union — an *almanah* to a *kohen gadol*, a *gerusha* or *chalutzah* to a regular *kohen*, a *mamzeret* to a *Yisrael*, or a *bat Yisrael* to a *mamzer* or *nasin* — none of these qualify. (The *gemara* will raise the question of why forbidden unions need to be excluded, and that discussion will be addressed below.)

Rabbi Yehuda adds that one who rebuilt his house on its original foundation — *al mechono* — does not return, because it is analogous to restoring a prior state rather than inaugurating something genuinely new, similar to the logic of *hamachazir gerushato*. Rabbi Eliezer adds that even one who builds a standard brick house in the Sharon Valley does not return, because the ground there is so unstable — as recalled in the Yom Kippur prayer for the inhabitants of the Sharon — that such houses require frequent rebuilding and are not reliably permanent.

### Complete Exemption

The third group is those who do not even go to the front at all and are entirely exempt from any form of military service. These are: one who built a house and *chanacho* — actually inaugurated it; one who planted a vineyard and performed *chilul*; one who betrothed a woman and completed the marriage (*nisu'in*); and one who performed *yibum* with his *yevamah*. The *pasuk* specifying this final level of exemption — *naki yiheyeh l'veiso shanah achas vesimach es ishto asher lakach* — grants a full year at home to a man who has actually married, not merely betrothed. The *mishnah* applies this principle to all three categories: once the house, vineyard, or marriage has been fully actualized, one receives a complete year off from all military obligation, including support services.

This is, as a careful reading makes clear, somewhat counterintuitive. One might have expected that unfinished business — the un-inaugurated house, the unmarried bride — would produce the greater exemption, while completion would return one to duty. The *mishnah* teaches the opposite: partial actualization leads to support service; full actualization leads to complete exemption for a year. This is a *milchemet reshut*, an optional war, and the Torah's provisions apply accordingly. In a *milchemet mitzvah*, an obligatory war, all go to battle.

---

## Officers' Communication

### Speaker Authority

The *gemara* now addresses the question of who speaks what. The *tanna* asks: when the Torah says *vedibru hashotrim* — and the officers shall speak — could this mean they speak entirely in their own words? Perhaps. But the Torah elsewhere says *veyasfu hashotrim* — and the officers shall add — which refers to the additional address about *hayarei verach halevav*, the fearful-hearted. That passage is clearly the officers' own speech. So what is the verse *vedibru hashotrim* referring to? The *gemara* concludes: *bedivrei meshuch milchama haksav medaber* — the Torah is speaking about the words of the *meshuch milchama*, which the officers communicate: *kohen medaber veshoter mashmia* — the *kohen* speaks and the officers amplify, projecting his words throughout the assembled ranks, precisely as a *tanna* (reciter) amplifies the words of an *amora* in the study hall.

### Three-Part Division

However, there is a difficulty: three *beraitot* seem to contradict one another. One says *kohen medaber veshoter mashmia*; a second says *kohen medaber vekohen mashmia*; a third says *shoter medaber veshoter mashmia*. Abaye resolves this by dividing the speech into three sections. From the moment the *kohen* draws near until the verse *vedibru hashotrim* — the section about courage and God's presence — the *kohen* both speaks and amplifies: *kohen medaber vekohen mashmia*. The section from *vedibru hashotrim* through the categories of house, vineyard, and betrothal is *kohen medaber veshoter mashmia* — the *kohen* speaks and the officers amplify. From *veyasfu* onward — the address about the fearful-hearted — it is *shoter medaber veshoter mashmia*, entirely the officers' domain.

The logic is coherent. The call for courage and divine presence appropriately comes entirely from the *kohen*, who embodies the sacred. The final section about the fearful soldier is entirely the officers', because it is the officers who will enforce order in the ranks — tradition records that deserters could be summarily punished — and it is they who must manage the question of who leaves and who stays. The middle section, dealing with the practical exemption categories, is a joint operation.

---

## House Analysis

### Hermeneutics

The *gemara* now probes the textual basis for each exemption category. A *baraita* addresses the house: *asher bana* — "who built" — I would know only about building. How do I know that purchasing, inheriting, or receiving as a gift are also included? *Talmud lomar: mi ha'ish asher bana* — the formulation *asher bana* is read as an expansion. Similarly: *bayit* — "house" — I would know only a house. How do I know that a barn (*beit hateven*), stable (*beit habakar*), woodshed (*beit ha'etzim*), or storehouse (*beit ha'otzarot*) are included? *Talmud lomar: asher bana mikol makom* — because the word *bana* precedes the word *bayit* in the verse, the act of building is mentioned before its object, allowing *bana* to encompass anything built that resembles a *bayit*.

### Habitable Test

However, one might then go too far and include even a gatehouse, colonnade, or porch. The *gemara* limits this: *talmud lomar bayit* — the word *bayit* sets the threshold. *Mah bayit haraui ledirah* — just as a house is something fit for habitation, *af kol haraui ledirah* — so too, only structures fit for habitation are included. A gatehouse or porch fails this test, even though a barn technically could serve as sleeping quarters if necessary. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov dissents from the broader reading and insists that *bayit* means a *bayit* literally: only a proper dwelling qualifies.

### Chanuch & Theft

The *gemara* then turns to the requirement of *lo chanacho* — that he did not yet inaugurate it. Why does the verse use the personal pronoun *chanacho* — "inaugurate it" — rather than the simpler *chanach*? The answer: *prat legazlan* — to exclude a thief. The inauguration must be something the person was legitimately entitled to perform; if the property was stolen, he has no right to inaugurate it, and it does not qualify for the exemption.

The *gemara* then asks whether this exclusion of the *gazlan* conflicts with the position of Rabbi Yosi haGelili, who interprets *verach halevav* — the fearful-hearted — as referring to one who fears his own sins: *zu hamityare me'aveirot shebeyado*. If so, a thief would already be excluded on those grounds — he is fearful of punishment for theft. Why state it separately? The *gemara* answers: the case under discussion is one where the thief has already done *teshuvah* and paid restitution. Since he has resolved his sin, he no longer qualifies as *verach halevav* due to his *aveirot*. Yet, the *gemara* counters, if he paid for it, he is now a legitimate purchaser — *havei lei lokei'ach* — and should be entitled to the exemption as one who purchased a house. The *gemara* responds: since the property originally came to him through theft — *keivan demeyikara betorat gezeilah ata lidei* — it remains outside the scope of this passage, regardless of subsequent payment.

One might ask: should we not apply *takanat hashavim* — the rabbinic principle of encouraging penitents — and allow him back from the *milchamah*? The *gemara* acknowledges the principle but maintains the exclusion nonetheless.

---

## Vineyard Analysis

### Five Trees Rule

The *gemara* applies the same hermeneutical method to the vineyard. *Asher nata* — "who planted" — I would know only planting. How do I know purchasing, inheriting, and receiving as a gift? *Talmud lomar: umi ha'ish asher nata kerem* — the word *asher* is expansive. And *kerem* — I would know only a vineyard. How do I know that five fruit-bearing trees of any species are included? *Talmud lomar: asher nata* — again, *nata* precedes *kerem* in the verse, allowing *nata* to encompass anything planted that resembles a *kerem*. One might then include even four fruit trees or five non-fruit-bearing trees. The *gemara* answers: *talmud lomar kerem* — it must resemble a *kerem*, and neither four trees nor barren trees constitute a *kerem*.

### Chilul & Fruit

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov again defends the plain meaning: *kerem kemashma'o* — a *kerem* means what it sounds like, literally a vineyard, not five fruit trees of another species. The *gemara* also treats the phrase *lo chilalo* as containing a textual exclusion: *prat lemavrich umarkiv* — to exclude one who performed *mavrich* (layering) or *markiv* (grafting). This is puzzling, since the *mishnah* itself listed *mavrich* and *markiv* as modes that qualify for the exemption. The resolution will come in the following section.

### Grafting Exclusions

The tension is significant: the *mishnah* includes *mavrich* and *markiv* in the exemption, yet the *baraita* derived from *lo chilalo* seems to exclude them. Moreover, why would grafting be worse than simply purchasing a vineyard? The *gemara* addresses this directly in the next section.

---

## Grafting & Orlah

### Prohibited Grafting

Rav Chisda, as transmitted by Rabbi Zeira, resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya, kan beharkavas issur, kan beharkavas heter* — there is no difficulty. The exclusion of *mavrich* and *markiv* from the exemption refers specifically to a case where the grafting was performed through a forbidden act — namely, *kilayim* (prohibited crossbreeding of species). When the *baraita* excludes it, it is referring to *harkavat issur*. When the *mishnah* includes *mavrich* and *markiv*, it refers to *harkavat heter*, a permitted grafting.

### Status Transfer

The *gemara* then asks: what exactly is a case of *harkavat heter* that would entitle one to the exemption? The *gemara* first considers *yeladah be-yeladah* — grafting a young vine (within three years, i.e., still in *orlah* status) onto another young vine. But this is rejected: *teipuk lei d'bamehadar mishum yeladah rishonah* — the exemption would apply anyway on account of the base vine itself, which is already in *orlah* status. That case requires no separate derivation from the graft.

The alternative is *yeladah be-zkeinah* — grafting a young shoot onto an older vine. Here Rabbi Abahu's ruling applies: *yeladah she-sibchah be-zkeinah batlah yeladah be-zkeinah* — a young vine that becomes incorporated into an old one takes on the status of the old vine and is no longer subject to *orlah*. If the exemption from war depends on having a vine in *orlah* status (as the *gemara* derives from *chililo*), then grafting a young vine onto an old one would not give the owner a new *orlah*-status vine; the graft loses its youth status by incorporation.

### Young on Young

Rabbi Yirmiya therefore proposes: *le-olam yeladah be-yeladah* — the case remains young-on-young, but with a critical distinction. The base vine, though young, was planted not for fruit but *li-syag u-le-kora* — as a fence or for its timber. A vine planted for non-fruit purposes is exempt from *orlah*, as the *mishnah* in another tractate teaches: *hanotei'a li-syag u-le-kora patur min ha-orlah*. So the base has no *orlah* status, and the owner of the base would have no military exemption on its account. Now someone grafts onto it a young shoot intended for fruit. That shoot is *chayav* in *orlah*, and through it the grafter earns his exemption from the war.

### Beams Exception

The case now presents a conceptual question: why does the grafted shoot retain its own *orlah* status rather than being absorbed into the base, which is *patur* from *orlah*? If — as Rabbi Abahu teaches for the opposite configuration — a young vine grafted onto an old vine loses its own status and takes on the status of the host, why doesn't the same logic apply here, so that the young shoot grafted onto the non-*orlah* base would become *patur* along with it?

### Bas Mahdar

The *gemara* answers with the principle of *bas mahdar* — the potential to cause a return from war. In the case of *yeladah be-zkeinah* (young onto old), if the owner were to reconsider and want the old vine to produce fruit, it would still not subject the old vine to *orlah* (it is too old), and so there is no scenario in which the old vine becomes *bas mahdar* — no scenario in which it could ever generate a reason to return from the *milchamah*. Therefore the young shoot is fully incorporated into it.

Here, by contrast — *yeladah be-yeladah*, with the base being *patur* because it was planted for timber — if the owner were to change his mind and decide to use the base vine for fruit, it *would* then become *chayav* in *orlah*, because it is still young. *Im mimlech aleih bas mahdar hi* — if he changed his mind about the base, it would be a basis for returning from battle. Since the base at least has the *potential* to become *chayav* in *orlah*, the grafted young shoot retains its own *orlah* status and is not absorbed. The *gemara* supports this with the ruling that fruit that grows spontaneously without any planting intention is still *chayav* in *orlah* — *olu me'eileihen chayavin b'orlah* — since the potential for *orlah* obligation inheres in youth regardless of the planter's purpose. The *gemara* acknowledges that this is something of a *chiddush*, since the *bas mahdar* reasoning would suggest that merely changing one's mind about the purpose of a fence-vine would be sufficient to both impose *orlah* and entitle one to return from war.

### Joint Ownership

The *gemara* then raises an alternative reading of the case of *harkavat heter*: perhaps the exemption applies to a *kerem shel shenei shutfin* — a vineyard with two partners — where one partner owns the base vine and another owns the grafted shoot. In such a case, the owner of the shoot would have a young vine in *orlah* status but could not claim exemption on account of the base. Rav Pappa derives from this discussion: *zo omeret, kerem shel shenei shutfin ein hozrin aleiv mei-orkhei hamilchama* — a jointly-owned vineyard does not entitle anyone to return from battle. One must have sole ownership to qualify for the exemption.

### Yibum Analogy

The *gemara* challenges this from a case discussed elsewhere: if five brothers go to war and one is killed, leaving a widow who requires *yibum*, all the remaining brothers return from the front, since any one of them might fulfill the obligation of *yibum*. Is this not analogous to the partnership case — multiple people sharing a kind of joint claim, none of whom has exclusive title? The *gemara* distinguishes: *hasam kochad vechad karinan bei ishto* — there, whichever brother ultimately performs *yibum*, that woman will be exclusively his wife. The claim is individual and exclusive in its realization, even if it is currently shared. *Hacha kochad vechad lo karinan bei karmo* — here, neither partner will ever be able to say "my vineyard" in an exclusive sense. The verse requires a sense of individual ownership, and joint partnership cannot supply that.

---

## Mavrich & Stunted

### Branch on Veg

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers yet another case of *harkavat heter* that would qualify for the exemption: *bemavrich ilan beyerek* — grafting a tree branch onto a vegetable plant. In such a case, the base is a vegetable, not a tree, so the grafted branch is not absorbed into a tree-host and retains its own status as a young tree, remaining *chayav* in *orlah*. This would therefore constitute a permitted grafting that carries *orlah* status and thus entitles the owner to return from battle.

### Vegetable Dispute

However, this case may itself be *harkavat issur* according to one opinion. A *baraita* records the dispute: Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel, in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Gamash of Kfar Akko, permits grafting a tree onto a vegetable; the Sages forbid it. According to the Sages, then, this would be a forbidden act, and the exemption derived from it would fall under *harkavat issur* rather than *harkavat heter*. According to Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel it is permitted, and in that case the branch retains its *orlah* status — since the vegetable host would never be subject to *orlah* — and the grafter would have a basis for returning from war.

### Stunted Trees

The *gemara* then shifts to a related discussion brought by Rav Dimi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. If a vine or tree is stunted, never growing more than a *tefach* in height, it is *chayav* in *orlah* for its entire life — *chayava b'orla kol shenoseha*. The reason is *d'michzi k'vas shata* — it always appears to be a one-year-old plant. Even if it is already five years old, observers will assume it is still within its first three years and therefore *orlah*, so it must always be treated as such to avoid causing others to sin. This ruling applies specifically when one has only a small stand of such stunted vines or trees — even a minimal *kerem* of five — because the configuration looks like a normal vineyard of young plants.

### Orchard Known

However, if one has an entire orchard of such stunted trees — *kula kerem* — the ruling changes. *Kala is lei* — the word gets out. Everyone in the area knows that this particular farmer has an unusual orchard of miniature trees. Since the reality is publicly known, there is no concern that observers will err, and the trees are not treated as perpetually in *orlah* status.

---

## Corpse Proximity

### Four Amos Rule

The *gemara* closes with one final tradition transmitted by Rav Dimi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov — collected here solely because it shares the same chain of transmission as the preceding rulings. *Meis tofes arba amos l'krias shema* — a corpse occupies four *amot* for the purpose of reciting *Shema*. One who is within four *amot* of a dead body may not recite *Shema*. The reason is the principle of *lo'eg l'rash chereif oseihu* — one who mocks the poor blasphemes his Maker — applied here to mean that reciting *Shema* in the presence of a *meis* who cannot himself fulfill the commandment is a form of mockery of the dead. This principle extends to other acts of religious observance as well.

---

---

# Sotah 44

## Meit Tofes Arba Amot

### Opening Statement

The daf opens in the middle of a statement transmitted by Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eleazar ben Yaakov: *meit tofes arba amot letumah* — that within four *amot* of a corpse, a person is considered *tamei*, this rule functioning as a mechanism to compel people to maintain distance from the dead.

### Chatzar HaKever

The Gemara marshals a corroborating teaching: *chatzar hakever* — the courtyard situated in front of a burial cave. If one stands in such a courtyard, *ha'omed betochah tahor* — he is *tahor*. The underlying rationale, as Rashi explains, is that the wall of the cave serves as a clear demarcation: a person standing in the courtyard can see exactly where the cave begins and therefore will not inadvertently enter the space of the dead. The qualifying condition is *vehu sheyiyu bah arba amot* — the courtyard must measure four *amot*. This minimum is not a distance requirement from the graves themselves but a size requirement for the courtyard as an independent space. If the courtyard is too small, it cannot be considered a genuinely separate domain, and one standing in it would effectively be considered co-located with the interior of the cave. This is the position of Beit Shammai.

### Beit Shammai v. Hillel

Beit Hillel disagrees, holding that *arbaah tefachim* suffice. Even a very small courtyard — provided it affords a person some place to stand — is adequate, since the wall itself provides the meaningful separation. The presence of the wall, on this view, does the primary halachic work, and the minimum size threshold can therefore be set much lower.

### Access Orientation

The Mishnah then introduces a distinction based on how one enters the courtyard: *bameh devarim amurim shepitchah milamalah* — when does the four-*amah* requirement apply? When the entrance to the courtyard is from above, meaning one must climb or drop down into the space. *Aval pitchah min hatzad, divrei hakol arba amot* — but if the entrance is from the side, then all opinions agree the courtyard must be four *amot*.

The Gemara immediately objects: *klapi laya* — this seems backwards. If entry is from the side — *madrik venafik* — one can navigate in and out smoothly without any part of the body passing over the cave. It is entry from above that is genuinely dangerous, since *iy efshar delo mayei* — it is virtually impossible to jump in and out without some part of one's body hovering over the burial space. The Gemara therefore reverses the ruling: the smaller size (*tefachim*) suffices when entry is from the side, because the risk of overhang is minimal; when entry is from above, the larger four-*amah* dimension is required so as to ensure the person can remain safely clear of the cave's interior space.

### Wall Demarcation

The Gemara draws the larger point together: *chatzar hakever, demisayma mechitzta* — the courtyard of a burial cave works because the wall is clearly delineated. One can see exactly where the boundary lies and stay clear of it. *Aval meit dealma, tefis* — but in the case of an ordinary corpse lying in an open space, there is no such demarcation, and the four-*amah* *tumah* zone takes hold automatically, compelling people to keep their distance. The proof from *chatzar hakever* is admittedly indirect — one might question whether the existence of a wall truly maps onto the rule of *meit tofes arba amot* — but the Gemara presents it as consistent with the principle: the extension of *tumah* to four *amot* functions precisely as a distancing mechanism in the absence of physical demarcation.

---

## Expansion Hermeneutics

### Who Betroths

Returning now to the *meshuach milchama* and the exemptions from military service, the Gemara takes up the phrase *mi ha'ish asher eiras isha* — "who is the man who betroths a woman." Just as the earlier sections expanded the categories of houses and vineyards beyond their most straightforward applications, so too the category of betrothal is subject to interpretive expansion.

### Betrothal Categories

*Tanu rabbanan*: *asher eiras* — "who betroths" — includes not only one who betroths a virgin (*betulah*), but also one who betroths a widow or divorcée, and even one whose connection to the woman is not through a formal act of *erusin* at all but through the bond of *yibum* — where a brother died and left a widow, making the surviving brother a *yavam* with an obligation to that woman.

### Multiple Brothers

Even more expansively: if five brothers fought together and one died in battle, having left a childless widow, all the remaining brothers return home — even though only one of them will ultimately perform *yibum*. Since at the time of departure any one of them might be the one to take her, all of them share the exemption. This holding is notable: the exemption attaches not to the certainty of the obligation but to the possibility of it.

### Forbidden Marriages

The phrase *velo lekacha* — "and did not take her" — functions as an exclusion. Just as the analogous phrases *velo chanacho* and *velo chilalo* excluded cases of *gezelah* or *issur* in earlier applications, so here the Torah excludes marriages that are halachically forbidden even while technically binding. The list includes: a widow (*almanah*) married to a *kohen gadol*, a divorced woman or *chalutzah* married to a regular *kohen*, a *mamzeret* or *netinah* married to an Israelite, and a daughter of Israel married to a *mamzer* or *natin*. In all these cases — unions that constitute a *lav* but where *kiddushin* nevertheless takes effect — the betrothed man does not receive the military exemption.

### Rabba's Transgression Ru…

This exclusion generates a *kushya*: given that Rabbi Yose HaGlili will say later that the *yarei verach halevav* — the fearful-hearted one — refers to someone who fears on account of *aveirot she'beyado*, sins presently in his possession, why do we need a special *pasuk* to exclude the man in a forbidden marriage? He has an *aveirah she'beyado* already! In the case of *gezelah* discussed earlier, the Gemara could say the person did *teshuvah* and repaid the theft, thereby clearing his slate. But here the man is still in the relationship — he cannot have rectified it without having divorced her. The *aveirah* should still be *beyado*. And yet the Gemara answers: *kiderabba* — this follows the view of Rabba.

Rabba holds: *le'olam eino chayav ad she'yiv'ol* — the man does not transgress at all until he actually consummates the union through *biah*. Although the *pesukim* governing *issurei kehunah* speak in the language of *kicha* — "taking," which sounds like *kiddushin* — Rabba maintains that the actual prohibition is only violated through the act of intercourse. His proof: the *pasuk* links *lo yikach* to *lo yechallel zaro be'amav* — the prohibition against "taking" is connected to the concern about desecrating his seed and altering her status. Neither of those consequences is possible without *biah*. Therefore: *mishum hachi eino lokeh ad she'yivol* — he is not flogged until *biah* has occurred. Prior to that act, whatever groundwork is being laid, no formal *aveirah* has yet been committed. This is why the *pasuk* of *velo lekacha* must explicitly exclude these cases — without it, since no *aveirah she'beyado* exists yet under Rabba's framework, they might otherwise qualify for the exemption.

Rashi notes that this point applies with even greater force to the case of *mamzer*, since the *pasuk lo yavo mamzer bikhal hashem* does not even employ the language of *kicha*. All of the *arayot* — the most severe forbidden relations, those carrying *karet* — are formulated exclusively in terms of *biah*, not *kiddushin*. It is specifically the *issurei kehunah* where the *pasuk* unusually employs the language of marriage-taking, and it is for that reason that Rabba's ruling is most needed there: even with language that sounds like *kiddushin*, the transgression only attaches at the point of *biah*.

A further point of interest arises in this context: there is a *machloket rishonim* about the converse scenario — a *kohen* who cohabits with a *gerushah* outside the context of *kiddushin* entirely. According to the Rambam, such a *kohen* is not *over* on *lo yikach*, since the prohibition technically requires both *kiddushin* and *biah* to be fully constituted. One might ask, finally, why a *kohen* is fighting in the army at all — a genuinely interesting question that warrants further analysis.

---

## Order of Life

### Torah's Derech Eretz

With the *halachot* of all three exemptions having been treated, the Gemara turns to a thematic reflection on the sequence in which the Torah presents them: *asher bana, asher nata, asher eiras* — who built, who planted, who betrothed. *Limdah Torah derech eretz* — the Torah is teaching the proper order of human life: first build a house, then plant a vineyard, then marry. The principle is that one should first establish the material capacity to support a family before undertaking the responsibility of one.

### Solomon's Wisdom

Shlomo expressed the same idea in his wisdom (Proverbs 24): *hachein bachutz melachtecha ve'atadah basadeh lach, achar u'vanita beisecha* — "Prepare your labor outside, ready it in the field, and afterward build your house." The peshat appears to counsel: first secure your livelihood and prepare your field, then establish your home. The Gemara proceeds to offer two *derashot* on this verse.

### Learning Stages

In the first interpretation: *hachein bachutz melachtecha* — prepare your labor outside — *zeh bayis*, this refers to building a house. *Ve'atadah basadeh lach* — prepare it in the field for yourself — *zeh karem*, this is the vineyard, one's source of livelihood. *Achar u'vanita beisecha* — afterward build your house — *zu isha*, this signifies marriage, since the Gemara equates *bayit* with *ishah*.

In the second interpretation — *davar acher* — the verse is read as a curriculum of Torah study: *hachein bachutz melachtecha* — *zeh mikra*, this is Scripture; *ve'atadah basadeh lach* — *zeh mishnah*, this is Mishnah; *achar u'vanita beisecha* — *zeh Gemara*, this is the study of Gemara. The point, made explicit by the Maharsha but already implicit in the Gemara, is that learning *mikra* and *mishnah* is preparatory groundwork — necessary stages, but ultimately in service of the genuine intellectual construction that is *talmud Gemara*. Just as one must first secure a livelihood and a house before starting a family, so one must traverse the prior stages of learning before engaging in the ultimate building, which is the *beit ne'eman* of Gemara study.

### Three Stages

A third reading — another *davar acher* — reframes the structure: *hachein bachutz melachtecha* — *zeh mikra u'mishnah*, Scripture and Mishnah together constitute stage one; *ve'atadah basadeh lach* — *zeh Gemara*, the study of Gemara is stage two; *achar u'vanita beisecha* — *eilu ma'asim tovim*, this is good deeds. On this reading, the ultimate goal beyond even the study of Gemara is the *ma'asim tovim* to which it should give rise — the classic question of whether the telos of Torah learning is the learning itself or the action it generates.

### Rabbi Eliezer View

Rabbi Eliezer, son of Rabbi Yose HaGlili, offers yet a fourth reading. For him, all of *mikra*, *mishnah*, and *Gemara* together constitute stage one — *hachein bachutz melachtecha*. Stage two — *ve'atadah basadeh lach* — is *ma'asim tovim*. And the culminating stage three — *achar u'vanita beisecha* — is *derosh u'kabel sachar*: theoretical analysis, for which one receives reward. This phrase, *derosh u'kabel sachar*, is typically invoked in contexts where a *pasuk* is being explained as existing purely for theoretical derivation without practical application — such as the case of *ben sorer u'moreh*. What does it mean here as the highest stage? The Maharsha understands it as *chochmah iyunit* — speculative philosophical wisdom, as distinct from the *chochmah* of Gemara study per se. The Rambam's *Moreh Nevuchim* offers the clearest framework: the entire structure of *mitzvot*, learning, and *ma'asim tovim* exists to cultivate sound character, a stable society, and disciplined intellect — all so that one may ultimately dedicate oneself to pure theoretical knowledge of God. That is the *derosh* — the pure contemplation — that constitutes the final, highest *bayit*.

It is worth noting that the three things invoked in these interpretations — Torah, *chuppah*, and *ma'asim tovim* — are the very same trio mentioned at a *brit milah*: *keshem she'nichnas la'brit kein yikanes le'Torah u'le'chupah u'le'ma'asim tovim*.

---

## Non-Returners

### Gatehouse Exception

The Mishnah turns to those who do *not* return from the front lines: among them is one who built only a *beit sha'ar* — a gatehouse — which does not constitute a true dwelling. The *Tanna* adds: if a man tore down his house and rebuilt it according to its original specifications, he does not return. However, *im hosif bo dimus echad, chozer* — if he added even a single row of bricks, departing even slightly from the original plan, he does return. Rabbi Eliezer adds: even one who built a *beit levenim* — a house of bricks — in the Sharon region would not return, because *mipnei shemechadeshin oto paamayim beshavua* — such structures require rebuilding twice every seven years, rendering the house insufficiently permanent to qualify as a stable dwelling.

### Full Completion

A separate and stronger category is *ve'elu she'einam zazim mimkomam* — those who do not even move from their position to provide support services. This category is derived from the *pasuk* concerning the newly married man: *lo yeitzei batzava velo yaavor alav lechol davar* — he shall not go out to the army and shall not be tasked with any matter. The expansion of this complete exemption to the cases of the house and vineyard requires that those cases have reached culmination: the house must have been dedicated (*chancho*), the vineyard must have reached its fourth year (*chillelo*), and the wife must have been fully married (*lekachah*).

---

## Complete Exemption

### New Wife Definition

*Tanu rabbanan*: the *pasuk* states *ki yikach ish ishah chadashah* — when a man takes a new wife — *lo yeitzei batzava velo yaavor alav lechol davar, naki yihyeh leveiso shanah achat veshimach et ishto asher lakach* — he shall be free for his home for one year and shall gladden the wife he has taken. The Gemara asks: *ein li ela ishah chadashah* — I only know this applies to a new wife. What of a widow or divorcée who has been married before? *Talmud lomar ishah, mikol makom* — the broader word *ishah* includes all women. Then: *im kein mah talmud lomar ishah chadashah* — if so, what is the point of the word *chadashah*? The answer: *ishah chadashah lo* — new to *him*. This serves to exclude *perat lemachazir gerushato* — a man who remarries his own divorcée; since she is not new to him, the full exemption does not apply.

### No Support Services

*Lo yaavor alav lechol davar* — he shall not be put to any service whatsoever. One might have thought the exemption is only from frontline combat while logistical support duties — supplying water, food, and maintaining roads — remain obligatory. The *pasuk* therefore adds *lechol davar* to indicate that not even auxiliary military service may be demanded of him.

### Culmination Requirement

Conversely, one might think the complete exemption — release from all army-related duty — should extend also to the person who built a house but did not yet dedicate it, or who planted a vineyard but did not yet reach the fourth year, or who betrothed a woman but did not yet marry her. The *pasuk* responds: *alav* — *velo yaavor alav lechol davar* — *alav iy atah maavir*, only upon *him*, upon the one who has reached full culmination, do you impose no obligation whatsoever. *Aval atah maavir al acherim* — but those in the preliminary stages are subject to support duties, even though they are exempt from frontline combat.

### Two Lavin

Why does the *pasuk* state both *lo yeitzei batzava* and *velo yaavor alav lechol davar*, given that once any obligation to support is removed, the prohibition against frontline service should be self-evident? The answer: *laavor alav bishnei lavin* — to teach that if such a man does go out to fight, he has transgressed two separate *lavin*. Whether this prohibition runs against the army authorities for sending him or against the man himself for going is an interesting question — though the language of *lo yeitzei* and *lo yaavor* does suggest personal prohibition, not merely entitlement. The Rambam's formulation in *Hilchot Melachim* (7:11) confirms: if the man provides water, food, or road service, or stands guard at the wall, or contributes in any capacity to the army's function throughout that year, *lo ya'avor alav shum davar ba'olam* — he violates *lo yeitzei* and *lo yaavor*, two *lavin*.

Two additional questions merit further attention: whether the man in the preliminary categories (*lo chancho*, *lo chillelo*, *lo lekachah*) can waive his exemption from frontline duty, and the underlying question of why a *kohen* would be fighting in the army at all — a point flagged earlier that remains unresolved and worth examining in the *Sefer Minchat Chinuch*.

---

## Hayrei Verach Halevav

### Rabbi Akiva Simple

The Torah commands: *veyasfu hashotrim ledaber el ha'am* — and the officers shall continue to speak to the people — and then introduces the case of *ha'yarei verach halevav*, the fearful and tender-hearted. Rabbi Akiva reads this straightforwardly, *kemashmao* — as it sounds: a person who is genuinely afraid, *she'eino yachol la'amod bekishrei milchama* — who cannot hold his place in the battle formation when soldiers bind together into a fighting unit — *velirot cherev shlufa* — and who cannot bear to face a drawn sword. According to Rashi, *kishrei milchama* refers to the moment when soldiers lock together to form a human wall or phalanx.

### R. Yose HaGlili Sin-Based

Rabbi Yose HaGlili disagrees, interpreting *ha'yarei verach halevav* as *ze hamityare me'aveirot she'beyado* — the one who fears on account of the sins presently in his possession. It is not physical fear of battle that the Torah addresses here but a consciousness of moral vulnerability: the awareness that one's sins have diminished one's merit and left one exposed on the battlefield.

### Divine Cover

*Ulfichach taltah lo hatorah et kol elu sheyachazor biglalan* — it is for this reason that the Torah provided all these other exemptions — the house, the vineyard, the wife — so that the person who must return on account of his *aveirot she'beyado* could do so without publicly disclosing the real reason. He can go back in the company of those who have built houses or betrothed wives, and no one need know that his departure is motivated by sin-fear rather than any qualifying material circumstance. This raises a striking implication embedded in the word *lefichach* — as if to say the Torah's entire framework of practical exemptions exists, at least in part, to provide cover for the *aveira*-bearing soldier. On this reading, there is no misrepresentation involved in availing oneself of a legitimate exemption even when one's actual motivation is different.

Rabbi Akiva, notably, is the one advancing the *pshat* reading here.

### R. Yose Addition

Rabbi Yose adds: *almanah lekohen gadol, gerushah vechalutzah lekohen hedyot, mamzeret unetinah leyisrael, bat yisrael lemamzer ulenatin* — all the cases of forbidden marriage discussed above — *harei hu ha'yarei verach halevav*. These men, too, fall under the category of the fearful-hearted, since their sin-laden situation makes them spiritually vulnerable. The Gemara had noted earlier that these cases seemingly present no *aveira she'beyado* under Rabba's framework (since the transgression only attaches at *biah*); Rabbi Yose is apparently disagreeing and treating the forbidden betrothal itself as an ongoing *aveirah she'beyado*.

The question of how Rabbi Yose differs from Rabbi Yose HaGlili in this regard is taken up directly: *ika beiniyahu aveira de-rabbanan* — the distinction lies in whether Rabbinic violations also qualify. Rabbi Yose HaGlili, who spoke in general terms of any *aveirot she'beyado*, would include even Rabbinic transgressions. Rabbi Yose gave specific examples that are all Biblical prohibitions, which suggests he would not extend the category to *aveirot de-rabbanan*. The Gemara confirms this by asking *keman azla* — according to whom is the *baraita* that teaches: one who speaks between the *tefillin shel yad* and the *tefillin shel rosh* has an *aveirah beyado* and returns from the battle array? The answer: this goes according to Rabbi Yose HaGlili, who extends the principle even to Rabbinic violations. Similarly, the Gemara asks the same question regarding the *baraita* that teaches: one who heard the sound of trumpets and trembled, heard the clashing of shields and trembled, heard the clashing of swords, and lost control of his bladder — *chozer* — he too must return. *Leima Rabbi Akiva hi* — perhaps this goes only according to Rabbi Akiva, who makes the category about simple physical fear? The Gemara answers: no, even Rabbi Yose HaGlili would agree in that extreme case, *mishum de'ksiv velo yimas levav achiv k'levavo* — because the Torah explicitly prohibits the melting of one's fellow soldier's heart; at that degree of visible fear, even Rabbi Yose HaGlili concedes the man must depart lest he infect the rest of the army.

---

## Officers & Deterrence

### Officer Placement

*Vahaya kechalot hashotrim ledaber el ha'am* — after the officers finish speaking — *upakdu sarei tzevaot berosh ha'am* — officers are appointed at the head of the force. The Gemara adds *ube'akeivo* — and also at the rear: *ma'amidin zekifim lifnehem ve'acherim me'achareihem* — they station strong officers both in front of the troops and behind them.

### Iron Staffs

*Vekashilin shel barzel beyadeihem* — and in their hands are iron implements — whether staffs, blades, or some form of weapon. The purpose: *vechol hamevakesh lachazor, hareshut beyado lekapeach et shokav* — anyone who seeks to retreat, it is within the officers' authority to cut him down at the knees. The rationale is the principle: *techilat nifila nisa* — the beginning of falling in battle is flight. The first instinct under fire is to turn and run; armies throughout history have recognized that the most dangerous moment is when soldiers begin to flee. The fear of the consequences of desertion must outweigh the fear of advancing into battle.

### Philistine Wars

The scriptural proof comes from two *pesukim* juxtaposed in the Gemara: *nass Yisrael lifnei Plishtim vegam mageifa gedolah haytah ba'am* — Israel fled before the Philistines and there was a great blow among the people; and *vayanusu anshei Yisrael mipnei Plishtim vayiplu chalalim* — they fled before the Philistines and fell as corpses. The pairing demonstrates the causal chain: flight *is* the beginning of slaughter.

---

## War Categories

### Discretionary v. Obligat…

*Bameh devarim amurim* — when do all these exemptions apply? According to Rabbi Yose HaGlili: in a *milchemet reshut*, a discretionary war. *Aval bemilchemet mitzvah, hakol yotzim* — but in an obligatory *mitzvah* war, all go out, without exemption. The paradigmatic example Rashi gives of a *milchemet mitzvah* is *kibush Eretz Yisrael bimei Yehoshua* — the conquest of the Land in the days of Joshua. The Rambam includes also *milchemet Amalek* and defensive wars — *lehoshia et Yisrael miyad tzar* — wars to rescue Israel from an attacking enemy.

### R. Y. HaGlili Discretion…

In a *milchemet reshut*, the exemptions operate fully, and those with unfinished houses, undedicated vineyards, and recent betrothals return home.

### Rabbi Yehuda Obligatory

Rabbi Yehuda frames the same dichotomy with different terminology: *bameh devarim amurim bemilchemet mitzvah* — when do the exemptions apply? In a *mitzvah* war. *Aval bemilchemet chovah, hakol yotzim afilu chatan mechedro vechallah mechupatah* — but in a *chovah* war, all go out, even the groom from his chamber and the bride from her canopy.

### Terminology Equivalence

The Gemara clarifies: are these two *tannaim* actually debating, or merely using different vocabulary for the same categories? Rabbi Yochanan states: *reshut de'rabbanan zu hi mitzvah de'Rabbi Yehuda* — what the *Rabbanan* call *reshut* is what Rabbi Yehuda calls *mitzvah*. *Mitzvah de'rabbanan zu hi chovah de'Rabbi Yehuda* — what the *Rabbanan* call *mitzvah* is what Rabbi Yehuda calls *chovah*. On this reading, the categories are substantively identical; the dispute is purely terminological.

### Three War Levels

Rava sharpens the analysis by introducing a tripartite framework. *Milchemet Yehoshua lichbosh — divrei hakol chovah*: the war of Joshua to conquer the Land is universally placed in the highest category. *Milchemet beit David l'rivachah — divrei hakol reshut*: expansionary wars fought by David and his successors for enlargement of territory are universally placed in the lowest category. The contested middle ground is preemptive war — *lema'utei ovdei kochavim delo leisu aleihu* — striking against enemy nations before they launch an attack. For such a war, *mar kari lei mitzvah umar kari lei reshut*: one authority calls it *mitzvah*, the other calls it *reshut*.

This is a striking Gemara. In terms of halachic outcome — whether the exemptions apply — both opinions agree: a preemptive war is not in the highest (*chovah*) category, so the exemptions for the newly built house, the vineyard, and the betrothed woman are all operative. The argument between them is not about the exemptions at all. Both the *Tanna Kamma* calling it *reshut* and Rabbi Yehuda calling it *mitzvah* agree that it is not *chovah* and thus the exemptions stand. This can be laid out concisely:

The *Tanna Kamma* operates with two levels — *reshut* and *mitzvah*. Rabbi Yehuda operates with two levels — *mitzvah* and *chovah*. Rabbi Yochanan equates these: the *Tanna Kamma*'s *reshut* = Rabbi Yehuda's *mitzvah*; the *Tanna Kamma*'s *mitzvah* = Rabbi Yehuda's *chovah*. In both systems, the lower level carries the exemptions; the upper level sends everyone to battle. Everyone agrees that Joshua's conquest belongs in the upper level and expansionary wars belong in the lower level. The preemptive war falls in the lower level for both — they simply name it differently.

### Nifka Mina

The practical implication of calling a preemptive war a *mitzvah* rather than a *reshut* is not about the exemptions but about an entirely different halachic principle: *osek bemitzvah patur min hamitzvah* — one engaged in a *mitzvah* is exempt from other *mitzvot*. If a preemptive war is classified as a *mitzvah*, then a soldier engaged in it need not interrupt his duties to perform other obligations — he would not be required to don *tefillin*, take a *lulav*, or fulfill other *mitzvot* during the campaign. If it is merely *reshut*, no such exemption applies. The *nafka mina* between the *Tanna Kamma* and Rabbi Yehuda on the question of preemptive war thus surfaces here: not in who fights, but in what obligations are suspended for those who do.

---

## Eglah Arufah Intro

### Opening Mishnah

With the conclusion of the discussion of *milchama*, the Gemara opens the final *perek* of the tractate with the *mitzvah* of *eglah arufah* — the decapitated heifer performed in response to an unsolved murder. When a corpse is discovered and the killer is unknown, the Torah prescribes a ritual in which the *zekanim* come forth and make the declaration: *yadeinu lo shafchu et hadam hazeh* — our hands did not shed this blood. This declaration is in *lashon hakodesh*, as the Gemara will address. The governing *pasuk* is *ki yimatze challal ba'adamah... veyatzu zekenecha veshoftecha*.

### Three v. Five

*Sheloshah mibeit din hagadol shebiyerushalayim hayu yotzin* — three representatives from the Great Sanhedrin of Jerusalem would go out. The *zekanim* referred to in the *pasuk* are not merely the elders of the local city but the elders of the entire nation — representatives of the central court. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *chamishah* — five are required. His derivation: *zekenecha* — your elders (plural, implying at least two) — *veshoftecha* — your judges (plural, implying at least two more) — totals four. *Ve'ein beit din shakul* — and since a *beit din* must have an odd number to avoid a deadlock, *mosifin aleihem od echad* — one more is added, yielding five.

### Disqualifying Scenarios

Certain circumstances disqualify the *eglah arufah* ritual altogether. *Nimtza tamun begal* — if the corpse was found buried under a heap of stones; *o talui be'ilan* — or hanging from a tree; *o tzaf al penei hamayim* — or floating on the surface of water — *lo hayu orfin*, the ritual is not performed. The *pasuk* requires *challal ba'adamah* — fallen on the ground: exposed on the ground (*lo tamun begal*), fallen rather than suspended (*lo talui be'ilan*), and on the ground rather than floating (*lo tzaf al penei hamayim*).

### Proximity & Beit Din

Additionally, if the corpse was found near a border city (*samuch le'sfar*), or near a city whose majority population is non-Jewish (*rubah ovdei kochavim*), or near a city that lacks a functioning *beit din* (*she'ein bah beit din*) — *lo hayu orfin*, the ritual is not performed. The measurement to determine which city is closest is conducted only with respect to cities that have a *beit din*: *ein modedin ela le'ir sheyesh bah beit din*. The significance of the local *beit din* here — distinct from the Great Sanhedrin representatives who come from Jerusalem — reflects the role of *ziknei ha'ir hahi*, the elders of that particular city, as participants in the ritual alongside the central court emissaries. The Gemara will elaborate on all of these requirements, and the discussion of *eglah arufah* will continue in the next session.

---

---

# Sotah 45

## Egla Arufah Overview

### Opening & Context

The final *perek* of *Sotah* turns to *egla arufa*, the ritual of the beheaded calf performed when a murder victim is found and the killer cannot be identified. Like the *sota* procedure, *egla arufa* involves an unresolved situation — in the case of *sota*, it is uncertainty about whether a woman committed adultery; here, the act of murder is known but the perpetrator is not. The *mishna* establishes that the declaration made by the elders over the calf must be recited in *lashon hakodesh*, and it cites the verse *ki yimatzei chalal* as its source. The *gemara*, however, immediately asks: *mai ka'amar*? What is the *mishna* actually saying? The verse *ki yimatzei chalal* does not appear to contain any indication that the declaration is made in Hebrew.

### Abbahu's V'anu V'amru

Rabbi Abbahu resolves the difficulty. The *mishna*'s citation of *ki yimatzei chalal* is not the source for the Hebrew-language requirement — that source is derived elsewhere, through a *gezerah shavah* based on the phrase *v'anu v'amru*. The verse in the *egla arufa* passage reads *v'anu v'amru: yadeinu lo shafchu es hadam hazeh* — "they shall respond and say: our hands did not spill this blood." The same linguistic formula, *v'anu v'amru*, appears in the context of the blessings and curses on *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eval*, where the *Levi'im* respond and say — a context already established as requiring *lashon hakodesh*. The parallel phrasing creates the equation: just as the response there is in Hebrew, so too here. The *mishna*'s citation of *ki yimatzei chalal* is therefore not addressing the language requirement at all.

### Procedure & Measurement

Rather, the *mishna* is introducing the procedure of *egla arufa* — *seder egla arufa keitzad*. The verse *ki yimatzei chalal ba'adamah v'yatzu zkeinecha v'shoftecha u'madadu svivos hachalal* describes how the elders and judges go out and measure around the corpse to determine which city is nearest. The *mishna* teaches that *shlosha mibeis din hagadol shebiYerushalayim hayu yotzin* — three representatives from the central *beis din* in Jerusalem would go out to perform this measurement. It is these central figures who are identified by the words *zkeinecha v'shoftecha*, not the *ziknei ha'ir*, the elders of the nearby city, who come later to perform the actual ritual once the measurement has established which city is closest.

---

## Three vs. Five Dispute

### Initial Positions

The *mishna* states that three representatives go out, but Rabbi Yehuda says five. A *braita* sets out the reasoning behind each position. The word *zkeinecha*, "your elders," is in the plural, indicating a minimum of two. The word *v'shoftecha*, "and your judges," likewise indicates two. But a *beis din* cannot have an even number — it requires an odd number to allow for a deciding vote and to structurally represent judicial authority. Therefore, one more is added: *masifin aleihem od echad harei kan chamisha* — that gives five, in the view of Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Shimon, identified as the *tanna kamma* of the *mishna*, holds three: he counts only from *zkeinecha*, yielding two, and adds one to make an odd number.

### Zkeinecha Analysis

The *gemara* presses Rabbi Shimon: the verse explicitly says *v'shoftecha* — what does he do with that word? The answer is that Rabbi Shimon reads *v'shoftecha* not as adding to the count but as identifying the character of those going out — *l'meyuchadim shebishoftecha*, the distinguished ones among your judges, meaning the central court, the *beis din hagadol*. The word tells you *who*, not *how many*.

Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, draws the identification of the *beis din hagadol* from a different source — the possessive form *zkeinecha* itself, which he parses in two stages. Had the Torah written simply *ziknei*, one might have thought this meant any elderly men found in the marketplace; the possessive "yours" signals that these are men of judicial standing. But even knowing they are judges, one might have assumed a local *beis din* — a *sanhedrei ktana* of twenty-three — suffices. The additional word *v'shoftecha* then clarifies that it must be the *hamiyuchadin shebishoftecha*, the most distinguished among your judges, meaning the *beis din hagadol*. Since Rabbi Yehuda uses *v'shoftecha* for this qualitative identification, he needs another mechanism to arrive at the count of five.

### Rabbi Yehuda Source

The *gemara* considers whether Rabbi Yehuda could learn both the identity of the *beis din hagadol* and the number five from *ziknei ha'eidah*, the verse in *Vayikra* concerning the *sanhedrin* that rules erroneously and must bring a special *korban*. From that context Rabbi Yehuda derives that only five members of the *beis din hagadol* need to be present — not the entire court. The *gemara* suggests that if Rabbi Yehuda learns both identity and number from that source, he would have no need to use *v'shoftecha* for numerical purposes at all. This challenge is acknowledged and the reasoning is refined accordingly.

### Vav Analysis

The *gemara* resolves the matter by focusing on the conjunction *vav* at the beginning of *v'shoftecha*. Had the verse read *zkeinecha shoftecha* — without the connecting *vav* — it would read naturally as an appositive: "your elders who are your judges," a single group described in two ways, yielding no additional count. The extra *vav* signals that *v'shoftecha* is to be counted as a distinct unit, adding two more to the two of *zkeinecha*, and requiring one more for an odd number — hence five. *V'shoftecha l'minyana*. Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, does not derive significant weight from the additional *vav*, and therefore holds three.

The *gemara* also considers whether the plural verbs *v'yatzu* ("and they shall go out") and *u'madadu* ("and they shall measure") should independently add to the count — potentially yielding nine for Rabbi Yehuda or seven for Rabbi Shimon. The answer is that those verbs are needed for their own teaching, as derived from a *braita*: *hen v'lo shlucheihen* — they themselves must go out, not send proxies, and *she'afillu nimtza ba'alil la'ir* — even if it is obvious which city is nearest, they are still required to measure, because *shemitzvah la'asok bemedidah*, the act of measurement is itself part of the *mitzvah*.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer Position

### Eliezer's Interpretation

The *gemara* notes that the *mishna* is not in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, as a *braita* teaches. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov reads the verse entirely differently: *zkeinecha zo sanhedrin* — "your elders" refers to the full *sanhedrin*; *shoftecha ze melech v'kohen gadol* — "and your judges" refers to the king and the *kohen gadol*. The textual support for each: the king is called *shofet* from the verse *melech bemishpat ya'amid aretz*, the king upholds the land through justice; the *kohen gadol* is likewise included under *shoftecha* from the verse *u'vata el hakohanim haleviyim v'el hashofet asher yihyeh bayamim hahem*.

### National Responsibility

This interpretation carries profound weight. It is already striking that when a body is found in some remote location, representatives of the highest court in the land must travel out to measure and identify the nearest city. But Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov takes this further: not only the *sanhedrin*, but the political leader and the religious leader of the entire nation must become involved. The reason lies in the nature of the ritual itself. A murder has occurred and gone unresolved — the killer has not been identified, justice has not been served, and the verse speaks of *v'nitchaper lahem hadam*, an expiation for the blood. The principle that *la'aretz lo yechuppar badam asher shupach bah ki im bedam shofcho* — the land cannot be fully atoned for without justice being done — means that this unresolved guilt operates at a national level. There is a murderer somewhere at large; responsibility for that has not been discharged. The entire national leadership — the courts, the king representing civil order, the *kohen gadol* representing divine law — must together take ownership of that failure. It is not simply that a crime occurred, which would be handled locally; it is that a crime occurred and was never resolved, and that demands a national response.

### Entire Sanhedrin Query

The *gemara* raises the further question: when Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says *zkeinecha zo sanhedrin*, does he mean only that *sanhedrin* representatives — three or five, as debated by Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda — must participate, with his dispute being only about the addition of the king and *kohen gadol*? Or does he mean the entire *sanhedrin* must go out? The phrasing *zkeinecha zo sanhedrin* seems to suggest the whole body, which would be consistent with the overarching theme of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position — that the entire national leadership must assume communal ownership of this unresolved murder. The question is left open for the *gemara* to resolve.

---

## Zaken Mamre Analogy

### Zaken Mamre Setup

Rav Yosef introduces a proof from the laws of *zaken mamrei*, the rebellious elder. If an elder of sufficient standing disputed a ruling of the central court, received their ruling against him, returned to his community, and continued to teach and rule in accordance with his own position, he is liable as a *zaken mamrei*. The case the *gemara* presents is: *matza zakein mamrei abei pagi v'himrah aleihem* — he encountered the *sanhedrin* not in the *lishkas ha-gazis*, their official chamber in the *beis hamikdash*, but in the *abei pagi*, the environs or surroundings of Jerusalem outside that chamber, and he voiced his dissenting position there. The question: *yachol tehei hamraso hamraah* — could that constitute actionable rebellion?

The answer is no, because the verse introducing *zaken mamrei* reads *v'kamta v'alisa el ha-makom asher yivchar*, you shall arise and ascend to the place that God has chosen — *melamed she-ha-makom goreim*, the place determines the law. Only when the court is sitting in their designated location does the confrontation carry the full weight of divine authority necessary to make defiance of their ruling a capital offense.

### Why They Left

This raises a critical question: for the *sanhedrin* to have been found outside the *lishkas ha-gazis* — which this scenario assumes — why were they there? The *gemara* cites the verse *sarech agan ha-sohar al yechsar ha-mazeg* from *Shir HaShirim*, understood as a metaphor for the *sanhedrin*. Rashi explains that the image of a round goblet corresponds to the *sanhedrin*'s semicircular seating arrangement. From the phrase *al yechsar ha-mazeg* — "the mixed wine shall not be lacking" — the *gemara* derives a rule: if any member of the *sanhedrin* needs to leave, it is permitted only if twenty-three members remain, corresponding to a full *sanhedrei ktana* capable of adjudicating capital cases. The proportion of twenty-three out of seventy-one approximates a one-to-three ratio, paralleling the one-to-three wine-to-water dilution of mixed wine.

Now, could the *sanhedrin* have left their chamber for a *dvar reshus*, an ordinary non-*mitzvah* purpose? The *gemara* concludes they could not have — at minimum, the scenario of the *zaken mamrei* encountering the entire court outside implies that the whole *sanhedrin* had left, and the entire *sanhedrin* cannot leave for a *dvar reshus*. They must have had a *mitzvah* purpose. What *mitzvah* purpose would bring the entire *sanhedrin* outside? *Lav lemedidat egla* — is it not for the measurement of the *egla arufa*? This, the *gemara* suggests, must be the position of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: that the entire *sanhedrin* goes out for the measurement, consistent with his view that *zkeinecha zo sanhedrin* means the full court.

Abaye challenges this inference: there is another *mitzvah* purpose for which the entire *sanhedrin* is required outside the chamber — the expansion of the sanctified boundaries of Jerusalem or the *azarot* of the *beis hamikdash*, as the *mishna* teaches, *ein mosifin al ha-ir v'al ha-azarot ela be-veis din shel shivim v'echad* — such expansion requires all seventy-one members. So the *zaken mamrei* scenario does not uniquely point to *egla arufa*; the *sanhedrin* might have left for boundary expansion. The question of whether Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov requires the entire *sanhedrin* for *egla arufa* therefore remains unresolved from this reasoning alone.

### Baraita Egla Evidence

A *braita* is then cited in support of Rav Yosef's original position: *tanya kevateih d'Rav Yosef*. The *braita* itself states — *matzan beis pagi v'himrah aleihem* — that if the *zaken* found the *sanhedrin* outside the *beis hamikdash* and rebelled against them, *kegon she-yatzu li-medidat egla o le-hosif al ha-ir v'al ha-azarot* — as for example when they went out for the measurement of the *egla* or to add to the city or the *azarot* — he is nevertheless not a *zaken mamrei*, since the verse requires that the confrontation occur in their designated place.

The significance of this *braita* is that it explicitly lists the measurement of *egla arufa* as a legitimate reason for the *sanhedrin* to be found outside — not as the only reason, but as a named scenario. And this scenario is coherent only on the view of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who holds that the entire *sanhedrin* participates in the *egla arufa* measurement. On the views of Rabbi Shimon or Rabbi Yehuda, where only three or five representatives go out, the remaining *sanhedrin* members would have no reason to leave the *lishkas ha-gazis*. The *braita* thus provides strong support that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov requires the full court, consistent with his broader vision of total national leadership assuming responsibility for unresolved murder.

---

## Body Conditions

### Chalal Definition

The *mishna* and accompanying *baraita* enumerate the conditions under which a body qualifies for *egla arufa*: it must be a *chalal*, understood as one killed by a sword (*be-chalal cherev*) and not merely strangled (*v'lo chanuk*); it must be fully still and not still convulsing on the ground (*v'lo mefarper ba-adamah*); it must not be buried under a pile (*v'lo tamun be-gal*); and it must be lying fallen on the ground (*nofel ba-adamah*) rather than suspended from a tree (*v'lo talui be-ilan*). The body must also be found in a field (*ba-sadeh*) and not floating on water (*v'lo tzaf al penei ha-mayim*).

### Tamun & Tzaf
