The *gemara* asks whether the *mishna*'s requirement that the body be exposed — not buried and not suspended — reflects the position of Rabbi Yehuda specifically, as against the *rabbanan*. The comparison is to the laws of *shichcha*, the forgotten sheaf: the verse *ki tikzor ketzircha besadecha v'shachachta omer basadeh* — when you harvest your field and forget a sheaf in the field — is the basis for *shichcha*. There, a *braita* records that the word *basadeh* is interpreted by Rabbi Yehuda as *perat le-tamun* — excluding a sheaf that is buried; whereas the *rabbanan* say *basadeh le-rabot et ha-tamun* — including even a buried sheaf within the laws of *shichcha*.

If so, the *mishna*'s apparent exclusion of a buried body from *egla arufa* sounds like Rabbi Yehuda. Rav responds: *afilu teima Rabbanan* — even the *rabbanan* could agree that the body must be exposed, because the derivation in each case depends on its own contextual logic. By *egla arufa*, the verse reads *ki yimatzei chalal ba'adamah* — "if a corpse is found on the ground." Before reaching the word *ba'adamah*, one would have assumed inclusively that the corpse could be found anywhere. The word *ba'adamah* therefore comes to narrow — *perat le-tamun*, excluding what is buried. The direction of the derivation is from broad to narrow.

By *shichcha*, the context is different. The verse reads *ki tikzor ketzircha* — your harvest — and then *v'shachachta*. The act of forgetting is juxtaposed to the act of cutting, and just as cutting involves grain that is exposed and visible, so too forgetting in that context initially suggests an exposed sheaf — narrow from the outset. The word *basadeh* then comes to broaden — *le-rabot et ha-tamun* — including even a buried sheaf. Each derivation responds to its own starting assumption, and the parallel positions by *shichcha* do not necessarily map onto *egla arufa*.

### Sheaves Analogy

The *gemara* then develops the *shichcha* analysis further. If the juxtaposition of forgetting to cutting already suggests that only an exposed sheaf qualifies — which is what Rabbi Yehuda holds — then why does he need the word *basadeh* to tell him so? The *gemara* answers: Rabbi Yehuda uses *basadeh* for a different purpose — *le-rabot shikchat kama*, to include the case of standing grain (*kama*) that has not yet been cut. If someone forgets unharvested grain still standing in the field, that too is *shichcha*. The word *besadecha* — "in your field" — teaches that even grain still *in* the field, not yet harvested, is subject to *shichcha*.

The *rabbanan*, who use *basadeh* to include buried sheaves, derive the inclusion of *shikchat kama* differently — from the juxtaposition *besadecha v'shachachta*, the very collocation of "your field" and "you forgot" suggesting that forgetting pertains to whatever remains *in* your field, including standing grain. Conversely, the *rabbanan* derive the exclusion of sheaves that flew into a neighbor's field — *perat le-shetzafu omarim le-toch sadeh chaveiro* — from the possessive *besadecha*, your field, not your neighbor's. Rabbi Yehuda, who does not place the same weight on the possessive, gets this exclusion from the juxtaposition rather than the possessive form.

### Tamun Resolution

Having worked through those exegetical debates, the *gemara* circles back to the question of *min b'mino* — whether being buried or suspended under an object of the same type affects the determination of *tamun* or *tzaf*. A *baraita* discusses the case of a sheaf that was picked up to be carried to the city, placed on top of a fellow sheaf, and then forgotten. The *tanna kamma* rules: *hatachton shichcha v'ha-elyon eino shichcha* — the bottom sheaf is *shichcha*, the top is not. Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon says both are exempt: *ha-tachton mipnei she-hu tamun*, the bottom because it is buried, *v'ha-elyon mipnei she-hu tzaf*, the top because it is floating.

The *gemara* initially assumes that both *tannaim* agree with Rabbi Yehuda that *tamun* creates an exemption for *shichcha*, and that their debate is specifically about *min b'mino* — whether being buried under a similar object (another sheaf) counts as *tamun*. On this reading, Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda holds that *min b'mino havei tamun*, while the *tanna kamma* holds it does not.

The *gemara* rejects this reading. If both agreed that *tamun* is an exemption, everyone would agree that being buried under another sheaf constitutes *tamun*, since that is clearly a form of burial. The more defensible reading is that they are not debating the definition of *tamun* at all — they are debating whether *tamun* creates any exemption from *shichcha* in the first place. The *tanna kamma* holds like the *rabbanan* — buried sheaves are still subject to *shichcha* — while Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda holds like his father Rabbi Yehuda — buried sheaves are exempt. The scenario involving one sheaf on top of another is chosen not to illustrate the minimum threshold of what counts as *tamun*, but to highlight the full scope of Rabbi Yehuda's position: *odi'acha kocho d'Rabbi Yehuda*, to show that even burial under a similar object — *min b'mino* — constitutes *tamun* in his view.

---

## Exposure & Location

### Nofel Ba'adamah

As enumerated in the *baraita*, the body qualifying for *egla arufa* must be *nofel ba'adamah* — fallen and lying on the ground. If it is buried under a pile (*tamun be-gal*) or suspended from a tree (*taluy be-ilan*), the obligation does not apply. These requirements parallel, in their structure, the *tamun* and *tzaf* conditions explored in the *shichcha* discussion, though as demonstrated above, the derivations for *egla arufa* and *shichcha* proceed from different contextual starting points and cannot simply be read across from one to the other.

---

## Stacked Corpses

### Problem Statement

Abaye, in a moment of confident self-assessment — declaring *hareini k'Ben Azai b'shukei Tveria*, I am ready to take on any question as Ben Azai was in the marketplaces of Tiberias — is challenged by Rabbah bar Abba with the following problem: *shenei chalalim zeh al gabei zeh* — two corpses, one lying on top of the other. *Meihechan hu moded* — from which one does one measure for the purposes of *egla arufa*, and does either, or both, or neither qualify for the ritual?

### Min B'Mino Issue

The question unfolds into multiple possibilities. Does one say *min b'mino havei tamun* — that being under another corpse counts as buried — such that the bottom corpse is excluded, while *min b'mino lavei tzaf* — being on top of another corpse does not count as suspended — leaving the top corpse as the qualified one, and one measures from it? Or conversely, *min b'mino havei tzaf* — the top one is considered suspended — but *min b'mino lavei tamun* — the bottom one is not considered buried — leaving the bottom as the qualified one? Or *min b'mino havei tamun u'min b'mino havei tzaf* — both determinations apply — leaving neither corpse qualifying, and no *egla arufa* is performed at all? Rashi adds the implicit fourth possibility: that *min b'mino* does not count as either buried or suspended, and both corpses qualify independently, potentially each triggering an obligation tied to a different nearby city.

Abaye responds by analogy to the sheaf *baraita*: the case of the sheaf placed on top of another sheaf and forgotten, where the bottom is *shichcha* and the top is not. At minimum, the *tanna kamma* of that *baraita* holds that the top sheaf is exempt while the bottom qualifies. This, Abaye suggests, reflects the debate about *min b'mino* that we explored in the *shichcha* context. However, the *gemara* has already established that the top sheaf's exemption in that case derives not from its being suspended but from the fact that the carrier had taken physical possession of it — *keivan de'achzik bah zachah bah* — and taken possession removes the category of *shichcha* entirely, regardless of where the sheaf comes to rest. The question of whether *min b'mino* suspension exempts for *egla arufa* therefore remains formally unresolved.

---

## Exposure & Location (II)

### Ba'Sadeh Requirement

The *baraita* further specifies *ba-sadeh* — the body must be in a field. The verse *ki yimatzei chalal ba'adamah* is read to exclude a body floating on the surface of water: *v'lo tzaf al penei ha-mayim*. Being on water is not *ba-sadeh* and not *ba'adamah*.

### Rabbi Elazar Position

Rabbi Elazar dissents from the collection of technical exclusions. He holds: *be-chulan im hayu chalal orfin* — in all of these scenarios, as long as the body is a *chalal* — killed by a sword — the *egla arufa* obligation applies. He does not accept the technical exemptions based on burial, suspension, or location on water. The *gemara* challenges him: surely he agrees that a strangled victim lying on a garbage heap would not trigger *egla arufa*, since the requirement of *chalal v'lo chanuk* — a sword-slain victim, not a strangled one — is derived from the repeated use of the word *chalal* throughout the *parasha*, and he accepts that *derasha*. If so, he should similarly accept the *drashot* derived from *ba'adamah v'lo tamun be-gal*, *nofel v'lo taluy be-ilan*, and *ba-sadeh v'lo tzaf al gabei mayim*. Rabbi Elazar replies: *chalal yeteira k'tiv* — the word *chalal* is written multiple times in the *parasha*, and he therefore gives weight to the *derasha* of *chalal v'lo chanuk*. The other words — *nofel*, *ba'adamah*, *ba-sadeh* — he does not accord the same exegetical significance.

### Border Town Exemption

If the body is found near a border town (*samuch le-sefer*) or near a city whose majority population is non-Jewish, *egla arufa* is not performed. The source is *d'chtiv ki yimatzei* — "if it is found" — *perat le-matzui*, excluding what is commonly found. Along a border with a hostile neighboring territory, corpses are a frequent occurrence from border conflicts; in a majority non-Jewish city under Roman rule, the unfortunate reality is that murders were not uncommon. In either case, the finding of a body is not a rare event that demands the extraordinary national response of *egla arufa*.

### Beis Din Requirement

Similarly, if the body is found near a city that has no *beis din*, the ritual is not performed — *d'ba'ina ziknei ha'ir v'leika*, because the verse requires the *ziknei ha'ir* to participate, and without a *beis din* there are no *zekeinim* of that city in the relevant sense. This leads to the final ruling: *ein modedin ela le-ir she-yesh bah beis din* — one measures only to a city that has a *beis din*. The *gemara* notes that this might appear obvious given the preceding rule, but it carries an independent teaching: if the closest city lacks a *beis din*, one does not simply abandon the entire ritual — one passes over that city and measures to the next-closest city that does have a *beis din*. The *talmud lomar* derives this from *v'lakchu ziknei ha-ir ha-hi mi-kol makom* — the *zekeinim* of *that* city, wherever it may be relative to the body, take responsibility. The point is not merely topographical proximity but judicial accountability: responsibility must remain anchored to a body capable of bearing it, even if that body is not the geographically nearest settlement.

---

---

# Sotah 46

## Equidistant Towns

### Body Equidistant

The *mishnah* before us concerns the ritual of *egla arufa*, the broken-necked calf performed when an unidentified murder victim is found in an open field. The procedure requires the elders of the *beit din hagadol* in Yerushalayim to come out and measure which nearby town — specifically, which town possessing its own *beit din* — is closest to the corpse, and it is that town's elders who must carry out the ritual.

The *mishnah* addresses a striking edge case: *nimtza mechuvon bein shtei ayarot* — what if the body is found precisely equidistant between two towns?

### R. Eliezer: Two Calves

*Shteihen mevi'ot shtei agalot divrei Rabbi Eliezer* — Rabbi Eliezer rules that each town brings its own calf. The phrasing makes clear that it is not both towns jointly bringing two calves, but each town independently bringing one. It is worth noting that the *mishnah* here cites this as *divrei Rabbi Eliezer* without recording a dissenting view — a formulation that clearly implies the ruling was contested, even if the opposing opinion is not spelled out.

This ruling might seem strange. After all, there is only one body and, one might think, only one responsible town. One could have suggested that the two *batei din* cooperate in bringing a single calf with a *tenai* — a stipulation that if the body is closer to one town, the calf counts as that town's *egla*, and if closer to the other, it counts as the other's. Alternatively, one might have argued for complete exemption: since the verse specifies *ha'ir hakerova*, the nearby city (in the singular), perhaps when no single city qualifies as definitively nearest, the entire obligation lapses. Rabbi Eliezer rejects both options and requires two calves.

### Precise Measurement

The *gemara* explains the reasoning: *kasavar efshar l'tzamtzem* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that precise equidistance is a real and legally cognizable possibility. The position of *i'efshar l'tzamtzem* would hold that in principle one town must always be fractionally closer, and our inability to measure with sufficient precision merely creates a *safek*. On that view, you would indeed bring one calf with a *tenai*. But Rabbi Eliezer maintains that *efshar l'tzamtzem* — genuine equidistance can exist, and when it does, each town bears its own independent obligation.

As for the concern that the singular language of *ha'ir hakerova* might exempt the case of two towns entirely, the *gemara* dismisses this: *v'afillu krovot* — the word *kerova* is not understood as excluding the scenario of multiple equidistant towns. There is no textual basis for such an exclusion.

### Jerusalem Exempt

The *mishnah* also states that Yerushalayim does not bring an *egla arufa*, even if it happens to be the nearest city. The *gemara* explains: *de'amar kra lerishtah* — the verse ties the obligation to a city given as an inheritance to one of the tribes, and Yerushalayim was never apportioned to any individual tribe. It remained, in a sense, an inter-tribal city, and therefore does not fall within the category of *lerishtah*.

---

## Separated Head

### Head vs. Body

The *mishnah* continues with another unusual case: *nimtza rosho b'makom echad v'gufo b'makom acher* — the head of the corpse is found in one location and the body in another. Rabbi Eliezer rules *molichin et harosh etzel haguf* — you bring the head to the body. Rabbi Akiva rules the opposite: *haguf etzel harosh* — you bring the body to the head.

At first glance this dispute seems to replicate the later dispute at the end of the *mishnah* about where one measures from. Rabbi Eliezer, who focuses on the body, says one measures from the belly button; Rabbi Akiva, who focuses on the head, says one measures from the nostrils. The positions appear perfectly parallel. However, the fact that the *mishnah* presents them as two separate disputes suggests that the earlier dispute — about which part of the body you bring to which — is dealing with a distinct question.

### Met Mitzvah

The *gemara* resolves the apparent duplication. Rabbi Yitzchak explains that the first dispute is actually about burial: *be'met mitzvah kanah mekomo* — a *met mitzvah*, a corpse with no one to bury it, acquires its place of rest where it lies. The question when the head and body are separated is therefore: to which location does the body "belong" for purposes of burial? Rabbi Eliezer says you bring the head to the body, since the body is buried where it is found. Rabbi Akiva says you bring the body to the head.

### Head or Body Moved

The *gemara* then asks: what is the underlying disagreement that drives these two rulings? *Mar savar gufa b'duchtei nafal reisha denada venafal* — one opinion holds that the body fell in place at the spot of the killing, and it was the head that flew off. Therefore the location of the body is the true location of the death, and the head must be brought there. *V'mar savar reisha heicha denafal nafal gufa hu derahit v'azal* — the other opinion holds that the head fell right where it was severed, while the body kept moving forward — as a body sometimes does when suddenly decapitated — before finally falling at a different spot. On this view, the head's location is the true locus of death.

### Measurement Points

Turning to the second dispute, the *mishnah* presents three views on which part of the body to measure from when determining which town is nearest. Rabbi Eliezer says *mitiburo* — from the belly button. Rabbi Akiva says *mechotamo* — from the nostrils. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says *mimakom shena'asah chalal* — from the place that made the person a *chalal*, a slain corpse — which he identifies as *mitzavaro*, the neck.

### Life Force

The *gemara* identifies the underlying question between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva: *mar savar ikar chayuta b'apei* — one holds that the essential life force of a person resides in the nostrils; *v'mar savar ikar chayuta b'tibura* — the other holds it resides in the belly button. This debate also arises in the context of *pikuach nefesh* in Yoma, specifically regarding how to determine whether a person trapped under rubble is still alive. Some wish to read this as a dispute about whether life is defined by respiration or by circulation — though the belly button's connection to circulation is unclear. It seems more likely that both positions are describing breath, with the belly button understood as relating to the diaphragm and the rhythmic rise and fall of breathing.

### Development & Life

The *gemara* entertains the possibility that this dispute parallels a separate *tannaitic* debate: *me'heichan ha'valad notzar* — from where does a fetus develop in the womb? One *tanna* says from the head; *Abba Shaul* says from the belly button, since the belly button is at the center, and development radiates outward in all directions. Each cites the verse *mi'mei immi atah gozi* in support.

The *gemara* concludes, however, that even *Abba Shaul* would agree that the locus of *chiyuta* — life force — is the nostrils. *Ad kan lo ka'amar Abba Shaul ela le'inyan yetzirah* — his position concerns *yetzirah*, fetal development, not the seat of life itself. *Aval le'inyan chiyuta dechulei alma b'apeih hu* — when it comes to the life force, everyone agrees it is in the nostrils, as the verse states: *kol asher nishmat ruach chayyim b'appav* — all in whose nostrils is the breath of life. The *gemara* thus consistently comes down on the side of breath in the nostrils as the defining measure of life — a point of considerable significance for contemporary halachic discussions surrounding the definition of death.

### R. Elazar: Neck

Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov's position — that one measures from the neck — derives from the verse *latet otcha al tzavverei challalei resha'im*, which locates the image of a *chalal*, a sword-slain corpse, at the neck. Since the typical *chalal* involves decapitation, the neck is the defining anatomical locus of that category of death.

---

## Ritual Procedure

### Elders Depart

Once the nearest city has been identified through measurement, *niftaru ziknei Yerushalayim v'halchu lahem* — the elders of Yerushalayim depart. The ritual itself is now the responsibility of the local elders of the identified town.

### Calf Requirements

*V'ziknei otah ha'ir mevi'in eglat bakar* — the elders of that town bring a calf. The calf must be *asher lo mashcha b'ol* — one that has not drawn a yoke, meaning it must never have been used for labor. Notably, however, *v'ein ha'mum posel bah* — a physical blemish does not invalidate it. The presence or absence of a *mum* is irrelevant; only prior *avoda*, labor, disqualifies.

### Wadi Eitan

*U'moridin otah l'nachal eitan* — they bring it down to a *nachal eitan*, a hard wadi. *Eitan k'mashma'o kasheh* — the word *eitan* in its plain sense means hard, referring to bedrock. Nevertheless, *af al pi she'eino eitan kasher* — even if the wadi is not actually of hard bedrock, it remains valid after the fact; the requirement of hard rock is only *lechatchilah*.

### Breaking the Neck

*V'orfin otah b'kofitz me'achoreha* — they break its neck from behind using a hatchet. This is done from behind the neck, not the front.

### Ground Forbidden

*U'mekomo assur milizro'a umila'avod le'olam* — the location where the ritual was performed is permanently forbidden for planting and agricultural work.

### Permitted Uses

*U'mutar lisrok sham pishtan ul'naker sham avanim* — it is, however, permitted to comb flax there or to clear stones from the area, since these activities do not involve working the soil itself. The prohibition falls specifically on uses that engage the ground; standing or sitting on the location, or conducting activities that merely take place upon it without making use of the earth, remain permitted.

---

## Declaration & Blessing

### Hand Washing

*Ziknei oto ir rochtzim et yedeihem b'mayim b'makom arifah* — the elders of the town wash their hands with water at the place where the neck was broken, over the calf. There is something visually striking about this: on the one hand, the washing of hands in a ritual context conveys assumption of responsibility, a cleansing of moral contamination; on the other hand, it calls to mind the idiom of "washing one's hands of" a matter, of disavowal. Perhaps both ideas are present — that there was a kind of defilement, a residual moral burden, that must be actively addressed and cleansed through the ritual act.

### Three Declarations

Following the hand washing, the elders declare: *yadeinu lo shafchu et hadam hazeh v'eineinu lo ra'u* — our hands did not shed this blood and our eyes did not see.

The *gemara* asks: surely no one suspected the *beit din* of murder — why must they declare that their hands did not spill the blood? The answer: *ela shelo ba leyadenu upatarnuhu belo mezonot velo ra'inuhu v'hinachnuhu belo levayah* — the declaration is not a denial of having committed murder, but an assertion of having fulfilled their communal obligations. They are affirming that this traveler did not come to them seeking help and get turned away without food; that they did not see him passing through and fail to accompany him.

This is a remarkable and demanding standard. The declaration does not merely address the question of direct culpability; it addresses the question of whether the community exercised sufficient care for the stranger in their midst. If a man had passed through town asking for shelter or assistance, and the *beit din* was aware of him and did nothing, they would be unable to make this declaration. The ritual thus encodes a positive communal responsibility for the welfare of travelers.

### Priestly Prayer

*V'hakohanim omrim kaper l'amcha Yisrael asher padita Hashem v'al titein dam naki b'kerev amcha Yisrael* — the *kohanim* then recite the prayer: atone for Your people Israel whom You have redeemed, God, and do not place the guilt of innocent blood in the midst of Your people.

### Divine Atonement

The *mishnah* notes that the final clause of the *pasuk* — *v'nichpar lahem hadam*, and the blood shall be atoned for them — is not part of the *kohanim*'s declaration. Rather, *ela ruach hakodesh mevasertam* — the divine spirit announces it to them as a promise: *eimatai sheta'asu kachah hadam yitkaper lahem* — when you perform this ritual, atonement for the blood will follow.

This raises a striking question about the theological structure of the *egla arufa* ritual. The *mishnah* earlier noted that the calf is killed by breaking its neck from behind — not by *shechitah* from the front, as in a *korban*. Why? The deliberate departure from the form of sacrifice signals that this is not a *korban* in the conventional sense. Yet the ritual does involve the shedding of blood in a context of atonement.

One way to understand this is that the *egla arufa* functions not as a sacrifice but as a substitute execution. The verse states *ki la'aretz lo yechupar ladam asher shupach bah ki im bedam shofcho* — the only true atonement for innocent blood is the execution of the murderer. Since the murderer is unknown and cannot be executed, the calf is slain in his stead. The blood being atoned for is the victim's innocent blood; the calf's blood is not what atones — rather, it is the act of execution, performed upon an innocent creature in place of the guilty one, that achieves atonement. This may be precisely why *avoda*, prior labor, disqualifies the calf: not only must it be young and never have borne offspring, it must also be wholly untarnished by human use — innocent, in the fullest sense.

---

## Mum & Avoda

### Blemish Permitted

The *mishnah*'s ruling that a *mum* does not disqualify the *egla* invites scrutiny. One might have expected the opposite conclusion based on a *kal v'chomer* from *parah adumah*.

### Kal VeChomer

The *gemara* constructs the argument: *u'mah parah she'ein ha'shanim posel bah mum posel bah* — by a *parah adumah* the age of the animal is irrelevant, and yet a *mum* disqualifies it. *Eglah she'shanim posel bah* — an *eglah* must be young (the word *eglah* itself implies a young animal), so age is a disqualifying factor. If even *parah adumah*, where age is not an issue, requires the absence of a *mum*, surely an *eglah*, which is already stricter with respect to age, should require the absence of a *mum* as well. The *kal v'chomer* seems compelling.

### Mum vs. Avoda

The *gemara* rejects it: *shani hatam de'amar kra asher ein bah mum* — by *parah adumah*, the Torah explicitly specifies *asher ein bah mum*, that there be no blemish in it. The word *bah* — "in it" — limits the requirement to *parah adumah* specifically. The absence of a *mum* is a requirement *bah*, in the *parah*, and need not be extended elsewhere.

But this immediately generates a counter-argument: if the word *bah* by *parah adumah* restricts the *mum* requirement to *parah* alone and prevents us from extending it to *eglah*, then by the same logic the word *bah* by *eglah* — which says *asher lo uvad bah*, that it was not worked — should restrict the *avoda* disqualification to *eglah* alone and prevent us from extending it to *parah adumah*. Yet we clearly do apply the *avoda* requirement to *parah adumah* (as seen from the ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav discussed below). How can we apply *avoda* from *eglah* to *parah* while simultaneously refusing to apply *mum* from *parah* to *eglah*?

### Avoda & Kodshim

The resolution is elegant and surprising. The *gemara* states: *hahi miba'ei lei l'mi'utei kodshim d'lo pasla behu avoda* — the word *bah* by *eglah* is not being used to exclude *parah adumah* from the *avoda* requirement. Rather, it is being used to exclude *kodshim* — sacrificial animals — from the *avoda* requirement. Remarkably, prior labor does not disqualify a *korban*.

This is counterintuitive. One would naturally assume that *kodshim* are subject to at least as stringent requirements as *eglah* and *parah adumah*. But the *gemara* holds the opposite: the disqualification of *avoda* is specific to these two non-*korban* contexts and does not apply to consecrated offerings. An animal that has been used for agricultural labor can still be brought as a *korban*, as long as it otherwise meets the required criteria.

The *bah* by *parah adumah* therefore functions as follows: it restricts the *mum* requirement to *parah adumah*, excluding *eglah* (which indeed has no *mum* requirement). The *bah* by *eglah* restricts the *avoda* requirement to *eglah*, excluding not *parah* but *kodshim*. The two *bah*s are doing different limiting work and are not in tension.

### Three Sources

The *gemara* then asks: is this really where we learn that *avoda* does not disqualify *kodshim*? Isn't that derived from the verse *iver o shavur o charutz o yavelet o garav o yalefet lo takrivu eleh la-Hashem* — a list of blemishes that disqualify offerings? *Eleh atah makriv* — only these disqualify, but an animal that was used for labor you may bring. So we already know *avoda* is not a problem for *kodshim* from this verse.

The *gemara* responds that this verse alone would not have been sufficient. Without the *bah* by *eglah*, one might have thought the *eleh* verse only exempts *avodat heter* — labor performed when it was still ordinary, unconsecrated property — but *avodat issur*, labor performed in a prohibited manner (such as being yoked in a forbidden mixture), might still create a metaphysical defect. The *bah* teaches that even *avodat issur* does not disqualify.

A second verse — *u'mi'yad ben nechar lo takrivu et lechem Eloheikhem mi'kol eleh* — also teaches the exemption. But even two verses would not have been enough: one might have thought the exemption applies only when the labor was performed while the animal was still *chullin*, unconsecrated property, but not when the labor was performed after the animal was already consecrated as *kadosh*. The third source — the *bah* by *eglah* — teaches that even labor performed on an animal after it was already consecrated as a *korban* does not disqualify it.

This is a remarkable ruling. Even if one violated the sanctity of the *korban* by using it for labor after it had been designated, the offering remains valid. It may well be that the person incurred *me'ilah* — misappropriation of consecrated property — but the *korban* itself retains its halachic status.

The overall picture is therefore illuminating: *eglah* has no *mum* requirement but does have an *avoda* requirement. *Korbanot* have a *mum* requirement but no *avoda* requirement. *Parah adumah* has both — and in this sense stands in the middle, sharing characteristics with both.

### Bundle of Sacks

The *gemara* now returns to examine the statement of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: *ha'maniach chavilah shel sakin al ha'parah* — if one placed a bundle of sacks upon the *parah adumah*, it is invalid. This is striking because a bundle of sacks is not an *ol*, a yoke — yet it disqualifies. Meanwhile, the rule by *eglah* is *u've'eglah ad she'timshoch* — by an *eglah* the animal must actually draw the load, actually walk with it, for the *avoda* to be operative.

Why the asymmetry? Why is *parah adumah* disqualified merely by having a burden placed upon it, while *eglah* requires the animal to actually move?

### Gezeirah Shava

The answer lies in the different legal sources for the two rulings. By *eglah*, the verse reads *asher lo mashcha b'ol* — which did not draw with a yoke. The term *mashcha*, drawing, connotes actual movement. And by *parah adumah*, the verse reads *asher lo alah aleha ol* — upon which no yoke has gone up. If we were to learn *parah* from *eglah* via a *gezeirah shavah* on the shared word *ol* — *ne'emar kan ol v'ne'emar lehalan ol* — then we would expect *parah* to also require actual movement, *meshichah*, just as *eglah* does.

The *gemara* confirms this logic: *mah lehalan ad she'timshoch af kan ad she'timshoch* — if the source is *eglah*, the threshold should be the same. Rav Yehuda's ruling that even placing a bundle of sacks without movement disqualifies the *parah* must therefore reflect an alternative source that does not derive from *eglah*.

This is indeed a *tannaitic* dispute: some derive the *avoda* disqualification for *parah* from *eglah* via the *gezeirah shavah*, in which case the definition is parallel — movement is required. Others derive it from the internal language of the *parah adumah* verse itself, in which case the conceptual framework is different.

### Ol vs. Avoda

According to the view that derives the rule from the *parah* verse itself, the operative phrase is not *avoda* at all. The disqualification comes from the words *asher lo alah aleha* — upon which nothing has gone up. The word *ol*, yoke, at the end of the phrase then has a specific additional function: *ol posel bein be'sha'at avoda bein shelo be'sha'at avoda* — a yoke disqualifies whether placed for the purpose of work or not. The mere presence of a yoke upon the *parah* is disqualifying, regardless of intent or use. For all other burdens, however, they disqualify only *be'sha'at avoda* — in the context of actual labor use. Rashi explains this to mean not that the animal must have walked, but that the burden must have been placed upon it for the purpose of work, not merely set down in passing.

On this reading, the conceptual framework for *parah adumah* is not fundamentally about *avoda* at all — it is about *alah aleha*, having anything placed upon it. The significance of the word *ol* in the verse is specifically to inform us that a yoke, even placed without any intent to use it for work, is immediately disqualifying.

### Tefach Movement

By contrast, for *eglah*, where the standard is *meshichah* — actual drawing — the *gemara* records a tradition from Rabbi Yochanan as transmitted by Rabbi Yaakov: *meshichat ol l'rochbo tefach* — the drawing of the yoke requires the animal to have moved the width of a yoke, which is a *tefach*. Rabbi Abbahu had posed the question of whether the relevant dimension was the length or the width of the yoke; Rabbi Yaakov transmitted that Rabbi Yochanan had specified the width, which is a *tefach*. This formulation also conveys a practical corollary for commercial purposes: a yoke that is less than a *tefach* in width does not qualify as a yoke at all and could be rejected in a sale transaction.

---

## Theology

### Never Produced

Rabbi Yochanan ben Shaul offers a theological reading of why the Torah requires both a calf and a wadi: *mipnei mah amra Torah hevi eglah b'nachal* — why did the Torah say to bring a calf down to the wadi? *Amar ha'Kadosh Baruch Hu yavo davar shelo asah peirot* — the Holy One said: let come something that has never produced fruit. The calf, young and never used for labor, is an animal that has produced nothing; the wadi, hard and barren, is a place that produces nothing.

### Wasted Potential

*V'ye'aref bimkom she'ein oseh peirot vichaper al mi shelo hinicho la'asot peirot* — and let it be killed in a place that does not produce anything, to atone for one who was not permitted to produce fruit. The victim — murdered, perhaps in youth — was a person whose potential was cut off before it could be realized.

### Fruit = Mitzvot

The *gemara* asks: *mai peiros* — what do we mean by "fruit" in this context? If it means *priyah v'rivyah*, children, then one would not perform *egla arufa* for an elderly man or a sterile person who could not have had children regardless — which is surely not the case. Rather, *ela mitzvot* — "fruit" means deeds, the good acts and *mitzvot* one might have performed in a lifetime. Every murder is an assault not merely on a life but on all the potential *mitzvot* that life would have generated. The calf and the wadi together form a symbolic tableau of unrealized potential, offering atonement for a world diminished by the act of violence.

### Ancient Ground

The *gemara* also explores the meaning of *nachal eitan*. One opinion derives from verses that *eitan* denotes hardness — a wadi of hard, rocky ground. Another opinion, *acherim omrim*, holds that *eitan* means ancient: *nachal eitan* is a wadi whose soil has never been disturbed, ground that goes back to primordial times, ground that carries with it no history of human cultivation. The two readings are not necessarily in conflict; Rashi reads *eitan* as ground that has never been dug up, which combines both the sense of hardness and antiquity.

---

## Ground Restrictions

### From Behind

*V'orfin otah b'kofitz me'achoreha* — the neck is broken from behind with a hatchet. The *gemara* derives this through *gezeirah shavah*: *gamar arifa arifa me'chatat ha'of* — the word *arifa* here is linked to the word *arifa* used in the context of *chatat ha'of*, the bird sin-offering, where the priest pinches the neck from behind. Just as there the action is performed from the nape of the neck, so here too the breaking of the neck is from behind.

### Past vs. Future

The verse states *asher lo ye'aved bah v'lo yizare'a* regarding the site of the *egla arufa*. A *tannaitic* dispute addresses whether this language refers to the past or the future. Rabbi Yoshiya reads it as describing the past: the wadi must be one that has not previously been worked or planted. Rabbi Yonatan reads it as prescribing the future: henceforth, this ground may not be worked or planted.

Rava clarifies: *lehaba d'chulei alma lo peligi* — on the future prohibition, there is no dispute. *V'lo yizare'a* means "shall not be seeded" — this is universally accepted as a prospective prohibition. The debate is only about *leshe'avar*, whether the verse additionally specifies that the ground must have been previously unworked. Rabbi Yoshiya argues that *asher* introduces a description of a past state; Rabbi Yonatan argues that had the Torah meant the past it would have said *ne'evad*, and the form used implies future obligation.

### All Soil Usage

A *braita* extends the scope of the future prohibition. The verse says *asher lo ye'aved bo* — it shall not be worked — and *lo yizare'a* — and it shall not be planted. From the combination, the *braita* derives: *ein li ela zri'ah, she'ar avodot minayin* — I know only that planting is forbidden; how do I know all other forms of soil work are also forbidden? *Talmud lomar asher lo ye'aved bo mikol makom* — the phrase "shall not be worked" encompasses all soil use. The specific mention of planting then teaches the principle: *mah zri'ah meyuchedet she'hi b'gufah shel karka, af kol she'hi b'gufah shel karka assur* — just as planting is distinctive in that it engages the body of the earth itself, so anything that engages the body of the earth is forbidden. *Yatza srikat pishtan v'nikur avanim* — excluded are combing flax and clearing stones, which take place upon the ground without working the earth itself.

---

## Accompaniment

### Declaration Details

Returning to the elders' declaration: *lo ba leyadenu upatarnuhu belo mezonot v'lo ra'inuhu v'hinachnuhu belo levayah* — the stranger did not come before us such that we dismissed him without food, and we did not see him pass through and leave him without accompaniment. The declaration contains within it two distinct communal obligations: the provision of sustenance (*mezonot*) and *levayah*, accompaniment.

### R. Meir: Enforcement

*Hachi darish Rabbi Meir omer kofin l'levayah* — Rabbi Meir taught: we coerce accompaniment. The obligation of *levayah* is not merely a matter of good character; it is of such fundamental importance that it may be enforced. *She'sechar ha'levayah ein lo shiur* — the reward for accompanying one's fellow has no measure.

### City of Luz

Rabbi Meir derives this from the story in *Shoftim* involving the city of Luz. When the Israelites were conquering the land, watchmen saw a man leaving a city. *Vayomru lo hareinu na et mevo ha'ir* — they asked him to show them the entrance to the city. *Ve'asinu imach chesed* — and we will deal kindly with you. He showed them, and while the entire city was put to the sword, *v'oto ha'ish umishpachto shilechu* — that man and his family were sent free. He went to the land of the Hittites, built a new city, and named it Luz — and the *gemara* identifies this as the Luz of later tradition, a city that dyed *techelet*, survived the campaigns of Sancheriv and Nevuchadnetzar undisturbed, and into which the Angel of Death has no entry. When its elders finally tire of life, they must leave the city walls in order to die.

This is an astonishing reward. The man had arguably betrayed his own people — he was a collaborator with the conquering force. Yet the *gemara* reads his act as one of *levayah*: he accompanied them toward their destination, showing them the way. The theological message is that the act of accompanying someone on their way carries merit of an almost unbounded kind, even when the context is fraught.

### Canaanite Pointer

The *gemara* then intensifies the lesson through a *kal v'chomer*: *uma kena'ani ze shelo diber befiv v'lo halach beraglav* — this Canaanite neither spoke aloud nor walked alongside them; he merely indicated the way — whether with his lips or with his finger, the *amora'im* dispute — *garam hatzalah lo ul'zar'o ad sof kol hadoros*. He brought salvation to himself and his descendants until the end of all generations. *Mi she'oseh levayah beraglav* — one who actually accompanies another on foot — *al achat kama v'chama* — how much more so will such a person merit.

### Torah Accompaniment

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi addresses the case of one who travels alone with no one to accompany him: *yiasok b'Torah* — he should occupy himself with Torah. The verse says *ki livyat chen hem l'roshecha* — for they are an ornament of grace for your head — a play on the word *levayah*, accompaniment. Torah accompanies the solitary traveler and affords the protection that human accompaniment would otherwise provide.

### Pharaoh & Abraham

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi further teaches: *bishvil arba pesi'ot sheleivah Paroh l'Avraham* — because Pharaoh walked four steps to accompany Avraham, as the verse states *vayetzav alav Paroh anashim vayishalchu oto v'et ishto v'et kol asher lo* — he commanded men to escort Avraham and his wife and all his possessions — *nishtabedu b'vanav arba meot shanah* — Avraham's descendants were enslaved for four hundred years, as the verse states *va'avaddum v'inu otam arba meot shanah*. Four steps of accompaniment yielded four hundred years of dominion. This is a striking and paradoxical formulation: the reward for Pharaoh's *levayah* was the power to subjugate the very family he had honored. The arithmetic — four steps, four hundred years — makes the principle vivid and arresting.

### Four Amot

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav teaches: *ha'malveh et chavero arba amot b'ir eino nizok* — one who accompanies a neighbor even four *amot* within a city will not be harmed. The protective benefit of *levayah* accrues to the one who accompanies. Beyond the formal spiritual merit, there is a practical logic: a traveler accompanied even briefly signals to bystanders that he has a protector and is not unguarded. Walking someone even a short distance out of one's home communicates care and connection, discouraging those who might otherwise take advantage of a stranger traveling alone.

### Ravina & Rescue

The *gemara* concludes this section with an illustrative incident: *Ravina alveiya l'Rava bar Yitzchak arba amot b'ir* — Ravina accompanied Rava bar Yitzchak four *amot* in the city. *Mata lideih hezika v'ishtaziv* — he subsequently encountered something that would have caused him injury, and he was saved from it. The protective promise of *levayah* materialized in a concrete and immediate way.

# Sotah 47

## Levayah

### HaRav LeTalmid

The daf begins on 46b, approximately twenty lines from the bottom, with a *baraita*: *tanu rabanan*, *harav letalmid* — even a rabbi who is hosting a student bears an obligation to accompany that student out of the city upon his departure. This is the *mitzvah* of *levayah*, rooted in the declaration of the *sanhedrin* in the *eglah arufah* ceremony: "our hands did not spill this blood" — meaning, we were not negligent in accompanying him out of the city. The *gemara* has been discussing this in the context of what declarations must be made in Hebrew, and now turns to the practical parameters of *levayah*.

### Distances: Ibburah, Tech…

How far must one accompany? The *baraita* specifies: *harav letalmid*, a rabbi accompanying a student, must go *ad ibburah shel ir* — until the outer houses of the city, the so-called "pregnancy" of the city, which corresponds to the measurement used for *techum shabbos*. *Chaver lechaver*, between equals, the obligation extends *ad techum shabbos* — two thousand *amot* beyond the city's edge, approximately one kilometer.

### Talmid LeRav

When the direction is reversed — a *talmid* accompanying his *rebbe* — the rule changes significantly. The *gemara* states *ein lo shi'ur*, there is no fixed limit. Yet immediately after asserting this, the *gemara* asks: *ein lo shi'ur vekama* — so how much really? Rav Sheshet answers: *ad parsah*, until a *parsah*, which equals four *mil*, roughly four kilometers — three times the distance of *techum shabbos*.

### Rebbe vs. Rabbo Muvhak

This limit of a *parsah* applies, however, only with respect to a *rebbe* who is not one's primary teacher. *Aval rabbo muvhak* — but for one's primary and most formative teacher — the obligation extends to *shalosh parsaot*, three *parsaot*, or twelve kilometers, approximately seven miles. This is a substantial distance, reflecting the depth of the relationship between a student and the teacher who shaped him most profoundly.

## Accompaniment Stories

### Rav Kahana & Tinisa

The *gemara* illustrates these principles with two brief accounts of *talmidim* who accompanied their *rebbes*. Rav Kahana would accompany Rav Shimi bar Ashi from Pum Nahara all the way to Bei Tinisa of Bavel — a location known for its distinctive groves of palm trees.

### Adam HaRishon Discussion

Upon arriving at Bei Tinisa, Rav Shimi bar Ashi remarked that people say these palm trees of Bavel go back to the days of *Adam HaRishon*. Rav Kahana responded: *idkeran milta* — you have reminded me of a Torah teaching. He then cited Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chanina on the verse, *be'eretz lo avar bah ish velo yashav adam sham* — in a land that no person passed through and no *adam* ever settled. The question is a classic one: if no one passed through, it is obvious that no one settled — why repeat the point? The answer reads *adam* literally: only the land that *Adam HaRishon* decreed for human settlement was ever settled. The regions he did not designate remained uninhabited throughout history. Thus the two terms are not redundant; one speaks of ordinary travelers and the other of the primordial decree of Adam. The story illustrates how even the act of accompanying a *rebbe* — what might seem like mere travel — becomes an occasion for *divrei Torah*.

### Rav Mordechai Story

Similarly, Rav Mordechai would accompany Rav Ashi from Hagronya to Bei Kifei — and some say all the way to Bei Dura.

## Shofech Damim

### Rabbi Meir Teaching

Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Meir: *kol she-eino melaveh u-mitlaveh ke'ilu shofech damim* — anyone who neither accompanies nor is accompanied is as though he spilled blood. The inclusion of *mitlaveh* — the one being accompanied — is noteworthy: it implies that even the person refusing accompaniment bears responsibility if harm results. The connection to *eglah arufah* is direct: the failure to accompany leaves a person vulnerable, exposed to attack, and the community becomes implicated in whatever violence follows.

### Elisha & Bears

The *gemara* now invokes a biblical narrative to drive this point home. *She'ilmalei livuhu anshei Yericho l'Elisha lo girah dubim batinokot* — had only the people of Yericho accompanied Elisha, he would not have sent the bears upon the young men. The verse (II Kings 2) recounts that Elisha traveled alone from Yericho to Beit El, at which point a group of young men emerged from the city, mocked him, and called out: *alei kerei'ach alei kerei'ach* — "get out of here, baldy." The *gemara* explains the word *kerei'ach* — baldy — as referring to: *shekeirachta lanu et hamakom*, you have stripped this place. These young men had been selling good water to the inhabitants; when Elisha performed a miracle sweetening Yericho's waters, he destroyed their livelihood. They were, in effect, accusing him of having impoverished them.

### Korach: Baldy

What does the word *kerei'ach* — "baldy" — signify beyond the surface insult? The *gemara* connects it to *shekeirachta lanu et hamakom*, as just noted. The taunts were not random cruelty but a grievance rooted in their economic loss from Elisha's miracle.

### Ne'arim & Ketanim

A deeper question surrounds the phrase *ne'arim ketanim* — literally "young lads who are small." Rabbi Eliezer explains: they are called *ne'arim* because they were *menue'arim min hamitzvot*, emptied of *mitzvot* — people with no serious religious commitment, which is why they could so callously insult the *navi*. They are called *ketanim* — small — because they were *m'katnei emunah*, of diminished faith, for rather than trusting that God would provide for them in other ways after the waters were sweetened, they attacked the man responsible.

Rav Yosef challenged this reading. Perhaps, he suggested, *ne'arim* simply designates their place of origin — there was a town called *Ne'urin*, and *ne'arim* would mean "people from Na'ar," not young men at all. He cites support from another verse (II Kings 5) describing a *na'ara ketana* — a young girl — captured from the land of Israel by Aram; perhaps there too, *na'ara* means she was from a place called *Ne'urin*.

The *gemara* responds: in the verse about the captive girl, her place of origin is not specified, so attributing *na'ara* to a geographical name is plausible. Here, however, the text explicitly states that these young men came from the city — from Yericho — *hacha mefareish mekumo*. The place is given; *ne'arim* therefore cannot be a geographical designation, and the original reading stands.

## Elisha's Curse

### Elisha's Ra'ah

The verse continues: *vayifen acharav vayar'em vayakalem beshem Hashem* — he turned, he saw them, and he cursed them in God's name. The *gemara* asks: *mai ra'ah* — what is meant by "he saw"? Was it simply that he looked at them?

Rav says: *ra'ah mamash* — he literally just saw them. Yet even this bare seeing is consequential, as we learn from a *baraita*: Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel teaches that whenever the Sages directed their gaze against someone — *kol makom shenasnu chachamim eineihem* — that person either dies or becomes impoverished. A look from a *navi* of this stature carries devastating force.

### Mitigating Factors

Shmuel offers a different reading: he saw that all of them had been conceived on *Yom Kippur* — their mothers had violated the sanctity of that day. This is the *gemara*'s attempt, however tentatively, to explain why such an extreme punishment befell them.

Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha adds another dimension: he saw that they wore their hair in a style called *blurei*, associated with the Amorites, suggesting involvement in idolatrous practices.

Rabbi Yochanan goes furthest in the prosecutorial direction: he saw that *lo hayta bahen lachluchit shel mitzvah* — there was not even a trace of moisture of *mitzvah* in them; they were entirely bereft of religious life.

Yet even this does not fully satisfy. One might still argue: *vedilma bezar'aihu nihavi* — perhaps from their descendants something good might have come? Rabbi Eliezer answers: he saw that neither from them nor from any of their descendants through all generations would any good emerge — *lo bam velo bezaram ad sof kol hadorot*. The *gemara* is not celebrating what Elisha did; it is straining to make some peace with a troubling text by marshaling every possible mitigating consideration.

### Bears & Casualties

*Vatetzeina shtayim dubim min haya'ar* — two bears emerged from the forest and mauled forty-two of the youths.

### Ness v. Ness B'Toch Ness

A dispute between Rav and Shmuel: one said it was a single miracle; the other said it was a miracle within a miracle. According to the first view, there was a forest but no bears in it — the bears themselves were miraculous. According to the second, there was neither a forest nor bears — both were created for the occasion, making it a miracle layered upon a miracle.

This raises an obvious question: if both forest and bears had to be created miraculously, why create the forest at all? Why not simply produce the bears? The *gemara* answers: *de'vi'isi* — because the bears would have been afraid to attack without a place of refuge. Even within a miracle, the bears behave like natural bears; they will only charge if they have somewhere to retreat. The forest was necessary to make the miracle function through natural-seeming animal psychology.

### Arba'im u'Shnayim

Rabbi Chanina notes that forty-two children perished — and this corresponds precisely to the forty-two sacrifices that Balak king of Moab offered in his effort to bring a curse upon Israel through Bilaam. *Bishvil arbaim ushnayim korbanot shehikriv Balak melech Moav hufka miYisrael arbaim ushnayim yeladim*. Even Balak's evil sacrifices had some effect — not the effect he intended, but they registered sufficiently to ultimately account for these forty-two deaths.

## Shelo Lishma to Lishma

### Shelo Lishma Ba Lishma

This leads to a teaching of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: one should always engage in Torah and *mitzvot* even *shelo lishma* — not for the right reason — because from *shelo lishma* one comes eventually to *lishma*, acting for the proper motive.

### Balak & Rut Legacy

The proof: *bishvil arbaim ushnayim korbanot shehikriv Balak melech Moav zacha veyatzta mimenu Rut* — in the merit of those forty-two sacrifices that Balak offered, he merited that Rut descended from him. Rav Yosef ben Choni specifies the lineage: Rut was the daughter of Eglon, who was the son of Balak. And from Rut came David and Shlomo — *elef olot ya'aleh Shlomo*, who brought a thousand burnt offerings to God for the purest of motives. Thus a chain beginning with Balak's deeply corrupted sacrifices ends with Shlomo's thousand offerings brought in perfect *lishma*.

### Ta'avato La'Kella

One might object: surely the parallel is strained. Normally we say *shelo lishma* means a self-interested but not malicious motive. Balak's intent was thoroughly evil. Can we say even evil sacrifices lead to good? Moreover, did those evil intentions have no effect at all?

The *gemara* responds: *ta'avaso miya lekilela hava* — his desire *was* for curse, and that too had its impact. The forty-two deaths attributed to those sacrifices are the evil effect that his evil intention generated. The good that ultimately flowed from it — Rut, David, Shlomo — was the *shelo lishma* becoming *lishma* across generations, but his wicked intention was not without consequence either.

## Yericho & Chen

### Moshav HaIr Tov

The *gemara* now circles back to the story of Elisha's arrival in Yericho. The people of the city addressed him: *hinei na moshav ha'ir tov ka'asher adoni ro'eh* — behold, the dwelling of the city is pleasant as my master can see. And yet the verse concludes that the waters are bad and the land causes miscarriage. The *gemara* presses: if the water is bitter and the land causes *shichlul*, what exactly is pleasant about the city? Why would they call it a good dwelling?

### Chen Makom

Rabbi Chanin answers: *chen makom al yoshvav* — a place has a certain charm upon those who dwell there. People who live somewhere develop a fondness for it that is not fully explicable from the outside. The inhabitants of Yericho found their city beautiful despite its obvious deficiencies, because familiarity and belonging produce an attachment that transcends objective assessment.

### Shlosha Chinot

Rabbi Yochanan extends this into a general principle: *shlosha chinot hein* — there are three types of *chen*, charm, that operate similarly. *Chen makom al yoshvav* — the charm of a place upon its inhabitants. *Chen isha al ba'ala* — the charm of a woman upon her husband; what an outsider might not appreciate, a husband finds profoundly attractive in his wife, because *chen* is relational, not objective. And *chen mekach al mikcho* — the charm of a purchase upon its buyer; a person who has acquired something finds it wonderful in a way that someone who hasn't bought it may not see. All three share the same logic: intimacy and commitment generate a subjective beauty that is real even if not universally perceptible.

## Elisha's Illnesses

### Shlosha Cholaim

A *baraita* teaches: *shlosha cholaim chala Elisha* — Elisha suffered three serious illnesses. The first was punishment for having sent the bears against the children. The second was for having pushed Geichazi away *bishtei yadayim* — with both hands — giving him only harsh rebuke without subsequently drawing him back. The third was simply the illness from which he ultimately died.

How does the *gemara* derive that there were three separate illnesses? From the verse: *ve'Elisha chala et chalyo asher yamut bo*. The *gemara* reads *chala*, *chalyo*, and *asher yamut bo* as three distinct expressions of illness — three episodes, three occasions of serious sickness.

### Smol Docha Yamin Mekarev…

From Elisha's error with Geichazi, the *gemara* derives a broader principle. *Le'olam tehei smol dochah ve'yamin mekarevet* — always let the left hand push away and the right hand draw close. When a person must rebuke and distance someone, the pulling close must ultimately be stronger than the pushing away. The *gemara* states explicitly: *lo ke'Elisha shedachafoto l'Geichazi bishtei yadav* — not like Elisha, who pushed Geichazi away with both hands. And the printed text says *velo ki-Yehoshua ben Perachiah shedachafoto le'echad mitalmidav bishtei yadav* — and not like Yehoshua ben Perachiah, who pushed away one of his students with both hands. The original text, which was censored to protect the Talmud from church persecution, names that student as Yeshu HaNotzri. The historical difficulty — Yehoshua ben Perachiah lived roughly a century before the common era, perhaps seventy years before Jesus — does not necessarily mean the *gemara* did not identify them; it may simply mean the *gemara*'s historical chronology does not align with ours.

## Geichazi Story

### Geichazi's Greed

What precisely was Geichazi's sin? The *gemara* recounts: after Elisha had healed Naaman the Syrian general of his leprosy and explicitly refused any reward — establishing the principle that one does not take payment for such a *mitzvah* — Geichazi ran after Naaman in secret and took silver and garments in Elisha's name. When Geichazi returned, Elisha confronted him: *lo libi halach ka'asher hafach ish me'al merkavto likrasecha* — was my heart not with you when that man turned from his chariot to greet you? *Ha'eit lakachas et hakesef* — is now really the moment to accept such gifts?

### Shmonah Sheratzim

The *gemara* notes that the verse mentions not only silver and garments but a long catalogue of goods: olives, vineyards, sheep, cattle, male and female slaves. But in fact Geichazi only took silver and garments — why does the verse enumerate so much more? Rabbi Yitzchak explains: *be'osa sha'ah hayah Elisha osek b'shmonah sheratzim* — at that very time, Elisha had been studying the laws of the eight *sheratzim*, the eight species of rodents that convey *tuma*. The eight items mentioned in the verse correspond to those eight categories. Elisha said to Geichazi: you have taken the reward for the *Torah* you studied — the reward you might have received in the World to Come for learning those laws you have now forfeited and will receive in this world in the form of material goods.

### Tzaraas Geichazi

The verse continues: *ve'tzaraas Naaman tidbak becha u-vezarcha le'olam* — the *tzaraas* of Naaman shall cleave to you and to your children forever. The *gemara* connects this to a later verse: *ve'arba'ah anashim hayu metzora'im petach hasha'ar* — four men afflicted with *tzaraas* sat at the gate. Rabbi Yochanan identifies them as Geichazi and his three sons.

### Elisha Seeks Teshuvah

A later verse records: *vayelech Elisha Damesek* — Elisha went to Damascus. Why did he go? Rabbi Yochanan answers: *shehalach lehachziro l'Geichazi b'teshuva* — he went to bring Geichazi back to *teshuvah*. Elisha had apparently come to feel some remorse about how he had handled his student and sought to repair it. He said to Geichazi: *chazor becha* — return, repent.

### Ein Maspikin B'Yado

Geichazi refused. He said: *kach mikublani mimcha kol mi shechata vehichti et harabbim ein maspikin b'yado la'asot teshuvah* — this is what I have received as tradition from you: anyone who sinned and caused others to sin does not receive the wherewithal to do *teshuvah*. It is not that *teshuvah* is metaphysically impossible, but that it becomes practically unattainable — the door feels permanently shut. One wonders, and the *gemara* implicitly raises this, whether teaching this principle so categorically to students is itself a form of pushing away with both hands. Geichazi took the teaching as license to give up entirely.

### Hichti Es HaRabim

In what way had Geichazi caused others to sin? The *gemara* records several traditions. One says he suspended the golden calves of Yerovam ben Nevat with lodestones — magnets arranged so the calves floated in midair — creating the illusion that they were genuine deities. Another says he engraved God's name on the mouth of the golden calves, so that they would supernaturally proclaim *Anochi Hashem Elokecha* and *Lo yiheyeh lecha*, mimicking the divine voice. Each of these represents an act of profound mass corruption.

A third tradition points in a slightly different direction: *rabbanan dacha mikamei* — he pushed away scholars from Elisha's presence, seeking to monopolize access to his master. How is this inferred? After Geichazi was sent away, the *bnei nevi'im* said to Elisha: *hinei na hamakom asher anachnu yoshvim sham lefanecha tzar mimenu* — the place where we sit before you has become too crowded. *Michlal de'ad idna lo hava dachik* — this implies that until then it had not been crowded, because Geichazi had been keeping people away. His removal opened the doors, and suddenly the place was full. His restricting access to Elisha constituted a form of *hichti et harabbim* — causing many to be deprived of Torah.

The broader lesson here is sobering. A small wrongdoing, handled with a heavy and unrelenting hand, can drive a person from occasional dishonesty into wholesale heresy and mass spiritual corruption. The consequences of pushing away entirely, without the right hand drawing close, are incalculable.

## Yehoshua ben Perachiah

### Yannai's Persecution

The *gemara* now tells the parallel story. During the period when King Yannai was killing the Sages and Pharisees, Shimon ben Shetach was protected because his sister had married Yannai and hid him. Yehoshua ben Perachiah, who was the *nasi*, had no such protection and fled — *azal arek l'Alexandria shel Mitzrayim* — he ran away to Alexandria in Egypt.

### Return & Inn

When the persecutions subsided, Shimon ben Shetach sent a message to his colleague, composed as a poetic epistle: from me, Jerusalem the Holy City, to you, Alexandria of Egypt — my sister — my husband dwells within you and I sit desolate. The message was at once poetic, coded, and emotionally resonant. Yehoshua ben Perachiah understood: *shema minah hava lei shlama* — it must now be peaceful. He set out to return.

On the journey back, he stopped at an inn. The innkeeper treated him with exceptional honor — *shapir avid lei yekara tuva*, with great and fitting respect. Yehoshua ben Perachiah sat and began praising the situation: *kama na'eh achsanya zo* — how beautiful is this inn. He meant, evidently, how beautiful is her manner of hosting.

### Student Rebuked

One of his students — the text preserves this as Yeshu HaNotzri in the original *girsa* — heard this and replied: *Rabbi, eineiha trutot* — her eyes are round, they are not beautiful. The student had interpreted the remark as a comment on the innkeeper's physical appearance.

Yehoshua ben Perachiah reacted immediately and harshly: *rasha, bekach ata osek* — wicked one, is this what occupies your mind? He was incensed that his student's thoughts had gone in that direction. He then took out four hundred *shofarot* and placed the student under *cherem*, the ban of excommunication.

### Repeated Rejection

Day after day the student returned, seeking to be readmitted. *Kol yoma ata lekamei velo kiblei* — every day he came and was not accepted. Then one day, as Yehoshua ben Perachiah was reciting *kri'at shema*, the student arrived once again. That very day, Yehoshua ben Perachiah had actually reached a change of heart — *hava be-da'ato lekablei* — he was prepared to accept him back. But as he was in the middle of *kri'at shema* he could not speak. He gestured with his hand — *achvei lei be-yadei*. The student interpreted the gesture as another rejection: *savar midche dachei lei* — he assumed he was being pushed away yet again.

### Stone Worship

*Azal zakfei livneita palcha* — the student went and erected a stone idol and worshipped it. He had crossed the line from estrangement to *avodah zarah*.

### Ein Maspikin (Repeated)

When Yehoshua ben Perachiah finally came to him and said *chazor becha* — return, repent — the student gave the same answer Geichazi had given: *kach mekublani mimcha, kol hachotei umachti et harabbim ein maspikin b'yado la'asot teshuvah* — this is what I have received as tradition from you: one who sins and causes others to sin is not given the opportunity to repent. The student invoked his teacher's own principle against his teacher's attempt at reconciliation.

As the *gemara* confirms: *kishef vehisit vehidiach vehichti et Yisrael* — he practiced sorcery, he seduced, he led astray, and he caused Israel to sin. This is how he had caused others to sin, making *teshuvah* practically foreclosed. And it confirms what the *gemara* already signaled: the dates in the story do not align historically with what we know of Jesus, yet the *gemara* clearly identifies the student as Yeshu HaNotzri and attributes to him the founding of a movement that led vast numbers away.

## Smol Docha Yamin

### Yeitzer, Tinok, Ishah

Having established the principle of *smol dochah ve'yamin mekarevet*, the *gemara* now extends it to other domains of personal life. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar teaches: *yeitzer, tinok, ve'ishah — tehei smol dochah ve'yamin mekarevet* — with regard to one's *yeitzer* (sexual desire), one's children, and one's wife, always let the left hand push away and the right hand draw close.

This is a distinctively Jewish teaching. The *yeitzer* is not to be annihilated — Judaism does not embrace asceticism — but moderated. Yet the moderation must always be in the service of embrace rather than rejection. The right hand, which draws close, must be stronger. A man's relationship with his children — even when a father must set limits — should ultimately be defined by closeness and warmth. The same applies to the relationship with one's wife. The principle is the same throughout: never push away so hard that the right hand cannot draw close again.

## Eglah Arufah

### Horeg Ad Lo Neerfah

The *gemara* now transitions to the *mishnah*. *Nimtza ha-horeig ad shelo neerfah ha-eglah* — if the murderer was discovered before the heifer's neck was broken, *teitzei vetireh ba-eider* — the heifer returns to the flock and may be used. It does not acquire the status of *eglah arufah* and is not forbidden. Rashi notes that there is an opinion in the *gemara* that once the heifer descends into the valley even before the neck is broken, it becomes forbidden — but the ruling here follows the view that it does not.

### Acharei Neerfah

If, however, the neck has already been broken — *misheneerfah ha-eglah tikaver bimkomah* — it is buried in place and remains permanently forbidden in benefit, even after the murderer is subsequently found. The reason is given in the next subsection.

### Kiphrah B'Safeik

*She'al safeik ba'ah mitchilatah* — it came originally on account of doubt. The entire purpose of the *eglah arufah* ritual is to achieve atonement for the community and the land during the period when no murderer is known and justice cannot be done. *Mitchilah kiphrah sefeika vehalchah lah* — it achieved its intended atonement during that period of uncertainty, and therefore it is not retroactively invalidated by the later discovery of the murderer. The ritual served its function; it may not be undone.

### Yehareg

*Neerfah ha-eglah ve-achar kach nimtza ha-horeig — harei zeh yeihareig* — if the neck was already broken and then the murderer is found, he is nevertheless executed. The *eglah arufah* provided communal atonement for the land; it did not substitute for the murderer's punishment. The verse is explicit: *ula-aretz lo yechupar la-dam asher shupach bah ki im be-dam shofcho* — the land cannot be atoned for spilled blood except through the blood of the one who spilled it. Performing the ritual does not spare the murderer; it only addresses the communal dimension of the crime.

## Edim v. Eglah

### Ed Echad Ra'iti

The *mishnah* continues: *eid echad omer ra'iti et ha-horeig* — if one witness says "I saw the killer" — even though a single witness cannot convict in *beit din* — the *eglah arufah* is suspended. This parallels what we saw with *sotah*: a single witness testifying to the adultery suspends the *sotah* ordeal. The Torah grants *ed echad* a form of credibility that prevents proceeding with these rituals even without the formal requirement of two witnesses for conviction.

### Neutralization Rules

The *mishnah* then presents a series of cases involving competing testimony. One witness says he saw and another says he did not: they neutralize each other and the neck is broken. A woman says she saw and another woman says she did not: the same, they neutralize. One witness says he saw and two say he did not: the two prevail, the neck is broken. Two witnesses say they saw and one says they did not: the two prevail, the neck is not broken.

### Mishe-Rabu Rotzchanim

*Mishe-rabu ha-rotzchanim batla eglah arufah* — when murders became rampant in Israel, the *eglah arufah* ritual was discontinued. The ritual presupposes a society where murder is an aberration that shocks the community into communal soul-searching. When murder had become routine — particularly associated with the period of the *sicarri* and the final decades of the Second Temple — the ritual could no longer carry its intended meaning. The *mishnah* mentions that this shift is associated with the rise of *Elazar ben Dinai*, who was originally known as *Tchina ben Perisha* and was later renamed *ben ha-ratzchan* — "son of the murderer."

## Batlu HaMitzvot

### Mishe-Rabu Menafim

*Mishe-rabu ha-menafim pasku ha-mayim ha-marim* — when adulterers became numerous, the bitter waters of *sotah* ceased to function. The *sotah* waters test a wife whose husband suspects her. But the waters only worked when the husband himself was innocent of adultery. Once men were routinely committing adultery, the waters would no longer have the power to check their wives.

### Yochanan ben Zakkai

*Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai hifsikan* — it was Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai who formally discontinued the *sotah* waters, citing the verse: *lo efkod al benoteichem ki tizneina ve'al kaloteichem ki tinafna* — I will not punish your daughters when they fornicate, nor your daughters-in-law when they commit adultery. When the men of the generation are themselves guilty, the divine mechanism of the *sotah* waters is suspended.

### Mishe-Meit Yosi

*Mishe-meit Yosi ben Yoezer ish Tsereidah ve-Yosi ben Yehudah ish Yerushalayim batlu ha-eshkolot* — when Yosi ben Yoezer and Yosi ben Yehudah died — the earliest *zugot* recorded in *Pirkei Avot* — the *eshkolot* ceased. *Eshkol* means a cluster of grapes; the *gemara* uses it to describe Torah scholars who were complete, containing within themselves the totality of the tradition. With their deaths, gaps began to appear in the transmission. Debates multiplied because the tradition was no longer perfectly intact from teacher to student, and subsequent generations were simply not at the same level of comprehensive mastery. The verse cited is *ein eshkol le-echol bikurah ivta nafshi* — there is no longer a cluster to eat, no one of that completeness to be found.

### Yochanan Kohen Gadol

Yochanan Kohen Gadol instituted several reforms. He discontinued the *viduy ma'aser* — the declaration that the Torah requires be made every third year confirming that one has properly distributed all *ma'aser* from one's home. He also abolished the *me'orerim* and the *nokfim* — practices associated with the Temple which the *gemara* will explain further. He stopped the practice of metalworkers hammering and smelting in Jerusalem during *Chol HaMoed*, as the constant noise of work undermined the spirit of the festival and created a false impression for the populace that labor during *Chol HaMoed* was entirely permitted. And in his time, *ein tzarich lish'ol al demai* — one no longer had to inquire about *demai* produce, because he instituted the systematic taking of *terumot u-ma'asrot* from doubtfully-tithed produce, rendering the question practically resolved.

## Gemara Analysis

### Lo Yichupuhr

The *gemara* now analyzes the *mishnah*'s rulings systematically. First, on the question of how we know that finding the murderer after the *eglah arufah* does not exempt him: *talmud lomar ula-aretz lo yechupar la-dam asher shupach bah ki im be-dam shofcho* — the land requires the blood of the murderer for atonement; the *eglah arufah* atones for the communal dimension but cannot replace the execution of the murderer.

### Ed Echad Ne'eman

On the rule that a single witness saying "I saw" suspends the *eglah arufah* ritual: *ta'ama demachish leh ha lo machish leh ed echad ne'eman* — the reason that when one contradicts him they neutralize is that when the first witness stands uncontradicted, one witness is believed. *Minani mili* — from where do we derive this? From the verse *lo noda mi hikahu* — the ritual is only done when it is not known who the killer was. *Ha noda afilu echad besof ha'olam lo hayu orfin* — if it is known at all, even through a single witness anywhere, the neck is not broken. This is the basis for *ed echad* being believed in this context. The *gemara* also cites Rabbi Akiva: from the elders' declaration *ve'eineinu lo rau* — our eyes did not see it — we derive that if the *sanhedrin* itself had witnessed the murder without identifying the killer, they too would not perform the *eglah arufah*, even without a named individual witness.

### Kashya on Neutralization

This creates a difficulty. If one witness is believed — and Ulla's principle is that *kol makom she-heimina Torah ed echad harei kan shnayim* (wherever the Torah believes one witness, that witness counts as two) — then how can a subsequent single witness come and neutralize him? The one who said he saw has the weight of two; the one who says he did not see has only the weight of one. They should not cancel each other out.

### Ulla's Girsa

Ulla therefore emends the *mishnah*: *teni lo hayu orfin* — read the *mishnah* as "they would not break the neck" even in the case of one against one. The first witness, having been believed and having the weight of two witnesses, cannot be neutralized by a second who merely contradicts him. Rabbi Yitzchak agrees and makes the same emendation. The *mishnah* should be read: one against one — they do not break the neck, the first witness's testimony stands.

### Garsot HaMishnah

Rabbi Chiya, however, maintains the standard reading of the *mishnah* — *hayu orfin*, one against one they do neutralize and the neck is broken. How does he resolve Ulla's principle?

### Bat Achat v. Zeh Achar Z…

The resolution: *lo kashya, kan be-vat achat, kan be-zeh achar zeh* — there is no contradiction. It depends on timing. When both witnesses testify simultaneously — or at least before the first has been formally accepted — they neutralize each other, and the *mishnah*'s ruling of *hayu orfin* applies. When the first witness testified and was already accepted and treated as credible, only then does Ulla's principle apply: the second witness cannot retroactively neutralize the first. Rashi understands simultaneity as *toch kidei dibbur*; Tosafot understand it more broadly as any testimony that occurred before the *beit din* had formally acted on the first witness's account.

## Mishnah Complications

### Mishnah Structure

The *mishnah* presents cases in both directions: one witness against two, and two witnesses against one — with different outcomes depending on which side has the majority. But the *mishnah* never explicitly states the baseline case of one against one. This creates an inferential problem, since each of the two cases involving two against one seems to imply something contradictory about what happens in the intermediate case.

### Psulei Edut Resolution

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction by observing: *ella matnitin kula bi-psulei edut* — the *mishnah*'s two-against-one cases are addressing witnesses who are *psulei edut*, disqualified witnesses. This connects to the principle of Rabbi Nechemya.

### Rabbi Nechemya

Rabbi Nechemya teaches: *kol makom she-heimina Torah ed echad halech achar rov deot* — wherever the Torah believed one witness with special standing, when we move outside the realm of that specially-believed witness and deal instead with *psulei edut*, we follow a simple numbers game — majority of opinions. *Ve'asu shtei nashim be-ish echad ki-shnei anashim be-ish echad* — two women count against one man as two men count against one man. Within the domain of *psulei edut*, the arithmetic applies straightforwardly: two beats one regardless of gender.

### Shnei Nashim v. Ish

An alternative reading, however, maintains: *kol heicha de-ata ed echad me-ikara afilu meah nashim ke-chad dami* — if a *kasher* male witness testified first, even a hundred women subsequently cannot neutralize him, because his testimony has the full weight of two *kasher* witnesses. In that reading, the *mishnah*'s cases of two against one must involve a *pasul* as the initial witness, so that the two *psulot* can effectively neutralize.

### Why Mention Zwei?

If the principle is simply that two *psulei edut* neutralize one, why does the *mishnah* need to state both directions — two saying they saw against one saying they didn't, and two saying they didn't against one saying they did? *Mahu de-teima ki azlinan batar rov deot le-chumra aval le-kula lo* — one might have thought that the majority rule among *psulei edut* is applied only stringently — that is, only in the direction that prevents breaking the neck — but not leniently, to permit breaking the neck when two *psulei edut* say the murderer was not seen. Therefore the *mishnah* states both cases explicitly to teach that the numbers game applies in both directions.

### Conclusion

The *gemara*'s ultimate position can be summarized as follows. When a single *kasher* witness testifies that he saw the killer, he is believed to the extent that the *eglah arufah* ritual is suspended; this parallels the *ed echad* who is believed regarding *sotah*. If that witness testifies first and is accepted, a subsequent single witness cannot neutralize him. If they testify simultaneously, or before formal acceptance of the first, they neutralize.
