Two *kasher* witnesses subsequently can neutralize one *kasher* witness. When the witnesses involved are *psulei edut*, the rule follows simple numerical majority in either direction. Whether two *psulei edut* can neutralize a single *kasher* male witness who testified first depends on the dispute between the readings of Rabbi Nechemya — some holding that two women cannot overcome the specially-believed man, others holding that they can, provided the first witness was not of that specially-elevated status.

---

---

# Sotah 48

## Egla Arufa & Sota

### Egla Arufa

The daf opens with a *mishnah* establishing that when murderers increased, the practice of *egla arufa* — the beheaded heifer brought in cases of an unsolved murder — was discontinued. The *Tanna* explains the reasoning directly: *egla arufa* was instituted only for cases of doubt, where the killer was unknown. Once murderers were acting openly and brazenly, killing with impunity in full public view, the entire institutional logic of the ritual collapsed. Even if a particular case remained technically unsolved, a society in which murder was rampant and unpunished could no longer sustain the moral outrage and communal responsibility that *egla arufa* was designed to express.

### Sota Discontinued

Similarly, the *mishnah* records that when adulterers multiplied, the *sota* water ordeal was discontinued — tying the discussion back to the central theme of the tractate. A *beraita* is cited: *venizka ha'isha me'avon bizman she'ish menuke me'avon* — the waters test the wife only when the husband himself is clean from sin.

### Husband's Purity Required

What is striking here is the scope of "clean from sin." When this principle was discussed earlier in the tractate, the focus was specifically on the husband having violated the laws of *sota* — for example, by continuing to live with his wife after she had been warned. Here, however, the *Gemara* broadens the requirement to encompass any type of sin. The *beraita* cites the verse: *lo efkod al benoseichem ki tiznena* — "I will not punish your daughters when they fornicate" — with the continuation of the verse making clear that the reason God withholds punishment is that the men themselves are running after prostitutes.

### Sexual Sin Affects Test

The *Gemara* then anticipates a series of potential limitations. One might argue that only the husband's own sexual transgression disqualifies the water test, but not the sins of his sons or daughters. The verse, however, speaks of both daughters and daughters-in-law — *ve'al kaloseichem ki tena'afena* — extending the husband's responsibility to encompass the sexual conduct of his household members. A further objection suggests that perhaps only adultery (*avon eshet ish*) disqualifies the test, not general sexual immorality with an unmarried woman. The verse again responds: *ki heim im hazonot yepareidu* — "for they go off with prostitutes" — which is ordinary sexual violation rather than technical adultery, yet it is precisely this that renders the *mayim ha-marim* inoperative.

The *Gemara* then cites Rabbi Elazar's reading of the prophet's message to Israel: if you are careful about your own conduct, the waters will test your wives; if not, they will not. It is worth noting that *Rashi* reads *yepareidu* as deriving from *pered*, a mule — signifying habitual, animal-like fornication.

---

## Justice Perverted

### Pleasure & Perversion

The *mishnah* shifts to a broader catalogue of societal decline and its institutional consequences. When *ba'alei hana'ah* increased — people who sought ease and pleasure, who preferred comfort to rigorous effort — justice became perverted. *Rashi* clarifies that this does not refer to extreme hedonism, but simply to people who preferred to take life a little too easy, who were unwilling to do the hard work that genuine adjudication demands. From this complacency, *nit'avu hadinim* — judgments were distorted — and *venitkalkelu hama'asim* — actions in general became corrupted — since people sensed they could act with impunity. The result: *ve'ein no'ach ba'olam* — there is no pleasantness in the world, which *Rashi* interprets as God no longer taking pleasure in the world.

What is striking about this entire catalogue is that it focuses overwhelmingly on the corruption of justice and the courts, not on ritual violations or even general moral failures. The point seems to be that once the justice system is compromised — once judges can be influenced, flattered, or financially entangled — the entire fabric of society unravels. The *dayan* and the *beit din* send the decisive signal to society both practically and symbolically, and their failure reverberates through every domain.

### Partiality in Court

When *roei panim* increased in judgment — judges who showed favor to litigants, not necessarily through outright bribery but through personal recognition and partiality — the prohibition *lo taguru mipnei ish* ceased to operate, and the injunction *lo takiru panim* was abandoned. Judges became responsive to who stood before them rather than to the demands of *din emet*. The consequence: they cast off the yoke of heaven and took upon themselves the yoke of *basar vadam* — flesh and blood — since the faces of the litigants now exerted more influence on their rulings than the awareness that they were conducting *din shamayim* and would answer to God.

### Lawyers' Influence

When *lochashei lechishot b'din* increased — those who whispered in court — divine anger intensified among Israel and the *Shechinah* withdrew. *Rashi* here clarifies that these are not practitioners of incantation but rather the legal advocates, *orchei dayanim*, who would whisper into the ears of the judges, attempting to find them an angle of acquittal for their client. The verse is invoked: *b'kerev Elohim yishpot* — judgment is conducted in the presence of God — and when it is subverted through this kind of behind-the-scenes manipulation, God is, as it were, removed from the proceeding.

### Profit Over Truth

When people's hearts followed after gain — *acharei bitzam libam holech* — the *Gemara* records that *rabu ha'omrim lara tov velatov ra*: people began calling bad good and good bad. The dynamic is recognizable: when profit is the dominant motivation, truth becomes a casualty, flattery replaces honest speech, and people say whatever is needed to get ahead. The *pasuk* in the *navi* continues with *hoy hoy ba'olam* — woe, woe to the world — and this, the *mishnah* observes, became the prevailing condition.

### Haughtiness & Marriage

When *moshchei harok* increased — those who draw out their speech in an act of self-important haughtiness — *rabu hayehirim*, the arrogant multiplied, and *venitma'atu hatalmidim*, Torah scholars decreased. *Rashi* invokes the principle that haughtiness is a sign of Torah poverty: *siman legasut haruach aniyut shel Torah*. Perhaps the connection is that when people are focused on external performance and on projecting status, the genuine internal investment that Torah learning demands is neglected. Consequently, *vehaTorah chozeret al lomdeha* — the Torah goes searching for those who will truly devote themselves to it.

The social consequence follows directly: when the haughty multiplied, *hitchilu bnot Yisrael lehinase layehirim* — women began marrying such men — because *she'ein dorenu ro'eh ela lifnim*, the generation sees only the external presentation and cannot perceive whether the status on display has been genuinely earned.

### Haughtiness Objection

The *Gemara* raises an obvious objection. We have a principle: *hai man demayahir afilu inish beiteih lo mikabli leih* — someone who is haughty is not even tolerated by the members of his own household. The verse is cited: *gever yahir velo yanveh* — the haughty man cannot even dwell in his own home, because his household sees through him and will not abide him. How then can it be said that women are attracted to such men?

The *Gemara* resolves the tension: *me'ikara kaftza leih* — initially, before the man is known, he appears distinguished and is eagerly sought in marriage. *Ulevasof mitzla leih* — but once he is married and his wife comes to know him for what he truly is, he becomes lowly in her eyes. The attraction and the disillusionment are sequential, not contradictory.

### Judges' Investments

When *matilei melai al ba'alei batim* increased — when judges began placing their money with businessmen to invest on their behalf — bribery increased and justice was perverted. The problem, it should be noted, is not anonymized investment in a general fund; it is the specific entanglement between a judge and particular businessmen who offer to handle his money as a personal favor. The judge who benefits from such an arrangement cannot adjudicate impartially in any dispute touching those businessmen or their interests. The result: *raba hashochar*, bribery increased, *vehatayas mishpat*, justice was tilted, *vepaska tova*, and all good ceased.

### Acceptance of Favors

When people multiplied who would say — in a context of judges and community members — "thank you for the favor you did for me," acknowledging and accepting kindnesses from those who might come before them in court, the consequence was *ish hayashar be'einav ya'aseh* — everyone acted as they saw fit, secure in the knowledge that the judges were indebted to them. *Shfalim hugbehu vehagvohim hushpelu* — the low were raised up and the high brought low — and *malchusa azla venavla*, governance collapsed entirely.

### Stinginess & Robbery

When the stingy (*tsarei ayin*) and those who seize what belongs to others (*torfei teref* — *Rashi* reads this simply as *gazlanim*, robbers) increased, *rabu ma'amitsei halev* — those of hardened heart multiplied — and *vekofsei hayadayim*, those who close their hands against lending, increased. The *Gemara* connects this explicitly to the Torah's warning: *hishamer lecha pen yihyeh im levavcha* — be careful that your heart does not harbor the miserly thought that withholds a loan, especially as *shemita* approaches. Whether stinginess produces robbery or the two are manifestations of the same underlying character, the *Gemara* groups them together as forces that produce a society of closed hearts and closed hands.

### Seductive Women

When *netuyot garon umeshakrot einayim* increased — women of outstretched necks and beckoning eyes, acting in a manner calculated to attract male attention — *rabu mayim hamarim* should, in theory, have increased as well, since the prevalence of such behavior would presumably generate more cases of suspected adultery warranting the *sota* ordeal. Instead, *pasku* — the ordeal ceased — because by that point the practice had already been suspended: the husbands themselves were not clean from sin, rendering the bitter water inoperative in any case.

### Gift-Taking

When those who accept gifts (*mekablei matanos*) increased, *nitma'atu hayamim veniktseru hashanim* — days diminished and years shortened. People lived shorter lives. The proof-text is direct: *veson'eh matanos yichyeh* — only one who hates gifts will live. It is notable that this consequence — shortened lifespan — is among the more overtly divine punishments in this catalogue, most of which operate through more recognizable social and political mechanisms.

### Arrogance & Disputes

When the arrogant of heart (*zechuchei halev*) increased, *rabu machlokes b'Yisrael* — disputes among Israel multiplied — because students no longer devoted their full energies to attending upon their teachers and mastering what they were being taught. The *mishnah* then makes this explicit with the famous statement: when the disciples of Shammai and Hillel who had not adequately served their teachers (*shelo shimshu kol tzorkan*) increased, debates multiplied and *na'asu Torah kishetei Toros* — the Torah became as though it were two Torahs. Until that moment, there had been virtually nothing debated in *Torah she-ba'al peh*; after it, the great controversies that characterize Talmudic literature took hold.

---

## Yosi ben Yoezer

### Eshkol Ceased

When Yosi ben Yoezer died, *batlu ha-eshkolos* — the *eshkolot* ceased. The *Gemara* asks: what is an *eshkol*? Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel explains: *ish she-hakol bo* — a person in whom everything is contained, a completely rounded *talmid chacham*. This connects directly to what was just said: the era of undisputed transmission ended, the unbroken *Mesorah* was disrupted — or even if not every *halacha* had been transmitted explicitly by *Mesorah*, there had been sufficient unanimity and consensus that any given question could be settled. After Yosi ben Yoezer's death, the great debates began.

### Yochanan Abolishes Viduy

The *mishnah* turns to the reforms of Yochanan the High Priest. He abolished the *viduy ma'aser* — the declaration made when presenting the tithe distribution after the three-year cycle, in which one attests to having distributed correctly.

### Ma'aser to Kohanim

The *Gemara* asks: what was his reason? One might have assumed the answer fits naturally into the theme of societal decline — perhaps people were no longer distributing correctly and the declaration had become a fiction. But Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina gives a different reason entirely: the problem was not individual dishonesty but a systemic departure from the Torah's prescription. The Torah requires *ma'aser rishon* to be given to *Levi'im* — *de-rachmana amar di-yehavi le-Levi'im* — but the practice had become to give it to *kohanim* instead. This shift had come about as a *kenas*, a penalty, against the *Levi'im* who had not returned to the land in the time of Ezra. Since *kohanim* are themselves *Levi'im*, the technical obligation was technically satisfied — but the declaration *vegam netativ la-Levi* could no longer be recited honestly, because the *ma'aser* was manifestly not going to the *Levi'im* as the Torah had specified.

What is remarkable about this juxtaposition is the way it complicates the preceding narrative of decline. Throughout that narrative, societal corruption produces institutional failure. Here, however, it is a *takkanah* of *Chazal* that caused the divergence from the Torah's ideal — and the reason for that *takkanah* was itself rooted in an earlier failure, the *Levi'im*'s failure to return with Ezra. Even five hundred years before the events under discussion, cracks were already appearing in the edifice of ideal Torah observance.

The *Gemara* raises a further question: if the *viduy* was blocked only by the first clause — *vegam netativ la-Levi* — why not recite the rest of the *viduy* formula while omitting that clause? Reish Lakish explains: a *viduy* that cannot begin with *ma'aser rishon* cannot continue with the rest of the *ma'asrot*. Abaye identifies the reason: since the *katuv* opens with *ma'aser rishon*, a declaration that cannot include it cannot proceed at all.

### Demai Ordinance

The *Gemara* adds that Yochanan also instituted the law of *demai* — the requirement that produce purchased from an *am ha'aretz* be treated as doubtful with respect to tithe separation.

### Am Ha'aretz Practices

The reason was empirical. Yochanan sent agents throughout all the borders of Israel and observed that *ammei ha'aretz* were routinely separating only *terumah gedolah*, while *ma'aser rishon* and *ma'aser sheni* were observed inconsistently — some separating them, some not. They assumed that *terumah gedolah* required attention, since eating it untithed is punishable by death at divine hands, but regarded the other obligations as less urgent.

### Heavenly Warnings

Yochanan gathered the people and delivered a striking teaching: just as *terumah gedolah* carries the sin of death, so too does *terumat ma'aser* and *tevel* — grain from which *terumat ma'aser* has not been taken. The underlying logic is precise: if one does not separate *ma'aser rishon*, the *terumat ma'aser* that the *Levi* would have been obligated to separate from that *ma'aser* remains embedded within the produce — and that *terumat ma'aser* renders the entire quantity *tevel* subject to the *chiyyuv mitah*. So the *am ha'aretz* who neglects *ma'aser rishon* is not merely failing to give the *Levi* his due; he is leaving the buyer's produce in a state of genuine *tevel*.

The question then arises: to whom exactly was Yochanan delivering this message? A close reading of *Rashi* suggests it was addressed not to the *ammei ha'aretz* themselves but to the *chaverim* — the observant scholars who were purchasing from them. They were the ones who needed to understand that when they bought produce from an *am ha'aretz*, they could not assume proper tithe separation had occurred; the obligation to complete the separation rested with them.

The *Gemara* then harmonizes the apparently contradictory accounts — one suggesting that *ammei ha'aretz* were in fact separating all required *ma'asrot*, another suggesting they were not — by concluding that Yochanan established two separate measures: first, he abolished the *viduy* even for *chaverim* separating from their own grain, because the first clause could not honestly be recited; second, he imposed the *demai* ordinance on produce purchased from *ammei ha'aretz*, requiring buyers to complete whatever tithe separations might have been omitted.

---

## Yochanan's Reforms

### Abolished Wake-Upers

Yochanan the High Priest also abolished the practice of the *me'orerim* — the "wake-upers." Every day the *Levi'im* would ascend the *duchan* and, before their singing, would call out: *urah lamah tishan Hashem* — "Awake, why do You sleep, O God?" Yochanan put an end to this. He argued: *vechi yesh sheinah lifnei hamakom*? Is there sleep before God? Has it not already been stated: *hinei lo yanum velo yishan shomer Yisrael* — "Behold, the Guardian of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps"?

His response was not to deny that the verse had a legitimate metaphorical meaning — the *Gemara* acknowledges that *urah lamah tishan* is appropriate language when Israel is suffering and the nations are at ease, as a way of saying, "How can You allow this to continue?" But that is not appropriate as a daily declaration in the *Beit HaMikdash*, and the fact that Yochanan needed to explain it as metaphor implies that the *Levi'im* had been reciting it in something closer to its literal sense. How this practice ever began in the middle of the Second Temple period, when the situation was not necessarily one of acute national tragedy, is a striking and somewhat disturbing question.

### Abolished Scratching

Yochanan also abolished the *nokfim* — the "bangers." Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel explains: they would scratch the animal between its eyes so that blood would run into them, confusing the animal and making it easier to slaughter without it thrashing. Yochanan abolished this because *demechazi kib'al mum* — it resembles a *mum*, a disqualifying blemish.

A *beraita* teaches a related practice: some would strike the animal with sticks — in the manner performed before pagan worship — to stun it before slaughter. Yochanan objected to this as well, decrying it with the words: "How long will you feed *neveilot* to the altar?" The *Gemara* objects: a properly slaughtered animal is not a *neveilah*. The *Gemara* corrects: not *neveilah* but *tereifot* — by striking the animal violently you may have perforated the membrane of the brain (*nikev krum shel moach*), rendering it a *tereifah*. It is worth noting that the *beraita* describes the striking as resembling pagan practice, connecting this concern back to the earlier abolition of the *me'orerim* — both practices had acquired an uncomfortably pagan appearance.

### Rings for Animals

In place of the striking with sticks, Yochanan instituted *tabaot bakarka* — rings fixed in the ground through which the animals' heads could be placed, holding them steady during *shechita* without any risk of injury.

### Blacksmith Hammer

He also stopped the sound of the blacksmith's hammer in Jerusalem on *Chol HaMoed*. Until his time, *devar ha'avad* — the principle that work which would cause irretrievable loss may be performed on *Chol HaMoed* — had been applied liberally enough that the hammer of the smithy was audible throughout the city. Yochanan found this too public and too permissive a signal, and he put an end to it.

---

## Sanhedrin & Song

### Sanhedrin Gone

The *mishnah* declares: *mishebatlah Sanhedrin batel hashir mibeit hamishtaot* — when the *Sanhedrin* ceased, song ceased from the drinking houses. The proof-text: *bashir lo yishtu yayin* — "they shall not drink wine with song." This is a striking formulation. The cessation of song is usually associated in the tradition with the *Churban Beit HaMikdash*, but here it is connected specifically to the *Sanhedrin*. The connection is not arbitrary: the entire arc of this section of the tractate has been about the corrupted justice system and the failure of the courts and their authority. The *Sanhedrin* is the apex of that system, and its disappearance extinguishes the institutional structure that had kept society intact — and with it, the capacity for genuine joy.

The *Gemara* then raises the question of whether this statement is purely descriptive — recording that joy ceased when the *Sanhedrin* fell — or also prescriptive, directing that song should not be practiced today.

### Biblical Proof

The verse establishing the connection between the *Sanhedrin* and song is supplied by Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua: *zkeinim misha'ar shavatu bachurim miginatam* — "the elders have ceased from the gate, and the young men from their music." The elders in the gate are the *beit din*, and their departure takes the young men's music with it.

### Song Prohibition

Rav then rules prescriptively: *ozna d'shama zimra te'aker* — an ear that hears song nowadays should be uprooted. One should not be listening to music at all, as an expression of mourning and loss. Whether this applies to all song or specifically to instrumental music is not spelled out here, though the term *zemer* could carry connotations of instrumental performance.

### Song Brings Destruction

Rava adds: *zimra beveita churba beseifa* — song in the household brings destruction at its threshold. The proof is from the verse: *kol yeshorer bachalon chorev basaf* — the sound of singing at the window, destruction at the threshold. Rabbi Yitzchak draws out the full force of this: even a house surrounded by cedars — seemingly impregnable and protected — will not be spared. *Mitro'eia*, it will be shattered. Rav Ashi adds: from this verse we also learn that destruction, when it comes, begins at the threshold — *ki matchali churba beseifa matchali*. An additional verse supports this: *vesha'iyah yukat sha'ar* — its desolation is smitten at the gate.

---

## Song Ban Failed

### Rav Huna's Attempt

Rav Huna attempted to move from the theoretical to the practical and actually annul song within his community. The result was economic devastation. A hundred geese could be had for a *zuz* and a hundred *sa'im* of wheat for a *zuz* — and yet no one wanted to buy. Prices collapsed not because supply had increased but because the prohibition on song had drained all joy from life, leaving people without the will to engage in normal commerce and consumption.

### Rav Chisda Reverses

Rav Chisda came and overturned the prohibition — disparaging it, or perhaps himself demonstrating that it was not to be enforced. The economic reversal was immediate: a single goose now cost a *zuz* and could not be found. Joy returned, demand surged, and prosperity was restored. The *Gemara* does not explicitly endorse either Rav Huna's stringency or Rav Chisda's reversal, but the narrative arc makes the practical lesson clear: however principled the mourning behind the song prohibition may be, its full enforcement produces consequences that are themselves destructive. Society cannot function in a state of enforced joylessness.

---

## Song Distinctions

### Permitted vs. Forbidden

Rav Huna himself, even while seeking to restrict song, draws a distinction: *zimra denagdei udevakrei shari* — song used to lead cattle is permitted, because it serves a functional purpose in the work. *Degarda'ei asir* — but song sung by weavers for their own entertainment is forbidden, because it is simply *stam* pleasure with no connection to any necessary task. This distinction also supports the observation that the prohibition is not limited specifically to musical instruments — the issue seems to be the nature and purpose of the singing rather than its medium.

### Mixed-Gender Singing

Rav Yosef introduces a distinction that is widely cited in *halachic* literature in discussions of *kol isha* and related matters. If men are singing and women respond to them responsively — *zimrei gavrei ve'anei nashei* — this is *pritzuta*, general sexual looseness. But if women are singing and men are responding — *zimrei nashei ve'anei gavrei* — the situation is far more serious: *ke'esh bene'oret*, like fire in flax. The men, waiting for their cue, focus intensely on the women's singing; the potential for genuine transgression is far greater.

### Priority Elimination

The *Gemara* then asks: what is the practical difference between the two levels? They are both problematic. The answer: *levatulei hai mikamei hai* — to tell us which to eliminate first if one cannot eliminate both. The *Gemara*'s realism here is notable. Not every wrong in society can be stamped out simultaneously; sometimes one must prioritize. If forced to choose, eliminate the women-led responsive singing, since it is the more combustible of the two. This principle — that practical *halacha* must account for what can and cannot be achieved — resonates directly with the earlier episode of Rav Huna and Rav Chisda.

---

## Five Punishments

### Music & Punishment

Rabbi Yochanan teaches: *kol hashoteh be'arba'ah minei zemer meivi chamesh puraniyot la'olam* — whoever drinks with four types of musical instruments brings five punishments upon the world. The verse is from the *navi*: *vehaya kinor vanevel tof vachalil veyayin mishteihem* — it was the *kinor* (harp), *nevel* (lyre), *tof* (cymbal), *chalil* (flute), and wine their drink — *ve'et po'al Hashem lo yabitu*, and the acts of God they do not see. It should be noted that the people described in these verses are not simply listening to music at a religious celebration; they are rising early in the morning to run after *shechar* and staying late into the night inflamed by wine. The music is a feature of a thoroughgoing lifestyle of excess and indifference.

### Exile & Famine

What follows from this? *Mah ketiv achrav* — what does the text say afterward? *Lachen gala ami mibli da'at* — therefore My people will go into exile for lack of knowledge: *she-gormim galut la'olam*, this behavior causes exile. *Ukhevodo metei ra'av* — and their honored ones will die of hunger: *she-mevi'im ra'av la'olam*, it brings famine. *Vehamono tzecheih tzamah* — and its multitude is parched with thirst — read metaphorically: *she-gormim la-Torah she-tishtakach mi-lomdeiha*, it causes Torah to be forgotten by those who learn it, since Torah is likened to water.

### Righteous Diminished

*Vayishach adam vayishpel ish* — a person is humbled and a man is brought low: *she-gormim shiflut le-son'o shel HaKadosh Baruch Hu* — it even brings humiliation to the One Who is called the enemy of sin, which is to say God Himself, since *ein ish ela HaKadosh Baruch Hu* — the term *ish* alludes to God, as the verse says *Hashem ish milchama*. And *veinei gevohim tishpalna* — the eyes of those held high will be brought low: *she-gormim shiflut shel Yisrael*, it diminishes Israel. The final consequence: *hirchiva she'ol nafsha ufa'ara piha livli chok* — the depths have opened their mouth without limit, consuming all glory.

---

## Urim & Tumim

### First Prophets Died

The *mishnah* records: *mishemetu nevi'im rishonim batlu urim vetumim* — when the first prophets died, the *urim vetumim* ceased to function. The phrasing is precise: it was not that the physical *urim vetumim* disappeared, but that they ceased to deliver answers.

### First Prophets Listed

Rav Huna identifies the "first prophets" as David, Solomon, and Samuel — an early and distinguished group. According to this view, the *urim vetumim* lost its efficacy already in that era. Rav Nachman qualifies: in the time of David it was not entirely defunct — *zimen solek vezimen lo solek*, sometimes an inquiry would receive a response and sometimes not. When Tzadok the *kohen* consulted it, he received an answer; when Avyatar did, he did not — as the verse implies when it records that Avyatar was removed from his position.

One might wonder whether David himself qualifies as a *navi*, since the *mishnah* uses the term *nevi'im rishonim*. It is a legitimate question; while David is known for his close association with prophets, he is not typically listed among them.

### First Destruction

The *Gemara* tests the claim that the *urim vetumim* ceased so early against a verse: *vayehi lidrosh Elokim kol yemei Zecharya hameivin bire'ot Elokim* — it was there to inquire of God all the days of Zecharya who understood the visions of God. This Zecharya — *Rashi* identifies him as the son of Yehoyada — lived very late in the period of the kings, well after David and Solomon. Does this not show the *urim vetumim* was operative until much later? The *Gemara* deflects: *lo, bineviim* — no, they would inquire of God through prophets, not through *urim vetumim*. The verse is about prophetic consultation, not the priestly oracle.

A second *tanna'itic* source proves more decisive: *mishecharav Beit HaMikdash rishon batlu arei migrash, upasku urim vetumim, upasak melech mibeit David* — from the time the First Temple was destroyed, the cities of the *Levi'im* ceased, the *urim vetumim* ceased, and kingship from the house of David ended. This connects the *urim vetumim* definitively to the destruction of the First Temple, not to the earlier era of David and Solomon.

A final text from the Second Temple period — the *tirshata's* declaration that certain *kohanim* of uncertain lineage must refrain from eating sacred food *ad amod kohen le-urim vetumim*, until a *kohen* arises who can consult the *urim vetumim* — might seem to suggest that restoration was imminent. The *Gemara* firmly rejects this reading: that phrase means nothing of the sort. It is like one person saying to another: "until the dead are revived and *Mashiach ben David* comes." It points to the eschaton, not to the near term.

In view of all this, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak redefines "first prophets" in the *mishnah*: the phrase means to the exclusion of the *last* prophets — Chaggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. These three prophesied at the very beginning of the Second Temple period, and the *urim vetumim* ceased no later than their time.

### Last Prophets

A *beraita* confirms: when Chaggai, Zechariah, and Malachi died, *nistalka ruach hakodesh miYisrael* — divine inspiration departed from Israel. These were the last of the *nevi'im*. After them, there was no more *nevuah*.

### Bat Kol

And yet — *ve'af al pi chen hayu mishtamshim bebat kol* — even after prophecy ceased, they would make use of a *bat kol*, a heavenly voice. This was not *ruach hakodesh* proper; it was a more attenuated form of divine communication, and its precise phenomenological character invites reflection. It is worth noting that while in the *Bavli* a *bat kol* is consistently presented as a miraculous heavenly voice, Saul Lieberman has demonstrated that in the *Yerushalmi* the term more often means something like a widely circulating report — a *shemuah* that spreads and acquires the status of near-certain information. The degree to which the *Bavli*'s *bat kol* was experienced as a literally miraculous auditory phenomenon or as a form of divinely inspired collective intuition is itself a question the text leaves open.

### Jericho Bat Kol

Once, the Sages were gathered at a meal in the upper room of the house of Gurya in Jericho, when a *bat kol* issued from heaven declaring: *yesh bachem adam echad sherauy shetishre Shechinah alav* — there is among you one person upon whom the divine presence could rest. The declaration itself is poignant in its implications: there is someone here worthy of *nevuah*, but the *bat kol* goes on to add — *ela she'ein doro rauy lekach* — the generation is not fit for it. The very vehicle of the announcement, the *bat kol*, thus serves simultaneously to identify prophetic potential and to explain why prophecy cannot be restored.

### Hillel Identified

All eyes turned to Hillel the Elder — the assembled Sages recognized immediately who was being described. When Hillel died, the eulogy over him invoked the language of loss: *hei chasid, hei anav, talmido shel Ezra* — woe to the pious man, woe to the humble man, disciple of Ezra. The designation *talmido shel Ezra* is not biographical but typological: as Ezra had embodied the transmission of *Torah she-ba'al peh* in his generation, so Hillel embodied it in his — the continuation of an unbroken spiritual lineage.

### Samuel the Small

A second *bat kol* came, this time at a gathering in Yavneh, with the identical declaration: one person among them is worthy of the *Shechinah*'s resting upon him, but the generation is not fit. This time all eyes turned to *Shmuel haKatan* — Samuel the Small — a student of Hillel in the same typological sense, spiritually his disciple even though Hillel had lived roughly a hundred and fifty years earlier. When Shmuel haKatan died, his eulogy echoed Hillel's: *hei anav, hei chasid, talmido shel Hillel*.

What is particularly remarkable is that at the moment of his death, Shmuel haKatan uttered a prophecy: *Shimon veYishmael lecharba, vachavro leketala, usha'ar ama leviza, ve'akan sagi'in atidin lemeti al ama* — Shimon and Yishmael are destined for the sword, their colleagues for slaughter, the rest of the nation for despoilment, and great travails will come upon the people. This refers to Rabban Shimon haNasi and Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha, among the *asara harugei malchut* — the ten martyrs of the Hadrianic persecutions, placing Shmuel haKatan at or near the time of the *Churban*. The *bat kol* had identified him as worthy of *nevuah*; this dying prophecy represents, it seems, at least a partial fulfillment of that verdict — something approaching, if not fully achieving, the *hashraat haShechina* that was declared his due.

### Yehuda ben Bava

A similar *hesped* was sought for Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava — they wished to say the same *hei chasid, hei anav* over him — but *nitrefa hasha'ah*, the opportunity was lost. Since he was among the *harugei malchut*, the martyrs executed by the Roman government, they could not deliver a public eulogy over him without incurring dangerous attention from the authorities.

---

## Shamir & Miracles

### Shamir Worm

With the destruction of the First Temple, the *shamir* was lost. A *beraita* records: *shamir shebo bana Shlomo et Beit HaMikdash* — the *shamir* was the means by which Solomon built the Temple.

### Metal Vessels Debate

The basis for this claim is the verse: *vehabayit behibanoto even shlemah masa nivnah* — the Temple was built with complete stones brought from the quarry. Rabbi Yehuda reads this literally: no metal tools were used at all; the stones were hewn from the quarry in their final form and brought as they were. Rabbi Nechemya objects: can this really be maintained? Another verse states clearly that the stones were *meGuzorot baMegeirah* — hewn with a metal saw. What then is the meaning of the prohibition on metal in the *Beit HaMikdash*? Rabbi Nechemya explains: *shehaya matkin mibachutz umachnis mibifnim* — the metal work was done off-site, and only the finished stones were brought to the Temple Mount, where no sound of metal was heard.

Rav attempts a synthesis: Rabbi Yehuda's position applies to the stones of the *Mikdash* proper — no metal was used on them at any stage — while Rabbi Nechemya's position, permitting off-site metal work, applies to the stones of Solomon's palace. On this reading, Rabbi Nechemya has no need of the *shamir* for the Temple stones at all.

### Shamir & Breastplate

But according to Rabbi Nechemya, who permits metal work off-site, why was the *shamir* needed at all? The answer comes from a *beraita*: the stones of the *efod* — the breastplate of the High Priest, upon which the twelve names of the tribes were engraved — presented a unique set of constraints. They could not be inscribed with ink, because the verse says *pituchei chotam*, carved engraving. But they also could not be cut with a metal awl, because the verse says *bimlu'otam*, they must be complete — nothing may be removed. The solution: the name was written in ink on the surface of the stone, the stone was then shown to the *shamir* — *umar'eh lahem shamir mibachutz* — and the *shamir*, following the path of the ink, caused the stone to split open precisely along those lines. *Vehen nivka'ot me'aleihen* — they would crack of their own accord, like a fig splitting in summer heat or a crevice opening in the earth during the rainy season, so that nothing was removed and the stone remained *malu'ot*, complete.

### Shamir Properties

The *shamir* was created at twilight on the eve of the first Sabbath — among the items listed in *Pirkei Avot* as created at *bein hashemashot*. *Ve'ein kol davar kashe yakhol la'amod befanav* — nothing hard can withstand it. This raises the obvious question: what vessel can contain it? If it eats through everything, what does one keep it in? *Korkhin oto bisfogin shel tzemer, uminichin oto be'itanei shel avar, mele'ah suvei se'orin* — it is wrapped in wool and placed in a lead container filled with barley bran. The logic is the same as — and apparently analogous to — the use of soft or pliable materials to contain highly corrosive or penetrating substances: the very softness of the material is what neutralizes the *shamir*'s destructive capacity.

---

## Lost Blessings

### Silk & Glass Lost

Rav Ami teaches: *mishecharav mikdash rishon batla shira paranda uzkhukhit levana* — from the destruction of the First Temple, *shira paranda* (a type of fine silk) and clear white glass were lost. A *beraita* confirms this and adds further losses: *rekhev barzel*, iron chariots, were also lost. Some say even *yayin karush haba mi-Shanir* — a congealed wine from Mount Senir that resembled pressed fig rounds — was lost. It could be used a little at a time and reconstituted with water, making it a kind of ancient concentrated wine.

### Nofet Tzufim

Also lost: *nofet tzufim*. Rav explains: *solet shetzafa al gabei nafa* — a finest flour so rich that it would adhere to the top of the sieve rather than passing through, and it resembled dough kneaded with honey and oil.

### Alternative Explanations

Levi offers a different interpretation: *shtei kikkarot hanidbakot batanur* — two loaves placed at opposite walls of the oven that would expand and rise until they touched each other in the middle. This recalls the discussion of the original blessing of dough, and the implication is clear: once the blessing departed from bread, loaves no longer expanded with such abundance.

### Wildflower Honey

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi identifies *nofet tzufim* as honey coming from *tzufim* — the highlands, the mountains. The word *nofet* suggests dripping, and *tzufim* here is read as the high places — hence wildflower honey gathered by bees from the mountain grasses. Rav Sheshet's *targum* of a verse about bees — *kema denitzan devyata veshaitan beruma alma, umaskan duvsha me'ishbei tura* — supports this: the finest honey comes from bees that soar to the heights and bring down honey from the mountain grasses.

The *Gemara* then connects this to a *mishnah* elsewhere: *kol hanitzok tahor* — anything poured from one vessel to another does not create a link (*tziruf*) that would transmit impurity back to the upper vessel. The exception is honey of *Zifim* and *tzapichin* — pressed honey cakes so thick and congealed they form a solid mass, so that if the lower portion becomes *tamei*, the upper portion is *tamei* as well. What is *dvash Zifim*? Rabbi Yochanan says it is honey so potent that one can adulterate other honey with it without the blend being detected — it can be used for "cutting" lesser honey. Reish Lakish maintains that *Zifim* is simply a place name, as the verse *Zif veTelem uVe'alot* confirms — a town in the territory of Yehuda, and the same place mentioned in the incident when the people of Zif informed Saul of David's whereabouts. Rabbi Yochanan, separately, interprets *anshei haZifim* in that narrative as people who falsify their words — *mezayefim divreihem* — while Rabbi Elazar maintains it is simply the place name.

---

## People of Faith

### Faith Ceased

*Upasku anshei amanah miYisrael* — the people of faith ceased from Israel. Rabbi Yitzchak explains: these are people who genuinely, fully believe in God — *ma'aminim b'HaKadosh Baruch Hu* in the deepest sense.

### High Faith Standard

What level of faith did they possess? Rabbi Eliezer the Great articulates the standard: *kol mi she-yesh lo pat besalo ve'omer mah ochal lemachaR* — whoever has bread in his pantry and says "what will I eat tomorrow?" — that person is among the *katnei emunah*, those of small faith. The bar is extraordinarily high: if you have food today and are already worrying about tomorrow, you lack complete trust in divine providence.

### Righteous Lack Faith

The consequence reaches even the *tzadikim* of later generations. Rabbi Elazar expounds the verse *ki mi vaz l'yom katanot* — who has despised the day of smallness? — as a question: what caused the righteous to have their table diminished in the world to come, not receiving the full reward they deserve? *Katanut she-hayah bahen* — the smallness that was in them; even the righteous of our time lack complete *emunah*, worrying about their material provision in this world. *She-lo he'eminu b'HaKadosh Baruch Hu* — they did not fully trust that God would provide. Measure for measure, their heavenly table in the world to come will not be complete either.

---

---

# Sotah 49

## Emuna & Yeridas Hadoros

### Eliezer: Bread & Faith

The final daf of Masechet Sotah picks up at the very bottom of 48b, and the overarching theme — that since the destruction of the *beit hamikdash* everything has gone to pot — frames the entire discussion. The Gemara opens with a statement attributed to Rabbi Yitzchak: *upasku anshei emuna* — the people of faith have ceased. Who are these people of faith? They are those who truly believe in God with complete trust. A *baraita* is cited: Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol says that anyone who has bread in his basket and worries about what he will eat tomorrow is among those of little faith — *mikatnei emuna*. God will provide for tomorrow; anxiety about tomorrow's sustenance reflects an incomplete trust in divine providence.

Rabbi Eliezer further interprets the verse *ki mi baz leyom katnut* — who has despised a day of smallness? — as referring to the righteous whose tables in the *olam haba* will not be fully laden. Why? *Katnut shehayah bahem* — because of the smallness that was in them, meaning that even they did not maintain complete faith in God. This is a striking formulation: even the righteous, if they harbored some anxiety about their livelihood, are measured accordingly, a case of *mida kneged mida*, in which their table in the future world is diminished because they did not fully trust that God would fill it in this world.

### Rava: Young Wicked

Rava offers a sharp reinterpretation of the very same verse. He says: *elu katnei bnei reshei Yisrael* — these are the young children of wicked Jews. These are children who died young, presumably on account of punishment visited upon their wicked fathers. The phrase *ki mi baz leyom katnut* is read by Rava as a reference to those who diminish the judgment deserved by the fathers in the world to come — *shemevazin dina deavihem leatid lavo*. These children argue before God: *Ribono shel olam*, if You were going to exact full punishment from our fathers in the future world, why did You blunt their teeth already — why did You cause us to die young? Our early death should count as partial atonement for our fathers' sins.

This is quite an interesting twist on the theme, and it does not obviously connect to the surrounding discussion of *emuna*. Normally one might be satisfied to see the wicked punished, yet here there is a note of compassion: even the wicked suffer when they lose young children, and at least that suffering ought to count for something as partial atonement *leatid lavo*.

### David's Prayer

Rabbi Ilai bar Yevarchia offers a statement: were it not for the prayer of David, all of Israel would have been reduced to selling *rivav* — some lowly commodity that only the poor are reduced to peddling. The verse cited is *shisa Hashem mora lahem* — God, place upon them a teacher, or give them mastery. Rashi explains this by tracing the context: the preceding verse reads *ki lo lanetzach yishachach evyon* — God will not eternally forget the poor — *tikvat aniyim tovad la'ad* — the hope of the lowly shall not be lost forever. Rashi reads *mora* as *marut* — mastery or status — and understands the verse as David's prayer on behalf of the poor, asking God to give them some standing in this world, so that the nations who look upon them with a degree of honor should know that they are merely human and not divine.

The precise connection of this statement to the theme of *emuna* is not entirely transparent. Perhaps the link is that David's prayer relates to anxiety about financial well-being, or to the general suffering of poverty discussed in the surrounding passages. Rabbi Ilai bar Yevarchia is mentioned again immediately for additional teachings, and the repeated citation of the same *amora* may itself be the editorial thread connecting these passages.

### Chabakuk Prayer

Rabbi Ilai bar Yevarchia further states: what was the function of the prayer of Chabakuk? *Habat talmidei chachamim shemiskasim betalis achas* — that Torah scholars so impoverished that they would share a single garment between them, and yet continue to learn Torah together, should be sustained. The image captures both their devotion and their destitution.

The verse cited is from Chabakuk: *Hashem shamati shimacha yarasi* — I have heard Your report and I was awed — *bekerev shanim chayeihu* — in the midst of years give it life. The Gemara reads *bekerev shanim* not as "in the midst of years" but as *bekiruv shnayim* — in the proximity of two people — *chayeihu* — give them life, give them *parnasa*. Who are those who hear God's message and witness God's deeds? Those who study Torah. So the prayer of Chabakuk on behalf of those two Torah scholars sharing a single garment is that God sustain them with a livelihood. This, too, connects to the broader theme of faith and sustenance: even in the most desperate circumstances, one who learns Torah out of poverty can trust that his prayer — or the prayer of the great — will be heard on his behalf.

### No Torah Discourse

Rabbi Ilai bar Yevarchia continues: two Torah scholars who travel together on the road and do not speak words of Torah between them are deserving of being consumed by fire — *re'uyim lehisharef ba'esh*. The proof is from the episode of Elisha and Eliyahu: *vayehi heima holchim haloch vedaber* — they were walking and speaking — *vehinei rechev esh* — and behold a chariot of fire. The Gemara infers: the reason the fire did not harm them is because they were speaking Torah. *Ta'ama de'ika dibur ha leika dibur re'uyim lehisharef* — had there been no Torah discourse, they would have been deserving of being burned.

### Two Sages Tallit

The image of two Torah scholars sharing a single *talis* is recalled precisely here in contrast to the next teaching: whereas the shared *talis* reflects an intimacy and mutual dedication in the pursuit of Torah, the following passage depicts the opposite dynamic.

### Scholars Without Respect

Rabbi Ilai bar Yevarchia adds: two Torah scholars who live in the same city and are not gracious and pleasant to one another in matters of *halacha* — *ein nochim zeh lazeh bahalacha* — such that there is no reciprocal respect, no willingness to say "you might also ask the other rabbi," no collegial discourse at all — will come to a bad end: *echad meis ve'echad goleh*, one will die and the other will go into exile.

The verse cited is *lanus shama rotze'ach asher yirtzach es re'eihu bevli da'as* — the city of refuge is for one who kills his friend *bevli da'as*, without knowledge. And *da'as* means Torah, as the verse says *nidmu ami mibli hada'as* — my people are struck down for lack of knowledge. So if there is no Torah shared between two scholars in the same city, it is as if one has killed the other through that absence, and the punishment of exile follows.

### Study in Hardship

Rabbi Yehudah bar breih de-Rabbi Chiya teaches: any Torah scholar who learns Torah out of *dachak* — out of pressing straits, in privation — *tefilato nishma'at*, his prayer will be heard. This builds on the foregoing: David and Chabakuk had to pray on behalf of the poor scholars; here the scholar himself, by virtue of learning in hardship, earns that his own prayers are answered directly.

The proof is from the verse *ki am be-Tziyon yeshev bi-Yerushalayim bacho lo tivke chanon yachnecha le-kol za'akecha ke-shom'ato anacha* — to the voice of your crying out, when God hears, He will answer. The next verse — *ve-natan lachem Hashem lechem tzar u-mayim lachatz* — God will give you bread of privation and water of oppression — is read as the situational context: these are people who have very little bread and very little water, yet learn Torah nonetheless. It is precisely because of that privation that God answers their cry immediately.

### Divine Presence

Rabbi Abbahu adds a further dimension. The question hovering over this entire passage is that *emuna* is all well and good, but the reality is that many Torah scholars do suffer, and the promises of answered prayer do not always seem to manifest materially. Rabbi Abbahu addresses this: *masbi'in oto mi-ziv Shechina* — such a person is sustained from the radiance of the Divine Presence itself. The verse cited is *ve-hayu einecha ro'ot et morecha* — your eyes will see your teacher. The experience of God's presence is itself a form of sustenance, even when it does not translate into food on the table. The comparison that naturally arises — Moshe Rabbeinu, who was literally in God's presence and did not eat — suggests that there are indeed souls capable of being sustained on something far beyond physical nourishment.

### Curtain Not Sealed

Rabbi Yochanan adds: *af ein ha-pargod nin'al be-fanav* — the heavenly curtain is not sealed before such a person, meaning his prayers have direct access. The verse cited is *ve-lo yikanef od morecha* — your teacher will no longer be hidden beneath a garment, covered from you. God will no longer be concealed. The spiritual access, even when material provision remains elusive, represents a real and sustaining form of divine response.

### Daily Curse

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua: from the day the *beit hamikdash* was destroyed, there is no day that does not carry within it some element of curse.

### Increasing Curse

Rava intensifies this: *be-chol yom va-yom meruba klalato mi-shel chaveiro* — not only is every day cursed since the destruction, but every single day the curse is greater than the day before. Every passing day is worse than the previous one. The verse cited is *ba-boker tomar mi yiten erev u-va-erev tomar mi yiten boker* — in the morning you will say, who will give evening, and in the evening you will say, who will give morning.

### Morning/Evening

The Gemara asks: when it is evening and you long for morning, which morning are you longing for? Perhaps the morning yet to come? But the Gemara dismisses this: maybe tomorrow morning will be even worse — *mi yada mai havi*. Rather, *ella dechalif* — you are longing for the morning that has already passed. When it is night, you wish it were yesterday morning, because yesterday morning things were not yet as bad as they are tonight. Every passing moment, a person wishes it were the moment before. Things are continuously getting worse.

### Kedusha & Kaddish

*Ve'ella alma amai mikayeim* — if the world is getting progressively worse, what sustains it? The Gemara answers: *a'Kedusha DeSidra ve'Yehei Shmei Rabba de'Agadata* — it is the *kedusha* of the *seder* recited during *U'va LeTziyon*, and the *Yehei Shmei Rabba* recited after a public teaching of *agadata*.

This is a striking Gemara, one of the very few places where these prayers are explicitly identified as sustaining the world. The *Kedusha DeSidra* is the *Kedushas Hashem* recited in *U'va LeTziyon* after *Shacharis*, where *kadosh kadosh* is recited along with its Aramaic translation. The *Yehei Shmei Rabba* refers to *Kaddish* recited specifically after public *agadata* teachings.

### Rashi: Universal Torah

Rashi's commentary here is essential. He explains: *seder kedusha shelo tiknuha ela sheyehu kol Yisrael oskin baTorah bechol yom davar mu'at* — this order of *kedusha* was established precisely so that all Jews would engage in Torah study each day, even if only a little. The key feature of *Kedusha DeSidra* is that the *pesukim* are recited together with their Aramaic translation, *targumo*. Aramaic was the vernacular, which meant that everyone — scholars and *amei ha'aretz* alike — actually understood what was being said. They were genuinely learning Torah, not merely reciting words. It created no hierarchy; it was accessible to all. And it combined two elements simultaneously: *Kedushas Hashem* and *Talmud Torah*. Rashi calls this *chaviva* — precious, beloved.

Similarly, the *Yehei Shmei Rabba* recited after *agadata* teachings has the same character: *agadata* was the form of Torah accessible to everyone, the public sermon of the *darshan* that would draw the whole community together on *Shabbos*. The people would gather, everyone would hear the Torah teaching, and everyone would respond with *Yehei Shmei Rabba*. Again: *Kedushas Hashem* combined with *Talmud Torah*, universal and egalitarian. It is this minimum — not some extraordinary spiritual achievement, but a daily communal practice accessible to all — that keeps the world going even as deeds continue to deteriorate.

The Gemara then cites the verse: *eretz afaisa kmo ofel tzalmaves velo sedarim* — a land shrouded in darkness and the shadow of death, without order. *Hayesh sedarim tofei'ah me'ofel* — if these orders of *kedusha* and *kaddish* are in place, then light breaks through the darkness.

### Taharah Loss

The Gemara continues: *v'lo yardah l'vrachah v'nitma'et ta'am peirot* — the rains have not descended for blessing since the destruction, and the taste of fruit has diminished.

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar teaches: *taharah batlah ta'am v'rei'ach* — the loss of *taharah* caused the loss of taste and smell in fruit. Rashi explains beautifully: because people were *tehorim* and conducted themselves in *taharah*, God purified their fruit of bad smell and bad taste — the metaphysical purity of the people generated a corresponding purity and sweetness in the produce of the land. When *taharah* was lost, that spiritual refinement of the fruit was lost as well.

The Gemara adds: *ma'aser bitlu shuman dagan* — the failure to give *ma'aser* caused the fatness of the grain to cease. The *ma'aser* is described in the *Torah* as *kol chelev dagan* — the fatness of the grain — because one gives from the best to God. If one withholds this, the fatness disappears. And indeed, *mida kneged mida*: the very fatness one tried to keep for oneself by not giving it is the fatness that is lost.

### Huna's Date

Rav Huna once found a particularly sweet and rich date — *tamarta d'chinunita*, a species known for its exceptional sweetness and juiciness. He took it, wrapped it in his handkerchief, and was going to give it to his son. His son Rabbah arrived and said: *murchina reicha d'chinunita* — I smell the fragrance of this amazing date. Rav Huna responded: *bni, taharah yesh becha* — my son, you must possess a special purity, because as we have seen, *taharah* enables one to perceive taste and smell. He gave it to him. Then Rabbah's own son Abba arrived, and Rabbah took the date and gave it to his son.

Rav Huna said to Rabbah: *bni, simachtani libi* — you made my heart rejoice that you could perceive the fragrance of the date, which speaks to your purity of soul. *Aval hikhita et shinai* — but you blunted my teeth, meaning you hurt me: rather than keeping what I gave you, you immediately passed it on to your own son. That is what people say: *rachamei d'abba a-vnei* — a father's love flows toward his children. *Aval rachamei d'vnei a-vnei d'havu lei* — but the love of children flows not back to the parent but downward to their own children. Parents give more and feel more for their children than children feel for parents — not that this is always so, and certainly there are exceptions, but it reflects a natural asymmetry in the direction of parental love.

### Grandson Dishonor

This theme finds a darker echo immediately after. Rav Aha bar Yaakov raised his daughter's son, Rav Yaakov bar bartei, as his own. When the boy grew up, Rav Aha said to him: *ashkin maya* — could you please pour me some water? The grandson replied: *lav avuna at* — you are not my father, and I owe you no honor. The Gemara comments: *vehainu d'amri inshi* — that is what people say: *rabi rabi verabi lei* — raise children, raise them up — *ubesof amar bar bartekh ana* — and in the end he says, I am your daughter's son, not your son, and therefore I owe you nothing. A dark coda to the theme of how things have declined.

---

## War Decrees

### Vespasian Decrees

The last *mishna* of Masechet Sotah turns to a related but somewhat different note: not merely the world going to pot of its own deterioration, but the communal response to the *churban* — the *gezeirot* enacted to limit expressions of joy as a *zecher l'churban*. It is worth noting, as Rav Soloveitchik emphasized, that there is a distinction between *zecher l'mikdash* — commemorating what the *beit hamikdash* was like in its glory — and *zecher l'churban* — commemorating the fact of its destruction. These decrees fall into the latter category.

*Bepulmus shel Vespasian* — in the wars of Vespasian — they decreed against *atarot hatanim*, the crowns worn by grooms, and against *hairus* (a kind of drum instrument, which we will return to).

### Titus Decrees

*Bepulmus shel Titus* — in the wars of Titus, who succeeded Vespasian — they decreed against *atarot kallot*, the crowns worn by brides, and *shelo yilamed adam et beno yevanit*, that a person should not teach his son Greek wisdom. The reasoning behind this latter decree will be explained in the *gemara* below.

### Carriage Decree

*Bepulmus ha'acharon* — in the last war, which may refer either to the destruction itself or, according to some opinions, to the great revolt concluded around the time of Bar Kochba — they decreed *shelo tetze kallah ba'apiryon betokh ha'ir*, that a bride should not go out in a carriage or litter through the city during her wedding procession. The *mishna* notes that subsequently *veraboteinu hitiru* — the Rabbis permitted it again. Indeed, in Masechet Ketubot, the public procession of the bride in such a litter was a marker of a first marriage.

---

## Deaths of Sages

### Meir Parables

The *mishna* continues with a litany of losses, enumerating what the world lost upon the death of each great sage. *Mishemmet Rabbi Meir batlu moshlei meshalim* — when Rabbi Meir died, those who could craft parables were gone, for he was known for his mastery of the *mashal*.

### Ben Azzai

*Mishemmet Ben Azzai batlu hashakdanim* — when Ben Azzai died, those characterized by unceasing, tireless diligence in Torah study were gone.

### Ben Zoma

*Mishemmet Ben Zoma batlu hadarshanim* — when Ben Zoma died, those who could derive teachings from *pesukim* were gone. Rashi explains that this refers not to *agadic* homiletics but to the kind of textual derivation associated with Ben Zoma himself, as in the famous teaching *ad she-darsha Ben Zoma*, where he derived the requirement to remember the Exodus at night from a careful reading of the verse.

### Akiva Power

*Mishemmet Rabbi Akiva batel kvod haTorah* — when Rabbi Akiva died, the honor of Torah departed — *v'nistatmu ma'ayanot hachachmah*, the wellsprings of wisdom were stopped up. This is because Rabbi Akiva was the supreme *mechadesh*, the one who drew new Torah from every extra letter and from every *kots shel yud*, and with his death that power of creative *chiddush* was lost.

### Chanina Miracles

*Mishemmet Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa batlu anshei ma'aseh* — when Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa died, those who performed wondrous deeds were gone. The stories surrounding Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa are replete with accounts of miraculous occurrences in his presence, and with his death that dimension of the world's experience was closed.

### Pious End

*Mishemmet Abba Yosi ben Katnuta batlu chasidim* — when Abba Yosi ben Katnuta died, the truly pious were gone. And why was he called *Katnuta* — the small one? *She-hayah mikatnei chasidim* — because he was even one of the most minor of the pious. The very fact that the smallest of the pious was still around had sustained the world; once even he was gone, the category of *chasid* was extinguished.

### Yochanan Wisdom

*Mishemmet Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai batal ziv hachochmah* — when Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai died, the luminous radiance of wisdom departed. Rashi acknowledges with characteristic honesty: *lo yadana mai hi* — I do not know precisely what the connection is.

### Gamliel Health

*Mishemmet Rabban Gamliel HaZaken batel kvod haTorah* — when Rabban Gamliel HaZaken died, the honor of Torah was lost, and *umesah taharah u'ferishut* — purity and asceticism ended. Rashi points to the Gemara in Megillah which records that after his death, people became far less healthy, and when people are not well, their Torah study necessarily diminishes.

### Yishmael Glory

*Mishemmet Rabbi Yishmael ben Pabi batlah ziv hakehunah* — when Rabbi Yishmael ben Pabi died, the glory of the priesthood departed. He was a wealthy man who supported the *kohanim*, and with him the *kavod* of the *kehunah* was extinguished.

### Rebbe Humility

*Mishemmet Rebbe batlah anavah v'yirat chet* — when Rebbe died — that is, Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, the final editor of the *Mishna* — both humility and true fear of sin departed from the world. This is a somewhat sobering note on which to end the *mishna*. Most final *mishnayot* of a *masechet* conclude on an uplifting note, and some *rishonim* indeed have a different *girsa* that includes additional lines here.

---

## Path to Mashiach

### Pinchas Ladder

Some versions of the *mishna* — though not in the standard printed *gemara* text — include the following statement from Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair, which in many *mishnayot* prints appears as the conclusion of the *masechet*:

*Zerizut mevia lidei nekiut, nekiut mevia lidei taharah, taharah mevia lidei perishut, perishut mevia lidei kedushah, kedushah mevia lidei anavah, anavah mevia lidei yirat chet, yirat chet mevia lidei chasidut, chasidut mevia lidei ruach hakodesh, ruach hakodesh mevia lidei techiyat hametim, u'techiyat hametim ba al yedei Eliyahu zachur latov.*

Diligence leads to cleanliness, cleanliness to *taharah*, *taharah* to *perishut*, *perishut* to *kedushah*, *kedushah* to *anavah*, *anavah* to fear of sin, fear of sin to *chasidut*, *chasidut* to *ruach hakodesh*, *ruach hakodesh* to the resurrection of the dead, and the resurrection will come through Eliyahu, may his memory be for blessing.

This is a profoundly different note on which to end the *masechet*. Everything may indeed be going to pot — but here is a ladder. Small, incremental steps of spiritual discipline, each one drawing the next, can reverse the entire process and lead ultimately to the coming of *Mashiach* and the resurrection of the dead. That this statement serves as the structural framework for the Ramchal's *Mesillat Yesharim* is well known. It is genuinely sad that it is not in our standard *girsa*, because it is such a powerful and necessary counterweight to everything that preceded it.

---

## Pre-Mashiach Chaos

### Chutzpah & Heresy

The *gemara* continues — whether as *baraita* or otherwise — with the famous passage about *ikveta d'Meshicha*, the footsteps of *Mashiach*, the period immediately preceding the redemption. *Be'ikvata d'Meshicha chutzpa yasga* — in the footsteps of *Mashiach*, insolence will proliferate. *Veyoker yaamir* — honor will be perverted. *Hagefen titein pirya vehayayin beyoker* — even though the vine will give its fruit, wine will be expensive, because people will be running after hedonistic pleasures. *U'malchut tahafech leminut* — the kingdom will turn to *minut*, heresy.

This last phrase requires explanation. Why should we care whether a non-Jewish government becomes heretical? Rashi — in the passage that appears in the outer margin of some editions, in text that was edited out of the standard Rashi — explains: the kingdom that rules over most of the world will turn toward *minut*, following the error of a particular figure and his disciples, who were called *minim*. Rashi is referring to the Roman Empire becoming the Christian Holy Roman Empire. The phrase *tahafech leminut* thus means the Christianization of Rome.

---

## Path to Mashiach (II)

### Ikvata Meshicha

The placement of these passages — everything getting worse right before *Mashiach* — is itself understood as a positive spin on the preceding litany of decline. The worse things get, the more they constitute the *ikveta d'Meshicha*, the footsteps, the foreshadowing of the redemption. The darkness is itself the sign that dawn approaches.

---

## Pre-Mashiach Chaos (II)

### No Rebuke

*Ve'ein tochecha* — there will be no one to remonstrate, because everyone is equally sinning and no one can rebuke another. *Beit va'ad yihiyeh liznut* — the house of assembly, formerly the place of Torah, will become a place of prostitution. *Vehagalil yecherav vehagavlan yaishom* — the Galil will be destroyed and this place called *Gavlan* will be desolate — *ve'anshei hagvul yesovevu me'ir le'ir velo yechonenu* — and the people of the border will wander from city to city and find no rest.

### Wisdom Lost

*Ve'chochmat sofrim tisrach* — the wisdom of the scribes will become corrupted and putrid. *Veyirei chet yimasu* — those who fear sin will be despised. *Ve'ha'emet tehei ne'ederet* — truth will be absent, will be a rarity.

### Youth Shame Elders

*Ne'arim pnei zekenim yalbinu* — youth will shame and humiliate elders. *Zekenim yaamdu mipnei ktanim* — elders will be expected to stand before the young. *Ben menavel av bat kama be'ima kala bachamota* — a son will disgrace his father, a daughter will rise against her mother, a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. *Oivei ish anshei beito* — a person's enemies will be the members of his own household — an image that conjures the world of informers and denunciations.

### Generation Face

*Pnei hador k'pnei hakelev* — the face of the generation will be like the face of dogs. Whether this means cruelty, indifference, or simply shamelessness is left somewhat open, though the following phrase clarifies the register.

### Son Shame

*Habein eino mitbayes me'aviv* — a son will not be embarrassed before his father. The breakdown of shame, of basic filial inhibition, is the culminating sign.

### Father Heaven

*Ve'al mah yesh lanu lehisha'en? Al avinu shebashamayim* — upon whom do we have to rely? Only upon our Father in heaven. This phrase serves as the conclusion of the *mishna* in some versions, and it is a genuine note of faith: despite the complete collapse of social and moral order, the only stable anchor that remains is God Himself.

---

## War Decrees (II)

### Groom Crowns

The *gemara* now returns to elaborate on the details of the *mishna*'s decrees. Rav says: the prohibition on grooms' crowns applies only to those made of salt and sulfur — some type of mineral formation used for such adornments. But crowns made of myrtle or rose — *shel hadas veshel vered* — are permitted.

### Crown Dispute

Shmuel disagrees: even a crown of myrtle and rose is forbidden. However, one made of reeds or some type of seaweed — *shel kanim veshel chilat* — is permitted. Levi goes further still: even reeds and seaweed are forbidden, and this is what he also taught in his *baraita*.

### Irus Drum

What exactly is the *irus* mentioned in the *mishna*? Rav Elazar says: *tavla dechad puma* — a tablet with one mouth, which Rashi understands as some type of clapper or gong. The discussion then turns to drums. Rabbah bar Rav Huna made a *tanbura* — a type of drum — for his son. His father came and broke it. He said: if you make that kind of drum, it will be confused with a *tavla dechad puma*, which is forbidden. If you want to make a drum for your son, make one on the mouth of a clay pot — *apuma dechatztzava* — or on the opening of some other household container, so that it will not be confused with the instruments that are actually prohibited.

### Bride Crowns

What were the *atarot kallot* — the brides' crowns — that were prohibited during Titus's wars? Rabbah bar bar Chana says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *ir shel zahav* — a golden city, some type of tiara made to look like the city of Jerusalem worked in gold. A *baraita* confirms this, and adds that what one may do instead is make *kippah shel milat* — some type of head covering of silk.

### Wedding Canopy

The *gemara* also records that a *tanna* taught that the prohibition extended to *chuppat chatanim* — a particular type of wedding canopy. What was this *chuppah*? *Zehorit mezuhevet* — a crimson fabric adorned with gold, a *tallit* dyed crimson with golden ornaments woven through it, which would be fashioned into a tent-like canopy. Rashi describes this in some detail. What remains permitted is a *papirit* — Rashi describes this as a frame of wooden arches upon which one can hang various ornaments and decorations as one wishes, which is the permissible alternative canopy.

### Permitted Alternatives

The *gemara* thus establishes that while the most ornate and elaborate forms of wedding adornment were prohibited in the wake of the various wars, the Rabbis permitted alternative forms that preserved the dignity and joy of the occasion without the extravagance associated with the pre-destruction era.

### Pig & Greek

A famous *baraita* is now cited to explain the prohibition on teaching Greek wisdom. When the Hasmonean kings were at war with one another — Hyrcanus on the outside of Jerusalem with Roman troops, and Aristobulus on the inside — the besieged would daily lower *dinarim* in a basket, and those outside would send up animals for the *temidim*, the daily sacrifices, because everyone still cared about the *avodah* in the *beit hamikdash*.

There was an elderly man on the inside of the walls who knew *chochmah Yevanis* — Greek wisdom, apparently a method of covert signaling. He communicated to those outside: as long as those inside continue performing the *avodah*, they will not be surrendered into your hands. The next day, when the besiegers lowered the *dinarim*, instead of sending up a lamb, they sent up a pig. When the pig reached halfway up the wall, it dug its claws into the wall, and the entire land of Israel shook for a distance of 400 *parsah*. At that moment they declared: *arur adam she-yigadel chazirim* — cursed is the person who raises pigs — *ve-arur adam she-yelamed livno chochmah Yevanis* — and cursed is the person who teaches his son Greek wisdom.

The Gemara adds that in that same year, *mavi'in ha-omer mi-gagots tzerifin* — they had to bring the *omer* from grain stored on rooftops or from distant places like *Bik'at Ein Socher*, since the besieging troops had burned all the fields around Jerusalem, and normal supplies were unavailable.

### Greek Language

Is the prohibition really absolute? The Gemara raises the question, for Rav teaches: Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi said that in Eretz Yisrael, one should not speak *Sursi* — Aramaic, a vernacular considered coarse — but rather either *leshon hakodesh* or Greek. If one is not going to speak the holy tongue, at least speak a refined and culturally elevated language. And Rav Yosef similarly teaches that in Bavel, one should not speak Aramaic but rather either *leshon hakodesh* or Persian — *leshon Parsi* — meaning Farsi, which was considered the elevated vernacular of that region.

The resolution: *leshon Yevanis lachud, chochmah Yevanis lachud* — the Greek *language* is one matter, Greek *wisdom* is quite another. One may speak Greek; what is forbidden is the study of *chochmah Yevanis* in its technical sense — the esoteric or philosophical wisdom that was used deceptively in the incident above.

### Gamliel Family

Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel cites a statement of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in explanation of the verse *eini olelah le-nafshi mi-kol benos iri* — my eye brings grief to my soul more than all the daughters of my city. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said: my father's household had a thousand children. Five hundred learned Torah and five hundred learned *chochmah Yevanis*. And of all of them, only I remain, and the son of my father's brother who is in Asia. Clearly, then, the Nasi's household itself had half its children studying Greek wisdom.

### Close to Govt

The Gemara explains: *shani shel beis Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel de-krovim le-malchus havu* — the household of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was different, because they were close to the Roman government and had to maintain those relations. A *baraita* confirms this principle: Avtolmos ben Reuven was permitted to wear his hair in the *komi* style — a particular Roman hairstyle that would normally constitute *darchei ha-Emori*, pagan practices — because he was close to the government and had to appear a certain way. Similarly, the household of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was permitted to learn *chochmah Yevanis* because of their proximity to the Roman government. The category of *karov le-malchus* — proximity to the government — thus functions as a recognized exception to otherwise forbidden practices.

---

## Halachic Details

### Crown Materials

The prohibition on grooms' crowns enacted during Vespasian's wars, the *gemara* clarifies, applies specifically to crowns made of salt and sulfur. This is the baseline position — not all materials are equally forbidden.

### Crown Dispute

The debate among Rav, Shmuel, and Levi, as detailed above, represents a spectrum of increasing stringency: Rav permits myrtle and rose; Shmuel forbids those but permits reeds and seaweed; Levi forbids even reeds and seaweed. Levi's position is supported by his own *baraita*.

### Drum Making

Rabbah bar Rav Huna's attempt to make a *tanbur*-style drum for his son, and his father's intervention, illustrates the concern about confusion with genuinely forbidden instruments. The practical ruling is to construct a simple drum from a household pot or similar vessel — *apuma dechatztzava* or *apuma dekafiza* — precisely so that no one mistakes it for a *tavla dechad puma*, which falls within the scope of the decree.

---

## Final Hope

### Yosef Humility

The Gemara concludes, following the *mishna*'s statement that when Rebbe died *batlah anavah* — humility departed — with a wonderful moment of humor. Rav Yosef said to the *tanna* reciting the *baraita*: do not recite that *anavah* is gone — *d'ika ana*, I am still here! This is the Gemara's way of not ending on pure despair. Humility does not mean denying one's own greatness; as the Gemara implies by bringing Rav Yosef's protest here, true *anavah* is about how one carries oneself, not false modesty. Moshe Rabbeinu was *anav mikol adam* and yet he knew his own stature. Rav Yosef's claim is itself a statement about what *anavah* means.

### Nachman Fear

Similarly, Rav Nachman said to the *tanna*: do not say that *yirat chet* has disappeared — *d'ika ana*, I am still around. Again, a note of hope: however grim the picture painted by the *mishna* and *baraita*, there is still someone left. Things are not completely lost. The Gemara ends with a gentle insistence that we are not yet beyond redemption.

### Hadran

*Hadran alach Masechet Sotah.*

הדרן עלך מסכת סוטה ודעתן עלך מסכת סוטה דעתך עלן לא נתנשי מינך מסכת סוטה ולא תתנשי מינן לא בעלמא הדין ולא בעלמא דאתי.

We return to you, Masechet Sotah, and our minds are upon you, Masechet Sotah. Your mind is upon us; we shall not forget you, Masechet Sotah, nor shall you forget us — neither in this world nor in the world to come.

---

---

# Gittin 2

## Intro to Gittin

### Masechet Overview

We begin a new *masechet*: Masechet Gittin. It is, in the fullest sense of the phrase, a classic *masechet* of the *gemara*. Unlike some of the more unusual tractates encountered elsewhere in the cycle — with non-standard language, absent *Rashi*, or unconventional structure — Gittin belongs to the heart of the *Shas* curriculum. Situated within *Nashim* and adjacent in spirit to *Nezikin*, it carries the full wealth of the *rishonim* and has been a staple of *yeshiva* education for centuries. And the reason it has remained so central is not merely because it is *halacha l'maaseh* — though of course the laws of delivering a *get* are of great practical consequence — but because it is extraordinarily rich in conceptual depth.

### Conceptual Themes

Masechet Gittin is packed with some of the deepest and most far-reaching themes in all of *Shas*. The laws of *shlichus* — agency — are explored here at length and in their most complex forms. So too are the laws of *shtarot*, legal documents, as well as questions of ownership, and the structure of conditions placed upon transactions. These are not parochial concerns; they are recurring themes throughout *Shas*, and Gittin becomes one of the primary sources to which the tradition returns again and again when working through them. It is a *masechet* with enormous conceptual reach.

### Divorce Context

There is, however, something almost melancholy about learning Masechet Gittin in the contemporary context. The *gemara*, like any legal document, focuses entirely on process: how does one write a *get*, how does one deliver it, what are the technical and conceptual requirements? And throughout, the social reality is simply taken for granted — of course a husband is giving a *get* to his wife. The complications are halachic, not social. Every page assumes that divorce is a natural and available option, and the legal analysis proceeds accordingly.

This stands in sharp contrast to the reality many Jewish women face today, where the process of obtaining a *get* is fraught with the possibility of extortion, refusal, and the tragedy of *iguna*.
