Part of what made the system more functional in Talmudic times was the absence of a parallel secular legal system: if you wanted to end a marriage, this was the only path. Just as today one cannot avoid obtaining a civil divorce if one wants legal dissolution, in that world a *get* was the sole mechanism. The tight-knit Jewish community, combined with a *beis din* that had real authority and the motivation to exercise it, created conditions in which the husband's cooperation was far more reliably obtained. That said, it is worth noting that in much of Western Europe and America, secular divorce was itself essentially unavailable until well into the twentieth century, owing in large part to Christian legal traditions. The contrast with the Talmudic system is therefore even more pointed.

### Perakim Structure

Masechet Gittin spans six *perakim* and does something characteristic of several *masechtot*: rather than beginning with the most fundamental questions — how does one write a *get*, what constitutes a valid *get* — it opens with what might appear to be a more peripheral topic. The first *perek* deals with *hameivi get mimedinat hayam*, the agent who delivers a *get* from overseas, and the testimony he must provide. The second *perek* continues this theme under the same heading, still concerned with the delivery of a *get* from afar — but midway through, it begins to address the specifics of how a *get* is written. We encounter *hakol kotvin*, the principle that one may write with all types of inks; the question of a *get* written by day and signed at night; what material the *get* may be written upon; and the rule that *ein kotvin bimchubar lakarka* — one may not write on something still attached to the ground.

It is also in this section that we encounter *lishmah* — the requirement that the *get* be written with the particular woman in mind. The third *perek* continues with questions relating both to the writing and delivery of the *get*, including the fascinating question of whether, while the *get* is being delivered, we may assume the husband who sent it is still alive. This opens into a broader digression: in general, when a *shaliach* has been dispatched to perform an act, what assumptions may he make about the one who sent him?

The fourth *perek*, called *ha-sholeach*, deals with a scenario of acute halachic danger: a husband who dispatches a *shaliach* to deliver a *get* to his wife, then subsequently cancels the agency — but does so not in the presence of the messenger. The messenger proceeds in good faith, the wife believes herself divorced, she remarries, and the children of that remarriage may be *mamzerim*. To prevent this catastrophe, the Rabbis intervened — and here we encounter one of the most celebrated concepts in the *masechet*: *tikkun haolam*. The Rabbis instituted certain enactments, and in some cases shaped or worked around biblical law, for the betterment of society. The fourth and fifth *perakim* are largely devoted to this theme — a wide-ranging survey, touching areas from *nashim* to *nezikin*, of things the Rabbis did *mipnei tikkun haolam*.

The sixth *perek* returns to the laws of giving a *get*, including the case of a *get* given conditionally — a topic that might sound like a technical curiosity, but which unfolds into a profound analysis of what constitutes a legally valid *tnai*. Toward the end of the *masechet* we reach the laws of how the woman receives the *get* and what constitutes valid receipt. And at the very end, in the final *mishnah*, we arrive at what might surprise a reader who has followed the tractate from the beginning: a discussion of under what circumstances a husband should divorce his wife in the first place. It is a rich and diverse *masechet* in every sense.

### Rambam's 10 Conditions

Before turning to the *daf* itself — which is notably short, with very few lines of *gemara* — it is worth pausing to appreciate a brilliant piece of systematic jurisprudence from the Rambam. His *Hilchos Gerushin*, particularly *perek* 1, offers a stunning overview of the entire subject. He opens by enumerating ten conditions, all *d'oraisa*, that must be met for a *get* to be valid. He then reveals the source: virtually all of them are derived from a single *pasuk* in the Torah, specifically from eight words.

The verse is from Devarim: *ve-kasav la sefer kerisus ve-nasan beyada ve-shilcha mibeiso* — "and he shall write for her a document of severance, and place it in her hand, and send her from his house." These eight words, combined with the general principle from *al pi shenayim eidim yakum davar*, underpin the entire architecture of *geirushin* from the Torah's perspective.

### Conditions Explained

The Rambam proceeds to derive each condition in turn. First, from *im lo timtza chen be'einav* — "if she does not find favor in his eyes" — we learn that the husband must act willingly: *melamed she-eino megaresh ela birtzono*. This distinguishes *gerushin* from ordinary transactions, where of course intent is always required; here the requirement of genuine consent carries particular weight. Importantly, the woman is divorced even against her will — *ha-isha mitgereshet birtzonah ve-she-lo birtzonah* — which is of course the pre-Rabbinic baseline, before the *cherem* of Rabbeinu Gershom.

Second, from *ve-kasav* — and he shall write — we learn that the *get* must be a written document: *eina mitgereshet ela bichtav*. Third, from *la* — for her — we derive *lishmah*: it must be written specifically with this woman in mind. A generic writ or one written without intention toward the particular woman does not suffice. Fourth, from *sefer kerisus* — a document of severance — we learn that the *get* must fully sever the relationship: *davar ha-koret beino u-veinah, she-lo yisha'er alav rashut*. If the husband appends an ongoing stipulation — some condition that leaves him with continued authority over her — the act is not one of complete severance. Fifth, from *ve-nasan beyada* — and he shall place it in her hand — we learn the obvious: the *get* must reach her, whether into her hand, into the hands of her *shaliach*, or into her property.

Sixth, from *ve-shilcha* — and he shall send her — the Rambam derives that the language of the *get* must be that *she* is being sent, not that *he* is leaving. The husband cannot formulate the *get* in terms of his own departure; the document must speak of her being divorced from him. Nor can the text be merely a declaration of freedom without reference to the act of divorce itself.

Seventh — and here the Rambam draws on the combination of *ve-kasav* and *ve-nasan* together — there must be no necessary intervening act between the writing and the giving. One may of course allow time to elapse, but there cannot be a situation in which some action is *required* between the writing and the delivery. The classic example is *mechubar lakarka*: one cannot write on a tree still attached to the ground, because the only way to give it would necessitate cutting the tree down first.

Eighth, from the combination of *sefer kerisus ve-natan beyada*, the Rambam derives that the *get* must be given explicitly as a *get*. One cannot hand a woman a piece of paper under false pretenses — "hold this for me" — and have that count as delivery of a *get*. It must be given as what it is.

The ninth condition — that there must be *eidim*, witnesses — is the one condition not derived from this *pasuk*, but rather from the general Torah principle of *al pi shenayim eidim yakum davar*. Whether this means witnesses must sign the document or witnesses must be present at the time of delivery is itself a dispute in the *gemara*. Tenth — and the Rambam closes the list here — the *get* must come from the husband himself, not from a court acting independently.

The elegance of this framework is remarkable: eight words of Torah, one additional *pasuk* about testimony, and the Rambam has mapped the entire *d'oraisa* architecture of *geirushin*. It is an ideal introduction to the *masechet*, and it is worth reading his *perek* 1 of *Hilchos Gerushin* in full before proceeding through the *daf yomi*.

---

## Hameivi Get

### Basic Requirement

The *mishnah* opens: *hamevi get mimedinat hayam* — one who brings a *get* from overseas. *Tosafos* immediately raises a point about this phrase. *Rashi* understands *medinat hayam* to mean simply *kol chutz la'aretz* — anywhere outside of *Eretz Yisrael*. *Tosafos* disagrees, arguing that if that were the intent, the *mishnah* would have said *hamevi get michutz la'aretz*. The use of the phrase *medinat hayam* suggests something more distant — a genuinely far-off place — and we will return to this distinction shortly.

The *mishnah* states: *tzarich she-yomar befanai nechtav uvfanai nechtam* — the agent delivering the *get* must declare, in front of witnesses or a *beis din*, "it was written in my presence and signed in my presence." The most natural question is: why? We have a *shaliach* standing before us, holding a *get*. We do not know who he is. We do not know who sent him. We have no way of verifying that the husband actually authorized this document, that the signatures on it are genuine, or that the *get* was written in accordance with *halacha*. The husband is not standing in front of us; the *shaliach* has not provided any prior affidavit of his agency. In that situation, the *shaliach* must testify — and his testimony that the *get* was written and signed in his presence serves as validation of the entire process. The *gemara* will go on to distinguish between the *nechtav* component and the *nechtam* component, attributing to each a different rationale. But at the *mishnah* level, both together constitute the required declaration.

### Geographic Debate

The *mishnah* then records a series of positions among the *tannaim* about what geographic distance triggers this requirement. *Rabban Gamliel* says: *af hamevi mi-Rekem umehager* — even one who brings from Rekem and Hager must make this declaration. These appear to be places very close to the border of *Eretz Yisrael*. *Tosafos* devotes considerable effort to identifying them, suggesting they may be in the region of the land of the *Plishtim*, though acknowledges some ambiguity. *Rashi* associates them with the biblical Kadesh and Bered, the location to which Hagar fled when driven out by Sarah — again pointing to proximity to *Eretz Yisrael*. *Rabban Gamliel*'s position, then, is that even these nearby locations trigger the requirement; one need not travel to genuinely distant overseas territories.

*Rabbi Eliezer* goes further: *afilu mikfar Ludim le-Lud* — even one who brings from the village of Ludim to Lud. This generates two puzzles. First, Lud is not on the border of *Eretz Yisrael* in any straightforward sense; why would its immediate vicinity even be considered *chutz la'aretz*? Second, and more textually puzzling, *Tosafos* asks: why does *Rabbi Eliezer* state where he is *bringing it to*? The point of these *tannaitic* positions is to define the place of *origin* — it doesn't matter where it is being delivered. *Tosafos* offers two resolutions. One is that *kfar Ludim* must be understood as so closely adjacent to Lud, so much like its suburb, that one might have assumed the two localities share a legal identity for these purposes — *Rabbi Eliezer* teaches that even so, if it technically falls over the line, the requirement applies. The other answer *Tosafos* offers is that *Rabbi Eliezer* himself was from Lud, and therefore chose this as his illustrative example.

What all three positions — *Rabban Gamliel*, *Rabbi Eliezer*, and the following *chachamim* — share is the underlying claim: the *mishnah*'s phrase *medinat hayam* need not refer to genuinely distant overseas territory. Even proximity to the border triggers the requirement.

*Ve-chachamim omrim*: the *chachamim* disagree, saying *ela hameivi mimedinat hayam* — only one who brings from genuinely overseas must make the declaration. The phrase *medinat hayam* means what it says: a distant place across the sea.

### Eretz Yisrael Borders

The *mishnah* continues with a separate question: how do we define the borders of *Eretz Yisrael* itself? This requires its own treatment, since knowing what is inside *Eretz Yisrael* is necessary to knowing when the requirement applies. *Rabbi Yehuda* provides the coordinates: from Rekem to the east — with Rekem counting as *outside* Israel; from Ashkelon to the south — with Ashkelon counting as outside; from Akko to the north — with Akko counting as outside Israel as well. This is immediately striking: Ashkelon is mentioned as one of the cities of Israel, and Akko is likewise associated with *Eretz Yisrael* in numerous other contexts.

*Rabbi Meir* takes a different position with respect to Akko: *Akko k'Eretz Yisrael legittin* — for purposes of the laws of *gittin*, Akko has the status of *Eretz Yisrael*. This raises a principle that will recur throughout the early *dappim* of the *masechet*: the borders of *Eretz Yisrael* may not be uniform across all areas of *halacha*. The borders relevant to *tumah* and *ma'asros* are generally those of the *Bayit Sheni* era. The borders associated with the *kedushah* of the land track the conquest of Yehoshua. But for the purposes of the *halacha* of *befanai nechtav uvfanai nechtam*, the relevant question may be more practical: is this a place where Jewish communities are established enough that *halachos* are reliably known, and where witnesses can be located if needed? If the concern driving the requirement is practical — that people far away do not know the laws of writing a *get*, or that one cannot find witnesses to validate signatures — then the borders of *Eretz Yisrael* for these purposes are drawn based on the cultural and communal realities of Jewish life, not necessarily on historical or sanctity-based demarcations.

### Within Eretz Yisrael

Finally, the *mishnah* closes: *hamevi get b'Eretz Yisrael eino tzarich lomar befanai nechtav uvfanai nechtam* — one who delivers a *get* within *Eretz Yisrael* does not need to make this declaration. When the entire transaction takes place internally within *Eretz Yisrael*, we have sufficient tools to verify everything, and the declaration is unnecessary. However, *v'im yesh alav orerim* — if a challenge is subsequently raised, if the husband appears and claims the *get* was a forgery — then *yitkayem be-chotmav*: the *get* is validated through its signatures. So within *Eretz Yisrael*, we do not validate proactively, but if and when a challenge arises, the mechanism of signature validation is available and sufficient.

### Mishnah Structure

This *mishnah* offers a remarkable illustration of a broader phenomenon in the structure of *mishnayos* — one that, once noticed, appears throughout the *Shas*. The *gemara* sometimes refers explicitly to a *mishnah rishona* and a *mishnah acharona*, cases where an earlier ruling was later superseded. But there is a more subtle and more common phenomenon: a later generation of *tannaim* received a simple, early *mishnah* containing basic terms, and then proceeded to debate what those terms meant. The apparent structure of *tanna kamma* versus *Rabbi Yehuda* versus *Rabbi Meir* often conceals what was really a simple original teaching, with the named opinions all being subsequent clarifications or debates about the scope of the original terms.

The phenomenon is visible even in the very first *mishnah* of Pesachim: *kol makom she-ein machnisin bo chametz ein tzarich bdikah* — wherever one does not bring *chametz*, one need not check. The *mishnah* then introduces the teaching about the two rows of the wine cellar (*shtei shurot ba-martef*), and *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel* debate what "two rows" means. Clearly, there was an early, simple teaching, and the later *tannaim* argued about what the term encompassed.

Apply this lens to our *mishnah*. Strip away every named position, and what remains is a strikingly elegant, minimal teaching: *hamevi get mimedinat hayam* — one who brings a *get* from overseas must say *befanai nechtav uvfanai nechtam*; and if one brings it from one *medinah* to another in *medinat hayam*, or from *Eretz Yisrael* to *medinat hayam*; but *hamevi get b'Eretz Yisrael eino tzarich*. That's the whole *mishnah* in its original form. Crisp, simple, complete.

Then come the named *tannaim*, and what are they doing? They are debating the meaning of the term *medinat hayam*. Does it mean genuinely distant overseas territory, or does it mean any place outside *Eretz Yisrael* — even places right at the border? *Rabban Gamliel* says even Rekem and Hager. *Rabbi Eliezer* says even the vicinity of Lud. *Chachamim* say no, only genuinely distant places. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* takes the term *mimedina limedina* and says it applies even to *hegmonia le-hegmonia* — even two jurisdictions within a single city. And *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Meir* are not adding new positions but simply defining, from different angles, what the borders of *Eretz Yisrael* are.

This structural observation enriches the reading considerably. Rather than a cacophony of competing voices, we see a simple early ruling, and a later generation systematically working through every ambiguous term. As one participant in the *shiur* observed, this is in a sense the same process that the *amoraim* perform explicitly in the *gemara* — with the difference that in the *gemara* the process of clarification and debate is transparent, while here it is embedded in the *mishnah* itself.

### Get Convention

Two brief textual notes are worth recording here. First, the word *get*: *Tosafos* points out that it is a generic term for a *shtar* — a legal document — but that without further qualification, it almost always refers to a *get nashim*, a bill of divorce. Why the word *get* came to be so closely associated with divorce specifically is not entirely clear. Second, *Tosafos* notes a widespread *minhag* to write a *get* with twelve lines. The basis offered is the *gematria* of the word *get*: *gimel* equals 3, *tes* equals 9, totaling twelve. An alternative explanation *Tosafos* considers is that between each of the five books of the *Sefer Torah*, there is a gap of four lines; the three such gaps between the first four books amount to twelve dividing lines in total. To this day, a *get* is written so that the text fills exactly twelve lines.

### Border Cities

Returning to the question of Ashkelon and Akko: *Tosafos* acknowledges that both cities are, in various sources, counted as part of *Eretz Yisrael*, and that Ashkelon is in the region of *Eretz Pelishtim*. Yet, *Tosafos* argues, even if these cities are technically within the boundaries of *Eretz Yisrael*, they may sit at the periphery in a meaningful sense. If the underlying concern of *befanai nechtav uvfanai nechtam* is practical — that people in certain places do not know the *halachos* of *gittin* or that witnesses cannot be located — then cities on the extreme margins of Jewish settlement may not enjoy the presumption of halachic reliability that the interior of the land does. The determination of which side of the line they fall on for purposes of this *halacha* is therefore not identical with the question of whether they are technically within the borders of *Eretz Yisrael*.

This question — whether we use standard definitions of *Eretz Yisrael*'s borders, or whether we draw the map based on the specific concerns underlying the law of *befanai nechtav* — will continue to animate the discussion across the first several *dappim* of the *masechet*.

### No Forgery Defense

*Tosafos* notes in its commentary to *im yesh alav orer mitkayem be-chotmav* that as long as the husband has not come forward to challenge the *get* — in the case of a *get* delivered within *Eretz Yisrael* — the woman may remarry on the strength of the *get* alone. We do not, on her behalf, raise the concern that perhaps the *get* is forged. One might have thought the opposite: since the husband is absent from the proceedings, should the *beis din* not represent his interests and challenge the document's authenticity? *Tosafos* answers: *de-mishum iguna akilu bah rabanan* — because of the concern for *iguna*, the Rabbis were lenient and declined to mount the forgery defense on the husband's behalf. The woman cannot be left in a state of uncertainty indefinitely because of an unsubstantiated concern.

### Ramban Property

The *Ramban* takes a fundamentally different approach to the same question. He argues that the reason the *beis din* does not represent the husband's interests and challenge the *get* is not because of any *leniency* born of the concern for *iguna* — it is because the entire framing of "representing the absent party's interests" does not apply here in the first place. In monetary matters, if one party is attempting to seize another's property and the owner is absent, the court will defend the owner's interests. But the *Ramban* says: *ein ha-ishah nichsei ha-ba'al* — the woman is not the husband's property. The act of divorce is not the taking of something from the husband. It is the definition of a woman's legal status — a question that lies outside the framework of *dinei mamonos* entirely.

This is a striking conceptual point to encounter on the very first *daf* of the *masechet*. The entire tractate is, in some sense, structured around the husband's power — he writes, he delivers, he sends. And yet here, at the outset, the *Ramban* insists that however we frame the halachic mechanics, the woman is not to be understood as her husband's property, and that framing must be kept entirely separate from the language of monetary law. As one participant noted, this is in some ways consistent with *Tosafos*'s position as well: even *Tosafos*, who invokes *iguna* as the *ta'am*, still presupposes that the husband is seen as a party who could be "injured" by the loss of the *get* challenge — something the *Ramban* rejects at the conceptual root.

---

## Two Reasons

### Rabbah Lishmah

The *gemara* opens with a simple question: *mai ta'ama* — what is the reason for the requirement of *befanai nechtav uvfanai nechtam*? Two *amoraim* offer two fundamentally different answers, each focusing on a different word of the declaration.

*Rabbah* says: *lefi she-ein beki'in lishmah* — because people in *medinat hayam* are not expert in the requirement of *lishmah*, the rule that a *get* must be written specifically for the sake of this particular woman. Since we are concerned that the *get* was not written with proper *lishmah* in mind, the *shaliach* must testify: *befanai nechtav* — it was written in my presence. *Rabbah* is focused on the writing of the *get*, and his concern is about whether the *get* was produced in accordance with *halacha*.

*Tosafos* raises the obvious question: why single out *lishmah* specifically? There are many other requirements for writing a valid *get*. The answer *Tosafos* gives is that *lishmah* was the most commonly neglected requirement — perhaps because people in distant lands were not fully persuaded of its necessity, or perhaps because it was simply less well-known. But *Tosafos* does note other possible framings, including the possibility that in *medinat hayam* the problem was not ignorance so much as non-acceptance: people who knew the law of *lishmah* but did not reliably observe it.

The practical question then arises: how does the *shaliach*'s statement *befanai nechtav* — "it was written in my presence" — actually establish that *lishmah* was observed? All he is literally saying is that it was written in front of him. *Rashi* offers two possibilities. Either the declaration opens a line of inquiry — we ask him to elaborate on how the *get* was written, and through that inquiry we establish that *lishmah* was observed — or, more elegantly, the statement *befanai nechtav* functions as an implicit claim that everything was done in accordance with *halacha*, without any need for further questioning. The implicit logic is reinforced by the sociological observation: if people in *medinat hayam* know they will have to make this declaration before the *get* can be received in *Eretz Yisrael*, they will know that they are testifying to *halachic* compliance, and will take care accordingly.

### Rava Signatures

*Rava* focuses on the other half of the declaration: *befanai nechtam* — it was signed in my presence. *Rava*'s concern is not about whether the *get* was written correctly, but about the practical problem of signature validation. We see at the end of the *mishnah* that a *get* delivered in *Eretz Yisrael* is subject to challenge: if the husband comes forward and claims the *get* is a forgery, the mechanism for resolving that challenge is *yitkayem be-chotmav* — signature validation, either through the witnesses themselves or through others who can identify their signatures.

Within *Eretz Yisrael*, this is manageable. One can locate witnesses, summon those who know the signatories, produce corroborating documents. But if the *get* was signed in a distant land and the challenge arises years later in *Eretz Yisrael*, how will one ever find witnesses to validate those signatures? They are back in *medinat hayam*, impossible to summon. *Rava* therefore says: we require upfront validation by the *shaliach* himself. He testifies at the point of delivery that the *get* was signed in his presence — and that testimony, even from a single witness as we will see, suffices to forestall the need for later signature validation.

### Nafka Mina Cases

The *gemara* then asks: *mai beinaihu* — what is the practical difference between these two reasons? And it proceeds to spell out several elegant *nafka minos*.

First: *de'asu bei trei* — two people brought the *get*. According to *Rava*, who is concerned about the ability to validate signatures at a later date, the presence of two witnesses delivering the *get* alleviates the concern. The two *messengers* together, by the very act of delivering the *get*, implicitly testify that it was legitimately dispatched by the husband; a subsequent forgery claim would be answerable through their testimony. But according to *Rabbah*, who is concerned about *lishmah*, the presence of two messengers solves nothing. The question of whether the *get* was written in accordance with *halacha* is entirely independent of how many people delivered it.

Second: *mimedina limedina b'Eretz Yisrael* — from one region to another within *Eretz Yisrael*, such as from *Yehuda* to *Galil*. According to *Rabbah*, everyone in *Eretz Yisrael* knows the requirement of *lishmah*, so there is no concern. But according to *Rava*, even within *Eretz Yisrael*, if the *get* was written in one region and delivered in another, the practicalities of locating witnesses for signature validation across those regions may still be difficult — one might need the declaration even there.

Third: *be-osah medinah b'medinat hayam* — within a single country in *medinat hayam*. According to *Rabbah*, who is concerned about *lishmah*, the problem exists even within one country abroad, since the concern is one of halachic knowledge. But according to *Rava*, if the *get* was written and delivered within the same country overseas, one will be able to locate witnesses for signature validation if needed — they are all in the same place.

These *nafka minos* are elegant because they isolate the exact axis of disagreement between the two *amoraim*: *Rabbah*'s concern is halachic competence, while *Rava*'s concern is logistical access.

### One Witness

The *gemara* now asks: according to *Rabbah*, who says the concern is that people in *medinat hayam* do not know the laws of *lishmah*, why does one witness suffice? If we genuinely doubt whether the *get* was produced in accordance with *halacha* — if we are uncertain of its *kashrus* — surely we require two witnesses to resolve that doubt, as is the case with all testimony in the Torah.

The *gemara* answers: *ed echad ne'eman b'issurin* — a single witness is trusted in matters of *kashrus* status. When the question is not one of conflicting factual claims but of an object's halachic status, the tradition holds that one witness suffices. *Rashi* notes the breadth of this principle: the Torah trusted every individual Jew to testify reliably about the separation of *terumah*, about the *shechita* of an animal, about the removal of *gid ha-nasheh* and *chelev*. When you purchase meat from a butcher, you do not require two witnesses to confirm it was properly slaughtered; the butcher's own representation suffices. As *Tosafos* puts it: *heicha anu somchin al neshoteinu* — we rely on our wives when they serve us food they have prepared, when they tell us meat was properly salted, when they report that they have attended the *mikvah*.

### Challenge Issued

The *gemara* immediately raises a sharp challenge. When we say *ed echad ne'eman b'issurin*, in what circumstances does that apply? The typical case is like a piece of fat: there is a piece of meat before us, and we do not know whether it is *chelev* — forbidden fat — or *shuman* — permitted fat. There is no prior known status of the piece, and a single witness can establish which it is. But — and this is the challenge — *aval hacha de-it-chazak issura d'eshet ish*: here, the woman was known to be married. She entered the situation with an established status of *eshet ish*, a forbidden relationship. We are not in a situation of mere uncertainty; we are in a situation of *chazakas issur* — a presumption of prohibition. Can a single witness overturn that?

Moreover, *havei davar she-b'ervah*: this is a matter of *arayos* — sexual prohibitions — and for those, the Torah's standard is *ein davar she-b'ervah pachos mishnayim*, not fewer than two witnesses. The woman's marital status, and therefore her permissibility to others, is a question of *arayos*, and *arayos* categorically requires two witnesses.

So there are, in fact, two independent reasons why one witness should *not* suffice here: first, the *chazakas issur* of being a married woman; second, the inherent requirement of two witnesses for all matters of *arayos*. How, then, does the *mishnah* permit the single declaration of the *shaliach* to suffice?

### Beyado Concept

*Tosafos* introduces an important conceptual tool in response to the first problem. The reason one witness suffices to overturn a *chazakas issur* in ordinary *issurim* — the piece of fat, the unsalted meat, the question of *shechita* — is the principle of *beyado*: the matter lies within the power of the person testifying to change. A butcher *can* shecht the animal. A householder *can* salt his own meat. A person *can* separate *terumah*. Because it was within their power to have done the permissible thing, they are believed when they testify that they did so, even against a background presumption of prohibition.

By contrast, neither the woman nor the *shaliach* can bring about a divorce independently. No matter how much effort or money is applied, unless the husband willingly gives the *get*, the woman remains married. The divorce is not *beyado* — not within their power to accomplish. And according to *Tosafos*, when the matter is *lo beyado* — not within one's power to change — a single witness does not suffice to overcome a *chazakas issur*.

### Unresolved Q

This leaves us with a compounded difficulty. The *gemara*'s challenge runs on two tracks: *chazakas issur* combined with *lo beyado*, and the categorical requirement of two witnesses for *arayos*. Even for those authorities who hold that a single witness *can* overcome a *chazakas issur* even when the matter is *lo beyado*, the second problem remains: this is *ervah*, and *davar she-b'ervah* always requires two witnesses. The woman was a *eshet ish*, and her permissibility to others is a matter of *arayos* by definition.

So the question stands in full force, and the *gemara*'s answer will have to address both dimensions simultaneously. The answer is left as a *cliffhanger* — to be resolved at the opening of the next *daf*.

---

---

# Gittin 3

## Rabbah vs. Rava

### Core Dispute Intro

The *mishna* at the opening of *Gittin* requires the *shaliach* — the agent delivering the *get* — to declare *bifanai nechtav bifanai nechtam*: "it was written before me and signed before me." The *gemara* explores this requirement through the lens of a foundational debate between Rabbah and Rava, two *amoraim* whose positions have become a touchstone for understanding the entire tractate.

### Rabbah's Lishma Focus

Rabbah's concern is *lishma* — that the *get* was written according to *halacha*, specifically for the sake of this woman and this divorce. His emphasis falls on *bifanai nechtav*, "it was written before me," because the writing is the act that must be performed with the proper intent and in accordance with the relevant laws. Rabbah's declaration is essentially a halachic certification: I witnessed that this document was executed correctly.

### Rava's Signature Focus

Rava's concern is different. His focus is on *eidim metzuyim lekaymo* — the practical problem that a *get* arriving from a distant place cannot easily have its signatures verified. Witnesses who know the signatories may simply not be available. Rava therefore emphasizes *bifanai nechtam*, "it was signed before me," because the *shaliach's* testimony addresses the authenticity of the signatures themselves. It preempts the possibility that the *get* will later be challenged as a forgery.

### Nafka Minot Examples

The *gemara* presents two elegant *nafka minas* — practical differences — that sharpen the distinction between the two positions. First: a *get* delivered from one province to another within *chutz l'aretz*, but within the same jurisdiction. Here there is no difficulty locating witnesses to verify signatures, so Rava's concern does not apply. But because it is *chutz l'aretz*, there remains a legitimate question whether the scribes and signatories were fully versed in the *halachos* of *lishma*. According to Rabbah, the declaration is required; according to Rava, it is not. Second: a *get* traveling from province to province within *Eretz Yisrael*. There, the *halachic* proficiency of those who wrote and signed the *get* is not in question — but geographic distance makes verification of signatures difficult. According to Rava, the declaration is required; according to Rabbah, it is not. Two positions, two sharply differentiated *nafka minas*.

---

## Ed Echad Question

### One Witness Problem

Having identified what the *shaliach's* declaration accomplishes, the *gemara* turns to a deeper structural question: why does a single witness suffice? Whether the *shaliach* is certifying *lishma* (Rabbah) or authenticating signatures (Rava), this would normally appear to require two witnesses. The *gemara* begins to press this question.

### Ed Echad Principle

The initial answer offered is the well-established principle of *eid echad ne'eman b'issurin* — a single witness is trusted in matters of *issur*, religious prohibition. Just as we trust one person to tell us that a piece of meat is *kosher*, we may trust one person to say that this *get* is halachically valid. The *get* is, from this vantage point, a question of permitted and forbidden — is this woman now permitted to remarry? — and in that domain, one witness carries sufficient weight.

### Itchazek Issura Issue

The *gemara* immediately raises a powerful objection. The principle of *eid echad ne'eman b'issurin* applies when the status of an object is genuinely unknown at the outset. A piece of meat whose identity is unclear — is it *chelev* or permitted fat? — may be ruled upon by one witness. But here, the woman's status is not unknown. She is a married woman. Her *issur* has been established: *itchazek issura d'eishet ish*. When a forbidden status is already fixed and certain, one witness is ordinarily insufficient to overturn it. This significantly complicates the initial answer.

### Tosafot Defense

*Tosafos* raises a further nuance in defense of *eid echad*. We do, in fact, trust single witnesses even regarding established forbidden statuses in certain contexts — the butcher, for instance, or one's wife who has prepared meat at home. We believe them that the *shechita* was performed, the fat removed, the meat properly treated. *Tosafos* explains the distinction: in those cases, the matter was *b'yado* — within the power and ability of that very person to perform or arrange. A butcher could kasher the meat; a wife could ensure it was done correctly. Here, however, no one can divorce this woman except her husband. The act is entirely outside anyone else's control. That is the *gemara's* point: *b'yado* is the key criterion, and it is absent here.

### Davar Shebe'erva

Even setting aside *itchazek issura*, there is a second, independent obstacle: the principle that *ein davar shebe'erva pachos mishnayim* — no matter touching on *arayos*, on forbidden sexual relationships and personal status, is decided with fewer than two witnesses. A married woman's status is not merely a standard *issur*; it is an *issur* rooted in *arayos*. The question of whether she is permitted or forbidden to other men always requires two witnesses as an absolute floor. This is the cliffhanger the *gemara* leaves us with: both on account of *itchazek issura* and on account of *davar shebe'erva*, one witness appears categorically insufficient.

---

## Rov Beki'in Solution

### Rov Principle

The *gemara* now offers its answer. The underlying premise of the concern — that perhaps the *get* was not written *lishma* — does not actually rise to the level of a genuine *safek* requiring formal resolution. This is because of *rov beki'in*: the majority of people, even in *chutz l'aretz*, are in fact familiar with and committed to the *halachos* of *lishma*. The majority rule allows us to simply assume that the *get* was performed correctly without requiring any formal verification.

### Rabbi Meir Mi'uta

A natural challenge arises from Rabbi Meir, who is known throughout *Shas* as one who is sensitive to minority possibilities — *de-chayeish le-mi'uta* — and does not dismiss them lightly. If there is a minority of people who do not know the relevant *halachos*, should Rabbi Meir not require that this concern be explicitly addressed? The *gemara* answers: *stam sofra de-dayanim migmar g'miri* — the scribes of the courts know the *halacha*. Who actually writes a *get*? Not the general population, but the *sofrim*, the professional scribes attached to *beis din*. The *hamon am* may not know the particulars of *lishma*, but the *sofrim* overwhelmingly do. As *Tosafos* frames it, the ignorant minority constitutes a *mi'uta de-mi'uta* — a minority of a minority — a category so small that even Rabbi Meir is not troubled by it.

### Sofrim Knowledge

The force of this answer depends on understanding who actually produces a *get*. Given the levels of literacy in the relevant era, the universe of those writing *gittin* was essentially coextensive with the *sofrim de-dayanim*, the court scribes. These are professionals embedded in the court system. Their knowledge of the *halachos* of *gittin* is virtually certain. The concern that a *get* may have been written by someone who did not understand *lishma* is therefore exceedingly remote.

### Mi'ut Categories

*Tosafos* articulates a formal halachic distinction that underlies this analysis. There is a *mi'ut d'shchiach* — a prevalent or significant minority, sometimes quantified as something above approximately five percent — and a *mi'ut lo shchiach*, a trivial or negligible minority. These two categories are treated fundamentally differently in *halacha*.

### Leidas Hasafek

A *mi'ut d'shchiach* generates a *leidas hasafek* — it raises a question that must be addressed. Once such a minority is acknowledged, one must find a way to resolve the doubt: through *rov*, *chazaka*, investigation, or some other mechanism. A *mi'ut lo shchiach*, by contrast, does not even create a *leidas hasafek*. It does not rise to the level of a problem requiring a solution; it is treated as though it simply does not exist as a halachic concern. The *gemara* is saying that the possibility of a *get* being written by someone unfamiliar with *lishma* falls into this latter category — so negligible that it does not register as a question needing to be addressed.

---

## Aguna Concern

### Rabbis' Initiative

Given the foregoing analysis, the *gemara* reaches a striking conclusion: from a purely technical standpoint, we should never have needed the *shaliach* to say anything at all. The *rov* of scribes know the *halacha*; the minority is too trivial to generate concern. And yet the Rabbis specifically created the requirement of *bifanai nechtav bifanai nechtam*. The *gemara* explains: *ve-rabbanan hu de-atzrich* — it is the Rabbis who imposed this additional demand, requiring that even a non-issue be formally addressed. They introduced a concern that strict halachic logic did not require. This is one of the first explicit invocations of the principle that will recur throughout the tractate: *mishum aguna akilu bah rabbanan* — because of the concern for *aguna*, a woman who would otherwise be unable to remarry, the Rabbis acted.

### Why Higher Standard

The Rabbis' reasoning is as follows. Even though the *rov* of scribes unquestionably know the *halachos*, personal status is profoundly consequential. The stakes involve not merely whether one person committed a transgression, but whether any subsequent children might be *mamzerim*. In a domain of such severity, the Rabbis felt it appropriate to demand a greater level of certainty — something beyond a mere inferential reliance on majority. They wanted something concrete, some act of testimony or verification that would stand behind the *get*. At the same time, they recognized that if they raised this concern they would need to respond to it.

### Rabbinic vs. Biblical

Critically, because the concern is Rabbinic in origin — it was the Rabbis who created the problem by raising it, not the Torah that mandated it — the Rabbis retained the latitude to decide how to resolve it. They determined that one witness would suffice. Requiring two witnesses to satisfy what is ultimately a Rabbinically-generated demand would have been disproportionate.

### Two Witness Problem

The practical consequences of demanding two witnesses would have been severe. A *get* arriving from *Medinat HaYam* — from overseas — would be blocked pending the production of two witnesses who could confirm the *get* was written and signed according to *halacha*. Who would those witnesses be? One would have to retrieve additional people from far away, a *tircha* — a burden — that might prove practically impossible. In many cases, the *get* simply would not be deliverable. That outcome is precisely what the Rabbis sought to prevent by accepting one witness.

---

## Defense of One Witness

### Apparent Stringency

The *gemara* now raises an incisive challenge: *hai kulla bu humra hu* — do you think this is a leniency? It is actually a stringency in disguise. By accepting only one witness rather than two, you have set the woman up for disaster. *De-im mas'rechet trei* — if you required two witnesses at the outset, a husband would have no opening to later challenge the *get* with any success. Two witnesses, properly testified before a *beis din*, are close to unassailable. But with only one witness, the *gemara* fears: *ati ba'al u'fasel lei* — the husband might come later and invalidate it. He might claim the *get* was not written *lishma*, that the process was flawed, that he had not truly understood what he was doing. If only one person stands behind the *get*, such a challenge might succeed. The woman might be left in the worst possible position — having lived as though divorced, now told the *get* is invalid.

### Shaliach Diligence

The *gemara* resolves this through a principle the later *rishonim* articulate as *me'ikara mi-dikdaik* — from the very outset, the *shaliach* is extremely careful. The reason is that, as the *gemara* notes — *bifnei kama nosna lah*, in front of how many does the *shaliach* deliver the *get*? — a debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina addresses this question: one holds the *shaliach* delivers before two witnesses, the other before three. The point is that the *shaliach* knows his declaration must be made before an audience. He is submitting what amounts to formal testimony. A person who knows he will have to formally testify is not cavalier about what he is testifying to; he makes absolutely certain in advance that the facts are as he will state them. Moreover, *v'lo ati l'irurei nafshei* — he will not put himself in the position of having his testimony publicly challenged and undermined.

### Rashi Refinement

Rashi adds an important dimension to what *me'ikara mi-dikdaik* actually entails. One might have assumed the *shaliach* is being careful to verify technical compliance — that the *get* was written *lishma*, that all the details were in order. But Rashi emphasizes something different. The more realistic concern, as Rashi reads the *gemara*, is that a husband who later challenges the *get* is typically not raising a genuine halachic defect that he happened to notice. He is almost certainly a husband who had misgivings, who is reconsidering the divorce, who is now motivated by regret. Given that reality, what the *shaliach* must be careful about — what his *dikduk* consists of — is ensuring that the husband was fully committed and resolute at the time of the *get*. The *shaliach* knows that his word may one day stand against the husband's, and so he makes certain the husband has no reservations, no hesitations, nothing that could later be dressed up as a halachic challenge.

### Shaliach Credibility

Rashi adds a second point. Even if a challenge does occur — whether based on legitimate concerns or on a husband's change of heart — *eino ne'eman*: the husband is not believed. *De-vadai dak be-milta ve-shapir* — the *shaliach* unquestionably knew what he was saying, and his claim carries more weight than the husband's belated challenge. This second point is crucial to the *gemara's* overall structure: not only is a challenge unlikely (because the *shaliach* has prevented it from arising), but even if it does arise, the *get* is protected because the *shaliach* will prevail.

### Mishna Support

*Tosafos* points out that this resolution finds implicit support in the *mishna* itself. The *mishna* states, regarding *gittin* in *Eretz Yisrael* — where no initial declaration is required — *im yesh alav orerim yitkayem be-chotmav*: if the *get* is challenged, it must be validated through its signatures. The contrast is instructive. In *Eretz Yisrael*, without an upfront declaration, a challenge can succeed in forcing signature validation. But in *chutz l'aretz*, where the *shaliach* has made the declaration of *bifanai nechtav bifanai nechtam*, the *mishna* strongly implies that a challenge does not open the door to re-examination. The upfront declaration serves as a shield against future challenge, precisely as the *gemara* has been arguing.

---

## Rava's Signature Valid

### Signature Validation Q

Having resolved the question for Rabbah's position — why one witness suffices to certify *lishma* — the *gemara* turns to the parallel question for Rava. Rava holds that the *shaliach's* function is to authenticate signatures, addressing the absence of *eidim metzuyim* who could verify them. Here too, the question immediately arises: *liba'ei trei* — why not require two? Signature validation is a formal halachic process; since when does one person suffice?

### Kiyum Shtarot

The process at issue is *kiyum shtaros* — the standard legal procedure for validating a document. Ordinarily, before a *beis din* acts on a document, the signatures must be authenticated. This is done either by the signatories themselves or by two witnesses who recognize the signatures. The number two is structural: it mirrors the requirement for testimony in general. Allowing one person to validate a document's signatures is not the norm in any other context.

### Ed Echad Issurin

The *gemara* offers the same answer as before: *eid echad ne'eman b'issurin*. One witness is trusted in matters of *issur*. This is a striking application of the principle. The *gemara* is not treating the *get* as an ordinary *shtar* in the domain of civil law — *mammonus* — where signature validation would clearly require two. Instead, it is recategorizing the authentication of this document as fundamentally an *issur v'heter* question. The *shliach* validating the signatures of a *get* is not doing *kiyum shtaros* in the technical civil-law sense; he is testifying that a document capable of changing a woman's halachic status is genuine. That is a question of *issur*, and in that domain, one witness can in principle suffice.

This is a significant *chiddush* in how the *gemara* frames the *get*. The *get* is simultaneously a *shtar* and an instrument of personal status. The *gemara* here chooses to see it through the lens of *issur v'heter* rather than through the lens of documentary law — and that reframing is what permits the testimony of one witness. The *gemara* thus consciously brackets the *shtar* identity of the *get* and foregrounds its *issur* identity.

### Woman Status Issue

The *gemara* immediately reasserts the same objection it raised for Rabbah's position: *itchazek issura d'eishet ish*. The woman's status as a married woman is established and known. *Eid echad ne'eman b'issurin* applies to cases of genuine uncertainty — a piece of meat of unknown identity, *safeik shel chelev safeik shel shuman*. It does not apply when the forbidden status has already been fixed. A woman who is a married woman is not in an uncertain state; her *issur* is established. One witness cannot overturn what is known and certain.

### Davar Shebe'erva

Beyond *itchazek issura*, the *gemara* reasserts the second independent obstacle: *havei davar shebe'erva*, and *ein davar shebe'erva pachos mishnayim* — no fewer than two witnesses suffice for any matter touching on *arayos*. Divorcing a woman is precisely such a matter. Whether approached through the *issur* angle or the *shtar* angle, two witnesses appear to be required on all fronts. The question of how one witness can validate the signatures of a *get* has now been posed in full force for Rava's position, just as it was for Rabbah's.

---

## Reish Lakish Principle

### Signatures on Document

The *gemara* resolves the impasse by invoking the principle of Reish Lakish: *edim hachatumim al hashtar* — witnesses who are signed on a document.

### Vetting Presumption

Reish Lakish states: *na'asu kemi shenachakra edusam beveis din* — it is as though their testimony has already been received and vetted in a court of law. This is a foundational principle about the nature of signed documents in Jewish law. When two people sign a document, the act of signing is treated as equivalent to appearing before a court and delivering testimony. The *chiddush* is that we do not then require a separate procedure to re-examine and validate what they have said.

The deeper implication, as the *gemara* develops it, is even more striking. Normally when a witness appears before a *beis din*, the court subjects him to *drisha ve-chakira* — rigorous examination and cross-examination. One might think: a person simply wrote something on a document and signed it; where is the cross-examination? Reish Lakish's principle is that the very act of signing constitutes a waiver of that process. The signed document is treated as testimony already vetted.

### Chiddush No Validation

The *gemara* takes this one step further. Not only does Reish Lakish eliminate the need for cross-examination of what the witnesses said — he also establishes that at a *de'oraisa* level, there is no requirement to independently verify that the signatures on the document are genuine. The presumption is that a document bearing two signatures is authentic. We do not, at a biblical level, suspect forgery. This is the *chiddush*: that at the level of Torah law, a signed document is presumed to be what it appears to be. We do not require two witnesses to come and confirm that these really are the signatures of the people named.

This may seem counterintuitive — forgeries are certainly possible. But the reasoning appears to be that the exposure to challenge and the social and legal consequences of a detected forgery create a sufficient deterrent. The *gemara* draws an implicit parallel to how signed instruments function in practice: we presume authenticity unless challenged.

### Rabbinic Requirement

It follows that the requirement to validate signatures before accepting a document — the entire institution of *kiyum shtaros* — is not a biblical requirement at all. It is a *derabbanan*, a Rabbinic enactment. The Rabbis, as a practical matter, imposed the requirement that documents be validated before a court acts on them. They were not willing to rely on the Reish Lakish presumption in practice without some gatekeeping. But at the *de'oraisa* level, none of this is required. The document, by virtue of its signatures, is presumed valid.

### Waive Validation

This distinction between *de'oraisa* and *derabbanan* is what resolves the difficulty for Rava's position. The need for two witnesses to validate signatures is Rabbinic. In the case of a *get*, the Rabbis chose to waive that Rabbinic requirement — *mishum aguna akilu bah rabbanan*. Rather than demand the full apparatus of *kiyum shtaros*, they accepted one witness. Because the underlying requirement is Rabbinic, the Rabbis retained the authority to relax it. One witness satisfies the Rabbinically-created concern without imposing an impossible burden that would prevent *get* delivery from distant places.

---

## Woman at Risk

### Husband Challenge

The *gemara* raises the same structural objection that it raised for Rabbah's position: this apparent leniency is in fact a stringency. *D'i atzreicht lah trei* — if you required two witnesses to validate the signatures, the husband would have no avenue to come later and challenge the *get*. *Lo ati ba'al u'ma'areer u'pasel lah* — he would not be able to come and contest it and render it invalid. But with only one witness standing behind the signature validation, *ati ba'al u'ma'areer u'pasel lah* — the husband could arrive and challenge the authenticity of the *get*, potentially leaving the woman in a devastating situation.

### One Witness Protection

The question sharpens: what exactly protects the woman if the husband does raise a challenge? If we have accepted only one witness's testimony that the signatures are genuine, what is the legal weight of that testimony when the husband, who is the *ba'al davar* — the principal and most directly interested party — appears and contests it?

### Delivery Witnesses

The *gemara's* answer parallels its earlier resolution for Rabbah: *bifnei kamma nosna lah* — in front of how many people does the *shaliach* deliver the *get*? Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina debate whether it must be two or three. Either way, delivery occurs before witnesses. This structural feature of the *get* delivery process is what protects against challenge. The *shaliach* knows he must deliver before an audience and that his declaration will be part of a formal, witnessed proceeding. Accordingly, *meikara meidakdeik* — from the very outset he takes every care to ensure that the husband was genuinely committed to the *get* and has no misgivings.

### Shaliach Credibility

Even if a challenge materializes, the *shaliach* is believed over the husband. *V'lo ati l'irurei nafshai* — the *shaliach* will not expose himself to reputational damage by making a claim he cannot support. Having been diligent from the outset, having ensured the husband had no second thoughts, having testified before witnesses, the *shaliach's* credibility prevails. The *gemara's* bottom line is the same as it was for Rabbah: the combination of the *shaliach's* diligence, the near-impossibility of a genuine challenge arising, and the *shaliach's* credibility in the event of a challenge together render the one-witness framework both practically sound and halachically defensible.

---

## Both Phrases Req'd

### Writing Phrase Q

Having established the theoretical foundation for each position, the *gemara* presses further. Rava holds that the *shaliach's* function is to authenticate the signatures. If so, the phrase *bifanai nechtam* — signed before me — is entirely appropriate. But why say *bifanai nechtav* — written before me — at all? If the issue is signature validity, the writing process is irrelevant to Rava's concern. This redundancy is the *gemara's* opening challenge.

### Confusion Risk

The *gemara* presents Rava's answer: if the *shaliach* said only *bifanai nechtam*, people observing this would conclude that one witness can validate signatures in the context of *kiyum shtaros* generally. *Ati l'achlufei b'kiyum shtaros de'alma b'eid echad* — people would confuse this with normal signature validation, conclude that one witness is sufficient for all documents, and halachic standards for document validation would erode. To prevent this confusion, Rava agrees that *bifanai nechtav* must be stated as well, signaling that something categorically different from standard *kiyum shtaros* is occurring.

### Three Factors

Rabbah pushes back on Rava's reasoning: are there not already enough distinguishing features to prevent this confusion? Rava himself articulates three. First, the language itself: in normal *kiyum shtaros*, witnesses say *yadina* — "we recognize these signatures." The *shaliach* says *bifanai* — "before me" — an entirely different formulation that already signals a departure from the norm. Second, women are eligible to serve as *shaliach* and make this declaration, whereas women cannot serve as witnesses in ordinary *kiyum shtaros*. Third, the *ba'al davar* — the principal, the interested party — can serve as *shaliach* here; under normal circumstances, an interested party cannot validate signatures. The wife herself could in principle serve as *shaliach* in a specially constructed case. These three differences, Rabbah argues, already mark this practice as sui generis, making *bifanai nechtav* unnecessary.

### Rabbah Counter

Rava's response is that these distinguishing factors are insufficient. The textual difference — *bifanai* versus *yadina* — does not actually preclude confusion, because if the *shaliach* were to say *yadina* rather than *bifanai nechtam*, we would still accept the testimony. As *Tosafos* clarifies: Rava's concern is not that a single *shaliach* saying *bifanai* would be confused with *kiyum shtaros*, but that if two people delivered the *get*, they could say *yadina* — and that would genuinely resemble standard signature validation with two witnesses. The public might then draw the wrong lesson. Because in practice the *shaliach* might fall back on *yadina* rather than *bifanai*, and because this would be accepted, there remains a real risk of confusion unless *bifanai nechtav* is also stated.

### Both Required

The resolution is that both phrases are necessary, each serving a distinct purpose. *Bifanai nechtav* addresses Rabbah's concern — certifying *lishma* — and also, for Rava, signals that this is not ordinary *kiyum shtaros*. *Bifanai nechtam* addresses Rava's concern — authenticating signatures — and also, for Rabbah, confirms that the *chasimah* was likewise performed according to *halacha*. Together, the two phrases reflect both dimensions of the *get's* validity, and together they make the declaration's unique character unmistakably clear.

---

## Writing vs. Signing

### Both Lishma Q

The *gemara* now turns to a foundational question about the nature of a *get* as a halachic instrument. If the concern is *lishma* and the declaration includes both *bifanai nechtav* and *bifanai nechtam*, the implication is that both the *kesivah* — the writing — and the *chasimah* — the signing — must be performed *lishma*. Who is the *tanna* who holds this? The *gemara* frames this as a search for the author of the *mishna's* formulation, and in doing so, introduces the most fundamental debate of *Masechet Gittin*.

### Rabbi Meir Position

Rabbi Meir, whose is the presumed view of unattributed *mishnayos*, holds that the *chasimah* is the essential act. The *get* is constituted by its signing, not its writing. The writing alone is merely words on paper; it is the signature that transforms the document into a legal instrument.

### Attached Ground

The *gemara* derives Rabbi Meir's position from the rule that *ein kosvin b'mchubar l'karka* — one may not write a *get* on something still attached to the ground. The rule is that nothing may intervene between the writing and the delivery in a way that could disqualify the *get*. Writing on attached material means the document cannot be handed over without first cutting it down — and that act of cutting intervenes between writing and delivery.

### Cutting Down Valid

However, if one violated this rule and wrote on something attached to the ground, and then *telasho v'chasamo u'nesano lah* — uprooted it, signed it, and delivered it — the *get* is *kasher*. This is the critical datum for understanding Rabbi Meir. Nothing occurred between the signing and the delivery. Even though something did intervene between the writing and the delivery — namely, the cutting down — this is irrelevant, because what matters is the signing. The *chasimah* is the *ikar*; it is the act that constitutes the *get*.

### Rabbi Eliezer Position

Rabbi Eliezer takes the opposite view: *kesivah ba'ei chasimah lo ba'ei* — the writing is the essential act; signing is not halachically necessary. The *get* is constituted by being written, not by being signed. Signatures are extrinsic to the document's essential validity.

### Three Gittin

The *gemara* introduces the position of Rabbi Eliezer by invoking the *mishna* of *shloshah gittin pesulin v'im nises ha-velad kasher* — three *gittin* that are rabbinically invalid, yet if the woman remarried, the child is not a *mamzer*. The fact that the child is not a *mamzer* reveals that the *get* is in fact valid at a biblical level; the disqualification is Rabbinic only. The three cases are: a *get* in the husband's own handwriting but without witnesses; a *get* with witnesses but without a date; and a *get* that is dated but bears only one signature.

### No Sig Valid

Rabbi Eliezer's position within this *mishna* goes further than any of those three cases. He states: *af al pi she-ein alav edim ella she-nasno bifnei edim* — even if there are no witnesses signed on the *get* at all, as long as it was delivered in the presence of witnesses, the *get* is *kasher*. She may even collect from encumbered property. The signature requirement is entirely dispensable for Rabbi Eliezer.

### Edei Mesirah

The reasoning Rabbi Eliezer offers is encapsulated in the principle the *gemara* will call *edei mesirah karti* — the witnesses of delivery effect the divorce. What validates a *get* is not the signatures on the document but the witnesses present at the moment of delivery. The witnesses of *mesirah* are what transform the act into a legally effective divorce. As a physical document, a *get* does not require signatures.

Why then do witnesses ever sign a *get*? Rabbi Eliezer explains: *she-mipnei she-ein edim chosmin al ha-get ella mipnei tikkun olam* — signatures on a *get* are only a Rabbinic enactment for the smooth functioning of society. If the *get* has no signatures and the delivery witnesses are unavailable twenty years later, the woman has no way to prove she was divorced. Signatures are a practical solution to that evidentiary problem — not a constitutive element of the divorce itself.

This brings the *gemara* back to its structural question. Rabbi Meir holds that *chasimah* is the *ikar* — so he requires signing *lishma* but not necessarily writing *lishma*. Rabbi Eliezer holds that *kesivah* is the *ikar* and signatures are Rabbinically unnecessary — so he requires writing *lishma*, but if signatures happen to be present, there would be no requirement that they be *lishma*, as they are superfluous in the first instance. Neither position straightforwardly supports requiring both writing and signing to be *lishma* simultaneously. The *gemara* pauses here, and this question — which *tanna* is the author of the formulation that demands both — carries us forward into the next *daf*.

---

---

# Gittin 4

## Rabbah vs. Rava

### Two Explanations

The discussion continues from the bottom of 3b, where the central debate between Rabbah and Rava is still unfolding — a debate that will occupy us for several more days. The question is: why does the *shaliach* who delivers a *get* need to declare *bifnei nichtav ubifnei nichtam*, that it was written and signed in his presence? Is this declaration meant to testify that the *get* was executed in accordance with the laws of *lishma* — that is, composed with the proper intention directed toward this specific woman — as Rabbah holds? Or is it meant to validate the signatures on the document, so that if the *get* is ever challenged in the future, one need not face the difficulty of locating people who can authenticate those signatures? That is the position of Rava, expressed through the phrase *edim metzuyim lekaymo* — that witnesses are readily available to confirm the document's validity.

### Rabbah: Lishma

As the Gemara has already pointed out, the declaration contains two distinct components: the *shaliach* testifies both that the *get* was *written* and that it was *signed* in his presence. The term "signed" seems naturally to support Rava's concern with authenticating the signatories, while the term "written" seems to emphasize that the proper procedures governing the composition of a *get* were followed. The question then becomes: how does each position account for the component that seems to support the other?

### Rava: Signatures

Rava, who holds that the concern is with validating the signatures, explains that *bifnei nichtav* — the testimony about the writing — serves a different purpose altogether. Since this declaration is made by a single individual, which is itself unusual (normally signature validation requires two witnesses), people might become confused about the ordinary rules of authentication. By having the *shaliach* add that it was also written in his presence, the declaration signals that this is something distinctive — a special institution unique to *gittin*, not a standard case of *kiyum shtarot*.

### Both Terms

For Rabbah, however, who holds that the entire institution is about testifying to the *lishma* requirements, the question runs in the opposite direction: if the whole point is the writing, why must the *shaliach* also testify about the signing? The Gemara therefore assumes that Rabbah understands the *Mishnah* as reflecting a view that demands compliance with the laws of *gittin* not only in the writing but equally in the signing. This leads the Gemara into a fundamental debate that will reverberate throughout the entire *masechet*: what is it, precisely, that transforms a piece of paper into a *get*?

---

## Get Validity

The question the Gemara now frames is foundational: is it the writing of the document — executed according to the proper *halachot* — that creates the *get*? Or does the paper remain legally inert until it is signed, with the signatures themselves being the act that constitutes the *get* as a valid instrument? The Gemara presents this as a debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer, and it uses the question of *mechubar* — whether a *get* is disqualified if it was written while attached to the ground — as a testing case to expose the underlying logic of each position.

---

## R. Meir: Signing

Rabbi Meir holds that it is the signatures alone that create the *get*. In his terminology, the signing is *karti* — from the root *karet*, meaning it "cuts," it effects the severance. Just as *koret habrit* refers to the act that seals a covenant, here the *chatima* is the act that seals the divorce. The legal consequence of this view is striking: if the *get* is nothing until it is signed, then there is no logical basis for demanding anything particular about how it was written. All the *halachic* requirements — including *lishma* — attach only to the signing. Before the signatures are affixed, the document is just paper; one could, in principle, take a pre-printed form off the shelf that happens to bear the correct names and have it signed. It is only the interval between signing and delivery where requirements like *mechubar* apply.

---

## R. Eliezer: Writing

Rabbi Eliezer takes the opposite position: the writing is what matters, and the signatures are not required at all. A *get* delivered without signatures is valid — apparently even *lechatchila*, at the Torah level, and certainly *bediavad*. What is required, however, is that the *get* be delivered in the presence of witnesses. Here an important conceptual question arises: is this witness requirement structurally parallel to the witnesses required for *kiddushin* — that is, witnesses who validate the *act* of divorce rather than the *instrument* — or do those witnesses themselves form a constitutive part of the *get*? In Rabbi Eliezer's language, this principle is *eidei mesira karti*: it is the witnesses to the delivery who "cut," who effect the divorce.

The Gemara then asks: if Rabbi Eliezer does not require signatures at all, why would *bifnei nichtam* — the testimony about the signing — ever be relevant to him? The Gemara answers by citing Rabbi Abba: *modeh Rabbi Eliezer b'mezuyaf mitocho shehu pasul* — Rabbi Eliezer concedes that a document that is "forged from within" is invalid. Rashi explains *mezuyaf mitocho* as meaning that the document was signed by relatives or otherwise disqualified witnesses. Even though one need not sign the *get* at all, if one chooses to sign it, one may not do so with invalid witnesses. The principle is that one should not create something that purports to be a valid legal instrument while building an intrinsic defect into it: if you do not want to have signatures, do not have them; but if you are going to sign, you cannot sign with disqualified witnesses.

---

## R. Meir: Lenient

Returning to Rabbi Meir, the Gemara now asks directly: does Rabbi Meir truly impose no requirements whatsoever on the writing? The Gemara cites Rav Nachman quoting Rabbi Meir: if someone found a pre-written *get* bearing the husband's and wife's names, had it signed by witnesses, and delivered it to the wife, it is *kasher*. The Gemara then asks whether this ruling is stated only at the Biblical level, while rabbinically the writing would still need to meet certain standards. The Gemara rejects this qualification: if Rabbi Meir's ruling were only Biblical, he would have said "from a Torah perspective it is *kasher*." Since he simply says it is *kasher*, with no qualification, it is clear that Rabbi Meir imposes no requirements on the writing even rabbinically. The practical implication follows directly: there would be no basis for a *shaliach* to testify about how the *get* was written. We are therefore still searching for the opinion that demands both the writing and the signing follow all the proper requirements.

---

## R. Eliezer: Conditional

The Gemara now revisits Rabbi Eliezer from this angle. It was shown above that Rabbi Eliezer does not require signatures. But if he does not require them, why would there be any demand that they be done *lishma* when they are affixed? The Gemara answers: it is precisely the logic of *mezuyaf mitocho* that carries this through. If one does sign, the signature must be valid — not only in the narrow sense that the witnesses must be halachically qualified, but also with regard to *lishma*. Rashi adds this point explicitly: *o shelo lishma*, or if it was done without the proper intent, that too would constitute a problem for Rabbi Eliezer.

Tosafot raises a challenge: how can one compare the case of invalid witnesses — where the invalidity is intrinsic and obvious — to the case of signing *shelo lishma*, where there is no apparent deficiency? There are valid witnesses; they simply lacked the proper intent. Tosafot's own answer is somewhat less structurally elegant: the concern is practical — that people will come to rely on those signatures to permit her to remarry or to collect her *ketubah*. His final resolution is that once signing occurs at all, we apply a rabbinic rule: *gazrinan chatima atu ketiva* — we extend the requirements of the writing to the signing, so that slippage in the one domain will not infect the other.

One might, however, suggest a more far-reaching approach. There are *Rishonim* who hold that according to Rabbi Eliezer, when signatures are affixed to the *get*, they do not merely serve as circumstantial evidence that witnesses were present — they become, at the Torah level, an integral part of the *get* itself, carrying the full testimonial weight of a classic *shtar*. If this is correct, then once one has chosen to sign the *get*, those signatures are recognized by the Torah as constitutive elements of the document, and they therefore require the same criteria — including *lishma* — as the writing itself. Under this reading, the demand for *lishma* in the signatures is not merely rabbinic caution against confusion, but potentially a Torah-level requirement that flows from the act of having incorporated testimony into the document. Tosafot's answer frames this as a rabbinic fence; but the conceptual logic could extend to the Biblical level.

A further point bears emphasis: the requirement of signatures is, in the final analysis, a *tikkun olam* — a rabbinic institution for the welfare of society. *Mideoraita*, Rabbi Eliezer would hold that an unsigned *get* takes full legal effect, and the woman is divorced. Practically, however, *beit din* will not permit her to remarry without some form of documentation. She cannot simply present herself and claim she was divorced; she bears the status of an *eshet ish*, and the court will demand proof. External witnesses could theoretically be summoned, but that is not always feasible or convenient. The practical, prudent course is always to have the document signed. The absence of a signature leaves her divorced in the eyes of Heaven but effectively unable to act on that status in this world. The institution of signed *gittin* is therefore the Rabbis' way of ensuring that *mide'oraita* validity translates into workable legal recognition.

The conclusion of this section: Rabbi Eliezer is the opinion whose framework supports requirements on both the writing and the signing. He does not require the signatures, but once they are affixed, they must follow the same rules as the writing — whether one understands this rabbinically or, as suggested above, potentially even Biblically.

---

## R. Yehuda: Both

The Gemara then offers a further possibility through Rav Ashi: *ha mani Rabbi Yehuda hi* — the *Mishnah* could reflect the position of Rabbi Yehuda. As taught in a *baraita*, Rabbi Yehuda invalidates the *get* unless both its writing and its signing take place when the document is *betalush* — detached from the ground. While it is somewhat difficult to construct a realistic scenario where a document is written while detached but signed while still attached, the theoretical point is clear: Rabbi Yehuda regards both the writing and the signing as independently essential to the validity of the *get*, and the requirement of *mechubar* applies to both stages equally. Whether he conceptualizes this as two independent acts that together constitute the *get*, or as a unique synthesis in which both the writing and the signing are jointly necessary, is left open, but the practical demand is symmetrical.

---

## Why Not R. Yehuda

The Gemara immediately asks: if Rabbi Yehuda provides the cleanest fit — requiring both writing and signing — why did the Gemara not simply begin there? The answer is twofold. First, *setam Mishnah Rabbi Meir*: an anonymous *Mishnah* is presumptively attributable to Rabbi Meir, and the opening requirement of *bifnei nichtav ubifnei nichtam* is stated anonymously. It was therefore natural to first attempt to reconcile it with Rabbi Meir's position. Second, and more significantly: *dekaiyma lan hilchata keva'tei b'gittin* — the *halacha* follows Rabbi Eliezer in *gittin*. This is a remarkable moment in the *sugya*: right at the outset, in what is only the second *daf* of the *masechet*, the Gemara announces the operative ruling on one of the most fundamental questions in the entire tractate. The *halacha* is that signatures on a *get* are not required. A *get* delivered before witnesses who did not sign the document is Biblically valid. Rabbi Yehuda, whose position is neither the *stam Mishnah* nor the accepted ruling, was therefore the option of last resort.

This explains why the *sugya* works through the positions in the order it does. The initial anonymous statement is matched first to Rabbi Meir, then to Rabbi Eliezer, and only when both prove problematic does the Gemara reach Rabbi Yehuda. It is a well-constructed opening *sugya* that introduces a major conceptual debate, maps out the positions of the *Tannaim*, and announces the *halacha* — all within the first pages of the tractate.

---

## Medina HaYam

The Gemara now transitions to examining the rest of the *Mishnah* through the lens of the Rabbah-Rava debate. The *Mishnah* contains an internal dispute about what qualifies as *medinat hayam* — the overseas region or distant diaspora — that triggers the *shaliach*'s obligation to declare *bifnei nichtav ubifnei nichtam*. The dispute involves three positions: Rabban Gamliel holds that the requirement applies even to cities *semuchot le-Eretz Yisrael* — adjacent to the Land of Israel — and Rabbi Eliezer extends this further to cities that are *muvlaot b'tehum Eretz Yisrael* — geographically enclosed or surrounded by the territory of Israel. The Sages, representing the view that the requirement applies only to genuinely distant locations, take the opposing position. Abaye explains that the debate concerns towns near the border of Israel, some of which are so closely surrounded by Israelite territory that they are described as "swallowed up" within it. Rabbah bar bar Hana adds that such a place was as short a distance as from Bei Kubi to Pumbedita.

Rashi depicts the geometry as follows: *semuchot* refers to a city right at the border; *muvlaot* refers to a city that is not merely adjacent but effectively enclosed — surrounded on multiple sides by Israelite territory. These are different degrees of closeness to Israel, and they are different degrees of removal from the category of *medinat hayam*. The Tanna Kamma says that only truly distant locations require the declaration; Rabban Gamliel says that even a city just at the border falls under the requirement; Rabbi Eliezer holds that even a *muvlaot* city — effectively surrounded by Israel — still requires it.
