The Gemara asks: is this dispute best understood as reflecting the Rabbah-Rava debate? If the concern is *lishma* — cultural and legal awareness of the proper procedures — then a city right over the border is probably still part of the same cultural orbit and would know the relevant *halachot*. But if the concern is the availability of witnesses for *kiyum*, then even a nearby city over a political border represents a distinct travel barrier, and we cannot assume that witnesses will be readily accessible across it. On this reading, the debate in the *Mishnah* about near versus far is really a debate about which underlying concern governs the institution.

The Gemara, however, rejects the premise that this dispute maps directly onto the Rabbah-Rava divide. Instead, it holds that each of Rabbah and Rava can explain the debate internally within their own framework.

---

## Rabbah on Lishma

According to Rabbah — who holds the concern is *lishma* — the underlying principle is agreed upon by all: the requirement exists because communities outside Israel may not be adequately familiar with the *halachot* of *lishma*. The debate is then about where to draw the line.

The Tanna Kamma holds that cities so close to Israel are still part of the same cultural and legal sphere; proximity means they have absorbed the relevant knowledge, and no declaration is required. Rabban Gamliel distinguishes: a *muvlaot* city, surrounded on multiple sides by Israel, may indeed be culturally integrated enough to know the law — he will concede that much — but a *semuchot* city, merely adjacent without being enclosed, might not have absorbed the same standards, and he requires the declaration there. Rabbi Eliezer pushes back against any such case-by-case evaluation: we cannot go city by city assessing knowledge levels. A formal, categorical rule is necessary. The rule is simple — anything over the border requires the declaration — and Rabbi Eliezer invokes the principle of *lo plug*: we do not make distinctions within the category of *medinat hayam* based on individual circumstances.

---

## Rava on Witnesses

Rava's framework — that the concern is the availability of witnesses to authenticate the document — can explain the same dispute with equal coherence. Here too, all *Tannaim* agree on the underlying principle: the requirement exists because witnesses may not be readily available to validate signatures across geographic distances. The Tanna Kamma holds that nearby cities have enough cross-border travel that witnesses are sufficiently accessible. Rabban Gamliel distinguishes *muvlaot* from *semuchot*: a city truly surrounded by Israel will have robust travel and available witnesses, but one merely adjacent will not. Rabbi Eliezer again invokes *lo plug* and *shelo tachlok b'medinat hayam* — we do not parse the category of *medinat hayam* into subcategories; the formalist rule applies uniformly to everything across the border.

The Gemara's broader methodological point is significant: one can hold a single principled position and still debate its application. Whether the issue is *lishma* or *edim metzuyim*, the underlying debate about near and far is really a debate about formalism versus context. A legal system cannot operate through purely contextual, case-by-case determinations. At some point, rules must be categorical. The question is merely where to set the threshold and how rigorously to apply it.

---

## Molich Issue

The Gemara turns to the next clause of the *Mishnah*: *vehamolich* — the obligation of a *shaliach* who carries a *get* outward from Israel to the diaspora, not merely inward. The *Chachamim* say that the declaration is required both of one who brings a *get* from *medinat hayam* to Israel and of one who carries it *out* — *hamolich*. The inference is that the Tanna Kamma required the declaration only for *hamevi*, bringing it in, and not for *hamolich*. The Gemara asks: is this dispute about *molich* a direct reflection of the Rabbah-Rava debate?

On the *lishma* theory, the concern is about people in the diaspora who lack the proper knowledge. A *shaliach* carrying a *get* from Israel outward is departing from a place of expertise; there is no *lishma* problem on his end. There would therefore be no intrinsic reason to require the declaration. On the *edim* theory, however, travel barriers exist equally in both directions: witnesses in the diaspora are no more accessible to those in Israel than vice versa. The requirement should therefore apply symmetrically, and *hamolich* should require the declaration just as *hamevi* does.

This appears to be a clean test case for the Rabbah-Rava debate, and the Gemara initially entertains this reading. It then pulls back: each position can explain both the Tanna Kamma and the *Chachamim* from within its own logic.

Rabbah explains: *dekulei alma lefi she-ein bekiyim b'lishma*, and the debate about *molich* is whether we extend the requirement through a *gezerah* of *molich atu mevi*. The Tanna Kamma says no such extension is necessary. The *Chachamim* say that to avoid confusion — someone seeing that *hamevi* always declares might assume the requirement is universal, and become confused when *hamolich* does not — we institute a symmetric requirement. If people in *medinat hayam* observe that every *shaliach*, regardless of direction, makes this declaration, this itself serves an educational function consistent with the *lishma* concern. The Tanna Kamma is not willing to make that extension; the *Rabbanan* are.

Rava explains more simply: *dekulei alma lefi she-ein edim metzuyin lekaymo*, and the *Chachamim* who add *hamolich* are not introducing a new dispute but merely clarifying what was already implied. When the Tanna Kamma said *hamevi*, he meant it to encompass both directions; when the *Chachamim* add *hamolich* explicitly, *rabbanan batrai lefirushei taama d'Tanna Kamma hu de-atu* — they are clarifying and unpacking what the earlier statement already included. This parallels the earlier discussion of *medinat hayam* itself: just as the debate about *semuchot* and *muvlaot* was a dispute about the scope of a general term, the addition of *hamolich* is similarly an elaboration on the scope of *hamevi*.

---

## Medina to Medina

The Gemara now examines the clause: *hamevi get mimedina limedina b'medinat hayam* — one who carries a *get* from one *medina* to another within the diaspora is required to declare *bifnei nichtav ubifnei nichtam*. The Gemara asks what can be inferred from this. Both Rabbah's and Rava's concerns are clearly present when crossing from one diaspora district to another: *lishma* problems exist throughout the diaspora, and witness availability diminishes with each additional border crossed. The question is what the *Mishnah*'s language implies about cases it does not explicitly state.

---

## Rava's Challenge

The Gemara notes that a straightforward reading of *hamolich mimedina limedina b'medinat hayam* implies that within a *single* diaspora *medina*, the declaration would not be required. For Rava, who grounds the requirement in witness availability, this is perfectly intelligible: witnesses are more accessible within a single administrative district, where travel is less restricted. But for Rabbah, who grounds the requirement in *lishma*, the implication is more troubling. The *lishma* problem does not disappear merely because one stays within a single diaspora *medina*; the lack of proper halakhic awareness pervades the entire diaspora regardless of internal administrative divisions.

The Gemara also raises a harder challenge for Rabbah. The *Mishnah* explicitly states that one who brings a *get* within *Eretz Yisrael* does not need to make the declaration at all — including, apparently, when traveling from one region (*medina*) to another within Israel. For Rava, who focuses on witness availability, this is easily explained: Israel has special characteristics that ensure witnesses are accessible. But for Rabbah, who focuses on *lishma*, why should Israel's internal geography matter? The *lishma* requirements apply everywhere; crossing from the Galil to Yehuda involves a change of district no less than crossing within the diaspora. The distinction between Israel and the diaspora is built into Rabbah's framework at the macro level, but the internal distinction — *medina* to *medina* within Israel — is harder to derive from *lishma* concerns alone.

---

## Rabbah's Answer

The Gemara resolves Rabbah's difficulty. One might have thought, based on the *diyuk*, that staying within a single *medina* of *medinat hayam* exempts one from the declaration — which would be inexplicable if the concern is *lishma*, since *lishma* problems exist uniformly across the diaspora. The Gemara rejects this inference: even within a single diaspora *medina* the declaration is required; the *Mishnah*'s statement about traveling between *medinot* in *medinat hayam* is meant to contrast not with same-*medina* travel in the diaspora, but with *medina*-to-*medina* travel within *Eretz Yisrael*, which does not require the declaration. The *lishma* framework then handles this contrast naturally: Israel as a whole is the domain of proper halakhic knowledge, and the internal structure of Israel is irrelevant to that determination.

For Rava, the analogous challenge is met by invoking the institution of *olei regalim* — the pilgrimage festivals that brought people to Jerusalem from throughout the land. This constant, large-scale movement across all regions of Israel ensured that witnesses were readily and regularly available throughout the country, making the *edim metzuyim* concern inapplicable to any intra-Israel transit. When the Temple no longer stands, the Gemara substitutes *batei dinin d'kevi'ei* — the presence of fixed, established courts — which similarly attracted regular travel and ensured that witnesses from any corner of Israel could be found without undue difficulty. The Gemara acknowledges that this explanation works better in one direction of travel than the other, but the basic answer is that Israel's unique institutional life — whether centered on the *Beit HaMikdash* or on its network of permanent courts — provided the structural conditions under which witnesses were always effectively available, and thus the concern animating the requirement of *bifnei nichtav ubifnei nichtam* simply did not arise within its borders.

The *sugya* of this *daf* has thus worked through the core of the *Mishnah*: the foundational debate between Rabbah and Rava, the major tannaitic dispute about what constitutes a *get*, the announced *halacha* following Rabbi Eliezer, and an analysis of how the geographic debates within the *Mishnah* — near versus far, coming in versus going out, one *medina* versus another — each reflect and are illuminated by the two competing rationales. The analysis will continue on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Gittin 5

## Rabba vs. Rava Debate

### Debate Overview

The daf begins at the bottom of 4b, still working through the debate between Rabba and Rava concerning the reason the Mishnah requires the messenger who brings a *get* from abroad to declare *bifnei nichtav u'bifnei nechtam* — that the *get* was written and signed in his presence. Rabba holds that the requirement addresses *lishmah* concerns, ensuring the *get* was written with proper intent for this specific couple. Rava holds that the requirement addresses *ein eidim metzuyim lekaymo* — the practical unavailability of witnesses to validate the signatures. The Gemara has already worked through several *mishnayot* that could neatly have fallen along these lines, and has managed to explain each according to both positions.

### Asasyos Case

The outstanding question at this stage concerned why Eretz Yisrael enjoys a special status — why, within Eretz Yisrael, the messenger need not make this declaration even according to the position that the requirement stems from concerns about witness availability. The answer offered was that travel within Eretz Yisrael is common, whether due to the *Beis Hamikdash* or, in later periods, the prevalence of *batei dinim*.

The Gemara now advances to a fresh challenge. We learn in the Mishnah that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: even from one *hegemonia* to another — that is, from one jurisdiction to another within a single divided city — the messenger must make the declaration. Rabbi Yitzchak explains that there was a city in Eretz Yisrael called Asasyos, which was divided between two governments that were at odds with one another (*makpidim zeh al zeh*), such that travel from one side of the city to the other was effectively impossible — like East and West Berlin. Therefore, even within that single city, moving from one political jurisdiction to the other required the declaration.

The critical point is that this case is situated in Eretz Yisrael. Since Eretz Yisrael is generally exempt from the requirement on Rava's account — witnesses being available there — the reason Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel reintroduces the requirement must be the practical impossibility of travel and the resulting unavailability of witnesses. This is *nichah l'Rava* — it fits Rava's position well — but *kashya l'Rabba*, it is difficult for Rabba. If the concern were *lishmah*, there would be no reason for Eretz Yisrael's general exemption to be overridden by a divided city, since *lishmah* concerns do not depend on the ease of travel.

### Rabba Concedes

The Gemara concludes: *Rabba is lei d'Rava* — Rabba concedes Rava's point. The one who holds *lishmah* as his primary rationale also acknowledges that there is a genuine problem of *ein eidim metzuyim lekaymo*. Rabba's position is therefore not simply *lishmah* alone, but rather *lishmah* plus *ein eidim metzuyim lekaymo*.

This is, in fact, a coherent and elegant position: the declaration has two components — *bifnei nichtav* and *bifnei nechtam*. One might understand *bifnei nichtav* as addressing the *lishmah* concern — how the *get* was written — and *bifnei nechtam* as addressing the witness-validation concern — how it was signed.

### Two Concerns

With Rabba now accepting both rationales, the question becomes: what remains between Rabba and Rava? The answer is that while Rabba agrees to Rava, Rava does not agree to Rabba. Rava maintains that signature validation is the *sole* concern; *lishmah* adds nothing. The remaining dispute therefore concerns cases where signature validation is not at issue but a *lishmah* concern might still apply.

### Remaining Debate

What would constitute such a case? The Gemara identifies two possibilities. The first is where two witnesses bring the *get* together. The second is when the *get* is brought within the same country in *Medinat Hayam*.

### Two Witnesses Case

If two witnesses bring the *get*, they themselves implicitly testify that the husband dispatched them, thereby eliminating any concern about the signatures being forged. There is no need for further validation. Yet for Rabba, a *lishmah* concern may still exist if the *get* originated in *Chutz La'aretz* — if it came from a place where the laws of proper writing were not well known.

### Lishmah Concerns

Similarly, when the *get* is brought within the same country of *Medinat Hayam*, there is no problem of signature validation since witnesses are accessible within that jurisdiction. But for Rabba, the *lishmah* concern persists wherever a *Chutz La'aretz* problem exists — even within one country, if it is a place where *lishmah* was not carefully observed, such as a distant location where Torah was not studied.

In short: whenever there is a signature-validation concern, everyone agrees the declaration must be made — *Rabba is lei d'Rava*. What Rabba adds is that even where there is no such concern, if the *lishmah* problem of *Chutz La'aretz* applies, he requires the declaration as well.

---

## Mute Messenger Case

### Aino Yachol Intro

The Gemara now turns to a Mishnah that will serve as further evidence in this debate. The Mishnah states: one who brings a *get* from *Medinat Hayam* and is *eino yachol lomar* — unable to say *bifnei nichtav u'bifnei nechtam* — may rely instead on having the signatures validated: *im yesh alav eidim yiskayem b'chosamav*, if there are witnesses, let it be confirmed through the signatories. The apparent implication is stark: if you cannot make the declaration, simply validate the signatures, and the *get* is valid. This reads as though the entire point of the requirement is signature validation — nothing more.

Before accepting this reading, however, the Gemara must clarify what *eino yachol lomar* — "unable to say" — actually means. The obvious first answer is that the messenger is a *cheresh*, a deaf-mute. But that cannot be right: the Mishnah elsewhere states explicitly that a deaf-mute may not bring a *get* in the first place — *hakol k'sherim l'havi es haget chutz micheresh shoteh v'katan* — since a deaf-mute lacks the legal competence (*bar da'as*) required to serve as a *shaliach*. How then could the case be a deaf-mute?

### Rav Yosef Explanation

Rav Yosef resolves this: *k'gon shenasno lo k'shehu pike'ach* — the *get* was given to a person who was fully competent, but before he could declare *bifnei nichtav u'bifnei nechtam* after delivering the *get*, he became a deaf-mute. He had a stroke on the spot. That is why he is unable to say the declaration — not because he was a deaf-mute at the time of appointment as *shaliach*, but because he became one immediately after delivery.

### Tosafot Alternative

This answer strikes Tosafot as unnecessarily extreme. Two far simpler explanations present themselves: the messenger is simply mute (*ilem*) — physically unable to speak but legally competent — or he was not present at the writing and signing and therefore genuinely cannot testify to it. Either of these would make better sense of the phrase *eino yachol lomar*. And if the Gemara wanted to convey a case of physical inability, why not say *v'lo amar* — "and he did not say" — rather than the charged language of *eino yachol*, which seems to emphasize an absolute incapacity?

### Signatures Primary

Whatever the precise identity of the messenger in the Mishnah, the substantive point stands: someone delivered a *get* and was unable or failed to make the declaration, and the solution is simply to validate the signatures. This is a clear statement that the primary — indeed, on this reading, the sole — operative concern is signature validation. The Gemara therefore notes: *l'Rava nicha, l'Rabba kashya* — it is good for Rava, whose entire position rests on the signature concern, but difficult for Rabba, who also insists on a *lishmah* concern. What became of *lishmah* in this case? The Gemara answers: *l'achar shelamdu* — this Mishnah addresses the period after the laws of *lishmah* became widely known in *Chutz La'aretz*, at which point the *lishmah* concern ceased to apply.

---

## Lishmah to Signatures

### Evidence Conflict

This Gemara is striking in its overall trajectory. What began as a clear, principled debate — is the requirement of *bifnei nichtav u'bifnei nechtam* about *lishmah* or about signature validation? — has evolved in a way that seems to progressively favor Rava. First, Rabba concedes that signature validation is also a concern. Then, confronted with a Mishnah that implies the *lishmah* concern has entirely lapsed, Rabba is forced to concede further: there was a period when the *lishmah* issue ceased to be operative.

The argument weighing in Rabba's favor remains the Mishnah's fundamental distinction between Eretz Yisrael and *Chutz La'aretz*. If the requirement were purely about signature validation, the geographic distinction should track witness availability — and witnesses are available in Eretz Yisrael because of the *Beis Hamikdash* or the *batei dinim*. This indeed explains Eretz Yisrael's exemption, and the Asasyos case showed that even within Eretz Yisrael, the requirement can be reinstated when travel is impossible. All of this fits Rava's account. The emphasis on Eretz Yisrael is thus Rabba's best evidence, and even that is accounted for by Rava.

Yet there is a tension worth noting. The evidence pointing toward *lishmah* is the structural emphasis on Eretz Yisrael as the default domain of exemption. The evidence pointing toward signature validation is the repeated pattern by which *ein eidim metzuyim lekaymo* explains case after case with precision. And crucially, when the two accounts come apart — as in the Mishnah of *eino yachol* — the Gemara explains it away as *l'achar shelamdu*, suggesting that the *lishmah* concern is temporally contingent in a way that the signature concern is not. This indicates that the parameters of the requirement are contextual, not purely formalistic: if circumstances change, what was once a concern may cease to be one.

### Gezeirah Yachzor

This contextual flexibility, however, raises a difficulty. If *lishmah* is no longer a concern, why not simply permit the messenger to skip the declaration entirely and rely on signature validation from the outset? Let the Mishnah say: *lechatchila*, if you want to validate the signatures instead, be our guest — that is the better option.

The Gemara answers with the principle of *gezeirah shema yachzor hadavar lekilkulo* — we fear that if we abandon the established practice, conditions may revert to the problematic state that originally necessitated it. Things were bad once; they got better; they can get worse again, as indeed we have witnessed in our own times. Therefore, we do not say *lechatchila* that the declaration is unnecessary. We maintain the original requirement in its place: the messenger should continue to declare *bifnei nichtav u'bifnei nechtam*. Only when this becomes impossible will we acknowledge changed circumstances and permit signature validation instead.

### Lechatachila Bedi'eved

This creates a formal distinction between *lechatchila* and *bedi'eved*. *Lechatchila*, the old practice is preserved — the messenger must make the declaration. *Bedi'eved*, if that is not possible, we acknowledge that *lishmah* is no longer an active concern and signature validation suffices. The *gezeirah* is maintained prospectively but not imposed retroactively in impossible cases.

### Unusual Cases Exempt

The Gemara presses further: if we maintain the old practice even when circumstances have changed, we should insist on the declaration even in a case like the *pike'ach shenishtatek* — the person who became a deaf-mute — where it is genuinely impossible. Should there not be no out? The Gemara responds: *milta d'lo shechicha lo gazru bah rabbanan* — the Rabbis do not extend their decrees to bizarre and highly unusual circumstances. The case of a person who was fully competent and then became a deaf-mute immediately after delivery is so extraordinarily rare that the *gezeirah* does not apply to it.

### Woman Get Case

One might think this creates a general exemption for unusual cases. But the Gemara challenges this immediately: what about the woman who brings her own *get*? That too is a bizarre scenario — the Mishnah explains it as a case where the husband appointed her as his *shaliach* to deliver the *get* to herself upon arriving in a particular place. Yet the Mishnah rules that she must still declare *bifnei nichtav u'bifnei nechtam*. If unusual cases are exempt from the *gezeirah*, why must she declare it?

The Gemara answers: *shelo tachlok b'shlichus* — we do not wish to introduce distinctions within the framework of *shlichus*. The principle of *lo plug* applies: we establish a uniform rule that every *shaliach* who is able to make the declaration must make it, regardless of whether the particular circumstances are usual or unusual. The *gezeirah* is maintained as a blanket requirement for all functioning *shlichim*, precisely to avoid the confusion that exceptions would generate.

### Resolution Balance

This brings the analysis to its resolution. Tosafot captures it concisely: *shelo tachlok b'shlichus*, *peirush b'shlichus d'yachol* — the rule applies uniformly when the *shaliach* is able to make the declaration. When, however, the *shaliach* is genuinely unable — as in the deaf-mute case — we do not impose an impossible standard. We acknowledge current realities: *lishmah* is no longer an active concern, and signature validation is sufficient. The woman bringing her own *get*, unusual as that scenario is, can still make the declaration, so the *lo plug* applies and she must.

The overall position, then, is this: *lechatchila*, every *shaliach* who can make the declaration must do so — not because *lishmah* is still a live concern, but because we maintain the old practice against the possibility of its recurrence. When it is genuinely impossible, we permit signature validation as a *bedi'eved* alternative. And unusual cases that fall entirely outside the normal *shlichus* paradigm — such as two messengers bringing a *get* together, as will emerge below — are treated differently.

---

## Husband Delivers Get

### Husband Question

The Gemara now raises a new question. If the principle is *lo plug* — we maintain the declaration uniformly to preserve the established practice — then even the husband himself, when he personally delivers the *get*, should be required to declare *bifnei nichtav u'bifnei nechtam*. After all, even if he is personally delivering it, and even if there is no concern about forgery, perhaps we should insist on his declaration as a hedge against the *lishmah* concern that might someday resurface. Yet a *braita* teaches explicitly: *hu atzmo sheheivi gito ein tzarich lomar bifnei nichtav u'bifnei nechtam* — if the husband himself brought his *get*, he need not make the declaration. Why not?

### Real Concern

The Gemara answers by clarifying what the underlying concern actually is. One might have thought that the requirement of *bifnei nichtav u'bifnei nechtam* exists because we genuinely worry the *get* was written *shelo lishmah*. In fact, this is not the case. The genuine concern of *shelo lishmah* is a *miuta d'miuta* — a vanishingly small concern. It is not a real fear that *gittin* are being written without proper intent. The actual concern, says the Gemara, is something more social and strategic: *dilma ati ba'al u'mearer u'fasil lei* — we fear that the husband will use *lishmah* as a pretext, a basis for later challenging the *get* and invalidating it. The declaration closes off that pretext: it establishes a record that the writing and signing were done properly.

### Husband Exception

With this clarification, the exemption for a husband who delivers his own *get* becomes entirely logical. *Minka naktei biyadei ve'ati ka'mearer lei?* — if he himself is physically delivering the *get* with his own hands, taking personal responsibility for it in public, is he then going to turn around and challenge it? The personal involvement eliminates both the factual basis and any credible pretext for a challenge. It would be absurd: he is the one who brought it.

This clarification is significant beyond the immediate case. It reveals that the *lishmah* concern was never primarily about the substantive risk that a *get* was actually written without proper intent. It was always about protecting the woman against a husband who might exploit a technical pretext. The requirement of *bifnei nichtav u'bifnei nechtam* is thus oriented toward the woman's interests, not toward a genuine fear that scribal practice was deficient.

---

## Two Messengers Get

### Shmuel Query

The Gemara introduces a query posed by Shmuel to Rav Huna: if two people bring a *get* from *Medinat Hayam* — *shnayim sheheviu get mimedinas hayam* — must they declare *bifnenu nichtav u'bifnenu nechtam*? Recall that two messengers together constitute one of the key *nafka mina* cases in the Rabba-Rava debate. Since two witnesses deliver the *get*, their combined testimony implicitly establishes that the husband sent them and that the *get* is genuine — there is no concern about forgery, and thus no *ein eidim metzuyim lekaymo* issue. The sole remaining concern, according to Rabba, would be *lishmah*.

Rav Huna answers: they need not declare. He reasons: *uma ilu yomru bifnenu gershah mi lo meheimni* — if they had stated that the divorce was carried out in their presence, they would be believed for everything. Certainly, then, they are believed to establish that the *get* was properly dispatched by the husband. This eliminates the signature concern entirely. The Gemara notes: *l'Rabba nicha, l'Rava kashya* — good for Rabba, whose position is driven by *lishmah*, but difficult for Rava, since on Rava's account the concern is signature validation, and here the two messengers eliminate that concern. The Gemara's characteristic response appears once more: *delamdu* — they already knew the laws of *lishmah* by this point, so that concern does not apply.

### Two Unusual

The Gemara then asks: if *lishmah* is no longer a concern, and we rely on *l'achar shelamdu*, why not simply say that even a single messenger need not declare — just let the signatures be validated? The answer returns to *gezeirah shema yachzor hadavar lekilkulo* — the fear that conditions may revert. We keep the old practice in place.

But then, why are two messengers exempt? The Gemara answers: *bei trei d'maisei gita milta d'lo shechicha* — two people bringing a *get* together is an unusual occurrence, and the Rabbis did not apply their decree to unusual circumstances. *Milta d'lo shechicha lo gazru bah rabbanan*.

### Woman Compare

The Gemara immediately challenges this with the familiar case: the woman who brings her own *get* is also unusual — *d'lo shechicha* — yet she must still declare. Why is two messengers different?

### Testimony Paradigm

The resolution, spelled out by Tosafot, rests on a fundamental distinction between *shlichus* and *edus*. In a standard case of one *shaliach*, the paradigm is purely one of agency: a single individual is empowered and sent. We do not want to make distinctions within that *shlichus* paradigm — *shelo tachlok b'shlichus d'yachol* — so we apply the requirement uniformly to all who are capable. The woman who brings her own *get*, unusual as that is, still falls squarely within the *shlichus* paradigm, and therefore *lo plug* applies.

Two people bringing a *get* together is qualitatively different. It is not merely an unusual instantiation of the standard *shlichus* model; it has the character of *edus* — testimony — rather than pure agency. When two people bring a *get*, the *get* delivery functions more like testimonial validation than like an act of *shlichus* alone. They are, to be sure, still *shlichim* in the sense that they are empowered to deliver, but the dual presence transforms the act into something that resembles a testimonial proceeding. It falls outside the standard *shlichus* paradigm entirely, and therefore *gazrinan chad d'lo shechiach atu chad d'shechiach — bei terei atu chad lo gazrinan*: we extend the decree from common cases of one messenger to less common ones, but we do not extend it to the fundamentally different case of two messengers together.

---

## Yehoshua Lishmah

### Yehoshua Proof

The Gemara now identifies the Rabba-Rava debate as a parallel to the *machloket* between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi — one holding *lishmah*, the other holding *ein eidim metzuyim lekaymo*. The Gemara seeks to determine which *amora* held which position. It concludes that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi is the one who said *lishmah*, on the basis of the following incident: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba brought a *get* before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and asked whether he still needed to declare *bifnei nichtav u'bifnei nechtam*. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi replied: you do not need to. *Lo amru ela b'doros harishonim*, it was only required in the earlier generations *she'ein beki'in lishmah* — when people were not expert in the laws of *lishmah*. But in these later generations, *d'beki'in lishmah*, when everyone knows the law, no declaration is required. This is the source of the Gemara's earlier phrase *l'achar shelamdu*.

### Contradiction

This ruling of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi seems to create a problem. We concluded above that everyone — including Rabba — agrees that the signature-validation concern is real and cannot be dismissed. If that is so, then even *l'achar shelamdu*, when the *lishmah* concern lapses, there should still be a requirement to make the declaration on account of *ein eidim metzuyim lekaymo*. And we further concluded that even after *l'achar shelamdu*, the old practice is maintained *lechatchila* because of *gezeirah shema yachzor*. Yet Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi told Rabbi Shimon bar Abba simply: you need not declare at all. This sounds like a *lishmah*-only position that recognizes no remaining concern once *lishmah* is resolved — which seems to contradict everything the Gemara established.

### Two Messenger Implicit

The Gemara resolves this in one stroke: *Rav Shimon bar Abba inish achrini havah bahadei* — Rabbi Shimon bar Abba was not alone; there was another person accompanying him. The *get* was being brought by two messengers together. The other person's presence is not mentioned in the account, as the Gemara explains, *mishum kevodo d'Rav Shimon* — out of respect for Rabbi Shimon bar Abba, the narrative focuses on him rather than noting the unnamed companion.

### Resolution Unusual

This resolves everything. When two people bring a *get* together, we already established that this is a *milta d'lo shechicha* — an unusual case falling outside the standard *shlichus* paradigm — and the Rabbis did not apply their decree to unusual cases. Therefore, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling that no declaration was needed does not reflect a *lishmah*-only position that ignores signature concerns. It reflects the specific exemption for two-messenger cases. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi is perfectly consistent with the Gemara's overall framework: the signature concern remains valid, the old practice is maintained *lechatchila*, but two messengers are exempt because they constitute an unusual case that the *gezeirah* never covered. The apparent contradiction dissolves.

---

## Witness Numbers

### Two vs Three

The Gemara now turns to a new question: *bifnei kamah notna lah* — in front of how many people must the *shaliach* deliver the *get* when making his declaration? Since the *shaliach* is testifying, presumably at least two witnesses must be present. But exactly how many? Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina debate the matter, one holding *bifnei shenayim* — before two — and the other holding *bifnei sheloshah* — before three.

### Rachavei Proof

The Gemara determines which *amora* held which position. An incident is cited: Rachavei bar Rav Chisda brought a *get* before Rabbi Yochanan, and Rabbi Yochanan instructed him, *zil havah lah b'apei trei* — go and deliver it to her in the presence of two — and say to them, *bifnei nichtav u'bifnei nechtam*. This demonstrates clearly that Rabbi Yochanan holds *bifnei shenayim* — two witnesses suffice.

### Theory Initial

The natural inference is that the debate of two versus three maps onto the underlying debate of *lishmah* versus signature validation. One might suggest: the position requiring two witnesses corresponds to the *lishmah* account, since a simple testimony before two witnesses is all that is needed to establish that proper intent was observed. The position requiring three corresponds to the signature-validation account, since validating signatures (*kiyum shtaros*) is done before a *beis din* of three.

### Theory Rejected

This mapping, however, does not survive scrutiny. We established above that Rabbi Yochanan himself is the one who holds *ein eidim metzuyim lekaymo* — signature validation — while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds *lishmah*. Moreover, we concluded that *Rabba is lei d'Rava* — everyone agrees at some level that signature validation is a concern. If signature validation requires a court of three, how can Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that the requirement is about signatures, rule that two suffice?

### Shliach Eid Dayan

The Gemara therefore proposes a different basis for the debate. The question is not about the underlying rationale for the requirement, but about the legal mechanics of validation. Everyone agrees that signature validation is necessary. The debate concerns whether *shaliach na'aseh eid v'eid na'aseh dayan* — whether the same individual can first act as the *shaliach* delivering the *get*, then switch roles to serve as a witness validating the signatures, and then switch roles again to serve as a *dayan* on the *beis din* that adjudicates his own testimony.

This triple role-shifting is the crux. The *shaliach* is delivering the *get*: that is his agency role. He simultaneously declares *bifnei nichtav u'bifnei nechtam*: that is his testimonial role — *shaliach na'aseh eid*. Now if he can also count as a *dayan* for the purpose of adjudicating his own testimony — *eid na'aseh dayan* — then the three-person *beis din* needed for *kiyum shtaros* can be constituted with only two additional people: the *shaliach* himself counts as one, and the two people before whom he delivers the *get* count as two, totaling three. Hence delivery before two people suffices.

If, however, *ein eid na'aseh dayan* — the witness cannot serve as a *dayan* for his own testimony — then the *shaliach*'s counting as a *dayan* is impermissible, and three additional people are needed.

### Eid Dayan Rabbinic

The Gemara notes that the accepted *halacha* is: *b'drabanan, eid na'aseh dayan* — in the domain of rabbinic enactments, a witness may indeed serve as a *dayan* for his own testimony. Since *kiyum shtaros* for a *get* delivered from abroad is a rabbinic requirement, the ruling should universally permit delivery before two, and the debate should collapse. The Gemara therefore looks for a different basis for the remaining dispute.

### Woman Dayan Risk

The debate, the Gemara concludes, concerns a concern about practical confusion. According to the view that requires three, the reasoning is: since a woman is valid to serve as a *shliach* and bring a *get*, if we establish a universal practice of delivering before two — relying on the *shaliach* himself counting as the third — people may eventually forget the nuance and begin relying on a woman to serve in that same counting role. A woman, however, cannot be a *dayan*, even for rabbinic proceedings. If she brings the *get* and people count her as the *shaliach*-turned-*eid*-turned-*dayan*, the *kiyum* will be defective. To prevent this confusion, the view of three insists that the required three people be present exclusively as witnesses and *dayanim*, separate from the *shaliach*.

The opposing view — Rabbi Yochanan's view of two — holds that *ishah meida yadiah velo samchi alah*: people know that a woman cannot serve as a *dayan* and will not make that error. Therefore, the nuance that the *shaliach* counts toward the three does not risk being misapplied.

---

## Failure Remedy

### Two Witnesses Accepted

The *braita* teaches the established practice: delivery before two witnesses suffices, in accordance with Rabbi Yochanan. The *braita* presents a case in which the *shaliach* delivered the *get* and gave it to the woman but did not declare *bifnei nichtav u'bifnei nechtam*.

### Meir Stringency

Rabbi Meir rules: *yotzi ve-havalad mamzer* — the husband must divorce her and any child born of a subsequent remarriage is a *mamzer*. The failure to declare invalidates the *get*, at least rabbinically, and the consequences are correspondingly severe. Rabbi Meir brooks no flexibility: the absence of the declaration, for whatever reason, is an irremediable defect. Even if she has already remarried and has children, the *mamzer* status follows.

### Sages Leniency

The Sages disagree sharply: *ein havalad mamzer* — the child is emphatically not a *mamzer*. The failure to declare is a *lechatchila* deficiency, not a fundamental invalidation of the *get*. The Sages then address the practical question of how to remedy the situation *lechatchila* for a woman who has received a *get* without the declaration and wishes to remarry: *yitlenu mimenu, v'yachzir v'yitnena lah bifnei shenayim, v'yomar bifnei nichtav u'bifnei nechtam* — the *get* is taken back from her, and the *shaliach* redelivers it in the presence of two, this time making the declaration. Since the declaration must accompany the act of delivery, a redelivery with proper declaration remedies the deficiency.

One might ask: if she is already divorced by the first delivery — which is valid *d'oraisa* — what is the point of redelivering? The answer employs a *mima nafshach* logic: if rabbinically the first delivery is not considered fully valid because the declaration was omitted, then rabbinically she is not yet divorced, and a second delivery with the declaration completes the rabbinic requirement. If *d'oraisa* she was already divorced by the first delivery, then certainly the second delivery causes no harm. Either way, the redelivery cures the problem *lechatchila*.

### Timing Declaration

Tosafot raises the question of when precisely the declaration must be made. The *braita*'s remedy of *yitlenu mimenu* — taking the *get* back from her and redelivering it — implies that the declaration must be contemporaneous with the act of delivery itself. One cannot simply say the words the next day while the *get* sits in the woman's possession. But how narrowly must "contemporaneous" be defined?

Tosafot anchors this from the case on the preceding daf: the *pike'ach shenishtatek* case, where the *shaliach* gave the *get* and became a deaf-mute before completing the declaration. That case implies that a moment after delivery — but still *toch kedei dibbur* — is acceptable, since the *shaliach* was in the process of speaking when he was stricken. Tosafot concludes: during delivery, certainly valid; immediately after delivery within *toch kedei dibbur* (*peirush b'shlichus d'yachol*), also valid; any time after *kedei dibbur*, no longer valid as a contemporaneous declaration, and the *get* must be redelivered.

As for the scene suggested by *yitlenu mimenu*, Tosafot observes that the language implies the *get* is still in her hands at the moment of taking it back — the parties are apparently still standing together, still engaged in the transaction. Once they have dispersed and the moment of the giving has fully passed, the declaration cannot be retroactively attached to it.

What remains unresolved, notes Tosafot, is whether the declaration is valid if made somewhat after *kedei dibbur* but while the parties are still actively engaged in discussing the *get*. The *Ri* remains uncertain — *mesapka lei l'Ri* — whether continued engagement with the subject matter of the *get* constitutes a prolonged moment of delivery. And similarly, whether a declaration made *before* the physical act of giving — moments before rather than during — would satisfy the requirement is also left unresolved.

### Meir Rationale

The Gemara explains Rabbi Meir's position by citing a principle attributed to him by Rav Hamnuna in the name of Ulla. Rabbi Meir used to say: *kol hameshaneh mi-matbe'a she-tav'u chakhamim b'gittin, yotzi ve-havalad mamzer* — anyone who deviates from the established mold (*matbe'a*) that the Sages coined for *gittin*, must have the woman divorce and any child of remarriage is a *mamzer*. For Rabbi Meir, the Sages established a precise and non-negotiable form for the *get* process. Any deviation from that form — including the failure to make the required declaration — is treated as a fundamental departure from the mold, with all its consequences. There is no *bedi'eved* leniency that mitigates the severity of the deviation. Any step outside the established *matbe'a* carries the full consequence.

---

---

# Gittin 6

## Rabbah & Rava Debate

### lishmah vs. Signatures

Our daf begins with a brief but essential summary of the debate developed in the preceding pages. The dispute between Rabbah and Rava concerns the reason for the requirement that a *shaliach* delivering a *get* from *medinat hayam* must declare *bifani nechtav u'bifani nechtam* — "it was written in my presence and signed in my presence." Rabbah's position focuses on *lishmah*: the declaration ensures that the proper intention required for a *get* — that it be written for the sake of this particular husband and wife — was indeed observed. This concern is reflected primarily in the phrase *bifani nechtav*, in my presence during the writing. Rava, by contrast, understands the declaration as a mechanism for validating the signatures, preventing the husband from later claiming the document was a forgery. His position is reflected more in *bifani nechtam*, in my presence during the signing.

### Both Positions Align

The *gemara* ultimately concludes that the distinction between these two positions is less stark than it initially appears. Rabbah, it emerges, is *also* concerned with the validation rationale that Rava emphasizes — he holds both reasons simultaneously. Rava, for his part, is concerned only with validation. Moreover, the *gemara* noted that since the laws of *lishmah* had come to be well known even in *medinat hayam*, Rabbah's *lishmah* concern was effectively reduced to a *lechatchila* standard. The result is that the two positions converge almost entirely in practice. With this summary established, the *gemara* now proceeds to examine the concrete details of how *bifani nechtav u'bifani nechtam* operates across a range of circumstances.

## Bar Hadaya Case

### Every Letter Present

The *gemara* introduces the case of Bar Hadaya, who wished to bring a *get* and came before Rabbi Achi, who had been appointed to oversee the proper execution of *gittin* in that city. As Rashi notes, the principle that one who does not know the intricacies of *gittin* and *kiddushin* should have no dealings with them demanded that a figure of genuine authority supervise the process. Rabbi Achi instructed Bar Hadaya: *tzarich at l'amod al kol ot ve'ot* — you must stand present as every single letter of the *get* is written, from the first stroke through the final signature. The requirement of *bifani nechtav* thus raises an immediate question: what does "in my presence" actually demand? How present must the *shaliach* be throughout the writing?

### Leniency & Chumras

Bar Hadaya brought this question to Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi, who ruled that Rabbi Achi's requirement was excessive — the *shaliach* need not be present for every single letter. One might nonetheless argue: even if it is not strictly required, why not adopt Rabbi Achi's stricter standard as a *chumra*? The *gemara* answers this decisively: *nimtza ata motzi la'az al gittin harishonim* — by insisting on a heightened standard, one implicitly casts ill repute upon all earlier *gittin* that were executed without such care. People will hear that one was *makpid* to supervise every letter and will begin to question the validity of documents delivered by *shelichim* who did not observe this practice. This is a critical principle about the real costs of unnecessary stringency: a *chumra* is never without consequences, and those consequences often fall upon others.

### Earlier Gittin Concern

The concern for *gittin harishonim* — not besmirching past practice — serves as an independent brake on the impulse toward stringency in this domain. Where the practical effect of stricter behavior is to impugn what has already been done and accepted, the *gemara* treats that as a sufficient reason to refrain.

## Partial Presence

### One Line Suffices

The *gemara* next records the case of Rabbah bar bar Chana, who brought a *get* in which half had been written in his presence and half had not — the *gemara* does not specify which half. He came before Rabbi Elazar, who ruled: *afilu lo katav bo ela shita achat lishmah shuv eino tzarich* — even if only one line was written *lishmah* in his presence, that is sufficient. The ruling is noteworthy for its invocation of *lishmah*, addressing the Rabbah dimension of the requirement. The reasoning would seem to be that if the *sofer* was observed declaring the proper intent for even one line, one may assume that the *sofer* understood and maintained that intent throughout. Tosafot explains the case somewhat differently: the reference to one line means the *shaliach* saw the first line being written, and from that beginning one may assume *lishmah* was maintained through the end. That reading is perhaps less straightforward than the plain sense of the *gemara*, which speaks of "any one line" and grants sufficiency regardless of position in the document.

### Hearing Quill/Klaf

Rav Ashi goes further still, requiring even less than one line of direct observation. *Afilu kan kulmusa vekan megilta* — even if one merely heard the preparation of the quill and the *klaf* being readied, that is sufficient. Rashi's variant reading is *kal kulmusa*, the sound of the quill, and he explains: if one heard the preparation and, in that context, heard them declaring that this was being done *lishmah* — for the sake of the husband and wife — even that degree of auditory awareness constitutes sufficient presence. The word *bifani* is thus stretched considerably: one did not see the writing, one did not witness the writing itself, one may not even have been present during the writing — and yet the awareness created by hearing the preparation in context suffices.

### Medinat Hayam Case

A *baraita* is cited in support of Rav Ashi's position. A *shaliach* bringing a *get* from *medinat hayam*: even if he was downstairs and the *sofer* was upstairs, or the *sofer* downstairs and the *shaliach* upstairs, and even if he was going in and out throughout the entire day — *kasher*. The document is valid and the declaration *bifani nechtav* may be made.

### Bifani Meaning

The *gemara* pauses to interrogate the *baraita*. If the *sofer* is on the upper floor and the *shaliach* is below, he cannot see anything. How does *bifani* — in my presence — apply? The *gemara* answers: *ela lav d'shama kan kulmusa vekan megilta* — it must mean that he could hear the activity upstairs, that there was some form of awareness even without visual contact. *Bifani*, in my presence, encompasses this kind of ambient awareness. It is also worth observing that this *baraita* does not mention *lishmah* at all. Consistent with the conclusion that Rabbah's concern is ultimately reducible in practical terms, and that the *lishmah* issue is primarily *lechatchila*, the *baraita* appears to address the requirement without any *lishmah* qualification.

## In & Out Motion

### Sofer Marketplace

The *gemara* now examines the phrase from the *baraita* — *afilu nichnas veyotzei kol hayom kulo kasher*, even going in and out all day, it is valid — and asks: who is going in and out? If it refers to the *shaliach*, the question answers itself: since even physical separation of floors is permitted, surely the case where the *shaliach* steps in and out of the room where the *sofer* is present poses no difficulty. That case is obvious and needs no ruling. The *gemara* therefore concludes that the *baraita* must be referring to the *sofer* — the scribe who steps out while the *shaliach* remains. The ruling then tells us that even when the *sofer* leaves the premises and returns, the *shaliach* may still declare *bifani nechtav*.

### Distraction Concern

But even this seems obvious — why would the *sofer* stepping out invalidate anything? The *gemara* answers: *lo tzricha* — the *baraita*'s ruling is needed for a specific case. *D'nafik l'shuka ve'asa* — the *sofer* went out to the marketplace and returned. One might have thought that while in the marketplace, another person approached him and asked him to write a *get* for his own wife. If, when returning, the *sofer* carried that second commission in mind, his *lishmah* intent may have become confused. The *baraita* teaches us that we are not concerned for this possibility. We note that this concern again touches on *lishmah* — suggesting that the question of intent remains relevant in evaluating the *sofer*'s conduct throughout the writing, even as the evidentiary threshold for the *shaliach*'s own presence has been set quite low.

## Bavel's Status

### Rav vs. Shmuel

The *gemara* now turns from the mechanics of *bifani nechtav* to the geographic question of which regions require it at all. The *mishnah* distinguished between Eretz Yisrael, where no declaration is needed, and *medinat hayam*, where it is. The question now is: what is the status of Bavel? At the time of the *Bavli*, Bavel was not a marginal outpost but the center of Jewish life, home to the majority of the Jewish population. The debate is presented thus: *Rav amar k'Eretz Yisrael l'gittin* — Rav holds that Bavel has the same status as Eretz Yisrael, and no declaration is required when transmitting a *get* from one location to another within Bavel. *Shmuel amar k'chutza la'aretz* — Shmuel holds it is like the diaspora, and the declaration is required.

### Two Explanations

The *gemara* initially proposes that this debate maps onto the Rabbah-Rava dispute: perhaps Rav focuses on *lishmah* and holds that Bavel's Torah knowledge is sufficient, while Shmuel focuses on *edim metzuyim lekaymo* — the availability of witnesses to validate signatures — and holds that travel between Babylonian cities is insufficient to ensure such availability. The *gemara* rejects this framing, however, on the grounds that Rabbah himself also holds of Rava's position. Everyone must address the question of witness availability; the *lishmah* issue alone cannot account for the debate. The *gemara* therefore reframes: *ela d'kulei alma edim metzuyim lekaymo* — everyone agrees the concern is about witness availability. The debate is about whether that concern is adequately answered in Bavel. Rav holds that because there are *yeshivot* in Bavel, there is constant travel from city to city; an industry of movement grows up around the great academies, and one can assume witnesses to signatures will be available when needed. Shmuel counters: *misiftei girsaihu tridi* — the *yeshiva* students are absorbed in their learning. The existence of academies does not translate into the kind of commercial and civic movement through which people become familiar with one another's signatures. There may be travel, but not the kind that ensures witnesses for *kiyum shtaros*.

### Rav Huna Statement

The *gemara* adds a tradition: *amar Rabbi Abba amar Rava amar Rav Huna asinu atzmeinu be-Vavel ke-Eretz Yisrael le-gittin* — we have established in Bavel that we treat ourselves as Eretz Yisrael for matters of *gittin*, from the time Rav arrived in Bavel. The same Rav whose ruling opened this section is identified as the pivotal figure: it was his arrival that transformed Bavel's practical status.

### Rashi: Yeshivot

Rashi explains: from the time Rav came to Bavel and established a *yeshiva* in Sura — while Shmuel's *yeshiva* was in Nehardea — there arose a permanent institutional framework driving movement throughout the region. The smaller communities flocked to these centers on days of Torah study; students traveled between Sura and Nehardea; traffic permeated the Babylonian Jewish world. It was this development, in Rashi's reading, that changed Bavel's status — not a pre-existing feature of the landscape, but an institutional transformation that Rav himself created. Although Torah had always been present in Bavel — Hillel himself came from there, and the exile of Yechanya brought *talmidei chachamim* in the aftermath of the first destruction — what Rav and Shmuel established was something qualitatively new: fixed, high-capacity academies generating the kind of constant movement that ensures witness availability.

## Yirmiya Challenge

### Borders & Geography

Rabbi Yirmiya challenges the foregoing from the *mishnah* itself. The *mishnah* enumerates the outer borders of Eretz Yisrael: Rekem to the east, Ashkelon to the south, Akko to the north — each of these border cities being treated as outside Eretz Yisrael for the laws of *gittin*. And we know from the *pesukim* that Bavel lies to the north of Eretz Yisrael: *mi-tzafon tipasach ha-ra'ah*, the evil shall open from the north — that was the prophecy of Bavel's destruction of the *Beis HaMikdash*. Moreover, the *mishnah* states that Rabbi Meir considers Akko equivalent to Eretz Yisrael for *gittin*, and even the sages who disagree with Rabbi Meir do so specifically because Akko is distant from the center — *d'merachka hi*. If even a border city like Akko requires debate, Bavel — which is far more distant — would certainly be treated as *chutz la'aretz*. How, then, can one declare that Bavel has the status of Eretz Yisrael?

### Exception Principle

Rabbi Yirmiya poses his own answer: *le-var mi-Bavel* — the mishnah's geographic framework applies to everything *other than* Bavel. Bavel is a distinct entity unto itself, not simply subsumed under the general category of *chutz la'aretz*. This resolution points to something structurally important. Just as *medinat hayam* had its own defined identity in the *mishnah*, Bavel — as Tosafot notes from the opening of the tractate — has its own category. One might object that since the changed status resulted from Rav's arrival, which postdates the *mishnah*, the *mishnah* cannot be used to challenge it. The answer would be that even before Rav, the *mishnah*'s framework implicitly allowed for such an exception — or alternatively, as Tosafot proposes, the status was always there, waiting to be articulated.

## Bavel's Status (II)

### Tosafot Alternative

Tosafot challenges Rashi's reading of the Rav Huna statement. If Bavel's status genuinely *changed* when Rav arrived — if it was formerly *chutz la'aretz* and became like Eretz Yisrael — then why does the *gemara* treat a challenge from the *mishnah* as meaningful? The *mishnah* predates Rav's arrival; of course it reflects the older reality. Tosafot therefore cites Rabbeinu Tam's alternative: when Rav arrived in Bavel and taught that Bavel has the status of Eretz Yisrael for *gittin*, he was not announcing a change but transmitting a pre-existing *halacha* — grounded in the foundational status of the exile of Yechanya and his *talmidei chachamim* — that Bavel had always carried this distinction. On this reading, there was no change in status, only a clarification of a status that always existed, which is why the *mishnah* remains a relevant source to engage. The *gemara* sounds more naturally like Rashi's reading, but the motivation behind Tosafot's approach is clear: to preserve the coherence of the *gemara*'s dialectic.

## Bavel Boundaries

### Yuchasin Parallel

Having established that Bavel has a distinct status, the *gemara* turns to the question of its precise geographic boundaries. *Ad heichan hi Bavel?* — how far does Bavel extend? Rav Papa rules: *k'machloket l'yuchasin kach machloket l'gittin* — whatever debate exists in tractate *Kiddushin* about the boundaries of Bavel for purposes of *yuchasin* — personal status and the reliability of genealogical records — the same boundaries apply for *gittin*. The considerations differ: *yuchasin* concerns where records were kept and personal status is most assured, while *gittin* concerns the availability of witnesses to validate signatures. One might ask whether these two criteria necessarily produce identical borders. Perhaps the *gemara*'s point is that for practical coherence — *kedei shelo tachalok* — a unified standard is preferable even if the underlying rationales do not map perfectly.

### Bridge Arch Limit

Rav Yosef disagrees. The debate in *Kiddushin* applies to *yuchasin*, but for *gittin* there is a different, universally agreed-upon boundary: *ad arba tinyana d'gashra* — until the second arch of the bridge. The *gemara* understood which bridge and which direction this referred to, and that specific landmark demarcates the extent of Bavel for purposes of the *bifani nechtav* exemption.

## Aktisphon Case

### One-Way Requirement

Rav Chisda introduces an asymmetric case: he required the declaration *bifani nechtav* for a *get* traveling from Aktisphon to Bei Ardashir, but not in the reverse direction. Two cities are thus in a relationship where one requires the declaration going one way but not the other. At first glance, one might explain this the same way Eretz Yisrael and *medinat hayam* differ: perhaps Aktisphon does not know *lishmah* and Bei Ardashir does, so when a *get* arrives from Aktisphon, Bei Ardashir requires the declaration to ensure proper intent, while the reverse is unnecessary. This explanation would work cleanly if *lishmah* were the only concern.

### Marketplace Effect

The *gemara* rejects this framing, again invoking the established principle that Rava holds of Rabbah — everyone must address the witness validation concern. The explanation instead focuses on commercial patterns: *vahani kimeizali beshuka lehasam hanach yadei bechasimeit yadei dehani* — the residents of one city go to the marketplace of the other. When people from city A regularly travel to buy and sell in city B, the residents of city B become familiar with the signatures of city A's residents through the commercial documents — IOUs, bills of sale — that the travelers sign while there. The buyers sign; they go home; the sellers of city B are left holding those documents and develop familiarity with those signatures. City B therefore knows city A's signatures and can perform *kiyum shtaros* if necessary. The reverse is not true: *vahani behanach lo yadei* — city A does not accumulate familiarity with city B's signatures, because city A's residents are busy with their own transactions when in city B and return home without a comparable record. *Mai ta'ama beshuka'i teridei* — they are preoccupied with the marketplace itself. This asymmetry in commercial traffic explains the asymmetry in the *halachic* requirement.

## Neighborhood Cases

### Reshus Division

Rav bar Avuha extends the logic further, requiring the *bifani nechtav* declaration even between opposite sides of a *reshus harabim* — a major thoroughfare. The reasoning, as Tosafot explains clearly, is that one is aware of the movements of those in one's immediate vicinity. If the witnesses to a *get* live on the same side of the street as the wife and her community, she and those around her will know if those witnesses are about to relocate, and can arrange *kiyum shtaros* in advance. But if the witnesses live across the major thoroughfare — the other side of the tracks, so to speak — that awareness is absent. Their departure may go unnoticed until it is too late to validate the signatures. The transience of population, and the limits of what one notices about one's neighbors, thus drives a requirement that would seem geographically trivial.

### Neighborhood Division

Rav Sheshes goes further: the declaration is required even between different neighborhoods within the same side of such a divide. The principle remains the same — one tracks the movements of those most proximate — but the zone of reliable awareness is narrowed further. Even within the same broad residential area, if the witnesses and the wife come from distinct neighborhoods, the risk of unnoticed departure applies.

### Transience Principle

Rava extends the requirement to within a single neighborhood itself. The transience of urban population is so pronounced that even neighbors may not know one another's plans, and a witness could depart without warning even to those living in the same *shechuna*.

### Mechuza Context

The *gemara* qualifies Rava's position: *shani benei Mechuza de'naidi* — Rava spoke from his own experience in Mechuza, a cosmopolitan commercial center with an unusually mobile population. His ruling applies specifically to cities of that character. The earlier, less sweeping positions reflect the realities of less transient communities, where one's neighborhood still provides meaningful notice of departures.

### Modern Application

Tosafot draws the practical conclusion directly from Rava's ruling and its grounding in transience: in all places of the medieval period, where Jewish populations were similarly mobile and cosmopolitan, one should always declare *bifani nechtav u'bifani nechtam*. Even though we rule like Rava that the concern is *edim metzuyim lekaymo* rather than *lishmah*, and even if the community is learned enough that *lishmah* poses no issue, the transience of population means the witness concern always applies. Everywhere in the world of the *Rishonim* resembles Mechuza, and the declaration should always be made.

## Rav Kahana Case

### No Need Statement

The *gemara* relates that Rav Kahana brought a *get* — Rav Chanin reported the incident — and did not know whether it had traveled from Sura to Nehardea or from Nehardea to Sura; both were major centers of Torah scholarship and, as established, of constant travel. He came before Rav and asked whether he needed to say *bifani nechtav u'bifani nechtam*. Rav ruled: *lo tzarichat* — you do not need to, because Bavel has the status of Eretz Yisrael for *gittin*, and the dense travel between these two great academies ensures that witness availability is not a concern.

### If Said, Works

The *gemara* adds: *ve'ee avad mahni* — and if one did say it, it works. This is not a trivial addendum. Even in cases where the declaration is technically unnecessary, making it protects the woman: if the husband were to later challenge the *get*, the declared *bifani nechtav u'bifani nechtam* ensures that his objection will not be entertained. According to Rashi, the risk in the absence of the declaration is that the husband's challenge could actually succeed in invalidating the *get*; according to Tosafot, the concern is rather the *la'az* — the cloud of suspicion — that such a challenge would create. Either way, the declaration, when made even unnecessarily, provides the woman with meaningful protection, and its use should be encouraged wherever possible.

## Kfar Sisai Case

### Witness Prevention

A *baraita* is cited: someone came before Rabbi Yishmael with a *get* he had brought from Kfar Sisai. He asked whether he needed to say *bifani nechtav u'bifani nechtam*. Rabbi Yishmael asked where he was from; upon learning it was Kfar Sisai, he instructed him: you must say it, *shelo tizakak l'edim* — so that she should not need to resort to witnesses. The framing is notable: the obligation is presented not as an inherent requirement of Kfar Sisai's status, but as a protective measure that spares the woman from having to produce witnesses.

### Ilai Challenge

After the *shaliach* departed, Rabbi Ilai entered and challenged Rabbi Yishmael: Kfar Sisai is swallowed within the borders of Eretz Yisrael — it is closer to Tzipori than Akko is, and Tzipori was a central location. The *mishnah* records that Rabbi Meir considers Akko itself to be like Eretz Yisrael for *gittin*, and even the sages who dispute Rabbi Meir do so only because Akko is distant — *d'merachka hi* — while Kfar Sisai is close. If Akko's proximity was sufficient for Rabbi Meir, Kfar Sisai's greater proximity should be sufficient for everyone. Why then require the declaration?

### Heter Established

Rabbi Yishmael responded: *shtok bni shtok* — hush, my son, hush. *Ho'il v'yatza davar b'heter yatza* — since the matter went forth as a *heter*, as a permission, let it stand. That is: the declaration was instructed not because it was technically required, but because making it activates the protective mechanism. Since the *shaliach* was told to say it and it is effective when said, the woman is now protected. Even if it need not have been required, the fact that it was said and is halachically operative means it serves its purpose.

### Incomplete Hearing

The *gemara* explains Rabbi Ilai's challenge: *lo siyem kamei* — Rabbi Ilai had not heard the complete statement Rabbi Yishmael made. He heard only the instruction to say *bifani nechtav u'bifani nechtam* and reacted before hearing the rationale — *shelo tizakak l'edim*, so that she not need witnesses — which would have clarified that this was protective guidance, not a statement of genuine requirement. Having heard only the ruling and not its explanation, Rabbi Ilai assumed Rabbi Yishmael was declaring Kfar Sisai to require the declaration on its own terms, and challenged accordingly.

## Avyasar Statement

### Travel Leniency

The *gemara* now turns to an entirely different axis of the question: not within Bavel or within Eretz Yisrael, but between them. Rav Avyasar sent a ruling to Rav Chisda: *gittin habaim misham l'kan* — *gittin* coming from there, Bavel, to here, Eretz Yisrael, *ein tzarich lomar bifanei nechtav u'bifanei nechtam*. No declaration is required. One might have thought that since these are two distinct regions — whatever their internal status — the movement between them would require the standard declaration applied to *medinat hayam*.

### Travel Rationale

The *gemara* again notes that a *lishmah*-only explanation is insufficient, since everyone holds of Rava's position requiring witness availability. The answer: *keivan d'ika rabim d'salki v'nechti* — since there are many who go up and come down, making *aliyah* and *yerida* between Bavel and Eretz Yisrael — primarily for purposes of Torah study — *mishkach shchichi*, witnesses are readily available. The volume of travel between the two great centers of Jewish life is so substantial that one can rely on finding someone who can perform *kiyum shtaros* when needed. The same logic that makes Bavel equivalent to Eretz Yisrael internally extends to the corridor between them.

## Yosef Challenge

### Trust Question

Rav Yosef raises a pointed objection to Rav Avyasar's ruling: *man lima lan d'Rav Avyasar bar samcha hu?* — who says that Rav Avyasar is a reliable authority? Since his ruling is a *kula* — a leniency, removing a requirement — the question of his credibility is directly relevant.

### Harsh Missive

Rav Yosef continues: this is the same Rav Avyasar who sent a harsh letter — apparently from Eretz Yisrael to Rav Yehuda in Bavel — condemning *bnei adam haolim misham l'kan*, the Torah scholars who came from Bavel to Eretz Yisrael to learn but neglected their responsibilities at home. They left wives effectively abandoned, failed in their obligations to provide *mezonot* for their families, and were absent from the responsibilities of building a household and having children.

### Verse Critique

The specific verse Rav Avyasar applied to these scholars was: *va'yitnu ha'yeled bazonah v'hayalda machru bayayin va'yishtu* — they gave the child to the prostitute and the girl they sold for wine and drank. The harshness of the charge attracted its own commentary. Tosafot understands *bazonah* as referring to *mezonot* — sustenance — meaning the children had to labor to support themselves because their fathers were gone. A tradition from the *Yerushalmi* goes further: there was an actual case of a man who sold his daughter into servitude in order to fund his Torah study. Rashi reads the critique differently: these scholars lingered in foreign lands, leaving their wives in a state resembling *agunot* — not refusing a *get*, but abandoned and bound — and neglecting the obligations of *pru u'rvu*, such that children who should have existed were never born. Whatever the precise meaning, the letter was a severe indictment, and its character speaks to the kind of authority Rav Avyasar was willing to project.

### Klaf Scoring

Rav Yosef's specific technical critique is this: Rav Avyasar wrote the letter *b'lo sirtut* — without scoring the *klaf*, without the preparatory lines grooved into the parchment to guide straight writing, which is required when writing a substantial text. And Rav Yitzchak taught: one may write two words without scoring, but not three. A *baraita* has a slightly different tradition — three words without scoring are permitted, but not four. Either way, Rav Avyasar wrote an extended text without observing this practice, and Rav Yosef takes this as evidence of a gap in his learning: if he is unaware of, or disregarded, this *halacha*, why should we trust his rulings on more consequential matters?

## Abaye Defense

### Authority Standards

Abaye responds to Rav Yosef's critique: *atu kuli alma lo yad'ei ha d'Rav Yitzchak lav gavra raba hu?* — does everyone know Rav Yitzchak's position, and if one does not, does that disqualify him as a major authority? The underlying principle is that gaps in knowledge of specific traditions do not determine overall reliability.

### Tradition vs. Logic

Abaye draws a principled distinction: *bishlama milta d'talya b'savra lechai* — if the failure were in something that depends on *savra*, on reasoning and logical analysis, that would be a valid critique of someone's reliability as a decisor. If someone cannot reason clearly, that calls into question the quality of his other rulings. But this is different.

### Tradition Knowledge

*Aval ha gmara gmara hi* — this is a matter of *gemara*, of received tradition. *U'gmara lo shmi'a lei* — he simply had not heard this particular tradition. Before the age of printed books and comprehensive libraries, one could not be expected to know every tradition that existed. Rav Yitzchak's teaching about *sirtut* may not have been widely circulated. Failure to have received a specific oral tradition says nothing about someone's analytical capacity or trustworthiness as a *posek*. On this note the *shiur* concludes, with the broader discussion of Rav Avyasar's authority — and the *gemara*'s continuation — to be taken up in the next session.

# Gittin 7

## Bifnei Nichtav Requireme…

### Bifnei Nichtav Basics

The daf begins at the bottom of 6b, picking up a discussion about the practical scope of the *shaliach*'s obligation to declare *bifnei nichtav uvifnei nechtam* — that the *get* was written and signed in his presence. The Gemara had recently established that even within *medinat hayam* one must reassess circumstances: if the population is highly transient or signatures are not recognizable, the declaration is required. This leads Tosafot and the *rishonim* to conclude that this is one of those *takanot* which do not remain fixed but must be continuously reevaluated based on prevailing conditions.

### Ramban's Question

The Ramban raises a question that bears noting here. The Gemara's reassessment is framed specifically in terms of *medinat hayam*. The Ramban asks: could one ever imagine a scenario in which even in Eretz Yisrael — if conditions deteriorated to the point where Torah knowledge was scarce and travel was limited, as was the case in the time of the *rishonim* — one would be required to state *bifnei nichtav uvifnei nechtam*? Or do we say that the question of whether the declaration is needed simply never applies to Eretz Yisrael, which is always categorically exempt? This remains an open question that the Ramban raises.

### Bavel's Special Status

The Gemara has already granted Bavel a special status comparable to Eretz Yisrael, such that the *shaliach* need not declare *bifnei nichtav uvifnei nechtam* within Bavel, owing to the regularity of travel and the widespread familiarity with *lishmah*. A further ruling attributed to Rabbi Avyasar held that when traveling between Bavel and Eretz Yisrael the declaration is likewise unnecessary.

### Rabbi Avyasar Authority

This ruling prompted the Gemara to challenge Rabbi Avyasar's reliability. The critique rested on the observation that in a letter he wrote — a blistering denunciation of the practice in Bavel of leaving home, wife, and children to study in Eretz Yisrael — he quoted a *pasuk* without scoring the parchment beneath it. In a *Sefer Torah*, the letters are suspended from scored lines indented into the parchment above them; the letters hang from the scoring rather than resting upon it. Failing to score a *pasuk* when writing it was taken as evidence that Rabbi Avyasar did not know this *halacha*, and therefore his authority could be questioned. The Gemara responds, however, that the absence of this practice is not necessarily disqualifying — not everyone is expected to know it. Indeed, this is likely the origin of the English word "underscore": to place the scoring beneath. In a *Sefer Torah* the scoring appears above, but the general concept of marking beneath a passage to highlight it flows from the same tradition.

---

## Rabbi Avyasar Defens (II)

### Avyasar Divine Alignment

The Gemara adds a further defense of Rabbi Avyasar. The verse states: *vatizneh alav pilegsho* — his concubine acted faithlessly against him — which is the opening of the story of *pilegeish b'Givah*. Rabbi Avyasar interpreted *vatizneh* not as literal adultery but as referring to a fly (*z'vuv*) found in the food — the word *z'vuv* possibly connecting etymologically to *mezonot*, as Tosafot suggests. Rabbi Yonatan, by contrast, said he found a strand of hair (*nima*).

Rabbi Avyasar then encountered Eliyahu and asked: what is God occupied with at this moment? Eliyahu replied that God is engaged in the *sugya* of *pilegeish b'Givah*. And what does He say? *Avyasar bni kach hu omer* — My son Avyasar says thus; *Yonatan bni kach hu omer* — My son Yonatan says thus. Rabbi Avyasar recoiled: *chas v'shalom* — can there really be a doubt before Heaven? Eliyahu answered: *eilu v'eilu divrei Elokim chayim* — both are the words of the living God.

### Fly vs. Hair Debate

The Gemara then clarifies how both positions can be simultaneously correct: *hein z'vuv matza v'lo hikpid* — he found the fly and was not particularly disturbed; *nima matza v'hikpid* — but he found the hair and became angry. The fly was disgusting but understandable; the hair provoked a sharper reaction. Even though Rabbi Yonatan's position was ultimately more precise, Rabbi Avyasar was nonetheless aligned with something genuinely true, and God's engagement with his view demonstrates that he cannot simply be dismissed.

### Negligence Theory

The Gemara elaborates. Rav Yehuda teaches: *z'vuv b'ke'ara v'nima b'oto makom* — the fly was in the bowl of food, but the hair was found in an intimate location. Based on a certain passage in the Gemara, it appears there was a practice of removing pubic hair, and the presence of such a hair there indicated either a potential physical danger (*sakanta*) or that the matter had not been properly attended to. A second opinion holds that both were found in the food (*ika d'amri idy v'idy b'ke'ara*): the fly was an *ones* — an unavoidable accident, for what can one do about a fly landing in food — while the hair reflected negligence (*pshiyuta*). The husband's disproportionate anger over a strand of hair, or his fury at finding a fly, drove his *pilegesh* from the house and set in motion a catastrophe.

### Undue Fear Lesson

From here the Gemara draws a broader moral lesson. Rav Chisda teaches: *le'olam al yatil adam eimah yeteirah b'toch beito* — a person should never impose excessive fear upon his household. The husband of the *pilegeish b'Givah* imposed such fear upon her, and as a result many myriads of Israel fell in the wars that followed.
