Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav extends this further: anyone who imposes excessive fear upon his household will ultimately come to three sins — *gilui arayot*, *shfichut damim*, and *chilul Shabbat*. Rashi explains the mechanism of each. *Gilui arayot*: the wife, afraid to admit that she did not immerse in the *mikvah* because the water was freezing cold — and one should not underestimate how arduous those immersions were historically, descending into deep wells in the dead of night in darkness and bitter cold — remains silent and her husband unknowingly cohabits with her while she is a *niddah*. *Shfichut damim*: as happened here, she flees from him in terror, falls into a pit or off a bridge, and dies. Or, as Rashi says, it is what the *pilegeish b'Givah* story itself exemplifies. *Chilul Shabbat*: she did not light candles and did not cook before nightfall, and out of fear of his reaction she lights the candles and cooks after dark — and he eats the food cooked on Shabbat without knowing it was forbidden.

Tosafot notes that *Seder Olam* records that the day of *pilegeish b'Givah* was itself a Shabbat, which would connect *chilul Shabbat* directly to that narrative. Rabbeinu Chananel has a variant reading: the three sins are *gilui arayot*, *shfichut damim*, and *chilul Hashem* — noting that *chillul Shabbat* and *chillul Hashem* are nearly the same word, and that all three were indeed present in the *pilegeish b'Givah* story.

It is striking that this *aggadata* appears at the opening of *Masechet Gittin*, a tractate deeply concerned with the husband's unilateral power over the *get* and the need to protect the wife's interests. From the very beginning the Gemara raises the specter of the husband who manufactures claims to make the wife's life impossible — and here too the story presents a husband whose disproportionate anger over a fly or a hair sets an entire catastrophe in motion.

---

## Domestic Ethics (III)

### Pre-Shabbat Statements

Rabbah bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: the Rabbis have said that a man must say three things in his household — to his wife — just as it begins to grow dark on *erev Shabbat*: *issartem* — have you taken *ma'aser*? *eiravtem* — have you made the *eiruv chatzeiros* or *eiruv techumin* (which is itself a dispute between Rashi and Tosafot)? *hadliku es haner* — light the candles. These three must be said *benichusa* — pleasantly, gently, without anger or yelling. The purpose is *ki heichi delikablu minei* — so that the members of the household will actually listen and act accordingly, rather than acting out of fear or being driven to sin precisely through the harshness of the tone.

### Abaye's Derivation

Abaye adds: *ana lo shmiyena le'ha de'Rabbah bar bar Chana* — I never heard that teaching — *v'kiyamtiyah misvara* — yet I arrived at the same conclusion independently through my own reasoning.

---

## Rabbi Avyasar Defens (II)

### Rabbi Chanina's Fear

Rabbi Abbahu continues the theme: *le'olam al yatil adam eimah yeseirah besoch beiso* — a person should never impose excessive fear upon his household. A great man once had his household so terrified of him that they nearly fed him something of enormous forbidden consequence: *eiver min hachai*, a limb torn from a living animal, because circumstances forced an emergency and they were too afraid to tell him. The Gemara asks: is it really possible that God would allow a *tzaddik* to stumble into such a sin? After all, the Gemara teaches elsewhere that *behemtan shel tzaddikim* — the very animals of the righteous — are protected by God from causing them to stumble, as with the donkey of Pinchas ben Yair, which was prevented from eating produce from which *terumos u'ma'asros* had not been separated. How much more so would God protect the *tzaddikim* themselves?

The answer: *ela bikshu le'ha'achilo davar gadol* — they sought to feed him, they were on the verge of it, but did not actually succeed. God intervened. The great man in question is identified as Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel.

Tosafot offers an important clarification here. It is not that *tzaddikim* can never stumble into sin. Rather, there is a specific tradition regarding food — *de'gnai hu le'tzaddik she'yochal davar issur* — that it would be a particular disgrace for a *tzaddik* to have a forbidden substance actually enter his body. It is for this reason, Tosafot explains, that the Gemara invokes divine protection specifically in cases of accidentally consuming *treif* food, while not making the same argument for other inadvertent transgressions. This concern connects to a broader sensibility about the singular gravity of what enters the body: the idea that feeding even an infant non-*kosher* food before the age of *chinuch* carries a kind of spiritual weight, the tradition of *Moshe Rabbeinu* refusing to nurse from an Egyptian woman, and the considerable hesitation found in various *teshuvot* regarding commerce in non-*kosher* goods, even in the difficult circumstances of the medieval period.

---

## Silence vs. Adversaries

### Mar Ukva's Question

Mar Ukva sent a question to Rabbi Elazar: *bnei adam ha'omedim alai* — there are people who stand against me and cause me harm — *u'veyadi le'mosram la'malchut* — and I have the means to hand them over to the government, as I possess information about them. What may I do? This is, of course, the question of *mesirah*. He wants to know whether protecting himself through this means is permitted.

### Guard Your Mouth

Rabbi Elazar scored the parchment and wrote him the following verse — and here the Gemara notes again the practice of scoring before writing a *pasuk*: *Amarti eshmerah derachai me'chato bi'leshoni, eshmerah le'fi machsom be'od rasha le'negdi* — I said I would guard my path from sinning with my tongue; I will watch my mouth, keeping it muzzled, while the wicked stands against me. Even though the wicked person is arrayed against you, guard your mouth and do not speak out against him.

### Anguish Concern

Mar Ukva wrote back: *ka mitza'ari li tuva* — he causes me tremendous anguish — *v'la mitzina de'eikum behu* — and I have no other means of protecting myself against him.

### Divine Silence Path

Rabbi Elazar wrote back again, scoring and writing: *dom l'Hashem v'hitcholel lo* — be silent to God and long for Him. Do not speak out; remain silent; God will cause them to fall, *v'hu yapilem lecha chalalim chalalim*. And if you wish to do something constructive: *hashkem v'haarev aleihem le'veit ha'midrash* — rise early and stay late over them at the *Beit ha'Midrash* — *v'inan kalin me'aleihen* — and they will disappear on their own. Tosafot connects *dom* here to *dimdumei chamah*, the early and late light of dawn and dusk, as a reading of *hashkem v'haarev*.

### Gneiva's Punishment

The Gemara then records: *ha'davar yatza mi'pi Rabbi Elazar v'natnuhu le'Gneiva be'kolar* — the matter had barely left the mouth of Rabbi Elazar when Gneiva — whose very name is suggestive — was put in chains. The parallel to *Haman chapu* — the moment in *Megillat Esther* when Haman was immediately seized as the words left the king's mouth — is notable. God acts swiftly when the righteous are silent and trust in divine justice.

---

## Music Prohibition

### Music Source

Mar Ukva was then asked a question: *zimra minalan de'assir* — from where do we know that playing music is forbidden? He scored parchment and wrote: *al tismach Yisrael el gil ba'amim* — do not rejoice, O Israel, in the rejoicing of nations — particularly after the *Churban ha'Bayit*. This verse was written even while the first Temple still stood, by the prophet Hoshea.

### Voice vs. Instrument

The Gemara asks: why did he not instead send the verse *be'shir lo yishtu yayin, yemar shechar le'shotav* — they shall not drink wine with song; the drink shall be bitter to those who drink it? The answer: had he sent that verse alone, one might have thought the prohibition applies only to *zimra de'mana* — instrumental music — while *de'puma*, vocal singing, would be permitted. By sending the verse from Hoshea instead, the Gemara establishes *ka mashma lan* — it teaches us — that even purely vocal music is included in the prohibition.

### Drinking Houses Context

Tosafot clarifies what is actually prohibited. Rashi explains that the prohibition is specifically directed at *shir be'veit ha'mishta'ot* — singing in drinking establishments. This reading is supported by the Gemara's very choice to ask why the verse about wine was not cited, and by the *mishnah* at the end of *Masechet Sotah* which states: *mishe'batla Sanhedrin batel ha'shir be'veit ha'mishta'ot* — once the Sanhedrin was abolished, song in the drinking houses was abolished. Tosafot notes, however, that the Yerushalmi speaks of one who rises and falls asleep to music — *dehavei kaei u'damich be'zimra* — suggesting the prohibition extends beyond the drinking house context to music used purely for pleasure and self-indulgence. *Shir shel mitzvah shari* — music in the context of a *mitzvah*, such as at a *chuppah* to gladden the groom and bride, or the recitation of *zemirot*, remains permitted. This area generated considerable literature among the *rishonim* and *poskim* regarding precisely where the prohibition applies and how strictly it is to be observed, with added complexity today given the difference between live and recorded music.

---

## Music Prohibition (II)

### Rabbinic Origin

Rav Huna bar Rav Natan asked Rav Ashi the meaning of the *pasuk* in *Yehoshua* listing the cities *Kinah, Dimonah, v'Ad'adah*. Rav Ashi replied that these are simply the cities of Eretz Yisrael being enumerated. Rav Huna responded that of course he knew they were cities — he was looking for a *derasha*. Rav Geviha from Argiza, he said, would offer one: *kol sheyesh lo kinah al chaveiro v'domeh* — anyone who has a grievance against his fellow and yet remains silent — *Kinah v'Dimonah* — and is silent, *shochney adei ad oseh lo din* — the One who dwells forever will execute judgment for him. This connects directly to the story of Gneiva: remain silent, do not hand him over to the government, and God will act. Rav Ashi then challenged Rav Huna bar Rav Natan to extend the *derasha* to the next verse: *Tziklag, Madmannah, v'Sansannah*. He replied that if Rav Geviha were present, he would have a *derasha* for that too. Rav Acha from Bei Choza'ah then supplied one: *kol mi sheyesh lo tza'akas legima al chaveiro* — anyone who has a cry of *legima* against his fellow, meaning his livelihood has been compromised to the point where he cannot put food on the table — *v'domeh* — and is silent and does not attack — *shocheyn ba'sneh oseh lo din* — the One who dwells in the bush will come to his defense.

---

## Wedding Crowns

### Crown Source

Reish Galuta asked Rav Huna: *kelila minalan de'assur* — from where do we know that the crown worn by a *chassan* at his wedding is forbidden? Rav Huna answered: it is *miderabbanan* — rabbinic — citing the explicit *mishnah* in *Masechet Sotah*: *be'fulmus shel Aspasyanos gazru al ataros chassanim v'al ha'irus* — in the wars of Vespasian they decreed against the crowns of grooms and against the drums.

### Mitre Crown Link

While Rav Huna stepped away momentarily, Rav Chisda was left with Reish Galuta and offered a biblical grounding. He cited the verse in *Yechezkel*: *koh amar Hashem Elokim, hasir ha'mitznefet v'hareim ha'atarah* — thus says the Lord God, remove the mitre and lift off the crown. *Zos lo zos* — this, not even this. *Ha'shpalah ha'gavoha v'ha'gavoha ha'shpil* — raise the lowly and bring down the exalted. What is the connection between the *mitznefet*, the High Priest's mitre, and the *atarah*, the crown? The verse teaches: *bizman she'mitznefet b'rosh kohen gadol, atarah b'rosh kol adam* — when the *mitznefet* rests upon the head of the *Kohen Gadol*, when the *Beit ha'Mikdash* stands, then crowns may rest upon the heads of all people at their weddings. *Nistalka mitznefet me'rosh kohen gadol, nistalka atarah me'rosh kol adam* — but once the *mitznefet* has been removed from the head of the *Kohen Gadol*, once the *Churban* has occurred, no one may wear such a crown.

### Huna's Objection

When Rav Huna returned and was told what Rav Chisda had said, he declared emphatically: *ha'elohim, miderabbanan* — by God, it is rabbinic, not a *pasuk*. The connection to *Yechezkel* is a support and a beautiful one, but it does not transform this into a biblical prohibition. He then added graciously: *ella chizer shimcha v'chazyan milach* — your name indeed suits you and your words are very pleasing. The point stands: the verse provides an *asmachta* and a conceptual underpinning, but the prohibition itself is a rabbinic decree. Tosafot notes that Rashi understood the *atarah* as a literal metal crown, but Tosafot challenges this from the first chapter of *Sotah*, which indicates the crowns in question were made of roses or myrtle — that is, wreaths.

### Braiding Wreath

Ravina found Mar bar Rav Ashi braiding a wreath for his daughter for her wedding — an *ateret kallah*, a crown for the bride. Ravina challenged him: does the master not hold by the verse *hasir ha'mitznefet v'hareim ha'atarah*, which would seem to prohibit crowns for women as well?

### Gender Distinction

Mar bar Rav Ashi replied: *dumya d'kohen gadol b'chasanei* — the prohibition is drawn by analogy to the *Kohen Gadol*, and therefore applies only to grooms (*chasanim*), not to women (*benashi lo*). Tosafot elaborates: what is prohibited for *kallos* according to the *mishnah* in *Sotah* is specifically an *ir shel zahav* — a golden tiara — while a wreath made of natural materials is a different matter entirely. The prohibition on the *kallah* wearing an *ir shel zahav* when she goes out in public derives from the general laws of jewelry on Shabbat treated in the chapter *bameh ishah*, not from the specific decree about wedding crowns — and even there, the prohibition is limited to the wedding context out of concern for *simcha yeteirah*, excessive festivity.

---

## Angels Plea Derasha

### Angels' Argument

Rav Avira expounded — sometimes citing the tradition in the name of Rav Ami, sometimes in the name of Rav Assi — on the phrase *zos lo zos*. When God declared to Israel *hasir ha'mitznefet v'hareim ha'atarah*, the ministering angels, the *malachei ha'shareis*, spoke before God: *Ribbono shel Olam, zos lahem l'Yisrael she'hikdimu lefanecha b'Sinai na'aseh v'nishma* — is this what Israel deserves, the very people who preceded *nishma* with *na'aseh* at Sinai?

### Sinai Connection

This is deeply evocative. The *midrashim* describe how at Sinai, when Israel declared *na'aseh v'nishma*, the *malachei ha'shareis* descended and crowned each Jew with two crowns — one for *na'aseh* and one for *nishma*. When they subsequently sinned with the *eigel*, the verse records *vayisnazlu b'nei Yisrael es adyam me'Har Choreiv* — Israel stripped off their ornaments from Har Choreiv — which the *midrashim* interpret as the removal of those very crowns. Here, in discussing the removal of the wedding crowns on account of the *Churban*, the *malachei ha'shareis* invoke the merit of *na'aseh v'nishma* as a reason to retain them.

### Crowns Removal Reason

God's response to the angels: *lo zos im zos* — is it not this very Israel who *hishpila es ha'gavoha v'higbiha es ha'shafel* — who brought low what was exalted and raised up what was lowly? They engaged in *avodah zarah*, they brought down the glory of the *Beit ha'Mikdash*, and they even erected an image in the *Heichal*. Therefore the crowns must be removed.

---

## Livelihood Derasha

### Limited Livelihood

Rav Avira expounded again — sometimes in the name of Rav Ami, sometimes in the name of Rav Assi — on the verse: *koh amar Hashem im shleimim v'chen rabbim v'chen nagozu v'avar*. If a person sees that his livelihood is *mtzumtzamin* — limited and barely sufficient — he should give *tzedakah* from it; and all the more so if he has abundant resources. The word *nagozu* is the key: it suggests shearing, and from it the Gemara derives the obligation to give charity even from constrained means.

---

## Domestic Ethics (III)

### Charity Derasha

*Tana d'vei Rabbi Yishmael* teaches: anyone who shears from his property — *kol ha'gozez mi'nechasav* — and gives *tzedakah* from it, is saved from the judgment of *Gehennom*, and the word *v'avar* — he passes through — indicates passage to safety.

---

## Livelihood Derasha (II)

### Shearing Property

*Tana d'vei Rabbi Yishmael* continues: anyone who shears from his property and gives *tzedakah* is saved from the judgment of *Gehennom*.

### Sheep Parable

This is illustrated through a parable of two sheep crossing a body of water. One is shorn and one is not. The shorn sheep passes through without difficulty; the unshorn sheep is weighed down by its waterlogged wool and cannot cross. So too: the one who has given away his wealth is unencumbered and can pass through, while the one who has hoarded it all is dragged down.

---

## Domestic Ethics (III)…

### Poor Giving Charity

The verse concludes *v'iniisicha* — and I have afflicted you. Mar Zutra teaches: *afilu ani ha'misparnes min ha'tzedakah ya'aseh tzedakah* — even a poor person who himself subsists on charity must give *tzedakah*. He too should recognize the blessing of whatever he possesses and share it with those in even greater need.

### Poverty Elimination

Rav Yosef teaches from the word *oni* in *lo a'aneich od* — I will no longer afflict you: *shuv ein marin lo simanei aniyus* — one who gives *tzedakah*, even from poverty, will no longer be shown the signs of poverty. With this concludes the lengthy *aggadata* that began from the attempt to vindicate Rabbi Avyasar and the principle that one need not declare *bifnei nichtav* when traveling between Bavel and *chutz la'aretz*.

---

## Eretz Yisrael Borders

### Yehuda's Boundaries

The Gemara now turns to the question of the boundaries of Eretz Yisrael as they pertain to *bifnei nichtav*. It is worth noting at the outset — and Tosafot's extensive discussion earlier in the *perek* addresses this — that the question of boundaries here might either reflect a completely independent definition tailored to the concerns of *get* delivery and *lishmah*, or it might assume that the boundaries used for *terumos u'ma'asros* and *kedushah* apply here as well. As will become clear, this *sugya* appears to adopt the latter approach, at least as a working framework.

Rabbi Yehuda sets the boundaries: from Rekem in the east, Ashkelon in the south, and Akko in the north.

### Tithes Boundaries

These boundaries map onto the standard halakhic definitions used for the laws of *terumot u'ma'asrot* and *shevi'it*. The Gemara appears to assume, or at least explore, the premise that the same area defined as Eretz Yisrael for those purposes defines it for the laws of *gittin* as well — not necessarily because they are identical definitions by principle, but because the areas of settlement with *kedushat Eretz Yisrael* and the areas relevant to *bifnei nichtav* can be assumed to overlap unless otherwise demonstrated.

### Akko vs. Kziv

The Gemara raises a difficulty: if Akko is the northern boundary of Eretz Yisrael, how do we account for the following *baraita*? One who walks from Akko northward to Kziv — with Kziv being further north than Akko — is told that the road to his east (*mi'yemino le'mizrach*, which confirms he is walking northward) is *tamei mishum Eretz ha'Amim* — impure as foreign territory — and exempt from *ma'aser* and *shevi'it*, while the road to his west is *tehorah* and *chayevet b'ma'aser u'v'shevi'it*, until Kziv is reached. This implies that the northern boundary extends to Kziv — beyond Akko. The traveler is walking north from Akko; to his right is the east, which is outside Eretz Yisrael; to his left is the west, a narrow strip between the road and the Mediterranean shore, which retains the sanctity of Eretz Yisrael. The picture becomes clearer when one considers the geography: Akko sits on the sea; the coastal path to Kziv runs along the shore, and to the left of the traveler is indeed a strip of land between the path and the sea that remains within the borders of Eretz Yisrael.

### Strip Explanation

Abaye answers: *retzu'ah nafka* — a small strip extends northward. The primary and substantial settlement of Eretz Yisrael ends at Akko; from Akko to Kziv there is only a narrow coastal strip remaining. When we define the northern border as Akko, we are identifying where the *ikkar yishuv* — the main inhabited region — ends. The strip beyond, while technically part of Eretz Yisrael, is too marginal to serve as the defining boundary marker. Tosafot raises the question of whether it is appropriate to devote an entire *mishnah* to describing the halakhic status of such a narrow strip. The Gemara answers that even a path can serve as a geographic marker, as demonstrated by a verse in the book of *Shoftim* that gives directions to Shiloh by reference to a road — *li'msila ha'olah mi'Beit El Shechema* — and Rav Pappa confirms that *lemizrachah shel mesila* means precisely to the east of the path, with the path itself serving as the boundary marker.

The underlying tension throughout this *sugya* is worth noting: some discussions in the first *perek* tailor the definition of Eretz Yisrael specifically to the concerns of *get* delivery — familiarity with signatures, reliability of witnesses, knowledge of *lishmah* — while this *sugya* appears to simply borrow the standard definitions from *terumot u'ma'asrot*. These two approaches do not seem to be in direct dialogue with one another.

---

## Get by Boat

### Boat Equivalence

The Gemara presents two contradictory *beraitot*. One teaches: *ha'meivi get bi'sfina kemevi b'Eretz Yisrael* — one who brings a *get* in a boat is like one who brings it in Eretz Yisrael, and need not declare *bifnei nichtav*. The other teaches: it is like one who brings it in *chutz la'aretz*, and the declaration is required. The case envisions the *get* being written or delivered while the *shaliach* is aboard a boat, without having disembarked — the question being whether his location counts as Eretz Yisrael or not.

### Foreign Soil Dispute

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by invoking a parallel dispute regarding *terumot u'ma'asrot*: the case of foreign soil brought in a boat into Eretz Yisrael — *afar chutz la'aretz haba bi'sfina l'aretz* — with something growing from that soil aboard the boat. Is the produce *chayav b'ma'aser u'v'shevi'it*? This is a dispute between the *Tanna Kamma* and Rabbi Yehuda.

### Rashi's Interpretation

Rashi understands the Gemara's case as involving a boat in one of the rivers of Eretz Yisrael — not on the open sea. The *get* was written in the boat while it was in such a river. The question is whether a boat in a river is considered "in Eretz Yisrael" in the relevant sense: *k'ilu mivi derech yavasha* — as if he were bringing it overland — or whether *ha'nahar eino tor yavasha l'chol toras ha'aretz* — the river does not count as dry land for all purposes of the Land's laws.

### Scraping Bottom

Rabbi Yehuda holds: *emasy? Bizman she'ha'sfina gosheshes* — when does the boat count as being in Eretz Yisrael? Only when the boat is scraping (*gosheshes*) along the riverbed — that is, when there is physical contact between the boat and the ground of Eretz Yisrael. In that case, the boat is considered connected to the land and the produce is *chayav*. If the boat is not scraping the bottom, the produce is *patur*.

Rabbi Yirmiah resolves the contradiction between the two *beraitot* accordingly: one *beraita* reflects the view of the *Tanna Kamma*, who holds that a boat in Eretz Yisrael is treated as part of the land regardless, while the other reflects Rabbi Yehuda's position, which requires contact with the riverbed. Abaye sharpens this: the two *beraitot* correspond to the two conditions — when the boat is scraping the bottom, and when it is not.

### Perforated Pot

Rabbi Zeira draws a comparison to a *perforated pot* (*atzitz nakuv*) suspended above the ground: just as there is a debate about whether such a pot, with its contents disconnected from the ground by air space, retains the agricultural sanctity of the land (*palugta de'Rabbi Yehuda v'Rabbanan*), so too the boat case mirrors that same structural question. The boat, like the *atzitz nakuv*, may be treated as porous — either literally, if Rashi's reading of the boat as made of pottery is accepted, or conceptually — such that contact with the ground below determines its status.

### Boat Movement

Rava draws a distinction between the two cases. One cannot simply assume they are parallel. Rabbi Yehuda's condition of *gosheshes* may apply specifically to a boat — *sefina ha'asuya livroach* — because a boat is designed to move; it is never truly settled in place. Since it is inherently mobile, the only moment when it can be treated as part of the land is when it is actively dragging along the bottom and thus physically connected. But an *atzitz* that stays in one location — *she'eino asui livroach* — Rabbi Yehuda might treat differently, granting it the status of connection to the land even without direct contact.

Alternatively, Rava suggests, the *Rabbanan* themselves might distinguish between the cases in the opposite direction. When they said the boat counts as part of Eretz Yisrael even without contact, their reasoning was that water is not truly a separation: *demaya de'ar'a semichta damya* — water is like thick, dense ground, still physically continuous with the earth beneath. Air, however, is a genuine separation; an *atzitz* suspended above ground by an air gap might be treated differently even by the *Rabbanan*. The irony throughout this entire *sugya* — and it is worth noting — is that while the debate about foreign soil in a boat is technically a dispute in the laws of *terumos u'ma'asros*, the Gemara is applying its resolution directly to the question of *get* delivery, even though the conceptual concerns underlying *bifnei nichtav* — familiarity with witnesses, knowledge of *lishmah* — bear no obvious relationship to whether a boat's hull is scraping the riverbed.

---

---

# Gittin 8

## Eretz Yisrael Borders

### Boat/Planter Debate

The daf picks up in the middle of a *gemara* discussing the parameters of *Eretz Yisrael* for the purposes of *gittin*. The question concerns someone who brings a *get* while on a boat traveling on a river in *Eretz Yisrael* — is that considered bringing it from within *Eretz Yisrael*, or does it have the status of *chutz la'aretz*, thereby requiring the messenger to declare *bifnei nichtav uvifnei nechtam*?

The *gemara* ties this debate to a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the *Chachamim* regarding a boat carrying soil on which crops are growing while the boat travels through a river in *Eretz Yisrael* — are those crops obligated in *terumot u'ma'asrot*? The *Chachamim* say yes; Rabbi Yehuda says only when the boat is actually scraping against the riverbed. The *gemara* also draws a comparison to the case of an *atzitz*, a flowerpot with a hole in it. Rashi understands the boat to be made of pottery, while Tosafot explains it is a wooden boat, which is considered porous. Regardless, the key question is why this agricultural consideration — whether the boat is touching the riverbed — has any bearing on the entirely separate question of *bifnei nichtav*, which concerns different practical matters such as *lishma* and the ability to validate signatures.

### Tosafot: Formal Definiti…

The answer becomes clear from Tosafot's explanation. The *gemara* is not examining whether the pragmatic concerns underlying the *takana* of *bifnei nichtav* are actually satisfied in any given case. Rather, it is drawing on a pre-existing, formal definition of what constitutes *Eretz Yisrael* — derived from the laws of *terumot u'ma'asrot* — and importing that definition wholesale into the context of *gittin*.

Tosafot, in the *tosafot* entitled *atzitz* toward the end of 7b, makes this point explicitly. He writes: *de'nehei de'hacha de'eina gosheses le'Rabbi Yehuda mi'de'hava lei Chutz La'aretz le'inyan ma'aser chashivnan Chutz La'aretz le'inyan get* — if the boat is not scraping the bottom, then since under Rabbi Yehuda's view the produce would not be obligated in *ma'aser*, it is treated as *chutz la'aretz* for *get* purposes as well. The logic is that the place itself is formally labeled *chutz la'aretz*, and Tosafot explains: *keivan desheim Chutz La'aretz al hamakom* — since that place is called *chutz la'aretz* in the formal sense, one must say *bifnei nichtav ubifnei nechtam*, even though from a purely practical standpoint, the *edim* are right there on the river, easily accessible, and presumably familiar with the laws of *lishma*. Tosafot acknowledges this practical observation and addresses it: *kedei shelo tachalok midinas hayam* — for reasons of formal consistency, the determination follows the label, not the practical reality.

Tosafot further clarifies a potentially confusing point. For something to be *chayav* in *terumot u'ma'asrot*, two separate conditions must be met: first, the produce must be growing in *Eretz Yisrael*; and second, the soil must be connected to the ground. For the purposes of *bifnei nichtav*, however, the second condition — soil connectivity — is irrelevant. That is a technical *terumot u'ma'asrot* concern. The only question that matters for *gittin* is the first: is this place formally considered part of *Eretz Yisrael* or not? We therefore borrow the *terumot u'ma'asrot* definition not to resolve questions about dirt connectivity, but as a formal indicator of whether one is standing inside or outside the land. And that formalistic determination, in turn, governs whether *bifnei nichtav* must be said.

One might ask about the upper floor analogy: does a person writing a *get* on a second floor in Israel need to say *bifnei nichtav* simply because dirt on an upper story would not be *chayav* in *terumot u'ma'asrot*? Tosafot addresses this: there at least the soil beneath the building is *chayav*, whereas on a boat in a river perhaps nothing below would be *chayav* — yet even then, Tosafot's point stands, because the question about the boat is not really about the dirt at all. It is about whether the location itself is formally designated as *Eretz Yisrael*.

### Rav Nachman: Rivers

The *gemara* resumes on 8a. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak states: *benaharot Eretz Yisrael kuli alma lo pligi* — when it comes to rivers within *Eretz Yisrael*, nobody disagrees. A river flowing through the land of Israel is unambiguously within the borders of Israel. Rashi confirms this: *kuli alma lo pligi de'Eretz Yisrael ninhu*, and even if the boat is not scraping the riverbed, that is irrelevant because, as Rashi explains, *ta'ama deget lav mishum yanika min hakarka hu* — the rationale for *gittin* is not about whether the soil is drawing nourishment from the ground of Israel, which is a *ma'aser* and *shvi'it* concern. Therefore, whether it is a river or dry land, *lo shna nahar velo shna yabasha*.

What, then, is the subject of the debate? *Ela ki pligi beyam hagadol* — the dispute concerns the Mediterranean Sea. If one is carrying a *get* on a boat in the Mediterranean, off the coast of Israel, at what point is that boat considered within *Eretz Yisrael* and at what point is it in international waters? This is where the *gemara* once again borrows a pre-existing formal definition from *terumot u'ma'asrot* — but now it is a more appropriate borrowing, because this is not about the technical question of soil connectivity. It is a genuine question about what constitutes the territorial boundaries of *Eretz Yisrael*.

### Turei Amnon Border

A *baraita* is cited: *eizehu Eretz Yisrael ve'eizehu Chutz La'aretz?* — which areas belong to *Eretz Yisrael* and which to *chutz la'aretz* for purposes of *terumah*? *Kol she'shofei'a v'yored mi'Turei Amnon v'lifnim Eretz Yisrael; mi'Turei Amnon v'lachutz Chutz La'aretz* — anything that slopes down from *Turei Amnon* inward is *Eretz Yisrael*; from *Turei Amnon* outward is *chutz la'aretz*. Rashi identifies *Turei Amnon* as the Aramaic equivalent of *Hor HaHar*, the mountain ridge mentioned in the Torah as part of the western border of the Land. The image is that of a mountain ridge: whatever slopes toward the interior of the land is *Eretz Yisrael*, and whatever slopes away is outside it.

### Island Definition

The *baraita* continues with the case of islands: *nasin she'ba'yam ro'in otan k'ilu chut matuach aleihen mi'Turei Amnon ad Nachal Mitzrayim* — for islands in the sea, one imagines a string drawn from *Turei Amnon* to *Nachal Mitzrayim* (understood as Wadi el-Arish at the southern coastal border). Anything within the arc between that string and the coastline is considered *Eretz Yisrael*; everything outside that string is *chutz la'aretz*. This is the position of the *Tanna Kamma*. Under this view, the northern and southern coastal borders are connected by a diagonal line, and the enclosed area of Mediterranean waters is considered part of the Land.

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees and expands this definition significantly. He derives from the verse *u'gvul yam v'hayah lachem haYam HaGadol u'gvul* — the redundancy of the word *u'gvul* teaches that more of the Mediterranean is to be included. His formulation: *kol she'keneged Eretz Yisrael harei hu k'Eretz Yisrael* — anything directly opposite Israel is counted as Israel. And for islands that fall to the sides, rather than drawing the diagonal connecting line of the *Tanna Kamma*, Rabbi Yehuda draws two parallel horizontal lines — one extending westward from *Turei Amnon* (which he terms *Kaflurya*) to the Atlantic, and one extending westward from *Nachal Mitzrayim* to the Atlantic. Everything between those two parallel lines is *Eretz Yisrael*, and everything outside them is *chutz la'aretz*.

The *gemara* asks: what does the *Tanna Kamma* do with the word *u'gvul* that Rabbi Yehuda uses for his expansion? Answer: the *Tanna Kamma* needs it to include islands at all — without it, one might not know islands are counted. Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, derives the inclusion of islands from the word *yam* itself, and therefore the additional *u'gvul* is available to teach the parallel-line rule.

Under Rabbi Yehuda's map, the territory between the two parallel lines extending across the entire Mediterranean would be extraordinarily vast — encompassing islands such as Sicily, Cyprus, and potentially parts of Greece. The debate between the *Chachamim* and Rabbi Yehuda about whether a boat is in *Eretz Yisrael* or *chutz la'aretz* therefore pertains to boats sailing in the farther regions of the Mediterranean: the *Chachamim* would call those waters *chutz la'aretz*, while Rabbi Yehuda would say they remain *Eretz Yisrael*.

### Tosafot: France Question

This leads to a question posed by Rabbeinu Peter to Rabbeinu Tam, cited in Tosafot: given Rabbi Yehuda's position, should communities in France be obligated in *ma'aser*, since they lie to the west of *Eretz Yisrael* and might fall within Rabbi Yehuda's expanded zone? Tosafot records three responses.

The first answer is simply that we do not rule according to Rabbi Yehuda — *delo kaima lan k'Rabbi Yehuda*. Tosafot then raises an additional question on the side: even granting Rabbi Yehuda's expansion, what does this have to do with *gittin*? Did Rabbi Yehuda really mean to say that all those regions — including apparently distant lands — had communities that were experts in *lishma* and that would not require *bifnei nichtav*? This question itself reinforces the point that this *gemara* is working with purely formal, pre-packaged definitions rather than the substantive concerns of the *takana*.

The second answer — which Tosafot identifies as closer to the plain sense of the *gemara* and as consistent with Rashi's commentary — is that Rabbi Yehuda is speaking only about islands in the Mediterranean, not about major continental land masses. *Delo havay beyabasha ad Kunas ela banasim shebaYam HaGadol davka* — his ruling applies only to islands in the sea. Sicily and certain Greek islands might be included, but France, Spain, and other major territories would not be. Tosafot supports this from a series of verses — *ad HaYam HaGadol mevo hashemesh yiheye gevulchem*, *veshatati gevulcha miYam Suf ve'ad Yam Pelishtim*, and so on — which indicate that the borders are defined in terms of surrounding seas and the territories they enclose, not unlimited projection across entire continents.

The third answer maintains that Rabbi Yehuda did actually know, in his time, that *lishma* requirements were being satisfied even in those regions, and that he knew specifically which communities would qualify. This third response, like the first, returns to the practical considerations of *lishma* and signature validation. Tosafot's most substantive resolution remains the middle one: the discussion concerns islands in the sea, and once the formal definition of which islands belong to *Eretz Yisrael* is established, that definition is imported wholesale into the context of *gittin* — not because it perfectly mirrors the needs of the *takana*, but because the *gemara* is working from a formalistic geographic definition.

---

## Three Definitions

### Rabbi Meir: Akko

The *gemara* now returns to the *mishna*: *Rabbi Meir omer Akko k'Eretz Yisrael l'Gittin* — Rabbi Meir rules that Akko counts as *Eretz Yisrael* for *gittin* purposes. This is a more specifically tailored definition — for *gittin* only, not for other purposes — which already reflects a different approach from the broad formalistic borrowing of the earlier discussion.

### Slave to Syria

The *gemara* then records a question posed to Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba: *hamocher avdo l'Surya k'mocher b'chutz la'aretz dami o lo?* — if someone sells his slave to *Surya* (Syria), is it treated like selling him to *chutz la'aretz*? This question introduces a third legal context in which the definition of *Eretz Yisrael* is relevant. There is a *halacha* that if a master sells his slave outside of *Eretz Yisrael*, the slave goes free as a *knas*, because an *eved kena'ani* is obligated in certain *mitzvot* tied to the land, and by selling him away the master is effectively determining that the slave will be unable to fulfill those obligations and will be cut off from the Jewish community's center of life. The question is whether *Surya* — understood as the territory broadly called Syria, which includes *Aram Tzova* and which was conquered by King David — is considered *chutz la'aretz* for this purpose.

### Graduated Definitions

The *gemara* answers by invoking Rabbi Meir's ruling: *l'Gittin in, l'avadim lo* — Akko is like *Eretz Yisrael* for *gittin* purposes but not for slave purposes. And if even Akko, which is immediately adjacent to the land, is considered *chutz la'aretz* for slave purposes, then *kol sheken Surya d'merachaka tuva* — how much more so Syria, which is much more distant from the central population of the land.

This establishes three distinct and graduated definitions of *Eretz Yisrael*. The first is the *terumot u'ma'asrot* definition, which turns on the formal question of which land was sanctified through conquest. The second is the *gittin* definition, which reflects where there is sufficient Jewish presence, knowledge of *lishma*, and ability to validate documents. The third is the *avadim* definition, which concerns where the primary Jewish community actually lives — the *ikkar yishuv* — such that selling a slave away from that center is genuinely disadvantaging him.

Conceptually, *Surya* may be *chayav* in *terumot u'ma'asrot* — because it was formally sanctified through conquest — yet it is treated as *chutz la'aretz* for both *gittin* and for the law of slaves. This is because the *gittin* definition asks where there is Jewish travel and communal life sufficient to ensure *lishma*, and the *avadim* definition asks where the primary Jewish population resides. *Surya* satisfies the criterion of formal sanctification but not the criteria of actual Jewish settlement and communal life. The three concentric definitions therefore correspond to three different underlying concerns, and each produces a different geographic result.

---

## Syria's Status

### Syria: Three Chutz

A *baraita* articulates the multi-layered status of *Surya* systematically. *Tanu Rabbanan bishlosha drachim shavsa Surya l'Eretz Yisrael u'vishlosha l'Chutz La'aretz* — in three ways *Surya* resembles *Eretz Yisrael*, and in three ways it resembles *chutz la'aretz*.

The three ways it is like *chutz la'aretz*: first, *afrah tamei k'Chutz La'aretz* — its soil is *tamei* like that of *chutz la'aretz*. The Rabbis decreed that the soil of lands outside *Eretz Yisrael* is *tamei*, based on the concern that non-Jews buried their dead throughout the land without demarcation, posing a risk of *tumah* to *kohanim* who traveled there. Beyond the practical concern, this decree also served as a communal mechanism to encourage Jews — and particularly *kohanim* — to remain in *Eretz Yisrael* rather than emigrate, giving *halachic* reality to the sanctity of living in the Land. *Surya*, despite its formal *kedusha* for *terumot u'ma'asrot*, is treated like *chutz la'aretz* in this regard. Second, *v'hamocher avdo l'Surya k'mocher b'Chutz La'aretz* — selling a slave there is like selling to *chutz la'aretz*. Third, *v'hameivi get mi'Surya k'meivi mi'Chutz La'aretz* — one who brings a *get* from *Surya* must declare *bifnei nichtav*, as it is treated as *chutz la'aretz* for *gittin*.

### Kibush Yachid

Three ways *Surya* is like *Eretz Yisrael*: *chayavet b'ma'aser u'vishvi'it k'Eretz Yisrael* — it is obligated in *ma'aser* and *shvi'it* like *Eretz Yisrael*. The *gemara* explains the underlying principle: *kasavar kibuish yachid shmo kibuish* — it holds that a conquest by an individual counts as a valid conquest for purposes of sanctifying land with the *kedusha* of *Eretz Yisrael*. It is this principle that makes *Surya chayav* in *terumot u'ma'asrot*, since the territories were conquered by David — an individual acting as king rather than through a full national enterprise.

### Rashi: Kibush Yachid

Rashi explains *kibuish yachid* as follows: *shelo hayu kol Yisrael b'yachad k'derech shehayu b'kibuish Yehoshua* — unlike Joshua's conquest, which was a fully national undertaking, David's campaigns were not carried out together with all of Israel. Rashi adds two related points: David's conquest lacked the participation of all twelve tribes as a national army, and it also lacked *Sanhedrin* authorization, which is what would have transformed a military campaign into a nationally sanctioned act of conquest. Additionally, Joshua's conquest was executed *l'tzorech kol Yisrael* — for the benefit of all Israel, for the purpose of division among the tribes. David's conquests, by contrast, were undertaken *l'tzorcho* — for his own purposes as king, not to serve an obvious national goal. That is what makes them *kibuish yachid*.

The *gemara*'s position here, that *kibuish yachid* does confer *kedusha* for *terumot u'ma'asrot*, means David's conquest of these territories sanctified them even without a full national enterprise. A striking question arises in this context: *terumot u'ma'asrot* as practiced is based on the sanctity established during the Second Temple period — we do not generally hold that the sanctity of the First Temple period persists for *terumot u'ma'asrot* purposes. Why, then, should what David did be the operative consideration? This question is worth noting, though the *gemara* proceeds on the assumption that it is.

### Tosafot: Kibush Yachid

Tosafot offers a fundamentally different understanding of *kibuish yachid*, derived from the *Sifrei* at the end of *Parshat Va'yihei Eikev*. For Tosafot, the problem is not that David's conquest was a private rather than national enterprise. Rather, the issue is that one cannot formally annex territory to *Eretz Yisrael* and endow it with *kedusha* until the primary land of Israel has itself been fully conquered. The *Sifrei* derives this from the verse *samuch l'pator yadcha shelo horashta* — you have not yet taken possession of that which is near you. Rashi there explains that this refers to the Jebusite enclave near Jerusalem, which had not yet been subdued. If the land adjacent to the capital had not been fully conquered, one cannot go off and conquer *Aram Naharayim* and *Aram Tzova* and incorporate those territories into the sacred land of Israel.

However, *aval achar shekol Eretz Yisrael kvusha* — once the entire primary land of Israel is conquered, *kol makom asher tidroch kaf raglchem lachem* — any territory subsequently conquered, even by an individual, attains the sanctity of *Eretz Yisrael*. So for Tosafot, *kibuish yachid* is not primarily about the absence of national participation; it is about the sequence of conquest. David conquered *Surya* before completing the conquest of the primary land, and that timing is what prevented full annexation. The conquered territories received some *kedusha* but not the full *kedusha* that would have come with a conquest occurring after *Eretz Yisrael* itself was fully in hand.

### Tahara in Syria

The second way *Surya* resembles *Eretz Yisrael* in its unique status: *v'harotzeh l'hikanes lah b'tahara nichnas* — if one wishes to enter *Surya* while remaining *tahor*, it is possible to do so. The *gemara* cites a *baraita*: one who enters *Eretz Ha'amim* (foreign lands) while enclosed in a box, chest, or tower — *Rebbe* says he becomes *tamei*; Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Yehuda says he remains *tahor*. The *gemara* then clarifies that even Rebbe only rules stringently in normal *chutz la'aretz*, where the Rabbis decreed *tumah* not only on the soil itself but on the very air — *al gusha gazru, avira lo gazru*. In Syria, however, the decree applies only to touching the soil, not to the air above it or to simply being present over the land. Therefore, everyone agrees that in *Surya* one can maintain *tahara* by avoiding direct contact with the ground, for example by being carried in an enclosed conveyance — though Tosafot notes that one riding a horse might similarly argue the same point.

The irony of this ruling is notable: the soil of *Surya* is formally *tamei*, and yet its *tumah* is categorically less severe than that of ordinary *chutz la'aretz*. This precisely reflects *Surya*'s middle position — more connected to *Eretz Yisrael* than the rest of the world, yet not fully part of it.

### Purchasing Fields

The third way *Surya* resembles *Eretz Yisrael*: *v'hakoneh sadeh b'Surya k'koneh b'parvarei Yerushalayim* — one who buys a field in *Surya* is like one who purchases property in the environs of Jerusalem itself. The *gemara* asks: *l'mai hilchasa* — what is the practical implication of this? Rav Sheshes answers: *lomar shekosvin alav ono va'afilu b'Shabbos* — it means that the deed of sale may be drawn up even on *Shabbat*. The *gemara* immediately asks: surely you do not mean that the Jew himself writes on *Shabbat*? The answer, as derived from Rava's ruling elsewhere, is *omer l'Akum v'oseh* — a non-Jew is instructed to draw up the document. Even though *amira l'Akum shvut* is normally prohibited as a Rabbinic prohibition, *mishum yishuv Eretz Yisrael lo gazru rabanan* — the Rabbis did not apply this prohibition when the purpose is settling the Land of Israel.

The tension here is striking. On one hand, the very same *Surya* whose dirt is *tamei*, whose slaves gain freedom if sold there, and from which a *get* requires *bifnei nichtav* — that same territory is valued so highly as an extension of *Eretz Yisrael* that purchasing fields there overrides the Rabbinic prohibition against *amira l'goy* on *Shabbat*. Perhaps the purchase of agricultural fields (*sadeh* suggests planting) in *Surya* serves the larger project of *yishuv Eretz Yisrael* by providing agricultural resources for the Jewish community in the Land proper. Or perhaps the *kedusha* inherent in the sanctified soil, even if Jews do not presently live there in large numbers, is sufficient to make Jewish ownership of that land a religious priority.

Tosafot notes the limits of this ruling. *Mishum yishuv Eretz Yisrael lo gazru rabanan* — only for the specific *mitzvah* of *yishuv Eretz Yisrael* is *amira l'goy* permitted even for a *melacha d'Oraisa*. For any other *mitzvah* purpose, *amira l'goy* remains permitted only for a *d'rabbanan* prohibition, not for a *d'Oraisa*. Tosafot does note that the *Halachot Gedolot* takes a broader view, permitting *amira l'goy* even for a *d'Oraisa* prohibition whenever it serves a *mitzvah* purpose — citing the case of *milah* as an example. We do not rule according to this position, though the Rema is prepared to rely on it *b'sha'at hadechak*. For *yishuv Eretz Yisrael*, however, the ruling of the *gemara* is clear and undisputed: *amira l'goy* is permitted.

---

## Slave's Get Shichrur

### Eved Brings Get

Since the discussion has introduced the laws of slavery and manumission, the *gemara* turns to a related *halacha* found in the *mishna*: *eved she'heivi gito v'kasuv bo atzmecha u'nechasai knuyim lach* — a slave who brings his own writ of manumission containing the language "you and all my property are given to you." The ruling: *atzmo kanah, nechasim lo kanah* — he acquires his freedom but does not acquire the property.

### Get vs. Gift

Rashi explains the underlying reasoning. The slave's declaration of *bifnei nichtav* — the very statement that the document was written and signed in his presence — functions as a *kiyum*, a validation of the signatures on the document. But it serves as a *kiyum* only in its capacity as a *get shichrur*, a writ of manumission, and not in its capacity as a *matan*, a gift instrument. The *gemara* introduced a parallel *takana* for *gitei shichrur* analogous to the *takana* for *gitei nashim*: the slave declaring *bifnei nichtav* is a special leniency granted to him with respect to validating his own document of freedom. There is, however, no such leniency for gift documents. A gift document requires standard *kiyum shtarot* — validation of its signatures by two witnesses. Since the single document performs two legal functions simultaneously — manumitting the slave and gifting him property — the *kiyum* achieved through *bifnei nichtav* is effective only for the manumission aspect. For the property transfer, the document must be independently validated through normal means.

### Abaye vs. Rava

A question is then raised: the case described above involves two statements — "you are given to yourself" and "my property is given to you" — phrased as two distinct phrases within one document. The *bifnei nichtav* can therefore potentially be understood as applying to one phrase and not the other, since there are two separable statements. But what if the document uses a single phrase: *kol nechasai k'nuim lach* — all my property is given to you? Here, "all my property" includes the slave himself, so the freedom and the gift are expressed in a single unified statement rather than two discrete ones. Does the *kiyum* achieved by *bifnei nichtav* then apply to the entire sentence — including the property — or only to the freedom element?

Abaye rules: *mitoch she'kanah atzmo kanah nechasim* — since the *kiyum* validates the sentence for the purpose of acquiring himself, it validates the sentence in its entirety, including the property. The sentence is one undivided legal act; either the *kiyum* applies to the whole sentence or it does not.

Rava disagrees: *bishlama atzmo liknei, midi d'hava a'get isha* — it is understandable that the *kiyum* works for his own freedom, just as *bifnei nichtav* works for a *get isha*. *Ela nechasim lo liknei, midi d'hava a'kiyum shtarot d'alma* — but for the property, from the vantage point of a gift document, the sentence requires standard validation of signatures, and *bifnei nichtav* does not supply that.

### Rava's Position

The debate continues as Abaye reconsiders. Unwilling to abandon the principle that the sentence is a single unified act, Abaye reverses the logic: *mitoch she'lo kanah nechasim lo kanah atzmo* — if the *kiyum* is insufficient to transfer the property, then by the same token it should not be sufficient to free him either. If the sentence stands or falls as a whole, then either it is fully validated or it is not validated at all.

Rava responds with equal firmness: *bishlama nechasim lo liknei* — I agree the property is not transferred, since that aspect of the document functions as a gift document requiring ordinary validation. *Ela atzmo liknei, midi d'hava a'get isha* — but he should acquire himself. The *kiyum* provided by *bifnei nichtav* is effective for the manumission aspect of the document, since that is precisely what the *takana* of *bifnei nichtav* was established to achieve.

In Rava's final ruling, *echad zeh ve'echad zeh atzmo kanah nechasim lo kanah* — whether the document phrases the two elements in two separate clauses or in a single unified clause, the result is identical: he is freed but does not acquire the property. Rava's position is that the legal effects of a document can be analyzed and split according to the distinct functions the document performs, even when those functions are expressed in a single sentence. A *get shichrur* and a *matan* are two categorically different types of legal instruments governed by different rules of validation. The fact that they happen to be expressed together — even in one sentence — does not merge them into a single legal act for the purposes of *kiyum*. Abaye, by contrast, insists that the physical sentence is the irreducible unit: either the *kiyum* validates the sentence or it does not, and one cannot selectively apply the *kiyum* to some of its legal ramifications while denying it to others.

---

---

# Gittin 9

## Rava vs. Abaye

### Property & Freedom

The sugya opens with a scenario involving a single document — a *get* — that simultaneously transfers property to a slave and frees him. The document contains one line stating that all of the master's property is given to the slave, and the question concerns whether the *kiyum* performed through *befanai nichtav uvefanai nechtam* — the declaration required and permitted specifically for a *shtar shichrur* — also validates the property transfer embedded in the same statement.

### Rava: Split Effect

Rava holds that it does not need to do both or neither. The effect of the *get* can be split: the aspect of the statement that applies to the slave's *shichrur* is validated by the *kiyum*, while the aspect that would transfer property to him is not. A single sentence can thus be partially effective.

### Abaye: All or Nothing

Abaye takes the opposing position: it is all or nothing. One cannot apply a *kiyum* selectively to one legal effect of a statement while leaving the other unaffected. Though notably, Abaye's position will shift over the course of the discussion.

---

## Palginan Dibura

### Rav Adda's Challenge

Rav Adda bar Matna challenges Rava directly: whose opinion are you following? Is this not the position of Rabbi Shimon, who maintains *palginan diburei* — that we split the words, or rather the legal effects of words?

### Mishnah: Reservation

The source for this principle is a *mishnah*: if one writes all his property to his slave, the slave goes free — because the slave's own person is included among the property, so the master is effectively giving the slave to himself, rendering the document both a gift and a writ of manumission. However, if the master reserves even a minimal amount of land — *kol she-hu* — the slave does not go free, because the reservation implies that the transfer is incomplete, that something is being held back, and there is a sense that the slave himself may not be fully released.

### R. Shimon's Exception

Rabbi Shimon qualifies this ruling. He says the slave is *always* freed — *le-olam hu ben chorin* — with only one exception: if the master says "all my property is given to my slave except for one part in ten thousand of it." The difference between this case and a reservation of a specific piece of land is significant. When an abstract, fractional percentage is withheld, we do not know what is being held back. It could be that the thing being withheld is the slave himself. In that case, there is genuine ambiguity as to whether the slave was ever given his own person. But when something concrete like a house is excluded, and there is nothing left to transfer other than the slave himself, the master is effectively just freeing the slave — and Rabbi Shimon holds that this works.

### Tosafot's Explanation

Rashi offers his own reading of how Rabbi Shimon's position relates to *palginan diburei*, but the discussion here follows Tosafot's explanation, which is more directly illuminating for the issue at hand.

Tosafot explains the connection as follows. Suppose the master owns a house and a slave, and he declares: "I am giving you all my property except for my house." According to Rabbi Shimon, the slave goes free. But why should this work? The statement, taken as a whole, is an attempted transfer of property. If we say that excluding the house effectively means there is nothing left to give other than the slave himself, then this statement is really only operative with respect to the slave's *shichrur* — it cannot function as a gift of property because no property, apart from the slave's person, is actually being conveyed. The *gemara* therefore identifies this as a form of *palginan diburei*: you have one statement, "all my property," but it is only going to take legal effect with respect to the slave's freedom, not with respect to any transfer of assets. That, says Tosafot, is what the *gemara* recognizes as analogous to Rava's position: one statement, *kol nechasai konuyim lach*, validated by *kiyum* only as a *shichrur*, not as a gift. The parallel is precise.

---

## Ruling: R. Meir

### Halacha: R. Meir

At this point the *gemara* raises a challenge from a ruling attributed to Rav Nachman, as cited by Rav Yosef bar Minyumi: even though Rabbi Yoshiyah praised Rabbi Shimon, the *halacha* follows Rabbi Meir — which here means following the *Tanna Kamma* who holds that if anything is held back, if the transfer is in any way incomplete, the slave does not go free. This would appear to reject *palginan diburei* entirely, and by extension, to undermine Rava's position.

### R. Yosei's Praise

A *baraita* records that when the words of Rabbi Shimon were brought before Rabbi Yosei, he applied to them the verse: *sefatayim yishak meshiv devarim nechochim* — "lips will kiss the one who returns proper words." The verse is a mark of high praise. Tosafot offers a striking reading of what *sefatayim yishak* means in this context: when someone says something truly correct and compelling, those around him press their lips together — that is, they fall silent, because they have nothing to say in response. The brilliance of the answer leaves no room for rebuttal. It is not a warm kiss, but the silence of intellectual defeat.

### Despite Praise

Yet despite this extraordinary praise, the *gemara* affirms: we still rule like Rabbi Meir. We do not apply *palginan diburei*, and if anything at all is held back within the text, the *get* or *shichrur* does not take effect. This appears to be a decisive ruling against Rava.

---

## Shachiv Mera

### Dying Donor Recovers

The *gemara* immediately presses back. Did Rav Nachman actually rule categorically against *palginan diburei*? There is another ruling attributed to him, also via Rav Yosef bar Minyumi: in the case of a *shachiv mera* — a person on his deathbed — who writes all his property to his slave, and then recovers, what is the outcome?

### Split Effect Outcome

The answer is striking: *chozer b'nechasim v'eino chozer b'eved* — he retracts the property but cannot retract the freeing of the slave. The property reverts because a deathbed gift is given on the assumption that the donor will die from his current illness; if he recovers, the gift returns to him. But the manumission does not revert, because *yatza lo shem ben chorin* — the slave has already been publicly proclaimed free, and once that status has been announced, it cannot be undone.

One might ask: if technically speaking the *shichrur* was part of a deathbed gift that reverts upon recovery, why should the slave's status be any different? The *gemara*'s invocation of *yatza lo shem* — a kind of proclaimed status — is admittedly unusual as a basis for *halacha*. The parallel offered in the shiur to a mistakenly announced Miss Universe winner captures the intuition: once the declaration has been made publicly, withdrawing it creates impossible social confusion. But how does that translate into hard *halachic* consequence?

### Tosafot on Institution

Tosafot addresses this directly. The entire institution of *matnas shachiv mera* is a rabbinic creation, and it operates under the parameters that the rabbis set for it. One of those parameters is that if you free a slave on your deathbed, even if you recover, the *shichrur* stands. That is simply how the rabbis structured the institution.

The key point for the present discussion, however, is what this ruling reveals about *palginan diburei*. The gift to the slave was made in a single statement — *kol nechasai knuyim lach*, all my property is given to you. And yet the outcome is that the slave receives his freedom but not the property. This is a classic application of *palginan diburei*: one sentence, two possible legal effects, and only one of them takes hold. It therefore appears that Rav Nachman himself — the very authority cited to rule against *palginan diburei* — applied it in the case of *shachiv mera*. This contradiction is what forces Abaye to clarify.

---

## Lav Krisus

### When It Applies

Abaye resolves the apparent contradiction. He concedes that Rava is correct: we do say *palginan diburei*. The *kiyum* of a *shtar shichrur* can free the slave even if it does not simultaneously effect a property transfer. Similarly, in the *shachiv mera* case, the *shichrur* holds even though the property reverts. These are genuine applications of *palginan diburei*, and they are valid.

### Qualified vs. Unqualified

The question then is: why, according to Rabbi Meir, does the slave *not* go free when the master says "all my property except for this plot of land"? If we apply *palginan diburei*, we should be able to let the *shichrur* take effect even if we disregard the property transfer — just as we do in the *shachiv mera* case.

Abaye draws a critical distinction. In the *shachiv mera* case, the text of the document is unqualified. The statement *kol nechasai knuyim lach* contains no internal reservation — the split in effect occurs externally, through the operation of the *shachiv mera* institution, not through anything embedded in the language of the document itself. Similarly, when Rava speaks of a *kiyum* that validates the *shichrur* but not the property transfer, the document's text is clean; it is the *kiyum* mechanism that selectively applies. *Palginan diburei* means that the effects of an otherwise unqualified statement are split — one effect is operative, another is not.

### Complete Severance

But when the text itself contains a qualification — "all my property *except for* this house" — the problem is not a failure of *palginan diburei*. The problem is *lav krisus*: it is not a complete severance. The concept of *krisus* — severance — which the Torah requires of a *sefer krisus*, applies equally to a *get isha* and to a *get shel eved*. The parallel between divorce and manumission is striking precisely here: just as a *get isha* must effect a total and unconditional severance of the marital relationship, so too a *shtar shichrur* must effect a complete and unconditional release from servitude.

When the document itself contains a reservation — when within the language of the *get* something is being held back — that is not a case of splitting effects externally. That is a document that, on its face, is not a full *krisus*. It is an incomplete severance, and no amount of *palginan diburei* can remedy that defect. The text itself is defective. This is the reason Rabbi Meir holds that the slave does not go free when a specific property is excepted: not because we reject *palginan diburei* in principle, but because the document's language is internally qualified, and an internally qualified document is *lav krisus* — it is not a *get* at all.

---

## Irur & Validation

### Mishnah: Challenge

The *mishnah* addresses a different scenario: a *get* given in *Eretz Yisrael*, where the declaration of *befanai nichtav uvefanai nechtam* is not required. If such a *get* is subsequently challenged — *yatza alav irur* — its signatures must then be validated.

### Number of Challengers

The *gemara* asks: how many challengers are needed to trigger this requirement? If only one person challenges the *get*, Rabbi Yochanan rules that universally, a single challenger does not constitute a valid *irur* — challenges require at least two people, and so a lone voice of protest should not require any validation. That seems to leave two challengers as the operative case. But if two people challenge the *get*, the *gemara* notes that we are now facing two witnesses against two witnesses — *trei u'trei ninhu* — and validation by an additional two witnesses would merely create an equal and opposite set of testimonies. *Mai chazit d'samchat ahani smoch ahani* — why should we favor one pair over the other? In that case, even successful validation would not seem sufficient.

### Husband's Challenge

The *gemara* resolves both difficulties by identifying the operative case: the challenger is the husband himself. The husband who issued the *get* now claims it was a forgery — that he never wrote it, that the signatures are not authentic. His challenge is weighty enough to require a response, and so we demand that the signatures be validated. But once validation is obtained through proper witnesses, those witnesses overcome even the husband's own objection. The husband's challenge demands validation; validation satisfies it.

---

## Get from Overseas

### Unable to Say

The *mishnah* states: one who brings a *get* from *medinat hayam* and is unable (*eino yachol*) to say *befanai nichtav uvefanai nechtam* — if there are witnesses whose signatures appear on the document, it may be validated through those signatures. This provides an alternative route: though the agent cannot offer the standard oral declaration, the *get* may still be delivered once the signatures are confirmed through independent testimony.

The *gemara* takes note of the language *eino yachol* — literally "he is unable" — and presses on its meaning. If the word is meant literally, suggesting a deaf-mute who is physically incapable of speech, then a prior question arises: can a deaf-mute (*cheresh*) serve as a *mevi get* at all? The *mishnah* in a different context explicitly excludes a *cheresh*, *shoteh*, and *katan* from delivering a *get*, since they lack the full intellectual standing — *bar deiah* — required for this role.

---

## Gittin & Manumission

### Agunah & Iguan

The *mishnah* states that in this regard — the requirement of *befanai nechtam* when bringing a *get* into or out of *Eretz Yisrael* — a *get* given to a woman and a *shtar shichrur* given to a slave are treated identically. This is introduced as one of the ways in which *gittei nashim* and *shichrurei avadim* are compared.

Tosafot raises an important question here. We understand why the rabbis instituted *befanai nechtam* for a woman: without it, there is a serious risk of *agunah* — a woman unable to remarry because her *get* cannot be properly authenticated. The concern for the *agunah* is a powerful and well-recognized institutional driver. But what parallel concern applies to the slave? What is the slave's *igun*?

One might argue the concern is marriage-related as well: if the slave has received a *shtar shichrur* of uncertain validity, he is caught in between — he cannot marry a free woman because he may still be a slave, and he cannot properly marry a slave woman because he may already be free. But Tosafot rejects this as a parallel to *agunah*, because the solution seems obvious: simply do not hand the *shtar shichrur* to the slave until the signatures have been validated. In the interim, the slave remains a slave and may continue living with a slave woman. There is no abandonment, no limbo — just a delay in delivery. The woman's situation is different: she is living apart from her husband without access to the *get*, with no recourse. That is *agunah*. The slave does not face the same predicament.

Tosafot answers that *igun* for the slave is not primarily about marriage at all. Simply withholding his freedom is itself an *igun*. The inability to live a fully free life — to enter into a normal marriage in the social framework of free people, and to take on the full complement of *mitzvot* — constitutes a deprivation that the rabbis wanted to address. When a master is in the process of freeing his slave, we want to facilitate that *shichrur* as smoothly as possible, in the same way that we work to prevent a woman from becoming an *agunah*. The slave's interest in freedom is weighty enough to justify parallel institutional protections.

---

## Get from Overseas (II)

### Deafness/Muteness

Returning to the question raised by the *gemara* regarding *eino yachol lomar*: the straightforward reading might be that the agent is mute, physically unable to speak. But as noted, the language of the *mishnah* specifically raises the scenario in the context of an agent who is otherwise qualified to bring the *get*, while the *mishnah* elsewhere explicitly excludes a *cheresh* — a deaf-mute — from serving in this role.

### Given While Able

Rav Yosef resolves this by clarifying the case: we are dealing with an agent who received the *get* and was fully competent — *pikeach* — at the time he took it. He was present, witnessed the writing and signing, and set out to deliver it. But before he could pronounce the declaration *befanai nichtav uvefanai nechtam*, he became a *cheresh*. He is therefore *eino yachol lomar* in the most literal sense: he was capable, he witnessed everything, but he is now physically unable to give voice to what he knows. In such a case, the *mishnah* permits the alternative route of signature validation. This is, admittedly, a peculiar case — the far simpler reading of *eino yachol* would be that the agent simply was not present at the writing. But the *gemara*'s insistence on the precise phrasing *eino yachol* pushes toward an interpretation of genuine physical incapacity.

---

## Gittin & Manumission (II)

### Befanai Nechtam

Returning now to the formal comparison between *gittei nashim* and *shichrurei avadim*, a *baraita* enumerates three ways in which they are alike. The first is the requirement of *befanai nechtam*: both a *get* delivered to a woman and a *shtar shichrur* delivered to a slave require the declaration when the document is being brought into or out of *Eretz Yisrael*. This was treated at length in the earlier part of the *masechet* and is now cited as the first formal point of parallel.

### Samaritan Witnesses

The second similarity — and a surprising one — is the rule regarding Samaritan witnesses. The *baraita* states: any document bearing a Samaritan (*Kuti*) witness is invalid — *except* for a *get isha* and a *shtar shichrur*. This is striking because these are precisely the documents one would expect to require the most rigorous standards, given that they effect fundamental changes in personal status. They are not merely evidentiary — they are the operative instruments of the status change itself.

Yet it is exactly this heightened significance that generates the *kula*. Because *gittei nashim* and *shichrurei avadim* are written with such extraordinary care and oversight, under so many more conditions and criteria than an ordinary commercial document, the mere fact that a Samaritan appears as a witness can itself be presumed to reflect carefulness. The assumption is that people involved in such a weighty process knew what they were doing — that this Samaritan witness was indeed a *kasher* witness, someone whose testimony can be relied upon. We will return to the specifics of this analysis, but the structural point is clear: the *chumra* of how *gittin* are written generates a *kula* in the assumptions we make about who signed them.

### Non-Jewish Courts

The third similarity is a *chumra*, and one that is entirely expected. As a general rule, documents produced by secular non-Jewish courts — *arkaot shel ovdei kochavim* — are valid, even when the signatories are non-Jews. For ordinary property documents, such as a bill of sale or a deed, we accept secular legal instruments as binding. However, *gittei nashim* and *shichrurei avadim* are explicitly excepted. A *get* or *shtar shichrur* issued by a non-Jewish court, signed by non-Jewish witnesses, is entirely invalid. These documents must conform to the requirements of *halacha*, and they cannot simply be processed through the general secular system as though they were property transactions.

### Dina D'Malchuta

Rashi's explanation of why secular property documents are valid is worth examining closely, because he identifies the conceptual foundation in an illuminating way. Rashi states simply: *dina d'malchuta dina* — the law of the land is law. In matters of property and commerce, the Jewish legal system defers to the governing civil authority, and therefore a secular document recording a property transaction between two Jews is fully binding under *halacha*. There is no requirement to conduct the transaction through Jewish legal mechanisms such as a formal *kinyan* under the rules of *Choshen Mishpat*; the secular system is sufficient.

But Rashi adds a further dimension. He notes: *aval hadinim nitztavu b'nei Noach* — matters of law and adjudication are among the *sheva mitzvot b'nei Noach*, the seven Noahide laws binding on all humanity. Among those seven is the commandment to establish courts and a functioning legal order. Rashi appears to be saying that the *Torah* itself validates the non-Jewish legal system in matters of property and civil law, precisely because the obligation to maintain such a system is itself divinely mandated for all nations. It is this divine mandate — the *sheva mitzvot b'nei Noach* — that provides the conceptual basis for *dina d'malchuta dina*: the secular legal order is not merely tolerated, it is endorsed by the *Torah* as a legitimate system for adjudicating property matters.

This, however, has its limits. Non-Jewish legal authority does not extend to matters of *halacha* and personal status. *Gittin* and *shichrurei avadim* are outside the *parsha* of non-Jewish law entirely — *lav bnei kritut ninhu*, non-Jews are not within the framework of *gittin* and *kidushin*, and their documents and signatures cannot effect the changes that only *halacha* can effect.

---

## Retraction Rights

### Both Retractable

Rabbi Meir identifies a fourth area of comparison between a *get* and a *shtar shichrur* — though on this point, Rabbi Meir and the *chakhamim* disagree. Rabbi Meir holds that if a man says "give this *get* to my wife" or "give this *shtar shichrur* to my slave," and then before delivery changes his mind, he may retract in both cases. Both a *get* and a *shtar shichrur* can be recalled before they are actually delivered.

### Sages' View

The *chakhamim* disagree on the second half. They agree that a *get* can be retracted before delivery — the act of divorce is not complete until the *get* reaches the woman's hand or domain, and the husband retains the ability to reconsider until that moment. But a *shtar shichrur* cannot be retracted once the agent has received it. Why? Because *zakhin l'adam shelo befanav* — one may represent a person's interests, and act on his behalf, even without being formally appointed and without the person's presence, when the act is unambiguously to that person's benefit.

### Zakhin Rationale

The logic is as follows. When the master hands the *shtar shichrur* to an agent and says "give this to my slave," there is no question whatsoever that the slave desires his freedom. Freedom is an obvious and unqualified benefit. Therefore, the moment the agent receives the *shtar*, he automatically becomes the slave's representative — not by the slave's appointment, not in the slave's presence, but by operation of the *zakhin* principle: since it is unambiguously in the slave's interest, the agent acquires it on his behalf. At the instant the agent takes the document, the slave's interests are already represented, and the *shichrur* effectively takes hold. The master can no longer retract.

### R. Meir Dissents

Rabbi Meir challenges this reasoning. He argues that one cannot simply assume it is in every slave's interest to be free. The *zakhin* principle applies when the benefit is certain and uncontested. But freedom carries obligations — a freed slave must now observe all *mitzvot*, enters a different social and legal world, and may in fact be leaving a situation of relative security and stability. Rabbi Meir's position is that we cannot automatically presume every slave wishes to be free, and therefore we cannot apply *zakhin* to represent the slave's presumed desire. Without *zakhin*, the agent is no more than the master's messenger, and the master may recall his messenger — and his *shtar* — until the moment of actual delivery.

It is worth noting the historical resonance of Rabbi Meir's position. The logic that a slave's interests are served by remaining enslaved was precisely the argument deployed by slaveholders in another era to justify the institution. That Rabbi Meir invokes a version of this reasoning as a matter of *halachic* analysis — questioning whether freedom is automatically and universally beneficial — is itself a striking feature of this passage, one that the *gemara* leaves for us to sit with.

---

---

# Gittin 10

## Get & Shtar Similarities

### Intro & Baraita

We begin on amud 10b, picking up from the *mishna*'s observation that both a *get* for a woman and a *shtar shichrur* — a writ of manumission for a slave — share the requirement of *befanai nichtav uvefanai nechtam*. The *gemara* had quoted a *baraita* listing several points of comparison between these two documents, and that *baraita* functions almost as a foreshadowing of the mishnayot that follow, since each case it enumerates will be addressed in turn. It is worth briefly reviewing the list.

### Befanai Requirement

*Tanu rabbanan*: in three ways are *gittei nashim* and *shichrurei avadim* alike. The first is *shetzarich lomar befanai nichtav uvefanai nechtam* — the delivering agent must declare that the document was written and signed in his presence.

### Samaritan Witnesses
