If the *mishnah* — by stating *b'fanai nechtam chetzyo pasul* — is meant to convey a genuine *chiddush* about partial signing testimony being invalid, the case it implies must be one where *something* was done to validate the second signature, not merely nothing. After all, if no attestation whatsoever was provided for the second signature, the *pesul* would be entirely trivial. Any meaningful reading of the *mishnah* requires us to assume that some attempt at validation was made for the second signature — and that it still failed.

But if so, the *mishnah* must be alluding to one of the specific cases debated by the *amoraim* — either *Rav Chisda*'s case, *Rava*'s, or *Rav Ashi*'s. The *gemara* suggests that the *mishnah* is therefore: *o k'Rava o k'Rav Ashi* — oriented toward one of those latter two positions. And this implies: *ule'apuki miderav Chisda* — to exclude *Rav Chisda*'s ruling. The argument is that if *Rav Chisda*'s case — where two complete, independent, qualified witnesses validate the second signature — were the *chiddush* of the *mishnah*, the *mishnah* would have stated it explicitly. Such a dramatic *chiddush* — that more witnesses can make things worse — would not be left as a mere implication of oblique phrasing.

### Rav Chisda Defense

*Rav Chisda* responds with a hermeneutical counter-principle. The *gemara* itself is employing the assumption that every case in the *mishnah* must convey a new *chiddush*. But this is not always the case. *Rav Chisda* points to the *mishnah*'s earlier line — *b'fanai nichtav aval lo b'fanai nechtam* — which states that if only the writing but not the signing was declared, the *get* is *pasul*. That is obviously *pasul*. There is no *chiddush* there at all. Yet the *mishnah* lists it.

The *mishnah* follows the rhetorical pattern of *lo zu af zu* — not only this, but also that. It lists cases in order, not because each individual case is a *chiddush*, but to build systematically through a range of scenarios, some obvious and some not. Accordingly, the *mishnah*'s mention of partial signing testimony being invalid does not necessarily imply that the second signature was validated by some additional means. It may simply be listing an obvious scenario as part of a larger progressive enumeration. *Rav Chisda*'s ruling — that even full, two-witness *kiyum* for the second signature is *pasul* when combined with the *takkanah* for the first — is therefore not excluded by the *mishnah*'s silence. The *mishnah* simply was not making a point of that specific case; it was following the *lo zu af zu* structure.

This is a characteristically striking exchange. Usually when the *gemara* argues that a *mishnah* does not make a *chiddush*, the purpose is to *deny* that something special is being communicated. Here, paradoxically, *Rav Chisda* uses the same argument to *defend* the largest *chiddush* of the three — by maintaining that the *mishnah* need not communicate it at all.

---

## Gidud/Mechitza Combinati…

### Rav Chisda Position

The *gemara* now applies the *o kulo... o kulo* — all-or-nothing — principle to an analogous case in the laws of *Shabbos*. *Rav Chisda* states: *gidud chamisha u'mechitza chamisha ein mitztarfin* — a ditch five *tefachim* deep combined with a fence five *tefachim* high does not constitute a *reshut hayachid*. To qualify as a *reshut hayachid*, an enclosure needs walls or barriers of ten *tefachim*. One might think that a five-*tefach* ditch and a five-*tefach* wall placed on its edge could combine — after all, from the inside of the ditch, the effective barrier height is ten *tefachim*. *Rav Chisda* says no: either the full ten *tefachim* must come from the ditch alone, or from the wall alone. Combining two different physical mechanisms, even when the arithmetic works out, does not suffice. *Ad d'ika o kulo b'mechitza o kulo b'gidud.*

### Mareimar & Halacha

*Mareimar* disagrees: *gidud chamisha u'mechitza chamisha mitztarfin* — they do combine. And the *halacha* is ruled in accordance with *Mareimar*: *v'hilchata mitztarfin*.

### Tosafos Distinction

*Tosafos* raises an interesting point here. *Tosafos* considers the case as *Rav Chisda* framed it — ditch plus fence on its edge — to be obvious: from inside the ditch, the entire surrounding barrier is ten *tefachim*, and of course this constitutes a *reshut hayachid*. For *Tosafos*, the less obvious case, and thus the one actually under discussion, involves a different configuration: a mound that is five *tefachim* high, with a five-*tefach* wall built atop it. In that scenario, someone standing at ground level outside the mound sees only a five-*tefach* wall; someone inside, atop the mound, also faces only a five-*tefach* drop on the outside. The combined barrier of ten *tefachim* is not experienced uniformly from any single vantage point, which is what makes the case genuinely debatable. Either way, the *halacha* is that they combine.

---

## Lashon Bnei Adam

### Lav Yaseira

The *mishnah* presents a case involving vow language. *Konam she'ani to'em* — may what I taste be forbidden like a *korban* — is a straightforward prohibition against tasting. But the *mishnah* then addresses *konam she'ani lo to'em* — *konam* that I do not taste — and rules that this formulation is *equally* a prohibition against tasting. This is surprising, since *she'ani lo to'em* would grammatically mean "if I do not taste," which should constitute a vow to taste rather than a vow not to.

The *gemara* explains: *lashon bnei adam* — we follow colloquial speech. People commonly insert an extra *lo* in their speech without intending a logical negation. Someone who says *she'ani lo to'em* colloquially means exactly the same thing as someone who says *she'ani to'em* — they are not eating. The additional *lo* is a *lav yaseira*, a superfluous negative, a speech pattern of ordinary people that does not reverse the meaning. Both formulations therefore express the same prohibition.

### Nedarim vs Shavuot

This raises a natural question: why should *nedarim* be treated differently from *shavuot*? In *shavuot*, precision of language is essential. *Shavuah she'ochal* — an oath that I will eat — obligates eating. *Shavuah she'lo ochal* — an oath that I will not eat — prohibits eating. The *lo* makes all the difference; its logical force is fully operative.

The *gemara* explains that *nedarim* and *shavuot* function on different linguistic bases. *Nedarim* follow *lashon bnei adam* — the way ordinary people actually speak. Since ordinary people speak loosely and sometimes insert extra negatives without intending to reverse meaning, the laws of *nedarim* accommodate that colloquial reality. *Shavuot*, by contrast, are governed by strict legal precision of language; the common speech patterns of *lashon bnei adam* do not override the logical content of the words used. The same phrase therefore produces opposite results depending on whether it appears in the domain of *nedarim* or *shavuot*.

---

---

# Gittin 16

## Half-Pure Hands

### Half-Pure Hands Query

The daf opens with a query posed by Ilfa: *yadayim tehorot lachata'in o ein tehorot lachata'in* — can hands be half *tahor*, or is that simply not a meaningful category? The question is, on its face, analogous to asking whether someone can be a little bit pregnant. To understand what the question is actually asking, the Gemara walks through a series of candidate cases, systematically eliminating each one before arriving at the genuine *sha'alah*.

### Eliminating Cases

The Gemara begins by asking *heichi dami* — what kind of case could this be? It first proposes that perhaps the question concerns two people washing from a single *kli* containing one *reviit*. But this is immediately dismissed: we have already learned explicitly (*umatnan*) that a *reviit* suffices for the *netilat yadayim* of one person, or even two. There is nothing unresolved there.

A second possibility is raised: perhaps he washes one hand at a time, sequentially. Again, this is set aside, because we have likewise already learned that if one hand is washed with *netila* and the other with *shtifa* — that is, dunking it in a body of water rather than having water poured from a vessel — both hands are nonetheless *tehorot*. Certainly if both hands are washed with proper *netila*, sequential washing would be fine. And a third possibility — washing half the hand at a time, in stages, with full drying in between — is dismissed by the statement of the school of Rabbi Yannai: *yadayim ein tehorot lachata'in*, hands simply cannot be purified in halves.

### Moisture Remaining Case

The Gemara therefore narrows the question: *lo tzericha d'ika mashkeh tofeach* — the case requires that there be residual moisture on the first portion of the hand when the second portion is washed. In other words, the person washed the hand in stages but did not fully dry the first section before washing the second. The moistness of the first section remains.

One might ask why that would change anything. After all, we have learned that *nitzok*, *katrafes*, and mere *mashkeh tofeach* are not considered *chibur* — connection — neither for *tuma* nor for *tahara*. A thin stream of liquid connecting two vessels, for instance, does not allow *tuma* to travel from one to the other, and similarly does not confer *tahara* upon the *tamei* one. So the residual moisture ought to be irrelevant.

But the Gemara refines the case further: the question is specifically where the moisture remaining on the first portion is *tofeach lehatfiach* — wet enough that if placed against another surface, it would render that surface wet as well. This is a higher threshold than mere dampness. And indeed, regarding *netilat yadayim*, we do have a tradition that *tofeach lehatfiach* constitutes *chibur*. So this particular category remains genuinely unresolved.

### Chibur & Mikvah

The Gemara then raises another possible dismissal: perhaps the *chibur* principle of *tofeach lehatfiach* is known only in the context of a *mikvah*, not for *netilat yadayim*. If that is so, there is no established ruling for the hand-washing case at all, and the question stands. This framing — that the *chibur* idea may belong exclusively to *mikvah* discussions — sets up the next step.

### Rabbi Yehuda Chibur

The *mikvah* source for *chibur* is introduced from a Mishnah: if a *mikvah* contains exactly forty *seah* — precisely the minimum required — and two people immerse, one after the other, some water will cling to the first person and leave the *mikvah* slightly deficient for the second. The *tanna kamma* rules that the first is *tahor* but the second is *tamei*. Rabbi Yehuda, however, rules that if the first person's feet are still touching the water — still in contact with the *mikvah* as he exits — then the water on his body is considered connected to the *mikvah* through *chibur*, and the second person's immersion is also valid.

The relevance to the *yadayim* question is this: the *chibur* principle in the hand-washing case may simply be an extension of Rabbi Yehuda's position regarding *mikvah*. If so, it is Rabbi Yehuda's view, not a universally accepted principle.

### Unresolved Question

The question is ultimately left unresolved. What we can say is that the answer likely follows party lines: Rabbi Yehuda, consistent with his *mikvah* position, would likely say the partially-washed hand is *tahor*, while the *tanna kamma* would not. As a practical note, the proper custom is to ensure a full *reviit* covers each hand completely — not to divide the water — precisely to avoid any such ambiguity, though the underlying legal question remains without a definitive answer in the Gemara.

---

## Drawn Water Decrees

### Head in Drawn Water

Rabbi Yirmeyah introduces two related rulings. First: one who immerses *rosho ve-rubo* — head and majority of the body — in *mayim she'uvim*, drawn water, is *tamei*. Second: a *tahor* person upon whom three *lugin* of drawn water are poured is likewise *tamei*. The question immediately arises: why should this be? In the first case, the person may have already been *tahor* — either they had just immersed in a valid *mikvah* or had never become *tamei* in the first place. Why would immersing in drawn water undo that?

### Rashi's Explanation

Rashi explains that such a person is *tamei l'terumah* — considered *tamei* with respect to *terumah* — until he immerses again in a valid *mikvah*. Rashi further notes that this is one of the eighteen things decreed during the famous confrontation between the disciples of Beit Shammai and the disciples of Beit Hillel, recorded at the beginning of Masechet Shabbat. These eighteen decrees were exceptional in that, notwithstanding the general principle that one does not issue a *gezeirah* upon the public unless the majority can uphold it (*ein gozerin gezeirah al ha-tzibur ela im ken rov tzibur yecholin la'amod bah*), these decrees were imposed because of the extraordinary intensity of feeling behind them at the time.

### Filthy Mikvah Caves

The Gemara explains the historical circumstance that gave rise to this *gezeirah*: *she-hayah lahem mei me'arot sruchim l'tevilah* — they used to immerse in the water of caves, which was foul and turgid. One can imagine the conditions: cave water, depending on what resided in or passed through those caves, could be thoroughly unpleasant. After immersing in such a *mikvah*, people would naturally cleanse themselves with drawn water — in effect, bathing after the immersion.

### Bathing Prohibition

This created a serious perceptual problem. Bystanders seeing this sequence of events might conclude that it was not the *mikvah* immersion but the subsequent bathing that effected *tahara* — *atu elu meta'arin elu meta'arin*, "is it these that purify, or these?" The concern was that people would simply skip the *mikvah* and rely on the drawn water alone. To prevent this, the Rabbis decreed that immersing in drawn water, or bathing with drawn water after a *mikvah*, renders one *tamei*, thereby preserving the *mikvah*'s exclusive role as the vehicle of *tahara*.

As a practical aside, this decree has contemporary relevance primarily in the context of ascending the Temple Mount or for a convert undergoing *tevilah* for conversion. For the purpose of marital *tahara*, where the *mikvah* is used for *niddah* and *zavah* restrictions rather than classic *tumah ve-tahara*, the question of a subsequent shower does not affect the woman's status vis-à-vis her husband. Rashi's formulation — *tamei l'terumah* — reflects that this *tuma* has practical significance only for *terumah* and *kodshim*, neither of which applies today outside of the Temple Mount context.

### Three Lugin Extension

The same *gezeirah* was extended to the case where three *lugin* of drawn water are poured over the head and majority of a person's body. The Gemara states: *de-ha u-me-ha chada hilcheta hi* — these two cases are governed by the same legal principle. Whether one enters a pool of drawn water or has it poured upon them, the rabbinic consequence is identical.

### Half Immersion Half Pour

Rami bar Abba poses a question about a hybrid case: *chatzyo be-shfichah ve-chatzyo be-vi'ah* — what if half was from immersion and half was from pouring? Does the *gezeirah* apply to a combination of the two modalities, each of which alone constitutes only half the triggering condition? The Gemara concludes *teiku* — the question stands unresolved.

---

## Takanat Ezra

### Nine Kabin Remedy

Rav Papa then introduces an analogous ruling: *ba'al keri choleh she-natnu alav tish'ah kabin mayim tahor* — a sick person who has had a seminal emission upon whom nine *kabin* of water are poured is rendered *tahor* in the relevant sense. This ruling is ancient and well established.

### Ezra's Decree

Stepping back to the broader context: Ezra enacted a *takkanah* requiring a *ba'al keri* to immerse in a *mikvah* before engaging in Torah study or prayer, as Rashi notes — *Ezra tiken tevilah le-ba'alei kerin k'dei shelo yehoyu k'tarnegalim*, so that they would not approach Torah with the casual, thoughtless attitude of roosters. The goal was to ensure that Torah study is approached with gravity and intentionality.

### Sick Exception

The exception allows a *ba'al keri* who is ill and unable to go to the *mikvah* to instead have nine *kabin* of water poured over him — even drawn water — and thereby fulfill the requirement sufficiently. The practical effect is essentially a shower. This *heter* applies only to the sick; a healthy *ba'al keri* would still be required to immerse in a proper *mikvah*.

### Modern Application

The *takkanah* of Ezra is generally not observed today. The underlying rationale was to ensure that Torah study is approached with the proper seriousness and composure that follows *tevilah*, as opposed to the levity that may have preceded the *keri*. The sad commentary embedded in this abandonment is that, since we do not in general approach Torah with the sustained gravity that would make the contrast meaningful, the *gezeirah* no longer has its intended effect and has effectively lapsed.

### Ritva Clarification

The Ritva adds an important clarification: the nine *kabin* do not actually purify the *ba'al keri* in the full *halachic* sense of *tahara*. Rather, they remove specifically the prohibition enacted by Ezra against Torah study and prayer. For purposes requiring actual *tahara* — such as going to the *Beit Ha-Mikdash* or its modern analog, ascending the Temple Mount — a full *mikvah* immersion remains necessary.

### Temple Mount Immersion

This point has direct practical implications. The only contexts today in which *mikvah* immersion for men carries concrete *halachic* weight are, first, ascending the Temple Mount, and second, conversion immersion for a convert. The nine *kabin* option of Ezra's *takkanah* would not suffice for these purposes, since the Ritva's distinction between removing a rabbinic prohibition and achieving actual *tahara* is operative there. For men who customarily immerse before *chag*, there is a view that *b'diavad* a shower might suffice based on this *takkanah*, though this remains a matter requiring consultation.

### Rav Papa Extension

Rav Papa extends the same logical question that Rami bar Abba asked about drawn water: *chetzyo be-tvila ve-chetzyo be-netina mah* — what if half the required quantity came from immersion and half from pouring, in the context of the nine *kabin* for a sick *ba'al keri*? Just as before, the Gemara answers *teiku* — the question is left without resolution.

---

## Get Witnesses

### Mishnah Setup

The Gemara returns to the *Mishnah* governing a *get* brought from outside of Israel (*medinat ha-yam*). The *takkanah* requires the messenger to declare *bifanai nictav uv'fanai nechtam* — "it was written in my presence and sealed in my presence" — a single person attesting to both the writing and the sealing. The Mishnah presents several cases involving multiple witnesses, each attesting to only one part of this declaration, and asks whether the *get* is valid.

### Three Cases

The Mishnah presents three configurations. In the first, one witness says *bifanai nictav* — it was written in my presence — and a different witness says *bifanai nechtam* — it was sealed in my presence. The *get* is *pasul*, invalid. In the second case, two witnesses attest to the writing and one attests to the sealing. The *tanna kamma* rules this *pasul*, while Rabbi Yehuda rules it *kasher*. In the third case, one attests to the writing and two attest to the sealing, and all opinions agree the *get* is *kasher*. These three cases form the framework for the ensuing analysis.

### Get Under Both Hands

Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *lo shanu ela she-ein ha-get yotzei mitachat yedei shneihem* — the Mishnah's ruling of *pasul* in the first case applies only where the *get* does not exit from under the hands of both witnesses, meaning the two individuals were not both appointed as *shlichim*, messengers. One person is the primary carrier; the other merely happened to be present and can attest to only part of the required declaration. Rashi explains: *mitachat yadei she-shneihem adukim bo u-shneihem shlichim* — if both are holding the *get* and both are designated as messengers, the situation is different.

### Foreign Get Takana

The *takkanah* for a *get* brought from outside Israel was specifically designed to require that one person testify to both the writing and the sealing together. The reason, as we shall explore, relates to either the *lishma* concern or the *edim metzuyim* concern — the two competing rationales that will be debated. The key structural point here is that the *takkanah* was crafted around a single person bearing full testimony, not a composite of partial attestations from multiple individuals.

### Two Messengers

If, however, both witnesses are formally appointed as messengers — *shneyhem shlichim*, both designated to carry and deliver the *get* — then the *get* is valid even according to the Mishnah's first case framing. *Amar kasavar shnayim she-heviu get mimedinas hayam ein tzrichim she-yomru bifanai nechtav uv'fanai nechtam* — when two people bring the *get* together as co-messengers, the *takkanah* requiring the combined declaration does not apply to them in the same way. The logic of why this should be the case, and how far the principle extends, is the subject of the dispute between Rava and Rabbah.

---

## Rava's Edim Principle

### Rava-Rabbah Dispute

The Gemara identifies two competing rationales for the *takkanah* requiring a messenger to declare *bifanai nictav uv'fanai nechtam*: the position of Rabbah and the position of Rava. This dispute, first introduced at the beginning of the tractate, is now directly applied to the Mishnah's cases. Rabbah holds that the *takkanah* was instituted because people outside of Israel were not expert in the requirement that a *get* be written *lishma* — for the specific purpose of the woman's divorce. Rava holds that the concern was *edim metzuyim l'kaymo* — the absence of available witnesses to authenticate the document through its signatures, since people in one country are not familiar with the signatures of witnesses from another.

### Edim Metzuyim

Rava's position — *lefi she-ein edim metzuyim l'kaymo* — generates a specific analytical framework. If the underlying concern is the availability of witnesses to establish the *get*'s authenticity, then when two people bring the *get* together as co-messengers, there are in fact two witnesses present and available. The *edim metzuyim* problem is solved. This explains why, under Rava's reasoning, two co-messengers need not make the declaration: they themselves constitute the available witnesses.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye challenges Rava by directing attention to the second case in the Mishnah: *shnayim omrim bifanaynu nictav ve-echad omer bifanai nechtam* — two say it was written in their presence, one says it was sealed in his presence. Under this configuration, you have three witnesses total, and certainly *edim metzuyim* are present. Yet the *tanna kamma* still rules *pasul*. How does Rava account for this? If *edim metzuyim l'kaymo* is the operative concern and that concern is satisfied here, why is the *get* still invalid?

### Confusion Concern

Rava resolves Abaye's challenge by clarifying the nature of the *takkanah*: the concern is not simply whether you have a sufficient number of witnesses in the abstract, but whether the particular configuration will lead to confusion with the authentication of regular documents (*kiyum shetarot d'alma*). Regular documents require two witnesses who together attest to the document's authenticity. If we permit this split-testimony arrangement for a *get* — where one group attests to writing and a different individual attests to sealing — people will begin to confuse that with the ordinary rules for authenticating *shetarot*, thinking perhaps that one witness can establish a document in general contexts. The *gezeirah* extends to prevent that confusion even where multiple people are present.

### Appointed vs. Present

The critical distinction in Rava's framework is between witnesses who are formally appointed as *shlichim* — designated messengers — and witnesses who are merely present and happen to be able to testify to one element or another. When both individuals are appointed as co-messengers, the *get* exits from under both their hands; they collectively bear the responsibility and function of the *shliach*, and the *takkanah* does not require them to make the composite declaration. But where they are not both formally appointed, even if their combined testimony covers all the required elements, the configuration is structurally flawed: no single person is standing fully behind the document, and the *gezeirah* against confusion with regular *kiyum shetarot* applies.

---

## Rabbah Lishma

### Lishma Common Ground

Rabbah advances a different framework: *d'chulei alma ba'inan lishma* — both the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Yehuda agree that the *takkanah* was instituted because of the *lishma* concern, that people were not expert in the requirement that a *get* be written specifically for the sake of this woman's divorce. This is Rabbah's operating principle, shared across all positions in the Mishnah.

### Gezeirah Lest Revert

Given that shared premise, Rabbah explains the disagreement: *v'hacha b'mai askinan le'achar she-lamdu u-gezeirah shema yachzor davar l'kilkulo* — the debate concerns a later stage, after knowledge of the *lishma* requirement has spread, and specifically whether we issue a *gezeirah* lest things revert (*davar ha-chozer l'kilkulo*) to the original state of ignorance. Originally, the *takkanah* was enacted because people did not know the *get* had to be written *lishma*. Eventually, this became widely understood. The question is whether, even after the principle became common knowledge, we maintain the original safeguards to prevent a future regression.

### Rabbi Yehuda Lenient

Rabbi Yehuda is lenient: since everyone already understands the *lishma* requirement, we need not worry that the situation will revert. The knowledge is sufficiently embedded that allowing some flexibility in how the testimony is arranged poses no risk of causing people to forget or disregard *lishma*. Rabbi Yehuda therefore permits the second case — two attesting to the writing and one to the sealing — because the concern that originally gave rise to the *takkanah* is no longer pressing.

### Tanna Kamma Stringent

The *tanna kamma*, by contrast, is *gazrinan* — we do issue the *gezeirah* against reversion. Even though everyone currently knows about *lishma*, the *tanna kamma* fears that if we relax the requirement, the structure that enforces awareness of *lishma* will erode, and future generations will lose sight of it. The *tanna kamma* therefore insists that the declaration of *bifanai nictav uv'fanai nechtam* by a single person must be maintained in all configurations, precisely because that unified declaration is the mechanism that keeps the *lishma* concern visible and enforced.

---

## Baraita Resolution

### Baraita Cases

Ulla's teaching is introduced in response to a logical pressure: if Rabbi Yehuda is not worried about *davar ha-chozer l'kilkulo*, he should be lenient not only in the second case but in the first case as well. *Ve-liflog nami Rabbi Yehuda b'reisha* — why does Rabbi Yehuda not disagree in the first case too? If the *lishma* concern is no longer operative, even one person saying *bifanai nictav* and another saying *bifanai nechtam* should be acceptable under Rabbi Yehuda's logic.

### Ulla Interpretation

Ulla resolves this: *chaluk hayah Rabbi Yehuda af b'rishona* — Rabbi Yehuda in fact does disagree in the first case as well. The Mishnah's formulation, which seems to show Rabbi Yehuda disagreeing only in the second case, is to be read as recording his leniency in that specific configuration while leaving his first-case position implicit. But this is complicated by a *Baraita* that was taught to Ulla by Rav Oshaya: *Rabbi Yehuda machshir b'zu ve-lo b'acheret* — Rabbi Yehuda validates *this* case and not *that* one. This *Baraita* explicitly limits Rabbi Yehuda's leniency, stating that there is one case he permits and another he does not.

### One Sealing Only

The question then becomes: what is the case that Rabbi Yehuda does *not* permit? If he disagrees in the first Mishnah case (one attests to writing, one to sealing) and permits the second (two attest to writing, one to sealing), then what is the "other" case the *Baraita* refers to that he rejects? The Gemara concludes that the missing case — not discussed in the Mishnah at all — is where a single witness says only *bifanai nechtam*, attesting solely to the sealing without any attestation to the writing. This configuration: zero witnesses to writing, one to sealing, is universally *pasul*. The *Baraita* is informing us that this is the case Rabbi Yehuda excludes, not one of the Mishnah's own cases.

### Salka Daatach

The Gemara explains why we might have thought otherwise: *salka daatach amina* — one might have assumed that since Rabbi Yehuda is not worried about *davar ha-chozer l'kilkulo*, he would extend his leniency all the way, validating even a case where only one person attests to only one element. After all, if the *lishma* concern is no longer pressing, and if we are not going to confuse this with regular *kiyum shetarot* — why not be maximally lenient?

### Rabbi Yehuda Limits

The answer is that Rabbi Yehuda, despite not being worried about *davar ha-chozer l'kilkulo*, still holds that there must be *some* substantive testimony to both elements of the declaration. He cannot simply accept half a job. The *takkanah* may have relaxed in one direction — Rabbi Yehuda does not require a single person to deliver the entire composite declaration — but it does not relax to the point of permitting a *get* where only one element is attested to at all. Attestation to sealing alone, without any testimony to writing, remains invalid even for Rabbi Yehuda.

### Final Resolution

The final resolution is thus clear. Rabbi Yehuda's leniency is structurally limited: it extends to cases where both persons delivering the testimony are appointed as *shlichim* — co-messengers formally charged with bringing the *get*. In that configuration, the *get* exits from under both their hands, and the functional requirements of the *takkanah* are satisfied through their shared appointment even if their testimonies are formally divided. What Rabbi Yehuda will not permit is a case where only one element is testified to in total, or where the individuals are not designated messengers and are merely bystanders attesting to fragments of what the *takkanah* requires as a unified whole.

---

---

# Gittin 17

## Two Witnesses Abroad

### Rabba bar bar Chana

The sugya opens by recalling the unresolved question from the previous amud: when two witnesses bring a *get* from *medinat hayam*, must they declare *bifnei nechtav uvifnei nechtam*, or not? Two versions of the ruling had been presented, and it was unclear which one to follow.

The Gemara now continues with a narrative set approximately six lines from the bottom of the prior daf. Rabba bar bar Chana fell ill, and Rabbi Yehuda and Rabba came to visit him — a *bikur cholim* call. They posed the question directly: if two witnesses bring a *get* from abroad, must they state *bifnei nechtav uvifnei nechtam* or not? Rabba bar bar Chana answered them: they need not.

### Edei Mesirah Logic

His reasoning is a clean logical argument. He said: if these two witnesses were to say simply, "*bifneinu geireshah*" — "in our presence he divorced her" — would they not be believed? Of course they would. If they were present at the actual act of delivery, they would function as *edei mesirah*, witnesses to the divorce itself, and their testimony would be fully accepted. All the more so, then, their failure to recite the formal declaration of *bifnei nechtav uvifnei nechtam* creates no disqualification.

### Chaveirim Incident

At that point the Gemara interpolates an incident that, as the text itself signals, has little to do with the halachic ruling just stated — yet it is colorful enough to record. The story continues: *ad hachi ata hahu chavara* — while this was going on, a group of *chaveirim* arrived. Here *chaveirim* does not refer to the learned scholars who earned that honorific in certain circles, but rather to Persian ruffians. They seized the candle from before the rabbis. As Rashi explains, it happened to be one of their festivals, during which only the temples were permitted to have light; the *beit midrash* was suddenly plunged into darkness.

Rabba bar bar Chana then cried out: *Rachmana, o vetulach o vetula d'var Eisav* — "Merciful One, either in Your shade or in the shade of the son of Esau." In other words: Master of the Universe, either protect us Yourself, or — implausible as it sounds — we would rather be living under Roman rule than under these Persians.

The Gemara challenges this immediately: are the Romans better than the Persians? Was there not a *baraita* in which Rabbi Chiyya expounded the verse, "*Elokim hevin darkah v'hu yada et mkomah*" — God understood its ways and knew its place — to mean that God, knowing Israel could not survive under the Romans, exiled them to Babylonia? That clearly implies Babylonian exile was preferable to Roman subjugation. Yet here, Rabba bar bar Chana was wishing they were under Rome?

The Gemara resolves the tension: *lo kashya* — there is no contradiction. One statement refers to the period before the *chaveirim* descended upon Babylonia; the other refers to after. In other words, the original Persian rulers were benign enough that exile there was preferable to Roman domination — but once this particular faction of Persian ruffians took hold, Rome was the better option. With that, the Gemara closes the historical digression and returns to the halachic analysis.

### Get Yotzei Mitachat

Rabbi Ami then cites Rabbi Yochanan with a significant qualification: *lo shanu ela sheget yotzei mitachat yedei edei chtivah* — the ruling that one witness saying *bifanai nechtav* combined with two witnesses saying *bifaneinu nechtam* is valid applies specifically when the *get* comes from the hands of the witness to writing — that is, when the one who declared *bifanai nechtav* is the primary bearer of the *get*.

The background here is the case from the Mishnah at the close of the prior discussion: one says *bifanai nechtav* and two say *bifaneinu nechtam*, which was declared valid. Rabbi Yochanan now explains why. That first witness, the one who declared *bifanai nechtav*, serves as the primary *shliach*; because he is the one in whose hands the *get* rests, he is elevated — functioning, as the Gemara puts it, *k'shnayim al zeh* — equivalent to two witnesses for that element. Combined with the two who declared *bifaneinu nechtam*, the result is effectively two-and-two, satisfying the requirement on both counts.

However, *aval mitachat yad edei chatima pasul* — if the *get* comes from the hands only of the signing witnesses, with that single witness merely a secondary figure rather than the primary bearer, it is invalid. In such a case you have only two and one, not two and two, and the requirement is not met.

The implication, as the Gemara draws it, is that two witnesses bringing a *get* from *medinat hayam* do need to declare *bifaneinu nechtav uvifaneinu nechtam*. This appears to contradict the lenient ruling of Rabba bar bar Chana.

### Rav Assi's Challenge

Rav Assi presses the point. He confronts Rabbi Ami (or the authority behind this ruling) with a challenge from the *reisha* of the Mishnah: the case where two say *bifaneinu nechtav* and one says *bifanai nechtam* — the *machloket* between the *Tanna Kamma*, who declares it invalid, and Rabbi Yehuda, who validates it.

Rav Assi's logic runs as follows: if you hold that two witnesses bringing a *get* from abroad *must* declare the full formula — and thus the requirement is strict — then even the case where the *get* comes from the hands of both of them would be disqualified by the Rabbanan, since you still only have two and one. But on the other hand, the Gemara elsewhere records an alternate version of the same teaching in which Rabbi Ami ruled more leniently — that even a *get* coming from the hands of the signing witnesses (*edei chatima*) is valid. If that is your position, then plainly you hold that two witnesses from abroad need *not* state the full formula, and in that case, why would the Rabbanan declare the Mishnah's case of two-and-one invalid? If two witnesses together are sufficient without any declaration, then even if the *get* rests primarily in their hands, the Rabbanan should validate it.

Rav Assi thus confronts Rabbi Ami with the inconsistency: you appear to have stated two irreconcilable positions.

### Final Resolution

Rabbi Ami's reply is crisp: *amar leh in* — yes, that is so — and then, regarding his earlier stricter formulation: *b'ha zimna lo amarta hachi* — on that occasion you did not say it this way. He had in effect reversed himself, and now he states clearly: *yated hi shelo tamut* — this is a peg that shall not be moved. The definitive position is the lenient one: two witnesses who bring a *get* from abroad need not recite *bifaneinu nechtav uvifaneinu nechtam*.

With this resolution in hand, Rav Assi's challenge dissolves. Why does the Rabbanan's ruling in the Mishnah case render it invalid? Because in that case, the *get* does not come from the hands of both of them — *she'ein haget yotzei mitachat yedei shneihem* — the two are not the primary bearers. It is that factor alone, not any failure to recite the formula, that creates the problem. But when two witnesses come together as the primary bearers of a *get* from abroad, they need not declare anything at all, because their joint presence would have sufficed even as *edei mesirah* — witnesses to the delivery — and no formal attestation is required.

---

## Get Mukdam

### Intro: Predating

With the foregoing questions settled, the Gemara opens a new Mishnah and a new topic of great practical importance: *get mukdam* — the predated *get*. The Mishnah lays out a grid of possibilities based on the timing of writing (*ketivah*) and signing (*chatimah*):

A *get* written by day and signed by day is valid. Written at night and signed at night is valid. Written at night and signed the following day is likewise valid — this presents no difficulty because the natural progression of time moves forward from night into the following day, so there is no discrepancy. The problematic case is the fourth combination: written by day and signed at night. Here the Mishnah presents a *machloket*.

To appreciate why this fourth case is contentious, one must understand the general problem with any document that bears two different dates — whether the gap is a day, a month, or a year. In ordinary loan documents (*shtarot chov*), the concern is this: a creditor holding a *shtar* has the power not only to collect from the debtor's own assets but also from land he has since sold to third parties, provided the sale took place after the *shtar* took effect. This is because the signing of the *shtar* creates a lien (*shiabud*) from its effective date. If a document purports to have taken effect on a date earlier than it actually did, the creditor can unjustly pursue property that was legitimately sold during the intervening period. The purchaser (*Jonathan*, in the lecturer's running example) bought the land fairly and had no way to know of any prior claim — yet if the document is predated, he loses his property when he should not have.

The same structural problem arises with a *get*, albeit with different stakes. The *get* involves the husband's rights to the produce (*peirot*) of his wife's property. From some point in the process — the precise moment being subject to dispute — those rights cease. If the *get* is predated, the apparent termination of those rights is pushed back artificially, potentially harming purchasers or creating other legal distortions.

### Mishnah Dispute

The Mishnah presents the following *machloket*. The *Tanna Kamma* holds that a *get* written by day and signed at night (*nichtav bayom venichtam balaila*) is invalid — *pasul*. Rabbi Shimon, however, is *machshir* — he validates it.

But Rabbi Shimon's position requires care. The Mishnah states: *kol hagittin shenichtevu bayom venichtamu balaila pesulin* — all *gittin* written by day and signed at night are invalid — and then immediately carves out the exception: *chutz migittei nashim*, with the exception of bills of divorce. So in the very breath in which he appears to disqualify such documents generally, Rabbi Shimon explicitly exempts *gittin* — the divorce documents for women — and validates them. Understanding the logic of this exemption is the central task of the ensuing Talmudic discussion.

### Yochanan: Bas Achoto

The Gemara then introduces a famous *machloket* between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish about the foundational reason the Rabbanan required a date in a *get* at all.

Rabbi Yochanan says: the reason is *mishum bas achoto* — on account of his niece. The concern is *shema yechapeh al bas achoto* — lest a husband, married to his own niece (which is permitted by Torah law), seek to cover up her adultery by producing a *get* antedated to before the act of infidelity occurred. Without a date, or with a manipulable date, she could claim to have been divorced before she committed adultery and thus escape punishment. To prevent this kind of cover-up, the Rabbanan required a clear and immovable date on every *get*.

### Lakish: Peirot

Reish Lakish gives an entirely different reason: *mishum peirot* — on account of produce. The husband, during the marriage, retains the right to benefit from his wife's property — specifically its yield, the *peirot*. Those rights do not persist indefinitely after the *get* process begins. The date in the *get* establishes precisely when those rights were severed. Without a date, the husband could claim to have retained his rights over the produce all along, or conversely the wife could claim he had none when in fact he did. The *zman* in the *get* thus functions as the halachic boundary of the husband's property entitlements.

### Lakish Rejects Bas Achoto

The Gemara then systematically asks why each of these Amoraim does not adopt the other's reasoning.

Why does Reish Lakish not hold like Rabbi Yochanan — that is, why does he reject the *bas achoto* rationale? His answer: *znus lo shechicha* — adultery is not common. The Rabbanan would not institute a universal requirement of dating every *get* throughout all of Israel for the rare scenario in which a man married his niece, she subsequently committed adultery, and he then sought to cover it up through a predated *get*. Such a chain of circumstances is too attenuated to serve as the foundation of a broad *takkanah*. Reish Lakish therefore insists that the reason must be something that arises routinely in every divorce: the *peirot* question.

### Yochanan: Until Netina

Conversely, why does Rabbi Yochanan not hold like Reish Lakish — why does he not ground the *zman* requirement in *peirot*?

Rabbi Yochanan's answer: *kasavar yesh l'baal peirot ad sha'at nesina* — he holds that the husband retains his rights to the *peirot* all the way until the moment of delivery (*netinah*), the final stage of the *get* process. If the husband's entitlement runs until the very moment the *get* is placed in his wife's hands, then the date inscribed in the document — which records only the writing or signing — is irrelevant to the *peirot* question. No matter what date appears in the *get*, the husband was legitimately exercising his rights until the last possible moment. There is thus no potential for injustice with respect to *peirot*, and no need to institute a *zman* for that reason. The only reason that remains, and the one Rabbi Yochanan therefore does invoke, is *bas achoto*.

### Shimon via Lakish

Now the Gemara turns to explaining the *machloket* between Rabbi Shimon and the *Tanna Kamma* through the lens of each Amora.

According to Reish Lakish, who holds that the entire institution of *zman* in a *get* is about *peirot*, what is the basis of the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the *Tanna Kamma*? The answer is elegant. They disagree about the precise moment at which the husband's rights to *peirot* are extinguished.

Rabbi Shimon holds *ein lo mizman ketivah* — the husband has no rights from the moment of writing. The instant the *get* begins to be written, the husband loses all entitlement to *peirot*. With this understanding, a predated *get* is unobjectionable. Suppose the *get* was written in the beginning of 2015 and signed and delivered at the end of 2015. The *get* is dated from the writing — the beginning of 2015. From that moment, says Rabbi Shimon, the husband's rights ceased. So if the wife comes to claim that the husband had no right to sell produce or encumber property after that date, she is correct, and anyone who purchased from him during that intervening period — even a legitimate third-party buyer — cannot claim to have acquired it free of her claim. Rabbi Shimon is therefore comfortable with a predated *get*: the date reflects the moment of writing, and from that moment all rights were already gone.

The *Tanna Kamma*, by contrast, holds that the husband retains rights to *peirot* until *sha'at chatimah* — the moment of signing. If the *get* is predated to the writing but the husband's rights actually ran until signing, then the wife can unjustly reach back into the period between writing and signing and dispossess legitimate purchasers. The predated *get* thus creates a false impression that the husband had no rights during a period when he actually did. The *Tanna Kamma* therefore declares such a *get* invalid.

To crystallize this in concrete terms: the produce that accrues between *sha'at ketivah* and *sha'at chatimah* is what stands between Rabbi Shimon and the *Tanna Kamma*. That is precisely what the Gemara states: *peirei d'vishaat ketiva ve'ad sha'at chatima ika beineihu* — the produce of that intervening period is the fulcrum of their dispute.

### Shimon via Yochanan

According to Rabbi Yochanan, however, the entire institution of *zman* has nothing to do with *peirot* — it is about *bas achoto*. So what, according to Rabbi Yochanan, is the basis of the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the *Tanna Kamma*?

This is more complex, and the Gemara addresses it directly. Rabbi Yochanan essentially says: *aliba d'Rabbi Shimon lo kamina, kamina d'Rabbanan* — I am not speaking according to Rabbi Shimon's view; I am speaking according to the Rabbanan, i.e., the *Tanna Kamma*. In other words, Rabbi Yochanan's *bas achoto* rationale explains why the *Tanna Kamma* instituted a *zman* in the *get*, but Rabbi Shimon himself does not accept this rationale. Rabbi Shimon does not share the concern about covering up adultery — whether because he considers it too uncommon, or for some other reason — and therefore he does not require the *zman* for that purpose.

But one might press the point: Rabbi Shimon presumably does agree that the husband has *peirot* rights that need to be protected by a date. Why then does he validate a predated *get* — does that not expose the buyer to an unjust claim? The answer, consistent with the framework already established, is that Rabbi Shimon holds the husband loses *peirot* rights from *zman ketivah*. So from his perspective, the predated *get* does not create any injustice with respect to *peirot*: the husband's rights ended when the writing began, and the date in the *get* accurately reflects that cutoff.

For the *Tanna Kamma*, by contrast, the husband retains *peirot* until *sha'at netinah* — the moment of delivery. Because rights persist until delivery, the *zman* in the *get* cannot be the writing date, since that would mislead buyers into thinking the husband's rights ended earlier than they did. But this *peirot* concern is not, on Rabbi Yochanan's account, the reason the *Tanna Kamma* requires a date; that reason is *bas achoto*. Rather, it is a separate, background consideration that runs through the whole system.

### Peirot Timing

With both accounts now laid out, the Gemara crystallizes the underlying positions. According to Reish Lakish, the entire *machloket* between Rabbi Shimon and the *Tanna Kamma* rests on when the husband's *peirot* rights terminate: Rabbi Shimon holds from *sha'at ketivah*, the *Tanna Kamma* holds from *sha'at chatimah*. According to Rabbi Yochanan, the *Tanna Kamma*'s rationale for requiring a *zman* is *bas achoto*, while Rabbi Shimon does not share that concern.

The broader framework that emerges is this: there are three temporally distinct moments in the *get* process — *ketivah* (writing), *chatimah* (signing), and *netinah* (delivery). Different authorities anchor the husband's rights to *peirot* at different points along this timeline, and those anchoring decisions determine whether a predated *get* is valid or creates a legal fiction that harms third parties.

### Peirot Sources

The Gemara then presents an alternate version of the dispute — *ve'ika d'amri*, there are those who state it differently. In this formulation, the question is not why the Rabbanan required a date in the *get*, but rather: from when does the wife begin to collect *peirot*? That is, from which moment do the husband's entitlements cease and the wife's property rights become fully operative?

Rabbi Yochanan says: *mishat ketivah* — from the moment of writing. Reish Lakish says: *mishat netinah* — from the moment of delivery.

This alternate version inverts the positions relative to what was stated earlier, and the Gemara notes that a *baraita* supports the *netinah* reading for one of them. The resolution is *efoch* — reverse the attribution. The precise assignment of which Amora holds which position in this alternate version requires the flip, bringing the positions back into alignment with the *baraita*'s evidence.

The sugya thus concludes with a rich, multi-layered dispute about the halachic timeline of a *get* — a dispute whose ramifications extend to the rights of buyers, the protection of wives, and the fundamental question of when a divorce takes legal effect in its various dimensions.

---

---

# Gittin 18

## Zman in Get Review

### Yochanan v. Lakish

The daf opens with a brief review of the central debate that occupied the preceding discussion: the argument between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish concerning when a *get* takes effect, and what precisely is the purpose of requiring a *zman* — a date — in a *get*. The *mishna* under examination deals with the permutations that arise when a *get* is begun on one day and completed on the following night, and whether such a document is valid given that technically the writing (*ketivah*) and the signing (*chatima*) occurred on different calendar days.

### Two Reasons for Zman

Two major reasons were proposed for why *chazal* instituted the requirement of a *zman* in a *get*. The first is to protect a wife from wrongful execution: if a husband were to predate a *get*, his wife could claim she was already divorced prior to any alleged act of adultery, thus escaping punishment she would otherwise deserve. Without a *zman*, she could always claim she was divorced earlier than the affair occurred. The second reason concerns the purchaser of *nichsei milog* — the wife's personal property over which the husband holds usufruct rights during the marriage. The question is until when the husband may legitimately sell the produce (*peirot*) of that property. If the *get* is predated, a buyer of those *peirot* might be disadvantaged, purchasing produce the husband was no longer entitled to sell. The later the husband's rights terminate, the more exposure the purchaser faces; the earlier the termination, the more circumscribed his ability to transact.

### Rabbi Shimon Get

These two foundational reasons allow us to understand the debate between Rabbi Shimon and the *Tanna Kamma*. The central question is: when does the husband's right to the *peirot* end? Rabbi Shimon, who is *machshir* — who validates — what is called a *get mukdam*, a predated *get*, holds that the husband loses his rights at the earliest possible time. If someone produces a *get* bearing an earlier date, Rabbi Shimon is unconcerned, because in his view the husband was in any case already divested of his rights to the *peirot* from the time of writing. Whether one follows Rabbi Yochanan or Reish Lakish regarding the precise moment this takes effect — the *ketivah*, the *chatima*, or the *netinah* — Rabbi Shimon places that cutoff earlier than either of them, and that is the basis of his leniency.

By contrast, the *Tanna Kamma* holds that the operative moment is later. Accordingly, if a *get* bears an earlier date than when it actually took legal effect, there is a problematic gap during which the husband might have sold *peirot* he should not have. It is precisely this gap that renders the predated *get* unacceptable to the *Tanna Kamma*, regardless of whether one follows Rabbi Yochanan or Reish Lakish on the specific timing question.

---

## Takanah Challenges

### Psulim Gets Kelali

The discussion turns to a pointed challenge against the entire framework of the *takanat chazal* requiring a *zman*. The *Gemara* introduces the teaching cited by Abaye to Rav Yosef: there are three categories of *gittin* that are *psulim* — invalidated — yet if a woman went ahead and remarried using one, the children born of that subsequent marriage are not considered *mamzerim*. One of those three defective *gittin* is a *get* that has witnesses but lacks a *zman*. This prompts the larger question: if such a *get* can in practice enable remarriage without producing *mamzerim*, what exactly did *chazal* accomplish with their *takanah* requiring a *zman*?

### Circumventing Zman

The *Gemara* then raises two ways a bad actor might circumvent the *takanah*, putting pressure on its effectiveness. First, one might simply instruct the *sofer* to write the *get* without any *zman* at all. The *Gemara* dismisses this: *l'chatchila* no one would do this, because the *sofer* would refuse. The requirement is well-known enough that a competent scribe would decline to write a *get* without a date. This practical deterrent gives the *takanah* real force.

But the *Gemara* presses further: what if the *sofer* writes the *get* with a proper *zman*, and then the husband physically cuts out the date and delivers the document without it? The *Gemara* responds: we do not suspect people for such games — *lo micheshvinan*. The concern does not rise to the level requiring us to legislate against every possible manipulation.

A third objection is then raised. What if the *zman* is written, but imprecisely — not the full date, but only the year, or the *shemita* cycle, or the month, or the week? Does such vagueness render the *takanah* ineffective? The *Gemara* rules that even such a document is *kasher*. And to the obvious follow-up — if so, what does the *takanah* accomplish if you can write something so general? — the *Gemara* answers: it at least delimits the time to the immediately preceding and immediately following units. If you wrote the *shemita* cycle but not the day, you know it was not the prior cycle and not the next one. That is meaningful precision, even if imperfect. And this is no different from the way we always write a *get* with the day but not the hour — we have always tolerated some degree of temporal imprecision. Writing the day tells us it was not yesterday and not tomorrow, and writing the *shemita* year tells us it was not the prior one and not the subsequent one. The *takanah* therefore always confers something, even when the *zman* is approximate.

### Takanah Effectiveness

A further challenge is posed by Ravina to Rava: what if the husband did everything correctly — wrote a proper *get* with a full *zman* — but then simply held onto it, placing it in his pocket in the hope that reconciliation might come? He thought things were rocky, wrote the *get* as a precaution, but then underwent a period of deliberation. Now the *get* is delivered much later than it was written. What did the *takanah* accomplish in this interval? Rava replies: a man does not hasten his own misfortune. If the husband genuinely hopes the marriage will work out, he would not write a *get* in the first place. The very act of writing signals resolve; one does not initiate divorce proceedings in anticipation of a trip to marriage counseling.

Then Ravina poses the question to Rav Ashi regarding *gittin* that arrive from *medinat hayam* — from overseas. A *get* written in Nisan may not be delivered until Tishrei, leaving six months or more between *ketivah* and *netinah*. How does the *takanah* help in such cases? The *Gemara* answers: *hani kala it lehu* — matters like this are publicly known. Rashi explains that the interim period raises concerns about both *zenut* and *peirot*, and in both cases the burden falls on her to bring proof of when the *get* was actually received. People will investigate and inquire, and the husband will not be able to transact freely with her property during the gap, because the community is aware of the circumstances. Whether the concern is adultery or the sale of *peirot*, public knowledge serves as a check: no one will be misled into thinking the *get* was delivered when it was not, because everyone knows it came from abroad and can calculate the timeline.

---

## Three-Month Wait

### Two Wives Case

The *Gemara* now pivots to a distinct question: from what point do we begin counting the three-month waiting period that a divorced woman must observe before remarrying? The question is introduced via a case of two wives living in the same courtyard, both given *gittin* by the same husband at the same time, but whose *gittin* bear different *zmanim* because they were written at different times. This would create an odd disparity — one wife appears to be divorced a month earlier than the other, despite both receiving their *gittin* simultaneously. Abaye resolves this by noting that *zmana mochiach aleha* — the date on each *get* speaks for itself. Since the *zmanim* are different, people can see that they were written at different times, and there is no confusion.

### Rav Netinah

Rav holds that the three-month waiting period begins at the time of *netinah* — delivery. A *baraita* supports this: if an agent was entrusted with a *get* to deliver to a man's wife, and the agent was delayed three months on the road, when the *get* finally reaches the wife she must wait an additional three months from the moment of delivery. If the period began from writing, she could remarry immediately upon receiving the *get*, since three months have already elapsed. The *baraita*'s ruling that she must wait further supports Rav's position that delivery is the operative moment.

The *baraita* adds that in this case we are not concerned about *get yashan* — the problem of an "old *get*" — because the husband did not have *yichud* with his wife in the interim. The concept of *get yashan* refers not necessarily to a *get* that is old in terms of calendar time, but to the concern that if the husband wrote a *get* and then cohabited with his wife before delivering it, we may infer that he reconsidered the divorce. Even if the *get* was written and delivered on the same day, if he slept with her in between, it becomes a *get yashan*. In the case of delivery from overseas, however, the parties are clearly not together, so there is no possibility of *yichud*, and the concern is entirely absent.

### Shmuel Ketivah

Shmuel holds that the three-month period begins at the time of *ketivah* — writing. A supporting *baraita* presents the case of a man who entrusted a *get* to an agent with the instruction not to deliver it for three months. The *baraita* rules that once the agent receives the *get*, the wife may remarry immediately upon delivery — because the three months have already been counted from the time of writing. This clearly supports Shmuel's position. The *baraita* likewise adds that we are not concerned about *get yashan* because the husband had no *yichud* with her in the interim.

### Final Ruling Ketivah

Among the later *amoraim*, Rav Kahana, Rav Pappa, and Rav Ashi ruled in practice according to the time of *ketivah*, while Rav Pappa and Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua ruled according to the time of *netinah*. The *Gemara* concludes: *v'hilchata mishaat ketivah* — the final ruling is that the three-month period begins from the time of writing.

---

## Ketubah Shemittah

### Ketubah Not Cancelled

The *Gemara* now raises a question that might seem surprising at first but proves remarkably relevant: is a *ketubah* cancelled by *shemita*? The *shemita* year cancels debts that are outstanding and collectable. However, not all financial obligations are treated as ordinary debts. Obligations that qualify as *tnai beis din* — conditions established by rabbinic enactment rather than purely private agreement — are not cancelled, because they are classified differently from personal loans. The *ketubah* is paradigmatically such an obligation: *chazal* instituted it as a condition of marriage, and a man is halachically forbidden to cohabit with his wife without one. It thus carries the character of a *beis din*-type imposition rather than a voluntary transaction.

In the ordinary case, therefore, a wife's *ketubah* is not cancelled by *shemita*. But what about a case in which the couple is no longer married — she is divorced or he has died — and the *ketubah* has become collectable but has not yet been paid? At that point, does it shift from a *tnai beis din* obligation to an ordinary private debt subject to *shemita*? That is the question the *Gemara* addresses.

### Rav Two Conditions

Rav holds that a *ketubah* becomes subject to cancellation by *shemita* only when two conditions have both been met. The first is *pegimah* — she has begun to collect, having received a partial payment of her *ketubah*. The second is *zekifah* — she has explicitly converted the remaining balance into a loan, declaring that what is owed to her should be treated as a monetary debt to be repaid. Only when both conditions are satisfied does the *ketubah* lose its *tnai beis din* character and become vulnerable to cancellation by *shemita*.

The logic is that *pegimah* alone — beginning to collect — signals that she is actively pursuing payment and the *ketubah* is now "live" in the sense of being processed. But the remaining unpaid balance is still a *tnai beis din* obligation unless she affirmatively converts it into a loan. Conversely, *zekifah* alone — declaring it a loan without yet having received any payment — also does not fully transform the obligation. Only when both are present has the *ketubah* truly migrated from the domain of *beis din* enactment into the realm of ordinary personal debt.

### Shmuel One Condition

Shmuel disagrees and holds that either condition alone is sufficient. If she has begun collecting (*pegamah*), even without declaring the remainder a loan, the *ketubah* becomes subject to *shemita*. And if she has declared it a loan (*zakfah*), even without having yet received any payment, that too is sufficient to render the remaining amount cancellable. Either act of converting the obligation from its *tnai beis din* status into something more like a private transaction is enough.

### Rav Baraita Support

The *Gemara* then cites a *baraita* that explicitly supports Rav's position. The *baraita* states: when is a *ketubah* cancelled by *shemita*? When she has both engaged in *pegimah* and performed *zekifah*. It then specifies: if she performed *pegimah* without *zekifah*, or *zekifah* without *pegimah*, the *ketubah* is not cancelled — not until she has done both. This is about as explicit as a *baraita* can be.

### Women's Obligations

The *baraita* cited in support of Shmuel enumerates several categories of obligations arising from situations involving women — *ones*, *knas*, *pitui*, and *ketuvat isha* — and states that these are cancelled by *shemita* when the obligation has been converted into a loan (*shezakfam b'malveh*). The process of *zekifah* is defined as *mishe'amda badin* — when the matter has been brought before a court and adjudicated, at which point the obligation is formally established as a monetary debt.

This *baraita* mentions only *zekifah* and says nothing about *pegimah*, which might appear to support Shmuel: perhaps *zekifah* alone, without *pegimah*, is sufficient to trigger *shemita* cancellation. However, the *baraita* does not explicitly say that *pegimah* is unnecessary — it simply does not address it. One could argue that the *baraita* presupposes that *pegimah* has already occurred, or at minimum that the absence of *pegimah* from the text does not prove that *zekifah* alone is enough. The *baraita* thus only partially supports Shmuel — it shows that *zekifah* without an explicit mention of *pegimah* can trigger cancellation, but it does not address whether *pegimah* alone, without *zekifah*, would also suffice. Shmuel claims both directions independently, and the *baraita* establishes only one leg of his position. Unlike the other debates discussed earlier in the *daf*, the *Gemara* here does not issue a final ruling between Rav and Shmuel.

---

## Ketubah Parallel

### Shmuel Parallel

Shmuel articulates an important principle: a *ketubah* is comparable to a *ma'aseh beis din* — an act of court. Just as documents issued by *beis din* may be written during the day and signed at night without the intervening time rendering the document invalid, so too a *ketubah* may be written during the day and signed at night. This is directly relevant to the question that has run throughout the *daf* — the concern about *get mukdam* and the gap between *ketivah* and *chatima*.

### Chiya Ketubah

A practical illustration is offered: the *ketubah* of Rabbi Chiya bar Rav was written on one day and signed on a different day, and Rav was present and raised no objection. One might infer from his silence that he agrees with Shmuel's position. However, the *Gemara* qualifies this inference.

### Same Matter Leniency

The reason Rav did not object in that case was not because he agreed with Shmuel's principle in the abstract, but because the parties were still *oskim b'oto inyan* — engaged in the same matter. When those writing and signing a document remain continuously involved in the same transaction or proceeding throughout, the gap between writing and signing does not introduce the kinds of concerns that would otherwise arise. A *tanna* from the school of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi supports this: the rule that writing in the day and signing at night is invalid applies only when the parties are no longer engaged in the same matter, but if they remain so engaged throughout, it is *kasher*. This leniency does not extend indefinitely — if the gap grows to ten days or more, or the parties are no longer involved in the same proceeding, the concern reasserts itself.

---

## Rabbi Shimon Scope

### Rabbi Shimon Reasoning

The *Gemara* now takes up the formal analysis of why Rabbi Shimon is *machshir* a *get mukdam*, a predated *get*. Rava explains: Rabbi Shimon holds that *keivan shenatan einav l'garshah, shuv ein lo piyus* — once the husband has set his mind to divorce, he can no longer be appeased or reconciled. The act of *piyus* — reconciliation — is no longer available to him. The concrete moment that marks this irreversible decision is the writing of the *get*. From that point forward, whatever appears in the *get* as the date is treated as though the divorce effectively began at that time, because the husband's intent was firm and irrevocable. This is why predating is tolerable according to Rabbi Shimon: no practical harm flows from an earlier date, since the husband's rights over the *peirot* were already forfeit from the moment he committed to the divorce through the act of writing.

### Lakish Limits Window

Reish Lakish, however, limits Rabbi Shimon's leniency sharply. He holds that Rabbi Shimon spoke only about the immediate case: the *get* was written that same day and signed that same night — *l'altar*, immediately. The window between *ketivah* and *chatima* that Rabbi Shimon permits is only that narrow span of a day and the following night. Extending the gap to ten days is something Reish Lakish does not permit under Rabbi Shimon's leniency. The concern is *shema piyes* — perhaps during that longer period the husband was reconciled with his wife, in which case the *get* would no longer represent a firm and irrevocable decision but a superseded one.

### Yochanan Expands

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees and permits a window of up to ten days even within Rabbi Shimon's framework. His reasoning: *ei ita d'piyes, kala it lehu l'milta* — if the parties had truly reconciled, people would know. Reconciliation is not a private matter; it manifests in behavior that the community observes. If a couple that was known to be headed for divorce is suddenly seen together again, going out, resuming their life — people talk. Since we would hear about a reconciliation, we are not concerned that one occurred silently during the ten-day gap. Rabbi Yochanan therefore permits relying on Rabbi Shimon's leniency for that extended period.

---

## Ten People Get

### Ten People Command

The *Gemara* introduces a new case: a husband instructs ten people to write a *get* for his wife. This requires interpretation. It cannot mean that all ten physically write the document — that would be neither practical nor halachically coherent. What then does he intend? The answer must lie in the signing. But a *get* requires only two witnesses to sign. So what role do the other eight play?

A *baraita* clarifies: if a husband says to ten people "write a *get* for my wife" without specifying *kulchem* — "all of you" — then one person writes and two sign. The other seven need not be involved at all. From this, we see that the act of addressing ten people does not inherently require all ten to participate. Rashi explains that in a case where all ten are indeed required to sign — without the word *kulchem* having been used — the husband's intention was to embarrass his wife publicly, using the gathering as a forum for the declaration of divorce. He wanted all those present to know about it. The *get* itself bears only the two standard witnesses, but the husband chose to make the matter public.

Given this, the case before us must be one in which the husband explicitly said *kulchem* — all of you — thereby creating an obligation for all ten to participate in the signing. The debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish turns on what that participation means.

### Yochanan Two Edim

Rabbi Yochanan holds: two of the ten sign as *edim* — as the actual halachic witnesses whose signatures give the *get* its validity — and all the rest sign because of a *tnai*, a condition. The husband, by saying *kulchem*, created a condition that all ten must sign, but only two of them function as witnesses in the technical sense. The remaining eight are satisfying a condition, not serving as witnesses.

### Lakish All Edim

Reish Lakish holds that all ten are *edim* — all ten function as full witnesses. The *get* is not valid until all ten have signed, because all ten were designated as witnesses when the husband invoked *kulchem*.

### Practical Differences

What practical difference emerges between these two positions? The *Gemara* identifies two.

The first: if two of the ten signed on one day and the remaining eight signed up to ten days later, according to Rabbi Yochanan — who holds the other eight are signing due to a *tnai* rather than as witnesses — this is unproblematic. A *tnai* carries no defined time requirement; the condition can be fulfilled whenever the parties get around to it. But according to Reish Lakish, who holds all ten are *edim*, all ten witnesses must sign at the same time. A *get* cannot have its witnesses sign across multiple days, and so this arrangement would render the *get* invalid.

The second difference: if one of the ten is found to be a *karov* or *pasul* — a disqualified witness — the consequences differ. According to Rabbi Yochanan, only the two designated *edim* need to be valid; if one of the other eight is disqualified, it is of no consequence, because they are signing due to a *tnai* and the *tnai* can simply be fulfilled by the remaining valid signatories. According to Reish Lakish, since all ten are *edim*, any disqualification among the ten affects the validity of the *get*.

A further sub-question arises: what if one of the *first* two to sign is found to be *karov* or *pasul*? According to those who say this is still *kasher*, the reasoning is that since the husband did not specify *which* two are the witnesses, the identity of the witnesses is determined by who among the ten is valid, not by the order in which they signed. The first two to sign are not inherently the designated witnesses; any two valid signatories from among the ten fulfill the requirement. The fact that a *pasul* signed first does not corrupt the *get*, because we look to the valid signatures as the operative witnesses. The opposing view holds that this creates a problem of *ati l'ichlofu b'shtar d'alma* — people may mistake the *get* for an ordinary legal document and validate other documents on the strength of a *pasul*'s signature appearing first.

---

## Rabbi Shimon Ten Days

### Two Days Signing

The *Gemara* now describes an actual case: a man said to ten people to write a *get* for his wife, and two of them signed on one day while the remaining signatories signed up to ten days later. The case came before Rabbi Shimon ben Levi.

### Rabbi Shimon Valid

Rabbi Shimon ben Levi ruled: *k'dai hu Rabbi Shimon lismoch alav b'sha'at had'chak* — Rabbi Shimon is sufficiently authoritative to rely upon in a time of pressing need. The validation requires invoking Rabbi Shimon's leniency that a *get* written and signed at different times can be valid.

### Sha'at Hadeichak

But the language of *sha'at had'chak* — a time of pressing need or hardship — is significant and calls for explanation. If Rabbi Shimon's position is a legitimate *l'chatchila* ruling, why frame reliance upon it as a concession to emergency? Rashi explains: *sha'at had'chak* here refers to cases such as where the husband has since departed and cannot be located to write a new *get*, or where the woman has already remarried on the basis of this *get* and has children — situations where retroactively invalidating the *get* would produce severe consequences, including stigmatizing her children and calling her subsequent marriage into question. These are not abstract halachic exercises but real human crises that require a practical resolution.

### Yochanan Leniency

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent tension: Rabbi Shimon ben Levi holds like Reish Lakish regarding the scope of Rabbi Shimon's leniency — that it applies only to the immediate day and night, not to ten days. But in this case he extends the window to ten days by relying on Rabbi Yochanan's position, which permits that longer interval under Rabbi Shimon's framework. This is a compound ruling: he relies on Rabbi Shimon's leniency for the validity of the *get* despite the gap between signings, and on Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that the window extends to ten days.

Why then is this only a *sha'at had'chak* ruling rather than a *l'chatchila* one? Because Rabbi Shimon ben Levi himself does not hold all these lenient positions *l'chatchila*. He holds primarily like Reish Lakish — who would require all the signatures to be contemporaneous and would limit Rabbi Shimon's window to the immediate day and night. It is only because the case already happened, and because invalidating the *get* would cause genuine hardship — *mishum iguna akilu bah rabanan*, the rabbis were lenient for the sake of preventing women from becoming *agunot* — that he is willing to reach across and rely on the more permissive opinions. This is not rabbi-shopping in the pejorative sense, but rather the established halachic principle that where the stakes involve freeing a woman from an uncertain marital status, authorities have greater latitude to adopt lenient readings than they would otherwise exercise *l'chatchila*.

---

---

# Gittin 19

## Perek Overview

### Masechet Framework

Daf 19 opens at the *mishna*, and it is worth pausing to appreciate how the *perakim* of *Gittin* have been structured and how the transition from the first *perek* to the second unfolds. The *masechet* begins in a somewhat indirect manner, organizing itself around the *takkana* of *bifanai nichtav ubifanai nechtam* — the requirement that the *shaliach* who delivers a *get* declare that it was written and signed in his presence. That framework dominates the opening *perek*, and it resurfaces at the beginning of the second *perek* as well, addressing variations on the same theme. But one can also read this structure as a way of approaching the central themes of the *masechet* obliquely — entering through a side door, as it were, before arriving at the heart of the matter.

One important thread that emerged throughout the first *perek* was a series of parallels between a *get* of an *isha* and a *shtar shikhrur* of an *eved*. The *bifanai nichtav* formulation applies to both, and this parallel itself underscores something significant: this is not merely any *shtar*. It is a document that changes personal status. That may be precisely why testifying about the *nichtav* — the writing itself — carries special weight: there are particular criteria governing the act of writing that do not apply to ordinary documents.

### Ketivat Haget Focus

Having established that broader framework, the second *perek* uses *bifanai nichtav ubifanai nechtam* as a bridge into the core concerns of *ketivat haget*. Where the first *perek* assembled a somewhat varied collection of topics — *arkha'ot*, *shtar shikhrur*, *shtar matana*, and the like — the second *perek* begins to focus squarely on the *get* itself and on what the Torah requires of its writing.

### Dating Requirements

The preceding *mishna* addressed the case of *nichtav hayom venechtam balaila* — what if the *ketiva* and the *chatima* occurred on different days? This was a natural transition from the *bifanai nichtav ubifanai nechtam* framework and led the *gemara* to explore the requirement to include a date in a *get* (*lamma hitkinu zeman begittin?*) as well as the particular *psul* of a *get mukdam* — a *get* bearing an earlier date than its actual execution. That discussion, emerging organically from the *nichtav-nechtam* framework, brought us to a central requirement of *ketivat haget*. Now, the current *mishna* moves even more concretely into the physical dimensions of that writing: what materials may be used, and on what surfaces may a *get* be written?

---

## Writing Materials

### Permitted Inks
