The *mishna* opens with the principle *bekhol kotvin* — one may write with everything — and then proceeds to enumerate: *bediyo* (ink), *besam*, *besikra*, *uvekomus*, *uvekhankantom*, and *uvekhol davar shehu kayyama* — with any substance that endures. These are all permitted writing materials for a *get*.

### Permanence Definition

There is an alternative *girsa* of the *mishna* which reads *bedik khol davar shehu roshem* — anything that leaves a mark — rather than *shehu kayyama*. The distinction is worth pondering. *Roshem* suggests an impression or mark, whereas *kayyama* emphasizes lasting permanence. One might ask whether carving or etching would be included under *roshem*, but the *mishna* does not address that case directly, and the *gemara* will have more to say about the question of permanence.

### Prohibited Liquids

The *mishna* then states: *ein kotvin lo bemashkin velo bemei peirot velo bekhol davar she'eino mitkayyem* — one may not write a *get* with liquids, fruit juices, or any substance that does not endure. The contrast with the permitted list is deliberate: *shehu kayyama* versus *she'eino mitkayyem*. This raises a natural question: precisely how long must something last? Is there a defined *shiur* of permanence? Does it need to resist erasure, or is it enough that it not evaporate immediately? The case of a *ketuba* whose ink has faded over decades, or of writing that disappears within moments of application — these represent very different points on the spectrum. The problem with *mashkin* and *mei peirot* appears to be that they are essentially ephemeral — they do not leave a genuinely lasting *roshem*. The word *roshem* itself may be instructive here: even if a substance does not endure for years, it should at minimum leave a visible, distinguishable mark that does not vanish instantaneously. The question of a pencil is interesting in this regard: a pencil certainly leaves a mark and does not fade on its own, though it can be erased. The *mishna* does not mention resistance to erasure as a criterion — that is a separate concern related to *davar sheyachol lehizdayef* — and so a pencil, or something like it, might not be disqualified on the grounds of *she'eino mitkayyem* alone.

### Permitted Surfaces

Turning to the surface, the *mishna* states *al hakol kotevin* — one may write on anything. The examples given are striking: *al ha'aleh shel zayit* — on an olive leaf — and *al hakeren shel parah* — on the horn of a cow. In the latter case, the *mishna* adds *venoten lo et haparah*: one must give her the cow itself along with the *get*. We will see in the *gemara* why this is so. Similarly, *al yad shel eved venoten lo et ha'eved* — one may write on the arm of a slave, but then the slave himself must be given to her. The operative rule is *vekhatvo venatano* — the *get* must be written and then delivered as a single act; if separating the document from its surface requires an additional act after the writing, complications arise, as the *gemara* will clarify.

### Rabbi Yose HaGalili

*Rabbi Yose HaGelili* disputes part of this ruling: *ein kotevin lo al davar she-yesh bo ruach chayim velo al ochlim* — one should not write a *get* on a living creature, and not on food. We will see his reasoning in the *gemara*, along with the question of whether his position is grounded in a *de'oraita* concern or a rabbinic one.

It is worth noting one structural asymmetry in the *mishna*: the requirement of permanence is stated explicitly for the substance used to write *with*, but not for the surface written *on*. Yet an olive leaf is hardly a permanent object. This tension points back to the question of what *mitkayyem* really demands: perhaps the concern is only with substances that are entirely ephemeral — that evaporate or vanish as soon as they are applied — rather than with materials that will eventually deteriorate under normal conditions.

---

## Ink Analysis

### Dyo & Sam

The *gemara* now turns to identify the materials listed in the *mishna*. *Dyo* is straightforwardly *dyuta* — ink. *Sam* is more elusive. Rashi identifies it as orpiment; the Steinsaltz commentary says arsenic; another tradition describes it as ink derived from a grass or root. Whatever the precise referent, it belongs to the category of plant- or mineral-derived colorants used as writing substances.

### Sikra & Kankantom

*Sikra*, according to *Rabbah bar Bar Hana*, is *sikrastah* — a transliteration that essentially concedes the difficulty of rendering the word in another language, illustrating the fundamental challenge of translation when no ready equivalent exists. Rashi understands *sikra* as a reddish substance, and that characterization will be important momentarily. *Kankantom*, as *Rabbah bar Bar Hana* reports in the name of Shmuel, is *khartsa d'ushkhasei* — the blacking used by shoemakers. The Steinsaltz commentary identifies it as copper sulfate, though it is likely iron sulfate.

### Kumos

*Kumos* is identified as *kuma* — gum arabic.

### Permanent Materials

Having listed these substances, the *mishna* concludes with the broader category of *bekhol davar shehu mitkayem* — anything that endures. The *gemara* asks: *le'atuyei mai* — what does this phrase come to include beyond the specific items already enumerated? The answer draws on a teaching of Rabbi Chiyya: if one wrote a *get* with *mei tarya*, it is *kasher*. Rashi explains *mei tarya* as water in which a fruit has been soaked — not fruit juice squeezed directly from the fruit, but rather a liquid in which some dye-bearing plant material has been steeped, producing something closer to an infusion or rudimentary ink. Rashi identifies the relevant substance with *afatzim* — gallnuts — a material that, as we will see later in the *gemara*, plays a significant role in the preparation of *kelafim* as well.

A separate *braita* cites Rabbi Chiyya teaching that if a *get* was written with *avar* (lead), with *shachor* (which Rashi understands as coals or charcoal), or with this shoemaker's dye, it is *kasher*. These may seem obvious, as all three are clearly permanent substances, but their explicit enumeration serves a purpose that will become clearer as the *gemara* proceeds.

---

## Writing Over Writing

### Dyeing on Sikra

The *gemara* now introduces a conceptually rich discussion about inking over existing writing, using the laws of *Shabbat* as a comparative framework. The case is *ha-madyo al gabei sikra be-Shabbat*: someone on *Shabbat* applies black ink (*dyo*) on top of writing that had already been done in *sikra* — the reddish, permanent but less visually distinct substance. Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish both agree: *chayav shtayim* — one incurs two violations.

### Kotev vs Mochek

The first violation is *mishum kotev* — writing. Even though the letters were already there in red, covering them with black ink constitutes a new and improved *ketiva*: black letters on white parchment are more crisp and legible than red ones, and so something qualitatively new has been produced. The second violation is *mishum mochek* — erasing. This is the striking part. The intuition might be that erasing means physically removing something; covering it up seems different. Yet the *gemara* holds that by applying black over red, one has in effect caused the red letters to disappear — and that counts as *mochek*.

This may be compared to the well-known discussion about lettering on cake on *Shabbat*. The *Maharach Or Zarua* discouraged eating it on account of *mochek*, though Rabbi Akiva Eiger called this position extreme. One objection is that eating the letters is *mitkalkel* — a destructive, not constructive, act — and also *eino mitkaven*. But one crucial difference is worth noting: eating the letters on a cake is a form of destruction, whereas inking over red letters with black is arguably an act of construction that simultaneously renders the red invisible. The classic *mochek* is *al menat lichtov* — erasing in order to write — because erasing makes the parchment beneath available for new writing. Here, by covering red with black, one is doing something analogous: the space that held red letters now holds black ones, and the surface has been put to productive use. That is the logic of the double liability.

*Tosafot* engages this question directly. In explaining why the *sikra-on-dyo* case (discussed below) might constitute *mochek al menat lichtov*, *Tosafot* argues that applying a red underlay actually improves the subsequent black layer — *ketiva elyona reshuma nikeret tefei mima'aseh tachtona levada* — the upper black writing will be even more legible when written over a red underlayer than if applied to bare parchment. This is a creative explanation, though its technical accuracy may be questioned.

### Red on Black

The case of *sikra al gabei deyo* — red applied over black — is more ambiguous. Here the *gemara* records a dispute: *amrei lah chayav ve'amrei lah patur*. Those who say *chayav* argue that this constitutes *mochek*: the black letters beneath have been rendered invisible. Those who say *patur* counter that this is *mekalkel* — a destructive act with no constructive purpose. The logic of *mochek* requires not merely that letters be made to disappear, but that their disappearance renders the parchment more usable for subsequent writing. When one covers black with red, the result is worse — red ink on top of black leaves the surface no more usable than before. The parchment has not become a blank slate ready for new writing; it now has red ink sitting atop black ink. One might respond that if the person *prefers* red, then covering black with red could be considered constructive — and in that case perhaps *chayav mishum kotev* would also apply — but the *gemara* leaves the matter as a dispute.

### Ink on Ink

The cases of *deyo al gabei deyo* and *sikra al gabei sikra* are more straightforward: if one adds fresh ink of the same color over existing ink of the same color, one is *patur*. Nothing qualitatively new has been produced. The letters were already there, the color is unchanged, and merely refreshing the same ink atop itself does not constitute a new act of *ketiva*. (If the underlying ink were fading, the analysis might differ — in that case one could argue that something genuinely new and improved has resulted — but the case under discussion assumes clearly legible, intact original writing.)

---

## Writing Over Writing (II)

### Pre-inked Signatures

With this *Shabbat* framework in view, the *gemara* transitions to a related but distinct question: what happens when witnesses who cannot sign their own names are offered pre-written letters in *sikra* over which they then trace in black ink? Does the result count as a valid *chatima*? The preceding discussion about *kotev* and *mochek* by *Shabbat* is the backdrop against which this question now unfolds.

---

## Signature Over Writing

### Witnesses Cannot Sign

Reish Lakish poses the question to Rabbi Yochanan: *edim she'ein yode'im lachtom* — witnesses who do not know how to sign — may one pre-write their names for them in *sikra* and have them sign over it with black ink? Is the resulting *chatima* valid?

### Is Upper Writing New

Rabbi Yochanan responds: *ktav elyon eino ktav* — the upper layer of writing is not considered writing. The names were already present in *sikra*; tracing over them in ink does not constitute a genuine act of signing.

### Shabbat Precedent

Reish Lakish presses back: but did our master not teach us that *ktav elyon ktav le'inyan Shabbat* — that by *Shabbat*, writing over existing writing is considered genuine *ketiva* and one is *chayav*? If it counts as writing for *Shabbat*, should it not count as writing for the *chatima* of a *get* as well?

### Analogy Limitation

Rabbi Yochanan's reply is striking: *veki mipnei she'anu m'damim na'aseh ma'aseh* — just because we can draw an analogy, does that mean we should act upon it? This is a remarkable methodological statement. The phrase *mipnei she'anu m'damim na'aseh ma'aseh* appears elsewhere in *halachic* literature as an expression of reluctance to translate a compelling argument into an actual ruling. Poskim sometimes construct an entire line of reasoning and then pull back with precisely this formulation — as if to say: the argument may be internally coherent, but I am not willing to cross the threshold from analysis to practical decision on its basis alone. But it is worth distinguishing two different contexts in which this reluctance can operate. In some cases, a *posek* builds an argument entirely within a single area of *halacha* and then hesitates to follow his own reasoning to its conclusion — that is a kind of general caution about the limits of one's own analysis. Here, however, something more specific is being said: we are making an analogy *across* two different areas of *halacha* — *hilkhot Shabbat* and *hilkhot gittin* — and Rabbi Yochanan is questioning whether the criteria operative in one domain can simply be imported into the other.

### Different Halakhic Areas

What might explain a difference in the definition of *ketiva* between *Shabbat* and the *chatima* of a *get*? One possible approach concerns the conceptual structure of *hilkhot Shabbat*. The framework of *avot* and *toldot* in *Shabbat* and the concept of *melekhet machshevet* together suggest that what matters in many cases is the *result* achieved rather than the precise mechanical process by which it was achieved. If the end result is that something of significance has been produced — if *nitkayma machshavto* — one may be *chayav*, regardless of the particular path taken. On this reading, inking over red letters to produce crisp black letters is a meaningful transformation: a new *cheftza d'ksav* has been created, even if the process was not a conventional act of writing from scratch. But for the *chatima* of witnesses on a *get* — or on any *shtar* — the question may be whether the witnesses performed a genuine *ma'aseh ketiva*. For a signature to be their signature, perhaps it must emerge from an act of writing something that was not already there, rather than from the act of filling in letters pre-formed by someone else. Writing on top of something that is already written may achieve a new result for the purposes of *Shabbat* while still not constituting a valid act of *chatima*. The *gemara* here leaves this distinction suggestive rather than fully resolved, noting that a more extended discussion of the *Shabbat* dimension will follow on the next *daf*.

---

## Illiterate Witnesses

### Stencil Method

The *gemara* now presents the practical solutions developed by the Amoraim for witnesses who cannot sign their names. Rav's approach: *mekarim lahem niyar chalak u-memalim et ha-keraim b'dyo* — one prepares for them a stencil of blank paper and they fill the cutout letters with ink. *Tosafot* understands this straightforwardly as a physical stencil. Rashi offers a different reading: one makes an indentation in the *klaf* itself and the witnesses fill the indentation with ink.

### Lead Underwriting

Shmuel's approach is different: *be-avar* — one pre-writes the letters for them in lead, and they write over it. This is similar in structure to the *sikra* case discussed above, but lead poses an even more pronounced difficulty.

### Lead Writing Status

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: *be-avar salka da'atach?* A *braita* of Rabbi Chiyya already established that writing with *avar* is *kasher* for a *get* — which means it constitutes valid *ksav*. If so, the letters are already written; how can the witnesses write over them and call it their *chatima*?

### Avar vs Mei Avara

The *gemara* resolves the difficulty by distinguishing between *avara* — actual lead rubbed directly onto the *klaf* — and *maya de-avara* — a liquid solution in which lead has been dissolved or processed, functioning as an ink. Rashi explains the distinction in terms that are illuminating. Lead rubbed onto parchment, like a pencil on paper, does not penetrate the surface; it remains on top and can be wiped away. A liquid solution, on the other hand, is absorbed into the *klaf* and becomes part of it, making it genuinely permanent. Rashi says explicitly: *be-avar leshafshef be-chatikha shel avar al ha-klaf umashchirah eino ksav* — rubbing an actual piece of lead across the parchment does not constitute *ksav*. The *maya de-avara*, by contrast, is *ksav*. This is a significant *chiddush*: something that leaves a visible mark — that is clearly *roshem* — and that does not disappear spontaneously, is nevertheless not considered *ksav* because it is not absorbed into the surface and is therefore erasable. This pushes back against the earlier reading of the *mishna* that did not seem to require deep permanence, and raises again the question of how precisely *mitkayyem* is to be defined.

### Gallnut Solution

Rav Abba proposes yet another approach: *be-mei milin* — using gallnut juice as the underlayer over which the witnesses sign. Rashi identifies *mei milin* with ground gallnuts soaked in water — an infusion that, in other contexts, functions as genuine ink. This creates an immediate problem: a *braita* of Rav Chanina teaches that writing a *get* with *mei tarya va-afatza* (gallnut water) is *kasher*, meaning it counts as valid *ksav*. If so, how can the *mei milin* underlayer be permissible?

### Gallnut Worked Klaf

The *gemara* resolves this with the distinction *ha de-afitz ha de-lo afitz* — it depends on whether the *klaf* was prepared (*afitz*) with gallnut juice. *Tosafot* explains this well: if the *klaf* itself was treated with a gallnut solution during its preparation, and one then writes on it with a gallnut-based ink, the ink will not leave a visible, distinguishable mark — *she'ein mei milin al gabei mei milin* — because the same substance has already saturated the surface. In this case, the underlayer effectively does not exist as a discernible *ksav*, and the witnesses' writing over it constitutes a genuine *chatima*. On a *klaf* that was not treated with gallnuts, the same gallnut solution would leave a permanent and visible mark, and writing over it would face the same problem as the *sikra* case.

This resolution also sheds light on the broader structure of the discussion. The *gemara* is consistent in assuming that whether a substance constitutes *ksav* for purposes of *get* writing is also the operative criterion for whether witnesses can write over an underlayer. That is itself a kind of *dimui* — an analogical application — but one the *gemara* accepts without hesitation. What the *gemara* refuses to accept is the analogical import of *Shabbat* liability into the definition of valid *chatima*. The distinction between these two analogical moves is itself instructive: the definition of *ksav* for *ketivat haget* presumably sets the threshold for the entire document, including the *chatima*, whereas *Shabbat* operates under a different conceptual architecture and different standards of what constitutes a meaningful act.

---

## Get vs Other Documents

### Saliva Method

Rav Pappa's practical solution for illiterate witnesses is the most striking of all: *be-rok* — using saliva. He demonstrated this method to a man called Pappa the ox-driver, showing him how to moisten the surface with spit and have the witnesses sign over it.

### Gets Only

Immediately the *gemara* qualifies: *vehanei milei be-gitten* — all of these accommodations apply only to *gitten*, not to other documents. *Aval bi-shtaros lo.*

### Agunah vs Fraud

Rashi articulates the reason: *be-gitten mishum agunah ke-dilekamman* — for *gitten*, these leniencies are justified because of the *agunah* problem. The scenario is familiar: a husband is about to depart on a sea voyage, there are witnesses present but they do not know how to sign, and without a *get* the woman risks being left an *agunah* — perhaps forever unable to remarry. Even a *yibbum* situation is treated as an *agunah* case if obtaining the *get* would forestall the need to locate an unwilling *yavam*. In such circumstances the rabbis were willing to accommodate witnesses who could not sign in the ordinary manner. For monetary documents, however, no such urgency exists — one simply waits until proper witnesses are available. More importantly, allowing unrecognizable or stenciled signatures in monetary matters would open the door to catastrophic fraud: anyone could produce a *shtar* with block-letter signatures and claim it was signed by illiterate witnesses.

### Rav Kahana's Lashes

The seriousness with which this was treated is illustrated by a vivid episode: a man who applied these methods of assisted signing to non-*get* documents was brought before Rav Kahana, who administered *malkot* — lashes. Rav Kahana apparently felt that the integrity of the institution of *shtarot* was so fundamental, and the risk of abuse so acute, that even without a specific Torah prohibition, the use of these techniques in monetary documents warranted corporal punishment. This is not a case of *akhal cheilev* — a classic Torah transgression — but Rav Kahana evidently regarded it as a threat to the entire structure of commercial documentation that required the strongest possible deterrent.

---

## Literacy Requirements

### Tanna Kamma

A *braita* consistent with Rav's position is cited: *eidim she'ein yod'im likhtom* — if witnesses do not know how to sign — *mekarim lahem niyar halak u-memalim et ha-keraim dyo* — one prepares a stencil and they fill it with ink. A further expansion: if the witnesses do not even know how to *read* the document, one may read it aloud for them (*korin lifneihem ve-khosmim*) and then have them sign with the stencil. The *tanna kamma* permits both accommodations — reading aloud by others and stenciled signatures — with no stated limitation to *gitten* specifically.

### Rabban Shimon Position

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees with the scope of this leniency. He agrees that both accommodations — reading aloud and stenciled signatures — are permitted, but limits them to *gittei nashim*. For *shichrurei avadim* (emancipation documents for slaves, which stand at the intersection of *mammonot* and personal status) and all other *shtarot*, he rules: if the witnesses know how to read and sign, they may sign; if not, they may not sign at all.

### Agunah Reason

Rav Elazar explains Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning: *shelo yehu bnot yisrael agunot* — so that Jewish women should not be left as *agunot*. The formulation focuses on what makes *gitten* exceptional rather than on what makes other *shtarot* consequential, though both considerations could have been stated.

### Accepted Ruling

Rava rules: *halacha ke-Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* — the law follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's distinction. This is the accepted position.

### Rav Gamda Rejected

Rav Gamda reports in Rava's name a contradictory ruling: *ein halacha* — we do not follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, apparently allowing these leniencies for all *shtarot*. But the *gemara* rejects this position immediately by invoking Rav Kahana's episode. If Rav Kahana administered lashes to someone who used these methods with ordinary documents, it is clear that the institution was considered inviolable. It is inconceivable that Rav Gamda intended to permit what Rav Kahana saw fit to punish with such severity.

---

## Reading Verification

### Reading Allowed

The *gemara* now resolves the apparent contradiction in Rav Gamda's ruling with the clarification *targema akria* — his statement was addressed only to the *kria* dimension, the reading aloud of a document. When Rav Gamda said the leniency applies to all *shtarot*, he meant only that one may have a document read aloud before signing it; he was not permitting stenciled or unrecognizable signatures in monetary documents. The *chatima* itself must still be the witness's own handwriting. The question now becomes how far the *akria* leniency extends and what safeguards must be in place.

### Trusted Readers

Two stories illustrate how senior Amoraim handled this. Rav Yehuda, apparently as his eyesight declined, would strain and squint to read documents himself before signing — suggesting he held that even having someone else read a document aloud is not fully reliable, and one should read it independently if at all possible. Ulla challenged this position, pointing out that Rav Elazar — considered *marei de'eretz yisrael*, the master authority of the Land of Israel, renowned in particular for his expertise in matters of *ketamim* and careful visual examination — would regularly have others read documents aloud before signing them. Similarly, Rav Nachman had the scribes of the *dayanim* read documents before him and then signed.

### Trusted Scribes

But the *gemara* immediately pulls back: *vedavka Rav Nachman vesafrey dayanei* — it was specifically Rav Nachman together with the judges' own scribes, *de'it lehu eimta* — because they were afraid of him and would not misrepresent what was written. With other scribes, or with other individuals, even Rav Nachman's presence would not have been sufficient to guarantee accuracy.

### Deception Concern

This qualification reveals how seriously the *gemara* takes the potential for abuse even in the apparently benign case of having a document read aloud. After all, the document is sitting right there — in theory, one could always take it to someone else to verify. But in practice, witnesses typically do not do that: they hear what is read to them, they trust the reader, and they sign. A dishonest reader can therefore misrepresent the content of a document with remarkable ease. The example is not difficult to imagine: a lender presents a document to the witnesses, reads it as stating that a borrower owes him money, when in fact it says the reverse. The witnesses sign, the document is right there for all to see, and yet they have been deceived. Because of this acute risk, the *gemara* restricts the *akria* leniency even for *shtarot* to circumstances where the reader can be trusted with near-absolute certainty — effectively limiting it to someone in a formal, accountable relationship with the signatory, like the judges' own scribes who feared the consequences of deceiving Rav Nachman.

---

## Foreign Languages

### Persian Documents

The *gemara* now turns to the case of documents in a foreign language. Rav Pappa would sometimes receive Persian *shtarot* that had been produced in non-Jewish courts (*arka'ot shel goyim*). Recall that an early *mishna* already established that documents executed in non-Jewish courts are valid as evidence that a transaction took place, even if they do not satisfy the full technical requirements of a Jewish *shtar*. But how could Rav Pappa know what was written in a document he could not read?

### Double Translation

His solution: *makrey lehu lishney kutim zeh shelo bifney zeh* — he would have two non-Jews each translate the document independently, not in each other's presence. If their translations matched, and they were *bemasiach lefi tumo* — casual, uninvolved individuals who had no prior knowledge of the case — there was no plausible explanation for the agreement other than that both were accurately rendering what the document actually said. Two strangers, unaware of the particulars of the dispute, could not coincidentally produce identical mistranslations.

### Liens Recognized

Rav Pappa's confidence in this method was such that he would collect even from *meshabedi* — property that was subject to a lien — on the basis of such a translated document. The concept of *meshabedi* is significant: a lien on a debtor's property attaches, and binds even subsequent purchasers of that property, only when there is a *shtar* that constitutes a matter of public record. Rav Pappa was willing to treat a properly verified Persian document as satisfying this standard — a striking endorsement of the method's reliability.

### Jewish Persian Get

Rav Ashi reports a related ruling in the name of Ameimar, via Rav Huna bar Natan: a Persian *shtar* written by Jews and bearing Jewish witnesses is *kasher* and supports collection from *meshabedi*. This is distinct from the *arka'ot* case — there we were dealing with documents from non-Jewish courts; here the document is Jewish in origin, executed by Jewish parties with Jewish witnesses, but written in Persian.

### Forgery Prevention

The *gemara* raises an objection: does this not require *ketav she'eino yakhol lehizdayef* — writing that cannot be forged or altered? Documents produced outside the formal Jewish legal system might be written with erasable materials, allowing subsequent alteration of amounts or names.

### Gallnut Protection

The *gemara* answers: *bi-defitzna* — we are speaking of a *klaf* that was treated with gallnut (*afitz*), which prevents erasure. The gallnut preparation bonds with the parchment in such a way that ink written on it cannot be erased without leaving visible evidence of tampering. In such a case, even a document written in Persian by a community less familiar with the full technical requirements of Jewish document law is protected against the specific vulnerability of forgery.

A further objection: a valid *shtar* must repeat the essence of its content in the final line (*tzarich lachzor me-inyano shel shtar be-shitah achronah*). Does such a Persian document satisfy this requirement? The *gemara* answers that in the case under discussion, *ahadreih* — it did repeat the key content in the final line. So the document is entirely congruent with a proper Jewish *shtar* in every respect except its language.

### Any Language Valid

This prompts the *gemara* to ask: *ela mai ka mashma lan* — what then is the ruling actually teaching us? The answer: *de-khol lashon kasher* — a *shtar* may be written in any language. But is that not already established by the *mishna* concerning a *get* written in Hebrew with Greek witnesses, or in Greek with Hebrew witnesses, which is *kasher*? The *gemara* responds: from that *mishna* alone, one might have concluded *hanei milei be-gittin* — that the latitude for different languages is a feature of *gitten* specifically, where the rabbis are more lenient across a range of dimensions, but that *shtarot* might require Hebrew or Aramaic. The ruling of Ameimar therefore adds *ka mashma lan* — that in *shtarot* as well, language is not a determinative criterion; what matters is that the document meet all the substantive requirements of a valid *shtar*.

To summarize the conclusions that emerge from this entire discussion: for *gitten*, the rabbis permitted both having the document read aloud to the witnesses and the use of stenciled or assisted signatures. For *shtarot*, stenciled signatures are absolutely prohibited — the risk of fraud is too great, as demonstrated by Rav Kahana's willingness to administer lashes. Having a document read aloud before signing is permitted in *shtarot*, but only in circumstances where the reliability of the reader can be established with near-certainty. And the language in which a document is written — whether Hebrew, Aramaic, Persian, or Greek — does not in itself determine the document's validity, provided all other substantive requirements are met.

---

---

# Gittin 20

## Blank Paper & Invisible…

### Shmuel's Blank Paper

The daf opens, technically, toward the end of Gittin 19b, roughly fifteen lines before the lines widen on the page. There, *Shmuel* presents a striking ruling: if a man gave his wife a blank piece of paper (*neyar chalak*), declared "this is your *get*," she is considered *megureshet* — divorced. The reason? *Chashishinan shema be'mei milin katava* — we are concerned that he may have written it in *mei milin*, water in which gallnuts had been steeped, a substance that produces a mark initially visible but prone to disappearing entirely.

This is a genuinely shocking proposition. The document is, by all appearances, blank. Why should there be any concern, and on what basis would such a claim be entertained? The *Gemara* does not immediately address those deeper questions; instead it first confronts a textual challenge from a *beraita*.

### Beraita Challenge

*Meitivei* — the *Gemara* raises a difficulty from a *beraita*: a man gives his wife a *get* saying *harei zeh gittech*, and she, in her anger, hurls it into the sea, or into fire, or destroys it in any manner. He then claims it was never a genuine *get* at all — it was a *shtar pasim*, a document he carried to project an appearance of wealth, or a *shtar amanah*, a pre-signed IOU before actual lending — in short, some other kind of document, not a bill of divorce. The *beraita* rules: *eino ne'eman* — he is not believed. Once he declared it a *get*, he cannot retroactively render her forbidden to remarry.

The *Gemara* draws an inference: *ta'ama de'ika ktav* — the reason the *beraita* works is that there *was* writing on the document, and his claim now contradicts that prior declaration. But the implication is sharp: *ha leka ktav* — had the document been blank, the outcome would presumably be different, and we would not consider the wife divorced. If *Shmuel*'s concern were correct — that even a blank document might constitute a *get* — the *beraita* would have taught the case of a blank document, where the *chiddush* would be even greater. The fact that it did not suggests that a blank document carries no such concern.

### Shmuel & Beraita

The *Gemara* resolves the tension: *hacha bamai askinan de'badkinan leh be'maya de'nara* — the *beraita* actually deals with a case where the document was subsequently processed with some other liquid that brought out previously invisible writing. When examined with this reagent, it became clear that something had in fact been written. So the *beraita*'s case was never truly blank; it always contained writing, merely invisible, and the processing revealed it.

But this resolution immediately softens the radicalism of *Shmuel*'s ruling. If the invisible writing can be made visible through processing, then we are no longer dealing with a document that is *entirely* blank — we now have actual evidence that something was written. The *Gemara* presses further: *ve'hashta de'pilit mai havei hashta hu de'pilit* — even if the writing emerges now under processing, what does that accomplish? At the moment the *get* was handed over, it was blank. We have established throughout the *mishna*'s discussion that writing must be visible to function as a valid *get*. What does it matter that it becomes visible only now?

The *Gemara* answers: *Shmuel nami chashinan ka'amar* — *Shmuel* too only means that we are *concerned*, not that she is definitively divorced. The concern is that the writing may have been visible at the precise moment of transfer and disappeared only afterward. *Tosafot* clarifies: had witnesses observed the document to be blank at the very moment of handover, there would be no concern at all, not even a *safek megureshet*. The case *Shmuel* contemplates is one where the document was examined only later and found to be blank, with no contemporaneous observation at the moment of transfer.

### Processing Invisible Ink

Building on this, the *Gemara*'s conclusion is that a completely blank document about which nothing further can be demonstrated raises no concern. The *beraita* at most suggested concern when there was writing. But where processing reveals that the document *had* been written in a disappearing ink, then *Shmuel* holds that there is at least a *safek megureshet* — for perhaps the writing was visible when the *get* was handed over. *I pali pali, ve'i lo pali lo*: if the processing reveals the writing, there is a concern; if nothing emerges, there is none.

---

## Witnesses Reading Get

### Reading Before Handing

The *Gemara* now cites *Ameimar* transmitting in the name of *Mareimar* in the name of *Rav Dimi*: *hani bei trei de'yahavi gita kamaihu tzerichinu lemikrei* — when two witnesses are present at the handing of a *get*, they are required to read it beforehand. This makes abundant sense. According to the view that *edei mesirah karsi* — the witnesses to the delivery are the operative legal witnesses — they must know what it is they are observing, for it is their observation that constitutes the testimony to the *get*'s content. And even according to *edei chasima karsi*, where the signed witnesses are primary, reading beforehand at least addresses the concerns already raised about invisible ink and disputed claims.

### Beraita Without Reading

*Meitivei* — the *Gemara* challenges this from the very same *beraita* cited earlier: a man gives a *get*, the woman destroys it, he claims it was something else, and the rule is *eino ne'eman*. But if witnesses had read the *get* beforehand, how could he possibly make such a claim? *Batar de'karyei mi matzei amar lei hachi* — once they have read it, his assertion that it was a different type of document is instantly refuted. The fact that the *beraita* must teach the ruling at all implies that no such reading had taken place.

### Resolution & Pockets

The *Gemara* resolves this: *lo tzericha de'batar de'karyei ayeilu le'vei yadei ve'afkeih* — the witnesses did read it, but after reading it, the husband put it back into his jacket pocket and withdrew it again before handing it over. His claim is not merely that the document was something else from the start, but that he performed an actual switch — he palmed a different document when he reached into his pocket. The *beraita* therefore teaches *kama mashma lan* that we are not concerned with such a claim, even if technically conceivable. The witnesses read it, they saw it handed over, and his assertion of a switcheroo is not believed.

### Tosafot Lechatchila Deba…

*Tosafot* raises an important question from this sugya. Why did the *Gemara* not simply explain the *beraita* as a *bedieved* case — one where the witnesses had failed to read it, the *get* is nonetheless valid *bedieved*, and the *beraita* therefore must address the consequent claim that it was a different document? The fact that the *Gemara* did not take that route implies that even *bedieved*, if the witnesses did not read the *get*, it is invalid. This is a highly practical question: if witnesses failed to read the *get* at the time of delivery, must one treat the divorce as ineffective even after the fact?

*Tosafot* works through the back and forth without settling it in a simple formula. What the *Gemara* does clearly establish is that the requirement to read is at least *lechatchila*, and there are strong grounds to view it as operative even *bedieved*.

### Reading Before & After

The final line of that *Tosafot* is worth highlighting. *Tosafot* records that the *Ri* had a standard practice: the witnesses would read the *get* both before the delivery and after — before, because the *Gemara* makes clear that the primary obligation is prior to handing, so that at the moment of transfer the witnesses know what they are observing; and after, to foreclose any claim that a switch had been made in the interval between reading and delivery, precisely the concern raised by the *Gemara*'s resolution.

*Tosafot* adds: it is *pshita* — obvious — that even if one holds that reading is necessary *bedieved*, if the witnesses read the document not before but after handing, and the woman returned it to them to examine, and they confirmed it was a *get*, that would suffice. For any evidentiary concern is resolved: there is no possibility of a pocket switch, and they can clearly testify to what was transferred. One might argue it is not so *pashut* — if the legal moment of transfer is the handing itself, and at that instant the witnesses had not yet verified the contents, perhaps their subsequent reading cannot retroactively complete the act. This touches broader questions about combining observations across time, analogous to debates about whether witnesses who observed a ring on a woman's finger after it was placed, having not directly seen the placement, can combine those perceptions. These remain significant questions in the laws of *gittin*.

---

## Found Document Cases

### Mezuza Case

The *Gemara* now presents a series of found-document cases that build on the earlier discussion. *Hahu gavra de'zarak leh gita le'deveiteih le'veini danei* — a man threw a *get* to his wife, and it landed among stacked barrels of wine in her space. When they went to retrieve it, they found not a *get* but a *mezuza*. The dimensions of a *mezuza* are, apparently, close enough to those of a *get* in this period to raise the question. Is this the very document he threw her, meaning he actually handed her a *mezuza* while claiming it was a *get* — perhaps withdrawing the real *get* from his pocket and substituting the *mezuza*, in light of what we just discussed — or did he genuinely throw a *get* that is now buried deeper in the barrel pile, while the *mezuza* had been there independently?

### Rav Nachman's Logic

*Rav Nachman* rules: *mezuzta be'vei danei lo shechicha* — it is not common to find a *mezuza* among wine barrels. The presence of this *mezuza* is therefore suspicious and must be explained. Since we know a document of that size was thrown, and this is the only such object found, the presumption must be that this *mezuza* is what he actually gave her — in which case she is not divorced.

However, this logic applies only when a single *mezuza* is found. *Aval bitartei u'tlat* — if two or three *mezuzot* are discovered among the barrels, then since some of them were clearly there before the incident, the reasonable assumption is that all of them were pre-existing, and that the document actually thrown was a *get* now unaccounted for.

### Lost Get Reasoning

As for the missing *get* in the two-or-three *mezuzot* case: *ve'gita eimar achbarim shakluho* — the *get* may simply have been dragged off by rats, as documents in such locations often were. The inability to produce the *get* is therefore no bar to treating the wife as divorced, especially in light of what was established earlier: once a *get* is properly given, declared by the husband, and — ideally — read by the witnesses, the absence of the document afterward need not undermine the divorce.

### Sefer Torah Get

The *Gemara* then describes a far more dramatic case. *Hahu gavra de'al le'vei knishta, shakal sefer torah yahav leh le'deveiteih ve'amar lah ha gitich* — a man entered a *beit knesset*, took a *Sefer Torah*, handed it to his wife, and declared it to be her *get*. *Rav Yosef* dismissed the concern that this could constitute a valid *get*, and then enumerated the reasons. Could we be concerned about *mei milin*? Perhaps he wrote a *get* in disappearing ink on the parchment of the *Sefer Torah*, it was visible at transfer, and now is no longer seen. The *Gemara* answers: *mei milin agabi mei milin* — the *klaf* of a *Sefer Torah* is itself treated with *mei milin* during its preparation, and therefore *mei milin* written on it would never be visible to begin with. There is consequently no moment at which such writing could have appeared, and no basis for the concern *Shmuel* raised.

Could the *Sefer Torah* itself serve as a *sefer kritut* by virtue of the very *parasha* containing *ve'chatav lah sefer kritut*? Perhaps the Torah's own text constitutes a bill of severance. The answer: *habe'inan ve'chasav lah lishmah ve'leka* — the *get* must be written *lishmah*, for the sake of this particular woman, and a *Sefer Torah* written by a *sofer* in the normal course of his work was not written with any such intention. Moreover, even if he had paid the *sofer* to write that *parasha* with his wife in mind, *habe'inan shino shemo ve'shemah ve'shem iro ve'shem irah ve'leka* — a valid *get* requires the names of the husband, the wife, and their respective cities, none of which appear in the text of the Torah. *Tosafot* notes that while the *lishmah* requirement in the context of *sota* may be more flexible — since the scraping itself is an integral part of the ritual, perhaps reducing the demands on the *ve'chasav* — the *lishmah* of a *get* is categorically different. It is an expression of the husband's will and intent, not merely a technical condition of the writing, and therefore cannot be satisfied by a generic text written by a *sofer* in the ordinary course.

So *Rav Yosef*'s statement that "there is nothing to worry about" is straightforward in all its components. What, then, is his *chiddush*?

### Mei Milin on Klaf

*She'ein mei milin agabi mei milin* — the *chiddush* is specifically the teaching that a *Sefer Torah*'s *klaf*, having been treated with *mei milin* in preparation, renders any writing in *mei milin* permanently invisible from the outset. This is not obvious. One might have thought that *mei milin* on *mei milin* could still produce some temporary visibility, analogous to *Shmuel*'s concern about disappearing ink on ordinary paper. *Rav Yosef* teaches that this is not the case, and that concern is therefore entirely inapplicable to a *Sefer Torah*.

---

## Lishmah & Overwriting

### Lishmah Overwriting

Having discussed the *lishmah* requirement in the context of the *Sefer Torah* case, the *Gemara* now turns to a related and practically significant question. *Rav Chisda* states: *get she'kesavo shelo lishmah ve'he'evir alav kolmos lishmah, banu lemachlokes Rabbi Yehuda ve'Rabanan* — if a *get* was written *shelo lishmah*, with all the correct names but without the particular intention toward this husband and wife, and the scribe subsequently passed the pen over the writing again with proper *lishmah* intention — writing directly on top of the existing letters — does that retroactively or effectively confer *lishmah*? *Rav Chisda* says this question is the subject of a *machlokes* between *Rabbi Yehuda* and the *Rabbanan*.

### God's Name Overwrite

The *Gemara* cites the relevant *beraita*: a *sofer* writing a *Sefer Torah* arrived at the divine name — *Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei* — but in his mind he had *yehudah* in mind. He wrote the letters *Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei* correctly, but his intention was for the word *Yehudah*, not for *shem Hashem*; he simply forgot to add the *dalet*. The name was thus written *shelo lishmah*. *Rabbi Yehuda* says: *ma'avir alav kolmos u'mikadsho* — pass the pen over the name again, this time with proper intention for *shem Hashem*, and this sanctifies it. *Va'chachamim omrim eino shem min hamuvchar* — the Sages say this is not the proper way to write God's name. The context of the ruling suggests this is a *bedieved* dispute, not merely a *lechatchila* preference. *Rav Chisda* holds that the same dispute governs the *lishmah* of a *get*: *Rabbi Yehuda* would permit overwriting to supply the missing *lishmah*, while the *Rabbanan* would reject it.

### Rav Acha Distinction

*Rav Acha bar Yaakov* pushes back: *dilma lo hi* — perhaps the two cases are not identical. The *Rabbanan*' rejection of the overwritten divine name may rest on a specific principle: *ad kan lo kamri rabbanan hasam de'be'inan zeh Eli ve'anveihu* — the Sages' stringency in that case derives from the demand for *noi mitzvah*, the glorification of God's name implied by the verse "this is my God and I will glorify Him." Writing the divine name by tracing over an improperly intended prior inscription is simply not dignified enough — the name ends up as a piggyback on a name that was not created with the proper sanctity, and the whole of *shem Hashem* was not formed *lishmah* from the outset. That specific demand of dignity and glorification may not apply to the *lishmah* of a *get*, and therefore *aval hacha lo* — here, perhaps everyone would agree that overwriting with *lishmah* intention is valid.

### Tosafot Missing Component

*Tosafot* notes a tension with an earlier discussion in the sugya. Earlier, the *Gemara* considered whether witnesses could effectively sign a *get* by tracing over letters that already bore their names, written in a light ink, with a darker ink. There, the *Gemara* was hesitant to accept ink-over-ink as constituting a valid signature. Yet here, *Rav Chisda* treats overwriting as at least the position of *Rabbi Yehuda* and perhaps universally valid. How are these consistent?

*Tosafot* distinguishes the two cases as follows. In the case of the *get*'s *lishmah*, the first writing — though physically correct — lacked the essential component of *lishmah*. Because *lishmah* was absent, the first writing in a certain sense did not fully constitute the act of writing required by the *get*. The second writing therefore comes to replace what was deficient with something properly accomplished; it creates something new, even though the letters look physically identical before and after. The earlier case of witness signatures is categorically different: the underlying writing was fully valid in every respect. There was no missing component. The act of writing the signature had already been completed — nothing was lacking. A second tracing of identical letters over a complete prior writing adds nothing, for nothing was absent to be supplied.

One could alternatively frame the distinction thus: in the signature case, the problem was whether the act of writing had occurred at all, and since writing had already occurred, the second pass added no new act. Here, the problem is not whether writing occurred but whether *lishmah* is present — and perhaps *lishmah* can be introduced by an act of rewriting even when the physical substrate already exists, precisely because *lishmah* is not the act of writing itself but a quality that can be inserted into an already-written text.

---

## Rav Chisda's Concern

### Invalidate All Gittin

The *Gemara* now records a remarkable theoretical statement. *Rav Chisda* says: *yachilna lemipsal lechol gittei de'alma* — I could construct an argument to invalidate every *get* in the world. He presents this as a theoretical observation, not a practical ruling. *Rava* asks: what is the argument?

### Woman's Payment Issue

*Rav Chisda*'s first suggestion: the Torah says the husband should write the *get* — *ve'chasav* — but in practice it is the woman who pays the *sofer*'s fees. If she is the one commissioning and paying the scribe, one might argue the scribe is functionally her agent, not the husband's, undermining the requirement that the husband be the effective author. *Rava* dismisses this: *vedilma aknoiyei aknu lei rabanan* — the *Rabbanan* may have established that even though the wife pays, the fee is legally assigned to the husband, so that the *sofer* is treated as an agent of the husband. The practical arrangement of payment does not determine the halakhic attribution of agency.

### Material Value & Issurei

The second possible argument: the Torah says *ve'natan* — he must *give* it to her — and perhaps this implies that the object given must have monetary value, at least a *perutah*. Yet the *mishna* permits writing a *get* on a leaf or other minimal-value material. Perhaps the *get* is therefore not a proper act of giving.

### Issurei Hana'ah Valid

The *Gemara* rejects this line of reasoning by citing a ruling sent from the West, from *Eretz Yisrael*: *ketavo al issurei hana'ah kasher* — a *get* written on an object from which benefit is forbidden is valid. This is a striking ruling. An object of *issurei hana'ah* has, by definition, no halakhic monetary value — indeed, there is a fundamental debate in the *poskim* as to whether such objects can even be considered property in a meaningful legal sense. Yet the *get* is valid. This demonstrates that *ve'natan* does not require a transfer of monetary ownership at all. The obligation is the physical act of handing the object, *netinat get*, not the conveyance of an item of value. The *get* belongs to a different conceptual framework from ordinary *kinyanim* — acquisition is not the operative act; the physical delivery is.

*Rav Ashi* notes that this principle might already be derivable from the *mishna* itself, which permits writing on an olive leaf. The *Gemara* responds that an olive leaf is still worth something — in aggregate, many such leaves have value, and a single leaf is therefore not literally worthless. An object of *issurei hana'ah* is a categorically more extreme case, and the ruling from *Eretz Yisrael* is therefore a genuine *chiddush*.

### Levi's Announcement

The *Gemara* records a *beraita*: *Rebbi* said that writing a *get* on *issurei hana'ah* is *kasher*. *Levi* went out to publicize this ruling *mishmeih de'Rebbi*, and the people did not praise it — presumably because they were uncomfortable accepting it as the position of a single authority. He then taught it *mishmei d'rabbanan* — as the consensus of the Sages — and it was praised. *Amar hilchata ke'vassai* — from this we derive that this is the operative *halacha*.

*Rashi* understands that we learn the *psak* from *Levi*'s own behavior: his insistence on teaching it as consensus opinion, and his discomfort with its being received as a *da'at yachid*, reflects his own conviction that it was the correct *psak*, and the *Gemara* accepts his determination. *Tosafot* disagrees: we learn from the audience's reaction. When the ruling was presented as a lone opinion they were not opposed to its substance — they simply disliked it being framed as a *da'at yachid*. When *Levi* reframed it as consensus, they accepted it enthusiastically, demonstrating that the community of scholars recognized it as the accepted *halacha*.

---

## Writing: Ink vs. Carving

### Writing Not Engraving

The *Gemara* now turns to the fundamental requirement of *ketivah* — writing — in the context of a *get*. A *beraita* teaches: *ve'chasav ve'lo chakak* — the verse says "he shall write," not "he shall engrave." *Chikuk* — engraving or carving — is not *ketivah*. The underlying distinction is clear: writing involves applying a substance to a surface to form letters; engraving involves carving away material, neither adding ink nor producing letters through deposition. The mode of creation is fundamentally different.

### Tablets Engraving

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this: *eved she'yatza bi'ktav she'al gabei tavla u'pinkas yatza le'cheirus* — a slave who received a *shtar shichrur* written on a tablet or *pinkas* goes free. These tablets — typically wood surfaced with wax — were written on with a stylus, a process that is inherently a form of *chakika*, engraving into the wax rather than depositing ink. Yet such a document is valid. Furthermore, the *beraita* specifies that writing on a *kipa* or *anduchtri* — some form of a garment — with sewn or attached letters is *not* valid. *Rashi* understands this as letters that have been cut out separately and affixed to the surface. The problem is not that they are engraved but that they are not integrated into the medium — the letters are merely incidentally attached and can be removed without disturbing the surface itself. This implies that the problem with the garment case is the lack of integration, not the mode of inscription, and therefore that *chakika* per se on a proper surface is acceptable.

### Chok Tocho & Yerechot

*Ulla* in the name of *Rabbi Elazar* resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between two types of carving. *Chak tochot* — carving out the interior space — means that rather than tracing the shape of the letter with the stylus, one removes the material *surrounding* the letter, so that the letter is left standing raised. *Chak yerachot* — carving the legs, i.e., the letter-form itself — means the stylus traces the actual shape of the letter directly, carving into the surface to form the letter's contours.

The critical distinction: in *chak yerachot*, the act of the hand traces the shape of the letter itself, analogously to the act of writing with ink. The instrument is working directly on the letter. In *chak tochot*, the instrument works on the space around the letter; the letter itself is never directly acted upon — it merely remains as what was not carved away. It follows that *chak yerachot* is *ketivah*, while *chak tochot* is not.

This distinction is also operative in laws of *Sefer Torah*. If a drop of ink fell into the interior of a *chet*, creating a solid rectangle rather than two legs joined by a roof, and one fixes it by scraping away the ink from the interior — the *chet* has been created by *chak tochot*, working on the interior space rather than forming the letter itself, and the letter is therefore invalid.

### Tzitz Protruding

The *Gemara* now challenges the ruling that *chak tochot* is invalid. The *tzitz* — the frontplate worn by the *Kohen Gadol* — bore the inscription *Kodesh l'Hashem*, and the *Gemara* states: *lo haya ketavo shoke'a ela bolet ke'dinrei zahav* — the letters were not sunken/engraved into the surface; rather they protruded, like the letters on a gold *dinar*. But the *tzitz* is described with the verb *ve'chatavta alav* — "you shall write upon it" — so the protruding letters must constitute *ketivah*. How? If letters protrude because the material *around* them has been pushed down or carved away, that is *chak tochot*, which we have said is not *ketivah*. And the analogy to *dinrei zahav* — minted gold coins — is itself problematic: coins are produced by pressing the material around the image down into a mold, so that the image remains raised — a paradigmatic case of *chak tochot*.

The *Gemara* answers: *ke'dinrei zahav ve'lo ke'dinrei zahav* — like *dinrei zahav* in that the letters protrude, but not like *dinrei zahav* in method. For coins, *de'ilu hatam tochot* — the protruding letters result from pushing down the surrounding material, which is *chak tochot*. For the *tzitz*, *ve'hacha yerachot* — the protruding letters were formed by engraving the letter-form itself from the *back* of the plate. When one engraves the letter from the reverse side, it causes the corresponding area on the front to protrude. The act of the hand was tracing the shape of the letter — *chak yerachot* — even though the visible result on the front is a raised letter rather than a sunken one. Working from the back, one is still directly forming the letter-shape, which constitutes *ketivah*.

This does raise a natural question: when engraving from the rear, one is working on the letter in reverse, relating to the mirror image of its form. The *Gemara* does not treat this as a disqualification, implicitly holding that working directly on the letter-form — even in reverse from behind — is a more genuine act of *ketivah* than working on the surrounding space from the front.

### Coins Minting

*Ravina* then raises a precise question to *Rav Ashi*: *rushma michratz charitz o kinufay michnaf* — when a metal-pressing die is used to mint a coin, what conceptually is occurring? Does the die push *down* the material around the image — carving out the space, which would be *chak tochot* — with the raised areas simply remaining as they were? Or does it push *in* the material that will become the raised image — pressing the metal into the indentations in the mold, so that one is effectively working on the letter-areas themselves? The conceptual answer matters for how we classify the act.

*Rav Ashi* answers: *michratz charitz* — the die pushes down the surrounding material. The raised letters remain raised not because they were pushed up but because the space around them was pushed down. This is *chak tochot* and, for purposes of *ketivah*, is not considered writing. This is consistent with everything said until now.

### Yerechot is Writing

The *Gemara* then raises the *tzitz* passage once more — the same challenge, the same answer. *Ve'lo ke'dinrei zahav de'ilu hatam migavai ve'hacha mibarai* — coins are made by working the die from the front, pushing down the surroundings; the *tzitz* was worked from the back, tracing the letter-form itself.

The conclusions of the sugya: a *get* does not require ink in the conventional sense — the physical deposit of a marking substance on a surface. Engraving without any liquid substance can constitute *ketivah*, provided the act of engraving directly traces the form of the letters themselves (*chak yerachot*). If instead the space around the letters is what is worked upon, leaving the letter raised by default (*chak tochot*), this is not *ketivah*. And sewing separately-cut letters onto a garment is likewise invalid, because the letters are not integrated into their background medium — they exist independently and are merely attached. The question of whether embroidered letters, sewn into the fabric of a garment by threading through it, would be more analogous to *chak yerachot* — as the needle traces the letter-form directly — or would suffer from the same lack of surface-integration as affixed cut-out letters, remains a question the *Gemara* leaves to further reflection.

---

---

# Gittin 21

## Value vs. Transfer

### Gold Plate Get

The daf opens with a question posed by Rava to Rav Nachman: what is the *halacha* in a case where a husband wrote a *get* on a gold plate — a *tass* of gold, some kind of gold foil — and then said to his wife, *hiskabli giteich v'hiskabli kesuvasech*, "receive your *get* and receive your *kesuva*"? The value of the gold on which the *get* is written is substantial, and the husband is proposing that this very value constitutes payment of her *kesuva*. What is the *halakha*? Is it a valid *get*, and does the value of the gold discharge the *kesuva* obligation?

The question turns on an issue already in play from the previous daf. The giving of a *get* requires a physical transfer of the object. But what exactly is the nature of that transfer — is it about the object's monetary value being conveyed, or is it simply the physical handing over of the thing? We established previously that even a leaf of an olive tree, worth less than a *perutah*, or even an item that is *issurei hana'ah* — something from which benefit is forbidden, which may not even be capable of being owned — nonetheless constitutes a valid *get* when physically handed over. That being so, if value is irrelevant to the act of giving a *get*, why can't the value of the gold *get* simultaneously serve as payment of the *kesuva*?

### Tosafot on Object

Tosafot addresses this directly. He acknowledges that we write a *get* on *issurei hana'ah* and it is valid — so value is clearly not the defining feature. Why, then, should attributing value to the *get* pose any problem? Tosafot answers: *hai mishum d'yehav la miah kol ha-get* — in the standard case, there is only one thing happening: the object is being given over entirely as a *get*. But here, *lo yehav la ela tofsa* — if you have a ten-thousand-dollar *get* and the focus is on the monetary value, the act of conveyance begins to look like the transfer of a valuable object rather than the giving of a *get*. The concern is that the nature of the act may be redefined by the monetary dimension. Tosafot ultimately concludes, however, that both things can be happening simultaneously — the physical giving constitutes the *get* and the taking of possession of the valuable object constitutes payment of the *kesuva*.

### Margins Teaching

The *Gemara* then introduces a *baraita* that raises a related question. Suppose the husband says to his wife: *hiskabli giteich v'hashar l'kesuvasech* — "receive your *get*, and the remainder goes toward your *kesuva*." That is, the *get* was written on a piece of gold, and the margins — the portions not covered by the writing — should serve as *kesuva* payment. This arrangement is ruled valid: it is a good *get* and the margins discharge the *kesuva*.

The *Gemara* infers from this that *taima d'ika shar* — the reason it works is precisely because there are margins. This implies that if the area of the *get* itself were to pay off the *kesuva*, that would not work — it would redefine the nature of the act. But the *Gemara* immediately rejects this inference: *hu hadin af al gav d'leka shar* — even with no margins at all, even if the entire *get* also serves as the *kesuva* payment, it is valid. The reason the *baraita* mentioned the case with margins is to teach something else entirely: that even when there are margins, the husband cannot unilaterally retain them. If he says nothing, *ada'ata d'megilta hu* — the margins are considered part of the scroll as a unified object, and she is entitled to the whole thing. Only if he explicitly specifies, before the giving, that the margins are to be credited toward the *kesuva*, does he retain that claim.

### Possession Principle

What emerges from these discussions is a consistent underlying principle: the giving of a *get* is not governed by the logic of *kinyan* — of acquiring monetary ownership. The *get* can be worth less than a *perutah*, can be worth nothing, and by some opinions, an item of *issurei hana'ah* may not even be capable of being owned at all. Nevertheless, the physical transfer of the *get* is valid. So complete is the separation between the act of giving the *get* and the logic of *dinei mamonot* that two entirely distinct acts can occur simultaneously: the physical giving of the *get* constitutes the divorce, while the taking of possession of the same object constitutes payment of the *kesuva*.

---

## Paper Ownership

### Husband Retains Paper

The *Gemara* now turns to a *baraita* that directly tests the limits of this principle. If a husband says *harei ze giteich v'haniyar sheli* — "here is your *get*, but the paper is mine" — she is not divorced. This is qualitatively different from the case of *issurei hana'ah*. In the *issurei hana'ah* case, no one can own the paper, and yet it is fully in her possession; he has no claim to it. Here, by asserting ownership, the husband is in effect not fully giving the object over. The retention of ownership means the transfer is incomplete.

### Conditional Return

By contrast, if he says *al menat she-tachziri li es haniyar* — "on the condition that you return the paper to me" — she is divorced. The giving is complete. She takes full possession of the *get*; she simply has a future obligation to return the paper. This is structurally like a *matana al menat lehachzir* — a conditional gift — in which the act of giving is whole and unimpaired even though the object must eventually be returned. The *get* is fully under her control at the moment of giving, and she is therefore divorced.

### White Space Question

Rav Pappa then poses a more refined question: what if the husband says he is retaining not the paper on which the letters are written, but only the white space between the words and between the lines — *bein shita l'shita, bein teiva l'teiva*? Is she divorced?

On the one hand, perhaps what he is retaining is not really the *get* itself, since she receives full possession of everything the letters are written on. On the other hand, if one were to physically remove the paper he is claiming — all the white space surrounding the letters — what would remain would be tiny, disconnected scraps. Can that truly be called a *get*?

### Teiku on Letters

The *Gemara* leaves this as *teiku* — unresolved.

The *Gemara* considers whether this should be obvious from the rule that a *get* must be a single, unified document — *safra echad Rachmana, v'lo shnayim u'shlosha sfarim* — and not multiple pieces. But it answers: *lo tzricha dime'ura* — the case is one in which the letters are written in an interwoven fashion, such that removing the claimed white space would still leave the letters physically connected. For example, a *lamed* from one line might extend into the space below, connecting with the next line, so that even after excision of the "white space," the document would remain one physical unit.

The difficulty with this answer, however, is not resolved neatly. If the document is truly constructed so that it would remain whole even after the husband's space is removed, it is not clear why it should not simply be valid. And if it cannot remain whole, it is not clear why the *Gemara* even entertains the possibility of validity. This is, in truth, a puzzling *teiku*, and it is not entirely clear what the *Gemara* finds genuinely uncertain.

### Interwoven Letters

Rashi explains *dime'ura* as meaning that the letters were intentionally written long so as to reach from line to line at the head of each word — *otiyot arukot hamagi'ot mishita l'shita b'rosh kol teiva v'teiva* — thereby creating physical connection throughout the document. On Rashi's reading, the construction is comprehensive enough to ensure continuity.

The *Ribam* — Rabbeinu Yitzchak bar Mordechai — draws a different conclusion. He argues there is no proof here, because *dime'ura* refers only to cases where letters from one line intrude naturally into the space of the adjacent line — a *regel kaf* of an upper line into the space of the line below, or a *lamed* into a *heh* or *chet* above it — not to letters that are actually touching one another. Moreover, the *Ribam* argues, there is no proof that letters touching is required in a *get* at all; that requirement may be specific to a *Sefer Torah*.

Tosafot, meanwhile, derives a broader principle from this passage: since the *Gemara* discusses the case of *dime'ura* — interwoven letters — and treats it as the operative scenario where the question becomes meaningful, it follows that the letters must actually be touching for the concern to be meaningful. The *Ribam* disputes this, maintaining that touching letters are not required, and that the concern arises simply from the structural configuration described. The question of whether letters in a *get* must have white space around them, or whether touching letters invalidate it, is left as a live debate between these *rishonim*.

---

## Slave as Medium

### Slave Holding Get

Rami Bar Chama poses the following question: it was known that a certain slave belonged to the husband; a *get* was written on the slave's arm; and now the slave is found in the possession of the wife — *harei hu yotze mitachas yada*. What is the *halakha*? Is she divorced?

The question is whether we say *akneiye aknei lah* — that the husband formally transferred the slave to her — or *dilma hu minafshei azal* — perhaps the slave simply walked over of his own accord, since slaves are capable of independent movement, and her physical possession of the slave proves nothing about whether it was deliberately given over as a *get*. This seems, on its face, to be a general question of evidentiary standards in ownership, not a *get*-specific question.

### Tattooing Objection

Rava interjects with a prior objection: before we even reach the question of whether the slave was transferred, the *get* written in ink on the slave's arm is susceptible to forgery — it could be erased and rewritten. That disqualifies it as a valid document, regardless of how it was transferred.

The *Gemara* responds: this is *kashia matnitin* — how does Rava explain the *Mishna*, which explicitly permits writing a *get* on a slave's hand? Rava answers: the *Mishna* is referring to a case of *eidei mesira* — witnesses present at the moment of transfer, who can testify to what was written. This is consistent with Rabbi Elazar's position. In such a case, the document's susceptibility to forgery is irrelevant because the witnesses themselves attest to the content and the transfer.

### Tattooed Resolution

Returning to Rami Bar Chama's question: since his case involves no witnesses to the transfer — the entire question is whether the slave's presence in her possession constitutes proof — the problem of forgery is real. The *Gemara* resolves this by stipulating that the case involves *biksivat ka'aka* — a tattoo. A tattooed *get* cannot be forged. The document is therefore valid and not subject to the forgery concern.

Tosafot notes that tattooing involves a potential *issur de'oraisa* only when performed with certain specific inks, as described in the third chapter of *Makkot*, and that even an *issur de'rabbanan* may attach in some configurations. However, Tosafot concludes that even if an *issur de'oraisa* were involved, it would not prevent the tattooed inscription from functioning as a valid *get*.

### Flocks Rule

The underlying question — whether the slave's presence in her possession is sufficient proof that it was transferred — is addressed by the principle stated by Resh Lakish: *ha-godot ein lahem chazakah* — flocks have no presumption of ownership based on possession alone. An animal that moves on its own can arrive in your yard without having been transferred. Accordingly, possession of a moving creature does not establish ownership the way possession of a static object does. For flocks — and similarly for slaves — one establishes ownership either through three years of uncontested possession or through a bill of sale.

### Slave Possession

Tosafot raises the question: if this rule is well established, what was the *safek* — the doubt — that prompted Rami Bar Chama's question? The answer Tosafot offers is that perhaps the combination of physical possession *and* the presence of a *get* written on the slave should together serve as proof that it was deliberately given over. But that argument ultimately fails, since the *halacha* of *ein lahem chazakah* is decisive.

There is, however, a more analytically interesting dimension to this question. We have established throughout this daf that the giving of a *get* does not require the kind of monetary transfer recognized by *dinei mamonot*. It can be given on *issurei hana'ah*, objects that may not be capable of conventional ownership. If that is so, perhaps the *standards of proof* for a *get* are also distinct from the standards of *dinei mamonot*. One might argue that even if physical possession of a slave does not prove ownership in *dinei mamonot*, it might nonetheless constitute sufficient evidence that she received the *get*, since for *get* purposes we are not operating within the framework of *Choshen Mishpat* but of *Even HaEzer*. The act of transfer might not need to mirror a monetary *kinyan*. 

Conversely, one could argue the reverse: that even if after three years she could establish ownership of the slave under *dinei mamonot*, that still would not retroactively prove that the *get* was given to her at the outset, since the evidence of *get* transfer must be apparent from the moment of giving — not established through a process that takes years to complete.

The *Gemara*'s resolution via *ein lahem chazakah* seems to cut across both frameworks, essentially holding that the slave was not even genuinely "in her possession" in any legally cognizable sense, and the question therefore fails on its own terms.

---

## Sefer Makneh

### Tablet Ownership

Rami Bar Chama poses a related question: it was known that a woman owned a particular *tavla* — a tablet — and a *get* was written on it. Now the husband is found holding it. What is the *halakha*? Can the *get* be valid?

The scenario is that she gave him the tablet specifically so he could write a *get* on it and give it back to her. But for a *get* to be valid, the husband must own the document — the principle of *sefer makneh* requires that the document be owned by the party transferring it. The question is whether she genuinely transferred ownership to him, or whether, since she expected to receive it back, her intention was never a full and complete transfer of ownership. This is analogous to the classic question of whether a bride can give her groom a family heirloom ring for him to give back to her under the *chuppa* — is the initial giving considered a real transfer if the return is anticipated from the outset?

### Woman's Knowledge

Abaye frames the uncertainty differently: *lo yad'ah la'akneye* — perhaps a person in this situation simply does not know that they are legally required to fully transfer ownership of the object even when expecting it back. The question is not only one of intent but of awareness.

### Elder Lender Case

Abaye then invokes a precedent: the testimony of Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava regarding a certain small village near Jerusalem, where there was one elder who would lend money to all the village residents. He would write the loan documents in his own handwriting — *bichtav yado* — and other people would sign as witnesses. This practice was brought before the *Chachamim* and validated.

The *Gemara* asks: how does this work? The concept of *sefer makneh* requires that the document be owned by the party from whom it passes. In a loan transaction, it is the borrower who must ultimately convey the document to the lender. But here, the lender was preparing all the documents himself. The answer implied by the *Gemara* is that the elder would prepare the document, hand it to the borrower, have witnesses sign it, and the borrower would then hand it back. Even though the borrower knew the document was coming back to the lender, the act of taking possession and returning it constitutes a valid transfer. We therefore conclude: *akneiye aknei lehu* — we presume that someone can and does fully transfer an object even knowing it will be returned to them.

### Tosafot Distinction

Tosafot questions whether *sefer makneh* truly applies to a loan document, as opposed to a document effecting a transfer of property. Tosafot's distinction is that the formal requirement of *sefer makneh* — which derives from a *pasuk* — applies to a *shtar* that itself operates as the instrument of transfer or change of status, such as a deed of sale or a *get*. A *shtar raya* — a document that merely serves as evidence that a transaction occurred, such as a simple loan record — may not carry the same formal requirement regarding which party must own the physical document, since it is the testimony of the witnesses, not the object itself, that does the legal work. Tosafot therefore suggests that the elder lender was also handling property transfer documents for his borrowers, not merely loan records, and those documents would indeed be subject to *sefer makneh*.

The plain reading of the *Gemara*, however, seems to apply *sefer makneh* across the board — whether the *shtar* effects a change or merely records evidence — requiring in all cases that the document be owned by the party conveying it.

### Co-signer Case

Rava challenges whether the precedent of the elder lender proves anything about a woman's knowledge and intent. Perhaps the elder was different — *zaken shani de-yada l'akneye* — he was the professional, the literate man of business, the one who arranged all the transactions in the village. It is reasonable to assume he knew precisely what legal formalities were required. One cannot extrapolate from his conduct to a case involving a woman who may not be versed in these requirements.

Rav Ashi therefore seeks a better precedent: the case of an *arev ha-yotze l'achar chitum shtarot* — a guarantor who signs a document after it has already been sealed and handed over to the lender. If I borrowed money from someone, signed a document and gave it over, and then a guarantor subsequently comes and signs it while the document is already in the lender's possession, this is a valid *halacha* under which the lender may collect from the guarantor. But how does that work?
