The *mishnah* records three opinions. The *Tanna Kamma* — the first, anonymous position — holds that one may write the boilerplate portion (*tofes*) of any document but must leave blank the essential particulars (*toref*).

### Rabbi Yehuda Position

*Rabbi Yehuda* takes a stringent view: *poseil bekullan* — he invalidates all of them. His position, as the *Gemara* will make clear, is that one may not write even the boilerplate portion of any document in advance, presumably out of concern that permitting the *tofes* will lead the scribe to inadvertently write the *toref* as well.

### Rabbi Eliezer

*Rabbi Elazar* presents a striking asymmetry: *machshir bekullan chutz migittei nashim* — he validates everything, except for bills of divorce. For *gittin*, he invokes the verse *bekosav lo lishmah* — the *lishmah* requirement — as the basis for a stringency that extends even to the boilerplate. But for all other documents, he permits the scribe to proceed freely.

The question this raises is what exactly *Rabbi Elazar* means by *machshir bekullan*. Is he merely restating what was already implicit — that the *tofes* of non-*get* documents may be written? *Rashi* reads him this way: *Rabbi Elazar* is not adding anything novel about other documents; he permits only the *tofes*, not the *toref*, exactly as the *Tanna Kamma* does. His distinctive position is solely his stringency about the *get*: even the boilerplate may not be pre-written there, as a protective measure (*gezeira*) against inadvertently writing the essential part without *lishmah*.

### Tosafot Reading

*Tosafot* offers a bolder reading — one that the *Gemara*'s subsequent discussion actually supports. According to *Tosafot*, *Rabbi Elazar* is simultaneously the most stringent and the most lenient of the three opinions. He is strictest regarding the *get*, where the *lishmah* requirement is paramount, and therefore prohibits even the boilerplate. But he is most lenient regarding everything else, precisely because *lishmah* is irrelevant there. In *Tosafot*'s reading, *machshir bekullan* means that for all non-*get* documents, the scribe may fill in the entire document — names, amounts, locations, everything — without any concern at all, provided only that the witnesses do not yet sign. There is no *lishmah* issue and no reason to withhold anything. The scribe who knows a land deal is being finalized may write out the entire document in full; the witnesses will sign when the transaction closes.

This produces a clean tripartite structure. The *Tanna Kamma* treats *get* and other documents symmetrically: *tofes* permitted, *toref* not, for all document types. *Rabbi Yehuda* treats them symmetrically in the opposite direction: nothing may be pre-written for any document, out of a cascading set of protective concerns. *Rabbi Elazar* distinguishes sharply: complete leniency for other documents, maximal stringency for a *get*.

One student raised the obvious practical concern: *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position, if followed as *halacha*, would invalidate the pre-printed forms that have been in universal use for centuries. The *Gemara* will confirm that we do not rule like *Rabbi Yehuda*.

---

## Gemara Resolution

### Harei at Muteret

The *Gemara* opens with a ruling from *Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel*: the *mishnah*'s requirement to leave blanks extends beyond the names and the date — *tzarich she'yaniach af makom harei at muteret le-chol adam*. The scribe must also leave blank the space for the essential phrase of the *get*: *harei at muteret le-chol adam*, "you are hereby permitted to any man." This is the punchline of the *get*, its operative declaration.

### Toref Requirement

This teaching clarifies the *lishmah* dimension of the *mishnah*. The *Tanna Kamma*'s requirement to leave blanks does not obviously signal a *lishmah* concern, since it applies equally to *shtarei milveh* and *shtarei mekach*, where *lishmah* is irrelevant. One might have concluded that the entire framework is about something else entirely. But *Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel* reads the *mishnah* as a *lishmah* ruling: the blanks must be left precisely because the essential content of the *get* must be written *lishmah*. And if *lishmah* applies, it applies not merely to the names — which could be seen as incidental — but to the *toref* proper, the operative declaration that constitutes the divorce.

Indeed, one might argue that the *lishmah* requirement, taken at face value from *vechatav lah*, should demand that every single word of the *get* be written *lishmah*. The *Gemara* is therefore being innovative in restricting the *lishmah* obligation to the *toref* alone and not the *tofes* — the boilerplate is explicitly excluded from the *lishmah* requirement. But within the *toref*, *lishmah* applies in full, and that includes *harei at muteret le-chol adam*.

### Gemara Attribution

The *Gemara* now makes explicit what *Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel* implies: the *mishnah*, including even the *Tanna Kamma*, is to be read according to *Rabbi Elazar*'s view — *k'Rabbi Elazar hi de-amar edei mesirah karti*. Since *Rabbi Elazar* holds that the witnesses of delivery (*eidei mesirah*) are what legally consummate the *get* rather than the witnesses who sign it, the essence of the *get* is its writing, not its signature. And since the writing is essential, *lishmah* in the writing is essential, which in turn explains why the blank for *harei at muteret le-chol adam* must be left unfilled: that phrase must be written *lishmah*.

### Three Cases

This reading of the *mishnah* as a *Rabbi Elazar* position is part of a broader interpretive project. *Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel* has made this attribution in three recent *mishnayot*, each presenting a distinct case. The first was the *mechubar* case — the rule that one should not write a *get* while the parchment is still attached to the ground. The second was the case of *hakol kesheirin lichtov et haget* — the rule that anyone, even a *cheresh*, *shoteh*, or *katan*, may write a *get*, because its validity rests on *ein kiyum haget ela bechotmav*. The third is the present *mishnah* regarding *tofsei gittin*.

In each case, *Shmuel* reads the *mishnah* as a *Rabbi Elazar* position, which requires reinterpreting certain words. In the *mechubar* case, the end of the *mishnah* uses the word *chatmu* — "they signed it" — but *Shmuel* reads this to mean they wrote the *toref*, not that they signed it. In the *hakol* case, the phrase *ein kiyum haget ela bechotmav* sounds entirely like *Rabbi Meir*'s position that the signatories are decisive — yet *Shmuel* reinterprets *bechotmav* to refer to the witnesses present at the moment of delivery rather than those who sign the document.

### Why Three Cases

The *Gemara* explains why each of the three cases was necessary to state. Had *Shmuel* attributed only the *mechubar* case to *Rabbi Elazar*, one might have accepted it: the emphasis on the writing in that *mishnah* — *ein kotvin bemechubar* — at least makes a *Rabbi Elazar* reading plausible, even if the end requires reinterpretation. But one might have insisted that the *hakol* case is genuinely a *Rabbi Meir* *mishnah*, since its explicit rationale — *ein kiyum haget ela bechotmav* — sounds precisely like *Rabbi Meir*'s view that the signatories are determinative. The *Gemara* notes the additional difficulty with the present *mishnah*: since *Rabbi Elazar* himself appears at its end — *chutz migittei nashim* — the implication is that the beginning is *not* his view. The *Tanna Kamma* permitting the *tofes* seems to contradict *Rabbi Elazar*, who at the end of the *mishnah* forbids even the *tofes* of a *get*. To assert that even the beginning of the *mishnah* reflects a *Rabbi Elazar* framework — albeit a position within that framework that countenances the *tofes* — required *Shmuel* to make the attribution explicit all three times. The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction between the *Tanna Kamma* and *Rabbi Elazar*'s end-of-*mishnah* position as a case of *trei tanna'ei aliba d'Rabbi Elazar*: two *tanna'im* debating the precise implications of *Rabbi Elazar*'s view.

---

## Three Takanos

### Rabbeinu Tam Practice

Before turning to the *Gemara*'s three explanations for the *takanah*, *Tosafot* raises a remarkable historical observation about the phrase *harei at muteret le-chol adam* itself. Throughout the *Gemara* this phrase is treated as the *ikar haget*, the essential declaration of the *get* — indeed, the next chapter will explicitly teach *gufo shel get harei at muteret le-chol adam*. Yet *Tosafot* notes that *Rabbeinu Tam* was the one who instituted the practice of including this language in *gittin*. The very fact that he had to institute it implies that *gittin* written prior to *Rabbeinu Tam* did not contain the phrase.

How is this possible? *Tosafot* explains that the standard boilerplate text of *gittin* before *Rabbeinu Tam*'s time did not include *harei at muteret le-chol adam* — not because the concept was absent, but because the operative language of divorce was expressed differently, often in Aramaic. The *Rif*'s text of a *get*, for instance, contains the phrase *l'hitnasva l'chol gvar di titzviyan* — "you may marry any man you wish" — which conveys the identical content in Aramaic. *Tosafot* then adds the crucial caveat: *ein l'hotzi la'az al gittin harishonim* — one must not cast aspersions on earlier *gittin*. The adoption of new stringent formulations, however well-grounded, does not retroactively invalidate prior practice, particularly when the earlier texts expressed the same substantive content through parallel Aramaic formulations. *Rabbeinu Tam* introduced the Hebrew phrase going forward, but the precedent from an earlier *Gemara* — that adopting new stringencies risks undermining the validity of what came before — remains relevant, and *Tosafot* is careful to address it.

### Takanat Sofrim

The *Gemara* now turns to the underlying rationale for the *takanah* mentioned in the *mishnah*. *Rav Yonatan* offers the first explanation: *mipnei takkanat sofer* — the *takanah* was enacted for the benefit of the scribes. The context is *Rabbi Elazar*'s position: since *Rabbi Elazar* requires *lishmah* in the writing, one might have thought that no part of a *get* — not even the boilerplate — could be prepared in advance. Writing anything before the proper moment might compromise the *lishmah* that the *get* demands. Yet pre-writing the *tofes* is extremely useful for scribes, enabling them to have forms ready for immediate use. The Rabbis therefore enacted a *takanah* permitting the *tofes* despite the general *lishmah* concern.

This framing also explains why the *mishnah* extends its requirements to other *shtarot*. Within a *Rabbi Elazar* framework, the temptation to fill in blanks by other documents might spill over into improper filling of blanks in a *get*. The *Tanna Kamma* therefore extends the restriction: just as you may not fill in the *toref* of a *get* — as that would compromise *lishmah* — so too you may not fill in the blanks of other *shtarot*, lest that practice migrate to the *get*. *Rabbi Yehuda* extends the concern further: since the *lishmah* requirement for a *get* is so demanding, he forbids even the *tofes* of a *get*, and once he forbids the *tofes* of a *get*, he forbids even the boilerplate of other *shtarot* by the same logic. *Rabbi Elazar* himself, by contrast, has no concern about other *shtarot* — there is no *lishmah* issue there — and is content to permit them entirely, while maintaining his stringency about the *get*.

Thus the three positions resolve into a coherent picture within the world of *Rabbi Elazar*. All three agree that the *get* is the locus of concern; they disagree only about how far the protective fences must extend.

### Takanat Ketata

*Rav Shabtai* cites *Chizkiya* with an entirely different reading of the *mishnah*: *mishum ketata* — the reason for leaving blanks is to prevent domestic quarrels. On this account, the *mishnah* has nothing to do with *lishmah* at all. The *mishnah* should be read as a *Rabbi Meir* position, where the *lishmah* requirement does not apply to the writing. Why then may one not fill in the blanks? Because a woman who overhears a scribe writing a *get* with her name in it will naturally assume her husband has commissioned the document, and the result will be fights in the household. More broadly, it is simply bad policy to have documents pre-filled with sensitive personal details — whether it is a loan, a sale, or a *get* — before the underlying transaction has actually occurred. No one wants a fully written document floating around that purports to record something that has not yet happened.

On this reading, the *takanah* is not one that *enables* the writing of the *tofes* despite *lishmah* concerns; it is rather a *takanah* telling scribes not to fill in the blanks even though there would be no technical prohibition in doing so. In principle, within a *Rabbi Meir* framework, one could pre-fill the entire document right down to the last detail and there would be no legal problem, since validity depends entirely on the signing. The *takanah* is a prudential restriction, not a *lishmah*-based one.

### Takanat Agunot

*Rav Chisda* cites *Avimi* with a third explanation: *mishum takkanat agunot* — the *takanah* is designed to prevent the creation of *agunot*. The *Gemara* notes that this rationale can be applied within either a *Rabbi Meir* or a *Rabbi Elazar* framework.

### Agunot Application

According to the *Rabbi Meir* reading, the *takanat agunot* rationale works as follows. Since all that matters in a *Rabbi Meir* world is the signing, there is in principle nothing wrong with having an entirely pre-written *get* ready to go — including names, date, and the operative declaration. The *takanah* says: do not do this. Why? Because having a fully written *get* immediately available makes it fatally easy for a husband to act in anger. He has a fight with his wife, runs to the scribe's shop, picks up the pre-filled document, gets witnesses to sign it on the spot, and throws it at her. What was a resolvable domestic dispute becomes an irreversible divorce. *Rav Dov* raised an alternative nuance worth considering: even if the *get* is technically invalid because the signing was rushed or incomplete, the act of throwing a *get*-like document at one's wife may shatter the marriage in practice — the husband storms off and never returns, leaving the woman in a state of abandonment that the *Gemara* characterizes as a form of *agunah*, even if her formal legal status has not changed. This broader use of the term is noteworthy.

According to the *Rabbi Elazar* reading, the *takanat agunot* works in the opposite direction. Since *Rabbi Elazar* demands *lishmah* in the writing, one might conclude that scribes may not pre-write even the boilerplate of a *get*. But this creates its own *agunah* problem: a husband who must travel overseas and wishes to leave his wife a conditional *get* — divorce to take effect if he does not return within a specified period — may be unable to find a scribe to write the entire *get* from scratch on short notice. *Lo ashkach safra* — he will not find a scribe, and he will depart without leaving any protection for his wife. If he fails to return, she becomes a genuine *agunah*. The *takanah* therefore permits the pre-writing of the *tofes* precisely to ensure that a *get* can be prepared quickly when circumstances demand it.

The *Gemara* thus presents two dimensions of *takanat agunot*: one aimed at preventing precipitous divorce when a *get* is too easily available, the other aimed at enabling divorce when the inability to prepare one quickly would leave a woman permanently bound.

---

## Pre-dating Problems

### Get for Arusa

The *mishnah* rules without distinction — *lo shna min hanisuin velo shna min ha'erusin* — that the requirement to leave the date blank applies equally to a *get* given after *nisuin* and to a *get* given after *erusin* alone, before the couple has established a shared household. The *Gemara* accepts the *nisuin* case without difficulty.

For the *nisuin* case, the prohibition on pre-dating has two well-established rationales. One, associated with the concern about a *bat achoso*, is that a husband might wish to protect his wife from a death penalty for adultery by backdating the *get* to make it appear she was divorced before the act occurred. The other rationale is about *peiros nichsei melog*: the produce of the wife's property that the husband is entitled to during the marriage. Pre-dating a *get* would distort the record of when the husband's entitlement ended, potentially harming third parties who relied on the husband's lien over those assets.

The *erusin* case is more difficult. The concern about adultery and misrepresentation of the divorce date applies equally whether or not the couple had established a household. But the *peiros* concern seems irrelevant: *arusa mi is lah peiri* — an *arusa* does not yet have *nichsei melog* producing fruit over which the husband has any rights, since that entitlement begins only from *nisuin*. If the only reason to prohibit pre-dating were the *peiros* issue, there would seemingly be no problem with a pre-dated *get* for an *arusa*.

### Takanas Valad

*Rav Amram* reports that he heard an explanation from *Ulla*, though he initially did not understand its application: *d'amar mishum takanas valad* — the rule exists for the protection of children. The relevant *braita* involves a husband who says: write a *get* for the woman I have just betrothed, and after we consummate the marriage I will divorce her. The *halacha* rules that such a *get* — written during *erusin* but intended for use after *nisuin* — is invalid.

### Reputation Concern

*Ulla* explains the reason: *gzeira shema yomru gita kodem livno* — a decree lest people say that her *get* predates her children. If the *get* is dated from the time of *erusin*, and the couple subsequently lives together and has children before the *get* is delivered, observers will see a *get* bearing a date that appears to precede the birth of the children. Even though the children are not *mamzerim* — their status is not affected — the appearance that they were born after their mother was divorced is a *pegam mishpacha*, a blemish on the family's reputation.

### Arusa Protection

This teaching resolves the *Gemara*'s question about the *erusin* case. When the *get* will be given to the woman while she is still an *arusa*, pre-dating is not intrinsically a problem: there are no *peiros* at stake, and the date makes no practical difference between January and March if she remains an *arusa* throughout. The *Gemara* concedes this. But the reason the *mishnah* prohibits writing the date before the *get* is actually given — even for an *arusa* — is that the scribe cannot know the *get* will actually be delivered during *erusin*. The husband may hold onto it. He may not give it until after *nisuin*. And if he then gives it after *nisuin*, the earlier date will appear to predate any children born from the marriage, creating precisely the *pegam mishpacha* that the *takanas valad* is designed to prevent.

---

## Halacha Ruling

### Rabbi Elazar Ruling

The *halacha* is ruled explicitly: *amar Rabbi Zeira amar Rav Abba bar Shila amar Rav Hamnuna Saba amar Rav Adda bar Ahava amar Rav halacha k'Rabbi Elazar* — the ruling follows *Rabbi Elazar*. This is a chain of five transmitters, underscoring the solemnity of the ruling. The practical implications are significant: we require *lishmah* in the writing of a *get*, we hold *eidei mesirah karti* — the witnesses of delivery are what legally consummate the *get* — and, most stringently, we do not permit even the boilerplate of a *get* to be written in advance. *Rav* even praises *Rabbi Elazar* as *tuveina d'hakimi* — the best of the sages. A brief clarification: the *Rabbi Elazar* at issue here is *Rav Elazar*, the student of *Rabbi Akiva* and colleague of *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Meir*. He is not to be confused with *Rabbi Eliezer*, *Rabbi Akiva*'s own teacher, whose stringent position resulted in a *cherem* and the designation *Shmuti*. Throughout this tractate the relevant figure for the *lishmah* discussion is *Rav Elazar*, and any prior confusion between the two names should be set aside.

### Other Documents

Having ruled like *Rabbi Elazar* regarding *gittin*, the *Gemara* raises the follow-on question: do we also rule like *Rabbi Elazar* regarding other documents, *l'kula* — in the direction of leniency? *Rabbi Elazar*'s position on other *shtarot* is that the scribe may fill in everything in advance — names, amounts, dates, all terms — so long as the witnesses have not yet signed.

### Mechezi k'Shikra

*Rav Pappa* cites *Rava* to raise a concern. The case involves a court's validation of witnesses' signatures — a form of notarization. Suppose the judges begin writing their certification before the witnesses have formally testified to their signatures; they intend to sign only after hearing the testimony. *Rava* rules that such a pre-written certification is *pesulah* — invalid — because it constitutes *mechezi k'shikra*: it has the appearance of falsehood. Writing a document that asserts as fact something that has not yet occurred, even if one intends to sign only when it becomes true, creates an inherently misleading document. By analogy, pre-filling any document before the underlying transaction occurs might be *mechezi k'shikra*.

### Non-Get Leniency

The *Gemara* resolves this concern by invoking the principle attributed to *Rabbi Meir* — that *rav nachman amar haya Rabbi Meir afilu matzo be-ashpah chasmo u-nosno lo kasher*: even a *get* found in a garbage heap, if signed and delivered, is valid. We do not rule this way for *gittin*, because we require *lishmah*. But the underlying principle — that writing a document does not itself constitute a legal act, and that validity depends on signing — applies to other *shtarot*. *Veafilu rabbanan lo pligi alei d'Rabbi Meir ela b'gitei nashim d'ba'inan ketivah lishmah* — the Sages dispute *Rabbi Meir* only regarding *gittin*, where *lishmah* in the writing is required. *B'sha'ar shtaros lo* — for other documents there is no such dispute, and the full leniency of pre-writing applies.

### Pre-writing Leniency

The *Gemara* thus confirms: for loan documents, bills of sale, and *kesuvot*, the scribe may write out the entire document in advance of the transaction, provided the witnesses do not sign until the transaction is complete. This is not *mechezi k'shikra*, because the document has no legal force until signed.

### Ketubah Practice

The *Gemara* adduces further support from a ruling of *Rabbi Yitzchak* citing *Rabbi Yochanan*: a promissory note with which one borrowed money and then repaid the loan on the same day may not be reused to borrow again, because *kvar nimchal shibudo* — the lien created by the document was already discharged. Critically, the *Gemara* notes: *ta'ama d'nimchal shibudo, aval mishum shikra lo chaishinan* — the only reason the document cannot be reused is that its legal effect was already exhausted, but the fact that it was written before being needed is not itself a problem. Concern about *shikra* — falsity in the pre-writing — does not apply.

The practical upshot is illustrated by the *kesuvah*. A *kesuvah* is written with the couple's names, the date, the amount, and all the stipulated terms before the *kinyan* has been performed. The text may even include the formula *ve-kanina minei* — "we acquired from him" — even before the *kinyan* takes place. Some scribes are careful to leave that particular word incomplete until after the *kinyan*, filling it in just before signing, out of an abundance of caution regarding *mechezi k'shikra*. But the *Gemara*'s ruling makes clear that this scruple, while understandable, is not required: the pre-writing of the entire document, including all terms and even the formula of acquisition, is permissible, and only the witnesses' signatures must wait until the transaction is finalized.

---

---

# Gittin 27

## Lost Get

### Mishnah Intro

The Mishnah at the top of the page opens with the case of *hamavi get ve-avda heimenu*: a *shaliach* who is transporting a *get* to deliver to the wife loses it along the way. The question is what he may do when he subsequently recovers it.

### Valid & Invalid

The Mishnah establishes a straightforward principle: *matza'o le-altar*, if he finds the *get* immediately — he dropped it, turned around, saw it, picked it up, and proceeded to deliver it — then it is *kasher*. *Ve-im lav pasul*: if he did not find it right away, it is invalid. The concern underlying this ruling is that after any meaningful interval, one cannot be confident that the recovered document is in fact the same *get* that was lost. However far-fetched it may seem, it is possible that another couple in the same city shares the husband's name, the wife's name, and the place name, and that what the *shaliach* has recovered is a different *get* altogether — one belonging to a different couple with identical names. It is on account of this worry that a *get* found only after some delay cannot be delivered.

### Recognition Markers

The Mishnah provides an exception: *matza'o be-chafisah o be-deluskama* — if the *get* is recovered inside a recognizable sack or purse. *Im makiro kasher*: if he recognizes it, it is valid. Rashi explains that this operates in two distinct ways. Either the *shaliach* recognizes the container itself — he lost his wallet, found his wallet, and the *get* was inside — or, even without a recognized container, he is able to identify the *get* itself through physical markers. What is required is not merely that he knows the names written within it, but that he can identify the document through some concrete physical characteristic. Recognition of the container is of course implicit in either case.

---

## Bava Metzia Cases

### No Return Rule

The Gemara now introduces a challenge from a Mishnah elsewhere. The teaching there reads: *matza gittei nashim ve-shichrurei avadim, diyateiki matanot ve-shovrin, harei zeh lo yachazir* — if one finds a woman's *get*, a writ of freedom for a slave, a deathbed bequest, a gift document, or a receipt, one may not return it to either party. The concern is expressed as *be-din omer*: one can argue that the document was written but perhaps the underlying transaction was never completed — the money was never lent, the *get* was never delivered. In the case of a loan document, returning it to the party written as the lender could prejudice the borrower if the money was never in fact advanced. Since one cannot determine from which party the document fell, it is held by *beis din* and returned to neither. In the case of a *get*, returning it to the wife risks allowing her to remarry if it was never actually delivered, while returning it to the husband would deprive her of evidence that she had received it. The document therefore remains with *beis din*.

### Writer's Approval

The Gemara infers that this prohibition is conditional: *ha amar tnu notnim* — implicitly, if the party who originally caused the document to be written were to say "give it," it would be given. In the case of a *get*, if the husband says to deliver it to the wife, one complies. The reasoning is *mimah nafshach*: whichever party the document fell from, the husband's instruction resolves the ambiguity. If it fell from the wife, she is now recovering what is hers; if it fell from the husband, he is now directing that it be given. *Ve-afilu zman merubeh* — the implication is that even after a considerable time has elapsed, once the doubt about delivery is removed, one would proceed. This, however, appears to conflict directly with our Mishnah, which invalidates a *get* found after any meaningful delay. The Mishnah in Bava Metzia is apparently unconcerned about the possibility that the recovered document might belong to a different couple entirely; it is concerned only with which party the document fell from. Our Mishnah, by contrast, worries that the recovered document may not be the same *get* at all.

### Document Identity

The apparent contradiction thus resolves into a distinction between two different concerns. The Mishnah in Bava Metzia addresses *ownership* — to which party does this document belong, and can we be sure it was delivered? It takes for granted that the document found is the same document that was lost. Our Mishnah raises an entirely different concern: *identity* — is this even the same *get*, or might it be a document from an entirely different couple who happen to share the same names? These are two separate problems, and the Gemara now turns to resolving why our Mishnah raises the identity concern while the Mishnah in Bava Metzia does not.

---

## Rava's Resolution

### High Traffic Concern

Rava resolves the tension as follows: *kan bemakom she-shayarot metsuyot, kan bemakom she-ein shayarot metsuyot* — the cases differ based on whether or not the location in question is a high-traffic area frequented by caravans. Our Mishnah's concern that the recovered *get* might belong to a different couple is, on its face, a remarkably remote possibility — that another man in the same city shares the husband's name, another woman shares the wife's name, and their *get* happened to be lost in the same vicinity. Rava explains that our Mishnah entertains this concern only in a setting with heavy foot traffic and caravan passage. If the *shaliach* loses the *get* in a bustling crossroads, the worry becomes at least conceivable. The Mishnah in Bava Metzia, which is unconcerned with document identity, addresses a case where there is no such heavy traffic — the question there is simply which party the document fell from, not whether it came from an entirely different couple.

### Duplicate Couples

The Gemara immediately adds a further limitation: *ve-afilu bemakom she-shayarot metsuyot, ve-hu she-huchzeku shenei Yosef ben Shimon be-ir achat* — even in a high-traffic area, the identity concern arises only where it is actually known that two couples bearing the same names exist in the same city. The concern, even in a busy location, must be grounded in a concrete known fact — that a second couple with identical names is present — not in mere theoretical possibility.

This two-part requirement emerges not only from Rava's stated position but is also demonstrated by the case of a *get* found in the *beis din* of Rav Huna. A *shaliach* had come to deliver a *get*, lost it, and wished to reclaim it. The *get* bore the name of a town, *Shiyurei*, situated on the river *Rakhis*, and named a man divorcing a woman. Rav Huna asked: ought one to be concerned that there is another city called *Shiyurei* — one we do not know of — where another couple bears the same names? Rav Hisda directed Rabbah, then a student of Rav Huna, to investigate relevant precedents in time for Rav Huna's deliberations that evening. Rabbah went and found the teaching in Bava Metzia: *kol ma'aseh beis din harei zeh yachazir* — any document that has been authenticated by *beis din* may be returned, since *beis din* authentication occurs only after delivery has been confirmed. From this, Rabbah inferred that one is not concerned about other cities of the same name harboring couples with the same names.

The Gemara observes that Rav Huna's *beis din* was itself a high-traffic venue — all documents passed through there, and it was precisely the sort of place where lost documents might turn up. Yet Rabbah was willing to infer from the Bava Metzia Mishnah that even in such a setting one returns the document, and apparently was not worried about an unknown city of the same name with a similarly named couple. This proves that Rabbah requires both criteria — high traffic *and* known duplicate couples in the same city — before entertaining the concern that a recovered document might be a different *get* entirely. High traffic alone is insufficient.

### Flax Marketplace Case

This two-pronged analysis is borne out by a practical ruling Rava issued. A *get* was found in the place of flax in Pumbedita, and Rava returned it to the *shaliach* following his own ruling, dismissing the concern that it might belong to a different couple. Two versions of the case are reported. According to some, *beduchta heicha d'tavu kitna* — it was a place where flax was processed, an industrial location outside the marketplace. Even if it were known that two couples with identical names both hailed from that town, there are no caravans there; the traffic criterion is not met, and so the concern does not arise. According to others, the case involved a place where flax was *sold* — a marketplace with genuine caravan traffic — yet it was not known that two couples with the same names existed in that city. Again, one criterion is absent. Either way, Rava returns the *get*, demonstrating that his position requires *both* high traffic and known duplicate couples before one withholds the document.

---

## Rav Zeira's View

### Mishnah vs Baraita

Rav Zeira now undertakes essentially the same exercise as Rava, but frames the contradiction differently. Rather than contrasting our Mishnah with the Mishnah in Bava Metzia, he sets our Mishnah against a *baraita* in Bava Metzia. The Mishnah is restated: *hameivi get ve-avado heimenu, matza'o le-altar kasher, ve-im lav pasul* — found immediately, valid; found after a delay, invalid. This is contrasted with the *baraita*.

### Husband Agreement

The *baraita* states explicitly: *matza get isha be-shuk, bi-zman she-ha-ba'al modeh yachzir le-isha* — if a woman's *get* is found in the marketplace, and the husband acknowledges it is hers, one returns it to the woman. *Ein ha-ba'al modeh lo yachzir lo le-zeh ve-lo le-zeh* — if the husband does not acknowledge it, one returns it to neither party. And critically, the *baraita* adds: *ve-afilu le-zman merubeh* — even after a long time has elapsed, once the husband concedes the *get* is hers, it is returned. The *baraita* is thus entirely unconcerned with the possibility that the document might belong to a different couple, even when considerable time has passed. This is the same tension Rava addressed, and Rav Zeira resolves it with the same solution: our Mishnah is the case of high traffic, the *baraita* addresses a case without such traffic.

Some report that Rav Zeira requires both criteria, just as Rava does — high traffic *plus* known duplicate couples — and holds that only when both conditions are met does one not return the *get*. Others say Rav Zeira may be stricter than Rava: once the location has heavy traffic, even without confirmed knowledge of a second couple bearing the same names, Rav Zeira may deem the concern sufficient to invalidate the *get*. On that reading, high traffic alone would be enough to worry that somewhere a similarly named couple exists, even if one has no concrete knowledge of them. This position, admittedly far-fetched in its scope, would then *pliga deRava* — stand in opposition to Rava's ruling.

### Implicit Language

The Gemara asks a pointed question about methodology: given that Rava accomplished the same reconciliation using two Mishnayot — which are more authoritative sources — why did Rav Zeira instead compare our Mishnah with a *baraita*? The answer is that Rav Zeira found the Mishnah in Bava Metzia inadequate as a proof text. *Mi katani im ha-ba'al modeh yachzir ve-afilu le-zman merubeh?* — does the Mishnah there actually state explicitly that when the husband agrees, one returns the *get* even after a long time? It does not. That inference is implicit. And since it is only implicit, one might argue that the Mishnah's permission to return the document when the husband agrees is limited to cases of immediate recovery. The Mishnah may simply mean: yes, under the right conditions — including immediacy — you return it if the husband agrees. Only the *baraita* states explicitly that one returns the *get* when the husband agrees *even after considerable time*. When a teaching states a rule explicitly without qualification, it communicates that the rule applies broadly; had immediacy been a required condition, the *baraita* would have said so. Therefore, Rav Zeira found the *baraita* a sharper proof of the genuine contradiction, even at the cost of using a less authoritative source.

---

## Stricter Approaches

### Witness Testimony

Rabbi Yirmiya takes a substantially stricter position. Rather than reading our Mishnah as the exceptional case warranting concern about document identity, he inverts the framing: the case in Bava Metzia where the document is returned is itself the exceptional situation, and the rule is one of pervasive concern about document identity. Under Rabbi Yirmiya's reading, a *get* may be returned only when the witnesses signed on it testify: *me'olam lo chasmanu ela al get echad she-Yosef ben Shimon* — we have never in our lives signed on any other *get* bearing this husband's and wife's names. Only that affirmative declaration suffices to remove all doubt that the document is the unique *get* it purports to be.

### Same-Name Witnesses

The Gemara raises an objection: *mahu d'teima leichosh shemma isromi shma ke-shma ve-edim ke-edim* — ought one not to worry that even the witnesses could by coincidence share their names with witnesses on a different *get*? Perhaps another couple bears the same husband's and wife's names, their *get* is signed by witnesses who happen to share the names of these witnesses, and we have only displaced the problem one level. The Gemara dismisses this: one does not entertain that degree of concern. The witnesses' testimony that they have never signed another such *get* is taken as decisive; the possibility that both the parties *and* the witnesses are coincidentally replicated is too remote to take seriously.

### Siman Muvhak

Rav Ashi offers yet another approach. He essentially applies the principle embedded in the end of our Mishnah to the case in Bava Metzia. For Rav Ashi, concern about document identity is the general rule, and one returns a *get* only when the *shaliach* is able to identify the specific document through a *siman muvhak* — an absolute, unambiguous identifying mark. The example given is: *nekev yesh bo be-tzad os ploni* — there is a hole directly beside a specific named letter. Such a marker is uniquely identifying and admits of no reasonable doubt.

### Siman Types

The Gemara draws a sharp distinction between a *siman muvhak* and an ordinary *siman*. A *siman* is an identifying marker that increases the likelihood that an object is the one claimed — for example, noting that a wallet had a hole in it somewhere near the top. While this certainly makes it more probable that the wallet is the claimant's, it is not conclusive: other documents may also have holes, and the description is insufficiently precise. A *siman muvhak*, by contrast, is an absolute identifier that removes all reasonable doubt — a hole beside a *specific* letter on a *specific* line, for instance. In the context of returning lost objects generally, even an ordinary *siman* suffices to return an *aveidah*. This practice, however, may be only a rabbinic accommodation; at the Torah level, one might require a *siman muvhak* to establish ownership conclusively. For a *get*, this distinction is critical. Even if *simanim* of the ordinary kind are sufficient to return a wallet — whether because *simanim* are *d'oraita* or because rabbinic law permits it for monetary objects — they may be insufficient when the validity of a divorce hangs in the balance. Rav Ashi's uncertainty about whether *simanim* are *d'oraita* or only *d'rabbanan* leads him to require the more exacting standard: only a *siman muvhak* permits returning a *get*.

---

## Siman vs Recognition

### Two Options

Rabbah Bar Bar Channah lost a *get* in the *beis midrash*. When the document was found, he declared that he could identify it in either of two ways: *i simanei it li bagah* — he could provide an identifying mark, some specific physical characteristic he could describe and that could be verified — or, alternatively, *i tvi'at eina it li bagah* — he could simply look at the document and recognize it through *tvi'at eina*, the impression of the eye. This mode of recognition is familiar from ordinary experience: one may be entirely certain that a garment is one's own without being able to articulate which specific feature makes it recognizable, because the knowledge arises from a gestalt of subtle accumulated cues. In Bava Metzia, the Gemara establishes that a *talmid chacham* may recover a lost object through *tvi'at eina*, because his reliability is trusted; extending this privilege to ordinary people would of course create an open-ended mechanism for fraudulent claims.

### Uncertain Grounds

The document was returned to Rabbah Bar Bar Channah. However, he himself expressed uncertainty: *lo yadana im mishum simana hadaruhu* — he did not know on what basis it had been returned to him. Was it because he offered a *siman*, and the *beis din* deemed that sufficient — thus implying a view that *simanim d'oraita* and adequate even for a *get*? Or was it *mishum tvi'at eina* — because he had asserted personal recognition?

### Torah Scholars Only

The uncertainty carries practical *halachic* weight. If the *get* was returned on the basis of *tvi'at eina*, then this procedure is available exclusively to a *talmid chacham* — *ve-davka tzurba me-rabbanan, aval inish de-alma lo* — but not to an ordinary person. If, however, the *get* was returned because the ordinary *siman* he offered was deemed sufficient, then an important and broader principle follows: even without a *siman muvhak*, a *siman* of the standard kind suffices to return a *get* — a ruling that would apply to any *shaliach*, not only to a scholar. The inability to determine which of these two grounds motivated the ruling leaves both the scope of *tvi'at eina* and the sufficiency of ordinary *simanim* for a *get* unresolved.

---

## Immediacy Measures

### Caravan Duration

Having established the framework of immediate versus non-immediate recovery, the Gemara presents a *baraita* in which Tannaim debate exactly what constitutes *she-lo le-altar* — a non-immediate interval. Rabbi Natan defines it functionally, within Rava's framework of caravans: *kedei she-tavor shayara ve-tishreh* — the amount of time it would take for a caravan to pass by and to spend some time encamped in the area. Once that interval has elapsed, the concern that the document might have arrived from an entirely different group is deemed relevant.

### Witness Requirement

Rabbi Shimon ben Eleazar does not define the interval by a fixed duration at all. Rather, *kedei she-yehei adam omed ve-ro'eh she-lo avar sham adam* — one must have a person who was standing watch and can testify that no one passed through the area between the moment the *get* was dropped and the moment it was recovered. This standard is inherently more demanding, since even a small number of passersby would disqualify the recovery absent such testimony.

### Tarrying Standard

Others offer an intermediate position: *she-lo shaha adam sham* — what matters is not whether anyone merely passed by, but whether anyone actually tarried in the area. If people walked through without stopping, the concern is not triggered; once someone stopped and remained, one worries that the document might have fallen from that person.

### Writing/Reading Time

Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi offers a time-based standard using a unit drawn from the subject matter itself: *kedei likhtov et ha-get* — the time required to write a *get*. There is no logical nexus between writing time and the risk of document confusion; Rabbi simply chose a time unit familiar to the context. Rabbi Yitzchak shortens this considerably: *kedei likroso* — the time it takes merely to read a *get*, a substantially briefer interval. Yet others combine the two: the time to write *and* read it.

---

## Simanim Evidence

### Marks Testify

The Gemara now turns to the role of identifying marks in recovering a *get* after what would otherwise be a disqualifying delay. The principle stated is: *va-afilu sha'ah, ve-yesh bo simanim, me'idim alav* — even if considerable time has elapsed, if the *get* bears identifying marks, those marks testify on its behalf. This restates and reinforces what the Gemara concluded in the analysis of Rav Ashi's position: where a sufficient identifier is present, the lapse of time does not render the document invalid.

### Hole Mark

The example of a qualifying *siman muvhak* is given: *nekev yesh bo be-tzad os ploni* — there is a hole positioned directly beside a specific named letter. The precision of this description — a particular hole in relation to a particular letter — is what elevates it to the level of an absolute identifier. It is not merely suggestive; it is conclusive.

### Insufficient Marks

By contrast, physical characteristics of the document as an object — *simanei ha-guf*, as it were — are insufficient: *ein me'idim al simanei ha-guf, d'amri aroch ve-gutz* — that the parchment is long or short, wide or narrow, dark or light in color. These are generic physical attributes that many documents may share and that cannot serve as identifying marks. They constitute at most an ordinary *siman*, not a *siman muvhak*, and as established earlier, an ordinary *siman* is inadequate to permit delivery of a *get*. The same principle that applies to the *baraita*'s analysis here parallels precisely the conclusion already reached in the immediately preceding sugya.

---

## Accepted Standard

### Tarrying Rule

The Gemara records two practical rulings on the question of non-immediacy. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *halacha she-lo shaha adam sham* — the accepted standard is that non-immediacy is constituted when someone actually *tarried* in the area. Mere passage is insufficient to trigger the concern; it is only lingering that creates the worry that the document might have fallen from another person.

### No Passerby

Rabbah bar bar Chana said in the name of Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel: *halacha she-lo avar adam sham* — the accepted ruling is stricter: the interval is non-immediate as soon as even a single person has *passed through*, not merely tarried. One might ask why these authorities stated the *positions* rather than simply ruling in favor of one of the named Tannaim above. The Gemara explains: *mishum d'aphlei* — because there were variant traditions about which Tanna held which view, it was cleaner to state the operative rule directly rather than risk confusion by citing a name associated with a disputed attribution.

---

## Wallet Definitions

### Chafisa

The Mishnah's mention of a *chafisah* and a *deluskama* as containers whose presence permits identification of the *get* invites a brief lexical clarification. What is a *chafisah*? Rabbah bar bar Chana explains: *cheima k'tana* — a small flask.

### Deluskama

And what is a *deluskama*? *Talika d'savi* — a purse carried by elderly people. In both cases, the point is the same: if the *get* is found within an object that itself can be recognized and identified as belonging to the *shaliach*, or if the document itself bears a *siman muvhak*, the combination of markers is sufficient to establish that this is indeed the same *get* that was lost. Without such markers — whether the container is unrecognized, the *siman* falls short of *siman muvhak*, or the claimant cannot offer *tvi'at eina* at the level the law requires — the document may not be delivered if found after any meaningful delay, given the concern, narrow as it may be, that it represents an entirely different *get* from a differently named couple who happen to share every relevant name.

---

---

# Gittin 28

## Get Delivery & Chazaka

### Opening & Mishnah Intro

Today's *daf* is dedicated to the learning in memory of Goldie, *Goldie bas Golda bas Yitzchak Yehuda*, on her third *yahrtzeit*. May it be in her memory and in her *zechus*.

We pick up with the *mishna* on 28a. The *mishna* opens: *hamavei get* — someone is delivering a *get*. The entire first *masechta* opens with the concept of *shelichus*, and that framework allows the Gemara to explore some genuinely interesting scenarios. We already dealt with what happens if the *get* is lost by the *shaliach*; now we confront a different problem.

### Chazaka & Status Quo

The *mishna* states: *hamavei get vehenicho zaken o choleh* — if the *shaliach* left the husband and at that time he was old or he was sick, *notno lah bechezkas shehu chayim* — the *get* may be delivered on the presumption that he is still alive. The wife is treated as divorced, with all the relevant consequences. Presumably the most immediate concern is *yibum* — but it is worth noting that even if one later discovers that the husband died, there may be no way to precisely date events, and the matter may simply never be determined. The operative principle is *chazaka*: he was alive then, and we presume he remains alive now.

### Wife of Kohen Overseas

The *mishna* then introduces a second case: *bas Yisrael hanesua leKohen vehalach baalah limdinas hayam* — an Israelite woman married to a *Kohen* whose husband travels overseas. *Ocheles baterumah bechezkas shehu chayim* — she continues eating *terumah* on the presumption that he is alive. The question naturally arises: for how long? A hundred years? The Gemara will address this to some extent, but the baseline ruling is that she continues indefinitely without being required to stop.

### Chattat from Overseas

The *mishna* adds a third case: *hasholeiach chataso mimdinas hayam* — someone who sends a *chatas* from overseas. *Makrivim osah bechezkas shehu chayim* — the offering is brought on the presumption that he is alive. Were he not alive, it would be a *chatas shemeisu baaleha* and would have to go *limisa*; it could not be brought as a *korban*. And yet the *chazaka* permits it.

### Terumah as Chidush

Of all these cases, *terumah* stands out as the most remarkable *chidush*. One might say that *gittin* is enormously weighty — the prohibition of *eishes ish* is at stake — though it bears noting that either way the woman is permitted, whether as a *gerusha* or an *almana*. And *terumah* consumed by a *zar* carries a penalty of *chiyuv misa bidei shamayim*, which is severe. But the deeper reason *terumah* is the greatest *chidush* is that it is ongoing. In the other cases, the *chazaka* is invoked at one moment in time — a single determination that he was alive when the *get* was sent or when the *korban* was dispatched. The *terumah* case, by contrast, requires an indefinite, open-ended presumption: she eats *terumah* continuously for years, without any terminus, on the basis of nothing more than the status quo.

---

## Rava on Age & Illness

### Rava's Limitations

The Gemara opens with a qualification from Rava: *lo shanu ela zaken* — the *mishna*'s ruling applies only to someone who is merely old in the ordinary sense, *shelo higia ligvurot*, meaning he has not yet reached the age of eighty. Similarly it applies to one who is merely sick, *sherov cholim lachayim* — because most sick people recover.

### Exceptions: Elderly & Go…

Rava continues: *aval zaken shehigia ligvurot* — if the man has already reached eighty years of age — *v'goses* — or if he is a *goses*, meaning he is actively in the process of dying — *sherov gosesim lemisa* — the majority of such people do die, and therefore one cannot invoke *chezkat chayim* on their behalf. In such cases the *chazaka* may be understood as *chazakah asuyah lehishtanot* — a status quo that is already in the process of changing.

### Braita Challenge

Abaye challenges Rava from a *braita*: *hamavei get vehenicho zaken afilu ben me'ah shanah* — even if the husband is a hundred years old, *notno lo bechezkas shehu kayam* — the *get* is delivered on the presumption that he is alive. This appears to directly contradict Rava's position that an elderly man who has reached *gevurot* cannot be presumed alive.

### Plateau Effect

Rava responds: *keivan de'ifrak ifrak* — once someone has made it that far, he has demonstrated genuine longevity. The concern with most people after eighty is that the probability of death is increasing; but once a person reaches an extremely advanced age — Rashi suggests around ninety — the risk plateaus. He is no longer at escalating risk of death on any given day, and therefore we can once again presume he remains alive.

### Gosses Status

There is, however, an important asymmetry between the case of old age and the case of a *goses*. Old age, even at eighty, does not carry a distinct *halachic* status as such — Rava creates the category of *gevurot*, but it is not a formal *halachic* classification. A *goses*, by contrast, carries a clearly defined *halachic* status: there is an explicit *halacha* that one may not move or handle a *goses*, out of concern that the very act of touching him will hasten his death. Because *goses* is a recognized *halachic* category in its own right, the argument that a *goses* has no *chezkat chayim* stands on considerably firmer ground than the argument about an old man.

---

## Get vs. Terumah

### The Contradiction

Abaye now presents Rava with a pointed internal contradiction. The *mishna* states that we deliver a *get* on the presumption that an old or sick husband is alive. Yet there is another ruling: if a husband says *harei zeh gitech sha'ah achas kodem lemisasi* — this is your *get*, to take effect one hour before I die — the wife is immediately prohibited from eating *terumah*. She cannot eat *terumah* because he might die in the next moment. This appears to be a direct conflict: in one case we are unconcerned about the husband's death, and in the other we are immediately concerned.

### Rava's Distinction

Rava responds: *terumah agittin karamis?* — why are you challenging a *terumah* ruling from a *gittin* ruling? These are not comparable cases. *Terumah efshar efshar velo efshar* — when it comes to *terumah*, she has a choice; she can simply refrain from eating *terumah* if there is any uncertainty. But the *get* — this woman needs to get on with her life. Just because we invoke the *chazaka* for purposes of *gittin* does not mean we apply the same standard to *terumah*.

### Tosafot Reframes

Tosafot notes, however, that this response does not go far enough, because the very next line of the *mishna* itself applies the *chazaka* to *terumah*. It is therefore better to compare *terumah* against *terumah*. The *mishna* says the wife of a *Kohen* who has gone overseas eats *terumah* on the presumption he is alive. Yet the ruling about *harei zeh gitech sha'ah achas kodem lemisasi* says she immediately cannot eat *terumah*. That is a direct contradiction within *terumah* itself, and it requires an answer.

### Rav Ada's Answer

Rav Ada bar Abba offers a response: *shani hasam sheharei asar aleha sha'ah achas kodem lemisaso* — the case of one hour before death is different, because in that case the husband has explicitly created a prohibition that will apply to her at some moment during his lifetime. Rashi acknowledges that this is more of a descriptive distinction than an explanatory one — the Gemara has identified that the two cases differ, but has not yet fully explained why the difference matters. As will become clear, the real distinction lies between a concern about whether he is already dead (*shema met*) versus a concern about whether he will die (*shema yamut*), but the Gemara at this stage has not yet articulated that distinction with full clarity.

### Rav Papa's Challenge

Rav Papa challenges: *midi de'ihu meiyas barishah dilma ihi meisa barishah* — how do you know he will die first? Perhaps she will die before him. The implicit reasoning behind the earlier analysis had been that since there will inevitably be a moment in this woman's life when she is prohibited from eating *terumah* — namely, that one hour before his death — we are always concerned that this might be that moment. Rav Papa's challenge dismantles this: if she dies before him, there will never be such a moment at all. The argument that *she must always be on guard because such a moment is coming* fails, because no such moment may ever arrive. This challenge lays the groundwork for the distinction the Gemara will draw between a concern about the present (*shema met*) and a concern about the future (*shema yamut*).

---

## Tannaitic Dispute

### Abaye's Proposal

Abaye proposes a different resolution: the apparent contradiction may simply reflect a *tannaitic* dispute. *Ha Rabbi Meir delo chaish lemisa, ha Rabbi Yehuda dechaish lemisa* — the permissive ruling of the *mishna* follows Rabbi Meir, who is not concerned about the possibility of death, while the stringent position about *sha'ah achas kodem lemisasi* follows Rabbi Yehuda and others who are concerned about such a possibility. This is somewhat ironic because, as a rule, Rabbi Meir is known for being *chaish lemi'uta* — attentive to minority cases — and yet here he is the lenient position.

### Barrel Case

This brings Abaye to cite the relevant *mishna*: someone who purchases wine from Samaritans just before *Shabbat*, when there is no time to properly separate *terumah* and *maaser*, may say: two *lugin* of this wine shall be designated as *terumah*, ten of the remaining hundred as *maaser rishon*, and nine of the remaining ninety as *maaser sheni*. He may then immediately proceed to drink from the wine. This is the position of Rabbi Meir. After *Shabbat*, he designates from the remaining wine what corresponds to the designated portions. Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosi, and Rabbi Shimon all prohibit this arrangement.

### Rabbi Meir Unconcerned

The Gemara elsewhere explains the basis for this dispute. When asked whether he is not afraid that the barrel might break before *Shabbat* ends — leaving no wine to be designated later, which would mean he had drunk *tevel* — Rabbi Meir responds: when it breaks, I will worry about it. He is not concerned the barrel will break. This parallels a concern about death or some other catastrophic change in circumstances: is one concerned that some tragedy will occur and transform the current state of affairs?

### Parallel to Death

The Gemara understands the case of the barrel as a close parallel to the concern about death — whether conceptually or because both reduce to the same question: are we concerned that some accident or unforeseen tragedy will upset the current status? According to this reading, the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about the barrel maps onto the question of whether we worry that the husband might die.

---

## Shema Met vs. Yamut

### The Distinction

Rava, however, offers a sharper analysis that goes beyond attributing the matter to a *tannaitic* dispute. Rava says: *shema met lo chayshinan, shema yamut chayshinan* — whether he is already dead, that we do not worry about; whether he will die, that we do worry about. This is a fundamental and practically significant distinction.

### Chazaka & Future

A *chazaka* speaks to the present status: it asserts that the status quo we knew to obtain continues to obtain now. It does not address the future. If we knew he was alive and have heard nothing to the contrary, we presume he remains alive — the *chazaka* resolves the question of his present status. But the *chazaka* cannot resolve a question about what will happen going forward.

### Present vs. Future

In the case of the wife eating *terumah* while her husband is overseas: the question is whether he is alive right now. We knew he was alive when he left; we presume he is still alive. The *chazaka* answers this question directly. In the case of *harei zeh gitech sha'ah achas kodem lemisasi*: the husband is sitting right there, alive. The question is not whether he is alive now — that is not in dispute — but whether he will die within the next hour. That is a question about the future, and the *chazaka* that he is presently alive says nothing about it. Since the *chazaka* provides no answer to the future question, one must remain concerned, and she may not eat *terumah*. This is *shema yamut*, a future concern, and the *chazaka* does not address it.

### Rav Ada Challenges

Rav Ada bar Matna challenges Rava's formulation: if *shema met* is universally not a concern and *shema yamut* is universally a concern, then why does the barrel case appear as a *tannaitic* dispute? If both matters are agreed upon by all, neither the leniency nor the stringency should be a point of disagreement. This challenge presses Rava to refine his position further.

---

## Rava's Resolution

### Barrel vs. Death

Rava begins to respond by noting a factual distinction between barrels and people: not every barrel breaks, and one can be careful to prevent it from breaking. Every person, by contrast, will eventually die — death is inevitable. This asymmetry might explain why the barrel case is disputed while the inevitability of death is not.

### Guardian Needs Guardian

Rav Mesharshiya pushes back: *shomer tzarich shomer* — your guardian himself needs a guardian. You cannot rely on someone's carefulness to guarantee that the barrel will never break; even the most careful guardian cannot be fully trusted to prevent all accidents. This undercuts the proposed distinction between barrels and human mortality.

### All Agree: No Shema Met

Rava therefore clarifies: *shema met lo chayshinan* — the concern that someone is already dead, that we are not concerned about, according to everyone. The *mishna*'s ruling that we deliver the *get* and permit the eating of *terumah* is agreed upon by all *tannaim*. The *chazaka* that a person remains in the status we last knew him to be in applies universally.

### Shema Yamut Debate

*Shema yamut* — the concern that some accident or tragedy will occur in the near term and cause a change in status — that is a *tannaitic* dispute. Rabbi Meir is not concerned that such events will occur imminently; Rabbi Yehuda and the other *tannaim* are. This is the correct framing of where the disagreement lies.

---

## Tosafot on Time

### Rabbi Meir & Long Term

Tosafot refines this picture significantly. Even Rabbi Meir, who is not concerned that the barrel will break before *Shabbat* is over, would still be concerned if asked whether something might go wrong over a span of ten years. Rabbi Meir's leniency is not absolute: it applies to short-term concerns, but not to the possibility of death or catastrophe over a genuinely long period of time.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Concern

Conversely, Rabbi Yehuda, who is concerned that the barrel might break in the short term — before *Shabbat* ends — is not concerned about *shema met le'altar*, that the husband dropped dead the very instant he walked out the door.

### Absurd Consequence

Tosafot demonstrates why this must be so with a reductio ad absurdum: if a wife of a *Kohen* were required to worry that her husband died the moment he stepped out of the house, she could never eat *terumah* once he left her presence — not even when he went to the synagogue. She would have to be watching him at all times. This is plainly unworkable and cannot be the *halacha*.

### Time-Qualified Dispute

Tosafot therefore concludes that the real dispute is more precisely framed as follows: the disagreement is not between *shema met* in the absolute and *shema yamut* in the absolute, but between *shema met lezman merubah* — the concern that after a substantial period of time he may be dead — and *shema yamut lezman mu'at* — the concern that he will die imminently or in the near term. The former is universally not a concern, the latter is universally a concern, and the *tannaitic* dispute occupies the middle ground: whether we worry about accidents or death occurring over the short-to-medium term. These are critical distinctions in *halacha* that find application in a number of areas, including *hilchos niddah*.

---

## Chattat & Smicha

### The Challenge

The Gemara now turns to a challenge against the *mishna*'s third case — the *chatas* sent from overseas. If we presume the sender is alive, should we not require *smicha* — the laying of hands on the *korban* — which demands the owner's physical presence? The fact that the *korban* is brought without *smicha* seems inconsistent with truly treating the owner as alive.

---

## Chattat & Smicha (II)

### Rav Yosef's Answer

Rav Yosef answers: the case involves a *korban nashim* — an offering brought by a woman. Women are not obligated to perform *smicha* on their offerings, and therefore the absence of *smicha* raises no difficulty.

### Rav Pappa's Answer

Rav Pappa offers an alternative: the case involves a *chatas ha'of* — a bird sacrifice — and *smicha* is simply not performed on bird offerings at all.

### Three Cases Explained

The Gemara then explains why all three cases in the *mishna* — *gittin*, *terumah*, and *chattat* — are necessary. Each one teaches something the others do not. The *get* case might have been explained by the urgency of the woman's situation — she has no alternative but to rely on the *chazaka*. If only *gittin* had been mentioned, one might have said that *terumah* is different because she could simply refrain from eating *terumah* and eat ordinary *chulin* instead. The *terumah* case is therefore needed to teach that even where an alternative technically exists, the *chazaka* permits her to eat. And the *chattat* case is needed to teach that even where there is no urgency — she can simply wait until the owner next comes to the *Beis HaMikdash* — we still permit the *korban* to be brought on the basis of *chezkat chayim*.

---

## Three Cases of Life

### Three Hazakas

The Gemara presents three cases introduced by Rabbi Elazar ben Parta, which the Sages affirmed. First, a city surrounded by a siege (*karkom*). Second, a ship caught in a storm at sea. Third, someone brought before a court on a capital charge. In all three of these cases, the person is presumed to still be alive — *bechezkat kayamin* — and one may proceed accordingly with respect to a *get*, *terumah*, and related matters.

### When Hazaka Fails

However, once the situation has been resolved in the worst direction — the city has actually been conquered, the ship has been lost at sea, the death sentence has been carried out — then we can no longer simply presume the person is alive. In these cases, we apply *chumrei chayim ve'chumrei meisim* — the stringencies of both life and death simultaneously — because there is genuine uncertainty as to whether the person is alive or dead.

### Consequences for Terumah

This dual stringency has concrete implications. Consider a *bas Yisrael* married to a *Kohen*: if her husband's fate is now uncertain — his city has been conquered, or he has been sentenced and the execution is imminent — she cannot eat *terumah*, because we must entertain the possibility that he is dead and she is no longer part of the *Kohen's* household. At the same time, she cannot remarry, because we must also entertain the possibility that he remains alive. Similarly, a *bas Kohen* married to an Israelite: if he might be dead, she might revert to her father's household and regain the right to eat *terumah*, but since he might be alive, she cannot eat *terumah* either. Either way, the uncertainty produces maximum stringency.

### Time Limits & Witnesses

As for time limits — whether there is any point at which the uncertainty is resolved — there is no simple rule. There is an entire chapter in Yevamos dealing with testimony about death, including the application of *eid echad* and *masiach lefi tumo* (innocent speech by a single witness). Those mechanisms allow for a lower evidentiary threshold in certain circumstances, enabling a determination that the husband has died. Until such testimony is available, however, the full dual stringency applies, and the most severe consequence is of course that she cannot remarry.

---

## Jewish vs. Non-Jewish Co…

### Rav Yosef's Position

Rav Yosef qualifies the third case of Rabbi Elazar ben Parta — the person brought to trial on a capital charge. The uncertainty as to whether such a person has actually been executed applies only when the trial was conducted before a Jewish court (*Beis Din shel Yisrael*), which retains the theoretical possibility of retracting even after judgment has been passed. A non-Jewish court, by contrast, once it has passed judgment, will not retract.

### Abaye Challenges

Abaye challenges: even a non-Jewish court can be bribed. How can one be certain they will not reverse the judgment in exchange for payment?

### Sealed Judgment

Rav Yosef responds: they are willing to accept bribes only before the judgment has been formally sealed — before the *pursishnamag* (whether this refers to a particular official or the act of affixing a formal seal, Tosafot explores the possibilities). Once the final seal has been affixed, they will not retract even for a bribe, because to do so at that stage would be too obvious and would undermine their credibility entirely.

### Baraita on Courts

A *baraita* is cited: if two witnesses come forward in any location and testify that they were present in a particular city, in a particular court, and they witnessed the formal sentencing of a named individual — that testimony is accepted and the man is executed on its basis. This shows that we are not concerned that a Jewish court's judgment may have been subsequently overturned.

On the other side: if one hears from a Jewish court that a certain man died or was executed, *yasiu es ishto* — his wife may remarry. But if the same announcement comes from a non-Jewish court, *al yasiu es ishto* — she may not remarry on that basis.

---

## Met vs. Neherag

### The Question

The Gemara now asks: when the *baraita* uses the words *met* (died) and *neherag* (was killed), does it mean that the man has literally already died or been executed, or does it mean that he is in the process of being led out to die?

### Logical Problem

If the *baraita* refers to a literal announcement of death or completed execution, a difficulty arises: we have an established principle that *kol masiach lefi tumo heimnuhu rabanan* — witnesses who speak in innocent, uncontrived speech are believed by the Rabbis for purposes of allowing a wife to remarry, and this applies even to non-Jewish witnesses. Why, then, would we not accept the announcement of a non-Jewish court that the man has been executed?

### Resolution

The resolution suggested is that *met* does not mean the man has literally died, but rather *yotzei lamus* — he is being led out to be left to die. Similarly, *neherag* means *yotzei le'hareig* — he is being led out to be executed, not that the execution has already occurred. They are announcing their intention, not a completed fact. Under this reading, the *baraita* is consistent with Rav Yosef's original formulation: when a Jewish court announces that a person is being brought out for execution, we are confident the execution will be carried out; when a non-Jewish court makes the same announcement, we are not equally certain.

### Alternative View

An alternative interpretation holds that *met* and *neherag* do mean literally dead and executed. Under this reading, the question becomes: why do we not accept the testimony of the non-Jewish court? The answer would have to be that the principle of *masiach lefi tumo* — believing witnesses who speak without a vested interest — does not apply here, because the non-Jewish court is not a disinterested party.

---

## Vested Interest

### Mesiach Lefi Tumo

The principle of *masiach lefi tumo* — believing those who speak innocently and without a stake in the matter — applies precisely because the speaker has no vested interest in the outcome. The reason such testimony is trusted even for so weighty a matter as allowing a woman to remarry is that someone speaking casually, without knowing the import of their words, has no reason to fabricate. Once a party has a vested interest, that reliability evaporates.

### Court's Vested Interest

The non-Jewish court is in exactly such a position. They announced that they would execute a particular individual. If they did not actually carry it out, they have failed to deliver on their formal judgment — a significant loss of institutional credibility. To avoid this embarrassment, they will claim they executed the person whether or not they actually did so. They are therefore not a disinterested party, and the principle of *masiach lefi tumo* cannot apply to their announcement.

### Jewish Court Finality

The Jewish court, by contrast, while technically capable of reopening a case even after *gmar din* — final sentencing — does so only in rare and exceptional circumstances in practice. Before *gmar din*, evidence and merit (*zchuta*) are actively considered; after the sentence is sealed, the case is effectively closed. It is this practical finality that allows us to rely on the testimony of witnesses who report that a Jewish court passed judgment, and that permits a wife to remarry on the basis of such testimony.

---

---

# Gittin 29

## Shaliach Appoints Shalia…

### Intro: Sick Shaliach

The *daf* opens with a *mishnah* addressing a scenario central to the laws of *gittin*: a *shaliach* who has been appointed to deliver a *get* in *Eretz Yisrael* becomes ill and cannot complete his *shlichus*. The *mishnah* rules that in such a case, *harei zeh m'shalcho b'yad acher* — he may appoint another person in his stead. What is notable at the outset is that the *mishnah* appears to require no *beit din* and apparently no witnesses for this reassignment, which raises an interesting broader question about how the *shaliach*'s status is established and verified in the first place.

There is a general question of *eidei kiyum hadavar* — whether witnesses must testify to the chain of agency in order for the delivery to be valid. If someone presents himself as an agent to deliver a *get*, how does one know that this is the right party, the actual *shaliach* of the husband? One answer may be that the very act of carrying the *get* itself provides sufficient evidence of the bearer's status. The *get* is not merely a document; it is, in a sense, the embodiment of the *shaliach*'s authority. This would leave open a related question for the woman's side: if the wife appoints a *shaliach* to receive the *get*, there is no comparable physical object to attest to that person's standing. The degree to which testimony is required to establish a *shaliach*'s identity, either on the delivering or receiving side, remains a question the *mishnah* does not fully resolve.

The second clause of the *mishnah* introduces a qualification. If the husband had instructed the *shaliach*, when you deliver the *get*, to also retrieve from the wife a particular object she has been holding — *ve'im amar lo tul li heimena cheifetz ploni* — then *lo yishlachenu b'yad acher*: he may not hand the *shlichus* over to someone else. The reason given is *she'ein retzono sheyehei pikdono b'yad acher* — it is not the husband's desire that his entrusted object be in the hands of another. Just because the husband trusted this particular *shaliach* to retrieve his prized possession does not mean he would be comfortable with a stranger doing so.

This immediately raises a structural question: are these two tasks — delivering the *get* and retrieving the object — one unified *shlichus* or two separate ones? The *mishnah* appears to treat them as intertwined: it says not to send the *get* at all under these conditions, rather than simply instructing the *shaliach* to deliver the *get* while forgoing the retrieval of the object. Whether the *get* itself would be valid after the fact, if the *shaliach* gave it without having retrieved the object, is something the *mishnah* leaves unresolved.

### Chala Tenan

The *Gemara* opens with an observation by Rav Kahana: *chala tenan* — our *mishnah* specifically says the *shaliach* got sick. The *Gemara* immediately asks: *peshita* — that is obvious, it says it right there in the text. Why does Rav Kahana feel the need to underscore this? Because one might have thought that *chala* is merely a common illustrative scenario and that the *halakha* would apply even if the *shaliach* did not fall ill — that he could appoint a substitute for any reason whatsoever. Rav Kahana is teaching that the *mishnah* means what it says: illness is a genuine condition, not merely an example. Absent such a circumstance, the *shaliach* is not entitled to appoint someone in his stead.

### Holech vs. At Holech

The *Gemara* then anticipates a tension with an upcoming *braisa* and introduces the key distinction between *holech* and *at holech*. If the husband said simply *holech get zeh l'ishti* — deliver this *get* to my wife — the *tanna kamma* of the *braisa* rules that the *shaliach* may appoint a substitute even without having fallen ill. If, however, the husband said *at holech get zeh l'ishti* — you deliver this *get* to my wife — the *shaliach* may not appoint another even if he does fall ill, since the use of the word "you" implies a personal designation. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* goes further, ruling that regardless of which formulation the husband used, *ein shaliach oseh shaliach* — a *shaliach* may never appoint a substitute. Neither the *tanna kamma* nor Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel invokes illness as a relevant condition, leaving the *mishnah* apparently in tension with the *braisa*.

### Three Reconciliations

The *Gemara* proposes three ways to harmonize the *braisa* with the *mishnah*.

The first and most restrictive reading holds that both conditions must be met simultaneously: the husband must have said *holech* (not *at holech*), and the *shaliach* must have fallen ill. Only under both conditions may he appoint a substitute.

The second reading is more permissive: either condition is sufficient. Even if the husband said *at holech*, if the *shaliach* fell ill, that changes matters — *chala shani*, illness is different. Conversely, if the husband said *holech* without the restrictive formulation, the *shaliach* may appoint a substitute regardless of illness.

The third reading applies this same logic to the position of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Even according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who rules that a *shaliach* may never appoint a substitute under ordinary circumstances, *chala shani* — illness creates an exception. His ruling stands only for the default case; when the *shaliach* is incapacitated, even Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel would permit reassignment.

### Husband's Intent

Underlying all three reconciliations is a single animating principle: the entire analysis is a question of the husband's intent and the scope of the authority he granted. Whether the governing factor is the specific word *at*, or the absence of illness, these are all tools for reading what the husband implicitly authorized when he empowered his *shaliach*. It is not a special dispensation triggered by illness as such — *chala* is not some independent *halacha l'Moshe m'Sinai*.
