Rather, when we say *chala shani*, we mean that in cases where it becomes genuinely impossible for the original *shaliach* to complete the task, we presume the husband — whose overriding interest is that the *get* be delivered — would have consented to a transfer of the agency. The same logic would presumably apply to any other *ones*, any other circumstance that genuinely prevents the *shaliach* from completing his mission. Whether this reasoning extends to a *shaliach* who simply changes his mind and refuses to complete the delivery, without any objective impediment, is a harder question whose answer is not clearly resolved.

---

## Shaliach Oseh Shaliach D…

### Two vs. Three People

The *Gemara* now introduces a challenge to the entire idea that a *shaliach* may appoint another *shaliach*. A *mishnah* elsewhere states: if the husband said to two people *tenu get l'ishti* — give a *get* to my wife — or to three people *kitvu get utenu l'ishti* — write a *get* and give it to my wife — those individuals themselves must carry out the task. They may not delegate it. *Inhu in, aval shaliach lo* — they yes, but a *shaliach* no.

The *Gemara* explains the internal logic of this *mishnah*. When the husband addresses three people with the word *tenu* — "give" or "see that it is given" — those three constitute a *beit din*, and the word *tenu* implies supervision rather than personal execution. They may therefore appoint someone to carry out the writing. But if he says *kitvu utenu* to those three, he is explicitly directing them to write it themselves, and personal execution is required. When he addresses only two, even if he says merely *tenu*, those two are simply agents — *shluchim* — not a *beit din*, and an agent cannot delegate his agency. The principle is stark: *ein shaliach oseh shaliach*, a *shaliach* cannot make a *shaliach*.

This apparently contradicts the *mishnah* that opened the *daf*, which permits the sick *shaliach* to appoint a replacement. The *Gemara* must explain the difference.

### Beit Din Exception

The *Gemara* draws a fundamental structural distinction. When the husband addresses a *beit din* and uses the language of *tenu*, he is not appointing them as personal agents; he is conferring upon them institutional authority to oversee the process. As a public institution, a *beit din* occupies a different role than an individual *shaliach*. They are not transmitting a personal agency they received; they are exercising a public institutional function that allows them to appoint an agent to carry out the delivery. By contrast, two individuals addressed as *shluchim*, even if told simply to "see that it is given," remain personal agents and cannot pass on what they received.

This distinction also explains something that might otherwise seem arbitrary. The husband does not need to sign a document or perform a *kinyan* appointing the *beit din*; a verbal instruction is sufficient. While the ephemeral quality of purely verbal appointment will soon become a central issue, the point here is that the *beit din*'s power derives not from a transferred personal agency but from its own institutional standing, once activated by the husband's directive.

### Bizayon D'Baal

Abaye offers the first of two answers to explain why a private *shaliach* — as opposed to a *beit din* — cannot delegate the writing of a *get*. His reasoning: *mishum bizyona d'baal* — because of the embarrassment of the husband. In contrast, when it comes to the delivery of the *get* across a distance, *hacha ba'al lo kapid* — there the husband does not mind.

What specifically is embarrassing about the writing stage? Rashi explains that there was a social presumption that a husband would write his own *get*. This may seem surprising today, when the involvement of a specialist *sofer* is entirely standard, but the underlying concept is that the *get* is fundamentally an expression of the husband's own will, much as a standard deed of sale — *sadi mechura lach* — is an expression of the seller's intent. When the husband delegates the writing to someone else, there is something inherently private about that act, and the presumption is that he wants to keep it contained. Anything short of a formal *beit din*, explicitly told to oversee the matter, is assumed to reflect the husband's desire for discretion. By contrast, when the *get* is being transported across a distance, the very nature of the situation requires an intermediary; there is no presumption of discretion to protect, and no embarrassment in passing on the task.

It is important to note the character of Abaye's answer: it is contingent and contextual, not intrinsic. There is nothing about the nature of *shlichus* itself that prevents delegation; it is a presumed preference of this particular husband under these particular circumstances.

### Mili Lo Mimsran

Rava offers a more fundamental answer: *mishum de-mili ninhu* — because an oral appointment consists of nothing but words, and *mili lo mimsran l'shaliach* — words cannot be handed over to a *shaliach*.

This gets to something structurally deeper. When the husband says "write a *get* for my wife," there is nothing tangible that the appointed *shaliach* receives. No object changes hands, no document of agency is produced. The appointment is entirely abstract, existing only in the verbal instruction. Because there is nothing concrete to pass on, there is no mechanism by which the *shaliach* can transfer his status to another. He received a verbal charge directly from the husband, and that charge has no form that can be re-transmitted.

The case of delivering a *get* is different precisely because the *get* itself exists as a physical object. The *shaliach* carries the *get*, and the *get* embodies his authority. Whoever holds it is manifestly empowered to deliver it, and that tangible embodiment allows the agency to be transferred along with the object.

The implications of Rava's principle extend further than the *get* case. It would also explain why a woman's *shaliach* to receive a *get* cannot appoint a substitute — she gave him no object to carry forward. And it would mean that even if the husband explicitly declared he has no objection to the *shaliach* delegating his role in the writing of the *get*, this declaration would not help; the inability to delegate is not rooted in the husband's *hakpada* but in the structural impossibility of transmitting a purely verbal appointment. The *beit din* remains the sole exception, because the *beit din* is not receiving a transmitted agency at all — it is exercising its own institutional authority once the husband has activated it.

### Matanah K'Get

The *Gemara* asks what the practical difference is between Abaye's and Rava's answers. The case that distinguishes them is a *shaliach* appointed to execute a gift — *l'shaliach matanah* — where the husband instructs one person to write a deed transferring a plot of land and give it to the recipient. There is no *bizayon* here; there is nothing private or embarrassing about making a gift. If Abaye's reasoning is correct, then in this case the *shaliach* could delegate the writing to someone else. But if Rava is correct, the structural impossibility of transmitting a verbal appointment applies here just as it does to the *get*, and the *shaliach* cannot delegate.

This becomes the debate of Rav and Shmuel. Rav holds that *matanah einah k'get* — a gift is unlike a *get*, and the *shaliach* for the writing of a gift deed may appoint another. Shmuel holds that *matanah harei hi k'get* — it is governed by the same principle, because the issue has nothing to do with embarrassment and everything to do with the inherent impossibility of transmitting a purely verbal appointment. In Shmuel's view, Rava's principle — *mili lo mimsran l'shaliach* — applies to any verbal agency that lacks a physical embodiment, whether the document in question is a *get* or a gift deed.

---

## Object Condition

### Borrower Comparison

The *Gemara* returns to the second clause of the *mishnah*: if the husband instructed the *shaliach* to retrieve a specific object from the wife, the *shaliach* may not appoint a substitute, because the husband does not want his *pikadon* in the hands of another person. Reish Lakish observes that the *mishnah* is teaching the same principle established elsewhere: *ein hasho'el rashai lehash'il ve'ein hasocher rashai lehaskir* — a borrower may not re-lend, and a renter may not sublet. Just as a person who entrusts an object to you does not thereby consent to having it in someone else's possession, so too the husband who entrusts the retrieval of his object to this *shaliach* does not consent to having another person handle it.

### Chiddush Identified

Rabbi Yochanan pushes back sharply: *zo afilu tinokos shel beis raban yode'in* — even young schoolchildren know that principle. It requires no *mishnah* to teach us that entrusting something to one person does not authorize that person to hand it to another. That is not the *chiddush* of the *mishnah* at all.

The true *chiddush*, says Rabbi Yochanan, is *zimnin de-gitta nami lo havei* — there are circumstances in which the *get* itself may be invalid as a result of this entanglement with the object. The *mishnah* is not merely saying that the *shaliach* violated a secondary duty by passing the object to someone else; in certain configurations, the very act of giving the *get* under the wrong conditions is an invalid giving. The *get* and the retrieval of the object can become so intertwined, depending on how the husband framed his instruction, that the *kashrut* of the *get* is conditional upon the object being handled correctly.

Rabbi Yochanan draws the analogy: it is as if the husband said "do not divorce her except in a house" and the *shaliach* divorced her upstairs, or "give it with your right hand" and he gave it with his left. When the husband frames an instruction as a condition on the manner of delivery, violating that condition invalidates the *get*.

### Woman Greeted

The *Gemara* proceeds to delineate the cases. Where there is no dispute: if the woman came out to greet the *shaliach* and proactively handed him the object, and he then gave her the *get* — *kulei alma lo peligi de-gitta gitta ma'alya havei* — everyone agrees it is a valid *get*. The object was received before the *get* was given, the order was preserved, and there is no concern. This scenario is uncontroversial.

### Order Debate

The dispute arises specifically when the husband framed the instruction in a particular order: *shekuli minach chefetz ve-hadar hav lah gitta* — first take the object from her, then give her the *get*. In this formulation, the husband is clearly treating the retrieval of the object as a precondition for the delivery of the *get*. Now if the *shaliach* reversed the order — *d'azil ihu ve-yahvei lah gita ve-hadar shakil minah chefetz* — he first gave her the *get*, forfeiting his leverage, and only then retrieved the object — this is where the debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish comes into focus.

### Rabbi Yochanan/Resh Laki…

Reish Lakish holds that the *get* and the retrieval of the object are always independent of one another. Even when the husband used the language of a specific order, Reish Lakish does not read this as creating a genuine condition on the *kashrut* of the *get*. Therefore, the *get* is valid whether delivered by the original *shaliach* himself in the wrong order, or by a substitute *shaliach* — *machshir b'shlucho ve-chol shekein bo*.

Rabbi Yochanan holds that when the husband framed the instruction with a specific sequence — first the object, then the *get* — the *kashrut* of the *get* is dependent on the correct order. *Posel bo ve-chol shekein b'shlucho*: the *get* is invalid even if the original *shaliach* himself delivers it in the wrong order, and certainly if a substitute does it.

The logic of Rabbi Yochanan's position deserves attention. Even if the *shaliach* first gave the *get* and then successfully retrieved the object two seconds later, this does not remedy the defect. At the moment the *get* was given, the *shaliach* was acting contrary to the husband's expressed intent — he was surrendering his leverage before securing the object. The invalidity attaches to the moment of giving, and what happens afterward cannot retroactively cure it.

Rabbi Yochanan's reading of the *mishnah* encompasses two distinct ways in which the *get* can be invalidated when the husband expressed this conditional order. First: the original *shaliach* himself delivers the *get* before retrieving the object. Second: the original *shaliach* appoints a substitute, and even if that substitute performs the acts in the correct order, the *get* is still invalid — because the husband never consented to having a stranger handle his object at all.

As one might observe, in practical life when two parties seek leverage over each other, the standard solution is a trusted neutral intermediary to whom both simultaneously deliver their respective obligations. Such a mechanism would in principle satisfy Rabbi Yochanan's framework, provided the husband had consented to the terms. But the asymmetry here is that the husband holds unilateral power over the *get*, making the dynamic structurally different from a bilateral exchange.

---

## Get from Overseas

### Overseas Scenario

The *mishnah* now turns to a more complex case. A *shaliach* bringing a *get* from overseas — *mimedinat hayam* — becomes ill and cannot complete the delivery. In *Eretz Yisrael*, where the *shaliach* is not required to declare *bifnei nichtav u-vifnei nechtam*, he may simply hand off the *get* to a substitute. But outside *Eretz Yisrael*, matters are more complicated: the original *shaliach* was the one who witnessed the writing and signing of the *get* and is therefore the one qualified to make the declaration. A substitute *shaliach* was not present at those events and cannot make that declaration in his own name.

### Beit Din Testimony

The *mishnah* provides the solution: the original *shaliach* must appear before a *beit din* and testify — *omer lifneihem bifnei nichtav u-vifnei nechtam* — he witnessed the writing and witnessed the signing. The *beit din* then appoints a new *shaliach* to carry the *get* forward. That second *shaliach* need not himself declare *bifnei nichtav u-vifnei nechtam*, because he was not a witness to those events; instead he declares *shaliach beit din ani* — I am an agent of the court. The court's appointment, grounded in the testimony of the original *shaliach*, supplies the necessary authentication.

This procedure also has an implicit bearing on the question of where and how *bifnei nichtav u-vifnei nechtam* must be recited — the *mishnah* presupposes that it is delivered before a *beit din*, a point that was subject to debate in the first *perek* of the tractate.

### Shaliach D'Shaliach

The rabbis posed a question to Avimi, the son of Rabbi Abbahu, to bring to his father: can the second *shaliach* — the one appointed by the *beit din* — in turn appoint a third *shaliach*, and so on down the chain?

### Multiple Shlichim

Rabbi Abbahu dismissed the question as unnecessary. The answer is evident from the *mishnah* itself, which refers to *shaliach acharon* — the final *shaliach* — rather than simply the second *shaliach*. The use of *acharon* implies that there can be any number of *shluchim* in the chain. From the *michlal* — from the logical implication — that it says "the last *shaliach*" rather than "the second *shaliach*," it is clear that the delegation may continue indefinitely, *shaliach* appointing *shaliach* in succession.

### Court Requirement

Rabbi Abbahu then identified what he considered the genuinely interesting question: when *shaliach* number two appoints *shaliach* number three, must that appointment also take place before a *beit din*, or may it be done informally? The second *shaliach* does not himself have a declaration of *bifnei nichtav u-vifnei nechtam* to offer — he can only say he was appointed by the *beit din*. The question is whether his ability to extend the chain depends on a court being involved at each successive stage, or whether having once established the chain through a *beit din*, subsequent transfers may proceed without one.

The *mishnah*'s language resolves this as well. Since every *shaliach* in the chain declares *shaliach beit din ani* — I am an agent of the court — this implies that a *beit din* must be involved at each stage of appointment. One might further suggest that the entire mechanism works precisely because at no stage is one personal *shaliach* transmitting his personal agency to another; rather, the court continuously reasserts its institutional appointment at each step, so that each *shaliach* is genuinely a direct appointee of the court.

---

## Eretz Yisrael Chain

### Rava's Ruling

Rava now addresses the parallel question for *Eretz Yisrael*. *Shliach b'Eretz Yisroel oseh kama shluchim* — a *shaliach* in *Eretz Yisrael* may make any number of *shluchim*, passing the *get* down an extended chain of agents.

### No Court Needed

This is not subject to the same requirements as the overseas case. Since there is no obligation to declare *bifnei nichtav u-vifnei nechtam* in *Eretz Yisrael*, the entire procedure is private rather than court-mediated. The first *shaliach* need not say *bifnei nichtav u-vifnei nechtam*, and the final *shaliach* need not say *shaliach beit din ani*. The chain is sustained without any *beit din* involvement at any stage. As Rashi spells out: none of those formal requirements apply in *Eretz Yisrael*, and yet the chain may extend as far as needed.

### Death of First

Rav Ashi raises a striking question about this chain. What if the first *shaliach* dies? Does the death of *shaliach* number one cause all the subsequent *shluchim* to become invalid — *im meis rishon batlu kulan*? This would be the case if each successive *shaliach* were understood as deriving his authority from the one who appointed him, making the chain's validity dependent on each link remaining intact.

### Power from Husband

Bar Rav Ashi swiftly and decisively refutes this position. *Ilu meis baal, midi mashasha is behu?* — if the husband died, would any of the *shluchim* retain validity? Of course not. The fact that a husband's death extinguishes all the *shluchim* simultaneously demonstrates that all of them derive their authority from the husband alone, not from any intermediate *shaliach*. *Kulam mi'koach d'baal ka'asu* — they all come from the power of the husband. *Isei l'baal isei l'kulehu* — as long as the husband lives, all the *shluchim* are valid. *Leisei l'baal leisei l'kulehu* — if the husband is gone, none of them have any standing regardless of how many intermediate *shluchim* remain alive.

This conclusion may seem intuitive, but it is worth noting that an analogous case — *shomer she'masar l'shomer*, where one guardian transfers an object to another guardian — is not quite so clear. There, the question is genuinely open as to whether the second *shomer* is watching the object on behalf of the first *shomer* or directly on behalf of the original owner. The *sugya* in Bava Metzia explores this in considerable depth, including the possibility that one could actually profit from the arrangement by converting a *shomer chinam* arrangement into a *shomer sachar* one at an intermediate step. But in the case of *gittin*, the logic is different: the act of divorcing one's wife is something that only the husband has standing to perform, and anyone empowered to carry out that act must necessarily be representing the husband directly. There is simply no other party they could be representing.

---

## Abba Bar Minyumi Case

### Scenario Setup

The *Gemara* now presents a practical case that tests these principles. A man sent a *get* to his wife via a *shaliach*. The *shaliach* said: I do not know who she is — *lo yadana lah* — I cannot identify the wife. The husband responded: go give it to Abba bar Minyumi, *d'ihu yada lah* — he knows who my wife is — and he will then go and give it to her. This was presumably a case involving *chutz la'aretz*, where the formal procedures of *bifnei nichtav u-vifnei nechtam* and *beit din* appointment would be implicated.

### Rabbis' Solution

The *shaliach* arrived at the destination but could not find Abba bar Minyumi. He did, however, encounter Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa, and Rabbi Yitzchak Napcha — and Rav Safra was also present. The three rabbis proposed a solution: testify before us *bifnei nichtav u-vifnei nechtam*. Once you have done so, we as a *beit din* will appoint Abba bar Minyumi when he is located — *de-chi atei Abba bar Minyumi ve-nispineih lei ve-leizil ve-lisveih nihala* — and he will go and deliver the *get* to the wife. The solution maps cleanly onto the procedure described in the *mishnah*: the first *shaliach* testifies before the court, the court appoints the next agent, and the chain continues.

### Rav Safra's Question

Rav Safra, who had been sitting alongside, raised a pointed objection: *ve-ha shaliach she'lo nitan l'geirushin hu* — but this *shaliach* is one who was not empowered to deliver the *get* himself. He was only empowered to hand the *get* to Abba bar Minyumi. If the *shaliach* was never fully invested with the authority to deliver the *get* directly, how can he appear before a *beit din* and transfer to them a responsibility he himself did not have?

### Full Empowerment

Rav Safra's challenge rests on a substantive principle: in order to confer upon a *beit din* the authority to oversee the delivery of a *get*, the transferring *shaliach* must himself have been fully empowered to deliver that *get*. It is a question of what he can give over — if you are only authorized to hand the *get* to a specific intermediary, you do not have the full role of a *shaliach l'gittin*, and therefore you cannot activate the *beit din*'s institutional authority in your stead. The three senior rabbis were visibly embarrassed — *ikhsifu* — by this challenge.

### Resolution

Rava then commented that Rav Safra had managed to embarrass three ordained *rabbanim* with his question. Rav Ashi, however, questioned whether the embarrassment was warranted — *bemai kaphinei* — what kind of a challenge was that really? *Mi amar lei Abba bar Minyomi velo at?* The husband never said "only Abba bar Minyumi and no one else." The instruction to find Abba bar Minyumi was practical advice — Abba bar Minyumi knows who my wife is — not a restrictive condition excluding the original *shaliach* from delivering the *get* himself. If the *shaliach* had happened to encounter the wife and identified her himself, there would have been no objection to his delivering the *get* directly. He was therefore *nitan l'geirushin* — fully empowered to deliver the *get* — and Rav Safra's challenge collapses.

There is an alternative reading in the *Rishonim* in which Rav Ashi reads the situation differently, concluding that the husband did indeed mean "Abba bar Minyumi and not you." But the more logical reading of the circumstances, as presented, is that the husband's specification of Abba bar Minyumi was a means of solving the *shaliach*'s practical problem — the *shaliach* did not know the wife — not an expression of distrust in the *shaliach* himself.

What makes this case enduringly interesting, however, is not merely its resolution but the principle it exposes. If a *shaliach* were truly appointed only to hand the *get* to a designated intermediary, and had no personal authority to deliver it himself, one would have to ask: in what sense is he a *shaliach* at all? His role would be indistinguishable from a messenger service. If all he is doing is conveying the *get* to the next person in line, one might argue that the husband has really appointed Abba bar Minyumi as the true *shaliach*, and the first person is merely a courier. The question then becomes whether one can appoint a *shaliach shelo b'fanav* — in the absence of the appointee — or whether that appointment requires a direct, face-to-face charge. If the courier is not actually a *shaliach*, what is the mechanism by which Abba bar Minyumi's appointment takes effect? These questions, which the *Gemara* raises implicitly in its closing discussion, remain open.

---

---

# Gittin 30

## Shliach shelo nitan

### Shliach empowerment

The daf is 30. We pick up at the bottom of 29b, continuing the discussion of a *shliach* appointing another *shliach*. When the delivery of a *get* takes place within Eretz Yisrael but originates from *chutz l'aretz*, the *shliach* must make the transfer before a *beis din* by declaring *befanai nechtav*. The preceding sugya had introduced the concept of a *shliach shelo nitan l'geirushin* — a messenger who has not yet been activated to deliver the *get* himself, and who therefore lacks the full empowerment necessary to transfer that responsibility to another.

### Thirty-day delay

The Gemara now turns to a new case: *hahu gavra dishadar leh gitta l'vei ittei* — a man sent a *get* to his wife through a *shliach*, instructing him, *lo titein lah ad t'latasin yomin* — do not give it to her until thirty days have passed. Within those thirty days, however, circumstances intervened and the *shliach* was compelled to leave before the thirty days elapsed. The *get* was not yet valid for delivery — not because it was literally postdated, but because the husband had placed a temporal hold on its delivery. Unable to wait, the *shliach* came before Rava.

### Rava's ruling

Rava reasoned as follows: the Mishnah had already established that a *shliach* may appoint a substitute when he falls ill — *chala ta'ama mai? mishum d'anus* — because illness is beyond his control, and we assume the husband would not object to the transfer of the *shliach*'s responsibility under such compelled circumstances. So too in this case — *hai nami anus hu* — this is equally a situation of *ones*. Rava therefore instructed the *shliach*: *mesoru milach kamei didan* — declare your appointment before us. The *beis din* would then, after thirty days, appoint a new *shliach* to deliver the *get*. The case maps neatly onto the Mishnah: a transfer of agency, declared before a *beis din*, under circumstances of *ones* — entirely in keeping with established procedure.

### Challenge to Rava

The Rabbis immediately challenged Rava: *ve'ha shliach shelo nitan l'geirushin hu* — is this not a *shliach* who has not yet been empowered to deliver the *get*? His *shlichus* is, as it were, on hold until the thirtieth day. He has not yet been activated. And if he is not yet empowered to deliver the *get* himself, how can he transfer that authority to the *beis din*?

### Empowerment debate

Rava responded by drawing a distinction between fundamental empowerment and temporal activation. *Kevan d'levatar t'latasin yomin matzi m'garesh* — since at the conclusion of thirty days he will have full authority to deliver the *get* — *k'shliach she'nitan l'geirushin hu*: he is fundamentally a *shliach* who has been empowered to deliver the *get*, merely waiting for the designated moment. The fact that the moment has not yet arrived does not redefine him as someone who lacks empowerment altogether. His agency is real; it is only the timing that is constrained. He may therefore transfer that responsibility to the *beis din*.

### Piyes concern

The Gemara now raises a different concern: *ve'neichosh shema piyes* — should we not worry that in the interim thirty days, the husband may have reconciled with his wife? Why would a husband put a *get* on hold for thirty days in the first place? Possibly because he was considering whether to go through with the divorce. If they reconciled, and then the husband and wife were in *yichud* together — or worse, actually cohabited — the *get* becomes disqualified *m'divrei sofrim*, because the *get* bears a date prior to that encounter. People seeing the *get*'s date will calculate that the child was born out of wedlock. This is the problem of a *get yashan*: the *get* is dated January first, delivered February first, and if they slept together on January fifteenth, observers will conclude from the *get* that she was divorced at the time of that encounter, creating a false impression about the child's status.

Concretely: the concern is not merely the general delay any *shliach* traveling from *chutz l'aretz* to *Eretz Yisrael* might experience — where the husband is distant and the delay is incidental — but rather a deliberate thirty-day hold explicitly imposed by the husband. The husband is not necessarily far away; the *shliach* was nearby, waiting. The deliberate withholding strongly suggests that the husband was allowing himself time to attempt reconciliation.

### 12-month condition

The Gemara draws a parallel to a case taught elsewhere: *me'achshav im lo basi mikan v'ad yud beis chodesh* — if a husband says "this is your *get* effective now if I do not return within twelve months," and he then died within that period, *harei zeh get* — it is a valid *get*, since he did not return. Yet the Gemara there already raised the same challenge: *ve'neichosh shema piyes* — perhaps before he died he secretly returned and reconciled? The Gemara answered that the resolution depends on a particular formulation: *be'omer ne'emenes alai lomar shelo basi* — the husband had declared that his wife is believed over a hundred witnesses to testify that he had not returned.

This principle of *ne'emenes alai* is a significant one. It has contemporary relevance in the context of halachic pre-nuptial agreements, where one of the provisions that can be included is a statement by the husband that his wife is believed even over his own counterclaims about what transpired or what conditions were set. It directly addresses the problem of disputed facts and counter-claims.

### Ne'emenes alai

The upshot of the parallel is clear: absent a specific declaration of *ne'emenes alai*, we would indeed be concerned that the husband returned and reconciled. In the case of the thirty-day hold, no such declaration was made. How, then, could Rava have proceeded to allow the *get* to be delivered?

### Arusa distinction

The Gemara resolves the difficulty by noting that *ichsof* — Rava was embarrassed by the question. And then it emerged: *u'lesof iglaei milsa de'arusa havaya* — it turned out that the woman in question was only an *arusa*, not a *nesuah*. Since they had never lived together as a married couple, there is considerably less reason to fear either that reconciliation is likely or that *yichud* and cohabitation would have occurred in the interim. Rava then stated: *im amru be'nesuah, yomru be'arusa?* — if they applied this concern about reconciliation in the case of a *nesuah*, would they apply it to an *arusa* as well? The concern does not extend to an *arusa* in the same way.

This passage raises a significant broader point: whenever a husband has had the opportunity to return and had explicitly put a *get* on hold, we face a potential concern — absent particular circumstances — that he may have returned and reconciled. This is not a trivial issue and applies across various scenarios.

### Shliach presence

The Gemara now raises a further procedural question: *ki mashvei bei dina shliach befanav v'shelo befanav* — when the *beis din* appoints a new *shliach* to replace the original one, must the first *shliach* be physically present at the time of that appointment? The Gemara then answers: *bein befanav bein shelo befanav* — whether in his presence or not. This ruling was also transmitted from Eretz Yisrael, confirming the same conclusion. The reasoning is clear: if the first *shliach* were himself a *shliach* of a *shliach*, one might think his presence necessary to formally demonstrate the transfer. But as established earlier, the *shliach* appointed by *beis din* is fundamentally the *shliach* of the husband — or at minimum the *shliach* of the *beis din* — and so there is no requirement for the first *shliach* to be present. The agency has been transferred to the *beis din*, and the *beis din* acts independently.

---

## Ones be-gitin

### Return condition

Having mentioned the case of "if I do not return within twelve months," the Gemara transitions into a self-contained sugya that also appears in Ketubot and elsewhere. The case: *hahu de'amar — ilu lo ateina taltin yomei, leihavei gita* — a man declared that his *get* should take effect if he does not return within thirty days. He then came back before the thirty days were up — *ata* — but *upaska mabara* — he found that the river crossing was blocked. The banks had risen and he could find no way to cross. As the deadline ran out, he called out from the other side: *chazu de'atai chazu de'atai* — "see, I'm here, I'm coming, I'm trying to return."

### Shmuel's ruling

Shmuel ruled: *lo shmei matya* — his calling out and trying to return does not count as having returned. The condition was formulated as "if I don't return," and he did not return. The *get* is therefore valid. His intention to return, his effort, his crying out — none of it satisfies the literal language of the condition.

### Ones doctrine

This ruling opens the sugya of *yesh ones be-gitin o ein ones be-gitin* — whether the doctrine of *ones* applies in the context of conditional divorces. The argument in favor of *ones* applying would run as follows: when a person frames a condition, he presumably means it to cover the range of situations he could foresee. If his intent was "if I willingly choose not to return, the *get* takes effect," then a case where he tried desperately to return but was physically prevented was never within the scope of what he meant. We ought to interpret his words in light of his evident intent.

Against this stands Shmuel's position: halacha must go by what a person says, not by the more nuanced intention one might retroactively attribute to him. If he wanted to exclude cases of *ones*, he should have said so explicitly. The condition as stated is unambiguous — he did not return.

### Reconciliation debate

A second case sharpens the debate. *Hahu gavra d'amar lehu — ee lo paisna lah tlasi yomin, leihavei gita* — a man told witnesses that if he does not reconcile with his wife within thirty days, the *get* should take effect. He then went to try to reconcile — *aza pisa velo ipisa* — but she refused to be reconciled.

Rav Yosef challenges the claim that this is a genuine *ones*: *mi yahiv lah tikra tarkava de-dinari velo paisa?* — did he send her a basket full of gold coins and she still refused? Perhaps he simply did not try hard enough. However, some report Rav Yosef's position in the opposite direction: *midi tarkava de-dinari baia u-maihava lah?* — does he have to give her a basket of gold coins? That would be excessive. He tried, and that should be sufficient.

Tosafot notes that even in the version where Rav Yosef questions whether he tried hard enough, the underlying point should really be: even if he had given her a basket of gold coins and she still refused, the condition still was not met. The issue is not the quality of the effort, but whether trying is sufficient at all.

### Ones conclusion

The Gemara concludes by mapping the two cases onto the two positions: *kad keman de'amar yesh ones be-gitin, ha keman de'amar ein ones be-gitin* — one case follows the view that *ones* is a valid consideration in *gitin*, the other follows the view that it is not. The question at stake is whether, when a person formulates a condition, we interpret that condition as implicitly excluding cases where he tried and was prevented — or whether we hold strictly to the letter of what was said. The sugya in Ketubot develops this at greater length; here we note the two positions and the cases that illustrate them.

---

## Teruma/Ma'aser loan

### Loan setup

The Gemara now turns to a Mishnah that, at first glance, has nothing to do with *gitin*. The connection lies in the theme of acting with a *chazakah* — a presumption — that someone is still alive, paralleling the earlier discussion of a *shliach* who delivers a *get* presuming that the husband remains living. This Mishnah introduces a range of similar scenarios and also serves as a bridge toward the next *perek*, which opens with a *get* case and then introduces the concept of *tikkun olam*, leading into two full chapters of material largely unrelated to *gitin* but connected through that broader idea.

The Mishnah: *hamalveh ma'os et ha-kohen ve'et ha-levi ve'et he-ani* — one who lends money to a *kohen*, a *levi*, or a poor person, with the following arrangement: the lender is a farmer who, after his crops come in, will separate *terumah* or *ma'aser* and designate it toward repayment of the loan, rather than physically delivering it to the *kohen* or *levi* and having it returned. Instead, he will simply separate it and retain it himself — since the debt is thereby offset, and there is no need to go through the formality of delivery and return.

The *halacha*: *mafrish aleihem b'chezkat she-hen kayamim* — he may go ahead and separate and retain it, acting on the presumption that the *kohen*, *levi*, or *ani* is still alive. He is not required to worry — *ve'eino choshesh shema meis ha-kohen o ha-levi o ha-ani o she'he'eshir he'ani* — that perhaps the *kohen* died, or the *levi* died, or the poor man died, or that the poor man became wealthy. If the *ani* became wealthy, he would no longer be eligible to receive *ma'aser ani*, and the arrangement would be undermined. Nevertheless, the lender may proceed on the presumption that the original circumstances still obtain.

### Separation mechanism

The mechanism works as follows. Rather than physically handing the *terumah* or *ma'aser* to the *kohen* or *levi* and having it handed back as repayment, the lender simply declares the separation mentally and retains the produce. In the case of *ma'aser ani*, the lender can himself eat *ma'aser* — it is not restricted to *kohanim* — and so the same logic applies. The arrangement was made in advance: when I separate, I keep it, and it counts as repayment of the debt.

### Presumption aliyah

The Mishnah permits this to proceed even when the *kohen*, *levi*, or *ani* is not present — operating on the *chazakah* that he is still alive, precisely as a *shliach* delivering a *get* presumes the husband still lives.

### Death of creditor

If, however, it becomes known that the *kohen*, *levi*, or *ani* has actually died, the situation becomes more complex. The question is whether the heirs assume the obligation. In general, heirs do not inherit the personal debts of their father as a personal obligation; rather, there is a *mitzvah al ha-yorshim liproa chov avihem* — a rabbinic obligation for heirs to repay their father's debts — but not a legally enforceable personal liability. If, however, there is a lien on inherited property — established through a *shtar chov* — then the lender retains rights against that property.

In the present case, since the arrangement was likely made orally rather than through a formal *shtar*, there probably would be no lien on the property. Nevertheless, the Mishnah provides a solution: if the heirs — who are themselves *kohanim* or *leviyim* — agree to honor their father's arrangement, the lender may retain the *terumah* or *ma'aser* as repayment. The mechanism is conceptually as though the lender gives the *terumah* to the heirs, and they return it as repayment. This requires the heirs' agreement — they are not legally obligated — but if they consent, the arrangement transfers smoothly. In the case of an *ani* who died, the same could apply in principle, though complications arise if the heirs are not themselves poor.

If the original loan was made *bifnei beis din* — in the presence of a *beis din* — the Mishnah rules *eino tzorich litol reshus min ha-yorshim*: the lender does not need the heirs' permission. The *beis din*, having official standing in matters of *dinei mammonos*, can in effect sanction the arrangement and speak on behalf of the heirs — analogous, in a certain way, to the institution of *prozbul*, which we will encounter later in Gittin.

### Possession problem

The Gemara raises a sharp challenge: *ve'af al gav de'lo asu le'yadei* — even though the *terumah* never came into the *kohen*'s possession — how does this arrangement work at all? There are two distinct problems. First, a straightforward *dinei mammonos* question: this *terumah* right now could be given to any *kohen*. How does this particular *kohen* acquire ownership over it such that the lender can then retain it as repayment of the debt? Second, there is a separate *mitzvah* of *nesina* — delivery — which requires actually handing the *terumah* to the *kohen*. When and how was that *mitzvah* ever fulfilled?

Rashi articulates both points explicitly: *maan zachye lei le-hai kohen* — who conferred ownership on this particular *kohen*? And *heicha yatza yedei nesina* — where did the lender ever fulfill the obligation of giving?

### Established families

Rav answers: *be-makirei kehuna u-leviya* — this applies to established families, where there is a longstanding and well-known practice of giving *terumah* and *ma'aser* to a specific household. In such a case, the very act of separating, given the firmly established pattern, is sufficient to confer ownership on that family automatically, even without a formal act of delivery. This was a known institution — families who had, across generations, given consistently to a particular *kohen* family or *levi* family. In that context, separation alone suffices.

### Third party

Shmuel offers a different explanation: *be-mezakeh lahem al yedei acheirim* — the lender calls over a third party, asks him to take possession of the *terumah* on behalf of the *kohen* or *levi*, and then the third party transfers it back to the lender as repayment. This fulfills both the ownership transfer and the act of giving, through the mechanism of *zechiyah* — acquiring on behalf of another. Shmuel's arrangement is simply more practical in cases where the *kohen* or *levi* is not nearby.

### Asu institution

Ulla offers a third explanation: *ha mani Rabbi Yossi hi — de'amar asu et she'eino zacheh ke'zacheh* — this Mishnah follows the view of Rabbi Yossi, who held that the Rabbis enacted that a person who has not formally acquired something is treated as if he has, in order to allow this institution to function. Ulla's explanation is frankly rabbinic: the Rabbis recognized that technically the *kohen* or *levi* does not own the *terumah* or *ma'aser*, but they enacted that it should be treated as though they did, in order to make this system viable.

The institution is in everyone's interest. The *kohen*, *levi*, or *ani* benefits enormously: they can borrow money and have it repaid with something they would likely have received anyway — or perhaps even something they would not have received had the lender not agreed to this arrangement. It is, in effect, free money. The lender benefits as well: he has confidence that his loan will be repaid, and the terms — as we will see — are quite favorable to him. The Rabbis therefore greased the wheels, as it were, and declared that the mechanics of *kinyan* are satisfied even without a formal act of delivery.

The Gemara notes that none of the three explanations fully satisfies the commentators' preference. *Ke-Rav lo amri* — Rav's explanation of *makirei kehuna* is not mentioned in the Mishnah. *Ke-Shmuel lo amri* — the third-party mechanism is also not mentioned. *Ke-Ulla nami lo amri* — why not like Ulla? Because *bi'yechida lo mokminan* — we prefer not to establish a Mishnah as following a single minority opinion. Nevertheless, one way or another, the institution of ownership transfer must be operative; the debate concerns only the precise mechanism.

A *baraita* then repeats essentially the same case, adding the detail of *posekin imahen ke-sha'ar ha-zol* — the exchange rate to be used when calculating repayment.

### Exchange rate

The *baraita* states: *ufosek imahem ke-sha'ar ha-zol* — one stipulates with them according to the lowest market rate. That is, when calculating how much produce the lender retains as repayment, the parties agree that the produce is valued at the lowest prevailing market price. If wheat, for instance, fluctuates between one and two dollars per bushel over the course of the season, the agreement stipulates the one-dollar rate. This maximizes the quantity the lender can retain — a hundred bushels repays a hundred dollars at one dollar per bushel, which at the higher market price might actually be worth two hundred dollars.

The Gemara initially observes *peshita* — this is obvious, since there is already a Mishnah in Bava Metzia permitting such arrangements. The underlying logic treats this less as a loan and more as a pre-purchase or forward transaction: the lender is in some sense pre-acquiring the *terumah* or *ma'aser* that will later be separated. The Gemara clarifies that the *chidush* is the implicit presumption: even if the parties did not explicitly fix the exchange rate, we assume the lowest market rate applies, since that is what benefits the lender and incentivizes the arrangement.

### Ribbis exemption

The *baraita* states: *ve-ein bo mishum ribbit* — there is no concern of *ribbit* in this arrangement. Even if the lender ends up retaining produce worth considerably more than the original loan — because the market price rose while the exchange rate was fixed at the low end — this does not constitute forbidden interest.

Tosafot extends this further: not only does the *sha'ar ha-zol* rule not raise a *ribbit* issue, but even if the parties agree to an exchange rate lower than anything the market actually reached — a rate more favorable to the lender than any prevailing price — there is still no *ribbit* violation. The Rabbis permitted this generously in order to make the institution as attractive as possible to both parties.

The Gemara explains the exemption: *keivan de-ki leis lei lo yahiv lei* — since if the crop fails entirely and there is nothing to separate, the borrower has no obligation to repay the loan at all. This fundamentally distinguishes the arrangement from a standard loan. In an ordinary loan, if the borrower cannot pay, the debt still exists. Here, if there is no crop, there is no debt. That feature makes the arrangement structurally closer to a forward sale than to a loan, and it is precisely that feature which removes the *ribbit* concern. *Ki it lei nami, ein bo mishum ribbit* — when the crop does come in and the lender retains more than he lent, we analyze it as the profit of a sale, not as interest on a loan.

### Shemita exception

The *baraita* further states: *ve-ein shevi'it meshamtattu* — the *shemita* year does not annul this debt. Normally, *shemita* annuls loans by prohibiting the creditor from pressing the borrower for repayment, which ultimately renders the debt uncollectable. Here, however, the borrower is essentially out of the picture — there is no creditor pressing anyone. The lender will simply separate *terumah* and retain it himself. Since the mechanism of *shemita*'s annulment — *lo yigos* — requires active pressure on a debtor, and no such pressure exists in this arrangement, *shemita* does not apply.

### Retraction rules

The *baraita* then states: *ve-im ba lachazor eino chozer* — if one wants to retract, he cannot. The Gemara, following Rav Pappa, clarifies which party is being addressed. The *ba'al ha-bayis* — the lender — cannot retract from the arrangement. But *aval kohen be-ba'al ha-bayis, im ba lachazor chozer* — the *kohen* can retract.

The reasoning draws on the principle that in a normal transaction, if the buyer has paid but has not yet taken possession of the object, he may retract — the transaction is not complete. The Gemara applies a parallel logic here. From the *ba'al ha-bayis*'s perspective, his side of the transaction is complete: he lent the money, and there is nothing further for him to do. He cannot claim that his act is unfinished and seek to reverse it. From the *kohen*'s perspective, however, his side of the transaction — the act of receiving the *terumah* and having it returned as repayment — is not yet complete. His portion of the transaction remains open, and that incompleteness gives him a degree of flexibility to withdraw.

Rashi formulates it this way: the *ba'al ha-bayis* has discharged his obligation on his end; the *kohen* has not yet fulfilled his end, and therefore retains the ability to reverse course. A student raised a helpful way of putting it: the lender has lent the money; the *kohen* effectively holds an option of repaying through this mechanism, but until the separation and retention actually occur, that side of the transaction is not complete, and the option remains his to exercise or not.

If the *kohen* does retract, the lender is entitled to a *mi she-para* — a rabbinic censure — but no more.

### Ye'ush concept

The *baraita* also states: *nityashu ha-be'alim, ein mafrishin aleihem* — if the lender has despaired of collecting, he may no longer use the *terumah* or *ma'aser* toward repayment of the debt. *Mipnei she-hu mafrish al ha-avud* — because he would be separating in relation to something already lost.

This is a surprising ruling. Normally, *ye'ush* — despair — does not in itself extinguish a debt. If a borrower absconds, the lender's despair does not cancel what is owed. What makes this case different is the concrete, specific nature of the anticipated payment. The repayment here was not a general monetary obligation but was tied to a particular object — the *terumah* and *ma'aser* from this lender's crop. When the lender despairs and considers that produce lost, he has effectively relinquished his claim on that specific object as a vehicle of repayment. It is a *ye'ush* directed at the thing itself, not merely at the hope of collection. Once that despair is registered, even if the crop recovers, the lender can no longer use it as repayment.

The Gemara further clarifies that this ruling is needed even in a case where the grain was already standing in the straw when it was damaged — one might have thought that such grain, which often recovers, was never truly lost, and that the lender's despair was therefore premature and ineffective. The Gemara teaches that even so, if the lender genuinely despaired, that *ye'ush* takes effect and forfeits his right to use that produce as repayment.

### Beis din takana

A *baraita* then cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: *hamalveh ma'os le-kohen u'le-levi bifnei beis din u'meisu, mafrish aleihem b'chezkas oso ha-shevet* — if the loan was arranged before a *beis din* and the *kohen* or *levi* subsequently died, the lender may still separate and retain the *terumah* or *ma'aser* by virtue of the status of that entire tribe. He does not need the heirs' permission.

The logic here is institutional. When the original arrangement was made formally and publicly before a *beis din*, the *beis din* implicitly speaks on behalf of the *kohanim* and *leviyim* as a class. The broader community of *kohanim* and *leviyim* has an interest in this institution functioning — after all, the ability to borrow money and have it repaid through *terumah* and *ma'aser* is a tremendous benefit for them. The *beis din*, acting in their collective interest, can therefore authorize the lender to retain the *terumah* even when the original *kohen* has died, without needing the specific heirs to consent.

A version in the Tosefta reads not *b'chezkat oso ha-shevet* but *bi-reshus oso ha-shevet* — by the permission of that tribe — capturing more explicitly the idea that the *beis din* speaks with the implicit authorization of the *kohanim* or *leviyim* as a group.

For an *ani*: *mafrish aleihem b'chezkat aniyei Yisrael* — one may presume on behalf of the poor of Israel generally. Rabbi Akiva extends this further: *b'chezkat aniyei olam* — on behalf of the poor of the world. The practical difference, as the Gemara notes, concerns *aniyei Kuti* — Samaritan poor in the town. If one holds like *aniyei Yisrael*, one speaks on behalf of Jewish poor specifically; if there are no Jewish poor in the town and only Samaritan poor, it may not work in certain configurations. Rabbi Akiva's formulation, reaching to *aniyei olam*, ensures that Jewish poor elsewhere can also serve as the relevant class.

### Death vs. wealth

The *baraita* adds: *he'eshir he'ani, ein mafrish alav* — if the *ani* became wealthy, the arrangement no longer applies, even when the loan was made before a *beis din*. The *beis din* speaks on behalf of the poor as a class in order to sustain this institution — but only in the case of death. If the *ani* merely got rich, the lender cannot retain the *ma'aser ani* and consider the debt repaid.

Why does the rabbinic enactment cover death but not wealth? The Gemara answers: *misa shchicha, ashirus lo shchicha* — death is common; getting rich is not. The Rabbis constructed the institution to address predictable and frequent occurrences. Death is universal and inevitable; the Rabbis therefore made provision for it, allowing the institution to continue functioning when the *kohen*, *levi*, or *ani* dies. But enrichment of a poor man is unusual enough that the Rabbis did not extend the *takkanah* to cover it. Rav Pappa encapsulates this with a folk saying: if you hear that your friend died, you can take it as true — as the *chazakah* holds, people do die. But if you hear that your friend got rich, do not be so quick to believe it.

### Heirs and land

The Mishnah had stated that if the *kohen* or *levi* dies, the lender must obtain permission from the heirs — *tzorich litol reshus min ha-yorshim*. A *baraita* citing Rebbi then stipulates: this applies to heirs who inherited — *yorshim she-yarshu*. The Gemara asks: are there heirs who did not inherit? Rabbi Yochanan clarifies: *yorshim she-yarshu karka v'lo she-yarshu kesafim* — heirs who inherited land, not merely cash. Only when there is actual landed property is there a lien upon which a debt can be collected; and only then is the permission of the heirs relevant in this framework.

Rabbi Yochanan then rules: *hiniah m'lo machat gove m'lo machat, m'lo kardom gove m'lo kardom* — if the deceased left an estate worth only a pin, the lender may collect only a pin's worth; if worth a hammer, he collects a hammer's worth. One can collect only proportionally to the actual land.

However, a further ruling — associated with the story of the small fields of Abaye in Ketubot — holds that even if the estate is tiny, one can collect the full debt through repeated cycles: take the land, accept the heirs' cash payment to redeem the land, apply that cash as partial payment of the debt, take the land again, and so on. Since this entire framework is a *takkanah d'rabbanan* aimed at making the institution work, Tosafot reads this position as applying even where the heirs have not formally consented — where there is a lien, the *beis din*'s institution ensures the debt can ultimately be collected even from a small estate.

---

---

# Gittin 31

## Lending to Kohen/Levi

### Unspecified Ma'aser

Today's daf begins at *Gittin* 31b, picking up in the middle of the discussion concerning the institution of lending money to a *kohen*, *levi*, or *ani*, whereby the borrower repays through *terumot* and *ma'asrot*. Within that context, the *gemara* introduces a related *baraita*: if a *Yisrael* says to a *levi*, "*ma'aser yesh lecha b'yadi*" — "you have *ma'aser* in my possession" — *ein chosheshin l'trumat ma'aser shebo*, we need not be concerned that there is *trumat ma'aser* within that *ma'aser*. The *halakha* is that there is no such concern. By contrast, if he specified a measure — "*kor ma'aser yesh lecha b'yadi*," you have a *kor* (thirty *se'ah*) of *ma'aser* in my possession — then *chosheshin l'trumat ma'aser shebo*, we are concerned about the *trumat ma'aser*. The *gemara* immediately protests: *mai ka'amar*? What is this even saying? The *baraita* seems impenetrable as stated.

### Abaye's Reading

Abaye steps in with a clarification: *hachi ka'amar* — here is what the *baraita* actually means. A *Yisrael* says to a *levi*: "*ma'aser yesh lecha b'yadi v'heilach damav*" — "I have separated *ma'aser* in my home, I have you in mind, it is yours; now here is money, let me buy it back from you." This fits squarely within the context of the *mishnah*, where a *Yisrael* separates *ma'aser* and then repurchases it from the *levi* in order to keep the grain in his own possession.

### Tosafot on Timing

Given this reading, *Tosafot* explains the concern as follows. The *levi* has agreed in principle to sell the *ma'aser* back, but the sale does not become binding until he takes the money — and in this case, since the grain is already physically in the *Yisrael*'s house, taking possession is effectively accomplished the moment he receives the money. Before the money changes hands, however, the *levi* still owns the *ma'aser*. *Tosafot* therefore asks: are we concerned that in that window of time, before the sale is binding, the *levi* might have used the separated *ma'aser* to perform *havdalah* — declaring it to be *trumat ma'aser* on behalf of *other ma'aser* he has at home? We are not concerned, says the *baraita* in the unspecified case.

### Switcheroo Concern

The concern that *Tosafot* is addressing is the following. Suppose the *levi* has a thousand bushels of *ma'aser* at home, and the *Yisrael* has just given him one hundred bushels of *ma'aser* (in some halakhically recognized manner, perhaps via a third-party *kinyan* on his behalf). The *levi* could say: "I will now designate these hundred bushels as *trumat ma'aser* on my other nine hundred bushels." He then takes the money from the sale — and the *Yisrael* discovers that what he bought back is now entirely *terumah*: ninety percent cannot be eaten by a non-*kohen* at all. In the unspecified case, we are not concerned that this occurred, because the *levi* did not know the precise amount of *ma'aser* involved, and one cannot properly designate *trumat ma'aser* without knowing the quantity. If, however, the *Yisrael* stated an exact measure — *kor ma'aser* — and that is also how the *levi* came to know the precise amount, then indeed we must be concerned: he knew exactly how much he had, and could have performed this "switcheroo," converting the full amount to *trumat ma'aser al makom acher*, on other *ma'aser* elsewhere.

### Wickedness Question

At this point the *gemara* objects sharply: *atu b'rishi'ei askinan*? Are we dealing with wicked people? *Deshaklu d'mei u'machlei lehu trumat ma'aser*? That they take money for the grain and yet turn it all into *trumat ma'aser* behind the buyer's back? If the *levi* did such a thing, the entire sale should be a *mekach ta'ut* — a transaction made in error — and void entirely. The *gemara* concludes that this reading, while it fits the language of the *baraita* elegantly, cannot be its true *pshat*.

---

## Deceased Levi Scenarios

### Rav Mesharshiya

The *gemara* therefore proposes an entirely different scenario, attributed to Rav Mesharshiya son of Rav Idi. The *baraita* now reads as follows: a *Yisrael* says to the son of a *levi*: "*ma'aser l'avicha b'yadi*" — "your father entrusted *ma'aser* to me before he passed away." The scenario has shifted: we are no longer dealing with a *levi* who might act improperly in the present, but with *ma'aser* that a now-deceased *levi* had left in someone else's possession. The *Yisrael* now wishes to purchase this *ma'aser* from the son. The question becomes: must we be concerned about what the *father* did to this *ma'aser* before he died?

### Trumat Ma'aser Question

The concern is whether the father, before his death, might have designated the entire sum of *ma'aser* as *trumat ma'aser al makom acher* — as *trumat ma'aser* on other *ma'aser* he possessed elsewhere. The *Yisrael* who wishes to buy the grain needs to know whether it is clean *ma'aser* (with only a tenth yet to be given to the *kohen*) or whether the whole amount has been converted to *trumat ma'aser*, leaving it entirely *terumah*. The *baraita* rules: if the amount was unspecified — "*ma'aser l'avicha b'yadi*" with no quantity stated — *ein chosheshin*, we need not be concerned. If a specific amount was named — "*kor ma'aser l'avicha b'yadi*" — then *chosheshin*, we are concerned.

There are in principle three possible states in which the father could have left the *ma'aser*: first, he did nothing at all, and it remains raw *ma'aser* awaiting *trumat ma'aser*; second, he removed the *trumat ma'aser* from within it, though we do not know where it ended up; and third, he converted the entire amount to *trumat ma'aser* on other grain elsewhere. The *gemara* treats the third scenario as the most extreme and the one animating the concern.

### Non-Standard Practice

The *gemara* then raises a pointed objection: *v'chi nechsh'du chaveirim litrom shelo min hamukaf*? Are we really to suspect scrupulous people — *chaveirim* — of separating *trumat ma'aser* in a manner that is not *min hamukaf*, not from grain that is all physically together in one place? The requirement that the grain being separated and the grain it serves as *terumah* for should be in the same physical space (*mukaf*) is the standard, normative procedure. Suspecting this *levi*, who was presumably a *chaver* scrupulous in his observance of *terumot u'ma'asrot*, of routinely designating grain in one location as *trumat ma'aser* for grain in an entirely different location seems unwarranted. The *gemara* accordingly dismisses this reading as well.

### Rav Ashi's Reading

Rav Ashi proposes a third interpretation. The *baraita* describes yet another scenario: a *ben Yisrael* reports to a *levi*: "*kach amar li Abba* — this is what my father told me before he died — '*ma'aser l'avicha b'yadi*,' that he had *ma'aser* in his possession belonging to your father." So here it is not the *Yisrael* himself reporting on grain entrusted to him, but the *Yisrael*'s son relaying what his deceased father said. Reuven says: my father Yaakov, before he died, separated *ma'aser* from his grain and designated it for you, the *levi*.

The question now is what Yaakov — the deceased *Yisrael* — might have done with that *ma'aser* before he died. Specifically, the concern here is not the *switcheroo* of *al makom acher*, but rather the opposite: did the father do the *levi* a favor and proactively separate the *trumat ma'aser* from within the *ma'aser*, so that the *levi* receives clean, ready-to-use *ma'aser*? Or does the *ma'aser* still contain its *trumat ma'aser* waiting to be taken?

### Articulation Effect

The *baraita* rules as follows: if the father said only "*ma'aser lecha b'yadi*" without specifying the amount, then *chosheshin l'trumat ma'aser shebo* — we are concerned that there is still *trumat ma'aser* within it, because since the amount was unspecified (*lo kayitz*), the father likely did not know the exact quantity and would not have taken the trouble of properly separating the *trumat ma'aser*. If, however, the father specified "*kor ma'aser lecha b'yadi*" — a precise measure — then *ein chosheshin l'trumat ma'aser shebo*: we need not be concerned, because since the amount was known and articulated, we assume the father fixed it up completely before he died.

### Father's Preparation

This reading, it should be noted, inverts the apparent direction of the original *baraita*. In the original text, the unspecified case triggered no concern and the specified case triggered concern; in Rav Ashi's reading, it is the specified case where we assume the father acted charitably on the *levi*'s behalf and there is no concern, while the unspecified case is where we remain concerned. As the *gemara* itself acknowledges, this does not map cleanly onto the literal language of the *baraita* — *adarabba* — but at least the underlying scenario is coherent. The operative principle is that just as we generally assume a *chaver* does not die and leave his grain in an unfixed state, so too if a *Yisrael* knew the exact amount of *ma'aser* he had designated for a particular *levi*, we presume he finished the job — that *tikkunei takniya baal habayis*, the householder fixed it up — separating the *trumat ma'aser* so the *levi* would receive clean grain, ready for use, what one might call *trumat ma'aser genummen*.

---

## Ba'al HaBayit Rights

### Question of Authority

Having established that the *ba'al habayit* is presumed to have separated *trumat ma'aser* from the *ma'aser* in his possession, the *gemara* pauses to ask a fundamental *halachic* question: *v'chi yesh lo reshut l'baal habayit litrom trumat ma'aser*? Since when does the *ba'al habayit* have the authority to separate *trumat ma'aser* from *ma'aser* that is not his? Once *ma'aser* has been separated, it belongs to the *levi* — or more broadly to *shevet Levi*. The *ba'al habayit* would normally need to be appointed as a *shaliach* to act on the *levi*'s behalf. The assumption in the previous discussion seemed to be that the *ba'al habayit* has an inherent entitlement: having separated the *ma'aser*, he simply finishes the job by separating the *trumat ma'aser*. But what is the basis for this?

### Abba Elazar View

The *gemara* answers: this is the position of Abba Elazar ben Gamla. As established in a *baraita*, Abba Elazar ben Gamla derives this authority from the *pasuk* concerning *trumat ma'aser*: *v'nechshav lachem trumatchem* — "and your *terumah* shall be considered for you."

### Scriptural Parallels

The *pasuk* in full (Bamidbar 18:26–27) reads: the *levi'im* shall take a *ma'aser min hamaaser* — a tenth of the tenth — and this shall be *v'nechshav lachem trumatchem k'dagan min hagoren uch'mleiah min hayekev* — "your *terumah* shall be considered as grain from the threshing floor and fullness from the winepress." Rashi explains that the verse is drawing a comparison between the two *terumot*: the *trumat ma'aser* that the *levi* gives is treated identically to the *terumah gedolah* that the *Yisrael* takes from his grain. The *baraita* makes this explicit: *bishtei trumos hakatuv medaber*, the *pasuk* is speaking of two *terumot* simultaneously and equating them.

### Estimation Method

From this equation the *gemara* derives: *keshem sheterumah gedolah nitelet b'omed uvemachshavah*, just as regular *terumah* is separated by estimation and by thought alone, *kach trumat ma'aser nitelet b'omed uvemachshavah* — so too *trumat ma'aser* may be separated by estimation and thought. Since *terumah* has no fixed Torah-mandated amount (even a single kernel exempts the entire pile, with the Rabbinic standard being approximately two percent), one cannot be expected to give a precise measure and is encouraged to estimate, presumably rounding up rather than coming up short. *Tosafot* notes that we specifically encourage estimation for this reason, similar to the practice of a merchant who heaps a measure generously. Even though *trumat ma'aser* does have a fixed amount — one tenth of the *ma'aser* — the Torah's equation to *terumah gedolah* teaches that a guesstimated tenth suffices and need not be precisely measured. Furthermore, *bemachshavah*: the entire act of separation can be accomplished through thought alone, without any verbal declaration. The source for this is the word *v'nechshav* in the *pasuk* — the root *cheshbon*, calculation or thought — indicating that a purely mental act of designation suffices.

### Conclusion

From this equation the *baraita* proceeds: *ukeshem sheyesh reshut l'baal habayit litrom terumah gedolah*, just as the owner of the grain separates *terumah gedolah*, *kach yesh reshut l'baal habayit litrom trumat ma'aser* — so too he has the authority to separate *trumat ma'aser* from the *ma'aser* in his possession. Having separated the *ma'aser*, he is entitled to complete the process by separating the *trumat ma'aser* as well. One might ask whether this entitlement also grants him the right to determine which *kohen* receives the *trumat ma'aser*, or whether that right remains with the *levi* — but the *gemara* does not explore this question, and at minimum the *ba'al habayit*'s authority to perform the separation itself is established.

---

## Setting Aside Produce

### Designated Room

The *gemara* now transitions to a new *mishnah*, which continues the overarching theme of the *masechet* — presuming that an agent remains alive and his actions valid — applied now to *terumot* and *ma'asrot*. The *mishnah* states: *hameniach peiros lihyos mafrish aleihen terumah uma'asrot* — one who sets aside produce in a specific location (say, a room) intending to use that stockpile as a source from which to separate *terumah* and *ma'asrot* over time. The practical scenario is this: a *Yisrael* fills a room with grain or fruit and maintains a running ledger as he processes batches from his fields. Each time he has new *tevel* grain and needs to separate *terumah*, he declares: "two more bushels in that room are *terumah*" — or *ma'aser* — until the entire room has been exhausted in designations. *Tosafot* notes that this arrangement is technically *shelo min hamukaf*, since the grain being designated and the grain it exempts are in different locations, and explains that the Rabbis permitted this specifically in cases of pressing need such as *erev Shabbat*, when one needs to prepare food quickly.

### Chazaka Status

*Mafrish aleihem bechezkas sheheim kayamim* — one may continue separating in the ordinary fashion with the presumption that the grain in the room still exists. There is no need to verify the continued existence of the stockpile every time one makes a designation; the *chazaka* that it was there permits the assumption that it remains.

### 24-Hour Window

*Im avdu, harei zeh choshesh me'es le'es* — if he goes back and discovers the stockpile is gone — whether rotted, stolen, or lost — he must be concerned for twenty-four hours. That is, any designations made in the last twenty-four hours are retroactively void, since the grain may have been gone during that window. Designations made before that point, however, stand. The reasoning behind this specific number is not obvious: if no one ever checked on the room, why should we assume the grain must have been present until twenty-four hours before discovery rather than having been lost months earlier? The *gemara* will address this tension directly, but the underlying conceptual framework is one of competing *chazakot*: the *chazaka d'meikara* — the original status quo that the grain was there — and the *chazaka d'hashta* — the inference from the current state that things may always have been as they are now. At what point does the current status override the original presumption? The *mishnah*'s answer is twenty-four hours. *Tosafot* notes this is reminiscent of the *me'es le'es* principle in the laws of *nidda*, but stops short of explaining why the twenty-four-hour figure works here — it simply observes the parallel without resolving the underlying rationale.

### Wine Checking Times

Rabbi Yehuda adds a further rule specifically for wine: *bishlosha perakim bodkin et hayayin* — one must check on wine designated in such a room at three specific times, because wine can turn to vinegar, and one cannot separate *terumah* from wine over vinegar. The three times are: when the east wind blows after *Sukkot* (specifically in a year where *Sukkot* falls after the fall equinox, as Rashi explains); when the grape blossoms (*smadar*) emerge; and when water begins to enter the unripe grapes (*boser*). These are moments when wine is particularly vulnerable to spoilage, and a *ba'al habayit* relying on a designated room of wine must verify at each of these junctures that his wine has not become vinegar.

---

## Me'es Le'es Debate

### Rabbi Yochanan

The *gemara* now examines precisely what the *mishnah*'s phrase *me'es le'es* means. Does it look backward from the moment of discovery, or forward from the moment of deposit? Rabbi Yochanan holds: *me'es le'es she-bdika* — the twenty-four hours run backward from the time of inspection. You discovered the problem now; you must be concerned that this problematic state began up to twenty-four hours ago. Everything done in the last twenty-four hours is potentially void; anything before that is presumed valid.

### Rabbi Elazar ben Tanchum

Rabbi Elazar ben Tanchum, citing Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yanai, takes a far more extreme position: *me'es le'es shel hanacha* — the twenty-four hours run forward from the time of deposit. From the moment the stockpile was set aside, you may only assume with confidence that the first twenty-four hours were good. Once that initial window closes, you must treat everything as potentially problematic, up through the present moment of discovery.

### Language Test

The *gemara* tests both positions against the language of the *mishnah*: *im avdu harei zeh choshesh me'es le'es* — if lost, one is concerned for *me'es le'es*. The word *choshesh* — concerned — clearly refers to the problematic state. Under Rabbi Yochanan's reading, the phrase fits naturally: you are concerned about the past twenty-four hours. Under Rabbi Elazar ben Tanchum's reading, however, if the good window is only the first twenty-four hours of deposit, the *mishnah* should have said *ad me'es le'es* — "until twenty-four hours" — rather than simply *choshesh me'es le'es*. The *gemara* concludes: *kashya* — this is indeed difficult for Rabbi Elazar ben Tanchum's position. The plain reading of the *mishnah* clearly supports Rabbi Yochanan.

### Mikva Analogy

The *mishnah* ends with *divrei Rabbi Elazar* (the *gemara* corrects the reading to Rabbi Elazar rather than Rabbi Eliezer). The *gemara* then fills in the implicit counterpoint: *chalukin alav chaveirav al Rabbi Elazar* — his colleagues dispute him. The proof comes from a *mishnah* in the laws of *mikva*: a *mikva* that was measured and found to be deficient — *nimdad v'nimtza chaser* — meaning it had been valid at some known past point and is now found lacking. The rule is: *kol taharos she-nasu al gabav l'mifrea*, all purifications performed in it retroactively — *bein b'reshut hayachid bein b'reshut harabbim* — whether in the private or public domain — are *teme'ot*, presumed invalid.

The logic here is crucial. Normally, in the public domain, a doubt about *tumah* is resolved leniently (*safek tumah b'reshut harabbim tahor*). But that rule applies when an object started as *tahor* and we are uncertain whether it became *tamei*. Here, the object — a vessel, a person — started as *tamei*. Its *chazaka* was *tumah*. It was brought to the *mikva* to achieve *tahara*, but now we discover that the *mikva* itself was in doubt. The *chazaka* of *tumah* has never been definitively broken. Therefore, even in the public domain, it remains *tamei*, and this is true retroactively for as long as the *mikva*'s validity was in question — without any twenty-four-hour limitation. The same logic, by extension, applies to the grain: the grain had a *chazaka* of being *tevel*. The householder's ongoing designations were meant to change its status. If the stockpile on which those designations depended was gone, the designations never took effect, and the grain retains its original *chazaka* of *tevel*.

### Chazaka Principle

The *gemara* anticipates a possible reconciliation: one might have tried to read the *mikva mishnah*'s word *l'mifrea* ("retroactively") through the lens of our *mishnah* and claim that *l'mifrea* means only the past twenty-four hours — thus limiting the retroactive reach in the *mikva* case as well and harmonizing it with the twenty-four-hour rule. The *gemara* rejects this: Rabbi Elazar's position is that the grain case goes all the way back, not merely twenty-four hours. His colleagues therefore apply the same logic to the *mikva*, rendering all past *tevilot* invalid without limit. In the *mikva* case, everything is *tamei* all the way back to the last verified measurement; there is no twenty-four-hour buffer. The competing *chazakot* are resolved decisively in favor of the original status: when an object's *chazaka* was *tumah*, a cloud of doubt over the act meant to purify it leaves the *chazaka* intact, indefinitely.

---

## Eastern Wind Effects

### Wind Characteristics

Because Rabbi Yehuda's rule about checking wine invoked the east wind (*ruach kadim*) blowing after *Sukkot*, the *gemara* takes up an extended discussion of the nature and effects of this wind. The point of departure is a *pasuk* from the book of Yonah: *vayeman Elokim ruach kadim charishit* — God appointed an east wind, *charishit*. What does *charishit* mean? Rav Yehuda says: when this east wind blows, *osa telamim telamim bayam* — it carves furrows in the sea, like a plow (*choreish*) carving rows in the earth. So powerful is its force that it produces these wave-furrows in the water. Rava objects: if that is what *charishit* means, how does it fit the context of the *pasuk*, which continues *vatach hashemesh al rosho shel Yonah vayitalaf* — the sun beat upon Yonah's head and he fainted? The context speaks of heat, not of the raw power of a wind at sea.

### Four Winds Balance

Before returning to resolve this, the *gemara* presents a tradition reported by Gneiva — who happened to pass by Rav Huna and Rav Chisda as they sat together. One of them suggested they rise for him as a great *talmid chacham*; the other demurred, noting that Gneiva was known for his contentious nature. While they deliberated, Gneiva approached them and, upon being told they were discussing winds, offered the following teaching in the name of Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav: *arba ruchot menashvot bechol yom* — four winds blow every day. *Ruach tzonit menashevet im kulam* — the northern wind blows in conjunction with all of them. *She'imalai kein ein ha'olam mitkaiyam afilu sha'ah achat* — were it not for the northern wind, the world could not endure even a single hour. Rashi explains that the northern wind has a tempering, balancing effect — neither too hot nor too cold — and without it, the other winds would be destructive.

### Southern Wind Danger

The southern wind, however, is the most powerful and dangerous of them all: *veruach dromit kashah mikulam* — the southern wind is the harshest. Were it not for an angel called Netz, who stands in its path and holds it back, *machrevet kol ha'olam kulo mipaneha* — it would destroy the entire world, presumably through an excess of cold. The scriptural basis is *hamavinatcha ya'aver Netz yifros knafav l'teiman* — "from Your understanding does Netz spread its wings to the south" (Iyov 39:26). This angel spreads its wings southward to restrain the southern wind and protect the world from its destructive force.

### Destructive Effects

Returning to the east wind and the context of Yonah, the *gemara* next reports a series of traditions about the damaging effects of the *ruach kadim*. Rava citing Rav states: *isha mapelet bo* — the east wind can cause a woman to miscarry. Shmuel says: *afilu margaliyot she'bayam markivot bo* — even the pearls in the sea rot because of it.
