And Rabbi Yochanan states: *afilu shichvat zera she'b'mei isha masrachet bo* — even semen within a woman's body spoils as a result of it, preventing conception.

### Scriptural Basis

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak then notes that all three Amoraim derived their respective positions from the same single *pasuk*: *ki hu bein achim yafria yavo kadim ruach Hashem, mimidbar ya'aleh v'yeivosh m'koro v'yecharav mayano v'hu yishasseh otzar keli chemdah* — "For he will cause division between brothers; the east wind of God shall come from the desert; his wellspring shall dry up and his spring shall wither; it shall plunder the treasure house of every precious vessel" (Hoshea 13:15). Rava then completes the exegesis: *adei Sura hu dedaykei kraei* — these are the scholars of Sura who know how to read *pesukim* in precisely this way. *V'yeivosh m'koro* — "his wellspring shall dry up" — refers to the womb of the woman, source of life; this is the miscarriage. *V'yecharav mayano* — "his spring shall wither" — refers to *shichvat zera she'b'mei isha*, the semen in the woman's body. *V'hu yishasseh otzar keli chemdah* — "it shall plunder the treasure house of precious vessels" — refers to *margaliyot she'bayam*, the pearls of the sea.

### Interpretations

The *gemara* finally returns to the opening of the *pasuk*: *ki hu bein achim yafria* — "for it will cause division between brothers; *yafria*." Rava interprets: *afilu shufsa bekufa demara rafya* — even the handle set into the head of an axe will be loosened and rotted by this east wind. The term *bein achim*, "between brothers," refers to the two sides of the axe-head through which the handle passes; and *yafria* is a rearrangement of the letters of *rafya* — weakening. Even that tightly fitted wood will be rotted away. Rav Yosef interprets the same verse differently: *afilu sachsa bedafna rafya* — even a peg driven into a wall will be loosened. And Rav Acha bar Yaakov: *afilu kanya bekufsa rafya* — even wicker woven into a basket will weaken and rot.

With that, we conclude our survey of the effects of the eastern wind, and complete *masechet Gittin*, chapter five — *hadran alach Kol HaGet*.

---

---

# Gittin 32

## Perek Hasholeach Intro

### Perek Overview

With Daf 32 we begin the fourth *perek* of Masechet Gittin, *Hasholeach*. While the *perek* opens with a discussion of *get*, what follows it moves into a range of topics that at first glance might appear unrelated to the laws of divorce. The unifying theme, however, is *tikkun olam* — the betterment of the world — a concept that motivates a series of rabbinic enactments throughout this *perek* and the ones that follow. Understanding what precisely is meant by *tikkun olam* here is itself one of the central tasks ahead of us.

The *perek* is also significant because it demonstrates the scope of rabbinic power. We will see how the rabbis could use their authority to shape, and in certain circumstances even to contravene, *d'Oraita* law. This is not a digression; it is the very point.

### Core Topics Preview

Beyond the question of *get*, the *perek* introduces core conceptual issues in a number of distinct areas. The most famous is *pruzbul*, the mechanism by which Hillel addressed the annulment of debts on *shemita*. To appreciate *pruzbul* properly, one must understand the underlying mechanics of how debts function during the *shemita* year — and this *perek* gives us that opportunity. Cases involving slaves and other varied and foundational topics will also arise, making this *perek* one of the richest in the masechet.

---

## Annulling Get Mishnah

### Get Nullification Concept

The *Mishnah* opens at the top of daf 32: *Hasholeach get l'ishto* — a man sends a *get* to his wife. We are still within the framework of *shlichut* established in the first *perek*, where the mechanics of delivering a *get* through an agent were laid out. What is new here, and immediately striking, is the concept of *bitul* — annulling the *get*.

When we hear that a husband can annul the *get* he sent, this demands some explanation. What does it mean to annul a *get*? One could straightforwardly annul the *shlichut* — tell the agent that he is no longer acting on your behalf — but the *Mishnah*'s emphasis seems to be on something more: changing the very status of this document, this piece of paper.

Given all that has been emphasized until this point about *lishmah* — that the *sofer* must write with the specific intent and under the direction of the husband, that the *get* must be a full and genuine expression of the husband's will — a certain logic emerges. The *get* is not merely a legal document the way an ordinary *shtar* might be; it is an expression of the husband's will. The text *harei at muteret lechol adam* is the verbal crystallization of that will. If the husband genuinely and formally retracts that will before the *get* has taken effect, does the document not cease to be what it was? Does it not become merely a piece of paper?

This idea is sometimes expressed in the *acharonim* literature in terms of the husband being *mevatel* the *lishmah* of the *get*. That formulation requires a moment's unpacking. The *lishmah* — the intent — is a fact; it was written with proper names and proper intent. But what it really means is that the *get* is an expression of the husband's ongoing will. The *acharonim* are saying: if that will is genuinely and formally retracted, the document no longer embodies it.

Consider the contrast with other *shtarot*. A *shtar kiddushin* — *harei at mekudeshet li* — is also an expression of one's will, and one might ask whether the same logic applies there. But a *shtar mecher* — *sadi mechurah lach* or *sadi netunah lach* — does not require *lishmah* in the same way. The *sofer* could theoretically pre-fill such a document, and the prohibition on pre-filling a *get* is by rabbinic *gezeirah* specific to *Gittin*. It is the *get* that demands this heightened sense of *lishmah* as an expression of the husband's will, and it is for that very reason that there seems to be this possibility of retracting it.

The *Mishnah* assumes, at least on its surface, that a verbal annulment suffices. One need not write a formal document of revocation. The verbal withdrawal of will, communicated to the right parties, is enough. The mechanics of how this works, and its limits, will be developed throughout the *Gemara*.

### Four Annulment Scenarios

The *Mishnah* describes four distinct scenarios of annulment. In the first, the husband himself catches up with the *shaliach* — *v'higia bashaliach* — and tells him: *get shenatati lecha batel, harei hu batel* — the *get* I gave you is annulled, behold it is annulled. In the second scenario, *o sheshalach acharav shaliach* — he sends a second *shaliach* after the first — and this second agent conveys the message of annulment to the first.

In the third scenario, *kadam etzlo ishto* — the husband races ahead and gets to his wife before the *shaliach* does — and tells her directly: *get sheshalachti lach batel* — the *get* I sent you is annulled, before she has received it. In the fourth, *o sheshalach etzlah shaliach* — he sends a second *shaliach* directly to his wife — and that second agent conveys the annulment to her before the *get* arrives.

All four scenarios are presented as valid forms of *bitul*. The *Gemara* will examine each in turn to explain why each one needed to be stated explicitly, since each one might have been thought ineffective for a different reason.

### Cutoff Point Rule

Before turning to the *Gemara*'s analysis of those scenarios, the *Mishnah* states the obvious but essential limit: *im meshehigia get leyadah, shuv eino yachol levatlo* — once the *get* has been placed in the wife's hand, he can no longer annul it. She is divorced. The document has taken effect and its work is done.

### Rabban Gamliel Takana

The *Mishnah* then records that *barishonah* — originally, in the earlier practice — a husband could convene a *beis din* in his own hometown and annul the *get* there, without notifying the *shaliach* or the wife. The *shaliach* would continue on his way thinking the *get* was valid; the wife would receive it thinking she was divorced; and no one in the relevant location would have any reason to doubt it — while back home, the husband and his small *beis din* knew otherwise.

The problem this creates is obvious. *Hitkin Rabban Gamliel HaZaken shelo yehu osin ken mipnei tikkun olam* — Rabban Gamliel the Elder enacted a *takana* that this practice is forbidden, for the sake of *tikkun olam*. A woman who believed herself divorced and remarried on the basis of a *get* that had been secretly annulled would be in a catastrophic halachic situation. The *takana* therefore requires that any annulment be communicated to the relevant parties — the *shaliach* or the wife — so that they are aware of it and the *get* cannot be acted upon in error.

The *Gemara* will raise the question: if someone defied Rabban Gamliel's *takana* and annulled the *get* secretly before a hidden *beis din*, is the *bitul* nonetheless effective — *batel o eino mevutal* — or does violating the *takana* invalidate the annulment itself?

---

## Gemara Analysis Early

### Higia Intentionality

The *Gemara* opens by noting that the *Mishnah* does not use the plural *higu* — they reached — but rather the singular *higia* — he reached. This is a reading about intentionality. *Higia* suggests that the husband simply happened to encounter the *shaliach*, perhaps coincidentally, without necessarily having set out to catch him. The *Gemara* raises the question of whether such an unintentional encounter could support a valid *bitul*. One might reason that since the husband was not focused on annulling the *get* — he just happened upon the *shaliach* — perhaps his subsequent words of *bitul* were not serious, or perhaps we should be concerned that he was not genuinely retracting his will but rather seizing an opportunity. The *Gemara* teaches: *afielu mimaila* — even if the encounter was unintentional — the *bitul* is valid. We do not say that the husband was acting on a whim or merely exploiting the moment to cause his wife difficulty.

### Second Shaliach Override

The second scenario — sending a second *shaliach* — requires explicit mention because one might have thought that *shaliach* number two lacks the standing to override *shaliach* number one. *Shaliach* number one carries the actual document; he is the embodiment of the husband's original will, and there is something to the idea that physical possession of the *get* invests that original *shlichus* with greater weight. Perhaps a mere verbal message carried by a second agent — himself not in possession of the document — cannot override the status conferred by the first *shaliach*'s role.

*Kamashmalan* — the *Mishnah* teaches that it can. The second *shaliach* effectively represents the husband's current will, and that current will takes precedence.

### Reaching Wife Directly

The third scenario — the husband himself races to his wife — also requires separate mention. Here, the concern cuts differently. When the husband goes directly to the woman who has been waiting for the *get*, and he appears before her and tells her that the *get* she was expecting is annulled, we might be deeply suspicious of his motives. *Vadai letzura d'achamchaman* — certainly we might suspect he is doing this purely to cause her anguish, not as a genuine retraction of his will. When he annuls through a messenger to the first *shaliach*, there is a degree of remove; but here he is confronting her directly, and the opportunity for cruelty is patent.

Nevertheless, the *Mishnah* teaches that we do not make that assumption. The *bitul* is valid regardless of how it was received emotionally.

### Second Shaliach to Wife

The fourth scenario — sending a second *shaliach* to the wife — requires mention for yet another distinct reason. One might have thought that hiring a *shaliach* to deliver the message of *bitul* to the wife suggests that the husband is not troubled by the effort and cost of causing her anguish at arm's length. He sits comfortably at home while someone else carries the distressing message. *Vadai letzura d'achamchaman* — perhaps in this configuration, where the husband incurs no personal inconvenience, we should certainly suspect his motives. The *Mishnah* teaches that we still do not invalidate the *bitul* on this basis.

### Running After Shaliach

Following the analysis of all four scenarios, the *Gemara* addresses a further case: *iglaei milta lemafreia d'bitulei batlei* — what if we discover in hindsight that the husband was clearly trying to annul the *get*? Specifically, the case imagined is one where the husband was visibly running through the marketplace after the *shaliach*, clearly trying to catch him, but the *shaliach* delivered the *get* to the wife a moment before the husband arrived. Should we reason that since it is now manifest what the husband's intent was — he was plainly trying to be *mevatel* — perhaps his running itself should count retroactively as an act of *bitul*?

The *Gemara* says: *ka mashma lan* — no. This does not work. And the reasons are multiple. First, we ordinarily say *devarim shebelev einam devarim* — unarticulated thoughts carry no halachic weight. The husband said nothing; he was thinking and running, but those inner intentions do not constitute a valid speech act. Second, even if one could somehow treat the running as equivalent to an articulation of will, the husband still did not communicate that will to the *shaliach*, the wife, or a *beis din*. He was shouting, so to speak, in the empty air of the marketplace. The *Mishnah*'s structure throughout is that valid *bitul* requires communication to the relevant parties. Without that, there is no *bitul*.

### Tosafot Devarim Shebelev

*Tosafot* engages this case with particular depth. *Tosafot* begins from the question of why *devarim shebelev einam devarim* — why do unarticulated thoughts carry no weight? The conventional answer is systemic: a legal framework cannot function if people can later claim "this is what I was thinking." Halachic acts require articulated, measurable, knowable expression.

But *Tosafot* notes a second rationale that appears in certain contexts: the reason unarticulated thoughts don't count is that if a person really meant them, they would have expressed them. The failure to articulate is itself evidence that the commitment was not firm enough to have legal weight.

*Tosafot* then points out that this second rationale fails to apply to the running-after-the-*shaliach* case. No one doubts that the husband was serious. He was running. He was making every effort. The failure to articulate was not a sign of ambivalence but a failure of logistics — he simply did not reach the *shaliach* in time. If the only problem were lack of seriousness, it would not apply here.

*Tosafot* further imagines a scenario in which the *shaliach* actually saw the husband running. At the time, the *shaliach* may have interpreted it as the husband urging him on — *hurry up and deliver it*. Only in hindsight, once the husband explains himself, does the *shaliach* understand that the running was an attempt at *bitul*. If *devarim shebelev havei devarim* in such a case — if we can treat the running as a form of articulation — should we not retroactively interpret what the *shaliach* witnessed as a communicated act of *bitul*?

*Tosafot* toys with this possibility seriously. Yet in the end, *Tosafot* concludes that the rabbis treated such a case as equivalent to *devarim shebelev* — even if the running was unambiguously sincere. *Shekeivan d'ktzas dami l'devarim shebelev lo chashiv akimas dibur min haTorah* — since it resembles *devarim shebelev* closely enough, it is not treated as a fully constituted speech act under Torah law. And *Tosafot* is explicit that this amounts to a rabbinic override: the rabbis effectively prevented what might technically have been a valid *bitul* from taking effect. As *Tosafot* notes — and this is a theme that will recur throughout the *perek* — the rabbis sometimes use their power to prevent something that would otherwise work under *d'Oraita* law, provided the contravention is not so blatant as to undermine the Torah structure.

The bottom line is that this does not constitute valid *bitul*, for a convergence of reasons: *devarim shebelev einam devarim*; even if it were treated as articulation, it was not communicated to the right parties at the right time; and even if the *shaliach* witnessed the running, a retroactive reinterpretation of that moment — based on later clarification — does not convert it into a contemporaneous speech act. Valid *bitul* requires explicit, timely communication to the *shaliach*, the wife, or a *beis din*.

---

## Annulment Formulas

### Valid Invalid Formulas

The *Gemara* now turns to the *Baraita* that addresses the question of what language suffices for valid *bitul*. A student had earlier asked whether there is a required formula. The *Baraita* teaches: if he said *batel hu* — it is annulled — or *ee efshi bo* — I do not desire it — *devarav kayamim*, it is effective. If he said *pasul hu* — it is invalid — or *eino get* — it is not a *get* — *lo amar klum*, he has said nothing.

The distinction is conceptually interesting. *Ee efshi bo* — I no longer desire it — does not explicitly void the document; it simply withdraws the will behind it. Yet that is enough. *Pasul hu*, on the other hand, is a statement of alleged fact — you are asserting that the *get* is halachically invalid. But by what grounds is it invalid? You are not making a declarative act of retraction; you are making a false assertion about its current legal status. That carries no weight.

### Batel Status vs Effect

The more subtle case is *batel hu* itself. The *Gemara* asks: *lemimra de-batel lishna de-livatel mashma* — does saying "it is *batel*" mean it shall become *batel*, i.e., I am hereby annulling it? Or is it a description of current status — it already is *batel*? Consider the language of *kiddushin*: *harei at mekudeshet li* — behold you are betrothed to me. Is that a description of a fact or the performance of an act? Obviously the latter. But the grammar is identical to a description. The question of whether language is constitutive or merely descriptive is not always resolved by the words themselves.

### Matana Gift Comparison

The *Gemara* brings a ruling of Rav Sheshet (also attributed to Rabba bar Abba or Rabba bar Avuh) concerning *matana* — a gift. If someone received a gift and thereafter said *matana zo mevutelet* — this gift that I have received shall be annulled — or *ee efshi bah* — I do not desire it — *lo amar klum*. Once you have received the gift, the gift is yours. If you wish to divest yourself of it, go give it away; you cannot retroactively annul the receipt. The language of *shall be annulled* is simply inapplicable to something already completed.

However, if the recipient said *beteila hi* — it is annulled — or *eina matana* — it is not a gift — *devarav kayamin*, that is effective. Here, the logic is essentially the reverse of the *get* case. By saying "it is not a gift, it was never a gift," you are articulating that you never accepted it as such; you are describing the status from its inception, not trying to effect a change now.

*Alma batel me'ikara mashma* — so when *batel* is used effectively in the *matana* context, it means "it was never valid from the outset." The *Gemara* thus faces a tension: by the *get*, *batel hu* seems to mean "I am hereby annulling it" — a future-oriented performative act. By the *matana*, *beteila hi* seems to mean "it was never valid" — a backward-looking description. Does *batel* mean one thing or two different things?

### Abaye Context Analysis

*Abaye* resolves this: *batel shtei leshonot mashma* — *batel* carries both meanings, and which meaning obtains depends entirely on context. *Le-gabei get lishna de-bahani beh ka-amar* — by a *get*, the clear purpose of the statement is to effect an annulment, so we interpret it accordingly; *batel hu* means it shall hereby be annulled. *De-gabei matana lishna de-bahani beh ka-amar* — by a *matana* already received, the only way the language can function effectively is if it refers to original status; so *beteila hi* means it was never a valid gift.

The straightforward explanation is simply that words are often ambiguous, and context disambiguates them. This is entirely parallel to the concept of *yadayim mokhichot* — when context is clear, it determines the meaning of an otherwise ambiguous expression. Under the *chuppah*, *harei at mekudeshet li* is unmistakably performative. Said in a different context, the same words might describe a fact. Here too: the intent behind the speech act in its context tells us which reading of *batel* is operative.

---

## Ravina Formula Questions

### Batel Without Hu

*Ravina* found Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak leaning in a doorway and posed him the following question: what if the husband simply said *batel* — without *hu*? He did not say *harei hu batel* or *batel hu*; he just uttered *batel*. Is that an effective formula? *Rashi* explains that the problem is the absence of *hu* — he did not even form a complete sentence.

The *Gemara* answers: *teiku* — the question stands unresolved. We do not know whether this stripped-down utterance suffices or not.

### Rav Sheshet Baraita

A *Baraita* is cited in the name of Rav Sheshet — some say it was taught in a *matnitta*: if he said *get zeh lo yoil* — this *get* shall not work — *lo yattir* — shall not render her permitted — *lo yaaziv* — shall not send her forth — *lo yishalach*, *lo yigoresh* — shall not divorce her — or *yehe kacheres* / *tehe kacheres* — it shall be like pottery — *devarav kayamim*, all of these are effective formulas.

What these formulations share is that they are forward-looking: they say what the *get* shall no longer do. They constitute a speech act of annulment. *Eino mo'il, eino matir, eino ma'aziv, eino meshaleach, eino megaresh* — it does not work, does not permit, does not send her forth, does not divorce — *lo amar klum*, these are not effective. These formulations merely describe what the *get* currently does not do — they are statements of alleged fact about its present status rather than acts of voiding it.

### Harei Hu Cheres

An ambiguous case is then raised: what of *harei hu cheres* — behold, it is pottery? Is this a performative declaration — I hereby declare it to be mere pottery, stripping it of its status as a *get* — or is it a description of current status — I am asserting that it already is nothing more than pottery? *Mahu* — what is the ruling?

### Hekdesh Hefker Compare

One *amora* said to another: *mai shena me-harei hu hekdesh, harei hu hefker* — what is the difference from "behold it is *hekdesh*" or "behold it is *hefker*"? In those cases, the declaration clearly effects a change in status; *harei hu hekdesh* is the paradigmatic performative speech act by which something becomes consecrated. Why should *harei hu cheres* not be read the same way?

*Tosafot* notes the difficulty with this comparison. The reason *harei hu hekdesh* or *harei hu hefker* are unmistakably performative is that *hekdesh* and *hefker* are statuses that exist exclusively through speech acts. When you say something "is *hekdesh*," the context makes clear that you mean you are making it *hekdesh*, because that is the only way *hekdesh* comes into being. *Cheres*, however — pottery — is a material description. Saying something "is pottery" does not inherently invoke a speech act that changes status; it might simply be identifying what the object is made of. Moreover, *Tosafot* points out, the parallel does not map cleanly: saying *kikar zeh hekdesh* — this loaf of bread is *hekdesh* — would clearly be effective, whereas *be-get zeh cheres* — this *get* is pottery — might certainly be saying nothing at all. One cannot mechanically substitute one predicate for another and assume the performative force transfers. The specific word matters enormously to the sense of the sentence, and *Tosafot* here does not arrive at a definitive resolution.

---

## Reversing Annulment

### Chozer Question

The *Gemara* now raises what is perhaps the most conceptually arresting question of the entire *sugiyah*: *chozer umegaresh bo o eino chozer umegaresh bo?* — once the husband has annulled the *get*, can he then reverse that annulment and use the *get* to divorce his wife, or has he effectively destroyed the *get* beyond recovery?

This is the equivalent of asking whether stopping a check and then un-stopping it would allow the check to be cashed. Can the *bitul* be undone?

### Nachman Sheshet Dispute

Rav Nachman says *chozer umegaresh bo* — he can reuse it; the *bitul* can be reversed and the *get* used. Rav Sheshet says *eino chozer umegaresh bo* — he cannot; the *get* has been rendered permanently void. *Vehilchata kevateih de-Rav Nachman* — the law follows Rav Nachman.

This ruling is striking. We have spent considerable time reading through formulas of *bitul* — *batel hu, harei hu cheres, lo yoil, lo yattir* — all of which are directed emphatically at the efficacy of the *get*, at stripping it of its status as an instrument of divorce. And yet the *halacha* says it can be un-done?

### Kiddushin Parallel

The *Gemara* draws a comparison to a case in *Kiddushin*. If a man says to a woman *harei at mekudeshet li be-tabaat zu le-achar sheloshim yom* — you are betrothed to me with this ring in thirty days — and then during those thirty days one of the parties retracts, *Rabbi Yochanan* rules that this retraction is effective. *Vekayma lan hilchata kevateih de-Rabbi Yochanan be-chozeret* — and the established ruling follows Rabbi Yochanan that she can retract. Furthermore, the kiddushin, once reversed in this way, is fully undone. The initial act, which created a pending kiddushin, can be annulled before it takes effect, and the annulment is complete.

The *Gemara* adduces this to support the idea that annulment before an act has fully taken effect is possible and reversible: just as the retraction of *kiddushin* before the thirty days expire is clean and complete, so too should a *bitul* of a *get* before delivery be reversible.

### Dibbur Umaseh Analysis

The *Gemara* immediately rejects this comparison. *Hatam dibbur u-dibbur hu* — there, in the *kiddushin* case, it is speech against speech. The *kiddushin* was created by a speech act conditioned on time, and it is undone by another speech act before the condition matures. *Ati dibbur u-mevatel dibbur* — one speech act cancels another. Nothing concrete has happened; no status has been effected in the world; the act is entirely in the realm of verbal declaration, and a subsequent verbal declaration can undo it.

*Hacha*, here, by contrast, the situation is different. *Nehi de-bitul li-shlichutei de-shaliach* — granted, when he said *batel hu*, he did annul the *shlichus* of the *shaliach*, the agency. But *gita gufiah mi ka batel?* — since when did he annul the *get* itself? This is the crucial move. The *Gemara* is suggesting that what the husband's words actually accomplished was the cancellation of the agency — nothing more. The *get* as a legal document was not changed. A valid document sitting in an agent's hand is not rendered legally void by the principal's subsequent verbal statement of displeasure with it. The words canceled the *shlichus*; they did not alter the status of the document.

And if all that was canceled was the *shlichus*, then the *shlichus* can simply be re-established. The document remains valid; appoint a new *shaliach* or take the document yourself, and deliver it. *Chozer umegaresh bo* — yes, he can reuse it — because nothing happened to the *get* itself.

### Tosafot Annul Get

*Tosafot* presses on this reading carefully. From the language of the *Gemara* — *gita gufiah mi ka batel* — *Tosafot* draws the inference that the *Gemara* is stating it is simply impossible to annul the *get* itself through speech. *Mitoch ha-lashon mashma de-afilu bitlo be-perush eino mevutal* — even if the husband had explicitly stated "I am not annulling the *shlichus*, I am annulling the *get* itself," it would be ineffective. *Ve-dibbur li-shlichuto hu de-batel* — whatever he said, we will interpret it as a cancellation of agency, not a change in the document's status.

This is significant because it means that all the rich analysis of formulas — *batel hu*, *harei hu cheres*, *lo yoil* — was really about the annulment of *shlichus*, not about changing the inherent legal status of the *get* as a document. The *get*, as a validly executed document, is beyond the reach of the husband's subsequent speech. *Ve-ka-amar gita gufiah mi ka batel — mashma de-ein lo koach levatel* — the language implies he simply does not have the power to annul it.

*Tosafot* also notes, however, that a parallel *sugiyah* reads slightly differently: *nehi de-batlei li-shlichutei, midei de-gita lo batlei* — granted he annulled the *shlichus*, but from the *get* itself he did not annul anything. *Tosafot* notes that this formulation only says he *did not* annul the *get*, not that he *could not*. Based on this, *Tosafot* argues that in a case where the *bitul* was explicit and unambiguous — where the husband clearly declared the *get* itself void — *Rav Nachman* would actually concede that it is *batel* and the *get* cannot be reused. Furthermore, *Tosafot* maintains that one necessarily must say that the *get* is not yet an irretractable completed act as long as it has not reached the woman's hand — otherwise, various other principles would be in tension. The upshot is that the *sugiyah* leaves genuine ambiguity: does Rav Nachman's ruling that *chozer umegaresh bo* rest on the view that annulment of the *get* itself is categorically impossible, or merely that in the ordinary case we interpret the husband's words as canceling *shlichus* rather than the *get*, while a fully explicit annulment could in principle still work?

---

## Original Beis Din

### Barishonah Original

The *Gemara* now takes up the second part of the *Mishnah* — the *barishonah* clause. Originally, before Rabban Gamliel's *takana*, a husband could annul the *get* by convening a *beis din* back in his hometown while the *shaliach* was en route, with no notification to the *shaliach* or the wife. This has now been prohibited. But the *Gemara* asks: in that original state, when this was permissible, how many people were required to constitute the *beis din* before which the *bitul* was made?

### Two Three Judges

Rav Nachman says *bifnei shnayim* — before two. Rav Sheshet says *bifnei gimel* — before three, a full *beis din*. Rav Sheshet's position is straightforward: the *Mishnah* says *beis din*, and a *beis din* is three. Rav Nachman counters that two are also called a *beis din* in certain contexts — *beis terei nami beis din kari lehu*.

*Tosafot* notes that Rav Nachman holds a position in Sanhedrin that *shnayim she-danu, dineihem din* — two who adjudicated, their ruling stands retroactively — but points out that other *amoraim* who agree with Rav Nachman here do not hold that position in Sanhedrin, suggesting that Rav Nachman's ruling here reflects a broader definitional claim about the term *beis din* in certain contexts, not merely a leniency about judicial quorums.

### Agency vs Document

The deeper question behind the dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet over two versus three is conceptual, and it connects elegantly to the earlier dispute between them. Why did the original procedure require a *beis din* at all? If all the husband is doing is retracting his will — annulling the *shlichus* — why not simply do it privately? The only reason to require witnesses is to establish proof that it occurred. In that case, two witnesses suffice, just as any other fact requiring proof requires two witnesses, not three judges. This is Rav Nachman's position: the *bitul* is fundamentally a retraction of *shlichus*, an act of the husband's will, which requires only *eidim* to authenticate it. The use of the term *beis din* is loose; two witnesses are all that is really needed.

Rav Sheshet, who holds that the *bitul* effects a genuine change in the status of the *get* itself — and who correspondingly holds that once done it cannot be reversed — sees this as a fundamentally judicial act. Something that changes the legal status of a document cannot be accomplished by a private expression of will, however witnessed. It requires a formal juridical proceeding, a *beis din* of three. The two positions — Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet — thus map perfectly: *chozer umegaresh bo* / *eino chozer umegaresh bo*, and *bifnei shnayim* / *bifnei gimel*, are two expressions of a single underlying conceptual disagreement about the nature of *bitul*.

---

---

# Gittin 33

## Shaliach Cancellation

### Two vs. Three Judges

The fourth chapter of *Gittin* opens with the *mishna* of *hasholeach get l'ishto* — the case of a husband who appoints a *shaliach* to deliver a *get* to his wife, and then seeks to cancel that appointment. Since the *shaliach* is no longer authorized to deliver the *get*, his doing so would render the *get* null, leaving the wife to believe she is divorced when she is not. To prevent this, *Rabban Gamliel HaZaken* enacted a *takana*: *hitkin Rabban Gamliel HaZaken shelo yehu osim ken mipnei tikkun ha-olam* — he ordained that a husband may no longer cancel the *shlichus* of the *shaliach*, for the sake of *tikkun ha-olam*.

The *mishna* records that originally — *barishona* — the husband could convene a *beit din* elsewhere, in a place where the *shaliach* was not present, and before that court announce the cancellation of the *shlichus*. This would nullify the *get* entirely. After *Rabban Gamliel*'s *takana*, this was no longer permitted.

There is a deeper conceptual point worth noting here. When a husband appoints a *shaliach*, he transfers the power to deliver the *get* to that agent. The question is: how independent does the *shaliach* then become? Does the initial command carry itself through to completion, or does the husband remain, so to speak, umbilically connected to the *shaliach* at every moment, retaining the capacity to withdraw authorization? The husband's power to cancel the *shaliach* mid-process reflects the latter understanding — that the *shlichut* continues to depend on the ongoing will of the husband. There are related *sugyot* in *Kiddushin*, in the second *perek*, that engage the question of how far a *shaliach* exercises his own independent judgment within the parameters granted to him.

The *gemara* at the bottom of 32b now takes up a new question: *bifnei kamah hu mevatlo* — in front of how many judges must the husband announce the cancellation? This refers to the era before *Rabban Gamliel*'s *takana*, when cancellation was still permissible.

*Rav Nachman* says *bifnei shnayim* — two judges suffice. *Rav Sheshet* says *bifnei shlosha* — three are required.

The conceptual underpinning of *Rav Nachman*'s position is that *le-bei trei nami beis din kari lehu* — even two people can be called a *beit din*. This is at least plausible, since the standard requirement for a *beit din* of three is rooted in the principle of *ein beit din shakol* — we do not allow an evenly divided court. That concern applies when the court is voting on a case and an even split would leave it deadlocked, as would occur with two judges. But here, no judgment is being rendered; the husband is simply making a declaration before a court that oversees it. It could therefore be argued that the concern of *ein beit din shakol* simply does not apply.

### Pruzbul Proof

*Rav Nachman* supports his position with a proof from the *mishna* in *Shevi'it* dealing with the institution of the *pruzbul*. The *pruzbul* is a legal document by which the *beit din* acquires the right to collect a loan even after the *shemita* year would otherwise cancel it. The text of the *pruzbul* as quoted in the *mishna* reads: *masrani lifneichem Ploni u-Ploni ha-dayanim she-be-makom Ploni* — "I hereby transfer [the loan] before you, so-and-so and so-and-so, the judges of such-and-such a place." Only two names appear — *Ploni u-Ploni* — suggesting that for the *pruzbul*, a court of two suffices.

*Rav Nachman* further adduces a proof from the same context: the *mishna* states that *ha-dayanim chotmin mi-lemata o ha-edim* — either the judges or the witnesses sign at the bottom of the *pruzbul*. He reasons: *mai lav dayanim dumya de-edim* — just as witnesses are two, so too judges in this context are two. The *mishna* equates the two tracks, implying that the same numerical threshold applies to both.

### Sheshet's Objection

*Rav Sheshet* objects to the first proof. He asks rhetorically: *atu tanna ki rukhla le-meichshav ve-leizil?* — Does the *tanna* have to go listing names like a peddler in the marketplace calling out his wares? Even if three *dayanim* were present, the *mishna* would not write *Ploni u-Ploni u-Ploni*; such repetition would be superfluous. The *mishna* mentions two names not to indicate that only two are required, but simply because that is sufficient to convey the formula. The reader is presumed to know that a *beit din* requires three.

To *Rav Nachman*'s second proof — the equation of judges and witnesses in the *pruzbul* — *Rav Sheshet* responds: *mi-di irya ha ke-dita ve-ha ke-dita* — the two tracks are simply independent. There is no implication that the two tracks share the same numerical requirement. Two witnesses are two; three judges are three. The *mishna* needed to mention both possibilities because the *shtar* can be drafted either in the voice of the witnesses or in the voice of the judges, and in either case the other party may sign. It is not that judges can replace witnesses with a reduced number; rather, the language of the document and the identity of the signatories are flexible, but the counts remain fixed at their respective minimums.

The *gemara* then works out the implications of this last point more carefully. The *mishna*'s ruling that *lo shena katuv bi-leshon dayanim ve-chatmu edim ve-lo shena katuv bi-leshon edim ve-chatmu dayanim* — it makes no difference whether the document is written in the voice of the judges and signed by witnesses, or in the voice of the witnesses and signed by judges — teaches that these two formalities are interchangeable. The judges and witnesses each retain their respective roles and numerical requirements, but the language of the document need not match the identity of its signatories.

### Halachic Conclusion

The *halacha* follows *Rav Nachman*: cancellation before two judges is sufficient. This is the general rule whenever *Rav Nachman* and *Rav Sheshet* dispute a matter — the *halacha* follows *Rav Nachman*. Both the *Rambam* and the *Shulchan Aruch* rule accordingly, as does the *Rif*.

One can observe that the proofs offered on each side are not particularly decisive. *Rav Nachman*'s argument from the *pruzbul* is answerable, and *Rav Sheshet*'s objections, while cogent, are not airtight either. The deeper question — what role this *beit din* plays when it oversees a cancellation of *shlichus*, a proceeding that involves no adjudication — remains somewhat open. Both positions carry internal logic. In practice, since *Rabban Gamliel*'s *takana* has closed off the entire mechanism of cancellation, the question is largely theoretical. Yet the later *amoraim* engage it seriously, and as will become clear, *Rabbi Yochanan*'s alignment with *Rav Nachman* and *Resh Lakish*'s alignment with *Rav Sheshet* gives this dispute an earlier, tannaitic resonance.

---

## Takanah Rationale

### Mamzerim Concern

The *mishna* states that *Rabban Gamliel* enacted his *takana mipnei tikkun ha-olam* — for the sake of fixing the world. The *gemara* now asks: what precisely is the *tikkun ha-olam* at stake?

*Rabbi Yochanan* says: *mipnei tikkun mamzerim* — to prevent *mamzerim*. When a husband secretly cancels his *shaliach* before a *beit din* of two — according to *Rav Nachman*'s position — the news of that cancellation may never reach the wife. She receives the *get* from the *shaliach*, believes she is divorced, remarries, and has children. Those children, born of what is in fact an adulterous union, would be *mamzerim*. The *takana* prevents this by blocking the husband's ability to cancel the *shlichus* altogether.

### Agunot Concern

*Resh Lakish* disagrees and says: *mipnei takkanat agunot* — to prevent *agunot*. He holds like *Rav Sheshet*, that cancellation must take place before three *dayanim*, and a formal court of three does generate a *kol* — *be-tlata it lehu kala* — a public voice sufficient to ensure that the wife hears of the cancellation before acting on the *get*. Given that, the problem is not that she will remarry and produce *mamzerim*; she will hear about it and refrain. The real danger, in *Resh Lakish*'s view, is the opposite: the husband, knowing that the court's announcement will reach her, will use the threat of cancellation to hold her hostage indefinitely. She cannot remarry even though she wishes to, and she remains an *aguna*. The *takana*, on this reading, is designed to protect women from being permanently chained.

This *machloket* recalls the broader tension in *Ketubot* between the concern for *tznuot* — women who are scrupulously careful about their marital status and may therefore wait indefinitely — and *prutzot* — women who may act on an invalid *get* and inadvertently commit adultery. *Rabbi Yochanan* is concerned with the second scenario; *Resh Lakish* with the first.

### Kol & Public Knowledge

*Tosafot* points out that the two positions are not simply in tension; they are logically nested. According to *Rabbi Yochanan*, even if the *takana* had merely changed the requirement from two witnesses to three, there would still be a concern — because even a court of three may not generate a *kol* sufficient to inform the wife in all cases. *Rabban Gamliel* therefore needed a two-stage response: first moving from two to three, and then eliminating the option entirely. The *takana* was not a minor procedural adjustment but a complete revocation of the husband's power to cancel.

A second *Tosafot*, on the phrase *be-tlata it lehu kala*, examines the broader assumption that three people sitting as a court create an effective public announcement. The suggestion is that the formality of a court proceeding — as distinct from a casual statement before two witnesses — is what generates the *kol*. *Tosafot* notes that in other areas of *halacha*, two witnesses are generally sufficient to establish public knowledge, and so the precise threshold at which something becomes widely known enough to protect the wife remains a matter of some delicacy.

---

## Bitulo Mevutal

### Rabbi's Position

The *gemara* now presents a *baraita* containing two separate *machlokot* between *Rabbi* (Judah the Prince) and *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*. The first: *bitalo mevutal, divrei Rebbe* — if the husband cancelled the *shaliach* [after *Rabban Gamliel*'s *takana*], the cancellation nonetheless works, according to *Rabbi*. Even though the husband is forbidden from cancelling the *shlichus* under *Rabban Gamliel*'s *takana*, *Rabbi* holds that if he did so, the cancellation is legally effective. This is an application of the general question — *kol mah de'asrah rachmana, ee avid mehani ee lo mehani* — whether an act that is prohibited nonetheless takes legal effect when performed. In some contexts, the act works despite being forbidden; in others, the prohibition also nullifies the act. *Rabbi* holds that here the cancellation falls into the first category: forbidden but effective.

### Rabban Shimon's Position

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* disagrees on two points. First, the husband cannot cancel the *shaliach* — and second, he cannot extend a *tnai* attached to the *get*. If the husband gave a *get* conditional upon some event within thirty days and then, on the twenty-ninth day, extended the condition for another month, this would effectively create a perpetual *tnai*, circumventing the requirement of *kritut* — the complete severing of the marital bond. While a finite *tnai* such as "on condition that you do not drink wine for thirty days" is valid — because at the expiration of the term the husband has no further control — indefinite extension undermines the entire structure of *kritut*. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* therefore prohibits this mechanism as well.

His overarching rationale is the principle of *mah koach beit din yafeh* — what then is the power of the court? If the husband can simply circumvent *Rabban Gamliel*'s *takana* by going ahead and cancelling anyway, with the cancellation remaining legally effective, then the *takana* accomplishes nothing. The *beit din* must have the authority to make its enactments effective, not merely advisory.

The *gemara* presses this position hard: *umi ika de-mide'oraita batel gita, u-mishum mah koach beit din yafeh sharina eshet ish le'alma?* — Is there really a case where the *get* is invalid at the *de'oraita* level and yet, in the name of *mah koach beit din yafeh*, we permit a married woman to remarry? The husband cancelled the *shlichus*; *de'oraita*, the *get* is void; this woman is still a married woman; and yet the rabbis step in and declare her permitted? The *gemara* answers: yes — and this is the striking principle at the heart of the *sugya*.

### Rabbinic Authority

The *gemara*'s answer is: *kol de-mekadesh ada'ata de-rabbanan mekadesh, ve-afke'inhu rabbanan le-kiddushin minei* — whoever gets married, marries on the basis of the rabbis' authority, and the rabbis therefore have the power to retroactively annul the *kiddushin*. This is a foundational principle, and a consequential one. Marriage is not simply a private affair between two individuals; it is a legal status change that takes place within the framework of a society governed by *halacha*. The *kiddushin* formula itself encodes this: *harei at mekudeshet li be-taba'at zu ke-dat Moshe ve-Yisrael* — according to Mosaic law and according to *dat Yisrael*, which includes the *halacha* as it exists at the time of the marriage, including rabbinic enactments. It is thus implicit in every marriage that it is contracted under, and subject to, the authority of *chazal*.

### Kiddushin Types

The *gemara* records *Ravina* posing a sharp question to *Rav Ashi*: *tenah de-kadesh be-kaspa* — this principle makes sense when a man betroths a woman with money, i.e., *kiddushei kesef*, such as a ring. Why? Because most *rishonim* invoke the principle of *hefker beit din hefker* — the court can declare property ownerless — and therefore the rabbis can retroactively nullify the monetary value used to effect the *kiddushin*, thereby undoing the *kinyan* at its root. But *kadish be-viah mai ika le-meimar* — what of *kiddushei biah*, one of the three forms of *kiddushin* recognized in the first *mishna* of *Kiddushin*, whereby marriage is effected through cohabitation? How can the rabbis retroactively declare that a sexual act did not effect *kiddushin*?

*Rav Ashi* responds: *shavveiyeh rabbanan le-beilato beilat zenut* — the rabbis recast that sexual act not as *kinyan kiddushin* but as mere *beilat zenut*, a licentious act. They strip it of its marital legal weight entirely. The mechanism is the following: there is a *chazakah* — a legal presumption — that *ein adam oseh beilato beilat zenut*, a man does not engage in cohabitation as a mere promiscuous act; he presumably intends it within a marital framework. The rabbis can reverse that *chazakah* and declare the opposite — that it was *beilat zenut* after all — and with that, the *kiddushin* falls away.

It is worth noting in this context that *Rav* famously placed a *cherem* on *kiddushei biah* because of its impropriety, which raises its own question: to what extent did the rabbis effectively close off this avenue of *kiddushin* entirely through their enactments, even though it is one of the three modes listed in the *mishna*?

### Rashi's Position

There is a lengthy and important *Rashi* on this page that deserves careful attention. *Rashi* cites his rabbis — the German scholars in whose *yeshivot* in Mainz and Worms he studied — who explain the principle of *kol de-mekadesh ada'ata de-rabbanan mekadesh* as follows: *de-kiddushei kesef de-rabbanan* — marriage by money is only a rabbinic institution to begin with. On this view, *kiddushei kesef* is not *de'oraita*, and therefore the rabbis' power to annul it is straightforward. The reason they give is that *kiddushei kesef* is derived through a *gezeirah shavah*, and a *gezeirah shavah* does not necessarily carry *de'oraita* force.

*Rashi* disagrees sharply and directly. He writes — and this is one of his characteristic moves in the commentary, where he explicitly parts ways with his teachers — that a *gezeirah shavah* is always *de'oraita*. He does not know what the basis for their view could be.

It is worth noting that the *Rambam* in *Hilchot Ishut* presents a related gradation. In at least some textual versions, the *Rambam* states that *kiddushei biah* and *kiddushei shtar* are *min ha-Torah*, while *kiddushei kesef* is *mi-divrei soferim*. The *Rambam*'s category of *mi-divrei soferim* occupies a middle zone in his system — learned through *drash*, but not explicitly stated in the *Torah*, and therefore not categorized as *de'oraita* in the strict sense of the *Rambam*'s taxonomy. The *Kesef Mishneh* has an important comment on this *Rambam* as well. This places the *Rambam* in a position somewhat related to, though not identical with, that of *Rashi*'s rabbis — and the debate between *Rashi* and his teachers over the *de'oraita* status of *kiddushei kesef* is directly relevant to interpreting the *Rambam*'s ruling.

---

## Multiple Messengers

### Ten Messengers

The *baraita* presents the second *machloket* between *Rabbi* and *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*. If a husband said to ten people, *amar l'asara kitvu get l'ishti* — write a *get* for my wife — in practice this means two of them will serve as witnesses and one will write, with the others largely superfluous to the formal process. Now, can the husband go to some of them — say, two of them, without the other eight present — and cancel the *shlichus*?

*Rabbi* says yes: *yachol le-vatel zeh shelo bifnei zeh* — he can cancel one without the other knowing. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* says no: *eino yachol le-vatel ela zeh bifnei zeh* — he can only cancel in the presence of all of them together.

### Witness Grouping

The *gemara* asks: *be-mai kamipalgi?* — what is the underlying *machloket*? The answer: they dispute the principle of *eidut she-batla miktzata batla kula* — if part of a group of witnesses is cancelled, is the entire group cancelled?

*Rabbi* holds *eidut she-batla miktzata lo batla kula* — cancelling two of the ten does not cancel the mandate of the other eight. If so, telling two that their *shlichus* is revoked does not prevent the other eight from proceeding. And therefore *Rabbi* permits it: it is not harmful to the process of giving the *get*, so there is no reason to prohibit it. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*, conversely, holds *eidut she-batla miktzata batla kula* — if two of the ten are cancelled, all ten are cancelled. Therefore, going to two of them and telling them the *shlichus* is revoked effectively voids the mandate of all ten. This is dangerous: the other eight do not know their mandate has been voided, and they will proceed to write and deliver the *get*, which is now invalid. Thus *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* forbids it.

### Formality Principle

An alternative reading is offered: *ve-iba'it eima, de-kulei alma eidut she-batla miktzata lo batla kula* — perhaps everyone agrees that cancelling part of the group does not cancel the whole. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*'s objection, on this reading, stems from a different principle entirely: *kasavar milta de-misavda be-apei asara tzricha be-asara le-mishlafa* — anything that was done in front of ten people requires the full ten to be present in order to undo it. This is a formality requirement: when a mandate is given to a group, it can only be revoked in front of that entire group. This is not about what will happen if the revocation is partial; it is about the inherent legal incapacity of a partial revocation to take effect at all.

*Tosafot* points out a striking consequence of this reading. Even the two to whom the husband privately declared the revocation are not actually revoked — because the announcement was not made before all ten. They remain bound by their mandate and may still proceed to write the *get*. This is a significant *chiddush*, and *Tosafot* highlights it explicitly.

### Two Messengers

The *gemara* then raises the question of the case where the husband said *kulchem* — "all of you." In the earlier case he instructed ten people and left open which of them would actually serve as witnesses and writer. But if he specified *kulchem kitvu get le-ishti* — "all of you write a *get* for my wife" — meaning all ten must sign, the analysis shifts.

If *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*'s reason is *eidut she-batla miktzata batla kula*, then in the *kulchem* case — where the entire group must function as a unified body — it would be even clearer that cancelling two of them cancels the entire enterprise, since the eight remaining cannot constitute the complete group the husband specified. But if *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*'s reason is the formality principle — that a group mandate requires a group revocation — then the *kulchem* case and the original case are equally governed by that rule.

The *nafka mina* between the two readings becomes apparent: according to the first reading, *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*'s ruling in the *kulchem* case would rest on the same *eidut* logic, whereas according to the second reading, the formality principle applies regardless of whether the husband said *asara* or *kulchem*.

A different formulation enters the analysis as well. The *gemara* asks: what if the husband appointed only two *shluchim* — not ten — and said *tenu get le-ishti*? Can he cancel one without the other present? *Rabbi* says yes; *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* says no, only *zeh bifnei zeh*. The *gemara* asks: are two *shluchim* comparable to the *kulchem* case of ten? They are somewhat analogous, but the analysis diverges — as *Rav Ashi* notes — depending on whether we are speaking of *edei holacha* (witnesses for the delivery of the *get*) or *edei ketiva* (witnesses involved in writing the *get*). Witnesses who sign the *get* must function as a group and satisfy the requirement that *ein eidutan mitztarefet ad she-yiru shnayim ke-echad* — their testimony only combines when both witnesses perceive the act together. *Shluchim* who merely deliver the *get*, on the other hand, need not function as a group in the same way, and cancelling one independently of the other is therefore less problematic.

### Shmuel's Uncertainty

*Shmuel bar Yehuda* reports: *shmi'a li minei de-Rabbi Abba tartei chad tartei* — I heard from *Rabbi Abba* [that the *halacha* is ruled] two ways, one like *Rabbi* and one like *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* — *chada ke-Rebbi ve-chada ke-Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*. But *ve-lo yadana hai ke-Rebbi ve-hai ke-Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* — he does not know which of the two *machlokot* is ruled like which *amora*. This uncertainty sets up the resolution that follows.

---

## Halachic Resolution

### Rabbi's Retraction

*Rav Yosef* introduces a crucial piece of evidence: when *Rav Dimi* came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he reported that there had been a case in which *Rabbi* retracted his opinion and ruled like *chachamim*. The *chachamim*'s position, as explained by *Rashi*, concerns the case of *shum ha-dayanim* — a court's assessment of property value for purposes of sale. If the judges over-estimated or under-estimated by more than a sixth — more than 120% or less than 80% of market value — the ruling of *chachamim* is *michran batel*, the sale is cancelled. This implies that the court's assessment, even when erroneous, is not shielded by the principle of *mah koach beit din yafeh* in that context. *Rabbi* originally held that *mah koach beit din yafeh* should protect the court's ruling even when mistaken, but he retracted and agreed with *chachamim* that in a case of significant error the sale is voided.

*Rabbi Prata*, son of *Rabbi Elazar ben Prata*, grandson of *Rabbi Prata haGadol*, challenged this retraction: *im kein mah koach beit din yafeh* — if the sale is cancelled even when the court made the error, what power does the court retain? To this, *Rabbi* responded by reversing to the position of *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* — affirming that *mah koach beit din yafeh* is indeed a weighty principle — *de-chazar Rebbi ve-assak ke-Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*.

The implication for our *sugya* is this: since *Rabbi* ultimately embraced *mah koach beit din yafeh* as a guiding principle, he must have held accordingly in the first *machloket* — i.e., that the husband cannot cancel the *shaliach* even after the *takana*, aligning with *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*. Consequently, in the second *machloket* — concerning the ten messengers — *Rabbi* must have reverted to his own original position, ruling that *yachol le-vatel zeh shelo bifnei zeh*.

*Rav Yosef* also cites *Rabbi Oshaya* and *Rabbi Yehoshua min Usha* as holding one *machloket* like *Rabbi* and one like *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*, though each is uncertain which ruling goes which way.

### Forced Get Case

The *gemara* then introduces a remarkable incident. Five *sages* were sitting before *Rabbi Yehoshua min Usha*, and a man was brought before them and compelled to give a *get* against his will — *ashkley gita al korchei*. This invokes the *halachic* mechanism of *kefauhu ad she'yomar rotzeh ani* — the court coerces the husband until he declares his consent, a power that *batei din* exercised in certain circumstances in that era, though not in ours. Once the husband was compelled to appoint two witnesses to write and deliver the *get*, the court instructed them: *zilu ve-itmeru ve-kitvu lah* — go, hide, and write the *get* for her. The concern was that the husband, having been coerced, would try to track down the witnesses after the court proceeding and cancel the *shlichus* before they delivered the *get*.

This is a telling detail: the court's instruction to the witnesses to hide makes sense only if the husband retains the power to cancel the *shlichus* by approaching the witnesses directly. If the husband had no power whatsoever to cancel — which would be the case if we held like *Rabban Gamliel*'s *takana* applies even to the cancellation-before-witnesses scenario — hiding would be unnecessary. The husband could simply cancel by appearing before a different court. Thus the instruction to hide tells us something about how this court understood the mechanism of cancellation.

### Case Inference

The *gemara* draws the inference: *ve-i salkha da'atach ke-Rabbi, ki mitmarei mai havvei?* — If we held like *Rabbi* that the husband can cancel even after *Rabban Gamliel*'s *takana*, why would hiding help? The husband could simply convene two other people and cancel the *shaliach* before them. The fact that hiding was the prescribed remedy implies that we must be holding like *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* in this context — that the husband cannot cancel the *shlichus* at all after the *takana*. Since the cancellation itself is blocked, the only way the husband could interfere is by physically locating the witnesses and cancelling in their presence; hiding prevents that.

But then, if *Rabbi Yehoshua min Usha* held like *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* in the first *machloket*, he must have held like *Rabbi* in the second: *shema mina chada ke-Rebbi ve-chada ke-Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*. This confirms the report of *Shmuel bar Yehuda* and resolves his uncertainty — at least as to which position *Rabbi Yehoshua min Usha* held.

### Rava's Ruling

*Rava* now delivers the authoritative ruling: *halacha ke-Rabbi bi-shteihen* — the *halacha* follows *Rabbi* in both cases. First, even after *Rabban Gamliel*'s *takana*, if the husband cancelled the *shlichus*, the cancellation is effective (*bitalo mevutal*). Second, if the husband appointed ten messengers and cancelled before two of them without the others present, that cancellation is effective as well.

This ruling directly overrules the analysis attributing one *machloket* to *Rabbi* and one to *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*. *Rava* also specifies that *Rav Nachman* does not hold *mah koach beit din yafeh* in this context — which is why he rules consistently like *Rabbi*.

### Monetary vs. Status

But this immediately raises a contradiction: *Rav Nachman* himself stated in the name of *Shmuel* that in a case of *yetomim* who come to divide their father's estate, the *beit din* appoints an *apitropus* for each of them and selects optimal portions on their behalf — *borin lahem chelek yafeh* — and *Rav Nachman* himself ruled that once the *yetomim* reach adulthood they cannot contest the division: *higdilu ein yecholim limchot*. This implies that *Rav Nachman* does hold *mah koach beit din yafeh* in monetary matters — because otherwise why would the court's assessment be binding on the adult orphans?

The *gemara* resolves: *hatam mamona, hacha issura* — there is a fundamental distinction between monetary cases and cases of *issurim*, matters of ritual prohibition and personal status. *Rav Nachman* accepts *mah koach beit din yafeh* in purely monetary contexts, where it is the court's role to manage and adjudicate property affairs with finality. But in matters of *issurim* — including marital status, which is governed not merely by convention and mutual agreement but by the direct laws of the *Torah* — *mah koach beit din yafeh* does not override the underlying *de'oraita* reality.

### Rambam's Ruling

The *sugya* concludes with a notable observation about the *Rambam*. The *Ran* on the *Rif* points out that on the one hand, the *Rambam* rules like *Rabbi* in both *machlokot* — consistent with *Rava*'s conclusion. Yet in the case of *shlichus she-batla miktzata batla kula* — the parallel principle to *eidut she-batla miktzata batla kula* but applied to *shlichut* rather than testimony — the *Rambam* rules against *Rabbi* and in accordance with *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*. This appears to contradict the *gemara*'s explicit statement: *halacha ke-Rabbi bi-shteihen*.

The *Ran* resolves this by drawing a principled distinction between *eidus* and *shlichut*. The *gemara*'s ruling — *halacha ke-Rabbi bi-shteihen* — addresses the *machloket* as it applies to testimony: *eidut she-batla miktzata la batla kula*. But the same principle does not automatically carry over to *shlichut*. *Shlichus she-batla miktzata lo batla kula* — cancelling one *shaliach* out of two does not cancel the other — is a separate proposition, and the *Rambam* holds that by *shlichut*, the parallel principle does not apply in the same way.

The *Ran* leaves this as a question without fully resolving the conceptual distinction, but it is possible to suggest one. A *shaliach* can operate as a *yachid* — a single individual agent. There is nothing in the nature of *shlichut* that requires two agents to function as a unified group. *Eidut*, by contrast, is structurally a group enterprise: the *halacha* of testimony requires that witnesses act together — *ein eidutan mitztarefet ad she-yiru shnayim ke-echad* — and the principle *eidut she-batla miktzata batla kula* flows naturally from that structural requirement. Since the two witnesses constitute a single composite unit of testimony, breaking part of that unit breaks the whole. *Shlichut* carries no equivalent structural requirement of group unity, and therefore the same principle does not follow. The *Ran* leaves the question hanging, but this conceptual distinction — that *eidus* demands collective integrity in a way that *shlichut* does not — offers a coherent basis for the *Rambam*'s position.

---

---

# Gittin 34

## Giddul & Gilluy Da'as

### Giddul's Regret

The daf opens six lines from the top of 34a, within the broader context of the *mishna*'s discussion of a husband's ability to be *mevatel* a *get* before it reaches his wife. Recall that *Rabban Gamliel Hazaken* had already reformed the older practice of nullifying a *get* without the wife's knowledge, as part of *tikkun olam*. The *gemara* now introduces a narrative that will occasion a major *machloket* between Abaye and Rava.

*Giddul bar I'lai shadru lei gita l'devitehu* — Giddul bar I'lai sent a *get* to his wife. The *shliach* arrived and found her sitting and weaving. He said: here is your *get*. She responded: go for now, come back tomorrow. The *shliach* obliged — though he was not technically required to, since a husband may divorce his wife against her will — and returned to Giddul bar I'lai to report what had happened. At that point, Giddul bar I'lai broke into the blessing *Baruch Hatov Vehametiv*, an expression of gratitude — transparently indicating his relief that the *get* had not yet been delivered and his clear regret at having sent it.

### Abaye: No Gilluy

*Abaye amar Baruch Hatov Vehametiv v'lo batil gita* — Abaye holds that despite this unambiguous expression of remorse, the *get* was not nullified. If the *shliach* were to proceed and deliver the *get*, it would still be fully effective. Abaye's formulation speaks of *bitul* of the *get* itself, though Rashi frames the analysis more in terms of *bitul* of the *shlichut*, the agency. Either way, for Abaye, both the *get* and the *shlichut* remain operative.

### Rava: Gilluy Works

*Rava amar Baruch Hatov Vehametiv u'batil gita* — Rava disagrees. Once Giddul bar I'lai's expressed delight makes his intent manifest, the *get* is *batel*. Rashi again emphasizes that it is primarily the *shlichut* that is *batel*, with the implication for the *get* being that if one wished to proceed with a divorce, a new *get* would be required.

### The Debate

*Bemai kamiflagi? Begilui da'ata begita kamiflagi* — the *gemara* identifies the crux: the dispute concerns whether *gilui da'as* — the public revelation of one's intent — is legally operative in the context of a *get*.

There is no ambiguity about Giddul bar I'lai's *da'as*. The question is whether demonstrating desire, without a formal speech act of revocation, carries legal weight. Abaye holds: *gilui da'as begita lav milta hi* — it is of no legal consequence. From a strictly formal legal standpoint, this is compelling: one must execute an actual act of *bitul* of the *get* and revoke the *shlichut* through a proper verbal declaration. The mere revelation of intent, however transparent, leaves everything in place.

Rava counters: *gilui da'as begita milta hi* — once the *shliach* can no longer be said to be acting on the husband's behalf, because the husband's contrary wishes are plain, the *shlichut* is dissolved.

---

## Rav Sheshet Proof

### Forced Divorce

Rava now offers a proof from a case involving Rav Sheshet. Rav Sheshet compelled a man to divorce his wife against his will — a practice recognized as legitimate when carried out through a *beis din* with proper grounds, even when the husband's compliance is extracted under duress. The man submitted under pressure, saying the requisite words of consent and directing witnesses to proceed with the *get*. Thereafter, however, he turned to the witnesses and declared: *hachi amar lacho Rav Sheshet l'vatulei gita* — so said Rav Sheshet to you, that the *get* should be nullified. And Rav Sheshet then found himself needing to produce a new *get* — implying that the first had somehow been undermined.

### Rava's Inference

Rava's argument is that the man's statement — though patently false, since Rav Sheshet had said no such thing and lacks the authority to nullify someone else's *get* — nonetheless served to manifest the man's lack of genuine desire to divorce. It was a declaration of intent, not a formally valid act of *bitul*. And yet it apparently sufficed to create a problem with the *get*, requiring a second one. This is Rava's evidence that *gilui da'as* is operative.

---

## Abaye's Rebuttal

### Active Bitul

Abaye responds with a complete reinterpretation of the case. *Atu Rav Sheshet mevatel gitta de'inshei havae?* — Rav Sheshet is certainly not in a position to nullify someone else's *get*. An ordinary person might not appreciate this — especially someone facing a *beis din* — but logically the story cannot be what Rava says it is. Abaye's reading is that the man actually did perform an act of *bitul*, a genuine formal revocation of the *get* after he had directed the witnesses to proceed.

### Lashes Defense

The reason the man invoked Rav Sheshet's name was simply a cover story. The *beis din*'s officers were lashing him for attempting to nullify the *get* he had been compelled to give. Under the pain of those lashes, he gave a pretextual excuse — he falsely claimed that Rav Sheshet had authorized the *bitul* — not because the *bitul* consisted of that claim, but because he needed a reason to make the lashing stop. In Abaye's account, the *gilui da'as* was incidental; the *bitul* was an actual formal act. The need for a second *get* is therefore no evidence that *gilui da'as* alone sufficed.

---

## Plugged Ears

### Forced Get

Abaye now marshals his own proof. The case involves Rav Yehuda, who sought to compel his son-in-law — the son-in-law of Rav Yirmiyah Birah — to divorce his wife. Each time Rav Yehuda applied sufficient pressure for the man to say he consented and direct the *sofer* and witnesses to write the *get*, the man would then formally be *mevatel* the *get* as soon as the pressure lifted. This happened repeatedly: *tana ashkaleih u'batlei, hadar tana v'ashkaleih al korchei* — again and again Rav Yehuda forced the declaration, and again and again the man performed *bitul*.

Finally, Rav Yehuda directed the witnesses: *otivu karrei b'oznaichu* — put a gourd in your ears. Write the *get* and ensure you are not in a position to hear him issue any further revocation directed at you, the persons charged with writing and delivering it.

### Formal Act

Abaye's inference is precise and elegant. The instruction to plug the witnesses' ears only makes sense if one holds that *bitul* or revocation of *shlichut* requires a formal speech act directed at those authorized to act. If *gilui da'as* sufficed — if merely demonstrating one's intent were enough — then plugging their ears would be useless. As the *gemara* states: *ve'ha chazu leih d'ka rahi batraihu* — they can plainly see him chasing after them, making every effort to communicate his desire to retract. His intent is manifest even without words. If *gilui da'as* worked, all of that visible, frantic effort would already constitute *bitul*. The only reason the plugged ears accomplish anything is if formal, audible speech is required — precisely Abaye's position.

---

## Conditional Gets

### Rava's Counter

Rava responds to the plugged-ears proof. He argues that one may reinterpret what the man was shouting as he ran after the witnesses. Perhaps he was not attempting *bitul* at all — perhaps he was calling out: *ashur havu lah* — go and give it to her quickly, already, so that I can be done with this ordeal. Once the witnesses' ears are stopped up, Rava argues, we are free to reinterpret ambiguous behavior. The man is running — perhaps out of urgency to complete the divorce, not to abort it. In Rava's view, *gilui da'as* must genuinely manifest the relevant intent, and under these circumstances that manifestation is contestable.

Rava's position is thus nuanced: he does not say *gilui da'as* is always sufficient regardless of context. He says it suffices when the intent is genuinely and unambiguously revealed — but the circumstances may sometimes allow for alternative readings that prevent *gilui da'as* from being established.

### Ferry Case

Abaye is not yet finished pressing his position. A man gave a *get* to his wife on a *tenai*, a condition: *ee lo ateina ad tlatin yomei leihavei gitta* — if I do not return within thirty days, let it be a *get*. This was perhaps motivated by concern that he might perish on a journey with no witnesses to testify, leaving his wife an *agunah*. The thirty days elapsed; the man actually did return and was attempting to cross the river back to the city. But the ferry was on the opposite bank, and by the time it could have reached him, the thirty-day limit would have passed. He stood at the water's edge, clearly within earshot, and called out: *chazu de'asai chazu de'asai* — look, I have arrived, I have come back!

### Shmuel Ruling

*Lav shemei matya* — Shmuel rules that this does not count as having returned. The condition was not met; the *get* takes effect. This is a striking ruling, because the man's desire that the *get* not take effect could not be more apparent. He is standing at the riverbank, calling out, clearly demonstrating with everything at his disposal that he does not wish to be divorced. And yet the *get* is effective.

Abaye draws his inference: even this transparent *gilui da'as* is insufficient to prevent the *get* from taking effect. Why, then, does it not constitute *bitul* according to Rava?

Rava's response, however, is subtle. *Atu hasam levitulei gitta baei? Hasam lekiyumei tnaia ka baei* — he is not attempting *bitul* of the *get*. He is attempting to argue that he fulfilled his *tenai*, that the condition of the *get* was satisfied on his end. His *gilui da'as* is not focused on the *get* itself; it is focused on the factual question of whether he returned. Moreover — and this is analytically significant — there is no *shlichut* in play here. He gave the *get* thirty days ago with a condition attached. There is no agent whose authority can be revoked. The only question is whether the condition was met, and the only mechanism by which *gilui da'as* could operate would be through an actual *bitul* of the *get* as an object. But his *gilui da'as* is not directed at the *get*; it is directed at the *tenai*. And even if one were to say that Rava holds *gilui da'as* suffices, it would have to be *gilui da'as* of an intent to perform *bitul* — which is not what is happening here.

### Nissuin Condition

Another case: a man gave a *get* to his betrothed — there being *kiddushin* already in place — on the condition that if they did not proceed to *nissuin* within thirty days, the *get* would take effect. When thirty days arrived without *nissuin* having been completed, he claimed to be working on it, trying to make the arrangements. Is that enough to stave off the effectiveness of the *get*?

### Debate Applied

*L'mai neichush lah* — what legal theory could help him? *Ei mishum ones ein ones b'gittin* — if the argument is that he was unable to satisfy the condition through no fault of his own, there is a well-established ruling in a separate *sugya* that a claim of *ones* does not operate to excuse an unmet *tenai* in a *get*. So the condition is simply unfulfilled. As for *gilui da'as* — *plugta d'Abaye v'Rava* — that is precisely the dispute between Abaye and Rava. And yet here too, as the *gemara* notes, following Rava's logic in the ferry case, one could argue that even Rava would concede: there is no *shlichut* to revoke and there is no *gilui da'as* directed at a *bitul* of the *get* itself. His *gilui da'as* is about the *tenai*, not the *get*.

### Month Confusion

A third case: a man similarly gave a *get* on condition that *nissuin* not occur by *Rosh Chodesh Adar*. When *Rosh Chodesh Adar* arrived without *nissuin*, he claimed: I said *Nissan*, not *Adar*. The witnesses clearly remembered he had said *Adar*; he was either lying or misremembering. In any event, it is manifest that he does not want the *get* to take effect.

Again the *gemara* asks: *l'mai neichush lah*? *Ei mishum ones ein ones b'gittin* — his inability or failure to satisfy the condition does not excuse him. *Ei mishum gilui da'as — plugta d'Abaye v'Rava* — and whether his clear manifest desire is legally operative is once again the debate. And as before, even granting Rava's position, the *gilui da'as* here is not a *gilui da'as* of *bitul*; there is neither *shlichut* to revoke nor a properly focused *gilui da'as* of the *get* itself.

---

## Final Halacha

### Ruled Like Abaye

*V'hilcheta k'Nachman* — the *gemara* now states the *halacha* on several related matters. It rules like Rav Nachman on the earlier questions concerning whether *bitul* before two or three witnesses is required and whether a *bedi'eved* *bitul* performed in violation of *Rabban Gamliel*'s *takanah* is nonetheless effective. And crucially: *v'hilcheta k'Nachmani* — the *halacha* follows Nachmani, which is a name for Abaye.

We rule like Abaye: *gilui da'as begita lav milta hi*. Revealing one's intent is not legally sufficient to effect *bitul* of a *get* or to revoke a *shlichut*. An affirmative speech act of revocation is required. This is one of the exceptional cases in which the *halacha* follows Abaye against Rava, enumerated by the mnemonic *ya'al kagam* — and this is the *gimel* of *ya'al kagam*: *gilui da'as begita*.

### Nachmani Etymology

Why was Abaye called Nachmani? Rashi, in the second line of his commentary here, explains: *nire b'einai d'al shem she-Rabbah bar Nachmani gidel Abaye b'veito v'limdo Torah* — it appears to him that Abaye was named after Rabbah bar Nachmani, who is otherwise referred to simply as *stam* Rabbah, because Rabbah raised the orphaned Abaye in his home and taught him Torah. Others reverse the relationship and suggest that Nachmani was actually Abaye's given name, but because it too closely resembled the name of Rabbah bar Nachmani — or Rabbah's own father — he was given the name Abaye instead. The *Maharsha* notes that the name *Abaye* carries a beautiful allusive quality as a *rashei teivos*: *asher b'cha yerucham yasom* — through You, O God, the orphan finds consolation. Either way, the *halacha* follows Abaye — Nachmani — that *gilui da'as begita* does not suffice.

---

## Multiple Names

### Rabban Gamliel

The *gemara* transitions to the next *mishna*, still within the thematic context of *tikkun olam* in the world of *gittin*. *Berishona haya mishane shemo v'shma shem iro v'shem ira* — originally, a *get* might be written using a name or a city name that was not the primary, fully established designation: a secondary name, a name recognized in one locale but not another, a nickname, without full transparency about all the names by which a party was known.

*Hitkin Rabban Gamliel Hazaken* — Rabban Gamliel the Elder enacted that the *get* should state: this man and any name that he has, and this woman and any name that she has — *mipnei tikkun olam*. This raises an important question that will recur throughout the *gemara*'s analysis: does the phrase *v'chol shum sheyesh lo* mean that one writes those words formulaically — a standard rubric inserted in all *gittin* — or does it mean that one must actually enumerate and list each additional name explicitly?
