That question, as the *gemara* makes clear, remains open to significant debate among the *rishonim*.

---

## Regional Names

### Name Problem

The *gemara* provides the historical context for Rabban Gamliel's enactment. *Shalchu leih bnei medinas hayam l'Rabban Gamliel* — the people of overseas communities sent a question to Rabban Gamliel in *Eretz Yisrael*. The problem was this: *shemo Yosef v'korin lo Yochanan, Yochanan v'korin lo Yosef* — people emigrating from *Eretz Yisrael* were known by one name at home and an entirely different name in their new community. Perhaps they had adopted a local name; perhaps the names were used interchangeably in different social contexts. The question was pointed: *heichi megarshin nishoseihem?* — if such a man wished to send a *get* back to his wife in *Eretz Yisrael*, which name should be used — the name by which he is known where the *get* is written, or the name by which he is known where it will be received?

This question illuminates precisely what the *mishna* meant by its concern about changing or misusing names. The ambiguity was real and consequential.

*Amar Rabban Gamliel v'hitkin* — Rabban Gamliel responded with his enactment: write the name and every other name, so that there is no ambiguity whatsoever. The question of which name takes priority — whether the primary name is determined by the location of writing or the location of delivery — is not resolved explicitly here; the *Tosafot* engage that question at length.

### Rav Ashi's Rule

*Amar Rav Ashi v'hu de-itchazak bitrei shemei* — Rav Ashi qualifies: the requirement applies only when it is *established* that a person goes by two different names. If only one name is known, the obligation to enumerate additional names does not apply.

One might wonder what this qualification adds — after all, one cannot be expected to list names one does not know. The practical significance, as Rashi explains, lies in the *bedi'eved* question. If a man is known by only one name at the time the *get* is written and someone later comes forward to assert that he also goes by another name, the *get* already delivered is nonetheless *kosher bedi'eved*. The *takanah* — and the consequence of *bitul* — applies only when both names were already *established* at the time of writing.

This in turn raises a significant question that will resonate through the rest of the discussion: is the *bitul* a rabbinic consequence that *Chazal* imposed through Rabban Gamliel's enactment — meaning *Chazal* are exercising their authority to invalidate a *get* — or is the invalidity rooted *de-Oraita*, in that a *get* lacking sufficient identification is inherently defective, and Rabban Gamliel's enactment was simply designed to prevent that underlying problem? The answer has significant implications for how broadly the *bitul* applies.

*Amar lei Rabbi Abba le-Rav Ashi* — Rabbi Abba confirmed to Rav Ashi that Rav Mari and Rav Elazar both hold in accordance with his view. And a *braita* is cited that supports Rav Ashi: *tanya kevathei de-Rav Ashi*.

---

## Two Wives Braita

### Two-Region Case

*Hayu lo shetei nashim* — a man had two wives, one in Judea and one in Galilee. Furthermore, he had two names: one name by which he was known in Judea and another in Galilee. This is the case that makes the *bedi'eved* ruling explicit.

### Both Names Required

*Gireish et ishah she-bi-Yehudah bishmo she-bi-Yehudah ve-et ishah she-ba-Galil bishmo she-ba-Galil — einah megureshet* — if he divorced his Judean wife using only his Judean name, or his Galilean wife using only his Galilean name, the *get* is invalid. The *braita* makes clear that to divorce his Judean wife, he must use his Judean name and include his Galilean name as well — *veshem de-Galil imo* — and vice versa for his Galilean wife. Failure to include both names produces a *batel get bedi'eved*.

This *braita* establishes two important points. First, the *bitul bedi'eved* is real and operative when both names were established and only one was included. Second — and here the *Tosafot* comment at length — the default name, the one written first, appears to be determined by the place where the *get* is being delivered: where the wife lives. Divorcing the Judean wife, one begins with the Judean name; divorcing the Galilean wife, one begins with the Galilean name.

### Third Place

*Yatza le-makom acher vegireish be-achad mei-hem megureshet* — now the *braita* introduces what appears to be a surprising ruling. If the same man leaves both Judea and Galilee and goes to a third place, and from there divorces one of his wives using only one of his names, the *get* is valid. This seems inconsistent. The same man, the same two names — why should his geographic location affect the validity of the *get*?

### Unknown Names

*Ela shema mina ha de-itchazek ha de-lo itchazek* — the *gemara* draws the inference: the distinction must rest entirely on whether the second name is *established* in the place of writing. In Judea, it is known that this man also goes by a Galilean name; in Galilee, his Judean name is known. In either case, writing only one name leaves a known gap. But if he travels to a third place — say, outside the land — that community knows him by only one name. His other name is not *established* there. Therefore, *bedi'eved*, the *get* is *kosher*.

This reasoning powerfully suggests that the *bitul* is rabbinic in nature. If the problem were a genuine *de-Oraita* lack of identification, the man's geographic location would be irrelevant — the ambiguity would exist regardless of whether the community writing the *get* was aware of it. The fact that ignorance of the second name renders the *get* valid implies that the requirement is imposed by *Chazal*, and *Chazal* calibrated the *takanah* to circumstances where the omission is blameworthy. Where one cannot be blamed — because the second name is simply unknown — the *get* stands.

---

## Majority Name

### Miriam vs Sarah

The *gemara* concludes with a case of a different character: *hahi d'hava karu lah Miriam v'ukmusa Sarah* — a woman was known by two names, Miriam and Sarah, and both names were used in the same locale. This differs from the earlier cases involving different names in different geographic regions; here, the two names coexist in a single community.

*Amar Nahardai: Miriam v'chol shum sheish lah v'lo Sarah v'chol shum sheish lah* — the sages of Nehardea rule that one writes Miriam — the majority name, the name by which she is predominantly known — as the primary name, and not Sarah. The logic is straightforward: the default name should be the one most widely recognized.

This ruling prompts further questions that the *gemara* does not fully resolve. The question of what happens *bedi'eved* if the names are reversed — if Sarah is written first and Miriam second — is left open. And importantly, this case extends Rabban Gamliel's *takanah* beyond the geographic scenario to the situation where a single person goes by multiple names in the same place. One must list all established names even absent any regional ambiguity.

Finally, the underlying structural question persists: does *v'chol shum sheish lah* mean that one writes those words as a formula, or that one actually lists each name by name? This question, raised at the outset of the *gemara*'s discussion, threads through every case and remains a central point of dispute among the *rishonim*.

---

---

# Gittin 35

## Tikkun Olam Overview

### Shift to General Tikkun

The daf opens on Gittin 35b, and we now transition from *tikkun olam* rulings that were specifically connected to *gittin* to *tikkun olam* rulings of a more general character — improvements to the world that extend beyond the narrow context of divorce. The phrase *tikkun olam* has, of course, acquired broad connotations in other cultural contexts — universal social justice and the like — but as it has been used throughout this sugya, it carries a far more specific and halachic meaning: protecting people from legal abuse, or from situations where the halacha itself places them in untenable circumstances, particularly to protect women from having their *get* challenged improperly or from other related hardships.

### Defining Tikkun Olam

This raises a genuine conceptual question: who exactly is the *olam* being improved? In the cases we have seen, the *olam* is a fairly local one — primarily women who find themselves in precarious legal positions. The *tikkun* is about managing a specific societal reality and making the halachic system function in a way that doesn't leave people stranded.

### Tikkun Olam Examples

The *mishna* presents several examples. The first — which will be the focus of the *gemara* — is the rule that a widow cannot collect from the orphans' estate except by taking an oath. The second is the already-familiar rule that witnesses sign a *get* for the sake of *tikkun olam*, enabling the woman to remarry without producing the original witnesses — the position of Rabbi Eliezer that biblically no signatures were required, but rabbinically they were instituted to protect the woman. The third is Hillel's institution of the *pruzbul* for the sake of *tikkun olam*. Notably, the phrase *mipnei tikkun olam* does not explicitly appear alongside the widow's case — the *mishna* simply says *hitkin Rabban Gamliel* — while it appears explicitly by the witnesses and the *pruzbul*.

### Who Benefits from Tikkun

The question of who constitutes the *olam* being addressed is worth pausing over. In one case it is widows; in another it is women being divorced; in the third it is the broader economic reality of lending and borrowing. In the final case, the *olam* encompasses the entire Jewish community's financial life. But in all cases, the *olam* remains the Jewish *olam* — it is the internal world of halachic society that is being ordered and improved.

---

## Widow's Kesuba Collection

### General Debt Collection…

The *gemara* immediately challenges the formulation of the *mishna*. Why does the *mishna* specify that an *almana* — a widow — cannot collect from the orphans without an oath? This rule ought to apply universally: anyone who comes to collect a debt from orphans after the father has died must take an oath, since the father is no longer alive to verify that the debt was never repaid. Perhaps he trusted the creditor and did not demand a receipt; perhaps he paid and the receipt was lost. The general rule is well established: *haba lipara minechasei yesomim lo yipara ela bishvua* — one who comes to collect from orphan heirs does not collect without an oath. So why single out the widow?

### Mishum China Doctrine

The *gemara* answers: *almana itztricha lei* — it was necessary to underscore that even the widow must take an oath, because one might have thought otherwise. The reasoning behind this assumption is the doctrine of *mishum china* — literally, finding favor. The idea is that because the *kesuba* was instituted to make marriage attractive and to protect the woman financially, one might have thought the rabbis would be lenient and not require her to take an oath, both to encourage women to marry with confidence that their financial interests would be protected, and to ensure the *kesuba* would genuinely function as a security. As Rashi explains: *mishum china sheyehei chen hanashim beeinei haanashim linasei lahem* — so that women would find favor in the eyes of men and be prepared to marry. Therefore, the *mishna* teaches us that notwithstanding this consideration, the oath requirement still applied to her — *ka mashma lan* — this leniency was not granted.

### Dinar-Bread Narrative

But then the situation changed. The *gemara* records that they stopped requiring the widow to take an oath — *nimne'u mil'hashbia* — because they became deeply concerned about the consequences of a false oath. The *gemara* introduces this concern through a famous story. Rav Kahana — and some say it was Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav — reports: there was an incident during years of famine in which a certain man deposited a gold *dinar* with a widow for safekeeping. She placed it in a pitcher of flour. She then forgot it was there, kneaded the dough, and baked it into bread. Given that it was a time of famine, she gave the loaf to a pauper. When the owner returned and asked for his coin, she could not produce it — she genuinely did not know where it had gone — and so she took what was intended as an oath: *yehaneh sam hamaves b'echad mibaneha shel osa isha im neheness midinaracha klum* — let poison take effect upon one of my children if I derived any benefit from your coin. A short time later, one of her children died.

When the sages heard of this, they said: if someone who swore truthfully — or at least believed she was swearing truthfully — suffered such consequences, how much more severe would be the punishment of one who swears falsely with intent. This incident crystallized the communal recoil from the oath and led to the reluctance to impose it upon widows.

### Benefit Analysis

The *gemara* then probes: why was she punished at all, if she swore truthfully? The answer is *d'ishtareshi lah makom dinar* — she did in fact benefit from the coin, since the coin displaced a volume of flour in the bread, meaning she effectively gained that volume's worth of flour. But the irony compounds: she did not even eat the bread herself — she gave it to a pauper. What benefit did she derive? The *gemara* holds that her voluntary decision to give away the bread does not negate the fact that she used another person's property without authorization. The benefit was incidental, but it was real. And yet in her own mind, she was swearing entirely truthfully — she genuinely believed she had derived no benefit. The *gemara* addresses this by characterizing her as *k'mi shenishba be'emes* — as if she had sworn truthfully — meaning her subjective intention was entirely honest. And even so, the consequences were severe. Hence the sages' alarm: if this is what befalls one who swears honestly but is factually mistaken, what will befall one who swears with deliberate falsehood?

---

## Why Widows Uniquely at R…

### Specificity Question

The *gemara* now presses the obvious question: if the concern is about the weight of oaths and the danger of swearing falsely — even innocently — why is this uniquely a problem for the *almana*? Why do we continue to allow *gerushos* (divorced women) to take oaths, or indeed any creditor collecting from orphans? The concern about inadvertent false oaths should apply universally.

### Widow's Rationalization

The *gemara* answers in the name of Rav Zeira citing Shmuel: *almana shani* — the widow is different. The reason is *debei hi na dekatarcha kmei dyasmei* — because she is there in the house, she exerts effort on behalf of the orphans. She is living in her late husband's home, cooking and cleaning, performing services for the orphans that no one is compensating her for. This creates the conditions for an almost unconscious rationalization: she may find a sum of money lying around and, having worked so hard without pay, tell herself she is entitled to take it as partial payment of her *kesuba*. She does not necessarily think of it as stealing — she genuinely believes she is owed this amount and that she is entitled to it. It is the kind of rationalization familiar from everyday life: the employee who takes home a notepad from the office because they have been working overtime without recognition.

### Divorced vs. Widow

The *gerusha*, by contrast, is not living in her former husband's home. She has no ongoing relationship with the estate, no daily proximity to the orphans, and no accumulating sense of uncompensated labor. There is therefore no analogous scenario in which she would take money and rationalize it as legitimate. Hence the concern is specific to the *almana*. The story of the *dinar* happened to involve a widow, but the widow's status was largely incidental to that narrative; the *ongoing* concern is structural and arises precisely from the widow's unique domestic situation.

### Tosafot on Negligence

Tosafot raises a pointed question based on a *gemara* in *Shevu'os* which states that an oath taken in good faith — believing oneself to be telling the truth — does not constitute a transgression, since the verse *lo yenakeh Hashem es asher yisa shemo lashav* applies only to those who take the name in vain, not to those who genuinely believe what they are saying. If so, why was the widow punished? Tosafot works through this at length and concludes: *veyesh lomar dehacha gabei pikadon haya lo lehizaher yoser leshomro heytev rauei lasukei adaitei shetavo lidei shvua* — here, since she was entrusted with the coin as a *pikadon* (a deposit), she bore a heightened responsibility to take adequate care of it. Because her error arose from negligence — she should have been more careful in tracking its location — the mistake cannot be considered entirely faultless, and therefore the normal exculpation for an unintentional false oath does not apply. The principle is significant: when one's false belief is itself the product of negligence, it is not treated with the same indulgence as a genuinely unavoidable error.

---

## Oath Types & Contexts

### Shift to Cherem

Tosafot continues with a remark that opens onto a broader practice. He notes that in the present era, the practice has shifted further: *ulekach nimneu milehashbia bishvua meruba* — because the oath is so weighty, they have moved away from it, *ela behadara delo chamir kuli hai* — toward the *neder*, which is not as weighty. And then Tosafot adds: *vehashata bizman hazeh tiknu lekabel cherem bemakom shvua shelo yehei hamichshol kol kach* — in our times they have instituted taking a *cherem* (a conditional curse) in place of the *shvua*, so that the potential for catastrophic consequences is diminished while still maintaining a form of solemn attestation. This observation is important not only for the specific case of the widow but for the entire institution of testimony and sworn statements. The deep-seated recoil from taking a *shvua* — even a *shvuas emes*, a truthful oath — has been a feature of Jewish practice for centuries. The practical question of what a *beis din* actually administers today follows from this entire trajectory of concern.

### Shvua vs. Alah

There is also a subtle distinction worth noting regarding the widow's statement in the story itself. A *shvua* proper is an invocation of God's name to attest to the truth of one's statement, anchored in the verse *lo yenakeh Hashem es asher yisa shemo lashav*. An *alah*, by contrast, is a conditional curse — "let such-and-such happen to me if I am lying" — which calls down consequences rather than calling God as witness. The woman's declaration in the story — *yehaneh sam hamaves b'echad mibaneha* — is linguistically an *alah*, not a *shvua*. It is possible, of course, that a proper *shvua* preceded it and is simply not quoted. But the distinction is interesting: the *gemara* treats it as a *shvua*, even though the precise language cited is that of an *alah*.

### Oath Context Distinction

The *gemara* introduces a further distinction regarding the differential weight of oaths depending on context. Rav Yehuda cites Rav and Shmuel as saying: *lo shanu ela b'beis din* — the restriction on making the widow take an oath applies only within *beis din*; *aval chutz leveis din mashbinan lah* — outside of *beis din*, she can be made to take an oath. Rashi explains the difference: a *beis din* oath is a Torah-level obligation, administered while holding a *sefer Torah* or *tefillin*, invoking God's name or an appellation thereof — as we find by Avraham who said *sim na yadecha tachas yerechi vehishvacha baShem* — and its consequences are correspondingly severe. Outside *beis din*, the oath is rabbinic in character: there is no holy object held, the formulation is more in the nature of an *arur* (a curse), and the penalty, while still real, is not as severe.

---

## Rav's Stringent Position

### Rav's Refusal

The *gemara* now raises a difficulty with this framework. If outside *beis din* the widow can be made to take an oath, then why does the *gemara* report that Rav refused to collect the *kesuba* for a widow — *lo magbi kesuba l'armalta* — at all? If there exists a lower-stakes mechanism (the oath outside *beis din*) that could enable collection, why did Rav block collection entirely?

The *gemara* initially treats this as a *kashya* — a genuine difficulty — against the version in which Rav himself stated that outside *beis din* an oath can be administered. It then presents an alternative version from *Neharde'a*: in *Sura* the teaching attributed the outside-*beis din* leniency to Rav; in *Neharde'a*, it is attributed exclusively to Shmuel. Under the *Neharde'a* version, Rav held a far more stringent position: *afilu chutz l'beis din nami ein mashbi'in osah* — even outside *beis din*, we do not make her take an oath. And Rav is then internally consistent — *Rav l'ta'ameih* — since he refused to collect the *kesuba* for widows altogether.

### Rav's Concerns

But then the question shifts: if Rav held that a *shvua* — whether in or out of *beis din* — cannot be administered to the widow, why didn't he simply follow the *mishna*'s *takanah* of Rabban Gamliel and have her take a *neder* instead? The *gemara* answers: *bishnei d'Rav kili nidrei* — in the time of Rav, people treated *nedarim* lightly. A *neder* was no longer weighty enough to function as a reliable instrument of truth-telling. The *takanah* of Rabban Gamliel had depended on the *neder* occupying a middle ground — weighty enough to keep the woman honest, but not so weighty as to carry the catastrophic consequences of a *shvuas sheker*. In Rav's era, that balance had shifted: *nedarim* had lost their gravitas, and Rav was therefore unwilling to use them. This left the widow with no viable instrument for collection, which is precisely what the *mishna*'s *takanah* was designed to prevent. The irony is not lost: the authority of Rav was now functioning as an obstacle to the very *tikkun* that Rabban Gamliel had worked to achieve.

### Woman's Workaround

Against this background the *gemara* relates the story of a woman who came before Rav Huna. He told her he could not help her — *d'Rav lo magbi kesuba l'armalta* — citing Rav's authority. The woman, without waiting to be asked, declared: *chai Hashem Tzevaos im nehenesi miksuvasi klum* — by the life of the God of Hosts, I did not derive any benefit from my *kesuba*. She simply took the oath unilaterally.

### Rav's Concession

Rav Huna responded: *modeh Rav b'kofetzes* — even Rav concedes in the case of one who "jumps in" and takes the oath voluntarily. The reluctance to administer the oath arose from rabbinic hesitation to impose it; but once the woman takes it on her own initiative, the oath is valid and she may collect. This creates a significant asymmetry: the court will not make her take the oath, but if she takes it herself, it is binding. Women needed to know this option existed.

### Widow Trapped

The second story is more troubling. A woman came before Rabbah bar Rav Huna seeking to collect her *kesuba*. He told her: *d'Rav lo magbi kesuba l'armalta* — and furthermore, *Abba Mari lo magbi kesuba l'armalta* — my father and teacher likewise did not collect a *kesuba* for a widow. The woman, finding this avenue closed, said: fine, then at minimum support me from my late husband's estate — *hav li mezoni*. He replied: *mezoni nami leis lach* — you cannot have that either. For Rav Yehuda had said in the name of Shmuel: *hatovasa kesuvashah b'veis din ein lah mezonos* — once a woman has gone to *beis din* to demand her *kesuba*, she has effectively declared her intention to sever her connection from her late husband's household, and she therefore forfeits the ongoing support that was premised on her continued identification with that household.

The woman was now caught between two rulings: she could neither collect her *kesuba* nor continue to receive support from the estate. She cursed Rabbah bar Rav Huna — *afchuah lekursai*, let your chair be turned upside down — and the *gemara* relates that they literally inverted his chair in an attempt to symbolically fulfill the curse and thereby neutralize it. Nevertheless, *va'afilu hachi lo ifrik mechulsha* — even so, he did not escape falling ill as a result of the curse. What the episode illustrates is how the invocation of Rav's authority, transmitted through generations of disciples without reassessment, had drifted entirely away from the animating concern of *tikkun olam* that motivated the original *takanah* of Rabban Gamliel.

---

## Rav Yehuda's Challenge

### Neder + Oath

Rav Yehuda said to Rav Yirmiyah Bira'a: *adra b'veis din* — have her take a *neder* in *beis din*, *ve'ashbe'uha chutz leveit din* — and have her take a *shvua* outside of *beis din*. The proposal is to combine both instruments. Given the concern that neither alone is fully reliable — the *neder* because it had lost weight in Rav's era, and the *shvua* outside *beis din* because it may not be sufficiently weighty — perhaps the combination of both would satisfy the competing concerns. The *neder* in the formal setting of *beis din* and the *shvua* in the more lenient extra-judicial context would together constitute a sufficient basis for collection.

### Demand for Action

Rav Yehuda did not stop at the theoretical proposal. He demanded: *velesei kalla velipo be'udni* — let the announcement go out and let me hear with my own ears that you have actually acted on this — *debe'inah keheichi de'avid bah ma'aseh* — I want to know that you have carried this through in practice and that she has in fact collected her *kesuba*. The frustration is palpable: this is not a theoretical discussion. There is a woman who is owed money and cannot collect it, and the whole purpose of Rabban Gamliel's *takanah* was to ensure she could. The response of Rav Yehuda reflects a reassertion of the *tikkun olam* imperative against the paralysis that had set in through excessive deference to Rav's stringency.

### Widow vs. Divorced

At this point the *gemara* circles back to reinforce the earlier distinction. The leniency for a *gerusha* — who can still take the standard oath — rests on the absence of the rationalizing dynamic. Unlike the *almana*, the divorced woman has no ongoing entanglement with her former husband's estate. She is not living there, not working there, not accumulating a sense of uncompensated labor. The scenario in which she would unconsciously take funds and tell herself she was entitled to do so simply does not arise. Hence the concern that drove the abandonment of the oath for widows does not apply to her.

---

## Sarah bat Yaakov Case

### Case Facts

The *gemara* then presents a concrete case transmitted from *Eretz Yisrael* to *Bavel*. A message was sent: how should we handle the case of a certain woman — Sarah the daughter of Yaakov — who received her *get* from Akha bar Kida, also known as Ayah Mari, and who took a *neder* regarding produce — that all the fruit of the world would be forbidden to her — attesting that the only things she had received from her *kesuba* were certain specified items? The case is therefore a *gerusha* who took a *neder* rather than a *shvua*, and the question sent to *Bavel* was: proceed to collect for her the remainder of her *kesuba*.

### Kesuba Contents

The items she admitted to having already received as partial payment of her *kesuba* deserve a moment's attention. They were: a coat, a scroll of *Tehillim*, a scroll of *Iyov*, and a scroll of *Mishlei* — worn and valued at five *maneh*. That a woman's *kesuba* included *Tehillim*, *Iyov*, and *Mishlei* is a striking window into the reality of women's learning. *Tehillim* and *Mishlei* might be expected — *Tehillim* for prayer, *Mishlei* for its *mussar* character. But *Iyov* is something else — a text of profound theological and philosophical inquiry. That these scrolls formed part of a woman's valued personal property speaks for itself.

### Rav Ashi Analysis

Rav Ashi intervenes: *hahu get yavmim hava* — that *get* she received was actually a *get yavmim*, a *get* given by a brother-in-law in the context of *yibum*. What this means is that the woman's husband died and she became subject to *yibum*; the brother-in-law gave her a *get* to prevent the *yibum* from occurring, but the case is in reality one of an *almana*, not a *gerusha*, since it is her first husband who died and from whose estate she is collecting. Tosafot points out that *chalitza* — not a *get* from the brother-in-law — is technically what would finalize her status, and raises the question accordingly. Tosafot's preferred resolution is that the brother-in-law in fact performed *yibum* and then divorced her, making her technically divorced from the *yavam* (the brother-in-law), but since *yibum* is understood as a continuation of the first husband's bond, she collects from the first husband's estate. Either way, her status is ultimately that of an *almana* with respect to the original estate — and the case therefore does not provide the proof one might have thought for allowing a *gerusha* to take a *neder* in lieu of an oath.

---

## Neder Timing Rules

### Rav Huna Position

The *gemara* now turns to the question of when, precisely, the widow may take the *neder* that enables her to collect. Rav Huna rules: *lo shanu ela b'shelo nises* — this applies only when she has not yet remarried. The *takanah* of Rabban Gamliel permitting her to take a *neder* and collect her *kesuba* is available only while she remains unmarried.

### Husband Annuls Neder

The reason is straightforward: once she has remarried, her husband acquires the right of *hafarah* — the power to annul her vows. If she takes a *neder* while already married to a second husband, he can simply annul it, and the *neder* provides no protection whatsoever. It cannot serve as the required instrument of attestation.

### Gemara Challenge

The *gemara* challenges: but even if she takes the *neder* before remarrying, why does this help? The moment she remarries, her new husband will learn of the *neder* and annul it on the day of their marriage. So even a pre-marriage *neder* would be vulnerable.

### Pre-Existing Vows Safe

The *gemara* answers: *ein haba'al meifer bikodmin* — a husband cannot annul vows that predate the marriage. His power of *hafarah* operates only on vows made during the marriage, or at most on the day he first hears of them if they were made just before the marriage. Vows that were established prior to the marriage relationship are beyond his reach. Therefore, if she takes the *neder* while still single, it will remain binding even after she remarries, and the instrument works as intended.

---

## Release from Neder

### Chacham Annulment Risk

The *gemara* raises a further concern: even if remarriage is not a problem — since the husband cannot annul pre-existing vows — what prevents her from going to a *chacham* and obtaining a release from the *neder* through the mechanism of *hatarat nedarim*? Unlike a *shvua* regarding a past event, which either was true or was false at the moment it was taken and admits of no subsequent "release," a *neder* remains technically open to annulment by a *chacham* who finds a legitimate *petach* (opening) for release. If she can simply obtain an annulment of the *neder* after collecting her *kesuba*, the entire instrument is undermined.

### Detailing Requirement

The *gemara*'s answer: *kasavar tzarich lefareit es haneder* — we hold that one must detail the circumstances of the *neder* when seeking release. The requirement of *leprat es haneder* means that the woman must explain to the *chacham* not merely the formal content of the vow but the conditions and circumstances that gave rise to it. The standard *hatarat nedarim* formula recited on *Erev Rosh Hashanah* — where we acknowledge that the *halacha* requires detailing but waive that requirement because the vows are too numerous — reflects awareness of this principle.

### Chacham's Logic

Once the circumstances are detailed, the *chacham* will immediately understand that the *neder* was taken precisely to enable collection of the *kesuba* — it is the very instrument that secured her right to collect. He cannot release her from it without invalidating the basis on which she collected. The release is therefore unavailable. The reasoning depends, of course, on the woman being truthful with the *chacham*. If she lies about the circumstances and the *chacham* annuls based on false information, the annulment would presumably not be valid — a genuinely interesting question, though one the *gemara* does not explore here.

---

## Rav Nachman Leniency

### Neder B'Rabbim

Rav Nachman takes a more lenient position: *afilu nises* — even if she has remarried, she can still take the *neder* and collect. The concern that her husband will annul the *neder* is addressed by ensuring that *demadrinan lah berabbim* — we have her take the *neder* publicly. Once taken in public, the *neder* can no longer be annulled.

### Berabbim Concept

The concept of *berabbim* rests on the principle that once a matter has become public, the private mechanisms of annulment no longer apply. A *neder* taken publicly is no longer a private affair susceptible to personal retraction; it belongs, in a sense, to the public record.

### Berabbim Types

The *gemara* distinguishes this from a related but distinct concept: *al da'as rabbim*. The *berabbim* principle holds that once a vow is publicly pronounced, the private mechanisms of annulment are structurally inapplicable — it is as if the vow has been "published." The *al da'as rabbim* principle is different: it means the vow is made not merely on the basis of the individual's own intent, but on the basis of what the community would desire for the conditions of the vow. This makes it resistant to annulment because the annulment would require addressing not just the individual's own circumstances but the communal understanding. These are two different tools, and the *gemara* will draw on both.

### Baraita Evidence

The *gemara* cites *baraisa* support for Rav Nachman's position. One *baraisa* states that if she has remarried — *nises govah kesuvashah im nadrah* — she collects her *kesuba* if she made a *neder*, which the *gemara* initially reads as meaning she made the vow after remarrying, and thus supporting Rav Nachman. A second *baraisa* is more explicit: *nises noderes v'govah kesuvashah* — she remarried, she takes a vow now, and she collects. Both *baraisas* clearly support the view that a post-marriage *neder* can work.

### Tannaitic Debate

The *gemara* resolves the tension between the two positions — Rav Huna's that she must be unmarried and Rav Nachman's that she can be married — by declaring *tannai hi*: this is a dispute among *tannaim*. The dispute hinges on a fundamental question in the laws of *nedarim*: does a *neder shehuddar berabbim yesh lo hafarah* — can a vow taken publicly be annulled — or *ein lo hafarah* — is it definitively beyond annulment? The opinion that she can take a *neder* even after remarrying must hold that a public *neder* cannot be annulled; the opinion that she cannot must hold that even public vows remain technically open to annulment, and the husband's power therefore remains a threat. The *beis din* context itself suffices to make the vow "public" — Rashi specifies *ba'asarah*, before ten, and in the *beis din* setting this is easily achieved.

---

## Detailing Debate

### Rav Nachman: No Detail

The *gemara* now presents a direct dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Papa on whether *leprat es haneder* — detailing the circumstances of the vow — is required when seeking release from a *chacham*. Rav Nachman holds: *eino tzarich* — one does not need to detail the circumstances. His reasoning is given in the negative: if you required detailing, *zimnin degayiz lei lediburei* — sometimes a person will abbreviate and not give the full circumstances, *vechacham bemai deshama meifer* — and the *chacham* will annul based only on what he heard, which may be incomplete. If the *chacham* annuls based on a partial account, the annulment may be technically valid even though the full picture would have led him to refuse. By not requiring detail, you avoid the problem of partial disclosures generating flawed annulments.

### False Release Risk

But this raises an obvious concern: if no detailing is required, then a woman who took a *neder* to enable collection of her *kesuba* could subsequently go to a *chacham*, give him no specifics, and obtain a release without his knowing the *neder* was the instrument of her collection. This is precisely the scenario the *gemara* had earlier invoked as a reason to worry about the effectiveness of the *neder* mechanism. Under Rav Nachman, the answer to this concern is the *berabbim* solution — the vow is taken publicly and is therefore not open to annulment, regardless of whether details are given.

### Rav Papa: Detail Required

Rav Papa disagrees: *tzarich* — one must detail the circumstances, *mishum milta de-issura* — because without the details, the *chacham* may release someone from a vow that was serving as a safeguard against a transgression. The illustration is sharp: if a person took a *neder* not to walk down a certain street in order to avoid the temptation of a forbidden establishment, and then goes to a *chacham* and simply says "I have a *neder* not to walk down such-and-such street" without explaining why, the *chacham* may well annul it — thereby inadvertently removing the person's protection against sin. Without knowing the purpose of the vow, the *chacham* cannot properly evaluate whether annulment is appropriate. In the *kesuba* context, the same logic applies: without knowing that the *neder* was taken to enable collection of the *kesuba*, the *chacham* cannot know that annulment would allow the woman to retain money she does not deserve.

---

## Kohein's Neder Case

### Kohein's Obligation

The *gemara* adduces a parallel case from the laws of *kehuna* to illuminate the same underlying tension. The *mishna* states: *hanosei nashim ba-aveira pasul* — a *kohen* who has married a woman he is forbidden to marry is disqualified from performing the *avoda* in the *Beis Hamikdash*. The mechanism to restore his eligibility is: *ad sheyidor hana'ah* — until he takes a *neder* forbidding himself any benefit from his wife, which will effectively compel him to divorce her since the marriage becomes untenable. Once he has taken that *neder*, a related *baraisa* states: *noder ve-oved* — he takes the vow and performs the *avoda*. He does his *avoda*, descends from the *mizbe'ach*, and then divorces her.

### Parallel Problem

The same question arises here: if one does not need to detail the circumstances of a vow, what prevents this *kohen* from going to a *chacham*, obtaining release from his *neder* without disclosing that the whole point was to secure his divorce from a forbidden wife, and thereby escaping both the obligation to divorce and the disqualification from *avoda*? The mechanism by which the *neder* was supposed to guarantee his behavior becomes hollow if it can be quietly annulled.

### Same Solution Applied

The *gemara* gives the same answer: *demadrinan lah berabbim* — we ensure that the *neder* is taken publicly, and a public vow cannot be annulled. The parallel reinforces the point that the two mechanisms — *leprat es haneder* and *berabbim* — are the twin pillars on which the effectiveness of these vows depends.

---

## Neder Protection Methods

### Detail Method

The two mechanisms that protect a *neder* from being circumvented operate in different contexts. The first — *leprat es haneder*, requiring that the circumstances be detailed when seeking release from a *chacham* — ensures that the *chacham* has full information and can decline to annul when doing so would enable a transgression or undermine the purpose for which the vow was taken.

### Berabbim Method

The second — taking the *neder berabbim*, in public — removes the vow from the domain of private arrangements amenable to personal retraction. A vow made in public is no longer susceptible to annulment by a *chacham* (according to the view that *ein lo hafarah*) and certainly not by a husband.

### Context Application

The two mechanisms are not interchangeable in all contexts. Where the concern is a *chacham* annulling the vow, either mechanism can in principle address the problem: requiring detail will prevent a well-intentioned *chacham* from annulling without full information, and a *berabbim* vow forecloses the option entirely.

### Husband Annulment

But where the concern is the husband exercising his power of *hafarah*, the *leprat es haneder* mechanism is simply irrelevant. The husband does not need to be informed of the circumstances or reasons for the vow; his right of annulment is a marital prerogative that operates independently of his knowledge of the vow's purpose. In that context, only the *berabbim* solution works: by taking the *neder* publicly, the wife removes it from the reach of the husband's unilateral power of annulment. We will continue to explore what types of vows can or cannot be annulled as we proceed in the sugya.

---

---

# Gittin 36

## Widow's Vow vs. Oath

### Vow instead of oath

We begin at the very top of 36a, picking up a topic that has been developing across the preceding pages: the substitution of a *neder* (vow) for a *shvuah* (oath) when a widow comes to collect from her deceased husband's estate. The reason for the substitution is the severity of a *shvuat sheker* — a false oath — even an unintentional one carries grave consequences. By switching to a *neder*, the Rabbis hoped to give the widow a viable path to collection while protecting her from the dangers of a potentially false oath. We have already seen how that institution experienced a certain pushback at a later stage, and we will continue to see that dynamic as we proceed.

### Vow annulment problem

The *gemara* now asks: why should a *neder* suffice? Two problems immediately present themselves. First, can she make the vow at all once she is already married, given that her husband has the power to annul it — in which case the vow would not accomplish anything? Second, even for an unmarried widow, what prevents her from going to a *chakham* (sage) and having the vow released, thereby undermining the entire mechanism?

### Married woman's vow

On the question of a married woman, the *gemara* records a dispute. According to one opinion, a married woman cannot make such a vow for precisely this reason: her husband will simply annul it and it will prove nothing. According to another opinion, it is possible — but only under certain conditions.

### Be-rabbim vs. al da'at

Before examining those conditions, a preliminary distinction is essential: the difference between *be-rabbim* and *al da'at rabbim*. *Be-rabbim* means the vow was made in public — *Rashi* defines the relevant quorum as ten people. *Al da'at rabbim* means the vow was made not merely on the basis of the individual's own *da'at* (intent or understanding) but in some sense on the basis of what the community would intend — it is grounded in communal, rather than personal, *da'at*.

### Tosafot on husband annul…

*Tosafot* observes that when it comes to the husband's power of annulment (*hafarah*), *al da'at rabbim* does not help. The mechanism of *hatarah* — going to a *chakham* to have a vow released — works by identifying an error in the vower's *da'at*: had I known this or that, I never would have made the vow; my intent was mistaken, and so the vow should be dissolved. If the vow is grounded not in my subjective *da'at* but in the community's *da'at*, that avenue is closed off, because the subjective circumstances that might have constituted my personal error are no longer operative. That is the power of *al da'at rabbim* in blocking *hatarah* by a *chakham*.

But *hafarah* by a husband operates on an entirely different principle. The husband does not dissolve the vow by identifying an error in his wife's intent. He has a legal power, independent of *da'at* altogether, to declare that this vow cannot stand within the marriage. The wife's intent — whether completely certain or completely ambiguous — is irrelevant to this mechanism. And if the wife's *da'at* is irrelevant, substituting the community's *da'at* for hers changes nothing. Accordingly, *al da'at rabbim* provides no shield against a husband's *hafarah*.

### Public vs. communal dist…

*Be-rabbim*, however, may work precisely because it operates on a different logic altogether. When a vow is made in public, it is no longer a private matter between husband and wife. The vow has entered the public domain — it is a matter of public record, so to speak — and is thereby removed from the private relational sphere in which the husband's power of annulment operates. According to the opinions that *be-rabbim* functions in this way, it would block both *hafarah* by a husband and *hatarah* by a *chakham*, and it would do so without exception, since the mechanism is not about *da'at* at all.

There are, however, opinions that *be-rabbim* does not help: merely pronouncing a vow in front of others does not alter the inherent nature of the vow. According to those opinions, *al da'at rabbim* remains the operative mechanism — effective against the *chakham*, ineffective against the husband, and, as we shall see, subject to its own internal limitations.

### Three solutions explained

Returning to the question of how to block a woman (married or not) from going to a *chakham* to dissolve the vow: the *gemara* presents multiple approaches. One answer is that when the vow is made for purposes such as these, she must specify the circumstances in which it was made (*tzarikh lefareit et haneder*), and once those circumstances are explicit, the *chakham* will recognize that this is not a vow he may dissolve — it is the very instrument by which she collects. A second answer holds that ordinarily one need not detail the conditions of the vow, and therefore we are concerned she may seek release. According to this view, the vow is only protected if made either *be-rabbim* or *al da'at rabbim*. These two mechanisms, and the interplay between them, are what the *gemara* now proceeds to examine in detail.

---

## Al da'at rabbim mechanism

### Gemara on two concepts

The *gemara* opens this discussion with a case that clarifies how *be-rabbim* and *al da'at rabbim* function in practice. Three lines from the bottom of 35b, the *gemara* frames its question around a case analogous to the widow's: a *kohen* who made a vow not to derive benefit from a woman he is forbidden to marry — say, a *gerusha* — in order to render himself eligible to perform the *avodah*. The concern is identical: perhaps he will simply go to a *chakham* and have the vow dissolved.

The *gemara* at the top of 36a proposes: *demadirin lei be-rabbim* — we have him take the vow in public. That will close off the avenue of *hatarah*. But the *gemara* immediately complicates this: *hani-cha le-man d'amar neder she-hudur be-rabbim ein lo hafarah* — this works well for the opinion that a vow made in public cannot be annulled. *Ella le-man d'amar yesh lo hafarah* — but according to the opinion that it can still be annulled, what solution remains? The *gemara* answers: *demadirin lei al da'at rabbim* — we have him take the vow on the communal *da'at*, not merely in their presence.

### Ameimar's position

This leads to a direct ruling. *Amar Ameimar*: the *halacha* is that even according to the opinion that a vow made *be-rabbim* can still be annulled, a vow made *al da'at rabbim* cannot be annulled (*al da'at rabbim ein lo hafarah*).

A clarification is in order here. *Tosafot* has already established that *al da'at rabbim* cannot prevent a husband's *hafarah*, since the husband's power is independent of *da'at* entirely. Therefore, the *hafarah* that *Ameimar* says is blocked must refer specifically to *hatarah* — release by a *chakham* — not to a husband's *hafarah*. *Ameimar*'s ruling is thus: *be-rabbim* may or may not block *hatarah* (it is disputed); *al da'at rabbim* blocks *hatarah* according to everyone. The mechanism, as noted above, is that *hatarah* works by identifying subjective error in the vower's *da'at*. When the vow is grounded not in one's individual *da'at* but in a communal one, the personal subjective circumstances that might have constituted error are simply no longer relevant.

It is worth pausing to note the difference in scope between the two mechanisms. If *be-rabbim* does work — and that remains disputed — it is arguably broader and more absolute than *al da'at rabbim*. Making a vow in public transforms it into a matter of public record, removing it entirely from the private sphere; this would block *hafarah* by a husband as well as *hatarah* by a *chakham*, and it would permit no exceptions. *Al da'at rabbim*, by contrast, operates through *da'at* — it replaces subjective individual intent with communal intent — and therefore it is only relevant where *da'at* is operative. This means it does not help against a husband's *hafarah*, and, as the *gemara* now demonstrates, it is not absolute even against a *chakham*.

### Dardeki case study

The *gemara* introduces an important limitation: *ve-hani milei le-dvar reshut* — this rule that *al da'at rabbim* prevents *hatarah* applies only when the vow pertains to a discretionary matter. *Aval le-dvar mitzvah, yesh hafarah* — but if keeping the vow would interfere with the performance of a *mitzvah*, it can be annulled despite having been made *al da'at rabbim*.

The illustrative case is the *mikri dardeki* — an elementary school teacher. *Rav Acha* imposed a vow on him *al da'at rabbim* — binding him, under communal *da'at*, to the effect that he would no longer be permitted to teach children. The background is that he had been negligent, apparently meaning he had been striking the children — a recognized form of discipline in that era, though one that the *gemara* treats as grounds for removal. The vow was structured as *al da'at rabbim* precisely to close off any avenue of release. Nevertheless, *Ravina* subsequently restored him to his position (*ahadrei Ravina*), because *lo ishtakach de-dayek ke-votei* — no other teacher could be found who was as exacting and demanding as he was, and the children's education was therefore suffering.

### Communal intent limits

The question naturally arises: how could *Ravina* dissolve a vow made *al da'at rabbim*? The answer lies in distinguishing between subjective and objective grounds for release. The mechanism of *al da'at rabbim* closes off the avenue of *ta'ut* (error) that is personal and subjective. If the vower says, "Had I known my own personal circumstances, I would not have made this vow," that subjective claim is not available — the community's *da'at* does not share those private circumstances. But there is a category of error that is not subjective at all: had we known that this vow would come to block the performance of a *mitzvah*, no community would ever have countenanced such a vow. The *rabim* never intend their communal *da'at* to be invoked in service of obstructing a *mitzvah*. That is an objective error — one that any community would universally recognize — and it therefore qualifies as a valid basis for *hatarah* even against a vow made *al da'at rabbim*.

This refines our understanding of what *al da'at rabbim* actually does and does not accomplish. It removes the vow from the domain of individual, subjective *da'at*, preventing release on the grounds of personal error or personal circumstance. But it does not insulate the vow against objective, universal errors — specifically, circumstances that no community would ever have wished to support. A *mitzvah* being impeded is precisely such a circumstance; the community, by definition, never would have wanted their *da'at* to stand in the way of Torah obligations. So *al da'at rabbim* is more limited than it might initially appear: it works against personal error, but not against objective necessity.

The overall picture, then, is as follows. *Al da'at rabbim* works according to everyone to block *hatarah* in ordinary discretionary cases. *Be-rabbim*, if it works at all (which is disputed), is a categorically different mechanism — it transforms the vow into a public matter and is therefore broader, more absolute, and operates even against a husband's *hafarah*. And *al da'at rabbim*, despite its power, has two significant limits: it does not block a husband's *hafarah* (as *Tosafot* established), and it does not prevent *hatarah* in cases where the vow obstructs a *mitzvah*.

### Oath vs. vow nature

It is worth stepping back to recall why this entire discussion is taking place in the register of *neder* rather than *shvuah*. The window of possibility for a *chakham* to release a vow, and for all of these mechanisms of *be-rabbim* and *al da'at rabbim* to become relevant, exists precisely because we shifted from *shvuah* to *neder*. A *shvuah* regarding a past event — "I never took any money from the estate" — is determined at the moment it is uttered. Either the words are true or they constitute a *shvuat sheker*. There is nothing for a *chakham* to act upon after the fact; no release is possible because the binding obligation exists only in the past. A *neder*, by contrast, creates an ongoing obligation that can be modified or dissolved. All the analytical machinery the *gemara* deploys in this section is a consequence of that initial substitution.

---

## Witness signatures

### Biblical requirement

The *mishnah* now turns to a second *tikkun olam*: *ve-ha-eidim chosmin al ha-get mi-pnei tikkun olam* — the witnesses sign on the *get* for the sake of *tikkun olam*. At first glance this is surprising. Surely the requirement that witnesses sign a document is biblical in origin? The verse says *ve-chasov be-sefer ve-chasom* — "write in a scroll and sign." Is this not a *de-oraita* requirement?

### Rabbi Elazar view

*Rava* explains: this *mishnah* is needed specifically according to the position of *Rabbi Elazar*, who holds *edei mesirah karti* — that biblically, the critical witnesses are those who are physically present at the moment the *get* is handed over, not those who sign the document. According to *Rabbi Elazar*, another *gemara* teaches, the verse cited is not a mandatory requirement for documents to be valid, but rather *eitzah tovah ka-mashma lan* — sound advice. The Torah recommends that signatures be included, but does not make them a biblical prerequisite for the legal efficacy of a *get*. Biblically, what is needed is the physical presence of witnesses at the moment of transmission — *edei mesirah* — whether understood as required for the *davar she-be-ervah* dimension, or as the witnesses whose observation of the handover constitutes the validating act of the *shtar* itself. Either way, their names need not appear in writing.

### Rabbinic innovation

It was the Rabbis who established *edei chasimah* — that witnesses must actually sign their names — *mi-pnei tikkun ha-olam*. The practical concern is stated plainly: *de-zimnin de-maisi sahadei* — sometimes witnesses die, or they travel far away (*azli li-medinas ha-yam*), and the woman is left with a document that divorces her but without any means of proving that she is indeed divorced. The signed *get* solves this problem elegantly: the very document she receives to effectuate her divorce simultaneously serves as her evidence of divorce. She need not locate the original witnesses; their names are there in the document itself.

An interesting structural point follows from this. One might have imagined an alternative arrangement: the *get* itself would not bear signatures, but a subsequent rabbinic *beit din* document would separately attest that the divorce occurred. The Rabbis' solution is more elegant: the single document that functions as the instrument of divorce also bears witness to its own execution.

### Original practice

One might ask how witness signatures were verified in earlier times. A *baraita* records the history: *ba-rishonah hayah kosev ani ploni chasamti eid* — originally, witnesses would write only their first name, something like "I, Reuven, have signed as a witness." This was sufficient *im kesav yado yotzei mi-makom acher* — if the person's handwriting was recognizable from another source, one could confirm the authenticity of the signature. *Ve-im lav, pasul* — but if the handwriting was not independently recognizable, the signature could not be verified. With a common name like Reuven, there could be any number of individuals who might have signed, and without a means of identifying the particular person, the *get* could be rendered invalid.

### Rabban Gamliel takana

*Amar Rabban Gamliel: takana gedola hiskinu* — they enacted a major *takana* that witnesses must spell out their names fully in *gittin*: the full name and patronymic, as in Reuven ben Yaakov. With this information, it becomes possible to identify the specific individual, to locate other exemplars of his handwriting, and to verify the signature properly. The *baraita* presents this as the content of the *tikkun olam* referred to in the *mishnah* — indeed, *Tosafot* notes that the conjunction in the *mishnah* (*ve-ha-eidim chosmin*) might suggest this was part of *Rabban Gamliel*'s own *takana*, but the *gemara* makes clear that witness signatures predated *Rabban Gamliel*; his contribution was the standardization of full identifying names.

### Symbols as signatures

The *gemara* then raises an apparent tension. If the concern is identification, what about those sages who signed with pictorial symbols rather than names? *Ve-ha Rav tziyer kavra* — *Rav* drew a little fish. *Rav Chanina tziyer charusa* — *Rav Chanina* drew a palm tree. *Rav Chisda* drew a *samech* (presumably for *Chisda*). *Rav Oshaya* drew an *ayin*. *Rabba bar Rav Huna tziyer makusa* — he drew a sail of a ship. These symbols, then, served as valid signatures among the *tanna'im* and *amora'im*.

This raises two distinct questions: first, are such symbols distinctive enough to prevent forgery, in the way a handwritten signature is? Second, how can a symbol adequately identify the signatory when, unlike a name with a patronymic, it gives no inherent information about who the person is?

### Symbol establishment

The *gemara* addresses the second concern: *shani rabbanan de-bekiei be-simanaihu* — the rabbinic class was distinguished by the fact that their symbols were publicly known. These scholars had recognizable, known symbols, such that people could identify the symbol as belonging to a particular sage. Once a symbol is publicly recognized and associated with a known individual, it functions no differently from a fully spelled-out name for purposes of identification and verification.

This prompts a further question: *me-ikara be-mai apteinu* — but how did they begin using their symbols in the first place? There is a circular problem: you cannot use a symbol on a *shtar* before people know it, but how do they come to know it before you use it? The *gemara* answers: *be-diskei* — through personal correspondence. Before a scholar began signing *shtarot* with his symbol, he would use it extensively in private letters and communications, such that the symbol became recognizable. Only once it was publicly known could it then be employed on legal documents.

---

## Prozbul introduction

### Hillel's takana

The *mishnah* in *Shevi'it* is cited: *pruzbul eino meshamet* — a loan protected by a *pruzbul* is not annulled in the *shemita* year. This is identified as one of the institutions that *Hillel ha-Zaken* established. The *mishnah* explains the motivation: *she-ra'ah ha-am she-nimnu mi-lhalvot zeh la-zeh* — Hillel saw that people were refraining from lending money to one another as the *shemita* year approached, thereby transgressing what is written in the Torah: *hishamer lecha pen yihyeh davar im levavecha beliya'al* — "Beware lest there be a treacherous thought in your heart" leading you to withhold a loan from the poor because the *shemita* year is near. Hillel responded by establishing the *pruzbul*.

### Mitzvah framing

A crucial point must be made about how this institution is framed, because it is commonly misunderstood. The *pruzbul* is not presented as a pragmatic concession to economic reality — as though the Torah's law of *shemita* had become too burdensome and a workaround was needed. Rather, it is framed entirely in terms of competing *mitzvot*. The existing situation — people refusing to lend — was causing active biblical violations. People were transgressing the commandment to lend to the poor. Hillel's *takana* is thus presented as a resolution to a conflict between two Torah mandates, not as an accommodation of human weakness against a Torah institution.

This framing matters significantly. Hillel does not start by saying this *mitzvah* is economically unworkable; he says that the current state of affairs is causing the transgression of biblical commandments. There is still a genuine trade-off: is it better that people transgress the prohibition against refusing to lend but that the *shemita* annulment functions properly, or is it better to preserve the lending relationship at the cost of not fulfilling the annulment? Hillel clearly judges that the well-being of the poor — who are better served by receiving loans that must eventually be repaid than by seeing their creditors refuse to lend at all — tips the scale toward protecting the lending relationship. But the entire analysis is conducted within the framework of Torah *mitzvot*, not against it.

### Prozbul text

The *gemara* records the formula of the *pruzbul*: *mosrani lachem ploni u-ploni dayanim she-bi-makom ploni* — "I am handing over to you, Reuven and Shimon, the judges in such-and-such a place, that any debt owed to me by so-and-so I retain the right to collect at any time I wish." The judges or witnesses then sign below.

### Debt transfer mechanism

The underlying legal mechanism, clarified by the *mishnah* in *Shevi'it* and by *Rashi* here, is *moseir shtarotav le-veit din* — handing the debt over to the *beit din*. By making this declaration before the court, the creditor is understood to transfer the authority to collect the debt to the *beit din* rather than retaining it as a personal claim against his neighbor. The verse *shamot* — "you shall release" — speaks of a personal claim: you shall not exact it from your neighbor. But once the debt is in the hands of *beit din* rather than of the individual creditor, it is the communal institution of the court, not the individual, that holds the right to collect. The *shemita* annulment operates against individual creditors; it does not apply to *beit din*. *Rashi* makes this explicit: *mosrani lachem* — "I am handing it to you, you will be the ones to demand it, and I will not."

---

## Legal basis for prozbul

### Gemara's challenge

The *gemara* presses with a fundamental question: *u-mi ika midi de-mi-d'Oraita meshamta shevi'it, ve-hiskin Hillel de-lo meshamta* — is there any case where the Torah biblically annuls a debt, and Hillel can simply establish by *takana* that it should not be annulled? How can a rabbinic institution override a biblical law of *shemita*?

### Abaye's answer

*Amar Abaye*: the entire discussion concerns *shemita* of our time, and it follows the position of *Rebbi* — that the annulment of money debts in our era is only rabbinic (*derabbanan*), not biblical. Since the Rabbis instituted the debt annulment in the first place, they retain the authority to create exceptions to it or workarounds from it. Hillel's *pruzbul* operates against a rabbinic institution, not a biblical one.

### Rabbi's teaching

The source for this claim is a *baraita* in which *Rebbi* expounds: *ve-zeh dvar ha-shemita shamot* — "this is the manner of the *shemita*, you shall release." The verse speaks of two *shemitot* simultaneously — *shemitat karka* (the sabbatical release of the land) and *shemitat kesafim* (the annulment of debts): *bizman she-ata meshamet karka, ata meshamet kesafim; bizman she-i ata meshamet karka, i ata meshamet kesafim* — when you observe the release of the land, you observe the release of money; when you do not observe the release of the land, you do not observe the release of money. The two *shemitot* are halakhically interdependent.

### No yovel status

Since there is no *shemitat karka* in force biblically in our era, there is correspondingly no biblical *shemitat kesafim*. But why is there no biblical *shemitat karka* nowadays? *Rashi* explains that *shemitat karka* is itself dependent on *yovel* — the Jubilee year — and *yovel* requires *kol yoshveha aleha*, all twelve tribes settled on the land. This condition was not met even during the Second Temple period (*Bayit Sheni*), and certainly has not been met since. Consequently, even during the period of *Hillel*, there was no biblical *yovel*, and without biblical *yovel* there was no biblical *shemita* of land, and without biblical *shemita* of land there was no biblical *shemita* of money. The entire framework at issue was already rabbinic before *Hillel* instituted his *pruzbul*.

### Prior puzzle

The *gemara* is still not satisfied. Even if we accept that the existing debt annulment was only rabbinic, there is a prior puzzle: how did the Rabbis come to institute a rabbinic *shemitat kesafim* in the first place? Before they acted, during *Bayit Sheni*, there was no biblical *shemita* of money — debts had to be paid. By what authority did the Rabbis institute a new obligation that people's debts would be annulled, effectively taking away the creditor's biblical right to collect?

### Shev ve'al ta'aseh

*Amar Abaye*: the institution of rabbinic *shemita* was possible because it operates in the mode of *shev ve-al ta'aseh* — passive non-action rather than active violation. The Rabbis did not actively compel anyone to violate a biblical obligation; they simply instructed creditors not to collect. This is analogous to the Rabbinic practice of setting aside the *lulav* when the relevant day falls on *Shabbat* — a passive restraint from action rather than an active override of the Torah.

### Hefker beit din

*Rava* offers a stronger answer: *hefker beit din hefker* — what a *beit din* declares ownerless becomes ownerless. The Rabbis have inherent authority to control the disposition of property. When it comes to monetary matters, the court can release people from their debts, reassign ownership, or restructure financial obligations. It was by virtue of this principle that the Rabbis were able to institute a rabbinic *shemitat kesafim* — they exercised their authority over property to declare debts annulled.

### Proof texts

*Rabbi Yitzchak* provides the biblical source for *hefker beit din hefker*: the verse in *Ezra*: *ve-chol asher lo yavo li-shloshet ha-yamim ke-atzat ha-sarim ve-ha-zekenim, yocharam kol rechusho* — anyone who does not appear within three days, in accordance with the directive of the officers and elders, shall have all his property put under the ban. This demonstrates that the court has the power to divest an individual of his property. *Rabbi Elazar* adduces a different verse: *eileh ha-nachalot asher nichalu Elazar ha-Kohen vi-Yehoshua bin Nun* — these are the portions that *Elazar ha-Kohen* and *Yehoshua bin Nun* apportioned. The text mentions *rashei ha-avot* — heads of the fathers — rather than heads of the tribes, which the *gemara* reads as a comparison: just as a father may bequeath to his children whatever he wishes, so too the leaders of the nation may apportion and redistribute the wealth of the people as they see fit.

The two proof texts point in somewhat different directions. The first (*Ezra*) demonstrates the punitive dimension of the court's power — property can be seized as a sanction. The second (*Yehoshua*) points to something broader: a fundamental, non-punitive authority to restructure ownership, comparable to a father's power to bequeath. *Hefker beit din hefker*, in *Rava*'s usage, invokes this broader principle.

---

## Tosafot critique

### Mechanism vs. will

*Rashi* notes that once *hefker beit din hefker* is introduced, it resolves not only the question of how the Rabbis could institute rabbinic *shemitat kesafim* in the first place, but also the original challenge of how *Hillel* could institute the *pruzbul* even against a potentially biblical *shemita*. If the court can control ownership, then even if the Torah's *shemita* voided the debt, *beit din* could simply reinstate it after *shemita*, and Hillel's institution is thereby justified even on a *de-oraita* level.

### Propriety concern

*Tosafot* takes sharp issue with this. Their question is not about mechanism but about propriety. As *Tosafot* puts it: even granting that Hillel had the mechanism of *hefker beit din hefker* available to him, *lo hayah lo le-Hillel la'akor shevi'it she-hi de-oraita* — it was not appropriate for Hillel to uproot a Torah institution of *shemita* in such a blatant way. The existence of a mechanism does not, by itself, justify its use. To openly deploy rabbinic power to directly override a foundational biblical institution is a different category of act than working within or around it.

### Fig leaf approach

*Tosafot* draws an illuminating parallel to the concept of *hafka'at kiddushin* — retroactive rabbinic annulment of a marriage. The *Rashba* holds that the Rabbis have the technical power to retroactively annul a marriage, but they will not exercise that power openly. To look back at twenty years of recognized marriage and declare it never existed would be a blatant and intolerable show of rabbinic power against a biblical institution. Therefore, the Rabbis will only invoke *hafka'at kiddushin* in the presence of a *get* — even if the *get* is technically invalid (*pasul*), its existence provides a cover: it looks as though the woman was divorced by the *get*, not as though the Rabbis voided the *kiddushin* by fiat. This is what might be called the *fig leaf* approach: the mechanism used must at least appear to be a non-confrontational resolution, not a naked exercise of power against the Torah.

### Prozbul as fig leaf

The same logic applies to *pruzbul*. *Tosafot* explains why the *gemara* frames the *pruzbul* around the mechanism of *moseir shtarotav le-beit din* — handing over the debt to the court — rather than simply invoking *hefker beit din hefker* directly. The transfer-to-*beit-din* framework provides the necessary appearance of legitimacy. Rather than openly declaring that the Rabbis are overriding *shemita*, the *pruzbul* presents itself as a structural change in who holds the debt: it is now the *beit din's* debt, not the individual creditor's, and *shemita* does not apply to *beit din*. Even if the underlying *takana* is really being driven by *hefker beit din hefker*, the *pruzbul* gives it a face that avoids the appearance of direct confrontation with a Torah law.

### Transfer doesn't work

Indeed, *Tosafot* goes further and suggests that the transfer to *beit din* may not actually be legally operative in the strict sense — it may be a legal fiction rather than a real transfer of the debt. But that does not undermine its purpose; if anything, it makes the point more sharply. The function of the *moseir shtarotav* framework is not primarily mechanical but presentational. We need a structure in which the *pruzbul* does not look like a straight override of a Torah institution, even if the underlying justification is ultimately rooted in the court's broader power over property.

This provides the proper lens through which to understand *tikkun olam* in the context of *pruzbul*. Several dimensions converge. First, the problem is framed not as economic hardship but as a competition of Torah *mitzvot* — the *pruzbul* resolves a clash between the commandment to lend and the institution of *shemita* by siding with what better serves the poor. Second, even where the Rabbis have the raw mechanism to act, they do not deploy it brazenly against a Torah institution; they require a framework — the *fig leaf* of the transfer to *beit din* — that presents the resolution as something other than a naked rabbinic override. These are not mere technicalities; they reflect a deeper commitment to operating within the spirit of Torah authority even when exercising the outer limits of rabbinic power.

---

---

# Gittin 37

## Pruzbul Foundation

### Hillel's Authority

Today's *daf* is 37, and we pick up in the middle of 36b, in the midst of the remarkable *sugya* of *pruzbul*. The preceding discussion addressed the fundamental question of how Hillel could establish *pruzbul* without undermining the *d'oraita* principle that *shmitta* annuls debts. The *Gemara* resolved this by noting that the annulment of debts nowadays is Rabbinic in nature. But that itself raised a further difficulty: how did the Rabbis create that Rabbinic annulment in the first place? The *Gemara*'s answer introduced the principle of *hefker bet din hefker* — the authority of a court to reassign questions of property ownership. For Rashi, this power was sufficient to ground *pruzbul* even if *shmitta* were biblical, since it gives Hillel the authority to restructure monetary obligations at their root.

Tosafot, however, pressed a deeper point. The problem was not merely mechanical — how *pruzbul* could circumvent a *d'oraita* — but ethical: how could Hillel have done such a thing at all? That is why it was a more satisfying answer that *shmitta* nowadays is Rabbinic. And this connects to the way Hillel himself framed the issue. Against the popular conception, Hillel did not frame *pruzbul* as a workaround because the law was too burdensome. Rather, he framed it as a weighing of one *d'oraita* against another.

### Balancing Obligations

Hillel recognized a genuine conflict: on one side, the *shmitta* annulment of debts; on the other, the prohibition against withholding loans from the poor. People were violating the latter because they feared the former. In order to prevent the ongoing violation of *that* commandment, Hillel found a means of addressing the debt annulment. The entire enterprise was framed as a *d'oraita* trade-off — one Torah obligation being preserved at the cost of circumventing another — and that framing is obviously critical when one is in the business of constructing such an institution.

### Hefker Bet Din

With that conceptual foundation in place, the *Gemara* continues. The principle of *hefker bet din hefker* is what gives a *beit din* the power to reassign ownership and thereby enable the mechanism of *pruzbul*. As we will see, this principle carries significant implications not only for *pruzbul* but for broader questions about the authority of rabbinic courts — including, parenthetically, the concept of *hafk'as kiddushin*, which at least according to Rashi in the case of *kesef kiddushin* may partly rest on this foundation, though the *Gemara* ultimately grounds *hafk'as kiddushin* in the principle of *al da'ata derabbanan mekadesh*.

---

## Temporal Scope

### Temporary vs. Permanent

The *Gemara* now raises a new question, approximately fifteen lines down on 36b, beginning *iba'u lehu*: when Hillel established *pruzbul*, did he do so only for his generation, or for all future generations? This question is notable because it was not asked about the other *tikkunei olam* instituted earlier in the tractate. Why should it arise specifically here?

One possibility is that *pruzbul* was framed as a response to a particular observed reality — *ra'ah Hillel she-nimnu ha-am mi-lilvot zeh et zeh*, Hillel saw that people were refraining from lending to one another — and this framing suggests a situational assessment rather than a permanent institutional change. A second possibility is that because *pruzbul* involves circumventing something that looks like a *d'oraita*, it was a radical step, and perhaps Hillel did not intend it as a permanent alteration.

The practical stakes of this question are made explicit: *l'mai nafka mina* — what difference does it make? The *Gemara* answers: *levatlohei*, the question is whether we can annul it. If Hillel established *pruzbul* only for his generation, then perhaps it is currently maintained only by force of habit, not by the binding authority of his enactment, and a later court could dissolve it. If, however, he established it for all generations, then no subsequent *beit din* could annul it unless it were greater in wisdom and number — *ein beit din yakhol levatel divrei beit din chavero ela im kein gadol mimenu be-chochma u-ve-minyan*.

### Shmuel's Restriction

The *Gemara* adduces evidence from a ruling of Shmuel: *lo katvinan pruzbul ela ei be-veit dina d'Sura ei be-veit dina d'Nahardei* — a *pruzbul* may only be written before the major *batei din* of Sura or Nahardea, the central courts of the region. The *Gemara* asks: if Hillel established *pruzbul* for all generations, why would it be limited to these central institutions? Surely Hillel wanted this tool to be broadly available, in which case he should have empowered all *batei din* to execute it.

The logic of the limitation seems to point toward a specific conclusion: perhaps the original authority of Hillel's enactment is no longer operative, and *pruzbul* now functions only by virtue of the power of a current central *beit din* exercising *hefker bet din hefker*. If that is so, only a *beit din* with the authority to be *motzi mamon* — to actually extract money — would have the standing to execute it. This would suggest not merely that Hillel's *takana* can be annulled, but that it has in effect already lapsed, and *pruzbul* now requires a fresh act of rabbinic authority each time it is invoked.

### Intentional Limitation

The *Gemara* rejects this inference, however. *Dilma ki takkin Hillel l'dorei alma, kegon beit dina didei* — perhaps when Hillel established *pruzbul* for all generations, he himself always intended it to be executed only before a *beit din* of sufficient authority to be *motzi mamon*, empowered with *hefker bet din hefker*, and not before every local court. In other words, the restriction to central *batei din* may have been part of Hillel's original design. Given how radical the institution was — circumventing what appears to be a *d'oraita* — perhaps Hillel deliberately chose to confine its use to courts of the highest caliber.

The question accordingly remains unresolved: is *pruzbul* still operative on the basis of Hillel's original enactment, or are we doing it on the independent authority of the current central *beit din*? This *Gemara* carries important implications beyond *pruzbul* — it suggests that *hefker bet din hefker* is limited to *batei din* of central and high authority, a point relevant to other applications of that principle.

---

## Shmuel's Opposition

### Olban Shel Dayanim
