The *Gemara* now introduces another statement of Shmuel, which is fully consistent with his restrictive posture toward *pruzbul*. *De-amar Shmuel: hai pruzbul ulbana de-dayyani hu* — this *pruzbul* is an embarrassment to the judges. Shmuel characterizes the institution as a disgrace, presumably because it involves circumventing what presents itself as a Torah law — even if *shmitta* nowadays is Rabbinic, it looks like a Torah law — and the judiciary is implicated in this circumvention.

### Shmuel's Chutzpah

Shmuel goes further still: *ve-ei yashar cheili, chaya, avatleinei* — if I had the strength, I would nullify it entirely. This statement likely motivated the *Gemara*'s earlier question about whether *pruzbul* can be annulled. Given that Shmuel expressed such displeasure and such a desire, the *Gemara* naturally wondered whether the institution was in fact susceptible to annulment.

What drove Shmuel's opposition? Several possibilities present themselves. He may have felt the weight of the appearance of circumventing Torah law. He may have believed that in his generation, people were willing to absorb the annulment of small debts and would have been prepared to do so, making *pruzbul* unnecessary. Or, much as one might observe about the institution of *mechirat chametz*, he may have felt that a well-intentioned workaround was being abused and applied far beyond the cases that genuinely warranted it — thereby undermining the very *mitzvah* it was designed to protect.

The *Gemara* at this point introduces an *aggadic* passage that may carry an implicit response to Shmuel. The phrase *ulbana* — embarrassment or disgrace — leads the *Gemara* to the *braita*: *ha-ne'elavin ve-einam olevim, shom'in cherpatam ve-einam meshivim, osim me-ahava u-semechim be-yisurin* — those who are shamed and do not return the shame, who hear themselves being disgraced and do not respond, who serve God out of love and rejoice in affliction — on them the verse says, *ve-ohavav ke-tzet ha-shemesh bi-gvurato*, those who love God shall be as the sun going forth in its strength. One might read this as a subtle pushback against Shmuel: rather than responding to the perceived embarrassment of *pruzbul* by seeking to dismantle it, the *Gemara* gestures toward the virtue of bearing that discomfort and maintaining the institution.

### Cannot Annul Unilaterally

The *Gemara* then asks explicitly: Shmuel said he would annul *pruzbul* — but how could he? *Ve-chi beit din yakhol levatel divrei beit din chavero ela im kein gadol mimenu be-chochma u-ve-minyan?* A *beit din* cannot annul the legislation of an earlier one unless it is greater. So what was Shmuel thinking?

The *Gemara* clarifies: *im yashar cheili yoter me-Hillel avatleinei* — Shmuel was not saying that he could annul it. He fully recognized that he could not, because *pruzbul* remains grounded in Hillel's authority, which Shmuel did not surpass. The statement was a wishful expression: if only I had the authority greater than Hillel's, I would do away with it. The practical reality is that as long as the institution rests on Hillel's enactment, no later *beit din* of lesser standing can dislodge it. Shmuel's two statements together — limit it to major courts, and wish it could be abolished — paint a consistent picture of an authority deeply uncomfortable with the institution and doing everything within his power to curtail it.

---

## Rav Nachman

### Automatic Pruzbul

Against Shmuel's restrictive posture, Rav Nachman says *akimnah* — I would affirm and establish it.

### Already Established

The *Gemara* responds with an obvious question: *ha-mekayem kayam* — what do you mean you would establish it? It's already established. Who are you to re-establish something already in force? This question, too, touches on whether *pruzbul* still rests on Hillel's original authority or whether it requires fresh affirmation.

### Rashi's View

The *Gemara* resolves this by explaining that Rav Nachman's intent was something more radical. *Eima bei milta de-af al gav de-la katav ki-katav dami* — he would declare that even if one did not write a *pruzbul*, it is treated as if it were written. As Rashi explains: *oshiv beit din ve-atkin de-stam malvin yihyu ke-mosrin shetaroteihen le-veit din de-af al gav de-la ketiv yehei ke-mi she-katav* — he would convene a *beit din* and establish that all lenders by default be considered as having transferred their documents to the *beit din*, such that even without any act of writing, a *pruzbul* would be automatically and implicitly in effect for every loan.

The contrast between the positions of Shmuel and Rav Nachman could not be starker. Shmuel wants to eliminate or radically restrict *pruzbul*; Rav Nachman wants to make it so universal that no affirmative act is required at all.

This range of opinion has direct *halachic* implications. Some *Rishonim* and *poskim* understand the ease with which certain *Amora'im* applied *pruzbul* as evidence that they regarded *shemittat kesafim* nowadays — particularly outside of *Eretz Yisrael* — as no more than *minhag chasidus*, a praiseworthy custom but not a binding obligation. On this view, even without a *pruzbul*, one may still collect one's loans. Others maintain that it retains at least Rabbinic force and requires some act, even if a minimal one. The question of how seriously to take *shemittat kesafim* today has also been explored by Rav Kook as a lens through which to understand the broader debate about the status of *shmitta* in our era, including the disputed mechanism of *heter mechira* for *shemitat karka*.

---

## Etymology

### Chisda's Meaning

The *Gemara* asks: *mai pruzbul* — what does the word *pruzbul* mean? Rav Chisda explains: *pruz buli u-buti*. The *pruz*, which Rashi understands as an establishment or enactment, is for both the *buli* and the *buti*. *Buli eilu ashirim* — the *buli* are the wealthy, as derived from the verse *ve-shavarti et ge'on uzchem*, and as connected with the *bulaot she-biYehuda*, the powerful class of Judea. *Buti eilu aniyim* — the *buti* are the poor, derived from *havet ta'avitenu*, you shall surely lend them. So *pruzbul* is an establishment that benefits both the wealthy, who can collect their loans, and the poor, who will now be lent to.

### Greek Origins

The actual etymology of the word is close to Rav Chisda's reading but not identical. The word *buli* is a Greek term for a council or assembly. As Klein's dictionary records, the word *pruzbul* is probably shortened from the Greek *pros boule bouleuteon* — meaning, presented before the assembly of counselors. The *Gemara* identifies the *buli* with the *ashirim*, the wealthy class, which reflects the social reality that the council members were typically the powerful elite. But the primary meaning of the full term is one who presents a matter before a court or council. This is why the institution is called *pruzbul* — the debt is, as it were, brought before the court. The lower house of the modern Greek legislature is still known as the *boule*, the same term.

One of the *Amora'im* suggests another etymology based on a foreign language: *porsa de-milta* — something that fixes or addresses the matter. Rashi seems uncertain about this derivation, but it is recorded alongside Rav Chisda's explanation.

---

## Land Requirement

### Mishna's Rule

The *Gemara* now turns to the *Mishna* from *Shevi'it*: *ein kotvin pruzbul ela al ha-karka* — a *pruzbul* may only be written if the debtor has land. This requirement is the focus of the next extended discussion.

### Limiting to Large Loans

Why does *pruzbul* require the debtor to hold land? Rashi and Tosafot both offer the following reasoning: the Rabbis established *pruzbul* only for the standard, common case of lending, which typically involves a debtor who owns land — since land is what allows the creditor to collect. One does not ordinarily lend large sums to someone with no assets at all. On small loans, without land present, people may well be content to have *shmitta* annul the debt.

This rationale suggests a secondary purpose as well: the land requirement serves to limit *pruzbul* to substantial loans, precisely the cases for which the institution was designed. Small debts, for which people are borrowing without any underlying assets, are arguably meant to be absorbed by *shmitta*. By requiring land, the Rabbis ensured that *pruzbul* would be used only where there is genuine need.

There is also a second explanation, which anticipates material the *Gemara* will develop later. Among the types of debt not annulled by *shmitta* even without a *pruzbul* is a loan for which the creditor holds collateral — because in such a case the creditor is not personally exacting payment, and the debt has, in a sense, already been partially collected. The combination of *pruzbul* with *karka* may similarly be designed to give the debt a quality of partial collection: real estate cannot be hidden, cannot be moved, and can always be seized by a court. The presence of *karka* may thus transform the debt from a pure obligation into something more concretely within the creditor's reach — lending the *pruzbul* a more substantive foundation.

---

## Land Requirement (II)

### Expanded Land

Having established the *karka* requirement, the *Gemara* addresses what happens when the debtor does not own land. *Im ein lo, mezakehu be-toch sodehu* — if the debtor has no land, the creditor may transfer even a tiny parcel of his own land to the debtor, thereby enabling the writing of a *pruzbul*. The *Gemara* establishes that *kol shehu*, even the most minimal amount, suffices. Rav Chiya bar Ashi citing Rav says: *afilu klach shel kruv* — even a single head of cabbage, even a square inch's worth of ground, is sufficient.

Rav Yehuda then extends this further: *afilu hishilo makom le-tanur ve-chirayim* — even if the debtor has merely borrowed space from someone on which to place his oven, that constitutes sufficient connection to land to permit writing a *pruzbul*. Borrowed land, not even owned, counts.

---

## Overcoming Requirement

### Transfer Strategy

The practical implication of the expanded definition of *karka* is that the creditor can always manufacture the land requirement by transferring a tiny parcel to the debtor. This transfer can be effected through a third party even without the debtor's active consent, since acquiring land is a *zechus* — a benefit — for the recipient, and one may confer a *zechus* upon a person in their absence. The *Gemara* does note the tension: this is ultimately a *zechus* that will be used against the debtor's interests, since it enables the *pruzbul* that will allow collection of the debt. Nevertheless, the act is effective.

### Perforated Pot

A *braita* citing Hillel himself specifies that one may write a *pruzbul* only if the debtor has an *atzis nakuv* — a perforated flower pot. A flower pot with a hole in the bottom is considered to have a connection to the soil beneath it and thus constitutes *karka*. One without a hole, *eino nakuv*, does not. The *Gemara* finds this striking: why should the unperforated pot not qualify?

### Borrowed Land

The *Gemara* raises a sharp objection: *ve-ha'ika mekomo* — wherever the debtor places his flower pot, he presumably has some right to that space of ground. If borrowed land suffices for *pruzbul*, as Rav Yehuda just ruled, then anyone who has so much as a place to set down any possession should have sufficient connection to land. Why, then, does Hillel's statement require specifically an *atzis nakuv*?

The *Gemara* answers: *lo tzricha de-manach asichi* — the case is one where the pot is placed on pegs rather than directly on the ground. In such a case, the debtor has rights to use someone's table or elevated surface, but has not been granted any rights to the ground itself. Therefore, despite the physical presence of his possession, he has no connection to actual land, and the *pruzbul* cannot be written. The distinction is fine but operative: it is specifically the right to *the ground* that matters, not merely any right of placement.

What the *Gemara* is doing throughout this discussion is working both sides of a tension. On one side is the impulse — consistent with Shmuel's view — to maintain *pruzbul* as a meaningful, somewhat restricted institution that is not available to everyone. On the other side is the impulse — consistent with Rav Nachman's view — to make it as widely available as possible. The progressive expansion of what counts as *karka* reflects the triumph of the latter tendency: in practice, anyone can always come up with some connection to land.

### Palm Tree Trunk

Consistent with that tendency, Rav Ashi in practice transferred a *gidma de-dikla* — the trunk of a palm tree — to a debtor through a third party and then wrote a *pruzbul* upon it. A trunk of a tree serves as the minimal *karka* equivalent sufficient to ground the institution.

---

## Verbal Pruzbul

### Academy Practice

The progression toward simplification reaches its endpoint in the practice of the scholars of Rav Ashi's academy. *Rabbanan d'bei Rav Ashi* did not write anything at all. They simply verbally transferred their loans to one another. In practice, one would walk over to three colleagues sitting nearby, say words to the effect of "you are my *beit din* and I am transferring my loans to you," and the matter was considered complete. No document, no transfer of land, nothing beyond a few words spoken informally among colleagues.

### Verbal Transfer

Rabbi Yochanan similarly transferred his loans verbally to Rabbi Chiya bar Abba. Having done so, Rabbi Chiya bar Abba asked whether anything further was required. Rabbi Yochanan replied: *lo tzrichas* — nothing further is needed.

The trajectory from a formal written document executed before a major *beit din*, to a verbal declaration before one's colleagues, reflects the dominant position that in practice *pruzbul* should be maximally accessible. Some *Rishonim* explain this extreme simplification by suggesting that for these *Amora'im*, the annulment of debts nowadays was regarded as no more than *midas chasidus* — a praiseworthy stringency — and therefore any minimal gesture acknowledging the institution was sufficient. Others suggest this leniency was confined to *talmidei chachamim* who could be trusted not to abuse the device.

---

## No Land Cases

### Basic Rule

Returning to earlier *mishnayot* from *Shevi'it* that address situations where the debtor lacks land, the *Gemara* now outlines the basic rule: *ein lo karka v'la-arev yesh lo karka* — if the debtor himself has no land but the guarantor of the loan does, one may write a *pruzbul*, since ultimately the creditor could collect from the guarantor's landed property. *Kotvin alav pruzbul* in such a case.

### Chain Debts

The *Gemara* extends this further: if neither the debtor nor the guarantor has land, but a third party who owes money *to the debtor* has land, that too suffices. I have lent money to Reuven, who has no land. Shimon, who guaranteed the loan, also has no land. But Levi owes money to Reuven, and Levi has land. Since I could ultimately reach Levi's property through the chain of obligations, *kotvin alav pruzbul* — a *pruzbul* may be written.

### Rav Natan

How does one jump over an intermediate link in a chain of debts? The *Gemara* cites Rav Natan: *mi-nayin le-noshe be-chavero maneh ve-chavero be-chavero maneh she-motzi'in mi-zeh ve-notnin le-zeh* — how do we know that if A is owed money by B, and B is owed money by C, we may collect directly from C to pay A? The *Gemara* derives this from the verse *ve-natan la-asher asham lo* — the money is given to the one to whom the guilt is ultimately due. Since that money is ultimately coming to me, I may go directly to the end of the chain and collect. This ability to bypass intermediate parties is what allows the creditor to have constructive access to Levi's land, thereby satisfying the *karka* requirement for *pruzbul*.

---

## Shmita's Scope

### All Annulled

The *Gemara* now surveys *Mishnayot* from the tenth chapter of *Shevi'it* — the chapter devoted entirely to *shemittat kesafim*, since there is no *Bavli* on *Shevi'it* itself. The *Mishna* states: *ha-shevi'it meshametet et ha-malveh bein be-shtar bein she-lo be-shtar* — the seventh year annuls loans, whether they were made with a document or without.

### Rav and Shmuel

Rav and Shmuel explain this *Mishna* together: *be-shtar* refers to *shtar she-yesh bo achrayut nechasim*, a document that has explicitly written into it liens on the debtor's property. *She-lo be-shtar* refers to *she-ein bo achrayut nechasim* — literally a document that lacks those explicit liens, or indeed a verbal loan with no document at all. On this reading, *shmitta* annuls everything — even a *shtar* with explicit liens, and *kal va-chomer* a purely verbal debt.

### Yochanan Position

Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish read the *Mishna* differently. *Be-shtar* refers to *shtar she-ein bo achrayut nechasim* — a document without explicit liens. *She-lo be-shtar* means a purely verbal loan with no document whatsoever. The implication of this reading is that there exists a third category: *shtar she-yesh bo achrayut nechasim*, a document with explicit liens written in, which is *not* annulled by *shmitta*, even without a *pruzbul*. That case is omitted from the *Mishna*'s list of what *shmitta* annuls, because according to Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish, *shmitta* does not touch it at all.

---

## Liens as Ownership

### Right vs. Ownership

This position of Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish rests on a fundamental conceptual distinction. How does one understand the nature of a lien? Is it a right that a creditor may exercise upon the debtor's property when collection becomes necessary, which crystallizes only at the moment of collection? Or is it an actual partial ownership of the property itself — present and real from the moment the *shtar* is written, even before any collection occurs?

Some *Rishonim* imply the latter view: when a *shtar* is written with *achrayut nechasim* explicitly stated, that *shtar* functions not only as a *shtar re'ayah* — a document of proof of the debt — but also as a *shtar mecher*, a document that transfers a form of property rights. The creditor does not merely have a claim against the debtor; he has a form of partial ownership in the debtor's real estate from the moment of the loan.

### Consequence

The consequence of this understanding is direct: *shmitta* annuls debts — obligations of one person to another — but it cannot annul what is already in a sense one's own property. If the written *achrayut* has already transferred a partial ownership in the land to the creditor, there is no longer a pure debt to be annulled. The debt has been, as it were, partially absorbed into a property right, and *shmitta* cannot reach it.

### Supporting Braita

The *Gemara* cites a *braita* in support of Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish: *shtar chov meshamet* — a loan document is annulled by *shmitta*. *Ve-im yesh bo achrayut nechasim eino meshamet* — but if it has liens written into it, it is not annulled. This *braita* is adduced independently of *pruzbul*; it reflects a baseline *halacha* that a document bearing explicit liens is not annulled by *shmitta* as a matter of principle.

A second *braita* reinforces this: *sicheid lo sadeh achat be-halvahato eino meshamet* — if the creditor specifically identified a particular field from which he would collect in the event of default, *shmitta* does not annul the debt. *Ve-lo od* — and furthermore, even if no specific field was identified but the debtor wrote *kol nechasai achra'in ve-arva'in lach*, all my property is encumbered and pledged to you — that too is not annulled by *shmitta*. This mirrors the position of Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish: the explicit written *achrayut*, whether specific or general, transforms the nature of the debt.

---

## Practical Hesitation

### Assi's Case

A practical case now arises. A relative of Rav Assi held a *shtar* with *achrayut nechasim* explicitly written into it, and sought to know: will *shmitta* annul this debt? The person was concerned — understandably, since if *shmitta* would annul it, he needed to act promptly, either by writing a *pruzbul* or otherwise protecting his claim.

### Initial Opinion

Rav Assi, consistent with the position of Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish, initially ruled that the debt would not be annulled. The written *achrayut* gave the creditor a form of property ownership that *shmitta* could not reach. The relative, apparently pleased with this answer but wanting authoritative confirmation — since the ability to actually collect the debt depends not merely on one opinion but on a reliable *halachic* consensus — went to Rabbi Yochanan himself.

### Reversal

Rabbi Yochanan ruled: *meshamet* — the debt *will* be annulled. Rav Assi, having heard this, went to Rabbi Yochanan directly and pressed him: but did you yourself, together with Resh Lakish, not rule that a *shtar* with *achrayut nechasim* is not annulled? Rabbi Yochanan acknowledged the argument but replied: *ve-chi mi-penei she-anu medamim na'aseh ma'aseh?* — just because we can construct an argument, does that mean we should act upon it? Of course, the entire enterprise of *Shas* is precisely the construction of legal arguments — but here Rabbi Yochanan is making a more pointed claim. Where there is no explicit textual grounding for a ruling, where it rests on *svara* alone, he is not prepared to issue a practical ruling on that basis. The consequence in this case is significant: without a firm ruling in his favor, the creditor must write a *pruzbul* to protect his debt.

### Beit Shammai

The *Gemara* pushes back on Rabbi Yochanan's reversal: but you had a *braita* supporting your position! It was not pure *svara*. Rabbi Yochanan responds: *dilma hi Beit Shammai hi* — perhaps that *braita* follows the opinion of Beit Shammai. Beit Shammai holds, in another context, that *shtar ha-omed li-gvot ki-gavuy dami* — a document ready for collection is treated as if already collected. If that principle underlies the *braita*'s ruling, then the *braita* may reflect a minority position we do not follow. According to Beit Hillel, until the money is actually paid, it is not in the creditor's possession, and no anticipatory ownership can be imputed. Rabbi Yochanan, therefore, could not rely on the *braita* to issue a practical ruling, lest it be grounded in Beit Shammai's rejected position. In the end, the wise counsel was to write a *pruzbul* and avoid the entire uncertainty.

---

## Other Exemptions

### Collateral and Court

The *Gemara* returns to the *Mishna* from *Shevi'it*: *ha-malveh et chavero chov al ha-mashkon, ve-ha-moseir shtarotav le-veit din — ein meshamtin* — a loan made against collateral, and a loan whose documents were actually handed over to *beit din*, are not annulled by *shmitta*. This is independent of *pruzbul*; it reflects the baseline *halacha* that these two categories of debt are simply not subject to *shmitta*'s annulment.

### Possession Logic

*Be-shlama moseir shtarotav le-veit din* — when the documents are genuinely handed over to *beit din*, the rationale is clear: it is the *beit din* that holds the documents and is empowered to collect, and the creditor is no longer personally exacting payment. The prohibition of *lo yigosh* — the creditor shall not press the debtor — is therefore not violated, and the debt, having been placed in the court's hands, is as if already somewhat collected. This is precisely the model on which Hillel constructed *pruzbul* as a legal fiction: the *pruzbul* works *ke-mosir shtarotav le-veit din*, as if one has handed the documents to the court, even though the actual giving over is a formal fiction.

But the *mashkon*, the collateral case, requires its own explanation. Why should holding collateral exempt a loan from *shmitta*?

### Living on Property

Abaye poses a sharp question: *ella me'ata hilvehu ve-dar be-chatzeiro, d'tafsilei, hachi nami ve-lo meshamet?* — if you lent someone money and happen to be living on his property, would we also say the debt is not annulled? As Tosafot clarifies, the case is one where you are not merely a tenant but are living there by virtue of a right connected to the loan — in essence, a physical presence in the debtor's property linked to the credit relationship. If mere possession is the logic, why does living on the debtor's property not equally protect the debt from *shmitta*?

---

## Mashkon Status

### Distinct Status

The *Gemara* answers through a distinction. Living on the debtor's property, even with a legal connection to the loan, does not create ownership in the property. But a *mashkon* — collateral — is different, because the creditor has a form of actual ownership over the collateral itself.

### Yitzchak Drasha

Rabbi Yitzchak derives this from a *pasuk*: *m'nayin le-ba'al chov she-koneh mashkon* — how do we know that the creditor owns the collateral to some degree? From the verse that describes the mitzvah of returning a pledge: *u-lecha tihiyeh tzedakah* — and it shall be accounted to you as righteousness. *Im eino koneh, tzedakah m'nayin?* — if you did not own it, where does the *tzedaka* come from? *Tzedaka* by definition involves giving away something of yours to another. The act of returning the collateral is described as *tzedaka* because the collateral belongs, in some sense, to the creditor. By returning it, the creditor is performing an act of generosity with property that is, at that moment, legally his.

### Already Collected

The consequence follows directly. Since the creditor has a form of ownership over the collateral, the debt has been, in a meaningful sense, already partially collected — it is no longer a pure obligation floating between two parties, but an obligation partially secured in the creditor's actual possession. Therefore, *shmitta* cannot annul it. The same *mechaber* of logic that produced the analysis of *achrayut nechasim* as partial ownership of land applies here: where a debt has been absorbed into some form of property right or actual possession, *shmitta* cannot reach it.

---

## Debt Ownership

### Spectrum

The *sugya* as a whole traces a spectrum of debt types, distinguished by the degree to which the creditor's claim has been absorbed into something more concrete than a pure interpersonal obligation. At one end sits the purely verbal debt — *milveh al peh* — a bare obligation with no documentation, no lien, no collateral, and no possession. *Shmitta* annuls this most readily. Moving along the spectrum: a *shtar* without explicit liens, a *shtar* with explicit *achrayut nechasim* debated by the *Amora'im*, a loan against which the creditor holds collateral and thereby has genuine ownership, and finally a debt whose documents have actually been transferred to *beit din* and are thus effectively in the court's hands. At the far end, the debt is as close to already collected as a debt can be without actually having been paid. The institution of *pruzbul* functions by positioning a debt, through legal fiction or actual transfer, somewhere toward the collected end of this spectrum — and thus out of *shmitta*'s reach.

---

---

# Gittin 38

## Shmitat Kesafim

### Creditor's Obligation

The Gemara opens by citing a *mishnah* from *Shevi'it*: *hamachzir chov lechaveiro bishmita tzarich she'yomar lo meshameit ani* — one who returns a debt to his fellow during *shmita* must be told by the creditor, "I release you." If the debtor then says *af al pi chen* — "nevertheless, I still wish to repay" — the creditor is permitted to accept the money, as derived from the verse *v'zeh dvar hashmita*: this is the "matter" of *shmita*, referring to speech — the creditor must verbally articulate the release.

This raises an immediate question about the mechanics of *shmitat kesafim*. We have generally assumed that *shmita* automatically annuls debts — *shamot kol ba'al masheh yado*. So what precisely is the relationship between the creditor's verbal declaration of *meshameit ani* and the automatic annulment? Is the debt erased by force of law, with the declaration serving merely as a reinforcement? Or is there some other structure at work?

### Rosh's Two-Stage View

The *Rosh* offers what is perhaps the most compelling resolution. He reads the term *bishmita* — during the *shmitta* year — with precision. According to the *Rosh*, during the year of *shmita* itself, the underlying debt still legally exists; what the Torah prohibits is the active demanding or exacting of that debt. The obligation of *meshameit ani* is thus the creditor's active participation in that prohibition: you declare "I release you," and your verbal release reflects the commandment not to press for payment. Only at the conclusion of *shmita* — at the onset of the eighth year — is the debt automatically and permanently annulled.

This reading elegantly explains the *mishnah*'s scenario. During *shmita*, the debt is real but uncollectable. If the debtor voluntarily appears and wishes to pay, the debt still technically exists, which is precisely why the creditor may accept the payment once the debtor says *af al pi chen*. An alternative reading — that the debt has already been erased and repayment is simply a moral gesture, like reciprocating a Shabbos invitation — is possible but less legally satisfying. The *Rosh*'s framework gives the entire structure a cleaner internal logic.

### Pressuring for Repayment

The *Gemara* pushes further on the concept of *af al pi chen* as a vehicle for recovering the debt. Rabba states: *talvei lei ad d'amar hachi* — one may "string him up" until he says *af al pi chen*, meaning one may apply pressure to get the debtor to voluntarily declare his intention to repay. The creditor is not demanding payment as a debt; he is urging the debtor to understand his moral responsibility.

### Abaye's Objection

Abaye challenges this directly. The *mishnah* elsewhere specifies that when the debtor does repay after the creditor has said *meshameit ani*, he should not say "I am giving this to you on account of my debt" — *be-chovi ani noten lach* — but rather "this is mine, and I am giving it to you as a gift" — *sheli hen u-v'matana ani noten lach*. If the very framing of the repayment must avoid any acknowledgment of debt, how can one pressure the debtor to pay at all? That pressure itself seems to acknowledge that a real debt is being pursued.

Rava responds: *talyuhu v'yahiv* — you pressure him until he gives it as a gift. The pressure is not framed as debt collection; it is an appeal to moral conscience. You are not saying "pay me what you owe me" but rather nudging him to understand that it is the right thing to do, and then he gives — voluntarily, framed as a gift. This is admittedly a fine line, and even a somewhat counterintuitive one. As the lecturer notes, it sits in obvious tension with the spirit of *shmitat kesafim*, much as the *pruzbul* does — it is the *Gemara* trying to balance the ideal of debt release with the practical reality that creditors have legitimate interests and debtors have genuine moral obligations. According to the *Rosh*'s reading, however, this is somewhat less strained: if the debt truly still exists during *shmita*, then the debtor is being encouraged to honor an obligation that is real, even if uncollectable.

### Abba bar Marta Story

The *Gemara* illustrates this tension through a vivid narrative. Abba bar Marta — also known as Abba bar Minyumi — owed Rabba money. During *shmita*, he came to repay the loan. Rabba did the right thing and said *meshameit ani* — "I release you." The debtor took Rabba at his word, pocketed the release, and left with his money. Abaye later found Rabba in a state of anguish and asked what was wrong. Rabba explained what had happened: he had done exactly what he was supposed to do, and the debtor had simply left without understanding the script he was meant to follow.

Abaye — the same Abaye who had challenged the legitimacy of applying pressure — went to the debtor and, with notable subtlety, walked him through the exchange. He asked: "Did you bring your money to the Master?" Yes. "What did he say?" *Meshameit ani*. "And did you say to him *af al pi chen*?" No. "Had you said *af al pi chen*, he would have happily accepted it." Abaye then instructed him: go back now, bring the money, and say *af al pi chen*. The debtor did so, and Rabba accepted it.

This story is striking on multiple levels. Rabba himself, after the fact, said that the debtor — a Torah scholar — should have known better, since the mechanism of *af al pi chen* is explicitly stated in a *mishnah* in *Shevi'it*. But more striking is Abaye's conduct: having challenged the very principle of pressuring debtors, he himself applied exactly such pressure — albeit gentle and indirect — in service of his own *rebbe*'s financial interests. The *Gemara* does not comment on this irony, but it is unmistakable.

---

## Pruzbul

### Rav Nachman's Leniency

The *Gemara* now pivots to the *pruzbul* — the mechanism instituted by Hillel to circumvent *shmitat kesafim* by transferring debts to a court, which is not subject to the *shmitta* release. Rav Nachman rules: *ne'eman adam lomar pruzbul hayah be-yadi ve-avad* — a person is believed to claim that he had a *pruzbul* and lost it, without having to produce the document. This is a significant leniency: previously we had seen opinions suggesting that certain *talmidei chakhamim* might not even need a formal written *pruzbul* or could rely on a verbal declaration; Rav Nachman does not go quite that far, but he does rule that production of the document in court is not required.

### Rationale: Presumed Dili…

The reasoning is straightforward: *keivan de-tikinu rabanan pruzbul* — since the Rabbis instituted the *pruzbul* as the legitimate and permitted path for collecting debts after *shmita*, *lo shevik heteира ve-achil issurah* — we presume that people would not abandon the permissible path and proceed in a transgressive manner. In other words, anyone who is claiming to collect a debt almost certainly wrote a *pruzbul*; we simply presume they did. This is a generalized principle used elsewhere in halakhic reasoning: where a straightforward permissible path exists, we assume people availed themselves of it.

### Rava's Suggestion

Rava applied this principle in practice. When a case came before him and the creditor had not produced a *pruzbul*, Rava asked him directly: *midi pruzbul havah lach ve-avad?* — "Is it possible that you had a *pruzbul* and you lost it?" This is the principle of *ptach picha le-ilem* — "open up your mouth to the mute" — the idea that someone who had indeed written a *pruzbul* and lost it might not even think to assert that fact. Rava's prompt invited the creditor to recall and state what was presumably the truth. There is, the lecturer acknowledges, something of a wink and nod in this exchange — Rava is actively facilitating the creditor's claim — but the underlying principle is sound: we presume people acted in the permitted manner.

### Mishnah Contradiction

A difficulty arises from a *mishnah* that seems to state the opposite: *ha-motzi shtaro ve-ein imo pruzbul harei elu lo yifare'u* — a creditor who produces his loan document without an accompanying *pruzbul* may not collect. This appears to require production of the *pruzbul*.

### Evolving Standards

The *Gemara* resolves this as a *tannaitic* dispute: a *baraita* cites the Sages as saying that the *pruzbul* need not be produced alongside the loan document. Beyond this formal resolution, there is a broader historical explanation available: the *pruzbul* at the time of the *mishnah* was a weightier and more formal institution, and its requirements were accordingly more stringent. Over time, as the institution developed and became more routine, the standards relaxed — consistent with the general pattern of the *pruzbul* becoming progressively easier to utilize, including the loosening of requirements around land ownership and other formal conditions. The principle of *lo shevik heteира ve-achil issurah* thus becomes ever more operative as the *pruzbul* becomes ever more accessible.

---

## Enslaved Captive

### Mishnah Case

The *Gemara* transitions to a *mishnah* in an entirely different domain, though it remains within the broader framework of *tikkun olam* — the organizing theme of this chapter. Interestingly, the *mishnah* itself does not mention *tikkun olam*, and it is not immediately clear from the *mishnah's* language which ruling constitutes the *takkanah* and what its social purpose is. That unpacking is left entirely to the *Gemara*.

The *mishnah* states: *eved she-nishba u-fadahu* — a slave who was taken captive and redeemed. *Im le-shum eved* — if he was redeemed for the purpose of returning to servitude — *yishtabed*, he goes back into servitude. *Im le-shum ben chorin* — if he was redeemed for the purpose of freedom — *lo yishtabed*, he does not return to slavery and goes free.

This is intuitively sensible. The slave is someone's property. Non-Jewish forces have captured him. If his own master or someone acting on the master's behalf ransoms him back, he returns to his master. But if third parties — people unconnected to the master — encounter this captive slave, take pity on him, and redeem him with the intention of setting him free, he goes free.

### Rabban Gamliel

Rabban Gamliel dissents: *bein kach u-vein kach yishtabed* — either way, he remains a slave. The rationale behind his position, and the question of which view constitutes the *tikkun olam*, will be developed by the *Gemara*.

### Ye'ush Question

The *Gemara* asks: *bemai askinan?* — what precisely is the case? The analysis turns on the concept of *ye'ush* — the master's renunciation of hope of recovering his slave. Since the slave is legally property, the same principles that govern lost or stolen objects apply. Before *ye'ush*, the master has not relinquished his claim; after *ye'ush*, he has, and the object can pass into the possession of a third party. The question is: in which of these two states does the *mishnah*'s case take place?

If it is before *ye'ush*, then when the slave is redeemed *le-shum ben chorin* — for freedom — why does he go free? He is still fully the master's property. A third party who purchases stolen property from a thief before the owner's *ye'ush* cannot claim ownership; similarly, why should these redeemers be able to grant the slave his freedom? The slave is still mine, regardless of what you intended when you paid the captors.

Conversely, if it is after *ye'ush*, then when the slave is redeemed *le-shum eved* — for servitude — why is he still enslaved? After *ye'ush*, he arguably should already be a free person, since no one owns him. These two questions create the central dilemma that Abaye and Rava each resolve in their own ways.

### Abaye: Before Ye'ush

Abaye says: *le-olam lifnei ye'ush* — the case is before *ye'ush*. Before *ye'ush*, *le-shum eved ishtabed le-rabo rishon* — obviously, if redeemed for servitude, he returns to the first master. He is still the master's property and the redemption simply restores him.

The harder question is *le-shum ben chorin*: if he is redeemed for freedom before *ye'ush*, why does he go free? *Lo ishtabed lo le-rabo rishon ve-lo le-rabo sheni* — he is enslaved neither to the first master nor to the second. That the redeemers cannot enslave him is straightforward — *de-ha le-shum ben chorin parkei* — they redeemed him to be free. But why does he not return to the first master? He was never subject to *ye'ush*; he remains the master's property. The answer lies in *tikkun olam*: *dilma mimnei ve-lo parkei* — we are concerned that if people know that a slave redeemed for freedom will simply be returned to his master, they will hold back and not redeem him at all. We wish to incentivize redemption. People may feel the pull of *pidyon shvuyim* — the obligation to redeem captives — but only if they perceive the captive as a potential free person do they feel sufficiently motivated to act. Rashi captures this: once a person knows that his redemption will result in the slave's freedom, he begins to see the slave as a would-be free man and feels the weight of *pidyon shvuyim* more acutely.

Therefore, as a *tikkun olam*, we rule that if someone redeems the slave *le-shum ben chorin* before *ye'ush*, the slave goes free — even though by strict law he should be returned to the first master.

### Rava: After Ye'ush

Rava takes the opposite position: *le-olam le-achar ye'ush* — the case is after *ye'ush*. After *ye'ush*, the first master has relinquished his claim. The slave does not automatically become free merely because of *ye'ush*, however; a third party who takes possession of him — *shinui reshut* combined with *ye'ush* — can acquire rights to him.

Thus, *le-shum eved ishtabed*: if redeemed for servitude after *ye'ush*, the redeemer acquires him through the mechanism of *ye'ush ve-shinui reshut*. *Le-shum ben chorin, lo yishtabed*: if redeemed for freedom, he goes free — the redeemer did not intend to acquire him, and the first master has been *meya'esh*. *Le-rabo sheni lo* — the redeemer cannot enslave him because that was not his intent. *Le-rabo rishon lama lo — de-ha le-achar ye'ush hu* — and the first master cannot reclaim him because *ye'ush* has already transpired.

On Rava's reading, the Sages (*chakhamim*) are simply stating the straightforward *din*: after *ye'ush*, the outcome depends on the redeemer's intent. There is no *tikkun olam* in the Sages' position; it is the plain law of *ye'ush ve-shinui reshut*. Rabban Gamliel, by contrast, is the one introducing a *tikkun olam*: *bein kach u-vein kach yishtabed* — either way, the slave goes back to the first master. This is not because of any legal logic, but because of the principle articulated by Chizkiyah.

As Chizkiyah explains: *shelo yehei kol echad ve-echad holech u-mapil atzmo le-gayyasot u-mafki'ah atzmo mi-yad rabo* — lest every slave deliberately allow himself to be captured by marauding troops as a strategy for escaping his master. If slaves know that capture leads to *ye'ush* and *ye'ush* leads to freedom, they have an incentive to manufacture the situation. The *tikkun olam* of Rabban Gamliel is therefore to ensure that whatever happens, the slave returns to his first master — according to Rashi, *le-rabo rishon* specifically, even if the second party intended to enslave him to himself.

This is a striking *Gemara* precisely because *tikkun olam* here is not the expansive, progressive concept it is sometimes romanticized to be. One version of *tikkun olam* incentivizes redemption by granting freedom. The other version of *tikkun olam* ensures runaway slaves are always returned to their masters, because social order depends on the stability of that institution. Both are *tikkun olam* in the technical sense: rabbinic enactments for the sake of societal welfare. They point in opposite directions.

### Baraita Challenge

The *Gemara* cites a *baraita* in which Rabban Gamliel himself says to the Sages: *keshem she-mitzvah lifdot bnei chorin, kach mitzvah lifdot ha-avadim* — just as there is a *mitzvah* to redeem free persons, so too there is a *mitzvah* to redeem slaves. This statement fits naturally with Abaye's reading: Abaye says the Sages' position is a *tikkun olam* to incentivize redemption, and Rabban Gamliel challenges it by saying people need no special incentive — there is already an obligation to redeem slaves, just as there is to redeem free persons. On Rava's reading, however, this statement seems out of place. According to Rava, the Sages are simply stating the *din* of *ye'ush*, and Rabban Gamliel is introducing a *takanah* to prevent runaways; in that context, his invocation of the *mitzvah* to redeem slaves seems entirely beside the point.

### Rava's Response

Rava resolves this by saying: *Rabban Gamliel lo hava yada mai kamri rabbanan* — Rabban Gamliel did not know what exactly the Sages were arguing. He was not responding to a specific position but rather laying out a comprehensive rebuttal to any possible rationale: if you are arguing that the slave goes free before *ye'ush* in order to incentivize redemption, you are wrong — there is already a *mitzvah* to redeem slaves, so no extra incentive is needed. And if you are arguing that after *ye'ush* the slave goes free because that is the plain *din*, I also disagree — we should override that *din* because of Chizkiyah's concern about slaves engineering their own capture. Either way, *bein kach u-vein kach yishtabed*.

---

## Non-Jewish Slave Ownersh…

### Captors' Rights

With the basic framework of the *mishnah* established, the *Gemara* turns to a foundational question: how do the non-Jewish captors acquire any ownership rights over the slave at all? This matters because, according to Rava, it is only after *ye'ush* that a third party can redeem the slave and enslave him to themselves through *ye'ush ve-shinui reshut*. For this to work, the captors must have some degree of recognized ownership over the slave. If the captors have no rights whatsoever, then the master's *ye'ush* would leave the slave simply ownerless — and one might argue he would go free at that very moment, with no mechanism for the second party to acquire him.

The *Gemara* answers: *in, kanei lei le-ma'aseh yadav* — yes, the captors do acquire him, but only for his labor — *ma'aseh yadav* — not as full property. This partial ownership is precisely the concept of *kinyan geneivah* or *kinyan gezeila*: when a thief or violent aggressor takes possession of someone's property, they acquire a de facto partial ownership. A well-known consequence of this principle is that a thief who steals an object and is later caught does not owe the owner rental fees for the period of use, because that de facto possession granted him some right of use, however illegitimate his acquisition. The same structure applies here: the captors, by seizing the slave, acquire rights to his labor, even without purchasing him and even without the master's consent. This partial ownership prevents the slave from being automatically freed by *ye'ush* and enables the subsequent transfer of possession to a Jewish buyer who wishes to enslave him.

### Reish Lakish

This raises a broader question about the structure of slave ownership in halakhic thought. Reish Lakish articulates a general principle: *minayin le-oved kochavim she-kanah oved kochavim le-ma'aseh yadav* — how do we know that a non-Jew who acquires a non-Jew does so only for his labor (*ma'aseh yadav*) and not as full bodily property (*kinyan guf*)? This is a striking halakhic distinction. Jews can own non-Jewish slaves as full property — *kinyan guf*. Non-Jews can own other non-Jews, or own Jews, only for their labor — *ma'aseh yadav*. Only a Jewish master holds full property rights over a non-Jewish slave.

This is deeply unsettling on its face. But one suggested rationale, offered in the course of discussion, is that Jewish law does not trust pagan society to exercise the kind of restrained mastery over another human being that full property ownership would entail. The experience of *shibud mitzrayim* — Egyptian bondage — and the ethical framework that follows from it means that the only context in which full property ownership of a person can be sanctioned is one governed by Torah law. It remains a troubling framework by any measure, but it is the halakhic structure the *Gemara* is operating within.

### Verse Derivation

The derivation for this distinction comes from the verse in *Vayikra*: *v'gam mi-bnei ha-toshavim ha-garim imachem, me-hem tiknu eved va-amah* — and also from the children of the resident aliens who dwell among you, from them you may purchase slaves. The *Gemara* reads this as a limiting verse: *atem konim me-hem* — you may purchase them as full property, *ve-lo hem konim mi-kem* — but they may not purchase you as full property. And *ve-lo hem konim zeh mi-zeh l'gufo* — nor may they purchase one another as full property. Non-Jews may own non-Jews and may own Jews, but only for *ma'aseh yadav*, not *kinyan guf*.

The implications of *kinyan guf* — full bodily ownership — go beyond mere economic rights. As Rashi emphasizes, *kinyan guf* is a matter of personal status. If a slave is owned *le-gufo*, then to change that status, a formal document of manumission — a *get shichrur* — is required. Merely renouncing one's economic claim is insufficient to alter the slave's halakhic identity. Furthermore, a slave owned *le-gufo* cannot simply choose to undergo conversion and thereby redefine his status; his identity is determined by the ownership relationship, and only the master can change it through formal manumission. A slave owned only *le-ma'aseh yadav*, by contrast, has a more fluid status: his labor belongs to another, but his person does not, and if that labor-obligation ends, his status adjusts accordingly.

### Kal va-Chomer

A *kal va-chomer* is then constructed. If a non-Jew can own a Jew for *ma'aseh yadav* — as we know from the *pesukim* in the Torah describing a Jew who sells himself into servitude to a resident alien — then certainly a non-Jew can own another non-Jew for *ma'aseh yadav*. The argument is: the *chumra* case (a Jew owned by a non-Jew for his labor) establishes the category; the *kal* case (a non-Jew owned by a non-Jew for his labor) follows *a fortiori*. 

A complication arises: we know a non-Jew can own a Jew for *ma'aseh yadav* through the mechanism of purchase (*be-kaspa*) — the Jew sells himself. But in our case, the captors did not purchase the slave; they seized him by force. What is the source for acquisition through forceful seizure — *chazakah* — rather than purchase?

### Kibbush Milchamah

The *Gemara* introduces the concept of *kibbush milchamah* — forceful conquest as a mode of acquisition. Rav Papa demonstrates this from the episode of Sichon: Sichon captured the lands of Ammon and Moab through military conquest. When the Jewish people subsequently conquered Sichon's territories, they were permitted to take those lands even though the Torah had commanded *al tetzer et Moav* — do not distress Moab. The resolution was that those territories were no longer Moab's; Sichon had acquired them through *kibbush milchamah*, and they had become Sichon's lands. When Israel conquered Sichon, they inherited lands that were legitimately Sichon's. This demonstrates that forceful seizure in war constitutes a recognized form of acquisition. Tosafot identifies this principle explicitly as *kibbush milchamah*.

If this is true of land, the same principle extends to people: a non-Jewish force that captures a slave by force acquires rights to him through *kibbush milchamah*, even without any purchase transaction.

### Captives Verse

The final step extends this principle from non-Jews seizing non-Jewish property to non-Jews seizing property belonging to Jews. For the former, the case of *Amon u-Moav* and Sichon is sufficient. For the latter — *akum mi-Yisrael minayin?* — the *Gemara* derives it from the verse *va-yishbi mimenu shevi* — and he took captives from them. The fact that the verse uses the noun *shevi* (captive) rather than merely saying that a person was taken implies that the captured person acquired the status of *shevi* — captive — as a result of being seized. The seizure itself changes the person's status, giving the captors recognized rights to him. This establishes that non-Jewish captors acquire rights — *ma'aseh yadav* — over Jewish-owned slaves whom they capture by force, and that those rights persist even after the master's *ye'ush*, enabling the subsequent transfer of possession.

---

## Escape & Manumission

### Escape Goes Free

Rabbi Yochanan, cited by Rabbi Shimon bar Abba, teaches: *eved she-barach mi-beit ha-asurin yatza le-cheirut* — a slave who escapes from captivity goes free. Moreover, *koфin rabo ve-kotev lo get shichrur* — we compel his former master to write him a writ of manumission, to ensure his freedom is formally and publicly established.

### Apparent Contradiction

This creates an apparent contradiction with Rabbi Yochanan's own stated position — recorded in the name of Rabbah bar bar Chana — that wherever Rabban Gamliel appears in the *mishnah*, the *halacha* follows him (with three specified exceptions, none of which is our case). Since our *mishnah* features Rabban Gamliel ruling *bein kach u-vein kach yishtabed* — he is always returned to slavery — and we rule like Rabban Gamliel, how can Rabbi Yochanan simultaneously hold that a slave who escapes goes free?

### Abaye Resolves

According to Abaye, the resolution is straightforward. Abaye's reading of the *mishnah* is *lifnei ye'ush*: before *ye'ush*, the slave is fully the master's property and Rabban Gamliel's ruling — that he always remains enslaved — is correct and we rule accordingly. But the case of Rabbi Yochanan — where the slave escapes his captors — is *le-achar ye'ush*. After *ye'ush*, the master has no claim, the captors own him only for *ma'aseh yadav*, and when he escapes, no one retains ownership over him. He goes free.

The need for a *get shichrur* even after *ye'ush* is not self-evident, since the master's monetary claim has lapsed. But this is precisely where the distinction between monetary ownership and personal status matters. Even if the master no longer owns the slave in any economic sense — cannot demand his labor, has no property rights — the slave's *halakhic status* may still be that of a slave. Personal status is not automatically altered by the lapse of property rights; it may require a formal document — the *shtar shichrur* — to effect the change.

### Rava: Escape Different

For Rava, the resolution is more complex, since on his reading, even *le-achar ye'ush* we apply the *takanah* of Chizkiyah — slaves are always returned to their masters, lest they engineer their own capture. If we rule like Rabban Gamliel based on Chizkiyah's concern, and Rabbi Yochanan says we always rule like Rabban Gamliel, how can Rabbi Yochanan simultaneously teach that an escaped slave goes free?

Rava answers: *barach shani* — escape is different. The reason we send slaves back to their masters after *ye'ush* is to disincentivize deliberate self-captivity. But a slave who escapes his captors has demonstrated the opposite: he risked his life — *le-katla masar nafsheih* — to get out of captivity. Presumably the penalty for escape was death. A person willing to accept mortal risk to flee captivity clearly did not seek out captivity as a means of liberation. The entire concern underlying Chizkiyah's *takanah* simply does not apply to this person. Therefore, even according to Rava, when a slave escapes rather than being redeemed, he goes free — and Chizkiyah's *takanah* does not operate.

---

## Ownership vs. Status

### Shmuel's Case

The *Gemara* now introduces a case involving the maidservant of Shmuel. She was taken captive — *ishtava'i* — and a group of people redeemed her *le-shum amahuta*, intending to restore her to Shmuel's service as a gift to him. They sent Shmuel a message: we follow the ruling of Rabban Gamliel (*ke-Rabban Gamliel sevira lan*), and even if you hold like the Sages, we redeemed her specifically for servitude — so please accept her back.

The difficulty is that they had assumed the case was *lifnei ye'ush* — before Shmuel had given up hope. But in fact, *le-achar ye'ush hava* — Shmuel had already been *meya'esh* from her. Once this is established, Shmuel had no interest in retaining her in any case, and no one wished to press a claim to her.

### Shmuel's Ruling

The *Gemara* records that Shmuel went further: not only would he not retain her in servitude, but she did not even require a *get shichrur* — a writ of manumission. This reflects Shmuel's consistent position: *ha-mafkir avdo yatza le-cheirut ve-eino tzarich get shichrur* — one who renounces ownership over his slave, the slave goes free without needing a formal writ. The renunciation of monetary ownership is sufficient to change the slave's halakhic status entirely.

### Verse Interpretation

Shmuel derives this from the verse *ve-chol eved ish miknat kasef* — the slave of a man. The phrase *eved ish* — slave of a man — implies: *eved she-yesh lo reshut rabo alav karui eved* — a slave is only called a slave when the master retains authority over him. *She-ein lo reshut rabo alav, ein karui eved* — when no such authority exists, he is no longer designated a slave, and his personal status changes accordingly without need for any further document. Monetary status and personal status are thus intertwined; one automatically implies the other.

### Rabbi Abba Case

The *Gemara* then brings the parallel case of the maidservant of Rabbi Abba bar Zutra. She was taken captive and redeemed by a non-Jew — *tarmuda'ah* — who intended to take her as a wife. Jewish community members sent word to Rabbi Abba: if you have been *meya'esh* from her, send her a *get shichrur*. But the *Gemara* asks: what would the *get shichrur* accomplish? If these community members have the financial means to redeem her, they can simply do so and return her to Rabbi Abba; there is no need for a writ. And if they cannot afford to redeem her, how does sending a writ of manumission help?

### Writ Purposes

The *Gemara* resolves this with two alternative explanations. The first: they do have the means to redeem her, but the point of the *get shichrur* is to incentivize broader communal participation. *Keivan de-mashdar lah gita de-cheiruta* — once a writ of manumission is sent and it becomes known that she is a free woman, people will feel a stronger obligation of *pidyon shvuyim* — redeeming a free person is more compelling than redeeming a slave — and they will pool their resources to buy her back. This parallels Abaye's *tikkun olam* reasoning from the *mishnah*: the prospect of freedom is what mobilizes people.

The second approach: they cannot afford to redeem her. But if Rabbi Abba sends a *get shichrur*, it becomes publicly known that she had been a slave. This embarrasses the non-Jew who wishes to take her as a wife — publicly known as the wife of a former slave is not a dignity he wishes — and he will therefore lower his asking price to a level they can afford. The *get shichrur* here is not about changing her status for its own sake, but about creating public information that changes the non-Jew's leverage. The *Gemara* qualifies: non-Jews may be privately happy to take advantage of opportunities involving Jewish-owned property, but *be-farhesia* — publicly — *zila behu milta* — such things are embarrassing to them. Public exposure thus becomes a tool for reducing the ransom price.

---

## Branded Woman Story

### Wedding Discovery

The *Gemara* concludes with a remarkable narrative drawn from *Bava Kamma* (daf 114). A man in Lod married off his son. Guests came to the celebration, and as the host's wife poured wine for the assembled guests, her sleeves shifted and her arms were exposed. The guests saw that she had a *kivuyah* — a brand — on her arm, the kind of mark used to identify slaves as property of their owner. The implication was immediate and devastating: if she was a branded slave who had never been formally freed, she could not legally marry a Jew. Her husband's marriage was no marriage. Their son, whose wedding was at that very moment being celebrated, was himself a slave. The entire gathering fell under a cloud.

### Martyrdom Explanation

The host addressed the whispers directly. He acknowledged the brand but offered an explanation: his wife had been taken captive by non-Jews who sought to compel her to serve their idols. She refused — categorically, repeatedly. In response, they tortured her; they took a red-hot iron and burned her arms to break her will. She endured the torture and still did not submit to *avodah zarah*. The brand on her arms was not a slave's mark; it was the mark of a *tzadeket*, a holy woman who had accepted physical torment rather than violate her faith.

### Acceptance

The guests believed him entirely. And the *Gemara* records that they not only accepted the explanation but honored him more after hearing it — contributing additional money and expressing greater esteem for him than they had before.

### Gemara's Lesson

The *Gemara* draws a careful lesson. Ordinarily, a woman who claims she was captured and mistreated is not simply believed to explain away evidence of slave status. The *mishnah* elsewhere makes clear that such claims require substantiation. Why was she believed here? Because there was tangible physical evidence that required explanation. The brand *existed*; it was visible to everyone. Given that evidence, the question was not whether to believe a claim out of nowhere, but how to interpret an observable fact. The choice was between two explanations — slave branding or torture for refusing idolatry — and given that she was a Jewish woman of apparent standing and reputation, the more favorable explanation was accepted. The underlying principle is that credible, corroborating physical evidence creates a context in which alternative explanations can be credited. Without such evidence — if a woman simply makes an unsubstantiated claim — she is not believed. The physical reality of the brand is what opens the door to the charitable reading. Without it, the door remains closed.

---

# Gittin 39

## Freeing Slaves

### Rav Yehuda/Shmuel

The daf opens at the very bottom of 38a, in the midst of a discussion concerning slaves and *tikkun olam* — though not necessarily in the direction one might have expected. The Gemara presents the following case: there was a female slave in Pumbedita (*hahi amata de'hava be-Pumbedita*) who was being sexually exploited (*de'hava kam'avdi ba issura*). Abaye declared that were it not for the ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel — *kol hamesachrer avdo over be-asei*, anyone who frees his slave transgresses a positive commandment — he would have compelled the master to write her a *get shichrur*, a writ of manumission, so that she could achieve full free status and thereby be protected from abuse.

The positive commandment in question derives from the verse *le'olam bahem ta'avodu* — you shall enslave them forever. The irony of this *mitzvat asei* is not lost: given the centrality of *Yetziat Mitzrayim* to the Jewish moral imagination, a positive obligation to maintain the institution of slavery is striking. One might distinguish between the Torah tolerating the institution of slavery — which could be understood as a concession to the realities of the ancient world — and actively reinforcing it through a prohibitory commandment. The latter is harder to account for. Perhaps the concern was systemic: freeing an individual slave without addressing the underlying economic structure may have been seen as disruptive in ways that were not necessarily in the slave's best interest. Or perhaps the commandment was understood as applying only when there is no legitimate purpose — a reading that several *Rishonim* favor, as we will see shortly.

### Abaye's Exception

Ravina qualifies the ruling: *ki ha modei Rav Yehuda* — Rav Yehuda himself would concede that in a case of ongoing transgression (*mishum milsa de'issura*), freeing the slave is permitted. Whether this means the prohibition is overridden or simply inapplicable when there is legitimate cause is a matter of debate among the *Rishonim*, and the Gemara returns to this question when it reaches the famous case of Rabbi Eliezer and the *minyan*.

### Half-Slave Woman

The Gemara now raises a challenge: there is a teaching (*ma'aseh b'ishah achas*) about a woman who was half-slave, half-free — owned jointly by two partners, one of whom freed her and the other did not. Her status was entirely ambiguous: she could not marry a Jewish man, nor could she marry a slave. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that people were treating her with contempt, exploiting her as if she were ownerless (*minhag hefker nahagu bah*). In that case the master was compelled to free her.

Does this case not demonstrate that Abaye should have acted similarly with the slave in Pumbedita? The Gemara distinguishes the two: in the case of the half-free woman, there was no alternative — *lo l'eved chazya v'lo l'ven chorin chazya*, she could neither marry a slave nor a free man. In the Pumbedita case, however, it would have been possible to arrange for her a slave husband who could protect her (*efshar d'meyachad lah avdi v'minatrah*). Since an alternative existed that did not require overriding the *mitzvat asei*, Abaye felt constrained from compelling her manumission.

### Rabbi Eliezer Minyan

The Gemara returns to examine the core ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel. It raises a well-known challenge: *ma'aseh b'Rabbi Eliezer shenichnas l'veit ha'knesses v'lo matza asarah* — Rabbi Eliezer entered the synagogue and did not find ten men to form a *minyan*. He freed his slave (*shichrar avdo*) and thereby completed the quorum (*v'hishlimo l'asarah*).

The Gemara responds: *mitzvah shani* — for a *mitzvah*, the case is different. This formulation invites scrutiny. If the prohibition against freeing slaves is a *mitzvat asei d'oraita*, how does a rabbinic obligation to maintain a *minyan* override it? The Ramban addresses this directly, citing the Gemara's teaching that when God arrives at a synagogue and finds fewer than ten people assembled, divine anger is immediate. The theological weight of the *minyan* thus transcends the technical question of whether it is *d'oraita* or *d'rabbanan*. Other *Rishonim*, however, favor the alternative reading: the prohibition against freeing slaves was never intended to apply when there is a legitimate purpose. On this reading, Rabbi Eliezer did not override the commandment — he simply did not transgress it, because the commandment is limited to gratuitous manumission.

One might further ask: when the slave is freed, does he not undergo a kind of *geirus*? In fact, the acts associated with conversion — *milah* and *tevilah* — were already performed when he was made a slave. But those acts were, in a sense, held in suspension by the reality of his enslavement. Upon manumission, that earlier status is released and given full expression. The Gemara does not view the prospect of the slave accumulating additional *mitzvot* through freedom as sufficient grounds by itself to mandate manumission; the concern about actively overriding a *mitzvat asei* remains the operative consideration.

### Yishmael vs Akiva

A *baraita* is then cited: *Tanu Rabbanan* — from the verse *le'olam bahem ta'avodu*, Rabbi Yishmael derives that maintaining a slave is merely permitted (*reshut*), not obligatory. Rabbi Akiva, by contrast, rules *chova* — it is an obligation. The Gemara then considers whether Rabbi Eliezer, who freed his slave for the *minyan*, might have held like Rabbi Yishmael. This is rejected: a *baraita* states explicitly that *Rav Elazar omer chova* — Rav Elazar himself rules it is an obligation, the position of Rabbi Akiva. His freeing of the slave must therefore be explained on other grounds, as discussed above.

### Three Ways Lose Wealth

Rava offers a related observation: *behani telat mili nacheti ba'alei batim minichseihon* — there are three ways in which wealthy householders descend from their wealth. First, freeing their slaves. Second, inspecting their property on *Shabbos* (*desayrei nichseihon beshabta*). Third, establishing their main meal on *Shabbos* at the time when the public should be attending the rabbinic lecture in the *beit midrash* (*dekeva'ei seudasa beshabta be'idna debei midrasha*).

The convergence of these three cases suggests something beyond mere economic observation. There is clearly a *mida kineged mida* dimension: in each case, the person imagines they are acting generously or properly, but in fact they are misusing what has been entrusted to them — their slaves, their property, or their table — and they are punished accordingly. In the case of *Shabbos* morning, a lavish *kiddush* scheduled to coincide with the public lecture is not *oneg Shabbos* — it is a violation of the communal obligation to learn.

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan adds a historical illustration: two prominent families in Jerusalem were destroyed (*ne'ekru*) because of misuse of their *Shabbos* meals — one made its major feast on *Shabbos* day at the wrong time, and one on *erev Shabbos*. Rashi offers two explanations for the problem with the *erev Shabbos* family. One is that they made their feast on Friday night; Rashi notes that the principle *kavod yom kodem le'kavod laila* — the honor of the day takes precedence over the night — means that by making Friday night more lavish than *Shabbos* day they inverted the proper hierarchy. When told not to feast during the *shiur* on *Shabbos* day, they shifted to Friday night — but introduced a new problem. Rashi's second explanation is that they feasted Friday afternoon, arriving at *Shabbos* already satiated and unable to honor *Shabbos* with the proper appetite.

---

## Methods of Freedom

### Sanctification Model

The Gemara now transitions from the permissibility of freeing a slave to the mechanisms by which a slave may actually become free. Rava cites Rav: *hamakdish avdo yatza l'cheirus* — if a person sanctifies (*makdish*) his slave, the slave goes free. The mechanism is not obvious, and Rashi and Tosafot understand it differently.

The Gemara's first step is to note *gufeih lo kadesh* — you cannot actually make the slave's body holy in the direct sense. Rashi understands this to mean that you cannot sanctify him as you would a beam designated for the *Beis Hamikdash* — he cannot be treated as a physical object consecrated to Temple use. Tosafot reads the principle differently: the slave cannot become *assur behana'ah*, forbidden in benefit, as consecrated property typically becomes, because he remains a human being. It is impossible for a person to be forbidden in benefit — he cannot refrain from benefiting himself, nor can others be categorically prohibited from all contact with him. Tosafot therefore understands *gufeih lo kadesh* to mean that he cannot acquire the standard legal character of *hekdesh* property.

Rashi then raises the obvious alternative: perhaps when one says *makdish avdo*, one means that the slave is transferred to the ownership of the *Beis Hamikdash* to be sold for his monetary value — *lidmei*. Rashi's answer to this is striking. He invokes the principle of automatic upgrade of holiness (*kedushah*): just as an unblemished animal designated to be sold by *hekdesh* automatically acquires full sacrificial sanctity rather than the limited sanctity one attempted to impose, so too a slave who is made *makdish* cannot have his *kedushah* artificially limited. The maximum expression of *kedushah* that can apply to a human being is membership in the holy people — *am kadosh*. Therefore, Rashi says, when one sanctifies a slave, the *kedushah* manifests itself as freedom: the slave becomes a free Jew.

### Renouncing Ownership

Rav Yosef then cites Rav's parallel teaching: *hamafkir avdo yatza l'cheirut* — if one renounces ownership (*mafkir*) of his slave, the slave goes free. This is in one sense more intuitive: if the slave is no longer owned by anyone, he is no longer enslaved as property. The Gemara notes the logical relationship between the two cases: whoever accepts the more counterintuitive proposition — that sanctification (*makdish*) results in freedom — will certainly accept the more straightforward case of renouncing ownership (*mafkir*). Conversely, one who begins only from the *mafkir* case need not accept the *makdish* case, since there the natural reading would be that the slave becomes owned by *hekdesh* for his monetary value.

### Status vs Property

This generates the central question of the sugya: *tzarich get shichrur o lo?* When an owner verbally renounces property ownership of a slave — whether by *makdish* or *mafkir* — is that declaration alone sufficient to change the slave's personal status? Or does the slave's personal status, his identity as an *eved*, require a separate *get shichrur* even after property ownership has ended?

The Gemara here revisits the position of Shmuel, mentioned previously in the sugya: *eved ish* — a slave is a slave only as long as he is owned by someone. On Shmuel's view, personal status follows property ownership automatically: the moment ownership ends, the personal status of slavery ends with it, and no writ is required. But this position is now placed in tension with other opinions.

### Get Required

The Gemara resolves the question with the ruling of Rav Chiyya bar Avin in the name of Rav: *echad zeh v'echad zeh yatza l'cheirus v'tzarich get shichrur* — in both the case of *makdish* and the case of *mafkir*, the slave is no longer enslaved in the property sense but still requires a *get shichrur* to change his personal status. This is an explicit rejection of Shmuel's position: property ownership and personal status are treated as legally distinct, and the cessation of one does not automatically entail the cessation of the other.

### Treasurers Authority

Rava then raises a challenge to Rav's position on *makdish*. A *baraita* teaches: if someone declares *hamakdish kol nechasai* — all my property is sanctified — and among that property are slaves, the *gizbarin* (the Temple treasurers, administrators of *hekdesh*) may not free those slaves. Rather, they may sell them to others, and those others may then free them. This *baraita* appears to assume that when a master sanctifies his property including slaves, the slaves become owned by *hekdesh* — they do not automatically become free. This directly contradicts Rav's position.

### Rashi Value Model

The Gemara's first response is that Rav, who was of the transitional generation between *tanna'im* and *amora'im*, is permitted to disagree with a *baraita* (*Rav tanna u'falig*). The Gemara then tries to find a reading of a subsequent source — a verse involving *cherem* — that would be consistent with Rav's position, and asks whether one could simply say that in all the problematic cases the owner specified *ledmai*, that he was sanctifying only for monetary value. If so, Rav would agree that the slave is not automatically freed, since the owner limited the consecration explicitly.

Rashi's answer to this question is distinctive. For Rashi, even an explicit *ledmai* — "I sanctify him for his monetary value" — does not avoid the automatic upgrade problem if the slave himself is being sanctified. The *kedushah* imposed on the slave himself will always express itself maximally as freedom. The only way to avoid the slave going free, on Rashi's reading, is if the owner never sanctified the slave at all — instead, the owner accepted a personal monetary obligation to pay the slave's value to the *Beis Hamikdash*. In that case, *ledmai* means not "the slave is consecrated for his value" but "I personally undertake to pay his value"; the slave himself is entirely unsanctified and remains enslaved.

This reading allows Rashi to explain why, in the case of the *gizbarin*, the *baraita* speaks of the treasurers selling the slave and others freeing him: clearly the slave himself has been consecrated and is owned by *hekdesh*, since the treasurers are transacting with him directly. That scenario is therefore one that Rav must reject — it represents a position incompatible with his own, and that is why the Gemara required the answer of *Rav tanna u'falig*.

### Rabbi Meir Principle

The Gemara then cites a further *baraita*: *hamakdish avdo oseh v'ochel shelo hikdish ela damav* — if one sanctifies his slave, the slave continues to work and consume as before, for the owner only sanctified his monetary value. Here the slave does not go free; the *baraita* seems to present a middle position in which the slave is not transferred to *hekdesh* ownership and is not freed, but the owner bears an obligation to pay his value.

The Gemara identifies this as the position of Rabbi Meir, based on his principle *ein adam motzi devarav l'vatala* — a person does not issue words for naught. The application here runs as follows: when an owner says *makdish avdo*, he cannot literally sanctify the slave's body (for the reasons discussed), so his words must be given some other valid legal meaning. Rabbi Meir's principle directs us to reinterpret the declaration as the owner accepting a personal financial obligation — to pay the slave's market value to the *Beis Hamikdash*. This is similar to Rabbi Meir's ruling elsewhere that if someone says *erko alai* — his assessed value is upon me — for a person whose *erech* under Torah law is zero (such as an infant under one month old), we do not conclude that nothing is owed; rather, we reinterpret the word *erech* to mean the person's market value.

Rashi explains that under this model, the slave himself is entirely unsanctified — *lo hikdish ela damav* means the owner assumed a personal debt, not that the slave acquired any sacred status. Accordingly, the slave continues to work, the master retains his labor, and no question of automatic upgrade arises. For Rav, there are thus two possible models when one is *makdish* a slave: either the sanctification applies to the slave himself and automatically results in freedom (the standard *makdish* case), or the owner's declaration is reinterpreted as a personal financial commitment and the slave is not sanctified at all (the Rabbi Meir model). The *baraita* of *hamakdish avdo oseh v'ochel* reflects the second model, and the Gemara confirms this by noting that a parallel clause — *v'chen hu she'hikdish atzmo*, if the slave sanctifies himself — makes sense only under Rabbi Meir's reading, since a slave has no external owner to transfer him to *hekdesh* ownership; the only coherent interpretation is that he undertook a personal monetary obligation.

---

## Holiness Debate

### All Agree Holy

The Gemara now introduces a *baraita* that shifts the framing entirely: *hamakdish avdo ein moalin bo* — if one sanctifies his slave, there is no transgression of *me'ilah* (misuse of sacred property) with respect to the slave. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds: *moalin b'sa'aro* — there is *me'ilah* with respect to his hair.

The Gemara asks whether this dispute tracks the fundamental question of whether the slave is sanctified at all. But this reading is rejected: *de'chulei alma kadosh* — everyone agrees the slave is sanctified. The debate is not about whether *kedushah* applies but about the legal category into which the slave falls for purposes of *me'ilah*. One opinion holds that *avda k'mankarkei dami* — a slave has the legal status of land — and the laws of *me'ilah* do not apply to land. The other holds *k'mitalteli dami* — a slave is like chattel — and *me'ilah* does apply. This entire discussion stands against Rav's position that the slave goes free upon *makdish*: according to this *baraita*, the slave is genuinely sanctified and remains enslaved.

### Hair Question

The question about hair — *se'ar ha'omed ligzoz* — arises because hair that is ready to be shorn occupies an ambiguous status.
