The *lah lah* comparison — a classic *gezerah shavah* linking the *lah* here to the *lah* in the verse *vechasav lah sefer kerisus*, which concerns a woman's bill of divorce — teaches that just as a woman is divorced by a writ, so too a slave is freed by a writ.

This yields the baseline: a slave can be freed both by money and by *shtar*. But the *baraita* goes further. From the monetary case we know partial freedom is achievable; but what of partial freedom by *shtar*? The verse contains both clauses — *vehispaday lo nifsasah* and *o chuphshah lo nittan lah* — and the *baraita* links them through *makish shtar lekessef*: the *shtar* is analogized to *kessef*. Just as monetary redemption can be total or partial, so too documentary freedom can be total or partial. This *baraita* is thus thoroughly consistent with Rabbi's position.

### Baraita Attribution

The *gemara* observes that according to Rav Yosef — who, after being challenged, conceded that the debate touches upon *shtar*, and then argued that it also extends to *kessef* — this *baraita* presents no difficulty: it is simply the view of Rabbi, while the Rabbanan would reject both halves of it.

The difficulty arises for Rabbah. According to Rabbah, partial redemption through *kessef* is a point of universal agreement, while the dispute concerns only *shtar*. If so, why does the *baraita* first establish the *kessef* rule as if it were an innovation, and then derive the *shtar* rule from it? Is the opening of the *baraita* *divrei hakol* while the conclusion is exclusively Rabbi's position?

Rava resolves this straightforwardly: yes, precisely that — *reisha divrei hakol, seifa Rebbi*. The first half, that partial monetary redemption is valid, is universally accepted. The second half, that a *shtar* can likewise effect partial freedom, represents Rabbi's contested position. The *baraita* naturally opens with the uncontested premise and then uses it as a platform for Rabbi's novel ruling.

Rav Ashi offers a slightly different formulation: the entire *baraita* is Rabbi's, and Rabbi himself is the one who opens with the agreed-upon *kessef* rule before extending it to *shtar*. There is nothing unusual about an author building from common ground toward his own distinctive position.

---

## Half-Slave Status

### Mishna Problem

The *gemara* turns to the *mishna*, which addresses a person who is half-slave and half-free — *mi she-chetzyo eved ve-chetzyo ben chorin* — and the question of whether the master is compelled to free him so that he may marry a woman and have children. According to Rava, the *mishna* poses no difficulty: it can be attributed to *divrei hakol*, since the half-slave status arose through partial monetary redemption, which all agree is valid.

The difficulty falls on Rav Yosef. Having maintained that the Rabbanan reject not only partial *shtar* freedom but also partial monetary redemption, Rav Yosef faces a *mishna* premised on the very phenomenon the Rabbanan supposedly deny. Can the *mishna* really represent only Rabbi's minority view and not the Rabbanan?

### Joint Ownership

Ravina resolves the difficulty — as Rashi had already noted on the earlier *mishna* — by identifying the *mishna*'s case as one of joint ownership: the slave belongs to two masters, and one of them frees his portion entirely. Each master divests himself completely of his own half-ownership. Since the act of the freeing master is total with respect to what he owns, even the Rabbanan agree it is effective. The resulting anomaly — that the slave is half-owned by a second master and half-free — arises not from a deficient act of liberation but from an external constraint on the outcome.

### Rava's Position

Rava now offers a more expansive formulation of the same principle: the dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbanan is confined to the case where a single master frees half and *retains* half — *shichrer chetzyo ve-hiniach chetzyo*. But if the master frees half and *sells* half, or gifts half to another person — *shichrer chetzyo u-machar chetzyo o nasan be-matanah chetzyo* — then, since he completely divests himself of the slave, *keivan de-nafik minei kulei*, even the Rabbanan concede that the act is effective, producing a half-slave half-free individual.

Rashi explains the underlying logic: the defect the Rabbanan identify in a partial *shtar* is not that it produces an intermediate status but that the act itself is incomplete — akin to a husband who divorces his wife while retaining some hold over her. The act of *shichrur* must mirror the totality of *gerushin*: a complete severance. Accordingly, even if the result is that the slave is now half-owned by someone else, what matters is that the master's own act of liberation was absolute. On this reading, simultaneously selling half and freeing half in a single moment also qualifies, since at the conclusion of the act the master retains nothing.

### Estate Division

Abaye challenges Rava's position with a *baraita*: one who writes over his entire estate to two of his slaves — *ha-kosev nechasav li-shnei avadav* — produces a situation in which each slave receives half the estate including half of the other slave. Since each is now half-free (by virtue of having received half of himself), each can own property and hold the other slave's half-ownership, and so *hem meshachrerim zeh es zeh* — they free one another by writing writs of liberation to each other. This *baraita* seems to validate Rava's view that full divestiture in a half-half arrangement works even according to the Rabbanan.

But a second *baraita* complicates matters: *ha-omer kol nechasai nesunim li-feloni u-feloni avadai* — one who says "all my property is given to Reuven and Shimon, my slaves" — *af atzman lo kanu*, they do not acquire even themselves. This sounds identical to the first case, yet the result is the opposite.

The *gemara* first proposes attributing the two *baraitot* to different authorities: the first to Rabbi, whose view permits partial *shichrur*; the second to the Rabbanan, who deny it. But the *gemara* then rejects this and argues that both *baraitot* can reflect the Rabbanan's view.

### Document Distinction

The resolution turns on two distinct variables. The first concerns the linguistic formula used: *kulhu* versus *chatzi chatzi*. When the master says to each slave "I give you *all* my property," each slave in principle receives the totality — including the full person of himself. Since, in one valid sequential arrangement, this would work (if you gave everything to one slave, he would own himself and be free), it also works simultaneously. But when the master says "I give you *half*" to each slave, this can never work sequentially: half-freeing a slave effects nothing in sequence, and therefore, by the same logic, it effects nothing simultaneously either. This distinction — articulated by Tosafot — underlies the difference between the two *baraitot*.

The second resolution (*ve-iba'it eima*) focuses on the number of documents: *kan bi-shtar echad kan bi-shnei shtarot*. A single *shtar* addressed jointly to two slaves is analogous to a single *get* issued to two wives simultaneously — a technical invalidity. Thus the case of *af atzman lo kanu* may involve a single document, which is defective for this reason alone, irrespective of the language used. Two separate *shtarot*, by contrast, each addressed to a single slave, would avoid this defect entirely — and according to Rava, if the formula is *kulhu* (all to each), even the Rabbanan would concede that it works.

The *gemara* ultimately preserves Rava's principle: the Rabbanan agree that full divestiture in a half-half arrangement is effective, provided the act of liberation meets the technical requirements of a valid *shtar shichrur* — one document per slave — and the formula used could function validly in sequence.

---

## Rav Ashi's View

### Terminology Issue

Rav Ashi proposes an entirely different explanation of why the second *baraita* — in which the master says "all my property is given to Reuven and Shimon, my slaves" — fails. The problem, he argues, is not structural or sequential: it is terminological. The master called them *avadai* — "my slaves" — thereby indicating that he conceived of them as remaining his slaves even as he transferred property to them. The word *avadai* reveals his intent: he did not mean to free them.

### Refram Objects

Rafram challenges this immediately: perhaps *avadai* merely describes their prior status — "who have been my slaves until now" — and carries no implication about their ongoing servitude. To support this, Rafram points to the *mishna*: *ha-kosev kol nechasav le-avdo* — one who writes all his property to his slave, the slave *yatza le-cheirus*, goes free. The *mishna* uses the identical construction *avdo* — "his slave" — and yet that slave undeniably goes free. The formula therefore cannot be read as evidence of intent to retain ownership.

### Mishna Evidence

The *gemara* confirms Rafram's objection. In the *mishna*, even when the text reads *le-avdo* — to his slave — the act is treated as a full *shichrur*. The term merely designates the person's prior status. The *gemara* therefore concludes that Rav Ashi's terminological argument fails: one cannot derive from the word *avadai* that the master intended to retain the slaves. The *mishna*'s use of *avdo* proves that such language does not negate the liberating effect of the transfer.

The consequence is that the terminological explanation is rejected, and the earlier resolutions — based on document structure or the *kulhu* versus *chatzi chatzi* distinction — remain the operative frameworks for understanding the two *baraitot*.

---

## Goring Damages

### Day-Based Ownership

The *gemara* now turns from the mechanism of half-freeing to its practical consequences. Before Beis Hillel agreed with Beis Shammai and ruled that the half-slave must be fully freed, the *halacha* was that he works half his days for his master and half for himself. The *gemara* raises the question: if an ox gores this slave on a day designated for his master, does the master collect the damages? And on a day the slave works for himself, does the slave collect?

The initial premise — *yom shel rabo lerabo, yom shel atzmo le'atzmo* — would suggest that his identity, at least in monetary terms, alternates based on the day: on the master's day he is entirely the master's, and on his own day he is entirely his own.

### Status vs. Labor

The *gemara* immediately rejects any extension of this principle to matters of personal status. The suggestion that he might therefore be permitted to marry a free woman on his own days and a slave woman on his master's days is dismissed out of hand: *issura lo ka'amrinan* — we make no such ruling regarding his personal status, which remains fixed as half-slave, half-free regardless of the day. The day-based framework applies only to the question of whose earnings he generates, not to who he is.

### Calya Karna

But even within the monetary domain, the day-based principle has limits. The *gemara* introduces the concept of *kalya karna* — destruction of the principal. If the slave is gored and killed, the *gemara* rules that the payment does not depend on whose day it was but is divided according to his permanent ownership structure: half a *knas* to the master and half a *kofer* to his heirs. This is because the death of the slave is not a question of whose earnings are lost on a given day — it is a permanent destruction of the property itself, and the question of who owns him is a permanent, fundamental one that must be assessed at the level of basic ownership. Since he is half-owned by himself and half by his master at all times, the payment is split accordingly.

The day-based rule, then, applies only to situations that are not *kalya karna* — not permanent damage. A temporary injury from which the slave will fully recover does not constitute a destruction of the principal. The slave will eventually return to full capacity, so the owners have not permanently lost anything; they have only lost his labor for the period of recovery. That lost labor is treated as earnings, and earnings go to whoever is entitled to them on the relevant day.

### Shevet Debate

Here the *gemara* surfaces a dispute between Abaye and Rava with significant implications for this framework.

Abaye holds that even in the case of a non-permanent injury, the payment takes the form of *shevet gedola ve-shevet ketana*. *Shevet gedola* — the major work-suspension payment — treats the temporary incapacity as a form of *nezek*: just as permanent injury is assessed by comparing the slave's market value before and after, so too is a temporary injury, even though he will recover. The comparison is made against the current condition of the slave while injured. *Shevet ketana* then covers the additional period of complete incapacitation — the time during which he cannot perform even minimal tasks. Under Abaye's view, an ox that gores a slave in a temporary injury would be liable for an assessable *nezek*, and this payment, since it concerns a valuation of the slave's current state rather than a permanent alteration of the principal, would go to whoever is entitled to his proceeds on that day.

Rava disagrees. In a case of non-permanent injury, there is no *nezek* to be assessed via the slave market. The injury produces no permanent diminution of value; once healed, the slave is worth exactly what he was before. The only payment owed is for *shevet* — time out of work — which is calculated day by day based on what work the slave is unable to perform relative to what he would otherwise do in his injured state. Crucially, *shevet* of this kind is a category of payment in cases of personal injury caused by a human being (*chavala*); an ox, however, only pays *nezek* — the actual, assessable cost of damage. Since under Rava's view a temporary injury produces no *nezek*, an ox that causes a non-permanent injury to a slave owes nothing at all under the laws of goring.

### Damage Split

This creates a tension in the *gemara*'s framework. We had said the day-based rule applies to non-permanent injuries — implying there is a payment from an ox in such cases that can then be allocated to the appropriate party. But according to Rava, an ox owes nothing for a non-permanent injury, because there is no *nezek* and an ox does not pay *shevet*. On what basis, then, would the day-based rule ever operate in an ox-goring scenario?

The *gemara* resolves this in two ways. First, *ee-ba'it eima keshe-hikahu adam*: perhaps the day-based rule applies not to a case of ox-goring at all, but to a case where the injury was caused by a human being. A human injurer does pay *shevet*, and if the injury is non-permanent, the *shevet* payment — being a function of lost labor rather than a destruction of the principal — goes to whoever was entitled to that labor on the relevant day. Second, *ee-ba'it eima memra hu*: the rule as stated is simply an independent teaching (*memra*), and Rava himself does not subscribe to it. It is not a *baraita* or *mishna* that demands his agreement.

The upshot is that permanent damage — whether death or lasting injury — is always allocated based on the slave's fundamental half-half ownership, split between master and slave. Temporary, non-permanent damage, if actionable at all, is allocated based on whose day it was, since it functions as a form of lost earnings rather than a diminution of the underlying property.

---

## Get Shichror Status

### Payment Question

The *gemara* now raises a distinct and unresolved *ibba'ya* concerning the slave who is *mechusar get shichrur* — one who lacks only a *get shichrur* to become free. The paradigmatic case is a slave whom the master has declared *hefker* (ownerless), or one whom Beis Hillel now compels the master to free: the master no longer holds any monetary claim over the slave, yet the slave's personal status has not changed, because a formal *get shichrur* has not yet been delivered. The master retains, in some sense, the residual status of *adon* — enough standing to write and deliver the liberating document — but no proprietary claim.

The question: if an ox gores this slave during the interim period, does the master collect the thirty-*shekel* *knas*? The Torah says *kesef shloshim shekalim yiten le-adonav* — the payment goes to "his master." Is this former master still an *adon* in the relevant sense? Or has he forfeited that status entirely along with his monetary ownership? Perhaps the *knas*, being a fixed fine rather than a payment for lost property, could be owed to whoever holds formal master-status — and the residual status needed to write a *get shichrur* might suffice. The *gemara* leaves the question open.

### Half-Slave Proof

The *gemara* attempts a proof from the earlier ruling: *hamamit mi she-chatzi eved ve-chatzi ben chorin nosei chatzi knas le-rabo ve-chatzi kofer le-yorshav* — an ox that kills a half-slave, half-free person pays half a *knas* to the master and half a *kofer* to the heirs. Perhaps this refers to the situation *after* Beis Hillel agreed with Beis Shammai — i.e., the master has effectively been compelled to free the slave and is now only awaiting the delivery of a *get shichrur*. If even in that situation the master collects half the *knas*, that would prove that the *mechusar get shichrur* retains enough master-status to collect *knas*.

The *gemara* rejects the proof: *lo, be-mishnah rishonah* — the ruling refers to the original situation (*mishnah rishonah*), before Beis Hillel reversed their position, when the half-slave arrangement was stable and the master fully owned his half. This case is not analogous to one in which the master has no monetary ownership at all.

### Blinding Proof

A second attempted proof: if the master knocks out the slave's tooth and blinds his eye, the slave goes free — *yotzei be-shino*, *yotzei be-eino*. This creates a *mechusar shtar shichrur* scenario: the master no longer exercises monetary dominion, yet a *shtar shichrur* remains to be written. Now, if an ox were to gore the slave during this interval, and if the rule is that the master collects the *knas*, then by parity of reasoning, personal injury (*chavala*) payments should likewise flow to the master. But the *halacha* is that when the master himself injures the slave in this state, the payment goes to the slave. Does this not prove that in the *mechusar get shichrur* scenario the master does not collect — neither *knas* nor *chavala*?

The *gemara* deflects: *eima keivan de-amar eino tzarich* — perhaps this *baraita* follows the opinion that a slave freed by loss of tooth or eye requires no *get shichrur* at all. He is automatically free the moment the tooth or eye is lost. In that case, when the master subsequently blinds the other eye, the slave is already a complete free person and collects as such. The scenario is not one of *mechusar get shichrur* at all — there is nothing to be awaited.

### Limb Loss

This leads the *gemara* to cite a *baraita* cataloguing the dispute among *tannaim* on precisely this question: when a master destroys one of the slave's limbs, does the slave need a *get shichrur* to effect his freedom, or does he go free automatically?

### Freedom Opinions

Rabbi Yishmael holds that in all such cases the slave goes free but requires a *get shichrur* from his master. Rabbi Meir holds he does not require one — freedom is automatic. Rabbi Eliezer says he does require one; Rabbi Tarfon says he does not; Rabbi Akiva says he does.

The *baraita* records that those who weighed the opinions before the sages (*ha-machri'in lifnei chachamim*) — Rashi notes he is uncertain of the precise referent — reached a compromise: *nir'im divrei Rabbi Tarfon be-shein va-ayin* — for tooth and eye, Rabbi Tarfon's position is compelling: the slave goes free without a *get shichrur*, since the Torah explicitly mandates his freedom in those cases. *Ve-divrei Rabbi Akiva bi-she'ar eivarim* — for other limbs, Rabbi Akiva's view is correct: a *get shichrur* is required, since the slave's freedom in those cases derives from rabbinic enactment (*knas chachamim*) rather than a direct biblical mandate.

The *gemara* objects: if it is *knas chachamim*, why call it a *knas*? It is derived from *pesukim*! The response: *ela eima ho'il u-midrash chachamim hu* — since it is known only through rabbinic *midrash* and not explicitly stated in the Torah, there is concern that the master might later find the slave in the marketplace and declare "you are still my slave — no limb-related freedom applies to you," since it is not as universally recognized as the explicit cases of tooth and eye. Tosafot (*Rabbeinu Tam*) makes the reasoning explicit: for tooth and eye, where the Torah states it openly, no one can plausibly deny it, and the slave needs no document for evidentiary protection; for other limbs, derived only by inference, the slave may be vulnerable to a master's bad-faith denial, and a *get shichrur* serves as his protective evidence.

### Unresolved Status

The *gemara* cannot complete its proof regarding the *mechusar get shichrur* because the tooth-and-eye case is disputed: according to several *tannaim*, that slave requires no *get shichrur* at all and goes free immediately, making the subsequent injury a case of injuring a free person entirely — not a case of *mechusar get shichrur*.

The fundamental question — whether a slave who is no longer the master's property but is still awaiting a *get shichrur* retains enough connection to the master for the master to collect *knas*, or *chavala*, on his behalf — remains *teku*, unresolved. The *gemara* leaves open what formal residue of master-status persists during that intermediate period and which monetary consequences, if any, attach to it. As the *gemara* closes the daf, the question of whether it is the *knas* (a fixed fine, perhaps more plausibly tied to formal status) or the *chavala* payment (a monetary loss that follows actual ownership) that the master might claim is left for further analysis.

---

---

# Gittin 43

## Half-Slave Monetary Stat…

### Half-Slave Intro

Today's *daf* is 43. We pick up in the middle of the bottom of 42b, dealing with the fascinating phenomenon of an *eved* who occupies a middle status: half-free and half-owned by his master. The practical arrangement was that he works for his master half the time and for himself the other half. Yet his personal status creates intractable problems — he cannot marry a free woman nor a slave woman. Beyond the realm of *issur*, monetary questions arise as well: what happens if he is gored?

### Permanent vs. Temporary

The *Gemara* on the previous *daf* established a distinction based on the nature of the damage. If the injury is permanent — his arm is severed, or he is killed — he is treated as being owned by both parties, and the award is split between himself (or his heirs, a point we will return to) and his master. If the damage is temporary — his arm swells and he cannot work for a period — and if that temporary incapacitation is classified as a form of injury rather than merely lost labor, then since the ox that caused it is not liable for lost labor, the payment goes to whichever party "owns" him on the day the goring occurred.

### Me'ukav Get Shichrur

A second scenario concerns a slave awaiting a writ of freedom — a *me'ukav get shichrur*. Two sub-cases arise. First, the slave who is half-owned: following the ruling of *Beis Shammai*, the master is compelled to free him. Second, and perhaps the cleaner case for isolating the conceptual issue: the master renounced ownership — *mafkir* him — or sold him to *Chutz La'aretz*, thereby incurring an obligation to free him. In these situations, monetary ownership has already dissolved; only the personal status of *eved* persists.

The *Gemara* raises whether even in this state the master can still collect *knas* — the fixed penalty paid when a slave is gored and killed. The *knas* of thirty *shekalim* need not be understood as compensation for the loss of property; it is a fixed punishment imposed on the negligent ox-owner, and conceivably it could still flow to the former master even absent ongoing property ownership. What is striking is that the *Gemara* entertains the further possibility that even personal-injury payments might still reach the master, despite the fact that he no longer owns the slave as property. That is genuinely difficult to understand, since any such payment would ordinarily be grounded in a proprietary relationship that has already lapsed.

---

## Terumah Eligibility

### Can He Eat Terumah?

The discussion now shifts from monetary matters to questions of status, beginning approximately twenty lines from the bottom of the *amud*, at the line opening with the words *u-midrash Chachamim hu*. The *Gemara* poses the question: a *me'ukav get shichrur* — a slave who no longer has any monetary ownership over him but is still awaiting his writ of freedom — may he eat *terumah* if his master is a *kohen*?

The *Gemara* frames the tension around the verse. The *pasuk* identifies the basis for a slave eating *terumah* as *kinyan kaspo* — he is the monetary acquisition of his master. Yet this slave is *lav kinyan kaspo* — he is no longer property in any meaningful sense. On the other hand, perhaps *terumah* is fundamentally about belonging to the household, a relational rather than strictly proprietary status, and perhaps that relationship persists. Yet the *Gemara* does not frame the question in those terms. The emphasis falls squarely on the *pasuk's* insistence on *kinyan kaspo*, and the question is whether that language can still apply to someone who is no longer owned.

### Mixed Babies Case

The *Gemara* offers a *ta shema* from a ruling of Rav Mesharshiya: a *kohenes* whose infant became mixed up with the infant of her *shifcha* — one of the babies is the master's heir and one is the slave, but no one knows which is which. The ruling is that *harei elu ochlin b'terumah* — both may eat *terumah* — because *terumah* may be eaten either as a *kohen* or as the slave of a *kohen*, and each child qualifies under one of those categories, even if the identities are uncertain. Furthermore, when they go to collect *terumah* at the threshing floor, they receive only one portion together — and the reason is that a slave may not collect *terumah* alone at the threshing floor, lest people mistake him for a *kohen*. He must therefore go together with his master. In this confused situation the two children must appear together.

### Babies Grow & Free

When the mixture grows up — *higdilu hata'arovet* — the father has died and one of them now owns the estate, which means one of them owns the other, though no one knows which is which. So they free one another: *meshachrerin zeh et zeh*. Each writes the other a *shtar shichrur* — if you are the slave, I am freeing you; if I am the slave, you are freeing me. The *Gemara* identifies this as a case of *me'ukav get shichrur* that eats *terumah*.

### Status Comparison

The *Gemara* immediately rejects the comparison, however: *hachi ata?* — is that really a parallel? *Hatam*, there, if *Eliyahu* would come and identify which child is the slave, we would say *kinyan kaspo karinan bei* — we still call him property in the full sense, because in reality one of them fully is. There is simply an unresolved *safek*. The reality beneath the uncertainty is intact. *Hacha*, here, by contrast, the *me'ukav get shichrur* is *lav kinyan kaspo hu kelal* — not owned as property at all. There is no underlying reality of ownership; only the procedural barrier of the missing *shtar shichrur* remains. The phrase *lav kinyan kaspo hu kelal* suggests the logic would point toward this person *not* eating *terumah* if the *pasuk* requires genuine property status. Yet the *Gemara* leaves the question unresolved.

---

## Selling for Knas

### Can Sell for Knas?

The *Gemara* now poses a fresh *iba'ya lehu*: can a master sell his slave specifically for the purpose of the buyer collecting future *knas*? Normally, when a slave is gored and killed, the owner collects the *knas*. The question is whether the owner can in effect sell off that future entitlement — you pay me something now, and if he is ever gored, you collect the *knas*, not me. This is analogous to a case in *Bava Metzia* regarding an object that is burgled: can the owner sell to a third party the right to collect *kefel*, the double payment, if the object is stolen? Or must the collector of *kefel* actually be the owner? Here the question is whether one can carve off this particular financial right and transfer it separately.

### Rabbi Meir Position

The *Gemara* frames the question as one that may be asked both according to Rabbi Meir and according to the *Rabbanan*, with different force in each direction. Even for Rabbi Meir, who holds that a person may sell *davar shelo ba le'olam* — something that does not yet exist in the world — one might argue that the *knas* cannot be sold. When Rabbi Meir permits selling future items, the paradigm case is buying the future dates of a palm tree: the fruit will naturally come into being, it is a predictable natural outcome. *Aval hacha mi yemar demingach* — but here, who says the slave will even be gored? It is not a natural eventuality arising from the slave himself. And further: *mi yemar demishalem* — even if the slave is gored, who says the tortfeasor will actually pay? If the person who was negligent admits to it, he is exempt from *knas* — *modeh umiptar*. The potential liability is therefore doubly speculative: the goring may never happen, and even if it does, admission forecloses payment.

### Rabbanan Position

Conversely, even for the *Rabbanan*, who generally hold that one cannot sell *davar shelo ba le'olam*, there may be grounds to permit this transaction. *Ad kan lo ka'amri Rabbanan hatam ein adam makneh davar shelo ba la'olam* — when did they say you cannot sell something that does not yet exist? In a case like *peires dekla* — selling the fruit of the palm tree — the fruit does not yet physically exist and one is attempting to transfer the fruit itself. *Aval hacha, ha kai shor ha kai eved* — here, however, the slave is present and the ox is present. As *Tosafot* explains, this is structurally different: everyone agrees that I can sell you ownership in the tree for the purpose of its fruit. I am giving you something concrete now — a present ownership — even though the fruit has not yet grown. So too here: perhaps I am not selling you a future right; I am selling you the slave himself for this purpose, and that constitutes a present transaction in a concrete object. Perhaps that works even for the *Rabbanan*. On the other hand, *knas* for goring is not a natural outgrowth of owning a slave the way fruit is a natural outgrowth of owning a tree. The *knas* arises from a tortious event inflicted by an outside party; it is a peculiar and unnatural basis for an ownership transfer. The question remains unresolved on both sides.

### Zero Value Evidence

Rabbi Abba then introduces a *ta shema* from an exegetical discussion of the *pasuk* about *terumah*, citing the phrase *v'yelid beiso hem yochlu belachmo*. The *Gemara* asks: why does the *pasuk* need to mention both *kinyan kesef* and *yelid bayis* — a slave purchased with money and one born into the household? If one who is purchased may eat *terumah*, surely one born into the house may eat all the more so. The answer is that if we had only the phrase *kinyan kesef*, we might have inferred: only a slave who currently has monetary value — *shaveh kesef* — may eat *terumah*, since the *pasuk* emphasizes the monetary dimension of the acquisition. The *yelid bayis* verse teaches that even a slave born into the household may eat regardless of whether he has present monetary value. But then one might argue the reverse: a *yelid bayis* eats *terumah* whether or not he has value, but a *kinyan kesef* — a purchased slave — perhaps requires present monetary value, and if after purchase he becomes worthless due to illness or disability, he may no longer eat *terumah*. Therefore the *pasuk* places *kinyan kaspo* and *yelid beiso* side by side to teach: just as one born into the house eats *terumah* even with no monetary value, so too one purchased eats *terumah* even with no monetary value — *af al pi she'eino shaveh klum ochel*.

The point for our purposes is that there exists a slave with zero monetary value who nonetheless eats *terumah*.

### Zero Value Objection

Now the *Gemara* asks: *v'i salka daiteich eved she'machro rabbo l'knas machur* — if one could sell a slave solely for the purpose of *knas*, then how could any slave ever have zero monetary value? A slave with no value — one whose upkeep exceeds his productivity, or one whom no one wishes to take into their household — could always be sold for at least a *perutah*, because someone would be willing to pay a small amount on the chance of eventually collecting thirty *shekalim* in *knas*. The logic resembles a lottery: the purchaser takes possession not in the ordinary sense but only for the *knas*, and pays a *perutah* for the possibility of collecting a substantial sum. Since someone would always take that wager, no slave could ever be worth less than a *perutah*, and the *Gemara's* premise of a slave with zero monetary value would be impossible.

This generates a productive discussion. One might ask: why would the owner sell for a *perutah* if the potential upside is entirely his? The answer is that the owner, doing the expected-value calculation, may conclude the risk is too small to bother holding — while a poorer party may rationally pay a *perutah* for the lottery-like chance at thirty *shekalim*. Conversely, if the arrangement allows the buyer to take the *knas* risk without actually taking the slave into his household — leaving all the upkeep obligations with the original owner — then the buyer has essentially pure upside, and the owner might prefer that arrangement. The *Gemara's* logic therefore stands: if such a sale is valid, the slave would always have at least minimal market value, and the case of *eino shaveh klum* would be impossible.

### Unfit Slave Exception

The *Gemara* responds: *in, ika avda treifa* — yes, there is a slave who is a *treifa*, one who has received an internal fatal injury. A *treifa* is halachically not considered fully *chai*, and accordingly, the *knas* for killing a *treifa* slave would not apply. Such a slave could not be sold for even a *perutah* on the basis of *knas*, since no *knas* would ever be owed. But the *Gemara* presses further: even a *treifa* slave can stand at your side and serve you — *chazi lemeikom kamei* — so how can any slave have zero value? The *Gemara* concludes with the limiting case: *bimnuval umukeh shechin* — a slave who is both a *treifa* and physically repulsive, afflicted with a skin disease so severe that no one wishes to be in his presence. In such a case he truly has zero value, no *knas* can ever be collected for him, and the *Gemara's* premise holds.

---

## Kiddushin Half-Status

### Half-Slave Man Marriage

The *Gemara* returns to the half-slave, half-free status — *mi shechetzyo eved v'chetzyo ben chorin* — presenting what is perhaps the most fascinating cluster of questions. Can such a man validly perform *kiddushin* with a free woman? The *eved* half of him is legally incapable of marrying a free woman, but is the marriage binding to the extent of his free half?

### Half Woman Marriage

Before resolving the question about the half-slave man, the *Gemara* introduces two analogous cases involving free persons. First: *ben Yisrael she'amar l'vas chorin hitkadshi bechetzi* — a fully free man who says to a free woman, "be married to half of me." The *Gemara* indicates this is *mekudeshes* — it works. The reason is that *kiddushin* restricts the woman, not the man. In a halachic framework that permits polygamy, marriage creates exclusivity for the woman but not for the man, and so the man being "half married" is coherent: his other half could theoretically be married to another woman. The woman is fully restricted by the relationship; the man speaking in halves is merely describing a social reality, not performing a defective act.

By contrast, if a man says to a free woman "half of you is married to me," that does not work — *einah mekudeshes* — because for the woman, marriage is fully exclusive. The half of her that is not married to this man could not be married to another man; therefore the category of "half a woman married" is incoherent.

Now the question is pressed in the more complex case. *Im timtzei lomar* — if the rule is that a free man marrying half a woman does not work because *shiyyer b'kinyano* — he held back, he performed only a half-act — perhaps the half-slave man who says to a free woman "I marry you" presents a different case. He did not hold anything back — *lo shiyyer b'kinyano*. He performed a full act; it simply could only take half-effect, because half of him is a slave. Does that make a difference?

On the other hand, one might argue: *dechazi lekulei* — in the case of the free man saying "half of me," the woman is in fact fully married to him, since his whole status is that of a free person who could potentially marry her entirely. The "half" is a manner of speaking. *Ha lo chazi lekulei* — here, by contrast, half of this man is fundamentally incapable of being married to her. Perhaps one cannot conceive of her being married to the free portion of him, *shebo*, and therefore the *kiddushin* is not binding.

### Full vs. Half Act

The distinction the *Gemara* is working toward is between two types of partial *kiddushin*. In the case where a man says "half of you is married to me," the act itself is defective — he performed a half-act, he held back. In the case of the half-slave man marrying a free woman, the act is complete and unqualified; the limitation is not in the act but in his status. Similarly, when a man says "half of me is married to you," he may be performing a full act that takes full effect, with the "half" being descriptive rather than constitutive of the act. These structural differences motivate the subsequent rulings regarding the half-slave woman.

### Half-Woman Evidence

The discussion of the half-slave woman proceeds as follows. רבא *Rava* states: *kesheim she-hamkadesh chatzi isha einah mekudeshes — kach chatzi shifcha v'chatzi bas chorin she-nitkadesha ein kiddusheha kiddushin*. Just as marrying half a woman produces no valid *kiddushin*, so too the *kiddushin* of a half-slave woman is not binding. Rabba bar Rav Huna subsequently delivers the same ruling publicly. Rav Chisda challenges him: *mi dami?* How can you compare? *Hasam shiyyer b'kinyano* — there, by marrying half a woman, the man held back and did not do a full act. *Hacha lo shiyyer b'kinyano* — here, in marrying the half-slave woman, the man held nothing back; he married her fully, as fully as he was able to. Rav Chisda implies this distinction should lead to the *kiddushin* being valid.

Rabba bar Rav Huna thereupon reversed his position entirely. He convened a public lecture and acknowledged the correction, prefacing his revised ruling with the famous dictum: *ein adam omed al divrei Torah ela im kein nichshal bahen* — a person does not truly come to stand on his Torah unless he has first stumbled in it. Having publicly erred and retracted, the lesson is genuinely internalized.

He then ruled: even though a free man marrying half a woman produces no *kiddushin*, by a half-slave half-free woman the *kiddushin* does take effect. *Hasam shiyyer b'kinyano, hacha lo shiyyer b'kinyano* — there he held back and performed a half-act; here he performed a full act that took half-effect. Since the act was complete and unqualified, it takes effect to whatever degree it can, and the half of her that is free is *mekudeshes*.

Rav Sheshet, however, did not accept this revision and maintained his original position: just as marrying half a woman produces no *kiddushin*, so too the half-slave half-free woman's *kiddushin* is not binding.

### Half-Woman Evidence

In response to Rav Sheshet's position, an interlocutor raises the case of *shifcha charufa* from the *Torah*: the passage describes a woman who is half-slave, half-free, designated to an *eved Ivri*, and refers to her as *me'ureset l'eved Ivri* — betrothed to a Hebrew slave. Does this not demonstrate that *kiddushin* is binding with a half-slave woman?

### Rabbi Yishmael View

Rav Sheshet replies: go and see what Rabbi Yishmael says. Rabbi Yishmael holds that the *Torah's* case of *shifcha charufa* is not about a half-slave woman at all — it is about a fully enslaved *shifcha Kena'anit*, one hundred percent a slave. And yet the *Torah* uses the term *me'ureset l'eved Ivri*. Now, a fully enslaved Canaanite woman is *not bat ishut* — she is legally incapable of *kiddushin* — so what does *me'ureset* mean in that context? *Meyushedet* — she has been designated to him, she is living with him in a recognized domestic arrangement, but there is no legally binding *kiddushin*. The master has assigned her to the *eved Ivri* to cohabit and produce slave-children; the word *me'ureset* denotes designation and cohabitation, not formal marriage.

Therefore, Rav Sheshet argues, the *Torah's* use of *me'ureset* proves nothing about whether *kiddushin* is valid for a half-slave woman. Even if the *Torah's* case involves a half-slave woman, the term means only *meyushedet* — designated — not *mekudeshes* in the legally binding sense.

### Heirs Contradiction

The *Gemara* had earlier cited a ruling about an ox that kills a *mi shechetzyo eved v'chetzyo ben chorin*: the payment is split — half *knas* to the master and half *kofer* to *yorshav*, his heirs. The difficulty is immediately apparent: *v'i amart kiddushav lav kiddushin — yorshin mena lei?* If the *kiddushin* of a half-slave is invalid, how does he have heirs?

Rav Adda bar Ahava proposes: *keshe'asa'o treifah* — the ox did not actually kill him; it merely rendered him a *treifah*, delivered a fatal internal injury but did not cause immediate death. Since he is still alive — Monty Python's "I'm not dead yet" — he collects himself; *nafshei*, he is his own heir. *Rava* objects with two responses: first, the text says *yorshav* — his heirs — not him; second, *kofer* by definition is only paid after death — *kofer ein mishtalem ela le'acher mitah*, as Reish Lakish rules — it is an atonement payment for a death, not for a wound, even a fatal one.

*Rava* therefore offers an alternative: *ra'uy liten v'ein lo* — those heirs should receive the *kofer* payment, but since in fact there are no heirs, that half of the *kofer* goes uncollected. No one receives it.

*Tosafot* notes a subtle point: why does the *Gemara* frame the question of heirs as dependent on *kiddushin* at all? Even illegitimate children — even a *mamzer* — are their father's heirs. One does not need *kiddushin* to have heirs. *Tosafot* explains that the issue is not legitimacy but the recognition of family structure. The principle *eved ein lo chiyus* — a slave has no legally recognized family — means that a slave's biological children are not halachically recognized as his children. It is analogous to the secular legal concept of a bastard child: biology alone was insufficient to establish legal parenthood; formal recognition was required. In *halacha*, a child born out of wedlock is legally recognized, but a slave's children are not. This applies even if the slave has children with a free woman — the *halacha* refuses to recognize the family structure of a slave, and the children are legally his master's slaves, not his heirs.

*Tosafot* therefore argues: the relevance of *kiddushin* here is that valid *kiddushin* is an affirmation that family structure is recognized for this person. If we say that the half-slave man is capable of *kiddushin*, we are simultaneously affirming that his family structure is legally cognizable — and therefore that children resulting from such a union would be legally recognized as his heirs. The question of heirs is thus not a question of legitimacy but of status-recognition.

---

## Kiddushin After Freedom

### Scenario Setup

Rav Chisda now introduces the further scenario: *chatziya shifcha v'chatziya bas chorin she-nitkadsha l'Reuven* — a half-slave half-free woman who was married to Reuven, and then *v'nishtachrerah* — the remaining half of her was freed — and *v'chazra v'nitkadsha l'Shimon* — she then went ahead and performed *kiddushin* with Shimon. She is now somehow half-married to Reuven and half-married to Shimon. Neither man could fully consummate the marriage while the other remained. Then both Reuven and Shimon died, and they happened to be brothers. Now Levi, their brother, has an obligation of *yibum*. And Rav Chisda says: *v'eini korei bah eishes shnei meisim* — I do not read about her as "the wife of two dead men," which would have been an obstacle to *yibum*. The *Gemara* in *Yevamos* establishes that a widow who comes to a surviving brother from two dead brothers — because one did *maamar* but not full *yibum*, leaving his connection to her overlapping with the first brother's — cannot perform *yibum* with the third brother. Yet here, even though she was seemingly half-married to two men, Levi can do *yibum*.

### Nullify or Complete?

The reason is that this situation cannot be characterized as her being half-married to both. When she was freed, one of two things necessarily happened to the original *kiddushin* with Reuven: either it expanded and completed, making her fully Reuven's wife, in which case the subsequent *kiddushin* with Shimon was entirely ineffective — or it dissolved entirely, making her fully available for Shimon's *kiddushin*, in which case the connection to Reuven is wholly gone. She is therefore either entirely Reuven's wife or entirely Shimon's wife. *Iy kiddushei d'Reuven kiddushei — kiddushei d'Shimon lav kiddushei; v'kiddushei d'Shimon kiddushei — kiddushei d'Reuven lav kiddushei.* She cannot be simultaneously half-married to each. And therefore she does not come to Levi as *eishes shnei meisim*. The question of which branch obtained remains unresolved — but either way, *yibum* with Levi is permissible.

### Kiddushin Bursts

The debate is now stated explicitly: *chatzi shifcha v'chatzi bas chorin sheniskadsha l'Reuven v'nishtachrerah v'chazra v'nitkadsha l'Shimon* — what is the law? Rav Yosef bar Chama in the name of Rav Nachman: *paku kiddushei rishon* — the original *kiddushin* burst. When she was freed, her legal identity changed so fundamentally that the half-*kiddushin* she had with Reuven dissolved. She became a new legal person, and Reuven's *kiddushin* evaporated. She is therefore fully available for Shimon's *kiddushin*.

### Kiddushin Completes

Rav Zeira in the name of Rav Nachman: *gamru kiddushei rishon* — the original *kiddushin* was completed. Once the impediment of her partial slavery was removed, there was nothing holding back the *kiddushin* from taking full effect. The half-*kiddushin* expanded to cover her entirely, and she is fully Reuven's wife. Shimon's subsequent *kiddushin* was therefore meaningless.

### Shifcha Charufa Text

Rav Zeira adds: *kavasi didi mistabra* — it makes sense like my position. The proof is from the *pasuk* of *shifcha charufa*: *lo yumsu ki lo chufasha* — they will not be put to death because she has not yet been freed. The *Gemara* reads this as a case of a half-slave half-free woman who is half-married to a man; another man sleeps with her and the *Torah* says it is not a capital crime because it is not fully adultery — she is only half-married, because she has not yet been freed. *Ha chufasha — yumsu*: had she been freed, they would be put to death, meaning had that other half of her been freed, the original half-*kiddushin* would have become full *kiddushin*, and adultery with her would have been a capital crime. This supports the view of *gamru kiddushei rishon*: freedom causes the original *kiddushin* to complete itself.

### Abaye Challenge

Abaye challenges Rav Zeira: *u'letana d'vei Rabbi Yishmael d'amar b'shifcha Kena'anit hame'ureset l'eved Ivri* — what does this *pasuk* say according to Rabbi Yishmael? Rabbi Yishmael holds that the woman in the *pasuk* is a fully enslaved *shifcha Kena'anit* with no valid *kiddushin* at all, only *eirusin* in the sense of designation and cohabitation. According to Rabbi Yishmael, then, how does the *pasuk* support *gamru kiddushei rishon*? There was no *kiddushin* to complete! Rav Zeira's reading of the *pasuk* collapses.

Abaye explains how Rabbi Yishmael reads the *pasuk*: *she'chufasha v'chazra v'nitkadsha* — had she been freed and then performed a new *kiddushin*, and then someone committed adultery with her, only then would it be a capital crime. The *pasuk* does not say that freedom automatically completes an existing *kiddushin*; it says that freedom followed by a new *kiddushin* would create a fully binding marriage. Therefore the *pasuk* cannot serve as evidence for *gamru kiddushei rishon* — it is equally compatible with *paku kiddushei rishon*, where freedom dissolves the original *kiddushin* and necessitates a fresh one. The question is left unresolved.

---

## Historical Precedent

### Forced Freedom

Rav Huna bar Chinena in the name of Rav Yitzchak reports: *maaseh b'shifcha she'chetziyah shifcha v'chetziyah bas chorin* — there was an actual case of a half-slave half-free woman, and *v'chafu es rabbo v'asah bas chorin* — the rabbinic authorities compelled her master to free her entirely.

### Childbearing Motive

This raises a question. Throughout our *sugya*, the case compelling the freeing of a half-slave *man* was justified by his inability to fulfill the *mitzvah* of *p'ru u'rvu* while trapped in this status. But does that reasoning apply to a woman? The *Gemara* asks: is this ruling in accordance with Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka, *d'amar al shneichem hu omer v'yevarech osam Elokim vayomer pru u'rvu* — who derives from the verse that the obligation of *p'ru u'rvu* applies to women as well? Perhaps the reason the rabbis forced the master to free this woman was specifically to allow her to fulfill that obligation by marrying and bearing children.

### Protection Motive

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, however, offers an entirely different explanation: *lo, minhag hefker nahagu bah* — that was not the reason at all. The actual motivation was that people were taking advantage of her. Because she was neither fully a slave nor fully free, her status was anomalous in both directions: she may not have been fully designated to a slave as a *shifcha* might be, and she could not be fully protected through marriage as a free woman could be. She had no man — whether master or husband — to protect her, and she was therefore being exploited. The rabbis freed her not to enable *p'ru u'rvu* but to protect her from that exploitation. The compelled manumission had nothing to do with the positive obligation of bearing children.

---

---

# Gittin 44

## Slaves: Status & Property

### Tikun olam & Slaves

The daf we take up today continues the *Gemara*'s sustained engagement with the laws governing slaves, which has emerged as a central preoccupation of the *tikun olam* enactments of *Gittin*. What makes this discussion particularly striking is the explicit and recurring comparison between the slave and the woman — a comparison that is not merely implicit but structurally built into the halacha itself. The *get shichrur*, the writ of manumission that frees a slave, is derived through a *gzera shava* of *la la* from the *get* that divorces a woman, and the level of the slave's obligation in *mitzvot* is likewise derived from this same verbal analogy.

At first glance, this parallel might seem to cast the woman in an unflattering light — as though she, like the slave, is a form of property being released. But the *Gemara* repeatedly uses the comparison to draw a careful contrast, and it is that contrast which animates much of this *sugya*.

### Issura & Mamona

The key analytical distinction is this: by a woman, there is only *issura* — a dimension of personal status. The laws governing her relationship to her husband are entirely about who she is and to whom she belongs in terms of personal, halachic standing. By the slave, however, there are two dimensions operating simultaneously: *issura*, personal status, and *mamona*, property ownership. The slave is both a person with a halachic identity and an item of property with a monetary value that can be bought, sold, pledged, and inherited.

A great deal of the *sugyot* in this chapter have explored precisely what happens when one of these two dimensions is altered without the other — when a master, for example, renounces monetary ownership (*mafkir*) of the slave without yet executing a formal act of manumission. The *Gemara* is consistent: changing the *mamona* dimension alone does not change the *issura*. The status change requires its own act, its own writ. This dual structure is what makes the slave's situation legally unique, and it is what makes the *tikun olam* concerns here far more complex than anything we encounter in the laws of divorce.

---

## Sale to Non-Jews

### Mishna: Slave Freed

The *mishna* at the opening of our discussion states: *ha-mokher avdo le-ovdei kokhavim o le-chutz la-aretz yatza ben chorin* — if someone sells his slave to a non-Jew or outside the Land of Israel, the slave goes free. The language sounds automatic: *yatza ben chorin*, he goes free, as though the sale itself operates the manumission. We will see that the *baraita* qualifies this considerably, but the broad principle is established here.

### Rationale: Mitzvot

The underlying rationale is that a slave is obligated in *mitzvot* to a degree comparable to that of a woman — again, the *la la gzera shava* at work. He is obligated in all negative commandments and in all positive commandments that are not time-bound. This partial but real level of *kedusha yisrael*, as it were, means that placing him under the dominion of a non-Jew creates a serious and ongoing violation. The non-Jew will compel him to work on *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*, will feed him food that is not *kosher*, and will in every practical sense prevent him from observing the *mitzvot* to which he is obligated.

The case of selling to *chutz la-aretz* is a lesser concern — the slave does not lose his obligation in all *mitzvot*, only in those that apply specifically in *Eretz Yisrael* — but it remains a genuine halachic problem. Notably, the comparison to the woman surfaces again here: there is an extensive halachic discussion about whether a husband can compel his wife to move to *chutz la-aretz*, and the answer is that he generally cannot force her to give up life in *Eretz Yisrael*. The parallel, though imperfect, reflects a shared underlying concern about the religious consequences of displacement.

### Jewish Presence

There is an additional dimension to the prohibition that goes beyond the individual slave's ability to observe *mitzvot*. *Chazal* were deeply invested in maintaining Jewish presence in the Land of Israel and issued broad *takanot* designed to prevent Jews living in Israel from transferring land, slaves, and cattle to non-Jews. All of these — land, animals, slaves — were understood as elements of an established, rooted presence in the land, and their transfer to non-Jewish ownership was seen as erosion of that presence. This communal concern does not displace the *mitzvot* rationale, which remains primary and most acute in the case of sale to a non-Jew, but it operates alongside it, especially in the case of sale to *chutz la-aretz*.

---

## Baraita: Writ Needed

### Get Shichrur

The *baraita* immediately clarifies that the *mishna*'s language of *yatza ben chorin* is not as automatic as it sounds: *ha-mokher avdo le-oved kokhavim yatza le-cheirus v-tzarich get shichrur me-rabo rishon* — he has gone out to freedom, but he requires a writ of manumission from his first master. The first master is the one who must act, since the non-Jew who now holds him cannot effect a change in the slave's halachic personal status. A non-Jew cannot write a *get shichrur* that alters the slave's *issura* dimension.

### Rabban Shimon

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* adds a nuance: *bameh devarim amurim ke-shelo katav alav ono* — when is this requirement for a formal writ applicable? When no document has already been written. *Aval katav alav ono zehu shichruro* — if a document has been written for him, that document itself constitutes his freedom. The question then becomes: what exactly is this *ono*, this document?

### Form of Writ

*Rav Sheshet* explains its content: the master writes to the slave before the sale the following language — *likshe-tivrach mimeni ein li esek bach* — if you ever manage to escape from the one to whom I am selling you, I make no claim upon you. Formally, this language sounds more like *hefker* — a renunciation of ownership — than like a declaration of *shichrur*, a change of personal status. And yet, when it is committed to writing and delivered to the slave as a writ, it can function as his *shtar shichrur*.

*Tosafot* raises the obvious difficulty: the writ cannot take effect at the moment of writing, because if the slave were freed at that moment, the subsequent sale to the non-Jew would be invalid — you cannot sell a free man. The document must therefore be conditional, taking effect only when the slave escapes. The phrase *likshe-tivrach mimeni* is exactly this: the freedom is triggered by the condition of escape.

### Hefker vs Shichrur

This brings us to a conceptually important distinction. *Hefker* and *shichrur* are not the same thing, even though both involve the master relinquishing his hold over the slave. *Hefker* addresses only the *mamona* dimension — the master renounces monetary ownership. But the *issura* dimension, the slave's personal status, is not altered by *hefker* alone. *Shichrur* — effected through the formal act of delivering a *shtar* — addresses the status dimension directly. What *Rav Sheshet* is telling us is that the language of the document need not explicitly say *harei atah ben chorin*; it can articulate the *mamona* dimension in the form of a renunciation, but because it is being delivered through the ritual act of *shtar* delivery, it effects the change of status as well. It is the formal act, the giving of the *shtar*, that carries the halachic weight, not merely the content of the declaration.

---

## Tosafot: Labor Only

### Non-Jew Labor Only

*Tosafot* addresses a deeper structural problem: how can the first master's writ take effect at all once the slave is under the control of the non-Jew and entirely outside the master's reach? The answer is grounded in an earlier principle established in the *Gemara*: *lo hem konin mikem* — non-Jews cannot acquire slaves from Jews in the full sense of ownership. More precisely, a non-Jew can only acquire *maasei yadayim*, the labor and work product of the slave, but cannot acquire the slave's *guf*, his body and person, as property.

### Master Owns Body

The practical consequence of this principle is far-reaching. Because the non-Jew acquires only the slave's labor and not his person, the original Jewish master retains full ownership of the slave as property — ownership of his *guf*. And since he retains that ownership, he retains the standing and the capacity to free the slave. The sale to the non-Jew transfers only one layer of the slave's dual status: the *mamona* dimension of his labor is transferred, but the *mamona* dimension of his body — and with it the *issura* dimension entirely — remains with the original master. It is precisely this retained ownership that allows the first master to write a *get shichrur* that has legal effect even after the sale has been completed.

---

## Loan & Collateral

### Nimuso Definition

The *Gemara* now moves to a related but distinct scenario governed by a new *baraita*: *laveh alav min ha-oved kokhavim* — you borrowed money from a non-Jew with your slave as collateral. The keyword here is *alav*: you borrowed specifically *against* the slave, designating him explicitly as the surety. This is crucially different from simply borrowing money and having the non-Jew later choose to collect against your slave. When you designate the slave as the collateral, you have in effect chosen to put him in harm's way, and the *Gemara* treats that as analogous to a sale.

The question the *baraita* poses is: at what point does the non-Jew's relationship with the slave rise to the level that triggers the obligation to free him? The *baraita*'s answer is: *keivan she-asah lo oved kokhavim nimuso* — once the non-Jew does for him his *nimuso*. The term *nomos*, from which *nimuso* derives, means law or custom, but what specific act or event does it describe?

### Nimuso = Seal

*Rav Huna bar Yehuda* proposes that *nimuso* refers to a *nashki* — some kind of seal, mark, or perhaps even a physical brand that the non-Jew places on the slave to indicate ownership. Once the non-Jew has marked the slave as his, the slave is considered effectively in his possession, and the obligation to free him is triggered.

### Sheshet's Objection

*Rav Sheshet* objects forcefully: the same word *nimuso* appears in the context of a field taken as collateral — *oved kokhavim she-mishkan sadeh le-Yisrael* — where a non-Jew has pledged his field to a Jew as surety for a loan. In that case as well, the *baraita* speaks of the *nimuso* occurring. But you do not place a seal on a field. A field cannot be branded or marked the way a slave can. Therefore, *nimuso* cannot mean a physical seal or mark; it must refer to something else that applies equally to slaves and to fields.

### Nimuso = Time

*Rav Sheshet* therefore redefines *nimuso* as *zman* — the time for repayment has arrived. When the loan comes due and the borrower has not repaid, the non-Jew is now legally positioned to take possession of the collateral. In the slave's case, this means the non-Jew can now claim the slave, and at that moment the obligation to free the slave is triggered. In the field case, the parallel language in the *baraita* refers to the same *zman* arriving — the time for collection — which is why the same term is used for both.

---

## Body vs Field

### Difficulty Posed

This resolution, however, generates a new difficulty. If *nimuso* means the *zman* has arrived in both cases, why does the arrival of the *zman* trigger the obligation to free the slave but not create an obligation regarding the field? The *Gemara* formulates this as *kashya zman a-zman*: the same moment in time is being described, yet the legal consequences differ. The *Gemara* proposes that perhaps in the slave case we are speaking of a moment when the *zman* has arrived, while in the field case the *zman* has not yet arrived — but this reading forces the same word to describe opposite temporal states in the same *baraita*, which is unsatisfying, and the *Gemara* rejects it.

### Tosafot: Slave In House

*Tosafot* offers the more coherent resolution. In both cases, the *zman* has not yet arrived — meaning the loan is not yet due. But the two situations differ structurally. When a slave is designated as collateral, the non-Jew typically takes physical possession of the slave before the loan comes due. The slave is already in the non-Jew's house, already under his daily control, already being forced to work on *Shabbat* and eat *treif* and violate *halacha* in every practical dimension of his life. The *guf* of the slave — his body, his person — has already been taken into the non-Jew's possession, even though the *zman* for formal collection has not yet arrived.

### Field: Fruit Only

By contrast, a field never moves. When a Jew holds a non-Jew's field as collateral, the Jew may be present on the field, farming it, enjoying its produce — its *peira* — but the *karka* itself, the land, remains exactly where it is. We say the Jew has possession only of the *peira*, the fruit, not of the *guf*, the body, of the field. Since the field itself has not been transferred into anyone's physical possession, there is no parallel to the slave situation.

### Conclusion

The operative distinction, then, is whether the *guf* has been physically transferred into the non-Jew's domain. Once the slave is living in the non-Jew's house and being subjected daily to violations of *halacha*, the obligation to free him is triggered — regardless of whether the formal *zman* of the loan has arrived. The ongoing nature of the violation, the daily compelled breach of *mitzvot*, is what creates the urgency and triggers the *takana*.

---

## Seizure vs Forced Sale

### Debt Seizure

A further *baraita* introduces two new scenarios that test the boundaries of when the master's choice is implicated. The first: *gevaho be-chovo* — if the non-Jew seized the slave as payment of a general debt, without the master having specifically designated the slave as collateral. In this case, *lo yatza le-cheirut* — the slave does not go free, and the master is not required to redeem and free him. The non-Jew chose to collect against the slave on his own initiative; the master did not choose to expose the slave to non-Jewish ownership. The *Gemara* reinforces this by comparing it to the case of grain seized from a threshing floor for taxes: if the seizure was in payment of a legitimate debt (*bechovo*), the owner has effectively benefited because his debt was discharged, making it akin to a voluntary transaction. But in that case *chamishtershi lei* — the benefit flowed to the owner — whereas in the slave case, even if the debt was discharged, the master did not specifically choose to submit the slave to non-Jewish possession, so we do not impute that choice to him.

The *Gemara* also notes the case of *sikrikon* — a strongman who forces the sale — in which the slave likewise does not go free, because the master was coerced without any meaningful choice or opportunity for alternatives.

### Forced Sale

The second scenario: *parhang* — a term understood, following *Rashi*, as a kind of strongman or blackmailer, and according to *Tosafot* a Persian term for someone who forces a sale but does pay for the slave. If someone forces you to sell your slave to him, the *Gemara* rules that *yatza le-cheirut* — the slave does go free. This is at first glance surprising: you were forced, so why are you held responsible?

### Responsibility

The *Gemara* answers: *havah lei le-fayusei ve-lo piyes* — you had the option of appeasing the person, of offering him alternative property, of paying him off or negotiating your way out of the situation. The assumption built into the ruling is that you were not entirely without options, and your failure to pursue those options makes you, at least partially, the agent of the slave's transfer into non-Jewish hands. Because you could have prevented it and did not, you are treated as though you chose it.

### No Liability

The contrast is clear: where the seizure was entirely beyond the master's control — through sheer military force or the like, where no negotiation or substitution was possible — the master is not held liable, and the obligation to redeem and free the slave does not arise. The threshold is meaningful choice and meaningful opportunity to act otherwise. When that opportunity existed and was not used, the master bears responsibility.

---

## Conditional Scenarios

### Thirty-Day Sale

*Rabbi Yirmiyah* poses a series of penetrating questions about cases that fall at the edges of these categories. The first: *machro li-shloshim yom mahu* — what if you sold the slave to a non-Jew for only thirty days, with the understanding that the slave returns to you afterward? The slave will be compelled to violate *halacha* for thirty days, but it is not a permanent sale. Are you required, when the slave returns at the end of the thirty days, to then free him? The *Gemara* attempts to resolve this from the case of the *parhang*, reasoning that in that scenario the non-Jew presumably intends eventually to resell the slave. But the *Gemara* rejects this inference because the *parhang* case involves a sale with no anticipated return (*she-eino chozer*), which is not comparable to an explicitly time-limited transaction. The question therefore remains unresolved.

### No Work Clause

A second question: *chutz mi-melachto mahu* — what if you sell the slave to a non-Jew on the explicit condition that the non-Jew does not put him to work? *Rashi* explains the realistic context: the non-Jew might want the slave not for labor but to have him breed with the non-Jew's own female slave, producing additional slaves. In such a case, the slave might not be compelled to violate *Shabbat* through labor. Does the condition change the master's obligation?

### Mitzvot Clause

A third question: *chutz min ha-mitzvos mahu* — what if you sell the slave on the explicit condition that he is permitted to observe his religious obligations? Or more specifically, *chutz mi-Shabbasos ve-yamim tovim* — on the condition that he is given *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* off? If all of this is written into the contract, does that now exempt the master from the obligation to redeem and free him?

### Mixed Status

*Rabbi Yirmiyah* then extends the inquiry to questions of the buyer's identity: *le-ger toshav o le-Yisrael mumar mahu* — what if the sale is to a *ger toshav*, a non-Jew living in the Land of Israel who observes the *sheva mitzvos b-nei Noach*, or to a *Yisrael mumar*, a Jew who is formally Jewish but entirely non-observant? And *le-Kuti mahu* — what about a Samaritan, whose status as Jew or non-Jew is itself debated?

These questions cut to the heart of a broader jurisprudential tension: do we apply formal categories — Jew versus non-Jew — regardless of the contextual reality of whether the slave will actually be able to observe *halacha*? Or do we take into account the practical circumstances? A *ger toshav* might in practice respect the slave's religious life far more than a non-observant Jew would. Does that practical reality count?

### Status Determinations

The *Gemara* partially resolves one of these questions: *ger toshav harei hu ke-oved kokhavim* — a *ger toshav* is treated like a non-Jew for our purposes. His observance of the Noachide laws does not give him the status of a Jew, and the formal rule applies. As for *Kuti ve-Yisrael mumar*, the *Gemara* records a dispute: *amri lei ke-ovdei kokhavim ve-amri lei ke-Yisrael* — some say they are treated like non-Jews, some say like Jews. That debate remains unresolved, as do the questions about the conditional sales and the clauses regarding *Shabbat* observance. The *Gemara* leaves *Rabbi Yirmiyah*'s questions as *teiku* — unresolved — reflecting the genuine difficulty of adjudicating between formal status and contextual reality.

---

## Accepting Compensation

### Money Instead

The *Gemara* now takes up a practical scenario of a different kind. A non-Jew has taken your slave without your consent — through force or coercion — and while you cannot recover the slave himself, the non-Jew offers you money in compensation. May you accept it? On the surface, accepting money might seem tantamount to ratifying the sale and abandoning your obligation to redeem and free the slave. But if recovery is genuinely impossible, is it permitted to at least salvage the monetary value?

### Investigation

*Rabbi Yirmiyah* instructs *Rabbi Zerika* to investigate the *tannaic* sources — his *michilta*, his collections of teachings — because *Rabbi Ami* has been asked this question and needs the relevant source material to render a ruling.

### House Analogy

*Rabbi Zerika* finds the following *baraita*: if someone sells his house to a non-Jew — which is itself prohibited, both because of the biblical *lo techonem* prohibition against giving non-Jews a foothold in the land and because of the broader rabbinic *takanot* about maintaining Jewish presence in *Eretz Yisrael* — the proceeds of such a sale are forbidden as *issur hana'ah*. However, if a non-Jew forcibly seized the house and *ein ba-alav yakhol le-hotzio lo be-dinei Yisrael ve-lo be-dinei ovdei kokhavim* — the owner cannot recover it through any legal means, neither in Jewish courts nor in non-Jewish courts — then *mutar litol dameihah*, the owner may collect monetary compensation. Furthermore, *ve-chotev u-ma'aleh be-arka'ot shelahem*, he may even register the transaction in non-Jewish civil courts to ensure the money is legally enforceable — because *mipnei she-hu ke-matzil mi-yadam*, this is considered salvaging what remains from their hands, not voluntarily selling to them.

### Slippery Slope

The *Gemara* raises the question of whether this precedent from the house can be applied to the slave. Perhaps they are not comparable. With regard to a house, people do not typically sell their homes freely; the loss of a house is a severe and unusual circumstance, and therefore permitting the monetary collection after the fact will not create a *slippery slope* toward people engineering such situations in order to profit. But a slave is more expendable — *sagi lei be-lo eved* — people can live without a slave, and if we allow the owner to simply collect money and walk away, it might encourage masters to arrange such forced seizures deliberately.

### Rabbi Ami Rules

Nevertheless, *Rabbi Ami* concludes that the house precedent is sufficiently analogous and issues a formal ruling — framed with the weight of a public proclamation, *mini Ami bar Natan Torah yotza le-khol Yisrael* — that from him the following teaching goes out to all of Israel: a slave who has fallen into the hands of soldiers (*geisot*), and whose master cannot recover him through any legal means, whether in Jewish courts or in non-Jewish courts — *mutar litol dameihav ve-chotev u-ma'aleh be-arka'ot shel ovdei kokhavim mipnei she-hu ke-matzil mi-yadam* — the master may collect the compensation and may register the arrangement in non-Jewish civil courts, because this is simply salvaging what can be salvaged. The formal prohibition on selling to non-Jews is not violated when the transaction is already a fait accompli that cannot be undone.

---

## Redemption Penalty

### Price Multiple

*Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* now introduces the mechanism by which the entire rabbinic system discourages the sale of slaves to non-Jews in the first place: *ha-mokher avdo le-ovdei kokhavim kohnsin oto ad me'ah be-dameihav* — if you sell your slave to a non-Jew, the court compels you to buy him back at up to one hundred times his value. The obligation to free the slave is not merely moral; it is backed by an extraordinary financial penalty designed to make the transgression so costly that no rational master would undertake it. Whether this penalty was ever successfully enforced in practice is a separate question, but as a statement of halachic principle it is remarkable.

### Precise or Approximate

The *Gemara* immediately asks whether the figure of one hundred is *davka* — a precise upper limit — or merely an approximation, an expression of "a very great multiple."

### Animal Comparison

*Reish Lakish* provides a parallel ruling: *ha-mokher behemah gasah le-ovdei kokhavim kohnsin oto ad asarah be-dameihah* — if you sell a large animal to a non-Jew, which is similarly prohibited (the *Gemara* in *Avodah Zarah* explains this is because animals can be worked on *Shabbat*, and there are also considerations of maintaining Jewish presence in the land), you are fined up to ten times the animal's value. Since the slave *baraita* says one hundred and the animal *baraita* says ten, these cannot both be approximations meaning the same thing. The numbers must be *davka*, and they differ.

### Slave vs Animal

The *Gemara* then wrestles with the direction of the reasoning. One version of *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi*'s statement has the slave at ten times and the animal at one hundred times — the mirror image of the other version. The *Gemara* considers whether the slave's penalty might be lower because the slave eventually must be freed rather than returned (*de-lo hadar lei*), meaning the master recovers nothing at the end of the redemption. But this reasoning is immediately questioned: if the animal *is* returned to the master upon redemption, why must the master pay up to one hundred times its value just to get it back? That seems disproportionate to the single unit of value gained from the return.

The *Gemara* ultimately resolves the matter differently: *eved milta de-lo shechicha* — selling a slave to a non-Jew is a rare transgression. *U-milta de-lo shechicha lo gazru bah Rabbanan* — the rabbis do not need to impose an extremely heavy fine on something that rarely occurs. Hence the slave's fine is ten times. The animal is one hundred times precisely because animal sales to non-Jews were more common and required a more powerful deterrent.

---

## Heir Liability

### Question Posed

*Rabbi Yirmiyah* poses the final major question of the *sugya* to *Rabbi Assi*: *machar avdo u-met mahu she-yiknasu et b-no acharav* — if a master sold his slave to a non-Jew and then died, are his sons obligated to buy the slave back — at the inflated price — and free him? Or does the penalty die with the transgressor?

### Tension

The question pulls in two directions. On the one hand, the rabbinic fine is a form of monetary punishment directed at the person who violated the prohibition. Fines of this kind are inherently personal — they target the sinner, not his estate or his heirs. On the other hand, the slave's situation is not resolved by the master's death. He continues, every single day, to be compelled to violate *halacha* while under non-Jewish ownership. The ongoing violation makes the children's inaction look like their own failure to remedy an existing wrong.

### Bechor Comparison

The *Gemara* examines analogous cases. One is *tzaram ozen bechor u-met* — a *kohen* who deliberately inflicted a blemish on a *bechor* animal in order to avoid the obligation of bringing it to Jerusalem as a sacrifice, thereby violating the biblical prohibition of *kol mum lo yihiyeh bo*, and who was therefore penalized by being forbidden to eat from that animal. If this *kohen* then died, was the fine imposed on his sons as well — *kohnsu b-no acharav*? The consideration is that this was an *issura de-oraisa*, a biblical violation. Perhaps the severity of the biblical transgression justifies extending the penalty to the next generation. But that would not necessarily help us with our case, where the prohibition against selling a slave to a non-Jew is *issura de-rabbanan* — of rabbinic origin.

### Chol HaMoed

A contrasting case: someone who intentionally delayed performing necessary work until *Chol HaMoed*, at which point he could claim it was a *davar ha-aved* — an unavoidable loss — and thereby permit himself to do labor that he should have completed before the holiday. Having thus circumvented the rabbinic prohibition on labor during *Chol HaMoed*, the person is not permitted to benefit from that labor. If he then died, are his sons also prohibited from benefiting?
