If the *katan*'s challenge carries no legal weight, why does it neutralize the debtor's *migo*? The *migo* should still apply: even facing a *katan*, I could simply have denied everything, so my partial admission should be credited.

### Ignorant = Katan

The Gemara reframes the case: *mai katan? gadol* — when we say *katan*, we do not mean a literal minor. We mean an adult who is ignorant of his father's financial affairs — one who does not know what debts his father held or was owed. *D'lgabei milei d'avuh katan hu* — with respect to his father's dealings, he is like a minor. This adult heir is pressing the debtor on a matter he does not fully understand. The debtor therefore cannot comfortably say he could have remained completely silent; the heir was making some kind of claim. Yet because the heir is effectively ignorant, his claim lacks the force of a genuine legal *ta'anah*. This is precisely why the Chachamim characterize the debtor's conduct as *meshiv aveida* — returning lost property — and exempt him from a *shvua*. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, by contrast, holds that the debtor's partial admission constitutes *modeh b'miktzat* regardless, and he must swear.

### Claim vs. Admission

The Gemara closes with an unresolved aporia. When Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says the person swears *al ta'anat atzmo* — on his own claim — the Gemara notes that this description is paradoxical. If there was a genuine claim by the other side, then calling it "his own claim" is misleading — it is the other side's claim. And if there was no genuine claim by the other side, then *modeh b'miktzat* should not apply, because the *migo* of silence was available. But if we say the heir's claim *was* legally meaningful, then describing the admission as self-generated seems wrong. *Kullehu ta'anata nami ta'anas acherim vehoda'as atzmo ninhu* — every case of *modeh b'miktzat* involves a claim by one side and an admission by the other. What is unique about this case?

The Gemara leaves this question open. Tomorrow's session will return to clarify precisely what Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Chachamim are debating, and why one side holds the debtor obligated while the other exempts him entirely.

---

---

# Gittin 52

## Modeh BeMiktzat

### Rabbi Eliezer vs. Rabanan

The discussion picks up approximately halfway through 51b, continuing the *machlokes* between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the *rabanan* regarding the circumstances under which one can compel another to take a *shvuah* in the cases we have been examining — and specifically, the question of *kemeshiv aveidah*: whether a minor can force someone to take a *shvuah*.

### Three Shvuot Categories

There is an interesting *machlokes rishonim* about which *shvuot* this exemption applies to. Three distinct categories of *shvuah* are relevant to the discussion. The first is *shvuas ed echad*: where a single witness testifies that a debt is owed, the witness cannot extract the debt but his testimony compels the defendant to take a *shvuah*. The second is *shvuas hapikadon*: where a *shomer* — someone watching over property — can be compelled to swear that he did not mishandle what was entrusted to him. The third, and the one the *gemara* now addresses directly, is *shvuas modeh bemiktzas*: where a person admits to part of a claim and is consequently compelled to take a *shvuah* regarding the remainder.

The *gemara* states: *ella keRabbah kamipalgei* — this *machlokes* is actually grounded in a principle articulated by Rabbah.

### Rabbah's Chazakah

Rabbah asks: *mipnei mah amrah Torah modeh bemiktzas hata'anah yishava* — why does the Torah require someone who admits to a partial debt to take a *shvuah*? One might wonder why Rabbah needs to inquire into the rationale at all; if it is *halacha*, it is *halacha*. But the reason Rabbah's rationale matters here is that it becomes the operative principle for determining how *modeh bemiktzas* intersects with the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the *rabanan*.

Rabbah's answer: *chazakah ain adam meiz panav bifnei ba'al chovo* — there is a *chazakah*, a presumption, that a person will not brazenly contradict someone to his face with a bald-faced lie. Tosafot formulates this sharply: *ain adam meiz kol makom she'oso kenegdo yode'a shehu meshaker* — a person will not be so brazen as to lie to someone who knows with certainty that he is lying. This *chazakah* is, admittedly, a claim about human psychology, and one might wonder whether it applies uniformly across all people and eras. Nonetheless, since *modeh bemiktzas* is a *halacha de'oraisa*, the operative rule certainly remains in force regardless.

### Delay Mechanism

The *gemara* then traces the psychological logic of the partial admission. Since *ain adam meiz panav bifnei ba'al chovo*, an honest person ought to have admitted to the entire debt. Why, then, does he admit only to part? Because *demishta­mutei hu dekamishta­mit lei* — he is trying to delay. He knows he owes the full amount, but he lacks the funds to pay it all right now, so he admits to part, pays that immediately, and hopes to buy time until he has the rest: *ad dehavu li zuzei ufarna lei*. He intends to pay eventually, but uses the mechanism of *modeh bemiktzas* to force a delay — against the lender's will.

It is this manipulation of the system that the Torah addresses. *Ve'amar Rachmana remei shvuah aleih* — the Torah imposes a *shvuah* on him, as a way of pressuring him to admit the full amount rather than engineer a delay. The *shvuah* is designed to make the partial denial untenable.

### Eliezer's Position

Having established Rabbah's rationale, the *gemara* explains the positions of the *tanna'im*. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds *lo shna bo velo shna bivno* — it makes no difference whether one is confronting the original creditor or that creditor's heir. *Eino meiz* — the debtor will not be brazen even in the presence of the son. The psychological restraint remains operative whether the opposing party is the original lender or his child, and therefore the same *shvuah* logic applies.

### Rabanan Counter

The *rabanan* disagree. In their view, *bo de'eino meiz aval livno meiz* — a person is indeed restrained from lying to the creditor himself, but he will be far more willing to stand up against the creditor's child, who was not party to the original transaction. Since the psychological impediment is diminished or absent, the very fact that the debtor admits to *part* of the claim is no longer surprising — he could easily have denied everything. His partial admission therefore resembles the conduct of a *meshiv aveidah*, someone voluntarily returning a lost object. Because the internal psychological pressure that would normally explain the partial admission is not in play, we give him greater benefit of the doubt, do not compel him to take a *shvuah*, and treat him as the honest person he appears to be.

## Apotropsin Powers

### Types of Apotropsin

With the beginning of the new *mishnah* at the top of 52a, the topic shifts entirely to *apotropsin* — appointed guardians who oversee the estates of orphans. The *mishnah* and subsequent *gemara* distinguish among three types of *apotropos*. The first is appointed by the father himself — anticipating his own death, a father may designate someone to administer the estate on behalf of his minor children. This has clear resonance for any case where a person can foresee his own death in advance; it is an interesting precedent for instruments akin to living wills and advance directives. The second type is self-appointed — someone who simply steps forward and assumes responsibility for the property. The third is appointed by *beit din*.

The *mishnah* opens: *yetomim shesamkhu etzel ba'al habayit* — orphans who have taken up residence with a householder, *o sheminah lahen avihen apotropos* — or whose father designated an *apotropos* for them — *apotropos chayav le'aser peroteihem* — the *apotropos* is obligated to separate *ma'aser* from their produce.

This immediately raises a question. The underlying issue is one of *zekhiyyah* and its relationship to ownership: who has the right to separate *terumah* and *ma'aser* from produce that belongs to someone else? The *gemara* in *Kiddushin* in the second *perek* distinguishes three different mechanisms by which land was apportioned when the Jewish people entered *Eretz Yisrael* with Yehoshua: *shelikhut* — formal agency; *zekhiyyah* — automatically doing something beneficial for another, with a *machlokes rishonim* as to whether *zekhiyyah* operates through the mechanism of *shelikhut*; and *apotropos* — a distinct category unto itself. The *apotropos* is not the owner of the produce. A *shaliach* can separate *terumah* from another's produce based on a special *drashah* from a *pasuk*, but the *pasuk atem* — "you," implying only owners — would seem to exclude an *apotropos* from this power.

One might ask: why does this matter so urgently, given that *katanim* are only obligated in *mitzvot* through *chinuch* anyway, making any *issur* at worst *derabanan*? Yet someone must manage their religious and financial lives, and that is precisely what motivates this entire institution of *apotropus* — the *yetomim* need someone to oversee their financial dealings and ensure their proper upbringing.

Regarding the underlying mechanism by which *apotropsus* functions: Rabbeinu Tam maintains that the *drashah* from *atem* is only an *asmachta*, and the principle excluding *apotropsin* from separating *terumah* is merely *derabanan*. The exception allowing the *apotropos* to separate *terumah* in the case of actively feeding the *yetomim* is itself a *derabanan* creation designed to protect them. Other *rishonim* propose different approaches. As we will see later, Tosafot Rid invokes *hefker beit din hefker* — the principle that a *beit din* can divest and reassign ownership — as the underlying mechanism that grants the *apotropos* his powers. That principle will resurface shortly.

### Tithes Separation

The *gemara* raises an apparent contradiction: *uvreminhu* — a *beraisa* that seems to exclude *apotropsin* from separating *terumah*. Rav Chisda resolves the tension with a distinction: *kan le-hachil, kan le-haniach* — one case concerns feeding the *yetomim* now, while the other concerns storing produce for the future. When the *apotropos* is separating *terumah* and *ma'aser* so as to actively feed the *yetomim* from the produce at hand, this is permitted. But to separate *terumah* from produce that will simply sit in storage for a decade until the orphans mature — that is not permitted, because they will be fully capable of separating it themselves when they are grown. The *gemara* confirms: *ve-hatanya apotropsin tormin u-maasrin le-hachil aval lo le-haniach* — the *beraisa* supports Rav Chisda's distinction, and Rashi notes that *ve-hatanya* here is used *be-nichuta*, as a supporting citation rather than a challenge.

### Braita's Restrictions

The *beraisa* continues with a comprehensive list of what *apotropsin* may and may not do. They may sell animals, slaves, houses, fields, and vineyards — *le-hachil*, to actively support the *yetomim*, but not *le-haniach*, not to build up a long-term reserve. Similarly, they may sell fruits, wine, oil, and flour for immediate support but not for storage. The language *u-mochrin lahem* encompasses both selling on behalf of the *yetomim* and purchasing for them — the *apotropos* manages active financial support in either direction.

### Fixed vs. Indefinite Pri…

The *beraisa* proceeds to enumerate *mitzvah* objects that may be purchased: the *apotropos* may make for the orphans a *lulav*, *arava* — notable since *arava* on its own is a *minhag* rather than a biblical *mitzvah*, though the *Rif*'s version of the text omits *arava* — a *sukkah*, and *tzitzit*. The *beraisa* then adds a general category: *kol davar sheyesh lo kitzvah* — anything with a fixed and defined cost; the *gemara* notes this includes *shofar* and, separately, *megillah*. Further, the *apotropos* may purchase for the orphans a *Sefer Torah*, *tefillin*, and *mezuzot*. Regarding a *Sefer Torah* in particular: there is a *mitzvah* for every Jewish man to write one, and beyond the ritual dimension, in antiquity a *Sefer Torah* was the means of Torah study itself — effectively, purchasing a *Sefer Torah* amounted to providing an education. The Maharam Shiff examines each item in this list individually, treating each as a *chiddush* in its own right.

### Court & Property Limits

Corresponding to these permissions, the *beraisa* specifies what *apotropsin* may not do: *ein poskin aleihen tzedakah* — they may not donate *tzedakah* from the orphans' inheritance; *ein podin aleihen et hashvuyim* — they may not use orphan funds to redeem captives; and *lo kol davar she'ein lo kitzvah* — nothing in the category of indefinite, open-ended expense. The paradigm case is *tanchumei aveilim* — bringing food to a house of mourning — since communal and charitable claims of this nature could arise indefinitely and drain the estate without limit. The governing principle is that any expenditure must be capped and predictable; anything unlimited falls outside the *apotropos*'s authority.

This typology raises an interesting question: does it apply uniformly to all types of *apotropos*, whether father-appointed, self-appointed, or *beit din*-appointed? The *mishnah* will address that shortly.

The *beraisa* further states: *ein apotropsin resha'im ladun lachov velizkos benichsei yetomim* — *apotropsin* may not litigate, whether the outcome would be adverse or favorable, with regard to orphan property. The *gemara* asks: if it is an entirely beneficial case, why may they not litigate? The answer: *ela lachov al menas lizkos* — even a case with long-term benefit may involve short-term detriment, and that suffices to prohibit it. But something that is unambiguously and entirely beneficial — that they may pursue. The practical difficulty, of course, is that no one can predict with certainty how litigation will resolve before the case is decided, which is why the *rishonim* struggle to define precisely what situations are contemplated here. The broader principle is clear: *katanim* cannot be brought to court, and active litigation of claims against their property must generally await their majority.

### Field Sale Restrictions

The *beraisa* further prohibits: *ein apotropsin resha'im limkor berachok velikhol bekarov* — they may not sell distant property and acquire nearby property in its stead, nor sell inferior property to acquire superior property. The rationale given by the *gemara*: *dilma mishta­dfin* — the newly acquired property might be struck by blight, flooding, or some other calamity. One thought it was good property; it may turn out to be ruinous. This reflects a broader awareness in *Chazal* — visible across several of the recent *dapim* — of the tension between objective assessments of property quality and the reality that property values fluctuate wildly over time.

### Slaves for Fields

The *beraisa* adds: *ein apotropsin resha'im limkor sadot velikaach avadim* — they may not sell fields to acquire slaves. And Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel goes further: *af lo limkor avadim velikaach sadot* — even selling slaves to acquire fields is prohibited. His rationale: *dilma lo mashpyan* — the fields may not produce abundantly. The *apotropos* may have thought that converting liquid assets into permanent productive land was a sound investment; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel warns that the field may yield little, rendering the transaction a net loss — and the *apotropos* is only authorized to act for the *yetomim*'s clear benefit.

### Freeing Slaves Prohibiti…

The *beraisa* states: *ein apotropin resha'im lehotzi avadim lacherut* — *apotropsin* may not free slaves; *aval mocherin otan la'acherim* — but they may sell them to others, *ve'acherim motzi'in otan lacherut* — and those others may then free them. Note that the *tanna kamma* permits selling slaves to acquire real estate, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disputes this.

Rashi and Tosafot Rid dispute the underlying reason for the prohibition on freeing slaves. Rashi holds that the *apotropsin* simply lack the requisite legal power — *ein gufan kanui lahen leshachreran* — freeing slaves is not within their authority. Tosafot Rid presses the point: if they can sell slaves, why can they not free them, since the two transactions are functionally nearly equivalent? Tosafot Rid's answer is grounded in the principle of *hefker beit din hefker*: the *apotropos*'s powers derive from a rabbinic framework in which *beit din* effectively takes the orphans' property and re-vests authority in the *apotropos* to act on their behalf — but only for the specific transactions within that authorization. Freeing a slave, though similar to selling, falls outside the scope of what the rabbinic framework empowers the *apotropos* to do. The alternative conceptual framework — that *apotropsus* operates through *zekhiyyah* or *shelikhut*, perhaps as a superpowered form of *zekhiyyah* capable of encompassing even temporary loss for long-term gain — would have different implications.

### Rabbi's Self-Redemption

Rabbi interjects with his own view: *omer ani af hu noten demei atzmo veyotze mipnei shehu kemochro lo* — even the slave himself may pay for his own freedom, since a slave buying his own freedom is legally equivalent to someone else selling the slave to him. This is an interesting extension of the earlier discussions regarding *avadim*.

### Accounting Requirements

The *beraisa* states: *vetzarich lechashev imahem ba'achronah* — the *apotropos* must render a full accounting to the orphans at the conclusion of his tenure, documenting how much was spent on their upkeep, food, and other expenditures, to ensure complete transparency and honesty.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: *eino tzarich* — no accounting is required. His reasoning, which the *gemara* will develop: if you impose the burden of detailed accounting, no one will be willing to serve as *apotropos*. This tension — between protecting the *yetomim* through oversight and ensuring that capable people are willing to take on the responsibility — runs throughout this entire discussion.

### Ineligible Apotropsin

The *beraisa* concludes: *ein osin apotropsin nashim va'avadim uketannim* — women, slaves, and minors are ineligible to serve as *apotropsin*. It is important to note that these three categories are disqualified for very different reasons. Rashi explains regarding women: *she'ein darchan latzeis ulavo ulitrach* — it was not the custom of women in that era to go out into the marketplace, engage in business dealings, and manage court cases. Rashi's formulation implicitly acknowledges that this rationale is circumstantial rather than inherent: were the relevant social conditions different, the application of this *halacha* might well look different.

However, there is a significant qualification: *ve'im minahu avi yatmei harreshut beyado* — if the father himself designated such a person as *apotropos*, that appointment stands. The father's authority over his own estate and his knowledge of those he trusts give him power to override what *beit din* would otherwise require. It is his estate, and he may exercise his own judgment as to whom he entrusts it.

## Apotropsin Case Studies

### Rabbi Meir's Dream

The *gemara* now turns to a series of narrative case studies illustrating *apotropsin* in practice. *Hahu apotropos dehava bishivvusei deRabbi Meir* — there was an *apotropos* in the town of Rabbi Meir who was selling real estate and selling slaves. Rabbi Meir did not intervene. *Itlai be-chelma* — the deceased father appeared to Rabbi Meir in a dream, crying: *ani leharos ve'atah livnot* — you are letting him destroy everything and I am left having to rebuild? Yet even after this dream, Rabbi Meir still did not act. *Amar divrei chalomot lo maalin velo moridin* — dreams carry no halakhic weight; they neither elevate nor diminish the legal standing of a matter. The *gemara* records many conflicting attitudes toward dreams across *Shas* — in *Yevamos*, *Nedarim*, and *Berakhot* dreams are sometimes taken with great seriousness — but Rabbi Meir here represents a position of firm dismissal.

### Satan Possession Case

The *gemara* interjects a famous story about Rabbi Meir. *Hanehu betrei de'igrei behu satana* — there were two men who were seized by *satana*, such that every *erev Shabbat* they would erupt in conflict. Rabbi Meir came and stayed with them for three consecutive *Shabbat* evenings until he brought peace between them. Upon his departure, he heard Satan cry out in frustration: *vai de'afkei Rabbi Meir lehahu gavra mibeisei* — woe, for Rabbi Meir has driven that man out of his house. The *satana* brings *machlokes*; it cannot coexist in a space where *shalom* prevails. The story reveals Rabbi Meir as a person who went out of his way to engage with people and intervene in their conflicts — a picture consistent with other accounts of him elsewhere in *Shas*.

### Oxen Sale Uncontested

A parallel case: *hahu apotropos dehava bishivvusei deRabbi Yehoshua ben Levi dehava kamazvin ar'a u-zavin tori velo amar lehu lei velo midi* — an *apotropos* in the domain of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was selling land and oxen, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said nothing to him. The *gemara* explains that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi followed the opinion of Rabbi Yosi. As the *beraisa* records, Rabbi Yosi said that in his life he never called his wife "my wife" but rather "my house," for she oversaw the entire household, and he never called his ox "my ox" but rather "my field," for the ox was indispensable to working all his fields. In other words, Rabbi Yosi regarded the ox as equivalent in importance to the field itself — and consequently Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi did not object to the *apotropos* selling the orphans' oxen.

### Widow's Ox Sale

Another case: *hanehu yasmei dehavu samchei gabei hahu sabta* — orphans who were under the care of an older woman. She had an ox belonging to them and sold it. The relatives came before Rav Nachman and protested. She invoked the case of *yetomim shesamkhu etzel ba'al habayit* from our *mishnah* — orphans who had taken up residence with a householder — arguing that she was acting within her authorized capacity to sell the ox for their support.

The *gemara* then notes: *veha ikar bireshusa delokeach* — but the ox had appreciated in value once it was in the buyer's possession. Moreover, *ve'ada lo nekiti damei* — the money had not yet been paid over. What could or should be done?

### Property as Hekdesh

Rav Nachman ruled on the basis of a principle transmitted by Rav Chanilai bar Idi in the name of Shmuel: *nichsei yetomim harei hen kehekdesh velo makni ela bechespa* — the property of orphans is like *hekdesh*, consecrated property, in that it can be acquired only through the transfer of money. This generates an important practical rule: just as a transaction involving *hekdesh* is not finalized until money changes hands, so too a transaction involving orphans' property.

This contrasts with the general rule for *metaltelin*, where there is a *machlokes* between Rav Yochanan and Reish Lakish — *ma'os konos* versus *eino nikneh ela bemeshicha* — whether acquisition of movable property takes effect through payment of money or through the act of *meshicha*, physically taking possession. For orphans' property, the rule is fixed: only cash completes the transaction, akin to *hekdesh*.

This principle operates in both directions, always to the *yetomim*'s benefit: if the price rises after *meshicha* but before payment, the *yetomim* collect at the higher price. The system is, in effect, rigged in their favor — whatever arrangement yields them the better outcome is the operative one.

### Wine Price Fluctuation

The *gemara* works through several scenarios. *Chamra de-rabna Ukva yatmei mashkhuhu be-arba'ah arba'ah* — wine belonging to the estate of the orphans of Rabna Ukva was drawn (*meshicha* was performed) when it was worth four per barrel. The price then rose to six per barrel. Rav Nachman invoked the ruling of Rav Chanilai bar Idi: since *nichsei yetomim* are like *hekdesh* and are acquired only through money, and money had not yet been paid, the transaction is resolved at the higher price — a very substantial windfall for the *yetomim*.

Conversely: if *meshicha* was performed on behalf of the *yetomim* when they were purchasing produce and the price then dropped — *lo yehei koach hedyot chamur mehekdesh* — the ordinary mechanism of sale must not work worse for them than *hekdesh* does. We give them the benefit of either form of acquisition, whichever is more advantageous.

### Merchant Incentives

This raises a practical concern: if sellers know that the price will always resolve against them when dealing with *yetomim*, people will simply refuse to do business with them. Moreover, applying the *hekdesh* principle in both directions — such that *yetomim* always pay the lower price when buying and receive the higher price when selling — creates a system that merchants will circumvent by waiting until payment and delivery coincide exactly. Rav Shisha, son of Rav Idi, identifies the countervailing risk on each side: if *yetomim* pay cash first before taking possession, the seller can always invoke *nisrefu chitechem ba'aliya* — your wheat burned in the attic — claiming the goods were destroyed before delivery, leaving the *yetomim* with no recourse. The *gemara* works through these tensions carefully, ultimately leaving the general principle of protecting the *yetomim* intact while acknowledging the practical complications.

Rav Ashi adds: he and Rav Kahana signed a document authorizing the sale of a field belonging to orphans to pay a tax, without performing *achrazata* — the public announcement calling for the best possible buyer that is normally required before selling orphan property. The *Nehardai* ruled that for three categories of pressing need — paying taxes, providing food, or funding a burial — *achrazata* is not required. Tosafot notes that the case of burial seems so self-evidently urgent as to be unworthy of explicit mention; the *gemara* must therefore be referring not to purchasing a burial plot itself but to repaying a debt incurred for a burial.

### Amram Tzeva Accusations

*Amram Tzeva* was serving as *apotropos* for orphans. Relatives came before Rav Nachman claiming he was dressing and clothing himself from the orphans' property. Rav Nachman's response was measured: perhaps he is eating and drinking from his own means — and if someone found an unexpectedly valuable lost object (*metzia*), one gives him the benefit of the doubt.

### Removing Negligent Guard…

The *gemara* then asks: but if he is in fact depleting their estate, that is a serious problem. Rav Nachman replied: bring me witnesses that he is causing loss, and I will remove him. The *apotropos* is entitled to a presumption of good faith — and that presumption serves a practical function. If an *apotropos* can be removed on bare accusation, no one will be willing to accept the responsibility.

Rav Huna stated in Rav's name: *apotropos demafsid mesalkinan lei* — an *apotropos* who causes loss to the orphans is removed. This is the subject of a direct *machlokes* among *amora'im*: Rav Huna citing Rav rules that he is removed; the school of Rabbi Shila says he is not removed. The *halacha* follows Rav Huna: he is removed.

## Shvuah for Apotropsin

### Tanna Kamma Position

The *mishnah* rules: *apotropos sheminahu avi yetomim yishava* — an *apotropos* appointed by the father must take a *shvuah*; *minahu beit din lo yishava* — one appointed by *beit din* does not.

### Incentive Rationale

The *gemara* explains the *tanna kamma*'s reasoning. The father-appointed *apotropos* is asked to take a *shvuah* precisely because *i lav de'is lei hana'ah minei lo hava lei apotropos* — if he were not receiving some benefit from the arrangement, he never would have agreed to take it on. The father must have offered him compensation or some special inducement. Accordingly, *mishum shvuah lo ati le'amnuyei* — the prospect of taking an oath at the conclusion of his tenure will not deter him from having accepted the position in the first place; the benefit still outweighs the burden. Therefore the *shvuah* can be imposed without creating a disincentive.

Conversely, the *beit din*-appointed *apotropos* does not take a *shvuah*. His motivation is simply *milta be'alma hu de'avid le'bei dina* — he is doing a favor for the court. *Ve'i ramit lei shvuah ati le'amnuyei* — if we burden him with the obligation of an oath at the end, the negatives will outweigh whatever public benefit he derives, and no one will agree to serve. The *beit din* does not pay its *apotropos*, making the deterrent effect of the *shvuah* far more pronounced.

This discussion invites reflection on how courts today think about foster care arrangements — with relatives versus non-relatives — and the degree to which financial incentives and public recognition affect people's willingness to step into caregiving roles for orphans.

### Abba Shaul Reversal

*Abba Shaul omer chiluf hadvarim* — Abba Shaul reverses the ruling entirely.

### Public Reputation Logic

Abba Shaul's rationale for his reversal: *minuhu beit din yishava be'hahi hana'ah de-nafik lei kala de'inish meheman hu* — when *beit din* appoints you, your appointment becomes publicly known. You become recognized in the community as a person of trustworthiness whom the court has seen fit to select. *Deha samchu lei beit din* — the court has placed its confidence in you. The public reputation you thereby acquire is itself a form of *hana'ah*, and it is sufficient to keep you motivated. Therefore *mishum shvuah lo ati le'amnuyei minehon* — the prospect of taking a *shvuah* will not deter you from having accepted the appointment.

Regarding the father-appointed *apotropos*, Abba Shaul argues the opposite: *milta be'alma hu de'avid le-hahu gavra* — he is doing a favor for a man who is now dead. A private appointment by a deceased father does not generate the same public recognition as a *beit din* appointment. The reputational reward is minimal, and therefore *ve'i ramit lei shvuah ati le'amnuyei* — the burden of a *shvuah* will indeed deter him from having agreed to serve.

### Shmuel's Ruling

Rav Chanan bar Ami reports in the name of Shmuel: *hilchata ke-Abba Shaul* — the *halacha* follows Abba Shaul. The *Rif* indeed rules accordingly.

### Rabbi Elazar's View

However, Tosafot raises a difficulty: a subsequent *beraisa* records that Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov says *zeh vezeh yishava* — both types of *apotropos*, whether appointed by the father or by *beit din*, must take a *shvuah*. The *beraisa* itself concludes: *halacha kidvarav* — the *halacha* is in accordance with his view. This appears to contradict the ruling of Shmuel following Abba Shaul, and Tosafot grapples with how to resolve the tension.

### Paid Guardian Status

Rav Tachlifa bar Ma'arava taught before Rabbi Abbahu: the reason the father-appointed *apotropos* takes a *shvuah* is *mipnei shehu nosei sachar* — because he is a *shomer sachar*, a paid guardian. Rabbi Abbahu challenges the precise formulation: he is not literally a *shomer sachar*; rather, he is *kenosei sachar* — like a paid guardian. He derives a certain *hana'ah* from the arrangement that places him in the functional position of someone who benefits from the *shmirah*, even if not technically a hired watchman.

There is a great deal more to be said about this *daf*. The *Ran* and the *Ra'avad* and *Rambam* on the *dapei ha-Rif* engage in a rich *machlokes* about how the institution of *apotropus* interacts with the various *halakhot* surveyed here. It is, in all, a remarkably dense and jam-packed *daf*.

---

---

# Gittin 53

## Hezek She'eino Nikar

### Three Cases Defined

The *mishna* on 52b introduces a new category of *tikkun olam* centered on the concept of *hezek she'eino nikar* — damage that is not visible. The *mishna* states: *hametameh vehamedameh vehamensach, beshogeg patur, bemeizid chayav* — one who contaminates, mixes, or pours a libation: if accidental, exempt; if intentional, liable. Before addressing the conceptual framework underlying these rulings, the *gemara* first examines the three specific cases.

*Metameh* refers to causing ritual impurity — for instance, touching *terumah* grain with a *sheretz* (a dead rodent), rendering it *tamei*. The grain, which could previously be eaten by *kohanim*, is now fit only to be burned. One may derive benefit from *tamei terumah* only as it burns, making it substantially less valuable. Yet nothing about the grain looks any different. *Medameh* refers to mixing separated *terumah* grain with *chullin* grain. Before the mixing, the *chullin* might be worth ten dollars a pound, available to anyone, while the *terumah* is worth five dollars a pound, restricted to *kohanim*. Once mixed, the entire pile is effectively restricted to *kohanim* and worth only five dollars a pound — yet to the eye, it is simply a large pile of grain. *Menasech* refers to pouring someone's wine as a libation to *avodah zarah*, rendering it *assur behana'ah* — prohibited even for any benefit — though again, nothing visible distinguishes it from ordinary wine. These three cases represent the distinctive phenomenon of a halakhic world where damage can be real, severe, and yet entirely invisible.

### Default Rule Debate

The central question raised by the *mishna* is: which direction does the *tikkun olam* run? For ordinary damages, one is liable whether the act was *beshogeg* or *bemeizid*. One might therefore assume that the same is true here, and that the innovation of the *mishna* is the exemption for *shogeg* — that *chazal* suspended the ordinary obligation as a social measure. Alternatively, one might hold that the baseline rule is exemption — *hezek she'eino nikar* is simply not considered actionable damage — and the innovation is that *chazal* imposed liability for intentional acts to prevent people from willfully harming others with impunity. As the *gemara* will make clear, this question is not merely academic: it determines the very nature of the obligation in the *meizid* case, whether it is a form of compensation or a fine.

---

## Menasech Interpretation

### Rav vs. Shmuel

Before reaching the fundamental conceptual debate, the *gemara* first clarifies a dispute between Rav and Shmuel about which act the *mishna* designates by the term *menasech*. Rav holds that the *mishna* refers to *menasech mamash* — literally pouring someone's wine as a libation to *avodah zarah*, thereby rendering it *assur behana'ah*. Shmuel, by contrast, holds that the *mishna* refers to mixing *yayin shel avodah zarah* into kosher wine — *me'arev*, an act analogous in structure to *medameh*, in that the wine's status is changed by admixture rather than by direct cultic act.

### Kam Leih B'Derabbah

The *gemara* asks why Shmuel does not simply accept Rav's reading of *menasech* as literal pouring. The answer is *kam leih biderabbah mineih*: one who performs *nisuch*, pouring wine as a libation to *avodah zarah*, incurs capital liability, and this greater punishment displaces any monetary obligation arising from the same act. The principle of *kam leih biderabbah mineih* holds that when a single act generates both a capital transgression and a financial obligation, the weightier punishment subsumes the lesser — the offender is "established" with the greater sanction.

This principle operates in two distinct modes. The first is the well-known rule of *ein adam lokeh umeshalem* — one is not both flogged and made to pay — where two actual punishments cannot be exacted for a single act. The second, and more far-reaching, mode is *kam leih biderabbah mineih* proper: even when no punishment is actually being administered — because there are no witnesses, no *hasra'ah* (forewarning), or no functioning court with capital jurisdiction — the sheer gravity of the religious transgression renders any concurrent monetary obligation legally inconsequential. The act of *avodah zarah* is so weighty that the accompanying financial damage becomes irrelevant in its shadow.

The *gemara* therefore asks: according to Rav, how is there any monetary liability at all? The answer is drawn from the principle stated by Rabbi Yirmiyah: *mishas hagbahah hu dekana* — the moment of acquisition, and hence the moment of financial liability, is the lifting of the vessel. *Mischayav b'nafsho lo havi ad sha'as nisuch* — capital liability for the act of *avodah zarah* does not attach until the moment of actual pouring. The financial act and the religious transgression thus occur at different moments, preventing *kam leih* from blocking the monetary claim.

### Tosafot Resolution

This resolution raises a further difficulty. If the financial liability arises at the moment of lifting — which is an act of *geneivah* or *gzeilah* — then the case in the *mishna* is simply one of theft, not of *hezek she'eino nikar*. The *mishna*'s entire concern is with invisible damage: an act that alters an object's halakhic status without any visible change. If the obligation tracks the lifting rather than the pouring, it is ordinary theft, not invisible damage.

*Tosafot* addresses this problem directly. He writes: *yesh lomar d'savar Shmuel dehagbahah tzorech nisuch hu* — one may say that Shmuel holds that the lifting is a necessary precondition for the *nisuch*, since pouring cannot occur without first lifting the vessel. The key insight of *Tosafot* is that the moment of liability is defined differently depending on which body of law is being applied. Through the lens of *hilchos avodah zarah*, the prohibited act begins at the moment of pouring. But through the lens of *hilchos nezek*, the damaging process begins earlier — from the moment the perpetrator took hold of the wine with the intent to harm it. He has already begun invading another's property and initiating the chain of damage. Accordingly, there are two overlapping but temporally distinct acts: the *nezek* process commences with the lifting, while the *avodah zarah* offense crystallizes at the pouring. Because they do not fully coincide, *kam leih biderabbah mineih* does not apply, and the financial liability stands as a genuine case of *hezek she'eino nikar* — not mere theft.

The *gemara* then inverts the question: why, according to Rav, does Shmuel not simply accept the plain reading of *menasech* as literal pouring? One answer is that the plain meaning of the word supports Rav's reading. A deeper answer is that if the *mishna* had only intended mixing wine — which is structurally identical to mixing *terumah* with *chullin* — it would be no new *chiddush*; we would have derived it directly from *medameh*. But the other side responds: *knasa hu* — all of these obligations are *kenasos*, rabbinic fines, and one may not draw inferences from one fine to another. The fact that *chazal* chose to impose a *kenas* in one case does not logically compel the same in a different case.

This response introduces a crucial conceptual point. The assertion that the obligation is a *kenas* implicitly affirms that the baseline rule is exemption — *me'ikar hadin*, one is *patur* in all these cases. The question of whether the *meizid* obligation is properly characterized as a *kenas* (a fine imposed for social control or deterrence) or as a form of rabbinic *tashlumim* (compensation instituted to close a gap in the law) carries significant implications. If it is compensation, then wherever the same injustice exists, the same remedy should logically follow. If it is a *kenas*, however, each case must be evaluated on its own terms: how prevalent is the problem, how severe is the harm, how pressing is the social need for deterrence? These factors vary, and a *kenas* instituted in one context cannot simply be extended to another by analogy.

---

## Why Three Cases?

### Baraita Progression

The *gemara* presses further: if one accepts that inferences can be drawn from one *kenas* to another, why does the *mishna* need to specify all three cases? A *baraita* attributed to the father of Rabbi Avin records that originally the ruling was stated only for *metamei* and *menasech*, and only later was it extended to include *medameh* as well. This progression is itself revealing: the fact that *medameh* was the last and apparently most difficult case to include reinforces the character of these obligations as targeted rabbinic interventions rather than applications of a general principle of compensation.

### Case Distinctions

The *gemara* explains why each case is indispensable and cannot be inferred from the others. Had the *mishna* stated only *metameh* — specifically, contaminating *terumah* — one might have thought the liability arises only because the loss is nearly total: *terumah temei'ah* can no longer be eaten at all and is useful only as fuel. One would not have extended the ruling to cases of partial loss. Alternatively, had the case been contaminating *chullin*, the monetary loss is minimal — *tamei chullin* is barely worth less than *tahor chullin* for most people — but there is the additional factor that causing *tumah* to *chullin* in *Eretz Yisrael* is itself a ritual transgression. One could not have known whether the fine was imposed because of the partial loss or because of this supplementary violation.

Had the *mishna* stated only *medameh*, one might have concluded that the obligation arises only because *medameh* is a common occurrence — people regularly separate *terumah* and maintain distinct piles, making accidental or deliberate mixing a practical and frequent hazard. One would not have extended the fine to *metameh*, which the *gemara* treats as a less common scenario.

And had the *mishna* stated only the first two without *menasech*, one might have concluded that these cases are straightforward because they do not implicate *kam leih biderabbah mineih*. Upon encountering *menasech*, one might have thought the capital dimension of *avodah zarah* exempts entirely. The *mishna* therefore includes all three to teach, in accordance with Rabbi Yirmiyah's principle, that the liability precedes the capital transgression, and the fine applies even there.

Each case is thus distinguished by a combination of factors: the degree of financial loss (total, near-total, or partial), the frequency with which the situation arises, and the presence or absence of additional ritual transgressions or competing legal doctrines. That all three parameters must be addressed independently confirms that what is operating here is a targeted series of rabbinic penalties, not a uniform principle of compensation.

---

## Damage Definition

### Chizkiyah Position

Having worked through the cases, the *gemara* now turns to the fundamental conceptual dispute. *Chizkiyah* holds: *devar Torah echad shogeg ve'echad meizid chayav* — as a matter of Torah law, whether one acted accidentally or intentionally, one is liable for this type of damage. The reasoning is *hezek she'eino nikar shemo hezek* — invisible damage is nonetheless called damage. An object whose halakhic status has been destroyed, rendering it worthless or severely diminished in value, has been damaged in the full legal sense, even if nothing visible has changed. The innovation of the *mishna*, on this reading, is not the liability for *meizid* but the exemption for *shogeg* — that is a departure from the ordinary rule and requires explanation.

### Disclosure Incentive

Why would *chazal* exempt an accidental damager? *Kedei sheyodi'o* — so that the person will disclose what happened. The concern is entirely practical: the damage caused by *hezek she'eino nikar* is not apparent to the victim. If the inadvertent damager knows that disclosure will result in financial liability, he faces a strong *yetzer hara* not to inform. He can simply stay silent, and the victim will never know — he will unknowingly consume *terumah temei'ah*, drink *yayin nesech*, or eat food that is halakhically forbidden. The financial harm is compounded by the ritual harm that follows from ignorance. To break this incentive structure, *chazal* removed the financial consequence for accidental acts, ensuring that the person has no monetary reason to conceal what occurred.

One might ask: if disclosure is the concern, should we not exempt even the intentional damager, so that he too will come forward and inform the victim? The *gemara* rejects this: when someone acts *bemeizid*, his motivation is to cause harm in this world — to make the victim's property worthless, to humiliate him, to damage him materially. Such a person will typically make sure the victim knows what has been done, either by informing him directly or by acting openly. The policy rationale for exemption applies only to the *shogeg*, who has no such motivation to inform and who faces a genuine financial disincentive to disclose.

### Yochanan Position

Rabbi Yochanan takes the contrary view: *devar Torah echad shogeg ve'echad meizid patur* — as a matter of Torah law, whether accidental or intentional, one is exempt. The reason is *hezek she'eino nikar lo shemei hezek* — invisible damage is not legally considered damage at all. On this view, there is no biblical obligation in these cases, and the *mishna*'s innovation is not the *shogeg* exemption but the *meizid* liability. The reason *chazal* imposed liability for intentional acts is precisely what was anticipated earlier: *shelo yehei kol echad ve'echad holech umetamei taharotav shel chaveiro ve'omer patur ani* — lest every person go and contaminate his neighbor's *taharos* and declare himself exempt. Without this rabbinic measure, anyone with malicious intent could willfully destroy another's property through invisible means and face no legal consequence whatsoever.

This framing is significant. By anchoring the obligation in the need to deter wrongdoers rather than in the victim's entitlement to compensation, Rabbi Yochanan's position strongly colors the liability as a *kenas* — a punitive fine aimed at social control — rather than a form of *tashlumim*. The question of whether the obligation is fundamentally about deterrence or about closing a gap of injustice is not merely theoretical: if it is deterrence, each case must be evaluated on its own social conditions; if it is compensation, any case in which the victim suffers and the damager was at fault would logically call for the same remedy. The *gemara*'s framing through Rabbi Yochanan's language — focusing on preventing the wrongdoer from acting with impunity — pushes toward the *kenas* characterization.

### Knas vs. Tashlumim

This distinction deserves further attention. One might have framed the same rabbinic intervention very differently: it is unjust that a person can willfully destroy another's property and the victim receives nothing; therefore *chazal* created a category of rabbinic compensation to close that gap. This framing would yield a *tashlumim* — an extension of the law's existing compensatory logic into a domain where Torah law had not yet reached. Under that model, the comparison between cases is natural: wherever someone suffers a loss attributable to another's willful act, the same logic compels compensation.

But the *gemara*'s language, and particularly Rabbi Yochanan's formulation, focuses on preventing the wrongdoer's impunity rather than on making the victim whole. That focus reflects a *kenas* mentality: we are not filling a gap in the law of compensation; we are imposing a deterrent penalty for socially dangerous behavior. And if it is a *kenas*, we cannot assume that the same penalty applies across all analogous cases. Different situations carry different degrees of risk, different frequencies of occurrence, and different social pressures — factors that determine whether a targeted fine is warranted. As *Rashi* puts it tersely: wherever they imposed a fine, they imposed it; wherever they did not, they did not. The apparent arbitrariness dissolves once one understands that the fine is a pragmatic instrument calibrated to specific social needs, not a logical extension of a general principle.

---

## Proofs & Parallels

### Pigul Case

The *gemara* now brings proofs from related cases to resolve the dispute between *Chizkiyah* and Rabbi Yochanan. A *mishna* in *Zevachim* states: *kohanim shepiggelu b'mikdash meizidim chayavim* — priests who rendered a sacrifice *pigul* (invalid by harboring an improper intention during its offering, such as intending to eat it at the wrong time or place) are liable if they acted intentionally. The Talmud notes: *vetanya alah mipnei tikkun ha'olam* — and a *baraisa* teaches that this obligation exists *mipnei tikkun ha'olam*. This is another case of *hezek she'eino nikar*: the sacrifice looks no different after the *kohen*'s improper thought, yet it is now *pasul* and the owner has suffered a real loss. The formulation — *meizidim chayavim mipnei tikkun ha'olam* — sounds like the innovation is the liability for intentional acts, implying that the baseline is exemption. This supports Rabbi Yochanan.

The *gemara* notes that if one follows *Chizkiyah* — that the baseline is liability and the innovation is the *shogeg* exemption — then the *baraisa* should have stated that *shogegim* are exempt *mipnei tikkun ha'olam*. The *gemara* deflects this by reading the *baraisa* as implicitly teaching the *shogeg* exemption through the *meizid* liability: since it says the intentional are liable, the accidental are implicitly exempt, and it is the exemption that is the *tikkun ha'olam*. This is a forced reading, and the proof-force leans toward Rabbi Yochanan.

### Parah Adumah

A stronger challenge comes from a *baraisa* concerning *parah adumah* and *mei chatat*: one who performs *melachah* with the red cow or with the purification waters is *patur midinei adam vechayav bidinei shamayim* — exempt from human courts but liable in the heavenly court. Performing *melachah* with the cow while it is still alive, or using the *mei chatat* (the waters mixed with the ashes of the *parah adumah*) as counterweights in a balance, invalidates them for their sacred purpose — again a case of *hezek she'eino nikar*. The *baraisa* does not distinguish between *shogeg* and *meizid*; it simply declares the person *patur midinei adam*. If *Chizkiyah* is correct that the baseline is liability, why is there no *meizid* obligation here? This seems to support Rabbi Yochanan: the default is exemption, and in this case *chazal* chose not to impose a fine.

*Rashi* notes that *chayav bidinei shamayim* here implies, at minimum, that a person who intentionally damaged another's property is answerable before God — and in another context, *Rashi* explains that this formulation may indicate a moral obligation to compensate the victim even though the human court cannot compel it.

### Cow Intention

The *gemara* offers a preliminary resolution. The case of the cow becoming invalid through *melachah* is distinguishable: the cow's activity (nursing from its mother, threshing grain on the floor) invalidates the *parah adumah* only because the owner *intended* for it to thresh. Without that intent, the cow's nursing would not be considered *avodah* (labor). The act of invalidation is thus mediated through the owner's thought, not through a direct physical act. This is not a case of *hezek she'eino nikar* in the usual sense — the problem is not merely that the damage is invisible, but that no direct physical action was performed at all; the invalidation occurred through mental intention alone. Accordingly, one cannot derive from this case that invisible damage carries no liability.

### Water Displacement

But the *gemara* presses further. What of the case of *mei chatat* used for water displacement — placing objects into the water to measure by displacement? There, the person performs a direct physical act and the water is invalidated. This is invisible damage caused by a real action. Why is the person still *patur midinei adam*? Does this not prove that *hezek she'eino nikar lo shemei hezek*?

The *gemara* offers a resolution: *lo kashya ha begufan ha bichenegdan* — it depends on the mode of use. Placing the *mei chatat* on one side of a balance with something on the other side (*bichenegdan*) is not considered *melachah* with the water itself, and therefore does not invalidate it. Placing an object *into* the water to measure displacement (*begufan*) does constitute a direct use of the water and would invalidate it. If so, the case of water displacement (*begufan*) should involve a direct act and yield liability — which would support *Chizkiyah*.

### Hesach Hada'at

The *gemara* ultimately resolves the tension by reframing both cases. It concludes that both the cow case and the water case can be explained as instances of *hesach hada'at* — a lapse in attentiveness — rather than as cases of direct physical action. With *mei chatat*, even the act of using the water as a counterbalance (*bichenegdan*) is not what produces invalidation through *melachah* per se; rather, the moment one turns one's attention to weighing grain, one is no longer fully focused on the *mei chatat*, and it is this *hesach hada'at* — the distraction from guarding its sanctity — that invalidates it. In other words, what makes the *mei chatat pasul* in that case is not the physical act but the absence of mindful attention. This is analogous to the cow case: the invalidation occurs through thought or the absence of thought, not through a straightforward physical act of damage.

The *gemara*'s conclusion is therefore that neither case succeeds as a proof about the nature of *hezek she'eino nikar*. In both instances, what is actually happening is that the invalidation is caused by a dimension of mental intent or attentional lapse, not by a direct physical act whose only deficiency is invisibility. The question of whether *hezek she'eino nikar shemei hezek* — whether Rabbi Yochanan or *Chizkiyah* has correctly identified the baseline — remains unresolved by these cases.

---

---

# Gittin 54

## Invisible Damage

### Mishna Setup

The daf opens on 53b, picking up the sustained discussion around the concept of *hezek she'eino nikar* — damage that is not visible. The *mishna* establishes the basic framework: when a person causes damage that is not perceptible to the eye — damage that exists in a halachic sense, because the object is worth less due to its legal status, yet cannot be seen — liability turns on intentionality. A *meizid*, one who acts willfully, must pay; a *shogeg*, one who acts accidentally, is exempt.

### Presumption

The *gemara*'s opening posture leans strongly toward treating *hezek she'eino nikar* as not constituting genuine damage at all. The reasoning is that *halacha* looks to an act of damage, not merely the causing of a loss; if the harm is invisible, it would not be classified as a true act of *mazik*, and one would be fundamentally exempt. The rabbinic intervention, then, is directed specifically at the *meizid*: in order to close the loophole that would allow a person to willfully damage another's property without consequence, the Sages decreed that intentional actors must pay. This is the *tikun olam* rationale — the rabbinic corrective is the imposition of liability in the *meizid* case. The competing position, that of Chizkiyah, runs in the opposite direction: fundamentally the actor is liable, and the Sages provided relief in the *shogeg* case so that the damaging party would have an incentive to inform the owner. The weight of the evidence accumulated thus far has been pointing toward the first view — *lo shemei hezek*, it does not constitute damage.

### Rav Pappa Challenge

At the two-dot marker near the top of 53b, Rav Pappa raises a challenge. The *gemara* cites three cases: one who steals a coin that subsequently becomes invalid, *teruma* that becomes *tamei*, and *chametz* over which Passover has passed and which is therefore worthless. In each of these cases, the thief may say to the victim *harei shelcha lefanecha* — here is your object before you, I am returning it — and this constitutes valid restitution despite the object now being essentially without value. The underlying principle is that the primary obligation of a thief is to return the stolen object itself, *v'heshiv et hagezeilah*. Since the object is being returned in the same physical state in which it was stolen, the obligation of return is discharged.

It is worth pausing to note that the three cases are not perfectly parallel. The invalid coin retains its precious metal value. *Teruma* that is *tamei* can still be burned, so it retains some use. And *chametz* that has passed over Passover is forbidden only by rabbinic decree. So none of them is truly and completely worthless — but the *gemara* treats them as functionally equivalent for purposes of this discussion.

### Harei Shelcha

The connection to *hezek she'eino nikar* is as follows. The *gemara* argues: if you maintain that *hezek she'eino nikar shemei hezek* — that invisible damage does constitute genuine damage — then this thief has caused real damage to the object, and *harei shelcha lefanecha* should not work. He would be obligated to pay full compensation, since he cannot be said to be returning the object in its original state if he has genuinely damaged it. The *gemara* therefore concludes *tiyuvta* — this is a decisive challenge — implying that the law of *harei shelcha lefanecha* proves that we do not treat such a changed object as truly different, and therefore the *mazik* would not have to pay.

### Tosafot Analysis

Tosafot presses on something genuinely puzzling here. Until this point, every proof brought in the debate about *hezek she'eino nikar* has come from the laws of *mazik*. This case, however, comes from the laws of the *gazlan* — the thief — and whether he can return a now-valueless object. These are distinct areas of *halacha*. Even if one were to say that a *mazik* who causes invisible damage must pay in the laws of damages, one might still argue that in the laws of theft — where the fundamental obligation is to return the object — the thief can say *harei shelcha lefanecha* as long as the physical object is unchanged, regardless of its changed halachic value. Why, then, does the *gemara* treat these two areas as mutually illuminating?

Tosafot answers that the comparison itself reveals something important: the question of *hezek she'eino nikar* is not merely a local question within the laws of *mazik*. It is a more fundamental and abstract question: when an object loses value without any physical change, do we consider the object itself to be different? Has it become, in some legally meaningful sense, a different object? If the answer is yes — if we say the object is substantively changed — then a *mazik* would have to pay and a *gazlan* could not say *harei shelcha lefanecha*. If the answer is no — if we say the object is not considered different — then the *mazik* is exempt and the *gazlan* may return it with that declaration. The fact that the *gemara* draws the proof from the *gazlan* case demonstrates that this is the underlying unified question, cutting across both bodies of law. The conclusion the *gemara* draws is that we do not consider the object to be changed, and thus the presumption is that a *mazik* is not liable.

---

## Tannaim Debate

### Mishna Positions

Having established that the weight of evidence favors *lo shemei hezek*, the *gemara* now asks whether this might nonetheless be a *tannaitic* debate. The *gemara* introduces a *baraita*: *ha-metamei*, *ha-medamea*, and *ha-menasech* — one who causes *tumah* to *teruma*, one who mixes *teruma* with *chullin*, and one who pours libation wine — whether done accidentally (*shogeg*) or intentionally (*meizid*), is liable according to Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda says: by *shogeg* one is exempt, by *meizid* one is liable. That is the position reflected in the *mishna* itself.

### Rabbi Meir Position

The natural reading would be that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda are debating the fundamental question of *hezek she'eino nikar* — Rabbi Meir holding *shemei hezek* (genuine damage, hence you pay even *beshogeg*) and Rabbi Yehuda holding *lo shemei hezek* (not genuine damage, hence you are fundamentally exempt but are fined in the *meizid* case).

### Rav Nachman Resolve

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, however, rejects this framing. He maintains that both opinions agree: *hezek she'eino nikar lo shemei hezek* — it does not constitute genuine damage. All the evidence has been pointing that way, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak insists the conclusion is universal. The debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda is therefore not about the fundamental nature of the damage. Rather, it concerns the scope of the rabbinic fine: given that we have already decided to impose a penalty on the *meizid*, do we extend that fine to the *shogeg* as well?

### Rabbi Yehuda Position

Rabbi Meir says yes: *knasu shogeg atu meizid* — the Sages fined the *shogeg* on account of the *meizid*. The reasons for extending the fine are practical: it is often impossible to distinguish between a *meizid* and a *shogeg*, and a willful actor could always claim accident; furthermore, even the inadvertent actor has caused real loss to another and may deserve some deterrent consequence. Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, says *lo knasu shogeg atu meizid* — the Sages did not extend the fine that broadly; they limited it to the *meizid* alone. Both positions treat the underlying liability as a *knas* — a rabbinic penalty — not a Torah-based obligation. The debate is only about how narrow or how broad that penalty should be.

---

## Reversals & Cases

### Shabbat Cooking

With this framework established, the *gemara* proceeds to demonstrate that when one examines other cases attributed to these same *tannaim*, their positions appear to reverse — sometimes dramatically. The *gemara* introduces a *baraita* about one who cooks on Shabbat. Rabbi Meir says: *beshogeg yokhal, bemeizid lo yokhal* — if done accidentally, one may eat the food; if done willfully, one may not. So here, Rabbi Meir does *not* impose a fine on the *shogeg*, only on the *meizid*. That appears to be the opposite of his position in the *hezek she'eino nikar* cases.

Rabbi Yehuda says: *beshogeg yokhal lemotza'ei Shabbat* — if done accidentally, one may eat after Shabbat ends, but not on Shabbat itself; *bemeizid lo yokhal le'olam* — if done willfully, one may never eat the food. So Rabbi Yehuda here does impose a consequence on the *shogeg* — he may not benefit from it during Shabbat itself — though not as severe a consequence as in the *meizid* case. A third opinion, that of Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar, holds that *bemeizid* neither the cook nor anyone else may ever eat the food, because from a Torah perspective the product of a willful *chilul Shabbat* is intrinsically forbidden, not merely subject to rabbinic fine. That is a separate *de'oraita* framework and is noted only in passing.

The chart that emerges is striking: in the *hezek she'eino nikar* case, Rabbi Meir fines *shogeg* and Rabbi Yehuda does not. In the Shabbat cooking case, Rabbi Meir does *not* fine *shogeg* and Rabbi Yehuda does. They have switched sides.

### Meir's Principle

The *gemara* resolves Rabbi Meir's apparent self-contradiction: *ki kanis bidrabbanan, bede'oraita lo kanis* — Rabbi Meir imposes the fine on a *shogeg* only in the context of a rabbinic violation, not a biblical one. The logic runs as follows: when the underlying prohibition is *de'oraita*, people are already vigilant; the weight of the Torah obligation creates its own deterrent, and there is no particular laxity to correct. By contrast, where the prohibition is only rabbinic, people are more likely to be casual, and there is a genuine slippery slope that requires the rabbis to step in and fine even the *shogeg* to tighten enforcement.

In the *hezek she'eino nikar* cases (*metamei*, *medamea*, *menasech*), the underlying acts — causing others financial loss — are in the domain of a rabbinic corrective, and so Rabbi Meir fines the *shogeg*. In the Shabbat cooking case, one has violated a *de'oraita* prohibition, and Rabbi Meir does not extend the fine.

### Avodah Zara Exception

The *gemara* immediately presses a difficulty: one of the cases in the *mishna* is *menasech* — pouring libations to *avodah zarah* — which is itself a *de'oraita* violation. Why does Rabbi Meir fine there? The *gemara* answers: *mishum chumra de'avodah zarah kanis lei* — because of the unique severity of *avodah zarah*, Rabbi Meir treats it as a special case and does fine. The very extremity of *avodah zarah* as a transgression overrides the general rule, and the fine is imposed regardless. This is structurally ironic — the gravity of the offense that would normally counsel against fining is here the very reason for the fine — but the *gemara* accepts this as the explanation.

### Yehuda's Reverse

Rabbi Yehuda's self-contradiction is resolved by applying the mirror-image principle: *ki lo kanis bidrabbanan, de'oraita kanis* — Rabbi Yehuda does *not* fine the *shogeg* for a rabbinic violation, but does fine him for a biblical one. Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning operates in the opposite direction from Rabbi Meir's: where the violation is biblical and weighty, Rabbi Yehuda feels there is both justification and need for imposing the fine even on the inadvertent actor. Where the violation is merely rabbinic, he limits the fine to the *meizid*.

Again the *gemara* presses: the *mishna* case of *menasech* is also biblical — why does Rabbi Yehuda not fine there? The answer is the same logic reversed: *mishum chumra de'avodat kokhavim mivdal badle minei* — the severity of idolatry is so extreme that people are simply not going to commit it; there is no need for a rabbinic deterrent, because *avodah zarah* is self-deterring by virtue of its theological weight.

### Planting Cases

The *gemara* is not yet satisfied. It introduces a *baraita* about planting on Shabbat and planting during *shemita* to demonstrate that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda appear to reverse themselves even within the category of *de'oraita* violations. The *baraita* states: one who plants on Shabbat — *beshogeg yekayem*, if done accidentally the planting may stand; *bemeizid ye'aker*, if done willfully it must be uprooted — according to Rabbi Meir. On *shemita*, however, whether *shogeg* or *meizid*, the planting must be uprooted — Rabbi Meir. And Rabbi Yehuda takes the opposite positions: on *shemita*, *beshogeg yekayem*; on Shabbat, whether *shogeg* or *meizid*, it must be uprooted.

This is more difficult to resolve through the *de'oraita*/*derabbanan* distinction because both Shabbat and *shemita* are *de'oraita*. The *gemara* points out that the problem actually emerges from within the *baraita* itself: why do both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda treat Shabbat and *shemita* differently from each other when both are biblical?

### Shemita Laxity

The *gemara* turns to a statement in the *baraita* where Rabbi Meir himself explains his reasoning. He says: why do I rule *beshogeg yekayem* for Shabbat but impose uprooting even for *shogeg* on *shemita*? One reason: *mipnei she-yisrael monin lishmita ve-ein monin leShabbasos* — because the Jewish people count years according to the *shemita* cycle but do not count by Shabbat weeks in the same way. The practical consequence is that if someone planted during *shemita* and one does the arithmetic from when the fruit becomes edible, it will be evident to everyone that the planting occurred during the *shemita* year. That public visibility is a violation of *shemita*'s sanctity, and therefore we force uprooting to prevent the impression that such planting was condoned. By contrast, there is no corresponding calculation that reveals whether a planting occurred on a weekday or on Shabbat.

An additional explanation is given: *necheshdu Yisrael al hashevi'is ve-lo necheshdu al haShabbatos* — Israel was suspected of laxity regarding *shemita* observance, but not regarding Shabbat. This is the more direct parallel to Rabbi Meir's general principle. Even though *shemita* is *de'oraita*, the actual observance level in the community was loose — there was practical laxity around *shemita* — and so it resembles a *derabbanan* situation in terms of behavioral patterns. Since people treat it with insufficient seriousness, Rabbi Meir applies the same logic that would normally attach to a *derabbanan* violation: fine the *shogeg* to create enforcement. The *gemara* offers a brief intermediate discussion about whether someone planting near the end of a year could be detected as having planted on Shabbat, before ultimately settling on the *necheshdu* principle as the operative reason.

Rabbi Yehuda's reverse position on *shemita* is explained by the local tradition in Rabbi Yehuda's locale: *be'atrei de-Rabbi Yehuda chamru lehu shevi'is* — in Rabbi Yehuda's region, *shemita* was observed with great stringency, and therefore there was no need for an additional rabbinic fine in the *shogeg* case. The *gemara* cites an anecdote about someone in that region who boasted to a neighbor that he did not eat *shemita* produce as others did, suggesting a culture of heightened *shemita* observance. Admittedly the connection is not entirely self-evident — the anecdote might equally demonstrate that violations were common enough to be noteworthy — but the *gemara* cites it as evidence of local stringency.

---

## Teruma Case

### Tashlumin Halakha

The *gemara* now introduces the laws of someone who eats a *kohen*'s *teruma*. The baseline *halacha* is that eating *teruma* intentionally (*meizid*) makes one liable to pay its monetary value. Eating it accidentally (*shogeg*), however, triggers a different mechanism: one must pay back in food, and that food, upon transfer to the *kohen*, itself becomes *teruma*. There is a debate about whether the quantity or the value must be matched, but the basic structure is that the repayment is made in food which takes on *teruma* status in the act of being given.

The present case involves someone who ate *teruma temeiah* — ritually impure *teruma*, which has substantially diminished value, since a *kohen* in a state of *tumah* can consume it but its general utility is limited. The question is what happens when this person repays with *chullin temeiim* — impure ordinary food — rather than *chullin tehorim*, which is what he should have given, since the latter would upon transfer become *teruma tehorah*, the more valuable form of *teruma*.

### Sumchus Position

Sumchus, in the name of Rabbi Meir, rules: *beshogeg, tashlumin tashlumin* — if done accidentally, the repayment counts and the obligation is discharged; *bemeizid, ein tashlumin tashlumin* — if done willfully, the repayment does not count. The *hakhamim* say: in both cases the payment counts as *teruma*, but in both cases the person must pay a second time with *chullin tehorim*. So Rabbi Meir fines only the *meizid*, whereas the *hakhamim* fine even the *shogeg*.

### Challenge to Fine

Before applying this to the larger debate, the *gemara* raises a striking logical question: why should willfully repaying *chullin temeiim* not count at all? The *kohen* ate *teruma temeiah*, which he could consume only in a state of *tumah* and which was of diminished value. The person repaying gave back *chullin temeiim*, which the *kohen* could likewise consume while *tamei*. Yes, the food became *teruma temeiah* upon transfer, but what exactly is the harm? The *kohen* has received back something functionally equivalent to what was taken.

### Rava Reinterprets

Rava, and some transmit it anonymously, responds with a radical solution: *chasuri michasra vehachi katani* — the *baraita* is incomplete as stated and must be reread. The entire scenario must be reframed. The *baraita* is not speaking of a case where one ate *teruma temeiah* and repaid with *chullin temeiim*. Rather, the case must be that one ate *teruma tehorah* — pure *teruma*, of full value — and then repaid with *chullin temeiim*. Now it is obvious why repaying with impure food is inadequate: the *kohen* had pure *teruma* taken from him, and he is now receiving back something far less valuable (whether measured by value according to Rashi, or by utility and convenience according to Tosafot, who holds the repayment is matched by value but notes that people prefer less *teruma tehorah* over more *teruma temeiah*). The *baraita* thus becomes: *achal teruma tehorah, meshalem chullin tehorim* — you ate pure *teruma*, you must repay with pure *chullin*. If instead you repaid with *chullin temeiim* (*shilem chullin temeim*), Sumchus in the name of Rabbi Meir says: *beshogeg, tashlumin tashlumin*; *bemeizid, ein tashlumin tashlumin*. And the *hakhamim* fine in both cases.

### Restitution Policy

Applying this to the Rabbi Meir / Rabbi Yehuda structure: the inadequate repayment is a *derabbanan* violation, and Rabbi Meir would normally fine the *shogeg* in *derabbanan* cases. Why then does Rabbi Meir not fine the *shogeg* here? The *gemara* says: *hatam gavra lishlumei ka michavein, anushei uveli knisa?* — there, the person is trying to make restitution; are we going to impose a fine on him? The critical distinction Rabbi Meir draws is between an act that is fundamentally bad — causing damage, acting destructively — and an act that is fundamentally good or remedial. Rabbi Meir's policy of fining *shogegin* in *derabbanan* cases is directed at curbing negligent harmful conduct. When someone is in the process of trying to make things right, even if he does it imperfectly, applying that fine is counterproductive. We do not penalize people who are genuinely trying to remedy a situation.

This principle is then applied to two additional cases the *gemara* had already addressed but which fit the same analysis. One who takes *maaser* on Shabbat (*hame'aser beShabbat*) — a rabbinic violation of Shabbat — is told *beshogeg yokhal, bemeizid lo yokhal*. Why is Rabbi Meir not fining the *shogeg* here, given that this is a *derabbanan* violation? *Hatam gavra letikuni kamikhaven* — the person was trying to do a *mitzvah*, separating *terumot u'maasrot*. Similarly, one who immerses vessels in a *mikvah* on Shabbat (*hamatbil kelim beShabbat*), again a rabbinic violation: *beshogeg yeshtamesh bahem, bemeizid lo yeshtamesh bahem*. Why no fine for *shogeg*? *Hatam gavra letahorei kamikhaven* — he was trying to purify his vessels.

### Dam & Meserech

There is one additional case that was returned to after it had initially been overlooked: *dam she-nitma ve-zarko* — blood of a *korban* that became *tamei* and was thrown on the *mizbeach*. The *halacha* is that even if such blood is thrown *bemeizid*, the *korban* is still valid because the *tzitz* worn by the *kohen gadol* has the power to render such service acceptable. Rashi clarifies that throwing *tamei* blood is itself only a rabbinic violation, since the presence of the *tzitz* makes it *de'oraita* permissible. The *baraita* rules: *beshogeg hurtzah, bemeizid lo hurtzah* — if accidental, the service is accepted; if willful, it is not, meaning the *kohanim* may not eat the meat. Why does Rabbi Meir not fine the *shogeg* here, given the *derabbanan* character of the violation? *Hatam gavra lechapporei kamikhaven* — the *kohen* is engaged in the *avodah*, trying to achieve atonement for the owners. One does not impose fines on people in the midst of performing *mitzvot* and the Temple service.

The corresponding case for Rabbi Yehuda's apparent reversal also involves the *derabbanan* category. In the case of *nafelu nitpatzu* — precious nuts, some of which are *orlah*, that all get cracked and thereby lose their *chashivus* (halachic significance) and become *batel* — Rabbi Meir says whether *shogeg* or *meizid*, the mixture remains forbidden. This is consistent with Rabbi Meir. But Rabbi Yehuda joins Rabbi Meir — which is inconsistent with Rabbi Yehuda's usual position of not fining in *derabbanan* cases. Rabbis Yose and Shimon, by contrast, are lenient and only disallow the mixture when it was *meizid*. The *gemara* explains Rabbi Yehuda's strictness: *mishum de-ati le'arumei* — because in this scenario there is a powerful incentive to scheme. If a person's entire stock of valuable nuts is ruined because of a single *orlah* nut, the temptation to deliberately crush them all and then claim it was an accident is enormous. Rabbi Yehuda therefore closes off this avenue by not distinguishing between *shogeg* and *meizid* at all.

Finally, regarding Rabbi Yose's reversal in the case of a shoot of *orlah* mixed with other plantings (*netia shel orlah she-nit'arba benetiot acherot*): Rabbi Yose there rules that even intentional picking (which creates *bitul*) is acceptable — *afilu mitkavein lilkot, ya'alu be'echad umatayim*. This seems far more lenient than his position on the nuts. The *gemara* resolves this by citing the principle of Rabbah and Rabbi Yochanan: *chazakah ein adam oser karmo benetiyah achat* — it is simply inconceivable that a person would allow an *orlah* shoot to be planted among his other vines without having taken precautions. The scenario is so implausible, so unlikely ever to arise in practice, that the rabbis did not impose their stricter rules upon it. The nuts case, by contrast, involves a genuinely common scenario, and there fining is warranted.

---

## Pigul & Testimony

### Pigul Definition

The *gemara* now pivots from the question of liability for *hezek she'eino nikar* to the question of testimonial credibility regarding invisible acts. The setting is *pigul*: a *korban* is rendered *pigul* — halachically disqualified — when the *kohen* performing the service harbors the intention at the wrong moment to eat it or offer it beyond its permitted time. This is an invisible act; no one can see what the *kohen* is thinking. The *mishna* says that *kohanim* who intentionally cause *pigul* are liable to the owners. The underlying *hezek she'eino nikar* question has already been resolved — we fine the *meizid*. But now the *gemara* turns to a different question: when will we believe someone who claims such an invisible act occurred?

### Abaye: Immediate

A *baraita* is introduced: if one was working together with another person on *taharot* (maintaining ritual purity) and declared *taharot she'asiti imcha nitme'u* — the pure items we were working on together have become *tamei* — he is believed (*ne'eman*). Similarly, a *kohen* who declares during or immediately upon the service that *zvachim she'asiti imcha nitpiglu* — the sacrifices I performed for you have been rendered *pigul* — is believed. But if the same person comes days later and says *taharot she'asiti imcha beyom ploni nitme'u* or *zvachim she'asiti imcha beyom ploni nitpiglu* — referring to events of a specific past date — he is not believed (*eino ne'eman*).

Abaye explains the distinction through the principle of *kol shebeyado ne'eman* — whoever has the matter in his control is believed. At the moment of the first declaration, the person is still actively working with the *taharot* or the *kohen* has shechted the animal but not yet thrown the blood.
