Because he retains control over the outcome — he could render them *tamei* or *pigul* at this very moment if he chose — this gives his claim a special credibility, somewhat analogous to a *migo*. According to Abaye, this principle applies strictly: the person must literally still have the matter in hand.

### Rava: Suspicion

Rava disagrees with Abaye's framework. It is not necessary that the act still be *mamash beyado* at the moment of the claim. Rather, the reason for disbelieving the later claim is not absence of control but suspicious delay: *keivan de'ashkechei velo amar lei velo midi* — since he encountered the person and said nothing at the time, and only later makes the claim, the delay itself is suspicious. Why would someone who witnessed or caused a problem fail to mention it immediately? The belated disclosure raises the inference of ulterior motive. But if someone reports the issue promptly after completing the service — even if it is technically no longer *beyado* — he would be believed under Rava's view.

### Delayed Claim

The practical upshot is that if someone waited and then came to another person saying, for instance, that three days ago the *taharot* became *tamei*, his claim is rejected. A case is brought before Rabbi Ami involving precisely this scenario, and Rabbi Ami rules *eino ne'eman* — he is not believed, because the claim concerns something that happened in the past with no immediate disclosure.

### Kohen Gadol

Rabbi Assi raises a counterposition in the name of Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yossi: *ma e'eseh she-haTorah he'eminaso* — what can I do, the Torah has believed him. The *gemara* asks: where does the Torah demonstrate this believability? Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna answers: the *kohen gadol* on Yom Kippur serves as proof. If the *kohen gadol* were to emerge from the *Kodesh Kodashim* and declare that something had gone wrong — that the service had been rendered *pigul*, for example — presumably we would believe him, even though the act occurred in a space where no other person was permitted. This shows that even after the fact, the Torah grants believability to such declarations.

The *gemara* challenges this: perhaps we would only believe the *kohen gadol* because we heard his voice from within, indicating something was said at the time of the service. The *gemara* responds: that would not suffice either, because the *kohen gadol* could have uttered those words after performing the service, intending to deceive. Therefore it must be that the Torah grants inherent credibility to such testimony. The *gemara* then raises a further challenge — perhaps there were peepholes through which observers could have seen the *kohen gadol* — and ultimately concedes *kashya*: it is not an airtight proof. The case of the *kohen gadol* may be consistent with Rava's position — that if the declaration came immediately upon emerging, there was no suspicious delay — so it does not definitively establish the broader point.

---

## Sefer Torah Cases

### Rabbi Ami Rules

A case is brought before Rabbi Ami: a scribe who had written a *Sefer Torah* for a client comes forward and admits that when writing the divine names (*azkarot*), he did not write them *lishmah* — with the proper intention. The *Sefer Torah* has already been transferred to the purchaser; it is no longer *beyado*. Rabbi Ami rules: *ne'eman atah lehafsid sekharekha ve-i atah ne'eman lehafsid Sefer Torah* — you are believed to the extent that you forfeit your fee, but you are not believed to render the *Sefer Torah pasul*. The *Sefer Torah* retains its *kasher* status in the hands of the purchaser, while the scribe loses his payment for having admitted to performing the work improperly.

This creates an apparent internal tension: if the *Sefer Torah* is going to be treated as valid for the purchaser's use, why should the scribe not be paid for a valid *Sefer Torah*? The *gemara* does not fully resolve this in this context; Rabbi Ami's ruling simply bifurcates the two consequences.

### Yirmiyah Question

Rabbi Yirmiyah presses the ruling further: granted that the scribe has forfeited some fee — but must he lose the entire fee for the *Sefer Torah*? He wrote the entire text correctly; only the *azkarot* were written without proper intention. Surely he should at minimum be paid for all the writing other than the *Shem Hashem* portions?

### Worthlessness

Rabbi Ami responds: *she-kol Sefer Torah she-ein azkaroteha ketuvot lishmah einah shaveh klum* — a *Sefer Torah* whose divine names were not written *lishmah* is worth nothing at all. The reason: one cannot simply rewrite the names. Erasing *Shem Hashem* is forbidden. There is no remediation available.

### Spotted Look

The *gemara* presses: why not simply re-ink over the names? Could Rabbi Yehuda's ruling be invoked here — that *ma'avir alav kulmus u-mekadesho*, one may re-ink and thereby sanctify the writing? The *gemara* answers that Rabbi Yehuda only permits re-inking a single name. To re-ink every instance of *Shem Hashem* throughout an entire *Sefer Torah* — *mishum de-mikhzei ke-menumar* — would make the scroll appear spotted, with every divine name visibly different from the surrounding text. A *Sefer Torah* that appears this way is not fit for use, whether this is a *de'oraita* or *derabbanan* disqualification. Either way, the scribe has produced something worthless, and accordingly forfeits his entire fee.

### Rabbi Abbahu Rules

A parallel case is brought before Rabbi Abbahu: a scribe comes forward and says that the *gevilin* — the parchment — of a *Sefer Torah* he wrote for a client were not processed *lishmah*, with the requisite intention during their preparation. The *Sefer Torah* is already in the purchaser's possession. Rabbi Abbahu rules: *mitoch she'ata ne'eman lehafsid sekharekha, ata ne'eman lehafsid Sefer Torah* — since you are believed to lose your fee, you are also believed to render the *Sefer Torah pasul*. This is the opposite of Rabbi Ami's ruling: Rabbi Abbahu believes the scribe not only about his financial loss but about the invalidity of the scroll.

### Reconciliation

The *gemara* confronts the apparent contradiction between Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Abbahu. It resolves the two cases by focusing on the scribe's financial exposure. In Rabbi Ami's case, where only the *azkarot* were written without *lishmah*, Rabbi Yirmiyah had raised a reasonable argument that the scribe should perhaps only lose the fee for writing the divine names, not the entire fee. One might say the scribe calculated that he was in a relatively favorable position — he could claim to lose only a small portion of his fee while the *Sefer Torah* would be disqualified. There was therefore an incentive to make the false claim: he would lose very little while harming the purchaser's *Sefer Torah*. Since the claim carried only limited financial self-damage, the *migo*-like circumstantial argument for truthfulness is not compelling, and we therefore do not extend his believability to *poseling* the scroll.

In Rabbi Abbahu's case, the *gevilin* themselves — every single piece of parchment — were not processed *lishmah*. There is no question of partial loss: the entire *Sefer Torah* is unambiguously worthless, and the scribe will forfeit his entire fee. *Kivan de-ka mafsid kula agrei* — since he knows he will lose everything and comes forward anyway, *eimar kushta ka'amar* — we must presume he is telling the truth. The magnitude of his financial self-sacrifice eliminates any plausible ulterior motive, and this circumstantial evidence of truthfulness is sufficient to believe him even though the matter is no longer technically *beyado*.

---

---

# Gittin 55

## R. Yochanan ben Gudguda

### Opening & Mishna

Daf 55 of *Gittin* opens by continuing the broader sugya of enactments made for *tikkun ha-olam* and similar *takkanot*. The *mishna* presents the testimonies of Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudguda — a *mishna* that appears as well in *Eduyos*, the tractate dedicated to collecting halachic traditions that various Sages transmitted. Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudguda testified to four distinct rulings, each of which, as we shall see, carries its own significance for the theme of rabbinic enactment.

### Chereshet & Divorce

The first testimony concerns a *chereshet* — a deaf woman. The term *chereshet* technically refers to one who is deaf-mute, though it does not necessarily mean she is entirely incapable of speech; rather, because she was born deaf and had no means of learning intelligible language in the manner of hearing people, *halacha* categorizes her as someone without sufficient *da'as* to be obligated in *mitzvos* or to execute binding legal transactions. This assumption, it should be noted, is rooted in pre-modern realities: until relatively recent centuries, when schools for the deaf were developed and sign language emerged, it was widely believed that deafness precluded the development of full intellect. *Halacha* operated within that understanding, and the reassessment of that assumption is itself a significant discussion of the past few hundred years.

In the case before us, the girl is both a minor and a *chereshet*, meaning she has two reasons why she cannot independently transact. However, a father has the authority to betroth his minor daughter, and that betrothal is binding *d'oraisa*. Now the husband wishes to divorce her, and the question arises: since we assume she lacks full *da'as*, does she have sufficient awareness to receive a *get* properly? Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudguda testified that yes, *yotzei b'get* — the delivery of a *get* does work. The reasoning: since a woman can be divorced even against her will, it follows that she can be divorced even without full cognizance of what is occurring. That conclusion is striking — not being willing and not being fully aware are not necessarily the same thing — yet that is the *halacha* as received.

### Ketana & Teruma

The second testimony involves a *ketana bat yisrael* married to a *kohen*. When a minor girl is married not by her father but through her mother and brothers, that marriage is only *d'rabbanan* — the Torah does not recognize it as a fully binding betrothal, but the rabbis established it to protect the interests of girls in a society where they could not generally provide for themselves independently. Despite being only a rabbinic marriage, Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudguda testified that *ocheles biterumah* — she may eat *teruma*. A *kohen*'s wife is permitted to eat *teruma*, and even though this marriage is not Torah-binding, it was treated with sufficient weight that she was allowed to eat it. The reasoning behind this, and how it is possible given the rabbinic nature of the marriage, is developed at length in the *gemara*.

The *mishna* also states *ve'im mesa ba'ala yorshah* — if she dies, her husband inherits her. Even for a *d'rabbanan* marriage, the inheritance follows the same rule as a Torah marriage.

### Marish Gazul

The third testimony concerns a stolen beam — *marish gazul* — that has been incorporated into a building. In principle, if a stolen object retains its identity and can still be identified, the owner has a right to reclaim it. In some cases, the beam might be embedded deep within a structure and yet technically still be the same beam it always was, with no sufficient *shinui* to sever the owner's claim. The *halacha* established was nevertheless that *shekinitahu* — the owner is simply paid the monetary value of the beam and cannot demand its physical return. The reason given is *mishum takanas hashavim* — because we wish to enable and encourage repentance. We do not want the practical consequences of returning stolen property to become so burdensome that they deter people from owning up to their wrongdoing.

### Chatas Gazula

The fourth testimony concerns *chatat hagzulah shelo nodah larabim* — a stolen sin-offering that was not publicly known to be stolen. The case in the *gemara* is specific: Reuven stole Shimon's unsanctified animal and then sanctified it himself as his own *korban*. The question is whether this *korban* — stolen and then sanctified by the thief — can function as a valid *chatat* for Reuven. The *mishna* rules that if the theft was not public knowledge, *hi mechaperes* — it does atone — *mipnei tikkun hamizbe'ach*, for the sake of the *mizbeach*. The precise import of this phrase, and the underlying question of what the *d'oraisa* rule actually is, occupies the *gemara* at considerable length.

### Mnemonic Pattern

It is worth noting that while these four testimonies may appear random, there is a mnemonic logic connecting them. The first case begins with *hisia aviha* — her father married her off — the *chereshet*. The next case flows naturally: *niset l'kohen* — she married a *kohen*, with the husband ultimately inheriting her. Then comes *hamarish hagazul*, the stolen beam. And finally *chatat hagzulah shelo nodah larabim*. Each testimony flows into the next through shared language or shared conceptual links, allowing one to remember the full sequence.

---

## Chereshet Divorce

### Undisclosed Get Case

The *gemara* opens its analysis with a ruling from Rava. From the testimony of Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudguda, Rava derives an additional *halacha*: if a man said to witnesses, "See this *get* — I am about to give it to my wife," and then folded it up and handed it to her while telling her it was a *shtar chov* — a promissory note — without disclosing it was a *get*, and she took possession of it, *harei zo megureshet* — she is in fact divorced. The delivery worked, even though she was entirely unaware that she was receiving a *get*.

### No Cognizance Needed

The source for this ruling is the principle derived from Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudguda: *lo bainan da'atah* — we do not require her full awareness. Just as the *chereshet*, who we assume lacks full *da'as*, can nonetheless receive a *get*, so too a woman who takes possession of a *get* without knowing it is a *get* is divorced. The *gemara* anticipates the objection that this should be obvious once the *chereshet* principle is established, but then raises a genuine concern.

### Nullification Question

One might argue that the two cases are not analogous. In the *chereshet* case, the husband simply did not inform her of the meaning of what was happening — a passive absence of communication. But here, when the husband says "take this *shtar chov*," he is actively calling it something other than a *get*. Perhaps this constitutes a *bittul* — a nullification — of the *get*'s status. Perhaps by reframing the act of giving, he has effectively undone the *get*.

### Witness Declaration

The *gemara* responds: *im ita d'vatleih, leadurei hava amar lehu* — if he truly intended to nullify the *get*, he would have gone back and told the witnesses. He had already declared to the witnesses that he was divorcing his wife. The fact that he did not update them demonstrates that the statement "take this *shtar chov*" was not meant as a *bittul*. *V'hai d'kamar hachi mishum kisufa* — he called it a *shtar chov* out of embarrassment, or perhaps simply to be particularly unkind, but it was not a formal reframing of the act. The *get* therefore stands.

---

## Ketana Teruma

### Why Ketana?

The *gemara* turns to the second testimony — the *ketana* married to a *kohen* who eats *teruma* — and immediately asks a pointed question. If the goal of this testimony was to establish that a *d'rabbanan* marriage to a *kohen* is sufficient to allow the wife to eat *teruma*, why did the *mishna* move to the case of a *ketana*? We had just been discussing the *chereshet*, whose marriage is also *d'rabbanan*. Why not remain with the *chereshet* and use her as the example? The implicit answer, which the *gemara* explores, is that *v'ilu hereshet lo achla* — the *mishna* is implying that a *chereshet* could not eat *teruma* in that situation. And the *gemara* sets out to explain why.

### Cheresh Gezeira

The concern is a *gezeira*: *shema ya'achil cheresh b'chereshet* — we are afraid that allowing a *chereshet* married to a hearing *kohen* to eat *teruma* will lead people to allow a *cheresh* — a deaf male *kohen* — married to a hearing, fully obligated woman to similarly feed her *teruma*. And why is this such a problem? The *gemara* clarifies: a *chereshet* married to a hearing *kohen* — the person eating is the *chereshet*, who is not halachically obligated, so one might argue the violation is tolerable given the practical need to validate the *d'rabbanan* marriage. But the mirror image — a *cheresh kohen* married to a *pikachat*, a hearing and fully obligated woman — in that case, *she* is eating *teruma*, and she is fully obligated, and her eating genuinely prohibited *teruma* is a real violation.

### Mirror Image Problem

Here lies the structural problem. The *chereshet* case and the *cheresh* case are natural mirror images of each other. If we permit the *chereshet* to eat, it will be easy to allow the analogous *cheresh* case as well — and in that case, a fully obligated woman would be eating *teruma* she is not permitted to eat. Since we cannot permit the *cheresh* case, we must also prohibit the *chereshet* case, to prevent one from leading to the other. The *ketana* case, by contrast, does not have this mirror-image problem. *Halacha* recognizes the marriage of an adult male to an underage female, both *d'oraisa* through the father and *d'rabbanan* through the mother and brothers, but it does not recognize the marriage of a minor male to an adult female — neither *d'oraisa* nor *d'rabbanan*. Since the reverse scenario does not exist, the fear of a problematic mirror image is eliminated, and we can permit the *ketana* to eat *teruma* without concern that this will lead to any genuine violation.

### Teruma Allowance

The *gemara* then asks: even if we concede that the *chereshet* case cannot work for *teruma d'oraisa*, why not allow her at least to eat *teruma d'rabbanan* — rabbinic-level *teruma*, applicable, for example, to produce not ordinarily subject to the full Torah prohibition? Then, even if the *cheresh* case were to arise in its mirror image, the woman eating would only be violating a rabbinic prohibition. The *gemara* responds: *gezeira shema ati l'meichal b'teruma d'oraisa* — we are nonetheless concerned that permitting *teruma d'rabbanan* in the *chereshet* case will ultimately lead to eating *teruma d'oraisa* in the *cheresh* case. Even though this requires two things to go wrong, sometimes two layers of protection are warranted, and here the rabbis chose to apply that stricter approach.

Rashi adds that even in the *ketana* case, we are likely dealing with *teruma d'rabbanan*, though the *gemara* itself seems comfortable suggesting that even *teruma d'oraisa* would be permitted in the *ketana* case, since as a minor she is not obligated, and there is no mirror-image scenario to fear.

---

## Marish Gazul Dispute

### Demolition vs. Payment

A *baraita* presents the dispute between Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel on the question of the stolen beam. If one stole a beam and incorporated it into a building, Beis Shammai rules *meka'ke'a kol habira kula u'machazir marish l'ba'alav* — he must demolish the entire building and return the actual beam to its owner. Beis Shammai, characteristically uncompromising in upholding strict legal entitlement, holds that the thief's practical difficulty is irrelevant. The owner's right to his property cannot be subordinated to the thief's interest in keeping his building intact.

### Takanas Hashavim

Beis Hillel, by contrast, rules *ein lo ela d'mei marish bilvad* — the owner is entitled only to the monetary value of the beam. The reason: *mishum takanas hashavim* — to encourage repentance. If the *halacha* demanded complete demolition, many thieves would be deterred from ever admitting their wrongdoing or seeking to make amends, calculating that the cost of restitution is too catastrophic. By limiting the obligation to a monetary payment, the rabbis removed that obstacle and made *teshuva* a realistic and accessible path.

---

## Chatas Gazula

### Ulla's Position

The *gemara* now presents two competing views on the underlying *d'oraisa* status of the stolen *korban*. Ulla holds: *devar Torah bein noda bein lo noda einah mechaperes* — by Torah law, whether the theft was publicly known or not, the stolen *korban* does not atone. His reasoning is *yeiush k'dei lo kani* — *yeiush* alone, without *shinui reshus*, does not transfer ownership to the thief.

To understand this, one must recall the general debate about *yeiush*. When an owner despairs of recovering a lost or stolen object, does that despair itself confer ownership on whoever holds it? In the case of a lost object found by a third party, *yeiush* combined with *shinui reshus* — a change of domain — does effect a transfer. But the *gazlan* is different. He was holding the object at the very moment the owner gave up hope. He cannot claim that the owner's despair freed up the object for him to acquire, since he took it while it was fully under the owner's control and he has an independent obligation to return it. So *yeiush* alone, while the object remains in the *gazlan*'s hands, does not work.

If Reuven's *yeiush* did not transfer ownership to him, then when Reuven sanctified the animal, he was sanctifying something that was not his. One could argue that the act of sanctification itself constitutes a *shinui reshus* — a transfer into the domain of *hekdesh* — or a *shinui hashem*, a change of identity, such that the animal becomes genuinely sanctified. The *gemara* entertains both possibilities. It is possible that the animal does become a valid *korban* but remains one that cannot atone for Reuven, since at the moment he sanctified it, it was still stolen — applying the principle of *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah*. Either way, according to Ulla, the *d'oraisa* baseline is that this *korban* does not atone.

### Kohanim Anxiety

Given that this is Ulla's position, the *gemara* asks: *uma ta'am amru lo noda mechaperes?* — why then did the rabbis say that if the theft was not publicly known, it does atone? The answer: *shelo yehu kohanim atzeivim* — so that the *kohanim* should not be filled with anguish. The *kohanim* eat from the *korban*, and if they are always anxious that they might have consumed from a stolen offering that was not truly valid — and therefore may not have been truly a *korban*, leaving them in a state of having eaten what was in effect *chullin she-nishchatu ba-azarah* — they would become paralyzed with worry. Their anxiety would disrupt the entire operation of the *mikdash*.

The *gemara* notes that the language of the *mishna* says *mipnei tikkun hamizbe'ach*, not *mipnei kohanim atzeivim*. Ulla responds: *keivan de-kohanim atzeivim nimtza mizbe'ach batel* — since if the *kohanim* are anguished, the *mizbeach* itself will be impaired. The two are inseparable: the functioning of the *mizbeach* depends on the *kohanim* being able to perform their service with confidence and wholeness. Therefore, when it is not publicly known, we declare the *korban* valid — even though *d'oraisa* it should not be — so that the *kohanim* will not be consumed by worry. However, when the theft is public knowledge, we cannot extend that protection, and the *korban* will not be accepted.

### Rav Yehuda Position

Rav Yehuda takes the opposite *d'oraisa* position: *bein noda bein lo noda mechapper* — by Torah law, it atones regardless of whether the theft was known. His reasoning: *yeiush k'dei kani* — *yeiush* does work to transfer ownership. The moment Shimon despaired of recovering his animal, Reuven became the owner. When Reuven then sanctified it, it was already his, and therefore it is a completely valid *korban* that should work in every case.

### Mizbeach & Theft

According to Rav Yehuda, the *takana* runs in the other direction. The *takana* is not to expand the circumstances in which the *korban* works, but to restrict it: *shelo yomru mizbe'ach ochel gezeilos* — so that people should not say that the *mizbe'ach* consumes stolen goods. If a thief can steal an animal and then bring it publicly as a *korban* and have it accepted, it creates a horrific impression: that the *mizbeach* is complicit in theft, that one can steal and atone through that very stolen object. The *pasuk* states *sonei gezel b'olah* — Hashem despises theft in a burnt offering — and this concern extends even to a *chatat*, where only the blood and fats go on the *mizbeach* while the *kohanim* eat the meat. Even in that case, the *gemara* concludes, it still models the *mizbeach* consuming stolen property, and we must not allow that when the theft is publicly known.

The *gemara* then asks: according to Rav Yehuda, why did the *mishna* specifically mention a *chatat*? If the concern is that the *mizbeach* appears to consume stolen goods, surely an *olah* — which is entirely consumed on the *mizbeach* — would be even more problematic. The *gemara* answers *lo mibaya ka'amar*: it goes without saying that a publicly stolen *olah* would not be accepted. The *mishna* chooses the *chatat* precisely because one might have thought it less objectionable — only the blood and fats go on the *mizbeach*, and the meat is eaten by the *kohanim* — and one might argue this does not really look like the *mizbeach* consuming stolen goods. The *mishna* therefore teaches that even so, the rabbis prohibited it, because it still gives the impression of the *mizbeach* endorsing theft.

---

## Slaughter Outside Mikdash

### Kereis Question

Rava now raises a powerful challenge against Ulla's position from a *mishna* elsewhere. The *mishna* states: *ganav vehikdish v'achar kach tavach umachar* — one stole, sanctified, and then slaughtered or sold the animal. He pays double (*tashlumei kefel*) for the theft, but does not pay the fourfold or fivefold payment (*tashlumei arba va-chamisha*) for slaughtering or selling, because by the time he slaughtered or sold it, it had already passed into *hekdesh* and was no longer in Shimon's ownership — therefore Shimon no longer has that claim. This much Ulla can accommodate.

But the *mishna* continues: *vetani alah, bachutz kehai gavna anush kares* — if he took this sanctified animal and slaughtered it outside the *beit hamikdash*, he is liable for *kares*, the penalty for *shichutei chutz* — offering a sanctified animal outside the *mikdash*. This is deeply problematic for Ulla. One is only liable for *kares* for slaughtering outside the *mikdash* something that would have been a valid *korban* inside the *mikdash*. If the animal is valid enough to generate *kares* when slaughtered outside, it implies that it would have worked as a valid *korban* inside — which is exactly what Ulla denies.

### Kereis Midvreihem

Rav Shizbi attempted to resolve this by suggesting that the *kares* here is *midivreihem* — a rabbinic enactment that treats it as if *kares* applies, even though it would not apply *d'oraisa*. 

### Kereis Cannot Be Rabbinic

This answer was met with laughter in the *beit midrash*, and Rava rebuked that response: *gavra rabba amar milta, lo techechu alei* — a great Sage said something; do not laugh at it. There must be something to it. But the substantive rejection stands: there is no such thing as *kares midivrehem*. Rabbinic enactments can prohibit actions, can impose lashes, but *kares* is a metaphysical reality — premature death at the hands of Heaven. The rabbis cannot create that. When the *mishna* says *kares*, it means *kares d'oraisa*.

Rava therefore reframes what Rav Shizbi must have meant: *kares al yedei divreihem ba lo* — the *kares* comes to him through the medium of a rabbinic enactment. It is a genuine *d'oraisa kares*, but it arrives as a consequence of what the rabbis did.

---

## Retroactive Ownership

### Before Sanctification

Tosafos provides the clearest explanation of what this means. When Ulla said that the *takana* is that a stolen *korban* will atone if the theft is not publicly known, the *takana* did not merely declare that we will *treat* it as if it atoned while secretly acknowledging it did not. Rather, the *takana* actually conferred ownership. At the moment Reuven sanctified this animal, the rabbis assigned him ownership — *d'rabbanan*, the rabbis have the authority to assign ownership — so that at the instant of sanctification, the animal was genuinely his. Now it becomes a fully valid *korban*: valid to atone inside the *mikdash*, and generating genuine *d'oraisa kares* if slaughtered outside. The *kares* is real and *d'oraisa*; it came to exist through the rabbinic enactment of assigning ownership.

### Timing Question

Rava now raises a further question: *de'okmuha rabbanan birshusei mishsha geneiva o mishsha hekdesh?* — when the rabbis assigned him ownership, did they do so from the moment of the theft, or only from the moment of sanctification? The practical difference: *ligizozeha ulvladoteha* — what happens to the wool shorn from the animal and the offspring born to it during the intervening period, while Reuven held the animal between stealing it and sanctifying it? If he owned it from the moment of theft, all of that belongs to him. If he owned it only from the moment of sanctification, then all of that remains Shimon's, and Reuven must return it when he does *teshuva*.

### At Sanctification

Rava himself resolves this: *mistabra mishsha hekdesh* — it is logical that the ownership was assigned from the moment of sanctification, and not retroactively from the moment of theft. The reason: *shelo yehei chotei niskar* — we will not allow the sinner to benefit. If we need to assign him ownership in order to make the *korban* valid, we will do so — but only for as long as necessary. There is no reason to reach further back and grant him ownership of the wool and offspring from the moment of theft. We assign him ownership only at the moment of sanctification, which is precisely when it is needed.

---

## Sikrikon Law

### Sikrikon Definition

The *mishna* now introduces the law of the *sikrikon*. *Sikrikon* were non-Jewish extortionists — Romans or others — who threatened Jews with death unless they sold their land. A Jew faced with such a threat would sell under extreme duress, almost certainly at a significant discount, simply to preserve his life. The *mishna* establishes that special rules apply to property that passed through the hands of such extortionists. The *gemara* notes that during the immediate period of active warfare and mass slaughter — *harugei milchama* — the law of *sikrikon* did not apply at all. Afterwards, once the killing subsided but the extortion continued, the rabbis ruled *yesh ba-sikrikon* — the law of *sikrikon* is now operative.

### Original Owner Retains

The original ruling — the *mishna rishona* — was that the original Jewish owner, call him Reuven, retained true ownership rights even after the forced sale. The *sikrikon* could not acquire the land in any meaningful halachic sense through coercion. In practice, though, anyone wishing to actually possess the land would have to deal with both parties: Reuven, the true owner, and the *sikrikon*, who physically controls it. The original ruling therefore focused on the order in which a third-party purchaser went about acquiring it.

### Sikrikon Then Owner

If one first paid the *sikrikon* and then went to Reuven to obtain his consent, the purchase is void — *mikcho batel*. The reason: Reuven's agreement in that scenario is not freely given. The *sikrikon* has already been paid; Reuven knows that if he creates difficulties, the *sikrikon*, who already received his payment and has a stake in the deal's completion, will make Reuven's life miserable. Reuven's ostensible consent is therefore coerced, and we do not treat it as genuine.

### Owner Then Sikrikon

By contrast, if one first approached Reuven — before any dealing with the *sikrikon* — and Reuven freely agreed, calculating that he may never recover the land and that at least he can salvage some value by selling his rights, then Reuven's consent is genuine and uncoerced. When the purchaser then goes to the *sikrikon* to pay him off and gain physical control, *mikcho kayam* — the purchase stands.

### Husband-Wife Analogy

The *mishna* draws an analogous case from property within a marriage. Where the wife has rights to certain property — whether brought as a dowry or secured through her *ketuba* — but the husband has practical control over it, the structure mirrors the *sikrikon* situation. The wife is like Reuven, the true holder of rights; the husband is like the *sikrikon*, with practical control. If a purchaser first bought from the husband and then sought the wife's consent, the purchase is void — her apparent agreement is suspect, as she would fear the consequences of opposing her husband. If he first approached the wife, who freely agreed, and then dealt with the husband, the purchase stands.

---

## Later Beit Din Ruling

### Sikrikon as Owner

*Zo mishna rishona* — that was the first ruling. A later *beit din* took a more pragmatic approach. Rather than treating Reuven as the true owner and requiring buyers to navigate the order-of-purchase rules, this later court ruled: *halokeach misikrikon nosein libaalim revia* — one who buys from the *sikrikon* must give the original owner a quarter of the value. In practice, the *sikrikon* is treated as the owner for purposes of the transaction, and the buyer deals only with the *sikrikon* — but must then compensate Reuven with one quarter of the purchase price, corresponding to the discount Reuven presumably suffered when he was forced to sell under duress. The assumption, somewhat remarkable, is that even with a gun to his head, the *sikrikon* only extracted a twenty-five percent discount.

The logic of this pragmatic shift is significant. The original ruling, while legally principled, created enormous practical obstacles to returning land to Jewish control. Requiring buyers to navigate competing claims, worry about the order of purchase, and secure Reuven's genuinely free consent may have been theoretically correct but was functionally paralyzing. The later *beit din* chose to treat the facts on the ground as given and devise a workable framework: acknowledge the *sikrikon*'s de facto control, compensate the original owner for his loss, and make it feasible for the land to change hands in an orderly way.

### Unable to Repurchase

The new rule applies specifically *bizman she'ein beyadam likach* — when the original owner does not have the wherewithal to repurchase the property himself.

### Right of First Refusal

If the original owner does have the means to buy it back, *heim kodmin lechol adam* — he retains the right of first refusal before any other purchaser. The later court thus preserved Reuven's priority where it was realistic, while removing it where it was not.

---

## Twelve-Month Rule

### 12-Month Cutoff

Rabbi convened a *beit din* and they voted on a further refinement: *shehasah bifnei sikrikon shenayim asar chodesh, kol hakodem likach zachah* — if the property remained in the hands of the *sikrikon* for twelve months, it is simply first come, first serve. Reuven's right of first refusal, which the later *beit din* had preserved where he had the means to buy, applies only within that twelve-month window. After twelve months, we no longer require any buyer to seek out Reuven and offer him priority.

### Quarter Payment

However, the obligation to pay Reuven one quarter of the transaction price remains in force even after the twelve months. The financial compensation to the original owner is not contingent on the time elapsed; it is a standing obligation.

### Practical Rationale

The rationale behind this further enactment is twofold: practical administration and the broader goal of returning property to Jewish control. Requiring buyers to locate Reuven and offer him priority indefinitely would create an impossible situation. At some point the process must be regularized. Rabbi's *beit din* drew the line at twelve months — a full year — and declared that beyond that point, the property may pass freely to whoever comes first, provided the quarter-payment obligation to the original owner is honored. This balance between principled protection of original ownership and practical functionality represents the culminating refinement of the *sikrikon* law on this daf.

---

---

# Gittin 56

## Three Edicts & Sicricon

### Sicricon Existence

The daf begins at the bottom of 55b, where the *Gemara* picks up a discussion emerging from the *mishnah*'s treatment of the *sicricon* — a type of assassin or violent extorter — and the question of when the legal framework governing property seized by such figures applies. The *Gemara* poses a pointed question: *hashta b'harugei milchama lo haya sicricon, me'harugei milchama v'ilech yesh sicricon?* If, during the very height of the killing during the destruction, the law of *sicricon* did not apply, how much more so should it not apply afterward? How is it possible that the phenomenon didn't generate legal consequences during the wars but did afterward?

Rav Yehuda resolves this apparent difficulty: the *mishnah* does not mean to say the *sicricon* himself didn't exist during the wars. Of course violent extorters were operating then. Rather, it means that the specific *din* — the legal doctrine — governing transactions involving *sicricon*-seized land did not apply.

### Rav Assi's Edicts

The reason for this is explained by Rav Assi, who teaches that there were three consecutive edicts — *gimmel gezeiros* — during the period of the *Churban HaBayis*. The first edict, *gezeira kamaisa*, was *kol d'lo katil liktlu'u*: any soldier who refused to kill a Jew would himself be killed. The second edict, *metzi'asa*, was *kol d'katil leisi arba zuzei*: killing a Jew would earn a reward of four *zuz*, but there was no longer a death penalty for failing to do so. The third edict, *basraisa*, reversed course entirely: *kol d'katil liktlu'u*, killing a Jew was once again punishable by death, as the Roman authorities sought to restore order following the wars.

### Sale Doctrine

The distinction between these three stages has direct *halachic* consequences. During the first and second edicts, when a *sicricon* threatened a Jew with death and demanded his land, the threat was entirely credible — the extorter either was obligated or at least rewarded for killing. Consequently, *keivan d'katlei, agav onseh gamur makni*: since the victim knew the threat was real, he genuinely and fully intended to transfer the land in exchange for his life. The sale was a complete *kinyan*. A third party who subsequently purchased that land from the *sicricon* acquired full ownership and need not return to the original owner to re-validate the transaction.

### Third Edict Rights

The third edict presents an entirely different legal picture. Under this edict, the *sicricon* was prohibited from killing the Jew. When the *sicricon* nonetheless demanded the land under threat, the owner reasoned: *idna lishkol, u'lemachar tavna lei b'dina* — let him take it today, and tomorrow I will pursue him in court. The owner never fully consented to the transfer; he merely yielded temporarily, expecting eventual legal redress. A third party who purchases such land from the *sicricon* therefore does not acquire good title. He must also go back and purchase it from the original owner in order for the transaction to be halachically sound.

### Narrative Setup

Notably, the *Gemara* does not linger on the further *halachic* details of the *mishnah* — the stages of *takkanah* governing whether a third party must pay the original owner a quarter of the land's value, and the proper order of purchase. Instead, it uses this brief legal excursus as a backdrop for the transition into the great *aggadata* of the *Churban HaBayis*, having established the violent historical context of soldiers killing Jews and the legal frameworks that emerged from it.

---

## Fear & Destruction

### Rabbi Yochanan's Verse

The *Gemara* opens its *aggadic* account of the destruction with a verse from Rabbi Yochanan: *ashrei adam m'fached tamid, u-maksheh libo yipol b'ra-ah* — praised is the person who is constantly in a state of fear, while the one who hardens his heart will fall into evil. This verse serves as the thematic key to everything that follows. The *m'fached tamid* is not mere anxiety; it is the posture of a person who is genuinely concerned about his actions, alive to the larger picture, aware of the possible ramifications of how he conducts himself. The *maksheh libo*, the one with the hardened heart, is the person moving through the world with blinders on, unable to see beyond the immediate moment.

### Causes of Destruction

Against this backdrop, the *Gemara* names three events that brought about three destructions: *a-Kamtza u-var Kamtza charuv Yerushalayim* — Jerusalem was destroyed on account of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza. *A-tarnagola v'tarnagolta charuv Tur Malka* — the city of Tur Malka was destroyed because of a hen and a rooster. *A-shaka d'rispak charuv Beitar* — Beitar was destroyed because of the axle of a carriage.

The stories to follow will be primarily concerned with Jerusalem, and the connection to the verse is already implicit. The destruction came not only through the hardness of heart of those who acted — the host who expelled his guest, the zealots who refused to make peace — but also through those who lacked the fear, the *yir'ah*, to stand up and intervene. Both forms of failure — active cruelty and passive acquiescence — find their indictment in this verse.

It is also worth noting the etymology of the name *Kamtza* itself. A *kometz* refers to a closed fist — the opposite of open-handed generosity. The very name telegraphs the theme of withholding, of miserly refusal to extend grace.

---

## Kamtza & Bar Kamtza

### Feast & Mistake

The story opens: *d'hahu gavra d'rachmei Kamtza u-va'al devaveih Bar Kamtza* — there was a man whose close friend was named Kamtza and whose enemy was named Bar Kamtza. He made a great feast and dispatched his attendant: *zil aysei li Kamtza* — go and invite Kamtza for me. The attendant went and by mistake invited Bar Kamtza. The host discovered his enemy sitting at his table.

### Bar Kamtza Pleas

The host confronted him directly: *mai ba-yis hacha* — what are you doing here? Get out. Bar Kamtza, acutely aware of the public shame that expulsion would bring him, pleaded: *ho-il v'asai shavkan* — since I am already here, simply let me stay. I will pay for whatever I eat and drink. The host refused. Bar Kamtza escalated his offer: I will pay for half the feast. Refused again. He offered to pay for the entire feast. *Amar lei lo* — still no.

*Naktye b'yadeih v'okmeih v'afkeih* — the host took him by the hand, stood him up, and drove him out. No offer of money, not even covering the full cost of the banquet, could overcome this man's commitment to his hatred. There is something almost parabolic here about the siege of Jerusalem itself — people so entrenched in their enmity that they cannot shift course even when an obvious path of accommodation presents itself.

### Public Expulsion

Bar Kamtza drew a conclusion that would have devastating consequences: *ho-il vehavu yatvi rabbanan velo machu bei, shema mina kanicha lehu* — since the rabbis were sitting there and did not protest his expulsion, evidently they found it acceptable. This raises one of the central themes of the entire passage. The rabbis bear responsibility not through what they did but through what they failed to do. The principle that evil flourishes when good people stand by in silence is directly implicated here. The rabbis' passivity is not a minor failing; the *Gemara* will return to it with force. The question is not only about the host who was cruel, or the zealots who forced the catastrophe — it is also about the leaders who could have intervened at multiple junctures and did not.

### Caesar & Sacrifice

Bar Kamtza decided to act: *izil eichol behu kurtza bei malka* — he went and spread a malicious report to Caesar, informing him that the Jews were in rebellion. Caesar was skeptical: *mi yeimar* — who says so? Bar Kamtza proposed a test: send them a sacrifice and see whether they offer it up.

Caesar sent a fine calf — *egla tilta*, a well-fattened animal. On the way to Jerusalem, Bar Kamtza introduced a blemish: *be-niv sefatayim* — in the upper lip, or according to another opinion, *be-dukin she-ba-ayin* — a tiny film over the eye. The halachic asymmetry was precise: *duchta de-ledidan havei muma, u-ledidehu lav muma hu* — by Jewish law this constituted a disqualifying blemish for a Temple offering, but by Roman standards it was not considered a blemish at all. The Romans would have no idea why the Jews refused to sacrifice it, and would take it as confirmation of rebellion.

The detail of the blemish on the lip — *niv sefatayim*, which also connotes speech — is not incidental. The power of speech, for both harm and good, runs as a thread through these stories.

---

## Sacrifice Debate

### Peace Consideration

When the blemished animal arrived, the rabbis found themselves confronted with a fateful choice. *Savar rabbanan le-kruvei mishum shelom malchut* — the rabbis considered offering the blemished animal for the sake of peace with the government. This reflects an important posture: the willingness to bend halachic norms for the sake of a larger national interest. The *Gemara* here implicitly endorses this flexibility — the wiser course, as will become clear, was to offer it.

### Zechariah's Refusal

Rabbi Zechariah ben Avkulos objected: *yomru ba'alei mumin kreivin legabi mizbeach* — people will say that it is permissible to bring a blemished animal to the altar. He could not look past the halachic precedent that might be set.

### Kill Bar Kamtza Plan

The rabbis then proposed an alternative: since they cannot offer the sacrifice and risk a diplomatic rupture, at least let them kill Bar Kamtza so he cannot carry back a negative report to Rome. Rabbi Zechariah objected to this as well: *yomru matil mum be-kodashim yehareg* — people will conclude that the punishment for blemishing a sacrifice is death.

### Yochanan Blames Zechariah

Rabbi Yochanan's verdict is famous and severe: *anvetanuto shel Rabbi Zecharia ben Avkulos hechriva et beiteinu ve-sarfa et heichaleinu ve-higlitnu me-artzeinu* — the humility of Rabbi Zechariah ben Avkulos destroyed our Temple, burned our sanctuary, and exiled us from our land.

The choice of the word *anvetanuto* — humility — is striking and deliberate. This was not simple obstinacy or stubbornness. Rabbi Zechariah's position can be framed as a kind of piety: who are we to override the *halacha*? Who are we to take such drastic action? His posture was the humble one, the *frum* one, the one that deferred to established norms rather than arrogating to himself the authority to deviate from them. And yet this very humility — this refusal to exercise rabbinic initiative and flexibility — was catastrophic.

But the criticism cannot be aimed at Rabbi Zechariah alone. The other rabbis were present and did not stand up to him. Their own passivity, their unwillingness to confront his position and override it, is equally implicated. This mirrors the passivity at the feast: again, the rabbis stand by. If Rabbi Zechariah's *anavah* destroyed the Temple, then the rabbis' reluctance to challenge him was its own form of failure. This forms a pointed contrast with the material on the preceding pages of the *masechta*, where the Rabbis exercised sweeping authority — employing *hefker beis din hefker*, overriding what would normally be the rules governing *korbanos*, redefining personal status — all for the sake of *tikkun olam*. The question the *Gemara* seems to be raising is: where was that boldness when it was needed most?

---

## Nero's Omens

### Arrow Divination

After the catastrophe was set in motion, *shadar alaihu le'Neron Keisar* — they dispatched Nero Caesar against Jerusalem. As he drew near, he engaged in a form of divination by shooting arrows. He shot to the east — *asa nefal bi'Yerushalayim*, the arrow fell toward Jerusalem. To the west — toward Jerusalem. *Le'arba ruchos ha'shamayim* — in all four directions — the arrow fell toward Jerusalem. The message was unambiguous: the divine will was pointing him to this city.

### Child's Verse

Nero then asked a child to recite whatever *pasuk* he happened to be studying at that moment. The child recited: *ve'nasati es nikmasi be'Edom, be'yad ami Yisrael* — I will take my vengeance against Edom through my people Israel. For the rabbis, Edom was the code for Rome.

### Nero Converts

Nero drew his own conclusion: *kudsha Berich Hu ba'ei le'charuvi beiseih* — God wants His Temple destroyed, *u-ba'ei le-kichuyei yadeih be-hu gavra* — and He intends to wipe His hands on me. God will use me to do His dirty work, and then I will bear the blame. This was not something Nero was willing to accept. *Arak va-azil ve-igaier* — he fled and converted to Judaism.

### Rabbi Meir Lineage

The *Gemara* adds a remarkable coda: *ve-nafik mineih Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Meir descended from Nero. Whatever one makes of this tradition in the rabbinic imagination, it is a striking claim — that one of the great Tannaim of the generation after the destruction traced his lineage to the Roman emperor who had been sent to destroy Jerusalem and refused.

---

## Siege & Wealthy

### Vespasian & Siege

With Nero gone, *shadreih ilaveih le-Aspasyanus keisar* — Vespasian was dispatched. He is called "Caesar" in the narrative, though at this point he was still a general. *Ata tzar alah telat shani* — he besieged Jerusalem for three years.

### Three Wealthy Men

Within the besieged city, three extraordinarily wealthy men were positioned to sustain the population. *Nakdimon Ben Guryon* — a figure known elsewhere in the Talmud, whose name derives from *shenakdah lo chamah ba-avuro*, as if the sun itself broke through the heavens for his sake, a reference to the miracle associated with him. *Ben Kalba Savua* — *she-kol ha-nichnas le-beiso keshehu ra'ev kekelev yetzei keshehu savei'a* — anyone who entered his house as hungry as a dog would leave fully satisfied. And *Ben Tzitzit HaKeset* — *shehayesah tzitziyaso nigreret al gabei kesasos* — whose fringes would drag along cushions, because servants would walk beneath his garment holding pillows so the fringes would never touch the ground. Another tradition holds that his seat was literally placed among the great of Rome.

### Support Offerings

Each man stepped forward to guarantee provisions for the entire besieged city. One offered to supply all of Jerusalem's wheat and barley. A second offered all the wine, salt, and oil. The third offered to supply firewood. The *Gemara* notes that the rabbis gave special praise to the one who offered the firewood — citing a teaching of Rav Chisda: *akliba de-chitei ba'eia shisin aklibei de-detzivi* — one storage warehouse of wheat requires sixty warehouses of firewood to bake it. The sheer volume and value of what was being pledged in firewood was staggering.

### Zealots Burn Food

Together, the three pledges were sufficient to sustain Jerusalem under siege for twenty-one years. But this immense resource was rendered worthless. *Havu behu hanahu biryoni* — there were zealots in the city. When the rabbis counseled making peace — *nafek vena'avid shelma bahadeihu* — the zealots blocked them. When the rabbis said that going to war would not succeed — *lo mistaye'a milta* — the zealots responded by going to war anyway. And to force the population's hand and eliminate any possibility of negotiated surrender, *kalin'hu lehannu ambarei dechitti usha'arei* — they burned down the warehouses of wheat and barley. The famine was now inevitable.

---

## Martha & Famine

### Martha's Flour Quest

Martha the daughter of Baitos was among the wealthiest women in Jerusalem. With the famine setting in, she dispatched her attendant: *zil aeiti li smida* — go get me fine flour. By the time he arrived at the market, it had sold out. He returned and reported: no fine flour, but white flour is available. She sent him for the white flour. By the time he arrived, that too was gone. He returned: no white flour, but coarser flour is available. She sent him for that. Gone by the time he arrived. Barley flour remained. Gone as well.

### Martha's Death

Finally, Martha decided to go out herself — barefoot, it would seem, since the text says *havah shalpa masana*, she had removed her shoe. She stepped into dung, and the shock and revulsion of it — she who had been so utterly refined — killed her.

### Martha's Verse

Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai applied to her the verse: *haraka becha vehanuga asher lo nista chaf ragla* — the tender and delicate woman who had never set the sole of her foot upon the ground. This was the very curse whose fulfillment she had now experienced.

An alternative tradition is offered: *ika de'amri grogerot deRabbi Tzadok achala* — some say she found and ate one of the dried figs that Rabbi Tzadok had discarded. Rabbi Tzadok, as will be described, was so emaciated from his decades of fasting that even illness clung to the scraps he rejected. She consumed one of these and died from the contagion.

### Rabbi Tzadok Fast

This brings the *Gemara* to Rabbi Tzadok himself. *Yativ arba'in shanin betanita* — he sat for forty years in a state of fasting, *dela licherav Yerushalayim* — so that Jerusalem might not be destroyed. When he ate at all, he was so thin that you could see the food going down from the outside of his body. When he was at his most recovered, they would bring him dried figs, *maitz meyayuhu* — he would suck out the juice, *v'shadileihu* — and throw them out. The contrast with Martha is pointed: Rabbi Tzadok is the *tzaddik* — in name and reality — who through private, invisible righteousness has been holding back the catastrophe. But his righteousness, as profound as it is, is not enough to reach others or redirect the course of events.

### Martha's Wealth Cast

As she lay dying, Martha did something extraordinary: *afikta lechol dahava vechaspa veshadisa beshuka* — she took out all her gold and silver and threw it into the marketplace. *Hai lemai mibaya li* — what use is any of this to me now? The *Gemara* connects this to the verse: *kaspam bachutzot yashlichu* — their silver they shall throw out into the streets.

---

## Yochanan's Escape

### Family Connection

*Abba Sikara* — whose name connects back to the *sicricon* with which the *daf* opened, and who is identified with the Sicarii, the dagger-men — was *reish biryonei diyerushalayim*, the head of the Jerusalem zealots. He was also *bar achtei d'Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai* — the nephew of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai.

### Confrontation

Rabban Yochanan sent for him privately: *ta betzina legabai* — come to me in secret. When Abba Sikara came, Rabban Yochanan confronted him directly: *ad matai avdisu hachi vekatlisu lehu l'alma dechafna* — how long will you continue like this, killing everyone through famine?

### Sikara's Dilemma

Abba Sikara's response was not defiance but despair: *mai avidei, de'amina lehu midi, katlu li* — what can I do? If I tell them to stand down, they will kill me. Even the head of the zealots was trapped by the logic of the movement he led.

### Fake Death Plan

Rabban Yochanan asked him to help engineer an escape: *chazi li takanta dididi, de'ipuk, efshar dehavi hatzalah purta* — find me some solution, that I might get out, perhaps there will be some small salvation. The phrase *hatzalah purta* — a little salvation — is significant and will recur.

Abba Sikara devised the plan. Rabban Yochanan was to take to bed feigning illness, let students and community come to pay their respects for many days, then arrange for something decomposing to be placed nearby so that the smell of death would be reported. *Denach nafshach* — it would be said that he had died. His students — who would be in on the scheme — would carry him out in a coffin. No one else could be admitted, because *dekalil at* — a live person is lighter than a dead one, and unfamiliar visitors would notice the difference in weight.

### Gate Escape

Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua — the two great students who would themselves become teachers of Rabbi Akiva — carried the coffin out of the city. At the gate, the zealot guards wanted to pierce the body to verify death. Abba Sikara deflected them: *yomru rabanan dakru* — do you want it said that you stabbed your own Rabbi? They then wanted at least to push the coffin around. *Yomru rabanan dachfu* — do you want it said that you shoved your Rabbi around even in death? The gate was opened. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai emerged.

### Vespasian Meeting

When he reached Vespasian's camp, Rabban Yochanan shed his disguise and greeted the general: *shlama aleichah malka, shlama aleichah malka* — peace to you, O king.

---

## Honey & Serpent

### Identity Challenge

Vespasian responded sharply: *mechayeivat trei katla* — you deserve two deaths. First, *delav malka ana* — I am not king, and you are mocking me by calling me one. Second, *ei malka ana, ad idna amai lo aseit legabai* — if I were king, why did you wait until now to come and pay your respects?

### Scripture Proof

Rabban Yochanan responded to both challenges. As for the first: you are indeed king, *de ee lav malka at, Yerushalayim lo mitnasyah be-yadach* — because only a king could receive Jerusalem into his hands. The proof is from scripture: *dechtiv vehalevanon beadier yipol* — the *Levanon* will fall to the *adier*, the mighty one. *Veein adier ela melech* — *adier* means king, as proven from the verse *vehaya adiero mimenu, umeshlo mikirbo yeitzei* — his ruler will come from within him. *Veein Levanon ela Beis HaMikdash* — and *Levanon* is the *Beis HaMikdash*, as proven from *hahar hatov hazeh vehalevanon* — the good mountain and the *Levanon*. Since Jerusalem and the *Beis HaMikdash* are being delivered into his hands, Vespasian must be king.

As for the second challenge: *biryonei deis behan lo shavkin* — the zealots would not permit me to come. They were the reason.

### Parable

Vespasian pressed back: *ilu chavis shel devash vedarkon karuch aleha, lo hayu shovrin es hachavis bishvil hadarkon* — if there is a barrel of honey and a serpent is coiled around it, would you not break the barrel open to get rid of the serpent? Here too: you should have broken the walls of Jerusalem, we would have come in, dealt with the zealots, and ended the whole matter far sooner.

### Response Failure

*Ishtik* — Rabban Yochanan was silent. He had no answer. Rav Yosef, and some say Rabbi Akiva, applied the verse *meishiv chachamim achor vedaatam yesakel* — God sometimes causes the wise to retreat and their wisdom to become folly. The proper response, they said, should have been: *shaklinan tzavta veshaklinan lei ledarkon vekatlinan lei vachavita shavkinan lah* — we would take tongs, remove the serpent, kill it, and preserve the barrel. Here too: the goal was to find a way to deal with the zealots without destroying Jerusalem.

---

## Caesar & Shoe

### Vespasian Crowned

While they were still in conversation, *asei pristaka miRomi* — a messenger arrived from Rome. *Kum, demeis lei keisar* — arise, the Caesar has died, *veamri hanu chashivei deRomi leoshivach bereisha* — and the senate of Rome has appointed you as the new Caesar.

### Swollen Feet

At that moment Vespasian was putting on his shoe. He went to put on the second shoe — it would not go on. He tried to remove the first — it would not come off. *Amar mai hai* — what is happening?

Rabban Yochanan explained: *shemuah tovah asya lach, dechtiv shemuah tovah tedashen atzem* — good news has come to you, and as the verse says, good news fattens the bone. The sudden swelling of pride and joy has caused his feet to expand so that neither shoe fits.

### Pride Deflation

The solution: *leisi inish dela misava daatach mineih vechalif kamach* — bring someone whose presence is distressing to you, let him walk before you, *dechtiv veruach necheiah tyavesh garem* — and a downtrodden spirit dries up the bones. He did so, and his feet returned to normal.

---

## Request for Yavne

### Why Not Sooner

Vespasian then turned to Rabban Yochanan: *umiaechar dechachmitu kulei hai, ad idna amai lo aseitu legabai* — since you are so wise, why did you not come to me sooner? Surely you could have found a way.

### Zealot Barrier

Rabban Yochanan repeated the answer: the zealots would not allow it. Vespasian's implied counter — that Rabban Yochanan should have found a means to neutralize them — reflects the same argument he had made with the serpent parable.

### Three Grants

Vespasian then told him: *meizal azilna*, I must return to Rome, *ve-inash achrina meshadrana*, and I will send another commander to complete the campaign. *Ela bei minai midi de-aten lach* — but ask of me something and I will grant it.

Rabban Yochanan's request: *ten li Yavne ve-chachameiha* — give me Yavne and its sages. And *shishulta de-Rabbi Gamliel* — preserve the chain of Rabban Gamliel's family, meaning the *nasi* line. This is the great pivot of the passage and, in a sense, of Jewish history: the recognition that the *Beis HaMikdash* will fall, and that what must be preserved in its place is a Torah center and the continuity of Jewish communal leadership. The phrase *hatzalah purta* — the little salvation — echoes back. Rabban Yochanan will not save Jerusalem. But he will save something. The shift from a Temple-centered Jerusalem to a rabbinic Judaism centered on Torah study begins here, at Yavne.

### Doctors Request

The third request is of a different register entirely: *ve-asvata de-masyan lei le-Rabbi Tzadok* — provide doctors who will heal Rabbi Tzadok. After the grand national requests — a Torah center, the continuity of leadership — Rabban Yochanan asks for the care of a single righteous individual. Rabbi Tzadok, who had fasted for forty years to prevent the destruction, now needs to be healed so he can live into whatever comes next. There is something deeply moving in placing this personal request alongside the national ones — an insistence that even amid catastrophe, the individual *tzaddik* matters and must be carried into the future.

---

## Akiva's Critique

### Wisdom Diminished

At this point the *Gemara* returns with a critique. Rav Yosef — and some say Rabbi Akiva — applied to Rabban Yochanan the verse *meishiv chachamim achor vedaatam yesakel*: God caused the wise to retreat, their wisdom diminished.

### Better Answer

What should Rabban Yochanan have asked for? *Ibei lei le-meimar lei shavkinehu hada zimna* — he should have asked Vespasian simply to leave Jerusalem alone entirely. If you will grant me something, leave. Do not destroy it at all.

### Yochanan's Fear

Why did he not ask this? *Dilma kulei hai lo avid, ve-hatzalah porta nami lo havei* — he was afraid that Vespasian would refuse even that, and then he would have gotten nothing at all. Not even Yavne. Not even the little salvation.

The voice of Rabbi Akiva here is characteristic. Rabbi Akiva, who would later support Bar Kochba and envision the full restoration of Jewish sovereignty, could not accept the compromise. He wanted to hold out for everything. Rabban Yochanan, with clearer eyes about what was politically achievable, chose to secure what he could. Neither position is without cost.

---

## Tzadok's Healing

### Gradual Nutrition

The *Gemara* then describes in clinical detail how the doctors went about healing Rabbi Tzadok. *Yoma kama ashkyuha maya defari* — on the first day they gave him water in which bran had been soaked: mostly water, a trace of nourishment, nothing more than his devastated body could absorb. The next day: *maya desipuka* — water with bran and a bit of flour. The day after: *maya de-kimcha* — water with flour. Each day the diet was slightly more nutritious than the day before.

### Stomach Expansion

*Ad deravach me'eih purta purta* — until his stomach expanded little by little. The word *purta* — a little, a small amount — is the same word used earlier for *hatzalah purta*, the little salvation. The gradual physical recovery of Rabbi Tzadok mirrors in miniature the gradual spiritual and communal recovery that the founding of Yavne represents. Just as Rabban Yochanan chose to accept a partial salvation rather than lose everything, the doctors choose to introduce nourishment gradually rather than overwhelm the body. The *Churban* has happened; the rebuilding must be slow and careful, one small step at a time.

---

## Titus Defilement

### Holy of Holies Act

With the transition to what follows, the *Gemara* completely skips over the military details of the siege's end and the burning of Jerusalem, moving directly to the figure of Titus. The verse *ei eloheimo tzur chasayu vo* — where is their God, the rock in whom they take refuge — is identified as referring to *Titus HaRasha*, the wicked Titus, who blasphemed toward Heaven.

*Tafas zonah beyado ve-nichnas le-veit kodshei kodashim* — he took a prostitute in his hand and entered the Holy of Holies. He spread out a *sefer Torah* and committed his act of desecration upon it. The specific detail of the *sefer Torah* is significant: not content with the physical destruction of the Temple, Titus enacts a deliberate symbolic desecration of the Torah itself.

### Parochet Pierce

He then took a sword — *ve-gider et ha-parochet* — and pierced the curtain, the *parochet* separating the Holy of Holies from the *heichal*. A miracle occurred, though not a saving one: *ve-hayah dam mivatzbetz ve-yotzei* — blood spurted from the curtain. According to Tosafot, this was to demonstrate how great and severe the destruction of the *Beis HaMikdash* was — or alternatively, it was intended to mislead Titus.

### God's Silence

*Kasavar harag et atzmo* — Titus thought, through the euphemism of *atzmo*, that he had killed God Himself. He saw this as confirmation, citing the verse *sha'agu tzorecha bekerev mo'adecha* — your enemies have cried out within your sanctuary. Abba Chanan responded: *mi kamocha chasin yah, mi kamocha chasin ve-kasheh* — who is like You in Your strength, who is like You in Your harshness and restraint, *she-attah shome'a ni'utzo ve-giduffo shel oto rasha ve-shotek* — that You can hear the blasphemies of that wicked man and be silent?

The Rabbis reframe God's silence as an expression of incomprehensible might — not weakness, but a restraint so great it staggers comprehension. The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: *mi kamocha ba'eilim Hashem* — who is like You among the mighty — *mi kamocha ba'ilmim* — who is like You among the silent ones?

---

## Titus Plunder

### Vessel Plunder

*Ve-asao kemin gargutni* — Titus took the *parochet* and made it into a sack, then filled it with all the vessels of the *Beis HaMikdash* — *kol keilim shebamikdash* — and loaded them onto a ship, intending to return to Rome and display his triumph.

The *Gemara* applies a verse from Kohelet: *ubchen raiti reshaim kburim* — I have seen the wicked buried. The *Gemara* re-reads this: *al tikrei kburim, ela kbutzim* — do not read "buried" but "gathered," meaning the wicked gathered together. *Al tikrei veyishtakchu, ela veyishtabchu* — do not read "and they were forgotten" but "and they praised themselves" in their cities, meaning Titus parading the Temple vessels through Rome. An alternative reading accepts *kburim* as meaning "buried" literally: *de'afilu mili demitamran iglei lehu* — even the buried treasures were revealed to Titus.

### Wave Challenge

Out at sea, a massive wave rose up to destroy him. Titus interpreted this theologically: *kmidumeh ani she'eloheihem shel elu ein gvurato ela bamayim* — it seems that the God of the Jews only exercises His power in water. He listed the precedents: Pharaoh was drowned, Sisera's forces were swept away by the waters of the Kishon — *nachal Kishon grefam* — so of course God tries to fight him in the sea.

### Gnat Plague

Titus then issued his challenge: *im gibor hu ya'ale layabasha veya'aseh imi milchama* — if God is truly mighty, let Him come up on dry land and fight me there. *Yatzta bat kol* — a heavenly voice issued forth: *lo larasha ben rasha ben bno shel Esav harasha* — wicked one, son of a wicked one, grandson of the wicked Esau — the connection to Edom and Rome is explicit. *Birya kala yesh li be'olami veyitush shma* — I have a tiny creature in My world called a gnat. *Ala layabasha veta'aseh ima milchama* — go up on land and fight it.

---

## Gnat Torment

### Gnat Entry

When Titus came ashore, the gnat entered his nose — *venichnas bechotmo* — and began boring into his brain — *venakar bemocho* — and this continued for seven years.

### Blacksmith Relief

One day Titus happened to pass the doorway of a blacksmith's forge. He heard the sound of hammering — *shama kol arzafta* — and the gnat, startled by the harsh clanging, stopped its drilling. *Amar ika takanta* — here, finally, was some relief.

### Daily Visits

Every day thereafter they would bring a blacksmith and have him bang before Titus. *Lenochri yahiv leih arba zuzei* — if the blacksmith was a non-Jew, Titus would pay him four *zuz*. *LeYisrael amar lei* — if the blacksmith was a Jew, Titus would say: *mistayach dekachazit besanach* — it is enough for you that you have seen your enemy in torment. No payment necessary.

### Immunity Develops

For thirty days this provided relief. Then, *keivan dedash dash* — once the gnat had grown accustomed to the sound, it developed an immunity, and the hammering no longer startled it. The relief ceased.

---

## Titus's Death

### Gnat Growth

Rabbi Pinchas ben Aruvah testifies: I was among the prominent people of Rome, and *ukshemet patzu et mocho umatzu bo* — when Titus died and they cracked open his skull, they found that the gnat had grown. According to one tradition it had reached the size of *ketzippor dror*, a free bird, *mishkalo shnei sela'im* — weighing two *sela'im*. A *Baraita* describes it as the size of a year-old pigeon, weighing two *litrin*. Abaye adds a received tradition: *piv shel nechoshet* — its mouth was of brass, *vetzipornav shel barzel* — and its claws of iron. The creature that had been growing inside Titus for seven years — fed, in a sense, by the same iron and brass of the blacksmith's forge that briefly gave him respite — had become a metallic instrument of divine retribution.

### Cremation Order

On his deathbed, Titus issued a final command: *liklyeh l'hahu gavra* — cremate me. *U'nivdrei l'kitmei ashivah yamei* — scatter my ashes across the seven seas.

### Afterlife Fear

The reasoning was explicit: *d'lo lishkachayeh eloha d'yehudai v'lyokmayeh b'dina* — so that the God of the Jews should not find me and bring me to judgment in the afterlife. Titus, who had blasphemed and desecrated with apparent impunity in this world, feared the accounting that awaited him in the next. His entire strategy of cremation and dispersal was an attempt to evade divine justice — a final act of defiance that itself testifies to his acknowledgment that such justice exists. The *Gemara* will continue this account on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Gittin 57

## Titus & Onkelos

### Churban Intro

Today's *daf* is 57, and we continue in the *aggadeta* — some of the most essential *aggadeta* about the *Churban ha-Bayit*. We pick up at the bottom of 56b, having just dealt with the downfall of Titus and the gnat that found its way into his nostril. One must acknowledge something almost darkly comic in this material: Vespasian's foot swells up, and Titus is undone by an insect in his nose. Even though Vespasian is something of a relatively sympathetic figure in these narratives, the theme running through all of this is very much the bringing low of the mighty — a note of mockery directed at the great powers of Rome.

### Titus & Gnat

By way of background: Titus, having destroyed the *Beis ha-Mikdash*, asked that after his death God would not be able to judge him, and requested that his ashes be scattered over the seven seas so that he could not be gathered for judgment.

### Onkelos Raises Titus

Picking up four lines from the bottom of 56b, the *Gemara* introduces *Onkelos bar Kalonikos bar achatei de-Titus* — Onkelos, the son of the sister of Titus. He *ba'ei le-giurei*, he wished to convert, and indeed the tradition identifies him as *Onkelos ha-Ger*, the famous convert who produced the authoritative Aramaic translation of the Torah.

*Azal askei le-Titus be-negida* — he went and raised Titus from the dead through a form of necromancy. He asked him: *man chashiv be-hahu alma* — who is important in the world to come? Titus replied: *Yisrael* — the Jewish people. Onkelos then asked: *ma lei devukei behu* — should I therefore cleave to them in this world? Titus replied: *milaihu nefishan velo matis le-kiyumaihu* — their commandments are many and you will not be able to fulfill them all. Rather: *zil igrei behu be-hahu alma* — go and attack them in this world, *ve-havis reisha* — and you will be a head, you will be a leader. As the verse says, *hayu tzareha le-rosh* — its enemies became the head. The implication, taken at face value, is almost troubling: afflict Israel and you will become a leader. The commentators struggle to reread this, suggesting it means that only one who is already a great leader will manage to oppress Israel — but that is admittedly not the plain *peshat* of the *Gemara* as it stands.

### Titus's Punishment

Onkelos then asked Titus: *dinei de-hahu gavra be-mai* — what is the judgment of that man, meaning yourself, in the world to come? Titus answered: *be-mai de-pasak anafshei* — whatever I decreed upon myself. *Kol yoma machneshi lei le-katmei* — every day my ashes are gathered from the seven seas, *ve-dayni lei* — I am re-judged, *ve-kalu lei* — I am burned again, *ve-mabdru a-shva yamei* — and my ashes are scattered once more over the seven seas. This cycle repeats daily. His counsel to Onkelos, then, is: you cannot win in the world to come, but you might as well be successful in this world by oppressing Israel.

---

## Onkelos & Balaam

### Balaam Summoned

*Azal askei le-Bilam be-negida* — Onkelos then went and raised Balaam from the dead through necromancy. He asked the same question: *man chashiv be-hahu alma* — who is important in the world to come? Balaam too answered: *Yisrael*. And again the follow-up: *ma lei devukei behu* — should I cleave to them?

### Balaam's Hatred

Balaam's answer was the opposite of what one might hope: *lo tidrosh shelomam ve-tovatam kol ha-yamim* — do not seek after their well-being or their good, ever. The counsel is straightforward hatred toward Israel in this world.

### Balaam's Torment

Onkelos asked Balaam as well: *dinei de-hahu gavra be-mai* — what is your punishment? *Be-shichvat zera rotachat* — in boiling semen. Two explanations are offered for this: one, that Balaam caused *Bnei Yisrael* to sin with *Benot Moav*, and the other, that it reflects his own personal licentiousness.

---

## Yeshu Raised

### Yeshu Summoned

*Azal askei be-negida le-poshei Yisrael* — the text as we have it reads "sinners of Israel," but the original *girsa* is *Yeshu ha-Notzri* — Jesus. Onkelos raised him through necromancy and asked the same question: *man chashiv be-hahu alma* — who is important in the world to come? The answer was again: *Yisrael*.

### Yeshu's Advice

Here, strikingly, the answer diverges from what both Titus and Balaam had said. Onkelos asked: *ma leidvuki behu* — should I cleave to them? And the reply was: *tovatam drosh ra'atam lo tidrosh* — seek their well-being and do not seek their harm. This does not necessarily mean one should convert, but the counsel is to be good to them in this world. *Kol hanogea bahen kenogea be-vavat eino* — anyone who harms them is as one who pokes at the pupil of his own eye.

### Yeshu's Torment

Onkelos asked about his punishment as well: *dinei de-hahu gavra be-mai* — what are you judged with? *Be-tzoa rotachat* — in boiling excrement. *De-amar mar kol ha-mal'ig al divrei chachamim nidon be-tzoa rotachat* — for anyone who mocks the words of the sages is judged in boiling excrement. It is notable that the sin attributed here is specifically mocking the sages — framing the figure as a Jewish heretic rather than as an external oppressor like Titus or Balaam.

### Heretic Contrast

The *Gemara* then draws the lesson explicitly: *ta chazi ma bein poshei Yisrael le-niviei umot ha'olam* — come and see the difference between sinners from Israel and the prophets of the nations who are idolaters. Even in the world to come, under harsh divine judgment, the idolaters — Titus and Balaam — still advise enmity toward Israel, while the Jewish heretic, even in his torment, says to seek Israel's well-being.

---

## Power of Shame

### Shame's Power

*Tanya*, it was taught in a *baraita*: *amar Rabbi Elazar, bo u're'eh kama gadol kocha shel busha* — come and see how great is the power of shame. This serves as a concluding reflection on the story of *Kamtza* and *Bar Kamtza*, which was covered previously, and which the *Gemara* now wraps up thematically.

### Kamtza Story

*She-harei siya HaKadosh Baruch Hu et Bar Kamtza* — God assisted *Bar Kamtza*, meaning He guided events through this story, *ve-hachiv et beito ve-saraf et heichalo* — and ultimately it led to the destruction of the *Beis ha-Mikdash* and the burning of the *Heichal*. This is worth pausing over. Earlier in the *Gemara*, the destruction was attributed to *Rabbi Zecharya ben Avkulas* and his excessive humility: *hechriv et bateinu ve-saraf et heichaleinu* — he destroyed our homes and burned our sanctuary. Here, God Himself is identified as the agent who destroyed His own house. And yet the *Gemara* also frames it as coming through *Bar Kamtza*'s shame. Who, then, bears the responsibility?

### Causes of Destruction

These layered attributions — the excessive humility of leadership, the shame of *Bar Kamtza*, and ultimately God's own guidance of events — all coexist in the *Gemara* without contradiction, and each illuminates a different dimension of the *churban*. There is also a case to be made that the entire story of *Kamtza* and *Bar Kamtza* is not merely a tale about the sin of shaming, however real and serious that sin is, nor only about *sinat chinam* in a narrow interpersonal sense. It reflects something more politically concrete: the factionalism and internal warfare of the period. The Zealots were spending their energy fighting one another. There was no compelling reason that the Jews had to rebel against Rome when they did, nor that they could not have negotiated a way to preserve the *Beis ha-Mikdash*. The destruction was in large measure brought about by internal strife and a failure of leadership — precisely the *Gemara*'s broader point about the rabbis of that generation who saw what was happening and did not act.

---

## Tur Malka Chickens

### Wedding Tree Custom

The *Gemara* now shifts to the story of *Tur Malka*, another city that was destroyed. *Aturnegoila ve-tarnegoilta chariv Tur Malka* — on account of a hen and a rooster, the city of *Tur Malka* was destroyed.
