The practice there was: *ki havu mapki chatan ve-challa*, when a wedding procession would go out, *mapki kameihu tarnegoila ve-tarnegoilta* — they would lead a rooster and a hen in front of the couple. *Kolomar pru u'revu ka-tarnegolim* — this symbolized the wish that they be as fruitful as hens and roosters.

### Caesar's Carriage

*Yoma chad hava ka chalif gunda de-Romai* — one day a troop of Romans was passing through. There happened to be a wedding procession at the time, and the hungry soldiers *shaklineihu mineihu* — grabbed the chickens.

### Jews Fight Back

*Naflu alaihu* — the people attacked the soldiers, demanding their chickens back. *Machunu* — they struck them. *Azlu amru lei le-Keisar* — the Romans went and reported to Caesar: *mardu becha Yehuda'ei* — the Jews are rebelling against you. *Ata alaihu* — and Caesar came with an army against them.

### Bar Droma Hero

*Havah behu hahu Bar Droma* — there was in this community a man called *Bar Droma*, *de-havah kafitz mila* — who could leap a *mila*, and *ve-katlu behu* — he would cut down the Romans as he vaulted through them. The imagery is almost of a superhero, and the parallel to the stories that may have inspired the Asterix comic series — a tiny village resisting Rome through what amounts to superhuman ability — is not difficult to see. Just as Asterix is a story of a small enclave that held out against Rome, Bar Kochba's revolt is clearly the historical event that gave rise to that imagination.

### Caesar Prays

*Shaklei Keisar le-tageih ve-asfeh a-ara* — Caesar took his crown and placed it on the ground. He prayed: *Ribonei de-alma*, Master of the world, *im nicha lach lo timsereih le-hahu gavra le-didei u-malchuteih be-yadei de-chad gavra* — if it please You, do not hand me and my entire kingdom over to one man. His prayer was heard: *achshaleih pumeih le-Bar Droma* — Bar Droma's mouth caused him to stumble. Bar Droma said: *halo atah Elohim zenachtanu ve-lo tetzei Elohim be-tzivotenu* — Have You not, O God, abandoned us, and You do not go out with our armies? This is a complaint against God rather than an expression of wonder.

The *Gemara* immediately raises an objection: this is a verse from *Tehillim* — David also said it! The *Gemara* responds that *David itmuhei ka-matmei* — David was expressing astonishment, as if to say, "Could it be that You have abandoned us?" It was a cry of disbelief. Bar Droma, by contrast, was leveling a charge: God, You abandoned us. And this distinction proved fatal.

### Bathroom Death

*Ala be-veit ha-kisei* — Bar Droma went to the bathroom. *Ata darkona* — a serpent appeared — and *shamteih le-karkashei* — his innards dropped out, *ve-nach nafshei* — and he died. The Superman of the Jewish resistance died in the bathroom. As with Titus's gnat and Vespasian's swollen foot, the manner of death is almost grimly comic.

### Caesar Returns

*Ho-il ve-itrachash li nisa* — Caesar acknowledged that a miracle had occurred for him. He declared: *ha zimna ishvakinhu* — this time I will leave them. *Ve-azal izdakar* — and when Caesar departed, the Jews rose up in celebration, *ve-achalu ve-shatu ve-adliku shragei* — eating, drinking, and lighting candles. So great was the illumination that *ad de-itchazi dilyona de-gushpanka be-richuk mila* — the impression of a signet ring could be made out from a distance of a *mila*. Caesar, observing this celebration as he withdrew, interpreted it as mockery: *michdi chadu be-Yehuda'ei* — the Jews are laughing at me. *Hadar ata alei* — and he turned back and attacked.

### Tur Malka Slaughter

*Amar Rav Assi: tlat me'a alfi shlifei saifa ailu le-Tur Malka* — 300,000 men with drawn swords entered *Tur Malka*, *ve-katlu bah tlata yoma ve-tlata leilavata* — and they killed there for three days and three nights.

### City Divided

*U've-hach gisa hilulei ve-chingei* — on one side of the city the slaughter was underway, while on the other side, celebrations and festivities continued. *Ve-lo hava yada hanei be-hanei* — the one half of the city did not know what was happening in the other. This detail is haunting in its own right. It may strain the imagination as to how such a thing is possible logistically, but its truth as a historical phenomenon — that in times of catastrophe communities in close proximity can remain entirely unaware of one another's fate — is well documented. One thinks of Jewish communities in Eastern Europe during the *Shoah*, where Jews in one country had no knowledge of the mass murder already underway in neighboring lands.

The deeper point of these stories about *Tur Malka* is often overlooked, because on *Tisha B'Av* people tend to stop the reading of this material before reaching it, since it no longer concerns the *Churban ha-Bayit* directly. But the *Gemara* is making precisely this point: the destruction was not only of the *Beis ha-Mikdash*. It was the destruction of a civilization, of cities, of an entire population and way of life. The rooster and hen, the wedding procession — these are prosaic details of traditional life, precisely the kind that are swept away in catastrophe. The Jews of *Tur Malka* could not adapt even slightly to the Roman presence, could not absorb even the minor disruption of the requisitioned chickens. And ultimately everything was destroyed.

---

## Yanai's Villages

### Jacob's Beauty

*U've-hach gisa hilulei ve-chingei* — having described the slaughter of *Tur Malka*, the *Gemara* now quotes the verse: *bala Hashem ve-lo chamal et kol ne'ot Yaakov* — God swallowed up and had no mercy on all the dwellings of Jacob. This verse from *Eicha* frames what follows.

### 600K Villages

*Ki ata Ravin amar Rabbi Yochanan: ailu shitin ribo ayarot she-hayu le-Yanai ha-melech be-Har ha-Melech* — these are the 600,000 villages that the Hasmonean king Yanai had on *Har ha-Melech*. *Ve-chol achat ve-achat hayu bah ke-yotzei Mitzrayim* — and each one of them had as many inhabitants as those who went out of Egypt, which is to say 600,000 males of fighting age, and by extension a total population of perhaps two million per village. The arithmetic, at 600,000 villages each with something like two million people, produces numbers that are frankly staggering.

### Three Villages

*Chutz mi-shalosh she-hayu bahen kiflayim ke-yotzei Mitzrayim* — with the exception of three villages that had double that number. These three were *Kfar Bish*, *Kfar Shichlayim*, and *Kfar Dichraya*. Their names are expressive. *Kfar Bish* — "the bad village" — *dela yahavi beis ushpiza*, because they did not provide lodging to wayfarers, in the manner of Sodom. *Kfar Shichlayim* — named for *shichlayim*, a type of watercress, because the residents made their living from that vegetable. *Kfar Dichraya* — "the village of males" — because, as Rabbi Yochanan explains, *she-hayu nesheihem yoldos zacharim techilla ve-yoldos nekeiva ba-achrona ve-poskos* — the women would first bear sons, then daughters, and then stop. The precise critique embedded in this last name is somewhat unclear.

### Ulla Challenges

*Amar Ulla: ledidi chazi li hahu atra* — Ulla said, I myself saw that place you are describing. *Ve-afilu shitin ribo kanei lo machzik* — it cannot even contain 600,000 reeds, let alone 600,000 villages. Ulla is directly calling out the exaggeration. In the *Gemara*'s version, a *min* — a heretic, though the parallel to *Tzadoki* in some texts suggests the original *girsa* was indeed *min* — challenges Rabbi Chanina: *shiku meshakritsu* — you people are lying.

### Land Expands

Rabbi Chanina responds: *Eretz Tzvi kesiv* — the land of Israel is described in Scripture as the land of the deer. *Mah tzvi zeh ein oro machzik et besaro* — just as a deer's hide, once removed, cannot be stretched back over the carcass that it once contained, because it shrinks outside the body, *af Eretz Yisrael, bi-zman she-yoshveha aleha ravcha* — so too the land of Israel, when its people dwell upon it, it expands. *U-vi-zman she-ein yoshveha aleha gamda* — and when its people are gone from it, it contracts. The physical smallness of the land today in no way contradicts the tradition that at its height it contained all those villages, because the land itself is of a different nature when inhabited by its people.

---

## Kfar Sekaniah

### Three Rabbis Query

*Rav Minyumi bar Chilkiya ve-Rav Chilkiya bar Tuvya ve-Rav Huna bar Chiya havu yasvei gabei hadadi* — three rabbis were sitting together and one of them said: *ika de-shamei lei milsa mi-Kfar Sekanya shel Mitzrayim leima* — if anyone has heard something about this place, *Kfar Sekanya* of Egypt, let him speak. A note on the geography: Soncino suggests that the original text may have read *Kfar Sekanya shel Notzrim* rather than *Mitzrayim* — that is, Nazareth — and that this was a place that later became associated with early Jewish-Christian sectarianism. Steinsaltz notes a city in the Galilee called *Sekanya*. Whatever the precise location, the tradition being invoked is of a place that had once been a model of piety and righteousness.

### Betrothed Couple

*Patach chad mineihu ve-amar: maaseh be-arus ve-arusa* — one of the three opened and said: there was a story involving a betrothed man and woman — meaning they had completed *kiddushin* but had not yet had *chuppah* and were not yet living together as husband and wife. *She-nishbu le-vein ha-ovdei kochavim* — they were taken captive by idolaters. *Ve-hisi'um zeh la-zeh* — and the captors, apparently not realizing the two were already married, put them together for the purpose of having them produce children as slaves.

One might think: they are already married, so what is the problem? The issue is that they had only *kiddushin* without *nisuin*, and one may not live as husband and wife without a *kesuva*. *Ve-amra lo: bevakasha mimcha al tiga bi, she-ein li kesuva mimcha* — she said to him: please do not touch me, for I have no *kesuva* from you. *Ve-lo naga bah ad yom moso* — and he did not touch her until the day he died.

When he died, she said to their captors: *sifdu la-zeh she-kipah et yitzro, ve-yoter mi-Yosef* — eulogize this man who subdued his desires, and he was greater than Joseph. *De-havah Yosef lo hava ela chada sha'ata* — Joseph resisted for only one moment. *Ve-da kol yoma ve-yoma* — this man, every single day. *U've-Yosef lav be-chada mita havu* — Joseph and Potiphar's wife were not sharing a bed. *Ve-ha be-chada mita* — but this couple were sharing a bed. *U've-Yosef lav ishto* — and Potiphar's wife was not Joseph's wife, *ve-ha ishto* — while this woman was his own wife. He resisted every day what Yosef resisted for a single moment, under far more intimate circumstances, and from his own lawful spouse.

### Grain Price Story

*Patach idach ve-amar: maaseh ve-amdu arbaim modiyot be-dinar* — the second rabbi opened and told: there was a time in this town when forty measures of grain could be bought for a dinar — grain was plentiful and cheap, a sign of prosperity. Then *nechsar ha-sha'ar* — the rate dropped, so that now only thirty-nine measures could be bought for a dinar. They investigated the cause. *U-vadeku u-matzu av u-veno she-vau al naara meurasah be-yom ha-kippurim* — and they found a father and son who had committed adultery with a betrothed young woman on Yom Kippur. The gravity of this sin is compounded at every level: the forbidden relationship, the sacred day, the violation of a betrothed woman, and the fact that it was father and son together. *Ve-heviyu le-veit din ve-sakalu* — they brought them to *beit din* and stoned them. *Ve-chazar ha-sha'ar li-mkomo* — and the grain price returned to its prior level. So thorough was their communal responsibility that even a single transgression had a measurable effect on the prosperity of the entire town — and so thorough was their justice that when the sin was addressed, the effect was reversed.

### False Accusation

*Patach idach ve-amar: maaseh be-adam echad she-natan einav be-ishto le-garesha* — the third rabbi told: a man wished to divorce his wife. *Ve-hayetah ketubatah merubah* — but her *kesuva* was very large, and he sought a way to avoid paying it. He arranged to manufacture evidence against her. *Halach ve-ziman et shoshvinav* — he invited his friends. *Ve-he'echilan ve-hishkan* — he fed them and plied them with drink until they were drunk. *Ve-hishkivan al mita achat* — he had them all lie together on one bed. *Ve-hevi loven beitza ve-hitipah beineihen* — he brought egg white and placed it among them, making it appear as semen. *Ve-he'emid lahen eidim* — and he stationed witnesses to observe. He then came before *beit din* claiming that these men had committed adultery with his wife. The staging of the scene recalls something almost theatrical in its calculated wickedness.

*Ve-haya sham zaken echad mi-talmidei Shammai ha-Zaken, Bava ben Buta shemo* — but there was present one elder from the disciples of Shammai the Elder, his name Bava ben Buta. *Amar lahem: kach mekubalni mi-Shammai ha-Zaken, loven beitza soled min ha-or, ve-shichvat zera docha min ha-or* — he said: this is the tradition I received from Shammai the Elder: egg white, when exposed to heat, shrivels and contracts, while semen is absorbed into cloth when brought near fire. *U-vadeku u-matzu ki-dvarav* — they tested it and found exactly as he had said: it was egg white, not semen. *Ve-heviuhu le-veit din ve-hilkuhu* — the husband was brought before *beit din* and flogged. *Ve-higbu ketubatah mimenu* — and they compelled him to pay his wife's *kesuva*.

The progression of the three stories is instructive. The first speaks to the personal righteousness of individuals. The second and third speak to the communal structures of justice: the *beit din* acting swiftly and correctly, the town taking full responsibility for the sins committed within its bounds. This stands in sharp contrast to the rabbinic failures described earlier in the tractate, where the leadership of Jerusalem saw what was unfolding and did not act.

### Abaye Questions

*Amar leih Abaye le-Rav Yosef: ve-achar de-havu tzaddikim kulei hai* — Abaye asked Rav Yosef: if they were so righteous, why were they punished?

### No Mourning

*Amar leih: mishum de-lo iabalu al Yerushalayim* — because they did not mourn over the destruction of Jerusalem. As the verse says: *simchu et Yerushalayim ve-gilu vah kol ohaveha, sisu itah masos kol ha-mitablim aleha* — rejoice with Jerusalem and exult in her, all who love her; be glad with her in gladness, all who mourned for her. Only those who share in the mourning will share in the rejoicing.

This is a historically grounded observation. The *Churban* was felt differently depending on proximity and circumstance. How much did a community in the Galilee, far from Jerusalem, truly feel the destruction of the *Beis ha-Mikdash* as having altered their daily lives? One can imagine a town — and Nazareth is in the Galilee, far from Jerusalem — that was genuinely righteous in its internal conduct but that did not cultivate the larger national and communal sense of loss. Highly responsible within their own *arba amos*, their own village, but without the broader sense that they were part of something larger whose destruction demanded mourning. This is the critique the *Gemara* levels at them: personal and communal righteousness alone is not sufficient. One must also feel the loss of *Yerushalayim* as one's own.

---

## Beitar Cedar Trees

### Tree Planting

The *Gemara* now moves to the destruction of *Beitar*. *De-hava nahigi ki avei misyalid yanuka* — the practice there was: when a baby boy was born, *shatlei arza* — they would plant a cedar tree; *yanukta* — when a baby girl was born, *shatlei turnisa* — they would plant a pine or cypress tree. It is a beautiful *minhag*, rooting the lives of the children literally in the land.

### Trees for Chuppah

*Ve-ki aveu minsevei* — when the boy and girl grew up and married, *kaitzei lo* — they would cut down their respective trees *ve-avdu ganana* — and construct a *chuppah* from them. The marriage canopy was thus built from trees planted at the moment of birth, intertwining the couple's origins with the culmination of their lives together.

### Caesar's Axle Breaks

*Yoma chad avei kachalfa bartei de-Keisar* — one day Caesar's daughter was passing through *Beitar* when *itbar ashaka de-rispak* — the axle of her carriage broke. *Katzu arza* — the soldiers cut down a nearby cedar tree to repair the carriage.

### Jews Defend Tree

*Asu naflu alaihu* — the Jews of *Beitar* attacked the Romans for cutting down the tree. *Machun* — they beat them. *Asu amri leh le-Keisar: mardu bach Yehuda'ei* — they went and told Caesar that the Jews were rebelling. *Asu alaihu* — and Caesar came with his army.

Once again, the inability to absorb even the slightest disruption to their traditional practices — however beautiful those practices were — proved catastrophic. The very qualities that made the community admirable in peacetime, their rootedness in custom and land, could not accommodate the realities of Roman occupation.

### Beitar Destroyed

*Gada be-chori af kol keren Yisrael* — God cut down in fierce anger all the horn of Israel. *Amar Rav Zeira amar Rav Abba amar Rabbi Yochanan: eilu shemonim elef karnei milchamah she-nichnasu le-krach Beitar* — these are eighty thousand horns of war that entered the city of *Beitar* when they conquered it, *ve-hargu bah anashim ve-nashim ve-taf* — and they slaughtered men, women, and children.

### Blood Flows

*Ad she-halach daman ve-naful le-yama ha-gadol* — until the blood flowed all the way to the Mediterranean. Lest one think the sea was nearby, the *Gemara* notes: *rechokah hayetah mil* — it was a *mil* away, and the blood flowed that distance. *Tanya, Rabbi Eliezer ha-Gadol omer: shenei nechalim yesh be-Bikat Yadayim* — there are two wadis in *Bikat Yadayim*, near *Beitar*, one flowing one direction and one the other, *ve-shi'aru chachamim shenei chalakim mayim ve-echad dam* — and the sages estimated that at that time these wadis ran two-thirds water and one-third blood. *Ve-masnista tana: sheva shanim batzru ovdei kochavim et karmeihem mi-daman shel Yisrael belo zevel* — and the *braita* teaches that for seven years afterward the non-Jews harvested their vineyards fertilized by the blood of Israel without any additional manure. The image is searing, and one cannot help but think of what is known about the soil of Auschwitz.

---

## Zechariah's Blood

### Elder's Testimony

*Amar Rabbi Chiya bar Avin amar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: sach li zaken echad mei-anshei Yerushalayim* — a certain elder from the men of Jerusalem told him: *be-vika zu harag Nevuzaradan Rav Tabachim* — in this valley Nevuzaradan, the head of the butchers, Nebuchadnezzar's chief general, slaughtered 211 myriads — 2.1 million — and in Jerusalem itself, 940,000. *Al even achas, ad she-halach daman ve-naga be-damo shel Zechariah* — all of them on one stone, until their blood reached and joined the blood of Zechariah. This Zechariah was a *kohein* who had been murdered by order of King Yoash because he refused to stop rebuking the people in the name of God — not the *Zechariah ha-Navi* of the *Tanach* who returned from Babylonian exile and figures in the second *Beis ha-Mikdash* period, but an earlier figure. *Ve-damim be-damim nagu* — and the bloods met one another, fulfilling the verse.

### Blood Bubbles

*Ashkechei le-damei de-Zechariah, de-hava kamartach ve-salik* — Nevuzaradan, upon entering the *Beis ha-Mikdash*, found the blood of Zechariah bubbling on the floor. *Amar: mai hai* — he asked, what is this? *Amru lei: dam zvachim de-ishtapuch* — the Jews told him it was sacrificial blood that had been spilled. *Ayise damma ve-lo dami* — he brought animal blood for comparison, and it did not match. He knew they were lying.

### Zechariah Confession

*Amar lehu: ei amritu li mutav, ve-ei lav masrikna le-visraichu be-masreki de-farzla* — tell me the truth, or I will flay your flesh with iron combs. *Amru lei: navi haya banu de-hava kamocheach lan be-milei de-shmaya, kaminnu alavei ve-katlinan lei* — they confessed: there was a prophet among us who rebuked us with words of Heaven, and we rose up against him and killed him. *Ve-ha kamma shanin de-lo ka nayach damei* — and for many years his blood has not stopped bubbling.

### Sanhedrin Slaughter

*Amar lehu: ana mefaysina lei* — Nevuzaradan said he would appease the blood. *Ayise Sanhedrin Gedolah ve-Sanhedrin Ketana ve-katlinhu alavei* — he slaughtered the Great Sanhedrin and the Small Sanhedrin over it, *ve-lo nach* — and the blood did not rest. The pattern of leadership bearing responsibility is reinforced: the very institutions of Jewish governance that had failed are the first to be called to account. *Bachurim u-vesulos ve-katlinhu alavei* — he slaughtered young men and young women over it, and still it did not rest. *Ayise tinokot shel beis rabban ve-katlinhu alavei* — he brought the schoolchildren and slaughtered them over the blood, and still it did not stop boiling.

### Blood Settles

*Amar lei: Zechariah, Zechariah, tovim she-bahen ibadtum* — Nevuzaradan said: Zechariah, Zechariah, I have destroyed the best among them. *Nicha lach de-avdinhu le-chulhu* — do you want me to wipe out all of them? *K'd-amar lei hachi, nach* — when he said this, the blood finally ceased to boil.

*U-ve-hahu sha'ata hirher teshuvah be-da'atei* — at that very moment, Nevuzaradan had a thought of *teshuvah* in his mind. He said: *u-mah al nefesh achas kach, hahu gavra de-katil kulei hanei nishmasa, al achas kamma ve-chamma* — if for one soul such vengeance is exacted, then I who have killed all these souls — how much more greatly will I be punished?

### Nevuzaradan Converts

*Arak* — he fled. *Shadar shetar partisa le-veiseh* — he sent a document home to distribute his property and settle his affairs. *Ve-isgayar* — and he converted.

---

## Enemies Convert

### Naaman & Nev.

*Tanu rabbanan: Naaman ger toshav haya* — the *Braita* teaches: Naaman, healed of his *tzara'at* by Elisha, became a *ger toshav* — he abandoned *avoda zara* but did not become a full Jew, as is evident from the plain meaning of the *psukim*. *Nevuzaradan ger tzedek havay* — but Nevuzaradan became a full convert. So the very general who destroyed the *Beis ha-Mikdash* in its first iteration ultimately entered the covenant of Israel.

### Haman's Line

*Mi-bnei banav shel Haman lamdu Torah bi-Vnei Brak* — the grandchildren of Haman studied Torah in *Bnei Brak*. The descendants of the man who sought to annihilate the Jewish people are found learning Torah in one of the great centers of Jewish life.

### Sisra's Line

*Mi-bnei banav shel Sisra limdu tinokot bi-Yerushalayim* — the descendants of Sisra taught schoolchildren in Jerusalem.

### Sancheriv's Line

*Mi-bnei banav shel Sancheriv limdu Torah ba-rabbim* — and the descendants of Sancheriv taught Torah in public. *U-man inun? Shmaya ve-Avtalyon* — and who are these? Shmaya and Avtalyon, the great rabbinic leaders who were the teachers of Hillel and Shammai themselves. The enemies of Israel — Haman a descendant of *Amalek* — ultimately find their descendants not only entering the Jewish people but becoming its greatest teachers. There is a *teshuvah* of Rav Oshry, *She'eilot U-Tshuvot Mi-Ma'amakim*, written in the aftermath of the *Shoah*, in which the question of whether a German soldier consumed by guilt might be permitted to convert is addressed. The precedent of Nevuzaradan and the descendants of Haman are part of the broader conversation about whether even one who participated in such evil can find a path to repentance and entry into the Jewish people. The *Rambam* takes up related questions regarding whether *Amalek*, if they do *teshuvah*, can become converts.

---

## Yaakov & Esav

### Zechariah Verse

*Haynu de-ksiv: nasati et damayich al tzhiach sela le-vilti hikasos* — this is the verse: I have placed your blood on the bare rock so that it cannot be covered over. The blood of Zechariah could not be absorbed, could not be hidden, lying exposed on the floor of the *Beis ha-Mikdash*, demanding justice.

### Hadrian & Vespa.

*Ha-kol kol Yaakov ve-ha-yadayim yedei Esav* — the voice is the voice of Jacob and the hands are the hands of Esau. The *Gemara* now interprets this verse in terms of the great destructions. *Ha-kol ze Adryanus Keisar she-harag be-Alexandrya shel Mitzrayim shishim ribo al shishim ribo* — the voice is Hadrian, who killed in Alexandria of Egypt 600,000 times 600,000, *kiflayim ke-yotzei Mitzrayim* — double those who went out of Egypt. Rashi explains: *ha-kol tzevacha u-vechi ola mi-Yaakov* — the voice, meaning the outcry and wailing, rises from Jacob, because of the hands of Esau. *Kol Yaakov ze Aspasyanus Keisar* — in another reading, the voice of Jacob refers to Vespasian, *she-harag bi-krach Beitar arba me'os ribo* — who killed in *Beitar* four million, *ve-amri lah arba'as alafim ribo* — or according to another version, forty million. *Ve-ha-yadayim yedei Esav zu malchus ha-resha'a she-hachriva et beisenu ve-sarfa et heichaleinu ve-higlisenu me-artzenu* — the hands of Esau, this is the evil kingdom of Rome, which destroyed our home, burned our sanctuary, and exiled us from our land.

### Prayer & War

*Davar acher: kol kol Yaakov, ein lecha tefilla she-mo'elet she-ein bo mi-zaro shel Yaakov* — another interpretation: you have no prayer that is effective unless it contains something of the descendants of Jacob. *Ve-ha-yadayim yedei Esav, ein lecha milchama she-notzachat she-ein bo mi-zaro shel Esav* — and you have no war that is won unless there is something from the descendants of Esau involved in it.

*Heinu de-amar Reb Elazar: be-shot lashon techavei, be-chirchurei lashon techavei* — and this is what Rabbi Elazar said: in the slander of the tongue it will be hidden, in the contentiousness of the tongue it will be hidden. Rashi connects this back to the story of *Kamtza u-Bar Kamtza* — the in-fighting, the *lashon hara*, that ultimately caused the destruction.

### Two Destructions

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav: mai de-chtiv, al naharot Bavel sham yashavnu gam bachinu be-zochreinu et Tziyon* — what does this verse mean? *Melamed she-her'ah HaKadosh Baruch Hu le-David churban bayit rishon ve-churban bayit sheni* — God showed David both the destruction of the First Temple and the destruction of the Second. *Churban bayit rishon: she-ne'emar al naharot Bavel* — the First Temple's destruction: *by the waters of Babylon*. *Bayit sheni: de-chtiv zechor Hashem li-vnei Edom et yom Yerushalayim ha-omrim aru aru ad ha-yesod bah* — the Second Temple: remember, God, against the children of Edom the day of Jerusalem when they said, destroy it, destroy it to its very foundation. The *bnei Edom* here is read not as the literal Edomites but as the figurative Edom — Rome — that destroyed the Second *Beis ha-Mikdash*.

---

## Four Hundred

### Children Captive

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel, ve-iteima Reb Ami* — it was taught: *maaseh be-arba me'ot yeladim u-me'ot yeladot she-nishbu le-kalon* — four hundred boys and girls were taken captive for degradation — meaning they were to be used for sexual purposes by their Roman captors. *Hirgishu be-atzmam lema hen mitbakshim* — they sensed why they were being taken.

### Eldest Interprets

They asked: *im anu tov'im ba-yam anu ba'im le-chayei ha-olam ha-ba* — if we were to drown ourselves in the sea, would we attain the world to come? *Darash lahen ha-gadol she-bahen* — the eldest interpreted for them the following verse: *Amar Hashem mi-Bashan ashiv, ashiv mi-metzulot yam* — the Lord said, from the Bashan I will bring back, I will bring back from the depths of the sea. *Mi-Bashan ashiv: mi-bein shinei arayot ashiv* — from the Bashan, meaning from the teeth of the lions. *Mi-metzulot yam: elu she-tvu'im ba-yam* — from the depths of the sea, these are those who drown themselves in the sea. God declares that He will bring back those who give their lives to the deep rather than surrender themselves to the lions — Rome.

### Children Jump

*Kivan she-shamu yeladot kach, kafzu kulan ve-naflu le-toch ha-yam* — when the girls heard this interpretation, they all jumped and fell into the sea. *Nas'u yeladim kal va-chomer be-atzmam* — the boys then made a *kal va-chomer* upon themselves: *ve-amru: u-ma halalu she-darkan le-kach, kach anu kach* — if the girls, for whom this form of abuse is in some sense more expected, were willing to do this, *anu she-ein darkenu le-kach, al achas kama ve-chama* — we, who would suffer what is even less natural, how much more so. *Af hen kafzu le-toch ha-yam* — they too jumped into the sea.

### Sheep Verse

*Ve-aleihem ha-katuv omer: ki alecha horagnu kol ha-yom, nechshavnu ke-tzon tivcha* — and upon them the verse says: for Your sake we are killed all the day; we are counted as sheep to the slaughter.

### Halakhic Debate

This *midrash* is of considerable *halachic* significance. *Tosafot* and the *chachmei Ashkenaz* drew upon it in the context of the Crusader persecutions, when Jews faced the prospect of forced baptism without any direct threat of death. The question is: is one permitted — or perhaps even obligated — to take one's own life in order to avoid being forced to commit *aveira*? The doctrine of *yehareg ve-al ya'avor* applies when the choice offered by the oppressor is: convert or die. But what if the oppressor will not kill you, only forcibly sin against you? May one actively choose death in that circumstance?

Haym Soloveitchik argued at length that there is no sound *halachic* basis for this, and that *Tosafot*'s reliance on *midrashim* like this one reflects a post-facto rationalization of what Jews had already done in extremis, rather than a genuine *halachic* derivation. His argument begins from the premise that *midrashim* are not a legitimate source for *psak halacha*.

One may question this premise at its root. Even conceding that a *midrash* is not a standard *halachic* text in the way a *sugya* of *Gemara* is, it nonetheless expresses the values and attitudes of *Chazal*. One cannot read this *midrash* without sensing clearly that *Chazal* regarded what these children did as not merely understandable but admirable — perhaps even praiseworthy. And if one knows what *Chazal*'s attitude toward a phenomenon is, that cannot be entirely excluded from the way one reads *halachic* texts bearing on the same phenomenon, even if the *midrash* itself does not constitute direct *halachic* evidence.

*Tosafot* on this *Gemara* reads: *kafzu kulan ve-naflu le-toch ha-yam*. The countertext they must address is the story of Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon, who when being burned said *mutav she-yitla mi she-netana ve-al yachavel be-atzmo* — better that God should take my soul and I should not injure myself. *Tosafot* explains the distinction: *hachi yere'im hayu mi-yisurim* — these children feared the torture. *De-amrinan: ilmale nigdu le-Chananya Mishael ve-Azarya palchu le-tzalma* — for we are told that had Chananya, Mishael, and Azarya been tortured, they would have worshipped the idol. The fear is not of death but of capitulation under torture. Furthermore, *Tosafot* notes: *ve-od al korcham hayu me'anim otam ve-lo hayu horgim otam klal* — in addition, they could have been raped without being killed. If the oppressor will neither kill them nor offer them the option of honoring *yehareg ve-al ya'avor*, and if the only escape from the sin is death, then *Tosafot* holds that what these children did was at least an acceptable course of action.

This remains an important *Gemara* in the larger conversation about martyrdom, the limits of *yehareg ve-al ya'avor*, and the circumstances — if any — under which *halacha* regards self-destruction as other than forbidden.

---

---

# Gittin 58

## Woman & Seven Children

### Seven Sons Refuse

The Gemara continues from the middle of 57b, following the *aggadata* about young children who threw themselves into the sea to avoid a life of moral degradation — a passage the Tosafot cites as evidence that, in extremis, even taking one's own life may constitute an act of *kiddush Hashem*, departing from the standard halachic framework that ordinarily governs martyrdom. With that context in mind, the Gemara introduces another story in the same spirit.

The verse that frames the entire discussion is from Tehillim: *ki alecha horagnu kol hayom, nechshavnu k'tzon tivcha* — "For Your sake we are slaughtered all day long, we are counted as sheep for the slaughter." Rabbi Yehuda applies this verse specifically to the story of a woman and her seven children.

They were brought before Caesar one by one and commanded to worship idols. The first son refused, citing *Anochi Hashem Elokecha* — "I am the Lord your God." He was taken out and executed. The second quoted *Lo yihyeh lecha elohim acherim al panai* — "You shall have no other gods before Me" — and was likewise killed. The third answered with *Zoveach la'elohim yochoram* — "Whoever sacrifices to foreign gods shall be destroyed." The fourth cited *Lo tishtachaveh l'el acher* — "Do not bow to another god." The fifth declared *Shema Yisrael Hashem Elokeinu Hashem Echad*. The sixth quoted *V'yadata hayom vahasheivota el levavecha ki Hashem hu ha'elokim bashamayim mima'al v'al ha'aretz mitachat ein od* — "You shall know today and take to heart that the Lord is God in the heavens above and on the earth below; there is no other." One notices here a progression: the earlier sons quoted the *lo ta'asehs*, the prohibitions against idolatry, while the later sons shifted to positive affirmations of faith.

### Seventh Son & Mother

When the seventh child was brought before Caesar, the emperor, frustrated by this point, tried a different strategy. He would throw down his imperial coin — bearing his own image — and instruct the boy to pick it up, so that onlookers would think he was bowing in submission to the emperor's authority. This was, of course, the imperial cult: the veneration of Caesar as a god. The child's response was striking: *Chaval alecha keisar, chaval alecha keisar* — "Woe to you, Caesar, woe to you." If you are so insistent on your own honor, he said, how much more is God insistent upon His honor? How then could I even make it *appear* that I am betraying God's honor?

The child was taken out to be executed. At that moment, his mother asked the soldiers to bring him to her for a moment so she could embrace him. She gathered all seven of her children — apparently before any of them had been killed — and spoke to them. She said: Go and tell Abraham your forefather, *Atah akadata mizbe'ach echad, va'ani akadeti shivah mizbachot* — "You bound one altar, while I have bound seven altars." Then she too went up to the roof, fell, and died. A *bat kol* then declared: *Em habanim smeichah* — "The mother of children rejoices." They had sanctified God's name.

It is worth pausing over the precise wording. The text uses *mizbe'ach* — altar — rather than *zevach* — sacrifice — which seems grammatically awkward. One senses that the language is deliberately softened, shifting away from the stark statement that Isaac was literally offered as a slaughter. This connects to a *midrash* in which Abraham did not actually slaughter Isaac — it says *al tishlach yadcha el hana'ar*, "do not lay your hand upon the lad" — but that the fire on the altar consumed him nonetheless, and a miracle reconstituted him. The *midrash* about the *eifer shel Yitzchak munach lifnei Hashem* — the ashes of Isaac resting before God — plays on exactly this reading.

This imagery proved extraordinarily potent. During the Crusades, Jewish communities facing forced conversion invoked the *akeidah* as a model for taking their own lives, and in some cases the lives of their children, rather than allow forcible baptism. The Crusade chronicles record parents using language almost identical to this passage — "Abraham offered one sacrifice; I offer all my children." It raises profound halachic questions: not merely taking one's own life, but actively taking a child's life. And the anguish was compounded when, on at least one occasion, the threatened assault never materialized, and the tragedy had been carried out in vain. Here in the Talmudic story, the mother took her own life but did not herself kill her children — and the text's use of *mizbe'ach* rather than *zevach* perhaps reflects that same hesitation about stating the thing too directly.

### Jeremiah's Lament

The Gemara now applies the verse from Tehillim — *ki alecha horagnu kol hayom* — to several other contexts, moving through a series of interpretations that carry us from literal martyrdom into the world of *talmud Torah*.

---

## Martyrdom Interpretations

### Brit Milah & Martyrdom

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reads *ki alecha horagnu kol hayom* as referring to *brit milah*, which was *nitnah bashmini* — given on the eighth day. During Roman persecutions, the Romans frequently prohibited circumcision, in part because they considered it a disfigurement of the body, and Jews were repeatedly prepared to risk their lives in order to perform the commandment. Rashi offers a somewhat different reading — that sometimes the surgical procedure itself could lead to complications and death — but it seems more compelling to read the verse as referring to the willingness to give one's life, or risk it, for the sake of *milah*.

### Torah Tent Slaughter

Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish offers a reading that is, on the face of it, startling. He says *ki alecha horagnu kol hayom* refers to *talmidei chachamim shemarim hilchot shechitah be'atzman* — Torah scholars who demonstrate the laws of *shechitah* on themselves. When learning *hilchot shechitah* and wanting to illustrate the proper movement of the knife on the animal's neck, one slips — and that is *ki alecha horagnu kol hayom*.

This is a jarring juxtaposition. From Roman persecution and the Caesar demanding emperor worship, we have suddenly shifted to the *beit midrash* and someone demonstrating slaughter techniques. The Gemara itself adds: *d'amar Rava, kol milei lachzei inish b'nafshei bar mishechitah* — one may demonstrate anything on oneself except *shechitah*. Do not try this at home. There is also mention of *tzara'at umar'ot nega'im* — one should not demonstrate the appearance of leprous afflictions on one's own body, presumably because of *ayin hara*.

Yet the shift itself is theologically significant. Recall the arc of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai: the entire camera of Jewish life pivoted from the *Beit HaMikdash* and Roman Caesar and martyrdom to *ten li Yavneh v'chachameha* — the world of Torah replacing that other world. Here too, a verse that once described literal death at Roman hands is now given new meaning in the *beit midrash*.

### Torah Devotion

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak completes the transformation. He reads *ki alecha horagnu kol hayom* as referring to *talmidei chachamim shememitim atzmam al divrei Torah* — Torah scholars who kill themselves, figuratively, over words of Torah. The literal martyrdom of the *churban* era becomes the self-sacrifice of the scholar who devotes himself entirely to learning.

This is grounded in the dictum of Reish Lakish: *ein divrei Torah mitkaymin ela bemi shememit atzmo aleihem* — words of Torah endure only in one who is willing to die for them — as the verse says, *zot hatorah adam ki yamut b'ohel* — "This is the Torah: when a person dies in the tent." The figurative death in the tent of Torah replaces the literal death *ki alecha horagnu kol hayom*.

---

## Destruction of Beitar

### Tefillin at Beitar

The Gemara now turns to the destruction of Beitar. Rabbah bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *arbaim se'ah ktzitzai tefillin nimtze'u berashei harugei Beitar* — forty *se'ah* of *tefillin batim* were found on the heads of those slaughtered at Beitar. Forty *se'ah* is the measure required for a *mikvah*, which one listener noted is perhaps symbolically resonant, though the precise import requires further thought.

Rabbi Yannai b'Rabbi Yishmael disputes the figure: it was not forty *se'ah*, but *shalosh kupot shel arbaim arbaim* — three containers each of forty *se'ah*, three times the amount. A *braita* teaches yet another version: *arbaim kupot shel shalosh shalosh* — forty containers of three *se'ah* each. The Gemara resolves that these two versions do not in fact contradict: *had'reisha had'dara* — one refers to *tefillin shel yad* and the other to *tefillin shel rosh*. Rashi explains that the *tefillin shel rosh*, which requires four compartments, cannot be made as small as the *shel yad*; anyone who has seen the tiny *tefillin* discovered at Masada will understand the difficulty of fitting four *batim* into a single very small housing, and so the *shel rosh* would necessarily be larger — roughly three times the size of the *shel yad*.

The image of all these slaughtered people still wearing their *tefillin* is arresting. People in those days wore *tefillin* throughout the day. The *tefillin* represents both the *mitzvah* and the *parshiyot* written within — a symbol of the *Torah* world. And so the image of the *tefillin* on the heads of the slain intersects the three themes woven throughout this passage: the destruction of the *Beit HaMikdash*, the destruction of the people, and the destruction of the world of *Torah*.

Rabbi Assi adds: *arba'a kabbin mo'ach nimtze'u al even achat* — four *kav* of brains were found on a single stone, from the smashing of skulls. Ulla says the figure was nine *kabbin*.

Rav Kahana (and some say it was Shila bar Mari) asks: what is the *pasuk* for this? The verse cited is from Tehillim 137: *Bat Bavel hashidudah, ashrei she-yeshalem lach, ashrei she-yo'chez venipetz et olalayich el hasala* — "O devastated Daughter of Babylon, praised is the one who repays you what you have done to us; praised is the one who seizes your infants and dashes them against the rock." This is a deeply challenging verse, one that has generated much contemporary discussion given its apparent expression of bloodlust. Here it is cited as evidence of what the Jewish people suffered — if this is what is considered appropriate repayment, then by inference this is what was done to them.

### Children of Zion

The Gemara turns to the verse in *Eichah*: *B'nei Tzion ha-yekarim ham'sula'im bapaz* — "The precious children of Zion, esteemed above gold." What does *m'sula'im bapaz* mean? Does it mean they were literally covered in gold jewelry?

The Gemara rejects this: *d'bei Rabbi Shila* reports that only two measures of the finest gold, *pizi*, descended into the world — one in Rome, and one distributed across the entire rest of the world. There was nowhere near enough for every child in Zion to be coated in gold. Rather, *m'sula'im bapaz* means *she-hayu meganim et ha-paz be-yofyam* — they shamed gold by the superiority of their beauty. Gold jewelry paled compared to how these children looked.

The Gemara continues: originally, prestigious Romans would keep an image of a handsome person — a seal or portrait — on the wall of their bedchambers during intercourse, believing that what one envisions at the moment of conception influences the appearance of the resulting child. This goes back to some degree to the story of Yaakov and the striped rods. After Israel was taken captive, the Romans would instead *maiti benei Yisrael ve-asrei be-charei de-puryeihu* — bring Israelite captives and tie them at the foot of their beds — in order to produce beautiful offspring.

One Roman asks his friend: where is this terrible humiliation actually prophesied? The friend responds with the verse *gam kol choli ve-chol maka asher lo katuv be-sefer ha-Torah ha-zot* — "also every illness and every plague that is not written in this book of Torah" will befall you. Even the unimaginable, the unprecedented degradations, were encompassed in that catch-all phrase. The first man says: how far was that verse from where I was up to in my learning? His friend answers: about a page and a half. The man replies: had I gotten there myself, I wouldn't have needed to ask you. A strange little exchange — but it perhaps lightens the devastating material slightly.

### Beitar Synagogues

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel: what does the verse *einai olela le-nafshi mi-kol benot iri* mean — "my eye afflicts my soul, more than all the daughters of my city"? *Arba mea batei kneisiyot hayu be-krach Beitar* — there were four hundred synagogues in the city of Beitar. Each synagogue had four hundred schoolteachers of young children. Each of those teachers had four hundred students. These are clearly hyperbolic numbers, but they evoke a vast and thriving world of Jewish education. When the enemy entered the city, they pierced the children with their staffs. When the enemy ultimately prevailed and captured the people, *karchum be-sifreihem ve-hitzitum ba-esh* — they wrapped the children and teachers in their books and set them ablaze. This is the same fate we associate with Rabbi Chananya ben Teradyon, but here it is depicted as happening to an entire civilization of Torah scholars and students. One cannot read this without thinking of later destructions.

---

## Rabbi Yehoshua Rescues

### Ransom from Prison

The Gemara presents the story of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya, who traveled to the great city of Rome. He was told: *tinok echad yesh be-veit ha-asurim* — there is one child in the prison, *yafeh einayim ve-tov ro'i ve-kvutzotav sdurot lo taltalim* — beautiful of eyes, handsome of appearance, his locks arranged in layers. Coming just after the discussion of the beauty of the *Benei Tzion*, the echo is unmistakable.

### Child's Knowledge

Rabbi Yehoshua went and stood at the entrance of the prison. He quoted the first half of a verse from Yeshayahu: *Mi natan limshisah Ya'akov ve'Yisrael le'vozezim* — "Who gave Jacob over to plunder and Israel to spoilers?" The child, from inside, responded with the second half of the verse: *Halo Hashem zo chatanu lo, velo avu bidrachav haloch, velo shamu betorato* — "Is it not the Lord, against Whom we sinned, in Whose ways they would not walk, and Whose Torah they did not heed?"

The child knew the end of the verse. Rabbi Yehoshua declared: *Muvtachni bo she-moreh hora'ah be'Yisrael* — I am confident that this child will rule on halachic matters in Israel. And he took an oath: *she'eini zaz mikan ad she'efdenu bechol mamon sheposkin alav* — I will not leave here until I redeem him, no matter the price demanded.

This raises an immediate question in light of the earlier *Gemara* about *tikkun olam* — the rabbinic enactment not to redeem captives for more than their worth, lest it encourage further taking of captives. Tosafot addresses this directly: *ki itcha sakanat nefashot podin shvuyim yoter mikdei dameihen* — when there is a genuine threat to life, one redeems captives for any sum. The earlier limitation applies only where life is not at risk. This is an important qualification of the earlier *Gemara* that had not been stated there explicitly.

Tosafot offers a second explanation: *mishum de'mufla be'chochmah hayah* — because this child was so obviously exceptional in his Torah knowledge, one might make an exception for him. This raises a perennial tension: on one hand, we resist distinguishing between lives based on social worth; on the other hand, *Mishnah Horayot* establishes that a *talmid chacham* takes precedence over all others.

### Rabbi Yishmael Identity

The Gemara reports: he did not leave until he redeemed him for a great sum of money, and it was not long before that child ruled on halachic matters in Israel. *U-manu* — and who was he? *Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha.*

---

## Rabbi Yishmael's Children

### Captors' Plan

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: there is a story about the son and daughter of Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha — himself a *kohen* of distinguished lineage — who were taken captive by two separate masters. We have just been told how beautiful these children were; their beauty made them desirable. *Liyamim nizdavgu sheneihem bemakom echad* — after some time, the two masters happened to meet. One said: I have a male slave of unparalleled beauty. The other said: I have a female slave more beautiful than any in the world. They agreed: let us have them marry one another, and we will divide the children between us. They placed them together in a room, treating them as commodities whose offspring would be split between owners.

### Siblings' Reunion

Each sat in a separate corner of the room. He said to himself: I am a *kohen*, descended from *kohanim gedolim* — shall I marry a slave woman? She said to herself: I am a *kohenet*, the daughter of *kohanim gedolim* — shall I marry a slave? They wept through the entire night, presumably unable to see one another in the dark. When dawn broke and they could finally see each other, *hikiru zeh et zeh* — they recognized one another as brother and sister. *Ve-nafalu zeh al zeh ve-ga'u bi-vchiyah* — they fell upon each other and cried out, *ad she-yatzta nishmatan* — until their souls departed.

There is something worth noting about their initial reasoning. Neither knew the other person was a Jew. They refused on the grounds of their priestly status — they could not marry a slave, even having themselves become slaves. It is this instinctive clinging to identity and dignity, before any recognition of kinship, that makes the reunion all the more devastating.

On them, Yirmeyahu composed his lament: *al eileh ani bochiya, eini eini yordah mayim* — "For these I weep; my eye, my eye runs down with water."

---

## Tzafnat Bat Pnu'el

### Tzafnat's Assault

Reish Lakish relates the story of a woman named *Tzafnat bat Pnu'el*. What does *Tzafnat* mean? *She-hakol tzofim be-yofyah* — everyone would gaze upon her beauty. *Pnu'el* means *bito shel kohen gadol she-shimesh lifnai ve-lifnim* — the daughter of a *kohen gadol* who served in the innermost chambers, the *lifnai ve-lifnim*, meaning the Holy of Holies. She was taken captive, and her captor abused her sexually the entire night. In the morning, he dressed her in seven garments and brought her out to sell her.

An exceedingly ugly man came and demanded to see her beauty before purchasing her. The captor said: if you want to buy her, buy her. The man insisted on seeing her. Six of her garments were stripped off. The seventh she herself tore away, rolled herself in the dust, and cried out to God.

### Challenge to God

Her words to God were: *Ribono shel olam, im aleinu lo chasata, al kedushat shimcha ha-gibor, lamah lo tachos* — "Master of the Universe, if You have no compassion on us, why will You not have compassion on Your great Name?" This is a striking moment in the Gemara — perhaps the first explicit articulation of what will become the central emotional register of *kinot*: a direct challenge to God, asking how He could allow this to happen.

For this, Yirmeyahu composed the lament: *biti ami chagri sak ve-hitpalshi be-afar* — "Daughter of my people, gird yourself with sackcloth and roll in the ashes; make mourning as for an only son, bitter lamentation." The phrase *ki pitom yavo ha-shoded aleinu* — "for the ravager will suddenly come upon us" — is notable: it says *aleinu*, "upon us," not *alayich*, "upon you." The Gemara observes: *ki kavyachol alai ve-alecha* — as if to say, it is upon Me and upon you. God Himself, as it were, is afflicted by the suffering of Israel. Yet this makes the challenge of the verse all the more acute: if God too is pained, how can God not defend His own name against the *shoded*?

---

## Societal Corruption

### Apprentice's Scheme

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: what does the verse *ve-ashku gever u-veito ve-ish ve-nachalato* — "they oppressed a man and his household, a man and his inheritance" — mean? There was a man who lusted after his master's wife. He was a carpenter's apprentice. One day his master found himself in need of a loan. The apprentice, who had more available cash, was approached for help. Instead of simply lending the money, the apprentice said: send your wife to me and she will receive the loan. The master sent his wife. She stayed three days.

Then the apprentice came to the master and asked about his wife's whereabouts. The master said: I sent her to you. The apprentice replied: I gave her the money right away and sent her off. But what I heard, he said, was that *ha-tinokot nit'allu bah ba-derech* — the young men had sport with her on the way back. The implication is clear: the three-day absence is to be understood not as anything that occurred in the apprentice's house, but as evidence that she had been faithless on the road. This is, of course, false — a trap.

### Marriage & Servitude

The master asked: what should I do? The apprentice said: divorce her. The master replied: her *ketubah* is too large; I cannot afford it. The apprentice said: I will lend you the money, and you can pay her *ketubah* with it. The master divorced his wife. The apprentice then went and married her. When the time came to repay the debt and the master had no means to do so, the apprentice said: come and work off your debt as my servant. And so there sat the apprentice and the former master's wife, eating and drinking, while the master stood and served them, pouring their wine.

### Master's Tears

His tears fell from his eyes into their cups. *U-ve-otah sha'ah nechtam gezar din* — and at that moment, the decree was sealed. The Gemara understands this not merely as the fate of these individuals but as a symbol of the moral corruption that had consumed the entire society, and it was this moment that triggered the irreversible judgment against them.

Some say the final *makkah be-pattish* was *shetei petilot be-ner echad* — two wicks in one candle — meaning when women began entering into relationships with two men simultaneously. Again, the emphasis falls on sexual corruption and on the exploitation of the vulnerable.

It is worth noting that many of these devastating narratives — the story of the apprentice, the story of the woman in Beitar and the children, and others — are attributed to the same *amora*, Rav Yehuda. He seems to have been deeply engaged in trying to provide some theological reckoning with the catastrophe: alternating between the incomprehensible suffering that defies explanation and the model of *schar va-onesh* that seeks to locate the destruction in human failure. The same oscillation runs through *Eichah* itself: God, how could You allow this? — followed by: because we did not listen, because we did not walk in His ways. Neither answer is sufficient on its own, and the Talmud does not pretend otherwise.

---

## Sikrikon Land Law

### Rav vs. Shmuel

With the *aggadata* of the *churban habayit* concluded, the Gemara returns to the *Mishnah* and to halachic analysis of the *sikrikon* laws.

The background: during and after the Roman destruction, Romans or their agents would seize Jewish land — sometimes under threat to the original owner's life — and then sell it. The Mishnah developed a *takana* governing under what conditions a purchaser from the *sikrikon* acquires valid title, which required in its first stage that the buyer also purchase the property from the original Jewish owner. A central question is how to determine whether the original owner's subsequent sale is genuine or merely performed under duress to avoid trouble with the *sikrikon*.

Rav rules: the distinction between valid and invalid turns on the form of the second transaction. If the original owner merely said verbally *lech chazek ukeni* — go take possession of it — this is insufficient; we presume he said so only to avoid confrontation, not because he genuinely wished to sell. But if he executed a written *shtar* of sale, *kana* — the transaction is valid, because the formality of a document demonstrates genuine intent.

Shmuel disagrees: *af beshtar nami lo kana ad she-yichtov lo achrayut* — even a written *shtar* is insufficient unless it explicitly includes a clause of *achrayut* — a guarantee of indemnification, whereby the seller undertakes liability if anyone later seizes the property from the buyer. Writing a liability clause demonstrates such a high level of commitment that it can only reflect genuine intent to sell, even following a coerced transaction with the *sikrikon*.

A *braita* is cited in support of Shmuel's position.

### Wife & Husband Order

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar applies the same logic to a parallel case involving a husband and wife. When a woman has a lien on property through her *ketubah*, and the buyer purchases from the wife first and then from the husband, *mekacho kayam* — the purchase stands. But if he purchases from the husband first and then from the wife, *mekacho batel* — the purchase is void — because we presume the wife sold only to please her husband and not of genuine free will. This remains invalid *ad she-yichtov lo achrayut* — unless she writes a guarantee of indemnification in the *shtar*.

The Gemara asks: does this not contradict Rav, who required only a *shtar* without an explicit *achrayut* clause? Rav responds: *mai achrayut nami shtar* — by *achrayut* we mean simply a *shtar*; the document itself is what makes it binding. Rashi explains that *achrayut* here does not mean a lien on property but simply that the *shtar* makes the transaction final. Tosafot, however, suggests that the dispute between Rav and Shmuel is precisely whether *achrayut* must be written explicitly in a document or whether it is implied — with Rav holding that any *shtar* carries *achrayut* by implication.

---

## Three-Year Rule

### Three-Year Possession

The Gemara presents a *baraita*: if someone purchased land from the *sikrikon*, ate its produce for three years in the presence of the original owners, and then sold it to a third party — *ein la-be'alim al lokeach sheni klum* — the original owners have no claim against the second purchaser.

This invokes the *halacha* of *chazakah* from Bava Batra: if one has been in possession of another's property for three years and the original owner lodges no objection, the possessor may, when challenged, claim that he purchased the property and has simply lost the *shtar*. One is not obligated to retain documents beyond three years when the owner watched and said nothing.

The Gemara presses: what exactly is the case? If the first buyer — who purchased from the *sikrikon* — is claiming to the original owner that he bought it from him and the three-year possession corroborates that claim, then even without involving the third party, the first buyer is already protected. And if the first buyer is *not* making that claim — if he says he never bought it from the original owner — then the three-year possession helps neither him nor any subsequent purchaser.

### Secondary Protection

Rav Sheshet resolves: *l'olam d'lo ka-ta'in lei* — the first buyer is simply not around or not making any claim at all. He has dropped out of the picture. The third party, having purchased the land, is now confronted by the original owner with a demand for return of the property, and does not know how to defend himself in *beit din*.

The Gemara explains that in such a case we assist the third party: we prompt him with the appropriate legal argument. We instruct him to say to the original owner: the man who sold you this land — from whom I purchased it — must have bought it from you, and he need not prove it because he was in possession for three years. The original owner saw him there for three years and made no objection; therefore we can presume the first buyer acquired it legitimately, and the third party holds it through him.

### Heirs & Claims

The Gemara extends this principle: *tainan le-yores ve-tainan le-lokeach* — we provide this guided claim both for an heir and for a subsequent purchaser. Neither necessarily knows the history of the property or what they would need to say to defend their claim in court. If someone challenges an heir — saying that the father never legitimately owned the land — we step in and instruct the heir: your father possessed this for three years without objection; therefore you can claim he bought it from the original owner. The heir, like the third-party purchaser, does not need to have independent knowledge of all the legal arguments required to defend the title.

However, the Gemara qualifies: *ve-idach ei ta'an in, ei lo, lo* — the original first buyer, *Shimon* in the example, must defend himself if he is the one being challenged. We do not provide *him* with a claim he has not himself made. The prompted claim is available only to subsequent parties — heirs and purchasers — who come to the property without full knowledge of the surrounding circumstances.

---

## Debt & Theft

### No Sikrikon

The Gemara presents a *baraita*: *haba machmat hov u-machmat amparut ein bo mishum sikrikon* — land seized for debt or taken by simple theft, without any threat to the original owner's life, does not fall under the *sikrikon* laws. The *sikrikon* framework — including the *takana* that after twelve months the original owner is presumed to have given up hope and the buyer need only compensate him a quarter of the land's value — applies only where the original transfer was coerced under threat to life. A simple creditor seizing land for debt, or a thief stealing it outright, does not trigger these provisions, and the original owner never loses his claim.

### Twelve Months

The *baraita* adds: *ve-amparut atzmo tzricha she-tisheh shneim asar chodesh* — and in a case of theft itself, twelve months are required. The Gemara clarifies: this means that the twelve-month waiting period before the second stage of the *takana* applies is itself a feature of the *sikrikon* law, not of the theft case. In theft, there is no *sikrikon* law at all — the original owner never loses his presumptive right to reclaim the property.

Rav Yosef then states: *naktinan, ein amparut be-Bavel* — we hold that there is no *din amparut* — no law of *amparut* — operative in Babylonia. The Gemara immediately challenges: surely theft of land occurs in Babylonia. Rav Yosef refines: what we mean is that there is no legal *din* of *amparut* in Babylonia. If someone seizes your land in Babylonia and you do not go to court to assert your claim — *keivan de-ika bei davar ve-lo azil kavel, amachulei achlei* — since there is a functioning court system and you chose not to file a claim in it, we presume you have waived your rights. The existence of a trustworthy legal framework changes the calculus entirely: a person who could have sought redress and did not is presumed to have relinquished the claim.

This is a striking observation about the relationship between legal systems and presumed intention. The Babylonian authorities commanded more trust in this respect than the Roman system — not necessarily because the Romans were unjust, but because Jews under Roman rule faced a very different relationship to imperial courts.

---

---

# Gittin 59

## Gido bar Re'ili

### Land Tax Arrangement

The daf opens in the middle of 58b with the case of Gido bar Re'ili, situated within the broader discussion of *sikrikon* — the legal framework governing property seized under threat of life and the various *takkanot* enacted to address it. By way of review: the first stage of the *takana* required a purchaser to acquire the property from both the *sikrikon* and the original owner, and in the correct order, so that the original owner would not feel coerced into a sale. The second stage, enacted later, permitted purchase from the *sikrikon* alone after twelve months, on the assumption that the owner had by then relinquished hope of recovering the land.

The case of Gido bar Re'ili unfolds as follows. A valley's land had been abandoned by its owners — perhaps they had left the region — yet the community as a whole remained liable for the land tax. To resolve this, the community arranged for Gido bar Re'ili to work the land in the owners' absence: he would keep the produce and pay the tax on their behalf. It was a reasonable arrangement for all parties.

### Prepayment Problem

The difficulty arose when Gido bar Re'ili, perhaps overeager, prepaid the land tax for three years in advance, presumably hoping to secure three years of produce. However, after only the first year, the original owners returned and reclaimed their land. Their position was entirely reasonable: you paid the tax and kept the produce for the first year while we were away — fair enough. But from this point forward, *anan yavnan va'anan achlinan* — we will pay the tax and we will take the produce. It is, after all, our land.

### Rav Pappa's Solution

The matter came before Rav Pappa, who considered writing Gido bar Re'ili a *turfa* — a writ of the *beis din* authorizing him to collect his prepaid taxes from the people of the valley. The reasoning was that the valley community had, in effect, appointed him to this role, and having paid out money on their behalf, he ought to be able to recoup it from them.

### Rav Huna Rejects

Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua objected to Rav Pappa's proposed remedy: *im ken asita sikrikon* — you have turned this into a case of *sikrikon*. The analogy Rashi draws, though admittedly somewhat difficult, is as follows. In the *sikrikon* scenario, a purchaser buys land that originally belonged to someone else, and the *takana* protects him from losing out simply because the land had previously belonged to the original owner. Here, Rav Pappa would be treating the valley people as though they had some right to grant Gido bar Re'ili a claim over the land — as if, now that the original owners have returned, Gido bar Re'ili is guaranteed not to lose out on his investment, analogous to the protection afforded by the *sikrikon takana*. But this analogy fails entirely. There was no seizure of land under threat of life, no *sikrikon* in any meaningful sense, and therefore no foundational presumption that this person had a right to buy the land such that the owners' return cannot be held against him.

### Sikrikon Analogy

The response of Rav Huna makes clear that the *sikrikon* framework cannot be extended by analogy to situations that lack its defining features. The *sikrikon* scenario involves a coercive seizure; the arrangements by the valley community involved no such thing. They simply needed someone to manage the land and pay the tax. There is no underlying structure that would generate a protected expectation of the kind that the *sikrikon takana* was designed to address.

### Heniah Maotav

Rather, Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua rules: *heniah maotav al keren hatzvi* — he placed his money on the horns of a deer. In other words, he effectively threw his money away. Nobody asked him to prepay three years of taxes in advance. He has no fundamental right, simply because the owners abandoned the land, to assume some protected status analogous to a *sikrikon* purchaser such that he will not lose out. One might ask: since those taxes were already paid to the government, shouldn't the returning owners at least reimburse him, since he saved them that expense? Rashi seems to suggest that the government would actually double-collect from the returning owners — a jarring result, but that appears to be how Rashi reads the case. More broadly, *heniah maotav al keren hatzvi* can apply even where there may be some moral responsibility to repay — the Gemara is addressing the question of legal obligation, and legally, Gido bar Re'ili is not owed anything. He acted unilaterally and must bear the consequences.

---

## Sikrikon Takana

### First Takana

The Gemara now returns to the *sikrikon* framework more directly, reviewing its two stages. The first *takana* — *mishna rishona* — required that a purchaser acquire the property from both the *sikrikon* and the original owner, and in the proper sequence, so the original owner would not feel compelled.

### Second Takana

The second *takana*, enacted by a later *beis din*, held that if the property sat in the hands of the *sikrikon* for twelve months and the original owner did not repurchase it, anyone could go ahead and buy it from the *sikrikon* — on the implicit assumption that after twelve months the owner had fully relinquished his expectation of recovery. However, the purchaser must still pay the original owners a *revi'a* — a quarter — because he acquired the property at a discount.

### Rav vs. Shmuel

The question then becomes: how exactly is this *revi'a* calculated? The Gemara presents a dispute between Rav and Shmuel on the matter.

### Quarter Calculations

Rav holds *revi'a bemaot* — a quarter of the purchase price. So if the purchaser paid one hundred for the land, which was really worth one hundred and twenty-five, he pays the original owners twenty-five — that is, a quarter of what he paid, representing the discount he received. *Revi'a bekarka*, in Rav's formulation, would mean that equivalent amount expressed in land: since the land is worth one hundred and twenty-five and the purchaser paid one hundred, returning a portion of the land worth twenty-five actually means returning a fifth of the land — hence the apparent paradox where *revi'a bekarka* in practice means a fifth of the land.

Shmuel, by contrast, holds *revi'a bekarka shehen shalish bemaot* — a quarter of the land, which works out to a third of the purchase price. In Shmuel's view, the discount was larger: the purchaser paid one hundred for land worth approximately one hundred and thirty-three, so he must pay the owners thirty-three — a full third of what he paid. In terms of land, thirty-three out of one hundred and thirty-three is one quarter, hence the phrase *revi'a bekarka*. The underlying dispute is simply whether the discount was one-fifth of the actual value (*nechi chumsha zavin*) or one-quarter of the actual value (*nechi revi'a zavin*).

A *braisa* is then cited: *zu mishna rishona* — after twelve months, anyone may purchase, *aval nosein l'baalim revi'a bekarka o revi'a bemaot*, and the owners may choose whether they want their portion in land or in cash. The *braisa* concludes with the phrase *revi'a bemaot*, which appears to support Rav's position — that a quarter of the purchase price, i.e., twenty-five out of one hundred, is owed to the owners.

### Rav Ashi Resolves

Rav Ashi reconciles the *braisa* with Shmuel's position as follows. Under Shmuel's formulation, the purchaser pays the *sikrikon* one hundred and then pays the owners thirty-three. Out of the total amount expended — one hundred and thirty-three — the owners received thirty-three. That is precisely a quarter of the total money spent. So when the *braisa* says *revi'a bemaot*, it can be read in Shmuel's terms as well: the owners receive a quarter of all the money the purchaser spent in total, counting both the payment to the *sikrikon* and the payment to the owners. For Rav, the quarter is of the purchase price alone; for Shmuel, the quarter is of the total expenditure. Both positions can be described as *revi'a bemaot*, resolving the apparent tension.

---

## Rav in Beit Din

### Rav Voted First

Rav now makes a striking personal disclosure: *ana hava b'minyana d'vei Rebbi* — I was present in the *beis din* that Rebbi convened, and *minai didi manu b'reisha* — they asked for my vote first. This is itself a remarkable datum, because Rav is the great transitional figure between the *tannaim* and *amoraim* — *Rav tanna hu u-falig* — and here he testifies that he participated in Rebbi's court when the vote on the *sikrikon* was taken.

### Voting Order Rules

The Gemara notes what appears to be a procedural irregularity. The *mishna* teaches: *dinei mamonot v'ha-taharot v'ha-tumos matchilin min ha-gadol* — in monetary cases and matters of *tumah* and *taharah*, the court begins with the most senior member voting first. The rationale is honor and respect for the senior authority. In *dinei nefashot* — capital cases — the procedure is reversed: *matchilin min ha-tzad*, voting begins from the side, from a more junior member. Two reasons are given for this: first, in a capital case where someone's life is at stake, you want every judge to feel maximally free to voice an independent opinion, without being overawed by the senior authority's position. Second, Rashi cites a *drasha* from the *pasuk* *lo sa'aneh al rav* — one may not simply acquiesce to a senior authority's ruling in *dinei nefashot*. So in capital cases, starting from the junior members protects the integrity of deliberation.

Since the vote on *sikrikon* was clearly not a capital case, Rebbi himself should have voted first. How, then, did Rav — presumably not the most senior member — cast the first vote?

### Rebbi's Humility

The Gemara answers, in the name of Rabbah son of Rabbah (or, some say, Rav Hillel son of Rav Vallas): *shani minyana d'vei Rebbi* — Rebbi's court was different. *D'kulei maminu lei min hatzad* — in all matters, they always began from the side, not from Rebbi. Tosafot explains this in light of the famous last *mishna* of *Sotah*: *batul anavah* — when Rebbi died, humility ceased. Rebbi was so humble that even in cases where he was entitled by right to vote first, he voluntarily stepped back and allowed others to begin deliberations. He was *mochel* on his prerogative, and the result — more open, more honest deliberation — was in every respect beneficial. This is why Rav could have voted first in a non-capital case: Rebbi chose, as a matter of *anavah*, to let others lead.

---

## Torah & Status

### Rebbi Unique

The implicit reference to Rebbi's *anavah* — and the account of his convening a *beis din* — leads the Gemara into an extended digression. Rabbah son of Rabbah (or Rav Hillel son of Rav Vallas) states: *mi-yemos Moshe v'ad Rebbi lo matzinu Torah u'gedulah bemakom echad* — from the time of Moshe Rabbeinu until Rebbi, we never find Torah greatness and worldly greatness (*gedula*, which Rashi explains as wealth, though one might also read it as broader societal authority and stature) combined in a single person. The claim is not that there were no great Torah scholars, nor that there were no figures of great status or wealth — but that the two were never unified in one individual to the degree they were in Rebbi. One might wonder whether this implies Rebbi was the greatest Torah scholar of his time in an absolute sense, or whether it is more a claim about the extraordinary degree of *both* qualities simultaneously residing in one person. The Gemara proceeds to test this claim historically.

### Early Examples

The Gemara raises a series of counterexamples. *Havei Yehoshua* — was Yehoshua not both a great Torah scholar (as Moshe's foremost student) and the political leader of Israel? The response: *havei Elazar* — Elazar was also present, a great Torah authority in his own right as Aharon's student, and therefore Yehoshua was not unchallenged in his combination of roles. The Gemara then asks: after Yehoshua's death, was not Elazar unrivaled? *Havei Pinchas* — Pinchas was also there. And when Elazar died and Pinchas remained, was he not uniquely combining these roles? *Havah zekenim* — the elders remained as political and religious authorities alongside him, a point reinforced by the repeated motif in *Sefer Shoftim* of *ein melech b'Yisrael* — suggesting that no single figure held unchallenged authority of both kinds.

A question worth raising in this context: this entire sugya seems to run counter to the principle of *yeridas hadoros* — the decline of generations. The response is that the claim is always relative: in any given generation, the question is whether one person towers above all others in both dimensions simultaneously, not whether they surpass figures of previous ages.

### Royal & Sage

The Gemara continues through the monarchic period. *V'ha Shaul* — Shaul was a king and, according to rabbinic tradition, a great Torah scholar. Response: *havah Shmuel*, who was the supreme religious authority of the age. But when Shmuel died while Shaul was still alive, was Shaul not then unrivaled? *Kulei shani ka'amina* — the claim is about someone who held this status throughout his entire career, not merely for a brief window.

*V'ha David* — David was a king and his Torah scholarship is well attested throughout *Masechet Brachos* and elsewhere. Response: *havah Ira haYairi*, who is, admittedly, a name one would not otherwise encounter, but whom rabbinic tradition regards as a great Torah scholar. This response feels somewhat weaker — Ira haYairi had no real authority comparable to David's — and Rashi limits his description simply to *gadol baTorah*, without addressing the *gedula* dimension. Again the Gemara responds that he did not hold this dual status throughout his entire career. The same pattern plays out with Shlomo: *havah Shimi ben Gera* — and when Shlomo had him killed, the response is again that Shlomo was not uncontested his entire reign.

*V'ha Chizkiyahu* — Chizkiyahu was a king and a great Torah scholar. Response: *havah Shevna*, a sage of his time. Shevna was killed, but again: *kulei shani ka'amina*, the whole-career qualification applies. Notably, the Gemara invokes Shevna rather than Yeshayahu as the counterweight to Chizkiyahu — why Yeshayahu is not cited here is unclear.

*V'ha Ezra* — Ezra HaSofer was both political leader and supreme Torah authority of the return from Babylonian exile. Response: *havah Nechemya ben Chilkiya*. With this, all the historical challenges have been answered.

### Later Period

The Gemara then adds the parallel claim for the later period: *mi-yemos Rebbi v'ad Rav Ashi lo matzinu Torah u'gedula bimkom echad* — from Rebbi's time until Rav Ashi, the same combination was not seen, until Rav Ashi, who was evidently a man of both great Torah stature and great wealth or societal standing. The Gemara anticipates a challenge: *v'ha havah Huna bar Nasan*, who also seemed to combine both qualities. The response: *d'mikaf havah kaif lei l'Rav Ashi* — Huna bar Nasan actually submitted himself to Rav Ashi's authority, and therefore he cannot serve as a genuine counterexample to Rav Ashi's unique status.

---

## Cheresh Status

### Definition Context

The Gemara now returns to the *mishnah*'s enumeration of rabbinic *takkanot*, moving from the *sikrikon* framework toward a broader set of measures addressing individuals with diminished legal capacity. The phrase *tikkun olam* has by this point largely receded from the discussion — we are now in the realm of rabbinic enactments addressing changing social circumstances and specific populations, though the *mishnah* we are about to examine is, in scope, as broad as some of the classic *tikkun olam* provisions.

The *cheresh* — the deaf-mute — is, as a matter of Torah law, not considered a *bar daas*, a person of full legal competency. As such, he cannot enter into legally binding transactions: buying and selling, *kiddushin*, *geirushin*, and so forth. He cannot discharge others' obligations such as blowing the *shofar*, and is not personally *chayav b'mitzvot* — his status is comparable in this respect to that of a minor.

That said, it is important to note that the Gemara does contain an opinion that regards the *cheresh* as having a meaningful degree of *daas*, or at least holds that competency ought to be assessed on a case-by-case basis.
