Even those who classify him as lacking full *daas* treat him differently from a *shoteh* — a person categorized as mentally ill in a more fundamental sense, perhaps unable to properly interpret reality. The *cheresh* is understood as diminished in *daas* but not entirely devoid of it, and this intermediate status is precisely what makes *takkanot* on his behalf possible.

An important historical observation is worth making here. One might wonder how frequently a person would be both deaf and mute. The answer is that in the pre-modern world, virtually every deaf person fell into this category — because individuals who cannot hear are generally unable to modulate their speech, and without education or training they could not speak intelligibly. The only exceptions were those who had been born hearing and later lost their hearing. As a result, nearly every deaf person was treated halachically as a *cheresh*. In recent centuries, as schools for the deaf developed and it became undeniable that deaf individuals can communicate with full intelligence through sign language, many *poskim* have revisited this categorization. Some have argued that a person communicating through sign language does not fall into the category of *ilemet* (mute) at all, and therefore is not a *cheresh* in the halachic sense. These developments lie beyond the scope of the Gemara, but they are essential background for understanding why the Gemara's enactments were designed as they were: the *cheresh* was understood to possess real, if imperfect, *daas*, enough to justify accommodating him in the normal functioning of society.

### Gesture Transactions

The *mishnah* states: *cheresh romez v'nirmas* — a *cheresh* can engage in buying and selling through gestures. If he points to an item he wants and holds out money, the transaction is valid at the rabbinic level, even though *d'Oraita* it would not be binding. This was enacted as a *takanna* precisely because of this intermediate status of the *cheresh*: he is not like a *shoteh*, and it would be untenable to deny him the ability to engage in basic commercial transactions.

### Ben Beteira

*U'ven Beteira omer kofetz v'nikpatz* — Ben Beteira holds that even jumping — an action less precisely expressive than hand gestures — constitutes a sufficient signal. The *chachamim*, by contrast, apparently regarded jumping as too ambiguous to be reliably interpreted as communicating transactional intent.

### Moveable Only

All of this applies only to *mitaltelin* — moveable property. The *takanna* was not extended to the purchase of land (*karka*). Two reasons converge: first, there was not the same pressing necessity, since the *takanna* for *mitaltelin* was grounded in the need for the *cheresh* to be able to function in everyday life — to buy basic provisions. Land transactions are qualitatively different in nature and not part of ordinary daily commerce. Second, land is far too weighty a matter, and the Rabbis were not willing to institute a *takanna* extending such capacity to a person who is not *d'Oraita* a full *bar daas*.

### Get Standards

The Gemara now addresses the question of the *get* — the divorce document. Rav Nachman explains: the dispute between Ben Beteira and the *chachamim* pertains to *mitaltelin*, as the *mishnah* explicitly states. When it comes to a *get*, by contrast, *divrei hakol b'remiza* — all agree that a proper hand gesture is required; jumping would not suffice.

The case of a *get* for a *cheresh* applies specifically when the man was already a *cheresh* when he entered into *kiddushin*. Since the *kiddushin* of a *cheresh* is only rabbinically valid — it is a rabbinic enactment parallel to the one permitting him to engage in transactions — the resulting marriage is dissolved through a corresponding rabbinic *get*. The *cheresh* husband can signal to the *sofer* his intention to write a *get* for his wife, and this suffices. But even in this context, which involves only rabbinic *kiddushin* and rabbinic divorce, the standard for gesture is higher than for *mitaltelin*: everyone requires clear *remiza*, proper hand signaling.

One might have thought the opposite: since the *get* is only undoing a rabbinic institution, perhaps the standards would be *lower*, and even jumping would suffice. The Gemara therefore clarifies that this is not the case — *mishnah* addresses *mitaltelin*, and for *get* the standards are uniformly higher, with everyone requiring *remiza*.

A second version (*ika d'amri*) of Rav Nachman's statement holds that the dispute between Ben Beteira and the *chachamim* applies equally to *mitaltelin* and to *gittin*. Under this reading, the *mishnah* mentioning *mitaltelin* simply addresses that context, but the dispute carries over to the *get* case as well, with Ben Beteira maintaining that jumping suffices even there.

---

## Pe'utot Minors

### Age Range

The *mishnah* also states that *pe'utot* — young children — may buy and sell *mitaltelin*, and such transactions are rabbinically valid. The Gemara asks: *v'ad kama* — until what age, or rather, down to what age? Rav Yehuda indicated to his son Rav Yitzchak: approximately six or seven years old. Rav Kahana says seven or eight. A *baraita* teaches nine or ten.

The Gemara resolves the apparent disagreement: *v'lo pligi* — these do not actually dispute one another. *Kol chad v'chad l'fi chorfei* — it depends on the sharpness of the individual child. There is no fixed biological age; what matters is whether the child has reached a sufficient level of understanding — knowing the value of money, understanding what a transaction means, being able to manage change appropriately. The different age ranges reflect the range of children's development rather than competing fixed thresholds.

### Rationale

Why was this *takanna* enacted? Rav Abba bar Yaakov said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *mishum k'dei chayyav* — because of his livelihood, so that he can function in society. In earlier periods, children as young as six or seven might be apprenticed or otherwise fending for themselves to a considerable degree. The inability to execute any valid commercial transaction would be practically untenable.

The Gemara at this point also brings a passage in which the same *baal memra* — Rav Abba bar Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yochanan — interprets the word *maltechah* (from 2 Kings 10:22: *vayomer la'asher al hamaltechah hotzei levush l'chol ovdei hab'aal*) as *davar hanimlal v'nimtach* — something spun and stretched by hand, i.e., a fine linen garment. This is connected to an account of Bunaya ben Nunaya sending Rebbi several types of extraordinarily fine fabrics — *sivni v'chumes* (folded to the size of a nut or half a nut), *salsala u'malmala* (folded to the size of a pistachio or half a pistachio) — with *malmala* receiving the same etymology: *davar hanimlal v'nimtach*, spun and stretched linen. The passage is cited here because of the shared *baal memra*, not because of topical relevance to the *pe'utot* laws.

### Overpayment Limits

If a *pe'utat* overpays, does the standard law of *ona'ah* apply? Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Zeira: *ad shtus k'gadol* — up to a sixth, as with an adult. The transaction stands but the excess must be returned; an overpayment exceeding a sixth would void the transaction, just as it would for a competent adult.

### Gift Validity

Abaye raises a further question: *matnaso mah* — what is the status of a gift given by a *pe'utat*? The *takanna* was enacted to allow children to participate in normal commercial life; a gift is outside that rationale, and there is greater opportunity for exploitation. Can a minor give a valid gift?

Rav Yeimar holds that it is not a valid gift; Mar bar Rav Ashi holds that it is. When the question was transmitted to Rav Mordechai for his view, the names were accidentally reversed — it was reported to him that Mar bar Rav Ashi held gifts were invalid and Rav Yeimar held they were valid, precisely the opposite of what each had actually said.

Rav Mordechai responded: go tell the son of my master — meaning Mar bar Rav Ashi, whose father Rav Ashi was Rav Mordechai's *rebbe* — don't you remember the incident? When Rav Ashi was walking up the steps to the *beis hamidrash* — one foot on the ground, one foot on the step — we asked him: *matnaso mah*, what is the law regarding a *pe'utat*'s gift? And he told us: *matnaso matnah* — it is a valid gift. This applies whether it is a gift of a *shechiv mera* (given on a deathbed), a *matnas bari* (given while healthy), a large gift, or a small gift — all are valid.

This of course confirms what Mar bar Rav Ashi had actually said — that gifts are valid — rather than the reversed version that had been reported to Rav Mordechai. Tosafot notes that the Gemara does not specify whether this ruling applies to *mitaltelin* only or also to *karka*; given the context — the entire discussion of *pe'utot* concerns *mitaltelin* — it is reasonable to assume only moveable property is intended, since there was no *takanna* extending transactional capacity to land.

---

## Darchei Shalom

### Aliyot Order

The *mishnah* now shifts to a new organizing principle: *mipnei darchei shalom* — for the sake of peaceful relations and social order. Where *tikkun olam* addressed deep systemic inequities, *darchei shalom* addresses the more quotidian need to establish conventions that minimize conflict. Having a recognized way of doing things — an acknowledged order or sequence — preempts many disputes before they arise. The opening example is the *aliyot* order: a *kohen* reads first, then a *levi*, then a *Yisrael*.

There is something worth pausing over in this institution. The authentic *halacha* of *krias hatorah* is that the most accomplished Torah scholar present should receive the first *aliyah*. Torah study is the great equalizer — as the Gemara elsewhere teaches, a *mamzer talmid chacham* takes precedence over a *kohen gadol am ha'aretz*. The institution of *krias hatorah* in principle reflects this: *hakol olim l'minyan shivah*, even a woman, even a minor. Torah is accessible to all, and greatness in Torah supersedes hierarchies of birth.

Yet this very egalitarianism creates a practical problem: precisely because greatness in Torah is a matter of achievement rather than birth, there is no predefined, unambiguous hierarchy. Disputes over who is the greater *talmid chacham* are endemic. The flip side of equal access is endless contest over rank. By instituting the *kohen-levi-Yisrael* sequence *mipnei darchei shalom*, the Rabbis introduced a clear, uncontested ordering that resolves at least the initial hierarchy of honors, even at the cost of some of the pure meritocracy that *krias hatorah* in principle demands.

### Torah Equalizer

As noted, while the *kohen-levi-Yisrael* order serves *darchei shalom*, the Torah itself is a domain of equal access. The priority of status applies in matters of *kavod*, but the very existence of Torah as the measure of worth means that a *talmid chacham* who is a *mamzer* takes precedence in Torah honor over a *kohen gadol* who is an *am ha'aretz*. This reflects a broader principle running through rabbinic Judaism: the shift from a *beis hamikdash*-centered hierarchy (which is about birth status, tribe, priestly lineage) to a Torah-centered hierarchy (which is about achievement and learning). The institution of *krias hatorah* lives in the tension between these two frameworks, and the *darchei shalom* ordering of *kohen-levi-Yisrael* is one resolution of that tension.

### Eiruv & Wells

Two further applications of *darchei shalom* follow. First: *eiruvin b'vayis yashan mipnei darchei shalom* — when an *eiruv chatzeros* has customarily been stored in a particular house, one should continue placing it there rather than shifting it to a different house. This preserves an established expectation and avoids disputes over whose home is used as the locus of the *eiruv*.

Second: *bor she'haya karov l'ama, mitmaleh rishon mipnei darchei shalom* — if a well was situated near an irrigation canal, the owner of the well closest to the water source has the first right to fill his well from the canal. In times of scarcity, when everyone wishes to store water in their wells before the canal level drops, having a recognized principle of priority by proximity prevents conflict.

### Traps Ownership

The *mishnah* states: *metzudot chayah v'ofot v'dagim yesh bahem mishum gezel mipnei darchei shalom* — traps set for wild animals, birds, or fish are protected *mipnei darchei shalom*, such that if another person comes upon the trap before the trapper returns and takes the animal, it is considered a form of theft. Strictly speaking, the trapper has not yet performed a formal *kinyan* — he has not physically taken possession of the animal, and depending on the circumstances, the trap may not function as a *kinyan kli* that transfers ownership automatically. Nevertheless, the Rabbis declared that one who takes from another's trap commits a form of *gezel*. The reason goes beyond mere conflict avoidance: the very institution of trapping as a livelihood depends on trappers being able to rely on ownership of their catch.

Rabbi Yose says: *gezel gamur* — it is real theft. The Gemara will explain that Rabbi Yose means rabbinic theft — the Rabbis enacted that taking from the trap constitutes genuine *gezel* rabbinically — rather than merely establishing a convention. The difference between the *tanna kama* and Rabbi Yose is thus not whether the trapper has a right, but whether the Rabbis articulated that right as a true *gezel* or merely as a *darchei shalom* convention.

### Lost Property

*Metziat cheresh shoteh v'katan yesh bahem mishum gezel mipnei darchei shalom* — lost objects found by a *cheresh*, *shoteh*, or minor are treated as their property for purposes of *darchei shalom*, even though these individuals lack the full legal capacity to effect a *kinyan* through finding. Taking from them what they have found is treated as *gezel*. Rabbi Yose again: *gezel gamur* — real rabbinic theft.

### Olive Knocker

*Ani hamenakef berosh hazayit* — a poor person who has climbed to the top of an olive tree and knocked olives down has not yet formally acquired them, since he has not yet performed *hagbahah* or another recognized *kinyan*. If someone passes by and takes the olives lying below, *ma shetachtav gezel mipnei darchei shalom* — what is beneath him is considered stolen *mipnei darchei shalom*. Rabbi Yose: *gezel gamur*. The pattern is consistent throughout this section.

### Non-Jewish Poor

*Ein memachin b'yad aniyei ovdei kochavim beleket shichcha u'peah mipnei darchei shalom* — one does not prevent non-Jewish poor from collecting *leket*, *shichcha*, and *peah* from the fields, for the sake of *darchei shalom*. It is important to situate this ruling within the context of what *darchei shalom* has meant throughout this *mishnah*. It is not simply about cultivating good relations with non-Jewish neighbors for self-interested reasons. *Darchei shalom* here expresses a value of peaceful, well-ordered society in which people's rights are respected and the vulnerable are not excluded. This reading is supported by the Rambam's use of the verse *deracheha darchei noam v'chol netivoteha shalom* in a related context — all the ways of the Torah are ways of pleasantness and peace.

---

## Kohen Honor

### Biblical Sources

The Gemara now asks: *mina hani milei* — what is the biblical source for giving *kohanim* the first *aliyah*? Three sources are offered. Rav Mattana cites: *vayichtov Moshe et hatorah hazot vayitnah el hakohanim bnei Levi* — Moshe wrote the Torah and gave it to the *kohanim bnei Levi*. The Gemara asks the obvious: we already know that *kohanim* are *bnei Levi* — why state both? The answer: to teach precedence — first *kohanim*, then *levi*. This functions as an *asmachta* for the ordering in *krias hatorah*.

Rabbi Yitzchak Napcha cites: *venigshu hakohanim bnei Levi* — and the *kohanim bnei Levi* shall draw near. Again, the doubling of the description teaches the order of precedence. Rav Ashi cites: *bnei Amram Aharon uMoshe vayibadel Aharon le'hakdisho kodesh kodashim* — Aharon was separated and sanctified as *kodesh kodashim*, above even Moshe, who was a *levi*. This establishes that the *kohen* occupies a higher level of *kedushah* than the *levi*.

### Honor Rights

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba derives the principle from the *pasuk* *ve'kidashto* — you shall sanctify him — applied to the *kohen*, *lekhol davar shebikdusha*: in every matter of sanctity or honor. This manifests in three specific honors: *liftoach rishon* — he opens first (gives the first speech or *drashah*); *ulvarekh rishon* — he leads *birkat hamazon*; and *ulitol manah yafah b'rishon* — at a meal, he has first choice of the food. These are matters of *kavod* in social settings, not financial matters like dividing an estate.

### De'oraisa Status

This sets up a striking exchange between Abaye and Rav Yosef. If *ve'kidashto* establishes a *d'Oraita* obligation to honor *kohanim* in these ways, then the *kohen*'s precedence in *krias hatorah* is not merely a rabbinic convention for *darchei shalom* — it reflects a *d'Oraita* principle. Abaye asks Rav Yosef directly: *mipnei darchei shalom, d'Oraita?*

Rav Yosef responds: *d'Oraita u'mipnei darchei shalom* — it is *d'Oraita*, and the Torah itself commands it *mipnei darchei shalom*. This is a puzzling formulation: the Torah's command to honor *kohanim* is rooted in their elevated *kedushah* and the recognition of their special role, not in *darchei shalom* as such.

Abaye pushes back sharply: *kol hatorah kulah nami mipnei darchei shalom* — if you use that reasoning, then every *d'Oraita* law is *darchei shalom*, since *de'chtiv deracheha darchei noam v'chol netivoteha shalom* — the entire Torah is characterized as ways of pleasantness and peace. This is an extraordinarily powerful statement. If every Torah obligation can be described as serving *shalom*, then *darchei shalom* becomes a vacuous explanation. Abaye's point is that one cannot collapse the specific category of *darchei shalom* into the general theological claim that Torah promotes peace.

Abaye therefore offers an alternative synthesis, citing what the *mar* — Rabbah bar Nachmani — taught. A *baraita* states: if two people are eating together, one waits for the other before beginning; with three, one need not wait. The one who recited *ha-motzi* has first access to the shared dishes, but may yield his priority to his *rebbe* or to someone of greater stature if he chooses. And on this Rabbah taught: *lo shanu ela b'seudah* — the option to waive one's *kavod* applies at a private meal. *Aval b'veit haknesset lo, de'atu le'intzuyei* — but not in *shul*, because it leads to fights.

### No Waiving

The synthesis now becomes clear. The *d'Oraita* obligation of *ve'kidashto* establishes that a *kohen* must be honored in settings involving *kedushah* — and *krias hatorah* in *shul* is such a setting. That honor manifests as receiving the first *aliyah*. However, were the *kohen* permitted to waive this honor at will — to say, I am *mochel*, let my friend take the first *aliyah* — the result would be precisely the competitive争 claiming of honor that the *darchei shalom* ordering was designed to prevent. People would lobby to be chosen, others would feel slighted for not being chosen, and communal harmony would break down. The rabbinic layer, then, is not the *kohen*'s honor itself — that is *d'Oraita* — but the prohibition on the *kohen*'s waiving that honor in *shul*. This prohibition is the *darchei shalom* element: it protects the institution by ensuring it remains stable and non-negotiable.

### Day Distinction

Rav Mattana adds a further refinement: the prohibition on the *kohen* waiving his *kavod* in *shul* applies specifically on *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* — *d'shechichi rabim*, when there is a large crowd in *shul*. On Mondays and Thursdays, when attendance is smaller, the *kohen* may be *mochel* on his *kavod* without generating the *darchei shalom* concerns that would arise in a full public setting.

Here the daf concludes. The discussion of *kohanim* and *aliyot* and the interplay between *d'Oraita* honor and rabbinic *darchei shalom* protections will continue in the following daf.

---

---

# Gittin 60

## Aliyot Order & Peace

### Kohen-Levi-Yisrael

The daf opens near the end of the *perek* dealing with *tikkun olam* and *darchei shalom*, before the tractate returns to the laws of *gittin* proper. The sugya at the bottom of 59b concerns the established order of *aliyot* — *kohen*, *levi*, *yisrael* — and the principle that this sequence exists as a function of *darchei shalom*, so that competition over communal honors not become a source of conflict. The Gemara acknowledges that the obligation to honor a *kohen* first derives from *de-Oraita* authority — the concept of *vekiddashto* — and that technically a *kohen* may be *mochel*, may waive his honor in favor of another. The Rabbis, however, instituted that he should not do so, since permitting such waivers opens the door to disputes.

### Shabbat vs Weekday

Rav Mattana introduces a qualification. The prohibition against a *kohen* ceding his *aliyah* to another applies only on *shabbatot* and *yamim tovim* — *deshehichi rabbim*, when the congregation is large and the potential for conflict correspondingly greater. On Tuesdays and Thursdays, however, where the minyan is typically small and intimate, the concern is less acute, and a *kohen* may be *mochel*. An important note is appended by Tosafot in the name of Rabbeinu Chananel: this distinction applied in Talmudic times when weekday attendance was sparse due to people being occupied with their work. Tosafot observes that in their own era, Tuesday and Thursday attendance could rival that of *Yom Tov*, and the leniency would not apply in such circumstances.

### Rav Huna Exception

The Gemara raises an objection: we know that Rav Huna, who was not a *kohen*, received the *kohen* *aliyah* on *shabbatot* and *yamim tovim*. This appears to contradict Rav Mattana's rule. The Gemara resolves the difficulty: Rav Huna was categorically different. Even Rav Ami and Rav Assi — the most distinguished *kohanim* in *Eretz Yisrael* — deferred to him. His preeminence was so universally acknowledged that calling him first was not an act of waiver at all; it was simply the objective recognition of his uncontested authority. The *kohen*'s honor was not so much conceded as it was superseded by an undisputed communal consensus.

---

## No Kohen Present

### Bundle Unravels

Abaye introduces the following tradition: *ein sham kohen, nisperdah hachavilah* — if no *kohen* is present, the bundle unravels. The entire edifice of hierarchical ordering rests on the premise that the *kohen* receives the first honor. Without a *kohen*, the structure loses its foundation, and the order collapses entirely. One might ask why, in such a case, one would not simply proceed to *levi* before *yisrael*. The answer lies in the nature of *vekiddashto*: the *mitzvah* of sanctifying and honoring applies fundamentally to the *kohen*. The *levi*, though assigned greater communal responsibility and role, does not carry the same *kedusha* in this regard. Without the *kohen*, there is no longer a basis for the hierarchy, and in principle any *aliyah* may be given to anyone.

---

## No Kohen Present (II)

### Rashi vs Rav Yitzchak

Rashi's first explanation of *nisperdah hachavilah* is striking: the *levi* loses his *aliyah* entirely — *eino korei kelal*. This is the position of *Mori ha-Zaken* and Rabbeinu Yitzchak ben Yehudah, and it accords with the *Siddur Rav Amram*. Rashi then cites a second view, from Rav Yitzchak ha-Levi, that there is simply no fixed order anymore — a *levi* may receive an *aliyah* somewhere in the middle, as may anyone else, but there is no reason to deprive the *levi* of an *aliyah* altogether.

### Tosafot Position

Tosafot takes a third position: Rav Yitzchak bar Yehudah maintains that the *levi* receives the second *aliyah*. That is, a *yisrael* is given the first *aliyah* — in the slot normally reserved for *kohen* — and the *levi* then reads second, in his proper position within the remaining order. The concern is that placing a *levi* in the first slot too closely mimics the role of *kohen*, creating a blurring of boundaries that might itself carry the character of *pegam kehunah*. A *yisrael* in the first slot signals more clearly that no status claim is being made. The practical custom — giving the remaining *aliyot* freely to *yisraelim* — reflects the *peshat* of the Gemara, though the precise practice when a *levi* is present varies, and the issue remains genuinely contested.

---

## Aliyot Order & Peace (II)

### Levi Without Kohen

To summarize the three positions: first, the *levi* receives no *aliyah* at all; second, the *levi* may receive any *aliyah* in any position, with no fixed order applying to anyone; and third, the *levi* receives the second *aliyah* specifically. The simple reading of the Gemara supports the second view — once the bundle has unraveled, *aliyot* are given without predetermined order. A related tradition from Abaye: *ein sham levi, kari kohen* — if there is no *levi*, the same *kohen* who received the first *aliyah* reads again in the second position, since a *kohen* is, by lineage, also a *levi*. Whether this constitutes a demotion in any sense is something the Gemara proceeds to examine.

---

## Kohen/Levi Stigma

### Double Status Rule

Rav Yochanan rules: *kohen achar kohen lo yikra* — one may not call up a second *kohen* immediately after a first *kohen* has already received an *aliyah*, because this will lead to *pegam* on the first: observers will assume that after the first was called, it was discovered that he was not truly a *kohen*, and a second genuine *kohen* had to be substituted. Similarly, *levi achar levi lo yikra* — a second *levi* may not be called after a first *levi* — but here the concern is *mishum pagmam shel sheneihem*, a stigma that falls on both of them, not merely on the first.

### Same Person Twice

This immediately raises the question posed above: if there is no *levi*, the Gemara instructs that the same *kohen* reads again — but does this not create the precise problem Rav Yochanan described? The Gemara resolves it: *ki ka'amrinan be'oto kohen* — when the same *kohen* reads twice, everyone understands the reason. The gabbai announces *ya'amod bimkom levi*, or makes it clear in some equivalent way, and there is no ambiguity. No one imagines that the first *aliyah* was invalid; it is simply understood that no *levi* is present.

### Stories

Two illustrative anecdotes bear on the practical reality of this rule. Hertzel Hefter, himself a *levi*, once studied this passage and was genuinely surprised to learn that the same *kohen* is truly called up twice — having never been in a *shul* when no *levi* was present, he had not encountered the practice. The other story involves Rabbi Weiss, who on a visit to a *Teimani shul* in Israel was given the *kohen aliyah* and discovered — unprepared — that the congregation expected him to read aloud himself. He managed to get through it. The following visit, he prepared the *aliyah* in advance, read it flawlessly, and immediately heard the *gabbai* announce: *ya'amod bimkom levi*.

### Pegam Analysis

The Gemara then probes why two *leviim* in succession generate a *pegam* on both, while two *kohanim* generate a *pegam* only on the first. The initial answer — that in both cases observers might question either individual's status — does not adequately distinguish the cases. The Gemara refines the analysis with reference to a specific scenario: suppose it is well established that the second *kohen*'s father was genuinely a *kohen*. Can that not also be stipulated for the second *levi*?

The Gemara's final answer is structural. If a *kohen* turns out to be a *chalal* — his father having married a *gerusha* and the son thereby losing his *kehunah* — he would receive a *yisrael aliyah*, not a *kohen* one. Therefore, when a second person receives the second *aliyah* after a *kohen*, there is only one available interpretation: the second person is the genuine *kohen* and the first was not. No observer can think the second person is a *chalal*, because a *chalal* would be receiving the *yisrael* slot, not the second position.

With *leviim*, by contrast, the second *aliyah* is also the slot a *yisrael* would receive if the *levi* had been demoted or disqualified. A *levi* who married a *mamzeret* and thereby blemished his descendants' status would produce offspring who might receive a *yisrael aliyah*. So when two people receive what look like consecutive *levi* slots, observers can read it either way: the first person may have been a non-*kohen* substitute later replaced by the real *levi*, or the second person may be a demoted *levi* whose true status is really *yisrael*. The stigma thus branches in two directions and lands on both.

The Gemara further asks: who exactly are these observers whose misinterpretation we fear? Those who remain through the entire *kriat haTorah* would presumably see the full sequence of *aliyot* and understand that the first one counted. The concern therefore applies specifically to those who leave *shul* in the middle, *leyotzim*, who see the second *kohen aliyah* without having witnessed the complete context.

---

## Higher Hierarchy

### Rabbi Helbo Query

The people of the Galilee sent a question to Rabbi Helbo: after *kohen* and *levi* have received their *aliyot*, how is the order determined among the remaining recipients? Rabbi Helbo did not have a ready answer and referred the question to Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha.

### Talmidei Chachamim

Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha replied that the post-*levi* *aliyot* go first to *talmidei chachamim* who are actually appointed as *parnasim al hatzibbur* — communal religious leaders. The *parnas* in this context is a figure of genuine Torah authority: elsewhere the Gemara defines one who is fit to be a *parnas* as someone who can answer a halakhic question from any area of Jewish law immediately and without hesitation. This is the model of the city's rabbinic authority, whether or not he formally holds that position.

### Full Hierarchy List

After the appointed *talmidei chachamim* come those who are *ra'uyim lemanotam parnasim* — scholars who are genuinely qualified for rabbinic leadership, but for whom the position is already filled. After them come the children of *talmidei chachamim* whose fathers are appointed as communal leaders. This introduces a notable intersection of two distinct principles: Torah scholarship, which is in theory a pure meritocracy, and inherited status, which mirrors the structure of *kehunah* and *leviyah*. The children of the religious leadership receive preferential standing — which, at a minyan where the same families appeared regularly, would have been a consistent and perhaps uncontested feature of the order.

### Status vs Merit

The hierarchy continues with the *rashei knesiyot* — the heads of the *shuls* — who in the relevant historical period appear to have occupied a civic or administrative role somewhat distinct from the rabbinic authority structure. Archaeological evidence from ancient synagogues in *Eretz Yisrael* confirms that synagogue leadership was not coextensive with rabbinic leadership; the *rosh knesset* was often a prominent communal figure whose authority derived from a different source. After the *rashei knesiyot*, the order is open: *vechol adam*, and from that point any reasonable allocation may be made. The interplay throughout is striking — a system rooted in inherited priestly status transitions, via an intermediate meritocratic hierarchy, back again to something resembling inherited communal prestige.

---

## Chumashim & Haftarot

### Chumashim Question

The *bnei Galila* also sent Rabbi Helbo a second question: *mahu likrot be-chumashin be-veit ha-knesset be-tzibbur* — may individual *chumashim* be used for public Torah reading? Here the term *chumash* does not refer to a printed codex; rather, as Rashi emphasizes, it refers to a scroll — but a scroll containing only one of the five books of the Torah rather than all five together. Each such scroll was written with the same technical requirements as a full *sefer Torah*, but it was only a fifth of the complete *chamisha chumshei Torah*. Rabbi Helbo did not know the answer, nor — when the question was referred onward — did Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha. The question was then brought to the *beit midrash* for resolution.

The attempted proof came from a ruling of Rabbi Shimlai bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: a *sefer Torah* from which one *yeri'ah* — one parchment section — is missing may not be read from publicly. If something that is ninety-nine percent complete is disqualified, surely a scroll containing only one-fifth of the Torah would be as well. The Gemara, however, rejects this reasoning: *hatam mechasar be-mileih* — in the case of the incomplete *sefer Torah*, something is actually missing from its contents. *Hacha lo mechasar be-mileih* — a complete *Sefer Bereishit* lacks nothing within itself; it is whole as what it is. The concern with a *chasar sefer Torah* is the *pegam* — the perception of brokenness — which differs from the case of a formally complete but partial scroll.

### Kavod HaTzibbur

The matter is ultimately resolved by Rabba and Rav Yosef, who rule jointly: *ein korin be-chumashin be-veit ha-knesset, mishum kevod ha-tzibbur* — one may not read from individual *chumashim* in *shul* because of the dignity owed to the congregation. The *tzibbur* deserves the full *sefer Torah*, and reading from a partial scroll, however internally complete, fails to meet that standard.

### Rambam Position

The Rambam's position introduces an important nuance. In *Hilchot Sefer Torah* Perek 10, the Rambam lists twenty things that invalidate a *sefer Torah*. He concludes: if any one of these defects is present, *harei hu ke-chumash min ha-chumashin she-melamdim bo ha-tinokot* — it has the status of a *chumash* used to teach children, it lacks the *kedusha* of a *sefer Torah*, and one may not read from it publicly. The implication is that a *pasul sefer Torah* and a *chumash* occupy the same halakhic category: suitable for private study but not for public reading.

### Beit Yosef

The *Beit Yosef* — Rav Yosef Karo, writing in the *Kessef Mishneh* — draws out a critical inference from the Rambam. A responsum attributed to the Rambam states that if a *sefer Torah pasul* is all that is available, one may read from it and even recite a *beracha* over it, and that *geonei olam* practiced accordingly. The *Rashba* found this startling and suspected a textual error. The *Beit Yosef* defends it by arguing that the Rambam's ruling — *ein korin be-chumashin be-tzibbur* — applies only *lechatchila*, as an ideal standard. Where no alternative is available, the *bidieved* situation invokes the framework of *lo efshar*, and reading from a *pasul sefer Torah* is permitted after the fact.

This distinction carries direct practical consequence. If, in the middle of *kriat haTorah*, an error is discovered in the *sefer Torah* — the reader is midway through an *aliyah* and a letter is found to be missing — a second *sefer Torah* is brought, and reading resumes from the point of the error. The *aliyot* already completed from the *pasul sefer Torah* are not repeated. The basis for this ruling, as the *Beit Yosef* explains in *Shulchan Aruch*, is precisely the Rambam's position: since those *aliyot* were read *bidieved* without a valid *sefer Torah*, and the prohibition is *lechatchila*, what was done stands.

One might further ask: if a community's only available *sefer Torah* is *pasul* and there is no time to repair it before *Shabbat*, may they read from it *lechatchila*? According to the *Beit Yosef*'s reading of the Rambam, the answer would be yes. How this plays out *halacha le-ma'aseh* given the resistance this approach encounters in practice remains a live question. One might add that all of this discussion still operates within the framework of a *chumash* understood as a genuine scroll — not a printed codex, which differs in parchment, form, script, and composition in so many dimensions that whether even the Rambam's *bidieved* leniency would apply to it is an entirely separate question.

---

## Haftara Books

### Haftara Prohibition

Rabba and Rav Yosef further rule: *ha-sefer aftarta asur le-mikrei bei be-shabbat* — it is forbidden to read the *haftarah* from a compiled book of *haftarot* on *Shabbat*. This refers to exactly the kind of volume familiar from contemporary *shul* practice: a convenient collection of *haftarot* with the relevant *berachot*, organized by *parasha*, in large and legible print.

### Out of Context Problem

The reason is that such a book *lo nitan le-hikatev* — it should not have been written. The concern is distinct from the *sefer Torah* discussion: this is not a question of ritual fitness or *kavod ha-tzibbur* in the same sense. The issue is that excerpting a *perek* of *Yeshayahu* or *Yirmiyahu* from its full context and presenting it as a standalone unit is itself problematic. One who wishes to learn *Sefer Yeshayahu* should learn it from the *sefer* in its entirety, not from an extracted chapter. Since the object was not appropriate to write, it is not appropriate to read from publicly.

### Muktzeh Status

Rav Ashi extends the ruling: since such a book may not be used for its intended purpose — reading the *haftarah* — it is also *muktzeh* on *Shabbat* and may not even be moved. The logic is that an item lacking any permitted use on *Shabbat* falls under the category of *muktzeh*. This implies a further dimension of concern: not merely that one should not read from it publicly, but that the very existence of the book, as a decontextualized excerpt of *Nach*, has a kind of problematic character even for private engagement.

### Aggadata Exception

A counterpoint is introduced immediately. Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish would study from a *sifra de-aggadata* — a written compilation of Rabbinic stories and homilies — on *Shabbat*. This presents a different but parallel challenge: such a book is *Torah she'baal peh* in written form, and *Torah she'baal peh* is in principle not to be written. Yet they used it. It is tempting to ask what it meant for the transmission of aggadic traditions in their era, and whether such material existed in written form from early on or emerged only gradually. One might also note that there were established traditions of *Shabbat drashot* of an aggadic character — works like the *She'iltot* blend *halacha* and *aggadata* in a homiletical framework, and portions of *Bereishit Rabbah* may themselves reflect sermon traditions. Whether Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish were encountering material outside their own area of expertise and therefore required a written text, or whether the oral transmission of *aggadata* was simply less rigorous than that of *halakha*, is an interesting open question.

### Lo Efshar Principle

The Gemara's resolution invokes a principle: *keivan de-lo efshar, eit la'asot l'Hashem heferu Toratecha* — since it is impossible otherwise, the time demands action for God's sake even at the cost of setting aside one aspect of Torah. This is the same rationale used to justify the writing down of *Torah she'baal peh* more broadly: the imperative to preserve Torah, when transmission by purely oral means becomes impracticable, overrides the formal prohibition against committing the oral tradition to writing.

The same logic applies, says the Gemara, to the *sefer haftarot*. Rashi explains: *she-ein kol tzibbur ve-tzibbur yachol lischir ve-likhtov nevi'im shalem* — not every community can commission and pay for complete scrolls of all the prophetic books from which *haftarot* are drawn. Given this practical impossibility, the compiled *haftarah* book — though not ideal — is permitted by the principle of *lo efshar*. This is precisely the rationale behind the contemporary practice. The speaker notes that he personally tries, when receiving an *aliyah* for *haftarah*, to read from a complete *Tanakh* rather than from a *haftarah* book, since that at least constitutes a *sefer shalem* in the relevant sense — and notes that publishers have even produced *Tanakhim* in which the *haftarah* sections are printed in larger type for exactly this purpose. Some *shulot*, particularly in Israel, have gone further and commissioned actual scrolls — individual *sefarim* of *Yeshayahu*, *Yirmiyahu*, and the other prophetic books from which *haftarot* are read — so that the reading is performed not merely from a *sefer shalem* but from a proper scroll. Whether the value of *shalem* applies equally to a printed book as to a scroll, and how it intersects with the contemporary reality of printed *chumashim* in schools, are questions the Gemara's discussion raises without fully resolving.

---

## Megillot for Learning

### Megillah Question

Abaye poses a question to Rabba: *mahu le-michtav megillah le-tinok le-hitlamed bah* — is it permitted to write a *megillah*, a subsection of the Torah, for a child to learn from? This is narrower than the *chumash* discussion: not a complete book such as *Sefer Bereishit*, but a segment of a book — say, *Parashat Bereishit* alone, or an even smaller unit. The context is pedagogical rather than liturgical; the question is not about public reading but about private study. Perhaps, one might think, the considerations of *kavod ha-tzibbur* and ritual propriety do not apply here, and a child who will spend the year learning a single *parasha* should be able to do so from a self-contained text.

### Megillah vs Chatumah

The question, Abaye notes, has different valences depending on how one understands the original transmission of the Torah. This introduces a fundamental debate about how the Torah was given: was it written down section by section as each passage was revealed — *megillah megillah nitnah* — or was the entire text preserved orally throughout the forty years and written down as a sealed, indivisible unit at the end — *Torah chatumah nitnah*?

If one holds that Torah was given *megillah megillah*, perhaps individual sections have always had a kind of independent identity, and writing a subsection for a child follows from that premise. Or perhaps even on that view, once the sections were joined together — *keivan de-idbik, idbik* — the composition became indivisible and may no longer be broken apart. Conversely, if Torah was given *chatumah* as a single sealed unit, perhaps the very difficulty of study and the principle of *eit la'asot l'Hashem* would nonetheless permit a pedagogical excerpt. The question, in other words, is not easily resolved by appeal to either premise — it is a genuine question either way.

### Tannaitic Debate

Rabba responds simply: *ein kotvin* — you may not write such a section. The rationale flows from the view that once the Torah was joined together it is *keivan de-idbik, idbik* — an indivisible unit. Even where *eit la'asot l'Hashem* permits certain accommodations, as in the writing of *Torah she'baal peh*, this leniency does not extend to fragmenting *Torah she'bikhtav*, which is treated as sacrosanct and utterly indivisible. The Gemara then brings a *Beraita* framing this as a *tannaitic* dispute. The first position: *ein kotvin megillah le-tinok le-hitlamed bah* — one may not write a section of Torah for a child to learn from it. The modification: *ve-im da'ato le-hashlim, mutar* — but if one intends to complete the full text, it is permitted. The interpretation of this condition is that one begins with the opening *parasha* and continues adding to the scroll as the child advances, ultimately producing a complete *sefer* — a kind of living scroll that grows along with the student's learning.

### Heleni Tablet

Rabbi Yehuda's position is then cited: he permits writing sections of specific lengths — from *Bereishit* through *Dor ha-Mabul*, or in *Torat Kohanim* through *Vayehi Bayom ha-Shemini* — implying that at least these natural units may stand on their own. Separately, the Gemara raises the case of the golden tablet of Heleni ha-Malka. Queen Helena had a golden tablet made, inscribed with *Parashat Sota*, so that the *kohen* could consult it when writing the *megillat sota* for the *sotah* ceremony. The Gemara initially understands this as a case of a Torah section written as an independent text — but Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai explains that the text on the tablet was written *be-seirugin*: not in full, but in a partial or abbreviated form, with the beginning of each *pasuk* written out and the remainder indicated only by *rashei teivot*. Rashi understands this to mean the opening words were complete while the endings were abbreviated. The point is that the tablet signaled the text rather than presenting it as a full, self-standing document. Presenting something as the actual, complete, authoritative text — such that it implicitly declares itself capable of standing alone — is precisely the problem. A text written in abbreviated or partial form avoids that declaration. This is what made the Heleni tablet acceptable.

### Modern Schools

The contemporary practice of using individual printed *chumashim* in schools is worth examining against these standards. The Gemara's concern was with a scroll — a *megillah* in the technical sense. A printed codex differs so dramatically in form, material, and script that it may constitute a categorically different object. Moreover, since *chumash* in the sense of a complete book of the Torah is in principle acceptable — it was the subject of the earlier discussion about public reading — a printed *Sefer Bereishit* may not qualify as the problematic *megillah* at all. There is also the *da'ato le-hashlim* consideration: if the school's intent is that students will eventually learn all *chamisha chumshei Torah*, the individual *chumash* may be understood as part of an ongoing, completable process. One might further note that a *chumash* is precisely a *chumash* — a fifth of the Torah — and the earlier discussion did acknowledge *chumashim* as a distinct category from a *megillah*, which is a sub-section of a *sefer*.

---

## Torah Transmission

### R. Yochanan vs Reish Lakish

The debate about how the Torah was given is now examined directly. Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Banna'ah, holds: *Torah megillah megillah nitnah* — the Torah was given section by section. His prooftext is from *Tehillim*: *Az amarti hinei vati be-megillat sefer katuv alai* — "Then I said, behold I come with a scroll-book written about me." The text calls it a *megillat sefer*, a scroll or sectioned book, and is understood as referring to the Torah — implying that the Torah is a composition of *megillos*, distinct sections. Reish Lakish disagrees: *Torah chatumah nitnah* — the Torah was given as one sealed, indivisible unit. His prooftext is from the end of *Devarim*: *Lakoch et Sefer ha-Torah ha-zot* — "Take this Sefer Torah," the singular *sefer* pointing to one complete and unified document.

### Prooftexts

The Gemara works through the counter-prooftexts in both directions. How does Rabbi Yochanan handle *Lakoch et Sefer ha-Torah*? *Hahu le-vatar de-idbik* — that verse refers to after the sections were assembled and joined together; by the end they formed one *sefer*, but that does not speak to how the text was originally transmitted. And how does Reish Lakish handle *megillat sefer*? *Chol ha-Torah kullah ikri megillah* — the word *megillah* can refer to the Torah as a whole, not to any particular section within it. He adduces a verse from *Zechariah*: *va-yomer elai mah attah ro'eh va-omar ani ro'eh megillah afah* — "And he said to me, what do you see? And I said, I see a floating scroll." There the word *megillah* clearly refers to a single whole scroll rather than a section of a larger work.

### Eight Parshiyot

Yet Reish Lakish concedes something to the structure of Rabbi Levi's tradition: *shemonah parshiyot ne'emru be-yom she-hukam bo ha-Mishkan* — eight *parshiyot* were communicated on the day the *Mishkan* was erected. These are: *Parshat Kohanim* — the laws of priestly status (*Emor el ha-kohanim*); *Parshat Leviyim* — the role of the *Leviyim* in the *Mishkan*; *Parshat Tme'im* — the laws of impurity (Rashi understands this as the narrative of those who were *tamei le-nefesh adam* and could not bring the *korban Pesach*; Tosafot reads it as the broader section of *tumat meit*, *tumas sheretz*, and *tumas neveilah*); *Parshat Shiluach Tme'im* — the *mitzvah* of sending the impure out of the camp; *Parshat Acharei Mot* — concerning *Yom Kippur*, understood by Rashi as connected to the tragedy of *b'nei Aharon* and the commandment limiting entry to the *kodesh*; *Parshat Shituyei Yayin* — the prohibition against entering the sanctuary in a state of intoxication, also linked to the death of *b'nei Aharon*; *Parshat Neirot* — the lighting of the *Menorah* (*Be-ha'alotecha*); and *Parshat Parah* — the laws of the *parah adumah*, necessary because the people needed a means of purification in order to enter the *Mishkan*. These eight sections, though dispersed across different locations in the Torah, were communicated together on a single occasion. Reish Lakish may acknowledge that these particular sections had a kind of distinct identity and communicative moment, while still maintaining that the Torah as a written text was given as one sealed unit.

---

## Written vs Oral (II)

### R. Elazar View

A further debate concerns the relative proportion of *Torah she'bikhtav* and *Torah she'baal peh*. Rabbi Elazar holds: *Torah rov be-chsav u-miut al peh* — the majority of Torah is written, a minority is oral. His prooftext: *Echtov lo rubei Torati* — "I will write for him the majority of my Torah" — and *kemo zar nechshavu*, taken by Rashi to mean "they have treated it like something foreign," i.e., they have not upheld the written Torah. The verse thus asserts that it is the *written* dimension that constitutes the majority.

### R. Yochanan View

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *rov al peh, u-miut be-chsav* — the majority of Torah is *Torah she'baal peh*, and only a minority is in written form. His prooftext: *ki al pi ha-devarim ha-eileh* — "by the mouth of these things," meaning the oral tradition is the primary medium of transmission. He handles Rabbi Elazar's verse by reading it as a rhetorical question with an exclamatory tone: *Echtov lo rubei Torati?* — could I possibly write down the majority of my Torah? *Halo kemo zar nechshavu* — that would be an extraordinary, even absurd, claim. He thus denies that the verse asserts what Rabbi Elazar took from it.

### Rashi Interpretation

The question as it stands seems almost unanswerable in its plain sense: there are roughly seventy volumes of Rabbinic literature against five books of the written Torah. On any raw count, the oral tradition is vastly larger. Rashi's interpretation resolves the difficulty ingeniously. The debate is not about sheer volume at all. The question is *from where* the content of *Torah she'baal peh* is derived. How much of *Torah she'baal peh* has its ultimate source in, and is derivable from, *Torah she'bikhtav* — through the mechanisms of *midrash*, *derashah*, textual analysis — versus how much exists independently of *Torah she'bikhtav*, whether as *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* or as tradition not anchored in a *pasuk*?

### Derivation Debate

This maps onto a question that occupies scholars of *Midrashei Halacha*: are the Sages genuinely *deriving* their halakhic conclusions from close reading of the text — that is, they did not know the *halacha* and went to the *psukim* to determine it — or did they begin with a received tradition and subsequently find support for it in the *pasuk*? If the former, the majority of *Torah she'baal peh* is ultimately rooted in *Torah she'bikhtav*; if the latter, the majority exists independently of what is written. Rabbi Elazar holds that the derivational source of most *halacha* is textual; Rabbi Yochanan holds that the tradition is primary and the textual connections secondary. This is a remarkable dispute about the epistemological structure of *Torah she'baal peh* itself.

---

## Written vs Oral (II)

### Separate Genres

Rabbi Yehuda bar Nachmani, the *meturgeman* — the formal announcer — of Reish Lakish, expounds the following *derasha*. One verse says *Ktov lecha et ha-devarim ha-eileh* — "Write these words for yourself." Another says *ki al pi ha-devarim ha-eileh* — "by the mouth of these things." The juxtaposition generates a principle: *devarim she-bi-chsav ee attah rashai le-omran be-al peh* — that which is written may not be transmitted orally, and *devarim she-be'al peh ee attah rashai le-omran bi-chsav* — that which is oral may not be committed to writing. Each genre must remain in its proper domain.

The power of this principle is not merely procedural. There is something theologically significant about the *Torah she'bikhtav* being fixed, concrete, and immutable — written in stone, as it were — while the *Torah she'baal peh* remains alive in the relationship between *rebbe* and *talmid*, transmitted by voice and internalized through engagement. Writing *Torah she'bikhtav* anchors it; the orality of *Torah she'baal peh* preserves its capacity for development, application, and response to circumstance. To collapse the boundary — to turn the written into an oral tradition or to freeze the oral in writing — would distort the nature of each.

There is a related tension worth noting: it is sometimes said that the Rabbis may have been pushing back against sectarian groups — such as those behind the Dead Sea Scrolls — who produced *pesharim*, written interpretive texts on *Torah she'bikhtav*. One might argue that writing down *derashot* directly tied to the text gave those interpretations a textual authority they did not deserve. If the *derashot* are presented in written form alongside *Torah she'bikhtav*, they may be mistaken for the original text itself — or at least accorded a similar standing. The school of Rabbi Yishmael's distinction, discussed next, addresses this very boundary.

### Drasha vs Halacha

The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: *eileh* — referring to the written *devarim* — *attah kotev, ve-ee attah kotev halakhot*. You may write *derashot* — the homiletical and exegetical engagements directly linked to the written text — but you may not write *halakhot*, the bottom-line legal rulings of the oral tradition. The *halakhot* as a genre — the kind of material later crystallized in the *Mishnah* — must remain oral. This represents resistance to codification: not merely to writing, but to the concretization of *halacha* into a fixed, authoritative written document. The *Mishnah* itself, it is worth recalling, was not published in written form but transmitted orally; its eventual writing down was itself an act of *eit la'asot l'Hashem*.

The distinction the school of Rabbi Yishmael draws may also reflect a different concern. *Derashot* are explicitly in conversation with *Torah she'bikhtav* — they are anchored in and point toward the text. Writing them alongside the text preserves their derivative status. *Halakhot*, by contrast, are presented as self-standing rulings without explicit textual reference. Writing them could make them appear equivalent in authority to the written Torah, or could give the false impression that human legal reasoning has the same standing as divine revelation. Keeping them oral preserves their character as *Torah she'baal peh* — transmitted, received, and applied through an ongoing human relationship with the tradition.

### Covenant & Oral

The sugya concludes with a statement of Rabbi Yochanan that is at once a legal observation and a theological declaration: *lo karat ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu berit im Yisrael ella bishvil devarim she-be'al peh* — the Holy One, Blessed be He, made His covenant with Israel only by virtue of *Torah she'baal peh*. The prooftext: *ki al pi ha-devarim ha-eileh karati ittecha berit ve-et Yisrael* — "for by the mouth of these things have I made a covenant with you and with Israel." Even if *Torah she'bikhtav* is immutable, fixed, and inviolable — the bedrock of the divine communication — the *brit*, the living covenantal relationship between God and the Jewish people, is constituted through *Torah she'baal peh*: through the ongoing human engagement with interpretation, derivation, and application. The process of *Torah she'baal peh* — its development, its transmission, its responsiveness to history — is not secondary to the covenant but is itself the very medium through which the covenant is enacted and sustained. On this striking note, the *daf* concludes.

---

---

# Gittin 61

## Eruv & Reputation

### Eruv Placement

The daf opens in the middle of Gittin 61b, returning to the halachic portion of the Mishnah and its discussion of *darkei shalom* — the principle of maintaining peaceful relations. The Mishnah states: *me'arvin b'bayit yashan mipnei darkei shalom* — one places the *eruv* in the established house, the house in which it has been kept until now, because of the ways of peace. The Gemara then asks: *mai ta'ama darkei shalom* — what precisely is the *darkei shalom* rationale here? If we suppose it is a matter of *kavod* — of honor, that the person in whose house the *eruv* is stored would feel slighted were it moved — we can challenge this from a case involving a *shippura*.

### Shippura Definition

The Gemara introduces the *shippura* that was kept in the house of Rav Yehuda and subsequently moved as the generations changed. Rashi explains that the *shippura* was a shofar blown to warn the public of the approaching Shabbat. Tosafot, citing one of the Geonim, offers an alternative reading: the *shippura* was a shofar-shaped charity box — a vessel with a narrow slot at the top and a wide base — used to collect donations for the students of the yeshiva. The Geonic source indeed reflects the reality of that era, when such collections were essential for the maintenance of the great academies.

### Shippura Succession

The Gemara traces the movement of the *shippura*: first it was kept in the house of Rav Yehuda, then in the house of Rabba, then Rav Yosef, then Abaye, and finally Rava. Rashi explains the succession in terms of the passing of each *rosh yeshiva* of Pumbedita: when one died and the next rose to lead the academy, the *shippura* was transferred to his household. Tosafot raises a geographic difficulty: Rav Yehuda was in Pumbedita while Rava was in Mechuza — these are different cities. Tosafot resolves this by suggesting that the *shippura* followed whoever held the position of primary *rosh mesivta*, wherever he happened to reside, since it was understood communally that the fund traveled with the leading authority and was his to distribute to the students.

### Suspicion Rationale

The Gemara concludes that the *darkei shalom* rationale for keeping the *eruv* in its established location is not *kavod* but rather *chashdah* — suspicion. Rashi explains: people are accustomed to seeing the *eruv* kept in a particular house. If it is moved and someone enters that house and does not find it there, they may assume the *eruv* was never made, and suspect the entire courtyard of carrying without an *eruv*. It is not an issue of dishonoring the original host; it is the concern for generating ill repute among the members of the *mavoy*.

Tosafot formulates the suspicion differently. According to Rabbeinu Tam, the concern is that if the *eruv* is removed from one house and placed in another, people will suspect that the original host can no longer be trusted — that he was suspected of stealing from the communal *eruv* chest. That is the reputational harm *darkei shalom* seeks to prevent. Tosafot then asks: if we are worried about such suspicion, how much more so should we be worried about moving the *tzedakah* box, where suspicion of misappropriation would be even more natural? Tosafot answers that everyone understands the charity fund follows the *rosh mesivta*, and so its movement from one leading scholar's home to the next raises no suspicion — it is a known and accepted practice.

## Water Rights Debate

### Well & Canal

The Gemara next takes up the Mishnah's case of *bor she-haya karov le-amah* — a well that is situated near a water channel — and the question of who has priority to draw from that channel first. The underlying dispute concerns which landowners along a waterway have preferential rights to its water.

### Rav vs Shmuel

The Gemara introduces a formal dispute: *beni nahara* — the people of the river. Rav says *tata'ei shatu maya be-reisha* — those at the bottom of the river have the first right to draw water. Shmuel says *ila'ei shatu maya be-reisha* — those at the top have priority.

The Gemara clarifies that when water flows freely and there is no concern of it running out — or when people are simply drawing from the moving river without damming it — there is no dispute; everyone may use the water freely. The debate is specifically about *be-miskar ve-ashkoyei* — the act of damming the river in order to irrigate one's fields from the pooled water. Who has the right to dam it up first?

Shmuel maintains that those upstream have priority, reasoning *de-amri anan mekarvinan tfei* — they are closer to the water's source and thus have a stronger natural claim. Rav disagrees, ruling in favor of those downstream: *nahara ke-fashtei leizil* — the river must be allowed to run its natural course. The phrase *ke-fashtei*, meaning "as it spreads," connects to the well-known expression *nahara nahara u-fashtei* — each river and its tributaries — used to acknowledge the legitimacy of varying practices. Rav's position is that you cannot stop the river at its upper reach before it has fed into the tributaries along the way; only after the river has done that may those downstream claim the right to dam it. Rashi elaborates: as the river descends it branches into tributaries, and the people upstream argue they must act first because by the time the water has spread into all those branches, little will remain. The people downstream counter that it is unjust to stop the flow before all those branches have been fed.

### Shmuel's Reading

Having stated their own positions, the Gemara now invokes the Mishnah: *bor ha-karov le-amah mitmalei rishon mipnei darkei shalom* — the well closest to the channel fills first because of *darkei shalom*. This would seem to favor Rav, since proximity to the channel would imply priority for those upstream. But *targumah Shmuel aliba de-Rav* — Shmuel, to his credit, interprets this Mishnah in a way that is consistent with Rav's position even though it appears to contradict his own. The Mishnah, Shmuel explains, is dealing with *amah ha-malechet al pi boro* — a channel that runs directly along the mouth of the well, such that the well fills naturally from the water's flow without any damming at all. Rashi: *she-mitmalei me-eilav ke-derech hillucho* — it fills on its own as the water runs its course. In such a case neither Rav nor Shmuel has anything to say; the water simply overflows into the adjacent well with no act of diversion.

The Gemara raises an objection: if that is so, what is the novelty of the ruling? What is the *chiddush*? The Gemara answers: one might have thought the well's owner is obligated to seal or cover his well so as to allow more water to flow downstream to those further along. The Mishnah tells us he is not required to do so. If water naturally flows into his well, he is permitted to allow it. This, however, says nothing about the separate question of whether one may actively dam the river — and it is only in that context that the dispute between Rav and Shmuel applies.

### Might Makes Right

Since neither Rav nor Shmuel's position was definitively ruled upon, Rav Huna bar Tachalifa states: *kol d'alim gavar* — whoever is stronger prevails. This is, as the Gemara implicitly acknowledges, the antithesis of *darkei shalom*. Rather than establishing orderly norms for communal resource allocation — perhaps alternating months or some other equitable arrangement — the outcome is effectively "go fight it out." It is both ironic and troubling that the discussion of *darkei shalom* ends at this juncture with a principle that is precisely the opposite of peaceful coexistence.

### Rav Shimi's Story

The Gemara then relates the story of Rav Shimi bar Ashi, which illustrates how *kol d'alim gavar* can be exploited. Rav Shimi bar Ashi came before Abaye and asked him to learn with him. Abaye replied that he had only his own study time left and could not spare it for teaching. Rav Shimi then asked about learning at night, and Abaye said he used his nights to water his fields. Rav Shimi offered a deal: he would water Abaye's fields during the day if Abaye would teach him at night. Abaye agreed.

To fulfill his end of the bargain conveniently, Rav Shimi went to the people upstream and told them the ruling was *tata'ei shatu be-reisha* — those downstream have priority. He then went to the people downstream and told them the ruling was *ila'ei shatu be-reisha* — those upstream have priority. Each group, deferring to his halakhic authority, held back from damming the river, whereupon Rav Shimi dammed it first himself and irrigated Abaye's fields.

When Rav Shimi returned to Abaye, Abaye confronted him: *k'bei trei avadt li* — you issued contradictory rulings on my behalf? This attribution to me is entirely inappropriate. As a consequence, Abaye refused to eat the produce of those fields for the entire year. Tosafot, sensing the need to explain how Rav Shimi could have done something so manifestly unjust, suggests he reasoned that since the law was *kol d'alim gavar* — a total free-for-all — any stratagem was equally valid. But Abaye clearly did not accept that justification.

### Beni Becharmach

The Gemara closes this section with the case of the *bnei Becharmach* — the people of that locale. They dug a canal diverting the river *Shanvata* so that it would flow around their fields and then return to the river's lower course, thereby ensuring their fields received the lion's share of the water. The people upstream, whose water supply was now cut off, came before Abaye complaining: *ka-matzli lana nahara* — they are destroying our river.

Abaye first suggested that they dig the channel deeper, perhaps allowing the water to flow below and reach them more readily; he acknowledged not fully understanding the mechanics but supposed it might help. They replied that digging deeper would lower the water level relative to their orchards and the fruit would dry out. Abaye then said *lizlu ve-lisalku nafshaikhu meihatam* — go and remove yourselves from there. The question is to whom this was addressed. Rashi reads it as directed at the *bnei Becharmach*, telling them they must remove their illegal diversion. But Tosafot reads it as addressed to the complainants — Abaye was telling them he could not help them, since the rule was *kol d'alim gavar*. This is a deeply unsatisfying conclusion. The entire *sugya* has been framed around *darkei shalom*, yet it ends with an outcome that encourages precisely the kind of deceptive and unjust behavior — and the sense of grievance — that *darkei shalom* was meant to prevent.

## Property & Possession

### Traps & Possession

The Gemara continues with further applications of *darkei shalom* in the domain of property: *metzudot chaya ve-ofot ve-dagim yesh bahem mishum gezel mipnei darkei shalom* — if one's animal traps catch something, taking what is in them constitutes a form of theft, but only *mipnei darkei shalom*, since full legal possession has not yet been acquired. Rabbi Yossi goes further, ruling it is actual theft. The Gemara asks how this can be real theft if the owner of the trap has not legally acquired the animal.

### Vessels vs Hooks

The Gemara distinguishes between types of traps. When it comes to *ozlei u-oharei* — nets and wicker baskets used for fishing — everyone agrees there is no debate about *darkei shalom* at all; the catch is actually owned by the trap's owner through *kinyan kli*, since the animal is fully enclosed within a vessel belonging to that person. The debate arises specifically with regard to *lechi ve-kukari* — hooks or spiked barriers against which fish or animals become caught without being contained. In such cases there is no *kinyan kli*, and taking what is caught there is prohibited only *mipnei darkei shalom*.

If Rabbi Yossi holds it is *gezel gamur* — actual theft — Rav Chisda clarifies that he means *gezel gamur mi-divreikhem*, real theft by rabbinic enactment rather than biblical law, since genuine acquisition cannot occur through a trap of this type. The practical difference between the two positions — *darkei shalom* versus *gezel midrabanan* — is whether a beit din can compel the return of what was taken. If the prohibition is merely one of *darkei shalom*, it is a behavioral norm without enforceable judicial consequence; if it is *gezel midrabanan*, a court may order restitution.

### Olive Tree Story

Similarly, a poor person perched atop an olive tree knocking down olives has not yet taken possession of them. This is prohibited only *mipnei darkei shalom*. However, the Gemara cites a *baraita*: if he plucked the olives with his hand, that is *gezel gamur* — genuine theft — because he has physically taken possession. Tosafot points out that this seems obvious and asks what the novelty is. Tosafot answers that the case involves someone who picked the olive off the branch with his hand but did not hold it in his palm — he simply pulled it from the tree and let it fall. One might have thought that since the olive never rested in his hand, there was no act of *kinyan*. The *baraita* teaches that even so, the act of *tlisha* — detaching it from the tree — constitutes sufficient acquisition, and it is *gezel gamur* at the biblical level.

### Dates Story

The Gemara then relates a story involving Rav Kahana. He was traveling and observed a man throwing palm branches up into a date palm, causing dates to fall. According to Rashi, the man was hurling the branches like javelins to knock down the dates. Rav Kahana went over and ate the dates, reasoning the man had not yet taken possession of them. The man then challenged him: *chazi mar de-vi-yadash dasin hu* — look, I knocked those down with my own hands. Whether the man was claiming *gezel gamur* or merely *darkei shalom* is not fully clear.

Rav Kahana responded: *m'atra de-Rav Yoshiya at* — you must be from the place where Rav Yoshiya teaches. He quoted the verse: *v'tzaddik yesod olam* — the righteous is the foundation of the world — implying that Rav Yoshiya's teachings had properly shaped this man's halakhic sensibility.

Tosafot offers a different reading of the story. In Tosafot's version, the man was not hurling branches to knock down dates but was cutting down the palm branches from atop the tree while the dates fell accidentally. Rav Kahana assumed the man was interested only in the branches and not the dates, so that the falling dates were *hefker* and he could take them. The man then corrected him: I am also shaking the tree in order to bring down the dates, so they are mine, and the *darkei shalom* prohibition applies.

## Non-Jewish Poor

### Braita Text

The Gemara turns to another dimension of *darkei shalom*: obligations toward non-Jews. The Mishnah states: *ein memachin be-yad aniyei nochrim be-leket shikha u-feah mipnei darkei shalom* — one does not prevent the non-Jewish poor from collecting *leket*, *shikha*, and *peah* because of *darkei shalom*. This is a relatively passive form of *darkei shalom*: one does not proactively give but simply does not obstruct.

The Gemara then quotes a *baraita*: *mefarnesin aniyei nochrim im aniyei Yisrael* — one sustains the poor of the non-Jews together with the poor of Israel; *u-mevakrin cholei nochrim im cholei Yisrael* — one visits the sick of the non-Jews together with the sick of Israel; *ve-kovrin metei nochrim im metei Yisrael* — one buries the dead of the non-Jews together with the dead of Israel; all of this *mipnei darkei shalom*. The word for non-Jews in the *baraita* is *nochrim* rather than *Akum*, signaling that this applies to all non-Jews without distinction.

### Rashi's Reading

A number of questions arise immediately. First, what does the word *im* — "with" or "together" — mean? Does it imply burying non-Jews in the same cemetery as Jews? Rashi rules it does not. Rashi explains that *im* means in the context of the same communal effort: if one is engaged in an effort of burying the dead and there are both Jews and non-Jews involved, one attends to both. Similarly, if one is feeding the poor, one includes the non-Jewish poor in that same effort. The primary obligation is oriented toward *Yisrael*, but one does not exclude the non-Jewish poor encountered in the same circumstances. This reading is careful and perhaps measured — it does not assert an independent primary obligation but rather a policy of inclusion within efforts already directed toward the Jewish community.

The question of what *darkei shalom* means in this context is itself significant. The most self-serving reading would be that we treat non-Jews well so they will treat us well — a kind of *mipnei eiva* logic. But it is worth noting that the *darkei shalom* of earlier portions of the chapter was not self-serving in that narrow sense. When it came to establishing priority for *aliyot* or setting norms for the *eruv*, the point was to build a society and community with less conflict, to establish conventions that allowed people to live together better. One can read the obligation toward the non-Jewish poor in the same light: *darkei shalom* as the cultivation of a broader peaceful social order, not merely an instrumental calculation.

### Rambam View

Maimonides' approach to this passage is striking. Recall that at the beginning of the broader *sugya* on *darkei shalom*, the Gemara considered whether honoring the *kohen* was biblical or only *darkei shalom*, and ultimately stated that the entire Torah is *mipnei darkei shalom* — for it says *dracheha darchei noam ve-chol netivoteha shalom*, its ways are ways of pleasantness and all its paths are peace. Rambam, when codifying the obligation to sustain the non-Jewish poor *mipnei darkei shalom*, invokes precisely this framework: *vaharei ne'emar tov Hashem la-kol ve-rachamav al kol ma'asav* — for it is said that God is good to all and His mercies extend over all His creatures — *ve-ne'emar dracheha darchei noam ve-chol netivoteha shalom*. For Rambam, *mipnei darkei shalom* is not a pragmatic accommodation but an expression of the core moral values of the Torah. Acting in accordance with *darkei shalom* means acting in accordance with God's own attribute of *rachamim* over all creation, and living a life shaped by Torah values of care and concern for others.

### Reciprocity Theme

A further dimension of this passage was noted by Suzanne Stone, who observed that the logic of *darkei shalom* is often presented as unidirectional: we are generous to non-Jews so they will be generous to us. But she proposed reversing the framing entirely: because of all that we receive from living within a broader society — all that we benefit from our participation in a larger human community — what are our reciprocal obligations toward that society? *Darkei shalom*, on this reading, is not primarily self-interested but arises from an awareness of what we owe to those alongside whom we live. The emphasis shifts from instrumental self-protection to genuine social responsibility. This is a considerably more demanding and more morally compelling reading, and it is worth appreciating that when the Gemara presents this principle it may have precisely this richer meaning in view.

### Tosefta Version

The *Tosefta* on this subject — in chapter 3, section 18 — goes considerably further than the Mishnah. It opens with the striking ruling that in a city containing both Jews and non-Jews, the *parnasim* — the communal charity collectors — collect from both Jews and *ovdei kokhavim* because of *darkei shalom*. This is not merely a case of not excluding non-Jews from what one is already doing for Jews; it is a statement of shared communal responsibility. The non-Jews are taxed alongside the Jews for communal welfare purposes. The *Tosefta* then lists the same obligations — feeding the poor, eulogizing and burying the dead, comforting mourners — but notably does not include the phrase *im Yisrael* in each case. The formulations stand independently, without the qualifier that limits the obligation to circumstances in which one is already acting on behalf of Jews. The *Tosefta* thus projects a more expansive and more egalitarian vision of *darkei shalom* than does the Mishnah. It is worth noting that the *Tosefta* was composed in Eretz Yisrael, as was the Mishnah — yet Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi chose in the Mishnah to articulate a considerably more limited version of this principle than the *Tosefta* contains.

## Lending & Suspicion

### Shemitah Lending

The Gemara returns to further applications of *darkei shalom*, now examining when one is permitted to lend tools or otherwise assist someone suspected of violating religious law. The Mishnah rules: *mash'elet ishah le-chavertah ha-chashudah al ha-shevi'it nafah ve-kevar ve-reichayim ve-tannur* — a woman may lend her neighbor who is suspected of disregarding the laws of *shemitah* a sieve, a colander, a millstone, and an oven, despite the fact that such neighbor may be using them to process *shemitah* produce she should not have. *Aval* — however — she may not actively grind or sift together with her, since that would cross the line into *mesayea yedei oveir aveirah*.

Tosafot brings into the discussion the parallel *sugya* in Avodah Zarah regarding *lifnei iver*. The question is how one can lend tools to someone when one knows, or strongly suspects, they will use them for a prohibited purpose. Tosafot notes that if there were genuine doubt about the intended use, no *darkei shalom* argument would be needed — the lending would be permitted in any case since the item might be used legitimately. Therefore, Tosafot concludes, the Mishnah must be dealing with a case where one is fairly certain the neighbor will use the tools for *shemitah* produce. This raises the difficulty: if so, why is it not *lifnei iver*? Tosafot does not fully resolve this, but one possible answer — developed by Tosafot in other contexts — is that since the borrower could obtain the same items from someone else, the lender is not the direct enabler of the violation. This principle became a major basis in the medieval period for permitting Jews to sell certain items to non-Jews: since the non-Jew could acquire the item from another source, the Jewish seller was not the cause of the prohibition. The Mishnah's ruling, then, permits lending but draws the line at active participation in the processing.

### Am Ha'aretz Wife
