The essential testimony, however, is that the *get* was received, not that it was torn.

### Tosafot's Challenge

Tosafot raises a serious question. The *Mishnah* then adds: *afilu hen ha-rishonim ve-hen ha-acharonim* — even if the same witnesses appear at both the appointment and the reception, that is sufficient. Tosafot asks: what is the force of *afilu* here? One might have expected the opposite — that the same witnesses who were present at both stages would be *preferable*, since they can testify as a single body to everything they witnessed without any concern about combining half-testimonies from different groups.

The problem Tosafot is pointing to is the principle of *davar v'lo chatzi davar*: witnesses testify to a matter, not to half a matter. If the witnesses who saw the *get* received knew nothing about the prior appointment, how can their testimony about reception alone constitute valid *eidut* on the act of *gerushin*? The *get* was given to some man by the husband, but those witnesses may not have known he was the wife's *shaliach*.

One might ask why the woman's own testimony cannot simply resolve the matter — she appointed him, after all. The answer is that her testimony alone does not constitute objective evidence. The husband may be contesting the validity of the *get*, and merely because he trusted the *shaliach* at the time of delivery does not mean his wife's word alone suffices to prove retroactively that the *shaliach* was properly authorized. A third party who held himself out as an agent and was believed at the time cannot thereby establish the transaction's validity if the principal later contests it without independent objective evidence.

Tosafot therefore explains the *afilu* differently: it tells us that we do not suspect the wife of having coordinated false witnesses. Ordinarily, the very reason one uses a *shaliach* is that the wife is in a distant location and cannot receive the *get* herself. Given that, it would be quite unlikely that the same witnesses happened to be present both in the location where she appointed him and in the entirely different location where he received the *get*. One might therefore suspect collusion. The *afilu* dispels this concern: even if the same witnesses appear at both events, they are believed and we do not suspect the wife of bribery.

As for the underlying question of *chatzi davar*, Tosafot notes that there are circumstances under which additional parties — such as the *shaliach* himself — could be believed to supply the missing information about his appointment, or the husband could be believed in certain respects. When such alternative means exist to fill the gap, it may not constitute a true case of *chatzi davar* that disqualifies the testimony.

### Same or Different Witnesses

The *Mishnah* further states: *v'echad min ha-rishonim v'echad min ha-acharonim v'echad mitztaref imahem* — even if a single witness overlaps between the two groups, that is also valid. Tosafot explains the novelty here as well: one might have suspected that a single individual who appears at both stages — say, Shimon — was hired by the wife to stitch together a false narrative, testifying alongside Reuven that the *shaliach* was appointed and alongside Levi that he received the *get*. The *Mishnah* tells us we do not entertain this suspicion. The upshot is that it does not matter whether the witnesses at the appointment and the reception are entirely the same, entirely different, or partially overlapping — the requirement is simply that there be witnesses at both stages.

### Shaliach's Credibility

The Gemara now asks: the *Mishnah* speaks of a *shaliach l'kabala* who received the *get* and tore it up. Since he is no longer holding the *get* intact, why are all these witnesses necessary? If he were still holding the *get* whole, might his own credibility suffice to establish what occurred?

### Rav Huna vs. Rav Chisda

A dispute is recorded regarding a *shalish* — a third party holding the *get* — where the husband claims he gave it to him only as a *pikadon*, for safekeeping, while the *shaliach* claims it was given to him as a *get* for the wife to be divorced through. Rav Huna rules that the husband is believed. Rav Chisda rules that the *shaliach* is believed, on the grounds of *d'haimneih* — by entrusting the document to him, the husband has implicitly accepted that whatever the *shaliach* says about it is reliable.

### Same Town Qualifier

Tosafot qualifies the entire dispute: it applies only when all three parties — the husband, the *shaliach*, and the wife — are present in the same town. Rav Huna's reasoning for believing the husband is that if he truly intended to divorce his wife, he could and would have handed the *get* to her directly without any intermediary. That argument collapses if the wife is in a distant city. When the wife is elsewhere, the husband obviously could not have given it to her directly, and therefore the very fact that he chose to use a *shaliach* cannot be taken as evidence against the *get* being for divorce. This also explains, Tosafot notes, why a *shaliach* delivering a *get* from overseas is believed when he says *b'fanai nichtav u-v'fanai nechtam* — the husband has no plausible argument that the *get* was only a *pikadon*, since the wife is plainly not available to receive it herself.

### Hemnei Principle

Rav Chisda's position rests on the principle of *hemnei*: when one entrusts an object to a third party, one implicitly agrees to be bound by whatever that third party later asserts about the nature of the transaction. Tosafot presses the point: even if we accept this principle of implicit trust, how does the *shaliach*'s say-so create an act of *gerushin*? The husband may have trusted him, but if no *get* was actually given as a *get*, the wife is simply not divorced regardless of what the *shaliach* claims.

### Money vs. Get Distinction

The Gemara addresses this through a *Baraita* that records: *hoda'at ba'al din k'me'ah edim dami* — an admission by a party against his own interest is equivalent to a hundred witnesses. And: *v'shalish ne'eman mishneihem* — the third-party custodian is believed more than either principal. The *Baraita* illustrates a case where two parties dispute the context in which funds were deposited with a third party, and the third party's account is definitive.

The Gemara draws the parallel: here too, the husband and wife dispute the context of the *get* entrusted to the *shaliach*, and by analogy the *shaliach* should be believed. The Gemara then asks whether this principle extends to *gittin*. The response is a critical distinction: *shani mamon d'it-yahiv l'mechila* — money is different because one can be *mochel* on it. By entrusting money to a third party, you can implicitly say: whatever he decides about this money, I will acquiesce, including simply giving it away. That implicit acquiescence — *hemnei* — works because money is transferable and the principal can effectively ratify whatever the custodian asserts retroactively, simply by choosing not to contest it.

A *get*, however, is different. Even if the husband implicitly trusted the *shaliach*, if he never actually gave the *get* as a *get* — with *da'at* to divorce his wife — the act of *gerushin* never occurred. The implicit agreement to trust the custodian cannot conjure a *da'at* of divorce where none existed. A *get* cannot be given away by mere acquiescence the way money can be waived. The Gemara does entertain the possibility that the *hemnei* principle could operate here as well — that when you hand a *get* to a *shaliach* you are implicitly saying that whatever he later says about its purpose will retroactively define your intent, meaning that if he says you meant to divorce your wife, that becomes your *da'at* at the time of the giving. But the Gemara acknowledges this is a far greater leap than the monetary analogy.

### Whole Get Held

Returning to the *Mishnah*'s requirement of witnesses, the Gemara asks: the *Mishnah* is discussing a case where the *shaliach* tore the *get*. But if he were still holding the *get* intact, why would witnesses be needed at all? If he is holding a whole, signed *get*, that fact itself constitutes circumstantial evidence that the husband gave it to him. Given that he is holding it, he should have the special standing of a custodian who is believed regarding the context of what he holds. The *shaliach* could then simply state that he received it as a *get*, and the wife would be divorced.

Tosafot refines this: why isn't the *shaliach* believed even when the *get* is torn, on the basis that we can see he is holding torn pieces? The answer is that torn pieces of paper could have come from anywhere — there is no way to verify that these particular fragments were once the husband's *get* and were torn only after reception. A whole, signed *get* in the *shaliach*'s hands is a different matter: it carries with it the implicit credential that the husband entrusted him with it, and that credential supports his believability about the circumstances of the transfer.

### Eidei Mesira Kartei

But even granting that a *shaliach* holding a whole *get* has enhanced credibility, there is a further requirement. The Gemara says: *ha mani? Rabbi Elazar hi d'amar edei mesirah kartei* — this reflects the position of Rabbi Elazar, who holds that witnesses to the actual handover are what effects the *get*, not the witnesses who signed the document. According to Rabbi Elazar, *edei mesira kartei* — it is specifically the witnesses who witness the act of the *get* being handed over that create the binding act of *gerushin*.

This is significant. It is not enough to have circumstantial evidence, however strong, that the *get* was received. Even if one could deduce from the *shaliach*'s possession of an intact document that he must have received it from the husband, that would not satisfy *edei mesira*, because *edei mesira* does not mean proving after the fact that a handover occurred. It means that witnesses must directly witness the act of the *get* being passed from hand to hand. The *gerushin* itself, not merely the evidentiary record of it, requires that act to have been witnessed.

It follows that even if a *shaliach* is holding a whole *get* and would be believed regarding what the husband intended, that would still not replace the need for witnesses to the delivery itself — at least according to Rabbi Elazar.

A note on what requires witnesses: there is an asymmetry worth observing. The husband's *shaliach* appears to carry his own credential in the form of the *get* itself — the fact that he possesses the document is in itself a form of testimony to his appointment. The wife's *shaliach*, by contrast, derives his status entirely from her words, which are unaccompanied by any physical credential. This may explain why the need for witnesses to the appointment was felt most acutely with respect to the wife's *shaliach*, while the husband's *shaliach* gains some implicit credibility from the document he carries.

### Torn Get, No Holdings

The Gemara now considers the situation where the *get* was torn, the *shaliach* is not holding it, and only testimonies are available. The husband says he gave the *get* to the *shaliach l'holacha* as his agent to deliver it. The *shaliach* says yes, the husband gave it to him as a *shaliach l'holacha*, and he duly delivered it to the woman. The woman says she received it and it has since been lost. The husband does not contest his having given it; no one challenges the basic facts. Yet there is a problem: how do we know the woman is actually divorced?

The husband's admission that he appointed the *shaliach* establishes that part of the chain. But the *shaliach*'s testimony that he delivered it is that of a single witness with no document in hand, giving him no special standing. The woman's testimony that she received it is also that of a single witness without a document. There are no *edei mesirah*. The Gemara asks why we cannot simply believe the *shaliach*, and the answer already established is that *mi ka nafik gita mi-tusei yadei l'heimneih* — the *shaliach* is believed only when the *get* is in his hands. Without it, he has no special credibility.

The Gemara then asks: let us at least believe the husband. Rav Chiya bar Avin said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: a husband who says "I divorced my wife" is believed, because he could do so now if he wished. By the same logic, the husband's statement that he appointed this man as his *shaliach* should be believed. Indeed, the Gemara accepts this: we believe the husband that he made the man a *shaliach l'holacha*. What we do not know is whether the *shaliach* actually delivered it, and for that we cannot rely on the *shaliach*'s unaccompanied word.

### Chazaka Shaliach

The Gemara asks: rather than requiring witnesses, why not simply invoke the *chazaka* that a *shaliach* performs his mission? Rabbi Yitzchak taught: if one says to his *shaliach*, "Go and betroth a woman for me," and the *shaliach* dies without reporting back, the husband is forbidden to marry any woman in the world, lest any one of them be his betrothed wife's relative. Tosafot notes that this seems extreme — one should also bear in mind that the woman, whoever she is, would herself presumably know she was betrothed. Tosafot therefore suggests this is a *knas*, a punitive measure for irresponsible conduct, but it is grounded in the underlying presumption that the *shaliach* did carry out his mission. This demonstrates the principle of *chazaka shaliach oseh shlichuso*.

Why then can that *chazaka* not resolve the present case? The Gemara answers: *hani mili l'chumra* — the *chazaka* is applied strictly, to create prohibitions. *Aval l'kula lo* — we do not invoke it leniently, to permit a woman to remarry. Presuming the *shaliach* delivered the *get* would mean permitting the woman as a divorced woman, and for that leniency one cannot rely on presumption alone.

### Woman's Chazaka

The Gemara then asks: why not believe the woman herself? Rav Hamnuna taught: a woman who says to her husband "you divorced me" is believed, on the basis of a *chazaka* — *ein isha me'izah paneiha bifnei ba'alah*, a woman would not be so brazen as to lie to her husband's face about something of this magnitude unless it were true. This is a striking ruling: after establishing that a very high standard of proof is required at every stage of this chain, the Gemara now considers whether a single *chazaka* about human behavior can replace all of that.

### Witness Synthesis

The Gemara resolves the tension. Rav Hamnuna's *chazaka* applies only when there is nothing that supports her claim — when she stands entirely alone in her assertion, she is presumed to be telling the truth because brazenness without any corroboration is implausible. But here, the *shaliach* is backing up her account, and the husband himself does not know whether the delivery actually occurred. Given that backdrop, she is not without support, and therefore it would not take unusual brazenness for her to make a false claim under these circumstances. The *chazaka* therefore does not apply.

This brings the discussion back to the *Mishnah*: witnesses are essential precisely in cases where neither the *shaliach* nor the woman holds the *get*, and neither has the special credibility that would otherwise come with possession of the document. The witnesses serve two functions simultaneously: they provide the objective evidence that the chain of *shlichus* was properly established and executed, and — depending on the position one holds regarding *edei kiyum* — they may also constitute the required witnessing of the act of *gerushin* itself. When the *get* is in someone's hands, that physical presence may supply some of what the witnesses would otherwise need to cover. When it is not — when the *get* has been torn, lost, or is otherwise unavailable — witnesses become indispensable to the entire construct.

---

## Minor Girl & Father

### Naara Me'urasa Status

The next *Mishnah* addresses a case of pre-assigned *shlichus* that arises naturally from a particular legal status. The subject is a *naara me'urasa* — a girl who is betrothed and who has reached the age of twelve but is not yet twelve and a half, and therefore has not yet achieved the status of *bogeres*. During this window, she is legally an adult in certain respects, yet her father retains authority over her. She is simultaneously *me'urasa* — betrothed — and still under paternal control. The reason the *Mishnah* focuses on this specific category is that it requires all three conditions at once: she must be an adult (*naara*), she must be under her father's authority, and she must be in a state of marriage from which a *get* is required. A *nesua* — one who has entered *chuppah* — would be fully out of her father's control and is therefore outside this particular category.

### Get Reception Authority

The *Mishnah* states: *hi v'aviha mekablin et gittah* — she and her father can receive her *get*. Both represent her interests. But Rav Yehuda rules: *ein shtei yadayim zachot ke'achat* — two hands cannot acquire simultaneously. The question then is whose hand prevails. Rav Yehuda rules: *aviha mekabel et gittah bilvad* — the father alone receives her *get*. Where the father is present, his authority is dominant, and the *get* must be given to him rather than to her.

The *Mishnah* then adds a general principle: *ve-chol she-eina yechola lishmor et gittah eina yechola l'hitgareish* — any woman who cannot safeguard her own *get* cannot be divorced.

### Rashi vs. Tosafot: Understanding Divorce

Rashi and Tosafot dispute the meaning of this principle. Rashi understands it to mean that even when the father receives the *get*, if the child is so young that she does not understand what *gerushin* means — if she cannot grasp that she is divorced and act accordingly, described in the Gemara with the phrase *meshaleches v'eina chozeres*, that she goes away and does not return the next day thinking nothing has changed — then the *get* cannot effect a divorce even through the father's reception. Rashi requires a minimal level of comprehension on the girl's part as a condition of the *gerushin* taking effect, even if she is not the one receiving it.

Tosafot disagrees. Tosafot argues that the issue of understanding pertains only to the act of reception by the girl herself. If the *get* is given to the father, it is entirely irrelevant how young or uncomprehending the girl is. After all, the Talmud elsewhere permits a father to betroth his daughter when she is extremely young — if one can be married off as an infant, one can presumably be divorced under the same conditions. For Tosafot, *yoda'at lishmor gittah* is a condition for when the girl herself receives the *get*, not for when the father does so on her behalf.

### Torah's Extra Hand Debate

The Gemara asks: what is the underlying dispute between the *Rabbanan* who say *hi v'aviha* and Rabbi Yehuda who says only the father? The *Rabbanan* hold *yadi yeseira zachei lah Rachmana* — the Torah granted her an extra hand. That is, the Torah provided her with her own independent capacity to receive the *get* in addition to, not instead of, the father's authority. Both hands are available. Rabbi Yehuda holds: *bimkom aviha yadah dilah lav klum hi* — when the father is present, her hand is nullified entirely. His authority does not merely supplement hers; it displaces it. She has no standing of her own as a recipient when her father is there to act on her behalf.

Tosafot raises a further dimension of this dispute: even regarding when the girl can receive the *get* on her own — either when there is no father or in a case where one might give it to her — when precisely does that right begin? Tosafot's view is that even as a *ketana*, she may receive a *get*, because receiving a *get* is a passive act requiring no legal capacity to transact. The point about *naara* is therefore not that she newly acquires this right upon reaching twelve; rather, it highlights that even once she becomes a *naara* and the father's authority would otherwise persist, the status of *naara* does not remove the father from the picture. We will continue with this discussion in the next session.

---

---

# Gittin 65

## Shlichus & Na'arah

### Father as Shaliach

The daf begins in the middle of 64b with the phrase *v'chol she'eina yachola lishmor gita* — any girl who cannot watch her own *get* cannot be divorced. To situate this discussion, we must recall the context: the Gemara is exploring the concept of *shlichus*, specifically the automatic or permanent *shaliach* that the Torah assigns to a father to represent his minor daughter. The Mishnah addresses the case of a *na'arah me'orasah* — a girl between twelve and twelve-and-a-half years old who is *me'orasah* but not yet *nisuah*. Since she has not yet begun living with her husband, she has not been emancipated from her father's authority. In this intermediate stage, she can receive her own *get* and represent herself, and simultaneously her father can receive the *get* on her behalf, given that he retains legal control over her and is entitled to her benefits during this period.

### Rashi vs. Tosafot

When the girl is a *ketanah* — a minor below the age of twelve — Rashi holds that only her father may receive the *get* on her behalf. Tosafot disagree sharply: even as a *ketanah*, the *get* may always be given to the girl herself. Since she is a passive recipient in the transaction, no *da'as* on her part is required. She always represents herself in this sense.

The practical debate between Rashi and Tosafot becomes sharpest when we examine the Mishnah's statement about *v'chol she'eina yachola lishmor gita*. Rashi reads this as a requirement of status: even if the *get* is given to the father, if the girl herself is so young that she would not understand that she has been divorced, the divorce is ineffective. For Rashi, it is not merely about the physical act of giving the *get* — there must be some comprehension on the part of the girl that she has achieved the status of being divorced.

### Understanding Get

Tosafot's reading is more compelling and will guide the analysis going forward. For Tosafot, *v'chol she'eina yachola lishmor gita* addresses solely the act of giving the *get* to the girl herself: if she does not understand what she has received, the act of delivery to her is meaningless. But if the *get* is given to the father, even a one-day-old infant can be divorced — just as a one-day-old infant can be married through her father's agency. If a girl can acquire the status of marriage at any age through her father, she can equivalently acquire the status of divorce through her father. The only constraint is whether giving the *get* to the girl herself constitutes a valid act of reception. Tosafot thus explains the Mishnah as speaking about cases where the *get* is delivered directly to the girl.

Under this reading, the phrase emphasizes whether she understands the physical object she has been given and appreciates its significance. It is not about the status of being divorced — that can happen regardless — it is about whether giving the *get* to her constitutes a legally meaningful delivery.

### Ketanah Yoda'at

The Gemara cites a *Tannaic baraita*: *ketanah yoda'at lishmor gita* — a minor who knows how to watch her *get* — *mitgareshet*, she can be divorced. *V'she'eina yoda'at lishmor gita* — if she does not know how to watch her *get* — *eina mitgareshet*, she cannot be divorced. The *baraita* then asks: what constitutes knowing how to watch her *get*? The answer given is: *kol she'meshameres gita v'davar acher* — whoever watches her *get* and something else.

Rabbi Yochanan clarifies this cryptic phrase: *kol she'meshameres davar acher machmat gita* — she watches something else on account of her *get*. Rashi explains that even if she loses her *get*, she has held onto another object in its place — a book, for instance — because she understood the *get* was something important. She grasps that it is a significant item even if she substitutes another object for it.

### Distinguishing Objects

Rav Huna bar Manoach rejects Rashi's reading forcefully: *ha shotah b'alma hi* — such a girl is essentially an imbecile! If she confuses a book with her *get* merely because she knows the *get* is important, that is hardly a relevant standard of knowledge. Accordingly, Rav Huna bar Manoach, citing Rav Acha the son of Rav Ika, reverses the reading: *kol she'mavchenes bein gita v'davar acher* — the girl who understands the *difference* between her *get* and something else. This means that if someone says to her, "Give me the *get*, I'll give you a different piece of paper in exchange," she refuses, insisting that her *get* is important and she must hold onto it specifically. It is not merely that she can watch the *get* as a physical object; she understands its unique importance and will not accept a substitute. This is the level of knowledge required for a valid delivery of the *get* to her directly.

---

## Minor Development

### Tzror & Egoz

Having established that intellectual development is a determining factor in whether a *get* given to a minor constitutes a valid act, the Gemara transitions to a broader discussion of levels of intellectual development in minors as they pertain to transactions and acquisitions generally. The first stage is described by the phrase *tzror v'zorko egoz v'notlo*: if a child finds a pebble and throws it away, but finds a nut and keeps it, the child has demonstrated an understanding of differential value. The pebble is worthless to him; the nut is something he wants to hold. He recognizes that not all objects are equivalent.

### Self vs. Others

At this first stage, the Gemara rules: *zocheh l'atzmo v'ein zocheh l'acherim* — the minor can acquire for himself but not on behalf of others. Rabbinically, once a child understands the difference between a pebble and a nut — a fairly young age — he can take possession of an object given to him. This is a rabbinic institution; a minor cannot take *de'oraita* possession until adulthood. Nevertheless, the Rabbis recognized this capacity and validated it. The rationale is that when someone gives the child an object, the adult is supplying the necessary *da'as* — the requisite intent to transfer ownership. The child need not himself be the fully competent party who initiates the transaction. He merely needs to do something that physically constitutes a meaningful act of taking — holding the object with some sense of what is occurring. The giver is the one effectuating the transfer. By analogy to *get*: the husband is the one effecting the divorce, but the recipient still needs to perform something that constitutes a meaningful reception.

At this stage, however, the minor cannot take possession on behalf of someone else. That requires a substantially higher level of *da'as*.

### Da'as Acheret

The case of *da'as acheret makneh oso* — another party providing the requisite intent — is relevant here. When you give the minor an object, you are the source of *da'as*. But for the minor to acquire on behalf of a third party, the minor would need to function as a conduit through which your intent reaches that third party. The minor would need to hold not only his own understanding but to represent another's interests — something beyond his current capacity.

---

## Minor Development (II)

### Object Permanence

The Gemara introduces a second and more advanced stage: *chefetz u'machziro l'achar sha'ah* — if you give the minor an object and an hour later ask him to return it, and he can retrieve it for you. This reflects something akin to object permanence: the child retains a mental representation of the object beyond the immediate present moment. He does not forget about it; he can locate it after an interval of time. This suggests a more developed cognitive capacity than the simple immediate recognition of the first stage.

At this stage, the Gemara rules: *zocheh bein l'atzmo bein l'acherim* — the minor can acquire both for himself and on behalf of others. Because the child has demonstrated an understanding that extends beyond the here-and-now, there is enough comprehension to serve as a vehicle through which another person takes possession when that other person is supplying the *da'as*.

### De'oraita Status

The question arises whether this capacity operates on a *de'oraita* level. Tosafot raises the issue: since it is the adult providing the *da'as* — similar to the *get* scenario, where the husband is the one effecting the divorce — perhaps even these rabbinic capacities of the minor could function on a *de'oraita* level. In general, however, the assumption is that all of this operates rabbinically. This is debated among the Rishonim. As will be seen, the Gemara's subsequent discussion will illuminate what the default assumption is and why.

---

## Rava's Gimmel Midot

### Stage Two

The Gemara records that when this analysis was presented before Shmuel, he responded: *da veda achat hi* — this and that are the same *halacha*. Rav Chisda explains: *echad zeh ve'echad zeh zocheh l'atzmo ve'ein zocheh l'acherim* — in both the first stage and the second stage, the minor can only acquire for himself; neither stage permits acquiring on behalf of others. Even the capacity to return an object after an interval does not elevate the minor to the status where his taking possession on behalf of a third party is meaningful, according to Shmuel as understood by Rav Chisda.

---

## Possession & Shituf

### Rav Chanina Challenge

Rav Chanina of Vardan challenges this ruling from a *baraita* concerning *shituf mavoi* — the joint acquisition used to create an *eiruv* for a shared alleyway.

### Shituf Mavo'ot

The *baraita* asks: *keitzad mishtatfin bemavoi* — how does one perform *shituf* of a *mavoi*? The answer is that one takes a barrel of wine (or another food), declares it to be for all the residents of the *mavoi*, and transfers possession of it to everyone through an intermediary. Specifically, the *baraita* lists the valid intermediaries: through one's adult son or daughter (*bno u'vito hagedolim*), or through one's Hebrew male or female slave (*avdo v'shifchato ha'ivrim*).

The Gemara immediately questions the case of the Hebrew female servant: *hai shifcha heichi dami* — what is the case of this maidservant? If she has already developed *shtei se'arot* — the two pubic hairs that mark puberty, typically around age twelve — she should already have been freed, since that is when a *shifchah ivriyah* goes free. It must therefore be that she does not yet have those signs of maturity — meaning she is a minor. Yet the *baraita* states that she can take possession on behalf of all the residents of the *mavoi*. This directly contradicts the position that a minor cannot acquire on behalf of others, even at the more advanced stage of *chefetz u'machziro*.

This challenge applies against Shmuel's understanding that *da veda achat hi* — that both stages only permit acquisition for oneself. Here is a minor girl taking possession for others.

### Derabbanan Pattern

The Gemara answers on behalf of Rav Chisda: *shani shitufei mavo'os derabbanan* — *shituf mavoi* is a rabbinic institution, and therefore the rules that apply to it need not mirror the *de'oraita* rules for acquisition. Because it is entirely a rabbinic creation, the Rabbis may permit a minor to serve as the acquiring agent even for others, in a context where the underlying institution itself has no *de'oraita* analog.

Rav Chisda reports that Rav Chanina of Vardan was silenced — *ishtik Vardan* — by this response. Yet the Gemara wonders what he should have said, implying his original question had force. His response could have been: *kol detikkun rabbanan ke'ein d'oraisa tikkun* — everything the Rabbis enacted is patterned after *de'oraita* law. If the Rabbis permitted it in *shituf mavoi*, it is because in general minors can acquire for others, and the Rabbis were following that principle.

The Gemara then articulates the counter-response that would defeat this rejoinder: *ke'ein d'oraisa tikkun* applies only when the rabbinic institution has a *de'oraita* root — *bemilta de'is lah ikar min haTorah*. When a rabbinic institution is built from whole cloth — *milta deleis lah ikar min haTorah* — as *shituf mavo'os* is, we cannot infer from it that the Rabbis were tracking a *de'oraita* principle. The case of, say, chicken and milk being rabbinic is modeled after the *de'oraita* prohibition of meat and milk; one can infer from the rabbinic extension that it tracks the original. But *shituf mavo'os* has no *de'oraita* analog at all, so we cannot use it as proof for *de'oraita* capacity.

Crucially, this entire exchange implies something significant: the premise throughout the Gemara seems to be that when an adult provides the *da'as* and gives an object to a minor, the minor can take possession even on a *de'oraita* level. The dispute is specifically about whether the minor can then serve as an agent for a third party. This point is not as obvious as it might appear, and it is noted as being debated among the Rishonim.

### Ma'aser Pidyon

The Gemara introduces a second challenge, this time concerning *ma'aser sheni*. The context involves a practice the Gemara terms *ma'arimin al ma'aser sheni* — "scheming" with respect to *ma'aser sheni*. When a person redeems his own *ma'aser sheni* onto coins, he is required to add a *chomesh* — the additional fifth (which in practice equals 25%, since the additional quarter becomes a fifth of the total). This obligation to add a *chomesh* applies only when the owner himself redeems his own *ma'aser sheni*. If, however, a different person redeems it — using his own money — no *chomesh* is required.

The *baraita* describes the permitted maneuver: one says to his adult son or daughter, or to his Hebrew male or female slave, *hei lachem ma'ot halalu* — here, I am giving you this money as a gift. It is now yours. You then use it to redeem my *ma'aser sheni*. Since they are now the owners of the money, and they are the ones performing the redemption, no *chomesh* is required.

The Gemara again asks: *hai shifcha heichi dami* — what is the case of this Hebrew maidservant? If she has already reached adulthood, she is no longer a *shifchah*. She must therefore be a minor. And yet here she is performing an act of *pidyon ma'aser sheni* — redeeming *ma'aser sheni* — which is not merely an act of taking possession on behalf of others; it is an independent legal act. This is an even stronger challenge.

### Tosafot Problem

Tosafot raises a pointed difficulty: in what sense does any analogy to acquisition on behalf of others — *zocheh l'acherim* — apply here? When we discussed acquiring for others, the model was that an adult provides the *da'as* and the minor serves as a conduit. But here, the minor herself is the active party. She owns the money (which was given to her) and she herself is performing the *pidyon*. There is no *da'as acheret makneh* at work — no external adult is supplying the intent. She is fully the agent of the transaction. Moreover, Tosafot notes, in general one requires adult status to perform *pidyon ma'aser sheni*. How, then, can a minor do it at all?

### Hafla'ah Theory

Tosafot resolves this through the principle of *mufla samuch l'ish* — the halacha that in the year before a minor reaches *bar mitzvah* or *bat mitzvah* (a twelve-year-old girl or a thirteen-year-old boy), his or her verbal declarations that change status — *nedarim* and *hekdesh* — take effect. This is a *de'oraita* principle. Now, how do we characterize *pidyon ma'aser sheni*? Is it a transaction — a *kinyan* — in which the owner of the *ma'aser sheni* acquires the coins in exchange for the food? Or is it more like *hafla'ah* — a verbal declaration that transfers a status? One might argue that the minor is not "buying" anything; she is merely transferring the *kedusha* from the fruit to the coin. It is not a *kinyan* of an object she did not previously own; it is a transfer of a sanctified status from one substrate to another. If we view *pidyon* as analogous to *hekdesh*, then just as a minor in the year before *bar/bat mitzvah* can consecrate objects through verbal declaration, she might also be able to transfer the sanctity of *ma'aser sheni* from fruit to coin.

The connection to the broader discussion of minors acquiring on behalf of others remains somewhat unclear even according to Tosafot — but the Gemara plainly treats the case as relevant.

The Gemara's response to the challenge is, once again: *hacha bemai askinan b'ma'aser b'zman hazeh d'rabbanan* — this is discussing *ma'aser sheni* in our era, which is only rabbinically obligatory. And the institution of the Hebrew maidservant (*amah ivriyah*) no longer applies at all in the present day, since *ein eved ivri noheg ella b'zman she'hayovel noheg* — the entire institution of Hebrew slaves operates only when *Yovel* is observed, and *Yovel* requires the Jewish people to be settled in the Land. So neither of these cases establishes that a minor can perform such acts when *de'oraita* stakes are involved. The Gemara thus successfully brackets each challenge as involving only rabbinic law, leaving open the question of the *de'oraita* position.

---

## Rava's Gimmel Midot (II)

### Stage One

With the preceding analyses as background, the Gemara now presents Rava's famous tripartite summary: *amar Rava gimmel middos b'katan* — Rava said there are three stages in the development of a minor's legal capacities. The first corresponds to *tzror v'zorko egoz v'notlo*: once a child recognizes that a pebble is worthless but a nut has value, he can take possession for himself — *zocheh l'atzmo v'ein zocheh l'acherim*.

### Girl's Stage One

Rava's formulation then turns to the female parallel: *v'knegedan b'ktana* — the corresponding stage for a girl. The male stage involves a child's recognition of differential value among objects. For a girl, the corresponding legal institution is *miskadeshes l'miyun* — she can be betrothed for the purpose of *miyun*. This requires explanation. By Torah law, only a father may betroth his minor daughter; if the father is deceased, the Torah provides no mechanism. The Rabbis enacted that when there is no father, the mother and brothers may arrange the girl's betrothal. Because this is a rabbinic institution, the girl may subsequently annul it through *miyun* — an informal verbal rejection, without the need for a *get*. At what age can this take effect? The girl must be old enough that if she were given the *kesef kiddushin*, she would understand that she received something of value. Rashi notes this is the capacity to preserve *kiddushin* the same way she preserves any other object of value — *kol tinokes she'eina yechola lishmor kiddusheha* — if she cannot protect the money of her betrothal, the betrothal enacted by the mother and brothers is not operative even rabbinically. Once she can, it is effective, and since it is only rabbinic, she retains the right of *miyun* to walk away.

Rashi goes further and says that at this stage, not only can the mother and brothers betroth her — if she is a complete orphan, she herself can accept the *kiddushin*. This is a remarkable position, though understandable in light of the desperate social realities that Tosafot elsewhere describes: the frequency of death and tragedy in medieval life was such that children required protection through betrothal arrangements as early as possible.

### Pautot Age

The second stage in Rava's scheme corresponds to *hapautot* — the age range of roughly six to nine years old — at which Rabbinic law permits minors to engage in buying and selling of movable goods (*mikach u'mimkar b'mitaltelin*, not land). The Gemara says this is permitted *kedei chayeihem* — to enable them to manage basic daily life. For a girl, the corresponding legal capacity is *miskadeshes b'kiddushei aviha* — she is old enough that if her father betroth her, it is a fully valid *de'oraita* betrothal. And crucially, this is the age that is the threshold for *yoda'at lishmor et gita* — knowing how to watch her *get*. The distinction here is illuminating: *yoda'at lishmor et kiddusheha* — knowing how to watch money of *kiddushin* — requires only that she recognizes physical value. But *yoda'at lishmor et gita* requires that she understand the *get* as an abstract symbol of a changed legal status. The *get* does not have intrinsic monetary value; its significance is conceptual. Therefore, understanding a *get* requires a more developed level of cognition than understanding a coin. The *pautot* age is when this higher threshold is reached.

### Stage Three

The third stage is *higi'u l'onas nedarim* — when minors reach the year before *bar* or *bat mitzvah* (a twelve-year-old girl, a thirteen-year-old boy). At this point, *nidra neder hekdesha hekdesh* — their vows take effect and their acts of *hekdesh* are binding. For a girl, the corresponding capacity is *choletzes* — she may perform *chalitza*. Tosafot notes that there is a Talmudic opinion that a woman performing *chalitza* need not be an adult, even if the man must be; this stage follows that view.

### Land Sale Limit

Rava adds a special rule regarding the sale of land inherited from one's father: *ul'makor b'nichsei aviv ad sheyehei ben esrim* — even after a boy reaches *bar mitzvah* at thirteen and is fully an adult, the Rabbis did not recognize the sale of inherited land as valid until he reached twenty. The concern was that a young man of thirteen, even legally an adult, lacked the life experience and judgment necessary to appreciate the full consequences of selling real property. Given that selling land was among the most consequential financial transactions possible, the Rabbis delayed full competence for this specific act until age twenty, regardless of *bar mitzvah* status.

---

## Minor Shaliach

### Location Conditions

The Mishnah presents the case of someone who says to his *shaliach*: *ten get l'ishti b'makom ploni* — give this *get* to my wife in a specific location — and the *shaliach* delivers it to her in a different location. The *get* is invalid, because the husband appointed him a *shaliach* specifically for that place, and outside that place the appointment does not hold.

### No Shaliach Power

The Mishnah then states: *ketanah she'amra hitkabel li giti eino get ad sheyagiya l'yadah* — a *ketanah* who said "accept my *get* for me" — this is not a valid *get* until it reaches her hand directly. The reason is that a minor cannot appoint a *shaliach*. If she attempts to appoint someone to receive her *get*, her attempt is legally ineffective. What happens instead is that when the husband gives the *get* to the agent, the husband has implicitly made that agent a *shaliach* for delivery (*shaliach holachah*). The *get* will only take effect when the agent delivers it to her hand. Since she cannot appoint a *shaliach*, the agent was never her representative — and the husband can retract his delivery *shaliach* at any point before the *get* reaches the wife. As the Mishnah states: *she'ein katan oseh shaliach* — a minor cannot create a *shaliach*.

### Father Appoints

If, however, the father says to an agent, *tzei v'hitkabel l'biti gita* — go and accept the *get* for my daughter — the father's appointment is valid. The father, who does legally represent his minor daughter, can appoint a *shaliach* to receive the *get* on her behalf. Once the husband gives the *get* to this agent, *im ratza lachazor lo yachazor* — the husband may not retract, because the father has validly appointed the agent as the daughter's representative for *kabbalah* (reception), and the *get* takes effect upon delivery to the agent.

---

## Place Conditions (III)

### Mar'eh vs. Hakpid

The Mishnah distinguishes between two types of location specifications in the context of *shlichus* for a *get*. When the husband says to his *shaliach*, *ten get l'ishti b'makom ploni* — give the *get* to my wife in a specific place — and the agent delivers it in a different place, the *get* is invalid. The husband specified the place, and we read that specification as a *hakpadah* — a genuine restriction on the terms of the *shlichus*. By contrast, if the husband says *harei hi b'makom ploni* — "she can be found at such-and-such a place" — and the agent delivers it elsewhere, the *get* is valid. Here the husband was merely offering logistical guidance — pointing the *shaliach* toward where to find his wife — not conditioning the *get* on a specific location.

The Mishnah then addresses the parallel case where the wife specifies a location: *ha'isha she'amra hitkabel li giti b'makom ploni* — a woman who said "accept my *get* for me in a specific place." If the agent receives it elsewhere, according to the *Rabbanam* the *get* is invalid. Rabbi Eliezer, however, validates the *get*. The disagreement concerns how to read the woman's specification of a place.

### Rashi's Logic

The Gemara asks: why does Rabbi Eliezer rule differently when it is the wife who specifies a location, compared to when it is the husband? The answer articulates the fundamental asymmetry: *ihu d'midaiteih megareish, kapid* — the husband, who is initiating the divorce entirely of his own will, can genuinely restrict the terms under which his *shaliach* operates. He can say: I only want to divorce her here. *Ihee d'al karchah migareshet* — she is being divorced against her will and cannot control the circumstances. Therefore, when she names a location, she is merely being *mareh makom* — pointing the *shaliach* toward where he can find her husband — not imposing a genuine condition.

Rashi elaborates the precise logic. Since the wife is appointing a *shaliach* and must presumably want the *get* to happen (otherwise, why appoint anyone?), she cannot realistically condition her appointment on a specific location, because the husband may simply refuse to cooperate there. The husband is the one with ultimate control over whether and where the *get* is given. Once we presume that the wife wants to be divorced — which her appointment of a *shaliach* demonstrates — we conclude that any location she names is guidance, not restriction. She cannot genuinely restrict it to one location because she cannot compel the husband to comply. Therefore, the *Rabbanam* read her specification as *hakpadah* while Rabbi Eliezer reads it as *mareh makom*.

This analysis is worth pausing over. One might argue that this is precisely the moment when a woman has actual agency: she is the one appointing the *shaliach*, and she can define the terms of her appointment. If she says "only accept it here," why should we ignore that because she is generally disempowered in *gittin*? Rashi's answer is practical: given that the husband controls whether the *get* happens at all, any condition she imposes is hollow — he can always simply decline to give the *get* in that location. Once she has made a *shaliach* and shown she wants the divorce, we presume she will accept it wherever it is offered.

One might add that in a post-*Cherem d'Rabbeinu Gershom* world, where a wife cannot be divorced against her will, these assumptions might shift — the fundamental asymmetry that drives Rashi's logic is no longer as stark.

---

## Hulkach vs. Kabbalah

### Husband's Hulkach

The distinction between *shaliach l'holachah* and *shaliach l'kabbalah* is clarified through the case introduced in the Mishnah. When the husband says to an agent *holech* — convey this *get* to my wife — he has made the agent a *shaliach* for delivery (*shaliach holachah*). The *get* does not take effect until it reaches the wife's hand.

### Wife's Hulkach

When the wife says to an agent *havei li giti* — bring me my *get* — she is not appointing him as a *shaliach* for *kabbalah* (reception) on her behalf. Rather, as the Gemara understands it through the principle of *holech k'zachi*, the wife is effectively making the agent a *shaliach holachah* for the husband — asking him to go and serve as the husband's delivery agent. The *get* does not take effect until it reaches her hands.

### Terumah Status

This distinction has an immediate practical consequence: if the wife is married to a *kohen*, she eats *terumah* while she is married and must stop once she is divorced. When she says *havei li giti*, since the agent is a *shaliach holachah* and she is not divorced until the *get* reaches her, she continues eating *terumah* until the *get* arrives — *ochelet b'terumah ad sheyagiya get l'yadah*.

---

## Place Conditions (III)

### Woman's Place

However, when she says *hitkabel li giti*, appointing the agent as a *shaliach l'kabbalah*, the moment the husband gives the *get* to the agent she is effectively divorced (since reception by her designated agent equals reception by her). Since she does not know when that moment will arrive, she must immediately stop eating *terumah* — *assur l'echol b'terumah miyad*.

---

## Place Conditions (III)…

### Mixed Places

The Mishnah states that if the wife says *hitkabel li giti b'makom ploni* — accept my *get* for me in a specific place — she may eat *terumah* until the *get* arrives at that place (*ochelet b'terumah ad sheyagiya get l'oto makom*). This phrasing is striking: it says until the *get* arrives at that place, not until the *shaliach* arrives at that place. The Gemara works to clarify this.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is describing a compound case: she says to the *shaliach*, "Accept my *get* for me in *Mata Machasia*, but sometimes you will find my husband in *Bavel*." In other words, she named a primary location but acknowledged that the husband could sometimes be found elsewhere. In such a case, the Gemara understands her to be saying: wherever you find my husband, take the *get* from him — but I do not want it to take effect until you arrive at the named location. The husband may give the *get* to the *shaliach* anywhere, but the *get*'s effect is suspended until the *shaliach* reaches *Mata Machasia*.

### Tosafot Problem

This is a genuinely strange reading, as Tosafot immediately observes. The mechanics are puzzling: the husband hands the *get* to the *shaliach* in *Bavel*, but the *get* does not yet take effect. So in what capacity does the *shaliach* hold the *get* while traveling to *Mata Machasia*? He cannot be the wife's *shaliach l'kabbalah*, since the *get* has already been received but not yet taken effect. Is he then the husband's *shaliach l'holachah*? But the husband gave it to him without making him a *shaliach* for delivery. Tosafot tries to resolve this by suggesting that since the wife stipulated this condition, and the husband plays into it, there is some sense in which the husband effectively delays the operation of the *get*. But how the wife can impose this delay — given that the *da'as* for the *get*'s effect belongs to the husband — remains mechanically unclear.

### Rabbi Eliezer

Rabbi Eliezer rules *oser miyad* — she must stop eating *terumah* immediately — because in his view, when a woman names a location it is merely *mareh makom*: guidance for finding the husband, not a genuine restriction. Since the *get* could be given anywhere at any time, she must stop eating *terumah* from the moment she appoints the *shaliach*. The Gemara adds a refinement: even if the wife told the *shaliach* "go east, you'll find him in the east," and he went west instead, Rabbi Eliezer would still require her to stop eating immediately — because *dilma bahadi deka'azal u'mati gabei*, perhaps as he walked out the door he happened to run into the husband and the *get* was given. Since there is no *halachically* enforceable restriction on where it takes place, there is always a theoretical possibility that it happened immediately.

---

## Eiruv Analogy

### Eiruv Dispute

The Gemara now applies the debate between the *Rabbanam* and Rabbi Eliezer beyond *gittin*, to the domain of *eiruv*. The Mishnah-level rule for *eiruv* involves designating specific food for the purpose. If a person instructs his *shaliach*, "Make my *eiruv* with dates," and the *shaliach* makes it with figs instead, or vice versa, two *beraitot* conflict: one says the *eiruv* is valid, the other says it is not. Rabba resolves this: *ha rabbanan ha Rabbi Elazar* — one *baraita* follows the *Rabbanam*, who read instructions as a *hakpadah* (and thus the *eiruv* with the wrong food is invalid), and the other follows Rabbi Eliezer, who reads instructions as *mareh makom* (and thus the *eiruv* is valid regardless).

### Rava's Synthesis

This suggests that the dispute between the *Rabbanam* and Rabbi Eliezer is not limited to the specific case of a woman appointing a *shaliach* for her *get*, but reflects a general jurisprudential disagreement: when a person specifies a particular detail in giving instructions to a *shaliach*, do we presume that specification is a genuine restriction (*hakpadah*) or merely helpful guidance (*mareh makom*)? The *Rabbanam* default to *hakpadah*; Rabbi Eliezer defaults to *mareh makom* based on contextual reasonableness.

### Rav Yosef

Rav Yosef offers an alternative resolution that avoids invoking the Rabbi Eliezer/*Rabbanam* dispute. He says both conflicting *beraitot* could represent the *Rabbanam*: *kan b'shelo kan b'shel chaveiro* — here we are dealing with the *shaliach*'s own food, and there we are dealing with the sender's food. If I tell a *shaliach* "make an *eiruv* with dates" and I am providing the dates, I am *makpid* about what is used — it is my property and I can restrict it. If, however, the *shaliach* is providing the food from his own stores, then even the *Rabbanam* would say I cannot genuinely be *makpid* about what he uses — I have no right to dictate which of his foods he employs.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye challenges Rav Yosef's framework from another *baraita*: the case where someone instructs his *shaliach* to make an *eiruv* in a tower (*migdal*) and the *shaliach* makes it in a pigeon coop (*shovach*), or the reverse. Again, one *baraita* validates the *eiruv* and one does not. If Rav Yosef's resolution is based on whose food it is, what does that have to do with whether the *eiruv* was made in the tower or the coop? The location of the deposit is not about ownership of food.

### Food Sources

Rav Yosef responds: in this case too, the reference to the *migdal* or *shovach* is not about the physical location of the *eiruv* deposit — it is about the *source* of the food. The *migdal* and the *shovach* are storage locations, and specifying one or the other indicates which stores of food the instruction refers to. "Make the *eiruv* from the tower" means "use the food stored in the tower," and "make it from the pigeon coop" means "use the food stored there." Thus the case is really still about whose food and which specific stores are being designated. If the *shaliach* uses the food from the wrong location, the question is whether the *ba'al* was genuinely restricting which of his stores should be used. Once understood this way, Rav Yosef's framework holds: when it is the sender's food, specification indicates *hakpadah*; when it is the *shaliach*'s food, the *Rabbanam* themselves concede that no *hakpadah* is imposed.

Abaye's own preferred resolution, by contrast, is simpler: the two *beraitot* reflect the straightforward disagreement between the *Rabbanam* and Rabbi Eliezer as general disputants over the presumption of *hakpadah* versus *mareh makom*, without any need to distinguish between whose food is involved.

---

---

# Gittin 66

## Two/Three Person Agency

### Language Assumptions

Today's study begins at the final line of Gittin 66a, where the *mishna* turns to a question that will occupy the bulk of the *daf*: when a husband appoints others to write and deliver a *get*, does his appointment bind those individuals personally, or may they in turn delegate that responsibility to someone else? The *mishna* explores this question through a series of cases distinguished by the number of people addressed and the precise language used.

### Two People Direct Action

The *mishna* opens: *amar lishnayim tnu get l'ishti* — if a husband says to two people, "give a *get* to my wife," and since one cannot give a *get* without first writing it, the instruction to give necessarily implies writing as well. Similarly, if he says to three people *kitvu get utnu l'ishti* — "write a *get* and give it to my wife" — then *harei elu yichtevu veyitnu*: those people themselves must both write and deliver it. They may not hand that responsibility to others.

### Three People/Beit Din

Here, however, the *mishna* introduces an important distinction, and it is precisely this distinction that explains why the *mishna* treats the two-person *tnu* case separately from the three-person *tnu* case. If a husband says to three people *tnu get l'ishti* — "give a *get* to my wife" — without specifying *kitvu*, the word *tnu* alone can plausibly be understood as "take responsibility to see that it is given," rather than as a directive to perform every step personally. When said to only two people, we would not interpret the instruction that way, because two people do not constitute a body that normally supervises and delegates; they would be expected to act themselves. Three people, however, constitute a *beis din*, and a *beis din* can be understood as a supervisory body that need not execute matters directly. Therefore, when a husband tells three people *tnu* without the concrete specification of *kitvu*, the *mishna* rules: *harei elu yomru l'acherim veyichtevu* — they may instruct others to write the *get*. This is because *she'asan beis din* — he has cast them in the role of a *beis din* — and that is the ruling of Rabbi Meir.

The *mishna* adds that this is also the *halacha* brought down by Rabbi Chanina Ish Ono from prison — a transmission from Rabbi Akiva, who was then incarcerated under the Roman decrees: *mekubal ani b'omer lishlosha tnu get l'ishti, yomru l'acherim veyichtevu, mipnei she'asan beis din* — I have received the tradition that when one says to three people "give a *get* to my wife," they may delegate to others, because he has made them a *beis din*.

### Rabbi Yose's View

Rabbi Yose, however, disputes this emphatically. *Nominu l'shaliach* — using an archaic term for "we said to the agent" — he declares: I too have a tradition. And his tradition is that *afillu amar l'beis din hagadol shebirushalayim tnu get l'ishti* — even if one says to the Great Court in Jerusalem, "give a *get* to my wife," since he used the word *tnu* and not *kitvu*, and those justices are obviously a *beis din* and one would never expect them to take out parchment and begin scribing themselves — nevertheless, if this *get* is to be given through this appointment, *she'yilmedu veyichtevu veyitnu*: they themselves must learn how to write a *get* and do it. They may always decline the appointment, but they cannot simply supervise and pass the task to others. *Harei elu yichtevu veyitnu* — it is they who must act.

This is a striking position. Rabbi Yose seems unconcerned with the husband's apparent intent, or at least he holds that whatever one's intent, the words of appointment bind only those who directly received them.

### Ten People Distribution

Shifting to a different scenario, the *mishna* takes up the case where the husband says to ten people *kitvu utnu get l'ishti* — "write a *get* and give it to my wife." Since he specifies *kitvu*, it is clear he does not mean mere supervision; he means they should execute it. How does this work in practice when addressing a group? *Echad kotev ushnayim chotmin* — one person writes, two people sign. The phrase "write and give," addressed to many, means simply: from among you, some combination should accomplish this. One person writes, two sign as witnesses, one delivers.

### Kulhon Requirement

A further case: *kulhon kitvu* — if he explicitly says "all of you write a *get*." Here, *echad kotev v'chulam chotmin* — one person writes and all of them sign. This prompts a question that will recur in the *Gemara*: if all of them must write, how is it that only one person does the actual scribing? The answer the *Gemara* will give is that when the husband says *kulhon*, the requirement is not that each person physically holds the pen, but that all are present while one writes — a kind of representative action, analogous to a *shaliach tzibur* who prays on behalf of the entire congregation. Everyone is present and constitutes the body; one person is the instrument through which the group acts.

### Invalidation by Death

The *mishna* closes this section with a consequential ruling: *im meit echad meihen harei zeh get batel* — if one of the ten dies before the *get* is written and delivered, the *get* is invalid. This flows directly from the husband's demand that all of them be part of the process. What is notable here — and worth pausing over — is how powerfully the husband's *da'at* and *ratzon* shape the very validity of the *get*. One might have assumed that a *get* has a fixed form: a specific text, signed by two witnesses, properly delivered. But in fact the husband controls far more than that. If he specified that ten people must all be involved and that requirement is not fulfilled, the *get* itself is *batel*. His will is not merely a preference; it is constitutive of the document's validity.

---

## Milei/Shaliach Question

### Scribe vs. Witness

The *Gemara* opens with a remarkable historical note: Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba reports that they sent a question *mi'bei Rav l'Shmuel* — from the academy of Rav to Shmuel. The very fact that the students of Rav would send a question to Shmuel is itself striking, given that the two were contemporaries generally regarded as peers.

The question: *amar l'shnayim kitvu utnu get l'ishti, v'amru l'sofer v'chatav v'chatmu hem mahu* — if a husband says to two people "write and give a *get* to my wife," and they do not write it themselves but instead have a *sofer* write it while they sign it as witnesses — what is the *halacha*? The question, at its core, is: when the husband says *kitvu* to these two people, does he mean that they must do the actual scribing, or does *kitvu* mean that they must sign? If it means scribing, they may not have the *sofer* do it. If it means signing, then having the *sofer* write it is merely finding someone to perform a task the husband implicitly left open.

Shmuel's reply: *teitzei v'hadavar tzarich talmud* — if she remarried on the basis of this *get*, she cannot remain with her second husband because the *get* is of questionable validity, but the matter requires further study. It is a *safek get*.

### Shmuel: No Delegation

The *Gemara* now asks: what exactly requires further investigation? One possibility is that the doubt concerns whether they are permitted to pass on their verbal appointment to someone else — the principle of *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach*, that words cannot be delegated to an agent. But this possibility is immediately challenged: *veha'amar Shmuel amar Rav halacha k'Rabbi Yose de'amar mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach* — Shmuel himself rules that we follow Rabbi Yose, who holds that a verbal appointment cannot be passed on. If that is already settled, why is there any doubt?

### Kitvu Meaning Debate

The *Gemara* therefore refocuses: Shmuel's real question is not about delegation but about the meaning of *kitvu* itself. When the husband says to the two people "write it," does he mean *kesav yadan* — that they must sign it — or does he mean *kesav haget* — that they must actually scribe the document? This is the live question.

### Ten-Person Proof

The *Gemara* attempts to resolve this from the *mishna* itself: *amar l'shnayim tnu get l'ishti, o lishlosha kitvu utnu get l'ishti, harei elu yichtevu veyitnu* — when the *mishna* says they must write it, doesn't that clearly mean they must scribe it? The *Gemara* rejects this, noting that the question about the meaning of *kitvu* is precisely what is at issue; the *mishna* cannot serve as its own resolution. More useful is the end of the *mishna*, where in the ten-person case the language *echad kotev ushnayim chotmin* suggests that someone in the group must be the actual scribe — which would imply that *kitvu* does include scribing.

### Signing-Only Rejected

The *Gemara* pushes toward clarification: *pishita dekesav haget hu* — it is obvious that *kitvu* means scribe the document. The proof: the *mishna* cites Rabbi Yose as saying that even the *beis din hagadol* in Jerusalem would have to *she'yilmedu veyichtevu* — learn how to write a *get* and do it themselves. If *kitvu* meant only signing, it would be absurd to say that the Supreme Court might not know how to sign their own names. That they would need to learn how to sign makes no sense; that they might need to learn the technical craft of scribing a *get* is at least intelligible.

The *Gemara* deflects this: *in, ika beis dina chadata* — perhaps it is a newly constituted court whose members have not yet signed anything. This is a forced answer, acknowledged as such, and the question remains live.

### Finding a Scribe

The *Gemara* now restates the issue in its proper form. If *kitvu* means sign — not scribe — then having the *sofer* do the writing is not a case of passing on one's agency (*mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach*); rather, it is a case where the two people are implicitly authorized to find a *sofer*, and their communication to that *sofer* is simply informing him that the husband has appointed him. That is the concept of *omer imru* — the husband is telling the two people, in effect, "tell the *sofer* to write it," meaning the husband is appointing the *sofer* through the intermediary of the two witnesses. The *sofer* has not received a sub-delegated appointment from the witnesses; he has received the husband's appointment, communicated through messengers. The question Shmuel is raising, then, is whether *omer imru* is permissible — and that depends on whether the *sofer* can be validly appointed through intermediaries rather than through direct communication from the husband himself.

---

## Milei vs. Omer Imru

### Milei Principle

The distinction being developed here is fundamental. *Mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach* — words cannot be delegated to an agent — addresses the following situation: I appoint Reuven, and Reuven, rather than performing the task himself, sub-delegates it to Shimon. Reuven has taken his own appointment, his *shlichus*, and attempted to pass it on. The question is whether he has the authority to do that. By a *get*, especially given the centrality of the husband's *da'at* and the verse *v'chasav lah sefer krisus* — "and he shall write for her a bill of divorce" — there are strong grounds to say that the appointment must remain with the original appointee. Reuven cannot make Shimon his substitute.

### Omer Imru Concept

*Omer imru* is a structurally different situation. Here the husband says to Reuven and Shimon: "go tell the *sofer* to write, and go tell Ploni and Ploni to sign." The husband himself is appointing the *sofer* and the witnesses; he is simply using Reuven and Shimon as messengers to communicate that appointment. They are not delegating their own agency; they are transmitting the husband's appointment to third parties. The question is whether this indirect form of appointment — *shlichus shelo befanav*, appointment not made in the presence of the appointee — is valid for a *get*.

---

## Chasam Sofer Issue

### Sofer V'Ed Valid

The *Gemara* now introduces a *mishna* from elsewhere that will generate significant discussion. Rabbi Yirmiyah reports: *chasam sofer shaninu* — the *mishna* speaks of a case where the *sofer* himself signs as one of the witnesses, together with one other witness. That configuration — *chasam sofer v'ed* — is valid.

### Validity Problem

But this raises an immediate difficulty. Rav Chisda states: *matnisin mani Rabbi Yose hi* — that *mishna* follows the position of Rabbi Yose. How so? Because the validity of *chasam sofer v'ed* presupposes that everything was arranged in a particular way, and the question is how that arrangement can be assumed to be legitimate under Rabbi Yose's stringent requirements.

### Embarrassment Scenario

The *Gemara* works through a troubling scenario. Suppose the husband, through *omer imru*, tells two intermediaries: "tell the *sofer* to write it and tell Ploni and Ploni to sign it." The intermediaries go to find the appointed witnesses, but the *sofer* objects — he is embarrassed that he is deemed fit to write the *get* but not fit to sign as a witness. Moved by concern for the *sofer's* dignity (*mishum kisufa d'sofer*), one of the intermediaries makes an adjustment: he has the *sofer* serve as one of the witnesses alongside only one of the originally designated witnesses. *U'va'al lo amar hachi* — but the husband said no such thing. The *get* is therefore *pasul*, yet those who rely on it may not know this and will assume it is *kasher*.

### Shouldn't Do/Valid

This is precisely the concern: if *omer imru* is permissible, one can readily imagine this corruption arising. The *Gemara* responds: *kivan d'amar mar kasher v'lo ta'aseh chen b'Yisrael* — since we rule that *chasam sofer v'ed* is valid but one should never do this in Israel, meaning the *sofer* himself is required to refuse such an arrangement. Since this practice is prohibited and the *sofer* ought not comply, we are not afraid that this scenario will in fact unfold. The prohibition makes the bad outcome sufficiently uncommon that we need not treat it as a standing concern.

### Witness Sign Alternative

But the *Gemara* is not satisfied. A second scenario: suppose the husband directly appoints the witnesses themselves and tells them to sign — he does not use *omer imru* for the witnesses at all — but he simply asks them to find someone to be the *sofer*. They are themselves committed to signing; only the scribing is left open. Now one might think this is clearly acceptable. Yet the same problem can arise: the witnesses, concerned about the *sofer's* feelings, have him sign as a witness instead of one of them — and again the husband never authorized this arrangement.

### Rava's Position

Rava concludes: *ha nami kasher v'lo ta'aseh hu* — this second scenario also falls under the rubric of *kasher v'lo ta'aseh*. One may not do this *lechatchila*, and the *sofer* should refuse to participate as a witness in such a circumstance. Since both scenarios are prohibited, neither presents a practical danger that should lead us to invalidate *chasam sofer v'ed* entirely.

### Rabbi Yose Explains It

At this point the *Gemara* draws a clean conclusion: *Rabbi Yose tarti amar* — Rabbi Yose holds both positions simultaneously. Not only does he hold *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach* — that a verbal appointment cannot be sub-delegated — he also holds that *omer imru* is invalid. No one can represent the husband in the writing, signing, or delivery of a *get* unless that person heard the appointment directly from the husband himself. This dual position is, upon reflection, entirely coherent. When the *mishna* says that even the *beis din hagadol* in Jerusalem must do it themselves, the implicit situation is one where the husband almost certainly intended them to delegate — and yet Rabbi Yose disallows it. This is not only about sub-delegation; it is about the principle that only those who heard directly from the husband can be part of the process. That is *omer imru* logic as much as *mili* logic.

---

## Milei vs. Omer Imru (II)

### Reconciliation

With Rabbi Yose's position now fully articulated, the *Gemara* returns to Shmuel's ruling: *halacha k'Rabbi Yose de'amar mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach*. The question is whether Shmuel adopts Rabbi Yose's position entirely — both *mili* and *omer imru* — or only partially. To understand the answer, it is worth being precise about the conceptual difference between the two principles.

*Mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach* addresses the internal authority of an agent: if I appointed Reuven, does Reuven have the power to take that appointment and transfer it to Shimon? The answer is no — the appointment stays with Reuven. *Omer imru* addresses a different question: can the husband appoint someone who is not in his presence, by having a messenger communicate the appointment? This is the question of *shlichus shelo befanav* — can you create agency in someone who did not directly hear the appointment from the principal?

These are distinct. In the first case, the appointed agent is fully empowered but lacks the authority to transfer his role. In the second case, the question is whether a valid appointment was ever created in the first place.

### Rabbi Yose Both Rules

Rabbi Yose holds that both are prohibited, and this is what makes his position internally consistent and explains the full force of the *mishna's* ruling about the *beis din hagadol*. Even in that case — where the implicit intent seems clearly to delegate — Rabbi Yose says no: the only people who can act are those who directly heard the appointment from the husband. *Mili lo mimsaran* prevents sub-delegation; the *omer imru* prohibition prevents indirect appointment altogether.

### Shmuel's Split

Shmuel, however, splits the difference. *U-Shmuel savar lah kevaseih b'chada u-palig aleih b'chada* — Shmuel agrees with Rabbi Yose on one point and disagrees on the other. Shmuel holds *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach*: if you are the appointed agent, you cannot pass your appointment on. But Shmuel disagrees regarding *omer imru*: the husband may appoint someone through an intermediary. An indirect appointment, where a messenger informs the prospective agent that the husband is appointing him, is valid. The appointee need not hear it directly from the husband himself.

This split is the key that unlocks Shmuel's original question. When the husband says to two people *kitvu utnu get l'ishti*, and Shmuel asks whether *kitvu* means sign or scribe — here is what depends on the answer. If *kitvu* means the actual scribing, then having the *sofer* do it would require them to transfer their own appointment to the *sofer*, which is *mili lo mimsaran*, and Shmuel would rule it invalid. But if *kitvu* means sign, then the husband never appointed these two to scribe at all; he implicitly left the scribing open, to be arranged through them as intermediaries. That is *omer imru*, which Shmuel permits. They are not sub-delegating their appointment; they are communicating the husband's appointment of the *sofer*. Hence the *get* would be valid. Shmuel's uncertainty about whether the *get* is valid — his response of *teitzei v'hadavar tzarich talmud* — reflects precisely his uncertainty about what *kitvu* means in this context.

---

## Lishnayim Agency

### Indirect Appointment

The *Gemara* now takes up a case directly related to *omer imru*. The husband says to two people: *imru l'sofer veyichtov, uleploni ploni veyachtimu* — tell the *sofer* to write it and tell so-and-so and so-and-so to sign it. Here the husband himself is not directly appointing anyone; he is using two intermediaries to communicate all of his appointments. Everything is transmitted indirectly.

### Concern: Bribed Witnesses

Rav Huna says in the name of Rav: *keshera v'lo ta'aseh chen b'Yisrael* — it is valid, but one should not do this in Israel. The *Gemara* asks: if it is valid, why should one not do it? The answer: *chayishinan shema tiskor edim* — we are concerned lest the woman have hired witnesses. If the husband does not directly appoint anyone and instead two intermediaries come to the *sofer* and the prospective witnesses claiming that the husband instructed them, there is no independent verification. Perhaps the woman bribed these two people to fabricate the husband's appointment, enabling the *get* to be written without the husband's genuine consent.

### Trust in Documents

The *Gemara* challenges this concern: is it not true that witnesses who sign a bill of sale or a *get* are trusted, and the Sages have no concern about forgery? *Edim hachatumim al sadeh mekach v'al get ishah, lo chashu chachamim l'davar zeh* — witnesses signed on a deed of sale or on a woman's *get*, the Sages had no such worry.

### Words vs. Writing

The *Gemara* resolves the tension: *ma'aseh lo avdi* — people will not actually forge a document. We are not afraid they will put their names to a fraudulent *get*. But *dibura ka'amri* — spoken messages are another matter. Finding someone willing to pass on a fabricated verbal message, without personally signing anything, is a realistic concern. The two intermediaries are not personally implicated by any written document; they are merely transmitting words. That is where the potential for corruption lies, and that is why the *sofer* and the witnesses should not agree to be appointed through such an indirect chain.

### Witnesses Self-Commit

The *Gemara* then considers a modified scenario: *amar lishnayim imru l'sofer veyichtov v'atem chatomu* — the husband tells the two directly that they themselves will sign, and only asks them to communicate to the *sofer* that he should write the *get*. Here the witnesses are personally committed — they are signing — so there is no concern that the woman hired them. The *sofer* can have confidence that the witnesses' word is genuine, since they are putting their own names on the document.

### Amoraic Dispute

Rav Chisda rules: *keshera v'lo ta'aseh* — even this is valid but should not be done, as a precautionary measure to prevent sliding into the broader prohibited practice. The *Gemara* then records a remarkable range of *Amoraic* opinions. Rabbah bar bar Chana says: *kasher veta'aseh* — it is permitted outright. Rav Nachman: *kasher v'lo ta'aseh*. Rav Sheshet: *kasher veta'aseh*. Rabbah: *kasher v'lo ta'aseh*. Rav Yosef: *kasher veta'aseh*. And the *Gemara* adds that some reverse the attributions to Rabbah and Rav Yosef. What emerges is that in practice we follow Rav Yosef, but the picture is complicated by Shmuel's earlier ruling, which acknowledged *omer imru* as technically valid while the subsequent *Amoraic* discussion introduces pragmatic concerns about reliability that counsel against it even where it would be *bedieved* valid.

---

## Counting Names

### Kulkhem Distinction

The *Gemara* now takes up the *braita* elaborating on the ten-person case from the *mishna*. *Amar l'asarah kitvu get utnu l'ishti, echad kotev al yedei kulam* — if he says to ten people "write a *get* and give it to my wife," one writes on behalf of all. By contrast, *kulchem kitvu* — if he says "all of you write it" — then *echad kotev bema'amad kulam*: one writes but all must be present.

### One Writes Distribution

The same logic applies to delivery. *Holichu get l'ishti, echad molich al yedei kulam* — if he says "bring the *get* to my wife," one person delivers on behalf of all. *Kulchem holichu* — if he specifies all of you — then *echad molich bema'amad kulam*: one delivers, but all must be present.
