The analogy to the *shaliach tzibur* is instructive: just as the prayer leader represents the entire congregation in *tefillat hatzibur* — each member present, one person as the mouthpiece — so here, one person performs the act while all are present as the constitutive body.

### Counting Effect

This leads to a novel question: *mana otan mahu* — if the husband does not say *kulchem* explicitly but instead counts them — one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten — does that counting carry the same legal weight as saying *kulchem*? Does enumerating each person individually signal an intent that all of them must participate, or does it merely mean "from among you"?

### Huna: No Effect

Rav Huna rules: *mana eino ke'kulam* — counting is not equivalent to saying *kulchem*. The counting does not impose the requirement that all must be present.

### Yochanan: Does Mean

Rav Yochanan, citing Rabbi Elazar from Rome, rules: *mana harei hu ke'kulam* — counting is indeed equivalent to *kulchem*. By identifying each person individually, the husband signals that each of them is specifically included and required.

### Papa Resolves

Rav Papa steps in to resolve the dispute: *v'lo pligi* — they do not actually disagree. The distinction is whether the husband counted all the people in the room or only some of them. *Ha d'mana kulhu ha d'mana miktzatayhu* — one ruling applies when he counted everyone present, and the other applies when he counted only some. Which case yields which ruling is itself debated — *amri lah l'hai gisa v'amri lah l'hai gisa* — with some holding that counting everyone means *kulchem* and counting some means "from among you," while others hold the reverse. The underlying logic in each direction is not entirely transparent, but the operative distinction is whether the counting was exhaustive or selective.

---

## Takanah for Formula

### Fixed Nusach

Rav Yehuda instituted a *takanah* to address the practical hazards created by the *kulchem* requirement. He established a fixed *nusach* — a standard formula — for the husband to use when appointing agents to write and deliver a *get*. The formula: *ktovu o kulchem o kol chad v'chad minchon, chatomu shtein o kulchem o kol trei minchon, ovilu o kulchem o kol chad v'chad minchon* — write it, whether all of you or any one of you; sign it, whether all of you or any two of you; deliver it, whether all of you or any one of you. By explicitly including the alternative of any individual, the formula ensures that the *get* will not be invalidated by the death or absence of one of the appointees.

### Rava's Caution

Rava raises a concern with this formula. *Lo zimnin degayiz lei l'diburei, v'omar kulchem v'lo amar kol chad v'chad minchon* — it sometimes happens that a person will cut off what he is saying and will say *kulchem* without completing the rest of the formula. If the husband says "all of you" and fails to add "or any one of you," the *get* will become *pasul*.

### Better Wording

Rava therefore proposes an alternative: do not begin with *kulchem* at all. *Ktovu kol chad minchon, chatomu kol trei minchon, ovilu kol chad minchon* — simply establish a text that opens with "any one of you" and does not introduce *kulchem* in the first place. If the formula never raises the problem of an all-inclusive requirement, there is no risk that the husband will inadvertently impose one. The word *kulchem* is the source of the difficulty; the better practice is to teach people a formula that avoids it entirely.

---

---

# Gittin 66b

## Multiple Messengers

### Two People: Write & Deli…

The present daf picks up with the final line of 66a, continuing the *mishna*'s discussion of the language a husband uses when appointing a *shaliach* and the scope of the word *kitvu*. The next *mishna* turns to a related but distinct issue: whether the individuals whom the husband has appointed must carry out the task personally, or whether they may delegate that responsibility to others.

The *mishna* opens with two cases. If the husband says to two people, *tnu get l'ishti* — give a *get* to my wife — then since *tnu* implies giving but necessarily also writing, the two must themselves carry out both actions. Similarly, if he says to three people, *kitvu get u'tnu l'ishti* — write a *get* and give it to my wife — then *harei elu yichtevu v'yitnu*: it must be precisely those individuals who do it.

### Three People: Delivery O…

There is, however, an important exception. If the husband says to three people, *tnu get l'ishti* — give a *get* to my wife — without specifying *kitvu*, then those three may in turn instruct others to write it: *harei elu yomru l'acherim v'yichtevu*. The *mishna* explains: *mipnei she'asah beis din* — because he has constituted them as a *beis din* — and this is *divrei Rebbi Meir*.

The distinction between two and three people rests on a conceptual difference in what a group of that size represents. Two people are not a constituted body; they are simply the individuals appointed, and the expectation is that they themselves perform the task. Three people, by contrast, constitute a *beis din*, and a *beis din* is understood as a supervisory body — one that takes responsibility for seeing that something is done, not necessarily one that performs every action directly. Accordingly, when the husband says *kitvu u'tnu* explicitly to a group of three, he is being concrete about the actions and means that they themselves must perform them. But when he says only *tnu* to three, the word is understood as conveying oversight and administrative authority, which they may then delegate.

### Beit Din Authority

The *mishna* adds that this ruling was transmitted by Rebbi Chanina ish Ono from prison — and Rashi explains that this means in the name of Rebbi Akiva, who was imprisoned at the time due to the Roman decrees. The report states: *mekubal ani b'omer lishlosha tnu get l'ishti sheyomru l'acherim v'yichtevu mipnei she'asah beis din* — I have a tradition that when one says to three people "give a *get* to my wife," they may transmit that to others, because he has made them a *beis din*.

### Rabbi Yosi's Tradition

Rebbi Yosi responds with a counter-tradition. *Af anu mekubalim* — we too have a received tradition — and his tradition is far more demanding. Even if the husband says *tnu get l'ishti* to the *beis din hagadol sheb'Yerushalayim* — the Great Court of Jerusalem itself — and says only *tnu* without *kitvu*, those distinguished jurists cannot delegate the task. If they wish to give the *get*, *sheyilmedu v'yichtevu v'yitnu* — they must learn how to write a *get* and write it themselves. The appointment, according to Rebbi Yosi, is non-transferable; only the individuals who heard the instruction directly from the husband may execute it.

### Ten People: Role Distrib…

The *mishna* then turns to a different scenario: the husband says to ten people, *kitvu get u'tnu l'ishti*. Since he has said *kitvu* explicitly, he cannot have meant mere oversight; he means they themselves should act. But how is that interpreted when there are more than the minimum number of required participants? The *mishna* rules: *echad kotev u'shnayim chotmim* — one writes it and two sign it. The word *kitvu* addressed to the group does not mean all ten must write and all ten must sign; it means that from among you, the necessary actions must be performed.

### Kulchem: All Present

If, however, the husband says *kulchem kitvu* — all of you write — then *echad kotev v'chulam chotmim*: one writes and they all sign. The word *kulchem* changes the character of the instruction.

### Kitvu: Write or Sign

At this point the *mishna* raises — or at least invites — the question that the *Gemara* will pursue explicitly: what is the primary meaning of the word *kitvu* in this context? Does it refer to the scribing of the *get*, or to signing it? It would seem from the *mishna* that signing is the more fundamental referent, since in the case of *kulchem kitvu* addressed to ten people, only one person actually scribes the document while all of them sign. The *mishna* is evidently not troubled by the fact that not all ten physically write the text. Rather, it seems to be the signing that constitutes the operative meaning of *kitvu* — or at least that signing is its core dimension. One might instead argue that even if *kitvu* also encompasses the scribing, the *mishna* interprets it practically: for the scribing, it suffices that one person writes on behalf of all, whereas for the signing, each must affix his own signature. The *Gemara* will analyze this more carefully.

### Death Invalidates Get

Finally, the *mishna* states: *im mes echad mehem harei zeh get batel* — if one of the group dies after the husband said *kulchem*, the *get* is invalid. This is striking, and worth pausing over. One might have thought that a *get* has a fixed form and fixed requirements — a particular text, two witnesses — and it would not be obvious how the husband's specifications could render an otherwise valid *get* invalid. But what we see here is how central the husband's *da'at* and *ratzon* are to the very nature of the *get*. The husband has shaped the conditions of his own *get*, and if those conditions are not fulfilled — if he required everyone's participation and one of them dies — then the *get* has not been executed according to his will, and it is therefore *batel*. The *get*'s validity is inseparable from the husband's intent as to how it is to be produced.

---

## Kitvu Meaning Debate

### Rav's Question to Shmuel

The *Gemara* opens with a remarkable report: *shalechu mibei Rav l'Shmuel* — they sent from the *yeshiva* of Rav to Shmuel. This is itself a striking phenomenon, since Rav and Shmuel were contemporaries of roughly equal stature, and yet the scholars of Rav's academy directed this question to Shmuel. The question they sent was: *amar l'shnayim kitvu u'tnu get l'ishti v'amru l'sofer v'chatav v'chatmu hem mahu* — if the husband said to two people "write and give a *get* to my wife," and they did not scribe it themselves but instead had a *sofer* write it while they themselves signed, what is the *halacha*?

The question is fundamentally about the meaning of *kitvu*. The two individuals were appointed, they signed the document, but the actual scribing was done by someone else. Does the husband's instruction *kitvu* require that they personally scribe the *get*, or does it require only that they sign it? If *kitvu* means scribing, then having the *sofer* do the scribing violates the husband's instruction. If *kitvu* means signing, then the two have fully complied.

### Shmuel: Needs Investigat…

Shmuel's response was: *tetzei v'hadavar tzarich talmud* — if she remarried on the basis of this *get*, she cannot remain with her second husband, because the *get* is of uncertain validity; but the matter requires further investigation. Shmuel was genuinely uncertain, and the *Gemara* now sets out to determine what the core of the investigation must be.

### Words & Delegation

The *Gemara* asks: what exactly is the issue Shmuel identified as requiring investigation? One possibility is that the question is whether *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach* — whether words, meaning a purely verbal appointment, can be passed on to another agent. This principle, which will be central to much of the remainder of the *daf*, holds that when an agency involves no physical object, only a verbal appointment, the agent may not delegate that agency to a further agent. When the husband gives the *shaliach* the physical *get* to deliver to the wife, the physical object in some sense represents and carries the agency. But the appointment of the *sofer* to write a *get* — before the *get* even exists — is purely verbal, and the question is whether that verbal appointment can be passed on.

### Verbal vs. Physical

To understand this, it is useful to recall the case of a *shaliach lekabbalah* — an agent appointed to receive the *get* on behalf of the wife — who becomes ill. The question of whether such an agent may appoint a substitute agent is precisely this problem: the agent has only a verbal appointment; there is no physical object that he received which he could now transfer. Without the physical object, the authority may not be transferable.

The *Gemara* raises a different formulation of the same issue. The concern of *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach* is that the originally appointed agents cannot pass on their appointment to the *sofer*; they were appointed, and they cannot on their own authority re-appoint someone to take their place. This is the position underlying the entire *mishna*: the whole structure of "you must do it yourselves" presupposes that the verbal agency cannot be transferred.

But if this is already the logic of the *mishna*, and if Shmuel himself rules that *halacha k'Rebbi Yosi d'amar mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach* — the *halacha* follows Rebbi Yosi who holds that a verbal agency cannot be passed on — then the question seems already answered: the *sofer* cannot have been used, because the two appointed agents could not delegate to him. Why then does Shmuel say *tzarich talmud*?

The *Gemara* therefore reframes the question. Shmuel is not uncertain about *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach* — that rule he knows and accepts. The question is rather: *hai kitvu, iksav yadan iksav haget?* — when the husband says *kitvu*, does he mean "sign it" or does he mean "scribe it"? These two possibilities lead to fundamentally different analyses.

If *kitvu* means "scribe it," then the two appointed agents were supposed to do the scribing themselves, and having the *sofer* scribe it is a violation of the appointment — a case of *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach*.

If *kitvu* means "sign it," then the husband never appointed the two to scribe anything. He told them to sign the *get* — and implicitly, to find someone to write it. In that case, they are not delegating their agency at all. They remain the signatories; they are merely communicating to the *sofer* that the husband wants him to write the *get*. That is a different concept entirely: *omer imru* — informing a third party of the husband's wish — rather than transferring one's own agency. And *omer imru*, as we will see, may be permitted even according to positions that prohibit *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach*.

### Mishna Presumption

The *Gemara* asks: can we not simply resolve this from the *mishna* itself? The *mishna* states that if the husband says to two people *kitvu u'tnu get l'ishti*, then *harei elu yichtevu v'yitnu* — they must write and give it. This suggests that *kitvu* means something they must do themselves, which would favor the interpretation that *kitvu* refers to scribing. The *Gemara* responds that the *mishna* itself is the subject of the question — the question of what *yichtevu* in the *mishna* means is precisely what we are investigating. The *mishna* does not independently resolve the ambiguity; it merely reuses the same term.

### Beit Din Learning

The *Gemara* then argues more forcefully that *kitvu* must mean scribing, drawing on Rebbi Yosi's ruling in the *mishna*. Rebbi Yosi says that even the *beis din hagadol shebiYerushalayim*, if told *tnu get l'ishti*, must *she'ilmedu v'yichtevu v'yachtemu* — learn how to write a *get* and do so themselves. If *kitvu* meant only signing, this passage would be absurd: *mi ika bei dina d'lo yadei michtav chasimas yedaihu* — is there conceivably a *beis din* whose members do not know how to sign their own names? The very premise of Rebbi Yosi's ruling — that they would need to *learn* — only makes sense if what they must learn is the scribing of a *get*, not the writing of their signatures.

### Signing Possibility

The *Gemara* deflects this argument. One could theoretically posit a newly constituted *beis din* whose members have not yet established their customary signatures. While the *Gemara* acknowledges this is a weak answer, it means the proof from Rebbi Yosi's ruling is not airtight. The possibility remains, at least formally, that *kitvu* refers to signing. The *Gemara* then approaches the issue from yet another angle: if *kitvu* means signing and therefore implies that the two signatories may find their own *sofer* to scribe the *get*, is that not itself a form of *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach*? The *Gemara* answers: no. If the husband said *kitvu* meaning "sign," then the husband himself implicitly authorized the signatories to procure a *sofer*. Whoever they find to write the *get* is, in effect, being appointed by the husband through the mode of *omer imru* — the husband is essentially saying, through his agents, "go tell someone to write it." The signatories are not re-delegating their own agency; they are transmitting the husband's appointment to the *sofer*. And *omer imru* — indirect appointment by informing a third party — may well be permitted.

---

## Chasam Sofer V'Ed

### Witnesses Inform Sofer

The *Gemara* now raises a new case to probe these distinctions. A husband says to two people: *imru l'sofer v'yichtov u'l'ploni u'ploni v'yachtemu* — tell the *sofer* to write it, and tell so-and-so and so-and-so to sign it. Here the husband himself is using *omer imru*: he is appointing the two people not to sign or scribe, but merely to convey his wishes to the *sofer* and to the designated witnesses. Rav Huna citing Rav rules: *keshera v'lo ta'aseh zo b'Yisrael* — it is technically valid, but this should never be done.

### Scenario Requirement

This scenario is worth noting. It only makes sense to entertain this case if *omer imru* is at least conceivably permitted. Were *omer imru* entirely invalid — were the rule that every participant must hear the appointment directly from the husband — then this entire arrangement would be obviously invalid and the *Gemara* would not need to say it is *keshera* while adding a caution against doing it. The very structure of the ruling — *keshera b'lo ta'aseh* — implies that *omer imru* is halachically operative.

### Embarrassment Problem

The *Gemara* asks: if it is *keshera*, why should one not do it? The answer is: *mishum kisufa d'sofer* — because of the embarrassment of the *sofer*. Consider: the two messengers approach the *sofer* and tell him to write the *get*, and then instruct him that Reuven and Shimon will sign it. The *sofer* may well feel affronted: you trust me to write this document but not to sign it? Am I not a fit witness? Out of concern for the *sofer*'s dignity, the messenger may quietly adjust the arrangement — he might tell the *sofer* to sign as well, and drop one of the originally designated witnesses. The resulting *get* would then have been executed in a manner the husband never sanctioned. The document would appear valid but would in fact be *pasul*, since the witnesses who signed it were not those the husband designated.

### Permitted, Not Done

The *Gemara* resolves this concern through the ruling itself: *kivan d'amar mar kasher v'lo ta'aseh kein b'Yisrael* — since we rule that it is *kasher* but should not be done, this means the *sofer* and the designated witnesses should refuse to participate in any arrangement where the embarrassment dynamic might lead them to deviate from the husband's instructions. Since they are expected to refuse such a scenario, the feared outcome is unlikely to materialize — *lo shechiach* — and the theoretical validity of *omer imru* does not, in practice, give rise to the feared abuse.

---

## Witnesses Find Sofer

### Direct Witness Appointme…

A related but distinct case now presents itself. Suppose the husband says directly to two people: *imru l'sofer v'yichtov v'atem chatomu* — tell the *sofer* to write it, and you yourselves sign it. Here the witnesses are directly appointed — they will personally sign the *get* — and they are only asking the *sofer* to write the text. The witnesses have a direct appointment, and the *sofer*'s involvement is not a re-delegation but a practical arrangement for the scribing.

### Permitted Debate

Whether this arrangement may be followed *lechatchila*, or whether it too falls under the prohibition of *lo ta'aseh*, is debated. The *Gemara* will return to this at the end of the *daf*. The general concern, as will become clear, remains that a woman might hire individuals to falsely report the husband's instructions, and any arrangement in which the *sofer* is not directly appointed by the husband is potentially vulnerable to that abuse.

---

## Mili vs. Omer Imru

### Two Concepts

Before proceeding, it is important to clearly distinguish between two concepts that run through this entire discussion. The first is *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach*: if I have appointed you as my agent, you may not pass that appointment on to another. Your agency is personal; it came to you directly from me, and the authority it carries cannot be transferred further. The second concept is the question of *shlichus shelo befanav* — can the husband appoint an agent without speaking to that agent directly? Can he tell Michael to inform Jenna that she is to write the *get*, so that Jenna becomes the husband's agent even though the husband never spoke to her personally?

These are conceptually distinct. *Mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach* addresses what happens after an appointment has been validly made — the appointee cannot re-delegate. The question of *shlichus shelo befanav* addresses whether a valid appointment can be made indirectly in the first place. *Omer imru* is precisely the question of *shlichus shelo befanav*: does the husband's instruction, conveyed through a third party, constitute a valid appointment?

---

## Mili vs. Omer Imru (II)

### Rabbi Yosi: Both

Rebbi Yosi, as the *Gemara* now establishes, holds both restrictions. He prohibits *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach* — once you are appointed, you cannot pass the agency on — and he also prohibits *omer imru* — the husband cannot appoint someone through an intermediary; the appointee must hear the instruction directly. This is precisely why, in Rebbi Yosi's ruling in the *mishna*, even the *beis din hagadol shebiYerushalayim* cannot delegate the writing of the *get*: the members of the *beis din* are the only ones who heard it from the husband, and only they may execute it. Any indirect appointment — even one where the husband clearly intended to confer authority on others — is invalid.

### Shmuel's Position

Shmuel, by contrast, accepts *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach* — he rules like Rebbi Yosi that you cannot re-delegate a verbal appointment — but he permits *omer imru*. The husband may communicate his appointment through a third party, and the person thus informed becomes a valid agent. Shmuel therefore occupies a middle position: tighter than the *tanna kamma* but not as restrictive as Rebbi Yosi across the board.

---

## Kitvu Meaning Debate (II)

### Shmuel's Split

This split in Shmuel's position is the key to understanding his original question. When the husband says *kitvu* to two people, if it means "scribe it," then they cannot have the *sofer* do it, because they cannot re-delegate their verbal appointment — *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach*. But if *kitvu* means "sign it," then implicitly the husband authorized the two to find a *sofer* through *omer imru*, which Shmuel permits. In that case, the *sofer* writes entirely validly, and the *get* is *kasher*. Shmuel's uncertainty — *tzarich talmud* — is thus the unresolved question of which meaning *kitvu* carries.

---

## Following Rabbi Yosi

### Rabbi Shimon's Question

The *Gemara* returns to the ruling cited earlier: *amar Shmuel amar Rebbi halacha k'Rebbi Yosi d'amar mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach* — Shmuel said in the name of Rebbi that the *halacha* follows Rebbi Yosi. Rebbi Shimon the son of Rebbi is surprised. Given that both Rebbi Meir and Chanina ish Ono — reporting in the name of Rebbi Akiva — disagree with Rebbi Yosi and hold that a group of three constituted as a *beis din* may delegate the task, what motivated Rebbi to rule like Rebbi Yosi? *Mah ra'ah Rebbi lomar halacha k'Rebbi Yosi?* — what did Rebbi see that led him to do so?

### Nimuko Imo

The response is: *shtok beni shtok. V'ei illu lo ra'isa es Rebbi Yosi* — be silent, my son. Had you ever merited to see Rebbi Yosi in person, you would understand. *Nimuko imo* — his reasoning is with him. This is the famous principle by which the *halacha* generally follows Rebbi Yosi: *halacha k'Rebbi Yosi shenimuko imo*. Whatever Rebbi Yosi ruled was backed by particularly thorough and well-grounded reasoning. Even when his position is outnumbered, even when the logic on the surface seems to favor his opponents, the presumption is that Rebbi Yosi's position has a depth of reasoning that justifies the ruling in his favor.

### Praises of Sages

The *Gemara* supports this by citing a *braisa* from *Avos d'Rebbi Natan*, in which Issi ben Yehuda would enumerate the distinctive qualities of the Sages. *Rebbi Meir chacham v'sofer* — Rebbi Meir was a sage and a scribe. Notably, he was literally a scribe, which lends an interesting resonance given our *sugya*'s concern with the scribing of a *get*. *Rebbi Yehuda chacham lecheshe'yirtzeh* — Rebbi Yehuda was wise when he chose to be; Rashi explains that when he took the time to think something through, he could be very wise. *Rebbi Tarfon gal shel egozim* — Rebbi Tarfon was like a pile of nuts: ask him something and everything comes cascading out, one thing flowing from the next in abundance. *Rebbi Yishmael chanut meyuzenet* — Rebbi Yishmael was like a well-stocked store; whatever you need, he has it, and he knows where to find it. *Rebbi Akiva otzar balum* — Rebbi Akiva was a warehouse organized into compartments. Rashi and Tosafos debate the precise meaning of *balum*, but *Avos d'Rebbi Natan* itself clarifies: Rebbi Akiva would receive teachings in a mixed, unsorted form — *midrash*, *halacha*, analysis — and then come home and sort everything into its proper category. This is indeed what his students did in editing the *midrashei halacha* — the *Sifra*, the *Sifrei* — systematizing the entire corpus, a feat not unlike what the *Rambam* later achieved.

*Rebbi Yochanan ben Nuri kupa shel rochlim* — Rebbi Yochanan ben Nuri was like the basket of traveling merchants, who carried unusual and varied wares from town to town. Unlike the stocked store with its staples, the merchant's basket contains the rare and the unexpected. *Rebbi Elazar ben Azarya kupa shel besamim* — he was like the spice merchant's basket; Rashi says this is similar in concept, though perhaps smaller in scope. *Mishnas Rebbi Eliezer ben Yaakov kav v'naki* — the teaching of Rebbi Eliezer ben Yaakov is only a *kav* — a small measure — but it is a very clean measure: few rulings, but each one carefully sifted and pure, so that what he does say carries correspondingly great weight.

And then: *Rebbi Yosi nimuko imo* — Rebbi Yosi's reasoning is with him. This is striking, because the reasoning is typically not spelled out explicitly in the *mishna*; on the surface, one might even think the more logical position belongs to Rebbi Meir and Chanina ish Ono, who held that a group constituted as a *beis din* may naturally delegate. Yet the received principle is that Rebbi Yosi's underlying reasoning, even when unstated, is so sound that we rule with him.

The *Gemara* also cites the description of Rebbi Shimon: *tochen harbeh u'motzi kim'a* — he grinds a great deal and produces only a little. This sounds like a criticism, but the *Gemara* clarifies: *mishake'ach kim'a* — he forgets only a little. The grinding is thorough; what he "produces" outward, what he actually forgets, is minimal — and even what he does forget is *suvin*, the chaff, the material that should have been discarded anyway. Rebbi Shimon himself told his students: *shanu midotai* — learn my methodology or my teachings — *sheymidotai trumot mitrumot midotav shel Rebbi Akiva* — for they are the choicest of the choicest of Rebbi Akiva's methods.

---

## Lo Ta'aseh Practice

### Rav Huna's Ruling

The *Gemara* now examines the practical ruling. The case is: *amar lishnayim imru l'sofer v'yichtov u'l'ploni ploni v'yachtemu* — the husband says to two people: go tell the *sofer* to write the *get*, and go tell so-and-so and so-and-so to sign it. Rav Huna citing Rav rules: *keshera v'lo ta'aseh zo b'Yisrael* — it is valid but should not be done this way.

---

## Lo Ta'aseh Practice (II)

### Woman Hiring Concern

The question is pressed: if it is *keshera*, why the prohibition? The answer is: *chaishinan shema tischor eidim* — we are concerned that the woman may have hired witnesses. If the husband did not personally appoint anyone, and two people come to the *sofer* and the witnesses claiming that the husband instructed them to arrange the *get*, there is a real concern that the woman herself hired those two people to make this claim. Since the intermediaries bear no direct personal responsibility — they are not signing the *get* themselves, they are merely conveying a message — they might be persuadable to lie. The *sofer* and the witnesses, by relying on these intermediaries, risk participating in the production of a fraudulent *get*.

### Dibbura vs. Ma'aseh

The *Gemara* challenges this concern: *eidim hachatumim al hasadeh mekach v'al get ishah lo chashu chachamim l'davar zeh* — witnesses who are signed on a bill of sale or on a *get* are not suspected of forgery; the Sages had no general concern that witnesses might falsify documents. The *Gemara* distinguishes: *ma'aseh lo avdi* — people will not commit an actual act of forgery, will not sign a false document. But *dibbura ka'amri* — they may be willing merely to convey a false oral message, to tell the *sofer* and the witnesses that the husband gave these instructions when in fact he did not. The act of signing a forged document is a categorical offense that people generally refuse. But repeating a message — even a false one — without personally being a signatory to the resulting *get*, carries a lower psychological threshold, and the concern that the woman's hired agents might do so is realistic. The prohibition of *lo ta'aseh ken b'Yisrael* addresses precisely this vulnerability.

### Amoraic Debate

A subsequent case introduces a further variation: *amar lishnayim imru l'sofer v'yichtov v'atem chatomu* — suppose the husband tells two people: go tell the *sofer* to write it, but you yourselves sign it. Here, the witnesses are directly appointed — they will personally sign the *get*, with full personal accountability — and they are only instructing the *sofer* to write. Rav Chisda rules: *keshera b'lo ta'aseh* — even this arrangement is valid but should not be done, though here the prohibition is only a *gezeira*, a protective extension, lest permitting this lead to permitting the prior case. Rabba bar bar Chana permits it outright: *kasher v'ta'aseh*. Rav Nachman rules *kasher v'lo ta'aseh*. Rav Sheshet says *kasher v'ta'aseh*. Rabba says *kasher v'lo ta'aseh*. Rav Yosef says *kasher v'ta'aseh*. The *Gemara* notes that some authorities reverse the positions attributed to Rabba and Rav Yosef.

The practical bottom line is nuanced. The *halacha* of *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach* is accepted, ruling like Rebbi Yosi. *Omer imru*, however — the indirect appointment through an intermediary — is technically valid according to Shmuel's position, which the *Gemara* does not fully abandon. Yet *omer imru* in practice should not be relied upon, not because it is halachically invalid in principle, but because of the risk that those conveying the message may not genuinely be representing the husband.

---

## Witnesses Find Sofer (II)

### Hired Witnesses Fear

This connects back to the case where witnesses are appointed directly but find their own *sofer*. There too, the real concern underlying the prohibition of *lo ta'aseh* is not the technical question of *shlichus shelo befanav* but the fear that the woman has hired witnesses to fabricate the husband's instructions. *Ma'aseh lo avdi* — people will not forge a signature on the document — but *dibbura ka'amri* — they may be willing to falsely represent a verbal instruction. The responsibility falls on the last link in the chain: the *sofer* and the witnesses who will ultimately produce the *get* must not rely on intermediaries whose report cannot be independently verified, lest the entire get rest on a fabricated mandate.

---

## Counting Ten People

### Enumeration Question

The *Gemara* raises a final question concerning the *mishna*'s case of ten people. If the husband did not say *kulchem* — all of you — but instead counted them one by one: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, give a *get* to my wife — what is the legal effect of enumeration? Does counting each person mean the same as saying *kulchem*, requiring all of them to participate? Or does it mean merely that he selected this group as the pool from which the requisite participants are to be drawn?

### Rav Huna on Counting

Rav Huna rules: *mana eino kechulam* — counting is not equivalent to *kulchem*. Enumerating the individuals simply designates the group; it does not require all of them to participate. Any of them may act on behalf of the group.

### Rav Yochanan on Counting

Rav Yochanan, citing Rabbi Elazar from Rome, rules: *mana harei hu kechulam* — counting is equivalent to *kulchem*. When the husband counts each person individually, he is singling out each one specifically, and the effect is the same as explicitly requiring all of them.

### Rav Papa's Resolution

Rav Papa offers a resolution: *velo pligi* — they do not actually dispute each other. The disagreement depends on a specific factual distinction: *ha demana kulhu, ha demana mikztayehu* — one ruling applies where the husband counted all the people present, and the other applies where he counted only some of them. The *Gemara* notes that there is a further dispute as to which direction the rule runs. Some say: if he counted all of them, it is equivalent to *kulchem*, since he specifically accounted for each one; if he counted only some, it merely designates a subgroup from which any may act. Others reverse this: if he counted all of them, it is not equivalent to *kulchem*, since that is simply how one refers to a group; but if he singled out a subset, the enumeration of that specific subset implies that each of the counted individuals is required.

### Rav Yehuda's Takanah

Rav Yehuda instituted a *takana* to address the ambiguity surrounding *kulchem*. He established a recommended text for cases where a husband wishes to involve multiple people, specifying: *ktovu o kulchem o kol echad v'echad michem* — write, either all of you or any one of you; *chatmu tarrei o kulchem o kol tarrei michem* — sign, either all of you or any two of you; *avilu o kulchem o kol echad v'echad michem* — deliver, either all of you or any one of you. By explicitly including both possibilities in the husband's instructions, the ambiguity is dissolved: whether all participate or only some, the *get* is valid.

### Rava's Practical Advice

Rava, however, objects to this formulation. *Zimnin d'gazlei le-diburei v'amar kulchem v'lo amar kol echad v'echad michem* — it sometimes happens that one seizes on the first part of the instruction and says *kulchem* without completing the formulation with *kol echad v'echad michem*, thereby inadvertently invoking the more restrictive requirement. The problem is that beginning with *kulchem* plants a word that, if the remainder of the formula is omitted or forgotten, will invalidate the *get*. Rava therefore advises: eliminate *kulchem* from the formula altogether. Simply instruct: *ktovu kol echad michem* — write, any one of you; *chatmu kol tarrei michem* — sign, any two of you; *avilu kol echad michem* — deliver, any one of you. By removing *kulchem* entirely from the husband's instructions, the risk of inadvertently imposing that requirement disappears.

With this practical guidance, the *perek* concludes: *hadran alach ha'omer*.

---

---

# Gittin 67

## Kitvu & Shlichim

### Two vs. Three People

The *daf* properly begins with the final line of 66a, where the *Mishnah* turns to a question of fundamental importance in the laws of *get*: when a husband appoints agents to write and deliver a *get*, must those specific individuals carry out the task themselves, or may they delegate to others?

The *Mishnah* draws a critical distinction based on both the number of people addressed and the precise language used. When a husband says to two people, *"tnu get l'ishti"* — give a *get* to my wife — they themselves must execute the task. Since giving a *get* necessarily implies writing it, they cannot hand that responsibility to anyone else. Similarly, if he says to three people, *"kitvu get u-tnu l'ishti"* — write a *get* and give it to my wife — the use of *kitvu* makes explicit that they must do it directly: *harei elu yichtevu v'yitnu*.

The more nuanced case arises when he says to three people simply *"tnu get l'ishti"* — without the word *kitvu*. Here the *Mishnah* reasons that three people constitute a *beis din*, and a *beis din* is understood as a supervisory body rather than a group expected to perform each action personally. Therefore, when *kitvu* is absent and the group is three, the husband may be understood as delegating oversight rather than direct execution, and those three may instruct others to write the *get*. This is *divrei Rabbi Meir*. The *Mishnah* further records a tradition transmitted by Rabbi Chanina ish Ono from prison — understood by *Rashi* as being in the name of Rabbi Akiva, who was then held under Roman imprisonment — confirming: *mekubalani b'omer lishloshah tnu get l'ishti she'yomru l'acherim v'yichtevu, mipnei she'asan Beis Din* — when three are told to give a *get*, they may delegate, because he constituted them as a *beis din*.

### Rabbi Yosi's Rule

Rabbi Yosi dissents sharply: *af anu mekubalin she-afilu amar l'Beis Din HaGadol she-bi-Yerushalayim tnu get l'ishti, harei elu yichtevu v'yitnu* — even if one said to the High Court in Jerusalem, "give a *get* to my wife," they themselves must write it and give it. Rabbi Yosi's position strips away any leniency based on the nature of the body addressed. Even the most eminent court in the world, if they received only a verbal instruction to give a *get*, must carry it out personally. If they do not know how to write a *get*, they must learn. They cannot delegate what was entrusted directly to them.

The *Mishnah* then shifts to a related but distinct case: when the husband addresses ten people. If he says *"kitvu get u-tnu l'ishti"* without the word *kulchem* — all of you — it means from among you: one writes and two sign. But if he adds *kulchem* — all of you — then all ten must be involved. The practical resolution, as the *Gemara* will clarify, is that one writes while all are present, analogous to the role of a *shaliach tzibur*, who acts on behalf of the entire assembled group. Crucially, *lifichach im meis echad meihem harei zeh get batel* — if one of them dies, the *get* is void — because the husband stipulated that everyone participate, and that condition was not met. This underscores a point worth pausing over: the husband's *da'at* and *ratzon* are so central to the nature of the *get* that failure to comply with his precise specification invalidates the document entirely.

### Signing vs. Scribing

The *Gemara* opens with a question sent from the academy of Rav to Shmuel — a remarkable fact in itself, given that Rav and Shmuel were contemporaries of roughly equal stature. The question: *amar l'shnayim kitvu u-tnu get l'ishti, amru l'sofer ve'chasav ve'chasmu hein mahu?* — if a husband told two people to write and give a *get*, and they instructed a *sofer* to scribe it while they themselves signed, what is the *halacha*?

The underlying question is what *kitvu* means when directed at a group. Does it refer to the physical scribing of the document, or does it refer to the signing — the affixing of witnesses' signatures? This distinction carries enormous practical weight. If *kitvu* means scribing, then having someone else write it violates the husband's instruction. If *kitvu* means signing, then having a *sofer* write the document is not a deviation at all — it was never their task to scribe it.

Shmuel's response was: *teitzei vehadavar tzarich talmud* — if she remarried on the basis of such a *get*, she must leave her second husband, because the *get* is uncertain; but the matter requires further investigation. The *Gemara* then explores what exactly requires investigation.

### Mili Lo Mimsaran

One possibility is that the question is about *mili*: can a verbal appointment be transferred to another agent? The *Gemara* immediately notes that this cannot be Shmuel's question, because Shmuel himself already rules *halacha keRabbi Yosi d'amar mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach* — the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yosi that a verbal agency cannot be passed on to another agent. If that principle is settled, why is there any uncertainty?

The concept of *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach* requires some unpacking, as it is the central analytical thread running through this entire *daf*. When a husband appoints a *shaliach* to deliver a *get*, he hands over a physical document. That physical object, in some sense, embodies and concretizes the agent's authority, and it may be possible in certain configurations to transfer that authority along with the document. But when the appointment consists only of words — as when the husband tells two people to write a *get* before the document exists — there is nothing physical to convey. The agent holds only a verbal mandate. The question is whether such a verbal mandate is one the agent can pass on to someone else. Rabbi Yosi's view, accepted by Shmuel, is that it cannot. If I appoint you to perform this task verbally, you must do it yourself; you cannot re-appoint another in your place.

This principle, however, does not answer the question Shmuel actually intends to investigate. That question is narrower and more precise: *hai ktovu, ktav yadam hu o ktav ha-get hu?* — when the husband says *kitvu*, does he mean "sign it" or "scribe it"?

If *kitvu* means "sign it," then the husband never directed these two people to do the scribing at all. What he implicitly said was: find someone to write the *get* and sign it yourselves. Having a *sofer* write it is not delegating their task — it is executing the husband's implicit instruction that someone else handle the scribing. This falls under a distinct concept: *omer imru*, the husband directing his appointees to communicate to a third party. In that framework, the two witnesses are not passing on their own agency; they are simply informing a *sofer* that he has been appointed by the husband. The husband effectively appointed the *sofer* through them.

If, on the other hand, *kitvu* means "scribe it," then having someone else do the scribing is forbidden — not as a violation of *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach* (since that concerns re-delegation of one's own agency), but simply because the husband told them to scribe it and they did not.

The *Gemara* attempts to resolve whether *kitvu* means scribing from the *Mishnah* itself: if it meant signing, why would the *Mishnah* say that members of the *Beis Din HaGadol* would have to *learn* to write the *get*? Surely they know how to sign their names. The *Gemara* deflects — perhaps it was a newly constituted court — but acknowledges the deflection is weak. The sugya thus arrives at two separate issues, which the *Gemara* now treats explicitly.

## Omer Imru Debate

### Omer Imru Basics

The concept of *omer imru* must be distinguished from *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach*, though both concern verbal agency. *Mili lo mimsaran* addresses whether an agent who received a verbal appointment can pass that appointment on to a third party. *Omer imru* addresses a different question entirely: can the husband direct his appointed agents to *inform* others that they have been appointed directly by the husband?

The distinction is this: in *mili lo mimsaran*, I appoint Michael, and Michael tries to hand off his role to Jenna — something he has no authority to do. In *omer imru*, I tell Michael to inform Jenna that I am appointing her — the appointment comes from me, and Michael is merely the messenger conveying it. If *omer imru* is valid, then the husband can appoint a *sofer* and witnesses without speaking to them directly, so long as he instructs an intermediary to relay the appointments. If *omer imru* is invalid, then every person involved in the *get* must hear their appointment directly from the husband himself.

The *Gemara* now asks: does Rabbi Yosi actually agree that *omer imru* is permissible? And if so, what does that imply for the case of *chasam sofer ve'eid*?

### Chasam Sofer Concern

The *Gemara* raises the ruling of *chasam sofer ve'eid* — where the *sofer* who wrote the *get* is also one of the two signing witnesses. Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba clarifies that the *Mishnah* here means *chasam sofer shaninu*: the *sofer* signed as a witness. And Rav Chisda notes that this *Mishnah* follows the position of Rabbi Yosi, for whom *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach*.

Now the *Gemara* presses: *ve'i salka da'atach modei Rabbi Yosi b'omer imru* — if Rabbi Yosi agrees that *omer imru* is valid, *nafka minah churbah*, disaster will follow. Here is the scenario: a husband says to two people, *"imru l'sofer veyichtov u-l'Reuven v'Shimon veyachtomu"* — go tell the *sofer* to write and tell Reuven and Shimon to sign. This is a legitimate use of *omer imru* if the concept is valid. But here is the problem: *mishum kisufa d'sofer* — out of embarrassment for the *sofer*. When the messenger approaches the *sofer* and says "write the *get*, but Reuven and Shimon are going to sign it," the *sofer* may feel slighted. "You trust me to write it but not to be a witness?" The messenger, anxious to avoid this embarrassment, decides to make the *sofer* one of the witnesses instead of Shimon. The result: the *get* is signed by witnesses whom the husband did not appoint, and *u'va'al lo amar hachi* — the husband never said this. The *get* is invalid, yet no one will know.

The *Gemara* attempts to deflect this concern by noting that *kasher v'lo ta'aseh kein b'Yisrael* has already been established — such appointments ought not be done in Israel, and the *sofer* should refuse to participate in this kind of arrangement. If no one is supposed to engage in it *lechatchila*, then we need not worry about the scenario. The *Gemara* then raises a second version of the same concern: even if the husband directly appoints the two witnesses but asks them to find a *sofer*, might the witnesses nonetheless rearrange the roles out of embarrassment — substituting the *sofer* for one of them? The same deflection applies: if witnesses who find their own *sofer* also fall under *lo ta'aseh kein b'Yisrael*, we are not concerned.

### Two Separate Issues

At this point the *Gemara* introduces a crucial clarification. The two concerns — *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach* and *omer imru* — are conceptually separate, even though they may both bear on the validity of a *get*. Shmuel holds both principles, but distinguishes between them. *Mili lo mimsaran* means that an agent cannot re-delegate a verbal appointment he himself received. *Omer imru* is a distinct question about whether the husband can appoint someone *shelo befanav* — not in their presence — by having a messenger relay the appointment.

### Rabbi Yosi Both Ways

The *Gemara* concludes that the only way to fully account for the *Mishnah*'s treatment of *chasam sofer ve'eid* — without concern that the *sofer* was substituted for a witness out of embarrassment — is to say that Rabbi Yosi holds *both* prohibitions. *Rabbi Yosi tartei amar*: Rabbi Yosi says both that *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach* and that *omer imru* is invalid. According to Rabbi Yosi, every participant in the *get* process must have heard their role directly from the husband. This resolves the *chasam sofer* concern entirely: if every appointment must be direct, there is no intermediary who could have rearranged things out of embarrassment.

This also explains Rabbi Yosi's position in the *Mishnah* far more coherently than it might first appear. When Rabbi Yosi says that even the *Beis Din HaGadol* in Jerusalem would have to write the *get* themselves if that is what was said, the implicit point is that no one may act as a conduit for an appointment. Even if the husband's practical intent was for the court to supervise and delegate, the *halacha* is that only those who heard the instruction directly from the husband may execute it. The reasoning of *mili lo mimsaran* and *omer imru* are conceptually distinct — the former concerns passing on one's own delegated authority; the latter concerns whether one can receive an appointment indirectly — but Rabbi Yosi holds that both are disqualifying. Together they constitute a comprehensive requirement that all agency in the writing and delivery of a *get* flow directly from the husband's own words to each individual actor.

## Shmuel's Psak

### Shmuel Splits

The *Gemara* now turns to the *gufa* of Shmuel's ruling: *ushmu'el savar lah keva'tei bechada u'falig alei bechada* — Shmuel agrees with Rabbi Yosi in one respect and disagrees in another. Shmuel accepts *mili lo mimsaran l'shaliach* — a verbal agency cannot be transferred by the agent who holds it. He does not accept that *omer imru* is prohibited. According to Shmuel, the husband may appoint a *sofer* or a witness by relaying the appointment through an intermediary; *omer imru* is valid, and one may make a *shaliach shelo befanav*, appointing someone who is not present, so long as the message is conveyed.

This is precisely what clarifies the original question from Rav's academy. Shmuel's uncertainty about the case where two people had a *sofer* write the *get* while they signed was not a question about *mili* — that is settled. It was a question about *kitvu*: if *kitvu* means signing, then the two appointees were only ever asked to sign, and by implicitly directing them to find a *sofer*, the husband was effectively using the mechanism of *omer imru*. Since Shmuel holds *omer imru* is valid, such a *get* would be valid in principle — hence the need to determine what *kitvu* actually means in the husband's instruction.

### Nimuko Imo

The *Gemara* then records an exchange that illuminates the general standing of Rabbi Yosi's rulings. Shmuel transmitted this *halacha* in the name of *Rebbi* (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi), prompting Rabbi Shimon, Rebbi's son, to object: given that Rabbi Meir and Chanina ish Ono — who brought the ruling from Rabbi Akiva in prison — both disagree with Rabbi Yosi, *mah ra'ah Rebbi lomar halacha keRabbi Yosi?* What motivated his father to rule like Rabbi Yosi against those other prominent opinions?

Rebbi's response is striking: *shtok beni shtok* — be silent, my son. Had you ever merited to see Rabbi Yosi in person, you would understand, because *nimuko imo* — his reasoning is with him. This is an ancient expression of confidence in Rabbi Yosi's intellectual authority, one that transcends the mere counting of opinions.

The *Gemara* then cites the famous passage from *Avot d'Rabbi Natan* in which Isi ben Yehudah catalogued the distinctive qualities of the great sages. Rabbi Meir: *chacham ve'sofer* — wise and a scribe (notably apt given the subject of this *daf*). Rabbi Yehudah: *chacham l'chesheyirtzeh* — wise when he chose to be, meaning when he took the time to reason things through carefully. Rabbi Tarfon: *gash shel egozim* — a heap of walnuts: ask him one thing and everything comes cascading out. Rabbi Yishmael: *chanut meyuzenet* — a well-stocked storehouse, anything one needed was available and organized. Rabbi Akiva: *otzar balum* — a sealed warehouse divided into compartments. The *Gemara* clarifies that this refers not to creativity — which one might naturally associate with Rabbi Akiva — but to his systematic organization: he would absorb traditions from his teachers in their mixed form (legal analysis, *midrash*, and *mishnah* all intertwined) and then sort them meticulously into their proper categories, a feat reflected in the work of his students who edited the *midrashei halacha*. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri: *kupat harochlim* — the basket of a traveling merchant, stocked with a variety of unusual wares. Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah: *kupat shel besamim* — the spice merchant's basket, similarly varied if somewhat smaller in scope. *Mishnat Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov*: *kav venaki* — a small measure, but clean: he taught little, but everything he taught was reliable and precise. And Rabbi Yosi: *nimuko imo* — his reasoning is with him.

The phrase is all the more striking because, as the *Gemara* itself notes, the reasoning is not always visible in the *Mishnah*. If anything, the surface logic might seem to favor Rabbi Meir and the tradition from Rabbi Akiva, who allow delegation when three people are addressed as a *beis din*. Yet the rule *halacha keRabbi Yosi she-nimuko imo* reflects a presumption that Rabbi Yosi's positions are grounded in deep, worked-out reasoning, even when that reasoning is not spelled out. The passage concludes with the description of Rabbi Shimon: *tochein harbeh u-motzi kima* — he grinds much and produces little. The *Gemara* clarifies that *motzi* here means "expels" rather than "produces": he forgets very little, and what he does forget was only the intellectual chaff.

## Two Appoint Sofer

### Kasher V'Lo Taaseh

The *Gemara* now examines the concrete case that had been hovering in the background. *Amar l'shnayim imru l'sofer veyichtov u-l'Ploni v'Ploni veyachtomu* — a husband says to two people: go tell the *sofer* to write, and go tell so-and-so and so-and-so to sign. Here the husband has appointed nobody directly; every appointment is conveyed through the intermediary of these two. Rav Huna citing Rav rules: *keshera v'lo ta'aseh zot b'Yisrael* — it is valid, but one should not do this in Israel.

### Hired Witnesses Fear

The reason for *lo ta'aseh*, when asked, is the concern *shema tiskor edim* — perhaps the woman has hired witnesses. In a case where the two appointed intermediaries are telling a *sofer* and witnesses what to do, and none of those actors are directly implicated by signing the document themselves, there is a real danger that the woman could find two people willing to falsely claim that the husband gave them this instruction. Unlike the case of forging signatures on a *get* — which the *Gemara* elsewhere says people will not do, since *ma'aseh lo avdi*, people will not commit an outright forgery by signing their names to a lie — here the two intermediaries are not signing anything. They are only transmitting a message. That lower threshold of personal implication makes bribery a credible concern.

### Dibura Kamari

The *Gemara* distinguishes this from the case of forged documents more precisely. By full document forgery, *ma'aseh lo avdi* — people will not place their own signatures on a fabricated document. But *dibura ka'amri* — mere speech is another matter. Relaying a false message, without signing one's name to any document, is exactly the kind of act that bribed witnesses might be willing to perform. This is the specific danger that makes *lo ta'aseh zot b'Yisrael* necessary even when the arrangement is technically valid.

## Witnesses & Sofer

### Rav Chisda Position

The *Gemara* then considers a variant: *amar l'shnayim imru l'sofer veyichtov v'atem chatomu* — what if the husband's two appointees are themselves the witnesses who will sign, and they only ask the *sofer* to write? In this case the hired-witness concern evaporates, since the witnesses are personally accountable — they are putting their own signatures on the *get*. Rav Chisda rules: *keshera v'lo ta'aseh* — valid, but should not be done. Here the only reason not to do it is prophylactic: if this is permitted, it may lead to the previous scenario being permitted as well.

### Amoraim Dispute

Several *Amoraim* then weigh in with differing positions. Rabba bar bar Chana holds the practice is *kasher ve-ta'aseh* — not only valid but permissible. Rav Nachman rules *kasher v'lo ta'aseh*. Rav Sheshet rules *kasher ve-ta'aseh*. Rava rules *kasher v'lo ta'aseh*. Rav Yosef rules *kasher ve-ta'aseh*. The *Gemara* adds that some authorities reversed the attributions of Rava and Rav Yosef. The practical upshot is that Shmuel's position — *halacha keRabbi Yosi* on *mili*, while accepting *omer imru* in principle — does not translate straightforwardly into permission *lechatchila*, since the *lo ta'aseh* concern about unverifiable messages applies even when *omer imru* is conceptually valid.

## Ten People Rule

### Without Kulchem

The *Gemara* turns to the rules governing a husband who addresses ten people. A *baraisa* teaches: *amar l'asara kitvu get u-tnu l'ishti, echad kotev al yedei kulam* — if he says to ten people to write a *get* and give it to his wife, one of them writes on behalf of all of them. The word *kitvu* without *kulchem* is interpreted as "from among you" — any one may scribe, any two may sign.

### With Kulchem

If he adds *kulchem* — *kulchem kitvu* — then *echad kotev bemaamad kulam*: one writes while all are present. The analogy to *shaliach tzibur* is instructive. Just as the prayer leader in the repetition of the *Shemoneh Esrei* represents the entire congregation — the entire *tzibur* prays as a single unit through one mouthpiece — so too here, when all ten are physically present and one writes on their behalf, it is as though all ten have written it. Similarly, *kulchem holichu* — all of you bring the *get* — means *echad molich bemaamad kulam*: one carries the *get* while all are present for the conveyance.

### Counting Question

The *Gemara* then raises a question: *mana otan mahu* — what if the husband counts them individually, naming each one? Does enumeration carry the force of *kulchem*, requiring all of them, or does it merely identify the pool from which some may act?

### Counting Debate

Rav Huna holds *mana eino kechulchem* — counting is not equivalent to saying *kulchem*; it means any one of them may act. Rav Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar demin Romi holds the opposite: *mana harei hu kechulchem* — counting is equivalent to *kulchem*, and all of them are required.

### Rav Papa Resolves

Rav Papa resolves the apparent contradiction: *velo peligi* — they do not actually disagree. The distinction lies in whether the husband counted all of the people present or only some of them. *Ha demana kulhu* — if he counted everyone in the group — and *ha demana miktzathu* — if he counted only some. The *Gemara* reports that there is disagreement about which direction the rule runs: some hold that counting everyone is like *kulchem* (since he addressed each individually), while counting a subset means only "from among those I counted"; others hold the reverse. Either way, Rav Papa's point is that the two *Amoraim* were addressing different factual scenarios.

## Takana & Text

### Rav Yehuda Takana

The *Gemara* concludes with a practical ordinance. *Atkin Rav Yehuda be-gitta de-kulchem* — Rav Yehuda instituted a standardized formula for a *get* involving the *kulchem* scenario, designed to avoid the pitfalls just discussed. The formula he proposed: *ktovu o kulcham o kol chad minichon* — write it, whether all of you or any one of you; *chasomu shnayim o kulcham o kol trei minichon* — two of you should sign, whether all or any two; *holichu o kulcham o kol chad minichon* — bring it, whether all or any one of you. By explicitly including both alternatives, the husband's instruction encompasses all possible configurations and prevents invalidation if not everyone is ultimately present or involved.

### Rava Correction

Rava objects to this formulation and improves upon it. The problem with Rav Yehuda's text is structural: *zimnin de-gazlei diburei* — it sometimes happens that the end of the sentence gets cut off. If the husband says *"kulcham"* first and then fails to complete the phrase *"o kol chad minichon"*, the instruction defaults to requiring everyone, and the *get* becomes vulnerable to invalidity if even one person is absent or dies. Therefore, Rava proposes an alternative formulation: begin with the permissive language rather than the restrictive. Say *ktovu kol chad minichon* — write it, any one of you; *chasomu kol trei minichon* — sign it, any two of you; *holichu kol chad minichon* — bring it, any one of you. By establishing the permissive formula first — without ever invoking *kulchem* — the text eliminates the risk entirely. If the husband never says *kulchem*, there is nothing to satisfy and no way for accidental omission to generate a *pasul* *get*.

---

# Gittin 68

## Kordyakos & Da'as

### New Perek Intro

Daf 68 marks the beginning of a new *perek*, one that is distinguished by an extended engagement with *aggadah* before returning to *halakha*. The daf in fact opens mid-discussion from the final lines of 67b, transitioning seamlessly into its first *mishnah*.

### Kordyakos Case

The *mishnah* introduces the case of *mi she'achazo kordyakos* — one who is seized with *kordyakos*, a condition that renders a person not in his right mind. The Gemara will eventually characterize it as a kind of spirit or demon, though it more likely refers to a specific illness producing mental incapacity. The governing principle is clear: such a person lacks *da'as*, and therefore when he says *kisvu get l'ishti* — write a *get* for my wife — *lo amar klum*, his words are legally meaningless. The appointment of *shlichus* requires genuine mental capacity, and that capacity is here absent.

### Retraction Valueless

The *mishnah* then presents a more striking case: *amar kisvu get l'ishti v'achazo kordyakos v'chazar v'amar lo tichtovenu* — he first said "write a *get* for my wife" while in his right mind, was then seized with *kordyakos*, and in that altered state retracted his instruction. The ruling is that *ein devarav ha'achronim klum* — his subsequent retraction is legally null. This is a considerable *chiddush*. One might have thought that the retraction, even if expressed during an episode of *kordyakos*, creates at minimum a *safek* sufficient to halt the writing of the *get*. Yet the Gemara rules that the wife is *vaday megureshes* — certainly divorced — and the retraction is treated as entirely without weight. The *shlichus* was validly constituted at the outset, and a declaration made while bereft of *da'as* cannot undo it.

This pair of cases illuminates a fundamental principle: what *halakha* requires is *da'as*, not merely verbal expression. One may speak without *da'as* — the first case — or one may lack the ability to speak while possessing full *da'as* — as the *mishnah* goes on to demonstrate. The two scenarios are mirror images of one another.

The *mishnah* then addresses *nishtatek* — one whose speech was silenced, whether through physical ailment or some other cause. If others ask him, "Shall we write a *get* for your wife?" and he nods, one tests him three times: *im amar al lav lav v'al hen hen* — if he can consistently signal no for things that are no and yes for things that are yes — then *yichtevu v'yitnu*, a *get* may be written and delivered. This procedure establishes two things simultaneously: that his signals can be interpreted reliably, and that his inability to speak does not reflect any deeper mental impairment.

### Kordyakos Definition

The Gemara then asks *mai kordyakos* — what precisely is this condition? Shmuel answers: *d'nachirei chamra chadta d'matzarta* — it is triggered by new wine fresh from the press. This appears to mean that the wine sets off something larger than ordinary intoxication, since the Gemara could simply have described the person as *shikor*, a drunk. The Gemara explicitly notes this: *v'lisni mi she'nashcho yayin chadash* — why not just say "one affected by new wine"? The answer is: *ha kamashma lan d'ha rucha kordyakos shema* — the text is teaching us that this particular spirit or illness has a name: *kordyakos*.

### Amulets & Names

*L'mai nafka mina?* — why does it matter that it has a name? *L'kameia* — because if one wishes to write an amulet against this affliction, one must know the name of the *shed* being warded off. The name is thus halakhically significant, not merely academically interesting.

---

## Medical Treatments

### Kordyakos Remedy

Immediately following the question of the amulet, the Gemara pivots to medical treatment — a striking juxtaposition that moves from the metaphysical to the practical. *Mai asusa* — how does one heal *kordyakos*? The prescription is *bisra sumka agumre* — lean red meat on coals — *vechamra marka* — and diluted wine.

### Sunstroke Treatment

Abaye then introduces a series of remedies transmitted in the name of his nursemaid, whom he calls *em*, mother — as Abaye was orphaned and reserved this term of endearment for the woman who raised him. For *shimsha bas yoma*, a sunstroke or fever of a single day, the remedy is a flask of water. If the condition persists for two days, *sikurei* — bloodletting is required. If it has lasted three days, one returns to the same regimen prescribed for *kordyakos*: lean meat on coals and diluted wine.

### Chronic Fever Cure

For *shimsha atikta* — a chronic or long-standing fever — the treatment is considerably more involved. One takes a black hen, cuts it lengthwise and widthwise, shaves the middle of one's head, and places the hen on the shaved area, leaving it there *ad demisrach* — until it begins to decompose. One then descends into the water, submerging up to the neck, remaining until faint, then swimming out and sitting down. If this does not suffice, one eats cress and repeats the water immersion in the same manner.

### Chills Remedy

The treatment for chills — *talga* — is characterized by Rashi as a condition of cold. As a kind of counterpart to the fever remedy, one prescribes *bisra shamina agumre* — fat meat on coals — and *vechamra chaya* — undiluted wine, the reverse of what is recommended for *kordyakos*.

### Rav Amram Story

Rav Amram Chasida suffered at the hands of the servants of the *Reish Galusa*'s household. The *Reish Galusa*, the political head of Babylonian Jewry, was not always surrounded by the most upright people, and Rashi explains that Rav Amram drew their hostility precisely because *mipnei shehaya chasid uparush umachmir aleihem be'isurin* — he was a pious and disciplined man who rebuked the household for its transgressions. In retaliation, they forced him to lie in the snow.

The next day, when they offered to make amends by bringing him whatever he wished, Rav Amram employed reverse psychology. Knowing that *hani kol de'amina lehu mafich apchi* — whatever he asked for they would give him the opposite — he requested lean meat on coals and diluted wine. They promptly brought him fat meat on coals and undiluted wine, which was precisely the remedy for chills that he required.

### Yalta & Bath

When Yalta, the learned wife of Rav Nachman and a member of the *Reish Galusa*'s family, heard of Rav Amram's condition, she took matters into her own hands. She brought him to the bathhouse and had him immerse in the waters until they turned red — the blood and fatty residue of the prescribed meat, Rashi explains, working their way out of his body. His flesh afterward showed markings that Rashi likens to coins, what we might describe as blotches, perhaps consistent with frostbite.

---

## Rav Sheshet & Trust

### Decline the Meal

The narrative shifts to Rav Sheshet, who was blind, and his interactions with the *Reish Galusa*'s household. When the *Reish Galusa* asked him why he had declined to eat at the household's table, Rav Sheshet replied without hesitation: *delo ma'alu avdei dechasidi eiver min hachai* — your servants are not trustworthy; they are suspect of tearing a limb from a living animal rather than producing properly prepared meat. The *Reish Galusa* challenged him: *mi yeimar* — who says so? Rav Sheshet replied: *hashta machveina lach* — I will demonstrate it to you now.

### Three-Leg Test

Rav Sheshet instructed his attendant to slip into the kitchen and steal one leg from the animal being prepared. When the servants then brought him a dismembered lamb, he had them place before him a full spread. They came with three legs, having failed to notice that one was missing. Rav Sheshet remarked: this animal had three legs? When they went and tore a leg off of another living animal to make up the count, Rav Sheshet had his attendant place the stolen leg on the table as well. He then observed: so this animal had five legs? The deception was fully exposed.

The episode illustrates with painful clarity the necessity of *mashgiach temidi* — constant supervision. Kosher establishments may operate with full integrity under normal conditions, yet the question is what happens when a shipment does not arrive, when a substitution must be made under pressure. The temptation to cut corners in such moments is precisely the vulnerability that requires constant oversight.

### Mashgiach Role

The *Reish Galusa*, rather than accepting Rav Sheshet's point as definitive, offered an alternative: let the preparations be done in front of Rav Sheshet himself, and he may supervise and eat. Rav Sheshet agreed to this arrangement.

### Dangerous Bone

A plate was set before him, and meat was brought out and placed at his place along with *ristana dechancha* — a particular bone near the thigh region which, Rashi explains, carries a small embedded bone capable of causing choking. The servants, now hostile after being publicly humiliated, were evidently hoping this bone would lodge in Rav Sheshet's throat. He sensed the danger before placing the meat in his mouth — apparently suspicious that they might attempt something — felt the piece carefully, identified it as the dangerous bone, and quietly wrapped it in his handkerchief, saying nothing.

When the meal ended, the servants accused him of having stolen a silver cup, using the charge as a pretext to search his belongings and expose what was wrapped in his handkerchief. They declared triumphantly: *chazi mar d'lo meichal ka be'ei ela l'tzaurin* — you see, you never intended to eat with us; you only came here to cause trouble.

### Disease Detection

Rav Sheshet responded that he had in fact eaten from the meat, but had detected from its taste that the piece he set aside had the flavor of *chivra* — a diseased, leprous quality. The servants denied this, insisting the animal had no such condition. Rav Sheshet told them: *bidku b'duchtei* — go examine the specific location on the animal where that piece came from, for Rav Chisda taught that *uchma b'chivra v'chivra b'uchma l'kishuta hu* — black spots on a white animal or white spots on a black animal indicate a diseased, *treif*-like condition. They examined the animal and found that Rav Sheshet was correct. Once again, the servants had been feeding guests from an animal with a problematic condition, and once again Rav Sheshet had caught them.

### Pit Trap Escape

As Rav Sheshet was departing from the *Reish Galusa*'s household, the servants dug a pit in his path and covered it with a mat, hoping he would lie down on it — as they suggested he do — and fall in. Rav Chisda, who was walking behind Rav Sheshet and could see, cleared his throat audibly — *nachar lei meachorei* — as a covert warning, since he apparently could not speak openly without risk.

Rav Sheshet, alerted, turned to a child traveling with him and asked: *psuk li psukecha* — tell me the verse you are studying. The child recited a verse from Shmuel 2: *neteh lecha al yeminecha o al semolecha* — turn to your right or to your left. Rav Sheshet understood the message and asked his attendant what he saw ahead. The attendant said: *tsifta deshadya* — a mat thrown on the ground. *Hadar minei* — go around it, Rav Sheshet instructed, and they did.

Afterward, Rav Chisda asked: how did you know there was danger? Rav Sheshet explained: your throat-clearing alerted me; the verse the child recited fit the situation exactly; and *de'chasidi avdei dela ma'alu* — I knew these servants were not to be trusted. Putting all those signs together, the conclusion was obvious.

---

## Demons & Shamir

### Singers vs Demons

The Gemara now turns to the world of *shedim*, entering through a verse in *Kohelet*: *asiti li sharim vesharot veta'anugot benei adam shida veshidot* — I made for myself male and female singers and all pleasures of humanity, *shida veshidot*. The Gemara parses the verse: *sharim vesharot* — male and female singers — refers to various types of music; *ta'anugot benei adam* — the pleasures of people — refers to pools and bathhouses. But what are *shida veshidot*?

Here the Gemara records a divergence between the Babylonian and Palestinian traditions. In Bavel, *hacha targimu shida veshidtin* — they translated it as male and female demons. In *Eretz Yisrael*, *amrei shidta* — the word denotes a kind of palanquin, a carriage. This divergence is not merely lexical; it reflects a broader cultural difference. The world of demons was far more prominent in the Babylonian *Gemara* than in the *Yerushalmi*, shaped by the surrounding Persian and Zoroastrian culture in which demonic figures played a significant role. The Roman milieu of *Eretz Yisrael* posed its own spiritual dangers, but demons were not their primary framework.

### Types of Demons

Rav Yochanan declares: *shlosh me'ot minei shedim hayu be'shichin* — there were three hundred different types of *shedim* in the place called Shichin. As for *shida* itself, Rav Yochanan says he does not fully know what it is — Rashi offering two readings: either that the nature of the *shed* remains uncertain to him, or that *shida* is the name of the mother or chief of all the *shedim*, and that identity he cannot determine.

### Building Challenge

The Gemara now explains why *Shlomo HaMelech* needed *shedim* at all. The verse in connection with the building of the *Beit HaMikdash* states that it was constructed with *even shlema masa* — whole, undressed stone — reflecting the prohibition of *lo tanif aleihem barzel* — you shall not raise iron over them. The rabbis therefore asked: how could the stonework of the Temple be accomplished without metal tools? The answer involves the *shamir* — a worm-like creature possessed of the capacity to split stone, which Moshe had used for the engraving of the names on the stones of the *ephod*, where similarly the stone had to remain whole while the letters were inscribed. The *shamir* would trace the path along the surface and the stone would crack along that line without being chipped, leaving the stone intact yet marked.

The *halakhic* question of whether iron implements were used outside the Temple precincts — at the quarry — and prohibited only within them is noted as a discussion among the *poskim*, but the Gemara's *aggadic* framework proceeds on the basis that the *shamir* was the operative solution.

### Finding Shamir

*Amru lei rabbanan* — the sages advised Shlomo: *ika shamira d'ayti Moshe l'avnei ephod* — there is the *shamir* that Moshe had for the stones of the *ephod*. But where is it now? *Heichi ishtakach?* They recommended: take a male and a female *shed* — *ayti shida v'shidtin* — press them against one another — *kavshinhu ahadadi* — cause them affliction — and *efshar d'yadei umaglu lach* — perhaps they will know and reveal it to you.

Shlomo had ordinary *shedim* at his disposal; capturing the king of demons would require a more elaborate stratagem. So he seized male and female *shedim* and coerced them. They responded: *anan lo yadinan* — we do not know. But, they said, *dilma Asmedai malka deshidi yada* — perhaps Ashmadai, the king of the *shedim*, knows. Shlomo asked: where is he? *Isei betur ploni* — at such and such a mountain. And here is what he does, which you may use to capture him.

### Ashmadai's Routine

Ashmadai digs for himself a pit — *karya lei bera* — fills it with water — *umali lei maya* — and covers it with a great rock — *umachsei lei betinra* — so that no one may tamper with his water supply. He seals it with his signet — *vachasmei begushpanka*. Every day he ascends to the heavenly *yeshiva* — *salik l'rakia v'gamar mesivta d'rakia* — and then descends to study in the earthly *yeshiva* as well — *v'gamar mesivta d'ara*. This dual engagement reflects the intermediate nature of *shedim*: they are partly human and partly divine, as the Gemara in *Berachot* notes that they resemble humans in three ways and angels in three. Having studied in both realms, Ashmadai returns, inspects his seal, uncovers the cistern, drinks, reseals, and departs.

---

## Capturing Ashmadai

### Well Scheme

Shlomo dispatched Benayahu ben Yehoyada, equipping him with a chain bearing the divine name — *shalshelta d'chakika aleh shem* — a signet ring also engraved with the divine name, bundles of wool, and skins of wine. Benayahu went to the mountain. He dug a pit below Ashmadai's cistern — *khara beira mittata'ei* — and opened a channel between them so the water from the upper cistern drained into the lower pit. He then stopped up the channel with wool — *vastminu b'gavvei d'amra* — so that the flow would not be visible. He then dug a pit above the cistern — *v'khara beira m'eila'ei* — and poured wine into it — *v'shafkhinu l'chamra* — so that the wine flowed down into the now-empty cistern. He then covered everything over so that no disturbance would be visible. He climbed a tree and waited.

### Wine Temptation

When Ashmadai returned, he inspected his seal, found it untampered, uncovered the cistern — and found wine where water had been. He immediately began to recite verses he had learned: *leitz hayayin homeh shechar v'chol shogeh bo lo yechkam* — wine is a mocker, strong drink is a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it will not be wise. And he cited the verse from Hoshea: *znus v'yayin v'tirosh yikach lev* — licentiousness and wine take away the heart. *Lo ishtei* — he would not drink. Yet *ki tzachi* — thirst overcame him, and *lo sagya leh* — he could not withstand it. He drank, became sated, and fell asleep.

It is worth noting the irony: just as new wine triggered the condition of *kordyakos* in a human being — diminishing his *da'as* — here the king of the *shedim* succumbs to wine despite his full awareness of its danger. And Ashmadai's refusal to drink was itself ironic: he was citing verses from *Kohelet*, the very book authored by Shlomo, whose name he would soon usurp.

### Chain Capture

Benayahu descended from the tree, approached, threw the chain around Ashmadai — *shada beh shalshelta* — and locked it. When Ashmadai woke and struggled — *hava ka mifarkes* — Benayahu told him: *shma d'marach alach* — the name of your Master is upon you. God's name on the chain held him, and he could not break free.

### Journey & Kindness

Benayahu now led Ashmadai back toward Shlomo. During the journey, as Ashmadai walked alongside or before his captor, he brushed against a palm tree and knocked it down — demonstrating the enormous physical force he contained even while restrained. He came close to a house and knocked it down as well simply by passing.
