When he came near the small hut of a widow who came out and implored him, he was moved by her entreaty — *itchanena leh* — and bent his enormous frame in the opposite direction to avoid harming her dwelling. In doing so he strained and broke a bone. He then cited the verse from *Kohelet*: *ulashon raka tishbor garem* — a soft tongue breaks a bone. He had been appeased by her gentle words, and look what it cost him.

---

## Ashmadai's Nature

### Acts of Kindness

Benayahu then began to ask Ashmadai about the curious behaviors he had observed along the way. Why, when you saw a blind man going astray on the path, did you set him right? Ashmadai replied: *machrezei aleih birki'a* — it was announced in heaven that *tzaddik gamur hu* — he was a completely righteous person, and *u'man de'avid leih nicha nafshia zachi le'alma de'ati* — anyone who did something good for him would merit a share in the world to come. Ashmadai, it seems, was not moved by compassion alone; he was moved by the knowledge, gained through his daily study in the heavenly *yeshiva*, of who this person was and what reward awaited those who helped him.

### Mortality Signs

Why, then, did you set right the drunk man who was wandering off the path? Here Ashmadai's answer was the reverse: *machrezei aleih birki'a de'rasha gamur hu* — it was announced in heaven that he was a completely wicked person. By doing him a kindness, Ashmadai ensured that he would receive his reward in this world — *ki heichi de'leikhalu le'alma* — so that in the world to come he would face only punishment, with no remaining merit to soften it. This reflects the classical *Chazal* understanding of *rasha ve'tov lo* — the wicked who prospers in this world is receiving his payment here, leaving nothing for the next.

The connection to *Kohelet* runs deep here. *Kohelet* wrestles with the apparent equivalence of *tzaddik* and *rasha*, the shared fate of the righteous and the wicked. Ashmadai's explanations pierce through that surface equivalence: the blind *tzaddik* and the wayward *rasha* receive the same outward act of assistance, but for entirely opposite reasons, with entirely opposite eschatological consequences.

Why did you weep at the wedding celebration? *Ba'ei mimat gavra be'go tlatin yomei* — the bridegroom is going to die within thirty days of the wedding. *U'va'ya mintar leih yavam katan* — and the bride will be bound in *yibbum* to a young brother-in-law who is still a baby, and she will wait thirteen years until he reaches adulthood to receive *chalitza* or *yibbum*. This too resonates with *Kohelet*'s *tov lalechet el beit avel milechet el beit mishteh* — better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting, for that is the end of all humanity. The wedding celebration conceals a coming tragedy that Ashmadai, with his heavenly knowledge, could already see.

Why did you laugh when the man ordered shoes to last for seven years? *Hahu shiva yomei leit leih masanei le'shava shanin ba'ei* — that man will not live seven more days; he is ordering shoes for seven years. Once more the theme: human beings make plans over vast horizons while they stand at the very edge of mortality.

Why did you laugh at the magician performing his divinations? *De'hava yativ avei gaza de'malka* — because he was sitting directly above a royal treasure buried in the earth beneath him, and he was attempting through his magic to discover hidden things — unable to find the treasure that lay immediately below him. *Liksum mai de'ika tuteih* — he should have tried to divine what was directly underfoot.

All of Ashmadai's observations during the journey function collectively as a kind of walking commentary on *Kohelet*: the vanity of human plans, the hidden decree of heaven, the tragic arc between celebration and mourning, the irony of the wise man who cannot see what is before him.

---

## Solomon's Fall

### Testing Power

Ashmadai was kept in Shlomo's presence even after the *shamir* had been obtained — perhaps to extract further heavenly knowledge, perhaps simply because Shlomo was reluctant to release him. One day they were sitting together, and Ashmadai posed a challenge. He cited the verse: *ke'to'afot re'em lo* — like the *to'afot* of the *re'em* are to God. The interpretation given is that *to'afot* refers to the ministering angels, and *re'em* refers to the *shedim*. So God is praised for his mastery over both angels and demons. Ashmadai then asked: *mai ravuteichu minan* — what makes you so much greater than us? How is it that God is praised for his dominion over you and over us together? You want to see how great I am? Take the chains off me. Give me your signet ring. *Ve'achvei lach ravutai* — I will show you my greatness.

### Casting Away

Shlomo removed the chains. He handed over the ring. Ashmadai swallowed Shlomo — or, as some versions read, swallowed the ring — spread one wing to the heavens and the other to the earth, spanning the full distance between them, and cast Shlomo *arba me'ah parsa* — four hundred *parasangs* away.

### Kohelet Realized

At that moment, Shlomo said the words of *Kohelet*: *mah yitron l'adam bechol amalo she'ya'amol tachas hashemesh* — what profit does a person have from all his labor under the sun? He had amassed everything — music, pleasure, wisdom, dominion over demons and kings — and a single moment of foolishness had stripped it all away. The verse *vezeh hayah chelki mikol amali* — this was my portion from all my labor — was interpreted by Rav and Shmuel as referring to what he had left: one opinion says *maklo*, his staff alone; the other says *gundo*, his cloak. After all his wealth, this was his portion.

---

## Solomon's Fall (II)

### Beggar King

Shlomo now wandered from door to door. *Kol heicha demati amar* — wherever he arrived, he would declare: *ani Kohelet hayisi melech al Yisrael biYerushalayim* — I, Kohelet, was once king over Israel in Jerusalem. The word *hayisi* — I used to be — is itself poignant: his very name had shifted; he was no longer Shlomo but Kohelet, the gatherer, the philosopher, now asking in exile what meaning underlies all human striving. The philosophizing of *Kohelet* takes on a new dimension here — it was born not from detached wisdom but from devastating loss. Only once he had been stripped of everything did the deep questions of the book become truly his own.

Meanwhile, Ashmadai was impersonating him in the palace.

---

## Impersonation Discovered

### Sanhedrin Inquiry

When Shlomo came before the Sanhedrin, the rabbis took note of something that did not fit the profile of genuine madness. *Shoteh bechada milta lo sarich* — a person who is genuinely deranged does not act sanely in all matters except one. Yet this man was entirely coherent in every regard, and his only apparent aberration was his insistence that he had once been Shlomo HaMelech. The sages recognized this inconsistency as grounds for investigation.

### Detection Methods

The rabbis asked Benayahu: *kabei lach malka legabei* — has the king summoned you recently? Benayahu replied that he had not been called to see the king in some time. They then sent word to the queens asking whether the king had visited them. The queens replied that yes, he had come. The rabbis then instructed the queens: *bidku bechar'ei* — examine his feet. The queens reported back that he keeps his feet covered at all times, wearing slippers in bed. Furthermore, they noted two profoundly disturbing behaviors: he was demanding relations even during *niddah*, and he had made advances toward Bat Sheva, his own mother. Something was deeply wrong.

### Restoration & Fear

The real Shlomo was brought back. He was given a signet ring and a chain engraved with the divine name — the same mechanism that had originally bound Ashmadai. When Shlomo entered, Ashmadai saw him and fled.

### Guards & Defense

Yet even after Ashmadai's flight, Shlomo was left with an ongoing fear — *havah lei bi'asusa minei* — a lasting dread of what Ashmadai could do. This explains the verse in *Kohelet*: *hinei mitaso shel Shlomo shishim giborim saviv lah migiborei Yisrael kulam achuzei cherev melumadei milchama ish charbo al yerecho mipachad baleilos* — behold, the bed of Shlomo, sixty warriors surrounding it from among the heroes of Israel, all grasping swords, trained in war, each man with his sword on his thigh because of the fear of the nights. That fear was the lingering shadow of Ashmadai.

---

## Final Status

### King or Beggar

The Gemara closes with a dispute between Rav and Shmuel. *Chad amar melech vehedyot* — one holds that Shlomo was first a king and then became a commoner, and never again regained his throne. *Vechad amar melech vehedyot umelech* — the other holds that he was king, then commoner, then king again, meaning the restoration described above represents a genuine return to his former status.

According to the first opinion, Shlomo spent the rest of his life wandering, declaring to anyone who would listen that he had once been king over Israel — a *Kohelet* indeed, gathering the meaning of everything he had lost, asking *mah yitron* with no answer forthcoming. According to the second opinion, the story has a restoration, though one shadowed permanently by fear. Either way, the lens through which the Gemara reads *Kohelet* is now fully in view: the book is not merely abstract philosophy, but the utterance of a man who had touched the heights of human achievement and learned from catastrophic personal experience that it could vanish in a moment.

---

---

# Gittin 69

## Blood/Migraine Remedies

### Blood in Head

The daf opens in the middle of an extended discussion of various *refuot* — medical treatments and remedies — that the Gemara presents in connection with a Mishnah dealing with a particular figure. We pick up following a remarkable *agadata* concerning Shlomo HaMelech and Ashmedai, and now arrive at the practical medical material beginning near the bottom of 68b.

*L'dama d'reisha* — for blood in the head — the Gemara prescribes an elaborate herbal preparation. One should bring *shorvina*, *vina*, fresh myrtle (*asa*), olives, poplar, sea willow, and cynodon, and boil them all together. The resulting mixture is then poured in 300 cups over one side of the head and 300 cups over the other side. Should this prove insufficient, one brings a white rose — specifically one where all the petals grow on a single side, as Rashi explains — boils it, and pours 60 cups of that mixture over each side of the head.

### Migraine Treatment

For *tzilchata* — which Rashi describes as a pain in half of the head, and which Koren translates as a migraine — the treatment is of a different character entirely. One takes a wild rooster and slaughters it with a sharpened silver coin (*zuza chivra*) on the side of the head where the pain is located. One must take great care that the blood does not enter the eyes, as Rashi warns it will cause blindness. The carcass is then hung on the doorpost so that one brushes up against it both upon entering and upon leaving the house, and that contact is understood to provide the therapeutic benefit.

## Eye Diseases

### Cataracts

At the top of 69a, the Gemara turns to eye diseases. For *frukita* — an eye ailment that Rashi identifies and which appears to correspond to something like cataracts — the treatment involves a scorpion. One takes a seven-colored scorpion, which Rashi understands to mean a very old one, and dries it out in the shade. One then grinds together two portions of *kuchla* — the substance used for eye application — and one portion of the powdered scorpion. Three applications of this mixture are placed in each eye using an eyebrush. The Gemara adds a clear warning: no more than three applications should be used, because too much will cause the eye to burst.

### Night Blindness

For *shavrire de-leilya* — night blindness — the Gemara prescribes an elaborate ritual that combines physical actions with incantation. One brings a rope made of animal hair, ties one end to one's own leg and the other end to the leg of a dog, and has a child follow behind banging on a pottery shard while reciting that the dog is old and the rooster is foolish. Seven pieces of raw meat are then collected from seven different houses, with the owners of each house placing the meat into the socket of their doorpost. The patient eats these pieces at the refuse heap of the city. Afterward, the rope is untied, and an incantation is recited in which the blindness of so-and-so son of so-and-so is declared to have departed from the patient and to have passed instead into the eyes of the dog. The treatment concludes by blowing into the pupils of the dog's eyes.

It is worth noting that the Gemara here clearly incorporates what it understood as incantation alongside physical remedies — presumably invoking some force associated with *shedim* or related phenomena. The Gemara evidently did not regard all of this as purely medical science in our sense of the term.

### Day Blindness

For *shavrire de-yami* — day blindness — one takes seven animal spleens from the innards of animals and roasts them on the pottery vessel used by a bloodletter to collect blood. The patient sits inside the house while another person sits outside. The blind person calls out to the outside person asking for food, and the outside person responds, handing him the meat to eat. After eating, the pottery must be broken, because if it is not, the condition will return.

## Nosebleed Remedies

### Nosebleed Treatment

For *dama de-asi mi-nichiri* — a nosebleed — the Gemara offers a graduated series of remedies of increasing complexity. First, a Kohen whose name is Levi should write the word *Levi* backwards. If that does not help, any ordinary man should write the phrase *ana Papi Shila bar Sumkei* — "I am Papi Shila bar Sumkei" — backwards. If that too fails, he should write the following words: *aton deli bemei chasaf, aton deli bemei pgam* — formulaic phrases about drawing from a bucket in silver water and in spoiled water.

If none of these inscriptions succeeds, the treatment becomes more physically involved. One takes the root of fodder, a rope from an old bed, a type of paper, saffron, and the red of a palm branch, burns them all together, takes a cluster of wool, spins two threads from it, soaks them in vinegar, rolls them in the ashes of the burned mixture, and places them in the nostrils. This is the first remedy in the sequence that involves actually introducing something into the nose.

Should that also fail, one finds a water conduit flowing from east to west and straddles it — one foot on each bank. One picks up a piece of clay with the right hand and holds it under the left arm, and simultaneously picks up another piece of clay with the left hand and holds it under the right arm. Two threads of wool are spun, submerged in this clay, and placed in the nostrils.

And if even that proves ineffective, the patient should sit beneath a drainpipe. Water is poured through the pipe so that it hits him, and he recites: just as this water has stopped flowing, so too may the blood of so-and-so son of so-and-so cease.

### Mouth Blood Diagnosis

For *dama de-asi mi-puma* — blood coming from the mouth — the Gemara first prescribes a diagnostic test before any treatment. A straw of wheat is introduced into the mouth to examine the blood. If the blood is viscous and sticky (*sarich*), it is coming from the *reeya* — the lungs — and there is a remedy. If it is not sticky and flows freely, it is coming from the *kavda* — the liver — and there is no remedy.

### Treifa Dispute

This diagnostic conclusion prompts an important exchange. Rav Ami challenges Rav Ashi: you are saying that blood from the lung is more treatable than blood from the liver, but this seems to contradict what we know from the laws of *treifa*. Regarding an animal, if the liver is removed entirely and nothing remains, it is a *treifa*. But a punctured or partially missing lung also renders the animal a *treifa*, and relatively minor damage to the lung is more significant halakhically than partial damage to the liver. So it would seem the lung is the more vulnerable organ — how can you say that lung bleeding is more treatable?

Rav Ashi responds by distinguishing the cases. The law of *treifa* addresses what we find when we open the animal and examine it — and indeed, if some liver remains, the animal is not a *treifa*. But when a person is spitting blood from the mouth, we are concerned that the liver has already dissolved entirely, which is why there is no remedy. So the comparison is not to partial liver damage but to total dissolution. The two cases are not parallel.

### Lung Bleeding

Now the Gemara returns to ask: what is the remedy when the blood is determined to be coming from the lungs? One brings seven handfuls of chopped beet (*silka*), seven handfuls of chopped leek (*karti*), five handfuls of a grass (*frada* according to Rashi), three handfuls of lentils (*talpachi*), a handful of cumin (*kamuna*), a handful of rope (*chavli*), and equal to the entire combined amount, the entrails (*kinsha petirta*) of a firstborn animal — Rashi explains this as the *peter rechem*. All of this is cooked together, eaten, and followed by drinking strong beer (*shichra charifa*).

## Tooth/Gum Care

### Toothache

For *kucha* — tooth pain — Rabba bar bar Chana states: take a single garlic bulb, specifically one in which only a single clove grew, as Rashi explains — though the practical difficulty of obtaining such a thing is evident. Grind it with olive oil and salt, and apply it to the thumbnail of the side of the body that is experiencing the pain. Then surround the thumbnail with a rim of dough as a barrier. One must be careful that the preparation does not touch the flesh directly, as it can cause boils.

### Gum Disease

For *chinchei* — a problem with the gums — Rabbi Yochanan prescribes *chumsei*, a plant similar to *mamru*, and notes that the root of *chumsei* is even more effective than *mamru* itself. This is placed in the mouth, and it serves to prevent the gum problem from spreading. That is the formula for *le-ukmei* — containing the disease. However, if the goal is *le-vshulei* — to draw the pus together so that it can be drained, as Rashi explains — one takes bran from the top of a sieve, lentils with the dirt they came from, fenugreek (*tavlulita*), and a piece of the hop plant (*chumasta de-chashuta*), combines them, and places an amount the size of a nut in the mouth.

### Gum Blister

If one then wishes to open the blister that has formed — *liftochi* — a friend blows a white seed through a straw of wheat, using it as a pea shooter aimed at the blister to cause it to burst. Once it has burst, for the purpose of healing and scabbing over — *le-asokei* — one takes dirt from the shade beneath an outhouse, kneads it with honey, and eats it, as this is said to be beneficial.

## Birsam Disease

### Birsam (Ammonia/Galbanum)

For *birsam* — an ailment that Rashi describes as coming to the head through the nose — the primary remedy involves the following preparation: a nut-sized amount of *nishtor*, which Jastrow identifies as ammonia and Rashi calls *ammonica*; a nut-sized amount of sweet galbanum (*chalbinisa dushana*); a spoonful of white honey; and a full measure of a vessel from Mechuza — which Rashi says held a *revi'is* — of clear wine. All of these are cooked together. One knows everything is properly cooked when the ammonia is done, since that ingredient takes the longest.

### Birsam (Milk Alternative)

If that does not work, one takes a *revi'is* of milk from a white goat and stirs three stalks of cabbage into it, using a twig of *maharmin* — apparently marjoram — as the stirring implement. Again, the dish is considered fully prepared when the marjoram twig is cooked through.

### Birsam (Excrement)

If that alternative also proves ineffective, one takes the excrement of a white dog and mixes it with balm. The Gemara adds a notable warning: as much as possible, one should avoid relying on this remedy, because overuse of it causes a separation of the limbs. The Gemara clarifies that this means the remedy does work and is to be consumed, but one should exhaust every other option first, given the dangerous side effect of excess use.

## Internal Ailments

### Gira Pain

For *gira* — described as a stinging pain — one takes a *gira de-lilasa*, which Rashi explains is a hailstone shaped like an arrow associated with Lilith, some form of demonic being. One turns it so that the point faces downward, pours water over it, and drinks the water. If that does not suffice, one takes water that a dog drank from at night and uses that — though one must be particularly careful to keep this water covered, since leaving things uncovered is in general problematic, and in this case may be especially dangerous.

### Uncovered Water

If one has already drunk uncovered water — *giluya* — the remedy is to drink a measure of *chamra chaya*, undiluted raw wine. For a blister or pustular sore (*mursa*), one drinks a *revi'is* of wine mixed with the plant *ahala tulana*.

### Heart Palpitations

For *pircha de-liba* — a fluttering or lightness of the heart — one takes three barley loaves, soaks them in *kimcha*, a yogurt-like substance that is no more than 40 days old, eats them, and then drinks diluted wine.

### Heart Remedy Dispute

Rav Acha of Difti raises an objection to Ravina: surely drinking diluted wine will only increase the fluttering of the heart, since such foods are considered light and would exacerbate rather than ground the condition. Ravina responds that the remedy he had described was actually for *yukra de-liba* — heaviness of the heart, not lightness. For heaviness, one wants precisely these lighter preparations — the barley loaves, the yogurt, and the diluted wine — to produce more lightness.

### Heart Pain

For *pircha de-liba* — the actual lightness — heavier foods are called for. One takes three wheat loaves rather than barley, soaks them in honey rather than yogurt, eats them, and then drinks *chamra chaya*, raw undiluted wine, rather than diluted wine.

### Heart Pain

For *tzircha de-liba* — pain in the heart — one takes three egg-worths of mint (*ninya*), one egg-worth of cumin, and one egg-worth of sesame, and eats them.

### Stomach Ache

For *kev maya* — a stomach ache — one takes 300 *pilpali arichta*, long peppers, and each day drinks 100 of them prepared with wine, doing this for three days. The Gemara notes that Ravina of Narsh made this remedy for the daughter of Rav Ashi, using only 150 of the Babylonian variety of pepper — which were apparently more potent than those of Eretz Yisrael — and she was healed.

### Roundworm

For *kirtza* — roundworm — one drinks a *revi'is* of wine in laurel leaves. For *kirtza chivra* — white worm specifically — one brings *bizra galglai*, cress seeds, ties them in a piece of cloth, soaks the bundle in water, and drinks the water. One must take great care not to consume the seed itself, because if one swallows the seed it will puncture the intestine.

### Bowel Remedies

For *maser* — the need to bind or stop diarrhea — one eats fresh, wet *sisin*, chamomile, in water. For *mishra* — the opposite problem, constipation requiring loosening of the bowels — one uses dried chamomile soaked in water rather than fresh. The Gemara offers a mnemonic: wet grass is used to dam rivers. Hence, wet chamomile stops flow, and dried chamomile releases it.

## Spleen Remedies

### Leeches Remedy

For *techla* — a disease of the spleen — the Gemara prescribes a graduated series of treatments, paralleling the structure seen earlier for the nosebleed. One begins by taking seven water leeches (*bani de-maya*), drying them out in the shade, and drinking two and a third each day with wine for three days. The Gemara notes in passing that some of the remedies across this entire sugya involve non-kosher materials — water leeches being one example — but since these illnesses were understood to be potentially life-threatening, presenting a consideration of *sakanas nefashos*, the Gemara records these treatments as valid.

### Goat Spleen (Oven)

If that does not work, one takes the spleen (*techla*) of a female goat that has never given birth (*shakun* as Rashi understands it), places it in the oven to dry out, and stands near it reciting: just as this spleen is drying out, so may the spleen of so-and-so son of so-and-so dry out.

### Goat Spleen (Bricks)

If that proves insufficient, one places the goat spleen between the bricks of a new house and recites the same incantation — the same logic of sympathetic drying applied through a different medium.

### Dead Hand Remedy

If still ineffective, one locates someone who died on Shabbat (*shichiv be-Shabbat*), takes that person's hand (*yad shachufa*), places it on the spleen of the sick person, and recites: just as this hand has dried, so may the spleen of so-and-so son of so-and-so dry.

### Blacksmith Water

If that does not work, one takes a fish, roasts it at the house of a blacksmith (*beit naphcha*), eats it with the water from the blacksmith's workshop, and drinks that water as well. The Gemara adduces an empirical proof for the efficacy of blacksmith water: there was a certain goat that regularly drank the runoff water from a blacksmith's shop, and when it was slaughtered, no spleen was found in it. The blacksmith water had evidently caused the spleen to disappear entirely — a striking piece of evidence that the Gemara brings to validate this remedy.

### Wine Barrel/Health

If none of the preceding remedies succeeds, one should open a new barrel of wine (*chavita dechamra*) for the sake of the sick person and drink liberally from it. Rava bar Rav objects to Rav Ashi that this remedy is impractical: if the patient had an entire barrel of wine available to him, he would not have needed to seek out the other remedies in the first place, since wine was understood as a reliable cure but required a substantial quantity. The Gemara concludes with a more general piece of advice: eating bread in the morning is beneficial for the whole body — a remark that seems to transcend the specific treatment for the spleen and offers general counsel for maintaining health.

---

---

# Gittin 70

## Medical Remedies

### Hemorrhoids Remedy

The daf opens with a series of medical remedies, beginning with a treatment for *leruchshasa* — hemorrhoids or a related condition in that area. The prescribed compound involves acacia wood, aloe, mercury (or, as Rashi understands it, raw silver, perhaps quicksilver), a silver dross, a small perfume vial containing an aromatic liquid mixture, and dog excrement. All of these are to be wrapped together in worn-out flax cloths — in summer using those cloths directly, and in winter or fall using cotton. Presumably the resulting package is applied to the affected area, though the Gemara does not spell this out explicitly. If this treatment proves unavailable or ineffective, the Gemara offers the considerably simpler alternative of drinking diluted beer.

### Hip Weakness

For *shiggrona* — a weakness or illness of the thighs or hips — the Gemara prescribes a pot full of fish brine. Rashi defines the vessel as one filled with *tzir dagim*, fish juice. The treatment involves rubbing it sixty times on one side and sixty times on the other.

### Bladder Stones

For *tzamirta* — a stone lodged in the bladder — the remedy calls for three drops of liquefied tar, three drops of leek juice, and three drops of clear wine. For a man, this mixture is applied to his member; for a woman, to the corresponding area. If that does not resolve matters, the next step is to take the ear of a pitcher and suspend it in the appropriate place — on the man's member, and for a woman on her breasts. If that still fails, one procures a purple string that was spun by a woman of ill repute, the daughter of a woman of ill repute, and suspends it in the same manner.

### Genital Ailments

If none of the above treatments work, the Gemara prescribes obtaining a louse — understood to mean one taken from a man and one from a woman, not a male and female louse per se — and applying it to the genital area. Additionally, when the afflicted person needs to urinate, they should do so onto a dried thorn bush near the doorpost frame, and then observe the stone that passes. The Gemara notes that such a stone, if retrieved, has health benefits for all manner of *tzimra*, fever.

For *tzimra barana* — an external fever, possibly a surface condition — the treatment involves three sacks of date pits and three sacks of alder leaves, each boiled separately. The person sits between the boiling vessels, then stands over one and bends toward the other, alternating, until sweating begins, at which point one bathes in the liquid. The Gemara adds an important warning: when one drinks from these preparations, drink from the alder-leaf water, not from the date-pit water — because the date-pit water causes sterility.

For *tzimra gavna*, an internal fever, one takes seven handfuls of beets from seven different garden rows, together with their soil, eats them, and then drinks alder leaves steeped in beer. Alternatively, one may drink or eat grapes from a vine that grew around a palm tree beside water.

### Skin Lesions

For *chazizta* — a skin lesion, something resembling anthrax — seven kernels of a particularly large type of wheat (*arzanita*, according to Rashi) are burned on a new iron hoe, allowing a liquid to emerge from them, which is then rubbed onto the affected area.

### Rav Shimi Case

The Gemara records that Rav Shimi bar Rav Ashi — the son of Rav Ashi — applied precisely this wheat-kernel ointment to a non-Jew (*nochri*) who suffered from a condition described obliquely as *davar acher*, leprosy, and the man was healed. This brief narrative closes out what is evidently a self-contained collection of anonymous remedies, likely originating in the circle of Ravina and Rav Ashi, as is indicated by the Gemara's own internal evidence: at one point Ravina himself clarifies his own position within the discussion. The style of this collection — formulaic, anonymous, and structured as "for this disease, do this" — stands in marked contrast to what follows.

---

## Fatal Conditions

### Persian Spear Poison

With the transition to named *amoraim* and a more narrative register, the Gemara shifts to a different category: not cures for recoverable ailments, but palliative care for conditions that are definitively fatal. Shmuel states that a person pierced by a Persian spear — whose tip was coated with poison — will not survive. However, in the time remaining, one should give him fatty roasted meat and raw wine; this may extend his life somewhat. The benefit of this extension is explicitly stated: it gives him enough lucidity to instruct his household and put his affairs in order — to give his last will and testament.

### Wasp Ingestion

Similarly, Ravidi bar Avin teaches that if a person swallows a wasp, he will not live. In the interim, however, he should drink a *revi'it* of *shamzag* — a particularly potent type of vinegar — which may keep him alive a little longer, long enough to make arrangements for his household. The underlying assumption is that a wasp, which causes severe damage through its sting on the outside of the body, would be catastrophically destructive from within.

---

## Diet & Prevention

### Beef & Moonlight

The Gemara now turns from emergency palliative measures to preventative medicine — identifying behaviors and foods that are dangerous and conditions to be avoided. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches: if a person eats beef (*basar shor*) together with a turnip (*lefet*), and then sleeps outdoors in the moonlight on the fourteenth or fifteenth of the month — the full moon — during the summer months (*tekufat Tammuz*), he will be seized by *achilu*. The Gemara will shortly explain what *achilu* is.

### Overeating Debate

The Gemara appends a *tanna*'s teaching: one who stuffs his stomach with any food whatsoever is likewise subject to *achilu*. Rav Pappa adds that this applies even if the overeating is with dates. The Gemara challenges this: is that not obvious, given that the teaching said "any food"? The Gemara explains that one might have thought dates are exempt, since the tradition praises them as a superfood — they cause satiety, they warm the body, they aid digestion, they strengthen, and they do not ruin the palate. One might therefore have supposed that dates, possessing all these remarkable properties, do not carry this risk. Rav Pappa therefore teaches us: even with dates, overstuffing oneself can bring on *achilu*.

The Gemara asks: what is *achilu*? Rabbi Elazar explains it as *eshet shel atzamot* — a fire of the bones. Abaye then glosses that with *eshet garmi* — which is simply the Aramaic equivalent, a fire of the bones. The Soncino suggests this may be arthritis, and the logic is not implausible: the heavier one becomes from overeating, the harder the joints must work to support the additional weight, and the worse the arthritic condition becomes.

### Achilu Treatment

The Gemara asks: what is the remedy? Abaye reports in the name of his mother — understood to mean his nursemaid — a comprehensive principle: all medicinal drinks are typically administered for a set period of three, seven, or twelve days; but the treatment for this *achilu* must continue until it is fully healed. Moreover, while all other medicinal drinks are taken on an empty stomach, this one is different.

The treatment is as follows: after eating and drinking a meal, the patient goes to the bathroom, relieves himself, comes out, and washes his hands. He is then given a fistful of lentil powder (*shasisa*), some sort of lentil-salt porridge, together with a fistful of aged wine. These are kneaded together and eaten — on a full stomach, after relieving oneself. The patient then wraps himself in his blanket and lies down to sleep; nobody should wake him until he rises on his own. When he does get up, he must make sure to remove the blanket immediately. If the blanket stays on him even after he wakes, the illness will return.

### Two-Thirds Full

The Gemara records that Eliyahu advised Rav Nassan: eat a third of your capacity, drink another third, and leave the final third empty — do not fill yourself completely. The rationale given is that when you become angry, your anger fills your belly; if the stomach is already full, the resulting tension may cause internal damage. The broader principle is one of calorie restriction: it is not merely a question of managing weight, but a more fundamental teaching about longevity. Indeed, the Rambam likewise rules that one should not eat until full. Studies on calorie restriction in animal populations have consistently shown significant extensions of lifespan, and researchers believe the same principle, applied to humans, could dramatically extend the human lifespan.

### Stomach Health

Rabbi Chiya taught in a *baraita*: one who wishes to avoid intestinal illness should make a habit of dipping foods in something — vinegar, oil, or the like — both in summer and in winter. At a meal that is particularly pleasurable, one should withdraw one's hand before eating one's fill. And one should never delay relieving oneself when the need arises. This last point is also recorded by the Rambam. These teachings from Rabbi Chiya belong to an earlier stratum than the extended anonymous remedies that opened the daf; their character is more that of general health advice than specific cures, and they are correspondingly more transparent and intuitive. The Rambam's general skepticism about the medical remedies in the Gemara — he regarded the rabbis as not being physicians, and therefore did not treat their remedies as normative — makes more sense when applied to the elaborate, often opaque prescriptions from earlier in the daf than to these straightforward principles. Notably, virtually none of this material appears in the *Shulchan Aruch*; whatever does survive in normative *halacha* was preserved selectively by the Rambam.

---

## Sexual Health

### White Wine Disease

Mar Ukva teaches that one who drinks inferior white wine (*tilaya chivra*) will be seized by a disease called *vitak*.

### Wine Quality

Rav Hisda elaborates: there are sixty types of wine in the world. The finest of all is red aromatic wine (*sumka richana*); the worst of all is precisely this inferior white wine.

### Morning Warmth

Rav Yehuda adds another cause of *vitak*: sitting in the mornings of Nisan beside a fire, rubbing oneself with oil, and then going outside to sit in the sun.

### Bloodletting Effect

A *baraita* teaches: one who lets blood and then has intercourse will have children who are *vitakin* — weak, a general sapping of their constitution. The Gemara understands *vitak* to describe a condition of pronounced weakness, and sees it as reflecting the state of the parents at the time of conception: after bloodletting, the body's strength is depleted, and that depletion is somehow transmitted to the child. If both parents had let blood before intercourse, the children will be still weaker, afflicted with *ra'atan*.

### Eating Mitigation

Rav Pappa qualifies this: the concern applies only when the person did not eat anything after letting blood. If one ate something between the bloodletting and the intercourse, the problem does not arise — a sensible precaution, corresponding to the contemporary practice of providing food to blood donors immediately after donation.

### Travel Exhaustion

Rava bar Rav Huna adds that if one engages in intercourse immediately upon returning from a long journey — when the body has been worn down by the physical exertion of travel — the children will similarly be *vitakin*, weakened.

### Bathroom Waiting

A *baraita* teaches that one who has just returned from the bathroom should not engage in intercourse until a time equivalent to walking half a *mil* has elapsed — roughly nine minutes or so. The reason given is that the *shed* of the bathhouse, the demon associated with that space, accompanies the person for a period of time after leaving. One should not engage in intimacy while that spirit is still attached.

One might ask how much of this translates into normative *halacha*. The principle *chamira sakanta me'isura* — that danger is treated more strictly than prohibition — would suggest these matters deserve serious consideration. However, a glance at the marginal notes confirms that virtually none of this is codified in the *Shulchan Aruch*, and the Rambam was highly selective.

### Standing Position

Another *baraita*: one who engages in intercourse while standing will be seized by *avit* — Rashi identifies this as *karnafa*, some form of spasms or cramps. If one does so while seated, one will be seized by *dulyaria* — delirium, or possibly the variant reading *uleria*. Similarly, if the woman is on top and the man below, the same *dulyaria* results. The Gemara notes that there are other discussions elsewhere concerning the effects of different positions on the nature of children conceived; here the concern is specifically for the health of the participants.

### Delirium Treatment

The Gemara asks: what is *dulyaria*? Rather than defining it, the Gemara provides the remedy: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says the cure for *dulyaria* is *dardura*. Abaye explains that *dardura* is *morika dechuchei* — a type of saffron that grows among thorns. Rav Pappa would chew it and swallow it; Rav Pappi would chew it and spit it out.

### Sexual Weakness

Abaye then teaches: one who is not capable (*baki bederech eretz*) — which Rashi understands to mean one who is too weak for intercourse — should take three *kafizim* of *kortamei dechuchei*, which Rashi again identifies as a saffron variety, growing from soil that has been fertilized with sheep dung. Tosafot explains that three *kafizim* equals three-quarters of a *log*. This is ground, boiled in wine, and drunk. Rabbi Yochanan testifies: this is what restored me to the strength of my youth — and Rashi specifies that this refers to his capacity for sexual intercourse.

---

## Health Principles

### Three Weakeners

The Gemara now moves to a series of general health principles structured as numbered lists. Three things weaken a person's strength: *pachad* — anxiety or fear; *derech* — travel; and *avon* — sin, or, as Tosafot suggests, anxiety over sin. Each is supported by a *pasuk*: for anxiety, "my heart has fluttered, my strength has abandoned me"; for travel, "God has sapped my strength on the path"; for sin, "my strength has stumbled through my sin."

### Three Shattering

Three things shatter the body: eating while standing, drinking while standing, and engaging in intercourse while standing.

### Five Fatal Things

Five things bring a person closer to death than to life: eating and then immediately standing up, drinking and then immediately standing up, letting blood and then immediately standing up, sleeping and then suddenly getting up, and having intercourse and then immediately standing up. The implication is not necessarily literal death, but that one will feel devastatingly ill.

### Six Lethal Acts

Six acts, performed in sequence, bring about actual death: coming home exhausted from a journey, letting blood, entering a bathhouse, drinking, becoming intoxicated, sleeping on the ground, and then having intercourse. If one performs all six in precisely that order, the outcome is death.

### Order Requirement

Rabbi Yochanan qualifies: it must be in exactly that order. Abaye adds: in that order, one dies; in a different order, one merely becomes seriously weakened. The Gemara then asks whether this is really true and cites a case: a woman named Me'arat did three of these things to her servant and he died. The Gemara deflects: that servant was already of a weak constitution to begin with.

### Eight Moderation

Eight things are harmful in large quantities but beneficial in small amounts: travel; *derech eretz* (sexual intercourse); wealth; work; wine; sleep; hot water (both for bathing and drinking, according to Rashi); and bloodletting. One might wonder whether the inclusion of wealth and work is a health statement or a moral-religious one. A little wealth is good — enough to meet one's needs and have modest comfort. Too much wealth, however, leads to indulgence and, critically, crowds out *Torah* study. Similarly, a certain amount of work is healthy; excessive work is harmful.

### Eight Semen

Eight things diminish semen production: salt, famine, a certain skin disease (*netek*), crying, sleeping on the ground, coriander (*gadgedaniyot*, which the Gemara identifies with *gad ha-sadeh*), and hops (*chsus*) consumed out of season. The Gemara adds that bloodletting from the lower part of the body — below the testicles — is doubly bad, as bad as any two of the items on this list, while bloodletting from the upper body is doubly beneficial.

A *baraita* confirms: just as lower-body bloodletting is doubly harmful, upper-body bloodletting is doubly beneficial. Rav Pappa defines the dividing line as the testicles. Regarding hops specifically: the Gemara teaches that just as hops out of season (*shelo bizmanah*) are harmful, hops in their proper season (*bizmanah*) are beneficial for the body. Rav Pappa defines the proper season as Tammuz — summer; the improper season as Teves — winter; and the months of Nisan and Tishrei — spring and fall — as neutral, neither beneficial nor harmful.

---

## Get & Seizure

### Mishna Case

The Gemara now returns to the *mishna*. The case: a husband instructs that a *get* be written for his wife, then is seized by *kordaikos*, and in that state retracts his instruction, saying not to write it. The *mishna* rules: his last words mean nothing. This is a striking ruling. It is one thing to say that the retraction during the seizure carries no weight. It is quite another — and a significant *chiddush* — to say that we proceed without any concern whatsoever for that retraction, and that the wife will be *vadai megureshet*, definitively divorced. The implication is that statements made during a *kordaikos* episode are entirely disregarded; the person in that state is not considered a *bar daas* whose expressed will has legal significance.

### Write Timing

Reish Lakish holds: the *get* is written and delivered immediately — even while the husband is still in the midst of the *kordaikos* episode — on the basis of his original instruction before the fit. Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: the *get* is written only once he recovers. Rabbi Yochanan does not mean that after recovery one must ask him again whether he still wishes to give a *get* — if that were so, the *mishna*'s ruling that the retraction counts for nothing would be superfluous. Rather, Rabbi Yochanan holds that the *get* can only be executed when the husband is a *bar daas*, a person of sound legal mind. His retraction during the episode is null, but the *get* itself cannot be written or given while he lacks that status.

The mechanism underlying Rabbi Yochanan's position is the principle of *shelichus*: an agent (*shaliach*) acts on behalf of the principal, and the rule is *kol milsa de'ihu lo matzi avid, shaliach lo matzi avid* — whatever the principal himself could not do, the agent cannot do on his behalf. This refers not to physical incapacity but to *halachic* incapacity. The husband, during his *kordaikos* episode, lacks the halachic standing to deliver a *get* himself; therefore his agent cannot deliver it for him either. Notably, this is different from physical paralysis: one who is physically unable to hand over the *get* can still appoint an agent, because physical disability does not affect one's *halachic* capacity. Only a deficit in *halachic* capacity — in *da'at* — prevents the use of an agent.

### Sleeping vs Shote

What is the root of the dispute? Reish Lakish compares the *kordaikos* victim to a sleeping person. A person who is asleep is temporarily unconscious and not in control of his *da'at*, but *begavra* — as a legal entity — he remains a *bar daas*. Rabbi Yochanan compares him to a *shote*, one who is genuinely of unsound mind and who is not considered a *bar daas* as a personal status.

The Gemara probes: why does Rabbi Yochanan not simply compare the case to a sleeping person? Because a person who is sleeping is not lacking any further act (*lo mechusar ma'aseh*) — he will simply wake up naturally, and his current unconsciousness does not change his legal status. The *kordaikos* patient, by contrast, is *mechusar maysa* — he lacks a treatment; his condition will not resolve on its own. That dependency on external treatment is what defines his status.

Conversely, why does Reish Lakish not compare the case to a *shote*? Because a *shote*'s condition is not in our hands to cure (*lo sami b'yadan*). The *shote* has no available remedy; his diminished status is effectively permanent or at least beyond our intervention. The *kordaikos* patient, however, does have a remedy in our hands (*sami b'yadan*): and here the earlier material pays off. The Gemara has just spent considerable time establishing a treatment for *kordaikos* — fatty roasted meat and diluted wine. The point of all that earlier medical material now becomes clear: we know that this condition is treatable, and therefore it does not define the person's status as a permanent *gavra* who lacks *da'at*. This is a fascinating conceptual question: at what point does a person's current state of mind define their *halachic* status as a legal entity, rather than merely representing a temporary condition that does not affect who they are?

### Treatability Test

The Gemara then considers a practical implication of Rabbi Yochanan's position. If the husband gives the instruction to write the *get*, is then seized by *kordaikos*, and never recovers, the *get* can according to Rabbi Yochanan never be delivered — the wife remains in legal limbo indefinitely. That consequence is precisely correct on Rabbi Yochanan's view.

The Gemara also notes that there is no expiration on the original *tzivuy* — the husband's instruction. As long as he has not retracted it while he was a *bar daas*, the instruction stands. The difficulty arises only at the moment of delivery: if at that moment the husband is not a *bar daas* as a status, no delivery can take place on his behalf.

---

## Mortal Wounds

### Slit Throat

The Gemara introduces a *baraita* cited by Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: if a person has had both his trachea and esophagus slit — or the majority of each — and he indicates (by gesture, since he presumably cannot speak) that a *get* should be written for his wife, it may be written and delivered. The clear motivation is to make the wife a *grusha* rather than an *almanah*, so that she need not worry about *yibum*.

This prompts a question on Rabbi Yochanan's position. Just as the *kordaikos* patient is *mechusar maysa* — lacking a treatment — so too is the person with a slit throat: his condition is certainly fatal and will not resolve. Should we not therefore say he lacks the status of a *bar daas* and the *get* cannot be written? Moreover, a further *baraita* teaches that even a person who was witnessed in a dismembered state (*meguyod*) or crucified (*tzaluv*), and who indicates that a *get* be written, may have the *get* written and delivered. These appear to be cases where the person is unambiguously dying and — one might think — will imminently lose coherent *da'at*.

The Gemara's answer is that these cases are distinguishable from *kordaikos*. In the case of the dying person — whether from a slit throat or from crucifixion — *chaziman da'atei tziluta*: we observe that their mind remains clear. Even if the person is physically incapacitated, wracked by pain, or unable to speak clearly, this is attributed to *kechishuta* — bodily weakness — rather than to any confusion or loss of mental capacity. The dying person retains *da'at* even as their body fails. The *kordaikos* patient is different: *da'atei shagishta* — his mind is actively confused. He is awake, but his thinking is disordered. It is this confusion of the mind — not physical weakness — that removes his status as a *bar daas*. Hence the cases of the mortally wounded, the dismembered, and the crucified are all in a different category and do not challenge Rabbi Yochanan's ruling.

### Death Testimony

This leads to a question on Shmuel's own position. Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel elsewhere: if a person has had both trachea and esophagus slit and then fled — presumably on a wagon — testimony can be given that he is dead and his wife may remarry. Does that not imply that once the throat is slit, the person is *halachically* already dead? If so, how can a *get* be written on his behalf?

The Gemara answers: the person is in the state of *chai hu vesofu lamut* — alive, but certain to die. The testimony about his death does not mean he is dead at this instant; it means that given his condition, witnesses may reliably testify after the fact that he did indeed die, without needing to observe the actual moment of death. As long as he is still visibly alive, he is *halachically* alive, and a *get* can be written.

### No Exile

This raises a further question. If the person is definitively going to die, why is the one who accidentally slits his throat exempt from *galus* — exile, the penalty for unintentional killing? If the death is certain, the causal chain from the act to the death seems unbroken, and exile ought to apply.

### Contributing Factors

The Gemara cites Rabbi Oshaya: even though death from a slit throat is certain, there may be contributing factors that complicate the causal attribution. Wind entering the wound may have accelerated the death (*ruach bilbelato*); or the victim himself, by trembling and convulsing, may have hastened his own end (*hu kirev et mitato*). The Gemara asks: what would be a case distinguishing these two possibilities? If the slitting took place in a sealed marble chamber — where no wind could enter — then the wind cannot be a contributing factor; only the shaking would be relevant. If it took place outdoors but the victim did not convulse, then the wind might be a factor, but the victim's own movements cannot.

Tosafot raises an important objection: if someone intentionally slits a person's throat, surely they are liable for murder and execution, regardless of whether the wound got infected or the wind sped up the death. Tosafot resolves this by noting that for *galus* — as opposed to execution — the halachic framework is significantly narrower. The categories eligible for *galus* require a specific configuration: not too close to *shogeg* that it borders on accident, not too close to *meizid* that it approaches intention. Beyond the specific requirements of proximity to a ladder and similar conditions, the principle can be understood through the concept of *misasek*: the classic case of unintentional killing eligible for exile is one where the person did not truly perform a directed *ma'aseh* of killing. He was chopping wood and the ax head flew; that is *misasek* — his act did not make contact with the victim in the directed sense.

In the case of unintentionally slitting a throat, if we work forward from the perpetrator's act, then the act itself constitutes a *ma'aseh retzichah* — a mortal wounding — and had it been intentional, execution would follow. But *galus* is established not from the forward direction but in reverse: we see that someone has died, and we trace responsibility back to this individual, who caused it without intent. Because we are working in reverse, any contributing factor — even one that logically would have occurred in any case, such as natural convulsing — suffices to break the direct line of attribution, and the person escapes *galus*. This framework elegantly accounts for why unintentional throat-slitting does not result in exile, even though the death is certain: the absence of a clean, unmediated causal chain, once we reason from outcome back to act, means that contributing factors remain relevant.

---

---

# Gittin 71

## Testing Non-Speakers

### False Nodding Problem

The daf opens by continuing a discussion from the preceding amud concerning a husband who has lost the ability to speak — *nishtatek* — and whether those around him may write a *get* on his behalf based on his nodding responses. The *mishna* had established that one may pose yes-or-no questions and, if he responds correctly and coherently, his nodded instructions may be followed. But the *gemara* immediately raises a difficulty: *v'lechosh d'lamma shita d'lav lav naktay* — perhaps the man has been seized by a fit of head-shaking and is simply nodding or shaking reflexively. If all the questions put to him happen to align with his involuntary movement, his responses prove nothing.

### Alternating Questions

Rav Papa's solution is to ask the questions *b'sirugin* — alternating between questions that should elicit a "yes" and questions that should elicit a "no." Rashi understands this to mean waiting an interval between each question; the approach suggested here, however, is that the questions themselves alternate in the type of answer they require, so that a man simply locked into a repetitive motion would immediately be exposed. But the *gemara* presses further: perhaps he is seized by a fit of *alternating* — first nodding, then shaking, then nodding again. The answer is that one should vary the pattern unpredictably: *chad lav u'trei hen, u'trei lav u'chad hen* — one question requiring "no," then two requiring "yes," then two requiring "no," then one requiring "yes," in no fixed sequence, so that no mechanical repetition could accidentally produce the correct results throughout.

### Fruit Test Questions

A *baraita* from the school of Rabbi Yishmael adds a further method: *amrinan leih devarim shel yemos hachama b'yemos hageshamim v'shel yemos hageshamim b'yemos hachama* — one asks him about things characteristic of summer during the winter, and about things characteristic of winter during the summer. The *gemara* questions what precisely this means. If you ask whether he wants a winter coat or a summer coat, that proves nothing, since a person might be cold in summer or warm in winter. Rather, says the *gemara*, the test is conducted through fruit — *b'peiri* — asking about seasonal produce that is simply unavailable out of season. Tosafot notes that some fruits can be preserved, and therefore suggests the question be posed in terms of going out to the orchards to pick fruit, which clearly cannot be done in the wrong season.

## Deaf-Mute Writing

### Writing = Speech

A statement of Rav Kahana in the name of Rav now introduces one of the most important and far-reaching *chiddushim* on the daf: *cheresh she'yachol l'daber mitoch haksav* — if a person who is deaf can "speak" through writing, then *kosvin venosin get le'ishto* — a *get* may be written and given to his wife.

To appreciate the full weight of this ruling, one must recall what the term *cheresh* means in the *gemara*. It refers not simply to a person who cannot hear, but specifically to the deaf-mute — someone who is both deaf and unable to speak intelligibly. The *gemara* operated under the presumption that most people born deaf never acquired intelligible speech, and were therefore classified as lacking *bar da'as* status. This is a categorical *halakhic* designation: such a person is considered to lack the intellectual competence required for binding legal transactions at the *d'oraisa* level. He may marry and be married *d'rabbanan*, but a marriage contracted before he became a *cheresh* — when he was a *pikeach*, a person of full faculties — is a full *d'oraisa* marriage, which would ordinarily require a valid *get* for dissolution.

Rav Kahana's ruling addresses precisely this case. If such a person can communicate through writing, he is no longer halakhically a *cheresh* at all. One might understand this in one of two ways. The formal reading is that writing constitutes an act of speech — *yachol l'daber mitoch haksav*, he can "speak" through writing — and therefore he is definitionally not mute. The functional reading is that the designation *cheresh* was always a proxy for lacking *da'as*, and that writing demonstrates unambiguously that he possesses *da'as*, rendering the category inapplicable. As will become clear, the distinction between these two framings is not merely theoretical.

### Rav Yosef Challenge

Rav Yosef challenges the novelty of this ruling: *tanina* — we already know this from a *braita* concerning a man who became silent (*nishtatek*), was asked whether a *get* should be written, nodded, was tested three times, and answered yes-and-no questions correctly, whereupon it was ruled that a *get* may be written. Is it not obvious that non-verbal communication suffices?

### Ilem vs. Cheresh

Rav Zeira responds that the *braita* is no precedent at all, because it speaks of an *ilem* — a person who is mute but can hear — and that case is entirely different. As a *braita* establishes: *medaber ve'eino shomea zehu cheresh* — one who can speak but not hear is a *cheresh*; *shomea ve'eino medaber zehu ilem* — one who can hear but not speak is an *ilem*. And *ve'ze ve'ze harei hen kepikechin lekhol divreihem* — both the person who is only deaf and the person who is only mute are treated as fully competent, *kepikechin*, in all respects. An *ilem* is unquestionably a *bar da'as*; the only question regarding him is whether his nodding constitutes a valid instruction. The *gemara* notes a scriptural support for the terminology from the verse *va'ani kacheresh lo eshma, ukhe'ilem lo yiftach piv* — "I was like a deaf person who did not hear, and like a mute person who did not open his mouth" — showing that the deaf person and the mute are designated by distinct terms in *Tanakh* as well.

The *chiddush* of Rav Kahana amar Rav, therefore, is not about a *bar da'as* who happens to be unable to speak. It concerns someone the *halakha* would categorize as an *eino bar da'as* — a *cheresh* — who ordinarily cannot engage in binding *halakhic* transactions. The ruling is that if this person can write, that recategorizes him entirely. That is a genuinely revolutionary position.

### Writing Testimony

Rav Zeira raises a further question from a different angle. The verse in *Vayikra* states *im lo yagid venasa avono* — if a person who was adjured to testify fails to come forward, he bears his sin and must bring a *korban shvua*. The verse adds *perat le'ilem she'eino yachol lehagid* — excluding a mute person who cannot speak. But according to Rav Kahana, writing is a form of speaking — *yachol lehagid mitoch haksav* — so why should a mute person who can write be excluded from the laws of testimony and the *korban shvua*?

Abaye responds: *shani eidus derachmana amar mipihem velo mipi ksavam* — testimony is different, because the Torah specifically requires *al pi shenayim eidim*, "by the mouth of two witnesses," and the *gemara* derives from this that testimony must come from their mouths and not from their writing. Even if writing constitutes a form of speech for other *halakhic* purposes, the specific demand of *mipihem* — from their mouths — requires actual verbal articulation. One might further note that this principle also underlies the requirement that a *beis din* know the seventy languages — *shivim lashon* — since testimony cannot pass through an interpreter, for *mipihem velo mipi hameturgeman*.

This exchange actually clarifies the formal nature of Rav Kahana's position. The *gemara* is not merely saying that writing is a reliable indicator of *da'as*; it is making the stronger claim that writing counts as speech *halakhically*. This is why the objection from testimony is worth raising at all — if writing were merely a *de facto* test of competence, there would be nothing to ask. But because writing is being declared a formal act of speech, Rav Zeira can legitimately ask whether it should satisfy *lehagid*, and Abaye must answer that the particular requirement of *mipihem* is more exacting than the general category of speech.

A subsequent *braita* cited in the *gemara* states: *keshem shebodkin oso l'gittin, kach bodkin oso l'massa u'mattanot, ul'eduyos, ul'yerushos* — the same testing procedure used for *gittin* applies to business transactions, testimony, and bequests. This seems to reintroduce the problem, since *eduyos* is listed. The *gemara* resolves: Rav Yosef bar Minyumi in the name of Rav Sheshet explains that the mention of testimony refers to *edus isha* — testimony concerning whether a woman's husband has died — where the rabbis were lenient and did not require the full standards of formal testimony. As for bequests (*yerushos*), Rabbi Abahu explains that it refers to a case where the person is declaring which of his sons is the firstborn — again not a case of formal *eidus*. And *massa u'mattanot*, business transactions, refers to his own transactions, not to his testifying about someone else's. So the principle that formal testimony requires verbal speech remains intact.

## Braita Contradiction

### Braita Rule

The *gemara* now introduces a *braita* that directly challenges Rav Kahana's position. The *braita* states that when it comes to a *cheresh*, the *chachamim* did not follow his signaling, his jumping, or his writing — *v'halchu bo achar remizosav v'achar k'fitzosav v'achar k'sav yado* — except for *mitaltelin*, transactions involving movable property, where a lower standard of *da'as* has always been accepted. But *aval lo l'gittin* — not for *gittin*. This directly contradicts Rav Kahana's ruling that a *cheresh* who can write may divorce his wife through that writing.

One might ask at this point: does this difficulty not arise only regarding a marriage that is *d'oraisa*? After all, the principle *keshem shekones bi'remiza kach motzi bi'remiza* — just as he married through signaling, so too he may divorce through signaling — seems to already allow a *cheresh* who married rabbinically to be divorced in the same mode. The *gemara* will confirm that this principle applies only to a woman he married as a *cheresh*, where the original marriage was *d'rabbanan*. The hard case is a woman he married before becoming a *cheresh*, or — as will emerge — a *yevama* who fell to him from a *pikeach* brother, where the relationship carries *d'oraisa* force.

### Tannaitic Dispute

The *gemara* resolves the contradiction: *tanna'ei hi* — it is a dispute between *tannaim*. The *braita* that denies writing any power to redefine a *cheresh* represents the position of the *chachamim*, while Rav Kahana's ruling follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

### Rabban Shimon Caveat

The *braita* records: *bameh devarim amorim b'cheresh mei'ikaro* — when is it true that writing does not help? When the person was *always* a *cheresh*. *Aval pikeach venischaraish* — but if he was originally a *pikeach* and then became deaf-mute — *hu kosev vehein chosmin* — he writes and others cosign the *get*, and it is valid.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel thus draws a distinction: a person who began life with full faculties and then lost them may be recategorized if he can communicate through writing. A person who was always a *cheresh* cannot be recategorized no matter how clearly he writes. The *chachamim* disagree and make no such distinction — for them, writing helps in neither case.

This also raises the question of how a *cheresh* who was *always* a *cheresh* could ever be in a situation where he needs a *get* from a *d'oraisa* marriage. If he was always a *cheresh*, any marriage he contracted himself was only *d'rabbanan*, and he could dissolve it the same way it was contracted. The answer is *yibbum* — levirate marriage. If his brother, a *pikeach*, died, leaving a wife, and this *cheresh* then had relations with her, the act of *yibbum* itself — which does not require *da'as* — would create a *d'oraisa* bond between them. Now he has a *d'oraisa* marriage he cannot dissolve through writing, according to the *chachamim*.

The implications for the *halachic* history of deaf people are significant. This is one of the most consequential *sugyot* on the matter, and the *gemara* — through this *braita* — has pushed back hard against Rav Kahana's liberating position. This deserves to be noted. The concern for *agunos* that Rav Kahana's ruling might have alleviated remains in tension with the outcome of the *sugya*.

## Yibum Case

### Rabbinic Marriage

The *gemara* now addresses the question head-on. If a *cheresh* was always a *cheresh*, then *keshem shekone'sa beremiza kach motzi'a beremiza* — the same way he married through signaling, he can divorce through signaling. His marriage was only *d'rabbanan*, so his divorce need only satisfy a *d'rabbanan* standard as well. This is not in dispute.

### Yibum Obligation

The problematic case is *yevamto* — his *yevama*, his sister-in-law who falls to him for *yibbum*. If his brother was a *pikeach* and was *d'oraisa* married to a woman, and that brother died, then this *cheresh* has a *d'oraisa* obligation of *yibbum*. The act of *yibbum* is effected through sexual relations, and that act does not require *da'as* to be binding at the *d'oraisa* level. Once the act occurs, she is his wife *d'oraisa*, and he cannot divorce her — not through signaling and not through writing, according to those who reject Rav Kahana.

### Wife vs. Sister

The *gemara* then asks: if his brother was himself a *cheresh* and had only a *d'rabbanan* marriage to this woman, then the entire framework remains rabbinic — her marriage to the brother was *d'rabbanan*, and consequently her status as a *yevama* is also only *d'rabbanan*. In that case, *keshem shek'nisata b'remiza kach yetziata b'remiza* should apply even to the *yibbum* scenario. 

The *gemara* offers an alternative answer: *gzeira achiv chereish atu achiv pikeach* — we make a decree that even the case where the brother was a *cheresh* is treated like the case where the brother was a *pikeach*, because the two situations — a *yevama* from a *cheresh* brother and a *yevama* from a *pikeach* brother — might be confused with one another.

But then the *gemara* asks: *ishto nami* — if we are concerned about such confusion, why not similarly prohibit divorcing one's wife when the marriage was *d'rabbanan*, lest it be confused with a *d'oraisa* marriage? The *gemara* answers: *yevamto b'yevamto michalfa, ishto b'yevamto lo michalfa* — a person can confuse one *yibbum* case with another *yibbum* case, since both involve the same category of relationship. But no one will confuse a wife with a *yevama*, as these are categorically distinct situations in the mind of anyone dealing with them.

### Two Deaf Siblings

The *gemara* now challenges the *gzeira* from a different direction. A *mishna* discusses the case of two brothers who are both *charashim*, married to two sisters who may be *pikchot*, *cherashot*, or one of each. In all these combinations, the marriages are *d'rabbanan*, and consequently the *gemara* rules that *harei elu peturot min hachalitza umin hayibbum* — they are entirely exempt from both *yibbum* and *chalitza*, because we treat the situation as analogous to a case of *arayos* in a full *d'oraisa* framework: just as two brothers married to two sisters cannot do *yibbum* when everything is *d'oraisa*, so too when everything is operating on the same *d'rabbanan* plane, we apply the same logic. Conversely, *v'im hayu nochriyot yichnesu* — if the two women are unrelated, *yibbum* is performed, and since the *yibbum* itself is only *d'rabbanan*, *v'im ratzu lehotzi yotzi'u* — the husband may afterward divorce her with a *get*, since the marriage is only rabbinic.

What is significant about this *mishna* for the present argument is that it treats the *cheresh* brother's case in its own right, without any concern that it will be confused with the *pikeach* brother's case. This directly undermines the *gzeira* reasoning. The *gemara* acknowledges this: *umi gazrinan chereish atu pikeach?* — are we really going to decree that a *cheresh* case be treated like a *pikeach* case? The *mishna* plainly does not do so.

The *gemara* therefore concludes: *ela michvarta kideshanin me'ikara* — the better answer is the original one. The case where the *cheresh* who was always a *cheresh* cannot divorce his *yevama* is specifically the case where his brother was a *pikeach*, making the *yibbum* a genuine *d'oraisa* bond. Where the brother was also a *cheresh*, there is no need for a *gzeira* because the two cases are not confused with each other, and divorce remains available.

## Recategorization Debate

### Rejection Clarified

Rav Yochanan makes explicit what was already implied: *chalukin alav chaveirav d'Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* — the *chachamim* disagree with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. This is not a case where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's leniency can be taken as a clarification of the majority view. His position stands alone, and the majority reject it entirely.

### Can Never Divorce

Abaye adds that this rejection can be seen from the *mishna* itself: *nishtatek lo yotzi, nitcharesh... lo yotzi olamit* — if a man becomes silent he may not divorce his wife, and if he becomes a *cheresh* or *shoteh* he may *never* divorce her. The word *olamit* — forever — is doing important work here.

### Forever = Writing

Rav Papa explains what he would have said had Rav Yochanan not clarified the matter: he would have read *olamit* as meaning that no matter how intelligent the man appears — *af al gav d'chazina d'charif* — as long as he cannot communicate, he can never divorce. But once he can write, he would no longer be classified as a *cheresh* and could divorce. In other words, Rav Papa would have read the *mishna* as consistent with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel — "*never*" means never *as a cheresh*, but writing exits the category. Only Rav Yochanan's explicit statement that the *chachamim* disagree with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel forecloses this reading. According to the *chachamim*, *olamit* means that even if he can write, it does not change his status, and he can never divorce her.

### Shotah Status

An alternative reading of *olamit* is offered in the name of Rav Yitzchak: *d'var Torah shota mitgereshes* — biblically, a *shotah* — a woman who is not of sound mind — can in principle be divorced. The reasoning is *midi d'hava a'pikeches ba'al korcha* — just as a woman who is fully competent can be divorced against her will, the same applies to a *shotah*, since the *get* takes effect regardless of her mental state, provided she can retain custody of it (*shomeres es gitah*). Why then did the rabbis prohibit divorcing a *shotah*? *Shelo yinhagu ba minhag hefker* — so that people should not treat her as ownerless property, exploiting her vulnerability. This concern reflects a sober awareness of the dangers to which cognitively impaired individuals are exposed.

Rav Yitzchak's reading thus proposes that *olamit* was said specifically about the *man* to emphasize that when *he* becomes a *cheresh* or *shoteh*, the prohibition is *d'oraisa* — unlike the case where the *woman* becomes a *shotah*, where the prohibition is only *d'rabbanan*. The word "forever" signals the absolute, *d'oraisa* nature of his incapacity to grant a *get*, in contrast to her case, where the incapacity is only rabbinic.

## Modern Challenge

### Logical Problem

The *sugya* leaves us with a genuine *halakhic* challenge that has only grown more acute in modern times. The *gemara* — according to the *chachamim* who reject even Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel — holds that a *cheresh* who was born a *cheresh* cannot grant a *get* even if he can write clearly and intelligently. This is a striking conclusion. We are not dealing with a person whose competence is ambiguous. We are dealing with a person who is demonstrably communicating precisely in writing — and yet the *gemara* still classifies him as a *cheresh*, lacking *bar da'as* status at the *d'oraisa* level.

The logical tension is acute. How can a person who writes clearly, reasons clearly, and communicates precisely be described as lacking *da'as*? This is not merely a formal inconvenience — it has profound human consequences, affecting the person's ability to give a *get*, receive an *aliyah*, serve as a *shaliach tzibbur*, or perform any *mitzvah* at a *d'oraisa* level. The *gemara* seems to be applying a rigidly formal category rather than a genuinely cognitive one.

### Tech Solutions

One interesting technological consideration that arises in this context is text-to-speech software. If a person types text that is then vocalized by a device — as Stephen Hawking famously did — one might argue that the result is actual audible speech, not merely writing. This could potentially provide a basis for satisfying even those authorities who require actual *mipihem*, verbal articulation, rather than merely writing, at least for purposes other than formal *eidus* where the *d'oraisa* requirement of *mipihem* applies.

### Poskim Redefine

In practical *halakha*, this *sugya* stands at the center of a major debate among contemporary *poskim* regarding the status of deaf individuals in the modern era. The development of schools for the deaf — dating back roughly two and a half centuries — and above all the emergence of sign language as a fully structured linguistic system with its own grammar, has prompted extensive *halakhic* reassessment. Many prominent *poskim* have ruled that a *cheresh* who can communicate through sign language is no longer classified as a *cheresh* for *halakhic* purposes. This is both a logically compelling and a practically important ruling.

At the same time, intellectual honesty requires acknowledging the difficulty this *gemara* poses. The *gemara* specifically discusses a *cheresh* who communicates through *writing* — precise, articulate, unambiguous communication — and yet still classifies him as a *cheresh* at the *d'oraisa* level if he was born that way. Any contemporary ruling in the direction of recategorization must engage with this *gemara* directly, whether by distinguishing sign language from writing on formal grounds, or by arguing that changed social circumstances alter the underlying presumptions about cognitive development that originally grounded the category.

## Direct Instruction

### Direct Instruction Rule

The *mishna* now turns to a different but related problem of *gittin*: the requirement that the husband give direct instructions to the *sofer* and witnesses. The case presented is: a man is told, "Should we write a *get* for your wife?" He answers, "Write it." They relay this to a *sofer*, who writes it, and to witnesses, who sign it. Even though the *get* is written, signed, and delivered to the husband who then gives it to his wife — *harei ha'get batel* — the *get* is invalid, *ad she'yomar le'sofer ktov ve'le'edim chasomu* — until he himself directly instructs the *sofer* to write and the witnesses to sign.

### Invalidity Reason

The reason, the *gemara* states, is *taima de'lo amar tenu* — his only word was "write it," not "give it." The word *ktovu* — write — is a more limited instruction; *tenu* — give — implies broader authorization and somewhat more latitude. The *gemara* will explore whether saying *tenu* would have made any difference.

### Rabbi Meir Latitude

The *gemara* asks who the *reisha* — the beginning of the *mishna* — is consistent with, in light of the implication that the *get* might have been valid had a different word been used. The answer: *Rebbi Meir, de'amar mili nimseran le'shaliach* — Rabbi Meir, who holds that verbal appointment can be transmitted through an agent. Under Rabbi Meir's view, if a husband says *tenu* to a *beis din* — three people — those three are empowered to pass on the appointment to others, including instructing a *sofer* to write and witnesses to sign. In that case, the *get* might be valid even without the husband's direct instruction to the *sofer*. The *reisha*'s implication that the defect was specifically the use of *ktovu* rather than *tenu* resonates with Rabbi Meir's position.

### Rabbi Yosi Strict

The *seifa* — the conclusion of the *mishna*, which requires that the husband personally instruct the *sofer* and witnesses — sounds like Rabbi Yosi, *de'amar mili lo nimseran le'shaliach* — who holds that verbal appointment is categorically non-transferable. According to Rabbi Yosi, there is no formulation — not *tenu*, not *beis din*, nothing — that can substitute for direct verbal instruction from the husband to the *sofer* and witnesses.

## Verbal Transmission

### Rabbi Meir Position

Rabbi Meir's position, *mili nimseran le'shaliach*, holds that words of appointment — verbal instructions — can be relayed through an agent. This means that when the husband says *tenu* to three people and designates them as a *beis din*, those three can themselves appoint a *sofer* and instruct witnesses, and the *get* produced through that chain is valid. The verbal appointment given to them can be "carried" and transmitted.

### Rabbi Yosi Position
