On the other hand, one might argue that even *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* would not accept *mechulim lach*. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* permitted money as a substitute precisely because it can purchase the item in the marketplace — a functional equivalence argument. But if nothing at all is given, there is no basis to say the condition was met. He permitted functional equivalence; he did not permit outright waiver.

### No Waiving Answer

*Rabbi Yochanan* answers: *einah megureshet* — the *get* does not take effect. Saying *mechulim lach* does not work, and this applies even according to *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*. It is one thing to accept money as the functional equivalent of a lost object; it is another thing entirely to simply declare the condition void without anything being given or treated as given.

---

## Neder Al Tnai

### Konam Case

Following from *Rabbi Yochanan*'s ruling, a challenge is raised from a *braita* involving a *neder al tnai*. The case: a man says to his fellow *konam she'atah neheneh li im atah noten livni kor echad shel chittin u'shtei chavyot shel yayin* — I make a vow that you may derive no benefit from anything of mine, unless you give my son a quantity of wheat and two barrels of wine.

### Vow Absolution

*Rabbi Meir* rules *asur ad sheyitein* — the other person remains forbidden from benefiting from this man's property until the condition is actually fulfilled. *Chachamim* say *af ze yachol lehatir et nidro shelo al pi chacham* — the one who made the vow can release it without the formal process of *hatarat nedarim* before a *chacham*.

### Ke'ilu Treatment

How? By saying *hareini ke'ilu hitkabalti* — I will treat it as if I have already received what was promised. So by the *chachamim*'s ruling, the person who made the vow can declare "it is as if I received the wheat and wine," and the *neder* is thereby dissolved. This appears to be precisely the mechanism the husband would need in the *get* case — saying "it is as if I received the two hundred *zuz*." If the vow-maker can invoke this formula, why can the husband who gave the *get* not do likewise?

### Intent Difference

The *gemara* asks *hachi hashta* — how can these cases be compared?

### Tzurah vs. Revacha

The *gemara* draws a fundamental distinction: *hatam letzi'ura ka michaven, hacha lerevacha ka michaven ve'lo letzi'ura*. In the *get* case, when the husband says "on the condition you give me two hundred *zuz*," we interpret his intent as being primarily about making her suffer — *letzi'ura*. It is not really about the money as money; it is about the principle, which in the context of an adversarial divorce we read as his desire to impose hardship on her. Therefore, even if he declares "I consider myself as having received the money," the condition is not satisfied, because the condition was never really about his benefit in isolation — it was about her suffering. Since she has not suffered (no money changed hands, no hardship was imposed), his declaration accomplishes nothing toward fulfilling the *tnai*.

In the *neder* case, by contrast, the one who made the vow wanted his son provided for — *lerevacha*, for benefit, not to impose suffering on the other party. Since the entire purpose of the condition was his own gain, he has the power to declare "I consider that gain as received," and that declaration genuinely resolves the condition.

### Final Conclusion

What emerges clearly from the *gemara* is a precise and important principle: one is not in a position to simply *waive* a *tnai*. A condition stands as it was articulated; it cannot be unilaterally dissolved. What one *may* be able to do — under specific circumstances — is to declare that the condition has been treated as fulfilled, *ke'ilu hitkabalti*. But that option is available only when the condition was framed entirely around one's own benefit (*revacha*), so that one may credibly say "I consider that benefit received." When the condition is framed around the other party's suffering (*tzi'ura*), no such declaration is meaningful — the condition is not met, and the *get* does not take effect.

---

---

# Gittin 75

## Tna'im Overview

### Cloak & Conditions

The *daf* opens by continuing a rich *gemara* about what constitutes satisfaction of *tna'im* — conditions — in *gittin*. The *gemara* has been reading the *Mishna* as presenting the following case: a husband says "give me my cloak" as the condition of a *get*. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that if the cloak is lost, giving its monetary value suffices. The *rabbanan* disagree, holding that the cloak itself must be returned.

### Waiving vs. Hana'ah

The *gemara* then compared this to a separate question: when a condition stipulates that the wife give 200 *zuz*, may the husband simply waive the *tnai* outright — *achulei machilna lach* — or alternatively, may he not waive it formally but instead declare that his *hana'ah* has been satisfied, treating the condition as though fulfilled? A parallel case from *nedarim* was introduced in which the latter approach does work. In the context of *gittin*, however, the *gemara* suggests a distinction may be warranted.

### Nedarim Parallel

The critical variable is what the husband had in mind when he formulated the *tnai*. If the 200 *zuz* were meant as an expression of his *hana'ah* — his personal benefit — then declaring that benefit received might well suffice, parallel to the *nedarim* case. But if the point of the *tnai* was that she must suffer, that she must endure the burden of satisfying his demand, then no declaration of *hana'ah* can substitute for that. The other person still has not suffered. This raises a deeper question about how we interpret any given *tnai*: what was the underlying purpose the party had in mind when formulating it?

---

## Sharecropper Case

### Rain & Irrigation

The *gemara* now presents the case of *hahu gavra de-amar lei le-ariseh* — a man who said to his sharecropper: "All other sharecroppers irrigate the field three times and receive a quarter of the produce. You irrigate it four times, and I will give you a third." The sharecropper agreed. At the end of the season, however, rain fell and rendered the extra irrigation unnecessary — indeed, counter-productive. Rav Yosef rules: *ha lo dala* — he did not irrigate as agreed, so he is not entitled to the extra share. Rava disagrees: *ha lo itztrecha* — it was not required. The purpose of the extra irrigation was achieved by the rain; the *tnai* is accordingly satisfied.

### Money vs. Cloak

The *gemara* proposes that this dispute maps onto the earlier one: perhaps Rav Yosef follows the *rabbanan* — a *tnai* must be fulfilled precisely as stated — while Rava follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who permits equivalents. Just as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says money may substitute for the cloak, so Rava holds that rain substitutes for irrigation. The *gemara* immediately rejects this alignment, noting that we generally rule like Rava, and yet we do *not* rule like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel regarding the cloak. The two cases must therefore rest on different logic.

### Gittin Specificity

The *gemara* resolves the tension as follows: even according to the *rabbanan*, who insist that the cloak itself must be returned, Rava's ruling regarding the irrigation remains valid — because the two situations are fundamentally different. In the *get* context, the *gemara* says, *delitzira kamichavein* — the husband's intent in imposing the *tnai* is to make demands of her, to impose hardship. Whether the condition involves money or a garment or anything else, we presuppose he wants no latitude given, no substitutes accepted. His *da'at* is to demand precisely what he stated.

By contrast, the sharecropper arrangement is a business transaction — *mishum arrucha*, it is all about profit — and the *tnai* is naturally read in terms of its economic purpose. If the rain accomplished exactly what the extra irrigation was meant to accomplish, then *ha lo itztrecha* — it simply was not required, and the *tnai* is satisfied. The irrigation was never the point; it was a means to an end. In a *get*, however, every *tnai* is presumed to be *davka*, precisely as stated, because we assume the husband is not in the business of granting the wife any latitude whatsoever.

---

## Hillel Takkana

### Hiding Practice

The *gemara* now introduces a *Mishna* from *Arachin* about a related phenomenon — the buyback right in a walled city during the period when *yovel* was operative. A seller retained the right to repurchase his house within a year of the sale. If a year passed and the right was not exercised, the sale became permanent. The practice that developed was that the buyer would hide on the last day of the year — *hayah nitman yom shenem asar chodesh kedei sheyehe chalut lo* — so that the seller could not find him, deposit the money, and thereby exercise the buyback.

### Deposit Institution

Hillel instituted a *takkana* addressing this abuse: *sheyehe cholesh ma'otav lalishkah* — the seller could deposit the money in a chamber (apparently at the *Beis HaMikdash* or a designated *lishkah*), then break down the buyer's door and reclaim the house. The buyer, wherever he might be hiding, was informed that the money had been deposited and was available for collection whenever he wished.

### Rava's Inference

Rava draws a *halachic* inference from Hillel's *takkana*: if a husband writes *harei zeh gittech al menas shetitni li masayim zuz* — "here is your *get* on the condition you give me 200 *zuz*" — and she gives him the money with his willing acceptance, she is divorced. But what if he refuses to accept it — *al korcho* — and she throws the money at him, or places it in his home? Rava says she is not divorced. The parallel to Hillel: the fact that Hillel needed to institute a *takkana* for the buyer-in-hiding implies that without it, depositing money against someone's will would not have constituted valid payment. *M'klal d'be'alma nethina ba'al korcho lo havya nethina* — ordinarily, giving something against a person's will does not count as giving. Rashi adds that Hillel's *takkana*, whatever its scope, cannot apply to *gittin*, because the personal status of a woman as married or divorced cannot be altered by rabbinic enactment the same way monetary matters can.

### Rav Pappa Challenge

Rav Pappa (or, in an alternative formulation, Rav Shimi bar Ashi) challenges Rava's inference. The premise is that Hillel's *takkana* was necessitated by *nesinat ba'al korcho* — the unwillingness of the buyer to accept payment. But perhaps, Rav Pappa suggests, Hillel's *takkana* was required solely because the buyer was not physically present — *shelo befanav*. Perhaps, had the buyer been standing there, payment against his will would have been fully effective even without any *takkana*. The buyer ran away precisely to avoid the embarrassment of refusing face-to-face, not because refusal would have been legally effective. If so, Hillel addressed only the problem of absence, not of unwillingness.

Tosafot explains that the buyer's motive for hiding was indeed to avoid the social humiliation of standing there and overtly refusing to accept money when the seller had a *Torah*-granted right to tender it. The buyer was not hiding because the law empowered him to refuse; he was hiding because the law did not clearly protect him if he refused in person.

### Ambiguity Remains

The *gemara* then presents an alternative version of the entire exchange — *v'ika d'amri* — in which Rava himself is the one who began by saying that from Hillel's *takkana* one proves that *nesinat ba'al korcho havya nethina*: giving against someone's will does work, and Hillel's *takkana* addressed only the problem of physical absence. Rav Pappa then challenges: perhaps even had the buyer been present and refused, it would not have worked, and Hillel's *takkana* covered both scenarios — presence-and-refusal as well as absence. The *gemara* leaves the question unresolved. We do not know definitively whether *nesinat ba'al korcho* — tendering against someone's will — constitutes valid *nesinat* in the context of a *get* condition. One might argue on principle that in a *Torah*-granted right, such as the seller's right to redeem his house, the right exists regardless of the buyer's preferences, whereas when a husband creates a *tnai* of his own accord, his implicit intent may be that he must willingly accept the money. But the *gemara* itself does not resolve the question on those grounds.

---

## Paper & Get

### Rabban Shimon Rule

Rabbah bar bar Chana cites Rabbi Yochanan: *kol makom sheshana Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel bemishnasenu halacha kemoso* — wherever Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel appears in *our Mishna* (i.e., the *Mishna* of the tractate under study), we rule in accordance with his view — *chutz* from three exceptions: *arev* (a *Mishna* about guarantors), *Tzidan* (our very case, the cloak *Mishna*), and *raya achrona* (a second debate in *Sanhedrin* concerning the deadline for producing evidence). So we do *not* rule like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in the cloak case of our *Mishna*.

### Paper Condition

A *baraisa* is then cited: *harei ze gittech vehaniyar sheli aina megureshes* — "here is your *get*, but the paper is mine," she is not divorced, because she has not received any physical object. She has not taken possession of a *get*. However, *al menas shetachziri li es haniyar megureshes* — "on the condition you return the paper to me," she is divorced. The *gemara* asks the obvious question: *mai shna reisha u'mai shna seifa* — what distinguishes the first clause from the second? In the first clause, he keeps the paper outright; in the second, he gives it to her but conditions the divorce on her returning it. If *al menas* does not mean *me'achshav* — from now — but only takes effect when the condition is fulfilled, then in the second clause, at the moment she returns the paper she no longer holds the *get*, and yet it is valid. How?

### Rav Chisda Explains

Rav Chisda offers an explanation: this *baraisa* follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, *de'amar titee lo et dameha* — who holds that the monetary value of the cloak can substitute for the cloak itself. By analogy, even without physically returning the *get* parchment, the wife could appease the husband with the monetary value of the paper, and the *tnai* is thereby satisfied. Rav Chisda uses the word *mifayes* — appease — which is notable, as it reintroduces the earlier question of whether payment against one's will suffices, or whether agreement is required.

### Abaye Challenge

Abaye challenges this explanation sharply: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel only allowed a substitute when the original object was unavailable — *heicha de'leisa be'einei*, where the cloak no longer exists. In such a case, money is a reasonable stand-in. But here, *heicha de'isa be'einei* — the paper is still extant. Would Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel really say money substitutes for an object that is right there in hand? The challenge stands, and the *gemara* turns to a series of explanations grounded not in the equivalence of substitutes but in the formal rules of *tna'im* — why the *tnai* itself is invalid and therefore does not bind her.

---

## Formal Rules

### Doubling Requirement

Abaye himself offers a new resolution: *Rabbi Meir hi de'amar beinan tnai kaful* — the *baraisa* follows Rabbi Meir, who requires that any *tnai* be stated in doubled form — *v'hacha lo kafla l'tna'ei* — and here the husband did not double the condition. Rabbi Meir's position derives from the model of *bnei Gad u'vnei Reuven*: when Moshe laid out their condition for receiving a portion in *Ever HaYarden*, the *Torah* stated both: if they cross the Jordan, they receive their portion in Canaan, and if they do not cross, they receive their portion there in *Ever HaYarden*. Both the positive and negative outcomes were spelled out explicitly. As Dov notes, in propositional logic the statement "if P then Q" does not entail "if not-P then not-Q," and Rabbi Meir requires that both possibilities be articulated. Since that doubling was not performed here, the *tnai* is invalid — and an invalid *tnai* means the *get* takes effect unconditionally.

This is a genuinely puzzling moment in the *gemara*. The *baraisa* is structured to contrast two cases — the husband who keeps the paper outright versus the husband who conditions return of the paper — and the implicit contrast suggests they have different *halachic* outcomes. Yet Abaye's resolution essentially collapses that contrast: the reason the second case works is not because the *tnai* was satisfied but because the *tnai* was never binding to begin with. The *chiddush* of the *baraisa* turns out to be a separate and entirely independent *halacha* about the invalidity of an improperly formulated *tnai* — which is a rather striking way to structure a *baraisa*.

### Rava Objection

Rava challenges Abaye directly: *ta'ama d'lo kaflia l'tna'ei* — you say the problem is that he did not double the *tnai*. But *ha kaflia l'tna'ei lo havi gitta* — had he doubled it, the *tnai* would have been binding, and the *get* would only take effect upon return of the paper. When she returns the paper she no longer holds it, and yet you want the *get* to work? Properly doubled, the *tnai* creates an insurmountable problem. So the doubling issue alone does not explain the *baraisa*'s ruling. Rava therefore turns to a different formal deficiency.

### Tnai Precedes Act

*Kol tnai me-heicha gamrinan lehu* — from where do we derive all the rules governing *tna'im*? From the *tnai* of *bnei Gad u'vnei Reuven*. *Mah hatam tnai kodem l'maaseh af kol tnai kodem l'maaseh* — there, the *tnai* preceded the *maaseh*: the verse first states "if they cross and you shall give them their portion," and only then the act. So too in every *tnai*, the condition must be formulated before the act. Here, however, the husband said *harei zeh gittech* — "here is your *get*" — and only afterward added *al menas shetachziri li es haniyar* — "on the condition you return the paper." The *maaseh* preceded the *tnai*. This renders the *tnai* invalid on formal grounds independent of the doubling requirement.

Rashi understands *tnai kodem l'maaseh* as a purely formalistic requirement about the order of words — the condition must be stated first. Some *Rishonim* understand it more substantively, but Rashi's reading is supported by the *gemara*'s treatment of the *shachiv meira* case below, where the requirement clearly concerns verbal formulation.

### Different Domains

Rav Adda bar Ahava presses further: even if we accept that *tnai kodem l'maaseh* explains the invalidity, there is yet another formal deficiency. *Mah hatam tnai bidavar echad u'maaseh bidavar acher* — in the *bnei Gad u'vnei Reuven* case, the *tnai* pertained to one domain (crossing the Jordan to fight) and the *maaseh* pertained to a different domain (receiving a portion in *Ever HaYarden*). This separateness is required: *af kol tnai bidavar echad u'maaseh bidavar acher*. In our case, however, *hatnai ve'hamaaseh bidavar echad* — the *tnai* and the *maaseh* concern the same thing, namely the *get* and its paper.

Rashi understands this as a prohibition on making a *tnai* about the same object as the *maaseh* — one simply cannot condition the *get* on something related to the *get* itself. Tosafot refines this: the problem is not mere topical overlap but logical self-contradiction. A *tnai* whose fulfillment would undermine the very *maaseh* it is meant to condition cannot be a valid *tnai*, since the entire purpose of a *tnai* is to enable the *maaseh*. A condition that, if satisfied, destroys what it was meant to activate defeats its own purpose and is therefore not recognized as a *tnai* at all.

The *gemara* thus accumulates multiple independent grounds — lack of doubling, *maaseh* preceding *tnai*, and *tnai* and *maaseh* in the same domain — each of which independently invalidates the *tnai* in the *baraisa*. This is also an opportunity for the *gemara* to rehearse the full body of *mishpatei ha-tna'im*, the formal rules governing conditions, which derive from the paradigmatic case of *bnei Gad u'vnei Reuven*.

---

## Tosafot Categories

### Tnai Kaful

Tosafot on *daf* 75a takes up the question of how we rule on these formal requirements. Tosafot concludes that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Meir and requires *tnai kaful* — the doubled condition — since Shmuel and Rava in the immediately following *sugya* both operate according to Rabbi Meir's position. As for all the *mishnas* in the tractate that deploy *al menas* — the condition that she give 200 *zuz*, that she nurse the child, and so on — Tosafot holds that those cases all involve a *tnai kaful*, even though the *Mishna* does not spell it out explicitly: *af al gav d'lo peireish*. The *gemara* later explains that the *tnai* is understood as doubled even when not stated in full. And this applies throughout *Shas*: wherever *al menas* appears and is assumed to be effective — for example, the *esrog* given *al menas l'hachazir* — we must assume the *tnai* was in fact doubled.

### Three Categories

Yet Tosafot acknowledges that this framework requires careful differentiation. At the end of that *Tosafot*, Rabbeinu Yitzchak articulates three distinct categories: *gimel inyanim yesh*. First, there are situations that require a fully formal *tnai* — *tnai gamur* — with all the formal rules including *tnai kaful* as per Rabbi Meir. Second, there are situations requiring only *giluy da'at* — disclosure of intent — without all the formal machinery of a *tnai*. Third, there are situations where not even *giluy da'at* is required, because the intent is assumed from context.

### Intent & Demands

This typology resolves what would otherwise be a bewildering proliferation of difficulty: if every *al menas* requires *tnai kaful* and *tnai kodem l'maaseh* and *tnai bidavar acher*, how have so many *mishnas* and *beraisos* deployed *al menas* without apparent concern for these rules? Tosafot's framework answers: the formal rules apply only when the *tnai* is genuinely external to the core *da'at* of the transaction. When a person truly desires to do something — marry, divorce, buy, sell — but is in a position to attach external demands, those demands are peripheral to his underlying intent. Because they are peripheral and could theoretically be dispensed with, the *Torah* requires that they be formulated with rigorous precision, following all the rules of *mishpatei ha-tna'im*, in order to override what would otherwise be an unconditional *maaseh*.

By contrast, when something is so central to a person's *da'at* that he would not have agreed to the transaction without it, this is not properly a *tnai* at all — it is a fundamental premise of his intent. Such a premise does not require the formal machinery of *tna'im*. It must, however, be articulated; otherwise it falls under *d'varim shebilev einam d'varim* — unexpressed inner thoughts have no legal standing.

The third category is *d'varim shebilev kol adam* — matters so universally understood that no articulation is needed. The classic *gemara* example is someone who sold all his possessions *adaita lemeisak l'ara d'Yisrael* — with the intention of making *aliyah* — and was subsequently prevented from going. The transactions he undertook in preparation are treated as void, even though he never explicitly conditioned each sale on his *aliyah* plans going through. No such articulation was necessary because every bystander understood perfectly well the assumption on which the sales were made.

Tosafot's framework thus creates an organic relationship between legal methodology and the reading of the *gemara*'s *pshat*. Beginning from the conclusion that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Meir on *tnai kaful*, Tosafot is impelled to read all the *mishnas* as implicitly involving doubled conditions, and then to construct a typology of which cases require those formal conditions at all. The legal methodology and the *pshat* reading of the *gemara* are not separable enterprises.

---

## Shachiv Meira

### Avoiding Evil Eye

Shmuel instituted a *takkana* for the *get* of a *shachiv meira* — a person on his deathbed who wishes to give a *get* contingent on his death. The text Shmuel prescribed is: *im lo meisi lo yehei get v'im meisi yehei get* — "if I do not die it shall not be a *get*, and if I do die it shall be a *get*." The reason for beginning with the negative — "if I do not die" — is *lo makdmi inish b'puranusa*: a person does not open by invoking a bad outcome for himself. Beginning with "if I die" has the character of *ayin hara*.

### Yes Before No

The *gemara* challenges: why not simply say *lo yehei get im lo meisi* — "it shall not be a *get* if I do not die" — and avoid the need to open with death at all? The answer is *be'ina tnai kodem l'maaseh* — the *tnai* must precede the *maaseh* in formulation. One cannot begin with the *maaseh* ("it shall not be a *get*") and then attach the *tnai* afterward.

Rava then challenges from a different angle: Shmuel's formulation opens with *im lo meisi* — "if I do not die" — which is the negative case. But the formal requirement derived from *bnei Gad u'vnei Reuven* is *hen kodem l'lav* — the affirmative must precede the negative. The "yes" — the case where the *tnai* is fulfilled — must come first. Shmuel's formulation violates this by leading with the negative.

The resolution: Shmuel's *takkana* addresses both requirements simultaneously in a way that avoids *ayin hara*. One opens with a statement that is technically the negative (*im lo meisi lo yehei get*), which is not the troubling part because it posits the hopeful outcome. Then one proceeds *im meisi yehei get v'im lo meisi lo yehei get* — stating the affirmative before the negative in the doubled portion, thereby satisfying *hen kodem l'lav*. The opening preliminary statement avoids the need to lead with "if I die" while the doubled formulation that follows preserves the formal requirement of affirmative before negative. This *sugya* makes clear that *tnai kodem l'maaseh* is indeed a matter of verbal formulation and word order.

---

## Nursing Condition

### Implicit Duration

The *Mishna* now turns to conditions regarding service and nursing: *harei zeh gittech al menas she-teshamshi es abba* — "here is your *get* on the condition you attend to my father," or *al menas she-teniki es beni* — "on the condition you nurse my son." These conditions are binding. The *Mishna* asks: *kamah hi menikaso* — for how long must she nurse? The answer is *shtei shanim* — two years, the conventional nursing duration. Rabbi Yehuda says eighteen months.

### Death Exemption

The *Mishna* then states that if the child or the father dies — *meis haben o she-meis ha-av* — the *get* remains valid. Rashi understands this to mean that she performed at least one act of nursing or one act of attending to the father, and once the subject of the condition is gone, the *tnai* is considered satisfied for its duration. Tosafot rejects this reading as too obvious to require a *Mishna*. Tosafot holds that the *chiddush* is precisely that she did nothing — the father or child died before she had an opportunity to attend to them at all — and yet the *get* is valid. This parallels the rain-and-irrigation case discussed earlier: when the purpose of the *tnai* has been rendered moot by circumstances, the *tnai* is treated as satisfied. That the husband said "nurse my child" and she never nursed him, yet the *get* holds because there was no longer a child to be nursed — this is a substantial *chiddush*.

### Explicit Duration

The *Mishna* then distinguishes: *harei zeh gittech al menas she-teshamshi es abba shtei shanim* — if he specified a duration of two years — then even if the father dies or the child dies before the time has elapsed, *eino get* — it is not a valid *get*. When a specific duration is stated, that duration is required to be served. The condition is no longer implicitly "as needed"; it is a fixed term. Similarly, if the father says *ee efshar she-teshamisheni* — "I do not wish her to attend to me" — without any fault on her part (*she-lo b'kapdah*), the *get* is still invalid, because the explicit duration was not satisfied.

### Rabban Shimon Rule

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dissents: *kol akavah she-einah heimena harei zeh get* — any failure to fulfill the condition that is not her fault renders the *get* valid. The principle is framed around *ones* — external compulsion. If the father refuses her attendance without cause, or if circumstances beyond her control prevent performance, it is as though the condition has been met. This may be understood not merely as a liberal reading of an implicit "as needed" provision, but as an application of *yesh ones b'gittin* — the doctrine that circumstances of compulsion count as fulfillment. Just as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was more liberal in the cloak case in accepting substitutes, he is more liberal here in accepting non-performance due to circumstances beyond her control.

---

## Liberal vs. Strict

### One Day Question

A *baraisa* is cited that appears to contradict the *Mishna*: *henikato yom echad shimshato yom echad harei zeh get* — if she nursed the child for one day or attended to the father for one day, the *get* is valid. If no duration was specified, a single day of fulfillment satisfies the *tnai*. But the *Mishna* said that nursing, even without a stated duration, runs until the child is two years old. The contradiction is direct.

### Lenient vs. Strict

Rav Chisda resolves it: *lo kashya ha rabbanan v'ha Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* — the *Mishna* and the *baraisa* reflect different opinions. The *Mishna*, whose opening section does not belong to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel (since he is only introduced at the *Mishna*'s end), follows the *rabbanan*. The *baraisa* follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who interprets the satisfaction of *tna'im* more liberally. Since Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was prepared to accept money in place of a cloak, he is prepared here to accept one day of nursing as satisfying a condition that mentioned no specific duration. The *rabbanan*, who demanded the cloak itself, demand the full implied duration.

### Interpretation Method

The *gemara* refines this further. The issue is not precisely one of leniency versus stringency, but of interpretive approach: do we read a *tnai* in a hyper-literal, maximally precise manner, or do we read it in terms of the evident purpose? The *rabbanan*, who read *tnai* language precisely — cloak means cloak, no substitute — also read "nurse" to mean "nurse for the full conventional duration" even when that duration is unstated. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who accepts functional equivalents, also reads the unstated duration liberally — one day of nursing fulfills the underlying intent of the condition. The *gemara* closes by noting that this framing in terms of hyper-literal versus liberal interpretation is more precise than simply mapping the positions onto leniency and stringency, since those categories shift depending on the case.

---

---

# Gittin 77

## Im vs. Al Menat

### Opening Cases

The daf opens by completing the previous perek's discussion of conditional language in the get, picking up from the mishna on 76b. The mishna presents the case of a husband who says *harei zeh gittech im lo bati mikan ad yod bet chodesh* — "Here is your get if I do not return from here within twelve months" — and then dies within those twelve months. The ruling is *eino get*: it is not a valid divorce. The reasoning turns on the word *im*. Without the qualifier *mehayom* ("as of now"), *im lo bati* means "when I do not come" — that is, the get is intended to take effect only at the end of twelve months, at which point the husband is already dead. A get that takes effect after death is a *get l'achar mita*, which is invalid.

By contrast, if the husband said *harei zeh gittech mehayom im lo bati mikan ad yod bet chodesh* — "as of now, if I do not return" — and then died within the twelve months, it is a valid get. Since the condition will certainly be fulfilled and the get was designated as effective from the present moment, the divorce is good.

A third case: the husband instructs others, *kitvu utnu get l'ishti im lo bati mikan ad yod bet chodesh* — "Write and give a get to my wife if I do not return within twelve months." Here the condition applies not only to the giving of the get but to its very writing. If they wrote it within the twelve months and gave it afterward, the get is invalid — the instruction was: write it, and give it, when I have not returned, meaning the writing itself was conditioned on the non-return.

The final case in this section is where the husband reversed the order of his statement: *kitvu utnu get l'ishti* first, then *im lo bati mikan ad yod bet chodesh*. The first ruling — that writing it early and giving it late renders it invalid — is the same. But Rabbi Yossi disagrees in this formulation. He reads the *kitvu* as grammatically severed from the conditional clause: "Write it" — then a pause — "and give it *if* I do not return." Because the instruction to write precedes the condition, Rabbi Yossi frees the writing from conditionality. Only the giving is conditional.

The mishna then addresses the case where the husband instructed *kitvu v'chatmu l'achar yod bet chodesh v'natnu l'achar yod bet chodesh* — write it and give it after twelve months — and he subsequently died. If the get was given before his death, it is valid; if death preceded the giving, it is not. If the sequence is unknown, she is in a state of *safek megureshes* — doubtfully divorced — which is, as the mishna acknowledges, the worst of all outcomes.

### Rabbi Yossi & Dating

The Gemara introduces a *baraisa*: *raboseinu* — "our teachers" — permitted the woman to remarry even in the case where the husband said simply *im lo bati*, without explicitly saying *mehayom*. The Gemara asks: who are these *raboseinu*? Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel identifies them as the *beis din* that permitted the oil of non-Jews — the court of Rabbi Yehuda Nesiah, known to have been willing to issue lenient rulings and occasionally criticized for it.

How did this *beis din* permit her to remarry when the language *im lo bati* would seem to mean "when I do not return," yielding a *get l'achar mita*? The Gemara answers: *sabri lah k'Rabbi Yossi* — they held in accordance with a different Rabbi Yossi, one cited in Bava Basra, who rules *zmano shel shtar mochiach alav* — the date of a document establishes its validity. Rabbi Yossi's principle is that when a *shechiv mera* gives a document that says *l'achar mita*, we read it as *mehayom v'l'achar mita* because the date written on the document anchors it to the present moment. Applied here: even though the *tnai* of *im lo bati* was stated verbally and thus might seem to stand on its own as meaning "when," the date inscribed in the get causes us to read it in conjunction with the condition, effectively transforming *im* from a temporal "when" into a conditional "if" effective as of the date.

Rabbi Abba the son of Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba then quotes Rabbi Yochanan: Rabbi Yehuda Nesiah — specifically identified as the son of Rabban Gamliel and grandson of Rabbi Yehuda Hanasi — could not get his colleagues to agree with him on this ruling. Throughout his life, no one from his circle concurred.

### Scope of Dating

Abbaye frames the positions of Rabbi Yossi more precisely. Everyone agrees on the two clear cases: if the husband says *lich'she'tetzei chama min hartika* — "when the sun rises" — and dies at night, it is unambiguously a *get l'achar mita*, since *lich'she* means "when." If he says *al m'nat she'tetzei chama min hartika* — "on the condition that the sun rises" — it is unambiguously a present-moment get with a future condition, because the principle articulated by Rav Huna in the name of Rav is *kol ha'omer al m'nat k'omer me'achshav dami* — whoever says "on condition" speaks as though saying "as of now." The debate of Rabbi Yossi applies exclusively to the word *im*. Without *zmano shel shtar*, *im* means "when." With *zmano shel shtar*, Rabbi Yossi holds that *im* is read as a conditional "if," and the date supplies the *me'achshav*; his colleagues disagree.

A student raised a sharp point: since *zmano shel shtar* — the date on the get — records only the day, not the hour, if the get was delivered at night and the husband dies that same night, even according to Rabbi Yossi the date cannot mean "as of this moment," since the date written on the document reflects only the day, which might refer to the daylight hours that follow. This would explain Rashi's position that when one says *lich'she'tetzei*, it is categorically a *get l'achar mita* even according to Rabbi Yossi — because the date, which marks a day, cannot reach back to anchor a nighttime death.

The discussion then turns to a technical ruling: in the formulation *kitvu utnu get l'ishti im lo bati*, Rav Yemar asks Rav Ashi whether Rabbi Yossi might hold that the *writing* of a get cannot be made conditional at all — that *ktav get al tnai* is fundamentally invalid. The Gemara rejects this: Rabbi Yossi agrees one can condition the writing. His point is purely grammatical and interpretive. When the husband says *kitvu utnu get l'ishti im lo bati*, Rabbi Yossi reads this as: "Write it now" — and then separately — "give it if I do not return." The condition attaches only to the proximate verb, the giving. Had he wanted to condition the writing as well, he should have said *im lo bati kitvu utnu* — placing the condition first. The Rabbis disagree and rule that regardless of word order, both the writing and the giving are conditioned on the non-return.

### Tosafot: Safek Get

The Gemara raises a question that is left without resolution: once it is known that the husband has died — and thus that the condition will certainly be fulfilled — can the wife remarry immediately, or must she wait until the twelve months have elapsed? The question is asked both about the case in the mishna (where *mehayom* was stated explicitly) and about the case of Rabbi Yehuda Nesiah's court (where the date of the document supplies the *me'achshav*). The Gemara notes that the question on the *beis din* case was posed to an elder who had actually participated in such a ruling, since a practical ruling would presumably have included thinking through its parameters — which makes the question more pointed than merely a theoretical one about the mishna. Nevertheless, the Gemara offers no answer.

Tosafot addresses this question directly. Tosafot asks: *le'alter mah yesh lachosh* — if he has died, what is there to worry about? He will not return. Tosafot answers that there is a concern about appearances. People are aware that the condition was "if he does not return in twelve months," and if they observe the woman marrying immediately, they will not know he has died and will conclude that the twelve-month condition need not be waited out in general — creating a false impression about how conditional divorces work. This is therefore a rabbinic-level concern about *mar'it ayin* or improper inference, not a question about the mechanism of conditional fulfillment.

Tosafot also addresses a further point: even if one holds like Rabbi Yossi that *zmano shel shtar mochiach alav*, the result in the case where *im* is combined with the date of the document is at best a *safek get* — a doubtful divorce — not a definite one. This is because there remains a question whether the date alone is sufficient to convert *im* from a temporal "when" to a conditional "if." Moreover, Tosafot notes that the question of whether we rule like Rabbi Yossi in these cases remains genuinely open. Even though it is reported that his colleagues did not agree with him, one cannot prove from that historical fact that the *halacha* rejects his position. Rabbi Yochanan, who reports that Rabbi Yehuda Nesiah could not convince his colleagues, may himself have agreed with Rabbi Yossi. And even if there is a basis to reject Rabbi Yossi where the *tnai* is external and verbal while the date is in the document, one might still apply his principle where both the date and the condition appear within the document itself.

---

## Timing Language

### After = Distance

With the transition to a new perek, the Gemara turns from questions about the content of conditional language to questions about temporal language — specifically, what it means to say that a document takes effect "after" (*l'achar*) a given unit of time.

A *baraisa* establishes the principle through a series of cases, each demonstrating that "after" does not mean immediately after but rather fully separated from. If one says a document takes effect *l'achar hashavua* — after the seven-year shmitta cycle — it takes effect a full *shana*, year, afterward. If one says *l'achar hashana* — after this year — it takes effect a *chodesh*, a month, into the following year. If one says *l'achar hachodesh* — after the month — it takes effect a full *Shabbos*, a week, later. And if one says *l'achar Shabbos* — after this Shabbat — the question arises: one day later?

Rav Zeira, and some say Rav Assi before Rabbi Yochanan, rules that Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday are still *batar Shabbos* — in the wake of the preceding Shabbat, still connected to it. One can still recite *havdala* in those days; one is still in the gravitational field of that Shabbat. Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday are already *kamei Shabbos* — oriented toward the coming Shabbat. The idea throughout is that "after" means when one is genuinely distant from the unit in question — when one is no longer in its shadow or afterglow. Just as someone writing a check in early January might still write the previous year out of habit, the period immediately following a major unit of time is still considered to be "of" that unit, not fully beyond it.

### Rabbi: 30 Days

A *baraisa* teaches in the name of Rabbi: *l'achar haregel shloshim yom* — "after the festival" means thirty days after the conclusion of Yom Tov. The festival's influence is understood to extend across an entire month.

### Attribution Issues

Rabbi Hiyya went out and taught this ruling in the name of Rabbi, and he was praised for doing so. When he subsequently taught the same ruling as though it represented a majority opinion rather than Rabbi's individual position, he was not praised — one does not present a *da'at yachid* as a consensus. The ruling, it seems, is not followed: the festival's shadow does not actually extend thirty days.

This prompts a brief observation: two instances appear in close proximity in this *sugya* where a rabbinic position fails to gain acceptance. Earlier, Rabbi Yehuda Nesiah could not convince his colleagues of Rabbi Yossi's principle regarding *zmano shel shtar*. Here, Rabbi's ruling on thirty days after the festival is likewise not accepted. In each case, the question of the correct *halacha* remains open — the non-acceptance of a position in a historical sense does not automatically determine the ruling, as Tosafot noted above.

---

## Giving the Get

### Mishna Cases

The new chapter opens with a mishna addressing how the get must physically be transferred to the wife. The central case is *hazorek get l'ishto vehi betoch beisah o betoch chatzerah* — if a man throws a get to his wife while she is in her house or in her yard, she is divorced. The get has landed in her domain, and that suffices. But if he threw it while they are in his house or his yard — even if she is lying beside him in bed — she is not divorced. The domain in which the get lands determines validity; his domain does not count as her receiving it.

However, if the get landed *betoch cheikah* — on her body, in her lap or bosom — or into her *kaltah*, her basket or purse, she is divorced even if they are standing in his domain. The get reached her person, not merely her property.

### Kinyan vs. Transfer

This mishna raises a fundamental conceptual question: is the act of giving a get an act of *kinyan* — of transferring legal ownership in a halakhically defined sense — or is it fundamentally a *ma'aseh netinah*, an act of physical giving? The question has practical implications. If it is a *kinyan*, then the conditions for valid transfer must mirror those of ordinary acquisition: the object must be capable of being owned, the domain must belong to the recipient, and so on. If it is an act of giving, perhaps more physical or interpersonal factors control validity rather than the formal mechanics of property transfer.

One test case mentioned earlier in the tractate is a get written on *issurei hana'ah* — objects from which benefit is forbidden. Some hold that such objects cannot be legally possessed at all, existing as it were outside the framework of ownership. If a get on such an object is valid, that would suggest the act is one of giving rather than of kinyan. But since other opinions hold that *issurei hana'ah* can in fact be possessed, the test case is not decisive. The question remains genuinely open, and the *sugya* here is best read as probing precisely this tension.

### Derasha

The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that the wife's roof, yard, and *karfif* — a smaller enclosure — can serve as a valid location for receiving the get? The verse says *ve-natan beyadah* — "and he shall give it into her hand." One might have thought only the hand is valid. The Gemara answers with a *derasha*: *talmud lomar ve-natan mikol makom* — the formulation of *ve-natan* by itself, separable from *beyadah*, extends the act of giving to any of her domains. Rashi explains that the verse could have written *beyadah yitnenah*, making the hand the exclusive object; by writing *ve-natan beyadah* the Torah allows *ve-natan* to be expounded independently.

A parallel *derasha* appears in the laws of theft. The verse *im himatzei timatzei beyado ha-geneivah* — "if the stolen object is found in his hand" — might suggest liability only when the thief holds the object directly. But the same *midrash* style extends liability to the thief's roof, yard, and *karfif* as well: *talmud lomar himatzei timatzei mikol makom*.

### Get vs. Theft

The Gemara then establishes that both *derashot* are necessary — one cannot be inferred from the other. If we had only the case of the get, one might think the wife's domain works because the husband divorces her against her will (*be'al korcha megarshah*) — the husband has greater power in the divorce context, so perhaps a broader range of situations counts as "giving to her." But for theft, where there is no such coercive power dynamic, one might have thought property acquisition would require more direct action. Conversely, if we had only the case of the thief, one might think his domain is implicated because the Torah penalized him — the rabbinic expansion of liability could reflect the punitive context — while for the get, perhaps the domain rule would not apply.

Rashi sharpens the novelty in the theft case. The obvious case — where the thief actively picked up the object and brought it to his yard — requires no *derasha* at all: the thief performed a direct act of *meshichah*, of drawing the object toward him, and is clearly liable. What the *derasha* comes to teach is the case where, say, a cow wandered into the thief's yard on its own, and the thief decided not to return it and locked the gate. He performed no direct act on the object. The *chiddush* is that closing the gate — a passive act relative to the object itself — nonetheless constitutes an act of *geneivah*. Just as if a baseball were thrown and accidentally landed in someone's hands and he refused to return it — that constitutes theft under this *derasha*. The willingness of the Torah to define such a passive situation as possession for purposes of theft liability is itself a striking *chiddush*.

---

## Husband Rights

### Rights Problem

The Gemara now asks the pointed question: the mishna says that throwing the get into the wife's yard effects a divorce. But *mah she'kaneta isha kanah ba'alah* — whatever the wife acquires, her husband acquires. So if the get lands in her yard, the yard's acquisitions belong to the husband — which means the get immediately becomes his property, not hers. How then does it constitute giving it to her?

As noted above, there are two ways to frame this problem. One reading focuses on the mechanics of ownership: when the get lands in her yard, it transfers to the husband. But this framing invites the response that surely he could waive those rights in advance. The other reading focuses on the nature of the yard itself: since the husband has full rights to the *peiros* — the produce and fruits — of his wife's property, the yard is not genuinely "hers" in the sense required for the verse *ve-natan beyadah*. On this reading, the question is not about who takes possession of the get, but about whether the yard can count as an extension of her person when he has such deep claims upon it.

The latter framing is more conceptually powerful. If we understand *ve-natan beyadah* as requiring that the get be given to *her* — to her as a person, to her domain — then a yard over which the husband has concurrent rights is not fully her domain. The analogy to the hand makes this vivid: giving something into her hand gives it to her because the hand is unambiguously her person. But a yard in which the husband has *kinyan peiros* — or perhaps even *kinyan haguf* on some views — is not unambiguously hers.

There is a broader halakhic backdrop here. The question of *kinyan peiros k'kinyan haguf dami* — whether the right to produce is equivalent to ownership of the body of the property — bears directly on this. If it is, then in a meaningful sense the husband is the owner of the yard during the marriage, and putting the get in that yard is like putting it in his own yard. If it is not — if *kinyan peiros* is merely a limited usufruct right — then the wife retains underlying ownership and the yard may still count as hers. Tosafot engages at length with these issues.

### Waiving Rights

Rav Elazar proposes that the case works when the husband has written her a document stating *din u'dvarim ein li benikhsayikh* — "I have no claim or dispute against your property." By waiving his rights in writing, he removes himself from the yard, leaving it fully hers.

The Gemara objects: a *baraisa* teaches that if a business partner tells his partner *din u'dvarim ein li al sadeh zu, v'ein li esek bo, yadi mesuleket heimena* — "I have no claim on this field, I have nothing to do with it, my hand is removed from it" — *lo amar klum*, it is legally meaningless. Rights and ownership are distinct categories. One can disclaim an adversarial claim (*din u'dvarim*) without transferring or relinquishing one's underlying ownership interest. To give up ownership, one must actually transfer it — a mere declaration of non-claim is insufficient. The same would apply to the husband's rights in the wife's yard.

### Timing of Waiver

The answer proposed by *d'vei Rabbi Yannai* is that the case works when the husband wrote the waiver *v'odah arusah* — while she was still betrothed, before the *nissuin*. The husband's rights to *kinyan peiros* in the wife's property do not attach until the *nissuin*. Therefore, if before the *nissuin* he declared in writing that he is waiving any rights he would otherwise receive over the fruits of her property, he never acquires those rights in the first place.

The mechanism is explained through two principles. First, *nachlah haba'ah lo l'adam mimakom acher* — an inheritance or benefit coming from an external source, not a biblical default of succession, can be declined in advance. A child cannot preemptively disclaim an inheritance from a parent because the Torah automatically transfers it; but a right that flows from rabbinic institution, arriving from an external source in a contingent way, can be refused before it takes effect. Second, Rava's principle: *ha'omer ee efshi b'takkanat chakhamim k'gon zu shom'in lo* — if someone declares that he does not want a rabbinic *takkanah* that was enacted for his benefit, we listen to him. Since the right of *kinyan peiros* was enacted as a rabbinic benefit for the husband, he may decline it before the marriage creates the entitlement.

Rav Huna in the name of Rav provides the paradigm: a wife may say to her husband *eini nizonet v'eini osah* — I will not be supported by you and I will not labor for you — because the arrangement of support in exchange for labor was enacted fundamentally for her benefit. She may therefore decline it. This refusal can even be toggled on and off during the marriage, since the arrangement is ongoing and personal.

The case of *kinyan peiros*, however, differs in an important respect. Once the *nissuin* occurs and the husband receives his *kinyan* in the wife's property, he cannot undo it merely by saying *din u'dvarim ein li* — that is the Gemara's earlier objection. To restore the property rights to her he would need to perform an actual *makneh*, a proper act of transferring ownership back. But before the *nissuin*, he can simply refuse the *takkanat chakhamim*, in which case he never acquires the right at all, and the yard remains unambiguously hers, allowing the get placed therein to count as given to her.

### Ba'im K'Echad

Rava, however, proposes a fundamentally different solution — one that does not require any prior waiver. *Atu yadah mi lo kanya leh l'baal?* — Is the hand of the wife not also, in a sense, "owned" by the husband? His rights to her labor might be understood as a kind of claim on her hand itself. Yet when the get is placed in her hand, it works. Why? Because *gito v'yadah ba'im k'echad* — the get and her hand come into effect simultaneously.

The insight is this: it is true that while the marriage subsists, the husband has rights to her hand through his entitlement to her labor, and rights to her yard through *kinyan peiros*. But the get and the divorce take effect at the same moment. At the instant the get is received, the divorce occurs — and at that same instant, her hand and her yard become entirely hers, free of any claim. The moment of reception and the moment of divorce are not sequential; they are simultaneous. Therefore, at the very moment that matters — the moment of reception — her hand and her yard belong to her fully.

Ravina then sharpens a question against Rava's formulation: granted, there is a meaningful analogy between the yard and the hand regarding simultaneity, but the cases are not truly parallel. The husband does not "own" her hand in any proprietary sense — his right to her labor (*ma'aseh yadeha*) is not the same as ownership of the hand as a physical object. Yet with the yard, the husband has something closer to a property interest. Is Rava's proof from the hand of the wife really compelling enough to extend to the yard?

Rava responds that his actual proof was never from the hand of the wife. It was from the hand of an *eved Kena'ani* — a Canaanite slave. The slave is legally property: *yad eved k'yad rabbo damya*, the slave's hand is like the master's hand. Yet the Gemara accepts that one can free a slave by handing him his writ of manumission directly — *le-man de-amar bi-shtar al yadei atzmo*. Why should that work? The slave's hand is entirely the master's property. The only possible answer is *gito v'yado ba'im k'echad* — the writ of manumission and the slave's hand become free simultaneously. At the moment of reception, the slave is freed, and at that same moment the hand is his own. The simultaneity principle is thus established on solid ground, independent of any ambiguity about the wife's hand.

From this principle, the application to the wife's yard follows: *hacha nami gito v'chatzerah ba'im k'echad* — here too, the get and her yard come into effect as one.

---

## Eved Case

### Freeing Eved

The case of the *eved Kena'ani* thus serves as the clearest proof of the *ba'im k'echad* principle. The slave is unambiguously property — his hand belongs to his master in a much more complete sense than the wife's hand or yard belong to her husband. There is no rabbinic *takkanah* to waive, no prior condition to arrange. The master simply hands the *shtar shichrur* to the slave, and it works. The only coherent explanation is that the act of freeing and the conferral of legal personhood upon the slave occur simultaneously — the hand that receives the document is, at that very instant, the hand of a free person.

### Divorce Timing

The same logic then resolves the problem of the wife's yard. Just as the slave's hand becomes legally his at the moment of reception, the wife's yard becomes legally hers at the moment the get is received. The husband's *kinyan peiros*, whatever its scope, is extinguished at the instant of the divorce — and since the divorce and the reception are simultaneous, the yard is hers at the relevant moment. *Gito v'chatzerah ba'im k'echad*. This is Rava's answer, and it operates independently of the solution proposed by *d'vei Rabbi Yannai*, which required a specific prior waiver.

---

## Shabbat Deathbed

### Case Setup

The final *sugya* on this daf presents a vivid practical scenario: a *shechiv mera* — a person on his deathbed — wrote a get for his wife on the eve of Shabbat but did not manage to give it to her before Shabbat came in. On Shabbat, his condition deteriorated severely. He needed to transfer the get urgently, both to spare her the ordeal of *yibbum* and because it was unclear how long he would survive.

The immediate problem is identified by the *rishonim* in accordance with Rashi's framing: the get is *muktzeh*. Giving a get or performing *kiddushin* on Shabbat is normally prohibited as a rabbinic restriction, but the *poskim* note that a *shechiv mera* is given latitude to perform acts on Shabbat that would ordinarily be impermissible — since we do everything possible to ease his distress. Therefore the concern is not the act of divorce per se on Shabbat, but the *muktzeh* status of the get document itself, which cannot simply be handed over.

### Kinyan Solution

They brought the question before Rava. Rava suggested: tell the *shechiv mera* to transfer ownership of the small piece of property on which the get is resting to the wife — *le-kanyei nihalah le-hahu duchsah de-yasiv beih gitta*. Then let her go and perform *kinyan chazakah* on that spot: *tisgor v'tiftach* — let her lock and open the enclosure — since the mishna and *baraisa* teach that locking a gate, closing a fence, or breaching one as needed constitutes *chazakah* on land — *na'al, gader, u-faratz, kol she-hu l'tikkuna, harei zu chazakah*. By acquiring the *makom* — the physical spot — through *chazakah*, she thereby acquires the get that sits upon it, since an object resting in one's *chatzer* is acquired along with the *chatzer* itself.

### Kinyan Problem

An immediate objection is raised: this solution seems to trade one rabbinic prohibition for another. If the problem is *muktzeh* — a rabbinic restriction — how does performing a *kinyan* on Shabbat, which is itself rabbinically prohibited, constitute a solution? The Ran addresses this by suggesting that the *kinyan chazakah* performed through opening and closing a door is experientially innocuous — it feels like an ordinary domestic act, not like a formal *kinyan* — whereas *muktzeh* involves an overt act of handling the forbidden object. The She'iltos offers a different explanation: the case is actually one where the get is located across a *reshut ha-rabbim* — a public domain — in another house, making it physically impossible to bring the get to the dying man on Shabbat. The problem is therefore not *muktzeh* per se but inaccessibility, and Rava's solution of having the wife acquire the spot through *kinyan chazakah* in the remote location is the only available mechanism.

### Arusa Not Nesua

Rava's solution was met with embarrassment when Rav Ilish pointed out the objection discussed above: *mah she-kaneta isha kanah ba'alah* — the husband would immediately acquire whatever she acquires, so her *kinyan* of the property would revert to him and the get sitting on it would become his. Rava was taken aback — *ikhsif*, he was embarrassed.

But then it emerged that the circumstances of the case were different from what had been assumed: the woman was an *arusa*, merely betrothed, not yet a *nesua*. The rule of *mah she-kaneta isha kanah ba'alah* and the husband's *kinyan peiros* apply only after *nissuin*; they do not apply to an *arusa*. Therefore, Rava had not actually made an error — the specific facts of the case meant that his solution was valid after all, since the *arusat*'s property was entirely her own.

### Final Position

Nevertheless, the Gemara records that Rava then retracted even this concession and reaffirmed his position without qualification: *lo shena arusa v'lo shena nesua — gita v'chatzerah ba'im k'echad*. Whether she is betrothed or married, the principle of simultaneity applies. The get and her domain — including a domain she acquires in the very act — come into effect as one.

The Gemara then notes that it had cited Rava's ruling of *gito v'chatzerah ba'im k'echad* earlier in the *sugya*, seemingly before this story was told. It explains: *mei-ikara ki amar Rava hai ma'isa amrah* — when Rava first formulated the principle of *ba'im k'echad*, it was this very story that gave rise to it. The deathbed Shabbat case was the original occasion for Rava's insight. What was presented earlier in the *sugya* as Rava's ruling was, chronologically, a conclusion that emerged from this episode — the story is the origin, and the earlier citation anticipated the result.

---

---

# Gittin 78

## Get Delivery Overview

### Daf Identification

Today's daf is 78, and we pick up in the middle of 77b — *v'hi b'toch beito* — dealing with the question of the act of giving of the *get*.

### Kinyan vs. Act of Giving

The *mishna* discusses giving the *get* directly to the woman — either on her body, as in her hand, or in her *chatzer*. The question that will continue for some time is: to what degree are we trying to define something that constitutes a classic act of *kinyan*, of taking possession of an object? And in what sense might this instead be a different definition entirely — a physical act of giving, distinct from acquisition? Complicating matters further, a *get* can be forced upon the wife, which makes this unlike a standard *kinyan* scenario.

### Two Models of Transfer

The *Gemara* had raised the question of why giving the *get* into her *chatzer* should count at all. The principle *kanta isha kanta ba'alah* — "what the wife acquires, the husband acquires" — can be framed in two ways: either because her taking possession transfers to the husband, which is the *kinyan* model, or because the *Gemara*'s deeper concern is why the *chatzer* is considered part of her in the first place, given that the husband has rights to it — *kinyan peiros* — and it is therefore not analogous to her hand.

Rava's resolution is *gita v'chatzeira ba'in k'echad*: we look a moment into the future and recognize that as a result of the *get*, the *chatzer* will become fully hers. That future reality renders the current delivery valid. This is the *chiddush* of *v'natan b'yadah* — that giving it into her property, and not only into her hand, constitutes giving it to her. With these two models in view — the act of giving versus the *ma'aseh kinyan* — we proceed.

---

## Chatzer & Mishtameret

### Mishna Emphasis

The *mishna* states *v'hi b'toch beitah* — she was standing in her house. The *mishna* emphasizes her actual physical location within her house or yard. Why?

### Ulla's Position

Ulla holds: *v'hi she'omedet b'tzad beitah, b'tzad chatzerah* — she must be physically on the property itself, just as the *mishna* implies.

### Oshaya's Position

Oshaya disagrees: *afilu shehi b'Tveria v'chatzerah b'Tzipori, hi b'Tzipori v'chatzerah b'Tveria* — even if she is in a different city entirely from her yard, it does not matter. She is *megureshet*; it works.

The *Gemara* immediately presses: but the *mishna* says *v'hi b'toch beitah b'toch chatzerah* — she is inside her house, inside her yard? The *Gemara* answers: *hachi ka'amar* — what the *mishna* means is *v'hi k'mi sheb'toch beitah, v'hi k'mi sheb'toch chatzerah*: wherever she is, it is as if she is in her yard. This is a strikingly forced reading of the *mishna* — if her physical presence is fundamentally not required, why would the *mishna* need to tell us that it is "as if" she were there? It is a very weak read, and the *Gemara* itself seems to acknowledge the difficulty.

### Mishtameret Principle

The *Gemara* then provides the conceptual foundation: *d'keivan d'chatzer mishtameret l'da'atah hi, mitgoreshet* — since the *chatzer* is guarded under her auspices, she is divorced. The requirement is not physical presence but rather that the yard is *mishtameret l'da'atah* — watched under her watch, through her, and not through someone else's control.

What would it mean for a yard to be guarded *not* under her auspices? The *Gemara* will address this later with the case of her slave. If the *get* is placed in the hand of her awake slave, even though the slave is her property, it is the slave who is fundamentally the watcher and controller of the object — not her. By contrast, if a person hires a watchman for their yard, the yard is still watched *through* the owner's arrangement and considered under their control. But a slave's body is his own, and so he is seen as the primary one watching and controlling whatever is placed on him. In any case other than this, the property is considered *mishtameret l'da'atah* and the *get* is valid even if she is not physically present.

### Chatzer Models Debate

The *Gemara* then raises the broader theoretical question: *leima b'ha kamipalgi* — perhaps this dispute between Ulla and Oshaya maps onto the general debate in all of *Shas* about the nature of *kinyan chatzer*. Is *chatzer* effective because it is like the owner's *yad* — an extension of the person — or is it effective because of *shlichus* — because it represents the owner's interests?

If *chatzer* works because it is like a *yad*, then just as a hand is attached to the person, the *chatzer* must be in physical proximity to the person, and Ulla's requirement that she stand on the property follows naturally. If *chatzer* works on the *shlichus* model, representing the owner's interests, then physical presence is unnecessary, and Oshaya's position makes sense.

One might further argue that by *get* specifically, even if in other contexts *chatzer* works via *shlichus*, here it must work on the *yad* model — because the *chiddush* of *natan b'yadah* seems to require something analogous to her hand, and a *get* is not given through a *shliach* in the usual sense.

### Chatzer Resolution

The *Gemara* resolves otherwise. *D'chulei alma chatzer mishum yad itrabai* — everyone agrees that *chatzer* is conceptually subsumed under *yad*. The debate is about what it means to be a *yad*. One view holds *k'yadah* literally: just as the hand is immediately adjacent to and attached to the body, so the *chatzer* must be spatially close, requiring her to stand on the property. The other view pushes back: if you insist on that level of physicality, you would require her to be *glued* to the yard — which is absurd. *Ela k'yadah* must mean something more conceptual: just as something in my hand is something I watch, protect, and control, *af chatzer mishtameret l'da'atah* — anything under my auspices and protected through me is considered like my hand. This is not a question of physical extension but of conceptual control. *L'afukei chatzer mishtameret she-lo l'da'atah* — the only exclusion is a *chatzer* watched under someone else's control, like the case of the awake slave.

---

## Hand & Vessel Principle

### Physical Proximity Model

The debate over what constitutes *yad* surfaces in two directions. One view treats *yad* as a physical, bodily concept — something on my person, attached to me, immediately adjacent to my body. On this model, the *chatzer* functions as a *yad* only when it is physically continuous with the person in some meaningful sense.

### Yad: Physical vs. Concep…

The two interpretations of *yad* map onto this debate directly. *Mah yadah b'sumucha* — just as her hand is next to her, attached to her, so the *chatzer* she must be adjacent to the *chatzer* for it to serve as an extension of her. The second view: *im mah yadah b'dvuka af chatzer b'dvuka* — if you take the analogy that far, you would require her to be literally connected to the yard, which is untenable. Therefore, we must read *yad* conceptually.

### Control Model

The conceptual reading grounds the *yad* principle in power and dominion rather than physical proximity. The metaphor of *hand* in Tanach itself points in this direction — the idea of *yad* as representing control and sovereign power: *af yadi yasdah aretz* — "my hand founded the earth." Something under her power and control is considered her *yad*. This is the principle of *mishtameret l'da'atah* — not as a physical proximity test but as a control test.

This is the position the *Gemara* ultimately endorses: *chatzer* as *yad* operates on the conceptual model of control and protection. Anything guarded and overseen through her is her *yad*; anything overseen by someone else — like the awake slave who is himself the primary controller — falls outside that category.

One might ask: what is the actual *halacha* on whether she must stand in the *chatzer*? The Rambam in *Hilchot Gerushin* 5 rules that she must be present: *im hayta omedet sham b'tzad chatzerah nitgareshet v'im lav lo nitgarsha ad she'ta'amod b'tzad chatzerah* — if she was standing beside her yard she is divorced, and if not, she is not divorced until she stands beside it — *v'af al pi she-hi chatzer she-mishtameret haget b'tochah*, even though the *chatzer* is guarded and the *get* is secured within it. The Rambam frames this not in terms of the *yad* requirement but around the inability of *chatzer* to function as a *shliach* against her interests — *she-chov hu lah*, divorce is a detriment to her, *v'ein chavin l'adam ela b'fanav*, and one cannot impose a detriment on a person in their absence. Interestingly, the Rambam rules differently for other *halachot* — in *Hilchot Aveidah* 17:10, it appears that *chatzer* works for *kinyan* without one's physical presence, presumably because those contexts are to the person's benefit and can function on the *shlichus* model.

This creates an interesting distinction: by *isha* — by the wife receiving a *get* — the *Gemara* sounds strongly as though the *yad* model is operative, as several *gemarot* confirm. By *kinyanim* generally, it may operate on the *shliach* model. And within the *yad* model itself, the debate remains: is the test physical adjacency, or conceptual control?

---

## Borrowed Space Case

### Get on Wood Piece

A certain man threw a *get* to his wife. She was standing in a yard, and the *get* rolled away and fell on a piece of wood. Rav Yosef ruled: *chazina* — we examine the situation. If the piece of wood is four *amos* by four *amos*, it constitutes its own domain — *palgei reshuta lenafshah* — and she is not divorced. If not, it is all one domain and the *get* reaches her.

### Space Boundaries

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this: *baheichi askinan* — what exactly is the case? If it is her *chatzer*, then what difference does it make if the piece of wood is four *amos*? It is in her yard and should work regardless. *Ela b'chatzer dideih* — the case must be that it is *his* yard. But then if the piece of wood is less than four *amos*, why does it work at all? It is his yard.

### Lending Space Concept

The *Gemara* answers: *lo tzricha de'ushlamah makom* — the case is that he lent her the space. He is throwing her a *get* and lending her the space to use for taking possession of it. This raises considerable questions. Must she do a *kinyan* on the space itself for it to become hers? The *Gemara* does not elaborate on what form of acquisition is required. The principle that rented or borrowed space can serve as one's domain for *kinyan* purposes is itself a *chiddush*, analogous to discussions about the *shechiv mera* who appears to have lent a space to be used. What constitutes sufficient ownership of property to function as *yad* for *gittin* remains an open question that the *Gemara* leaves imprecise.

The logic of the four-*amot*-or-not analysis is this: when he lends her a space, he lends her *one* space — the specific area he designated. If the piece of wood is four by four *amos*, it constitutes a distinct, separate domain within the larger area. Having lent her *one* space, he did not implicitly lend her two spaces. The *get* now rests on the second space — the piece of wood — which is not hers, and she is not divorced.

### Four Amot & Names

Two further refinements follow. *V'lo amran ela delo gavo'ah asarah* — all of this, the rule that a piece of wood less than four by four *amos* is treated as part of the same domain, applies only when the piece of wood is less than ten *tefachim* off the ground. If it is higher than ten *tefachim*, even if it is not four by four *amos*, it constitutes its own separate domain — analogous to the rules about *reshuyot* and height thresholds in *Shabbat*.

Additionally: *v'lo amran ela deleis lei shem levai* — even when the piece of wood is less than four *amos* and within ten *tefachim*, it is treated as the same space only if it does not have its own name. *Aval is lei shem levai* — if the piece of wood has its own accompanying name, an identity of its own — like "Fred rock" or "Pooh corner" — then even without meeting the four-by-four or the ten-*tefachim* threshold, it is treated as its own domain. Whether an analogous principle applies in *Shabbat* contexts is worth exploring, but the fundamental point here is clear: named objects with their own recognized identity may function as separate domains regardless of size or height.

---

## Bed & Vessel Cases

### Husband's Bed Problem

The *mishna* states that if the husband placed the *get* on his own bed — even while the wife is there — it does not work. This is striking. One might have thought that the husband's physical presence alongside the wife would, if anything, add to the immediacy of the transfer. Yet the *mishna* says *afilu* — even in this case — it fails.

### Rava's Distinction

Rava clarifies: *lo shanu ela b'mita shelo* — the *mishna*'s ruling that it does not work applies only to his bed. *Aval mita shela megureshet* — but if it is her bed, she is divorced. This presumably holds even if he is physically present alongside her, just as dropping a *get* into someone's yard does not fail merely because the husband is also standing in that yard.

A *baraita* confirms: *Rabbi Eliezer omer b'mita shelo eina megureshet b'mita shela megureshet* — in his bed she is not divorced, in her bed she is divorced.

### Vessel in Seller's Domain

This raises a fundamental question: why does her bed work at all if it is inside his house? The *Gemara* invokes the principle of *kelay shel lokeach birshut mocher* — the vessel of the buyer within the domain of the seller. If you bring your jug to a seller's premises and he pours wine into your jug, does that constitute a *kinyan* for you? Your jug is yours, but it sits within his domain. This is an open question in *halacha*, and the *Gemara* asks whether the case of her bed working might teach us that *kelay shel lokeach birshut mocher* — the buyer's vessel in the seller's domain — acquires for the buyer.

The *Gemara* deflects: perhaps the case of her bed is special not because of the general *kelay shel lokeach* principle but because of the height of the bed.

### Ten Tefachim Height

*De-gavoah asarah* — the bed is more than ten *tefachim* off the ground. As with the piece of wood in the previous case, an object elevated more than ten *tefachim* constitutes its own domain. Though in *Shabbat* law everything within a house is treated as *reshut hayachid* regardless of height, for these purposes the ten-*tefachim* threshold applies: her vessel, elevated above ten *tefachim*, is sufficiently its own space that placing the *get* in it works even within his domain.

The *Gemara* then asks: but what about the legs of the bed? *Ve'ika makom karay* — the legs of the bed rest on the floor, which is his domain. Is the bed truly independent? The *Gemara* answers: *makom karay lo kapid inish* — a person does not object to his wife's bed occupying space in the house.

### Lo Makpid Principle

This introduces the principle of *lo makpid* — that the husband does not object to his wife's presence and use of space in the household. However, the exact interaction between *lo makpid* and the ten-*tefachim* requirement is somewhat unclear. If *lo makpid* alone were sufficient, one would not need the ten-*tefachim* threshold at all — any vessel of hers on the ground should work. If ten *tefachim* alone were sufficient, there would be no need to add *lo makpid*. It seems that both factors work together: the elevation creates enough of a distinct space, and the husband's non-objection means his domain does not overwhelm the independence of her vessel within it.

Tosafot specifies: *makom karay lo kapid inish le'chol hapachot be'ishto* — at minimum, a man does not object to his wife's bed occupying space in his home, and the same applies to the airspace of the bed itself. With others, he might be more particular, but not with his wife.

We thus see two considerations intersecting: on the one hand, the classic *kinyan* framework of *kelay shel lokeach birshut mocher*; on the other, special considerations about what constitutes sufficient establishment of a woman's presence — whether through verbal permission, *lo makpid*, or physical thresholds. The question remains how fully the *get* framework tracks normal *kinyan* rules versus constituting a distinct model of giving.

---

## Lap & Basket Cases

### Lap Case

The *Gemara* turns to the case of throwing the *get* into the wife's *cheika* — her lap or bosom — or into her basket (*kaltah*). The lap seems straightforward: it is on her body. The basket raises the same issues as the bed. Where is the basket?

### Lap Explanation

The *Gemara* asks: *amai* — why does the basket work? *Kli shel lokeach bireshut mocher hu* — it is the vessel of the buyer within the domain of the seller. Again, the question of *kelay shel lokeach birshut mocher* surfaces. Because if the basket were in her yard, the discussion would be unnecessary.

### Suspended Basket

Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: *kegon she-hayta kaltah tluyah bah* — the case is that her basket is actually suspended on her. It hangs from her, like a chain or a strap around her neck or body, and is therefore truly an extension of her person — analogous to her hand. Indeed, *kaltah* was sometimes a form of head covering involving a basket-like structure worn on the body. If physically attached and suspended, it functions unambiguously as an extension of her person.

### Tied Basket
