Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya agrees that suspended suffices. Reish Lakish adds: *kshurah af al pi she'einah tluyah* — if it is tied to her, even if it is not suspended. Even if the basket drags on the ground but is connected to her by a string tied to her leg, it works. Notably, a third possibility would be *tluyah* without *kshurah* — suspended but not tied, like holding it — but the *Gemara* will explore this further.

### Between Thighs Case

Rav Adda bar Ahava: *kegon she-hayta kaltah munachat lah bein yarkoteha* — the basket was placed between her thighs while she was seated. This is apparently distinct from the cases of suspension or tying.

### Rashi's Lo Makpid

Rashi explains: *bein yarkoteha* — even if the basket rests on the ground between her thighs, *eino makpid al kol makom moshav ishto* — the husband does not object to wherever his wife sits or places herself. Analogous to the earlier ruling about the bed, his not objecting means his domain does not override the fact that the *get* is in her vessel. Rashi even says *vead achshav hayta oto makom kanuy lah* — up to now that space was, in a sense, hers — though this language of *kanuy lah* seems to push further than a mere *lo makpid* rationale. The operating principle, however, is that it is in her vessel (*keilim*), and his sense of domain does not overpower that because he fundamentally does not object to her being there.

### Basket Seller Case

Rav Mesharshiya bar Rav Dimi: *kegon she-haya ba'alah mocher kaltot* — the husband sells baskets for a living. Rashi explains: therefore anywhere a basket appears in the house, the husband is unbothered, since the house is full of baskets in any event. The implication is that in this household, a basket on the ground is the default and not a special indulgence — making her basket entirely unremarkable in the space.

This raises an important conceptual question. Why must we identify a special scenario — the husband selling baskets, or the basket being between her thighs — in order for *lo makpid* to apply? Should we not say that in *any* scenario where the wife is in the house, the husband implicitly allows her to set things down wherever she likes? Why would we presume that he *would* object in an ordinary case? If the principle is that special permission is needed, that implies his ownership is fundamentally established and her use is merely tolerated by exception — which would not adequately ground her presence as her own domain. But if, as seems more natural, his *not* objecting is a default rather than a special grant, then it reflects something like her established right to be in that space — and that is what enables the *get* in her vessel to work.

### Yochanan: Woman's Right

Rabbi Yochanan states this most broadly: *makom cheika kanuy lah, makom kaltah kanuy lah* — just as the space for her lap belongs to her, so too the space wherever her basket is belongs to her. This suggests not a special permission scenario but a general right: wherever the wife places her basket, that space is effectively hers.

### Rava on Lo Makpid

Rava explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: *lefi she'eino makpid lo al makom cheika velo al makom kaltah* — the husband does not object to where his wife sits or where she places her basket. It is an ongoing allowance, a default state, not a particular permission. As long as it is not a special case of permission that was granted for this moment, but rather a continuous background allowance, his domain does not override the fact that the *get* is in her vessel.

### Baraita on Baskets

A *baraita* confirms: *zarko lah letoch cheika o letoch kaltah o letoch kol davar shehu kekaltah harei zu megureshet* — anything similar to her basket is valid. The *Gemara* asks: *kol davar shehu kekaltah lribuyei mai* — what does "like her basket" add? *Lribuyei taska de'achla bah tamrei* — to include a basket she uses to eat dates from. The *tanya nami hachi* here presumably serves to confirm that the category extends to items she habitually uses and has implicit permission to place wherever she wishes — not just her primary basket but analogous vessels that share the same character of ongoing permitted presence.

---

## Get Identification

### Debt Document Case

The *mishna* now addresses framing. *Amar lah kinsi shetarach zeh* — if the husband said "take this business document," and then she opened it and discovered it was her *get*, *eino get ad she'yomar lah hileich gitteich* — it is not a valid *get* until he says to her "here is your *get*." The *get* must be identified as a *get* at the time of giving.

### Sleeping Wife Case

Similarly: *natan beyada vehi yeshena* — if he placed the *get* in her hand while she was asleep, and she woke up, read it, and found it to be her *get*, *eino get ad she'yomar lah hileich gitteich* — it is still not valid until he tells her. She must be awake and aware.

This prompts an important question. Michael raises the scenario from the earlier *Gemara* where Oshaya ruled that she could be in *Tzippori* while her yard is in *Tveria* — physically absent — yet the *get* is valid. If she need not even be present, why is a sleeping wife's reception invalid? Apparently there is a conceptual distinction: when she is physically elsewhere, there is a sense in which the *get* is objectively knowable — anyone present can see that it is a *get* being delivered — and we combine the pieces into a valid act. But when she is present yet unconscious, the necessary awareness of the act is entirely absent, and no one who is an active party to the exchange is aware of its character.

### Why Explicit Naming

The *Gemara* surprisingly does not press the question of the textual or logical derivation of this requirement — that the *get* must be framed as a *get*. Tosafot and the Rambam supply different foundations.

### Tosafot Position

Tosafot holds that the husband who gives a *get* must state *hileich gitteich v'harei at miteret lechol adam* — this is your *get* and you are permitted to any man — both as a verbal declaration and as part of the standard formulation, as is implied in the section of *Hamgaresh*. However, Tosafot acknowledges a difficulty from the case in *Nezikin* involving Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgada: a man told witnesses "see this *get* that I am giving my wife," and then delivered it to her without her knowledge that it was a *get*. The *Gemara* there indicates it is valid. Tosafot reconciles: *v'yeish lomar d'hasam nami achar kach yagidu lah ha'eidim shehi megureshet* — even there, the witnesses will subsequently inform her that she is divorced. 

The underlying principle for Tosafot is derived from *v'shalachah mibeito v'halcha v'haysa l'ish acher* — she must leave his home and go to another man — meaning she must understand the consequences of the divorce. Therefore she must know she is divorced. On this reading, the statement need not accompany the act of giving simultaneously — it can come after — as long as she ultimately knows. This also explains why Rabbi's ruling in the *baraita* allows a later declaration to retroactively validate the act.

### Witnesses Case

The Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgada case illustrates the tension directly. The husband told the witnesses — not the wife — that this document is a *get*. He then delivered it to her under false pretenses. The witnesses have objective knowledge; she does not. Tosafot says the witnesses will eventually tell her. This is not an entirely comfortable resolution — combining a misrepresented delivery with a subsequent correction — but it demonstrates that objective knowability, even without the recipient's immediate awareness, can be a factor.

### Rambam Position

The Rambam, in *Hilchot Gerushin* Perek 1, Halachah 10, derives the requirement differently. *Uminan she'eina nitna lah ela b'torat geirushin* — from where do we know it must be given in the framework of divorce? *Shene'emar sefer kritut v'natan b'yadah* — the verse says *sefer kritut* and *natan b'yadah*: the act of giving must be clearly defined as the giving of a *sefer kritut*. *Sheyeiteinu otah b'torat sefer kritut* — it has to be given in that capacity. *Aval im nitan lah b'torat shtar chov o mezuzah eino get* — but if given as a debt document or a mezuzah, it is not a *get*.

The Rambam then addresses the *eidim* case — why does that work? *Sheharei hodia et ha'eidim shenitan b'torat geirushin* — he informed the witnesses that it is being given as a *get*. For the Rambam, the requirement is not that *she* knows she is divorced, but that the act itself is objectively defined as an act of *get*-delivery. If witnesses know, the act is objectively framed correctly, even if she is ignorant. The distinction from Tosafot is precise: Tosafot requires the witnesses to eventually tell the woman so that she knows; the Rambam does not require her subjective knowledge at all — only that the act be objectively constituted as a *get*-transfer. This also explains why, for the Rambam, a sleeping woman's case is more difficult: if none of the necessary parties — not she, not any present witness — is aware of the act in the moment, one might question whether the act is sufficiently defined.

---

## Active Giving & Release

### Picking Up Issue

The *Gemara* now turns to the case where the wife picked up the *get* from behind the husband — *she-shalafto me'achorav*. The *mishna* says this is not valid. The *Gemara* asks: surely the problem is not merely that he failed to name it a *get* — the deeper problem is that *he* did not give it to her. She plucked it from behind him. *Havei lei tli giteich me'al gabi karka* — it is equivalent to telling her "pick your *get* up off the ground."

### Ground Pick-up Ruled Out

Rava rules explicitly: *tli giteich me'al gabi karka lo amar klum* — if he says "pick your *get* up off the ground," it is nothing. He must give it to her; she cannot be the one to take it. It must come actively from him to her, not be lifted by her off the ground.

### Jutting Out Solution

The *Gemara* therefore reframes the case of picking it from behind him: *lo tzricha d'arkei leh chartzei* — he jutted out his side, his body, and she then took it from him. He performed an active physical motion, extending himself toward her; she received it from that extension. This counts as an act of giving.

This remains a *chiddush*. If he extends his hand to her holding the *get* and she plucks it from his hand, one would naturally think she is the primary actor — she is the one taking, not he. The typical image of giving is that he actively drops it in her hand or places it there. Here, what is required of him seems quite minimal — jutting out his body. That this constitutes *natan b'yadah* is worth noting as something the *poskim* would need to develop and clarify.

### Baraita Parallel

The *baraita* states the two scenarios in parallel: if he told her "take this debt document" or she took it from behind him — *she-shalafto me'achorav* — the *baraita* clarifies that she did not pick it up from the ground but took it from his person, and then he said *kirtzonach veharei hu gittech* — as you wish and here is your *get*. *Eino get ad she'yomar lah harei zeh gittech* — it is not valid until he says "this is your *get*." *Divrei Rabbi.*

### Rabbi's Position

The *chiddush* of Rabbi's ruling is that the declaration can come *after* the act of giving. Once we establish that the act must be framed as a *get*, one might think the framing must coincide with the moment of delivery. Rabbi says it need not. If she was conscious throughout and he says "here is your *get*" afterward, that later statement can retroactively define the whole process. The reasoning: she was conscious and engaged when the document was placed in her hands, capable of being divorced at that moment; when he subsequently says "here is your *get*," we read the statement backward through the continuous interaction and view it as defining the earlier act.

### R. S. ben Elazar

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar disagrees: *le'olam eino get ad she-yitlena heimena ve-yachzor ve-yitnena lah ve-yomar lah harei zeh gittech* — it is never valid until he takes it back from her and gives it again properly, with the correct declaration. A subsequent statement cannot retroactively reframe an earlier act of giving.

### Consciousness Factor

The *Gemara* explains why both cases — the debt-document misrepresentation and the sleeping wife — are necessary. Had we only the case of misrepresentation, one might think Rabbi rules as he does because she was conscious throughout and capable of receiving a *get* in that moment — *bat gerushin hi* — such that the later statement can define the earlier act as part of a continuous exchange. When she is asleep, she is *lav bat gerushin* — incapable of receiving a *get* at the moment of delivery — and perhaps even Rabbi would agree with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar that the *get* must be re-given.

Conversely, had we only the sleeping case, one might think Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar requires a re-giving only because of the unconsciousness — but in the debt-document case, where she was awake, perhaps he would concede to Rabbi. *Tzricha* — both cases are needed to establish the full scope of the dispute.

The underlying question for Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar is coherent: how can a later statement reframe an earlier act? An act was done in one capacity; how does a subsequent declaration transform its identity? For the case of misrepresentation where she was conscious, one can at least argue for a continuous, unified interaction in which the later statement gives meaning to the whole. For the sleeping case, the acts are separated by time and states of consciousness, making the retroactive reframing far harder to sustain.

---

## Slave Intermediary

### Sleeping Slave Works

Rava rules: if a man wrote a *get* and placed it into the hand of his wife's slave — *yashen u-mesharmato harei zeh get* — if the slave is asleep and she is watching it, it is a valid *get*.

### Awake Slave Fails

*Ne'or eino get* — if the slave is awake, it is not valid. This is counterintuitive. One would think that an awake, alert slave is *more* capable of guarding the *get*. But the problem is precisely that: *de-havei leh chatzer ha-mishtameret she-lo le-da'atah* — the slave's wakefulness means *he* is the one in control of the *get*, not her. An awake slave is watching the object through his own conscious agency; the *chatzer* is therefore not *mishtameret l'da'atah* — not guarded under her auspices — and fails.

### Slave as Moving Domain

Why does even the sleeping slave case not fail on a different ground? *Chatzer mehalechet hi* — it is a moving *chatzer*. The principle that *chatzer* only functions when stationary rules out placing a *get* in an object that moves of its own accord. Vessels (*keilim*) can be moved by an external force but do not move on their own — so placing the *get* in her vessel works. But a slave moves himself. How then does the sleeping slave ever work?

### Rava on Movement

Rava presses further: *kol she'ilu mehalach lo kanah omed v'yoshev lo kanah* — anything that would not acquire when moving would not acquire when standing still or seated. Even seated or standing, a slave who can move of his own volition remains a *chatzer mehalechet* in principle, because at any moment he might walk away. The distinction between sleeping and seated is insufficient to resolve the problem.

### Bound Slave Solution

*V'hilchata b'chafut* — the practical ruling is that the slave must be bound. When the slave's legs are bound and he cannot walk even if he wills it, two problems are resolved simultaneously: the *chatzer mehalechet* problem disappears because he cannot move, and the *mishtameret she-lo l'da'atah* problem is addressed because — being bound and asleep — he is not the active controller. The *chatzer* is then *mishtameret l'da'atah* and stationary, and the *get* is valid. This ties together the earlier discussion of *chatzer* with the specific difficulties raised by the use of human agents as intermediaries.

---

## Public Domain Get

### Proximity Rule

The *mishna* states: *hayta omedet bireshut harabim* — if she was standing in the public domain and he threw the *get* to her — *karov lah megureshet, karov lo eina megureshet* — if it lands closer to her she is divorced, if it lands closer to him she is not divorced. *Mekhtza al mekhtza megureshet v'eina megureshet* — if it lands exactly equidistant, she is doubtfully divorced.

### General Application

The *mishna* adds that the same rule applies to *kiddushin* — if a ring was thrown — and to a debt. These extensions will be significant later.

### Debt Parallel

The debt case is instructive. If a creditor said *zerok li chovi* — throw me the money you owe — and the borrower threw it: *karov l'malveh zachah malveh* — if it landed closer to the creditor, the creditor has acquired it and bears the loss if it is subsequently lost. *Karov l'loveh, haloveh chayav* — if it is closer to the borrower, the debt has not yet been transferred and the borrower remains liable. *Mekhtza al mekhtza shneihem yachloku* — if exactly equidistant and then lost, the borrower must repay half.

### Kinyan Question

This *mishna* is striking on its face. Since when is there a *kinyan* based on physical proximity in a public domain? Normally, acquiring something requires *hagbahah* — lifting — or *meshichah* — drawing toward oneself. The mere fact that an object lands closer to me than to you in the middle of a public thoroughfare does not, by ordinary *kinyan* law, vest it in me. This would seem to be strong evidence that *get* delivery does not operate on the normal *kinyan* model — it is a distinct act of giving, not an acquisition.

However, the *mishna*'s extension to *kiddushin* and *chov* complicates this. If the proximity rule also governs *kiddushin* and debt-payment, it presumably reflects some general *kinyan* principle applicable across contexts — not only a *get*-specific rule. Yet proximity in a public domain as a *kinyan* is something we have never encountered.

### Rav's Four Amot

Rav resolves this: *arba amos shelah zehu karov lah, arba amos shelo zehu karov lo* — "closer to her" means within her four *amos*, and "closer to him" means within his four *amos*. The *mishna* is not speaking of literal physical proximity but of the rabbinic *kinyan* of *arba amos* in a public domain. The Sages created the rule that an ownerless object within someone's four *amos* in the public domain is acquired by that person — analogous to the concept that carrying an object four *amos* in a public domain constitutes a form of displacement. Something within my immediate environs is considered under my control. Rav thus reads the *mishna* as invoking this established *kinyan* and not introducing anything novel.

### Half and Half Case

The *Gemara* asks: *heichi dami mekhtza l'mekhtza* — what is the half-and-half case according to Rav? Rabbi Shmuel bar Avtigon answers: *b'shneihem omdim b'arba amos* — the case is where the two are close enough that their respective four-*amos* zones overlap. The *get* lands in a space that falls within both her four *amos* and his four *amos* simultaneously — a Venn diagram of contested space. That is why it is a *safek* — not because we lack factual information about where it landed, but because it objectively falls within both parties' domains.

The *Gemara* then asks: could we not resolve this by asking who was in the public domain first? The first person there establishes the priority of their four *amos*, and whoever arrived later entered into the other's space. *V'chi teima d'asu tarvaihu bahadi hadadi v'ee efshar l'tzamtzem* — one might say they arrived at exactly the same time, but perfect simultaneity never occurs in practice, so this should always be determinable in principle. The implication would be that the *safek* is merely epistemic — a lack of facts — not a genuine indeterminacy. This is less interesting as a legal case.

### Conflicting Witnesses

Rabbah and Rav Yosef resolve differently: *hakha b'shnei kitei edim askinan* — the *mishna* is speaking of a case with two sets of witnesses offering conflicting testimony. One pair testifies the *get* landed closer to her; another pair testifies it landed closer to him. The *safek* is purely a matter of disputed evidence — not an objective overlapping of domains. If the instant replay were available, the question would be resolved. Fine as a legal mechanism; it makes the *mishna* more a procedural curiosity than a substantive doctrine about contested space.

---

## Yochanan's Literal Read

### Rejects Four Amot

Rabbi Yochanan takes a more *pshat*-oriented reading of the *mishna* and explicitly rejects Rav's four-*amos* interpretation. *Rabbi Yochanan omer karov lah shaninu* — "closer to her" is what we taught — literally. *Afilu meah amah* — even a hundred *amos* away, as long as it is closer to her than to him. And *karov lo shaninu, afilu meah amah* — "closer to him," even a hundred *amos* away.

### Protection Model

The *Gemara* asks: according to Rabbi Yochanan, what then is the half-and-half case? Rav Himnuna bar Abba answers: *lididi meparsha li minei d'Rabbi Yochanan* — it was explained to me directly from Rabbi Yochanan: the operative question is not rulers and distances but who can protect the object. *Hi yechola l'shomro v'hu einu yachol l'shomro* — if she is able to protect it and he is unable, that is "closer to her" and she is divorced. Even though Rabbi Yochanan initially sounds purely literal, his actual principle is conceptual: it is about control, access, and the ability to protect — not raw physical distance.

### Clarification

So Rabbi Yochanan's read is "literal" in rejecting the four-*amos* framework, but "conceptual" in how he defines proximity: proximity means the capacity to control and protect. The categories then emerge clearly.

### Protection Categories

Three categories follow from this: if she can protect it and he cannot — *zehu karov lah*, it is considered near to her, and she is divorced. If he can protect it and she cannot — *zehu karov lo*, it is near to him, and she is not divorced. If both can protect it equally, or neither can — *zehu mekhtza al mekhtza*, that is the half-and-half case of doubt.

This approach departs dramatically from normal *kinyan* logic. Under standard acquisition rules, the ability to run over and grab an object does not vest ownership. For Rabbi Yochanan, by contrast, the ability to access and protect — even from a hundred *amos* away — constitutes the relevant standard for *get* delivery. This points strongly toward the view that *get* transfer operates on a sui generis model, distinct from ordinary *kinyanim*.

### Praise from Babylon

When the scholars in Israel told Rabbi Yochanan that Rabbi Yonatan in Bavel had arrived at the same reading, Rabbi Yochanan responded: *yodin chavran b'vavlayi l'forushei ki hai ta'ama!* — our Babylonian colleagues know how to give good *pshat* to a *mishna*! This is a telling remark. In general, the scholars of Eretz Yisrael tended toward more literal, text-faithful readings of earlier sources, while the Babylonians were more comfortable with interpretive departures. Here Rabbi Yochanan praises the Babylonian for having arrived independently at what he regards as the true *pshat* of the *mishna*.

### Dog Example

The *Gemara* brings a *baraita* in support: Rabbi Eliezer says — *kol shehu karov lah mi lo* — if it is closer to her than to him, and *uba kelev v'natlo* — a dog came and took it, *einah megureshet* — she is not divorced. The *Gemara* clarifies: surely Rabbi Eliezer does not mean she must guard it forever. The *baraita* means: if the object is physically closer to her than to him, but *v'im ba kelev v'natlo v'hu yachol l'shomro v'hi einah yechola l'shomro* — if a dog were to come and he could stop it while she could not, then even though it is physically nearer to her, she is not divorced. Perhaps a river or a large boulder lies between her and the *get*, giving her the appearance of proximity but not the actual capacity for control. Physical measurement is never the test; the protection and access test is always determinative.

---

## Practical Stringency

### Bending Down Test

Shmuel said to Rav Yehuda: *shinana* — sharp one — *kdei she-tishoch v'titlennu* — the *halacha* in practice is that it must be close enough to her that she can bend down and pick it up. This is more stringent than either Rav's four-*amos* framework or Rabbi Yochanan's hundred-*amos* protection model. Given the gravity of a woman's marital status, Shmuel insists that in practice we require genuine physical proximity.

### Direct Hand Requirement

And even that is not the final word: *v'at lo ta'avid uvda ad d'mati gita l'yadah* — you should not rule in practice that she is divorced until the *get* actually reaches directly into her hand. The progression tightens dramatically: from the theoretical possibility of a hundred *amos* away, to the requirement of four *amos* as per Rav, to the requirement of close enough to bend and pick up, to the requirement that it actually come into her hand directly.

### Chalitza Case

Mar bar Ammi told Rav Ashi: there was an actual case where the *get* was thrown close to the wife — perhaps close enough that she could have bent down to pick it up — and nonetheless *v'atzrichua chalitza* — they required her to undergo *chalitza*. She was not ruled to be definitely divorced, because the *get* had not reached directly into her hand. This shows how stringently the practical ruling was applied.

### Tosafot Limit

Tosafot limits this stringency: *dehaynu davka bireshut harabim* — this applies specifically in the public domain. In a public domain, a person has no real, established presence. Without a *chatzer*, without a vessel, without any grounded connection to the space, the delivery must be maximally direct. But in a *chatzer* — her yard — the analysis is different.

### Yard Exception

*Aval bechatzer ein tzarich sheyagia liyada* — in the yard, the *get* need not reach her person at all. The *chatzer* itself is her domain; a *get* deposited anywhere within it, provided the *chatzer* is *mishtameret l'da'atah*, reaches her in the legally required sense. Tosafot notes that the *Aruch* appears more stringent even in the yard case, requiring the *get* to reach her person, but Tosafot rejects this position.

### Summary Arc

The arc traced by this sugya is remarkable. We began with the theoretical possibility — under Rabbi Yochanan — that a *get* thrown a hundred *amos* away, but in a position where she can protect it and he cannot, constitutes a valid delivery. We moved to Rav's position that the four-*amos kinyan* framework applies. We arrived, through Shmuel's stringency, at the requirement that in practice, for a ruling to be issued, the *get* must reach the woman's hand directly. In the public domain, the practical ruling effectively requires direct personal delivery.

---

## Get Model Distinct

### Non-Kinyan Model

The *sugya* of 78 reveals a radical element in the laws of *get* delivery: the transfer of a *get* need not conform to the ordinary rules of *kinyan*. Under Rabbi Yochanan's model, proximity is measured by the capacity to protect — not by the formalities of *hagbahah*, *meshichah*, or even *arba amos*. A *get* can be delivered into a space the husband lent for the purpose; it can be delivered into her vessel elevated above ten *tefachim* in his house; it can be delivered by a bound, sleeping slave. These are not standard modes of acquisition.

### Definition vs. Awareness

At the same time, the *sugya* reveals a deeper debate about what *get* delivery requires beyond the physical transfer. For Tosafot, the wife must ultimately be aware that she is divorced — *v'shalachah mibeito v'halcha* — she must understand the consequence of the act, which is why the witnesses in the Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgada case must eventually inform her. For the Rambam, the requirement is objective rather than subjective: the act of giving must be constituted and framed as the giving of a *sefer kritut* — and if witnesses know, the act is properly defined, regardless of the wife's awareness.

### Forward Question

Tomorrow, we will take up the question posed by the end of the *mishna*: the same proximity rule is stated to apply to *kiddushin* and to the repayment of a *chov*. If the proximity model of delivery is a special rule for *get* — not conforming to ordinary *kinyanim* — how can the *mishna* apply it equally to *kiddushin* and debt? Normal *kinyanim* do not work this way. We will see what the *Gemara* makes of that extension.

---

---

# Gittin 79

## Get in Reshus HaRabim

### Gittin Only

The daf opens in the middle of the previous discussion on 78b, concerning the scenario in which a husband throws a *get* in *reshus ha-rabim* and it falls near the woman. The earlier sugya established a debate about what "near her" means: one position holds it must land within her *arba amot*, the classic mode of rabbinic *kinyan*; the other, attributed to Rabbi Yochanan, holds that as long as she is in a position to guard and protect it — even if it is far from her — it is considered under her control. Rabbi Yochanan's reading underscores a fundamental principle: the act of giving a *get* need not conform to the same formal requirements as *kinyan* of an ordinary object. It can be a *netina* without a conventional *kinyan*. At the same time, the *Gemara* closed with a significant practical stringency — endorsed by Tosafot — that in practice the *get* must reach her hand directly, or at minimum land in her yard. None of the more lenient constructions of the *Mishnah* are relied upon *le-halacha*.

Against this backdrop, the *Gemara* on our daf turns to the final clause of the *Mishnah*, which extends the same rule — that throwing works — not only to *gittin* but also to *kiddushin* and repayment of a debt. This raises a sharp question: if Rabbi Yochanan's position is that the *get* works even when it lands far away, provided she can protect it, why would such a non-standard act of transfer function in *kiddushin* or debt repayment, which are governed by ordinary *kinyan* principles?

The *Gemara* opens with Rav Assi citing Rabbi Yochanan: *L'Gittin amru v'lo l'davar acher* — this principle was stated for *gittin* alone and does not apply to anything else. This amounts to reading the *Mishnah* as if its additional cases simply do not mean what they appear to say.

### Kiddushin & Debt

Rabbi Abba immediately challenges Rav Assi: the *Mishnah* explicitly states *v'chein l'inyan kiddushin* — and likewise for *kiddushin*! How can Rav Assi, in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, simply bracket the plain text of the *Mishnah*?

### Yatza V'Hayata

The *Gemara* responds that *kiddushin* is not a true counter-example. The verse in Devarim reads *v'yatza v'hayata* — she leaves one husband and becomes the wife of another — which links *geirushin* and *kiddushin* as conceptually mirrored. If the mechanism works for *gittin*, it works for *kiddushin* as well, because the Torah itself draws this parallel.

This linkage is less surprising once one recalls that *kiddushin* already operates differently from ordinary *kinyan*. *Kiddushei kesef*, for instance, can be effected through *bahahi hana'ah* — the abstract benefit a woman derives from some act done on her behalf — without any concrete object passing into her possession at all. There are even opinions that one can perform *kiddushin* with a stolen object, since the woman acquires certain rights in it even absent formal ownership. Given these anomalies, it is not so strange to say that just as *gittin* can be effected through a protected-but-not-formally-transferred object, *kiddushin* can parallel it.

### Debt Condition

The debt case, however, is different and cannot be resolved so easily. The *Mishnah* says: *Zrok li chovi v'zarko lo, karov l'malveh zachah lo* — if the debtor throws the money and it lands near the creditor, the creditor has acquired it; if it lands nearer to the debtor, the debtor remains liable; and if it falls midway, they split. This appears to be a genuine application of the "proximity-as-acquisition" principle in an ordinary property context, which directly contradicts Rabbi Yochanan's insistence that this mechanism is unique to *gittin*.

The *Gemara* answers: *hacha b'mai askinan d'amar lei zrok li chovi v'tipater* — the *Mishnah* is discussing a case where the creditor specifically stipulated, "Throw it to me and you will be exempt." In other words, it is not that throwing near the creditor is inherently an act of debt repayment; rather, the creditor himself created a special condition under which the throw would discharge the obligation.

The *Gemara* immediately objects: if that is all that is happening, *mai le-memra* — what is the *chiddush*? Of course if the creditor declared that the throw would suffice, it works. The *Gemara* then refines the case further: *d'amar lei zrok li chovi b'toras gittin* — the creditor said, "Throw me my debt in the manner of a *get*," i.e., as if you were giving me a *get*. The *Gemara* again presses: still, what is the novelty? And the final answer is: *mahu d'teima mechi amar lei meshachek ani bach* — one might have thought the debtor could later claim he was joking, that he never seriously meant to frame the payment in those unusual terms. The *Mishnah* therefore teaches that once he made that declaration, he cannot retract it.

This is, as the lecturer notes, a strikingly forced reading of the *Mishnah*. The plain implication of the *Mishnah* is that throwing a debt payment near the creditor functions as a valid act of repayment — yet Rabbi Yochanan, through Rav Assi, refuses to accept this, driven by the conviction that his radical reading of *gittin* (that a *get* can work even without a conventional *kinyan*) is so exceptional that it cannot bleed into normal monetary law. He is therefore willing to impose a nearly impossible reading on the *Mishnah* rather than concede that this mechanism is a general mode of acquisition.

It is worth pausing to note that a debt repayment is arguably not identical to an ordinary *kinyan*. When one sells a basketball, the object was never the buyer's, and acquisition requires a formal *ma'aseh kinyan*. But when repaying a debt, the money in some sense already belongs to the creditor — it is merely being returned. Whether that distinction would affect the formal requirements of repayment is an independent question the *Gemara* does not resolve here, but it sharpens why Rabbi Yochanan's position, however forced as a reading of the *Mishnah*, has internal logic.

### Direct Handover

Rabbi Yochanan's stringency bears revisiting in light of all this. The same Rabbi Yochanan who expands the *get's* validity to cover situations where the woman can merely protect the document — even a hundred *amot* away — also insists, in practice, that the *get* must reach her hand directly. Whatever theoretical latitude the *Mishnah* provides, *le-ma'aseh* Rabbi Yochanan does not rely on it, and a woman who received a *get* by any of these indirect means would be in a state of doubt. This is a significant practical *chumra*, one that transforms what might seem like a liberalization of the *Mishnah* into a stringency that renders her status as *megoreshet* uncertain unless the *get* came directly to her.

---

## Physical Control

### Get & Strings

Rav Chisda addresses a case of a *get* given with strings still attached: *get beyada u-meshicha beyado* — the *get* is in her hand, but the husband is holding a string connected to it. The rule is: *im yachol lenatko u-lehavyo etzlo einah megureshet* — if he can yank the string and retrieve the *get*, she is not divorced. If the string is effectively slack — if he cannot use it to reclaim the document — she is divorced. The reasoning is *ba'inan kerisus* — the Torah requires a complete severance between husband and wife, and if he retains the ability to reclaim the document, that severance has not been achieved. This is, of course, entirely literal, but it lends itself naturally to the metaphorical expression of a divorce "with strings attached."

### Sloped Hands

Rav Yehuda addresses another scenario: *haysah yada asuya ke-tafres* — her hand was positioned like a slope, angled downward. The husband threw the *get* into her sloped hand, and despite physically reaching her hand, it immediately slid off. The ruling is *af al pi she-higi'a le-yada einah megureshet* — even though it reached her hand, she is not divorced.

### Did Not Settle

The *Gemara* asks: even if we accept that the *get* slipping from her hand means she did not acquire it *via* her hand, why does it not take effect by virtue of landing within her *arba amot* once it hits the ground? The *Gemara* answers: *delo nach* — it did not come to rest. According to Rashi, before the *get* reached the ground it was blown away, or perhaps burnt, and never actually settled within her *arba amot*.

A further question arises: even if it did not come to rest, should she not acquire it *me-avira de-arba amot* — from the airspace of her *arba amot*? This raises an open question: when the Rabbis instituted *kinyan arba amot* in *reshus ha-rabim*, did that *kinyan* include the airspace above those four *amot*, or only the ground level?

The *Gemara* notes that this question — *yesh lahen avir ein lahen avir* — was itself posed by Rabbi Elazar and left unresolved. One might think the sloped-hands case resolves it: since the *get* in the airspace did not effect a divorce, perhaps *arba amot* has no airspace rights. But the *Gemara* deflects this inference: the case involves a woman standing at the edge of a river, so that when the *get* slid off her hands, it immediately passed over the airspace above the river. Since the riverbed is not a surface on which something can come to rest, the airspace above it does not belong to her *arba amot* — *mi-ikara le-ibud ka'ei*, it was headed for destruction from the outset.

### Airspace Rights

The broader principle — that airspace above a space where objects cannot come to rest does not constitute protected domain — carries implications for the subsequent discussion of rooftops and enclosed areas. The question of whether *arba amot* includes airspace thus remains formally unresolved, but the practical direction of the sugya leans toward excluding it, with the rooftop cases relying instead on property-based airspace rather than the rabbinic *kinyan* of *arba amot*.

---

## Rooftop Scenarios

### Woman Above

The next *Mishnah* (79a) opens with two scenarios involving different vertical positions. In the first: *haisah omedes al rosh ha-gag* — the woman is standing on the rooftop and the man is at ground level; he throws the *get* up to her. The rule is: *keivan she-higi'a le-avir ha-gag harei zu megureshet* — once the *get* reaches the airspace of the rooftop, she is divorced, even before it lands. This introduces airspace of one's own property as a mechanism distinct from the *arba amot* discussed earlier. One's property certainly carries airspace rights, and once the *get* enters that airspace, if under normal circumstances it would have come to rest, she is already divorced — even if something intervenes (a wind, a fire) and it never actually lands.

### Unprotected Airspace

The second scenario reverses the positions: *hu mi-lema'ala ve-hi mi-lematah* — he is on the rooftop and she is below in the yard; he throws it down to her. The *Mishnah* states that once the *get* leaves the domain of the rooftop — *keivan she-yatza me-reshus ha-gag* — and enters the airspace of the yard below, even if it is subsequently erased or burnt in mid-air, she is divorced.

The *Gemara* immediately raises the obvious difficulty: *lo mintar* — the rooftop has no fence. It is a flat roof, open to wind and other elements. What makes the airspace above it or the airspace below it "protected"? The whole theory of airspace-as-acquisition rests on the concept of *chatzer ha-mishtameres* — a guarded domain that keeps things within it. An open rooftop, or the open air above a yard with no enclosing walls sufficiently high, is not inherently protective in this sense.

### Fenced Airspace

Rav Papa resolves this: *begag she-yesh lo ma'akeh askinan* — we are dealing with a rooftop that has a fence around it. Once there is a fence, the *get* must enter the space *within* the fence — not merely above the level of the fence — and then it is genuinely contained and protected. The *Mishnah*'s statement that she is divorced once it enters the airspace of the rooftop is predicated on the existence of such an enclosure.

The same principle applies to the second case, where the woman is below. The airspace through which the *get* travels after leaving the rooftop must be enclosed and protected. The *Gemara* cites Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: *kegon she-hayu mechitzot ha-tachtonot odofot al ha-elyonot* — the walls of the lower yard are higher than the walls of the rooftop building. If one imagines a building standing in the middle of a large courtyard whose surrounding walls are taller than the rooftop, then the moment the *get* leaves the rooftop it is already within the enclosed, protected airspace of the courtyard below. This ruling is stated in parallel by Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya, and by Rabbi Ami in the name of Rabbi Yochanan.

Rav Papa then asks Abaye: *ke-man ke-Rabbi?* — is this position consistent only with the view of *Rebbi*, who holds *kluta ke-mi she-hunchah damya* — that an object absorbed into a domain's airspace is legally equivalent to having landed there? And this would mean that only according to *Rebbi* does the *get* take effect the moment it enters the protected airspace, even before it comes to rest.

Abaye responds: *afilu tima rabbanan* — even the *Rabanan* who dispute *Rebbi* on this point do so only for *Shabbat* purposes. The *Rabanan* hold that for *Shabbat*, being in the airspace of *reshut ha-yachid* is not equivalent to resting there — so one who throws an object into the airspace of a private domain but does not land it has not violated *Shabbat* according to the *Rabanan*. But here the concern is not about *Shabbat* at all. The question for *gittin* is whether the object is *mintar* — protected — and once it is in the enclosed protected airspace, *ve-ha kamintar*, it is protected. The two frameworks operate by entirely different criteria.

### Three Tefachim Rule

Ulla bar Manashya, in the name of Avimi, offers a further approach: even without a fence, if the *get* is within three *tefachim* of the rooftop surface, it works — *d'chol pachot mi-shlosha samuch le-gag ke-gag dami* — because within three *tefachim* of the ground (or of a surface), halachic law treats the object as if it were already resting on that surface. This principle, familiar from other areas, means that for the first case — the woman above — even without an enclosure, if the *get* clears the lip of the roof and is within three *tefachim* of the roof surface, it is as though it has landed and she is divorced.

### Man Above

In the second case — the man above, woman below — the *Gemara* applies the same framework of higher surrounding walls. This is described by Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, and repeated by Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya and by Rabbi Ami in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *kegon she-hayu mechitzot ha-tachtonot odofot al ha-elyonot*.

Rava articulates three distinct principles that emerge from comparing *gittin* to *Shabbat* law in this area. First, *Rebbi's* ruling that *kluta ke-mi she-hunchah damya* — an object is treated as having landed once it enters a domain's airspace — is disputed by the *Rabanan* for *Shabbat* purposes, but applies for *gittin* because in *gittin* the criterion is protection, not rest. Second, Rav Chisda had earlier ruled that placing an object atop a hundred-*amah* pole in *reshut ha-yachid* renders one liable for *Shabbat* — *reshut ha-yachid olah ad la-rakia*, private domain extends upward to the heavens — so even at that height, if the object has landed, one is liable. But that ruling is *hani milei l'inyan Shabbat*; by *gittin*, *mishum neturei hu*, the *get* must be in a protected space, and an object balanced on the top of a hundred-*amah* pole is not protected from forces that could dislodge it, regardless of its technical presence within *reshut ha-yachid*. These two cases are mirror images of one another: the first involves an object that is protected but has not rested; the second involves an object that has rested but is not protected. For *Shabbat*, the object in the first case does not create liability (lacking rest), while the object in the second does (having rested within *reshut ha-yachid* regardless of protection). For *gittin*, precisely the opposite: the first case works (protected space suffices), and the second does not (lack of protection disqualifies it).

### Trajectory

Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha rules that the case of *nimchak* — the *get* being erased in mid-air — depends critically on the direction of travel at the moment of erasure. *Lo shanu ela she-nimchak derech yerida* — the ruling that she is divorced applies only when the *get* was erased on its downward trajectory. *Aval nimchak derech aliyah lo* — if it was erased while still going upward, she is not divorced, *me-ikara lo le-minach ka'ei* — because at that moment it was not yet headed toward coming to rest in the yard. An object on an upward trajectory, even if gravity will eventually bring it down, is directionally oriented away from the receiving domain and cannot be considered as entering that domain's space at the moment of erasure. Only when the object is descending is it definitively in the process of landing within the protected space.

### Burning Get

Similarly, the case of *nisraf* — the *get* catching fire — depends on timing relative to when the fire began. If the *get* was thrown before the fire broke out, and the fire then destroys it in mid-air, she is divorced. But if there was already a fire burning in the yard when the husband threw the *get*, she is not divorced: *me-ikara le-sreifah ka-azil* — from the outset it was thrown into a fire, not into a protected domain. If a wind subsequently blew the *get* into a fire that was not in its path when thrown, that would presumably be treated as *kadam get le-dleikah* — the *get* preceded the fire — and she would be divorced, since the throw itself had nothing to do with the conflagration.

---

## Separate Domains

### Different Buildings

Rav Chisda introduces the principle of *reshuyot chalukot be-gittin* — separate domains in the context of *gittin*. The case involves a structure or courtyard above which the rooftop appears as a single continuous surface, but below which different sections are owned by different people. Rav Chisda's ruling is that the separate ownership below creates separate domains above as well, such that even if on the roof it all looks like one flat space, the airspace over one building's section is distinct from the airspace over another's.

### Source Question

Rami bar Chama asks Rava: *mina lei le-saba ha?* — from where does Rav Chisda derive this principle? Rava responds: *masnitin hi* — it comes from the *Mishnah* itself.

### One Space

The *Gemara* works through the logic as follows. The *Mishnah* presents two scenarios: (1) she is on the rooftop and he throws from below — once it reaches the airspace of the roof she is divorced; (2) he is on the rooftop and she is below — once the *get* leaves the domain of the roof she is divorced. In both cases, the *Mishnah* simply describes where each party is standing without specifying who owns which space.

Now, who owns what? If she owns both the rooftop and the yard below, there is no *chiddush* in the airspace of the rooftop — the entire space is hers and of course she acquires whatever enters it. Conversely, if he owns both rooftop and yard, neither scenario makes sense, because neither the airspace of the roof nor the airspace of the yard is hers. The *Gemara* therefore says: in the first scenario (*reisha*), she must own the roof and he owns the yard; in the second (*seifa*), he owns the roof and she owns the yard.

But this creates a difficulty: how can the *Mishnah* switch the ownership arrangements between the first and second clauses without saying so? Rava's resolution is: in truth, *all* the space is his — both the roof and the yard. What the *Mishnah* is describing is a case of *d'oshla makom* — he has granted her the use of whichever space she is currently standing in for the purpose of receiving the *get*. When she is above, he is effectively lending her the rooftop as her domain for the *get*. When she is below, he is lending her the yard.

This reading has a further implication: *chad makom moshli inshi, trei mekomot lo moshli inshi* — people ordinarily lend one space, not two. Therefore, if there are two distinct buildings below, even if the rooftop looks like one unbroken surface above, the husband's permission to use "a space" grants her rights in only one of those spaces. If the *get* lands in the airspace over the other building's section, she has not acquired it, even though from above it appears to be the same continuous roof. This is the derivation of Rav Chisda's principle of *reshuyot chalukot be-gittin*.

Rava's challenger responds: *dilma hachi ve-dilma hachi* — perhaps the two clauses of the *Mishnah* simply describe two different factual scenarios, each with its own ownership configuration, without requiring the harmonized reading. In the *reisha* she owns the roof; in the *seifa* he owns the roof. The *Mishnah* switched cases without announcing it — a reading that, while less elegant, requires no theory of implicit permission-granting. The *Gemara* acknowledges this alternative without definitively rejecting it, leaving Rava's reading as a compelling but not exclusive interpretation.

### Gittin vs. Shabbat

The third of Rava's principles addresses the analogue in *Shabbat* law. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules: one may not stand on one rooftop and collect rainwater from a neighbor's rooftop — *she-keshem she-diyurin chalukin mi-lematah, kach diyurin chalukin mi-lema'alah* — because just as the inhabitants are separate below, the domains are separate above, even though the two rooftops form one continuous surface. This is a *Shabbat* ruling: carrying from one section of the roof to the other constitutes carrying between separate *reshuyot* and requires an *eiruv*.

However, Rava notes: *hani milei l'inyan Shabbat, aval l'inyan get, mishum kepeida hu ve-chulei hai lo kapdi inshi* — this rule applies for *Shabbat*, but for *gittin* the analysis differs. The rationale in *gittin* is about what the husband actually intends when he tells her she may use "a space." When it comes to a rooftop, *ein tashmisham kavu'a* — people do not regularly use rooftops — and the two halves of a flat rooftop are not meaningfully distinct in the way a yard and a room are. A husband who says "you may use this space" for her *get* would not typically distinguish between the two halves of a continuous rooftop. *Lo kapdi inshi* — people are not particular about that. Therefore, the *reshuyot chalukot* principle that prohibits carrying across rooftop sections for *Shabbat* does not disqualify a *get* received on the "wrong" half of a flat rooftop. This is a meaningful divergence between the rules for *gittin* and the rules for *Shabbat*, reflecting the different underlying concerns of each framework.

### Connected Roofs

Rashi spells this out explicitly: even if the husband specifically named one rooftop when granting her permission — *hish'il lah makom be-zeh le-kabel et gittah* — and she received the *get* on the other rooftop, the *Gemara* says *lo amrinan hacha reshuyot chalukot*. This is because *mishum kepeida hu* — it is about what he cares about, and regarding adjacent rooftops that share one flat surface, *ein tashmisham kavu'a ve-gas*, people do not invest particular significance in which half of the roof is being used. The contrast is with the earlier principle that *yesh mash'il chatzeiro u-makpid al beito* — one who lends a yard does not thereby grant use of the inner rooms. There, the distinction is functionally obvious and significant. On a flat rooftop, it is not. Therefore, *lo kapdi inshi* — he would not be *makpid* about which half of his own connected rooftops she used — and a *get* received on either half is valid.

---

## Yards & Baskets

### Nested Yards

Abaye presents a case of two concentric yards: *pnimit shelah ve-chitzonah shelo* — the inner yard belongs to her and the outer yard belongs to him. The walls of the outer yard are higher than those of the inner yard, such that the inner yard is fully enclosed within and protected by the outer walls. The husband throws the *get* to her. The ruling: *keivan she-higi'a le-avir mechitzot ha-chitzonah harei zu megureshet* — once the *get* enters the airspace of the outer walls, she is divorced. The rationale is *pnimit gufah be-mechitzot ha-chitzonah kamintara* — the inner yard itself is what is protected by the outer walls. Her property (the inner yard) is implicitly shielded by his enclosure. This is a case where she acquires the *get* while it is still technically over his property (the outer yard), but because her property is the beneficiary of the protection his walls provide, it counts as sufficiently within her domain.

### Nested Baskets

The *Gemara* then draws a pointed contrast: *ma she-ein ken be-kupot* — this is not true for baskets. If she has the inner basket and he has the outer (larger) basket, and he throws a *get* into the nested baskets: *afilu higi'a le-avir pnimit einah megureshet* — even if the *get* reaches the airspace of the inner basket, she is not divorced, because it has not yet landed. She must wait until it actually comes to rest.

### Property vs. Vessels

The reason is fundamental: *de-ha lo nach* — it has not come to rest. The concept of acquiring something through airspace is a feature of real property and enclosed domains, not of movable vessels. A basket has no airspace rights. *Kinyan kli* — acquisition through a vessel — requires the object to actually land in the vessel; the airspace above a basket conveys nothing. Yards and property have airspace. Baskets do not.

A further complication arises: *kli she-lokeach be-reshut mocher hu* — if her basket is sitting inside his basket, then her vessel is sitting within his domain, which raises a question about whether it counts as her domain at all. The *Gemara* addresses this by positing that the outer basket has no bottom — *kuppa she-ein lah shulayim* — so that it does not constitute a closed domain in which her basket is "sitting." But as the *Gemara* makes clear, the operative *chiddush* throughout is the first one: even the airspace of her own basket, standing alone, conveys no acquisition. The contrast between *chatzer* and *kli* in this regard is the defining line: property carries airspace rights; movable vessels do not.

---

## Old Get

### Definition

The daf concludes with a new *Mishnah* addressing the *get yashan* — an old *get*: *kol she-nityached imah mei-achar she-ketavo lah* — a *get* that was written, not yet given, and during the intervening period the husband was secluded (*yichud*) with the wife.

### Shammai & Hillel

*Beit Shammai* permit the husband to divorce his wife with such a *get*: they do not invoke the concern *shema yomru gitah kodem livnah* — that people will say the divorce preceded the child she may have conceived during the *yichud*. *Beit Hillel* forbid using it — *osrim* — out of precisely that concern. If the *get* is eventually used and she later has a child, people looking at the date on the *get* might conclude that she was pregnant after the formal date of the divorce, creating a false impression about the circumstances of the birth.

### Forbidden Not Invalid

Critically, *Beit Hillel* said *osrim* — they forbid it — not *pasul* — they do not invalidate it. This distinction is legally operative: a prohibition against using the *get* is a rabbinic *gezeirah*, but it does not go so far as to invalidate the *get* retroactively if it was used.

### Retroactive Validity

Rabbi Abba in the name of Shmuel rules accordingly: *im nise'it lo tetze* — if she used this *get* and remarried, she need not leave the second marriage. *Be-di'eved* the *get* is entirely valid. A second version of the ruling goes further: *im nitgarshah tinasei le-chatchilah* — once the *get* has been given (even though it should not have been), she may remarry *le-chatchilah*. The rabbinic concern of *Beit Hillel* was never about the validity of the divorce itself, only about the social misperception that might follow. Once the *get* has been given and the divorce has taken effect, she is fully and retroactively divorced, with no restrictions on her remarriage.

---

---

# Gittin 80

## Defects Beyond Giving

### Shift in Focus

Today's daf is 80, and we pick up with the *mishna* at the bottom of 79b. Until now, the extended *mishna* — really at least two *mishnayot* joined together — has been occupied with the act of giving the *get*: what constitutes the woman's domain, the man's domain, and the precise mechanics of the act of giving itself, with enormous discussion among the *rishonim* about whether these definitions parallel those of standard *kinyanim* or operate according to independent principles. We have now completely switched gears. The brief *mishna* encountered yesterday about an old *get* — a *get* written before *yichud* — had nothing to do with the act of giving; it introduced the topic of *psulim*, of problems internal to the *get* document itself. That transition marks the character of the current *mishna*, which addresses additional categories of defects in the *get*.

### Get Yashan Review

That earlier case of the *get yashan* — the old *get* — served as the threshold to this new domain. Where previously we asked questions about the giving, we now ask questions about the document. The *mishna* before us identifies specific categories of textual problems and their consequences, and it is worth keeping in mind from the outset that these are not all cases of equal severity. The *gemara* will later probe whether every category of *psul* generates the same grave consequences, or whether different degrees of defect carry different legal weight.

---

## Improper Government

### Mishna: Wrong Dating

The *mishna* states: *kasav lishum malchus she'eino hogenet* — if the *get* was written in the name of an improper government, it is invalid. The *gemara* will explain that this refers specifically to dating by the Roman *caesar*, and will call Rome a *malchus she'eino hogenet* — an improper government — even if the year written is technically accurate.

### Historical Problem

This immediately raises a striking historical difficulty. The *mishna* was authored in Roman Palestine. The Jews of that period lived under Roman sovereignty. How, then, can dating by Rome be characterized as naming a *malchus she'eino hogenet*? Rashi appears to frame the *gemara*'s reasoning as follows: the problem is that one is dating by a government that is not one's own — not one's recognized local authority — giving a kind of recognition to a competing sovereign. But this framing seems historically incoherent. If the *mishna* was composed under Roman rule, Rome *was* the local authority. It is difficult to understand how dating by Rome could constitute using the wrong government's dating system. This tension cannot be fully resolved, and the *gemara*'s explanation — which we will see centers on *shalom malchus*, on giving proper acknowledgment to the reigning power — presupposes that the relevant authority and the Roman regime are distinct, which historically seems hard to sustain.

### Alternative Datings

The *mishna* continues: *lishum malchus Madai, lishum malchus Yavan* — if the *get* was dated by the Median kingdom or by the Greek kingdom, it is similarly invalid. The *gemara* will treat this as a separate and significant *chiddush*, since these are dead kingdoms — the Medians and the Greeks have long since ceased to exist as sovereign powers. One might have thought that invoking a long-defunct monarchy poses no *shalom malchus* problem at all, since there is no living competing government whose honor is at stake. The *mishna* therefore teaches that even naming a *get* after an ancient, dead *malchus* is problematic.

Notably, the *mishna* includes two further categories: *u'v'vinyan habayit* and *u'v'churban habayit* — dating by the construction of the *Beit Hamikdash* or by its destruction. These would seem to be purely Jewish, internally religious datings with no political valence at all, yet they too are invalid. It is worth observing that it was precisely these categories — *minyan shtarot* (the Seleucid dating system, which began with the establishment of the Seleucid monarchy in 311 BCE and is what the *mishna* likely means by *malchus Yavan*), *binyan habayit*, and *churban habayit* — that constituted the historically known and commonly used Jewish dating systems. The *mishna* invalidates all of them. The clear implication is that there is no intrinsic prohibition against dating a *get* by these systems; the problem is contextual. In the environment the *mishna* envisions, these datings were simply not the appropriate ones to use.

### Principle: Current Authority

The consistent principle that emerges from all these cases is that a *get* must be dated according to the government and country under which the parties currently live, not by a foreign power, a competing authority, or a dead kingdom. This, as the *gemara* will explain, reflects the requirement of *shalom malchus* — giving proper fealty and acknowledgment to the existing ruling authority. The same logic extends even to one's own Jewish historical datings, since using them instead of the current government's calendar fails to provide that acknowledgment.

---

## Wrong Location

### Mishna Case

The *mishna* also addresses a separate set of problems: a *get* written in the wrong city — specifically, where the scribe and witnesses indicated the wrong location for where the *get* was being written.

### East-West Problem

The *gemara* clarifies the precise scenario. *Haya bamizrach v'chasav bama'arav* — the *sofer* and *edim* were in the east of the city but wrote in the *get* that they were in the west, or vice versa. To use a contemporary analogy: the *get* begins, as a *ketubah* does, by specifying the place — we are here in New York, New York, on such-and-such a date — but the *sofer* wrote a city where he was not actually sitting when he wrote the document. That constitutes an error of location.

### Consequences Apply

These location errors generate the same severe legal consequences as the government-dating errors described above. The *gemara* will identify this entire set of stringent rulings with the position of Rabbi Meir, and we will see the full range of those consequences in the following section.

---

## Rabbi Meir's Position

### Paradoxical Status

The severity of the consequences in these cases derives from a paradoxical status created for the woman. In cases where the *get* is *batel miderabbanan* — invalid by Rabbinic law — yet valid *mide'oraita* — by Torah law — she finds herself in the worst of both worlds. From the Torah's perspective she remains married to her first husband; from the Rabbinic perspective the *get* is treated as so problematic that she is regarded as no longer married to him either. When she then marries a second man, she is simultaneously considered married to two people by two different legal frameworks, and the consequences cascade from that compound status.

### Mamzer Consequence

Rabbi Meir articulates his foundational principle: *kol hamishaneh mimatbei'ah shetavu chachamim begittin havlad mamzer* — anyone who deviates from the formulation established by the Sages for *gittin*, the child is a *mamzer*. Rabbi Meir is extraordinarily exacting about adherence to the precise text and form of the *get*. Any deviation from that established form — even if the *get* remains valid *mide'oraita* — triggers these consequences according to his view. It is worth pausing on the phrase *mimatbei'ah shetavu chachamim* — from the coin-stamp that the Sages minted. This type of language appears in other halachic contexts as well, such as the fixed texts of prayer, and carries the implication that the Sages have established a precise formulation that may not be varied. In *gittin*, where the formulation is in some respects variable — the *sofer* cannot know in advance which *malchus* will be relevant, or exactly what city he will be in — there are nonetheless very precise rules about how the text is to be constructed. When those rules are violated, the text has been changed, and Rabbi Meir treats such a change as maximally consequential.

### Double Divorce

The first consequence is *tetzei mizeh umizeh* — she must leave both men and receive a *get* from each. She cannot remain with the second husband because, from the Torah-law perspective, she was still married to the first husband when she married him, making the second marriage adulterous. She cannot return to the first husband because, from the Rabbinic perspective, the first *get* is being treated as valid, meaning she committed adultery with the second man, which permanently bars her from returning to the first. She therefore needs a *get* from both: from the second man because we treat her as having been married to him, and from the first man because we treat his original *get* as though it effected a divorce.

### Financial Loss

Beyond this, *ve'ein lah lo ketubah, velo peiros, velo mezonot, velo bl'ot, lo mizeh v'lo mizeh* — she does not collect her *ketubah* from either husband, she does not receive *peiros* (the produce proceeds that would otherwise be a husband's entitlement during marriage, which Rashi understands here as what she would receive in exchange), she does not receive *mezonot* from either party while awaiting her *get*, and she does not receive reimbursement for worn-out clothing from either husband.

### Unfair Burden

What is striking, and deeply troubling, is that the woman bears the overwhelming weight of all these consequences despite having played no active role in the defect. It was the scribe who wrote the wrong date or the wrong location. She passively received the *get*. Yet she loses her *ketubah* from both husbands, her *mezonot*, her *bl'ot*, and more. Rashi, drawing on the *gemara* in *Yevamot*, attempts to explain this as a kind of penalty, arguing that she should have been more careful. But this explanation is difficult to accept. The more literate party in ancient society was the man; she had no ability to verify the technical details of the *get* text she received. Rashi's explanation makes more sense in the parallel case in *Yevamot*, where a woman remarried on the basis of a single witness's testimony that her husband had died, and the husband subsequently reappeared — there, one can at least argue she should have been more cautious before relying on a single witness. But in the case of a defective *get*, the fault lies entirely elsewhere.

A more honest reading may be that this is not a punishment at all, but simply an unfortunate consequence of her indeterminate legal status. Consider the *ketubah*: how could she collect her *ketubah* from the second husband if, from one legal lens, she was committing adultery with him and was never validly married to him? How could she collect it from the first husband if, from another legal lens, she was committing adultery against him? The financial deprivations are not the product of moral blame; they are the structural result of a status that is simultaneously married and unmarried. That said, one must acknowledge the profound unfairness of the situation.

Furthermore, *im nitla mizeh umizeh tachzir* — if she was actually given any of these payments, she must return them. This is not merely a case of *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'ayah*, where the burden of proof rests on the party seeking to extract money; she must proactively return it even if she is already in possession. This detail does suggest something more than a neutral consequence and more than a mere technical result of her status — though why she should bear such an active obligation remains difficult to explain satisfactorily.

### Impurity & Property

*V'lo zeh v'zeh mitam'im lah* — if she dies and either husband is a *kohen*, he does not become *tamei* to bury her. *V'lo zeh v'zeh zaka'im lo bimtziatah v'lo bima'aseh yadeha v'lo b'hafarat nedareha* — neither husband is entitled to her found objects, her labor, or the right to annul her vows. Here, at least, the husbands too lose something; they have no rights over her, even as she remains legally entangled with both of them.

### Priesthood Disqualification

*Haytah bat Yisrael nifselah min hakehunah* — if she was a *bat Yisrael*, she becomes disqualified from marrying a *kohen*, since she is considered to have committed relations with someone who was not her husband while she was still married — rendering her a *zonah* in the technical sense. The point is somewhat complicated by the fact that the first *get*, even if Rabbinically defective, is technically valid *mide'oraita*, meaning she is already a *gerushah* by Torah law and would in any case be disqualified from *kehunah*. But the additional disqualification follows as a consequence of the adulterous union. *Bat Levi min hama'aser* — a daughter of a Levite loses her right to *ma'aser*, which requires its own analysis in *Yevamot*. *Bat Kohen min hatrumah* — a daughter of a *kohen* loses her right to eat *terumah*, since the verse *v'nitma'ah* is stated three times in connection with a woman who commits adultery, each instance disqualifying her from a different priestly privilege.

### Inheritance & Children

*V'ein yorshim shel zeh v'yorshim shel zeh yorshim ktuvatah* — neither husband's heirs inherit her *ketubah*. This refers to the institution of *ktuvat benin dichrin*: when a woman brings a dowry into a marriage, that property, if she predeceases her husband, passes through him but then descends specifically to her children rather than to all of the husband's heirs from various wives. In this case, because she is in a status of double marriage, that protection is lost. Each husband does inherit from her while she is alive (which itself raises questions, since she receives nothing from them), but upon their deaths, the property descends equally to all heirs rather than being reserved for her children. This seems manifestly unfair — she loses the very protection the *ketubah* institution was designed to provide — but it reflects the logical consequence of a status that cannot be resolved cleanly into either marriage.

Regarding the *mamzeirim*: an important clarification is necessary. The *mamzer* status for children from the first husband applies only to children born after she married the second man — not retroactively. The *gemara* makes this explicit: a woman who commits adultery and returns to her first husband does not produce *mamzeirim*; *mamzeirim* result from a union where she is married to a second man. It is specifically children born to her by the first husband after she went through the second marriage (without a proper *get* from the second man) who are *mamzeirim*. Children from the second husband are *mamzeirim* because she is considered still validly married to the first husband at the time of those relations. But the first husband's children are *mamzeirim* only if she returned to him while still married to the second — not simply because she received a defective *get*.

### Yibum Issues

*V'im meis achiv shel zeh v'achiv shel zeh choltzin v'lo meyabmin* — if either husband dies before giving her a *get*, his brother must perform *chalitzah* and may not perform *yibbum*. Since she is in a *safek* status with respect to each husband — possibly married, possibly not — *yibbum* cannot be performed, for she might not be a true *yevamah* to the brother; yet since she might be, *chalitzah* is required.

---

## Changing Names

### Mishna Case

The *mishna* continues: *shina shemo u'shmah, shemo u'shemah, o shemo v'shem iro* — if the *get* changed the name of the husband, the wife, or their cities, the same consequences apply and she must leave both men.

### Definition of Change

Tosafot clarifies: *lo shina mamash* — this does not mean a complete and obvious substitution of one name for another (writing a completely different name is clearly invalid on its face). Rather, the *mishna* speaks of a change that is subtle — a nickname, a slight variation in spelling, an imprecise rendering of a name. The *gemara* at 34b discusses this in the context of *ramya aspasta*, where the issue is that all secondary names and nicknames must be included, or that the name given was slightly imprecise. The principle is that it is worse to do it incorrectly than to omit it entirely, and Tosafot engages with that problem in detail.

### Same Consequences

The *gemara* attributes this ruling — *tetzei mizeh umizeh v'chol hadrachim ha'elu bah* — to Rabbi Meir's position, consistent with his general principle about any deviation from the established *matbei'a* of *gittin*. All the consequences catalogued above apply equally to cases of name changes or location changes in the names of the parties.

---

## Arayot & Ailonit

### Arayah Exemption

The *mishna* now turns to a different category of cases that generate the same severe consequences, though these have nothing to do with a defective text. The principle of *kol ha'arayot she'amru tzaroteihen mutarot* — that whenever one woman is an *ervah* to the surviving brother (and thus forbidden to him for *yibbum*), her co-wife is also exempt from both *yibbum* and *chalitzah* — is central to the opening *mishna* of *Yevamot*. The classic example: a man married his brother's daughter (his niece). Since a niece is an *ervah* to the surviving brother (who is her uncle), she is exempt from *yibbum*, and her co-wife is consequently also exempt and may freely remarry without *chalitzah*.

### Ailonit Discovery

The scenario the *mishna* presents: the co-wife, relying on her exemption, went and married another man. Subsequently, the woman who was the *ervah* — say, the niece — grew up and was discovered to be an *ailonit*, a woman who never developed sexually, and who would have been a *mekach ta'ut* — a mistaken transaction — had her condition been known at the time of marriage. Since presumably neither party knew, the marriage is retroactively voided. There was no deliberate deception; the facts simply became apparent later. But the legal consequence is that retroactively he was never married to his niece. She was therefore never an *ervah* to the surviving brother. When the first husband died, the co-wife was therefore always obligated in *yibbum* or *chalitzah* — she simply did not know it.

### Co-Wife's Problem

The co-wife's situation is that she has been married to her second husband, perhaps for twenty years, in the genuine belief that she was free to do so. Nobody deceived her; she had every legal reason to believe she required neither *chalitzah* nor *yibbum*. Yet retroactively, because the *ailonit* determination voids the original marriage, the co-wife was always *zekukah l'yibbum* — bound to the surviving brother — before she remarried. The prohibition she violated is *lo tihyeh eishet hamet hachutzah le'ish zar*, and the *gemara* understands the resulting child as a *mamzer* according to the position of Rabbi Akiva, who holds that a child born from a union prohibited by a *lav* is a *mamzer*. This may reflect Rabbi Akiva's general position on all *issur lav* relationships, or it may reflect something more specific to *yibbum*, where the status of *zekukah leyibbum* creates a quasi-*kiddushin* bond between the woman and the surviving brother, making her union with another man more analogous to adultery.

### Consequences Apply

*Tetzei mizeh umizeh v'chol hadrachim ha'elu bah* — she must leave both men and suffers all of the consequences catalogued by Rabbi Meir. The unfairness here is, if anything, more acute than in the *get* cases. At least in those cases one could say the parties should have had expert supervision of the *get* text. Here, the co-wife did everything correctly given the information available to her, and she is still subjected to all these consequences. What she was supposed to do to prevent this is unclear: as one might ask, was the court supposed to wait, however many years it takes, to determine whether the *ervah* was an *ailonit* before permitting the co-wife to remarry? Or should the *ervah* have been brought to perform *chalitzah* just in case — which itself would have entailed disqualifying her from *kehunah* and attendant consequences? The situation is genuinely without good remedy.

---

## Yibum with Ailonit

### Scenario Setup

A further variation: a man performed *yibbum* with one of two *yevamot*. The co-wife, understanding herself to be freed by the *yibbum*, went and married another man. Subsequently, the woman with whom *yibbum* was performed was discovered to be an *ailonit*.

### Nullification

The retroactive consequence: the *yibbum* never legally occurred, since the *ailonit*'s original marriage was a *mekach ta'ut* and she was therefore never truly the *yevamah*. The *zikah* — the levirate bond — was never discharged. The co-wife therefore still required *yibbum* or *chalitzah* from the original brother-in-law before she could remarry.

### Unfair Penalty

*Tetzei mizeh umizeh v'chol hadrachim ha'elu bah* — she must separate from her second husband and suffers all the consequences. As in the previous case, she did nothing wrong; the situation arose through no fault of hers. Yet the severity of the consequences follows her.

---

## Mistaken Documents

### Mix-up Scenario

The *mishna* presents a case of scribal error of a different kind: *katav sofer get la'ish v'shovar la'ishah* — the *sofer* prepared the *get* for the husband and a *shovar* (a receipt acknowledging payment of the *ketubah*) for the wife. The design was that the wife, upon receiving payment of her *ketubah*, would hand the receipt to the husband; the husband would hand the *get* to her. The *sofer* inadvertently delivered the documents in reverse: the wife received the receipt and the husband received the *get*. *V'natnu zeh lazeh* — and they exchanged documents, each believing they had the correct one. Perhaps both parties were not fully literate, or perhaps the documents were handled quickly and without close inspection.

### Unmarried Status

The result is that she is not actually divorced — she received a receipt, not a *get* — and yet she believes herself to be divorced. If she subsequently married another man, she remained, from the Torah's perspective, married to her first husband throughout.

### Later Discovery
