*V'le'achar zman harei haget yotzei miyad ha'ish v'hashovar miyad ha'ishah* — some time later, someone examines the documents and discovers that the husband is holding the *get* and the wife the receipt — the reverse of what they should have.

### Consequences

*Tetzei mizeh umizeh v'chol hadrachim ha'elu bah* — she must leave her second husband and suffers all the consequences. She married her second husband genuinely believing she was divorced, and yet all the penalties attach.

### Immediate Discovery

Rabbi Eliezer offers a partial exception: *im l'altar yatza ein zeh get* — if the mistake is discovered immediately, when the documents are examined right away at the time of exchange, then plainly no valid *get* was given, the error is clear, and the relevant consequences follow straightforwardly.

### Delayed Discovery

However, *v'im l'achar zman yatza* — if the error surfaces only after a significant period has elapsed — Rabbi Eliezer rules differently: *lo kol heimenu min harishon l'abeid zchuto shel sheni* — the first husband does not have the power to retroactively destroy the second husband's rights. If the first husband, a year after giving what purported to be a *get*, asks to examine the document and it turns out to be a *shovar*, Rabbi Eliezer does not accept the resulting claim that the *get* was never given. After the passage of time, who can verify that these are the same documents as were originally exchanged? Perhaps the first husband himself swapped the documents in order to reclaim his wife and undermine the second marriage. The *gemara* will discuss how much time must elapse for this rule of Rabbi Eliezer to apply.

---

## Contemporary Dating

### City of Origin

Tosafot raises an important practical question about the *mishna*'s prohibition on giving the wrong city. Rabbeinu Yitzchak (*Ri*) observes that the requirement to give the correct city applies specifically to the city where the parties currently reside — *ir she'darim bah*. However, *ir she'nolad bah* — the city of birth, the city of origin — is a different matter: *afilu shina kasher*, even if the city of origin is written incorrectly, the *get* is valid, *keivan she'ein tzarich le'kotvo klal* — because there is no obligation to write the city of origin at all.

### Historical Context

Tosafot notes that older practice did include the city of origin: *ve'hakadmonim nahagu le'kotvo* — the earlier generations customarily wrote it. The reason was identification: *mishum shema yihiyeh arar she'yesh sham Yosef ben Shimon acher yihiyeh shemo v'shem iro mekom leida* — because if there might be a challenge and another man named Yosef ben Shimon existed elsewhere, having the city of birth as well would serve to identify the correct individual. It is analogous to the function of a family name. Indeed, as was noted, these place-names very often became the basis for family names over time.

Since the city of origin was never required, one might have thought that if one writes it and gets it wrong, that is worse than not writing it at all — a case of doing the optional thing incorrectly. But Tosafot rejects this conclusion on practical grounds.

### Practical Evidence

*De'chazinan de'kama pe'amim kotvim mekom leida pi ha'ba'al o ha'ishah* — Tosafot observes that in practice, the city of birth was simply written on the basis of what the husband or wife stated, without any independent verification. No proof of origin was demanded. Tosafot argues this demonstrates that the city of origin cannot be *pasul be'di'avad* if incorrect: if getting it wrong would invalidate the *get*, one would not simply accept the husband's word without some form of objective evidence. In fact, *Ri* himself validated a *get* where the city of birth turned out to be incorrect. And in cases where the city of birth was simply not known — the family had moved when the person was young, for instance — *Ri* ruled that the city of origin should be omitted entirely rather than guessed at.

---

## Improper Government (II)

### Gemara: Rome's Definition

The *gemara* now formally addresses the opening clause of the *mishna*. *Mai malchus she'eina hogenet?* — what is an improper government? *Malchus ha'romim* — Rome. And why call it *malchus she'eina hogenet*? *Mishum de'ein lahem ktav v'lo lashon* — the *gemara*'s stated reason is that the Romans have no writing or language of their own. This claim is historically puzzling, to say the least: Latin is distinctly Rome's own language, and the Latin alphabet, derived from the same part of Italy, was Rome's own as well. The precise meaning of the *gemara*'s statement here is difficult to resolve.

Setting that aside, the deeper historical difficulty remains: if the *mishna* was composed in Roman Palestine, and the Jews lived under Roman sovereignty, how can dating by Rome represent dating by an *improper* government — a government that is not one's own? The *gemara*'s framing of the issue as a *shalom malchus* problem — you are supposed to date your *get* according to the government under which you live, and using a different dating system fails to show proper fealty — seems to presuppose that Rome is *not* the government under which one lives. If the rule is that one must date by the local authority, and the local authority *is* Rome, then one should be writing the Roman date. The problem, as the *gemara* understands it, apparently lies somewhere else, but the *gemara* does not resolve this historical tension cleanly.

### Shalom Malchut Rationale

*Amar Ula: mipnei mah tiknu malchus be'gittin? Mishum shalom malchus* — why did the Sages require that *gittin* be dated by the reigning government? For the sake of peace with the government — *shalom malchus*. Tosafot adds that this requirement seems to apply specifically to *gittin* and not to other *shtarot*; other documents were historically dated by *minyan shtarot* and *binyan habayit* without concern. The reason *gittin* are singled out is that *gittin* are so consequential — they determine personal status, they separate husband and wife — that they more than any other document warranted official, government-recognized dating. The government has an interest in such documents being precisely and officially dated; dating them by an unrecognized system fails to provide that.

This rationale then drives the *gemara*'s analysis of the other cases in the *mishna*. The *gemara* frames each case as a question of how much the government would be *makpid* — how much it would object — to the dating used. If you named the *get* after Rome (a currently existing other sovereign): *mishum de'malicha* — because it is an active, competing *malchus*, you are giving recognition to a rival power, and the local government would be distinctly offended. If you named it after Median or Greek kingdoms: *mah de'havah havah* — those kingdoms are gone, yet one might still argue that invoking them implies their greatness — *mishum de'malchuta havu* — they were great kingdoms and you are, in some fashion, honoring them over the current sovereign. If you named it after *binyan habayit*: *de'amri ka madcharei shivcheihu* — you are evoking your own ancient sovereignty and greatness, which can feel like a challenge to the current government. If you named it after *churban habayit*: *de'tza'ara hu* — that is purely an expression of mourning; the government would not feel threatened by it. Yet even this, the *gemara* concludes, is problematic from a *shalom malchus* perspective. The *gemara* thus frames the entire *mishna* as a unified teaching about the government's *hakpada*, and the *tzricha* — the necessity of including each case — lies in the fact that one might have thought each case less serious than the previous.

---

## Contemporary Dating (II)

### Question Posed

Tosafot now raises the central practical question for post-Talmudic practice: how do we justify dating our contemporary documents, including *gittin*, *l'vriat olam* — according to the count from the creation of the world — rather than by the reigning government's calendar? The *mishna* and *gemara* have just established that failing to date by the current *malchus* is a significant problem, and yet our standard practice for centuries has been to date by the Jewish calendar rather than by the regnal year of whatever king or government is currently in power.

### Government Indifference

Tosafot cites Rav Yosef's explanation: *de'achshav ein hamalchus makpedet* — nowadays the government simply does not care how Jews date their documents. The concern that gave rise to the requirement — that the government has a strong interest in *gittin* being dated by the official calendar — no longer applies in the historical circumstances Tosafot is addressing. Since the *shalom malchus* concern has lapsed, the requirement to date by the regnant government's calendar has correspondingly lapsed.

### Practical Ruling

*V'kayma lan k'Chachamim* — and we rule according to the Sages, not according to Rabbi Meir, in this matter. The *mishna*'s stringent position, which the *gemara* attributes to Rabbi Meir, is not the operative *halacha*. The Sages' more lenient position is the practical ruling.

### No Malchut Issue

The conclusion Tosafot draws is two-fold: first, even if one were to rule like Rabbi Meir, dating *l'vriat olam* would not be problematic today because there is no *shalom malchus* issue — the government is indifferent, and therefore the underlying rationale for the requirement does not apply. Second, independent of the *shalom malchus* question, we do not rule like Rabbi Meir in this matter. Dating by *briat olam*, Tosafot concludes, is entirely permissible on both grounds.

---

## Wrong Location (II)

### Written vs. Given

The *gemara* returns to the issue of the wrong location in the *get*. The question arises: when the *get* specifies a location, what moment does that location refer to — when the *get* was written, or when it was given? The *gemara* considers the possibility that the *baal* (the husband) is the one referred to in *haya bamizrach v'chasav bama'arav*, meaning he comes from the east but wrote that he is from the west. But the *gemara* dismisses this reading: that would just be a case of the wrong city of residence for the husband, which is already addressed in the later clause of the *mishna* (*shina shemo u'shem iro*). The correct reading is that it refers to the *sofer* — specifically, where the *sofer* was physically located at the moment of writing. The location written in the *get* should reflect where the scribe was when he wrote it. What matters is where the document was created, not where the husband gave the instruction.

A natural question arises: who really cares where the *sofer* was? Tosafot engages with this extensively, noting that the purpose of writing a location in a *get* — as in a *ketubah* — is to record where the event took place. The difficulty is that sometimes the writing and the giving are separated: a *ketubah* might be written a year before the wedding and in a different city, yet reflect the location of the wedding. Similarly, a *get* might be written before it is given. Tosafot grapples with what happens if the *sofer* wrote it in one location but it was given in another, and whether the date and place should reflect the writing or the giving.

### Rav's Rule

*V'hilchta safra k'de'amar leh Rav l'safrei, v'chein amar leh Rav Huna l'safrei* — the practical ruling follows what Rav said to his scribe, and what Rav Huna similarly said to his scribe: *ki yasvitu b'Shili ktuvu b'Shili* — when you are sitting in Shili and writing, write that you are in Shili. *V'af al gav d'mimsaran l'chu mili b'Hini* — even if the husband communicated his instructions to you when you were all in Hini, if you are now writing the document in Shili, write Shili. The location to be recorded is where the *sofer* physically sits at the moment of writing — not where he received the instruction, and not where the husband was standing. The converse applies equally: *v'chi yasvitu b'Hini ktuvu b'Hini, v'af al gav d'mimsaran l'chu mili b'Shili* — if you are in Hini when you write it, write Hini, even if the instruction was given in Shili.

---

## Rabbi Meir vs. Sages

### Rabbi Meir Strict

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel: zu divrei Rabbi Meir* — the entire set of severe consequences we have been discussing is the position of Rabbi Meir. As the *gemara* restates it: *kol hamishaneh mimatbei'ah shetavu chachamim begittin havlad mamzer* — anyone who changes the established form of *gittin*, the child is a *mamzer*. This returns the *gemara* to the question of which cases are governed by Rabbi Meir's principle and which are agreed upon by all.

---

## Governor Cases

### Local Official

The *gemara* now considers a case involving a local official rather than the king: what if the *get* was dated in the name of a *santar* — a local city official — rather than in the name of the reigning monarch? The Sages rule: *afilu lo katav ela shem santar shebe'ir harei zu megureshes* — even if the *get* was written only in the name of a local city official, the divorce is valid. To use a contemporary analogy, dating a *get* "in the third year of the reign of the mayor of the city" would, according to the Sages, be acceptable.

### Royal Appointee

There was a particular *get* that came before Rava, having been dated in the name of a governor of Bashkar who was an appointee of the king — not the king himself. *Shalchu Rav Nachman v'Rav Chisda l'kamei d'Rava: ki hai gavna mai?* — is such a dating valid or not? *Shalach lehu: be'ha afilu Rabbi Meir modeh* — even Rabbi Meir agrees that this is valid. *Me'ota malchus hu* — he is an official of the same government. You have not given honor to a foreign power; you have simply named the official agent of the legitimate authority.

### Official Rank

The distinction between the governor of Bashkar and the *santar* of the city is then established. *U'mai shna mi'santar shebe'ir?* — how is the appointed governor different from the petty city official, given that the Sages accept both and Rabbi Meir accepts the governor? *Hatam zila leh milta* — in the case of the *santar*, the matter is considered disrespectful to the *malchus*: the *santar*, as Rashi describes him, is a minor, perhaps insignificant local functionary, possibly not even a government official in any meaningful sense. Dating a *get* after him is almost a mockery of the idea of government dating. *Hacha shevicha leh milta* — in the case of the appointed governor, the matter redounds to the honor of the *malchus*, since he is a significant official formally appointed by the king. The distinction, then, is not merely between a local and a national official, but between an important, formally appointed official and a petty functionary of no real standing.

---

## Rabbi Meir vs. Sages (II)

### Sages Lenient

*Amar Rav Abba amar Rav Huna amar Rav: zu divrei Rabbi Meir. Aval Chachamim omrim ha'vlad kasher* — the position that wrong dating results in *mamzer* status for the child belongs to Rabbi Meir alone. The Sages hold that even if the dating was done incorrectly — even if the wrong *malchus* was named — the child is *kasher*, not a *mamzer*.

### Areas Agree

However, *u'modim Chachamim l'Rabbi Meir she'im shina shmo u'shmah shem iro v'shem irah she'havlad mamzer* — the Sages concede to Rabbi Meir that if the names of the husband or wife, or their cities, were changed, the child is a *mamzer*. Changing the name of a party to the *get* or the name of their city is far more central to the document than the dating system used — these names identify the very people between whom the divorce is effected. Even if such a change does not necessarily render the *get* invalid *mide'oraita* (since it may be a small variation rather than a wholesale substitution), it is sufficiently central to the document that the Sages join Rabbi Meir in applying the *mamzer* consequence.

### Mishna Structure

*Amar Rav Ashi: af anan nami tanina* — Rav Ashi notes that this agreement between the Sages and Rabbi Meir on the name-and-city issue is evident from the structure of the *mishna* itself. The *mishna* states the case of wrong dating and its consequences, and then separately states: *shina shemo u'shmah shem iro v'shem irah tetzei mizeh umizeh v'chol hadrachim ha'elu bah* — if he changed the names or locations, she must leave both and all these consequences apply. *Man tana lah?* — who is the author of this second clause? If we say it is Rabbi Meir, then it should simply have been listed together with the first clause and all the other cases of wrong dating. The fact that the *mishna* states the name-and-city clause separately — as a distinct addition — indicates *shma mina rabbanan*: this reflects the position of the Sages as well, not only Rabbi Meir. The Sages, even in their leniency regarding dating errors, agree that changing the names of the parties or their cities carries the full severity of consequences. This explains the extraordinary care taken in the drafting of a *get* with respect to names and locations — because on this point, the consequences are severe according to all opinions.

---

---

# Gittin 81

## Co-Wife Status Dilemma

### Invalid Co-Wife Setup

The opening sugya of today's *daf* continues the *Mishnah*'s discussion of cases in which a woman suffers severe consequences — *teitzei mizeh umizeh*, *uvalad mamzer*, and all the attendant prohibitions — despite being entirely innocent. Having treated the case of an incorrectly written *get* and the case of mistaken names or locations, the *Mishnah* now addresses a situation arising from *yibbum* law. A woman was waiting for either *yibbum* or *chalitzah* from her brother-in-law, but the obligation was in fact void because her co-wife turned out to be an *erva* — a woman forbidden to the brother-in-law — meaning there was never a genuine bond of co-wife status to begin with. Under that misapprehension, however, the waiting woman went ahead and remarried. When the truth emerged, all of the severe consequences applied.

### Rav Hamnuna's Rule

The *Gemara* notes that the *Mishnah* specifies *nisu'in* — actual marriage — as the triggering act, but says nothing about a case where the woman merely had sexual relations with another man (*zinu*). This omission prompts the *Gemara* to ask whether this silence constitutes a challenge to Rav Hamnuna, who rules that a *shomeret yavam* — a woman awaiting *yibbum* — who commits a sexual act with another man is thereby forbidden to the *yavam*. If sexual relations with another man render her forbidden to the brother-in-law, then that act should carry the same severity as remarriage, and the same catalogue of negative consequences ought to follow.

### Consequence Discrepancy

The *Gemara* thus frames the discrepancy sharply: if sexual relations suffice to create the forbidden status described by Rav Hamnuna, why does the *Mishnah* restrict the consequences to the case of *nisu'in*? The implication seems to be that the *Mishnah* holds sexual relations short of marriage do not trigger these consequences — which would undercut Rav Hamnuna's position.

### Clean Language Explanati…

The *Gemara* resolves this by invoking the principle of *lishna ma'alya* — clean or elevated language. The *Mishnah* chose to phrase the case in terms of *nisu'in* out of linguistic propriety. The actual law, however, is identical whether she married another man or merely had sexual relations with him; in either case, *vehu hadin lezinus*, the same negative consequences apply. The *Mishnah*'s use of the term "married" is not *davka* — it is simply the more refined way to express the matter.

### Alternate Version

An alternative version of this teaching frames the relationship between *nisu'in* and *zinus* in reverse: since the *Mishnah* says *nisu'in*, and *nisu'in* presumably also implies sexual relations, this version reads the *Mishnah* as supporting Rav Hamnuna — *leima mesayeya leih l'Rav Hamnuna* — since even sexual relations short of formal marriage would generate these consequences.

The *Gemara* then pushes back on this alternative reading and insists that the *Mishnah* should be read *davka* — only *nisu'in* triggers the consequences, not sexual relations alone. The reason is that the paradigm case underlying all these rulings is the scenario of a woman who heard her husband had died, remarried, and then the husband reappeared — *mishum demichalfa b'eishes ish shehalach ba'alah l'medinat hayam*. That model case involves remarriage, not mere sexual relations, and therefore the *Mishnah* deliberately frames matters in terms of the woman having taken a second husband.

---

## Invalid Yibum Case

### Yibum with Invalid

The *Mishnah* then presents a companion case: a man actually performed *yibbum* with one of his late brother's wives, which led the other wife to conclude she was free from any further obligation and entitled to remarry. It subsequently emerged that the wife with whom *yibbum* was performed was not in fact obligated — she was, for example, an *aylonit* — rendering the *yibbum* retroactively invalid. Nevertheless, the other wife who had remarried is subject to all the same severe consequences.

### Two Cases Necessity

The *Gemara* explains why both cases — the *erva* co-wife and the invalid *yibbum* — are necessary and cannot be collapsed into one ruling. With respect to the first case alone, one might have reasoned that because no act of *yibbum* or *chalitzah* was ever performed, the woman bore some residual responsibility to investigate before simply walking away from the situation. In the second case, by contrast, an act of *yibbum* was actually carried out — *dikayim mitzvas yibbum* — and one might have said that since everyone did everything correctly, the other wife should be entirely free of negative consequences. Conversely, had only the second case been stated, one might have concluded that because the situation did carry a genuine obligation of *yibbum* from the outset, people who participated in it are held to a higher standard even when they acted in good faith. Hence *tzricha* — both cases are required.

### Innocent Yet Punished

This leaves standing what the *Gemara* itself acknowledges is a deeply troubling reality: these women are entirely innocent, yet they bear the full weight of consequences as severe as any deliberate transgression. The *Gemara* offers no fully satisfying resolution to this basic moral difficulty, and it is important not to paper over that discomfort.

---

## Scribe's Document Mix-Up

### Mixed Documents Setup

The *Mishnah* turns to a scenario of scribal error: a scribe was asked to write a receipt (*shover*) for a man and a *get* for a woman, and he accidentally reversed the documents, giving the receipt to the woman and the *get* to the man. Since the woman received a receipt rather than a *get*, she is not divorced — *lo megureshet*. Rabbi Elazar, however, introduces a temporal qualification: the problem with the incorrect documents can be raised only *l'alter* — immediately — but not after a period of time has passed.

### Immediacy Requirement

Rabbi Elazar's ruling generates an obvious question: what constitutes *l'alter* and what constitutes *l'achar zman*?

### L'Alter Definition

Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel defines *l'alter* as the period during which the parties are still sitting and engaged in the same matter — *kol zman sheyoshvin v'oskin b'oto inyan*. As long as the parties remain present and the conversation has not concluded, discovering the error falls within *l'alter* and the problem can be raised.

### After Meeting Breaks

Once the meeting breaks — *amdu* — any moment thereafter constitutes *l'achar zman*. From that point forward, we cannot know with certainty what transpired between then and the time the document is inspected, and the first husband therefore loses the ability to challenge the divorce. This definition effectively limits the window of challenge to the duration of the transaction itself, a remarkably narrow timeframe.

### Alternative: No Remarria…

Rav Adda bar Ahava offers a substantially different definition. *L'alter* extends for as long as the woman has not yet remarried — *lo niset zehu l'alter*. Under this reading, even ten years later, as long as she has not taken a second husband, the problem can still be raised. Once she marries a second man, *niset zehu l'achar zman*, that constitutes the temporal threshold beyond which the first husband can no longer upend her new marriage.

### Right to Remarry

The *Gemara* notes that the *Mishnah* specifically mentions a second husband — *lo kol heimenu min harishon l'aved zchuto shel sheni* — the first husband cannot act to destroy the rights of the second. This language fits naturally with Rav Adda bar Ahava's view, since it is the existence of the second marriage that blocks the challenge. The *Gemara* then asks how Shmuel's view accounts for the *Mishnah*'s mention of a second party. Shmuel answers: *zchut harauya l'sheni* — once she leaves the meeting, she has acquired the right to remarry. The *Mishnah*'s reference to the second husband is not about a second marriage already having occurred, but about the right that crystallizes the moment the meeting concludes. Once she walks out the door with the right to remarry, the first husband cannot retroactively vitiate that right on the basis of a document discrepancy.

---

## Get Written Then Retract…

### Beit Shammai Stringent

The *Mishnah* now presents the case of a man who instructed a scribe to write a *get* for his wife and then changed his mind — *v'nimlach* — and the divorce never took place. Beit Shammai rules: *pasla min hakehuna* — she is disqualified from marrying a *kohen* even though no *get* was ever given and the marriage remained intact.

### Rumor Problem

The reasoning is striking and worth examining carefully. The moment a man approaches a scribe and commissions a *get*, word begins to circulate — *yatza alav kol* — a rumor spreads that the husband is divorcing his wife. Even if the *get* is ultimately never delivered, even if the couple continues living together, the perception that a divorce occurred or was in process has been created. Beit Shammai holds that once this *rei'ach* — this whiff — of divorce has been generated, we must take it seriously: if the husband subsequently dies and the woman seeks to remarry a *kohen*, people who heard the rumor will assume she is a *gerusha* and conclude that the children of that marriage are *chalalim*. Because the perception cannot be reliably dispelled, Beit Shammai rules preemptively: do not allow her to marry a *kohen* in the first place.

The difficulty with this position is obvious, and the *Gemara* acknowledges it. The woman has done nothing wrong. Her husband wrote something and changed his mind. Yet Beit Shammai would impose a lifelong restriction on who she may marry based solely on a rumor generated by her husband's momentary intention. A student correctly notes that this concern would make much more sense if the *get* had been written on the husband's deathbed, where there would be little time for the couple's continued cohabitation to publicly dispel the rumor. If they lived together openly for years afterward, it is hard to understand how anyone would seriously believe she had been divorced.

### Beit Hillel Lenient

Beit Hillel takes the opposing position, framed as an even stronger case: *af al pi she-nasnu lah tnai v'lo na'asa hatnai, lo pasla min hakehuna* — even if he actually handed her a conditional *get* and the condition was not fulfilled, she is not disqualified from marrying a *kohen*. If the condition goes unsatisfied and she is therefore not actually divorced, there is no divorce and the law treats her accordingly. Beit Hillel refuses to impose legal consequences on the basis of a perceived status that does not correspond to reality. If she is not divorced, she is not divorced — and no rumor or perception changes that.

It is worth noting the concept of *rei'ach hagget* — the whiff of a *get* — which does exist in the *Gemara* in other contexts. There are cases where a *get pasul*, a *get* that was invalid but close enough to a valid *get*, does render a woman *pesulah min hakehunah*. This makes Beit Hillel's position all the more striking: Beit Hillel's principle is that if a *get* was not actually given and did not actually effectuate a divorce, no consequence follows.

---

## Dispelling Get Rumor

### Kohen Get Rumor Query

A question was sent from Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of Dovila to Shmuel: a rumor had spread in town that a certain *kohen* had written a *get* for his wife — *yatza alav kol ish ploni kohein kasav get l'ishto* — and yet the couple was still living together, *yosheves tachtav umeshamashto*. What is the law?

The case is more complex than it might appear. If the *kohen* did in fact give the *get*, he is now living with his divorced wife, which would constitute a serious prohibition for a *kohen* — *machzir grushato*. The question concerns how to respond to this rumor in the absence of established facts.

### Investigation Needed

Shmuel's response is: *teitzei v'hadavar tzarich bdika* — she should leave the marriage and the matter requires investigation. The *Gemara* notes that in other contexts, Shmuel used the phrase *hadavar tzarich talmud* — the matter requires further *halachic* analysis. Here, the matter requires *bdika* — factual investigation — since the question is not what the law is, but what actually occurred.

### Dispel Rumor Strategy

The *Gemara* then addresses what kind of investigation *bdika* refers to. Is the question whether, when a rumor exists, we attempt to *mevatel* the rumor — to publicly dispel it — or whether we accept the rumor and act accordingly?

There is a genuine policy question embedded here. If we know the rumor is false and we publicly declare so, we might successfully neutralize it. Alternatively, attempting to fight the rumor might backfire: people who believe the rumor strongly will suspect that the *beit din* has been co-opted — that the husband has the rabbis in his pocket — and the attempt to dispel the rumor will only entrench the perception further. The question is therefore not merely factual but strategic: is it ever effective to fight perception with official declarations?

### Naharda'a Doesn't Dispel

The *Gemara* notes that *Naharda'a* — Shmuel's own city, the locus of his *halachic* authority — does not attempt to be *mevatel* rumors of this kind. If even in Shmuel's home community the policy is not to dispel such rumors, what does Shmuel have to say to the questioner? The practical import is that if one does not dispel rumors, one must act on them — which in this case means imposing some consequence on the couple.

### Language Ambiguity

Before reaching that conclusion, the *Gemara* interrogates the language of the rumor itself. When people say a man "wrote a *get*" for his wife, does that necessarily mean he *gave* the *get*? It is entirely possible that *kasav* — "wrote" — means only that: he composed a document, not that he delivered it. If the rumor is only that he wrote a *get* and not that he gave one, there may be no rumor of actual divorce at all, and consequently no allegation that he is living with a *gerusha*.

### Double Uncertainty

Even granting that in common usage "wrote a *get*" might sometimes mean "gave a *get*" — *de-migalya milta de-karu li-nisuei ketiva* — this only means the rumor *might* refer to delivery. The result is a *safek* within a *safek*: there is a rumor, and the rumor might mean he gave the *get*, but it might not. This double uncertainty would seem to substantially weaken any grounds for imposing consequences.

### Rav Ashi Principle

At this point Rav Ashi's principle enters the discussion: *kol kala devatar nisuin lo chaishinan leih* — we do not give halachic weight to rumors that arise after a marriage has already taken place. This is a significant and welcome clarification. The concern about rumors — *kol* — is a *lechatchila* concern, a prospective one. We say: do not enter into a marriage if there is a credible rumor of prior divorce. But we do not use a rumor to undo a marriage that has already been contracted. The implications for Beit Shammai's ruling in the *Mishnah* are directly relevant: the perception created when a man commissions a *get* might lead us to restrict whom the woman may marry *going forward*, but it does not require dissolving any existing relationship.

### Second Marriage Bar

The *Gemara* thus clarifies what *teitzei* means in Shmuel's response: it does not mean she must be divorced from her current husband. Rather, *teitzei mi-sheni* — if the first husband were to die and she sought to remarry, she would not be permitted to marry a second husband, specifically a *kohen*. The consequence is prospective and limited, not retroactive and destructive.

---

## Perception Creates Reali…

### Rabbis Shape Perception

The *Gemara* then raises a striking counter-argument. If the consequence is only that she may not marry a second man — a *kohen* — while remaining with her first husband, there is a paradox: people will observe that the rabbis are permitting her to stay with her first husband while barring her from remarrying after his death. That combination of rulings will itself generate a perception. People will not say "the rumor was false." They will construct a narrative to explain the rabbis' behavior.

### Samuch L'Misa Logic

Specifically, the *Gemara* says people will say *samuch l'misa gershah* — he must have divorced her just before he died. People will reason: the rabbis would not bar her from remarrying unless there was something to the rumor; and since she lived with her husband until his death, the divorce must have occurred right at the end. The ruling itself thus generates a new and more damaging perception than the original rumor.

This is a genuinely unsettling passage. The *Gemara* is acknowledging that the rabbis' response to perception can itself shape perception — and yet rather than concluding that we should therefore impose no consequence at all (which would send the clearest message that the rumor was false), the *Gemara* proceeds to analyze which consequence is tolerable. The answer is: the limited consequence of barring remarriage to a *kohen* is tolerable because people who observe it will assume *samuch l'misa gershah* — and in that case they will understand that she was with her first husband until the end, which at least does not impugn the children of that marriage as *chalalim*.

This is, as acknowledged, a deeply difficult passage. The *Gemara* openly grapples with the fact that rabbinic rulings create as well as respond to social perception, and yet does not reach a fully satisfying resolution of how this interplay should be managed.

### Yeridat Hadorot

The *Gemara* introduces a teaching attributed to Rabbi Ami bar Chama citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yehuda the son of Rabbi Ilai: come and see that the later generations are not like the earlier generations — *bo r'eh shelo kedoros rishonim doros ha'achronim*. The contrast drawn is between Beit Shammai as representative of the *doros rishonim* and Rabbi Dosa as representative of the *doros achronim*.

This is a *yeridat hadorot* type of observation — a romanticization of the stringency and purity of earlier generations relative to later ones. But what is notable is that the particular example chosen complicates any simple evaluation of who was "better."

### Rabbi Dosa Example

The *baraita* records that a woman taken captive — *shvuya* — who was married to a *kohen* may, according to Rabbi Dosa, continue eating *terumah* upon her return. We do not presume she was raped. Rabbi Dosa's reasoning is direct and almost startling in its humanity: *v'chi mah asah lah aravi zeh? b'shvil shemeichah bein dadeiha — tifsel m'unakehunah?* What did this Arab do to her? Because he may have fondled her — should she be disqualified from *kehunah*? Rabbi Dosa refuses to presume rape even in conditions where it was entirely possible, in order to protect the woman's status and her marriage.

The contrast with Beit Shammai is therefore not straightforward. Beit Shammai, the *doros rishonim*, imposed restrictions on a completely innocent woman based on the faintest whiff of a rumor. Rabbi Dosa, the *doros achronim*, refused to strip a woman of her status based on a presumption of violation she may never have suffered. In this framing, the "later" generation actually shows greater sensitivity to human dignity and real consequences.

The *Gemara* cites a second contrast — that the *doros rishonim* would bring their produce through the main gate in order to be *chayiv* in *maaser*, while the *doros achronim* would bring it in through rooftops and courtyards to avoid the obligation. This is a less ambiguous case of decline. But the contrast with the *shvuya* case is worth sitting with: sometimes what looks like a relaxation of standards is actually a greater moral clarity. It is not that we think the *doros achronim* are doing wrong; it is, as framed here, more of a sense of loss — are we losing some dimension of *kedusha* and *tahara* even as we do the right thing by human beings? That tension is what the *Gemara* appears to be naming.

---

## Overnight Together Probl…

### Overnight Inn Scenario

The *Mishnah* now presents the case of a man who divorces his wife and then spends the night with her in an inn — *hamigaresh es ishto v'lan imah b'pundaki*.

### Beit Shammai No Second

Beit Shammai rules: she does not need a second *get* from him — *eina tzricha heimenu get sheni*. We do not presume from the fact that they spent the night together that they had sexual relations and thereby entered into a new marriage.

### Beit Hillel Requires Sec…

Beit Hillel rules more stringently here: she does require a second *get*, but only *bizman shenitgarsha min hanisu'in* — when the divorce follows a full marriage (*nisu'in*) in which the couple had actually lived together and been intimate.

### Eirusin Agreement

Both schools agree, however, that if the divorce followed only *eirusin* — betrothal, prior to cohabitation — no second *get* is required: *mipnei she'ein libo gas bah*. He is not sufficiently at ease with her — having never yet lived with her as a wife — to make it plausible that after granting her a *get* he would have sex with her the same night, let alone with the intent of remarriage.

This formulation makes clear that the *Mishnah*'s debate turns on whether we presume sexual relations occurred, since the presence of *nisu'in* versus *eirusin* is relevant only to the probability of sex, not to the legal significance of sex if we already know it happened.

It is worth noting the *Yerushalmi*'s insight cited here: this debate may be connected to the famous *Mishnah* at the end of *Gittin* (*daf* 90), where Beit Shammai rules that a man may not divorce his wife unless she has committed a sexual transgression — *ervas davar* — while Beit Hillel permits divorce even if she merely burnt his food. If Beit Shammai believes divorce only occurs because of a serious transgression, it follows naturally that Beit Shammai would not assume the divorced couple desired to reunite sexually. Beit Hillel, who permits divorce for minor reasons, must account for the possibility that the divorce was over something trivial and the couple, having spent a night together, may have reconciled.

---

## Edei Yichud vs. Edei Biah

### Sex Witnessed Version

Rabbah bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan offers a different version of the debate. He says the *machloket* between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel arises specifically in a case where witnesses actually observed the couple having sexual relations — *beshero'uha shenivala*.

### Beit Shammai Zenut

On this reading, Beit Shammai holds: *adam oseh beilato beilat zenut* — a person may engage in a sexual act that is not intended to constitute marriage. The sexual act itself does not imply matrimonial intent, and therefore we do not retroactively treat the couple as having remarried.

### Beit Hillel No Zenut

Beit Hillel holds: *ein adam oseh beilato beilat zenut* — we presume that when a man has sexual relations, particularly with a woman who was formerly his wife, he intends it as an act of marriage, not mere fornication. The couple should therefore be treated as having remarried, and a second *get* is required.

### Rashi Clarification

Rashi clarifies an important limitation: this presumption — *ein adam oseh beilato beilat zenut* — applies specifically to a woman who was previously his wife, *nashim shenitgarsha min hanisu'in*. In that case, the prior marital relationship provides the context in which we interpret the sexual act as matrimonial. The principle does not mean that any two people observed having sexual relations are thereby presumed married. Without the prior marital context, there is no basis for such a presumption.

### Seclusion Witnesses

The *Gemara* then recasts the *Mishnah* itself. If the debate is about a case where witnesses actually saw them have sexual relations, why does the *Mishnah* distinguish between *nisu'in* and *eirusin*? If we witnessed the act, the only question is its legal meaning — not whether it occurred. The *Mishnah*'s distinction based on whether they had a prior *nisu'in* relationship (*libo gas bah*) makes sense only if the question is whether sex occurred at all, not what the sex means. The *Gemara* therefore concludes: *ella matnitin beshelo ro'uha shenivala* — the *Mishnah* must be dealing with a case where witnesses did not directly observe sexual relations. Rather, there were *edei yichud* — witnesses to seclusion — who saw the couple enter a private space together. The debate is whether seclusion witnesses are treated as tantamount to witnesses to sexual relations.

### Shammai Seclusion Only

Beit Shammai holds: *lo amrinan hein hein edei yichud hein hein edei biah* — we do not say that the witnesses to seclusion are the same as witnesses to sexual relations. Seclusion witnesses testify only to what they saw: the couple entered a private space. They cannot be treated as having implicitly testified to sex, and therefore no presumption of remarriage arises.

### Hillel Seclusion = Sex

Beit Hillel holds: *amrinan hein hein edei yichud hein hein edei biah* — witnesses to seclusion are implicitly witnesses to sex. Since we presume that a man does not intend a sexual act with his former wife as mere fornication, and since seclusion is treated as equivalent to the act itself, the couple is presumed to have remarried and a second *get* is required.

### Eirusin Exception

Even according to Beit Hillel, however, when the prior divorce followed only *eirusin* and not *nisu'in*, we do not make this presumption — *ein libo gas bah*, he is not sufficiently comfortable with her. Without the intimacy of prior cohabitation, even Beit Hillel does not extend the *edei yichud* presumption to cover the act of sexual relations.

The *Gemara* closes this section by noting a tension in Rabbi Yochanan's positions: elsewhere Rabbi Yochanan is reported to hold that the *halacha* follows a *stam Mishnah* — an unattributed *Mishnah*. But here Rabbi Yochanan's formulation aligns with the *baraita*'s version of the debate (witnesses saw sex), not the *Mishnah*'s version (witnesses saw only seclusion). The *Gemara* resolves this by saying these represent two *amoraim* debating what Rabbi Yochanan's view actually was: the *amora* who reports Rabbi Yochanan's opinion in line with the *baraita* does not accept the general principle that Rabbi Yochanan always follows the *stam Mishnah*.

---

## Get Kereiach Folded

### Accordion Structure

The final *Mishnah* of today's *daf* introduces the *get kereiach* — the "bald" or "folded" *get* developed specifically to slow down *kohanim* who might impulsively divorce their wives. Since a *kohen* may not remarry a divorced woman — even his own wife — the rabbis wanted to make the act of writing a *get* for a *kohen* significantly more laborious than for an ordinary Israelite.

The mechanism they devised was an accordion-style document. A sheet of parchment was written upon for a few lines, then folded over, and the fold was tied shut with a knot. A witness then signed on the back of that folded section. The process was repeated: more text was written, another fold was made, another knot was tied, another signature was affixed. The result was a document with multiple sealed sections, each bearing a witness signature on its exterior. The minimum number of such folds — and signatures — required by the rabbis for a *get kereiach* was three, as opposed to the two witnesses required for an ordinary *get*.

If a *kohen* chose to add more folds — say, ten — then ten sections needed to be signed. A *get kereiach* is defined as one in which the number of folds (*kesharav*) exceeds the number of signatures (*edav*) — *kol shekesharav merubim me'adav*. A fold left blank — unsigned — renders the *get* defective and treated as *pasul*, with all the attendant consequences.

### Ben Nanas Position

Ben Nanas rules that when there is a blank section — a fold without a signature — beyond the minimum three, *psulim* can fill in the blank: *hakol mashlimin alav*. Even witnesses who are disqualified for normal testimony may sign the surplus sections, and the *get* is nevertheless valid. The reasoning is that these extra signatures are not functioning as genuine *eidus* — testimony — but merely as a formal fulfillment of the requirement that no fold be left unsigned.

### Rabbi Akiva Restrictions

Rabbi Akiva disagrees. He rules: *ein mashlimin alav ela kerovim hara'uyim leha'id bemakom acher* — only those who would be valid witnesses in other contexts may fill in the blank sections, specifically relatives (*kerovim*). Relatives are disqualified in cases involving their own family members, but in other contexts they are perfectly valid witnesses. Slaves (*avadim*) and thieves (*gazlanim*) may not sign, even for surplus sections.

### Kereiach Definition

The definition of *get kereiach* flows directly from this structure: it is any *get* in which the number of folds exceeds the number of signatures. The name *kereiach* — "bald" — evokes the image of a fold that has been left bare, without its requisite signature.

### Kulchem Fear

Why is a blank fold such a serious problem that it renders the entire *get* invalid and triggers all the negative consequences? The *Gemara* answers: *gezeira mishum kulchem* — a rabbinic decree arising from the concern that "everyone sign." The reasoning is as follows: if a man creates a *get* with ten folds, the creation of ten fold-sections implies that ten witnesses were originally designated to sign. If only three signatures appear and seven folds are blank, an observer might conclude that seven witnesses who were supposed to sign did not — and the *get* is therefore defective for having failed to gather all its designated witnesses. To eliminate this concern entirely, every fold must bear a signature. Leaving any fold blank invites the misperception that a witness who was supposed to sign failed to do so.

Interestingly, the fact that the *Gemara* permits *psulim* to sign the surplus folds demonstrates that the concern is not that the *get* will be seen as requiring more *kosher* witnesses. The worry is purely one of perception — that blank spaces will look like an incomplete process. Even an invalid signature fills the visual gap and eliminates the *gezeira*'s concern.

### Slave Freed Misconception

The *Gemara* then asks why Rabbi Akiva excludes a slave (*eved*) from signing even surplus sections. The initial suggestion is that people will say: "Look, a slave signed — slaves must be valid for *eidus*!" But this reasoning would equally apply to a relative signing, since people might say: "A relative signed — relatives must be valid!" So that cannot be the full explanation.

The *Gemara* therefore reformulates Rabbi Akiva's reasoning for excluding a slave: *dilma asu l'assukei l'yuchsin* — people will not say slaves are generally *kosher* for testimony, since everyone knows they are not. Instead, they will say: "How could a slave sign? He must have been freed!" If people believe the slave was freed, they will treat him as a free man for purposes of *yichus*, potentially allowing him to marry a free woman in contexts where that would be problematic.

### Thief Teshuvah Misconcep…

The analogous concern for a *gazlan* — a thief — is: *asu l'meimar teshuva avad* — people will assume he did *teshuva* and was thereby rehabilitated as a valid witness. This would cause people to trust him and have him sign other documents, leading to a reliance on invalid testimony in consequential halachic matters.

### Relatives Safe

For a *karov* — a relative — neither of these concerns applies. *Karov kulei alma yadei dekarov hu* — everyone knows he is a relative, and everyone knows that relatives are disqualified only in matters involving their own families. No one will draw any anomalous conclusions from seeing a relative's signature. It simply means this is a supplementary fill-in signature from a family member, and the situation is self-explanatory.

### Two Witnesses Dispute

The *Gemara* then cites a *baraita* that extends the analysis: seven folds with six signatures, six with five, five with four, four with three — in each case, the debate between Ben Nanas and Rabbi Akiva applies. As long as there are at least three *kosher* signatures, the question is merely what categories of people may fill in the surplus blanks. *Ad kan machlokes Ben Nanas v'Rabbi Akiva* — up to this point is the debate.

However, if there are three folds and only two witnesses — *shachrech sheloshah v'eideh shenayim* — *divrei hakol ein mashlimim alav ela karov* — everyone agrees that only a relative may sign the missing third position. The logic is that the minimum required for a valid *get kereiach* is three *kosher* signatures; without that minimum, the entire *get* is deficient in a more fundamental way, and the standards for filling the gap are consequently higher.

### Basic Three Challenge

This ruling, however, immediately raises a challenge. Rav Zeira poses it directly to Rabbah bar Shilas, from whom he had received this teaching: *michdi kol sheloshah bi-mekushar k'shenayim bi-pashut dami* — three witnesses on a folded *get* are the equivalent of two witnesses on a plain *get*, since the minimum threshold of valid witnesses is set at three for this document. *Mah hasam karov lo, af hacha nami karov lo* — just as on a plain *get* a relative may not serve as one of the two required witnesses, so too here, when you are down to the basic three required signatures, how can a relative serve as one of them?

Rabbah bar Shilas replied that he had asked the very same question of Rav Hamnuna, who had received the ruling from Rav Adda bar Ahava. Rav Adda's answer was: *hanicha sheloshah bi-mekushar delav de-oraisa* — indeed, the requirement of three signatures on a *get kereiach* is only of rabbinic origin; biblically, two witnesses suffice. But even granting that the three-signature requirement is rabbinic, the question remains: if the rabbis defined three as the minimum for this *get*, and one of those three is a relative, has the rabbinic minimum actually been met?

The *Gemara* then cites a confirming *baraita* and reads a specific case: if a *get kereiach* had a surplus blank filled in by a slave, Ben Nanas says it is *kasher* (at least *bediavad*), while Rabbi Akiva says *ha-vlad mamzer* — the child is a *mamzer* — the most stringent possible consequence. When the *Gemara* reaches the case of three folds with two witnesses, it reports that Rav Yosef reads the text differently: where the tradition says *karov*, Rav Yosef rules *kasher* — meaning that when you are down to the basic three, one cannot rely on a relative at all, and if the third signer was a relative, the *get* would only be treated as valid (*kasher*) if that position is filled by a proper *kosher* witness. Rav Pappa endorses this correction: *tani kasher* — the reading should be *kasher*, not *karov*.

The resolution emerging from this discussion is that for surplus blank sections — beyond the minimum three — the debate between Ben Nanas and Rabbi Akiva governs what categories of invalid signatories may fill in. For the basic three signatures themselves, however, the standards are categorically higher, and the question of whether a relative may serve as one of those three remains a serious difficulty that the *Gemara* is still pressing at the close of the *daf*. This discussion will continue on the following *daf*.

---

# Gittin 82

## Get Kereach

### Structure & Definition

The daf opens at the bottom of 81b with a teaching of Rabbi Yochanan concerning the *get kereach* — the "bald get," which originated from the *get mekushar* developed for *kohanim* to slow the process of divorcing their wives. In the *get mekushar*, the scribe writes several lines of text and folds the document over a blank space, with witnesses signing on the outer panel. This accordion-like structure is then repeated — fold upon fold, each sewn shut, each bearing a witness signature on its panel. A minimum of three such folds with three signatures is required for the *get* to be valid.

The *get kereach* arises when a husband prepared many such folds but failed to obtain signatures on all of them. He may have created ten folds but secured only nine signatures, for example. The *braita* treats this as a serious defect — according to Rabbi Meir, the woman must leave the marriage and the offspring is a *mamzer*, the gravest of consequences.

### Validity Requirements

Despite the severity of this defect, the *halacha* allows the blank spots to be filled in with *psulei edim* — disqualified witnesses — perhaps even a *karov*, a relative. The underlying rule is that the basic minimum of witnesses that the Rabbis required must themselves be *kasher*, but beyond that core, the remaining folds may be completed with otherwise disqualified signatories. The question raised at the close of the previous session was whether, when only two valid signatures exist — which suffices on a Torah level — the third must also be *kasher*, or whether the third may be filled in by a *karov* or other *pasul* witness.

### Disqualified Witnesses

The *gemara* is operating with the principle that even disqualified witnesses may fill the remaining blank spots in a *get kereach*, provided the foundational two or three valid signatures are in place. What requires further clarification is the scope of this leniency.

### One Disqualified Maximum

Rabbi Yochanan states explicitly: *lo huchsharu bo ela ed echad karov bilvad* — only one disqualified witness is permitted. All the other folds must bear the signatures of *kasher edim*. The permission to use a *pasul* extends to one slot only, not two or more.

### Validation Logic

The reason is elegant and practical. When *beis din* comes to validate a *get* bearing, say, ten signatures, it will seek out people who can identify the handwriting and confirm the signatures. Any three confirmations will suffice. If more than one *pasul* witness had signed, there is a real danger that *beis din* might validate the *get* on the basis of two *pasul* signatures — leaving only one valid witness among the three. Since we cannot guarantee which three of the ten signatures will be brought forward for validation, allowing two *pasulim* to sign creates an unacceptable risk that the woman will be permitted to remarry on the strength of invalid testimony. Restricting the *pasul* signature to one ensures that any three signatures that *beis din* selects will include at least two *kasher* witnesses.

### Abaye's Proof

Abaye adds a corroboration from a careful reading of the *braita* itself: *matniten nami dika* — the *braita* can be read to support this. The *braita* lists its cases as "seven folds and six witnesses, six folds and five witnesses, five folds and four witnesses," always speaking of a shortfall of exactly one witness. It never envisions filling in more than one missing signature. *Shma mina*, Abaye concludes: this confirms that only one *pasul* signature is ever contemplated.

One might ask whether it matters where in the sequence the *pasul* witness signs — must he be at the beginning, middle, or end? The answer flows from the same *braita*. Since it never specifies a location for the *pasul* signature, we infer that he may sign in any fold. As the *gemara* puts it: *midlo kavah lei makom* — because no particular location was specified, the *pasul* may sign anywhere — at the beginning, middle, or end.

### Non-Consecutive Validati…

A second inference follows from the same logic: *beis din* need not validate three consecutive signatures. If *ratsufin* — consecutive signatures — were required, one could simply mandate that the *pasul* witness sign only in a position immediately following two *kasher* witnesses. In that arrangement, any sequence of three consecutive signatures would necessarily include two valid ones. Since the *gemara* instead limits the *pasul* to a single occurrence regardless of position, it must be that *beis din* may validate any three signatures it chooses, not only consecutive ones. This is the rule of *mikol tlasa d'mekaymin* — validation may be drawn from any three confirmable signatures in the document.

### Rashi's Interpretation

Rashi's reading of this passage is remarkable — remarkable enough that at the end of his commentary he acknowledges it openly. His explanation is as follows: one might have supposed that a *pasul* could sign freely, so long as he was always preceded by two *kasher* witnesses. Under such an arrangement — *kasher*, *kasher*, *pasul*; *kasher*, *kasher*, *pasul* — the sequence would be repeatedly anchored in valid testimony, and a rule requiring consecutive validation would make the arrangement safe no matter how many *psulim* signed. Since the *gemara* rejects that approach and insists on only a single *pasul* signature, it necessarily follows that validation is not limited to consecutive groupings. Any three signatures may be used, and therefore even one *pasul* among ten signatories poses a risk if a second *pasul* is also present.

At the end of his commentary, Rashi writes with characteristic directness: *k'ein zu ikara shel sugya zu v'lo shimatiha ken* — "This, in my view, is the true meaning of this passage; that was not the tradition I received. But the version I previously had, from my teacher's written commentary, did not seem correct to me — and so I am presenting what I believe to be the proper explanation."

### Rabbi Ammi Case

The practical upshot is illustrated by a case that came before Rabbi Ammi. When presented with a *get kereach* bearing a blank spot, he ruled: *tzei v'hashleima lav afilu min hashuk* — go and complete it, even with someone from the marketplace, meaning even a slave could fill in the last missing signature. This reflects the ruling attributed to Ben Nanos, that one *pasul* signature — even that of a slave — suffices to complete the document.

One might have supposed that allowing a *pasul* as the *first* signer would set the wrong tone, or that there is something structurally significant about where in the sequence he appears. That intuition is understandable, but the *gemara* gives it no footing. What saves the document from the principle of *nimtza echad mehem karov o pasul* — that discovering a *pasul* among the signatories invalidates the group — is the context: it is understood that this particular signature serves a distinct purpose and is not part of the core witnessing group. The *Rama* applies a parallel logic to the practice in his time of passing a *ketuba* around for relatives and disqualified persons to sign after the two valid witnesses, as an honor to the *chatan* and *kallah*. Because the context makes clear that these additional signatories are functioning differently, they do not invalidate the *ketuba*.

---

## Conditional Divorce

### Exclusionary Get

With the conclusion of this *perek*, the *gemara* transitions to a new and altogether different set of questions. The new *perek* opens with *Hamgaresh et ishto* — a case in which a man divorces his wife and adds: *harei at muteres l'chol adam ela l'ploni* — behold, you are permitted to every man except Frank. He excludes one specific individual from the divorce's effect. Is this a valid *get*?

### R. Eliezer vs. Chachamim

Rabbi Eliezer rules that it is valid (*matir*), while the *Chachamim* forbid it — meaning they do not recognize it as a valid *get* at all. The core objection of the *Chachamim* is that a *get* must constitute *kritut* — a complete severance — and a *get* that leaves the woman still bound to even one person in the world fails that standard.

### Remedial Procedure

If the *get* as given is invalid, what should the husband do? The *mishna* prescribes: *yitlena mimena veyachzor veyitnena lah* — he takes the *get* back from her and gives it to her again, this time saying *harei at muteret lechol adam* without restriction. The underlying principle is that an invalid *act* of delivery does not consume the *get* itself as an instrument. The *cheftza* — the physical document — remains a valid instrument, and can be re-delivered with proper language.

However, if the exclusionary language was written *into the body of the get* — *katvo betocho* — then even if it is subsequently erased, the *get* is *pasul*. The witnesses signed a document that was from the outset an invalid *krisus*, and that defect cannot be undone. The distinction is between a problem with the *act* of delivery, which is remediable, and a problem with the *instrument* itself, which is not.

### Exclusion vs. Condition

At this point the *gemara* poses its fundamental analytical question: *hai ela — chutz o al menat?* What is the nature of the exclusion expressed by the word *ela* ("except")? Does it mean *chutz* — that the *get* takes effect for the whole world with the actual exception of Reuven, so that vis-à-vis Reuven she remains a married woman — or does it mean *al menat* — on the condition that she not marry or have relations with Reuven, so that the *get* takes full conceptual effect for everyone, but is retroactively annulled if she violates the condition?

The practical consequences are sharply different. Under the *chutz* reading: she sleeps with Shimon — not adultery; she sleeps with Reuven — adultery, because vis-à-vis Reuven she is still *eishet ish*. Under the *al menat* reading: she sleeps with Shimon and subsequently sleeps with Reuven. Once she has violated the condition, the *get* is retroactively void — which means her prior relations with Shimon were also adulterous.

### Practical Consequences

Beyond the question of adultery, the framing has implications for the *kehunah* status of the *get* as well. As one interlocutor notes, there is a meaningful difference between excluding a *kohen* from the *get* and excluding an ordinary Israelite. Ordinarily, a *kohen* already faces an *issur lav* against marrying a *grusha*; but if the husband explicitly says she is forbidden to that *kohen*, the act would constitute adultery, not merely an *issur kehunah*. Moreover, the question of whether the *issur kehunah* applies even to relations outside of marriage — a matter of dispute between the *Rambam* and the *Ra'avad* — gives the exclusion additional force in the case of a *kohen*.

One might also ask about excluding someone she could never marry regardless — say, a *chayav kares* relative, whose *kiddushin* would not take effect at all. In that case, excluding that person from the *get* would arguably have no legal consequence. The case of a *kohen*, by contrast, clearly does have a profound effect, as it transforms what would have been an *issur kehunah* into outright adultery.

### Word Ela Meaning

So which reading is correct — *chutz* or *al menat*? The *gemara* now argues that the plain meaning of *ela* is *chutz*. If the two are equivalent, the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and the *Chachamim* is most naturally cast as a dispute over whether *chutz* — actual exclusion — can produce a valid *get*. *Chutz* is obviously the problematic case: how can a *get* that is not effective vis-à-vis one person in the world qualify as *kritut*? If the dispute were only about *al menat*, it would be far less surprising, since any ordinary conditional transaction works, and Rabbi Eliezer would simply be applying standard rules of *tenai*. The *chiddush* would be minimal.

To confirm the meaning of *ela*, the *gemara* invokes a proof from an entirely different domain.

### Negaim Proof

Ravina brings the following *braita*: *kol habatim mitamim b'negaim ela shel ovdei kochavim* — all houses can become *tamei* through *nega tzaraas*, except the houses of non-Jews. The word *ela* there is structurally identical to the *ela* in our *mishna*. The question: does *ela* here mean "with the exception of" (*chutz*), or "on the condition that" (*al menat*)? If *ela* meant *al menat*, the sentence would read: all Jewish houses are susceptible to *negaim* only on the condition that the houses of non-Jews are not susceptible. And if the condition were violated — if non-Jewish houses could become *tamei* — then Jewish houses would not become *tamei*. This is obviously absurd. Who is one making this condition with? And further, the condition cannot be violated in any case, since a separate *braita* derives from the verse *v'nasati nega tzaraas b'veit eretz achuzaschem* — "I will place a plague of *tzaraas* in a house in the land of your inheritance" — that only property held as inheritance is susceptible; houses of non-Jews, even within *Eretz Yisrael*, are never susceptible to *negaim*. The *al menat* reading is thus completely incoherent in that context. *Ela* must mean *chutz* — "with the exception of." *Shma mina*, so too in our *mishna*.

This produces a substantial *chiddush* for Rabbi Eliezer's position: he holds that a *get* can take effect even when it is not effective vis-à-vis a particular person. The *get* is, in Rabbi Eliezer's view, valid as a document of divorce even though it leaves an island of continued marriage to one individual.

### R. Yose Braita

The *gemara* then notes that our *mishna*, now established as framing the dispute in terms of *chutz*, does not accord with a *braita* of Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah. That *braita* frames the dispute differently: Rabbi Yose states that Rabbi Eliezer and the *Chachamim* do not disagree at all about *chutz*. If a man says *harei at muteret l'chol adam chutz miploni* — you are permitted to everyone except so-and-so — everyone agrees she is not divorced. *Al mah nechleku?* — about what do they disagree? About *al menat*: if a man says *harei at muteret l'chol adam al menat she-lo tinassei l'ploni* — you are permitted to everyone on the condition that you not marry so-and-so. There, Rabbi Eliezer says the *get* is valid, while the *Chachamim* forbid it.

On Rabbi Eliezer's view in this *braita*, the *get* functions like any standard conditional transaction. The conceptual effect of the *get* is total — she is completely divorced from everyone — and the condition is simply an external restriction, like any other *tenai*. The *Chachamim* respond: any ordinary condition (*kol tenai d'alma*) works because the conceptual act is not compromised. But here, even if the *get* is conceptually complete, it does not in practice make her *muteret l'chol adam*. A *get* must produce actual freedom to marry anyone, and if in practice she is barred from one person, that practical limitation renders it an inadequate *kritut* — *hacha shiyyer lah b'get*.

*Tosafot* raises a further nuance: even if the condition is formulated as prohibiting both marriage and intercourse with the excluded person — making the exclusion as total in practice as the *chutz* formulation — Rabbi Eliezer would still say the *get* is valid. The reason: Rabbi Eliezer looks at the conceptual structure. The *get* itself is one hundred percent effective; the condition is an external layer. The *Chachamim* look at practical reality. If she cannot in practice be with that person, the *get* has not produced full *kritut*.

This is a genuine and deep *machloket*. The question is whether the effectiveness of a legal instrument is measured by its conceptual structure or by its practical outcome. One analogy: if one sells another the fruits of an olive tree — clearly the whole purpose of the transaction — but conditions the sale on the buyer not consuming ten percent of the fruits, has the sale accomplished what a sale of this type is supposed to accomplish? The *Chachamim* say no; Rabbi Eliezer says yes.

### Rav Yannai Verse

Returning now to the *mishna* as established — that the dispute concerns *chutz* — the *gemara* asks: how does Rabbi Eliezer justify his position? How can a *get* that explicitly leaves the woman married to one person constitute *kritut*?

Rav Yannai, citing an unnamed elder, points to the verse: *v'yatza mibeito v'halcha v'hayta l'ish acher* — she leaves his house and goes and becomes the wife of another man. Rav Yannai derives: *afilu lo hutrah ela l'ish echad harei zu megureshes* — even if the *get* makes her permissible to marry only one man, this constitutes a valid divorce. The Torah does not say the *get* must make her *muteret l'chol adam*; it says she goes and marries *ish acher* — another man. So long as some door opens, the *get* has done its work.

This is a striking *gemara*. It challenges the intuition that a *get* must fully sever. And it raises a further difficulty: what is the nature of the remaining marriage? Can a man be married to a woman vis-à-vis himself but not vis-à-vis the rest of the world? Is marriage a binary status, or can it be partial?

### Chachamim Response

The *Chachamim* respond to the verse: *l'chol ish v'ish* — *ish acher* does not mean some particular man she now has license to marry. It means any man she chooses. A *get* must open the door to the entire world; it must make her *muteret l'chol adam* in the full sense. If it cannot do that, it fails as *kritut*.

It is noted that the language of *sefer kritut* has not been invoked explicitly, but it is implicit throughout — it is clearly what drives the objection, and it is why Rabbi Eliezer must resort to a *pasuk* to defend his position.

### R. Yochanan Verse

Rabbi Yochanan offers a different Scriptural basis for Rabbi Eliezer's position. The verse in *Vayikra* regarding *kohanim* reads: *v'isha grusha me'isha lo yikachu* — a woman divorced from her husband, a *kohen* may not take. Why does the verse say "divorced from her husband" rather than simply "a divorced woman"? Rabbi Yochanan derives: *afilu lo nitgarsha ela me'isha nifsela min hakehuna* — even if a woman was only "divorced from her husband" — meaning she was given a *get* with the declaration *harei at megureshes mimeni v'i at muteret l'shum adam*, you are divorced from me but not permitted to anyone else — she is nonetheless *pasul l'kehunah*.

This is a remarkable *drasha*. Normally, *reiach haget* — the "scent of a *get*," the taint of divorce-like circumstances — is a rabbinic concept: certain types of *gittin* that are close to valid create a *derabanan* prohibition for *kohanim*. Rabbi Yochanan's *drasha* suggests that *reiach haget* can operate *mid'oraita*. Even a *get* that divorces her from her husband while permitting her to no one — which everyone agrees is not a valid *get* — creates a Torah-level disqualification from *kehunah*.

As *Tosafot* and Rashi explain, the *nafka mina* in such a case would be, for instance, whether the husband's brother could perform *yibum* if the husband subsequently died. It is *pashut* that he could, since the *get* was entirely ineffective. But the *chiddush* is the *kehunah* disqualification. And from this, the *gemara* builds the following argument: if even a *get* that excludes the entire world — which is obviously void — still creates a Torah-level *kehunah* problem, then a *get* that excludes only one person, while leaving her permissible to everyone else, might actually be a real *get*. If it were so hopelessly invalid that no concept of divorce were in play at all, the Torah would not have bothered to create a *kehunah* disqualification for it. The Torah's response implies there is something real here.

The *Chachamim* counter: *issur kehunah shani* — *kehunah* law is different. The *kehunah* disqualification reflects only *reiach haget* considerations and carries no implication about the *get*'s underlying validity. No inference about what constitutes a valid *get* can be drawn from it.

---

## Polyandry Scenarios

### Partial Kiddushin Questi…

Rabbi Abba now poses a question that pushes the sugya into still more remarkable territory: if Rabbi Eliezer allows a *get* that is only partially effective — that divorces the wife vis-à-vis everyone except Reuven — then what is the status of *kiddushin* given with a similar exclusion? If one can end up in a reality where a woman is "a little divorced," can one create the reverse reality at the outset — a "partial marriage"?

The question is asked *tiba'ei leRabbi Eliezer tiba'ei leRabanan* — both against the view of Rabbi Eliezer and against that of the *Rabanan*.

### Kiddushin-Gerushin Link

The *gemara* identifies the nexus between *kiddushin* and *gerushin* in the verse *v'yatza v'hayta* — the verse links the process of leaving one marriage to the process of entering another. If by *gerushin* the Torah tolerates a partial dissolution, then by *kiddushin* as well, one might argue, a partial acquisition is possible.

### Two Men Scenario

The *gemara* raises the possibility — now fully explicit — that two men could each perform *kiddushin* on the same woman, each excluding the other from his stipulation. Reuven says *harei at mekudeshes li chutz miShimon*, and Shimon says *harei at mekudeshes li chutz miReuven*. Neither man's *kiddushin* forecloses the other's. The result, within Rabbi Eliezer's framework, would be a woman simultaneously married to two men — a form of polyandry created not through violation but through structured exclusion.

### Abaye's Resolution

Abaye resolves the question: *bein leRabbi Eliezer bein leRabanan ba'inan v'yatza v'hayta* — both Rabbi Eliezer and the *Chachamim* agree that *kiddushin* is linked to *gerushin* through *v'yatza v'hayta*. The implication cuts in both directions: the same way Rabbi Eliezer tolerates a partial *get*, he would also allow partial *kiddushin*. And by the same token, for the *Chachamim*, if a partial *get* is invalid, a partial *kiddushin* is equally unavailing. The *kiddushin* and *gerushin* regimes are structurally symmetric.

The *chiddush* for Rabbi Eliezer's position is now fully stated: one may say to a woman *harei at mekudeshes li chutz miReuven*, and thereby create a partial marriage that coexists with Reuven's access to her.

### Two Brothers Case

The *gemara* now works through the strange case of two brothers. Reuven says *harei at mekudeshes li chutz miShimon*, and Shimon responds *harei at mekudeshes li chutz miReuven*. Each brother excludes the other from his *kiddushin*, allowing both relationships to coexist. In principle — within this framework — she would be married to both simultaneously. (It is worth noting that the Torah's prohibitions address a man married to two sisters, not a woman married to two brothers, so there is no Biblical *issur* on that dimension — though the questions of adultery, *onah*, and inheritance that would attend such an arrangement are substantial, and the *gemara* does not engage them here.)

### Yibum Problem

To test whether these dual *kiddushin* are actually legally effective, the *gemara* raises the *yibum* scenario. If both Reuven and Shimon die, is their third brother Levi obligated in *yibum* through both of them? This would constitute *zikas shenei yevamim* — the *zika* of two *yevamim* — which is already a category the *gemara* in *Yevamos* discusses in its rabbinic form. By way of background: if Reuven dies and Shimon performs *ma'amar* — a rabbinic-level act resembling *kiddushin* for *yibum* — but then dies before completing *yibum*, Levi's obligation runs through both brothers, creating a *zikas shenei yevamim* at the rabbinic level. The *gemara* here asks whether the same phenomenon can arise on a Torah level, through the dual *kiddushin* we have just described.

### Shimon Ineffective

The *gemara* answers that this does not produce *zikas shenei yevamim*, because Shimon's *kiddushin* was ineffective. When Reuven married her and said *chutz miShimon*, she became forbidden to the entire world except Shimon. When Shimon then came and said *harei at mekudeshes li chutz miReuven*, his act made no change to her legal status whatsoever. Before his *kiddushin*, she was forbidden to everyone in the world except Shimon. After his *kiddushin*, she remained forbidden to everyone in the world except Shimon. His act did not alter whom she was permitted to marry or with whom she was forbidden. A legal act that changes nothing in the world has no legal effect. *Kidushei d'Reuven ahannu, kidushei d'Shimon lo ahannu* — Reuven's *kiddushin* was effective; Shimon's was not.

The *gemara* thus uses the *yibum* question as a test case: not to show that she is married to two men, but to show that in the scenario as described, the second *kiddushin* simply does not take hold.

### Effective Marriage Case

There is, however, a scenario in which both *kiddushin* would be effective. Suppose Reuven said *harei at mekudeshes li chutz miShimon v'Frank* — you are married to me, except that Shimon and Frank remain accessible to you. She is now forbidden to everyone in the world except Shimon and Frank. Shimon now says *harei at mekudeshes li chutz miReuven* — but makes no exception for Frank. Shimon's *kiddushin* does something: it closes the door to Frank. Before Shimon's *kiddushin*, Frank was accessible; after it, Frank is excluded. Shimon's act changed her status in a meaningful way. In this case, she is genuinely married to both Reuven and Shimon simultaneously — each marriage having had a distinct legal effect.

The *gemara* also frames the *eshet shenei meitim* case — a woman who would truly be classified as the wife of two deceased men for purposes of *yibum* — as follows: Reuven marries her with *chutz miShimon*, and then Shimon comes and marries her *stam*, without any exclusion. Shimon's *stam kiddushin* has the effect of closing the door to Reuven — whom Reuven's own *kiddushin* had left accessible. *Kidushei d'Reuven ahannu lemisra achulei alma* — Reuven's *kiddushin* made her forbidden to everyone except Shimon. *Kidushei d'Shimon ahannu lemisra a'Reuven* — Shimon's *kiddushin* then made her forbidden to Reuven as well. The resulting state: she is bound to Reuven as a married woman but cannot have relations with him (Shimon's *kiddushin* made her *asura* to him), while she is also bound to Shimon but with Reuven still technically present as her husband. When both die, she is classified as *eshet shenei meitim*, the wife of two deceased men.
