*Tosafot* raises a pointed question in the name of Rabbeinu Yitzchak: if Shimon's *kiddushin* makes her *asura* to Reuven, why doesn't that act knock Reuven's *kiddushin* out altogether? Should not Shimon's act, which purports to override Reuven's rights, dissolve the first marriage? The *gemara* apparently holds that both marriages coexist: she is married to Reuven, and Shimon's *kiddushin* forbids her to Reuven — a configuration that is strange on its face, but that this *sugya* apparently accepts as coherent within Rabbi Eliezer's framework.

It is worth noting that this scenario has been cited in discussions of *hafka'at kiddushin* — retroactive annulment of *kiddushin* — in particular the *agunah* context. Whether the model could ever be implemented practically is a separate matter entirely.

### Simultaneous Marriage

Abaye raises a final question in this vein: if the two brothers' *kiddushin* scenarios are being entertained, what exactly is the woman's legal status when both men are alive and both *kiddushin* are effective? The *gemara* does not resolve who she can be with — it treats the *yibum* and *agunah* implications as the operative test cases, not the question of whom she may actually have relations with. The *gemara*'s concern throughout is the formal legal question of whose wife she is "on paper," not an adjudication of permitted relations. Whether any of this is practically relevant is left aside; the *gemara* is working through the implications of Rabbi Eliezer's position to their logical conclusion.

---

## Ambiguous Language

### Gap-Filling Scenario

With the *kiddushin* discussion concluded, the *gemara* turns to a series of cases involving a husband who partially fills the gap in an exclusionary *get*. The scenario: the husband said *harei at muteres l'chol adam chutz miReuven v'Shimon* — you are permitted to everyone except Reuven and Shimon. He has excluded both men. He then added — before delivering the *get* — the words *leReuven v'Shimon*. He handed her the *get* with both statements included. What do those closing words mean?

### Two Interpretations

The *gemara* poses the fundamental ambiguity: *mi amrinan mah d'asar shara?* — do we say that by saying *leReuven v'Shimon* he reversed his own exclusion, making her now permitted to Reuven and Shimon as well as everyone else, filling in the gap he had created? Or do we say *mah d'asar shara u'mah d'shara asar* — he completely inverted the earlier statement, so that now she is permitted only to Reuven and Shimon and forbidden to everyone else, having reversed the original formulation entirely?

### Single Name Case

The *gemara* then subdivides the question. If, under the first reading, saying *leReuven v'Shimon* fills the gap and permits her to everyone: what if he said only *leReuven*? Does *leReuven* mean he was speaking elliptically — naming Reuven because Reuven came first in his original list, but intending to restore permission to both Reuven and Shimon? *Lehu hadin leShimon* — and the same naturally applies to Shimon. Or does *leReuven* mean *leReuven davka* — exclusively Reuven, leaving Shimon still excluded?

### Shimon Only Case

If he said only *leShimon* — the reverse: does *leShimon* mean he is restoring permission to both men, choosing Shimon's name because it was the last word of his original exclusion (*mishum desalik mineih* — it was the word most recently in his mouth), and he intends by implication to fill in all the gaps? Or does *leShimon* mean only Shimon is now permitted, while Reuven remains excluded?

### Even For Case

Finally, Rav Ashi raises an additional layer: suppose the husband said *af leShimon* — "even Shimon." Does *af* here refer backward to Reuven — meaning you are permitted to Reuven and *even* Shimon, so both are now permitted? Or does *af* refer forward to the rest of the world — meaning you are permitted to everyone in the world and even to Shimon, but Reuven remains excluded?

### Rav Ashi Question

*Teiku* — all of these questions are left unresolved. The *gemara* does not provide answers to any of the cases Rav Ashi raises. It is worth noting that these questions can be read according to either Rabbi Eliezer or the *Chachamim*. According to Rabbi Eliezer, the operative question is whether she remains *asura* to one of the excluded men even after the follow-up statement — which affects whether she can actually marry those individuals. According to the *Chachamim*, the follow-up statement's meaning is critical to whether the *get* is valid at all: if it successfully fills all the gaps and makes her *muteret l'chol adam*, the *get* becomes *kasher*; if any exclusion remains, it is *pasul*.

The *daf* closes on these open questions, but the deeper issue running through the entire *perek* remains: what is the nature of marriage and divorce? Is either a binary status, or can one be partially married and partially divorced? Can a legal instrument that is not one hundred percent effective still be a valid *get* or a valid *kiddushin*? These are the questions Rabbi Eliezer forces us to confront — and they will continue into the next *daf*.

---

---

# Gittin 84

## R. Eliezer's Chutz

### R. Eliezer Intro

The daf opens in the middle of 83b, continuing with the remarkable and legally strange position of Rabbi Eliezer that a woman can be divorced *vis-à-vis* everyone except one specific person — a *get* that reads *chutz mi-ploni*, "except for so-and-so." A series of *Tannaim* responding to this position after Rabbi Eliezer's death are discussed, and we pick up with *Heishiv Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar*.

Before turning to that response, however, the *gemara* establishes an important internal concession that Rabbi Eliezer himself makes. *Modeh Rabbi Eliezer ben Horkenus*: even Rabbi Eliezer agrees that if the husband said "you are permitted to all men except Reuven," and she went ahead and married someone else — and was then widowed or divorced from that second man — she is subsequently permitted to marry Reuven. The logic is as follows. When the husband declared *chutz mi-Reuven*, this was not an *al menat* condition but a *chutz* exclusion: she remained in some sense his wife *vis-à-vis* Reuven. But once she entered into a complete new marriage with another man, that marriage entirely supplants and extinguishes whatever residual marital bond existed toward Reuven from the first husband. With the second marriage, she becomes fully the second man's wife, with no remnant of the first marriage. When the second man dies, she is therefore fully free — including *vis-à-vis* Reuven.

### R. Shimon ben Elazar

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar then offers a formal challenge to Rabbi Eliezer's entire position. He asks: *heich matzinu she-zeh oser ve-zeh matir?* — how can we find that one person prohibits and a second person permits? The first husband said she is forbidden to Reuven; how can a second husband, by marrying and then releasing her, make her permitted to Reuven?

The *gemara* immediately tests whether this principle holds universally. Is there truly no case where one party's action creates a prohibition and a different party's action dissolves it? Two apparent counterexamples are raised.

First, the case of a *yevamah*: the husband who married her caused her to become forbidden to the rest of the world upon his death, since the *mitzvah* of *yibbum* creates a *zikah* that restricts her. Then the *yavam* comes and performs *chalitzah*, releasing her to everyone. Is this not a case of one person restricting and another permitting? The *gemara* answers: no, because it is actually the *yavam*, not the husband, who creates the restriction in the first place. Had there been no brother-in-law, the wife would have been fully free upon the husband's death. It is the *yavam*'s existence that generates the *zikah*, and so it is the *yavam* himself who both creates and resolves the problem through *chalitzah*.

Second, the case of *nedarim*: a person makes a vow, restricting something upon themselves, and a *chacham* comes and annuls it. Is that not a second party lifting what the first party imposed? The *gemara* invokes Rabbi Yochanan's principle: *ein chacham matir klum ela be-charatah* — the sage does not annul anything except through *charatah*, remorse. The mechanism of *hatarat nedarim* requires that the person who made the vow articulate genuine regret for having done so, which retroactively reframes the vow as having been made in error. The sage serves as an instrument, but it is ultimately the original maker of the vow who is undoing it through remorse.

### Undoing Restrictions

A third challenge: the case of *hafarat ha-ba'al*, the husband's power to void his wife's vows. Here the wife makes a vow and the husband annuls it — with no requirement of *charatah* on her part. The husband simply declares that he does not accept it, and the vow is voided. Is this not a genuine case of one person restricting and another person lifting that restriction?

The *gemara* responds by invoking the ruling of Rav Pinchas in the name of Rava: *kol ha-noderet al da'at ba'alah hi noderet* — any time a woman makes a vow, she makes it implicitly with the understanding that her husband accepts it. The underlying presumption is that a woman does not intend her vow to take effect if her husband objects. Therefore, even in *hafarat ha-ba'al*, it is conceptually the woman herself who is undoing her vow, because she never truly intended it to bind without his acquiescence. The husband's annulment, on this reading, is simply the activation of a condition already embedded in the way she made the vow.

This is, admittedly, a striking way to frame *hafarat ha-ba'al*. The principle of *charatah* and the construction that the woman "makes her vow on her husband's *da'at*" are presented here as responses to a dialectical challenge, not necessarily as exhaustive accounts of these institutions. The *gemara* is not claiming this is the only way to understand *hatarat nedarim* or *hafarat ha-ba'al* — it is pushing back against the analogy to Rabbi Eliezer's case, where there is no plausible construction under which the first husband's restriction dissolves: he explicitly wanted her to remain bound to him *vis-à-vis* Reuven, and no subsequent act by a third party can be read as an expression of his original intent.

### Kerisus Argument

The *gemara* now introduces what it describes as the sharpest and most direct challenge to Rabbi Eliezer's position. Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah argued from the word *kerisus* — the Torah's description of a *get* as a *sefer kerisus*, a document of severance. *Kerisus* means something that cuts completely. *Almah de-shein zeh kerisus* — if the divorce excludes one person, it is not a complete severance. A *get chutz mi-Reuven* fails at the most fundamental level: it is definitionally not a *get*.

### Rabbis' Approach

If Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah's *kerisus* argument is the strongest and most decisive, why did all the other *Tannaim* bother giving their more elaborate and complex critiques of Rabbi Eliezer? Why didn't they simply cite this verse?

The answer is that the other rabbis could not freely deploy the *kerisus* argument because they needed the word *kerisus* to teach something else. The *gemara* cites a *baraita*: if a husband says *harei zeh gittech al menat shelo tishti yayin* — this is your *get* on the condition that you never drink wine — *al menat shelo telchi le-veit avich le-olam* — on the condition that you never go to your father's house for all time — *ein zeh kerisus*, that is not a *get*, because the condition perpetually hovers over her head and binds her to her first husband for the rest of her life. But if he stipulates a condition for only thirty days, *harei zeh kerisus* — that is a valid *get*. This ruling, which delimits what qualifies as a complete severance in the context of temporal conditions, is derived from *kerisus*.

Thus, for the other rabbis, the word *kerisus* is already committed to teaching that a condition hovering over her head for her entire lifetime is not a valid *get*. They cannot simultaneously use it to prove that excluding one individual is impermissible. Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah, by contrast, derives both teachings from the fuller expression *karet kerisus* — the word could have been written simply as *karet*, but the term *kerisus* teaches two things: that an eternally hovering condition is not a *get*, and that excluding a specific person is not a *get*.

The other rabbis, however, do not accept this double *derasha* from *karet/kerisus*. They read the textual elaboration as yielding only one teaching. Since they need that teaching for the hovering-condition case, they must argue against Rabbi Eliezer on other grounds.

---

## Temporal Conditions

### Hovering Conditions

Having established that a condition hovering over a woman's head for her entire life is not *kerisus*, the *gemara* now explores the precise parameters of this rule with greater care.

### Duration Analysis

Rava poses the following case: *harei zeh gittech al menat shelo tishti yayin kol yemei chayai* — this is your *get* on the condition that you do not drink wine for all the days of my life. This is not *kerisus*, because the condition perpetually hangs over her and maintains a residual bond to her first husband. But what if he says *kol yemei chayai ploni* — for the entire duration of Reuven's life? The *gemara* initially suggests that this *is* valid *kerisus*, because Reuven might die and the condition would then be permanently satisfied. The condition is not necessarily eternal and therefore does not perpetually subjugate her to the first husband's authority.

The *gemara* immediately challenges this distinction: *mai shna chayei ploni* — why is Reuven's lifetime different from the husband's own lifetime? Perhaps the husband will also die before her, in which case the condition would similarly resolve. If the possibility of Reuven's death makes the condition temporally limited and thus valid, the same logic should apply when the husband stipulates the duration of his own life, since the husband himself might die before the wife.

The *gemara* therefore revises the formulation. The operative distinction is: if the husband says *kol yemei chayaichi* — for all the days of *your* life — that is not *kerisus*, because then the condition will necessarily last as long as she lives and will never cease to hang over her. If the condition is tied to the husband's own lifespan or to that of a third party, it is *kerisus*, because the death of the husband or the third party — while they are both still alive — could satisfy or dissolve the condition.

This distinction, however, is not entirely satisfying. *Tosafot* points to a different *gemara* which appears to hold that both *kol yemei chayai* (the husband's life) and *kol yemei chayaichi* (the wife's life) are invalid as conditions, while only *kol yemei chayei ploni* — a third party's lifespan — is valid *kerisus*. The reasoning there is that a condition tied to the husband's lifespan provides no meaningful divorce at all: if the husband must die for her to be free of the condition, his death would have made her a widow and freed her regardless, rendering the *get* superfluous. For a *get* to have practical meaning — to free her from him while they are both still alive — the condition cannot be dissolved only by his death. That version of the rule makes considerably more intuitive sense than what the *gemara* here appears to conclude.

### One-Day Get

Rav Ami posed a question to Rav Nachman: what is the law in the case of *hayom at ishti u-le-machar at ishti* — today you are my wife, and tomorrow you are my wife again? That is, a husband gives a *get* that is valid for one day only, expiring at the end of that day, after which the marriage automatically resumes. Does this constitute a valid *get*?

The question can be framed in two directions. From Rabbi Eliezer's perspective: Rabbi Eliezer permits dividing a marriage along certain lines — she is divorced *vis-à-vis* everyone except Reuven. But in that case, at least those from whom she is divorced are divorced from her permanently. Here the division is temporal: for all people simultaneously, she is free today and not free tomorrow. Perhaps Rabbi Eliezer would not extend his leniency to this kind of on-and-off arrangement. Conversely, the rabbis reject Rabbi Eliezer's position because when he says *chutz mi-Reuven* she is never completely severed from her husband — the *get* never achieves full *kerisus*. But here, for one full day, she is completely and unconditionally divorced. Perhaps that momentary complete divorce is itself sufficient.

### Severance Principle

After deliberation, the *gemara* resolves the question and concludes: *keivan de-paska, paska* — once severed, severed. This applies equally according to Rabbi Eliezer and according to the rabbis. If a complete and unconditional divorce took effect — even for a single day — that divorce cannot be undone. The state of full *kerisus*, once actualized, is permanent. The husband's stipulation that the marriage would resume the following day is simply ineffective, because a divorce that has fully taken effect cannot be unilaterally reversed by the husband's subsequent declaration.

---

## Marriage Conditions

### Reuven Marriage Condition

The *gemara* now presents a *baraita* with a sharply different kind of condition: *harei zeh gittech al menat she-tinasi le-ploni* — this is your *get* on the condition that you marry so-and-so. The *baraita* states: *harei zo lo tinasei* — she should not marry him — and *ve-im nis'et, lo teitzei* — but if she did marry him, she does not need to leave. The precise meaning of this ruling is far from obvious, and the *gemara* will require two attempts to clarify it.

The reason to be concerned about actually fulfilling such a condition relates to appearances: *shema yomru nesheihem notnim bematana* — people will say that husbands are trading wives as gifts. If Reuven divorces his wife on the condition that she marry Shimon, and Shimon divorces his wife on the condition that she marry Reuven, the result is an exchange of wives — a practice deemed morally and socially unacceptable.

### Rav Nachman's Reading

Rav Nachman offers a first interpretation of the *baraita*. *Harei zo lo tinasei lo* — she should not marry Shimon (the specified party). The concern is the wife-swapping appearance. And *ve-im nis'et lo, lo teitzei* — if she did in fact marry Shimon, she need not leave. Although the rabbis discourage the marriage because of appearances, if she went ahead and fulfilled the condition, the *get* was valid and the new marriage stands. We do not uproot a completed marriage simply because of the societal concern.

But the *gemara* challenges this first reading. It reads *lo tinasei* as applying only to Shimon — implying that she *may* marry someone else. But how can she marry someone else? If the condition is that she marry Shimon, and the condition has not been met, she may not yet be divorced from her first husband. If she marries another man, she is potentially an *eshet ish* committing adultery. One might answer that she could marry the other man temporarily, eventually divorce him, and then go and marry Shimon to satisfy the condition — but this raises the problem of control: can she really guarantee that this chain of events will unfold? The *gemara* draws a comparison to the case of *konam einai be-sheina hayom im ishan lemachar* — my eyes are forbidden from sleep today if I sleep tomorrow — where Rav Nachman ruled that one may sleep today and trust oneself not to sleep tomorrow.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava objects to this comparison sharply. In the sleeping case, the matter is *be-didi ka'ima* — within the person's own control. *De'i ba'ei mavriz nafshei be-silu'asa* — if he really wants to, he can scratch himself with a thorn, stand under cold water, do whatever it takes to remain awake the next day. But here, *be-dida ka'ima l'garushei?* — can she get herself divorced from the other man if she wants to? Can she get Shimon to marry her? These things depend on other people's decisions entirely.

### Control Analysis

The *gemara* accepts Rava's point: the sleeping case and this case are fundamentally dissimilar because in the sleeping case the person retains direct control over the triggering condition, whereas here the woman has no meaningful control over whether the *tnai* of marrying Shimon will ever be satisfied. She cannot compel Shimon to marry her. Even if Shimon were willing, she cannot compel her interim husband to divorce her. And even if all of that were somehow achieved, Shimon might die before any of it could occur.

### Resolution

Rava therefore offers the only coherent reading of the *baraita*. *Harei zo lo tinasei — lo lo ve-lo le-acher* — she should not marry Shimon, and she should not marry anyone else either. She should not marry Shimon because of the wife-swapping appearance. She should not marry anyone else because she cannot guarantee she will ever be able to satisfy the condition, and until the condition is satisfied she may never have been divorced — meaning any children from such a union could be *mamzerim*.

*Ve-im nis'et lo, lo teitzei* — if she did marry Shimon, she does not leave, because in that case the *tnai* was in fact satisfied and the *get* was valid. *D'mishum gezeirah lo mafkinan* — we do not force her out of the marriage simply because of the appearance concern. *Aval le-acher teitzei* — but if she married someone other than Shimon, she must leave him, because *de-ba'ei kiyumei le-tnai* — the condition has not been met and may never be met, and we cannot allow the marriage to stand given the probability that she was never actually divorced. The *gemara* notes that a *baraita* confirms Rava's reading precisely: *harei zo lo tinasei lo lo ve-lo le-acher; ve-im nis'et lo, lo teitzei; le-acher, teitzei*.

This resolution raises a broader and troubling observation. The structure of this *tnai* effectively makes it impossible for the woman to marry anyone. She cannot marry Shimon because of the prohibition against the appearance of wife-swapping. She cannot marry anyone else because she cannot guarantee fulfillment of the condition. The practical result is that a husband, simply by attaching this kind of condition to a *get*, has made it impossible for his wife to remarry — while she cannot be certain she is even divorced. This is precisely the mechanism by which a *get* can simultaneously exist and create an *agunah*. Unlike the explicit *chutz mi-Reuven* of Rabbi Eliezer, which the rabbis openly reject, here the condition has the same practical effect by a more indirect route: she is, in practice, bound.

*Tosafot* pushes the analysis even further. Given that the condition is not within the woman's control to satisfy — she cannot ensure that she will marry Shimon — *Tosafot* argues that she should be considered a fully married woman (*eshet ish*) from the outset, since the *get* is conditioned on something that may never occur. If she is still considered married to her first husband, then any purported *kiddushin* to Shimon would be ineffective. Yet if she is considered *eshet ish*, then when she does go and marry Shimon to satisfy the condition, she is doing so as a married woman — and yet, by satisfying the condition, retroactively the *get* takes effect and she was divorced... but then she has left Shimon without a *get* and would need one. *Tosafot* works through these loops without fully resolving them here, but the question itself is illuminating.

---

## Impossible Condition (II)

### Absurd Conditions

The *gemara* now turns to a *baraita* dealing with conditions that are not merely difficult to satisfy but physically impossible. Examples given: *al menat she-ta'ali la-rakiya* — on the condition that you ascend to heaven; *al menat she-terdi li-tehom* — that you descend to the depths; *al menat she-tivle'i kaneh shel arba amot* — that you swallow a pole four *amot* long; *al menat she-tavi'i li kaneh bein me'ah amah* — that you bring a pole a hundred *amot* in length; *al menat she-ta'avri et ha-yam ha-gadol be-raglayich* — that you cross the Mediterranean Sea on foot. The anonymous view of the *baraita* holds that this is *eino get* — not a valid *get*, because the condition is perpetually unmet, and she remains in suspended uncertainty.

### R. Yehuda ben Teima

Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima disagrees: *kaze get* — this is a valid *get*. His reasoning: *kol tnai she-ei efshar lo le-kayemo be-sofo, ve-hitnah alav mi-techilato, eino ela ke-miflig bi-devarim ve-kasher* — any condition that is impossible ever to fulfill, yet was stipulated at the outset, is merely an exaggerated empty utterance and does not constitute a real *tnai*. We therefore discard it, and the *get* stands unconditionally. The *tnai* is so obviously absurd that no reasonable person could have intended it as a genuine legal condition — it must be understood as hyperbole or bluster, and the *get* is therefore valid from the moment it was given.

### Rav Nachman's Ruling

Rav Nachman rules in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that the *mishnah* in Bava Metzia corroborates this position by implication: it states *kol she-efshar lo le-kayemo be-sofo... tnao kayam* — any condition that *can* eventually be fulfilled is binding. The inference — *ha ei efshar, tnao batel* — if it cannot be fulfilled, the condition is void. This is taken as independent support for Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima's ruling.

---

## Impossible Condition (II)

### Abaye vs. Rava

With the ruling in favor of Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima established, the *gemara* now probes the precise scope of what "impossible to fulfill" means. The critical question: does the category of conditions that are voided as impossible extend only to physically impossible acts, or does it also include acts that are physically possible but *halakhically* forbidden?

---

## Forbidden Acts

### Abaye's Position

Abaye holds that *hi hi* — the case of a forbidden act is the same as the case of a physically impossible act. A condition such as *al menat she-tochli basar chazir* — on the condition that you eat pig meat — is thrown out and the *get* is valid unconditionally. While the woman could physically eat the *chazir*, she is not permitted to do so, and Abaye treats this as functionally equivalent to impossibility. The general principle stated in the *baraita* — "any condition that cannot be fulfilled" — is understood by Abaye to include forbidden acts, since they cannot legitimately be performed.

### Rava's Position

Rava disagrees. *Efshar de-achla ve-lakya* — it is possible that she will eat it and receive *malkot*. The act is physically executable. The fact that it carries a penalty does not remove it from the category of possible conditions. A condition that can in principle be met — even through violation — is a binding *tnai*, and the *get* is not valid unless the condition is actually fulfilled.

The *gemara* then maps out the implications of each position for the general rule (*klal*) stated by Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima. According to Abaye, the *klal* — "anything that cannot be fulfilled" — includes even a case like *basar chazir*, which is physically possible but forbidden. The phrase *kaze* ("like this," referring to the paradigmatic absurd cases of going to heaven) is understood to establish that only the most extreme physical impossibilities are the paradigm; the *klal* extends further to include forbidden acts. According to Rava, *kaze* refers precisely to absurd physical impossibilities, and the *klal* does not extend to forbidden acts. Rather, *basar chazir* — physically possible even if forbidden — remains a binding *tnai*.

### Sexual Conditions

The *gemara* cites a *baraita* that addresses sexual conditions: *harei zeh gittech al menat she-tiv'ali le-ploni* — this is your *get* on the condition that you have sexual relations with so-and-so. If the condition is met, the *get* is valid. If not, it is not a *get*. This *baraita* presents the condition as binding, consistent with Rava's position that a physically possible act — even one that may entail legal or moral problems — remains an enforceable *tnai*.

### Others' Violations

The *baraita* continues with a contrasting case. If the husband stipulates: *al menat shelo tiv'ali le-aba u-le-avich* — on the condition that you do not have sexual relations with my father or your father — *ein chosheshin shema ni'valah lahem* — we are not concerned that she might violate this. The implication is that we treat compliance with this condition as essentially guaranteed, and it is therefore a valid *get*.

The *gemara* then asks: what if the formulation were reversed — *al menat she-tiv'ali le-aba u-le-avich* — on the condition that you *do* have relations with my father or your father? Would that be a binding condition? The *gemara* implies it would not be, and this seems to support Abaye's view that forbidden acts cannot be conditions. But Rava responds by distinguishing between this case and the *basar chazir* case.

### Rava's Synthesis

Rava's answer: *bishlama basar chazir, efshar de-achla ve-lakya* — eating *chazir* is physically possible; she does it, she gets *malkot*. Similarly, *al menat she-tiv'ali le-ploni* — on the condition that she has relations with some other man — that too is physically possible; *efshar de-mishachda bei be-mamona* — perhaps she could pay him, persuade him, and the act could occur. But *aba ve-avich mi avdi issura?* — can she ensure that her father-in-law or her own father will commit this sin? Here it is not merely that the act is forbidden; it is forbidden by someone *else*, over whom she has no control. The combination of the act being prohibited *and* requiring a violation by another person places it in the category of impossibility. One who is merely being asked to violate *herself* can still choose to do so — the condition is physically executable. But a condition requiring another person to commit a serious violation is treated as tantamount to impossible, because one cannot realistically compel another person to transgress. Rava thus draws a line: a violation that the woman herself commits can be a binding *tnai*; a violation that depends on someone else committing a transgression is not a realistic condition and is voided.

---

## Torah Violations

### Tosefta Challenge

The *gemara* raises a challenge from a *Tosefta* that directly addresses the *basar chazir* case. The *Tosefta* states: *harei zeh gittech al menat she-tochli basar chazir* — this is your *get* on the condition that you eat pig meat. Similarly: if she was a non-*kohen* — *al menat she-tochli bi-terumah* — on the condition that she eat *terumah* (which a non-*kohen* is forbidden to eat). And if she was a *nezirah* — *al menat she-tishti yayin* — on the condition that she drink wine. In each of these cases, the *Tosefta* rules: *yitkayem ha-tnai harei zeh get; ve-im lav eino get* — if the condition is fulfilled, it is a valid *get*; if not, it is not. This confirms Rava's position that a forbidden act, being physically possible, constitutes a binding *tnai*. For Rava, the ruling is clear. But for Abaye it is difficult, since Abaye holds that such conditions should be voided.

### Abaye's Response

Abaye responds: *mi savrat divrei ha-kol hi?* — who says this *Tosefta* represents everyone? The *Tosefta* reflects only the view of the *Rabbanan*, not that of Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima. And recall: even the *Rabbanan* hold that an impossible condition is still binding — meaning the woman is simply stuck, unable to fulfill an impossible *tnai* and unable to remarry. According to the *Rabbanan*, the *tnai* is always enforced, regardless of whether it is possible or forbidden. Therefore the *Tosefta*'s ruling that *basar chazir* is a binding condition tells us nothing about Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima's view — which Abaye applies to forbidden acts as well, treating them as non-binding.

### Matne al Mah Shekatuv

At this point the *gemara* poses a more fundamental objection. Rather than debating whether forbidden acts are binding *tnai'im*, perhaps the entire category should be invalidated on a different basis entirely: the principle of *matneh al mah she-katuv ba-Torah* — stipulating against what is written in the Torah. The rule is *kol ha-matneh al mah she-katuv ba-Torah, tnao batel* — any stipulation that runs contrary to Torah law is void. A condition requiring a violation of *halakha* would seem to fall squarely within this principle and should therefore be voided automatically, prior to any debate between Abaye and Rava.

Rav Adda bar Rav Ika addresses this challenge. The principle of *matneh al mah she-katuv ba-Torah* does not apply to every condition that touches upon a Torah law. Rather, it applies specifically when someone is attempting to alter or eliminate the fundamental legal structure of a Torah institution. The classic example is *she'erah, kesutah, ve-onatah* — a husband who says "you are my wife, but I am exempt from providing you food, clothing, and conjugal rights." There, the husband is trying to maintain the institution of marriage while stripping out its Torah-mandated obligations. He is not merely attaching a condition to his marriage; he is attempting to restructure the institution itself, removing components that are intrinsic to it. That is *matneh al mah she-katuv ba-Torah*, and it is voided.

But here — a *get* conditioned on eating *chazir* — the husband is not trying to alter the structure of *gittin*. He is issuing a fully normal *get*; he is simply conditioning its effectiveness on a specific act. The institution of *gittin* itself is unchanged. The husband is not saying "I give you a *get* but without some Torah obligation of divorce"; he is saying "here is a complete *get* that takes effect under a certain condition." That the condition happens to require a transgression does not transform it into a *matneh al mah she-katuv ba-Torah* in the technical sense.

### Rav Adda's Clarification

The distinction Rav Adda draws is thus structural: *matneh al mah she-katuv ba-Torah* refers to attempts to *uproot* a Torah institution — to have the institution exist but without one of its Torah-defined parameters. It does not refer to conditions that require a violation in order for an institution to take effect. In the case of *she'erah, kesutah, ve-onatah*, the institution of marriage is being invoked while simultaneously eliminating obligations that are constitutive of what Torah marriage means. That is an attempt to create a Torah institution on non-Torah terms. In the case of a conditional *get*, no Torah institution is being restructured. The *get* is a complete and ordinary *get*; it simply has not yet taken effect. Once the condition is met, the *get* will function exactly as the Torah envisions.

### Ravina's Objection

Ravina challenges this framework. When the woman eats the *chazir* in order to satisfy the condition of the *get*, who is causing the violation? It is the husband who stipulated this condition. *Shehu sachar deideh* — his benefit, the divorce, is what drives her to transgress. Can one really say the husband is not implicated in the violation she commits in order to satisfy *his* condition? Is this not itself a form of *matneh al mah she-katuv ba-Torah* — using the mechanism of a Torah institution to compel a violation?

Ravina ultimately resolves this by refining the application of the principle. *Matneh al mah she-katuv ba-Torah* applies only when the Torah institution *certainly* and *definitively* uproots a Torah obligation — as in *she'erah, kesutah, ve-onatah*, where the husband's declaration of marriage is simultaneously and unconditionally a declaration that those obligations do not apply. In the *basar chazir* case, there is no certainty that any violation will occur. *Lo teichol ve-lo tisgaresh* — she need not eat the *chazir*, and she simply will not receive the *get*. The Torah violation is not embedded in the transaction; it is something she may or may not choose to do. The condition does not force a violation; it offers a choice. Therefore, one cannot say the husband's condition is itself a *matneh al mah she-katuv ba-Torah* — the Torah is not being overridden, because nothing in this transaction definitively requires that it be violated.

---

---

# Gittin 85

## Reregiving & Framing

### Reregiving Question

The daf opens in the middle of 84b, with the *gemara* asking *keitzad ya'aseh* — what should a man do if he gave his wife a *get* with a *chutz* clause, declaring her permitted to all men except Reuven? Assuming that such a *get* is invalid, as the rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Eliezer hold, what is the remedy? The *gemara* answers: *yitlena heimena* — he takes it back from her and gives it again, this time simply declaring *harei at muteret l'chol adam*, without any exclusion.

### Rebbe vs. R. Shimon

The *gemara* then asks: who is the *tanna* behind this requirement to physically redeliver the *get*, rather than simply reframing the original giving with a new verbal declaration? Chizkiya answers that this position belongs to Rabbi Shimon Elazar, as taught in a *baraita*: Rabbi Shimon Elazar holds that one must take the *get* back and give it anew, declaring *ha'geiteich*. This connects to a prior dispute: if a man gives a document to a woman framing it as a promissory note (*shtar chov*), and she opens it to discover it is a *get*, the *chachamim* hold that he may simply declare *ha'geiteich* while it remains in her hand, whereas Rabbi Shimon Elazar requires that he take it back and redeliver it. The *chutz* case, where he must redeliver and declare *harei at muteret l'chol adam* without exclusion, seems to align with Rabbi Shimon Elazar's more demanding position.

Rabbi Yochanan, however, says: *afilu teima Rebbi* — one can maintain that even Rebbi, who disagrees with Rabbi Shimon Elazar, would require regiving here. How so?

### Rav Kahana's Framework

Rabbi Yochanan invokes the position of Rav Kahana — referred to here as "that one of yours" (*dichon amar*), reflecting Rav Kahana's origins in Bavel when Rabbi Yochanan addressed his Eretz Yisrael audience — who offers a principled distinction. In the *chutz* case, the woman has already acquired a degree of *pesul* for *kehunah* even from the invalid giving, on account of *rei'ach haget*. This is the crux of the conceptual framework: was the original act of giving *not a giving of a get at all*, or was it *a giving of a get, but a bad one*?

### Rei'ach Haget

This distinction carries significant analytical weight. If the original giving was not a giving of a *get* at all — as in the *shtar chov* case, where the husband explicitly framed the document as something entirely different — then the act of giving a *get* was never performed. In that circumstance, a subsequent declaration of *ha'geiteich* may suffice to frame the holding of the document as an act of giving a *get*, without requiring a new physical delivery. But if the original giving *was* an act of giving a *get*, albeit a defective one — as in the *chutz* case, where the husband said *harei at muteret l'chol adam chutz mi'Reuven* — then the act of giving was already performed, and performed badly. To correct it, one cannot merely reframe; the entire act must be redone from the start.

This framework also maps onto the question of *rei'ach haget*: where the original giving was not a giving of a *get* at all, there is no *rei'ach haget* and no residual *pesul* for *kehunah*. Where it was a defective giving of a *get*, the *rei'ach haget* takes effect. The two phenomena — whether a restatement suffices, and whether *rei'ach haget* applies — are expressions of the same underlying question about the nature of the original act.

One might consider that the opposite conclusion would be equally defensible: if it was not a giving of a *get* at all, one should have to redo everything from scratch; whereas if it was a bad giving, perhaps one can simply correct it. The *gemara* runs the other way: a bad giving, precisely because it was an act of giving a *get*, cannot be patched over by words alone — the act must be re-executed. This is the position of Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rav Kahana, and it provides a coherent account of why even Rebbi would require redelivery in the *chutz* case, while remaining consistent with Rebbi's more lenient stance in the *shtar chov* case.

---

## Erasing Conditions

### Chutz Cannot Be Erased

The *gemara* turns to a related problem: if the *chutz* exclusion was written inside the body of the *get*, erasing it does not remedy the defect. Even if the text is subsequently corrected and no trace of the *chutz* remains, the *get* remains invalid. The reason is that the *get* was never written as a valid instrument of divorce — at the moment of its composition, it lacked the *da'as gerushin* necessary to function as a *get krisus*. No later correction to the text can retroactively supply what was absent at the time of writing.

### Tosafot on Erasures

*Tosafot* uses this ruling as a springboard to clarify the general rule regarding erasures in a *get*. The implication of the *gemara* — *davka chutz* — is that the prohibition on erasure applies specifically to the case of *chutz*, because *chutz* fundamentally compromises the *krisus* of the *get* and cannot be undone. For other erasures, however, correction is in principle valid, provided procedural requirements are met. The reason we are not concerned that an ordinary erasure represents a tampering with the document is that such corrections can be properly authenticated.

### Before Sharir V'Kayam

*Tosafot* specifies the mechanism: the correction must be documented before the words *sharir v'kayam*, which serve as the closing formula of the document. Any alteration to the text — whether in a *get* or a *ketubah* — must be noted within the body of the document, ahead of the final *hakol sharir v'kayam*, so that the attesting witnesses can validate the correction. For example, if a name was written incorrectly and then changed, a notation such as "in line two, there is an erasure" would be written before *sharir v'kayam*, and the *edim* would sign with awareness of that correction. Alternatively, if the notation appears separately, the *edim* must themselves authenticate what was written there.

*Tosafot* acknowledges the practical concern: without such safeguards, there would be no barrier to altering a document after the fact — changing a sum, a name, or any other material detail. The requirement that corrections precede *sharir v'kayam* or be independently attested by *edim* is precisely what prevents such abuse. *Tosafot* further notes that while erasure is technically permissible in a *get* under these conditions, the practice (*nahagu ha'olam*) is to be stringent, and in practice a *get* with an erasure would ordinarily be rewritten. *Ketubot*, by contrast, are not treated with the same stringency.

The important caveat, however, remains: none of this applies to *chutz*. Where *chutz* was written into the *get*, erasing it does nothing, because the defect is not in the text but in the fundamental nature of the instrument as written.

One might ask: if it is the signatures of the *edim* that give the *get* its legal force — whether one holds *edei mesirah karsei* or *edei chasimah karsei* — why can we not say that as long as the *chutz* is erased before the *edim* sign, their signature would then ratify a valid instrument? The *gemara*'s focus on the act of writing, and Tosafot's emphasis on the *sofer*'s commission from the *ba'al*, suggests that the writing itself — and the frame of mind and instruction under which it was composed — carries independent significance, at least according to the view that *edei mesirah karsei*, where even the writing must reflect the direct *tzivuy* of the husband. But the question is not entirely without force.

---

## Verbal vs. Written Chutz

### Rav Safra: Written Only

The *gemara* now addresses a fundamental question about the scope of the ruling. Rav Safra notes pointedly: *k'tavo b'tocho tnan* — "we taught: if it was written inside." His emphasis is deliberate: only if the *chutz* is physically written within the *get* does it compromise the instrument. One might think this is obvious — after all, that is precisely what the *mishna* says — but Rav Safra is forestalling an expansive reading.

### Objection: Before Toref

The *gemara* raises the objection: one might have thought that the rule *k'tavo b'tocho* — that writing *chutz* in the *get* invalidates it even after erasure — applies specifically when the *chutz* was written *after* the *toref*, the key operative line of the *get* (i.e., *harei at muteret l'chol adam* and its equivalent). In that case the core line was written without the taint of *chutz*, and the invalidation comes from what surrounds it. But if the *chutz* instruction was given *before* the *toref* was written — even if only verbally, communicated to the *sofer* before he composed the central line — perhaps even that verbal framing would invalidate the *get* as an instrument, since the *toref* itself was written in the context of a *chutz* intent.

This is not a frivolous concern. If the husband instructed the *sofer* — "write *harei at muteret l'chol adam*, but understand that my intention is to divorce her *chutz mi'Reuven*" — and the *sofer* then wrote the *toref* under that directive, there is a reasonable argument that the *toref* was never written as an expression of *da'as gerushin*. The key operative line of the *get* would have been composed without the proper intent, even if nothing problematic appears in the text.

Rav Safra's point is: do not say this. A verbal instruction — even one given before the *toref* was written — does not affect the validity of the instrument. The *get* as an object is defined by what is written in it, not by what was said to the *sofer* in the course of its composition. If nothing invalid appears in the document, the document is valid.

### Rava: Before Toref

Rava disagrees sharply. He holds: *lo shanu ela l'achar hatoref* — the ruling that writing *chutz* inside the *get* invalidates it even after erasure applies only when the *chutz* was written *after* the *toref*. But if the *chutz* instruction was given *before* the *toref* was written, even a verbal instruction invalidates the *get*. In that case, the *toref* itself was composed without proper *da'as gerushin* — the husband's framing of the entire act was as a *chutz* divorce, and the *sofer* wrote the key line under that direction. The instrument is therefore invalid, even though the words *chutz mi'Reuven* never appear in the text.

This is a striking position, and at first blush it seems to contradict the plain sense of the *mishna*, which focuses on what is written. Rava's reading is admittedly interpretive, locating the *mishna*'s ruling in the context of *l'achar hatoref* rather than treating it as a general statement. This is not the simple *pshat* of the *mishna*, but the *gemara* accepts it as Rava's position.

### Silence the Husband

Rava's practical corollary follows from this: *d'amar lehu Rava l'hanei d'chasvei gitei* — Rava instructed the *soferim* who write *gittin*: keep the husband silent (*shatku shutku l'ba'al*) until the *toref* of the *get* has been written. If the husband is going to say something problematic before the *sofer* reaches the key line, he can retroactively compromise the validity of the *get* as an instrument. The practical solution is to keep the husband occupied and quiet — distracted from making any declarations or conditions — until the *toref* has been composed, at which point the core of the instrument is already established and any subsequent statements can be managed separately.

This teaching also opens onto the broader concern that follows: even instructions that are not technically *chutz* may be problematic if given before the *toref*. The reason Rava counsels general silence, rather than simply warning against *chutz* specifically, anticipates the discussion of *gezeirah atu chutz* — a protective decree extending the concern about *chutz* to all conditions stated before the *toref* is written.

---

## Conditions & Chutz

### Rebbe: No Erasure

A *baraita* is cited: *kol hatna'im poslin baget* — all conditions invalidate a *get*. This is the position of Rebbi. The *chachamim* respond differently.

### Chachamim: Chutz Only

The *chachamim* state: *kol shepasul al peh pasul bichtav* — anything that is problematic when stated orally is problematic when written, and anything that is not problematic orally is not problematic when written. The application: *chutz*, which invalidates the *get* when stated verbally at the moment of delivery, likewise invalidates it when written into the document. An *al mnat* condition — a standard conditional clause — which does not invalidate the *get* when stated verbally, does not invalidate it when written either.

Before the *gemara* explains how Rebbi is to be understood, it is worth noting that one might have read Rebbi's position as a principled claim about the *cheftza* of the *get* itself: a *get* that is written without reservation expresses an absolute *krisus* in its very text, whereas a *get* that incorporates a condition — even a standard *al mnat* — is itself a qualified instrument, and the instrument as an object no longer expresses absolute severance. That reading has genuine force as a *svara*. However, as *Tosafot* explains, this is not how the *gemara* actually understands the dispute.

*Tosafot* frames the issue as follows: the practical question is whether a condition *written* into a *get* and subsequently *erased* before delivery can be treated as though it never existed. The *chachamim* hold that only *chutz* is irredeemably problematic — *chutz* written into the *get* compromises the instrument fundamentally, and erasing it does not help. Any other condition, however, if written and then erased, simply goes away; it does not taint the instrument, because the *chachamim* hold that the equivalence between verbal and written applies symmetrically, and a standard condition stated verbally is not a problem. Rebbi, by contrast, extends the logic of *chutz* to all written conditions: just as erasing a written *chutz* does not help, so too erasing any other condition that was written into the *get* does not help. This is not because all conditions are intrinsically as severe as *chutz*, but because of a *gezeirah atu chutz* — a protective decree that, once anything has been written and erased, we do not permit, lest it lead to doing the same with *chutz*.

### R. Zeira: Before/After

Rabbi Zeira offers a further refinement. He holds that the debate between Rebbi and the *chachamim* applies specifically to the case of a condition written *before the toref* — the key operative line — and subsequently erased. In that zone, Rebbi is concerned: *gazminan al mnat atu chutz* — we fear that permitting the erasure of a standard condition will lead to erasing a *chutz* written before the *toref*, or will otherwise be too close to scenarios where verbal *chutz* before the *toref* also causes problems. The *chachamim* are not worried and permit the erasure of any non-*chutz* condition.

But after the *toref* — *divrei hakol kasher* — everyone agrees that a standard condition written after the key line and then erased is entirely valid. The whole debate, on Rabbi Zeira's reading, is confined to the pre-*toref* zone.

The *gemara* cites a teaching presented before Rabbi Avin before Rabbi Zeira: if a *get* was written conditionally (*al tnai*), it is invalid — *divrei hakol*. The *gemara* challenges this: surely there is a recorded dispute? After correction, the teaching is reformulated: *divrei hakol kasher* — everyone agrees it is valid. The context must be a condition written and erased *after* the *toref*, where Rabbi Zeira's framework places consensus. The *gemara* explains that the tradition bearer remembered that the ruling was *divrei hakol* on something, but may have confused whether it was *pasul* or *kasher* — *kasher b'pasul michelef* — whereas confusing *divrei hakol* with *Rebbi alone* is not the kind of mistake one makes.

### Rava on Toref

Rava disagrees with Rabbi Zeira's limitation. Rava holds that Rebbi's concern applies even *after* the *toref*: *de'Rebbi savar gazrinan atu lifnei hatoref* — Rebbi worries that permitting erased conditions after the *toref* will lead to doing the same before the *toref*, and so Rebbi prohibits erased written conditions throughout the *get*. The *chachamim* are untroubled by that slippery slope and allow erased conditions after the *toref*.

But before the *toref*, both Rava and Rabbi Zeira agree: *divrei hakol pasul*. The difference between them is only in how far back they locate the consensus zone. For Rabbi Zeira, before the *toref* is where the debate lies; after the *toref* all agree it is valid. For Rava, before the *toref* all agree it is invalid; after the *toref* is where the debate lies.

### Gezeirah Concern

The concluding summary of this entire passage identifies the layered structure of the analysis. At the core is *chutz*, which fundamentally compromises the identity of the *get* as an instrument of *gerushin* — whether stated verbally at the moment of giving or written into the document. Around that core sits a series of protective extensions. Rava's instruction to keep the husband silent before the *toref* is written reflects the concern that even a verbal *chutz* before the *toref* would invalidate the instrument. The debate between Rebbi and the *chachamim* about erasing conditions reflects the concern that permitting erased conditions will lead people to treat a written *chutz* as erasable. And the zone before the *toref* is treated with particular severity — *divrei hakol* — because that is where the *chutz* concern is most acute.

The two fundamental positions to keep distinct are those of Rav Safra and Rava. Rav Safra holds that verbal instructions to the *sofer*, even if framed in terms of *chutz*, do not affect the validity of the *get* as an instrument — only what is written inside matters. Rava holds that verbal instructions given before the *toref* was composed do affect the instrument, because the key line was written without proper *da'as gerushin*. Everything else in this section — the debates about erasing conditions, the *gezeirah atu chutz*, the scope of Rebbi's concern — is secondary to that foundational disagreement.

---

## Categories of Exclusions

### Relatives & Slaves

A new *mishna* opens with a series of cases in which a husband declares *harei at muteret l'chol adam* followed by an *ela* — "except for" — excluding specific categories of men. The first group of exclusions: except for my father, your father, my brother, your brother, a *eved*, a non-Jew (*ovdei kochavim*), and anyone with whom *kiddushin* would not be binding — all of these exclusions leave the *get* valid (*kasher*). The reason, which the *mishna* will clarify through its concluding general principle, is that none of these men are people she could have entered into a binding marriage with. Excluding them from the scope of the *get* therefore does not genuinely limit the practical effect of the *gerushin*. The *kiddushin* with relatives and with *ovdei kochavim* or a *eved* would not take effect even without the exclusion — the *get* is not withdrawing anything real.

### Kohanim & Gerusha

The *mishna* then presents the contrasting category: except for a *almanah* vis-à-vis a *Kohen Gadol*, a *gerushah* or *chalutzah* vis-à-vis a *Kohen hedyot*, a *mamzeret* or *netinah* vis-à-vis a Jew, or a *bas Yisrael* vis-à-vis a *mamzer* or *nasin* — in all of these cases, the *get* is invalid (*pasul*).

The key question is why these exclusions are different. In the case of the *eved* or non-Jew, there is also a prohibition, so why is excluding the *Kohen* worse? The answer is not simply the severity of the prohibition. Even an *eved* or non-Jew may involve a *lo ta'aseh*; the distinction does not lie in the weight of the prohibition. The critical difference is that *kiddushin* with a *Kohen* would be *binding* even though prohibited. If a *gerushah* — a divorced woman — were to marry a *Kohen hedyot* in violation of the prohibition, the marriage would nonetheless take effect as a valid *kiddushin*, because the prohibition is an *issur lav*, not one that negates the binding force of the *kiddushin*. By contrast, *kiddushin* with a non-Jew or an *eved* does not take effect at all.

Accordingly, when the husband says "this is your *get* except with respect to *Kohanim*," he is doing something real: without that exclusion, if she had chosen to marry a *Kohen* in violation of the prohibition, the marriage would have been binding. By carving out the *Kohen*, he is preventing a binding *kiddushin* from taking effect — that is a genuine limitation on the effect of the *gerushin*. In the case of the *eved* or non-Jew, there is nothing real to limit; the *kiddushin* was never going to be binding in any case.

### Binding Kiddushin

The *mishna* states its general principle explicitly: *kol mi she'yesh lo alav kiddushin* — anyone with whom *kiddushin* would be binding — even if that *kiddushin* would only be binding through a transgression (*afilu ba'aveirah*) — excluding such a person from the *get* invalidates it. And conversely, anyone with whom *kiddushin* is not binding at all, excluding that person leaves the *get* valid.

### Minor's Future Status

The *gemara* records a question posed by Rava to Rav Nachman: *chutz mi'kiddushei katan mahu*? If the husband says "this is your *get* except with respect to a minor" — what is the ruling? The *kiddushin* of a *katan* cannot take effect right now; he is simply not in the category of one who can effect *kiddushin* at present. So perhaps this exclusion does not limit the *get* at the moment of giving. Or perhaps, since he will eventually reach the age at which *kiddushin* can take effect — *ati l'khlal havayah* — the exclusion is real even now.

Rav Nachman responds: we have already been taught this, from the case of *ketanah misgarshet b'kiddushei aviha*. A minor girl whose father had married her off can be divorced even before she reaches adulthood. One might have questioned this on the grounds that *gerushin* should parallel *kiddushin* — just as *kiddushin* without a father requires adulthood, so too perhaps *gerushin* without a father should require adulthood. But the *gemara* answers: *ati l'khlal havayah* — since she will naturally mature and enter the category of those who can be given in marriage, she is already treated as within that category. The same logic applies to the *katan*: since he will naturally mature and enter the category of those who can effect *kiddushin*, he is considered within that category now, and excluding him is a real exclusion that invalidates the *get*.

### Unborn Children

The *gemara* next asks: *chutz min hanoladim mahu*? If the husband says this is your *get* except with respect to anyone born from today onward, is that a real exclusion? Right now there are no such people. Or do we say that since people will inevitably be born — *asidei d'miyalid* — this is an anticipated future that renders the exclusion real even now?

The *gemara* attempts to resolve this from the *mishna*'s ruling that excluding an *eved* or *oved kochavim* does not invalidate the *get*. If future status were always relevant, one should worry even about the *eved* or non-Jew, since either might eventually convert or be freed, after which *kiddushin* would be binding. Since the *mishna* is not concerned about that future, perhaps future status is never relevant.

The *gemara* rejects this inference: *hanahu lo l'giyurei kaimei* — a non-Jew cannot be assumed to be on a path toward conversion; *hani l'ileyudei kaimei* — but children will be born, that is simply the natural course of events. The future arrival of new people in the world is an anticipated certainty; the conversion of a particular non-Jew is not. Accordingly, the question of *chutz min hanoladim* remains unresolved.

A conceptual point follows from this entire discussion. The *chachamim* who dispute Rabbi Eliezer generally hold that one cannot be *muteret* to one person and *asurah* to another — the *gemara* earlier invoked the principle *lo matzinu muteret lazeh va'asurah lazeh*. Yet in these *teku* cases, the *gemara* is entertaining the possibility that a *chutz* clause directed at people who are not currently present may in fact leave the *get* valid — which would mean the woman could be a *gerushah* vis-à-vis most people and something more like an *eishes ish* vis-à-vis those specified in the *chutz*. This is a more permissive stance toward conditional *gerushin* than one might have expected from the *chachamim*'s position — the key criterion being not an absolute bar on partial divorce but whether the exclusion limits the effect of the *get* in the here and now.

### Sister's Husband

The *gemara* poses a further question: *chutz miba'al achosah mahu*? If the husband says this is your *get* except with respect to your sister's husband — right now she cannot marry her sister's husband in any case, since her sister is alive. But if her sister were to die, he would become available. Does the possibility of the sister's death render this a real exclusion? Or does the uncertainty of whether that will occur mean it is not a genuine limitation right now?

The *gemara* attempts to draw an analogy to the *eved* and *oved kochavim* — they too might convert or be freed — and the *mishna* is not concerned about that future. But the *gemara* distinguishes: *geirus lo shchicha* — conversion is uncommon and cannot be assumed; *misah shchicha* — death is common. Death is an anticipated event; the question is only who dies first. Accordingly, the possibility that the sister will predecease makes the exclusion of the sister's husband potentially real, and the question of whether it constitutes an invalidating *chutz* is left unresolved.

---

## Marginal Exclusions

### Sexual Exclusion

The *gemara* now turns to exclusions that concern not the act of marriage (*nisuin*) but something more marginal. The *mishna*'s entire framework has focused on whether the husband is excluding someone from the scope of *kiddushin* — from the possibility of a binding marriage. What if the exclusion is directed not at marriage but at something else?

### Anal Intercourse

*Chutz miznus'ayich mahu*? If he says this is your *get* except with respect to extramarital sex with a certain man — is that a real *chutz*? The *mishna*'s framework seems to focus on marriage: the question has always been whether certain men are excluded from the scope of the *get* in terms of their ability to marry her. If no marriage is excluded, perhaps this is not a real limitation on the *gerushin*. Or perhaps even limiting certain acts of sex constitutes a holding back on the full effect of the divorce.

The *gemara* then asks the parallel question: *chutz mishelo kedarkah mahu*? If the only thing excluded is *biah shelo kedarkah* — anal intercourse — while *biah kedarkah* is not excluded, is that a limiting exclusion? The Torah considers both forms of intercourse to constitute *mishkevei ishah*, and therefore perhaps even excluding one form of sex constitutes a limitation on the completeness of the *gerushin*. The *gemara* envisions — strikingly — the possibility that a *gerushin* could take partial effect with respect to one form of sexual union and not another.

### Annulling Vows

*Chutz mehafarat nedarayich mahu*? If he says this is your *get* except that he retains the right to annul her vows — is that a real *chutz*? In terms of marriage, she is entirely free: she may marry anyone. But the Torah states *ishah yekimenu v'ishah yeferenu* — it is the husband who upholds or annuls her vows. If he is still exercising that prerogative, perhaps the Torah considers him still to be her husband, and the *get* is therefore not complete.

### Terumah Rights

*Chutz mitrumasayich mahu*? If he says this is your *get* except that she may continue to eat his *terumah* — perhaps the *get* is valid since she remains free to marry anyone. Or perhaps the right to eat *terumah* is rooted in the verse *kinyan kaspo* — she is still considered his *kinyan*, his wife, and therefore the *get* is not genuine.

### Inheritance Rights

*Chutz meyerushasayich mahu*? If he says this is your *get* except that when she dies he will still inherit her — she may marry anyone she chooses, but he retains the right of inheritance. Perhaps this is fine since no marriage is excluded. Or perhaps, since the verse establishes *lishero yirash osah* — his flesh inherits her — if he inherits her she remains considered his, and the severance is not real.

### Document Kiddushin

*Chutz mikidushayich beshtar mahu*? If he says this is your *get* except that if someone tries to effect *kiddushin* with her through a *shtar* — a document — it will not take hold, though *kiddushin* by money or by *biah* remains possible. She can in fact enter a new marriage by other means; perhaps this is sufficient. Or perhaps, since all three modes of *kiddushin* are equated — *huksha havayah leyetziah*, the modes of marriage are parallel to the modes of divorce — she must be fully free in all modes simultaneously, and any limitation on even one mode prevents the *get* from being effective.

The *gemara* leaves all of these questions as *teku* — unresolved. What emerges from this remarkable sequence is that the *gemara* is genuinely entertaining the possibility that a *get* could be valid while leaving some marginal aspect of the marital relationship intact, as long as the core function of the divorce — freeing her to enter a new binding marriage with any man — remains intact. At the same time, the *gemara* is uncertain whether even these marginal retentions might, on close reading of the relevant verses, indicate that the marital bond has not been fully severed.

---

## Core Language

### Standard Punchline

A new *mishna* states: *gufo shel get* — the essential text of the *get* — is *harei at muteret l'chol adam*: you are hereby permitted to marry any man. This is the minimal statement required at the core of the instrument of divorce.

### Testify About Itself

Rabbi Yehudah adds a further requirement. He cites the *Aramaic* text: *v'dein dei l'hevei lichi minai sefer teiruchin v'igert shivuchin v'get piturin l'meihach l'hitnasba l'chol gevar d'titzabyan* — "and this shall be from me a document of dismissal, a writ of separation, and a letter of release, to go and marry any man you desire." The *gemara* will explain that Rabbi Yehudah's primary contribution is the word *v'dein* — "this." Rabbi Yehudah holds that the *get* must testify about itself as the instrument of divorce. If the *get* merely declares *harei at muteret l'chol adam*, one might suppose that the divorce was effected through some other means and that this document merely records or proves the fact — that the *get* demonstrates she is divorced, rather than being itself the cause. Rabbi Yehudah requires that the document identify itself — *v'dein*, this very document — as the instrument through which the divorce is effected.

The *mishna* concludes by noting the parallel text for a *get shichrur*: *harei at bat chorin, harei at l'atzmech* — you are a free woman, you belong to yourself — which constitutes the essential language of a writ of emancipation for a *shifchah* or *eved*.

---

---

# Gittin 86

## Core Get Language

### Mishna & R. Yehuda

The *daf* begins in the middle of 85b, where the *mishna* establishes that the key line of a *get* is *harei at muteret le-chol adam* — "behold, you are permitted to all men." Rabbi Yehuda, however, requires that the *get* be more explicit and self-referential, stating *v'dein* — "and this" — should serve as an instrument of divorce. Not only does his formulation contain additional language, but it explicitly declares that the document itself is functioning as the instrument of divorce.

### Leatzimech Analysis

The *Gemara* then explores which formulations are valid and which are not. If a man says to his wife *harei at bat chorin* — "you are a free woman" — that is meaningless as a *get*, because *bat chorin* carries the specific meaning of being free as opposed to being a slave, and is not a language of divorce. Conversely, if he says to his female slave *harei at muteret le-chol adam*, that too is ineffective, since the language of permissibility to all men is not relevant to the slave's status of bondage or freedom.

The more interesting case arises when a man says to his wife *harei at le-atzmech* — "you are under your own control." This formulation works for freeing a slave, but is it general enough to function as divorce language as well? The *Gemara* frames the question: does *le-atzmech* mean *legamrei* — fully and completely — such that it severs all connection including marriage, or does it mean only that he is releasing her from his rights to her labor, which would be relevant only to a slave?

Ravina raises a proof for Rav Ashi from the *mishna*: the essence of a *get shichrur* is either *harei at bat chorin* or *harei at le-atzmech*. The *Gemara* reasons: *uma avda dekani lei gufei* — by a slave, over whom the master owns the body entirely, if one says *harei at le-atzmech*, the slave acquires ownership of himself or herself. This demonstrates that the phrase means a full withdrawal of control, not merely a waiver of labor rights. *Isha d'lo kani lei gufei* — by a wife, over whom the husband's control is less comprehensive than that of a master over a slave — *kal va-chomer* that *harei at le-atzmech* constitutes a complete removal of ownership. The *Gemara* thus establishes that any formulation lacking the specific semantic content of "slave versus free person" — meaning one that expresses a full severance of ownership and control in general terms — can function for both manumission and divorce.

### Ein Li Esek

Ravina then poses to Rav Ashi a further question: if a man says to his slave *ein li esek bach* — "I will have no dealings with you" — what is the status? This language sounds like a waiver of rights rather than a positive grant of freedom or a fundamental change of status. Rav Chanan, or according to another version Rav Chanin of Mechuza, brings a proof from a *baraita*: one who sells his slave to a non-Jew — the slave goes free, and the first master must still write a *get shichrur*. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel qualifies: when is a second document needed? Only when the master had not already written a document at the time of sale. If he had written one, *zehu shichruro* — that earlier document serves as the writ of manumission. What was this document? Rav Sheshes explains: it was a document stating that should the slave ever escape from the non-Jew, *ein li esek bach* — "I waive all rights to you." This establishes that *ein li esek bach* functions as a valid *shtar shichrur*.

This is a genuine *chiddush*, because the phrase "I will have nothing to do with you" does not on its face convey a positive transfer of self-ownership or a change of status — it sounds more like a unilateral withdrawal. Yet we find that it works for a slave. The natural follow-up question is whether it similarly works in a bill of divorce, and given the *Gemara*'s reasoning that a language effective for freeing a slave — as long as it does not carry the specific meaning of slave-versus-free — is sufficient for divorce as well, the presumptive answer is yes.

### Explicit vs Implicit

The *Gemara* now addresses the heart of the debate between Rabbi Yehuda and the *tanna kamma*. Rabbi Yehuda requires the *get* to state *v'dein di yehavi lichi minai sefer teiruchin v'igeret shivukin* — "and this shall be to you from me a book of divorce and a writ of release." One might ask why any document should need to declare itself the instrument it constitutes — a standard *shtar mechira* simply says *sadi mechura lach* and is handed over; a *shtar kiddushin* says *harei at mekudeshet li*. Neither describes itself as the instrument of transfer. The *Gemara*, however, does not frame the debate this way.

*Rabbanan savri yadayim she-einan mochichos haviyan yadayim* — the Rabbis hold that even an implicit or non-explicit indication (*yad*) suffices. The document need not explicitly state that it is the instrument of divorce; it is sufficiently clear from context. *Mochiach milta de-be-hai gitta kama-garesh lah* — the fact that this document is being given as a *get* makes the matter apparent. Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, holds *yadayim she-ein mochichos lav havyan yadayim* — an implicit indication that falls short of being fully evident does not qualify. Without the explicit *v'dein*, one might argue *be-dibura girsheha* — he is divorcing her verbally — *ve-shtara re'aya be-alma* — and the document is merely serving as evidence of that verbal act. Rabbi Yehuda thus requires both that the *get* make clear it is the instrument of divorce and that it do so explicitly. Both of these are genuine *chiddushim*, but the first — that a *get* must identify itself as the instrument at all — is arguably the more striking one.

---

## Nusach & Letters

### Spelling Rules

The *Gemara* now turns to extreme precision in the drafting of the *get*. Abaye enumerates a series of spelling hazards. The word *v'dein* must be written without a *yod* — *v'den* — lest it be read as *v'din*, suggesting "it is the law" that the *get* be given, which is both inaccurate and misleading. The word for letter or writ must be written *ageret* without a *yod*, not *igeret* with one, lest it be misread as *igra* — a roof — yielding the absurd meaning "this should be to you a roof of divorce." The word for "to go," *le-meihach*, must be written with a *heh*, not *le-mihach* with a *chet*, lest it be read as *le-mihach* — "to mock" — turning the *get* into something of a Purim joke.

### Rashi Nusach

Rashi provides the complete standard *nusach ha-get*, which runs as follows. *Petirus ychi lichi* — I have freed you to yourself — *ant plonit bat ploni*, you, such-and-such daughter of such-and-such, *de-haveit inteti min kadmat de-na* — who were my wife prior to this — *ve-chadu* — and with this — *petirat u-shvakat ve-taricat ychi* — I have released and divorced you — *di te-haveyan rasha'a u-shalta'a be-nafshichi* — that you should be permitted and under your own authority — *le-meihach u-le-hitnasba le-chol man di tetzbayan* — to go and be married to whomever you desire — *ve-inash lo yimchei be-yadaichi* — and no man shall protest or stand in your way — *min yoma de-nan u-le-alam* — from this day forward — *ve-den di ye-havei lichi minai* — and this shall be to you from me — *get piturin ve-sefer teiruchin ve-igeret shevukin* — a bill of release, a book of divorce, and a writ of abandonment — *ke-dat Moshe ve-Yisrael*.

One notable observation: Rashi's *nusach* does not explicitly include *harei at muteret le-chol adam*, even though the *mishna* identifies this as the core line of the *get*. The complete *nusach* as cited by both Rashi and the *Rif* is clearly the product of a received *mesora*, which is why Tosafot references the concept of a *tikun gittin* — an established authoritative text for the formulation of a *get*.

The *Gemara* continues with a requirement that the *get* contain three *yudin* in the word *de-yihavyan* — "that you should be" — and three in *de-yitzbayan* — "that you should desire." The reasoning is that with only two *yudin*, the phrase could be read impersonally — that women generally may desire or may be permitted — whereas three *yudin* make the language personal and direct, referring specifically to this woman. Tosafot adds that there must be five *yudin* in total: three at the end of *de-yihavyan* and one each before and after the *taf* of *de-yitzbayan*.

### Tosafot Letters

Tosafot raises several fine points regarding letter formation. The *vav* in *teiruchin* must be written long enough that it is not mistaken for a *yod*; if read as a *yod*, the word would become *terichin* — divorced women — rather than the abstract noun meaning "of divorce," yielding the absurd phrase "a book of divorcees." Similarly, the *vav* in *chadu* must be sufficiently elongated that it is not confused with a *yod*, which would transform *chadu* — "with this" — into *chadi*, meaning "for nothing" or "for naught." The word *le-hitnasba* must be written with a *heh* rather than an *alef*, lest *l'itnasva* be misread as *lo yitnasva* — "she shall not marry" — precisely the opposite of the intended meaning. The *heh* in *le-meihach* must be written with its leg sufficiently separated from the roof that it does not look like a *chet*.

Tosafot is careful to clarify what these requirements actually entail. The *vav* need not be dramatically elongated relative to other letters — it simply must not be so short as to resemble a *yod*. Similarly, the leg of the *heh* need not be made especially prominent; it must simply not be attached to the roof so as to resemble a *chet*. As for whether extreme elongation is required or merely preferred, Tosafot concludes that *vadai ein ha-get pasul im lo he'erikh* — certainly the *get* is not invalid if the letter was not given extra emphasis, as long as it does not actually look like the wrong letter.

This last point leads to a practical ruling. Tosafot records an actual incident: a *get* was brought before Rabbi Eliyahu in which it was unclear whether a particular letter was a *vav* or a *yod*. Rabbi Eliyahu employed the *tinok* test — bringing a child who is neither especially bright nor especially slow-witted to read the word, paralleling the procedure described in *Menachot* regarding letters in *tefillin*. If the child reads it correctly, the *get* is *kasher*; if not, it is *pasul*. This is the same standard applied to *sifrei Torah*, and it can raise real questions in the context of *gittin*.

### Rava Takana

The *Gemara* then asks whether we rule like Rabbi Yehuda — whether the *v'dein* line is in fact required. The *Gemara* notes that Rava, in formulating his *takana* for the standard *nusach* of a *get*, stated: *eich planya bar planya pattar ve-tarich yat plonisa ittati de-havas ittati min kadmat de-na, min yoma den u-le-alam* — so-and-so releases and divorces so-and-so my wife who has been my wife until now, from this day forward — but did not include the *v'dein* line. This would suggest he did not rule like Rabbi Yehuda.

The *Gemara* pushes back: *u-le-ta'ameicha kulhu mi ka'amar?* — by your reasoning, did Rava say everything? That formulation was only one particular addition Rava was establishing; the absence of *v'dein* from his stated formulation cannot serve as proof that he excluded it, any more than the absence of *harei at muteret le-chol adam* means he excluded that. *Ela ba'inan* — we require the other parts as well even though he did not mention them, and *hachi nami ba'inan* — similarly, perhaps we also require *v'dein* and he simply did not mention it.
