The *Gemara*'s conclusion, given the extraordinary attention to every letter and every word throughout this discussion, is that the *nusach* requires explicit inclusion of *v'dein de-yihavi lichi minai*, ruling in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda. Whether the absence of *v'dein* renders the *get* invalid *bedi'avad* is perhaps less clear, but *lechatchila* the standard demands full explicitness.

What Rava did explicitly insist upon, however, are two additions. First, *miyoma de-nan* — from this day — *la-apoukei mi-d'Rabbi Yosei*, to avoid relying on Rabbi Yosei's position that the date of the document implicitly establishes its effective date, making explicit retroactive conditions unnecessary. Rava required that the effective date be stated unambiguously. Second, *u-le-olam* — and forever — *la-apoukei mi-de-ba'ei minei Rava me-Rav Nachman*, in order to preempt the kind of question Rava once posed to Rav Nachman about whether one could be divorced only for a single day. Even though the *halacha* ultimately holds that such a conditional divorce does not work, Rava wanted the *get* to state explicitly that the divorce is permanent, so that no one could raise the claim that she was only divorced for that day.

---

## Three Invalid Gittin

### Handwriting No Edim

The *mishna* states: *shelosha gittin pesulim ve-im nisset ha-vlad kasher* — there are three invalid *gittin* such that nevertheless the children are not *mamzerim* if the woman remarried on the basis of them. The *Gemara* will discuss whether this *mishna* goes against Rabbi Meir — who holds that any deviation from the rabbinic standard of *gittin* renders the child a *mamzer* — or whether it represents Rabbi Meir's own concession that these particular cases, while invalid, do not produce a *mamzer*.

This is striking, because some of these defects seem far more serious than defects Rabbi Meir was willing to hold produce a *mamzer* in earlier contexts. Rabbi Meir had ruled that even dating a *get* according to the wrong foreign government or according to the *binyan beit ha-mikdash* renders the child a *mamzer* — extraordinarily exacting standards. Yet here, with defects that seem more substantive, the child will not be a *mamzer*.

The first case: *katav bi-chtav yado ve-ein alav eidim* — it was written in the husband's own handwriting but has no witnesses. Whose position is this? The *mishna* ends by introducing Rabbi Eliezer with his *edei mesira kartei* position, which implies that the beginning of the *mishna* is not Rabbi Eliezer's view. Two possibilities are offered. The first — attributed to Tosafot — is that this reflects Rabbi Meir's view that *edei chasima kartei*, signatures are required; yet the husband's own handwriting constitutes a form of *eidus*, since *hoda'as ba'al din ke-me'ah eidim dami* — the admission of a litigant is equivalent to a hundred witnesses. One's own handwriting is one's own testimony. The second — attributed to Rashi — is a more radical suggestion: perhaps no *eidus* is required in a *get* at all. If written by the husband himself as his own direct expression of divorce, perhaps that suffices without any testimony. Rashi entertains this as a possibility, which is, as noted, quite shocking given that the necessity of *eidus* has been among the most stable assumptions of the entire tractate. The more natural reading, as Tosafot argues, is that one's own handwriting constitutes self-testimony.

### No Date/One Witness

The second case: *yesh alav eidim ve-ein bo zman* — it has witnesses but no date. Dating was critical, as extensively discussed, to establish precisely when the *get* took effect. The third case: *yesh bo zman ve-ein bo ela eid echad* — it has a date but only one witness.

Regarding the third case, the *Gemara* presents a debate. Rav holds that *ktav yado shaninu* — what the *mishna* is discussing is the husband's own handwriting combined with one witness, not the scribe's handwriting with one witness. His reasoning: if a *get* is found in the street and a single witness attaches his name to it, one cannot know whether it is genuine. The scribe's handwriting alone carries no testimonial weight about the validity of the *get*. But if the husband himself wrote it in his own hand, that handwriting functions as his own testimony, and adding one witness creates a combination of his testimony and one external witness — sufficient *bedi'avad*.

Shmuel disagrees: *afilu ktav sofer ve-eid* — even the scribe's handwriting combined with one witness is *kasher bedi'avad*, relying on a later *mishna* that validates such a combination. Shmuel understands that later *mishna* as dealing with the scribe's handwriting, and holds that the scribe's writing counts as one form of testimony plus one signature equals two.

Rav responds that the later *mishna* is not discussing *ktav sofer* — the scribe's handwriting — but *chatam sofer* — the scribe's signature alongside one other witness. The proof: that later *mishna* says the woman may remarry *lechatchila*, whereas in our *mishna* she may only do so *bedi'avad*. Clearly they discuss different cases. Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Rav's position that *ktav yadcha shaninu* — it is the husband's handwriting that is at issue in the third case of our *mishna*.

Shmuel responds that there is no contradiction: *ha be-sofer mufhak ha be-sofer delo mufhak* — when the later *mishna* permits remarriage *lechatchila*, it refers to an expert scribe, *sofer mufhak*, whose writing of the *get* carries implicit testimonial weight because an expert scribe would not allow a *get* to leave his hands unless it was going to be properly used. A non-expert scribe might write a *get* for practice and discard it — his handwriting carries no such presumption. The scribe's handwriting combined with one witness therefore suffices *lechatchila* only when the scribe is *mufhak*.

### Rav Positions

Rav's two positions can be reconciled as follows: *zimnin amar Rav tetzei* — sometimes Rav said that if a woman married on the basis of any of the three *gittin* in the *mishna*, she must be divorced — and *zimnin amar Rav lo tetzei* — sometimes he said she does not need to be divorced. The resolution is circumstantial: *yesh la banim lo tetzei* — if she has already had children, she does not need to be divorced, because forcing a divorce would cause people to declare the children *mamzerim*. *Ein la banim tetzei* — if she has not yet had children, she must obtain a proper *get*.

### Tannaitic Proofs

A *baraita* is cited as a possible challenge to the position that she does not need to be divorced: all cases involving doubtful betrothal or doubtful divorce — *sefek kiddushin* or *sefek gerushin* — require *chalitzah* but not *yibbum*. The *baraita* specifies that the three *gittin* of our *mishna* constitute *sefek gerushin*. If she does not need to be divorced upon remarriage, the *Gemara* objects, then people will conclude she is fully divorced and a *yavam* may come to perform *yibbum* with her co-wife, thinking the marriage to the deceased brother's daughter was certainly severed. The *Gemara* deflects: *tityabem bein kach u-vein kach* — let him do *yibbum* either way; since *bedi'avad* the divorce is merely a rabbinic problem, the marriage was effectively severed and *yibbum* would be technically permissible. The concern is only a *chashasha de-rabbanan*, a rabbinic precaution.

The *Gemara* also examines whether these three *gittin* should be listed together with other problematic *gittin* such as *get yashan* — an old *get*, written before the couple later cohabited and then given afterwards — or *get kerei'ach* — the bald *get* in which not all of a folded *get*'s folds were signed. Neither fits neatly with the three of our *mishna*. A *get yashan* is not listed because, according to the view that in our *mishna* she must be divorced, the *get yashan* is less weighty — once given, she may even remarry *lechatchila*. A *get kerei'ach* is not listed because there the child is a *mamzer*, whereas here the child is *kasher*. However, the *Gemara* notes a tension: if our *mishna* follows the *Rabbanan*, who never declare a child a *mamzer*, then the distinction from *get kerei'ach* must rest on whether *tetzei* applies. This works only for the opinion that in our *mishna* she does not need to be divorced; if she does need to be divorced here just as in *get kerei'ach*, then there is no basis to omit *get kerei'ach* from the list according to the *Rabbanan*. The *Gemara* is forced to concede: *okimta ke-Rabbi Meir* — one can explain the separate lists only by attributing the *mishna* to Rabbi Meir, who maintains two distinct categories, one in which the *vlad* is a *mamzer* and one in which it is not. By the *Rabbanan*, who never declare a *mamzer*, the lists should be combined, and no fully satisfying answer is given unless one holds that in our *mishna* she does not need to be divorced.

The *mishna* also closes with Rabbi Eliezer's position: even a *get* that bears no witnesses at all is valid if it was given in the presence of witnesses — *edei mesira kartei* — and the woman may even collect from encumbered property on the basis of it, since the witnesses at the moment of delivery confer upon it the full legal weight of a witnessed document.

### Remarriage & Divorce

Levi states: *l'olam lo tetzei* — she never needs to be divorced, regardless of whether she has had children. Rabbi Yochanan agrees: *l'olam lo tetzei*. Rabbi Yochanan conveyed this also to the sons of Rav Chalafta of Minhuna — "this is what your father said: *l'olam lo tetzei*." Once a woman has remarried on the basis of one of these three *gittin*, she does not need to be divorced, with or without children, *l'olam* meaning even absent children.

The *daf* concludes with a brief appendix conveyed alongside this ruling — Rabbi Yochanan also told the sons of Rav Chalafta another ruling in their father's name: a certain type of locust (*kartzi*) that dwells among bundles of wheat does not invalidate the waters of a *parah adumah* if it drinks from them. The *Gemara* asks what a *kartzi* is, and identifies it as a small insect or flying grasshopper found between grain bundles. A challenge is raised from a *baraita* stating that all birds invalidate *mei chatat* if they drink from them, with the sole exception of the dove, which sucks in and does not spit back. If the *kartzi* were always valid, the *baraita* should have listed it alongside the dove. The *Gemara* resolves: the ruling is not absolute — *gedola lo pasla, ketana pasla* — a large one does not invalidate the water but a small one does. How small must it be to still pose a problem? Until the size of an olive, according to Rav Yirmiya, or according to another version, Rav Ami. This brief digression aside, the substantive *halacha* of the *daf* concludes with the ruling of Levi and Rabbi Yochanan: once a woman has remarried on the basis of any of the three *gittin* of our *mishna*, she does not need to be divorced — *l'olam lo tetzei*.

---

---

# Gittin 87

## Edei Mesira Krati

### Intro: Edei Mesira

The daf opens in the middle of 86b, where the *mishnah* has been discussing three types of *gittin* that are *pasul* — those lacking full *eidus*. The cases involved either the husband's own handwriting, a single *eid*, or various combinations thereof. That discussion proceeded according to Rabbi Meir's position that *edei chatima krati* — the witnesses who sign the document are the essential ones — and raised questions about what counts as valid signatures. At the close of the *mishnah*, however, Rabbi Eliezer articulates a fundamentally different position: a *get* requires no signatures at all. As long as it was delivered in front of witnesses, it is valid *l'chatchila*. And Rabbi Eliezer extends this principle beyond *gittin* — even a *shtar chov*, a loan document, if given in front of witnesses without signatures, creates liens on encumbered property. His principle is *edei mesira krati*: the witnesses who observe the transfer are the essential ones, and their *eidus* effectively combines with the physical document to constitute it as a document of testimony.

### Gittin vs. Shtarot

One might have expected the *halacha* to follow Rabbi Eliezer more readily in monetary matters than in *gittin*. After all, *dinei mamonot* is a more flexible area of law — *hefker beis din hefker* and similar principles give the rabbis wider latitude — whereas *gittin* involves personal status, which typically demands stricter standards. Yet the *gemara* will demonstrate the opposite, and for a compelling reason. A *get* is an instrument that, once it meets its technical requirements, effects a change in status. A *shtar*, by contrast, creates liens partly because it constitutes a matter of public record — buyers of property need to know that liens may exist against what they are purchasing. There is therefore a pragmatic reason to demand more objectively accessible documentation in monetary matters than in *gittin*, where the instrument's function is more purely technical.

### Halacha k'Rabbi Eliezer

The *gemara* opens with Rav Yehuda citing Rav: *halacha k'Rabbi Eliezer begittin* — we rule like Rabbi Eliezer for *gittin*, that witnesses of delivery without signatures suffice. When Rav Yehuda transmitted this ruling before Shmuel, Shmuel extended it: *af b'shtarot* — even by monetary documents. The *gemara* then asks whether Rav himself disagreed with Shmuel on this point, since the *mishnah* mentions collection from *nechasim meshubadim*, which implies that Rabbi Eliezer's position creates binding liens even in monetary matters. The *gemara* resolves this: Rabbi Eliezer himself said both — both for *gittin* and for *shtarot*. Nobody disputes what Rabbi Eliezer held. The question is only how we rule. Rav rules like him for *gittin* but not for *shtarot*; Shmuel rules like him in both domains.

### Rabbi Yannai's Challenge

The *gemara* then cites Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *halacha k'Rabbi Eliezer begittin*. Rabbi Yannai, however, says: *afilu reiach haget ein bo* — a *get* without signatures does not even have the whiff of a *get*. A *get* lacking any *reiach haget* is so completely invalid that it does not even create the usual complications for *kehunah* that a questionably valid *get* would generate.

The *gemara* immediately objects: does Rabbi Yannai not hold like Rabbi Eliezer? The answer is that of course he does. What Rabbi Yannai is saying is that *for the rabbanan* who disagree with Rabbi Eliezer — and that *rabbanan* is no small figure, being Rabbi Meir — the position is not merely that such a *get* is *pasul*, but that it is diametrically and categorically invalid. If you believe that a *shtar* is fundamentally a signed document, then a document delivered in front of witnesses but bearing no signatures is not a defective *get* — it is simply not a *get* at all. The analogy is apt: if someone handed you an unsigned check and told you two people had watched the transaction, you would rightly say that is not a check. That is Rabbi Meir's position — and Rabbi Yannai is articulating it faithfully, while personally ruling like Rabbi Eliezer.

The *gemara* thus presents an extreme polarity: Rabbi Eliezer validates such a *get* entirely, while those who oppose him regard it as having no legal status whatsoever.

### Amoraic Consensus

The *gemara* proceeds to accumulate a striking series of rulings all affirming *halacha k'Rabbi Eliezer begittin*. Rabbi Yochanan bar Rabbi Yannai cites Reish Lakish: *halacha k'Rabbi Eliezer begittin*. When Rabbi Yochanan's own name appears immediately after with the statement *afilu reiach haget ein bo*, the *gemara* again clarifies in the same way: Rabbi Yochanan is articulating the position of the *rabbanan* who oppose Rabbi Eliezer, not his own ruling.

The *gemara* then relates that Rabbi Abba bar Zavdi sent a message to Mari bar Mar: ask Rav Huna whether we rule like Rabbi Eliezer for *gittin* or not. Before the question could be put to him, Rav Huna died. His son Rava then reported: this is what my father said — *halacha k'Rabbi Eliezer begittin*. Some transmit this in the name of Rav directly. Additionally, *raboseinu habeki'im b'dvar halacha* — the rabbis who are expert in matters of law, identified as Rav Chama bar Guria citing Rav — rule the same way. And some say that not just those experts but the students of Rav, *mishum Rabbeinu*, transmitted the same ruling. Finally, when Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael, he reported that Rabbi Elazar said in the name of Rav: *halacha k'Rabbi Eliezer begittin*.

The cumulative effect is remarkable. The *gemara* is thoroughly insistent that this is the unanimous ruling of the *Amoraim* — that we rule like Rabbi Eliezer for *gittin* — while simultaneously emphasizing, through the careful limitation *begittin*, that this ruling does not extend to monetary *shtarot*.

---

## Mixed-Up Gittin

### Setup: Two Identical

The *gemara* turns to a new *mishnah*: *shnayim she'shaltchu shnei gittin shavin* — two men sent two *gittin* that are identical, because by coincidence both husbands and both wives happened to share the same names. This raises a preliminary question not addressed by the *mishnah* directly — can a *get* be valid if it is not *mochiach mitocho*, not self-evidently identifiable as referring to one particular couple? If there are multiple men in a city named Reuven ben Yaakov married to women named Sarah bat Rachel, can the document serve as valid written testimony? This question bears more acutely on Rabbi Meir's position, where the document itself must function as written *eidus*, but the *mishnah* sets this aside and assumes the *gittin* are otherwise valid. The scenario is simply that both husbands gave their identical *gittin* to a single *shaliach*, who was to deliver them to the respective wives — and the *shaliach* mixed them up and no longer knows which belongs to which.

The *mishnah*'s solution is elegant: *notnin shnayhem l'zu v'shnayhem l'zu* — give both *gittin* to one wife and then both to the other. Each wife thereby receives the *get* that was written for her, even if neither she nor the *shaliach* knows which one it is. However, if one of the *gittin* is lost — *avad echad meihem, harei hasheni batel* — the remaining *get* cannot be used. Giving it to each wife individually would render each one a *safek gerushah*, a woman of uncertain divorced status, which is the worst possible outcome, and so the remaining document is simply invalidated.

---

## Five Husbands, One G (II)

### One Date, Multiple Names

The *mishnah* then introduces a distinct case: *chamisha shekatvu klal b'toch haget* — five husbands who incorporated all their names within a single *get*, listing each man and his wife: *ish ploni megaresh plonit, v'ploni plonit*, and so on, with the witnesses signing below. The ruling is *kulam kesherim* — they are all valid — and the *get* is given to each wife in turn.

However, if *haya chosev tofes l'chol echad v'echad* — if there was a separate text for each individual — and the witnesses sign below, then only the one most proximate to the witnesses is valid: *es she'ha'eidim niktamim imo kasher*. The question that will occupy the *gemara* is: what exactly distinguishes a single unified statement, for which the witnesses' signatures validate the whole, from multiple separate statements, for which the signatures apply only to the bottommost?

---

## Mixed-Up Gittin (II)

### Why Problematic?

The *gemara* asks: *man tana* — according to which *tanna* is the case of the two mixed-up *gittin* a problem? Rabbi Yirmeyah answers: *d'lo k'Rabbi Eliezer* — it is not according to Rabbi Eliezer. This is initially surprising, because one might have expected the opposite: if the *get* is ambiguous as to which person it refers to, that seems more problematic under Rabbi Meir, for whom the document must constitute clear written *eidus*. Yet the *gemara* argues that it is specifically Rabbi Eliezer's position that creates the difficulty.

Rabbi Eliezer holds that *edei mesira krati* — the witnesses who observe the delivery are the essential ones; their testimony combines with the physical document and makes it an instrument of *eidus*. For this to work, there is a logical requirement: the witnesses must be able to know which document is doing the divorcing. If two identical *gittin* are handed over together and neither the witnesses nor anyone else knows which one was written for this particular woman, how can the witnesses' testimony be said to combine with *this* document? The witnesses observed a delivery, but they cannot attest that *this* document is the one that was written for *this* woman. Their *eidus* would need to attach specifically to a document that they can identify as the operative one.

*Tosafot* articulates this precisely: the witnesses did not know that *this* document — as opposed to the other one — was the one written for this woman. And since Rabbi Eliezer's entire mechanism requires that the witnessing of the delivery combine with the specific document that was designated for her, the uncertainty about which document is which is fatal to his framework. For Rabbi Meir, by contrast, the witnesses signed the document at the time of writing, when everything was clear. The signing was done *lishmah*, with the correct parties in mind, producing a complete and valid instrument. Whatever happens at the time of delivery — even if the *shaliach* is uncertain about which *get* to hand over — is irrelevant to the document's validity, because the *eidus* is already embedded in it.

*Rashi* approaches this from the verse *v'chatav lah sefer keritut* — for Rabbi Meir, the word *v'chatav* refers to the signing, which was performed *lishmah* and completed the instrument. For Rabbi Eliezer, the *v'natanah b'yadah* — the delivery — also bears *halachic* weight, and one might argue it too must be *lishmah*. But the deeper logic is structural: if it is the act of witnessed delivery that constitutes the document as testimony, then the witnesses' awareness of what they are witnessing — specifically, *which* document is being activated — is an essential component of that act.

### Abaye's Answer

Abaye rejects this analysis: *afilu teima Rabbi Eliezer* — the *mishnah* can be understood even according to Rabbi Eliezer. *Ketivah lishmah, netinah lishmah mi bei?* — writing must be *lishmah*, but does delivery require *lishmah* as a separate condition? Abaye maintains that the requirement is simply that it be delivered *as a get* — not, say, as a *shtar chov* — and the witnesses' uncertainty as to which document was written for this particular woman does not undermine their testimony about the delivery itself. The document was written correctly and *lishmah* at the time of writing; the fact that the witnesses at delivery cannot distinguish between two identical *gittin* does not invalidate either one.

---

## Five Husbands, One G (II)

### Yochanan: Zman Echad

The *gemara* now returns to the five-husbands *mishnah* and asks *heichi dami klal* — what constitutes a unified statement for which the witnesses validate all five *gittin*? And *heichi dami tofes* — what constitutes separate statements for which the witnesses apply only to the last?

Rabbi Yochanan answers: *zman echad l'kullan zehu klal* — a single date for all of them makes it one unified statement. *Zman l'chol echad v'echad zehu tofes* — a separate date for each makes them individual statements. On Rabbi Yochanan's view, the key variable is the date. If the entire document bears one date at the outset — "on the first of the week, I, Reuven ben Yaakov, divorce my wife... and I, Yaakov ben Yitzchak, divorce my wife..." — the shared date pulls the entire document together as one continuous statement, and the witnesses at the bottom validate everything. But if each section bears its own date — even if all the dates are identical — the repetition of the date marker makes each section self-contained, and the witnesses apply only to the bottommost statement.

The underlying logic is that a separate date makes a statement *self-referential* and therefore independent. Without its own date, a statement must look back to the single date at the top, and that shared reference point unifies the whole document. With its own date, each statement stands alone.

### Lakish: Klal Needed

Reish Lakish goes further: *afilu zman echad l'kulam nami avei tofes* — even with a single date for all, the result is still multiple separate statements. On Reish Lakish's view, the mere sequence of individual declarations — even connected by conjunctions — does not by itself constitute one unified statement. Each declaration "I divorce my wife" is an independent legal act; stringing them together with *vav*s does not make them one.

What then constitutes the *klal* — the unified statement — according to Reish Lakish? *D'kasvu anu ploni u'ploni gerashnu nishoseinu plonit u'plonit* — you would need to begin with a collective declaration: "We, Reuven and Shimon and Levi and Yehuda, divorce our wives..." That opening collective statement — *anu* — is what transforms the document into a single unified act, allowing the witnesses' signatures at the bottom to validate everything that follows.

But there is an immediate difficulty: if everything is so tightly bound into one statement that the witnesses validate the whole, doesn't that mean one *get* is divorcing multiple women? And the Torah says *v'chatav lah* — *lah v'lo l'chavertah* — a *get* must be for *her*, not for her and her friend simultaneously. The *gemara* resolves this for Reish Lakish: after the collective opening, you then write out individual statements — *ploni geiraish plonit, v'ploni geiraish plonit* — spelling out each husband's divorce separately. The collective opening creates the unity that allows the witnesses to cover everything, while the subsequent individual statements preserve the separateness of each *get* for each woman.

### Klal vs. Tofes

Rav Abba challenges Rabbi Yochanan's position. Rabbi Yochanan holds that the conjunction — the *vav* connecting the individual declarations under a single date — is sufficient to make everything one statement. But why should that be so? Perhaps the witnesses signed only on the final, most proximate statement. The *gemara* supports this concern by citing a *baraita*: *edim she-chotmin al she'elat shalom b'get pasul* — if witnesses sign at the bottom of a *get* that concludes with a social pleasantry ("and please send my regards to so-and-so"), the *get* is invalid, because we suspect the witnesses may have signed only on that closing pleasantry rather than on the *get* itself.

This principle establishes that witnesses' signatures are presumed to apply only to what is most immediately proximate to them. If an interpolated phrase — even a formulaic one — can sever the witnesses from the *get*, then surely separate individual declarations should do the same.

Rav Abba then clarifies that he had the position of Rabbi Yochanan explained to him directly. The case of *she'alat shalom* is *pasul* because the final line reads "and ask after the welfare of so-and-so" — a separate sentence that the witnesses could plausibly have been signing. But if the closing reads "and you should ask" — *v'sha'alu* — then it is *kasher*, because the conjunction makes it part of the same sentence as the *get* itself. Similarly, for Rabbi Yochanan, individual declarations joined by *vav* — "and I, Yaakov, divorce my wife... and I, Shimon, divorce my wife..." — are one run-on statement. The *ands* make it all one sentence, and the witnesses at the bottom validate the whole.

However, the *gemara* raises a further difficulty with Rabbi Yochanan's position. If the declarations are joined by *vav* but each bears its own date — even the identical date — does the redundant dating create a problem? The *gemara* observes that having a repeated date entry is even more self-contained than simply having a new sentence, because the date marker signals a fresh, independent statement. Moreover, if different dates were used, the earlier sections would be invalid on entirely separate grounds: a *get* signed on a different day from the one on which it was dated is *pasul*, because it was effectively signed on a day other than its stated date. The *gemara* resolves this by noting that in Rabbi Yochanan's case, all the dates are the same — the same day is simply repeated for each line. The repetition itself, even of the same date, is what signals that each is a self-contained statement — which is all the more reason it would function as a *tofes* even within Rabbi Yochanan's framework.

Ravina asks Rav Ashi: according to Reish Lakish, who says that even a single date is insufficient to create a *klal* — and that what is needed is the collective opening statement — what would a *klal* look like in practice? The *gemara* answers: *anu ploni u'ploni gerashnu nishoseinu plonit u'plonit* — the collective "we" followed by all the names and their wives. But this immediately generates the problem already noted: *nimtze'u shtei nashim misgarshos b'get echad* — two women are being divorced by one *get*, which violates *v'chatav lah v'lo l'chavertah*. Hence Reish Lakish's requirement that the collective opening be followed by individual statements for each husband.

The *gemara* considers whether this is analogous to the case of a master who gives all his property to two slaves, which would free both of them, since each owns half of the other as part of the property. Might that case demonstrate that one document can effect a legal change for two people? The *gemara* dismisses this: *v'okimna bishnei shtarot* — that case was long since explained as involving two separate documents, one given to each slave. One document for one slave and another for the other; the combined effect is joint ownership and mutual freedom. One *shtar* for two people remains impermissible. The conclusion stands: you cannot have one *get* for two women, and the collective statement in Reish Lakish's model must be accompanied by individual declarations.

### Baraita Consensus

The *gemara* confirms both positions with *tannaic* support. In favor of Rabbi Yochanan: if five men write *ish ploni megaresh plonit v'ploni plonit* — each name connected by *vav* with a single date — and the witnesses sign below, *kulam kesherim*, and the *get* is given to each wife. If each section has its own date, the witnesses apply only to the final section. This is precisely Rabbi Yochanan's framework.

In favor of Reish Lakish: if five men write the collective *anu ploni u'ploni gerashnu nishoseinu*, followed by the individual *ploni geiraish plonit*, with a single date and witnesses below — *kulam kesherim*. If each individual section has its own date and its own line-space, the witnesses apply only to the final section. This is precisely Reish Lakish's framework.

### ben Beteira: Revach

Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira then weighs in with a position more lenient than anything encountered so far. He says: *im yesh revach beneihem pasul, v'im lav kasher* — if there is a blank line-space between the sections, they are *pasul* as separate units; if there is no such space, they are *kasher* as one unit. Crucially: *she'ein zman mafsikan* — a separate date is not sufficient to create separation. Only a physical gap in the text — a blank line — constitutes a break.

On Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's view, the natural reading of a continuous text is that it is all one document, and a separate date-entry alone does not sever that continuity. One needs an actual physical interruption — a *revach* — to signal that what follows is a distinct and independent statement.

The *gemara* then raises a sharp internal question against Reish Lakish's supporting *baraita*: Reish Lakish requires a collective statement to create a unified *klal*. But if that collective statement is what makes the whole thing one, why does the *baraita* then say that you can break it back into separate units by means of separate dates and line-spaces? If you needed the collective to unify them, the simple absence of the collective should be sufficient to produce separate units — why the need for dates and *revach* as well?

The *gemara* answers: the two cases are distinct. Where no collective statement was ever made, the individual declarations are simply multiple separate units from the outset, and no further mechanism is needed to establish their separateness. But where a collective statement *was* made at the outset — *anu ploni u'ploni gerashnu* — that collective creates a presumption of unity. To overcome that presumption and re-establish the separateness of the individual sections, something affirmative is needed: *mipalgu zman u-shita* — a separate date-entry and a line-space for each section. The combined force of these two elements can overcome the unifying effect of the initial collective statement. Without both, the collective statement continues to bind the whole document together.

---

## Parallel Columns

### Setup: Hebrew, Greek

The final *mishnah* of the daf introduces another scenario: *shnei gittin shek'tavam zeh b'tzad zeh* — two *gittin* written side by side in parallel columns on one piece of paper. Below them are four signatures in total: two Hebrew witnesses and two Greek witnesses. The question is which signatures belong to which *get*.

### Language & Direction

The key to the *mishnah*'s ruling lies in the direction in which each script is written. Hebrew runs from right to left, so a Hebrew signature that begins at the right will be aligned with — and is presumed to belong to — the right-hand *get*. Greek runs from left to right, so a Greek signature that begins at the left will be aligned with and presumed to belong to the left-hand *get*. If the two Hebrew signatures appear directly beneath the two *gittin* — spanning both columns — and the two Greek signatures appear below them, the Greek witnesses are two lines removed from the *get* on the right. In that configuration, only the right-hand *get* is valid: the Hebrew witnesses are proximate to it, and the Greek witnesses, though displaced, are aligned with and proximate to the right-hand column as well by virtue of where they begin. The *mishnah*'s underlying presumption is that signatures must be immediately proximate — directly beneath — the *get* they are validating.

### Alternating Pattern

The *mishnah* then presents the case where the signatures alternate: one Hebrew witness, one Greek witness, one Hebrew witness, one Greek witness. In this arrangement, *sheneihem pesulim* — both *gittin* are invalid. No two signatures for the same *get* are proximate to one another, and there is a *hefsek* — an interruption — between any pairing. The *mishnah* thus assumes that valid *eidus* on a *get* requires the two witnesses' signatures to be proximate both to the document and to each other.

### Proximity Problem

The *gemara* asks a pointed question about the case of two Hebrew witnesses followed by two Greek witnesses: why can't we simply let both sets of witnesses validate both *gittin*? After all, we know from a prior ruling that a *get* written in one language with witnesses who signed in another is valid — language itself is not a barrier. If so, why not say the Hebrew witnesses validate the right *get* and the Greek witnesses, even though displaced by two lines, validate the left *get*?

The *gemara* cites Chizkiyah to address this: *mil'o b'krovim kasher* — if the gap between a *get* and its witnesses was filled in with additional text, even signatures of relatives (who are *pasul* as witnesses but whose names in writing fill the space), the *get* is valid. Chizkiyah's ruling establishes that proximity is about continuity: a blank gap breaks the connection between document and witness; filled space — even with legally useless text — maintains it. But if filled space suffices to maintain connection, why can't the Hebrew signatures in the middle, which are themselves writing between the top *get* and the bottom Greek signatures, serve as the filling that keeps the Greek signatures proximate?

### Chizkiyah: Fill Gaps

Chizkiyah's principle is that a gap is problematic because it visually and legally detaches the witnesses from the document they are meant to validate. Once the gap is filled — by any writing, even non-*kasher* signatures — the document runs continuously from beginning to witness, and the connection is maintained. The implication for our case is that the Hebrew signatures physically separating the *gittin* from the Greek signatures might constitute just such a fill — maintaining continuity rather than severing it.

### Ziri: Both Valid

*Ziri* has a variant text of the *mishnah* itself. According to Ziri, in the case of two Hebrew witnesses followed by two Greek witnesses, *shnayim kesherim* — both *gittin* are valid. On Ziri's reading, there is no requirement of strict proximity; each set of witnesses is associated with its respective *get* regardless of the gap, and both *gittin* are therefore fully valid.

### Our Tanna's View

Our *tanna*, however, maintains that only the proximate *get* is valid and not the other. The *gemara* explains our *tanna*'s concern: *dilma gundali chasam* — perhaps the signatures were written in an unusual orientation. *Rashi* explains *gundali* as referring to some strange or reversed manner of signing. The possibility is that even the Greek signatures, written in some aberrant fashion, may be oriented toward the right-hand *get* rather than the left — meaning all four signatures could be attaching to the same *get*, leaving the other without valid witnesses at all. Because we cannot rule out this possibility, we cannot confidently say which *get* has two valid witnesses and which does not, and therefore only the *get* that is certainly proximate to identifiable signatures is valid.

The same logic applies to the alternating case. One might suggest that the first Hebrew witness and the first Greek witness together constitute two witnesses for the right *get*, and the second Hebrew and second Greek together constitute two witnesses for the left *get*. The *gemara* notes that Ziri again says *shnayim kesherim* — both are valid. Our *tanna*, however, again raises the concern that one of the signatures might be written in an unusual direction — *gundali* — such that instead of the alternating pattern yielding one witness per document, three signatures might be attaching to one *get* and only one to the other. Since we cannot determine which *get* has two valid witnesses and which has only one, neither can be definitively validated.

The fundamental principle underlying our *tanna*'s position, then, is that a signature must be unambiguously aligned with — visually, directionally, and proximately — the *get* it is meant to validate. Ambiguity in any of these dimensions, whether caused by physical gaps or uncertain orientation, is sufficient to undermine the validity of the *get*. The *gemara* will continue with the next *mishnah* in the following session.

---

---

# Gittin 88

## Two-Column Get

### Two Columns, Signatures…

The *mishna* before us — located on 88b, roughly in the middle of the page — opens with a case that is in many ways a continuation of the previous day's discussion, albeit the simpler version of it. The case is: *shi'er miktzat haget uchtavo bedaf hasheni vehayedim milmata kasher* — he wrote part of the *get* in one column and the remainder in a second column, and the witnesses signed at the bottom of the second column. Here *daf* carries the sense of *yeri'ah*, a column, as in a column of a Torah scroll. The ruling is *kasher*: the witnesses sign at the conclusion of the *get* after the entire text has been written across both columns, and that is sufficient.

### Signatures Top/Side

The *mishna* then presents variations on signature placement. *Chatmu ha-eidim berosh ha-daf* — if the witnesses signed at the top of the second column rather than the bottom — or *min ha-tzad*, at the side, meaning in the margins of the document rather than at its conclusion — these are problematic. The intuition is straightforward: a contract is signed at its end. Signing in the margins or at the top does not follow the expected structure of a legally executed document.

### Signing on Back

A third case: *o me'achorav beget pashut pasul* — if they signed on the back of a plain *get*. This is distinguished from a *get mekushar*, the folded-style *get* treated in earlier passages where signing on particular external sections was the correct practice. For a standard *get*, signing on the back is *pasul*.

### Heads Touching Invalid

The *mishna* then introduces cases requiring illustration, and those following along without a visual aid will need to hold the picture in mind. The first case: *hikif rosho shel zeh betzad rosho shel zeh veha-eidim ba-emtza sheneihem pesulin* — imagine two *gittin* placed so that the top (*rosh*) of one faces the top of the other, with the witnesses signing in the middle between them. Both *gittin* are invalid. The reason, as becomes clear, is that the witnesses appear at the head of one of the documents rather than at its conclusion.

### Tails Touching Valid

The next case: *sofo shel zeh betzad sofo shel zeh veha-eidim ba-emtza* — the tail (*sof*) of one *get* faces the tail of the other, with the witnesses between them. The ruling is *et she-nikra'im imo kasher* — the one that can be read together with the witnesses is valid. Visually: if *get* one is written normally and the witnesses appear at its bottom, and *get* two is written upside-down below the witnesses, then *get* one's witnesses are properly placed at its conclusion, and it is valid. The second *get*, read from the other direction, has the witnesses at its head — which is invalid.

## Two-Column Get (II)

### Head-Tail Adjacent

The final configuration: *rosho shel zeh betzad sofo shel zeh* — the head of one *get* is adjacent to the tail of another, with a single set of witnesses. Again, the ruling is *et she-nikra'im imo basof kasher* — the one for which the witnesses appear at the end is valid, and the other is not, for the same reason. In each of these cases, the governing principle is that witnesses must appear at the conclusion of the document they are signing.

## Hebrew-Greek Mix

### One Get, Two Languages

The *mishna* continues with a series of cases involving language. *Get she-ketavo Ivrit ve-chatamo Yevanit, o Yevanit ve-chatamo Ivrit, ed echad Ivri ve-ed echad Yevanit* — a single *get* written in Hebrew and signed in Greek, or the reverse, or one witness signing in Hebrew and the other in Greek — all of these are valid. This is the simple version of what was treated in more complex form in the previous day's material: so long as it is a single *get*, the mixing of languages and scripts presents no problem.

### Scribe + Witness

Then: *katav sofer ve-ed kasher* — the scribe wrote and signed, along with one additional witness. As the *gemara* clarifies, *katav* here really means *chatam* — the scribe himself signed the document in addition to writing it. This is not a case of only one witness; rather, the scribe's signature counts as one of the two required signatures.

The *gemara* identifies this ruling as the position of Rabbi Yossi: *ve-amar Rav Chisda man Rav Yossi hi*. The underlying logic relates to the rule that a *shliach* may not deviate from the husband's instructions. If a *shliach* could alter arrangements, one would worry that the scribe, having written the entire *get*, might be permitted to sign out of courtesy — even though the husband never designated him as a witness — and that a proper witness might then be displaced. But if a *shliach* cannot change what the husband specified, then the only way the scribe could be signing is if the husband himself, speaking directly, authorized it. Under those circumstances, the scribe's signature is entirely legitimate.

## Witness Name Variations

### Name Forms Valid

The *mishna* turns to different forms of witness identification. *Ish ploni ed kasher* — if a witness signed simply using his first name without his father's name, this is valid. *Ben ish ploni ed* — if he signed only as "son of so-and-so," giving his father's name but not his own first name, this too is valid. *Ish ploni ben ish ploni* without writing *ed* at all — simply his full name without the word "witness" — is also *kasher*, since it is self-evident why one would sign a *get* if not as a witness.

### Jerusalem Practice

*V'kach hayu nikkei ha-da'at she-bi-Yerushalayim osim* — this was the practice of the scrupulous and refined people of Jerusalem. The connection to the next clause, *katav chanichato va-chanichato kasher* — if one wrote a nickname or family surname — may indicate that what the people of Jerusalem did was to sign using family names, emphasizing the family lineage rather than drawing attention to themselves individually. Either way, the ruling stands: all of these forms of identification are valid.

## Get Continuity Issues

### One or Two Gets?

With the basic cases of the two-column *get* established, the *gemara* raises a pointed question. How do we know that two columns constitute a single *get* rather than two separate *gittin*? The concern is concrete: perhaps someone cut part of one *get* and part of another and assembled them together, so that what appears to be a continuous document is actually a patchwork of two different instruments.

### Rava: Space Below

*Amar Rava ke-she-yihye revach milmata* — Rava answers that there is a visible space at the bottom of the first column, indicating that the text continues and the column simply ran out of room. This space signals continuity — the document picks up where it left off.

### Cut and Paste Risk

The *gemara* immediately pushes back: *u-dilma zman d'batra migaz gayiz* — perhaps someone cut off the date from the second column. The space below is still there, but the authenticity of the connection between the two columns remains in doubt.

### Rav Papa: Space Above

*Amar Rav Papa ke-she-yihye revach milmata, hacha nami ke-she-yihye revach mil'mala* — Rav Papa adds a parallel answer: just as there is a space below the first column, so too there is a space above the second column, indicating it begins mid-text. Both columns show visible evidence of continuation. For both spaces to be coincidentally present in two fraudulently combined documents would be extremely improbable.

### Dating Problem

Yet another concern is raised: *u-dilma imlochi imlach ve-katav* — perhaps the husband changed his mind mid-composition, and the *get* was written across two different days, completing the first column on one day and the second on another. This would create a problem of *get yashan* — an old *get* — where there is a meaningful gap between the date written on the *get* and when it was actually completed, with all the attendant difficulties: the wife might be considered divorced from the earlier date, potentially creating issues around her subsequent conduct, or questions about property rights. The *gemara* entertains this concern but then asks: if the text ended in the middle of a sentence — say, the first column ended with *harei at* and the second began with *muteret le-chol adam* — is one really to worry that the husband changed his mind mid-sentence and resumed writing months later? The *gemara* acknowledges that such a scenario would be far-fetched.

### Parchment Proof

Rashi offers a more fundamental answer: *de-yada bei mi-tachtah de-megilta* — one can tell from the physical characteristics of the parchment itself. In antiquity, writing surfaces such as *klaf* or vellum were individually prepared, and each piece had its own distinctive texture and grain, much as one can tell from the grain of wood that a plank has not been joined from two separate pieces. If both columns share the same physical characteristics — the same coloration, the same grain, the same aging — it is evident that they constitute a single original document and are not a cut-and-paste fabrication. Rashi's answer thus addresses the foundational concern: the very materiality of the document testifies to its integrity.

## Signature Orientation

### Top/Side Signing Invalid

Returning to the case of witnesses signing at the top of the page or to the side: the *mishna* ruled this invalid. The *gemara* expresses surprise — *eini*? Is that really so?

### Rav's Practice

*Ve-ha Rav chatam min ha-tzad* — but Rav himself used to sign from the side! If signing to the side were categorically invalid, how could Rav have done so?

### Letter Roof Orientation

The *gemara* resolves the question: *de-hatam bi-shgago kelapei ha-ktav* — the roof (*shigago*, meaning the top edge) of Rav's letters faced toward the text of the *get*. That is, Rav signed sideways, but oriented so that the heads of the letters pointed inward toward the document. The *mishna*'s invalidation applies to the opposite orientation — when the letters face away from the text. There is thus a meaningful distinction between a signature that is laterally placed but directed toward the document versus one that faces outward.

### Vertical vs Horizontal

This resolution, however, raises a further question from a *baraita*: the case of *hikif rosho shel zeh betzad rosho shel zeh ve-ha-eidim ba-emtza sheneihem pesulin* — heads facing heads, witnesses in the middle, both invalid. In that case, the roof of the letters of the witnesses' signatures does face the text of one of the *gittin*. If facing inward is sufficient to validate the signature, why are both *gittin* invalid? The *gemara* answers: *hatam d'dami lei ke-ivura* — in the case of the *mishna*'s invalidation, the problem is not the orientation of the letters but that the signatures were written vertically, running up and down the page rather than across it horizontally. Written that way, the signature is ambiguous — one cannot determine which *get* it belongs to, since it is perpendicular to both. Hence: *lo adin nikarim imo* — neither document can clearly claim the witnesses as its own.

### Conclusion: Rav Not Signing Gets

Having exhausted attempts to harmonize Rav's practice with the cases involving multiple documents, the *gemara* concludes: *ela Rav be-duchti hava chatim* — Rav was signing in a different context entirely. He was signing court summonses or judicial orders, not *gittin*. His lateral signature was an authorization or approval on a court document, not the witnessing signature on a *get*. The *mishna*'s rules about signature placement apply to *gittin* specifically; Rav's practice was in an entirely separate domain and poses no challenge. Rashi notes that the term for such documents is something like a summons — an order confirming that a party may be summoned before the court — and that Rav's signature was simply his judicial approval, not a witnessing act governed by the laws of *get* signatures.

## Language Variants

### Language Variants OK

The *gemara* briefly revisits the *mishna*'s cases of language variation. A *get* written in one language and signed in another — Hebrew written, Greek signed, or the reverse — is valid in all its combinations. These rulings require little elaboration, as the principle is clear: for a single *get*, the language of composition and the language of signature are independent of one another.

### Scribe Signs

The case of *katav sofer ve-ed kasher* — the scribe who also signed — is now taken up in the *gemara*'s own voice. *Amar Rabbi Yirmiyah: chatam sofer u-shnei eidim* — Rabbi Yirmiyah specifies that this means the scribe signed and there are additionally two other witnesses, totaling two signatures alongside the scribe's.

### Direct Speech Requirement

*Ve-amar Rav Chisda: man Rav Yossi hi* — Rav Chisda identifies this as the position of Rav Yossi. The scribe is permitted to sign only if the husband spoke directly to him — directly commissioning the *get* and thereby implicitly authorizing the scribe's participation as a signatory. If the husband's instruction reached the scribe through intermediaries, the concern returns: perhaps the scribe was added as a signatory by those intermediaries without the husband's explicit authorization, which is impermissible under Rav Yossi's view that a *shliach* may not unilaterally alter the arrangements specified by the husband.

## Ketubah Recognition

### Recognizing One Witness

A practical case is now introduced. A *ketubah* came before Rabbi Abbahu, and those present recognized the handwriting of the scribe who had written it and the signature of one of the witnesses. The question arose: since the scribe's handwriting and one witness's signature were both recognizable, could the *ketubah* be validated on that basis alone, without verifying the second witness's signature? Rabbi Abbahu was inclined to validate it — *savar Rabbi Abbahu le-achshurah*.

### Two Signatures Required

Rabbi Abba objected: *lav chatam sofer u-shnei eidim tnan* — did we not learn in the *mishna* that the operative case is the scribe's signature plus two additional witnesses? The *mishna*'s permission applies when the scribe himself is a signatory and there are two recognized witness signatures. You cannot substitute recognition of the scribe's handwriting as a *writer* for recognition of his signature as a *witness*. Two proper witness signatures are required; the handwriting of the scribe in his capacity as a scribe is not equivalent.

## Family Names Limits

### Nicknames Valid

*Katav chanichato va-chanichato kasher* — if one recorded a nickname or family surname as the identifier of the parties, this is valid for purposes of a *get*.

### Generations Dispute

A *baraita* is cited on how far back one may reach for ancestral identification: *tanu rabbanan chanichat avot be-gittin ad yud dorot* — one may identify a party by an ancestral family name for up to ten generations. *Ve-Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar omer: gimmel dorot kasher* — Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says three generations suffice and beyond that it is invalid. After ten or three generations — depending on which opinion one follows — the ancestral name may no longer serve as a legal identifier: *mi-kan ve-ilech pasul*.

The logic of the ten-generation position may be connected to a well-known phenomenon in Tanach: the genealogy of Shaul in Divrei HaYamim spans ten generations, even though the Torah in Parshat Lech Lecha telescopes four generations into what Divrei HaYamim shows are actually ten, skipping six intermediate generations because Shaul's more distant ancestor was sufficiently famous that intervening generations could be omitted. The ten-generation limit may reflect this principle — that ancestral identification retains legal currency for up to ten generations.

### Three Generations Pasuk

*Ka-man azla ha d'amar Rav Chanina: chatav chanichat avot be-gittin ad gimmel dorot?* — whose opinion does Rav Chanina follow when he rules that ancestral family names in *gittin* are valid for three generations? *Ke-Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar* — he follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. *Amar Rav Huna: mai kra?* — Rav Huna asks what scriptural basis supports the three-generation position.

The *pasuk* cited is from Devarim: *ki tolid banim u-vnei vanim ve-noshantem* — when you have children and grandchildren and you have grown old in the land, and then you will sin and be driven out. The word *ve-noshantem* carries the sense of becoming ancient, of staleness — and Rav Huna reads the sequence as: you, your children, and your grandchildren; after that, the ancestral name has grown too old and too stale to serve as current identification. Beyond three generations it is *noshen* — antiquated — and may no longer be used. A scriptural proof for the ten-generation position is not offered in the *gemara* here, which is conspicuous.

## Seven Kingdoms Aggada

### Seven Kingdoms

At this point the *gemara* takes an *aggadic* turn. *Amar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: na'atzei de-aggadata* — here is a fine *aggadic* teaching. *Lo chavah Eretz Yisrael ad she-ba'u vah shiv'ah batei dinim shel avodah zarah* — the Land of Israel did not become desolate until seven successive dynasties of *avodah zarah* had arisen within it. The seven are: Yeravam ben Nevat, Acha ben Achiyah, Achav ben Omri, Yehu ben Nimshi, Pekach ben Remalyahu, Menachem ben Gadi, and Hoshea ben Elah. *Va-ilu hein* — these are the seven.

The scriptural basis: *umlala yoledet ha-shiv'ah* — the one who bore seven is desolate. The *gemara* reads *yoledet ha-shiv'ah* not as a mother of seven children but as the land that gave rise to seven royal dynasties of idolatry. *Nafcha nafshah, ba'ah shamshah be-od yomam, bosha va-chafrah* — she breathed her last, her sun set while it was still day, she was covered in shame and disgrace. After seven such dynasties, the Land is left empty of its inhabitants, driven into exile.

*Amar Rav Ashi: mai kra?* — Rav Ashi asks how one derives the number seven from the same *pasuk* of *ki tolid banim u-vnei vanim* cited earlier. The derivation counts as follows: you yourself are one; *banim*, children, adds two; *bnei vanim*, grandchildren of grandchildren — following out the tree — adds four more. One plus two plus four equals seven. Tosafot notes that this arithmetic, while somewhat loose, follows the branching of a genealogical tree, with each generation doubling.

### Hoshea ben Elah

Rav Kahana raises a pointed question to Rav Ashi: it is written of Hoshea ben Elah that *va-ya'as ha-ra be-einei Hashem rak lo ke-malchei Yisrael* — he did evil in the eyes of God, but not like the kings of Israel before him. And yet it is also written that Shalmaneser came up against him and exiled his people. If Hoshea was less wicked than his predecessors, why was he the king under whom the final exile took place? Why did God not wait for a worse king?

The answer: *otan prosda'ot she-hoshiv Yeravam ben Nevat she-lo ya'alu Yisrael la-regel, ba Hoshea u-vitlan* — those border checkpoints that Yeravam ben Nevat had established to prevent the people of Israel from going up to Jerusalem for the *regalim*, the pilgrimage festivals, were abolished by Hoshea. Hoshea ben Elah actually removed the blockade. In this respect he was genuinely less wicked: he gave the people back the ability to go to the *Beit HaMikdash*. So why was exile decreed specifically in his time?

*Afilu hachi lo alu Yisrael la-regel* — even so, the people did not go up. It was no longer the king who was stopping them; they simply no longer wanted to go. The sin had become internalized. God's response: *otan shanim she-lo alu Yisrael la-regel yelchu ba-shvi* — for all those years in which Israel chose not to ascend for the *regel*, they would now go into captivity. They had forfeited their connection to the Land, and so the Land would be taken from them. The blame ultimately traces back to Yeravam ben Nevat — *chata ve-hichti et ha-rabbim* — who sinned and caused the many to sin, as stated in Pirkei Avot, though the particular detail about the people's continued non-attendance after Hoshea lifted the restriction goes beyond what Pirkei Avot records.

### Divine Haste

*Amar Rav Chisda amar Mar Ukva* — and some say *amar Rav Chisda amar Rav Yirmiyah darash Mareimar*: *mai de-chtiv vayishkod Hashem al ha-ra'ah vayevi'eha aleinu ki tzaddik Hashem Elokeinu?* — what does it mean that God was *vayishkod*, that He hastened the evil and brought it upon us, and that this demonstrates that God is righteous? The root *sh-k-d* is the same as in *shekedia*, the almond tree, the first to blossom — suggesting swiftness. But in what sense is it an act of righteousness to hasten punishment?

### Exile Preparation

The answer involves the structure of the exile itself. The exile did not occur all at once. There was first the exile of Yechonyah — *im ha-golah asher hogleitah im Yechonyah melech Yehudah*, as recalled in Megillat Esther — and then afterward the exile of Tzidkiyahu. *She-dikdek HaKadosh Baruch Hu mi-Yisrael she-heglah galut Tzidkiyahu ve-adain galut Yechonyah kayemet* — God was precise: by the time the exile of Tzidkiyahu arrived, the earlier exiles of Yechonyah were already established in Babylon and had prepared the way.

As the verse records of the exile of Yechonyah: *hacharash ve-ha-masgeir elef* — a thousand *charash* and *masgeir*. Homiletically: *charash she-be-sha'ah she-posachin na'asu ha-kol ke-chereshin* — the *charash* are the *chachamim*, the great sages, so called because when they speak, everyone else becomes as if deaf to all else, silenced by the authority of their words. And *masgeir: keivan she-sogrin, shuv ein poschin* — the *masgeir* are those whose rulings, once closed, are not reopened. A thousand such figures were already in Babylon by the time the second wave arrived. The scholarly infrastructure — the *batei midrashos*, the *chachamim*, the capacity for Torah life — was already in place. The later exiles arrived not into a spiritual vacuum but into a functioning community. This is the righteousness of God: the hastening of the first exile allowed the second exile to survive with their identity intact.

### 850-Year Mercy

*Ulla amar she-hikdim shtei shanim le-ve-noshantem* — Ulla offers a different reading of God's righteousness. The *gematria* of *ve-noshantem* is 852. Yet God brought the exile after only 850 years — two years early. *Vayishkod Hashem al ha-ra'ah*: God hastened the evil by two years. Why is this righteous? Because the full text of the verse concludes with a warning of total annihilation: *ki avod toveidun* — you will utterly perish. Had God waited the full 852 years, the verse implies there would be nothing left of the Jewish people. By hastening the exile by two years, God cut short the countdown before the point of no return, ensuring that something of the Jewish people would survive. The *tzedakah* was in the timing: a slightly earlier, less complete punishment rather than a delayed, total destruction.

*Amar Rav Acha bar Yaakov: shema mina meheirah* — we learn from this what "quickly" means from God's perspective: 850 years. As the verse says elsewhere, *elef shanim be-einecha ke-yom etmol* — a thousand years in God's eyes are like yesterday. On a divine timescale, 850 years is barely a moment. The compassion embedded in the word *maher* — quickly — is not that God acted immediately, but that He acted before the situation became irreversible, giving centuries for *teshuvah* while still ensuring that when the judgment came, it came before the point of utter destruction.

## Coerced Get

### Jewish vs Non-Jewish Cou…

The *gemara* moves to an entirely new topic: the *get me'useh*, the coerced *get*. This subject gained notoriety in recent years when a group of individuals in New Jersey were prosecuted for using coercion to extract *gittin* from recalcitrant husbands — a reminder that these laws carry real contemporary stakes. Rashi's gloss on *me'useh* is a single word: *be-chezakah* — by force.

The *mishna* states: *get me'useh be-Yisrael kasher, uv'ovdei kochavim pasul* — a coerced *get* administered by a Jewish court is valid; one administered by a non-Jewish court is invalid. There is however a nuance: *ovdei kochavim chovtin oto ve-omrim lo: aseh mah she-Yisrael omrim lecha — kasher* — if the non-Jewish court beats the husband and says to him, "Do what the Jewish court is telling you to do," the resulting *get* is valid. The non-Jewish enforcement acts as the arm of Jewish judicial authority, not on independent grounds. Only when the non-Jewish court acts entirely on its own initiative, without reference to the Jewish court's ruling, is the *get* invalid.

### Acting on Authority

This distinction is crucial. A non-Jewish court that serves as an enforcement mechanism for a legitimate Jewish *beit din* ruling is effectively an extension of that ruling. The *get* produced under such circumstances is as if it were produced under direct Jewish court compulsion. The invalidity arises only when the non-Jewish court operates on its own legal authority without grounding in Jewish law.

### According to Din

Rav Nachman, citing Shmuel, introduces a further grid of distinctions: *get ha-me'useh be-Yisrael ke-din kasher, she-lo ke-din pasul u-posel*. When a Jewish court coerces a *get ke-din* — according to law — the *get* is fully valid. When the coercion is *she-lo ke-din* — not in accordance with law — the *get* is *pasul u-posel*. This phrase requires careful parsing. *Pasul* means the *get* does not function to dissolve the marriage — she remains married. *Posel*, however, means that despite the *get*'s failure to actually divorce her, it renders her ineligible to marry a *kohen* — she is, so to speak, partially affected. The *get* has done something, just not the right thing.

For a non-Jewish court: if it acted *ke-din*, the result is *pasul u-posel* — the same partial effect as a Jewish court acting improperly. If it acted *she-lo ke-din*, the *get* has absolutely no effect: *pircha ein bo* — it accomplishes nothing whatsoever. She remains fully and unambiguously married.

### Din Criteria

What does *ke-din* mean in the context of a coerced *get* by a Jewish court? Rashi specifies: *ke-gon hanach d'amrinan behu: yotzi ve-yiten ketubah, o she-hayetah asurah lo* — cases in which the *beit din* had already ruled *yotzi ve-yiten ketubah*, that he must divorce and pay the *ketubah*, or cases where the wife was forbidden to him in the first place, where the marriage itself was halachically impermissible. In other words, the paradigmatic case of a coerced *get ke-din* is not the common contemporary scenario of a husband who refuses to give a *get* to a wife seeking divorce in an otherwise permissible marriage. It is specifically a case where the marriage should not have continued — or perhaps should never have occurred — and the *beit din* had formally ruled that the husband was obligated to give a *get*, but he refused to comply with that ruling. The court's coercion in such a case is the enforcement of a pre-existing legal obligation, not the imposition of a new one.

Whether this framework can be extended by analogy to the modern problem of the recalcitrant husband in an otherwise valid marriage is a question the *gemara* raises implicitly but does not resolve in this passage, and one must be cautious about abstracting too freely from the specific cases the *rishonim* describe to broader contemporary applications.

# Gittin 88b

## Get Me'useh

### Mishna Get Me'useh

The penultimate daf of *Gittin* opens with a *mishna* whose legal and moral weight belies its brevity. The *mishna* states: *get me'useh biYisrael kasher* — a *get* that is compelled by a Jewish *beis din* is valid. *Uv'ovdei kochavim pasul* — if non-Jews are the ones compelling it, the *get* is invalid. However, *uv'ovdei kochavim chovtin oto v'omrim lo asei mah sheYisrael omrim lach* — non-Jews may beat the husband and tell him to do what the Jews instruct him. The final word *ve-kasher* appears in the text in parentheses, reflecting a certain ambiguity. Tosafot raises the possibility that even when non-Jews are doing the physical coercion on behalf of a Jewish *beis din*, the *get* might still be problematic. Tosafot ultimately rejects that reading, reasoning that the *dayanim* themselves need not personally carry out the coercive act — they may delegate the unpleasant work. The simple reading, and the one Tosafot endorses, is that if the non-Jewish court is merely doing the dirty work under the supervision of a Jewish *beis din*, the *get* is valid.

### Rav Nachman Ruling

The *gemara* then introduces the ruling of Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel: *ha-get me'useh biYisrael kadin kasher* — a *get* compelled by a Jewish *beis din* where there is a genuine legal mandate, meaning where the law actually obligates the husband to give a *get*, is valid. *Shelo kadin pasul u'posel* — if the court compelled it without a legitimate legal mandate, it is an invalid *get*, but it creates a *re'ach haget* problem: if the husband subsequently dies, the wife would be prohibited from marrying a *kohen*, as there is enough of a "whiff of a *get*" to affect her status for *kehunah*. Turning to the non-Jewish court scenario — again, assuming the non-Jewish court is acting on its own authority, not merely as the arm of a Jewish *beis din* — *kadin pasul u'posel*: if there is a legal mandate, the *get* is invalid because it was not done under Jewish auspices, but it still creates a *re'ach haget* problem. *Shelo kadin* — if it is doubly removed, both non-Jewish and without legal mandate, *afilyu re'ach haget ein bo*: there is not even the faintest whiff of a *get*, and there is no *kehunah* consequence whatsoever.

Notably, the *gemara* throughout this entire discussion does not raise what might seem like the most obvious question: how can a forced *get* be valid at all, given that a *get* must be given *mirtsono*, of the husband's own free will, and a coerced transaction is ordinarily void? The *gemara* elsewhere does address forced transactions — *talu v'zavin*, where a person was strung up until he agreed to sell his property, and the ruling is *zvinei zvin*, the sale is valid — because even under compulsion, at some level the person is choosing to act. Similarly, *talu v'kideish kiddushei kiddushin*: a shotgun *kiddushin* is valid *b'diavad*. One could simply have placed this case in that same category.

### Rambam Yetzer Hara

The Rambam, however, offers an additional reason specific to the *get*. He explains that deep down, every Jew wishes to do what is right. The husband's *yetzer hara* is simply getting in the way. When the *beis din* coerces him, it is not overriding his will — it is wearing down the *yetzer hara* and liberating his true, inner will to do the right thing. In that sense, he is ultimately acting *mirtsono*.

The question arises: why did the Rambam need this additional reason rather than simply relying on the general rule that coerced transactions are valid? The answer may lie in the Rambam's own formulation at the beginning of *Hilchos Gittin*, where he lists ten criteria for a valid *get*, one of which is that it must be *mirtsono*. The *rishonim* and *acharonim* ask: isn't *mirtsono* simply the standard requirement for any valid legal act? The answer seems to be that there is a distinction between *da'as* — consenting to something — and actually *wanting* it in the deeper sense that the Torah describes when it says *ki matza bah ervat davar v'chatav lah sefer kiritut*: the husband is motivated, not merely consenting. It is not enough that he agreed; he must on some level want to give the *get*. It is for this reason that the Rambam required his special explanation: the beating does not merely produce *da'as*, it reveals the husband's genuine, latent will to fulfill his *halachic* obligation.

This explanation also illuminates why a *get* compelled without a legal mandate is invalid. The entire justification for treating the forced *get* as truly voluntary is anchored in the existence of a *halachic* mandate. Without that mandate, there is no basis to say that the husband's "true will" is to give a *get*, and so the *get* is not *mirtsono* in any meaningful sense.

### Four-Case Matrix

The structure of valid and invalid *get me'useh* cases can be mapped as a matrix of two variables: the source of compulsion (Jewish *beis din* or non-Jewish court) and whether there is a legal mandate (*kadin* or *shelo kadin*). Only one of the four cells produces a genuinely valid *get*: a Jewish *beis din* acting with a legal mandate. The two cells that combine one condition with its absence — a Jewish *beis din* without legal mandate, or a non-Jewish court with legal mandate — each produce a *re'ach haget* problem: close enough to the real thing to affect *kehunah* status, but not valid as a *get*. The fourth cell — a non-Jewish court acting without a legal mandate — is so far removed from any legitimate *get* that *afilu re'ach haget ein bo*: it carries no halakhic weight whatsoever.

### Rav Mesharshaya Rejected

The *gemara* probes the logic of this framework by introducing a position of Rav Mesharshaya, which it will ultimately reject. Rav Mesharshaya proposes: *dvar Torah*, as a biblical matter, *get me'useh b'ovdei kochavim kasher* — if there is a genuine legal mandate, a *get* compelled by a non-Jewish court is in principle valid. The reason *chazal* declared it invalid is merely rabbinic: *shelo t'hei kol achas v'achas holches v'tolah atzma b'ovdei kochavim u'mafka'as atzma miyad ba'alah* — so that women would not hire non-Jewish courts to pressure their husbands into giving a *get* without a legitimate *halachic* basis, particularly since non-Jewish courts may be more susceptible to being paid off.

The *gemara* immediately challenges this position: if in principle a *get* compelled by a non-Jewish court is biblically valid, then the combination of a non-Jewish court and no legal mandate should still generate a *re'ach haget* problem, since *shelo kadin* under a valid Jewish *beis din* also creates *re'ach haget*. But the *mishna* says in that fourth case there is not even a *re'ach haget*. The *gemara* therefore concludes: *ella hadar Rav Mesharshaya b'dusiah hi* — this position of Rav Mesharshaya is sheer foolishness; it is rejected entirely. A *get* compelled by a non-Jewish court acting on its own authority is completely invalid on any level.

The *gemara* then asks: given that a non-Jewish court has no authority, what explains the *re'ach haget* problem even when there is a legal mandate? The answer is *k'din b'k'din d'Yisrael mechalaf*: when there is a legal mandate, the non-Jewish scenario resembles closely enough the one case that genuinely works — a Jewish *beis din* with a legal mandate — that it creates concern for *kehunah* status. *Shelo k'din b'k'din d'Yisrael lo mechalaf*: when there is neither a Jewish *beis din* nor a legal mandate, the case is too far removed to create any concern at all.

---

## Semicha & Shlichus

### Abaye Challenge

The *gemara* next records that Abaye found Rav Yosef sitting and compelling husbands who were obligated to give *gittin*, using various forms of pressure and leverage. Abaye challenged him: *vaanen hedyotot anan* — we are mere commoners. We do not possess the *semicha* that traces back to Moshe Rabbeinu.

### Rabbi Tarfon

In support of this concern, the *gemara* cites a *baraita* in the name of Rabbi Tarfon: wherever you find gatherings of non-Jews — *Rashi* understands this as referring to non-Jewish courts — even if their substantive laws are identical to Jewish law, *i atah rashai lehizakek lahem*: you are forbidden to submit to their authority. The verse states *ve'eleh hamishpatim asher tasim lifneihem* — before *them*, the Jewish judges — *velo lifnei ovdei kochavim*. This is not merely a question of substantive law. Even if the law itself is the same, the critical question is who is recognized as the empowered legal authority. It is the Jewish court system that is divinely empowered, not merely correct in its rulings.

The *baraita* adds a second clause: *davar acher*, before them and not before *hedyotot* — commoners. To exercise coercive authority as a *beis din*, one requires *semicha*. This seemingly creates a grave problem for Rav Yosef's practice. One might think that if the requirement of *semicha* applies to ordinary legal proceedings, it applies with even greater force to cases of compelling a *get*, where the court authorizes actual physical force over a transaction that on its surface appears involuntary.

### Common Case Exception

Rav Yosef responds: *anan shelichutaihu ka avdinan* — we act as agents of the court that does possess *semicha*. The *gemara* supports this by analogy to ordinary cases of loans and admissions of debt, which courts without *semicha* handle regularly, on the grounds that they represent the authority of the courts that did have *semicha*.

### Theft Pushback

The *gemara* immediately presses: *i hachi gezeilos vachavalos nami* — if that is so, should courts today not also handle cases of theft and personal injury as agents of the *semicha* court? The *gemara* answers: *ki avdinan shelichutaihu bemilsa deshchicha* — we only function as agents of the *semicha* court in matters that are common occurrences. *Bemilsa d'lo shchicha lo avdinan shelichutaihu* — in uncommon cases, we do not claim that agency.

This generates an extensive body of *poskim* literature about the scope of contemporary *beis din* authority. The *gemara* here implies that theft and personal injury cases fall outside this agency. This is in tension with sources elsewhere in the *gemara* that suggest courts did handle such cases. Tosafot addresses the apparent contradiction and suggests that perhaps the agency applies only when certain conditions are met jointly. Additionally, some note a distinction between *knas* — punitive fines, which represent the coercive power of a court of full authority — and pure restitution in cases of loans and debts, which is more a matter of compensating actual loss and restoring the status quo. The concept that *shlichus* applies only in matters of *chisaron kis*, where someone has actually suffered a monetary loss, is raised elsewhere, though it is not made explicit in this *gemara*.

What is striking, as the *gemara* implicitly acknowledges, is that forcing a *get* — which involves actual physical coercion to produce a document that on its face looks involuntary — would seem to be the most demanding case requiring formal authority. Yet the *gemara* concludes that this too falls within the common-case *shlichus*. That forcing a *get* is classified as *milsa deshchicha*, a common occurrence, is itself a painful commentary on the frequency with which husbands refuse to give *gittin* — a reality that has not changed since the time of the *gemara*.

### Tosafot Semicha

Tosafot raises two further questions in this context. The first concerns the acceptance of converts: accepting a *ger* requires three expert *mumchin* with *semicha*, as derived from the word *mishpat* written in connection with *chalitza* in *Hacholetz*. Yet we accept converts today, without any court possessing *semicha*. Tosafot answers, again invoking the agency principle, *d'avdinan shlichuseihu*, and adding that acceptance of converts is considered sufficiently common — *d'chashiv k'shchicha* — to fall within the scope of that agency. Tosafot notes that the *gemara* in *Hacholetz* itself implies that they would accept converts in *Bavel* even in the absence of *semicha*.

The second and more fundamental question is this: to say we are agents of a court with *semicha* presupposes there is such a court to represent. In the era of the *gemara*, courts with *semicha* existed in Eretz Yisrael and the later Babylonian courts could claim to represent them. But today, *v'hashta ein mumchin b'Eretz Yisrael* — there are no ordained judges in Eretz Yisrael at all. Of whom are we agents? Tosafot answers: *d'shlichus d'kama'i avdinan* — we act as agents of the earlier courts, the ancient courts that no longer exist. This is a remarkable conceptual claim: contemporary *batei din* derive their authority from their status as the continuing institutional expression of an ancient court whose *semicha* has long since lapsed, yet whose transmitted authority is still, in some sense, operative.
